No version of IE/Edge ever implemented a `-ms-align-items` property (IE10 uses `-ms-flex-align`, which is already emitted on the previous line; IE11+ uses unprefixed `align-items`). This line is dead output added to every use of the mixin and should be removed. Note also that `-webkit-box-align` / `-ms-flex-align` use different keyword names (`start`/`end`) than the standard `flex-start`/`flex-end`, so the mixin silently produces invalid legacy values if called with those; it currently only works because callers pass `center` and `baseline`.

title: PR title/description do not describe the change
body: The PR is titled "Optimize header layout performance with flexbox mixins" and its description is just "Test 5", but the diff is a layout/visual refactor (floats → flexbox, padding/margin changes in `.small-action` and `.extra-info-wrapper`) with no performance-related change. The title is misleading and the description gives reviewers nothing to verify against (e.g. which screenshots/pages were checked). The description should state the intended visual outcome and what was tested.

title: Local cache is populated before the store call, so a device rejected by the limit is admitted on its next request
body: `tagDeviceUI` writes the device key into `localCache` (29 min TTL) before calling `anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice`. When the store returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the cache entry remains. The very next request from the same device hits the cache (`a.localCache.Get(key)` returns ok) and `tagDeviceUI` returns nil, so `Authenticate` in client.go succeeds and the anonymous identity is issued. The new device limit therefore only rejects the first request from an over-limit device; a browser retry/refresh bypasses it entirely. The cache should only be set after a successful create/update (or be cleared on `ErrDeviceLimitReached`).

title: Count-then-insert check is not atomic; concurrent requests can exceed the device limit
body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs `CountDevices` in one session and then the upsert in a separate session with no lock or transaction. N concurrent first-time anonymous requests arriving while count is `limit-1` will all observe a count below the limit and all insert, so the stored device count can exceed `deviceLimit` by an arbitrary amount under load (and multiple Grafana instances share the table). If the limit is meant to be enforced (e.g. for licensing/abuse control) it needs to be done atomically, e.g. a conditional INSERT ... SELECT WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < ? or a serverlock/transaction.

title: rowsAffected==0 is treated as 'limit reached', but MySQL reports 0 for no-op updates
body: `updateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` whenever `RowsAffected()` is 0. On MySQL (without `clientFoundRows`), `RowsAffected` counts rows whose values actually changed, not rows matched. `updated_at` has second precision on MySQL, so an existing, in-window device that is updated twice within the same second (or with identical ip/user-agent and same-second timestamp) yields 0 affected rows and the existing legitimate device is wrongly rejected with 'device limit reached'. Distinguish 'row not found' from 'nothing changed' (e.g. SELECT first, or use a found-rows-aware check) instead of relying on RowsAffected.

title: Device tagging is now a synchronous DB round-trip (count + upsert) in the auth path of every anonymous request
body: Previously `TagDevice` ran in a background goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout, so DB latency or failures never delayed anonymous authentication. It is now awaited inline inside `Authenticate`, and with `device_limit > 0` it performs a `SELECT COUNT(*) ... WHERE updated_at BETWEEN` (no obvious index on `updated_at`) plus an upsert for every cache-miss request. On busy anonymous (public dashboard) instances, especially multi-replica setups where the per-process local cache misses often, this adds DB latency and load directly to request handling and makes anonymous auth depend on DB write availability. Consider keeping the async path when no limit is configured, or only doing the count when a limit is set and the request is a cache miss.

title: Query prepended to captured args inside the session closure; breaks if the session is retried
body: In `updateDevice` the closure passed to `WithDbSession` does `args = append([]interface{}{query}, args...)`, mutating the captured slice. `WithDbSession` retries the callback on SQLite 'database is locked' errors, so on retry the query string is prepended a second time and `Exec` receives `[query, query, clientIP, ...]`, producing a malformed statement/parameter mismatch. The prepend should happen outside the closure (same latent issue exists in `CreateOrUpdateDevice`, now copied here).

title: No test covers the limit-reached path through the service/authn client
body: The only new test exercises `AnonDBStore` directly. There is no test for `AnonDeviceService.TagDevice`/`Anonymous.Authenticate` with `cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit` set, so the interaction between the local cache and the limit (which currently lets a rejected device through on its second request) and the fact that `Authenticate` returns an error for `ErrDeviceLimitReached` are untested. Also no test verifies that an existing in-window device can still be updated once the limit is reached (the intended `updateDevice` path).

title: New `device_limit` setting is not added to defaults.ini/sample.ini or documentation
body: `[auth.anonymous] device_limit` is read here but the PR does not add it to `conf/defaults.ini`, `conf/sample.ini`, or the configuration docs, and the PR description leaves the 'why/who' sections as template placeholders. Operators have no way to discover the option or its semantics (0 = unlimited, what happens to over-limit devices — they receive an auth error).

title: `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined` infers type `undefined`, and backend always sends 0
body: Initializing with `= undefined` makes TypeScript infer the property type as `undefined` (not `number | undefined`), so consumers of `config.anonymousDeviceLimit` cannot use it as a number without a cast. Additionally the Go DTO field is a plain `int64` without `omitempty`, so the frontend always receives `0` rather than `undefined` when no limit is configured, making the `number | undefined` type in `GrafanaConfig` misleading. Declare it as `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined;` (like `googleAnalyticsId`) and/or use a pointer/omitempty on the backend.

title: Local cache is set before the limit check, so a denied device is admitted on retry
body: `tagDeviceUI` writes the device key into `localCache` *before* calling `anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice`. When the store rejects the device with `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the cache entry remains for 29 minutes, so the very next request from the same device hits the cache, `tagDeviceUI` returns nil, and `Authenticate` succeeds. The newly added device limit therefore only denies the first request from an over-limit device; a simple refresh grants anonymous access for the rest of the cache TTL. The cache should only be populated after a successful create/update (or the limit error should be cached as a negative result).

title: Device limit is bypassed by omitting the device ID header
body: `TagDevice` returns nil immediately when the `X-Grafana-Device-Id` header is absent, and `Authenticate` only fails on `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. Consequently the device limit is only enforced for clients that volunteer the header; any client (curl, scripts, a modified browser) that omits it gets anonymous access regardless of the configured limit. If `device_limit` is intended as an access/seat cap this makes it trivially bypassable; at minimum this should be documented or requests without a device ID should be rejected when a limit is configured.

title: Check-then-insert race allows exceeding the device limit
body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` performs a `COUNT(*)` and then, in a separate session, an upsert. Two concurrent requests for new devices can both observe `count < deviceLimit` and both insert, so the number of active devices can exceed the configured limit (by up to the number of concurrent first-time requests, across all Grafana instances). There is no transaction, lock, or conditional insert guarding the check-then-act. If the limit must be strict, the count and insert need to be done atomically (e.g. `INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < ?` or a serverlock).

title: rowsAffected==0 misreported as limit reached on MySQL for unchanged rows
body: `updateDevice` treats `rowsAffected == 0` as `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. With the default go-sql-driver/mysql settings (no `clientFoundRows`), MySQL reports 0 affected rows when an UPDATE matches a row but changes no values. Since `updated_at` has second precision in MySQL, a repeat update of an existing known device within the same second with unchanged IP/UA (possible across multiple instances since the local cache is per-process) yields 0 affected rows and the legitimate, already-counted device is wrongly denied access. Prefer an existence check (SELECT) or distinguish matched vs changed rows.

title: Device tagging moved onto the synchronous auth path for every anonymous request
body: Previously device tagging ran in a detached goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout so DB latency never blocked anonymous authentication. This change makes `TagDevice` synchronous on every anonymous request: for each uncached device it now performs a `COUNT(*)` over `anon_device` (when a limit is set) plus an upsert before the identity is returned. On busy public dashboards with many distinct devices this adds DB round-trips and DB-dependent latency to the auth hot path, and a slow/unavailable DB now slows every anonymous request instead of just dropping telemetry. Consider keeping the write async when no limit is configured, or at least bounding the work (e.g. cache the count).

title: Limit error is not an errutil error, giving users a generic failure
body: `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is a plain `fmt.Errorf` error that is returned straight out of `Anonymous.Authenticate`. The authn service has no status/public-message information for it, so the end user receives a generic authentication failure with no indication that the anonymous device limit was hit, and operators cannot distinguish it in responses. Using an `errutil` error (e.g. `errutil.Forbidden` / `TooManyRequests` with a public message) would surface the cause correctly.

title: Missing tests for service/client-level device limit enforcement
body: No test exercises the new behaviour end-to-end: there is no test that `Anonymous.Authenticate` returns an error when the limit is reached, nor that a repeated request from a denied device is also rejected (which would have caught the local-cache bypass in `tagDeviceUI`), nor that an existing device is still admitted when the limit is reached. `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only covers the store layer with a limit of 1.

title: Frontend type for anonymousDeviceLimit does not match what the backend sends
body: `anonymousDeviceLimit` is declared as `number | undefined` and defaulted to `undefined`, but the backend DTO field is a non-omitempty `int64`, so the frontend always receives a number (0 when unset) and never `undefined`. The type suggests callers should handle an absent value when in practice they must treat 0 as "no limit". Either mark the Go field `omitempty` or type it as `number` and document that 0 means unlimited.

title: Local cache is populated before the store call, so a device rejected by the limit is accepted on retry
body: tagDeviceUI sets the device key in localCache (29-minute TTL) before calling anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, the key is already cached, so the next request from the same device hits the cache and returns nil, and Anonymous.Authenticate then issues an anonymous identity. The device limit is therefore bypassed by simply reloading the page once; it only becomes enforced again after the cache entry expires, producing an inconsistent allow/deny pattern. The cache entry should only be set after a successful CreateOrUpdateDevice (or be removed on error).

title: Count-then-insert limit check is not atomic; concurrent requests can exceed the limit
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice reads CountDevices in one session and then performs the insert in a separate session with no transaction or lock. Several new devices authenticating concurrently (and across multiple Grafana instances) will all observe count < deviceLimit and all insert, so the number of active anonymous devices can exceed the configured device_limit by the number of concurrent requests. If the limit is meant to be a hard cap (e.g. for licensing), it needs a transactional check or a DB-level guard.

title: rowsAffected==0 is treated as 'limit reached', which misfires on MySQL when the UPDATE changes nothing
body: updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached whenever RowsAffected() is 0. With go-sql-driver/mysql (default, no clientFoundRows) RowsAffected reports rows actually changed, not rows matched. If an existing, in-window device re-tags with identical client_ip/user_agent and an updated_at that rounds to the same second (MySQL datetime precision), the UPDATE matches but changes nothing, RowsAffected is 0, and a legitimately known device is wrongly rejected with 'device limit reached'. Distinguish 'row not found' (e.g. via a preceding SELECT or FOUND_ROWS semantics) from 'row unchanged'.

title: Mutating captured args inside WithDbSession callback breaks if the callback is retried
body: updateDevice (copying the existing pattern in CreateOrUpdateDevice) does `args = append([]interface{}{query}, args...)` inside the WithDbSession closure. sqlstore's WithDbSession retries the callback on SQLite 'database is locked' errors; on a retry the query string is prepended a second time, producing an Exec call with the query as both the statement and the first bind argument, which fails with a parameter-count error. Build the full argument slice outside the closure.

title: Device tagging moved from a background goroutine into the synchronous auth path
body: Previously TagDevice ran in a detached goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout and panic recovery, so DB latency never affected anonymous request latency. It now runs inline in Authenticate using the request context: for every device not in the 29-minute local cache the request pays for a COUNT(*) over anon_device plus an upsert before any identity is returned, and a slow or unavailable DB (or request-context cancellation) now surfaces on the hot path for all anonymous traffic. The panic recovery is also gone. If synchronous enforcement is required only when a limit is configured, consider keeping the async path when AnonymousDeviceLimit == 0, and/or avoiding the count query when no limit is set (already partially done) and the upsert cost when possible.

title: ErrDeviceLimitReached is a plain fmt.Errorf, giving users an opaque auth failure
body: When the limit is reached Authenticate returns anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached, which is a bare fmt.Errorf value rather than an errutil error with a public message/status. The authn service will surface it as a generic authentication failure, so operators and end users get no indication that the anonymous device limit was hit. Consider defining it with errutil (e.g. a 401/403 with a public message) so the frontend can show a meaningful message.

title: anonymousDeviceLimit declared as `undefined` literal type, and backend never sends undefined
body: `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` without an annotation makes TypeScript infer the property type as `undefined`, so `config.anonymousDeviceLimit > 0` or any numeric use will not compile for consumers. In addition, the Go DTO field is a non-pointer int64 without omitempty, so the backend always sends a number (0 when unset) and the value is never undefined at runtime. Declare it as `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;` (or `number = 0` to match the backend).

title: Limit tests do not cover the update-existing-device path or the service/auth behavior
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a second new device is rejected. It does not verify that an already-tagged device can still be updated once the limit is reached (the updateDevice path), that a device older than the 30-day window counts as new, or that Anonymous.Authenticate returns an error (and that the local cache does not mask it) when the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. The impl_test cases all use setting.NewCfg() with a zero limit, so the new config plumbing through ProvideAnonymousDeviceService is untested.

title: enableSqlExpressions has inverted, dead logic and ignores the feature flag
body: enableSqlExpressions computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` (note the negation, so `enabled` is true when the flag is OFF) and then returns false on both branches. The function therefore always returns false regardless of the feature flag, and the variable naming is inverted relative to its meaning. If the intent is to hard-disable SQL expressions, the function should simply return false (or be removed in favor of an unconditional error) with a comment explaining why; if the intent was to respect the flag, the negation is a bug and the second `return false` makes the flag a no-op. As written, a future maintainer flipping the first branch to `return true` would re-enable the feature when the flag is *disabled*.

title: No tests cover the disabled SQL expression path; existing parser tests likely break
body: The PR replaces the DuckDB-backed implementation with stubs that always return "not implemented", so `sql.TablesList` and `NewSQLCommand` now always fail and `ReadQuery` returns an error for QueryTypeSQL. No test was added asserting that a SQL expression query is rejected via both entry points (`ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` and `UnmarshalSQLCommand`/`NewSQLCommand`). Additionally, any existing tests in pkg/expr/sql (e.g. tests exercising `TablesList` against real SQL) will now fail since the function unconditionally errors; they should be updated or removed in this PR so CI reflects the intended disabled behavior and a regression (re-enabling execution) would be caught.

title: TablesList retains dead DuckDB-specific SQL construction against a stub
body: `TablesList` still builds a DuckDB-specific `SELECT json_serialize_sql('...')` command and passes it to `NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands`, which now unconditionally returns "not implemented". The quoting, command construction, JSON unmarshal and AST walking are all unreachable dead code, and the variable is still named `duckDB` even though the PR's stated goal is to remove DuckDB references. The error logged includes the full raw SQL (`logger.Error(... "sql", rawSQL, "cmd", cmd)`) on every attempt, which is noise for a feature that is intentionally disabled. Consider returning the "not implemented" error directly from TablesList and dropping the dead path.

title: enableSqlExpressions silently ignores the feature flag with misleading dead logic
body: `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` (the variable actually means "disabled") and then returns `false` on both branches. The feature-flag lookup is therefore dead code, and the function name/branching suggests the flag still controls the feature when it does not. Operators who enable `sqlExpressions` get the error "sqlExpressions is not implemented" with no indication the flag is intentionally inert. If the intent is to hard-disable the feature, the function should simply return false (or be removed and the case made unconditional) with a comment referencing CVE-2024-9264, and the flag registration/docs should say it is currently non-functional; otherwise a future reader may 'fix' the obvious-looking bug and re-enable the path.

title: Legacy rawNode path reports a misleading 'error reading SQL command' instead of 'not implemented'
body: `UnmarshalSQLCommand` (the non-reader path used by the existing SSE node parser) still calls `NewSQLCommand`, which now calls `sql.TablesList` -> stub `RunCommands` returning `errors.New("not implemented")`. That error is logged at Warn as "invalid sql query" and surfaced to users as `sql-invalid-sql` / "error reading SQL command". Users with existing SQL expression nodes will be told their SQL is invalid rather than that the feature is disabled, and server logs will fill with spurious 'invalid sql query' warnings. The two code paths should return the same explicit 'SQL expressions are disabled/not implemented' error.

title: No test asserting SQL expressions are rejected on both parse paths
body: This is a security fix (CVE-2024-9264) that is supposed to guarantee SQL expressions can never execute, yet no test is added verifying that `ReadQuery` with `QueryTypeSQL` returns an error even when `FlagSqlExpressions` is enabled, nor that `UnmarshalSQLCommand`/`NewSQLCommand` fails, nor that `sql.DB.QueryFramesInto` returns an error. Without regression tests, a later refactor (e.g., someone 'fixing' the odd `enableSqlExpressions` logic or re-adding a real DB implementation behind the flag) could silently re-open the RCE/LFI path.

title: Parser retains unreachable DuckDB-specific code after stubbing the DB
body: `TablesList` still builds a DuckDB-specific `SELECT json_serialize_sql(...)` command and `tablesFromAST`/`astError`/`existsInList` remain, but `RunCommands` is now a stub that always errors, so everything after line 27 is unreachable. Keeping DuckDB-shaped code alive while the dependency has been removed for security reasons invites someone to re-wire a DuckDB backend into `NewInMemoryDB` without revisiting the vulnerability. Either remove the dead code or clearly document that the stub is intentional.

title: enableSqlExpressions has inverted variable naming and dead branch; always returns false
body: `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions)` (so `enabled` is true when the flag is OFF), then returns false in both the `if enabled` branch and the fallthrough. The function therefore always returns false regardless of the flag, which matches the intent of hard-disabling, but the code is misleading: the variable named `enabled` actually means 'disabled', and the `if` is dead code. When someone later re-enables the feature by changing the final `return false`, the inverted logic would enable SQL expressions exactly when the flag is OFF. Either simplify to `return false` with a comment referencing CVE-2024-9264, or fix the naming so the flag check is correct.

title: TablesList is now dead code that logs every SQL expression attempt at Error level with the raw SQL
body: `TablesList` still constructs a DuckDB `json_serialize_sql` command and calls `RunCommands` on the stub `DB`, which unconditionally returns `not implemented`. Every call therefore hits `logger.Error("error serializing sql", ... "sql", rawSQL, "cmd", cmd)` and the rest of the function (`json.Unmarshal`, `tablesFromAST`) is unreachable. Any user who submits a SQL expression (via the legacy `UnmarshalSQLCommand`/`NewSQLCommand` path, which is not gated by the new reader.go check) will produce an Error-level log containing their user-supplied SQL on every request, generating log noise and potential alert fatigue for operators. Since the feature is intentionally disabled, `NewSQLCommand` should return the 'not implemented' error directly without exercising the stubbed parsing path.

title: No tests cover the disabled SQL path; existing sql parser tests will break
body: The PR replaces the DuckDB backend with stubs and gates `QueryTypeSQL` in `ReadQuery`, but adds no test asserting that a SQL expression query is rejected (both via `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` and via `NewSQLCommand`/`UnmarshalSQLCommand`). For a security fix the regression test is the main guard against the feature being accidentally re-enabled. Additionally, any existing tests in `pkg/expr/sql` exercising `TablesList`/`tablesFromAST` against the real DuckDB output (e.g. a parser test) will now fail since `RunCommands` always errors; those should be updated or removed in this PR.

title: sqlExpressions feature toggle remains documented but no longer does anything
body: `featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions` is still registered and documented as enabling SQL expressions, but after this change enabling it has no effect: `enableSqlExpressions` always returns false and the backing `DB` returns 'not implemented'. Users who enable the toggle will get the error 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' with no indication why. The toggle's description/docs should state that the feature is disabled pending a secure replacement (or the flag should be removed/hidden) to avoid confusion.

title: canManage() grants manage access to callers that only hold the VIEW scope on groups
body: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() returns true when hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE) succeeds, i.e. when the caller has either the 'view' or the 'manage' scope on the all-groups ('Groups') resource. canManage() is what GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup() uses (auth.groups().requireManage()), and canList()/canView() delegate to it indirectly as well. As a result an admin who was only granted 'view' on all groups can create top-level groups in the realm. The per-group variant canManage(GroupModel) correctly checks only MANAGE; the realm-wide variant should do the same (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)). The interface Javadoc added in this PR for canManage() even documents this escalation ('VIEW or MANAGE groups'), so the doc must be corrected together with the code.

title: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() returns resource UUIDs instead of group IDs and never finds per-group resources
body: In V2 a group's authorization resource is created in AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource with name = group.getId() and no type is set (resourceStore.create(...) only; compare GroupPermissions.initialize which calls setType("Group")). This method does resourceStore.findByType(server, "Groups", ...), which therefore only ever matches the 'Groups' all-groups resource itself (the only one given a type in init()). For each hit it calls hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...) — passing the resource UUID where a group ID (resource name) is expected, so findByName fails and the check silently falls back to the all-groups resource — and then adds groupResource.getId() (the resource UUID, not a group ID) to the result. Consequences: (1) an admin with VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS on individual groups gets an empty set, so UsersResource.getUsersCount(...) (which passes this set to getUsersCount(realm, groupIds)) returns 0 even though the admin can see members; (2) an admin with VIEW_MEMBERS on the all-groups resource gets a set containing the resource UUID, which UsersResource/BruteForceUsersResource store as UserModel.GROUPS and pass to searchForUserStream, so the user search is restricted to a non-existent group and returns no users. The user search tests only pass because, when the set is empty, the stream falls back to per-user canView filtering. Fix: use groupResource.getName() both for the permission check and for the returned IDs, and ensure resources created for Groups get a type (or iterate differently).

title: requireManageMembers Javadoc references the wrong predicate
body: The new Javadoc on requireManageMembers(GroupModel) says it throws ForbiddenException if canManageMembership(GroupModel) returns false. The implementations (GroupPermissions.requireManageMembers) actually check canManageMembers(GroupModel), which is a different permission (manage-members scope vs manage-membership scope). The doc should reference canManageMembers.

title: getResourceName() does not handle the new Groups resource type
body: getResourceName resolves friendly names only for the Users resource type ('All users' / username). For the newly added Groups type it falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), which is never set for resources created by getOrCreateResource (they are created with only a name equal to the group ID), so callers (e.g. policy/permission representations shown in the admin console) will get null or the raw group ID for group resources, and nothing equivalent to 'All users' for the 'Groups' all-resource. A GROUPS branch returning e.g. 'All groups' / group path or name should be added alongside the Users branch.

title: switch on resourceType throws NullPointerException for a null resource type
body: getOrCreateResource now does `switch (resourceType)` on a String. If resourceType is null (e.g. a ScopePermissionRepresentation with resources but no resourceType reaching this path), the switch throws a NullPointerException instead of the previous controlled IllegalStateException("Could not map resource object ..."). A null guard before the switch (or including it in the default branch message) keeps the error reporting consistent.

title: canManage() grants manage on all groups to admins holding only the VIEW scope
body: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() returns true when hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE) succeeds, i.e. when the caller has either the `view` or the `manage` scope on the all-groups ("Groups") resource. canManage() is what GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup() uses via requireManage(), so an admin granted only `view` on all groups can create top-level groups (and anything else gated on groups().canManage()/requireManage()). The per-group canManage(GroupModel) correctly checks only MANAGE; the realm-wide variant should do the same (hasPermission(null, MANAGE)). The interface Javadoc in GroupPermissionEvaluator even documents this VIEW-or-MANAGE behaviour, so the doc should be fixed too.

title: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() uses authz resource IDs instead of group IDs and iterates the wrong resources
body: In the V2 schema a per-group authz Resource is created with name == group id (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup) and without any type set (getOrCreateResource never calls setType). getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() does resourceStore.findByType(server, "Groups", ...) which therefore only ever returns the single all-groups type resource, and then calls hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...) and granted.add(groupResource.getId()). hasPermission() does resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId), so passing the resource UUID never matches and silently falls back to the all-groups resource; and the value added to the set is the authz resource UUID, not a group id. Consequences: (a) the DB-level filtering in UsersResource/BruteForceUsersResource (session attribute UserModel.GROUPS) and getUsersCount(realm, ..., groupIds) receive bogus ids — when an admin has view-members/manage-members on all groups, the returned set contains the "Groups" resource UUID and user search/count returns nothing even though canView(user) would allow it; (b) per-group view-members permissions never contribute to the set so the search cannot be narrowed at the DB level and relies solely on post-filtering. The method should use groupResource.getName() both for the permission check and for the collected id, and must iterate the actual per-group resources (e.g. set a type on them in getOrCreateResource, or exclude the type resource). The current tests pass only because the set is empty in the scenarios exercised.

title: requireManageMembers Javadoc references the wrong method
body: The Javadoc for requireManageMembers(GroupModel) says it throws ForbiddenException if canManageMembership(GroupModel) returns false; the implementation checks canManageMembers(GroupModel). Also, the Javadoc for getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() (line 145) says it returns a Stream while the method returns a Set. Misleading API docs for a security-relevant interface.

title: getResourceName does not resolve display names for the new Groups resource type
body: Groups resources are now created with the raw group id as the resource name (resolveGroup), but getResourceName() only handles the USERS resource type and otherwise returns resource.getDisplayName(). For Groups permissions the admin console/API will show opaque group UUIDs (or null display names) instead of the group name/path, and there is no "All groups" equivalent to the "All users" label. A GROUPS branch mirroring the USERS one should be added.

title: canManage() grants manage on all groups when caller only has VIEW scope
body: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() returns true when hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE) succeeds, i.e. a permission on the 'all groups' resource granting only the 'view' scope is enough. canManage() is used by GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup (requireManage()) and by V1-inherited paths, so an admin granted only view on all groups can create top-level groups and perform other manage operations. The check should be hasPermission(null, MANAGE) only, mirroring canManage(GroupModel) which correctly checks just MANAGE. The matching javadoc in GroupPermissionEvaluator.canManage() ('VIEW or MANAGE groups') repeats the same mistake.

title: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns authz resource IDs instead of group IDs and never finds per-group resources
body: In V2 per-group resources are created by AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource with name = group ID and no type set, so resourceStore.findByType(server, "Groups", ...) will not return them (it only returns the 'Groups' all-resource whose type was set in init). For whatever it does return, the callback passes groupResource.getId() (the authz resource UUID) to hasPermission(), which does resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId) — the lookup fails and silently falls back to all-groups evaluation — and then adds the resource UUID (not the group ID) to the returned set. UsersResource/BruteForceUsersResource put this set into session attribute UserModel.GROUPS to restrict the DB user search, so the returned values are meaningless as group IDs. Current tests pass only because the post-filter usersEvaluator::canView happens to compensate; the DB-level filter (and getUsersCount(realm, ..., groupIds)) is broken. Should use getName() and ensure per-group resources carry the resource type.

title: All-groups fallback is skipped whenever any permission exists for the specific group
body: hasPermission only falls back to the 'Groups' resource-type resource when no resource named after the group exists. Once any permission is created for a specific group (e.g. granting only manage-members), that group gets its own resource and subsequent checks for other scopes (view, manage, manage-membership) are evaluated solely against it; an existing all-groups permission granting those scopes is ignored. So adding a narrow per-group permission silently revokes broader all-groups grants for that group. Evaluation should consider both the specific resource and the resource-type resource (or document this as intended, with tests).

title: getResourceName does not resolve display names for Groups resource type
body: getResourceName special-cases only USERS (mapping the resource name, which is a user ID, to the username, and 'Users' to 'All users'). For the newly added GROUPS type the method falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), but group resources are created by getOrCreateResource with name = group ID and no display name, so permission listings for groups will show null/empty names instead of the group name (or 'All groups'). A GROUPS branch resolving the group by ID is needed.

title: Wrong javadoc on requireManageMembers
body: The javadoc for requireManageMembers(GroupModel) says it throws when canManageMembership(GroupModel) returns false, but the implementation checks canManageMembers(GroupModel). Also the javadoc of getGroupIdsWithViewPermission says '@return Stream of IDs' while the method returns a Set.

title: testManageGroupMembership does not isolate the group MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP scope
body: The test grants both the all-users manage-group-membership permission and the group manage-membership permission before asserting that joinGroup succeeds, so it would pass even if the group-side MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP check were missing or ignored. There is also no test for canManage()/requireManage() rejecting a caller who only has VIEW on all groups, which is exactly the case GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() currently gets wrong.

title: Post-validation bookkeeping is meaningless for federated recovery-code credentials
body: `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` now prefers the credential returned by the user storage's `getCredentials()`. For such a credential the `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` is built by the provider (in the test provider via `createFromValues`, so it has no id and all codes are always unused). The authenticator then calls `allCodesUsed()` on it, which can never be true, and if it ever were, `removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())` would target the local DB (with a possibly null id, which `em.find` rejects) rather than the user storage. Consequently a user whose codes live in user storage is never forced to `CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES` when codes run out, and the 'remove exhausted credential' logic silently does nothing. The federated branch needs its own semantics (delegate consumption/removal to the storage) or this code path should be restricted to locally stored credentials.

title: Test storage never consumes recovery codes and the test doesn't check code consumption or the displayed code number
body: `isValid` for recovery codes only checks `anyMatch` against the stored raw list and never marks a code as used, and `getCredentials` rebuilds the model with `createFromValues`, so `getNextRecoveryAuthnCode()` is always code 0. The new `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` therefore only logs in once with code 0 and cannot detect regressions where codes are not consumed, where a second login is asked for the wrong code number, or where an invalid/reused code is accepted. At minimum the test should attempt a second login (expecting a different code number / rejection of the reused code) and a login with a wrong code, with the test provider tracking used codes.

title: getCredentials dereferences possibly-null MyUser
body: `getCredentials` calls `getMyUser(user)` and immediately accesses `myUser.recoveryCodes` / `myUser.otp` without a null check, unlike `isConfiguredFor`, `isValid` and `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream` which all guard against `myUser == null`. If the user was removed from the in-memory map while a cached/federated `UserModel` still exists (e.g. during cleanup or `getFederatedCredentialsStream()` calls from other tests), this throws a NullPointerException instead of returning an empty stream.

title: Backwards-compatibility provider now uses APIs that did not exist in the version it claims to represent
body: The class Javadoc states this provider was written against Keycloak 4.8.3 and must keep compiling unchanged to prove compatibility. This PR adds an override of `CredentialInputUpdater.getCredentials(...)` and support for `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel`, neither of which existed in 4.8.3, so the provider no longer demonstrates what its documentation says. Either update the Javadoc to reflect the new mixed purpose or put the recovery-code support into a separate test storage provider so the backwards-compatibility guarantee is still meaningfully exercised.

title: Raw (unhashed) recovery codes are handed to arbitrary user storage providers without documenting it
body: `createRecoveryCodesCredential` serializes the plaintext generated codes into the `UserCredentialModel` challenge response and passes it to `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)`, i.e. to any `CredentialInputUpdater` that claims to support the `recovery-authn-codes` type. The local path stores only hashes. Any existing third-party storage provider that returns true from `supportsCredentialType` for this type (or generically) will now receive plaintext recovery codes, which is a behavior change not called out in the Javadoc or the PR. The method's Javadoc should state that the raw codes are delivered to the storage and that the storage is responsible for hashing/consuming them.

title: Exhausted federated recovery-code credential is removed with removeStoredCredentialById, which neither targets user storage nor tolerates a null id
body: `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` now returns the credential from the user storage (federated) first. When `allCodesUsed()` is true for such a credential the code still calls `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())`. That method only operates on the local Keycloak DB, so the exhausted credential stays in the user storage (and `isConfiguredFor`/`isValid` on the storage keep treating it as valid). Worse, federated models built with `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...)` (as in the test provider) have a null id, so the local store is queried with a null primary key (JPA `em.find` throws `IllegalArgumentException`), failing the login after a correct code was entered. For federated credentials the removal should go through `disableCredentialType(RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE)` (or be skipped and left to the provider).

title: Login form bean calls Optional.get() unconditionally; user storages that validate recovery codes without exposing them via getCredentials crash the login page
body: With this PR a user storage provider can own the recovery-codes credential (`updateCredential` returning true, `isConfiguredFor` true). The authenticator is then offered in the browser flow, and rendering its form constructs `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean`, which does `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user).get()` and then `getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get()`. A provider that implements `CredentialInputValidator`/`CredentialInputUpdater` for this type but does not return a fully-formed `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` (with hashed codes in secretData/credentialData) from `getCredentials` — a perfectly legal, and probably the most common, implementation — causes `NoSuchElementException` or a JSON/NPE inside `createFromCredentialModel`, producing a 500 on the recovery-code login page. The bean should handle an absent/opaque credential (e.g. fall back to not showing a code number) instead of assuming the storage surfaces the full model.

title: getCredentials dereferences getMyUser(user) without null check
body: `getCredentials` does `var myUser = getMyUser(user); ... if (myUser.recoveryCodes != null)`. All other methods in this provider (`isConfiguredFor`, `isValid`, `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream`) guard against `getMyUser` returning null (user removed from the in-memory map while a UserModel/cached entry is still referenced). Here it will throw a NullPointerException from `credentialManager().getFederatedCredentialsStream()`, which is now invoked on every recovery-code login via `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential`.

title: Test user storage never consumes recovery codes nor supports disabling them, so key behaviours of the new federated path are untested
body: `isValid` for recovery codes only checks `anyMatch(key.equals(challengeResponse))` and never marks the code as used, `getCredentials` rebuilds a fresh model from the raw list each call (so `getNextRecoveryAuthnCode()` is always code 0 and `allCodesUsed()` is never true), and `disableCredentialType`/`getDisableableCredentialTypesStream` ignore `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE`. Consequently `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` only covers a single login with code 0 and cannot exercise code consumption, the 'all codes used → CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action' branch in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator`, re-use of an already used code, or removal of the credential by admin/account REST — exactly the areas where the federated path diverges from the local one.

title: Recovery codes stored in user storage are never consumed and remain reusable
body: The user-storage `isValid` branch for `recovery-authn-codes` only checks `anyMatch(key.equals(challengeResponse))` and never marks the code as used or removes it from the stored list. Combined with `getCredentials` rebuilding a fresh `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` from the raw list on every call, a recovery code accepted once stays valid forever and `allCodesUsed()` can never become true. This silently breaks the single-use contract of recovery codes for federated users (the local `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider` consumes codes; the federated path introduced by this PR has no mechanism to do so). At minimum the test provider should consume the code so the test exercises realistic behaviour, and the production design should document/handle that `CredentialInputUpdater`-backed storages must consume codes themselves.

title: Code number prompted to the user is always 0 when credential comes from user storage
body: `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` now prefers `getFederatedCredentialsStream()`. A model returned by a user storage (e.g. via `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues`) has no usage state, so `getNextRecoveryAuthnCode()` always yields code #0 and the login form keeps asking for the first code on every login. The new test even hard-codes `expectedCode == 0`, which masks this rather than catching it. The sequential-code UX is therefore lost for federated users without any error.

title: getCredentials dereferences possibly-null MyUser
body: `getCredentials` calls `getMyUser(user)` and immediately accesses `myUser.recoveryCodes` / `myUser.otp` without a null check, unlike `isConfiguredFor`, `isValid` and `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream` in the same class. If `getFederatedCredentialsStream()` is invoked for a user that is not (or no longer) in the in-memory map, this throws a NullPointerException instead of returning an empty stream.

title: User label and generation timestamp are dropped when storing in user storage
body: `createRecoveryCodesCredential` passes only the raw code list (as JSON) to `updateCredential`; the `userLabel` and `generatedAt` values the user submitted (and that are stored in the local path via `credentialModel`) are not forwarded. The test provider consequently reads `getUserLabel()` which is always null. Storages cannot preserve the label, so the federated and local behaviour diverge for the same required action.

title: No negative or fallback coverage for recovery codes in user storage
body: The new test only verifies a single successful login with code #0. It does not verify that a used code is rejected on a second attempt, that an invalid code is rejected, that a second login prompts for the next code, or that a storage which does not support `recovery-authn-codes` falls back to local creation (the `else` branch in `createRecoveryCodesCredential`). The `delayed-authenticator` execution copied into the flow with delay 0 also adds nothing to the test.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and cannot be instantiated
body: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` was changed to subclass `StatefulDetectorHandler` with a bare `pass` body, dropping its previous concrete `evaluate` implementation. `StatefulDetectorHandler` declares four abstract members (`counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the newly added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`) that are not implemented here, so the class is abstract. `Detector.detector_handler` (src/sentry/workflow_engine/models/detector.py:86) does `group_type.detector_handler(self)`, which will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class` for any `Detector` whose `type` is `metric_alert_fire`, instead of returning a handler or `None`. `process_detectors` does not catch this, so a single metric-alert detector in the list would crash processing for the whole data packet. Either implement the abstract methods or keep a concrete stub implementation. The `# TODO: This will be a stateful detector` comment above the class is also now stale.

title: Expected occurrence built with wrong group key in TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe
body: In `TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe` the expected occurrence is built via `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)` while `evaluate_group_key_value` is invoked with group key `"group_key"`. The handler's real `build_occurrence_and_event_data` call will produce a fingerprint of `[f"{detector.id}:group_key"]`, whereas the expected one has `[f"{detector.id}:val1"]`. `IssueOccurrence` is a frozen dataclass whose equality includes `fingerprint`, so either this assertion fails, or (if it passes) the comparison is not actually verifying the fingerprint, meaning the new occurrence hook is not meaningfully tested for correct group-key-based fingerprinting. Use `"group_key"` when building the expected occurrence.

title: evaluate() docstring still says it returns a list
body: `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` was changed to return `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, but its docstring still states "Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`". The docstring should be updated to describe the dict keyed by group key so implementers of the abstract `DetectorHandler.evaluate` are not misled about the contract.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and cannot be instantiated
body: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` was changed to subclass `StatefulDetectorHandler` with a bare `pass`, but `StatefulDetectorHandler` declares four abstract members (`counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, `build_occurrence_and_event_data`). The class is therefore abstract, and `Detector.detector_handler` (which does `group_type.detector_handler(self)`) will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class` for any `Detector` whose `type` is `metric_alert_fire`. `MetricAlertFire` still registers this class as its `detector_handler`, so `process_detectors` will crash on such detectors instead of logging/skipping. Either implement the abstract methods (even with stub bodies) or remove `detector_handler` from `MetricAlertFire` until a real implementation exists.

title: Expected occurrence in test_dedupe is built with the wrong group key
body: In `TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe` the expected occurrence is built via `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)`, but the handler is invoked with group key `"group_key"`. The real call to `build_occurrence_and_event_data` will produce a fingerprint of `["<detector_id>:group_key"]` while the expected `IssueOccurrence` has `["<detector_id>:val1"]`. Since `IssueOccurrence` is a dataclass with field equality, the `== expected_result` assertion compares different fingerprints; the test either fails or, if it currently passes, indicates the comparison is not actually checking the occurrence. The expected occurrence should be built with `"group_key"`.

title: Mock occurrence builder ignores `value`, so tests cannot detect wrong values passed to the hook
body: `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` accepts `value` but never uses it in the produced `IssueOccurrence` or event data. Several tests (e.g. `test_results_on_change` evaluating with value 100, `test_dedupe` with 8, `test_state_results_multi_group` with 10 for `group_2`) build the expected occurrence with a hard-coded `6`, and they pass only because `value` is discarded. This means a regression that passes the wrong `value` into `build_occurrence_and_event_data` (the new hook this PR adds) would go unnoticed. Include `value` in the mock output (e.g. in `evidence_data`) and pass the actual evaluated value in the expectations.

title: evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` was changed to return a `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, but its docstring still states 'returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`'. Implementers reading the docstring will be misled about the contract; update it to describe the dict keyed by group key.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and cannot be instantiated
body: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` was changed from a concrete `DetectorHandler` (with a stub `evaluate`) to `class MetricAlertDetectorHandler(StatefulDetectorHandler[QuerySubscriptionUpdate]): pass`. `StatefulDetectorHandler` declares four abstract members (`counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the newly added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`), none of which are implemented here. Because `Detector.detector_handler` does `group_type.detector_handler(self)`, any `Detector` whose `type` is `metric_alert_fire` will now raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class` inside `process_detectors`, instead of the previous behaviour of returning no results. Either keep a concrete stub implementation of the abstract methods or do not point `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler` at an abstract class until it is implemented.

title: Expected occurrence built with wrong group key in TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe
body: In `TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe` the expected `IssueOccurrence` is built with `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)`, but `evaluate_group_key_value` is invoked with group key `"group_key"`. The handler's `build_occurrence_and_event_data` will therefore produce a fingerprint `["<id>:group_key"]` while the expected occurrence has `["<id>:val1"]`. Since `IssueOccurrence` is a frozen dataclass compared field-by-field, this equality assertion either fails outright or, if it passes, indicates the comparison is not actually verifying the produced occurrence. The mock should be built with `expected_result.group_key` ("group_key").

title: evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` now returns `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]` keyed by group key, but its docstring still states "returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`". Implementers reading the docstring will get the wrong contract; update it to describe the dict keyed by group key.

title: Hung/dead flusher processes are never killed because isinstance check against multiprocessing.Process fails for SpawnProcess
body: `_ensure_processes_alive` now only calls `process.kill()` when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. Processes are created via `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which yields `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` subclasses `process.BaseProcess`, not `multiprocessing.context.Process` (which is what `multiprocessing.Process` refers to), so the isinstance check is False and `kill()` is never invoked. Previously `self.process.kill()` was called unconditionally. Consequence: when a flusher process is detected as hung (`cause == "hang"`), it is left running while a new process for the same shards is spawned, leading to leaked processes and two flushers concurrently flushing the same Redis shards (duplicate produces to buffered-segments). The same faulty check at line 346 means `terminate()` is never called in `join()` either. Use `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)` or `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`.

title: join() breaks out of the loop on deadline, skipping terminate() for remaining processes
body: In `join()`, when the deadline has passed the loop does `break` before reaching `process.terminate()` for the current and all remaining processes. The inner `while process.is_alive() and (deadline is None or deadline > time.time())` already handles the deadline, so the early `break` only serves to skip termination. Any flusher processes still alive after the timeout are therefore left running after the strategy is joined (e.g. on rebalance), rather than being terminated as the single-process version did. Remove the early break (or move terminate before it).

title: time.sleep(0.1) in test_basic is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
body: `test_basic` monkeypatches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None` at the top, and then later calls `time.sleep(0.1)` with the comment "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change". Since the module-level `time.sleep` attribute is patched, this call does nothing, so the test does not actually give the flusher thread any time; it merely relies on `step.join()` blocking until the thread finishes. Either the comment is misleading or the intended wait is not happening. Use a real sleep (e.g. bind `from time import sleep` before patching, as test_flusher.py does) or remove the line and comment.

title: Inconsistent metric tag key: "shards" vs "shard"
body: `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is tagged with `{"shards": shard_tag}` while the adjacent `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` use `{"shard": shard_tag}`. This makes dashboards/queries across flusher metrics inconsistent and is likely a typo. Also note `shard_tag` is a comma-joined list of shards (e.g. "0,1,2"), so the `shard` tag no longer identifies a single shard, unlike the `spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy` metric which is emitted per individual shard.

title: _create_process_for_shard is dead code
body: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is defined but never called anywhere in the module or tests; restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards` directly from `_ensure_processes_alive`. Dead code adds maintenance burden and may confuse readers into thinking per-shard restarts are supported. Remove it.

title: Unrelated documentation change bundled into flusher PR
body: The CLAUDE.md edit (adding a hasattr vs isinstance anti-pattern) is unrelated to the multiprocessed flusher change described in the PR. Bundling unrelated changes makes review and potential reverts harder; it should be a separate PR.

title: isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is never true for spawn-context processes, so hung flushers are never killed
body: Processes are created via `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which yields `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` subclasses `BaseProcess` but is NOT a subclass of `multiprocessing.Process` (= `multiprocessing.context.Process`), so `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` evaluates to False in production. In `_ensure_processes_alive`, the old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally; the new guard means a process detected as hung (`cause == "hang"`) is never killed, yet a replacement process for the same shards is started immediately. The still-running old process and the new one then both flush and produce the same shards concurrently, leading to duplicate segments on buffered-segments and leaked processes/Redis+Kafka connections on each restart (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per index). The same false check in `join()` (line 346) means `terminate()` is also never called there. Use `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)` or check `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`.

title: join() stops iterating at the deadline and leaves remaining processes un-terminated
body: In `join()`, once `remaining_time <= 0` the loop `break`s, so any processes later in `self.processes` never get `process.terminate()` called. Previously the single process was always terminated after the wait. With several flusher processes and a slow first process, subsequent processes are left running past join, continuing to flush against Redis while the consumer is rebalancing/shutting down. The deadline check should only skip the waiting, not the terminate call.

title: Inconsistent metric tag key: "shards" vs "shard"
body: `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is tagged with `{"shards": shard_tag}` while `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` use `{"shard": shard_tag}` (and `flusher_unhealthy` uses `shard` with a single int). This splits the same dimension across two tag keys, breaking dashboards/queries that group by `shard`. Also note `shard_tag` is a comma-joined list, so the value set differs from the per-shard int used by `flusher_unhealthy`.

title: _create_process_for_shard is dead code
body: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is defined but never called anywhere in the module or tests. It also would create a second process for an index without killing/replacing the existing one. Remove it or wire it in.

title: time.sleep(0.1) in test is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
body: The test monkeypatches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None` at the top, then calls `time.sleep(0.1)` with the comment "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change". The call does nothing, so the test does not actually give the flusher thread any time; whether the segment is flushed before `step.join()` sets `stopped` is left to scheduling luck, making the test flaky rather than fixed. Use the original sleep (e.g. save a reference before patching) or poll until `messages` is non-empty.

title: Docstring claims one process per shard but default is a single process
body: The class docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but the CLI option `--flusher-processes` defaults to 1 and `num_processes = min(max_processes, len(shards))`, so by default all shards share one process exactly as before. Additionally, `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` means passing `0` silently selects one-process-per-shard rather than being rejected. The docstring and help text should describe the actual behaviour (shards are distributed round-robin over at most N processes).

title: Unrelated documentation change bundled into flusher PR
body: The hasattr/isinstance guidance added to CLAUDE.md has no relation to the span-buffer flusher refactor described in the PR. Bundling unrelated changes makes review and revert harder; it should be split into its own PR.

title: Hung/dead spawn processes are never killed because isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is False for SpawnProcess
body: `_ensure_processes_alive` now only calls `process.kill()` when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. Processes are created via `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which yields `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` and `multiprocessing.Process` (`multiprocessing.context.Process`) are sibling subclasses of `BaseProcess`, so the isinstance check is False and `kill()` is skipped. The previous code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. Consequence: when a flusher process hangs (cause="hang"), it is left running and a second process is spawned for the same shards, so two processes flush the same Redis shards concurrently and leak until the consumer dies. The same wrong check in `join()` (line 346) means `terminate()` is also never called on real processes. Use `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)` or check `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`.

title: join() stops terminating remaining processes once the deadline passes
body: In `join()`, when `remaining_time <= 0` the loop `break`s before reaching `process.terminate()` for the current and all following processes. Processes that haven't exited by the deadline are thus never terminated (intent of the original code was to terminate after waiting). The `break` should instead skip the wait but still terminate each process.

title: _create_process_for_shard is dead code
body: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is never called anywhere; `_ensure_processes_alive` calls `_create_process_for_shards` directly. It also would create a duplicate process without killing the old one. Remove it to avoid confusion.

title: Inconsistent metric tag key ('shards' vs 'shard') and high-cardinality comma-joined tag
body: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` use tag key `shard` while `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` uses `shards`, making the metrics impossible to correlate by the same tag. Additionally the value is a comma-joined list of all shards in the process (e.g. "0,4,8,12"), whose cardinality depends on partition assignment and process count and will fragment dashboards. Use a consistent key and consider tagging with the process index instead.

title: time.sleep(0.1) in test is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
body: The test monkeypatches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None` at the top, then calls `time.sleep(0.1)` with the comment "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change". Since `time.sleep` resolves to the patched attribute, this sleep does nothing, so the comment is misleading and the test only works because `step.join()` waits for the flusher thread. Either remove the sleep or capture the original `sleep` before patching (as `test_flusher.py` does via `from time import sleep`).

title: No test exercises end-to-end flushing with multiple flusher processes/shards
body: `test_flusher_processes_limit` only asserts structural properties (process count and shard assignment) and never submits spans or checks that segments from shards handled by different processes are actually flushed and produced. The multi-process restart path in `_ensure_processes_alive` (per-process healthy_since/restart counters, re-creating a `SpansBuffer` for the shard subset) is also untested. Given this PR changes the core flushing topology, an end-to-end test with >1 process that verifies all shards' segments are produced would catch regressions such as the kill/isinstance bug.

title: Docstring claims one process per shard but default is a single process
body: The class docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but the CLI option `--flusher-processes` defaults to 1 and `num_processes = min(max_processes, len(shards))`, so by default all shards share one process and in general shards are round-robined across at most `max_processes` processes. The docstring should describe the actual behaviour.

title: Google credential key is overwritten with a zod SafeParseReturnType wrapper object
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the full zod safeParse result (`{ success: true, data: {...} }`), not the parsed token. In `refreshAccessToken` the return value is assigned to `key` and written directly with `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. Previously `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` returned the token object itself. After the first token refresh, every Google Calendar credential in the DB becomes `{success: true, data: {...}}`; the next `GoogleCalendarService` construction calls `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` which throws, breaking Google Calendar (and Google Meet) for the user until they reconnect. This happens in all modes, not just when credential syncing is enabled. The callers in office365/zoom/salesforce correctly use `.data`; Google must do the same (`key: parsed.data`).

title: `prisma` used without being imported in Salesforce CalendarService
body: The new refresh-and-persist logic calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` but the file never imports `prisma` from `@calcom/prisma` (the import list only has jsforce, rrule, zod, lib helpers, types, `getAppKeysFromSlug` and `parseRefreshTokenResponse`). This is a TypeScript error and, if it ever ran, a `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined` on every Salesforce service instantiation, making the Salesforce integration unusable. Add `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma";`.

title: minimumTokenResponseSchema computed keys evaluate to "[object Object]" and strip every field except access_token
body: `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()` do not create wildcard keys; `ZodType` has no custom `toString`, so both evaluate to the literal key `"[object Object]"` (the second overwriting the first). The resulting schema is effectively `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), "[object Object]": z.unknown().optional() })`, and because `z.object` strips unknown keys, in sync mode `data` contains only `access_token` (plus the injected placeholder `refresh_token`). Consequences: Zoom computes `key.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + undefined * 1000)` = NaN which is persisted as `null` and makes `zoomTokenSchema.parse(credential.key)` fail on the next call; Office365 never gets a new `expires_in` so it refreshes on every request; Salesforce loses `instance_url`/`id`/`signature` from the stored key so the next connection has `instanceUrl: undefined`. Use `.passthrough()`/`.catchall(z.unknown())` and explicitly handle expiry rather than computed keys.

title: Sync mode returns a raw fetch Response while several callers expect SDK-specific response shapes
body: When `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is set, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the `fetch` `Response` object regardless of what the wrapped `refreshFunction` would have returned. Several integrations were converted assuming the original shape: Google expects a gaxios response and reads `res.data.access_token` (undefined → TypeError, swallowed by the catch, so the stale expired auth is returned and calls fail); HubSpot expects a `HubspotToken` object and reads `.expiresIn`/`.accessToken` then stores the `Response` object as the credential key; Zoho CRM and Zoho Bigin expect an axios response and read `tokenInfo.data.error` (TypeError). So for Google Calendar, HubSpot, Zoho CRM and Zoho Bigin the credential-sync feature cannot work at all, and in some cases corrupts the stored key. Either normalize the sync response to JSON and adapt each caller, or make the sync branch return the same shape as the provider SDK.

title: appStoreMetadata is keyed by app directory name, not slug, so the webhook 404s for most apps
body: `appStoreMetadata` (from `apps.metadata.generated.ts`) is keyed by the app's directory name (`googlecalendar`, `office365calendar`, `zoomvideo`, `office365video`, `larkcalendar`, ...), not by `slug` (`google-calendar`, `office365-calendar`, `zoom`, `msteams`, `lark-calendar`). The handler looks up `appStoreMetadata[app.slug]` after confirming the slug exists in the `App` table, so for every app whose dirName differs from its slug the lookup is `undefined` and the request returns 404 "App not found. Ensure that you have the correct app slug" even though the slug is correct. Only apps where dirName === slug (hubspot, salesforce, zohocrm, webex, zoho-bigin) work. Use `getAppFromSlug(slug)` from `@calcom/app-store/utils` (which searches by `slug`) instead.

title: Zoho Bigin passes the credential id as the user id to refreshOAuthTokens
body: `refreshOAuthTokens(fn, "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` — the third parameter is `userId: number | null` and is sent to the self-hoster's sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. `refreshAccessToken(credentialId, credentialKey)` only has the credential id in scope, so the sync endpoint will receive a credential id and return (or fail to return) tokens for the wrong user. Every other integration passes `credential.userId`; this method needs access to the credential's `userId` as well.

title: Injected placeholder refresh_token overwrites the real refresh token stored in the DB
body: When the parsed response lacks `refresh_token`, the function sets `data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. Callers then merge this into the stored credential: Zoom does `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token` and Office365 does `o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }`. In sync mode (where the self-hoster is told to return only access token and expiry) this replaces the user's real refresh token in Cal.com's DB with the literal string `"refresh_token"`, so if syncing is later disabled or the endpoint is unavailable the credential is permanently unusable without reconnecting. In non-sync mode Office365's `refresh_token` is optional in `refreshTokenResponseSchema`, so a response without it would also destroy the stored token (previously the spread simply left the existing value untouched). Do not fabricate a refresh token; leave the field absent so callers keep the existing value.

title: Request to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT carries no authentication
body: The POST to the self-hoster's credential sync endpoint sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` as form fields with no secret, signature or bearer token. The endpoint must return live OAuth access tokens for arbitrary users, so unless the self-hoster adds out-of-band protection (network allowlisting), anyone who discovers the URL can obtain any user's third-party access tokens by posting a user id. The inbound webhook already has `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`/`CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME`; the outbound call should at minimum send the same secret header so the endpoint can authenticate Cal.com.

title: Salesforce now refreshes on every instantiation, uses fragile statusText check, and connects with the stale access token
body: `getClient` previously just constructed a `jsforce.Connection` (jsforce refreshes lazily on 401). It now unconditionally POSTs to `login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` every time the service is constructed (every booking, availability check, etc.), adding latency and a Salesforce API call per operation. The success check `response.statusText !== "OK"` is unreliable (status text is optional/empty for HTTP/2 and some proxies); use `response.ok`. After persisting the new token, the connection is still created with `accessToken: credentialKey.access_token` (the old one) instead of `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`, so the refresh result isn't even used for the current request. Also, the refresh does not go through `refreshOAuthTokens`, so in sync mode Salesforce still contacts Salesforce directly while every other app contacts the self-hoster, which contradicts the feature's intent.

title: Sync request uses "zoomvideo" while the webhook requires the DB slug "zoom"
body: The `appSlug` sent to the credential sync endpoint for Zoom is the directory name `"zoomvideo"`, but the inbound `/api/webhook/app-credential` endpoint validates `appSlug` against `App.slug` in the DB, which is `"zoom"`. Other apps send their real slug (`google-calendar`, `office365-calendar`, `msteams`, `lark-calendar`). Self-hosters implementing the sync endpoint will have to special-case Zoom. Use `"zoom"` for consistency.

title: Webex and Lark refresh paths route through the sync endpoint but keep provider-specific strict response validation
body: Webex now calls `refreshOAuthTokens` (so in sync mode the response comes from the self-hoster) but still validates with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema`, which requires `scope` to be the exact literal `"spark:kms meeting:schedules_read meeting:schedules_write"`, `token_type: "Bearer"`, `refresh_token` and `refresh_token_expires_in`. Lark similarly passes the sync response through `handleLarkError`, which expects Lark's `{ code: 0, data: { access_token, refresh_token, expires_in, refresh_expires_in } }` envelope. The comment in `refreshOAuthTokens` tells self-hosters the response "should only contain the access token and expiry date", so a conforming endpoint will be rejected by both apps. Either use `parseRefreshTokenResponse` (once fixed) in these apps or document the full provider-shaped response they require.

title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time `!==` and no method restriction
body: The shared secret is checked with a plain string inequality, which is vulnerable in principle to timing side channels; use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers (as other webhook handlers in the repo do for signatures). The handler also accepts any HTTP method (GET included) and will read `req.body`; it should reject non-POST requests with 405.

title: Body validation and decryption errors surface as unhandled 500s
body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a `ZodError` on malformed input, and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` throws on a wrong key or non-JSON payload. Neither is caught, so the self-hoster receives a generic 500 with no indication of what was wrong. Use `safeParse` and wrap decryption in a try/catch, returning 400 with a message.

title: Updating an existing credential does not clear the `invalid` flag
body: Google Calendar and Zoom/Webex mark a credential `invalid: true` when the provider returns `invalid_grant`. When the parent application pushes fresh keys via this webhook, the update only sets `key`, so a previously invalidated credential stays flagged invalid and the UI/booking flows continue to treat it as broken even though it now has working tokens. The update should also set `invalid: false`.

title: No tests for the new webhook or the shared refresh/parse utilities
body: The PR adds a new public API route and two shared OAuth utilities used by ~10 integrations, and modifies the token-refresh path of every OAuth app, but ships no tests (the checklist explicitly says none were added). Even a minimal unit test of `parseRefreshTokenResponse` would have caught that the computed-key schema strips all fields, and an integration test of the Google refresh path would have caught the SafeParseReturnType being stored as the credential key. Please add unit tests for `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, `refreshOAuthTokens` (both branches), and the webhook handler (auth failure, unknown slug, create vs update).

title: Google Calendar stores the zod SafeParse wrapper object as the credential key
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse()` returns the raw `safeParse` result (`{ success: true, data: {...} }`), not the parsed data. Previously this line was `const key = googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` which returned the token object directly. Now `key` is the wrapper object and it is written to `credential.key` on line 98-101. The next time this credential is loaded, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` (line 75) will fail because `access_token`, `refresh_token`, `expiry_date` etc. are nested under `data`. This corrupts every Google Calendar credential on its first token refresh and happens regardless of whether credential sharing is enabled. Use `.data` from the return value (or have the helper return the parsed data).

title: `prisma` is used but never imported in Salesforce CalendarService
body: The new `getClient` code calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` on line 96, but there is no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` in this file (imports are lines 1-20). This is a type-check failure and, at runtime, a `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined` thrown from `getClient`, which runs in the constructor via `this.conn = this.getClient(credential)`. Every Salesforce booking operation will fail. Add the missing import.

title: `minimumTokenResponseSchema` uses `z.string().toString()` as keys, which evaluates to "[object Object]" and strips every field except access_token
body: Computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the literal string `"[object Object]"` (ZodType does not override `toString`), so the second overwrites the first and the schema is effectively `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), "[object Object]": z.unknown().optional() })`. The intended 'any numeric property is the expiry' / 'allow other properties' behaviour does not exist.
