This PR adds an override of `CredentialInputUpdater.getCredentials` (an API that did not exist in 4.8.3), uses `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel`/`KeycloakModelUtils.generateId()`, and changes the OTP path to assign an id. After this change the test no longer demonstrates that an unmodified legacy provider still works; it only demonstrates that a provider written against the current API works. The recovery-code support should live in a separate test provider (or the Javadoc/intent of this class must be revised).

title: Test storage accepts any stored code, never consumes codes, and keeps them in plaintext
body: `isValid` for `recovery-authn-codes` returns true if the input matches *any* of the stored codes and never removes the used one; `getCredentials` rebuilds the model from the full list each time, so `getNextRecoveryAuthnCode()` always yields code 0. Consequently `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` can only ever assert `expectedCode == 0` and does not exercise code consumption, the `allCodesUsed()` branch, or the required-action re-trigger for a federated credential, which are exactly the paths the production changes touched. Also, `getCredentials` dereferences `getMyUser(user)` without the null check used elsewhere in this class, so an unknown user yields an NPE instead of an empty stream.

title: Recovery-code login is never completed, so the final logout is a no-op
body: Unlike the OTP tests in this class, `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` calls `enterRecoveryAuthnCodePage.clickSignInButton()` and then `testAppHelper.logout()` without first calling `testAppHelper.completeLogin()`. `TestAppHelper.logout()` logs out using the refresh token obtained in `completeLogin()`; without it the logout request is sent without a token, fails, and the result is not asserted. The authorization code is never exchanged either, so the test does not verify the login actually yields tokens, and the browser SSO session for `otp1` is left behind for subsequent tests in the class.

title: Old locally-stored recovery codes stay valid when new codes are accepted by the user storage
body: `createRecoveryCodesCredential` first calls `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)`; if the user storage returns `true`, it logs and returns without touching Keycloak's own store. Before this change recovery codes for federated (non-import) users were always written to Keycloak's federated-storage tables via `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential`, which also deletes any previously stored recovery-code credential. After upgrading, a federated user who already has such a local credential and regenerates codes will get the new set stored in the user storage while the old set remains in Keycloak DB. `UserCredentialManager.isValid` falls through to the local `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider` when the storage rejects the input, so the old, supposedly replaced codes continue to authenticate the user, while the login page (driven by `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential`, which prefers the federated credential) asks for a number from the new set. The method should remove existing stored credentials of this type (e.g. via the credential provider's delete path) when the user storage accepted the new codes.

title: removeStoredCredentialById is applied to a credential that may come from the user storage
body: `optUserCredentialFound` is now obtained from `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential`, which returns the user-storage credential first. When that credential reports `allCodesUsed()`, the code calls `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())`. A credential produced by a `CredentialInputUpdater.getCredentials` implementation is not a stored Keycloak credential: its id is provider-defined or null (e.g. `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues` never sets an id, as the test provider in this PR shows). With a null id the JPA federated store's `em.find(..., null)` throws `IllegalArgumentException`, failing the login after the code was already accepted; with a foreign id the call is a silent no-op and the exhausted credential is never cleared in the storage. For federated credentials the removal should go through `disableCredentialType(RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE)` (or be skipped), and the local removal should only run for credentials actually obtained from `getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream`.

title: User label and generation timestamp are dropped on the user-storage path
body: The `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` passed in carries the user-chosen label (`userLabel` hidden field) and the `generatedAt` timestamp, but the `UserCredentialModel` handed to `updateCredential` only contains the type and the JSON list of raw codes. A user storage provider therefore has no way to persist the label or the real generation time (the test provider ends up with `userLabel == null` and `createdDate = now`). When the storage accepts the credential, the label the user typed is silently lost, which is a behavioral regression versus the local path where both are stored.

title: New user-storage SPI contract for recovery codes is undocumented and unverified
body: This method introduces a new, implicit contract for `CredentialInputUpdater` implementations: for type `recovery-authn-codes` the `CredentialInput.getChallengeResponse()` is a JSON-serialized array of plaintext codes, and `getCredentials(realm, user)` is expected to return a `CredentialModel` whose `credentialData`/`secretData` can be parsed by `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel` (otherwise `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` and the authenticator will throw). None of this is documented on the method, in `CredentialInputUpdater`, or in release notes. Additionally, unlike `createOTPCredential` which returns a boolean and validates the result, this method is `void` and trusts a `true` from `updateCredential` without any check, so a provider that answers `supportsCredentialType` liberally but does not persist the codes leaves the user with no recovery codes while the required action is marked complete.

title: Federated recovery-code test covers only a single login; consumption, exhaustion and removal are untested
body: `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` sets up codes and performs one login with code #0. The companion test storage never marks a code as used (`isValid` is a plain `anyMatch` over all codes), always rebuilds the credential with all codes remaining, never exposes an id, and does not support `disableCredentialType`/`getDisableableCredentialTypesStream` for this type. Consequently the new production paths are not exercised for federated storage: that the next requested code number advances after use, the `allCodesUsed()` branch in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` (which now operates on a federated credential), re-generation replacing an older set, and removal via admin/account REST. A test that re-logs with a second code and asserts the requested code number, plus one exercising exhaustion, would catch the id/removal problem in the authenticator.

title: getCredentials dereferences getMyUser(user) without a null check
body: Every other method in this provider (`getDisableableCredentialTypesStream`, `isConfiguredFor`, `isValid`) guards against `getMyUser(user)` returning null, but `getCredentials` immediately accesses `myUser.recoveryCodes`. `getCredentials` is reached via `getFederatedCredentialsStream()` from the account REST endpoint and from `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential`, so a `UserModel` adapter whose backing entry has been removed from the shared map (e.g. after `removeUser` in test cleanup while a session still holds the adapter) produces a `NullPointerException` instead of an empty stream.

title: Recovery-code credential returned from getCredentials has no id; id generated in updateCredential is discarded
body: `updateCredential` assigns `KeycloakModelUtils.generateId()` to the stored `recoveryCodesModel`, but `getCredentials` rebuilds the credential with `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...)`, which never sets an id, so consumers receive a credential with `getId() == null`. This makes the credential unaddressable through the account REST API (`/credentials/{id}`) and feeds a null id into `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator`'s `removeStoredCredentialById` branch. The stored id (and label) should be copied onto the rebuilt model so the test provider reflects what a real provider must return.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now an abstract class and cannot be instantiated
body: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` was changed to subclass `StatefulDetectorHandler` with a bare `pass` body. `StatefulDetectorHandler` declares four abstract members (`counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the newly added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`), none of which are implemented here, so the class is abstract. `MetricAlertFire` is a registered `GroupType` whose `detector_handler` points at this class, and `Detector.detector_handler` does `group_type.detector_handler(self)`; for any `Detector` row with `type="metric_alert_fire"` this will now raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class ...` from inside `process_detectors`, whereas before this PR `evaluate` simply returned an empty list. Either implement the abstract members (even as stubs), keep the old concrete `DetectorHandler` subclass until the real implementation lands, or remove `detector_handler` from `MetricAlertFire`. The `# TODO: This will be a stateful detector when we build that abstraction` comment is also now stale.

title: Expected occurrence in TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe is built with the wrong group key
body: In `TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe` the expected occurrence is produced via `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)`, but `evaluate_group_key_value` is invoked with group key `"group_key"`, so the handler's hook builds an occurrence whose fingerprint is `[f"{detector.id}:group_key"]` while the expected one has `[f"{detector.id}:val1"]`. `IssueOccurrence` is a frozen dataclass with field-wise equality (and `DetectorEvaluationResult` compares its `result` field), so `== expected_result` cannot hold and the assertion will fail. The call should pass `"group_key"` (i.e. `expected_result.group_key`) so the fingerprints line up.

title: Hook arguments `value` are never verified; several tests pass incorrect values and still pass
body: `MockDetectorStateHandler.build_occurrence_and_event_data` delegates to `build_mock_occurrence_and_event`, which ignores the `value` argument entirely. As a result nothing in the suite checks that `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate_group_key_value` forwards the correct value (or priority) to the new hook. This is already masking mistakes in the expectations: `test_state_results_multi_group` builds the expected `group_2` occurrence with value `6` although the packet carries `10`, and `test_results_on_change`/`test_dedupe` build expectations with `6` while evaluating `100`/`8`. A regression that passed the wrong value or wrong `PriorityLevel` into the hook would go undetected. Consider having the mock embed `value`/`new_status` in `evidence_data` (or asserting on a `mock.patch.object` of the hook) so the forwarded arguments are actually checked.

title: evaluate() docstring still says it returns a list
body: `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` was changed to return `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, but its docstring still states "returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`". Implementers reading the docstring will get the wrong contract; update it to describe the dict keyed by group key.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and cannot be instantiated
body: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` was changed to subclass `StatefulDetectorHandler` with an empty body (`pass`). `StatefulDetectorHandler` declares four abstract members (`counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the newly added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`), none of which are implemented here, so the class remains abstract under `ABCMeta`. `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler` still points at it, and `Detector.detector_handler` does `group_type.detector_handler(self)`, which will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler ...` for any `Detector` whose `type` is `metric_alert_fire` (which is also the default type produced by the `create_detector` test fixture). Previously this handler was a working no-op (`evaluate` returned `[]`); now `process_detectors` will crash instead of skipping. Either implement the abstract members (even as stubs) or leave the class as a concrete `DetectorHandler` until the real implementation lands.

title: Expected occurrence built with wrong group key in TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe
body: In `TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe` the expected occurrence is built with `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)`, which sets `fingerprint=handler.build_fingerprint("val1")` -> `["<id>:val1"]`. The code under test is then invoked with group key `"group_key"`, so the real hook produces `fingerprint=["<id>:group_key"]`. `IssueOccurrence` is a frozen dataclass with field-wise equality, so `DetectorEvaluationResult(...) == expected_result` will be False and the assertion on line 546-560 fails. The expected occurrence must be built with the same group key (`"group_key"`) that is passed to `evaluate_group_key_value`.

title: Mock occurrence builder ignores `value`, so tests don't verify the value passed to the hook
body: `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` accepts a `value` argument but never uses it, so the tests cannot detect whether `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate_group_key_value` passes the correct value into `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. This is already masking inconsistencies in the new tests: `test_results_on_change` evaluates `{"val1": 100}` but builds the expected occurrence with `value=6`, and `test_state_results_multi_group` evaluates `group_2` with `10` but builds the expected occurrence with `6`. Include `value` in the mock occurrence (e.g. in `evidence_data` or `subtitle`) so a regression in the argument passed to the hook would actually fail a test, and fix the mismatched values in those tests.

title: evaluate() docstring still says it returns a list
body: `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` was changed to return `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, but its docstring still reads "returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`". Implementers reading the docstring will get the wrong contract; update it to describe the dict keyed by group key.

title: Stale TODO comment about becoming a stateful detector
body: The comment `# TODO: This will be a stateful detector when we build that abstraction` is now wrong: this PR makes `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` subclass `StatefulDetectorHandler`. The stale TODO should be removed or replaced with a note about the abstract methods that still need to be implemented.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now an uninstantiable abstract class
body: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` was changed to subclass `StatefulDetectorHandler` with a bare `pass` body. `StatefulDetectorHandler` declares four abstract members (`counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the new `build_occurrence_and_event_data`), none of which are implemented here, so the class retains a non-empty `__abstractmethods__` and `MetricAlertDetectorHandler(detector)` raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class`. `Detector.detector_handler` calls `group_type.detector_handler(self)` unconditionally, so any `Detector` row with `type="metric_alert_fire"` fed to `process_detectors` will now crash instead of returning no results as it did before this change (the previous implementation had a concrete no-op `evaluate`). Either implement the abstract members (even as stubs that raise `NotImplementedError` with a clear message) or keep a concrete handler until the metric-alert detector is actually built. The `# TODO: This will be a stateful detector when we build that abstraction` comment on line 10 is also now stale.

title: Expected occurrence in TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe is built for the wrong group key
body: In `TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe`, the expected `IssueOccurrence` is produced via `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)`, but `evaluate_group_key_value` is invoked with `expected_result.group_key == "group_key"`. The handler's `build_occurrence_and_event_data` therefore calls `build_fingerprint("group_key")` producing `["<id>:group_key"]`, while the expected occurrence has fingerprint `["<id>:val1"]`. `IssueOccurrence` is a dataclass whose generated `__eq__` compares `fingerprint`, so `expected_result` cannot equal the actual `DetectorEvaluationResult` and the assertion on line 546-560 should fail (if it somehow passes, the comparison is not actually verifying the occurrence contents). The expected occurrence should be built with the same group key (`"group_key"`) and value (`10`) that are passed to `evaluate_group_key_value`.

title: evaluate() docstring still describes a list return value
body: `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` was changed in this PR to return `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, but its docstring still reads "Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`" and "There will be one result for each group key". The docstring should be updated to say it returns a dict keyed by group key, so implementers of other handlers aren't misled about the contract (which `process_detectors` now relies on via `.values()`).

title: isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is never true for spawn-context processes, so hung flushers are never killed
body: `self.mp_context.Process` (from `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")`) returns `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`, which subclasses `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` but is NOT a subclass of `multiprocessing.Process` (`multiprocessing.context.Process`). The guard `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.kill()` added in `_ensure_processes_alive` is therefore always False in production. Before this PR `kill()` was called unconditionally. Consequence: when a flusher is detected as hung (`cause == "hang"`), the restart counter is bumped and a brand-new process is spawned for the same shards, but the hung original is left running. It leaks (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS times per process index), and if it later unblocks, two processes concurrently run `flush_segments`/`done_flush_segments` against the same Redis shards and both produce to buffered-segments, causing duplicate segments and racy queue updates. The same broken check at line 346 in `join()` means `terminate()` is never invoked either (pre-existing, but now multiplied by N processes), and the early `break` on deadline at line 341 skips cleanup for the remaining processes entirely. Use `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)` or `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`. There is also no test exercising the restart/kill path to catch this.

title: Comma-joined shard list used as a metric tag value corrupts statsd/Datadog tags
body: `shard_tag = ",".join(map(str, shards))` is passed as the tag value for `spans.buffer.flusher.produce`, `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` and `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce`. The DogStatsD wire format separates tags with commas (`|#k:v,k2:v2`) and Sentry's Datadog backend does not escape tag values, so with the default `--flusher-processes 1` a single process handles all assigned shards and emits e.g. `shard:0,1,2,...,31`, which the agent parses as tag `shard:0` plus bare tags `1`, `2`, ... This both breaks the intended per-shard breakdown and injects garbage tags with unbounded cardinality (the value changes with every rebalance). Additionally the tag key is inconsistent: `shard` on lines 185/195 but `shards` on line 199. Either emit one metric per shard with an integer tag, or tag with `process_index` and drop the joined list.

title: Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched, leaving the flush race unaddressed
body: `test_basic` monkeypatches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None` at line 15, and the newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` at line 62 resolves the attribute on the `time` module at call time, so it does nothing. The comment "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change" is therefore wrong: there is still a race between setting `current_drift.value = 9000` and `step.join()` setting `stopped`, and if the flusher thread observes `stopped` before completing one `flush_segments` round-trip with the new drift, `messages` is empty and `(msg,) = messages` fails. `test_flusher.py` avoids this by using `from time import sleep` (bound before the monkeypatch). Either do the same here, or poll until `messages` is non-empty with a timeout.

title: submit() now issues N× redundant Redis INFO/ZCARD round-trips, one per flusher buffer
body: `submit()` iterates over `self.buffers` (one `SpansBuffer` per flusher process) calling `record_stored_segments()` (line 270) and `get_memory_info()` (line 301). `SpansBuffer.get_memory_info` returns memory usage for every node of the Redis cluster regardless of `assigned_shards`, so with N flusher processes every submitted batch now sends N× the `INFO` commands to every Redis node (and the summed `used`/`available` are both inflated N×; the ratio is unchanged only by coincidence). `record_stored_segments` similarly goes from one pipeline to N pipelines. With `flusher_processes=None` (the factory default) N equals the number of assigned shards, so a consumer with 32 partitions issues 32× the previous Redis control traffic on every batch. Call `get_memory_info()` on a single buffer and either keep the original full-shard buffer for `record_stored_segments` or dedupe the calls.

title: flusher_unhealthy counter is now incremented once per shard per event, inflating existing alerts
body: Previously `spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy` was incremented once per detected crash/hang. The new code loops over every shard handled by the unhealthy process and increments once per shard, so with the default single flusher process covering all assigned partitions a single crash produces e.g. 32 increments. Any dashboards or alert thresholds based on this counter will see an N× jump unrelated to actual failure rate. Emit once per process (tagged with process index or shard count) instead.

title: _create_process_for_shard is dead code
body: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is never called anywhere; the restart path in `_ensure_processes_alive` calls `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly. The `if not process: continue` check at line 222 is likewise unreachable since process/thread objects are always truthy. Dead code in the restart path makes the already-subtle lifecycle logic harder to audit; remove it.

title: max_processes=0 silently means 'one per shard' and negative values crash with KeyError
body: `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats `--flusher-processes 0` as "use as many processes as shards", which is undocumented (the CLI help only says it is a maximum, default 1) and the opposite of what a user passing 0 likely intends. A negative value (e.g. `--flusher-processes -1`) yields `num_processes = -1`, `range(-1)` creates an empty map, and `i % -1 == 0` makes `self.process_to_shards_map[0]` raise `KeyError` in `__init__` on every partition assignment. Validate the option (`>= 1`) in the click option or constructor.

title: Docstring claims one process per shard, but processes are capped by max_processes (default 1)
body: The class docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but `num_processes = min(max_processes, len(shards))` and the CLI default for `--flusher-processes` is 1, so in the default deployment a single process handles all shards round-robin. The docstring also still documents a non-existent `:param topic:` and omits `max_processes`. Misleading documentation on the concurrency model of a component that was just made multiprocess will confuse operators tuning it.

title: `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is never true for spawn-context processes, so hung flushers are never killed
body: `_ensure_processes_alive` now only calls `process.kill()` when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. The flusher processes are created via `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which returns `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` derives from `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, not from `multiprocessing.Process` (`multiprocessing.context.Process`), so the check is always False in production and the kill is silently skipped. Consequences: for the `hang` cause, a new process is started for the same shards while the old one is left running; when the old process unblocks (e.g. Kafka/Redis recovers) two processes flush the same shards concurrently and both produce the same segments to buffered-segments (duplicates), and each restart leaks a process plus its Redis connection and KafkaProducer (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per index). The previous code called `kill()` unconditionally, so this is a regression introduced by the guard. Use `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)` (or `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`), and add a test for the restart path, which currently has no coverage.

title: join() never terminates spawn processes and skips cleanup of remaining processes after deadline
body: In `join`, `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.terminate()` has the same problem as the kill path: `SpawnProcess` is not a subclass of `multiprocessing.Process`, so `terminate()` is never invoked. Additionally the loop `break`s as soon as the deadline has passed, so any processes after the first one in iteration order are neither waited on nor terminated. Shutdown therefore relies entirely on the `stopped` flag and `daemon=True`; a process stuck in `future.result()` or a Redis call will not be stopped by `join` and will only die when the parent exits.

title: `time.sleep(0.1)` added to fix a race is a no-op because `time.sleep` is monkeypatched earlier in the same test
body: `test_basic` starts with `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` and then later calls `time.sleep(0.1)` with the comment "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change". Because the test references `time.sleep` through the module attribute, it resolves to the patched lambda and returns immediately, so no time is actually given. The race the comment describes (flusher thread must observe `current_drift = 9000` and flush before `step.join()` sets `stopped`) is unchanged, and the test remains timing-dependent/flaky. Bind the real sleep before patching (as `test_flusher.py` does with `from time import sleep`) or wait on an explicit condition (e.g. poll until `messages` is non-empty).

title: Inconsistent metric tag key (`shard` vs `shards`) and comma-joined shard list used as a tag value
body: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` are tagged with `{"shard": shard_tag}` while `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` uses `{"shards": shard_tag}` for the same value, so the three metrics cannot be grouped/filtered by the same tag key in dashboards. Also `shard_tag` is `",".join(shards)`; with the CLI default of one flusher process this becomes a value like `0,1,2,...,31`. Commas are the tag separator in the statsd/DogStatsD wire format and are either mangled by the client or split into bogus tags, and the set of possible combinations changes with every rebalance, creating unbounded tag cardinality. Prefer a stable key and either a per-process index tag or per-shard emission.

title: Redis memory info is fetched once per flusher process and summed, duplicating cluster-wide data
body: `SpansBuffer.get_memory_info()` reports Redis node memory via `INFO memory` on every node of the cluster; it is not shard-scoped. Iterating `self.buffers.values()` and extending `memory_infos` therefore issues the same INFO calls N times (N = number of flusher processes) and sums N copies of `used` and `available` on every `submit()` when `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage < 1.0`. The ratio happens to come out the same, but the Redis round trips scale with process count for no benefit. Similarly `record_stored_segments()` is now N pipeline round trips instead of one. Keeping the original full-shard `buffer` on `self` for these two calls avoids the duplication.

title: Docstring claims one process per shard; actual behaviour depends on `max_processes` with a CLI default of 1 and a `None` default of per-shard
body: The class docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but `SpanFlusher` creates `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` processes with shards distributed round-robin, and the `process-spans` CLI option defaults `--flusher-processes` to 1, so in production the default is a single process handling all shards. Conversely, constructing `SpanFlusher`/`ProcessSpansStrategyFactory` directly with `flusher_processes=None` (or `0`, because of `max_processes or len(...)`) silently spawns one Django-initialized process per assigned shard, which for consumers with many partitions can be dozens of processes. The docstring should describe the real mapping and document the `max_processes` parameter (the existing `:param topic:` also refers to a parameter that does not exist).

title: `--flusher-processes` accepts 0 and negative values with surprising results
body: The new `--flusher-processes` option is a plain `int` with no range validation and help text "Defaults to 1". Passing `0` is treated as falsy by `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` and results in one process per shard rather than zero or an error. Passing a negative value makes `num_processes` negative, `process_to_shards_map` empty, and `i % num_processes` evaluate to 0 (or negative), so `self.process_to_shards_map[process_index]` raises `KeyError` during `create_with_partitions`, i.e. the consumer crashes on partition assignment with an unhelpful error. Use `click.IntRange(min=1)` or validate in the factory.

title: New multi-process test only checks counts; no test exercises flushing across multiple processes or the restart path
body: `test_flusher_processes_limit` asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2` and that the total shard count is 4, then joins. It never submits spans, so nothing verifies that segments on shards handled by the second process are actually flushed, that each shard is assigned to exactly one process (a shard appearing twice would still satisfy the sum check), or that per-process backpressure/health values propagate to `submit()`. `_ensure_processes_alive` (unhealthy detection, kill, re-spawn, MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS) is also untested, which is how the non-functional `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` guard went unnoticed.

title: `_create_process_for_shard` is dead code
body: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is defined but never called anywhere in the module or elsewhere in the diff; restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly from `_ensure_processes_alive`. Dead helpers that look like public-ish API on the strategy add maintenance burden and can mislead future callers (it does not kill the existing process before starting a new one, so calling it would double up flushers for those shards). Remove it or wire it in with the kill logic.

title: Unrelated documentation change bundled into the flusher refactor
body: The PR adds a new `hasattr()` vs `isinstance()` anti-pattern section to `CLAUDE.md`. This has nothing to do with the span-buffer flusher change described in the PR title/description and is not mentioned there. Mixing unrelated guidance edits into a behavioural consumer change makes the commit harder to review and revert; it should be split into its own PR.

title: isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is False for spawn-context processes, so hung flusher processes are never killed
body: In `_ensure_processes_alive`, the PR wraps `process.kill()` in `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. Production flusher processes are created via `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which yields `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` subclasses `BaseProcess` directly and is NOT a subclass of `multiprocessing.Process` (`multiprocessing.context.Process`), so the check is always False for real processes and `kill()` is never invoked. The previous code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally and worked. Consequence: when a process is detected as hung ("hang" cause after `max-unhealthy-seconds`), the old process is left running while a replacement is spawned for the same shards. A slow-but-alive process will then flush the same shards concurrently with the new one (both can read the same expired segments from the Redis queue before `done_flush_segments` removes them, producing duplicate segments to Kafka), and up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS+1 processes can pile up per shard group. The same wrong check at line 346 in `join()` means `terminate()` is also never called on spawned processes (pre-existing, but this PR touched that code). Use `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)` or `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)` instead.

title: join() breaks out of the process loop on deadline, leaving remaining processes un-terminated
body: In `SpanFlusher.join`, once `deadline - time.time() <= 0` the loop does `break`, which skips `process.terminate()` for every process not yet visited. Previously (single process) the wait loop was always followed by `terminate()`. With multiple flusher processes, if the first process consumes the whole join timeout, all later processes are neither waited on nor terminated, and will keep running (potentially hung, which is precisely when join times out) across a rebalance alongside the newly created flusher for the same shards. The `break` is also redundant since the inner `while` already respects the deadline; remove it so that each process is at least terminated.

title: Redis memory info is queried once per flusher process on every submit
body: `submit()` now iterates `self.buffers.values()` and calls `buffer.get_memory_info()` on each. `SpansBuffer.get_memory_info` reports cluster-wide node memory (it is not scoped to the buffer's assigned shards), so each of the N per-process buffers returns the same node list. The used/available ratio is unaffected (both sums scale by N), but the number of Redis INFO/MEMORY round trips per `submit()` now scales linearly with `--flusher-processes`, and with per-shard processes this can mean dozens of redundant cluster-wide queries per batch. Query memory info once (e.g. from a single buffer) rather than per process.

title: Inconsistent metric tag keys ("shard" vs "shards") and high-cardinality comma-joined tag values
body: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` are tagged with `{"shard": shard_tag}` while `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` on line 199 uses `{"shards": shard_tag}`. The same value is emitted under two different tag names, which breaks consistent filtering/grouping in dashboards. Additionally `shard_tag` is a comma-joined list of all shards handled by the process (e.g. "0,1,2,...,31" when `--flusher-processes 1`), so the tag value changes with every assignment/partition count and is not comparable with the per-shard integer `shard` tag used by `spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy` at line 244.

title: The added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched in this test
body: `test_basic` monkeypatches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None` at the top, and the new `time.sleep(0.1)` (commented "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change") resolves to the patched function at call time, so it sleeps for zero time. The test therefore still depends on the flusher thread happening to run an iteration between `current_drift.value = 9000` and `join()` setting `stopped`; if the thread observes `stopped` first it exits without flushing and `(msg,) = messages` fails. Either use a pre-import `from time import sleep` (as `test_flusher.py` does) or poll until `messages` is non-empty with a timeout instead of a fixed sleep.

title: New multi-process flusher behaviour is only asserted structurally; no end-to-end or restart coverage
body: `test_flusher_processes_limit` only checks `len(flusher.processes) == 2` and that shard counts add up; it never submits spans to the different shards and verifies that each process's `SpansBuffer(shards)` actually flushes its own shards (and not others), nor that backpressure/health state is tracked per process. The restart path in `_ensure_processes_alive` (which was rewritten and now contains the broken `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` guard) has no test at all, and both tests run with `produce_to_pipe` so only the thread code path is exercised, never real spawned processes or pickling of per-shard buffers.

title: Docstring claims one process per shard, but default is a single process
body: The class docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but the actual behaviour is `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` processes with shards round-robined across them, and the CLI option `--flusher-processes` defaults to 1, so production runs a single process unless configured otherwise. The `max_processes` parameter is also undocumented in the `:param:` list while `topic` (which does not exist) is documented. This will mislead operators about resource usage and about what `--flusher-processes` controls.

title: Password show/hide toggle is broken by forced type="password"
body: The password field was switched to `PasswordField` but still passes `type="password"`. In packages/ui/components/form/inputs/Input.tsx, `PasswordField` sets `type={isPasswordVisible ? "text" : "password"}` and then spreads `{...props}` after it, so the caller's `type="password"` always wins. The eye toggle on the password step therefore does nothing and the password can never be revealed. Remove the explicit `type` prop.

title: Unrelated accessibility regression: password visibility toggle removed from tab order
body: The `tabIndex={-1}` added to the show/hide password button is unrelated to backup codes. It makes the toggle unreachable by keyboard for every PasswordField in the app, a regression for keyboard and screen-reader users. It should be reverted or put in a separate PR.

title: Backup code can be replayed by concurrent logins (read-modify-write race)
body: The backup code is consumed by decrypting the list, nulling the entry, and writing the whole list back with a plain `prisma.user.update`. There is no transaction, row lock, or conditional update. Two concurrent login requests that submit the same valid code can both read the unused list, both pass the `indexOf` check, and both succeed. This defeats the single-use guarantee. Consuming the code should be atomic, for example by re-reading inside a transaction with a version check or using a conditional update on the stored value.

title: Closing the dialog on the backup codes step loses the codes and leaves parent state stale
body: 2FA is enabled server-side when the TOTP code is accepted, but `onEnable()` (which updates the parent switch) is only called from the "Close" button on the backup codes step. Closing via the X, Escape, or overlay (`onOpenChange`) skips it, so the settings page still shows 2FA as off until reload. The one-time backup codes are also shown with no warning or confirmation, so the user can lose them permanently with no way to regenerate them without disabling 2FA.

title: Enable test leaves the backup codes dialog open and does not handle the new step
body: The enable test now lands on the backup codes screen after entering the TOTP code, but it never clicks `backup-codes-close` and then asserts the switch state. The assertion at this line relies on a FIXME-noted weak check that passes even when the switch is unchecked, so the test does not verify the real end state. There is also no test for the backup code login path, which the PR's own TODO acknowledges. The PR checklist states no tests were added for the feature.

title: Interactive button nested inside an anchor element
body: The download control renders a `<Button>` inside `<a download href=...>`. Nesting interactive content inside a link is invalid HTML and gives inconsistent keyboard and screen-reader behavior (two focusable targets for one action). The anchor should carry the styling or the button should be the link.

title: Backup code single-use is not enforced atomically
body: The backup code is consumed by reading the encrypted list, setting the matched entry to null in memory, and writing the whole list back with a plain update. Nothing ties the write to the value that was read. Two concurrent login requests that present the same valid code (both pass the password check and read the same list) will both succeed, and the second write will simply overwrite the first. A code documented as 'can be used exactly once' can therefore be redeemed more than once. A conditional update (compare-and-swap on the stored ciphertext, or a transaction with a re-check) is needed.

title: missing_backup_codes message points to a settings option that does not exist
body: The message tells users 'No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings.' No regenerate or view-codes UI is added by this PR. Codes are only created during the initial 2FA setup, and disabling 2FA is required to get new ones. Users who see this message are sent to a place where they cannot act on it, so the text is misleading.

title: Backup codes are unrecoverable if the dialog is dismissed without clicking Close
body: Backup codes are shown only in the DisplayBackupCodes step, and the dialog's own close control (onOpenChange / Escape / overlay click) bypasses the 'backup-codes-close' button. The codes are stored hashed-to-nothing (encrypted only, and never shown again). Once the user dismisses the dialog, the codes can no longer be retrieved, and the only way to get new ones is to disable and re-enable 2FA. Nothing in the flow forces the user to acknowledge or save the codes before dismissal.

title: Copy button reports success even if the clipboard write fails
body: navigator.clipboard.writeText(...) is not awaited or caught, and the success toast is shown unconditionally. The Clipboard API rejects in insecure contexts or when permission is denied, so the user gets a 'Backup codes copied!' toast while nothing was copied, and an unhandled promise rejection is produced.

title: Interactive Button rendered inside an anchor element
body: The download control nests a <Button> (a <button> element) inside an <a download> element. Interactive content inside <a> is invalid HTML, has inconsistent keyboard and click behaviour across browsers, and is an accessibility problem. The anchor should carry the styling or the button should be the link.

title: Password visibility toggle removed from keyboard tab order for all PasswordField uses
body: tabIndex={-1} is added to the show/hide password button inside the shared PasswordField component. This affects every password field in the app, not only the 2FA flow, and makes the toggle unreachable by keyboard users. The change is unrelated to backup codes and is an accessibility regression.

title: Non-string backupCode in request body causes an unhandled exception
body: req.body.backupCode.replaceAll(...) assumes a string. A client sending a number, object, or array as backupCode (the body is unvalidated JSON) throws a TypeError, which surfaces as a 500 rather than a 400 IncorrectBackupCode. The same pattern exists in next-auth-options.ts for credentials.backupCode.

title: Backup-code login path has no test coverage
body: The new login flow (Lost access, backup code submission, incorrect and missing backup code errors, and single-use consumption) is not exercised by any test. The only backup-code assertions are that the download, copy, and close buttons exist in the setup dialog. The PR description says the feature is untested, and the TODO only defers this. The core behaviour of the feature, including the single-use guarantee, is unverified.

title: missing_backup_codes message points to a settings option that does not exist
body: The message says "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." Nothing in this PR adds a way to generate or regenerate backup codes from settings. Codes are only created during the initial 2FA setup, and disabling 2FA is the only way back to setup. Users who enabled 2FA before this change have no codes, and the "Lost access" path shows this message with no working next step. The text should not promise a settings action that is not implemented.

title: Backup code can be redeemed more than once under concurrent logins
body: The backup code is read from the DB, checked with indexOf, nulled in memory, and written back in a separate prisma.user.update with no transaction, row lock, or conditional update. Two concurrent login attempts with the same valid code (for example a double-submit or a parallel request) both read the old list, both pass the check, and both write back. A single-use code is therefore accepted twice. The consume step should be an atomic conditional update or run inside a transaction that re-checks the stored value.

title: Backup codes can be dismissed without being saved, leaving the user locked out
body: The dialog is opened with onOpenChange, so Escape or clicking the overlay closes it during the DisplayBackupCodes step without going through the Close button. The codes are only shown once, and nothing forces the user to copy or download them or confirm they have been saved. Since 2FA is already enabled at this point and there is no regeneration path, a user who loses their authenticator and never saved the codes is locked out of the account. The backup-codes step should block dismissal or ask for confirmation.

title: type="password" prop overrides PasswordField's show/hide toggle
body: PasswordField sets type from its visibility state and then spreads {...props}. Passing type="password" here overrides that value, so the visibility toggle on this password field never reveals the text. This is a regression from the TextField it replaced, which had no toggle. Remove the explicit type prop.

title: Password visibility toggle removed from keyboard tab order
body: The new tabIndex={-1} takes the show/hide password button out of keyboard navigation for every PasswordField in the app. Keyboard and screen-reader users can no longer reach the toggle. The change is not related to backup codes and is an accessibility regression for all password inputs.

title: Backup code login, the main new login feature, has no test
body: The PR's stated purpose includes logging in with a backup code via "Lost access", and the test-plan step asks for this. The only e2e changes cover setup and the download/copy/close buttons. Nothing tests that a backup code logs in, that it is single-use after login, that a wrong code shows the error, or that disabling 2FA with a backup code works. The TODO acknowledges this, but the feature ships untested, and the consumption logic in next-auth-options.ts has no unit test.

title: Non-string backupCode in request body causes an unhandled exception
body: req.body.backupCode.replaceAll(...) assumes a string. A client sending a number or object for backupCode (it is truthy, so the branch is taken) throws a TypeError outside any try/catch, producing a 500 rather than a 400 error response. The same pattern is in next-auth-options.ts line 144. Validate the type before calling string methods.

title: Backup codes stored reversibly encrypted instead of hashed
body: Backup codes are stored as a symmetric-encrypted JSON array, so anyone with the encryption key (or a DB read plus key access) can recover all unused codes in plaintext. Single-use credentials are normally stored as salted hashes, which lets the server verify them without retaining the secrets. Because the codes are only needed for comparison, hashing them is the expected approach.

title: Unguarded property access crashes create() when no destination calendar exists
body: `mainHostDestinationCalendar` comes from `evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` destructuring, so it is `undefined` when the array is empty. The next line reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining. For a Google Meet location with no destination calendar (for example a booking where the organizer has no destinationCalendar row), this throws a TypeError and the booking creation fails. It should be `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.

title: updateEvent/deleteEvent fallback lookup compares against the wrong value and always resolves to undefined
body: In the fallback branch (externalCalendarId falsy), the code does `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. Since externalCalendarId is falsy here, the comparison can never match a real externalId, so the result is always undefined. The same broken expression is at line 317 in deleteEvent. Consequences: updateEvent sends `calendarId: undefined`, and deleteEvent falls back to "primary", so events stored on a non-primary calendar are not updated or deleted. The lookup should match on credentialId, as createEvent does.

title: Lark createEvent always uses the first destination calendar, so multi-host collective events are not created per host
body: Lark's createEvent, createAttendees, updateEvent and deleteEvent all take `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = event.destinationCalendar` and ignore which credential is calling. CalendarManager calls each credential's createEvent with the full destination array. In a collective event with two hosts, every host's Lark credential therefore writes to host #1's calendar, and host #2's calendar gets no event. The same pattern applies to Office365 (createEvent, line 73 of that file) and CalDAV (createEvent filter in packages/lib/CalendarService.ts). The PR's stated goal of letting each host receive the event is not met for these integrations.

title: The destination externalId is attached to the result but never passed to the calendar services
body: createEvent now receives `externalId` and calls `calendar.createEvent(calEvent, credential.id)`, dropping the externalId. Only the Google service uses the credential to pick a calendar. Other services read event.destinationCalendar[0] or filter by it, so the per-destination externalId is lost. EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents (line 370) passes `destination.externalId` into createEvent, which is then discarded, so each destination entry results in the same write. The result's `externalId` field is also set from an argument that does nothing for these integrations, so the references stored for the booking will not match the calendars actually written to.

title: Team destination calendars are silently dropped when the organizer has no destination calendar
body: `evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither eventType nor organizer has a destination calendar. The following line does `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`, which is a no-op on null. For a collective event where the organizer has no destination but other hosts do, the other hosts' calendars are never used, which is the exact scenario this PR is meant to fix. The array should be initialised rather than optionally pushed to.

title: Team destination calendars can be duplicated and are collected inside a parallel map
body: teamDestinationCalendars is pushed inside `users.slice(1).map(async ...)`. The push happens before the await in each callback, so ordering is nondeterministic. Also, if multiple hosts share a destination calendar or an existing entry is already in evt.destinationCalendar, duplicates are not removed, so createAllCalendarEvents will write the same event more than once. Collecting the calendars synchronously after the users list is built, then de-duplicating by id, would avoid both problems.

title: Recurring cancellation deletes the same events once per calendar reference
body: The loop now iterates over every calendar reference. Inside the recurring branch, for each reference it maps over all user calendar credentials and deletes every updated booking's calendar event again. With two calendar references (the multi-host case this PR enables), each booking's event is deleted twice or more, and the duplicate deleteEvent calls push extra promises into apiDeletes. The recurring deletion should run once, outside the per-reference loop.

title: Inverted condition on slug and requestedSlug, unrelated to the PR
body: The original code was `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })`. The new code is `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`, which includes slug when billing is enabled and omits it when disabled. This is a logic inversion, and the same inversion applies to `requestedSlug` on the following line. It changes organization creation behaviour for every installation and is not mentioned in the PR description.

title: Office365 createEvent ignores the credential and writes every destination to the first calendar
body: createEvent reads `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = event.destinationCalendar ?? []` and uses that calendar's externalId for the URL. With multiple destinations, each per-destination createEvent call writes an event to the first calendar rather than the one belonging to its credential. This creates duplicate events on one account and none on the others.

title: No tests added for the multi-host collective behaviour being fixed
body: The PR adds a new multi-destination code path in EventManager, CalendarManager and the booking handlers, but the checklist says no tests were added and the testing section relies on manual Loom recordings. Given how many call sites changed from a single destination to an array, unit tests for EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents and updateAllCalendarEvents with multiple destinations would be needed to catch the regressions above.

title: Inverted condition for organization slug and requestedSlug
body: The original code spread `slug` when `!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED` and `requestedSlug` when billing was disabled. The rewrite `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {}` flips that logic, so with billing enabled the org gets a real slug immediately and with billing disabled it doesn't. This is an unrelated behavior change to organization creation that the PR description does not mention. Revert to the original semantics.

title: Unguarded access to first destination calendar can throw
body: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` can yield `undefined` when the array is empty, but line 119 then reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining. Any event with location Google Meet and no destination calendar (e.g. organizer has no destinationCalendar, or the array is `[]`) will throw a TypeError during create. Use `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.

title: updateEvent loses calendar id when no externalCalendarId is passed
body: The fallback is now `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. When `externalCalendarId` is falsy, this compares each destination's externalId against null/undefined, which matches nothing, so `selectedCalendar` becomes undefined. The previous code used `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. Google's `events.update` then gets an undefined calendarId for bookings without a stored external calendar id. The lookup should match on the destination's credential or simply take the main destination's externalId.

title: deleteEvent has the same broken destination lookup
body: `calendarId = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` only matches when externalCalendarId is truthy, but in the fallback branch it is falsy, so the lookup always returns undefined. Deletes for bookings without an explicit external calendar id silently go to 'primary' instead of the booked calendar, leaving the event behind on the real calendar.

title: Lark always uses the first destination calendar, ignoring the per-credential target
body: createEvent (and createAttendees/updateEvent/deleteEvent) derive the calendar id from `event.destinationCalendar[0]` only. Since EventManager now calls createEvent once per destination (passing `destination.externalId`), every Lark credential creates its event on the first host's calendar. For collective events with multiple hosts, the second host's Lark event is created in the wrong calendar and duplicates are placed on the first host's calendar. The explicit externalId/credential is never used.

title: Office365 createEvent ignores the per-host destination calendar
body: createEvent always uses `event.destinationCalendar[0]` for the target calendar. With multiple destinations (collective event), EventManager invokes createEvent for each host credential, but the Office365 service ignores which credential it belongs to and writes every host's event into the first host's calendar. The PR's goal of inviting each host correctly is not met for Outlook.

title: updateAllCalendarEvents may pass undefined credential to updateEvent
body: After the DB fallback, `credential` may still be undefined (the DB lookup can return null or a credential without app slug). The code then unconditionally pushes `updateEvent(credential, ...)`, which calls getCalendar(undefined) and will throw inside an un-awaited promise, or be caught as a generic error. Unlike the create path, there is no `if (credential)` guard. Also, `credential` is a shared outer variable reused across loop iterations, so a stale value from a previous reference can be used.

title: Recurring cancellation deletes events once per calendar reference
body: The bookingCalendarReference loop now iterates every calendar reference. Inside, the recurring branch (`allRemainingBookings`) re-runs the whole loop over all user calendar credentials and all updatedBookings, so with N calendar references each remaining booking's event is deleted N times. Duplicate deleteEvent calls push duplicate promises into apiDeletes and can produce spurious errors. The recurring deletion should run once outside the per-reference loop.

title: Dynamic-user query drops organization select and adds broad error mapping
body: In the loadUsers rewrite, the `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` clause was removed from the dynamic user findMany. Downstream code that relies on organization slug for dynamic group bookings will now get undefined. The new try/catch also converts every non-HttpError/non-Prisma error into a generic 500 'Unable to load users', hiding the real cause, and treats an empty dynamicUserList as a 400 that previously could have been handled differently.

title: Collective co-host destination calendars dropped when organizer has none
body: Team destination calendars are appended with `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...)`. If the organizer has no destinationCalendar, `evt.destinationCalendar` is `null` and the push is silently skipped, so the other collective hosts' calendars are never added, which is the exact case this PR is meant to fix. The array should be initialized before pushing.

title: PR ships no tests for multi-destination behavior
body: The PR changes the destinationCalendar contract across ~20 files (array shape, per-credential selection, fallbacks) but adds no unit or e2e tests. The checklist explicitly says tests were not added. The collective multi-host scenario and the array-to-single fallbacks are untested, which is how the regressions above slipped through.

title: Unguarded property access on possibly-undefined first destination calendar
body: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` can yield `undefined` when the array is empty or null, but the next line reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining. For any event with a Google Meet location and no destination calendar (for example a user with no destinationCalendar set), `create()` throws a TypeError and the booking fails. It should be `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.

title: Inverted condition for organization slug (and requestedSlug) after refactor
body: The original code was `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` and `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { requestedSlug: slug })`. The rewrite to `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {}` and `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { requestedSlug: slug } : {}` flips the logic. When billing is disabled the org is no longer created with its slug, and when billing is enabled the slug is written to the wrong field. This is unrelated to the PR's stated goal and changes org creation behavior.

title: updateEvent calendar lookup returns undefined when no externalCalendarId is passed
body: The fallback is `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. When `externalCalendarId` is falsy (null/undefined), this searches for a destination whose externalId equals null/undefined, which never matches. The previous code fell back to `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. So `selectedCalendar` becomes undefined and `calendar.events.update` is called with no calendarId, which breaks updates for bookings lacking an external calendar id. The same faulty `find` is repeated in deleteEvent (around line 317), where it causes the calendarId to fall back to 'primary' instead of the booking's calendar.

title: Calendar references lose externalCalendarId for non-destination-specific creates
body: `externalCalendarId: isCalendarType ? result.externalId : undefined` relies on `createEvent` returning `externalId`. But in `createAllCalendarEvents`, the branch without `destination.credentialId` calls `createEvent(c, event)` with no externalId, and the fallback branch does the same. Those results have `externalId` undefined, so the stored BookingReference has no externalCalendarId. Previously it was taken from `evt.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. Later reschedule, cancel, and update operations then target the wrong or default calendar.

title: Recurring cancellation deletes the same events once per calendar reference
body: The calendar references are now iterated with `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)`. In the recurring-all-remaining branch, the inner logic loops over every `updatedBookings` and every calendar credential and deletes each one. With N calendar references, each remaining event is deleted N times, producing duplicate deleteEvent calls and duplicate pushes into apiDeletes. The recurring branch should run once, not once per reference.

title: loadUsers error mapping misclassifies errors and turns a missing-list case into a hard failure
body: The rewritten loadUsers throws a plain Error when dynamicUserList is empty or not an array. That plain Error is not an HttpError, so the catch converts it to a 500 'Unable to load users'. The catch also maps `Prisma.PrismaClientKnownRequestError` (a database failure) to a 400 Bad Request, which blames the client for server-side errors. Previously an empty list just returned no users. This changes status codes and error semantics in the booking path.

title: Dynamic user query dropped the organization select
body: The rewritten `findMany` for dynamic users removed the `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` clause that was in the original query. Any downstream code that reads `organization.slug` from these users will now get undefined. The removal is not explained by the PR's description.

title: Team collective calendars are silently dropped when organizer has no destination calendar
body: `evt.destinationCalendar` is set to null when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destinationCalendar. Later, `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is a no-op in that case, so the collective team members' calendars are never added and those hosts are not invited on their calendars. The array should be initialized as `[]` and the team calendars appended regardless.

title: createEvent passes credentialId but Google createEvent's calendarId falls back inconsistently between insert and patch
body: In the Google createEvent path, insert uses `selectedCalendar || "primary"`, but the follow-up `calendar.events.patch` uses the raw `selectedCalendar`, which can be undefined. When the patch is issued for a hangoutLink event without a matched destination calendar, the patch targets an undefined calendarId and fails silently, because its errors are not handled.

title: `prisma` is used but never imported in the Salesforce calendar service
body: `getClient` now calls `prisma.credential.update(...)`, but the file's import list has no `prisma` import (only jsforce, rrule, zod, CalEventParser, constants, http-error, logger, types, getAppKeysFromSlug, parseRefreshTokenResponse). This is a ReferenceError at runtime and a type error at build time, so every Salesforce calendar operation fails.

title: Salesforce now refreshes its token on every client construction, bypassing the sync endpoint
body: `getClient` unconditionally POSTs to login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token and writes the result to the DB, for every user and every service instantiation. It does not go through `refreshOAuthTokens`, so self-hosters with `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` never get their sync endpoint used for Salesforce, and non-sync installs gain an extra network round trip and a DB write each time. Its `statusText !== "OK"` check is also brittle, since HTTP/2 responses may have an empty statusText.

title: Minimum token schema uses a computed key from `z.string().toString()`, which is not a pattern
body: `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` builds an object key from a schema's string representation (a fixed literal such as "[object Object]"), not a wildcard for 'any numeric property'. The resulting schema requires a property with that literal name, so real token responses fail `safeParse`. In sync mode every refresh then throws 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned'. The same applies to the `[z.string().optional().toString()]` entry on line 10.

title: Real refresh token is overwritten with the placeholder string "refresh_token"
body: When the parsed response lacks `refresh_token` (the minimum schema strips it, and it is absent from many refresh responses), this code sets it to the literal "refresh_token". The caller then persists that value to the credential, destroying the working refresh token. The sync-mode check here also uses only the global env flag, while `refreshOAuthTokens` additionally requires a userId, so for team-owned credentials (userId null) the real refresh path runs but the minimum schema still strips fields and the placeholder still gets written.

title: Sync branch returns a raw fetch Response while the other branch returns the provider's token shape
body: The sync path returns the `fetch` Response, but the non-sync path returns the value of `refreshFunction()`, which callers expect in provider-specific shapes (e.g. Google reads `res.data`, Zoho reads `tokenInfo.data.error`, HubSpot reads `expiresIn`). With sync enabled, Google's `res?.data` is undefined, so `token.access_token` throws. That error is swallowed by the catch, and the stale token is returned silently. Zoho Bigin's `tokenInfo.data.error` throws an uncaught TypeError in `refreshAccessToken`, breaking event creation. The sync response is also never checked for `response.ok`, so an error from the sync endpoint is handled as if it were a successful token refresh.

title: Expiry computed from `expires_in` becomes NaN when sync mode omits that field
body: After switching to `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, in sync mode the parsed data may not contain `expires_in`. `Date.now() + newTokens.expires_in * 1000` is then NaN. The stored `expiry_date` becomes NaN, and `isTokenValid` (`(expires_in || expiry_date) < Date.now()`) evaluates false, so the adapter never refreshes the token again.

title: Decrypted keys are unvalidated and JSON.parse can throw an unhandled error
body: `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` is not wrapped in try/catch, so a wrong key or malformed payload produces an unstructured 500. The parsed value is then written directly to `credential.key` with no per-app schema check, so any JSON shape is stored and can break the app's CalendarService when it later parses the credential.

title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time `!==`
body: The shared secret from the request header is compared with `!==` against the env value. This is a timing-sensitive comparison for an authentication secret; `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers should be used. The header lookup also depends on the configured header name being lowercase, which Node enforces for incoming headers.

title: New webhook endpoint and token-refresh changes have no tests
body: The PR adds an authenticated endpoint that writes credentials, plus new refresh logic in parseRefreshTokenResponse and refreshOAuthTokens that branches on env vars and userId. The checklist confirms no tests were added. The bugs above (placeholder refresh token, NaN expiry, the broken schema) would be caught by unit tests on these helpers.

title: Moved OAuth utilities may leave other importers of the old paths broken
body: encodeOAuthState, decodeOAuthState and createOAuthAppCredential were moved to `_utils/oauth/`. Only the listed app files were updated. If other apps or shared code still import `_utils/encodeOAuthState`, `_utils/decodeOAuthState` or `_utils/createOAuthAppCredential`, they will fail at build time. The diff does not show a full repository search.

title: Sync-mode schema uses computed keys from zod instances, so it never matches real token responses
body: `[z.string().toString()]` evaluates to the literal key "ZodString", and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` to "ZodOptional". The minimum schema therefore requires a numeric property named "ZodString" and does not describe the token response at all. When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, every refresh fails with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". The intended expiry-field check needs to be written differently (for example with z.record or a passthrough object).

title: Placeholder refresh_token string is written into stored credentials
body: When the refreshed token response has no refresh_token, this assigns the literal string "refresh_token" to it. The caller then persists that value to the credential row. The next refresh will send "refresh_token" as the refresh token and fail, so the integration is silently broken. The original refresh token should be kept instead of a fake value.

title: parseRefreshTokenResponse return value (SafeParse result) is stored as the credential key
body: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the zod safeParse wrapper `{ success, data }`, not the parsed data. Here that wrapper is assigned to `key` and saved with `data: { key }`. The stored Google credential becomes `{ success: true, data: {...} }`, so googleCredentialSchema.parse on the next construction fails. The code should use `.data` as the other callers do.

title: refreshOAuthTokens returns a raw fetch Response in sync mode, but the caller reads `.data`
body: In sync mode refreshOAuthTokens returns the fetch Response. `res?.data` is undefined, so `token.access_token` on line 95 throws a TypeError, and the refresh fails. The same mismatch affects hubspot, zoho-bigin and zohocrm, which read `.data` or `.expiresIn` from a value that is a Response in sync mode.

title: Sync-mode Response is treated as a token object, producing NaN expiry and an empty stored credential
body: refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response when syncing. `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` is then undefined, so expiryDate becomes NaN. Line 198 then persists a Response object, which serializes to an empty object, as the credential key, and `setAccessToken(undefined)` is called on line 202. Hubspot tokens are lost after the first sync-mode refresh.

title: Sync-mode Response is read through `.data`, which is undefined
body: refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response in sync mode, so `tokenInfo.data` is undefined. `tokenInfo.data.error` on line 96 throws a TypeError, and the Bigin token refresh fails whenever credential sync is enabled.

title: credentialId is passed where refreshOAuthTokens expects userId
body: refreshOAuthTokens takes `userId: number | null` and sends it to the self-hoster endpoint as calcomUserId. Bigin passes `credentialId`, a credential row ID, so the sync endpoint receives the wrong user. The field should be the owning user's ID (credential.userId), as in the other integrations.

title: `prisma` is used but never imported
body: getClient now calls `prisma.credential.update` (line 96), but the file has no import of prisma. Every SalesforceCalendarService construction throws a ReferenceError, which breaks all Salesforce calendar operations, not just sync-enabled setups.

title: Salesforce token refresh runs on every client construction regardless of sync configuration
body: The refresh call to login.salesforce.com and the credential write now run unconditionally in getClient. Previously the stored access token was used. Every service construction now hits the token endpoint and rewrites the credential, which adds latency and rate-limit pressure. It also bypasses refreshOAuthTokens, so self-hosters' sync endpoint is never used for Salesforce. The statusText === "OK" check is also unreliable, since HTTP/2 responses have no status text.

title: Updating an existing credential does not clear the invalid flag
body: When a credential was previously marked `invalid` (for example after invalid_grant), the sync update only replaces the key. The credential stays invalid even though fresh credentials were just synced, so the app remains unusable until the user reconnects manually.

title: Webhook secret compared with a non-constant-time string comparison
body: The secret is compared with !==. A timing-safe comparison (for example crypto.timingSafeEqual over equal-length buffers) should be used for webhook authentication.

title: Invalid request bodies cause an unhandled 500 instead of a 400
body: appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse throws a ZodError when the body is malformed. It is not caught, so the handler returns 500. JSON.parse of the decrypted keys on line 57 has the same problem for invalid ciphertext or non-JSON plaintext. Both should return 4xx with a clear message.

title: Sync request to the external endpoint carries no authentication and no timeout
body: The POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends the user ID and app slug with no shared secret, auth header, or timeout. The self-hosted endpoint cannot verify that the caller is Cal.com, and a hung endpoint blocks the token refresh indefinitely. Its response is also not validated before being trusted.

title: No tests added for the new webhook, sync refresh path, or encryption handling
body: The PR adds a new authenticated write endpoint, a new refresh branch used by about 15 integrations, and new encryption logic, with no unit or integration tests. The PR checklist confirms this. The sync-mode bugs above (wrong return types, missing import, placeholder token) would have been caught by even basic tests of refreshOAuthTokens and parseRefreshTokenResponse.

title: `prisma` is used but never imported, so the module fails to compile
body: The new credential update in `getClient` calls `prisma.credential.update(...)`, but the file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. The file's import list only includes jsforce, rrule, zod, lib helpers and the app-store util. This is a TypeScript/runtime error that breaks the whole Salesforce calendar integration, not just token refresh.

title: Computed keys use `z.string().toString()`, so the minimal schema requires a literal "[object Object]" key
body: `[z.string().toString()]` evaluates to the string "[object Object]", not a pattern matching any key. The minimum schema therefore requires a property literally named "[object Object]" and fails on any real token response. When `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` and `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` are set, every refresh that goes through this helper (Zoom, Office365, Salesforce) will be rejected with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned".

title: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns a SafeParse result, but its return value is stored as the credential key
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns `{ success, data }` (the safeParse wrapper), but this call stores that wrapper as the key: `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(...)` followed by `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. The credential JSON then becomes `{ success: true, data: {...} }` and the actual access_token/expiry_date fields are no longer at the top level, so the next `googleCredentialSchema.parse` on the stored key will fail. Other callers (Office365, Zoom, Salesforce) correctly use `.data`.

title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token"
body: When the provider's refresh response omits `refresh_token`, this code writes the placeholder string "refresh_token" into the response. Callers persist this as the credential's refresh token, so the next refresh attempt sends a bogus token and fails with invalid_grant, which then marks the credential invalid. The original token should be kept, or the case should be an error.

title: In sync mode it returns a raw fetch `Response`, which callers treat as a parsed token object
body: The sync branch returns the `fetch` Response from the sync endpoint, while the fallback branch returns the provider's native result (e.g. googleapis `res`, a HubSpot TokenResponse, an axios response). Callers read token fields directly: Google reads `res?.data.access_token`, which is undefined on a Response, so it throws. HubSpot sets `expiryDate` from `expiresIn`, which is undefined and yields NaN. Zoho Bigin and Zoho CRM read `tokenInfo.data.error`/`.data.expires_in`, which are not on a Response. The sync endpoint's response is also never checked for `ok`, so an error body would be treated as valid tokens.

title: Outbound sync request carries no authentication and the response is trusted
body: The request to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` as form data, with no shared secret, signature or auth header. Anyone who can reach or impersonate that endpoint can return arbitrary tokens, which are then persisted to the credential. The request also doesn't validate the status or content type before use.

title: Salesforce token refresh now runs unconditionally on every service construction
body: `getClient` now always POSTs to login.salesforce.com and writes the credential, regardless of whether credential sync is enabled. Every Salesforce calendar operation performs a network round-trip and a DB write, and a failed refresh fails the whole service.
