title: 'next' can set offset to user_count, which produces an empty page
body: offset is computed as Math.min(offset + limit, user_count). Offsets should step by whole pages. Combined with the totalPages off-by-one, paging forward can land on an offset equal to user_count, and findMembers then requests an empty page. Offsets should advance by limit and be bounded by the last page start, not by user_count.

title: Offset clamp to user_count yields an empty page after removing the last member on a page
body: findMembers clamps offset to user_count. If a page is at offset 50 with 51 users and one member is removed, user_count becomes 50. The clamp then keeps offset at 50, so the reloaded page is empty even though page 1 has members. The offset should be moved back to the start of the last existing page, not left at user_count.

title: findMembers now returns undefined instead of a promise when the group has no name
body: The early return was changed from Ember.RSVP.resolve([]) to a bare return. Callers that chain .then on the result, which is a common pattern in this codebase, will throw a TypeError for unnamed groups. Returning a resolved promise keeps the contract.

title: Client-controlled limit has no upper bound and no validation
body: limit comes straight from params as (params[:limit] || 50).to_i. A caller can request an arbitrarily large page of members, which defeats pagination and allows bulk enumeration of group membership in one request for any visible group. Negative values also reach SQL LIMIT and raise an error. The limit should be clamped to a sane maximum and a minimum of 1, and offset should be clamped to be non-negative.

title: Members endpoint response shape changed for all groups
body: The members action now returns {members:, meta:} instead of a bare serialized array for every group, including automatic groups that previously returned a plain array. Any other client of /groups/:name/members, not just the updated admin and group templates, will break. This is an API change that is not called out.

title: automatic flag is looked up on the member, so the remove link shows for automatic groups
body: Inside an itemView the context is the individual member (a User), not the group. {{#unless automatic}} therefore checks member.automatic, which is undefined, so the remove link is always rendered. Clicking it on an automatic group yields a 422 from the server. The parent group's automatic flag needs to be passed into the item view or the controller.

title: remove_member spec uses PUT while the route is DELETE
body: The 'cannot remove members from automatic groups' example calls xhr :put, :remove_member, but the route is defined as delete "members" => "groups#remove_member". The spec does not exercise the real HTTP verb and could pass for the wrong reason. It should use :delete.

title: No specs for the new paginated members endpoint or for the non-admin path
body: The PR rewrites GroupsController#members to add pagination, limit/offset handling, and a meta payload, but no spec covers it. It also removes the 'cannot patch automatic groups' and incremental-membership tests without replacement for the public members endpoint. Pagination edge cases (limit bounds, offset past end, total count) are untested.

title: Stale selector references the removed group-users id
body: The rule `input#group-users { width: 600px; }` still targets the id that the template no longer uses (it now uses user-selector). The rule is dead and the intended width for the member input is no longer applied.

title: Member routes bind :id, but the controller and spec read :group_id
body: `delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"` and `put "members" => "groups#add_members"` sit directly inside `resources :groups` without `collection do`, so they generate `/admin/groups/:id/members`. `Admin::GroupsController#add_members` and `#remove_member` read `params.require(:group_id)`, which is never supplied on that path, so every real call raises ParameterMissing (400/500). The frontend `Discourse.Group#addMembers`/`removeMember` call `/admin/groups/{id}/members.json`, so the feature is broken end to end. The controller spec passes `group_id:` directly, which masks the mismatch.

title: remove_member and add_members read group_id but the route supplies id
body: `Group.find(params.require(:group_id).to_i)` in `remove_member` (and the same pattern in `add_members`) requires a `group_id` parameter, but the only route that reaches these actions uses `:id` as the path segment. Requests from the admin UI therefore fail before any membership change happens.

title: totalPages is off by one when user_count is an exact multiple of limit
body: `totalPages` computes `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`. With 100 users and limit 50 this yields 3 pages instead of 2. `showingLast` is then false on the real last page, so `next` sets offset to min(offset+limit, user_count) = 100 and loads an empty page. The same formula is used in `currentPage`'s counterpart, so the pager shows a phantom page.

title: members endpoint accepts unbounded or negative limit/offset
body: `limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i` has no upper bound, so any visible group can be dumped in one request, which the previous automatic-only cap was meant to prevent for large groups. A negative `limit` or `offset` is passed straight into SQL LIMIT/OFFSET, which PostgreSQL rejects, producing a 500. Clamp limit to a sane maximum and floor both values at 0.

title: findMembers returns undefined for empty names and callers ignore the promise
body: `findMembers` returns nothing when `name` is empty, while the rest of the method returns a promise. Callers such as `admin_group_route.js` `setupController` and `group-members.js.es6` call `model.findMembers()` without handling the result, so errors from the AJAX request are unhandled and the loading state is never observable.

title: Stale selector targets a removed element id
body: `.row.groups input#group-users { width: 600px; }` still references the `group-users` id, which this PR removed from `group.hbs` (the user selector now uses `id="user-selector"`). The rule is dead and the intended width for the member input is no longer applied.

title: Specs pass parameters that do not match the real routes and HTTP verbs
body: The spec calls `xhr :put, :remove_member, group_id: 1, user_id: 42` although the only remove route is DELETE, and it uses `group_id` where the route provides `:id`. Controller specs do not check routing, so these tests pass while the actual endpoints are broken. There is also no test for the groups#members pagination (limit/offset/meta), which is the other main behavior change.

title: Unfinished TODO left in addMembers
body: The `// TODO: should clear the input` comment marks a known UI bug: after adding members the username selector keeps its previous value, so a repeated click re-submits the same usernames. The defect is shipped rather than fixed.

title: removeMember and addMembers have no error handling
body: Both methods return an AJAX promise that only reloads members on success. A failed request (e.g. 422 for automatic groups) is not surfaced to the user, and the admin controller's `removeMember` action does not handle the rejection, so the UI silently does nothing.

title: PR description is a placeholder
body: The description reads only "Test 8", so reviewers have no statement of the intent, the removed update/PATCH API, or the new member pagination contract (meta.total/limit/offset). The API change needs documenting.

title: totalPages is off by one when user_count is an exact multiple of limit
body: totalPages computes Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1. For user_count = 100 and limit = 50 this gives 3 pages, but only 2 pages of members exist. The pager shows a phantom page 3, and clicking next moves to offset 100, which returns an empty list. Use Math.ceil(user_count / limit), with a minimum of 1 when user_count > 0.

title: next() clamps offset to user_count instead of the start of the last page
body: offset is set to Math.min(offset + limit, user_count). With user_count = 120 and limit = 50, the sequence goes 0, 50, 100, then 120. Offset 120 is past the end and returns no rows. The offset should be capped at the start of the last page, for example (totalPages - 1) * limit, not at user_count.

title: alias_level chosen for a new group is never persisted
body: For a new group, save() calls group.create(), which posts asJSON() including alias_level. The controller's create action ignores alias_level, and the JS create() does not follow up with a save. The user's alias level selection is silently dropped on creation and the group keeps the default.

title: create action ignores alias_level sent by the client
body: The client's asJSON() sends alias_level, but create only reads name and visible. Any alias_level value is discarded, so the admin UI cannot set alias level at creation time, and the behaviour differs from update.

title: automatic flag is read from the member, not the group, so remove links show on automatic groups
body: group_member.hbs is rendered as an itemView of each member, so its context is the User, not the group. {{#unless automatic}} therefore always evaluates true, and the remove link appears even for automatic groups. The server rejects those removals with a 422, but the UI still offers an action that cannot succeed. The automatic flag must be passed in from the group.

title: limit and offset are unvalidated and can produce SQL errors or unbounded queries
body: params[:limit] and params[:offset] are converted with to_i and used directly. A negative offset yields a negative SQL OFFSET, which raises a database error and a 500. A very large or negative limit is also accepted with no cap. The endpoint is public for visible groups, so both should be clamped (for example limit between 1 and 200, offset >= 0).

title: members response shape changed from a bare array to an object
body: GET /groups/:id/members previously returned a JSON array, and it was unpaginated for non-automatic groups. It now returns {members, meta}. Any existing client of this public endpoint breaks, and the change is not called out in the PR description. Either version the endpoint or document the break.

title: findMembers requests /members.json, changing the URL contract
body: The request now adds the .json suffix and query parameters, and it always expects result.meta. Any caller relying on the old response (a plain array) or on the older URL form gets a different shape. This coupling to the new server response should be documented or covered by a test.

title: coverage removed for non-existent usernames and incremental operations
body: The deleted specs covered that adding a non-existent user succeeds silently, that removing a non-member succeeds, and that PATCH on automatic groups is rejected. The new add_members and remove_member specs do not cover these cases, and nothing covers the GroupsController#members pagination or meta output. Behaviour changes in these paths are now untested.

title: PR description is not meaningful
body: The description reads 'Test 8' and does not explain the large change: removing PATCH/PUT member updates, changing the create and update param shapes, changing the members API response, and adding paging. A reviewer cannot judge the API break from the description.

title: Translation LRU cache ignores the fallback chain, so cached results go stale when the default locale changes
body: The cache key on line 72 is built from the key, `config.locale`, and the backend object_id only. With this PR, `translate_no_cache` resolves through `FallbackLocaleList#[]`, whose result depends on `SiteSetting.default_locale` (initializers/i18n.rb line 17). Once a lookup falls back to the site locale or :en, the cached string is keyed as if it were a direct hit for the user's locale. If the admin changes `default_locale`, or a fallback translation is later loaded, existing cache entries keep serving the old result until the process restarts or `reload!` is called. Changing a site setting does not call `I18n.reload!`, so nothing clears the cache. Include the effective fallback chain (or default_locale) in the cache key, or invalidate the cache when the setting changes.

title: ensure_loaded! runs on every request and walks all fallback locales, taking the global mutex each time
body: `ApplicationController#set_locale` now calls `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` on every request. That builds the fallback array (including a SiteSetting lookup) and calls `I18n.ensure_loaded!` for each locale. `I18n.ensure_loaded!` in translate_accelerator.rb calls `load_locale`, which takes `LOAD_MUTEX` whenever the locale is not yet in `@loaded_locales`. After warm-up the check is a cheap array include, so the real cost is small, but the fallback list is recomputed per request on the hot path. It also means set_locale can block on the mutex during a cold load. This is worth a look, but it is not a blocker.

title: Fallback list is computed from SiteSetting at call time without a nil guard for default_locale
body: `SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym` on line 17 is evaluated on every `I18n.fallbacks[locale]` call, including during early boot and in the `ensure_loaded!` path. If the setting is not yet available or is blank in some environments (for example during asset precompilation or in a rake task that runs I18n before the DB is ready), `to_sym` on nil raises NoMethodError, and the failure appears far from its cause. Consider guarding for a blank default_locale.

title: Translation cache key ignores the site default locale that now drives fallbacks
body: The LRU cache key is built from the key, `config.locale` and the backend object_id only. With this PR, the result of `translate` also depends on `SiteSetting.default_locale`, because `FallbackLocaleList#[]` inserts that locale into the fallback chain. After the site default locale changes, cached entries for user locales that fell back to the old default (or to :en) keep being served until they are evicted or `reload!` runs. The key should include the fallback chain or the default locale.

title: Fallback chain is rebuilt and reads SiteSetting on every lookup and every request
body: `FallbackLocaleList#[]` allocates a new array and calls `SiteSetting.default_locale` on each call. `set_locale` in ApplicationController calls `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` on every request, which invokes `self[I18n.locale]` and so repeats that work. The Fallbacks backend also calls `I18n.fallbacks[locale]` for every missing-key translation. This is small per call but runs on the hot path.

title: ensure_loaded! only loads the chain for the current locale, not for an explicitly passed locale
body: `ensure_loaded!` loads only `self[I18n.locale]`. Lookups made with an explicit `locale:` argument, or from background jobs that switch locale without going through `set_locale`, will use a fallback chain whose translation files may not be loaded yet. The lazy `load_locale` in the accelerator only covers `config.locale`, so the fallback locales can be missing without any error.

title: Pull request description is a placeholder
body: The PR description reads only 'Test 9'. It gives no explanation of why fallbacks move from environment configs into an initializer, why `pluralization.rb` is merged into `i18n.rb`, or how the fallback chain is meant to behave. Reviewers cannot check the intent of the change from the PR itself.

title: Fallback locales are only loaded per request, so non-request code paths can miss English and default-locale strings
body: `FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded!` loads translations for the fallback chain, but it is only called from `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Background jobs, mailers, rake tasks and other code that calls `I18n.t` without going through a controller request never load the fallback locales. The patched `translate` in lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb only calls `load_locale(config.locale)`, so when the requested locale lacks a key, the fallback lookup for `:en` or the site default hits an unloaded backend and returns a missing-translation string. The fallback behaviour is therefore request-dependent and inconsistent. Loading the fallback chain inside `translate` (or in the fallback lookup itself) would make it hold everywhere.

title: ensure_loaded! runs on every request and allocates a new fallback array each time
body: `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` is executed on every request. Each call builds a fresh array via `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact` and iterates it, calling `I18n.ensure_loaded!` for each entry. It reads `SiteSetting.default_locale` each time. This is cheap but unnecessary per-request work that could be memoised or moved to a single load step.

title: ensure_loaded! reads and lazily initialises @loaded_locales outside the mutex
body: `ensure_loaded!` performs `@loaded_locales ||= []` and an unsynchronised `include?` check before calling `load_locale`. Two threads can race on the lazy initialisation, and the first check reads the shared array without the LOAD_MUTEX that protects writes. `load_locale` re-checks inside the mutex so the final result is correct, but the unlocked read and the `||=` initialisation are inconsistent with the locking discipline used elsewhere in the same file.

title: FallbackLocaleList overrides only [] on a Hash, so other Hash accessors return inconsistent results
body: `FallbackLocaleList < Hash` overrides `[]` to compute a computed fallback chain, but the underlying hash is never populated. Methods such as `fetch`, `key?`, `has_key?` or `dig` still use the empty stored data, so they disagree with `[]`. Any caller that uses these methods, including I18n internals that may check membership, gets different answers. A plain object with a single `[]` method would be clearer and safer.

title: Denial cache short-circuits before the DB fallback, so a cached denial can keep hiding a newly granted permission
body: The denial cache is checked first in Check and returns deny immediately, before the cached-permission lookup and the DB fallback that this PR adds. A denial is written with a 30s TTL (shortCacheTTL) whenever the DB result is not allowed. If a user is checked on a resource before its permission row exists (for example, a dashboard or folder just created by that user, or a frontend poll), the denial is cached for 30s. Once the permission is written, every Check for that same user/action/name/folder returns false until the entry expires, which is the exact symptom this PR is meant to fix. The denial entry should be bypassed or invalidated when the permission is granted, or the check should go to the DB before trusting a denial. At minimum this trade-off needs to be documented and covered by a test.

title: Denial cache key concatenates unescaped fields, so distinct requests can collide
body: userPermDenialCacheKey joins userUID, action, name and parent with '_' and no escaping. Different tuples produce the same key: name "a_b" with empty parent and name "a" with parent "b" both yield "...._a_b_" / "...._a_b"-style collisions. The key also shares the "perm_" prefix with userPermCacheKey. A collision makes a denial for one resource apply to another, so an unrelated resource is wrongly denied until the TTL expires. Use a separator that cannot appear in the fields (or a hash of a structured tuple).

title: Permission denials are cached for 30s with no invalidation, so a newly granted permission stays denied
body: When the DB check returns not-allowed, the result is stored in permDenialCache for shortCacheTTL (30s), keyed by user, action, name and parent folder. Nothing invalidates this entry when permissions change. The PR's stated goal is that a creator can access a dashboard or folder they just created. If the user is first denied on that name (for example a fetch before creation), the denial is then served from cache for up to 30s even though the DB now grants access. The denial cache check at line 116-121 returns before the DB fallback runs, so the new-permission fallback never applies during that window. Either skip caching denials, use a much shorter TTL, or invalidate the entry when a permission or resource is created.

title: Denial cache key is ambiguous because fields are joined with '_' and names can contain '_'
body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates name and parent with '_' separators without escaping. Different tuples produce the same key, e.g. name="a_", parent="b" and name="a", parent="_b" both yield "...action_a__b". A denial recorded for one resource then short-circuits Check for another resource with a colliding key, returning a wrong deny. Dashboard and folder UIDs can contain underscores, so this can happen. Use an unambiguous encoding (length prefix, or a separator that cannot appear in UIDs).

title: Folder tree stays cached for 30s after folder creation, so inherited access to new nested folders is denied
body: buildFolderTree caches the namespace folder tree for shortCacheTTL and nothing invalidates it on folder creation. The fallback to the DB only refreshes permissions, not the folder tree. For a folder created within the TTL, e.g. grandchild C under a newly created child B under a folder A the user already has access to, the tree lacks C (and possibly B). checkInheritedPermissions then calls tree.Ancestors(C), which cannot reach A, so the creator is denied on a dashboard in C even though they hold a grant on A. This is the same user-facing bug the PR aims to fix, and it is not covered by the new fallback. Refresh the folder tree on a miss for the requested folder, or invalidate it on folder creation.

title: New cache tests do not cover the behaviour the PR is meant to fix
body: TestService_CacheCheck covers cache hits, DB fallback on a miss or outdated map, and a pre-set explicit denial. It never checks that a DB denial populates the denial cache, nor that a permission granted after a denial is honoured (the creator scenario). It also has no test for inherited access through a folder created after the tree was cached, and no test for denial key collisions. These are the scenarios that would catch the staleness and key issues above.

title: Denial cache is consulted first and not invalidated when permissions are granted, so creators can still be denied right after creating an item
body: Check() now returns a cached denial before consulting the permission cache or the DB (lines 116-121). A denial is written for 30s whenever a check fails (line 153-155), keyed by user, action, name and parent folder. If a user is denied on a dashboard or folder name (for example a get attempted before creation), then creates that resource, the stale denial is served for up to 30s. The DB-requery fallback added in this PR never runs in that window, so the exact scenario the PR is meant to fix ('dashboard/folder creator can't access what they just created') can still fail. Creation paths should invalidate or bypass the denial entry, or the denial should be checked only after the permission cache miss path has been ruled out.

title: Denial cache key concatenates unescaped fields, so different resources can collide
body: userPermDenialCacheKey joins userUID, action, name and parent with '_' and no escaping. Dashboard and folder UIDs can contain underscores, so distinct requests map to the same key. Example: (name="a_b", parent="") and (name="a", parent="b_") both produce '...._a_b_'. A denial recorded for one resource then denies access to the other for 30s, causing false denials. Use a separator that cannot appear in UIDs, or a hash/structured key.

title: List serves cached permissions with no DB requery, so newly created items are missing from lists
body: The PR adds a DB fallback on cache miss for Check, but List only falls back when the user's permission map is absent from the cache (lines 180-192). If the map is cached (up to 30s), a newly created dashboard or folder is missing from the List response, because the stored permission set predates it. The creator therefore cannot see the new item in listings for the TTL window, even though Check now succeeds. This inconsistency between Check and List should be either addressed or explicitly documented.

title: Test setupService uses a different TTL for basicRoleCache than NewService
body: NewService creates basicRoleCache with shortCacheTTL, but setupService (line 1338) uses longCacheTTL. Tests therefore exercise a configuration that production does not use. The test helper should mirror NewService.

title: Delete and Pause menu items never render in the list view
body: The abilities for delete and pause are now computed from promRule, so canDelete and canPause can be true in the list view. But the Delete item is gated on `canDelete && rulerRule`, and the Pause item (line 123) is gated on `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`. In the list view rulerRule is always undefined, so users with delete or pause permission never see those actions. The Delete handler also still requires a RulerRuleDTO to call handleDelete(rulerRule, ...), so the delete flow is not wired to the Grafana prom rule path at all.

title: Pause action gated on rulerRule, which is absent in the list view
body: canPause is computed from grafanaPauseAbility (promRule-based), but the MenuItemPauseRule is only rendered when `rulerRule` is a Grafana ruler rule. In the list view rulerRule is undefined, so the pause item is silently dropped even when the user is allowed to pause.

title: Silence drawer never opens from the list view
body: The Silence menu item is shown when canSilence is true (now derived from promRule), and clicking it calls setShowSilenceDrawer(true). But SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer is only rendered when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` holds, and rule is undefined in the list view. The click therefore does nothing.

title: Grafana rule list item rendered without a key
body: The previous GrafanaRuleLoader element had `key={key}`, and the diff removes it while rendering GrafanaRuleListItem. The list items are rendered from an array, so React will warn about missing keys. Reconciliation can also mix up rows when the list grows or re-sorts. The other branches in this switch still pass key.

title: Federated rule group check removed from ruler abilities
body: useAllRulerRuleAbilities now hardcodes `isFederated = false` with a TODO. The previous useAllAlertRuleAbilities used isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group), so federated Mimir rule groups were treated as immutable (no edit, delete, pause or duplicate). Now they are shown as editable and deletable. Note that this hook also serves the data source rule path through AlertRuleMenu and RuleActionsButtons, so the regression is not limited to Grafana rules.

title: View link drops the returnTo parameter
body: The removed GrafanaRuleLoader built the href with `createRelativeUrl(..., { returnTo })`, which lets the rule view page navigate back to the list. The new GrafanaRuleListItem drops returnTo, so the view page loses the back-navigation context for rules opened from the list.

title: Test asserts the buggy menu contents, hiding the missing Delete item
body: The test grants AlertingRuleDelete and then asserts exactly 4 menu items (silence, copy link, duplicate, export). That expectation locks in the regression where Delete is never rendered in the list view. The test should expect Delete (and Pause where applicable), and it should check that the action performs the expected behaviour, not just that the items exist. The tests for silence also do not verify that the drawer opens.

title: Delete menu item is never shown in the alert list view
body: The Delete item is rendered only under `canDelete && rulerRule`. In the list view the component is now called with `promRule` and no `rulerRule` (the ruler API is no longer queried), so the item is hidden even when `grafanaDeleteAllowed` is true. Users who can delete a Grafana rule from the list lose that action. The new permission logic computes `canDelete` from the Prometheus abilities, but the render condition still depends on the ruler rule. The same gating also applies to the Pause item at line 123 (`rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`), so Pause is also hidden in the list view.

title: Silence menu item appears in list view but its action does nothing there
body: `canSilence` is now true from the Prometheus-based abilities, so the 'Silence notifications' item is shown in the list view. Clicking it calls `handleSilence`, which sets `showSilenceDrawer` in RuleActionsButtons.V2. That drawer only renders when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` holds (RuleActionsButtons.V2.tsx line 104), and `rule` (the ruler rule) is undefined in the list view. The user gets a menu item that silently does nothing.

title: GrafanaRuleListItem rendered in a list map without a key
body: The previous code passed `key={key}` to the Grafana rule loader. The replacement `<GrafanaRuleListItem>` has no key, although it is rendered inside `rules.map(...)`. React will warn about missing keys, and reconciliation can reuse the wrong DOM nodes or component state when the list is paginated or reordered. The `key` computed by `getRuleKey` is still available in the destructuring on line 152.

title: Federated rule group check was removed, so federated rules are treated as editable
body: In `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` the check `isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` was replaced by a hard-coded `const isFederated = false;` in `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`. This is a behavior change for Mimir data source rule groups that have `source_tenants`. Those rules were previously marked immutable and their Update/Delete/Duplicate/Pause actions were disabled. They now become available. The TODO does not justify removing a working check from a path that is still in use. `isFederatedRuleGroup` is only passed a group, and the hook now receives only the rule.

title: View link no longer carries the returnTo parameter
body: The removed `GrafanaRuleLoader` built the view href with `createRelativeUrl(..., { returnTo })` using `createReturnTo()`. The new `GrafanaRuleListItem` drops `returnTo`, so navigating from the list to the rule view and back no longer restores the list position or filters. Other rule list items in this repo keep this behavior.

title: Test asserts the buggy 4-item menu, so the missing Delete action goes unnoticed
body: This is the list-view test for AlertRuleMenu. The test in GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx asserts that the menu has exactly 4 items (line 207). The user is granted AlertingRuleDelete and the `delete` menuitem selector is defined (line 42) but never used. The test therefore locks in the absence of Delete (and Pause) in the list view. Nothing checks that Silence actually opens a drawer.

title: Delete menu item is never shown in the list view
body: The Delete item is gated on `canDelete && rulerRule`. The list view (GrafanaRuleListItem) no longer passes `rulerRule`, so Delete is hidden even for users with delete permission, which the new `grafanaDeleteAbility` check was meant to allow. The same gating hides Pause (line 123, `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` and `MenuItemPauseRule` requires `rulerRule`). The updated GrafanaGroupLoader test asserts exactly 4 menu items, which locks in the missing Delete action instead of catching it.

title: Silence menu item in the list view does nothing when clicked
body: `canSilence` is now true from the promRule-based ability, so the Silence item is shown in the list view. Its handler `handleSilence` only sets `showSilenceDrawer` in RuleActionsButtons. The drawer is rendered only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` holds, and in the list view `rule` (the ruler rule) is undefined, so clicking Silence silently does nothing.

title: Missing React key on GrafanaRuleListItem in the filter view
body: The `grafana` case returns `<GrafanaRuleListItem>` inside `rules.map` without a `key` prop. The previous `GrafanaRuleLoader` had `key={key}`, and the datasource branch still has it. React will warn about missing keys and may mis-reconcile list items when the filtered list changes.

title: Federated rule group immutability check was dropped
body: `useAllRulerRuleAbilities` now hardcodes `isFederated = false`. The previous `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` used `isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`, which made federated groups non-editable/non-deletable/non-duplicable. Since `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` now delegates to this hook, federated rules that used to be locked will now show Edit/Delete/Pause as allowed, which is a permission regression. The TODO does not restore the old behaviour.

title: Rule view link drops the returnTo parameter
body: The removed GrafanaRuleLoader built the href with `createRelativeUrl(..., { returnTo })` using `createReturnTo()`. The new `GrafanaRuleListItem` builds `/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view` without `returnTo`, so the rule view page loses the ability to navigate back to the list with its filters.

title: Test asserts the regression instead of the intended behaviour
body: The GrafanaGroupLoader test 'should render correct menu actions' expects exactly 4 menu items (silence, copy link, duplicate, export) and omits Delete. Because it encodes the current missing-Delete behaviour, it will not flag the regression. No test covers clicking Silence or Delete from the list view.

title: Interpolation runs before the $__range check, so the no-split guard may stop working
body: `runSplitQuery` now interpolates every target with `applyTemplateVariables` (line 299) before `partition(queries, (query) => !querySupportsSplitting(query))` at line 300. `querySupportsSplitting` relies on `isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)` to keep `$__range` queries unsplit, and the comment there says that variable must stay un-interpolated because the backend fills it in for the split time range. If `applyTemplateVariables` replaces `$__range` with a concrete duration, the check no longer matches and such queries get split, producing wrong per-chunk results. The guard should inspect the raw expression, or the interpolation should happen after partitioning for the non-splitting path.

title: Targets are interpolated twice on the shard-splitting path
body: `runShardSplitQuery` interpolates each target here, and every sub-request then calls `runSplitQuery` (line 163 of this file), which interpolates the same targets again at querySplitting.ts line 299. Interpolation is not idempotent: a variable value containing `$` (for example a regex or a literal like `$foo`) gets substituted a second time, and the final query can differ from what the user wrote. The existing test asserting `applyTemplateVariables` was called 5 times is evidence of this repeated work. Interpolate once, at one layer.

title: Test asserts the redundant interpolation call count as expected behavior
body: The assertion changed from 1 call to `toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)`. That locks in the repeated interpolation (one call in `runShardSplitQuery` plus one per sub-request) as intended behavior rather than catching it. If the double interpolation is fixed, this test will fail for the wrong reason, and it does not check that the interpolated values are correct.

title: No test covers the $__range guard after interpolation moved earlier
body: The new 'Interpolates queries before execution' test only checks `$__auto` and `$step`. Since interpolation now happens before `querySupportsSplitting`, nothing verifies that a query using `$__range` is still excluded from splitting. The regression described above would go unnoticed.

title: Queries are interpolated a second time when shard splitting delegates to runSplitQuery
body: runSplitQuery now calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables on every target. shardQuerySplitting.ts already interpolates its targets in runShardSplitQuery (line 52) and then calls runSplitQuery(datasource, subRequest, ...) with the already-interpolated and shard-selector-injected expressions (shardQuerySplitting.ts line 163). Those expressions are interpolated again here. Any value that survives the first pass and contains a '$' (regex anchors, literal dollar signs in label values, escaped variable-like text) can be rewritten a second time, so the query sent to Loki can differ from what the user wrote. Interpolation should happen in exactly one place for each request path.

title: Test asserts applyTemplateVariables is called 5 times, locking in redundant double interpolation
body: The updated expectation `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` counts the calls made by runShardSplitQuery plus the repeated calls made inside runSplitQuery for each shard sub-request. The test encodes the redundant interpolation as expected behaviour, so it will fail to catch the double-interpolation regression, and it will break if the redundancy is correctly removed. The test should assert the observable query text sent to runQuery rather than the number of interpolation calls.

title: $__range detection now runs on interpolated expressions, so range-variable queries may be split
body: querySupportsSplitting checks isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) to avoid splitting queries that use $__range, because $__range must be evaluated over the full request range. Interpolation now runs before this check (line 299), so the check sees the expression after applyTemplateVariables has rewritten it. If interpolation replaces or removes the $__range token, the check no longer matches and such queries get split, which is the exact case the guard was meant to prevent. The ordering needs to be verified, and the detection should run on the original expression or the test suite should cover a $__range query through runSplitQuery. No test in querySplitting.test.ts covers this path.

title: Shard path interpolates each target twice, once here and again in runSplitQuery
body: runShardSplitQuery now calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables on every target, and splitQueriesByStreamShard then passes each sub-request (whose expr already has the shard selector inserted) into runSplitQuery. runSplitQuery in querySplitting.ts (line 299) calls applyTemplateVariables again on those targets. The expression is interpolated twice. For values containing '$', regex metacharacters, or values that Loki's formatter escapes, a second pass can change or corrupt the query. The second pass is not needed for correctness, and the two call sites should not both interpolate.

title: $__range guard in querySupportsSplitting now sees interpolated expressions
body: querySupportsSplitting (line 287) checks isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) to keep queries using $__range out of splitting, and the comment explains that the variable must stay un-interpolated. Interpolation now runs before partitioning (here, before querySupportsSplitting is called), so if applyTemplateVariables resolves $__range to a concrete range, the guard no longer matches and such queries get split, which the comment says breaks them. The guard should be evaluated on the raw expression, or the PR should confirm that $__range is not resolved by applyTemplateVariables.

title: Empty-expression filter runs before interpolation
body: The filter `query.expr` (line 298) is applied before applyTemplateVariables (line 299). A query whose expr is a template variable that interpolates to an empty string is not dropped and is sent to the backend as an empty query. The emptiness check should happen after interpolation, as the stated goal of this PR is to interpolate first.

title: Test asserts an exact applyTemplateVariables call count that couples it to internals
body: The assertion `toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` depends on how many times interpolation happens across the top-level call and each nested runSplitQuery sub-request. It does not check the behavior the test name describes (interpolated before running), and it will break on any refactor that changes the number of passes, including the double-interpolation fix. It also hides the double-interpolation problem, since the count of 5 is the symptom of it.

title: traceID and plugin/datasource fields dropped from the 'Plugin Request Completed' log
body: The refactor removes pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName, dsUID and traceID from the completed-request log params and relies entirely on the context logger. ContextualLoggerMiddleware (contextual_logger_middleware.go) only adds endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID and uname; it never adds traceID. The traceID field that the old code attached via tracing.TraceIDFromContext is therefore lost from this log line, which breaks correlation of plugin egress logs with traces for anyone querying on traceID. Either add traceID to the contextual attributes or keep it in logRequest.

title: LoggerMiddleware now silently depends on ContextualLoggerMiddleware being placed earlier in the chain
body: Fields that were previously explicit in logRequest now only appear if the context carries them, which only happens when ContextualLoggerMiddleware runs before LoggerMiddleware. In CreateMiddlewares this ordering is implicit and undocumented, and the removed doc comment on MetricsMiddleware ('this middleware should live at the top of the middleware stack') gave no replacement. Reordering the list, or using LoggerMiddleware without the contextual middleware, will silently drop all identifying fields from the log with no error or test failure.

title: New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no tests
body: The attributes that were previously covered by the instrumentation path (endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, uname) are now produced by this new middleware, but there is no test verifying that the contextual logger is attached to the context or that the attributes are correct. The existing metrics test was only renamed and does not exercise any logging context. Similarly, the changed LoggerMiddleware output has no test.

title: TestLogger.FromContext ignores the context and returns a fresh logger
body: FromContext discards its context and returns a new TestLogger, so the logs recorded by tests are not connected to the logger returned for a given context. Any test that wants to assert that LoggerMiddleware logs via a context-derived logger will see its calls on a different instance than the one it inspects, making such assertions impossible or misleading.

title: FromContext silently discards the context when the type assertion fails
body: If the underlying infra logger's FromContext does not return a *log.ConcreteLogger, the wrapper falls back to d.New() which carries none of the context attributes. This is a silent loss of all contextual fields with no log or error, and it is not covered by any test.

title: Logger name 'plugin.instrumentation' is stale after the rename
body: The middleware is now named MetricsMiddleware and the logging concern lives in LoggerMiddleware, yet the logger is still named 'plugin.instrumentation'. This keeps the old 'instrumentation' terminology the PR aims to remove and makes the log source inconsistent with the new naming.

title: Test function still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware after rename
body: The file and constructor were renamed to MetricsMiddleware, but the test function keeps the old TestInstrumentationMiddleware name, leaving the rename incomplete and making it harder to find the test for the renamed type.

title: traceID field silently dropped from plugin request completion log
body: The old logRequest explicitly appended a "traceID" field to the log params when a trace ID was present in the context. That code is removed, and the new contextual logger (ContextualLoggerMiddleware/instrumentContext) only attaches endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID and uname. Unless the infra logger's FromContext adds the trace ID on its own, completion logs for plugin requests lose the traceID, which breaks correlating these log lines with traces. The PR description says it only moves the contextual logger, so this is an unintended regression.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, so logs written through it are lost
body: FromContext ignores the receiver and returns NewTestLogger(). LoggerMiddleware now calls m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so with a TestLogger injected, the "Plugin Request Completed" entry is recorded on a throwaway logger and the test's InfoLogs stay empty. Any test asserting on the logged output of LoggerMiddleware will silently pass or fail for the wrong reason. FromContext should return the receiver (or share its log storage) so calls are visible to the test.

title: New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no test coverage
body: This file is new and takes over the contextual-attribute enrichment that was previously tested as part of the instrumentation middleware. Nothing in the PR adds a test for ContextualLoggerMiddleware, and the existing metrics test no longer exercises instrumentContext. Its attribute assembly (endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, uname) and its placement in the chain are therefore unverified.

title: Test function name still refers to the old InstrumentationMiddleware name
body: The file was renamed to metrics_middleware_test.go and the type is now MetricsMiddleware, but the test is still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware. This is inconsistent with the rename the PR is meant to do and makes the test harder to find when searching for MetricsMiddleware.

title: traceID is no longer logged with plugin request completion events
body: The old logRequest explicitly appended a "traceID" field from tracing.TraceIDFromContext, plus pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName and dsUID. The new code removes all of these and only calls m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...). The new ContextualLoggerMiddleware adds endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID and uname, but not traceID. Unless the infra logger injects the trace ID itself (nothing in this diff shows that), completion logs lose the trace ID, which breaks log-to-trace correlation for plugin requests. The PR is titled and described as a rename, so this user-visible logging change is not called out.

title: FromContext silently drops all contextual attributes when the type assertion fails
body: FromContext does d.l.FromContext(ctx).(*log.ConcreteLogger) and, on failure, falls back to d.New() with no context. If the infra logger ever returns a different concrete type (wrapper, interface change), every LoggerMiddleware log line silently loses the plugin/datasource/user context that the new design now depends on, and nothing reports it. The fallback should at least preserve the logger, or the mismatch should be surfaced.

title: LoggerMiddleware now depends on ContextualLoggerMiddleware being earlier in the chain, with no enforcement
body: The rename moved the context enrichment out of the metrics middleware into a separate ContextualLoggerMiddleware. LoggerMiddleware now emits pluginId, endpoint, dsName and similar fields only through the context. That only works if ContextualLoggerMiddleware is placed before LoggerMiddleware in CreateMiddlewares. The removed doc comment ('this middleware should live at the top of the middleware stack') was the only warning about this ordering. Reordering the list, or enabling LoggerMiddleware in another stack, will silently strip those fields from logs.

title: New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no tests
body: contextual_logger_middleware.go is a new file with an instrumentContext helper and eight middleware methods, but no test covers it. Nothing checks that the contextual attributes (endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, uname) are attached for each endpoint, or that the optional DataSourceInstanceSettings and User branches behave correctly. The behaviour that moved from the metrics middleware and the LoggerMiddleware change are also untested. The LoggerMiddleware field change and the FromContext wrapper (pkg/plugins/log/logger.go) have no test either.

title: Test function name still refers to the old InstrumentationMiddleware
body: The file was renamed to metrics_middleware_test.go and the type is now MetricsMiddleware, but the test is still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware. This keeps the old name in test output and makes it harder to find the test for the renamed type.

title: Device is cached before the DB write, so a rejected device is let through for 29 minutes
body: tagDeviceUI marks the device key in localCache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, but the cache entry stays. Every later request from that device hits the early `localCache.Get` return and skips the DB check entirely, so Authenticate succeeds. The first request is rejected, and retries within the cache TTL are allowed. The device limit is therefore not enforced. The cache entry should be set only after a successful write, or removed when the write fails.

title: Device limit check is a non-atomic count followed by insert
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts devices and then inserts in separate statements with no transaction or lock. Concurrent first-time requests from distinct devices can all read a count below the limit and all insert, so the number of devices can exceed deviceLimit. The limit is only a soft bound under concurrency, which matters because the feature exists to cap devices.

title: Anonymous login now does DB work synchronously on every request, without a timeout
body: Authenticate previously ran TagDevice in a goroutine with a 2-minute timeout and a panic recover. Now it calls TagDevice inline with the request context. When deviceLimit is set, each anonymous request runs a COUNT query on anon_device, then an UPDATE or upsert, before authentication can complete. Slow DB latency now directly slows or fails every anonymous page load. The async behaviour and timeout were removed without a replacement.

title: Runtime field typed as `undefined` instead of `number | undefined`
body: `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` gives the class property the literal type `undefined`, which contradicts the `number | undefined` declared in GrafanaConfig. Any code reading `config.anonymousDeviceLimit` through the class type will be treated as always undefined. It should be declared as `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;`.

title: TypeScript type says the limit may be undefined, but the backend always sends a number
body: The Go DTO field `AnonymousDeviceLimit` is `int64` without omitempty, so it is always serialized, defaulting to 0. The `number | undefined` type suggests the field may be absent, which the frontend never receives. The type should be `number`, with 0 meaning no limit documented.

title: No tests for the existing-device update path or the anonymous login rejection path
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit covers only a new device being rejected at the limit. It does not check that an already-tagged device still updates when the limit is reached, which is the purpose of updateDevice. It also does not test that TagDevice or Authenticate returns the error, nor the cache bypass described above. The cache bypass in particular would have been caught by a test that repeats the rejected request.

title: Device is cached before the limit check, so a rejected device is later let in
body: tagDeviceUI stores the device key in localCache (line 87) before CreateOrUpdateDevice runs. When the limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached and the device is not tagged, but the key stays cached. For the next ~29 minutes, every request from that device hits the cache hit at line 83 and returns nil, so Authenticate succeeds without the device ever being counted. The first rejection is effectively followed by a bypass of the limit. The cache key should only be set after a successful tag, or removed on error.

title: Device limit check is a non-atomic count followed by insert
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts devices (line 110) and then separately inserts or updates (lines 115-118 and below). Concurrent first-time requests from distinct devices can all read a count below the limit and all insert, so the number of devices can exceed deviceLimit. A correct enforcement needs a single atomic statement or a transaction/lock, and the race should be acknowledged or tested if it is not fixed.

title: rowsAffected == 0 is treated as limit reached, which misfires on MySQL
body: updateDevice treats zero affected rows as ErrDeviceLimitReached. On MySQL, the default driver behaviour reports only changed rows, so an UPDATE that rewrites identical client_ip and user_agent values (common for a returning device) reports 0 rows and is wrongly rejected as if the limit were reached. Also, a device whose updated_at is older than the 30-day window matches nothing and is rejected, even though it already exists and should be updated. The error conflates 'row not found in window' with 'limit reached'.

title: Device tagging is now synchronous on every anonymous authentication
body: The previous implementation ran TagDevice in a goroutine with a 2-minute timeout. It now runs inline on the request path. For any device not in the local cache, each request performs a COUNT over the 30-day window and then a write, so database latency is added directly to every anonymous page load and API call. Slow or contended DB writes now slow or block authentication, and the panic recovery that the goroutine had is also gone.

title: Device-limit tests miss the update path, MySQL behaviour and the cache bypass
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only covers a new device being rejected. It does not check that an already-registered device under the limit is still updated when the limit is reached, that a device outside the 30-day window is handled, or that re-tagging with unchanged values succeeds on MySQL. There is also no test at the client.go Authenticate level verifying that a limit rejection fails authentication, nor one for the cached-device bypass.

title: New auth.anonymous device_limit option is not documented
body: A new user-facing config key [auth.anonymous] device_limit is read here, but the diff adds no entry to conf/defaults.ini or conf/sample.ini and no docs. Operators have no way to discover that the option exists or what value 0 (unlimited) means.

title: Rejected device is cached, so the device limit is bypassed after the first rejection
body: tagDeviceUI sets the local cache entry (line 87) before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the device limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, but the cache entry is already set. For the next ~29 minutes, every request from that device hits the cache at line 83 and returns nil, so Authenticate succeeds. Only the first request is rejected. The limit is therefore not enforced consistently, and a new device can authenticate on its second request. The cache should only be set after a successful write, or the entry should be removed on error.

title: Device limit check is a non-atomic count followed by an insert, so concurrent logins can exceed the limit
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice first runs CountDevices and only then inserts or updates. Under concurrent anonymous requests from different new devices, several goroutines can read a count below the limit at the same time and all insert, so the number of devices can exceed deviceLimit. Enforcing the limit needs a transactional check-and-insert, or an accepted and documented best-effort tolerance.

title: Device tagging moved into the synchronous auth path, adding a COUNT query and a DB write to every anonymous request
body: The previous implementation tagged devices in a goroutine with a 2-minute timeout and panic recovery. This change calls TagDevice synchronously with the request context. When deviceLimit > 0, every anonymous request that is not served from the local cache now runs a COUNT over anon_device for the last 30 days before the write. Slow DB responses now directly delay or fail the anonymous login path. Consider keeping the work off the request path, or at least documenting the latency impact.

title: No test covers the new Authenticate behaviour when the device limit is reached
body: The new branch in Authenticate that returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, and the change from fire-and-forget to synchronous tagging, are untested. The only new test exercises the store directly (TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit). Nothing checks that Authenticate fails for a rejected device, that a non-limit error is only logged, or that the cache issue above is handled. The existing impl_test tests also do not set a device limit.

title: Frontend type says the device limit may be undefined, but the backend always sends a number
body: anonymousDeviceLimit is typed as `number | undefined`, and GrafanaBootConfig initializes it to undefined. The Go DTO field is a non-pointer int64 with no omitempty, so it is always serialized as a number (0 when unset). The TypeScript type should be `number`, or the field should be made optional on the backend if undefined is intended.

title: New auth.anonymous device_limit option is not documented
body: cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit is read from the new `device_limit` key in [auth.anonymous], but no default or documentation was added to conf/defaults.ini or the docs. The PR's own checklist marks docs as unchecked. Operators have no way to discover the option, and the semantics (0 meaning unlimited, negative values treated as unlimited) are not stated anywhere.

title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, unrelated to the annotation fix
body: The ticker interval for the whole cleanup service was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This is not mentioned in the PR description and has nothing to do with the annotation deadlock. Every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, user invites, short URLs, query history, temp files, annotations) now runs ten times as often. That is a production behaviour change that looks like a leftover debugging edit and should be reverted or justified separately.

title: Routine per-batch cleanup progress is logged at Error level, including full ID lists
body: The new fetch/delete loops log every batch with r.log.Error, both before and after the delete (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579). These are normal informational messages, and on a healthy system they fire on every batch, even when err is nil. Each message also includes the full `ids` slice, which can hold up to the batch size (up to 32767 IDs). This floods error logs and makes real errors hard to find. The messages should be Debug or Info, the ID list should be dropped or truncated, and the `err` field should only be logged when there is an error.

title: Quadratic string building of IDs for SQLite large-batch delete
body: In deleteByIDs, the SQLite branch builds the IN list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` in a loop. Each iteration copies the whole accumulated string, so building a list of N IDs costs O(N^2) bytes. With batch sizes up to 32767 (as exercised by the new 40003-annotation test), this produces hundreds of megabytes of intermediate copies per batch. Use a strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt to build the list in linear time.

title: Cleanup ticker silently changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The ticker interval for the whole cleanup service is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. Nothing in the PR description mentions this, and it is unrelated to the annotation deadlock fix. It increases how often every cleanup job runs (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, invites, short URLs, query history, annotations) by 10x. This looks like a leftover debugging change and should be reverted or justified separately.

title: Per-batch cleanup logs at Error level and dump full ID lists
body: CleanAnnotations logs every batch with r.log.Error, including the entire slice of IDs ("ids", ids) and the SQL condition. Batches can be up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize (default and max in tests is 32767) and the loop runs until no rows remain, so a single cleanup run can emit many error-level log lines with large ID lists. Success paths are not errors, so this floods error logs and inflates log volume on every cleanup cycle. The same pattern is used at lines 536-537, 554-557 and in CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags (576-579). These should be Debug logs without the ID list.

title: Logged 'err' field is always nil in the batch log lines
body: The log calls after the batch use "err", y where y is the deleteByIDs error, but the line at 534 logs "err", err from fetchIDs, which is always nil at that point because errors return early. Logging err=nil on success is harmless but the field is misleading. It is not needed on the success path since errors are already returned to the caller.

title: Quadratic string building for SQLite inline ID list
body: The SQLite branch builds the IN-list with values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) inside a loop. Each iteration copies the whole accumulated string, so building a list of up to 32767 IDs is O(n^2) in bytes copied, on every batch. Using strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt would avoid this. The IDs are int64 from the database, so there is no injection risk here.

title: Cleanup of inserted rows is registered after the inserts and assertions that can fail
body: createTestAnnotations and the count assertions run before t.Cleanup is registered for each subtest. If any of those assertions fail (require calls call t.FailNow), the annotation and annotation_tag rows are left in the shared fakeSQL database and subsequent subtests start with unexpected data, producing misleading follow-on failures. The cleanup registration should come before the inserts.

title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, unrelated to the annotation deadlock fix
body: The ticker interval in CleanUpService.Run is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. Nothing in the PR description or the annotation changes calls for this. It makes every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, short URLs, query history) run ten times as often, which raises DB load on every instance. It looks like a leftover debugging change and should be reverted or justified separately.

title: Routine cleanup progress is logged at Error level, including full ID lists, on every batch
body: CleanAnnotations logs 'Annotations to clean by time' (and the matching 'by count', 'Tags to clean', and 'cleaned ...' messages in the other cleanup paths) with r.log.Error. These are normal successful operations, so they pollute error logs and can trigger error alerting. Each line also includes the full list of up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize IDs, which can be tens of thousands of values per batch, and the 'err' field is always nil on these lines. These should be Debug (or Info) messages, and the ID list should not be logged at that size.

title: Quadratic string building of ID list for SQLite delete
body: In deleteByIDs, the SQLite path builds the IDs list with values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) inside a loop. Each iteration copies the whole accumulated string, so building a list of N IDs costs O(N^2) bytes copied. With the batch size allowed to reach 32767 (as in the new 40003-annotation test), this copies gigabytes of data per batch and runs on every cleanup cycle. Use strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt to build the list in linear time.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and will be cancelled when the request finishes
body: The legacy write runs in a goroutine but uses a context derived from the request ctx (`context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). Once the HTTP handler returns, the request context is cancelled, so the legacy Create (and the same pattern in Delete, Update and DeleteCollection, lines 110, 135, 163) can fail spuriously with 'context canceled' before it completes. The legacy write is then silently dropped, which defeats the purpose of the 'safe measure' write. Detach from cancellation with context.WithoutCancel(ctx) before adding the timeout.

title: Legacy Create receives the same obj that Storage.Create already mutated, concurrently
body: `obj` is passed to `d.Storage.Create` synchronously and then to `d.Legacy.Create` in a goroutine. Storage create implementations commonly mutate the object (name generation, resourceVersion, timestamps). The goroutine reads and possibly mutates the same object concurrently with any remaining work on the request path, which is a data race. The object should be deep-copied before the async legacy call.

title: Legacy write failures in Create are only recorded as a metric, never logged
body: In the Create goroutine the legacy error is passed to recordLegacyDuration but never logged. With writes now fire-and-forget, the metric is the only signal, and nothing identifies which object failed to reach legacy storage. Other methods also lack logging on the async path. Failures in the async safety writes should be logged with object identity.

title: Delete puts the base logger into the context instead of the per-call logger
body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` discards the `log` built just above with name/kind/method values. Downstream logs from the storage and legacy calls lose the request-specific fields that the other methods keep.

title: Delete records the object name as the kind label on the storage duration metric
body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes `name` where the kind (`options.Kind`) is expected, as used on every other call. This corrupts the metric's label cardinality and makes per-kind dashboards wrong; each deleted object creates a new label value.

title: Update records a Storage failure as a legacy duration metric
body: When `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)`, not `recordStorageDuration`. Storage failures are counted against the legacy store, and the storage metric is never incremented for these failures, so both dashboards are wrong.

title: Legacy Update reuses objInfo from the Storage update in a goroutine
body: `objInfo` is consumed by `d.Storage.Update` synchronously and then passed to `d.Legacy.Update` in a goroutine. UpdatedObjectInfo implementations may be stateful or read the old object they were given. Calling UpdatedObject again concurrently and out of band with the request can race and can apply the change against the legacy store's old object, which may differ from unified storage. The previous implementation resolved the updated object once and passed it explicitly, and this change removes that.

title: DeleteCollection records the legacy duration through the storage metric
body: The async legacy path calls `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)`. Legacy timings and failures are counted as storage. It should call `recordLegacyDuration`, as the other legacy goroutines do.

title: Create error case sets up a legacy expectation but no storage expectation
body: In the 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' case, the mock expectation is attached to the legacy store (setupLegacyFn) and setupStorageFn is nil. Mode 3 calls Storage.Create first, so the storage mock has no expectation and the test fails for the wrong reason or panics. The expectation should be on storage. The test also never checks that the legacy write happens in the success case.

title: Tests do not verify the asynchronous legacy writes
body: The mode 3 tests configure legacy mock expectations (Create, Update, Delete, DeleteCollection) but never assert they were called, and the legacy calls now run in goroutines that may not finish before the test returns. The tests therefore pass whether or not the legacy write happens, which is the core behaviour of this PR. Tests should wait for or synchronise with the goroutine and assert the legacy calls with AssertExpectations.

title: Tests now share one global Prometheus registry
body: The PR removes the per-test `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` in Mode1 Get and makes mode 3 tests use the package-level `p`. NewDualWriter registers metrics on the given registry, so every test now registers into the same registry. If the metrics are registered with MustRegister this will panic with AlreadyRegistered on the second test. Each test should use a fresh registry.

title: Mode 3 integration runs assert immediately on legacy state that is written asynchronously
body: In mode 3 the legacy write happens in a goroutine after the unified storage write returns. doPlaylistTests then checks the legacy `/api/playlists` endpoint immediately after k8s creates or updates, for example listing legacy results after creating playlists. Those checks can run before the async legacy write lands, making the new mode 3 subtests flaky. The tests should poll or wait for the legacy side to converge in mode 3.

title: Unrelated checksum entries added to go.work.sum
body: The diff adds many go.sum lines for unrelated modules (grafana-azure-sdk-go/v2, a prometheus-alertmanager fork, otel exporters and sdk v0.x, otlp proto, genproto rpc). These come from incidental dependency resolution, not from the mode 3 change. They should be dropped from this PR so the review and dependency surface stay focused.

title: Async legacy writes run on the request context, so they are cancelled once the request returns
body: Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection launch the legacy write in a goroutine using a context derived from the request ctx (e.g. line 51 `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). The HTTP request context is cancelled when the handler returns, which happens right after the storage write succeeds. The legacy write will therefore often fail with context canceled, and the failure is only recorded in metrics. Legacy writes can silently be skipped, which defeats the purpose of mode 3's safety copy. The goroutine should use a detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx)) plus the timeout.

title: Object passed to the async legacy Create is shared with the storage Create and may be mutated concurrently
body: The same `obj` is handed to d.Storage.Create (line 42) and then to d.Legacy.Create inside a goroutine (line 55). Storage create implementations typically mutate the object (set ResourceVersion, UID, creationTimestamp, name generation). The legacy goroutine therefore reads an object that may be written concurrently or is already modified, which is a data race and can write inconsistent data to legacy. The legacy path should get a DeepCopy taken before the goroutine starts, or the storage result should be used.

title: Async legacy Update reuses objInfo that the storage Update has already consumed
body: objInfo is passed to d.Storage.Update (line 126) and then reused in the legacy goroutine (line 139). UpdatedObjectInfo.UpdatedObject is typically called once per store and may consume or mutate the old object; calling it concurrently from the goroutine races with the storage path. Also the legacy update may compute its update from a different base object than the one storage used, so the two stores can diverge without any error being surfaced.

title: Storage Update failure is recorded as a legacy duration metric
body: In the Update error path, the failure is recorded with d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) and startStorage, even though the failing call was the storage write. This corrupts legacy metrics and hides storage failures from the storage metric.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection duration and errors are recorded as storage metrics
body: In the goroutine, the legacy DeleteCollection result is recorded via d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...) (line 166) instead of recordLegacyDuration. Legacy failures are counted as storage and legacy metrics stay empty for this method.

title: Delete success metric uses the object name in the kind label position
body: recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) passes `name` where the other calls pass options.Kind. The kind label of the metric is therefore set to the object name, creating unbounded label cardinality and making the metric inconsistent with the other methods.

title: Delete builds the context from d.Log, dropping the per-request log values
body: Delete creates a local `log` with name/kind/method values but then attaches `d.Log` (line 97) to the context instead of `log`. Logs emitted by downstream code for delete lose the name, kind and method values that every other method attaches.

title: Legacy write failures in async goroutines are not logged
body: Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection run the legacy write in a goroutine and only record a metric on error. There is no log call, so a failed legacy write leaves no trace in logs and divergence between the stores is invisible to operators. The old code logged these failures, so this is a regression in observability.

title: Update goroutine creates its timeout context before startLegacy and without a defer on the same line
body: In the Update goroutine (lines 135-138) the timeout context is created before the timer starts and the cancel is deferred after an unrelated statement. This is harmless today but is inconsistent with the other goroutines and makes the cancel easy to miss if the function is edited. Low priority.

title: Error test for Create passes only because the legacy expectation matches the storage call
body: The 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' case registers no storage expectation (setupStorageFn is nil). The storage Create call therefore matches the legacy mock expectation at line 41 and returns the error by accident. The test does not check what it claims to check, and a change in the call pattern would make it panic instead of asserting.

title: Mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy write or wait for it
body: The tests set legacy mock expectations but never assert they were called (AssertExpectations is not used), and the goroutines are not awaited. Tests pass even when legacy is never written, and goroutines can call mocks after the test has finished. The behavior that defines mode 3 (legacy write happens and does not fail the request) is not tested.

title: Get test creates its own registry while the other tests share the package-level registry
body: TestMode3_Get creates a new prometheus registry (line 119) while all other tests, and the mode1 test after this change, use the shared package-level `p`. Mixing the two patterns is inconsistent and makes it unclear whether the dual writer metrics are registered more than once on the shared registry across subtests.

title: Mode 3 playlist integration tests check legacy consistency immediately after writes that are now asynchronous
body: doPlaylistTests asserts legacy API results right after k8s creates, updates and deletes (for example the legacy list check after Create, and getFromBothAPIs after Update). With mode 3 the legacy write runs in a background goroutine, so these checks can race with it and fail intermittently. The new mode 3 subtests need a wait or retry before comparing the legacy store, or the assertions must be relaxed for mode 3.

title: Unrelated module checksum entries added to go.work.sum
body: The go.work.sum diff adds checksums for unrelated modules (grafana-azure-sdk-go/v2, prometheus-alertmanager, otel exporters, genproto rpc, etc.) that have nothing to do with the dual writer change. These look like incidental tooling output and should be removed from this PR to keep the change focused.

title: Async legacy writes are derived from the request context and may be cancelled
body: The legacy goroutines in Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection build their timeout context from the caller's `ctx`. That context belongs to the incoming API request and is cancelled as soon as the response is returned. The 'fire-and-forget' legacy write can therefore be aborted almost immediately after the unified-storage write succeeds, leaving the legacy store silently out of sync. The legacy write should run on a context detached from the request, for example `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` plus the timeout.

title: Object shared with an asynchronous goroutine while storage may still mutate it
body: In Create, `obj` is passed to `d.Legacy.Create` inside a goroutine while the same object was already handed to `d.Storage.Create`. The storage layer may set fields such as name, UID or resourceVersion on it, and the caller may keep using it after returning. This is a data race on a shared runtime.Object. The legacy write should receive a deep copy.

title: Legacy Update reuses objInfo that was already consumed by the storage update
body: `objInfo` is passed unchanged to both `d.Storage.Update` and the asynchronous `d.Legacy.Update`. The UpdatedObjectInfo's UpdatedObject is typically applied to the current old object. Calling it a second time from another goroutine, against the legacy store's view of the object, can produce a different result from what unified storage stored (or fail), and the two stores can diverge. The legacy write should use the object that storage actually persisted, as the previous implementation did with updateWrapper, and not re-run the mutation.

title: Storage failure in Create is recorded as a legacy failure metric
body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the error is recorded with `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)`, so unified-storage errors are counted against the legacy store. The same mistake appears in Update (line 129). This corrupts the metrics used to compare the two stores.

title: DeleteCollection legacy timing is recorded with the storage metric
body: The DeleteCollection goroutine reports its outcome via `d.recordStorageDuration` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy delete-collection failures and durations are therefore counted as storage metrics, and the legacy metric stays empty.

title: Delete success metric is labelled with the object name instead of the kind
body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes `name` in the kind label position. Every other call passes `options.Kind`. Using the object name gives unbounded label cardinality and breaks the per-kind metric series.

title: Delete attaches the base logger to the context instead of the request-scoped logger
body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` ignores the `log` value built just above with name/kind/method. Every other method attaches `log`, so Delete logs lose their contextual fields downstream.

title: Legacy delete of an object missing from legacy is reported as a failure
body: The previous implementation ignored NotFound errors from the legacy delete. The new goroutine treats any error as a legacy failure and logs or records it. Objects that were created only in unified storage will now generate spurious legacy errors and failure metrics on every delete.

title: Destroy calls Legacy.Destroy without a nil check and while async writes may still run
body: Destroy tears down both stores immediately, while fire-and-forget legacy goroutines may still be running against Legacy. Calling Destroy can race with those in-flight writes. There is no tracking (WaitGroup or similar) of pending async writes.

title: Tests cannot observe the asynchronous legacy writes
body: The mode 3 tests register `Legacy` mock expectations (Create, Update) but never wait for or assert the goroutine calls. The legacy path is never verified, and the mock may be invoked after the test has finished. The tests therefore pass even if the legacy write is never made, cancelled, or made with the wrong object.

title: Test case name says 'not implemented' but List is implemented
