body: limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i and offset = params[:offset].to_i are used directly. A negative offset is passed to SQL OFFSET and causes a database error (500). A very large or negative limit is also accepted without a cap, so a single request can dump an entire large group's membership. Clamp limit to a sane maximum (e.g. 1..200) and clamp offset to >= 0.

title: members endpoint now runs a COUNT on every page request
body: Each request runs group.users.count plus the paginated query. Combined with the unbounded limit above, this makes large groups expensive to page through on every click. The removed code paginated only automatic groups, so non-automatic groups are now paginated too, which changes behaviour for all callers.

title: Admin group create/update request contract changed without compatibility
body: The controller now reads top-level params (params[:name], params[:usernames] is gone) instead of params[:group][...]. PUT /admin/groups/:id no longer accepts usernames, and PATCH with changes[:add]/[:delete] was removed. Any external API client or script using the previous nested format will silently break. This is not called out in the PR description.

title: update does not strip the group name, unlike create
body: create does (params[:name] || '').strip, but update assigns group.name = params[:name] unchanged. Names with surrounding whitespace can be saved through edit but not through creation, so the two paths disagree on validity.

title: add_members does not trim usernames and silently ignores unknown ones
body: usernames.split(",") keeps whitespace, so 'alice, bob' looks up ' bob' and silently skips it. Unknown usernames are dropped with no error returned to the UI, so the admin sees success with no member added.

title: Coverage for updating non-automatic groups was removed and not replaced
body: The old '.update' tests covering membership changes and name/visibility updates on regular groups were deleted. The new update spec only covers the automatic-group rename case. Nothing tests alias_level or visible changes on a normal group, and the pagination added to GroupsController#members has no spec.

title: Stale selector for the old group-users element
body: The rule 'input#group-users' under .row.groups targets an element id that the template no longer renders (the user-selector now uses id="user-selector"). The rule is dead code and misleads future maintainers.

title: Fallback chain reads SiteSetting on every lookup
body: `FallbackLocaleList#[]` calls `SiteSetting.default_locale` each time it is invoked. Once `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` is included, every translation miss or lookup goes through `I18n.fallbacks[locale]`, so this adds a SiteSetting read (and a `uniq`/array allocation) per translation call, on a hot path. The result could be memoized or derived from a cache that is invalidated when default_locale changes.

title: LRU translation cache key ignores the fallback chain and default locale
body: `translate` caches results keyed only by `key`, `config.locale` and the backend object id. With fallbacks now enabled, the resolved string depends on `SiteSetting.default_locale` (the second element of the fallback chain). If the site default locale changes, cached translations for locales that previously fell through to the default will keep returning the old text until the cache is evicted or `reload!` is called. The cache key should include the fallback chain or the cache should be cleared when default_locale changes.

title: Fallback locales are loaded only for web requests
body: `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` is called only in `set_locale`, a controller before_filter. Background jobs, mailers, and rake tasks that call I18n will get the fallback chain from `FallbackLocaleList` (site default and :en) but those locales' YAML files are only loaded when `translate` is called for them, and the chain is not explicitly loaded there. Those contexts can silently return missing-translation text when the user locale is missing a key. Consider loading the fallback chain in the accelerator's `translate` path or in the job/mailer setup.

title: Removing i18n fallback config in some environments but not others
body: The `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` setting is removed from production, profile and cloud66 configs, while the fallback module is now enabled unconditionally by the new initializer. Other environments (development/test) may still set the Rails config, so behavior is now split across environments and the Rails setting is dead/misleading in the ones that still have it. Either remove it everywhere or document the intent.

title: ensure_loaded! runs on every request
body: `set_locale` calls `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` on every request, which builds the fallback array and calls `I18n.ensure_loaded!` for each locale. `ensure_loaded!` performs an Array `include?` check each time. This is cheap individually but is per-request work that could be skipped once the locales are loaded.

title: PR description is missing
body: The PR description is just 'Test 9' and gives no rationale for enabling fallbacks globally, moving the pluralization require into a new initializer, or the cache implications. A maintainer reviewing this cannot tell what behavior change is intended.

title: Fallback chain reads SiteSetting on every lookup
body: FallbackLocaleList#[] calls SiteSetting.default_locale on every invocation. I18n consults the fallback list on each missing-translation lookup, and set_locale now also calls ensure_loaded!, which calls [] on every request. This adds a settings read (possibly cached but still non-trivial) on hot paths, and it can also touch the database during boot or in rake/console contexts where the initializer runs before SiteSetting is usable.

title: Removing config.i18n.fallbacks from all environments relies solely on the initializer
body: The config.i18n.fallbacks = true lines are removed from production, profile and the cloud66 production file, and the only replacement is the initializer that patches the backend and assigns I18n.fallbacks. If the initializer's include or assignment is not applied in some boot path (for example one that skips initializers or loads the backend earlier), fallbacks silently stop working in production with no error. The change is not reflected in any environment-specific check or test.

title: ensure_loaded! runs on every request and can trigger file loading inside a global mutex
body: set_locale now calls I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! on every request. The first request for each fallback locale (user locale, site default, :en) triggers load_locale, which holds LOAD_MUTEX while reading and parsing YAML files. Concurrent requests for a new locale serialize behind that lock, causing latency spikes. Preloading these locales at boot would avoid this on the request path.

title: Ordering comment refers to a file that may not match the load order
body: The header comment says 'order: after 02-freedom_patches.rb', but the initializer now depends on translate_accelerator.rb behaviour (I18n.ensure_loaded!) and also replaces the separate pluralization initializer that was deleted. The comment does not describe these dependencies, so a future reordering could break fallbacks or pluralization silently.

title: No tests cover the new fallback behaviour
body: The PR adds locale fallback ordering (user locale, site default, :en), a new ensure_loaded! API on both I18n and FallbackLocaleList, and moves the pluralization include. No spec verifies that a missing key in a user locale falls back correctly, that pluralization still works after the move, or that the fallback chain follows the site default locale.

title: PR description is a placeholder
body: The description reads 'Test 9' and gives no explanation of why fallbacks moved from environment configs to an initializer, what behaviour changes, or how to verify it. Reviewers cannot assess the intent or risk from the PR text.

title: Fallback chain reads SiteSetting on every translation lookup
body: FallbackLocaleList#[] builds a new array by reading SiteSetting.default_locale and calling to_sym each time it is invoked. I18n consults the fallback list on every missing-key lookup, and ensure_loaded! calls it again on every request via set_locale. This adds avoidable work on a hot path. Memoizing the value, or invalidating it when default_locale changes, would avoid repeated lookups.

title: ensure_loaded! runs on every request
body: I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! is called in set_locale for every request. It walks the fallback list and calls I18n.ensure_loaded! for each locale, which takes the LOAD_MUTEX path when a locale is not yet marked loaded. The work is cheap once loaded, but it repeats the SiteSetting read and array construction on every request. Loading could happen once per locale instead of per request.

title: Translation cache key ignores the fallback chain, so cached results can be stale
body: The LRU cache key is built from key, config.locale and the backend object_id only. With fallbacks now dependent on SiteSetting.default_locale, a translation resolved through the fallback chain is cached under a key that does not include the default locale. If default_locale changes at runtime, previously cached fallback results keep being served for that process until reload!. The key also concatenates without a separator, so distinct (key, locale) pairs can collide, for example key 'a' with locale 'en' versus key 'ae' with locale ''.

title: ensure_loaded! relies on I18n.locale being a Symbol for the fallback lookup
body: ensure_loaded! calls self[I18n.locale], which builds [locale, default.to_sym, :en]. If I18n.locale is ever a String, the list contains both 'en' and :en, so the same locale can be loaded twice, and the uniq does not dedupe them. The code assumes symbols everywhere without normalizing the input.

title: Fallback behaviour is not covered by any test
body: The PR changes global I18n fallback configuration, removes the Rails i18n.fallbacks config from three environment files, deletes the pluralization initializer, and adds a per-request loading hook. No spec exercises the fallback chain (user locale, then site default, then :en), missing-key behaviour, or the interaction with the accelerator's lazy loading. Regressions here would only surface in production.

title: Deletion of the pluralization initializer is not mentioned in the PR
body: The pluralization initializer is removed and its include moved into the new i18n.rb. The PR description is just 'Test 9' and does not explain this move, the removal of config.i18n.fallbacks from three environment files, or the behaviour change. Reviewers cannot verify intent from the PR text.

title: Denial cache short-circuits before the DB requery, so a new dashboard/folder stays denied for up to 30s
body: Check first consults permDenialCache and returns Allowed=false before any permission lookup. A denial is written at line 154 whenever a check fails, keyed by user, action, name and parent folder, with a 30s TTL. The PR's stated goal is that a creator can access a dashboard or folder they just created. But if the creator (or anyone) requests that resource before it exists, the denial is cached. After creation, the same Check hits the denial entry and returns false without reaching the new fallback-to-DB path. Nothing invalidates the denial entry when permissions or the resource change. The bug the PR is meant to fix therefore persists for the TTL window. The denial lookup should be skipped or invalidated when the resource is not present in the cached permissions, or the denial should not be cached for name-specific checks.

title: Denial cache key concatenation is ambiguous and can collide across resources
body: userPermDenialCacheKey joins action, name and parent with "_" without escaping. Resource names may contain underscores, so distinct requests produce the same key. For example name="x_y" with parent="" and name="x" with parent="y" both yield the suffix "x_y_". A cached denial for one dashboard then denies a different dashboard for the same user for 30s. Use an unambiguous separator or hash the tuple.

title: Denial cache keeps a creator denied on a just-created resource for the full TTL
body: Check() caches a denial keyed by user, action, name and parent folder for shortCacheTTL (30s) whenever the check is denied (line ~154). The PR's stated purpose is to let a dashboard/folder creator access the resource they just created. If a check for a not-yet-existing resource is denied, the denial is cached. When the resource is created and the permission is granted, the next Check hits the denial cache at line 117 and returns Allowed=false before any permission lookup. Access is therefore still refused for up to 30 seconds, so the reported bug is not fixed. The denial entry is also never invalidated when permissions change. Consider not caching denials for resources that may be newly created, or bypassing the denial cache when the permission set is refreshed.

title: No test covers the actual regression scenario (deny, then grant, then allow)
body: TestService_CacheCheck only checks that a pre-seeded denial entry wins over a permission cache entry. It never performs a denied Check, then grants the permission in the store, then checks again and expects Allowed=true. That sequence is the scenario this PR exists for, and the test would have caught the stale denial described above. The test also seeds a permCache value that contradicts the denial, so it does not exercise a realistic cache state.

title: Denial cache key built by underscore concatenation can collide
body: userPermDenialCacheKey joins userUID, action, name and parent with '_' without escaping. Folder and dashboard UIDs may contain underscores, so different tuples can produce the same key (for example name "a_b" with parent "" versus name "a" with parent "b"). A collision would deny a request that should be allowed for up to the TTL. Use an unambiguous separator or a hash of the tuple.

title: Denial cache is consulted before permissions, so a cached denial defeats the fix for newly created resources
body: Check now returns a cached denial (keyed by user, action, name and parent folder) before looking at permissions. The denial is written at line ~153 whenever a check is denied and lives for shortCacheTTL (30s). The PR's stated goal is that a creator can access a dashboard or folder they just created. If the creator (or anyone) is checked for that name before it exists, the denial is cached. Once the resource is created and the user gets access, the next Check still hits the denial cache and returns Allowed=false for up to 30s. The new 'requery from DB on cache miss' logic never runs in that window. Name-less checks (create verbs, where Name is empty) are cached the same way, so a denied create can block a subsequent allowed create for 30s. Denials should not be cached for resources that may be created, or the denial cache should be invalidated when permissions change.

title: Negative results are cached for every denied check, including name-less checks
body: The denial entry is set for every denied request, with no regard for whether the target exists yet or whether Name is empty. For verbs like create (Name empty), checkPermission returns len(scopeMap)>0, so a user with no permissions is denied and that denial is cached under a key with an empty name. Any later create within 30s is denied from cache even after the user is granted permissions. Caching negatives this broadly also means permission revocations are not reflected for the TTL of the denial, which is not documented.

title: Denial cache key concatenates unescaped fields, so distinct requests can collide
body: userPermDenialCacheKey joins userUID, action, name and parent with '_' and no escaping. Names and folder UIDs can contain underscores, so (name='a_b', parent='') and (name='a', parent='b') produce the same key. A denial for one resource would then be applied to another. The key also shares the '.perm_' prefix with userPermCacheKey, so it can collide with permission-cache entries if identifiers contain '_'. A separator that cannot appear in these fields, or a hash of the tuple, is needed.

title: No test covers the actual regression: denial then creation then allow
body: TestService_CacheCheck covers an explicit denial entry, a cache miss, and an outdated cache, but none checks the scenario this PR targets. A user is denied for a resource, the resource is then created and the permission granted, and the next Check must allow. The 'explicit deny' test seeds the denial cache by hand and only checks that denial wins. Without a test for the denial-then-grant sequence, the bug above goes unnoticed. The removed getUserPermissions cache-hit case also leaves no test that exercises the cache path through getIdentityPermissions.

title: Pause menu item can never appear from the list view
body: The pause item is gated on `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`. The list view now passes only `promRule` (GrafanaRuleListItem renders RuleActionsButtons with no `rule`), so `rulerRule` is undefined and the item is hidden even when `canPause` is true from the Grafana prom-rule ability. The new Grafana abilities are computed but the pause action is unreachable in the list view.

title: Delete menu item is hidden in the list view even when the user is allowed to delete
body: The delete item requires `canDelete && rulerRule`. In the alert list view `rulerRule` is always undefined, so the item is never rendered even when `grafanaDeleteAllowed` is true. The new promRule-based delete ability is therefore dead in the list, and users cannot delete Grafana rules from the list view despite the PR's stated intent.

title: Silence menu item shown in list view but does nothing
body: `canSilence` now includes the promRule-based ability, so the Silence item renders in the list. Its handler calls `setShowSilenceDrawer(true)`, but RuleActionsButtons.V2 only renders `SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer` when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` holds, and `rule` is undefined in the list view. Clicking Silence silently does nothing.

title: Rule link drops the returnTo parameter
body: The removed GrafanaRuleLoader built the href with `createRelativeUrl(..., { returnTo })` using createReturnTo(). The new GrafanaRuleListItem drops returnTo, so opening a rule from the list no longer lets the user return to the filtered list view.

title: Tests do not cover Pause/Delete/Silence through the promRule path
body: The RBAC tests mock the ability hooks and only check Edit and Delete visibility in the table. Nothing verifies that the Delete, Pause, or Silence menu items actually render or act when only promRule is supplied, which is how the list view uses the component. The bugs above pass the existing test suite.

title: Silence menu item shown in list view but its drawer never opens
body: In the list view `rulerRule` is undefined, but `canSilence` now also comes from the Grafana prom-rule ability, so the 'Silence notifications' item renders. Its click calls `handleSilence`, which sets `showSilenceDrawer`. In RuleActionsButtons.V2.tsx the drawer is rendered only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true, and `rule` is undefined here, so nothing opens. The menu item is a dead control for every Grafana rule in the list view.

title: Delete and pause items are unreachable in list view despite Grafana abilities
body: `canDelete` now includes the prom-rule ability, but the Delete item is still gated by `canDelete && rulerRule`. The list view never passes `rulerRule`, so Delete is never rendered for Grafana rules there, even when the user has permission. Likewise the pause item (line 123) requires `rulerRule` via `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`, so the new `canPause` grafana branch has no effect in the list view. The abilities were wired up but the rendering conditions were not updated, so the feature is silently incomplete.

title: GrafanaRuleListItem rendered in list without a React key
body: The diff removed `key={key}` from the `GrafanaRuleListItem` element in the filtered results map, while the `datasource` and `unknown` branches still set keys. Rules are rendered from an array that grows via concat, so React will warn about missing keys and may reuse or misplace DOM/state between items when the list is updated. The `key` was already computed (`ruleWithOrigin.key`) and should be kept.

title: Link to rule view drops the returnTo parameter
body: The previous GrafanaRuleLoader built `href` with `createRelativeUrl(..., { returnTo })`. The new GrafanaRuleListItem uses `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`)` without returnTo, so navigating from the list to a rule and pressing back/cancel no longer returns the user to the list with its filters.

title: Removed coverage for Creating/Deleting states and matchRules logic
body: The tests for rules that exist only in the ruler (Creating) and only in Prometheus (Deleting), and the matchRules unit tests, were deleted together with the behaviour. Nothing replaces them, and the list view no longer surfaces rules in these transitional states at all. The PR does not add tests that cover the new behaviour where ruler-only actions are unavailable, such as Silence and Delete from the list.

title: Delete action is never shown in the list view for Grafana rules
body: The Delete menu item is gated on `canDelete && rulerRule`. The list view now passes only `promRule` (GrafanaRuleListItem no longer supplies `rulerRule`), so `rulerRule` is always undefined there. `canDelete` can be true from the Grafana prom abilities, but the item is still not rendered. Users with delete permission lose the Delete action in the alert list, and the Delete button wired to `handleDelete(rulerRule, ...)` is effectively dead for this path.

title: Pause menu item is gated on rulerRule and disappears in the list view
body: `MenuItemPauseRule` is rendered only when `canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`. In the list view `rulerRule` is undefined, so the pause option is hidden even when the Grafana prom abilities grant pause. The ability was computed from `promRule` but the render condition still depends on the ruler rule.

title: Silence button in list view opens nothing because the drawer requires rulerRule
body: `handleSilence` sets `showSilenceDrawer`, but the `SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer` is rendered only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` holds. In the list view `rule` is undefined, so the drawer never mounts. The Silence menu item (now enabled via `grafanaSilenceAbility`) appears and does nothing when clicked.

title: Test asserts the broken 4-item menu as the expected behavior
body: GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx expects exactly 4 menu items (silence, copy link, duplicate, export) and never checks pause or delete. The test therefore locks in the missing Delete and Pause actions instead of catching them, and the silence test does not verify the drawer opens.

title: Removed matchRules tests with no replacement coverage
body: The matchRules unit tests were deleted along with the ruler matching logic, but no tests were added for the new list-item path that handles Grafana rules without a ruler rule. Behaviour such as provenance (now read from promRule.provenance) and the is-paused source change is not covered.

title: Rule view link drops the returnTo parameter
body: The previous GrafanaRuleLoader built the href with `createReturnTo()` so navigating from the list back to the list works. The new href is `createRelativeUrl('/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view')` with no returnTo, so the back navigation from the rule view is lost.

title: Targets are interpolated twice on the sharded path
body: runShardSplitQuery now calls applyTemplateVariables on every target, and the resulting targets are passed into splitQueriesByStreamShard, which builds subRequest and calls runSplitQuery(datasource, subRequest, ...). runSplitQuery in querySplitting.ts (line 299 in the head) now also calls applyTemplateVariables on each target, with the same scopedVars and filters. Every sharded sub-request is therefore interpolated a second time. Any value that survives the first pass but is changed by a second pass (a value containing '$', regex-escaped label values, or adhoc filters applied again) gets corrupted or duplicated. The fix is to interpolate in exactly one layer, or to skip interpolation in runSplitQuery when the caller has already done it.

title: runSplitQuery interpolates unconditionally, including for callers that already interpolated
body: The map to applyTemplateVariables was added to runSplitQuery, which is a public entry point. Besides shardQuerySplitting (see the double-interpolation finding), any other caller that passes already-interpolated targets now gets them interpolated again. There is no flag or contract documenting which layer owns interpolation, so the behaviour depends on the call path.

title: Call-count assertion hard-codes an implementation detail
body: The 'Interpolates queries before running' test now asserts applyTemplateVariables was called exactly 5 times. That count only holds because of the nested runSplitQuery re-interpolation, so the test encodes the double-interpolation behaviour as expected and would not catch a regression in either direction. It should assert what the sharded path must do (interpolate each original target once) rather than an incidental call count.

title: Shard path interpolates queries twice, once here and again inside runSplitQuery
body: runShardSplitQuery() now calls applyTemplateVariables on every target (line 52), and splitQueriesByStreamShard() then builds subRequest with those already-interpolated targets. Each subRequest is passed to runSplitQuery(), which calls applyTemplateVariables again on every target (querySplitting.ts line 299). Interpolation is therefore applied twice to the same expression. Any value that contains a '$' or other template-like text after the first pass gets interpolated a second time. The test change that expects applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times reflects this double application rather than a deliberate design. Interpolation should happen in exactly one place for the sharded path.

title: Interpolation before querySupportsSplitting breaks the $__range check
body: querySupportsSplitting() relies on isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) to keep $__range queries from being split. The comment on that check says the range must not be split because $__range is interpolated on the backend against the split time range. Now that applyTemplateVariables runs at line 299, before partition() at line 300, the expr seen by isQueryWithRangeVariable is already interpolated. If the Loki datasource resolves $__range on the frontend, the variable is gone by the time the check runs, so $__range queries would be split and get an incorrect range. The check should run on the original expression, or the test suite should cover a $__range query to confirm the behaviour is preserved.

title: Empty-expression filter runs before interpolation, so a variable that expands to empty is not dropped
body: The filter `.filter((query) => query.expr)` runs at line 298, before applyTemplateVariables at line 299. A target whose expr is a variable that interpolates to an empty string passes the filter and is sent as an empty query. Filtering after interpolation, or filtering both before and after, would avoid this.

title: $__range check now runs on already-interpolated expressions, so range queries get split
body: Queries are now interpolated at the top of runSplitQuery, before querySupportsSplitting() runs at line 300. querySupportsSplitting() relies on isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) to keep $__range queries out of splitting, and its comment says the $__range variable must not be split because it is computed for the full time range. Once $__range has been replaced with a concrete duration, the check no longer matches, so such queries are split and each sub-request gets an incorrect $__range value. The range-variable check should run on the original expression, or the query should be classified before interpolation.

title: Queries are interpolated twice on the sharded path
body: runShardSplitQuery now calls applyTemplateVariables on every target, and the result is passed to splitQueriesByStreamShard. That code then calls runSplitQuery for each subRequest, and runSplitQuery calls applyTemplateVariables again on the same targets. Values that contain `$` or other template syntax can be expanded a second time, and the interpolation is not idempotent in general. Interpolation should happen in one place only.

title: Assertion pins the exact applyTemplateVariables call count
body: The test expects applyTemplateVariables to be called exactly 5 times. That count depends on how many shard groups and sub-requests the implementation creates, and it will break on unrelated refactors while not checking that interpolation happens before execution. The test should assert on the interpolated expressions passed to runQuery instead.

title: Trace ID is no longer logged on plugin request completion
body: The removed code explicitly appended `traceID` from `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` to the completion log line. The new code only calls `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`, so the trace ID now appears only if the infra contextual logger happens to carry it. Nothing in this PR adds the trace ID to the contextual logger (`ContextualLoggerMiddleware.instrumentContext` does not include it). Trace correlation for 'Plugin Request Completed' logs is therefore silently lost.

title: Nil request is dereferenced without a guard
body: QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth and CollectMetrics read `req.PluginContext` unconditionally, while the sibling LoggerMiddleware explicitly handles `req == nil`. A nil request will panic here before reaching the downstream client, which previously did not happen on this path for the logger. The nil handling should match LoggerMiddleware, or the behavior should be justified.

title: New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no tests
body: The logging context enrichment (endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, uname) was moved out of the metrics middleware into this new file, but no test covers it. The existing metrics test was only renamed and no longer exercises context propagation. A regression in the attributes or in the ordering dependency with LoggerMiddleware would go unnoticed.

title: Adding FromContext to the Logger interface breaks any other implementers
body: `FromContext` is added to the exported `plog.Logger` interface. Any other implementation of this interface elsewhere in the repo or in plugins/extensions that is not updated will fail to compile. The PR only updates `TestLogger` and `grafanaInfraLogWrapper`, so the blast radius should be confirmed across the codebase.

title: Trace ID no longer appears in the plugin request completion log
body: logRequest used to add a `traceID` field explicitly via tracing.TraceIDFromContext. That was removed, and the log now relies entirely on m.logger.FromContext(ctx) to carry it. Nothing in this PR adds trace ID to the contextual attributes (instrumentContext only adds endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, uname). Unless the infra logger's FromContext happens to include the trace ID, completed-request logs silently lose their trace correlation, which is a regression in observability.

title: TestLogger.FromContext discards recorded calls
body: FromContext returns a brand-new NewTestLogger(), so anything logged through the contextual logger is recorded on a throwaway object. LoggerMiddleware now logs via m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so tests that inject TestLogger and assert on InfoLogs will see zero calls and pass or fail for the wrong reason. The fake should return the receiver (or share its log state) so that calls are observed.

title: No test covers the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware or the moved logging behavior
body: The contextual logger logic was moved out of the metrics middleware into a new file, and LoggerMiddleware now depends on it for endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID and uname. None of the tests in this PR verify that ContextualLoggerMiddleware adds these attributes to the context, or that LoggerMiddleware's output still includes them. The existing test still only exercises metrics, with the test name still TestInstrumentationMiddleware.

title: Nil request is dereferenced without a guard
body: QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth and CollectMetrics read req.PluginContext unconditionally. LoggerMiddleware explicitly guards against a nil req, but this middleware does not. Any caller that passes a nil request into this layer will panic here, which is inconsistent with the rest of the logging chain.

title: Plugin request log line no longer includes traceID
body: The old logRequest explicitly appended a "traceID" field from the context (via tracing.TraceIDFromContext) to the "Plugin Request Completed" log line. That block was removed. The new ContextualLoggerMiddleware (contextual_logger_middleware.go, instrumentContext) only adds endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID and uname, and does not add traceID. Unless the infra logger's FromContext happens to add trace IDs (nothing in this diff shows that), completed-request logs lose their trace correlation, a regression for anyone correlating plugin egress logs with traces.

title: Logger middleware now depends on ContextualLoggerMiddleware being earlier in the chain
body: LoggerMiddleware no longer adds pluginId, endpoint, dsName, dsUID or uname itself. It relies entirely on m.logger.FromContext(ctx) picking up attributes injected by ContextualLoggerMiddleware. That ordering is only enforced by the comment-free slice in pluginsintegration.go CreateMiddlewares. Any future reordering, or any caller composing LoggerMiddleware without the contextual middleware (or with metrics removed), silently drops all plugin/datasource identifiers from the egress log, and nothing fails at compile time or in tests.

title: New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no tests
body: The middleware and the moved instrumentContext logic are new in this file, and the logging contract (which attributes are attached to the context, and that LoggerMiddleware picks them up) has no unit test. metrics_middleware_test.go was only renamed, and its test still covers only metrics. Since the change moves log-enrichment responsibility across middlewares, a test asserting the contextual attributes reach the logger would catch the ordering and traceID regressions above.

title: Test still named for the old InstrumentationMiddleware
body: The test function is still TestInstrumentationMiddleware even though the file and type were renamed to MetricsMiddleware. This leaves the naming inconsistent with the stated goal of the PR.

title: Logger still registered under the old 'instrumentation' name
body: The LoggerMiddleware is still constructed with log.New("plugin.instrumentation"), which keeps the old naming this PR is meant to clean up. Log consumers filtering on the logger name will see the stale name.

title: Device is cached as tagged before the limit check, so a rejected device is let through on its next request
body: tagDeviceUI sets the local cache key (SetDefault) before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the device limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, and Authenticate rejects the request. But the key is already cached for about 29 minutes, so the next request from the same device hits the cache, tagDeviceUI returns nil, and Authenticate succeeds. The limit is therefore enforced only on every other attempt. The cache entry should be set only after a successful write, or removed on error.

title: Device limit check is a non-atomic count followed by insert, so concurrent logins can exceed the limit
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice first runs CountDevices and then performs a separate INSERT/UPDATE. Under concurrency, many new devices can pass the count check before any of them is inserted, so the number of devices can exceed deviceLimit. The check and insert need to be done in one transaction or as a conditional insert, or the overshoot must be accepted and documented.

title: updateDevice treats zero rows affected as 'limit reached', which MySQL reports for no-op updates
body: updateDevice relies on RowsAffected()==0 to mean the device is outside the window. MySQL reports changed rows by default, so if an existing device sends the same client_ip, user_agent and an updated_at within the same second, the UPDATE affects 0 rows. The function then returns ErrDeviceLimitReached for a device that already exists and should be allowed, and the user is locked out. The check should use a select or a matched-rows connection setting instead.

title: Tagging is now synchronous on the authentication path, so every new anonymous request waits on a DB write and can fail login
body: Previously TagDevice ran in a goroutine with a timeout. It now runs inline with the request context. Each first request from a device adds a count query plus a write to login latency. If the DB is slow or the request context is cancelled, the write fails. The error is only logged for non-limit errors, but the limit error now blocks authentication. Also, the removed goroutine had panic recovery, and the new call has none.

title: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now builds its own store, bypassing the injected AnonStore
body: The constructor previously took an anonstore.AnonStore from dependency injection. It now takes db.DB and calls anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore internally with cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit. Any other provider that depends on the AnonStore binding in the wire graph now gets a different instance than the one used by the service. This is a wiring change that can cause two stores with inconsistent config and should be made through DI.

title: TagDevice now returns the tagging error, but the logging and return path are inconsistent with the caller
body: TagDevice logs at Debug and returns the error for every failure, while Authenticate only propagates ErrDeviceLimitReached and logs the rest at Warn. Other DB errors are logged twice at different levels. The return value of TagDevice is therefore not a clear contract for callers and should be documented or narrowed.

title: Tests do not cover the update path when the limit is reached, or the limit being unset
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only checks that a new device is rejected. It does not check that an existing device in the window can still be updated at the limit, which is the behavior updateDevice is designed for. It also does not check the RowsAffected edge case or the concurrent case. No test covers the TagDevice cache interaction that allows a rejected device through on retry.

title: anonymousDeviceLimit is typed number | undefined in the interface but initialised to undefined, while the backend always sends a number
body: The Go DTO serializes anonymousDeviceLimit as int64 and always includes it, with 0 meaning no limit. The TS side is declared `number | undefined` and defaulted to undefined. Frontend code checking for truthiness or a limit will treat 0 and undefined inconsistently, and the type does not match what the server sends.

title: Device limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert (TOCTOU race)
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts devices and then inserts in a separate statement. Concurrent new anonymous requests can all observe count < deviceLimit and insert, so the limit can be exceeded by the number of concurrent requests. The limit is not enforced under concurrency, which is the core purpose of the feature.

title: Count window differs from the window used in the update path and in the API
body: The limit count uses [now-30d, now+1m] while updateDevice uses [updatedAt-30d, updatedAt+1m] keyed on the device's own timestamp. Both are fine individually, but the count also includes stale rows that the cleanup job has not yet removed (cleanup keeps 61 days), so the count is based on devices updated in the last 30 days only while rows are deleted at 61 days; the semantics of 'device limit' are inconsistent with the stored data. Worth confirming the intended window.

title: Limit-reached is signaled via RowsAffected, which is zero when the row is unchanged
body: updateDevice treats rowsAffected == 0 as ErrDeviceLimitReached. On MySQL, RowsAffected returns 0 when the UPDATE sets values identical to existing ones (unless CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS is set), so an existing device re-tagged with the same IP and user agent within the same timestamp window is reported as limit reached and the request is rejected with an error. The error also misidentifies the cause, since a non-matching row (device expired/updated outside window) is also reported as limit reached.

title: Device limit error now fails the whole anonymous login
body: Authenticate now returns the ErrDeviceLimitReached error, so once the limit is hit every anonymous request (including ones from already-known devices that go through the update path) is rejected at authentication. Combined with the update path returning the same error for any non-matching row, users may be locked out instead of being served as anonymous without tagging. Confirm this is the intended behavior and that the error does not leak as an unhandled 500.

title: Synchronous TagDevice on the request path adds DB latency and removes the timeout
body: The tagging was previously run in a goroutine with a 2 minute timeout and panic recovery. It is now called synchronously with the request context, so every anonymous authentication performs DB writes (a COUNT plus an insert/update) in the hot path, and the panic recovery was removed. A slow database now slows or fails all anonymous page loads.

title: TagDevice now returns DB errors but the caller ignores them for the device-ID path, and the ID-less case still returns nil silently
body: The new 'return err' in TagDevice is only reached after tagDeviceUI, but tagDeviceUI marks the local cache before the DB write succeeds. If CreateOrUpdateDevice fails (including the limit error), the device key stays in the local cache for 29 minutes, so later requests from that device are skipped without retry and are not tagged, even after space frees up.

title: Device limit is read from cfg in the service constructor but the store is no longer injected
body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now constructs the store internally with cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit instead of receiving it via Wire. This bypasses dependency injection, makes the store impossible to mock in service-level tests, and the service's anonStore is now a concrete type while the API is passed a.anonStore, so the cleanup/ListDevices behavior cannot be substituted in tests.

title: New device_limit setting is undocumented and not validated
body: The new [auth.anonymous] device_limit key is read with MustInt64(0) but negative values are silently accepted, which the store treats as no limit (>0 check). No documentation or conf/defaults.ini entry is added for the new option, which the PR checklist requires.

title: Limit test does not cover the update-allowed path or the race
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only checks that a second new device is rejected. It does not verify that an existing device can still be updated when the limit is reached, nor that the limit holds under concurrent inserts, nor the API-level behavior of the anonymous client returning an error.

title: Device is cached as tagged before the limit check, so a rejected device gets in on its next request
body: tagDeviceUI sets the local cache entry (`a.localCache.SetDefault(key, ...)`) before calling `CreateOrUpdateDevice`. If that call returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, the device stays cached for about 29 minutes. The next request for that device hits the cache check at the top of tagDeviceUI, returns nil, and Authenticate lets the anonymous login through without the device ever being stored. The device limit can therefore be bypassed. The cache entry should be set only after a successful store, or removed when the store returns an error.

title: Count-then-insert device limit check is racy and can exceed the limit
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts devices with CountDevices and then inserts in a separate statement. Concurrent first-time requests from different devices can all read a count below the limit and all insert, so the number of devices can overshoot deviceLimit. The check and insert need to be atomic, for example a conditional INSERT ... SELECT with a count subquery under a transaction or lock, or the limit should be documented as approximate.

title: Existing devices older than the window are reported as limit-reached
body: When the limit is hit, updateDevice only updates rows whose updated_at lies in [now-30d, now+1min]. An existing device whose record is older than 30 days matches no row, so rowsAffected is 0 and the function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. That user is then rejected even though the device is already known and the limit was not exceeded for it. Also, on MySQL RowsAffected counts changed rows, so an update that changes nothing would also be misreported. The function should distinguish a missing row from an unchanged one.

title: Device tagging moved from a background goroutine to the request path, adding DB work to every anonymous login
body: The previous code tagged the device asynchronously with a 2-minute timeout and panic recovery. The new code calls TagDevice synchronously with the request context. Every uncached anonymous request now runs a COUNT query over anon_device and then an insert or update before login completes, so DB latency or contention directly slows authentication. The removal of the timeout and recover also means a slow DB can block the request until the client gives up.

title: Constructor signature change may break dependency wiring
body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now takes db.DB instead of anonstore.AnonStore and builds the store internally. If the wire provider set (or any other caller) still provides an anonstore.AnonStore, wire generation or compilation will fail, or the store will be built twice with different configurations. The wire definitions should be checked and regenerated to match.

title: Device-limit tests don't cover the update path or the bypass case
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only checks that a new device is rejected at the limit. It does not check that an already-known device is still allowed to update when the limit is reached, which is the main purpose of updateDevice. It also doesn't check that a rejected device is not treated as tagged on a later request (the cache bypass), and it doesn't cover the limit being 0 with concurrent inserts. The new branch of the logic is therefore largely untested.

title: Unrelated change: background cleanup ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The ticker interval for the whole cleanup service is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This is not mentioned in the PR description and has nothing to do with the annotation deadlock fix. It makes every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, invites, short URLs, query history, annotations) run ten times as often on every instance, adding DB load. It looks like a leftover debugging change and should be reverted unless it is intentional and documented.

title: Routine per-batch progress is logged at Error level, including full ID lists
body: Every batch of the time-based cleanup logs at Error level ("Annotations to clean by time", with the full "ids" slice and the SQL "cond"), and then logs again at Error level after deletion (line 536). The same happens for the count-based cleanup (lines 554, 556) and for orphaned tags (lines 576, 579). A healthy cleanup run therefore emits error-level logs for every batch, and each line can contain up to batch-size IDs. This floods logs and triggers error alerts on success. Also, the 'err' field in these calls is always nil at that point. These should be Debug-level and should not include the ID list.

title: Quadratic string building when inlining IDs for SQLite
body: For SQLite with batch sizes above 999, the IDs are concatenated with repeated fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v). Each iteration copies the whole accumulated string, so building a 32767-element list is O(n^2) work and allocation on every batch. Use strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt into a byte slice.

title: Test with 40003 annotations is slow and is the only coverage for the large-batch SQLite path
body: The new case inserts 40003 annotations and 80006 tags through InsertMulti on every run, and it is the only test that exercises the inlined-ID SQLite branch in deleteByIDs. This makes the integration suite noticeably slower. Also, the new integration tests are now skipped under testing.Short(), so the cleanup logic has no unit-level coverage in short runs. Consider a smaller test that still crosses the 999 threshold, or a unit test for deleteByIDs that does not need the DB.

title: Test cleanup does not clear annotation_tag rows
body: TestIntegrationOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst removes only the annotation table in its t.Cleanup, while the other test in this file removes both annotation and annotation_tag. Leftover tag rows can leak into other tests in the package that count annotation_tag, making results depend on test order.

title: Cleanup ticker interval silently changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The ticker in Run was changed from time.Minute * 10 to time.Minute * 1. This is unrelated to the annotation deadlock fix described in the PR and is not mentioned in the description. It makes every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, invites, short URLs, query history, annotations) run ten times as often, which is a production behaviour change. It looks like a leftover from debugging and should be reverted unless it is intentional and documented.

title: Routine cleanup progress is logged at Error level, including full ID lists, on every batch
body: In CleanAnnotations (and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags) the normal per-batch progress messages ("Annotations to clean by time", "cleaned annotations by time", "Tags to clean", "cleaned tags", and the by-count equivalents) are emitted with r.log.Error. Successful routine work is not an error, so this will flood error logs and trip error-based alerting on every cleanup cycle. The ids slice is also logged in full: with batch sizes up to 32767 that is a very large log line per batch. These should be Debug (or Info) and should not dump the ID list. The "err" field is also always nil at the first log call, since err was just checked and returned, so it is misleading.

title: Unrelated change: cleanup ticker interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The diff changes `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)` to `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)` in `Run`. This is not mentioned in the PR description and has nothing to do with the MySQL deadlock fix. It makes every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, invites, short URLs, query history, annotations) run ten times as often, with a 9-minute timeout per run. This should be reverted or split into its own PR with a stated rationale.

title: Routine progress messages logged at Error level on every batch
body: The new fetch-then-delete loops log informational messages with `r.log.Error(...)`: 'Annotations to clean by time', 'cleaned annotations by time', 'Annotations to clean by count', 'cleaned annotations by count', 'Tags to clean', and 'cleaned tags'. These run for every batch, including batches that delete nothing, and they fire every cleanup cycle (once a minute now). This will flood error logs and trigger error alerting even on healthy systems. They should be Debug (or Info) messages. The `err` key is also always nil in the success-path log lines, which is misleading.

title: Full ID lists logged on every batch, potentially up to the batch size
body: Each batch logs the full `ids` slice (`"ids", ids`), and the batch size is configurable and can be as large as 32767 in the new test. Each cleanup batch therefore writes tens of thousands of IDs into the log, repeated on every batch and every cycle. Log the count only, or log IDs at Debug level.

title: Fetched IDs are deleted without re-checking the condition, so the delete is not guarded
body: The IDs are selected in one statement and deleted in a separate one with no transaction. Between the two, a concurrent update could change a row so it no longer matches (for example, a row's `created` changes). This is probably acceptable for cleanup, and the comment acknowledges the under-delete case, but the delete statement does not repeat the age or type condition, so a row that no longer qualifies can still be removed. Consider including the original condition in the DELETE, or document this explicitly as accepted behaviour.

title: Large-batch test inserts about 40k rows on every run and is gated only by -short
body: The new case inserts 40003 annotations and 80006 annotation_tag rows through the store in 500-row batches for each of the three cleanup cases. This is slow on every integration run and is the only coverage of the SQLite parameter limit path in `deleteByIDs`. The SQLite-specific inline-ID branch has no unit test that checks the generated SQL or the case where the batch size exceeds 999 on a non-SQLite database. Consider a unit test for `deleteByIDs` SQL generation.

title: Async legacy writes run on the request context, which is cancelled once the request returns
body: Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection launch the legacy write in a goroutine using a context derived from the request ctx. When the HTTP handler returns, that ctx is cancelled, so context.WithTimeoutCause produces an already-cancelled context and the legacy write fails or is aborted. Mode 3 relies on these writes to keep legacy in sync, so they will often silently not happen. The goroutines should use a detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx)) before applying the timeout.

title: Legacy Create races on the same obj and options that Storage.Create already used
body: The goroutine passes the same obj pointer and options to Legacy.Create while Storage.Create may still be reading or mutating them (e.g. setting ResourceVersion, name generation, or DryRun handling). This is an unsynchronized data race on shared objects. Similarly Update passes the same objInfo to both storage and legacy concurrently, and UpdatedObject may be invoked twice on a one-shot objInfo.

title: Update error path records a legacy metric for a storage failure
body: When Storage.Update fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recordStorageDuration. This corrupts the legacy error/latency metrics and hides storage failures. The same mistake is in Create's error path (line 45).

title: Create error path records a storage failure as a legacy metric
body: On Storage.Create failure, recordLegacyDuration is called. Storage failures should be recorded with recordStorageDuration, otherwise dashboards show legacy errors for unified-storage failures.

title: Delete records the object name as the resource kind label
body: recordStorageDuration is called with `name` in the kind position (`mode3Str, name, method`), while every other call uses options.Kind. This produces high-cardinality, wrong metric labels per object.

title: DeleteCollection records legacy duration using the storage metric
body: The goroutine calls d.recordStorageDuration for the legacy DeleteCollection result instead of recordLegacyDuration, so legacy failures are counted against storage.

title: Legacy update errors are only counted, never logged
body: Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection drop the legacy error after recording the metric. Failures to write to legacy are therefore invisible to operators except as a counter, and the object is left inconsistent with no log line with the object name to reconcile it.

title: Delete attaches the bare logger to ctx instead of the named one
body: ctx is set with klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log), discarding the `log` built with name/kind/method values that is used for the error logs. Downstream logs lose the context fields.

title: Update goroutine: cancel is not deferred on every path and ctx is created before the goroutine's timer starts
body: The timeout context is created outside the start timer and cancel is deferred after startLegacy; this is inconsistent with the other goroutines and makes the timeout include unrelated work. Minor, but it is an unexpected pattern.

title: Tests never verify the asynchronous legacy writes happen
body: The mode 3 tests set up legacy mock expectations but never wait for or assert the goroutine calls (no AssertExpectations/AssertCalled, no sync). The legacy path could be entirely broken and the tests would still pass. The removed legacy-failure cases (e.g. Create error from legacy) are no longer covered either, since legacy errors no longer affect the result.

title: Misleading test name for List error case
body: The case 'error when listing an object in the unified store is not implemented' now asserts a real storage error path, not a not-implemented stub; the name is stale.

title: Unrelated dependency checksums added to go.work.sum
body: The diff adds checksums for grafana-azure-sdk-go, prometheus-alertmanager, and several OpenTelemetry modules that have nothing to do with dual-writer mode 3. These look like incidental go tooling churn and should be explained or dropped from this PR.

title: Async legacy Create shares the request object and context with the storage write
body: Create hands the same `obj` to Storage.Create and then to a goroutine calling Legacy.Create. Storage may mutate that object (e.g. set ResourceVersion, UID, or timestamps) while the goroutine reads it, which is a data race. The goroutine also uses `ctx` from the request; once the HTTP handler returns, the request context is cancelled, so the legacy write can fail or be cut short with the 10s timeout unrelated to the actual work. The legacy copy should get a deep copy of the object and a context detached from request cancellation (e.g. context.WithoutCancel).

title: Async legacy Update reuses objInfo that storage has already consumed
body: Update passes the same `objInfo` to Storage.Update and then to Legacy.Update in a goroutine. UpdatedObjectInfo.UpdatedObject is typically invoked with the stored old object and may mutate state or be non-reentrant; calling it again concurrently with the storage path is unsafe. The legacy update may also be computed from a different base object than the one storage used, so the two stores can diverge silently. The same request ctx is also reused after the handler returns.

title: Delete records the object name as the kind label in metrics
body: The storage duration metric on success is called with `name` in the kind position (`d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, ...)`), while every other call uses `options.Kind`. This pollutes the metric label cardinality with per-object names and breaks dashboards that group by kind.

title: Storage failure in Update is recorded as a legacy failure
body: When Storage.Update returns an error, the code calls recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recordStorageDuration. The unified storage error is therefore counted against the legacy store and the storage metric is not updated, making both metrics wrong. Create's storage error path has the same mislabeling issue on the legacy side.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection duration recorded with the storage metric
body: In the DeleteCollection goroutine the legacy result is reported via d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...) rather than recordLegacyDuration. Legacy timings and errors are then mixed into the storage metrics.

title: Delete attaches the base logger to the context, dropping the name and method fields
body: Delete builds a scoped `log` with name, kind and method, but then calls `klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`, so downstream logs from the storage/legacy calls lose the context fields that every other method in this file keeps.

title: Fire-and-forget legacy writes have no way to surface failures or bound concurrency
body: All mutating methods launch an unbounded goroutine per request for the legacy write, and failures are only logged as a metric (and the goroutine's log is not used). Under sustained write load goroutines and legacy writes can pile up without limit, and divergence between stores is only visible through metrics. At minimum a bounded worker or queue is needed, and the legacy error should be logged with the object identity.

title: Mode 3 playlist tests assume legacy writes are synchronous
body: In mode 3 the legacy write happens asynchronously, but doPlaylistTests checks the legacy /api/playlists list and per-item legacy GETs immediately after the k8s create/delete calls. These assertions will be flaky or fail whenever the goroutine has not finished, so the new mode 3 integration cases are unreliable. They need to poll/eventually-assert on the legacy side, or the test should check the legacy store only after waiting.

title: No tests verify the legacy write happens or that legacy failures are ignored
body: The mode 3 unit tests mock the legacy store with expectations but never assert they were called (no AssertExpectations), and the legacy goroutine may run after the test returns. There is no test that a legacy failure does not change the returned result, and none for the Create/DeleteCollection legacy paths. The core behaviour of mode 3 (sync storage, async legacy) is therefore not actually tested.

title: Unrelated checksum entries added to go.work.sum
body: The go.work.sum change adds many entries for unrelated modules (grafana-azure-sdk-go, prometheus-alertmanager, otel exporters, etc.) that this feature does not touch. This looks like an accidental tooling side effect and should be dropped from the PR or explained.

title: Async legacy write uses the request ctx, which is cancelled when the request returns
body: The goroutines launched in Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection derive their context from the request ctx via context.WithTimeoutCause. When the HTTP request finishes, the request context is cancelled, so the legacy write is aborted almost immediately after the response is sent. The 'asynchronous safe measure' write will frequently fail silently (only logged/metric'd), leaving legacy out of sync. The background goroutine should use a detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx)) plus the timeout.

title: Create passes the same obj to legacy asynchronously after storage may have mutated it
body: The goroutine calls d.Legacy.Create with the same obj and options that were just passed to Storage.Create, concurrently with the returned object being used by the caller. Storage Create/Update implementations can mutate the object (e.g. set ResourceVersion, UID, generated name), so the legacy write races with those mutations (data race detected by -race) and may write different content than what was stored in unified storage.

title: Update reuses objInfo for legacy after storage consumed it
body: objInfo is an UpdatedObjectInfo whose UpdatedObject is typically called by Storage.Update, and the same objInfo is then passed to the async legacy Update. The legacy update will run the transform again against the current stored state of legacy (or a different old object), and it may race with the storage call that is still using objInfo. The previous implementation carefully wrapped the storage result for the legacy write; that was removed, so legacy may get a different object than what was written to unified storage.

title: Update goroutine leaks the context cancel on a path that never calls cancel promptly
body: In Update, the context.WithTimeoutCause is created in the goroutine, but cancel is deferred after the timer is set and it is fine; however the cancel is only called after Legacy.Update returns. The ctx variable is shadowed correctly, but the timeout starts before startLegacy is measured; minor, though combined with the request ctx cancellation the goroutine has no independent lifetime control.

title: Delete storage duration metric records the object name as the kind label
body: In Delete, recordStorageDuration is called with `name` in the kind position instead of options.Kind, so the metric label cardinality explodes per object name and the kind dimension is wrong, unlike every other method.

title: Update error path records a legacy metric for a storage failure
body: When Storage.Update fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recordStorageDuration, so storage failures are counted as legacy errors and storage error metrics are never incremented for update.

title: DeleteCollection async legacy duration is recorded with the storage metric
body: The legacy DeleteCollection goroutine records its outcome with recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration, corrupting storage vs legacy metrics.

title: Delete attaches the parent logger instead of the scoped log
body: ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) in Delete discards the log with name/kind/method values that was just built, so downstream logs lose context. Inconsistent with other methods.

title: options.Kind dereferenced for nil-safe access and CreateOptions has no Kind field used reliably
body: log uses options.Kind on *metav1.CreateOptions etc.; these option types' Kind is set only via TypeMeta and is often empty, so the logs/metrics label is frequently blank. Mode 3 metrics labels depend on this.

title: Mode 3 tests do not verify the asynchronous legacy write happens
body: The tests set up legacy mock expectations but never assert they were called, and the goroutine can race with test teardown. Failures in the legacy write (the core of mode 3 behavior) are untested; the Update failure test has no legacy expectation at all.

title: New mode 3 integration cases are not tied to legacy consistency checks
body: The new mode 3 cases run the same doPlaylistTests, which asserts only unified-storage results; since legacy writes are asynchronous and not awaited, the tests cannot detect the legacy write being lost, so the added coverage does not validate the feature.

title: Cache miss is re-checked only by the fast path, so concurrent callers all rebuild the manifest
body: The read lock is released at line 43 and the write lock is taken at line 48 without re-checking `entryPointAssetsCache`. When the cache is empty or in dev mode, every goroutine that misses the cache at the same moment proceeds to call readWebAssetsFromFile (or the CDN path) and rebuilds the manifest, one after another. The usual fix is to re-read the cache after acquiring the write lock and return early if it is already populated. This only matters at startup or in dev mode, so the impact is limited to redundant file reads and parsing.

title: Write lock is held across file and network I/O, blocking all readers
body: The exclusive lock taken at line 48 is held for the whole rebuild, including the HTTP request in readWebAssetsFromCDN and the file read. Every concurrent GetWebAssets call, including ones that would otherwise hit the cached fast path, blocks on RLock until the rebuild finishes. A slow or hung CDN request, bounded only by the context, can stall all page renders. Consider doing the load outside the lock and only publishing the result under the lock.

title: No regression test for the data race fix
body: The PR fixes an unsynchronized read of the package-level `entryPointAssetsCache`, but adds no test that exercises GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines. A test run under `go test -race` that calls GetWebAssets concurrently (with the cache populated and in dev mode) would catch a regression of this fix. Without one, the lock discipline could be broken again silently.

title: No double-check after acquiring the write lock, so cold-start loads repeat
body: After the RLock fast path misses, the code takes the write lock but does not re-check entryPointAssetsCache. If N requests arrive while the cache is nil (or in Dev mode on every call), each one that acquires the write lock in turn re-reads the manifest from disk or re-fetches it from the CDN, even though the first call has already populated the cache. The fix is to re-read entryPointAssetsCache under the write lock and return early when it is non-nil and cfg.Env != setting.Dev.

title: Write lock is held across file I/O and the CDN HTTP request
body: The exclusive lock is held for the whole duration of readWebAssetsFromCDN (an HTTP GET with only the caller's ctx as a bound) and readWebAssetsFromFile. Until that finishes, every other GetWebAssets caller blocks on RLock, including ones that would otherwise have hit the fast path. A slow or hung CDN therefore stalls all requests that need the page assets. In Dev mode, every request takes the exclusive lock and serializes on disk and network reads. Consider doing the load outside the lock and publishing the result under a short write lock, or at least documenting this trade-off.

title: Write lock is held across CDN and file I/O, blocking all readers
body: The write lock is acquired at line 48 and held via defer for the whole rebuild, including `readWebAssetsFromCDN`, which performs an HTTP request bounded only by the caller's context. While a cache miss or dev-mode reload is in progress, every concurrent `GetWebAssets` call blocks on `RLock` at line 41, even though a valid cached value may exist. Before this change, readers never blocked. A slow or hung CDN can therefore stall all page renders that go through this function.

title: No double-check after acquiring the write lock
body: After the RLock check at lines 41-47 fails, the goroutine takes the write lock without re-reading `entryPointAssetsCache`. Every goroutine that observed a nil cache at the same time will repeat the full manifest load and CDN fetch, and each will overwrite the global in turn. The lock prevents a data race, but it does not prevent this duplicated work or the last-writer-wins churn on a cold start.

title: No test covers the concurrent access this change is meant to fix
body: The PR fixes a data race on the package-level cache, but it adds no test that exercises `GetWebAssets` from multiple goroutines. Without a `-race` test, nothing guards against regressions. A test that runs concurrent calls in both dev and non-dev modes would verify the fix.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false, so the feature flag check is dead logic
body: enableSqlExpressions computes `enabled := !IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions)`, then returns false on both branches of `if enabled`. The result is that SQL expressions are unconditionally rejected regardless of the flag. The function reads as if it honours the flag but it does not, so anyone who later re-enables the feature will be confused, and the flag check is misleading. If the intent is a hard disable, the function and the flag lookup should be removed and the SQL case should return the error directly. If the intent is to gate on the flag, the negation and the second `return false` are wrong.

title: Stub DB silently replaces the SQL engine and its errors are not tied to the gate
body: DB, TablesList, RunCommands and QueryFramesInto are now stubs returning 'not implemented'. TablesList in parser.go and SQLCommand.Execute depend on these. The gate lives only in reader.go's ReadQuery. Other entry points such as UnmarshalSQLCommand and NewSQLCommand reach sql.TablesList without the gate, so they fail with an opaque 'error serializing sql' or 'not implemented' rather than the explicit disabled message. The stub also has an unused receiver and parameter names in TablesList. Consider making the disable explicit at NewSQLCommand/Execute too, so every path reports the same reason.

title: Module checksums moved between go.sum and go.work.sum without a clear reason
body: The diff removes checksum lines for apache/thrift, klauspost/asmfmt, JohnCGriffin/overflow and others from go.sum and adds them to go.work.sum. Those modules are removed from go.mod as indirect dependencies, so the moves are inconsistent with the stated change. Running `go mod tidy` and `go work sync` should be verified so the checksum files match the module graph and the build is reproducible.

title: enableSqlExpressions ignores the feature flag and always returns false
body: The function computes `enabled` from the feature flag but then returns `false` on both branches, so the flag has no effect. Enabling `FlagSqlExpressions` cannot re-enable SQL expressions. This is probably intended as a hard kill switch, but the code reads as if the flag is honored and is misleading. Replace it with an explicit disabled path (or a comment stating the feature is unconditionally off) and remove the dead flag lookup. The `if enabled` check at line 130 also becomes dead logic.

title: Error message says 'not implemented' for a feature that is disabled
body: The user-facing error `sqlExpressions is not implemented` is misleading: SQL expressions are implemented but disabled for security reasons. Users and support staff will be confused about why a previously working query now fails. The message should say the feature is disabled.

title: Stubbed DB methods break existing SQL command and parser behavior without updated tests
body: All DB methods now return 'not implemented', so `sql.TablesList` always errors, and `NewSQLCommand`, `SQLCommand.Execute`, and the SQL parsing tests that depend on table extraction will fail. The PR adds no tests for the disabled path, and it does not update or remove the existing SQL tests. Either remove or skip those tests explicitly, or add tests that assert the disabled behavior.

title: Unused stub DB path remains reachable from SQLCommand execution
body: `UnmarshalSQLCommand` and `Execute` construct commands directly through `sql.NewInMemoryDB()` without going through the reader gate in `reader.go`. The gate is therefore the only protection, and a future caller that uses `NewSQLCommand` directly would bypass the disable check. Put the disable check in `NewSQLCommand` or in the stub layer so it cannot be bypassed.

title: Variable name `duckDB` no longer refers to DuckDB
body: After the change `duckDB` holds the stub `*DB`, which has no DuckDB backing. The name is misleading to future readers, and the `TablesList` comment still implies DuckDB-based parsing. Rename the variable and update the comment.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false, so the feature flag has no effect
body: The function computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(...)`, returns false if enabled, and then returns false unconditionally. The result is that SQL expressions are disabled regardless of the flag. The logic is confusing and suggests a half-finished edit. If the intent is a hard kill switch, the function should simply return false with a comment saying so, and the feature-flag lookup should be removed. As written, a maintainer reading the flag check would believe the flag gates the feature.

title: The SQL gate is only in the reader; NewSQLCommand and UnmarshalSQLCommand have no gate
body: The disable check lives only in ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery. `UnmarshalSQLCommand` in sql_command.go calls `NewSQLCommand` directly and never checks the gate. Any other caller that builds an SQL command bypasses the disable. It currently fails only because the stubbed `sql.TablesList` always returns an error. That is incidental, not a guard, so a future change to the DB stub would reopen the vulnerability. The check should be enforced in `NewSQLCommand` or at the execution boundary.

title: Error message says 'not implemented' for a deliberate security disable
body: Users who enable sqlExpressions will get 'sqlExpressions is not implemented', which misstates the situation. The message should say the feature is disabled for security reasons and point to the advisory. Operators trying to diagnose it will be misled.

title: Stub DB makes every SQL expression fail, including legitimate ones
body: TablesList, RunCommands and QueryFramesInto all return 'not implemented'. Because `sql.TablesList` in parser.go depends on RunCommands, `NewSQLCommand` now fails for every query. The SQL expression type is therefore completely non-functional, not just locked down. This is a deliberate hotfix, but nothing in the PR documents that the feature is gutted, and the stubbed DB type is named as if it were a real in-memory database. This should be an explicit, documented temporary state.

title: Quote-escaping is still used to build SQL via fmt.Sprintf
body: TablesList still interpolates user SQL into a string with fmt.Sprintf after only doubling single quotes. This is the injection-prone pattern that the RCE/LFI issue is about. It is currently unreachable because RunCommands is stubbed, but it will be dangerous as soon as a real engine is reconnected. Keeping this code path unchanged in a security fix is risky.

title: tablesFromAST indexes ast[0] without checking length
body: `flatten.Flatten(ast[0], ...)` panics if the slice is empty, for example if the JSON decodes to `[]`. The code is unreachable today, but the panic would become reachable as soon as the stub is replaced.

title: No tests added for the disabled SQL path
body: The PR changes the reader's behaviour for QueryTypeSQL and removes a dependency, but adds no test asserting that SQL expression queries are rejected. A regression test is needed so that the gate cannot be silently removed, and a test for UnmarshalSQLCommand to confirm the bypass is closed.

title: Removing the BuildIndex-wide lock allows duplicate concurrent builds of the same key
body: BuildIndex previously held b.cacheMu for the whole build, serializing builds. Now the lock is only taken around the final map write. Two callers that miss the cache for the same NamespacedResource (for example a Search request via getOrCreateIndex racing with a watch event handled by handleEvent, or init racing with either) will both run the full build. For file-backed indexes (size > FileThreshold), bleve.New on the same directory will fail for the second caller, or the two indexes will each be built and one silently overwrites the other in b.cache, leaking an open bleve index. The fix needs per-key singleflight or a check-again under lock before building, not just finer locking around the cache write.

title: TotalDocs iterates the cache map without holding cacheMu
body: TotalDocs ranges over b.cache with no lock, while BuildIndex now writes to b.cache under cacheMu. Concurrent map read and write is a data race and can crash the process with 'concurrent map iteration and map write'. TotalDocs is called from searchSupport.init for logging. The read should take cacheMu.RLock().

title: init goroutines write shared variables without synchronization
body: Inside group.Go, the closure does `totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(...)`. Both `totalBatchesIndexed` and the outer `err` are shared across the errgroup goroutines, so this is a data race on each increment and assignment. A failing build can also overwrite another goroutine's error, so group.Wait may return the wrong error. Use a local err variable inside the closure and an atomic counter.

title: Partially initialized resources leak when Init fails in NewResourceServer
body: If s.Init returns an error, NewResourceServer returns nil without calling s.cancel() or Stop. The background context created earlier, and any watcher goroutines already started by initWatcher or search init, are never torn down.
