A key missing from the user's locale then resolves to 'translation missing' there, while the same key falls back correctly in a web process that happened to serve a request first. Because translate() caches zero-argument results per locale (lines 71-76) and only clears that cache on reload!, the 'translation missing' string can stay cached for the life of that process. Fallback targets should be loaded on demand by translate(), not only in the controller filter.

title: Every translation now reads SiteSetting.default_locale through the fallback backend
body: FallbackLocaleList#[] calls SiteSetting.default_locale and allocates a new array each time it is invoked. The i18n Fallbacks backend calls I18n.fallbacks[locale] on each I18n.translate call, not only on a miss. Calls with arguments (count:, interpolation) bypass the LRU cache in translate_accelerator.rb, so they hit this path on every invocation, including in tight render loops. Site setting access is also DB-backed on a cache miss, so translation now depends on the settings store being readable, including during boot, migrations, or asset precompilation, where it previously was not needed. The default locale should be read once per request or cached, not recomputed on every lookup.

title: Locale fallback behaviour change is shipped without any specs
body: This PR replaces Rails' configured i18n fallbacks with a custom FallbackLocaleList (fallback order, on-demand loading via ensure_loaded!), removes config.i18n.fallbacks from three environment files, moves the pluralization include, and adds a new ensure_loaded! path to the I18n accelerator. None of this is covered by a spec. There is no test that a missing key in a user's locale falls back to the site default and then to :en, that fallback targets are loaded, or that the removed environment settings are not needed. Regressions in i18n fallback would only show up in production.

title: Translation cache key ignores the fallback chain, which depends on default_locale
body: The LRU cache key is built from key, config.locale and the backend object_id only. Results for zero-argument translations now depend on the fallback chain, which includes SiteSetting.default_locale. If the site's default locale is changed at runtime, cached results that were resolved through the old fallback chain are still returned for that process until it restarts or I18n.reload! is called. Nothing in this diff invalidates the cache on a default_locale change, so the cache can serve stale fallback text after an admin change.

title: Fallback locales are only loaded during web requests, not for background or console lookups
body: translate() only calls load_locale(config.locale). The fallback chain (default locale and :en) is loaded only by ApplicationController#set_locale via I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!. Outside a web request (background jobs such as Sidekiq email delivery, rake tasks, the console, or a process that has not served a request yet), I18n.locale is e.g. :fr, so only :fr translations are loaded. Fallbacks#translate then asks the Simple backend for :en or default-locale strings that were never loaded, and keys missing from the non-English locale come back as 'translation missing' instead of the English text. That is the exact case this feature is meant to fix. The fallback chain should be loaded from the translate path (for example by loading I18n.fallbacks[config.locale] here), not only from the controller filter.

title: LRU translation cache key ignores the fallback chain it now depends on
body: With fallbacks enabled, the value returned for (key, locale) depends on the fallback chain, which depends on SiteSetting.default_locale and on which fallback locales happen to be loaded at lookup time. The cache key is only key + config.locale + backend object_id, and nothing in this change invalidates entries when default_locale changes or when a fallback locale is loaded later. The first computed value, including a 'translation missing' string that is frozen and cached at line 75, is then served until LRU eviction (300 entries) or reload!.

title: Every I18n lookup now reads SiteSetting and allocates a fallback array
body: Fallbacks#translate, included into the backend at line 9, calls I18n.fallbacks[locale] on every lookup that reaches the backend. That means this method runs for every translation, including calls with interpolation arguments that bypass the LRU cache (translate_accelerator.rb line 69). Each call reads SiteSetting.default_locale and builds and uniq/compacts a new array. I18n previously had no dependency on SiteSetting, so any I18n.t during boot or in tasks where settings are not yet readable (asset precompile, migrations) can now trigger a SiteSetting load and hit the database. Memoizing the chain per (locale, default_locale) would remove both costs.

title: No specs cover the new fallback behavior or the load path
body: This change affects global translation behavior: a new fallback chain, the fallback backend module included globally, pluralization moved from pluralization.rb into this file, config.i18n.fallbacks removed from three environment files, and a new ensure_loaded! path in set_locale and the accelerator. The PR adds no specs. Nothing verifies that a key missing in a non-English locale resolves through the site default and then :en, that the fallback works when the fallback locale has not been loaded (the gap described in translate_accelerator.rb line 68), or that pluralization still works after the include was moved. A unit test for FallbackLocaleList#[] and a request spec exercising set_locale with a missing key would catch these regressions.

title: Fallback locales are only loaded by the controller filter, not by I18n.t
body: The translate override loads only `config.locale` (`load_locale(config.locale)`). The fallback chain's other locales (the site default and :en) are loaded only by `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!`, which is called from `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Any translation made under `I18n.with_locale` outside a web request (Sidekiq jobs, mailers rendered in jobs, rake tasks) therefore has no guarantee that the fallback yml files are loaded. If the key is missing in the requested locale, the lookup falls back to a locale whose translations were never loaded and returns a 'translation missing' string. The fallback behavior depends on which entry point ran first, which is fragile.

title: Loading fallback locales does not invalidate the LRU translation cache
body: The cache at line 71 is keyed only on key, locale, and backend object_id, and is cleared only in `reload!`. Results now depend on which fallback locales are loaded and on `SiteSetting.default_locale`, but neither is in the key. If a lookup runs before the fallback locale (e.g. :en) has been loaded, the 'translation missing' result is frozen into `@cache`. When `ensure_loaded!` later loads :en, that stale entry is still served for that locale until the process restarts. The same staleness applies when an admin changes `default_locale`, since cached fallback output for other locales is not recomputed.

title: Fallback chain is rebuilt and SiteSetting is read on every backend lookup
body: Fallbacks#translate in the i18n gem calls `I18n.fallbacks[locale]` on every backend translate, including the interpolated translations that bypass the LRU cache (`args.length > 0`). Each call reads `SiteSetting.default_locale`, calls `to_sym`, and allocates a new array with `uniq.compact`. This is a small per-translation cost on a hot path. Computing the chain once per locale, or caching it in the hash, would avoid it.

title: No specs for the new fallback chain, ensure_loaded!, or the set_locale change
body: This PR changes locale resolution for the whole application: it adds a custom fallback order (user locale, site default, :en), a new `ensure_loaded!` path in the I18n accelerator, a new call in `set_locale`, and it removes `config.i18n.fallbacks` from three environment files. None of this is covered by a spec. Nothing checks that a missing key falls back in the expected order, that fallback locales get loaded, or that the behavior holds in production and profile environments after the config removal. Given the cache and loading issues above, targeted specs are needed before merge.

title: Denial cache key concatenates name and folder with '_' and can collide
body: userPermDenialCacheKey joins userUID, action, name and parent with unescaped '_' separators. Grafana resource UIDs can contain underscores (the tests themselves use UIDs like 'some_dashboard' and 'some_folder_parent'). Dashboard 'a_b' in folder 'c' and dashboard 'a' in folder 'b_c' both produce the key '...perm_<uid>_<action>_a_b_c'. Check consults the denial cache before any permission lookup and returns deny on a hit (service.go lines 116-121), so a denial recorded for one resource causes a false deny for the other for up to the 30s TTL, even when the user has access to it. The key needs an unambiguous encoding (a delimiter that cannot appear in UIDs, or a hash of a structured tuple).

title: Cached denial is checked first and never invalidated, so it can keep blocking a just-created resource
body: The denial cache is consulted before cached or DB permissions and is only cleared by TTL (30s). The PR's fix for newly created resources is the DB fallback on a permission-cache miss, but that fallback is bypassed whenever the same (user, action, name, folder) was denied within the last 30s. A plausible sequence: a client checks access to a dashboard UID before it exists (authz runs before the storage lookup), gets Allowed=false, and that denial is written at lines 153-155. After the dashboard is created and the creator's permission is written, the creator's check for the same name/folder still returns false until the entry expires. The same staleness applies to any later grant of access. Denials should not short-circuit fresher permission data, or they should be invalidated on create/permission changes.

title: DB fallback re-reads permissions but still uses the cached folder tree
body: When the permission cache misses, Check calls getIdentityPermissions and then checkPermission, which reaches checkInheritedPermissions and buildFolderTree (called at line 590). buildFolderTree returns the folderCache entry (TTL 30s) if present (this line). A subfolder created after the tree was cached is absent from that tree, so Ancestors() does not walk through it and grants inherited from its parent folder are not found. Dashboards in the new subfolder are then denied for up to 30s, even though this fallback was added precisely so newly created resources are picked up. The fallback only refreshes the permission map, not the folder data it depends on.

title: Every denied check missing the permission cache now queries the DB
body: Before this change, a denied check with a warm permission cache returned without touching the DB, since getUserPermissions read permCache first. Now, when the cached map does not contain the resource, Check always falls through to getIdentityPermissions (line 139), which runs the full permissionStore.GetUserPermissions query for the action. The 30s denial cache only suppresses repeats for the same (name, folder). Each distinct resource a user is denied on, such as a client probing many UIDs or a user hitting resources they cannot access, therefore produces a full permission query, and sequential checks are not coalesced by singleflight. DB load now scales with the number of distinct denied resources. The fallback should be rate-limited or coalesced per user/action, or the cost should be accepted explicitly.

title: Denial-precedence test sets the permission cache to false, so it does not exercise the denial cache
body: The test 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' says the permission cache entry allows access 'to prove this is not checked', but the value is false, so the cached permission path also denies. The DB fallback (fakeStore with no userPermissions) also returns nothing, so the request is denied even if the permDenialCache lookup in Check were removed. The assertion assert.False therefore passes without the new code path. Setting the permission cache value to true would make the test fail unless the denial entry takes precedence, which is what the test is meant to guard.

title: Denial cache short-circuits before the DB refresh, so a fresh grant is ignored for up to 30s
body: Check() returns a cached deny as soon as the denial key is present, before it tries the cached permissions or re-queries the DB. The denial entry is written from a fresh DB result (line 154) but is never invalidated when permissions are granted. Sequence: user U checks dashboard X and is denied (denial entry stored, 30s TTL); U is then granted access to X (or X is created by U and U gets access); U checks X again within 30s. The denial hit returns Allowed=false, so the new 'requery DB when the resource is not in cached permissions' fallback never runs. That is exactly the 'creator cannot access what they just created' symptom this PR is meant to fix, and the denial cache re-introduces a stale-deny window that the fallback removed. The same applies to name-less checks (create flows, where the result only depends on whether any permission exists for the action). No test covers denial-then-grant.

title: "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" passes even if the denial cache is ignored
body: The test is meant to prove that the denial cache short-circuits the check. But the permCache entry it sets is {"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}, a deny, so the cached-permission path also denies. The fallback then reads the DB, where setupService's fakeStore has no permissions, so it denies too. Removing the permDenialCache lookup in Check() leaves this test green. The comment on line 981 ('Allow access ... to prove this is not checked') contradicts the value set. There is also no test that a denial is written after a DB deny and then bypassed once the permission exists.

title: Denial cache key is ambiguous because '_' separates fields that can contain '_'
body: userPermDenialCacheKey joins namespace, user UID, action, name and parent with '_', and Grafana UIDs and names often contain underscores. Different tuples collide: name "a_b" with parent "c" and name "a" with parent "b_c" both produce "...perm_<uid>_<action>_a_b_c". If the first is denied and cached, the second (which the user may be allowed) is wrongly denied for the 30s TTL. The key needs an unambiguous encoding (length prefix, escaping or a hash).

title: Every DB denial is cached under a request-controlled key with no size bound
body: The denial key is built from the request's name and parent folder, and an entry is written for every denied request. The local cache used here (authlib cache.NewLocalCache) has no size cap in its configuration. A user can issue requests with many distinct names (including nonexistent ones) and fill the cache with entries for 30s each. Denial entries also add a write per denied request on top of the DB query. A bounded cache or a cap on what is cached would limit this.

title: Failed user lookup is performed twice per request in Check and List
body: getCachedIdentityPermissions calls GetUserIdentifiers, and its error is then ignored. The fallback getIdentityPermissions path calls GetUserIdentifiers again. Failed lookups are not cached, so for an unknown or deleted user every request issues two identical DB queries (Check at line 123 then line 139; List at lines 180 and 186). The identifier lookup should be done once and reused.

title: Remote/cloud client still keeps the 30s authlib client cache, so the stale-result symptom remains there
body: The PR removes the authlib client cache only for the in-proc client (ProvideAuthZClient). newRemoteRBACClient still wraps the client in a 30s LocalCache, which caches Check results on the client side. A creator using a remote or standalone authz server will therefore still see stale results for a newly created resource for up to 30s, regardless of the server-side fallback. The PR description only mentions in-proc, so either this is intentional and should be documented, or the remote path is not fixed.

title: Recorded denials pin a deny for 30s, bypassing the new requery and surviving grants
body: Check consults permDenialCache before anything else and returns Allowed=false on a hit, without consulting the permission cache or the DB. Entries are written whenever a DB-backed check denies (line 154) and are removed only by the 30s TTL; nothing clears them when a grant is written or a resource is created. The requery added by this PR only runs on a permission-cache miss, so a denial recorded before the creator's permission was visible (for example a GET racing the permission write, or any read of the UID before it existed) keeps returning denied for up to 30 seconds. That is the exact symptom the PR says it fixes, so the fix is incomplete for that window.

title: Denial cache key is ambiguous: different resources can collide
body: userPermDenialCacheKey joins name and parent folder with '_' without escaping. Grafana UIDs can contain underscores, so the tuple is ambiguous: dashboard 'a_b' in folder 'c' and dashboard 'a' in folder 'b_c' both produce '...perm_<uid>_<action>_a_b_c'. A denial recorded for one resource then makes Check return denied for the other for 30s without consulting permissions. The result is false denials of legitimate access for the feature this PR targets. Encode the tuple unambiguously (length-prefixed fields, a JSON array, or a hash of the tuple).

title: Requery on permission-cache miss still reads a stale folder tree
body: The requery only refreshes the permission set. checkInheritedPermissions (line 590) calls buildFolderTree, which returns the folderCache entry for up to 30s with no bypass. A folder created in that window is missing from the tree, so its ancestors cannot be resolved and a user whose access is inherited from an ancestor folder is denied for resources inside it. That denial is then cached (line 154). The requery therefore does not cover inherited access to newly created folders, and no test covers this case because the folder tests seed a complete tree.

title: Every unmatched name now triggers an uncached permissions query
body: On a permission-cache miss for a name, which is the normal case for any resource the user cannot access, Check always runs the uncached GetUserPermissions query. Before this PR those denials were answered from the cached permission map with no DB access. The denial cache is keyed by exact (action, name, folder), so a caller checking many distinct names the user cannot access costs one DB permissions query per name per 30s. The DB cost of this path should be considered or documented.

title: Explicit denial-cache test passes without the denial cache
body: The test is meant to show the denial entry short-circuits the check, but it cannot fail if that logic is removed. The permission cache entry for dash1 is set to false (line 982), so checkPermission returns false, and the DB fallback also denies because setupService's fakeStore has no userPermissions. The result is false with or without permDenialCache. The comment 'Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked' contradicts the value set. Set the cached permission for dash1 to true so only the denial entry produces the deny, and/or assert the store was not called. No test also checks that a DB-confirmed denial actually populates permDenialCache.

title: List has no requery path, so newly created items stay out of results for up to 30s
body: List answers from the 30s permission-map entry on a hit and never requeries, because it cannot tell which resources are missing from the cached set. Dashboards and folders created by the user therefore stay absent from list results for up to 30 seconds, the same class of problem this PR claims to fix for Check. The PR does not mention or test this limitation.

title: Delete (and Pause) disappear from the alert list menu even though permissions allow them
body: The Delete item is rendered only when `canDelete && rulerRule`. The list view no longer passes `rulerRule` (GrafanaRuleListItem renders RuleActionsButtons with only `promRule`), so the item is never shown, even though `canDelete` now correctly comes from the promRule-based ability. Users with AlertingRuleDelete lose Delete from the list, which the previous GrafanaRuleLoader path offered. The same gating applies to Pause at line 123 (`MenuItemPauseRule rule={rulerRule}` requires a ruler rule), so Pause is also unreachable while `canPause` is true. Either wire delete/pause to the identifier-based path or stop computing these abilities for the list view; as written, the abilities and the rendered menu disagree.

title: Silence item is shown in the list view but clicking it does nothing
body: `canSilence` is now true in the list view via the promRule-based ability, so the 'Silence notifications' item renders and calls `handleSilence`. That handler sets `showSilenceDrawer` in RuleActionsButtons.V2.tsx, but the drawer is only mounted when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true (see RuleActionsButtons.V2.tsx line 104). In the list view `rule` is undefined, so the drawer never renders and the click is a silent no-op. Either migrate SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer to accept the Grafana prom rule, or hide the item when no ruler rule is present.

title: Silence drawer is gated on the ruler rule, which is always undefined in the list view
body: The condition `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) && showSilenceDrawer` requires the ruler DTO. The list view intentionally passes only `promRule`, so `rule` is undefined and the drawer (which also takes `rulerRule`) can never open. Combined with the new silence ability in AlertRuleMenu, this exposes a control that visibly does nothing.

title: Federated-group check was dropped, so federated rules become editable through useAllAlertRuleAbilities
body: Previously useAllAlertRuleAbilities computed `isFederated` from `isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`. The refactor routes that hook through useAllRulerRuleAbilities(rule.rulerRule, groupIdentifier), which has no access to the group's `source_tenants`, and hard-codes `const isFederated = false` (TODO). useAllAlertRuleAbilities is still exported and used by callers (it is only marked deprecated), so for federated rule groups Update/Delete/Pause/Restore/DeletePermanently are now treated as mutable whenever the user has permission. This is a regression of existing behavior for those callers. The federation information should be passed through the new signature rather than removed.

title: Test asserts the 4-item list menu, locking in the missing Delete/Pause actions, and does not exercise the actions
body: The test grants AlertingRuleDelete and expects exactly four menu items (silence, copy link, duplicate, export), so it codifies the omission of Delete (and Pause) in the list view. The comment at line 191 says 'all 4 menu actions should be available' while the user has delete permission, which is misleading. No test verifies that clicking Silence opens the drawer, that Delete is reachable, or that Pause works from the list. The unused `ui.menuItems.delete` helper suggests the delete case was meant to be tested. Tests should reflect the intended list-view action set and cover the click behavior.

title: GrafanaRuleListItem rendered in a mapped list without a key
body: The grafana branch previously passed `key={key}` (the computed rule key). The refactor to `<GrafanaRuleListItem rule={rule} ... />` drops the key while the other branches still use it. React will warn about missing keys and fall back to index identity, and component-local state (silence drawer, clone redirect in RuleActionsButtons) is then keyed by position rather than by rule. Pass `key={key}` to restore consistent identity.

title: Link to the rule view no longer carries returnTo
body: The removed GrafanaRuleLoader built the view href with `createRelativeUrl(..., { returnTo })` using `createReturnTo()`. The new component builds `/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view` without returnTo, so rule-view navigation back to the list (which relies on returnTo, e.g. via useReturnToPrevious) is lost. This is an unmentioned behavior change; restore the returnTo parameter or document its removal.

title: Doc comment still says the loader reads from the Ruler endpoint
body: The doc comment says 'Loads an evaluation group from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints', but after this change the component only queries the Prometheus endpoint (the ruler query was removed). Line 19 in the `expectedRulesCount` prop docs similarly refers to the ruler response, which is no longer consulted. Update the comments to match the implementation.

title: Every list row now computes both ruler and Grafana ability sets, twice
body: AlertRuleMenu calls useRulerRuleAbilities (with rulerRule undefined in the list view) and useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities, and RuleActionsButtons.V2 separately calls useRulerRuleAbility and useGrafanaPromRuleAbility. Each of these runs the full useAll*RuleAbilities computation, including folder lookups and the silence-status query, so each rule row runs the ability logic about four times, even though the ruler-based results are always neutral in the list view. The list page's own comment notes this hook is already called for ~80 rules, so the duplication scales poorly. Compute the abilities once per row or skip the ruler path when rulerRule is absent.

title: Immutability of list-view rules now depends on a provenance field the Prometheus endpoint must return
body: `provenance` was added to GrafanaPromRuleDTOBase, and isProvisionedPromRule uses it to disable Update/Delete/Pause for provisioned rules in the list view (previously read from the ruler). If the Prometheus-compatible groups endpoint does not populate `provenance`, provisioned rules will appear editable in the list and editing them will fail server-side. This PR does not include the backend change, so the dependency should be confirmed and called out.

title: Delete (and Pause) never render in the list view even though their abilities are computed from promRule
body: canDelete is now computed from the Grafana promRule abilities, but the Delete item is rendered only under `canDelete && rulerRule`. The list view no longer passes rulerRule (GrafanaRuleListItem passes only promRule), so Delete never appears in the list-view menu. Pause has the same gating on line 123 (`rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`), so Pause also disappears. Before this PR both were available in the list view, and the new promRule-based ability code for them is effectively dead. The GrafanaGroupLoader test asserts exactly 4 menu items (silence, copy link, duplicate, export), which locks in the missing Delete/Pause instead of catching the regression.

title: Silence notifications menu item is a no-op in the list view
body: In the list view AlertRuleMenu now shows 'Silence notifications' when the Grafana promRule silence ability is true, and its handler `handleSilence` sets showSilenceDrawer=true. But the drawer is rendered only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true, and `rule` (the ruler DTO) is always undefined in the list view after this PR. Clicking Silence therefore sets state and nothing appears. No test clicks this item, so the gap is not caught.

title: GrafanaRuleListItem rendered in a list without a key
body: The grafana branch of the switch now renders <GrafanaRuleListItem> without a key prop, while the datasource and unknown branches still use key={key}. React emits 'unique key' warnings for this list. The component comment explicitly says the keys exist to prevent duplicates, so the removal looks accidental. Since rules are append-only today the visible impact is small, but row-level state is then keyed by index.

title: Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable
body: useAllAlertRuleAbilities previously derived isFederated from isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) (source_tenants). It now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes `const isFederated = false` with a TODO. Federated groups therefore lose the immutability guard, so Update/Delete/Pause/DeletePermanently can be enabled for them. The isFederatedRuleGroup import was also dropped. This affects every caller of useAlertRuleAbility/useAlertRuleAbilities, not only the list view.

title: Duplicate is offered for data-source rules via the Grafana-side fallback, bypassing ruler and datasource permission checks
body: For non-Grafana rules AlertRuleMenu passes skipToken to useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities. With an undefined rule, useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities sets Duplicate to [AlwaysSupported, hasPermission(AlertingRuleCreate)] (useAbilities.ts line 318). canDuplicate ORs this with the ruler result, so Duplicate is shown for datasource-managed rules whenever the user holds the Grafana-wide create permission. This bypasses the ruler-availability check (duplicateSupported = isRulerAvailable) and the isPluginProvided check, and ignores the datasource's own write permission (AlertingRuleExternalWrite). The other OR'd actions (Edit, Delete, Silence, Export, Pause) are false on this path, so Duplicate is the only leak.

title: Rule view link drops the returnTo parameter
body: The previous GrafanaRuleLoader built the view href with `createRelativeUrl(..., { returnTo })` using createReturnTo(). The new GrafanaRuleListItem silently drops returnTo, so navigating from the list to the rule view and back no longer returns to the list context. This is unrelated to removing the ruler and appears accidental.

title: Every list row now evaluates both ruler and Grafana ability hooks, duplicating folder and silence-config subscriptions
body: AlertRuleMenu (and RuleActionsButtons.V2 the same way) now calls useRulerRuleAbilities and useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities for each row. Each full evaluation calls useFolder, the Grafana alerting-config RTK query, and folder permission lookups. For Grafana rows the ruler evaluation runs with an undefined rule and contributes nothing useful, so each row ends up with about four full ability evaluations. The hook comment already warns about ~80 rows on the list page. Only the applicable hook should be invoked per row.

title: Doc comments still describe the removed ruler request
body: The component docstring says it loads 'from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints', and the expectedRulesCount prop doc (line 19) says the ruler response may contain a different number of rules. After this change the component uses only the Prometheus endpoint, so both comments are wrong.

title: Pause and Delete disappear from the alert list menu
body: In the list view `rulerRule` is now always undefined, but the Pause item is gated on `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` here and the Delete item is gated on `rulerRule` at line 165. The new Grafana (promRule) abilities compute canPause/canDelete as allowed, yet the menu items are never rendered, so users lose pause and delete from the list view (they only remain on the details page). The regression is locked in by GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx line 207, which asserts exactly 4 menu items, and the `ui.menuItems.delete` helper defined in that test is never used. The menu gating needs to use the promRule path for these actions, or the abilities should not be advertised.

title: Delete item is gated on rulerRule, which is always absent in the list view
body: `{canDelete && rulerRule && (...)}` hides Delete whenever rulerRule is undefined. Since the list view no longer fetches ruler rules, Delete is never shown for Grafana rules there even when the user has delete permission on the folder and canDelete is true via the promRule abilities. Delete is silently removed from the list view.

title: Silence menu item in the list view does nothing
body: In the list view `rule` (the RulerRuleDTO) is undefined. AlertRuleMenu shows the Silence item based on the Grafana promRule silence ability, and clicking it calls handleSilence, which sets showSilenceDrawer to true. But the drawer is rendered only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true, which is false when rule is undefined. Also SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer is passed `rulerRule`, which doesn't exist here. The result is a visible, permitted Silence action that silently does nothing. The drawer needs to be driven from promRule, or the menu item must be hidden when no ruler rule is present.

title: GrafanaRuleListItem in the filter list has no key
body: The diff removed `key={key}` from the grafana branch of the rules.map in FilterView, while the datasource and default branches still set key. React will warn about missing keys for this list and can misreconcile rows when the list grows or items reorder, because row identity and component state are no longer tied to the stable key computed by getRuleKey.

title: Federated rule group check dropped from useAllAlertRuleAbilities
body: useAllAlertRuleAbilities previously computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`. It now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which only has the group identifier and hardcodes `const isFederated = false` here. Every caller of useAlertRuleAbility, useAlertRuleAbilities and useAllAlertRuleAbilities therefore loses the immutability check for federated groups, so Update, Delete, Pause and related actions can be enabled for federated rules that cannot be modified.

title: Duplicate becomes allowed for non-Grafana rules via skipToken
body: When promRule is not a Grafana rule, AlertRuleMenu and RuleActionsButtons pass skipToken, so useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities receives undefined. With no rule, MaybeSupported is AlwaysSupported and isPluginProvided is false, so Duplicate returns [true, user has AlertingRuleCreate]. AlertRuleMenu ORs this with the ruler-based ability (canDuplicate = ruler || grafana), so any data source rule in the list shows Duplicate for users with Grafana create permission. This bypasses the ruler-availability check and the plugin-provided check (the ruler path marks plugin-provided rules as unsupported). The grafana hook should return NotSupported when no rule is supplied.

title: Grafana rule links drop returnTo, breaking navigation back to the filtered list
body: The previous GrafanaRuleLoader built the view href with `{ returnTo }` from createReturnTo(). The new href is just createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`), so navigating to a Grafana rule and back no longer returns to the filtered list. Data source rule links still pass returnTo, so behavior is now inconsistent between rule types. This is an unmentioned navigation regression.

title: New Grafana promRule abilities hook has no direct test coverage
body: useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities, useGrafanaPromRuleAbility(ies) and the skipToken path contain new permission logic that determines what the user can do in the list view (silence, export, duplicate, pause, delete). RulesTable.test.tsx mocks the whole hook surface, and GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx only checks that a few menu entries exist. None of the tests exercise the real decisions, including the skipToken/non-Grafana case where Duplicate is incorrectly allowed, or the federated check that was dropped.

title: Comment says this is a copy of RuleActionsButtons.tsx, which is no longer true
body: The header comment describes this file as a copy of RuleActionsButtons.tsx with only the View button removed. After this change it takes promRule, uses useGrafanaPromRuleAbility and getEditableIdentifier, and has different identifier and provenance logic, so it has diverged. The stale comment will mislead maintainers about which file to change.

title: Shard sub-requests are interpolated a second time, with request.filters applied again
body: runShardSplitQuery() already calls applyTemplateVariables on every target (shardQuerySplitting.ts:52). Each shard sub-request is then passed to runSplitQuery(), which calls applyTemplateVariables again on the already-interpolated targets, and passes the same request.filters. The updated shard test confirms this: it now expects applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times for one target (1 from the shard entry point plus 4 sub-requests). The PR's goal is to interpolate once at the start, but the change repeats the work for every sub-request. Interpolation is not guaranteed idempotent: any value that contains a '$' token after the first pass gets substituted again, and ad-hoc filter handling that appends matchers would run once per sub-request. Fix by interpolating in only one place, for example by having the shard path call an internal runner that skips interpolation.

title: $__range check now runs on the interpolated expression, so $__range queries can be split
body: querySupportsSplitting() uses isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) to stop queries that use $__range from being split. The comment says $__range must reach the backend so it is computed over the split time range. With this PR, runSplitQuery interpolates each query with applyTemplateVariables (line 299) before partition() calls querySupportsSplitting. If request.scopedVars contains __range, the token is already replaced when the check runs, so the check no longer matches. The query is then split, and each chunk is computed over the whole range's value of $__range, so the merged result differs from the unsplit query. The new test only covers $__auto and $step, so nothing catches this. Fix by checking the range variable on the raw expression before interpolation, and update the comment, which becomes misleading.

title: Empty-expression filter now runs before interpolation, so variables resolving to empty are sent
body: The filter on query.expr used to run after interpolation, so a target whose expression was a variable resolving to an empty string was dropped. It now runs on the raw expression, before the map that interpolates it. A target such as '$query' whose value is empty is kept, and an empty expression is sent to Loki, which returns a parse error that shows up in the panel. Previously that target was silently skipped. Filter again after interpolation, or keep the previous order.

title: Test asserts the redundant interpolation count instead of guarding against it
body: The test now expects applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times for a single target. That count encodes the double interpolation of shard sub-requests (one call in runShardSplitQuery plus one per runSplitQuery sub-request), so the test locks in the behavior the PR should avoid. No test checks that each target is interpolated exactly once, and none checks that request.filters is applied once. Those assertions are needed once the double interpolation is fixed.

title: $__range queries are now split because the range check runs after interpolation
body: querySupportsSplitting() (line 287) exists so that queries containing $__range are not split, because $__range has to be evaluated against the full time range of the request. Before this change it saw the raw expression. Now runSplitQuery interpolates first (line 299) and partitions on the result (line 300). Any $__range that applyTemplateVariables resolves from request.scopedVars (Grafana supplies __range for panel queries) has already been replaced by a literal, so isQueryWithRangeVariable() returns false and the query is split. Each time chunk then runs with the full-range literal as its window and combineResponses merges the chunks, which gives wrong results for range aggregations. No test in the PR covers this exclusion.

title: Shard path no longer drops targets whose expression interpolates to empty
body: The old code interpolated first and then filtered on expr, so a target whose expression is a variable expanding to an empty string was dropped. The filter now runs on the raw expression (line 50), before the map on line 52, so such targets survive. They are passed to runSplitQuery as a subrequest, where the empty expr is filtered out (querySplitting.ts line 298). If nothing is left, runSplitGroupedQueries reads requests.filter(...)[0].partition (querySplitting.ts line 96) on an empty array and throws a TypeError. On the sharded path that throw happens inside the groupTargetsByQueryType().then() callback, so the rejection is unhandled and the observable never emits. For example, a panel with a metric query plus a query like $q, where $q is empty, would hang instead of returning the metric results.

title: Empty-expression filter runs before interpolation, so expressions that expand to empty are not dropped
body: The filter on line 298 checks query.expr before applyTemplateVariables runs on line 299. A target such as $query whose variable expands to an empty string passes the filter and goes to runQuery with an empty expr, which the backend will reject. If that target is the only one, the requests array ends up empty and runSplitGroupedQueries throws a TypeError at line 96. The empty check should run after the interpolation step, as the old shard code did.

title: Targets are interpolated twice on the sharded path
body: runShardSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts line 52) already calls applyTemplateVariables on every target. Each shard subrequest is then passed to runSplitQuery, which calls applyTemplateVariables again on the already expanded expression (line 299) with the same scopedVars and filters. Expansion is not idempotent: if a variable value contains a $name token that matches a template variable, it gets expanded a second time and the query changes. The test change shows the redundancy: 'Interpolates queries before running' went from toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1) to toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5), which codifies the repeated calls instead of removing them. Interpolation should happen once per request, with the sharded path skipping the second pass.

title: Ad-hoc filters are now passed on the sharded path and then applied again per subrequest
body: The removed call interpolateVariablesInQueries(request.targets, request.scopedVars) did not pass request.filters. The new applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters) does. The subRequest built at line 154 keeps the original request's filters, so runSplitQuery applies them again (querySplitting.ts line 299). If applyTemplateVariables applies ad-hoc filters to the expression, sharded queries get the filter matchers added twice, and that behavior change is not covered by any test, because the mock in shardQuerySplitting.test.ts ignores the third argument.

title: New interpolation test checks only runQuery arguments, not the splitting decisions
body: The added test asserts only the expr and step passed to runQuery. The point of the fix for #107530 is that interpolated values drive splitting: calculateStep reads query.step (used for metric partitioning) and querySupportsSplitting reads the expression. Nothing checks that a $step value changes the metric stepMs grouping, or that a $__range query is excluded from splitting after interpolation.

title: $__range guard now checks the interpolated expression and can be silently bypassed
body: querySupportsSplitting() is documented (lines 285-286) as refusing to split queries containing `$__range`, because `$__range` must be resolved on the backend against the split time range. This change interpolates templates at the start of runSplitQuery (line 299), so the guard on line 287 now tests the already-interpolated expression. If template replacement resolves `$__range` (it does when request.scopedVars carries `__range`), the token is gone, isQueryWithRangeVariable() returns false, and queries like `count_over_time({a="b"}[$__range])` get split into chunks. Their results then no longer match what the guard was meant to protect. No test in the diff covers a `$__range` query, so this regression would not be caught. The guard should check the pre-interpolation expression, and the comment at lines 285-286 needs updating since its premise no longer holds.

title: Shard sub-requests are interpolated a second time (and the test locks this in)
body: runShardSplitQuery() (shardQuerySplitting.ts line 52) already applies applyTemplateVariables to each target. splitQueriesByStreamShard() then passes every shard sub-request to runSplitQuery() (shardQuerySplitting.ts line 163), and this line interpolates those targets again. The updated shard test asserts applyTemplateVariables is called 5 times (1 for the original target plus 4 sub-requests), which confirms the double application, and the assertion makes it look intended. Template replacement is not idempotent: a substituted value containing a `$name` token gets expanded on the second pass. Ad hoc filters are also passed on every pass, and the shard path now forwards request.filters, which it did not do before. The interpolation should happen at one point, or sub-requests should bypass it through an option.

title: Empty-expression check runs before interpolation, so variables that resolve to empty still execute
body: The `.filter((query) => query.expr)` runs on the raw expression, but the emptiness that matters is the one after interpolation, which this PR now introduces. A query whose expr is a variable resolving to an empty string (e.g. `$query` with an empty value) passes the filter, is classified by isLogsQuery('') as a metric query, and is sent to the backend with an empty expression. The same ordering exists in shardQuerySplitting.ts lines 50-52. Moving the empty-expr filter after the map in both places would make the check match the interpolated value the PR is meant to use.

title: New test only checks the runQuery arguments, not the splitting decisions the change is meant to fix
body: The new 'Interpolates queries before execution' test only asserts that the expr and step passed to runQuery are interpolated. It does not exercise what interpolating first changes: the isLogsQuery partitioning, querySupportsSplitting (including the $__range guard), and the step/resolution grouping computed by calculateStep. There is no case where a variable expands into a logs query, a step variable drives grouping, or a $__range query stays unsplit. Those are the behaviors the PR is supposed to fix, and they are untested.

title: traceID dropped from the 'Plugin Request Completed' log line
body: The old logRequest appended a traceID field (from tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)) to the completed-request log. That block is removed and the new log call m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...) does not add a traceID. The new ContextualLoggerMiddleware's instrumentContext also does not add traceID (it only adds endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID and uname). Plugin request logs therefore lose trace correlation, which is a user-visible regression for debugging. The traceID should be carried into the contextual attributes or appended here again.

title: New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no tests and the moved logging behaviour is untested
body: This PR moves the plugin context attributes (endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, uname) out of LoggerMiddleware and into a new ContextualLoggerMiddleware, and changes LoggerMiddleware to log via FromContext. No test covers that the contextual attributes are attached for QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth and CollectMetrics, or that LoggerMiddleware's completed-request log picks them up. The only test touched is the renamed metrics test, which checks only metrics. A regression in the attribute set would go unnoticed.

title: Undocumented ordering dependency: request log fields now depend on ContextualLoggerMiddleware running earlier
body: LoggerMiddleware no longer adds pluginId, endpoint, dsName, dsUID or uname itself. It relies on the contextual logger already being in the ctx, which requires ContextualLoggerMiddleware to be placed before LoggerMiddleware in CreateMiddlewares. If someone reorders the stack or omits the contextual middleware, the completed-request log silently loses these fields with no error. The removed MetricsMiddleware comment ('this middleware should live at the top of the middleware stack') is not restated for the new middleware, and neither NewContextualLoggerMiddleware nor NewLoggerMiddleware documents the requirement.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, so recorded calls are lost
body: FromContext returns NewTestLogger(), a new instance whose InfoLogs/WarnLogs/etc. are not connected to the receiver. LoggerMiddleware now writes 'Plugin Request Completed' via m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so a test that injects a TestLogger and then inspects its InfoLogs will see nothing. Such assertions would fail or pass vacuously after this change. The fake should return the receiver (or share its recording state) so the contextual calls are observable.

title: Stale test name after the rename
body: The file was renamed to metrics_middleware_test.go and the type is now MetricsMiddleware, but the test is still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware. The rename is incomplete and the test name now refers to a type that no longer exists.

title: PR description says the contextual logger moved into LoggerMiddleware, but it is a separate middleware
body: The PR description says the contextual logger was moved 'to the LoggerMiddleware'. In the code, the contextual logger is a new, separate ContextualLoggerMiddleware (this file), which is wired as its own entry in CreateMiddlewares. Anyone relying on the description when reviewing or reverting this change will be misled about where the behaviour lives.

title: Plugin request completion log no longer includes traceID
body: The old logRequest appended traceID from tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false) to the 'Plugin Request Completed' log entry. That block was removed, and the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware (instrumentContext) does not add traceID to the contextual attributes either. Nothing in this diff puts the trace ID into the log record, so completed plugin requests lose log-to-trace correlation for data egress logs. Either add traceID to the contextual attributes in instrumentContext or keep the field in logRequest.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a detached logger, so recorded calls are lost
body: FromContext returns NewTestLogger(), a fresh logger whose calls are never recorded on the receiver. LoggerMiddleware now logs via m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so with this fake the Info call goes to a throwaway logger and the parent's InfoLogs.Calls stays 0. Any test asserting on the fake's InfoLogs after exercising LoggerMiddleware will see no calls and fail, or will be unable to verify that the request was logged. FromContext should return f (or otherwise share the recorded state) so the fake captures the call.

title: LoggerMiddleware silently depends on this middleware being outer to it; no tests cover either
body: LoggerMiddleware no longer adds pluginId, endpoint, dsName, dsUID or uname itself. It relies on this middleware running before it so that m.logger.FromContext(ctx) returns those attributes. The only enforcement is the list order in pluginsintegration.go. If the order changes, or LoggerMiddleware is used without this middleware, completed-request logs silently lose these fields with no error. The doc note that the instrumentation middleware had to sit at the top of the stack was removed with the rename and not replaced here. No test covers ContextualLoggerMiddleware, and none checks that the attributes reach the emitted log record.

title: traceID dropped from the grafana-data-egress log line
body: The old logRequest explicitly appended a traceID field (tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)) to the 'Plugin Request Completed' event. That code is removed in this PR, and the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware/instrumentContext does not add a trace ID either. The egress event therefore no longer carries traceID, so plugin request logs can no longer be correlated with traces unless the infra logger injects trace IDs from ctx on its own, which this diff does not show. The event loses a field it previously always emitted when a trace was present.

title: Moved egress-log fields have no test coverage and depend on implicit ordering
body: instrumentContext now carries pluginId, endpoint, dsName, dsUID and uname that LoggerMiddleware used to emit directly. They reach the 'grafana-data-egress' event only if (a) ConcreteLogger.FromContext renders contextual attributes from ctx, and (b) ContextualLoggerMiddleware is ordered outside LoggerMiddleware in CreateMiddlewares. Nothing in this PR tests either condition: there is no unit test for ContextualLoggerMiddleware, and the existing metrics test no longer covers the enrichment it used to exercise. Reordering the middleware list or changing FromContext would silently strip plugin and datasource identifiers from the data-egress event with no failing test.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, so its output is invisible to the test
body: FromContext returns a brand-new NewTestLogger() instead of the receiver. LoggerMiddleware now emits its only log line via m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so messages go to a throwaway object and never reach the TestLogger's InfoLogs/ErrorLogs counters. Any test that uses plog.TestLogger to assert on the egress log will observe zero calls. Returning f, or sharing the Logs state, would keep the fake observable.

title: FromContext silently discards context attributes when the type assertion fails
body: If d.l.FromContext(ctx) does not return a *log.ConcreteLogger, the wrapper falls back to d.New(), which drops ctx entirely and logs nothing about the failure. The data-egress log now relies on FromContext to carry pluginId, endpoint, dsUID and similar fields, so this path would silently remove them from every plugin request log line. The fallback should preserve the attributes or surface the mismatch.

title: FromContext doc comment is copied from New and misdescribes the method
body: The comment 'returns a new contextual Logger that has this logger's context plus the given context' is the New() description. FromContext takes a context.Context and derives its attributes from that context value, which the comment does not say. Callers implementing the interface are given a misleading contract.

title: Rejected device is cached as tagged, so later requests bypass the limit
body: tagDeviceUI sets the device key in localCache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice and never removes it when that call fails. When the limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached and the first request is rejected, but the key stays cached for about 29 minutes. Every later request from that device ID hits the cache check at the top of tagDeviceUI, returns nil, and Authenticate succeeds. The device is never counted, so after one rejection it keeps anonymous access for the rest of the cache window. The fix is to cache the key only after a successful tag, or to delete it on error. No test covers a second request after a rejection.

title: Requests without a device ID or a parseable IP skip the limit entirely
body: TagDevice returns nil before any limit check when the X-Grafana-Device-Id header is empty (line 121), and also when the remote address cannot be parsed (line 128). Authenticate then proceeds and grants anonymous access. The device ID is fully client-supplied, so a client that omits the header is never counted or rejected, and the limit cannot be enforced for those requests once it is reached. Anonymous requests that are not tagged should be checked against the limit, or rejected when the limit is reached.

title: Device tagging moved onto the synchronous login path using the request context
body: Previously tagging ran in a goroutine with a detached 2-minute context and panic recovery. Now Authenticate waits for TagDevice on the request context. For every device not in the cache, login blocks on a DB write and, when a limit is configured, on a COUNT over the 30-day window (CreateOrUpdateDevice). If the client disconnects, the request context is cancelled and the write may fail with context canceled. The device key has already been cached at impl.go:87, so the device stays untagged for about 29 minutes. Only the limit check needs to be synchronous. The tagging write should not depend on the request context, or the cache entry should be cleared on failure.

title: Device limit check is not atomic with the insert
body: CountDevices and the following INSERT are separate statements with no transaction or lock. Concurrent first-time requests from distinct devices can each see count < deviceLimit and all insert, so the number of devices can exceed the configured limit by up to the number of concurrent first requests. The limit is therefore soft. If it is meant to be strict (for example for licensing), the check and insert need to be a single conditional statement or a transaction.

title: Constructor signature changed for a DI-wired provider without any wire changes
body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now takes db.DB instead of anonstore.AnonStore, and ProvideAnonDBStore now requires a deviceLimit argument. These are Wire providers, but no wire.go or wire_gen.go file is in the change set. If the generated injector still passes an AnonStore into this constructor, the build breaks. In either case the service now constructs its own store, so the AnonStore can no longer be injected or replaced in tests. The generated wiring needs to be checked and regenerated.

title: New device_limit option is not documented
body: The [auth.anonymous] device_limit key is parsed here, but it is not added to conf/defaults.ini or the configuration docs, and the PR's docs checkbox is unchecked. Operators cannot discover the option or its semantics: 0 means unlimited, the count covers devices updated in the last 30 days, and negative values are treated as unlimited.

title: Device limit tests miss the update path and the request-level behavior
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only checks that a new device is rejected at the store level with limit 1. It does not cover an already-known device still being updated once the limit is reached (the updateDevice path). It also does not test TagDevice or Authenticate, where the rejected-device caching bug at impl.go:87 lives, so a retry after rejection is never checked. There is no test for a limit above 1 either.

title: updateDevice comment and error description do not match behavior
body: The comment says the function updates a device 'that has been updated between the given times', but it takes no time arguments. The window is hard-coded relative to device.UpdatedAt (30 days back to 1 minute ahead). The function also returns ErrDeviceLimitReached whenever no row matches, which includes devices that simply expired or were deleted concurrently. The comment and the error meaning should be corrected.

title: Device is cached as tagged before the limit check, so a rejected device is admitted on its next request
body: tagDeviceUI sets the local cache entry for the device before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice, and never removes it when the store fails. When the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, Authenticate rejects the request, but the device key stays cached for the default 29-minute expiry. The device's next request hits the cache check at the top of tagDeviceUI, returns nil, and Authenticate succeeds without any database record. A rejected device is therefore admitted on retry and stays admitted for up to ~29 minutes, so the configured device limit is not enforced for that device. The cache entry should only be set after a successful tag, or be deleted when CreateOrUpdateDevice returns an error.

title: Device limit keys off a client-supplied, unverified header
body: The device identity is the raw X-Grafana-Device-Id request header, accepted without any server-side verification. A client that sends a fresh ID on each request is counted as a new device every time, so the cap can be bypassed trivially. Clearing browser storage has the same effect. If the limit is meant to be enforced rather than advisory, the device identity needs a server-verifiable basis; otherwise the limit should be documented as not being a security control.

title: Limit check is a separate COUNT followed by a separate insert, so concurrent requests can exceed the limit
body: The check at lines 110-116 counts devices, then the insert/upsert runs later in a separate statement with no transaction or lock. Concurrent first requests from different new devices can all read count < deviceLimit and all insert, so the stored device count can overshoot the configured limit by up to the number of concurrent requests. The limit is only soft under load. If it is meant to be strict, the check and insert must be atomic (for example a conditional insert within a transaction).

title: Device tagging moved from a background goroutine onto the synchronous auth path
body: Previously TagDevice ran in a goroutine with a 2-minute timeout and panic recovery, so anonymous authentication never waited on the database. Now it runs inline with the request context. Each device that misses the local cache (the first request per device and again every ~29 minutes) performs a COUNT(*) over the 30-day window plus an upsert or update before the request can be authenticated. With many devices or a slow database this adds latency to those requests and holds request goroutines and DB connections. The cap check makes this worse because it adds a COUNT to the hot path. Consider keeping the non-blocking write for the normal path, or bounding the synchronous call with a timeout.

title: Tests only cover rejection of a new device at the limit, not the update path or the authentication flow
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only asserts that a brand-new device is rejected when the table is at the limit. Not covered: (a) an existing in-window device being updated successfully while the limit is reached, which is the updateDevice success path; (b) devices outside the 30-day window not being counted; (c) TagDevice or Authenticate actually returning ErrDeviceLimitReached to the caller; (d) a rejected device retrying. The retry bug in impl.go (device cached after rejection) would be caught by a test that calls TagDevice twice for a rejected device.

title: RowsAffected()==0 used as 'device not found' is unreliable on MySQL
body: updateDevice treats RowsAffected()==0 as meaning the device is not in the window, and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. MySQL reports changed rows by default (unless clientFoundRows is set on the connection), so an UPDATE that sets the same client_ip and user_agent and a updated_at with the same second-precision value reports 0 even though the row matched. In that case an existing, legitimate device is wrongly rejected. The window is narrow (a same-second retag), so the impact is limited, but the check should not rely on affected rows on MySQL, for example by verifying existence with a SELECT.

title: New [auth.anonymous] device_limit option is undocumented
body: The new device_limit option is read here, but the PR does not touch conf/defaults.ini, conf/sample.ini or the docs, and the docs checkbox in the PR description is unchecked. Operators cannot discover that 0 means unlimited, or that the limit counts devices seen within a rolling 30-day window.

title: Device is cached as tagged before the DB write, so a limit-rejected device is admitted on its retry
body: tagDeviceUI sets the local cache key (line 87) before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice (line 93). When the limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, TagDevice returns that error, and Authenticate rejects the login. The cache entry is not removed, so it stays for 29 minutes. The next request from the same device ID hits the cache check at lines 83-85, tagDeviceUI returns nil, and the anonymous login succeeds without the device ever being stored or counted. The same happens after any transient DB error. The cache entry should be set only after a successful write, or deleted when the write fails.

title: Requests without the device ID header are never counted or limited
body: TagDevice returns nil when X-Grafana-Device-Id is absent (lines 120-122). Authenticate only fails on ErrDeviceLimitReached, so an anonymous request that omits the header is neither stored nor rejected, and the limit does not apply to it. The header is client-supplied, so clients can also rotate IDs to get fresh slots. Before this change, tagging was only analytics and this gap did not matter. Now the feature is meant to enforce a limit, so the missing-header case should either be rejected while the limit is active or be documented as outside the limit.

title: Count-then-insert is not atomic, so concurrent new devices can exceed the limit
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts devices (line 110) and compares with the limit (line 115), then runs the upsert (lines 120-155) with no transaction or lock. Many concurrent logins from new devices can all read a count below the limit and all insert, so the number of stored devices can exceed deviceLimit by up to the concurrency level. The check-and-insert needs to be atomic, for example in one transaction with a conditional insert, or the overshoot must be documented as acceptable.

title: Device tagging moved from a background goroutine onto the synchronous auth path
body: Previously TagDevice ran in a goroutine with a 2-minute timeout, off the request path. Now Authenticate calls it synchronously with the request context and no timeout. Each first request per device per instance performs a DB write during login, and when a limit is configured each new device also runs a COUNT over the updated_at range (database.go line 110). Slow DB calls now delay or block anonymous page loads, and the panic recovery from the goroutine is gone. The limit-enforcement design needs the synchronous write, but the cost on the hot path, including the uncached COUNT, should be assessed.

title: No tests cover the Authenticate path, the cache interaction, or updates to existing devices at the limit
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only checks that the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached for a new device. Nothing tests that a rejected device retried within the cache window is still rejected, which would have caught the cache bypass in impl.go. Nothing tests that Authenticate returns the error to the caller, or that an existing device still gets its updated_at refreshed (the updateDevice path) once the count has reached the limit. The new enforcement behaviour is therefore only covered at the store level.

title: New auth.anonymous device_limit option is not documented
body: The device_limit key is read here, but the PR changes no configuration documentation such as conf/defaults.ini or the docs for the [auth.anonymous] section, so operators have no way to learn that the key exists, that 0 means unlimited, or how the 30-day window counts devices. The PR description is also still the unfilled template, including the docs and feature-toggle checklist items.

title: Dependency injection signature changed; wire files are not part of this diff
body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now takes db.DB and builds the store itself, and anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore now requires an int64 that no provider in the graph supplies. If the wire provider set (wire.go or wire_gen.go) still binds anonstore.AnonStore or lists ProvideAnonDBStore, wire generation or compilation will fail. Those files are not in the changed list, so this should be checked.

title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, unrelated to the PR
body: The change from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1` alters how often every background cleanup job runs (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, user invites, short URLs, query history, and annotations), not just annotation cleanup. The PR description does not mention it, and it looks like a leftover debugging change. It raises the periodic DB load of all cleanup jobs roughly tenfold, and the annotation job can run for up to the 9-minute clean timeout. Revert it unless the new interval is an intentional, separately reviewed change.

title: Routine batch progress is logged at Error level, including full ID lists
body: The informational logs added in CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags use r.log.Error for every batch, including successful ones (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576 and 579). Every cleanup batch therefore emits error-level entries even when nothing failed. The 'Annotations to clean by time/count' and 'Tags to clean' entries also include the whole `ids` slice, up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize IDs per line. With a large backlog this floods the error log with thousands of IDs and hides real errors. The `err` field logged at these points is always nil, because errors already return earlier. These should be Debug-level messages without the ID list.

title: Quadratic string concatenation when building the inline SQLite ID list
body: `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` copies the entire accumulated string on every iteration. For a batch of up to 32767 IDs, which is the case the new test exercises, this copies on the order of several GB of bytes and performs tens of thousands of allocations on every cleanup iteration. Build the list once with strings.Builder, strconv.AppendInt, or strings.Join over strconv.FormatInt.

title: Non-SQLite delete now binds one parameter per ID, which breaks for large batch sizes
body: The non-SQLite branch builds one `?` placeholder and one bind argument per ID. The previous DELETE only inlined LIMIT, so the statement did not depend on the batch size. MySQL prepared statements and the Postgres wire protocol reject more than 65535 bind parameters. AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is an unbounded int64 config value, so a batch size above that limit would make every cleanup batch fail on MySQL/Postgres, where it previously worked. Validate or cap the batch size, or chunk the DELETE IN list to a bounded number of parameters.

title: Cleanup logs every batch at Error level, including successes, with full ID lists
body: The new per-batch closures log at Error level on every batch, including successful ones. This applies to 'Annotations to clean by time' and 'cleaned annotations by time' here (lines 534 and 537), to 'Annotations to clean by count' and 'cleaned annotations by count' (554 and 557), and to 'Tags to clean' and 'cleaned tags' (576 and 579). Each message includes the full ID slice, which can be up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize entries (32767 in the new test). A large backlog therefore produces many very large error-level log lines per cleanup cycle, and error-based alerting will fire on routine success. The "err" field is also always nil at these points, because fetchIDs errors return earlier. These should be Debug-level, without the full ID list.

title: Quadratic string building when inlining IDs for SQLite
body: In the SQLite branch, `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` rebuilds the entire string on every iteration, so building an IN list of n IDs copies O(n^2) bytes. For the 32767-ID batch exercised by the new test, each id adds about 7 bytes, so the total copying is roughly 7*n^2/2, about 3.8 GB of allocation and copying per batch. This repeats for every batch of the cleanup loop whenever the batch size exceeds 999 on SQLite. Use strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt to build the list in linear time.

title: Unrelated change: cleanup ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The ticker interval is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This is not mentioned in the PR description and has nothing to do with the annotation deadlock fix. It makes every cleanup job in this loop (temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, old annotations, user invites, short URLs, query history with its row-limit enforcement) run about 10 times as often in production, adding continuous DB load. It looks like a leftover debugging change and should be reverted, or split into its own justified PR.

title: IN list with one placeholder per ID can exceed MySQL's 65535 placeholder limit
body: On non-SQLite databases the DELETE uses one placeholder per ID, and the batch size is the configured annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size. MySQL prepared statements are limited to 65535 placeholders, so a batch size above that makes the DELETE fail on every batch and stops cleanup. The previous LIMIT-based statement had no such limit. The only special handling in this diff is for SQLite. Either cap the batch size or chunk the IDs for this case.

title: Subtest cleanup is registered after setup and assertions that can fail
body: t.Cleanup is registered only after createTestAnnotations and the assertAnnotationCount/assertAnnotationTagCount calls (lines 116-118). Those helpers call require, which stops the test with FailNow. If any of them fails, the rows are never deleted, and every following subtest starts with leftover annotations and fails on counts, which hides the real failure. The cleanup should be registered before the data is created, as the previous top-level version did.

title: Unrelated change: cleanup ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: This PR is about annotation-cleanup deadlocks, but it also changes the cleanup ticker from 10 minutes to 1 minute. The ticker drives srv.clean(), which runs every cleanup job (temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, user invites, short URLs, query history) as well as annotation cleanup. The change is not mentioned in the description and is not needed for the deadlock fix. It multiplies the periodic DB load of all these jobs by ten and changes operator-visible behavior. If it was left in by accident (for example a debugging tweak), it must be reverted. If it is intended, it needs to be called out and justified.

title: Routine per-batch progress logged at Error level, including full ID lists
body: The new logging uses r.log.Error for routine progress: 'Annotations to clean by time' (with the full ids slice, up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize entries), 'cleaned annotations by time' (line 537), the matching 'by count' calls (lines 554 and 557), and 'Tags to clean' / 'cleaned tags' (lines 576 and 579). untilDoneOrCancelled always runs at least one batch, including the final empty one, so every cleanup cycle emits error-level entries even when nothing was deleted. A large cleanup dumps up to 32767 IDs per batch into the error log. The 'err' field is always nil at the first call. These look like debugging leftovers. They will flood error logs and alerting, and the problem is worse now that the job runs every minute. They should be Debug-level without the ID list, or removed.

title: Quadratic string building of the SQLite ID list
body: The SQLite branch builds the IN list with values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) inside a loop. Each iteration copies the whole accumulated string, so building a list of n IDs costs O(n^2) bytes copied and allocated. With the batch size used in the new 40003-annotation test (32767), the final string is roughly 200KB and the loop copies several GB per batch, repeated for every batch and every annotation type. Use strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt into a byte slice.

title: One bind parameter per ID breaks large batch sizes on MySQL and PostgreSQL
body: The non-SQLite branch sends one bind parameter per ID. Previously the batch size was a literal in the LIMIT clause and could be any value. MySQL prepared statements and the PostgreSQL wire protocol cap bind parameters at 65535 per statement. A configured AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize above that now makes the DELETE fail on every cycle, and the diff adds no upper bound on the setting. The SQLite workaround only covers SQLite. Either cap the batch size or split the DELETE into statements of bounded parameter count.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context, which is cancelled when the handler returns
body: The goroutine derives its context from the request ctx via context.WithTimeoutCause. Create returns immediately after the storage write, and net/http cancels the request context when ServeHTTP returns. The legacy Create therefore usually runs with an already-cancelled context, and SQL-backed legacy stores abort the write. The resulting error is only recorded in a metric, so the legacy copy silently diverges. The same pattern is used in Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163). The fix is to detach the context first, e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx), before adding the 10s timeout.

title: Legacy Update recomputes the update from the same objInfo, so legacy can persist a different object than unified
body: The previous implementation computed the updated object once and handed the same result to both stores. This version passes the raw objInfo to d.Storage.Update and then, in a goroutine, to d.Legacy.Update. The legacy call invokes objInfo.UpdatedObject a second time, against the legacy store's current object, and after the handler may have returned. A patch-style or stateful UpdatedObjectInfo can then yield a different result than the one written to unified storage, so the two stores diverge with no error surfaced.

title: Errors from async legacy writes are discarded without logging
body: In the Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection goroutines the legacy error is only passed to a duration metric as a boolean (e.g. line 56 errObjectSt != nil). The error value and the object identity are never logged. The previous synchronous code logged these failures. Operators have no way to find which objects failed to reach legacy storage, which matters because this is the only signal that the 'safe measure' copy is missing data.

title: Fire-and-forget legacy writes can be applied out of order relative to later writes
body: Each write spawns an independent goroutine with no per-object ordering. A Create followed quickly by a Delete of the same name can run the legacy Delete before the legacy Create. The Delete then hits NotFound (ignored), and the Create lands, leaving a legacy copy of an object that unified storage has already deleted. Update/Delete races can similarly leave resurrected or stale legacy objects. Nothing reconciles these because the error is not surfaced.

title: Untracked goroutines have no panic recovery and Destroy does not wait for them
body: The legacy goroutines have no recover(). A panic in a legacy implementation inside a goroutine terminates the whole process, whereas the previous synchronous calls ran in the request handler where net/http recovers the panic. Destroy() (lines 172-175) also tears down d.Legacy while these goroutines may still be using it, and there is no WaitGroup or other tracking to drain in-flight writes at shutdown.

title: Delete passes the object name where the kind label is expected in the storage duration metric
body: The call is d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage). The third argument is the kind/resource label used by the other calls (options.Kind). Passing the object name produces wrong metric labels and creates one time series per deleted object, which is an unbounded cardinality explosion in Prometheus.

title: Storage failures are recorded as legacy failures (Create and Update)
body: In Create (line 45) and Update (line 129) the error branch for the storage write calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...). Failures of the unified storage write are therefore counted against legacy, which misattributes errors and sends operators to the wrong backend. These should be recordStorageDuration calls.

title: DeleteCollection records the legacy duration as a storage duration
