body: The goroutine at line 166 calls d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). The legacy latency and error are attributed to the storage metric, which corrupts the storage/legacy comparison this dual-writer is meant to produce. It should be recordLegacyDuration.

title: Unified NotFound now skips the legacy delete, which the previous code deliberately did not do
body: The removed code tolerated IsNotFound from the storage Delete and still deleted from legacy. This version returns immediately on any storage error (lines 101-105), so a NotFound from unified never reaches legacy. An object that exists only in legacy stays there forever. A later Create succeeds in unified, and its async legacy Create fails with AlreadyExists, silently. This behavior change is not mentioned in the PR and needs an explicit decision and a test.

title: Delete attaches the bare logger to the context, dropping name/kind/method fields
body: Line 96 builds a 'log' with name, kind and method values, but line 97 stores d.Log in the context instead. Storage implementations that log via klog.FromContext therefore lose the per-request fields that the other methods (Create, Get, Update) propagate.

title: Method comments describe synchronous dual writes that are no longer synchronous
body: The comment on Create says it writes to LegacyStorage and Storage, and the DeleteCollection comment says it deletes from both. The legacy write is now asynchronous and its failures are not reported to the caller. The comments should say so, otherwise readers will assume legacy consistency guarantees that do not exist.

title: Each write spawns an unbounded goroutine with a 10s timeout and no backpressure
body: Every successful write starts a goroutine that holds the object and context for up to 10 seconds. If the legacy store is slow, goroutines and held objects accumulate proportionally to write rate with no concurrency cap or queue. This can increase memory usage and goroutine count under write load.

title: Mode 3 tests share one mock between storage and legacy, so they cannot verify which backend was called
body: The tests use one mock.Mock for both legacyStoreMock and storageMock, so an expectation set for one backend also matches calls to the other. The Create error case sets up no storage expectation, yet passes because the legacy expectation for failingObj matches the storage call. Async legacy calls are never awaited or asserted, and there is no AssertExpectations or AssertNotCalled check. The tests therefore do not verify the core Mode 3 contract: reads hit only storage, and writes go to storage first and then to legacy.

title: Test name says 'not implemented' but the case tests a storage error
body: The case named 'error when listing an object in the unified store is not implemented' now exercises a normal List path where the storage mock returns an error. The name is a leftover from the old stub and misdescribes the behavior under test.

title: New mode 3 integration subtests assert legacy state immediately after writes that go to legacy asynchronously
body: The new 'file, mode 3' and 'unified storage, mode 3' subtests run doPlaylistTests. That helper checks the legacy /api/playlists endpoint right after k8s creates and checks legacy GETs right after k8s PUT/PATCH (for example the list at line 523 and getFromBothAPIs). In mode 3 the legacy write happens in a goroutine after the response, so these assertions race with it and the subtests will be flaky. The helper needs to poll or wait for legacy convergence in mode 3.

title: Unrelated go.work.sum churn, including a duplicated checksum line
body: The go.work.sum changes add checksum entries for grafana-azure-sdk-go, grafana-plugin-sdk-go, prometheus-alertmanager, otel exporters/sdk and others that have nothing to do with the dual-writer feature. The grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery go.mod line at 408 duplicates the unchanged line just above it. These changes look like a stale workspace file and should be dropped from this PR.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context, which is canceled when the handler returns
body: The legacy write runs in a goroutine but its context is derived from ctx, the incoming request context. net/http cancels a request's context when ServeHTTP returns, which happens right after Storage.Create returns and the response is written. The 10s timeout wrapper is built on that already-canceled context, so Legacy.Create typically fails with context canceled before it writes anything. Legacy writes will be lost for most requests, silently, which defeats the purpose of mode 3. The same pattern appears in Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163). The background write should detach from the request context first, e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx), before applying the timeout.

title: Legacy write failures are no longer logged anywhere
body: The goroutine only feeds a boolean into a duration metric and drops the error. The base code logged legacy failures with the object attached. Now a failed legacy create (including a timeout) produces no log line and no error detail, so the unified/legacy divergence this mode is meant to guard against is invisible to operators. The same omission exists in Delete (line 113), Update (line 140) and DeleteCollection (line 166).

title: Fire-and-forget legacy writes are not ordered per object
body: Each write spawns an independent goroutine with no per-object serialization. Two quick successive operations on the same playlist (for example update then update, or update then delete) can reach the legacy store out of order, leaving legacy with the older state while unified storage holds the newer one. Nothing detects or repairs this, and the 10s timeout makes it more likely. This needs either per-key serialization or an explicit, documented eventual-consistency guarantee with tests.

title: Legacy update recomputes the change from its own state instead of writing the unified result
body: The base code wrapped the Storage.Update result in updateWrapper so the legacy store received exactly what unified storage produced. This version passes the raw objInfo to Legacy.Update. objInfo.UpdatedObject is then applied to the legacy store's current object, which can differ from the unified object (different resourceVersions, stored fields, defaults, or a patch applied against a different base). Both writes can succeed and the stores still diverge. The same objInfo is also consumed a second time after the first UpdatedObject call.

title: Delete records the object name as the kind label on storage metrics
body: recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) passes name where every other call passes options.Kind. Each distinct object name becomes a new Prometheus label value, which creates unbounded metric cardinality and breaks per-kind dashboards and alerts.

title: DeleteCollection records the legacy outcome in the storage metric
body: The goroutine calls recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ..., startLegacy), so legacy delete-collection latency and failures are counted under the storage series, and the legacy histogram is never updated for this method. It should be recordLegacyDuration.

title: Unified storage failures are recorded as legacy failures
body: When the storage write fails, Create (line 45) and Update (line 129) call recordLegacyDuration(true, ...). The failed unified write is counted in the legacy metrics and the storage error metric is never set, so storage error rates are under-reported and legacy stats are polluted.

title: Delete puts the base logger into the context instead of the request-scoped logger
body: Delete builds log with name, kind and method, then calls klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) using the base logger. Downstream logs from the storage and legacy calls lose those fields, unlike the other methods, which pass log.

title: Destroy tears down Legacy while fire-and-forget writes may still be running
body: Destroy calls Storage.Destroy and Legacy.Destroy immediately, but background legacy goroutines may still be executing against the legacy store. Those writes then run against a destroyed backend and fail or panic. Destroy has no way to wait for in-flight legacy writes.

title: Background legacy goroutines have no panic recovery
body: Legacy calls used to run on the request goroutine, where net/http recovers panics per request. The bare goroutines added here have no recover, so a panic in any legacy storage method crashes the whole Grafana process instead of failing one request.

title: Tests never verify the asynchronous legacy write
body: Storage and Legacy share a single mock.Mock, so the test cannot tell which store was called. The tests never call AssertExpectations, so the legacy expectations set up in TestMode3_Create, _Update and _DeleteCollection are never checked. Nothing verifies that Legacy is called, or with what object, which is the core of this change. The background goroutine can also call the mock after the test returns, so those calls are not observed at all.

title: Legacy-side reads run immediately after writes that are now asynchronous
body: In mode 3, the k8s create at line 496 returns before its legacy write completes. getFromBothAPIs then reads the legacy endpoint right away (and the legacy list comparison around line 523 does the same). These checks race the background write and will be flaky. If the legacy endpoint is actually served from unified storage, the checks do not exercise the legacy write at all. Either way the assertion does not test what it claims without waiting or polling for the legacy write.

title: Test case name says List is not implemented, but it is
body: The case is named 'error when listing an object in the unified store is not implemented', but List is now implemented in this PR and the case only checks that a storage error is propagated. The name is misleading to future readers.

title: Create test name contradicts its setup
body: The case is named 'creating an object only in the unified store', but its setup registers a legacy Create expectation and the implementation writes to legacy as well. The name describes the old behavior.

title: Duplicate go.work.sum entry and unrelated checksum additions
body: The line 'github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery ... /go.mod' is added a second time, duplicating the entry immediately above it. The hunk also adds checksums for unrelated modules (grafana-azure-sdk-go, prometheus-alertmanager, several otel exporters and genproto rpc), which this dual-writer change does not touch. These look like an accidental go mod tidy or merge artifact and should be removed or verified.

title: Async legacy writes run on the request context, which is cancelled when the handler returns
body: The legacy write goroutine derives its context from the request ctx via context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...). The request context is cancelled when the HTTP handler returns, which happens right after the unified-storage write completes. The legacy Create therefore almost always sees context.Canceled, the legacy copy is never written, and the only trace is a metric. The same pattern appears in Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163). The detached goroutine should use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) (or a background context) before applying the timeout.

title: Legacy write failures in mode 3 are counted but never logged
body: In Create the goroutine stores the legacy error in errObjectSt and only records a duration metric; no log line is emitted. Update (line 140), Delete (line 113) and DeleteCollection (line 166) have the same gap. The previous synchronous code logged legacy failures. Since the async legacy write is now the only safety net, failures become invisible except as a counter with no object name or error text, so diverged objects cannot be identified.

title: Delete passes the object name as the resource label on the storage duration metric
body: recordStorageDuration is called with name where every other call passes options.Kind. Object names are unbounded, so each deleted object creates a new label value and a new time series that stays in the metrics registry for the life of the process. On a long-running server this grows metric cardinality and memory without bound.

title: Storage failures are recorded in the legacy duration metric
body: In Create, when the unified-storage write fails, the code calls recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recordStorageDuration, so storage errors are counted against the legacy series and the storage error metric is not updated. Update (line 129) makes the same mistake. Dashboards and alerts comparing the two stores will report wrong numbers.

title: DeleteCollection records legacy results under the storage metric
body: The legacy DeleteCollection goroutine calls recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration. Legacy results are counted as storage results, and the legacy metric never sees delete-collection calls.

title: Legacy create mutates the same object the storage write used, racing with the response
body: The goroutine passes obj, the same pointer given to Storage.Create at line 42, to Legacy.Create while the handler continues to serialize the returned object. Legacy create paths typically assign UID, creationTimestamp and other metadata to the object in place. If the storage result shares memory with obj, this is an unsynchronized write concurrent with response encoding, and it can alter metadata of the object the storage already persisted. The goroutine should receive a deep copy (obj.DeepCopyObject()).

title: Mode 3 update no longer sends the legacy store the object unified storage persisted
body: The previous implementation wrapped objInfo with the object produced by unified storage so that legacy stored exactly that result. Now the raw objInfo is passed to Legacy.Update, so UpdatedObject is evaluated again against the legacy store's own copy. For patch and apply requests the legacy result can differ from what unified stored. Any resourceVersion precondition is checked against the legacy RV, which differs from the unified RV, so legacy updates can fail with a conflict. Both outcomes are silent (see the logging finding), so the two stores can silently diverge.

title: Delete puts the bare logger into the context, dropping name, kind and method
body: Every other method stores the request-scoped log (with name, kind and method values) in ctx. Delete uses d.Log, so anything downstream that logs via klog.FromContext, including the storage Delete path, loses those key/values. This is inconsistent with the rest of the file.

title: Dry-run requests are still dispatched to the legacy store
body: Create, Update, Delete and DeleteCollection never check options.DryRun before spawning the legacy write. A dry-run request is meant to have no side effects. Unified storage honors it, but the legacy call is dispatched unconditionally with the same options, and this file does not rely on the legacy store honoring DryRun. The legacy goroutine should be skipped when len(options.DryRun) > 0.

title: One unbounded goroutine per write, not tracked and not drained on shutdown
body: Each successful write spawns a goroutine that holds the request object and options until the legacy call returns. There is no bound on in-flight legacy writes. Nothing waits for them on shutdown, and Destroy (line 172) calls Legacy.Destroy while those goroutines may still be using Legacy. A slow legacy store causes goroutines and retained objects to grow with the write rate.

title: Update doc comment describes the old synchronous ordering
body: The comment says Update writes first to Storage and then to LegacyStorage, which implies the legacy write is part of the synchronous call. It is now fire-and-forget in a goroutine and its errors are not returned. The Create comment (line 35) also does not say that the legacy write is asynchronous and best-effort, which callers need to know.

title: Legacy writes in mode 3 are never verified by the tests
body: Each success case sets up a legacy expectation (for example here), but nothing asserts that it was called: there is no AssertExpectations and no wait for the goroutine. Legacy and storage also share one mock object (lines 53-54 construct legacyStoreMock and storageMock with the same m), so a legacy call would satisfy a storage expectation with the same method name and arguments. A regression that never calls Legacy, or calls it with the wrong object, passes these tests. Since asynchronous legacy behavior is the point of mode 3, tests should wait for the legacy call and check it against a separate legacy mock.

title: List test is named as 'not implemented' although List is implemented
body: The case name says listing 'is not implemented', but this PR implements List by calling Storage.List. The case only checks that an error returned by the storage mock is propagated. The name should describe that, for example 'error when listing from the unified store fails'.

title: New mode 3 subtests assert legacy state immediately after asynchronous writes
body: The new mode 3 subtests call doPlaylistTests, which reads the legacy API right after k8s writes (getFromBothAPIs at lines 535 and 547, and later). With legacy writes now fire-and-forget, those reads race the goroutine and nothing waits for convergence. The subtests can be flaky, or fail deterministically if the legacy write fails (see the cancelled-context finding). The legacy-visibility checks should poll (for example with require.Eventually), or the test should document why these reads are unaffected in mode 3.

title: go.work.sum gets unrelated checksum entries and a duplicated line
body: The change adds checksums for modules unrelated to mode 3 (grafana-azure-sdk-go/v2, prometheus-alertmanager, several otel exporter and SDK versions, genproto rpc). This suggests a dependency tool was run and its output was committed. The github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery /go.mod line is also added even though an identical line already appears as context just above it, so it is duplicated. The unrelated lines should be reverted and the duplicate removed, or the PR should explain why they are needed.

title: Dev mode now serializes every request behind a write lock held across file and network I/O
body: In dev mode the condition `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && ret != nil` is always false, so every call falls through to `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` and holds the exclusive lock for the whole reload. That reload can call `readWebAssetsFromCDN` (an HTTP request made with `http.DefaultClient`, which has no timeout) and then read and parse the manifest from disk. Before this change, concurrent dev-mode requests ran in parallel. Now they queue behind one another, and a slow CDN response stalls every caller, including ones that only need the read path. Waiting callers also ignore their own `ctx` cancellation while blocked on the lock. Consider doing the reload outside the lock, or only holding the lock while publishing the result.

title: No double-checked read after acquiring the write lock, so concurrent cold-start callers each reload the manifest
body: The RLock check at lines 41-47 happens once, and the write lock is taken at line 48 without re-checking the cache. If several goroutines miss the cache at the same time, they each acquire the write lock in turn and each re-read the manifest file (and possibly the CDN) even though the first one has already populated `entryPointAssetsCache`. Re-checking `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` after `Lock()` would avoid the redundant work in non-dev mode.

title: Data race fix has no regression test
body: The PR fixes a data race on the package-level `entryPointAssetsCache`, but no test is added or changed. A test that calls `GetWebAssets` concurrently from multiple goroutines (in both dev and non-dev environments, run under `go test -race`) would confirm the fix and keep the race from coming back. Without it, nothing in CI exercises the locking path.

title: No double-checked cache lookup after acquiring the write lock
body: The fast path reads entryPointAssetsCache under RLock, then releases it and takes the write Lock with no re-check. Any goroutine that missed the cache while another goroutine was already populating it will still re-read and re-parse assets-manifest.json from disk, one at a time, even though the cache is now filled. At startup, N concurrent requests produce N serialized manifest reads. Re-checking `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` after taking the Lock would return the cached value immediately.

title: Exclusive lock held across file I/O serializes all dev-mode calls and ignores caller context
body: The write Lock is taken on every call in dev mode (cfg.Env == setting.Dev), because the early return is skipped. Each call then reads and parses the manifest from disk while holding the exclusive lock, so concurrent dev requests that previously ran in parallel now run one at a time. In non-dev mode, while the cache is nil (for example, the manifest is missing or failed to load), every request blocks on Lock without honouring its ctx, so a slow operation inside readWebAssetsFromCDN (which uses http.DefaultClient with no timeout) holds up all waiters. The CDN path is currently unreachable because cdn is the constant "", so this is latent, but the lock scope is wider than the data race requires. Doing the I/O outside the lock and only taking the lock to publish the result would avoid both problems.

title: No regression test for concurrent access to the cached web assets
body: The PR fixes a data race on the package-level entryPointAssetsCache, but adds no test that exercises GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines. Without a test run under `go test -race`, nothing guards against the race being reintroduced, for example by a future change that reads the global outside the lock. A small test that calls GetWebAssets concurrently with a temp manifest, with the cache reset between cases, would lock in the fix.

title: Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock, so waiters redo the full load
body: After Lock() at line 48, the function unconditionally reads and parses assets-manifest.json and then overwrites entryPointAssetsCache at line 69. It does this even when a goroutine that held the lock just before has already populated the cache. On a cold start, or after a failed load, N concurrent requests queue on the write lock and each performs the full file read and JSON decode, one after another. The redundant work existed before this change, but the lock now serializes it, so request latency grows with the number of waiters. Re-checking entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the lock in the non-dev case would complete the double-checked pattern that the RLock fast path starts.

title: Dev mode now serializes every request through the exclusive lock
body: When cfg.Env == setting.Dev, the RLock fast path at lines 45-47 is never taken, so every GetWebAssets call acquires the exclusive write lock at line 48 and holds it across the file open, JSON decode and cache write. Concurrent dev-mode requests that previously ran in parallel are now fully serialized. The impact is limited to local development, but the change in concurrency behaviour is not mentioned and could be avoided by only taking the write lock when a reload is actually needed.

title: No regression test for the concurrent access fix
body: The change fixes a data race on the package-level entryPointAssetsCache, but no test is added. The race is only detectable by calling GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines under `go test -race`. A test that uses a temporary static root with a valid assets-manifest.json, runs concurrent calls in both dev and non-dev configurations, and checks the cache behaviour would prevent a regression. Without it, removing the RWMutex would not be caught by CI.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false, so the feature flag check is dead logic
body: The helper reads FlagSqlExpressions, then returns false on both branches of `if enabled`. The flag value has no effect, so the SQL case always returns 'sqlExpressions is not implemented'. The name suggests flag-driven enablement, which misleads anyone who later wants to re-enable SQL expressions by flag. They would have to rewrite the helper, and the flag lookup is still evaluated on the SQL path, which the previous code did not do. If h.features is ever nil, this now panics for SQL queries where it previously did not. Replace the helper with an unconditional rejection, or keep the flag check and drop the forced false.

title: Existing SQL expression parsing and execution tests will fail, and no test covers the new rejection
body: TablesList now always fails because DB.RunCommands in db.go always returns an error, so NewSQLCommand also always fails. Any existing test expecting TablesList or NewSQLCommand to return table names, or expecting SQL command execution to produce frames, will now fail. The PR does not touch any test files. Nothing in the diff asserts that a SQL query is rejected at ReadQuery (reader.go, SQL case), or that the stub DB returns errors. Either the affected tests are left broken, or the PR is missing coverage for the new behavior. Update or remove the old SQL tests and add a test for the rejection path.

title: UnmarshalSQLCommand bypasses the ExpressionQueryReader gate
body: The new check lives only in ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery. UnmarshalSQLCommand is exported and calls NewSQLCommand directly with no feature or enable check. Right now SQL execution is blocked only because the stub DB returns errors. If a real engine is reintroduced in pkg/expr/sql/db.go, this path would reach it without the gate. Put the guard in NewSQLCommand or UnmarshalSQLCommand too, so the protection does not depend on a single call path.

title: Nil pointer dereference when building the unloading threshold fails (pre-existing)
body: This is not introduced by the PR, but it is in the same file. `unloading, err := NewThresholdCommand(...)` is followed by `unloading.Invert = true` before the `if err != nil` check on the next line. If NewThresholdCommand returns a nil pointer on error, a user-supplied invalid unloadCondition evaluator type causes a panic while parsing the query. Move the error check above the field assignment.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false and its flag check is misleading
body: The helper always returns false. `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(...)` names the disabled state 'enabled', and both branches return false, so the flag lookup has no effect on the result. This is a security gate, and the inverted naming makes it easy to misread or to 'fix' later by flipping the wrong condition. It also adds a dereference of h.features on the SQL path, which previously never touched the feature toggles, so a reader constructed with nil features would now panic on any SQL expression instead of returning the intended error. A plain hard-coded rejection with a comment explaining the disable would make the intent obvious.

title: SQL command construction and execution have no disable gate of their own
body: The only enforcement of the disable is the new check in ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery (reader.go). NewSQLCommand, the exported UnmarshalSQLCommand, and SQLCommand.Execute remain callable with no check. The current safety depends entirely on the stub in pkg/expr/sql/db.go returning 'not implemented' from TablesList/QueryFramesInto. Any caller that builds a SQLCommand without going through ReadQuery, or any future change that reimplements the DB stub, reopens the RCE/LFI path the PR is closing, with no second check to catch it. The disable should also be enforced at the command boundary (for example in NewSQLCommand or Execute) so the protection does not rest on one stub's error return.

title: No test covers the rejection of SQL expressions and no test files were updated
body: This security fix adds a new early return for QueryTypeSQL but no test asserts that a SQL expression query is rejected, with or without the sqlExpressions flag. None of the changed files are test files. Existing tests for sql.TablesList, NewSQLCommand, or SQLCommand.Execute, if any exist, previously exercised DuckDB behaviour and will now fail against the stub, and nothing in the PR updates them. A regression test for the reader rejection is needed so that re-enabling the path cannot happen silently.

title: sqlExpressions flag is now a no-op, but its documented meaning and error text are inconsistent with that
body: After this change, enabling the sqlExpressions feature flag does nothing: every SQL expression is rejected with 'sqlExpressions is not implemented'. The flag is still registered and documented as enabling SQL expressions, which the PR description acknowledges it is leaving unchanged. Users who enable the flag will get an error that points at the flag as if it were the problem, and operators reading the flag docs will be misled. At minimum the flag description and this message should say that SQL expressions are disabled for security reasons regardless of the flag.

title: enableSqlExpressions ignores the feature flag and always returns false
body: enableSqlExpressions computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`, then returns false in both branches of the following `if`. The flag value is discarded, so the function is dead logic that reads as if it honours the flag. Anyone later restoring a flag-based gate will find an inverted-looking expression that never reaches a true result. It also dereferences `h.features` on every SQL query, so a nil feature set would panic on the SQL path, which previously never touched features. A plain rejection with a comment explaining the disablement would be clearer.

title: No regression test asserts that SQL expression queries are rejected
body: This is a security hotfix for RCE/LFI, but the PR adds no test showing that ReadQuery returns an error for QueryTypeSQL regardless of feature flags, and none that NewSQLCommand or UnmarshalSQLCommand fail for arbitrary SQL. Without such a test, a future change could silently re-enable the path (for example by restoring the DuckDB implementation in pkg/expr/sql/db.go) and nothing would catch it.

title: Existing SQL parsing and execution tests will fail, and no test files were updated
body: TablesList now always errors because DB.RunCommands is a stub returning "not implemented", and NewSQLCommand and SQLCommand.Execute depend on it. The PR changes no test files. If the repository's existing tests for TablesList, NewSQLCommand, SQL command execution, or the reader's SQL path (pkg/expr/sql, pkg/expr, reader tests) expect DuckDB results, they will fail in CI. Those tests should be removed, skipped with an explanation, or converted to assert the disabled behaviour.

title: Error message says 'not implemented' for a deliberate disablement
body: When a user enables the sqlExpressions flag, every SQL query now fails with "sqlExpressions is not implemented". That is misleading: the feature is disabled by policy after a security fix, not missing. Users and support will read it as a bug. The feature toggle and its docs still describe SQL expressions as enabled by the flag, which the PR explicitly leaves untouched. The message and the flag documentation should say the feature is disabled for security reasons.

title: DuckDB-era string-built SQL is left in place; the fix depends entirely on the stub
body: TablesList still builds a SQL command with fmt.Sprintf and only escapes single quotes before sending it to the engine. The security property now relies entirely on the stub DB in db.go returning errors. Nothing in the reader or parser enforces the gate if the real engine is restored. Anyone who reinstates the DuckDB backend would reintroduce the injection surface without any warning in the code path. Either remove the dead parser code or add a comment and a guard tying its use to the feature gate.

title: Stub DB named like a working in-memory engine with no doc comment
body: NewInMemoryDB and the DB type suggest a functional in-memory SQL engine, but every method unconditionally returns "not implemented". The type has no doc comment saying it is an intentional fail-closed stub that disables SQL expressions. A maintainer reading only this file could mistake the failures for a bug, or reinstate a DuckDB backend without knowing the stub is the security boundary.

title: Checksum removals unrelated to go-duck are unexplained
body: The go.work.sum hunk removes checksum lines for github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-go/sdk/storage/azblob v1.3.2 and github.com/google/go-replayers/grpcreplay and httpreplay. These are not part of the go-duck removal, and nothing in the PR explains them. This looks like side effects of a tidy run on a different module graph. Removing needed checksums can cause 'missing go.sum entry' failures in builds that run with -mod=readonly. Reviewers should confirm these modules are not needed, or drop the unrelated churn.

title: Shared err variable written from concurrent index builds can swallow errors
body: In init, the errgroup closure writes the outer err (declared at line 181) and increments totalBatchesIndexed (line 189) from up to initWorkers goroutines at once. The closure returns that shared variable, so a failing build can be overwritten by another goroutine's successful s.build (which sets err to nil) before the closure's return value is read. group.Wait() then reports nil and startup continues with a namespace's index missing. The race detector also flags this. Because init now runs synchronously inside NewResourceServer, a swallowed error means the server starts with incomplete search results. Use a closure-local err and an atomic or mutex-protected counter.

title: Constructor now performs DB init and full index build synchronously with no deadline
body: NewResourceServer now synchronously runs lifecycle.Init (for the sql backend: DB provider init and ping) and the full search index build via search.init, then returns any failure as a constructor error. The context is a background context with no deadline, so a slow or unreachable database, or a long index build, now blocks construction indefinitely instead of failing individual RPCs. Any dependency-injection graph that constructs ResourceServer now runs this I/O at construction time, before service Init phases, and fails startup on any init error. The PR does not show that every caller constructs it after the database is ready. Add a startup timeout and confirm construction order for all callers.

title: Lazy-to-eager init change ships with no tests
body: The change removes the Init guard from about ten handlers, reorders initialization (search init now runs before initWatcher), and makes NewResourceServer fail on init errors. No unit tests are added or updated; the only test touched adds a postgres skip. Nothing verifies that the constructor returns the init error, that the broadcaster is ready for Watch immediately after construction, or that mocked backends in existing server tests tolerate the eager GetResourceStats, WatchWriteEvents and lifecycle calls now made during construction.

title: Watch consumer does not check channel close and panics on nil event during shutdown
body: The goroutine consuming the watch channel does 'v := <-events' without checking the ok flag. The sql backend's poller closes its stream when the backend is stopped (deferred close after <-b.done), so after Stop every receive yields nil. handleEvent then dereferences evt.Type on its first line and panics in a background goroutine, which takes down the process during graceful shutdown. The context used here is context.Background() and is never cancelled, so nothing stops the loop. This predates the PR, but it is the init path the PR changes and now runs at construction. Check ok and return when the channel closes.

title: Missing indexes are still built under the gRPC request context
body: The PR's goal is to stop index builds from being cancelled by request contexts, but Search still builds any index missing from the cache with the request context: Search calls getOrCreateIndex(ctx), which calls s.build(ctx, key, 10, 0), which calls BuildIndex(ctx) and ListIterator(ctx). Namespaces skipped at startup (count at or below InitMinCount) and namespaces created after startup still take this path, so a client disconnect or deadline mid-build still aborts the build. The hard-coded size of 10 is also far below any realistic FileThreshold, so these indexes are always memory-only even when large. Build missing indexes with a server-lifetime context, or document that this path remains request-scoped.

title: TotalDocs iterates the cache map without holding cacheMu
body: TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without taking cacheMu, while BuildIndex writes b.cache under cacheMu.Lock. The PR adds a TotalDocs call to searchSupport.init (search.go line 216) that runs right after the watch goroutine starts, and that goroutine can call BuildIndex for a namespace with no index yet. A concurrent map iteration and map write is a fatal, unrecoverable runtime error in Go, so this can crash the process. Take cacheMu.RLock in TotalDocs.

title: Removing the build lock lets duplicate builds for the same key run concurrently
body: Removing cacheMu from BuildIndex means concurrent builds for the same NamespacedResource now run in parallel, and nothing dedupes them (the TODO in getOrCreateIndex notes this gap). Two concurrent Search requests on a new namespace each run a full build, roughly doubling CPU and memory for that namespace. For file indexes, the second caller gets bleve's path-exists error from bleve.New at this line while the first build is still in flight. The old lock did not dedupe either, but it serialized the work. The speedup holds only for distinct keys, so the PR should add per-key deduplication or state this limitation.

title: Post-Stop rejection of RPCs was lost when the Init guards were removed
body: Previously every RPC called s.Init, which returned s.initErr, and Stop sets initErr to 'service is stopping' or 'service is stopped', so RPCs after Stop were rejected. With the Init guards removed from Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search, History, Origin, IsHealthy, PutBlob and GetBlob, nothing reads initErr after construction. This assignment is now dead, and requests arriving after Stop are served against a stopped service: writes still reach the database and watch streams run on a cancelled context. Keep a post-stop check in the handlers or document the new behavior.

title: Constructor error path does not release context or lifecycle resources
body: When Init fails, NewResourceServer logs and returns without calling s.cancel() or stopping the lifecycle. The background context and any resources opened by lifecycle.Init (for the sql backend, the DB handle from dbProvider.Init) are never released. Now that construction performs real I/O, the error path should clean up, for example by calling s.cancel() and stopping the lifecycle when Init fails.

title: WriteEvent discards the span context, so the PR's trace fix is incomplete
body: The PR claims to fix trace propagation, but only GetResourceStats was changed to use the derived context. WriteEvent still does '_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)' and then passes the original ctx to create/update/delete, so those spans become siblings of the WriteEvent span rather than children. The same pattern remains in ReadResource (line 353) and ListIterator (line 388). Either fix all of them or stop describing the trace propagation as fixed.

title: BuildIndex span context is discarded, so the span has no children
body: BuildIndex starts its span with '_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)' and never passes the derived context to bleve.New, the builder, or the flush. The span therefore has no children, which is inconsistent with the trace-propagation fix this PR describes in search.go's build and init. Use 'ctx, span :=' and pass ctx onward.

title: Poller span is never ended on the listLatestRVs error path
body: In poller, the span started at line 580 is ended only at the bottom of the tick. The error branch at lines 583-586 logs, resets the ticker, and executes 'continue' without calling span.End(), so the span is never ended and is never exported on every failed tick. Call span.End() before continue, or end the span in each branch.

title: Postgres skip removes the only storage-server startup test for postgres runs
body: This skip disables TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer for every postgres run. That test exercises the storage-server startup path that this PR moves into the NewResourceServer constructor, so the PR now has no coverage of that path on postgres. The skip is unrelated to the PR description, has no tracking issue, and removes coverage rather than fixing the test. Link an issue or keep the test running.

title: Storage init failures now abort NewResourceServer and block startup on the full index build
body: NewResourceServer now calls s.Init synchronously. Init runs lifecycle.Init (DB connect and ping) and the search init, which builds an index for every namespace above InitMinCount, and returns the error to the caller. Previously these failures only surfaced as errors on the first gRPC call and never stopped construction. Now a transient DB error or any index build error makes the constructor fail, which fails whatever wires the server, and startup (including HTTP and metrics) is blocked for the entire index build. Init is also never retried. This is the behavior change the PR description asks about. It should be called out explicitly, and the module init order should be checked to confirm the DB and dependencies are ready when the provider runs.

title: On-demand index build still runs under the gRPC request context
body: getOrCreateIndex still builds a missing index with the request context: s.build(ctx, key, 10, 0). The build's ListIterator and builder calls use that ctx. Namespaces at or below InitMinCount at startup are not indexed at init. If such a namespace has since grown, the first Search builds the whole index inside the RPC, and a client cancel or deadline aborts the build mid-way. The index is then never cached, so the same failure repeats on every request. This is the failure mode the PR says it fixes, and it remains on this path. The fixed size hint of 10 also always selects the memory-only index.

title: Removing the BuildIndex lock allows concurrent duplicate builds for the same key
body: BuildIndex no longer serializes builds: the lock was removed from the whole function and only the final cache write is locked. Nothing deduplicates concurrent builds for one key, and getOrCreateIndex's GetIndex-then-build sequence is not atomic. Two concurrent cold Search or watch-event calls for the same namespace now build two full indexes in parallel, roughly doubling memory and CPU. The second 'b.cache[key] = idx' silently replaces the first index, which is never closed. For file-backed indexes, the second bleve.New on the same directory races the first and can fail. The previous code built twice too, but serially. Use per-key singleflight or re-check under the lock.

title: TotalDocs iterates the cache map without holding cacheMu
body: TotalDocs ranges over b.cache with no lock, while GetIndex takes RLock and BuildIndex writes the map under Lock. The new log line in search.go init (line 216) calls TotalDocs after the watch goroutine has started (lines 207-213). That goroutine can call handleEvent, then getOrCreateIndex, then BuildIndex, which writes the map concurrently. A concurrent map iteration and write is a fatal runtime error in Go and cannot be recovered. TotalDocs should take cacheMu.RLock().

title: Data race on shared err and counter in the parallel init workers
body: Pre-existing, but it is in the function being edited. The errgroup closure assigns the outer function's err variable ('_, _, err = s.build(...)') and increments totalBatchesIndexed (line 189), and both run concurrently in up to initWorkers goroutines. That is an unsynchronized write from multiple goroutines, which the race detector flags and which can tear an interface value. The closure should use a local error (the return value already reaches group.Wait), and the counter should be atomic.

title: GetResourceStats never checks rows.Err, so a mid-iteration failure returns partial stats as success
body: The loop ends when rows.Next() returns false. If that was caused by an error (for example a dropped connection), rows.Err() holds it, but the code never checks it. The callback then returns err, which is nil at that point, and the function returns partial res with a nil error. search init then indexes only the namespaces that were read, logs success, and never retries. rows is also not closed on the early Scan-error return. Check rows.Err() after the loop and defer rows.Close().

title: Trace propagation fixed only in GetResourceStats; sibling methods still drop the span context
body: The PR says it fixes trace propagation, but only GetResourceStats was changed. WriteEvent (line 158), ReadResource (line 353) and ListIterator (line 388) still do '_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)' and then pass the parent ctx down. As a result the create, update and delete spans and the DB transaction spans are siblings of the wrapper span, not children. bleve.go BuildIndex (line 88) has the same pattern. Either finish the change in these methods or narrow the PR description.

title: Removing the Init gate from every RPC silently allows requests after Stop
body: Before this change, each RPC called s.Init, which returned s.initErr. Stop sets initErr to 'service is stopped', so every request after Stop was rejected. With the gates removed, initErr is dead state and RPCs keep being served after Stop, even though the broadcaster context has been cancelled. This behavior change is not mentioned in the PR. Either keep a stopped check in the RPCs or document the change.

title: Postgres skip removes the only startup test for the storage target in CI
body: The new skip disables the only test that exercises starting the storage-server target, for postgres, with a TODO and the reason 'Works locally'. This PR changes exactly that startup path, because Init now runs inside NewResourceServer. CI therefore has no coverage of the new startup behavior on postgres. The PR description does not mention this test change. Either fix the test or track the skip with an issue and explain why the change is safe.

title: NewResourceServer leaks its context and started goroutines when Init fails
body: The context and cancel func are created at line 229, but on the Init error path the constructor returns without calling s.cancel(). If initWatcher failed after the broadcaster started, its goroutines keep running on s.ctx. The lifecycle hooks, which may already have been initialized, are not stopped either. The same applies to the error return at line 254. Call s.cancel() (and stop the lifecycle) before returning the error.

title: Watcher goroutine dereferences nil event when the backend stops, panicking at shutdown
body: Pre-existing, but in the function being edited. When the backend stops, the poller returns and runs 'defer close(stream)'. The loop 'v := <-events' then receives nil forever, and handleEvent reads evt.Type on a nil pointer, which panics and crashes the process during shutdown. The same pattern exists in server.go initWatcher (around lines 762-765, where v.Type is read). Use 'v, ok := <-events' and return when !ok.

title: Build errors in init's errgroup closures are shared-variable races and can be silently dropped
body: The errgroup closure assigns to the outer `err` (declared at line 181) and increments the shared `totalBatchesIndexed` from up to `initWorkers` goroutines at once. The closure then does `return err`, which reads that shared variable, so a failing build's error can be overwritten by a concurrent successful build's nil. `init` then reports success while a namespace is missing from the index. `totalBatchesIndexed++` is also an unsynchronized write (lost updates, and the race detector flags it). This now runs inside NewResourceServer, which the code comments say must block startup on failure, so a swallowed error means a silently incomplete index. Use a closure-local error and an atomic counter.

title: Watch loop dereferences nil event when the events channel is closed, causing a panic
body: The loop does `v := <-events` and passes `v` to handleEvent without checking whether the channel is open. The SQL poller does `defer close(stream)` when the backend is stopped (b.done). After that, every receive yields nil, and handleEvent immediately reads `evt.Type` (line 226), which panics with a nil pointer dereference. The same pattern in server.go initWatcher (`v.Type` on a possibly nil v) panics too. The watch context is context.Background(), so this loop never exits on its own. Use `v, ok := <-events` and return when ok is false.

title: TotalDocs iterates the index cache without the lock, racing with BuildIndex writes
body: TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without taking cacheMu, while BuildIndex writes b.cache under cacheMu.Lock. This PR adds a new caller of TotalDocs in init (search.go line 216), which runs right after the watch goroutine has started. That goroutine can call getOrCreateIndex, then build, then BuildIndex, and write b.cache concurrently. A concurrent map iteration and write is a fatal runtime error that cannot be recovered. Take cacheMu.RLock() in TotalDocs.

title: Removing the BuildIndex lock allows concurrent duplicate builds for the same key with no dedupe
body: The whole-function lock was the only serialization in BuildIndex. GetIndex returns nil for concurrent first requests, so each one runs a full ListIterator build. For file-backed indexes (size above FileThreshold), two builds now call bleve.New on the same directory at the same time (line 98). Previously the second build ran after the first and failed cleanly on the existing path. Now the two can interleave on-disk creation and fail or leave a bad store. For memory indexes, the second build replaces the first in the cache, orphaning it, and the IndexTenants and IndexedKinds metrics are double counted. Add a per-key guard (the TODO in search.go mentions this) or re-check the cache under the lock.

title: Writes made during the initial index build are never indexed
body: init lists and builds each namespace first, and only afterwards calls WatchWriteEvents. The SQL WatchWriteEvents takes its starting point from the latest resource versions at subscription time (listLatestRVs), so any write committed after a namespace was read but before the subscription is never delivered to the index. The object stays missing from search until it is modified again. This PR makes the build window longer, since the whole build for all namespaces now runs synchronously at construction. The rv returned by build (line 309 onward) is computed for exactly this purpose but discarded here. Subscribe first, build, then replay events with a resource version above each namespace's list version.

title: Construction now performs DB init, full index build and watcher start synchronously, and can fail
body: NewResourceServer now synchronously runs lifecycle Init (DB open and ping), the full search index build for every namespace above the threshold, and starts the watcher. Any error makes construction fail. Previously this work happened on first RPC, so construction was cheap and a failure only affected calls. The consequences: the caller (module wiring) blocks for the entire build with no timeout (only Stop cancels, and that is not reached during startup); one bad namespace or a transient DB error prevents the whole storage module from starting; and any code that constructs a server before its DB or blob dependencies are ready now fails at construction. The PR asks what this could break, but the diff shows no update to callers and no bounded context for the build. This needs an explicit decision.

title: Stop no longer gates RPCs, since the Init calls that returned the stop error were removed
body: Stop stores 'service is stopping' or 'service is stopped' in s.initErr. Before this PR every RPC called s.Init, which returned that stored error, so calls after Stop failed fast. This PR removes every s.Init call from the handlers, so nothing reads initErr anymore. After Stop, Create, Update, Delete, Read, List and Search keep reaching the backend. backend.Stop only cancels the poller and does not close the DB. This silently removes the shutdown guard. If it is still needed, check a stopped flag in the handlers or in a shared helper.

title: Error path after the new Init call leaks started resources
body: If any step after the new Init call fails, NewResourceServer returns nil without calling cancel. The lifecycle backend may already be initialized, and search init may already have started the event goroutine (search.go line 207), which loops on a context.Background() watch forever. Nothing calls Stop on the discarded server. Call s.cancel() and the lifecycle Stop on the error path.

title: Span context is still discarded in WriteEvent, ReadResource and ListIterator
body: The PR is described as fixing trace propagation by passing span contexts down, but this file still discards the span context in WriteEvent (`_, span := b.tracer.Start(...)` followed by `b.create(ctx, event)`). ReadResource (line 353) and ListIterator (line 388) do the same. The WriteEvent span is therefore not the parent of the create, update or delete spans, and the DB spans attach to the request instead. Only GetResourceStats was fixed here. Use `ctx, span :=` in these functions.

title: Postgres skip disables the storage-server startup test without a tracked issue or mention in the description
body: A postgres branch is added that skips the only test in this file covering the storage-server startup path this PR changes. The skip has a TODO and no tracking issue, and the PR description does not mention disabling it. If construction-time init broke postgres startup, that regression is now hidden rather than fixed. Either fix the test or document the skip with an issue link in the description.

title: No tests cover the new construction-time failure and concurrency behaviour
body: The PR changes several behaviours without adding tests: NewResourceServer now returns an error when lifecycle init or the index build fails, RPCs no longer gate on initialization, and the BuildIndex lock was removed. Nothing checks that a failing index build makes NewResourceServer return an error, which would have caught the lost-error race in search.go. Nothing exercises concurrent BuildIndex and TotalDocs under the race detector, which would catch the cache races above.

title: Conditional passkey UI is no longer set up on the username-less login page
body: The guard `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())` returns false whenever no user is set, because the helper at line 161 requires `user != null`. Before this PR, passkey setup ran when `context.getUser() == null` (the first login page). This change inverts that: `fillContextForm` now runs only when a user is already set, which is the re-authentication case. The same inverted guard appears in `challenge(context, error, field)` at line 137. Consequence: on the initial login page the conditional-UI attributes are never set, so the 'username webauthn' autocomplete and the passkey form disappear, discoverable-key auto-login stops working, and invalid-username error pages lose passkeys. Existing and new tests that assert the first-page autocomplete and webauth form (e.g. PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest.webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey, passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey, and the first-page checks in PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest) would fail. Passkeys should be gated only on passkeys being enabled; the re-authentication case should be added on top of the existing null-user behavior, not replace it.

title: Call to isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments does not compile
body: `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` is called with no arguments, but the only definition in UsernamePasswordForm (the superclass) is `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)`, and no zero-argument overload exists in the class hierarchy shown. The services module will fail to compile. The call was probably meant to be `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`.

title: NoSuchElementException import is now unused
body: The two `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, ...)` calls were replaced in this PR, and no other use of `NoSuchElementException` remains in this file. The import is left dangling, which a checkstyle unused-import check would flag.

title: PasswordCredentialModel import added but never used
body: This PR adds the `org.keycloak.models.credential.PasswordCredentialModel` import, but nothing in the file references it. Unused imports are lint failures in this codebase.

title: Negative webauthn-form check swallows every exception, so it can pass vacuously
body: The check wraps `findElement` in `try { ... fail(...) } catch (Exception nsee) { // expected }`. Any exception, including a WebDriverException from a broken page or session, makes the assertion pass. The same pattern is repeated at line 315. The rest of the suite uses `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, ...)` or `driver.findElements(...).isEmpty()`, which would catch only the intended condition.

title: Test comment and name misattribute why passkeys are hidden
body: The comment says passkeys are not shown 'as this user does not have passkey', and the test is named reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey. But the test actually disables passkeys at realm level (line 282), and the production check is realm-only (isConditionalPasskeysEnabled checks the realm policy, not the user's credentials). As a result, no test covers a passkeys-enabled realm with a user who has no passkey, which is the case the name and comment describe.

title: SHOULD_DISPLAY_AUTHENTICATORS stays true for conditional UI when a user is set
body: WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator overrides only shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators to suppress the authenticator list. shouldDisplayAuthenticators (lines 147-149) still returns context.getUser() != null, so during re-authentication fillContextForm sets SHOULD_DISPLAY_AUTHENTICATORS=true while ALLOWED_AUTHENTICATORS is never set. Whether the template then renders an empty list or fails depends on the webauthn FTL, which is not in this diff. The override looks incomplete, and the template behavior should be checked.

title: Call to non-existent no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() breaks compilation
body: The new condition calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments. The only definition in this change is `protected boolean isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` in UsernamePasswordForm.java, and no no-arg overload exists in the class hierarchy. The `services` module will not compile, so the whole PR (including all the new tests) cannot build or run. The intended call is presumably `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`, which is already non-null inside this branch.

title: Re-auth skip is disabled for every user whenever passkeys are enabled in the realm
body: The shortcut that skips the username form during re-authentication is now bypassed for any user as soon as passkeys are enabled for the realm, regardless of whether that particular user has a passkey. A password-only user re-authenticating with prompt=login in a passkey-enabled realm is now shown the username page and must submit it, where previously they were skipped. The only new UsernameForm re-auth test uses a passkey-only user, so this regression for password-only users is not covered. If the intent is to only show the form when the user can use a passkey, the condition should check the user's passkey credentials rather than only the realm flag.

title: Negative webauthn-button check uses catch(Exception), so it can pass vacuously
body: In `reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey` (and again around line 312), the absence of the webauthn form is checked with `try { assertThat(driver.findElement(...), nullValue()); fail(...) } catch (Exception nsee) { }`. Any Exception thrown while looking up the element, such as a WebDriverException from a stale or not-yet-loaded page, is swallowed and the check passes without verifying anything. The same PR and file already use `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, ...)` for this kind of check, which only accepts the expected exception.

title: Unused import NoSuchElementException left behind
body: The two `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, ...)` uses were replaced by `MatcherAssert.assertThat(...)` in this PR, so the `org.openqa.selenium.NoSuchElementException` import is now unused. This can fail a checkstyle or unused-import check in the build.

title: Unused PasswordCredentialModel import added by this PR
body: The import `org.keycloak.models.credential.PasswordCredentialModel` is added in this PR, but nothing in the file references it (the new tests only use string/nullValue checks). It should be removed to keep the build's unused-import checks clean.

title: Call to nonexistent no-argument isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() breaks compilation
body: The condition calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments. The only definition in this PR (protected, in UsernamePasswordForm) takes a `UserModel` parameter, and no no-arg overload appears in the shown code. The services module will not compile, so nothing in the PR can be built or tested. It should pass the user, i.e. `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`, or use the helper as intended.

title: Passkey conditional UI is no longer set up on the initial login page
body: The passkey fill was moved out of the `user == null` branch and is now guarded by `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`. That helper (lines 160-162) returns `webauthnAuth != null && isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null`, so it is false whenever no user has been identified yet. The normal first login page therefore never gets `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm`, and the webauth form and 'username webauthn' autocomplete disappear. Existing tests that expect these on the first page will fail, e.g. PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest.passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey (around line 145-146) and PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest.passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey (line 192). The fill must run both when the user is unknown and when it is already set, so these call sites should check only `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()`.

title: Passkey UI dropped when the username/password challenge is re-rendered with an error and no user is set
body: `challenge(context, error, field)` now gates the webauthn fill with `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`, which is false when no user is set. Before this PR the fill ran exactly when `context.getUser() == null`. That is the case for an invalid username on the conditional-UI page, which reaches this method through testInvalidUser/getUserFromForm. After this change the error page is rendered without the webauthn setup, so the passkey autofill and 'username webauthn' autocomplete are lost after the first failed username. This is the same root cause as the line 115 regression and needs the same fix.

title: configureTestRealm() call has no definition visible in this change
body: `configureTestRealm(realmRepresentation)` is newly called here, but the method is neither defined in this file nor added by the diff. If it is not inherited from AbstractWebAuthnVirtualTest or another base class with a matching signature, the test module will not compile. This should be verified.

title: No test covers a failed passkey attempt during re-authentication
body: createErrorResponse now calls setupReauthenticationInUsernamePasswordFormError, which changes the page shown when a passkey fails for a user already set in the flow (username hidden, registration disabled). None of the added tests exercise this path. They cover wrong-password followed by passkey success, but never a failed passkey during a prompt=login re-authentication. A test should fail a passkey in that flow and assert the username field is hidden and the error is shown.

title: update() judges the 'before' state with the org-aware wrapper, so login-cache invalidation is skipped for IDPs of disabled orgs
body: update() gets idpById via getById(), which returns the organization-aware wrapper from createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel. That wrapper's isEnabled() returns false whenever the owning organization is disabled. So when the org is disabled, getLoginPredicate().test(original) is false even though the IDP is raw-enabled and its id is in the cached ORG_ONLY/ALL login lists (the DB query does not check org enablement). If the update then also makes the IDP non-login (hideOnLogin=true, linkOnly, BROKER_PUBLIC=false, or enabled=false), both predicates are false and registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate returns without invalidating. When the org is later re-enabled, getForLogin returns the stale entry; the wrapper now reports enabled, and OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean only re-checks isEnabled(), so a hidden or link-only IDP is shown on the login page. remove() avoids this by using the raw idpDelegate.getByAlias(), so the 'original' state should likewise come from the raw model (e.g. idpDelegate.getById) rather than the wrapped getById().

title: Cleanup removes an IDP named literally 'alias' instead of the IDPs created in the loop
body: The cleanup registers testRealm().identityProviders().get('alias')::remove, which targets a nonexistent provider with the literal alias 'alias', so the 'idp-alias-N' providers created in the loop are never removed (the same mistake is repeated at line 425 for 'idp-alias-20'). The leftover IDPs stay linked to the organization and can leak into other tests in the class or leave the cleanup itself failing with a 404. The cleanup should capture the actual alias in a final local and call get(thatAlias)::remove.

title: testCacheIDPForLogin never checks that creating or removing a login-eligible IDP invalidates the login caches
body: Step 1 only creates a hidden IDP and removes a disabled IDP, and asserts that the caches survive. Neither operation qualifies for login, so the registerIDPLoginInvalidation calls in create() and remove() are never shown to invalidate anything. A regression that drops those calls would pass this test. The test also has no scenario where the owning organization is disabled, which is the case where the wrapper changes login eligibility and where update() currently skips invalidation incorrectly. Add steps that create and remove a login-eligible IDP, and one that changes a linked IDP's login status while its org is disabled.

title: getForLogin Javadoc omits the new requirement that org-linked IDPs must be public
body: The Javadoc says an IDP can be used for login if it is enabled, not link-only, and not hidden on login. The PR adds to getLoginPredicate a rule that IDPs bound to an organization must have BROKER_PUBLIC=true, and the ORG_ONLY query filters on the same flag. Neither this Javadoc nor the LoginFilter enum documentation mentions it, so SPI implementers and callers reading the contract will not know that org-bound IDPs need the public flag to be listed for login.

title: Cache search key maps null and empty organizationId to the same entry, although the underlying queries differ
body: searchKey is computed as organizationId != null ? organizationId : "". The default getForLogin only adds the ORGANIZATION_ID criterion when organizationId is non-null, so a null argument (all organizations) and an empty-string argument (criterion applied with an empty value) are different queries. Both are cached under the same cacheKey and searchKey, so a call with one value can return the cached result of the other, depending on call order. No current caller passes an empty string, so the impact is latent, but the key construction is ambiguous. Use a distinct sentinel for the null case.

title: Login-cache invalidation on update evaluates the stored IDP through the org-aware wrapper, so updates to IDPs in a disabled org skip invalidation
body: In update(), `idpById` comes from getById(), which wraps the model in createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel. That wrapper's isEnabled() returns false whenever the bound organization is disabled, while `model` (the updated raw representation) reports the IDP's own enabled flag. For an IDP bound to a disabled org, getLoginPredicate().test(original) is therefore always false. The login lists are built from the JPA query, which does not consider org state, so such an IDP can be cached. If the update then disables it (or hides it / makes it link-only), both sides evaluate to false, registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate returns early, and the cached login list keeps the now-disabled IDP. A later getForLogin cache hit returns it; the uncached path would exclude it. The stale entry persists after the org is re-enabled. Callers that do not re-check isEnabled() will expose a disabled IDP. The login decision should use the raw stored model (e.g. idpDelegate.getById), not the org-aware wrapper.

title: Cleanup never removes the created IDPs (get("alias")::remove), leaking 21 IDPs into the shared test realm
body: `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` binds the method reference to a resource for the literal alias "alias", which does not exist. Each registered cleanup therefore targets a nonexistent IDP, and the idp-alias-0..20 providers created by this test are never deleted. The same bug exists at line 425 for idp-alias-20 and at line 303 in testCacheIDPByOrg, which this test copies. The leftover IDPs (several of them enabled, public, and linked to an organization) remain in the realm for later tests. Any test that asserts exact login or organization IDP counts can then fail depending on test execution order. The cleanup should reference each created alias.

title: getForLogin javadoc omits the new organization BROKER_PUBLIC requirement
body: The javadoc says an IDP can be used for login if it is enabled, not link-only, and not hidden on login. The getLoginPredicate() change in this PR adds a further rule: an IDP bound to an organization must also have BROKER_PUBLIC=true to qualify. The public contract documented here is now incomplete, and callers of getForLogin cannot learn the rule from the interface.

title: REALM_ONLY lookups get separate cache entries per organizationId even though the organization is ignored
body: searchKey is derived from organizationId for every mode. For FetchMode.REALM_ONLY the delegate ignores organizationId, so getForLogin(REALM_ONLY, orgA) and getForLogin(REALM_ONLY, null) produce identical results but are stored under different searchKeys in the same IdentityProviderListQuery. The same realm-only list is duplicated per distinct organization id that is passed in. Normalising searchKey to "" for REALM_ONLY would avoid the duplicate entries.

title: No test covers the invalidation cases the new BROKER_PUBLIC predicate and org disable handling exist for
body: The new `idp.getOrganizationId() == null || BROKER_PUBLIC` clause in getLoginPredicate() is only exercised indirectly. Step 4 links a realm-level login IDP to an organization, but nothing checks that flipping BROKER_PUBLIC from true to false on an organization-bound login IDP invalidates the login caches. Nothing covers an IDP bound to a disabled organization either, which is the case where the stored-state evaluation in update() goes wrong. Regressions in either path would leave stale login lists undetected.

title: Login-cache invalidation on update evaluates the stored IdP through the org-aware wrapper
body: update() obtains `idpById` via getById() (line 91), which returns the model wrapped by createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel. That wrapper's isEnabled() returns false whenever the linked organization (or the OrganizationProvider) is disabled. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() then runs getLoginPredicate() on this wrapper, but the login caches were built from raw DB rows where org state is irrelevant. Consequence: for an enabled, public IdP linked to a disabled org, an update that makes it not login-eligible (e.g. setHideOnLogin(true) or setLinkOnly(true)) gives test(original)=false and test(updated)=false, so no invalidation is registered. The cached ALL/ORG_ONLY lists still contain the IdP id. The consumer (OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean) only re-checks isEnabled(), not hideOnLogin/linkOnly, and enabling an org does not invalidate login caches. Once the org is re-enabled, the hidden IdP is shown on the login page. The original state should be taken from the raw stored model (not the org-aware wrapper) before evaluating the predicate.

title: Test cleanup removes the literal alias "alias", so the 20 IdPs created in testCacheIDPForLogin leak
body: The cleanup `testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove` (copied from the pre-existing testCacheIDPByOrg) never references the IdP that was created (`"idp-alias-" + i`). The 20 IdPs therefore remain in the realm after the test, and 10 of them (idp-alias-10..19) stay linked to orga. testCacheIDPByOrg asserts exact membership counts for orga (e.g. 6) and the new test asserts exact login counts, so their results depend on JUnit method execution order and can fail once the other runs first. The cleanup should reference the created alias.

title: Cache search key conflates null and "" organizationId, which the delegate treats differently
body: searchKey maps both null and "" to "". The delegate's default getForLogin only adds the ORGANIZATION_ID filter when organizationId != null. With null, ORG_ONLY/ALL return IdPs of any organization. With "", it adds an explicit ORGANIZATION_ID="" filter with different results. Because both share the same cache slot, a result computed for one input can be served for the other. Use a key that distinguishes null from the empty string.

title: remove() now always performs a DB lookup of the IdP
body: `idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)` was moved out of the `isInvalid(cacheKey)` branch, so every remove() now issues an extra DB query even when the alias entry is served from cache. The result is needed only for the new login invalidation and for the invalid branch. The lookup could be deferred or the cached model could be used for the login check.

title: No test covers invalidation when a login-eligible IdP is created or removed
body: testCacheIDPForLogin only creates a hidden IdP (line 424) and removes a disabled IdP (line 428). Both are paths where login caches must NOT be invalidated. The new registerIDPLoginInvalidation calls in create() and remove() for IdPs that are actually login-eligible are never exercised, so a regression there would go unnoticed. Also untested is the scenario where an org-linked IdP's login eligibility changes while its organization is disabled, which is where the wrapper-based classification in update() goes wrong.

title: Equal-order crypto providers are now resolved silently by classpath order, including FIPS vs default
body: detectProvider now sorts by order() descending and takes the first entry. The old guard that threw 'Multiple crypto providers loaded' was removed, but no tie-breaking rule was added. DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider and WildFlyElytronProvider all return order() == 200. If two of them are on the classpath, the winner is whichever ServiceLoader lists first, with no error or warning. In a FIPS deployment where the non-FIPS default provider jar is also present, this can silently select the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider. The javadoc for order() in CryptoProvider does not say what happens on ties. Also, every discovered provider is instantiated before selection. FIPS1402Provider's constructor inserts BCFIPS and BCJSSE into the global java.security provider list and modifies security properties, so those side effects happen even when the provider is not selected. Previously this configuration failed fast.

title: New abstract order() method breaks every existing CryptoProvider implementation
body: order() is added as an abstract interface method with no default implementation. Any CryptoProvider implementation not updated in this PR, including out-of-tree providers and any in-repo test or helper implementations not shown in the diff, will fail to compile. A default method (for example returning 0) would keep the SPI source-compatible while still letting providers override the priority.

title: Every AuthzClient.create() now requires CryptoProvider SPI discovery to succeed
body: create(Configuration) now calls CryptoIntegration.init(...) unconditionally. Before this change, a plain token or HTTP client needed no crypto provider. Now, if ServiceLoader finds no CryptoProvider, init throws IllegalStateException and client construction fails even for non-ECDSA use. This can happen when the authz-client jar's META-INF/services entry is dropped by a shade or fat-jar build, or when the classloader does not expose it. Initialization is also process-wide and first-wins, so the first AuthzClient created fixes the JVM-wide provider for every other library. Consider initializing lazily only on the ECDSA signing path, or handling discovery failure.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns an unrelated JDK keystore provider, not BouncyCastle
body: The method returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is typically the SUN provider for PKCS12/JKS. The CryptoProvider contract documents this method as returning the BouncyCastle provider. Any caller that uses it to register or look up the BC provider silently gets the wrong provider. The other unimplemented methods in this class throw UnsupportedOperationException, so this is also inconsistent with the class's own pattern. It should throw UnsupportedOperationException, or return the real BC provider if one is available.

title: ECDSA test uses a P-256 key for ES384/ES512 and only checks a round-trip
body: The key pair is always generated with the default EC size (P-256), including for the ES384 and ES512 cases. For ES512 the coordinates are then only 32 bytes, so the 66-byte coordinate path in integerToBytes is only exercised with padding and never with real P-521 values. The test also only asserts that RS -> DER -> RS is the identity. It never verifies that the DER produced by concatenatedRSToASN1DER is accepted by java.security.Signature.verify, and never checks an independently produced DER signature. A bug where both directions are wrong in a consistent way would still pass. The test should generate a curve matching each algorithm (P-256/P-384/P-521) and verify the reconstructed DER signature with the JDK verifier.

title: Code appears adapted from Bouncy Castle without attribution
body: The readTagNumber/readLength logic and comments, such as the quotation of X.690 8.1.2.4.2 and the 'Note: -1 will pass' comment, look taken from Bouncy Castle's ASN1InputStream. ASN1Encoder.writeLength looks similarly derived from DEROutputStream. Bouncy Castle is MIT-licensed. If this code is adapted, the source's license notice and attribution must be kept.
