body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin sets up codes in user storage and logs in once with the first code. It does not check that a wrong code is rejected, that a used code cannot be reused, that exhausting all codes forces regeneration, or that the local-DB fallback still works when the user has no federated codes. The reuse and exhaustion gaps are exactly where the user-storage path differs from the local path, so the test would not catch the replay and cleanup problems in this change.

title: Plaintext recovery codes are persisted in user storage
body: createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generated codes into a JSON array and passes that as the credential value to user storage via updateCredential. The local path does not do this: RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode and verifyRecoveryCodeInput (which compares against a hashed saved code) show that local storage keeps only hashes. Recovery codes act as a second factor that bypasses OTP/WebAuthn, so after this change they sit in plaintext in whatever external store backs the user storage (LDAP attribute, external DB). Anyone with read access to that store can obtain usable recovery codes for the user. The codes should be hashed before leaving Keycloak, or the trade-off should be explicitly justified and documented.

title: Exhausted federated recovery-code credential is never removed
body: getCredential now returns credentials from user storage first. When all codes are used, this calls removeStoredCredentialById with the id of that credential. removeStoredCredentialById only operates on the local store (and on user-storage providers that implement UserCredentialStore). For a federated credential the call is a silent no-op, so the spent credential stays in user storage. The CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is still added, but the spent credential is not cleaned up for user-storage-backed users. The test provider does not implement UserCredentialStore and keeps returning the credential. No test covers this path.

title: Undocumented, asymmetric data format for user-storage recovery codes
body: updateCredential receives a JSON array of raw codes (CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential). But getCredential passes whatever the provider returns from getCredentials into RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel (RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator around line 83 and RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean line 19), which expects the local serialized model. The test provider has to convert its stored list via createFromValues inside getCredentials to make this work. Nothing documents this contract for SPI implementers. A provider that returns the stored credential data unchanged, the natural round trip, will likely fail to parse at login or make the login bean throw.

title: Reference provider never consumes recovery codes; single-use is untested
body: The recovery branch of isValid returns true for any stored code and never removes or marks it as used, so this reference provider accepts the same recovery code indefinitely. The new test logs in once with code 0 and never checks that a reused code is rejected or that the next login asks for a different code. Single-use behaviour for user-storage recovery codes is therefore untested, and the provider silently demonstrates the wrong semantics for anyone copying it.

title: Class Javadoc claims this is an unchanged 4.8.3 fixture
body: The Javadoc says this is the Keycloak 4.8.3 implementation and that future versions should work without any change to this provider. This PR adds recovery-code support to the class, a credential type 4.8.3 never had. The comment is now wrong, and the class no longer serves as a frozen 4.8.3 compatibility baseline.

title: Switching to user storage leaves stale local recovery-code credentials
body: When updateCredential succeeds, the local recovery-codes credential is not removed. getCredential then prefers the federated credential, so any previously created local set becomes unreachable for authentication, but it remains in the local store and in stored-credential listings. Regenerating codes after user storage starts supporting the type leaves duplicate, dead recovery credentials.

title: Recovery codes held in user storage are never consumed, so they can be replayed
body: isValid for RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE only checks whether the submitted code is in the stored list and never removes or marks it as used. The core RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator (lines 80-92) decides when to retire the credential and force regeneration solely from the credential's allCodesUsed() state. For a federated credential that state is rebuilt from the raw stored list by getCredentials (new model, no used-state), so allCodesUsed() can never become true. The result is that a recovery code which logged a user in once keeps working indefinitely, while the local provider consumes codes. Nothing in the core flow writes used-state back to user storage either. The new test performs only one successful login and never attempts a second use, so this goes undetected.

title: Recovery codes are sent to user storage in plaintext while local storage keeps only hashes
body: generatedCodes are the raw codes shown to the user. They are serialized to JSON and passed unhashed to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...), so any external user storage provider (LDAP, a custom DB) persists usable bearer login secrets. The local path stores only RS512 hashes (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues hashes via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode). A read of the external store therefore yields directly usable recovery codes, and the test provider compares raw strings. Either hash the codes before handing them to user storage (and hash the input on verification) or explicitly document and accept the difference.

title: New recovery-codes test covers only the happy path
body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin sets up codes, logs in once with code 0 and stops. It does not check that a wrong code is rejected, that a used code cannot be reused (which the user-storage path currently fails, see the isValid comment), that the stored codes are visible through the account/admin credential APIs (the new getCredentials override is not exercised), or that the local fallback still works when a storage provider does not support recovery codes. The reuse gap in particular is exactly what this test should catch.

title: getCredentials dereferences a possibly null MyUser
body: getMyUser(user) returns null when the user is not in the users map, and getCredentials immediately dereferences myUser.recoveryCodes and myUser.otp with no null check. The sibling methods getDisableableCredentialTypesStream and isConfiguredFor guard against this case, so this one throws NullPointerException where the others return empty results.

title: supportsCredentialType throws NPE for a null type
body: The previous implementation was null-safe (CredentialModel.PASSWORD.equals(null) and isOTPType(null) return false). The new clause credentialType.equals(RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE) is evaluated for a null argument and throws NullPointerException instead of logging and returning false. Comparing against the constant (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE.equals(credentialType)) would avoid this.

title: Recovery codes in user storage cannot be disabled or listed as disableable
body: disableCredentialType only handles OTP and logs 'Unsupported' for anything else, and getDisableableCredentialTypesStream never includes the recovery type. Admin disable-credential requests for a federated user therefore silently leave the stored recovery codes in place, and the admin API does not offer them as disableable. The local path supports revoking these codes, so the behaviour is inconsistent with the feature being added.

title: userLabel and generatedAt are silently dropped in the user-storage branch
body: The credentialModel passed in carries the user-provided userLabel and the generatedAt timestamp, and the local branch persists them. The user-storage branch builds only a UserCredentialModel from the type and the JSON codes, so these values are discarded. The test provider then stamps createdDate with the current time and has no label. Users who set a label or check creation dates will see different metadata depending on where the codes ended up, without any indication.

title: Same concurrent-deletion NPE remains in the getSubGroupsStream overloads
body: The PR guards only getSubGroupsCount(). The three paged/searching getSubGroupsStream overloads at lines 256, 262 and 268 still call modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...) with no null check. When the group has been deleted in the database but the cache has not yet been invalidated, modelSupplier.get() returns null and these methods throw the same NullPointerException the PR is meant to fix. The issue is only partly fixed unless these are guarded too.

title: getSubGroupsCount silently returns null instead of a count or an error
body: The NPE is replaced by a null Long. Callers that unbox the result (for example comparisons or arithmetic on getSubGroupsCount()) will now fail with a different NPE far from the cause. The rest of this adapter treats the same condition, a group that is missing from the database, as IllegalStateException("Not found in database") (lines 61 and 74). The behaviour is also inconsistent: when `invalidated` is true, isUpdated() throws, but in the window before invalidation this method returns null. Throwing the same IllegalStateException here, or otherwise defining the contract for a missing group, would be consistent.

title: parentModel can be null in populateGroupHierarchyFromSubGroups and is still dereferenced
body: Line 47 fetches the parent with session.groups().getGroupById(...), which returns null if the parent was deleted concurrently. The null is then passed to groupEvaluator.canView(parentModel) (line 51), to toRepresentation(groupEvaluator, parentModel, full) inside computeIfAbsent (line 57) and to populateSubGroupCount(parentModel, parent) (line 60). The last two dereference it, so this is the same concurrent-access NPE class the PR claims to fix, left unhandled in the group listing path this PR touches.

title: Reader thread is never joined, so the test can pass with exceptions still pending
body: The reader thread is started at line 139 and never joined. After deletedAll.set(true) at line 155, the assertion at line 157 runs immediately. A request that is in flight when the flag is set can still fail and add to caughtExceptions after the assertion has already passed, so the test can report success when the bug is present. The thread should be joined before asserting on caughtExceptions.

title: Stop flag is set outside try/finally and the reader is a non-daemon thread
body: If any groups().group(...).remove() call in the loop at lines 152-154 throws, deletedAll.set(true) at line 155 is never reached. The reader thread then loops forever, hitting the server with no delay, and as a non-daemon thread it keeps the test JVM alive, so a single failure can hang the whole test run. The stop signal should be set in a finally block, the thread should be a daemon or be joined, and the reader should be stopped on failure.

title: Regression test depends on an unguaranteed race and may not reproduce the NPE
body: The NPE needs the reader to hit the window where a group is deleted in the database but still present in the cache, and nothing here forces that interleaving or confirms that the brief listing reaches getSubGroupsCount(). Without the fix the test can still pass on most runs, so it is not a reliable guard. A deterministic check, for example a run-on-server test that removes the group in a second session while the adapter is held, would catch the regression reliably.

title: Paged subgroup listing still dereferences a possibly-null model
body: getSubGroupsStream(search, firstResult, maxResults) calls modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...) with no null check. The supplier resolves to null when another request has deleted the group, which is the race this PR targets, so this still throws the same NPE. The same unguarded pattern appears at lines 262 and 268 in the other two paged overloads. Only getSubGroupsCount was guarded, so the reported bug is only partly fixed.

title: Deleted group silently reports a null subgroup count
body: The NPE is replaced by returning null from a method whose contract is a count. The missing group is swallowed here and the null propagates into representations (populateSubGroupCount assigns it directly). Callers that unbox the Long or compare it will now throw NPE far from the cause. Other methods in this adapter throw IllegalStateException('Not found in database') when the group is gone, so behavior is inconsistent. Pick one defined behavior and document it on GroupModel.

title: Null guard in getRoleMappings tests the supplier instead of the group
body: The check 'if (group == null)' tests the Supplier<GroupModel> parameter. GroupAdapter always passes its non-null modelSupplier, so the guard never fires. When the underlying group has been deleted, the supplier returns null, and that null reaches the lazy loader. The comment describes exactly the case this guard was meant to handle, so the intended protection is missing and the PR does not address it. The check should be on group.get() == null before calling the loader.

title: getAttributes and getSubGroups have no null handling for a deleted group
body: Unlike getRoleMappings, getAttributes (lines 66-68) and getSubGroups (lines 90-92) pass the supplier straight to DefaultLazyLoader. The loaders at lines 55 and 57 dereference the source (source.getAttributes(), source.getSubGroupsStream()). Assuming the loader runs on the supplied source when the value is not yet loaded, a group deleted before its first attribute or subgroup access makes the supplier return null and the loader throws NPE. That affects getFirstAttribute, getAttributes, getAttributeStream and getSubGroupsStream() in GroupAdapter, so the concurrent NPE remains reachable.

title: Parent lookup result used without a null check during hierarchy build
body: session.groups().getGroupById(realm, currGroup.getParentId()) returns null if the parent was deleted between listing and this lookup. parentModel is then passed to groupEvaluator.canView(parentModel) at line 51 (when admin permissions are off), to toRepresentation inside computeIfAbsent at line 57, and to populateSubGroupCount(parentModel, parent) at line 60, which calls getSubGroupsCount() on null. This is the same concurrent-deletion NPE in the group listing path, and the PR edits this file without handling it. A null check that drops the orphaned child or skips the parent is needed.

title: Reader thread is not joined, so late failures are ignored
body: deletedAll is set and the assertion runs at line 157 without joining the reader thread started at line 139. The reader may still be inside an in-flight request, and any exception it records after the assertion is evaluated is never checked. The test can therefore pass despite the failure it is meant to catch. The thread should be joined, with a timeout, before asserting.

title: Exception during deletion leaves a non-daemon busy-looping thread running
body: If group(...).remove() at line 153 throws (for example a 500 from the bug under test), the exception escapes the forEach and deletedAll.set(true) at line 155 never runs. The reader thread (lines 139-149) then loops forever issuing HTTP requests. As a non-daemon thread it also keeps the JVM alive, so the run hangs instead of failing cleanly. The flag should be set in a finally block, and the reader should be a daemon or be stopped explicitly.

title: Race-based test may not reproduce the NPE and has no deterministic interleaving
body: The NPE requires a cached adapter with a loaded group, a concurrent deletion, and then a lazy access. This test depends on timing between one reader thread and 100 sequential deletes, and it only asserts that no exception reached the client. Nothing shows it fails on the base commit, so it may pass without the fix. The author should confirm it reproduces the failure without the change, or drive the interleaving deterministically (for example by deleting the group on the server between the read and the access).

title: Reader thread spins on HTTP requests with no pause
body: The reader loop at lines 139-149 issues back-to-back list requests over 100 groups for the whole deletion phase with no sleep or backoff. This saturates the shared test server, slows the test, and adds load that can cause timeouts on CI. A short pause between iterations would avoid this.

title: Same concurrent-deletion NPE remains in the paged/searched subgroup methods
body: The fix only guards getSubGroupsCount(). Three sibling methods still dereference modelSupplier.get() without a null check: getSubGroupsStream(search, firstResult, maxResults) at line 256, getSubGroupsStream(firstResult, maxResults) at line 262, and getSubGroupsStream(search, exact, firstResult, maxResults) at line 268. If the group was deleted concurrently, isUpdated() is false (the adapter was not invalidated), modelSupplier.get() returns null, and the call throws NullPointerException. This is the same race the PR claims to fix, so the issue is only partially resolved.

title: Parent lookup can return null and is then dereferenced in the hierarchy builder
body: At line 47 parentModel comes from session.groups().getGroupById(...) and can be null if the parent was deleted concurrently. It is then used unguarded: at line 51 in canView(parentModel) when admin permissions are disabled; at line 57 in toRepresentation(groupEvaluator, parentModel, full) when the parent is not yet in the map; and at line 60 in populateSubGroupCount(parentModel, parent), which calls group.getSubGroupsCount() whenever subGroupsCount is true, even when the parent was already in the map. Each of these is an NPE in the same concurrent-access scenario the PR targets. The PR edits this file (only removing an unused helper) but does not add a null check here.

title: getAttributes and getSubGroups lack the null-supplier guard that getRoleMappings has
body: getRoleMappings (lines 70-76) returns an empty set when the group supplier is null, with a comment about groups not being loaded. getAttributes (lines 66-68) and getSubGroups (lines 90-92) pass the supplier straight to DefaultLazyLoader. If the group has been deleted and the value is not yet loaded, the loader will call methods such as source.getAttributes() or source.getSubGroupsStream() on null. This reaches GroupAdapter.getAttributes, getFirstAttribute, getAttributeStream and getSubGroupsStream() (line 240) through the same concurrent-deletion race, and the PR does not guard it. This assumes the loader dereferences the supplied source without a null check, which the guard in getRoleMappings suggests.

title: Missing group now yields null count while sibling paths throw IllegalStateException
body: For a group deleted concurrently, getSubGroupsCount now silently returns null (line 275). In the invalidated path, isUpdated() at lines 73-74 throws IllegalStateException("Not found in database") for the same situation, so the class handles concurrent deletion inconsistently. A null Long is also not a count, so any caller that unboxes the result (for example, comparing it with > 0) will still throw NullPointerException. The change moves the NPE rather than defining the contract for a missing group.

title: Reader thread is not joined before the assertion, and not stopped on failure
body: The reader thread (lines 139-149) is never joined. The assertion at line 157 runs right after deletedAll.set(true) at line 155, so any exception from a read still in flight when the flag is set is never checked, and the test can pass despite an NPE. Also, the flag is set only on the happy path. If remove() at line 153 throws, deletedAll is never set, the reader loops forever against the server on a non-daemon thread, and the test fails without cleanup. Wrap the deletions in try/finally that sets the flag and joins the thread before asserting.

title: Test depends on timing and does not deterministically reproduce the NPE
body: The NPE is a race between a group lookup and a concurrent deletion. The test only has a chance to catch it if the reader thread happens to hit the window while groups are being removed. It can pass on unfixed code, and nothing targets getSubGroupsCount or the subgroup overloads specifically. A deterministic regression test, for example a run-on-server test that obtains a group adapter, deletes the group in another session, and then calls getSubGroupsCount and getSubGroupsStream, would show the fix works and would cover the other unguarded paths.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator applies math.floor/ceil to a datetime key and raises TypeError
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator inherits BasePaginator's cursor machinery but overrides get_item_key with math.floor/math.ceil on getattr(item, self.key). The endpoint uses order_by="-datetime", so self.key is "datetime" and the value is a datetime object, which math.floor rejects with TypeError. build_cursor calls key(results[0]) whenever the first page has results, so every request with optimized_pagination=true from an admin that returns at least one audit log row fails with a 500. Unlike DateTimePaginator, this class also lacks the strftime-to-milliseconds conversion, and value_from_cursor returns the raw integer, so cursors could not be used for datetime comparisons even if the TypeError were avoided. The new code path cannot work for its only intended use.

title: Negative-offset branch always fails inside Django slicing and is reachable from user input
body: The 'advanced' branch passes a negative cursor.offset directly into queryset[start_offset:stop]. Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ rejects negative indices with ValueError('Negative indexing is not supported.'), so this branch never returns data. The offset comes from Cursor.from_string, which accepts any integer from the request's cursor parameter (cursors.py line 59). An admin who sends an opted-in request with a cursor such as 0:-1:0 gets a 500 instead of a 400. The comment says the branch gives access to data beyond normal bounds, which it does not do. Negative offsets are never validated, so the branch is dead code that also turns malformed input into a server error.

title: Base paginator silently clamps negative next-cursor offsets for all paginators
body: BasePaginator.get_result now uses start_offset = max(0, offset) for next cursors but leaves prev cursors unclamped. This shared base class is used by DateTimePaginator, which the audit log endpoint uses on every default request, so the change alters behavior well beyond the opt-in path. A forged next cursor with a negative offset is now silently served from the start of the result set instead of failing, while a forged prev cursor with a negative offset still raises from Django slicing. Invalid input is now accepted inconsistently. The inline comment that this is 'safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions' is wrong: the queryset rejects negative slices, and the clamp is what changes the outcome. The existing code validates offsets elsewhere (for example the `if self.offset < 0` checks in other paginators), so this should be an explicit validation or be reverted.

title: enable_advanced dereferences organization_context.member, which may be None, on every request
body: enable_advanced is evaluated unconditionally, not only when optimized_pagination=true. RpcUserOrganizationContext.member is optional. For a caller that is not a superuser and has no organization membership record (for example a non-member who passes OrganizationAuditPermission through another grant), `organization_context.member.has_global_access` raises AttributeError, so the whole endpoint returns a 500, including the default pagination path that previously worked. Guard the access with `organization_context.member is not None`, or evaluate the flag only when use_optimized is true.

title: Comment claims permissions are enforced at the queryset level, which this branch does not do
body: The comment says 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level'. Nothing in this branch checks permissions. The endpoint's permission class has already run, and the queryset is only filtered by organization_id. The comment justifies a deliberately wider access path, which would mislead future maintainers into treating unchecked negative-offset access as vetted. The claim should be removed, and the branch should be removed unless a real use case is demonstrated.

title: The 'optimized' path issues the same query as the default path, so it gives no performance benefit
body: The opted-in branch uses the same queryset, ordering, and slicing as DateTimePaginator. The only differences are the broken get_item_key and the unreachable negative-offset branch. The PR title and comments claim high-performance, efficient traversal, but no query, index, or benchmark change supports that. The PR description is just 'Test 1', so there is no stated rationale or measurement. The comments and title should not claim a performance gain unless one is demonstrated.

title: Comment says negative cursor offsets are supported, but nothing validates or handles them
body: The added comments state that negative offsets are allowed and 'enable efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions'. The change here is only a comment, and Cursor accepts whatever int() returns, including values parsed from untrusted request input via from_string. The paginators either raise on negative slices or silently clamp them, so the comment describes behavior that does not exist and documents an input the server never validates. Remove the comment or add real validation.

title: New paginator, new query parameter, and changed base behavior have no tests
body: The PR adds a public experimental query parameter (optimized_pagination), a new OptimizedCursorPaginator class with its own get_result and get_item_key, and changes BasePaginator.get_result, which every DateTimePaginator caller relies on. No tests are added or updated. A single request from an admin with at least one audit log row would have exposed the TypeError in get_item_key. Tests should cover: the opted-in admin path with rows, the non-admin fallback to DateTimePaginator, the member-less caller case, and how negative cursor offsets are handled on both the next and prev paths.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor/ceil to a datetime, crashing any non-empty page
body: The endpoint sends `order_by="-datetime"` to this paginator, so `getattr(item, self.key)` returns a `datetime` for each AuditLogEntry. `math.floor()`/`math.ceil()` raise TypeError on a datetime. `build_cursor` calls this key function on the results, so with `optimized_pagination=true` every organization that has at least one audit entry gets a 500. Only the empty-result case avoids the call. DateTimePaginator.get_item_key avoids this by converting the datetime to a millisecond epoch value. This class did not copy that logic, so it cannot serve its only use case. Subclassing DateTimePaginator or porting its conversion would fix it.

title: value_from_cursor returns the raw integer cursor value, which is then bound against a DateTimeField
body: DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor converts the millisecond cursor value back into a timezone-aware datetime. This class returns `cursor.value` unchanged. `build_queryset` then appends that int to the `extra(where=...)` params against `auditlogentry.datetime`, so any request carrying a next/prev cursor either fails at the database (timestamp compared with integer) or fails Django's DateTimeField validation. Pagination past the first page cannot work on this path.

title: Negative cursor offset is passed straight into a queryset slice, which Django rejects
body: When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, `start_offset` is the raw negative offset and `queryset[start_offset:stop]` is evaluated. Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative start indices and raises an error, so the request returns a 500. The branch that is supposed to reach data beyond normal pagination bounds therefore never returns data. A user can reach this with any crafted cursor string whose offset is negative, provided the advanced flag is set.

title: Comments justify exposing data beyond pagination bounds on the claim that queryset-level checks exist, which is false
body: The comments at lines 878-879 say the negative-offset branch 'enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds' and that this 'is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level'. The queryset here is only filtered by organization_id (organization_auditlogs.py line 48). The role check that enables the mode is in the endpoint (line 71). Nothing checks permissions at the queryset level. The intent is a privilege-gated path that widens what an admin can reach, and its safety argument is wrong and unreviewed. The branch should be removed or its authorization model explicitly designed and documented.

title: Negative offsets are silently clamped to 0 in BasePaginator for every paginator, not only the new one
body: The change to `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` affects BasePaginator.get_result, which DateTimePaginator, Paginator and every other cursor paginator inherit. It is not gated by the new query parameter. Before this change, a non-prev cursor with a negative offset (reachable through Cursor.from_string) raised a slicing error. Now it silently returns the first page with a cursor built from the original negative offset. The comment at lines 179-181 says negative offsets are being allowed, but the code does the opposite, clamping them. The comment and the global behavior change both need to be reconsidered, and the change should be separated from this feature.

title: organization_context.member is dereferenced without a None check
body: RpcUserOrganizationContext.member is optional, since a requester may not be a member of the organization. The expression `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` only avoids the dereference when the user is a superuser. For any other requester with no membership record, this raises AttributeError and returns a 500. Whether OrganizationAuditPermission guarantees membership for non-superusers is not visible in this diff, so this needs a None guard or a confirmed invariant.

title: Privileged mode is gated on the raw is_superuser flag rather than an active superuser session
body: The gate uses `request.user.is_superuser` directly. Sentry's superuser pattern normally checks an elevated, session-scoped superuser state (for example via is_active_superuser(request)). Using the raw user flag can grant the advanced mode to a superuser who has not elevated in this session. The impact is limited while the advanced path is broken, but the gate should follow the codebase's superuser convention.

title: Comment claims a Cursor behavior change that the diff does not make
body: The added comment says the Cursor now 'allows negative offsets ... enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets'. The code line below it, `self.offset = int(offset)`, is unchanged. The class already accepted negative offsets, and nothing in the change makes pagination more efficient. The comment documents a nonexistent optimization and should be removed.

title: New paginator, query-parameter path and negative-offset behavior change have no tests
body: The PR adds OptimizedCursorPaginator, a new `optimized_pagination` branch in the endpoint, an advanced-features gate, and a global change to BasePaginator offset handling, but adds no tests. The first basic use (one page of audit entries with the param set) crashes, as described in the get_item_key and value_from_cursor findings. A simple endpoint test would have caught it. Tests are also needed for the default DateTimePaginator path, which the BasePaginator change now affects.

title: PR description is a placeholder and the 'performance' framing is unsupported
body: The description is only 'Test 1', so nothing explains why the endpoint gets an undocumented `optimized_pagination` query parameter or who it is for. The code comments at lines 68-75 call this a performance optimization, but the optimized branch issues the same ORM queries as DateTimePaginator (its only real difference is the broken negative-offset branch), and no measurements are included. The title and comments overstate what the change does.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes with TypeError on every non-empty datetime page
body: get_item_key copies the numeric logic from Paginator: `value = getattr(item, self.key)` followed by `math.floor(value)` / `math.ceil(value)`. The endpoint sorts by `-datetime`, so self.key is 'datetime' and the value is a datetime.datetime. math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError. build_cursor calls this key on the first result whenever a page has any rows (via _build_next_values), so with `?optimized_pagination=true` from a superuser or global-access user, every non-empty audit log page returns a 500. DateTimePaginator avoids this by converting to a millisecond timestamp. value_from_cursor here also returns the raw cursor integer, which build_queryset would compare against a datetime column even if the key function worked. The optimized path is unusable as written.

title: Negative cursor offsets are passed straight to queryset slicing and raise
body: On the enable_advanced_features branch, `start_offset = cursor.offset` can be negative and is used in `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django QuerySet does not support negative indexing and raises ('Negative indexing is not supported'), so any cursor with a negative offset produces a 500. The cursor comes from the client-supplied query string, so an admin can trigger this by crafting a cursor. The comments at lines 876 and 878-879 say Django 'properly handles negative slicing automatically' and that this grants access 'beyond normal pagination bounds'; both claims are false, and the advertised behavior never works.

title: Shared BasePaginator silently clamps negative next-page offsets, leaving cursor arithmetic inconsistent
body: For next-page cursors, the query now starts at max(0, offset), but build_cursor still receives the raw negative cursor.offset. When the key value is unchanged, _build_next_values computes next_offset = offset + limit from the negative value. The returned page therefore starts at row 0 while the next cursor is computed as if it started at a negative position, so consecutive pages can overlap. Before this change such cursors raised an error; now they return wrong pages silently. BasePaginator is shared by DateTimePaginator, Paginator and every other endpoint using them, so this changes behavior well beyond the audit log endpoint. The change is also not a performance optimization, and no tests cover it.

title: Advanced pagination gated on bare User.is_superuser instead of an active superuser session
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` checks the User model flag directly. Sentry gates superuser behavior on an active superuser session (is_active_superuser(request)), so this bypasses the session-level elevation check. It also introduces a new authorization decision (superuser or global-access member unlocks a different paginator and negative-offset handling) outside the endpoint's permission class, controlled by a client-supplied `optimized_pagination` query parameter.

title: New pagination path and gating logic have no tests and the PR description is empty
body: The PR adds a new paginator class, a new query-parameter switch, a superuser/global-access gate, and changes to the shared BasePaginator offset handling, but adds no tests. The description is just 'Test 1'. A single test requesting `optimized_pagination=true` with a non-empty audit log would have exposed the datetime TypeError in OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key. Tests should also cover negative cursor offsets, permission gating for non-admin members, and the unchanged default DateTimePaginator behavior.

title: Performance claims in comments are not backed by any change in query behavior
body: The comments describe the optimized path as 'high-performance' and 'efficient browsing of large audit datasets'. For non-negative offsets the optimized path issues the same queryset, ordering and slice as DateTimePaginator, and it adds no index, query or caching change. The only behavioral difference is the negative-offset path, which crashes. The comments and the PR title overstate what the change does.

title: Comment claims negative offsets are allowed, but this diff changes no code here
body: The only change in Cursor.__init__ is a comment saying it 'allows negative offsets' and 'enables efficient reverse pagination'. The code (`self.offset = int(offset)`) is unchanged and already accepted negative values before this PR. Rejection of negative offsets happens in the paginators, so the comment describes a behavior that does not come from this line and misleads readers about where the behavior lives.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor/ceil to a datetime, so every non-empty page raises
body: The audit log endpoint sends `order_by="-datetime"`, so `self.key` is `datetime` and `getattr(item, self.key)` returns a datetime. `math.floor(datetime)` and `math.ceil(datetime)` raise TypeError. `build_cursor` and `_build_next_values` call `key(results[0])` whenever results exist, so any request with `?optimized_pagination=true` from an admin with a non-empty audit log returns a 500. `DateTimePaginator.get_item_key` converts datetimes to a timestamp first; this class does not. `value_from_cursor` also returns the raw int cursor value, which `build_queryset` would compare against a datetime column. The path is untested (no test covers `OptimizedCursorPaginator` or the endpoint flag), which is why this was not caught.

title: Negative cursor offsets are passed straight to queryset slicing, which Django rejects
body: When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start. Django QuerySets raise AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported') for negative slice bounds, so any caller who supplies a cursor string such as `0:-1:0` gets a 500. The `Cursor` parser accepts negative offsets from the client, so this is reachable by any user for whom the flag is on (superusers or members with global access). The comments on this branch say it 'enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds' and that 'permissions are checked at the queryset level'. Neither is true: the queryset is only filtered by organization_id, and negative slicing cannot be executed.

title: Unrelated, undocumented pagination switch added to the audit log endpoint
body: This PR is about the spans buffer, but it adds an `optimized_pagination` query parameter to the audit log endpoint that routes to the new paginator. Enabling it for superusers and has_global_access members turns on the negative-offset path (see paginator.py line 877), which crashes. The parameter is not validated by the serializer, has no tests, and is not documented. The duplicated `paginate` call also means the endpoint has two code paths to keep in sync. This change should be split out and either removed or fixed and tested separately.

title: Switching span-buf:s:* from Redis sets to sorted sets breaks in-flight keys during deploy
body: The key names `span-buf:s:{...}` are unchanged, but the type changes from SET (`sadd`/`sscan`) to ZSET (`zadd`/`zscan`). Keys written by the old code remain in Redis for up to `redis_ttl` (3600s) and are still being read and written. During that window, `p.zadd` here raises WRONGTYPE for any group whose key already holds a set. The pipeline `execute()` raises on the first error by default, so the whole batch fails and the consumer retries or crashes. The flusher's `p.zscan` at line 434 fails the same way on old set keys. There is no key versioning or migration step to prevent this.

title: ZUNIONSTORE uses default SUM aggregation, so re-delivered spans get doubled scores
body: `zunionstore` defaults to `AGGREGATE SUM`. When the same span payload exists in both the source and destination sets (for example, Kafka redelivers a span), its score becomes 2x the end timestamp. The score is the eviction key for `zpopmin`, so duplicated spans are treated as the newest and are never evicted, and eviction order is wrong for those members. The same problem applies to the second `zunionstore` at line 53. Using `AGGREGATE MIN` or `MAX` would keep the timestamp. This only matters once a segment exceeds 1000 spans, but the eviction is the feature this PR adds.

title: Span eviction silently truncates segments and removes the old max_segment_spans guard
body: Previously, `_load_segment_data` skipped segments over `max_segment_spans` and logged an error plus a metric. That check is removed in this PR, and the Lua script now `zpopmin`s the oldest spans beyond 1000 with no log or metric. Flushed segments are now silently incomplete. The Python limit `max_segment_spans` (default 1001 in buffer.py line 150) is now dead, and it disagrees with the hard-coded 1000 in the script. Operators have no way to see or tune the eviction. At minimum, the eviction should emit a counter, and the cap should come from configuration.

title: Redirect-chain depth limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 and its explanatory comment removed
body: The loop bound changes from 10000 to 1000, and the comment that documented the depth limit and its consequence is deleted. Redirect chains deeper than 1000 will now stop resolving early, so their spans land in a separate segment instead of being joined. This is unrelated to the eviction work and is not mentioned anywhere in the PR.

title: Comment claims negative offsets are now allowed, but no code changed
body: The added comment says the Cursor 'Allow[s] negative offsets for advanced pagination' and 'enables efficient reverse pagination'. The only change in this hunk is the comment, and `self.offset = int(offset)` is unchanged. Downstream, Django slicing rejects negative bounds, so the comment describes a capability that does not exist.

title: Comment says negative offsets are safe and efficient, but they are clamped or crash
body: The comment says negative offsets are allowed for 'efficient bidirectional pagination without full dataset scanning' and that 'this is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions'. The code clamps negative offsets to 0 for next-page cursors, which silently changes the result. For previous-page cursors (`is_prev`), `offset` is still passed unclamped, so a negative value raises AssertionError from Django. The comment misstates both the behavior and the safety.

title: No test exercises the eviction that this PR is about
body: The PR is titled 'eviction during insert' and adds a hard 1000-span cap in the Lua script, but no test inserts more than 1000 spans into a segment. Nothing verifies that the oldest spans are evicted, that the newest are kept, that the cap holds across multiple batches, or that duplicate payloads are scored correctly (see the SUM aggregation finding). The tests only add `end_timestamp_precise` fields, so the behavior change is untested.

title: Module docstring still describes span-buf:s:* as plain sets
body: The glossary says `span-buf:s:*` are 'the actual set keys', and the flow description says spans are added to 'the set'. After this change they are sorted sets scored by end timestamp, and eviction depends on that ordering. Future readers will be misled about the data type, which is exactly the mismatch that breaks in-flight keys during deploy.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes on datetime sort keys (auditlog optimized_pagination path)
body: The auditlog endpoint uses OptimizedCursorPaginator with order_by='-datetime', but get_item_key applies math.floor/math.ceil to the raw attribute value. That attribute is a datetime, so math.floor raises TypeError. build_cursor calls key(results[0]) whenever cursor.value is 0 and there are results, so the first page of any superuser or global-access request with optimized_pagination=true and at least one audit log returns a 500. value_from_cursor also returns the raw integer cursor value, which build_queryset would compare against a datetime column on later pages. The paginator needs DateTimePaginator-style handling (strftime/timestamp conversion) or the endpoint must not route datetime keys to it.

title: Negative-offset branch relies on Django negative slicing, which is unsupported
body: When enable_advanced_features is set and cursor.offset < 0, the code slices queryset[start_offset:stop] with a negative start. Django QuerySet.__getitem__ rejects negative indices ('Negative indexing is not supported'), so this raises instead of returning data. The comment 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false, and the claim 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level' is unsupported. Any admin request with a crafted cursor carrying a negative offset gets a 500, and the feature the branch advertises does not work.

title: Previous-page cursor with negative offset still passes a negative start index to queryset slicing
body: For is_prev cursors, start_offset is set to the raw offset, which Cursor.from_string allows to be negative from user input. The slice queryset[start_offset:stop] then raises on a negative index, so a user-supplied cursor such as '0:-1:1' produces a 500. The crash predates this PR, but the PR adds a comment at lines 179-181 calling this behavior safe and intentional, and clamps only the next-page direction, so the inconsistency is now written down as design.

title: Span eviction at 1000 is silent: no log or metric when spans are dropped
body: When span_count exceeds 1000, zpopmin silently removes the lowest-scored (oldest by end timestamp) spans from the segment. The Python side previously logged 'Skipping too large segment' and emitted spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded, and that guard was removed in buffer.py. Dropped spans are now invisible to operators, and the limit is hardcoded here rather than configured. Emit a metric (and ideally a log) from the script or the caller when eviction occurs.

title: Key type change from Redis set to sorted set breaks in-flight buffers during deploy
body: The span-buf:s:* keys change from SET to ZSET but keep the same name prefix. Any segment key written by the old code is a SET. After deploy, ZADD in process_spans, ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE in add-buffer.lua, and ZSCAN in _load_segment_data all fail with WRONGTYPE. Ingestion raises for those traces, and flush_segments raises before done_flush_segments runs, so the queue entries are not cleared until the keys expire (redis_ttl, default 3600s). The PR needs a new key prefix or a drain/migration plan.

title: ZUNIONSTORE uses default SUM aggregation, doubling scores of duplicate payloads
body: zunionstore is called without AGGREGATE, so the default SUM applies. When the same payload already exists in the destination (for example a redelivered Kafka message, or a span present in both merged sets), its score becomes the sum of the two end timestamps. That corrupts the eviction ordering, which relies on score = end_timestamp_precise. Use AGGREGATE MIN or MAX so the score is preserved.

title: Redirect-chain depth limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 and caveat comment removed
body: The loop bound changed from 10000 to 1000 with no mention in the PR description, and the comment explaining the limit's consequence was deleted. Redirect chains deeper than 1000 are now cut off silently, so their spans are attached to an intermediate segment rather than the root. Either keep the old limit or document the change and keep the caveat.

title: Hard key access on end_timestamp_precise can fail an entire batch
body: val['end_timestamp_precise'] is a strict lookup, and the cast(SpanEvent, ...) is type-only and does not validate anything at runtime. Before this PR the field was not read. A single message missing it raises KeyError inside process_batch, which fails the whole batch and can leave the consumer retrying the same poison batch. Use val.get with a fallback, or validate and skip the bad message with a metric.

title: max_segment_spans config is now dead and disagrees with the hardcoded Lua limit
body: After this PR the span-count check in _load_segment_data was removed, so the max_segment_spans constructor argument (default 1001) is never read. The effective limit is the hardcoded 1000 in add-buffer.lua. Configuration that appears to control the limit no longer does, and the two defaults disagree. Remove the parameter or wire it into the script.

title: No test covers the new 1000-span eviction, the set-to-zset change, or the redirect depth change
body: The headline feature of this PR, evicting spans beyond 1000 during insert, has no test. The added lines only add end_timestamp_precise to existing fixtures, so nothing checks that the segment is capped, that the oldest spans are the ones evicted, that merges keep the right scores, or that the loop limit behaves as intended. Add tests that insert more than 1000 spans through process_spans and assert the resulting count and which payloads survive.

title: optimized_pagination path is untested and crashes on the first page
body: The new branch gated by optimized_pagination=true has no test. Such a test would immediately expose the datetime TypeError in OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key, so the endpoint's new path is broken and unverified. Add a test for a superuser request with that parameter and at least one audit log entry.

title: Comment claims a negative-offset feature that this change does not implement
body: The added comment says Cursor now allows negative offsets for advanced pagination and enables reverse pagination from arbitrary positions. The diff changes nothing in this constructor (self.offset = int(offset) is unchanged), and the paginators that consume negative offsets crash on them. The comment describes behavior that does not exist, so it should be removed or corrected.

title: Module docstring still describes span-buf:s:* keys as sets
body: The glossary says span-buf:s:* are 'the actual set keys', but after this PR they are sorted sets (ZADD, ZUNIONSTORE, ZSCAN, ZPOPMIN). Update the docstring so future readers do not assume SET commands.

title: Unrelated pagination changes and an undocumented query parameter are bundled into a spans PR
body: The PR title is about span buffer eviction, but this file, paginator.py, and cursors.py add an experimental audit-log paginator switch. That switch is an undocumented optimized_pagination query parameter, and the PR description is just 'Test 2', so reviewers have no rationale for it. Split these changes into their own PR with a description, or revert them from this one.

title: Segment key type changed from SET to ZSET without migration, so in-flight keys break on deploy
body: The per-segment key type changes from a Redis SET to a sorted set: sadd becomes zadd here, sscan becomes zscan in _load_segment_data, and sunionstore becomes zunionstore in add-buffer.lua. The key names (span-buf:s:{...}) are unchanged and segment keys live for up to redis_ttl (3600s). During a rolling deploy, or for up to an hour after, old-version SET keys still exist. New code then hits WRONGTYPE on zadd, on zcard/zunionstore/zpopmin inside the Lua script, and on zscan in the flusher. redis-py pipelines raise on command errors, so process_spans fails for any batch touching a legacy key, and flush_segments can fail for every segment in the same batch. That stalls ingestion and flushing until the old keys expire. The fix needs a new key prefix or explicit handling of the type mismatch.

title: zunionstore uses default SUM aggregation, corrupting scores of members present in both sets
body: ZUNIONSTORE without an AGGREGATE option sums scores. When a member (same payload) already exists in set_key and is also in the source key, for example a redelivered span, its score becomes the sum of two end timestamps (about 3.4e9) instead of end_timestamp_precise. zpopmin uses these scores to choose which spans to evict, so eviction order is corrupted. The same problem applies at line 53 for the parent key. Use AGGREGATE MAX or MIN so scores remain timestamps.

title: Span eviction at 1000 is silent: no metric or log, and it replaces an observable limit
body: When a segment exceeds 1000 spans, zpopmin silently deletes the lowest-scored (earliest-ending) entries. The buffer.py change also removes the old flush-time guard, which logged an error and emitted spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded. Segments that used to be dropped and logged are now silently truncated, and operators have no signal that spans are being discarded. Add a counter or log for the number of evicted spans.

title: Redirect-chain walk bound lowered from 10000 to 1000 without explanation
body: The loop bound changed from 10000 to 1000 and the comment that documented the limit was deleted. The change is unrelated to span eviction and is not mentioned in the PR. Redirect chains deeper than 1000 now stop early, leaving set_span_id at an intermediate span, so later spans are attached to the wrong segment with no error or metric. Restore the original bound or justify the change explicitly.

title: Forward-cursor offset clamp changes BasePaginator behavior for all paginated endpoints
body: BasePaginator.get_result is shared by DateTimePaginator and Paginator, which many endpoints use. The new line clamps negative offsets to 0 for forward cursors. Previously a negative offset made queryset slicing raise. Now it silently returns the first page. The same negative offset on a prev cursor still passes through unchanged and still raises, so the behavior is inconsistent. The comment on lines 179-181 says negative offsets are 'allowed' for bidirectional paging, but forward pages now do the opposite. No tests cover this change, and it is not gated behind the new optimized path.

title: Negative cursor offset is passed to queryset slicing, which Django rejects with a 500
body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is set and cursor.offset is negative, start_offset is passed unchanged to queryset[start_offset:stop]. Django QuerySet does not support negative indexing and raises ValueError ('Negative indexing is not supported'). An admin who sends optimized_pagination=true with a negative cursor offset gets an unhandled 500. The comments at lines 874-880 claim the ORM 'handles negative slicing automatically' and that this exposes data 'beyond normal pagination bounds'; neither is true. The class also copies BasePaginator.get_result (line 821 onward) almost line for line, so the two implementations will drift.

title: organization_context.member is dereferenced without a None check
body: RpcUserOrganizationContext.member is Optional. For a non-superuser, the expression organization_context.member.has_global_access raises AttributeError if there is no membership record. Whether this is reachable depends on OrganizationAuditPermission admitting non-members, which this diff does not show. Guard with a None check, or confirm the permission guarantees membership.

title: New optimized_pagination branch and its admin gating have no tests
body: The branch that switches to OptimizedCursorPaginator with enable_advanced_features=True, the superuser/global-access gate, and the fallback to DateTimePaginator are all untested. The negative-offset path that 500s for admins (paginator.py line 882) would be caught by even a single endpoint test. Add tests for the admin path, the non-admin fallback, and a negative cursor.

title: Comment claims a capability that this change does not implement
body: The added comment says it is a 'performance optimization' that allows negative offsets for 'efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions'. The only change is this comment: int(offset) was already unvalidated. Downstream, forward pages clamp negatives to 0 and prev pages pass them into queryset slicing, which raises. The comment advertises behavior that does not exist and will mislead future readers.

title: Module docstring still describes span-buf:s:* keys as sets
body: The glossary says span-buf:s:* keys are 'the actual set keys', and the flow above says payloads are added to 'the set'. After this change these keys are sorted sets scored by end_timestamp_precise, which is what the eviction and flush logic depends on. The docs should say so.

title: max_segment_spans is now a dead parameter; the eviction limit is hard-coded to 1000 in Lua
body: SpansBuffer still accepts max_segment_spans (default 1001), but nothing reads it. Its only use, the span-count check in _load_segment_data, was removed. The real limit is the hard-coded 1000 in add-buffer.lua line 62. Callers tuning this parameter get no effect, and the two limits disagree. Either pass the limit to the script through ARGV or remove the parameter.

title: Tests do not cover eviction, score ordering, or the set-to-zset change
body: The PR's purpose is eviction above 1000 spans, but no test inserts more than 1000 spans or checks which spans survive. Every fixture uses the same constant end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0, so score-based ordering is never exercised. The zunionstore SUM collision is also untested, as is the old-SET-key compatibility problem. Add a test that inserts more than 1000 spans with distinct end timestamps and checks that the latest 1000 survive, plus a case where the same payload arrives twice.

title: Unrelated audit-log, paginator, and cursor changes are bundled into a spans-buffer PR with a placeholder description
body: The PR title describes a spans buffer optimization, and the description is only 'Test 2'. The diff also changes the audit-log endpoint, adds an experimental pagination class to api/paginator.py, and changes utils/cursors.py. Nothing in the description explains why these belong together or how they are meant to behave. Split them into separate PRs with descriptions, or document the intent.

title: Substring match treats negated or OR'd event.type:error filters as error-only
body: `_is_error_focused_query` returns True whenever the raw query string contains the substring `event.type:error`. That also matches `!event.type:error` (selects non-error rows such as transactions) and `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`. For such queries on the discover dataset with all projects allowlisted, `count()` is rewritten to `upsampled_count()` = `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. Transaction rows carry no sample_weight, so the result is zero or wrong counts presented as upsampled error counts, with no error raised. The unit test only covers a positive case and an unrelated query, so this is not caught. The check should parse the query and look for a standalone, non-negated `event.type:error` term.

title: upsampled_count is exposed as a general-purpose aggregate with no guard
body: The new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is registered in the global discover function converter, so any user can type `upsampled_count()` in any discover/events query on any dataset. There is no allowlist or dataset check. The aggregate is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`, which is null or zero for events without sample_weight (non-allowlisted projects, transactions). Users therefore get silently low numbers, or a query error on datasets lacking the column. The comment 'assumes sample_weight exists' is not enforced anywhere, and the function has no unit test.

title: 'upsampled_count() as count' is an alias form the other column paths don't use
body: The transformed column string `upsampled_count() as count` is passed directly as a selected/y-axis column to `timeseries_query` and `top_events_timeseries`. Every other aggregate in these paths is a bare `func(args)` string, and this change adds no parsing for an ` as alias` suffix. If the field parser rejects this string, every upsampled request fails with an invalid-field error instead of returning counts, and the endpoint test expecting `count == 10` would fail. This needs verification against the parser. Either confirm the alias form is supported or use the bare function and map the result key separately.

title: Only an exact count() is upsampled, so mixed column lists produce inconsistent values
body: The transform rewrites a column only when it equals `count()` after lowercasing and stripping. Equations that reference count (for example `equation|count() / 2`) are passed through unchanged. A single chart can therefore show an upsampled `count` series next to an equation computed from the raw, un-upsampled count. Nothing in the code or tests handles this mixed case, and the function silently leaves those columns alone.

title: Upsampling eligibility is re-evaluated on every _get_event_stats call, even for non-count queries
body: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` runs unconditionally at the start of every `_get_event_stats` call. For dashboard widgets this happens up to four times per request, each doing a cache read and possibly a cache write plus an options lookup. It runs even when no requested column is `count()`, which is the only thing the transform affects. The check should be skipped unless a count column is present.

title: Allowlist lookup and cache write happen before the cheap dataset check
body: `is_eligible` (an options read plus a cache write on a miss) is computed before `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, which is a simple dataset comparison. For transactions, spans, or metrics queries, which never upsample, every call still reads options and writes the cache. The final result is `is_eligible and ...` with the cheap check second. The dataset/query check should run first and short-circuit.

title: Allowlist changes take up to 60s to apply and the invalidation helper is never called
body: The eligibility result is cached for 60 seconds (`cache.set` at line 38), keyed only on organization and project set. Allowlist edits therefore take up to a minute to affect counts. `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined to be called 'when the allowlist configuration changes', but nothing in the diff calls it, so it is dead code and the consistency it promises does not exist. Either wire it into the option-change path or remove it and document the staleness window.

title: Upsampling decision uses the outer dataset, not the dataset actually queried
body: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` receives the outer `dataset`, but `_get_event_stats` runs against `scoped_dataset`, and the widget split path passes a different `split_dataset` (for example `discover` with `event.type:transaction`). The decision therefore describes a different dataset from the one queried. The split path currently only runs when the outer dataset is a metrics dataset, so this is latent. If that gating changes, a transactions-only split query would be upsampled whenever the outer dataset is errors. The dataset actually being queried should be passed.

title: Comments claim caching and performance guarantees the code does not provide
body: The comments describe an 'early upsampling eligibility check for performance optimization' whose 'cached result ensures consistent behavior across query execution', and say storing the decision 'allows for better query optimization and caching'. None of this holds. `should_upsample` is a local boolean, nothing is cached at this level, and the check is re-run on every `_get_event_stats` call. The 'late transformation ensures we use the most current schema assumptions' comment is also unsupported. These should be corrected so maintainers don't assume a caching guarantee that doesn't exist.

title: Unrelated change to a public error message
body: The `topEvents` validation message changes from 'If topEvents needs to be at least 1' to 'topEvents needs to be at least 1'. This is unrelated to upsampling and changes the `detail` string returned by the public API. Any client or existing test matching the old text will break. The fix should be split into its own change, or confirmed safe with a check of existing tests and consumers.

title: Stray submodule-pointer file committed at repository root
body: The PR adds a regular file named `sentry-repo` whose content is `Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a`. This is not a real submodule: no `.gitmodules` entry or gitlink is added, so git treats it as an ordinary text file. It pollutes the repository root with a pointer to the base commit, and it can confuse checkout or any later real submodule setup under that name. It is almost certainly an accidental commit and should be removed.

title: Bare exception swallowing in test helper that runs for every store_event
body: Both `try/except Exception: pass` blocks in `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` silently discard any error, including a malformed `contexts` value or an unparsable rate. A malformed test event then just loses its sample_rate, and the test depending on it fails far from the cause, or passes incorrectly. Because the helper is called from `store_event` for the whole test suite, this hides problems globally. The handling should be narrowed to the expected cases, or errors should be allowed to surface.

title: Modified topEvents, RPC, and widget-split paths have no test coverage
body: The new test class only exercises the plain timeseries path with `count()`. The `topEvents` branch (where `top_events_timeseries` now receives transformed columns), the RPC branches, and the dashboard widget split path in `get_event_stats_factory` are all modified by this PR but have no tests. There are also no tests for negated or OR'd `event.type` queries, which is why the substring bug in error_upsampling.py went unnoticed, and no direct tests for the `upsampled_count` aggregate or the cache behavior. Coverage should be added for `topEvents=` and a widget-split case, plus the negation case.

title: Allowlist option read via options.get with no registration in the diff
body: The allowlist comes only from options.get('issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist', []). None of the eight changed files registers this key in the options defaults. Sentry's options manager raises an UnknownOption error for unregistered keys, so on a cache miss _are_all_projects_error_upsampled would raise. That call happens in is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects before any dataset gating, so every events-stats request with a project could fail, not only error queries. The tests patch options in this module, so the real lookup never runs and CI would not catch it. Register the option or confirm it already exists.

title: Substring match classifies negated and compound event.type filters as error queries
body: The check 'event.type:error' in query is a substring test. Queries such as '!event.type:error', 'event.type:errors', or '(event.type:error OR event.type:transaction)' all return True. For those queries the count is rewritten to sum(sample_weight), but non-error rows have no sample_weight, so the sum drops them and the count is wrong (for '!event.type:error' it can come out as 0). The filter should be parsed as a token rather than matched as a substring. No test covers negation or compound queries.

title: sum(sample_weight) silently drops events that lack a weight
body: sum() ignores NULLs, so any error event without a sample_weight contributes 0 instead of 1 to upsampled_count. This includes events ingested before the rollout and events with no client sample rate. The docstring in error_upsampling.py (lines 85-86) says no null handling is needed because the schema guarantees the column, but nothing in the diff enforces that. Time ranges spanning the rollout would silently undercount for allowlisted projects. The fallback for a missing weight should be defined explicitly, for example coalesce(sample_weight, 1).

title: Upsampling eligibility is evaluated against the request dataset, not the dataset actually queried
body: The check passes the request-level dataset, but the query runs against scoped_dataset, which differs in the dashboard split path (discover for the errors-only and transactions-only sub-queries). The errors/transactions/discover guard in _should_apply_sample_weight_transform is therefore evaluated for the wrong dataset. The split path requires metrics_enhanced, so the outer dataset is always a metrics dataset there. The guard returns False and the errors-only discover sub-query is never upsampled, while the same query outside the split path would be. The decision should be made from the dataset the query actually runs on.

title: Transform is not gated on metrics or on-demand routing
body: The count() rewrite to upsampled_count() is applied regardless of use_metrics, has_metrics, use_metrics_layer, or on_demand_metrics_enabled, which can route a discover-dataset query to a metrics or on-demand builder. upsampled_count is registered only in discover.py's function converter, so in those routes the function would not resolve, or the query would silently fall back to a non-upsampled count. The transform should be gated on the builder actually used.

title: Equations containing count() are not upsampled alongside the rewritten yAxis
body: Only the exact count() entries in query_columns are rewritten. Equations passed through equations=self.get_equation_list(...) are not transformed, so an equation such as equation|count() * 2 returns un-upsampled values while the plain count() yAxis returns upsampled values in the same response. The inconsistency is not handled or documented.

title: Upsampling branch in the RPC path is unreachable
body: use_rpc is true only when dataset is spans_rpc or ourlogs. _should_apply_sample_weight_transform returns False for both, so upsampling_enabled is always False when this block runs. The block is dead code, and it gives the false impression that RPC datasets get upsampled. Remove it, or rework the gating if RPC upsampling was intended.

title: Allowlist check and cache write run before the dataset gate
body: On every cache miss, _are_all_projects_error_upsampled runs options.get and cache.set, even for spans, metrics, and transactions queries. The dataset check on line 40 then discards the result. The cache get and set happen on every _get_event_stats call. Checking the dataset and request gate first, then returning early, would avoid the Redis round trips and the option lookup for queries that can never be upsampled.

title: invalidate_upsampling_cache is dead code, so allowlist changes are only picked up after 60s
body: invalidate_upsampling_cache is never called in the diff, and no allowlist write path invokes it. Its docstring says it should be called when the allowlist changes, but nothing does. An allowlist change therefore takes up to 60 seconds to affect upsampling, because of the cache.set at line 38. Either wire it to the option update path or remove it and correct the docstring.

title: Comments claim caching and consistency that the code does not provide
body: The comments say the cached result 'ensures consistent behavior across query execution' and that storing the decision 'allows for better query optimization and caching'. Nothing is cached at this point. The decision is recomputed on every _get_event_stats call, and the underlying eligibility is a 60-second cache in error_upsampling.py. Calls within one request can therefore disagree if the cache entry expires between them. The comments should be corrected.

title: Unrelated change to an existing error message
body: The topEvents validation message changes from 'If topEvents needs to be at least 1' to 'topEvents needs to be at least 1'. This has nothing to do with upsampling and is not mentioned in the PR. Any client matching the exact string will see a change. It should be split out or called out in the description.

title: Bare except blocks silently ignore malformed sample rates
body: _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling wraps dict access and float conversion in bare 'except Exception: pass'. A malformed client_sample_rate is silently dropped and the event is stored without sample_rate. This helper runs inside store_event, which many tests use, so a bad test payload gives no signal. The try around a plain dict .get chain is unnecessary. Validation should be explicit or errors should surface.

title: upsampled_count is a public aggregate with a different result type from count()
body: The function is registered without private=True, so users can request upsampled_count() in any discover query, including transaction queries the upsampling guard is meant to exclude. Its default_result_type is 'number' while count() is 'integer', so the field type reported in meta changes for upsampled responses. Either mark it private or document and validate the new public aggregate and its result type.

title: Stray file committed at repository root
body: A regular file named sentry-repo containing 'Subproject commit a5d29095...' is added at the repository root. It is not a real gitlink and appears to be an accidental artifact that pins the base commit. It should not be part of this change and should be removed from the PR.

title: Query-classification and cache paths are untested
body: test_is_error_focused_query and test_should_apply_sample_weight_transform only check the exact strings 'event.type:error' and 'event.type:transaction'. Nothing covers negated filters ('!event.type:error'), compound queries, or 'event.type:errors', which is exactly where the substring check goes wrong. is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects itself is not tested, so the cache hit and miss paths and the dataset gate are unverified. The endpoint tests also never exercise the topEvents or RPC branches where the transform is applied.

title: Error-focus gate is a substring match on the raw request query
body: `"event.type:error" in query` is True for `!event.type:error` (exclude errors) and for `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`. In both cases `count()` is rewritten to `upsampled_count()` (sum of sample_weight) even though transaction rows are in scope and carry no sample weight, so counts come out wrong or the query fails. The gate also reads `request.GET['query']` (line 135) rather than the query string that actually executes. The split paths in organization_events_stats.py append `AND !event.type:transaction` or `AND event.type:transaction` to the query, so the gate's decision and the executed query can disagree.

title: Upsampling decision uses the request's dataset instead of the dataset the call runs against
body: is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(...) receives `dataset`, the closed-over variable from get(), not `scoped_dataset`, which is the parameter this _get_event_stats call actually runs on. The dashboard split path calls _get_event_stats with `discover` for errors_only_query and transactions_only_query, and with split_dataset elsewhere. When the request dataset is `errors`, _should_apply_sample_weight_transform returns True, so the transactions-only discover query also gets count() rewritten to upsampled_count(). That result feeds has_transactions and therefore the split decision. scoped_dataset is accepted by _get_event_stats but never used for this check.

title: Reads an option that this change does not register
body: options.get('issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist', []) is called here, but the diff does not register this key in sentry/options defaults. Sentry's options manager raises for unregistered keys. This call runs on every cache miss for any events-stats timeseries request, before the dataset check. If the option is not registered elsewhere, those requests fail. The endpoint and unit tests mock sentry.api.helpers.error_upsampling.options, so they cannot catch this. Confirm the registration exists or add it.

title: Rewritten column uses an alias suffix that the field grammar does not accept
body: The rewrite produces the literal string 'upsampled_count() as count'. Sentry's field grammar takes function(args) with nothing after the closing paren, so this string will not match the function form and will be treated as an unknown field or fail to parse. That turns affected requests into errors. The upsampled_count aggregate is only registered in DiscoverDatasetConfig (discover.py), yet _should_apply_sample_weight_transform also enables the rewrite for the `errors` dataset. Nothing in the diff shows this resolves through the errors query builder.

title: sum(sample_weight) silently undercounts events that have no weight
body: The docstring says the schema guarantees sample_weight for all events in allowlisted projects, so no null checks are needed. Nothing enforces that: the allowlist is per project, not per event. An event whose SDK does not send contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate may have a NULL or zero sample_weight. sum() skips NULLs, so such events contribute 0 instead of 1 to the count, silently, in any allowlisted project with mixed traffic.

title: Gate tests miss the negated and OR cases the substring check gets wrong
body: The discover gate is tested only with a plain 'event.type:error' query and a plain 'event.type:transaction' query. It is not tested with '!event.type:error', with 'event.type:error OR event.type:transaction', or with the split-path query shapes. Those are exactly the inputs where the substring check gives the wrong answer, so the bug above would pass this suite.

title: Endpoint tests skip topEvents, dashboard split, and mixed-row queries
body: The new class covers only plain count() timeseries for an error query, an all-allowlisted and a partial-allowlist case, and a transaction-only query. Not covered: topEvents with upsampling (the top_events_timeseries branch rewrites columns too), the dashboardWidgetId split path (where the dataset-scope bug lives), dataset=errors routing, and queries that mix error and transaction rows. test_error_upsampling_with_transaction_events checks only a transaction-only query, which never reaches the rewrite, so it does not exercise the case the gate exists to block. The upsampled_count aggregate is also not tested directly.

title: upsampled_count is a public aggregate with no allowlist gate
body: The new aggregate is registered without private=True, unlike the adjacent function in the same converter. Any discover or events query can therefore call upsampled_count() on any project. The allowlist check exists only in the count() rewrite, so users can request an upsampled value for non-allowlisted projects, where sample_weight is typically absent and the result is 0 or misleading. Gate it or mark it private.

title: invalidate_upsampling_cache is dead code and the 60s staleness is unmitigated
body: invalidate_upsampling_cache is defined but nothing in this change calls it. The eligibility cache set at line 38 has a 60 second TTL and is keyed only by org and project set. Removing a project from the allowlist therefore keeps upsampling it for up to a minute.
