Arroyo keeps polling Kafka while a slow group accumulates work. Each queued WorkItem also keeps a reference to the full Message and its payload (WorkItem.message, which is never read). This is exactly the slow-item scenario the PR is meant to address, and it turns it into unbounded memory growth rather than backpressure. Either bound the queues and pause consumption when they are full, or correct the docstring.

title: Error-handling test asserts the partition is NOT committed, contradicting its own docstring and the implementation
body: The test docstring says errors in processing must not block offset commits for other messages. The implementation marks the failed offset complete in the worker's finally block, so the second message's offset (101) is committed as 102. The assertion instead requires that test_partition is absent from committed_offsets. It passes only because the commit thread ticks once per second and the test checks within about 0.3 seconds, before the first tick. If the tick lands earlier, the test fails. The assertion encodes the opposite of the intended behavior and should check that the partition is committed past the failed message.

title: Offset-gap test does not check gap blocking, and the implementation only blocks on the first batch
body: test_offset_gaps_block_commits claims gaps block commits, but nothing asserts that. After offset 100 is committed, the next tick computes start = max(last_committed+1, min(all_offsets)) = 102. The missing 101 is therefore skipped, and 103 is committed on the next tick even if 101 never arrives. So the gap blocks the first batch but not later ones. The test only waits for commits that happen after 101 has already been submitted, so it passes either way. The same mismatch makes test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps in test_results_consumer.py (about line 1982) pass only because it exits before the next commit tick. The intended gap semantics should be decided and asserted.

title: test_preserves_order_within_group never checks the order
body: The test submits five messages for the same subscription and asserts only len(self.processed_results) == 5. The recorded list is never compared to the expected sequence, so the test would still pass if ordering within a group were broken. Since per-group ordering is the core guarantee of this design, the test should assert the processed sequence.

title: Racy assertion that total_items > 0 right after submitting
body: Worker threads start consuming as soon as items are put, so by the time get_stats() runs, they may already have drained the queues. The assertion assert stats['total_items'] > 0 can then fail intermittently. It is a timing assumption, not a guarantee.

title: --mode help text is wrong and does not describe the new thread-queue-parallel mode
body: The help says 'Parallel uses multithreading', but the 'parallel' mode uses MultiprocessingPool (see result_consumer.py, create_multiprocess_worker). The PR adds the 'thread-queue-parallel' choice but does not describe it in the help text, so operators cannot tell the modes apart.

title: queue.ShutDown and Queue.shutdown() require Python 3.13; earlier interpreters fail silently
body: queue.ShutDown and Queue.shutdown() exist only on Python 3.13+. If this code can run on an earlier interpreter, q.shutdown() raises AttributeError, which the except at line 239 swallows, so queues and workers are never stopped. Also, on older versions the 'except queue.ShutDown' clause in the worker (line 142) raises AttributeError whenever result_processor raises, which kills the worker thread and stalls its queue. The minimum supported Python version should be confirmed.

title: close() shuts down the factory-owned queue pool, so messages are silently dropped after the first rebalance
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), but the FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and passed to every strategy that create_with_partitions() builds. Arroyo closes the current strategy on partition revocation and creates a new one on assignment, so after the first rebalance the pool's queues are already shut down and its workers have exited. The new strategy's submit() calls FixedQueuePool.submit -> queue.put(), which raises queue.ShutDown. The except branch in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit (lines 317-325) then marks the offset as added and completed, so the message is never processed but its offset becomes committable. Work that was still queued when the old pool shut down keeps its offsets in `outstanding` forever, which stalls commits for those partitions. Net effect: uptime results are silently lost after any rebalance and the commit point stops advancing. No test runs close() followed by create_with_partitions() on the same factory, so this is not caught. Pool ownership should stay with the factory; the strategy's close() should only stop its own commit thread.

title: Enqueue failures mark the offset as completed, so unprocessed messages get committed
body: In SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit, any exception raised while decoding, grouping, or enqueueing a message reaches an except block that calls add_offset and then complete_offset for that message. The message is never handed to a worker, yet its offset is now treated as processed, so the commit loop advances past it and the message is dropped with only a log line. This is the mechanism that hides the ShutDown failure described above. Poison messages (decode or grouping errors) may reasonably be skipped, but a failure to enqueue must not mark the offset complete. Failed enqueues should keep the offset outstanding or propagate the error.

title: Per-queue work queues are unbounded, contradicting the documented backpressure
body: Each per-queue work queue is created as queue.Queue() with no maxsize (line 185), so FixedQueuePool.submit() never blocks. The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring (line 255) promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but nothing ever fills. If the handlers are slower than the Kafka fetch rate, the main thread keeps polling and queued WorkItems (each holding a full Message) accumulate without bound. Because commits are contiguous, the last committed offset stays pinned behind the slowest item, so the outstanding and all_offsets sets also grow. Either bound the queues and make submit block or pause the consumer, or remove the backpressure claim.

title: A hole in the offset sequence permanently stalls all commits for that partition
body: get_committable_offsets breaks out of the scan on any offset that is not in all_offsets (line 90), so a missing offset blocks commits forever. Within a partition, Kafka delivers messages in offset order, so if offset 102 arrives after 100, offset 101 will never arrive later; it is a hole from compaction or a transaction marker, and the tracker waits for it indefinitely. Consequences: the committed point never moves past the hole, mark_committed never prunes all_offsets so it grows without bound, and every restart reprocesses everything after the hole. test_offset_gaps_block_commits in the queue consumer tests only passes because it submits offset 101 after 102 and 103, which real delivery cannot produce. The tracker should treat offsets skipped by a newer delivered offset as complete.

title: Arroyo commit callback is invoked from a background thread without synchronization
body: _commit_loop runs on its own thread and calls commit_function (line 287), which is the Arroyo commit callback from create_with_partitions. Arroyo's consumer is driven from the StreamProcessor thread (poll, stage, commit); nothing here coordinates with that loop, so commits can race with the main thread's consumer calls. There is also a shutdown race: after shutdown_event is set, the loop does not re-check the flag after shutdown_event.wait(1.0) (line 276), so it can run one more get_committable_offsets and commit_function after close() has begun or returned, and close() only joins for 5 seconds. Commit calls should be made from the processor thread (for example from poll()), and the loop should exit once the event is set.

title: Sequential 5-second joins make shutdown block for up to 100 seconds per rebalance
body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown joins each worker with a 5-second timeout, one after another (line 243). With the default 20 queues, if the workers are all stuck in slow result handlers (the exact case this PR targets), shutdown can block for up to 100 seconds. Because the strategy's close() also calls this shutdown (see the close() bug above), this delay occurs on every rebalance. That risks exceeding the consumer's poll or session timeouts and getting the consumer evicted from the group. Use one shared deadline for all joins, or avoid blocking joins on the rebalance path.

title: Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its stated intent and depends on timing
body: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling says errors in processing must not block offset commits for other messages. Its final assertion requires that the partition is NOT committed: `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`. By the design (the finally block completes the failed offset 100), both offsets 100 and 101 complete, so a later commit should reach 102. The assertion passes only because the test exits about 0.2 seconds after submission, before the commit thread's first one-second tick. The test therefore neither verifies the intended behavior nor is stable. It should wait for a commit and assert that the partition is committed at 102.

title: Racy assertion that queued items remain right after submission
body: test_stats_reporting asserts stats['total_items'] > 0 immediately after ten submits (line 200), while worker threads are already draining the queues. If the workers dequeue everything before this line runs (possible under CI load or GIL switching), the test fails intermittently. The check adds no coverage that the later == 0 assertion does not already provide, so either remove it or make the precondition deterministic, for example by blocking the workers first.

title: Test named for concurrency does not check concurrency
body: test_concurrent_processing_across_groups claims to verify that different groups are processed concurrently, but its only assertion (line 173) is that three group labels appear in the processed output. That would pass if every item ran serially on one thread, and with only three queues the groups can hash onto the same queue. The name and the assertion disagree, so the test gives false confidence about concurrency.

title: Worker transaction is named with a 'monitors.' prefix copied from another consumer
body: The worker transaction name is built as monitors.{identifier}.worker_{id} (line 138). This module is generic remote-subscription code used by the uptime results consumer, and the same prefix is copied into the result processor. Performance data for these workers will be filed under the monitors namespace, which misleads anyone looking at traces. The prefix should reflect the actual consumer or be derived from the identifier alone.

title: Strategy created in test is never closed, leaking a commit thread
body: test_factory_creates_thread_queue_parallel_strategy creates a SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy through the factory (line 415) but only calls factory.shutdown(), which stops the pool and not the strategy. The strategy's commit thread loops every second for the rest of the test session because its shutdown event is never set. The test should call strategy.close() so the thread is stopped and the test does not leak threads into later tests.

title: Closing one strategy shuts down the factory-wide queue pool, so messages are dropped after a rebalance
body: The FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__, and create_thread_queue_parallel_worker (result_consumer.py:255) passes that same pool to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy the factory builds. close() here calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which permanently shuts down every queue and stops every worker. join() (line 345) delegates to close(). Arroyo closes the old strategy and calls create_with_partitions again on the same factory on each partition reassignment, so the new strategy gets an already-shut-down pool. Its submit() then calls FixedQueuePool.submit, which records the offset as outstanding and then queue.put() raises queue.ShutDown. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches that in its broad except, logs 'Error submitting message to queue', and marks the offset complete, so the commit loop advances past it. The net effect is that after the first rebalance every consumed result is silently discarded (only logged) while its offset is still committed. No test creates a second strategy from one factory, so this is not caught. The pool should live for the factory's lifetime and be shut down only in ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown(), or each strategy should own its own pool.

title: An offset that never arrives permanently stalls commits for its partition
body: get_committable_offsets walks offsets from last_committed+1 and stops at the first offset that is either outstanding or absent from all_offsets (the else/break at lines 92-93). Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be contiguous (log compaction and transaction control markers leave holes). A hole is never added via add_offset, so the loop breaks at it on every cycle and last_committed never advances again for that partition. Everything after the hole keeps accumulating in all_offsets, which mark_committed never prunes, and every one-second commit cycle runs min()/max() over that growing set. Consequences are a frozen committed offset, unbounded consumer lag, and unbounded memory growth. The unit test test_offset_gaps_block_commits only passes because it later submits offset 101 to fill the hole, which a real gap never does. test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps in the results consumer tests asserts the stall as expected behavior.

title: Worker queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure, contrary to the docstring
body: queue.Queue() is created without maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit never raises MessageRejected, so Arroyo never pauses polling. If a worker stalls (a slow result handler or a DB hiccup), every subsequent message is still polled, decoded, and queued, and each WorkItem keeps the full Kafka message alive. Memory grows with the backlog until the process is killed. The class docstring at line 253 ('Natural backpressure when queues fill up') is therefore false. Either bound the queues and reject when full, or remove the claim.

title: Docstring promises no item is lost and commits only after success, but failed items are logged and committed
body: OrderedQueueWorker.run catches Exception and logs it, and the finally block (line 149) completes the offset anyway, so the offset is committed and the failed result is never retried. The result processor also swallows its own exceptions. The guarantees 'No item is lost' (line 252) and 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' (line 254) therefore do not hold. This may match the existing batched modes, but the docstring should not claim otherwise.

title: Error-handling test asserts the failing batch is NOT committed, contradicting its own docstring
body: The docstring says errors 'don't block offset commits for other messages'. Offsets 100 and 101 both complete: the first raises, the worker logs it and completes the offset in its finally, and the second succeeds. The commit loop should therefore commit 101+1=102 for the partition. The final assertion `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` requires the opposite. It passes only because the commit thread's first cycle fires about one second after creation while the test checks after roughly 0.2 seconds. On a slower run the commit happens and the test fails. The test should wait for the commit and assert committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102.

title: Graceful-shutdown test runs the real result processor in worker threads and asserts almost nothing
body: Unlike the other thread-queue tests, this one does not patch result_processor.__call__. The worker threads run the real ResultProcessor, which hits the database through get_from_cache from threads outside the test transaction, and the queued results can still be running after the test returns. The only assertion is factory.queue_pool is None, which does not verify that queued results were processed or that the workers stopped. The processor should be mocked, and the test should assert that all results were handled before shutdown completed and that the worker threads are no longer alive.

title: test_preserves_order_within_group never checks order
body: The test name and docstring claim messages for the same subscription are processed in order, but the only assertion is the count of processed results. Ordering is never checked. Similarly, test_concurrent_processing_different_groups (line 314) does not verify concurrency, only the count. Assert the processed sequence for the group, as the unit test test_ordered_processing_within_group does.

title: test_stats_reporting asserts total_items > 0 after submitting, which races with the workers
body: The workers consume concurrently with the submitting thread, so the queues can be fully drained before get_stats() runs. The assertion `stats["total_items"] > 0` is therefore timing-dependent and can fail intermittently. The check should be dropped or made deterministic, for example by blocking the result processor on an event while the stats are read.

title: Shutdown joins worker threads one after another with 5s timeouts, which can block for about 100s
body: The join loop calls worker.join(timeout=5.0) sequentially for each of the default 20 workers. If workers are still finishing slow items, the worst case is about 5s times the number of queues, all blocking inside close()/join(), which Arroyo invokes on the processing thread during rebalance and shutdown. This can exceed the consumer's poll interval. Use a single shared deadline, or join all workers against one timeout.

title: Backup-code branch allows login without password verification
body: In `authorize()` the password is only verified when `credentials.totpCode` is empty (`if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)` at line 121). The new backup-code branch at line 131 is evaluated for `user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode` regardless of whether a password was checked, and it takes precedence over the TOTP branch. A request that sends any non-empty `totpCode` (e.g. "000000") together with a valid `backupCode` therefore skips password verification entirely and also never validates the TOTP code, so the backup code alone grants a session. Backup codes are meant to be a second factor (they are even downloaded to a plain text file / copied to the clipboard), so this turns a leaked backup code into a full account takeover. The backup-code path should require successful password verification before accepting the code.

title: Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write
body: The code decrypts `user.backupCodes`, nulls the matched entry in memory and writes the whole re-encrypted array back with `prisma.user.update`. Two concurrent login attempts using the same backup code can both read the array before either writes, so the same single-use code is accepted twice. Likewise, two concurrent logins using two different codes will each write back their own copy of the array, and the last write resurrects the code consumed by the other request. Consuming the code should be done atomically (e.g. inside a transaction with a conditional update / row lock) so a code can be redeemed exactly once.

title: Unvalidated backupCode body field can crash the endpoint
body: `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` assumes the field is a string. A client sending a non-string JSON value (number, array, object) makes the handler throw a TypeError, which surfaces as an unhandled 500 instead of a 400 validation error. The same pattern exists for `credentials.backupCode` in next-auth-options.ts. The field should be validated (type and expected format) before use. Also note `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` is unguarded and will throw a 500 if the stored value cannot be decrypted/parsed.

title: "missing_backup_codes" message points to a settings flow that does not exist
body: The new string `missing_backup_codes` says "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." but there is no UI anywhere in this PR to generate or regenerate backup codes: codes are only created inside `/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup`, which rejects users who already have 2FA enabled (`TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled`). Every user who enabled 2FA before this change (and any user who closed the dialog without saving the codes) will hit this error and will be told to do something that is impossible without first disabling 2FA. Either add a regeneration endpoint/UI or change the message to tell the user to disable and re-enable 2FA.

title: Assertion on the 2FA switch is a no-op and is left unfixed
body: `expect(page.locator('[data-testid=two-factor-switch]').isChecked()).toBeTruthy()` asserts on the unawaited Promise returned by `isChecked()`, which is always truthy, so the first test never verifies that 2FA was actually enabled (the PR adds a FIXME acknowledging this instead of fixing it). With the new backup-codes step inserted into the flow this assertion is the only post-enable check in that test, so a regression in the enable flow would not be caught. Use `await expect(locator).toBeChecked()` or the `[data-state="checked"]` locator as the second test does.

title: No test covers logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code
body: The core new behaviour of this PR — authenticating with a backup code in `next-auth-options.ts` (including single-use consumption) and in the disable endpoint — has no automated coverage; the added test only clicks the download/copy/close buttons on the new dialog and the file notes this as a TODO. Regressions such as a code being reusable, or the "Lost access" flow sending the wrong field, would go undetected.

title: Dismissing the backup-codes dialog skips onEnable(), leaving the parent UI stale
body: 2FA is already enabled on the server when the `DisplayBackupCodes` step is shown, but `onEnable()` is only called by the "Close" button. If the user dismisses the dialog with the X / Escape / overlay (which goes through `onOpenChange`), the parent's enable callback never runs, so the two-factor switch and any cached profile data keep showing 2FA as disabled until a reload, and the user loses the codes without any warning. The enable callback should also run when the dialog is closed from this step.

title: Backup code can be used to log in without the account password
body: The credentials provider only verifies the password when `credentials.totpCode` is empty (`if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)` a few lines above). The new backup-code branch is entered whenever `user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode` is true, regardless of `totpCode`. An attacker can therefore POST `email` + empty `password` + any garbage `totpCode` (e.g. "000000") + a valid `backupCode` and be logged in without ever proving knowledge of the password. Unlike a TOTP code, a backup code is static and never expires, so a single leaked/stolen backup code becomes a standalone, long-lived credential for the account. The backup-code check should require a successful password verification (or at minimum must not be reachable on the password-skipping path).

title: Backup code consumption is a read-modify-write and can be raced
body: The code list is read in the earlier `prisma.user.findUnique`, mutated in memory (`backupCodes[index] = null`) and written back with a full `update`. Two concurrent login attempts that both read the same ciphertext can both succeed with the *same* backup code, and the second write will also resurrect codes consumed by the first attempt (last write wins). Backup codes are meant to be single use; this allows replay of a code that was already spent. Consumption needs to be atomic (e.g. a transaction with a conditional update / optimistic version check on the stored value).

title: Backup codes are stored reversibly encrypted instead of hashed
body: Backup codes are persisted as `symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes), CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY)`, i.e. recoverable plaintext for anyone with the DB dump and the shared app encryption key (the same key used for many other things and typically present in the app environment). Because a backup code bypasses 2FA entirely, these should be stored as one-way hashes and compared by hashing the submitted value, so a database/key compromise does not immediately yield usable 2FA-bypass credentials. Additionally each code carries only 40 bits of entropy (`crypto.randomBytes(5)`), which is low for a credential that is checked by an endpoint reachable by unauthenticated callers.

title: onEnable() is now deferred to the Close button, so dismissing the dialog desyncs UI and loses the codes
body: Previously `onEnable()` was invoked as soon as the enable request succeeded; now it is only called from the "Close" button on the `DisplayBackupCodes` step. If the user dismisses the dialog with ESC/outside click/X after 2FA was already enabled server side, the parent is never notified: the two-factor switch stays in the "off" state even though 2FA is enabled on the account, and the backup codes are gone forever (there is no regenerate path). Notify the parent as soon as the server confirms enablement, and/or handle `onOpenChange` on this step.

title: "missing_backup_codes" tells users to generate codes in settings, but no such option exists
body: The message "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." is shown (login page and disable modal) when `user.backupCodes` is null. Every user who enabled 2FA before this migration has null `backupCodes` (the migration does not backfill), and this PR adds no UI to generate codes for an already-enabled 2FA account — codes are only created by `totp/setup`, which rejects users with `twoFactorEnabled` true. Users following this instruction will find nothing in settings; the only route is disabling 2FA (which requires a working authenticator) and re-enabling. Either add a regeneration flow or change the message to reflect reality.

title: resetState leaves stale backup codes and leaks the blob object URL
body: `resetState()` clears only `password`, `errorMessage` and `step`. `backupCodes` and `backupCodesUrl` are kept, so after closing and reopening the dialog the previously generated codes and download URL remain in component state (and are still reachable by the download anchor until a new setup overwrites them). The object URL created with `URL.createObjectURL` is only revoked on the next successful setup, so dialogs that are cancelled leak the blob for the lifetime of the document. Clear `backupCodes` and revoke/clear `backupCodesUrl` in `resetState` (and on unmount).

title: No test covers the actual backup-code authentication paths
body: The only added coverage exercises the download/copy/close buttons on the new setup screen. The security-critical new logic — logging in with a backup code via the credentials provider (including single-use consumption) and disabling 2FA with a backup code in `totp/disable.ts` — has no test at all, as the added TODO acknowledges. Given this code path can authenticate a user, at least one test that logs in with a stored code and asserts the code cannot be reused should be added.

title: Assertion on the 2FA switch is a no-op and was documented rather than fixed
body: `expect(page.locator('[data-testid=two-factor-switch]').isChecked()).toBeTruthy()` asserts on the returned Promise, which is always truthy, so the first test never verifies that 2FA was actually enabled (the added FIXME admits this). Use `await expect(locator).toBeChecked()` or the `[data-state="checked"]` selector used in the second test so the test can actually fail.

title: Unvalidated/unguarded backup code handling can throw an unhandled 500
body: `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, key))` and `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` are not guarded: if the stored ciphertext was written with a different `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (decrypt/parse throws) or if a client sends a non-string `backupCode` (e.g. a number or object), the handler throws a raw exception and returns an unhandled 500 instead of a meaningful error code. Validate the request body type and wrap the decrypt/parse in a try/catch returning a defined ErrorCode.

title: tabIndex={-1} makes the password reveal toggle unreachable by keyboard
body: Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the show/hide password button removes it from the tab order globally for every `PasswordField` in the app, so keyboard-only and screen-reader users can no longer toggle password visibility (the `sr-only` label and tooltip become unreachable). If the intent was only to keep focus out of the way in the 2FA modals, this should not be applied to the shared component unconditionally.

title: Backup-code login path lets a caller skip password verification entirely
body: Password verification only runs in the block at line 121 (`if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)`), i.e. it is skipped whenever a non-empty `totpCode` is submitted. The new backup-code branch at line 131 (`if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode)`) takes precedence over the TOTP branch, so a request that sends a dummy non-empty `totpCode` together with a valid `backupCode` has neither its password nor its TOTP code verified: the password check is skipped because `totpCode` is set, and the TOTP check is skipped because the backup-code branch ran instead. The result is that possession of a single backup code (e.g. from the downloaded `cal-backup-codes.txt`) is enough to sign in with just the e-mail address, downgrading 2FA from 'second factor' to 'only factor'. The branch should require that the password was actually verified (or verify it explicitly) before accepting a backup code.

title: Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write
body: The code decrypts `user.backupCodes`, nulls out the matched entry in memory and then writes the whole re-encrypted array back with `prisma.user.update`. Two requests that arrive concurrently both read the same pre-update array, so (a) the same backup code can be redeemed more than once (breaking the 'each code can be used exactly once' guarantee stated in `backup_code_instructions`), and (b) if two different codes are redeemed concurrently the second write resurrects the code invalidated by the first. Consuming the code needs to be atomic (e.g. a conditional/compare-and-set update inside a transaction, or storing codes in their own rows and deleting by unique key).

title: Backup codes are matched case-sensitively and without trimming
body: `backupCodes.indexOf(credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""))` only strips dashes. The generated codes are lowercase hex (`crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")`), but users typically retype them from a printout and mobile keyboards auto-capitalise the first character, and copy/paste frequently adds surrounding whitespace. Any uppercase character or stray space makes a valid code be rejected with `IncorrectBackupCode`, consuming the user's rate-limit budget and potentially locking them out of the very recovery path this feature adds. Normalise with `.trim().toLowerCase()` (same issue exists in `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts` line 61).

title: onEnable() is only invoked by the Close button, so dismissing the backup-code dialog leaves the parent UI stale
body: Previously `onEnable()` was called as soon as the enable request succeeded (old line 135). Now success only advances to `SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes`, and `onEnable()` is called exclusively from the `backup-codes-close` button handler. If the user dismisses the dialog any other way (the Dialog's close/X control, Escape, clicking the overlay — all of which go through `onOpenChange`), 2FA is enabled server-side but the parent never runs its `onEnable` callback, so the two-factor switch / cached query is not refreshed and the settings page reports 2FA as disabled until a manual reload. `onEnable()` should also be fired when the dialog closes from the DisplayBackupCodes step.

title: Submitting an empty backup code silently does nothing
body: `BackupCode.tsx` relies on the HTML `required`/`minLength` attributes, but the login form is rendered with `noValidate` and the zod schema only validates `email`/`password` (`.passthrough()` for everything else), so an empty backup code is submitted. Server-side an empty `backupCode` is falsy, so the TOTP branch runs and returns `ErrorCode.SecondFactorRequired`, which this handler maps to `setTwoFactorRequired(true)` and shows no message at all. From the user's point of view pressing Submit on the 'Lost access' screen does nothing — no error, no feedback. Validate `backupCode` in the form schema (or map `SecondFactorRequired` to a visible error while in lost-access mode).

title: Unvalidated request body can crash the disable endpoint
body: `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` is called on whatever JSON the client sent. A non-string value (e.g. `{"backupCode": 1234567890}` or an array) makes `replaceAll` throw a TypeError that is not caught, producing an unhandled 500 instead of a 400. Similarly `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` at line 58 throws if the stored blob cannot be decrypted/parsed. Validate the body (zod/typeof check) and wrap the decrypt/parse in a try/catch returning a proper error code.

title: Backup codes are stored reversibly encrypted instead of hashed
body: `backupCodes` is persisted as `symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes), CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY)`, so anyone who obtains a database dump plus the (usually env-deployed, long-lived) `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY` recovers every user's usable recovery credentials in plaintext. Unlike `twoFactorSecret`, backup codes never need to be displayed again after setup — only compared — so they should be stored as one-way hashes (e.g. per-code hash, compared by hashing the submitted code) to limit the impact of a DB/key compromise.

title: resetState() leaves backup codes in memory and leaks the blob URL
body: `resetState()` clears only `password`, `errorMessage` and `step`; `backupCodes`, `backupCodesUrl`, `dataUri` and `secret` persist. The `URL.createObjectURL` blob is only revoked on the next successful `handleSetup` call, so closing the dialog (or navigating away) leaks the object URL for the page's lifetime, and the plaintext recovery codes stay in component state after the dialog is closed. Revoke the URL and clear the code state in `resetState()`/on unmount.

title: Assertion is a no-op and the new backup-code auth paths are untested
body: `expect(page.locator('[data-testid=two-factor-switch]').isChecked()).toBeTruthy()` asserts on the returned Promise, which is always truthy, so this step passes even when 2FA was not enabled — the PR adds a FIXME comment acknowledging this but leaves the broken assertion in place (use `await expect(locator).toBeChecked()` or the `data-state="checked"` selector as the second test does). In addition, the only new coverage is clicking download/copy/close on the backup-code screen; the actual security-relevant paths added by this PR — logging in with a backup code, single-use invalidation of a redeemed code, and disabling 2FA with a backup code — have no tests at all (only a TODO), which is how issues like the password-bypass and case-sensitivity problems go unnoticed.

title: TypeError when evt.destinationCalendar is empty and location is Google Meet
body: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` yields `undefined` whenever the event has no destination calendar (now a common case: handleNewBooking sets `destinationCalendar: null` when neither the event type nor the organizer has one). The very next line dereferences it unconditionally: `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"`, which throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'integration')` and aborts `EventManager.create()` for any Google Meet booking made by a user without a destination calendar. Use optional chaining (`mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`).

title: Video booking references no longer store credentialId
body: `credentialId: isCalendarType ? result.credentialId : undefined` drops the credentialId for non-calendar (video) results; the previous code used `result.credentialId` in that branch. Video meeting references are therefore persisted with `credentialId: null`. Cancellation logic depends on it: `handleCancelBooking` only deletes the meeting when `bookingVideoReference.credentialId` is truthy (see packages/features/bookings/lib/handleCancelBooking.ts ~line 491), so Zoom/MS Teams/etc. meetings will silently stop being deleted when a booking is cancelled.

title: updateLocation creates booking references without externalCalendarId/credentialId
body: `externalCalendarId: result.externalId` and `credentialId: result.credentialId ?? undefined` are read from the results of `updateAllCalendarEvents`, but `CalendarManager.updateEvent` (packages/core/CalendarManager.ts:313-323) does not return `externalId` or `credentialId` at all — only `createEvent` was changed to return them. Previously these values came from `evt.destinationCalendar`. As a result, every booking reference created by an "edit location" action loses its calendar linkage, and subsequent updates/cancellations can no longer resolve the right credential/calendar (they fall back to iterating all credentials or to "primary").

title: Organization slug assignment logic inverted
body: `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})` inverts the previous condition `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })`. The intent is: when billing is enabled the slug is only *requested* (stored in `metadata.requestedSlug` until payment), otherwise the slug is set directly. With this change, a billing-enabled instance sets both `slug` and `metadata.requestedSlug`, and a non-billing instance (self-hosted) creates the organization with **no slug at all**, so org subdomain resolution/`orgDomains` lookups break for newly created orgs. This change is also unrelated to the PR's stated purpose.

title: updateEvent fallback calendar lookup can never match
body: `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` is only evaluated when `externalCalendarId` is falsy (the ternary's else branch), so it compares each `cal.externalId` against `undefined`/`""` and always returns `undefined`. The previous code used `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. Consequently, when no external calendar id is passed, `calendar.events.update({ calendarId: undefined })` is issued instead of targeting the destination calendar, and the update fails. The intent was presumably to fall back to the first (main host) destination calendar.

title: deleteEvent fallback calendar lookup can never match
body: Same self-defeating condition as in `updateEvent`: `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)` only runs when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so it always resolves to `undefined` and the code silently falls back to `"primary"`. Previously it used `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. Events stored in a non-primary destination calendar will therefore not be found/deleted (Google returns 404, which the handler swallows), leaving orphaned calendar events after cancellations.

title: createEvent ignores destination calendars that have no credentialId
body: `selectedCalendar` is now resolved only by `cal.credentialId === credentialId`. `DestinationCalendar.credentialId` is nullable, and `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents` explicitly handles that case by calling `createEvent(credential, event)` without an externalId. For those rows the `find` returns `undefined` and the event is created in `"primary"` instead of the user's configured destination calendar — a regression from the previous `calEventRaw.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. A fallback to the destination calendar matching this integration (or the first one) is needed.

title: Hangout-link patch sends calendarId: undefined
body: In `createEvent`, the follow-up `calendar.events.patch({ calendarId: selectedCalendar, ... })` uses `selectedCalendar` directly, but `selectedCalendar` can now be `undefined` (the `|| "primary"` default was moved to the insert call only). When the destination calendar can't be resolved, the insert succeeds against `primary` while the patch that adds the Meet link to the description is sent with no calendarId and fails.

title: Duplicate calendar events created for multiple destination calendars without credentialId
body: For each destination with no `credentialId`, the code filters *all* of the organizer's credentials of that integration type and creates an event with each. With the new multi-destination array (e.g. two collective hosts both having a Google destination calendar with `credentialId: null`), this loop runs once per destination using the same credential set, producing N duplicate events in the same calendar. The per-destination branch should create at most one event for the destination it is iterating over.

title: updateAllCalendarEvents error message computed but never logged
body: The catch block still builds the diagnostic `message` (including credential type, userId and bookingId) but the `console.error(message)` call was removed in this change. Calendar update failures are now swallowed entirely with no log output, making production debugging of failed reschedules/updates impossible.

title: Collective team destination calendars silently dropped when organizer has none
body: `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` uses optional chaining, and `evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar. In that case all the collected host destination calendars are discarded, so collective hosts get no calendar invite — exactly the scenario this PR aims to fix. Initialize the array (e.g. `[]`) before pushing, or build the array in one expression.

title: Dynamic-booking user select no longer fetches organization slug
body: The rewritten `loadUsers` dropped `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` from the `prisma.user.findMany` select used for dynamic (no eventTypeId) bookings. This field was added deliberately for org-aware booker URLs; without it any downstream use of `user.organization?.slug` resolves to undefined (or fails type-checking because the two branches of `loadUsers` now return different shapes), producing wrong links for dynamic group bookings in organizations. The removal is unrelated to the destinationCalendar refactor.

title: Empty dynamicUserList surfaces as a 500 instead of a 400
body: `throw new Error("dynamicUserList is not properly defined or empty.")` is a plain `Error`, so the catch below (which only re-wraps `HttpError` and Prisma errors as 400) converts it into `HttpError({ statusCode: 500, message: "Unable to load users" })`. A malformed/empty client-supplied user list is a client error and previously did not produce a 5xx; this will pollute error monitoring and give the booker no useful message.

title: Recurring-cancellation deletion repeated once per calendar reference
body: The recurring + `allRemainingBookings` block (which itself loops over every user calendar credential and every updated booking) is now nested inside the new `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)` loop. With multiple calendar references (the normal case for the new multi-host destination calendars) the same delete calls are issued refs × credentials × bookings times, multiplying external API calls against Google/Office and relying on 404/410 swallowing for correctness. The recurring branch should run once, outside the per-reference loop.

title: Webhook payload destinationCalendar shape is now inconsistent (null vs []) and breaking for consumers
body: `destinationCalendar` in the webhook payload changes from an object/null to an array, but the code paths are inconsistent: BOOKING_REJECTED/confirm now emits `[]` (this assertion), while BOOKING_CREATED and BOOKING_REQUESTED still assert `null` (lines 119 and 373) because handleNewBooking sets `null` when there is no destination calendar. External webhook consumers parsing `payload.destinationCalendar.externalId` will break, and they now have to handle three shapes (object-less array, empty array, null). The shape should be normalized (always an array) and the payload change documented as breaking.

title: Calendar.createEvent credentialId made a required parameter
body: `createEvent(event: CalendarEvent, credentialId: number)` adds a required second parameter to the public `Calendar` interface. Any caller outside of `CalendarManager` (other packages/apps, third-party calendar app implementations in the app store that are invoked directly) that calls `createEvent(evt)` now fails type-checking, and at runtime receives `undefined` for `credentialId` — which in GoogleCalendarService makes the destination-calendar lookup fail and silently writes to `primary`. Making the parameter optional and defensively handling `undefined` would avoid both the contract break and the silent misrouting.

title: Organization slug logic inverted (unrelated change)
body: The condition was changed from `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`, which inverts the behaviour: the team's `slug` is now only persisted when team billing *is* enabled, and in that case both `slug` and `metadata.requestedSlug` are set simultaneously. On self-hosted/billing-disabled instances the organization is now created with `slug = null`, so its subdomain/org lookup (`orgDomains`, `slugCollisions` checks, org URLs) will not resolve. This change is unrelated to the destinationCalendar refactor and should be reverted or corrected to `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })`.

title: TypeError when location is Google Meet and no destination calendar exists
body: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` yields `undefined` when the array is empty or null, and line 119 then reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining. For any booking whose location is Google Meet and whose organizer/event type has no destination calendar (previously handled safely via `evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`), `EventManager.create()` throws `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'integration')`, failing the whole booking instead of falling back to Cal Video.

title: credentialId is no longer stored for video booking references
body: `credentialId: isCalendarType ? result.credentialId : undefined` drops the credentialId for non-calendar (video) results; the previous code stored `result.credentialId` for video results. Cancellation logic in `handleCancelBooking` only deletes the meeting when `bookingVideoReference.credentialId` is set (`if (bookingVideoReference && bookingVideoReference.credentialId)`), so video meetings created after this change will never be deleted on cancellation, and other code paths that resolve a video credential from the reference will also break.

title: Destination-calendar fallback in updateEvent/deleteEvent can never match
body: `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` is only evaluated in the branch where `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so the predicate compares each `externalId` against `undefined`/`null` and always returns `undefined`. The pre-change fallback was `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. Consequence: when a booking reference has no `externalCalendarId`, `calendar.events.update` is called with `calendarId: undefined` (request fails / wrong target) instead of the configured destination calendar. The same broken predicate is used at line 317 in `deleteEvent`, where it silently falls back to `primary` and the event in the destination calendar is never deleted.

title: createEvent falls back to "primary" when destination calendar has no credentialId
body: `selectedCalendar` is now resolved only by `cal.credentialId === credentialId`. Destination calendars stored without a `credentialId` (legacy rows, and the event-type destination calendar path in `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents` which calls `createEvent(c, event)` without an externalId) will not match, so the event is created in the account's `primary` calendar instead of the user-selected destination calendar. Previously `calEventRaw.destinationCalendar.externalId` was used unconditionally. Consider keeping an `externalId` fallback when no credentialId match is found.

title: events.patch uses possibly-undefined calendarId
body: The insert call guards with `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"`, but the follow-up `calendar.events.patch` (used to write the hangout link into the description) passes `calendarId: selectedCalendar` directly. When `selectedCalendar` is undefined (no destination calendar matching the credentialId), the event is created in `primary` but the patch request targets an undefined calendar and fails, so Google Meet links are missing from the calendar event description.

title: Team destination calendars dropped when organizer has none
body: `evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` exists, and the collective branch then does `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`. Because of the optional chaining the collected host calendars are silently discarded in exactly the case the PR aims to fix (organizer without a destination calendar, other collective hosts with one). Initialize the array (e.g. `[]`) and push, or build the array from all sources before assigning.

title: updateLocation no longer records externalCalendarId on references
body: `referencesToCreate` in `updateLocation` now uses `result.externalId`, but `CalendarManager.updateEvent` never sets `externalId` on its `EventResult` (only `createEvent` does). Previously the value came from `evt.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. As a result, booking references recreated after a location change get `externalCalendarId: undefined`, so later updates/cancellations can no longer target the correct external calendar (see the Google `deleteEvent`/`updateEvent` fallbacks, which require it).

title: Recurring cancellation deletes every event once per calendar reference
body: The recurring-event branch (iterating all of the user's calendar credentials × all `updatedBookings` × each booking's first calendar reference) is now executed inside the new `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)` loop. With N calendar references the same delete requests are issued N times, multiplying external API calls and producing repeated 404/410 responses. The recurring branch should be hoisted out of the per-reference loop (or keyed on the current reference) instead of re-running for each one.

title: updateAllCalendarEvents error is no longer logged
body: The `catch` block still builds the diagnostic `message` string (including credential type, userId and bookingId) but the `console.error(message)` call was removed, so `message` is now dead code and calendar-update failures are swallowed with no trace in the logs. Either log the message or remove it.

title: updateEvent may be called with an undefined credential
body: Inside the `reference.credentialId` branch, if neither `this.calendarCredentials` nor the DB lookup yields a credential (e.g. credential deleted, or app slug missing), `credential` stays `undefined` and `updateEvent(credential, ...)` is still invoked, which will throw when it dereferences `credential.appName`/`credential.type`. Guard with `if (credential)` and push a failed `EventResult` otherwise so the booking flow reports the app status instead of hitting the generic catch.

title: organization.slug removed from dynamic-booking user select
body: The rewritten `loadUsers` for dynamic (no eventTypeId) bookings no longer selects `organization: { select: { slug: true } }`, which the previous query included. Any downstream consumer of the organizer's `organization.slug` (org-aware booker/webapp URLs) will now see `undefined` for dynamic group bookings. This change is unrelated to the destinationCalendar refactor; restore the field unless it is provably unused.

title: Invalid dynamicUserList surfaces as 500 instead of 400
body: `throw new Error("dynamicUserList is not properly defined or empty.")` is caught by the new try/catch, which only maps `HttpError` and `Prisma.PrismaClientKnownRequestError` to a 400; a plain `Error` falls through to `new HttpError({ statusCode: 500, message: "Unable to load users" })`. A malformed client request therefore reports a server error and the real reason is lost. Throw `new HttpError({ statusCode: 400, ... })` directly for this validation.

title: Webhook payload shape for destinationCalendar is now inconsistent (null vs [] vs array)
body: `CalendarEvent.destinationCalendar` changed from an object to an array, which is a breaking change for webhook/API consumers. The payload is now inconsistent across triggers: BOOKING_REJECTED expects `[]` (confirm.handler returns `[]`), while BOOKING_CREATED/BOOKING_REQUESTED still expect `null` (handleNewBooking assigns `null` when no calendar is found). Normalize to a single representation (always an array) and document the breaking payload change.

title: No tests for multi-destination-calendar creation/update paths
body: `createAllCalendarEvents` and `updateAllCalendarEvents` were substantially rewritten (loops over multiple destination calendars, per-reference credential resolution, DB credential fallback), and `EventResult.externalId`/`credentialId` now drive `referencesToCreate`. There are no unit tests covering: multiple destination calendars producing one reference per calendar with the correct `externalCalendarId`/`credentialId`, the empty destinationCalendar fallback, and the video-reference credentialId. Given the regressions these fields cause in cancel/reschedule flows, tests here would prevent silent breakage.

title: Unguarded access to first destinationCalendar crashes Google Meet fallback
body: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` yields `undefined` whenever the event has no destination calendar (empty array or null, which is now a very common case — several call sites build `destinationCalendar: []`). The very next line dereferences it: `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"`. For any booking whose location is Google Meet and whose organizer/event type has no destination calendar, this throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'integration')` and the whole booking creation fails. Use optional chaining (`mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`).

title: Video booking references no longer store credentialId
body: In `create()`, `referencesToCreate` now sets `credentialId: isCalendarType ? result.credentialId : undefined`. Previously the non-calendar branch used `result.credentialId`, i.e. the video credential id returned by `createMeeting`. With this change every `_video` booking reference is persisted with `credentialId = null`. Cancellation code (`handleCancelBooking`: `if (bookingVideoReference && bookingVideoReference.credentialId)`) only deletes the meeting when that id is present, so video meetings will silently never be deleted on cancellation for all new bookings.

title: updateLocation creates booking references without externalCalendarId/credentialId
body: `updateLocation()` builds `referencesToCreate` from `result.externalId` and `result.credentialId`, but these results come from `CalendarManager.updateEvent()`, which never sets `externalId` or `credentialId` on its returned `EventResult` (only `createEvent` does). Both fields are therefore always `undefined`, whereas the previous code fell back to `evt.destinationCalendar?.externalId` / `.credentialId`. The references written by `editLocation.handler.ts` will have no external calendar id or credential id, so subsequent updates/deletes of that booking will target the credential-less legacy path / the "primary" calendar instead of the real destination calendar.

title: updateAllCalendarEvents can call updateEvent with an undefined credential
body: Inside the new per-reference loop, when `reference.credentialId` is set but neither `this.calendarCredentials` nor the DB lookup yields a usable credential (e.g. credential deleted, or `credentialFromDB.app?.slug` missing), `credential` stays `undefined` and `updateEvent(credential, event, bookingRefUid, calenderExternalId)` is still pushed. `CalendarManager.updateEvent` dereferences `credential.appName`/`credential.type` when building its result, throwing a TypeError. Because `return Promise.all(result)` is not awaited inside the `try`, that rejection escapes the surrounding try/catch and surfaces as an unhandled rejection rather than the intended degraded result. Skip the reference when no credential could be resolved.

title: Error diagnostics removed from updateAllCalendarEvents catch block
body: The catch block still computes the detailed `message` string but the `console.error(message)` call was deleted, so `message` is now dead code and calendar update failures are swallowed completely with no log output. Debugging multi-host calendar failures (the exact scenario this PR targets) becomes impossible; keep a log statement.

title: updateEvent destination-calendar fallback can never match
body: `const selectedCalendar = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;` — the `find` only runs when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so it compares `cal.externalId === undefined/""` and always returns `undefined`. The previous code fell back to `event.destinationCalendar.externalId`. Result: for bookings whose reference has no `externalCalendarId` (legacy bookings, and references created by `updateLocation`, see above), `calendar.events.update` is called with `calendarId: undefined`, so the Google request is malformed and the update fails instead of hitting the host's destination calendar. Should fall back to the first destination calendar's `externalId`.

title: deleteEvent destination-calendar fallback can never match
body: Same inverted predicate as in `updateEvent`: `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)` is only evaluated when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so it always resolves to `undefined` and `calendarId` degrades to `"primary"`. Events that live in a non-primary destination calendar and whose booking reference lacks `externalCalendarId` will no longer be deleted (Google returns 404, which the handler swallows), leaving orphaned calendar entries.

title: Hangout-link patch uses possibly-undefined calendarId
body: `selectedCalendar` can now be `undefined` (when no destination calendar matches `credentialId`); the insert call guards this with `selectedCalendar || "primary"`, but the follow-up `calendar.events.patch({ calendarId: selectedCalendar, ... })` that writes the Meet link into the description does not. When `selectedCalendar` is undefined the patch request is malformed and the event description will be missing the hangout link. Use the same `selectedCalendar || "primary"` value for the patch.

title: createEvent now ignores destination calendars that have no credentialId
body: The target calendar is resolved exclusively via `calEventRaw.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.credentialId === credentialId)`. `DestinationCalendar.credentialId` is nullable and is null for rows created before credential linking, so for those users the event is now written to `"primary"` instead of their configured destination calendar — a behaviour regression from the previous `destinationCalendar.externalId` lookup. Worse, `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents` still records `externalId: destination.externalId` in the booking reference for the credential-ful branch, so the stored reference can disagree with the calendar actually used, breaking later update/delete.

title: Organization slug condition inverted (unrelated change)
body: `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` was changed to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`, inverting the condition. With team billing enabled the org now gets both a real `slug` and `metadata.requestedSlug` (the requestedSlug flow exists precisely because the slug must not be claimed until payment), and with billing disabled (self-hosted default) the organization is created with no slug at all, so org subdomain resolution breaks. This change is also unrelated to the destinationCalendar refactor and should be reverted.

title: Collective hosts' destination calendars are dropped when there is no primary destination calendar
body: `evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` exists, and the collective handling is `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`. With optional chaining on `null`, the push is a no-op, so for a collective event where the organizer has no destination calendar but other hosts do, none of the host calendars are used — exactly the multi-host case this PR is meant to fix. Initialise the field to an array (or assign the collected list) instead of relying on `?.push`.

title: Invalid dynamicUserList surfaces as a 500 instead of 400
body: `throw new Error("dynamicUserList is not properly defined or empty.")` is thrown inside the new `try` in `loadUsers`, but the catch only maps `HttpError` and Prisma errors to a 400; everything else becomes `new HttpError({ statusCode: 500, message: "Unable to load users" })`. A malformed client request (empty dynamic user list) is therefore reported as a server error and the actual reason is lost. Throw an `HttpError` with status 400 directly.

title: organization relation removed from the dynamic-booking user select
body: In the `!eventTypeId` (dynamic group booking) branch of `loadUsers`, the `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` sub-select was dropped. Any downstream consumer of `user.organization` for dynamic bookings (e.g. building org-scoped booker URLs) will now see `undefined`, and the two branches of `loadUsers` return structurally different user shapes, which weakens the inferred type the comment claims to rely on. Re-add the select unless you have verified no consumer reads it.

title: Recurring cancellation now issues duplicated delete calls per calendar reference
body: The recurring branch (iterate all of the user's calendar credentials × all `updatedBookings`' first calendar reference) was moved inside the new `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)` loop. With N calendar references on a booking the whole credential×booking deletion matrix is executed N times, sending the same `deleteEvent` request repeatedly to each provider (and pushing N× duplicate promises into `apiDeletes`). For multi-host collective recurring events this multiplies external API calls and the risk of rate limiting. Hoist the recurring handling out of the per-reference loop.

title: Credential-less destinations create events in every credential of that integration
body: For each destination without a `credentialId`, the code creates an event in every calendar credential of the matching integration type (`this.calendarCredentials.filter((c) => c.type === destination.integration)`). Now that `destinationCalendar` is an array and is populated with each collective host's calendar, two hosts with credential-less Google destination calendars cause 2 × (number of google credentials) event creations, i.e. duplicate calendar entries for the same booking. Additionally the resulting `EventResult`s carry no `externalId`, so the persisted booking references lose the external calendar id. De-duplicate destinations and pass the destination's `externalId` through.

title: No tests for the array-based destinationCalendar behaviour
body: This PR changes `CalendarEvent.destinationCalendar` from a single object to an array across ~20 files and adds new branching in `createAllCalendarEvents`/`updateAllCalendarEvents` (per-destination credential resolution, DB credential fallback, collective host aggregation), yet no unit/integration tests were added and the only test touched is an e2e expectation value. Given the number of null/empty-array edge cases introduced (see the Google Meet crash and the dropped collective calendars), at least tests covering: empty destinationCalendar, destination without credentialId, and a collective event with two hosts, are needed before merge.

title: minimumTokenResponseSchema is built with bogus computed keys and strips every field except access_token
body: The schema is declared as `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), [z.string().toString()]: z.number(), [z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional() })`. The computed keys evaluate `ZodString.toString()` / `ZodOptional.toString()`, which both produce the same literal string (`"[object Object]"`), so the resulting schema is just `{ access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown? }`. The intended behaviour ("assume any property with a number is the expiry" and "allow other properties") is not implemented at all. Worse, because `z.object` strips unknown keys by default, parsing a credential-sync response discards `expires_in`/`expiry_date`/`refresh_token`, so callers that merge `tokenResponse.data` into the stored key (office365calendar, zoomvideo) end up with no expiry at all — the token is treated as permanently expired and refreshed on every request, and zoom computes `expiry_date = Date.now() + NaN`.

title: Injecting the literal string "refresh_token" overwrites valid stored refresh tokens
body: When the parsed response has no `refresh_token`, the function sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. Several callers spread the parsed data over the existing credential key and persist it, e.g. `packages/app-store/office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` does `o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }` and writes it to the DB. Microsoft legitimately omits `refresh_token` on some refresh responses (the schema marks it optional), so the user's real refresh token is replaced in the database by the useless string "refresh_token" and the integration breaks permanently until re-installed. The same happens for zoomvideo, where `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token` is persisted.

title: Google credential key is overwritten with the zod safeParse wrapper object
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the result of `schema.safeParse(...)`, i.e. `{ success: true, data: {...} }`, but the result is assigned to `key` and written straight to the DB (`prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`). Previously the code stored `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` (the credential object itself). After the first token refresh every Google Calendar credential will be stored as `{"success":true,"data":{...}}`, which no longer satisfies `googleCredentialSchema`, so subsequent constructions of GoogleCalendarService throw and the calendar connection is broken for the user.

title: Credential-sync branch returns a fetch Response while callers expect provider-specific shapes
body: In the sync branch the helper returns the raw `fetch` `Response`, but the wrapped `refreshFunction` of most callers returns something completely different: google returns a Gaxios response (caller reads `res.data.access_token`), hubspot returns a parsed `HubspotToken` (caller reads `.expiresIn` and stores the object as the credential key), zoho-bigin and zohocrm return an axios response (callers read `tokenInfo.data.error` / `tokenInfo.data.access_token`). With app-credential syncing enabled these callers will read `undefined` off the `Response`, throw TypeErrors, compute `NaN` expiry dates, or persist a serialized `Response` as the credential key. The helper must normalise the sync response (await `response.json()`) into the same shape the refresh function returns, or each caller must be adapted.

title: Credential-sync request is unauthenticated and its status is never checked
body: The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` with no shared secret/signature header (unlike the inbound webhook, which verifies `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`), so the self-hoster's endpoint has no way to tell that the request really came from Cal.com — anybody who knows the URL can harvest access tokens for arbitrary user ids if the endpoint trusts the caller. In addition the response status is never checked, so a 4xx/5xx body is passed to the token parsers as if it were a token response, producing confusing downstream failures instead of a clear error.

title: `prisma` is used but never imported in salesforce CalendarService
body: The newly added code calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` inside `getClient`, but this file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. This is a compile error (and a `ReferenceError` at runtime if type-checking is bypassed), so every Salesforce booking/calendar operation fails as soon as the service is instantiated.

title: Salesforce connection still uses the old access token after refreshing
body: `getClient` now performs a refresh_token exchange and persists the new token, but the `jsforce.Connection` is still created with `accessToken: credentialKey.access_token` (the stale value read from the credential before refreshing) and `instanceUrl: credentialKey.instance_url`. The refresh is therefore pointless: if the stored access token was expired, every Salesforce API call still fails. The newly parsed `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token` / `instance_url` should be used.

title: Salesforce token is refreshed unconditionally on every service instantiation
body: `getClient` issues a refresh_token request to `login.salesforce.com` and a `credential.update` write every time a `SalesforceCalendarService` is constructed, with no expiry check on the stored token. Since the service is constructed per booking/availability operation this adds a blocking round trip plus a DB write to every request and will hit Salesforce's refresh-token rate limits on busy instances.

title: Error detection via `response.statusText !== "OK"` is unreliable
body: The refresh result is validated with `if (response.statusText !== "OK") throw ...`. `statusText` is an empty string for HTTP/2 responses (undici does not synthesize a reason phrase), so a perfectly successful refresh can be rejected with an `HttpError` whose message is empty, while a non-2xx response with reason phrase "OK" would be accepted. Use `response.ok` / `response.status` instead.

title: Zoho Bigin passes a credential id where a user id is expected
body: `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` passes `credentialId` as the third argument, which the helper uses as `calcomUserId` in the credential-sync request body. The self-hosted endpoint will receive a credential id instead of the Cal.com user id, so it will either return the wrong user's tokens or fail. `refreshAccessToken` should receive and forward `credential.userId`.

title: Zoom sends appSlug "zoomvideo", which is not the app's slug
body: `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoomvideo", credential.userId)` sends `appSlug=zoomvideo`, but the Zoom app's slug used everywhere else (callback stores `appId: "zoom"`, and the new `/api/webhook/app-credential` endpoint looks the app up with `prisma.app.findUnique({ where: { slug } })`) is `zoom`. A self-hoster keying off `appSlug` will not be able to map the sync request back to the credential the webhook created, so Zoom credential syncing silently fails.

title: Webex refresh still validated with the strict provider schema, so credential sync cannot work
body: Webex was switched to `refreshOAuthTokens` but the response is still validated with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema.safeParse(...)`, which requires an exact `scope` literal, `token_type: "Bearer"`, `refresh_token` and `refresh_token_expires_in`. A self-hosted sync endpoint is documented to return only the access token and expiry, so the parse always fails and `refreshAccessToken` rejects with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". Either use `parseRefreshTokenResponse` here (as done for zoom/office365) or don't wire Webex into the sync flow.

title: Webhook handler has no method guard and throws raw errors on malformed input
body: The handler accepts any HTTP verb (GET/DELETE included) and uses `schema.parse(req.body)` plus `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` without try/catch. A malformed body, a payload encrypted with the wrong key, or non-JSON plaintext results in an unhandled exception and a 500 with a stack trace instead of a 400/422 with a useful message. Restrict to POST and use `safeParse` / wrap the decryption in a try/catch.

title: Updating synced credentials does not clear the `invalid` flag
body: When a credential already exists the handler only writes `key`. Credentials that were previously marked `invalid: true` (e.g. google/zoom/webex set this on `invalid_grant`) stay invalid after fresh keys are pushed in, so Cal.com keeps treating the connection as broken even though valid tokens were just synced. The update should also reset `invalid: false`.

title: Webhook secret compared with a non-constant-time `!==` and header may be an array
body: The shared secret check uses a plain string inequality, which short-circuits on the first differing byte and is therefore vulnerable to timing analysis; use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers. Additionally `req.headers[name]` can be `string[]` when the header is sent twice, in which case the comparison always fails and legitimate callers get a 403 with no explanation.

title: findFirst + update can leave duplicate credentials out of sync
body: Because the lookup is `findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })`, when a user has more than one credential row for the same app (which happens for several apps that historically allowed duplicates) only one row is updated; the stale rows keep their old keys and may still be selected by other code paths (`findFirst` is used in several adapters). Two concurrent webhook deliveries can also both see no credential and create two rows. Consider a unique constraint or an `updateMany`/transaction.

title: No tests for the new credential webhook or the token-parsing helpers
body: This PR adds a publicly reachable endpoint that decrypts a payload and writes third-party OAuth credentials for arbitrary user ids, plus two new shared helpers (`parseRefreshTokenResponse`, `refreshOAuthTokens`) used by ~10 app integrations, with no unit tests. Basic tests covering secret mismatch, unknown user/app, bad ciphertext, create-vs-update behaviour, and the token-schema fallback would have caught the schema and response-shape defects noted elsewhere in this review.

title: Google credential key is overwritten with the zod SafeParse wrapper object
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse()` returns the result of `schema.safeParse(...)` (i.e. `{ success: true, data: {...} }`), not the parsed object, but the return value is assigned to `key` and written straight into `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. Previously the code used `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` which returned the credential object itself. As a result, after the first token refresh the stored Google Calendar credential becomes `{"success":true,"data":{...}}`, which no longer satisfies `googleCredentialSchema` on the next load, permanently breaking Google Calendar for that user. It should store `...data` (and ideally only after checking `success`).

title: minimumTokenResponseSchema computed keys are nonsense and strip every token field except access_token
body: `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the string `"[object Object]"` (Zod types have no `toString` override), so the object literal ends up with a single extra key literally named `"[object Object]"`, with the second definition overwriting the first. The resulting schema is effectively `{ access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown }`. Because `z.object` strips unknown keys by default, when credential sharing is enabled the parsed data loses `expires_in`/`expiry_date`/`refresh_token`/`scope`/etc. Callers that spread `tokenResponse.data` into the stored credential (e.g. office365calendar) will therefore persist a credential with no expiry and a bogus refresh token. The intent ("allow any extra properties, require access_token plus a numeric expiry") needs `.passthrough()` / `z.record()`, not computed keys.

title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token", destroying valid stored refresh tokens
body: When the provider response has no `refresh_token`, the function sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. This runs on the normal (non credential-sharing) path too. For providers whose schema makes `refresh_token` optional — e.g. `packages/app-store/office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts`, where the result is spread with `{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }` and persisted — the real, still-valid refresh token in the DB is overwritten with the useless string `"refresh_token"`, so the next refresh fails and the user must reconnect. Only inject a placeholder when it is actually needed, or leave the field absent so the spread keeps the existing token.

title: Credential-sync path returns a fetch Response where callers expect an axios/SDK/gaxios response
body: When credential sharing is enabled the helper returns a raw `fetch` `Response`, but the call sites consume very different shapes: `zoho-bigin` and `zohocrm` read `tokenInfo.data.error` / `tokenInfo.data.access_token` (axios response), `hubspot` assigns the return value to a `HubspotToken` and reads `expiresIn`/`accessToken` (SDK object), and `googlecalendar` reads `res?.data` (gaxios response). A `Response` has none of these properties, so with `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` configured these refresh paths throw `TypeError` or silently store `undefined` tokens. The helper needs to normalise the sync response per call site (or each call site must handle both shapes).

title: `prisma` is used but never imported in Salesforce CalendarService
body: `await prisma.credential.update(...)` was added to `getClient`, but there is no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` in the file (the import list only adds `zod` and `parseRefreshTokenResponse`). This is a compile error under type-check and a `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined` at runtime, which means every Salesforce CalendarService instantiation (i.e. every booking/availability call involving Salesforce) will throw.

title: Salesforce connection is built with the stale access token after refreshing
