Loki's real `applyTemplateVariables` deliberately removes `__auto`, `__interval`, `__range` (and their variants) from `scopedVars` so that they are interpolated on the backend with the *split* time range; a real `templateSrv.replace` would leave `$__auto` untouched here. The test therefore asserts behaviour that does not occur in production and would not catch a regression where `$__auto` is prematurely resolved against the full range. Using a non-range variable (like the `$step` part of the test) or a real templateSrv stub with defined variables would make the test meaningful.

title: Queries are now interpolated twice (runSplitQuery + DataSourceWithBackend.query)
body: `runSplitQuery` now maps every target through `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)`. The sub-requests built from these targets are executed with `datasource.runQuery(subRequest)`, which calls `super.query()` (DataSourceWithBackend.query), and that method already applies `applyTemplateVariables(q, request.scopedVars, request.filters)` to every target it sends to the backend. As a result each query is interpolated twice: `templateSrv.replace` runs over an already-substituted expression (so a variable whose value itself contains `$something`/`[[something]]` will be expanded a second time) and `addAdHocFilters` is applied a second time to an expression that already contains the ad hoc matchers, which is at best redundant LogQL parsing per sub-request and at worst produces duplicated label matchers in the selector. If interpolation must happen up front for partitioning/step calculation, the second pass should be avoided (e.g. by stripping scopedVars/filters from the sub-request or by only using the interpolated copies for partitioning decisions).

title: Shard path re-interpolates already sharded expressions
body: `runShardSplitQuery` interpolates the targets, `splitQueriesByStreamShard` then rewrites them with `interpolateShardingSelector()` (adding `__stream_shard__=~"..."` and `| drop __stream_shard__`) and hands the result to `runSplitQuery`, which (after this PR) interpolates them again, and `datasource.runQuery` interpolates a third time inside `DataSourceWithBackend.query`. So for every shard group the sharded expression is re-parsed and re-processed by `addAdHocFilters`/`templateSrv.replace` twice more. The new test assertion `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` (shardQuerySplitting.test.ts line 112) confirms this: one interpolation became five for a single query. Besides the wasted work, re-applying ad hoc filters and variable substitution to an already-interpolated, shard-annotated expression risks duplicated matchers and double expansion of variable values that contain `$`.

title: New test asserts client-side interpolation of $__auto, which the real code must not do
body: The test mocks `templateSrv.replace` with a blind string replacement (`input.replace('$__auto', '5m')`) and then asserts that the expression reaching `runQuery` is `count_over_time({a="b"}[5m])`. In the real `LokiDatasource.applyTemplateVariables`, `__auto`/`__interval`/`__interval_ms`/`__range*` are deliberately removed from the scoped vars so that they are interpolated on the backend with the *sub-request's* time range; a frontend interpolation of `$__auto` based on the full range would yield a wrong step/range for each split chunk. The test therefore validates behaviour that neither happens nor should happen in production and gives false confidence; it should instead cover a user-defined variable (e.g. `$step`) and explicitly assert that `$__auto` is left untouched.

title: Assertion hard-codes redundant interpolation count
body: `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` encodes the number of times the (now repeated) interpolation happens for a single query: once in `runShardSplitQuery` plus once per shard-group sub-request via `runSplitQuery`. This number has no functional meaning, is coupled to the number of shard groups produced by the mocked label values, and will break on unrelated changes to grouping/shard-size heuristics. Prefer asserting that the interpolated expression reaches `runQuery` (or that it is called at least once per target) instead of an exact call count that documents the redundant interpolation.

title: Targets are now interpolated two to three times before being sent
body: `runSplitQuery` now maps every target through `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)`, but the same method is still applied later by `DataSourceWithBackend.query()` for every target of the sub-request created in `runSplitGroupedQueries` (via `datasource.runQuery`). In the shard-splitting path it is worse: `runShardSplitQuery` interpolates once (shardQuerySplitting.ts:52) and then calls `runSplitQuery` for each shard group, which interpolates again, and the backend wrapper interpolates a third time. Concrete consequences: (1) `applyTemplateVariables` calls `addAdHocFilters`, so ad hoc filters are re-applied to an expression that already contains them; for non-indexed labels the filter is appended as a pipeline stage, producing duplicated stages such as `| env="prod" | env="prod"` in the executed query; (2) `templateSrv.replace` runs over already-substituted text, so any variable value that itself contains `$name`/`${name}` syntax is substituted a second time and the resulting query differs from what the user wrote; (3) each pass re-parses the LogQL expression (lezer) per sub-request, which is pure overhead – the updated shard test even asserts 5 calls where there was previously 1. Consider adding an option/flag so the splitting code interpolates exactly once (e.g. skip interpolation in nested `runSplitQuery` calls and in the request sent to the backend).

title: New interpolation test asserts behaviour that does not hold with the real template service
body: The test stubs `replace` with a blind `input.replace('$__auto', '5m')`, and then asserts that the expression sent to `runQuery` is `count_over_time({a="b"}[5m])`. The real Loki `applyTemplateVariables` deliberately strips `__auto`/`__interval`/`__range` from the scoped vars handed to `templateSrv.replace` so that those variables are interpolated on the backend with the *split* time range; with the production template service `$__auto` would still be present in the expression at this point. The test therefore encodes incorrect expectations and gives false confidence. It also does not cover the regression the PR fixes: that the interpolated `step` is used when computing the partitions (e.g. asserting the number/size of sub-requests changes when `step: '$step'` resolves to a large interval). The same applies to the equivalent new test in shardQuerySplitting.test.ts.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a brand-new logger, discarding recorded logs
body: `TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()` instead of a logger that shares the receiver's `DebugLogs/InfoLogs/WarnLogs/ErrorLogs` counters. Since `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` now emits its log line via `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`, any test that injects a `*TestLogger` into the middleware and then asserts on `logger.InfoLogs.Calls`/`Message`/`Ctx` will observe zero calls — the log is recorded on a throwaway instance. This silently makes log assertions for the logger middleware (and any other code that logs through `FromContext`) impossible, so regressions in the log output will go undetected. The fake should return the same instance (or one sharing the `Logs` structs).

title: Logger middleware silently depends on ContextualLoggerMiddleware being installed above it
body: `logRequest` no longer adds `pluginId`, `endpoint`, `uname`, `dsName`, `dsUID` or `traceID` to the log parameters; it relies entirely on `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)` picking up the attributes injected by the new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` (and, for `traceID`, on the tracing package having registered a contextual log provider). This dependency is implicit and unchecked: if `NewLoggerMiddleware` is used without `NewContextualLoggerMiddleware`, or if the two are ordered so that the contextual middleware runs after the logger middleware, the 'Plugin Request Completed' lines degrade to just status/duration with no plugin, datasource, user or trace identification — a silent loss of operational data. Consider adding the key fields back explicitly, or documenting/enforcing the ordering requirement (and covering it with a test).

title: ContextualLoggerMiddleware dereferences req without nil checks
body: `QueryData`, `CallResource`, `CheckHealth` and `CollectMetrics` access `req.PluginContext` unconditionally. The sibling `LoggerMiddleware` in the same package explicitly guards `if req == nil { return m.next... }`, which indicates nil requests are considered possible in this chain; with this new middleware sitting above the logger middleware, such a request would panic here instead of being forwarded. Add the same nil guards for consistency and robustness.

title: FromContext silently drops contextual attributes when the type assertion fails
body: `grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext` asserts the result of `d.l.FromContext(ctx)` to `*log.ConcreteLogger` and, on failure, falls back to `d.New()` — a logger with no contextual attributes at all. If `infra/log` ever returns a different `Logger` implementation, all plugin request logs would quietly lose pluginId/endpoint/traceID context with no warning. Prefer wrapping the returned `log.Logger` interface (or at least logging/annotating the fallback) rather than silently discarding the contextual logger.

title: No tests for the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware
body: The newly added middleware is responsible for all plugin/datasource/user attributes that now appear in the plugin request logs, but there is no test asserting that `instrumentContext` puts `endpoint`, `pluginId`, `dsName`, `dsUID` and `uname` into the context for each endpoint. Given that the logger middleware lost its explicit field list in the same PR, a regression here would silently drop these fields from logs with nothing failing in CI.

title: Test name still refers to the removed InstrumentationMiddleware
body: The test function is still called `TestInstrumentationMiddleware` while the middleware it exercises is now `MetricsMiddleware` (`newMetricsMiddleware`). Since the whole point of the PR is the rename, leaving the stale name makes the test hard to locate and contradicts the new naming.

title: Logger name 'plugin.instrumentation' not updated after the rename
body: `NewLoggerMiddleware(cfg, log.New("plugin.instrumentation"))` keeps the old 'instrumentation' naming, so emitted log lines are tagged with a logger name that no longer corresponds to any middleware in the code (instrumentation was split into metrics + contextual logger + logger middlewares). Operators grepping logs by logger name will be misled; rename it to something like 'plugin.logger' / 'plugin.request'.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, so log assertions no longer observe records
body: `TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()` instead of the receiver. `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` now emits its log line via `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`, so every record is written into a throwaway `TestLogger` that the test holds no reference to. Any test that injects a `plog.TestLogger` into the middleware and then asserts on `InfoLogs.Calls`/`Message`/`Ctx` will see zero calls, meaning the assertions either fail or (if written as "no error") silently stop verifying anything. `FromContext` (and arguably `New`) should return the same instance (or at least share the `Logs` state) so captured logs remain observable.

title: LoggerMiddleware silently loses pluginId/endpoint/dsName/dsUID/uname/traceID when used without the contextual logger middleware
body: The explicit log params (`pluginId`, `endpoint`, `uname`, `dsName`, `dsUID`, `traceID`) were removed and the middleware now relies entirely on contextual attributes injected by the separate, exported `NewContextualLoggerMiddleware()` plus a registered contextual log provider for the trace ID. There is no compile-time or runtime guarantee of that coupling: `NewLoggerMiddleware` is exported and any stack that omits the contextual logger middleware, or places it after the logger middleware, will produce "Plugin Request Completed" lines with no plugin/datasource/user identification at all — an operationally significant log regression that will not be caught by tests. Also note the trace ID previously came from `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` (unsampled spans included); it now depends on whatever the registered contextual log provider does, so the field can disappear for unsampled traces. Either keep the identifying fields in the middleware or document/enforce the ordering dependency and add a test asserting the fields are present in the final log line.

title: Adding FromContext to the exported plugins log.Logger interface is a breaking change
body: `log.Logger` in `pkg/plugins/log` is an exported interface consumed across the plugin packages (and by downstream/enterprise code). Adding the `FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger` method means every existing implementation outside this repository (or in a repo that vendors it, e.g. grafana-enterprise fakes/wrappers) fails to compile until updated. If the intent is only to let middleware derive a contextual logger, consider a narrower optional interface (type-asserted at the call site) instead of widening the shared interface.

title: New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no tests
body: `contextual_logger_middleware.go` is new behaviour that the logger middleware now depends on (it is the only source of `pluginId`, `endpoint`, `dsName`, `dsUID`, `uname` in plugin request logs), yet no test file was added. There is no coverage asserting that the attributes are attached to the context for QueryData/CallResource/CheckHealth/CollectMetrics, nor that downstream logging actually picks them up, so a regression in either this middleware or its position in the stack would go unnoticed.

title: TestLogger.FromContext discards recorded logs, making log assertions useless
body: `TestLogger.FromContext` returns a brand new `TestLogger` instead of `f` (or a logger that writes back into `f`'s `Logs` fields). After this PR `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` logs via `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`, so any test that injects a `TestLogger` into `NewLoggerMiddleware` and then asserts on `InfoLogs.Calls`/`Message`/`Ctx` will always see zero calls, even though the code logged. This silently removes the ability to unit-test the plugin request logging (and any other code path that uses `FromContext`). It should return the same instance (or a child that records into the parent's slices).

title: ContextualLoggerMiddleware dereferences req without nil check
body: `QueryData`, `CallResource`, `CheckHealth` and `CollectMetrics` access `req.PluginContext` unconditionally. `LoggerMiddleware` in the same package explicitly guards with `if req == nil { return m.next.X(...) }`, which indicates nil requests do reach the middleware chain (at minimum in tests). With this new middleware always inserted into the chain in `CreateMiddlewares`, a nil request now panics with a nil-pointer dereference instead of being forwarded. Add the same nil guards for consistency and safety.

title: LoggerMiddleware silently loses pluginId/endpoint/dsName/uname unless ContextualLoggerMiddleware runs before it
body: The log parameters `pluginId`, `endpoint`, `uname`, `dsName`, `dsUID` were removed from `logRequest` and are now expected to come from the contextual logger installed by the new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware`. This creates an undocumented ordering dependency: if `NewLoggerMiddleware` is used without `NewContextualLoggerMiddleware`, or the latter is registered after it in the chain (e.g. other call sites building their own middleware list, Enterprise code, or tests), the "Plugin Request Completed" egress log silently degrades to status/duration only, breaking log-based dashboards/alerts on these fields. At minimum document the requirement on both middlewares (the old `InstrumentationMiddleware` carried a "should live at the top of the middleware stack" comment, which was dropped), and ideally add a test asserting the egress log contains the plugin fields.

title: Explicit traceID log field removed; now depends on a globally registered contextual provider
body: The explicit `traceID` log parameter (previously added via `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)`) was deleted from `logRequest`. The field now only appears if a contextual log provider that injects the trace ID has been registered globally with `pkg/infra/log`. In setups/tests where the tracing service (and therefore that provider) is not initialized, the `traceID` field disappears from the `grafana-data-egress` log line, breaking correlation between egress logs and traces. Verify the provider is always registered, or re-add the field explicitly.

title: No test coverage for the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware
body: The PR extracts contextual-logging behaviour into a new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` and makes `LoggerMiddleware` depend on it, but no test is added for either. Nothing verifies that `endpoint`, `pluginId`, `dsName`, `dsUID` and `uname` end up in the context (and thus in the egress log line), so a future regression in this middleware or in middleware ordering would go unnoticed. Also, the renamed test still declares `func TestInstrumentationMiddleware`, which no longer matches the `MetricsMiddleware` name it exercises.

title: Adding FromContext to the Logger interface breaks all existing implementors
body: `FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger` is added to the `plugins/log.Logger` interface. Every type implementing this interface must now provide the method; only `grafanaInfraLogWrapper` and `TestLogger` are updated in this PR. Any other implementation in the repository (fakes/mocks in other packages, embedded wrappers) will fail to compile, and out-of-tree implementations break. Confirm there are no other implementors, or provide an embeddable base/no-op implementation.

title: Device limit is bypassed after the first rejection because the local cache is populated before the store write
body: `tagDeviceUI` writes the device key into `a.localCache` (`a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})`) *before* calling `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice`. When the device limit is reached, `CreateOrUpdateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` and `Anonymous.Authenticate` denies the request — but the key is already cached. Every subsequent request from the same device ID hits the `if _, ok := a.localCache.Get(key); ok { return nil }` early-return for the next 29 minutes, so `TagDevice` returns nil and the anonymous user is authenticated normally. The configured limit therefore only blocks a device's very first request and is effectively unenforced afterwards. The cache entry should only be set after a successful store write (and removed/not set on error).

title: Check-then-insert race allows the device limit to be exceeded
body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` reads the current device count with `CountDevices` and then, if `count < s.deviceLimit`, performs an unconditional upsert. Multiple concurrent requests (and multiple Grafana instances sharing the database) can all observe `count == limit-1` and all insert, so the number of distinct anonymous devices can exceed `AnonymousDeviceLimit`. If the limit is meant to be a hard cap, the count and insert need to be in a single transaction/statement (e.g. an `INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < limit`) or the overshoot needs to be acknowledged as acceptable.

title: rowsAffected == 0 is reported as ErrDeviceLimitReached, conflating distinct conditions
body: `updateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` whenever the UPDATE affects zero rows. Zero rows also occurs when the row exists but its `updated_at` falls outside the `[now-30d, now+1m]` window, and on MySQL an UPDATE that writes values identical to the stored ones reports 0 affected rows (the driver does not enable CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS), which can happen when `updated_at` is truncated to second precision and the same device is written twice within the same second. In those cases an already-known device is incorrectly refused authentication with a "device limit reached" error. The limit-reached condition should be distinguished from "row not updated" (e.g. check existence explicitly or treat 0 rows for a pre-existing device as success).

title: New auth.anonymous.device_limit key missing from conf/defaults.ini, breaking env-var override and documentation
body: `cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit = anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0)` adds a new configuration key, but `conf/defaults.ini` (and `conf/sample.ini`) are not updated in this PR. Grafana applies environment-variable overrides by iterating the keys that exist in the loaded ini files, so a key that is absent from defaults.ini cannot be set via `GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_DEVICE_LIMIT` — operators running in containers (the common case) would silently get the default of 0/unlimited. The option is also undocumented, so users have no way to discover it or its semantics (0 = unlimited).

title: Raw ErrDeviceLimitReached returned from Authenticate yields an opaque 500 to the user
body: `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is a plain `fmt.Errorf` value, and it is returned directly from `Anonymous.Authenticate`. The authn broker/HTTP layer has no mapping for it, so an anonymous visitor who is rejected because of the device limit receives a generic internal-server-error rather than a meaningful status/message. Use an `errutil` error with an appropriate status (e.g. 429/403) and a user-facing message so the rejection is diagnosable and does not look like a server fault.

title: Provider signature changes are not reflected in the DI/wire configuration
body: `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` now takes `sqlStore db.DB` instead of `anonStore anonstore.AnonStore`, and `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` gained a second `deviceLimit int64` parameter. The wire configuration (pkg/server/wire.go and generated wire_gen.go), which registers `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` and binds it to `anonstore.AnonStore`, is not part of this PR. Unless those files are updated, wire generation/compilation fails (no provider for `int64`, and the old call `ProvideAnonDBStore(sqlStore)` no longer matches). Also, because the store is now constructed inside the service, the previously injectable `anonstore.AnonStore` binding becomes dead/unsatisfiable for any other consumer.

title: Device tagging moved onto the synchronous authentication path
body: `TagDevice` was previously executed in a background goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout; it is now called inline during `Authenticate`. Every anonymous request whose device ID is not in the 29-minute local cache now performs a `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM anon_device` (when a limit is configured) plus an upsert before the response can proceed, adding database round-trips to request latency. With randomly generated device IDs (cache misses on every request) this turns each anonymous request into at least two synchronous DB statements, which is a cheap amplification vector against the database. Consider keeping the write asynchronous and only performing the limit check synchronously, or caching the count.

title: Device-limit tests do not cover the important paths
body: `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only asserts that a second, new device is rejected. There is no test that an *existing* device can still be refreshed once the limit is reached (the main purpose of `updateDevice`), no test that a device whose `updated_at` is older than the 30-day window behaves as intended, and no test of the service-level behaviour (the local-cache interaction in `tagDeviceUI`, which currently lets rejected devices through on subsequent requests). These are the cases most likely to regress.

title: anonymousDeviceLimit is typed as `undefined` on the boot config and can never actually be undefined
body: `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined` has no type annotation, so TypeScript infers the property type as `undefined` on `GrafanaBootConfig`; any consumer writing `config.anonymousDeviceLimit > 0` will fail to type-check even though the value is a number at runtime. Additionally the backend DTO field is a non-pointer `int64` with no `omitempty`, so the frontend always receives a number (0 when no limit is configured) and the declared `number | undefined` in `GrafanaConfig` is misleading. Annotate the field (`anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;`) or make the type `number` to match what the server actually sends.

title: Local cache entry is written before the DB write, letting devices bypass the limit
body: In `tagDeviceUI` the cache key is stored (`a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})`) before `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice` is called. Now that `TagDevice` propagates the store error (impl.go:147) and `Anonymous.Authenticate` rejects the request on `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the first request from an over-limit device fails, but the cache entry is already present. Every subsequent request from the same device within the 29-minute cache TTL short-circuits at the cache check and returns nil, so the device is authenticated anonymously and never recorded. The configured device limit is therefore trivially bypassed by retrying the request, and transient DB errors are also "cached" as success.

title: Count-then-insert is not atomic, so the device limit can be exceeded
body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` reads the device count with `CountDevices` and then performs the upsert in a separate session. Concurrent anonymous requests (and multiple Grafana instances sharing a DB) can all observe a count below `deviceLimit` and then each insert a new row, so the number of anon devices can exceed the configured limit by the number of concurrent requests. If the limit is meant as a hard cap (e.g. for licensing/billing), this check needs to be done inside a transaction or enforced by a conditional insert.

title: updateDevice reports ErrDeviceLimitReached when the UPDATE matched but changed nothing
body: `updateDevice` maps `rowsAffected == 0` to `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. On MySQL, `RowsAffected` for an UPDATE returns the number of *changed* rows, not matched rows (unless CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS is set). Since MySQL DATETIME columns have second precision, an existing, known device that re-tags within the same second with the same client IP and user agent produces 0 changed rows and will be wrongly rejected with "device limit reached", denying anonymous access to a device that is already counted. The condition conflates "row not found" with "nothing changed".

title: Raw error returned from Authenticate yields an opaque 5xx instead of a proper status/message
body: `Anonymous.Authenticate` returns `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached`, which is a plain `fmt.Errorf` value. Other authn clients return `errutil`-based errors so the HTTP layer can produce a correct status code (e.g. 401/403/429) and a stable messageId. As written, a user hitting the device limit will get a generic internal-error response (and the error will be logged as an unexpected failure) rather than a meaningful "too many anonymous devices" response, making the feature hard to diagnose and inconsistent with the rest of authn.

title: Device tagging moved onto the synchronous auth path, adding DB round-trips per anonymous request
body: The previous implementation tagged the device in a background goroutine with its own timeout; now `a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, ...)` runs inline during authentication. For every cache miss (cache TTL is 29 min, and the cache is per-instance) this executes a `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM anon_device WHERE updated_at BETWEEN ? AND ?` plus an upsert before the request can proceed, so anonymous page loads now block on DB latency and the count scan grows with the number of stored devices. On a busy anonymous instance (or after a restart, when the cache is empty) this can noticeably increase request latency and DB load.

title: New auth.anonymous device_limit setting is undocumented
body: `cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit` is read from `[auth.anonymous] device_limit`, but the option is not added to `conf/defaults.ini`, `conf/sample.ini`, or the configure-grafana documentation. Operators have no discoverable way to learn the option exists, its default (0 = unlimited), or that reaching the limit blocks new anonymous devices from authenticating.

title: No test for the main intended behaviour: updating an already-known device when the limit is reached
body: `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only asserts that a *new* device is rejected once the limit is reached. The core of the feature — that an existing device (one already counted) can still be refreshed via `updateDevice` and does not get `ErrDeviceLimitReached` — is untested, as is the behaviour for a device whose row exists but is older than `anonymousDeviceExpiration`. Given the `rowsAffected == 0` heuristic used in `updateDevice`, regressions here would silently lock out already-counted anonymous users.

title: args slice is mutated inside the session callback, corrupting the query on retry
body: Inside `updateDevice` the closure does `args = append([]interface{}{query}, args...)`, mutating the captured outer `args` variable. `WithDbSession` can invoke the callback more than once (e.g. sqlite "database is locked" retries); on a second invocation the query string would be prepended again, producing `Exec(query, query, ...)` and a malformed statement/argument mismatch. Build the exec argument slice as a new local variable instead of reassigning the captured one.

title: anonymousDeviceLimit field is typed as `undefined`, not `number | undefined`
body: `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` has no type annotation, so TypeScript infers the field type as `undefined`. The backend always sends a numeric `anonymousDeviceLimit` (no `omitempty` on the DTO), and the value is injected via `merge(this, defaults, options)` which bypasses type checking. Consumers reading `config.anonymousDeviceLimit` will see the type `undefined` and cannot compare it to a number without a cast. Declare it as `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;` to match `GrafanaConfig`.

title: Local cache is populated before the store call, so the device limit is bypassed after the first rejection
body: In `tagDeviceUI` the cache entry is written (`a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})`) before `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice` is invoked. With the new limit logic, the first request from an over-limit device returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` and is denied, but the cache key is already set, so every subsequent request from that same device for the cache TTL (29 min) short-circuits with `return nil` and is authenticated without ever consulting the limit. The result is that the configured `device_limit` is enforced only on the very first request per device per cache window, i.e. effectively not enforced, and users see a confusing "fails once then works" behaviour. The cache should only be populated after a successful store call (or the failed key removed on error).

title: rowsAffected == 0 wrongly reported as ErrDeviceLimitReached for existing devices on MySQL
body: `updateDevice` maps `rowsAffected == 0` to `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. On MySQL, `RowsAffected()` reports *changed* rows, not matched rows (unless CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS is set), so an UPDATE that matches an already-tracked device but writes identical column values (same client_ip/user_agent and an `updated_at` that truncates to the same second — MySQL DATETIME has second precision here) returns 0. In that case an existing, already-counted device is denied access with "device limit reached" even though it is within the limit. Additionally, this error value conflates two distinct conditions ("device not found/expired" vs "limit reached"), which makes the surfaced error misleading; the device-not-found case should be distinguished or detected via a SELECT/matched-rows check.

title: Check-then-insert on device count is racy and can exceed the configured limit
body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` performs `CountDevices` and then, in a separate session, an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT. Concurrent anonymous requests for new device IDs can all read a count below `deviceLimit` and then all insert, so the stored device count can exceed the configured limit by the number of concurrent requests. Since the limit is a licensing/abuse control, this is an enforcement hole. Consider doing the count and insert inside one transaction, or enforcing the limit with a conditional INSERT (e.g. `INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < limit`) so the check and write are atomic.

title: Device tagging moved into the synchronous auth path, adding DB round-trips to every anonymous request
body: `TagDevice` was previously executed in a background goroutine with its own timeout; it is now called synchronously inside `Authenticate`. Every anonymous request whose device ID is not in the 29-minute local cache now blocks on a `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM anon_device` (when `device_limit > 0`) plus an INSERT/UPDATE before authentication completes. For instances with high anonymous traffic and many distinct device IDs this adds DB load and request latency on the hot login path, and a slow/locked DB now stalls (rather than merely fails to record) anonymous requests. If synchronous behaviour is required only to enforce the limit, consider only doing the blocking path when a limit is configured, and/or caching the device count.

title: ErrDeviceLimitReached is a plain error, so clients get an opaque 500 instead of an actionable status
body: `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is created with `fmt.Errorf`, and `client.go` returns it directly from `Authenticate`. Because it carries no `errutil` status/public message, the authn broker will surface it as a generic internal error (HTTP 500 with no meaningful message) to the browser, so an operator-configured device limit looks like a server failure to the end user and is hard to diagnose from the response. Define it with `errutil` (e.g. a 429/403-style status with a public message) so the limit rejection is reported as an intentional, documented condition.

title: New auth.anonymous device_limit option is not added to defaults.ini/sample.ini or documented
body: `cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit = anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0)` introduces a new user-facing configuration key `[auth.anonymous] device_limit`, but the PR does not add it to `conf/defaults.ini`/`conf/sample.ini` nor to the configuration docs. Without the defaults.ini entry the option is undiscoverable (and the documented-config consistency checks Grafana runs over defaults.ini/docs will flag it), and operators have no documentation of the behaviour when the limit is hit (new devices are rejected, existing devices continue to work).

title: Provider signature change (AnonStore -> db.DB) requires DI wiring updates not included in this PR
body: `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` no longer accepts an `anonstore.AnonStore` and instead takes `db.DB`, constructing the store internally, while `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` gained a second `deviceLimit int64` parameter. No changes to the wire provider sets (`pkg/server/wire.go` and the enterprise equivalents) are included. If `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` / `wire.Bind(new(anonstore.AnonStore), ...)` are still listed there, wire generation will fail (no provider for `int64`, and/or an unused provider), breaking the build; conversely any other consumer that relied on injecting an `AnonStore` now loses it. The DI configuration needs to be updated in the same change.

title: No test for the main intended path: updating an already-tracked device while at the limit
body: `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only asserts that a *new* device ID is rejected once the limit is reached. The core behaviour of the feature — that an already-stored device keeps working (its client_ip/user_agent/updated_at are updated) when the count is at or above `deviceLimit` — is untested, as is the expiry window in `updateDevice` (a device older than `anonymousDeviceExpiration` should not be revived). These are exactly the paths where the `rowsAffected == 0` heuristic can misfire, so they should be covered.

title: anonymousDeviceLimit initialised to undefined narrows its type to `undefined`
body: `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` with no type annotation makes the class property's inferred type `undefined`, so any frontend code that tries to use it numerically (e.g. `config.anonymousDeviceLimit > 0`) will be a type error even though the backend always sends a number. Note also that the Go DTO field has no `omitempty`, so the value is `0` (not absent) when the limit is disabled; annotate as `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined` (or `number`) and make the frontend contract explicit about 0 meaning "no limit".

title: Cleanup job ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The background cleanup loop's ticker was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This makes every cleanup job (temp file scans, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history) run 10x more often on every Grafana instance, which is a significant and unrelated increase in DB and filesystem load for a PR whose purpose is to avoid annotation deadlocks. Given the per-run timeout is still 9 minutes, this looks like leftover debugging to make the annotation cleanup fire quickly during testing and should be reverted to 10 minutes.

title: Leftover debug logging emitted at Error level on every cleanup batch
body: `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", ...)` (and the equivalent calls at lines 537, 554, 557, 576, 579) log normal, successful operation at Error severity. Every cleanup cycle will therefore emit error-level log lines even when nothing is wrong, which pollutes logs and triggers error-based alerting/monitoring for operators. In addition, these lines dump the full `ids` slice, which can be tens of thousands of integers per batch (the new test uses a batch size of 32767), producing very large log records. These should be removed or demoted to Debug without the full ID list.

title: Quadratic string concatenation when inlining IDs for SQLite
body: In `deleteByIDs`, the SQLite fallback builds the `IN (...)` list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside a loop, re-allocating and copying the whole accumulated string on each iteration. With the batch sizes this code path is designed for (the new test exercises 32767 IDs per batch), this is O(n^2) in allocations and bytes copied and runs for every batch of every cleanup cycle. Use `strings.Builder` (or `strconv.AppendInt` into a byte slice, as done in `getAccessControlFilter`) instead.

title: Parameterized delete can exceed placeholder limits on non-SQLite databases
body: The parameter-limit workaround in `deleteByIDs` is gated on `r.db.GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite`. For other backends the code always emits one `?` placeholder per ID. PostgreSQL has a hard limit of 65535 bind parameters per statement, so an operator who sets `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` above that value will get a driver error on every cleanup batch and annotation cleanup will stop working, with no indication that the batch size is the cause. Either cap the number of IDs per DELETE statement (chunking) regardless of backend, or base the inline-values decision on `len(ids)` against a per-dialect limit.

title: Table cleanup registered after assertions that can abort the subtest
body: `t.Cleanup` that truncates `annotation`/`annotation_tag` is registered only after `createTestAnnotations` and the two `assertAnnotationCount`/`assertAnnotationTagCount` calls, which use `require` and abort the subtest on failure. If any of those assertions fail, the rows inserted by this subtest are never deleted, and because `fakeSQL` is shared across all subtests in the table the subsequent cases will see leftover rows and fail with confusing counts, masking the original failure. Register the cleanup immediately after obtaining the session / before inserting the test data.

title: Comment states an outdated SQLite parameter limit inconsistent with the new test
body: The comment says "SQLite has a parameter limit of 999" and the constant is `sqliteParameterLimit = 999`, while the new test case is named "should not fail if batch size is larger than SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER for SQLite >= 3.32.0" (which is 32766). The two descriptions disagree about what limit is being guarded against; a reader cannot tell whether 999 is intentionally conservative (pre-3.32 builds) or simply wrong. Clarify the comment to state that 999 is the pre-3.32.0 limit and is used conservatively.

title: Cleanup job interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The background cleanup ticker was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This makes *every* cleanup job (temp file scanning, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, annotation cleanup, user invites, short URLs, query history row-limit enforcement) run 10x more frequently, multiplying DB and filesystem load on all installations. The `clean()` function also uses a 9-minute timeout, so a long-running cleanup cycle now overlaps with ticks that are simply dropped, making the effective schedule unpredictable. Nothing in the PR description justifies this change; it looks like leftover debugging and should be reverted to 10 minutes (or made configurable deliberately).

title: Debug logging left in at Error level, dumping entire ID batches
body: Six `r.log.Error(...)` calls were added in `CleanAnnotations` (lines 534, 537, 554, 557) and `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` (lines 576, 579). These are informational/debug traces, not errors: they fire on every cleanup batch even on full success, and they log the complete `ids` slice, which can contain up to `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` entries (the test in this PR uses 32767). Consequences: log files and alerting pipelines keyed on ERROR level will be spammed every cleanup cycle (now every minute), with multi-hundred-KB lines. Additionally the `"err", err` field in the pre-delete log statements is always nil, since a non-nil error has already returned. These statements should be removed or downgraded to Debug without the full ID dump.

title: Placeholder-limit workaround keyed on config value and only applied for SQLite
body: `deleteByIDs` decides whether to inline IDs based on `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit` and `GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite`, not on `len(ids)` or on the actual driver's limit. Two problems: (1) for non-SQLite backends there is no guard at all, so an operator who sets `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` above the backend's bind-parameter limit (65535 for PostgreSQL and MySQL's protocol) will get hard failures from the new `DELETE ... IN (?,?,...)` statement, where the previous sub-query-based DELETE used no parameters at all; (2) the condition is driven by configuration rather than the real number of IDs, so the behaviour is inconsistent with the statement actually being built. Consider chunking `ids` into fixed-size groups (e.g. 999/65535) independently of the configured batch size, for all dialects.

title: Quadratic string concatenation when inlining IDs for SQLite
body: The SQLite inline-IDs path builds the value list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside the loop, reallocating and copying the whole accumulated string on each of up to `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` iterations. With the 32767 batch size exercised by the new test this copies on the order of gigabytes per batch and allocates tens of thousands of intermediate strings, for every cleanup batch. Use a `strings.Builder` (or `strconv.AppendInt` into a byte slice, as `getAccessControlFilter` already does) instead.

title: Per-subtest table cleanup is registered after assertions that can abort the subtest
body: `t.Cleanup` that deletes rows from `annotation`/`annotation_tag` is registered only after `createTestAnnotations`, `assertAnnotationCount` and `assertAnnotationTagCount` have run. Those helpers use `require`, which aborts the subtest immediately on failure; in that case the cleanup is never registered and the inserted rows persist in the shared `fakeSQL` database, causing all following subtests (which assert absolute row counts and insert explicit primary keys) to fail with cascading, misleading errors. Register the cleanup before inserting the fixtures.

title: New subtest inserts 40003 annotations and 80006 tags, making the suite much slower
body: The added "should not fail if batch size is larger than SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER" case inserts 40003 annotations plus 80006 annotation_tag rows and then deletes 40000 of them, in a test that also runs against MySQL/Postgres in CI. This is a large fixed cost on every run of the integration suite. The parameter-limit behaviour could be exercised with a far smaller dataset (e.g. batch size just above 999 with a few thousand rows), since the threshold in `deleteByIDs` is 999, not 32767.

title: Debug logging left in at Error level, dumping every ID of every batch
body: Six new `r.log.Error(...)` calls were added in `CleanAnnotations` (lines 534, 537, 554, 557) and `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` (lines 576, 579). These are informational/debug messages ("Annotations to clean by time", "cleaned tags", ...) emitted at ERROR level on every batch iteration of a job that runs continuously, and they include the full `ids` slice (up to `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` entries, 32767 in the new test) plus a nil `err`. Consequences: operators' error logs/alerting will fire on normal cleanup activity, and log volume/allocation becomes huge on large installations. These should be removed or downgraded to Debug without the full ID list.

title: Cleanup job ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: `ticker := time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)` changes the global cleanup service interval from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This is unrelated to the annotation deadlock fix and looks like leftover local debugging. It makes every cleanup job (tmp file scan, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history row-limit enforcement) run 10x more often, multiplying DB and filesystem load on all Grafana instances; note also that `clean()` has a 9-minute timeout, so a long-running sweep is immediately followed by another. This change should be reverted unless intentional and documented.

title: O(n^2) string building for SQLite inline ID list
body: In `deleteByIDs`, the SQLite branch builds the ID list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside a loop. Each iteration reallocates and copies the whole accumulated string, so for a batch of ~32k IDs (the size exercised by the new test) this performs ~32k allocations and copies of an ever-growing ~200KB string, i.e. gigabytes of memcpy per batch, repeated for every batch of the cleanup loop. Use a `strings.Builder` (or `strconv.AppendInt` into a byte slice, as done elsewhere in this file) instead.

title: Placeholder-limit workaround only covers SQLite; large batch sizes can fail on MySQL/Postgres
body: `deleteByIDs` only avoids bind parameters when `GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite && AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999`. For MySQL and Postgres the code always emits one `?` per ID, but both have a hard limit of 65535 bind parameters per statement. An operator who sets `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` above 65535 will get a hard driver error on every cleanup cycle instead of a degraded-but-working job. Either cap the number of IDs per DELETE statement (chunking) regardless of dialect, or gate on `len(ids)` against a per-dialect limit.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and will be cancelled when the handler returns
body: All four write paths (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) spawn a goroutine and build the goroutine's context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the inbound apiserver request context. net/http cancels the request context as soon as the handler returns, which typically happens before/while the goroutine runs. The legacy store call therefore receives an already-cancelled context and its DB work will be aborted, so the "safe measure" legacy write silently never happens for most requests, leaving legacy storage permanently out of sync. The goroutine must detach from the request context (e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` or a fresh background context carrying only the needed values) before applying the timeout.

title: Legacy write errors in goroutines are swallowed with no logging
body: In Create (line 55), Delete (line 112), Update (line 139) and DeleteCollection (line 165) the error returned by the legacy store is only used as a boolean for the duration metric; it is never logged. The previous implementation logged these failures. Since the caller has already received a success response, a failed legacy write now produces no error, no log line and no retry — divergence between unified and legacy storage becomes undiagnosable. Log the error (with name/kind) in each goroutine.

title: Goroutines have no panic recovery; a legacy store panic crashes the process
body: The four goroutines spawned in Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection call into legacy storage without a `defer recover()`. Synchronous calls were previously protected by the apiserver's per-request panic handler; a panic on a bare goroutine terminates the whole Grafana process. Any panic in a legacy store (e.g. nil map/SQL layer bug) is now fatal instead of a 500 for one request. Add recovery (and log) around the goroutine body.

title: Delete records object name in the `kind` metric label, causing unbounded cardinality
body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. This creates one Prometheus label value per deleted object name, producing unbounded time-series cardinality in the metrics registry (memory growth / scrape bloat) and making the storage-duration metric unusable for deletes. It should be `options.Kind`.

title: Create failure path records a legacy-duration metric for a storage error
body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with the storage start time. No legacy call happened, so the legacy error/duration metric is polluted with storage failures and the storage failure itself is never recorded in the storage metric. Should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

title: Update failure path records a legacy-duration metric for a storage error
body: On `d.Storage.Update` failure the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`, but the failing call was the unified storage one and no legacy call was made. The legacy error metric is inflated with storage errors and storage failures are not counted, which will make the dual-writer dashboards misattribute failures. Should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

title: DeleteCollection's legacy call records a storage-duration metric
body: Inside the async goroutine the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is reported via `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration`. The legacy delete-collection latency/errors are therefore never visible in the legacy metric, and the storage metric double-counts with a legacy duration, skewing both series.

title: Legacy Update is given the raw objInfo instead of the object produced by unified storage
body: The previous implementation wrapped objInfo (`&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}`) so legacy storage persisted exactly the object unified storage had written. Now the original `objInfo` is replayed against the legacy store. For PATCH/apply requests the transformation is recomputed against the legacy copy, and for requests carrying a resourceVersion precondition the version comes from unified storage, which does not match the legacy row's version — legacy updates will fail with conflicts or write a different object than unified storage, silently diverging the two stores.

title: Object passed to the async legacy Create may be mutated concurrently with response serialization
body: `d.Legacy.Create(ctx, obj, ...)` runs on a goroutine with the same `obj` pointer that was handed to `d.Storage.Create`. The generic registry store mutates the input object in place (name generation, resourceVersion, UID, creationTimestamp) and typically returns that same pointer as `created`, which the apiserver serializes into the HTTP response after this function returns. The legacy store also mutates the object it is given. Two goroutines therefore read/write the same object without synchronization — a genuine data race that can corrupt the response body or the persisted legacy record. Deep-copy the object before handing it to the goroutine.

title: Tests never verify (or wait for) the asynchronous legacy write
body: Every mode-3 write test (Create line 63, Delete line 228, DeleteCollection line 282, Update line 343) returns as soon as the dual writer returns, with no synchronization on the goroutine that performs the legacy write and no assertion that the legacy store was called. The core behaviour this PR introduces — "write to unified storage, then asynchronously write to legacy" — is untested; the context-cancellation bug above would not be caught. In addition, because legacy and storage share a single `mock.Mock`, a legacy call cannot be distinguished from a storage call, and the goroutine can still be running (touching the mock) after the subtest finishes, which can race with test teardown. Use separate mocks per store plus a channel/WaitGroup (or `mock.AssertExpectations` after waiting) to assert the legacy call happened.

title: Delete stores the wrong logger in the context
body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` puts the bare base logger into the context instead of `log`, which was just built with name/kind/method values. Downstream code that pulls the logger from the context loses all the request-scoped fields, unlike every other method in this file which passes `log`.

title: go.work.sum gains a duplicate entry and unrelated dependency hashes
body: The diff re-adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod h1:...`, which already exists a couple of lines above, and adds hashes for modules (azure sdk, prometheus-alertmanager, old otel sdk/metric v0.39.0, otlp protos) that are unrelated to this change. This looks like an accidental/mechanical `go work sync` from a different module set; it makes the dual-writer PR carry unrelated dependency churn and the duplicate line will keep reappearing/disappearing in future diffs. Revert go.work.sum unless the change is actually required to build.

title: Misleading List test case name
body: The case is named "error when listing an object in the unified store is not implemented" but mode 3 List is now implemented and the case simply asserts that a store error is propagated. The stale name (copied from the previous not-implemented behaviour) will confuse readers about what is covered.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled when the handler returns
body: In Create (line 51), Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163) the background goroutine builds its context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the incoming request context. As soon as the handler returns (which happens immediately, because the goroutine is fire-and-forget), net/http cancels the request context, and every context derived from it is cancelled too. The legacy store call will therefore frequently fail with `context canceled` (or never reach the DB at all), silently losing the legacy write that mode 3 exists to keep as a safety copy. The derived context must be detached from the request, e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` before applying the timeout (while still carrying the request's auth/user values).

title: Delete records the object name in the `kind` metric label
body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. Object names are unbounded (one per resource instance), so each successful delete creates a new Prometheus label value, causing unbounded metric cardinality growth in the dual-writer histogram and skewing/polluting all dashboards built on the `kind` label. It should pass `options.Kind`.

title: Create error path records a legacy-store duration for a storage failure
body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)`. The failure happened in unified storage, not legacy, so the error is attributed to the wrong store and no storage-error sample is recorded at all. Any alert/dashboard on storage error rate will miss these failures while the legacy error rate shows phantom errors. Should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

title: Update error path records a legacy-store duration for a storage failure
body: On a failed `d.Storage.Update` the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. The failing call was against unified storage, so storage errors are never recorded and legacy error metrics are inflated with failures that did not occur in legacy. Should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

title: DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine records a storage duration
body: Inside the background goroutine that calls `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection`, the result is reported with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`. Legacy delete-collection latency/errors are therefore invisible, and the storage histogram is polluted with timings of legacy calls, making mode-3 metrics unusable for detecting broken legacy writes.

title: Delete puts the wrong logger in the context
body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` stores the bare writer logger instead of the `log` built one line above with `name`, `kind` and `method` values. Downstream code that pulls the logger out of the context (`klog.FromContext`) loses all request-specific fields, making delete failures much harder to correlate. Every other method in this file passes `log`.

title: Fire-and-forget goroutines have no panic recovery and no lifecycle tracking
body: The four write paths spawn bare goroutines calling into the legacy store. (1) A panic inside a legacy store implementation (e.g. nil map/pointer in the SQL layer) is not recoverable from the goroutine and will take down the whole Grafana process, whereas in the previous synchronous code the apiserver's handler recovery would have converted it to a 500. (2) Nothing tracks in-flight goroutines, so `Destroy()` (line 172) can tear down `d.Legacy`/`d.Storage` while a goroutine is still calling into them, and in-flight legacy writes are silently dropped on shutdown. A `defer recover()` plus a WaitGroup/semaphore drained in `Destroy()` is needed.

title: Create passes the caller's object to the legacy store from a goroutine without deep-copying
body: `d.Legacy.Create(ctx, obj, ...)` runs concurrently with the request handler while `obj` is the very object the apiserver handler chain passed in; registry stores and legacy stores mutate the passed object (name from generateName, UID, resourceVersion, creationTimestamp). Sharing the pointer with a goroutine while the handler may still read/serialize or further mutate it is a data race (and makes the legacy row depend on timing). The object should be `obj.DeepCopyObject()`ed before handing it to the goroutine.

title: Legacy update now reuses the raw objInfo instead of the object written to unified storage
body: The previous implementation fetched the current object from storage and wrapped `objInfo` in an `updateWrapper` carrying the object actually persisted, so the legacy store received the same final state. The new code calls `d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...)` with the original `objInfo`, which re-runs `UpdatedObject` against the legacy store's own old object. Consequences: for PATCH/apply requests the patch is re-applied to a possibly different base, and for requests that carry a resourceVersion the value refers to the unified-storage revision, so the legacy update can fail with a conflict. Either way legacy silently diverges from unified storage (the error is only counted in a metric, not even logged). Also note `objInfo` is a request-scoped object being invoked concurrently from the goroutine, which is not guaranteed to be safe for reuse.

title: No test verifies that the asynchronous legacy write happens
body: All mode-3 tests only assert the value returned from the unified-storage mock. Because the legacy write now happens in a detached goroutine, nothing in Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection tests waits for or asserts `Legacy.*` was invoked (and `legacyStoreMock`/`storageMock` share one `mock.Mock`, so a legacy call cannot even be distinguished from a storage call). The whole point of mode 3 — that writes eventually reach legacy — is untested, so defects such as the cancelled-context issue in the goroutines cannot be caught by this suite. Use separate mocks for legacy and storage plus a channel/`assert.Eventually` to assert the legacy call.

title: "unified store fails" test case only configures the legacy mock
body: The case named "error when creating object in the unified store fails" sets up the failure via `setupLegacyFn` and leaves `setupStorageFn` nil; it only passes because `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` wrap the same `mock.Mock`, so the legacy expectation also satisfies the storage call. The test therefore does not actually exercise a unified-storage failure and would keep passing if the storage error path regressed. The same pattern appears in the List test case whose name still says "is not implemented" even though List is now implemented.

title: go.work.sum changes look accidental and add a duplicate entry
body: The diff re-adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod` even though the identical line already exists immediately above, and adds hashes for unrelated modules (grafana-azure-sdk-go, prometheus-alertmanager, older otel versions) that have nothing to do with the dual writer change. These lines are probably the result of a local `go work sync` with a different module set; they are out of sorted order and the duplicate will be removed again by tooling. Revert the go.work.sum changes unless a dependency actually changed in this PR.

title: Async legacy writes derive from the request context, which is cancelled when the handler returns
body: All four write paths (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) spawn a goroutine that does `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` using the *request* context. The apiserver cancels the request context as soon as the HTTP handler returns, which in practice happens before or right after the goroutine starts. The derived context is therefore already (or immediately) cancelled, so the legacy store call will typically fail with `context canceled` and the legacy database will never be updated. Since mode 3's whole purpose is to keep legacy storage in sync as a safety net, this silently defeats the feature (errors are only recorded in a duration metric, never logged). Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (preserving user/identity values) as the parent before applying the timeout.

title: Create records a legacy-storage duration on a unified-storage failure
body: In `Create`, when `d.Storage.Create` fails the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with `startStorage`. This attributes a unified-storage failure/latency to the legacy backend metric, so the legacy error rate/latency dashboards will show failures that never happened in legacy, and unified-storage create failures are invisible in the storage metric. It should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

title: Update records a legacy-storage duration on a unified-storage failure
body: In `Update`, the error branch calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` even though the failure came from `d.Storage.Update`. Same consequence as in `Create`: legacy metrics get polluted with unified-storage failures and storage failures are not counted. Should be `recordStorageDuration`.

title: Object name passed as the `kind` metric label in Delete causes unbounded label cardinality
body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object's `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. Because `name` is a per-object identifier, each deleted resource creates a new Prometheus time series on the storage duration histogram, leading to unbounded cardinality and potential memory blow-up in both Grafana and the scraping Prometheus. It also makes the metric unusable for comparison with the other label values. Use `options.Kind`.

title: DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine records a storage duration instead of a legacy duration
body: Inside the background goroutine of `DeleteCollection`, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded via `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` with `startLegacy`. This reports legacy latency/errors under the unified-storage metric, double counting storage observations for delete-collection and leaving legacy delete-collection completely unmeasured. Should be `recordLegacyDuration`.

title: Legacy Update is given the raw objInfo instead of the object already persisted in unified storage
body: The previous implementation wrapped `objInfo` with `&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}` so that legacy storage persisted exactly the object that unified storage had stored. Now the original `objInfo` is handed to `d.Legacy.Update` from a goroutine. `objInfo.UpdatedObject` will be re-evaluated against legacy's own `old` object, which has a different resourceVersion than unified storage, so for PUT (which carries a resourceVersion) legacy updates can fail with a conflict, and for PATCH/apply the transformers run a second time against a different base producing a different result. The net effect is silent divergence between unified and legacy data – the opposite of what mode 3's legacy mirror is for. Additionally `objInfo`/`obj` are request-scoped values that are now read concurrently after the handler has returned, which is not guaranteed to be safe.

title: Fire-and-forget goroutines have no panic recovery and no error logging
body: Each write path launches a bare `go func()` that calls into the legacy store. If the legacy implementation panics (e.g. nil map, nil pointer in a legacy service), the panic is not recovered inside the goroutine and the whole apiserver process crashes – unlike the synchronous path, where the apiserver's handler-level recovery would convert it to a 500. The goroutines also discard the legacy error entirely (only `err != nil` is folded into a histogram label), so operators have no way to find out which objects failed to mirror. Add `defer recover()` with logging and log the legacy error with the object name/kind.

title: Delete puts the base logger in the context instead of the enriched one
body: `Delete` builds `log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method)` but then does `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`. Downstream code that retrieves the logger via `klog.FromContext(ctx)` loses the name/kind/method values, making delete-path logs from the storage and legacy layers unattributable. Should be `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)` as in the other methods.

title: NotFound from unified storage now aborts the legacy delete, leaving orphan legacy rows
body: The previous mode 3 `Delete` explicitly tolerated `apierrors.IsNotFound` from unified storage and still attempted the legacy delete. The new code returns early on any storage error, so an object that exists only in legacy (e.g. created before the migration, or whose earlier async legacy mirror failed) can never be deleted from legacy via the API. These orphan rows will resurface if the deployment is ever moved back to a mode that reads from legacy (modes 0–2).

title: Mode 3 integration tests assert legacy state immediately after k8s writes, which is now asynchronous
body: The three new mode-3 sub-tests (file line 132, unified line 191, etcd line 287) run `doPlaylistTests`, which after creating playlists through the k8s client immediately queries the legacy endpoint `/api/playlists` and requires the same UIDs (line 523-531), and after each k8s update calls `getFromBothAPIs` comparing legacy DTO fields (line 547). In mode 3 the legacy write happens in a detached goroutine with no synchronization, so these assertions race against the background write and the tests will be flaky – and given the cancelled-context problem in the goroutine they are likely to fail deterministically. The tests need to poll/retry the legacy endpoint, or mode 3 must flush legacy writes before responding.

title: Unit tests never verify (or wait for) the asynchronous legacy write
body: All mode-3 write tests (`Create`, `Delete`, `Update`, `DeleteCollection`) assert only on the value returned from unified storage and return immediately; nothing calls `m.AssertExpectations`/`AssertCalled` or waits for the goroutine that performs the legacy write. The central new behaviour of mode 3 – that legacy is also written – is therefore completely untested (the cancelled-context bug above would not be caught). Worse, the goroutine may invoke the shared `mock.Mock` after the sub-test has finished; if the arguments don't match a registered expectation testify panics from that goroutine and takes down the whole test binary. Add a synchronization point (e.g. a channel closed from the mock's Run function) and assert the legacy call happened with the expected arguments.

title: go.work.sum contains a duplicated entry and unrelated dependency churn
body: The added block duplicates the line `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod h1:...` that already exists a few lines above, and inserts entries out of sorted order (grafana-azure-sdk-go after grafana/pkg/apimachinery). This indicates the file was hand-edited rather than regenerated with `go work sync`/`go mod tidy`; it is also unrelated to the dual-writer change and will churn/conflict with other PRs. Regenerate the file or drop these hunks from this PR.

title: Missing re-check of cache after acquiring write lock (no double-checked locking)
body: After the RLock fast path fails, the function takes the write lock but never re-reads `entryPointAssetsCache`. If N requests arrive concurrently before the cache is populated (e.g. at startup), all N will block on the write lock and each will in turn re-open and re-parse `assets-manifest.json` (and, when the CDN branch is enabled, perform an HTTP request) and overwrite the cache, even though the first one already populated it. Re-checking `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after `Lock()` would make the cache actually serve concurrent callers and avoid the redundant I/O.

title: Blocking file/network I/O performed while holding the exclusive lock
body: `readWebAssetsFromCDN` (HTTP GET with the request context) and `readWebAssetsFromFile` are executed while the write lock is held, so every other caller of `GetWebAssets` — including readers that would otherwise hit the cache — is blocked for the duration of a network round trip or disk read. In dev mode, where the cache is bypassed on every call, this fully serializes all asset-manifest lookups across requests. Consider loading into a local variable outside the lock and only taking the lock to publish the result.

title: No test exercising concurrent GetWebAssets calls
body: The PR fixes a data race but adds no test. A simple test that calls `GetWebAssets` from multiple goroutines (runnable under `-race`), covering both `setting.Dev` and non-dev configs, would prevent regression if the locking is later removed or the global is reintroduced elsewhere.

title: Missing re-check of the cache after acquiring the write lock
body: `GetWebAssets` reads the cache under `RLock`, releases it, and then takes the write lock without re-checking whether another goroutine populated `entryPointAssetsCache` in the meantime (classic double-checked-locking recheck). Consequence: on startup, if N requests arrive concurrently with an empty cache, all N serialize on the write lock and each one re-reads and re-parses `assets-manifest.json` (or performs a CDN HTTP fetch) even though the first one already produced a valid result. In addition, every one of those late writers overwrites the already-published pointer; if a later read fails (file transiently unavailable, CDN error) the code unconditionally executes `entryPointAssetsCache = result` with `result == nil`, discarding a previously valid cached value and making subsequent callers re-do the work / receive `nil`. Adding `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` right after `Lock()`, and only assigning the cache when `err == nil`, fixes both.

title: Cache is overwritten with nil when manifest loading fails
body: `entryPointAssetsCache = result` is executed unconditionally, including when `err != nil` and `result == nil`. This makes a load failure poison/clear the cache rather than leaving the last known-good assets in place, so every later request repeats the failing file/CDN read and callers get a nil `*dtos.EntryPointAssets`. Guard the assignment with `if err == nil && result != nil`.

title: No test covering the concurrent access the PR claims to fix
body: The PR is specifically a data-race fix on the `entryPointAssetsCache` global, but no test was added that exercises `GetWebAssets` from multiple goroutines (e.g. a `t.Parallel`/`sync.WaitGroup` test runnable under `-race`). Without such a test, a future refactor can silently reintroduce the unsynchronized access.

title: Double-checked locking is missing the second check inside the write lock
body: After the fast path with the read lock fails, the function takes the write lock but never re-reads `entryPointAssetsCache`. If N goroutines reach this point concurrently at startup (the common case, since the cache is cold while the first requests arrive), each one in turn will acquire the write lock and redo the full manifest load (file read + JSON decode, or an HTTP fetch to the CDN) and overwrite the cache, even though the first one already populated it. Re-checking `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after `Lock()` removes this thundering-herd work.

title: A failed load overwrites a previously valid cache with nil
body: `entryPointAssetsCache = result` is executed unconditionally, including when `readWebAssetsFromFile`/`readWebAssetsFromCDN` returned an error and `result == nil`. In that case a previously successfully cached value is destroyed and the function returns `nil, err`, so every subsequent call must retry the load and callers that don't check the error can get a nil pointer. The assignment should only happen when `err == nil && result != nil`.

title: Blocking I/O performed while holding the write lock
body: The file read and the (currently dead, but still reachable) CDN HTTP request at lines 54-67 are executed while the exclusive `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` is held, so all other callers of `GetWebAssets` — including those that would be served from cache in dev mode or during cache refreshes — block on network/disk latency. Loading outside the lock and only taking the write lock to publish the result would avoid serializing request handling on I/O.

title: No test covering the concurrent access being fixed
body: The PR fixes a data race on the `entryPointAssetsCache` global but adds no test. A simple test that calls `GetWebAssets` from multiple goroutines (which fails under `-race` before the fix) would prevent the race from being reintroduced, e.g. by a future refactor that drops the mutex.

title: enableSqlExpressions() is dead logic that can never return true and misreads the feature flag
body: `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` (note the negation, which inverts the flag's meaning), then returns `false` in both the `if` branch and the fall-through. The feature-flag lookup result is therefore completely discarded and the function is a constant `false`. Even if the intent is to hard-disable SQL expressions, this shape is dangerous: a future reader will assume the flag is honoured and the inverted condition means a one-line "re-enable" change would turn the feature on when the flag is *disabled*. It is also the kind of ineffectual assignment that staticcheck/golangci can flag and break CI. Prefer an explicit `return false` with a comment referencing CVE-2024-9264, or remove the helper and return the error unconditionally.

title: Disabled SQL expression returns a plain error with a misleading message
body: When a `QueryTypeSQL` node is encountered the reader returns `fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")`. Unlike the other error paths in this package (e.g. `NewSQLCommand` uses `errutil.BadRequest`), a bare error carries no status/public-message metadata, so an operator-enabled `sqlExpressions` toggle will surface as an opaque server error rather than a 400 with a clear reason. The wording is also misleading: the feature is intentionally disabled for security, not merely unimplemented, which will send users chasing a non-existent bug. Use `errutil.BadRequest` with a public message stating the feature is disabled.

title: No regression test asserting SQL expressions are rejected
body: This PR is a security fix (CVE-2024-9264) that disables server-side SQL expressions, but no test is added covering either entry point: `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` with `type: sql` (should error even with `FlagSqlExpressions` enabled) and `UnmarshalSQLCommand`/`NewSQLCommand` (which now fails because `sql.TablesList` errors). Without such tests, a later refactor of `enableSqlExpressions` or of the `sql.DB` stub can silently re-enable the RCE/LFI path with no CI signal.

title: TablesList is now permanently broken dead code that still contains the unsafe SQL string interpolation
body: `TablesList` builds `SELECT json_serialize_sql('<rawSQL>')` by string concatenation with only naive `'` doubling and then calls `DB.RunCommands`, which the new stub in db.go always fails with `errors.New("not implemented")`. So the whole function can only ever return an error, and everything after line 26 (`tablesFromAST`, `astError`, `existsInList`, the `flatten` dependency) is unreachable. This leaves the exact query-construction code that was part of the vulnerability in the tree while providing no functionality, and any existing unit test asserting that `TablesList` extracts table names from a query will now fail. Either delete the parser together with the DuckDB removal or keep it behind a clearly-dead-code marker and update/remove its tests.
