title: tablesFromAST indexes ast[0] without a length check
body: `flatten.Flatten(ast[0], ...)` will panic with an index-out-of-range if the deserialised AST JSON is an empty array (e.g. `[]`). The function is currently unreachable because `RunCommands` always errors, but if the DuckDB-backed implementation is ever restored this is an attacker-influenceable panic in a request path. Add a `len(ast) == 0` guard returning an error.

title: Stub DB silently degrades SQLCommand.Execute into an opaque runtime error
body: `NewInMemoryDB()` returns a struct whose `QueryFramesInto` always returns `not implemented`. `SQLCommand.Execute` (pkg/expr/sql_command.go:100-105) assigns that to `rsp.Error` and returns a nil error, so if any code path ever reaches execution (for example a query constructed without going through `NewSQLCommand`/`ReadQuery`) the user sees a bare "not implemented" in the query result instead of a clear "SQL expressions are disabled" message. Consider returning a descriptive, user-facing error from the stub that names the feature and the reason it is disabled.

title: sqlExpressions feature toggle remains documented/registered while being a no-op
body: `featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions` is still registered and documented as enabling server-side SQL expressions, but after this change enabling it has no effect other than producing an error on every SQL expression query. Operators who follow the existing docs will enable the toggle and get a confusing failure. The toggle's description (and the generated feature-toggle docs) should state that the feature is currently disabled/unavailable, or the toggle should be marked deprecated/hidden in this PR rather than deferred.

title: enableSqlExpressions is dead, self-contradictory logic that ignores the feature flag
body: `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`, then returns `false` in both the `if enabled` branch and the fall-through, so the function unconditionally returns `false` and the computed value (and the feature toggle itself) has no effect. The result is a function whose name says "enable" but which can never enable anything, a branch that can never do anything, and a feature-toggle read that is pure noise. If the intent is to hard-disable SQL expressions, this should be an explicit unconditional rejection (with a comment explaining the CVE-2024-9264 context); as written, the next person touching it cannot tell whether the double `return false` is deliberate or a typo, and static-analysis/dead-code linters are likely to flag it.

title: Error text "sqlExpressions is not implemented" is misleading for users who enabled the toggle
body: When a SQL expression query is received, the reader now always returns `fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")`, even for operators who have explicitly enabled the still-existing `sqlExpressions` feature toggle. Those users will see a message implying the feature was never built rather than that it has been disabled for security reasons, which will generate support noise. The message should state that the feature is currently disabled (and the toggle has no effect), and the feature-toggle documentation/registry description should be updated to match, since the toggle is now inert.

title: DuckDB-specific SQL string interpolation of user input left behind in dead code path
body: `TablesList` still builds `SELECT json_serialize_sql('<rawSQL>')` by string-interpolating the user-supplied query after only a naive `strings.Replace(rawSQL, "'", "''", -1)`, and `tablesFromAST` still parses a DuckDB AST shape (`json_serialize_sql` output, `table_name` keys). This whole path is now dead because `RunCommands` is a stub that returns an error, but it is the exact code shape that led to CVE-2024-9264: if anyone later re-implements `DB.RunCommands`, the injection-prone interpolation is silently re-armed. Since the goal of the PR is to remove DuckDB, this parser (and the unused `DB.TablesList` method added in db.go) should be deleted rather than left as a trap. Note also `tablesFromAST` indexes `ast[0]` without a length check, so it would panic on an empty AST if it ever became reachable.

title: No test asserts that SQL expressions are rejected
body: This change disables SQL expressions in two places (the query reader in reader.go and the stubbed `sql.DB` methods here), but no test is added that asserts a `QueryTypeSQL` query is rejected by `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` or that `NewSQLCommand`/`SQLCommand.Execute` fail. Given this is a fix for a critical RCE/LFI (CVE-2024-9264), a regression test is important: without one, a future change that restores `DB.RunCommands`/`QueryFramesInto` or rewrites `enableSqlExpressions` can silently re-enable the vulnerable path with a green CI. Any existing tests that exercised `sql.TablesList` or SQL expression execution against DuckDB also need to be updated/removed, since they will now hit the "not implemented" stubs.

title: enableSqlExpressions() is dead, self-contradictory logic
body: `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` (note the inverted sense: `enabled` is true when the flag is *off*) and then returns `false` from both branches, so the feature-flag lookup has no effect at all. The intent (always disable SQL expressions) is achieved only by accident of the final `return false`. This is a trap for the next maintainer: anyone re-enabling the feature by deleting the `if` block would end up enabling SQL expressions exactly when the toggle is disabled, and vice versa. It should be a plain unconditional disable (or a correctly-oriented flag check) with a comment referencing CVE-2024-9264.

title: Error message does not explain that the feature was intentionally removed
body: Returning `fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")` for `QueryTypeSQL` is misleading for operators who have explicitly enabled the still-registered `sqlExpressions` feature toggle: it reads like a missing implementation rather than a deliberate security-driven disable. Users will have no indication why their previously working queries fail. Mention that SQL expressions are disabled in this build/version (and consider removing or marking the feature toggle as non-functional so the documented toggle doesn't advertise a capability that no longer exists).

title: Legacy SQL command path now fails with an opaque 'error reading SQL command'
body: `NewSQLCommand` still calls `sql.TablesList`, which now unconditionally fails because `DB.RunCommands` returns `errors.New("not implemented")`. The caller converts this into `errutil.BadRequest("sql-invalid-sql")` with public message "error reading SQL command", so any existing panel or alert rule using a SQL expression (through `UnmarshalSQLCommand`, the non-reader path) breaks with a message suggesting the user's SQL is malformed rather than that the feature has been disabled. It also logs the full raw SQL at Warn level on every such request. Prefer short-circuiting with an explicit "SQL expressions are disabled" error.

title: NoData result is immediately overwritten by TableData
body: In `Execute`, when `frame.Rows() == 0` the code sets `rsp.Values = mathexp.Values{mathexp.NoData{Frame: frame}}` but the following statement unconditionally reassigns `rsp.Values = mathexp.Values{mathexp.TableData{Frame: frame}}`, so the NoData branch can never take effect and empty results are always reported as an empty table. The second assignment needs to be in an `else` branch. (Pre-existing, but this file is being touched and the dead branch will mislead future readers.)

title: DB.TablesList stub is unused dead code
body: `DB.TablesList` is never called: `pkg/expr/sql/parser.go` uses the package-level `TablesList` function, which goes through `DB.RunCommands`. Keeping an unused method on the stub type adds confusion about which entry point actually gates SQL execution; either remove it or make the package-level function delegate to it.

title: No regression test asserting SQL expressions are rejected
body: This change is a security fix (CVE-2024-9264) whose entire effect is that `QueryTypeSQL` queries must be rejected and that `sql.DB` never executes anything. There is no test covering `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` with `type: sql` returning an error (with the feature toggle both on and off), nor one covering `NewSQLCommand`/`sql.TablesList` failing. Without such a test, a future refactor of `enableSqlExpressions` or re-introduction of a real `DB` implementation can silently reopen the RCE/LFI path.

title: TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu, racing with BuildIndex writes
body: `TotalDocs()` ranges over `b.cache` without taking `b.cacheMu` (read) lock, while `BuildIndex` now writes into `b.cache` under a short-lived write lock (lines 137-139). This is a genuine data race that Go turns into a fatal runtime error ("concurrent map iteration and map write"), which crashes the process. The new call site makes it reachable: `searchSupport.init` starts the watch-event goroutine (search.go lines 207-213) and only afterwards logs `s.search.TotalDocs()` (search.go line 216); any watch event handled in that goroutine can call `getOrCreateIndex` -> `build` -> `BuildIndex`, writing the map while `TotalDocs` is iterating. `TotalDocs` should take `cacheMu.RLock()`.

title: Removing the BuildIndex-wide lock allows two concurrent builds of the same key
body: `BuildIndex` no longer holds `cacheMu` for the duration of the build; it only locks when inserting into the cache. Because `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` checks `GetIndex` and then calls `BuildIndex` without any per-key serialization, two callers (e.g. a search request and a watch event for the same namespace/group/resource) can now build the same index concurrently. For file-backed indexes both goroutines call `bleve.New` on the same directory `b.opts.Root/<ns>/<resource>.<group>` at the same time, which can fail or corrupt the on-disk index; both also increment `IndexMetrics.IndexTenants` and the second cache write silently discards the first index (leaking its open bleve index/file handles). Some form of per-key locking (e.g. a keyed mutex / single-flight) is needed to keep the previous mutual exclusion while still allowing different keys to build in parallel.

title: Cancel function leaked when Init fails in NewResourceServer
body: `ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)` is created at line 229, but on the new error path `s.Init(ctx)` -> `return nil, err` (lines 258-262) `cancel()` is never called. The context is never cancelled, so any background work tied to it (and the context itself) is leaked, and the partially-initialized server's goroutines (e.g. the SQL poller / watch goroutines started during `search.init`) keep running for the lifetime of the process even though the constructor reported failure. `go vet`'s lostcancel check will also flag this. Call `cancel()` before returning the error.

title: Full index build now happens synchronously inside the constructor with no deadline or cancellation
body: `NewResourceServer` now calls `s.Init(ctx)` with the server's own background context, which runs `lifecycle.Init`, the complete search index build over every namespace, and `initWatcher`. The constructor is invoked from the service-wiring path, so Grafana/storage-server startup is blocked for as long as indexing takes (minutes for large installations) and there is no way for the caller to pass a deadline or cancel the work - the caller's context is ignored and the internal context is only cancelled by `Stop`, which can't run yet. Consider accepting a context (or running the index build in the background and gating only search on it) so startup cannot hang indefinitely.

title: After Stop(), requests are no longer rejected because no method checks initErr anymore
body: `Stop` communicates shutdown exclusively by setting `s.initErr` to "service is stopping"/"service is stopped", which used to be surfaced because every RPC method began with `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil`. Those checks were all removed in this PR, so `s.initErr` is now write-only dead state: after `Stop` cancels the background context, Create/Update/Delete/Read/List/Watch/Search/blob calls still execute and will fail with opaque "context canceled" errors or operate against a torn-down backend instead of returning the clear "service is stopping" error. A explicit stopped/closed flag checked by the public methods (or returning an error from the entry points) is needed to preserve the previous contract.

title: Shared err and totalBatchesIndexed are mutated from errgroup goroutines (data race)
body: Inside `init`, each `group.Go` closure assigns to the enclosing `err` variable (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and increments the enclosing `totalBatchesIndexed`. With `initWorkers > 1` these run concurrently, so both are unsynchronized writes to shared variables: `go test -race` will flag it, the reported batch count can be wrong, and the `err` returned by one goroutine can be overwritten by another before `group.Wait()` observes it, so a build failure may be silently hidden or a spurious error attributed. Use local variables inside the closure (`idxErr := ...; return idxErr`) and an atomic counter.

title: BuildIndex span context is still discarded, so child spans do not nest under it
body: This PR's stated goal is fixing trace propagation (the callers in search.go and sql/backend.go were changed from `_, span :=` to `ctx, span :=`), but `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` still does `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)` and the builder callback keeps using the caller's context. As a result the storage `ListIterator` spans emitted while building are siblings of the `unified_search.bleve.BuildIndex` span rather than children, leaving BuildIndex as a leaf in traces and defeating the purpose of the change.

title: Postgres integration coverage for the storage-server target is silently disabled
body: The only integration test that boots the `StorageServer` target (and therefore exercises the new eager `NewResourceServer` initialization path) is now skipped for postgres with only a TODO comment. Combined with the existing sqlite skip, this leaves mysql as the sole DB covered, so a startup regression specific to postgres - plausible given init now runs synchronously at construction - would go undetected. The skip should reference a tracking issue or the failure should be diagnosed before merge.

title: Removing the BuildIndex-wide lock allows duplicate concurrent builds of the same index
body: Previously `BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for its whole duration, which made a concurrent `GetIndex` (RLock) block until the build finished, so a second caller observed the finished index instead of starting its own build. Now the lock is only taken around the final `b.cache[key] = idx` write, so two callers (e.g. the startup indexing goroutines in `searchSupport.init` and a watch event going through `getOrCreateIndex`) can both see `GetIndex == nil` for the same NamespacedResource and build in parallel. For file-based indexes this means two goroutines call `bleve.New(dir, ...)` on the same directory (`Root/namespace/resource.group`), and the second one fails (path already exists) or corrupts the on-disk index; for memory indexes the work is duplicated and one index is silently dropped from the cache while documents may still be written to it. The duplicate-build window needs to be guarded per key (e.g. keyed mutex / singleflight) rather than removed entirely.

title: TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu
body: `TotalDocs()` ranges over `b.cache` with no lock, while `BuildIndex` now writes to that map from many concurrent goroutines (the lock was narrowed to just the map write). Concurrent map read + write causes a fatal `concurrent map read and map write` runtime panic. This path is newly exercised on every startup by the added log line in `searchSupport.init` (`s.search.TotalDocs()`), and can also be hit at any time if metrics/logging call it while a watch event triggers a lazy index build. `TotalDocs` should take `cacheMu.RLock()`.

title: init() goroutines write shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` without synchronization
body: Inside `group.Go(...)` the closures do `totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(...)`, both of which mutate variables declared in the enclosing function from up to `initWorkers` goroutines running in parallel. This is a data race (detectable by `-race`, and the counter reported in the `namespaces indexed` span event can be wrong/undercounted), and assigning to the shared `err` instead of returning the value through the errgroup can also overwrite an error from another worker. Use a local `err :=` inside the closure (returning it) and an atomic counter.

title: Stop()'s initErr is no longer surfaced; requests are served after shutdown
body: All the per-RPC `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil { return ... }` guards were removed, but `Stop()` still communicates shutdown exclusively by setting `s.initErr = "service is stopping"` / `"service is stopped"`. Since nothing reads `initErr` after construction anymore, calls arriving during or after shutdown no longer fail fast; they proceed against a backend whose lifecycle hooks have been stopped and whose watcher context has been cancelled, producing confusing internal errors instead of a clear "service is stopping" response. Either add an explicit closed/stopped check on the request paths or drop the now-dead initErr mutation in Stop().

title: Context cancel func leaked when Init fails in NewResourceServer
body: `ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)` is created a few lines above, and on the new `s.Init(ctx)` error path the function returns `nil, err` without ever calling `cancel()`. The cancel func is also only reachable through the discarded `server` value, so the derived context (and any timer/goroutine attached to it) is leaked for the lifetime of the process. Call `cancel()` before returning the error (also applies to the `newSearchSupport` error return just above).

title: Index build now blocks server construction and makes startup fail hard
body: `NewResourceServer` now runs the full `Init` (lifecycle init + building every namespace's search index) synchronously before returning. Two consequences worth confirming: (1) process/DI startup is blocked for as long as indexing takes (the PR description says it can exceed a gRPC deadline, i.e. potentially minutes on large installs), so nothing else that depends on this constructor — including the HTTP server/readiness endpoint in single-binary mode — comes up during that time; (2) any transient failure during index build (DB hiccup, bleve directory error) now aborts construction and prevents the server from starting at all, whereas before only the failing request errored and a later request would retry `Init`. Consider doing the index build in the background with a readiness gate, or at least bounding it with a timeout and tolerating per-namespace failures.

title: BuildIndex still discards the span context, breaking the trace fix for builder work
body: The PR fixes trace propagation in `searchSupport.build` and `GetResourceStats` by assigning the derived context, but `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` still does `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)`. The builder callback invoked at line 126 uses the context captured from `searchSupport.build`, so all storage/list spans produced during the actual index build are siblings of the `BuildIndex` span rather than children, and the BuildIndex span appears empty in traces. Propagate the derived context into `builder(idx)` (e.g. by making the builder accept a ctx or by assigning `ctx, span := ...`).

title: Postgres integration coverage for the storage-server target is silently disabled
body: `TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer` now skips whenever `GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres`, leaving only MySQL exercising the storage-server module path. Given this PR changes when unified storage initializes (now inside `NewResourceServer`, i.e. during module startup), postgres is exactly the configuration where a startup regression would go unnoticed. The skip reason ("works locally") suggests the test is actually failing with these changes in CI; the root cause should be understood before merging, and the TODO should reference a tracking issue so the coverage is restored.

title: Removing the BuildIndex-wide lock allows concurrent duplicate index builds for the same key
body: BuildIndex previously held `b.cacheMu` for the whole function, which serialized builds and guaranteed that only one index per NamespacedResource was ever constructed. Now the lock is only taken around the final `b.cache[key] = idx` write. Nothing prevents two goroutines from calling BuildIndex for the same key concurrently (e.g. `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` does an unsynchronized GetIndex-then-build, and it is reachable from both the watch-event handler and concurrent Search calls). Consequences: (1) for file-backed indexes both goroutines call `bleve.New(dir, ...)` on the same directory, so the second call fails with a 'path already exists' error and the request errors out; (2) duplicated full index builds waste CPU/IO; (3) the loser's bleve index is overwritten in the cache and never closed, leaking file handles/memory. If the goal is finer-grained locking, a per-key lock (or singleflight) is needed rather than no mutual exclusion at all.

title: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without holding cacheMu
body: `TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` with no lock while `BuildIndex` now writes to that map under `b.cacheMu` from arbitrary goroutines (index builds triggered by watch events or search requests). Concurrent map read and map write is a fatal, unrecoverable Go runtime error ('concurrent map read and map write') that crashes the process. Previously this was partially masked because BuildIndex held the write lock for its whole duration; with the finer locking, writes happen far more often and at unpredictable times. TotalDocs should take `b.cacheMu.RLock()`.

title: errgroup goroutines share the outer `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` variables (data race, lost errors)
body: Inside `group.Go(...)` the code does `_, _, err = s.build(...)` assigning to the `err` declared in the enclosing function, and increments the shared `totalBatchesIndexed`. With `initWorkers > 1` these are concurrent unsynchronized writes: a genuine data race (will be flagged by `-race`) and, worse, one goroutine's error can be clobbered by another goroutine before `group.Wait()` returns, and `err = group.Wait()` can be overwritten by a still-running assignment. Since this function now runs at server construction and its error aborts startup, misreporting matters. Use a local `err :=` inside the closure and an atomic counter.

title: Init failure in NewResourceServer leaks the server context and background goroutines
body: `NewResourceServer` creates `ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)` and stores `cancel` on the server. When `s.Init(ctx)` fails, the function returns `nil, err` without calling `cancel()`. Anything already started during Init — the storage backend's watch poller started by `searchSupport.init` via `WatchWriteEvents`, and the broadcaster/watcher if `initWatcher` partially succeeded — keeps running against a context that is never cancelled, leaking goroutines, DB connections and the context itself for the lifetime of the process. Call `cancel()` (or `s.Stop`) on the error path.

title: Removing per-request Init() checks means requests are still served after Stop()
body: `Stop` communicates shutdown by setting `s.initErr = "service is stopping"` / `"service is stopped"`, and the only thing that ever read `initErr` on the request path were the `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil` guards that this PR deleted from Create/Update/Delete/Read/List/Watch/Search/History/Origin/IsHealthy/PutBlob/GetBlob. After this change, requests arriving after `Stop()` no longer fail fast; they fall through to a backend whose context has been cancelled, producing confusing 'context canceled' errors (or, for blob/diagnostics paths, operating on torn-down state) instead of the intended shutdown error. Either keep a cheap state check at the entry of the handlers or drop the now-dead `initErr` shutdown signalling in `Stop`.

title: Index build now runs synchronously in the constructor with an uncancellable, unbounded context
body: `s.Init(ctx)` is invoked from `NewResourceServer` with a `context.Background()`-derived context that has no deadline, and it performs the full search index build (`searchSupport.init`, which lists every resource of every namespace). Constructing the resource server therefore blocks Grafana/storage-server startup for as long as indexing takes, with no timeout and no way for the caller to cancel; a slow or unresponsive database makes startup hang indefinitely rather than failing or degrading. Consider a bounded context or kicking the index build off asynchronously while keeping the lifecycle/backend init synchronous.

title: Storage-server integration test now skipped for postgres, leaving only mysql coverage
body: With sqlite3 already skipped, adding an unconditional skip for postgres means `TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer` only ever runs against mysql in CI. Given this PR changes resource-server startup to initialize unified storage (including index building) inside `NewResourceServer`, the postgres startup path is exactly what this test would have covered. The TODO has no tracking issue; at minimum reference one so the coverage gap is not forgotten.

title: Call to non-existent no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() will not compile
body: `authenticate()` now calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments, but the only method defined is `UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` (added in this PR), and no no-arg overload exists in `UsernamePasswordForm`, `AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator` or `AbstractFormAuthenticator`. The services module therefore fails to compile. The intended call is presumably `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`.

title: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires a non-null user, disabling conditional passkeys on the anonymous login page
body: `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` returns true only when `user != null`. It replaces the previous checks which deliberately filled the WebAuthn conditional-UI data when `context.getUser() == null` (the normal, ID-less login). As a result, on a fresh login (no user in the context) `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` is no longer invoked at line 115, so the login page gets no challenge/RP-ID/conditional-UI attributes and discoverable-key (passkey) autofill/auto-login no longer works at all for first-time authentication. This contradicts the feature's main flow and the existing tests that assert `//form[@id='webauth']` and autocomplete `"username webauthn"` on the initial login page. The condition should not require a non-null user (it most likely should just be `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()`).

title: Error-challenge no longer re-fills passkey data when no user is established
body: The `challenge(context, error, field)` override previously filled the WebAuthn conditional-UI data when `context.getUser() == null`; it now does it only when the user is non-null (`isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())` requires `user != null`). Consequently, when an unauthenticated login attempt fails (e.g. unknown username, empty password), the re-rendered login form loses all passkey attributes and the user can no longer authenticate with a passkey from that error page — a regression of the previously working behaviour covered by existing tests (e.g. PasskeysUsernameFormTest.passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey asserts the webauthn autocomplete after an invalid-user error).

title: Test named reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey actually only disables realm passkeys
body: `reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey` sets `setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(FALSE)`, i.e. it verifies that the passkey form is hidden when the realm does not have passkeys enabled — not that it is hidden for a user who has no passkey credential. Since `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled` only checks the realm/feature flag and never whether the user owns a WebAuthn credential, a passkeys-enabled realm will now render the passkey option during re-authentication for users with no (or no discoverable) passkey, and `WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator.shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators()` returns false so no `allowCredentials` is sent, making the option unusable for such users. There is no test covering that combination, and the misleading test name hides the gap.

title: Call to non-existent no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() breaks compilation
body: UsernameForm.authenticate() calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments, but the only method added in this PR is `UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` (UsernamePasswordForm.java:160), and no no-arg overload exists in this class or in AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator. This does not compile, so the whole services module fails to build. Either add a no-arg overload (e.g. `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()`) or pass `context.getUser()` here.

title: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires a non-null user, inverting the previous behaviour and disabling conditional passkeys on the first login screen
body: `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` returns true only when `user != null`. Before this change, `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` was executed exactly when `context.getUser() == null` (authenticate(), old else-branch) and in `challenge(context, error, field)` when the user was not yet selected. With the new helper, both call sites (lines 115 and 137) now do the opposite: the WebAuthn/conditional-UI data is only filled when a user is already set (re-authentication), and is never filled for a plain login where no user has been established yet. Consequently the normal passkeys autofill/conditional-UI on the initial username+password page disappears (no challenge, no rpId, no ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI), which breaks the primary passkeys login flow and the existing assertions in these tests that expect `//form[@id='webauth']` on the first login page. The condition most likely should be `user == null || user has a passwordless WebAuthn credential` rather than `user != null`.

title: Unconditionally returning false removes the guard that skipped the passkey form for users without WebAuthn credentials
body: `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators()` is overridden to always return false. In `WebAuthnAuthenticator.fillContextForm()` this branch also contained the check `if (authenticators.getAuthenticators().isEmpty()) return null;`, which prevented rendering passkey UI for an identified user that has no WebAuthn credential. Since the conditional-UI authenticator is now also used while a user is already set (re-authentication), a user who only has a password but belongs to a realm with passkeys enabled will now get the passkey/conditional-UI markup rendered on the re-authentication form (with IS_USER_IDENTIFIED=false and no allowCredentials), so any passkey attempt can only fail or, worse, let the browser offer a discoverable credential of a different user which then aborts the flow with WEBAUTHN_ERROR_DIFFERENT_USER. The 'no credentials' case should still suppress the passkey UI.

title: No test for re-authentication of a passkey-less user while passkeys are enabled for the realm
body: `reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey` only sets `setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(FALSE)`, i.e. it verifies the trivial case where passkeys are disabled realm-wide. The behaviour actually changed by this PR is re-authentication with passkeys *enabled* for the realm: in that case `fillContextForm` is now invoked for an already-identified user, and because `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators()` returns false the previous 'user has no WebAuthn credential' short-circuit no longer applies. There is no test covering a user that has only a password while realm passkeys are enabled, which is exactly the regression-prone path.

title: Broad catch(Exception) around element lookup can make the assertion vacuous
body: The two `try { assertThat(driver.findElement(...), nullValue()); fail(...); } catch (Exception nsee) { }` blocks (lines 291-296 and 312-317) swallow any RuntimeException from WebDriver, not just NoSuchElementException (e.g. StaleElementReferenceException or a WebDriver timeout), so the test can pass without ever proving the webauthn form is absent. Use `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, () -> driver.findElement(...))` as done in the other tests in this package.

title: Call to non-existent no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()
body: `UsernameForm.authenticate()` now calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments, but the only method with that name declared in the hierarchy is `UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` (added in this PR, see UsernamePasswordForm line 160). `AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator` declares no such method either. As written this does not resolve to any accessible method and the services module will fail to compile. If a no-arg overload is intended (e.g. "passkeys enabled for the realm" without the user check), it must be added explicitly; otherwise the call should pass `context.getUser()`.

title: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires user != null, disabling conditional passkeys on the anonymous login page
body:
`isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` returns true only when `user != null`. Both call sites previously had the opposite user condition:

- In `authenticate()` (line 115) `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` used to be executed in the `context.getUser() == null` branch; now it is executed only when a user is already set. Consequence: on the regular (anonymous) login page no WebAuthn challenge/RP-ID/conditional-UI attributes are put on the form any more, so conditional-UI/passkey autofill login (the main passkeys flow, covered by `webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey`) no longer works.
- In `challenge(context, error, field)` (line 137) the previous condition was `context.getUser() == null && ... isPasskeysEnabled()`; now it is `user != null`. Consequence: error re-renders of the anonymous login form (e.g. unknown username) lose the passkey form/autocomplete, while re-auth error pages gain it.

The intent of the PR (make passkeys available during re-authentication) requires the form to be filled in both cases, so the `user != null` term should be dropped (or replaced by a check that the known user actually has a passwordless WebAuthn credential).

title: SHOULD_DISPLAY_AUTHENTICATORS set to true while ALLOWED_AUTHENTICATORS is never set
body: `WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator` overrides `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators()` to always return `false`, so `WebAuthnConstants.ALLOWED_AUTHENTICATORS` is never put on the form, but `shouldDisplayAuthenticators(context)` is still inherited from `WebAuthnAuthenticator` and returns `context.getUser() != null`. With this PR `fillContextForm()` is now invoked with a non-null user (re-authentication), so the form gets `SHOULD_DISPLAY_AUTHENTICATORS=true` without the corresponding authenticators bean. Templates that gate the authenticator list on that flag will then dereference an undefined `authenticators` variable, producing a FreeMarker/template error (500) instead of the login page. `shouldDisplayAuthenticators()` should be overridden to `false` as well (or the two flags kept consistent).

title: reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey does not test a user without a passkey
body: The test name and the inline comment at line 304 ("Passkeys login should not be available on the page as this user does not have passkey") claim the scenario is a user without a passkey credential, but the test disables passkeys at the realm level (`setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(Boolean.FALSE)`), so the WebAuthn form is absent simply because the feature is off for the realm. The behavior actually changed by this PR - `fillContextForm()` now being called during re-authentication whenever the realm has passkeys enabled and a user is set, regardless of whether that user owns a passwordless WebAuthn credential - is therefore untested. A test with realm passkeys enabled and a password-only user re-authenticating should be added (and the misleading comment/name fixed).

title: Broad catch(Exception) can hide unrelated WebDriver failures in absence assertions
body: The two "webauthn form must not be present" checks wrap `driver.findElement(...)` in `try { ... fail(...) } catch (Exception nsee) { /* expected */ }`. Any exception, not just `NoSuchElementException` (e.g. stale element, timeout, driver/communication errors), is silently treated as the expected outcome, so the assertion can pass for the wrong reason. Other tests in this package use `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, () -> driver.findElement(...))`; the same pattern should be used here.

title: Login IDP cache key omits organizationId, causing repeated invalidation/rebuild of one shared entry
body: `cacheKeyForLogin(realm, mode)` only includes the realm id and the fetch mode, while the per-organization dimension is pushed into the `searchKey` of a single `IdentityProviderListQuery` entry. Consequently all organizations of a realm share one cache entry for `ORG_ONLY`/`ALL`. Each time a login happens for an organization whose id is not yet in that entry, the code takes the `cached == null` branch and calls `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)` and then re-adds a copy of the whole query object (lines 234-241). In a realm with many organizations this means (a) one cache entry that grows linearly with the number of organizations, (b) a full invalidate-and-rebuild of the shared entry on the first login of every new organization, and in a cluster nodes repeatedly discard each other's accumulated entry for different orgs. Contrast this with `getByOrganization`, where the organization id is part of the cache key, so each org gets its own entry. Including `organizationId` in the cache key (or keeping the entry append-only) would avoid the thrashing.

title: Cleanup registers removal of a hard-coded alias "alias", so the 21 created IDPs are never deleted
body: `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` (also at line 425) uses the literal string "alias" instead of the alias that was just created (`idp-alias-<i>` / `idp-alias-20`). The cleanup therefore targets a non-existent identity provider (producing a 404 on every cleanup callback) and none of the 21 identity providers created by `testCacheIDPForLogin` are removed. The leftover providers pollute the shared test realm, and since this test asserts exact counts of login-eligible providers (5, 10, 6, 11), leftovers from this or other tests in the same class (`testCacheIDPByOrg` has the same copy/paste defect at line 303) make the assertions dependent on JUnit method execution order and prone to intermittent failures.

title: New invalidation paths on remove() and for non-public org brokers are untested
body: The test only removes `idp-alias-1`, which is disabled and therefore not login-eligible, so the newly added `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp)` call in `InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.remove()` is never exercised with a provider that actually appears in the login caches; a regression there (e.g. looking up the alias after deletion, or not invalidating at all) would leave a removed broker in the cached login list and would not be caught. Likewise, the new clause added to `LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate()` (organization-linked IDPs only count as login IDPs when `kc.org.broker.public` is true) is never covered: no test creates/removes an org-linked provider with `BROKER_PUBLIC=false` and asserts that the login caches are *not* invalidated.

title: Update comparison mixes an organization-aware wrapper with a raw model, causing spurious cache invalidation
body: `update()` obtains `original` via `getById(...)`, which (when the ORGANIZATION feature is enabled) returns the anonymous `IdentityProviderModel` subclass from `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel()` whose `isEnabled()` additionally reflects the state of the linked organization and of the OrganizationProvider. `updated` is the raw model coming from the caller, whose `isEnabled()` only reflects the IDP's own flag. So for any IDP linked to a *disabled* organization, `getLoginPredicate().test(original)` is false while `getLoginPredicate().test(updated)` is true, and `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate` will invalidate all three login cache entries on every unrelated update of that provider (e.g. a display-name change). This is only a performance/noise issue (over-invalidation), but it defeats the purpose of the fine-grained check; comparing the unwrapped model (or comparing only the persisted flags) would avoid it.

title: Login-cache invalidation decision uses the organization-aware wrapper, so updates can leave stale entries
body: `update()` obtains `idpById` from `getById()`, which returns the anonymous `IdentityProviderModel` subclass created by `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel()`. That wrapper's `isEnabled()` returns false whenever the owning organization (or organizations support for the realm) is disabled, regardless of the IDP's own `enabled` flag. `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate()` then evaluates `getLoginPredicate().test(original)` on this wrapper, so for any org-linked IDP whose organization is currently disabled the predicate is false. If the update also leaves the *new* model ineligible (e.g. only `hideOnLogin` is flipped to true, or `linkOnly` toggled) the method early-returns and no login cache key is invalidated, even though the cached id list (built from a DB query that only filters on the IDP's own attributes) does contain / should now contain that id. After the organization is re-enabled the login lists are served from the stale cache: a `hideOnLogin=true` provider keeps being rendered on the login page, or a newly un-hidden provider stays missing. The comparison should be done against the raw delegate model (e.g. `idpDelegate.getById(...)`) rather than the org-aware wrapper.

title: Login query cache keyed only by realm+mode grows with the number of organizations and is rebuilt per new org
body: `getForLogin` stores all results for a realm/fetch-mode in a single `IdentityProviderListQuery` whose internal map is keyed by `organizationId`. For `FetchMode.ALL` each per-organization entry contains the full set of realm-level login IDP ids plus that org's ids, so memory is O(#organizations * #realm login IDPs) per realm. Worse, every time a not-yet-cached organization id is seen the code calls `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)` and re-adds a merged query (lines 236-240), i.e. the whole entry for the realm is discarded and rebuilt on the hot login path. In realms with many organizations this means repeated full rebuilds instead of a stable cache. Note also that for `REALM_ONLY` the `organizationId` argument is ignored by the implementation, yet it is still used as the search key, producing redundant duplicate entries for every organization.

title: Cleanup registered for the literal alias "alias" instead of the created providers
body: `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` (lines 381 and 425) registers 21 cleanup tasks against a provider whose alias is the literal string `"alias"`, which never exists. The 21 providers actually created (`idp-alias-0` ... `idp-alias-20`) are therefore never removed, and the cleanup call itself will hit a 404. Depending on whether the realm is re-imported per method this either fails the cleanup phase or leaks providers into other test methods — e.g. `testCacheIDPByOrg` asserts exact counts (6 IDPs for orga) and `testCacheIDPForLogin` asserts 5/5/10, so leftovers make the suite order-dependent and flaky. Use the real alias variable (the same bug exists at line 303 and should be fixed there too).

title: No coverage for login-cache invalidation on create/remove of a login-eligible provider
body: The new test only exercises `create()` and `remove()` with providers that are *not* eligible for login (`hideOnLogin=true` provider created, disabled `idp-alias-1` removed) and asserts the caches survive. The two new `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(...)` call sites in `create()` and `remove()` for an eligible provider are never verified, so a regression where creating or deleting a login-visible IDP fails to invalidate the per-realm login caches (leaving the login page showing a deleted broker, or hiding a new one) would not be caught.

title: getLoginPredicate no longer matches LoginFilter/getLoginSearchOptions contract
body: `LoginFilter` is documented as the enum that "contains all fields that are considered when deciding if a provider should be available for login or not", and `getLoginSearchOptions()` is used to build the equivalent DB query. The predicate now additionally requires `organizationId == null || config[kc.org.broker.public] == true`, a condition that is not represented in the enum nor in `getLoginSearchOptions()`. Callers that rely on the two being equivalent filters (query vs. in-memory predicate) will now get different result sets for org-linked providers; the javadoc/enum should be updated or the organization condition expressed as part of the filter set so both paths stay in sync.

title: Cleanup registers removal of a non-existent IDP alias ("alias") instead of the created one
body: `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` uses the literal string "alias" rather than the alias actually created (`idp-alias-<i>`, and `idp-alias-20` on line 425). Consequently (a) the cleanup call targets a provider that never exists, so it will fail/throw at teardown, and (b) the realm-level providers created by this test (`idp-alias-0`..`idp-alias-9`, which are not linked to an organization and therefore not removed together with the organizations) are left behind in the shared test realm. Any other test in the class that counts identity providers or login-eligible providers can then fail depending on JUnit method ordering. The alias must be captured in a local final variable and used in the cleanup lambda.

title: Login-cache invalidation on update is decided from the organization-aware wrapper, so it depends on transient organization state
body: `update()` passes `idpById` (obtained from `getById()`, which returns the anonymous `IdentityProviderModel` subclass created by `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel`) into `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate`. That wrapper's `isEnabled()` returns `false` whenever the linked organization (or the organization provider for the realm) is disabled, even though the stored IDP row is enabled. As a result `getLoginPredicate().test(original)` can evaluate to `false` for an IDP that *is* present in the cached login ID sets (the DB query behind `getForLogin` only filters on the IDP's own `enabled` flag, not on the organization state). In that situation an update that really removes the IDP from the login set (e.g. setting `hideOnLogin=true` or clearing `kc.org.broker.public`) takes the `!test(original) && !test(updated)` early return and does *not* invalidate `*.idp.login.*`. Because enabling/disabling an organization (a group attribute change) also does not invalidate those keys, after the organization is re-enabled `getForLogin` keeps returning the now hidden/non-public provider - `getForLogin` never re-applies the login predicate to the re-resolved models, and callers only re-check `isEnabled()`. Note the inconsistency with `remove()`, which correctly uses the unwrapped `idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)`; `update()` should likewise use the raw stored model (or compare only the IDP's own fields).

title: New invalidation paths in create()/remove() are only tested for the negative case
body: The test only removes `idp-alias-1` (a disabled provider, i.e. not login-eligible) and only creates `idp-alias-20` with `hideOnLogin=true`, so both assertions verify that the login caches are *not* invalidated. The newly added `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(model)` in `create()` and `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp)` in `remove()` are therefore never exercised in their positive branch: a regression that drops either call (leaving the login caches stale after adding or deleting a login-eligible broker) would not be caught. Add a case that creates an enabled, non-hidden provider and one that removes a login-eligible provider, and assert the `*.idp.login.*` entries disappear.

title: Search key includes organizationId even for REALM_ONLY, and per-organization entries accumulate without bound
body: The search key is always derived from `organizationId`, but for `FetchMode.REALM_ONLY` the delegate ignores `organizationId` entirely (it forces `ORGANIZATION_ID=null`). Any caller invoking `getForLogin(REALM_ONLY, someOrgId)` therefore creates a distinct search key for a logically identical result, and each new key triggers `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)` plus a full re-query before being merged back. For `ORG_ONLY`/`ALL`, one cached `IdentityProviderListQuery` per realm accumulates one entry per organization id ever queried, with no bound or pruning, so memory grows with the number of organizations that are used for login. Consider using an empty search key for REALM_ONLY and bounding/keying per-organization results separately.

title: getForLogin now returns providers in non-deterministic order
body: The cached implementation collects internal ids into a `HashSet` and returns `new HashSet<>(...).stream()`, so the order of the returned providers is unspecified and can differ between calls/JVMs. Before this change the stream order followed the underlying query order (realm-level providers first, then organization providers, in the order produced by JPA). Callers that rely on a stable order or that take `findFirst()` on the result will now behave unpredictably; the login page happens to re-sort, but the SPI contract change affects every other consumer. Either preserve ordering (e.g. `LinkedHashSet`/list) or document that the order is undefined.

title: getLoginPredicate dereferences getConfig() which may be null
body: The new predicate does `Boolean.parseBoolean(idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC))` whenever `idp.getOrganizationId() != null`. `IdentityProviderModel.getConfig()` is not guaranteed to be non-null (it can be set to `null` via `setConfig`, e.g. when a representation without a config is converted), so this can throw a `NullPointerException` from `create()`/`update()` in the Infinispan provider, which now calls the predicate on the caller-supplied model. Use a null-safe access (e.g. `idp.getConfig() != null && Boolean.parseBoolean(...)`) or `getConfig().getOrDefault` on a guaranteed map.

title: Removing the multi-provider failure allows silently picking the wrong crypto provider when orders tie
body: detectProvider() previously threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was found on the classpath ("Multiple crypto providers loaded ... Make sure only one cryptoProvider available"). It now sorts by order() and silently takes the first. However DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order() == 200, so if two of them end up on the same classpath the tie is broken by ServiceLoader/classpath ordering, which is not deterministic across environments and builds. Concretely, a FIPS deployment that accidentally still contains the non-FIPS crypto/default jar would no longer fail loudly; it could silently initialise the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider and run outside FIPS mode. Either give the built-in providers distinct orders and/or keep a hard failure (or at least a WARN) when two providers report the same highest order.

title: New abstract order() method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: `int order();` is added as an abstract method to the public CryptoProvider interface. Any existing implementation outside this repository (e.g. the copies/implementations in the keycloak-client repository, custom or vendor FIPS providers, adapters compiled against an older keycloak-common) will no longer compile and will fail at runtime with AbstractMethodError. Since a sensible fallback exists, declare it as `default int order() { return 100; }` (or similar) so the interface stays backwards compatible.

title: Test only round-trips the new encoder/decoder against itself and uses a P-256 key for ES384/ES512
body: test() converts the DER signature to concatenated R||S and back, then only asserts that the two concatenated forms are equal. A systematic encoding bug (e.g. wrong DER length bytes or wrong integer padding) would be symmetric and the assertion would still pass, while the produced DER would be rejected by a real verifier - which is exactly the interop the new provider exists for. The test should at minimum feed the re-encoded DER into `Signature.verify()` with the public key, and/or compare the output byte-for-byte with the existing BouncyCastle-based ECDSACryptoProvider. Additionally the key pair is generated with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` default parameters (P-256) and reused for ES384/ES512, so the long-curve paths (48/66-byte R and S) are never exercised with realistic values; the curve should match the algorithm (secp384r1 / secp521r1).

title: Indefinite-length encoding leads to NegativeArraySizeException instead of IOException
body: readLength() returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding (0x80). readInteger() and readNext() pass that value straight into read(int length), which does `new byte[length]` and therefore throws an unchecked NegativeArraySizeException (readNext can also compute a bogus positive length). The decoder processes attacker-supplied signature bytes, and callers typically only expect IOException for malformed input, so a crafted/garbled signature surfaces as an unexpected runtime exception instead of a clean "invalid signature" error. Reject length == -1 (and negative lengths) with an IOException in readLength()/read().

title: Dead code: two ASN1Encoder writes whose results are discarded
body: Lines 114-115 create two throw-away ASN1Encoder instances and write rBigInteger/sBigInteger into them; the results are never used because the returned DER sequence is built from freshly created encoders on lines 117-120. These statements only waste work and suggest a leftover from refactoring; they should be removed to avoid confusing future readers into thinking the encoding is stateful.

title: logger.debugf() called with a dynamically built string as format
body: `logger.debugf(builder.toString())` passes a runtime-built message (containing provider class names) as a format string with no arguments. jboss-logging will run it through String.format, so any '%' character appearing in the message would raise an UnknownFormatConversionException/MissingFormatArgumentException from a logging call. Use `logger.debug(builder.toString())` or `logger.debugf("%s", builder)` instead.

title: Removing the multiple-provider error makes provider selection silent and non-deterministic on order ties
body: detectProvider() previously threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was found on the classpath. Now it just sorts by order() and takes the first, logging the rest at debug level. All three real providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, WildFlyElytronProvider) return the same order value of 200, so if two of them ever end up on the same classpath (e.g. keycloak-crypto-default accidentally present in a FIPS deployment) the selection depends purely on ServiceLoader iteration order and the deployment silently runs with the wrong crypto stack (non-FIPS BouncyCastle instead of BCFIPS) instead of failing fast. Either keep a hard failure for equal-order providers, or give the providers distinct orders and log the ignored ones at WARN.

title: New abstract method order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: order() is added to the public CryptoProvider SPI interface without a default implementation. Any third-party or downstream implementation of CryptoProvider (including the copies maintained in the keycloak-client repository) will no longer compile and will fail at runtime with AbstractMethodError after upgrading. Adding `default int order() { return 100; }` (or some documented baseline) would keep the SPI backward compatible.

title: logger.debugf() called with a dynamically built string as the format
body: `logger.debugf(builder.toString())` passes a runtime-built message as the format string with no arguments. If any provider class name ever contains a '%' (or the message is changed later) the formatting throws/produces garbage inside logging. Also the message is concatenated unconditionally even when debug logging is disabled, and it ends with a dangling ", ". Use `logger.debugf("Ignored crypto providers: %s", ...)` with the joined names instead.

title: Malformed ASN.1 input causes unchecked exceptions instead of IOException
body: readLength() returns -1 for the indefinite-length encoding (0x80) and can return 0. readInteger() then calls read(length) with that value: read(-1) allocates `new byte[-1]` and throws NegativeArraySizeException, and for length 0 `new BigInteger(new byte[0])` throws NumberFormatException. Both are unchecked exceptions escaping methods declared to throw IOException, so an attacker-supplied/corrupted ECDSA signature propagates an unexpected runtime exception to callers of asn1derToConcatenatedRS instead of a handled IOException. Validate length > 0 and reject indefinite-length encodings with an IOException.

title: Dead encoder calls in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
body: Lines 114-115 create two ASN1Encoder instances, write rBigInteger/sBigInteger into them and discard the results; the actual DER output is built from freshly created encoders on lines 117-121. These two statements have no effect (only wasted allocations) and are confusing to readers; they should be removed.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default KeyStore provider, not a BC provider
body: The implementation returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, i.e. typically the JDK SUN provider. BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER is initialized from this method's return value and is then used as the provider name in provider-specific lookups elsewhere in keycloak-core (Signature.getInstance(alg, PROVIDER) etc.). With this provider installed, those lookups resolve against SUN and can fail with NoSuchAlgorithmException for algorithms only offered by BC, which is hard to diagnose. It also instantiates a KeyStore on every call just to read a provider. Returning null (as WildFlyElytronProvider does) or caching an explicit provider reference would be clearer.

title: ES384/ES512 tests use a 256-bit EC key and only round-trip the new code against itself
body: The key pair is generated with the default EC curve (P-256) and reused for ES384 and ES512, so r/s are always ~32 bytes and the 48/66-byte component paths of integerToBytes/concatenatedRSToASN1DER are never exercised with realistic values. In addition the test only checks that asn1derToConcatenatedRS -> concatenatedRSToASN1DER -> asn1derToConcatenatedRS is self-consistent; it never verifies the produced DER/concatenated bytes against a known-good encoding or against the existing BC-based ECDSACryptoProvider, so an encoding bug that is symmetric in both directions would pass. Generate P-256/P-384/P-521 keys per algorithm and assert the DER signature verifies with java.security.Signature (or compare with the BC implementation output).

title: No test covers the new provider-selection ordering logic
body: detectProvider() changed from fail-fast on multiple providers to order-based selection, which is the core behavioural change of this PR (the Keycloak testsuite now has both DefaultCryptoProvider and AuthzClientCryptoProvider on the classpath). There is no unit test asserting that the higher-order provider wins, that the list is correctly sorted, or what happens when the orders are equal, so a regression in this selection (silently picking the wrong crypto provider) would go unnoticed.

title: `order()` added as abstract method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: `int order();` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` interface without a `default` implementation. `CryptoProvider` is an SPI loaded via `ServiceLoader`, so any implementation outside this repository (adapters, downstream/3rd-party crypto providers, test doubles) will fail to compile and will throw `AbstractMethodError` at runtime when `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` sorts providers. Giving the method a sensible `default` (e.g. `return 100;` or `0`) would keep the SPI backward compatible while still allowing providers to override the preference.

title: Equal-order providers are now silently resolved instead of failing fast (FIPS vs non-FIPS)
body: The previous code threw `IllegalStateException` when more than one `CryptoProvider` was found, which protected against a misconfigured classpath. Now the list is sorted by `order()` and the first entry is used unconditionally. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return `order() == 200`, so if e.g. both the default (non-FIPS BouncyCastle) and the FIPS provider jars end up on the classpath, the selection depends on undefined `ServiceLoader` iteration order and the server may silently start with the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider in a deployment that must be FIPS-compliant, with only a debug-level log line. Either keep failing on an order tie, or give the server-side providers distinct orders and log at WARN when multiple providers of the same order are present.

title: Dynamic string passed as format to logger.debugf
body: `logger.debugf(builder.toString())` passes a dynamically built message as the format string of a formatting logger method (with no arguments). Any `%` character appearing in a provider class name would cause an `UnknownFormatConversionException`/`MissingFormatArgumentException` from the logging call. Use `logger.debug(builder.toString())` or `logger.debugf("%s", builder)` instead.

title: concatenatedRSToASN1DER does not validate the input signature length
body: `System.arraycopy(signature, 0, r, 1, len)` / `System.arraycopy(signature, len, s, 1, len)` assume `signature.length == signLength`. For an attacker-supplied token whose signature part is shorter (or where the wrong algorithm length is used), this throws an unchecked `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` out of a method declared to throw `IOException`, so callers doing signature verification will see an unexpected runtime failure instead of a clean "invalid signature" error. The BouncyCastle-based implementations validate the length and throw `IOException`; the same check should be added here.

title: Indefinite-length encoding (-1) leads to NegativeArraySizeException instead of IOException
body: `readLength()` returns `-1` for the indefinite-length form (0x80), but callers do not handle it: `readInteger()` passes it directly to `read(length)`, which does `new byte[-1]` and throws an unchecked `NegativeArraySizeException`. Since this decoder parses attacker-controlled DER signature bytes, malformed input escapes as an unchecked exception rather than the declared `IOException` (and in `readSequence()` an indefinite length silently yields an empty list). DER does not allow indefinite lengths at all here, so `readLength()` should reject 0x80 with an `IOException`, or every caller must check for `-1`.

title: Dead encoder calls in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
body: Lines 114-115 create two `ASN1Encoder` instances, write `rBigInteger`/`sBigInteger` into them and discard the results; the actual DER sequence is built from freshly created encoders on lines 117-121. These two statements have no effect and only allocate; they should be removed to avoid suggesting the encoders are stateful/shared.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default keystore's JDK provider
body: `getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, i.e. typically `SUN`, not a BouncyCastle provider. `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER` is derived from this provider's name and is used elsewhere as the explicit provider argument for `Signature.getInstance(alg, PROVIDER)`, `KeyFactory.getInstance(alg, PROVIDER)` etc. If any code reached with this crypto provider active uses `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER`, it will request algorithms from a provider that does not implement them and fail with `NoSuchAlgorithmException`. Returning `null` (as `WildFlyElytronProvider` does) or throwing `UnsupportedOperationException` would make the unsupported nature explicit.

title: ECDSA conversion test uses one default curve and never verifies the produced DER
body: The key pair is generated once with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` default parameters (P-256), so the ES384 and ES512 cases are exercised with 32-byte r/s values zero-padded to 48/66 bytes; the real cases (secp384r1/secp521r1 signatures, including the 521-bit odd byte length that is the usual source of off-by-one bugs) are never covered. In addition the test only asserts a round-trip of the new implementation against itself (`rsConcat` vs `rsConcat2`), so a systematic encoding error would pass. The test should generate a key per curve (`ECGenParameterSpec` secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) and verify the DER output with `Signature.verify()` (and/or compare with the BouncyCastle-based provider output).

title: Client/role/group removal fails when both FGAP v1 and v2 features are enabled
body: The provider-event listener is now only executed when `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` (v1) is enabled, but inside it still calls `management(session, realm)`, which returns `MgmtPermissionsV2` as soon as `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` is enabled (see `AdminPermissions.management`). With both features enabled, `ClientModel.ClientRemovedEvent` handling calls `clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false)` which in the new `ClientPermissionsV2` throws `UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2")`. The result is that deleting any client (and, via the same path, deleting roles/groups once those evaluators get V2 implementations) aborts with a server error and a rolled-back transaction. The event handler must pick the v1 implementation explicitly (or the v2 class must tolerate the call).

title: V1 client management-permission endpoints break whenever the V2 feature flag is on
body: `MgmtPermissionsV2` is selected purely from the global `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` feature flag, not from `realm.isAdminPermissionsEnabled()`. Consequently, for every realm in the installation (including realms that only use the v1 fine-grained admin permissions), `clients()` now returns `ClientPermissionsV2`, whose `isPermissionsEnabled`, `setPermissionsEnabled`, `resource`, `getPermissions`, `managePermission`, `configurePermission`, `viewPermission`, `mapRoles*Permission` all throw `UnsupportedOperationException`. The admin REST endpoints `/admin/realms/{realm}/clients/{id}/management/permissions` (GET and PUT) and the corresponding console screens therefore return HTTP 500 instead of working or returning a clear error. These methods should either delegate to the v1 behaviour when the realm does not have FGAP v2 enabled, or throw a mapped exception (e.g. `BadRequestException`/`ModelValidationException`) with a meaningful message.

title: canExchangeTo throws UnsupportedOperationException, breaking token exchange
body: `canExchangeTo` is invoked from the token-exchange flow (`AdminPermissions.management(session, realm).clients().canExchangeTo(...)`) independently of whether a realm uses fine-grained admin permissions. Because `MgmtPermissionsV2` is chosen based on the global `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` feature flag, enabling that feature makes every client-to-client token exchange hit this `UnsupportedOperationException` and fail with HTTP 500 instead of being allowed/denied. Either implement the check (deny/allow explicitly) or fall back to the v1 implementation when the realm does not have FGAP v2 enabled.

title: No migration for realms that already have the admin permissions client: new scopes and Clients resource are missing
body: `init()` creates the authorization scopes (`configure`, `map-roles-client-scope`, `map-roles-composite`, ...) and the per-resource-type "all resources" resource only once, when the admin permissions client is first created, and returns early if the client already exists. Realms that enabled FGAP v2 before this change therefore have neither the new scopes nor the `Clients` resource. In such realms: (1) `getOrCreateResource` for a client permission hits `scopeStore.findByName(...) == null` and throws `ModelException("No scopes found.")` (HTTP 500 on permission creation), and (2) `hasPermission(scope)`/`getResourceTypeResource` always return false/null so all-clients permissions can never be granted. A migration/upgrade step that adds missing schema scopes and resource-type resources to existing admin permission clients is needed.

title: getClientsWithPermission never returns client ids and leaks the aggregate "Clients" resource name
body: `resourceStore.findByType(server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)` only matches resources whose `type` is set to `Clients`. Per-client resources are created by `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` via `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, owner)` which never sets the resource type, so individual client resources are never visited. The only resource with that type is the aggregate resource named `Clients` (created in `AdminPermissionsSchema.init`), so the method returns either an empty set or the literal string `"Clients"`, which callers interpret as a client id. Any caller relying on this contract (set of client ids the caller has the scope for) gets wrong results; no test covers it.

title: Possible NullPointerException when the Clients resource-type resource cannot be resolved
body: In `hasPermission(ClientModel, String)`, when no per-client resource exists the code falls back to `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...)`, which returns `null` when the realm does not support the authorization schema (e.g. `realm.isAdminPermissionsEnabled()` is false while an admin-permissions client still exists) or when the `Clients` resource has not been created (realms created before this change). The returned value is used immediately in `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` and, if that does not blow up, in `resource.getScopes()` on line 224, producing a NullPointerException / HTTP 500 during an authorization decision. The null case must be handled by returning false.

title: getResourceName not extended for the new Clients resource type
body: `getResourceName` only resolves human-readable names for the `Users` resource type. Since per-client resources are stored under the client's internal UUID (see `resolveClient`), permission representations for `Clients` permissions fall through to `resource.getDisplayName()`, which is not set for these generated resources and will therefore be null/empty in the admin REST responses and console, instead of the aggregate name ("All clients") or the client's clientId.

title: Javadoc on void require* methods documents a return value
body: `requireView()` (line 96-98) and `requireViewClientScopes()` (line 100-103) are `void` methods but their new Javadoc says "Returns {@code true} if {@link #canView()} returns {@code true}". They should state that a ForbiddenException is thrown when the corresponding can* method returns false, as done for the other require* methods. Also, the Javadoc of `canList()` (line 72-76) mentions `AdminRoles#QUERY_USERS`, which is unrelated to client listing and looks copy-pasted from the user evaluator.

title: Dead code left over from copy/paste
body: `getEvaluationContext(ClientModel, AccessToken)` is private and never referenced (the only caller would have been `canExchangeTo`, which now throws). Likewise the `logger` field, and the imports `Scope`, `ClientModelIdentity`, `DefaultEvaluationContext`, `EvaluationContext` and the static import of `AdminPermissionManagement.TOKEN_EXCHANGE` are unused. This dead code suggests an incomplete copy from `ClientPermissions` and should be removed to avoid confusion about token-exchange support in V2.

title: New Clients scope map-roles-client-scope is untested
body: The schema now exposes six scopes for the `Clients` resource type, but the added tests only cover `manage`, `configure`, `view`, `map-roles` and `map-roles-composite`. There is no test for `map-roles-client-scope` (`canMapClientScopeRoles`), nor for the all-clients variants of `map-roles*`/`configure`, so regressions in those evaluation paths would go unnoticed.

title: NPE when the "Clients" resource-type resource does not exist
body: In `hasPermission(ClientModel, String)` the code falls back to the resource-type resource: `resource = AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE);` and then immediately calls `authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource)`. `getResourceTypeResource()` returns `null` in several realistic cases: the realm does not have admin permissions enabled (but an admin-permissions client still exists from a previous activation), or the `Clients` resource was never created for that resource server (e.g. realms whose admin permissions client was initialized before this resource type existed). The result is a NullPointerException (HTTP 500) on every client admin REST call that evaluates a client permission instead of simply returning `false`. A null check is needed before the policy lookup (and before the subsequent `resource.getScopes()` call).

title: getClientsWithPermission() cannot return individual clients and returns the literal "Clients" name
body: `getClientsWithPermission(scope)` collects resources via `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)` and adds `resource.getName()` to the result set. However, the per-client resources created by `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource()` are created with `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, owner)` and never get a `type` assigned, so `findByType(..., "Clients", ...)` matches only the single resource-type resource whose name is `"Clients"`. Consequently this method (a) never returns the ids of clients that have an individual permission, and (b) returns the bogus entry `"Clients"` when an all-clients permission is granted. Callers treat the returned strings as client identifiers, so client filtering/listing based on this method is wrong in both directions.

title: Client removal fails with UnsupportedOperationException when V1 and V2 fine-grained authz are both enabled
body: The `ClientRemovedEvent` branch calls `management(session, realm).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false)`. `management()` returns `MgmtPermissionsV2` whenever `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` is enabled, and `MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()` now returns `ClientPermissionsV2`, whose `setPermissionsEnabled()` throws `UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2")`. Since the new guard only checks `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` (V1), a deployment with both features enabled will throw on every client deletion, failing the delete with a server error. The listener should resolve the V1 management implementation explicitly (or skip when V2 is active).

title: V1-only entry points now throw UnsupportedOperationException and surface as HTTP 500
body: `canExchangeTo()`, `isPermissionsEnabled()`, `getPermissions()` and `resource()` throw `UnsupportedOperationException`. These are still reachable while `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` is enabled: the token-exchange code path calls `clients().canExchangeTo(...)` when the V1 feature is enabled, and the admin endpoint `/admin/realms/{realm}/clients/{id}/management/permissions` calls `isPermissionsEnabled()`/`getPermissions()` unconditionally. With V2 enabled these calls now produce an uncaught runtime exception (HTTP 500) instead of a meaningful 400/404 response, and token exchange breaks outright when both features are enabled.

title: New schema scopes are not created for already-initialized admin permission clients
body: `init()` creates the authorization scopes from the schema only when the admin permissions client does not yet exist (it returns early otherwise). Adding `configure`, `map-roles-client-scope` and `map-roles-composite` to the schema therefore leaves realms whose admin-permissions client was already initialized without those scopes. In that state `getOrCreateResource()` throws `ModelException("No scopes found.")` when creating a resource for a Clients permission (line 108), and creating any client permission with the new scopes fails with a validation error from `getScope()`. A migration/upgrade step that adds missing schema scopes (and the new `Clients` resource) to existing resource servers is required.

title: getResourceName() has no handling for the new Clients resource type
body: `getResourceName()` resolves friendly names only for the `Users` resource type ("All users" / username). For the newly added `Clients` resource type it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`, which is `null` for resources created by `getOrCreateResource()` (only name and owner are set). As a result, permissions created for clients expose a null/empty resource name through the admin API (and in the console), unlike user permissions; the name should be resolved to the client's clientId, with `"All clients"` for the resource-type resource.

title: V1 permission cleanup is now skipped when the V1 feature is disabled
body: Wrapping the whole listener body in `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)` means that when the V1 feature is turned off, removal of roles, clients and groups no longer disables/cleans up their V1 fine-grained permission policies. Data created while the feature was enabled (policies/resources referencing the removed role/client/group) is left behind as orphaned authorization objects, which can resurface or break if the feature is re-enabled.

title: Javadoc for requireView()/requireViewClientScopes() describes a return value instead of the thrown exception
body: `requireView()` is documented as "Returns {@code true} if {@link #canView()} returns {@code true}." and `requireViewClientScopes()` as "Returns {@code true} if {@link #canViewClientScopes()} returns {@code true}." Both methods are `void` and throw `ForbiddenException` when the corresponding `can*` check fails, like the other `require*` methods documented in this file. The documentation is misleading for implementers/callers of this SPI-like interface and should state the ForbiddenException behaviour.

title: Dead code left in new class
