A storage provider that returns true from updateCredential for this type but does not persist the codes would leave the user with no working recovery codes even though the required action reports success; and if a local credential already existed, it stays in the DB while RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() always prefers the federated one, leaving a stale, still-valid set of codes in local storage.

title: Optional.get() without presence check leads to server error
body: credentialModelOpt.get() is called unconditionally. If neither the user storage nor local storage returns a recovery-codes credential (e.g. the credential was removed between authenticator selection and form rendering, or the storage provider fails to deserialize it as in BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials where an IOException just logs and returns nothing), this throws NoSuchElementException while building the login form, producing an internal server error page instead of a proper authentication error.

title: Login assertion incomplete and no coverage of code consumption/reuse
body: Unlike testOTPUpdateAndLogin, this test never calls testAppHelper.completeLogin() after submitting the recovery code, so the authorization code is never exchanged; the subsequent testAppHelper.logout() result is also ignored (other tests wrap it in assertTrue), meaning a failed logout goes unnoticed. More importantly the test only performs a single login with code #0 and never verifies the core property of recovery codes: that the used code is rejected on a second login and that the next requested index advances. With the user-storage path this currently does not happen, so the gap hides a real regression.

title: Unrelated 'delayed-authenticator' execution copied into the test flow
body: configureBrowserFlowWithRecoveryAuthnCodes adds a REQUIRED "delayed-authenticator" execution (with the misspelled alias "delayed-suthenticator-config" and delay 0) into the browser flow used by testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin. This authenticator has nothing to do with recovery codes; it only couples the new test to another testsuite provider and will break flow creation if that provider is not deployed. The parameter `delay` is always 0, so it adds no value.

title: Possible NPE on null credential type and no support for disabling recovery codes
body: supportsCredentialType() uses `credentialType.equals(RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE)` (same pattern at line 275 in isConfiguredFor), which throws NullPointerException for a null credentialType, while the surrounding checks are written null-safely (`CredentialModel.PASSWORD.equals(credentialType)`). Additionally, disableCredentialType() and getDisableableCredentialTypesStream() were not extended for the new type, so a recovery-codes credential created in this storage can never be disabled/removed via admin or account REST.

title: New, undocumented user-storage contract: all raw recovery codes passed as a JSON array in the credential value
body: createRecoveryCodesCredential() serializes the full list of *raw* (unhashed) recovery codes into a JSON array and passes it as the challenge-response/value of a UserCredentialModel of type `recovery-authn-codes` to `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)`. This establishes a brand new, completely undocumented contract that every UserStorageProvider must now implement to receive recovery codes (the JSON encoding, the fact that the value is a list and not a single code, that the provider is responsible for hashing them and for invalidating individual codes after use). Nothing in the SPI javadoc, the UserStorage documentation, or a migration note describes it; the only example is the testsuite provider, which stores the codes in clear text and compares them with `String.equals`. Without documentation, third-party providers will either reject the update (silently falling back to local storage) or mis-store the codes. At minimum the method javadoc should specify the wire format and the provider's obligations (hashing, single-use invalidation).

title: Federated-first credential lookup can disagree with credential validation order and with an existing local credential
body: getCredential() returns the federated recovery-codes credential if the user storage exposes one, and only otherwise the locally stored one. A user can legitimately have both (e.g. codes were created locally before the federation provider started supporting the type, or a previous `updateCredential` returned false). In that case the login form renders the "next code number" taken from the federated model while `credentialManager().isValid()` may validate against the other credential, so the user is asked for code N but only code M is accepted, making login impossible. The helper should either take the credential from the same source that will validate it, or the creation path should delete the stale local credential when the credential is stored in the user storage.

title: Unguarded Optional.get() breaks the recovery-code login form for providers that don't expose credentials
body: The bean calls `credentialModelOpt.get()` without checking presence. A UserStorageProvider can fully support recovery codes by implementing `supportsCredentialType`/`isConfiguredFor`/`isValid` (which is what makes `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.configuredFor()` return true) while not implementing the optional `getCredentials()` method. In that case `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()` returns an empty Optional and rendering the recovery-code login page throws NoSuchElementException, producing an HTTP 500 error page instead of a login form. Since this PR makes federated recovery codes a supported scenario, this path is now reachable in a supported configuration and must degrade gracefully (or the requirement to implement getCredentials must be enforced/documented).

title: removeStoredCredentialById() is called with a federated credential id
body: After the lookup was switched to `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()`, the credential returned here may come from the user storage (federated) instead of the local credential store. The code then calls `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())`, which only operates on the local store, so for a federated credential the call silently does nothing (and the id may even be null, as it is for the testsuite provider which rebuilds the model with `createFromValues`). Consequence: when a federated provider reports all codes as used, the exhausted credential is never removed and the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action will be re-added on every subsequent login, leaving the user in a loop. The removal/reset needs to be delegated to the user storage (e.g. via disableCredentialType/updateCredential) when the credential is federated.

title: getCredentials() dereferences a possibly null MyUser
body: `var myUser = getMyUser(user);` can return null (getMyUser is a plain map lookup by username, and every other method in this class — isConfiguredFor, getDisableableCredentialTypesStream, isValid — explicitly null-checks it). `myUser.recoveryCodes` on line 235 then throws NullPointerException whenever getCredentials is invoked for a user that is no longer in the in-memory map (e.g. after removeUser, or for a stale cached UserModel), which will surface as a 500 in account/admin endpoints that list credentials and make tests flaky. Add the null check and return Stream.empty().

title: Federated recovery-codes credential is rebuilt on every call, losing id and used-code state
body: getCredentials() builds a fresh `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...)` from the raw codes on each invocation. The returned model therefore has no id and always reports every code as unused, and the provider never marks a code as consumed in isValid(). As a result this reference provider models recovery codes as infinitely reusable, the credential cannot be addressed by id (account console delete, removeStoredCredentialById), and the new test cannot detect a regression in the single-use semantics of recovery codes.

title: New test only covers one successful login; no coverage of code consumption, wrong code, or fallback to local storage
body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only sets up codes and performs a single successful login with code #0. It does not verify that the used code is rejected on a second login / that the form then asks for the next code, does not verify that an invalid code is rejected, does not assert that no credential leaked into the local DB *after* the login, and does not cover the other branch of the new code in CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential (a federated user whose storage does not support `recovery-authn-codes`, which must fall back to the local credential store). The two behaviours this PR is about — storing in user storage and falling back to local — are therefore only half covered.

title: Unneeded 'delayed-authenticator' execution (with typo'd config alias) added to the test browser flow
body: configureBrowserFlowWithRecoveryAuthnCodes adds a REQUIRED `delayed-authenticator` execution with delay 0 and a config alias typo ("delayed-suthenticator-config"). The delay serves no purpose for this test, but it makes the flow (and the test) depend on an extra testsuite authenticator being deployed and on the `delay` config being accepted; if that provider is unavailable the flow fails at authentication time for reasons unrelated to recovery codes. The parameter and the execution should be dropped (or at least the alias typo fixed).

title: Unchecked Optional.get() breaks login form for user-storage recovery codes
body: `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user)` returns an `Optional`, and the result is dereferenced with `.get()` without an `isPresent()` check. With this PR, recovery codes can now be owned by a user-storage provider: `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.configuredFor()` only asks `isConfiguredFor(RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE)` (a `CredentialInputValidator` call), while `getCredential()` relies on the provider also exposing the credential through `getFederatedCredentialsStream()`. A provider that validates the credential but does not expose it (a very common combination, e.g. a provider implementing only `CredentialInputValidator`/`CredentialInputUpdater`) will make the authenticator render this bean, and the empty `Optional` throws `NoSuchElementException`, resulting in a 500 error page instead of a login challenge. The same applies to `getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get()` on line 21. Both need a graceful fallback/error path.

title: Pre-existing local recovery-codes credential is left valid after codes are stored in user storage
body: `createRecoveryCodesCredential()` calls `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` and, when the user-storage provider handles it, skips creating/replacing the local credential entirely. Any previously stored *local* recovery-codes credential for that user is neither removed nor overwritten. This is exactly the upgrade scenario this PR targets: a federated user who configured recovery codes before the provider supported the type keeps the old local credential, and `SubjectCredentialManager.isValid()` will still accept those old codes via the local `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider`. Re-generating recovery codes must invalidate the previous set; here the old codes stay valid indefinitely. Additionally `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()` now prefers the federated credential, so the stale local credential is invisible in the UI while remaining usable for authentication.

title: User label and generation timestamp are dropped when codes are stored in user storage
body: The credential handed to the user-storage provider is built as `new UserCredentialModel("", type, recoveryCodesJson)`, i.e. only the raw codes are transferred; the `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` (which carries the user-entered label from the `userLabel` form field and the `generatedAt` timestamp) is used only on the local-storage branch. Consequently, for federated users the label the user typed in the required-action form is silently discarded and cannot be shown in the account/admin console. The new value format (a JSON array of raw codes in `getChallengeResponse()` on update, versus a single raw code on validation) is also completely undocumented in the method javadoc, so third-party provider authors cannot implement `updateCredential` for this type correctly.

title: Exhausted federated recovery-codes credential is removed from the wrong store
body: `getCredential()` can now return a credential coming from the user-storage provider (via `getFederatedCredentialsStream()`), but when `allCodesUsed()` is true the code still calls `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())`, which only addresses Keycloak's local credential store. For a federated credential this is a no-op (and the id may even be null, since providers typically build the model with `createFromValues(...)` which does not set an id), so the exhausted credential is left in the user storage. Removal/disabling for federated credentials has to go through the provider (`disableCredentialType`), otherwise the stale credential stays reported as configured.

title: getCredentials() dereferences a possibly null MyUser
body: `var myUser = getMyUser(user);` is immediately dereferenced (`myUser.recoveryCodes`) without the null check that every other method in this class performs (`isConfiguredFor`, `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream`, `isValid` all handle `null`). `getMyUser()` returns null whenever the username is not in the in-memory map (e.g. a user still cached/linked in Keycloak after being removed from the provider), which turns a credential listing into a NullPointerException propagated to the caller.

title: Recovery codes cannot be disabled/removed although the type is now reported as supported
body: `supportsCredentialType()` (line 114) and `isConfiguredFor()` (line 275) were extended for `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE`, but `disableCredentialType()` (line 217) still only handles OTP and `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream()` (line 255) only ever reports `CredentialModel.OTP`. As a result, a recovery-codes credential stored in this provider can never be deleted or disabled through the admin/account REST APIs, and the new tests do not cover removal at all (unlike the OTP flows, which have `testOTPSetupThroughAdminRESTAndLogin` / `testDisableCredentialsInUserStorage`). Since this provider doubles as the reference for user-storage credential support, the gap will be copied by implementors.

title: New test never verifies that a recovery code is consumed/single-use
body: `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` logs in once with code index 0 and asserts the requested code number is 0. Because `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid` (line 340) merely checks membership in the stored list and `getCredentials` (line 237) rebuilds the model with `createFromValues`, which marks all codes unused, every login will accept the very same code forever and the prompt will always ask for code #1. The single-use semantics of recovery codes — the core security property of the feature, and the behaviour `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean`/`allCodesUsed()` depend on — are therefore neither exercised nor supported by the reference provider. At minimum a second login should assert that the previously used code is rejected and/or that the requested code index advances.

title: Login in new test is not completed and logout result is ignored
body: Unlike the sibling OTP test (`testOTPUpdateAndLogin`, which calls `testAppHelper.completeLogin()` before `appPage.assertCurrent()` and wraps logout in `assertTrue(...)`), `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` never calls `completeLogin()` after submitting the recovery code and discards the `testAppHelper.logout()` return value. The code-to-token exchange is thus never performed and a failing logout is silently swallowed, leaving the user session behind and potentially affecting subsequent tests in this class (which all reuse the username "otp1").

title: Reader thread is never joined, making the regression test racy and unreliable
body: `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti` starts a background thread that records exceptions into `caughtExceptions`, then sets `deletedAll` and immediately asserts the list is empty without ever joining the thread. Consequences: (a) an exception raised by the in-flight request (exactly the NPE this PR fixes) can be appended after the assertion has already run, so the test can pass even when the bug is present — the regression coverage is illusory; (b) if the thread has not yet issued a single request before the deletions complete, nothing is exercised at all. The thread reference should be kept, `Thread.join()` (with timeout) called before asserting, and the test should also assert that at least one read actually completed.

title: Background thread can spin forever if group deletion throws
body: `deletedAll.set(true)` (line 155) is only reached if every `groups().group(groupUuid).remove()` call succeeds. If any delete throws (e.g. 404/500 during the concurrent read load), the exception propagates out of the test method and `deletedAll` is never set, leaving the started non-daemon thread looping and continuously issuing admin REST calls. That hangs the surefire JVM / build instead of failing cleanly. Set the flag in a `finally` block (and/or create the thread as a daemon).

title: getSubGroupsCount() now returns null, moving the NPE to callers
body: The fix changes `getSubGroupsCount()` to return `null` when the group no longer exists in the store. `GroupModel.getSubGroupsCount()` returns a boxed `Long` that callers routinely use in arithmetic/comparisons or propagate into `GroupRepresentation.setSubGroupCount(...)` (see `GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount`). Any caller performing auto-unboxing (`getSubGroupsCount() > 0`) will now throw an NPE instead, and the admin REST response will contain a null/absent `subGroupCount`, which the admin console uses to decide whether a group is expandable. Returning `0L` for a group that has been concurrently removed keeps the contract non-null and avoids simply relocating the NPE.

title: Unthrottled busy loop requesting Integer.MAX_VALUE groups
body: The reader thread calls `groups(null, 0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, true)` in a tight loop with no sleep. Each iteration asks the server for an unbounded page of groups, so the test saturates a CPU core and floods the server with large queries for the whole duration of the delete loop, slowing the test suite and increasing the chance of unrelated timeouts. Add a small sleep and a realistic page size.

title: getSubGroupsCount() may now return null, moving the NPE to callers
body: `getSubGroupsCount()` now returns `null` when the group has been removed concurrently (`modelSupplier.get()` returns null). `GroupModel.getSubGroupsCount()` declares `Long`, and callers are not prepared for a null value: any caller that auto-unboxes the result (e.g. comparisons such as `getSubGroupsCount() > 0`) will throw exactly the NPE this PR is trying to fix, just one frame higher, and REST representations will silently report a missing/null `subGroupCount`. Returning `0L` (or throwing a well-defined model exception that the REST layer maps to 404) would keep the contract non-null and make the behaviour predictable.

title: Other methods using modelSupplier.get() still NPE on concurrently removed groups
body: The same concurrent-removal race fixed in `getSubGroupsCount()` exists unguarded in `getSubGroupsStream(String, Integer, Integer)` (line 256), `getSubGroupsStream(Integer, Integer)` (line 262) and `getSubGroupsStream(String, Boolean, Integer, Integer)` (line 268): each dereferences `modelSupplier.get()` directly, which returns `null` when the group row was deleted by another transaction after the cache entry was created. Listing subgroups while a group is being deleted will therefore still produce a NullPointerException / HTTP 500, so the reported issue is only partially fixed.

title: Reader thread is not joined before asserting, so failures can be missed
body: `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti()` starts a reader thread and asserts `caughtExceptions` is empty immediately after setting `deletedAll` to true. The reader thread may still be inside an in-flight `groups(...)` call at that moment; if that call fails (the exact failure this test is supposed to detect) the exception is appended after the assertion has already passed, making the test silently green. The thread must be joined (with a timeout) before the assertion.

title: Reader thread can spin forever if a group removal throws
body: `deletedAll.set(true)` is only reached if every `groups().group(groupUuid).remove()` succeeds. If any removal throws, the flag is never set and the non-daemon reader thread keeps looping and hammering the admin API indefinitely, which can hang the surviving JVM/test run instead of producing a clean failure. Set the flag in a `finally` block and/or create the thread as a daemon.

title: Created groups are not registered for cleanup
body: The 100 groups created in `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti()` are only removed by the explicit delete loop at the end of the test. If the test fails or an assertion/exception aborts it before the loop completes, the leftover groups stay in the shared `@InjectRealm` realm and can break the other tests in this class (several of which assert on exact group listings/names). Registering each created group with `managedRealm.cleanup()` would make the test self-contained.

title: Shared admin client used concurrently from two threads
body: The reader thread and the main thread both use `managedRealm.admin()`, i.e. the same `Keycloak` admin client instance. The admin client's token manager is not designed for concurrent use; a token refresh happening while both threads issue requests can produce spurious 401/`NotAuthorizedException`s that would be recorded in `caughtExceptions` and fail the test for reasons unrelated to the group NPE, making the test flaky. Use a separate admin client instance per thread.

title: getSubGroupsCount() can now return null, shifting the NPE to callers
body: `getSubGroupsCount()` now returns `null` when the group has been removed concurrently (`modelSupplier.get()` returns null). `GroupModel.getSubGroupsCount()` previously never returned null for a live adapter, and callers treat it as a value: e.g. `GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount` passes it straight into `GroupRepresentation.setSubGroupCount(...)` (producing a `subGroupCount: null` in the admin REST payload) and any caller that compares/unboxes the result (`count > 0`, `long c = group.getSubGroupsCount()`) will throw NPE at a point further from the cause. Returning `0L` (or re-checking invalidation and delegating) would keep the contract intact; if null is intentional, the `GroupModel` javadoc should document it and the known consumers should be audited.

title: Same concurrent-removal NPE remains in the three getSubGroupsStream overloads
body: Lines 256, 262 and 268 (`getSubGroupsStream(search, first, max)`, `getSubGroupsStream(first, max)`, `getSubGroupsStream(search, exact, first, max)`) call `modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` with no null check. `modelSupplier` resolves via `cacheSession.getGroupDelegate().getGroupById(realm, cached.getId())`, which returns null exactly in the race this PR fixes for `getSubGroupsCount()` (group deleted while a cached adapter is still in use). So listing subgroups concurrently with a group deletion still throws NPE inside the cache layer, i.e. the fix is incomplete for the reported issue.

title: populateGroupHierarchyFromSubGroups dereferences a possibly-null parent group
body: `session.groups().getGroupById(realm, currGroup.getParentId())` can return null when the parent group is removed while the hierarchy is being built (the very concurrency scenario this PR targets). `parentModel` is then passed to `groupEvaluator.canView(parentModel)` (line 51), `toRepresentation(groupEvaluator, parentModel, full)` (line 57) and `populateSubGroupCount(parentModel, parent)` (line 60), all of which dereference it, producing an NPE/500 from the admin groups endpoint. A null check that breaks out of the while loop (and drops the orphaned child) is needed.

title: Reader thread is never joined, so the assertion races with the thread it validates
body: `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti` starts a reader thread and asserts `caughtExceptions` is empty immediately after `deletedAll.set(true)`. The reader can still be in the middle of an HTTP request at that moment, so an exception recorded after the assertion is silently lost (false pass), and a failure recorded in a later test's execution window produces confusing noise. The thread is also left running after the test method returns, continuing to call `managedRealm.admin()` while the test framework may already be tearing down/closing the admin client. The thread should be joined (with a timeout) before asserting, and the test should fail with the captured exception's stack trace.

title: Shared admin client used from two threads and no guarantee the race is hit
body: The reader thread and the main thread both use `managedRealm.admin()` (the same injected Keycloak admin client / underlying JAX-RS client), which is not documented as thread-safe for concurrent request submission; failures from client-side state corruption would be indistinguishable from the server-side NPE this test is meant to catch. In addition the test has no synchronization that guarantees a read overlaps a delete, so it can pass even with the bug present (and the created groups are not registered with `managedRealm.cleanup()`, so a mid-test failure leaves 100 groups behind for other tests in the realm).

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key crashes on datetime keys
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key()` does `int(math.floor(value) ...)` on the raw attribute value, which only works for numeric keys. The only caller (`OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`) passes `order_by="-datetime"`, so `value` is a `datetime` and `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`. `build_cursor()` always invokes `key=self.get_item_key` on the results, so any request with `optimized_pagination=true` that returns at least one row will 500. The class should subclass/reuse `DateTimePaginator`'s key handling (or at minimum not be wired to a datetime-ordered queryset).

title: value_from_cursor returns raw int for a datetime column
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor()` returns `cursor.value` unchanged (integer/float), but `BasePaginator.build_queryset()` injects it into a raw SQL `WHERE "datetime" <= %s` clause. Since the endpoint orders by `-datetime`, the value must be converted back to a `datetime` as `DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor()` does. As written, following any cursor will either raise a database type error or silently compare a timestamp column against an integer, returning wrong pages. Additionally, cursor values produced by `DateTimePaginator` (milliseconds) and this paginator are not interchangeable, so a client toggling `optimized_pagination` between requests will feed incompatible cursors to the other paginator.

title: Negative slice on a QuerySet raises ValueError, not supported by Django
body: In the `enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0` branch, `start_offset` (and often `stop`) are negative and used as `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` for negative slice bounds, so the comment claiming "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false. Since `offset` comes straight from the user-supplied `cursor` query parameter (`Cursor.from_string` accepts negative integers), any authorized caller can trigger an unhandled 500 by sending e.g. `cursor=0:-1:0` with `optimized_pagination=true`. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError` instead.

title: Silently clamping negative offsets masks invalid cursors and is inconsistent for prev cursors
body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes `BasePaginator.get_result()` for every paginator in the codebase: a forward cursor with a negative offset, which previously surfaced an error, now silently returns the first page as if the cursor were `offset=0`, while the cursors returned in the response are built from the original negative `cursor.offset` (see `_build_next_values`/`_build_prev_values`), producing inconsistent/incorrect next/prev links. For `is_prev` cursors the negative offset is still passed through and will raise Django's `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` (a 500) rather than a `BadPaginationError`. Negative offsets should be validated and rejected explicitly in one place.

title: Extra-row trimming uses raw offset instead of the slice offset
body: The check `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra:` compares the number of fetched rows against the un-clamped `offset`, but the rows were fetched with `start_offset` (which can differ from `offset` after clamping or in the negative-offset branch). When they differ, the extra look-ahead row is not dropped, so a previous-page response can contain `limit + 1` items / an item that belongs to the adjacent page. Use `start_offset` consistently (same issue exists in the `BasePaginator` copy at line 192).

title: organization_context.member can be None -> AttributeError 500
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences `organization_context.member` unconditionally when the requester is not a superuser. For requests authenticated with an org API key/auth token (or any caller that passes `OrganizationAuditPermission` without being a member), `member` is `None`, so this raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'` and the endpoint returns a 500 for every GET, not just optimized ones. Guard with `organization_context.member is not None` and only evaluate the flag when `use_optimized` is actually requested.

title: "admin-only" gate is actually satisfied by any member of an open-membership org
body: The comment says the optimized path is enabled only for "authorized administrators", but the condition uses `member.has_global_access`, which is true for every member of an organization with open membership (and for any member whose role grants global access), not just admins/owners. Combined with the new unvalidated negative-offset path in `OptimizedCursorPaginator`, this lets ordinary members reach code that bypasses the normal offset bounds and crashes the request. If this is meant to be admin-only, check the actual role/permission (e.g. superuser or `org:admin`); the claim that "permissions are checked at the queryset level" in paginator.py is also unsupported for this path.

title: New paginator and endpoint branch have no tests
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (including the negative-offset branch) and the new `optimized_pagination=true` endpoint branch are added with no unit or API tests. Given that the class as written raises `TypeError` on datetime keys and `ValueError` on negative slices, even a single test exercising the new query parameter would have caught the breakage. Tests should cover: optimized path with/without a cursor, negative offsets, and unauthorized callers falling back to `DateTimePaginator`.

title: Misleading comment documents negative offsets as a supported feature
body: The added comment states that `Cursor` now "allows negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios", but no behavior changed here (offsets were never validated) and downstream consumers cannot handle negative offsets: Django querysets reject negative slice bounds and `OffsetPaginator`/`ChainPaginator` explicitly raise `BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`. Documenting an unsupported, user-controllable value as a feature invites more code to rely on it; either add real validation here or drop the comment.

title: `organization_context.member` can be None, raising AttributeError on every request
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated unconditionally for every GET on this endpoint, before checking `use_optimized`. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is optional and is `None` when the requester is not a member of the organization (e.g. a superuser/staff user, or an org-auth-token/API-key request that passes the `OrganizationAuditPermission` check without membership). Because Python's `or` short-circuits only when the left side is truthy, a non-superuser non-member will dereference `None.has_global_access` and the endpoint will return a 500 instead of the audit log page. Guard with `use_optimized and organization_context.member is not None` (and only compute the flag inside the optimized branch).

title: "authorized administrators" gate actually grants the feature to ordinary members
body: The comment says the optimized path is for "authorized administrators", but the condition uses `organization_context.member.has_global_access`, which is true for any member of an organization with open membership (and for members whose role grants global access) — not just admins. Any such user can set `?optimized_pagination=true` and reach `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `enable_advanced_features=True`, which deliberately bypasses the offset lower-bound (see `paginator.py`). The access-control intent and the implemented check do not match; use an explicit admin/owner scope check if the feature is meant to be privileged, and fix the misleading comment.

title: Negative queryset slice is not supported by Django and will raise, not "handled automatically"
body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is set and the client supplies a cursor with a negative offset, `start_offset = cursor.offset` is negative and `queryset[start_offset:stop]` is executed. Django QuerySets explicitly reject negative indices (`ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.`), so this path can never work: it turns a user-controlled cursor value into an unhandled 500 instead of a `BadPaginationError`/400. The inline comment claiming "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is factually wrong. Either validate `offset >= 0` and raise `BadPaginationError`, or remove the feature.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key crashes for datetime sort keys
body: `get_item_key` applies `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly to `getattr(item, self.key)`. The only caller added in this PR (`OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`) uses `order_by="-datetime"`, so the value is a `datetime` and `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime`. Every request with `?optimized_pagination=true` from an eligible user will 500 as soon as a cursor is built. Either subclass `DateTimePaginator`'s key conversion or do not use this paginator for datetime columns.

title: value_from_cursor returns a raw number for a datetime column, producing an invalid WHERE clause
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` unchanged (integer/float), but `BasePaginator.build_queryset` injects it into `WHERE "auditlogentry"."datetime" >= %s`. For the audit-log endpoint the sort key is a timestamp column, so comparing it against a bare millisecond integer either raises a database error or silently filters wrong rows. `DateTimePaginator` converts the cursor value back to a `datetime` for exactly this reason; this subclass must do the same.

title: Silent clamping of negative offsets changes pagination semantics and is inconsistent for prev cursors
body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` in `BasePaginator.get_result` silently rewrites a client-supplied negative forward offset to 0, so the response no longer corresponds to the requested cursor; the next/prev cursors produced by `build_cursor` are still derived from the original (negative) `cursor.offset`, so clients can get duplicated or skipped rows instead of a clear error. Meanwhile the `is_prev` branch still passes a negative offset straight into the queryset slice, which Django rejects with `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` (500). Invalid offsets should be rejected uniformly with `BadPaginationError` rather than half-clamped.

title: Comment claims a behavior change that the code does not make
body: The added comment in `Cursor.__init__` ("Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios") describes a change, but the only code here is the pre-existing `self.offset = int(offset)`; nothing about negative offsets was enabled or validated. The comment misleads future readers into believing negative offsets are an intentionally supported/validated feature of `Cursor`, when in fact consumers such as `OffsetPaginator` still raise `BadPaginationError` for them. Remove or correct it.

title: No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the new query parameter
body: The PR adds a new public paginator class with its own `get_result` implementation and a new request-controlled branch in `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` (`?optimized_pagination=true`), but no tests are added for either. The paginator's datetime key handling and negative-offset path are both broken (see other findings), which a single test exercising the endpoint with the new parameter would have caught. Add tests covering: the optimized branch for an eligible user, a non-member/superuser requester (where `organization_context.member` is None), and a negative-offset cursor.

title: get_result duplicated from BasePaginator, dropping explanatory invariants
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` is a near-verbatim copy of `BasePaginator.get_result` (~60 lines) with the inline documentation about the extra before-row fetch removed. Any future fix to the base implementation (e.g. the cursor-value comparison edge case documented in the base method) will silently not apply here. Prefer overriding only the slice computation via a small hook instead of copying the whole method.

title: Negative slice start passed to a Django QuerySet raises ValueError
body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing/slicing – `QuerySet.__getitem__` raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`. The inline comment "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is factually wrong. Any client-supplied cursor with a negative offset (cursors are parsed with `int()` in `Cursor.from_string`, so `0:-5:0` is accepted) will produce an unhandled 500 on the audit log endpoint rather than a 400, making this a trivially reachable error/DoS path.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator uses integer key semantics but is wired to a datetime-ordered queryset
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `math.floor(getattr(item, self.key))` and `value_from_cursor` returns the raw cursor value, i.e. it assumes the sort key is numeric (the `Paginator` semantics). The new audit-log code path instantiates it with `order_by="-datetime"` on `AuditLogEntry`, whose `datetime` field is a `datetime` object. `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError`, and `build_queryset` would compare the datetime column against a raw integer cursor value in the generated `WHERE ... <= %s` clause, producing a database error. The optimized path therefore cannot work for this endpoint at all; it needs to derive from `DateTimePaginator` (or convert values) and have tests covering datetime keys.

title: Advanced pagination gated on has_global_access / non-elevated is_superuser
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is described as enabling the feature for "authorized administrators", but `has_global_access` merely means the member has access to all teams (it is true for every member in an organization with open membership), so any ordinary org member can turn on the unbounded/negative-offset pagination path. In addition, `request.user.is_superuser` is the raw staff flag; Sentry requires the active-superuser check (`is_active_superuser(request)`) so that superuser privileges are only honored when the superuser session is elevated. Both checks should be replaced with a proper permission/feature check.

title: organization_context.member may be None -> AttributeError 500
body: `organization_context.member.has_global_access` assumes `member` is always populated. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is optional and is `None` when the requester is not an organization member (e.g. authentication via an org auth token/integration token, or a non-member with elevated permissions). Because `or` only short-circuits when `request.user.is_superuser` is true, a non-member request will raise `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'` and return a 500 for a previously working endpoint. Also `request.user` can be `AnonymousUser` for token auth, so relying on its attributes here is fragile.

title: Offset clamping in BasePaginator is inconsistent and leaves invalid cursors in the response
body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` silently clamps negative offsets only for forward cursors; a previous-page cursor with a negative offset is still passed straight into the queryset slice and will raise `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` from Django. For the clamped forward case the negative `cursor.offset` is still handed to `build_cursor`, where `_build_next_values` computes `next_offset = offset + limit` from the negative value, so the returned next/prev cursors keep propagating out-of-range offsets. Invalid cursor offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError` (400) rather than partially clamped.

title: Extra-row trim uses raw cursor offset instead of the effective start offset
body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` the check `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` compares the fetched row count against the raw `cursor.offset`, but the rows were fetched using `start_offset` (which may differ from `offset` after clamping, and is negative in the "advanced" branch). When they diverge the extra look-ahead row is not dropped, so a previous-page response can include a row that belongs to the adjacent page.

title: New paginator and offset-clamping behavior have no tests
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` and the new offset-clamping logic in `BasePaginator.get_result` change pagination semantics (negative offsets, boundary trimming) but no tests are added. Given the class is dead-on-arrival for datetime keys and crashes on negative offsets, basic unit tests for zero/negative/large offsets and for the audit-log endpoint with `optimized_pagination=true` are needed before merging.

title: Comment claims negative offsets are supported although nothing validates or supports them
body: The added comment in `Cursor.__init__` states that negative offsets are allowed as a "performance optimization ... enables efficient reverse pagination". No validation or support was added here, and every consumer (Django queryset slicing, `OffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`) either rejects negative offsets or crashes on them. The comment will mislead future readers into believing negative offsets are a supported contract.

title: `organization_context.member` can be None, causing a 500 on every audit-log request
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated unconditionally for every GET. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is `None` whenever the requester is not an organization member (e.g. org auth token / integration token auth, or a staff/superuser request that resolves no membership). Because `request.user.is_superuser` is `False` for non-user auth (and `AnonymousUser`), the second operand is evaluated and raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'`, turning a previously working endpoint into a 500 for those auth paths. The flag should only be computed inside the `optimized_pagination` branch and must null-check `member`.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator is numeric-keyed but is used with the `datetime` column
body: The endpoint passes `order_by="-datetime"` to `OptimizedCursorPaginator`, whose `get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(getattr(item, self.key)))` and whose `value_from_cursor` returns the raw cursor integer. `AuditLogEntry.datetime` is a `datetime`, so `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`, and a cursor value would be compared against a timestamp column as a bare integer in the generated `WHERE` clause. Any request with `?optimized_pagination=true` from an authorized user will therefore fail with a 500 instead of returning a page. Date-keyed querysets require `DateTimePaginator`-style key handling (the `multiplier` conversion).

title: Negative slice start on a Django QuerySet raises ValueError, not "handled automatically"
body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is on and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django explicitly rejects this: `QuerySet.__getitem__` raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`. Since `Cursor.from_string` happily parses a negative offset from the user-supplied `cursor` query parameter, a request like `?optimized_pagination=true&cursor=0:-5:0` produces an unhandled exception / 500 rather than a 400. The inline comment claiming "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is factually wrong. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError` like `OffsetPaginator` does.

title: BasePaginator now silently clamps negative cursor offsets, producing inconsistent cursors
body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes the behavior of every paginator derived from `BasePaginator` (issues, audit logs, many list endpoints). Previously a negative offset in a client-supplied cursor surfaced as an error from the ORM; now the query silently starts at row 0 while `build_cursor` is still handed the original negative `cursor.offset`. `_build_next_values` then computes `next_offset = offset + limit` from the negative value and `_build_prev_values` treats the negative offset as "has_prev", so the returned next/prev cursors point at positions that do not correspond to the rows actually returned, causing skipped or duplicated rows on subsequent pages. Negative offsets should be rejected explicitly rather than clamped.

title: Prev-page trimming uses raw offset instead of the slice start
body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, the extra-row trim condition `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra:` uses the raw `cursor.offset`, while the rows were fetched with `start_offset` (which may differ, e.g. clamped to 0 or negative). When `offset` is negative the comparison can never be true (or is true for the wrong row count), so the extra look-behind row fetched for `is_prev` cursors is not dropped and leaks into the returned page, duplicating a row the client already saw. The condition should compare against `start_offset + limit + extra`.

title: Redirect-chain limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000
body: The loop bound was changed from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000` and the explanatory comment ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. This is an unannounced 10x reduction in the maximum redirect-chain depth: traces whose parent/child redirect chains exceed 1000 hops will stop resolving to the correct `set_key`, so their spans get split across multiple segments and are emitted as separate (incorrect) segments. If the reduction is intentional it should be stated in the PR and the caveat comment kept; otherwise the original bound should be restored.

title: Eviction silently drops spans with a hardcoded limit and no metric/log
body: `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000) end` trims segments to a hardcoded 1000 spans. Two problems: (1) the limit is hardcoded in Lua while `SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans` (default 1001) is the configured value and is no longer used anywhere, so the setting has no effect and the two numbers disagree; (2) the previous code path in `_load_segment_data` that dropped oversized segments emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and `logger.error`, and that observability was removed in this PR. Now span data is discarded with no metric, log, or configuration, making truncated segments undetectable in production.

title: zunionstore uses the default SUM aggregate, corrupting span timestamps/scores
body: `zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` (and the same call for `parent_key` on line 53) uses Redis' default `AGGREGATE SUM`. The scores are `end_timestamp_precise` values used to order spans for eviction. If the same span payload exists in both source sets (e.g. a redelivered/duplicated span that landed under a different key before the redirect was established), its score becomes the sum of two ~1.7e9 timestamps, making it the newest member forever and causing `zpopmin` to evict legitimate newer spans instead. The merges should specify `AGGREGATE MIN` (or MAX) to preserve timestamp semantics.

title: `max_segment_spans` is now dead configuration
body: The span-count guard in `_load_segment_data` was removed, so the `max_segment_spans` constructor parameter (default 1001) is no longer read anywhere; the effective limit is the literal `1000` inside `add-buffer.lua`. Callers that set this parameter will silently get no behavior change. Either wire the value through to the Lua script as an ARGV, or remove the parameter.

title: Module docstring still describes Redis sets after the switch to sorted sets
body: The storage layout changed from Redis sets (`sadd`/`sscan`/`sunionstore`) to sorted sets (`zadd`/`zscan`/`zunionstore`) scored by `end_timestamp_precise`, and spans are now evicted at insert time when a segment exceeds the limit. The docstring (step 3 "Add the ingested span's payload to the set under `set_key`" and the glossary entry "span-buf:s:* -- the actual set keys") still describes plain sets and says nothing about scoring or eviction, so readers will have the wrong mental model of the key types and of the fact that spans can be dropped.

title: No test for the new insert-time eviction behavior
body: The headline change of this PR is eviction during insert (`zpopmin` once a segment exceeds 1000 spans) plus the set→sorted-set migration, but no test exercises a segment larger than the limit. Existing tests only cover 4-5 span segments, so neither the trimming threshold, the choice of which spans are discarded (lowest `end_timestamp_precise`), nor the removal of the old `max_segment_spans` guard in `_load_segment_data` is verified. A regression in the Lua arithmetic (e.g. off-by-one in `span_count - 1000`, or the `span_count == 0` fallback) would go unnoticed.

title: New OptimizedCursorPaginator has no tests
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` is a new public paginator with non-trivial branching (negative-offset path, prev-cursor extra-row trimming, `enable_advanced_features` flag) and it is already wired into a production endpoint, yet no tests are added for it or for the audit-log endpoint's new `optimized_pagination` code path. The datetime/negative-slice failures in this class would have been caught by a single test.

title: Misleading comment claims a behavior change that was not made
body: The added comment says "Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios" above `self.offset = int(offset)`, but no code changed here — `Cursor` always accepted negative offsets, and callers (e.g. `OffsetPaginator`) are the ones that validate them. The comment implies `Cursor` now intentionally supports negative offsets as a feature, which will mislead future readers into assuming downstream paginators handle them safely (they do not; Django rejects negative slice starts).

title: Negative slice start raises ValueError in Django, not a handled pagination error
body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code slices the queryset with a negative start (`queryset[start_offset:stop]`). The inline comment claims "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically", which is false: Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly rejects negative indices with `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` Every other paginator in this file guards this with `raise BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`. The result is an unhandled exception and a 500 response that is trivially triggered by any client passing a cursor such as `-5:0:0`, i.e. a cheap error/DoS vector on the audit log endpoint.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot paginate datetime columns, but is used with order_by="-datetime"
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `math.floor(value)/math.ceil(value)` on the raw attribute and `value_from_cursor` returns the raw cursor value, i.e. it only works for numeric keys (it is a copy of `Paginator`, not `DateTimePaginator`). The audit-log endpoint instantiates it with `order_by="-datetime"` on `AuditLogEntry.datetime` (a DateTimeField). `build_cursor` calls `key(results[0])`, so `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError`, and on a follow-up request `build_queryset` injects an integer into `WHERE "datetime" <= %s`, comparing an int against a timestamp column. Any request to the new code path fails with a 500 or a database error.

title: BasePaginator silently clamps negative offsets, producing inconsistent cursors
body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes `BasePaginator.get_result` so that a negative forward offset is silently clamped to 0 instead of surfacing an error. Two problems: (1) an invalid/garbage cursor now returns page-1 data as if it were valid, masking client bugs; (2) the raw negative `offset` is still passed on to `build_cursor` and still used in the `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` check further down, so the drop-extra-row logic and the generated next/prev cursor offsets no longer correspond to the rows actually fetched. For `is_prev` cursors the negative offset is still handed to Django and will raise. If clamping is desired it should be applied consistently (and the invalid case rejected with `BadPaginationError`).

title: organization_context.member may be None, causing a 500 on the audit log endpoint
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences `organization_context.member` unconditionally whenever `is_superuser` is false. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is `None` for callers that are not org members — notably org auth tokens / integration tokens and staff or superuser-flagged users accessing an org they do not belong to — so the expression raises `AttributeError` and turns a previously working GET into a 500. This runs for every request, not just when `optimized_pagination=true` is passed.

title: "Advanced pagination" gate is not an admin check
body: The comment says the feature is enabled for "authorized administrators", but the gate is `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`. `request.user.is_superuser` is the raw DB flag and bypasses Sentry's required active-superuser/elevated-session check (`is_active_superuser(request)`), and `has_global_access` is true for ordinary members in open-membership organizations. So the out-of-bounds pagination path (negative offsets, no `BadPaginationError` guard) is reachable by regular org members and by superuser-flagged sessions that have not elevated. Feature flags that relax pagination bounds should be gated on an explicit permission check, not on these two signals.

title: No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the new endpoint query parameter
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (including the negative-offset branch) and the new `optimized_pagination=true` branch in `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` are added with no test coverage in this PR. Both are trivially broken (negative slice raises in Django, `get_item_key` cannot handle datetimes) which a single endpoint test with `?optimized_pagination=true` would have caught.

title: Set keys switched to sorted sets without renaming, breaking rolling deploys with WRONGTYPE
body: `span-buf:s:{...}` keys change type from Redis SET to ZSET (`p.zadd` here, `zcard`/`zunionstore`/`zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua, `p.zscan` in `_load_segment_data`) while keeping the exact same key names. During a rolling deploy (and for up to `redis_ttl` = 1h after it) old SET keys written by the previous version still exist; `zadd`/`zcard` against them return `WRONGTYPE`, which aborts the Lua script and raises out of `p.execute()`, crash-looping the consumer. Old pods still running will likewise get `WRONGTYPE` from `sadd`/`sscan` on the new ZSET keys. The key prefix needs a version bump (e.g. `span-buf:z:`) so the two formats cannot collide.

title: zunionstore uses default SUM aggregation, corrupting timestamp scores
body: `zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` (and the same call for `parent_key`) uses Redis' default `AGGREGATE SUM`. Any span payload present in both source zsets — which happens on duplicate deliveries / reprocessing of the same span — gets its score set to the sum of the two `end_timestamp_precise` values, roughly doubling it. Since the score is used as the eviction ordering key for `zpopmin`, such a span becomes effectively un-evictable while legitimate newer spans are dropped instead. Pass `AGGREGATE MIN` (or MAX) explicitly to keep scores meaningful.

title: Eviction limit hard-coded at 1000 while max_segment_spans config is now dead
body: The new eviction (`if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)`) hard-codes the segment span limit in Lua, while `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` which, after the removal of the count check in `_load_segment_data`, is no longer referenced anywhere. Operators changing `max_segment_spans` now silently get no effect, and the two values disagree (1000 vs 1001). The limit should be passed to the script as an ARGV, or the unused parameter removed.

title: Span eviction is now silent: no metric or log when spans are dropped
body: The removed block in `_load_segment_data` emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and logged when a segment exceeded the span count limit. The replacement — `zpopmin` inside add-buffer.lua — drops spans with no counter and no log, so oversized-segment truncation becomes invisible in production and silent data loss cannot be detected or quantified. The script should return the number of evicted members so the consumer can emit a metric.

title: Redirect-chain limit silently lowered from 10000 to 1000
body: The loop bound was changed from `0, 10000` to `0, 1000` and the explanatory comment ("segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. This is an unannounced behaviour change: segment trees with redirect chains deeper than 1000 will no longer be joined into a single segment, producing split segments for deep traces. If the reduction is intentional it should be documented and the retained comment updated; the PR description mentions nothing about it.

title: Module docstring/glossary still describes plain Redis sets
body: The module docstring ("Add the ingested span's payload to the set under `set_key`", and the glossary entry "span-buf:s:* -- the actual set keys") is now wrong: these keys are sorted sets scored by `end_timestamp_precise`, and the scoring is what drives the new eviction behaviour. Readers relying on the docstring will not know spans are evicted lowest-timestamp-first once a segment exceeds 1000 spans.

title: Unguarded access to end_timestamp_precise can crash the consumer
body: `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` uses direct indexing (unlike the neighbouring `val.get(...)` calls), so any message on the ingest-spans topic missing this field raises `KeyError` inside `process_batch` and kills the consumer rather than dropping/DLQ-ing the bad message. Given this is a newly required field, in-flight messages produced by older Relay versions would take the consumer down.

title: Negative queryset slicing raises in Django, so the "advanced" path always 500s
body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code slices the queryset with a negative start (`queryset[start_offset:stop]`). Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly rejects negative indices/slice bounds (`ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.`), so the comment "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false. Any request with a negative cursor offset on this code path results in an unhandled 500 rather than a 400/BadPaginationError. Negative cursor offsets are reachable because `Cursor.from_string` parses `int(bits[1])` without a sign check.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator uses integer key semantics on a datetime column
body: The audit log endpoint orders by `-datetime` (a `DateTimeField`) but the optimized branch passes `paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator`, whose `get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(getattr(item, self.key)))` and whose `value_from_cursor` returns the raw cursor value. `math.floor()` on a `datetime` raises `TypeError`, and feeding a raw integer cursor value into `build_queryset`'s `datetime >= %s` extra-where produces a SQL type error. The original code used `DateTimePaginator` precisely because the key needs the millisecond-multiplier conversion. As written, `?optimized_pagination=true` returns a 500 for any request that reaches this branch; there is no test covering it.

title: Superuser check bypasses active-superuser verification and can crash on non-member actors
body: `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is used to unlock the alternate pagination path. Two problems: (1) Sentry gates privileged behaviour on `is_active_superuser(request)` (which honours superuser session elevation / staff requirements), so reading `request.user.is_superuser` directly grants the privileged path to any account with the flag regardless of elevation state; (2) `organization_context.member` is `None` for requestors that are not org members (e.g. API-token/integration auth where `request.user` is anonymous), so evaluating `.has_global_access` raises `AttributeError` and returns a 500 on an otherwise valid request.

title: BasePaginator silently clamps negative offsets and then uses the unclamped value
body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` silently turns an invalid (negative) forward cursor offset into page 0 instead of failing with `BadPaginationError` as every other paginator in this module does, hiding malformed/tampered cursors from callers. Worse, the clamped value is only used for the slice: further down, the prev-page trim still compares `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` using the raw (possibly negative) `offset`, so the two values can disagree and the extra row is trimmed incorrectly. For `is_prev` cursors the negative offset is still passed straight into the slice and will raise in Django, so the clamp doesn't even fix the crash it appears to target.

title: Span cap hardcoded to 1000 in Lua, ignoring SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans
body: The new eviction logic hardcodes `1000` both as the threshold and as the retained size, while `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts `max_segment_spans` (default 1001) which is now referenced nowhere after the removal of the count check in `_load_segment_data`. The configuration knob is therefore dead and silently ineffective, and changing the limit requires editing the Lua script. The limit should be passed to the script as an ARGV value derived from `max_segment_spans`, and/or the unused constructor parameter removed.

title: zunionstore defaults to AGGREGATE SUM, corrupting end-timestamp scores on merge
body: `zunionstore` is called without `AGGREGATE`, so Redis sums the scores of members present in both source zsets. Since the score is `end_timestamp_precise` and used for eviction ordering (`zpopmin`), any span payload that exists in both the span's own set and the target set (e.g. a re-delivered/duplicated span, which the comments elsewhere acknowledge can happen when partitioning assumptions break) gets a score of roughly twice the timestamp. That span then sorts as the newest and is retained while genuinely newer spans are evicted. Use `AGGREGATE MIN` (or MAX) to keep scores meaningful.

title: Span eviction is now silent: metric and error log for oversized segments were removed
body: The previous code emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and logged an error when a segment exceeded the span-count limit. That branch is deleted and the new behaviour (dropping the oldest spans via `zpopmin` inside add-buffer.lua) emits no metric or log at all. Segments silently lose spans in production with no way to detect or quantify the data loss. Add a counter/metric for evicted spans (e.g. return the evicted count from the Lua script and record it).

title: Redirect-chain limit lowered 10x without explanation
body: The redirect-resolution loop bound was changed from `0, 10000` to `0, 1000` and the comment documenting the consequence ("segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. This is an unrelated, undocumented behaviour change: segment trees deeper than 1000 redirects will now be split into multiple segments instead of being joined. Either restore the previous bound or keep the comment and justify the new value.

title: No test for the new in-insert eviction path
body: The headline change of this PR is eviction during insert (set -> sorted set, `zpopmin` when a segment exceeds 1000 spans), but no test exercises a segment larger than the cap, verifies which spans are kept (newest by `end_timestamp_precise`), or verifies that scores survive the `zunionstore` merge path. All existing tests use 1-5 spans and therefore never reach the eviction branch, so a regression in the eviction arithmetic (`span_count - 1000`) or score handling would go unnoticed.

title: New public paginator class has no tests and duplicates BasePaginator.get_result
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` is added with no unit tests in `tests/sentry/api/test_paginator.py` even though it is wired into a production endpoint. Its `get_result` is a near-verbatim copy of `BasePaginator.get_result` with one extra branch, so any future fix to the base implementation (cursor trimming, hit counting) will silently not apply here. Prefer overriding only the offset computation, and add tests covering the forward, prev and negative-offset cases.

title: Module docstring still describes Redis sets and omits the new span cap
body: The module docstring (steps 3 and the glossary line "span-buf:s:* -- the actual set keys") still says spans are added to a Redis set, but the implementation now uses sorted sets keyed by `end_timestamp_precise`, and segments are capped at 1000 spans with the oldest evicted during insert. Someone reading this docstring will have the wrong model of both the data structure and the data-loss behaviour.

title: Unguarded access to end_timestamp_precise can crash the consumer
body: `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` is read with a hard subscript while every other field that may be absent uses `.get()`. If any message on `ingest-spans` lacks the field (older producer, replayed backlog, malformed payload) this raises `KeyError` inside `process_batch`, which fails the whole batch and puts the consumer into a crash loop rather than dropping or defaulting the single message. Consider defaulting (e.g. to the message timestamp) or explicitly rejecting the individual span.

title: Upsampling eligibility uses outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`
body: `_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` as its first argument, but the eligibility check passes the closure variable `dataset` to `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(...)`. In the dashboard-widget split path (`get_event_stats_factory`), `_get_event_stats` is deliberately invoked with a different dataset (e.g. `discover` for the errors-only/transactions-only probe queries) while the outer `dataset` is still the originally requested one (e.g. `metrics_enhanced_performance`). As a result the upsampling decision is computed for a dataset that is not the one being queried: upsampling is silently skipped for the split errors query (under-reported counts for allowlisted projects) and could conversely be applied to a dataset whose query builder has no `upsampled_count` function. The check should use `scoped_dataset`.

title: `upsampled_count()` only registered for the discover dataset, but applied to the errors dataset
body: `upsampled_count` is added only to `DiscoverDatasetConfig.function_converter`, yet `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` in `src/sentry/api/helpers/error_upsampling.py` returns `True` unconditionally when `dataset is sentry.snuba.errors`. The errors dataset is resolved through its own `ErrorsDatasetConfig` function registry, which does not contain `upsampled_count`, so any `yAxis=count()` request with `dataset=errors` for allowlisted projects will be rewritten to `upsampled_count() as count` and then fail with an "is not a valid function" search error instead of returning data. There is also no test exercising `dataset=errors`, so this path is completely uncovered.

title: `_is_error_focused_query` substring match also matches negated error queries
body: `_is_error_focused_query` does `"event.type:error" in query`. This matches `!event.type:error` (a query that explicitly excludes errors, i.e. transactions) as well as occurrences inside quoted free-text/message filters. For such queries the discover `count()` is rewritten to `upsampled_count()` (`sum(sample_weight)`), producing wrong (or null/zero) numbers for non-error rows where `sample_weight` is absent. The check needs to parse the query (or at least exclude negations) rather than do a raw substring test.

title: Error-focus detection reads `request.GET['query']` instead of the query actually executed
body: `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` / `_is_error_focused_query` inspect the raw `request.GET["query"]`, but `_get_event_stats` is frequently called with a *modified* query string: the dashboard widget split path builds `f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction"` (errors-only) and `f"({query}) AND event.type:transaction"` (transactions-only). Because the helper never sees these, the errors-only probe query is not recognized as error-focused (upsampling skipped, counts under-reported) while the transactions-only query inherits the decision made from the original request. The query string that is actually executed should be passed into the helper.

title: 60s eligibility cache has no working invalidation; option changes are ignored and the cache adds little value
body: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches the allowlist decision for 60 seconds keyed by org + project ids. `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined to clear it but is never called from anywhere in the codebase, and it requires knowing the exact project-id set used in the cache key, so it cannot realistically invalidate all affected entries when `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` changes. Consequence: adding or (more importantly) removing a project from the allowlist — e.g. to stop emitting inflated counts during an incident — takes effect only after up to 60s, with no way to force it. Note also that `options.get` is already backed by the options cache, so the extra caching layer buys little while introducing this staleness and a stale-data risk. The surrounding docstring claiming "we always have the latest configuration state" contradicts the caching behaviour.

title: Cache key built from Python `hash()` of project ids can collide
body: The cache key is `f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))}"`. Using an opaque 64-bit hash instead of the sorted ids themselves means two different project sets in the same organization can map to the same key, in which case one set inherits the other's eligibility verdict and the returned counts are silently wrong (either inflated or not upsampled). Since this cache is shared across processes, the wrong value is served broadly. Serialize the sorted ids (or a stable digest with low collision risk) into the key instead.

title: `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` can yield NULL and is exposed as a public function
body: Two problems with the new `upsampled_count` SnQL function: (1) `sample_weight` is not guaranteed to be populated for all error rows in an allowlisted project (events ingested before the feature was enabled, or SDKs not sending `contexts.error_sampling`); for a nullable column ClickHouse `sum` over all-NULL rows returns NULL, and `toInt64` of that stays NULL, so the timeseries can return `null` counts where consumers (zerofill, frontend charts, alert comparisons) expect integers. The docstring's assumption that "sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects" is not enforced anywhere — consider `ifNull(...)`/`sumIf` semantics. (2) Unlike the neighbouring internal helpers, it is not marked `private=True`, so any user can request `yAxis=upsampled_count()` on discover for non-allowlisted projects and get meaningless zero/null results, a new public API surface that was presumably not intended.

title: Test factory fabricates `sample_rate` and silently swallows all errors
body: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` injects `normalized_data["sample_rate"]` from `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` in `store_event`, bypassing the real ingest path (relay/event manager) that is responsible for deriving the sampling weight in production. The new endpoint tests therefore validate upsampled counts against a value the test harness itself invents, so a regression in the real normalization/ingest logic would not be caught. Additionally both `try/except Exception: pass` blocks hide genuine problems (e.g. a non-numeric `client_sample_rate`), silently producing events without a sample rate and turning a meaningful assertion failure into a confusing count mismatch.

title: Stray git submodule entry `sentry-repo` committed
body: The PR adds a gitlink (`Subproject commit a5d2909...`) at path `sentry-repo` with no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry. This is clearly an accidental artifact of local tooling: it pollutes the repository tree, makes `git submodule status/update` and some clone/CI tooling report errors for an unregistered submodule, and pins a commit of the repository inside itself. It should be removed from the PR.

title: Misleading comments on upsampled count assertions
body: `assert data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10  # First bucket has 1 event` (and the following line) claim the bucket contains 1 event while asserting a count of 10. The value 10 is the upsampled count (1 event at a 0.1 client sample rate); the comment makes the assertion look wrong and will mislead the next person debugging a failure here. State that the raw event count is 1 and the expected upsampled count is 10.

title: `setUp` overwrites `self.user` after `login_as`, and no coverage for errors dataset / caching
body: In the new `OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest.setUp`, `self.user` is reassigned to a freshly created user after `self.login_as(user=self.user)`, so `self.user` no longer refers to the authenticated user; any later use of `self.user` for auth assertions in this class would be wrong (the workaround `self.authed_user` hints at the confusion). The class also lacks tests for the two riskiest new behaviours: requests with `dataset=errors` (where `upsampled_count()` is applied unconditionally) and the newly added 60-second eligibility cache (stale allowlist results), both of which are currently unverified.

title: Substring match treats negated `!event.type:error` queries as error-focused
body: `_is_error_focused_query` does a raw substring test `"event.type:error" in query`. A query such as `!event.type:error` (exclude errors) or `event.type:error_foo` also contains that substring, so the function returns True. For the `discover` dataset this causes `count()` to be rewritten to `upsampled_count()` (i.e. `sum(sample_weight)`) for a query that explicitly excludes error events, producing wrong numbers for transaction/other rows (or a Snuba error because `sample_weight` is not populated for non-error rows). The check needs to parse the search query (or at least exclude negations) rather than a naive substring test.

title: Upsampling eligibility computed from outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`
body: `_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` as its first argument but passes the closure-level `dataset` to `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`. In the dashboard-widget split path (`get_event_stats_factory`) `_get_event_stats` is deliberately invoked with a different dataset (`discover`, `split_dataset`, etc.) while the outer `dataset` is still the metrics/transactions dataset. As a result the dataset-based gate (`_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`) is evaluated against the wrong dataset: upsampling can be skipped for error queries actually run against `discover`, or applied to a run that was switched to a transaction-like dataset. The check must use `scoped_dataset`.

title: Caching a global option behind a per-org/per-project key yields stale, inconsistent results
body: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches the result of `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` for 60s under a key built from `organization.id` plus a hash of the project id set. The underlying data is the *global* option `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`, which Sentry's options layer already caches in-process; writing/reading a remote cache entry per org+project-set combination adds a cache round trip per query (and the split-dataset path calls this up to 4 times per request) while providing no real speedup. Worse, when the allowlist is changed, queries keep returning the previous decision for up to 60 seconds, so the same chart can flip between upsampled (x10) and raw counts between adjacent requests - a visible data-correctness problem for a counting API. Either drop the cache or key it on the option value/version.

title: `hash()` of project ids in the cache key can collide and return another project set's decision
body: The cache key uses `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. `hash` is a 64-bit (32-bit on some builds) value with no collision guarantees, so two different project-id sets inside the same organization can map to the same key.
