body: `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is emitted with tag key `shards` while `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` use `shard` for the same value, so dashboards/queries cannot filter uniformly. Additionally, `shard_tag` is a comma-joined list of all shards owned by the process (e.g. `"0,4,8,12"`); since the shard→process grouping changes with partition assignment, this produces a combinatorial set of tag values on `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` (a per-segment metric), which inflates metric cardinality and breaks continuity with the previously untagged series.

title: Dead method `_create_process_for_shard`
body: `_create_process_for_shard(shard)` is not called from anywhere after the refactor (restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` in `_ensure_processes_alive`). It should be removed; leaving it invites a future caller to restart a process by shard id, which would silently restart the whole shard group and overwrite `self.processes`/`self.buffers` entries.

title: Zero assigned shards results in no flusher process at all
body: `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` followed by `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))` yields `num_processes == 0` when `buffer.assigned_shards` is empty (also when `max_processes` is explicitly passed as 0, which the CLI `--flusher-processes 0` allows). In that case `process_to_shards_map` is empty, no process is started, and `submit()` silently never flushes anything while still accepting messages. Guard with `max(1, ...)` / validate the CLI option so a misconfiguration fails loudly instead of running a consumer that writes to Redis but never produces segments.

title: New multi-process test only checks internal bookkeeping, not that all shards are flushed
body: `test_flusher_processes_limit` asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2` and that the total count of mapped shards is 4, but never submits spans and never asserts that segments from shards owned by *both* processes are produced. The count assertion also passes for an incorrect mapping (e.g. shard 0 duplicated and shard 3 missing would still total 4) — comparing the union of mapped shards to the assigned shard set would catch that. As written, the multiprocessed flusher path (>1 process actually flushing distinct shards) is untested.

title: kill() is never called on unhealthy spawn processes (isinstance check is always False)
body: `_ensure_processes_alive` only kills the old worker if `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. The processes here are created via `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which produces `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` objects. `SpawnProcess` derives from `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, not from `multiprocessing.context.Process` (which is what the module-level `multiprocessing.Process` alias resolves to), so the isinstance check is always False and `kill()` is never invoked. The previous code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. Consequence: when a flusher is detected as hung (`cause == "hang"`) the old process keeps running while a replacement is started for the same shards, so two processes concurrently flush the same Redis shards and produce duplicate/fragmented segments to `buffered-segments`, and leaked processes accumulate on every restart. Use `process.kill()` guarded by `hasattr`/`BaseProcess` instead.

title: join() aborts the shutdown loop, leaving the remaining processes unterminated
body: In `join()`, when the deadline has passed the loop `break`s out before reaching the `process.terminate()` call for the remaining entries of `self.processes`. With more than one flusher process, a timed-out join therefore terminates only the processes iterated before the deadline expired; the rest are left running and continue flushing segments while the consumer is shutting down/rebalancing. (Additionally, `remaining_time` is computed but never used, and the `terminate()` call itself is dead for spawn processes because of the same `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` problem.) Terminate every process unconditionally after the wait loop.

title: Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
body: `test_basic` monkeypatches `time.sleep` to a no-op at line 15, so the newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` ("Give flusher threads time to process after drift change") does nothing. The test still relies on the flusher thread having produced the message before `step.join()` returns, so the intended synchronization is absent and the test remains timing-dependent/flaky. Use a real sleep (e.g. `from time import sleep as real_sleep` captured before patching, as `test_flusher.py` does) or poll until `messages` is non-empty.

title: New multi-process flusher test only asserts bookkeeping, never exercises flushing across shards
body: `test_flusher_processes_limit` creates 4 partitions with `flusher_processes=2` but never submits a message and never asserts that segments from all 4 shards are produced. It only checks `len(flusher.processes)`, `max_processes`, `num_processes` and the total shard count. The behaviour this PR actually changes — several shards being flushed by one worker, and all shards being covered by the shard->process mapping — is untested. Consider submitting spans for each partition and asserting that one produced message per shard arrives, and that `process_to_shards_map` is a partition of `assigned_shards` (no duplicates/omissions).

title: Dead method `_create_process_for_shard` left behind
body: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is never called anywhere (restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`). Dead code that duplicates restart logic is a maintenance hazard — a future caller would restart a whole process group from a single shard id. Remove it.

title: Class docstring claims one process per shard and documents a non-existent param
body: The docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but the number of processes is `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))`, and the consumer CLI defaults `--flusher-processes` to 1, so the normal configuration is a single process handling all shards. The docstring also still documents `:param topic:` which is not an argument, and does not document the new `max_processes` argument. This misleads operators about the default parallelism.

title: Inconsistent metric tag key and high-cardinality tag value for shard tags
body: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` are tagged with `shard=<comma-joined shard list>` while `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` uses the key `shards` for the same value. Dashboards/alerts filtering on `shard` will silently miss `wait_produce`, and a comma-joined value such as `"0,4,8"` is a different tag value for every shard-to-process assignment, which breaks aggregation by shard and inflates metric cardinality whenever partition assignment changes. Pick one key and emit a stable, low-cardinality value (e.g. the process index) or emit per-shard series.

title: A new SpansBuffer (and its Redis clients) is created in the parent on every restart without releasing the old one
body: `_create_process_for_shards` constructs a fresh `SpansBuffer(shards)` and stores it in `self.buffers[process_index]`, overwriting the previous instance. The parent process keeps using these buffers for `record_stored_segments()` and `get_memory_info()`, so each unhealthy-process restart (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per process) leaves the previous buffer's Redis connections unclosed in the parent. Reuse the existing buffer for the process index, or close the old one before replacing it.

title: Queue pool is owned by the factory but shut down by the strategy, breaking the consumer after the first rebalance
body: `FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and shared via `self.queue_pool`, but `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` (queue_consumer.py lines 335-342), which sets `worker.shutdown = True` and calls `queue.shutdown()` on every queue. Arroyo closes the current strategy on every partition revocation and then calls `create_with_partitions()` again on assignment. The second strategy therefore gets a pool whose worker threads have exited and whose queues are shut down, so every `work_queue.put(...)` raises `queue.ShutDown`. That exception is swallowed by the `except Exception` block in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, which then marks the offset as added *and* completed - so messages are silently dropped and their offsets committed. After the first rebalance the consumer stops doing any work while continuing to advance offsets, i.e. permanent data loss. The pool must be created per strategy (or not shut down in `close()`).

title: Queues are unbounded and submit never applies backpressure
body: `queue.Queue()` is created without `maxsize` and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`. The class docstring claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing ever blocks or rejects: if the result processor is slower than the incoming message rate, arroyo will keep reading from Kafka and the strategy will buffer the entire backlog (decoded results plus the full `Message`/`KafkaPayload` kept on `WorkItem.message`) in memory until the process OOMs. Give the queues a bounded size and raise `MessageRejected` (or block) when full, and fix the docstring.

title: close()/join() do not drain queues or perform a final commit
body: `join(timeout)` ignores its timeout and just calls `close()`; `close()` sets `shutdown_event`, joins the commit thread and then shuts down the pool. Because `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before shutting down the queues, each worker exits after finishing at most one more item, so all still-queued work items are discarded. Additionally no commit is attempted after the workers stop, so offsets for items that completed since the last 1-second commit tick are never committed. Arroyo's contract for `join(timeout)` is to flush outstanding work and commit before returning; as written every shutdown/rebalance drops in-flight work and re-reads a window of messages (duplicate processing) on restart.

title: Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread
body: `_commit_loop` runs in its own daemon thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which is arroyo's `Commit` callback. That callback mutates the StreamProcessor's staged-offset state and the underlying consumer, which the main poll thread is using concurrently; arroyo's consumer/commit path is not documented as thread-safe. This can corrupt the staged offset bookkeeping or raise (e.g. committing offsets for a partition that was just revoked), and the only handling is a broad `except Exception: logger.exception(...)` that will then spin once per second. Offsets should be handed back to the main thread (e.g. via a thread-safe queue drained in `poll()`), which is also where arroyo expects commits to happen.

title: OffsetTracker state is never reset on partition reassignment
body: `OffsetTracker` is owned by the long-lived `FixedQueuePool` and keeps `last_committed`, `all_offsets`, `outstanding` and `partition_locks` for every partition it has ever seen. On rebalance a new strategy is created but the tracker still holds the old `last_committed` values; if a partition is reassigned and the consumer must restart from an earlier offset (or the partition is assigned to another consumer and later returned), `get_committable_offsets()` will refuse to return anything `<= last_committed`, permanently stalling commits for that partition. Entries for revoked partitions are also never dropped, so the dicts grow for the lifetime of the process.

title: Any offset that is never submitted permanently stalls commits for the partition
body: `get_committable_offsets()` walks `range(start, max_offset + 1)` and breaks as soon as an offset is not present in `all_offsets`. Offsets can be missing for reasons other than slow processing: arroyo can hand the strategy messages whose `value` is not a `BrokerValue` (the `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` fails and the `except` branch then also skips recording because of the same `isinstance` check), transaction/control markers consume offsets on some topics, and anything that throws before `add_offset` leaves a hole. Once a hole exists the partition can never advance: no offsets are ever committed again, `all_offsets` grows without bound, and on restart the whole backlog is reprocessed. Track a per-partition "next expected" watermark from the messages actually received rather than requiring offset contiguity.

title: Failed work items are marked complete, so failures are committed and lost
body: `complete_offset()` is called in the `finally` block of the worker, so a work item whose `result_processor` raised is treated exactly like a successfully processed one: its offset becomes committable and is committed, with only a log line. There is no retry, no DLQ and no metric, so a transient failure (e.g. a DB hiccup) silently drops the check result. If this at-most-once behaviour is intended it should at least emit a failure metric; otherwise the offset should not be completed on error.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the opposite of the implemented behaviour and is timing-dependent
body: The test is documented as "errors in processing don't block offset commits" but asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, i.e. that nothing was committed. The implementation marks the offset complete in the worker's `finally` block even when processing raised, so offsets 100 and 101 become committable and the 1-second commit loop will commit them. The assertion only passes because the test breaks out of its wait loop ~0.2-0.3s after submitting, before the commit thread's first tick - it will flake as soon as timing shifts, and it does not verify the behaviour its docstring describes.

title: Kafka integration test relies on private arroyo APIs, wall-clock sleeps and a second consumer in the same group
body: `ProcessResultThreadQueueParallelKafkaTest` drives the consumer with `processor._run_once()` / `processor._shutdown()` (private arroyo APIs that can change without notice), busy-loops for a fixed 5 wall-clock seconds and then asserts an exact committed offset of 5 - this depends on the background commit thread and ONCE_PER_SECOND policy firing within that window, so it will flake on a loaded CI machine. It also creates a second `confluent_kafka.Consumer` with the same `group.id` to read committed offsets, which joins the group and can trigger a rebalance/return stale offsets, and `verify_consumer.committed(partitions)` is called without a timeout so it can block indefinitely.

title: Per-message gauge emitted from every worker with identical tags
body: Every processed item emits `remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth` as a gauge tagged only with `identifier`. All N workers report their own queue's depth under the same metric name and tag set, so the values overwrite each other and the resulting series is meaningless, while the emission rate equals the message rate. Either tag by `worker_id`/queue index or report queue depth periodically from `poll()` instead.

title: close()/join() destroys the shared queue pool, breaking the consumer after any rebalance
body: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` (and `join()`, which just calls `close()`) calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which permanently stops every worker thread and calls `queue.shutdown()` on every queue. The `FixedQueuePool` is however owned by the factory (`ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` creates it once, see result_consumer.py:133) and is reused for every `create_with_partitions()` call. Arroyo closes/joins the strategy on every partition revocation/rebalance and then builds a new strategy from the same factory, so after the first rebalance the new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` is wired to a dead pool: `work_queue.put()` raises `queue.ShutDown`, which is swallowed by the broad `except Exception` in `submit()` (line 317-325), where the offset is then marked complete. The result is that every message after the first rebalance is silently dropped *and* its offset committed — permanent data loss plus a consumer that appears healthy while doing no work. The pool must be created/torn down per strategy instance (or close() must not shut it down).

title: Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread
body: `_commit_loop` runs in a daemon thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which is arroyo's `Commit` callback (it stages offsets on the `KafkaConsumer` and may commit them). Arroyo's `StreamProcessor`/`KafkaConsumer` offset staging is not thread-safe and expects the commit callback to be called from the thread driving `poll()`/`submit()`. Concurrent staging from this thread while the main loop polls/commits can corrupt or lose staged offsets, and if a partition has just been revoked the staged partition is no longer assigned, raising inside the loop (swallowed by `except Exception`, so commits silently stop). Offsets should be collected in the worker threads and actually committed from `poll()`/`submit()` on the main thread.

title: Queues are unbounded: no backpressure, unbounded memory growth
body: Each work queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with the default `maxsize=0`, i.e. unbounded, and `submit()` never raises `arroyo.processing.strategies.MessageRejected`. That means the strategy accepts messages as fast as Kafka delivers them regardless of how far the workers are behind, so a slow result processor leads to unbounded in-memory growth (each `WorkItem` also retains the full Kafka `Message`) and eventually OOM, plus an ever-growing `OffsetTracker.all_offsets`/`outstanding` set. The class docstring at line 253 explicitly claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", which is not true with the current configuration. Bound the queues and raise `MessageRejected` when full.

title: OffsetTracker state is never reset between partition assignments
body: The `FixedQueuePool` (and therefore its `OffsetTracker`) is created once in the factory `__init__` and shared by every `create_with_partitions()` call. On a rebalance the tracker keeps `last_committed`, `all_offsets` and `outstanding` for partitions that may no longer be assigned, and for partitions that are re-assigned it keeps a stale `last_committed`. Consequences: (a) the background commit loop will keep trying to commit offsets for partitions this consumer no longer owns, and (b) if a re-assigned partition resumes at an offset lower than the retained `last_committed`, `get_committable_offsets()` computes `start = last_committed + 1` and will never find a contiguous run, so that partition's offsets are never committed again. The tracker needs to be rebuilt (or pruned to the new assignment) in `create_with_partitions`.

title: shutdown() discards queued work instead of draining it
body: `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` first sets `worker.shutdown = True` for every worker and only then calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. Because the workers' loop condition is checked before each `get()`, each worker finishes at most its current item and then exits, leaving all remaining queued items unprocessed and discarded — despite the docstring saying "Gracefully shutdown all workers". Additionally `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` stops the commit thread *before* calling `queue_pool.shutdown()`, and `join(timeout)` ignores its timeout argument entirely (arroyo uses it to flush in-flight work). Net effect: on every graceful shutdown/rebalance an arbitrary amount of already-consumed work is dropped and must be reprocessed after restart (duplicate processing), and the documented drain semantics of `join()` are not honoured.

title: A single untracked offset stalls commits for the partition forever
body: `get_committable_offsets()` walks offsets from `last_committed + 1` and `break`s on the first offset that is missing from `all_offsets`. There is no mechanism to ever skip a hole, so if any offset is consumed but never registered with `add_offset()`, that partition's committed offset freezes permanently and `all_offsets`/`outstanding` grow without bound. This is reachable from `submit()`: if `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` fails, the `except Exception` handler at line 317 only tracks the offset when `message.value` is a `BrokerValue`, so the offset is dropped from tracking while later offsets continue to be added. Consider tracking the offset before any decoding/validation can fail, or detecting and logging/advancing past permanent holes.

title: Per-message gauge emission from every worker
body: `metrics.gauge("remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth", ...)` is emitted in the `finally` block of every single work item, from every worker thread, with only an `identifier` tag. For a high-throughput uptime results topic this is one statsd emission per message (on top of the per-poll `total_queued` gauge), which adds measurable overhead and produces a meaningless aggregate because all N queues report into the same gauge name/tags. Emit it periodically (e.g. in `poll()`) or tag by worker id.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts behaviour the code does not implement
body: The test (`assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`) asserts that a processing exception prevents the offset from being committed. The implementation does the opposite: `OrderedQueueWorker.run` calls `offset_tracker.complete_offset()` in a `finally` block, so a failed item is treated as done and its offset becomes committable. The test only passes when the 1-second commit loop happens not to have ticked within the short polling window, i.e. it is an inherently racy test that will flake and that documents the wrong contract. Either change the implementation to not complete offsets for failed items (and make the test deterministic), or fix the test to assert the real at-most-once-on-error behaviour.

title: test_stats_reporting races against the worker threads
body: After submitting 10 items with a no-op `result_processor`, the test immediately asserts `stats["total_items"] > 0`. The three worker threads are already running and can drain all 10 items before the assertion executes, making this assertion flaky in CI. Either block the processor (e.g. with an event the test releases) before checking depth, or drop the `> 0` assertion.

title: Queue pool is destroyed on strategy close and then reused after rebalance
body: `FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__`, but the per-assignment strategy's `close()`/`terminate()`/`join()` call `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets `worker.shutdown = True`, calls `queue.shutdown()` on every queue and joins the worker threads. Arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on every partition revocation (rebalance), and then calls `create_with_partitions()` again for the new assignment. On that second call `assert self.queue_pool is not None` still passes, so a strategy is built around a pool whose worker threads are dead and whose queues are shut down: every `work_queue.put()` raises `queue.ShutDown`, which `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` swallows in its generic `except Exception` handler and then marks the offset as completed. The consumer will therefore silently drop all messages while still committing their offsets after any rebalance. The pool must be created per assignment (or re-created in `create_with_partitions`) rather than shared across strategy lifetimes.

title: Unbounded queues mean no backpressure, contradicting the documented guarantee
body: Each queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` never raises `arroyo.processing.strategies.abstract.MessageRejected`. As a result the strategy accepts messages from the Kafka consumer as fast as they arrive regardless of worker progress: work items (which also retain the full `Message`/`KafkaPayload`) and their tracked offsets accumulate in memory without bound when a group's processing is slow, which is exactly the scenario this PR is meant to address. This also contradicts the class docstring ("Natural backpressure when queues fill up"). A bounded queue plus `MessageRejected` on `queue.Full` is needed for arroyo to actually throttle consumption.

title: close() stops the commit thread before draining queues, losing committable offsets
body: `close()` sets `shutdown_event`, joins the commit thread, and only then calls `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which drains the remaining queued items (`shutdown(immediate=False)` lets queued work finish). Any item processed during that drain completes its offset after the only thread that commits offsets has already exited, so those offsets are never committed. On restart/rebalance all of that work is reprocessed. Additionally `join(timeout)` ignores the supplied timeout and just calls `close()`, so arroyo's shutdown deadline is not honoured. The order should be: stop accepting work, drain the queues, perform a final `get_committable_offsets()` + commit, then stop the commit thread.

title: Arroyo commit callback is invoked from a background thread
body: `commit_offsets` (passed as `commit_function`) is called from `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop`, a separate daemon thread, while the arroyo `StreamProcessor` concurrently polls and commits on the main thread. The `Commit` callable given to `create_with_partitions` stages/commits offsets on the shared consumer state and is expected to be called from the processing (main) thread; calling it concurrently races with the processor's own offset staging/commit and with partition revocation (where it can raise `ConsumerError` for unassigned partitions, silently swallowed by the loop's `except Exception`). This can produce lost or incorrect offset commits. Offsets should be collected by the background workers and committed from `poll()`/`submit()` on the main thread instead.

title: A single missing offset permanently blocks all commits for the partition
body: `get_committable_offsets()` walks offsets contiguously from `last_committed + 1` and `break`s on the first offset that is not present in `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be contiguous as seen by a consumer (transactional/control records, compaction, or any message that never reaches `submit` because an upstream wrapper such as the DLQ/stale-message wrapper consumed it). If one offset in the sequence is never added, that partition can never advance its commit point: `all_offsets` grows without bound and the consumer group lag never decreases, causing full reprocessing of everything after the gap on restart. There needs to be a mechanism to advance past offsets that will never be seen (e.g. seed the committed position from the assignment and treat unknown offsets below the current max as done).

title: Generic exception handler in submit() drops messages and commits their offsets
body: `submit()` wraps decoding, grouping and enqueueing in one `try/except Exception`; on any failure (including a failing `grouping_fn`, a `FilteredPayload` payload which trips the `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)` in `decode_payload`, or `queue.ShutDown` from a shut-down pool) it logs and then marks the offset as both added and completed. The message is silently discarded and its offset is committed, so the data is lost with no DLQ and no visible failure other than a log line. Expected non-processable cases (filtered payloads, decode failures) should be handled explicitly, and unexpected enqueue failures should either raise (so arroyo can DLQ/stop) rather than ack the offset.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts behaviour the implementation does not provide and is timing dependent
body: The test's docstring says errors should not block offset commits, yet it asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`. `OrderedQueueWorker.run` catches the processing exception and still calls `complete_offset` in its `finally`, so offsets 100 and 101 become committable and the commit loop (which ticks every ~1s) will commit them. The test only passes because it breaks out of the wait loop after a 0.2s sleep, before the first commit tick — i.e. it is flaky and encodes the opposite of the real behaviour. Either assert that failed messages are committed (documenting the at-most-once semantics) or implement and test actual retry/DLQ handling.

title: Distribution test depends on randomized string hashing
body: `test_different_groups_distributed` asserts that 20 group keys hash into exactly all 3 queues (`len(queue_indices) == 3`). `get_queue_for_group` uses `hash()` on a `str`, which is salted per interpreter run (PYTHONHASHSEED), so there is a small but non-zero chance (~0.1%) that one bucket receives no key and the test fails for unrelated reasons. Assert something weaker (e.g. `len(queue_indices) > 1`) or use a deterministic hash function.

title: Per-worker queue-depth gauge is emitted with identical tags from all workers
body: Every `OrderedQueueWorker` emits `remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth` with only an `identifier` tag, so all N workers (20 by default) report the depth of their own queue under the same metric series. The values overwrite each other and the resulting gauge is meaningless for diagnosing a backed-up individual queue — which is the main failure mode this design is meant to surface. Add a `worker_id`/queue index tag or emit the max/aggregate from one place.

title: Worker transaction name hardcodes the "monitors" prefix
body: The sentry transaction created per work item is named `f"monitors.{self.identifier}.worker_{self.worker_id}"`, but this strategy is generic to remote subscriptions and is being enabled for the uptime consumer. Transactions for uptime results will be grouped under a `monitors.` namespace, making performance data misleading/hard to find.

title: Backup code consumption is a read-modify-write race
body: The backup code is validated and then invalidated via a separate `prisma.user.update` using the decrypted array read earlier. Two concurrent login attempts with the same backup code can both pass the `indexOf` check before either write lands, so a single backup code can be redeemed more than once (and the second write can also resurrect codes nulled by the first, since the whole array is re-serialized from stale data). Use an atomic conditional update or a transaction with row locking so each code can only be consumed once.

title: Backup codes are overwritten on every setup call and can never be regenerated afterwards
body: `/totp/setup` unconditionally regenerates and stores new `backupCodes`, and `/totp/disable` nulls them. There is no endpoint or UI to view or regenerate codes once 2FA is enabled. Consequently, if the user closes the "Backup Codes" dialog (e.g. via the dialog X / `onOpenChange`) without copying or downloading, the codes are permanently unrecoverable while 2FA stays enabled, leaving the user with no recovery path. A regenerate endpoint (or showing codes again from settings) is needed.

title: backupCodes state typed as never[] and blob URL never revoked
body: `useState([])` infers `never[]`, so `setBackupCodes(body.backupCodes)` and `backupCodes.map(formatBackupCode)` only type-check because the response body is `any`; any future typing of the response will break. Additionally the object URL created with `URL.createObjectURL` is only revoked when a new one is created — it is never revoked when the modal unmounts, leaking the blob (containing the plaintext backup codes) for the lifetime of the document.

title: Download button is nested in an anchor inside a form without type="button"
body: The download `Button` is rendered inside an `<a download>` which itself is inside the `<Form>` for `handleEnable`, and the button sets no `type` and no `preventDefault`. If the shared Button does not default to `type="button"`, clicking Download will also submit the enable form (re-running `handleEnable` with an empty totpCode) and may interrupt the download. Add `type="button"` explicitly, as done for the copy/close buttons via `preventDefault`.

title: No test covers logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code
body: The new authentication path (backup code verification in `next-auth-options.ts` and in `/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable`) including single-use invalidation is untested; the test only clicks the download/copy/close buttons on the setup screen (with TODOs for content). A regression that accepts an invalid code, fails to invalidate a used code, or breaks the backup-code login screen would not be caught.

title: Component exported as `TwoFactor` in BackupCode.tsx
body: The default export in `BackupCode.tsx` is named `TwoFactor` (copy-paste from the TOTP component). This misleads readers and shows up as `TwoFactor` in React DevTools/stack traces for two different components. Rename to `BackupCode`.

title: Backup codes stored reversibly encrypted instead of hashed
body: Backup codes are persisted as `symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(codes))` (setup.ts) and compared by decrypting and `indexOf` here. Backup codes are password-equivalent second-factor secrets; storing them in a reversibly encrypted blob means a DB dump plus the (often co-located) CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY yields plaintext second factors for every user. They should be hashed individually (e.g. bcrypt/argon2) and compared by hash, as is done for passwords.

title: Backup code login unusable for non-CAL identity providers
body: For users whose identityProvider is GOOGLE/SAML, 2FA is completed via the `/auth/login?totp=...` flow. In that flow the user submits only `backupCode` with an empty `totpCode`, so the earlier guard at line 113 (`user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode`) throws `ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled` before the new backup-code branch is reached. SSO users therefore can never use the "Lost access" backup-code path even though the UI offers it.

title: Consumed backup code replaced by null, leaving holes in array
body: `backupCodes[index] = null` keeps a `null` entry in the stored JSON instead of removing it. Any future code that counts remaining codes, displays them, or validates the array shape must handle nulls; `JSON.parse` of this array also makes `indexOf` semantics depend on nulls never being produced by user input. Filtering the code out (or storing a per-code used flag) would be safer.

title: No rate limiting or brute-force protection on backup-code verification when disabling 2FA
body: The login path calls `checkRateLimitAndThrowError` before verifying credentials, but this endpoint verifies an attacker-supplied `backupCode` against the decrypted code list with no rate limit and no invalidation of failed attempts. With a stolen session cookie plus known password this allows unlimited guessing of 10-char hex codes. Add rate limiting consistent with the login flow.

title: JSON.parse / symmetricDecrypt of backupCodes can throw an unhandled error
body: If `user.backupCodes` was written with a different encryption key or is otherwise corrupt, `symmetricDecrypt`/`JSON.parse` throws a raw exception that surfaces as a generic 500 rather than a meaningful ErrorCode, breaking login for that user with no diagnostic. Wrap in try/catch and map to `ErrorCode.InternalServerError` (same applies to disable.ts line 58).

title: backupCodes state typed as never[] and blob URL leaked on unmount
body: `useState([])` infers `never[]`, so `setBackupCodes(body.backupCodes)` and `backupCodes.map(formatBackupCode)` are only accepted because the payload is `any`; this silently defeats type checking. Additionally the object URL created with `URL.createObjectURL` is only revoked when a new one is created — if the modal unmounts the URL is never revoked, leaking the blob (which contains the plaintext backup codes) for the lifetime of the document. Type the state as `string[]` and revoke the URL in a cleanup effect.

title: No test covers logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code
body: The new feature's core behavior (authenticating with a backup code, single-use invalidation, rejecting an already-used or wrong code) is untested; only the backup-code display/download/copy UI is exercised. The TODO acknowledges this. Without a test, regressions in the authorize() backup-code branch would silently allow or block logins.

title: Component exported as `TwoFactor` in BackupCode.tsx
body: The default export in `BackupCode.tsx` is declared as `function TwoFactor(...)`, which is misleading in React devtools/stack traces and confusing for anyone searching for the backup-code component. Rename to `BackupCode`.

title: backupCodes state typed as never[]
body: `const [backupCodes, setBackupCodes] = useState([])` infers `never[]`, so `setBackupCodes(body.backupCodes)` and `backupCodes.map(formatBackupCode)` are type errors (and `code` in the render map is `never`). This will break the TypeScript build / requires implicit any. Should be `useState<string[]>([])`.

title: Download button inside <Form> can submit the form
body: The "download" Button is rendered inside the `<Form handleSubmit={handleEnable}>` element and, unlike the adjacent close/copy buttons, does not call `e.preventDefault()`. If the button resolves to type="submit" it will re-trigger `handleEnable` (another /enable API call with a stale/empty totpCode) while also performing the download, producing an unexpected error state. Give it `type="button"` (or preventDefault and trigger the download programmatically).

title: Object URL for backup codes is never revoked on unmount/close
body: `URL.createObjectURL` is only revoked when a new setup is started. Closing the dialog or unmounting leaves the blob (containing plaintext backup codes) alive in memory for the page lifetime. Revoke it in a cleanup effect / in resetState.

title: Used backup code replaced with null, leaving JSON nulls in array
body: Setting `backupCodes[index] = null` re-encrypts an array containing nulls. The stored type is then `(string|null)[]`, which breaks the invariant assumed by other consumers (e.g. disable.ts parses and indexOf's the same array) and makes it impossible to distinguish 'used' from 'never generated'. Consider storing a sentinel string or filtering/regenerating consistently and typing the parsed value.

title: Backup code consumption is not atomic (race allows reuse)
body: The code is verified from a read copy and the remaining codes are written back with a plain `update`. Two concurrent login attempts with the same backup code both read the same array, both succeed, and the second write overwrites the first, so a single-use code can be used more than once. Use a conditional/transactional update (e.g. transaction with re-read, or update guarded by the previous backupCodes value) to make consumption atomic.

title: Unvalidated req.body.backupCode can throw 500
body: `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` assumes a string. A client sending a number/object/array for `backupCode` passes the truthiness check and then throws a TypeError, returning an unhandled 500 instead of a 400. Validate the body type (e.g. zod) before use.

title: Backup codes persisted at setup time even if 2FA is never enabled
body: The setup endpoint writes `backupCodes` while `twoFactorEnabled: false`. If the user abandons the flow, stale codes remain stored; each repeated setup silently invalidates previously shown codes. Consider persisting the codes only when 2FA is actually enabled, or documenting/clearing the abandoned state.

title: "Lost access" toggle button lacks type="button"
body: This Button is inside `<Form form={form} handleSubmit={handleDisable}>`. If it is rendered as a submit button it will submit the disable form (with empty code) when the user just wants to switch to the backup-code input, showing a spurious error. Explicitly set `type="button"` to be safe.

title: Clipboard assertion likely flaky in headless browsers
body: The test clicks the copy button and waits for a success toast, but `navigator.clipboard.writeText` requires clipboard-write permission and a focused document; in headless CI it can reject, so the toast never appears and the test fails intermittently. Grant clipboard permissions via the browser context or skip this assertion.

title: Component exported as `TwoFactor` in BackupCode.tsx
body: The default export in BackupCode.tsx is named `TwoFactor`, which is misleading in stack traces/devtools and when debugging the login flow where both components are rendered. Rename to `BackupCode`.

title: Destructuring an empty destinationCalendar array causes TypeError
body: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` can yield `undefined`, and the next line dereferences it unguarded: `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"`. For any booking with Google Meet as location and no destination calendar (now commonly `[]` or `null`, e.g. handleCancelBooking and the stripe/paypal webhooks pass `[]`), `EventManager.create` throws `Cannot read properties of undefined`, breaking booking creation. Use optional chaining.

title: updateEvent/deleteEvent fallback lookup is always undefined
body: `const selectedCalendar = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;` — the `find` branch only runs when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so it compares each `cal.externalId` against `undefined` and can never match. The previous code fell back to `event.destinationCalendar.externalId`. Result: when no externalCalendarId is stored on the reference, `calendarId` becomes undefined and the Google update/delete targets the wrong (default) calendar or fails. The same pattern exists in `deleteEvent` (line 317), where it then silently falls back to `primary`.

title: externalId not recorded for destinations without credentialId
body: In the `else` branch (destination without `credentialId`), `createEvent(c, event)` is called without the third `externalId` argument, so `EventResult.externalId` is undefined and the booking reference gets `externalCalendarId: undefined` (line 169 now derives it from `result.externalId` instead of `evt.destinationCalendar.externalId`). Subsequent updates/cancellations then cannot locate the event in the right calendar.

title: Possible duplicate event creation for *_other_calendar destinations
body: After the destination loop, all credentials whose type includes `other_calendar` are unconditionally used to create another event. If a destinationCalendar entry points to one of those credentials (its `credentialId` matches, or its `integration` equals the credential type), the event is created twice for that integration, producing duplicate calendar entries and duplicate booking references.

title: Team destination calendars dropped when evt.destinationCalendar is null
body: `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is a no-op when `destinationCalendar` is `null` (which happens when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar). In a collective event where only the non-organizer hosts have calendars connected, their calendars are silently ignored — exactly the case this PR aims to fix. Initialize to `[]` and push instead.

title: Dynamic booking user select lost `organization.slug`
body: The rewritten `loadUsers` drops `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` from the dynamic (no eventTypeId) user query that the previous code selected. Any downstream code relying on `user.organization?.slug` (e.g. booker/organizer URL construction for org users) will now see it missing for dynamic group bookings.

title: BOOKING_CREATED/BOOKING_REQUESTED webhook assertions not updated for array payload
body: Only the BOOKING_REJECTED expectation was changed to `destinationCalendar: []`. The BOOKING_CREATED (line 119) and BOOKING_REQUESTED (line 373) expectations still assert `destinationCalendar: null`, but `CalendarEvent.destinationCalendar` is now an array (`[]` or a list). These assertions will fail or, worse, pass accidentally and no longer verify the payload shape.

title: Legacy-reference cancellation path now deletes once per reference per credential
body: The loop over all `_calendar` references combined with the inner `else` branch (iterating every user calendar credential) means for N legacy references with M calendar credentials, M*N delete calls are issued, each using that reference's `uid`/`externalCalendarId` against unrelated credentials. This multiplies API calls and generates spurious 404s compared to the previous single-reference behavior.

title: Destructuring empty destinationCalendar array then dereferencing causes TypeError
body: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` followed by `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"` dereferences `undefined` whenever `destinationCalendar` is null or an empty array (common: user/event type with no destination calendar). Since `handleNewBooking` can now pass `null`, any booking whose location is Google Meet without a destination calendar will throw `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'integration')` and the booking fails. Use optional chaining (`mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`).

title: Video booking references lose credentialId
body: `credentialId: isCalendarType ? result.credentialId : undefined` drops the credentialId for non-calendar (video) results, whereas the previous code used `result.credentialId` for them. `handleCancelBooking` only deletes a video meeting when `bookingVideoReference.credentialId` is set, so newly created bookings will no longer have their video meetings cancelled/updated. Keep `result.credentialId` for the non-calendar branch.

title: updateEvent/deleteEvent fallback lookup is logically impossible
body: `const selectedCalendar = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;` — the `find` only runs when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so it searches for a calendar whose `externalId` equals `undefined`/`""` and always returns undefined. The previous code fell back to the event's destination calendar externalId. Consequence: updates without an explicit externalCalendarId are sent with `calendarId: undefined` (API error), and deletes silently fall back to `"primary"`, leaving events in other calendars. Same bug at line 317 in `deleteEvent`.

title: Non-Google calendar services ignore credentialId and always use the first destination calendar
body: `createAllCalendarEvents` now iterates every destination calendar and calls `createEvent(credential, event, destination.externalId)` with the full multi-entry `event.destinationCalendar`. Only GoogleCalendarService selects the entry matching `credentialId`; Office365 (here), Lark and the CalDAV base service take `destinationCalendar[0]`. For a collective event with hosts on different accounts, each host's credential will attempt to write into the first host's calendar id, producing 404/permission errors or duplicate events in the wrong calendar. These services need the credentialId-aware selection too.

title: Team destination calendars are dropped when there is no event-type/organizer calendar
body: `evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` exists, and then `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is a no-op. Collective hosts' calendars are silently discarded in that case — exactly the scenario this PR aims to fix. Initialize to an array before pushing.

title: loadUsers rewrite drops organization select and changes error semantics
body: The rewritten dynamic-user query no longer selects `organization: { select: { slug: true } }`, which downstream code (org-aware booker URLs / org slug resolution) relies on, so dynamic group bookings for org users may lose organization context. Additionally, the thrown plain `Error("dynamicUserList is not properly defined or empty.")` is neither `HttpError` nor a Prisma error, so it is converted to a 500 instead of the former 400-style validation failure.

title: Recurring cancellation now deletes each event once per calendar reference
body: The recurring-cancellation block (iterating all user calendar credentials × all updatedBookings) is now nested inside the new `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)` loop. With N calendar references the same delete calls are issued N times per booking occurrence, multiplying external API calls and producing repeated 404/410 responses. The recurring branch should be executed once, outside the per-reference loop.

title: updateEvent called with possibly undefined credential
body: After the DB lookup, `credential` can still be undefined (credential missing or `app.slug` null), yet `result.push(updateEvent(credential, event, bookingRefUid, calenderExternalId))` is executed unconditionally. `updateEvent` immediately reads `credential.appName`/`credential.id`, so this throws inside the try block and the whole update is reported as failed for all references. Guard with `if (credential)` as the create path does.

title: Organization slug assignment logic inverted (unrelated to this PR)
body: Changed from `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`. This inverts behavior: with billing enabled the org now gets a real `slug` immediately (bypassing the pending `requestedSlug` flow, and setting both at once), and with billing disabled the org is created with no slug at all, breaking org subdomain resolution. This change is unrelated to the destinationCalendar fix and looks accidental.

title: Inconsistent expected destinationCalendar across webhook tests
body: BOOKING_REJECTED now expects `destinationCalendar: []` while BOOKING_CREATED (line 119) and BOOKING_REQUESTED (line 373) still expect `null`. The payload shape is now an array-or-null depending on the code path, which indicates the API contract is inconsistent for webhook consumers; it should be normalized (always array) and the tests updated accordingly.

title: Destructured destinationCalendar element dereferenced without null check
body: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` yields `undefined` when the event has no destination calendars (array empty or null). The next line accesses `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining, so any booking whose location is Google Meet and which has no destination calendar will throw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`, failing the whole create flow. Use `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.

title: Organization slug logic inverted (unrelated to PR purpose)
body: The condition was changed from `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`. This inverts behaviour: with team billing enabled the org is now created with a live `slug` *and* `metadata.requestedSlug`, while with billing disabled it gets no slug at all (previously the opposite). This bypasses the paid-slug reservation flow and leaves non-billing instances with slug-less organizations. The change also appears unrelated to the destinationCalendar refactor.

title: Dead fallback lookup in updateEvent/deleteEvent always returns undefined
body: `const selectedCalendar = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;` — the `find` only runs when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so it compares `cal.externalId === undefined` and can never match. The previous code fell back to `event.destinationCalendar.externalId`. Result: when no externalCalendarId is stored on the reference, `calendarId` is `undefined` for `events.update` (request fails) and falls back to `primary` in `deleteEvent` (wrong calendar). Same pattern at line 317.

title: createEvent called without externalId for credential-less destination calendars
body: In the `else` branch (destination calendar without `credentialId`) `createEvent(c, event)` is called without the third `externalId` argument. Since `referencesToCreate` now takes `externalCalendarId` from `result.externalId` (instead of `evt.destinationCalendar.externalId` as before), these bookings will be persisted with `externalCalendarId: undefined`, so later updates/cancellations cannot target the right calendar — a regression for legacy destination calendars that have no credentialId.

title: Collective team destination calendars silently dropped when organizer has none
body: `evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar, and then the collective hosts' calendars are appended with `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...)`. Because of the optional chaining, when the value is `null` all collected `teamDestinationCalendars` are discarded, so co-hosts get no calendar event — exactly the case this PR aims to fix. Initialise an array instead.

title: loadUsers rewrite drops organization select and the no-user guard for dynamic bookings
body: The new dynamic-user query no longer selects `organization: { select: { slug: true } }`, which the previous version included and which downstream code uses (e.g. for org-aware booker URLs/links). Additionally, there is no check that the queried users actually exist/match `dynamicUserList.length`, so a booking for a non-existent username now proceeds with fewer (or zero) users instead of failing clearly.

title: Recurring cancellation now deletes each event once per calendar reference
body: The recurring branch (which already loops over all of the user's calendar credentials and all updated bookings) is now nested inside the new `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)` loop. With N calendar references the same delete requests are issued N times, multiplying API calls to the calendar providers and producing repeated 404/410 handling. The recurring handling should be hoisted out of the per-reference loop.

title: updateEvent may be called with undefined credential
body: If `this.calendarCredentials` has no match and the DB lookup returns nothing (or the credential has no `app.slug`), `credential` remains `undefined` but `updateEvent(credential, ...)` is still invoked, leading to a runtime failure inside `getCalendar`/`credential.appName` rather than a skipped reference. Guard with `if (credential)` before pushing.

title: Inconsistent destinationCalendar expectations across webhook tests
body: BOOKING_REJECTED now expects `destinationCalendar: []` while BOOKING_CREATED (line 119) and BOOKING_REQUESTED (line 373) still expect `null`. Since `CalendarEvent.destinationCalendar` is now an array type, these payloads are shape-dependent on which code path built the event; the inconsistency makes the contract ambiguous for webhook consumers and leaves the array-with-multiple-hosts case untested.

title: Google credential key stored as zod SafeParse wrapper object
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse()` returns the result of `schema.safeParse(...)`, i.e. `{ success: true, data: {...} }`, not the parsed key. The previous code used `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` which returned the key itself. The result is now written directly to `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`, so the stored credential becomes `{"success":true,"data":{...}}` and will fail `googleCredentialSchema.parse` on the next use, breaking every Google Calendar connection after a token refresh.

title: `prisma` is used but never imported in salesforce CalendarService
body: `prisma.credential.update(...)` is called in `getClient`, but there is no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` in this file. This is a compile/runtime error (ReferenceError at request time), breaking every Salesforce calendar operation.

title: Credential-sync path returns a fetch Response where callers expect axios/SDK shapes
body: When credential sharing is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` always returns a `fetch` Response. Callers such as zoho-bigin, zohocrm (`tokenInfo.data.*`) and hubspot (expects a `HubspotToken` object with `expiresIn`/`accessToken`) read properties that do not exist on a `Response`. With syncing enabled those apps will throw or silently write `undefined` keys to the credential. The sync response must be normalized per-caller or parsed as JSON.

title: credentialId passed where userId is expected to the credential sync endpoint
body: `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` passes the credential's id as the `userId` argument. The helper sends it as `calcomUserId` to the self-hosted sync endpoint, so the wrong user's credentials would be fetched/refreshed. `credential.userId` should be threaded through `refreshAccessToken` instead.

title: minimumTokenResponseSchema computed keys are meaningless and strip required fields
body: `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` evaluate to the same stringified object key (e.g. "[object Object]"), so the schema does not "assume any numeric property is the expiry" nor allow arbitrary extra properties. Because zod strips unknown keys by default, the parsed `data` when credential sharing is enabled contains only `access_token`, dropping `refresh_token`, `expiry_date`/`expires_in` and provider-specific fields. Callers then persist an incomplete credential key, breaking subsequent refreshes.

title: Fake literal "refresh_token" injected into credential keys
body: If the parsed response has no `refresh_token`, the code assigns the literal string `"refresh_token"`. Callers store this value in the DB credential, so a real missing/omitted refresh token is replaced by a bogus value instead of preserving the existing one. Future refresh attempts will send `refresh_token=refresh_token` and fail with invalid_grant, requiring users to reconnect.

title: Unvalidated input paths throw unhandled errors (500) and no HTTP method check
body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` can throw, producing an unhandled rejection / opaque 500 instead of a 400 with a useful message. The handler also accepts any HTTP method (GET included), so credentials could be mutated via a GET with a query-shaped body. Use `safeParse`/try-catch and restrict to POST.

title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time equality and no length guard
body: The shared secret is compared with `!==` against a header value, which is vulnerable to timing analysis, and `req.headers[name]` may be an array if the header is repeated (comparison then always fails/succeeds unpredictably). Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on normalized string values.

title: Salesforce refreshes token on every client creation and then ignores the new token
body: `getClient` unconditionally POSTs to the Salesforce token endpoint on every service instantiation (no expiry check), which wastes a request and risks rate limiting. Worse, the returned `jsforce.Connection` is still built with the stale `credentialKey.access_token` / `instance_url` rather than `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`, so the refresh has no effect on the connection. It also bypasses `refreshOAuthTokens`, so Salesforce is excluded from the credential-sync feature this PR adds.

title: Fragile `response.statusText !== "OK"` success check
body: `statusText` is not guaranteed to be "OK" (it is empty on HTTP/2 and varies across runtimes/proxies), so successful refreshes can be rejected with a 400 HttpError. Check `response.ok` / `response.status` instead.

title: App slug "zoomvideo" does not match the Zoom app slug used elsewhere
body: `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoomvideo", ...)` sends `appSlug=zoomvideo` to the sync endpoint, but the app's slug in the DB/app store (and the value the new `/api/webhook/app-credential` endpoint looks up) is `zoom`. A self-hoster implementing the sync endpoint will receive an unknown slug and cannot map it back, breaking Zoom credential syncing.

title: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is a string, not a boolean
body: The expression returns `process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (string) or `undefined`/empty string rather than a boolean. It is consumed in boolean contexts and typed as such by consumers; wrap with `!!(...)` to avoid leaking the encryption key value into a client-importable constant module and to keep the type honest.

title: Google credential key is overwritten with the Zod safeParse wrapper object
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the result of `schema.safeParse(...)`, i.e. an object of the form `{ success: true, data: {...} }`. Here the return value is assigned to `key` and written straight into `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. The stored credential therefore becomes `{"success":true,"data":{...}}` instead of the Google token object, so `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` will fail on the next use and the user's Google Calendar integration breaks permanently until re-installed. The value must be `...data` (previously `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)`).

title: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses nonsensical computed keys and validates nothing useful
body: `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` evaluate to the string `"[object Object]"` for both entries (a ZodString stringifies to `[object Object]`), so the object literal collapses to a single property named `"[object Object]"` of type number/unknown. The comment claims 'any property with a number is the expiry' but Zod cannot express that this way. Effectively the credential-sharing path only validates `access_token` presence and silently accepts responses with no expiry, so expired tokens will be stored and reused.

title: Missing refresh_token is replaced by the literal string "refresh_token"
body: When the parsed response has no `refresh_token`, the code sets it to the literal string `"refresh_token"`. Callers (e.g. zoom, office365) persist the parsed data as the credential key, so a bogus refresh token is written to the DB, silently destroying the real refresh token stored previously and making future refreshes fail with invalid_grant. It also mutates `refreshTokenResponse.data` when `success === false`, which will throw since `data` is undefined (though the preceding throw usually prevents this).

title: `prisma` used but never imported in Salesforce CalendarService
body: The new code calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` but there is no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` in this file. This is a compile/runtime error (ReferenceError) that breaks every Salesforce calendar operation, since `getClient` is called in the constructor path.

title: Salesforce refresh result is discarded; stale access token still used
body: A refresh_token grant is now executed on every `getClient()` call (every service instantiation, even when the existing token is still valid — an unnecessary API round trip and rate-limit risk), but the returned connection is still built with `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` from the old credential rather than `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`. The refresh therefore has no effect on the request that triggered it. It also bypasses `refreshOAuthTokens`, so Salesforce is not actually covered by the credential-sync feature this PR adds.

title: Sync endpoint always returns a fetch Response, incompatible with axios/SDK callers
body: `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw `fetch` `Response` when credential syncing is enabled, but several callers expect the shape produced by their own refresh function: zoho-bigin and zohocrm read `tokenInfo.data.*` (axios response), hubspot expects a `HubspotToken` object with `expiresIn`/`accessToken`. With syncing enabled these will read `undefined` and store broken credentials (or throw). The sync branch needs per-app normalisation or each caller must handle both shapes.

title: Credential-sync request is sent unauthenticated and response status is never checked
body: The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` with no shared secret / signature header (the PR introduces `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` but does not use it here), so anyone who can reach the self-hoster's endpoint can request tokens for an arbitrary user id. There is also no `Content-Type` header for the URL-encoded body and no `response.ok` check, so error pages are passed downstream as if they were token responses.

title: zoho-bigin passes credentialId where userId is expected
body: `refreshOAuthTokens(fn, "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` passes the credential's primary key as the third argument, which the helper treats as the Cal.com user id and forwards as `calcomUserId` to the sync endpoint. This will request tokens for the wrong user (or a non-existent one). `refreshAccessToken` must receive and forward `credential.userId`.

title: Wrong app slug "zoomvideo" sent to credential sync endpoint
body: The Zoom app slug in the app store / credential records is `zoom` (see `createOAuthAppCredential({ appId: "zoom", ... })` in zoomvideo/api/callback.ts), but the refresh call passes `"zoomvideo"`. A self-hoster's endpoint keyed on the Cal.com app slug (and the `app-credential` webhook, which looks up `prisma.app` by slug) will not match, so Zoom token sync silently fails.

title: Webhook handler has no method check and unhandled parse/decrypt errors
body: `handler` accepts any HTTP method (GET included) and calls `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` plus `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` without try/catch. Malformed bodies, a wrong encryption key, or a non-JSON plaintext throw and produce an unhandled 500 with a stack trace rather than a 400. Validate the method and return structured 400s.

title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time equality and no empty-secret guard
body: The shared secret check uses `!==` on the header value, which is vulnerable to timing analysis; use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers. Additionally, if the header is absent `req.headers[...]` is `undefined`; this is only safe because `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` requires the secret to be set, but that constant is a truthy string expression rather than a boolean, so any future refactor could allow `undefined === undefined` to pass.

title: Diagnostic logging for failed Outlook token refresh removed
body: The previous code logged the Zod error and the raw Microsoft response when the refresh token response did not parse. Now `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws a generic `Error("Invalid refreshed tokens were returned")` with no detail, making Outlook refresh failures much harder to diagnose in production.

title: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is a string, not a boolean
body: The expression `process.env.A && process.env.B` yields `undefined`/`""`/the second string rather than a boolean, so the exported constant's type is `string | undefined`. Consumers use it in boolean contexts today, but the name implies a boolean and it would serialize oddly if ever returned from an API. Wrap in `!!`.

title: minimumTokenResponseSchema is built from invalid computed keys and strips all fields except access_token
body: `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the same literal string (`"[object Object]"` – ZodString has no toString override), so the resulting schema is effectively `{ access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown }`. It does not validate the expiry at all, and because `z.object` strips unknown keys, parsing a real token response in credential-sharing mode returns only `{ access_token }` – `expires_in`/`expiry_date`/`refresh_token` are discarded. Every caller that writes `tokenResponse.data` into the credential key will therefore persist a credential with no expiry and no refresh token, breaking subsequent refreshes.

title: Fake refresh_token placeholder overwrites valid stored refresh tokens
body: When the parsed response has no `refresh_token` (common: Microsoft/Office365 and others only return one sometimes, and the schema marks it optional), the code assigns the literal string `"refresh_token"`. Callers spread `tokenResponse.data` over the stored credential key (e.g. office365calendar CalendarService), so the previously valid refresh token is replaced by the dummy string and all future token refreshes for that user fail permanently, requiring re-installation of the app.

title: Credential key is written as a SafeParseReturnType object instead of the parsed key
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the zod `safeParse` result (`{ success, data }`), not the parsed value, yet the result is stored directly: `data: { key }`. Previously `googleCredentialSchema.parse()` returned the key object. This persists `{"success":true,"data":{...}}` into `credential.key`, which no longer matches `googleCredentialSchema`, so Google Calendar breaks for the user after the first token refresh.

title: `prisma` is used but never imported in salesforce CalendarService
body: `prisma.credential.update(...)` is called in `getClient`, but the file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. This is a ReferenceError (or a TS compile error) hit on every Salesforce calendar operation, making the integration completely non-functional.

title: Salesforce token is refreshed unconditionally on every client creation and the new token is not used
body: `getClient` now performs a refresh_token request on every instantiation regardless of expiry (extra latency and Salesforce rate-limit pressure), and then builds the jsforce Connection with the *old* `credentialKey.access_token`/`instance_url` instead of the freshly obtained `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`. So the refresh is wasted work and an already expired access token is still used.

title: Response success checked via `statusText !== "OK"`
body: `response.statusText` is empty for HTTP/2 responses and is not guaranteed to be "OK" otherwise. Using it as the success check can throw an HttpError with an empty message on perfectly successful refreshes. Use `response.ok`/`response.status` instead.

title: refreshOAuthTokens returns heterogeneous types; callers expecting axios/googleapis shapes break when sync is enabled
body: In the sync branch the function returns a raw `fetch` Response, while in the fallback branch it returns whatever the provider SDK returns (an axios response with `.data` for hubspot/zohocrm/zoho-bigin, `fetchTokens.res` for googleapis, a Response for fetch-based apps). With credential sharing enabled, hubspot does `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` on a Response (NaN expiry), zoho reads `tokenInfo.data.error` (undefined) and persists a Response-shaped object as the credential key, and googlecalendar reads `res.data` (undefined). Each affected app needs to parse the sync endpoint response consistently.

title: Request to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT is unauthenticated and the response status is never checked
body: The POST to the self-hoster's sync endpoint carries no shared secret/authorization header, so any party able to reach that endpoint can request tokens for an arbitrary `calcomUserId`; symmetrically Cal.com has no way to verify it is talking to the right endpoint. The returned Response is also forwarded without checking `response.ok`, so a 4xx/5xx body is passed to parsing/persistence paths.

title: credentialId passed where userId is expected in refreshOAuthTokens
body: `refreshAccessToken(credentialId, credentialKey)` passes `credentialId` as the third argument of `refreshOAuthTokens(fn, appSlug, userId)`. With credential sharing enabled the sync endpoint will be called with `calcomUserId = <credential id>`, returning tokens for the wrong user (or failing). The credential's `userId` must be plumbed through instead.

title: appSlug "zoomvideo" does not match the Zoom app slug used elsewhere
body: The credential/app slug for Zoom is `zoom` (see `createOAuthAppCredential({ appId: "zoom", ... })` in zoomvideo/api/callback.ts and the webhook handler which looks up `prisma.app.findUnique({ where: { slug } })`). Passing `"zoomvideo"` to `refreshOAuthTokens` means the self-hosted endpoint receives a slug that does not exist in the app store, so self-hosters can't correlate it with the slug they must send back to `/api/webhook/app-credential`.

title: Unvalidated zod parse and missing HTTP method check cause 500s instead of 400s
body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a ZodError for malformed payloads, which surfaces as an unhandled 500 rather than a 400 with a useful message. Likewise `symmetricDecrypt`/`JSON.parse` on line 57-59 will throw on a bad ciphertext or wrong key. There is also no method restriction, so a GET with the right secret reaches the body parse. Wrap in try/catch and use `safeParse` plus a `req.method !== "POST"` guard.

title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time equality and no length guard
body: The shared secret is compared with `!==`, which short-circuits and leaks timing information; for a long-lived static secret this is a realistic oracle for an attacker who can send many requests. Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on buffers of equal length. Additionally, `req.headers[...]` may be a string array when the header is sent twice; that case silently fails rather than being rejected explicitly.

title: Existing invalid credentials are not revalidated and multiple credentials are ignored
body: When updating an existing credential only `key` is set; if the credential had previously been flagged `invalid: true` (e.g. by the zoom/webex invalidateCredential paths), it stays invalid and the freshly synced keys will never be used. Set `invalid: false` on update. The `findFirst` also silently ignores additional credentials for the same user/app, leaving stale duplicates that other code paths may pick up.

title: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is a string, not a boolean
body: `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` evaluates to `string | undefined`, so the exported constant has a misleading name and type for a flag that is consumed in boolean contexts and could be serialized/compared elsewhere. Wrap in `!!(...)`.

title: Diagnostic logging for failed Outlook token refresh removed
body: The previous code logged the zod error and the raw Microsoft response when the refresh token response failed validation. Now `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws a generic `new Error("Invalid refreshed tokens were returned")` with no provider detail, making Outlook refresh failures much harder to diagnose in production.

title: Team permission check uses AND of isTeamAdmin and isTeamOwner
body: `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`, which is only true for a user who is both admin and owner. Despite the name, team admins (and in most role models, owners who are not reported as admins) will be denied and get FORBIDDEN. It should be `||`. Additionally, when `booking.eventType?.teamId` is null, `?? 0` queries a non-existent team on every personal booking — two wasted DB round trips.

title: Duplicate guest emails within the request are not de-duplicated server-side
body: `uniqueGuests` only filters emails that already exist as attendees; it does not remove duplicates inside the incoming `guests` array, and the trpc schema (`addGuests.schema.ts`) does not enforce uniqueness. Uniqueness is only validated in the client dialog, so any other caller (or a crafted request) can create several attendee rows with the same email on one booking, resulting in duplicated calendar attendees and duplicated emails.

title: Blacklist comparison is case-sensitive on the guest side, allowing bypass
body: `blacklistedGuestEmails` is lowercased, but the incoming guest email is compared as-is (`!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`). A guest email with different casing (e.g. `Blocked@x.com`) bypasses the BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS protection. Lowercase the guest email before comparison. The existing-attendee comparison is similarly case-sensitive, so `Foo@x.com` can be added when `foo@x.com` is already an attendee.

title: sendAddGuestsEmails receives the raw input list instead of the actually added guests
body: `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` passes the unfiltered input. In email-manager the list decides who receives the full "scheduled" email vs the "guests added" notice, so any email that was filtered out (already an attendee, or blacklisted) will incorrectly receive a brand-new booking confirmation email. Pass `uniqueGuests` instead.

title: Email failure is swallowed without the error details
body: The catch block logs a fixed string via `console.log` and discards `err`, so email delivery/render failures for this new flow are effectively invisible in production. Use the project logger and include the error and bookingId.

title: No restriction on booking state; any attendee can add guests to any booking
body: The handler permits the action when the caller is simply one of the booking's attendees, with no check that the booking is ACCEPTED/not cancelled and not in the past, and no check for seated events (`seatsPerTimeSlot`). Adding attendees to a cancelled/past booking sends out CONFIRMED ICS invites, and adding guests to a seats-based event bypasses the seat accounting.

title: MultiEmail imports from its own package barrel, creating a circular import
body: `packages/ui/form/MultiEmail.tsx` imports `Button, EmailField, Icon, Tooltip` from `@calcom/ui`, while `packages/ui/index.tsx` re-exports `MultiEmail` (via MultiEmailLazy). This module cycle can yield undefined components at runtime depending on evaluation order/bundler. Import the components from their concrete paths (e.g. `../components/button`, `../components/form`) as the sibling form components do.

title: Add button silently does nothing when all email rows are removed
body: `handleAdd` returns early when `multiEmailValue.length === 0`, with no toast or validation message, so after removing every row the Add button appears unresponsive. Also, the initial value is `[""]`, so pressing Add immediately validates an empty string and shows "Emails must be unique and valid" rather than a clearer empty-input message.

title: "Add guests" action id/label mismatch and shown for past bookings
body: The new action uses `id: "add_members"` with label `t("additional_guests")`, which is inconsistent and makes the test id (`add_members`) misleading. More importantly, `editBookingActions` is also rendered for past and pending bookings (lines 553-554), so users are offered "add guests" on bookings that already happened, which triggers new CONFIRMED invite emails for a past event.

title: Organizer email subject can render "undefined"/empty name
body: The subject uses `this.calEvent.attendees[0].name`. Newly added guests are created with `name: ""`, and if attendee ordering places a new guest first the subject becomes "Guests Added:  with  at ...". It also throws if `attendees` is empty. Fall back to the booker name/email as other organizer templates do.

title: No tests for the new addGuests mutation
