Under concurrent requests on a threaded server, two threads can simultaneously see nil/stale arrays and `@loaded_locales << locale` from different threads can lose entries, causing redundant loads or a locale being considered loaded while its translations are only partially installed. Perform the check and initialization under the same mutex.

title: No tests for fallback behaviour
body: This PR introduces a new fallback chain (user locale -> site default locale -> :en) plus lazy loading of fallback locale files, but adds no specs. There is no coverage asserting that a key missing in the user locale resolves from the site default locale and then from English, nor that fallback locale YAML is actually loaded before lookup. Given the silent-failure mode (missing translation strings shown to users), a spec for FallbackLocaleList#[] and an end-to-end translation fallback spec should be added.

title: nil default_locale raises NoMethodError in fallback list
body: `SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym` is called before `.compact`, so if `SiteSetting.default_locale` is nil (or SiteSetting is unavailable, e.g. during asset precompile/early boot or a misconfigured site), `nil.to_sym` raises NoMethodError and every translation lookup through the fallback chain blows up. Guard the value (e.g. `SiteSetting.default_locale.presence&.to_sym`) before calling to_sym, and compact before uniq.

title: Fallback locale keys may be strings, causing mismatched/unloaded locales
body: `[](locale)` returns `[locale, ...]` without normalizing `locale` to a symbol. I18n may pass strings (e.g. 'de'), so the chain can contain a String while `ensure_loaded!`/`@loaded_locales` in translate_accelerator compares symbols (`config.locale`). This results in the same locale being loaded twice or not matched at all, and `uniq` failing to dedupe 'de' vs :de. Normalize with `locale.to_sym`.

title: Translation LRU cache key ignores fallback chain / site default locale (multisite leakage)
body: With fallbacks enabled, a translation result now depends on `SiteSetting.default_locale` in addition to `config.locale`, but the cache key is only `key + config.locale + backend.object_id`. The LRU cache is process-wide, so in multisite (or after changing the site's default locale) a value resolved via one site's fallback chain will be served to another site/request with a different default locale, producing wrong-language strings. Include the fallback chain (or site identifier) in the cache key, or clear the cache when default_locale changes.

title: Fallback locales only loaded in web requests
body: `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` is invoked solely from ApplicationController#set_locale. Code paths that set I18n.locale outside a controller (Sidekiq jobs, mailers, rake tasks, console) will have the fallback locales unloaded, so lookups that should fall back to the site locale or :en will return missing-translation output instead. Loading should be hooked where locale is set globally (e.g. inside the patched translate/load path).

title: ensure_loaded! initializes shared state outside the mutex
body: `@loaded_locales ||= []` and the subsequent `include?` check run outside LOAD_MUTEX, so two threads can concurrently assign different arrays to @loaded_locales, losing load bookkeeping and causing duplicate/missed locale loads. Move the initialization and check inside the synchronized block.

title: Hash subclass only overrides #[], other Hash API returns empty
body: `FallbackLocaleList` subclasses Hash but overrides only `#[]`; `fetch`, `keys`, `each`, `empty?` etc. still reflect an empty hash. Any I18n (or plugin) code that uses those methods on `I18n.fallbacks` will see no fallbacks, silently bypassing this feature. Also, defining it at top level without a namespace risks constant collisions.

title: Denial-cache test does not actually prove the denial cache short-circuits
body: The test "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" claims to "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked", but it seeds the permission cache with `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`, i.e. the scope maps to false, so `checkPermission` would deny anyway (and with no store configured the fallback path would also deny). The test therefore passes even if the permission-denial cache lookup were removed entirely, so the new behaviour is untested. Set the scope to `true` so that a deny result can only come from the denial cache.

title: Every negative Check for a new resource name triggers a full permission DB query
body: Check now falls through to `getIdentityPermissions` (DB query for basic roles, teams and permissions) whenever the cached scope map does not grant access, and only caches the negative result per (namespace, user, action, name, parent). Since `name` is caller-supplied, a client repeatedly checking distinct resource names the user cannot access produces one full permissions query per distinct name within each 30s window, bypassing the permission cache entirely. This is a significant and attacker-influenceable increase in DB load compared to the previous behaviour where the cached scope map answered denials. Consider caching a "permissions freshly loaded" marker per user/action so at most one DB refresh happens per TTL.

title: Denial cache key can collide between distinct (name, parent) pairs
body: `userPermDenialCacheKey` joins namespace, user, action, name and parent with a single `_` separator and name/parent are arbitrary UIDs that may contain `_`. For example name="a", parent="b_c" and name="a_b", parent="c" produce the same key, so a denial recorded for one resource can deny a different resource for up to the cache TTL. Use a separator that cannot appear in UIDs or length-prefix the components.

title: permissionCacheUsage metric records a miss on cache hits that denied
body: When `getCachedIdentityPermissions` succeeds but `checkPermission` returns false, execution falls through to line 137, which increments `permissionCacheUsage` with label "false" (miss) even though the permission cache was actually hit. The cache hit-rate metric will therefore understate hits for all deny paths, making it unreliable for tuning the cache.

title: Denial cache delays visibility of newly granted permissions with no invalidation path
body: A negative result is cached for `shortCacheTTL` (30s) keyed per resource, and nothing invalidates it when a permission is granted (e.g. a user is added to a role/team or given access to an existing dashboard). Previously such a grant became visible when the per-user permission cache expired; now the deny answer is sticky for up to 30s after the grant with no way to clear it. Worth documenting, or wiring an invalidation on permission writes.

title: Denial cache key omits identity type, risking cross-identity collisions
body: userPermDenialCacheKey is built from namespace, userUID, action, name and parent only. Subjects of different identity types can share the same UID string (e.g. `user:0`, `anonymous:0`, `render:0`, or a service account whose UID equals a user UID), so a denial recorded for one identity can be returned as a cached deny for a different identity in Check (service.go:116-121). Unlike permCache, which uses distinct key builders per identity type (anonymousPermCacheKey vs userPermCacheKey), the denial key has no type discriminator. This produces incorrect authz decisions (wrongful denials, and incorrect caching semantics). Include the identity type in the key.

title: Cached denials are not invalidated when permissions are granted
body: Check now stores a positive deny entry (permDenialCache, shortCacheTTL=30s) for every (namespace, user, action, name, parent) that is denied after a DB query, and returns early on a hit without consulting the DB. There is no invalidation path when a permission is subsequently granted (e.g. a user is given access to an existing dashboard/folder immediately after being denied), so the user will keep receiving 403s for up to 30 seconds even though the fresh DB state allows access. This is the inverse of the problem the PR fixes; consider a shorter TTL or an invalidation hook.

title: Per-resource denial cache entries can grow unboundedly
body: The denial cache key includes the resource name and parent folder, so every distinct denied resource for every user creates a separate entry in the shared local cache. In workloads where many checks are denied (e.g. scanning/listing a large number of dashboards per user), this produces a very large number of cache entries with no bound other than the 30s TTL and 2–10 min cleanup interval, increasing memory pressure on the shared cache that also holds permissions, teams and folder trees.

title: permissionCacheUsage metric double-counted / wrongly labelled in Check
body: In Check, a denial-cache hit increments permissionCacheUsage with label "true" and returns; on a permission-cache hit that results in allow it also increments "true"; but on a permission-cache hit that results in deny the code falls through and increments "false" at line 137 even though the cache was hit. The metric therefore no longer reflects cache hit ratio and mixes denial-cache hits with permission-cache hits, making it unusable for tuning.

title: Non-ErrNotFound errors from getCachedIdentityPermissions are silently ignored
body: getCachedIdentityPermissions can return real errors (e.g. GetUserIdentifiers store failure, or 'unsupported identity type'). In Check (line 123) and List (line 180) any error is treated the same as a cache miss, so genuine backend failures are swallowed and the code proceeds to a second lookup; the error cause is lost from logs/traces. Distinguish cache.ErrNotFound from other errors.

title: cacheHit test field is now dead and cached-permission path untested in getUserPermissions
body: The 'should return permissions from cache if available' case was removed from TestService_getUserPermissions, leaving the cacheHit field always false and the `if tc.cacheHit` branches (lines 367-369, 388-392) unreachable. Since getUserPermissions no longer reads permCache, there is no test asserting that it always re-queries the store (the behaviour change this PR relies on), nor that the permission cache is still written. Add an explicit assertion that the store is queried even when permCache is populated.

title: Denial cache key is ambiguous and omits group/resource
body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, user UID, action, name and parent folder with '_' separators. Since resource/folder UIDs may legally contain underscores, two different (name, parent) pairs can produce the identical key (e.g. name="a_b", parent="c" vs name="a", parent="b_c"), causing a denial cached for one resource to be returned for a different one. The key also does not include group/resource, so two different group/resource pairs that map to the same action string would share denial entries. The consequence is incorrect (false) denials for up to the cache TTL. Include a non-ambiguous separator/encoding (e.g. length-prefixed or escaped segments) and the group/resource in the key.

title: Error from getCachedIdentityPermissions silently swallowed
body: In Check, the error from getCachedIdentityPermissions is only compared against nil; real errors (e.g. GetUserIdentifiers DB failure or 'unsupported identity type') are indistinguishable from cache.ErrNotFound and are neither logged nor traced. This hides genuine failures and makes debugging cache/identity-store problems hard. Distinguish cache.ErrNotFound from other errors and log/return the latter.

title: permissionCacheUsage metric counted twice for a single Check
body: When cached permissions are found but do not grant access, the code increments permissionCacheUsage with label "false" at line 137 after having consulted the cache successfully; conversely a denial-cache hit at line 118 increments "true" and then returns. The 'false' bucket therefore counts cache hits that simply didn't grant permission, so the cache hit-rate metric no longer reflects actual cache hits and will look much worse than reality.

title: Denial-cache test does not prove the permission cache is bypassed
body: The comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked" but the permCache entry is set to map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}, i.e. a deny, so the assertion assert.False(resp.Allowed) would pass even if the denial cache were not consulted at all. Set the value to true (an allow) so the test actually verifies that the denial cache short-circuits before the permission cache.

title: Missing React `key` on GrafanaRuleListItem in list map
body: In the `rules.map(...)` render, the `grafana` branch renders `<GrafanaRuleListItem ...>` without a `key` prop, while all other branches pass `key={key}`. The previous `GrafanaRuleLoader` usage had `key={key}`. This triggers React key warnings and, more importantly, causes element identity to be positional, which can lead to incorrect re-use/reset of component state as new pages of results are appended during infinite scrolling.

title: Delete and Pause menu items are unreachable in the list view
body: The menu now computes `canDelete`/`canPause` from either ruler or Grafana Prometheus abilities, but the rendering still requires a ruler rule: Delete is gated on `canDelete && rulerRule` and Pause on `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`. Since the whole point of this PR is that the list view no longer fetches ruler rules (`rulerRule` is undefined there), users will never see Delete or Pause in the rule list, even with full permissions — a functional regression for the new list view.

title: Silence menu item does nothing without a ruler rule
body: `AlertRuleMenu` can now enable the 'Silence notifications' item based solely on Grafana Prometheus abilities, but the drawer is only rendered when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true. In the list view `rule` (ruler rule) is undefined, so clicking Silence sets state but no drawer is shown — a dead UI action.

title: Federated rule-group check removed, allowing edits/deletes of federated groups
body: `useAllRulerRuleAbilities` (which now backs the deprecated `useAllAlertRuleAbilities`) hardcodes `const isFederated = false` and the former `isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` call was deleted. Federated Mimir rule groups were previously treated as immutable (Update/Delete/Pause unsupported). Now the UI will offer edit/delete for federated groups, which will either corrupt or fail against the ruler. This is a behaviour regression for all existing consumers of `useAllAlertRuleAbilities`.

title: Grafana recording rules lose Pause/Export abilities in the prom-based hook
body: In `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`, `Pause`, `Restore`, `DeletePermanently` and `ModifyExport` are gated on `isAlertingRule = prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)`. The ruler equivalent used `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(...)`, which is true for Grafana recording rules as well. As a result, Grafana-managed recording rules can no longer be paused or exported from the list view, although the backend supports both.

title: `returnTo` dropped from rule view link
body: The removed `GrafanaRuleLoader` built the href as `createRelativeUrl('/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view', { returnTo })` using `createReturnTo()`. The new component drops the `returnTo` query param, so navigating back from the rule detail view will no longer return the user to their filtered list position.

title: Silent empty render when Prometheus returns no matching group
body: `promResponse.data.groups.at(0)?.rules.map(...)` renders nothing if the response contains no groups (e.g. group not yet propagated or wrong folder/group). Previously the ruler response provided a fallback and 'Creating' operation items. Users now see an empty group with no explanation or error.

title: Removed coverage for rule matching and creating/deleting states without replacement
body: This diff deletes all `matchRules` unit tests plus the 'creating' (ruler-only) and 'deleting' (prom-only) rendering tests, and replaces them with assertions about the More button/menu. The eventual-consistency behaviour that the component still conceptually supports (`RuleOperation` prop on `GrafanaRuleListItem`) is now completely untested, and no test covers the new ability resolution via `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` for recording rules or provisioned rules.

title: Missing React `key` on GrafanaRuleListItem in filtered list
body: In the `rules.map(...)` render, the `grafana` branch returns `<GrafanaRuleListItem ... />` without `key={key}`, while all other branches pass a key. React will emit a key warning and, more importantly, lose element identity across incremental page loads of the infinite-scroll list, which can cause incorrect re-use/re-ordering of list item state as new batches are appended.

title: Pause/Delete/Silence menu items still gated on rulerRule, so they never show in the list view
body: The abilities are now computed from either the ruler rule or the Prometheus rule, but the rendering conditions were not updated: the Pause item requires `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` (line 123) and the Delete item requires `rulerRule` (line 165). Since the list view no longer fetches the Ruler API, `rulerRule` is undefined there and Pause/Delete will never render even when `canPause`/`canDelete` are true from the Grafana Prom abilities. This is a functional regression for the new rule list.

title: Silence action is a no-op when only promRule is available
body: `handleSilence` sets `showSilenceDrawer`, but the drawer only renders when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true. In the list view `rule` (ruler rule) is undefined, yet AlertRuleMenu now enables the Silence item based on Grafana Prom abilities. Clicking "Silence notifications" will therefore do nothing at all.

title: Federated rule-group check dropped; federated rules now appear editable/deletable
body: `useAllRulerRuleAbilities` hardcodes `const isFederated = false` (replacing the previous `isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` used by `useAllAlertRuleAbilities`). Federated Mimir rule groups were previously treated as immutable; now Update/Delete/Pause are reported as supported for them, exposing edit/delete UI for rules that cannot be modified. This affects the existing (non-list) views that use the deprecated hook too.

title: `returnTo` query param dropped from rule view link
body: The removed `GrafanaRuleLoader` built the href as `createRelativeUrl(.../view, { returnTo })` using `createReturnTo()`. The new component omits it, so navigating into a rule from the list and back loses the "return to previous" context.

title: Loss of Creating/Deleting rule operation indicators
body: Removing the Ruler query and `matchRules` means rules that exist in the Ruler but not yet in Prometheus (Creating) and rules removed from the Ruler but still in Prometheus (Deleting) are no longer surfaced; the former simply disappear from the group listing until Prometheus catches up. The tests for these behaviours were deleted rather than replaced, so there is no coverage of the new behaviour either.

title: Missing React `key` on GrafanaRuleListItem in list rendering
body: In the `rules.map(...)` loop the `grafana` branch renders `<GrafanaRuleListItem rule={rule} .../>` without passing `key={key}`, while all other branches do. React will emit a key warning and, more importantly, lose element identity across incremental page loads of the infinite-scroll list, which can cause incorrect re-use/re-ordering of rule rows and lost component state. Pass `key={key}` as before.

title: Delete and Pause actions silently disappear in the new rule list view
body: Abilities are now also derived from `promRule` (`useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`), so `canDelete`/`canPause` can be true when only a Prometheus rule is available. However the Delete menu item is still gated on `canDelete && rulerRule` and the Pause item on `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`. Since the list view no longer fetches ruler rules (GrafanaRuleListItem passes only `promRule`), Delete and Pause are never rendered there — a functional regression versus the previous GrafanaRuleLoader which supplied `rulerRule`. Either keep fetching the ruler rule for these actions or implement prom-rule-based variants.

title: Silence menu item is a no-op when only a Prometheus rule is provided
body: `canSilence` in AlertRuleMenu can now be satisfied via the Grafana prom-rule abilities, so the "Silence notifications" item is rendered in the new list view. Clicking it sets `showSilenceDrawer`, but the drawer is only rendered when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true, i.e. when a ruler rule exists. In the list view `rule` is undefined, so the user clicks Silence and nothing happens.

title: Federated rule-group check dropped, allowing edit/delete of federated rules
body: `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` previously computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`; it now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, where `isFederated` is hard-coded to `false`. Federated (Mimir cross-tenant) rule groups were intentionally treated as immutable; with this change Update/Delete/Pause abilities are reported as supported for them, exposing edit/delete UI for rules that cannot be modified.

title: View link no longer carries returnTo parameter
body: The removed `GrafanaRuleLoader` built the href with `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`, { returnTo })` using `createReturnTo()`. The new component drops `returnTo`, so navigating back from the rule detail view loses the user's previous list position/filters.

title: Removed coverage for Creating/Deleting rule operation states without replacement
body: The tests for "ruler-only rule shows Creating state", "prom-only rule shows Deleting state" and the whole `matchRules` suite were deleted. `GrafanaRuleListItem` still accepts an `operation` prop and `RuleOperation.Creating/Deleting` still exist, but nothing now exercises or verifies the eventual-consistency UI behaviour, so regressions there will go unnoticed.

title: Rule-type check placed in the 'allowed' slot of the Silence ability
body: `[AlertRuleAction.Silence]: [silenceSupported, canSilenceInFolder && isAlertingRule]` puts `isAlertingRule` (a support condition, not a permission) into the 'allowed' position. Callers that only inspect `supported` (e.g. to decide whether to render a disabled control) will treat recording rules as silenceable. Move `isAlertingRule` into the supported flag to match the ruler-based implementation semantics.

title: Stale comment/variable name after removing ruler prefetch
body: The ruler `prefetch('getGrafanaRulerGroup')` dispatch was removed, but the surrounding comment still says "This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules..." and the variable is still named `cacheAndRulerPreload`. This is misleading for future readers since no ruler data is preloaded anymore.

title: Queries are interpolated twice in the shard-splitting path
body: runShardSplitQuery() now calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables() on every target, and then passes the resulting (already interpolated) targets down to runSplitQuery() (line 163), which in querySplitting.ts:299 applies applyTemplateVariables() again to each target. Any non-idempotent part of applyTemplateVariables — notably ad-hoc filter / scope injection into the LogQL selector and label-filter addition — will be applied twice, producing duplicated filters in the final expression (and, with the shard selector already injected, interpolation runs over an expression that already contains `__stream_shard__`). The new test asserting `applyTemplateVariables` is called 5 times for a single target (shardQuerySplitting.test.ts:112) documents this repeated interpolation rather than preventing it. Interpolation should happen once; e.g. pass a flag/option to runSplitQuery to skip re-interpolation when called from the shard splitter.

title: Queries are interpolated twice when shard splitting delegates to runSplitQuery
body: runShardSplitQuery now applies datasource.applyTemplateVariables to each target, and the resulting sub-request is handed to runSplitQuery (line 163), which in querySplitting.ts (line 299) applies applyTemplateVariables again to every target. Every shard sub-request therefore goes through template/ad-hoc-filter interpolation twice (the updated test even asserts applyTemplateVariables is called 5 times for a single query). This can duplicate ad-hoc filters / label filters injected by applyTemplateVariables, re-interpolate values that themselves contain `$`-like text, and recompute `$__auto`/step against the already-substituted expression, producing incorrect queries. One of the two interpolation points should be removed (e.g. let runSplitQuery skip interpolation when called from shard splitting).

title: runSplitQuery may re-interpolate already-interpolated targets from other callers
body: runSplitQuery unconditionally calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables on request.targets. Callers that already interpolate before calling runSplitQuery (shard splitting, and any datasource.query path that pre-processes targets) will now have variables/ad-hoc filters applied a second time. There is no guard or flag to opt out, so the function's contract silently changed: passing pre-interpolated targets is no longer safe. Consider adding an option (e.g. `skipInterpolation`) or documenting/enforcing that callers must pass raw targets.

title: Assertion on interpolation call count codifies the double-interpolation behaviour
body: The test was changed from expecting interpolation once to `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)`. That number is exactly 1 (shard splitting) + 4 (re-interpolation inside runSplitQuery per sub-request), i.e. the test now locks in the duplicate interpolation described above instead of verifying that each query is interpolated exactly once. If the duplication is fixed this assertion must change; as written it hides the defect.

title: Queries are now interpolated twice in the shard-splitting path
body: runShardSplitQuery() now calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables() on every target, and the resulting sub-requests are handed to runSplitQuery() (querySplitting.ts:296-299), which was changed in the same PR to also call applyTemplateVariables() on request.targets. Every shard sub-query therefore gets interpolated a second time (the new shard test even asserts applyTemplateVariables is called 5 times for a single target). Double interpolation re-runs variable/ad-hoc-filter/regex-escape logic over already substituted text: variable values that themselves contain `$`/`{{}}` syntax get expanded again, and ad-hoc filters (request.filters) can be appended twice to the selector, producing wrong queries. Interpolation should happen in exactly one place.

title: Pre-interpolation can defeat the $__range split guard
body: querySupportsSplitting() relies on isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) to avoid splitting queries that use $__range (because the backend interpolates it per split range). Now that targets are interpolated before this check, any `$__range`/`$__range_ms`/`$__range_s` occurrence that templateSrv resolves on the frontend will already be substituted, so the guard no longer matches and the query gets split anyway — reintroducing the exact incorrect-range bug the guard was added for. The range check should run against the original, un-interpolated expression (or the guard moved before interpolation).

title: Assertion on applyTemplateVariables call count encodes the double-interpolation behaviour
body: The test now asserts `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` for a single target. This number is an artifact of interpolation being re-applied inside runSplitQuery for each shard sub-request; it locks in the duplicate-interpolation behaviour and will break on any unrelated change to the number of shard groups, rather than testing that interpolation happens once up front.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, breaking log assertions
body: TestLogger.FromContext(ctx) returns NewTestLogger() instead of the receiver. LoggerMiddleware.logRequest now calls m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so any test that injects a *TestLogger and then asserts on InfoLogs.Calls/Message/Ctx will observe zero recorded calls, since the log goes to a throwaway instance. Return `f` (or propagate recorded logs) so logging through FromContext remains observable; otherwise existing/future logger middleware tests silently stop validating anything.

title: traceID no longer guaranteed in plugin request log
body: The explicit `traceID` log param (from tracing.TraceIDFromContext) was removed and now depends entirely on the contextual logger installed by ContextualLoggerMiddleware, which does not add a traceID attribute. If the infra logger's FromContext does not inject the trace ID (or if the contextual attributes were never set, e.g. for stream endpoints), the 'Plugin Request Completed' log loses trace correlation, which is a regression for debugging.

title: Stream endpoints get no contextual logger attributes
body: SubscribeStream/PublishStream/RunStream pass the context through without calling instrumentContext, so logs emitted downstream for streaming calls lack pluginId/endpoint/dsUID/uname attributes. Since this middleware exists solely to attach the contextual logger, these endpoints silently lose all contextual log fields.

title: Test name and missing test for new ContextualLoggerMiddleware
body: The test function is still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware after the rename to MetricsMiddleware, and the newly extracted ContextualLoggerMiddleware (which now owns instrumentContext) has no test coverage verifying the contextual attributes are added to the context for each endpoint.

title: TestLogger.FromContext discards recorded logs
body: TestLogger.FromContext returns a brand-new TestLogger instead of the receiver, so any log calls made through it are recorded on a throwaway object. Since LoggerMiddleware.logRequest now calls m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), tests that inject a *log.TestLogger and then assert on InfoLogs.Calls/Message/Ctx will always observe zero calls, silently losing coverage of the logging middleware (and existing assertions would fail). FromContext (and New) should return the same instance so recorded logs are observable.

title: Logger interface extended with FromContext (breaking for implementers)
body: Adding FromContext(context.Context) Logger to the exported plugins/log.Logger interface breaks any existing implementation of that interface outside this package (e.g. in enterprise or test helpers), which will no longer compile. Worth confirming all implementers are updated in this PR or that the interface is internal.

title: Stream endpoints get no contextual logging attributes
body: SubscribeStream, PublishStream and RunStream pass the context through without calling instrumentContext, so logs emitted during stream handling (and by LoggerMiddleware for these endpoints) carry no pluginId/endpoint/dsUID attributes. Since the contextual logger is now the only source of these fields (they were removed from LoggerMiddleware's log params), this leaves stream requests unidentifiable in logs.

title: Log fields now depend on a separate middleware being installed
body: pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName, dsUID and traceID were removed from LoggerMiddleware's logParams and now come only from the contextual logger installed by ContextualLoggerMiddleware. Anyone constructing middlewares without NewContextualLoggerMiddleware (e.g. other callers/tests building their own stack) will emit 'Plugin Request Completed' lines with no plugin identification at all, a silent regression in log usefulness. Consider keeping the essential fields here or documenting the hard ordering dependency.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, discarding recorded logs
body: TestLogger.FromContext (and New) returns a brand-new TestLogger instead of the receiver. Since LoggerMiddleware now logs via m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), any test using log.TestLogger to assert on InfoLogs/ErrorLogs counts and messages will observe zero calls, because the log is recorded on a throwaway instance. This silently makes existing/future logger-middleware assertions vacuous. Return the same instance (or one sharing the same Logs state).

title: Contextual logger not applied to stream endpoints
body: SubscribeStream, PublishStream and RunStream pass the context through unchanged, so logs emitted downstream for streaming requests get no pluginId/dsUID/endpoint attributes. Since this middleware's sole purpose is enriching the context, adding instrumentContext for these three endpoints would make logging consistent across all client methods.

title: traceID may be dropped from plugin request logs
body: The explicit `traceID` log param (previously added via tracing.TraceIDFromContext) was removed and replaced by m.logger.FromContext(ctx). This only preserves the traceID field if the infra logger's FromContext injects it and the span is recording; otherwise plugin egress logs lose correlation with traces, breaking existing log queries/dashboards that filter on traceID.

title: localCache is populated before the store write, so the device limit is silently bypassed
body: tagDeviceUI() calls a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{}) before CreateOrUpdateDevice(). When the device limit is reached and CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, the cache entry remains, so every subsequent request with the same device id returns nil early (for the 29-minute cache TTL) and the anonymous client authenticates successfully. The limit is therefore enforced only for the first request of each new device and then effectively bypassed, and behaviour differs per Grafana instance (each has its own local cache). The cache entry should only be set after a successful store write.

title: updateDevice reports ErrDeviceLimitReached when MySQL reports 0 changed rows for an existing device
body: updateDevice treats rowsAffected == 0 as ErrDeviceLimitReached. With MySQL, UPDATE reports the number of *changed* rows, so an existing, known device whose client_ip/user_agent/updated_at values are unchanged (e.g. repeated requests within the same second, since MySQL datetime precision is seconds) yields 0 and the user is wrongly rejected as over the device limit even though the device is already tracked. Consider checking for row existence separately or relying on a SELECT before deciding.

title: Count-then-insert is not atomic; the device limit can be exceeded
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts devices and then performs the upsert in two separate sessions. Concurrent requests (same instance or multiple Grafana instances sharing the DB) can all read count < deviceLimit and then each insert a new device, exceeding the configured limit by an arbitrary amount. Also, a COUNT(*) query is now executed on every tagged request, adding DB load on the authentication hot path.

title: Device tagging moved onto the synchronous authentication path
body: TagDevice is now called inline in Authenticate with the request context instead of in a background goroutine. Every anonymous request now blocks on a COUNT query plus an upsert/update against the database before authentication completes, which increases request latency and DB pressure for anonymous-heavy instances. If synchronous behaviour is required for limit enforcement, at least the non-limit path should avoid the extra COUNT.

title: Raw ErrDeviceLimitReached returned from Authenticate yields an opaque 500
body: ErrDeviceLimitReached is created with fmt.Errorf and returned directly from Authenticate. The authn layer has no status mapping for it, so a user hitting the device limit gets a generic internal error instead of a meaningful message/status (e.g. errutil with 429/403 and a user-facing message). This makes the new limit undiagnosable for operators and users.

title: New auth.anonymous device_limit setting is undocumented and missing from defaults.ini
body: cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit reads [auth.anonymous] device_limit, but conf/defaults.ini, conf/sample.ini and the anonymous-auth documentation are not updated in this PR. Users have no discoverable way to learn about or configure the new limit, and the setting won't appear in the shipped config files.

title: Frontend type declares anonymousDeviceLimit as possibly undefined while backend always sends a number
body: The backend DTO field AnonymousDeviceLimit is a non-pointer int64 with json tag "anonymousDeviceLimit" (no omitempty), so the value is always present and is 0 when no limit is configured. Typing it as `number | undefined` in GrafanaConfig (and initialising it to `undefined` in GrafanaBootConfig) means consumers must handle a state that never occurs while the real "no limit" signal (0) is untyped/undocumented. Either make it `number` with a documented 0 meaning, or omit the field server-side when unset.

title: rowsAffected==0 wrongly treated as device limit reached on MySQL / unchanged rows
body: updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached whenever the UPDATE affects 0 rows. With MySQL (default CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS off) an UPDATE that matches an existing row but sets identical values reports 0 affected rows, so an already-registered anonymous device whose client_ip/user_agent/updated_at are unchanged would be denied authentication even though it is within the limit. The error is also semantically wrong for the 'device not found' case; a known device should succeed. Consider checking existence explicitly (SELECT) instead of relying on rows affected.

title: localCache is populated before the store write, letting over-limit devices bypass the limit
body: tagDeviceUI calls a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{}) before CreateOrUpdateDevice. If the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached (and the request is therefore rejected in Anonymous.Authenticate), the device id is nevertheless cached, so for the next ~29 minutes tagDeviceUI returns nil early and the same unknown device is granted anonymous access without ever being recorded. The limit is effectively bypassed by retrying. The cache should only be set after a successful write.

title: Count-then-insert is not atomic, limit can be exceeded
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice reads the device count and then inserts in a separate statement/session. Concurrent anonymous requests (or multiple Grafana instances sharing the DB) can all observe count < deviceLimit and each insert, so the stored device count can exceed the configured device_limit. A transaction with appropriate locking, or an atomic INSERT ... SELECT guarded by the count, is needed if the limit is meant to be enforced.

title: Device tagging moved onto the request path adds a DB count+write per anonymous request
body: TagDevice was previously executed in a background goroutine with its own timeout; it is now called synchronously inside Authenticate. For every anonymous request that misses the local cache this now performs a SELECT COUNT(*) on anon_device plus an upsert before the request can proceed, and any DB latency/failure directly affects anonymous page loads. Under high anonymous traffic with a configured limit this COUNT query over a large table is a notable added cost.

title: Raw ErrDeviceLimitReached returned from Authenticate yields an unhelpful 500/opaque error
body: ErrDeviceLimitReached is created with fmt.Errorf and returned directly from Authenticate. The authn layer expects typed errutil errors to produce a correct HTTP status and user-facing message; a plain error will surface as a generic internal error rather than a clear 'anonymous device limit reached' response, and gives no way for the frontend to show the limit message implied by the new anonymousDeviceLimit frontend setting.

title: New auth.anonymous device_limit option not documented in defaults.ini/sample.ini or docs
body: cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit is read from [auth.anonymous] device_limit, but no entry was added to conf/defaults.ini, conf/sample.ini, or the configuration docs. Users have no discoverable way to learn about the setting or its default (0 = unlimited), and Grafana convention is that every ini option is listed in defaults.ini.

title: ProvideAnonDBStore signature change may break wire DI registration
body: ProvideAnonDBStore now takes an extra int64 argument and AnonDeviceService constructs the store itself instead of receiving anonstore.AnonStore. If ProvideAnonDBStore is still registered as a provider in pkg/server/wire.go (not included in this PR), wire will fail to build because there is no provider for int64, and any other consumer of the injected AnonStore loses it. Verify the DI graph was updated.

title: Device limit tests do not cover the update path for an existing device at the limit
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only asserts that a *new* device id is rejected once the limit is hit. There is no test that an already-registered device still succeeds (updates its updated_at/client_ip) when the limit is reached — exactly the path that is broken by the rowsAffected==0 logic on MySQL/unchanged rows. Add a case re-tagging the existing device id after the limit is reached.

title: Local cache is populated before the device is persisted, allowing the device limit to be bypassed
body: In tagDeviceUI the cache key is set with a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{}) before CreateOrUpdateDevice is called. When the device limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice/updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached and the request is rejected, but the key stays in the local cache for ~29 minutes. On the next request with the same X-Grafana-Device-Id, tagDeviceUI returns nil early (cache hit) and the anonymous user is authenticated without ever being recorded, effectively bypassing the new limit for the whole cache TTL. The cache entry should only be stored after a successful store call.

title: Count-then-insert device limit check is not atomic
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice reads CountDevices and then performs the insert in a separate session. Under concurrent anonymous requests several goroutines can all observe count < deviceLimit and all insert, so the configured device_limit can be exceeded by an arbitrary amount. Enforcement needs to be done inside a transaction (or via a conditional insert) if the limit is meant to be a hard cap.

title: rowsAffected == 0 is wrongly reported as ErrDeviceLimitReached for known devices on MySQL
body: updateDevice maps rowsAffected == 0 to ErrDeviceLimitReached. On MySQL, an UPDATE that matches a row but changes no column values reports 0 affected rows (CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS not set), so an existing, within-expiry device whose client_ip/user_agent/updated_at are unchanged (same second precision) will be treated as over the limit and the user will be denied access. Use rows-matched semantics or an explicit existence check instead.

title: Device tagging moved onto the synchronous auth path, adding DB round-trips per request
body: TagDevice was previously executed in a background goroutine with its own timeout; it is now called inline in Authenticate. Every anonymous authentication that misses the local cache now blocks on a COUNT query plus an upsert against anon_device, and any DB slowness/latency now directly affects anonymous request latency and can fail authentication (errors other than ErrDeviceLimitReached are only logged, but the latency remains). Worth confirming this is intended and bounding it (context timeout).

title: ErrDeviceLimitReached surfaces as a generic 500 to clients
body: ErrDeviceLimitReached is created with fmt.Errorf and returned verbatim from Authenticate. The authn layer has no mapping for it, so a user blocked by the device limit gets an opaque internal error rather than a meaningful status/message (e.g. 429/403 with explanation). Define it with errutil so the API returns an actionable response.

title: New auth.anonymous device_limit option is undocumented
body: cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit is read from [auth.anonymous] device_limit but the option is not added to conf/defaults.ini, conf/sample.ini, or the configuration docs. Operators have no discoverable way to learn about the setting or its default (0 = unlimited).

title: anonymousDeviceLimit initialized to undefined infers type `undefined`
body: `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined` without an explicit annotation gives the property the type `undefined`, while the backend always sends a number (0 when unset) via merge(). Consumers that read it as a number will fail type checking, and the declared `number | undefined` in GrafanaConfig never actually becomes undefined. Annotate as `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined`.

title: Cleanup job interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The background cleanup ticker was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This is unrelated to the deadlock fix and makes all cleanup jobs (temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history) run 10x more often, which increases DB load substantially on large installs. Also, the per-run timeout is 9 minutes, so runs can now overlap/queue behind each other. This looks like a leftover debugging change and should be reverted.

title: Debug logging left in at Error level, dumping all IDs on every batch
body: `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", ..., "ids", ids, ...)` and the equivalent calls at lines 537, 554, 557, 576 and 579 log normal successful operation at ERROR severity, and include the entire batch of IDs (up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize, default in the thousands) in each message. This will spam error logs/alerting on every cleanup cycle and produce huge log lines. These should be removed or downgraded to Debug without the full ID slice.

title: Parameter-limit workaround only guards SQLite; other drivers can exceed placeholder limits
body: deleteByIDs inlines IDs only when `GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite && AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999`. For Postgres (pq limits a statement to 65535 parameters) and MySQL (max_prepared_stmt / packet limits), a large configured AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize will produce a DELETE with that many placeholders and fail at runtime. Additionally the condition is based on the configured batch size rather than `len(ids)`, so behaviour depends on config rather than the actual statement being built. Consider chunking the ID list to a fixed safe size (e.g. 999) for all dialects.

title: Cleanup job ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The background cleanup ticker was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This makes all cleanup jobs (temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, query history) run 10x more often, which is a significant and unrelated behavior/load change — and because each `clean()` run has a 9-minute timeout, runs can now overlap/stack up. This looks like leftover debugging from testing the annotation cleanup and should be reverted.

title: Debug logging left in at Error level, logging full ID lists
body: `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", ..., "ids", ids, ...)` (and the analogous calls at lines 537, 554, 557, 576, 579) log routine, successful cleanup progress at ERROR severity, and include the entire batch of IDs. With a batch size of up to tens of thousands this produces huge log lines every cleanup cycle and will trigger error alerting/noise for operators. These should be removed or downgraded to Debug without dumping the ID slice.

title: SQLite parameter-limit check uses configured batch size instead of actual ID count
body: The decision whether to inline IDs into the DELETE statement is based on `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit` rather than `len(ids) > sqliteParameterLimit`. Also, the limit is applied only for SQLite; other drivers have their own limits (e.g. Postgres allows at most 65535 bind parameters), so a batch size above that would fail at runtime on Postgres. Basing the branch on `len(ids)` and applying a safe limit for all backends (or chunking the deletes) would be more robust.

title: fetchIDs builds SQL by string concatenation of caller-provided condition
body: `fetchIDs` interpolates both the table name and a free-form `condition` string directly into the SQL text, and callers build the condition with `fmt.Sprintf` including `annotationType` and `cutoffDate`. Current callers pass constants/ints so there is no live injection, but this pattern is fragile: any future caller passing user-derived input creates an injection. Parameterizing the cutoff date and keeping the condition to a fixed set of templates would avoid this.

title: Cleanup job interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The background cleanup ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. The clean() routine itself has a 9-minute timeout, so runs can now overlap/queue up, and all cleanup jobs (temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, annotations, query history) will execute 10x more often, increasing DB load significantly. This looks like leftover debugging from reproducing the deadlock and is unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR.

title: Debug logging left in at Error level, dumping full ID lists
body: r.log.Error(...) is used in CleanAnnotations (lines 534, 537, 554, 557) and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags (lines 576, 579) for purely informational messages, including the entire slice of IDs being deleted. On a busy instance with large batch sizes (e.g. 32767 IDs per batch) this will spam error-level logs with huge messages every cleanup cycle, trigger alerting on error logs, and is pure debug leftover. These should be Debug level (or removed), and the ID list should not be logged.

title: SQLite parameter-limit workaround keyed on batch size instead of actual ID count
body: deleteByIDs decides between inlined literals and bound parameters based on r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999, not len(ids). The condition is also tied to GetDBType()==SQLite only. If any other code path (or a future caller) passes more IDs than the configured batch size, or if the configured batch size is unset/zero while a large slice is passed, the parameterized branch will be used with >999 placeholders and SQLite will fail with "too many SQL variables". Base the decision on len(ids) instead, and chunk the deletes so the statement is always within the driver limit.

title: Non-atomic fetch-then-delete can loop extra times and miscount
body: fetchIDs and deleteByIDs run in separate sessions, so rows found by the SELECT may already be gone when the DELETE runs. untilDoneOrCancelled only stops when affected==0, so in a concurrent scenario a batch that selects N ids but deletes 0 terminates the loop early (under-delete, as documented), but a batch that selects ids and deletes a subset keeps looping; combined with the MaxCount offset query this can repeatedly re-read the same rows. Consider terminating on len(ids)==0 rather than affected==0 so the loop semantics match the actual work remaining.

title: Async legacy writes derive from request context and get cancelled
body: All four goroutines (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) build their timeout context from the incoming request `ctx`. The apiserver cancels the request context as soon as the HTTP handler returns, which typically happens before the goroutine completes its legacy write. The legacy store write will therefore frequently be aborted mid-flight, silently losing the data that mode 3 is supposed to keep in sync. Use a detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or a fresh background context carrying the needed request values) before applying the timeout.

title: Storage failure recorded as legacy duration in Create/Update
body: In Create (line 45) and Update (line 129) the error path for the *storage* call calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)`. This attributes unified-storage failures/latency to the legacy backend metric, making the dashboards and error rates for both backends wrong. Should be `recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

title: Delete passes object name as the 'kind' metric label
body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the resource `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. This both mislabels the metric and causes unbounded label cardinality (one time-series per object name), which can blow up the Prometheus registry.

title: DeleteCollection legacy goroutine records storage duration
body: Inside the async legacy DeleteCollection the code calls `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` with `startLegacy`. This records legacy latency/errors under the storage metric, double-counting storage and hiding legacy failures. Should be `recordLegacyDuration`.

title: Delete puts the un-enriched logger into the context
body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` uses `d.Log` instead of the `log` built on line 96, so downstream code reading the logger from the context loses the name/kind/method values. Every other method passes `log`.

title: Tests never synchronize with the async legacy write (data race + no coverage)
body: Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection in mode 3 spawn a goroutine that calls the legacy mock. The tests return immediately after the call, so (a) the legacy write is never asserted — mode 3's core behaviour is untested, and (b) the shared `*mock.Mock` is read/written concurrently by the goroutine and by the test's assertions/teardown, which `go test -race` can flag as a data race and causes intermittent panics (mock calls after test completion). Add a synchronization point (e.g. wait channel from the mock's Run/ `assert.Eventually`) and assert the legacy call happened.

title: Async legacy writes inherit request context and get cancelled
body: All four goroutines (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) build their timeout context from the incoming request ctx (`context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). The apiserver cancels the request context as soon as the HTTP handler returns, which typically happens before the goroutine completes. The legacy write will then fail with context canceled, silently dropping the legacy copy that mode 3 exists to maintain. Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (preserving auth/user values) as the parent before applying the timeout.

title: Storage error path records legacy duration metric
body: In Create, when `d.Storage.Create` fails the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` even though the failing call was to unified storage. Same in Update (line 129). This mislabels failures: storage error rates/latencies will be missing and legacy metrics will be polluted with storage failures. Should be `recordStorageDuration`.

title: Delete success passes object name as the 'kind' metric label
body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the resource name instead of `options.Kind`. Since the name is unbounded per-object, this creates an unbounded-cardinality Prometheus label, risking memory blowup in the metrics registry, and makes the metric unusable for per-kind aggregation.

title: DeleteCollection legacy goroutine records storage duration
body: The goroutine measuring the legacy DeleteCollection calls `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `recordLegacyDuration`, so legacy delete-collection latency/errors are never recorded and storage metrics are double-counted with legacy timings.

title: Delete puts the un-enriched logger in the context
body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` uses the base logger rather than `log`, so downstream code logging from the context loses the name/kind/method values that every other method in this file propagates.

title: Legacy Update receives the raw objInfo, re-applying the patch against the legacy object
body: The previous implementation wrapped objInfo with the already-updated object (`updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}`) before calling legacy. Now the raw `objInfo` is passed, so legacy will call `UpdatedObject` against its own stored object. For patch/apply requests this can produce a different result than what was written to unified storage (and resourceVersion precondition checks are evaluated against legacy's RV), causing the two stores to diverge or the legacy update to fail with a conflict.

title: Tests never synchronize with the async legacy write
body: Mode 3 now performs the legacy write in a goroutine, but the tests return immediately after the storage call. Nothing asserts that Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection is invoked, so the core behaviour of this PR is untested. Worse, the shared `mock.Mock` is read/written by the goroutine after the test function finishes, which is a data race (will fail under -race) and can cause 'mock called after test completion' panics. Add a synchronization hook (e.g. a channel/WaitGroup signalled from the mock's Run function) and assert the legacy calls.

title: Local registry shadows package-level one inconsistently
body: `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` inside TestMode3_Get shadows the package-level `p` used by every other test here, while the mode1 test removed exactly this pattern. All other subtests reuse one global registry across many NewDualWriter calls; if the metrics registration uses MustRegister this repeated registration of the same collectors will panic. Pick one approach (fresh registry per test is safest) and apply it consistently.

title: Unrelated and duplicated go.work.sum entries
body: This PR adds ~16 go.work.sum lines unrelated to the dual-writer change, including a duplicate `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod` entry that already exists two lines above. These look like accidental local-tooling churn and should be dropped from the PR.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and will be cancelled
body: All four goroutines (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) derive their timeout context from the incoming request `ctx`. As soon as the HTTP handler returns (which happens immediately, since the goroutine is fired and the response is returned), the apiserver cancels the request context, which cancels the derived child context. The legacy write will then frequently fail with `context canceled` instead of running for its intended 10s budget, silently losing the legacy copy of the data. Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (preserving auth/user values) before applying the timeout.

title: Storage failure recorded as legacy duration in Create and Update
body: On the storage error path of Create (line 45) and Update (line 129) the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with `startStorage`. The failing call was to unified storage, so this inflates the legacy error/duration metric and leaves storage failures unrecorded, making the mode-3 dashboards misleading.

title: DeleteCollection goroutine records legacy call as storage duration
body: Inside the async legacy DeleteCollection goroutine the result is recorded via `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` with `startLegacy`. This attributes legacy latency/errors to the storage metric; it should be `recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy delete-collection failures will therefore never show up in the legacy error metric.

title: Object name used as metric label in Delete success path
body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. Since names are unbounded (one per resource), this creates an unbounded number of Prometheus label values, causing cardinality explosion / memory growth in the metrics registry, and it also breaks comparability with the other recorded durations.

title: Delete puts the base logger in the context instead of the enriched one
body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` uses the base logger rather than `log`, so downstream code reading the logger from the context loses the name/kind/method values that were just attached. Every other method in the file passes `log`.

title: Mode 3 tests race with the async legacy goroutine and never assert it ran
body: The implementation now performs the legacy write in a goroutine, but the tests return as soon as the synchronous call completes. The same `*mock.Mock` is shared between the legacy and storage mocks, so the goroutine calls `m.Called(...)` concurrently with (or after) the test's assertions — a data race that `-race` will flag, and possibly a call into a `t` that has already finished. Additionally no test asserts that the legacy store was actually written to (e.g. via `mock.AssertExpectations` after waiting), so the core behaviour of mode 3 is untested. The tests need synchronization (e.g. a channel/WaitGroup signalled from the legacy mock) before asserting.

title: Legacy Create is given the pre-create object which storage may have mutated
body: The goroutine passes the original `obj` to `d.Legacy.Create`. `d.Storage.Create` may have mutated `obj` in place (resourceVersion, UID, generated name) or the legacy store may generate a different name/UID, so the two stores can diverge in identity — exactly what mode 3's background legacy write is meant to prevent. Consider passing the returned `created` object (as mode 2's update path did with `updateWrapper`).

title: Duplicate go.work.sum entry added
body: `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod` is added at line 408 while the identical line already exists a few lines above. These go.work.sum additions look like unrelated/accidental churn for a dual-writer change and should be dropped or regenerated.

title: Cache is overwritten with nil/partial result on error
body: `entryPointAssetsCache = result` is executed unconditionally, even when `err != nil` and `result == nil`. A transient failure (e.g. CDN/file read error) therefore clears a previously valid cached value, forcing every subsequent request to re-read the manifest and potentially return errors. Only assign the cache when `err == nil && result != nil`.

title: No re-check of cache after acquiring write lock
body: After the RLock fast path fails, the code takes the write lock but does not re-check `entryPointAssetsCache`. Under concurrent startup load, N goroutines queued on the write lock will each re-read and re-parse assets-manifest.json even though the first one already populated the cache. Add a double-checked `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return ... }` after acquiring the lock.

title: Cache overwritten with nil on read failure
body: When readWebAssetsFromFile/CDN fails, result is nil and it is still assigned to entryPointAssetsCache, clobbering a previously good cached value and forcing every subsequent request to re-read the manifest (and return nil). Guard the assignment with `if result != nil` / `err == nil`.

title: No re-check of cache after acquiring write lock
body: After taking the write lock the function does not re-verify that entryPointAssetsCache is still nil. Concurrent cold-start requests will each serialize on the mutex and redundantly parse/fetch the manifest (including an HTTP request in the CDN case) even though an earlier goroutine already populated the cache.

title: No re-check of cache after acquiring write lock
body: After the read-lock fast path fails, the function takes the write lock but never re-reads entryPointAssetsCache. If N requests arrive concurrently on a cold cache, each one in turn will re-read and re-parse assets-manifest.json (or hit the CDN) while serialized on the mutex, instead of the first filling the cache and the rest returning it. Re-checking `entryPointAssetsCache != nil` (for non-Dev env) right after Lock() avoids the redundant I/O and the resulting latency spike at startup.

title: Failed load overwrites a previously valid cached value with nil
body: `entryPointAssetsCache = result` is executed unconditionally, including when readWebAssetsFromFile/CDN returned an error and result is nil. A single transient failure (e.g. file temporarily unreadable, CDN error) wipes an already-good cached value, so every subsequent call must reload and will return nil assets until a load succeeds. The assignment should be guarded by `if err == nil && result != nil`.

title: enableSqlExpressions contains unreachable/dead logic and always returns false
body: `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` (note the inverted logic), then returns false in both branches. The feature-toggle read has no effect and the inverted expression is misleading: a future reader may 'fix' the branch and accidentally re-enable SQL expressions when the flag is *disabled*. If the intent is to hard-disable the feature, the function should simply `return false` (or the QueryTypeSQL case should error unconditionally) with a comment explaining the CVE; the dead flag check should be removed.

title: Misleading error message for disabled SQL expressions
body: Returning "sqlExpressions is not implemented" to users who have the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle enabled is confusing, since the feature previously worked and the toggle still exists and is documented. The message should state that SQL expressions are currently disabled/unavailable so operators don't file bugs about a toggle that silently does nothing.

title: No test asserting SQL expressions are disabled
body: This PR is a security fix that disables a code path leading to RCE/LFI, but adds no test. A regression test asserting that `ReadQuery` with `QueryTypeSQL` returns an error (even with the `sqlExpressions` toggle enabled) and that `sql.NewInMemoryDB().QueryFramesInto`/`RunCommands` return errors would prevent an accidental re-enable of the vulnerable path.

title: enableSqlExpressions is dead logic that unconditionally returns false
body: `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns `false` in both branches, so the feature-flag read has no effect and the variable is pointless. The function is effectively `return false`. This is confusing (a reader could think the flag re-enables the feature, and the inverted `!` suggests the opposite of the intent) and is prone to breaking if someone 'fixes' the branch later. Replace with an explicit unconditional rejection (or a correctly polarised flag check) and drop the unused feature lookup.

title: Stub DB silently keeps SQL expression code path alive with runtime errors
body: The new stub `sql.DB` returns "not implemented" from `TablesList`, `RunCommands` and `QueryFramesInto`. In `SQLCommand.Execute` (pkg/expr/sql_command.go:100) this error is placed into `rsp.Error` and `nil` is returned, so the legacy (non-reader) SQL expression path returns a generic opaque "not implemented" to the user instead of a clear 'feature disabled' message. Consider short-circuiting in `NewSQLCommand`/`UnmarshalSQLCommand` with an explicit disabled error so behaviour is consistent across both entry points.

title: No test asserting SQL expressions are rejected
body: This change is a security fix disabling the SQL expression query type, but no test was added verifying that `ReadQuery` with `QueryTypeSQL` returns an error (both with and without the `sqlExpressions` feature flag enabled), nor that `UnmarshalSQLCommand`/`SQLCommand.Execute` no longer executes SQL. Without such a test, a future change to `enableSqlExpressions` could silently reintroduce CVE-2024-9264.

title: enableSqlExpressions is dead logic that always returns false
body: `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns false on both branches, so the feature-flag read has no effect and the function is a constant `false`. While the intent (hard-disabling SQL expressions) is achieved, the code is misleading: a reader/linter can't tell whether the flag is honoured, and a future edit to one branch could silently re-enable the vulnerable path. Replace with an explicit `return false` plus a comment referencing CVE-2024-9264, or remove the helper and return the error directly.

title: Error message 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' is misleading
body: Users enabling the still-present `sqlExpressions` feature toggle will get 'sqlExpressions is not implemented', which suggests a missing feature rather than a deliberately disabled one. Since the toggle remains documented, the message should state that SQL expressions are currently disabled, so operators don't file bugs or assume a build problem.

title: Legacy (non-reader) SQL expression path is not blocked, only stubbed
body: `UnmarshalSQLCommand`/`NewSQLCommand` still accept SQL expression nodes; the feature-flag gate was only added in `reader.go` (ReadQuery). On the legacy query path, `sql.TablesList` now fails inside `NewSQLCommand`, returning a generic 'error reading SQL command' BadRequest, and `Execute` would return an opaque 'not implemented' as a query error. This makes the disable behaviour inconsistent and the failure mode confusing; the legacy path should explicitly reject SQL expressions with the same clear message.

title: No test asserting SQL expressions are disabled
body: This PR disables a security-sensitive feature purely by stubbing out the DB implementation and adding an always-false flag check, but no test asserts that a QueryTypeSQL query is rejected. Without such a test, a future refactor (e.g. reintroducing an engine or 'fixing' enableSqlExpressions) can silently re-enable the RCE/LFI path. Add a unit test for ReadQuery with QueryTypeSQL expecting an error.

title: Removing the BuildIndex lock allows concurrent builds of the same index key
body: BuildIndex previously held b.cacheMu for its whole body, which serialized index creation. Now only the cache write is locked, so two callers for the same NamespacedResource (e.g. a watch event handler plus startup build, or two concurrent search requests that both see a nil index via GetIndex) can run bleve.New() against the same on-disk directory concurrently. bleve.New fails or corrupts state when the directory already exists/is open, and the second winner overwrites the cache entry while the first index is still referenced by a caller. Some per-key coordination (e.g. a keyed mutex / singleflight) is needed, not just a cache-write lock.

title: TotalDocs reads b.cache without holding cacheMu
body: TotalDocs iterates b.cache with no lock while BuildIndex now writes to the map under cacheMu from worker goroutines and from the watch-event path. Concurrent map read/write panics the process. This is newly reachable because search.init() now logs s.search.TotalDocs() and index builds can be triggered asynchronously by the watch goroutine. Take cacheMu.RLock() in TotalDocs.

title: Init failure in NewResourceServer leaks the server context and background resources
body: When s.Init(ctx) returns an error, NewResourceServer returns nil without calling cancel() on the context created above (and without stopping any lifecycle/blob resources already initialized). The context and any goroutines started during partial init (e.g. the storage watch poller started by backend WatchWriteEvents) are leaked for the life of the process. Call cancel() (and ideally s.Stop) before returning the error.

title: Shared `err` variable written from concurrent errgroup goroutines
body: Inside the `for _, info := range stats` loop, each goroutine assigns to the outer `err` (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and also increments the shared `totalBatchesIndexed` counter without synchronization. With initWorkers > 1 these are concurrent writes to the same variables — a data race that can be detected by -race and can mask or mis-report build errors (one goroutine's error being overwritten by another's nil). Use a goroutine-local `err :=` and an atomic counter.

title: Postgres path of the storage-server integration test is now skipped
body: The only integration test exercising the storage server target is disabled for postgres with a TODO. Since this PR changes initialization to happen eagerly at ResourceServer construction (the riskiest behavioral change here), the test that would catch startup regressions no longer runs on postgres in CI, leaving that configuration uncovered.

title: Removing the write lock around BuildIndex allows concurrent builds for the same key
body: BuildIndex previously held b.cacheMu for the whole function, serializing all index builds. Now only the final cache write is locked. Two concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same NamespacedResource (e.g. a watch event triggering getOrCreateIndex while the startup indexing is still building, or two concurrent searches for the same key) will both call bleve.New on the same directory path (b.opts.Root/namespace/resource.group). bleve.New fails if the path already exists, so the second build errors out; for the mem-only case both builds complete and one index is silently discarded while duplicating all the indexing work and double-counting the IndexTenants metric. Consider per-key locking (e.g. an in-flight map or singleflight) rather than dropping the lock entirely.

title: TotalDocs reads b.cache without holding cacheMu
body: TotalDocs iterates b.cache with no lock while BuildIndex now writes to the map under b.cacheMu. Previously builds held the lock for their whole duration, which reduced the window; with the finer-grained locking, concurrent builds (startup indexing workers, watch-event driven builds) can write to the map while TotalDocs ranges over it, which is an unsynchronized map read/write and will trigger a fatal 'concurrent map iteration and map write' panic. TotalDocs is called from searchSupport.init logging, so this is reachable. Take b.cacheMu.RLock() in TotalDocs.

title: Shared err and counter written from concurrent errgroup goroutines
body: Inside the errgroup in searchSupport.init, each goroutine assigns to the enclosing `err` variable (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and increments the shared `totalBatchesIndexed` counter. With initWorkers > 1 these are unsynchronized writes from multiple goroutines: a data race, and `err` is also read after group.Wait() (line 195), so a failure in one namespace can be masked or an unrelated error reported. Use a goroutine-local `err :=` and an atomic/locked counter.

title: NewResourceServer leaks the server context and background goroutines when Init fails
body: s.Init(ctx) is now called in the constructor, but on error the function returns nil without calling the cancel func created at line 229. Any goroutines already started by the search watcher (searchSupport.init starts a watch goroutine on context.Background()) and by the backend poller keep running, and the cancelable context is never released. Call cancel() (and ideally s.Stop) before returning the error.

title: Stop() no longer has any effect on request handling since Init checks were removed
body: Stop sets s.initErr to 'service is stopping'/'service is stopped' as a guard, but every request handler's `if err := s.Init(ctx)` check was removed in this PR. After Stop, Create/Update/Delete/Read/List/Watch/Search/blob calls will proceed against a cancelled context and a stopped backend instead of returning a clear 'service is stopped' error. Either add an explicit stopped/served state check in the handlers or drop the now-dead initErr mutation in Stop.

title: Postgres path of the storage-server integration test is skipped without a tracking issue
body: The only integration coverage for running the storage server target with Postgres is now unconditionally skipped with a 'works locally' comment. Since this PR changes when unified storage initialization happens (now during server construction), this is exactly the path that would catch startup regressions on Postgres. At minimum reference a tracking issue so the skip does not become permanent.

title: Data race on shared `err` variable in index-build errgroup
body: In `searchSupport.init`, each `group.Go` closure assigns to the function-scoped `err` variable (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and `totalBatchesIndexed++` is incremented without synchronization. With `initWorkers > 1` these run concurrently, producing a genuine data race: build errors can be lost or overwritten (and `group.Wait()`'s result can be confused with a stale value), and the counter can be wrong. This matters more now that the coarse lock in `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` was removed, so the goroutines actually run in parallel. Use a local `err :=` inside the closure and an atomic counter.

title: Concurrent BuildIndex for the same key can collide on the bleve directory and cache entry
body: BuildIndex no longer holds `cacheMu` for the whole function; the lock is only taken when writing the cache. Two concurrent calls for the same NamespacedResource (e.g. a watch event triggering `getOrCreateIndex` while startup indexing runs) will both call `bleve.New(dir, ...)` on the same path, which fails (or corrupts) for file-backed indexes, and both will write to `b.cache[key]`, so one fully built index is silently discarded while readers may already hold it. Consider per-key locking / single-flight instead of no lock at all.

title: TotalDocs reads the cache map without holding cacheMu
body: `TotalDocs` iterates `b.cache` without taking `cacheMu` (even read lock). Previously writes to the map happened while BuildIndex held the exclusive lock for its entire duration; now writes are short but can occur from watch-event-driven builds at any time. `init()` in search.go now calls `s.search.TotalDocs()` while such builds can be in flight, so a concurrent map read/write panic is possible. Take `cacheMu.RLock()` in TotalDocs.

title: Context/goroutine leak when Init fails in NewResourceServer
body: `NewResourceServer` now calls `s.Init(ctx)` and returns `nil, err` on failure, but the `cancel` from `context.WithCancel` created a few lines above is never called on this path. The derived context stays alive, and any goroutines already started by `s.search.init` (the watch-event consumer goroutine started before the failure point) are never stopped. Add `defer`/explicit `cancel()` before returning the error.

title: Stop() no longer prevents further request handling
body: `Stop()` sets `s.initErr = "service is stopping"/"service is stopped"` as the mechanism to reject requests, but all the `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil` guards were removed from Create/Update/Delete/Read/List/Watch/Search/Blob handlers. After `Stop()` those handlers will keep serving requests against a cancelled background context and a stopped backend, instead of returning an error. Either re-add a lightweight 'is running' check to the handlers or drop the now-dead initErr mutation in Stop.

title: Call to isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments does not match any method
body: `UsernameForm.authenticate` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` but the only definition added in the parent class `UsernamePasswordForm` is `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)`. There is no no-arg overload, so this will not compile. Either add the no-arg variant or pass `context.getUser()`.

title: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires a non-null user, disabling conditional UI on the initial login page
body: `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` returns true only when `user != null`.
