The result is that interpolation runs twice on the same query: (a) `addAdHocFilters` is applied a second time to an expression that already contains those matchers, so ad hoc/adhoc-variable label matchers end up duplicated in the LogQL sent to Loki (e.g. `{app="x", env="prod", env="prod"}`), and (b) `templateSrv.replace` is re-run over a string that already contains substituted variable values, so any value that itself contains `$name`/`${name}` is expanded a second time, silently changing the query. Either strip `scopedVars`/`filters` from the sub-request, or flag the request as already interpolated so the downstream call is skipped.

title: Shard splitting path interpolates each query three times
body: `runShardSplitQuery` interpolates the targets with `applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)`, then hands the resulting sub-request (which still contains `scopedVars` and `filters`) to `runSplitQuery`, which interpolates again (querySplitting.ts:299), and finally `datasource.runQuery` -> `DataSourceWithBackend.query` interpolates a third time. The new assertion `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` in shardQuerySplitting.test.ts confirms the repeated calls (1 up-front + 1 per sub-request). Beyond wasted work (each call re-parses the LogQL expression in `addAdHocFilters`), repeated application of ad hoc filters duplicates label matchers and repeated `templateSrv.replace` can re-expand `$`-containing variable values in the already-interpolated expression, including the injected `__stream_shard__` selector context. Interpolation should happen exactly once per query.

title: Assertion locks in redundant interpolation count
body: `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` asserts that a single target is interpolated five times (once in `runShardSplitQuery` plus once per shard sub-request inside `runSplitQuery`). This encodes the redundant re-interpolation as expected behaviour, so a future fix that interpolates only once will fail this test, and the test is coupled to the number of shard groups rather than to the thing being verified (that queries are interpolated before being run). Prefer asserting that the targets reaching `runQuery` are interpolated, or `toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)` once the duplicate interpolation is removed. Note also that the mock mutates `query.expr` in place and is only correct because the substitution happens to be idempotent.

title: New test does not cover the actual regression (step used for partitioning)
body: The bug being fixed is that an un-interpolated `step` (e.g. `step: '$step'`) does not match the interval regex in `calculateStep`, so the metric time-range partitioning falls back to `intervalMs` and produces wrong split boundaries. The new test only asserts that `targets[0].expr`/`targets[0].step` on the first `runQuery` call are interpolated; it never asserts that the partitions/ranges (or the number of sub-requests) now reflect the interpolated step. The existing 'Correctly splits queries with step' test shows how range boundaries differ by step, so the fix could regress (e.g. interpolation moved back after partitioning) while this test still passes.

title: Test's replace mock ignores scopedVars, so `$__auto` substitution is unrealistic
body: The test's `replace: (input = '') => input.replace('$__auto', '5m')...` ignores the `scopedVars` argument. The real Loki `applyTemplateVariables` deliberately passes macros such as `$__auto`, `$__interval` and `$__range` through by overriding them in the scopedVars it hands to `templateSrv.replace`, so in production `count_over_time({a="b"}[$__auto])` is left untouched on the frontend and interpolated on the backend. The test therefore asserts a substitution that cannot happen in the real data source and gives false confidence about macro handling. Using a user-defined variable (e.g. `$range`/`$step`) would exercise the same code path realistically.

title: Queries are now interpolated twice (runSplitQuery + DataSourceWithBackend.query)
body: `runSplitQuery` now maps every target through `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)`, but each resulting sub-request is executed via `datasource.runQuery(subRequest)` → `super.query()` (`DataSourceWithBackend.query`), which already calls `applyTemplateVariables` on every target. So each split query is interpolated at least twice. Two concrete consequences: (1) ad hoc filters (`request.filters`) are applied by `addAdHocFilters()` a second time to an expression that already contains them, which can duplicate label matchers / pipeline stages (e.g. `| key="value" | key="value"`); (2) `templateSrv.replace()` runs again over values that were already substituted, so any variable whose value contains `$name`, `${name}` or `[[name]]` is expanded a second time and the final LogQL is wrong. If the interpolated query is only needed to make splitting decisions (step parsing, logs-vs-metric classification, `$__range` detection), keep it locally for those decisions and send the original targets downstream, or mark the request/targets as already interpolated so the backend data source layer skips the second pass.

title: Shard splitting path now interpolates each query three times
body: `runShardSplitQuery` interpolates all targets here; `splitQueriesByStreamShard` then builds `subRequest` from those interpolated + shard-annotated targets and hands it to `runSplitQuery` (line 163), which after this PR interpolates again, and `runQuery`/`DataSourceWithBackend.query` interpolates a third time. Besides the correctness problems of repeated interpolation (ad hoc filters re-appended to an expression that already carries them, template values containing `$`/`${}`/`[[]]` re-expanded), the expression handed to the 2nd/3rd pass already contains the injected `__stream_shard__=~"..." | drop __stream_shard__`, so `addAdHocFilters()` re-parses and re-modifies a mutated query whose stage ordering is no longer the user's. There is also avoidable cost: `addAdHocFilters` parses the LogQL expression per target, now once per shard group in addition to the per-sub-request pass.

title: Test asserts applyTemplateVariables is called 5 times for a single target, locking in redundant interpolation
body: `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` is for a request with a single target. The 5 calls come from one interpolation in `runShardSplitQuery` plus one per sub-request created by `runSplitQuery`, i.e. the assertion codifies that the same query is interpolated repeatedly instead of exactly once. This makes the test both a brittle magic number (it changes whenever the shard grouping or the number of split requests changes) and a guard that prevents noticing the double/triple interpolation problem. The intent of the test ("Interpolates queries before running") would be better expressed by asserting interpolation happened once per user target.

title: applyTemplateVariables mock mutates the query and is idempotent, masking repeated interpolation
body: The new mock `datasource.applyTemplateVariables = jest.fn().mockImplementation((query) => { query.expr = query.expr.replace('$SELECTOR', '{a="b"}'); return query; })` mutates the target object in place and performs a replacement that is a no-op the second time it runs. The real implementation returns a new object and is *not* idempotent (it re-applies ad hoc filters and re-runs template replacement). Because of this mock, the tests cannot detect that the same target is now interpolated multiple times, and they also silently mutate the shared `request.targets` fixture used by subsequent assertions in the same test.

title: New interpolation test is unrealistic and does not cover the risk introduced
body: The stubbed `replace: (input = '') => input.replace('$__auto', '5m').replace('$step', '5m')` ignores `scopedVars`, whereas the real Loki `applyTemplateVariables` deliberately strips `__auto`/`__interval`/`__range` from the scoped vars so that these are interpolated by the backend; so in production `$__auto` is still present in the expression at this point and the assertion `expr === 'count_over_time({a="b"}[5m])'` does not reflect real behavior. More importantly, the actual risk of this change — the target being interpolated again by `DataSourceWithBackend.query` inside `runQuery`, duplicating ad hoc filters from `request.filters` and re-expanding variable values that contain `$` — is untested. Add a test with `request.filters` set asserting the ad hoc filter appears exactly once in the final expression sent to `runQuery`, and one with a variable value containing `$`/`${}` to assert it is not re-expanded.

title: Targets are now interpolated twice (runSplitQuery + DataSourceWithBackend.query)
body: `runSplitQuery` now maps every target through `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)`, but each sub-request is later executed with `datasource.runQuery(subRequest)`, which goes through `DataSourceWithBackend.query()` and applies `applyTemplateVariables(q, request.scopedVars, request.filters)` again to the same (already interpolated) target. The second pass is not a no-op: Loki's `applyTemplateVariables` calls `addAdHocFilters(target.expr, adhocFilters)`, so ad-hoc filters are injected into the expression a second time (duplicated label matchers / duplicated `| key="value"` stages), and `templateSrv.replace` runs again over the already-substituted expression, so a variable value that itself contains a `$`-prefixed token gets expanded a second time. It also costs an extra LogQL parse/rewrite per sub-request. Either the pre-interpolation needs a way to mark targets as already interpolated, or the interpolation must stay in a single place.

title: Shard path interpolates, then delegates to runSplitQuery which interpolates again
body: `runShardSplitQuery` interpolates all targets here, builds a sub-request whose expressions already contain the shard matcher (`__stream_shard__=~"..."` / `| drop __stream_shard__`), and then passes it to `runSplitQuery` (line 163), which — after this PR — interpolates every target once more, and `datasource.runQuery` triggers a third pass inside `DataSourceWithBackend.query`. The repeated `applyTemplateVariables` calls re-run `addAdHocFilters` on the shard-rewritten expression, so ad-hoc filters can be added two or three times (duplicated matchers, and for non-indexed labels filter stages appended after the injected `drop` stage). The updated test at shardQuerySplitting.test.ts:112 (`applyTemplateVariables` expected to be called 5 times for one target) is direct evidence of this redundancy; it only passes because the mock returns the same object unchanged after the first call.

title: New interpolation test mocks replace() so it cannot show $__auto is actually resolved up-front
body: The test supplies a `replace` implementation that unconditionally rewrites `$__auto` and `$step` regardless of the `scopedVars` it is given. Loki's `applyTemplateVariables` deliberately strips `__auto`/`__interval`/`__interval_ms`/`__range*` from `scopedVars` because those are interpolated on the backend, so in production `$__auto` will still be present in the expression after this new front-end interpolation step and will be resolved per sub-request range on the backend — i.e. the behaviour the linked issue complains about. With the current mock the assertion on `count_over_time({a="b"}[5m])` passes no matter what `applyTemplateVariables` does with `$__auto`, giving false confidence that the issue is fixed. The test should drive interpolation through realistic `scopedVars` (including `__auto`) and a `replace` that honours them.

title: Test asserts a magic call count that encodes redundant interpolation, and the mutating mock hides repeat interpolation
body: `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` locks in the fact that one target is interpolated once in `runShardSplitQuery` plus once per sub-request inside `runSplitQuery`. Because the mock mutates and returns the same query object (`query.expr = query.expr.replace('$SELECTOR', ...)`), the extra calls are no-ops and the test cannot detect side effects of repeated interpolation such as duplicated ad-hoc filters. Any future change to the number of shard groups will also break this assertion for reasons unrelated to interpolation. A test asserting that ad-hoc filters/variables are applied exactly once to the final expression would be more meaningful.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, discarding recorded logs
body: `TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()` instead of the receiver, so the returned logger writes its `InfoLogs`/`DebugLogs`/... counters into a throwaway instance. Since `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` now always goes through `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info("Plugin Request Completed", ...)`, any test that injects `plog.NewTestLogger()` into the middleware and then asserts on `logger.InfoLogs.Calls`/`Message`/`Ctx` will observe zero calls — either failing outright or, worse, silently passing assertions that expect nothing to be logged. The fake should return `f` (optionally recording the ctx) so logging through the contextual path remains observable.

title: New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no tests and the moved log fields are unverified
body: This PR moves the `pluginId`, `endpoint`, `dsName`, `dsUID` and `uname` fields out of the explicit log params in `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` and into context attributes set by the brand-new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware`, but no test is added for the new middleware and no test asserts that the "Plugin Request Completed" log line still carries those fields. The correctness now depends on (a) the middleware being registered ahead of `LoggerMiddleware` in the chain and (b) `log.WithContextualAttributes` attributes being picked up by `Logger.FromContext`. A silent regression here would drop fields that log-based dashboards/alerts rely on, with nothing in CI to catch it.

title: Adding FromContext to the exported plugins/log.Logger interface is a breaking change
body: `plugins/log.Logger` is an exported interface consumed across the plugin packages and by out-of-tree code (e.g. grafana-enterprise). Adding the `FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger` method breaks every existing implementation that is not updated in this PR; only the two in-tree implementations (`grafanaInfraLogWrapper` and `TestLogger`) were adjusted, and the `var _ Logger = ...` compile checks only cover those. Any external or generated implementation will fail to compile after this change, so it needs to be coordinated/announced or the method should be introduced via an optional extension interface.

title: FromContext silently drops contextual fields if the concrete type assertion fails
body: `grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext` asserts the result of `d.l.FromContext(ctx)` to `*log.ConcreteLogger` and, on failure, falls back to `d.New()` — a logger with no context attributes at all. The failure path is silent: if `infra/log` ever returns a different `Logger` implementation from `FromContext`, every plugin request log line would silently lose `pluginId`, `endpoint`, `dsName`, `dsUID`, `uname` and `traceID`, with no error or warning to indicate why. Consider storing the `log.Logger` interface in the wrapper instead of the concrete `*ConcreteLogger`, so no assertion is needed.

title: Logger name still "plugin.instrumentation" after the rename
body: `NewLoggerMiddleware` is still constructed with `log.New("plugin.instrumentation")`, so the emitted log lines carry `logger=plugin.instrumentation` even though the instrumentation middleware has been renamed to the metrics middleware and the contextual logging has been split out. Since the goal of this change is naming consistency, and this name is user-visible in logs (and used for per-logger level configuration), it should be updated to something that matches the new structure (e.g. `plugin.logger`/`plugin.request`), keeping in mind that changing it affects existing log filters.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, discarding recorded logs
body: `TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()` instead of the receiver (or a logger sharing its `Logs` state). `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` now emits its only log line via `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`, so any test that injects a `*TestLogger` and then asserts on `InfoLogs.Calls`/`Message`/`Ctx` will observe zero calls, because the log is recorded on a throwaway instance. This makes the fake unusable for verifying the middleware's logging behaviour and will silently pass tests that are meant to catch regressions. Return `f` (or a logger that writes into the same `Logs` fields).

title: New ContextualLoggerMiddleware is untested and the ordering dependency it creates is unguarded
body: The log fields `pluginId`, `endpoint`, `dsName`, `dsUID`, `uname` and `traceID` were removed from `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` and are now expected to come from contextual attributes injected by this new middleware (plus the tracing contextual log provider). No test exercises `ContextualLoggerMiddleware`, and no test asserts that the "Plugin Request Completed" log line still contains those fields. If this middleware is omitted from a chain, or ordered after `NewLoggerMiddleware` in `CreateMiddlewares`, every plugin egress log line silently loses all plugin/datasource/user identification and nothing fails. Add a test that runs the real middleware chain (or at least ContextualLogger + Logger) and asserts the emitted log parameters.

title: Adding FromContext to the exported Logger interface breaks out-of-tree implementations
body: `log.Logger` in `pkg/plugins/log` is an exported interface that is passed around the plugin management code (e.g. `NewLoggerMiddleware`). Adding the `FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger` method is a breaking change for any implementation outside this package (Grafana Enterprise, other modules, custom fakes), which will fail to compile until updated. If these implementations exist, they must be updated in lockstep; consider documenting this in the PR or providing an embeddable default implementation.

title: LoggerMiddleware still uses the stale "plugin.instrumentation" logger name
body: After the rename, there is no instrumentation middleware any more, yet the logger handed to `NewLoggerMiddleware` is still created as `log.New("plugin.instrumentation")`, so every plugin egress log line is emitted with `logger=plugin.instrumentation`. This is misleading for anyone grepping logs for the middleware that produced them. If the name is kept for backwards compatibility with existing log queries/dashboards, that should be stated in a comment; otherwise rename it to match the middleware.

title: Test function name not renamed along with the middleware
body: The file and the type under test were renamed to `MetricsMiddleware`/`metrics_middleware_test.go`, but the test is still called `TestInstrumentationMiddleware`. Since the whole point of the PR is consistent naming, leaving the old name makes the test harder to locate by name (`go test -run TestMetricsMiddleware` finds nothing).

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a throwaway logger, so log calls become unobservable in tests
body: `TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()` — a brand new, unrelated instance — instead of the receiver (`f`). Since `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` now logs via `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`, every log line recorded by the middleware is written into a discarded logger. Any test that injects `plog.NewTestLogger()` into the logger middleware and asserts on `InfoLogs.Calls`/`InfoLogs.Ctx` will see zero calls, so the fake silently hides regressions (and will break existing assertions, if any). `FromContext` (and arguably `New`) should return `f` so recorded logs remain inspectable.

title: New method added to exported log.Logger interface is a breaking change for other implementations
body: `FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger` is added to the exported `plugins/log.Logger` interface. Every existing implementation of this interface must now implement the new method or compilation fails; only `grafanaInfraLogWrapper` and `TestLogger` are updated in this PR. Any other in-tree fake/adapter (e.g. fakes in plugin manager packages) or out-of-tree implementation of `plugins/log.Logger` is broken by this change. Verify all implementers are updated, and consider whether this interface is part of a stable surface that needs a non-breaking path.

title: traceID may disappear from the "Plugin Request Completed" log line
body: The explicit `traceID` field (previously obtained with `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)`, i.e. including non-sampled traces) was removed from `logParams` and is now expected to come from the contextual logger via `FromContext`. The contextual attributes added by `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` do not include a trace ID, so the field is only present if a globally registered contextual log provider injects it — and if that provider requires a sampled span, non-sampled requests will no longer have `traceID` in the `grafana-data-egress` log line. This silently breaks log queries/dashboards that correlate plugin egress logs with traces. Either keep adding `traceID` explicitly or confirm the provider semantics match the previous `requireSampled=false` behaviour.

title: Lost documentation of the ordering constraint for the contextual logger
body: The removed comment on `InstrumentationMiddleware` explicitly stated that it enriches the context with a contextual logger and therefore "should live at the top of the middleware stack". The new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` carries no such note, yet the same constraint applies: it must be registered before (outside of) `LoggerMiddleware` and anything else that logs from the request context, otherwise `pluginId`, `endpoint`, `dsName`/`dsUID` and `uname` silently vanish from plugin request logs. Re-add the ordering requirement to the type/constructor doc comment so a future reordering in `CreateMiddlewares` does not regress logging unnoticed.

title: New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no test coverage
body: The contextual-attribute logic (`instrumentContext`) is now the sole responsibility of a new middleware, and the only behaviour that makes plugin request logs useful (`pluginId`, `endpoint`, `dsName`, `dsUID`, `uname` reaching the log line) is untested: there is no `contextual_logger_middleware_test.go`, and the renamed metrics test no longer exercises it. A regression such as dropping an attribute or placing the middleware in the wrong position would not be caught by CI. Add a test asserting the attributes are present in the context passed downstream for each instrumented endpoint.

title: Device limit is bypassed after the first rejection because the cache is populated before the DB write
body: `tagDeviceUI` writes the device key into `localCache` (`a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})`) *before* calling `anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice`. With the new limit enforcement, the first request from a device that exceeds the limit returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` (and `Anonymous.Authenticate` rejects it), but the key is already cached. Every subsequent request from the same `X-Grafana-Device-Id` within the cache TTL (29 min) short-circuits at the cache check, returns nil, and the anonymous user is authenticated without ever being recorded. So the limit only blocks a single request per device per ~29 minutes and is trivially bypassed by a page reload. The cache entry should only be set after a successful store write (or removed on error).

title: Raw `ErrDeviceLimitReached` returned from Authenticate yields an opaque 500 to the user
body: `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is created with `fmt.Errorf("device limit reached")` in anonstore/database.go and is returned verbatim from `Anonymous.Authenticate`. The authn stack maps non-`errutil` client errors to a generic internal server error, so a user hitting the configured anonymous device limit gets a 500 with no actionable message instead of a well-defined 4xx/403 with a user-facing reason. Define the error with `errutil` (public message, proper status) so the rejection is reported correctly to the browser and logs.

title: Count-then-insert is not atomic, so the device limit can be exceeded
body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` first runs `CountDevices` and then, if under the limit, performs the upsert in a separate session. Concurrent requests from different new devices (very likely for anonymous traffic across multiple Grafana instances or goroutines) can all read a count below the limit and all insert, pushing the stored device count above `AnonymousDeviceLimit`. Enforcement needs to be atomic (e.g. insert guarded by a conditional statement/transaction with appropriate locking) if the limit is meant to be a hard cap.

title: Exported provider signatures changed without updating DI wiring / generated code
body: `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` no longer takes `anonstore.AnonStore` but a `db.DB`, and `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` gained a second `deviceLimit int64` parameter. These are the providers referenced by the checked-in wire graph (`pkg/server/wire.go` and the generated `wire_gen.go`), plus enterprise wiring. Neither file is part of this PR, so the generated code still calls the old signatures and the build will fail (and/or wire now has a stale `ProvideAnonDBStore` provider with no `int64` binding). Regenerate wire and update all callers. Note this also removes the ability to inject a fake `AnonStore` into the service, which reduces testability of `AnonDeviceService`.

title: Any zero-row UPDATE is reported as "device limit reached"
body: `updateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` whenever `RowsAffected() == 0`. That is true not only for unknown devices but also for a device row that exists yet whose `updated_at` falls outside the `[now-30d, now+1m]` window (rows are only purged after 61 days), and on MySQL for an update that changes no column values. The caller turns this into an authentication failure, so legitimate but stale devices are denied with a misleading error that makes the real cause impossible to diagnose from logs. Distinguish "row not matched" from "limit reached", or at minimum log the device id/reason.

title: New `[auth.anonymous] device_limit` option is undocumented
body: `cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit` is read from `auth.anonymous.device_limit`, but the PR does not add the key to `conf/defaults.ini` / `conf/sample.ini` nor to docs/sources/setup-grafana/configure-grafana. Operators have no way to discover the option, its default (0 = unlimited), or the fact that exceeding it blocks anonymous authentication. Grafana convention requires every new ini setting to appear in defaults.ini and the configuration docs. Also consider rejecting/normalizing negative values, which are currently silently treated as "unlimited" by the `s.deviceLimit > 0` check.

title: Limit-enforcement tests do not cover the update path or the client behaviour
body: `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only asserts that a *new* device is rejected when the limit is reached. The core new logic — that an *existing* device is still updated successfully (and therefore still authenticates) once the limit is hit, including the `updated_at BETWEEN` window boundaries — is untested, as is the new synchronous `Anonymous.Authenticate` behaviour (returns error for `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, logs and continues for other errors) and the interaction with the local cache. Without those tests the limit-bypass via the local cache and the stale-row rejection path go unnoticed.

title: Device tagging moved into the synchronous auth path, adding a COUNT query per cache miss
body: The previous implementation tagged devices in a background goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout and panic recovery; tagging is now done inline on the request's context during `Authenticate`. For every cache miss (once per device per 29 min) an anonymous request now blocks on `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM anon_device WHERE updated_at BETWEEN ? AND ?` plus the upsert. `anon_device` has no index supporting a range scan on `updated_at`, so on instances with many anonymous devices this is a table scan in the request path, and any DB slowness/latency is now visible to the user instead of being absorbed asynchronously. Consider caching the count or indexing `updated_at`, and only performing the count when the limit is configured.

title: Backend sends 0 for "no limit" while the frontend type declares `number | undefined`
body: `AnonymousDeviceLimit int64` has no `omitempty`/pointer, so when no limit is configured the payload contains `anonymousDeviceLimit: 0`, yet `GrafanaConfig.anonymousDeviceLimit` is typed `number | undefined` and `GrafanaBootConfig` initialises it to `undefined`. Frontend code that distinguishes "unset" via `=== undefined` will treat an unlimited instance as having a limit of 0. Use `*int64` with `omitempty` (or document that 0 means unlimited) so the two sides agree.

title: Device-limit rejection is cached, so the limit is bypassed on the next request
body: `tagDeviceUI` writes the cache key (`a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})`) *before* calling `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice`. With the new behaviour, when the device limit is reached `CreateOrUpdateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, which now propagates out of `TagDevice` and makes `Anonymous.Authenticate` fail. But the cache entry stays in place for the cache lifetime (29 min). On the very next request with the same `X-Grafana-Device-Id`, `tagDeviceUI` hits the cache, returns nil, `TagDevice` returns nil, and the anonymous identity is granted even though the device was never persisted and the limit is exceeded. Net effect: the device limit can be trivially bypassed by reloading the page once, and the device is invisible to `ListDevices`/usage stats. The cache key must be removed (or only written after a successful store call) when `CreateOrUpdateDevice` fails.

title: Check-then-insert on device count allows exceeding the configured limit
body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` reads the device count and then performs the upsert as two separate statements with no transaction, locking, or unique constraint on the aggregate. Concurrent requests (and in HA setups, concurrent Grafana instances) can all observe `count < deviceLimit` and then each insert a new row, so the number of tracked anonymous devices can exceed `auth.anonymous.device_limit`. If the limit is meant to be an enforced cap (it is used to reject authentication), the count and insert need to be done atomically, e.g. inside a single transaction with appropriate locking or an `INSERT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(...)) < limit` style statement.

title: Unauthenticated requests now trigger a synchronous COUNT(*) plus write on the auth path
body: When `deviceLimit > 0`, every `CreateOrUpdateDevice` first runs `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM anon_device WHERE updated_at BETWEEN ? AND ?`, and since `client.go` no longer performs tagging in a background goroutine, this query plus the upsert/update now runs inline during authentication of the request. The device id comes from the attacker-controllable `X-Grafana-Device-Id` header, and the in-memory dedup cache is keyed by that header, so an unauthenticated client can force a fresh COUNT + UPDATE round-trip (and a new 29-minute cache entry) on every single request. On an instance with many anonymous devices this adds unbounded DB load and request latency on the hot auth path. Consider caching/throttling the count or enforcing the limit without a per-request aggregate query.

title: DI signatures changed but wire registration/generated code not updated in this PR
body: `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` no longer accepts `anonstore.AnonStore` (it now takes `db.DB` and constructs the store itself), and `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` gained a required `deviceLimit int64` parameter. Both functions are wired via Google Wire (`pkg/server/wire.go` / `wire_gen.go`), which is not part of this changeset: the generated code still calls the old signature, and if `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` is still in a provider set, wire now has to resolve a bare `int64` dependency, which it cannot. This will break the build / wire generation unless the provider sets and generated files are updated in the same PR. Constructing the store inside the service also removes the ability to inject an alternative `AnonStore` implementation (e.g. for tests or enterprise).

title: Device-limit error returned as an untyped error, producing an opaque failure for the user
body: `Authenticate` returns `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached` (a plain `fmt.Errorf` value) straight to the authn broker. Grafana's authn layer expects `errutil`-typed errors to derive an HTTP status and a user-facing message; an untyped error yields a generic internal/unauthenticated failure with no indication that the anonymous device limit was hit. Given this PR also ships `anonymousDeviceLimit` to the frontend (presumably to display a message), the error should be wrapped in an `errutil` error with an explicit status (e.g. 403/429) and message id so the UI and API clients can react meaningfully.

title: `rowsAffected == 0` is reported as "device limit reached" for unrelated cases
body: `updateDevice` maps any update that matched no rows to `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. Besides the intended "this device is not among the tracked devices" case, zero affected rows also occurs when the row exists but its `updated_at` falls outside the `[now-30d, now+1m]` window used in the WHERE clause (e.g. a device last seen 31 days ago, or clock skew between HA instances pushing a stored timestamp past the +1m bound), and — on MySQL connections without CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS — when the update is a no-op. In those cases the caller/user is told the device limit was reached, which is misleading and makes debugging and metrics harder. Distinguish "no matching device" from the limit condition, e.g. by checking existence explicitly.

title: New `auth.anonymous.device_limit` option is undocumented
body: `cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit` is read from `auth.anonymous.device_limit`, but the option is not added to `conf/defaults.ini`, `conf/sample.ini`, or the configuration reference docs. Grafana users discover configuration through defaults.ini and the docs page; an option that silently rejects anonymous authentication once the limit is reached is especially important to document (including that 0 means unlimited and what happens to users beyond the limit).

title: Device-limit tests omit the main success path and the limit-bypass scenario
body: `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only asserts that a *new* device is rejected once the limit is hit. There is no test that an already-tracked device can still be refreshed while the store is at the limit (the whole point of the `updateDevice` branch — a regression there would lock out every existing anonymous user), no test for `deviceLimit` boundary values (e.g. count exactly equal to vs. below the limit, negative/0 limit), and no test at the `AnonDeviceService`/client level covering the new error propagation from `TagDevice` or the local-cache interaction, which is where the limit is currently bypassable.

title: `anonymousDeviceLimit` is inferred as type `undefined`, making it unusable from TypeScript
body: `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` is an initializer without a type annotation, so TypeScript infers the field type as `undefined` on `GrafanaBootConfig` (unlike the neighbouring `googleAnalyticsId: undefined;` declarations, which are annotations). Any consumer writing `config.anonymousDeviceLimit > 0` will fail to compile, even though the backend always serialises a number (`AnonymousDeviceLimit int64`, 0 when unset) — so the value is in fact never `undefined` at runtime. Annotate it as `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;` (or just `number`) to match the `GrafanaConfig` interface and the actual payload.

title: Device limit is bypassed on retry because the local cache is populated before the store call
body: `tagDeviceUI` inserts the device key into `localCache` (`a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})`) *before* calling `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice`. When the new device limit is hit, `CreateOrUpdateDevice` -> `updateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` and `Authenticate` fails, but the cache entry has already been written with a 29 minute TTL. On the very next request from the same device, `tagDeviceUI` short-circuits at the cache hit, returns nil, and anonymous authentication succeeds even though the device was never recorded and the instance is over its limit. The net effect is that the limit only rejects the first request of each device and is trivially bypassed by a page refresh, while the device is also never counted in `anon_device` (so usage stats under-report). The cache entry should only be set after a successful store write, or be explicitly removed on failure.

title: Count-then-insert is not atomic, so the device limit can be exceeded
body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` reads the device count with `CountDevices` and then performs the INSERT ... ON CONFLICT in a separate statement/session. Concurrent requests (including across multiple Grafana instances sharing one database) can all observe `count < deviceLimit` and then all insert, so the stored number of devices can exceed `AnonymousDeviceLimit` by the number of concurrent requests. If the limit is meant to be a hard cap (it is enforced by failing authentication), the check and the insert must happen in a single transaction/statement (e.g. an INSERT guarded by a count sub-query) or the overshoot must be documented as acceptable.

title: rowsAffected == 0 is reported as ErrDeviceLimitReached, blocking existing devices
body:
`updateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` whenever the UPDATE affects zero rows, but zero affected rows does not only mean "this is a new device":

1. The WHERE clause restricts the match to `updated_at BETWEEN now-30d AND now+1m`. Devices are only purged after 61 days (`keepFor` in impl.go), so a device row that exists but was last seen 31-60 days ago will not match, and the returning user is rejected with "device limit reached" even though no new row would be created.
2. On MySQL `RowsAffected()` reports *changed* rows. If two instances (or a request after a cache expiry within the same second, given MySQL's second-granularity timestamps) write identical `client_ip`, `user_agent` and `updated_at`, the UPDATE changes nothing and returns 0, producing a spurious limit error for a device that is already tracked.

In both cases a legitimate anonymous session is denied access. The existence check should be explicit (e.g. SELECT by `device_id`) rather than inferred from affected rows.

title: Device tagging moved into the synchronous auth path, adding DB round-trips to every anonymous request
body: The goroutine that previously performed `TagDevice` asynchronously (with its own 2 minute context) was removed, so `Anonymous.Authenticate` now performs the device-tagging database work inline on the request path. With `device_limit > 0` each cache miss issues a `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM anon_device` plus an INSERT/UPDATE before the request can proceed. Anonymous request latency is now bound to database latency, and a slow or saturated database directly slows down (or, with the request context being cancelled, fails) anonymous page loads. Previously these failures were fire-and-forget warnings. If synchronous enforcement is required, consider at least caching the count instead of querying it per new device.

title: Limit error returned from Authenticate is an untyped error, surfacing as a 500 to end users
body: `Authenticate` returns the raw `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached` (created with `fmt.Errorf`) instead of an `errutil`-based error with a status code and public message. The authn broker maps unknown errors to a generic internal server error, so a user hitting the configured anonymous device limit gets a 500 "Internal Server Error" rather than a meaningful 429/403 with an explanatory message, and operators will see this as a server fault in logs/metrics. Wrap the error with `errutil` (e.g. a 429/403 with a public message) so the limit is reported as a client-visible, actionable condition.

title: New `device_limit` option is missing from conf/defaults.ini, sample.ini and docs
body: `cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit` is read from `[auth.anonymous] device_limit`, but the key is not added to `conf/defaults.ini` / `conf/sample.ini` nor to the configuration documentation. Besides being undiscoverable, Grafana's environment-variable override mechanism iterates over the keys that actually exist in the loaded ini files, so a key absent from `defaults.ini` cannot be set with `GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_DEVICE_LIMIT` — the option would silently be ignored for env-var based deployments (Docker/Kubernetes). The semantics of `0` (unlimited) and the fact that exceeding the limit causes anonymous authentication to fail also need to be documented.

title: Service now builds its own store; AnonStore provider/injection not updated
body: `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` no longer accepts an `anonstore.AnonStore` and instead constructs one via `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore(sqlStore, cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit)`, while `ProvideAnonDBStore` gained a primitive `int64` parameter. The dependency-injection wiring (pkg/server/wire.go, which previously had to provide `anonstore.AnonStore` for this constructor) is not touched by this PR: if `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` is still registered in the provider set, wire has no provider for the new `int64` argument, and any other consumer that injects `anonstore.AnonStore` now receives a second, independently constructed store rather than the instance the service uses. The wire graph needs to be updated (or the store kept as an injected dependency), and taking `db.DB` directly also removes the ability to inject a fake store in tests.

title: Only the rejection path of the device limit is tested
body: `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` asserts that a *new* device is rejected once the limit is reached, but the main purpose of the new `updateDevice` code path — allowing an already-known device to keep refreshing `client_ip`/`user_agent`/`updated_at` while at the limit — is never exercised. There is also no test for a device whose `updated_at` falls outside the 30-day window while the limit is reached (which currently returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` for an existing row), and no service-level test with a non-zero `AnonymousDeviceLimit` covering the interaction with the local cache in `tagDeviceUI`. As written, a regression that rejects every request at the limit would pass the suite.

title: Cleanup job interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute (looks like leftover debug change)
body: The background cleanup ticker was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This is unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (splitting the annotation cleanup query) and has broad consequences: every cleanup job (temp files, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history) now runs 10x more often, increasing database and I/O load on every Grafana instance. It also interacts badly with the 9-minute timeout in `clean()`: a cleanup pass that takes longer than one minute will be immediately followed by another pass, effectively making cleanup run continuously. Unless this is intentional and documented, it should be reverted to 10 minutes.

title: Debug logging left in at Error level, dumping entire ID batches
body: Six new log calls use `r.log.Error(...)` for purely informational progress messages (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579), e.g. `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, ...)`. Consequences: (1) every cleanup cycle emits error-level log lines on a healthy system, which pollutes logs and will trigger error-rate alerting/monitoring; (2) the full `ids` slice is logged, so with a configured `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` (the test in this PR uses 32767) each iteration writes tens of thousands of IDs per log line, which can be megabytes of logs per cleanup run; (3) the `"err", err` field in the "to clean" messages is always nil at that point because the error path returned earlier, so it is misleading. These should be `Debug` level without the raw ID list (or removed).

title: Quadratic string concatenation when inlining IDs for SQLite
body: In `deleteByIDs`, the SQLite inline-values path builds the ID list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside the loop. Each iteration reallocates and copies the whole accumulated string, giving O(n^2) copying. With the batch sizes this code path is specifically designed for (>999, and the new test uses 32767 IDs), this copies on the order of gigabytes per batch and allocates one string per ID, for every cleanup iteration. Use a `strings.Builder` (or `strconv.AppendInt` into a byte slice, as done in `getAccessControlFilter`) instead.

title: Bind-parameter path can exceed Postgres/MySQL parameter limits for large configured batch sizes
body: For non-SQLite databases `deleteByIDs` always builds `DELETE ... WHERE id IN (?,?,...)` with one placeholder per ID. Postgres and MySQL cap the number of bind parameters in a statement at 65535, so an operator who sets `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` above that will make annotation cleanup fail permanently with a driver error ("extended protocol limited to 65535 parameters" / "Prepared statement contains too many placeholders"). The previous implementation used a single parameterless DELETE with a subquery, so any batch size worked; this is therefore a regression. Also note the branch condition tests `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit` instead of `len(ids)`, which couples the delete path to an assumption about how many IDs the caller fetched; checking `len(ids)` (and applying an inline/chunked strategy for all dialects above the limit) would be safer.

title: Test cleanup registered after data creation and assertions, leaking rows across subtests on failure
body: `createTestAnnotations` and the two `assertAnnotationCount`/`assertAnnotationTagCount` calls run before `t.Cleanup` is registered, and all subtests share the single `fakeSQL` database. If insertion or either initial assertion fails (they use `require`, so the subtest aborts immediately), the `DELETE FROM annotation` / `DELETE FROM annotation_tag` cleanup is never registered, leaving rows behind and causing every subsequent subtest to fail with confusing count mismatches instead of a single clear failure. Register the `t.Cleanup` before creating the test data.

title: Cleanup job ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The background cleanup loop's ticker was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This makes every cleanup job (temp files, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, annotations, user invites, short URLs, query history) run ten times more often in production, which is a significant and unrelated change in DB/IO load for all Grafana installations. Note also that `clean()` has a 9-minute timeout, so a long-running cleanup cycle will be immediately followed by another one. This looks like a leftover from local reproduction of the deadlock and should be reverted to 10 minutes (or made configurable) before merge.

title: Leftover debug logging at Error level, including full ID lists
body: `CleanAnnotations` and `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` log six messages per batch via `r.log.Error(...)` (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579), e.g. `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, ...)`. These are informational/debug messages, not errors: they will fire on every cleanup batch for every healthy installation, polluting error logs and triggering alerting on error-level log volume. They also serialize the entire ID slice into the log line — with the documented batch sizes (e.g. the 32767 used in the new test) each line can be hundreds of kilobytes. In addition, the `"err", err` field is always nil at these call sites because the error path returns earlier. These calls should be removed or downgraded to Debug without the full ID slice.

title: Quadratic string concatenation when inlining IDs for SQLite
body: In `deleteByIDs`, the SQLite path builds the IN-list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside a loop over all IDs. Each iteration reallocates and copies the whole accumulated string, so building the list is O(n^2) in bytes copied. With a batch size such as the 32767 exercised by the new test, this copies on the order of gigabytes per batch and allocates 32k intermediate strings, for every delete batch of the cleanup job. Use a `strings.Builder` (or `strconv.AppendInt` into a byte slice, as done elsewhere in this file) instead.

title: Placeholder-limit workaround only covers SQLite and keys off config instead of actual ID count
body: `deleteByIDs` only avoids bind parameters when `r.db.GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite && r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999`. MySQL and Postgres have their own hard limit of 65535 placeholders per statement, so an operator who sets `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` above 65535 will get every cleanup batch failing with a driver error on those backends. The condition also tests the configured batch size rather than `len(ids)`, which couples correctness of the statement to a config value instead of the data actually being deleted. Consider branching on `len(ids)` and applying a placeholder cap for all dialects (or chunking the delete).

title: Per-subtest data cleanup is registered after the assertions that can abort the subtest
body: `createTestAnnotations` is called, then `assertAnnotationCount`/`assertAnnotationTagCount` run (both use `require`, which calls `FailNow`), and only afterwards is `t.Cleanup` registered to delete from `annotation`/`annotation_tag`. If either pre-condition assertion fails, the subtest aborts before the cleanup is registered, so the inserted rows stay in the shared `fakeSQL` database and every subsequent subtest (which now assumes an empty table and asserts exact counts) fails with confusing cascading errors. Register the `t.Cleanup` immediately after creating the annotations, before asserting.

title: Cleanup ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute (apparent debug leftover)
body: The background cleanup loop's ticker was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This makes *all* cleanup jobs (temp files, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, annotations, user invites, short URLs, query history) run 10x more often, multiplying background DB load on every Grafana instance. Nothing in the PR description mentions changing the cleanup cadence, and the per-run timeout is still 9 minutes (sized for the 10-minute cadence), so a long-running cleanup now blocks the loop while ticks are dropped. This looks like a leftover from local testing of the annotation cleanup and should be reverted (or justified and documented) before merge.

title: Debug logging left in at Error level, dumping every deleted ID
body: Six new `r.log.Error(...)` calls were added in the cleanup paths (lines 534, 537, 554, 557 in `CleanAnnotations` and 576, 579 in `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags`). These log normal, successful operation at ERROR severity, which will trigger operator alerting/dashboards that watch for error logs. They also log the full `ids` slice and the raw SQL condition on every batch: with the default cleanup cadence and a batch size that can be tens of thousands (the new test uses 32767), each cycle emits log lines containing tens of thousands of IDs, which is a serious log-volume and formatting-cost problem. Additionally, the `"err", err` field in the "to clean" lines is always nil (the error was already returned above), and the error from `deleteByIDs` is logged *and* returned, so failures get double-reported. These statements should be removed or demoted to Debug without the full ID list.

title: Quadratic string concatenation when inlining IDs for SQLite
body: In `deleteByIDs`, the SQLite inline-values branch builds the IN list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside the loop. Each iteration reallocates and copies the whole accumulated string, making the construction O(n^2) in the number of IDs. With the batch sizes this branch is specifically meant for (it only triggers when `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999`; the new test uses 32767) this copies hundreds of megabytes to gigabytes per batch and burns CPU/GC on every cleanup cycle. Use a `strings.Builder` (or `strconv.AppendInt` into a byte slice, as done elsewhere in this file) instead.

title: Placeholder-count limit only handled for SQLite; large batch sizes now break MySQL/Postgres cleanup
body: `deleteByIDs` only falls back to inlining IDs when the driver is SQLite and the configured batch size exceeds 999; otherwise it emits one `?` placeholder per ID. MySQL and PostgreSQL cap a single statement at 65535 bind parameters, so an operator who sets `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` above that value will now get a hard failure from every cleanup batch, where the previous sub-query-based DELETE had no such limit. Consider chunking `ids` to a safe maximum (e.g. a few thousand) inside `deleteByIDs` regardless of driver, instead of relying on the configured batch size staying small.

title: Per-subtest DB cleanup is registered after the data is inserted and asserted
body: `t.Cleanup` that truncates `annotation`/`annotation_tag` is registered only after `createTestAnnotations` and the two `require`-based pre-assertions have run. Since all subtests share one `db.InitTestDB` instance and now seed rows with fixed primary keys (`ID: int64(i+1)`), a failure inside `createTestAnnotations` or in the pre-condition assertions aborts the subtest without ever registering the cleanup, leaving rows behind and causing every subsequent subtest to fail with confusing duplicate-key/count errors instead of just the original failure. Register the cleanup before inserting the test data.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and will be canceled when the request finishes
body: All four async legacy writes (`Create` line 51, `Delete` line 110, `Update` line 135, `DeleteCollection` line 163) build their context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the incoming request context. In net/http (and therefore in the apiserver), the request context is canceled as soon as the handler returns, which happens immediately after the dual writer returns the unified-storage result. The spawned goroutine therefore usually starts or continues with an already-canceled context, so the legacy write is aborted (and silently only shows up as an error in the duration metric). Since the whole point of mode 3 is to keep legacy in sync as a safety net, legacy would systematically fail to be written. Use a detached context (e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` as the parent, preserving the auth/user values) before applying the timeout.

title: Unrecovered panic in async legacy write will crash the whole process
body: The legacy writes are now executed in bare `go func()` goroutines (lines 50, 108, 134, 161) with no `defer recover()`. Previously these calls were synchronous and any panic inside the legacy store was caught by the apiserver's panic-recovery filter for that request. Now a panic in `d.Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection` (or in the validation callbacks it invokes) happens on a goroutine with no recovery and takes down the entire Grafana process. Wrap the goroutine body with a recover (e.g. `runtime.HandleCrash` semantics) or a helper that logs and swallows panics.

title: Delete records the object name in the metric's `kind` label, causing unbounded cardinality
body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. Each distinct resource name becomes a new Prometheus label value on the storage duration histogram, so the series count grows with the number of objects ever deleted. This is a metrics cardinality explosion that can blow up the registry and the scraping backend. It should be `options.Kind`.

title: Storage failures in Create/Update are recorded as legacy-storage durations
body: In `Create` (line 45) and `Update` (line 129) the error path calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` even though the failure came from `d.Storage`. The success paths correctly call `recordStorageDuration`. As a result the legacy histogram is polluted with unified-storage failures and the storage error rate is under-reported, which makes the mode-3 dashboards/alerts misleading. Both should call `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

title: DeleteCollection records the legacy call duration into the storage metric
body: Inside the async goroutine of `DeleteCollection` the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration`. The legacy delete-collection latency/error rate is therefore never visible in the legacy metric and instead corrupts the storage metric (which was already recorded a few lines above for the same request), double-counting storage observations.

title: Delete puts the bare logger in the context instead of the enriched one
body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` uses `d.Log` rather than the `log` built one line earlier with `name`, `kind` and `method` values. Downstream code that retrieves the logger via `klog.FromContext(ctx)` loses all of the request-specific context, unlike every other method in this file which stores `log`. Should be `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`.

title: Legacy update now re-runs the caller's objInfo instead of applying the object already written to storage
body: The previous implementation fetched the current object, computed `updated`, and passed `&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}` to the legacy store so that legacy received exactly the object persisted in unified storage. The new code hands the raw `objInfo` to `d.Legacy.Update`, so the legacy store re-evaluates the update/patch against *its own* copy of the object, including resource-version precondition checks. For PUT requests the resourceVersion in the request body comes from unified storage and will generally not match the legacy row, so the legacy update can fail with a conflict, and for PATCH/Apply the transformation is applied to a possibly divergent legacy object. Either way legacy silently drifts from unified storage, defeating the purpose of the mode-3 safety write. The failure is only visible as a metric label, since the error is not even logged.

title: The input object is shared with the async legacy write without a deep copy
body: `d.Legacy.Create(ctx, obj, ...)` is called from the goroutine with the same `obj` pointer that was just passed to `d.Storage.Create` and that the request handler still owns (admission/audit layers may read it, and generic registry code mutates object metadata in place such as resourceVersion/UID/name on name generation). Writing to that object from the legacy store concurrently with the handler's continued use is a data race that can also mean the legacy store persists metadata mutated by the unified store. Pass `obj.DeepCopyObject()` to the goroutine.

title: Destroy can tear down the stores while async legacy writes are still in flight
body: `Destroy()` immediately calls `d.Storage.Destroy()` and `d.Legacy.Destroy()`, but nothing tracks the goroutines spawned by Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection. On shutdown an in-flight legacy write can run against an already-destroyed store (closed DB handles/connection pools), producing errors or panics. A WaitGroup (or a shared lifecycle context) that Destroy waits on would make shutdown deterministic.

title: New mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy write
body: All of the new tests share a single `mock.Mock` between `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock`, so an expectation registered by `setupLegacyFn` is indistinguishable from the one registered by `setupStorageFn` (e.g. in `TestMode3_Update` both register `"Update"` with identical argument matchers). Combined with the fact that no test waits for (or asserts on) the goroutine that performs the legacy write, and no `AssertExpectations`/`AssertCalled` is used, the tests cannot show that the legacy store is written at all — which is the core behaviour this PR adds. They also cannot show that a legacy failure does not affect the response. Separate mocks per store (or distinct expectations) plus a synchronization point (channel/WaitGroup signalled from the legacy mock) are needed.

title: Unrelated, duplicated and unsorted go.work.sum entries
body: The added block contains `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod` which is already present a few lines above, and inserts `github.com/grafana/grafana-azure-sdk-go/v2` out of sort order. These entries are unrelated to the dual-writer change and look like a hand-edited/stale generated file; they should be regenerated (`go work sync`) or dropped from this PR to avoid confusing future dependency updates.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled when the request finishes
body: All four background goroutines (Create l.51, Delete l.110, Update l.135, DeleteCollection l.163) build their timeout context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the incoming request context. A child context is cancelled as soon as its parent is cancelled, and the apiserver cancels the request context the moment the handler returns — which happens immediately after `return created, err`. So in practice the legacy write will frequently (often always, for fast handlers) be aborted with `context.Canceled` before or during execution, which silently defeats the whole point of mode 3 (writing a safety copy to legacy). Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (preserving auth/user values) as the parent before applying the timeout, so the write survives the request lifecycle.

title: Errors from the asynchronous legacy writes are never logged
body: In Create (l.55-56), Delete (l.112-113), Update (l.139-140) and DeleteCollection (l.165-166) the error returned by the legacy storage is only fed into a duration histogram and then dropped. The previous implementation logged these failures. Since mode 3 reads exclusively from unified storage, a failing legacy write produces a silent divergence between the two stores with no diagnostic trail (no object name, no error message), making it impossible to reconcile later. Log the error with the object identity (and the timeout cause when the ctx expired).

title: Storage failures are recorded in the legacy duration metric
body: In `Create`, when `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with `startStorage`. The same mistake exists in `Update` (l.129). This attributes unified-storage latency/failures to the legacy histogram, so the storage histogram never records any failures and the legacy histogram is polluted with samples for an operation legacy never performed. Both should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

title: Delete records the object name in the `kind` metric label (unbounded cardinality)
body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. Each deleted object therefore creates a new time series in the duration histogram, which is an unbounded-cardinality label and will blow up the Prometheus registry/scrape payload on any workload that deletes many objects. It also makes the metric unusable for per-kind aggregation. Should be `options.Kind`.

title: DeleteCollection goroutine records legacy latency as storage latency
body: Inside the async goroutine of `DeleteCollection` the legacy call's duration is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` using `startLegacy`. This means the legacy DeleteCollection duration/errors appear under the unified-storage metric, double-counting storage samples for the same request and leaving the legacy metric with no data for delete-collection. Should be `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`.

title: Legacy Update is given the raw objInfo instead of the object actually persisted in storage
body: The previous implementation wrapped `objInfo` in `updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}` so that legacy received exactly the object that was written to unified storage. Now the raw `objInfo` is handed to `d.Legacy.Update`, so legacy recomputes the updated object from *its own* stored copy. For PATCH/Apply requests, or when the client sent a resourceVersion precondition (the RV now belongs to unified storage, not legacy), this either fails with a conflict or writes a different object than the one in unified storage, producing a silent divergence between the two stores. Pass the storage result through `updateWrapper` as before.

title: Request-scoped object and validation callbacks are used from a goroutine after the request completed
body: The goroutines pass the caller-owned `obj` (Create, l.55) and the request's `createValidation`/`updateValidation`/`deleteValidation` funcs (l.55, 112, 139, 165) into the legacy store after the handler has returned. `obj` has already been mutated in place by the unified-storage create path and is still reachable from the handler, and the validation closures run admission, which writes audit annotations onto the request's audit event — an event the audit backend may be serializing concurrently once the request finished. This is a real data race / mutation-after-response hazard. Deep-copy the object before handing it to the goroutine and avoid re-running request-scoped validation/admission on the async path.

title: Delete stores the base logger in the context instead of the enriched one
body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` uses `d.Log` rather than the `log` built one line above with name/kind/method values. Any downstream code that pulls the logger from the context (`klog.FromContext`) loses the request identifying fields for deletes only, making delete failures hard to correlate. Should be `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`.

title: Tests never verify (or wait for) the asynchronous legacy writes
body: Every mode 3 test only asserts on the value returned from the unified store; no test waits for or asserts that `Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection` was invoked (e.g. via `m.AssertExpectations`/`AssertCalled` after synchronization). Because the legacy goroutine is fire-and-forget, the core behaviour added by this PR — the safety write to legacy — is completely untested, and the regression described above (the goroutine's context being cancelled with the request) would not be caught. The goroutines also outlive the subtest, so the mock is exercised after the test function returns, which makes any future expectation mismatch surface as a panic in a background goroutine rather than a test failure.

title: Storage-failure test case is configured through setupLegacyFn and only works because both mocks share one mock.Mock
body: In the "error when creating object in the unified store fails" case the failing `Create` expectation is registered via `setupLegacyFn` while `setupStorageFn` is nil. It only produces the expected error because `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` are constructed around the same `*mock.Mock`, so the storage call matches the legacy expectation. The test therefore cannot distinguish a legacy failure from a storage failure and is misleading for anyone adding cases later; register the expectation on the storage setup function.

title: go.work.sum contains a duplicated entry and unrelated dependency hashes
body: The added block re-adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod` which already exists two lines above, and adds hashes for modules unrelated to this change (grafana-azure-sdk-go, prometheus-alertmanager, several otel versions). This looks like a locally dirty workspace file committed by accident rather than a regenerated one; it will churn/conflict on the next `go work sync`. Regenerate the file or drop these lines from the PR.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled as soon as the request completes
body: All four write paths (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) spawn a goroutine whose context is derived from the incoming request context via `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`. net/http cancels the request context as soon as the handler returns, which will normally happen before (or shortly after) the goroutine gets scheduled. The derived context is therefore already cancelled, so the legacy SQL store call will abort with `context canceled` and the 10s timeout is effectively meaningless. The whole point of mode 3 is to keep legacy storage in sync as a safety net, so this silently drops most legacy writes. The goroutine needs a context detached from the request lifetime (e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` or a fresh background context carrying the requester/identity values) before applying the timeout.

title: Errors from the asynchronous legacy writes are never logged
body: In the goroutines for Create (line 55), Delete (line 112), Update (line 139) and DeleteCollection (line 165) the error returned by the legacy store is only fed into a duration histogram's `isError` label; nothing is logged. The previous implementation logged these failures (`unable to create object in legacy storage`, `could not delete from legacy store`, ...). With mode 3 this means legacy and unified storage can silently drift apart with no operator-visible signal other than an aggregate metric label, making divergence impossible to diagnose per object. Log the error together with the object name/kind.

title: Spawned goroutines have no panic recovery, so a legacy store panic kills the process
body: The four `go func()` blocks (lines 50, 108, 134, 161) call into legacy storage without a `defer recover()`. Panics inside an HTTP handler are recovered by the apiserver's panic middleware, but a panic in a detached goroutine terminates the entire Grafana process. Since these goroutines run arbitrary legacy storage code (including validation callbacks passed in from the request), a single bad object can now crash the server instead of failing one request. Add a recover (and log) wrapper around the goroutine bodies.

title: Delete records the object name in the `kind` metric label, causing unbounded cardinality
body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. Each distinct deleted object therefore creates a new histogram label value in the storage duration metric, so the time series count grows without bound with the number of deletes, bloating the Prometheus registry and scrape payload. It also makes the metric unusable for comparing with the other operations. Should be `options.Kind`.

title: Create error path records a legacy duration for a storage failure
body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with `startStorage`. The failure came from unified storage, not from legacy, so the error is attributed to the wrong backend and the storage histogram never records the failed call. This makes the dual-writer dashboards report phantom legacy errors and hide unified-storage errors. Should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

title: Update error path records a legacy duration for a storage failure
body: `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` is called when `d.Storage.Update` returns an error. As in Create, a unified-storage failure is recorded against the legacy backend's histogram and the storage histogram misses the failure entirely, producing misleading metrics. Should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

title: DeleteCollection goroutine records the legacy call under the storage metric
body: Inside the async goroutine, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is reported with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)`. This double-counts the storage histogram (it was already recorded at line 159 for the real storage call) with the legacy latency, and the legacy histogram records nothing for delete-collection, so legacy failures for this operation are invisible. Should be `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`.

title: Delete injects the bare logger into the context instead of the enriched one
body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` uses `d.Log` rather than the `log` created on line 96. Every downstream component that pulls the logger out of the context via `klog.FromContext(ctx)` loses the `name`, `kind` and `method` values, which is inconsistent with every other method in this file and makes delete-related log lines unattributable.

title: Legacy Update is now driven by the raw objInfo instead of the object written to storage
body: The previous implementation wrapped objInfo (`&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}`) so legacy received exactly the object that was persisted to unified storage. Now the unmodified `objInfo` is handed to `d.Legacy.Update`, so legacy re-evaluates the update against the *legacy* copy of the object. For PATCH/apply requests the transformers are re-run against a different base object, and for requests carrying a resourceVersion the precondition is checked against the legacy resourceVersion (which is not the same value space as unified storage), so the legacy write can fail with a spurious conflict. Combined with the fact that the error is only counted in a metric, this silently diverges the two stores.

title: NotFound from unified storage now aborts the legacy delete, leaving orphaned legacy rows
body: The old Delete explicitly tolerated `apierrors.IsNotFound` from unified storage and still issued the legacy delete. The new code returns early on any error, so an object that exists only in legacy (e.g. written before the mode switch, or whose unified write failed) can never be deleted: reads come from unified storage, so the row is invisible, and the delete never reaches legacy. Consider keeping the NotFound passthrough so legacy cleanup still happens.

title: Mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy write, and leak unsynchronized goroutines
body: The new tests use a single `mock.Mock` instance shared by `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock`, so a call to legacy is indistinguishable from a call to storage, and no test asserts that the legacy store was written at all. The central behaviour of mode 3 (write to unified, then asynchronously mirror to legacy) is therefore untested; the mislabeled metrics and the context-cancellation problem in dualwriter_mode3.go would not be caught. In addition, nothing waits for the spawned goroutine, so the mock is invoked after the subtest finishes - any future assertion on legacy calls will be flaky, and an unmatched expectation would panic in a background goroutine and abort the whole test binary. Use separate mocks for legacy and storage and add synchronization (e.g. a channel/WaitGroup signalled from the legacy mock) so the async write can be asserted deterministically.

title: Duplicate go.work.sum entry added
body: `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod h1:...` is added at line 409 although the identical line already exists a few lines above (line 405). The duplication indicates the file was hand-edited or generated with a mismatched toolchain rather than produced by `go mod tidy`/`go work sync`; the whole set of added hashes is unrelated to this dual-writer change and should be dropped or regenerated.

title: Write lock acquired without re-checking the cache (no double-checked locking)
body: After the fast path under `RLock` sees a nil cache, every goroutine falls through, takes the exclusive `Lock`, and unconditionally re-reads `assets-manifest.json` (or performs the CDN HTTP request) before setting the cache. There is no second check of `entryPointAssetsCache` after the write lock is acquired, so on a cold start with N concurrent requests the manifest is parsed N times, serialized one after another while holding the exclusive lock. Re-checking `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after `Lock()` makes the load happen exactly once and avoids the serialized duplicate I/O.

title: Cache is overwritten with nil when loading the manifest fails
body: `entryPointAssetsCache = result` runs unconditionally, including when `readWebAssetsFromFile`/`readWebAssetsFromCDN` returned `nil, err`. A transient failure therefore stores nil in the shared cache and the function returns a nil `*dtos.EntryPointAssets` together with the error; any caller that logs the error but still dereferences the returned pointer will panic. Guard the assignment with `if err == nil && result != nil` (and return the previous cached value on error) so a failed reload cannot poison the cache.

title: No test exercising concurrent GetWebAssets calls
body: The PR fixes a data race but adds no test that calls `GetWebAssets` from multiple goroutines, so the race fix is not covered and a future refactor (for example removing the lock or mutating the cached struct) could reintroduce the race without any CI signal. A small `t.Parallel`/`sync.WaitGroup` test run under `-race` would pin the behaviour.

title: No double-check after acquiring the write lock: duplicate loads and a valid cache can be clobbered with nil
body:
`GetWebAssets` reads the cache under `RLock`, releases it, and then takes the write lock without re-checking whether another goroutine has already populated `entryPointAssetsCache` in the meantime. Two consequences on a cold start where many requests arrive concurrently (the common case, e.g. several browser tabs hitting the index page):

1. Every goroutine that observed `ret == nil` re-runs the full manifest load (disk read / JSON decode, and the CDN HTTP fetch if `cdn` is ever non-empty), serialized one after another behind the exclusive lock, instead of just reusing the value the first goroutine stored.
2. More importantly, line 69 unconditionally assigns `entryPointAssetsCache = result`. If a later goroutine's reload fails (file transiently unreadable, truncated manifest during a rebuild, CDN error), `result` is nil and the already-published, valid cache is overwritten with nil, so subsequent callers fall back to re-reading from disk again.

Fix by re-checking `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` right after acquiring the write lock, and by only assigning to the cache when `err == nil`/`result != nil`.

title: Exclusive lock is held across blocking I/O (file read and CDN HTTP request)
body: The write lock acquired at line 48 is held (via `defer`) for the whole duration of `readWebAssetsFromCDN` (an HTTP request whose only bound is the request context) and `readWebAssetsFromFile` (open + JSON decode). All other callers of `GetWebAssets` block on the mutex during that time. In `setting.Dev` mode the early return is skipped, so *every* index-page request takes the exclusive lock and does a disk read + JSON decode while holding it, fully serializing page loads.
