Consider loading outside the lock (or using `sync.Once`/`singleflight`) and only taking the lock for the pointer assignment.

title: Double-checked locking is incomplete: cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock
body: After the fast-path read-lock check fails, the function takes the exclusive write lock but never re-reads `entryPointAssetsCache`. During a cold start, every goroutine that got past the read-lock check (because the cache was still nil) will, one after another, acquire the write lock and re-open/parse `assets-manifest.json` even though the first one already populated the cache. Adding a `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` check immediately after `Lock()` would make the initialization happen exactly once instead of once per concurrent request.

title: Failed manifest read caches nil and now serializes every request on the write mutex
body: When `readWebAssetsFromFile` fails, `result` is nil and `entryPointAssetsCache = result` stores nil, so the fast path never short-circuits. Previously these repeated retries were lock-free; now every single request that renders the index page must take the exclusive `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` and perform a failing `os.Open`/JSON decode while holding it. A missing or malformed `assets-manifest.json` therefore turns into a global serialization point (all HTTP handlers queueing on one mutex plus disk I/O), which is far worse than a plain error. Consider only overwriting the cache when `result != nil` (and/or caching the failure with a backoff).

title: Blocking network I/O performed while holding the global write lock
body: `readWebAssetsFromCDN` issues an HTTP GET with `http.DefaultClient` (no explicit timeout) while `entryPointAssetsCacheMu` is held exclusively. If the CDN path is ever enabled (the `cdn` variable is currently hardcoded to ""), a slow or hanging CDN would block every other caller of `GetWebAssets` for the duration of the request, since readers also need the same mutex. The I/O should be done outside the lock, with the lock only taken to publish the result.

title: No test covers the concurrent access that this PR fixes
body: The PR is a race-condition fix but adds no test. A small test that calls `GetWebAssets` from several goroutines concurrently (both with `cfg.Env == setting.Dev`, which always rewrites the cache, and with the production env) would fail under `-race` before the change and pass after, preventing a future regression when the `// TODO: get rid of global state` cleanup happens.

title: enableSqlExpressions has unreachable logic and silently neutralises the feature toggle
body: `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns `false` from both the `if enabled` branch and the fall-through, so the function is a constant `false` and the feature-flag lookup is completely dead. The negation is also inverted relative to the variable name (`enabled` is true when the flag is *off*), which makes the code read as a logic error rather than an intentional kill switch. Consequences: (a) the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle no longer has any effect on this code path, which is surprising for anyone later trying to re-enable the feature by flipping the flag; (b) static analysis/lint (ineffectual assignment, identical branch returns) is likely to flag it. If the intent is a hard disable, the function should simply `return false` with a comment explaining why, or the type case should return the error directly.

title: User-facing error says "not implemented" while the sqlExpressions toggle is still registered and documented
body: Requests of `QueryTypeSQL` are now rejected with `sqlExpressions is not implemented`. The `sqlExpressions` feature toggle remains registered in featuremgmt and documented as an available (experimental) flag, so an operator who enables it, and users who already have saved SQL expression queries, will get an error that contradicts the documentation and gives no hint that the feature was deliberately removed/disabled for security reasons. Either the toggle/docs should be marked as unavailable, or the message should state that SQL expressions are currently disabled.

title: Feature gate only added to the new reader path; legacy UnmarshalSQLCommand path relies solely on the stubbed DB
body: The explicit disable check was added only in `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` (pkg/expr/reader.go). The other entry point, `UnmarshalSQLCommand` -> `NewSQLCommand` (used by the classic/non-apiserver expression pipeline), has no toggle or disable check at all; it is only prevented from working because `sql.DB.RunCommands`/`QueryFramesInto` in the new `pkg/expr/sql/db.go` stub return `errors.New("not implemented")`. If `sql.DB` is ever re-implemented (which is the obvious next step for this package), that path silently becomes reachable again with no gate, re-opening the vulnerable surface. The gate should be applied at command construction/execution as well, not just in the query reader. Additionally, every such request now takes the `logger.Warn("invalid sql query", "sql", rawSQL, ...)` branch and surfaces an opaque `error reading SQL command` BadRequest, which both logs user-supplied query text on every attempt and gives no indication the feature is disabled.

title: No test asserts that SQL expressions are rejected
body: This change is a security fix that disables a code path, but no test is added or updated. There is nothing verifying that `ReadQuery` returns an error for `QueryTypeSQL` (with the toggle both on and off), nor that `NewSQLCommand`/`SQLCommand.Execute` fail safely against the new stub `sql.DB`. Without such a test, a future refactor (e.g. "fixing" the obviously odd `enableSqlExpressions` helper, or implementing `sql.DB`) can silently re-enable the vulnerable path with a green CI.

title: tablesFromAST indexes ast[0] without a length check
body: `tablesFromAST` does `flatten.Flatten(ast[0], ...)` immediately, so an empty JSON array (`[]`) returned from the serialization step causes an index-out-of-range panic. Today this is unreachable because `DB.RunCommands` is a stub that always errors, but the DuckDB-specific code in `TablesList` (the `SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')` command, the single-quote escaping) is left in place and will be the starting point if/when a real backend is wired up again. Either add a length guard, or remove this now-dead DuckDB-specific parser along with the dependency it was built for so it cannot be reactivated by accident.

title: enableSqlExpressions() contains dead and inverted logic
body: `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns `false` on both branches, so the computed value and the `if` are dead code and the function is a constant `false`. Two problems: (1) the polarity is inverted — `enabled` is true when the flag is *disabled* — so if anyone later re-enables the feature by deleting the trailing `return false`, SQL expressions would be permitted exactly when the toggle is off and rejected when it is on; (2) static analysis / linters commonly flag the unreachable branch and unused assignment, which can fail CI. Since this is the kill-switch for CVE-2024-9264, it should be written unambiguously (e.g. `return false` with a comment explaining that SQL expressions are disabled for security reasons), or the flag check removed entirely.

title: Error text "sqlExpressions is not implemented" is misleading for an intentionally disabled feature
body: When a query of type `QueryTypeSQL` arrives, the reader returns `fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")`. The feature *is* implemented in the codebase and the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle still exists and is documented as enabling it; the code path is deliberately disabled for security. Users who enable the toggle will get an error claiming the feature does not exist, with no hint that it was disabled on purpose, making the behaviour hard to diagnose and contradicting the toggle documentation. Either reword the error (e.g. "SQL expressions are currently disabled") or update/remove the toggle documentation accordingly.

title: No tests guard the newly disabled SQL-expression path
body: This PR disables SQL expressions (the fix for CVE-2024-9264) by stubbing `sql.DB` so every method returns "not implemented" and by short-circuiting `QueryTypeSQL` in `pkg/expr/reader.go`, but it adds no test. There is nothing that asserts that `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` rejects a `sql` query (including when `FlagSqlExpressions` is enabled) or that `NewSQLCommand`/`SQLCommand.Execute` fail, so a future refactor could silently re-enable the vulnerable path. Conversely, any pre-existing unit tests that exercise `sql.TablesList` or the SQL command end-to-end will now fail because `RunCommands` always errors — those need to be updated in this PR as well.

title: Dead DuckDB-specific SQL string interpolation left behind in parser
body: `TablesList` still builds `SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')` by interpolating the user-supplied `rawSQL` after only replacing `'` with `''`. This is unreachable today (the stubbed `DB.RunCommands` always errors), but it is the exact pattern that made arbitrary SQL/DuckDB execution possible, and the escaping is engine-specific and incomplete (it does not handle backslash escapes or dollar-quoting). Leaving it in place means that whenever a real `DB` implementation is wired back into `NewInMemoryDB`, the injection surface is restored silently. Consider deleting the DuckDB AST parsing code along with the dependency, or at minimum parameterising the statement and adding a comment that this code is intentionally inert.

title: enableSqlExpressions() is dead logic that always returns false
body: `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns `false` on both branches, so the feature-toggle lookup has no effect and the function is a constant `false`. Besides being unreachable/dead code (which some linters such as `unparam`/`gocritic` will flag and which can fail CI), the inverted condition reads like a mistake: a future reader may "fix" the inversion and accidentally re-enable the code path this PR is meant to kill. If the intent is to hard-disable SQL expressions, the function should be a plain `return false` (or the branch removed entirely) with a comment referencing CVE-2024-9264 explaining why the toggle is deliberately ignored.

title: Disabled SQL expressions produce inconsistent, misleading error messages
body: The new guard returns `sqlExpressions is not implemented` for the typed-query path, while the legacy path (`UnmarshalSQLCommand` -> `NewSQLCommand` -> `sql.TablesList`, which now hits the stubbed `RunCommands` returning `not implemented`) surfaces `error reading SQL command` (pkg/expr/sql_command.go:34) and the execute path surfaces a raw `not implemented` from `QueryFramesInto`. Users who have the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle enabled will therefore get three different and non-actionable errors, two of which look like a malformed-query problem rather than "this feature is disabled". A single, explicit message such as "SQL expressions are disabled" in all paths would avoid support confusion.

title: No regression test asserting SQL expressions are rejected
body: This PR is a security fix that disables an RCE/LFI-capable code path, but no test is added. Nothing locks in the new behaviour, so a later refactor of `enableSqlExpressions` or of `pkg/expr/sql/db.go` could silently re-enable SQL expressions. Tests should cover both entry points: `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` with `QueryTypeSQL` (with the `sqlExpressions` toggle both on and off) must return an error, and `UnmarshalSQLCommand`/`NewSQLCommand` must fail rather than construct a usable command.

title: tablesFromAST indexes ast[0] without a length check
body: `flatten.Flatten(ast[0], ...)` will panic with an index-out-of-range if `ast` unmarshals to an empty slice (e.g. if `RunCommands` ever returns `"[]"`). Today the new stub always returns an error so this is unreachable, but the function is still exported-by-use and the DuckDB-specific `json_serialize_sql` command construction in `TablesList` (line 25) is now dead code against a stub that cannot execute SQL. Either guard `len(ast) == 0` or strip the now-meaningless parser/DuckDB SQL generation so it cannot be reintroduced as a live path.

title: NoData result is immediately overwritten by TableData
body: In `Execute`, the `if frame.Rows() == 0 { rsp.Values = mathexp.Values{mathexp.NoData{...}} }` assignment is unconditionally overwritten by the following `rsp.Values = mathexp.Values{mathexp.TableData{...}}`, so the empty-result branch has no effect and an empty frame is always reported as table data. This is pre-existing and currently unreachable (the stub DB always errors), but since the file is being touched it is worth either fixing with an `else`/early return or deleting along with the rest of the now-dead execution body.

title: Index/lifecycle init failure now aborts server construction (and therefore process startup)
body: `NewResourceServer` now calls `s.Init(ctx)` and returns the error. Previously initialization was lazy, so a failure only broke the individual gRPC call that triggered it. Now any failure in `lifecycle.Init`, `search.init` (which lists all resource stats and builds every index), or `initWatcher` makes the constructor fail, which propagates up through DI and prevents the storage server / Grafana from starting at all. This is a real, reachable scenario: for file-backed bleve indexes `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` (pkg/storage/unified/search/bleve.go:98) returns `ErrorIndexPathExists` when the directory from a previous run is still on disk (the code itself has a TODO about not yet checking the persisted RV), and transient DB errors during `GetResourceStats` have the same effect. Startup also now blocks for the full duration of indexing all namespaces. Consider keeping init asynchronous/retryable, or at least making index build failures non-fatal.

title: cancel() is not called when Init fails in NewResourceServer, leaking goroutines
body: The cancelable context created at line 229 is only cancelled via `server.Stop`. On the new error path (`err := s.Init(ctx); if err != nil { return nil, err }`), the constructor returns without calling `cancel()`, so the context (and anything already started under it) is leaked. This matters because `search.init` may already have called `storage.WatchWriteEvents` and started the SQL poller/event-handling goroutines before the error occurred; nothing will ever stop them, and the caller has no handle to the server to call `Stop`. Call `cancel()` (and ideally `lifecycle.Stop`) before returning the error.

title: Removing per-request Init() checks makes the shutdown guard dead code
body: `Stop` sets `s.initErr` to "service is stopping" / "service is stopped", which used to be surfaced to clients because every handler started with `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil { return nil, err }`. All of those checks were removed in this diff, so no handler ever reads `initErr` again. After `Stop()` has cancelled the background context and the backend lifecycle has shut down, Create/Update/Delete/Read/List/Watch/Search now proceed into a stopped backend instead of returning a clear "service is stopping" error, producing confusing driver-level errors (or worse, work against a closed DB). Either keep a lightweight state check in the handlers or remove the now-misleading `initErr` assignments in `Stop`.

title: Data race on shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` in searchSupport.init
body: Inside `group.Go(...)` the closure writes the function-scoped `err` variable (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and increments `totalBatchesIndexed++`. With `group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers)` these closures run concurrently, so both are unsynchronized writes from multiple goroutines: a genuine data race (the race detector will flag it), an undercounted `namespaced_indexed` span attribute, and — worse — error misattribution: one goroutine can overwrite `err` with `nil` before another returns it (swallowing a build failure) or a goroutine can return an error produced by a different build. Since init failure now aborts server startup (server.go:258), a spuriously propagated error can block the whole process. Use a local `err :=` inside the closure and an atomic/counter for the batch count.

title: TotalDocs reads b.cache without holding cacheMu — concurrent map read/write panic
body: `TotalDocs()` iterates `b.cache` with no lock, while `BuildIndex` now writes the map (line 138) outside any long-held lock, from the N concurrent index-build workers and from lazy builds triggered by search/watch events. A concurrent map read and map write is a fatal runtime panic in Go (not just a benign race), taking down the process. This path is newly exercised by the `s.search.TotalDocs()` call added in search.go:216 and by any metric/diagnostic caller. Take `cacheMu.RLock()` in `TotalDocs` (and avoid holding it while calling `index.DocCount()` if that is expensive, e.g. snapshot the slice of indexes first).

title: Dropping the BuildIndex-wide lock allows concurrent duplicate builds of the same key
body: The write lock that previously covered the whole of `BuildIndex` is now only taken around the cache assignment. `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` does a lock-free `GetIndex` followed by `build`, so two concurrent requests (or a watch event plus a search) for the same NamespacedResource can now execute `BuildIndex` for the same key at the same time. Consequences: (a) for file-backed indexes both goroutines call `bleve.New` on the identical directory `Root/namespace/resource.group`, which at best fails with ErrorIndexPathExists and at worst leaves two writers on the same on-disk index; (b) both perform a full re-list/re-index of the resource (wasted DB and CPU work); (c) the loser's index object silently overwritten in the cache is never closed, leaking its file handles/memory, while callers that already got the old handle keep searching a discarded index. Finer-grained locking is fine, but it needs to be per-key (e.g. a per-key build mutex or singleflight) rather than removed.

title: BuildIndex still discards the span context, so the indexing work is not under its span
body: This PR's stated goal includes fixing trace propagation (`ctx, span := ...` in search.go and sql/backend.go), but `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` still uses `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)` and never passes the derived context anywhere. The `builder(idx)` callback executed at line 126 captures the caller's context instead, so all the list/iterate/document-build spans produced during the actual indexing attach to the parent `unified_search.Build` span rather than to `unified_search.bleve.BuildIndex`, leaving BuildIndex as an empty leaf span and making it impossible to attribute index build time in traces.

title: Storage-server integration test silently disabled for postgres in CI
body: The only integration test that boots the `StorageServer` module target is now skipped for postgres with the comment "test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally." This PR moves unified storage initialization (index build, watcher start) into `NewResourceServer`, i.e. into module startup — exactly the code path this test exercises — so disabling it removes CI coverage of the change for one of the supported databases and hides whatever failure prompted the skip (it may well be caused by this PR's startup-blocking init rather than by Drone). The root cause should be identified before the skip is merged, or the skip should link to a tracking issue with the observed failure.

title: Data race and lost errors in the index-build errgroup
body: In `searchSupport.init`, the goroutines started via `group.Go` all write to the function-scoped variables `err` (line 190: `_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and `totalBatchesIndexed` (line 189) without synchronization. Up to `initWorkers` goroutines run concurrently, so these are genuine data races (detectable by `-race`, and the counter will under-count). Worse, each goroutine returns the shared `err`, so one goroutine can observe another goroutine's value: a real build failure can be clobbered by a concurrent `nil` assignment (startup then proceeds with a partially built index) or a successful goroutine can return someone else's error (startup aborts spuriously). This was largely masked before because `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for its whole body and serialized the builds; this PR removes that lock, so the goroutines now really overlap. Use goroutine-local variables (`if err := s.build(...); err != nil { return err }`) and an atomic counter.

title: TotalDocs reads the index cache map without holding cacheMu
body: `bleveBackend.TotalDocs()` iterates `b.cache` with no lock, while `BuildIndex` now writes to the same map under `cacheMu` (lines 137-139). Concurrent map read + write is a fatal, unrecoverable Go runtime error (`concurrent map read and map write`), i.e. a process crash. This PR makes it reachable: `searchSupport.init` starts the watch-event goroutine (search.go line 207) and then calls `s.search.TotalDocs()` in the new log line (search.go line 216); a watch event handled in that goroutine can trigger `getOrCreateIndex` -> `BuildIndex` -> cache write at the same moment. Take `cacheMu.RLock()` in `TotalDocs` (and copy out the indexes before calling `DocCount`).

title: No per-key build guard: concurrent BuildIndex for the same key can corrupt a file-backed index
body: Previously `BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for its entire body, which serialized index creation. With the lock now only held around the cache write, two concurrent callers that both saw `GetIndex() == nil` (e.g. two Search requests for the same namespace/group/resource, or a watch event racing with a search) can run `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` on the same directory at the same time when `size > FileThreshold`. That means two processes/goroutines writing the same on-disk bleve index concurrently (undefined behaviour/corruption, or a spurious "path already exists" error), plus duplicated full re-index work and a cache entry that is overwritten by the loser. The TODO in `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` acknowledges this; a per-key lock (or singleflight) is needed now that the global lock is gone.

title: Requests are no longer rejected after Stop(): initErr is now write-only
body: `Stop()` still sets `s.initErr` to "service is stopping"/"service is stopped", but every RPC handler's `s.Init(ctx)` guard was deleted, so nothing reads `initErr` any more. After `Stop()` cancels the background context, `Create`/`Update`/`Delete`/`List`/`Watch`/`Search` etc. will happily keep executing against a backend whose watcher/poller has been shut down: writes still reach the DB but no write events are broadcast or indexed, and watchers silently receive nothing. Previously these calls returned an error. Either keep an explicit "stopped" check at the entry of the handlers or drop the now-dead `initErr` mutations in `Stop` and document the new contract.

title: Init failure in constructor leaks the cancel func and background watcher
body: `ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)` is created at line 229, but the new error path `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil { return nil, err }` returns without calling `cancel()`. Anything already started during `Init` (the sql backend poller started by `search.init`'s `WatchWriteEvents`, and `initWatcher`'s broadcaster goroutine if it got that far) keeps running for the lifetime of the process, and the context is leaked (this is also what `go vet`'s lostcancel check flags). Call `cancel()` (or `s.Stop`) before returning the error.

title: Synchronous, unbounded index build now blocks/aborts server construction
body: Moving `s.Init(ctx)` into `NewResourceServer` makes the full search-index build (all namespaces, via `searchSupport.init`) part of object construction, with no timeout and no way to serve traffic while it runs. Two consequences the PR should address explicitly: (1) startup latency - the PR itself states the build exceeds a gRPC request deadline, so Grafana/the storage-server target will not accept any request (not even `/metrics` via the gRPC health service) until indexing finishes; (2) a single transient failure (DB not reachable yet, one namespace failing to index) now aborts `NewResourceServer` and therefore the whole process startup, whereas previously only the first request failed and the next one retried via `sync.Once`... note that with `sync.Once` a retry was never possible either, but at least the server existed. Consider building the index asynchronously and gating readiness/search on it rather than blocking construction.

title: Postgres storage-server integration test silently skipped with no tracking issue
body: The only integration test that boots the `StorageServer` module target is now skipped for postgres with the comment "test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally." This is the exact code path changed by this PR (unified storage now initializes - including the full index build - inside `NewResourceServer`, before the module reports running), so disabling the test may be hiding a regression introduced here rather than a pre-existing CI quirk. At minimum the skip needs a linked issue and an explanation of the failure mode; ideally the failure should be root-caused before merging, otherwise postgres deployments of the storage server have no coverage of startup at all.

title: BuildIndex still discards the span context, breaking trace nesting
body: The PR's stated goal is fixing trace propagation, but `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` keeps `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, tracingPrexfixBleve+"BuildIndex")` and never passes the span context to `builder(idx)` (line 126). The builder closure in `searchSupport.build` uses the caller's context, so the `sql.resource.List`/`GetResourceStats` spans produced while populating the index become siblings of the `BuildIndex` span instead of children, which makes the index-build timing breakdown unreadable in traces. Either plumb the new context into `builder` (changing the callback signature) or document why the span is intentionally a leaf.

title: BuildIndex is no longer serialized per key, allowing duplicate/conflicting index creation
body: Previously `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for the whole function, so two callers that both saw a cache miss in `getOrCreateIndex` were at least serialized. Now only the final `b.cache[key] = idx` write is guarded. Two goroutines (e.g. the startup indexer and a `handleEvent`/`Search` triggered lazy build, or two search requests for the same namespace) can now build the same key concurrently: for the file-backed path both call `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` on the same directory, which will fail for one of them (path already exists) or race on the on-disk index; for the memory path both succeed and the second write silently replaces the first in the cache. The replaced index is never `Close()`d, leaking memory/file handles, and any documents written to it (including watch events already applied) are lost. Consider a per-key lock or single-flight so only one build per key runs and the previous index is closed when replaced.

title: TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu
body: `TotalDocs()` ranges over `b.cache` with no lock while `BuildIndex` now writes to that map under `cacheMu` from potentially many worker goroutines. A concurrent map read and map write is a fatal runtime error in Go (`concurrent map read and map write`), which would crash the process. This became reachable in a new place by this PR: `searchSupport.init` now logs `"total_docs", s.search.TotalDocs()`, and lazy builds triggered by watch events or search requests can still be writing the cache at that time. Take `cacheMu.RLock()` in `TotalDocs`.

title: Shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` written from concurrent errgroup goroutines
body: Inside the `group.Go` closure the code does `totalBatchesIndexed++` and assigns to the function-scoped `err` (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) instead of using local variables. With `group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers)` and multiple namespaces these closures run in parallel, so both the counter increment and the `err` assignment are unsynchronized data races (detectable by `-race`, and the counter will under-report). Worse, the outer `err` is also the variable later checked after `group.Wait()` (`err = group.Wait()` overwrites it, but the races remain) and a build error written by one goroutine can be clobbered by another. Declare `err` locally in the closure and use an atomic counter.

title: Eager Init in the constructor blocks startup, ignores caller context, and turns transient failures into hard startup failures
body: `NewResourceServer` now runs the full initialization (lifecycle hook -> DB init, full search index build over every namespace, watcher start) synchronously and with the server's own `context.Background()`-derived context. Two consequences: (1) the caller cannot bound or cancel this work - there is no deadline, so the constructor can block for minutes while all indexes are built, delaying everything downstream of it in the wiring graph (including HTTP/readiness for the embedded single-binary mode); (2) any error (a single namespace failing to index, DB not yet reachable) now aborts construction and therefore process startup, whereas before the error was retried on the next request. At minimum the init should accept a caller-supplied context/timeout, and index building should not be a fatal startup error.

title: Removing per-request Init() calls removes the post-Stop request guard
body: `Stop()` sets `s.initErr` to "service is stopping" / "service is stopped" and relies on every RPC calling `s.Init(ctx)` (which returns the cached `initErr`) to reject requests after shutdown. With all `s.Init(ctx)` calls removed from `Create`, `Update`, `Delete`, `Read`, `List`, `Watch`, `Search`, `History`, `Origin`, `IsHealthy`, `PutBlob` and `GetBlob`, requests arriving after `Stop()` now proceed and hit a canceled context / closed database, returning arbitrary internal errors instead of a clear "service is stopped". Either keep an explicit stopped-state check at the top of the handlers or document/remove the now-dead `initErr` assignments in `Stop`.

title: Constructor error path never calls cancel, leaking the context and any started goroutines
body: When `s.Init(ctx)` fails, `NewResourceServer` returns `nil, err` without calling the `cancel` created at line 229. The derived context is never canceled, and anything already started during the partially completed init (e.g. `initWatcher`'s broadcaster goroutine and the `WatchWriteEvents` poller goroutine, or the watch goroutine started inside `searchSupport.init` before a later error) keeps running for the lifetime of the process with no owner. Call `cancel()` before returning the error.

title: Postgres integration test is skipped instead of diagnosing why it now fails
body: The only integration test that exercises booting the `StorageServer` module is now skipped for postgres with the comment "test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally." Given that this PR moves unified-storage initialization into `NewResourceServer` (so module startup now performs DB init and full index building), a newly failing startup test for one database is exactly the signal that should be investigated rather than suppressed; skipping it leaves the eager-init path untested for postgres in CI and can hide a real startup regression (e.g. ordering versus migrations, or a timeout during index build).

title: Remaining spans discard the returned context, so child spans are not nested
body: This PR fixes the `_, span :=` pattern in `GetResourceStats`, `searchSupport.init` and `searchSupport.build`, but the same defect remains on the hot indexing path: `ListIterator` (line 388), `ReadResource` (line 353) and `WriteEvent` (line 158) start a span and then pass the original `ctx` to `listLatest`/`listAtRevision`/`create`/`update`/`delete`, so all the DB query spans attach to the caller's span instead of the `sql.resource.List`/`Read`/`WriteEvent` span. `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` (pkg/storage/unified/search/bleve.go:88) has the same issue. The result is that the traces this PR is trying to fix still show a flat/mis-parented structure for index builds.

title: Call to non-existent no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() does not compile
body: `UsernameForm.authenticate()` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments, but the only method added in this PR is `UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` (UsernamePasswordForm.java:160), and no no-arg overload exists in the super-class hierarchy (`UsernamePasswordForm` -> `AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator` -> `AbstractFormAuthenticator`). As written this is a compilation error and the `services` module (and therefore the whole build) will not compile. Either add the no-arg overload or pass `context.getUser()`.

title: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires user != null, disabling passkeys on the normal login page
body: `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` returns true only when `user != null`. Both call sites use it to decide whether to call `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)`: `authenticate()` (line 115) and the error `challenge(context, error, field)` override (line 137). Before this change the condition was exactly the opposite (`context.getUser() == null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()`), i.e. the webauthn/conditional-UI data was filled when the user had not yet been identified. `fillContextForm` is what sets the challenge auth note and the `enableWebAuthnConditionalUI`/challenge/rpId form attributes that the login template needs to render the `webauth` form and start conditional mediation. With the new condition, a first-time visitor (user == null) no longer gets any of that, so the primary ID-less passkey login (auto-login with a discoverable key, 'Sign in with passkey' link, passkey autofill on the username/password page) is silently removed, and the same happens on the error re-render after a bad username/password. Existing tests in all three Passkeys* test classes assert the presence of `//form[@id='webauth']` on the initial login page and auto-login with a discoverable key, so they will fail. The condition most likely needs to be 'passkeys enabled AND (user == null OR user has a passwordless webauthn credential)'.

title: Overriding shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators() to false removes the 'user has no passkey' guard during re-authentication
body: `WebAuthnAuthenticator.fillContextForm()` used the `user != null` branch not only to publish `ALLOWED_AUTHENTICATORS`, but also to bail out (`return null`) when the identified user has no credential of the relevant type. By overriding `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators()` to always return `false` in the conditional-UI authenticator, that branch is never taken, so during re-authentication (where the user is already known) the passkey/conditional-UI markup is now injected unconditionally for every user in a passkeys-enabled realm, including users that have no passwordless WebAuthn credential at all. Combined with the `UsernameForm` change (which no longer skips the username form during re-authentication when passkeys are enabled), such users get an extra, useless screen with a passkey prompt, and any passkey they pick from the platform list that belongs to another account ends in a WEBAUTHN_ERROR_DIFFERENT_USER error page. A check that the already-identified user actually has the passwordless credential configured is needed before enabling the conditional UI.

title: reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey does not test a user without a passkey
body: The test name and the inline comment at line 304 ('Passkeys login should not be available on the page as this user does not have passkey') claim it covers re-authentication of a user that has no passkey, but the test sets `setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(Boolean.FALSE)`, i.e. passkeys are disabled for the whole realm. The absence of the `webauth` form therefore proves nothing about per-user credentials. The actually interesting (and currently unverified) scenario introduced by this PR - passkeys enabled for the realm, user already identified for re-authentication but owning no passwordless WebAuthn credential - remains untested, which is exactly the path where the conditional UI is now shown unnecessarily. Either rename/retarget this test or add a second test with passkeys enabled and a user without a passkey credential.

title: Overly broad try/catch(Exception) used to assert element absence
body: The blocks at lines 291-296 and 312-317 call `driver.findElement(...)` inside `try { ...; fail(...); } catch (Exception nsee) { /* expected */ }`. Catching `Exception` swallows any WebDriver failure (e.g. TimeoutException, StaleElementReferenceException, WebDriverException from a broken page), so the assertion can pass for a completely unrelated reason and hide a real regression. The rest of the suite uses `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, () -> driver.findElement(...))`; use that here so only the expected exception type satisfies the assertion.

title: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() requires a non-null user, disabling conditional passkeys for normal (first-time) login
body: `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` returns `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null`. Both new call sites use it with `context.getUser()`: in `authenticate()` (line 115) and in `challenge(context, error, field)` (line 137). On a regular login the authentication context has no user yet, so the condition is false and `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` is never invoked. Consequences: the `ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI` attribute, the WebAuthn challenge (`AUTH_CHALLENGE_NOTE`), RP id and timeout are never put on the login form, so passkey/conditional-UI login from the initial login page stops working entirely (previously it was enabled exactly in the `context.getUser() == null` case). This also contradicts the existing assertions in `PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest.webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey` and `passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey`, which expect the `webauth` form and `username webauthn` autocomplete on the first login page. The user check should be dropped (the method should only test that the webauthn authenticator exists and passkeys are enabled).

title: Call to isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments does not match the declared signature
body: `UsernameForm.authenticate()` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` without arguments, but the only declaration in the hierarchy is `UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` (added in this PR, UsernamePasswordForm.java:160); neither `AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator` nor `AbstractFormAuthenticator` declares a no-arg variant. As written this does not compile. Either add a no-arg overload that only checks `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()` (which appears to be the intent here, since the user is already known to be non-null in this branch) or pass `context.getUser()`.

title: Re-authentication now always renders the username form when realm passkeys are enabled, even for users with no passkey
body: The new condition only checks the realm-level passkeys flag, not whether the already-known user actually has a passkey credential. With passkeys enabled on the realm, any re-authentication (e.g. `prompt=login`) will no longer short-circuit the username step; instead the username form is rendered with `usernameHidden=true`, i.e. a page with no input field and just a submit button, for every user including those who have only a password. That is a pointless extra click/step and a confusing screen for all password-only users. Consider also checking that the user has a passwordless WebAuthn credential (as `WebAuthnAuthenticator.fillContextForm` used to do by returning null when the user has no registered authenticators) before keeping the form.

title: New shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators() hook decouples the branch from the null-user guard
body: The branch that builds `new WebAuthnAuthenticatorsBean(session, realm, user, ...)` is now guarded by the overridable `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators(context)` instead of `user != null`, while `user` is still read from `context.getUser()` above. Any subclass that overrides the hook to return `true` for an unidentified user will pass a `null` user into `WebAuthnAuthenticatorsBean`, causing an NPE while rendering the login form. Since this is a new protected extension point, the null check on `user` should be kept inside the branch (or documented as a precondition of the hook).

title: reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey does not cover a password-only user in a passkeys-enabled realm
body: The test name suggests coverage for re-authenticating a user that has no passkey, but it disables passkeys for the whole realm (`setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(FALSE)`), so it only verifies that WebAuthn markup is absent when the realm feature is off. The behaviour actually changed by this PR - passkey/conditional-UI markup is now rendered during re-authentication whenever the realm has passkeys enabled, regardless of whether the known user owns a passkey credential (see `WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator.shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators` returning `false`, which removes the previous "no registered authenticators" short-circuit) - remains untested. Add a case with passkeys enabled on the realm and a user holding only a password.

title: try/catch(Exception) around findElement can silently pass on unrelated WebDriver errors
body: The 'webauthn elements not available' checks are implemented as `try { assertThat(driver.findElement(...), nullValue()); fail(...); } catch (Exception nsee) { }`. Any exception other than `NoSuchElementException` (e.g. `StaleElementReferenceException`, `TimeoutException`, a session error) is swallowed and the assertion silently passes, so the test can report success without having verified anything. Use `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, () -> driver.findElement(...))` as done elsewhere in these tests.

title: UsernameForm calls a no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() that does not exist
body: `UsernameForm.authenticate()` evaluates `!isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments, but the only method introduced by this PR is `UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` (UsernamePasswordForm.java:160) and neither `AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator` nor `AbstractFormAuthenticator` declares a no-arg variant. As written this does not compile. If the intent was the realm-level check, a parameterless helper has to be added; if the intent was the user-aware check, it must be called as `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`.

title: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires user != null, disabling conditional-UI passkeys on the anonymous login page
body: `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` returns true only when `user != null`. It is used as the gate for `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` in `authenticate()` (line 115) and in the error `challenge()` override (line 137). Before this change the fill was executed exactly in the opposite situation (`context.getUser() == null`), i.e. for the normal, not-yet-identified login. With the new gate, the first login page (user == null) no longer gets the WebAuthn challenge/RP-ID/conditional-UI attributes, so passkey conditional UI / autofill login is silently turned off for regular logins — the very feature this class implements. This also contradicts existing assertions in the test suite, e.g. PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest.passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey asserts `//form[@id='webauth']` is present on the initial login page. The condition for the re-authentication case should be added without dropping the `user == null` case (e.g. `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && (user == null || userHasPasskey(user))`).

title: Overriding shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators to always false removes the "user has no passkey" guard
body: In `WebAuthnAuthenticator.fillContextForm()` the branch guarded by `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators(context)` also performs the check `if (authenticators.getAuthenticators().isEmpty()) return null;`, i.e. it signals that the identified user owns no WebAuthn credential of the required type. By hard-coding `false` here, that guard is never reached for the conditional-UI authenticator, so during re-authentication (where the user is already known) the passkey UI/conditional-UI attributes are emitted even for users that have no passkey credential at all. Those users are offered a "sign in with passkey" option that can only fail. Consider still inspecting the identified user's credentials and skipping the passkey setup when none exist (note that `UsernamePasswordForm.authenticate()` also ignores a `null` return from `fillContextForm`).

title: SHOULD_DISPLAY_AUTHENTICATORS and ALLOWED_AUTHENTICATORS can now disagree
body: `shouldDisplayAuthenticators(context)` still returns `context.getUser() != null`, while the newly extracted `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators(context)` is overridden to `false` in `WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator`. During re-authentication (user != null, conditional UI) the form therefore gets `SHOULD_DISPLAY_AUTHENTICATORS=true` but never gets the `ALLOWED_AUTHENTICATORS` bean, a combination that was impossible before (both flags were derived from `user != null`). Templates that use `shouldDisplayAuthenticators` to render the authenticator selection list will have no bean to iterate over, which at best renders an empty selector and at worst raises a FreeMarker reference error. `shouldDisplayAuthenticators` should be overridden consistently in the conditional-UI authenticator.

title: Test comment claims to cover "user without passkey" but the realm policy disables passkeys entirely
body: `reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey` sets `setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(Boolean.FALSE)`, so no passkey UI is rendered for any user in that realm; the inline comment "Passkeys login should not be available on the page as this user does not have passkey" describes a different scenario than the one actually exercised. The interesting (and newly changed) case — re-authentication of a user who has no passkey credential in a realm where the passkeys policy is enabled — is not covered by any test, even though the new `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators() == false` override in WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator changes exactly that behaviour. Please fix the comment and add a test with the passkeys policy enabled and a user without a passkey credential.

title: try/fail/catch(Exception) for absent element can mask unrelated WebDriver failures
body: The blocks at lines 291-296 and 312-317 assert absence of the webauthn form by calling `driver.findElement(...)` inside a `try` and catching plain `Exception`. Any WebDriver exception (stale element, timeout, broken page, session error) is treated as "element absent", so the assertion can pass for the wrong reason; the `assertThat(element, nullValue())` line can also never succeed. The same files already use `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, () -> driver.findElement(...))` (e.g. PasskeysUsernameFormTest:202); use that instead so only the expected exception is accepted.

title: Login-cache invalidation decision uses the org-aware wrapped model, so required invalidations can be skipped
body: In `update()` the "original" model passed to `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate()` comes from `getById(model.getInternalId())`, which returns the model wrapped by `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel()`. That wrapper's `isEnabled()` returns `false` whenever the linked organization (or the realm's organization support) is disabled, even though the underlying IDP row is enabled. The login cache, however, is populated from the JPA query, which only filters on the IDP's own `enabled` flag and therefore *does* contain such IDPs. The result is an asymmetry: for an org-linked IDP whose organization is currently disabled, `getLoginPredicate().test(original)` is `false`, so an update that also makes the raw model non-eligible (e.g. setting `hideOnLogin=true`, `enabled=false`, or `broker_public=false`) takes the first early-return branch and no login cache is invalidated, while the cached id list still contains the provider. After the organization is re-enabled (organization updates do not invalidate the login keys), `getForLogin()` keeps returning that id from the cache, so a hidden or non-public (private) organization broker is still offered on the login page. Note that `create()` and `remove()` evaluate the predicate on raw models (`model`, `idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)`), so only `update()` is inconsistent; the fix is to evaluate the predicate on the unwrapped model (e.g. `idpDelegate.getById(...)`).

title: One login cache entry per realm+fetch mode aggregates all organizations, causing cluster-wide invalidation churn
body: `getForLogin()` stores all results for a given realm and `FetchMode` in a single cache object keyed by `cacheKeyForLogin(realm, mode)`, using the organization id as the inner search key. Whenever a request asks for an organization that is not yet present in that object, line 236 calls `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)`, which drops the entry locally and broadcasts an invalidation to the whole cluster, then re-adds a merged copy. `OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean` calls `getForLogin(ALL, organization.getId())` on the login path, so in a realm with many organizations the first login for each new organization on each node wipes every other node's cached login IDP lists for that fetch mode, which must then be rebuilt from the database; the merged entry itself also grows with one id set per organization without any bound. Keying the cache per `(mode, organizationId)` (as `getByOrganization` does per organization) would avoid the shared-entry contention. Additionally, for `FetchMode.REALM_ONLY` the `organizationId` argument is documented as ignored, yet it is still used as the search key, so passing different organization ids creates redundant duplicate entries with identical content.

title: Cleanup registers a non-existent alias, leaking 21 identity providers into the shared test realm
body: `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` (lines 381 and 425) uses the literal string "alias" instead of the alias of the provider just created (`idpRep.getAlias()`). Consequently the 20 providers `idp-alias-0..19` plus `idp-alias-20` are never deleted after the test, and the cleanup action itself targets a provider that does not exist (404 at teardown). Because `OrganizationCacheTest` uses the shared test realm across test methods, these leftover providers change the IDP counts other tests in this class rely on (e.g. `testCacheIDPForLogin` asserts exactly 5/5/10 login providers and `testCacheIDPByOrg` asserts 6/2/4), making results order-dependent and flaky. Note that the same mistake already exists at line 303 and is being copied here.

title: No coverage for the new create/remove login-cache invalidation
body: The new test only exercises the negative cases for the invalidation hooks added to `create()` and `remove()`: it creates an IDP with `hideOnLogin=true` and removes a disabled IDP, then asserts the login caches are still present. There is no case that creates a login-eligible IDP (enabled, not link-only, not hidden) or removes one and asserts that all three `cacheKeyForLogin(realm, mode)` entries are invalidated. Those are exactly the paths added by `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(model)` in `create()` and `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp)` in `remove()`, so a regression that drops either call (leaving stale login lists that hide a new broker or still advertise a deleted one) would not be caught.

title: Test asserts only on cache internals, never on what getForLogin returns
body: `testCacheIDPForLogin` discards the stream returned by `session.identityProviders().getForLogin(...)` and only inspects the sizes of the internal `IdentityProviderListQuery` entries. Nothing verifies that the cached code path returns the same providers as the uncached delegate path (for example that the aliases match, that disabled/hidden/non-public providers are excluded, or that the second, cache-hit call returns the same result as the first). A bug in the cache-hit branch (e.g. the `getById` loop returning wrapped models whose `isEnabled()` is false, or the fallback on a missing id) would pass this test unnoticed.

title: getLoginPredicate() silently gains an organization/BROKER_PUBLIC criterion that getLoginSearchOptions() does not have
body: `LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate()` now additionally rejects any IDP that is linked to an organization and does not have `BROKER_PUBLIC=true`. This criterion is not represented by any `LoginFilter` constant and is therefore absent from `getLoginSearchOptions()`, so the query-based and predicate-based helpers of the same enum no longer agree on what "available for login" means; the enum's javadoc ("contains all fields that are considered when deciding if a provider should be available for login") is now inaccurate. The change also affects every existing caller of `getLoginPredicate()` (e.g. `IdentityProviderBean.federatedProviderPredicate()`, which `OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean` builds on): non-public organization brokers that previously passed the predicate are now filtered out. If that behavior change is intended it should be documented; otherwise the extra condition belongs in the Infinispan invalidation logic rather than in the shared SPI predicate.

title: Cached getForLogin returns providers in non-deterministic order, unlike the delegate path
body: On a cache hit, `getForLogin()` returns `identityProviders.stream()` built from a `HashSet`, so the iteration order is arbitrary, whereas the fallback paths (lines 218 and 249) return the delegate's stream, which for `FetchMode.ALL` is realm-level providers followed by organization providers in query order. The order of providers returned by the same call therefore differs depending on whether the cache is warm or cold. Current login beans sort the result, but any consumer that relies on the stream order (or picks the first element) will behave non-deterministically; this should at least be documented in `IdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin`, which says nothing about ordering.

title: Login-cache invalidation decision uses the organization-aware wrapper, so updates can be silently skipped
body:
`update()` obtains `original` from `getById(model.getInternalId())`, which (when the ORGANIZATION feature is on) returns the anonymous wrapper created by `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel`. That wrapper's `isEnabled()` returns `false` whenever the linked organization (or the realm's organization support) is disabled, while `updated` is the raw model. `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate` therefore compares a model whose enabled state depends on *external* org state against a raw model, and bails out of invalidating when both sides fail the login predicate.

Concrete failure: organization X is disabled; IDP `idp1` is linked to X with `BROKER_PUBLIC=true`, raw `enabled=true`, `hideOnLogin=false`. The login caches were populated from the JPA query (which filters on the raw DB columns), so `idp1`'s id is in the `ORG_ONLY`/`ALL` entries. An admin now sets `hideOnLogin=true`: `test(original)` is false (org disabled ⇒ wrapper reports disabled) and `test(updated)` is false (hidden), so the first early-return triggers and no login cache is invalidated. When organization X is re-enabled, `getForLogin` keeps returning `idp1`'s id and `getById` returns a non-null model, so the IDP that is explicitly hidden on login is rendered on the login page (the bean only re-checks `isEnabled()`, not `hideOnLogin`/`linkOnly`).

Use the unwrapped model (e.g. `idpDelegate.getById(...)`) or compare the raw fields (`enabled`, `linkOnly`, `hideOnLogin`, `organizationId`, `BROKER_PUBLIC`) when deciding whether to invalidate. Note `remove()` correctly uses the raw delegate model, so the two paths are inconsistent today. There is also no test covering a disabled organization combined with a cached login list.

title: Single per-realm login cache entry keyed by organizationId is rebuilt/invalidated for every unseen organization
body:
`getForLogin` uses one cache key per realm+FetchMode (`cacheKeyForLogin`) and stores the per-organization result sets inside a single `IdentityProviderListQuery` under `searchKey = organizationId`. When a request arrives with an organizationId that is not yet present in that entry, the code calls `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)` (bumping the revision) and re-adds a merged query containing all previously cached search keys plus the new one.

On the login hot path this means: (a) the first login for each of N organizations in a realm invalidates and rebuilds the shared entry, so the realm's login IDP lookup is re-queried and the entry re-serialized O(N) times, and concurrent first-logins for different orgs will repeatedly drop each other's entry and re-hit the DB; (b) the entry grows monotonically with the number of organizations, so a realm with thousands of orgs ends up with one very large cache object that the realm cache's eviction policy treats as a single element. For `FetchMode.REALM_ONLY` the problem is gratuitous: `organizationId` is ignored by the query, yet it is still used as `searchKey`, so each distinct org id creates another identical result set (and another invalidate/rebuild cycle). Consider putting the organization id in the Infinispan key itself, or at least using a constant search key for `REALM_ONLY`.

title: Cleanup registers the literal alias "alias", so the 21 IDPs created by the new test are never removed
body:
`getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` (lines 381 and 425) references a hard-coded alias `"alias"` instead of the alias that was just created (`idp-alias-<i>` / `idp-alias-20`). At cleanup time the admin client targets a non-existent provider, so either the cleanup throws `NotFoundException` or it silently does nothing; in both cases none of the 21 identity providers created by `testCacheIDPForLogin` are deleted, and `idp-alias-20` stays linked to organization `orga`.

Because the test realm is imported once per class, this leaks state into the other methods of this class: `testCacheIDPByOrg` asserts exact counts (`assertEquals(6, ...)`, `assertEquals(2/4, ...)`) for the IDPs of orga/orgb, and `testCacheIDPForLogin` itself asserts exact counts (5/5/10, 6/5/11, 5/6/11) that are only valid in a clean realm. Depending on JUnit's method order, one of the two tests will fail or produce misleading results. (The same mistake exists in the pre-existing line 303 and should be fixed there too.)

title: Login-cache invalidation decision uses the organization-aware (wrapped) model
body: `update()` obtains `idpById` from `getById(...)`, which (when the ORGANIZATION feature is enabled) returns the anonymous `IdentityProviderModel` subclass created by `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel()`. That wrapper's `isEnabled()` returns `false` whenever the linked organization is disabled or the realm's organization provider is disabled, regardless of the IDP's stored `enabled` flag. `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate()` then evaluates `LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate()` (which includes `isEnabled`) on this wrapper for `original` and on the raw REST model for `updated`. Consequence: when an org-linked IDP is edited while its organization (or the realm's organization support) is disabled, `test(original)` is false for org reasons and, if the update also makes `test(updated)` false (e.g. setting `broker.public=false` or `hideOnLogin=true`), the login caches are not invalidated at all. The cached ID list, however, was produced by the JPA query which ignores organization enablement, so it still contains that IDP; once the organization is re-enabled, `getForLogin` returns it and consumers only re-check `isEnabled()` (not `hideOnLogin`/`linkOnly`/`broker.public`), so a hidden or non-public broker can be rendered on the login page. The comparison should be done against the raw stored model (e.g. `idpDelegate.getById(model.getInternalId())`).

title: Login cache key omits organizationId, so one entry accumulates one search key per organization
body: `cacheKeyForLogin()` only includes the realm id and the `FetchMode`, and the organization id is used as the *search key* inside a single `IdentityProviderListQuery` entry. For `ORG_ONLY`/`ALL` the organization id varies per login (see `OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean` which calls `getForLogin(ALL, organization.getId())`), so every distinct organization adds a new search key to the same cached object. Each first-time organization hits the `cached == null` branch, which calls `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)` (a cluster-wide invalidation that wipes the login cache for that fetch mode on all nodes) and then rebuilds the query copying all previously cached search keys. With N organizations this is O(N^2) copying, one unboundedly growing cache entry per fetch mode, and continuous cluster-wide cache thrashing plus DB re-loads on all nodes. Including the organization id in the cache key (as `getByOrganization` does with `cacheKeyOrgId`) avoids both the growth and the repeated invalidations.

title: Cleanup registered for literal alias "alias" leaks the created identity providers
body: `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` (also at line 425) references the hard-coded alias `"alias"` instead of the alias that was just created (`idp-alias-<i>` / `idp-alias-20`). Consequently (a) none of the 21 identity providers created by `testCacheIDPForLogin` are removed after the test, so they leak into the other test methods that share the same realm and make the exact-count assertions (e.g. `assertEquals(5, ...)` for `REALM_ONLY`) dependent on JUnit method execution order, and (b) the cleanup task itself targets a provider that never existed and will fail with a 404 NotFoundException. Use the actual alias when registering the cleanup.

title: getLoginPredicate() now embeds organization semantics for all its callers
body: `LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate()` is public API in server-spi and is used outside the new invalidation logic (e.g. as the base of `IdentityProviderBean.federatedProviderPredicate()`). Adding `idp.getOrganizationId() == null || Boolean.parseBoolean(idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC))` silently changes the result for every existing caller: any IDP that carries an organization id but no `broker.public=true` config is now considered not available for login. Unlike `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel()` in the Infinispan provider, this check is not guarded by `Profile.Feature.ORGANIZATION`, so in a deployment where the organization feature is disabled but IDPs still carry an organization id (left over from when it was enabled) those brokers disappear from the login/account paths that rely on this predicate. If the organization condition is only needed for cache-invalidation decisions, it should live in the caller or be feature-guarded.

title: No coverage for invalidation on create/remove of a login-eligible IDP, nor for returned results
body: The new test only exercises the negative paths of the invalidation logic added to `create()` and `remove()`: it creates a `hideOnLogin=true` provider and removes a disabled one and asserts the caches survive. The positive paths added in this PR - creating a provider that qualifies for login, and removing one that qualifies - are never exercised, so a regression in `registerIDPLoginInvalidation()` (e.g. stale login lists after adding or deleting a visible broker) would not be caught. The test also only asserts the size of the cached id sets and never compares the stream actually returned by `getForLogin` against the uncached delegate result, so an incorrect set of ids or dropped entries would go unnoticed.

title: Multiple crypto providers are now silently tolerated, with non-deterministic tie-breaking
body: detectProvider() no longer throws when more than one CryptoProvider is found on the classpath; it just sorts by order() and picks the first. All three in-tree providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, WildFlyElytronProvider) return order() == 200, and Stream.sorted() is stable, so when two of them are on the classpath the selected provider is decided purely by ServiceLoader/classpath discovery order. The removed IllegalStateException was the guard that caught exactly this misconfiguration; now a deployment that accidentally has both the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider and the FIPS provider on the classpath can silently run non-FIPS crypto (or vice versa) with no error, and the behaviour can change between environments or build layouts. Either keep failing when two providers share the same order, or give the real providers distinct orders and log at WARN/ERROR when more than one is present.

title: order() added as a non-default interface method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: CryptoProvider is a public SPI in keycloak-common. Adding the abstract method `int order();` is a source- and binary-incompatible change: any out-of-tree implementation (and, per the PR description, the authz-client copy maintained in the keycloak-client repository which compiles against a released keycloak-common) will no longer compile, and pre-compiled implementations will fail at runtime with AbstractMethodError when CryptoIntegration sorts the providers. Declaring it as `default int order() { return 0; }` (or some neutral baseline) keeps compatibility while still allowing the new provider to lower/raise its precedence.

title: logger.debugf() called with a dynamically built string as the format
body: `logger.debugf(builder.toString())` passes runtime-constructed text as the format string. If any ignored provider class name ever contains a '%' the formatter will throw or produce garbage, and static analysis/IDE format checks cannot validate it. Use `logger.debugf("%s", builder)` (or logger.debug(Object)). The message should also be built lazily (guarded by isDebugEnabled) and, given that silently ignoring a crypto provider used to be a fatal error, logged at WARN rather than DEBUG so misconfigured classpaths are visible. The message also ends with a dangling ", ".

title: Dead code: two ASN1Encoder instances created and discarded in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
body: Lines 114-115 (`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);`) build encoders whose results are thrown away; the actual DER sequence is produced from freshly created encoders on lines 117-121. These two statements have no effect and only confuse readers (they look like they are part of the encoding). They should be removed.

title: integerToBytes silently truncates integers larger than the expected signature half-length
body: When `qLength < bytes.length` the method keeps only the low-order qLength bytes of the BigInteger, silently discarding high-order bytes. The BouncyCastle-based implementation this replaces uses BigIntegers.asUnsignedByteArray(len, value), which raises an error when the value does not fit. With this implementation a DER signature containing an r/s value wider than the algorithm's half-length (corrupt input, or a mismatch between the key curve and the declared ES* algorithm) is converted to a wrong concatenated R||S value instead of failing, which turns a detectable error into a silently invalid signature. It should throw IOException when the value does not fit in qLength bytes.

title: Indefinite-length encoding (-1 from readLength) is not handled by readInteger/readSequence
body: readLength() returns -1 for the indefinite-length form (0x80). readInteger() passes that value straight to read(length), which executes `new byte[-1]` and throws NegativeArraySizeException - an unchecked exception escaping a method that declares IOException, so callers that catch IOException will not handle it. readSequence() with a -1 length simply skips the while loop and returns an empty list, hiding the malformed input. Malformed or BER-encoded input (asn1derToConcatenatedRS is called with externally supplied bytes) should be rejected with a clear IOException instead.

title: Test uses the default EC curve for ES384/ES512 and never validates the produced DER with a verifier
body: The key pair is generated once with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` using the JDK default curve (P-256 on current JDKs), so testES384/testES512 sign with a P-256 key while asserting against signature lengths 96/132. The round-trip assertion still passes because r/s are simply zero-padded, so the real P-384/P-521 r/s widths produced by concatenatedRSToASN1DER are never exercised. Additionally the test only asserts rsConcat == rsConcat2; it never feeds the DER output of concatenatedRSToASN1DER into Signature.verify(), which is the actual production use of that method (JWS signature verification), so an encoder that produces structurally parseable but non-DER output would not be caught. Generate keys with the curve matching each algorithm (secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) and verify the re-encoded DER with a JCA Signature.

title: New abstract `order()` method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: `int order();` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` interface as an abstract method. `CryptoProvider` is an SPI that is implemented outside this repository (e.g. the keycloak-client repo, adapters, custom/vendor crypto modules). Any existing implementation that is not recompiled will fail at runtime with `AbstractMethodError` as soon as `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider()` calls `CryptoProvider::order`, and sources will no longer compile. Declaring it as a `default` method (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) would keep the SPI backward compatible while still allowing the authz-client provider to lower/raise its priority.

title: Multiple crypto providers on classpath are no longer rejected; ties resolved nondeterministically and only logged at debug
body: The previous code threw `IllegalStateException` when more than one `CryptoProvider` was found on the classpath. Now the list is sorted by `order()` and the first entry is used silently. All three real providers (`DefaultCryptoProvider`, `FIPS1402Provider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider`) return the same order `200`, so if two of them end up on the same classpath (e.g. BC non-FIPS jar accidentally present in a FIPS deployment) the winner depends on `ServiceLoader` iteration order, and the fact that a provider was ignored is only reported via `logger.debugf` (off by default). That turns a previously loud, deterministic failure into a silent, non-deterministic choice of crypto backend — in a FIPS deployment it can mean silently running with non-approved crypto. At minimum, equal-order collisions should still fail (or be logged at WARN) rather than being resolved arbitrarily.

title: `logger.debugf(String)` used as a format string with no arguments and built unconditionally
body: `logger.debugf(builder.toString())` resolves to the varargs `debugf(String format, Object... params)` overload with an empty parameter array, so the message is passed through `String.format`. Any `%` character in the message (class names normally have none, but the message is data-driven) would raise `UnknownFormatConversionException`/`MissingFormatArgumentException` from a logging call. In addition, the `StringBuilder` is populated and `toString()` is invoked even when debug logging is disabled. Use `logger.debug(...)` (optionally guarded by `isDebugEnabled()`), or a proper format string with parameters.

title: Dead statements in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
body: Lines 114-115 (`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);`) create encoders, write into them and discard the results; the actual DER is produced by the `writeDerSeq(...)` call below with freshly created encoders. These two statements have no effect and only add confusion (a reader may believe the first encoders are the ones serialized). They should be removed.

title: Malformed DER input causes unchecked exceptions instead of IOException
body: `readInteger()` uses the value returned by `readLength()` without validating it. `readLength()` returns `-1` for the indefinite-length form (0x80), so `read(-1)` executes `new byte[-1]` and throws `NegativeArraySizeException`; a zero-length INTEGER (`02 00`) yields an empty array and `new BigInteger(new byte[0])` throws `NumberFormatException` ("Zero length BigInteger"). Both are unchecked exceptions escaping a method declared `throws IOException`, which is what callers of `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` handle. Since the input is an attacker-supplied token signature, this turns a verification failure into an unexpected runtime error propagating out of the verification path. `readInteger()` (and `readNext()`) should reject negative/zero lengths with an `IOException`.

title: Test only round-trips through the new encoder/decoder, so a wrong DER encoding would not be detected
body: The test asserts `asn1der -> concat -> asn1der -> concat` self-consistency using only `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`'s own `ASN1Encoder`/`ASN1Decoder`. If `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` produced structurally wrong DER (wrong tag, wrong length form, missing leading-zero for negative-looking values), the matching custom decoder would still accept it and the assertion would pass. The produced DER should be validated against the JDK, e.g. by calling `Signature.verify(asn1Des)` with the public key (and/or comparing against the BC-based provider output). Additionally, the key pair is created with the JDK default EC curve (P-256) for all three tests, so ES384/ES512 never exercise the real r/s sizes, and the leading-zero-stripping branch of `integerToBytes` (`qLength < bytes.length`) is only hit by chance depending on the randomly generated key; the test should use P-256/P-384/P-521 keys matching each algorithm.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns an unrelated JDK provider, making BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER point to e.g. "SUN"
body: `getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, i.e. typically the JDK's `SUN`/`SunJSSE` provider, although the interface contract states it must return a BouncyCastle (FIPS or non-FIPS) provider. `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER` is derived from this value, so any keycloak-core code reachable from the authz client that does `Xxx.getInstance(algorithm, BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER)` will be routed to a provider that does not implement the requested algorithms and will fail with a confusing `NoSuchAlgorithmException` instead of the clear `UnsupportedOperationException` the rest of this class raises. Consider returning a provider that actually matches the contract or documenting/handling the null case in `BouncyIntegration` instead of this workaround.

title: New abstract method order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: `int order()` is added as a non-default method on the public `CryptoProvider` SPI interface in `keycloak-common`. Any implementation that lives outside this repository (keycloak-client repo, adapter/distribution forks, custom FIPS integrations) will no longer compile, and pre-compiled implementations will fail at runtime with `AbstractMethodError` as soon as `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider()` sorts the loaded providers by `order()`. Since the whole point of the change is to allow extra providers to coexist, this should be declared as a `default` method (e.g. returning the current 200 baseline) so existing implementations remain binary- and source-compatible.

title: Silently picking a provider when several share the same order hides classpath misconfiguration
body: The previous code threw `IllegalStateException("Multiple crypto providers loaded ... Make sure only one cryptoProvider available on the classpath")`. It is now replaced by a debug-level log and `foundProviders.get(0)` is used. All three in-tree providers return `order() == 200` (`DefaultCryptoProvider`, `FIPS1402Provider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider`), so when two of them end up on the classpath the winner is decided by `ServiceLoader` iteration order, i.e. by classpath ordering, which is not deterministic across environments. In a FIPS deployment where both `keycloak-crypto-fips1402` and `keycloak-crypto-default` are present, this can silently select the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider instead of failing loudly, producing a non-compliant installation that is very hard to diagnose. Either keep a hard failure for ties in `order()`, or give the providers distinct orders (fips > default) and log the ignored ones at WARN.

title: Test uses a P-256 key for all algorithms and never validates the produced DER
body: The key pair is created with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` (default curve, P-256) and reused for ES256, ES384 and ES512. Consequently r/s are always 32 significant bytes, and after padding to 48/66 bytes the re-encoded DER sequence stays below 128 bytes, so `ASN1Encoder.writeLength()`'s long-form branch (`length > 127`) and the decoder's multi-byte length branch are never exercised – exactly the paths that real P-521/ES512 signatures hit. In addition the test only asserts that `asn1derToConcatenatedRS(concatenatedRSToASN1DER(x)) == x`, i.e. the new encoder is only checked against the new decoder; a malformed DER output would still round-trip and pass. The test should generate keys with `ECGenParameterSpec("secp256r1"/"secp384r1"/"secp521r1")` matching each algorithm and verify the generated DER with `Signature.verify()` (and/or compare it byte-wise with the signature produced by the JDK).

title: Indefinite-length / empty encodings cause unchecked exceptions instead of IOException
body: `readLength()` returns `-1` for the indefinite-length form (0x80), but no caller handles that value: `readInteger()` passes it to `read(length)` which executes `new byte[-1]` and throws `NegativeArraySizeException`, and `readNext()` computes a bogus length. Similarly, a zero-length INTEGER makes `new BigInteger(new byte[0])` throw `NumberFormatException`. These are unchecked exceptions escaping methods declared to throw `IOException`, so callers of `ECDSACryptoProvider.asn1derToConcatenatedRS()` that only catch `IOException` will propagate a runtime exception for malformed input. Reject indefinite length (and empty integer content) with an `IOException` instead.

title: Dead no-op statements in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
body: Lines 114-115 create two `ASN1Encoder` instances, write `rBigInteger`/`sBigInteger` into them and discard the results; the actual DER is built again on lines 117-121. These statements have no effect other than extra allocations and they suggest to a reader that something is being accumulated into shared state. They should be removed.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default keystore provider, not a BouncyCastle provider
