body: `normalizeValue` runs `StringEscapeUtils.unescapeHtml4(value)` on the raw property value before sanitizing. A translation that correctly escapes markup, e.g. `<div>`, is thereby converted into real `<div>` markup, removed by the policy, and reported as "Illegal HTML" even though the stored value is safe. The unescape step is only needed on the sanitizer output (to undo the sanitizer's own escaping); applying it to the input changes the semantics of the value being checked.

title: No test asserts that a compliant bundle produces zero findings
body: All four tests only use `Matchers.hasItem(...)`, so any additional (false-positive) message is silently ignored, and there is no test at all that runs `verify()` on a well-formed translation and asserts the returned list is empty. The newly added fixtures `noHtml_en.properties` and `changedAnchor_en.properties` are only used as English sources. Without a happy-path test, the many heuristics in the new code (identical anchors allowed, `{n,choice,...}` normalisation, `<!-- -->` stripping, entity unescaping, `br/p/strong/b` whitelist) can regress into false failures across hundreds of bundles without any test detecting it.

title: Italian text introduced into the Lithuanian account bundle
body: `totpStep1` was replaced with `Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:`, which is Italian, not Lithuanian. Lithuanian users will see an Italian sentence on the OTP setup page. The surrounding keys (`totpStep2`, `totpStep3`) are in Lithuanian, so the intended replacement text should be a Lithuanian equivalent of "Install one of the following applications on your mobile".

title: Italian text introduced into the Lithuanian login bundle
body: `loginTotpStep1` was replaced with `Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:`, which is Italian while the rest of this file (and the following `loginTotpStep2`/`loginTotpStep3`) is Lithuanian. Lithuanian users configuring OTP at login will see an Italian instruction line.

title: Traditional Chinese text added to the Simplified Chinese (zh_CN) bundle
body: `totpStep1=在您的手機上安裝以下應用程式之一：` uses Traditional Chinese wording/characters (手機, 應用程式), whereas this file is the zh_CN (Simplified) bundle and neighbouring entries use Simplified forms (e.g. `totpStep2=打开应用扫描二维码输入验证码`). The Simplified equivalent (e.g. 在您的手机上安装以下应用之一：) should be used instead.

title: isAccessTokenId() grant-shortcut check is inverted and reads the wrong characters
body:
The new matcher is supposed to assert that the `jti` of an access token encodes the expected grant shortcut. Two defects make it a no-op:

1. The condition is inverted: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` fails the match when the shortcut *matches* instead of when it differs.
2. The offsets are wrong. The encoded prefix is `<sessionType:2><tokenType:2><grantType:2>`, so the grant shortcut is `substring(4, 6)`, not `substring(3, 5)`. `substring(3,5)` returns the second char of the token type plus the first char of the grant type (e.g. for `onrtac` it returns `"ta"`).

Because of (2) the comparison can never be true for any currently defined shortcut, so with (1) the method always falls through to the UUID check and never verifies the grant type at all. Every call site (`expectCodeToToken`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, `expectAuthReqIdToToken`) therefore silently passes, leaving the main new behaviour of this PR untested. Fixing only the offsets without fixing the inversion would invert all those assertions and break the suite.

title: Null check for rawTokenId actually re-checks grantType
body: `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed");` validates `grantType` a second time instead of `rawTokenId`. As a result a `null` rawTokenId is accepted, and the failure only surfaces later as a token id literally ending in `":null"` produced by `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId()` (string concatenation of null), i.e. a corrupt `jti`, instead of failing fast at construction time with a clear message.

title: testIncorrectGrantType passes on a NullPointerException, not on the intended validation error
body: The test sets up the factory by calling only `init(null)` and populating the maps directly; `postInit()` is never called, so `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.sessionFactory` stays `null`. Decoding `"ofrtac:5678"` misses the cache and `getGrantTypeByShortcut()` dereferences `sessionFactory`, throwing a `NullPointerException`. Since the test catches the broad `RuntimeException`, it passes for the wrong reason and never exercises the intended `IllegalArgumentException("...Unknown value 'ac' for grant type")` path. Assert on the concrete exception type and make the factory usable (or inject a session factory) so the real validation path is covered.

title: getShortcut() javadoc says 3 letters, but the decoder requires exactly 2
body: The javadoc states the shortcut is "usually like 3-letters shortcut of specific grants", while `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider` encodes/decodes a fixed 6-character prefix (2 chars session type + 2 chars token type + 2 chars grant type) and rejects anything else with `IllegalArgumentException("...Expected length of 6")`. A custom grant factory that follows the javadoc and returns a 3-character shortcut will produce token ids that this very provider cannot decode (and a 1-character shortcut would silently shift the grant type characters). Fix the javadoc to require exactly 2 characters and validate the length (and the absence of the `:` delimiter) in `postInit()` so misbehaving providers fail at boot rather than producing undecodable token ids.

title: New abstract SPI method breaks existing grant-type factories and can fail server startup
body: `getShortcut()` is added as a non-default abstract method to the `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` SPI interface. Existing third-party grant type factories no longer compile and, if deployed as an already-compiled jar, will fail with `AbstractMethodError` when `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit()` iterates all grant factories. Additionally, `postInit()` puts the returned shortcut into a `ConcurrentHashMap` without a null check, so a provider returning `null` makes `postInit()` throw a bare `NullPointerException` and the whole server fails to boot with no indication of which provider is at fault; the same code also blindly casts every `ProviderFactory<OAuth2GrantType>` to `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory`, which would throw `ClassCastException` for a factory implementing only `ProviderFactory`. Consider a `default` implementation and defensive handling/validation in `postInit()`.

title: Lazy shortcut-map refresh bypasses duplicate-shortcut validation and can map a shortcut to the wrong grant
body: `postInit()` validates that no two grants share a shortcut (by comparing map sizes), but `getShortcutByGrantType()` and `getGrantTypeByShortcut()` later mutate the same maps at runtime for "newly deployed" grant types without re-running that validation. `getGrantTypeByShortcut()` simply takes `findFirst()` of all factories whose shortcut matches, and `getShortcutByGrantType()` unconditionally overwrites the `grantsByShortcuts` entry for that shortcut. If a newly registered grant collides with an existing shortcut, decoding a token id will silently resolve to the wrong grant type (and the reverse mapping becomes inconsistent) instead of being rejected.

title: Format change of the access token `jti` is not documented / no upgrade note
body: Every access token's `id` (`jti` claim, and the `token_id` event detail) changes from a plain UUID to `<6-char-context>:<uuid>`. This is a client-visible contract change: integrations that store `jti` in a UUID column, parse it with `UUID.fromString()`, or assume a 36-char value will break after upgrade. The PR contains no documentation or upgrading/release-note entry describing the new format, its stability guarantees, or the fact that old (pre-upgrade) tokens still carry a bare UUID that decodes to `UNKNOWN`. Add the corresponding documentation/upgrade note before merging.

title: isAccessTokenId matcher checks the wrong characters and inverts the comparison
body:
The new matcher is supposed to assert that an access-token id looks like `<session><token><grant>:<uuid>` and that the grant shortcut matches `expectedGrantShortcut`. Two defects make the check useless (and potentially wrong):

1. Wrong offset: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4 and 5 of the 6-char prefix (`on`+`rt`+`ac`), so it must be read with `substring(4, 6)`. `substring(3, 5)` reads the last char of the token-type plus the first char of the grant type (e.g. "ta" for "onrtac").
2. Inverted condition: `if (items[0].substring(3,5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` fails the match when the shortcut *equals* the expectation; it should be `if (!....equals(...)) return false;`.

Combined, the matcher currently always skips the grant check (the garbled 2-char slice never equals a real shortcut), so `expectCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken` and `expectAuthReqIdToToken` no longer verify anything about the encoded grant type — the main thing this PR introduces. Conversely, if `expectedGrantShortcut` ever happened to equal the garbled slice, every such assertion would fail. Additionally, `substring(3,5)` throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException (instead of returning false) for a prefix shorter than 5 chars, turning a mismatch into an error.

title: New abstract getShortcut() breaks existing OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations
body: `getShortcut()` is added to the `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` SPI interface without a `default` implementation. Any existing implementation of this SPI (third-party grant providers, and any grant factory in the repo/testsuite that was not updated in this PR) will no longer compile, and a pre-compiled provider JAR deployed into the server will fail at runtime. The failure is not localized to the grant itself: `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit()` iterates over *all* `OAuth2GrantType` factories, casts them to `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` and calls `getShortcut()`, so a single stale provider throws `AbstractMethodError` during server startup. Providing a `default` implementation (e.g. returning a neutral/unknown shortcut) and handling that value in the encoder would keep the SPI backwards compatible.

title: Grant shortcut length is never validated, yet decoding hard-codes a 6-char prefix
body: `getTokenContextFromTokenId()` requires the prefix before ':' to be exactly 6 characters (2 for session type + 2 for token type + 2 for grant type) and throws `IllegalArgumentException` otherwise, while `encodeTokenId()` happily concatenates whatever `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` returns. Nothing validates that a shortcut is exactly 2 characters — and the Javadoc of `getShortcut()` even states "usually like 3-letters shortcut", which actively invites 3-character values. A provider (or a future built-in grant) returning a shortcut of any other length will produce access-token IDs that this very provider can never decode, i.e. permanently undecodable tokens in the wild. Validate the shortcut length in `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit()` (fail fast at startup) and fix the Javadoc to state the exact required length.

title: postInit can fail with a bare NPE if a grant factory returns a null shortcut
body: `grantsByShortcuts`/`grantsToShortcuts` are `ConcurrentHashMap`s, which reject null keys and values. If any `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` implementation returns `null` (easy to do, since the method has no contract enforcing non-null), `postInit()` throws a `NullPointerException` from inside `ConcurrentHashMap.put`, aborting server startup with a message that gives no hint about which provider is at fault. An explicit null/length check with a descriptive `IllegalStateException` naming the offending factory id (similar to the existing duplicate-shortcut check below) would make the failure diagnosable.

title: Copy-paste in constructor validation leaves rawTokenId unchecked
body: `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` checks `grantType` for the second time instead of `rawTokenId`. As a result a `null` raw token id passes validation and later produces an access-token id literally ending in ":null" (`encodeTokenId` concatenates it), instead of failing fast at construction. The message is also misleading if `grantType` is the actual null argument. Should be `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, ...)`.

title: Session type derived from client session instead of the user session used for the token
body: The provider resolves the session type via `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getUserSession()`, while `TokenManager.initToken` already has the authoritative `UserSessionModel` parameter that the rest of token creation uses (subject, session id, persistence state). Any code path that builds a `ClientSessionContext` whose client session is not (yet) attached to a user session, or where the passed `userSession` differs from the one on the client session, will either NPE during token issuance or encode the wrong session type into every access token of that flow. Passing the `userSession` already available in `initToken` into `getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext` removes this divergence.

title: Decoding a malformed token id throws instead of degrading to UNKNOWN
body: `getTokenContextFromTokenId()` returns an all-UNKNOWN context for ids without ':' (legacy tokens), but throws `IllegalArgumentException` for ids that contain ':' with an unexpected prefix length or unknown shortcuts. Token ids come from client-supplied tokens (the stated goal is to call this from introspection/userinfo/admin endpoints), so once wired up any crafted or foreign `jti` turns into an unhandled runtime exception, i.e. an HTTP 500 instead of an invalid-token response. Treating unparseable prefixes the same way as legacy ids (UNKNOWN context) or wrapping the call in explicit error handling at the call sites is needed before these endpoints start consuming it.

title: Format change of access-token jti is not documented in upgrading/release notes
body: Access tokens no longer carry a plain UUID in `jti`; the value becomes `<6 chars>:<uuid>` (and `Details.TOKEN_ID` in events changes accordingly). This is an externally visible, behaviour-changing contract: resource servers, log/SIEM pipelines and client libraries that parse or store `jti` as a UUID (fixed 36-char column, `UUID.fromString(...)`) will break on upgrade. The PR contains no upgrading/release-note documentation for this change, nor any statement that the prefix is opaque and must not be relied upon by third parties.

title: Negative test accepts any RuntimeException and ignores the result
body: `testIncorrectGrantType` catches `RuntimeException`, so the test would also pass if the code threw an unrelated `NullPointerException` instead of the intended `IllegalArgumentException` about an unknown grant shortcut; the declared `ctx` variable is unused. Assert the expected exception type (and ideally the message) so the test actually pins the contract of `getTokenContextFromTokenId`.

title: No test coverage for the context values actually encoded during token issuance
body: The only tests are unit tests that decode hand-written token ids; nothing verifies the mapping performed by `getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext`, i.e. that an offline-session token really gets `of`, a transient session `tr`, a lightweight access token `lt`, and that the grant-type attribute is populated for every grant that now sets `Constants.GRANT_TYPE` (authorization code, refresh, password, token exchange, pre-authorized code, device, CIBA). Given that the AssertEvents matcher that was supposed to cover this in integration tests is broken (grant check never executes), the whole encoding path is effectively untested end to end.

title: isAccessTokenId matcher never validates the grant shortcut (wrong offset + inverted condition)
body:
The new matcher is supposed to assert that the access-token id has the form `<sessionType><tokenType><grantType>:<uuid>` with the expected grant shortcut. Two defects make it a no-op:

1. The grant shortcut occupies characters 4-5 of the 6-char prefix (`substring(4, 6)`), not `substring(3, 5)`; for `onrtac:...` the code reads "ta" instead of "ac".
2. The comparison is inverted: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` returns a mismatch when the value *equals* the expected shortcut.

As a result every token id of the right shape passes regardless of the encoded grant type, so `expectCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken` and `expectAuthReqIdToToken` silently stop verifying the feature introduced by this PR. The condition should be `if (!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` (plus a length check on `items[0]` to avoid StringIndexOutOfBoundsException on unexpected ids).

title: Copy-paste error: rawTokenId is never null-checked
body: `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` checks `grantType` twice instead of checking `rawTokenId`. A `null` raw token id therefore passes construction and only surfaces later: `encodeTokenId()` produces an id ending in the literal string "null" (e.g. `onrtac:null`), which would be used as the `jti` of a real access token. Should be `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")`.

title: New abstract getShortcut() breaks existing OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations
body: `getShortcut()` is added as an abstract method on `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory`, which is a documented extension point for custom grant types. Any third-party factory built against a previous release will fail to compile, and an already-built provider jar will fail at runtime with `AbstractMethodError` when `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit()` iterates all grant factories and calls `getShortcut()` — i.e. the whole server fails to start. Consider providing a `default` implementation (e.g. returning the "unknown" shortcut) and handling it gracefully in the encoder factory, or at minimum document this as a breaking SPI change.

title: Public copy constructor OAuth2GrantType.Context(Context) removed without deprecation
body: The `public Context(Context context)` copy constructor is deleted in this change. `OAuth2GrantType` is an extension SPI, so any external grant-type implementation that wrapped/copied the context (a natural pattern for decorating contexts) will no longer compile against this version. If removal is required because the new `grantType` field cannot be derived in a copy, either keep the constructor and copy `grantType` too, or state the removal explicitly in the upgrading notes.

title: Javadoc for getShortcut() says '3-letters' but the encoder requires exactly 2 characters
body: The Javadoc states the shortcut is "usually like 3-letters shortcut of specific grants", while all in-tree implementations return 2 characters and `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId()` hard-requires the encoded prefix to be exactly 6 characters (2 for session type + 2 for token type + 2 for grant type). A custom grant type that follows the Javadoc and returns a 3-character shortcut would produce access-token ids that the very same provider cannot decode (`IllegalArgumentException: ... Expected length of 6`). The contract must state exactly 2 characters (and ideally be enforced).

title: No validation of grant shortcut (null / wrong length) during postInit
body: `postInit()` puts `gtf.getShortcut()` directly into a `ConcurrentHashMap`. If a (third-party) `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` returns `null`, `ConcurrentHashMap.put(null, ...)` throws a bare `NullPointerException` during `postInit`, aborting server startup with no indication of which provider is at fault. Similarly a shortcut whose length is not exactly 2 is accepted here but produces token ids that `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId()` rejects. Validate non-null and length==2 here with a message naming the offending factory, analogous to the existing duplicate-shortcut check.

title: testIncorrectGrantType passes because of an NPE, not the expected validation
body: The test constructs the factory without calling `postInit()`, so `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.sessionFactory` is `null`. For the unknown shortcut "ac", `getGrantTypeByShortcut()` misses the map and dereferences `sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream(...)`, throwing a `NullPointerException`. Because the test catches the broad `RuntimeException`, it reports success while never exercising the intended `IllegalArgumentException("Unknown value 'ac' for grant type")` path. Catch `IllegalArgumentException` specifically (and assert its message), and make the fixture supply a non-null session factory so the refresh-on-miss code path is actually covered.

title: Access-token jti format change is not documented in release/upgrading notes
body: From this change on, every access token's `jti` (and the `token_id` event detail) is no longer a plain UUID but `<6 chars>:<uuid>`, e.g. `onrtac:1f65761e-...`. Relying parties that validate/store `jti` as a UUID (UUID columns, regex validation, replay caches keyed by UUID) will break, and no release note or upgrading guide entry is included in this PR. A user-visible format change of a standard claim needs an explicit documentation entry describing the new format and the fact that older tokens keep the plain-UUID form.

title: Credential from user storage is removed via local removeStoredCredentialById()
body: `isRecoveryAuthnCodeInputValid()` now obtains the credential through `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()`, which may return a credential that comes from the external user storage (`getFederatedCredentialsStream()`), not from the local/federated credential store. When all codes are used the code still calls `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())`. For a credential returned by a user-storage provider the id is not a local credential id, and providers that build the model with `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...)` (as the new `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials()` does) do not set an id at all, so `getId()` is `null`. Calling `removeStoredCredentialById(null)` on the JPA store performs an `em.find()` with a null primary key, which throws `IllegalArgumentException`, turning the last successful recovery-code login into a server error; at best it is a silent no-op and the exhausted codes are never removed from the user storage. The removal must be skipped (or delegated to the provider) when the credential originates from user storage.

title: Existing local recovery-codes credential is not removed when codes are stored in user storage
body: `createRecoveryCodesCredential()` writes the new codes to the user storage when `updateCredential()` returns true and in that case does nothing with any recovery-codes credential already present in the local (federated) credential store. `UserCredentialManager.isValid()` consults both the user storage and the local providers, so a previously stored local set of recovery codes stays valid indefinitely after the user regenerates codes (e.g. after the user-storage provider gained recovery-code support, or after the required action is re-run). The user believes the old codes were replaced while they can still be used to authenticate. The local credential of type `recovery-authn-codes` should be deleted when the codes are successfully stored in the user storage.

title: Undocumented credential-input format for recovery codes; user label and generatedAt are dropped
body: The code passes the generated codes to the user storage as a JSON array of plaintext codes in the `UserCredentialModel` value, while validation later passes a *single* raw code (`UserCredentialModel.buildFromBackupAuthnCode`) with the same credential type. Third-party `CredentialInputUpdater`/`CredentialInputValidator` implementations therefore have to distinguish between two completely different payload formats for the same credential type, and nothing in the SPI or javadoc documents this contract. In addition, the user-supplied label and the `generatedAt` timestamp that are present in `credentialModel` are not transmitted at all, so a provider cannot store them (the account console will show no label and a provider-invented creation date). Either send the full `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` data or document the expected format explicitly.

title: NPE in getCredentials() when the user is not present in the in-memory map
body: `getCredentials()` dereferences the result of `getMyUser(user)` (`myUser.recoveryCodes`, `myUser.otp`) without a null check, unlike every other method in this class (`getDisableableCredentialTypesStream`, `isConfiguredFor`, `isValid` all guard for `myUser == null`). The backing map lives only in the factory's memory, so after a server restart (or if the federated link survives removal from the map) `getMyUser()` returns null and any call going through `SubjectCredentialManager.getFederatedCredentialsStream()` – which is now on the login path via `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()` – fails with a NullPointerException instead of returning an empty stream.

title: Test does not cover one-time use / rotation / exhaustion of user-storage recovery codes
body: `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` only sets the codes up and logs in once with code #0 (`enterRecoveryCodes(..., 0, recoveryKeys)`). The stub provider's `isValid()` (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage, ~line 340) just checks list membership and never marks a code as used, and `getCredentials()` rebuilds the credential from the complete list on every call, so `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` will always request code #0 and the very same code can be replayed forever. Nothing in the test asserts that a code cannot be reused, that the next login asks for the next code, or that the exhaustion path (`allCodesUsed()` -> credential removal + `CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES` required action) works for credentials held in user storage. As written the test would pass even if one-time-use semantics are completely broken for user-storage-backed recovery codes.

title: Recovery codes stored in user storage cannot be disabled/removed
body: `disableCredentialType()` and `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream()` were not extended for `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE`, although `updateCredential()`/`isConfiguredFor()`/`isValid()` now support it. Consequently once recovery codes are written into this provider they can never be removed through the admin or account APIs, and the exhaustion path in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` has no way to clear them. Since this provider is the reference implementation exercised by the new test, the removal/disable side of the feature is both unimplemented and untested.

title: getCredentials() also exposes the OTP credential, changing behaviour of existing OTP tests
body: Beyond the recovery codes needed for this PR, `getCredentials()` now also returns the stored OTP credential (and `updateCredential` assigns it a generated id). This makes the OTP credential visible through `SubjectCredentialManager.getFederatedCredentialsStream()` where previously nothing was returned, which can change what the account/admin credential endpoints list and which id the client receives — exactly what `testOTPSetupAndRemoveThroughAccountMgmtAndLogin` asserts (`assertEquals(1, otpCreds.size())` and deletion by that id expecting 204). This unrelated change should be dropped or its impact on the existing OTP tests verified.

title: Unnecessary 'delayed-authenticator' execution in the test browser flow
body: `configureBrowserFlowWithRecoveryAuthnCodes` adds a REQUIRED `delayed-authenticator` execution (with the config alias typo "delayed-suthenticator-config") to the copied browser flow, and the only call site passes `delay = 0`. The delay serves no purpose for this test while adding a hard dependency on an unrelated test-only authenticator provider: if `delayed-authenticator` is not deployed, flow creation/login in this test fails for reasons unrelated to recovery codes. Either drop the extra execution or explain/exercise the delay.

title: Pre-existing local recovery-codes credential is left behind when codes are written to user storage
body: `createRecoveryCodesCredential` delegates to `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` and, as soon as some user storage provider accepts the codes (`userStorageCreated == true`), it returns without touching Keycloak's own credential store. If the user already has a `recovery-authn-codes` credential stored locally (codes configured before the federation provider supported the type, while the provider was disabled, or for a user whose provider capabilities changed), that stale credential is never removed. `SubjectCredentialManager.isValid` falls back to the local credential providers when the user-storage validator rejects an input, so the *old* codes keep authenticating the user indefinitely even after the user regenerated codes. The helper should delete existing local credentials of this type when the provider takes over (and vice versa), otherwise credential rotation can be bypassed.

title: Undocumented and asymmetric value format passed to user storage providers for recovery codes
body: The credential value handed to the user storage provider is a Jackson-serialized JSON array of the raw recovery codes (`JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes)`), whereas validation of the very same credential type passes a *single* raw code (`UserCredentialModel.buildFromBackupAuthnCode(...)` in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator`). This asymmetric wire format is not documented anywhere (no javadoc on the new method, no provider documentation in this PR). Any existing third-party `CredentialInputUpdater` that returns true from `supportsCredentialType("recovery-authn-codes")` - which today is only needed for validation - will now silently receive the JSON blob in `updateCredential` and will most likely store it as if it were a single code, corrupting the user's credential. The contract (JSON array of raw, unhashed codes on update; single raw code on validate) must be documented, or a dedicated structured input type used.

title: User label and generation timestamp are dropped when the credential goes to user storage
body: `createRecoveryCodesCredential` receives a fully built `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` (containing the user label entered in the required-action form and the `generatedAt` timestamp validated against the auth-session note), but when delegating to user storage it only forwards the codes JSON in `new UserCredentialModel("", type, recoveryCodesJson)`. The provider therefore cannot store the label or creation date (the test provider in this PR invents `Time.currentTimeMillis()` and leaves the label null), so the label a user typed is silently lost and credential metadata shown in the account console differs from the local-storage behaviour.

title: removeStoredCredentialById called with the id of a credential that may live in user storage
body: After the lookup was changed to `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(...)`, the returned credential can originate from the user storage provider (`getFederatedCredentialsStream()`). Such a model is built by the provider and generally carries no Keycloak credential id (the test provider in this PR builds it via `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...)`, which leaves `id == null`). Calling `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(null)` on the exhausted-codes path either throws (JPA `find` with a null id raises `IllegalArgumentException`, producing a 500 during login) or is a no-op, and in no case does it clear the exhausted codes from the external store. The removal must be restricted to locally stored credentials (or delegated to the provider).

title: Unguarded Optional.get() can now fail for credentials held in user storage
body: `credentialModelOpt.get()` throws `NoSuchElementException` when no credential model is found. With this PR the codes may be stored in a user storage provider, and providers are not required to expose them: `CredentialInputUpdater.getCredentials` defaults to an empty stream, so a provider that stores and validates recovery codes but does not implement `getCredentials` makes `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` return `Optional.empty()` while `isConfiguredFor` is still true. The authenticator then renders this login bean and the recovery-code login page fails with a 500 instead of asking for a code. The bean must handle the empty case (e.g. fall back to code number 0 / render without a specific index).

title: Reference user-storage implementation never consumes a recovery code, and no test covers single use
body: `isValid` for `recovery-authn-codes` only checks membership in the stored list and never invalidates the matched code; `getCredentials` additionally rebuilds the credential from the raw list each time, so every code is always reported as unused and the login form always requests code #0. Recovery codes are single-use by definition, so this provider (which is the de-facto reference implementation other provider authors will copy) accepts the same code an unlimited number of times. The new `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` only logs in once and therefore does not verify that a used code is rejected, nor that the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is re-triggered once all codes are consumed - exactly the behaviour that distinguishes recovery codes from a static secret.

title: getCredentials dereferences a possibly null MyUser
body: `var myUser = getMyUser(user);` is used without a null check at line 235 (`myUser.recoveryCodes`), while every other method in this class (`getDisableableCredentialTypesStream`, `isConfiguredFor`, `isValid`) explicitly guards against `getMyUser(user) == null`. If `getCredentials` is invoked for a user that is no longer in the in-memory map (e.g. after `removeUser`, or for a cached `UserModel`), the provider throws a NullPointerException instead of returning an empty stream, which will surface as a server error in whatever credential listing triggered the call.

title: Credential returned by getCredentials loses its id and user label
body: The `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` built in `getCredentials` is created with `createFromValues(...)`, which does not carry over `myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()` (nor the stored label, which is always null because `updateCredential` never sets one). Consumers therefore get a credential with a null id: the browser authenticator passes exactly this id to `removeStoredCredentialById` on the exhausted-codes path, and account/admin REST cannot reference or delete the credential. The stored id should be set on the returned model.

title: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin never completes the login and ignores the logout result
body: Unlike the sibling tests (`testOTPUpdateAndLogin`, `testLoginSuccess`), this test calls `testAppHelper.startLogin(...)` but never calls `testAppHelper.completeLogin()`, so the authorization code is never exchanged and the test only checks the redirect URL rather than that the login actually produced tokens. It then calls `testAppHelper.logout()` without asserting the result; since no id token/refresh token was obtained, the logout can silently fail, leaving the SSO cookie and user session alive for the following tests in this class (which reuse the same realm, browser and username `otp1`), making those tests order-dependent.

title: Unguarded Optional.get() produces a 500 when the recovery-code credential cannot be read back
body: `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user)` returns an `Optional`, but the bean immediately calls `credentialModelOpt.get()` (and then `getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get()`). With the new user-storage support, a provider can legitimately report `isConfiguredFor(recovery-authn-codes) == true` (so `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.configuredFor()` shows the form) while exposing no credential object at all through `getFederatedCredentialsStream()`/`getCredentials()` – that is exactly the default for any existing `CredentialInputUpdater` that does not implement credential listing. In that case the Optional is empty and rendering the login page throws `NoSuchElementException`, which surfaces as an internal server error instead of a login form. The bean should handle the empty case (e.g. fall back to code number 0 / a generic prompt) rather than dereferencing blindly.

title: New user-storage credential contract for recovery codes is undocumented and asymmetric
body: `createRecoveryCodesCredential()` hands the user-storage provider a `UserCredentialModel` of type `recovery-authn-codes` whose value is a JSON array of all 12 *raw* codes, while validation (`UserCredentialModel.buildFromBackupAuthnCode()` in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator`) hands the same provider a single raw code with dashes stripped. Nothing in the javadoc or in any SPI documentation states this format, that the codes arrive unhashed (so the provider is responsible for hashing them), or that the provider must mark a code consumed after a successful validation. Third-party providers implementing `CredentialInputUpdater.supportsCredentialType(recovery-authn-codes)` will silently store/compare the wrong thing. Please document the expected serialization and the one-time-use obligation on this method (and ideally use a stable constant instead of the hardcoded provider id "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes").

title: User label and generation timestamp are dropped when codes go to user storage
body: The `UserCredentialModel` built here carries only the type and the JSON of the raw codes. The `credentialModel` argument, which holds the user-supplied label (`userLabel`) and the `generatedAt` timestamp collected by `RecoveryAuthnCodesAction`, is only used for its type on the user-storage path and is discarded. As a result a user who names their recovery-code set loses that label whenever the credential ends up in the user storage (the test provider indeed returns `getUserLabel() == null`), and the created date becomes the provider's own clock value rather than the generation time shown to the user.

title: removeStoredCredentialById() is now called with an id that may come from (or be missing in) user storage
body: After the switch to `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()`, `optUserCredentialFound` may be a credential returned by the user-storage provider via `getFederatedCredentialsStream()`. Its id is not a local/federated-store credential id, and in the reference implementation added in this PR (`BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials`, which builds the model with `createFromValues` and never copies the id) it is `null`. Calling `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(null/foreign-id)` therefore cannot delete the exhausted credential: it silently no-ops (or fails), while the user is pushed into the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action. The exhausted credential stays in the user storage and the new one is written on top of it, so state can diverge. The removal path needs to distinguish federated credentials from locally stored ones.

title: getCredentials() NPEs for users not present in the provider map
body: `getCredentials()` does `var myUser = getMyUser(user); if (myUser.recoveryCodes != null)` with no null check, unlike every sibling method (`getDisableableCredentialTypesStream`, `isConfiguredFor`, `isValid`) which all guard against `getMyUser(user) == null`. Because this method is reached from `credentialManager().getFederatedCredentialsStream()` (account console credential listing, the new `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()`), any call for a user id that is no longer in the in-memory map (removed user, stale cache entry, different factory instance) throws a NullPointerException out of the provider instead of returning an empty stream.

title: Recovery-code credential exposed by getCredentials() has no id
body: `updateCredential()` assigns `recoveryCodesModel.setId(KeycloakModelUtils.generateId())`, but `getCredentials()` rebuilds the model with `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...)`, which does not set an id, and the stored id is never copied over. Consumers of `getFederatedCredentialsStream()` therefore see a credential with `id == null`: the account console renders/deletes credentials by id, and `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` calls `removeStoredCredentialById(model.getId())` with that null. The same bug was explicitly fixed for OTP in this diff (`newOTP.setId(...)`), so the recovery-code model should propagate the id too.

title: Reference provider never invalidates a used recovery code, so one-time-use is not covered by any test
body: `isValid()` for `recovery-authn-codes` simply checks whether the submitted value is contained in the stored plaintext list and returns true, without removing/marking the code as used. Consequently the same recovery code can be replayed an unlimited number of times against this provider, and the new integration test (`testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin`) cannot detect that the critical one-time-use semantics of recovery codes are preserved when the credential lives in user storage. Please consume the code on successful validation (and add an assertion that re-using the same code fails, and that the next login asks for the following code number).

title: supportsCredentialType()/isConfiguredFor() can NPE on a null credential type
body: The new conditions are written as `credentialType.equals(RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE)` (lines 114 and 275), dereferencing the parameter. The pre-existing checks in the same expressions (`CredentialModel.PASSWORD.equals(credentialType)`, `isOTPType(...)`) are null-safe, so a null type used to be handled gracefully and now throws NullPointerException. Invert the comparison to `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE.equals(credentialType)`.

title: Recovery codes stored in the provider cannot be disabled/removed
body: `disableCredentialType()` only clears OTP and `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream()` only reports `CredentialModel.OTP`, yet `getCredentials()` now exposes the recovery-code credential to the account console and admin REST. The credential is therefore listed but there is no way to delete or disable it through the standard credential-management paths, which also means the new feature has no test for removing user-storage recovery codes (the OTP equivalent is covered by `testOTPSetupAndRemoveThroughAccountMgmtAndLogin`).

title: Login is never completed and logout result is ignored in testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin
body: Unlike the sibling tests, this test never calls `testAppHelper.completeLogin()` after submitting the recovery code, so the authorization code is never exchanged and no tokens (incl. the id/refresh token used by `TestAppHelper.logout()`) are obtained. The subsequent `testAppHelper.logout()` is then very likely a no-op/failure and its boolean result is discarded (other tests use `assertTrue(testAppHelper.logout())`). The result is that the test neither verifies a complete, token-producing login via a user-storage recovery code nor reliably tears the SSO session down, which can leak session state into the other tests in this class that log in as the same user `otp1`.

title: Reader thread is never joined, so the regression test can pass while the NPE happens
body: `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti` starts a background thread that repeatedly lists groups and records exceptions into `caughtExceptions`, but the main thread only sets `deletedAll = true` and immediately runs `assertThat(caughtExceptions, Matchers.empty())`. There is no `Thread.join()` (and no synchronization between setting the flag and the assertion), so an exception thrown by the very iteration that races with the last deletions – exactly the window this test is meant to cover – can be appended after the assertion has already run, making the test green even when the regression is present. In addition the thread is non-daemon and keeps issuing admin requests after the test method returns (until it observes the flag), which can produce errors/log noise or interfere with teardown of the managed realm and admin client. The thread reference should be kept and joined before asserting.

title: Same concurrent-removal NPE still present in the getSubGroupsStream overloads
body: The fix only guards `getSubGroupsCount()` against `modelSupplier.get()` returning `null`. The three `getSubGroupsStream(...)` overloads (lines 256, 262 and 268) call `modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` with no null check, and `modelSupplier` resolves to `cacheSession.getGroupDelegate().getGroupById(realm, cached.getId())`, which returns `null` for a group removed by a concurrent transaction after the cache entry was obtained. Under the same race that motivated this PR (listing groups while groups are being deleted) those paths will still throw a NullPointerException, so the reported bug is only partially fixed for group tree/search endpoints.

title: getSubGroupsCount() now returns null, which is not part of the GroupModel contract
body: `GroupAdapter.getSubGroupsCount()` returns `null` when the underlying group no longer exists. `GroupModel.getSubGroupsCount()` returns a boxed `Long` but no implementation (e.g. the JPA adapter) ever returns `null` and the interface documents no nullability, so callers are free to unbox or compare the result. Any such caller now gets a NullPointerException at the call site instead of here – i.e. the NPE is relocated rather than removed – and REST responses can silently carry `subGroupCount: null`. Prefer returning `0L` (or handling the removed-group case explicitly, e.g. by skipping the group) instead of leaking `null` through the model API.

title: populateGroupHierarchyFromSubGroups still dereferences a possibly-removed parent group
body: In `populateGroupHierarchyFromSubGroups`, `session.groups().getGroupById(realm, currGroup.getParentId())` can return `null` when the parent group is deleted concurrently with the listing request. `parentModel` is then passed to `groupEvaluator.canView(parentModel)` (line 51), to `toRepresentation(groupEvaluator, parentModel, full)` (line 57) and to `populateSubGroupCount(parentModel, parent)` (line 60) without any null check, producing a NullPointerException on exactly the concurrent read/delete path this PR aims to fix (and unconditionally when fine-grained admin permissions are enabled, since the `canView` block is skipped). A null `parentModel` should abort the walk for that branch (e.g. remove the current group from the map and break), analogous to the existing not-viewable handling.

title: Shared admin client used from two threads may yield spurious failures
body: The background reader calls `managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(...)` while the main thread performs deletes through the same injected `Keycloak` admin client. The admin client's token manager/JAX-RS proxy is not documented as thread-safe; concurrent token refresh from two threads can produce intermittent 401/`NotAuthorizedException`, which this test would record in `caughtExceptions` and report as a failure of the group-listing code. Using a separate admin client instance (or at least a dedicated token) for the reader thread would avoid attributing client-side races to the server fix being tested.

title: Tight busy loop issuing unbounded group queries
body: The reader thread loops with no pause, each iteration requesting `groups(null, 0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, true)`. This saturates a CPU and floods the server with full-table group listings for the whole duration of the 100 deletions, slowing the test suite and making timing-sensitive neighbouring tests more flaky. A small sleep between iterations (and a bounded `maxResults`) would keep the race window without the load.

title: Created groups are not registered for cleanup
body: The 100 groups created in `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti` are only removed by the explicit delete loop; nothing is registered with `managedRealm.cleanup()`. If any `remove()` call or an earlier assertion fails, the remaining `Test Group N` entries stay in the realm, which is shared by all other test methods in this class, so a single failure here can cascade into unrelated failures in group-listing tests.

title: getSubGroupsCount() can now return null, breaking callers that unbox the Long
body: `GroupAdapter.getSubGroupsCount()` now returns `null` when the underlying group can no longer be loaded from the store (concurrent deletion). `GroupModel#getSubGroupsCount()` is declared as `Long` but every other provider implementation returns a real count, and consumers such as `GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount()` forward the value straight into `GroupRepresentation#setSubGroupCount(...)`; any caller that compares or unboxes the value (e.g. `count > 0`, assignment to `long`) will now throw a NullPointerException instead of the original one, i.e. the NPE is only moved. It also silently produces representations with a missing/null `subGroupCount`, which the admin console uses for lazy-loading sub-groups. Prefer a defined behaviour for a vanished group: return `0L`, or follow the pattern used elsewhere in this class (`getDelegateForUpdate()` / registering an invalidation) so the stale cache entry is dropped.

title: Same concurrent-deletion NPE remains in the getSubGroupsStream(...) overloads
body: The three `getSubGroupsStream(...)` overloads (lines 256, 262, 268) still call `modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` without a null check. `modelSupplier` resolves to `cacheSession.getGroupDelegate().getGroupById(realm, cached.getId())`, which returns `null` exactly in the scenario this PR fixes (group removed by another transaction while a stale `CachedGroup` entry is still served). Listing sub-groups concurrently with a group deletion therefore still produces a NullPointerException / HTTP 500, so the fix is incomplete and the added test only covers the count path.

title: Reader thread is never joined and can outlive/hang the test
body: The test starts a plain (non-daemon) thread that loops on `managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(...)` until `deletedAll` is set, but it is never joined. Consequences: (1) `deletedAll` is only set at the end of the happy path, so if any `group(groupUuid).remove()` call throws, the flag is never set and the non-daemon thread spins forever issuing admin requests, hanging the build; (2) the thread keeps issuing requests against the shared `managedRealm` after this test method returns, which can interfere with subsequent tests and with realm cleanup. Set the flag in a `finally` block and `join()` the thread (with a timeout) before leaving the test.

title: Assertion on caughtExceptions races with the reader thread, so the test can pass vacuously
body: `assertThat(caughtExceptions, Matchers.empty())` is executed immediately after `deletedAll.set(true)` without any synchronization with the reader thread. Exceptions added by the reader after this point (including the very NPE this PR fixes, which is most likely to occur during the last deletions) are never observed, and if the reader thread had not yet issued a request overlapping a deletion the list is trivially empty. The result is a test that is both flaky and able to pass even when the regression is present; join the thread before asserting.

title: Same NPE race remains in the getSubGroupsStream overloads
body: The fix only guards `getSubGroupsCount()` against `modelSupplier.get()` returning `null` (group concurrently removed from the DB while a cached entry is still served). The three `getSubGroupsStream(...)` overloads (lines 256, 262 and 268) dereference `modelSupplier.get()` unconditionally, so the very same race that produced the reported NPE still throws `NullPointerException` there, e.g. when the admin endpoint lists sub-groups with paging/search while another request deletes the group. Either handle `null` consistently (empty stream / delegate invalidation) or centralize the null handling in one helper so all accessors are protected.

title: getSubGroupsCount() can now return null, an undocumented value for GroupModel
body: `GroupModel.getSubGroupsCount()` is declared to return `Long` but no provider (JPA, map) ever returns `null`; callers therefore assume a non-null count. After this change the cached adapter returns `null` when the group has vanished from the store, which only moves the failure: any caller that unboxes the value (`long c = group.getSubGroupsCount()`, arithmetic or comparison) will throw NPE at a less obvious place, and `GroupRepresentation.subGroupCount` will be serialized as null/absent for that group, which the admin console does not expect. Prefer returning `0L` (or invalidating/handling the missing group explicitly) instead of leaking `null` through the model API.

title: Regression test is racy: reader thread is never joined before asserting
body: `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti` starts a reader thread and then immediately asserts `caughtExceptions` is empty after `deletedAll.set(true)`, without joining the thread. The thread may not even have issued its first request before the deletions finish, and an exception thrown by an in-flight request can be added to the list after the assertion has run. The test can therefore pass even when the NPE it is supposed to cover is still present (false negative), and it can also fail spuriously. Join the thread (or use an ExecutorService/Future and get its result) before asserting.

title: Non-daemon reader thread can leak/hang the test JVM
body: The reader thread spins on `while (!deletedAll.get())` and `deletedAll` is only set after the delete loop completes. If any `groups().group(groupUuid).remove()` call throws (404, 500, connection error) the flag is never set, and since the thread is a plain non-daemon `Thread` with no timeout it keeps looping forever, hammering the server and preventing JVM/test-run termination. Set `deletedAll` in a `finally` block, mark the thread as daemon, and/or bound the loop with a deadline.

title: Reader thread busy-loops admin REST calls with no pause
body: The reader thread repeatedly calls `groups().groups(null, 0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, true)` in a tight loop with no sleep for the whole duration of 100 group deletions. This issues an unbounded number of full group listings (each with maxResults=Integer.MAX_VALUE), consuming CPU on both test and server side and slowing CI considerably. A small sleep between iterations, or a bounded iteration count, would reproduce the race just as well.

title: New test does not drain the 200 admin events it generates
body: The realm used by this class has `eventsEnabled(true)` and other tests in the class assert on specific entries from `adminEvents.poll()` / call `adminEvents.skipAll()`. `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti` creates and deletes 100 groups (200 admin events) without polling or skipping them; if the injected admin-events queue is shared across tests in the class this leaves stale events that will make the subsequent `adminEvents.poll()` assertions fail or match the wrong event. Add `adminEvents.skipAll()` at the end of the test (or clear the queue) to be safe.

title: `organization_context.member` can be None, causing AttributeError on every request
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated unconditionally for every GET, before the `use_optimized` check. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is `None` whenever the caller is not an organization member — e.g. requests authenticated with an org-level/integration token (where `request.user` is an AnonymousUser and `is_superuser` is False), or a staff/superuser-less service account. In those cases the short-circuit does not fire and `None.has_global_access` raises `AttributeError`, turning a previously working audit-log listing into an unhandled 500. Guard with `organization_context.member and organization_context.member.has_global_access`, and only compute the flag when `use_optimized` is true.

title: Authorization gate does not restrict the feature to administrators
body: The comment says the new pagination path is for "authorized administrators", but the check is `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`. Two problems: (1) `request.user.is_superuser` is the raw DB flag; Sentry requires `is_active_superuser(request)` (or the staff equivalent) so that superuser powers only apply within an elevated/validated superuser session — using the raw flag bypasses that elevation requirement; (2) `member.has_global_access` is not an admin signal at all: it is true for ordinary members in organizations with open membership / global access, so essentially any regular org member can turn on the "admin-only" code path by appending `?optimized_pagination=true`. The gate should use an explicit permission/scope check.

title: Negative queryset slicing raises ValueError; the "Django handles it" comment is wrong
body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset` (and often a negative `stop`, since `stop = start_offset + limit + extra`). Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly rejects negative start/stop values with `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`; there is no SQL equivalent of a negative OFFSET. So the inline comment "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is factually false, and any request carrying a cursor with a negative offset on this path returns an unhandled 500. Since cursor strings are fully client-controlled (`Cursor.from_string` accepts negative offsets), this is a trivially reachable error/DoS vector. The whole negative-offset branch should be removed, or negative offsets rejected with `BadPaginationError`.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle datetime sort keys, which is what the audit-log endpoint uses
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(getattr(item, self.key)))` and `value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` unchanged — i.e. it copies `Paginator`'s numeric-key semantics. The only caller, `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`, instantiates it with `order_by="-datetime"` on `AuditLogEntry`, whose `datetime` field is a `datetime` object: `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`. Even if the first page somehow succeeded, `value_from_cursor` would hand an integer to `build_queryset`, which injects it into `WHERE "datetime" <= %s` against a timestamp column, producing a database error. The optimized path therefore fails for every request that reaches it; it needs `DateTimePaginator`-style key/value conversion (or should subclass `DateTimePaginator`).

title: Cursors are not interchangeable between the two paginators selected by a query param
body: The endpoint switches between `DateTimePaginator` (cursor value = epoch milliseconds) and `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (cursor value = floor/ceil of the raw sort value) based on the client-supplied `optimized_pagination` flag. A cursor minted by one paginator is meaningless to the other, so a client that follows a `Link` header while the flag changes (or that caches cursors) will get wrong pages, skipped/duplicated rows, or a query error. Pagination state must not depend on a mutable request flag; pick one cursor encoding or namespace the cursors.

title: BasePaginator silently clamps negative forward offsets, changing behavior for every paginated endpoint
body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes the shared `BasePaginator.get_result` used by most paginated Sentry endpoints: a forward cursor with a negative offset, which previously surfaced as an error from Django slicing, now silently returns the first page's rows. That masks malformed/tampered cursors and can produce duplicated results across pages. Note also that the clamp is deliberately not applied when `cursor.is_prev`, so the previous-page path still crashes with `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` — the stated justification ("the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions") is incorrect. Invalid offsets should raise `BadPaginationError` consistently for both directions.

title: No tests for the new paginator or the new endpoint branch
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (including its negative-offset branch) and the new `optimized_pagination` branch in `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` ship with no tests, and the behavior change in `BasePaginator.get_result` (offset clamping) is likewise untested. Basic tests would have caught the `math.floor(datetime)` TypeError, the negative-slice `ValueError`, and the `organization_context.member is None` AttributeError. Add paginator unit tests for negative/zero/positive offsets plus endpoint tests covering member, non-member-token and superuser callers.

title: Comment documents a non-existent feature of Cursor
body: The added comment claims "Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios", but no code changed here — `int(offset)` has always accepted any integer and nothing validates or makes use of negative offsets. The comment asserts that negative offsets are a supported, intentional capability, which is false: every consumer eventually feeds the offset into a Django queryset slice, which rejects negative values. This will mislead future readers into producing negative-offset cursors. Remove the comment or, better, add explicit validation that rejects negative offsets.

title: Negative-offset slicing of a Django QuerySet raises ValueError (500)
body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code slices the queryset with a negative start: `queryset[start_offset:stop]` where `start_offset = cursor.offset`. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing/slicing; this raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` The endpoint's `paginate()` helper only converts `BadPaginationError` into a 400, so any client that supplies a cursor with a negative offset (cursors are user-supplied strings and `Cursor.from_string` happily parses `-5`) gets an unhandled 500. The inline comment "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is factually wrong and should not be used to justify this branch.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator key handling is numeric-only but is used with a datetime order_by
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `math.floor/ceil(getattr(item, self.key))` and `value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` unchanged (the integer/float `Paginator` semantics). The only caller, `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`, uses it with `order_by="-datetime"`. Consequences: (1) `math.ceil(datetime)` raises `TypeError` for any non-empty result page, so the first optimized request 500s; (2) even if that were fixed, `value_from_cursor` would feed a raw number into the raw SQL comparison built by `build_queryset` (`"datetime" <= %s`), which fails/compares wrongly against a timestamp column. For a datetime sort key the class must derive from `DateTimePaginator` (or override these two methods with the timestamp-multiplier logic).

title: Privilege gate uses request.user.is_superuser and member.has_global_access
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is described as gating "authorized administrators", but neither condition expresses that. Sentry requires superuser mode to be actively elevated for a request; the correct check is `is_active_superuser(request)` (or an explicit scope check). Reading `request.user.is_superuser` grants the privileged code path to any staff account with a normal, non-elevated session. Additionally, `has_global_access` on an org member only means "access to all teams" and is implicitly true for every member of an organization with open membership, so the second clause makes the gate effectively 'any member', not 'admin'. If the advanced pagination path is meant to be restricted, gate it on an explicit permission/scope instead.

title: organization_context.member can be None -> AttributeError 500
body: `organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated whenever `request.user.is_superuser` is false. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is optional and is `None` for requests that are not made by an org member (e.g. token/integration or org-auth-token authenticated requests, or a user acting through superuser without membership). In that case this line raises `AttributeError` and the endpoint returns a 500 instead of the audit log. The attribute access also needs verification that `has_global_access` exists on the RPC member model at all, since it is a property of the Django `OrganizationMember` model rather than a field of the RPC payload.

title: Cursor values become incompatible depending on an undeclared query parameter
body: The new `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter switches between `DateTimePaginator` (cursor values are millisecond timestamps) and `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (cursor values are raw numeric keys). Cursors returned by one paginator are therefore meaningless to the other, so a client that follows a `Link` header but drops/keeps the flag inconsistently (or a cached/bookmarked cursor) will silently page to the wrong position rather than erroring. The parameter is also not declared in `AuditLogQueryParamSerializer`, so it is undocumented and unvalidated (any value other than the exact string "true" silently falls back). Either encode the mode in the cursor/Link headers or drop the request-level switch.

title: Inconsistent and silent clamping of negative offsets in BasePaginator
body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes behaviour for every paginator derived from `BasePaginator`. For forward cursors an invalid negative offset is now silently clamped to 0, so a malformed/tampered cursor returns page 1 instead of surfacing an error - and the `next`/`prev` cursors are then built from `cursor.offset` (still negative) in `build_cursor`, producing further inconsistent cursors. For `is_prev` cursors the negative offset is still passed straight into `queryset[offset:stop]`, which raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` and yields a 500. Negative offsets should be rejected explicitly (e.g. `raise BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`, as `OffsetPaginator` and `ChainPaginator` already do) rather than half-clamped; the comment claiming "the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions" is incorrect.

title: No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the new endpoint branch
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (including the negative-offset branch and the `enable_advanced_features` flag) and the new conditional path in `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` are added with no accompanying tests. Nothing exercises the optimized path, which is why the datetime/`math.ceil` TypeError and the negative-slice ValueError went unnoticed; there is also no test asserting that unprivileged callers cannot activate the path. Tests covering: optimized path with results, cursor round-tripping, negative offsets, and the authorization gate are needed before merging.

title: Comment claims a behaviour change that the code does not make
body: The added comment in `Cursor.__init__` states "Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios", but the code is unchanged (`self.offset = int(offset)`) - no validation was removed or added, and nothing in `Cursor` makes negative offsets usable (consumers slice QuerySets, which reject negative starts). A comment that describes a non-existent feature will mislead future readers into assuming negative offsets are a supported, safe input. Remove it or replace it with an accurate note (ideally a validation that rejects negative offsets).

title: Negative slice start raises ValueError in Django — "advanced" negative-offset path always 500s
body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code slices the queryset with a negative start (`queryset[start_offset:stop]`, where `start_offset = cursor.offset`). Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` for any slice whose `start` or `stop` is negative, so this branch can never succeed. The inline comment "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is factually wrong. Because `Endpoint.paginate` only converts `BadPaginationError` into a 400, this ValueError propagates and the request returns an unhandled HTTP 500 for any client-supplied cursor such as `?cursor=0:-5:0&optimized_pagination=true`. If negative offsets are meant to be rejected, they should raise `BadPaginationError`; if they are meant to be supported, they must be translated into a real positive offset/ordering flip.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator key handling is incompatible with the datetime ordering it is used with
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(value))`/`math.ceil(value)` on `getattr(item, self.key)` and `value_from_cursor` returns the raw `cursor.value`. The only caller (`OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`) instantiates it with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `value` is a `datetime`: `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`, which happens inside `build_cursor` on every request that takes this path. Additionally, when a cursor value is present, `build_queryset` will emit raw SQL comparing the `datetime` column to an integer (`"datetime" <= %s` with an int param), producing a database type error on Postgres. The optimized path therefore cannot work at all for this endpoint; it needs `DateTimePaginator`-style key conversion (multiplier + `datetime.fromtimestamp`) or must not be used with a datetime sort key.

title: `organization_context.member` may be None, causing AttributeError/500
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences `organization_context.member` unconditionally. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is optional and is `None` for requests that are not made by an org member — e.g. org-level auth tokens / integration tokens, or a superuser-style actor with no membership (in that case `request.user.is_superuser` is False for token auth because `request.user` is anonymous). The short-circuit does not protect those cases, so the expression raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'` and the audit log endpoint returns a 500 instead of the normal paginated response. Guard with `organization_context.member is not None and ...`.

title: Privilege gate uses `request.user.is_superuser` and `has_global_access`, so it is not an admin-only gate
body: The new branch is gated on `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`, and the comments describe it as "for authorized administrators" that "enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds". Two problems: (1) Sentry's convention is `is_active_superuser(request)` — reading `user.is_superuser` directly ignores the superuser session/elevated-privilege requirement, so a superuser account without an active superuser session (and without the usual staff checks) passes the check; (2) `has_global_access` is true for ordinary members of organizations with open membership, so effectively any regular member can toggle the alternative code path by adding `?optimized_pagination=true`. The gate therefore does not restrict the behavior to administrators as the comment claims. The toggle is also an undocumented, unvalidated query parameter (it is not part of `AuditLogQueryParamSerializer`) rather than a feature flag/option, so there is no way to turn it off operationally.

title: BasePaginator offset clamping is inconsistent and leaves the is_prev crash in place
body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes behavior for every endpoint that uses `BasePaginator`. For forward cursors a client-supplied negative offset is now silently clamped to 0 (returning page-one rows instead of surfacing an error for a malformed cursor), while for `is_prev` cursors the negative value is still passed straight into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, where Django raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` and the request 500s. The accompanying comment ("This is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions") is incorrect — the queryset rejects negative slices. Either validate the offset once and raise `BadPaginationError` (yielding a 400), or clamp in both branches; note also that the subsequent `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` check still uses the unclamped `offset`, so the two values can disagree.

title: Comment documents negative cursor offsets as a supported optimization, which is false
body: The added comment on `Cursor.__init__` claims negative offsets are allowed as a "performance optimization" enabling "efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions". No validation was added or removed here, and negative offsets are not supported anywhere downstream: Django refuses negative slice starts (`ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.`) and the offset-based paginators explicitly raise `BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`. Leaving this comment in a shared utility invites future callers to construct negative-offset cursors that will crash at query time; either remove the comment or add an explicit validation/rejection of negative offsets here.

title: No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the new endpoint branch
body: A new public paginator class (`OptimizedCursorPaginator`) and a new request-driven branch in `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` are introduced without any tests. The behaviors that most need coverage are exactly those that are currently broken: a negative `cursor` offset with `optimized_pagination=true`, pagination with the `-datetime` sort key (which raises `TypeError` in `get_item_key`), and the permission gate when `organization_context.member` is `None`. Without tests these regressions reach production as 500s on a customer-facing endpoint.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result duplicates BasePaginator.get_result and will drift
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` is a near-verbatim copy of `BasePaginator.get_result` with one branch added, and it dropped the explanatory comments about the extra fetched row and the `post_query_filter` semantics. Any future fix to the base implementation (for example the offset clamping just added, or the `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` off-by-one when offset is clamped) has to be applied in two places and will silently diverge here. Override only the slicing step (e.g. a `_slice_bounds` hook) instead of copying the whole method.

title: `organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated for every request and crashes when member is None
body: Line 71 unconditionally dereferences `organization_context.member`, regardless of whether `optimized_pagination` was requested. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is optional (`RpcOrganizationMemberSummary | None`) and is None whenever the caller is not an organization member — e.g. org auth tokens, API keys, or a superuser acting on an org they don't belong to. Those requests now raise `AttributeError` and return a 500 for a previously working endpoint. Additionally, `has_global_access` is not a field on `RpcOrganizationMemberSummary` (global access is exposed on the request's `Access` object, i.e. `request.access.has_global_access`), so this attribute lookup will fail even when `member` is populated. Move the check behind the `use_optimized` flag and use a real, existing access API.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator's item key/cursor conversion is numeric-only and breaks the audit log's `-datetime` ordering
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(getattr(item, self.key)))` and `value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` verbatim. The only caller (`organization_auditlogs.py`, `order_by="-datetime"`) sorts on a `DateTimeField`, so `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError`, producing a 500 as soon as the optimized path is taken. Even if that were fixed, `value_from_cursor` would hand an integer millisecond value to `build_queryset`, which injects it into `WHERE "datetime" <= %s` and compares a timestamp column against an integer, causing a database error. `DateTimePaginator` exists precisely to do these conversions; the new class cannot be used with a datetime sort key.

title: Negative, user-controlled cursor offsets are passed straight into a Django queryset slice
body: When `enable_advanced_features` is set, a cursor with `offset < 0` (cursors come from the untrusted `?cursor=` query parameter via `Cursor.from_string`, which accepts negative integers) is used as the slice start: `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with `start_offset` negative. Django raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` on querysets, which is not caught by `Endpoint.paginate` (only `BadPaginationError` becomes a 400), so any request with a negative cursor offset returns an unhandled 500. The in-code justification ("the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically", "permissions are checked at the queryset level") is incorrect, and it deliberately removes the negative-offset guard (`BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`) that every other paginator in this module enforces. Negative offsets should be rejected, not forwarded.

title: Silent offset clamping in BasePaginator yields incorrect pagination instead of a clear error
body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes behaviour for every paginator derived from `BasePaginator`. For forward cursors a negative offset is now silently clamped to 0, but the raw negative `offset` is still used to build the next/prev cursors in `build_cursor` (e.g. `_build_next_values` computes `next_offset = offset + limit`), so a client passing a negative offset gets page-0 rows together with cursors that skip or repeat rows rather than a deterministic error. For `is_prev` cursors the negative offset is still passed unclamped to the queryset slice, which raises `ValueError` from Django. Also note the subsequent check at line 192 (`len(results) == offset + limit + extra`) still uses the unclamped `offset`, so it no longer matches the number of rows actually fetched.

title: Comment claims negative offsets are supported, contradicting the paginators
body: The added comment states that negative offsets are allowed as a "performance optimization ... enables efficient reverse pagination", but no code changed here and every paginator in `sentry/api/paginator.py` (`OffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`, `CombinedQuerysetPaginator`, `CallbackPaginator`) explicitly rejects negative offsets with `BadPaginationError`. Leaving this comment in `Cursor.__init__` will mislead future readers into assuming negative offsets are a supported contract of the cursor type.
