title: Redirect-resolution loop bound silently reduced from 10000 to 1000
body: The loop bound was changed from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000` and the explanatory comment ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. This is an unrelated, undocumented behaviour change: traces whose redirect chains are deeper than 1000 will stop resolving to their real root, so those segments get split into multiple partial segments and are emitted as if complete, with no error or metric to signal it. Either keep the previous bound or document/justify the reduction and add observability for hitting the cap.

title: zunionstore uses the default SUM aggregate, corrupting end-timestamp scores on duplicate payloads
body: `zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` (and the same call for `parent_key` on line 53) uses Redis' default `AGGREGATE SUM`. Scores here are `end_timestamp_precise` values, and merges happen repeatedly as spans arrive. If the identical span payload is present in both merged keys — which happens with Kafka at-least-once redelivery or when a span is written under a parent key and later re-resolved — the resulting score becomes the sum of two epoch timestamps (~3.4e9), making that member permanently "newest". Since the new eviction logic (`zpopmin`) relies on these scores to drop the oldest spans, inflated scores cause the wrong spans to be evicted. Pass `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) so the score keeps timestamp semantics.

title: Span eviction limit is hardcoded to 1000 and drops spans with no metric or log
body: `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)` silently discards spans. Two problems: (1) the limit is hardcoded in Lua while `SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans` (default 1001) is the configured knob — that parameter is now dead code and operators cannot tune the limit, and the two values disagree by one; (2) the previous behaviour logged an error and emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` when a segment was too large, whereas the new path emits nothing, so oversized segments are now published as silently truncated segments that downstream consumers cannot distinguish from complete ones. Pass the limit in as an ARGV from `max_segment_spans` and emit a metric/return value when eviction occurs.

title: `max_segment_spans` is now unused dead configuration
body: The span-count guard in `_load_segment_data` was removed, so `self.max_segment_spans` (set from the constructor parameter on line 158) is no longer read anywhere; the span limit now lives as a hardcoded `1000` in `add-buffer.lua`. Anyone constructing `SpansBuffer(max_segment_spans=...)` will have their setting silently ignored. Either wire the value through to the Lua script's ARGV or remove the parameter.

title: Unguarded `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` can crash the consumer on messages lacking the field
body: `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` raises `KeyError` for any ingest-spans message that omits the field; the `cast(SpanEvent, ...)` on line 134 is a type-checker-only assertion and performs no validation, so a single malformed/older-format payload aborts batch processing and stalls the partition. Previously no span field beyond trace/span/project ids was mandatory. Consider defaulting (e.g. to the message/produce timestamp) or explicitly dropping such messages with a metric.

title: No test covers the new insert-time eviction or score ordering
body: The buffer tests were only mechanically updated to pass the new required `end_timestamp_precise` field. The core behaviour this PR introduces — zset-based storage, the 1000-span cap with `zpopmin` eviction of the oldest spans, and the removal of the old "skip too large segment" path — is completely untested. A regression in the Lua eviction arithmetic (e.g. popping too many spans, or evicting the root span) or in the zunionstore score aggregation would not be caught. Add a test that inserts more than the cap into one segment and asserts which spans survive, plus one asserting eviction keeps the highest `end_timestamp_precise` members.

title: New OptimizedCursorPaginator has no tests
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` duplicates ~70 lines of `BasePaginator.get_result` and adds a new `enable_advanced_features` code path, yet no tests were added in this PR for the class or for the modified offset handling in `BasePaginator.get_result`. Given the class is already broken for datetime keys and forwards negative offsets to the ORM, tests covering normal paging, prev cursors, and rejection of negative offsets are required before this can be relied on by an endpoint.

title: `organization_context.member` can be None, causing a 500 on every audit-log request
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated unconditionally for every GET, before it is known whether the optimized path is even requested. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is `RpcOrganizationMember | None` and is None whenever the caller is not an organization member of record — e.g. requests authenticated with an organization auth token / API token that carries `org:write`/`org:admin`, which `OrganizationAuditPermission` accepts. For those callers `request.user.is_superuser` is False (AnonymousUser), so the right-hand side is evaluated and raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'`, turning a previously working endpoint into a hard 500. At minimum the check must be guarded (`organization_context.member and ...`) and only evaluated when `use_optimized` is true.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator is an integer paginator but is used with a datetime sort key
body: The endpoint sorts by `-datetime` (a `DateTimeField`). `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(getattr(item, self.key)))` and `value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` unchanged — i.e. the integer semantics of `Paginator`, not the millisecond-timestamp conversion that `DateTimePaginator` implements. Consequently, when `optimized_pagination=true` is honored, `build_cursor` calls `get_item_key` on a `datetime` and raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`, and any follow-up cursor value is injected raw into the `WHERE datetime >= %s` clause built by `build_queryset`, comparing an integer against a timestamp column. The optimized path therefore cannot work for this endpoint at all; it only produces 500s (and would silently mis-page if it did not crash).

title: Negative offsets are passed straight into a Django queryset slice and raise ValueError
body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly rejects this with `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` for any slice whose start or stop is negative, so the request ends in an unhandled exception / HTTP 500. The inline comment “The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically” is factually wrong, and the comment “enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds … safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level” documents behaviour that does not exist. Since `Cursor.from_string` accepts any integer offset from the `cursor` query parameter, this is a user-triggerable error path. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError` instead.

title: Silently clamping negative cursor offsets masks invalid cursors and is inconsistent for prev cursors
body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` in `BasePaginator.get_result` silently rewrites an invalid (negative) forward cursor offset to 0, so the caller gets page 1 data while `build_cursor` still derives the next/prev cursors from the original negative `cursor.offset` (e.g. `next_offset = offset + limit`), producing further bogus cursors. For `is_prev` cursors the negative offset is still handed to the Django slice, which raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`, so the fix is only half applied. Other paginators in this file (`OffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`, `CombinedQuerysetPaginator`) raise `BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`; `BasePaginator` should do the same rather than clamp.

title: New OptimizedCursorPaginator has no tests
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` is a brand-new public paginator wired into a production endpoint, but no tests were added in this PR (neither for the paginator itself nor for the new `optimized_pagination=true` branch of `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`). As a result the broken datetime key handling and the negative-offset ValueError path described in the other findings would not be caught by CI. Tests should cover: default behaviour parity with `DateTimePaginator` for the audit log ordering, and the behaviour for negative/invalid cursor offsets.

title: Misleading comment added to Cursor.__init__
body: The added comment claims that `self.offset = int(offset)` is a “performance optimization” that “allows negative offsets … enables efficient reverse pagination”. No code changed here; `int(offset)` has always accepted negative values, and negative offsets are not a supported feature — most paginators reject them and Django refuses negative slices. The comment documents a non-existent and unsafe capability and will mislead the next reader into thinking negative offsets are intentional and handled.

title: zunionstore defaults to AGGREGATE SUM, corrupting the end-timestamp scores used for eviction
body: Both merge steps use `redis.call("zunionstore", set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` without an `AGGREGATE` option, so Redis sums the scores of members present in both sorted sets. Scores here are `end_timestamp_precise` values, so a span payload that happens to exist in both the destination set and the merged set (e.g. a duplicate delivery, or a span already zadd'ed under the top-most parent key by `process_spans` and also present under its own span key) ends up with a score of roughly 2×1.7e9. That value is no longer a timestamp, and because the new trimming logic uses `zpopmin` (lowest score evicted first), duplicated spans become effectively un-evictable while legitimate newer spans are dropped. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) to keep scores meaningful.

title: Segment span limit hardcoded to 1000 in Lua, conflicting with the now-dead max_segment_spans setting
body: The new eviction uses the literal `1000` in two places (`if span_count > 1000` / `zpopmin set_key, span_count - 1000`), while `SpansBuffer.__init__` still exposes `max_segment_spans: int = 1001`, which this PR leaves completely unused after removing the span-count check in `_load_segment_data`. The effective limit is therefore no longer configurable, differs from the previous 1001 threshold, and the stale constructor parameter will mislead operators who try to tune it. Either pass the configured limit into the script as an ARGV, or remove `max_segment_spans` from the buffer.

title: Redirect-chain depth limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 and the explanatory comment deleted
body: The loop bound was changed from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000`, and the comment explaining the consequence (“theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly”) was removed. With the lower bound, traces whose redirect chains exceed 1000 hops will stop resolving to their real root set and will be emitted as separate, incorrectly split segments. This is a behavioural change unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (eviction on insert), is not mentioned in the description, and now has no comment documenting the limitation.

title: max_segment_spans is now dead code and the over-size-segment metric/log was dropped
body: `_load_segment_data` no longer checks `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans`, so the constructor parameter `max_segment_spans` is unused, and the `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` metric plus the accompanying `logger.error` are gone. Any dashboards/alerts built on that metric will silently go to zero, and there is no longer any signal when a segment is truncated — trimming now happens silently inside the Lua script. Add an equivalent metric for evicted spans (e.g. the `zpopmin` count) and remove or honor the unused parameter.

title: Module docstring still describes plain Redis sets and no eviction
body: The storage layout changed from Redis sets (`sadd`/`sscan`/`sunionstore`) to sorted sets keyed by `end_timestamp_precise`, and spans are now evicted on insert once a segment exceeds 1000 members, but the module docstring was not updated: step 3 still says “Add the ingested span's payload to the set under `set_key`” and the glossary still says “span-buf:s:* -- the actual set keys”. Nothing documents that spans can now be silently dropped from a segment, which is the most important semantic change in this PR for anyone debugging missing spans.

title: No test covers the new eviction-on-insert behaviour
body: The PR's headline change is trimming segments to 1000 spans during insert (`zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua) and the switch from sets to sorted sets scored by `end_timestamp_precise`, yet the only test changes are mechanical additions of `end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0` to existing fixtures. There is no test that pushes more than the limit of spans into one segment and asserts that the oldest-ending spans are the ones dropped, nor any test that the score is preserved correctly across the `zunionstore` merges. The previously-tested-by-implication span-count guard in `_load_segment_data` was removed with no replacement coverage, so a regression in the eviction logic (wrong aggregate, wrong pop count, off-by-one on the threshold) would go unnoticed.

title: Redis value type change from SET to ZSET on the same key prefix breaks in-flight segments
body: `span-buf:s:{project:trace}:span_id` keys are switched from plain Redis SETs (`sadd`/`sscan`/`sunionstore`/`scard`) to sorted sets (`zadd`/`zscan`/`zunionstore`/`zcard`) while keeping the exact same key names. Keys written by the previous code version live for `redis_ttl` (default 3600s), and during a rolling deploy old and new consumers write to the same keys. Any `ZADD`/`ZCARD`/`ZUNIONSTORE`/`ZSCAN` against a key that is still a SET returns `WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value`, which raises out of the pipeline in `process_spans`/`_load_segment_data` and will crash-loop the consumer (or permanently fail those batches) until every legacy key expires. The key prefix needs to be versioned (e.g. `span-buf:z:`) or the data explicitly migrated/flushed as part of the rollout.

title: zunionstore uses default SUM aggregation, corrupting span scores on duplicate payloads
body: `zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` (and the same call for `parent_key` on line 53) uses Redis' default `AGGREGATE SUM`. If the identical span payload is a member of both source sorted sets — which happens with at-least-once Kafka redelivery where the same payload was first buffered under the parent key and later under the redirect-resolved set key — the resulting score becomes the sum of the two `end_timestamp_precise` values (~2x epoch seconds). That span then sorts as the "newest" member forever, so the new `zpopmin` eviction will evict legitimate recent spans instead, and the score is no longer a meaningful timestamp. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) explicitly.

title: Eviction limit hardcoded to 1000 and silently drops spans with no metric or log
body: The new trimming logic hardcodes `span_count > 1000` / `zpopmin set_key span_count - 1000`, while `SpansBuffer.__init__` still exposes `max_segment_spans` (default 1001) which is now never used, so the limit is neither configurable nor consistent with the Python config. In addition, the previous behaviour emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and an error log when a segment exceeded the span count; now spans are dropped silently inside Lua, so there is no metric, log, or dashboard signal that data loss occurred. Please make the limit a script argument driven by `max_segment_spans` and return/emit an eviction count so the loss is observable.

title: Redirect-resolution loop limit silently lowered from 10000 to 1000 and its warning comment deleted
body: The loop bound was changed from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000`, and the comment explaining the consequence ("segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was removed. This 10x reduction means segment trees deeper than ~1000 redirects now stop resolving and get split into separate segments, which is a user-visible behaviour change unrelated to the stated purpose of this PR (insert-time eviction). Either keep the previous bound or document the new limit and the reason for lowering it.

title: Negative-offset slicing raises ValueError on Django querysets (comment is wrong)
body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, the advanced branch passes a negative `start_offset` into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` for negative slice starts/stops before any result cache is consulted, so this path cannot work: a client supplying a cursor with a negative offset (e.g. `?cursor=0:-5:0&optimized_pagination=true`) gets an unhandled 500 instead of a 400. The in-code comment claiming "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false, and the sibling comment "enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds" describes behaviour that paginators elsewhere in this file deliberately reject with `BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`. Negative offsets should be rejected, not forwarded.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator uses integer key semantics but is wired to a datetime-ordered queryset
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `math.floor(getattr(item, self.key))` and `value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` unchanged — these are the integer `Paginator` semantics. The only caller (`OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`) uses it with `order_by="-datetime"`. `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError`, so any request with `optimized_pagination=true` that returns at least one row 500s inside `build_cursor`. Even if that were fixed, `value_from_cursor` would hand a raw integer to the `WHERE "datetime" <= %s` clause built in `build_queryset`, comparing a timestamp column against an integer and producing a database error. For a datetime-ordered queryset this class must derive from/replicate `DateTimePaginator`'s key conversion.

title: organization_context.member can be None, causing an AttributeError 500
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences `organization_context.member`, which is `RpcOrganizationMember | None` and is `None` for requesters who are not org members (e.g. org auth token / integration token authenticated requests, or staff access without membership). Because `request.user.is_superuser` is `False` for those requests, the `or` does not short-circuit and the endpoint raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'`, turning a previously working audit-log request into a 500.

title: Superuser check uses request.user.is_superuser instead of is_active_superuser(request)
body: The gate for the new pagination mode uses the raw `request.user.is_superuser` flag. In Sentry, holding the superuser flag is not the same as having an elevated/active superuser session; the supported check is `sentry.auth.superuser.is_active_superuser(request)` (or staff equivalent). Using the raw flag grants the privileged code path to any account with the flag set regardless of whether superuser mode was activated, bypassing the elevation requirement that the rest of the codebase enforces. Note also that `has_global_access` is true for every member of an open-membership organization, so the "authorized administrators" framing in the comment does not match what is actually checked.

title: BasePaginator now silently clamps negative forward offsets instead of failing
body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes behaviour for every endpoint using `BasePaginator`: a forward cursor with a negative offset, which previously surfaced as an error, now silently returns the first page while `build_cursor` still derives the next/prev cursors from the original negative `cursor.offset`, producing inconsistent pagination links. Negative offsets for `is_prev` cursors are still forwarded into the slice and will raise `ValueError` from Django. This unrelated change to a widely used base class should either validate and reject negative offsets (as `OffsetPaginator` does with `BadPaginationError`) or be dropped from this PR.

title: Comment claims negative cursor offsets are a supported feature, which they are not
body: The added comment on `Cursor.__init__` states that negative offsets are allowed as a "performance optimization" for "efficient reverse pagination". Nothing in `Cursor` was changed, and the rest of the codebase explicitly rejects negative offsets (`OffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`, `CallbackPaginator` all raise `BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`) while Django querysets raise `ValueError` on negative slices. The comment will mislead future readers into believing negative offsets are a validated, supported input.

title: max_segment_spans config is now dead code
body: `self.max_segment_spans = max_segment_spans` is still set in `SpansBuffer.__init__` (default 1001) but the only consumer of it — the span-count guard in `_load_segment_data` — was deleted, and the new limit is hardcoded as `1000` in `add-buffer.lua`. Anyone tuning `max_segment_spans` will silently have no effect. Either thread the value into the Lua script as an ARGV or remove the constructor parameter.

title: Module docstring still describes plain sets and omits insert-time eviction
body: The module docstring (steps 2-3 around line 38-39 and the glossary entry on line 58: "span-buf:s:* -- the actual set keys") still describes the span buffers as Redis sets and says the payload is added "to the set". They are now sorted sets scored by `end_timestamp_precise`, and spans are evicted (oldest-first) once a segment exceeds 1000 spans. Since this docstring is the primary explanation of the buffer's Redis layout, it should document the new type and the lossy eviction behaviour.

title: Unguarded access to end_timestamp_precise can hard-fail a whole batch
body: `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` uses direct indexing while neighbouring optional fields use `val.get(...)`. Any message lacking the field (older producers, replayed/spillover topics, malformed payloads) raises `KeyError` inside `process_batch`, which fails the entire arroyo batch rather than a single message and will crash-loop the consumer on a poison message. Consider defaulting (e.g. to the message timestamp) or explicitly invalidating the single span.

title: No test for the new insert-time eviction, the headline change of this PR
body: All changes to `tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py` are mechanical additions of `end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0`. Nothing exercises the new behaviour: no test pushes more than 1000 spans into a segment to verify that `zpopmin` trims to the limit, that the lowest-`end_timestamp_precise` spans are the ones evicted, that the root/segment span survives, or that merging two over-limit sub-segments via `zunionstore` still trims correctly. The eviction path (and the score-based ordering it depends on) is therefore completely untested.

title: New OptimizedCursorPaginator and the audit-log code path have no tests
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (~90 new lines, including a dedicated negative-offset branch) and the new `optimized_pagination=true` branch in `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` ship with no tests at all. Basic coverage would have caught that `get_item_key` cannot handle the `datetime` field the endpoint orders by and that negative slice starts raise `ValueError` in Django. At minimum there should be tests for: the paginator with the endpoint's actual order_by, the permission gate (member=None, non-superuser, non-privileged member), and the rejection of negative offsets.

title: Upsampling eligibility uses the outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`
body: `_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` as its first argument (the dataset actually queried), but the eligibility check passes the enclosing `dataset` variable: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)`. In the dashboard-widget-split code path, `_get_event_stats` is intentionally invoked with a different dataset (`discover`, or the widget's split dataset) while the outer `dataset` is the metrics/discover dataset selected from the request. As a result the `count()` -> `upsampled_count()` decision is made for a dataset that is not the one being queried: upsampling can be skipped for an errors query that should be upsampled, or (when the outer dataset is errors-like and the scoped dataset is not) `upsampled_count()` can be sent to a dataset that has no `sample_weight` column, producing a Snuba error or wrong numbers. The check should use `scoped_dataset`.

title: Caching allowlist eligibility for 60s can serve 10x-wrong counts and cannot be invalidated
body: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` stores the result of the allowlist check in the shared cache under `error_upsampling_eligible:{org}:{hash(project_ids)}` for 60 seconds. The underlying value comes from `options.get("issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist")`, which is already cached by the options store, so there is no meaningful performance gain; what it does add is up to a minute of stale behavior. After an operator removes a project from the allowlist (e.g. to stop bad data or roll back the feature), charts keep returning `sum(sample_weight)` values that are inflated by the inverse sample rate (10x in the tests here) — and conversely, newly allowlisted projects keep returning raw counts. Because the cache key is per (org, exact project-id set), there is no practical way to purge all affected entries. Additionally, if the cache backend (redis/memcached) outlives a database reset in CI or local dev, project ids can be reused and a stale `True`/`False` will be applied to an unrelated project set. Consider removing the cache entirely or keying it on the option value/version.

title: Cache key uses `hash()` of the project tuple, so distinct project sets can collide
body: The cache key embeds `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))` rather than the project ids themselves. Two different project sets within the same organization that hash to the same value will share a cached eligibility verdict, which means a non-allowlisted project set can be treated as upsampled (counts multiplied by the sample weight) or vice versa. Serializing the ids (e.g. `"-".join(map(str, sorted(ids)))`, or a cryptographic digest if length matters) removes this failure mode at no cost.

title: Docstring claims the allowlist is read fresh on every call, which the caller's cache contradicts
body: `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`'s docstring states: "This function reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time... This is intentional to ensure we always have the latest configuration state." Its only caller, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, caches the result for 60 seconds, so the system does not always see the latest configuration. The comment in the caller ("This is safe because allowlist changes are infrequent and eventual consistency is acceptable") asserts the opposite guarantee. A future maintainer reading either docstring will reason incorrectly about staleness; the two must be reconciled.

title: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is dead code and cannot invalidate in practice
body: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is not called from anywhere in this PR, and by construction it can only delete the single key for one exact (organization, project-id set) combination. Eligibility is cached per distinct project-id set, so a single allowlist option change would require enumerating every combination of project ids that has ever been queried. Shipping it gives the false impression that the cache is invalidated on configuration changes; either wire up a real invalidation (option-value-based cache key / option update hook) or drop the function.

title: `upsampled_count` has no fallback when `sample_weight` is missing/NULL
body: The new aggregate is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` with a comment asserting the schema guarantees `sample_weight` exists for all events in allowlisted projects. That guarantee does not hold for data stored before a project was allowlisted or before the SDK started sending `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` (the test factory change in this PR only sets `sample_rate` when that context is present). For such rows `sample_weight` is NULL/0, so `sum` silently drops them and a chart over a time range that spans the rollout collapses to zero or badly undercounts — with no error surfaced to the user. Wrapping the column, e.g. `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))`, makes unweighted events count as 1.

title: `upsampled_count` is registered as a public function, exposing it to arbitrary user queries
body: Unlike the neighbouring internal aggregates, the new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is not marked `private=True`, so any user can put `upsampled_count()` in a Discover/dashboard field or yAxis. This (a) lets users obtain sample-weight-scaled counts for projects that are not on the `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`, bypassing the gating this PR builds, and (b) will fail at the Snuba layer (500 / SnubaError) for datasets or storages where the `sample_weight` column does not exist, since nothing validates dataset or project eligibility at resolution time. Mark it private, as this is an implementation detail of the server-side column rewrite.

title: `default_result_type="number"` conflicts with the integer result it replaces
body: `upsampled_count` is declared with `default_result_type="number"` even though the aggregate is wrapped in `toInt64` and it is substituted for `count()`, which declares `"integer"`. Because the rewrite aliases the result back to `count`, clients receive meta `fieldType`/`type` of `number` for a field they previously got `integer` for, which changes formatting/axis handling in the UI for the same logical series. Use `"integer"` for consistency.

title: Top-events path upsamples only the series, not the top-N selection or orderby
body: In the `top_events > 0` branch only `timeseries_columns`/`y_axes` are rewritten to `upsampled_count()`; `selected_columns=self.get_field_list(...)` and `orderby=self.get_orderby(request)` keep the raw `count()`. The top-N groups are therefore selected and ordered by un-upsampled counts while the plotted series are upsampled. When the per-event sample rates differ across groups/projects, the chosen top groups and their ordering do not match the magnitudes shown in the chart.

title: Sample-rate extraction silently swallows all errors and drops a 0 rate
body: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` wraps both the context lookup and the `float()` conversion in bare `except Exception: pass`, and gates on `if client_sample_rate:` (falsy), so a malformed or zero `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` results in no `sample_rate` on the event with no signal at all. A test that intends to store an upsampled event but passes a slightly wrong value will instead silently assert against raw counts, making failures hard to diagnose. Narrow the exception handling (e.g. `(TypeError, ValueError)`) and check `is not None` rather than truthiness.

title: Accidental git submodule (gitlink) `sentry-repo` committed without a .gitmodules entry
body: This PR adds a gitlink entry `sentry-repo` pointing at `a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a` (the base commit of this very repository) with no corresponding `.gitmodules` mapping. Git will report "no submodule mapping found in .gitmodules for path 'sentry-repo'" and `git submodule update`/`clone --recurse-submodules` will fail, and the self-referential pointer serves no purpose. This looks like a local working-directory artifact and should be removed from the commit.

title: No test covers the public entry point, its cache, or the errors-dataset path
body: The unit tests only exercise the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`) and the column transform. The public function `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` — which contains the new cache key construction, the `cache.get`/`cache.set` logic, and the combination of eligibility with the dataset check — is never called in any test, so the cache-hit path, cache-staleness behavior, and the empty-`project_ids` case are unverified. Separately, no test issues a request with `dataset=errors`, even though `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns `True` unconditionally for that dataset and `upsampled_count` was only registered in the Discover dataset's `function_converter`; if the errors dataset config does not inherit that function, the primary intended path raises an invalid-function error and nothing here would catch it.

title: Misleading comments on upsampled count assertions
body: In `test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects` the assertions `assert data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10` / `== 10` are annotated "# First bucket has 1 event" / "# Second bucket has 1 event". The value 10 is the upsampled count derived from `client_sample_rate: 0.1`, not an event count; the comments make the expected values look like a bug to anyone reading the test. Reword to state that one stored event at a 0.1 sample rate is expected to be upsampled to 10.

title: Trailing whitespace and an over-length line will fail the repo's formatting checks
body: Several added lines contain trailing whitespace (e.g. the blank-but-indented lines inside the docstrings and between statements in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, and similar lines added in `organization_events_stats.py` around the `upsampling_enabled`/`final_columns` blocks), and the `cache_key = f"error_upsampling_eligible:..."` assignment exceeds the 100-character limit configured for black in `pyproject.toml`. The pre-commit/lint CI job will reject the branch until these are reformatted.

title: Accidental git submodule/gitlink `sentry-repo` committed
body: This PR adds a gitlink entry `sentry-repo` pointing at commit a5d2909 (the PR's own base commit) with no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry. A gitlink without submodule configuration leaves the repository in a broken state: `git submodule update --init --recursive` fails or silently leaves an empty directory, tooling that walks the worktree sees a phantom directory, and CI checkouts can fail. This is clearly an accidental artifact of local development and must be removed from the PR.

title: Upsampling eligibility computed from outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`
body: `_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` as its first argument and runs the query against it, but the eligibility check passes the enclosing `dataset` variable to `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(...)`. In the dashboard discover-split path (`get_event_stats_factory.fn`) `_get_event_stats` is deliberately called with a different dataset (`discover` for the errors-only probe, `split_dataset`, etc.), so the decision whether to rewrite `count()` into `upsampled_count()` is made for the wrong dataset. Result: the errors-only split probe against `discover` will not be upsampled when the request dataset is metrics/transactions, and conversely a transform decided for `errors` can be applied to a query actually executed against another dataset. Use `scoped_dataset` for the check.

title: Comment claims cached/consistent decision, but eligibility is re-evaluated per call and can flip mid-request
body: The comments say "Early upsampling eligibility check ... This cached result ensures consistent behavior across query execution" and "Store the upsampling decision to apply later", but `should_upsample` is recomputed on every invocation of `_get_event_stats`, and the helper's cache has a 60s TTL. In the discover-split flow `_get_event_stats` is called 2–3 times per request (errors-only probe, original query, transactions-only probe). If the cached entry expires or the allowlist option changes between those calls, one series will be `sum(sample_weight)` based and another plain `count()`, so `check_if_results_have_data` / `save_split_decision` compares incomparable magnitudes and the widget split decision is made on inconsistent data. The decision should be computed once per request and passed down.

title: Cache key built from `hash()` of project ids and omits the allowlist value
body: The cache key is `f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))}"`. Two different project-id sets in the same organization that hash to the same value will share a cache entry, which can make a query over non-allowlisted projects be treated as eligible and silently multiply reported error counts by the sample weight (or vice versa, suppressing upsampling). The key also does not incorporate the allowlist option value, so the cached answer is not tied to the input that produced it. Use the explicit sorted project id list (or a stable digest such as md5 of the joined ids) in the key, and include an allowlist version/hash.

title: 60s eligibility cache with no invalidation path returns stale upsampling decisions
body: `cache.set(cache_key, is_eligible, 60)` caches the allowlist decision for 60 seconds, and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (defined below at line 67) is never called from anywhere in the codebase — nothing hooks option updates for `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`. Consequently, after a project is removed from the allowlist, event-stats responses keep returning upsampled (inflated by 1/sample_rate) counts for up to a minute, and after a project is added the counts stay un-upsampled. Given `options.get` is already option-cached in Sentry, the extra cache buys little while introducing a correctness window; either drop the cache or wire the invalidation to option changes.

title: Docstring states allowlist is read fresh every call, contradicting the new cache
body: `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`'s docstring says the function "reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time ... This is intentional to ensure we always have the latest configuration state", but its only caller caches the result for 60 seconds, so callers do not see the latest configuration. The docstring will mislead the next person debugging stale upsampling behaviour and should be corrected or removed.

title: `_is_error_focused_query` substring match also matches negated/unrelated queries
body: `_is_error_focused_query` returns True whenever the lowercased raw query string contains the substring `event.type:error`. A query such as `!event.type:error` (an explicitly non-error query) or a free-text/message search that happens to contain that substring also matches, so `count()` is rewritten to `upsampled_count()` (i.e. `sum(sample_weight)`) for a result set that includes transactions/other event types. That yields wrong numbers, and on entities where `sample_weight` is unavailable it can fail the Snuba query outright. Parse the search query (e.g. with the event search parser) and require a positive `event.type:error` term instead of a substring check.

title: `upsampled_count` sums `sample_weight` with no null/zero fallback
body: The new SnQLFunction resolves to `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` with no `ifNull`/default. Events in an allowlisted project that were ingested without a client sample rate (older events already in retention, SDKs that don't emit `contexts.error_sampling`, or server-side generated events) have no sample weight, so they contribute 0 to the sum and vanish from the chart entirely — an undercount that looks like data loss. The helper docstring in error_upsampling.py ("We rely on the database schema to ensure sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects, so no additional null checks are needed") is an assumption, not an enforced invariant. Use something like `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))` or an explicit default.

title: `upsampled_count` is exposed publicly in the discover function registry
body: Unlike the neighbouring internal helper functions, the new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is registered without `private=True`, so it immediately becomes a user-callable aggregate on every endpoint using the discover dataset config (events, events-stats, dashboards, alerts). Users can request `upsampled_count()` for projects that are not allowlisted (producing meaningless or inflated numbers), and for queries that include transaction events, where `sample_weight` is not available — the very case `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` deliberately avoids — which surfaces as a Snuba error rather than a validation error. Mark it `private=True` since the only intended caller is the internal column transform.

title: `upsampled_count` declares `default_result_type="number"` for an integer aggregate
body: The aggregate is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` and it replaces `count()` (which declares `integer`), yet it declares `default_result_type="number"`. The declared result type is echoed in the response `meta`, so the frontend will format the upsampled count as a float/number rather than an integer, making charts and tables render differently depending on whether upsampling was applied. Use `"integer"`.

title: Added lines contain trailing whitespace that will fail lint/black checks
body: Several newly added lines consist of or end with trailing whitespace (e.g. line 223 after the `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(...)` call, line 234 after the first `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling(...)` assignment, and line 278 in the RPC branch); the same pattern exists in `src/sentry/api/helpers/error_upsampling.py` docstrings/blank lines. The repository enforces black and flake8 via pre-commit, so CI will reject these as formatting failures until the files are reformatted.

title: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` swallows all exceptions, silently dropping the sample rate
body: Both the context lookup and the `float()` conversion are wrapped in bare `except Exception: pass`. If a test supplies `client_sample_rate` in an unexpected shape (string, nested differently, typo'd context key), the sample rate is silently not set, the event is stored with weight 1, and the upsampling assertions in tests degrade to asserting the non-upsampled path without any signal that the fixture was wrong. Validate/convert explicitly and let bad fixture data raise, or at minimum narrow the exception types.

title: No test covers the new public entry point or its caching logic
body: The unit tests only exercise the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`) and the column transform. The actually new and risky behaviour introduced by this PR — `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` with its cache key derivation, 60s TTL staleness, and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` — has no coverage at all, so regressions such as a cached `True` being returned after a project is removed from the allowlist, or a cache key collision, would not be caught. Note also that cached entries persist across tests in the same process, so any future test of this function must clear the cache in `setUp`.

title: Upsampling end-to-end tests only cover the default discover dataset
body: `OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest` only issues requests without `dataset` (discover) plus one `dataset=discover` transaction case. The `errors` dataset — for which `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` unconditionally returns True and which is the primary production path for error charts — is never exercised, nor is the `topEvents` branch where the transform is also applied. This matters because the `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction was registered only in the discover dataset config; if the errors dataset config does not inherit that registry, every upsampled errors-dataset request would fail with an unknown-function error and no test would notice. Add coverage for `dataset=errors` and for a `topEvents` request.

title: `upsampled_count` is only registered for the discover dataset but is applied to the errors dataset
body: The new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is added only to `DiscoverDatasetConfig.function_converter` in `discover.py`. However `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform()` in `src/sentry/api/helpers/error_upsampling.py` returns `True` unconditionally when `dataset is errors`, so for `?dataset=errors` requests the endpoint will send `upsampled_count() as count` to a builder backed by `ErrorsDatasetConfig`, which maintains its own independent `function_converter`. If that config does not also register `upsampled_count`, every errors-dataset timeseries request from an allowlisted project will fail with `InvalidSearchQuery: upsampled_count() is not a valid function` (HTTP 400) instead of returning data. Either register the function for the errors dataset config too, or restrict the transform to datasets that actually expose it. Note that the added tests only exercise the default (discover) dataset, so this path is completely uncovered.

title: Upsampling eligibility is computed from the outer `dataset`, not the `scoped_dataset` actually queried
body: `_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` as its first parameter and executes the query against it, but the eligibility check passes the enclosing `dataset` variable: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)`. In the dashboard-widget split path, `_get_event_stats` is deliberately invoked with a different dataset (`discover` for the errors-only probe, `scoped_dataset` for the original), so the transform decision can be made for the wrong dataset: e.g. the errors-only probe against `discover` is evaluated with `dataset == metrics_enhanced_performance` (never upsampled), and conversely a query executed against a non-error dataset can be evaluated as `discover`. The result is counts that are inconsistently upsampled (or a transform sent to a dataset lacking `upsampled_count`). Pass `scoped_dataset` instead.

title: Error-focus detection reads the raw request query instead of the query actually executed
body: `_is_error_focused_query()` inspects `request.GET["query"]`, but the query string that is actually executed is passed into `_get_event_stats` as the `query` argument and can differ from the request parameter. In the dashboard split path the endpoint builds `f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction"` (error-only) and `f"({query}) AND event.type:transaction"` (transaction-only); both are evaluated using the same unmodified `request.GET["query"]`. So an error-only split query will not be upsampled unless the user happened to type `event.type:error`, and a transaction-only split query *will* be upsampled if the user's original query contained `event.type:error`, summing `sample_weight` over transactions where the column does not exist. The detection should operate on the query string handed to the dataset, not on the request parameter.

title: Cross-request cache of allowlist eligibility is stale, never invalidated, and keyed by `hash()`
body: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches the allowlist decision in the shared cache for 60s under `error_upsampling_eligible:{org_id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))}`. Three problems: (1) the option value `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` is not part of the key and `invalidate_upsampling_cache()` is dead code (no caller anywhere in this PR), so after an operator changes the allowlist—including turning it off because counts are wrong—requests keep returning 10x-inflated or non-upsampled counts for up to 60s with no way to flush; (2) `options.get` is already backed by an option cache, so this adds a correctness window for no measurable gain; (3) using `hash()` of the project-id tuple makes different project sets collide into the same key, which silently applies the wrong upsampling decision (use a deterministic, collision-free key such as the sorted ids joined by commas).

title: `sum(sample_weight)` silently returns 0 for events without a sample weight
body: `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` replaces `count()` with `upsampled_count()`, which is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. The docstring asserts "we rely on the database schema to ensure sample_weight exists", but a project only gets a `sample_rate`/`sample_weight` once the SDK sends `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate`; events ingested before upsampling was enabled, events from SDKs that do not send it, and events from other event sources in the same (allowlisted) project will have a NULL/0 weight. For those rows `sum(sample_weight)` contributes 0 instead of 1, so adding a project to the allowlist silently zeroes or undercounts historical and non-instrumented error counts in charts and alerts. The aggregate should fall back to 1 per row when `sample_weight` is absent (e.g. `sum(if(sample_weight > 0, sample_weight, 1))` or an equivalent coalesce).

title: `upsampled_count` is exposed as a public discover function
body: Unlike the neighbouring internal helper functions, the new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is not marked `private=True`, so any API consumer can request `field=upsampled_count()`/`yAxis=upsampled_count()` on discover/transaction queries. Since it compiles to `sum(sample_weight)` and `sample_weight` does not exist for transaction rows, this is a user-reachable path to a raw Snuba/ClickHouse "unknown column" error (500/snuba error surfaced to the client), and it becomes an unintentionally supported public API surface. Also, the aggregate returns `toInt64(...)` but declares `default_result_type="number"`; `"integer"` matches the actual value type and the result type reported for `count()`.

title: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` swallows all exceptions, hiding mis-set sample rates
body: Both the context lookup and the `float()` conversion are wrapped in bare `except Exception: pass`, and invalid/zero values are dropped by the `if client_sample_rate:` guard. If a test supplies a malformed `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate`, `sample_rate` is silently not set and the stored event gets `sample_weight = 1`; the upsampling assertions (e.g. `count == 10`) then fail with no indication of why. Let the conversion raise (or assert) so test authors get an actionable error instead of a mysterious count mismatch.

title: No test covers the public entry point or its caching behaviour
body: The unit tests only exercise the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`) and the column transform. `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` — the only function the endpoint actually calls, and the one containing the new 60s shared-cache logic — is never tested, nor is `invalidate_upsampling_cache`. As a result, the cache-hit path (including the `cached_result is not None` handling of a cached `False`, and the key-building logic duplicated between the two functions) is unverified, and regressions in the caching layer would silently change query results in production.

title: Accidental git submodule/gitlink `sentry-repo` committed
body: The PR adds a gitlink entry `sentry-repo` pointing at commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a (the PR's own base commit) with no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry. This is clearly a local workspace artifact: it makes `git submodule update`/`git clone --recurse-submodules` fail or warn about an uninitialized submodule with no URL, and pollutes the repo tree. It must be removed before merging.

title: New file violates the repo's formatting rules (will fail lint/CI)
body: `pyproject.toml` configures black/flake8 with `line-length = 100`, but the `cache_key` assignment on this line is ~110 characters, and the new file plus the edits in `organization_events_stats.py` contain trailing whitespace on several blank/comment lines (e.g. after `should_upsample = ...` and inside the docstrings). Pre-commit/black and flake8 will reject the diff as-is; run the formatter before merging.

title: Feature-flagged table widget path renders hardcoded empty data
body: In `tableResultComponent`, when `organization.features.includes('use-table-widget-visualization')` is true the component renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />` instead of passing `result`/`fields`/`result.meta`. Because `columns` is an empty array (not nullish), `TableWidgetVisualization`'s fallback to derive columns from `tableData.meta.fields` is also bypassed. The consequence is that every table widget on a dashboard renders completely blank (no headers, no rows) for any organization that has this flag enabled, silently hiding real widget data. Either wire the real data through or keep the new component behind code that is not reachable from a user-facing flag.

title: zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes nodestore preserves input ordering
body: `fetch_error_details` builds `node_ids` from `error_ids`, calls `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` (which returns a dict keyed by node id), and then pairs them positionally with `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. This relies on the backend returning values in exactly the same order as the requested ids and on never omitting missing keys. Some backends (e.g. Bigtable, which returns rows sorted by row key) do not guarantee that, and any omitted/missing entry shifts the pairing. The result is `ErrorEvent.id` being attached to the wrong error's title/message/timestamp, so the summary sent to Seer references incorrect event ids. Iterate `node_ids` and look up `events.get(node_id)` per id instead.

title: Error/breadcrumb merge compares timestamps in different units
body: `gen_request_data` interleaves errors and replay events with `error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)`. Error timestamps come from the nodestore event payload and are epoch *seconds* (e.g. 1718900000.0), while rrweb replay event `timestamp` values are epoch *milliseconds* (e.g. 1718900000000). With real data every error timestamp is ~1000x smaller than every breadcrumb timestamp, so all errors are emitted before all breadcrumbs regardless of when they actually occurred, defeating the purpose of the chronological merge (and the log text prints raw, mismatched numbers). Normalise both to the same unit before comparing. The new unit test passes only because it uses hand-written second-scale event timestamps.

title: React Query key no longer includes the organization
body: The hook was switched from `useApiQuery([path, options])` (where `path` contained `/organizations/${organization.slug}/...`) to `useQuery({queryKey: ['use-trace-item-attribute-keys', queryOptions]})`, and `makeTraceItemAttributeKeysQueryOptions` only contains itemType, attributeType, project ids and the datetime range. When the project selection is "all projects" (`projects: []`), two different organizations produce an identical cache key, so attribute keys fetched for one org can be served from cache to another org. Add the organization slug (and ideally the endpoint path) to the query key.

title: 60s processing deadline is likely too short for a 100-identity chunk
body: `check_auth_identities` is scheduled by `check_auth` with `chunk_size=100` and sequentially calls `check_single_auth_identity` for each id; each call does a DB read, an RPC membership check and `provider.refresh_identity()`, which performs an external IdP request. A 60s `processing_deadline_duration` gives ~0.6s per identity. If the deadline is hit, the task is killed mid-chunk and (a) the remaining identities were already stamped with `last_synced=now` in `check_auth`, so they will not be re-selected for roughly another AUTH_CHECK_INTERVAL, and (b) the trailing `check_auth.apply_async(...)` that chains the next chunk never runs, stalling the whole sweep. Either raise the deadline substantially or reduce the chunk size.

title: Both saved-search conversion migrations turned into no-ops pointing at a migration not in this change
body: `0917_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views` and `0920_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views_revised` both have their `RunPython` bodies replaced with `return` and a comment saying "See 0921_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views_rerevised.py for the correct migration". No such migration is added in this PR, and the only test covering the conversion (`tests/sentry/migrations/test_0917_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views.py`) is deleted. If 0921 does not exist, organization-visibility `SavedSearch` rows are never converted into `GroupSearchView` rows anywhere, and the codebase is left with two dead migrations whose comments reference a nonexistent file plus zero test coverage for the conversion logic.

title: One invalid report rejects the entire browser report batch
body: The loop validates each report and returns `422` for the whole request as soon as any single report fails validation, so all other valid reports in the same batch are dropped. Browsers send Reporting API payloads as batches and will retry the whole batch, meaning a single persistently malformed/unsupported report (e.g. a `type` not in `BROWSER_REPORT_TYPES`, or a `url` the `URLField` regex rejects) permanently blocks metrics for every other report delivered with it. Prefer skipping/counting the invalid entries (with a metric or log) and returning 200 for the rest.

title: age/timestamp mutual-exclusion checks use truthiness instead of presence
body: `validate_timestamp` checks `self.initial_data.get("age")` and `validate_age` checks `self.initial_data.get("timestamp")`. Since both use truthiness, a value of `0` counts as absent: a report containing both `timestamp: 0` and `age: 0` passes both validators even though the stated rule is that exactly one of the two fields may be present, and a report with `timestamp: <valid>` plus `age: 0` produces an error only on the `age` field. Use `"age" in self.initial_data` / `"timestamp" in self.initial_data` instead.

title: get_environment_info issues a per-issue recommended-event lookup while building PR comments
body: `get_environment_info` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` for every issue included in a merged-PR comment. That helper runs a search/Snuba query plus a nodestore fetch per group, so building one comment now performs up to 5 extra event lookups (per PR, for both GitHub and GitLab comment workflows) purely to render an environment name. Consider resolving environments with a single cheap query (e.g. GroupEnvironment) instead of fetching recommended events, and note that the broad `except Exception` silently degrades to no environment on any failure.

title: Issue titles are interpolated into a markdown link without escaping
body: `MERGED_PR_SINGLE_ISSUE_TEMPLATE = "* \u203c\ufe0f [**{title}**]({url}){environment}\n"` now puts the (truncated) issue title inside markdown link text, whereas the previous template only bolded it. Issue titles frequently contain `[` / `]` (e.g. `KeyError: 'items[0]'`), which terminates the link text early and renders a broken link/raw brackets in the PR comment. Escape `[`, `]` (and backslashes) in the title before formatting.

title: Analytics event recorded before the feature check and request validation
body: `analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` is the first statement in `post()`, so it fires even when the organization lacks `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` (404 response) or when the body fails schema validation (400 response). The resulting metric therefore counts rejected calls as assemble attempts. Move the `analytics.record` call after the feature/validation gates (or after the task is queued) so it reflects actual assembles.

title: Custom cell renderers returning falsy React nodes are silently overridden
body: Both `renderDefaultHeadCell` and `renderDefaultBodyCell` do `const cell = render...(...); if (cell) return cell;`. The documented contract (see tableWidgetVisualization.stories.tsx and the prop JSDoc) is that only `undefined` falls through to the default renderer, but `null`, `''` and `0` are valid React nodes meaning "render this" and will instead be replaced by the default rendering. Check `cell !== undefined` so a custom renderer can intentionally render nothing.

title: Dead _handle_regex_match helper left in parametrize_w_experiments
body: After removing `ParameterizationRegexExperiment`, the experiment loop always calls `experiment.run(content, _incr_counter)`, but the inner `_handle_regex_match` closure (lines 335-343) is still defined and is now unreachable dead code duplicating the helper in `parametrize_w_regex`. Remove it to avoid confusion about which callback experiments use.

title: Error IDs are zipped against unordered nodestore results
body: `fetch_error_details()` builds `node_ids` from `error_ids`, calls `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` and then pairs them with `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. `get_multi()` returns a mapping keyed by node id; its iteration order is an implementation detail (several backends merge cache hits and DB fetches into a new dict), so `events.values()` is not guaranteed to be in the same order as `error_ids`. Worse, missing events are filtered with `if data is not None` *after* zipping, so a single missing event shifts every subsequent pairing. The result is `ErrorEvent.id` values attached to the wrong title/message/timestamp, which is then fed to Seer for summarization. Pair explicitly instead, e.g. iterate `for error_id, node_id in zip(error_ids, node_ids)` and look up `events.get(node_id)`.

title: Error/breadcrumb merge compares timestamps in different units
body: `gen_request_data()` interleaves errors and replay events with `error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)`. The error timestamps come from the nodestore event payload (epoch **seconds**, e.g. 1.75e9), while the top-level timestamp of an rrweb replay event is epoch **milliseconds** (e.g. 1.75e12). The comparison is therefore always true for real data, so every error is emitted before the first breadcrumb instead of being interleaved chronologically, defeating the purpose of the merge. The new unit tests use hand-written second-based event timestamps (1.5, 2.0), which hides the mismatch. Normalize both sides to the same unit before comparing.

title: Feature-flagged table widget renders hardcoded empty data
body: When `organization.features.includes('use-table-widget-visualization')` is true, the widget renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />`, completely ignoring the `result` that was just fetched. Any organization with this flag enabled will see every dashboard table widget render as an empty table with no columns and no rows, with no error or loading state to explain it. Either wire the real `result`/`fields` into the new component or keep the branch out of the shipped code path.

title: age/timestamp mutual-exclusion validation is incomplete and falsy-sensitive
body: The serializer is meant to accept exactly one of `age` (Editor's Draft) or `timestamp` (Working Draft), but: (1) both fields are `required=False` with no object-level check, so a report containing *neither* passes validation; and (2) the cross-checks use truthiness (`if self.initial_data.get("age")` / `.get("timestamp")`), so `age: 0` (a perfectly valid age for a freshly generated report) or `timestamp: 0` bypasses the mutual-exclusion check and both fields are accepted together. Use `is not None` checks and add a `validate()` that requires exactly one of the two fields.

title: get_environment_info triggers a recommended-event lookup per issue in PR comments
body: `get_environment_info()` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` for every issue included in a merged-PR comment. That helper runs a Snuba query plus a nodestore fetch per issue, so building a comment for the top 5 issues now issues up to 5 extra event lookups (each able to time out or return a stale 'recommended' event) inside the PR comment task, for a single word of decoration in the comment. Consider resolving environments from data already fetched (e.g. the group's environments or the snuba row) instead of fetching full events. Also note the `except Exception` branch logs the raw exception object in `extra={"error": e}`; `str(e)` serializes more reliably.

title: Issue list template produces blank lines and a trailing newline in PR comments
body:
`MERGED_PR_SINGLE_ISSUE_TEMPLATE` ends with `
`, but both the GitHub and GitLab workflows join the rendered entries with `"
".join(...)`. Every bullet is therefore separated by a blank line (which Markdown renders as a 'loose' list with extra paragraph spacing) and the list ends with an extra newline immediately before the `<sub>Did you find this useful?</sub>` footer. The updated tests encode this double spacing, so the formatting regression will ship silently. Drop the trailing `
` from the template.

title: Hook now returns possibly-undefined attributes instead of an empty TagCollection
body: Previously `attributes` was derived through a `useMemo` that always produced a `TagCollection` object (`{}` when there was no data). Now it is `isFetching ? previous : data`, where both `previous` (first render) and `data` (query disabled or not yet resolved) are `undefined`. Callers that are not updated in this PR and treat the value as always-present (spreading is fine, but `Object.keys(attributes)` / `attributes[key]` is not) can now hit runtime errors, in particular when the hook is used with `enabled: false`. Fall back to an empty object (`data ?? {}`) to preserve the previous contract.

title: Custom cell renderers fall back on any falsy return, not just undefined
body: Both `renderDefaultHeadCell` and `renderDefaultBodyCell` decide to use the custom renderer with `if (cell)`. The documented contract (see the prop JSDoc in `tableWidgetVisualization.tsx` and the storybook text: 'If the function returns `undefined`, fallback renderer will run') is that only `undefined` falls through. In practice a renderer that intentionally renders nothing by returning `null`, or that returns `''`/`0`/`false` for a cell value, will be silently overridden by the default renderer. Check `cell !== undefined` instead.

title: Inconsistent optional chaining on required tableData prop
body: `Object.keys(tableData?.meta.fields)` mixes optional chaining with a non-guarded member access and an unguarded `Object.keys`. If `tableData` is ever undefined (the surrounding code defends against it with `tableData?.data ?? []`), this throws `Cannot convert undefined or null to object` instead of rendering an empty table. Either treat `tableData` as truly required (drop the `?.`) or guard the fallback column computation.

title: Analytics event recorded before feature gate and payload validation
body: `analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` is the first statement in `post()`, before the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` feature check and before schema validation. Every request from an org without the feature (which gets a 404) and every malformed request is counted as an assemble event, so the metric no longer reflects actual assemble attempts. Move the call after the feature/validation checks. Note also that with org-auth-token authentication `request.user` is anonymous, so `user_id` will be `None` for the main machine-to-machine use case.

title: Unauthenticated endpoint loops over an unbounded report array
body: This endpoint has `permission_classes = ()` and is CSRF exempt, yet the new code iterates the entire posted array with no cap on the number of reports: it logs the full request body, logs each invalid report (`extra={"raw_report": report}`) and emits one metric per valid report at `sample_rate=1.0`. A single large request can therefore flood logs and the metrics pipeline with attacker-controlled content. Add a maximum list length (and ideally a body size limit) before processing.

title: Tests no longer exercise the application/reports+json content type
body: The rewritten `test_basic` and `test_handles_multiple_reports_both_specs` post without `content_type="application/reports+json"` (the previous tests passed it explicitly). The custom `BrowserReportsJSONParser` exists precisely to accept the Browser Reporting API media type, and that is the content type real browsers send, yet it is now only covered indirectly by the negative `test_rejects_invalid_content_type` case. Keep at least one success-path test that posts with `application/reports+json`.

title: Dead code left behind after removing regex experiments
body: With `ParameterizationRegexExperiment` deleted, the nested `_handle_regex_match` helper inside `parametrize_w_experiments` is no longer referenced by anything (the loop now always calls `experiment.run(content, _incr_counter)`), and `ParameterizationRegex.compiled_pattern` / `_compiled_pattern` were only used by the removed class. Removing them keeps the module from accumulating unreachable branches that future readers assume are live.

title: Dead `enabled` condition and default refetching on an LLM-backed endpoint
body: `normalizeDateTimeParams(...)` always returns an object, so `Boolean(normalizedDateRange)` is always `true` and contributes nothing to the `enabled` guard — the intent (don't query without a date range) is not implemented. Additionally the query uses `staleTime: 5000` with default refetch behaviour, so the `/feedback-summary/` endpoint (which generates an LLM completion server-side) can be re-hit every few seconds on remount/refocus, multiplying model cost. Consider a substantially larger `staleTime` and an explicit guard on the date range.

title: Feature-flagged TableWidgetVisualization renders a hard-coded empty table
body: When `organization.features.includes('use-table-widget-visualization')` is true, the widget table is rendered as `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />`. The actual query result (`result.data`, `result.meta`, `fields`, `fieldAliases`, title, loading state, custom field renderers) is never passed through, and because `columns` is `[]` (not nullish) the component's fallback to derive columns from `tableData.meta.fields` is also bypassed. Any organization that gets this flag will see completely blank table widgets instead of their data. Either wire the real `result`/`fields` into the new component or keep the branch out of the released code path.

title: fetch_error_details pairs error IDs with nodestore values by dict order
body: `zip(error_ids, events.values())` assumes `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns its results in the same order as the input list and includes an entry for every requested node id. That is only true for the naive dict-comprehension backend; other backends (e.g. Bigtable, which returns rows in row-key order, and caches that skip misses) can return a differently ordered and/or shorter mapping. The result is `ErrorEvent.id` values attached to the wrong event payload, and silently dropped/mismatched errors. Iterate over `node_ids`/`error_ids` and look the data up by node id instead (`events.get(node_id)`).

title: Error/breadcrumb interleaving compares seconds against milliseconds
body: `gen_request_data` orders errors relative to replay events with `error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)`. The error timestamp comes from nodestore event data, which is a Unix timestamp in seconds (~1.7e9), while rrweb recording events carry `timestamp` as epoch milliseconds (~1.7e12). Every error will therefore compare as "earlier" than every breadcrumb and all error log lines will be emitted before any breadcrumb, destroying the chronological context the feature is built to provide. The new tests don't catch this because the fixtures build segment events with second-resolution timestamps; please normalize units (and add a test with realistic millisecond rrweb timestamps).

title: HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES filter is skipped unless a search query is typed
body: `sortedAndFilteredAttributes` returns `sorted` early when `searchQuery` is empty, and only applies the `!HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES.includes(attribute.name)` filter in the search branch. As a result `is_segment`, `project_id` and `received` are shown in the attributes tree by default and disappear only while the user is searching — the opposite of the intent, and visibly inconsistent behavior. The hidden-attribute filter should be applied to the base list before the search short-circuit.

title: get_environment_info issues a Snuba + DB query per issue inside comment generation
body: `get_environment_info` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` (a Snuba event lookup) followed by `event.get_environment()` (a DB/environment lookup) for every issue, and both GitHub and GitLab `get_comment_body` call it once per issue in a list comprehension. That adds up to 5 extra Snuba queries plus environment fetches per PR/MR comment, on a path that previously only used already-loaded `Group` fields. Consider resolving the environment in bulk (or from data already available on the group) instead of per-issue, and note that the broad `except Exception` silently degrades to no environment, so these failures would be hard to notice.

title: One nonconforming report causes the entire batch to be dropped with 422
body: The loop validates each report and returns `422` for the whole request as soon as any single report fails, so all other (valid) reports in the same POST are discarded and never counted. This is risky for a data-collection endpoint: the serializer requires `destination` and `attempts` (fields the Reporting API spec does not include in the delivered payload — browsers send `age`/`type`/`url`/`user_agent`/`body`) and restricts `type` to a fixed `BROWSER_REPORT_TYPES` choice list, so newly introduced or spec-variant report types will now fail hard instead of being measured. Prefer validating per report and skipping/counting invalid ones (with a metric/log) while still returning 200 for the rest.

title: Custom cell renderers returning falsy nodes are silently replaced by the default renderer
body: `TableWidgetVisualization`'s prop docs (and the story) state that returning `undefined` from `renderTableBodyCell`/`renderTableHeadCell` falls back to the default renderer, but the implementation checks `if (cell)`. A custom renderer that legitimately returns `null`, `''`, `0` or `false` (e.g. to render an intentionally blank cell) will be overridden by the default field renderer. Check explicitly for `undefined` (`if (cell !== undefined)`).

title: Header alignment is derived from the display name instead of the column key
body: `fieldAlignment(column.name, column.type as ColumnValueType)` passes the human-readable column label. When a caller supplies custom display names without an explicit `type` (the documented use case — e.g. `{key: 'count(span.duration)', name: 'Count of Span Duration'}` in the spec fixture), `fieldAlignment` falls back to name-based detection and cannot recognize the aggregate/numeric field, so numeric columns are left-aligned. Use `column.key` for the field argument.

title: Assemble analytics recorded before the feature check and payload validation
body: `analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` runs at the top of `post`, before the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` feature gate and before schema validation. Every probe/404 and every malformed request is therefore counted as an assemble call, which makes the metric unusable for measuring real usage. Move the record after the feature check (and ideally after validation succeeds).

title: 60s processing deadline may be too short for a 100-identity chunk, silently skipping identities
body: `check_auth_identities` processes up to `chunk_size=100` identities serially, each performing an external IdP `refresh_identity` network call, under the new `processing_deadline_duration=60`. That is a ~0.6s budget per identity. If the deadline is hit the task is killed, but `check_auth` has already bumped `last_synced` for the whole batch, so the unprocessed identities will not be re-selected until the next ~24h cutoff and their SSO validity silently goes unchecked. Either raise the deadline, lower the default chunk size, or only update `last_synced` after an identity is actually processed.

title: No-op migration comments point to a migration that isn't in this change
body: Both 0917 and 0920 are gutted to `return` with the comment "See 0921_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views_rerevised.py for the correct migration." No such migration is added in this PR, so unless 0921 already exists on the base branch the comment is a dangling reference and a future reader cannot find the replacement migration. Please land the referenced migration together with these no-ops or fix the pointer.

title: `Boolean(normalizedDateRange)` guard is always true
body: `normalizeDateTimeParams(selection.datetime)` always returns an object, so `Boolean(normalizedDateRange)` is unconditionally `true` and the `enabled` option is effectively just the feature-flag check. If the intent was to avoid firing the request before page filters are ready, the guard needs to inspect an actual field (e.g. `statsPeriod`/`start`/`end`) or use `usePageFilters().isReady`; otherwise drop the dead condition.

title: Merged-PR comment template's trailing newline produces blank lines between issues
body:
`MERGED_PR_SINGLE_ISSUE_TEMPLATE` now ends with `
`, while both GitHub and GitLab build the list with `"
".join(...)`. The rendered comment therefore has a blank line between every issue and an extra blank line before the trailing `<sub>Did you find this useful?...</sub>` footer (visible in the updated test expectations as `


<sub>`). Drop the trailing newline from the template (or join with `""`) so the bullet list renders as a compact list.

title: Error context silently empty for replays older than the default stats period
body: `self.get_filter_params(request, project)` falls back to the default stats period (14 days) when the caller doesn't pass `statsPeriod`/`start`/`end`, and those bounds are used for the `query_replay_instance` lookup that produces `error_ids`. For a replay older than the default window the Snuba query returns nothing, `error_ids` is empty, and the summary is generated without any error context with no indication to the caller. Derive the time range from the replay itself (or require explicit bounds and return an error when the replay isn't found).

title: OAuth `state` uses `pipeline.signature`, which is not a per-session nonce
