body: `OAuthLoginView.dispatch` sends `state = pipeline.signature` to GitHub and then validates the callback with `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature` (line 412). `Pipeline.signature` is derived from the pipeline view definitions, not from the user's session, so it is the same constant for every user and every installation attempt of the provider — the new tests hardcode `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3` and reuse it across different users and organizations, which demonstrates this. As a result the `state` check provides no CSRF/replay protection (any party can supply the correct value), contrary to what the PR description claims. The established pattern in `sentry/identity/oauth2.py` (`OAuth2LoginView`) is to generate `secrets.token_hex()`, `pipeline.bind_state("state", ...)` it, and compare the callback value against the bound state; this view should do the same.

title: Unguarded `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` can raise KeyError/TypeError
body: The new user check indexes `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` directly. `GitHubIntegrationProvider.build_integration` only sets `metadata["sender"]` when `state.get("sender")` is present (line 376-377), so integrations created through the normal pipeline have no `sender` key at all (see `test_basic_flow`, which asserts the metadata dict without `sender`). This branch is reached whenever an `Integration` row exists but no `OrganizationIntegration` does (e.g. the org integration was removed while the Integration row survived, or legacy rows), and it will raise an unhandled `KeyError` (or `TypeError` if `sender` is stored in a different shape), producing a 500 instead of the intended failure page. Use `(integration.metadata.get("sender") or {}).get("login")` and fail closed.

title: Token exchange and user-info request can raise unhandled exceptions
body: `safe_urlopen(...)` on line 423 is outside the try/except, and `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` on line 434 is not wrapped at all. `sentry.identity.github.get_user_info` performs an HTTP request and calls `raise_for_status()`, so a revoked/invalid token, a GitHub outage, or any network error raises out of the pipeline view and yields a 500 error page rather than the user-facing `github-integration-failed.html` page this PR is designed to show. Both calls should be wrapped and converted into the `error(request, self.active_organization)` response (ideally with logging so these failures are observable).

title: GitHub user validation is skipped when no local Integration row exists
body: In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, if `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `DoesNotExist` the pipeline continues immediately (`return pipeline.next_step()`) without comparing the OAuth-authenticated GitHub user to the owner/sender of the installation. `installation_id` is attacker-controllable (it is read straight from the query string at line 448, or from state bound from the query string in `OAuthLoginView`) and GitHub installation ids are small sequential integers. Whenever Sentry has no Integration row for a live GitHub installation (installation webhook never delivered/processed, row deleted while the GitHub-side installation remains, self-hosted installs), an attacker can submit someone else's installation id and `build_integration` will fetch it from the App API and attach it to the attacker's Sentry org, exposing the victim's repositories. The ownership check should be made against the installation data fetched from GitHub (e.g. `installation["account"]`), not only in the branch where a local Integration happens to exist.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer verifies the installation-not-found error
body: The assertion was changed from `b"The GitHub installation could not be found."` to the generic `b"Invalid installation request."`, which is the default `error_short` emitted by nearly every failure path in the new code (state mismatch, failed token exchange, missing `login`, user mismatch). In addition, the `state` value hardcoded here (`ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`) differs from the value every other test uses (`9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`) even though `pipeline.signature` does not depend on bound state, so this request almost certainly fails the new `state` check in `OAuthLoginView` and never reaches the installation lookup. The 404 stub installed by `responses.replace` is therefore dead, and the regression this test used to cover (GitHub returning 404 for `/app/installations/{id}` surfacing a specific message) is no longer tested.

title: No tests for the state-mismatch and failed-token-exchange failure modes
body: The PR description lists three new failure modes (GitHub user mismatch, `state` mismatch, and GitHub not returning an `access_token`), but only the user mismatch is covered by `test_github_user_mismatch`. There is no test asserting that a tampered/missing `state` or an access-token response without `access_token` (e.g. `error=bad_verification_code`, which GitHub returns with HTTP 200) renders the failure page, so regressions in those branches would go unnoticed. There is also no test for an existing `Integration` whose metadata lacks a `sender` key, which currently crashes (see the `metadata["sender"]` finding).

title: Hardcoded pipeline signature makes the setup tests brittle
body: `assert_setup_flow` asserts the exact redirect query string including `state=9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`, and five other tests hardcode the same md5 value as the `state` parameter. This value is an implementation detail of `Pipeline.signature` (a hash over the pipeline views): adding, removing or renaming a pipeline view will silently change it and break all of these tests with an opaque "Invalid installation request." failure rather than a clear assertion error. Reading the `state` out of the redirect `Location` (or binding a real nonce, as suggested elsewhere) would make the tests robust and self-explanatory.

title: KeyError when integration metadata has no `sender` (500 during install)
body: `GitHubInstallation.dispatch` compares the pipeline-stored GitHub login against `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` with direct subscripting. `sender` is only ever written by `GitHubIntegrationProvider.build_integration` when the incoming state carries it (`if state.get("sender")`), i.e. only for Integrations created from the GitHub `installation` webhook. Integrations created through the install pipeline itself have no `sender` key (see `test_basic_flow`, which asserts metadata without `sender`), and all Integration rows that pre-date the webhook handler also lack it. Any time this branch is reached for such a row (Integration exists, no OrganizationIntegration — e.g. a re-install after the org integration was removed, or a self-hosted instance where webhooks are not delivered), the view raises `KeyError` and the user gets an unhandled 500 instead of the intended error page. Use `.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and decide explicitly how to behave when it is absent.

title: Identity check uses mutable GitHub login instead of immutable user id
body: The new authenticity check compares the OAuth-authenticated GitHub `login` string to the `login` stored in `integration.metadata["sender"]` at webhook time. GitHub usernames are renameable and, once freed, re-registerable by anyone. Consequences: (a) a legitimate installer who renames their GitHub account is permanently locked out of re-installing (generic "Invalid installation request."), and (b) an attacker who registers the installer's abandoned username passes the check. The webhook stores the sender's numeric `id` alongside the login and `get_user_info()` returns `id` as well; comparing the immutable numeric ids would close both holes.

title: User validation is skipped when the Integration row does not exist yet
body: The GitHub-user equality check only runs in the branch where an `Integration` row for the `installation_id` already exists. If `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `DoesNotExist` (line 481-482) the pipeline advances with no validation at all, so a caller who supplies someone else's `installation_id` can still bind that installation to their own Sentry org. This happens whenever the `installation` webhook has not been processed yet (race between the user finishing the pipeline and webhook delivery), was never delivered, or webhooks are not configured (self-hosted). A validation that does not depend on previously stored webhook data — e.g. calling `GET /user/installations` with the freshly obtained user access token and asserting the `installation_id` is listed — would cover this branch too.

title: OAuth `state` is the pipeline signature, not a per-session nonce
body: `state` is set to `pipeline.signature` and later compared against `request.GET["state"]`. The pipeline signature is derived from the pipeline's view set, so it is a constant value shared by every user and every organization — the tests hard-code it (`state=9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`). A constant, publicly discoverable `state` provides no CSRF / authorization-code-injection protection for the OAuth callback: an attacker can always craft a callback URL with the correct `state`. The PR description lists this as one of the security checks, which overstates what it provides. Generate a random nonce per pipeline run, store it with `pipeline.bind_state(...)`, and compare that instead.

title: Unhandled exception from get_user_info on GitHub API failure
body: `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` (from `sentry.identity.github`) performs a `GET /user` and raises on a non-2xx response rather than returning a payload. Unlike the surrounding code paths (bad state, missing access token), this call is not wrapped in try/except, so a transient GitHub 5xx, rate limit, or revoked token turns the install flow into an unhandled 500 instead of the intended "Invalid installation request." page. Wrap the call and return `error(request, self.active_organization)` (ideally with logging/metrics so these failures are observable).

title: Hard-coded redirect_uri must be registered as the GitHub App callback URL
body: The authorize redirect sends `redirect_uri=<absolute_uri>/extensions/github/setup/`. GitHub rejects an authorize request whose `redirect_uri` is not under the callback URL registered for the app ("The redirect_uri MUST match the registered callback URL for this application"). Instances whose GitHub App/OAuth App is configured with a different callback URL (self-hosted setups are documented to point the user-authorization callback elsewhere, and single-tenant deployments use custom apps) will fail at the very first step of the integration install after this change. The PR contains no documentation or setup-instruction update for the newly required callback URL.

title: Re-install now blocked for non-ACTIVE integrations
body: After the `installations_exist` check, the code re-fetches the integration with `status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE` and renders the generic error if it is missing. Previously this branch (Integration row exists, no OrganizationIntegration) simply advanced the pipeline, so an Integration left in `PENDING_DELETION`/`DISABLED` with its org integrations already removed could be re-installed. Now such users get "We could not verify the authenticity of the installation request", which does not describe the real cause and gives them no actionable path. Either reuse the row already fetched on line 478 or report a status-specific message.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer covers the 404 path
body: The test passes `state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`, which differs from the valid pipeline signature used by every other test in this file (`9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`). The request therefore short-circuits in `OAuthLoginView` on the state-mismatch branch and the assertion `b"Invalid installation request."` passes for that reason alone. The behaviour the test is named for — `get_installation_info` returning 404 and `build_integration` raising `IntegrationError("The GitHub installation could not be found.")`, previously asserted — is now completely uncovered, and the 404 `responses.replace` setup is dead. Either use the correct state so the flow reaches `build_integration`, or rename the test to reflect that it only exercises state mismatch and add a separate test for the 404 case.

title: No coverage for token-exchange failure branches
body: The PR introduces two new failure branches in `OAuthLoginView` — the access-token exchange returning a body without `access_token` (wrong or reused `code`) and `get_user_info` returning a payload without `login` — and both are listed as intended failure modes in the description, but no test stubs a failing `https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token` or `/user` response. Regressions in these paths (e.g. an exception leaking a 500 instead of the error page) would go unnoticed.

title: error_short strings are not extractable for translation
body: `error()` takes `error_short` as a plain string and calls `_(error_short)` at runtime (line 141). Because the argument is a variable, `makemessages` cannot extract the literals ("Invalid installation request.", "GitHub installation pending deletion.", "Github installed on another Sentry organization."), so these user-facing strings will never be translated even though the code implies they are. Mark the literals with `_()` at their definition/call sites and pass the already-lazy objects through.

title: OAuth `state` is the static pipeline signature, so the new identity check can be bypassed
body: `OAuthLoginView` sends `state=pipeline.signature` to GitHub and then validates `request.GET["state"] == pipeline.signature` (line 412). `Pipeline.signature` is an md5 of the fully-qualified class names of the pipeline views, i.e. a value that is identical for every user and every session (the new test even hard-codes it as `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`). It is therefore not a per-session nonce and provides no CSRF/session binding: an attacker who authorizes the GitHub OAuth app themselves can hand a victim a URL such as `/extensions/github/setup/?code=<attacker_code>&state=<known_signature>`. The victim's pipeline will accept it, exchange the attacker's code, and bind `github_authenticated_user` to the attacker's login — which then matches `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` and defeats exactly the installer-identity check this PR adds. Follow the existing pattern in `sentry.identity.oauth2` (`OAuth2LoginView` generates `secrets.token_hex()`, binds it with `pipeline.bind_state("state", ...)`, and `OAuth2CallbackView` compares it with `constant_time_compare`).

title: `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` can raise KeyError and return a 500
body: The new check indexes `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` unconditionally. `sender` is only written by `build_integration` when the incoming state contains it (currently only the GitHub `installation` webhook path), so integrations created before that metadata existed, or by any flow where the webhook did not supply a sender, have no `sender` key. In that case the installation pipeline raises `KeyError` and the user gets an unhandled 500 instead of the intended "Invalid installation request." dialog. Use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` (and fail closed) instead.

title: Installer-identity check is skipped when the Integration row does not yet exist
body: The comparison between `github_authenticated_user` and the installing GitHub user only happens in the branch where an `Integration` row already exists (lines 493-505). If `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `DoesNotExist` the pipeline immediately advances (line 482) and `build_integration` creates the integration with no identity validation at all. Since that row is created asynchronously by the GitHub `installation` webhook, an attacker who completes the Sentry pipeline before the webhook is processed (or on an instance where the webhook is not delivered) still gets the previous, unvalidated behaviour. Consider validating the authenticated user against the installation data returned by `get_installation_info()` (e.g. the account/sender) in that path as well, so the protection does not depend on a webhook race.

title: Unhandled exception from `get_user_info` / `safe_urlopen` yields a 500 instead of the error dialog
body: `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` performs an HTTP call and raises on non-2xx responses (`raise_for_status`), and `safe_urlopen` on line 423 can raise on network/timeout errors. Neither is wrapped in a try/except, so a transient GitHub failure or a revoked/invalid token during installation surfaces as an unhandled 500 in the setup popup rather than the `github-integration-failed.html` dialog that the rest of this view carefully returns. Wrap both calls and return `error(request, self.active_organization)` on failure (ideally with logging so these failures are diagnosable).

title: `test_installation_not_found` no longer tests installation-not-found
body: The test still stubs a 404 for `/app/installations/{id}` but now passes `state="ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"`, which does not match the pipeline signature used everywhere else in this file (`9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`). The request therefore fails in `OAuthLoginView` on the state check and the assertion only verifies the generic "Invalid installation request." message. The previously covered behaviour — `build_integration` raising `IntegrationError("The GitHub installation could not be found.")` for a 404 from GitHub — is now untested, and nothing covers the missing-`access_token` or user-mismatch-in-OAuthLoginView branches separately. Use the correct state so the test reaches `GitHubInstallation`/`build_integration`, and add a distinct test for the state-mismatch path.

title: Authorize URL built by string interpolation without URL-encoding
body: `client_id`, `state` and `redirect_uri` are interpolated raw into the authorize URL. `redirect_uri` comes from `absolute_uri(...)` and can contain characters that must be percent-encoded in a query value (e.g. when the install URL carries a query string or when a custom `SENTRY_URL_PREFIX`/subdomain introduces reserved characters), which would silently corrupt the redirect GitHub uses. Build the query with `urlencode({...})` as `OAuth2LoginView` does.

title: `_(error_short)` cannot be extracted for translation
body: `error()` calls `_(error_short)` on a runtime variable. The literal strings passed by callers ("Invalid installation request.", "GitHub installation pending deletion.", "Github installed on another Sentry organization.") are no longer wrapped in `_()` at their definition sites, so `makemessages` will not extract them and they will never be translated (the long messages are correctly marked, the short ones are not). Mark the short strings with `gettext_lazy` at the call sites and drop the runtime `_()`.

title: `queued` default is evaluated once at import time, so every AssignmentSource shares the same timestamp
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a dataclass default, which Python evaluates a single time when the class body executes (i.e. at module import). Every `AssignmentSource` created for the lifetime of the process therefore carries the process-start timestamp rather than the time the assignment was queued, making the field useless for debugging/ordering and misleading to anyone who later relies on it (e.g. to expire stale sources). Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead. As a secondary effect, evaluating `timezone.now()` in the class body touches Django settings (`USE_TZ`) at import time of a module that is imported by `sentry/models/groupassignee.py`.

title: AssignmentSource round-trip through Celery kwargs corrupts the `queued` type and silently drops the source on any mismatch
body: `to_dict()` (via `asdict`) emits a raw `datetime` for `queued`, and that dict is passed as a Celery task kwarg in `sync_group_assignee_outbound`. With the JSON task serializer the datetime is encoded as an ISO string and is never decoded back, so `from_dict` reconstructs an instance whose `queued` field is a `str` even though it is annotated `datetime` (and with a stricter serializer the publish would fail outright, breaking assignee sync). `from_dict` performs no type validation and only catches `ValueError`/`TypeError`, returning `None` without logging, which means any future schema drift (renamed/extra key) silently yields no assignment source and re-enables the sync loop this PR is meant to fix. Serialize `queued` explicitly (e.g. isoformat string) and log when parsing fails.

title: Abstract `sync_assignee_outbound` was not updated for the new `assignment_source` kwarg that the task now passes
body: `sync_assignee_outbound` in `src/sentry/integrations/tasks/sync_assignee_outbound.py` now calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(external_issue, user, assign=assign, assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)`, but the abstract declaration here still only lists `external_issue, user, assign, **kwargs`. The new keyword is only tolerated because concrete implementations happen to declare `**kwargs`; any implementation (current or third-party/plugin shim) that does not will raise `TypeError`, which the `@retry` decorator will retry and then drop, silently disabling outbound assignee sync for that provider. The contract should declare `assignment_source` explicitly so implementers know it exists.

title: `assignment_source` added to abstract `sync_status_outbound` but never passed or implemented
body: The abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature gains `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None` before `**kwargs`, yet no call site (e.g. `sentry/integrations/tasks/sync_status_outbound.py`) passes it and no concrete integration implementation declares it. The result is a parameter in the published contract that is positionally inconsistent with subclass signatures (`(external_issue, is_resolved, project_id, **kwargs)`), so a positional call would bind the value to the wrong argument in subclasses, and keyword calls are silently swallowed into `**kwargs`. Either wire status sync through the same loop-breaking check or drop the parameter until it is implemented.

title: `should_sync` is called with the new argument positionally, breaking any one-argument override
body: `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)` passes the new source positionally. Only `IssueBasicIntegration.should_sync` and `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync` were widened in this PR; any installation class that overrides `should_sync(self, attribute)` with the old single-argument signature will now raise `TypeError` inside a retried task, disabling assignee sync for that provider. Passing it as a keyword (and/or defaulting it) would at least make such breakage explicit and greppable.

title: No test covers the task-level dict round trip, and `test_to_dict` cannot detect the frozen `queued` default
body: `assert result.get("queued") is not None` always passes because `queued` has a class-level default, so the test gives no coverage of the timestamp actually reflecting when the source was created, nor of the dict surviving a serialize/deserialize cycle (`to_dict()` -> Celery JSON -> `from_dict()`), which is the path that actually breaks the loop. Tests using `self.tasks()` run tasks eagerly and skip kwarg serialization, so the datetime handling is untested end to end. Add a test that feeds `to_dict()` output through JSON encode/decode into `from_dict` and asserts the resulting `integration_id`/`queued` types, plus a deassign-with-matching-source case mirroring the new assign test.

title: `queued` default is evaluated once at import time
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a dataclass field default, so `timezone.now()` is called exactly once when the module is first imported. Every `AssignmentSource` created afterwards (including all instances built by `from_integration`) carries the process-start timestamp instead of the time the assignment was actually queued. Any logging/debugging or future staleness check based on `queued` will be wrong, and `__eq__` (which includes `queued`) will differ between processes for otherwise identical sources. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead.

title: AssignmentSource does not survive a serialization round-trip through the task queue
body: `to_dict()` (via `asdict`) puts a raw `datetime` into the dict that is passed as celery task kwargs in `sync_group_assignee_outbound`, and `from_dict()` just splats the dict into the constructor with no coercion. Depending on the configured task serializer this either (a) fails to serialize the task payload, breaking all outbound assignee syncs, or (b) round-trips `queued` as an ISO string, which `from_dict` happily accepts because dataclasses perform no type validation — leaving a field annotated `datetime` holding a `str`. Tests only exercise the eager/in-process path, so neither case is covered. Serialize `queued` explicitly (e.g. `isoformat()`) and parse it back in `from_dict`.

title: from_dict silently returns None, disabling cycle protection
body: When the payload is malformed, `from_dict` swallows the error and returns `None`. In `sync_assignee_outbound` a `None` source means `should_sync("outbound_assignee", None)` falls back to the old behaviour and the change is propagated back to the originating integration — i.e. the exact sync loop this PR is meant to break — with no log line or metric to indicate it happened. At minimum log a warning here so a serialization regression is detectable.

title: `assignment_source` added to abstract sync_status_outbound but never passed or implemented
body: The abstract `sync_status_outbound` now declares `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`, but no caller passes it (the status-sync task is unchanged) and none of the concrete implementations (Jira, Jira Server, VSTS, Example, ...) were updated to accept or use it. The parameter is dead code that suggests inbound status webhooks are protected against sync cycles when they are not. Either wire the status path through (task -> `should_sync("outbound_status", source)` -> implementations) or drop the parameter.

title: New `assignment_source` kwarg passed to duck-typed installations that may not accept it
body: The task resolves `installation` by `hasattr(installation, "sync_assignee_outbound")` and now always passes `assignment_source=...`. The abstract declaration in `IssueSyncIntegration` was not updated to include this parameter, so it is only tolerated by implementations that happen to declare `**kwargs`. Any installation implementing `sync_assignee_outbound(self, external_issue, user, assign=True)` without `**kwargs` will raise `TypeError`, which is not in the task's `retry(exclude=...)` list and will therefore burn 5 retries for every assignment. Declare the parameter explicitly on the abstract method (and in the implementations) rather than relying on `**kwargs`.

title: Task kwarg is always sent, breaking old workers during rollout
body: `assignment_source_dict` is included in the `apply_async` kwargs unconditionally (as `None` when there is no source). During a rolling deploy, workers still running the previous revision of `sync_assignee_outbound` do not accept this keyword and the task will fail with `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument`, dropping assignee syncs for the duration of the rollout. Only include the key when `assignment_source` is not `None`.

title: No test that a different integration's assignment source still syncs outbound
body: The new tests cover source=None and source==the same integration, but not the case the PR explicitly claims to preserve: an assignment originating from integration A must still be propagated outbound to integration B. Since the guard in `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync` compares `sync_source.integration_id` to `org_integration.integration_id`, a mistake there (e.g. comparing against `org_integration.id`) would silently suppress all outbound syncs for every integration and no test would catch it. Add a case with two linked integrations where the source is one of them.

title: `queued` default is evaluated once at import time
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` makes the default value a class-level constant computed when the module is first imported, not when an `AssignmentSource` is constructed. Every `AssignmentSource` created via `from_integration()` (which never passes `queued`) will therefore carry the process start/import timestamp, which can be hours or days stale. Any present or future logic that reasons about how long ago the assignment was queued (e.g. expiring the cycle-breaking context) will be silently wrong, and the field's value is misleading in logs/payloads. Use `dataclasses.field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead.

title: `to_dict`/`from_dict` do not survive a Celery JSON round-trip with a typed `queued`
body: `to_dict()` returns `asdict(self)`, so `queued` is a raw `datetime` that is handed to `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs={... "assignment_source_dict": ...})`. Celery/kombu's JSON serializer will encode it as an ISO-8601 string (and a stricter serializer would reject it outright), and `from_dict` simply does `cls(**input_dict)` with no coercion, so the reconstructed object's `queued` is a `str` even though it is annotated `datetime`. Anything that later compares or arithmetics on `queued` will raise `TypeError` at runtime. Serialize `queued` explicitly (e.g. `isoformat()`) and parse it back in `from_dict`.

title: Malformed assignment source is silently dropped, re-enabling sync cycles
body: `from_dict` swallows `ValueError`/`TypeError` and returns `None`. In `sync_assignee_outbound` the returned `None` is passed to `should_sync("outbound_assignee", None)`, which means the cycle-prevention check is skipped entirely and the change is propagated back to the originating integration — exactly the loop this PR is meant to break. Since this failure mode is invisible (no log, no metric), a payload-shape change (e.g. the `queued` serialization issue above, or an added/renamed field during a deploy) would silently reintroduce the sync loop. Log/capture the parse failure instead of returning `None` silently.

title: `sync_status_outbound` gains an `assignment_source` parameter that is never passed or implemented
body: The abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature now declares `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`, but no caller passes it (the status-sync task still calls `sync_status_outbound(external_issue, is_resolved, project_id)`), no concrete integration implementation was updated, and `should_sync("outbound_status")` is still invoked without a source. The parameter is dead API surface that suggests status sync cycles are now broken when they are not; subclasses that only accept `**kwargs` would silently swallow the argument if someone starts passing it. Either wire the status path through (task kwarg + `should_sync` call + implementations) or drop the parameter from this signature.

title: New positional second argument to `should_sync` can break duck-typed installations
body: The task only checks `hasattr(installation, "should_sync")` and now calls `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)` with two positional arguments. Any installation class that defines `should_sync(self, attribute)` with the old single-argument signature (only the two definitions in `mixins/issues.py` were updated here) will now raise `TypeError`, which the `@retry` decorator will retry 5 times before giving up — silently breaking outbound assignee sync for that provider. Additionally the parameter is named `sync_source` in `should_sync` but `assignment_source` everywhere else, so keyword calls will not be interchangeable; align the names and verify no other `should_sync` overrides exist.

title: No test covers the dict round-trip or the per-instance `queued` default
body: The new tests only assert that `to_dict()["queued"]` is not `None` and that `from_dict` works for a dict without `queued`. They never (a) assert that `queued` differs between two instances created at different times, which would have caught the import-time default evaluation bug, nor (b) round-trip `to_dict()` through JSON serialization and back into `from_dict`, which is exactly how the value travels in `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async`. Both the real failure modes of this dataclass are therefore untested.

title: Cycle-breaking is only tested for assign, not deassign, and never through the task boundary
body: There is a new test for `assign(..., assignment_source=AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration))` not triggering outbound sync, but no equivalent test for `deassign(..., assignment_source=...)`, even though `sync_group_assignee_inbound` now passes a source on the unassign path. Also, all tests run under `self.tasks()` (eager execution), so `assignment_source_dict` is handed to the task as a live `dict` with a `datetime`; the serialize/deserialize path used in production (and therefore `AssignmentSource.from_dict` receiving a string `queued`) is never exercised. A regression in that path would silently restore the sync loop without failing any test.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and cannot be instantiated
body: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` is redefined as `class MetricAlertDetectorHandler(StatefulDetectorHandler[QuerySubscriptionUpdate]): pass`, but `StatefulDetectorHandler` is an `abc.ABC` with four abstract members: `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the newly added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. None of them are implemented here, so the class retains its `__abstractmethods__` and any attempt to construct it raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler ...`. `Detector.detector_handler` (src/sentry/workflow_engine/models/detector.py:86) instantiates the registered handler unconditionally, so `process_detectors()` will blow up for any detector of type `metric_alert_fire` instead of the previous no-op (`evaluate` returning `[]`). Either keep a concrete stub implementation of the four abstract members or leave the handler on the non-stateful `DetectorHandler` base until the real implementation lands.

title: evaluate() docstring still describes a list return value
body: `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` now returns `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, but its docstring still says "returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`. There will be one result for each group key result in the packet". The same wording is misleading for implementers of the abstract `DetectorHandler.evaluate` contract, which also changed to a dict. Update the docstring to describe the dict keyed by group key.

title: Stale TODO comment about stateful detectors
body: The comment `# TODO: This will be a stateful detector when we build that abstraction` sits directly above a class that now subclasses `StatefulDetectorHandler`, so the abstraction already exists and the TODO is misleading. It should be removed or replaced with the actual remaining work (implementing the abstract methods).

title: Mock occurrence builder ignores `value`, so tests can't detect wrong arguments to the new hook
body: `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` takes `value` but never uses it when constructing the `IssueOccurrence`, and the returned occurrence/event_data only depend on `group_key` and `new_status`. As a result the assertions in `TestProcessDetectors.test_state_results_multi_group` (line 190 passes `6` for `group_2`, whose actual value is `10`) and in `TestEvaluate`/`TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue` (which pass `6` while the data packets contain `100`, `8`, `200`, `10`) pass regardless of what value `evaluate_group_key_value` actually forwards to `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. The main new behaviour of this PR — forwarding the correct group value and priority to the occurrence hook — is therefore untested. Encode `value` (e.g. in `evidence_data` or `subtitle`) and pass the real values in the assertions.

title: get_group_key_values type annotation disallows the `None` group key that is actually used
body: `get_group_key_values` is annotated as returning `dict[str, int]`, but `evaluate()` feeds those keys straight into `get_state_data`/`evaluate_group_key_value`, which are typed with `DetectorGroupKey` (`str | None`), and the new tests exercise exactly that case (`DataPacket("1", {"dedupe": 2, "group_vals": {None: 6}})`). The mismatch means type checking will not catch implementations that return `None` keys (legitimate) or will force implementers to lie about the type. Annotate it as `dict[DetectorGroupKey, int]`.

title: get_state_data raises KeyError when a detector declares no counters
body: `counter_updates` is only populated inside `if self.counter_names:`; when a `StatefulDetectorHandler` subclass legitimately declares `counter_names = []`, the dict stays empty and `counter_updates=counter_updates[gk]` raises `KeyError` for every group key. Since this PR documents/encourages new `StatefulDetectorHandler` subclasses (and adds a required `build_occurrence_and_event_data` hook), it would be worth defaulting to `counter_updates.get(gk, {})` so counter-free detectors work.

title: process_detectors return type changed from list to dict of results without updating consumers
body: `process_detectors` now returns `list[tuple[Detector, dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]]]` instead of a list of results per detector. Any existing call site that does `for result in detector_results:` keeps working syntactically but silently iterates group keys (strings/None) instead of `DetectorEvaluationResult` objects, which fails only later and confusingly. Confirm all callers of `process_detectors()`/`DetectorHandler.evaluate()` outside this diff were updated to the dict contract.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler can no longer be instantiated (abstract methods unimplemented)
body: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` now subclasses `StatefulDetectorHandler` with only `pass`, but `StatefulDetectorHandler`/`DetectorHandler` declare four abstract members: `counter_names` (abstract property), `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the newly added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. Because none are implemented, `MetricAlertDetectorHandler(...)` raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class ...`. `Detector.detector_handler` instantiates the registered handler (`group_type.detector_handler(self)`), so any code path that touches a `metric_alert_fire` detector handler will now raise instead of returning an empty result list as it did before this change. mypy will not catch this since subclassing an ABC without implementing abstract methods is legal at definition time. Either keep a trivial concrete implementation or mark the class abstract and remove it from the registered group type until it's implemented.

title: Stale TODO comment contradicts the code
body: The comment "TODO: This will be a stateful detector when we build that abstraction" sits directly above a class that now *is* a `StatefulDetectorHandler`. Leaving it there is misleading for the next reader; it should be removed or replaced with the remaining work (implementing the abstract hooks).

title: PriorityLevel(new_status) can raise ValueError for non-priority condition results
body: `build_occurrence_and_event_data(group_key, value, PriorityLevel(new_status))` converts the computed status to `sentry.types.group.PriorityLevel`. `new_status` is derived from `max(new_status, condition.evaluate_value(value))`, and `DataCondition.condition_result` is DB/user-configured and not constrained to `DetectorPriorityLevel` values (it can be a bool or an arbitrary int). Any such value (e.g. `True` -> 1, or 10) makes `PriorityLevel(...)` raise an unhandled `ValueError`, aborting evaluation of the whole data packet (and leaving already-enqueued dedupe/state updates uncommitted). Validate/clamp the value, or only build an occurrence when `new_status` is one of the known `DetectorPriorityLevel` members.

title: Occurrence fingerprint contract with build_fingerprint is neither enforced nor documented
body: Resolution is emitted by the base class as a `StatusChangeMessage` whose fingerprint comes from `self.build_fingerprint(group_key)` (line 293), but the new `build_occurrence_and_event_data` hook lets subclasses construct the `IssueOccurrence` fingerprint however they like, and the abstract method has no docstring stating that it must use `build_fingerprint(group_key)`. If a subclass picks a different fingerprint, the firing occurrence and the resolving status change will target different groups and issues will never auto-resolve. Document the requirement on the abstract method (or build/inject the fingerprint in the base class).

title: evaluate() docstring still says it returns a list
body: `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` now returns `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, but the docstring still reads "returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`". Update it to describe the dict keyed by group key, otherwise implementers of the hook will be misled about the contract.

title: get_group_key_values type annotation disallows the None group key that the code and tests use
body: `get_group_key_values` is annotated `-> dict[str, int]`, but group keys are `DetectorGroupKey = str | None` everywhere else (`build_occurrence_and_event_data`, `get_state_data`, `build_dedupe_value_key`), and the new test `test_state_results` returns `{None: 6}` from this method. The annotation should be `dict[DetectorGroupKey, int]`; as written, type checking gives implementers wrong guidance about whether a `None` (ungrouped) key is allowed.

title: get_state_data raises KeyError when a handler has no counters
body: `counter_updates` is only populated inside `if self.counter_names:`; when a `StatefulDetectorHandler` subclass legitimately declares `counter_names = []`, `counter_updates` stays `{}` and `counter_updates[gk]` on this line raises `KeyError` for every group key, breaking all evaluation for that detector. Default to `{}` per group key (e.g. `counter_updates.get(gk, {})`).

title: Expected occurrences are built with the wrong value, so value/priority propagation is untested
body: In `test_state_results_multi_group` the expected occurrence for `group_2` is built with value `6` while the packet supplies `10` (similarly `TestEvaluate` builds expectations with `6` while packets carry `100`/`8`). The assertions still pass only because `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` ignores `value`, which means the tests never verify that `evaluate_group_key_value` passes the correct `value` (or the correct `new_status`) into the new `build_occurrence_and_event_data` hook. Make the mock occurrence depend on `value`/`new_status` (e.g. in `evidence_data`) and use the real values so a regression in the hook arguments would be caught. There is also no test that `process_detectors` produces a `PayloadType.STATUS_CHANGE` payload for the resolution path.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and will raise TypeError when instantiated
body: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` was changed to subclass `StatefulDetectorHandler` with only `pass` as a body. `StatefulDetectorHandler` declares four abstract members (`counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the newly added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`), none of which are implemented here, so the class remains abstract. `Detector.detector_handler` instantiates the registered handler via `group_type.detector_handler(self)`; for any detector of type `metric_alert_fire` this now raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler ...` instead of returning a handler (previously it returned a no-op handler whose `evaluate` returned an empty list). Any code path that resolves the handler for a metric alert detector will crash rather than no-op. Either implement the abstract methods (even as stubs raising NotImplementedError only when actually called) or keep it on the non-abstract base until the real implementation lands.

title: get_state_data raises KeyError when counter_names is empty
body: In `get_state_data`, `counter_updates` is initialized to `{}` and only populated inside `if self.counter_names:`. The result loop then unconditionally does `counter_updates=counter_updates[gk]`, which raises `KeyError` for every group key when a subclass legitimately declares `counter_names = []`. With the new `StatefulDetectorHandler` hook being the intended base for real detectors (e.g. metric alerts, which may not need counters), this will blow up during evaluation. Use `counter_updates.get(gk, {})` or build a default dict of `{name: None}` per group key.

title: Docstring still says evaluate returns a list
body: `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` now returns `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, but its docstring still reads "returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`. There will be one result for each group key result in the packet". This misdescribes the return contract for implementers/callers; update it to describe the dict keyed by group key.

title: Stale TODO comment about stateful detector
body: The comment `# TODO: This will be a stateful detector when we build that abstraction` sits directly above a class that now subclasses `StatefulDetectorHandler`, so the TODO is already satisfied and is misleading. It should be removed or replaced with the remaining work (implementing the abstract hooks).

title: Multi-group test builds expected occurrence with the wrong value
body: `test_state_results_multi_group` sends `{"group_1": 6, "group_2": 10}` but constructs the expected occurrence for `group_2` with `value=6` (`build_mock_occurrence_and_event(detector.detector_handler, "group_2", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)`). The assertion only passes because the mock builder ignores the `value` argument entirely, so the test does not verify that `evaluate_group_key_value` passes the correct group value into `build_occurrence_and_event_data` — a regression in that argument would go undetected. Either pass 10 and make the mock occurrence depend on `value` (e.g. in `evidence_data`), or assert on the hook arguments directly.

title: get_monitor_environment_context returns the raw config, discarding the schedule_type display conversion
body: `get_monitor_environment_context` builds a copy of the monitor config and rewrites `schedule_type` to its human-readable display value (`config["schedule_type"] = monitor_environment.monitor.get_schedule_type_display()`), but the returned dict sets `"config": monitor_environment.monitor.config` — the original object, not the modified copy. The local `config` variable is therefore dead code and the occurrence's monitor context always carries the raw integer `schedule_type` instead of e.g. "crontab"/"interval". Since this code is being lifted into a new module as part of a refactor, it is a good moment to fix it: return `config` instead of `monitor_environment.monitor.config`.

title: get_failure_reason docstring shows an output string the function can never produce
body: The docstring lists `"A failed check-in was detected"` as example output, but `SINGULAR_HUMAN_FAILURE_MAP` only contains "An error check-in was detected", "A missed check-in was detected" and "A timeout check-in was detected"; there is no generic "failed" variant. The second example ("... were detected") also doesn't match the template `"%(problem_checkins)s check-ins detected"`. Also note the typos "humam readible". Misleading docs here make it harder to reason about the user-visible failure reason text.

title: Public helpers removed from mark_failed without re-export; external importers will break
body: `mark_failed.py` no longer defines `mark_failed_threshold`, `create_issue_platform_occurrence`, `get_failure_reason`, `get_monitor_environment_context` or `SimpleCheckIn`, and they are not re-exported from the module. Any other module, task, or test that does `from sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed import <one of these>` (or patches e.g. `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed.create_issue_platform_occurrence` in a test) will now fail with ImportError/AttributeError. The PR touches only these four files, so no callers/tests were updated — the whole tree should be grepped for the old names (including mock patch targets, which are string-based and won't be caught by static checks) before merging.

title: get_monitor_environment_context returns the unmodified monitor config
body: `get_monitor_environment_context` copies `monitor.config` into a local `config` and replaces `config["schedule_type"]` with the human-readable display value, but the returned dict uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` (the original object) rather than the modified `config` copy. As a result the `monitor` context attached to the issue occurrence event always contains the raw integer `schedule_type` instead of the display string, and the whole copy/mutate block is dead code. (The defect is carried over from `mark_failed.py`, but this PR is the natural place to fix it since the function is being moved.) Fix by returning `"config": config`.

title: Public helpers removed from mark_failed with no re-export and no test updates
body: `mark_failed.py` no longer defines `mark_failed_threshold`, `create_issue_platform_occurrence`, `get_failure_reason`, `get_monitor_environment_context`, `HUMAN_FAILURE_STATUS_MAP`, `SINGULAR_HUMAN_FAILURE_MAP` or `SimpleCheckIn`, and two of them were also renamed (`mark_failed_threshold` -> `try_incident_threshold`, `create_issue_platform_occurrence` -> `create_incident_occurrence`). No compatibility aliases are left behind and the PR touches no test or caller files. Any module or test that does `from sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed import ...` or patches `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed.create_issue_platform_occurrence` / `...get_failure_reason` will now fail at import time or silently patch a non-existent attribute (mock.patch raises AttributeError). Before merging, grep for these names across `src/` and `tests/` and update the references (or add re-exports).

title: Public names removed from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` with no importers updated
body: This PR deletes the module-level names `mark_failed_threshold`, `create_issue_platform_occurrence`, `get_failure_reason`, `get_monitor_environment_context` and the `SimpleCheckIn` TypedDict from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` and re-homes them (under new names in some cases) in `sentry/monitors/logic/incidents.py`, `sentry/monitors/logic/incident_occurrence.py` and `sentry/monitors/types.py`. No other file in the PR is updated. Any production module or test that imports these symbols from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed`, or that monkeypatches them by path (e.g. `mock.patch("sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed.create_issue_platform_occurrence")`), will now raise ImportError/AttributeError, or worse, silently patch nothing and let real Kafka occurrences be produced in tests. The reorganization should be accompanied by updates to all call sites/patch targets (grep for the old names) before merging.

title: `get_monitor_environment_context` returns the raw config, discarding the humanized `schedule_type`
body: The function copies `monitor.config` into `config` and replaces the numeric `schedule_type` with its display value, but the returned dict sets `"config": monitor_environment.monitor.config` — the original object, not `config`. The computed copy is dead code, so the monitor context attached to the issue occurrence event contains the raw integer `schedule_type` instead of the human readable one (e.g. `0` rather than `crontab`). Since this code is being moved into a new module anyway, it is a good time to return `config` instead.

title: `get_failure_reason` produces a malformed string when no statuses are recognized
body: `status_counts` only counts statuses present in `HUMAN_FAILURE_STATUS_MAP` (error/missed/timeout). If `failed_checkins` is empty or contains only other statuses (e.g. `IN_PROGRESS`/`OK`), the counter is empty, the `sum(...) == 1` branch is skipped, `get_text_list([])` returns an empty string and the function returns the nonsensical " check-ins detected", which is then shown to users as the issue's "Failure reason" evidence. A fallback such as the generic "A failed check-in was detected" message mentioned in the docstring should be returned for the empty case.

title: Docstring of `get_failure_reason` is misspelled and documents output the function cannot produce
body: The docstring reads "Builds a humam readible string" (should be "human readable") and lists example outputs that do not match the implementation: "2 missed check-ins, 1 timeout check-in and 1 error check-in were detected" (the code emits "2 missed, 1 timeout and 1 error check-ins detected") and "A failed check-in was detected", which is never returned by any branch. Since the code is being moved into a new module, the docstring should be corrected so it doesn't mislead future readers about the generated user-facing text.

title: Unhealthy flusher process is never killed before being restarted
body: `_ensure_processes_alive` now guards the kill with `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. The processes are created via `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, i.e. `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`, which derives from `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` and is *not* a subclass of `multiprocessing.Process` (`multiprocessing.context.Process`). The isinstance check is therefore always False, so `process.kill()` is never executed — the previous code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. Consequence: when a flusher is detected as hung (`cause == "hang"`, process still alive but `healthy_since` stale), the old process keeps running while `_create_process_for_shards` spawns a second process for the same shards. Two processes then flush the same Redis shards concurrently, which can produce duplicate/partial segments to the buffered-segments topic, and up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS+1 processes can accumulate per shard group. Use `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` (or check for `threading.Thread` instead) in the guard.

title: join() skips termination of remaining processes once the deadline expires
body: In `join`, the loop over `self.processes.items()` does `if remaining_time <= 0: break` before waiting on each process. If the first process consumes the whole timeout budget, every remaining process is skipped entirely — it is neither waited for nor terminated. Combined with the `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` check at the end of the loop (always False for spawn-context `SpawnProcess`, see the kill() issue), `terminate()` is effectively never called on any flusher process, so hung flusher processes can outlive the shutdown/rebalance path. `remaining_time` is also computed and then unused except for the comparison. Consider terminating all processes after the wait loop regardless of which ones timed out, and fixing the isinstance check.

title: Per-segment metric now tagged with a high-cardinality shard-list tag
body: `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` is emitted for every flushed segment and is now tagged with `shard=shard_tag`, where `shard_tag` is the comma-joined list of all shards handled by that process (e.g. `"0,3,6,9"` or, with the default `--flusher-processes 1`, the full assigned-partition list). That tag value changes on every Kafka rebalance and differs per consumer instance, so this high-volume metric gains an effectively unbounded set of tag values. The same tag is added to the `spans.buffer.flusher.produce`/`wait_produce` timers and to `spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy`. This risks cardinality blowup/cost in the metrics backend; consider emitting a per-shard tag only where the value is a single bounded shard id, or dropping the tag from the per-segment metric.

title: Inconsistent metric tag key: "shards" vs "shard"
body: `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is tagged with `{"shards": shard_tag}` while `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` use `{"shard": shard_tag}` for the same value. Dashboards/alerts grouping by `shard` will silently miss the `wait_produce` timer. Pick one key.

title: Class docstring claims one process per shard, which is not what the code does
body: The docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing." In practice the number of processes is `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` and shards are round-robined onto processes, and the CLI default for `--flusher-processes` is 1, so the default behaviour is a single process handling all shards. The new `max_processes` parameter is also undocumented while the docstring still documents a non-existent `topic` parameter. This misleads operators about the default behaviour.

title: Dead method _create_process_for_shard
body: `_create_process_for_shard(shard)` is not called anywhere after the refactor (`_ensure_processes_alive` calls `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly). It duplicates restart logic and will silently drift out of sync; remove it or wire it up.

title: --flusher-processes 0 silently means "one process per shard"
body: `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats 0 as falsy, so passing `--flusher-processes 0` (or any code path passing 0) results in one process per assigned shard rather than an error or a single process. The click option has no range validation. Use an explicit `if max_processes is None` and/or validate `>= 1` in the click option.

title: Redis memory info is now queried once per flusher buffer on every submit
body: `submit` previously called `self.buffer.get_memory_info()` once; it now iterates `self.buffers.values()` and calls `get_memory_info()` on each of the N per-process buffers (plus `record_stored_segments()` on each). Since each `SpansBuffer` holds its own client, these calls duplicate the Redis INFO round trips N times per submitted message batch when `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage < 1.0`, scaling with `--flusher-processes`. If a given Redis node is reported by more than one buffer, both `used` and `available` are also counted multiple times. Consider keeping a single buffer in the parent for memory/stat reporting.

title: Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
body: Line 15 does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, so the newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` on line 62 ("Give flusher threads time to process after drift change") does nothing at all. The comment is misleading and the test still relies entirely on `step.join()` busy-looping for the flusher thread to produce the message, so it remains timing-dependent. Either drop the sleep/comment or use an unpatched sleep (e.g. capture the original `time.sleep` before monkeypatching) / poll until `messages` is non-empty.

title: New multiprocess flusher test only asserts bookkeeping, not behaviour
body: `test_flusher_processes_limit` submits no messages and only asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `max_processes`, `num_processes` and that the shard map totals 4. It does not assert that shards are partitioned without overlap (e.g. `{0,1,2,3}` exactly once across `process_to_shards_map`), nor that segments from all 4 shards are actually flushed/produced when more than one process is used. The core risk of this PR — multiple flushers each owning a disjoint shard subset and producing all segments exactly once — is untested. There is also no test for the unhealthy-process restart path that this PR rewrote.

title: isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is never true for spawn-context processes, so hung flushers are never killed
body: `self.mp_context = multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")` creates `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` instances, which subclass `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, *not* `multiprocessing.context.Process` (what `multiprocessing.Process` resolves to). Therefore the guard `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.kill()` in `_ensure_processes_alive` is always False and `kill()` is never executed. Consequences: (a) a process detected as hung (`cause == "hang"`, i.e. it is still alive but has not updated `healthy_since`) is left running while a replacement process is spawned for the *same* shards — two flushers then flush/produce the same shard set, risking duplicate and/or fragmented segments on `buffered-segments`; (b) dead processes are never reaped (no `kill`/`join`/`close`), leaving zombies; (c) the same broken check at line 346 in `join()` means `terminate()` is never called on shutdown. The intent was clearly to distinguish processes from threads — use `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)` (or `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`).

title: No validation of flusher process count; 0/negative values silently disable flushing
body: `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` followed by `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))` has two bad edge cases reachable from the new `--flusher-processes` CLI option: passing `0` falls through the `or` and silently means "one process per shard" (the opposite of what the help text 'Maximum number of processes ... Defaults to 1' implies), and passing a negative number yields `num_processes <= 0`, so `process_to_shards_map` is empty and **no flusher process is started at all**. In that case spans keep being written to Redis but no segments are ever flushed or produced, until Redis memory backpressure stalls the consumer. The same happens if `assigned_shards` is empty. Validate the option (require >= 1) and/or clamp `num_processes` to at least 1.

title: Metric tag contains the comma-joined list of all shards, causing high-cardinality tags (and a tag key typo)
body: `shard_tag = ",".join(map(str, shards))` is used as the value of the `shard` tag on `spans.buffer.flusher.produce`, `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` (emitted per segment) and `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce`. With the default `--flusher-processes 1`, a single process owns all assigned shards, so the tag value becomes e.g. `"0,1,2,...,63"` and differs per pod/partition assignment, producing a distinct time series per consumer instance — a cardinality explosion on a per-segment distribution metric, and it makes the previously untagged `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` unusable for simple aggregation. Additionally line 199 uses the tag key `shards` while lines 185/192 use `shard`, so the three metrics are not tagged consistently. Prefer emitting per-shard tags (or no shard tag) with a stable, low-cardinality value.

title: Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
body: Line 15 does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, which replaces the attribute on the `time` module itself. The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` at line 62, with the comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change', therefore does nothing at all. The test still depends on the flusher thread happening to flush before `step.join()` sets the stop flag, i.e. it is racy, and the comment misleads future readers into thinking a wait was added. Either don't patch `time.sleep` globally (e.g. patch it only in the flusher module) or wait on an actual condition (poll until `messages` is non-empty with a timeout).

title: New multi-process flusher test only asserts internal bookkeeping, not that all shards are flushed
body: `test_flusher_processes_limit` asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `max_processes`, `num_processes` and `sum(len(shards)) == 4`, then immediately joins without submitting any spans. It never verifies the behaviour the PR introduces: that spans landing on each of the 4 shards are actually flushed and produced by the two flusher workers, and that shards are partitioned without overlap (the `sum == 4` assertion would also pass for a duplicated mapping such as `{0: [0, 0], 1: [1, 1]}`, which would cause double-production). It also exercises only the thread path (`produce_to_pipe` is set), so the real spawn-process path with multiple workers remains untested. Add a test that writes spans for several shards, advances the drift, and asserts every segment is produced exactly once, plus an assertion that the union of `process_to_shards_map` values equals `assigned_shards` with no duplicates.

title: Dead method _create_process_for_shard is unused
body: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is never called anywhere after the refactor (restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` in `_ensure_processes_alive`). Leaving it in place is confusing — it suggests per-shard restart is supported, and if someone later calls it, it restarts the whole process group for the shard without resetting the restart counter bookkeeping that `_ensure_processes_alive` relies on. Remove it.

title: A new parent-side SpansBuffer (and Redis client) is created on every process restart and never released
body: `_create_process_for_shards` constructs `shard_buffer = SpansBuffer(shards)` in the parent process and stores it in `self.buffers[process_index]`, replacing the previous instance without closing it. Each restart (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per worker) therefore leaks the Redis client/connection pool of the discarded buffer in the consumer process. In addition, the parent now holds one buffer per worker group on top of the buffer passed in from the factory, so `submit()` performs N `record_stored_segments()`/`get_memory_info()` round trips per call instead of one. Consider reusing a single parent-side buffer for stats/memory checks and only creating per-shard buffers for the children.

title: isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is always False for spawn processes, so unhealthy flushers are never killed
body: `self.mp_context = multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")` creates processes of type `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`, which is *not* a subclass of `multiprocessing.Process` (that name resolves to `multiprocessing.context.Process` of the default context). Therefore the guard `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.kill()` never fires, and the previous unconditional `self.process.kill()` behaviour is lost. Consequence: when a flusher is declared unhealthy (hang or non-responsive), the old OS process is left running and `_create_process_for_shards()` immediately starts a second process for the *same* shards. Two processes then call `flush_segments()`/`done_flush_segments()` on the same Redis shards, which can produce duplicated segments to `buffered-segments` and leaks a process on every restart (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per shard group). The same wrong check is used in `join()` (line 346), so `terminate()` is also never called on shutdown. Use `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` (or `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`) instead.

title: No validation of flusher_processes; negative value raises KeyError, 0 silently means one process per shard
body: `--flusher-processes` is parsed as a plain int with no range validation and is used as `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` / `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))`. With `--flusher-processes 0`, `0 or N` evaluates to `N`, so the operator silently gets one process per assigned shard instead of the obvious interpretation. With a negative value, `range(self.num_processes)` is empty while `i % self.num_processes` still evaluates to 0, so the shard assignment loop raises `KeyError: 0` and the consumer crashes at startup with an opaque error. Validate the option (>= 1) in the click option or in `__init__`.

title: Inconsistent metric tag key and high-cardinality tag value for shard groups
body: The produce timer and segment size metrics are tagged `{"shard": shard_tag}` (lines 185, 195) while the wait_produce timer is tagged `{"shards": shard_tag}` (line 199) — two different tag keys for the same dimension, which will silently split dashboards/queries. Worse, `shard_tag` is a comma-joined list of all shards owned by the process (e.g. `"0,3,6"`), whose value depends on the Kafka partition assignment of each consumer instance and changes on every rebalance. `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` is emitted per segment, so this adds a per-assignment, unbounded-cardinality tag to a very high-volume metric. Use a single stable tag key and either omit the shard tag or emit one metric per concrete shard.

title: time.sleep(0.1) in test_basic is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
body: Line 15 does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, which replaces `time.sleep` globally for the duration of the test. The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` on line 62, whose comment claims to "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change", therefore returns immediately and provides no synchronisation at all. The test still races: if the flusher thread has not observed the new `current_drift` before `step.join()` sets `stopped`, `messages` stays empty and `(msg,) = messages` fails with a ValueError. Either use a real sleep (e.g. capture the original `time.sleep` before patching) or poll on `messages` with a timeout.

title: New flusher test asserts a tautology and never exercises the multiprocess path
body: `total_shards = sum(len(shards) for shards in flusher.process_to_shards_map.values()); assert total_shards == 4` is trivially satisfied by the construction loop and would still pass if a shard were assigned twice while another was dropped. The meaningful invariant — that the union of `process_to_shards_map` values equals the assigned shards exactly once each — is not checked. In addition, because `produce_to_pipe` is passed, `SpanFlusher` takes the `threading.Thread` branch, so the test does not cover the actual `SpawnProcess` path this PR introduces (process creation, pickling of the per-shard `SpansBuffer`, restart/kill logic), and the factory is never shut down (`fac.shutdown()` is not called).

title: Dead method _create_process_for_shard is unused and silently no-ops for unknown shards
body: `_create_process_for_shard(shard)` has no callers anywhere after the refactor (health checking now goes through `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`). It is also subtly unsafe: if the shard is not found in `process_to_shards_map` it silently does nothing. Leaving it in invites a future caller to use the wrong restart path; delete it.

title: Parent-side SpansBuffer per process is replaced on restart without closing the old one
body: `_create_process_for_shards()` constructs a new `SpansBuffer(shards)` in the parent process on every (re)start and stores it in `self.buffers[process_index]`, overwriting the previous instance. The parent uses these buffers for `record_stored_segments()` and `get_memory_info()`, so they hold live Redis connections; the overwritten buffer is never closed, so each flusher restart leaks the old buffer's Redis client(s) in the main consumer process until GC. Note also that the `buffer` argument passed to `SpanFlusher` is now used only for `assigned_shards` — the extra parent-side buffers duplicate the Redis clients already held by the span-writing buffer.

title: Docstring claims one process per shard and omits the new max_processes parameter
body: The class docstring now says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but the actual behaviour is `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` processes, and the `process-spans` consumer defaults `--flusher-processes` to 1, i.e. a single process handling all shards. The docstring's parameter list documents `topic` (which is not a parameter) and `produce_to_pipe`, but not the new `max_processes` argument or its `None` default (one process per shard). This will mislead operators tuning the flusher.

title: join() abandons remaining processes once the deadline expires
body: In `join()`, the per-process loop computes `remaining_time` only to `break` out of the whole loop when the deadline has passed. Processes later in the iteration order are then neither waited on nor terminated, so on a timed-out shutdown an arbitrary subset of flusher processes is left running (they are daemons, so they die only when the parent exits). The computed `remaining_time` is otherwise unused — the inner wait loop re-checks `deadline` instead, so the first process can consume the entire timeout. Terminate every process regardless of the deadline.

title: Queue pool is destroyed on strategy close, so the consumer silently drops every message after a rebalance
body: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` (and `terminate()`/`join()`) calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets `worker.shutdown = True` and calls `queue.shutdown()` on every queue. The `FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` (result_consumer.py:133) and reused for every `create_with_partitions()` call. Arroyo invokes `close()`/`join()` on the strategy whenever partitions are revoked and then builds a new strategy on the next assignment. After the first rebalance the factory hands the new strategy the already-shut-down pool: the worker threads are dead and `work_queue.put()` raises `queue.ShutDown`, which is swallowed by the broad `except Exception` in `submit()` (line 317) where the offset is then marked complete and committed. The result is that every subsequent message is committed without ever being processed – permanent, silent data loss after any rebalance or partition reassignment. The pool (and its workers) needs to be created per assignment, or `close()` must not destroy state owned by the factory.

title: OffsetTracker state is never reset between partition assignments
body: The `FixedQueuePool` (and therefore its single `OffsetTracker`) is created once per factory and shared across all `create_with_partitions()` calls. `OffsetTracker.last_committed` and `all_offsets` therefore survive partition revocation. If a partition is revoked and later reassigned at a lower offset (offset reset, another consumer having made less progress, topic re-creation), `get_committable_offsets()` computes `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)` and only reports an offset when `highest_committable > last_committed`, so no offset for that partition will ever be committed again and the consumer group silently stops advancing. In-flight work items belonging to the previous assignment also remain tracked and can be committed by the new strategy for partitions the consumer no longer owns.

title: Offsets are committed from a background thread, outside arroyo's single-threaded strategy contract
body: `_commit_loop` runs in its own daemon thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which is arroyo's `commit` callable wired to `StreamProcessor`/`KafkaConsumer`. Arroyo strategies are only ever called from the main consumer thread, and `KafkaConsumer.stage_offsets`/`commit_offsets` mutate consumer state (staged offsets, assignment/state checks) without locking. Committing from this thread races with `poll()`/rebalance callbacks on the main thread and can stage offsets for partitions that were just revoked, which arroyo rejects with `ConsumerError`, or corrupt the staged-offset bookkeeping. The exception is merely logged by the loop's `except Exception`, so the failure is invisible while offsets stop advancing.

title: Failed work items have their offsets committed, contradicting the documented at-least-once guarantee
body: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, any exception raised by `result_processor` is logged and the `finally` block still calls `offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)`, so the offset becomes committable. The same happens in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` (lines 317-325) when `grouping_fn` or the queue put fails. This makes processing at-most-once: a transient failure (DB blip, timeout) permanently drops the message, while the class docstring claims "No item is lost" and "Only commits offsets after successful processing". Either failures must block the commit / be routed to a DLQ, or the documented guarantee must be corrected.

title: Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure and memory can grow without limit
body: `queue.Queue()` is created with the default `maxsize=0` (unbounded) and `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`, so arroyo will keep feeding messages as fast as it can poll regardless of how far behind the workers are. The docstring of `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", which cannot happen. Each queued `WorkItem` additionally retains the full `Message[KafkaPayload]` (field `message`, never read anywhere), so a slow group pins both the decoded result and the raw Kafka payload in memory, and a backlogged consumer will OOM instead of applying backpressure.

title: Shutdown sets the worker stop flag before queue.shutdown(immediate=False), so queued items are discarded instead of drained
body: `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` first sets `worker.shutdown = True` for every worker and only then calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. Because the worker loop is `while not self.shutdown:`, each worker exits right after finishing the item it currently holds, so the "non-immediate" shutdown that is supposed to let queued items drain has no effect and all pending items are dropped. Combined with `close()` joining the commit thread before the pool shuts down, the final set of completed offsets may also never be committed, so a normal restart re-reads and re-processes more messages than necessary.

title: Worker threads can block forever on queue.get(); shutdown failures are swallowed and leak threads
body: `OrderedQueueWorker.run` uses a blocking `self.work_queue.get()` with no timeout, so the `self.shutdown` flag is only observed after an item arrives. Termination relies entirely on `queue.Queue.shutdown()` succeeding, but `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` wraps that call in `except Exception: logger.exception(...)` (line 239). If it raises for any reason (e.g. the method is unavailable on the running Python version), every idle worker stays blocked in `get()`, `worker.join(timeout=5.0)` is executed sequentially for each worker, and shutdown stalls for 5s × num_queues (100s with the default of 20) before leaking the threads. Using `get(timeout=...)` would make the stop flag effective.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts behaviour the implementation does not provide
body: The test makes the result processor raise and then asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, i.e. that a processing error prevents the offset from being committed. The implementation does the opposite: `OrderedQueueWorker.run` completes the offset in its `finally` block even when processing raises, so offsets 100 and 101 become committable. The assertion only holds because the polling loop breaks within ~0.3s while the commit thread ticks once per second; if the commit tick lands first the test fails. This test is both flaky and encodes a guarantee that does not exist – it should assert the real behaviour (or the behaviour should be fixed).

title: Commit assertions race with the 1-second commit loop and will flake
body: `test_offset_committing` and `test_handles_invalid_messages` wait for the first `commit_event` and then assert an exact final offset (104, resp. 101).
