The limit therefore only rejects a device's first request and is not actually enforced. Fix by evicting the key on error, or by setting the cache only after a successful store call.

title: Count-then-insert is not atomic; limit can be exceeded under concurrency
body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs `CountDevices` and then does a separate INSERT, with no transaction or lock. Concurrent first requests from new devices, or several Grafana instances sharing one DB, can all read `count < limit` and all insert. The configured limit can then be exceeded by an arbitrary amount.

title: rowsAffected==0 treated as limit reached; false positives on MySQL
body: `updateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` whenever `RowsAffected()` is 0. By default MySQL reports only rows whose values actually changed, not rows matched. `updated_at` has second precision, so an existing, already-counted device re-tagged within the same second with the same IP and user agent changes nothing and gets 0 rows. That device is then wrongly rejected as over the limit.

title: Device limit bypassed by omitting the device ID header
body: `TagDevice` returns nil when the `X-Grafana-Device-Id` header is missing, and it also returns nil when the IP cannot be parsed. In both cases anonymous authentication succeeds without any limit check. Any client can get unlimited anonymous access by not sending the header, so the limit is advisory at best.

title: Device tagging moved onto the synchronous auth path
body: Tagging used to run in a background goroutine with its own timeout and panic recovery. It now runs inline in `Authenticate`, using the request context. When a limit is configured, each new device costs an extra COUNT(*) query plus a write. Slow-DB latency, or a panic in this path, now directly affects every anonymous request. The previous panic protection was also removed.

title: Provider signature changes likely break wire DI
body: `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` now takes `db.DB` instead of `anonstore.AnonStore`. `ProvideAnonDBStore` now takes an extra `int64` that wire cannot supply. No wire set (wire.go / wireexts) is updated in this PR. If `ProvideAnonDBStore` is still registered as a provider there, wire generation fails. Otherwise the unused binding should be removed.

title: anonymousDeviceLimit inferred as type `undefined`
body: `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` has no type annotation, so TypeScript infers the class property type as `undefined`, not `number | undefined`. Consumers of `config.anonymousDeviceLimit` cannot use it as a number without casting. Declare it as `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;`.

title: No test that existing devices can still be updated at the limit
body: `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only checks that a new device is rejected once the limit is reached. No test checks that an already-registered device is still updated successfully at the limit, which is the `updateDevice` path. No test covers the authn client behaviour either, including repeat requests after a rejection.

title: Device cached before store call, so the device limit only blocks the first request
body: `tagDeviceUI` writes the device into `localCache` (line 87) before calling `CreateOrUpdateDevice`. When the store returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the key stays cached. For the next 29 minutes, every request from that device hits the cache and gets `nil` back. `Authenticate` then succeeds, so a device over the limit is rejected once and then let in. The device should only be cached after a successful store call, or the cache entry should be removed on error.

title: Non-atomic count-then-insert lets concurrent new devices exceed the limit
body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs `CountDevices` and then does the upsert in a separate statement, with no transaction or lock. Several new devices arriving at the same time can all read `count < deviceLimit` and all insert. The configured limit is therefore not enforced under concurrency, including across multiple Grafana instances.

title: Zero RowsAffected is treated as limit reached even for existing devices
body: `updateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` whenever `RowsAffected()` is 0. On MySQL, RowsAffected counts only rows actually changed by default. `updated_at` has second precision there, so updating an existing device with the same IP, user agent and second-truncated timestamp reports 0 rows. A legitimate, already-registered device would then be rejected as over the limit.

title: Device tagging moved from a background goroutine into the synchronous auth path
body: Before this change, `TagDevice` ran in a goroutine with its own timeout. Now it runs inline in `Authenticate` using the request context. A cache miss now adds a COUNT query plus an upsert to request latency when a limit is set (just the upsert otherwise), and slow DB calls directly block anonymous logins. A cancelled request context will also make tagging fail.

title: ProvideAnonDBStore signature change can break the wire dependency graph
body: `ProvideAnonDBStore` now takes a bare `int64`, and `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` builds the store itself instead of receiving `AnonStore`. If the wire provider sets still list `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` and the `AnonStore` binding, wire cannot satisfy the `int64` parameter and code generation or build fails. The wire files are not updated in this PR.

title: Tests miss key device-limit behaviours
body: The new test only checks that a second new device is rejected. Nothing checks that an existing device can still be updated once the limit is reached. Nothing covers the service or client path, where caching currently bypasses the limit. None of the bugs above would be caught.

title: New device_limit setting is undocumented and missing from default config
body: `[auth.anonymous] device_limit` is read in code, but this PR adds no entry to `conf/defaults.ini` or `sample.ini` and no documentation. Users have no way to discover the option or learn that 0 means unlimited.

title: Device limit bypassed: cache entry set before the limit check fails
body: `tagDeviceUI` writes the device key to `localCache` before calling `CreateOrUpdateDevice`. When the limit is reached, the first request from a new device gets `ErrDeviceLimitReached` and authentication is rejected, but the cache entry stays. For the next 29 minutes every request from that device hits the cache, `TagDevice` returns nil, and the client authenticates successfully. The limit only blocks one request per device per cache window. Set the cache entry only after the store call succeeds, or don't cache when the error is `ErrDeviceLimitReached`.

title: Count-then-insert is not atomic, so the limit can be exceeded
body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs `CountDevices` and then does a separate INSERT, with no transaction or lock around them. Concurrent first requests from different new devices can all see `count < deviceLimit` and all insert. The configured limit is therefore not enforced under concurrent load, including across multiple Grafana instances.

title: rowsAffected==0 wrongly reports limit reached for existing devices on MySQL
body: Once the limit is reached, `updateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` whenever the UPDATE affects 0 rows. By default MySQL reports affected rows as changed rows, not matched rows. If an already-registered device is updated with the same IP and user agent within the same second (DATETIME has second precision), nothing changes and 0 is returned. That legitimate device is then denied anonymous access. Check existence with a SELECT, or treat matched rows as success.

title: ProvideAnonDBStore now takes a bare int64, which breaks wire injection
body: `ProvideAnonDBStore` now requires an `int64` argument, and `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` no longer consumes `AnonStore`. If the wire provider sets still list `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` and bind `AnonStore`, wire generation fails because nothing provides `int64`. No wire.go changes are part of this PR. Remove the provider from the wire sets, or have it take `*setting.Cfg`.

title: Device tagging moved from async to the synchronous auth path
body: `TagDevice` used to run in a background goroutine with a timeout. It now runs inline in `Authenticate`. On every cache miss, the anonymous request now waits for DB writes, plus a full COUNT over `anon_device` when a limit is configured. This happens even when `device_limit` is 0 and enforcement isn't needed. Slow or locked DBs now directly add latency to, or stall, anonymous page loads.

title: Limit test doesn't verify existing devices still work at the limit
body: `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only checks that a new device is rejected. It never checks that the already-registered device can still be updated once the limit is reached, which is the core path through `updateDevice`. It also has no service-level test that rejection persists across repeated requests, which would have caught the cache bypass.

title: New `device_limit` setting is undocumented
body: `[auth.anonymous] device_limit` is read here, but it is not added to conf/defaults.ini, conf/sample.ini, or the docs. Operators have no way to discover the option, or to learn that 0 means unlimited.

title: Debug logging left at Error level, dumping full ID lists every batch
body: Each cleanup batch logs at Error level with the full slice of fetched IDs, the SQL condition and a nil error. This happens at lines 534/537 (by time), 554/557 (by count) and 576/579 (orphaned tags). With batch sizes up to tens of thousands, every batch writes huge log lines. Healthy runs will flood the logs and trigger error-based alerting. The final no-op batch also logs at Error level. These look like leftover debugging statements and should be removed or lowered to Debug without the ID list.

title: Cleanup interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The ticker for all cleanup jobs went from 10 minutes to 1 minute, while each run still has a 9-minute timeout. This affects snapshots, dashboard versions, images, invites, short URLs, query history and annotations. It is unrelated to the deadlock fix, is not mentioned in the PR description, and looks like a leftover local testing change. It multiplies DB load by 10x and makes contention with the annotation write path more likely, which works against the stated goal of reducing deadlocks. Revert it.

title: Quadratic string building when inlining IDs for SQLite
body: The SQLite inline path builds the ID list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` in a loop. Each iteration copies the whole accumulated string, so the cost is O(n^2). This path only runs when the batch size exceeds 999, i.e. for large batches such as the 32767 used in the test, so tens of thousands of IDs mean hundreds of MB of copying per batch. Use a strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt instead.

title: Placeholder path can exceed MySQL/Postgres bind-parameter limits for large batch sizes
body: On non-SQLite databases, each ID becomes a bound parameter. MySQL and Postgres cap prepared statements at 65535 parameters. If `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` is configured above that, the DELETE fails on every run and cleanup never progresses. The old subquery-based statement had no such limit. Either chunk the IDs or inline them for all dialects.

title: Debug logging left in at Error level, including full ID lists
body: Every cleanup batch logs at Error level: `Annotations to clean by time/count`, `cleaned annotations ...`, `Tags to clean`, `cleaned tags` (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579). Each message includes the full `ids` slice, which can hold up to `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` entries (tens of thousands), and the `err` value, which is always nil at the fetch log sites. The final batch of every loop logs an empty result at Error too. In production this floods logs with huge false error entries on every cleanup run and can trigger error-based alerting. These look like debugging leftovers and should be removed or moved to Debug level without the ID lists.

title: Cleanup interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The ticker driving all cleanup jobs changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This is unrelated to the PR's stated goal and is not mentioned in the description. It makes every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, short URLs, query history) run 10x more often, adding database load and more chances for lock contention, which is the problem this PR is trying to reduce. It also no longer fits the 9-minute per-run timeout in `clean()`, which was sized for a 10-minute interval. This looks like a testing leftover and should be reverted.

title: Bound-parameter path can exceed placeholder limits on MySQL/Postgres
body: Only SQLite falls back to inlining the IDs. On MySQL and Postgres, `deleteByIDs` always binds one placeholder per ID. Both databases cap a prepared statement at 65535 parameters. If an operator sets `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` above that limit, every cleanup batch fails, whereas the previous subquery-based statement had no parameter limit. Consider capping or chunking the IDs per statement, or inlining the integer IDs for all dialects.

title: Quadratic string building for inlined SQLite IDs
body: The loop at lines 610-612 runs `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` once per ID. Each iteration copies the whole accumulated string, so building the list is O(n²) in the number of IDs. With the large batch sizes this branch exists for (e.g. 32767, as in the new test), that means heavy allocation and CPU work on every batch. Use a `strings.Builder` or `strconv.AppendInt` into a single byte buffer instead.

title: Leftover debug logging at Error level dumps every ID batch
body: Every cleanup batch logs at Error level, both before and after the delete. Each entry includes the full `ids` slice, which can hold up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize entries (tens of thousands), plus the raw SQL condition. The `err` field is always nil at the point it is logged. The same happens at lines 537, 554, 557, 576 and 579. In production this floods logs with huge lines and raises false Error alerts on every run, even when nothing failed. These look like debugging leftovers and should be removed, or reduced to Debug level without the ID list.

title: Cleanup interval silently changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The ticker for the whole CleanUpService was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This change is unrelated to the deadlock fix and is not mentioned in the description. It makes every cleanup job run 10x more often across all instances: snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs and query history. That adds DB load and more chances for the very lock contention this PR tries to reduce. It also no longer matches the 9-minute per-run timeout, which was sized for a 10-minute interval. This looks like a debugging leftover and should be reverted.

title: Quadratic string building for inlined SQLite ID list
body: In the SQLite large-batch path, the IN list is built with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` in a loop. This copies the whole growing string on every iteration, so cost is O(n^2) in the batch size. For the batch sizes this path targets (e.g. 32767 IDs), that means hundreds of MB of copying per batch. Use a strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt into a byte slice instead, as is already done in getAccessControlFilter.

title: Placeholder path can exceed MySQL/Postgres bind-parameter limits
body: For non-SQLite databases, the delete always binds one placeholder per ID. Both MySQL and PostgreSQL cap prepared statements at 65535 parameters. With an AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize above that, every delete batch fails and cleanup never makes progress. The old single-statement subquery had no such limit. Either chunk the IDs, or use the inlined-integer approach for any batch above the dialect's limit.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and get canceled when the request returns
body: Each background goroutine builds its context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` from the incoming request context. The method returns as soon as the unified-storage write succeeds, and the apiserver then cancels the request context. That cancellation reaches the derived context, so the legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection is often aborted or never runs (same pattern at lines 110, 135, 163). Legacy storage silently drifts from unified storage, which defeats the stated 'safe measure'. Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` before applying the timeout.

title: Legacy write failures in background goroutines are never logged
body: The goroutines only record a duration metric with an error flag. The error itself is discarded in Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection. The old code logged legacy failures. Now a divergence between legacy and unified storage leaves no trace of which object failed or why.

title: Storage create failure recorded as a legacy duration
body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `recordStorageDuration`. Unified-storage failures are therefore reported as legacy failures. The same mistake is in Update at line 129.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection recorded as a storage duration
body: The background legacy DeleteCollection calls `d.recordStorageDuration` rather than `recordLegacyDuration`. Each delete-collection is counted twice as a storage operation and never as a legacy one, which skews both metric series.

title: Object name used as the metric 'kind' label in Delete
body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object name where the kind belongs. Every object name becomes a separate label value, causing unbounded Prometheus cardinality and wrong kind attribution. It should be `options.Kind`.

title: Delete puts the base logger in context instead of the enriched one
body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` stores the base logger rather than `log`. Downstream storage logs therefore lack the name, kind and method values, unlike the other methods.

title: Legacy update re-applies objInfo against legacy state instead of the unified result
body: The previous code wrapped the unified-storage result in `updateWrapper`, so legacy received exactly the object written to unified storage. Now the raw `objInfo` is replayed in a goroutine, and the update or patch is applied to whatever old object legacy holds. For PATCH/apply, or when the stores already differ, legacy ends up with different content than unified storage. Reusing `objInfo` concurrently after the request has finished is also unsafe.

title: Request object shared with a background goroutine while the handler keeps using it
body: `obj` and `options` are passed to `d.Legacy.Create` in a goroutine after the method has already returned `created`, which may be the same pointer or derived from `obj`. The apiserver goes on encoding or mutating the response while legacy storage reads or mutates the same object, which is a data race. The object should be deep-copied before handing it to the goroutine.

title: Unit tests never verify the async legacy write and race with it
body: The tests return right after the dual-writer call without waiting for the background goroutine, so nothing asserts that the legacy write happens. Legacy and storage mocks share a single `mock.Mock`, so expectations meant for one store satisfy calls to the other. For example, the 'unified store fails' Create case only fails because the legacy expectation for `failingObj` is matched by the storage call. A goroutine can also invoke the mock after the subtest finishes.

title: Mode 3 integration tests check legacy reads immediately after async writes
body: `doPlaylistTests` creates or updates through k8s and then immediately queries the legacy `/api/playlists` endpoints via `getFromBothAPIs` and the search check. In mode 3 the legacy write is asynchronous, so these assertions race the background goroutine. If the legacy endpoint reads legacy storage, the test will be flaky; if it reads unified storage, legacy consistency is not being tested at all.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled when the request returns
body: Each background goroutine builds its context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`, where `ctx` is the incoming request context. The handler returns right after starting the goroutine, and the apiserver then cancels that request context. The legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection calls will therefore often fail with `context canceled` before they finish, so legacy storage silently drifts out of sync. The same pattern is at lines 110, 135 and 163. The parent should be `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` so logger values are kept but cancellation is not.

title: Legacy write failures in background goroutines are never logged
body: The goroutines only record a duration metric with an error flag. They never log the error from the legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection call. The previous code logged legacy failures. Now a failed safety write to legacy storage leaves no diagnostic trace beyond a counter, which makes divergence between the two stores hard to investigate.

title: Storage create failure is recorded as a legacy metric
body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `recordStorageDuration`. Unified-storage errors are therefore reported as legacy errors, and storage error metrics are missing. Update has the same mistake at line 129.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection result recorded as storage metric
body: The background goroutine runs `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` but records the result with `d.recordStorageDuration`. Legacy latency and errors are attributed to unified storage, which skews both metric series.

title: Delete success metric uses object name as the kind label
body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` where every other call passes `options.Kind`. This produces wrong labels and unbounded label cardinality, since there is one series per object name.

title: Delete attaches the base logger to the context instead of the enriched one
body: Delete builds `log` with name, kind and method, but then calls `klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`. Downstream code that pulls the logger from the context loses those fields. Every other method uses `log` here.

title: Legacy update reapplies the raw objInfo instead of the result from unified storage
body: The old code wrapped the unified-storage result in `updateWrapper` so legacy received exactly the stored object. The new code passes the original `objInfo` to `Legacy.Update` asynchronously. `UpdatedObject` is then re-evaluated against legacy's own current object. For patch or apply requests this can produce a different result, and resourceVersion preconditions may fail. It also reuses a request-scoped `objInfo` after the request has completed.

title: Request object shared with background goroutine while the handler continues using it
body: `obj` (and `options`) are handed to a goroutine that calls `d.Legacy.Create`, while the apiserver keeps processing and serializing the response, which may reference the same object returned by storage. Legacy create implementations may mutate the object, for example by setting metadata. This creates a data race. A deep copy (`obj.DeepCopyObject()`) should be passed to the goroutine.

title: Mode 3 integration tests check legacy reads immediately after async writes, so they are racy
body: `doPlaylistTests` creates, updates and deletes through the k8s API, then immediately checks `/api/playlists` and `getFromBothAPIs` for matching legacy results. In mode 3 the legacy writes happen in a goroutine with no synchronization. These assertions can therefore run before legacy has been updated, making the new mode 3 file and unified test cases flaky.

title: Unit tests never verify the async legacy writes
body: The mode 3 Create, Update, Delete and DeleteCollection tests do not wait for the background goroutine and do not assert that the legacy store was called. Goroutines may also outlive the test. Legacy store and storage share one mock, so legacy calls silently match the storage expectations. Bugs in the legacy path, such as the context cancellation issue, go undetected.

title: Duplicated go.work.sum entry
body: The line `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod` is added again even though it already appears a few lines above. The go.work.sum changes look like unrelated local churn that should not be in this PR.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and get cancelled when the request ends
body: Each background legacy write (Create here, and likewise Update line 135, Delete line 110, DeleteCollection line 163) builds its context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`, where `ctx` is the incoming request context. The apiserver cancels that context as soon as the handler returns, which is right after the goroutine is started. The legacy write will therefore often fail with `context canceled` or never complete, so legacy storage silently drifts from unified storage. That defeats the stated 'safe measure'. Detach the context, e.g. `context.WithTimeoutCause(context.WithoutCancel(ctx), ...)`.

title: Legacy write errors in the background goroutines are never logged
body: The async goroutines in Create, Update, Delete and DeleteCollection only feed the error into a duration metric (an error boolean). They never log it or include the object, name or cause. The old code logged legacy failures. Now a failed legacy write leaves no trace in the logs, so divergence between the two stores is very hard to diagnose.

title: Storage failure is recorded as a legacy duration in Create
body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `recordStorageDuration`. The same mistake is in Update at line 129. As a result, unified-storage errors show up in the legacy-storage metrics and are missing from the storage error metrics, which makes the dashboards misleading.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection duration is recorded as a storage duration
body: The background goroutine times `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` but records it with `d.recordStorageDuration`. Legacy latency and errors are therefore counted as unified-storage metrics, and the legacy metric never sees delete-collection.

title: Delete records the object name as the metric 'kind' label
body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object name where every other call passes `options.Kind`. This puts per-object names into the kind label, producing unbounded Prometheus label cardinality and wrong kind attribution.

title: Delete stores the base logger in the context instead of the enriched one
body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` drops the `name`, `kind` and `method` values that were just added to `log`. Every other method uses `log`, so storage/legacy code that logs from the context during Delete loses that context.

title: Legacy Update re-applies the original objInfo instead of the object stored in unified storage
body: The previous implementation wrapped objInfo in `updateWrapper` with the object returned by Storage.Update, so legacy received the same final object. Now legacy gets the raw `objInfo` and computes the update against its own (possibly divergent) current state. Patches or apply operations can therefore produce a different result in legacy than in unified storage, or fail. This also re-invokes objInfo asynchronously after the request has completed.

title: Mode 3 tests share one mock for both stores and never verify the async legacy write
body: `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` are built on the same `mock.Mock`, so an expectation such as `Create` or `Delete` is satisfied by either store. The tests cannot tell which store was called, and in Delete/DeleteCollection they set up only storage expectations. The tests never wait for or assert the background legacy call, so the core mode-3 behavior (legacy is written asynchronously after unified storage) is untested. The goroutine may also still be calling the mock after the test returns. Case names like 'creating an object only in the unified store' do not reflect what is actually verified.

title: No re-check of the cache after taking the write lock
body:
`GetWebAssets` reads the cache under `RLock`, releases it, then takes the exclusive `Lock`. It never re-checks `entryPointAssetsCache` after acquiring that lock.

When the cache is empty (startup, or after a failed load), every concurrent caller that saw `nil` queues on the write lock. Each one then re-reads and re-parses `assets-manifest.json` in turn, even though the first one already filled the cache.

This redundant reload can also lose a good value. If a later goroutine's reload fails (e.g. a transient read error), it sets `entryPointAssetsCache = result` with `nil`. That overwrites the valid cache the first goroutine just stored, and the caller gets an error that a simple re-check would have avoided.

Fix: after `Lock()`, add `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }`. Alternatively, only assign the cache when `err == nil`.

title: No re-check of cache after acquiring write lock causes redundant manifest reloads
body:
The fast path reads `entryPointAssetsCache` under RLock and releases it. It then takes the write lock and unconditionally reloads, without checking the cache again.

At startup or after a cache miss, many concurrent requests can all see `nil`. Each one then queues on the write lock and re-reads and re-parses `assets-manifest.json` in turn, even though the first goroutine already populated the cache. If the CDN path is enabled, each would also issue an HTTP request.

Add a second check after `Lock()` (`if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }`), or use `sync.Once`/singleflight for the non-dev case.

title: Cache is not re-checked after taking the write lock, so concurrent callers each reload the manifest
body:
On a cold cache, several goroutines can see `ret == nil` under the read lock and then queue on `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()`. After acquiring the write lock, none of them re-checks `entryPointAssetsCache`. Each one in turn re-reads and re-parses `assets-manifest.json` (or would hit the CDN), even after the first goroutine has already filled the cache.

This disk or network I/O runs while holding the exclusive lock. Every other request, including ones that would hit the cache, is serialized behind it.

Fix: after `Lock()`, add the usual double-check, `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }`. Alternatively, use `sync.Once` or singleflight for the non-dev path.

title: Existing SQL parser/command tests will break against the stub DB
body: `TablesList` now goes through the stub `DB.RunCommands`, which always returns "not implemented". `TablesList` therefore always fails, and `NewSQLCommand` always returns the `sql-invalid-sql` BadRequest. The existing tests that assert parsed table names and successful SQL command creation (in `pkg/expr/sql` parser tests and `pkg/expr` SQL command tests) were not updated or skipped in this PR, so CI will fail. Those tests should be skipped or rewritten to assert the new disabled behaviour.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false; the feature flag is silently dead
body: `enableSqlExpressions` negates the `sqlExpressions` flag, then returns false in both branches. The flag lookup has no effect, and the function name suggests the flag still controls the feature. The `sqlExpressions` toggle is still registered and documented, so operators who enable it get "sqlExpressions is not implemented" with no hint that the flag was intentionally neutered. Replace this with a plain `return false` (or remove the check) plus a comment referencing CVE-2024-9264. Also mark the flag as deprecated or no-op in the registry and docs.

title: Dead DuckDB code path left in place, including SQL string building and logging of raw user SQL
body: `TablesList` still builds a hand-escaped `json_serialize_sql('%s')` command, which was the injection vector. On every call it now logs the full user SQL and the command at Error level, because the stub always fails. The variable is still named `duckDB`. Leaving the vulnerable command construction in place makes it easy to re-enable accidentally by swapping the DB implementation back. It also spams error logs on the `UnmarshalSQLCommand` path, which does not go through the reader's flag check. The function should return an error immediately.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false; the feature-flag check is dead code
body:
`enableSqlExpressions` reads `FlagSqlExpressions`, negates it, and then returns `false` on both branches. The flag lookup has no effect, and the function name and structure suggest the toggle still controls the feature when it does not.

This is easy to 'fix' later into `return true` while the backend is only a stub, or to misread during review. If the intent is a hard disable, replace it with an explicit constant (or remove the helper) and add a comment that SQL expressions are disabled for CVE-2024-9264 regardless of the flag.

title: Existing SQL expression tests will now fail against the stub DB
body:
`TablesList` now uses the stub `DB`, whose `RunCommands` always returns "not implemented". `sql.QueryFramesInto` also always errors.

Existing tests in `pkg/expr/sql` and `pkg/expr` (e.g. parser tests expecting table names, and SQL command tests calling `NewSQLCommand`/`Execute`) previously ran against DuckDB. They will now fail unless they are removed or skipped.

The PR changes no test files. Either CI breaks, or those tests should be updated to assert the disabled behaviour, for example that a SQL expression query is rejected.

title: Non-reader code paths report a misleading 'error reading SQL command' instead of 'disabled'
body:
`UnmarshalSQLCommand` is used by the legacy node-building path and does not go through `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery`. On that path, the SQL query reaches `NewSQLCommand`, where `sql.TablesList` fails with "not implemented".

The user then gets a 400 "error reading SQL command", which suggests their SQL is malformed rather than that the feature is disabled. The 'disabled' check should be applied centrally, e.g. in `NewSQLCommand`, so every entry point returns a clear, consistent error.

title: Error message 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' is inaccurate
body:
The feature is implemented but has been deliberately disabled for security reasons. The message will confuse users who enabled the `sqlExpressions` feature flag.

A message such as "SQL expressions are disabled" would be accurate. Returning a proper `errutil` BadRequest, consistent with the other SQL errors, would also help.

title: Existing SQL expression tests will fail against the stubbed DB
body: `TablesList` now always fails, because `NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands` returns "not implemented". `NewSQLCommand` therefore always returns a BadRequest error. Existing tests in `pkg/expr/sql` and `pkg/expr` (e.g. parser tests and SQL command tests) expect table extraction and SQL execution to work, and none of them are updated or skipped in this PR. CI will break, or those tests will silently stop meaningful coverage. They should be removed or skipped, and replaced with a test asserting that SQL expressions are rejected.

title: enableSqlExpressions has dead feature-flag logic and always returns false
body: The function reads `FlagSqlExpressions`, inverts it, and then returns `false` in both branches. The flag lookup has no effect, and the name and structure suggest the toggle still controls the feature. Since the flag still exists and is presumably documented, operators enabling `sqlExpressions` will be confused when it silently does nothing. Make the hard disable explicit, e.g. `return false` with a comment referencing CVE-2024-9264. Also consider deprecating the flag or updating its docs to say it is non-functional.

title: TotalDocs iterates cache map without lock while builds can now write it concurrently
body:
`BuildIndex` no longer holds `cacheMu` for its whole body; it now writes `b.cache[key]` under a short lock. `TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` without taking `cacheMu` at all.

In `searchSupport.init`, the watch goroutine is started (search.go:207) before `s.search.TotalDocs()` is called (search.go:216). `handleEvent` -> `getOrCreateIndex` -> `BuildIndex` can therefore write the map while `TotalDocs` is iterating it. Search requests can do the same once the server is up.

Concurrent map iteration and write is a fatal runtime error in Go and will crash the process. `TotalDocs` should take `cacheMu.RLock()`.

title: Removing the BuildIndex lock allows duplicate concurrent builds of the same key
body:
With the coarse lock gone, nothing stops two callers from building the same NamespacedResource at once. Callers include `getOrCreateIndex` from Search (including federated lookups) and from `handleEvent`, and the init workers. Each caller sees `GetIndex == nil` and calls `BuildIndex`.

For in-memory indexes, one fully built index silently replaces the other. Writes applied to the losing index by a concurrent watch event are lost, and the IndexTenants/IndexedKinds metrics are double counted.

For file-based indexes (`size > FileThreshold`), both callers run `bleve.New` on the same directory and the second fails. A per-key singleflight or lock is needed to keep the speedup without this race.

title: Init worker goroutines race on shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed`
body:
Inside `group.Go`, each goroutine assigns the outer `err` variable (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and increments `totalBatchesIndexed` with no synchronization. Both are data races.

This PR's goal is to make these builds actually run in parallel by removing the backend lock, which makes the races far more likely to bite. One goroutine's error can be overwritten by another, and the reported count is unreliable.

The goroutine should use a local `err` and an atomic counter.

title: Requests are no longer rejected after Stop
body:
`Stop` still sets `s.initErr` to "service is stopping" / "service is stopped". Previously every handler called `s.Init(ctx)`, which returned that `initErr`, so requests were rejected after shutdown.

This PR removes those `Init` calls from all handlers. After `Stop`, Create/Read/List/Watch/etc. now run against a stopped backend instead of returning a clean error. `initErr` is effectively dead after construction.

Either keep a cheap stopped/initErr check in the handlers or remove the now-meaningless assignments.

title: Context cancel leaked when Init fails in constructor
body:
`NewResourceServer` creates `ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)` and then returns `nil, err` if `s.Init(ctx)` fails, without calling `cancel`.

Any goroutines or watchers started during partial initialization keep running. For example, the search watch goroutine may already be started if only `initWatcher` failed. They are never cancelled.

`cancel()` should be called on the error path.

title: Postgres integration test skipped instead of fixed
body:
The storage-server module test is now skipped for postgres in CI. This likely follows from the behaviour change to eager initialization in the constructor, which is exactly what the test exercises.

Skipping it removes coverage for eager init against postgres, the scenario the PR description itself asks reviewers to worry about. It should be fixed, or the root cause should be documented.

title: No per-key guard against concurrent BuildIndex now that the global lock is removed
body:
`BuildIndex` used to run entirely under `cacheMu`. Now the lock is taken only to store the result. `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` does a check-then-build (`GetIndex` returns nil, then `build`), so two callers can build the same `NamespacedResource` concurrently. Typical callers are two `Search` requests, or a `Search` request racing the async `handleEvent` watcher. The consequences are:
- Duplicate full ListIterator scans.
- The second cache store silently replaces the first index, so writes made to the losing instance are lost.
- `IndexTenants` and `IndexedKinds` metrics are double-counted.
- For file-based indexes, `bleve.New` on the same directory fails because the path already exists.

The code needs per-key build deduplication, e.g. singleflight or a per-key mutex, rather than either one global lock or none.

title: TotalDocs iterates the cache map without holding cacheMu
body: `TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` with no lock. Builds can now run concurrently and write to the map under `cacheMu.Lock`, from `handleEvent` or `Search` triggering `getOrCreateIndex`. A concurrent map read/write is a data race and can crash with a fatal "concurrent map iteration and map write". Take `cacheMu.RLock()` while iterating.

title: Shared variables mutated from errgroup goroutines in init
body: Each goroutine in `init` assigns the outer `err` (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and increments `totalBatchesIndexed` without synchronization. Both are data races. The PR's goal is to raise indexing concurrency, which makes this more likely to trigger. Use a local `err` inside each goroutine and an atomic counter.

title: Stop no longer causes requests to be rejected
body: All per-request `s.Init(ctx)` checks were removed, but `Stop` still sets `s.initErr` to "service is stopping" / "service is stopped". That error used to be returned to callers via `Init` after stop. Now nothing reads it, so requests after `Stop` reach the backend after the watch context is cancelled and the backend's `Stop` has run, instead of failing cleanly. The `initErr` writes in `Stop` are dead code, and the shutdown contract has silently changed.

title: Context and lifecycle resources leaked when Init fails in the constructor
body: If `s.Init(ctx)` fails, `NewResourceServer` returns nil without calling `cancel()`. It also does not stop a lifecycle that may already have been initialized, such as the DB backend. The background context and any goroutines started during partial init, like the search watch poller, are leaked. Call `cancel()` (and `lifecycle.Stop` where appropriate) on the error path.

title: Integration test disabled for postgres without a tracked fix
body: The storage-server module test is now skipped on postgres, with the note "Works locally". This lands alongside a change that moves DB initialization and index building into server construction, which is exactly what this test exercises. Skipping it removes coverage that could catch startup regressions caused by this PR.

title: Removing the BuildIndex lock allows duplicate concurrent builds of the same index
body:
`BuildIndex` used to hold `cacheMu` for its whole body, which serialized index builds. Now the lock is only taken around the final cache assignment. `getOrCreateIndex` does an unlocked check-then-build (`GetIndex` returns nil, then `build`). Search requests and watch events (`handleEvent`) can therefore build the same NamespacedResource at the same time.

Consequences:
- For file-backed indexes, two `bleve.New` calls race on the same directory, and one fails or corrupts the other.
- For memory indexes, the last writer silently replaces the cached index. Watch-event writes that went to the discarded instance are lost.
- `IndexTenants` and `IndexedKinds` metrics are double-counted.

The lock needs to become per-key (e.g., singleflight or a per-key mutex), not just narrower.

title: TotalDocs iterates cache map without holding cacheMu
body: `TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` without taking `cacheMu`. Builds triggered by Search requests or watch events can write to the map at the same moment (line 138). This is a concurrent map read/write, which can crash the process with a fatal `concurrent map iteration and map write`. `TotalDocs` should take `RLock`.

title: Stop no longer prevents further requests from being served
body: Every handler used to call `s.Init(ctx)`. After `Stop` set `s.initErr` to "service is stopping" or "service is stopped", those calls returned that error and new requests were rejected. With the `Init` calls removed, nothing reads `initErr` anymore. After `Stop`, requests now go straight to a stopped backend whose lifecycle and poller have been cancelled. The result is undefined errors or hangs instead of a clean "service is stopped" error. Either add an explicit stopped check to the handlers or drop the now-dead `initErr` bookkeeping in `Stop`.

title: Constructor now blocks on full index build and fails hard on any index error
body:
`NewResourceServer` now runs lifecycle init and builds every search index synchronously, with no timeout, before returning. Any indexing error for a single namespace or resource (e.g., a document builder failure) now prevents the whole storage server from being constructed. Previously such an error only affected requests.

It also means every caller and test that constructs a server pays the full indexing cost at construction time. The description explicitly asks what lazy init callers might break, and this failure-mode change is not handled or tested.

title: Data race on shared err and counter in parallel init workers
body: Each errgroup goroutine assigns the outer `err` variable (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and increments `totalBatchesIndexed` without synchronization. The PR's goal is to raise effective build concurrency, which makes these races more likely to occur. As a result, the reported `namespaced_indexed` count is wrong and the race detector will flag this code. Use a local `err :=` and an `atomic.Int64` counter.

title: Integration test disabled for postgres instead of being fixed
body: The storage-server integration test is now skipped for postgres, in addition to the existing sqlite skip. This probably masks a regression from moving initialization into the constructor: the server now blocks on init before the metrics endpoint comes up within the 500ms sleep. Postgres coverage of the startup path is lost exactly when startup behavior changes.

title: Call to non-existent no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() breaks compilation
body: `UsernameForm.authenticate` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments. The only method with that name, defined in `UsernamePasswordForm`, is `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)`, and there is no no-arg overload. The services module will not compile. The check should probably be `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()` or call `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`.

title: Conditional passkeys UI now only rendered when a user is already set, disabling it for normal login
body: `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(user)` returns `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null`. Previously `authenticate()` filled webauthn data only when no user was selected, and `challenge(..., error, field)` did so only when `context.getUser() == null`. The PR's goal is to also show passkeys during re-authentication, when a user is set. Instead, the `user != null` condition drops the regular login case, where no user is set yet. On a fresh login page the passkey challenge, the conditional-UI attribute and the `webauth` form are no longer emitted, so discoverable-key auto login and the 'username webauthn' autocomplete break. The tests asserting `//form[@id='webauth']` on the initial page would fail. The user condition should be removed (or the method should return true regardless of user).

title: Call to non-existent no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() will not compile
body: `UsernameForm.authenticate` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments. The only method with that name, added in `UsernamePasswordForm` (line 160), takes a `UserModel` parameter. No zero-argument overload exists in the class hierarchy, so this is a compilation error and the services module will not build. It should probably be `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()`, or a dedicated no-arg helper.

title: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires user != null, so passkeys are dropped from the normal login page
body:
Previously the conditional-UI webauthn data was filled when no user was selected yet (the normal first-login case). The new helper returns true only when `user != null`. Both `authenticate` (line 115) and `challenge(context, error, field)` (line 137) now skip `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm` on the initial username/password page. They also skip it on error pages after a failed login, because `getUser` clears the context user before the error challenge.

Result: discoverable-passkey and conditional-UI login no longer work for regular (non re-authentication) logins. The new tests on initial login (e.g. `webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey`, `passwordLoginWithExternalKey`) expect the `webauth` form there. The fix was meant to also enable passkeys when a user is set, not only then; the `user != null` clause should be removed.

title: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires user != null, which drops passkeys from normal login
Call to non-existent no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() does not compile
body:
`UsernameForm.authenticate` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments. The only method added to the superclass `UsernamePasswordForm` is `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)`, and no zero-argument overload exists in the class hierarchy.

This is a compilation error, so the services module will not build. It needs to pass `context.getUser()` or a no-arg overload must be added.

title: Disabled-org wrapper on the original IDP skips needed login-cache invalidation
body:
`update()` gets `idpById` through `getById()`, which returns the organization-aware wrapper. That wrapper's `isEnabled()` returns false whenever the linked organization is disabled. So for an IDP of a disabled org, `getLoginPredicate().test(original)` is false even though the DB row (what the JPA `getForLogin` query uses) is enabled, and the IDP id is in the cached login list.

If an admin then sets hideOnLogin=true, linkOnly=true or BROKER_PUBLIC=false, the updated model also fails the predicate. The first early-return fires and the login caches are not invalidated. Only `isEnabled()` is re-checked when the cached list is read, so once the org is re-enabled the cached `ORG_ONLY`/`ALL` lists still contain an IDP that is hidden, link-only or non-public. It is then shown on the login page.

The predicate for the original state should be evaluated against the raw stored model (e.g. `idpDelegate.getById`), not the org-aware wrapper.

title: Test cleanup removes the literal alias "alias", so created IDPs are never cleaned up
body:
`getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` binds the cleanup to an IDP whose alias is literally "alias". It does not refer to the `idp-alias-N` providers created here. The same mistake is at line 425.

The 21 IDPs created by `testCacheIDPForLogin` therefore leak into later tests in the realm. That can skew counts and assertions in tests that run afterwards, such as the login-list sizes and `testCacheIDPByOrg`. Use the actual alias variable in the cleanup.

title: Update skips login-cache invalidation when the org-aware wrapper reports the IDP disabled
body:
`update()` passes `idpById` to `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate`. `idpById` comes from `getById()`, so it is wrapped by `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel`, and its `isEnabled()` returns false whenever the linked organization is disabled. The JPA `getForLogin` query does not look at organization state, so the cached login list can still contain this IDP's id.

Scenario:
1. The organization is disabled.
2. An admin sets `hideOnLogin=true` (or `linkOnly=true`) on one of its IDPs.
3. The original model fails the login predicate because the wrapper says disabled, and the updated model fails it because it is hidden. Both are false, so the method returns early and nothing is invalidated.
4. The organization is re-enabled. Organization updates do not invalidate the login keys.

The stale cached id is then resolved through `getById`. `OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean` only re-checks `isEnabled()`, so the hidden or link-only IDP appears on the login page.

Fix: evaluate the predicate against the stored model without the wrapper (e.g. `idpDelegate.getById`). Alternatively, invalidate whenever any `LoginFilter` field or `BROKER_PUBLIC` changes.

title: Cleanup registers removal of literal alias "alias" instead of created IDPs
body:
`getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` targets an IDP named "alias", not the `idp-alias-N` providers this test creates. The same mistake is repeated at line 425 for `idp-alias-20`.

None of the 21 created IDPs are cleaned up. They leak into the realm for subsequent tests, which can change IDP counts and login-page results in other tests and cause order-dependent failures. Use the actual alias variable in the cleanup.

title: Cleanup registers removal of literal alias "alias" instead of the created IDPs
body: The cleanup is registered as `testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove`, which targets an IDP whose alias is the literal string "alias". The IDPs the test actually creates (`idp-alias-0`..`idp-alias-20`) are never removed. The same mistake appears at line 425 and was copied from `testCacheIDPByOrg` (line 303). Leftover IDPs can make other tests in the class order-dependent, for example tests that count IDPs or check login caches. It should be `get("idp-alias-" + i)` and `get("idp-alias-20")`, with the loop variable captured in a final local.

title: remove() now always performs an extra uncached DB lookup
body: `idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)` is now called unconditionally before the delegate removal, even when the cached entry is available. Before this change the DB lookup only happened when the cache key was already invalidated. Every IDP removal now issues an extra JPA query, used only to decide on login-cache invalidation. The cached model, when present, could be used for the login predicate instead, falling back to the DB only when nothing is cached.

title: Ignored providers are still instantiated and mutate global JCA state
body:
`detectProvider` now iterates the whole `ServiceLoader` and sorts the results. That instantiates every `CryptoProvider` on the classpath, including the ones that end up ignored. These constructors have global side effects:
- `FIPS1402Provider` calls `Security.insertProviderAt` to put KeycloakFipsSecurityProvider, BCFIPS and BCJSSE at positions 1-3, and changes the ssl.KeyManagerFactory/TrustManagerFactory security properties.
- `DefaultCryptoProvider` registers BouncyCastle.

Before this change, having several providers on the classpath was a hard error, so the side effects could not go unnoticed. Now a provider that is 'ignored' (only reported in a debug log) can still reorder JVM security providers and TLS defaults. Ordering should be resolved without instantiating every provider, for example via `ServiceLoader.stream()` or a static order, or the side effects should be moved out of the constructors.

title: Equal-order providers now resolve silently and nondeterministically
body: `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return order 200. If two of them are on the classpath (e.g. FIPS plus default), selection depends on ServiceLoader iteration, which is effectively classpath order. Previously this case threw an `IllegalStateException`. Now it only logs at debug level. As a result, a deployment intended to run in FIPS mode could silently pick the non-FIPS provider. Keep failing when more than one provider shares the highest order, or give the providers distinct orders.

title: New abstract interface method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: `int order()` is added as an abstract method on the public SPI interface `CryptoProvider`. Any third-party or out-of-tree implementation (custom crypto providers, older keycloak-client copies) will fail to compile. Already-compiled implementations will hit `AbstractMethodError` when `detectProvider` calls `order()`. A `default` method returning a neutral value would preserve compatibility.

title: Test uses a P-256 key for ES384/ES512 and never verifies the re-encoded DER
body: The key pair is generated with the default EC size (P-256) and reused for ES384 and ES512. As a result, r and s are always about 32 bytes, and the 48- and 66-byte cases (including P-521 values with leading bytes) are never exercised. The test also only checks that DER -> RS -> DER -> RS round-trips to the same RS. It never checks that the produced DER is accepted by `Signature.verify`, or that it matches the existing BC implementation, so a symmetric encoding bug would pass. Use curve-appropriate keys (secp384r1, secp521r1) and verify the reconstructed DER signature.

title: Dead code: encoders created and discarded
body: Lines 114-115 create two `ASN1Encoder` instances, write the r and s integers into them, and then discard the results. The real encoding is done again on lines 117-121. These two lines do nothing except allocate, and they should be removed.

title: Equal-order providers are now picked silently instead of failing
body: Detection used to throw an IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath. It now sorts by `order()` and silently takes the first entry. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return 200, so the sort is stable and ties fall back to ServiceLoader/classpath order. The only notice is a debug log. If a FIPS deployment accidentally ships both the FIPS and default (non-FIPS BouncyCastle) providers, it can now quietly run on the non-FIPS provider. The old fail-fast guard should be kept for ties at the highest order, or the FIPS provider should be given a distinct higher order.

title: New abstract interface method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: `int order()` is added as an abstract method on the public `CryptoProvider` SPI. Any third-party or downstream implementation (custom crypto providers, the separate keycloak-client repository) will no longer compile. Already-compiled implementations will throw AbstractMethodError when `detectProvider` calls `CryptoProvider::order`. Declaring it as a `default` method returning a baseline value would keep compatibility.

title: Test uses one default-curve key for every algorithm and only checks self round-trip
body: A single key from `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` (JDK default curve: P-256 or P-384 depending on JDK version) is reused for ES256, ES384 and ES512. The test only asserts that DER→RS→DER→RS gives the same result as the first RS conversion. Because `integerToBytes` truncates or pads, a lossy conversion still passes: on a JDK whose default is P-384, ES256 truncates r/s to 32 bytes and both sides match. The test never checks that a converted DER signature still verifies with `Signature.verify`, never uses the curve that matches each algorithm, and never compares output against the BC-based provider. Encoding bugs would go undetected.

title: integerToBytes silently truncates values longer than the expected length
body: When `bytes.length > qLength`, the high-order bytes are dropped without any check. This is correct only when the extra byte is the 0x00 sign byte. For a malformed or mismatched-curve signature where r or s really exceeds `signLength/2` bytes, the method returns a corrupted value instead of throwing an IOException. That produces wrong JWS signatures or misleading verification results. It should reject the value when the dropped bytes are non-zero.

title: Dead code: ASN1 encoders created and discarded
body: Lines 114-115 build ASN1Encoder instances for r and s and throw the results away. The same encoding is done again in the return statement. This is leftover code that wastes allocations and should be removed.

title: Conflicting providers with equal order are now silently resolved instead of failing
body: Before this change, finding more than one CryptoProvider was a hard error. Now the list is sorted by `order()` and the first entry is used. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return 200. If two of them are on the classpath (for example FIPS and default/BC), the winner is whatever ServiceLoader returns first, because the sort is stable. Only a debug log records the ignored providers. A misconfigured deployment can therefore run non-FIPS crypto when FIPS was intended, with no visible error. Ties at the highest order should still raise an error, or these providers should get distinct orders.

title: Ignored providers are still instantiated, with global Security side effects
body: Sorting by `order()` requires ServiceLoader to instantiate every CryptoProvider on the classpath. The constructors have JVM-wide side effects: DefaultCryptoProvider calls `Security.addProvider(BC)`, and FIPS1402Provider inserts KeycloakFipsSecurityProvider, BCFIPS and BCJSSE at positions 1-3 and rewrites the ssl.*ManagerFactory security properties. These run even for providers that are then ignored. Previously this setup was rejected outright. Now the JVM security configuration is altered by providers that are not used. Expose order without instantiation (e.g. `ServiceLoader.stream()` with an annotation or static metadata), or keep ambiguous setups as an error.

title: New abstract interface method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: `int order()` is added as an abstract method on a public SPI interface. Any third-party or downstream CryptoProvider implementation, including the separately released keycloak-client repo this is meant to sync with, will fail to compile or throw AbstractMethodError at runtime. Making it a `default` method returning a baseline value would keep compatibility.

title: ES384/ES512 tests use a P-256 key, and the round trip is never checked against JCA
body: `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` generates a key on the default curve (P-256) for every test. ES384 and ES512 are therefore exercised with 32-byte r/s values, never with the 48- or 66-byte values those algorithms produce; the P-521 case, where values can have a leading 0x00 and exceed the length, is not covered. The test also only checks that DER->RS->DER->RS is self-consistent. It never verifies that the DER produced by `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` is accepted by `Signature.verify`, or that it equals the original JCA DER. An encoder bug that is symmetric with the decoder would pass. Initialize the generator with the matching curve and verify the re-encoded signature.

title: Dead encoder calls and no input length validation in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
body: Lines 114-115 build ASN1Encoder instances and discard them; this is leftover dead code. The method also never checks that `signature.length == signLength`. A malformed or truncated JWS signature surfaces as an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException rather than the declared IOException, which callers may not handle.

title: Client removal no longer cleans up V2 permissions; V1+V2 combination throws on delete
Possible NPE when the all-clients resource is not found
body:
`getResourceTypeResource` returns null in several cases, for example when `supportsAuthorizationSchema` is false because the realm has admin permissions disabled or the 'Clients' resource is missing. `root.realmResourceServer()` can still be non-null in that case.

The result is passed straight to `findByResource(server, resource)` and then used as `resource.getScopes()`. Any client permission check for a client without its own resource then throws a NullPointerException instead of returning false.

title: getClientsWithPermission returns wrong names / misses per-client resources
body:
Per-client resources are created in `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` via `resourceStore.create(...)` without setting a type. Only the 'Clients' type resource has type `Clients`.

As a result, `findByType(server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)` never finds individual client resources. It can only return the type resource itself, whose name is the literal string "Clients", not a client id.

Callers relying on `getClientsWithPermission` therefore get an empty set or a bogus id instead of the clients the admin is actually allowed to access.

title: All-clients VIEW short-circuits per-client deny permissions
body:
`canView(ClientModel)` returns true as soon as `canView()` is true. `canView()` checks the all-clients VIEW permission.

Because of this, a per-client permission that denies VIEW (NEGATIVE logic or a negative policy) on a specific client is never evaluated. The pattern of granting all and denying one, which is supported and tested for users (`testViewUserPermission`), does not work for clients and over-grants access.

title: getResourceName not extended for Clients resource type
body:
`getResourceName` only maps USERS resources to readable names. For the newly added CLIENTS type it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`.

Per-client resources are created with no display name and are named by the client internal UUID. The "Clients" all-resource is also not mapped to an "All clients" label.

Consumers such as the admin UI will show null or a UUID instead of the clientId.

title: Javadoc for void require* methods says 'Returns true'
body: The Javadoc for `requireView()` (line 95) and `requireViewClientScopes()` (line 100) says "Returns {@code true} if ...". Both methods are void and throw ForbiddenException on failure, as the other `require*` docs describe.

title: Tests leave state behind (roles, client name, client scopes) without cleanup
body:
These tests permanently mutate the shared managed realm and never register any cleanup:
- `testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient` creates the client roles 'myclient-role' and 'myclient-subRole' on myclient. The returned Responses are not closed or checked.
- `testManageOnlyOneClient` renames myclient/realmClient and moves default client scopes to optional.

Other tests, or reruns, may see altered state. For example, `getDefaultClientScopes().get(1)` may refer to a different scope, and role creation would return 409.

title: getClientsWithPermission returns the schema resource name instead of client ids and misses per-client resources
body:
`getClientsWithPermission` uses `findByType(server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)` and adds `resource.getName()` for each match.

Two problems follow:
- Per-client resources are created in `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` via `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, owner)`, which never sets a type. Only the "Clients" all-resource (created in `init` with `setType`) is ever found.
- When an all-clients permission is granted, the returned set contains the string "Clients" rather than any client id.

Callers that use this set to filter or list clients will either see nothing or get a bogus id. Per-client grants are never reflected.

title: Possible NPE when the all-clients resource is missing
body:
`AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource` can return null, for example when the schema is not supported for this resource server or the "Clients" resource was never created. Realms initialized before this PR added the Clients type would have no such resource.

The result is passed straight to `findByResource(server, resource)` and then `resource.getScopes()` without a null check. A permission check would then fail with a NullPointerException (500) instead of returning false.

title: Client removal no longer cleans up V2 per-client FGAP resources/permissions
body:
The removal listener is now gated on the V1 `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` feature. Nothing replaces it for V2.

When a client that has a per-client resource in the admin-permissions client is deleted, that resource and its scope permissions stay behind as orphans referencing a non-existent client id. They also keep showing up in permission listings.

If both features were enabled at once, `management()` would return `MgmtPermissionsV2`, whose `clients().setPermissionsEnabled` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. That would break client deletion.

title: getResourceName not extended for Clients resource type
body:
`getResourceName` only maps the Users type to a human-readable name. For the new Clients type it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`.

Per-client resources are created without a display name, so the admin API and console will show null or a raw internal UUID instead of the clientId. The all-clients resource will not get a friendly label like "All clients" either.

title: Javadoc for void require* methods says 'Returns true'
body: The new Javadoc on `requireView()` (line 96) and `requireViewClientScopes()` (line 101) says "Returns {@code true} if ...". These methods return void. They should say they throw `ForbiddenException` when the corresponding `can*` check returns false.

title: getClientsWithPermission returns "Clients" instead of client IDs and skips per-client permissions
body:
`getClientsWithPermission` iterates `resourceStore.findByType(server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)` and adds each `resource.getName()` to the result.

The only resource with type `Clients` is the schema's all-clients resource, whose name is the literal string "Clients". Per-client resources are created in `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` via `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, owner)` with no type set.

Consequences:
- Callers that expect a set of client IDs receive "Clients" when an all-clients permission is granted.
- Clients granted through individual per-client permissions are never returned.
- Any list filtering based on this method is wrong.

title: Possible NPE when the all-clients resource cannot be resolved
body:
When no per-client resource exists, the code falls back to `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...)`. That method returns null in several cases: when the schema is not supported for the realm (admin permissions disabled), when the type is unknown, or when the resource is missing.

The result is passed straight to `getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource)` and then dereferenced via `resource.getScopes()` without a null check. A null here produces an NPE, and the admin request fails with a 500 instead of a simple deny.

The sibling `hasPermission(String)` does null-check its resource; this path should too.

title: Client removal listener can throw UnsupportedOperationException under V2
body:
The listener is now gated on `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` (V1), but `management()` returns `MgmtPermissionsV2` whenever `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` is enabled.

`ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. If both features are enabled, every `ClientRemovedEvent` triggers that exception, which can make client deletion fail.

The gate should either check that V2 is not active, or V2 should implement or no-op cleanup.

title: Dead code and unused imports in new class
body:
`getEvaluationContext` is a private method that is never called. The `logger` field and the imports `TOKEN_EXCHANGE`, `Scope` and `Collections`-adjacent helpers are also unused.

`canExchangeTo` throws, so this token-exchange context code is leftover copy-paste. It should be removed to avoid confusion.

title: getResourceName not updated for Clients resource type
body:
`getResourceName` only maps the Users type to a human-readable name: "All users" or the username.

For the newly added Clients type it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`. For per-client resources that is null or the internal UUID, so permissions on clients will display UUIDs rather than clientId or "All clients".

title: Javadoc on void require* methods says "Returns true"
body:
The Javadoc for `requireView()` and `requireViewClientScopes()` says "Returns {@code true} if ...", but both methods are void.

They actually throw `ForbiddenException` when the corresponding `can*` check fails. The text should read like the other `require*` docs: "Throws ForbiddenException if ... returns false".

title: Created roles not cleaned up and responses not closed
body:
`testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient` creates client roles `myclient-role` and `myclient-subRole` with `roles().create(...)`. The returned Response is never closed, and no cleanup is registered via `realm.cleanup()`.

The roles leak into the shared managed realm, which can break re-runs or other tests that create roles with the same names (409 conflict).

title: Exit code 4 changes meaning from 'recreate needed' to 'feature disabled'
body:
`RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE` moves from 4 to 3, and the new `FEATURE_DISABLED` takes over 4. Any script or pipeline written against the previous behavior treats exit 4 as "rolling upgrade not possible, do a recreate". After this change, those scripts will:

- read a missing-feature configuration error (4) as a legitimate recreate decision;
- not recognise the new recreate code (3).

Reusing a code with a different meaning silently breaks existing consumers instead of failing loudly. Either use a previously unused code for `FEATURE_DISABLED` or clearly call out the exit-code change in the release/migration notes.

title: Feature-disabled test checks neither exit code nor the `check` subcommand
body: `testFeatureNotEnabled` only runs the `metadata` subcommand and only asserts the error message. It never verifies that the process exits with the documented `FEATURE_DISABLED` code (4). It also never exercises the identical guard added to `UpdateCompatibilityCheck`. A regression in the exit code (the very contract the docs tell scripts to rely on) or in the `check` guard would go unnoticed.

title: Appending --features=rolling-updates to the documented command can silently override the user's feature configuration
body:
The `updatecompatibility` macro now appends `--features=rolling-updates` to every documented `update-compatibility` invocation. A CLI `--features` value takes precedence over `KC_FEATURES` or a `features=` entry in keycloak.conf.

A user who already enables other features would copy this command and replace their feature list with only `rolling-updates`. The `metadata` and `check` commands would then capture or compare a configuration that differs from the real deployment. The guide itself warns that omitted configuration leads to incorrect results.

The docs should tell users to add `rolling-updates` to their existing feature list rather than hardcoding the flag.

title: Docs claim the Operator fails if rolling-updates is not enabled, but this PR adds no such check
body:
The new CAUTION block says that if the `rolling-updates` feature is not enabled, "the {project_name} Operator will fail." No operator code in this PR checks the feature or fails on it.

The example also enables the feature through the Keycloak CR `features` list, which configures the server and not the Operator. The test `UpgradeTest` only enables the feature when a strategy is set.

As written, the statement misleads users about what happens. Either the Operator should validate `spec.update` against the enabled features, or the text should describe the actual behavior.

title: Exit code 4 is repurposed from 'recreate upgrade' to 'feature disabled'
body:
`RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE` changes from 4 to 3, and 4 now means `FEATURE_DISABLED`. Any script or automation written against the previous behavior that treats exit code 4 as "recreate required" will now get that meaning for a different condition.

The new value does align with the docs table, but the renumbering should be called out, for example in release or upgrade notes.

title: Feature-disabled path tested only for 'metadata' and without checking the exit code
body: `testFeatureNotEnabled` only runs the `metadata` subcommand and only asserts the error message. It does not check that the exit code is `FEATURE_DISABLED` (4), which is the documented, scriptable contract. The `check` subcommand's feature-disabled branch is not tested at all.

title: Recreate exit code silently changed from 4 to 3, and 4 now means something else
body: `RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE` changes from 4 to 3, and 4 is reused as `FEATURE_DISABLED`. Scripts or pipelines written against the previous release treat exit code 4 as "recreate upgrade required". After this change they will read 4 as recreate when the real cause is that the feature was not enabled. They will also no longer recognise the actual recreate signal (3). Reusing a code that previously had another meaning makes the mismatch silent instead of failing loudly. Either keep 4 for recreate and pick a new code for feature-disabled, or call out the change explicitly in the release and upgrade notes.

title: Feature-disabled test checks neither the exit code nor the `check` subcommand
body: `testFeatureNotEnabled` only asserts the error message for the `metadata` subcommand. It does not assert the new documented exit code 4 (`CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED`). It also does not exercise the same guard in `UpdateCompatibilityCheck`, which is the command whose exit code scripts rely on. A regression in either the exit code or the `check` guard would go unnoticed.

title: Exit code 4 is described as "Rolling Upgrade is not possible"
body: The table describes exit code 4 as "Rolling Upgrade is not possible". In reality no compatibility check is performed: the command exits immediately because the feature is not enabled. Automation that maps every non-zero, non-error code to "recreate" will choose an unnecessary downtime upgrade because of this wording. The entry should say this is a usage/configuration error and that no compatibility decision was made.

title: Test overwrites any enabled features from the base test deployment
body: `setEnabledFeatures(List.of(...))` replaces whatever features `getTestKeycloakDeployment` may already have enabled instead of appending `rolling-updates`. If the base deployment enables features (now or later), the RECREATE variant of this test silently runs with a different feature set than the null-strategy variant.

title: canManage() is granted by VIEW permission on all groups
body: `canManage()` falls back to `hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE)`. An admin who only holds the VIEW scope on the all-groups resource therefore passes `canManage()`. That check guards top-level group creation and moving groups (`GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup` → `requireManage()`), and it is also reached through `canView(group)`-style checks in the parent class. This is a privilege escalation from view to manage. It should check only `AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE`.

title: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses resource ids and the wrong type lookup
body:
In V2, per-group resources are created by `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource`. Their name is the group id and no type is set, so `findByType(server, "Groups")` only returns the all-groups resource named "Groups".

The callback then does `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...)`, which looks the resource up by name using its id. That lookup always misses and falls back to the all-groups resource. It then adds `groupResource.getId()`, a resource id rather than a group id, to the result.

Consequences:
- Groups with individual VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions are never enumerated.
