title: Hostnames compared case-sensitively
body: URI#host preserves the case of the input, so a website like `http://Example.com/user` will not match a Discourse host of `example.com`. Both hosts should be downcased before comparison.

title: Light-theme lightness changed from 30% to 70% for embedded post author links
body: The original rule was scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%). The new light branch uses 70%, which changes the existing light-theme color and makes embedded post usernames much fainter. Every other conversion in this PR keeps the light value and uses (100 - x) for the dark one, so this should be (30%, 70%).

title: Light-theme value inverted for .custom-message-length
body: The original rule was scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%). The new code uses 30% for the light branch, so the hint text becomes noticeably darker on light themes. The desktop version of this rule correctly uses (70%, 30%); the mobile one should match.

title: Topic map h3 lightness changed from 20% to 50%
body: The original rule was scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%). The new code uses 50% for light and 50% for dark, which visibly lightens mobile topic-map headings on light themes. The desktop equivalent correctly uses (20%, 80%), so this should match.

title: group-member-info .name lightness changed from 30% to 50%
body: The original rule was scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%). The new light branch uses 50%, which changes the existing light-theme appearance. It should be (30%, 70%) to preserve current behavior.

title: group-member-info .name lightness changed from 30% to 50%
body: Same issue as on desktop: the original rule used 30% lightness, but the light branch is now 50%. This changes the light-theme color and should be (30%, 70%).

The pattern used elsewhere in the PR would give `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 70%))`. The dark branch uses 30% instead of the complementary 70%. The two values appear swapped; the expected form is dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 70%)).

The expected form is dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 80%)).

title: create ignores alias_level
body: The client's asJSON sends alias_level, and update applies it, but create only sets name and visible. A group created with a non-default alias level silently gets the default instead.

title: totalPages off by one when count is a multiple of limit
body: totalPages uses Math.floor(user_count/limit)+1, so 50 users with limit 50 gives 2 pages. The Next button stays enabled and leads to an empty page. It should use Math.ceil(user_count/limit).

title: Unbounded limit on public members endpoint
body: The limit parameter is user-controlled with no cap. A request such as limit=1000000 on a large automatic group serializes every user, which is a cheap DoS vector. Clamp it to a sane maximum, and also guard against negative or zero values.

title: Breaking change to members.json response format
body: /groups/:id/members.json used to return an array and now returns an object with members and meta keys. Any other consumers that expect the old array shape will break, such as the user-selector, plugins, or API clients.

title: automatic not in scope of item view
body: Inside the each itemView, the template's context is the view, not the group. The `automatic` binding there likely does not resolve to the group's automatic flag, so the remove link may be shown for automatic groups. Clicking it would only produce a 422 error.

title: remove_member automatic test uses wrong HTTP verb
body: The test calls `xhr :put, :remove_member`, but the route is DELETE. Controller specs bypass routing, so the test passes without exercising the real route.

title: addMembers errors unhandled and input not cleared
body: addMembers has no error handler, so a 422 response (for example on an automatic group) fails silently. The usernames field is also never reset after adding, as the TODO in the code notes.

title: totalPages off by one when user_count is a multiple of limit
body: totalPages is computed as floor(user_count/limit)+1. When user_count is an exact multiple of limit (e.g. 50 users, limit 50), this yields 2 pages instead of 1. The page indicator is then wrong, showingLast stays false on the real last page, and 'next' navigates to an empty page. Use Math.ceil(user_count/limit).

title: create ignores alias_level
body: The client sends alias_level in asJSON, but create only sets name and visible. Any alias level the admin picks when creating a group is silently discarded.

title: Unbounded limit on public members endpoint
body: limit comes straight from params with no cap. Any user who can see the group can request limit=1000000 and load every member in a single query. Negative values are also passed through unchecked. Clamp limit to a sane range, e.g. 1..200.

title: Stale pagination offset when revisiting a group
body: Group models are cached in the adminGroups list, so offset persists between visits. Returning to a group can show a later page rather than page 1. findMembers also clamps offset against the old user_count, which may be out of date.

title: automatic not resolvable in item view context
body: Inside the `each ... itemView` item view, `automatic` is looked up on the item context rather than the group. It may be undefined, so remove links can appear for automatic groups. Clicking one fails with a 422 from the server.

title: remove_member automatic test uses wrong verb
body: The 'cannot remove members from automatic groups' test sends PUT, but the route for remove_member is DELETE. The test therefore does not exercise the actual routed request.

title: No error handling for add/remove member
body: The promises returned by addMembers and removeMember have no rejection handler. A failure such as a 422 is not reported to the admin, and the usernames input is never cleared after a successful add.

title: create ignores alias_level
body: The client sends `alias_level` in `asJSON` when creating a group, but `create` never assigns `params[:alias_level]`. Any alias level chosen when creating a new group is silently dropped and the group gets the default.

title: totalPages off by one when count is a multiple of limit
body: `totalPages` is computed as `floor(user_count/limit)+1`, so 50 members with a limit of 50 shows 2 pages. Because `showingLast` compares `currentPage` with this inflated total, the next button stays enabled on the last real page. Clicking it sets offset to `user_count` and fetches an empty member list. Use `Math.ceil(user_count/limit)`.

title: Unbounded limit on public members endpoint
body: The public `members` endpoint takes `limit` straight from the request with no maximum. Any user can request e.g. `limit=1000000` on a large automatic group and force a huge query and serialization. Negative `limit`/`offset` values are not rejected either. Clamp both values to a sane range.

title: findMembers returns undefined instead of a promise
body: When the group name is empty, `findMembers` now returns `undefined` instead of a resolved promise. The `next`/`previous` actions return its result, so any caller that chains `.then()` on it will throw.

title: `automatic` not resolved in item view context
body: Inside the `each ... itemView` the template context is the item view, so `automatic` likely does not resolve to the group's property. The remove link may then be shown for automatic groups; the server rejects the request with a 422, so the user sees a broken action.

title: remove_member bypasses group.remove
body: `remove_member` calls `group.users.delete(user_id)` with a raw id instead of the existing `group.remove(user)` API used elsewhere. Removing by integer id on a has_many through association is unreliable, and any callbacks or side effects in `group.remove` are skipped.

title: Test uses wrong HTTP verb
body: The test "cannot remove members from automatic groups" sends `xhr :put` to `remove_member`, but the route is DELETE. It therefore does not exercise the real routed request.

title: addMembers has no error handling and doesn't clear input
body: `addMembers` has no failure handler, so failed additions (e.g. the 422 for automatic groups) fail silently with no message to the admin. The username input is also never cleared after a successful add (noted by the TODO), so it can be resubmitted by accident.

title: Fallback chain built from SiteSetting at runtime; loaded fallback locales only ensured in controllers
body: FallbackLocaleList#[] reads SiteSetting.default_locale on every lookup. Fallback locales are only loaded by ensure_loaded!, and that is called only from ApplicationController#set_locale. In jobs, mailers, and rake tasks, I18n.translate loads only config.locale, so a missing key falls back to a locale that was never loaded and returns 'translation missing'. Load the fallback locales inside I18n.translate / load_locale instead of relying on the controller.

title: Translation cache key ignores the fallback chain
body: The LRU cache key is key + locale + backend id. The fallback chain depends on SiteSetting.default_locale, which can change at runtime or differ per site in multisite. A cached fallback result, or a cached 'missing' result computed before the fallback locale was loaded, keeps being served afterwards. Users can get stale or wrong-language strings until the cache is evicted.

title: Hash subclass only overrides [] for fallbacks
body: I18n::Backend::Fallbacks calls I18n.fallbacks[locale], which works here. Other code (e.g. Rails' I18n railtie or gems) may call fetch, defaults=, or expect an I18n::Locale::Fallbacks instance. A plain Hash subclass returns nil or empty results from those calls, which can break lookups in subtle ways.

title: Fallback locales are never loaded outside controller requests
body: The I18n patch loads locales lazily, and `translate` only loads `config.locale`. The fallback locales (the site default and `:en`) are loaded only by `ensure_loaded!`, which is called only from `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Jobs, mailers, rake tasks and console code that call `I18n.t` never load those locales, so lookups that should fall back still return 'translation missing'.

title: Translation cache can store a missing result before fallbacks are loaded
body: The LRU cache key combines the translation key, the locale and the backend object id. If a translation is requested before its fallback locale has been loaded, the 'missing' result is cached. It is then served from the cache even after the fallback locale loads. Changing the `default_locale` setting also leaves stale fallback results in the cache.

title: Fallback lookup does not normalize the locale argument
body: `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq` does not convert `locale` to a symbol. If it is passed as a string, e.g. 'en', the list contains both 'en' and :en and is not deduplicated. That locale is then loaded and looked up twice, which can also pollute `@loaded_locales`.

title: Fallbacks module is included into whatever backend class is current
body: `I18n.backend.class.send(:include, ...)` depends on which backend is active when the initializer runs. The pluralization line above targets `Simple` explicitly. If a plugin or a later initializer swaps the backend, fallbacks silently stop applying.

title: No tests for the new fallback behaviour
body: The PR adds no specs covering the fallback order (user locale, then site locale, then English) or the loading of fallback locales.

title: Translation cache key ignores the fallback chain, which depends on site default locale
body: Cached translations are keyed only by key, locale and backend. With fallbacks, the result for a missing key now depends on SiteSetting.default_locale. When the default locale changes, or differs between multisite sites in the same process, the LRU cache keeps serving stale or wrong-site fallback strings.

title: Fallback locales are not loaded outside controller requests
body: translate only loads config.locale. The fallback locales are loaded only by I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! in ApplicationController#set_locale. Jobs, mailers, rake tasks and any other non-controller code never load the site-default or :en translations. In those contexts, fallback lookups to unloaded locales return 'translation missing'.

title: Fallback list may contain a locale string alongside its symbol
body: The current locale is passed through unchanged while the site default is converted to a symbol. If the locale arrives as a string (for example 'en'), uniq does not collapse it with :en. The same locale is then looked up twice, and ensure_loaded! tracks both forms.

title: Denial cache defeats the newly-created-resource fix
body: When a check is denied, the result is cached for 30s under (user, action, name, parent). If a user checks a resource before its permission is written, as happens in the create flow, every later check for that resource returns deny from this cache without querying the DB. The resource only becomes accessible once the entry expires, which is the stale-access problem this PR is meant to fix. Nothing ever invalidates the cache when permissions change.

title: Denial cache key is ambiguous and keyed on raw subject UID
body: The key is built by joining fields with '_', and names, folder UIDs and actions can themselves contain '_'. Two different requests can therefore produce the same key and wrongly share a cached denial. The key also uses the raw request subject, which may be a numeric ID or a UID, so it is inconsistent with the normalized UID used for permCache keys. In addition, the key omits identity type, so for anonymous subjects it uses the subject ID rather than the anonymous namespace key.

title: Cache usage metric double-counted / misreported
body: A cached-permission miss records cache usage 'false' at line 137. On a denial-cache hit, line 118 records 'true' but nothing records the permission-cache lookup. As a result, the cache hit-rate metric is skewed.

title: Deny-cache test doesn't prove precedence
body: The test seeds permCache with dashboards:uid:dash1 set to false, so the cached-permission path would deny anyway. The fallback path would also deny because the fake store has no permissions. The test therefore passes even without the denial cache and does not verify the behavior its comment claims.

title: Denial cache defeats the newly-created-resource fix and blocks grants for 30s
body: When a check is denied, Check writes a denial entry for (user, action, name, folder) with a 30s TTL, and every later Check returns deny from that entry before looking at permissions. Nothing invalidates the entry when permissions change. A user who checks a resource just before its permission row is visible (for example, a creator racing dashboard creation), or before being granted access, stays denied for up to 30s. This brings back the exact problem the PR is meant to fix.

title: Denial key uses raw subject UID and ambiguous concatenation
body: The denial key is built from checkReq.UserUID, the raw subject string, which can be a numeric ID or a UID. The permission cache instead uses the resolved userIdentifiers.UID, so the two caches key the same user differently. The key also omits the identity type, so a user and an anonymous or service-account identity with the same ID would share denial entries. Finally, name and parent are joined with '_', which also appears in names, so different (name, parent) pairs can produce the same key. Any of these collisions can deny the wrong subject or resource.

title: Every cached deny now triggers a DB query, cache hits double-counted
body: When cached permissions deny a request, Check falls through to getIdentityPermissions, which now always queries the DB. The singleflight cache-check was removed from it. So every first-time denied check hits the database. When the denial cache returns, permissionCacheUsage is incremented with the label "true". On the fallthrough path, the "false" label is incremented even when the cache was actually hit. Both make the cache metrics misleading.

title: Denial test does not prove the cache bypass
body: This test is meant to show that the denial cache short-circuits the permission check. However, it sets the permission cache to map{dash1: false}, which would deny the request anyway. The test therefore passes whether or not the denial cache works. It should set dash1 to true so that only the denial cache can explain the deny.

title: Denial cache defeats the purpose of fresh requery for newly created resources
body: When the DB requery still returns no grant, a denial is cached for 30s. Permissions for a newly created dashboard or folder can be written after the first Check, for example when the frontend checks before the creator's grant is persisted. In that case every later Check short-circuits on the denial key and never reaches the DB. The creator stays locked out for up to the TTL, which is the bug this PR is meant to fix. Nothing invalidates the denial key when permissions change.

title: Denial cache key collides with permission cache key namespace
body: `userPermDenialCacheKey` builds keys with the same `ns.perm_<uid>_<action>` prefix as `userPermCacheKey` and joins parts with `_`. UIDs and folder names can themselves contain `_`, so different (name, parent) pairs can produce the same key. A denial for one resource can then be applied to another. The two typed caches also share one store, and a key from one can be read by the other and fail to unmarshal. Use a distinct prefix and an unambiguous separator.

title: Denial key uses raw subject UID, not resolved identifier; anonymous/renderer share keys
body: The denial key is built from `checkReq.UserUID` as supplied, which may be a numeric ID or a UID, so one user gets inconsistent keys. Every anonymous subject also maps to one key. The renderer path's denials are cached as well, even though they are static. The permission cache uses the resolved `userIdentifiers.UID`, so the denial cache keys should match it.

title: Cached-permission miss always triggers full DB refetch, including for genuinely denied requests on fresh entries
body: Any cached negative result now bypasses the cache and queries the DB, through singleflight but still per request. This lasts until the denial cache absorbs it. For list-like access patterns with many distinct names the denial keys never repeat, so every denied Check costs a DB round trip. Cache hit metrics are also double-counted: a miss is recorded after a cache hit that did not allow.

title: In-proc client caching fully removed
body: The in-proc client now uses a NoopCache, so every authz check goes through the server path. That path does at least the GetUserIdentifiers and permCache lookups plus JSON unmarshal. The earlier 30s client cache may have been hiding a high volume of these calls.

title: Missing key prop on GrafanaRuleListItem in list
body: The rewrite of the 'grafana' branch in FilterView drops `key={key}` from the rendered `GrafanaRuleListItem`. These items are rendered in a list that grows as more pages load. Without a stable key, React logs warnings and falls back to index-based reconciliation, so component state and hooks can attach to the wrong rule as rules are appended.

title: Pause and Delete menu items never render in list view
body: The list view now passes only `promRule` to the menu, so `rulerRule` is undefined. Even when `canPause` or `canDelete` comes out true from the prom-based abilities, the render conditions still require `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` (Pause, line 123) and `rulerRule` (Delete, line 165). As a result, users can no longer pause or delete Grafana rules from the alert list.

title: Silence drawer never opens for prom-only rules
body: The Silence menu item is shown based on the prom abilities. However, the drawer only renders when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true. In the list view `rule` is undefined, so clicking 'Silence notifications' does nothing.

title: Export ability excludes Grafana recording rules
body: `ModifyExport` uses `isAlertingRule`, whereas the ruler version uses `isGrafanaManagedAlertRule`, which covers any Grafana rule including recording rules. Pause and Restore have the same narrowing. This silently drops these actions for Grafana recording rules in the list view.

title: View link lost returnTo parameter
body: The rule link previously included `returnTo` via `createReturnTo()`; the new href omits it. As a result, navigation back from the rule view to the filtered list no longer preserves the user's position and filters.

title: Missing key prop on GrafanaRuleListItem in list
body: When `GrafanaRuleLoader` was replaced with `GrafanaRuleListItem`, the `key={key}` prop was dropped. This element is rendered inside `rules.map(...)`. Without a key, React warns and reconciles items by index. Since the list grows incrementally as pages load, items can be mismatched and lose state such as an open menu or modal.

title: Pause and Delete never shown in list view despite prom-based abilities
body: `canPause` and `canDelete` now include the prom-rule abilities, but the menu items still require a `rulerRule`. Pause is gated on `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` and Delete on `canDelete && rulerRule`. The list view no longer passes a ruler rule, so users with permission silently lose the Pause and Delete actions there. The new test asserts exactly 4 items, which locks in this regression.

title: Silence menu item does nothing without ruler rule
body: The silence drawer is rendered only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true. In the list view `rule` is undefined, yet `canSilence` can be true via the prom abilities, so the 'Silence notifications' item is shown. Clicking it sets `showSilenceDrawer` to true but nothing renders, so the action is a no-op for the user.

title: Export ability excludes Grafana recording rules
body: For prom rules, ModifyExport is supported only when `isAlertingRule` is true. The ruler-based version uses `isGrafanaManagedAlertRule`, which also covers recording rules. As a result, Grafana recording rules lose the Export option in the list view.

title: Missing React key on GrafanaRuleListItem in list
body: The refactor dropped `key={key}` when GrafanaRuleLoader was replaced with GrafanaRuleListItem. Without a key, React reconciles these list items by index. As rules are appended or reordered, component state such as open menus, drawers and modals can attach to the wrong rule. React will also emit key warnings.

title: Silence drawer never opens in list view
body: The list view now passes only `promRule`; `rule` (the ruler rule) is undefined. AlertRuleMenu still shows 'Silence notifications' because canSilence is computed from promRule abilities. However, the drawer only renders when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true. Clicking Silence therefore does nothing.

title: Pause and Delete menu items silently disappear without rulerRule
body: canPause and canDelete now come from promRule abilities, but rendering still requires `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` for Pause and `rulerRule` for Delete (line 165). In the list view no rulerRule is passed, so users with permission lose Pause and Delete entirely. The new test even asserts that only 4 menu items appear, which encodes this regression.

title: ModifyExport not supported for Grafana recording rules
body: `isAlertingRule` is used as the 'supported' flag for ModifyExport, Pause, Restore and DeletePermanently. The ruler version uses isGrafanaManagedAlertRule, which is true for any Grafana rule, including recording rules. With this change, Grafana recording rules lose export, pause and restore capabilities in the list view.

title: returnTo dropped from rule view link
body: The previous implementation built the view href with `{ returnTo: createReturnTo() }`. The new link omits it, so navigating back from the rule detail page no longer returns the user to the filtered list state.

title: Queries are interpolated more than once, so ad-hoc filters can be appended repeatedly
body:
`runSplitQuery` now calls `applyTemplateVariables` on every target. In the sharding path, `runShardSplitQuery` (shardQuerySplitting.ts:52) has already called `applyTemplateVariables`. It then passes a sub-request that still carries `request.filters` into `runSplitQuery`, which applies it a second time.

The sub-requests also go through `datasource.runQuery`. If that ends up in `DataSourceWithBackend.query`, it calls `applyTemplateVariables` per target again, which would make a third pass.

`applyTemplateVariables` is not idempotent. It injects ad-hoc filter matchers from `request.filters` into the expression, so those label matchers can be duplicated. Values containing `$` or regex-escaped multi-value variables can also be re-processed and corrupted.

The new shard test asserts 5 calls for a single target, which reflects this repeated application. Interpolation should happen exactly once: drop it from one entry point, or strip `filters`/`scopedVars` from the request after interpolating.

title: Mocked applyTemplateVariables mutates input and hides double-interpolation effects
body:
The mock replaces `$SELECTOR` in place and returns the same object. Applying it a second time is therefore a no-op. Because of that, the tests cannot detect the duplicated filter/escaping problem caused by calling `applyTemplateVariables` several times per query.

The mock also mutates `request.targets`, which a non-mutating real implementation would not do. A test with ad-hoc filters that asserts the final expression contains each filter only once would catch the regression.

title: Queries are interpolated twice in the sharding path
body: runShardSplitQuery now calls applyTemplateVariables on each target and then passes the subrequests to runSplitQuery, which calls applyTemplateVariables again on every subrequest. The test confirms this: the call count goes from 1 to 5. Running interpolation a second time on already-interpolated expressions can double-apply ad-hoc filters (request.filters) or re-escape values. It also adds per-shard overhead.

title: Queries interpolated twice in shard path (shard + runSplitQuery)
body: runShardSplitQuery applies applyTemplateVariables, then each sub-request goes to runSplitQuery, which applies applyTemplateVariables again. Ad-hoc filters (request.filters) can be added to the expression twice. The second pass also runs on expressions that already carry injected shard selectors and `| drop __stream_shard__`. The test confirms this: it expects 5 calls to applyTemplateVariables for a single query. Interpolation should happen in only one place, or the sub-request filters should be cleared before delegating.

title: Removed traceID from plugin request completion log
body: The old logRequest appended a traceID field via tracing.TraceIDFromContext. This PR removes it and relies on logger.FromContext(ctx), but nothing visible in the diff adds traceID to the contextual attributes. If the infra logger's FromContext does not inject the trace ID itself, the 'Plugin Request Completed' egress log loses its traceID field. That would break log/trace correlation for anyone querying on it.

title: FromContext fallback discards contextual attributes
body: If infra log's FromContext returns something other than *log.ConcreteLogger, the wrapper silently falls back to d.New(), which carries no context attributes. The log line would then lose pluginId, endpoint, dsName and the other fields with no warning.

title: Adding method to exported Logger interface breaks implementers
body: FromContext is added to the exported plugins Logger interface. Any other implementations, such as fakes in other packages or enterprise code, will fail to compile. The doc comment is also inaccurate: it says the method adds 'the given context', but it actually derives the logger from attributes stored in the context.Context.

title: traceID no longer included in plugin request log
body: The explicit `traceID` log param was removed. The replacement, `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)`, adds only contextual attributes such as endpoint, pluginId and dsName. Whether it also adds traceID depends on the infra logger's context providers, and the plugin log wrapper's FromContext falls back to `d.New()` when the type assertion fails, which drops all context. In that fallback case, "Plugin Request Completed" logs lose the traceID and all plugin and request details.

title: Adding a method to the exported Logger interface breaks other implementations
body: `FromContext` is added to the public `plugins/log.Logger` interface. Any other implementations, such as fakes in other packages, test loggers or enterprise code, will stop compiling until they implement the new method.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, so logged calls cannot be asserted
body: `FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()`, a new instance, instead of `f`. Since LoggerMiddleware now always logs through `FromContext(ctx)`, tests that use TestLogger will never see the recorded Info calls. Returning `f` would keep those calls observable.

title: traceID no longer included in plugin request log lines
body: The old logRequest appended `traceID` from `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` to every "Plugin Request Completed" line. That was removed on the assumption that the contextual logger supplies it. The new ContextualLoggerMiddleware only adds endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID and uname, not traceID. Unless infra log's FromContext adds the trace ID on its own, the data-egress logs lose trace correlation.

title: Adding FromContext to the exported Logger interface breaks other implementations
body: Adding a method to the exported `plog.Logger` interface breaks every other implementation of it, including mocks and enterprise or external wrappers, at compile time. Only TestLogger and grafanaInfraLogWrapper are updated in this PR. Separately, `TestLogger.FromContext` returns a fresh TestLogger, so any logs written through the returned logger cannot be asserted on the original test logger. Tests of LoggerMiddleware will silently see zero calls.

title: Device tagging now synchronous on every anonymous request
body: TagDevice used to run in a background goroutine. It now runs inline with the request context. Each anonymous request that misses the local cache now waits on DB writes before authenticating. When a device limit is set, that includes an extra COUNT query. A slow or failing DB therefore adds latency to anonymous authentication. Request cancellation can also abort the tagging.

title: Cache set before store write lets rejected devices bypass the limit
body: tagDeviceUI writes the cache key before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice. If the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, the first request fails. Later requests from the same device hit the cache, get nil back, and authenticate successfully for the 29-minute cache TTL. The limit is effectively enforced only once per cache period.

title: Race between count and insert lets the limit be exceeded
body: CountDevices and the upsert run as separate statements with no transaction or lock. Concurrent new devices can all read a count below the limit and all insert. The number of stored devices can then exceed the configured limit.

title: Zero rows affected misreported on MySQL
body: On MySQL, RowsAffected counts only rows whose values actually changed. If an existing device is updated with identical values (same IP, user agent and second-precision timestamp), it returns 0. A legitimate existing device is then rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached.

title: Device tagging moved from async goroutine to synchronous request path
body: TagDevice used to run in a background goroutine with its own timeout. It now runs synchronously on every anonymous authentication. When a device limit is set, each uncached request does a COUNT query and then an INSERT or UPDATE against the DB. This adds DB latency to every anonymous request. A slow or failing DB now delays or degrades anonymous auth, even when no limit is configured.

title: Cache set before store write lets rejected devices bypass the limit
body: tagDeviceUI writes the device to localCache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice. If the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, the cache entry stays in place. For the next 29 minutes, requests from that device hit the cache and return nil. Authentication then succeeds, so the device limit is only enforced on the first request.

title: Count-then-insert race allows exceeding device limit
body: The limit check counts devices and then inserts in a separate statement, with no transaction or lock. Concurrent requests from new devices across goroutines or instances can all see count < limit and all insert. The configured limit can therefore be exceeded.

title: RowsAffected==0 misreported as limit reached on MySQL
body: By default, MySQL reports only changed rows in RowsAffected. When an existing device updates with identical client_ip, user_agent, and updated_at (second precision), 0 rows are reported as affected. ErrDeviceLimitReached is then returned for a device that is already registered, and authentication is denied.

title: Raw error returned on limit with no proper authn error/status
body: When the limit is reached, Authenticate returns a plain error instead of a typed authn/errutil error. The client gets a generic failure with no clear HTTP status or message explaining that the anonymous device limit was reached.

title: Device tagging moved onto the synchronous authentication path
body: TagDevice used to run in a background goroutine with its own timeout. It now runs synchronously inside Authenticate, so every anonymous request whose device is not in the local cache waits on DB writes. With a device limit configured it also runs a COUNT query first. This adds latency to anonymous requests. A slow or failing database now delays anonymous authentication, and the request context's cancellation can abort the tag.

title: Cache set before DB write lets rejected devices bypass the limit
body: tagDeviceUI writes the cache key before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the call returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, the key stays cached. For the next ~29 minutes, requests from that device hit the cache, return nil, and authenticate successfully. Only the first request is rejected, so the limit is effectively not enforced. The key should be cached only after a successful write, or removed when the write fails.

title: Racy count-then-insert allows exceeding device limit
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts devices and then inserts, without a transaction or lock. Concurrent requests from new devices can all see count < limit and all insert, so the limit can be exceeded. Each new device also adds a full COUNT query.

title: Existing device with an unchanged-timestamp update reports limit reached
body: updateDevice treats rowsAffected==0 as ErrDeviceLimitReached. On MySQL, RowsAffected by default counts only rows that actually changed. An existing device re-tagged with the same IP, user agent and second-precision timestamp therefore returns 0 rows and is wrongly rejected even though it is already a registered device.

title: Store construction bypasses DI; wire providers likely broken
body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now takes db.DB and builds the store itself, instead of receiving the injected anonstore.AnonStore. ProvideAnonDBStore now takes an extra int64 argument, which wire cannot provide. Any wire set that still references anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore or binds AnonStore will fail to build, and the change was not updated in this PR.

title: Debug logging left at Error level, dumping full ID lists
body: Each batch in the cleanup loops logs at Error level, including the full slice of IDs, at lines 534/537, 554/557 and 576/579. This happens even on success and even when there are zero IDs. With large batch sizes (e.g. 32767) every cleanup cycle emits enormous error-level log lines. That floods logs and triggers false alerts. These look like leftover debugging and should be removed or lowered to Debug without the ID list.

title: Cleanup interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The ticker was reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which looks like a debugging leftover unrelated to the deadlock fix. All cleanup jobs (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, query history, etc.) now run 10x more often, increasing DB load. The per-run timeout is still 9 minutes, so runs can overlap or queue behind each other. That also increases contention with the very writes this PR aims to stop deadlocking.

title: SQLite inline-ID path is quadratic
body: On SQLite with a large batch size, the IN list is built by calling fmt.Sprintf repeatedly on a growing string. That is O(n^2) in the number of IDs, which is expensive for batches of ~32k. A strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt (as used elsewhere in this file) should be used instead.

title: MaxCount loop can delete annotations inserted concurrently
body: The MaxCount pass fetches IDs with ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT batch OFFSET maxCount and loops until nothing is deleted. Because the fetch and the delete are now separate statements, and repeated without a transaction, concurrent inserts shift the offset window between iterations. The loop keeps going while new rows arrive, so it can run for a long time under steady insert load.

title: Debug logging left at Error level, dumping full ID lists
body: Each batch of the cleanup loops logs at Error level (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579), including the entire `ids` slice. These logs fire on every run even when nothing goes wrong. With large batch sizes (e.g. 32767), they write enormous error log lines, flood logs and alerting, and add overhead. They look like leftover debugging and should be removed or lowered to Debug without the ID list.

title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The interval for all cleanup jobs went from 10 minutes to 1 minute, and the PR description does not mention or justify it. Each job still has a 9-minute timeout, so runs can now overlap or queue back to back. That means 10x more DB load for snapshots, dashboard versions, query history and the rest. This looks like a leftover debugging change.

title: MaxCount cleanup can delete the wrong rows when inserts run concurrently
body: The IDs are fetched with ORDER BY id DESC plus an OFFSET of MaxCount, then deleted in a separate statement outside any transaction. This already happens every batch. Concurrent inserts shift the offset between batches, so the result is no longer one consistent cut. The comment only claims under-deletion, but this offset behaviour should be considered and documented.

title: Quadratic string building for SQLite IN list
body: `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` rebuilds the whole string on every iteration. That is O(n^2) for batches of tens of thousands of IDs. Use a strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt instead.

title: SQLite inline path keyed on configured batch size instead of actual ID count
body: The check for whether to inline IDs or use placeholders looks at the configured batch size, not at how many IDs this batch actually has. The placeholder path is still correct as long as len(ids) never exceeds the batch size. Checking len(ids) instead would make the limit handling more robust.

title: Debug logging left at Error level, including full ID lists
body: The new cleanup loops log every batch at Error level and include the full `ids` slice. These calls are at lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576 and 579. A batch can hold tens of thousands of IDs, so each run floods the logs with huge Error entries even when nothing went wrong. That breaks error alerting and inflates log volume. These look like leftover debug statements; remove them or lower them to Debug without the ID list.

title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute while job timeout is still 9 minutes
body: The global cleanup interval drops from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This change is unrelated to the deadlock fix and looks like leftover debugging. Every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, query history, and so on) now runs ten times as often. That adds database load and makes contention with inserts more likely, which works against the goal of this PR. The per-run timeout is still 9 minutes, much longer than the new interval, so the timeout no longer matches the schedule. Revert to 10 minutes.

title: SQLite parameter-limit check uses configured batch size instead of actual ID count
body: The code decides whether to inline IDs based on `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize`, not on `len(ids)`. When the batch size is above 999 it always inlines, which is safe but inconsistent with the stated reason. The check also assumes no other code path ever passes more IDs than the batch size. Base the decision on `len(ids)`. In addition, building the inlined list with repeated `fmt.Sprintf` copies the whole string on every ID, which is quadratic for 32k IDs. Use `strings.Builder` or `strconv` instead.

title: MaxCount cleanup can loop indefinitely under concurrent inserts
body: Each MaxCount batch re-runs `ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT batch OFFSET MaxCount` and keeps looping while rows are deleted. While annotations keep being inserted, every new row pushes an older row past the offset, so the loop may never see zero affected rows. Only the 9-minute context timeout would stop it, and it runs one SELECT and one DELETE per batch the whole time. The old single-statement version behaved the same way, but the extra round trip per batch makes it costlier. Consider capping the number of iterations.

title: Async legacy write derives from request context and gets canceled
body: Each background goroutine wraps the request `ctx` with `context.WithTimeoutCause`. The request context is canceled as soon as the handler returns, which happens right after the goroutine is spawned. The legacy write will therefore often be canceled before or while it runs. The context also carries request-scoped values whose lifetime ends with the request. Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` as the base, then apply the timeout. The same pattern appears at lines 110, 135 and 163.

title: Legacy write errors are silently dropped
body: Errors from the async Legacy Create, Update, Delete and DeleteCollection calls only feed the duration metric. They are never logged. Legacy store divergence will go unnoticed and be hard to debug. Log the error, using the `log` logger, inside each goroutine.

title: Storage failure recorded as legacy duration
body: When the Storage Create call fails, the code calls `recordLegacyDuration` instead of `recordStorageDuration`. Unified-storage failures are therefore attributed to the legacy store in metrics. Update has the same mistake at line 129.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection recorded as storage duration
body: The async legacy DeleteCollection goroutine calls `recordStorageDuration` instead of `recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy timings end up in the storage metric and skew it.

title: Delete metric uses name as kind label
body: In Delete, the success path passes `name` where `options.Kind` is expected. Every object name becomes its own value of the kind label, which creates unbounded metric cardinality. Separately, line 97 calls `klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` instead of passing `log`, so the logger stored in the context loses the name, kind and method fields.

title: Legacy update re-applies objInfo against a different base
body: The async legacy Update reuses the original `objInfo` instead of wrapping the object that unified storage returned. The previous code used `updateWrapper` for this. Patch-style updates will be recomputed against the legacy object, which can produce divergent data between the two stores.

title: Tests are racy and don't verify async legacy calls
body: The goroutines may call the shared mock after the test returns, and nothing asserts that the legacy methods were actually invoked. In the Create error case, the setup function registers the failing expectation on the legacy mock rather than on storage. That case only passes because the shared mock answers storage calls too.

title: Async legacy write derives from request context which is canceled after response
body: The goroutine wraps the request ctx with a timeout. The apiserver cancels the request context as soon as the handler returns, which is immediately after the goroutine is spawned. The legacy Create, Update, Delete and DeleteCollection calls will therefore often fail with context canceled, and legacy storage silently diverges. Use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) before applying the timeout. The same pattern appears at lines 110, 135 and 163.

title: Storage failure recorded as legacy duration metric
body: In Create, a failure from d.Storage.Create is recorded with recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration. Update has the same mistake at line 129. As a result, storage errors are attributed to the legacy store in metrics.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection recorded as storage metric
body: The asynchronous legacy DeleteCollection result is recorded with recordStorageDuration rather than recordLegacyDuration. This skews storage metrics and hides legacy failures.

title: Delete metric uses name instead of kind label
body: On success, Delete calls recordStorageDuration with `name` in the kind position. This produces a metric label per object name, which is a cardinality explosion, and the label value is wrong.

title: Delete puts base logger in context, dropping fields
body: Delete calls `klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` with the base logger instead of `log`. The name, kind and method values built on the line above are therefore lost for downstream logging.

title: Async legacy write errors are never logged
body: Errors from the background legacy writes are only counted in metrics, never logged. The previous synchronous code logged legacy failures. Divergence between the stores is now invisible in logs.

title: Legacy update reuses objInfo concurrently/after request
body: objInfo is passed unchanged to the background legacy Update, while the old updateWrapper with the storage-updated object is no longer used. Patch-based objInfo is evaluated against the legacy object, so the legacy store may end up with different content than unified storage. The same objInfo is also used across goroutines after the request has finished.

title: Create error case mocks legacy, not storage; async calls unasserted
body: The case named "unified store fails" sets up the failure on the legacy mock via setupLegacyFn. The legacy and storage mocks share one mock instance, so the test passes by accident. None of the tests wait for or assert the asynchronous legacy calls.

title: Async legacy write derives from request context that is cancelled when the request returns
body: Each goroutine builds its timeout context from the request ctx. The apiserver cancels that ctx as soon as the handler returns, which happens right after the goroutine is launched. The legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection therefore often runs with an already-cancelled context and fails, so legacy storage silently stops being written. Use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or a background context that carries the needed values.

title: Storage failure recorded as legacy duration
body: In Create, a failure of the Storage write is recorded with recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration. Update has the same mistake at line 129. As a result, failures of the unified store show up under the legacy metric.

title: Name passed as kind label in Delete metric
body: recordStorageDuration is called with `name` where `options.Kind` should be. This mislabels the metric and creates one label value per object name, giving unbounded metric cardinality.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection recorded as storage duration
body: The async legacy DeleteCollection call records its result with recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration. Legacy deletecollection results are therefore counted under the unified-storage metric.

title: Delete context uses base logger without request fields
body: In Delete, the context is built with klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) rather than the `log` built just above it. Downstream logs lose the name, kind and method fields.

title: Legacy async errors are not logged and goroutines race with test mocks
body: Errors from the background legacy writes are only counted in metrics and never logged, so divergence between the stores is hard to diagnose. In the unit tests, Delete and DeleteCollection set no legacy mock expectations. The goroutine then calls an unexpected mock method, which panics or races with test completion. The tests also never assert that the legacy write happened.

title: Create error case does not exercise a storage failure
body: The failing case only sets up a legacy expectation. The storage mock's Create has no expectation, so the test passes or fails based on mock behaviour rather than on a configured storage error.

title: No re-check of cache after acquiring write lock
body: When several goroutines miss the cache at once, they all queue on Lock(). Each one then re-reads and parses the manifest, because the code does not check `entryPointAssetsCache` again after acquiring the write lock. This is redundant work on cold start. It is also needless serialization in Dev mode, where every request reloads the manifest while holding an exclusive lock. Fix it by adding a double-checked read under the write lock when not in Dev mode.

title: No re-check after acquiring write lock; concurrent callers all reload the manifest
body: After the read-locked check misses, the code takes the write lock but does not check the cache again. Several goroutines that miss at the same time line up on the lock. Each one then re-reads and re-parses assets-manifest.json, or makes the CDN request, one after another. They also overwrite the cache each time. A double-checked pattern (re-check `entryPointAssetsCache != nil` when not in Dev, after taking `Lock`) would avoid this redundant serialized I/O. In production this happens at startup, or after an earlier failure has left the cache nil.

title: Error result overwrites a previously cached valid value with nil
body: `entryPointAssetsCache = result` runs even when `err != nil`. If a reload fails, the cache is set to nil and the error is returned. This happens in Dev mode on every call, or with a transient file or CDN error. Any good assets cached earlier are lost, and later callers get errors or trigger reloads. Only update the cache when `err == nil`.

title: Missing re-check after acquiring write lock causes redundant manifest loads
body: After the read lock finds the cache empty, the code takes the write lock but does not check `entryPointAssetsCache` again. When the cache is cold, several concurrent requests can all miss under RLock. Each then takes the write lock in turn and re-reads and re-parses the manifest from disk or the CDN. This is wasted work, and the cached pointer gets replaced several times. Add a double-check after `Lock()`: if not in Dev mode and the cache is non-nil, return it.

title: Load failure overwrites a previously cached value with nil
body: `entryPointAssetsCache = result` runs even when loading fails, in which case `result` is nil. In Dev mode, a single transient read or parse error, for example while the frontend build is rewriting the manifest, wipes out the good cached value. Only assign the cache when `err == nil`.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false; logic is inverted and misleading
body: `enableSqlExpressions` sets `enabled := !IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns false on both branches. It always returns false, so the feature-flag check does nothing. Disabling the feature unconditionally is the intent here, but the code reads as if it honours the flag, and the variable name is the opposite of what it holds. It should simply return false, with a comment explaining that SQL expressions are disabled because of CVE-2024-9264. As written, a future maintainer could easily "fix" the branch and re-enable the vulnerable path.

title: Dead SQL-building code left behind the not-implemented stub
body: `TablesList` still builds `SELECT json_serialize_sql('...')` by string concatenation and passes it to a stub DB that always errors. Every call fails, and each failure logs at error level with the raw user SQL. Leaving the injection-prone command construction in place invites someone to wire up a real DB again without re-checking it. Return a not-implemented error up front instead.

title: SQL commands still constructible via UnmarshalSQLCommand path bypassing reader gate
body: The disable gate was added only in `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery`. `UnmarshalSQLCommand` (the legacy `rawNode` path used by the expression service and alerting) still calls `NewSQLCommand` without any check. Execution now fails because the DB is a stub, so this is safe today. However, the only protection on that path is the stub, which is fragile. Add the same explicit disable check in `UnmarshalSQLCommand`/`NewSQLCommand`, and add tests asserting that SQL expressions are rejected on both paths.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false; logic is misleading
body: enableSqlExpressions negates the feature flag check and then returns false in both branches, so the flag has no effect. Disabling the feature is intentional, but the code reads as if the flag gates it. A future maintainer who 'fixes' the inverted negation could re-enable the DuckDB path without noticing. Replace this with a plain `return false` and a comment explaining the security reason.

title: Error message misleading for SQL expressions
body: Users receive "sqlExpressions is not implemented", even when the sqlExpressions feature flag is on. In reality the feature was implemented and then deliberately disabled for security reasons. A clearer message such as "SQL expressions are disabled" would tell users that turning on the flag will not help.

title: Existing SQL parser/command tests now fail against the stub DB
body: TablesList now calls the stub DB, whose RunCommands always returns "not implemented". The other legacy SQL path, UnmarshalSQLCommand, calls NewSQLCommand and so fails the same way. Any existing tests that parse SQL table lists or execute SQL commands will fail. The PR does not update or skip those tests and adds no test asserting that SQL expressions are rejected.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false; logic is misleading
body: `enableSqlExpressions` returns false on both branches, so the `FlagSqlExpressions` toggle has no effect. The negated flag check stored in a variable named `enabled` reads as a mistake. A later maintainer could "fix" the inversion and re-enable a path whose backend is now a stub. Make it an explicit unconditional `return false` (or drop the case) and add a comment explaining it is deliberately disabled for CVE-2024-9264.

title: Error message is misleading
body: When SQL expressions are requested, users get the error "sqlExpressions is not implemented". The feature exists but was deliberately disabled for security reasons, so the message is confusing. A clearer message such as "SQL expressions are disabled" would help users and support.

title: Other SQL command construction paths still reachable; existing tests likely broken
body: `UnmarshalSQLCommand` (the legacy rawNode path) is not gated by the feature check. It is now harmless only because `TablesList` returns an error. Existing tests in `pkg/expr/sql` (e.g. parser tests that expect table lists) and the SQL command tests probably fail now. They should be removed or updated, and a test added asserting that SQL expressions are rejected.

title: Concurrent BuildIndex for same key now races and duplicates work
body: BuildIndex is no longer serialized; the lock is only taken around the cache write. getOrCreateIndex calls GetIndex and then build, so two concurrent requests or watch events for the same key can both see nil and build the index at the same time. Both writes go to the same on-disk dir (bleve.New fails if it exists) or produce duplicate in-memory indexes. The last writer wins, so the other index leaks, and its IndexTenants and IndexedKinds metrics are double-counted. A per-key lock or singleflight is needed.

title: TotalDocs reads cache map without lock
body: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without taking cacheMu. Now that builds run concurrently and write the map under the lock, this read is a data race. A concurrent map write during iteration can crash the process. It should hold RLock.

title: Shared err and counter written from multiple goroutines
body: Inside group.Go, the closures assign to the outer `err` variable and increment `totalBatchesIndexed` concurrently, which is a data race. Since this PR is meant to raise build concurrency, the race is more likely to occur. Use a local `err :=` in the closure and an atomic counter.

title: Init errors are now fatal at construction and Stop no longer gates requests
body: Init now runs in NewResourceServer, and the Init checks were removed from every handler. As a result, Stop setting initErr ("service is stopping") no longer prevents requests from being served after shutdown. Building all indexes synchronously in the constructor also blocks startup. On error, the context created with WithCancel is never cancelled, so it leaks.

title: Data race on shared err and totalBatchesIndexed in parallel init workers
body: Inside the group.Go closures, `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` are variables captured from the enclosing scope and written by several goroutines at once. Now that BuildIndex no longer holds a global lock, builds really do run concurrently, so these writes race. The result can be a wrong indexed count and corrupted error state. Use goroutine-local variables (`_, _, err := ...`) and an atomic counter.

title: Concurrent builds of the same key and file index collisions
body: The cache lock is now taken only for the final map write. Two callers that both miss in getOrCreateIndex (for example, watch events or searches arriving during startup) will build the same key at the same time. For file-based indexes, both call bleve.New on the same directory, which can fail or corrupt the index. One built index also overwrites the other, and IndexTenants and IndexedKinds metrics get double-counted. Add per-key singleflight or re-check the cache under the lock.

title: TotalDocs iterates cache map without lock
body: TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without holding cacheMu. Other goroutines can write to the map concurrently via BuildIndex. A concurrent map read and write can make the Go runtime throw a fatal error.

title: Search init now runs before the watcher, so events between index build and watch start are lost
body: Init now builds every index synchronously in the constructor. WatchWriteEvents is subscribed only after the indexes are built and starts from the latest RV at that moment. Any writes made while the indexes were being built are therefore never applied to the index. Init also now blocks NewResourceServer startup for the whole index build, with no timeout.

title: Integration test disabled for postgres
body: This PR skips the storage server integration test on postgres instead of fixing the failure. The new startup-init behaviour therefore goes untested on postgres.

title: Data race on shared err and totalBatchesIndexed in errgroup goroutines
body: Every worker goroutine assigns its result to the `err` variable captured from the enclosing `init` function (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and increments `totalBatchesIndexed` with no synchronization. With initWorkers > 1 these are data races, which this PR makes more likely by removing the global BuildIndex lock. One goroutine can return another goroutine's error, so a failure can be hidden or reported against the wrong resource, and the reported indexed count is wrong. Declare a local `err` inside each goroutine and use an atomic counter.

title: Concurrent builds of the same key now race; duplicate indexes and file-dir conflicts
body: Without the whole-function lock, two callers of getOrCreateIndex for the same key (concurrent Search requests, or watch events arriving while init is still building) can both miss the cache and build in parallel. For file-based indexes, both call bleve.New on the same directory, and one of them fails or corrupts it. The last writer also overwrites the other's index in the cache, leaking it and double-counting the IndexTenants and IndexedKinds metrics. A per-key lock or singleflight is needed.

title: TotalDocs iterates cache without lock
body: TotalDocs ranges over `b.cache` without holding `cacheMu`. It is now called from init via the new log line, and other goroutines (watch handling, concurrent builds) can write the map at the same time. That is a concurrent map read/write, which can make the Go runtime throw a fatal error. Take `cacheMu.RLock()` while iterating.

title: Search init now blocks constructor; Stop/cancel unavailable and ctx never cancelled on failure
body: NewResourceServer now runs the full index build synchronously, so module startup blocks for the whole build, which can be long. If Init fails, the server is discarded but `cancel` is never called. The background contexts are leaked, along with any watcher or poller goroutines that were already started (for example the search watch on context.Background()).

title: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires user != null, so passkeys are disabled on first login
body: `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(user)` returns true only when `user != null`. In `authenticate()` (line 115) and `challenge()` (line 137) it is called with `context.getUser()`, which is null on a fresh login. As a result `fillContextForm` is never called for unauthenticated users. Conditional-UI passkey login on the initial username/password page is lost, which is the main passkeys scenario; previously that case was explicitly supported. The condition looks inverted or misplaced: it should probably not depend on the user at all.

title: No-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() call doesn't match the defined overload
body: `UsernameForm.authenticate` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments. The only method added in `UsernamePasswordForm` is `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)`, so this either fails to compile or depends on an overload that isn't shown. Even if it is changed to pass `context.getUser()`, the semantics differ from the intended check of whether passkeys are enabled.

title: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires user != null, disabling passkeys on initial login
body:
`isConditionalPasskeysEnabled` returns true only when `user != null`. Before this change, `authenticate()` and `challenge()` filled the WebAuthn conditional UI data whenever passkeys were enabled and no user was selected yet.

Now, on a normal first login (no user in the context), `fillContextForm` is never called. The conditional passkey UI therefore disappears from the username/password form, which is the main passkeys use case. The check looks inverted or wrongly scoped: the intent was likely to always allow passkeys when enabled.

The initial-login tests that assert the `webauth` form is present should fail with this change.

title: UsernameForm calls an isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() overload that does not exist
body:
`UsernameForm.authenticate` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments. The superclass only defines `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)`, so this does not compile.

It should probably pass `context.getUser()` or call a separate check of whether passkeys are enabled.

title: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires user != null, disabling passkeys on normal login
body: The new helper returns true only when `user != null`. Before this change, passkeys were set up only when the user was not yet identified. In `authenticate()` and `challenge()` the call is now `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`. On a fresh login the user is null, so `fillContextForm` is never called and the conditional passkey UI is gone. That breaks the main passkeys login path, which several existing tests expect to show the webauth form before the username is entered. The condition looks inverted, or the null check should simply be removed.

title: UsernameForm calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no argument
body: `UsernameForm.authenticate` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments. The only method defined, in `UsernamePasswordForm`, takes a `UserModel` parameter, so this code will not compile. It should pass `context.getUser()`, or a no-argument overload should be added.

title: Cached login IDPs bypass the org enabled check for REALM_ONLY callers
body: Cached results are returned from getById, and those models are wrapped so that isEnabled also checks the linked organization. Disabling an organization does not invalidate the login cache keys, so cached lists can still contain IDPs of a disabled org. Only the ORG_ONLY and ALL callers re-check isEnabled. Any other caller of getForLogin, such as the base IdentityProviderBean or third-party code, will now receive IDPs that are effectively disabled. The cache should either filter by isEnabled before returning, or the organization enable/disable path should invalidate the login cache keys.

title: Login cache invalidation on update misses changes that alter list membership
body: Invalidation is skipped when the IDP qualifies for login both before and after the update with the same organization. Changes that the predicate does not cover can still affect the cached results, for example the delegate's search semantics like a null orgId match. In addition, `idpById` is the org-aware wrapper whose isEnabled depends on the organization state, while `updated` is not wrapped. The two sides of the comparison can therefore disagree, so the cache can be wrongly skipped or wrongly invalidated.

title: Cleanup removes literal alias "alias" instead of created IDPs
body: `get("alias")::remove` refers to a non-existent IDP, so none of the 21 created IDPs is cleaned up. They leak into other tests that run in the same realm.

title: Login cache keeps stale IDP data after updates that leave login availability unchanged
body:
In `update()`, `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate` skips invalidating the login caches when an IDP stays login-eligible with the same organization. The cached query stores only internal IDs, and those are re-resolved through `getById`, so changed attributes like the display name are picked up. Ordering and membership stay correct too.

The gap is the `getById` path: `update()` calls `getById(model.getInternalId())`, which can return an org-aware wrapped model. The predicate is tested against that wrapper, whose `isEnabled()` also depends on the organization being enabled. So the decision to skip invalidation is based on org state, not only on the IDP's own fields.

The cached list is also not invalidated when an organization is disabled or enabled. That is why the bean has to re-check `isEnabled()`. However, the `onlyRealmBrokers` path in `OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean` (line 58) does not re-check it.

title: Login cache not invalidated when organization is removed or IDP is unlinked via org provider
body:
The `ORG_ONLY` and `ALL` login caches are keyed only by realm and fetch mode. Invalidation happens only from this provider's `create`, `update` and `remove`.

Removing an organization or deleting its IDPs through other paths, such as `removeAll` on realm deletion, never registers a login-cache invalidation. The `getById` null check only catches IDPs that have been deleted outright.

When an organization is removed but its IDPs remain, possibly unlinked, the cached `ALL`/`ORG_ONLY` results can still include IDPs that are no longer org-linked. The `REALM_ONLY` results can also miss IDPs that should now appear there.

title: Cleanup registers removal of literal alias "alias"
body: Each cleanup is registered with `get("alias")::remove` instead of the actual alias created in the loop. As a result, the created IDPs are never removed, and test state leaks into other tests. The same mistake appears at line 425.

title: removeAll does not invalidate login caches
body:
removeAll() invalidates only the count key. The new cacheKeyForLogin entries for each FetchMode are left in place. A cached login IDP list can then outlive the deletion of all IDPs.

The per-ID fallback partially masks this, because a missing IDP triggers a reload. The keys still remain stale, and any cross-node behaviour depends on that fallback path.

title: Cleanup removes literal alias "alias" instead of created IDPs
body: The cleanup is registered as `get("alias")::remove` instead of using the alias that was actually created. The created IDPs are therefore never cleaned up. The cleanup call targets a nonexistent IDP, which can fail or leak state into other tests.

title: Login cache not invalidated when an organization changes
body:
Unlike getByOrganization, getForLogin does not check isInvalid(organizationId). It also never registers a login-cache invalidation when organization membership or org state changes, such as an IDP being linked or unlinked through the organization API.

Correctness then depends on update() being called with an organizationId change. If the org link is changed through a path that bypasses this provider's update(), the cached login IDP list goes stale.

title: New abstract interface method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: `int order()` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` interface as an abstract method with no default. Any third-party or out-of-tree implementation stops compiling, or throws AbstractMethodError at runtime when CryptoIntegration sorts the providers. Declaring it as a default method (for example returning 0) would keep compatibility.

title: Providers with equal order are silently chosen nondeterministically
body: The old code failed fast when multiple providers were found. The new code sorts by order and picks the first one, logging the rest only at debug level. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return 200. If two of them end up on the classpath, for example FIPS plus default, the one selected depends on ServiceLoader iteration order. This can silently run Keycloak in non-FIPS mode. The code should still throw when the top two providers have the same order.

title: Indefinite length (-1) not rejected
body: `readLength` returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding. `readNext` then computes a wrong length, and `readInteger` calls `new byte[-1]`, which throws NegativeArraySizeException instead of IOException. A malformed signature can therefore surface as an unexpected runtime exception rather than a verification failure.

title: Dead encoder calls
body: Lines 114-115 build two ASN1Encoder objects and throw them away. This is wasted work and should be removed.

title: New abstract interface method breaks third-party CryptoProvider implementations
body: `int order()` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` interface as an abstract method with no default. Any existing external implementation of `CryptoProvider` will fail to compile, and at runtime an `AbstractMethodError` is thrown when `detectProvider` calls `order()` during sorting. Making it a `default` method (for example returning 0) would keep backward compatibility.

title: Ties between equal-order providers resolved silently and nondeterministically
body: Default, Elytron and FIPS providers all return 200. Previously, having more than one on the classpath was a hard error. Now the first one in ServiceLoader (classpath) order wins and the others are only mentioned in a debug log. A misconfigured deployment, for example FIPS and the default provider both present, could quietly run with the non-FIPS provider. Consider still failing when the top two providers have the same order.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns an arbitrary keystore provider
body: This method returns the provider of the default KeyStore type (for example SUN or SunJSSE), not a BouncyCastle provider. Code that calls `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER` or uses this provider for cipher or signature operations may get an unexpected provider or fail with `NoSuchAlgorithmException`.

title: Indefinite length returns -1 and causes NegativeArraySizeException
body: `readLength` returns -1 for the indefinite-length form (0x80). `readInteger` then calls `read(-1)`, which throws `NegativeArraySizeException` instead of an `IOException`. In `readSequence` the loop is skipped and an empty list is returned. Malformed signatures therefore produce unchecked exceptions rather than a clean verification failure.

title: New abstract interface method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: `order()` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` interface as an abstract method with no default. Any third-party or out-of-tree implementation will stop compiling, or throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when `detectProvider` sorts the providers. Make it a `default` method returning a neutral value.

title: Providers with equal order are chosen nondeterministically and silently
body: Default, Elytron and FIPS providers all return order 200. Previously, multiple providers on the classpath failed fast. Now the stable sort keeps ServiceLoader order, which depends on classpath ordering, and the others are ignored with only a debug log. A FIPS deployment that accidentally has the default provider present could silently run non-FIPS crypto. Detect ties at the top order and throw, or at least warn.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns an arbitrary keystore provider
body: It returns the provider of the default KeyStore type (e.g. SUN for PKCS12). Callers that expect a BouncyCastle provider for algorithms such as ECDSA or PSS lookups will get a provider that lacks them, causing NoSuchAlgorithmException. It would be safer to return null, as Elytron does, or to document the behaviour.

title: Indefinite length or malformed sequence handling
body: `readLength` returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding, and `readSequence` then silently returns an empty list. `readInteger` would call `new byte[-1]` and throw NegativeArraySizeException instead of IOException. Malformed signatures therefore produce unexpected runtime exceptions. Reject -1 explicitly.

title: Possible NPE when the all-clients resource is missing
body: `hasPermission(ClientModel, String)` falls back to `getResourceTypeResource(...)` when the client has no specific resource. That method can return null, for example in realms whose admin-permissions client was initialized before the Clients type was added to the schema. The null resource is then passed straight to `findByResource`, and later `resource.getScopes()` is dereferenced. The result is a NullPointerException, which surfaces as a 500 error, instead of a plain denial.

title: canMapRoles and related checks ignore MANAGE_CLIENTS role and per-client manage
body: `canMapRoles`, `canMapCompositeRoles` and `canMapClientScopeRoles` only evaluate the specific scope. They do not check whether the caller has the manage-clients admin role or the manage scope, which the V1 behaviour and other V2 methods honour. As a result, admins holding the manage-clients role lose the ability to map roles, which is a regression.

title: Removal listener now runs only when the V1 feature flag is on, but still dispatches to V2
body: The listener is now gated on `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` (V1). However, `management()` still returns `MgmtPermissionsV2` whenever V2 is enabled. If both features are enabled, a client removal event calls `ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled`, which throws `UnsupportedOperationException` and breaks client deletion. In addition, V2 resources for deleted clients or users are never cleaned up.

title: getClientsWithPermission relies on resource type that per-client resources don't have
body: `getOrCreateResource` creates per-client resources without setting their type; only the all-clients resource has type Clients. As a result, `findByType` returns only the "Clients" resource, so `granted` contains the string "Clients" instead of client IDs. Per-client grants are therefore never listed.

title: getResourceName not updated for Clients type
body: For the Clients resource type, `getResourceName` falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`. That value is null or the raw client UUID, unlike Users, which resolves to a readable username. Permission listings therefore show unhelpful resource names for client permissions.

title: getClientsWithPermission only finds resources whose type is 'Clients'
body: Per-client resources are created in `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` via `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, owner)`, and no type is ever set on them. Only the 'Clients' all-resource has type 'Clients'. `findByType` therefore returns at most that all-resource, so the method returns {"Clients"} instead of client IDs. As a result, listing clients will not work through per-client permissions.

title: Possible NPE when all-clients resource missing
body: `getResourceTypeResource` can return null, for example when a realm's admin-permissions client was initialized before 'Clients' was added to the schema. The null is passed to `findByResource` and then dereferenced in `resource.getScopes()`, which throws an NPE. That would surface as a 500 on admin client endpoints.

title: Removal listener gated on V1 feature only
body: The listener is now gated on `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ`, which skips cleanup when only V2 is enabled. That avoids the UnsupportedOperationException from `ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled`. However, if V1 and V2 are both enabled, `management()` returns MgmtPermissionsV2, so deleting a client calls `setPermissionsEnabled` and throws. Separately, V2 per-client resources and permissions are never removed when their client is deleted, leaving orphaned resources.

title: Per-client permission shadows all-clients permission
body: If a per-client resource exists, only that resource is evaluated and the 'Clients' all-resource is never checked. For example, a per-client VIEW permission removes a MANAGE grant the admin has through an all-clients permission, because the fallback only runs when no specific resource exists. Note that the caller's `canManage` short-circuit does not cover this case.

title: Per-client resource shadows all-clients permission
body: When a client-specific resource exists (created by any permission for that client, e.g. one granting only CONFIGURE), only that resource is evaluated and the 'Clients' all-resource permission is never consulted. An admin holding an all-clients MANAGE/VIEW permission is denied on that client as soon as someone adds an unrelated per-client permission. The fallback should also evaluate the type resource, as UserPermissionsV2 does.

title: Removal listener now runs in V2 and throws UnsupportedOperationException
body: The listener is gated on ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ, but management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever V2 is enabled. If both features are enabled, deleting a client calls ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled, which throws UnsupportedOperationException. The client deletion then fails.

title: getClientsWithPermission includes the 'Clients' type resource
