The cache is process-wide, so the first fallback result is stored and reused for everyone. Example: an `:es` user on site A (default `:fr`) hits a key missing in `es`, and the French text is cached. An `:es` user on site B (default `:de`) then gets French instead of German. After an admin changes `default_locale`, stale fallback text is served until `I18n.reload!`.

A 'translation missing' result, or an `en` result produced before the site locale was loaded, is also cached permanently. The cache key should include the fallback chain (or at least `SiteSetting.default_locale`), or fallback results should not be cached.

title: Fallback locales are only loaded in the controller before_filter
body:
Translations are lazy-loaded per locale. `translate` only calls `load_locale(config.locale)`. The fallback locales (site default and `:en`) are loaded only by `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` in `ApplicationController#set_locale`.

Any code path that translates outside a controller request gets no loaded fallbacks. That includes Sidekiq jobs, mailers run from jobs, rake tasks, and code that sets `I18n.locale` or uses `I18n.with_locale`. When `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` iterates over those unloaded locales it finds nothing and returns 'translation missing'. Because of the LRU cache, that result is then stuck for the process.

The fallback chain should be ensured inside `translate` (e.g. `I18n.fallbacks[config.locale].each { |l| ensure_loaded!(l) }`) rather than only in a controller filter.

title: FallbackLocaleList does not normalize locale to a symbol
body:
`I18n::Locale::Fallbacks` normally calls `to_sym` on the locale it is given; this replacement does not. When a caller passes `locale: 'en'` (a String), the result is `['en', :fr, :en]`. `uniq` does not remove the duplicate, so the same locale is looked up twice.

In `ensure_loaded!` a string locale would also miss the `@loaded_locales.include?` check, which stores symbols. Use `[locale.to_sym, ...]` (guarding for nil) before `uniq`.

title: No tests for the new fallback behaviour
Denial cache key omits identity type, so anonymous denials also deny the renderer
body:
The denial key is built from `checkReq.UserUID`, the raw id parsed from the subject, and does not include `checkReq.IdentityType`. Different identity types can share that id. Anonymous (`anonymous:0`) and the render service (`render:0`) both parse to UserUID "0".

If an anonymous user is denied `dashboards:read` on dashboard X, the entry `<ns>.perm_0_dashboards:read_X_<folder>` is cached. A renderer check for X within the next 30s then hits that entry and is denied, even though `getRendererPermissions` would grant `*`. This breaks alert screenshots and reports. The reverse also applies: renderer denials leak to anonymous checks.

Include the identity type in the key, or the resolved internal user UID for users and service accounts.

title: Ambiguous '_' separator in denial key causes collisions between different resources
body:
`userPermDenialCacheKey` joins name and parent folder with `_`. Grafana dashboard and folder UIDs may themselves contain underscores, so distinct (name, parent) pairs map to the same key. For example, dashboard `abc` in folder `def_ghi` and dashboard `abc_def` in folder `ghi` both produce `..._abc_def_ghi`.

A denial on one resource then wrongly denies the other for the cache TTL.

The key also reuses the `.perm_` prefix of `userPermCacheKey` in the same underlying cache, which makes the key spaces harder to reason about.

Use a separator that cannot appear in UIDs, or encode or length-prefix the components, and use a distinct prefix such as `.perm_denial_`.

title: Denial cache is consulted before the fresh DB re-query, re-introducing stale denials
Every not-allowed Check now triggers a full permission DB query
body:
Previously a cached permission map answered both allows and denials. Now any Check whose cached scopes don't grant access falls through to `getIdentityPermissions`, which always runs `permissionStore.GetUserPermissions` against the DB. The denial cache is keyed per (name, folder), so it only protects repeat checks of the same resource.

A user with restricted access who triggers checks over many distinct resources pays one permission query per unseen denied resource. This happens with search results filtered item by item, or batch checks over hundreds of dashboards. Singleflight only dedupes concurrent identical calls.

This is a significant DB load amplification compared to before.

title: Denial-cache test seeds a non-granting permission, so it passes without the denial cache
body:
The comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked", but the seeded map is `{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`. `checkPermission` treats a false value as no access.

Without the denial cache, the flow would still end in a deny. The cached perms don't allow access, the fallback DB query on the default fakeStore returns no permissions, and the result is `Allowed: false`. The test therefore passes regardless of whether the denial cache works.

The value should be `true` so that only the denial entry explains the deny. There is also no test that a DB-confirmed denial actually writes a denial entry.

title: Disabling the client-side cache in-proc makes every Check deserialize full cached permission maps
body:
With `NoopCache` on the in-proc client, every access check goes through the in-proc gRPC server. Each one performs several cache `Get`s, and each `Get` JSON-unmarshals its value: the denial entry, the user identifiers, and the full scope map for the action, which can contain thousands of entries for large instances.

Previously the authlib client cached per-check results. For hot paths such as batch or item checks this adds noticeable CPU and allocation overhead per request.

Meanwhile the remote/cloud client (line 162) still caches results, including denials, for 30s, so the newly-created-resource problem this PR targets remains in cloud mode.

title: Denial cache key omits identity type, so anonymous and render identities share denials
body:
The denial key is built from namespace, `checkReq.UserUID`, action, name and parent folder. The identity type is not part of it.

Anonymous (`anonymous:0`) and the render service (`render:0`) both parse to UserUID "0", so they get the same denial key. If an anonymous Check on a dashboard is denied, the entry is cached for 30s. A following `render:0` Check for `dashboards:read` on that dashboard then hits the denial cache and is refused, even though the renderer is meant to be granted read on everything. Image rendering breaks for that window.

The reverse also happens. The renderer is denied every non-read action, so a renderer denial can block an anonymous identity whose configured role (e.g. Editor) should allow the action.

Fix: include the identity type in the denial key (and ideally the resolved user UID), or skip the denial cache for render/anonymous.

title: Ambiguous '_' delimiter in denial cache key lets different resources collide
body:
`userPermDenialCacheKey` joins userUID, action, name and parent with "_". Grafana dashboard and folder UIDs may contain underscores, so different requests can produce the same key.

Example: dashboard `a_b` in folder `c` and dashboard `a` in folder `b_c` both map to `<ns>.perm_<uid>_<action>_a_b_c`. A cached denial for one makes Check return `Allowed:false` for the other for up to 30s, without ever looking at the user's permissions.

The key also reuses the `.perm_` prefix of `userPermCacheKey`, which mixes two value types (bool vs map) in the same key space.

Fix: use a distinct prefix and an unambiguous encoding, such as a separator that cannot appear in UIDs, length-prefixing, or hashing the tuple.

title: Every denied check on a new resource now forces a full DB permission fetch
body:
Before this change, a cached permission set answered Check entirely from cache. Now, when the cached set does not allow the request, Check always calls `getIdentityPermissions`. That path no longer consults `permCache` and re-runs the permission store query, plus basic-role and team lookups once those 30s caches expire.

The denial cache only short-circuits repeats of the exact same (user, action, name, folder) tuple. So each distinct resource a user cannot access costs one DB round trip, and singleflight only merges concurrent calls.

For anonymous access (one shared permission set for all anonymous users), requests for many distinct or random dashboard UIDs each trigger a DB query and each add a new denial-cache entry. That is a cheap load-amplification path compared to before.

Possible mitigations: rate-limit or bound the fallback, e.g. only re-query if the cached perms are older than some threshold, or refresh once per user/action rather than per resource.

title: Denial-cache test seeds a non-granting permission, so it passes without the denial cache
body:
The test "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" says it sets an allowing permission "to prove this is not checked". It actually stores `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`. `checkPermission` treats a false value as not granted.

Without the denial cache, the flow would be: cached perms deny, the DB fallback runs, the default `fakeStore` returns no permissions, and the result is deny. So the test passes whether or not the denial cache works.

The value should be `true`, so the cached perms would allow access and only the denial entry can produce `Allowed:false`.

There is also no test that a denial is written to `permDenialCache` after a DB-backed deny, and none for the collision cases above.

title: Denial cache key omits identity type, so render:0 and anonymous:0 share deny entries
body:
`userPermDenialCacheKey` is built from `checkReq.UserUID` only; the identity type is not part of the key. The renderer identity (`render:0`) and the anonymous identity (`anonymous:0`) both parse to UserUID "0", so they produce identical denial keys.

If anonymous is denied `dashboards:read` on dashboard X, that cached deny is then returned for the renderer's `dashboards:read` check on X, for up to 30s. The denial cache is consulted before `getRendererPermissions` runs, and that function grants `*` for reads. Rendering then fails even though the renderer is always supposed to be allowed. The reverse also happens: renderer denials poison anonymous checks.

Include the identity type (or the full subject) in the denial key.

title: Un-invalidated denial cache short-circuits the new DB fallback and reintroduces the staleness the PR targets
body:
The denial cache is checked before both the cached permissions and the DB requery. It is never invalidated when permissions change.

Any Check that is denied before a grant lands is answered `Allowed: false` for the full 30s TTL without consulting the DB. This includes a GET on a UID before the dashboard or folder is created, e.g. an import or uniqueness probe, a UI poll, or a request racing the creator's permission write.

The PR's stated goal is that a creator can immediately fetch what they just created. For any resource that was checked before its permission was written, the denial cache defeats exactly that, because the fallback to the DB is skipped.

Consider one of:
- not caching denials for specific names;
- keeping the denial TTL much shorter;
- invalidating or bypassing the denial entry when permissions or resources are written.

title: Every new denied (name, folder) pair now forces a full permission DB query
body:
`getUserPermissions` and `getAnonymousPermissions` no longer read `permCache`. On a cached deny, `Check` therefore always calls `getIdentityPermissions`, which runs `permissionStore.GetUserPermissions` against the DB.

Previously, all denials for a user and action were answered from the 30s permission cache. Now each distinct resource name (and parent folder) that a user lacks access to costs one DB permission query before its denial entry is written. Singleflight only dedups concurrent identical requests.

A restricted user, or a client issuing GETs for many arbitrary or non-existent names, turns each request into a DB query. This is a load amplification compared to before. The per-name keys also grow the local cache without bound within the TTL window.

Consider rate-limiting the refresh per user and action, e.g. refresh the permission set at most once per short interval, instead of once per denied resource.

title: Ambiguous '_' delimiter in denial cache key causes collisions between different resources
body:
The key is `namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent`. Dashboard and folder UIDs may contain underscores, so different (name, parent) pairs can map to the same key. For example, name="a_b" with parent="c" and name="a" with parent="b_c" both produce `..._a_b_c`.

A denial for one resource is then returned for an unrelated resource the user may actually have access to, for 30s. Use a delimiter that cannot appear in UIDs, or encode or length-prefix the components.

title: Denial-cache test passes even without the denial cache
body:
The test claims to "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked", but it seeds `permCache` with `{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`. `checkPermission` treats a false value as no permission.

The default `fakeStore` from `setupService` also returns no permissions, so the DB fallback denies too. The test would pass if the denial-cache lookup in `Check` were removed entirely.

To actually exercise the short-circuit:
- seed `true`, or configure the fake store to grant dash1;
- assert that the store was not called.

There is also no test that a DB-confirmed denial is written to `permDenialCache`, or that a subsequent Check skips the DB.

title: Silence menu item does nothing in the new list view
body:
AlertRuleMenu now shows "Silence notifications" for Grafana prom rules, because `canSilence` is ORed with `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`. Clicking it calls `setShowSilenceDrawer(true)`.

The drawer is only rendered when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true. In the list view (GrafanaGroupLoader and FilterView), `rule` (the ruler rule) is now always undefined, so the drawer never opens.

Users with silence permissions see a menu item that silently does nothing. The new test only asserts the item exists and never clicks it. The drawer needs to work from the prom rule, or the item should be hidden when no ruler rule is available.

title: Delete and Pause actions are lost in the list view despite being computed from promRule
body:
`canDelete` and `canPause` are now ORed with the Grafana prom-rule abilities. However, the menu items are still gated on the ruler rule:
- `canDelete && rulerRule`
- `canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`

RuleActionsButtons.V2 no longer passes a ruler rule in the list view. As a result, users with delete or update permissions on the folder can no longer delete or pause/resume rules from the list. Previously they could, because the ruler rule was fetched.

The prom-based Delete/Pause abilities are effectively dead code. GrafanaGroupLoader.test ("exactly 4 menu items" while granting AlertingRuleDelete) locks this regression in. Either support delete/pause from the prom rule (fetch the ruler rule lazily on click) or stop computing these abilities from promRule.

title: skipToken path returns Duplicate as supported+allowed, leaking into non-Grafana rules
body:
When `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` gets `skipToken`, `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined)` runs. Then `useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable` returns `loading: false`, so `MaybeSupported = AlwaysSupported` and `duplicateSupported = true`.

`Duplicate` therefore becomes `[true, hasPermission(AlertingRuleCreate)]` even though there is no rule.

AlertRuleMenu ORs this with the ruler ability. For data-source rules (Mimir/Loki/vanilla Prometheus), or any case where `promRule` is not a Grafana rule, the Duplicate item now appears for any user with Grafana `alert.rules:create`. This happens even when the ruler is unavailable or the user lacks external-rule write permission.

The skip case should return all-NotSupported abilities. The RulesTable cloud-rule tests miss this because `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` is mocked to always return `[false,false]`.

title: Federated rule groups no longer treated as immutable in legacy ability hook
body:
`useAllAlertRuleAbilities(CombinedRule)` previously computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` and marked federated Mimir groups as immutable, so Update, Delete and Pause were not supported.

It now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, which hardcodes `isFederated = false` with a TODO. Every consumer of `useAlertRuleAbility`/`useAlertRuleAbilities` (legacy rule list, RuleDetails, rule viewer actions) will now offer Edit/Delete on federated rule groups.

That is a behavioural regression. Editing such groups through the UI is unsupported and can drop `source_tenants`. The federated check should be preserved, e.g. by passing the group or computing it in the CombinedRule wrapper.

title: Missing React key on GrafanaRuleListItem in rules.map
body:
The previous `GrafanaRuleLoader` was rendered with `key={key}`. The replacement `<GrafanaRuleListItem ... />` inside `rules.map(...)` has no `key` prop, even though `key` is destructured right above and used for the other branches.

Consequences:
- React emits a missing-key warning.
- Reconciliation falls back to index, which can mix up component state (open menus, delete modals, silence drawer state) between items.

Add `key={key}`.

title: Rule view link lost the returnTo parameter
body:
The removed implementation built the link as `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`, { returnTo: createReturnTo() })`. The new component drops `returnTo`.

Navigating from the (filtered) list to a rule's detail page no longer returns the user to the same list/filter state via the back/return link. This is a UX regression unrelated to removing the ruler request.

title: Prom-based abilities exclude Grafana recording rules from Export/Pause, unlike the ruler version
body:
In `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, `ModifyExport`, `Pause` and `Restore` are gated on `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)`, which includes Grafana recording rules.

The new `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` gates them on `prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)`. So Grafana-managed recording rules lose Export (and Pause) in the list view, while they keep them in the rule viewer, where the ruler rule is available.

The two ability sources should agree. Use `prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)` for these actions.

title: Provisioned detection for prom rules depends on a field not added server-side in this PR
body:
`isProvisionedPromRule` relies on the newly typed `provenance` field of `GrafanaPromRuleDTO`. The list view now uses it to decide whether Edit, Update and Delete are immutable, and AlertRuleMenu ORs it with the ruler result.

This PR changes no backend code. If the Grafana Prometheus-compatible rules endpoint does not serialize `provenance`, provisioned rules will be reported as mutable: the Edit button will show for them in the list. Because of the OR, ruler-side immutability can also be overridden in the rule viewer.

Please confirm the API returns this field, or add backend support and a test.

title: Legacy ability hook can now throw during render via groupIdentifier.fromCombinedRule
body:
`useAllAlertRuleAbilities` previously derived the source name with `getRulesSourceName`, which never throws. It now calls `groupIdentifier.fromCombinedRule(rule)`.

For data-source rules that function resolves the datasource UID and throws when the datasource cannot be found. That is why the tests had to be changed to pass a real `mimirDs`.

Any CombinedRule whose rulesSource isn't resolvable (e.g. a removed or renamed datasource, or test fixtures) now crashes the component tree instead of degrading gracefully.

title: Stale docstring still says the group is loaded from Ruler endpoints
body:
The component comment still reads "Loads an evaluation group from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints." The `expectedRulesCount` prop doc also still refers to the Ruler response.

The Ruler query was removed in this PR and only the Prometheus endpoint is used. The comments should be updated to avoid misleading future maintainers.

title: "Silence notifications" menu item does nothing in the new list view
body: The list view now passes only `promRule` to `RuleActionsButtons`, so `rule` (the ruler rule) is undefined. `AlertRuleMenu` still shows "Silence notifications" whenever `canSilence` is true, and here that comes from `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`. The click handler sets `showSilenceDrawer`, but the drawer only renders when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true. With no ruler rule, the drawer never opens and the menu item is a dead button. The new GrafanaGroupLoader test asserts the item is present but never clicks it, so this is not caught. The drawer needs to work from the prom rule (UID/labels), or the item should be hidden when it can't be acted on.

title: Delete and Pause actions silently disappear from the list view
body: `canDelete`/`canPause` can now be true via the prom-rule abilities. Rendering, however, still requires a ruler rule: `canDelete && rulerRule` here, and `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` for Pause at line 123. The list view no longer loads ruler rules, so users with delete/update permission can no longer delete or pause/resume Grafana rules from the list. The new GrafanaGroupLoader test grants AlertingRuleDelete/Update yet asserts exactly 4 menu items, which locks in this regression. Delete and Pause should work from a GrafanaRuleIdentifier/prom rule (e.g. fetch the ruler rule on demand), or the regression should be made explicit.

title: skipToken path grants Duplicate based on Grafana create permission, leaking into data-source rules
body: When `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` gets `skipToken` (rule is undefined), `loading` is false and `isPluginProvided` is false. That makes `duplicateSupported` true, so Duplicate becomes `[true, ctx.hasPermission(AlertingRuleCreate)]`. `AlertRuleMenu` ORs this with the ruler abilities. For any data-source (cloud) rule, which always takes the skipToken path, "Duplicate" is therefore shown whenever the user has the Grafana rule-create permission. This happens even when the ruler-based check says it is unsupported (ruler unavailable/loading) or not allowed (no external write permission). This affects the existing RulesTable and rule viewer, not just the new list. A skipped rule should return NotSupported for every action. RulesTable tests mock the prom hook to `[false,false]` for cloud rules, which hides this.

title: Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable
body: `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` previously computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` from the CombinedRule. It now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, which hardcodes `isFederated = false`. Every consumer of `useAlertRuleAbility`/`useAlertRuleAbilities` loses that guard, including the default (non-V2) RulesTable list and rule details. Edit/Delete/Pause are now offered for Mimir federated rule groups (`source_tenants`). Editing those groups through the Grafana form is not supported and risks rewriting the group without its federation settings. The CombinedRule's group is still available in `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` and should be used to keep the check.

title: Prom-based abilities exclude Grafana recording rules from Export/Pause/Restore
body: The ruler-based hook gates ModifyExport/Pause/Restore/DeletePermanently on `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)`, which covers any Grafana-managed rule including recording rules. The new prom-based hook gates them on `prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` instead. In the list view only the prom path is evaluated, so Grafana recording rules lose the "Export" menu entry and the pause ability. The two hooks now disagree for the same rule. Use `prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)` for these actions to keep parity, and keep `alertingRule` only for Silence.

title: Missing React key for Grafana rule items in filtered list
body: The previous `GrafanaRuleLoader` received `key={key}`. The replacement `<GrafanaRuleListItem ... />` inside `rules.map` has no key, although `key` is destructured on the line above for exactly this purpose and the other branches still pass it. React will emit missing-key warnings and fall back to index-based reconciliation for these stateful items, which hold delete-modal and silence-drawer state.

title: Rule detail link no longer carries returnTo
body: The removed implementation built the link as `createRelativeUrl('/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view', { returnTo: createReturnTo() })`. The new component drops `returnTo`. Navigating from the list (including a filtered search) to a rule's detail page no longer lets the viewer return to the same list state/filters, which is a UX regression unrelated to removing ruler calls.

title: Stale doc comment says group is loaded from Ruler endpoint
body: The JSDoc still says the component "Loads an evaluation group from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints", but this PR removes the ruler query and it now only uses the Prometheus endpoint. The comment in `prometheusGroupsGenerator.ts` ("preload ruler rules", variable `cacheAndRulerPreload`) is similarly stale now that the ruler prefetch was removed.

title: "Silence notifications" menu item does nothing in the list view
body:
The list view now renders `RuleActionsButtons` with only `promRule` and no ruler rule. `AlertRuleMenu` still shows "Silence notifications", because `canSilence` is true via `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`. Clicking it calls `setShowSilenceDrawer(true)`.

However, the drawer only renders when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) && showSilenceDrawer`. Since `rule` is undefined here, `SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer` is never mounted and the click is a silent no-op.

The new GrafanaGroupLoader test checks that the silence item exists but never clicks it, so the bug is not caught. The drawer needs to work from the prom rule (e.g. by uid/labels), or the menu item should be hidden when no ruler rule is available.

title: skipToken still reports Duplicate as supported, enabling Duplicate for data-source rules via Grafana permissions
body:
With `skipToken`, `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` receives `undefined`. In that case `useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable` returns `loading: false`, so `MaybeSupported` becomes `AlwaysSupported`. Duplicate then resolves to `toAbility(true, AlertingRuleCreate)`, meaning `[true, true]` for any user with the global Grafana rule create permission.

`AlertRuleMenu` ORs this with the ruler result: `canDuplicate = rulerDuplicate || grafanaDuplicate`. For a data-source-managed rule (which always gets skipToken), Duplicate is therefore shown whenever the user can create Grafana rules. This holds even when the ruler is unavailable (e.g. vanilla Prometheus) or the user lacks external rule write permission. It affects the rule viewer, RulesTable and the v2 list.

When the rule is skipped, the hook should return `[false, false]` for every action.

title: Delete and Pause actions silently disappear from the list view
body:
Both menu items still require a ruler rule:
- Pause: `canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) && ...` (line 123)
- Delete: `canDelete && rulerRule`

The list view (`GrafanaRuleListItem`) no longer passes a ruler rule. So even when the prom-based abilities say the user can pause or delete, these items are never rendered. Previously both actions were available from the list.

`canPause` also still feeds `showDivider`, so a divider can appear without a pause item. The new GrafanaGroupLoader test grants delete permissions yet asserts exactly 4 menu items, which locks this regression in.

Either support pause/delete from the prom rule (identifier + groupIdentifier are available) or document the removal explicitly.

title: Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable
body:
`useAllAlertRuleAbilities` used to compute `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`, which made Mimir federated groups (those with `source_tenants`) non-editable and non-deletable.

It now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, which hardcodes `const isFederated = false`. All existing consumers of `useAllAlertRuleAbilities`/`useAlertRuleAbility` (rule details, RulesTable, rule viewer) will now offer Update/Delete/Pause for federated rules. Editing those through the UI was previously blocked deliberately.

The federated check should be kept in the CombinedRule path, e.g. by passing the group or a flag.

title: Prom-based abilities exclude Grafana recording rules from Export/Pause/Restore
body:
The ruler version gates ModifyExport, Pause, Restore and DeletePermanently on `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)`, which is true for any Grafana-managed rule including recording rules.

The new prom version uses `isAlertingRule = prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` for all of these, despite the comment saying "All GrafanaPromRuleDTO rules are Grafana-managed by definition".

In the list view, which now relies only on these prom abilities, Grafana recording rules lose the Export menu item, and Pause/Restore are reported as unsupported. Only Silence should be restricted to alerting rules; the others should use `prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)`.

title: Missing React `key` on Grafana rule items in filtered list
body:
The previous `<GrafanaRuleLoader key={key} .../>` was replaced with `<GrafanaRuleListItem .../>` without carrying over `key={key}`. The other branches (`DataSourceRuleLoader`, `UnknownRuleListItem`) still set it.

Grafana-origin items in this `rules.map` therefore have no key. React will emit "Each child in a list should have a unique key" warnings and fall back to index-based reconciliation, which can mis-associate per-item state (open menus, modals, silence drawer) as the list changes.

Add `key={key}` back.

title: Rule view link lost the `returnTo` parameter
body:
The removed implementation built the rule link as `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`, { returnTo })` using `createReturnTo()`. The new component drops `returnTo`.

After opening a rule from the list (including a filtered search), the rule viewer's back navigation can no longer return the user to the same list/filter state. This is a UX regression unrelated to removing ruler requests.

title: Stale doc comment says the group is loaded from the Ruler endpoint
body:
The JSDoc still reads "Loads an evaluation group from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints", but this PR removed the ruler query. The component now only uses `useGetGrafanaGroupsQuery`.

The `expectedRulesCount` comment also still refers to the Ruler response. Similarly, `prometheusGroupsGenerator.ts` still says "preload ruler rules" and names the variable `cacheAndRulerPreload`, though no ruler prefetch happens anymore.

title: Template variables and ad hoc filters are applied twice in the split path
body:
`runSplitQuery` now runs `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)` on every target. Each sub-request is built as `{ ...request, range, targets }`, so it still carries `scopedVars` and `filters`. `datasource.runQuery()` then calls `super.query()` (DataSourceWithBackend), which runs `applyTemplateVariables(q, request.scopedVars, request.filters)` again on the already-interpolated targets.

`applyTemplateVariables` is not idempotent:
- `addAdHocFilters` → `addLabelToQuery` only de-duplicates when the filter goes into the stream selector. When the query has a parser or existing label filters, it appends ` | key=`value`` with no duplicate check. For example, `{app="x"} | json` with an ad hoc filter `level=error` becomes `{app="x"} | json | level=`error` | level=`error``. That query is what reaches Loki and what users see in the query inspector.
- A second `templateSrv.replace` pass also re-interpolates variable values. Suppose a textbox line-filter value contains `$host` and `host` is also a dashboard variable; the literal text gets substituted on the second pass.

Before this PR, interpolation happened only once, in `super.query`. Possible fixes: interpolate only what the splitting logic needs (e.g. `step` for `calculateStep`), or strip `filters` from the request passed downstream after interpolating.

title: Shard path now interpolates and applies ad hoc filters three times
body:
`runShardSplitQuery` now calls `applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)`. The previous `interpolateVariablesInQueries` call did not pass filters, so ad hoc filters were not applied at this stage before.

It then passes `{ ...request, targets }` (with `filters` intact) to `runSplitQuery`. That function now calls `applyTemplateVariables` again on every sub-request. `runQuery` → `super.query` applies it a third time.

For queries with a parser or label filters, each ad hoc filter is appended three times to the expression sent to Loki. Variable values are also re-templated twice. The updated test asserting `applyTemplateVariables` was called 5 times (1 + 4 sub-requests) codifies this redundant re-interpolation instead of catching it. Interpolation should happen once, e.g. by clearing `filters` on the request handed to `runSplitQuery`, or by having `runSplitQuery` skip interpolation when called from the shard path.

title: New interpolation test asserts `$__auto` frontend substitution that doesn't happen in production
body:
The new test 'Interpolates queries before execution' stubs `templateSrv.replace` to unconditionally replace `$__auto` with `5m`. It then asserts that the expression sent to `runQuery` is `count_over_time({a="b"}[5m])`. The real `LokiDatasource.applyTemplateVariables` deliberately strips `__auto` (and `__range*`, `__interval*`) from scopedVars so these are interpolated on the backend. In production `$__auto` stays as-is.

The test therefore documents behaviour that doesn't exist. The same pattern is copied into `shardQuerySplitting.test.ts` (around line 88). Neither test covers the realistic case: a dashboard variable in `step` affecting `calculateStep` grouping, or ad hoc filters combined with splitting. As a result they would not catch the duplicated-filter regression.

title: Empty-expr filter now runs before interpolation; a variable that resolves to empty can leave the panel loading forever
body:
`runShardSplitQuery` used to interpolate first (`interpolateVariablesInQueries`) and then drop queries with an empty `expr`. The PR reverses this: `.filter((query) => query.expr)` checks the raw expression and only then calls `applyTemplateVariables`.

A target such as `$query`, where the variable resolves to an empty string, now passes the filter and becomes `expr: ''`. The failure path:
- `requestSupportsSharding([query])` is false for an empty expr, so the query lands in the non-shard `otherQueries` group.
- `runSplitQuery` is called for that group and filters it out, because its `expr` is now empty.
- `runSplitGroupedQueries` receives an empty `requests` array. There `requests.filter(...)[0].partition` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`.
- The throw happens synchronously inside the `groupTargetsByQueryType(...).then(...)` callback. It becomes an unhandled promise rejection, and the returned Observable never emits or completes.

Result: any panel mixing a shardable query with a query whose variable resolves to empty hangs in the loading state. Filter on `expr` after interpolating, in both `runShardSplitQuery` and `runSplitQuery`, so empty interpolated queries are dropped. Consider also guarding `runSplitGroupedQueries` against an empty `requests` array.

title: Ad-hoc filters and template variables are applied repeatedly to the same query
body:
`runSplitQuery` now calls `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)`. The sub-requests it builds keep `request.filters` and are passed to `datasource.runQuery`, which goes through `DataSourceWithBackend.query` and calls `applyTemplateVariables(q, scopedVars, request.filters)` again. On the sharding path it happens a third time: `runShardSplitQuery` also applies the variables and filters, then forwards the request, filters included, into `runSplitQuery`.

Loki's `applyTemplateVariables` adds ad-hoc filters to the expression. Filters added to the stream selector are de-duplicated. For queries with a parser or label filter, though, `addFilterAsLabelFilter` appends a new `| key=`value`` stage on every pass, with no de-duplication. For example, `{app="x"} | json` with ad-hoc filter `level=error` becomes `{app="x"} | json | level=`error` | level=`error`` (three copies on the shard path). The queries sent and shown in the inspector are bloated, and they differ from what the non-split path produces.

Re-running `templateSrv.replace` on already-interpolated text can also re-expand `$name` sequences that came from variable values. The updated shard test expecting `applyTemplateVariables` to be called 5 times encodes this redundant work.

Interpolate once and strip `filters` (or otherwise mark the request as already interpolated) on the sub-requests passed down to `runSplitQuery` and `runQuery`.

title: New interpolation test does not cover the behaviour the fix targets and relies on unrealistic `$__auto` replacement
body:
The test only checks that the targets passed to the mocked `runQuery` are interpolated. In production, `runQuery` (via `DataSourceWithBackend.query`) already interpolated targets before this change. So the assertion does not exercise what the PR actually fixes: `calculateStep`, `isLogsQuery` and `querySupportsSplitting` now see interpolated values, e.g. a `$step` variable changing the step-aligned partition boundaries.

The mock `replace` also rewrites `$__auto` to `5m` unconditionally. The real `applyTemplateVariables` deliberately removes `__auto` from scopedVars so the backend interpolates it, so the test asserts frontend behaviour that never happens. The same pattern is copied into `shardQuerySplitting.test.ts`.

Assert on the computed ranges or grouping for an interpolated `step` instead, and use a regular dashboard variable in place of `$__auto`.

title: Queries that interpolate to an empty expr are no longer dropped, which can leave the shard observable hanging
body:
The old code interpolated first and then ran `.filter((query) => query.expr)`. The new code filters on the raw `expr` and only then calls `applyTemplateVariables`. A query such as `expr: '$var'` whose variable resolves to an empty string now passes the filter and comes out with `expr: ''`.

What happens next:
- `groupTargetsByQueryType` puts it in the `otherQueries` group, because `requestSupportsSharding` rejects empty exprs.
- `runNextRequest` calls `runSplitQuery` with that group. `runSplitQuery` filters out empty exprs, so `requests` is `[]`.
- `runSplitGroupedQueries` then throws synchronously at `requests.filter(...)[0].partition` (querySplitting.ts line 96).
- The throw happens inside the `.then()` of `groupTargetsByQueryType`, so it becomes an unhandled promise rejection. The subscriber is never completed or errored, and the panel stays in loading state forever.

This triggers when the request has a shardable query plus a non-shardable query whose variable is empty. Fix: filter `query.expr` after interpolation, here and in `runSplitQuery`, as the previous implementation did.

title: applyTemplateVariables (including ad-hoc filters) now runs multiple times per query
body:
`runSplitQuery` now calls `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)`. Each sub-request then goes through `datasource.runQuery` → `DataSourceWithBackend.query`, which calls `applyTemplateVariables` again with the same `request.filters`. In the shard path, `runShardSplitQuery` interpolates as well, so each query is processed three times.

Loki's `applyTemplateVariables` is not idempotent: it calls `addAdHocFilters`, which appends ad-hoc filters to the expression. Stream-selector placement de-duplicates via `labelExists`. For queries with a parser (e.g. `{app="x"} | json`), filters go through `addFilterAsLabelFilter`, which has no dedup. The result is queries like `| level=`error` | level=`error` | level=`error`` sent to Loki and shown in the inspector.

Variable values containing `$name` text, and ad-hoc filter values, are also re-interpolated on each pass. The previous shard code deliberately used `interpolateVariablesInQueries` without filters, leaving ad-hoc filter application to the backend-query step.

The updated test asserting `applyTemplateVariables` is called 5 times codifies this redundant processing. Consider interpolating only variables (no `filters`) here, or marking targets as already interpolated so later passes skip ad-hoc injection.

title: New interpolation test relies on a mock that interpolates `$__auto`, which the real code never does
body:
The test's `replace` mock replaces `$__auto` unconditionally and ignores the scopedVars passed in. The real `LokiDatasource.applyTemplateVariables` explicitly strips `__auto`, `__interval`, `__range`, etc. from scopedVars so they pass through to the backend. In production, `$__auto` therefore stays uninterpolated at this stage.

The test asserts behaviour that cannot happen with the real template service. It also does not check what the change is supposed to fix: that splitting decisions (log vs. metric partitioning, `calculateStep` grouping by `step`) are made on interpolated values.

The same pattern is copied into `shardQuerySplitting.test.ts`. Use a regular dashboard variable and assert on the grouping or partition outcome instead.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, so logs sent through it are never recorded
body: `TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()`, a new, unrelated instance. `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` now logs only via `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`. As a result, the "Plugin Request Completed" entry never shows up in the injected TestLogger's `InfoLogs`/`ErrorLogs`. Any test that checks that this middleware logs, or checks the status/error params it logs, will see zero calls. The fake should return itself, or a logger sharing the same `Logs` storage, so that context-derived logs stay observable in tests.

title: Moving pluginId/endpoint/dsUID/uname into context-only logging is untested and relies on middleware order
body: `LoggerMiddleware` no longer logs `pluginId`, `endpoint`, `uname`, `dsName`, `dsUID` or `traceID` explicitly. These fields now appear on the `grafana-data-egress` log line only if `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` ran earlier in the chain and stored them via `log.WithContextualAttributes`. The PR adds no tests for the new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware`, and none checking that the final log line still has these fields. If the middleware is reordered, omitted by another caller of `NewLoggerMiddleware`, or `FromContext` stops picking up the attributes, the egress log silently loses the plugin and datasource identifiers. A test that runs the real chain and asserts the logged key/values would catch such a regression.

title: Single MetricsMiddleware instance has its `next` field overwritten on every request (data race)
body:
`NewMetricsMiddleware` creates one `*MetricsMiddleware` up front. The returned `ClientMiddlewareFunc` then sets `imw.next = next` and returns that same shared instance.

`client.Decorator` rebuilds the middleware chain on every QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth and CollectMetrics call through `clientFromMiddlewares`. So concurrent plugin requests write `imw.next` at the same time other goroutines read it via `m.next.QueryData(...)` and similar calls. That is a data race the race detector will flag, and request A may end up running request B's downstream chain.

This pattern was carried over unchanged from `NewInstrumentationMiddleware`. Since this code is being reworked anyway, the middleware should return a fresh struct per call instead, e.g. `&MetricsMiddleware{pluginMetrics: imw.pluginMetrics, pluginRegistry: imw.pluginRegistry, next: next}`.

title: LoggerMiddleware now silently depends on ContextualLoggerMiddleware running before it
body:
`logRequest` used to add `pluginId`, `endpoint`, `uname`, `dsName`, `dsUID` and `traceID` to the "Plugin Request Completed" (`grafana-data-egress`) log line itself. It now relies entirely on `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)` and on attributes that `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` placed in the context earlier in the chain.

If `NewLoggerMiddleware` is used without `NewContextualLoggerMiddleware` ahead of it, those identifying fields disappear from the egress log with no error. That includes tests, enterprise or other compositions, and any future reordering of `CreateMiddlewares`.

The old doc note saying the instrumentation middleware must sit at the top of the stack was removed, and no replacement documents the new ordering requirement. Either document the requirement on `NewLoggerMiddleware`/`CreateMiddlewares`, or keep the explicit fields in the logger middleware.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a new empty logger, so logged calls cannot be asserted
body:
`TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()`, a fresh instance, not the receiver. `LoggerMiddleware` now always logs through `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`.

A test that injects a `TestLogger` and checks `InfoLogs.Calls`, `Message` or `Ctx` will therefore always see zero calls. The fake cannot be used to verify the middleware's logging. Returning `f`, or a logger that shares the recorded state, would make the fake usable for this purpose.

title: New ContextualLoggerMiddleware and changed log composition are untested
body:
The PR adds a new middleware and moves the source of the egress log's identifying fields (pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName, dsUID, traceID) from explicit parameters to context-derived attributes.

No test checks either of these:
- that `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` attaches the expected attributes for each endpoint;
- that the "Plugin Request Completed" log still carries them when the middlewares are chained in production order.

A regression here, such as a reordering or a missing attribute, would silently degrade the data-egress logs.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, so logs written through it are lost
body: `TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()` instead of the receiver `f`. `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` now logs via `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`, so with this fake the "Plugin Request Completed" call is recorded on a throwaway instance. The `InfoLogs`/`ErrorLogs` counters on the logger a test injected stay at zero. Any current or future test that checks the middleware's logging with this fake cannot observe the log call. Returning `f`, or a child that shares the parent's `Logs` storage, would keep the fake usable for this path.

title: LoggerMiddleware now silently relies on ContextualLoggerMiddleware being earlier in the chain
body: `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` used to add `pluginId`, `endpoint`, `uname`, `dsName`, `dsUID` and `traceID` to the "Plugin Request Completed" (`grafana-data-egress`) log line itself. It now relies entirely on context attributes that `NewContextualLoggerMiddleware` sets upstream. `NewLoggerMiddleware` is exported and nothing enforces or documents this ordering. Any middleware stack built without `NewContextualLoggerMiddleware` before it (custom/enterprise stacks, tests, or a future reorder in `CreateMiddlewares`) will emit egress log lines without plugin or datasource identifiers, and nothing will fail. Consider documenting the dependency on `NewLoggerMiddleware`, or keeping a fallback that adds these fields when they are missing.

title: New ContextualLoggerMiddleware and the moved log attributes have no test coverage
body: This PR adds `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` and moves the plugin/datasource/user attributes out of both the old instrumentation middleware and `LoggerMiddleware`. No test checks that requests passing through the stack still carry `endpoint`, `pluginId`, `dsName`, `dsUID` and `uname` in the context. Nor does any test check that the `LoggerMiddleware` log line still includes them via `FromContext`. A regression here would drop identifying fields from production data-egress logs and no test would catch it.

title: Device is cached before the limit check, so the limit is bypassed after the first request
body: `tagDeviceUI` calls `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, ...)` before `CreateOrUpdateDevice`, and keeps the entry when that call returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. Only the first request from a new device over the limit is rejected. For the next ~29 minutes (cache TTL), `localCache.Get(key)` hits, `tagDeviceUI` returns nil, and `Anonymous.Authenticate` lets the device in. The device is never stored or counted, so a user who just reloads the page is admitted. The cache entry should only be set after a successful create/update, or removed on `ErrDeviceLimitReached`.

title: Check-then-insert race lets the device count exceed the limit
body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs `CountDevices` in one session and the INSERT/upsert in a separate session, with no transaction or locking. When the count is just under the limit, several concurrent requests from new devices (on one instance or across HA instances) can all see `count < deviceLimit` and all insert. The limit can therefore be exceeded by the level of concurrency. If it is meant as a hard cap, the check and insert need to be atomic, e.g. a conditional INSERT ... SELECT with the count in the WHERE clause, or a transaction with appropriate locking.

title: Device limit is trivially bypassed by omitting the device ID header
body: Enforcement depends on `TagDevice` returning `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. `TagDevice` returns nil early when the client-controlled `X-Grafana-Device-Id` header is missing (and also when the remote address can't be parsed). In both cases `Anonymous.Authenticate` succeeds. Any client that does not send the header (curl, scripts, a modified frontend) gets anonymous access regardless of the configured limit, and is never counted. If the limit is meant to be enforced, requests without a device ID should be handled explicitly once the limit is reached.

title: Device tagging moved into the request path unconditionally, even when no limit is set
body: The goroutine with its own timeout and panic recovery was replaced by a synchronous `TagDevice(ctx, ...)` call for every deployment, including the default `device_limit = 0`. Every anonymous request that misses the local cache now waits for a DB upsert before authentication completes. With a limit set, it also waits for an extra `COUNT(*)` over `anon_device`. The panic recovery was also dropped. Consider keeping the asynchronous path when `AnonymousDeviceLimit == 0` and only blocking when enforcement is needed.

title: DI wiring for AnonStore likely broken by the ProvideAnonDBStore signature change
body: `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` used to receive `anonstore.AnonStore` via dependency injection, so a provider for it (`anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` plus a bind) was registered in the wire set. `ProvideAnonDBStore` now requires an `int64`, which wire cannot supply, and the service no longer consumes `AnonStore`. `pkg/server/wire.go` is not updated in this PR. Wire generation will fail either on the unsatisfiable `int64` or on an unused provider, unless that registration is removed. Any other single-argument callers of `ProvideAnonDBStore` will also fail to compile.

title: New `device_limit` setting is undocumented and missing from the default/sample config
body: `[auth.anonymous] device_limit` is read here, but the PR adds no entry to `conf/defaults.ini` / `conf/sample.ini` and no documentation. Operators have no way to discover the option. Nothing tells them that 0 means unlimited, that devices are counted over a 30-day window, or that anonymous users over the limit are rejected at authentication.

title: anonymousDeviceLimit is inferred as type `undefined` on GrafanaBootConfig
body: `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` has no type annotation, so with strictNullChecks TypeScript infers the property type as `undefined` rather than `number | undefined`. It still satisfies `implements GrafanaConfig`, but consumers of `config.anonymousDeviceLimit` see a type that can never hold a number. The backend always sends an int64 (0 when unset), so the value is never actually undefined. Annotate it, e.g. `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;`.

title: Limit tests don't cover updating existing devices at the limit or the service/cache path
body: `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only checks that a second, new device is rejected. It does not check that an already-registered device can still be updated (the `updateDevice` happy path) once the limit is reached. No test exercises the limit through `AnonDeviceService.TagDevice` / `Anonymous.Authenticate`. Such a test would have caught that the local cache lets a rejected device through on its next request.

title: Device is cached before the limit check, so a rejected device is let in on its next request
body: `tagDeviceUI` calls `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, ...)` before `CreateOrUpdateDevice`, and it caches whether or not the call succeeds. When the store returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the first request is rejected in `Anonymous.Authenticate`. The device ID is now in the local cache, though, so every following request within the 29-minute TTL returns nil early from `tagDeviceUI` and authenticates. The limit therefore blocks only one request per device per cache period (per instance) and does not really enforce anything. The cache entry should be set only after a successful create/update, or the rejection should be cached and checked.

title: Device limit is bypassed by omitting the client-controlled X-Grafana-Device-Id header
body: `TagDevice` returns nil when the `X-Grafana-Device-Id` header is missing. It also returns nil when the remote IP cannot be parsed. In both cases `Anonymous.Authenticate` succeeds without any limit check. The header is fully client-controlled, so any client that leaves it out (curl, scripts, or a modified frontend) gets anonymous access no matter how many devices are already registered. Only cooperating UI clients are affected by the limit. If the limit is meant as an access control, requests without a device ID need a defined policy, such as rejecting them once the limit is enabled and reached.

title: Non-atomic count-then-insert lets the device limit be exceeded
body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs `CountDevices` and then, in a separate statement with no transaction or lock, runs the upsert. Concurrent requests from new devices, within one instance or across HA replicas, can all see `count < deviceLimit` and all insert. The stored device count can end up well above the configured limit. The check and the insert need to be atomic, for example a conditional INSERT ... SELECT with a count guard, or a transaction with appropriate locking.

title: Device tagging moved into the synchronous auth path for all deployments, adding a COUNT(*) per new device
body: Tagging used to run in a background goroutine. It now runs inline in `Authenticate` with the request context for every deployment, including the default `device_limit = 0`. On each local-cache miss the request waits for a DB upsert. When a limit is set, it also waits for a `SELECT COUNT(*) ... WHERE updated_at BETWEEN` over the whole anon_device table. The cache key is the client-supplied device ID, so a client sending random IDs forces these queries on every request and adds DB load and latency to anonymous auth. Consider keeping the async path when no limit is configured, and caching the device count instead of counting per request.

title: ProvideAnonDBStore now requires an int64, which breaks wire injection of anonstore.AnonStore
body: `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` used to receive `anonstore.AnonStore` through dependency injection, which implies `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` is registered as a wire provider (in `pkg/server/wire.go`). The provider signature is now `ProvideAnonDBStore(db.DB, int64)`. Wire cannot resolve a bare `int64`, so code generation fails if the provider is still registered. Any other consumer that injects `anonstore.AnonStore` also loses its provider, or gets a separately constructed store without the limit. wire.go is not part of this change and needs updating, or the limit should come from `*setting.Cfg`.

title: rowsAffected==0 is treated as limit reached, but MySQL reports 0 for unchanged rows
body: `updateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` whenever `RowsAffected()` is 0. With the default go-sql-driver/mysql settings (no clientFoundRows), MySQL counts only rows whose values actually changed. `updated_at` is a second-precision DATETIME, so an update with the same IP, user agent and second (for example, the same device tagged by two HA instances, whose local caches are separate) reports 0 rows. An already-registered device is then rejected as over the limit.

title: Limit test does not cover updating an existing device at the limit or the auth-level behavior
body: `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only checks that a second, new device gets `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. It does not check the main intended behavior: an already-registered device must still be able to update when the limit is reached. No test covers `Anonymous.Authenticate` rejecting a device over the limit, or repeated requests from a rejected device. Such a test would have caught the local-cache bypass in `tagDeviceUI`.

title: New `device_limit` setting not added to defaults.ini/sample.ini or documentation
body: The new `[auth.anonymous] device_limit` key is read here, but `conf/defaults.ini`, `conf/sample.ini` and the configuration docs are not updated. Operators have no way to discover the option, or to learn that 0 means unlimited and that devices over the limit lose anonymous access.

title: `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined` infers type `undefined` on GrafanaBootConfig
body: With strictNullChecks, a class field initialized to `undefined` without a type annotation gets the type `undefined`. Code using `config.anonymousDeviceLimit` (typed as `GrafanaBootConfig`) therefore cannot treat it as a number; for example, `config.anonymousDeviceLimit > 0` is a type error. The backend always sends an int64 (0 by default), never undefined. The field should be annotated, e.g. `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined`, or simply default to 0.

title: Device limit bypassed because rejected devices are cached as already tagged
body:
`tagDeviceUI` writes the device key into `localCache` (29-minute TTL) before calling `CreateOrUpdateDevice`. When the store returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the key stays cached.

The device's next request hits the cache, `tagDeviceUI` returns nil, and `Anonymous.Authenticate` grants access. The limit is enforced only on the first request from a new device; a reload or retry gets in.

The same ordering means a transient DB error suppresses re-tagging for 29 minutes. Fix: on `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, cache a negative marker and return the error on later cache hits. On any other error, delete the key.

title: ProvideAnonDBStore signature change likely breaks the Wire dependency graph
body:
Before this PR, `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` took an `anonstore.AnonStore` argument, so the Wire set (pkg/server/wire.go or the enterprise wireexts) must contain `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` plus a `wire.Bind` to `AnonStore`. That file is not in this PR.

`ProvideAnonDBStore` now needs an `int64`, which Wire cannot supply. If the provider stays in the set, code generation fails with either a missing int64 provider or an unused-provider error.

If another component still injects `anonstore.AnonStore`, it would get a second store instance that silently ignores the limit. Update or remove the Wire provider and binding in the same change.

title: Limit keyed on a client-supplied header: trivially bypassed and abusable for lockout
body:
Enforcement relies entirely on the `X-Grafana-Device-Id` header, which the client controls.

1. A request without the header returns nil from `TagDevice` and is authenticated anonymously. Unparseable IPs also return nil. So any non-browser client skips the limit entirely.
2. An unauthenticated attacker can send requests with random device IDs until `device_limit` is reached. Every new legitimate anonymous visitor is then rejected for up to 30 days, until rows age out of the `updated_at` window.

At minimum, document this behaviour. Ideally, rate-limit device creation or treat a missing device ID consistently with the limit.

title: Check-then-insert lets concurrent requests exceed the device limit
body:
`CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs `CountDevices` and then a separate upsert, with no transaction or lock around them.

Concurrent first requests from different devices can all read `count < deviceLimit` and all insert. This is especially likely across multiple Grafana instances sharing the DB, or a burst of new visitors. The stored device count can therefore exceed the configured limit.

If the limit is meant as a hard cap, the count and insert need to be atomic, for example a conditional `INSERT ... SELECT` with a count predicate or a serialized transaction.

title: Device tagging moved onto the synchronous auth path even when no limit is configured
body:
Tagging used to run in a background goroutine with its own timeout and panic recovery. It now runs inline in `Authenticate` using the request context.

Every cache-miss anonymous request now waits for the DB upsert, plus a `COUNT(*)` when a limit is set, before it is authenticated. This applies even with the default `device_limit = 0`, where nothing needs to be enforced.

The panic recovery is also gone, and a client disconnect now cancels the write. Consider staying asynchronous when `AnonymousDeviceLimit == 0`.

title: Tests don't cover existing devices at the limit or repeated requests from rejected devices
body:
`TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only checks that a second new device is rejected.

It does not check that an already-registered device can still update once the limit is reached, which is the `updateDevice` path's main purpose. No test at the service or client level checks that a rejected device stays rejected on later requests, and such a test would have caught the local-cache bypass.

`Anonymous.Authenticate` returning an error on `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is also untested.

title: anonymousDeviceLimit is inferred as type `undefined` on GrafanaBootConfig
body:
`anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` has no type annotation, so TypeScript infers the property type as literal `undefined`, not `number | undefined`.

At runtime the backend sends a number, which is merged into the config. Code that reads `config.anonymousDeviceLimit` and treats it as a number, such as `config.anonymousDeviceLimit > 0`, will not type-check.

Declare it as `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;`.

title: New device_limit setting not documented in defaults.ini/sample.ini or the docs
body:
`[auth.anonymous] device_limit` is read here, but conf/defaults.ini, conf/sample.ini and the configuration docs are not updated.

Operators have no way to discover the option. Nothing tells them that exceeding it makes new anonymous visitors fail authentication.

title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, a likely leftover debug change
body: The cleanup service ticker went from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. The PR description does not mention or justify this. Every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, user invites, short URLs, and the query-history row-limit enforcement) now runs 10x more often, which multiplies background DB load on every installation. The 9-minute `timeout` in `clean()` was sized to fit inside the 10-minute interval, so with a 1-minute ticker that relationship no longer holds. This looks like a local-testing change and should be reverted.

title: Leftover debug logging at Error level dumps full ID lists on every batch
body: `CleanAnnotations` (lines 534, 537, 554, 557) and `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` (lines 576, 579) call `r.log.Error` on every batch, including successful ones and empty ones. Each call logs the whole `ids` slice, which can hold up to `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` entries (tens of thousands), plus the SQL condition. Every cleanup run therefore emits several Error-level lines per annotation type even when nothing is deleted. That floods logs and trips error-based alerting. The `"err", err` field in the fetch log is always nil at that point, which further suggests this is debug code. These lines should be removed or downgraded to Debug without the ID list.

title: Quadratic string building when inlining IDs for SQLite
body: The SQLite inline path builds the IN list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` in a loop. Each iteration reallocates and copies the whole growing string, so the cost is O(n²). With a large batch size such as the 32767 used in the new test, this copies gigabytes of data and adds heavy GC pressure on every batch. A `strings.Builder` or `strconv.AppendInt` into a `[]byte` would make it linear, as `getAccessControlFilter` already does in this file.

title: Bound-parameter limit is now a hard cap on batch size for MySQL/Postgres
body: The old cleanup used a single subquery with no bound parameters, so `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` had no upper limit. `deleteByIDs` now binds one placeholder per ID on every non-SQLite database. MySQL prepared statements and Postgres both reject more than 65535 parameters. A user with a batch size above that will see every cleanup run fail and annotations never get cleaned. Either chunk the delete or inline integer IDs for all dialects, since they are int64 values read from the DB and safe to inline.

title: Per-subtest DB cleanup is registered only after setup assertions succeed
body: All subtests share one DB. `t.Cleanup` (which deletes from `annotation` and `annotation_tag`) is registered only after `createTestAnnotations`, `assertAnnotationCount` and `assertAnnotationTagCount` have run, and those helpers call `require`. If any of them fails partway, for example after some rows were inserted, the cleanup is never registered. The leftover rows then make every later subtest fail with misleading counts. Registering the cleanup before creating test data avoids these cascading failures.

title: Cleanup ticker silently changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body:
The interval for all background cleanup jobs drops from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This covers temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs and query history, not only annotations. The PR description does not mention this, and it looks like a debugging leftover.

`clean()` still uses a 9-minute timeout, which was sized to fit inside the 10-minute interval. With a 1-minute ticker, a slow run is followed almost immediately by the next one, so cleanup can run nearly continuously.

There is no server lock around `clean()`, so every replica in an HA setup now hits the database 10x more often. This adds load and contention on exactly the tables (annotation) where the PR is trying to reduce deadlocks. It should be reverted to 10 minutes.

title: Debug logging left in at Error level, dumping full ID lists every batch
body:
Every batch in CleanAnnotations (lines 534, 537, 554, 557) and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags (lines 576, 579) logs via `r.log.Error`. This happens even on the normal path, including the final empty batch where count is 0.

The log lines include the full `ids` slice, which can be up to `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` entries (tens of thousands in the new test). They also include an `err` field that is always nil at lines 534/554/576.

In production this produces many spurious ERROR entries on every cleanup cycle, multiplied by the new 1-minute ticker. That pollutes logs, can trigger error-based alerting, and can create very large log lines. These should be removed or downgraded to Debug without the ID list.

title: Quadratic string building when inlining IDs for SQLite
body:
`values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside the loop allocates and copies the whole accumulated string on every iteration, so the total work is O(n²) in the number of IDs.

This branch only runs when the batch size is above 999, which is exactly the large-batch case. At the batch size of 32767 used in the new test, this amounts to gigabytes of allocation and copying per batch, repeated for every batch until cleanup is done.

Use a `strings.Builder` or `strconv.AppendInt` into a `[]byte` instead, as `getAccessControlFilter` already does in this file.

title: Bound-parameter DELETE breaks on MySQL/Postgres for very large batch sizes
body:
The old implementation used a subquery with no bind parameters. The new code binds one `?` per ID for every database except SQLite-with-large-batch.

MySQL prepared statements and PostgreSQL both cap a statement at 65535 bind parameters. A user who has configured `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` above that will now get an error on every cleanup run, and annotations will never be cleaned.

The parameter-limit workaround only covers SQLite. Either chunk `ids` into sub-batches below each dialect's limit, or apply the inlining approach (the IDs are trusted int64s read from the DB) for all dialects when the batch is large.

title: Per-subtest cleanup registered after data creation and assertions
body:
`t.Cleanup` that empties `annotation`/`annotation_tag` is registered only after `createTestAnnotations` and two `require`-based count assertions. All subtests share one DB.

If insertion or either count assertion fails, `FailNow` aborts the subtest before the cleanup is registered. The leftover rows then make every later subtest fail its initial count assertion, which hides the original failure.

The cleanup should be registered before inserting the data.

title: Debug logging left in at Error level, dumping full ID lists on every batch
body:
Every batch in the three cleanup loops logs twice with `r.log.Error` (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579), including the complete `ids` slice and the SQL condition. This happens on every run even when nothing is deleted (count 0), so each cleanup cycle emits at least 6+ error-level log lines per annotation type. With a large batch size (the new test uses 32767) each line carries tens of thousands of IDs.

The `"err", err` field on the 'to clean' lines is always nil at that point, which suggests these are leftover debug statements. In production this floods error logs, triggers log-based error alerting and wastes CPU and I/O. They should be removed or lowered to Debug without the ID payload.

title: Cleanup interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute (unrelated, likely debug leftover)
body:
The ticker for the whole CleanUpService was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. The PR description does not mention or justify this.

The interval is coupled to `clean()`'s 9-minute timeout, which was sized to fit inside the 10-minute tick. With a 1-minute tick, a long-running cleanup is followed immediately by the buffered tick, so cleanup can run almost continuously.

The change also affects every cleanup job, not just annotations: temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, invites, short URLs and query history. They now run 10x more often on every Grafana instance (there is no server lock here), which significantly increases database load in HA setups. This should be reverted.

title: Bound-parameter IN list can exceed MySQL/Postgres placeholder limits for large batch sizes
body:
The old implementation used a subquery with no bind parameters. The new `deleteByIDs` binds one `?` per ID on every non-SQLite database. MySQL and Postgres both cap prepared statement placeholders at 65535.

Any user who sets `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` above 65535 will now get a 'too many placeholders' error on every cleanup run, and annotations will stop being cleaned. Before this change, such a setting worked.

Only SQLite has the inline-values fallback. The batch should be chunked per dialect limit, or the IDs inlined as integers for all dialects (they are int64, so inlining is safe).

title: Quadratic string building for inline ID list
body:
On the SQLite large-batch path, the IN list is built with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` in a loop. Each iteration copies the whole accumulated string, so building N IDs is O(N²).

With the batch size used in the new test (32767 IDs, roughly 200KB of text), this copies several gigabytes and creates heavy GC pressure on every batch. A `strings.Builder` or `strings.Join` over `strconv.FormatInt` results makes this linear.

title: Per-subtest cleanup registered after data creation, so failures leak rows into later subtests
body:
`t.Cleanup` that deletes annotation and annotation_tag rows is registered only after `createTestAnnotations` and the two count assertions. All of these use `require`, which calls `FailNow`.

If insertion or an initial count assertion fails, or if a previous subtest left rows behind, the cleanup is never registered. The rows then remain in the shared DB. Every subsequent subtest then fails its initial count assertion and does not register cleanup either, which cascades failures and hides the original cause. Registering `t.Cleanup` before inserting data avoids this.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled when the request finishes
body:
Each background goroutine builds its context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`, where `ctx` is the incoming request context. This happens in Create (line 51), Delete (110), Update (135) and DeleteCollection (163).

The handler returns right after spawning the goroutine. net/http and the apiserver then cancel the request context, and the derived context is cancelled with it.

As a result, the legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection calls race with cancellation and will often fail with `context canceled`. The "safety" copy into legacy storage silently never happens.

Fix: derive the context with `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` before applying the 10s timeout. That keeps the identity/logger values but drops the parent's cancellation.

title: Errors from async legacy writes are dropped without logging
body:
In all four async goroutines (Create line 55-56, Delete 112-113, Update 139-140, DeleteCollection 165-166), the legacy error is only used as a boolean for a duration metric. It is never logged.

The previous implementation logged legacy failures. Now, when legacy diverges from unified storage (e.g. due to the context cancellation issue or a conflict), there is no record of which object failed or why. That makes reconciliation and debugging impossible.

The error, along with the object name and kind, should be logged in each goroutine.

title: Storage create failure recorded as a legacy duration metric
body:
When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

Unified-storage create failures are therefore reported as legacy errors. This skews both the legacy and storage metrics and hides storage failures, which are the source of truth in mode 3.

title: Storage update failure recorded as a legacy duration metric
body:
On `d.Storage.Update` error, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` although the timed operation is the unified-storage update.

Storage update failures are misattributed to legacy, and the storage error rate is under-reported. It should call `recordStorageDuration`.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection result recorded as a storage metric
body:
Inside the async goroutine that calls `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection`, the result is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `recordLegacyDuration`.

Legacy delete-collection latency and errors end up in the storage metric. Each successful delete-collection is counted twice in storage and never in legacy.

title: Object name used as the `kind` metric label in Delete (cardinality explosion)
body:
`d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` where every other call passes `options.Kind`.

Because this metric label is supposed to be the kind, every deleted object creates a new Prometheus time series. That produces unbounded label cardinality and memory growth in the metrics registry. It also mislabels the data. Use `options.Kind` here.

title: Legacy Update re-applies the original objInfo instead of the object persisted in unified storage
body:
The previous implementation wrapped `objInfo` in `updateWrapper{updated: obj}`, so legacy received exactly the object that unified storage persisted.

The new code passes the raw `objInfo` to `d.Legacy.Update`. Legacy therefore calls `objInfo.UpdatedObject` against its own (possibly stale) old object. For PATCH and server-side apply, this recomputes the patch (and admission) against different state, which can produce a different result than what unified storage stored. Preconditions and resourceVersion carried from the client may also not match legacy's state.

This causes silent divergence between the stores, which mode 3 writes to legacy precisely to avoid. Pass `&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: res}` instead.

title: Fire-and-forget legacy writes have no ordering, allowing out-of-order application
body:
Each write spawns an independent goroutine with no ordering or serialization per object.

Suppose a client creates and then quickly deletes (or updates twice) the same object. The legacy goroutines can run in any order. A Create that runs after the Delete leaves an orphaned object in legacy, and an older Update can overwrite a newer one.

The goroutines are also unbounded and not tracked, so Destroy() does not wait for in-flight writes on shutdown. Together this undermines legacy as a safe fallback. Consider a per-key queue or worker, or at least document and reconcile this.

title: Delete stores the base logger in the context instead of the enriched one
body:
`ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` puts the base logger into the context, while every other method uses the `log` enriched with name, kind and method.

Logs emitted downstream by storage/legacy during Delete lose those fields. It should be `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`.

title: Tests share one mock for legacy and storage and never verify the async legacy write
body:
`legacyStoreMock{m, l}` and `storageMock{m, s}` wrap the same `*mock.Mock`. Any expectation such as `"Create"` or `"Delete"` is satisfied by either store, so the tests cannot tell which store was called.

For example, the Delete and DeleteCollection tests only set up storage expectations, yet the legacy goroutine silently consumes them. The "error ... unified store fails" Create case actually configures its failure via `setupLegacyFn`.

The main new behavior of this PR is never asserted:
- legacy is written asynchronously after a successful storage write;
- legacy is not written when storage fails;
- reads never touch legacy.

The tests return without waiting, so the spawned goroutines also outlive the test. Use separate mocks and wait for (e.g. `assert.Eventually`) or assert the legacy call.

title: Duplicate and unrelated go.work.sum entries
body:
