The diff adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod` a second time; the identical line already exists a few lines above.

It also adds unrelated checksums such as `otel/exporters/prometheus v0.37.0` and `otel/sdk/metric v0.39.0` that have nothing to do with this change. These look like accidental local `go work` artifacts and should be dropped or regenerated cleanly.

title: Async legacy writes derive from the request context and get cancelled when the request returns
body:
Each background goroutine (Create here, and likewise Delete at 110, Update at 135 and DeleteCollection at 163) wraps the incoming request `ctx` with `context.WithTimeoutCause`. The apiserver/net/http cancels that context as soon as the handler returns, which happens right after the goroutine is spawned.

As a result, the legacy SQL write will very often fail with `context canceled` before or while it runs. The 10s timeout never applies. The "safe measure" legacy copy silently goes stale, and the only trace is a metric, because the error is not logged.

Fix: use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` as the parent. That keeps request-scoped values such as identity and the logger, but drops the cancellation.

title: Unordered fire-and-forget legacy writes can apply out of order and leave legacy inconsistent
body:
Every write spawns an independent goroutine for the legacy store, with no ordering, serialization or retry.

A create quickly followed by an update or delete of the same object (as the integration tests do) can reach legacy in any order. For example, the legacy Delete goroutine may run before the legacy Create goroutine. That leaves an orphaned row in legacy that is never cleaned up. An Update can likewise run before the Create and fail.

Since mode 3 keeps legacy as a fallback for rolling back modes, this silently corrupts the fallback data. A per-object ordering mechanism, or at least logging and reconciliation, is needed.

title: Legacy write errors are no longer logged
body:
The previous implementation logged failures from the legacy store. In the new goroutines (Create here, and also Delete, Update and DeleteCollection), the legacy error is used only as a boolean for the duration metric and then discarded.

There is no log entry with the object name or kind or the error cause. Divergence between unified and legacy storage, including the context-cancellation failures, cannot be diagnosed. Log the error inside each goroutine.

title: Storage Create failure is recorded as a legacy metric
body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. Unified-storage create failures are therefore reported as legacy failures, and the storage error metric never sees them. Dashboards and alerts on dual-writer health will be wrong.

title: Storage Update failure is recorded as a legacy metric
body: When `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. Unified-storage update errors are therefore attributed to legacy storage in the metrics.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection duration recorded as storage metric
body: Inside the background goroutine, the legacy `DeleteCollection` result is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(...)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`. Legacy delete-collection timings and failures are therefore counted as unified-storage observations, which skews both series.

title: Object name used as the `kind` metric label (unbounded cardinality)
body:
The success path of Delete calls `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`. It passes the resource `name` where every other call passes `options.Kind`.

This mislabels the metric. Worse, it creates a new Prometheus time series for every distinct object name deleted, which is unbounded label cardinality and can blow up memory in Grafana and in the metrics backend. Use `options.Kind`.

title: Delete stores the base logger in context instead of the enriched one
body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` attaches the base logger rather than the `log` built on the previous line, which carries the name, kind and method values. Every other method uses `log`. Logs emitted by downstream storage code during Delete lose the object name and method context.

title: Legacy Update re-applies the raw objInfo instead of the object persisted in unified storage
body:
The previous code wrapped `objInfo` in `updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}` so legacy received exactly the object stored in unified storage. The new code passes the original `objInfo` to `d.Legacy.Update`.

That makes legacy compute its own result via `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, legacyOld)`. For patches, the patch is applied against the legacy copy, which may differ from storage. For PUTs, the object carries unified-storage resourceVersion and preconditions, which legacy may reject.

The two stores can therefore silently diverge, or legacy updates can fail. It also reuses a request-scoped objInfo after the request has completed. Restore the wrapper so legacy receives `res`.

title: Delete no longer removes legacy copy when the object is missing in unified storage
body:
The old implementation treated `NotFound` from unified storage as non-fatal and still deleted from legacy. Now any storage error, including NotFound, returns early and skips the legacy delete.

Objects that exist only in legacy, such as ones never migrated or ones whose async create to unified storage was lost, can no longer be removed through the API. They remain as stale data in legacy.

title: Mode 3 unit tests never verify the legacy write happens
body:
Legacy and unified storage share one mock, and the legacy calls run in untracked goroutines that may execute after the test returns. None of the Mode3 tests assert that the legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection was invoked, or with which arguments.

The core new behavior, asynchronous propagation to legacy, is untested. That is why bugs like the cancelled-context issue and the wrong metric calls go unnoticed.

The failure case also configures the error via `setupLegacyFn` even though it is named "unified store fails", so the test only passes because the mock is shared. Consider separate mocks and a synchronization point, for example `assert.Eventually` on `AssertCalled`.

title: Duplicate and unrelated go.work.sum entries
body: The diff re-adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod`, which already exists on the line directly above it in the same hunk. It also pulls in unrelated older otel and plugin-sdk sums that have nothing to do with the dual writer change. This looks like accidental local tooling churn and should be reverted or regenerated cleanly.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are canceled when the request ends
body:
Each background goroutine (Create, Update, Delete, DeleteCollection) builds its timeout with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`, where `ctx` is the incoming request context.

The k8s handlers wrap that context in `context.WithTimeout` and `defer cancel()` it. net/http also cancels the request context as soon as ServeHTTP returns. So once the dual writer returns the storage result, the parent context is canceled almost immediately. The legacy write then races against that cancellation and will often fail with `context canceled`, which leaves legacy storage permanently out of sync.

The 10s timeout adds nothing, because the parent is canceled first. Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` as the parent: it keeps request values such as the user identity but drops the cancellation.

title: Storage create failure is recorded as a legacy metric
body:
When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

As a result, storage create errors are reported as legacy-store errors and never show up in the storage error metric. That makes the dual-writer dashboards and alerts misleading.

title: Storage update failure is recorded as a legacy metric
body:
When `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with the storage start time. The failure should go to `recordStorageDuration`.

Storage update errors are therefore misattributed to legacy storage and missing from the storage metrics.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection result recorded via recordStorageDuration
body:
Inside the async goroutine that calls `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection`, the outcome is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ..., startLegacy)` instead of `recordLegacyDuration`.

Legacy delete-collection latency and errors are counted as storage metrics. This pollutes the storage series and hides legacy failures.

title: Object name passed as the `kind` metric label
body:
On successful storage delete the code calls `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`. It passes the object `name` where every other call passes `options.Kind`.

This mislabels the metric. It also creates a new Prometheus label value for every deleted object name, which is unbounded label cardinality and can blow up memory and storage in the metrics backend.

title: Legacy update re-applies the raw objInfo instead of the object written to storage
body:
The previous implementation wrapped `objInfo` in `updateWrapper` so legacy received exactly the object persisted in unified storage. The new code passes the original `objInfo` to `d.Legacy.Update` in a background goroutine.

The legacy store then calls `objInfo.UpdatedObject` against its own copy of the old object. For PATCH and server-side apply, the patch is applied to legacy's possibly different state, so the two stores can diverge. The patcher's transformers (patch application, mutating admission) also run a second time, asynchronously, after the request has completed. Keep using `updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: res}` for the legacy write.

title: Unordered fire-and-forget goroutines can apply legacy writes out of order
body:
Every write spawns an independent goroutine for the legacy write, with no ordering or serialization.

Take a create or update followed quickly by a delete of the same object. The legacy Delete goroutine can run before the earlier Create/Update goroutine finishes. Legacy then ends up with a resurrected or stale object even though unified storage is correct. Because mode 3 never reads from legacy, the divergence goes unnoticed until a rollback to a lower mode. There is also no bound on the number of in-flight goroutines, and `Destroy` does not wait for them.

title: Legacy write errors are silently dropped (no logging)
body:
In all four async goroutines the legacy error only sets a boolean on a metric; it is never logged. The previous implementation logged legacy failures together with the object.

If legacy writes fail (for example from the context cancellation issue, validation, or conflicts), operators get no error message, object name, or cause to diagnose the divergence. Log `errObjectSt` / `err` with the request logger.

title: Delete puts the base logger into the context instead of the enriched one
body:
`Delete` builds `log` with name/kind/method values but then calls `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`.

Downstream storage code that logs via `klog.FromContext(ctx)` loses the name, kind and method fields. Every other method in this file passes `log`.

title: Tests share one mock for both stores and never verify the async legacy write
body:
Both `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` wrap the same `mock.Mock`, so the tests cannot tell which store was called.

For example, the "error when creating object in the unified store fails" case only configures `setupLegacyFn`. It passes only because the storage Create call matches the expectation registered for legacy.

No test checks that:
- the legacy write is actually issued after a successful storage write,
- it is skipped when storage fails,
- Get and List never touch legacy.

The background goroutines also outlive the test. The core mode 3 behavior is effectively untested, which is how the canceled-context and metric bugs got through.

title: Duplicate and unrelated go.work.sum entries
body: The diff re-adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod`, which is already present on the line above. It also adds a number of unrelated dependency checksums (azure sdk, alertmanager, older otel exporters). This is accidental churn from a local `go work sync` and should be dropped from a dual-writer change.

title: Cache is not re-checked after taking the write lock, so concurrent misses reload and can overwrite a good cache with nil
body:
`GetWebAssets` checks the cache under `RLock`, releases it, then takes the exclusive `Lock` without checking `entryPointAssetsCache` again.

In production (`cfg.Env != setting.Dev`), N requests that arrive while the cache is empty (e.g. at startup) all pass the read check. Each then takes the write lock in turn and re-reads and re-decodes `assets-manifest.json`. That is a serialized thundering herd on every cold start.

The redundant reloads can also lose data. Goroutine A loads the manifest and stores a valid cache. Goroutine B, queued behind it, reloads anyway. If B's read fails (transient I/O error, file being replaced during a deploy), line 69 sets `entryPointAssetsCache = nil` and B returns an error. B has thrown away a valid cached value that A had just stored.

Fix: after acquiring `Lock`, check again (`if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }`). Also consider not overwriting the cache when `err != nil`. Alternatively use `sync.Once` or `singleflight` for the non-dev path.

title: Cache not re-checked after taking the write lock
body:
`GetWebAssets` checks the cache under `RLock`, releases it, then takes the exclusive `Lock`. Once it holds the exclusive lock it never checks again whether another goroutine has already filled `entryPointAssetsCache`.

Outside dev mode, many requests can arrive while the cache is still nil (cold start, or after a failed load that cached nil). All of them queue on the write lock. Each one then re-opens and re-parses `assets-manifest.json` (or would re-fetch from the CDN), one after another, instead of using the value the first holder just stored.

The standard double-checked pattern fixes this: after `Lock()`, do `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }`. Alternatively, use `sync.Once` for the non-dev path.

title: No regression test for the data race being fixed
body: The PR fixes a data race on the package-level `entryPointAssetsCache`, but adds no test that would catch it coming back. A small test that calls `GetWebAssets` from several goroutines against a temp `StaticRootPath` containing a valid `build/assets-manifest.json`, run under `go test -race`, would verify the fix and guard against regressions.

title: Cache is not re-checked after taking the write lock, so waiting callers reload and overwrite it
body:
In non-dev mode, `GetWebAssets` reads the cache under `RLock`, releases it, and then takes the exclusive `Lock`. It never checks `entryPointAssetsCache` again after acquiring that lock.

At startup, every request that saw a nil cache queues on `Lock()`. Each one then re-opens and re-parses `assets-manifest.json` in turn, although the first holder already filled the cache.

Worse, a later waiter whose read fails transiently runs `entryPointAssetsCache = result` with `result == nil`. That wipes out the good value the earlier goroutine stored and returns an error to that caller. Subsequent requests then have to reload again.

Fix: add the standard double-check after `Lock()`, e.g. `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }`. Optionally, only assign to the cache when `err == nil`.

title: No regression test for the data race being fixed
body: The PR's stated purpose is to fix a data race on `entryPointAssetsCache`, but it adds no test. A small test would lock in the fix: call `GetWebAssets` from several goroutines concurrently against a fixture manifest and run it under `go test -race`. Without it, a future refactor (for example, removing the TODO'd global state, or adding another unguarded access) could reintroduce the race unnoticed.

title: Existing SQL parser/command tests will fail now that TablesList always errors; no regression test added
body:
`TablesList` now always fails, because `NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands` returns "not implemented". `NewSQLCommand` calls `TablesList`, so it now always returns a BadRequest error.

The existing tests are not modified in this PR. These are `pkg/expr/sql/parser_test.go`, which asserts the table names extracted by `TablesList`, and `pkg/expr/sql_command_test.go`, which expects `NewSQLCommand("a", "select a from foo, bar")` to succeed. They will now fail and break CI.

The tests should be skipped or rewritten to assert the disabled behaviour. A regression test should also be added that a SQL expression is rejected, through both the reader and the `NewSQLCommand` path, even when the `sqlExpressions` flag is on. That locks in the security fix.

title: enableSqlExpressions looks like a flag check but always returns false
body:
The function reads `FlagSqlExpressions`, stores the *negation* in a variable named `enabled`, and then returns `false` from both branches. The flag lookup is dead code.

The name and structure suggest the feature honours the toggle, but it is unconditionally disabled. The misleading `enabled := !...` inversion makes it easy for a future change, such as switching the final `return false` to `return true`, to silently re-enable the code path.

Because this is a security kill-switch, it should be explicit. Either return `false` with a comment referencing CVE-2024-9264, or drop the flag lookup entirely. As written, users with the flag on get "sqlExpressions is not implemented" from code that appears to check whether they enabled it.

title: Main query path is not gated; it still runs SQL-building code on user input and relies only on the stub
body:
The new disable check is only in `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery`, which serves the query-service path. The regular expression path (`buildCMDNode` → `UnmarshalSQLCommand` → `NewSQLCommand`) has no such gate.

On that path, raw user SQL still goes into `sql.TablesList`. That function still builds `SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')` by string formatting user input. It then logs at Error level ("error serializing sql", parser.go:28) together with the raw user SQL on every request.

The only thing preventing execution is that the `DB` stub returns "not implemented". If anyone restores a real `NewInMemoryDB` implementation, the RCE/LFI vector comes back immediately. Meanwhile, users get a misleading 400 "error reading SQL command", and any user can generate Error-level log noise.

Put the hard disable at the top of `NewSQLCommand` (or `UnmarshalSQLCommand`), so no path reaches the SQL parsing or execution code, and return a clear "SQL expressions are disabled" error.

title: Existing DuckDB-backed tests for TablesList/NewSQLCommand will now fail
body:
`TablesList` now calls the stub `NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands`, which always returns "not implemented". `NewSQLCommand` then always fails with `sql-invalid-sql`.

The existing unit tests in `pkg/expr/sql` (parser tests) and `pkg/expr/sql_command_test.go` call `TablesList`/`NewSQLCommand` with real SQL and assert on the returned table names. This PR does not update, skip or remove them, so they will fail and break CI.

They should be skipped or rewritten to assert the new disabled behaviour.

title: No regression test that SQL expressions are rejected on both code paths
body:
This is the in-repo fix for CVE-2024-9264, but no test asserts that SQL expressions are refused.

There are two entry points:
- `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` (the new gate at line 129).
- The legacy `UnmarshalSQLCommand` -> `NewSQLCommand` path. It does not go through the reader gate and is protected only by the stub DB.

Without tests for both, someone could later restore a real DB implementation or change `enableSqlExpressions`, and nothing would fail to flag the reintroduced RCE/LFI. Add tests that a `type: sql` query fails in `ReadQuery`, and that `NewSQLCommand`/`Execute` cannot run SQL.

title: enableSqlExpressions reads the feature flag but always returns false
body:
The function computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions)`, so the variable named `enabled` actually means the flag is disabled. Both branches then return `false`.

The flag lookup is dead logic, and the function name, variable name and control flow all suggest the feature can be enabled by the toggle when it cannot. That misleads future maintainers and anyone debugging why enabling `sqlExpressions` has no effect.

Replace it with an explicit hard-disable plus a comment referencing the CVE, or make the intended re-enable condition explicit and correct.

title: Misleading and inconsistent errors when SQL expressions are used
body:
On the reader path the user gets "sqlExpressions is not implemented". That is inaccurate: the feature exists but has been deliberately disabled for security.

On the legacy `UnmarshalSQLCommand` path (used when the expression parser toggle is off), the request fails inside `TablesList`. The user gets a BadRequest "error reading SQL command", which implies their SQL is invalid. Each attempt also logs at Error level in `parser.go` (and Warn in `sql_command.go`), including the raw user SQL.

Users who enabled the `sqlExpressions` flag get confusing feedback, and logs get noisy. Return a single clear "SQL expressions are disabled" error from both paths, ideally before calling `TablesList`.

title: Existing SQL expression tests will fail against the new stub DB
body:
The new stub `RunCommands` and `QueryFramesInto` always return "not implemented". As a result `sql.TablesList` and `expr.NewSQLCommand` now always return an error.

Existing tests still assume they succeed and were not updated or skipped in this PR:
- `pkg/expr/sql/parser_test.go` (e.g. `TestParse`, which expects `TablesList("select * from foo")` to return `foo`).
- `pkg/expr/sql_command_test.go` (`TestNewCommand`, which expects `NewSQLCommand("a", "select a from foo, bar")` to succeed).

These tests will fail CI. They should be skipped or rewritten to assert the new disabled behaviour.

title: enableSqlExpressions has inverted naming and ignores the feature flag
body:
`enableSqlExpressions` sets `enabled := !IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions)`, so `enabled` is true when the flag is OFF. Both branches then return false, so the toggle is read but has no effect.

This is misleading. A future maintainer who edits one branch to "re-enable" the feature could easily get the polarity wrong and turn SQL expressions on when the flag is off, re-opening the RCE/LFI.

It also adds a needless dereference of `h.features` (a nil-features reader now panics on the SQL path).

User-facing problems:
- The `sqlExpressions` toggle is still registered and documented as enabling the feature, but it is now a silent no-op.
- The returned error says "sqlExpressions is not implemented" rather than that the feature is disabled.

Replace the function with an unconditional, clearly commented disable and a clear error message. Also update or deprecate the toggle docs.

title: Legacy SQL expression path is not explicitly gated; relies only on the stub
body:
The explicit disable check was added only in `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery`. The legacy graph-building path (`buildCMDNode` -> `UnmarshalSQLCommand` -> `NewSQLCommand`) has no equivalent gate. It is blocked today only because the stub `sql.TablesList` happens to fail.

On that path users get a generic "error reading SQL command" BadRequest instead of a clear "disabled" error. The security fix also depends on the stub never being replaced with a real engine.

Add the same explicit rejection in `UnmarshalSQLCommand`/`NewSQLCommand` so both entry points are covered consistently.

title: No regression test for the security disable
body:
This PR is the in-repo version of the CVE-2024-9264 fix, but it adds no test asserting that a `type: sql` expression is rejected. That should be checked both with the `sqlExpressions` toggle on and off, and through both the `ReadQuery` and `UnmarshalSQLCommand` paths.

Without such a test, a future change could silently re-enable SQL expressions and nothing would catch it.

title: Every SQL expression attempt now logs at Error level
body:
With the stub DB, `RunCommands` always fails. So every SQL expression that reaches `TablesList` (e.g. via the legacy `UnmarshalSQLCommand` path) logs `logger.Error("error serializing sql", ...)`, which includes the full user-supplied SQL. `NewSQLCommand` then logs an additional Warn.

This is expected, permanent behaviour for a disabled feature, not an error condition. It creates log noise and records arbitrary user query text at error level.

Short-circuit before calling the stub, or lower the log level.

title: New TotalDocs() log call can crash the process via unsynchronized map iteration
body:
The new log line calls `s.search.TotalDocs()`. By then the goroutine at lines 207-213 is already consuming watch events. `bleveBackend.TotalDocs` (bleve.go:146) ranges over `b.cache` without taking `cacheMu`.

A watch event for a namespace that has no index yet goes through `handleEvent` -> `getOrCreateIndex` -> `BuildIndex`, which writes `b.cache[key]` under `cacheMu.Lock()`. That write can overlap with the lock-free iteration in `TotalDocs`. Concurrent map iteration and write is a fatal Go runtime error, so it crashes the process; it is not a recoverable panic.

The window is roughly as long as `DocCount()` takes across all indexes. Namespaces skipped at startup because they are below `initMinSize` make this path reachable.

Fix: have `TotalDocs` take `cacheMu.RLock()`, or compute the total before starting the watch goroutine.

title: Stop() no longer prevents requests from being served after shutdown
body:
Before this PR, every handler (Create, Read, List, Watch, Search, IsHealthy, blob calls, etc.) called `s.Init(ctx)` and returned `s.initErr`. Since the `sync.Once` had already run, that meant returning whatever `Stop()` had stored ("service is stopping" / "service is stopped").

This PR removes all those calls, so `Stop()` writing `s.initErr` no longer has any effect. After `Stop()` cancels the server context and stops the backend lifecycle, handlers keep running against a stopped backend and a cancelled broadcaster. Callers no longer get a clear "service is stopped" error.

Fix: add an explicit stopped/ready check in the handlers, or have `Stop` close the gRPC service, instead of relying on the now-unused `initErr`.

title: Index-build goroutines race on shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed`, so errors can be lost
body:
Each goroutine started by `group.Go` does `totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(...)`; `return err`. Both variables are the outer function's locals and are shared by all workers.

Before this PR, `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for its whole body, which largely serialized builds. With the lock narrowed, the builds now run truly in parallel. Two consequences:
- The race detector will flag it.
- One goroutine can overwrite another's error with nil before it is returned. A failed namespace build can then be silently dropped instead of failing startup as the comment on `init` promises.
- `namespaced_indexed` will be miscounted.

Fix: use a goroutine-local `err :=` and an `atomic.Int64` for the counter.

title: Narrowed lock lets concurrent builds of the same key run in parallel and overwrite each other
body:
`getOrCreateIndex` checks `GetIndex` and then calls `BuildIndex` with no per-key guard. With the function-wide lock removed, a Search request and a watch event for the same uncached key can build two indexes at once.

The last `b.cache[key] = idx` wins. Any watch-event writes already applied to the losing index are discarded. `IndexTenants` is also incremented twice. For file-backed indexes, the second `bleve.New` on the same directory fails.

Fix: re-check the cache under the write lock before storing, or use a per-key singleflight so finer-grained locking does not introduce lost updates.

title: Failed Init in constructor leaks the cancel func and the already-initialized backend
body:
When `s.Init(ctx)` fails, `NewResourceServer` returns `nil, err` without calling `cancel()` or `s.lifecycle.Stop`.

If `lifecycle.Init` succeeded (for example, the DB connection was opened) and then `search.init` or `initWatcher` failed, the backend's resources and any pollers started are never cleaned up. The caller has no handle to clean them up either, because the server is returned as nil.

The same error is also logged twice: once inside `Init` and again here.

title: Integration test skipped for postgres instead of fixed, possibly masking a regression from eager init
body:
This PR makes unified storage initialize (DB init, full index build, watchers) synchronously inside `NewResourceServer`, which changes storage-server startup behavior. In the same PR, the only module-server integration test is disabled for postgres with "not working in Drone. Works locally."

If the failure is caused by the new eager initialization (for example, slower startup or blocking DB init beyond the 500ms sleep), skipping the test hides exactly the regression the PR description asks reviewers about. Nothing else in the PR adds coverage for the new init-at-construction behavior.

title: TotalDocs ranges over the index cache without a lock while the watch goroutine can write to it
body:
`TotalDocs` iterates `b.cache` without taking `cacheMu`. This PR adds a call to it in `searchSupport.init` (search.go:216), and that call happens after the event-handling goroutine has already started (search.go:207).

That goroutine runs `handleEvent` → `getOrCreateIndex` → `BuildIndex`, which writes `b.cache[key] = idx`. A write event for a resource not indexed at startup can therefore mutate the map while `TotalDocs` is iterating it. Go treats concurrent map iteration plus write as a fatal, unrecoverable runtime error, so the process crashes at startup.

Fix: take `b.cacheMu.RLock()` in `TotalDocs`, or compute the total before starting the watch goroutine.

title: Narrowing the lock allows duplicate concurrent builds of the same index key
body:
Previously `BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for the whole build, and `GetIndex` (RLock) blocked until a build finished, so callers rarely built the same key twice. Now the lock covers only the final map assignment.

`getOrCreateIndex` does an unsynchronized check-then-build. Concurrent `Search` requests and `handleEvent` calls for a namespace not indexed at startup can therefore each run a full build for the same key. Consequences:
- Wasted work.
- `IndexTenants` and `IndexedKinds` metrics incremented multiple times.
- For file-based indexes, the second `bleve.New(dir, ...)` fails because the path already exists.
- The last build overwrites the cache entry, so documents that `handleEvent` wrote into an earlier, now-discarded index instance are lost.

A per-key lock or singleflight around build would give the speedup without these races.

title: Stopped server no longer rejects requests
body:
`Stop` sets `s.initErr` to "service is stopping" / "service is stopped". The only way that error reached callers was through the `s.Init(ctx)` check at the top of every gRPC handler, and this PR removes all of those checks.

After `Stop` cancels the server context and stops the backend, `Create`/`Update`/`Delete`/`Read`/`List`/`Watch`/`Search`/blob/health calls will still run against the stopped backend instead of failing fast with a clear error. `initErr` is now effectively dead state outside of `Init`.

Keep a cheap check of a stopped flag (ideally atomic) in the handlers, or remove the misleading `Stop` bookkeeping.

title: Init failure in constructor leaks the context and background goroutines
body:
When `s.Init(ctx)` fails, `NewResourceServer` returns `nil, err` without calling `cancel()`.

If `search.init` succeeded but a later step such as `initWatcher` failed, the search watch goroutine and the backend poller started by `WatchWriteEvents` keep running with no owner that can stop them. The search watch uses `context.Background()`.

Call `cancel()` on the error path. Ideally also tear down anything that `search.init` started.

title: Integration test disabled for postgres instead of being fixed
body:
The PR skips `TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer` on postgres with the note "works locally". This PR changes startup behaviour: `NewResourceServer` now runs DB init, search index build and watcher setup synchronously.

The skip likely hides a regression or timing problem introduced by that change. For example, the test only sleeps 500ms before probing the HTTP server, and startup now blocks on indexing.

The postgres storage-server startup path loses CI coverage exactly when its behaviour changes.

title: Data races on shared counters/err in parallel init workers
body:
Inside the `errgroup` workers, two shared variables are written from multiple goroutines without synchronization:
- `totalBatchesIndexed++`
- `_, _, err = s.build(...)`, which writes the outer `err`

Before this PR the global `BuildIndex` lock serialized most of each worker's run. Now that the lock is removed so that builds run in parallel, these races are much more likely to be hit. The reported `namespaced_indexed` span attribute can be wrong, and the race detector will flag the code.

Use a local `err` in the closure and an `atomic.Int64` (or count after `Wait`).

title: TotalDocs iterates the index cache without a lock while the watch goroutine can write to it
body:
`bleveBackend.TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` without holding `cacheMu`. This PR adds a call to it in `searchSupport.init` (search.go:216), after the watch goroutine has already started at search.go:207.

That goroutine calls `handleEvent` -> `getOrCreateIndex` -> `BuildIndex`, which now writes `b.cache[key]` under `cacheMu.Lock()` (bleve.go:137-139). If a write event arrives for a resource that has no index yet, the map write can overlap with the unlocked iteration in `TotalDocs`.

Go treats concurrent map iteration and write as a fatal, unrecoverable runtime error, so this can crash the process at startup. `TotalDocs` should take `b.cacheMu.RLock()`, or the log line should run before the watcher is started.

title: Errgroup workers share and overwrite the outer `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` variables
body:
Inside `group.Go`, each worker assigns to the enclosing function's `err` (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and returns it, and also increments `totalBatchesIndexed++` without synchronization.

Before this PR, `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for its entire duration, which effectively serialized most of the work. This PR removes that lock so builds really run in parallel with up to `initWorkers` goroutines, which widens the race window considerably.

One worker can overwrite `err` between another worker's assignment and its `return err`. A failed index build can then be reported as success, letting startup continue with a missing index, or a successful worker can return another worker's error. The `namespaced_indexed` span attribute is also racy.

Fix: use a local variable (`_, _, err := s.build(...)`) and an atomic counter.

title: Stop() no longer causes requests to be rejected because handlers stopped checking Init
body:
`Stop` sets `s.initErr` to "service is stopping" / "service is stopped". This was the mechanism that made subsequent gRPC calls fail, because every handler called `s.Init(ctx)` and the already-completed `sync.Once` returned `initErr`.

This PR removes the `Init` call from all handlers (Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search, History, Origin, IsHealthy, PutBlob, GetBlob), and nothing else reads `initErr`. After `Stop`, requests are still served against a backend whose lifecycle has been stopped and whose watch context is cancelled. `IsHealthy` also keeps reporting healthy during shutdown.

If stop semantics are still wanted, keep a cheap check of a stopped/initErr flag in the handlers (protected against the data race with `Stop`).

title: Init failure in the constructor leaks the cancel func and background watchers
body:
`NewResourceServer` now runs `s.Init(ctx)` and returns `nil, err` on failure without calling `s.cancel()` or `lifecycle.Stop`.

If `search.init` succeeds and `initWatcher` then fails, the search watcher has already been started: it called `WatchWriteEvents` with `context.Background()`, and its backend poller goroutine runs until the backend is stopped. Because the server is never returned, nobody can stop it. The cancelable context created for the server is also never cancelled.

Call `cancel()` and stop the lifecycle hooks on the error path.

title: Postgres integration test disabled instead of fixed
body:
This PR adds an unconditional skip for postgres in `TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer`, noting that it "works locally".

The PR moves resource server initialization (DB init and migrations, building indexes for every namespace, starting watchers) into the constructor, which runs during `InitializeModuleServer`. A CI failure that appears together with this change is likely related to it, for example a timeout or a connection issue at construction time.

Skipping the test removes postgres coverage of the storage-server target exactly when its startup behaviour changes. The root cause should be investigated, or at least tracked with an issue link, rather than silently skipped.

title: Call to non-existent no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() breaks compilation
body:
`UsernameForm.authenticate` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments. The only method this PR adds to the superclass `UsernamePasswordForm` is `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)`, and there is no no-arg overload. The services module therefore does not compile.

The call should pass the current user: `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`. Even after that fix, the skip decision for re-authentication depends on the predicate in `UsernamePasswordForm`, which is itself wrong (see the separate finding).

title: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires user != null, disabling passkeys on normal login
body:
The new helper returns `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null`. Both `authenticate()` and the error `challenge()` now gate `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` on it. On a fresh login `context.getUser()` is null, so the conditional-UI passkey data (challenge, `ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI`, the webauth form) is never added. That is the primary passkey use case, and the old code explicitly filled it when the user was null.

The same applies after a failed initial login. `validateUserAndPassword` clears the context user, so the error re-challenge also drops passkeys.

The new tests that expect automatic discoverable-key login or the `//form[@id='webauth']` element on the initial page would fail, e.g. `webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey` and the first half of the `_reauthentication` tests.

Conversely, when a user is set (re-authentication), the passkey UI is enabled for any user, even one with no passkey credential. `UsernameForm` would then never skip the username step during re-auth for such users.

The intended condition is likely `user == null || user.credentialManager().isConfiguredFor(webauthnAuth.getCredentialType())`.

title: reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey disables passkeys realm-wide instead of testing a user without a passkey
body:
The test name and the comment at line 304 ("Passkeys login should not be available on the page as this user does not have passkey") claim to verify that a user with no passkey credential does not see passkey UI during re-authentication. The test, however, sets `setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(Boolean.FALSE)` for the whole realm, so the webauth form is absent only because the feature is off.

The case this PR actually changes is never covered: passkeys enabled for the realm, re-authenticating user has only a password. In that case the current `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled` would show the passkey UI.

The comment at line 280 ("set passwordless policy for discoverable keys") is also wrong for this block. A test with passkeys enabled and a password-only user (e.g. test-user@localhost) should be added.

title: Call to non-existent no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() breaks compilation
body: `UsernameForm.authenticate` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments. The only declaration, in `UsernamePasswordForm` (line 160), takes a `UserModel` parameter, and no no-arg overload exists in the class hierarchy. The `services` module will not compile. The call should pass the user, e.g. `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`.

title: `user != null` turns off conditional passkeys for normal (unidentified) login
body:
`isConditionalPasskeysEnabled` returns `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null`. Before this change, webauthn data was filled exactly when no user was selected (`context.getUser() == null`). The new check does the opposite: on a first login there is no context user, so `authenticate()` (line 115) never calls `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm`. Passkey conditional UI and the discoverable-key auto login therefore no longer appear on the initial login page.

The error path is affected too. `getUser()` calls `context.clearUser()`, and `validateUser` only sets the user after the password is validated. So `challenge(context, error, field)` (line 137) also sees a null user after an invalid username or invalid password, and passkeys vanish from the error page.

This breaks the main passkeys feature; existing tests such as `webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey` should fail. The check should allow `user == null` (for example `user == null || <user has passkey credential>`) rather than require a non-null user.

title: Re-authentication enables passkeys for any identified user, even one with no passkey credential
body:
For an already-identified user, the new condition depends only on the realm setting. It never checks whether that user has a passwordless/passkey credential (e.g. `user.credentialManager().isConfiguredFor(webauthnAuth.getCredentialType())`). Two problems follow:

1. During re-authentication (e.g. `prompt=login`), users without passkeys are shown the passkey UI and a browser WebAuthn prompt they cannot complete.
2. In `UsernameForm.authenticate`, the shortcut that skips the username step for an already-identified user is disabled whenever the realm has passkeys enabled. Every re-authenticating user, including those without passkeys, gets an extra username form with the username hidden and nothing to fill in.

The condition should also require that the current user actually has a passkey credential.

title: "User without passkey" test actually disables passkeys for the whole realm
body:
`reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey` and its comment claim to check that passkeys are not shown during re-authentication "as this user does not have passkey". The test, however, sets `setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(Boolean.FALSE)`, which turns the feature off realm-wide.

The case that matters is not covered: a realm with passkeys enabled and a user who has no passkey credential re-authenticating. That is exactly where the new `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled` logic misbehaves, showing the passkey UI and no longer skipping `UsernameForm`. The test should keep passkeys enabled and log in as a user without a WebAuthn credential.

title: Call to non-existent no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() breaks compilation
body: `UsernameForm.authenticate` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments. The only method added in the superclass `UsernamePasswordForm` is `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)`, and no no-arg overload exists anywhere in the hierarchy. The services module will not compile, so neither the fix nor the new tests can run. The call should pass the current user, e.g. `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`.

title: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires user != null, disabling passkeys on normal login and enabling them for every re-auth
body:
The new helper returns `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null`. Before this PR, the conditional UI was filled only when no user was selected yet (the normal identity-first login). It is used in `authenticate()` (line 115) and in `challenge(context, error, field)` (line 137), and with this condition:
(1) On a fresh login where `context.getUser()` is null, `fillContextForm` is never called. The webauthn challenge and conditional UI are no longer rendered, so passkey login is broken for all first-time and logged-out logins.
(2) During re-authentication it returns true for any identified user, so the passkey UI is shown even to users with no passkey credential.
The intended condition is `user == null || user.credentialManager().isConfiguredFor(webauthnAuth.getCredentialType())`.

title: Re-auth test for user without passkey disables passkeys realm-wide, so the per-user check is never tested
body:
`reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey` sets `setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(Boolean.FALSE)` for the whole realm. The webauthn form is therefore absent simply because the feature is off, not because the user lacks a passkey. Yet the inline comment at line 304 says passkeys are unavailable "as this user does not have passkey".

The important case is never exercised: passkeys enabled in the realm, and a user without a passkey credential re-authenticating with prompt=login. That case is exactly where the `user != null` logic in `UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled` misbehaves. The test should keep passkeys enabled and assert the webauthn form is absent for test-user@localhost.

title: Login-cache invalidation decision uses org-aware isEnabled(), which can leave a stale login IDP list
body:
In `update()`, `idpById` comes from `getById()`, which returns the `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel` wrapper. Its `isEnabled()` returns false whenever the linked organization is disabled. `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate` feeds this into `getLoginPredicate()`. The cached ID set, however, is built by `idpDelegate.getForLogin`, which filters on raw DB fields (enabled, hideOnLogin, linkOnly, BROKER_PUBLIC) and ignores organization enablement.

Repro: an IDP linked to org A is public, enabled and shown, so it is in the cached ORG_ONLY/ALL lists. Org A is then disabled. An admin sets `hideOnLogin=true`, `linkOnly=true` or removes `BROKER_PUBLIC`. The original evaluates as not-login (wrapper reports disabled) and the updated model is also not-login, so the first early return fires and nothing is invalidated. The cached list still holds the IDP's id.

Once org A is re-enabled, `getForLogin` returns the IDP from cache. `OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean` only re-checks `isEnabled()`, not hideOnLogin, linkOnly or public. A hidden, link-only or non-public broker is therefore displayed on the login page until something else invalidates the key.

Fix: base the original-state check on the raw stored model (e.g. `idpDelegate.getById`), or always invalidate when any `LoginFilter` field, `BROKER_PUBLIC` or the org link changes.

title: Single per-mode login cache entry grows with every organization and is rebuilt on each new org lookup
body:
All `getForLogin` results for a fetch mode share one cache key (`<realm>.idp.login.<mode>`), with the organizationId only used as a sub-key inside `IdentityProviderListQuery`. The first lookup for each new organization calls `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)`, which bumps the revision. It then re-adds a new query object that copies every previously cached org result set.

For `FetchMode.ALL`, each per-org set also duplicates all realm-level login IDPs. In realms with many organizations, the entry grows roughly as O(orgs × IDPs). Login traffic for different orgs keeps invalidating and rewriting the same entry, and concurrent requests race on the revision, so their caching attempts are discarded. Consider keying the cache by mode and organizationId instead.

title: Test cleanup removes literal "alias" instead of the created IDPs
body: `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` binds the cleanup to an IDP whose alias is the string "alias", not to `"idp-alias-" + i`. The same mistake appears again at line 425 for `idp-alias-20`. None of the IDPs created by `testCacheIDPForLogin` are cleaned up. Instead, cleanup issues repeated removals of a non-existent IDP, which may fail with 404 or be silently swallowed. Use the actual alias, e.g. `final String alias = "idp-alias-" + i; ... get(alias)::remove`.

title: Login-cache invalidation on update uses the org-aware wrapped model, so changes to IDPs of disabled orgs are missed
body:
In `update()`, `idpById` comes from `getById()`, which returns the model wrapped by `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel`. That wrapper's `isEnabled()` returns false whenever the linked organization is disabled. The cached login lists, however, are built from `idpDelegate.getForLogin`, which only checks the IDP's own `enabled` column. So IDPs of a disabled org are in the cached sets; this is why the bean now re-checks `isEnabled()`.

Scenario: org A is disabled and has a public, enabled IDP X that sits in the `ALL`/`ORG_ONLY` login cache. An admin sets X's `BROKER_PUBLIC` to false (or `hideOnLogin` / `linkOnly` to true). `getLoginPredicate().test(original)` is false because of the wrapper, and `test(updated)` is also false, so the early return at line 405 skips invalidation. When org A is re-enabled, which does not touch the login keys, the stale cached set still contains X. `getById` returns a fresh model whose `isEnabled()` is now true, and the bean only re-checks `isEnabled()`. A private, hidden or link-only broker is then shown on the login page until something else invalidates the cache.

Fix: evaluate the predicate against the raw stored model, e.g. `idpDelegate.getById(...)` or the unwrapped cached model, as `remove()` already does with `idpDelegate.getByAlias`.

title: Merge path can re-cache stale per-org results after a concurrent invalidation
Single cache entry per FetchMode shared across all organizations causes churn and unbounded growth
body: `cacheKeyForLogin` keys only on realm and mode, while `organizationId` is stored as a searchKey inside one `IdentityProviderListQuery`. Every first login lookup for a not-yet-seen organization invalidates and rebuilds the whole entry for that mode, merging in all previous orgs' sets. In realms with many organizations, this causes repeated invalidation of the shared entry. Concurrent lookups for different orgs race and drop each other's results. The entry also grows roughly as (#orgs × #realm-level login IDPs) for `ALL` mode. Including the organization id in the cache key would avoid both problems.

title: Test cleanup removes literal alias "alias" instead of the created IDPs
body: `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` registers a cleanup for an IDP whose alias is literally "alias". It does not target the `idp-alias-N` providers created in the loop, and line 425 repeats the same mistake for `idp-alias-20`. None of the created IDPs are cleaned up by these registrations, and the cleanup targets a non-existent resource. The cleanup should use the actual alias, e.g. `get("idp-alias-" + i)`.

title: Update decides login-cache invalidation using the org-aware model, which disagrees with what the cached list contains
body:
In `update`, the 'original' IDP comes from `getById()` (line 91). That method returns `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(...)`, whose `isEnabled()` returns false when the linked organization is disabled, or when organizations are disabled for the realm.

The cached login ID lists, however, are filled from `idpDelegate.getForLogin(...)`. That is a raw DB query on the ENABLED/LINK_ONLY/HIDE_ON_LOGIN/BROKER_PUBLIC columns and ignores organization status.

Example: an org is disabled and one of its public, enabled IDPs is in the cached list. An admin then sets that IDP to hideOnLogin=true, linkOnly=true, or removes BROKER_PUBLIC. `getLoginPredicate().test(original)` is false because the wrapped `isEnabled()` is false. `test(updated)` is also false. So `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate` returns early (line 405) and nothing is invalidated.

The stale ID stays in the cached list. Once the org is re-enabled, `getForLogin` keeps returning it. `OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean` only re-checks `isEnabled()`, so a hidden, link-only, or non-public broker appears on the login page until some other change invalidates the cache.

Fix: evaluate the original with the raw model (e.g. `idpDelegate.getById(...)`), so the comparison uses the same view as the cached query.

title: Merging a previously read query can re-insert stale search results after a concurrent invalidation
body:
When the cached `IdentityProviderListQuery` exists but lacks the current `searchKey`, the code proceeds in this order:
1. It reads `query` (line 222).
2. It calls `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)`.
3. It reads a fresh revision.
4. It builds a new query that copies all of the old query's searches (`new IdentityProviderListQuery(..., query)`).
5. It adds the result with `cache.getCurrentCounter()`.

If another transaction invalidates `cacheKey` between steps 1 and 2, the old searches are already stale. They still get merged in and stored with an up-to-date revision, so `addRevisioned` accepts them. Typical triggers are creating, removing, or relinking a login IDP.

The login cache can then keep serving outdated ID lists for other organizations: newly added brokers go missing, or brokers that became hidden or unlinked still show. This copies the pattern from `getByOrganization`, but it now affects the login page. The merge should be dropped, or the code should verify the entry was not invalidated between the read and the re-add.

title: Single cache entry per fetch mode accumulates one result set per organization and is rebuilt on every new org
body:
The cache key is only realm + FetchMode, and the organization ID is used as a search key inside one `IdentityProviderListQuery`. For `ALL`/`ORG_ONLY` with an organizationId, each organization not yet seen does three things:
- triggers `invalidateObject` on the shared entry,
- copies the entire existing map of searches,
- re-adds it.

In realms with many organizations, this entry grows without bound, since it holds a set per org. It is also repeatedly invalidated and copied during normal login traffic. Any login-relevant IDP change then discards all of it at once. Consider keying the cache entry by organization (as `getByOrganization` does with `cacheKeyOrgId`), or bounding the stored searches.

title: Test cleanup removes IDP with literal alias "alias" instead of the created IDPs
body:
`getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove);` points at an IDP named "alias", which does not exist. The same mistake appears again at line 425. None of the 21 IDPs created by `testCacheIDPForLogin` (`idp-alias-0`..`idp-alias-20`) are ever cleaned up.

If the realm is not re-imported, they leak into other tests. Re-running the test would also make the `create(...)` calls fail with conflicts that go unnoticed, because the responses are closed without checking status. The cleanup should use the real alias (e.g. `get("idp-alias-" + i)`).

title: Removed fail-fast for multiple crypto providers; equal-order providers now resolved silently
body:
`detectProvider` used to throw when more than one `CryptoProvider` was on the classpath. It now sorts by `order()` and silently returns the first one, logging the rest only at DEBUG.

`DefaultCryptoProvider`, `FIPS1402Provider` and `WildFlyElytronProvider` all return the same order (200). If two of them end up on the classpath (for example default and fips1402), the choice now depends on ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order. A FIPS setup can silently fall back to the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider, or the reverse, with no visible warning.

It gets worse because ServiceLoader instantiates every provider before sorting. The constructors of the "ignored" providers still run their global side effects: `Security.addProvider(BC)`, and `insertProviderAt` of KeycloakFipsSecurityProvider/BCFIPS/BCJSSE plus `ssl.*ManagerFactory.algorithm` property changes. Previously that misconfiguration made startup fail. Now the JVM keeps running with mixed security-provider state.

The ordering should only be used to break ties between different priorities. If several providers share the highest order it should still throw, or at least log a WARN.

title: New abstract `order()` breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations (source and binary)
body:
`int order()` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` SPI as an abstract method.

Any third-party or extension implementation of `CryptoProvider` no longer compiles. Worse, an implementation compiled against the previous keycloak-common will throw `AbstractMethodError` at runtime when `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` calls `CryptoProvider::order` in the comparator. That error surfaces during crypto initialization and breaks startup.

This should be a `default` method returning a sensible base value, so existing implementations keep working and only the providers that need a different priority override it.

title: ES384/ES512 tests use a P-256 key and only check self-round-trip
body:
The key pair comes from `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, which uses the JDK default curve (P-256). `testES384` and `testES512` therefore sign with a P-256 key, so r and s are always about 32 bytes and are just zero-padded to 48/66.

A real ES512 (P-521) signature has a DER SEQUENCE body over 127 bytes. That requires the long-form length encoding in `ASN1Encoder.writeLength` and the long-form parsing in `ASN1Decoder.readLength`, and neither path is ever exercised.

The assertion is also weak. It only checks that decode → encode → decode through the same new code is self-consistent. It never compares the re-encoded DER with the original `sign` bytes (DER is canonical, so they should be identical), and it never verifies the signature with `Signature.verify`. A symmetric bug in the encoder and decoder would pass.

The test should generate keys on the matching curve (secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) and assert `assertArrayEquals(sign, asn1Des)` and/or verify the re-encoded signature.

title: Leftover dead code in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
body: Lines 114-115 (`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger); ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);`) build two encoders and throw the results away. The real encoding is done again on lines 117-121. This is leftover code that adds allocations on every signature conversion and should be removed.

title: Multiple-provider guard removed; equal-order providers are now picked silently by classpath order
body:
`detectProvider` used to throw `IllegalStateException` when more than one `CryptoProvider` was found. That check protected against a misconfigured classpath, for example one containing both `keycloak-crypto-default` and `keycloak-crypto-fips1402`.

Now the list is sorted by `order()` and the first entry is used. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return 200, and the sort is stable, so a tie between them is broken by ServiceLoader/classpath order. The other providers are reported only at DEBUG level.

Consequences:
- A FIPS deployment that accidentally has the default provider on the classpath can silently run with the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider instead of failing fast.
- `ServiceLoader` instantiates every provider before sorting. The ignored providers' constructors still run their global side effects: FIPS inserts BCFIPS/BCJSSE at JVM security-provider positions 1-3 and rewrites `ssl.*ManagerFactory.algorithm`, and Default registers BC. The JVM can end up in a mixed state.

Suggested fix: keep failing (or at least log at WARN) when two or more providers share the highest order. Only allow silent fallback when the winner has a strictly higher order, such as 200 vs the authz-client's 100.

title: New abstract interface method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body:
`int order();` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` interface in keycloak-common without a default implementation. Any `CryptoProvider` implemented outside this repository stops compiling, or fails at runtime with `AbstractMethodError` when `CryptoIntegration` calls `order()` while sorting. This includes custom providers and implementations in keycloak-client or other downstream projects built against a newer keycloak-common.

A `default int order() { return 0; }` (or similar) would keep compatibility and still let the bundled providers override it.

title: ES384/ES512 tests use a P-256 key, so real curve sizes and long-form DER lengths are never tested
body:
The key pair comes from `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, which defaults to P-256. The same 32-byte r/s values are reused for ES384 and ES512; they are only zero-padded to 48/66 bytes.

As a result:
- P-384 and P-521 signatures are never exercised.
- A P-521 DER signature is about 139 bytes. That is the only case that triggers the long-form length (>127) path in `ASN1Encoder.writeLength` and `ASN1Decoder.readLength`, and it stays untested.

The test also only checks that the custom encoder and decoder agree with each other. It never compares `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` output with the JDK-produced DER (`sign`), and never checks that the result passes `Signature.verify`. Symmetric bugs in the hand-written ASN.1 code would therefore go unnoticed.

Suggested fix: initialize the generator with `secp256r1`/`secp384r1`/`secp521r1` per algorithm, and assert `Arrays.equals(asn1Des, sign)` or verify the re-encoded signature.

title: Leftover encoder calls whose results are discarded
body:
`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` (lines 114-115) build encoders and throw them away. They are re-created inside the `writeDerSeq` call just below.

This is dead code that does extra allocation and encoding on every signature verification, and it makes readers wonder whether something was meant to use those results. Remove both lines.

title: Multiple equal-order crypto providers are now silently resolved by classpath order
body:
`detectProvider` used to throw when more than one `CryptoProvider` was found. It now sorts by `order()` and takes the first. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return 200, so a tie between them is broken only by the stable sort, i.e. by `ServiceLoader`/classpath order. The ignored providers are logged at DEBUG only.

Consequence: a deployment that relies on `CryptoIntegration.init` (not `setProvider`) and has both the FIPS and the default crypto jars on the classpath now silently picks one at random instead of failing. It may run in non-FIPS mode without any visible warning.

All discovered providers are also instantiated before sorting. The constructors of `FIPS1402Provider` and `DefaultCryptoProvider` change JVM-global state: they insert BCFIPS/BCJSSE/KeycloakFipsSecurityProvider at positions 1-3, add BC, and rewrite `ssl.KeyManagerFactory.algorithm`. A provider that loses the tie still leaves those changes behind. Before this PR startup aborted in that case.

Suggested fix: keep the hard failure (or at least WARN) when the two highest-ranked providers have the same `order()`, and only drop lower-ranked ones.

title: New abstract `order()` breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body:
`int order()` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` SPI as an abstract method. Any external or custom implementation no longer compiles.

Binaries compiled against the previous `keycloak-common` are worse: when such a provider is discovered, `Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order)` in `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` throws `AbstractMethodError` during the sort. That aborts crypto initialization entirely, even if a valid built-in provider is also present.

A `default int order() { return 0; }` (or similar) would keep the SPI backward compatible while still letting the built-in providers take precedence.

title: ES384/ES512 tests use a P-256 key, so long-form DER lengths are never tested and only a self-roundtrip is checked
body:
The test builds one key pair with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, which defaults to P-256, and reuses it for ES256, ES384 and ES512. With a P-256 key, r and s are at most 33 bytes and the DER SEQUENCE is under 128 bytes. So the long-form length paths in the new `ASN1Encoder.writeLength` and `ASN1Decoder.readLength` (needed for P-521/ES512, where the sequence is about 136-139 bytes) are never executed. The 48- and 66-byte component sizes are only checked as zero padding of 32-byte values.

The test also compares only the output of the hand-written decoder against itself after a round trip through the hand-written encoder. A symmetric encoding bug would pass. It never checks the re-encoded DER with `Signature.verify`, and never compares against a reference implementation such as BC.

Suggested fix: generate a key on the matching curve (secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) for each algorithm, and assert that `signature.verify(asn1Des)` succeeds.

title: Possible NPE when the all-clients resource is missing
body:
When there is no client-specific resource, `hasPermission(ClientModel, String)` falls back to `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...)` and passes the result straight into `getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource)`. `getResourceTypeResource` returns null in two cases:
- `supportsAuthorizationSchema` is false, e.g. admin permissions were disabled on the realm but the admin-permissions client still exists.
- The "Clients" resource does not exist. This is the case for any realm whose admin-permissions client was initialized before this change, because `init()` returns early when the client already exists.

In both cases the store dereferences a null resource and throws an NPE. The call chain is `canView(client)` → `canConfigure` → `canManage(client)`, so any FGAP-only admin (without the manage/view-clients roles) gets a 500 on basic client endpoints. Add a null check that returns false, as the sibling `hasPermission(String)` already does.

title: New Clients scopes/resource are never provisioned for existing admin-permissions clients
body:
`init()` returns immediately if `realm.getAdminPermissionsClient()` is non-null. Scopes and the per-type 'all-resource' resources are only created on first initialization.

Realms that enabled FGAP v2 before this change keep their old setup: they have no `Clients` resource and no `configure`, `map-roles-client-scope` or `map-roles-composite` scopes. For those realms:
- Creating a Clients permission with those scopes fails in `getScope` with "Scope [...] does not exist".
- Creating a per-client resource fails in `getOrCreateResource` with "No scopes found."
- Evaluation hits the null `Clients` resource path.

There is no migration or reconciliation step that adds the missing schema elements.

title: getClientsWithPermission returns the resource-type name instead of client IDs
body:
Per-client resources are created by `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` via `resourceStore.create(...)` without setting a type. So `resourceStore.findByType(server, "Clients", ...)` only finds the 'all-clients' resource whose type was set in `init()`. The method then adds `resource.getName()`, which is the literal string "Clients", to the result set.

Callers expect a set of client IDs, as the V1 implementation returns. They will get either an empty set or `{"Clients"}`, never the clients the admin actually has the scope for. Any filtering based on this method is therefore wrong.

title: Global canView() ignores all-clients MANAGE, inconsistent with canView(ClientScopeModel) and V1 semantics
body:
`canView()` only checks the `view` scope on the all-clients resource. An admin granted MANAGE on all clients therefore gets `canView()` == false.

The inherited `canViewClientScopes()`, `canListClientScopes()` and `requireList()` all delegate to `canView()`. As a result, such an admin can manage every client scope (`canManageClientScopes`/`canManage(ClientScopeModel)` accept MANAGE) and `canView(ClientScopeModel)` explicitly accepts MANAGE. Yet the same admin gets 403 when listing client scopes or clients, unless they also hold a query-* role.

In V1, manage implies view (`canManageClientsDefault() || canViewClientDefault()`). Consider `hasPermission(VIEW) || hasPermission(MANAGE)` here. This also lets client listing use the paginated fast path instead of loading every client and evaluating it individually.

title: Same resource evaluated repeatedly per client check
body:
`canView(ClientModel)` calls `canView()`, then `canConfigure(client)`, which calls `canManage(client)`, then `hasPermission(client, VIEW)`. That is up to four full policy evaluations for one client:
- one of the all-clients resource;
- three of the same client resource, each evaluating all of its scopes and then discarding all but one.

The fallback path also runs a `findByResource` policy lookup each time. Client listing calls this for every client when global view is not granted, multiplying policy-evaluation cost. Evaluate the resource once and check for any of the accepted scopes.

title: getResourceName not extended for the Clients resource type
body:
`getResourceName` only special-cases `USERS`, returning "All users" or the username. For Clients-type permissions it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`.

Neither the 'Clients' all-resource nor the per-client resources (created with only a name) set a display name. Permission resource listings for client permissions will therefore show null instead of "All clients" or the clientId.

title: Client deletion leaves orphaned V2 client resources/permissions
body:
The removal listener is now a no-op unless V1 `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` is enabled. Nothing replaces it for V2.

With this PR, V2 creates per-client resources in the admin-permissions client, named after the client UUID. When a client is deleted, its resource and the scope permissions referencing it stay in the admin-permissions resource server indefinitely. The gate also silently removes the cleanup of leftover V1 data that previously ran regardless of the feature flag.

title: Existing management/permissions endpoints now fail with 500 under V2
body:
`isPermissionsEnabled(ClientModel)`, `setPermissionsEnabled` and `getPermissions` now throw `UnsupportedOperationException`. `ClientResource`'s `management/permissions` GET/PUT endpoints call these via `AdminPermissions.management(...).clients()`.

Before this PR, under V2 those endpoints returned a disabled reference. Now they surface as an unhandled 500 instead of a meaningful client error.

title: Javadoc for void require* methods says "Returns true"
body: The Javadoc on `requireView()` (line 96) and `requireViewClientScopes()` (line 101) says "Returns {@code true} if ... returns {@code true}". These methods are void and actually throw ForbiddenException when the corresponding `can*` method returns false.

title: Test mutates the admin's own login client by removing an arbitrary default scope
No test that Users permissions don't leak to Clients via shared scopes
body:
`init()` collapses scope names across resource types into a single Scope entity. 'manage', 'view' and 'map-roles' are now shared between the Users and Clients resource types, so isolation depends entirely on permissions being bound to the correct type resource.

No test checks either direction:
- that an all-users MANAGE/VIEW permission does not grant `canManage`/`canView` on clients;
- that a Clients permission does not grant user access.

`testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient` grants both types at once, so it cannot detect leakage. The `MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE` scope and per-client negative overrides are also untested.

title: getClientsWithPermission returns "Clients" instead of client IDs and misses per-client resources
body:
`getClientsWithPermission` iterates `resourceStore.findByType(server, "Clients", ...)` and adds `resource.getName()`.

Per-client resources created in `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` never get a type. They are made with `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, owner)` and no `setType`. Only the all-clients resource from `init()` has type `Clients`.

As a result:
- Individual client permissions are never found.
- When the all-clients permission is granted, the returned set contains the literal string "Clients" rather than any client id.

Any caller that treats the result as a set of client IDs gets wrong data. Either nothing is found, or a bogus id is returned.

title: canView(client) short-circuits on all-clients VIEW, so per-client deny permissions cannot restrict view
body:
`canView(ClientModel)` returns true as soon as `canView()` is true. `canView()` includes `hasPermission(VIEW)`, which evaluates only the all-clients "Clients" resource.

So if an admin is granted VIEW on all clients, a per-client NEGATIVE VIEW permission for a specific client is never consulted. The admin can still view that client.

This contradicts the resource-specific-overrides-type semantics used elsewhere in V2. For users, `testViewUserPermission` shows a per-user deny overriding the all-users allow. Here an administrator cannot hide individual clients from someone holding all-clients VIEW.

`canView(client)` should only short-circuit on the admin roles (`canViewClientDefault`). The VIEW decision should go through `hasPermission(client, VIEW)`, which already falls back to the all-clients resource.

title: NPE when the "Clients" type resource is absent
body:
When no per-client resource exists, the code loads the type resource via `getResourceTypeResource(...)` and passes it straight to `getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource)`. Later it calls `resource.getScopes()`. Neither use is null-checked.

`getResourceTypeResource` returns null in several cases:
- `supportsAuthorizationSchema` is false, e.g. the realm's admin permissions were disabled while the admin-permissions client still exists.
- The "Clients" resource does not exist. `AdminPermissionsSchema.init()` returns early when the admin-permissions client already exists, so realms initialized before this change never get the new "Clients" resource or the new scopes (configure, map-roles-composite, map-roles-client-scope).

In those cases every client access check by a non-manage-clients admin throws a NullPointerException (500), because the store dereferences `resource.getId()`. The method should return false when the type resource is null.

title: getResourceName not updated for the Clients resource type
body:
`getResourceName` maps only `Users` resources: "All users" for the type resource, or the username for a user. For policies of type `Clients` it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`.

Neither the per-client resources (created with only a name) nor the "Clients" type resource have a display name. Permission representations for client permissions will therefore show null resource names instead of the clientId or an "All clients" label.

Add a `CLIENTS` branch that resolves the client by id and returns its clientId.

title: Removal listener now does no cleanup under V2 (or when FGAP v1 is disabled)
body:
The whole listener is now gated on `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` (v1). This was needed because `ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled` throws.

As a result, when V2 is enabled, deleting a client leaves behind its per-client resource (named by the client UUID) and any scope permissions referencing it in the admin-permissions resource server. No V2 cleanup was added.

Also, previously the v1 cleanup ran unconditionally. Realms that once used v1 and later disabled the feature will now accumulate orphaned v1 resources and policies for deleted clients, roles and groups.

title: Javadoc for void require* methods says they "Return true"
body:
`requireView()` is documented as "Returns {@code true} if canView() returns true", and `requireViewClientScopes()` (line ~101) as "Returns {@code true} if canViewClientScopes() returns true".

Both methods are `void` and throw ForbiddenException when the check fails. The other `require*` methods in this interface are documented that way. These two docs are wrong.

title: Repeated full policy evaluations per client check
body:
Each `hasPermission(client, scope)` call:
- performs a full policy evaluation over all scopes of the resource, then discards everything but one scope;
- on the fallback path, also runs a `findByResource` query.

`canView(client)` chains `canView()`, then `canConfigure` → `canManage` → `hasPermission(MANAGE)`, then `hasPermission(CONFIGURE)`, then `hasPermission(VIEW)`. That is up to four evaluations of essentially the same resource. `getAccess(client)` repeats this for view, manage and configure.

When listing clients without the view-clients role, this runs for every client in the realm. Evaluate once and check the granted scopes set, or cache per request.

title: New client scopes and override semantics are not actually verified
body:
`testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient` grants `CONFIGURE` together with `MAP_ROLES` and `MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE`. The composite-mapping success may therefore come from configure/manage-role checks rather than the new `MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE` scope.

Other gaps:
- No test covers `MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE`.
- No test covers `getClientsWithPermission`.
- No test covers a per-client NEGATIVE permission combined with an all-clients permission, as is done for users.

These tests would have exposed the canView short-circuit and the getClientsWithPermission bug.

title: Tests mutate shared realm state without cleanup
body:
Some tests change realm state and never restore it:
- `testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient` creates client roles `myclient-role` and `myclient-subRole`, maps one to `myadmin`, and adds a composite. It registers no `realm.cleanup()` actions.
- `testManageOnlyOneClient` renames `myclient` and moves a default client scope to optional without reverting.

Other tests in the class index into `getDefaultClientScopes()` and depend on `myclient`'s state. These changes make results order-dependent, and a role-create conflict will occur if the realm is reused.

title: NPE when the 'Clients' all-resource is missing
body:
When no per-client resource exists, `hasPermission(ClientModel, String)` falls back to `getResourceTypeResource(...)`.
