- The thread outlives the test method and may keep issuing admin requests while the framework cleans up or reuses the realm for the next test.

Keep a reference to the `Thread` and `join()` it (with a timeout) before asserting. Also consider asserting that at least one read actually overlapped the deletions.

title: If a deletion throws, the reader thread spins forever
body:
`deletedAll.set(true)` (line 155) only runs if every `remove()` call in the loop at lines 152-154 succeeds. If any `remove()` throws, for example a 500 or 404 caused by the very race under test, the flag is never set.

The non-daemon reader thread then loops indefinitely. It keeps hammering `GET /groups` for the rest of the test run, interferes with other tests, and can keep the test JVM from exiting. Set the flag in a `finally` block, or make the thread a daemon and bound its lifetime.

title: Created groups are not registered for cleanup
body:
The 100 groups are created directly via the admin API without `managedRealm.cleanup().add(...)`. Other tests in this class register their cleanup this way.

If creation fails partway (the `fail(...)` branch), or the deletion loop aborts, the leftover "Test Group N" groups stay in the shared managed realm. They can break later tests that count or list top-level groups. Register a cleanup for each created id.

title: Same concurrent-delete NPE remains in the paginated getSubGroupsStream overloads
body:
The PR null-guards `modelSupplier.get()` only in `getSubGroupsCount()`. Three sibling methods still call `modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` with no null check:
- `getSubGroupsStream(search, firstResult, maxResults)` (line 256)
- `getSubGroupsStream(firstResult, maxResults)` (line 262)
- `getSubGroupsStream(search, exact, firstResult, maxResults)` (line 268)

`getGroupById` on the delegate returns null once the group is deleted in the database while the cached adapter is still in use. In that window these methods throw the same NullPointerException the PR is meant to fix. A realistic trigger is listing a group's children (the admin console's children endpoint) while another request deletes the group. The fix is incomplete; these methods should get the same null handling, e.g. return `Stream.empty()`.

title: Reader thread is never joined, so exceptions can be missed and the thread leaks
body:
After the deletes, the test sets `deletedAll` to true and immediately asserts that `caughtExceptions` is empty. It never waits for the reader thread to finish.

The reader may still be inside a `groups()` request at that moment. That last request is the one most likely to hit the race, and any exception from it is added after the assertion has already passed, so the regression can go undetected.

The thread is also non-daemon and unmanaged. It can keep sending requests to the shared managed realm while cleanup or the next test runs, which causes cross-test interference.

Keep a reference to the thread and `join()` it (with a timeout) before asserting.

title: Test does not ensure reads actually overlap with deletes
body:
The reader thread is started and the main thread begins deleting right away. Nothing guarantees the reader has started, or completed any request, before or during the deletions. On a fast or loaded machine the deletes can finish before any concurrent read happens, and the test passes without exercising the fix.

A latch or counter would fix this, for example:
- wait for the first successful read before starting deletes, and/or
- assert that at least N reads happened while deletes were in progress.

Without it, the regression test is nondeterministic and can pass vacuously.

title: getSubGroupsCount now returns null, unlike other GroupModel implementations
body:
Other `GroupModel` implementations return an actual count and never null: the default method counts the subgroup stream, and JPA runs a count query. The cached adapter now returns `null` when the backing group has disappeared. Any caller that unboxes or compares the `Long` (e.g. `getSubGroupsCount() > 0`) would trade the original NPE for a new one.

Returning `0L` for a deleted group would keep the contract consistent. Alternatively, document that null means "group no longer exists".

title: Hierarchy population still NPEs if a parent group is deleted concurrently
body:
`populateGroupHierarchyFromSubGroups` looks up each parent with `session.groups().getGroupById(realm, currGroup.getParentId())` and uses the result without a null check. The result is passed to `groupEvaluator.canView(parentModel)`, `toRepresentation(groupEvaluator, parentModel, full)` and `populateSubGroupCount(parentModel, parent)`.

This code path runs when groups are searched. If a parent is deleted between loading the child and walking up the tree, the lookup returns null and the request fails with a NullPointerException. This is the same class of bug the PR addresses, and this file is touched by the PR, but the path is left unguarded. The new test only covers the non-search listing, so it does not catch it.

title: Same NPE remains in the paginated getSubGroupsStream overloads
body: The fix null-guards only `getSubGroupsCount()`. The three paginated `getSubGroupsStream(...)` overloads (lines 256, 262, 268) still call `modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` directly. `modelSupplier.get()` returns null when the group has been deleted in the database but the cached adapter is still in use. That is exactly the concurrent-deletion race this PR targets. Listing or paginating subgroups of a group deleted by another request will still throw a NullPointerException and return HTTP 500. These call sites should get the same null handling, e.g. return `Stream.empty()` when the model is null.

title: Reader thread is never joined, so its exceptions can be missed
body: The test sets `deletedAll` to true and then asserts on `caughtExceptions` right away, without joining the reader thread. At that moment the reader may still be inside a `groups()` request that overlapped the last deletions. An exception from that request is added to the list after the assertion has already passed, so a regression can go undetected. Nothing guarantees the reader issued any request during the deletion window either, so the test may pass without exercising the race at all. Keep a reference to the thread, `join()` it after setting the flag, and ideally check that at least one read overlapped the deletions.

title: Background thread loops forever if a deletion throws
body: `deletedAll.set(true)` runs only after every `remove()` call succeeds. If any deletion throws (e.g. a 500 or a 404), the flag is never set. The non-daemon reader thread then keeps calling the admin API in a tight loop indefinitely. It leaks into later tests and can keep the JVM from exiting. Put the deletion loop in try/finally so the flag is always set, and make the thread a daemon or join it.

title: `organization_context.member` can be None and is dereferenced on every request
body: `enable_advanced` is computed for every request, even when `optimized_pagination` is not set. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is Optional; it is None when the caller is not an org member, for example API-key/token auth where `request.user` is AnonymousUser, or staff accessing an org they don't belong to. For any such non-superuser caller, `organization_context.member.has_global_access` raises AttributeError. That turns the previously working default (DateTimePaginator) path into a 500. At minimum, only evaluate this when `use_optimized` is true and guard against `member is None`.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator key handling is incompatible with the `datetime` ordering it is used with
body: The endpoint uses this paginator with `order_by="-datetime"`, but `get_item_key` does `math.floor/ceil(getattr(item, 'datetime'))`. Calling `math.floor` on a `datetime.datetime` raises TypeError, so any non-empty page crashes inside `build_cursor`. `value_from_cursor` also returns the raw integer cursor value. `build_queryset` then emits `"sentry_auditlogentry"."datetime" <= <int>`, which Postgres rejects (timestamp vs integer). The optimized path therefore fails on the first page and on every cursor-based page. It needs DateTimePaginator-style conversion, e.g. by subclassing DateTimePaginator.

title: Negative queryset slicing raises in Django; 'advanced' path always 500s
body: When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` for negative slice bounds. So the advertised feature can never return results and turns any crafted cursor like `0:-5:0` into an unhandled 500. The comment claiming the ORM 'properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. The comment saying this gives 'access to data beyond normal pagination bounds' describes an intent that should not ship. Negative offsets should be rejected with BadPaginationError (as OffsetPaginator does), not passed through.

title: Admin gate uses raw `is_superuser` flag and `has_global_access`, not an admin check
body: The code says advanced pagination is restricted to 'authorized administrators', but the gate is `request.user.is_superuser or member.has_global_access`. Sentry requires an active superuser session (`is_active_superuser(request)`) for superuser privileges; checking the raw user flag bypasses that elevation step. `has_global_access` is also true for ordinary members in orgs with open membership (allow_joinleave), so it is not an admin check at all. Any privilege-gated behavior here is reachable by far more users than intended.

title: BasePaginator change and comment are misleading; prev cursors with negative offsets still crash
body: The new line `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` only clamps negative offsets for next-cursors. A prev-cursor with a negative offset is still passed straight to `queryset[offset:stop]`, and Django raises ValueError (500). The comment says negative offsets are allowed for 'efficient bidirectional pagination' and that 'the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions'. Neither is true, and this shared base class is used by many endpoints. Clamped negative offsets are also still fed into `build_cursor` via `cursor.offset`, producing nonsensical next/prev offsets. Negative offsets should be rejected with BadPaginationError instead.

title: Comment claims a behavior change that the code does not make
body: The added comment says negative offsets are allowed 'for advanced pagination scenarios', but `self.offset = int(offset)` is unchanged and does no validation either way. The comment documents a nonexistent feature, and negative offsets are not actually usable because Django rejects negative slicing. Remove the comment, or add explicit validation that rejects negative offsets.

title: No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the new endpoint branch
body: The PR adds a new paginator class, a new branch in the audit log endpoint, and changes BasePaginator slicing semantics without any tests. Even a basic test requesting `?optimized_pagination=true` as a superuser with one audit log entry would fail with TypeError from `math.floor(datetime)`. A test with a non-member/API-key caller would hit the AttributeError on `member.has_global_access`.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle the datetime key it is used with; the optimized path always errors
body:
`OptimizedCursorPaginator` copies the integer `Paginator` key logic. `get_item_key` calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` on `getattr(item, self.key)`, and `value_from_cursor` returns the raw cursor value.

The audit log endpoint uses this paginator with `order_by="-datetime"`, so:
- On any non-empty page, `build_cursor` calls `key(results[0])`, i.e. `math.floor(datetime)`, which raises `TypeError`.
- Any request carrying a cursor puts an integer millisecond value into `WHERE datetime <= %s`, which Postgres rejects (timestamp vs integer).

As a result, `?optimized_pagination=true` returns a 500 for every organization that has audit log entries. The paginator needs `DateTimePaginator`'s key and value conversion, e.g. by subclassing `DateTimePaginator`.

title: Negative-offset slicing of a Django QuerySet raises instead of paginating
body:
The "advanced" branch passes `cursor.offset < 0` straight into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing and raise `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`.

The comment claiming "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false. A client-supplied cursor such as `0:-10:0` therefore produces an unhandled 500 instead of results or a 400.

The stated intent, "enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds", is also not something a pagination cursor should provide. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError`, not passed through.

title: BasePaginator change leaves negative prev-cursor offsets unvalidated and miscomputes next cursors for clamped offsets
body:
This shared code path is used by every endpoint that paginates with `Paginator` or `DateTimePaginator`, and it has two problems with negative offsets.

- **Prev cursors (`is_prev`):** a negative user-supplied offset is still passed to `queryset[offset:stop]`. That raises `ValueError` and surfaces as a 500, not as the `BadPaginationError` that `paginate()` converts to a 400. The comment "This is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions" is incorrect.
- **Next cursors:** the offset is silently clamped to 0, but `build_cursor`/`_build_next_values` still use the original negative `cursor.offset`. For example, `next_offset = offset + limit` with offset -5 yields 95 after returning rows 0..100, so the next page overlaps the current one.

The fix is to raise `BadPaginationError` when `cursor.offset < 0`, rather than clamping or passing it through.

title: AttributeError when organization_context.member is None
body:
`organization_context.member` is optional. It is None for requests authenticated without an org membership, e.g. org-level API keys/tokens where `request.user` is anonymous and `is_superuser` is False.

In that case `organization_context.member.has_global_access` raises `AttributeError`. The check is evaluated on every request, before the `use_optimized` flag is consulted, because the `if use_optimized and enable_advanced` comes after it. So such clients get a 500 on every call to this endpoint, even without `optimized_pagination=true`.

Guard for `member is None` and compute this only when `use_optimized` is true.

title: Authorization check for "administrators" uses the wrong signals
body:
The comment says the advanced features are for authorized administrators, but the check does not enforce that.

- **Superuser:** `request.user.is_superuser` is the raw DB flag. Sentry requires an active superuser session, checked via `is_active_superuser(request)`. Using the flag grants the privilege to superuser accounts that have not elevated.
- **Members:** `member.has_global_access` is not an admin indicator. It is true for every member of an org with open membership (allow_joinleave), so ordinary members qualify.

If this gate is meant to restrict a privileged capability, it does not do so.

title: Comment claims negative offsets are supported, but nothing in the code supports them
body:
The added comment says `Cursor` allows negative offsets to enable efficient reverse pagination. The code is unchanged and still accepts any int.

Downstream, negative offsets crash queryset slicing in Django, and other paginators (`OffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`, etc.) explicitly reject them with `BadPaginationError`. The comment documents a nonexistent and unsafe capability and will mislead future maintainers.

title: New paginator, endpoint branch and BasePaginator behavior change ship without tests
OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle the datetime sort key, so the optimized path always fails
body:
The audit log endpoint uses `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `order_by="-datetime"`. Its `get_item_key` calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly on `item.datetime`. That raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`.

As soon as the first page has any rows, `build_cursor` → `_build_next_values` calls `key(results[0])` and the request fails with a 500.

`value_from_cursor` also returns the raw integer cursor value. `build_queryset` then emits `sentry_auditlogentry.datetime <= <int>`, which Postgres rejects, so any request carrying a cursor also errors.

The result is that the whole `optimized_pagination=true` path is unusable. This contradicts the docstring's claim of backward compatibility: cursors issued by `DateTimePaginator` (millisecond timestamps) cannot be consumed here.

Fix: reuse `DateTimePaginator`'s key and cursor conversion, e.g. subclass `DateTimePaginator` instead of re-implementing it.

title: Negative-offset branch slices a QuerySet with a negative index, causing an unhandled error
body:
With `enable_advanced_features=True` and a client-supplied cursor such as `0:-10:0`, the code runs `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`.

Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing; they raise `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`. The comment claiming "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false.

`Endpoint.paginate` only converts `BadPaginationError` into a 400. So any client can trigger a 500 by crafting the cursor.

The stated intent, "access to data beyond normal pagination bounds", is also not a legitimate feature. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError`, as `OffsetPaginator` and `ChainPaginator` already do.

title: Unconditional `organization_context.member.has_global_access` crashes when there is no member
body:
`enable_advanced` is computed on every request, even when `optimized_pagination` is not requested. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is optional. It is `None` for callers that pass `OrganizationAuditPermission` without an org membership, for example:
- staff users who are not superusers
- legacy API keys / token-authenticated requests where `request.user` is anonymous

For those callers, `None.has_global_access` raises `AttributeError`, so the previously working default `DateTimePaginator` path now returns a 500.

Fix: guard on `member is not None`, and only evaluate this when `use_optimized` is true.

title: Admin gating uses the raw superuser flag and `has_global_access`, which is not an admin check
body:
The feature is described as being for "authorized administrators", but the gate does not enforce that.

`request.user.is_superuser` bypasses Sentry's active-superuser-session requirement; the codebase uses `is_active_superuser(request)` for this.

`has_global_access` is also true for every member of an org with open membership (`allow_joinleave`), not just owners or managers.

As a result, the extra paginator behaviour, including the negative-offset path, is exposed more broadly than intended.

title: BasePaginator change still passes negative offsets to the QuerySet for prev cursors
body:
`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` silently clamps negative offsets for next cursors. This behaviour change affects every endpoint using `BasePaginator`.

For prev cursors it still passes the negative value to `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, which raises `ValueError` from Django and returns a 500 for a crafted cursor such as `123:-5:1`.

The accompanying comment ("This is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions") is incorrect.

Fix: raise `BadPaginationError` for any negative offset.

title: Comment claims negative offsets are supported, but nothing changed
body:
The added comment says Cursor now allows negative offsets for "efficient reverse pagination". No code was changed: `int(offset)` already accepted negatives.

No paginator actually supports negative offsets either; Django slicing rejects them, and other paginators raise `BadPaginationError`.

The comment misleads future maintainers into thinking negative offsets are a supported, safe contract.

title: New paginator and endpoint branch have no tests
body:
No tests were added for:
- `OptimizedCursorPaginator`
- the `optimized_pagination=true` branch of the audit log endpoint
- the modified `BasePaginator` offset handling

A single request through the new branch with at least one audit log entry would have surfaced the `TypeError` on the datetime key. A cursor with a negative offset would have surfaced the Django `ValueError`.

The new class also duplicates `BasePaginator.get_result` almost verbatim, which increases the surface that needs coverage.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes on the datetime key it is used with
body:
`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly on `getattr(item, self.key)`. The audit log endpoint uses it with `order_by="-datetime"`, so the value is a `datetime`. `build_cursor` calls the key function on the first result, which raises `TypeError` and returns a 500 for any non-empty page.

`value_from_cursor` (line 843) has a related problem. It returns the raw integer cursor value, and `build_queryset` then emits `datetime <= <int>`, which Postgres rejects.

The optimized path is therefore unusable. It needs the `DateTimePaginator` key/cursor conversion, e.g. by subclassing `DateTimePaginator`.

title: Negative queryset slicing raises in Django; comment's safety claim is false
body:
When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start. Django querysets do not support negative indexing and raise `ValueError` ("Negative indexing is not supported"). Any admin-supplied cursor with a negative offset, e.g. `?cursor=0:-5:0`, therefore produces a 500.

The comments state the ORM "properly handles negative slicing automatically" and that this "enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds". Both are wrong, and the second describes an intent to bypass pagination bounds that should not ship. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError`, as the other paginators do.

title: AttributeError on default path when organization_context.member is None
body:
`enable_advanced` is computed unconditionally, even when `optimized_pagination` was not requested, and dereferences `organization_context.member.has_global_access`. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is `None` for callers that are not org members, such as staff sessions and API-key/token authenticated requests.

For these callers `request.user.is_superuser` is False, so the expression raises `AttributeError` and the endpoint returns 500. This is a regression to the existing, non-optimized audit log listing. Only evaluate this when `use_optimized` is true, and guard for `member is None`.

title: Privilege gate uses raw is_superuser flag instead of active superuser session
body:
The gate uses `request.user.is_superuser`, which is true for any account with the superuser flag. It does not check whether the superuser session is active (sudo/elevated). Sentry's convention is `is_active_superuser(request)`.

As written, a flagged user with no active superuser session who has org access gets the "admin-only" pagination behaviour.

title: Spans are silently evicted with no metric or log
body:
Before this change, oversized segments were detected at flush time and reported via the `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` metric plus `logger.error`. That check was removed from `_load_segment_data`.

The new `zpopmin` eviction in the Lua script drops the lowest-scored spans whenever a segment exceeds 1000. Nothing is returned to the caller and nothing is emitted, so span data is lost with no observability.

The script should return the evicted count so Python can emit a metric, or the old metric should be kept in some form.

title: max_segment_spans config is now dead; limit hardcoded in Lua with a different value
body:
`SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans` (default 1001), but nothing reads it anymore. The actual cap is the literal `1000` hardcoded in `add-buffer.lua`.

Callers that tune `max_segment_spans` will see no effect, and the default disagrees with the enforced value. Pass the limit to the script as an ARGV, or remove the parameter.

title: ZUNIONSTORE uses default SUM aggregate, corrupting scores on duplicate payloads
body:
`zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` (and the parent_key merge on line 53) uses the default `AGGREGATE SUM`. If the same payload is present in both sets, its score becomes the sum of two timestamps (~3.4e9), for example after a Kafka redelivery of a span.

That inflated score makes the duplicate effectively unevictable and breaks the end-timestamp ordering that `zpopmin` relies on. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or `MIN`) to keep scores meaningful.

title: Evicted spans leave stale entries in the redirect hash
body:
`zpopmin` removes payloads from the segment set, but their `span_id -> set_span_id` entries in `span-buf:sr:{...}` are never removed. `done_flush_segments` only `hdel`s the span IDs of spans actually flushed.

Since the redirect hash's TTL is refreshed on every insert for the trace, these entries linger. Late children of an evicted span can also be redirected into an already-flushed segment key.

title: Redirect depth limit silently reduced 10x and explanatory comment removed
body:
The redirect-following loop limit was cut from 10000 to 1000. The comment explaining that trees deeper than the limit may not be joined correctly was also deleted.

This behaviour change is unrelated to eviction and is not mentioned in the PR. Segment trees deeper than 1000 levels will now be split into separate segments.

title: No tests for span eviction or the new optimized audit-log pagination
body:
The tests were only updated to pass `end_timestamp_precise`. Nothing exercises the new core behaviour: inserting more than 1000 spans into a segment and asserting which spans are evicted (lowest end timestamp), including across merges via `zunionstore`.

Likewise there are no tests for `OptimizedCursorPaginator` or the `optimized_pagination=true` audit log path. Even a basic test would have caught that the path crashes on its datetime key.

title: Comment claims negative offset support but no code changed
body:
The new comment says negative offsets are allowed for "efficient reverse pagination". `Cursor` was already doing a plain `int(offset)`, and no behaviour changed.

The similar comment added in `BasePaginator.get_result` (paginator.py line 179) is also misleading. A negative offset with `is_prev` is still passed straight to the queryset slice, which raises in Django.

These comments misdocument the pagination contract and should be removed.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator uses numeric keys but the endpoint orders by a datetime column
body:
`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` on `getattr(item, self.key)`. The audit log endpoint passes `order_by="-datetime"`, so the value is a `datetime`. When the first page has any rows, `build_cursor` calls the key function and raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime`, which returns a 500.

`value_from_cursor` has the same problem: it returns the raw integer cursor value. `build_queryset` then emits `WHERE datetime <= <int>`, which Postgres rejects.

The class copies `Paginator`'s integer-key logic instead of `DateTimePaginator`'s (multiplier plus `fromtimestamp`). The optimized audit-log path cannot work for any non-empty organization.

title: User-controlled negative cursor offsets are passed straight into queryset slicing
body:
When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code slices `queryset[cursor.offset:stop]`. The offset comes directly from the client-supplied `cursor` query parameter.

The comment says "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically". That is false: Django raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`, so any such request is an unhandled 500.

The stated intent, "enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds", is itself a red flag. Pagination bounds should never be bypassable by crafting a cursor. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError`, as `OffsetPaginator` and `ChainPaginator` already do.

This audit-log/pagination change is also unrelated to the PR's stated purpose (spans buffer eviction) and should not ride along in it.

title: Dereferences organization_context.member unconditionally; crashes when member is None
body:
`enable_advanced` is computed on every request, even when `optimized_pagination` is not requested. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is `None` for callers that are not org members, such as API-key or org-auth-token requests where `request.user` is anonymous.

For those callers `request.user.is_superuser` is False, so `organization_context.member.has_global_access` raises `AttributeError` and the endpoint returns a 500. This regresses audit-log access for existing token-based integrations.

Compute this only inside the `use_optimized` branch and guard against `member is None`.

title: Privilege gate uses raw is_superuser flag and has_global_access, not an admin check
body:
The comment says the advanced paginator is for "authorized administrators", but neither check actually restricts it to admins.

- `request.user.is_superuser` is the raw DB flag. Sentry requires `is_active_superuser(request)`, an active superuser session, before granting superuser powers, and this bypasses that.
- `has_global_access` is true for every ordinary member in organizations with open membership (`allow_joinleave`), so it is not an admin check either.

The gate therefore exposes the "advanced" negative-offset behavior to far more users than intended.

title: Redis key type changes from SET to ZSET with no migration; WRONGTYPE errors during rollout
body:
Segment keys `span-buf:s:*` were Redis SETs (`sadd`/`scard`/`sunionstore`/`sscan`). They are now ZSETs (`zadd`/`zcard`/`zunionstore`/`zscan`) under the same key names.

Existing keys survive up to `redis_ttl` (3600s) and stay referenced from the flush queues. During and after deploy:
- New consumers will hit `WRONGTYPE` on `zadd` (pipeline raises), on `zcard`/`zunionstore` inside the Lua script, and on `zscan` in `_load_segment_data`.
- Old consumers still running during the rolling deploy will hit the same errors on keys written by new ones.

This crashes the span consumer and can drop or duplicate segments. The change needs a new key prefix or version, or a drain/flush plan, before rollout.

title: Span eviction silently drops data with no metric or log, and can evict the root span
body:
`zpopmin` removes the spans with the smallest `end_timestamp_precise` whenever a segment exceeds 1000 spans. The previous code emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and logged an error. Now spans are discarded with no signal, so data loss in production is invisible.

Eviction is purely by end time, so a segment/root span that ends before 1000 of its children can be evicted. The segment is then flushed with no span marked `is_segment`, even though the `hrs` flag says it has a root.

The `span-buf:sr` redirect entries of evicted spans are never `hdel`'d in `done_flush_segments`, because only flushed spans are cleaned. They linger until the hash TTL lapses.

At minimum, return the eviction count from the script and emit a metric.

title: max_segment_spans config is now dead; Lua hardcodes a different limit
body:
`SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans` (default 1001), but nothing reads it after the Python-side check was removed.

The effective cap is the literal `1000` hardcoded in `add-buffer.lua`. Anyone tuning `max_segment_spans` will see no effect, and the defaults already disagree (1001 vs 1000).

Pass the limit to the script as an ARGV, or remove the parameter.

title: ZUNIONSTORE default SUM aggregation corrupts scores for duplicate members
body:
`zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` uses the default `AGGREGATE SUM`. If the same payload is present in both sets, for example after a Kafka redelivery, its score becomes the sum of the two end timestamps (about 2x).

That breaks the end-timestamp ordering the new `zpopmin` eviction relies on: such members effectively become un-evictable while legitimately later spans get evicted. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or `MIN`) so the score remains a timestamp. The same applies to the `parent_key` union on line 53.

title: No tests for the new eviction behavior or the optimized audit-log paginator
body:
The PR's headline feature, evicting spans beyond 1000 during insert, has no test.

Nothing covers:
- a segment exceeding the cap, or which spans survive;
- that redirect and queue keys are cleaned afterwards;
- interaction with the root span.

The tests only add `end_timestamp_precise` to existing fixtures.

Likewise there are no tests for `OptimizedCursorPaginator` or the `optimized_pagination=true` path of the audit log endpoint. A single test there would have caught the `math.floor(datetime)` TypeError and the negative-slice ValueError.

title: BasePaginator negative-offset change is inconsistent and its comment is misleading
body:
This change affects every endpoint using `Paginator`/`DateTimePaginator`. The comment claims it "allow[s] negative offsets", but it does the opposite for forward cursors: they are silently clamped to 0.

For prev cursors the negative offset is still passed to the queryset and Django raises `ValueError` (a 500). The clamped forward case also feeds the original negative `cursor.offset` into `build_cursor`, so the next cursor's offset is wrong and rows get skipped or repeated.

The matching comment added in `utils/cursors.py` describes behavior that doesn't exist. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError` instead.

title: Unconditional access to organization_context.member crashes when requester is not an org member
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` runs on every request, not only when `optimized_pagination=true` is passed. `organization_context.member` is None when the caller is not an org member, for example staff users or API-key/token auth where `request.user` is anonymous. If the caller is not a superuser, this raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'`. The default audit-log listing path, which worked before this PR, then returns a 500 for those callers. At minimum, evaluate this only when `use_optimized` is true and guard against `member is None`.

title: "Admin-only" gate uses raw is_superuser and has_global_access, neither of which identifies administrators
body: The comment says advanced pagination is limited to authorized administrators, but the check does not enforce that. `request.user.is_superuser` ignores whether the user has an active superuser session; Sentry normally requires `is_active_superuser(request)`. `member.has_global_access` is true for ordinary members whenever the org has open membership enabled, and for any role with global access. So regular members can opt into the paginator that is explicitly designed to read "beyond normal pagination bounds" via user-controlled negative offsets. Use a proper permission or role check, or drop the feature.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle the datetime key it is used with
body: The audit-log endpoint uses `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `order_by="-datetime"`. However, `get_item_key` calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly on the field value, which is a `datetime`, and that raises `TypeError`. `build_cursor` calls the key on the first result whenever any results exist, so every non-empty optimized request returns a 500. `value_from_cursor` also returns the raw integer cursor value instead of converting it to a datetime as `DateTimePaginator` does. A follow-up cursor would therefore generate `datetime <= <int>` SQL, which fails in Postgres. The optimized path is non-functional for this endpoint.

title: User-controlled negative offsets are passed to QuerySet slicing; the "safe" claim is false
body: With `enable_advanced_features` set and `cursor.offset < 0`, which the client controls through a cursor string like `0:-50:0`, the code runs `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing and raise `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`, so any such request is a 500. The comment says the ORM "properly handles negative slicing automatically"; that is wrong. The comment also says this "enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds" and is "safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level". That describes a deliberate bound-bypass feature driven by untrusted input, which should not exist. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError` (400), as `OffsetPaginator` does.

title: BasePaginator still slices with negative offsets for prev cursors; comment is misleading
body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` only clamps non-prev cursors. A prev cursor with a negative offset, such as `123:-5:1`, still reaches `queryset[negative:...]` and raises `ValueError`, giving a 500 instead of a 400. Next cursors with a negative offset are now silently coerced to the first page instead of being rejected. The comment says negative offsets enable bidirectional pagination and that the queryset handles boundaries, but neither is true. The same misleading comment was added to `Cursor.__init__` in `utils/cursors.py` with no code change. Validate and reject negative offsets instead.

title: Switching span-buf:s:* keys from SET to ZSET breaks on existing keys during deploy (WRONGTYPE)
body: Segment keys written by the previous version are plain Redis sets with TTL up to `redis_ttl` (3600s). After deploy, `ZADD` here, `ZCARD`/`ZUNIONSTORE` in add-buffer.lua, and `ZSCAN` in `_load_segment_data` will hit those keys and fail with `WRONGTYPE`. During a rolling deploy, old consumers likewise run `SADD`/`SCARD` against new ZSET keys. Pipelines raise on the first error, so both the process step and the flusher will crash-loop on any batch or flush touching such a key, potentially for up to an hour until the keys expire. This needs a migration or compat strategy, such as new key prefixes, type-checking with fallback, or draining or flushing the buffer before rollout.

title: Spans beyond 1000 are silently evicted with no metric or log
body: `zpopmin set_key span_count - 1000` permanently drops the earliest-ending spans of a segment with no visibility. The removed Python code at least emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and logged an error. Now there is no signal that data was discarded. Eviction is by `end_timestamp_precise` only, so it can also remove the segment/root span when children end after it, while the `hrs` flag still marks the segment as having a root. Return the evicted count from the script and emit a metric in `process_spans`.

title: max_segment_spans is now dead configuration; limit is hard-coded to 1000 in Lua
body: The `max_segment_spans` constructor parameter (default 1001) is no longer read anywhere, because the span-count check was removed from `_load_segment_data`. The actual limit is a hard-coded `1000` in add-buffer.lua, which also differs from the old default. Callers configuring `max_segment_spans` will get no effect. Pass the limit as an ARGV to the script, or remove the parameter.

title: ZUNIONSTORE uses default SUM aggregation, corrupting scores for duplicate payloads
body: `zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` (and the same call at line 53) defaults to `AGGREGATE SUM`. If the same span payload exists in both sets, for example after Kafka redelivery or reprocessing a batch, its score becomes the sum of the timestamps (about 2x the end timestamp). That breaks the end-timestamp ordering the new `zpopmin` eviction relies on, and makes such spans effectively un-evictable. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) to keep a real timestamp.

title: Redirect-depth limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000
body: The loop bound for following span redirects drops from 10000 to 1000, and the comment explaining the consequence was removed. The consequence is that segment trees deeper than the limit are not joined correctly. This behavior change is unrelated to eviction, is not mentioned in the PR, and now applies to much shallower trees.

title: No test covers the new insert-time eviction
body: The core behavior change, trimming a segment to 1000 spans via ZPOPMIN by `end_timestamp_precise` including after merges via ZUNIONSTORE, has no test. The existing tests only add `end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0` to fixtures, with every span sharing the same score, so the eviction order is never exercised. Add a test inserting more than 1000 spans with distinct timestamps across batches and merges, and assert which spans survive. Similarly, the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` and the audit-log `optimized_pagination` path have no tests, which is how the datetime TypeError and negative-slicing crash went unnoticed.

title: Substring check treats negated `!event.type:error` queries as error-focused
body:
`_is_error_focused_query` lowercases the raw query string and checks whether it contains `"event.type:error"`. That substring also appears in the negation `!event.type:error`, in `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`, and in free text such as `message:"event.type:error"`.

For these discover-dataset queries in allowlisted projects, `count()` is rewritten to `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` even though the matched rows are not (or not only) errors. Transactions and other non-error rows have no meaningful `sample_weight`, so the chart silently shows wrong counts, typically 0 or undercounted.

The check should parse the query (e.g. with the event search parser) and require a positive `event.type:error` filter, not a substring match.

title: Upsampling decision uses outer `dataset` and `request.GET['query']` instead of the per-call dataset and query
body:
`_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` and `query`, but the eligibility check is called with the closed-over outer `dataset` and `request`. `_is_error_focused_query` then reads `request.GET['query']` rather than the query actually being executed.

In the dashboard split path, `_get_event_stats(discover, ..., f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction")` and the ERROR_EVENTS split both run against discover. However, the decision is made against the outer metrics dataset, which always returns False, so error counts there are never upsampled.

Conversely, the upsampling verdict for any call reflects the user's original query string, not the modified split query. Results for the same widget can therefore differ depending on which code path served them.

Pass `scoped_dataset` and the effective `query` to the eligibility check.

title: "Performance" cache adds a remote cache round-trip to every events-stats call, even for non-error datasets
body:
`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` does `cache.get` (and `cache.set` on a miss) before checking the dataset. Every `_get_event_stats` call therefore hits the shared cache backend (memcached/redis), including spans, transactions, metrics, logs and RPC queries that can never be upsampled.

Dashboard split requests call `_get_event_stats` up to four times, so they pay several round-trips.

The value being cached is a single `options.get` lookup, which Sentry's options manager already serves from an in-process cache. The "optimization" replaces a local lookup with a network call and writes one cache key per distinct project-id combination.

Check `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` first and drop the extra cache layer, or at minimum short-circuit before touching the cache.

title: Allowlist changes are served stale for 60s and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is unusable/never called
body:
Eligibility is cached for 60 seconds per (org, project-set). The docstring says `invalidate_upsampling_cache` "should be called when the allowlist configuration changes", but nothing calls it.

It also cannot be called meaningfully. The allowlist is a single global option, and the cache is keyed on arbitrary combinations of project ids. An options change has no way to enumerate which keys to delete.

As a result, removing a project from the allowlist (e.g. because upsampled data is wrong) keeps producing upsampled counts for up to a minute across all workers. Adding one keeps returning raw counts for the same period. Mixed results within a dashboard are possible.

The key also embeds `hash(tuple(...))`, which can in principle collide between different project sets. Either remove the cache or key and invalidate it on the option value itself.

title: `options.get(key, [])` passes `[]` as `silent`, not as a default; real option path is never tested
body:
`OptionsManager.get(key, silent=False)` has no default-value parameter. The `[]` is interpreted as `silent=[]` and is not used as a fallback value.

If `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` is not registered in this codebase, `options.get` raises `UnknownOption`. Because the helper is now called on every events-stats request, that would turn every request into a 500.

All new tests patch the whole `options` module, so the real lookup is never exercised. Drop the misleading second argument, ensure the option is registered, and add a test that does not mock `options`.

title: Top-events ranking uses raw `count()` while the plotted series are upsampled
body:
For top events, only `timeseries_columns` are transformed. `selected_columns=self.get_field_list(...)`, `orderby=self.get_orderby(...)` and `equations` still use plain `count()`.

The top-N groups are therefore chosen and ordered by raw (sampled) counts, while the plotted values are upsampled. Groups with different client sample rates can display in an order that contradicts their plotted values, and equations referencing `count()` mix raw and upsampled numbers.

title: `upsampled_count` is exposed as a public function and changes the `count` result type to `number`
body:
Unlike the neighbouring internal helpers, the new `SnQLFunction("upsampled_count", ...)` is not marked `private=True`. Any user can call `upsampled_count()` directly in discover or errors queries, including against data where `sample_weight` is not populated. That makes an internal implementation detail part of the public query API.

It also declares `default_result_type="number"`, while `count()` is `integer`. The response meta for the `count` column now changes type for allowlisted projects, which affects frontend formatting and any API consumer relying on the type.

title: Accidental gitlink/submodule `sentry-repo` committed
body: The PR adds `sentry-repo` as a subproject commit pointing at the base commit, with no `.gitmodules` entry. This is clearly an accidental artifact of a local checkout. It adds a broken submodule to the repository root, which can confuse clones, CI checkouts and tooling. It should be removed from the PR.

title: Docstrings/comments contradict actual caching behavior
body:
The `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` docstring says it "reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time… intentional to ensure we always have the latest configuration state". Its only caller caches the result for 60s, so this is false.

In the endpoint, "This cached result ensures consistent behavior across query execution" and "late transformation ensures we use the most current schema assumptions" also describe nothing the code actually does. The decision is recomputed per `_get_event_stats` call, and `upsampling_enabled = should_upsample` is a no-op alias.

The transform branches inside the `use_rpc` paths are dead code, because `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` always returns False for `spans_rpc`/`ourlogs`. These comments will mislead future maintainers.

title: Main entry point and its caching are untested; key edge cases missing
upsampled_count sums raw sample_weight without a NULL fallback, undercounting events
body:
`upsampled_count` compiles to `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. Any error event without a `sample_weight` is effectively dropped from the count, because ClickHouse `sum` ignores NULLs. That includes events ingested before the project was allowlisted, events from SDKs that don't send `error_sampling` context, and events in an allowlisted project that weren't client-sampled.

Once a project is added to the allowlist, every chart that covers older data, or mixes sampled and unsampled events, shows a lower count than plain `count()` would. The comment says the code "assumes sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects", but nothing in ingestion guarantees that.

The aggregate should treat a missing weight as 1, e.g. `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))`. The endpoint test only stores events that carry a sample rate, so it cannot catch this.

title: Substring check treats negated `!event.type:error` queries as error-focused
Upsampling decision uses the outer `dataset`/request query instead of `scoped_dataset`/`query`
body:
`_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` and `query`, but the eligibility check passes the outer `dataset`, and the helper reads `request.GET['query']`.

In the dashboard discover-split path, `_get_event_stats` is called with `discover` and an errors-only query such as `(...) AND !event.type:transaction`, or with the widget's `ERROR_EVENTS` split. Because the outer `dataset` there is `metrics_enhanced_performance`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns False. Error counts from those split queries are therefore never upsampled, while the same widget on the errors dataset would be.

Conversely, the decision ignores the rewritten `split_query`. Pass `scoped_dataset` and `query` to the eligibility check.

title: 60s eligibility cache serves stale allowlist decisions and the invalidation hook is never called
body:
Eligibility is cached per (org, project set) for 60 seconds. When a project is removed from `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`, queries keep returning upsampled counts for up to a minute, and the reverse is also true.

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined but never called anywhere. It also cannot realistically be called on an allowlist change, because the cache key space is every combination of project IDs any user has queried.

This also contradicts the `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` docstring (lines 50-53), which says the allowlist is read "fresh each time ... to ensure we always have the latest configuration state".

title: Added cache lookup is likely slower than the option read it replaces
body:
The docstring justifies the cache as avoiding "expensive repeated option lookups". However, `options.get` is already served from an in-process cache, and the uncached work is a list membership check.

The new code adds a `cache.get`, plus a `cache.set` on miss, against the shared cache backend (Redis or memcached). That is a network round trip on every `_get_event_stats` call, and in the dashboard split and fallback paths there can be several calls per request.

This adds latency and load rather than removing it. Either drop the cache or rely on the options layer's existing caching.

title: Cache key uses `hash()` of the project tuple, so different project sets can collide
body:
The cache key embeds `hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))` instead of the IDs or a cryptographic digest. Two different project sets in the same org that hash to the same value share a cache entry for 60s.

That can upsample a query over a non-allowlisted project set, or fail to upsample an allowlisted one. Use a stable digest such as md5 or sha1 of the joined sorted IDs if key length is the concern.

title: Stray gitlink/submodule `sentry-repo` added to the repository
body:
The PR adds a `sentry-repo` entry that is a gitlink (`Subproject commit a5d2909...`, which is the base commit itself). There is no `.gitmodules` entry and it is unrelated to the feature.

It looks like an accidental commit of a nested checkout. It will confuse clones and submodule tooling and break `git submodule` operations, so it should be removed.

title: Top-events ranking still uses raw count() while the series show upsampled counts
body:
In the top-events path only `timeseries_columns` are rewritten to `upsampled_count() as count`. `selected_columns` (from `get_field_list`) and `orderby` (e.g. `-count()`) are left untouched.

The top N groups are therefore chosen by unweighted event count, while the plotted values are weighted counts. When client sample rates differ between groups, the ranking can disagree with the displayed values, and a group with a higher upsampled count can be excluded from the top N.

title: No tests for the cached entry point or for negated/compound queries
body:
The unit tests only exercise the private helpers. `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` is never tested, so its cache hit/miss behaviour and staleness are uncovered. The `self.snuba_params` built in `setUp` is unused.

`_is_error_focused_query` is only checked against `event.type:error`, `event.type:transaction` and an empty query. A case such as `!event.type:error`, which currently returns True, would have exposed the substring-matching bug.

The endpoint tests also don't cover allowlisted projects containing events without `sample_weight`, which is where `sum(sample_weight)` undercounts.

title: upsampled_count ignores events with NULL sample_weight, so they are silently dropped
body:
`upsampled_count` compiles to `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. ClickHouse `sum` skips NULL values, so any matched error without a `sample_weight` contributes 0 instead of 1. Such events include ones ingested before a project was allowlisted, ones sent without `error_sampling.client_sample_rate`, and rows from storages that never populate the column.

The comment says the schema guarantees `sample_weight`, but nothing enforces that; the allowlist is just a project-id option. Enabling a project would make historical buckets drop to near zero, and unsampled errors would vanish from charts.

Fix: aggregate `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))` so unweighted events still count as one.

title: Error-focused detection is a raw substring match and also matches negated `!event.type:error`
body:
`_is_error_focused_query` returns True whenever the lowercased query contains `event.type:error`. That is also true for `!event.type:error`, which explicitly excludes errors, and for `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` or a quoted message containing that text.

On the discover dataset those queries return transactions or mixed events. They would still be rewritten to `upsampled_count()`, summing a weight column that is absent or NULL for transactions, which gives wrong counts. The docstring claims this errs "on the side of caution", but the negated case is the opposite.

Fix: parse the query, e.g. with `event_search`, and require a positive `event.type:error` filter, with no negation and no OR containing other types.

title: Upsampling decision uses outer `dataset` and the raw request query instead of the dataset/query actually being executed
body:
Inside `_get_event_stats` the eligibility check is passed the closed-over `dataset`, not the `scoped_dataset` argument. The helper also inspects `request.GET["query"]` rather than the `query` argument.

In the dashboard discover-split path, `_get_event_stats` is called with `discover` and a rewritten query (`({query}) AND !event.type:transaction`, or ERROR_EVENTS split widgets). The outer `dataset` there is always metrics_performance or metrics_enhanced_performance, so `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns False. Error-only results for split widgets are therefore never upsampled, while the same query from a non-dashboard request is.

The same mismatch can let a transactions-only sub-query be judged by the original request's query text.

Fix: pass `scoped_dataset` and the effective `query` into the eligibility check.

title: Stray submodule gitlink committed to the repository root
body:
The PR adds `sentry-repo` as a gitlink (`Subproject commit a5d2909…`, the base commit of this repo) with no `.gitmodules` entry. This looks like an accidental nested checkout.

It creates a dangling submodule that breaks or warns in `git submodule` operations and CI checkouts that recurse submodules, and it has nothing to do with the feature.

It should be removed from the PR.

title: 60s eligibility cache is never invalidated and contradicts the 'fresh read' contract
body:
The eligibility result is cached for 60 seconds per org and project set. `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is never called anywhere, and it cannot practically be: invalidation needs every project-id combination that was cached, but option changes are not tied to orgs or project sets.

After a project is removed from `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`, for example to roll back a bad rollout, its counts stay inflated for up to a minute. That inconsistency is per project set.

The docstring of `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` says the allowlist is read fresh each time "to ensure we always have the latest configuration state", which the caching wrapper defeats. The cache key also relies on the Python `hash()` of the project tuple, so distinct project sets can in principle share an entry.

Options:
- Drop the cache, since options are already cached in-process.
- Wire up invalidation and use the full sorted id list or a stable digest in the key.

title: "Performance" cache adds a remote cache round-trip to every events-stats call
body:
`options.get` is normally served from an in-process cache, so the check it guards is a cheap list-membership test. Wrapping it in `cache.get` and `cache.set` (memcached/redis) adds a network round-trip per `_get_event_stats` call, which is several calls per request in the dashboard-split and comparison paths.

The check also runs even when no `count()` column is requested. Net effect: added latency and cache load with no benefit.

title: Top-events ranking uses raw count() while plotted series use upsampled counts
body:
For top events only `timeseries_columns` are rewritten to `upsampled_count() as count`. `selected_columns` (from `field`), `orderby` (e.g. `-count()`) and equations still reference the raw `count()`.

The top-N groups are therefore chosen by raw event count, while the values shown are weighted sums. When events carry different client sample rates, the displayed series can be out of order or omit a group that would be in the top N by upsampled count. Equations based on `count()` will also disagree with the plotted count.

title: upsampled_count is exposed as a public user-callable function
body:
Unlike neighbouring internal helpers, the new `SnQLFunction` is not marked `private=True`. Any user can request `upsampled_count()` directly in any discover-based query, including the transactions dataset where `sample_weight` does not exist. That produces Snuba errors.

The endpoint also bypasses all of the allowlist gating, so the function becomes part of the public query surface unintentionally.

title: Public entry point, caching and negated queries are untested
Error timestamps (seconds) are compared and logged against replay event timestamps (milliseconds)
body:
`fetch_error_details` takes `timestamp` straight from the nodestore event payload, which is in seconds since epoch (~1.7e9). `gen_request_data` (lines 153-155) then compares it with the rrweb replay event's top-level `timestamp`. The replay SDK emits that value in milliseconds (~1.7e12), and `as_log_message` prints the same value.

As a result, every error is "earlier" than the first breadcrumb. All errors are emitted at the start of the log instead of being interleaved in chronological order. The LLM also receives error times and breadcrumb times on different scales.

The unit test and `test_get_with_error` only pass because they use seconds for both values. Convert the error timestamp to milliseconds (e.g. `* 1000`) before comparing and logging.

title: zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes get_multi preserves order and returns every key
body:
`nodestore.backend.get_multi` returns a dict keyed by node id. It deduplicates ids, returns uncached items first and then cached ones, and omits ids that are not found on some backends.

Zipping the original `error_ids` list with `events.values()` can therefore pair an event id with another event's data. Results are also silently truncated or shifted when some ids are missing or duplicated.

Iterate over `zip(error_ids, node_ids)` and look up `events.get(node_id)` instead. Separately, `node_ids` are built with the replay's own `project_id`, so errors linked to the replay from other projects (e.g. backend errors) are never found.

title: Snuba replay query runs even when error context is disabled, and its failure fails the whole summary
body:
`query_replay_instance` is called unconditionally before the `enable_error_context` check, so `enable_error_context=false` still pays for a Snuba query whose result is thrown away.

In addition, unlike `fetch_error_details`, this query is not wrapped in error handling. A Snuba failure or rate limit therefore turns the optional error-context enrichment into a 500 for the entire summarize request.

Move the query inside the `else` branch and treat its failure as "no error context".

title: HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES are only hidden while a search query is entered
body:
The early return `if (!searchQuery.trim()) return sorted;` runs before the `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` filter. In the default view with an empty search box, `is_segment`, `project_id` and `received` are still displayed. They only disappear once the user types a search.

Apply the hidden-attributes filter before the early return so it covers both cases.

title: Feature-flagged TableWidgetVisualization renders with hardcoded empty columns and data
body:
When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, the table widget renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />`. It ignores `result.data`, `result.meta`, the loading state and field aliases.

Any organization with the flag enabled sees every table widget as an empty table. Wire `result` into `tableData`/`columns`, or keep the flag off until the wiring exists.

title: Assemble analytics event recorded before feature check and validation
body:
`analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` fires before the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` feature check and before schema validation. Requests that end in 404 (feature disabled) or 400 (invalid body) are still counted as assemble events, which inflates the metric.

Recording after the feature check, or after successful validation, would make the event reflect actual assemble attempts.

title: React Query key for attribute keys omits the organization
body:
The new cache key is `['use-trace-item-attribute-keys', queryOptions]`. `queryOptions` contains only itemType, attributeType, project ids, substring and datetime, not the organization slug.

When the project selection is empty (all projects / my projects), two organizations produce identical keys. Cached attributes from one org can then be served for another after switching orgs.

The previous `useApiQuery` key included the org-scoped URL. Add `organization.slug` to the key.

title: Per-issue get_recommended_event() adds N extra Snuba/nodestore lookups per PR comment; titles inserted unescaped into link text
body:
`get_environment_info` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` once per issue when building the merged-PR comment. Each call runs its own Snuba query plus a nodestore fetch, all just to read an environment name; the `Group` row may already carry enough information to avoid this.

Separately, the truncated issue title is now placed inside markdown link text (`[**{title}**]({url})`) without escaping. Titles containing unbalanced `[`/`]` break the link. This includes balanced pairs that become unbalanced after the 50-character truncation.

title: Removed overflow constraint lets long attachment names blow out the table column
body:
The removed `FlexCenter` applied `overflowEllipsis`, which includes `overflow: hidden`. That made the grid item's automatic minimum width 0, so `Name` could truncate within the `1fr` column.

The replacement `<Flex align="center">` has visible overflow. The grid item's min-content width is now the full nowrap file name, so long attachment names expand the column and push Size/Actions out instead of truncating.

Add `min-width: 0` or `overflow: hidden` to the wrapper.

title: FlexBox replacement drops `height: 100%`
body:
The removed `FlexBox` styled component set `display:flex; flex-grow:1; flex-direction:column; height:100%`. The replacement `<Flex direction="column" flex={1}>` does not set `height: 100%`.

If the parent is not itself a flex container, `flex={1}` has no effect. The waterfall container can then collapse to its content height instead of filling the available space.

title: Flex replacement loses align-items:center and gap
body:
The old `Container` extended `FlexBox`, so it had `align-items: center; gap: space(1)` plus `justify-content: space-between`. The replacement `<Flex ref={setRef} justify="space-between">` drops both alignment and gap. The tabs and vitals are no longer vertically centered or spaced.

Similarly, the second placeholder group at line 27 (`<Flex>`) lost its `align-items: center` and `gap`, so the three placeholders now render touching each other.

title: None max_segment_id case is not actually exercised
body:
The row's `max_segment_id` was changed to `None` to cover the new early-return in `_make_recording_filenames`. However, this test patches `delete_matched_rows`, so `_make_recording_filenames` is never called and the new branch has no coverage.

The pre-fix crash (`range(None + 1)`) would also not have been caught here. Add a direct unit test for `_make_recording_filenames`/`delete_matched_rows` with `max_segment_id=None`.

title: Mutual-exclusion checks use truthiness, so age=0 or timestamp=0 bypass them
body:
`validate_timestamp` rejects only when `self.initial_data.get("age")` is truthy, and `validate_age` only when `timestamp` is truthy. `age: 0` (a valid value for a just-generated report) and `timestamp: 0` (allowed by `min_value=0`) are falsy. A report containing both fields therefore passes validation.

Use `"age" in self.initial_data` / `"timestamp" in self.initial_data`. Also note that a report with neither field is accepted, which contradicts the docstrings saying one must be present.

title: Tests no longer exercise the application/reports+json content type
body:
The previous tests posted with `content_type="application/reports+json"`, the media type browsers actually send. The rewritten success tests post with the default (JSON) content type.

No test now covers `BrowserReportsJSONParser`, so a regression in parsing real browser submissions would go unnoticed. Keep at least one success-path test using `application/reports+json`.

title: Shows 'Project not found' while the projects store is still loading
body:
`useProjectFromId` returns `undefined` until the projects store has loaded. The new check `if (replayRecord?.project_id && !project)` runs before the loading check. When projects are not yet loaded, the tab renders an error alert instead of a loading indicator, even though the project exists.

Gate this error on the projects having finished loading.

title: Error timestamps (seconds) compared against rrweb event timestamps (milliseconds)
body:
`gen_request_data` merges errors into the breadcrumb stream by comparing `error_events[i]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)`. The error timestamp comes from nodestore event data, which is float seconds (~1.7e9). The top-level `timestamp` on recorded replay events is in milliseconds (~1.7e12); the SDK writes breadcrumb custom events with `timestamp = breadcrumb.timestamp * 1000`.

Because of the unit mismatch, every error compares as "before" the first recording event. All error messages are emitted at the start of the log list instead of in chronological order. The log lines also carry inconsistent time units, which degrades the Seer summary.

The new tests mask this by using second-based timestamps for the recording events. Normalize both sides to the same unit before comparing, e.g. multiply the error timestamp by 1000.

title: zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes nodestore get_multi preserves input order
body:
`nodestore.backend.get_multi` returns a dict. The base implementation fills it with cache hits first and then adds backend-fetched items, so the value order does not follow `node_ids`. Backends may also omit missing keys.

Zipping `error_ids` against `events.values()` can therefore attach the wrong event ID to an event's data, and can drop or shift entries when some IDs are missing.

Iterate over `zip(error_ids, node_ids)` and look up `events.get(node_id)` instead.

title: All replay errors are injected into every paginated page
body:
`analyze_recording_segments` is bound with the full `error_events` list and is called once per page of segments by `GenericOffsetPaginator`. `gen_request_data` yields any errors not consumed by the page's events at the end.

For replays spanning more than one page, every page's Seer request contains the complete set of errors, including errors outside that page's time range. Those errors are duplicated across pages and misattributed in the summaries.

Filter `error_events` to each page's time window, or fetch all segments in one request.

title: Snuba replay query runs even when error context is disabled
body:
`query_replay_instance` and `process_raw_response` run unconditionally before the `enable_error_context` check. When the caller passes `enable_error_context=false`, the endpoint still pays for a Snuba round-trip whose result is discarded.

When error context is enabled, nodestore payloads for every error ID on the replay are fetched up front on each request.

Move the Snuba query inside the enabled branch.

title: HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES only filtered while a search query is active
body:
The `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` filter is applied only in the branch after `if (!searchQuery.trim()) { return sorted; }`.

With an empty search box, the default view, `is_segment`, `project_id` and `received` are still shown. They disappear only once the user types a query.

Apply the hidden-attribute filter before the early return.

title: Mutual-exclusion checks for age/timestamp use truthiness
body:
`validate_timestamp` uses `self.initial_data.get("age")` and `validate_age` uses `self.initial_data.get("timestamp")`. A value of 0 is falsy, and `age: 0` is common for freshly generated reports. A report carrying both `age: 0` and a `timestamp` therefore passes validation, contrary to the stated intent.

Neither field is required either, so a report with neither one is accepted, even though the docstrings say one must be present.

Use `"age" in self.initial_data` / `"timestamp" in self.initial_data`, and add an object-level `validate()` that enforces exactly one of the two.

title: One invalid report causes the whole batch to be rejected with 422
body:
Browsers send reports in batches, and the Reporting API retries non-2xx deliveries. Returning 422 as soon as any single report fails validation drops all the valid reports in the same request.

The browser will then retry the entire batch, including the bad report that will never validate. That produces repeated failed deliveries and lost data for the valid reports.

Consider skipping or recording invalid reports individually and still returning 2xx.

title: Feature-flagged TableWidgetVisualization ignores the actual table results
body:
When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, the widget renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />`. It ignores `result.data`, `result.meta`, the loading state, field aliases and custom renderers.

Any org with the flag on sees an empty table for every table widget. Wire `result` into `tableData` and derive `columns` from `fields`, or keep the flag off until that is done.

title: Per-issue recommended-event lookup when building PR comments
body:
`get_environment_info` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` for every issue in the comment. That method does a Snuba query plus a nodestore fetch, and `get_environment()` adds a DB lookup.

This runs serially inside the PR comment task for every issue listed, adding several round-trips per issue. Any failure is swallowed by a broad `except Exception`.

Consider batching the lookups or using a cheaper source of environment information, such as the group's tag values.

title: Null max_segment_id case isn't actually exercised
body:
The test now passes a row with `max_segment_id: None`, but `delete_matched_rows` is mocked. The new `None` guard in `_make_recording_filenames` is never executed.

If the guard were removed, this test would still pass. Add a direct unit test of `_make_recording_filenames` / `delete_replay_recordings` with `max_segment_id=None`.

title: Assemble analytics event recorded before feature/validation checks
body:
`analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` runs before the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` feature check and before body validation.

Every request is counted as an assemble event, including requests from orgs without the feature that get a 404 and requests with invalid bodies that get a 400. Polling requests are counted too. This inflates the metric.

Move the call after the feature check, and ideally after successful validation.

title: Error timestamps (seconds) are compared with rrweb event timestamps (milliseconds)
body:
`fetch_error_details` takes `timestamp` from the nodestore event payload, which is float seconds since epoch (~1.7e9). `gen_request_data` compares it against the top-level `timestamp` of replay recording events (lines 153-155). The JS SDK writes those in milliseconds (`breadcrumb.timestamp * 1000`, ~1.7e12).

With real data every error looks earlier than every breadcrumb. All errors are emitted at the start of the log instead of being interleaved chronologically, which is the main point of this change. The emitted messages also mix units (`at 1.7e9` for errors, `at 1.7e12` for breadcrumbs), which misleads the LLM.

The tests hide this because they use seconds for both. Convert the error timestamp to milliseconds (`* 1000`) before sorting and comparing, and use ms in the tests.

title: zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes nodestore get_multi preserves input order
body:
`nodestore.backend.get_multi` returns a dict keyed by node_id. Its order is not guaranteed to match `error_ids`: cached items come first, then fetched ones, and missing entries may be omitted entirely. Zipping `error_ids` with `events.values()` can therefore attach the wrong event id to each payload, or shift every id after a missing one.

Look up each payload by its generated node_id instead, e.g. `events.get(Event.generate_node_id(project_id, event_id))`.

title: HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES are only hidden while a search query is entered
body:
The memo returns `sorted` unfiltered when `searchQuery` is empty. The `!HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES.includes(attribute.name)` check only runs in the search branch.

In the default view (no search) `is_segment`, `project_id` and `received` are still shown. They disappear only once the user types something, which is inconsistent and almost certainly not intended. Filter out hidden attributes before the early return.

title: Mutual-exclusion check for age/timestamp uses truthiness
body:
`validate_timestamp` checks `self.initial_data.get("age")` and `validate_age` checks `self.initial_data.get("timestamp")`. A legitimate value of 0 is falsy, so a report carrying both `timestamp` and `age: 0` passes validation even though the fields are meant to be mutually exclusive. `age` is in milliseconds, so 0 is realistic.

Nothing requires at least one of the two to be present either, despite the docstrings. Use `"age" in self.initial_data` / `"timestamp" in self.initial_data`, and add a `validate()` that requires exactly one.

title: One invalid report rejects the whole batch, so valid reports are dropped and retried
body:
The endpoint returns 422 as soon as any report in the array fails validation, for example an unlisted or new report type in the strict `ChoiceField`. Per the Reporting API, any non-2xx response marks delivery as failed, and the browser retries the entire batch.

As a result, the valid reports in that batch are never counted, and the same payload is re-sent repeatedly. Consider counting the valid reports and logging or skipping the invalid ones instead of failing the request.

title: No remaining test exercises the application/reports+json content type
body:
The removed `test_logs_request_data_if_option_enabled` and the old multiple-reports test were the only tests that posted with `content_type="application/reports+json"`. Every test now uses the default JSON format.

The custom `BrowserReportsJSONParser` is the content type real browsers send, and it is no longer covered. A regression in parser registration would go unnoticed. Keep at least one success-path test using that media type.

title: Data migrations turned into no-ops pointing to a migration not included in this PR
body:
Both 0917 and 0920 now just `return` and point readers to `0921_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views_rerevised.py`. That migration is not added in this PR, and the migrations lockfile is unchanged.

If 0921 does not already exist, organization-visible saved searches are never converted to GroupSearchViews. This affects every environment that has not run these migrations yet, including self-hosted. The comment would also be a dangling reference. Either include the replacement migration or confirm it exists.

title: Feature-flagged TableWidgetVisualization always renders an empty table
body:
When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, the widget renders `TableWidgetVisualization` with `columns={[]}` and hard-coded empty `tableData`. It ignores `result.data`, `result.meta`, the loading state and the field aliases.

Any org with the flag on sees empty table widgets on every dashboard, with no loading indicator. Map `result` into `TabularData` and columns before gating real users onto this flag.

title: Query key omits organization, allowing cached attributes to leak across orgs
body:
The new react-query key is `['use-trace-item-attribute-keys', queryOptions]`. `queryOptions` contains item type, attribute type, project ids and datetime, but not the organization slug, while the queryFn fetches `/organizations/${organization.slug}/...`.

When switching organizations with the same page filters (e.g. `projects: []` for "My Projects" and the same period), the cached attribute keys from the previous org are served until the refetch completes.

This refactor also dropped the previous `retry: false` / `refetchOnWindowFocus: false`, so failures now retry with backoff by default. Include `organization.slug` in the key and restore the intended query options.

title: Container lost align-items and gap during Flex migration
body:
