The removed `Container` was `styled(FlexBox)`, so it had `align-items: center` and `gap: space(1)` in addition to `justify-content: space-between`. The replacement `<Flex ref={setRef} justify="space-between">` sets only the justify.

The tabs and `TraceContextVitals` are no longer vertically centered and have no gap between them, which is a visual regression from what was meant to be a no-op refactor. Add `align="center" gap={space(1)}`.

title: KeyError when existing Integration metadata has no `sender`
body:
The new check reads `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` with no fallback. `sender` is only written when the Integration is created by the installation webhook (`state.get("sender")` in `build_integration`). Integrations created through the pipeline itself never get it; `test_basic_flow` asserts the metadata has no `sender` key. Integrations created before sender tracking also lack it.

Common case: an org uninstalls the GitHub integration in Sentry. The OrganizationIntegration is deleted but the Integration row stays. On reinstall, the code reaches this branch and raises an unhandled KeyError, so the user gets a 500 and cannot reinstall.

The lookup is also not filtered by `provider`, so a non-GitHub integration with a colliding `external_id` would fail the same way. Use `.get()` with a defined fallback (verify another way, or error cleanly), and filter by `provider="github"`.

title: User/installation ownership check skipped when no Integration row exists
OAuth `state` is a static, predictable value (pipeline.signature)
body:
`pipeline.signature` is an md5 of the pipeline view class names. It is the same for every user, org and session; the tests hard-code `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3` across different users and orgs. Using it as the OAuth `state` gives no CSRF or code-injection protection: anyone can compute it, so a forged callback `?code=<attacker code>&state=<constant>` passes the check at line 412.

The PR description presents state validation as a security property, but it doesn't provide one. Generate a random nonce (for example `secrets.token_hex()`), store it in pipeline state, and compare it with `constant_time_compare`, as `OAuth2LoginView`/`OAuth2CallbackView` already do.

title: Network/HTTP failures in token exchange or user lookup cause unhandled 500s
body: `safe_urlopen(...)` on line 423 sits outside the try block, so connection errors or timeouts propagate. `get_user_info()` calls `raise_for_status()` internally, so a 401 or 5xx from `api.github.com/user` (for example a revoked token or a GitHub outage) raises an uncaught HTTPError. In both cases the user sees a 500 instead of the integration-failed dialog. That dialog is what the opener window expects for its postMessage. Wrap these calls and return `error(...)` on failure.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer tests the not-found path
body:
The test now sends a deliberately wrong `state` (`ddd023...`). The new state-mismatch check rejects it before the GitHub 404 is ever reached, and the assertion was changed to `"Invalid installation request."`.

As a result, the `build_integration` 404 path (`"The GitHub installation could not be found."`) is untested. The test name is also misleading. Use the correct state so the flow reaches the 404, and add a separate test for state mismatch.

There is also no test where an Integration exists with a matching `sender` and the install succeeds, and none where `sender` is missing (the KeyError case).

title: Error strings no longer extractable for translation
body: The old code wrapped literals directly, for example `_("GitHub installation pending deletion.")`. The new helper calls `_(error_short)` on a variable, and callers pass plain string literals. `makemessages` only extracts literals passed to `_()`, so "Invalid installation request.", "GitHub installation pending deletion." and "Github installed on another Sentry organization." drop out of the translation catalogs. Wrap the literals at the call sites or in the default argument.

title: OAuth `state` is the static pipeline signature, not a per-session nonce
body:
The OAuth `state` sent to GitHub, and later checked at line 412, is `pipeline.signature`. That value is an md5 of the pipeline view class names, so it is identical for every user, session and installation. The tests confirm this by hardcoding "9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3".

Because it is constant and publicly derivable, the `state` check gives no CSRF or login-CSRF protection. An attacker can build a valid callback URL with their own `code` and the known state. The victim's pipeline would then bind the attacker's GitHub identity as `github_authenticated_user`.

The existing `OAuth2LoginView` already does this correctly: it generates `secrets.token_hex()`, binds it with `pipeline.bind_state("state", ...)`, and compares the callback against the stored value. The same should be done here. As written, the PR description's claim that a `state` mismatch is detected is not meaningfully true.

title: User verification is bypassed when the Integration row does not yet exist
body:
The check that the authenticated GitHub user matches the installer only runs on the branch where the Integration exists and has no OrganizationIntegration. When `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises DoesNotExist, the view returns `pipeline.next_step()` with no check. `build_integration` then creates the integration from the attacker-supplied `installation_id`.

This happens whenever the `installation` webhook has not arrived yet, is delayed, or failed. In those cases anyone who supplies another account's installation_id (these are sequential integers) can still link that GitHub installation to their own Sentry org.

The fix is to validate the installer independently of the local DB row, for example by fetching the installation sender from GitHub or by rejecting the request. Otherwise the protection this PR describes is incomplete.

title: KeyError (500) when existing Integration metadata has no `sender`
body:
`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes every Integration was created by the installation webhook. `build_integration` only adds `sender` when it is present in state, and the pipeline path never puts it there. Integrations created through the pipeline (see `test_basic_flow`'s expected metadata, which has no `sender`) or older ones therefore lack this key.

If such an org removes the Sentry-side installation, leaving the Integration in place without an OrganizationIntegration, and later reinstalls, this line raises KeyError. The user gets an unhandled 500 instead of either a successful install or the error page. Use `.get()` and decide on explicit handling for a missing sender.

title: Network/HTTP failures in the OAuth exchange are not handled and surface as 500s
body:
Two calls in the OAuth exchange are not handled:

- `get_user_info()` calls `raise_for_status()`, so a non-2xx from GitHub's `/user` endpoint (revoked token, rate limit, outage) raises `requests.HTTPError`.
- `safe_urlopen` at line 423 sits outside the try block and can raise on connection errors or timeouts.

Neither is caught. Instead of the intended `github-integration-failed.html` page with `postMessage` back to the opener, the user gets a server error and the setup dialog breaks. Wrap both calls and return `error(...)` on failure.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer tests the installation-not-found path
body:
The test now sends a `state` value ("ddd023d8...") that does not match the pipeline signature. The OAuth view therefore rejects the request with "Invalid installation request." before the GitHub 404 for `/app/installations/{id}` is ever reached.

The previous assertion on "The GitHub installation could not be found.", i.e. the `IntegrationError` raised in `build_integration` on a 404, is gone. That path no longer has coverage, and the test name is now misleading. Use the valid state, finish the flow, and assert the 404 message; add a separate test for the state mismatch.

title: No test for the success path where the webhook-created sender matches the authenticated user
body:
`test_github_user_mismatch` covers only the rejection case. No test covers an Integration created by the webhook, with no OrganizationIntegration, whose `sender.login` equals the OAuth-authenticated user and so completes successfully. That is the main path the new check affects.

The existing success tests all go through the `Integration.DoesNotExist` branch, so a regression that blocks legitimate installs on the sender-match branch would not be caught.

title: OAuth `state` is the static pipeline signature, so it gives no CSRF protection
body:
`pipeline.signature` is an md5 hash of the pipeline view class names. It is the same for every user and every session. That is why the tests can hardcode `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`, and why `ddd023...` was the old one-view value.

The OAuth2 `state` parameter must be an unguessable, per-session value that is bound to the session. Sentry's own `OAuth2LoginView` uses `secrets.token_hex()` stored via `bind_state`.

With a constant state, anyone can build a valid callback URL `/extensions/github/setup/?code=<attacker_code>&state=<known constant>`. The comparison at line 412 then always passes, so the 'state mismatch' protection described in the PR is ineffective and the OAuth step is open to login-CSRF and code injection.

Fix: generate a random token, `bind_state` it, and compare against the stored value with a constant-time compare.

title: GitHub user verification is skipped when no Integration row exists
body:
If `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `DoesNotExist`, the view returns `pipeline.next_step()` without comparing `github_authenticated_user` to anyone.

`build_integration` then fetches the installation from GitHub with the app JWT and links it to the current Sentry org. So the new check only runs when the installation webhook has already created the Integration row. It is bypassed in two cases:
- when the user's redirect beats the webhook (a normal race);
- for any installation_id whose Integration row is absent, e.g. a webhook failed or the row was deleted while the app is still installed on GitHub.

An attacker supplying such an installation_id can still link someone else's GitHub installation. The installer identity should be verified in this path too, for example by checking the installation/sender via the GitHub API or by requiring the webhook-created row.

title: KeyError when the existing Integration has no `sender` in metadata
body:
`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes every Integration was created by the installation webhook. Integrations created through the pipeline itself never get a `sender` key: `build_integration` only sets it when `state.get("sender")` is present, and `test_basic_flow` asserts the metadata has no `sender`. Older integrations created before this field existed also lack it.

When such an Integration still exists but has no OrganizationIntegration, the reinstall path reaches this line and raises `KeyError`, returning a 500. This happens, for example, after an org uninstalls and tries to reinstall. Use `.get()` and treat a missing sender explicitly instead of crashing.

title: Network/HTTP errors in token exchange and user lookup are uncaught and cause 500s
body:
`safe_urlopen(...)` at line 423 sits outside the `try` block, so connection errors or timeouts propagate. `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` at line 434 calls `raise_for_status()` internally and raises on any non-2xx response from GitHub, such as a revoked token, rate limiting or a GitHub outage.

None of these are handled, so the installation dialog shows a server error instead of the intended `github-integration-failed.html` page that posts a failure message to the opener. Wrap both calls and return `error(request, self.active_organization)` on failure.

title: Authorize URL query string is built without URL-encoding
body:
The redirect to GitHub is built with an f-string, `?client_id=...&state=...&redirect_uri=...`. Nothing is encoded, and `redirect_uri` is an absolute URL containing `:` and `/`.

If the configured base URL, client id or redirect URI ever contains `&`, `?`, `#` or `%`, GitHub will receive a malformed or truncated parameter. The other OAuth views use `urlencode(params)`; this one should too.

title: test_installation_not_found now tests a state mismatch, not the 404 installation path
body:
The second request uses `state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`, which does not match the current pipeline signature (`9cae5e88...`). `OAuthLoginView` therefore returns the generic 'Invalid installation request.' error before `GitHubInstallation` or `build_integration` ever runs.

The mocked 404 on `/app/installations/{id}` is never exercised. The 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' error path from `build_integration` has lost its test coverage, while the test name still suggests it is covered.

Separately, there is no test for the success path where a webhook-created Integration's `sender.login` matches the authenticated user. There are also no tests for a failed token exchange or a missing `login`.

title: `queued` default is evaluated once at import time, so every instance shares the same timestamp
body:
`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a plain dataclass default. It is computed once, when the class body runs at module import, not on each instantiation.

Every `AssignmentSource` built without an explicit `queued` (including all those from `from_integration`) gets the worker process's import time. In a long-lived worker that can be hours or days stale. Any current or future use of `queued` for staleness, ordering or debouncing of rapid assignee changes (the scenario this PR targets) will be wrong.

Use `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

`test_to_dict` only asserts `queued is not None`, so it cannot catch this.

title: `to_dict` puts a raw `datetime` into Celery task kwargs; the round-trip is not type-safe
body:
`to_dict()` returns `asdict(self)`, which contains a `datetime` object. That dict is passed as `assignment_source_dict` to `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs=...)`.

Task payloads should be JSON-safe primitives. Under a JSON serializer the datetime is either rejected at enqueue time or converted to an ISO string. `from_dict` does `cls(**input_dict)` with no type coercion, so after the round-trip `queued` silently becomes a `str` despite its `datetime` annotation.

Serialize `queued` explicitly (e.g. `isoformat()` or epoch) in `to_dict` and parse it back in `from_dict`.

title: Cycle guard compares integration IDs, so syncs to other linked issues in the same integration are dropped
body:
`should_sync` returns False whenever `sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id`. The outbound task runs once per linked `ExternalIssue`.

If a Sentry group is linked to two issues in the same Jira integration (A and B), an inbound change on A now blocks the outbound update to B as well. Previously B would be kept in sync; this is a silent regression.

The loop being fixed is between Sentry and the specific external issue that sent the webhook. Carrying the originating external issue key/id in `AssignmentSource` and skipping only that issue would break the cycle without suppressing legitimate propagation.

title: `from_dict` silently returns None on malformed input, which re-enables the sync loop
body:
`from_dict` catches `ValueError`/`TypeError` and returns None without logging. In `sync_assignee_outbound`, a None source means `should_sync` skips the cycle check and proceeds with the outbound sync.

Any schema drift in the payload (an added or renamed field, or tasks enqueued by a different code version during deploy) silently brings back the exact cycle this PR fixes. Log or emit a metric when parsing fails so this is observable.

title: `sync_status_outbound` gains an `assignment_source` parameter that nothing passes or honors
body:
The abstract signature of `sync_status_outbound` now declares `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`. No caller supplies it, no implementation uses it, and the status outbound path does not consult the source in `should_sync`.

This suggests to readers and implementers that status-sync cycles are also prevented when they are not. Either wire it through the status sync path or remove it from this PR.

title: No test that a different integration still receives the sync, or that the inbound path breaks the cycle
body:
The new test only covers the case where the source matches the target integration and the outbound call is skipped.

Two behaviors are untested:
- An `AssignmentSource` from a different integration still triggers `sync_assignee_outbound` on the linked integration.
- `sync_group_assignee_inbound` (the real webhook entry point) does not call back out to the originating integration.

The existing inbound tests run without `self.tasks()` and without mocking outbound, so the end-to-end cycle break is not verified.

title: `queued` default is evaluated once at import time, not per instance
body:
`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a plain dataclass default. Python evaluates it once, when the class is defined at module import.

As a result, every `AssignmentSource` created via `from_integration()` or `from_dict()` without an explicit `queued` gets the same timestamp: the moment the web or worker process imported the module. That can be hours or days old. Any future use of `queued` (staleness checks, ordering of rapid assignment changes, debugging/logging) will silently get wrong data.

`test_to_dict` only asserts `queued is not None`, so it does not catch this.

Fix: use `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

title: Cycle check is per-integration, so other linked issues in the same integration stop syncing
body:
`should_sync` returns False whenever `sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id`. The task runs once per linked ExternalIssue, but the check ignores which external issue triggered the change.

If a Sentry group is linked to two issues in the same Jira integration (e.g. APP-1 and APP-2), a webhook assigning APP-1 updates the Sentry assignee. The outbound sync to APP-2 is then skipped too, because it shares the integration id. Before this change APP-2 would have received the new assignee, so this silently regresses assignee propagation.

The nearby comment says other targets should still get the change, but that only holds across different integrations, not across different issues in one integration.

Fix: carry the originating external issue (key or id) in `AssignmentSource` and skip only that external issue.

title: Task kwargs now contain a raw `datetime` object
body:
`assignment_source.to_dict()` uses `dataclasses.asdict`, so the `queued` value passed to `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async` is a `datetime` instance. This works only under pickle (or serializer-specific datetime handling).

Under plain JSON task serialization, which Sentry is moving toward, it will either fail to serialize or arrive as a string. `from_dict` then passes that string straight into the dataclass without parsing, leaving `queued` as a `str` despite its `datetime` annotation.

Fix: serialize `queued` explicitly (e.g. isoformat or epoch) in `to_dict` and parse it back in `from_dict`.

title: `sync_status_outbound` abstract signature changed but never wired up
No test covers the actual inbound→outbound cycle or other-integration propagation
body:
The new test calls `GroupAssignee.objects.assign` directly with an `AssignmentSource`. Nothing verifies the real fix path, i.e. that `sync_group_assignee_inbound` (assign and deassign), run under `self.tasks()`, does not enqueue an outbound sync back to the originating integration.

There is also no test that a different integration linked to the same group still receives the outbound assignee sync when the source is another integration. The PR description explicitly claims that behavior.

`test_assignee_sync_inbound_assign` and `test_assignee_sync_inbound_deassign` run without `self.tasks()` and without asserting on outbound calls, so a regression in the source propagation would go unnoticed.

title: `queued` default is evaluated once at import time
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` runs a single time, when the module is imported. Every `AssignmentSource` built without an explicit `queued`, including all of those from `from_integration`, gets the same timestamp: the process start time. On long-running web and worker processes that value can be hours or days stale, so `queued` never reflects when the assignment was queued. Use `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. The new `test_to_dict` only checks that `queued` is not None, so it cannot catch this.

title: Raw datetime passed in Celery task kwargs
body: `assignment_source.to_dict()` uses `dataclasses.asdict`, so the `queued` value is a raw `datetime`. That dict is passed as `assignment_source_dict` in `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async` kwargs. Sentry expects task parameters to be JSON-safe primitives, and a datetime is not. With a JSON serializer this either fails to serialize, gets flagged as a bad-pickle parameter, or reaches the worker as a string. In the string case `from_dict` still builds the object, because dataclasses do no type checking, and `queued` silently ends up as a `str` despite its `datetime` annotation. The tests run tasks eagerly with `self.tasks()`, so the serialization round-trip is never exercised. Serialize `queued` as an ISO string or epoch int and parse it back in `from_dict`.

title: Cycle suppression works per integration, so other linked issues on the same integration stop syncing
body: The new check returns False whenever `sync_source.integration_id` equals the installation's integration id. A Sentry group can be linked to several external issues on the same integration, for example two Jira tickets on one Jira install. If the assignee changes on ticket A, the outbound sync to ticket B is now skipped too, because B shares A's integration. Before this change B would have been updated, so B is left with a stale assignee. The suppression should target the originating external issue (for example by carrying the external issue key or id in `AssignmentSource`) rather than every issue on that integration.

title: `assignment_source` added to abstract `sync_status_outbound` but never passed or used
body: The abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature gains an `assignment_source` parameter. No caller passes it, the status sync path never builds an `AssignmentSource`, and concrete implementations don't consume it. The signature suggests status sync cycles are also prevented, but inbound status webhooks still trigger outbound status syncs back to the same integration. Either wire it through the status path or drop the parameter so the abstract signature doesn't mislead implementers.

title: `from_dict` silently returns None on any unexpected key, turning off cycle protection
body: `from_dict` does `cls(**input_dict)` and swallows `TypeError`/`ValueError` by returning None. The task then calls `should_sync(..., None)`, which skips the source check and syncs back to the originating integration. This will happen if the payload ever gains a field during a mixed-version deploy, or if `queued` cannot be handled. The sync-cycle protection is lost without any log or metric. At minimum, log when parsing fails. Better, ignore unknown keys and build the object from the known fields.

title: No end-to-end test that inbound sync suppresses outbound to the same integration
body: The new test only calls `GroupAssignee.objects.assign` directly with a hand-built `AssignmentSource`. Nothing checks that `sync_group_assignee_inbound` actually attaches the source for both assign and deassign, which is the code path that fixes the reported loop. Nothing checks that a different integration linked to the same group still receives the outbound sync. There is also no deassign test with a matching source. The inbound tests at the end of this file don't mock or assert on `sync_assignee_outbound` at all.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and cannot be instantiated
body:
`MetricAlertDetectorHandler` used to subclass `DetectorHandler` and implement `evaluate` (returning `[]`). It now subclasses `StatefulDetectorHandler` with only `pass`. It does not implement any of the abstract members: `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, or the new `build_occurrence_and_event_data`.

`MetricAlertFire.detector_handler` points at this class. So `Detector.detector_handler` (`group_type.detector_handler(self)`) raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class` for any detector of type `metric_alert_fire`.

In `process_detectors` that exception is not caught. It aborts processing for every remaining detector in the list. Before this PR the handler was a harmless no-op.

The abstract methods need stub implementations, or the class should stay a concrete `DetectorHandler` until it is ready. The TODO comment above the class is also now stale.

title: Expected occurrence built with wrong group key in TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe
body:
The expected occurrence is built with `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", ...)`, so its fingerprint is `["<id>:val1"]`. The code under test is called with group key `"group_key"`, so the real `build_occurrence_and_event_data` gives fingerprint `["<id>:group_key"]`.

`IssueOccurrence` and `DetectorEvaluationResult` are dataclasses that compare all fields. The `== expected_result` assertion should therefore fail on the fingerprint mismatch. If it somehow passes, the test is not checking that the occurrence is built for the right group key.

The expected occurrence should be built with `expected_result.group_key` (and value 10).

title: Tests never verify the value passed to build_occurrence_and_event_data
body:
In `test_state_results_multi_group`, `group_2` has value 10, but the expected occurrence is built with value 6. `TestEvaluate` cases do the same: they evaluate with 100 or 8 but build expectations with 6.

These tests only pass because `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` ignores `value`. No test checks that the hook gets the actual group value. A regression that passes the wrong value, such as the threshold or another group's value, would go unnoticed.

The mock should encode `value` into the occurrence (for example in `evidence_data`), and the expectations should use the real values.

title: PriorityLevel(new_status) raises for non-standard condition results, aborting the whole packet
body:
`new_status` is computed as `max(DetectorPriorityLevel.OK, evaluation)` over `condition.evaluate_value(value)`. `DataCondition.get_condition_result` can return raw ints that are not valid `DetectorPriorityLevel` members, and it can also return bools or floats.

The new conversion `PriorityLevel(new_status)` raises `ValueError` for any such value, for example `True`→1 or an arbitrary int like 100. The exception propagates out of `evaluate` and `process_detectors`. It aborts evaluation for every group key in the packet and every later detector, with no state committed.

The condition result should be validated or mapped first, or the bad value logged and skipped, instead of crashing.

title: evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: The docstring for `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` still says it "returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`". This PR changed the return type to `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]` keyed by group key, so the docstring now misdescribes the contract implementers and callers rely on.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and raises TypeError when instantiated
body:
`MetricAlertDetectorHandler` used to implement `evaluate` and return `[]`. It now subclasses `StatefulDetectorHandler` with only `pass`. That leaves four abstract members unimplemented: `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values` and the new `build_occurrence_and_event_data`.

`Detector.detector_handler` instantiates the handler via `group_type.detector_handler(self)`. For any detector of type `metric_alert_fire`, that call raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class`.

`process_detectors` does not catch this. One such detector therefore aborts processing of every detector in the batch, and pending state commits are lost. mypy does not flag this because the instantiation goes through a `type[DetectorHandler]` variable.

Either keep a concrete stub implementation, or leave it on `DetectorHandler` until the real implementation exists.

title: Expected occurrence uses group key 'val1' but evaluation uses 'group_key'
body:
In `TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe`, the expected occurrence is built with `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", ...)`. Its fingerprint is therefore `["<detector_id>:val1"]`.

`evaluate_group_key_value` is then called with group key `"group_key"`. The handler builds the real occurrence with fingerprint `["<detector_id>:group_key"]`.

`IssueOccurrence` and `DetectorEvaluationResult` are frozen dataclasses compared field by field. The `== expected_result` assertion should therefore fail on the fingerprint mismatch. If it somehow passes, it is not checking that the occurrence is built for the right group key.

The expected occurrence should be built with `"group_key"`.

title: evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: The PR changes `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` to return a `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]` keyed by group key. The docstring still says it "returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`". It should describe the dict return value, which is the contract change this PR introduces.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and cannot be instantiated
body:
`MetricAlertDetectorHandler` now subclasses `StatefulDetectorHandler` with only `pass`. It inherits several abstract members it does not implement: `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values` and the new `build_occurrence_and_event_data`.

`MetricAlertFire.detector_handler` points at this class. As a result, `Detector.detector_handler` (`group_type.detector_handler(self)`) raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class` for any detector of type `metric_alert_fire`.

In `process_detectors` that exception is not caught. One such detector aborts processing for every detector in the batch, and `commit_state_updates` never runs for detectors already evaluated.

Before this change the handler was a concrete no-op that returned `[]`. Either keep it concrete (stub the abstract methods) or don't register it as the group type's handler yet. The TODO comment on line 10 ("This will be a stateful detector when we build that abstraction") is also now stale.

title: Expected occurrence built with wrong group key; fingerprint won't match
body:
In `TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe`, the expected occurrence is built with `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", ...)`, so its fingerprint is `["<id>:val1"]`.

The call under test is `evaluate_group_key_value("group_key", 10, ...)`. That invokes `build_occurrence_and_event_data("group_key", ...)`, which produces fingerprint `["<id>:group_key"]`.

`IssueOccurrence` is a frozen dataclass with field-wise equality, and only `StatusChangeMessage.__eq__` is patched. The `DetectorEvaluationResult` comparison therefore fails on the fingerprint. The expected occurrence should be built with `"group_key"`.

title: evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: The `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` docstring still says it "returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`". This PR changed the return type to `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]` keyed by group key. The docstring should be updated so implementers and callers aren't misled about the contract.

title: Monitor context returns the raw config, not the copy with the readable schedule_type
body: `get_monitor_environment_context` copies the monitor config into `config` and replaces `schedule_type` with its display value (e.g. "crontab" or "interval"). The returned dict then uses `"config": monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead of the local `config`, so the conversion is computed and thrown away. As a result, the `monitor` context on every incident occurrence event shows the raw integer `schedule_type` rather than the readable label. This bug existed before, but the function is being moved into a new module, so this is a good time to change it to return `config`.

title: `get_failure_reason` docstring examples don't match the strings it produces
body: The docstring gives examples like "3 missed check-ins detected", "2 missed check-ins, 1 timeout check-in and 1 error check-in were detected" and "A failed check-in was detected". The code actually produces "2 missed, 1 timeout and 1 error check-ins detected" for mixed statuses: it never says "were" and never adds a per-status "check-in". For a single failure it produces "An error/A missed/A timeout check-in was detected", never "A failed check-in". The docstring also misspells "human readable" as "humam readible". Since the function now lives in its own module and will be extended, the documented contract should match the real output.

title: Monitor context returns raw config, discarding the schedule_type conversion
body: `get_monitor_environment_context` copies the config into a local `config` and replaces `schedule_type` with `get_schedule_type_display()`. The returned dict then uses `"config": monitor_environment.monitor.config`, so the converted copy is never used. As a result, the monitor context attached to every incident occurrence carries the raw integer `schedule_type` instead of the human-readable label. The bug existed before, but this PR moves the function into a new module, which is a cheap point to fix it: return `config` instead.

title: get_failure_reason docstring examples don't match actual output
body: The docstring says outputs look like "2 missed check-ins, 1 timeout check-in and 1 error check-in were detected" and "A failed check-in was detected". Neither can be produced. The plural branch formats "%(count)d %(status)s" with no per-item "check-in(s)" and ends with "check-ins detected" (no "were"). The singular branch only yields "An error/A missed/A timeout check-in was detected". It also contains typos ("humam readible"). Anyone reading the new module's docs will be misled about the strings shown in the issue evidence. Update the examples to the real outputs, e.g. "2 missed, 1 timeout and 1 error check-ins detected".

title: Prepared config copy is discarded; raw monitor config is sent in the monitor context
body: `get_monitor_environment_context` copies `monitor.config` and replaces `schedule_type` with its human-readable display value. The returned dict then uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead of the local `config`, so that copy is never used. As a result, the `monitor` context on every issue occurrence carries the raw integer `schedule_type` rather than the display name. The bug was carried over from mark_failed.py, but the function now lives in a new module. Fix: return `"config": config`.

title: Moved helpers removed from mark_failed without re-exports or test updates
body:
Several names were removed from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed`:
- `mark_failed_threshold`, renamed to `try_incident_threshold`
- `create_issue_platform_occurrence`, renamed to `create_incident_occurrence`
- `get_failure_reason`
- `get_monitor_environment_context`
- `SimpleCheckIn`

No compatibility re-exports were added, and no tests were updated in this PR. Any code or tests that import these names from `mark_failed`, or use them as `mock.patch` targets, will fail with ImportError/AttributeError. Either update those references and the tests in the same change, or keep temporary aliases.

title: get_failure_reason docstring examples don't match actual output
body:
The docstring has typos ("humam readible") and its examples don't match the code.
- It claims output like "2 missed check-ins, 1 timeout check-in and 1 error check-in were detected". The code actually produces "2 missed, 1 timeout and 1 error check-ins detected".
- It claims "A failed check-in was detected". No such string exists in `SINGULAR_HUMAN_FAILURE_MAP`; the singular forms are status-specific ("A missed check-in was detected", etc.).

The docstring is now in a fresh module and should describe the real behavior.

title: Hung flusher processes are never killed, so a duplicate flusher is started for the same shards
body:
The kill is now guarded by `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. Real processes are created with `self.mp_context.Process`, i.e. `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` subclasses `BaseProcess` directly, not `multiprocessing.Process` (`multiprocessing.context.Process`), so the check is always False and `process.kill()` never runs.

The old code called `kill()` unconditionally. Now, when a process is detected as hung (`cause == "hang"`), it keeps running and `_create_process_for_shards` spawns a second process for the same shards. Both processes share the same `stopped`, `healthy_since` and `backpressure_since` Values.

Consequences:
- Two flushers can flush the same shards concurrently, which risks duplicate segments on buffered-segments.
- Processes leak on every restart, up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per process index.
- A recovered zombie keeps updating the shared health and backpressure values.

Fix: check against `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` or the concrete `SpawnProcess` class, or test `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`.

title: join() stops early on deadline without terminating the remaining flusher processes
body:
In `join()`, if the deadline has passed when the loop reaches a process, it does `break`. Every later process is skipped and never gets `terminate()` called.

With a timeout, the whole budget can be spent waiting on the first process, so the other N-1 processes are simply abandoned. On a rebalance, the next `create_with_partitions` immediately spawns new flushers, so hung or still-running old processes can overlap with the new ones.

Separately, the `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` check at line 346 never matches `SpawnProcess`, so `terminate()` is effectively never called for real processes.

Fix: keep the wait loop bounded by the deadline, but always terminate every process, and use a correct type check.

title: Redis memory info is queried once per flusher buffer on every submit, multiplying INFO calls on the main thread
body:
`get_memory_info()` on `SpansBuffer` walks the memory usage of every node in the Redis cluster; it does not depend on `assigned_shards`. Looping over `self.buffers.values()` therefore runs the same full-cluster INFO sweep `num_processes` times on each `submit()` and sums the duplicated results.

The used/available ratio comes out the same, but the main consumer thread now pays N times the Redis round-trips. That works against the PR's stated goal of keeping the main thread minimal.

Fix: query memory info once, e.g. from the original `buffer` or from just one of the shard buffers.

title: Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
body:
The test calls `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at the top and then calls `time.sleep(0.1)` through the `time` module. That call hits the patched lambda, so no time passes.

The comment "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change" is false. The test still depends on the flusher thread happening to flush before `join()` sets `stopped`, so it can be flaky. If a real wait is needed, use a saved reference to the real `sleep` or poll until `messages` is non-empty.

title: Inconsistent metric tag key: 'shard' vs 'shards'
body:
Three metrics in this PR tag the shard list:
- `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` uses the tag key `shard`.
- `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` uses `shard`.
- `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` uses `shards`.

Dashboards and queries that group by shard will silently miss the `wait_produce` metric. Use one tag key consistently.

title: Docstring says one process per shard, but processes are capped and default CLI value is 1
body:
The class docstring says the flusher "Creates one process per shard". In fact shards are distributed round-robin across `min(max_processes, len(shards))` processes.

The CLI option `--flusher-processes` defaults to 1, so by default a single process handles all shards. The docstring should describe the capped, round-robin assignment.

title: Unused method _create_process_for_shard
body: `_create_process_for_shard` is never called anywhere; restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards` directly. This dead code should be removed to avoid confusion about the restart path.

title: Hung flusher process is never killed because the isinstance check never matches spawn processes
body:
Processes are created with `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which is `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`. `multiprocessing.Process` is `multiprocessing.context.Process`, and `SpawnProcess` is not a subclass of it (both derive from `BaseProcess`). So `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is always False and `process.kill()` is never called.

The old code called `kill()` unconditionally, so this is a regression. When a process is restarted for the `hang` cause, the hung process keeps running while a replacement is spawned for the same shards. It also shares the same `healthy_since` and `backpressure_since` Values.

If the old process resumes, two flushers work on the same Redis shards concurrently, which can produce duplicate segments to `buffered-segments`. Each further hang leaks another process, up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS.

Use `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)`, or check `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`.

title: join() never terminates spawn processes (same isinstance mismatch)
body:
In `join()`, `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is False for `SpawnProcess` objects, so `process.terminate()` is never called. Flusher processes that do not exit before the deadline keep running after the strategy is joined.

On rebalance the consumer process stays alive and builds a new SpanFlusher. Old flusher processes can then keep flushing alongside new ones for the same shards. With N processes per flusher, the number of leaked processes now scales with shard count. Check against `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` instead.

title: join() breaks out of loop on deadline, skipping cleanup of remaining processes
body:
When the deadline has passed, the loop does `break`. Every remaining process in `self.processes` is then neither waited on nor terminated.

The previous single-process code always reached the terminate step after the wait. Now, if the first process consumes the timeout, processes 2..N are silently left running. The remaining processes should still be terminated when the deadline is exceeded: skip the wait but not the terminate.

title: Redis memory info and stored-segment queries are now repeated per flusher process on the consumer main thread
body:
`submit()` now loops over `self.buffers` and calls `get_memory_info()` and `record_stored_segments()` on each per-process SpansBuffer. `get_memory_info()` reports memory for the whole Redis cluster, not per shard. With N flusher processes, every submit therefore issues N times the INFO round-trips to every Redis node.

The ratio is unaffected because `used` and `available` are both multiplied by N, so the work is purely redundant. `record_stored_segments()` likewise goes from one pipeline to N.

This cost lands on the consumer main thread, which the PR is trying to keep minimal. Query memory once, for example via the original full-shard buffer, and batch the ZCARDs in a single pipeline.

title: Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
body:
The test does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at the top. The new `time.sleep(0.1)`, meant to "give flusher threads time to process after drift change", resolves through the patched `time` module attribute and does nothing.

The race the comment describes is still present. `join()` sets `stopped` immediately, and the flusher thread can exit its loop before it flushes with the new drift. `(msg,) = messages` can then fail intermittently.

Use a real sleep captured before patching (e.g. `from time import sleep` as test_flusher.py does), or better, poll until `messages` is non-empty with a timeout.

title: Inconsistent metric tag key: 'shard' vs 'shards'
body: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` are tagged with `shard`, but `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is tagged with `shards`. The value is the same comma-joined shard list. Dashboards and queries that slice by shard will not work uniformly across these related flusher metrics. Use the same tag key for all of them.

title: Docstring claims one process per shard, but processes are capped and the CLI default is 1
body: The class docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing." The implementation actually creates `min(max_processes, len(shards))` processes and round-robins shards across them. The `--flusher-processes` CLI option defaults to 1, so production behaviour by default is still a single flusher process handling all shards. Update the docstring to describe the capped, shared-process behaviour.

title: Hung flusher processes are no longer killed before a replacement is spawned
body:
The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. The new code only kills when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is true. Processes come from `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which builds `SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` subclasses `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, not `multiprocessing.Process` (that is `context.Process`), so the check is always False in production.

When a process is flagged as a `hang`, the still-alive old process is left running and a second process is started for the same shards. Both share the same `stopped`, `current_drift`, `healthy_since` and `backpressure_since` Values. Consequences:
- Two processes can call `flush_segments` on the same shards concurrently and produce duplicate segments to buffered-segments.
- The stale process can keep refreshing `healthy_since`, masking the new one's health.
- Up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS orphan processes can leak.

The same broken check at line 346 means `terminate()` in `join()` never runs either. Use `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` (or check for not being a `threading.Thread`) instead.

title: join() breaks out of the loop on deadline and skips terminating the remaining processes
body:
In `join()`, once the deadline has passed, `if remaining_time <= 0: break` exits the loop entirely. Every process after that point never reaches the `process.terminate()` call. Before this change, terminate was always attempted after the wait.

With several flusher processes, a timed-out join (e.g. during rebalancing) leaves the later processes running unsupervised. They can keep flushing shards that may now belong to another consumer. A stuck process would never exit, because it is only stopped via the `stopped` flag.

The deadline check should only skip the waiting, not the termination.

title: Cluster-wide Redis memory info is queried once per flusher buffer on every submit
body:
`get_memory_info()` reports memory for the whole Redis cluster, not for a shard. The new loop calls it once per per-process buffer, so every `submit()` issues N times as many INFO calls to every cluster node.

The used/available ratio comes out the same only because both sums are multiplied by N. The extra calls are pure overhead on the consumer's main thread, which this PR is trying to keep minimal.

`record_stored_segments` is likewise split into N separate pipelines. Query memory info once (e.g. from a single buffer) instead.

title: Inconsistent metric tag key: 'shards' vs 'shard'
body: `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is tagged with `{"shards": shard_tag}`. `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` use `{"shard": shard_tag}` for the same value. Dashboards that group or filter these flusher metrics by one key will silently miss the other metric.

title: Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
body: The test calls `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at the start, so the new `time.sleep(0.1)` does nothing. The comment says it gives the flusher threads time to process the drift change, but it doesn't. The test still races: `join()` sets `stopped=True` and the flusher thread may exit before it ever observes the new drift, which makes the test flaky. A real wait (e.g. the original `sleep` saved before patching, or polling until `messages` is non-empty) is needed.

title: Strategy close() shuts down the factory-owned queue pool, so every message after the first rebalance is dropped and committed
body:
`FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__`, and every strategy returned by `create_with_partitions` gets the same instance (result_consumer.py:133 and :255). On any partition revocation, arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the current strategy. That calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets every worker's `shutdown` flag, calls `Queue.shutdown()` on every queue and joins the workers.

On the next assignment, arroyo calls `create_with_partitions` again and the new strategy wraps the same dead pool. Each `submit` then goes through `FixedQueuePool.submit`: `add_offset` succeeds, but `work_queue.put` raises `queue.ShutDown`. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` catches that exception and marks the offset completed, so the commit thread commits it.

Result: after the first rebalance (deploy, scale event, pod restart), no uptime result is processed, yet all offsets are committed. This is silent data loss.

The shared `OffsetTracker` makes it worse. Stale outstanding or committable offsets for revoked partitions survive into the new assignment. They can block commits forever, or be passed to arroyo's `stage_offsets` for unassigned partitions; that raises, and the whole commit batch fails every tick.

Fix: the pool and tracker should be owned per strategy, or reset on assignment. `close()` should not tear down a resource owned by the factory.

title: Arroyo commit callback is invoked from a background thread
body:
`_commit_loop` runs on its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which ends up in arroyo's `StreamProcessor` commit callback. That callback calls `KafkaConsumer.stage_offsets`/`commit_offsets` and updates the commit-policy state. Arroyo expects it to be called only from the processing thread, inside `submit`/`poll`/`join`. Here it runs concurrently with the main thread's `consumer.poll()` and with rebalance callbacks, with no synchronization.

Consequences:
- Races on arroyo's unsynchronized internal state (staged offsets, policy timestamps).
- Exceptions when staging offsets for partitions that were just revoked.
- Commits with `force=False` under `ONCE_PER_SECOND` may only be staged. Because the loop calls commit only when new offsets become committable, the trailing offsets can sit staged indefinitely once traffic pauses.

The committable offsets should be computed and committed from `poll()` on the main thread, as arroyo's `CommitOffsets` step does. `join()` should do a final forced commit.

title: Unbounded queues mean no backpressure, despite the docstring's claim
body:
Each worker queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`. `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`, so arroyo never pauses the consumer. If processing is slower than ingestion (slow DB or cache, one hot queue), the consumer keeps reading the topic into memory. Every message, with its full `Message` object, is held in `WorkItem`, and the `OffsetTracker` sets grow alongside.

This can OOM the consumer. Because commits stay behind the slowest item, a crash also forces reprocessing of a very large backlog.

The class docstring (line 253) promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", which is not true. Bound the queues, and raise `MessageRejected` from `submit` when the target queue is full.

title: join() ignores its timeout, shutdown blocks up to 5s per worker, and no final commit is made
body:
`join(timeout)` discards the timeout and calls `close()`. `close()` waits up to 5s for the commit thread. It then calls `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()`, which calls `worker.join(timeout=5.0)` on each worker in turn. With the default of 20 queues and workers stuck in slow processing, a rebalance or shutdown can block for about 100s, regardless of arroyo's `join_timeout`. That risks exceeding `max.poll.interval.ms` and triggering further rebalances.

`terminate()`, which is meant to be immediate, also goes through the same blocking `pool.shutdown()`.

In addition, the commit thread is stopped before the workers finish, and no final commit is issued. Offsets completed since the last 1s tick are never committed and will be reprocessed after every rebalance.

Honor the timeout, shut workers down in parallel, and force-commit completed offsets in `join()`.

title: Error-handling test contradicts its docstring and passes only because of timing
body:
`test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` says errors "don't block offset commits for other messages". It then asserts that nothing was committed for the partition.

In the implementation, the worker's `finally` always calls `complete_offset`, even when processing raised. The commit thread will therefore commit offset 102 about 1s after the strategy is created.

The assertion holds only because the test checks around 0.2–0.3s, before the first commit tick. On a slow CI run (for example, slow DB fixture setup) the commit lands first and the test fails. The test is both flaky and asserting the opposite of its stated intent.

title: Offset-gap tests assert behaviour the tracker only exhibits for one commit tick
body:
`test_offset_gaps_block_commits` (and `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps` in the uptime tests) assert that a missing offset 101 prevents committing past 100.

The tracker does not keep blocking. After committing 100, `mark_committed` prunes `all_offsets` to {102, 103}. On the next tick, `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)` jumps to 102, and the tracker commits 103 without 101 ever arriving.

The unit test only reaches 103 on its second wait because of this, not because 101 was submitted. The uptime test passes only because it stops observing before the second 1s tick.

These tests give false confidence about the gap semantics and are timing-dependent. Either change the semantics or make the tests assert what the code actually guarantees.

title: Queue-depth gauge emitted for every message, and worker gauges overwrite each other
body:
Every processed item emits `metrics.gauge("remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth", ...)` in the worker's `finally` block. On a high-volume topic like uptime results, that is one statsd call per message per worker.

The gauge is tagged only with `identifier`, not with the worker or queue id. The values reported by different workers therefore overwrite each other, and the metric does not show any particular queue's depth.

`poll()` already reports total queue depth; per-queue depth could be emitted there, tagged by queue index.

title: Shared queue pool is shut down on strategy close, then reused after rebalance, silently dropping and committing all messages
body:
`ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` creates one `FixedQueuePool` and every `create_with_partitions` call (result_consumer.py:254) hands that same pool to a new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`. On any partition revocation, arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the old strategy, and `close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`. That stops all worker threads and calls `Queue.shutdown()` on every queue.

The next strategy created on reassignment uses the dead pool:
- `work_queue.put()` raises `queue.ShutDown`.
- `submit`'s blanket `except Exception` (lines 317-325) catches it and calls `add_offset` + `complete_offset`.
- The message is therefore treated as successfully processed, and the new commit loop commits past it.

After the first rebalance the uptime consumer stops processing results entirely while still advancing Kafka offsets. This is silent data loss. The pool needs to be owned per strategy, or must not be shut down in `close()`. Enqueue failures must not be marked complete.

title: Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread
body:
`_commit_loop` runs on its own thread and calls `commit_function` -> arroyo's `Commit` callable. That callable (`StreamProcessor.__commit`) is not thread-safe and is meant to be called from the consumer thread during `submit`/`poll`. It mutates the DLQ buffered-messages state, calls `KafkaConsumer.stage_offsets` (which checks assignment state) and may call `commit_offsets` synchronously.

Those run concurrently with the main thread's `poll()`, rebalance callbacks and `close()`. During revocation, `close()` sets the event, which wakes the commit thread. The thread then does one more commit while the main thread is inside the revoke callback, so offsets can be staged for partitions being revoked, which raises or races.

Completed offsets should be collected in a thread-safe structure and committed from `poll()`/`submit()` on the consumer thread.

title: OffsetTracker state is never reset per assignment; revoked partitions poison future commits
body:
The `OffsetTracker` lives on the factory-scoped pool and is never cleared when partitions are revoked. Two failure modes follow on a later assignment:

1. If a revoked partition still has completed-but-uncommitted offsets, the new strategy's commit loop includes that partition in `committable`. Arroyo's `KafkaConsumer.stage_offsets` raises for unassigned partitions, so the whole commit fails. Because `mark_committed` is never reached, the same failure repeats every second and no partition ever commits again.
2. Outstanding offsets abandoned at shutdown stay in `outstanding`. If the partition comes back starting at a higher offset, `get_committable_offsets` starts from the stale minimum, hits a permanently outstanding offset and breaks. Commits for that partition stall forever while `all_offsets` grows.

Tracker state should be scoped to the strategy/assignment and pruned on revoke.

title: Unbounded queues with no backpressure, contrary to the docstring
body:
Each work queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `submit` never raises `MessageRejected`. The strategy docstring nevertheless claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up".

If `result_processor` slows down (slow DB/cache, one hot subscription clogging a queue), arroyo keeps polling and the consumer reads the backlog into memory without limit. Every message's `WorkItem` (holding the full `Message`) and the `OffsetTracker` sets grow until the process OOMs.

The queues should be bounded, or the total in-flight count capped, raising `MessageRejected` from `submit` when full.

title: join() ignores timeout, never flushes final commit, and shutdown abandons queued work
body:
`join(timeout)` just calls `close()` again. It ignores the timeout, does not wait for in-flight items, and does not make a final (forced) commit of offsets completed since the last 1-second tick. Every rebalance or shutdown therefore re-delivers up to a second's worth of already-processed results to the next owner.

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before shutting the queues, so workers exit after their current item instead of draining, despite the "Gracefully shutdown" docstring.

It then joins each worker sequentially with a 5s timeout. With the default 20 queues and slow processors, a revoke callback can block for up to ~100s, which can exceed the rebalance/poll timeout and get the consumer kicked from the group.

title: Commit logic requires strictly contiguous offsets; any gap stalls the partition forever
body:
`get_committable_offsets` walks `range(start, max_offset + 1)` and breaks at the first offset not present in `all_offsets`. Kafka does not guarantee contiguous offsets for delivered messages: transactional control markers and compacted topics leave gaps.

The same happens for a message whose `value` is not a `BrokerValue`, which `submit` never tracks (the except branch skips it).

A single such gap means the partition never commits again, `all_offsets` grows without bound, and a restart reprocesses everything since the gap. The tracker should track the highest contiguous completed offset relative to submitted offsets, e.g. an ordered deque of submitted offsets, rather than assuming offset+1 always exists.

title: Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its stated behavior and passes only by timing
body:
`test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` is documented as "errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages". It then asserts that no commit happened (`len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`).

With the implementation, both offsets are marked complete in the worker's `finally`, so a commit of 102 is expected. The assertion only passes because the check runs before the commit thread's 1-second tick fires. On a slow CI run (DB writes for result creation, scheduling) the tick lands inside the window and the test fails.

The test should wait for the commit and assert `committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102`.

title: Thread-queue tests leak commit threads and run real processors on worker threads against the DB
body:
None of the new `test_thread_queue_parallel*` tests call `close()` on the strategy returned by `create_with_partitions`. Each leaves a daemon commit thread polling every second for the rest of the test run.

`test_thread_queue_parallel_graceful_shutdown` also submits results without mocking the processor. Worker threads then execute real `handle_result` DB/cache queries on separate connections outside the test transaction. They cannot see the test's fixtures, and they leave connections open across tests.

That test also only asserts `queue_pool is None`. It never verifies that queued items were drained or committed.

title: --max-workers help text is inaccurate
body:
The help text was changed to "The maximum amount of parallelism to use when in a parallel mode." However, `--max-workers` is ignored in `parallel` mode, which uses `--processes`.

In `thread-queue-parallel` it means the number of queues/worker threads, defaulting to 20 when unset. That default is not documented.

title: Shared queue pool is shut down on first rebalance, then reused: every later message is dropped and committed
body:
`self.queue_pool` is created once in the factory `__init__`, and every `create_with_partitions` call hands that same pool to a new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`. On partition revocation, arroyo calls `strategy.close()`/`join()`, which run `queue_pool.shutdown()`. That stops all worker threads and calls `Queue.shutdown()` on every queue.

After the next assignment, the new strategy's `submit` reaches `work_queue.put(...)`, which raises `queue.ShutDown`. The generic `except Exception` in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` catches it, logs it, and marks the offset as added and completed. The commit loop then commits it.

Result: after the first rebalance (any deploy or scale event), the consumer silently discards every uptime result while advancing committed offsets, until the process restarts. The pool (and its offset tracker) needs to be created per assignment, or must not be shut down by the strategy.

title: Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread
body:
`_commit_loop` runs on its own thread and calls `commit_function`, which calls arroyo's `commit`. That is the StreamProcessor's `__commit`, which calls `consumer.stage_offsets()`, `commit_offsets()` and the DLQ policy flush.

Arroyo's StreamProcessor and KafkaConsumer are not thread-safe. Their staged-offset dicts, consumer state machine (ASSIGNING/REVOKING) and commit-policy state are mutated by `poll()` and the rebalance callbacks on the main thread. Calling into them concurrently can corrupt or lose staged offsets, or raise `InvalidState`/`ConsumerError` mid-rebalance.

The `close()` path makes this worse: when the shutdown event is set, the loop still runs one more iteration and commits while the main thread is inside the revoke callback. Offsets should be handed back to the main thread, e.g. committed from `poll()`/`join()`.

title: Offset tracker never forgets revoked partitions, so commits can fail permanently for all partitions
body:
`OffsetTracker` lives on the shared `FixedQueuePool` and is never cleared or filtered when partitions are revoked. `get_committable_offsets` iterates every partition ever seen, so after a rebalance the committable map can include a partition this consumer no longer owns. This happens whenever completions land after the last commit, and workers keep running after close.

Arroyo's `KafkaConsumer.stage_offsets` raises "cannot stage offsets for unassigned partitions" if any key is unassigned. The commit loop catches that and skips `mark_committed`, so the same stale entry is returned and fails again every second. Commits for all currently assigned partitions are blocked as well.

Separately, outstanding offsets left behind for a revoked partition would block that partition's commits forever if it is later reassigned. Tracker state must be scoped to the current assignment.

title: Unbounded queues with no backpressure; docstring claims otherwise
body:
Each work queue is `queue.Queue()` with no maxsize, and `submit` never raises `MessageRejected`. The strategy docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing applies it.

When any worker is slow or stuck (the exact scenario this PR targets), the main thread keeps polling Kafka at full speed. Messages pile up in memory, each WorkItem holding the full arroyo `Message`. The `OffsetTracker` sets also grow without bound, because commits cannot pass the stuck offset.

At uptime-results volume this can OOM the consumer, and every buffered item is reprocessed after a restart. Bound the queues or the number of outstanding offsets, and raise `MessageRejected` when the limit is exceeded. The docstring claims "No item is lost" and "Only commits offsets after successful processing" are also inaccurate: failures and decode errors are committed.

title: Commit logic requires contiguous Kafka offsets and stalls forever on a gap
body:
`get_committable_offsets` walks `range(start, max_offset + 1)` and stops at the first offset not in `all_offsets`. After the first commit, `start` is `last_committed + 1`.

Kafka offsets are not guaranteed contiguous: transactional producers write control records, compaction removes offsets, and retention can skip ahead. If an offset is never delivered to `submit`, `highest_committable` never advances again for that partition. Commits stop permanently while the in-memory tracker keeps growing.

Arroyo delivers messages in order per partition, so the tracker should track offsets in arrival order. It can then commit up to (but excluding) the earliest still-outstanding received offset, instead of assuming every integer offset will appear. The new tests (`test_offset_gaps_block_commits`) codify the problematic behavior.

title: Shutdown blocks up to 5s per worker sequentially and ignores arroyo's join timeout
body:
`FixedQueuePool.shutdown` joins each worker with `timeout=5.0` in sequence. With the default 20 queues, close/join during a rebalance can block for up to 100 seconds, which risks exceeding rebalance/poll timeouts and being kicked from the group. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(timeout)` ignores the timeout arroyo passes.

Workers still busy after their join times out keep processing items for partitions that have been revoked. Another consumer may already be processing the same partition, so the same subscription can be handled concurrently and out of order.

In addition, the commit thread is stopped before the workers finish, so results completed during shutdown are never committed and get reprocessed.

title: Error-handling test asserts no commit happened, contradicting its docstring and the implementation
body:
`test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` says errors "don't block offset commits for other messages". It then asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, i.e. that nothing was committed.

The worker's `finally` marks the failed offset complete, so after the commit loop's 1-second tick both 100 and 101 become committable and offset 102 is committed. The test only passes because it checks about 0.3s after processing, before the first commit tick. It is timing-dependent (it will fail on a slow CI run) and verifies the opposite of the intended behavior.

The test should wait for a commit and assert the partition was committed to 102.

title: Two Sentry transactions started per message
body:
Every work item is wrapped in `sentry_sdk.start_transaction(op="queue_worker.process")`, and `ResultProcessor.__call__` immediately starts another transaction. Each Kafka message therefore produces two transactions, compared with one per batch in batched-parallel mode.

At uptime-results throughput this multiplies tracing volume and overhead. It also adds a per-message `metrics.gauge` call in the `finally` block. A span, or reusing the processor's transaction, would be more appropriate.

title: Racy/probabilistic assertions make tests flaky
body:
`test_stats_reporting` asserts `stats["total_items"] > 0` right after submitting 10 trivially-fast items. The three worker threads may have already drained the queues, so the assertion can fail nondeterministically.

Similarly, `test_different_groups_distributed` (line 106) assumes 20 keys hashed with the per-process randomized `hash()` always cover all 3 queues. That fails with roughly 0.1% probability depending on PYTHONHASHSEED.

title: --max-workers help text implies it applies to all parallel modes
body:
The help text now reads "The maximum amount of parallelism to use when in a parallel mode." However, `--mode parallel` ignores `max_workers` and uses `--processes`.

`max_workers` means thread count in batched-parallel mode and number of queues/threads in thread-queue-parallel mode. The text should name the modes it actually affects.

title: Backup codes stored with reversible encryption instead of one-way hash
body: Backup codes are encrypted with symmetricEncrypt/symmetricDecrypt using CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY (see also setup.ts line 68), the same way the TOTP secret is stored. Unlike the TOTP secret, backup codes never need to be recovered in plaintext for comparison — they only need equality checking, so they should be hashed with a one-way function (e.g. bcrypt/argon2) like passwords. Storing them with reversible encryption means that if CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY is ever compromised, every user's full set of backup/recovery codes can be recovered in plaintext, defeating the purpose of a second factor recovery mechanism.

title: Backup code component incorrectly named 'TwoFactor'
body: The default-exported function in BackupCode.tsx is declared as `function TwoFactor({ center = true })` instead of `function BackupCode(...)`. This is clearly copy-pasted from TwoFactor.tsx and not renamed. While the default export still works at the module level, React DevTools, error stack traces, and displayName-based debugging will show 'TwoFactor' for what is actually the backup-code input component, causing confusion when diagnosing issues in either component.

title: backupCodes state is untyped, inferred as never[]
body: `const [backupCodes, setBackupCodes] = useState([]);` has no generic type argument, so TypeScript infers the state type as `never[]`. The code later calls `setBackupCodes(body.backupCodes)` and `backupCodes.map((code) => ...)` where `code` is typed as `never`, relying on `body` being implicitly `any` to avoid a compile error. This should be `useState<string[]>([])` to get proper type safety for the `code` parameter and avoid incorrect typing silently propagating through the component.

title: No e2e coverage for the actual backup-code login/disable flows
body: The PR adds the ability to log in with a backup code and to disable 2FA using a backup code (the core new functionality described in the PR), but the only test change exercises the backup-code download/copy UI during setup. The TODO comment itself acknowledges 'add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup', and the PR checklist states no tests were added proving the feature works. This leaves the primary new behavior (backup-code authentication, IncorrectBackupCode/MissingBackupCodes error handling) completely untested.

title: Backup codes are persisted to the DB before 2FA setup is confirmed
body: setup.ts generates and stores encrypted backupCodes (and the TOTP secret) in the database immediately after password confirmation, while twoFactorEnabled remains false. If the user abandons the setup flow (e.g. closes the modal after seeing the QR code without entering a valid TOTP code), the newly generated backup codes remain stored against the user's account indefinitely even though 2FA was never actually enabled, until the user restarts setup (which overwrites them) or disables 2FA. This leaves sensitive recovery codes persisted for an account state that doesn't reflect them being issued/used.

title: Backup codes Blob URL is leaked if the dialog is closed without restarting setup
body: `URL.createObjectURL(textBlob)` is called in handleSetup and only revoked via `if (backupCodesUrl) URL.revokeObjectURL(backupCodesUrl)` the next time handleSetup runs. If the user completes the enable flow (closing the modal via the Close button) or cancels without re-opening setup, the created object URL is never revoked, leaking the Blob for the lifetime of the page/session.

title: Misleading 'missing_backup_codes' message references a non-existent settings feature
body: The string `missing_backup_codes`: "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." implies there is a dedicated settings action to regenerate backup codes. No such feature was added in this PR — the only way to get a fresh set of backup codes is to fully disable and re-enable two-factor authentication. This message will confuse users looking for a 'regenerate backup codes' option in settings that doesn't exist.

title: Backup code verification/consumption is not atomic, allowing reuse
body: In the credentials authorize() callback, the backup code is read from `user.backupCodes`, checked for a match, and only afterwards persisted back with the matched code nulled out (lines 131-156). There is no transaction or row lock between the read and the write. If two concurrent login attempts submit the same backup code before either update completes, both requests will see the code as still valid and both will succeed, effectively allowing a single-use backup code to be used more than once. This defeats the 'exactly once' guarantee stated in the backup_code_instructions translation string.

title: Explicit type="password" prop breaks the password visibility toggle
body: The password field was switched from a plain TextField to the PasswordField component, but an explicit `type="password"` prop is still passed (line 176). PasswordField (packages/ui/components/form/inputs/Input.tsx) computes `type={isPasswordVisible ? "text" : "password"}` and then spreads `{...props}` afterward, so any caller-supplied `type` prop overrides the computed value. Because `type="password"` is passed here, clicking the show/hide-password eye icon in this dialog will never reveal the password, unlike other usages of PasswordField (e.g. in DisableTwoFactorModal) that don't pass a type prop.

title: Backup code login unavailable for identity-provider (SSO) 2FA flow
body: When `totpEmail` is set (the identity-provider/SAML/Google 2FA redirect flow), the footer renders `ExternalTotpFooter` instead of `TwoFactorFooter` (line ~182). `ExternalTotpFooter` has no 'Lost access' control, so `twoFactorLostAccess` can never be toggled to true for these users, and the BackupCode component is effectively unreachable even though it's referenced in the render logic. Users who signed up via Google/SAML, enabled 2FA, and then lose access to their authenticator have no way to use a backup code to regain access through this login path, unlike regular CAL-identity users.

title: No test coverage for logging in with a backup code
body: The PR adds backup-code-based login as a core part of the feature (per the PR description and demo video), but the only e2e coverage added exercises the backup codes display/download/copy UI during setup, not the actual login-with-backup-code flow or disabling 2FA via a backup code. The added comment '// TODO: add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup' explicitly acknowledges this gap. Given this is a security-sensitive account-recovery mechanism, lacking a test that verifies a backup code can actually authenticate a user (and that it is single-use) is a significant gap.

title: Used backup codes are nulled rather than removed, leaving stale entries
body: After a successful backup code login, `backupCodes[index] = null` is used to invalidate the used code instead of filtering it out of the array (line 148). Over repeated logins the encrypted backupCodes JSON blob accumulates null placeholders indefinitely instead of shrinking, which is unnecessary data bloat and makes it harder to reason about how many valid codes remain without decrypting and counting non-null entries.

title: Backup codes download Blob URL is never revoked on modal close/cancel
body: `URL.createObjectURL(textBlob)` is called in handleSetup (line 99) and only revoked the next time `handleSetup` runs again (line 98: `if (backupCodesUrl) URL.revokeObjectURL(backupCodesUrl);`). If the user cancels the dialog or closes it via the 'close'/'enable' flow without starting a new 2FA setup, the object URL is never revoked, leaking the Blob for the lifetime of the page.

title: Backup code consumption is not atomic, allowing a code to be reused
body: The backup-code validation reads the encrypted backupCodes blob, decrypts it, finds a matching code, and then writes back the updated list with that entry nulled out (lines 131-156). This read-decrypt-modify-write sequence is not performed inside a transaction or with any locking/compare-and-swap. If two requests present the same backup code concurrently (e.g. an attacker retrying, or a double form submission), both can read the code as still valid before either write completes, so the same backup code can authenticate twice. This defeats the stated guarantee ("each backup code can be used exactly once") and is a security-relevant data integrity bug.

title: Backup codes stored with reversible symmetric encryption instead of one-way hashing
body: Backup codes are generated in apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts and stored via symmetricEncrypt (reversible) using CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY, the same key used for the TOTP secret.
