Logging routine success at Error level will pollute error logs/alerting dashboards with false positives and generate excessive log volume (each call also logs the full `ids` slice, which can be as large as the configured batch size, e.g. tens of thousands of entries). These should be logged at Debug level and only actual failures logged as errors.

title: Splitting fetch-then-delete-by-ID can delete rows that no longer match the cleanup criteria (potential over-deletion)
body: CleanAnnotations/CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags now fetch a batch of IDs matching the cleanup WHERE clause in one DB session/transaction (fetchIDs), then delete strictly by those IDs in a separate, later DB session/transaction (deleteByIDs). Between the two round-trips, a row that matched the original condition (e.g. an annotation older than the cutoff, or one past the max-count threshold) could be concurrently updated (e.g. via Update(), which changes `epoch`/`epoch_end`/`updated`) so that it no longer satisfies the cleanup criteria, yet it will still be deleted because deleteByIDs only filters on `id IN (...)` without re-validating the original condition. This is the opposite of the under-deletion risk called out in the code comment ("This may under-delete when concurrent inserts happen") — in fact it can over-delete rows that were concurrently modified out of the cleanup scope, which is a data-integrity regression relative to the original single-statement subquery approach that evaluated the condition and deletion atomically.

title: Raw integer concatenation into SQL string instead of parameterized query for SQLite large-batch delete
body: In deleteByIDs, when running on SQLite with a batch size greater than the SQLite parameter limit (999), IDs are concatenated directly into the SQL string via fmt.Sprint/fmt.Sprintf instead of using bound parameters, unlike the normal placeholder path used otherwise. Although the values originate from fetchIDs (trusted int64 database IDs) rather than external user input, this pattern departs from parameterized-query best practice used elsewhere in the same function and is worth tightening (e.g. chunking into sub-batches of <=999 parameterized placeholders) to avoid any future risk if this code path is ever reused with less-trusted input.

title: Async legacy write uses request-derived context that is likely canceled before the goroutine runs
body: In Create (and similarly in Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) the goroutine does `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, ...)` where the outer `ctx` is the context passed into the handler, derived from the original request context. Once the HTTP handler returns (which happens right after this goroutine is spawned, since Create/Update/Delete return immediately), the apiserver typically cancels the request context. Because the goroutine's context is a child of that same request context, it will be cancelled almost immediately, well before the intended 10s timeout, causing `d.Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection` to fail with 'context canceled' on virtually every call. This defeats the entire purpose of Mode 3 (writing to legacy asynchronously 'as a safe measure'), since the legacy write will essentially never complete successfully. The context used in the goroutine should be detached from request cancellation (e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` combined with the timeout, or a fresh background context carrying only the relevant values).

title: Storage Create error incorrectly recorded as a legacy-duration metric
body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration`. This mislabels a unified-storage failure as a legacy-storage failure in metrics, corrupting the dual-writer observability data used to monitor Mode 3 health. The same pattern recurs in Update's error branch (line 129).

title: Storage Update error incorrectly recorded via recordLegacyDuration
body: On the error path after `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`, mislabeling a unified-storage error as a legacy error. This should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`, consistent with the Delete and DeleteCollection error paths.

title: Metric label uses object name instead of resource kind, risking unbounded metric cardinality
body: In Delete, the success path calls `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`, passing the deleted object's `name` where every other call site (and the metric's label semantics) expects `options.Kind`. Besides being inconsistent, feeding a per-object name into a metric label can create unbounded cardinality in Prometheus (a new label value per deleted object), which can bloat metric storage and cause performance/memory issues on the metrics backend.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection error recorded through recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration
body: In the async goroutine in DeleteCollection, after calling `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection`, the result is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)`. Since this measures the Legacy store call, it should use `d.recordLegacyDuration`, not `d.recordStorageDuration`. This causes legacy failures/timings to be misattributed to storage in metrics.

title: Async legacy writes silently drop error details, losing observability on failures
body: The previous (synchronous) implementation logged errors from the Legacy store calls (e.g. `log.Error(errLS, "could not delete from legacy store")`). The new async goroutines in Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection only record a boolean into a duration metric and never log the actual error returned by the Legacy store call. Since these goroutines are fire-and-forget with no caller visibility, failing legacy writes become effectively invisible except through aggregate metrics, making it hard to diagnose data drift between the legacy store and unified storage.

title: Delete uses d.Log instead of the request-scoped logger with additional context fields
body: In Delete, `log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method)` is created, but then `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` stores `d.Log` (without the added name/kind/method values) into the context instead of the local `log` variable. This means any logger retrieved from the context downstream loses the name/kind/method fields that were just added, unlike the Create, Get, List, Update, and DeleteCollection methods which correctly propagate their local `log` variable.

title: Tests do not wait for the async legacy goroutine before asserting, making legacy-write verification unreliable
body: TestMode3_Create (and the Delete/Update/DeleteCollection tests) set up mock expectations on the shared `mock.Mock` for the Legacy store call, but `DualWriterMode3.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection` fire the legacy write in a goroutine and return immediately. The tests assert results and move on without any synchronization (e.g. a WaitGroup or channel) to ensure the goroutine has completed. This means the tests don't actually verify the legacy write happened, and since the same `mock.Mock` instance (`m`) can continue to be accessed by a lingering goroutine after the subtest finishes, running tests with `-race` can surface data races, and leftover goroutines can interact with mocks from a subsequent subtest case.

title: Duplicate go.work.sum entry introduced
body: The diff re-adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod h1:DkxMin+qOh1Fgkxfbt+CUfBqqsCQJMG9op8Os/irBPA=` as a new line even though an identical line already exists immediately above (unchanged context). This creates a duplicate checksum entry, which is a symptom of an unclean dependency sync/rebase and should be cleaned up (e.g. by re-running `go work sync`/`go mod tidy`) rather than merged in with a duplicate line.

title: Async legacy writes derive their timeout context from the (soon-to-be-canceled) request context
body: In Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection, the background goroutine does `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10*time.Second, ...)` where the outer `ctx` is the original request context. In the k8s apiserver/net-http stack, the request context is typically canceled as soon as the HTTP handler returns (which happens right after the main Storage write succeeds and the goroutine is spawned). As a result, the derived child context used for the async Legacy write is very likely already canceled (or about to be) by the time the goroutine runs, causing the 'safety measure' legacy write to fail with context-canceled errors almost every time instead of actually mirroring data to legacy storage. The context passed into the goroutine should be detached from the parent's cancellation (e.g. via `context.WithoutCancel`) before applying the new timeout, while still carrying trace/log values.

title: Async legacy Update uses the raw UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the object actually persisted to Storage
body: Previously, Mode3's Update fetched the old object, resolved `objInfo.UpdatedObject`, and explicitly wrapped the resolved object before writing to Legacy, guaranteeing Legacy received exactly what was written to Storage. The new implementation calls `d.Storage.Update(...)` and then, asynchronously, calls `d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...)` with the same unresolved `objInfo`. Since `objInfo.UpdatedObject` is re-evaluated independently inside Legacy's own Update call (against Legacy's own 'old' object, which can have a different resourceVersion/content than Storage's), the final object written to Legacy can diverge from what Storage has, or the update can fail outright (e.g. on resourceVersion conflict checks), defeating the purpose of the safety-net replication.

title: Storage.Create failure incorrectly recorded via recordLegacyDuration
body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` even though this is a Storage (not Legacy) failure. The success branch correctly calls `d.recordStorageDuration`. This mislabels the dual-writer metrics, making it look like a Legacy error occurred when it was actually a Storage error, corrupting any dashboards/alerts used to gauge readiness for progressing dual-write modes.

title: Delete success metric uses object name instead of resource Kind as the label
body: On success, `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the per-request object `name` where every other call site in this file passes `options.Kind`. This both mislabels the metric (wrong semantic value for the 'kind' parameter) and risks high-cardinality Prometheus labels if `name` is used as a label value, since resource names are unbounded unlike Kind.

title: Storage.Update failure incorrectly recorded via recordLegacyDuration
body: When `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration`, mirroring the same mislabeling bug as in Create. This pollutes dual-write metrics by attributing Storage failures to Legacy.

title: DeleteCollection async legacy call duration recorded via recordStorageDuration
body: Inside the goroutine that calls `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection`, the resulting duration/error is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration`. This mixes Legacy timing/error data into the Storage metric series, making it impossible to accurately monitor Legacy write reliability for DeleteCollection in mode 3.

title: Errors from async Legacy writes are no longer logged
body: In Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection, the background goroutine that performs the Legacy write only records a metric (`d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`) when the Legacy call fails; there is no `log.Error` call anywhere in these goroutines. The previous implementation explicitly logged failures such as 'unable to create object in legacy storage'. Now, failures of the async safety-net write are silent except via metrics, making it much harder to diagnose why Legacy storage has drifted out of sync with Storage.

title: Delete's context logger omits the per-request fields set on `log`
body: In `Delete`, a `log` variable is built with `WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method)`, but the context is updated with `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` (the bare, field-less logger) rather than `log`. Every other method in this file (Create, Get, List, Update, DeleteCollection) correctly injects the enriched `log` into the context. As a result, any code downstream that pulls the logger from context during a Delete call loses the name/kind/method fields, producing inconsistent log output for Delete versus the other operations.

title: Mode3 tests never verify the asynchronous Legacy write actually happens
body: Mode 3's defining new behavior is firing an async write to Legacy storage after a successful Storage write (Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection). None of the updated tests synchronize with or assert on the Legacy mock being invoked (no waitgroup/channel, no `AssertExpectations`/`AssertCalled` on the Legacy mock). Since the goroutine can run after the test function returns, these tests provide no actual coverage of the new async replication behavior and would not catch a regression that broke or removed the Legacy write.

title: New mode3 integration test asserts legacy search results immediately after k8s writes, racing the async legacy replication
body: The 'Do CRUD via k8s (and check that legacy api still works)' subtest (exercised against the newly added mode3 configurations 'with dual write (file, mode 3)' and 'with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)') creates playlists through the k8s/unified API, then immediately queries the legacy `/api/playlists` endpoint and `getFromBothAPIs` (legacy GET) and expects them to already reflect the just-created/updated data. Under Mode3, writes to Legacy storage are explicitly asynchronous ('safe measure' goroutine with up to a 10s timeout), so there is no guarantee the legacy copy has been written by the time these assertions run. This test has no retry/eventual-consistency handling and is likely to be flaky (intermittently failing in CI) specifically for the new mode3 configurations this PR adds.

title: Async legacy writes derive from the request-scoped context, which is canceled once the handler returns
body: In Create (and similarly in Delete line 110, Update line 135, and DeleteCollection line 163), the goroutine that performs the asynchronous Legacy write does `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` using the `ctx` that was passed into the outer method, i.e. the request's context. The outer function returns immediately after the Storage write succeeds (it does not wait for the goroutine), so the HTTP handler completes and the underlying request context is typically canceled by the server right after the response is sent. Because the 10s timeout context is derived from (a child of) that request context, it will also be canceled as soon as the parent is canceled, aborting the legacy write before it has a chance to run or complete. This defeats the entire purpose of Mode 3's 'best effort' async legacy write, since legacy writes will routinely fail with context-canceled errors instead of actually persisting data. A decoupled context (e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` or a fresh context carrying only the needed values) should be used as the parent for the goroutine's timeout context.

title: Storage.Create failure incorrectly recorded as a legacy-storage duration metric
body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. This mislabels a Unified Storage failure as a Legacy Storage failure in the metrics, corrupting the duration/error metrics used to monitor dual-write health. The same bug exists in `Update` (line 129) where a Storage.Update failure is also recorded via `recordLegacyDuration` instead of `recordStorageDuration`.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection result recorded using the Storage duration metric
body: Inside the async goroutine of `DeleteCollection`, after calling `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection`, the result is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration`. This mislabels the legacy-store outcome as a unified-storage outcome, corrupting dual-write metrics that are meant to distinguish storage vs legacy performance/error rates.

title: Delete records object name instead of resource kind as a metric label
body: In `Delete`, the successful-storage-delete metric call is `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`, passing the object's `name` (e.g. "foo") where every other call site in this file passes `options.Kind` (the resource kind, e.g. "playlists"). This introduces an unbounded, high-cardinality label value (one per deleted object name) into the metric instead of the intended bounded resource-kind label, which can blow up metric cardinality in Prometheus and also makes the recorded data inconsistent with the rest of the dual-writer metrics.

title: Delete attaches the un-enriched logger to the context instead of the local contextual logger
body: In `Delete`, `log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method)` is built but then `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` attaches the base `d.Log` (without the name/kind/method values) to the context instead of the enriched `log`. Every other method in this file (Create, Get, List, Update, DeleteCollection) correctly propagates the enriched logger. As a result, any code downstream that pulls the logger via `klog.FromContext(ctx)` during a Delete call loses the name/kind/method structured fields, reducing log traceability specifically for deletes.

title: Async legacy write failures are only recorded as metrics, never logged
body: In the goroutines for Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection, the error returned from the Legacy store call (e.g. `errObjectSt` in Create) is only fed into `recordLegacyDuration`/`recordStorageDuration` as a boolean; it is never logged (e.g. via `log.Error(...)`). Previously (pre-PR) these failures were logged with contextual detail. Since these writes now happen asynchronously and their result is not surfaced to the caller at all, silently dropping the error message removes the only way an operator could discover/debug data divergence between Legacy and Unified storage, beyond a boolean metric increment.

title: Mode3 tests never verify that the asynchronous legacy write actually occurs
body: TestMode3_Create (and similarly TestMode3_Delete, TestMode3_Update, TestMode3_DeleteCollection) set up `m.On("Create"/"Delete"/"Update"/"DeleteCollection", ...)` expectations on the legacy mock, but since the real implementation now fires the legacy write in a goroutine, the test function can return before the goroutine executes. The tests never call `m.AssertExpectations(t)` / `m.AssertCalled(t, ...)` nor synchronize with the goroutine (e.g. via a channel/WaitGroup), so the test will pass whether or not the legacy write ever runs or succeeds. This leaves the core 'asynchronously write to legacy as a safety measure' behavior of Mode 3 effectively untested.

title: Missing double-check after acquiring write lock causes redundant work
body: After acquiring entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock() at line 48, the code does not re-check whether entryPointAssetsCache was already populated by another goroutine that raced to the lock first (and whether cfg.Env != setting.Dev). If multiple goroutines call GetWebAssets concurrently while the cache is still nil (e.g., first requests at startup), each will block on the lock sequentially and then each will redundantly re-read the manifest file (or hit the CDN) and overwrite entryPointAssetsCache again, even though another goroutine already populated it moments earlier. This is a 'thundering herd' / wasted-work issue; the fix correctly removes the data race but does not restore the original single-computation behavior for concurrent cold-cache calls.

title: No test added for the race fix or concurrent-access behavior
body: The PR fixes a data race on entryPointAssetsCache but does not add any test (e.g., a test run with -race exercising concurrent calls to GetWebAssets) to verify the race is actually fixed or to guard against regressions. Without such a test, a future refactor could reintroduce the race undetected by CI.

title: Double-checked locking pattern is incomplete, causing redundant work under concurrent cold-cache access
body: After acquiring the write lock at line 48, the code does not re-check `entryPointAssetsCache` before proceeding to re-read/parse the manifest file. If multiple goroutines call `GetWebAssets` concurrently while the cache is empty (e.g., at startup) and `cfg.Env != setting.Dev`, each goroutine will serialize on the write lock but still redundantly re-read and re-parse the assets manifest (or hit the CDN) instead of reusing the result already computed by the first goroutine. This isn't a correctness bug (the lock does prevent the data race), but it defeats the purpose of caching under concurrent first-access and should re-check `entryPointAssetsCache != nil` right after acquiring the write lock to return early.

title: No test added to verify the data race fix
body: The PR fixes a data race on the global `entryPointAssetsCache` variable by introducing `entryPointAssetsCacheMu`, but no test (e.g., one exercised with `go test -race` under concurrent calls to `GetWebAssets`) was added to validate the fix or guard against regressions. Without such a test, a future refactor could reintroduce the race undetected by CI unless the race detector happens to catch it in another path.

title: No double-check after acquiring write lock leads to redundant work and thundering herd on cache miss
body: After acquiring entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock() (line 48), the code does not re-check whether entryPointAssetsCache was already populated by another goroutine that got the lock first. Every goroutine that passed the initial RLock-based nil check will proceed to recompute the result (reading the manifest file or hitting the CDN) even though another goroutine may have just finished populating the cache. Under concurrent initial access (e.g. many simultaneous requests hitting GetWebAssets before the cache is warm), this causes redundant file reads and, worse, redundant outbound HTTP requests to the CDN in readWebAssetsFromCDN, which is both wasteful and could amplify load on an external CDN endpoint.

title: Write lock held across blocking I/O (file read / HTTP call) serializes all callers
body: The entryPointAssetsCacheMu write lock (acquired at line 48 and released via defer at line 49) is held for the entire duration of readWebAssetsFromFile/readWebAssetsFromCDN, including a network round-trip when a CDN URL is configured. While this does fix the data race, it means every concurrent call to GetWebAssets that misses the cache (or is in Dev mode, which always recomputes) will serialize behind a potentially slow network call, which can increase request latency under load compared to a design that only locks around the shared variable assignment.

title: No regression test added for the data race fix
body: The PR fixes a data race on the global entryPointAssetsCache variable but does not add any test (e.g. a test exercising GetWebAssets concurrently, ideally run with -race) to verify the fix or guard against future regressions. Without such a test, a future refactor could easily reintroduce the race undetected.

title: enableSqlExpressions() is dead code that always returns false regardless of input
body: The function computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then has `if enabled { return false }` followed unconditionally by `return false`. Both branches return false, so the computed `enabled` value is never actually used to determine the result — the function always returns false no matter the feature-toggle state. While this currently achieves the intended 'always disable SQL expressions' behavior, the code reads as if it is still gating on the feature flag, which is misleading. A future maintainer (or an automated 'bug fix' from a linter/refactor) could easily 'simplify' this by flipping the dead branch (e.g. to `return true`) believing they're restoring flag-based behavior, silently re-enabling the vulnerable SQL expressions path. The function should be simplified to explicitly `return false` with a comment explaining this is a deliberate, permanent disablement pending further hardening, rather than leaving confusing unreachable logic tied to the feature flag.

title: No test added verifying SQL expressions are blocked regardless of feature toggle state
body: This PR is a security fix meant to permanently disable SQL Expressions (to close an RCE/LFI vulnerability), but no test was added to pkg/expr covering ReadQuery with QueryTypeSQL for both FlagSqlExpressions enabled and disabled, asserting that an error is always returned. Given the severity of the vulnerability being fixed and the confusing logic in enableSqlExpressions, a regression test is necessary to prevent this security control from being accidentally removed or inverted in a future change.

title: Stub DB implementation always errors, likely breaking existing SQL expression tests not updated in this PR
body: The new DB struct's TablesList, RunCommands, and QueryFramesInto methods unconditionally return 'not implemented' errors, replacing the previously functional github.com/scottlepp/go-duck/duck implementation. If pre-existing tests in pkg/expr (e.g. sql_command_test.go, pkg/expr/sql/parser_test.go) assert successful SQL parsing/execution results, they will now fail since every call returns an error instead of a parsed table list or query result. None of these test files appear in the diff, so it is unclear whether they were removed/adjusted; if they still exist unmodified, CI would break.

title: No documentation update reflecting that SQL Expressions are now permanently non-functional
body: The PR description explicitly states the FlagSqlExpressions feature toggle is left untouched and existing docs that only mention the flag's existence are not updated. However, after this change, enabling the toggle has no effect — SQL Expressions will always fail with 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' (and now also always fail internally via the stubbed DB in pkg/expr/sql/db.go). Users/admins who toggle FlagSqlExpressions on, expecting functionality based on existing docs, will be confused by always-failing behavior with no documentation explaining why. At minimum a brief doc or code comment update is warranted to avoid confusion during the period this feature is dead code.

title: Confusing dead-code logic in enableSqlExpressions makes the security gate fragile
body: The function `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` (note the inverted naming — `enabled` actually means 'feature flag is NOT set') and then has an `if enabled { return false }` followed by an unconditional `return false`. Both branches return `false`, so the function always disables SQL expressions regardless of the feature-flag state — which is presumably the intent (to patch the RCE/LFI vulnerability), but the code reads as if it is supposed to check the flag and enable the feature when set. This is highly confusing: a future maintainer looking at this code will likely 'fix' the apparent dead branch/unused logic, assuming it's a bug, and could inadvertently re-enable the vulnerable SQL-expression execution path. Given this function is the primary gate preventing exploitation of the CVE, it should be a single explicit `return false` with a clear comment explaining why SQL expressions are permanently disabled, not an inverted boolean with unreachable branches.

title: No tests added/updated verifying SQL expressions are now blocked
body: The PR introduces a security-critical change (fully disabling SQL expression execution via `enableSqlExpressions` and stubbing out the SQL engine) but does not add or update any tests in `pkg/expr` to assert that: (1) `ReadQuery` returns the 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' error for `QueryTypeSQL` regardless of feature flag state, and (2) `SQLCommand.Execute`/`NewSQLCommand` fail safely now that `sql.TablesList`/`QueryFramesInto` always return errors. Without such tests, a future refactor could silently reintroduce the vulnerable code path (e.g., by 'fixing' the dead logic in `enableSqlExpressions`) without any test catching the regression.

title: Leftover 'duckDB' variable name contradicts PR's stated goal to remove DuckDB references
body: The PR description states the goal is to 'Remove reference to DuckDB', but `TablesList` still assigns `duckDB := NewInMemoryDB()`, keeping a DuckDB-specific variable name even though the underlying DuckDB dependency (`scottlepp/go-duck`) has been removed and replaced by the stub `DB` struct. This is a minor but visible inconsistency with the PR's own description and could confuse future readers into thinking a DuckDB engine is still in use.

title: Stub error messages ('not implemented') obscure that the feature is intentionally and permanently disabled for security reasons
body: All methods on the new stub `DB` type (`TablesList`, `RunCommands`, `QueryFramesInto`) return a generic `errors.New("not implemented")`. Combined with the feature-flag check that also always disables SQL expressions, this gives operators/support staff no indication that the feature was intentionally and permanently removed due to a security vulnerability (CVE-2024-9264) rather than simply unfinished. This can lead to confusing support tickets or well-meaning future attempts to 'finish implementing' the stub, inadvertently reopening the vulnerability if not accompanied by a code comment or clearer error message explaining the deliberate removal.

title: enableSqlExpressions() has confusing, inverted-looking dead logic that always returns false
No test coverage added to assert SQL expressions remain disabled regardless of feature flag
body: The whole point of this PR is to make `QueryTypeSQL` always fail with 'sqlExpressions is not implemented', including when `FlagSqlExpressions` is toggled on, in order to close CVE-2024-9264. No test was added (or updated) in this diff to lock in that behavior — e.g. a test that enables `FlagSqlExpressions` via a feature-toggle test double and asserts `ReadQuery` still returns an error for `QueryTypeSQL`. Without such a regression test, a future refactor of `enableSqlExpressions` (see the dead/inverted logic noted separately) could silently re-enable the vulnerable code path and nothing in CI would catch it.

title: Stub DB implementation has no tests verifying it always errors
body: `pkg/expr/sql/db.go` replaces the real DuckDB-backed implementation with a stub whose `TablesList`, `RunCommands`, and `QueryFramesInto` methods unconditionally return `errors.New("not implemented")`. This is the second line of defense against the vulnerability (independent of the feature-flag gate in reader.go), but there are no unit tests asserting these methods always fail, nor any test exercising `sql.TablesList`/`SQLCommand.Execute` end-to-end to confirm no code path can execute arbitrary SQL/filesystem access anymore. Given this is a direct mitigation for a critical CVE, this logic should be explicitly covered by tests rather than relying on incidental callers getting an error.

title: Error message is misleading about why SQL expressions are unavailable
body: The error returned when `QueryTypeSQL` is requested — `"sqlExpressions is not implemented"` — is factually inaccurate: SQL expressions are implemented but intentionally disabled for security reasons (per the PR description, this is a hard-disable to close CVE-2024-9264), and the feature flag `FlagSqlExpressions` still exists and can be toggled with no effect. Returning a message implying the feature doesn't exist yet (rather than that it is disabled) can confuse users/operators who previously relied on it, and conflicts with any surviving documentation that still describes the flag as functional.

title: NewResourceServer now blocks synchronously on full index build during startup
body: NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) directly in the constructor, which in turn calls searchSupport.init(), which builds the search index for every namespace returned by GetResourceStats before returning. Previously this cost was paid lazily inside the first gRPC call (with its own deadline); now it is paid unconditionally at construction time with no timeout. If NewResourceServer is invoked anywhere besides the dedicated storage-server module (e.g. during normal Grafana app-server bootstrap for unified storage), overall process startup can block for an arbitrarily long time while every namespace's index is built, and any failure during that build (e.g. a transient DB error) now causes server construction itself to fail outright rather than only a particular RPC. The PR description explicitly raises this as an open question ('What could this break?') but does not resolve it — there is no bound on index-build time nor any fallback/async option.

title: Stop() no longer gates any RPC after shutdown
body: Previously every RPC handler (Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search, History, Origin, IsHealthy, PutBlob, GetBlob) called s.Init(ctx) first; since Init used sync.Once, after Stop() set s.initErr to "service is stopping"/"service is stopped", those calls to Init(ctx) would surface that error to callers. This PR removes the s.Init(ctx) calls from all RPC handlers, so the initErr set in Stop() is now write-only dead state — no code path reads it anymore. As a result, after Stop() is called, in-flight or new RPCs will no longer get a clean 'service is stopping/stopped' error; they will instead proceed against a server whose background context (s.ctx) has already been cancelled (e.g. broadcaster/watch loops torn down), leading to inconsistent or silent failures instead of a clear error to the caller.

title: Removing the full-function lock in BuildIndex allows concurrent duplicate builds for the same key
body: BuildIndex previously held cacheMu.Lock() for its entire duration, which incidentally serialized all builds, including two concurrent calls for the same NamespacedResource key. The new code only takes cacheMu when writing the final result into b.cache (near the end of the function), so two goroutines can now run BuildIndex concurrently for the same key (this is a real possibility because searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex in search.go checks GetIndex and calls build() without any per-key lock, a gap already flagged by a TODO comment in that file). Concurrent builds for the same key can both call bleve.New()/bleve.NewMemOnly() and write documents independently, then race to overwrite b.cache[key], silently discarding one index's work or, for file-backed indexes sharing the same directory, causing on-disk index corruption/contention.

title: TotalDocs() reads the cache map without holding cacheMu
body: TotalDocs() iterates over b.cache directly without acquiring cacheMu (not even RLock), while BuildIndex now performs genuinely concurrent writes to b.cache under its own lock (enabled by the finer-grained locking introduced in this PR, combined with the worker pool in searchSupport.init that builds multiple namespaces in parallel). Because real concurrent map writes now happen during startup/runtime, a concurrent call to TotalDocs() (e.g. from a metrics scrape or another caller) racing with a BuildIndex write to the same map can trigger Go's 'concurrent map read and map write' fatal error, crashing the process. This hazard existed before but is made materially worse by the increased real concurrency this PR introduces for cache writes.

title: Postgres integration test disabled instead of fixed, losing coverage for the exact startup-init change
body: This PR adds a skip for dbType == "postgres" in TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer with only the comment 'test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally.' No root cause or follow-up ticket is referenced. Since this PR's core change is moving unified-storage initialization into server startup (which can now block or fail at NewResourceServer time), disabling exactly the integration test that exercises a real storage-server startup against postgres removes the only regression coverage for that scenario, rather than investigating why it fails under the new init-at-startup behavior.

title: Resource server construction now blocks indefinitely with no timeout on index build
body: NewResourceServer() calls `s.Init(ctx)` synchronously before returning, and `ctx` here is derived from `context.WithCancel(context.Background())` with no deadline. If building the search index (or any lifecycle hook) takes a very long time or hangs (e.g. due to a slow/unavailable DB), NewResourceServer will never return, blocking the whole process startup indefinitely with no way to time out or recover. Previously this work happened lazily on the first gRPC call, so a slow index build at least allowed the server/process to start and expose health endpoints; now the entire service construction is gated on this unbounded operation. This directly matches the question raised in the PR description about what could break by making init eager, and should be addressed with a startup timeout/cancellation strategy or by running Init in the background with a readiness gate.

title: Postgres integration test skipped without root-causing a likely regression from this PR
body: The test `TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer` is now skipped for postgres with the comment 'test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally.' This test exercises exactly the module-server startup path that this PR changes (ResourceServer now blocks on Init() synchronously at construction instead of lazily). It's very plausible the test now fails/times out because startup takes longer or behaves differently with the new eager initialization, and the fix should be to address the underlying timing/behavior rather than silently skip the only integration test covering this startup path for a specific backend.

title: Data race on shared `err` variable across concurrent goroutines in search index init
body: Inside `searchSupport.init()`, multiple goroutines spawned via `group.Go(...)` all read and write the single shared `err` variable declared outside the loop (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and then `return err`. Because the assignment and the `return` are two separate statements, one goroutine's assignment can be overwritten by another goroutine's assignment before its own `return err` executes, causing errgroup to receive the wrong goroutine's result (potentially losing a real build error, or reporting an unrelated one). This is also a plain data race flagged by `go test -race`. This bug is now far more consequential because `init()` is invoked synchronously during `NewResourceServer`, directly gating process startup — an incorrect/lost error here can mask a failed index build or incorrectly fail startup.

title: Unsynchronized increment of totalBatchesIndexed across goroutines
body: `totalBatchesIndexed++` is incremented inside each `group.Go` closure, i.e. concurrently from multiple goroutines (bounded by `initWorkers`), with no mutex or atomic operation. This is a data race that can produce an incorrect count used in the subsequent `span.AddEvent` call, and will be flagged by Go's race detector. Given this PR's goal of increasing indexing concurrency, this latent race becomes more likely to actually manifest/be hit by the race detector in CI.

title: Removing the whole-function lock in BuildIndex allows duplicate concurrent builds for the same key
body: Previously `BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for its entire duration, which (as a side effect) serialized all builds, including duplicate builds for the same `NamespacedResource` key. Now the lock is only taken when writing the final result into `b.cache` (lines 137-139). If two callers (e.g. two concurrent requests to `getOrCreateIndex`) trigger a build for the same key before either completes, both will independently build a full index (including, for file-backed indexes, opening/writing to the same directory via `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` at line 98), and only the last one to finish 'wins' the cache slot — the other built index is silently discarded without being closed, leaking memory/file handles, and the two concurrent file-based bleve.New calls on the same directory can also conflict/fail. There is no key-level locking (the existing TODO at the top of getOrCreateIndex acknowledges this), so this PR's removal of the broader lock increases the chance of this duplicate-build race actually occurring under load.

title: TotalDocs() reads the cache map without holding cacheMu, racing with concurrent writers
body: `TotalDocs()` iterates over `b.cache` (line 146) without acquiring `cacheMu` (not even RLock), while `BuildIndex` and other paths write to the same map under `cacheMu.Lock()`. This is an unsynchronized concurrent map access, which can produce a 'concurrent map read and map write' runtime panic if `TotalDocs()` is called (e.g., from metrics scraping or from `searchSupport.init()`'s log line at the end of initialization) while another goroutine is still building/caching an index. The PR's stated goal of enabling more concurrent index building increases the odds of this race being hit in practice.

title: Removing per-call Init() checks breaks shutdown gating
body: Previously every RPC handler (Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search, History, Origin, IsHealthy, PutBlob, GetBlob) called s.Init(ctx) before doing work. Because Init() uses sync.Once, after the server was already initialized this call cheaply returned the cached s.initErr, which Stop() deliberately sets to "service is stopping"/"service is stopped" to make in-flight and new RPCs fail once shutdown begins. This PR removes all of those Init() calls from the handlers (since init now happens once synchronously in NewResourceServer), but Stop() still mutates s.initErr and nothing reads it anymore. As a result, after Stop() is called, handlers (including IsHealthy, used for liveness/readiness) no longer reflect the stopped state and will keep processing requests normally until the underlying resources themselves start failing, defeating the graceful-shutdown mechanism that existed before this change.

title: Removing the backend-wide lock around BuildIndex allows duplicate/corrupting concurrent builds for the same key
body: Previously bleveBackend.BuildIndex held cacheMu.Lock() for the entire function (including running the builder callback that populates the index), which serialized all builds. This PR removes that lock and only takes cacheMu briefly at the very end to insert into b.cache. getOrCreateIndex() in search.go checks GetIndex() for a cached entry and, if absent, calls build()/BuildIndex() -- there is no synchronization preventing two concurrent callers for the *same* NamespacedResource key from both seeing a cache miss and both calling BuildIndex concurrently. For disk-backed indexes (size > FileThreshold), two goroutines would call bleve.New(dir, mapper) on the same directory concurrently, which can fail or corrupt index data; for memory-backed indexes, the loser's bleve.Index is simply overwritten in the cache map and never closed, leaking resources. The intended optimization (finer-grained locking) should still serialize builds per-key (e.g., per-key mutex/singleflight) rather than removing the serialization entirely.

title: Synchronous, unbounded Init() in NewResourceServer can block startup indefinitely
body: NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) synchronously before returning, and the ctx passed in is derived from context.Background() with no deadline. Init() runs s.search.init(ctx), which builds the full search index over every namespace found via GetResourceStats — the exact operation the PR says 'takes too long' inside a gRPC call's context. Moving this work earlier removes the gRPC-context-cancellation symptom, but now the entire module/server construction blocks for however long indexing takes, with no timeout or cancellation path exposed to the caller. In orchestrated environments this can cause startup/readiness probes to fail or force restarts before initialization completes, and there's no way for an operator to bound or cancel this work.

title: Unsynchronized shared variables mutated by concurrent errgroup goroutines
body: In searchSupport.init(), totalBatchesIndexed++ and the outer err variable (declared from `stats, err := s.storage.GetResourceStats(...)`) are both written inside group.Go closures that run concurrently (errgroup limited to s.initWorkers, which can be >1). Both totalBatchesIndexed and err are shared, non-atomic variables written from multiple goroutines without any mutex/atomic, which is a data race (will be flagged by `go test -race`) and can produce an incorrect/non-deterministic final totalBatchesIndexed count used in the trace span attribute, and a lost/overwritten err value. Given this PR's explicit goal of increasing indexing concurrency, this race becomes more likely to actually manifest and should be fixed (e.g., use atomic counters and let errgroup.Wait() be the sole source of the returned error).

title: Swapped order of watcher init and search init can drop events in HA setups
body: Init() previously started the broadcaster watcher (initWatcher) before building the search index; this PR swaps the order so the (potentially long-running) search.init() runs first and initWatcher() runs only after it completes. The main broadcaster's starting resource version is determined at the moment initWatcher() calls WatchWriteEvents, so any WriteEvents produced by other instances during the lengthy index-build window (explicitly a supported HA scenario per StorageBackend's WatchWriteEvents doc: 'For HA setups, this will be more events than the local WriteEvent above!') will not be observed by this instance's broadcaster and will be missed by clients subscribing via Watch() once the server comes up. This should be verified/tested, since it directly affects correctness of the watch stream in multi-replica deployments.

title: Postgres integration test silently skipped with vague TODO
body: The newly added skip for the `postgres` dbType disables the only integration test that exercises module server startup with the storage server target against Postgres, with just a TODO comment ('test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally.') and no linked issue or root-cause explanation. Given this PR changes resource-server initialization timing (synchronous init at startup) which this very test is meant to validate, losing Postgres coverage reduces confidence that the new startup behavior works correctly on that backend.

title: Call to isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments does not match any method signature
body: UsernameForm.authenticate() calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with zero arguments, but the only method with that name is `protected boolean isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` defined in the parent class UsernamePasswordForm. There is no no-arg overload defined anywhere in the class hierarchy shown in this PR. This will not compile ("cannot find symbol"), breaking the build. The call should almost certainly be `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`.

title: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() inverts the condition that gates filling WebAuthn form attributes, breaking passkeys on fresh (non-reauth) logins
body: The new helper `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` requires `user != null` to return true. It replaces the previous explicit check `context.getUser() == null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()` in both `authenticate()` (line ~115) and `challenge(context, error, field)` (line ~137), which used to call `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` precisely when there was NO pre-selected user (the normal, first-time login/conditional-UI discovery flow). With the new helper requiring `user != null`, `fillContextForm` is now only invoked when a user is already set (i.e., during re-authentication), and it is never invoked for the standard first-time login case where `context.getUser()` is null. This removes the WebAuthn challenge/RP-id/conditional-UI attributes from the rendered login form for all normal (non-reauthentication) logins, which would break the passwordless/passkeys discoverable-credential login flow entirely for the common case and contradicts existing tests (e.g. webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey, passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey) that expect the webauthn form to be present on a fresh login page where no user has yet been identified.

title: Unused import left after replacing assertThrows(NoSuchElementException) assertions
body: The import `org.openqa.selenium.NoSuchElementException` is retained even though both usages of `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, ...)` were replaced by `MatcherAssert.assertThat(..., notNullValue())` assertions (lines ~200 and ~211 area in the diff). The import is now dead code; depending on the project's checkstyle configuration this may fail the build or is at least confusing dead code that should be removed.

title: Call to isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with wrong arity will not compile
body: UsernameForm.authenticate() calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments, but the only method with that name defined in the parent class UsernamePasswordForm is `protected boolean isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)`, which requires a UserModel parameter. There is no no-arg overload anywhere in the diff. This is a method signature mismatch that will fail to compile, breaking the entire build (and therefore all the new tests added in this PR as well).

title: fillContextForm no longer called for anonymous/new login, breaking normal passkeys conditional UI
body: The new `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` helper returns true only when `user != null`. In `authenticate()`, the call `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())` is now used (unconditionally, replacing the previous `else`-branch-only check) to decide whether to call `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)`. Previously, this fill happened precisely when `context.getUser() == null` (i.e. during a fresh/anonymous login, to populate the conditional-UI webauthn attributes on the initial challenge). With the new condition requiring a non-null user, the webauthn/conditional-UI attributes will no longer be set for normal (non-reauthentication) logins where no user has been identified yet, which is the primary passkeys use case. This directly contradicts the assertions in the already-existing/updated tests (e.g. PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest.passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey) that still expect the webauthn form element to be present on the initial, unauthenticated login page.

title: challenge(context, error, field) stops refilling webauthn data for anonymous users on error
body: The overridden `challenge(AuthenticationFlowContext, String, String)` previously called `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` when `context.getUser() == null` (i.e. to keep the webauthn/passkeys UI available on the error page shown after an invalid username or an invalid password attempt where the user was never set in the auth context). It now uses `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`, which requires `user != null` and will therefore be false in exactly that anonymous-user error scenario. As a result, after a failed login attempt where the user isn't set in the auth context (e.g. wrong password for a non-reauthenticated session, where context.setUser() is only invoked on success), the webauthn conditional-UI attributes are no longer populated on the retry/error page, even though this scenario is explicitly asserted to still show the webauthn form in the updated test `PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest.passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey`.

title: Unused import left after replacing assertThrows usages
body: The import `org.openqa.selenium.NoSuchElementException` is no longer used anywhere in this file after the two `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, ...)` calls in `passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey` were replaced with `MatcherAssert.assertThat(..., Matchers.notNullValue())`. This leaves a dead/unused import that should be removed.

title: Call to isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments does not match the method signature
body: UsernameForm.authenticate() calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments, but the only method with that name, defined in the parent class UsernamePasswordForm, is `protected boolean isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` which requires a UserModel parameter. There is no no-arg overload anywhere in the diff. This will not compile, breaking the build for this module (and any module that depends on it).

title: fillContextForm gated on isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()) incorrectly requires a non-null context user
body: In authenticate(), `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` is now only invoked when `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())` is true, and that helper explicitly requires `user != null`. Previously the fill was done precisely when the user was NOT yet selected (the normal, non-reauthentication login case), guarded only by `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()`. With the new gating, on a fresh/initial login (context.getUser() == null) the webauthn/passkeys conditional-UI attributes (challenge, rpId, ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI, etc.) will never be populated, so the webauthn form will not be rendered for the ordinary login flow. The same regression occurs in the overridden `challenge(context, error, field)` method a few lines below (previously filled only when `context.getUser() == null`, now filled only when it's non-null), which is invoked from badPasswordHandler/testInvalidUser while context.getUser() is still unset for non-reauthentication flows (context.setUser() is only called later, inside validateUser(), after password validation succeeds). As a result, retrying login via passkeys after an invalid username or invalid password in a normal (non-reauthentication) flow will lose the webauthn UI, contradicting the explanatory comment "setup webauthn data when passkeys enabled" which says nothing about requiring an already-identified user.

title: Unused import left after replacing assertThrows assertions
body: The import `org.openqa.selenium.NoSuchElementException` is no longer used anywhere in the file after the two `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, ...)` calls in passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey were replaced with `MatcherAssert.assertThat(..., Matchers.notNullValue())`. This leaves a dead import that may trigger checkstyle/unused-import failures in CI.

title: Unnecessarily widened visibility of internal auth-note constant to public
body: USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH was widened from protected to public solely so that AuthenticatorUtils (a different package) could reference it via static import. This exposes an internal implementation-detail constant as part of the public API surface of an abstract authenticator class, increasing the risk of external code depending on it and constraining future refactors. A narrower approach (e.g., exposing it through a dedicated accessor method, or moving the shared logic into AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator itself) would avoid broadening the public API.

title: remove() now unconditionally calls the backend delegate, defeating the cache
body: In remove(String alias), `IdentityProviderModel storedIdp = idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias);` is now executed unconditionally before checking cache validity. Previously, the delegate (JPA) lookup only happened when `isInvalid(cacheKey)` was true; when the cache entry was valid, the code used the already-cached `CachedIdentityProvider` via `realmCache.getCache().get(cacheKey, ...)` without hitting the backend. With this change, every call to remove() now performs an extra backend lookup even in the common case where the idp is already cached and valid, which is a performance regression that partially defeats the purpose of this caching layer. The fetched `storedIdp` is only actually needed for the `registerIDPLoginInvalidation` call and for the (already-existing) invalid-cache branch; it should be computed lazily/only when needed instead of unconditionally up front.

title: Cleanup uses a hard-coded wrong alias, so created IdPs are never removed
body: In the new testCacheIDPForLogin test, cleanups are registered as `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove);` (lines 381 and 425), using the literal string "alias" instead of the actual alias that was just created (e.g. "idp-alias-" + i, or "idp-alias-20"). As a result, the cleanup callback attempts to delete a non-existent identity provider named "alias" instead of the ones created by the test, so the 20+ identity providers created in this test are never actually removed after the test runs. This can leak test data across test executions/tests in the suite (the same organization "orga"/"orgb" are reused by other tests in this class) and may also cause cleanup-time failures (404 on delete) that mask the real test result.

title: remove() now always performs an extra storage lookup
body: In remove(), `IdentityProviderModel storedIdp = idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias);` is now executed unconditionally before checking `isInvalid(cacheKey)`. Previously, `idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)` was only invoked inside the `isInvalid(cacheKey)` branch; when the cache entry was valid, the code relied solely on the already-cached `CachedIdentityProvider` without hitting the underlying storage. With this change, every call to remove() now performs an unconditional read against the delegate storage provider (JPA), even when a valid cached copy is already available, just to determine whether to invalidate the login caches. This is a measurable regression on a hot path (IDP removal) and could have been avoided by reusing the already-fetched `cached.getIdentityProvider()` when present.

title: Login cache invalidation is always applied to all three fetch modes, causing cache thrashing for multi-organization realms
body: registerIDPLoginInvalidation() and registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() always invalidate the cache keys for all three FetchMode values (REALM_ONLY, ORG_ONLY, ALL) whenever any IDP crosses login-eligibility, regardless of which organization (if any) is actually affected. Unlike getByOrganization(), which caches/invalidates per specific organization id (cacheKeyOrgId), the getForLogin() cache stores results for ALL organizations' queries inside a single IdentityProviderListQuery keyed only by realm+mode. This means a single IDP update unrelated to a particular organization wipes out cached login results for every organization in the realm, causing unnecessary cache misses and re-queries in realms with many organizations.

title: Single cache entry per mode can accumulate unbounded per-organization result sets
body: getForLogin() caches results under a single key per FetchMode (cacheKeyForLogin), with per-organization result sets stored inside the same IdentityProviderListQuery object (keyed internally by organizationId as the search key). In realms with many organizations, repeated getForLogin(ORG_ONLY/ALL, orgId) calls for different organizations will keep adding entries to the same cached object indefinitely, since there is no per-org eviction — only a full invalidation of the whole mode-level entry. This can lead to unbounded growth of a single cache entry in multi-tenant/many-organization deployments.

title: Asymmetric isEnabled() evaluation between original and updated model in login invalidation check
body: registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate(original, updated) is called from update() with `original` being the result of getById(), which wraps the model through createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel (its isEnabled() depends dynamically on the linked organization's current enabled state). The `updated` parameter, however, is the raw model passed into update() and uses the static isEnabled() field value. When the organization is currently disabled, getLoginPredicate().test(original) and getLoginPredicate().test(updated) can diverge purely due to this wrapping difference rather than due to an actual change in the IDP, leading to unnecessary cache invalidations. While this does not appear to cause stale caches (it only triggers extra invalidation), the asymmetry is inconsistent and could mask more serious issues if the wrapping logic changes in the future.

title: Public static predicate semantics changed without versioning/compat note
body: LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate() is a public static method on a server-spi interface, and its behavior has been changed to additionally require that organization-linked IDPs have BROKER_PUBLIC=true. Any existing external code (custom providers, extensions) that already calls this public API expecting the old semantics (only ENABLED/LINK_ONLY/HIDE_ON_LOGIN checks) will now silently get different results. Since server-spi is a public extension point, this behavior change should be called out explicitly (e.g., in release notes or javadoc) as it is a backward-incompatible semantic change to a public method, not just an internal implementation detail.

title: No test coverage for the isEnabled() re-check fix introduced in the login IDP bean
body: This PR adds `idp.isEnabled()` re-checks in searchForIdentityProviders() for the ORG_ONLY and ALL branches, specifically to handle the case where a cached IDP model is wrapped and its effective isEnabled() depends on live organization enablement status that may differ from what was cached. No test was added (in OrganizationCacheTest or elsewhere) that exercises this specific scenario, e.g. disabling an organization after the login IDP list has been cached and verifying that disabled-org IDPs are filtered out of the rendered login page bean. Without such a test, a regression in this filtering logic (e.g. someone removing the re-check) would not be caught.

title: Test cleanup registers wrong (literal) alias, leaking created identity providers
body: In the new testCacheIDPForLogin test, the cleanup callback is registered as `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove);` instead of using the actual alias that was just created (e.g. "idp-alias-" + i). Because the literal string "alias" never corresponds to a real identity provider, the cleanup lookup will fail (404) and the 20 identity providers created in the loop are never actually removed after the test runs. The same bug is repeated at line 425 for the 21st identity provider ("idp-alias-20"). This leaves stale identity providers in the test realm, which can pollute subsequent tests in the same class (counts/assertions depending on realm state) and makes cleanup unreliable.

title: Second occurrence of wrong cleanup alias for idp-alias-20
body: Same issue as above: `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove);` uses the literal string "alias" rather than the alias of the identity provider actually created ("idp-alias-20"), so this provider is never cleaned up after the test, leaving residual data.

title: remove() now always performs an extra unconditional storage lookup
body: `remove(String alias)` now unconditionally calls `idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)` at the top of the method to obtain `storedIdp`, even in the branch where the entry is already present in cache (`cached != null`, lines 105-108) and `cached.getIdentityProvider()` is used instead for the invalidation logic. Previously, the delegate lookup only happened when the cache entry was invalid. This adds an unnecessary database round-trip to every call to remove(), even when cache data is readily available, which is a performance regression on a path that previously avoided redundant delegate queries.

title: Login cache invalidation always clears all FetchModes regardless of relevance
body: registerIDPLoginInvalidation() and registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() both iterate over all FetchMode values and invalidate cacheKeyForLogin for REALM_ONLY, ORG_ONLY and ALL whenever any login-eligibility-affecting change occurs, even if the change only affects one mode (e.g., a realm-only IDP toggling enabled state cannot possibly affect the ORG_ONLY cache, yet that cache is invalidated and must be rebuilt anyway). This causes unnecessary cache rebuilds for unrelated fetch modes on every qualifying create/update/remove operation, which could be avoided by selecting the specific FetchMode(s) impacted by the change.

title: Silent resolution of multiple CryptoProviders removes a useful safety check
body: Previously detectProvider() threw an IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was found on the classpath, which caught classpath/packaging misconfigurations early and loudly. Now it silently sorts by order() and picks the highest, logging the ignored providers only at debug level (which is typically filtered out in production). Worse, DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order()==200, so if two of these full-featured providers accidentally end up on the same classpath (e.g. a packaging mistake bundling both the default and elytron crypto modules), the chosen provider now depends on ServiceLoader iteration order (effectively classpath/jar ordering), which is not guaranteed to be stable across environments. This can silently select the wrong crypto backend instead of failing fast, which is a real risk for a security-sensitive subsystem.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider() does not actually return the BouncyCastle provider
body: The CryptoProvider interface documents getBouncyCastleProvider() as returning the BouncyCastle (or FIPS) security provider. This implementation instead returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), i.e. whatever provider happens to back the JVM's default keystore type (e.g. the SUN or PKCS12 provider), which has nothing to do with BouncyCastle. Any caller that relies on this method to obtain the actual BC provider (e.g. to reference its name or algorithms) will get a misleading/incorrect result when this is the active CryptoProvider.

title: Dead code creates and discards ASN1Encoder instances
body: In concatenatedRSToASN1DER, the lines `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` construct encoders, write into them, and then discard the result without using it anywhere. This is leftover/dead code that wastes cycles and allocations on every signature conversion and should be removed.

title: Single shared EC key reused for ES256/ES384/ES512 tests does not match expected curve sizes
body: The test generates a single EC key pair with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` (no curve specified, defaulting typically to a 256-bit curve) and reuses it for testES256, testES384 and testES512. For ES384 and ES512, the real signature r/s values will actually be ~32 bytes (P-256 sized), not the 48/66 bytes implied by algorithm.getSignatureLength(). The round-trip only passes because integerToBytes() zero-pads/truncates to the expected length, masking the fact that the conversion logic is never exercised with genuinely 384-bit or 521-bit curve signatures. This reduces the test's value and could hide bugs that only manifest with real P-384/P-521 keys.

title: New mandatory CryptoIntegration.init() call changes AuthzClient.create() behavior/contract
body: AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now unconditionally calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()), which throws IllegalStateException if no CryptoProvider implementation can be located via ServiceLoader on that classloader. Previously AuthzClient did not require any CryptoProvider to be present at all. Consumers that shade/repackage the authz-client jar in a way that drops or fails to merge META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider, or that load AuthzClient with a restrictive classloader, will now get a hard failure on client creation where they previously worked fine. This is a backward-incompatible behavior change that should be called out/tested explicitly.

title: readInteger/readLength does not guard against indefinite-length (0x80) DER encoding producing negative array size
body: readLength() returns -1 for the indefinite-length form (0x80) but this is not validated by callers. In readInteger(), `int length = readLength();` followed by `byte[] bytes = read(length);` will attempt `new byte[-1]` if length is -1, throwing an unchecked NegativeArraySizeException instead of a handled IOException. Since this decoder parses externally supplied DER-encoded signature bytes (attacker-influenced JWT/token signatures), malformed input can trigger an unexpected unchecked exception instead of a predictable IOException, which callers may not be prepared to catch.

title: New abstract method order() breaks binary/source compatibility for existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: CryptoProvider is a public SPI interface. Adding `int order();` as a plain abstract method (no default implementation) means any third-party or external implementation of CryptoProvider that does not implement order() will fail to compile/load (AbstractMethodError at runtime for compiled classes). Since CryptoProvider is loaded via ServiceLoader and is explicitly designed to allow multiple implementations on the classpath (per this PR's own rationale), existing external providers will break. A default method (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) would preserve backward compatibility while still allowing the new ordering feature.

title: Multiple-provider conflict is now silently resolved instead of failing fast
body: Previously, detecting more than one CryptoProvider on the classpath threw an IllegalStateException, forcing the user to fix a misconfigured/ambiguous classpath. Now the code silently picks the provider with the highest order() value and only logs the ignored ones at debug level (which is often disabled in production). If two providers happen to have the same order() value (e.g. DefaultCryptoProvider and FIPS1402Provider both return 200), the selection becomes non-deterministic (dependent on ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order), which can silently select the wrong crypto backend (e.g., non-FIPS instead of FIPS) without any error, which is a serious regression for environments that require strict crypto provider guarantees.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider() does not actually return a BouncyCastle provider
body: The implementation returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, i.e. whatever JCA provider backs the JVM's default keystore type (typically the JDK's built-in provider, not BouncyCastle). This contradicts the documented contract of the method ("BouncyCastle security provider. Can be either non-FIPS or FIPS based provider") and is misleading for any caller (e.g. via BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER in the common module) that assumes the returned provider name/behavior matches a BC-compatible provider. This could cause obscure NoSuchProviderException or incorrect algorithm resolution wherever generic code paths (not overridden with UnsupportedOperationException in this class) rely on this provider.

title: Dead/leftover code in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
body: Lines 114-115 create two throwaway ASN1Encoder instances (`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);`) whose results are discarded and have no effect on the method's output - the actual DER sequence is built again right afterwards on lines 117-121. This is clearly leftover debugging/refactoring code that should be removed; it wastes allocations and makes the method harder to review/maintain.

title: Inconsistent use of format.name() instead of format.toString() for KeyStore lookup
body: getKeyStore() calls `KeyStore.getInstance(format.name())`, whereas every other CryptoProvider implementation in this PR (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider) consistently uses `format.toString()`. If KeystoreUtil.KeystoreFormat overrides toString() to return a value different from the enum constant name() (which is a common pattern for such enums, e.g. to map to the exact JCA keystore type string), this implementation will request a different/incorrect keystore type than intended, potentially throwing KeyStoreException at runtime for formats where name() and toString() diverge.

title: No test coverage for the new provider-ordering/selection logic
body: The detectProvider() method's behavior changed significantly: it now sorts providers by order() and silently picks the highest, logging the rest. There is no unit test added in this PR verifying that, given multiple CryptoProvider implementations with different order() values on the classpath, the correct (highest-order) one is selected, nor a test for the tie-break behavior when two providers share the same order(). This is core logic for the stated goal of the PR (allowing multiple CryptoProvider instances) and should be covered by a dedicated test.

title: Removed fail-fast check for multiple CryptoProviders on classpath, now silently resolved with non-deterministic tie-breaking
body: Previously detectProvider() threw an IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was found on the classloader, which protected against misconfiguration (e.g. accidentally having both a FIPS and a non-FIPS provider on the classpath, which has real compliance/security implications). Now the providers are simply sorted by order() and the highest-order one is silently picked, logging the rest only at debug level (logger.debugf, line ~69). If two providers happen to have the same order() value (e.g. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all use order()==200), the choice between them depends on ServiceLoader enumeration order, which is unspecified and can vary across JVMs/classloaders. This can silently select a FIPS or non-FIPS provider unintentionally, with no error raised and only a debug-level log that is typically not visible in production, defeating the original safety check.

title: New abstract method order() breaks binary/source compatibility for existing CryptoProvider implementors
body: The interface CryptoProvider now declares `int order();` as an abstract method with no default implementation. Any existing third-party or custom implementation of CryptoProvider (e.g. custom SPI providers maintained outside this PR) will fail to compile/load until updated to implement order(). Since CryptoProvider is a public SPI loaded via ServiceLoader, this is a breaking API change that should either provide a default method (e.g. default int order() { return 0; }) or be called out explicitly as a breaking change in release notes.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider() does not return a BouncyCastle provider, violating the interface contract
body: CryptoProvider#getBouncyCastleProvider() is documented as returning 'BouncyCastle security provider. Can be either non-FIPS or FIPS based provider'. This implementation instead returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is simply whatever JCA provider implements the platform default keystore type (e.g. the JDK's built-in PKCS12 provider), not BouncyCastle at all. Any caller relying on the documented contract (e.g. to register BC-specific algorithms, or pass 'BC' as a provider name) will get unexpected/incorrect behavior rather than a clear UnsupportedOperationException like the rest of the unimplemented methods in this class.

title: Dead code: throwaway ASN1Encoder instances created and discarded
body: In concatenatedRSToASN1DER(), lines 114-115 create two separate ASN1Encoder instances and call write(rBigInteger)/write(sBigInteger) on them, but the results are never used (new encoders are created again a few lines later to actually build the returned bytes). This is dead code left over from development that performs unnecessary work on every signature conversion and is confusing to maintain; it should be removed.

title: AuthzClient.create() triggers global static CryptoIntegration initialization as a side effect
body: AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()). CryptoIntegration keeps a process-wide static singleton (cryptoProvider) that, once set, cannot be changed except via explicit setProvider(). If AuthzClient.create() is invoked before the hosting application performs its own CryptoIntegration.init() (e.g. when authz-client is embedded inside a larger application/server that shares the same classloader or class-loading hierarchy), the singleton can get permanently locked to whatever CryptoProvider is visible to AuthzClient's classloader at that moment — potentially the minimal AuthzClientCryptoProvider, which throws UnsupportedOperationException for almost every operation except order(), getBouncyCastleProvider(), getEcdsaCryptoProvider() and getKeyStore(). Any later, unrelated code path in the same classloader that needs other crypto features (PEM utils, certificate utils, key generation, etc.) would then fail with UnsupportedOperationException instead of using the application's intended full-featured provider.

title: No test coverage for the new multi-provider ordering/tie-breaking logic
body: This PR introduces a significant behavioral change to CryptoIntegration.detectProvider(): instead of failing when multiple CryptoProvider implementations are found, it now sorts by CryptoProvider.order() and silently picks the highest. No unit test is added anywhere in the diff to verify this sorting logic, the tie-breaking behavior when two providers share the same order value, or that a provider is correctly ignored/logged. Given this is core logic that determines which cryptographic backend the whole application uses, it should have direct test coverage.

title: getClientsWithPermission only matches the 'all-clients' meta-resource, not individual client resources
body: getClientsWithPermission() calls resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...) to find resources of type 'Clients'. However, the per-client resources created in AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource() (resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId())) never call resource.setType(...); only the single meta resource representing the whole resource type ('Clients') gets its type set during AdminPermissionsSchema.init().
