As a result, findByType will only ever return that one meta resource, so getClientsWithPermission() cannot discover individual per-client grants and would at best add the literal resource name 'Clients' (not an actual client id) to the result set when an 'all clients' permission is granted. Any caller relying on this method to filter/list clients a caller has permission for (e.g. client listing endpoints) will silently miss clients granted via individual resource permissions.

title: getResourceName() was not updated to handle the new CLIENTS resource type
body: getResourceName() has special-case handling that maps a 'Users' resource to a friendly display ('All users' for the all-resource meta entry, or the username for a specific user resource). No equivalent branch was added for the new CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE/CLIENTS resource type introduced by this PR. For permissions scoped to 'Clients' it falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), which is never set when the resource is created in getOrCreateResource() (displayName isn't populated there), and there's no 'All clients' label for the all-resource meta entry either. This results in blank/unclear resource names being shown for Client-type permissions (e.g. in the admin console or REST responses), unlike the equivalent User-type permissions.

title: Potential NullPointerException when the 'all-clients' meta resource is missing
body: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), when the per-client resource is null, the code falls back to AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) to get the 'all-clients' resource, then immediately calls authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) without checking whether that call returned null. getResourceTypeResource() returns null if the resourceType is unknown or if resourceStore.findByName() doesn't find the meta resource (e.g. the admin-permissions client's resource server hasn't been fully initialized). In that case findByResource is invoked with a null resource, which is likely to throw a NullPointerException instead of gracefully denying the permission.

title: Role/Client/Group removal cleanup gated only by legacy (V1) feature flag, not V2
body: The provider event listener that disables permissions on RoleRemovedEvent/ClientRemovedEvent/GroupRemovedEvent is now wrapped in `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))`, checking only the legacy V1 feature. When only ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled (V1 disabled), this block never executes, so no cleanup/disable logic runs at all when a client, role, or group is removed under the V2 fine-grained authorization model. Since the corresponding V2 permission classes (e.g. ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled) throw UnsupportedOperationException, this avoids a crash, but it also means there is no equivalent cleanup path for V2 schema data (e.g. orphaned per-client/per-user resources or policies referencing a removed client, role, or group), risking stale/orphaned authorization data over time.

title: New MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE scope added to Clients schema has no test coverage
body: AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS now includes the MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE scope (used by ClientPermissionsV2.canMapClientScopeRoles), but PermissionClientTest only imports and exercises MAP_ROLES and MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE (see testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient). There is no test validating that granting/denying MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE actually controls the ability to map client-scope roles for a client, leaving this new capability unverified.

title: Several ClientPermissionEvaluator methods unconditionally throw UnsupportedOperationException in V2
body: canExchangeTo, exchangeToPermission, mapRolesPermission, mapRolesClientScopePermission, mapRolesCompositePermission, managePermission, configurePermission, viewPermission, isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, resource, and getPermissions are all overridden to throw UnsupportedOperationException('Not supported in V2'). If any existing call site (e.g. token exchange flow calling canExchangeTo, or admin console code retrieving a client's permission map via getPermissions/resource) is invoked while ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, this will propagate as an unchecked RuntimeException resulting in a 500 Internal Server Error instead of a controlled 403/empty response, rather than failing gracefully.

title: New CLIENTS resource type/scopes are never created for realms that already have an admin-permissions client
body: init() only performs the full setup (creating scopes and the per-resource-type 'all-resource' resources, including the newly added CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE scopes CONFIGURE/MANAGE/MAP_ROLES/MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE/MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE/VIEW and the 'Clients' resource) when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is null; otherwise it returns immediately (lines 226-228). Any realm that already enabled ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 before this PR already has a non-null admin permissions client, so after upgrading, init() will no-op for that realm and the new 'Clients' scopes/resource will never be created. As a result the whole new Clients permission feature is silently non-functional (and, combined with the missing null-check described elsewhere, can throw NPEs) for any realm that adopted V2 admin permissions prior to this change. There is no migration logic added to retrofit the new resource type/scopes into already-provisioned admin-permission resource servers.

title: NullPointerException risk when the 'Clients' all-resource type resource is missing
body: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), when no per-client resource exists, the code falls back to AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and immediately calls authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) without checking whether the returned resource is null. getResourceTypeResource can legitimately return null (e.g. unsupported schema, or the 'Clients' resource not yet created for pre-existing admin-permission realms, see the related init() migration gap). Passing a null resource into findByResource is very likely to throw an NPE in the underlying store implementation, causing permission evaluation (canManage, canConfigure, canView, canMapRoles, etc. for a specific client) to fail with an unhandled exception instead of gracefully denying access.

title: Cleanup listener for removed clients/roles/groups is now skipped entirely when only V2 admin permissions are enabled
body: The ProviderEventListener body (handling RoleContainerModel.RoleRemovedEvent, ClientModel.ClientRemovedEvent, GroupModel.GroupRemovedEvent) is now wrapped in `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))`, i.e. it only runs for the legacy V1 feature. Previously it ran unconditionally. This change appears necessary because, under V2, ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled/isPermissionsEnabled throw UnsupportedOperationException, which would otherwise crash on every client removal when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled. However, by gating the whole handler behind the V1 flag instead of adding an equivalent V2 cleanup path, no corresponding cleanup of V2 authorization resources happens when a client, role, or group is deleted while only V2 is enabled. This leaves orphaned 'Clients'/'Users' resources and related policies referencing deleted entities in the authorization store, a data-integrity regression with no compensating implementation added in this PR.

title: getClientsWithPermission queries resources by type, but per-client resources are created without their type being set
body: getClientsWithPermission() calls resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...) to enumerate per-client resources. However, AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource() (server-spi-private/.../AdminPermissionsSchema.java) creates the individual client resource via resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId()) and only calls resource.updateScopes(...); it never calls resource.setType(resourceType). Only the pre-created 'all-resource' resources built in init() have their type explicitly set. Unless the resource type is populated some other way, findByType will not match the individual per-client resources, so getClientsWithPermission() would return an incomplete/incorrect result (at best only the 'all-clients' aggregate resource, whose name is the literal string 'Clients', not a real client id).

title: canList() javadoc references QUERY_USERS role which is unrelated to listing clients
body: The newly added javadoc for canList() states: 'Or if the caller has at least one of the AdminRoles#QUERY_CLIENTS or AdminRoles#QUERY_USERS roles.' This appears to be a copy/paste mistake from the analogous Users permission evaluator documentation; QUERY_USERS has no obvious relation to listing clients and is likely to mislead readers about the actual authorization requirements for this method.

title: Roles created in testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient are not cleaned up
body: This test creates a client role ('myclient-role') and a sub-role ('myclient-subRole') directly via the admin API but, unlike similar tests elsewhere in this PR (e.g. UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest.testMapRoles, which registers realm.cleanup().add(...) for the created role), it registers no cleanup. If the managed realm/test fixtures are reused across test methods in this class, the created roles and their composite relationship will persist beyond the test, which can affect subsequent tests or leave stale data.

title: Role/client/group removal cleanup listener now gated by the V1 feature flag only
body: The ProviderEventListener body that disables permissions for a removed role/client/group (calling management(...).roles()/.clients()/.groups().setPermissionsEnabled(..., false)) used to run unconditionally. This PR wraps the whole block in `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))`, i.e. it now only runs when the (older) V1 fine-grained-authz feature is enabled. The `management(...)` factory itself selects V1 vs V2 based on `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2`, so if a deployment only enables the V2 feature (without V1), this cleanup listener will be skipped entirely and permission/resource cleanup for deleted roles/clients/groups will no longer happen for V2 permissions. This change is unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (adding Clients resource type) and is not covered by any new test.

title: getClientsWithPermission cannot find per-client resources and leaks the catch-all resource name
body: `getClientsWithPermission` looks up resources via `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)`, which filters on the resource's `type` attribute. However, `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` (used to create the per-client resource when a scoped permission is created for a specific client) never calls `resource.setType(...)`; only the catch-all 'all-resource' entry created in `AdminPermissionsSchema.init()` has its type set to `CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE`. As a result: (1) individual per-client resources will never be returned by `findByType`, so clients with a specific scoped permission are silently omitted from the result set, and (2) if the catch-all 'Clients' resource itself has the scope granted, its resource name ('Clients') is incorrectly added to the returned set as if it were a client id. Any caller treating the returned set as a list of client ids will get wrong/empty results.

title: No migration path to add the new Clients resource/scopes for realms that already enabled admin permissions
body: `init()` only creates the schema resources/scopes (including the newly added 'Clients' resource type and its scopes) when `realm.getAdminPermissionsClient()` is null, i.e. only the very first time admin permissions are enabled for a realm. For any realm that already had admin fine-grained permissions (V2) enabled before this change was deployed, `init()` returns immediately and the 'Clients' resource/scope set is never created. Consequently, `ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission(...)` will call `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(..., CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE)`, which returns null because the resource doesn't exist, and that null is then passed into `authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource)`, risking an NPE (or at least silently returning no permissions) for any existing realm upgrading to this version. There is no migration/upgrade step shown to retrofit existing admin-permission-enabled realms with the new resource type.

title: Missing tests for client-scope role mapping and for all-vs-single resource interaction
body: There is no test exercising `canMapClientScopeRoles`/`MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE` for clients (only MAP_ROLES and MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE are covered in PermissionClientTest.testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient), and no test for `getClientsWithPermission`, nor for the interaction between an 'all clients' grant and a resource that already exists for a specific client due to an unrelated scope permission (the analogous scenario is tested for Users in UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest.testImpersonatePermission but has no Clients counterpart). Given the fallback logic in `hasPermission` only triggers when no per-client resource exists at all, this combination is an important but untested code path.

title: RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE value changed from 4 to 3, repurposing 4 for FEATURE_DISABLED
body: The constant RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE is changed from 4 to 3, and the previously-used value 4 is now repurposed to mean FEATURE_DISABLED. Anyone who has already scripted around the previous exit-code contract (where 4 meant 'recreate upgrade required') will now get a different, incompatible meaning for the same exit code. Even though the docs for this preview tool already described code 3 for recreate-required (meaning the running implementation and docs were previously inconsistent), this PR silently changes the runtime behavior of an already-usable CLI command. Given the documentation explicitly instructs consumers to rely on the exit code contract ('they should rely only on the exit code of the check command'), this is a user-facing behavioral change that should be called out clearly in release notes / changelog, not just silently fixed.

title: Feature key hardcoded as string literal instead of using the Feature enum
body: printFeatureDisabled() hardcodes the string 'rolling-updates' in the error message instead of referencing Profile.Feature.ROLLING_UPDATES.getKey(). If the feature's enum name or generated key is ever changed, this message will silently become inconsistent with the actual required feature flag, misleading users on how to enable the feature.

title: testFeatureNotEnabled does not assert the exit code
body: The new test testFeatureNotEnabled only asserts the printed error message but never verifies that the command exits with CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED (4), which is the actual contract this PR introduces/relies on (also documented in update-compatibility.adoc). Without an exit-code assertion, a regression that changes or removes the picocli.exit(CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED) call in UpdateCompatibilityCheck/UpdateCompatibilityMetadata would not be caught by this test.

title: CAUTION block wording overstates scope of failure
body: The CAUTION note states 'the feature rolling-updates must be enabled. Otherwise, the {project_name} Operator will fail,' which reads as if the entire Operator stops working without this feature. Based on the accompanying NOTE and the UpgradeTest.java changes (where the default/null update-strategy path does not enable the rolling-updates feature and still works, mimicking old behavior), the feature is only required when the update.strategy field is explicitly configured. The CAUTION text should clarify that only configuring spec.update.strategy requires the feature, to avoid readers believing they must always enable the preview feature flag for the Operator to function at all.

title: Exit code semantics changed for an already-shipped preview CLI tool
body: RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE is changed from 4 to 3, and the previously-unused value 4 is now repurposed for the new FEATURE_DISABLED constant. The update-compatibility command (and its exit codes) were already documented/shipped as a preview feature before this PR. Any automation or CI scripts already built against the prior exit code (4 == recreate required) will now get a different, misleading result: exit code 4 now means 'feature disabled' instead of 'recreate needed', and exit code 3 now means what 4 used to mean. This silently changes the contract of a tool meant to be consumed by scripts/pipelines, which is explicitly called out in the docs as a GitOps-friendly, scriptable tool.

title: New FEATURE_DISABLED exit code is not asserted
body: testFeatureNotEnabled only checks the printed error message via cliResult.assertError(...) but never asserts cliResult.exitCode() == CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED (4). Since this PR also changes which numeric exit code is used for 'recreate' vs 'feature disabled' (3 vs 4), a future regression that swaps these codes again would not be caught by this test even though the exit code is the primary machine-readable contract of this command per the documentation.

title: No negative test for rolling-updates feature being disabled on the operator
body: The updated test only exercises the scenario where the 'rolling-updates' feature is enabled via FeatureSpec. The newly-added documentation (docs/guides/operator/advanced-configuration.adoc) explicitly states in a CAUTION block that 'While on preview stage, the feature rolling-updates must be enabled. Otherwise, the {project_name} Operator will fail.' No test in this PR verifies that the Operator actually rejects/fails when update.strategy is configured but the feature is not enabled, so this documented behavior is unverified and could silently regress or never have been correctly implemented.

title: Reassigning exit code 4 silently changes CLI contract
body: RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE was changed from 4 to 3, and the previously-used value 4 is now repurposed as FEATURE_DISABLED. Any existing automation/scripts built against the earlier shipped behavior (where exit code 4 meant 'rolling upgrade not possible, recreate required') will now silently misinterpret a 'feature disabled' result as 'recreate required', or vice versa. Even though update-compatibility is a preview feature, this is a behavior-changing contract break for the exit codes documented in docs/guides/server/update-compatibility.adoc and should be called out explicitly (e.g., in release notes) rather than silently swapped as a side effect of this PR.

title: Missing test for feature-disabled path on the 'check' subcommand
body: testFeatureNotEnabled only exercises UpdateCompatibilityMetadata.NAME without the rolling-updates feature enabled. The same feature-gating logic was also added to UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run() (in UpdateCompatibilityCheck.java), but there is no corresponding test verifying that running 'check' without the feature enabled prints the expected error and exits with CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED. This leaves part of the newly introduced gating logic untested.

title: ROLLING_UPDATES feature auto-enables with the generic 'preview' profile
body: ROLLING_UPDATES is declared as Type.PREVIEW rather than Type.PREVIEW_DISABLED_BY_DEFAULT. Per Profile.isEnabledByDefault(), any Type.PREVIEW feature is automatically turned on whenever the server-wide profile is set to PREVIEW (e.g. via a general '--profile=preview' or env var toggle), without the operator/administrator explicitly opting into 'rolling-updates'. Since this flag changes default update/rollback behavior for update-compatibility commands and the Operator's update strategy, silently enabling it alongside unrelated preview features could cause unexpected behavior changes for users who only intended to try other preview features.

title: Operator enforcement of rolling-updates feature flag not verifiable in this change set
body: The new CAUTION block states 'While on preview stage, the feature rolling-updates must be enabled. Otherwise, the {project_name} Operator will fail.' However, none of the files included in this PR implement an operator-side check that fails when the update stanza is used without the feature enabled (only the CLI update-compatibility commands gained such a check in AbstractUpdatesCommand/UpdateCompatibilityCheck/Metadata). If the enforcement logic lives in a file not touched by this PR, that's fine, but reviewers should confirm the Operator actually performs this validation; otherwise the documentation overstates the current behavior and the CR update stanza being used with the feature disabled could silently fall back to unintended behavior instead of failing as documented.

title: canManage() for groups treats VIEW permission as MANAGE permission
body: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() (no-arg), when the admin role check fails, the code calls `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)` instead of checking only the MANAGE scope. This means any admin who was granted only a VIEW permission on the 'all-groups' (or an individual group that falls back to the all-groups resource) will pass `canManage()`. This method gates mutating operations such as `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup()` (`auth.groups().requireManage()`), so a user with read-only access to groups can create/manage groups - a privilege escalation. Compare with `GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(GroupModel group)` which correctly checks only `AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE`, and with `UserPermissionEvaluator#canManage()`'s javadoc which only mentions MANAGE. The added javadoc on `GroupPermissionEvaluator#canManage()` documents this VIEW/MANAGE behavior as intentional, which is misleading and should be corrected along with the implementation.

title: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() uses Resource's internal id instead of the group id
body: In `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()`, the iteration does `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, groupResource -> { if (hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...)) { granted.add(groupResource.getId()); } })`. However, per `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource`/`resolveGroup`, the actual group id is stored as the resource's *name*, not its (randomly generated) *id*. `hasPermission(groupId, ...)` subsequently does `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)`, so passing `groupResource.getId()` will never find the per-group resource and will always fall back to the 'all-groups' schema resource evaluation. Consequently: (1) per-group permissions are effectively ignored for this method, with results only reflecting whether an 'all-groups' permission exists for any of the requested scopes, and (2) the returned Set contains internal resource IDs rather than real group IDs. These IDs are used verbatim by callers such as `UsersResource.getUsersCount(realm, search, groupIds)` and session attribute `UserModel.GROUPS`, so downstream filtering by group membership is broken (counts/filters will not match real groups). It should use `groupResource.getName()` both for the permission check and for the value added to the result set.

title: Removed global-view short-circuit causes a per-group authorization evaluation
body: Previously `canViewGlobal = groupsEvaluator.canView()` was computed once and used as `g -> canViewGlobal || groupsEvaluator.canView(g)`, so when the caller has a blanket view permission, no further per-group evaluation was needed. The change to `stream.filter(groupsEvaluator::canView)` removes this optimization: for FGAP V2 (`GroupPermissionsV2.canView(GroupModel)`), each call performs a fresh policy-engine evaluation (`hasPermission(group.getId(), VIEW, MANAGE)`) per group instead of reusing a single global result, which can significantly degrade performance for realms with many groups when the admin's visibility is granted at the all-groups level rather than via a role.

title: Removed global-view short-circuit in getSubGroups causes a per-group authorization evaluation
body: Similar to GroupsResource.getGroups, `getSubGroups` previously hoisted `canViewGlobal = auth.groups().canView()` out of the filter loop (`g -> canViewGlobal || auth.groups().canView(g)`), but now uses `.filter(auth.groups()::canView)` directly. Under FGAP V2, this forces a separate policy evaluation for every subgroup instead of computing the global permission once, which is a performance regression for groups with many subgroups when the caller only holds a blanket (all-groups) view permission rather than a role.

title: No negative test verifying VIEW-only permission does not grant manage capability
body: `testManageAllGroups()` only verifies that granting the MANAGE scope allows group creation/management; there is no test asserting that granting only the VIEW scope at the all-groups (or per-group) level does NOT allow create/update/delete operations. Such a test would have caught the bug in GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() where VIEW permission is mistakenly treated as sufficient for MANAGE-gated operations like creating top-level groups.

title: Tests only exercise a single group, hiding getGroupIdsWithViewPermission correctness issues
body: The membership-based tests (testCanViewUserByViewGroupMembers / testCanViewUserByManageGroupMembers) only create a single group with a single permission. Because `GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` incorrectly falls back to an 'all-groups' evaluation for every resource it iterates (see separate finding), a scenario with multiple groups - one with a scoped permission and one without - would be needed to detect that the method does not correctly restrict visibility to only the permitted group, and that the returned IDs are not valid group IDs usable by callers such as `getUsersCount`.

title: canManage() for Groups grants management rights with only VIEW scope
body: GroupPermissionsV2#canManage() (no-arg) calls hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE) - exactly the same call used by canManage()'s sibling canView(). This means a caller who was only granted the VIEW scope on the all-groups ('Groups') resource (and not MANAGE) will have canManage() return true. Since GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup() and other mutating endpoints call auth.groups().requireManage(), a user with view-only permission on groups can create/modify top-level groups, which is a privilege escalation. Compare with canManage(GroupModel) in the same file which correctly only checks AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE. The no-arg canManage() should only check the MANAGE scope, not VIEW+MANAGE.

title: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() uses Resource.getId() instead of Resource.getName() when looking up/collecting group IDs
body: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission(), the lambda passed to resourceStore.findByType(server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...) receives Resource objects whose 'name' field holds the actual Group ID (per AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource/resolveGroup, which creates the resource with name=group.getId()). The code instead uses groupResource.getId() (the Resource entity's own internal id) both as the key passed into hasPermission(groupId, ...) - which does resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId) - and as the value added to the 'granted' set. Because the Resource's internal id generally does not equal the group id used as the resource name, the findByName lookup fails for every resource, hasPermission() falls back to checking only the 'all-groups' permission (which is usually absent in the per-group-permission scenario), and the returned set either stays empty or (worse) contains bogus resource IDs rather than real group IDs. This breaks group-scoped user visibility/search (UsersResource/BruteForceUsersResource rely on these IDs to filter users by group membership), and should make the newly added GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest#testCanViewUserByViewGroupMembers/testCanViewUserByManageGroupMembers tests fail or behave incorrectly. The fix is to use groupResource.getName() instead of groupResource.getId() in both places.

title: getResourceName() not extended for the new Groups resource type
body: getResourceName() special-cases USERS_RESOURCE_TYPE to return a friendly label ('All users') for the all-users resource and the username for individual user resources, but no equivalent branch was added for GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE even though this PR introduces Groups as a full resource type with the same 'all-resource vs individual resource (named by id)' pattern. As a result, scope permissions for groups will fall through to resource.getDisplayName(), which for group resources is just the raw group id/UUID rather than a readable group name or an 'All groups' label, unlike the symmetric handling added for Users.

title: Per-subgroup canView() re-evaluation replaces a cached global check
body: getSubGroups() previously computed `boolean canViewGlobal = auth.groups().canView();` once and used `.filter(g -> canViewGlobal || auth.groups().canView(g))`, so when the caller already has global view rights, no further permission evaluation was performed per subgroup. The change to `.filter(auth.groups()::canView)` calls canView(GroupModel) for every subgroup, and that method internally re-invokes canView() (role check, and for V2 FGAP a full authorization policy evaluation) for every single element. For realms with many subgroups and FGAP V2 enabled, this turns one policy evaluation into N policy evaluations per request, which is a real performance regression. The same pattern was also introduced in GroupsResource.getGroups().

title: Public utility method removed without deprecation
body: The public static method `ModelToRepresentation.searchGroupModelsByAttributes(KeycloakSession, RealmModel, Map<String,String>, Integer, Integer)` was removed entirely (its one-line body was simply inlined into GroupsResource). Since this is a public static method on a widely-used utility class, any external code (custom providers/extensions) calling it directly will fail to compile/link against the new version. If this method is intended to be internal-only, it should at least be deprecated before removal rather than removed outright in the same change.

title: canManage() grants management rights to callers that only have VIEW scope on groups
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() uses the resource's internal id instead of the group's id, breaking per-group view filtering
body: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission(), for each group-type Resource found, the code calls hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...) and adds groupResource.getId() to the granted set. However, resources created for groups via AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource() store the actual GroupModel id in resource.getName() (see resolveGroup()), not in resource.getId() (which is the authorization store's own generated identifier for the Resource entity). All other methods in this class (canView(GroupModel), canManage(GroupModel), canViewMembers, canManageMembers, canManageMembership) correctly pass group.getId() which matches resource.getName(). Because hasPermission()'s internal lookup does resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId), passing the resource's own id instead of its name will almost never find the resource, so permission checks for individual groups silently fail and fall back to the (usually absent) all-groups permission. Additionally, even where hasPermission did succeed, the method would return the wrong identifiers (resource ids, not group ids) in the resulting Set<String>. Since this set is used by UsersResource/BruteForceUsersResource to filter the user search by group membership (session.setAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS, groupIds)), real group ids never show up there, so admins granted per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions will not see any users through this path, defeating the feature added by this PR (the exact scenario covered by GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest#testCanViewUserByViewGroupMembers / testCanViewUserByManageGroupMembers).

title: No negative test ensures VIEW-only group permission cannot perform management actions
body: testManageAllGroups() only exercises the case where the policy is granted the MANAGE scope and verifies group creation/management succeeds. There is no test that grants only the VIEW scope for all-groups (or a specific group) and asserts that management actions (create group, add child, map roles) are forbidden. Given the canManage() bug in GroupPermissionsV2 (treats VIEW as sufficient for MANAGE), such a negative test would have caught the privilege-escalation regression before merge.

title: getResourceName() has no special-cased display for Groups (or Clients) resource type
body: getResourceName() special-cases USERS_RESOURCE_TYPE to resolve a friendly name ("All users" or the username) for display purposes (e.g. in the admin console permission UI). No equivalent handling was added for the newly introduced GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE (or for CLIENTS), so for group-scoped permissions the method falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), which for individually-scoped group permissions is the raw group UUID (the resource name) rather than a human-readable group name/path. This is inconsistent with the Users handling added in the same method and will show opaque IDs instead of group names wherever this helper is used to render permission resource names.

title: Fragile string-based resolution of the English reference file
body: The English counterpart file is located by doing a plain string replace on the absolute path (`resources-community`→`resources`, then `_<locale>.properties`→`_en.properties`). This assumes every verified properties file lives in a `resources`/`resources-community` theme tree with a sibling `_en.properties` file following exactly this naming convention. If a file doesn't match this pattern (e.g. is not itself under one of these two trees, has a differently-formed locale suffix, or has no English counterpart at all), `new FileInputStream(englishFile)` will throw `FileNotFoundException`, which is wrapped in a `RuntimeException` (see line 78-79) instead of a clear Maven error. This makes the verifier brittle to any directory/naming variation and produces a confusing stack trace rather than an actionable build failure.

title: Unchecked RuntimeException bypasses the MojoExecutionException contract
body: verify() declares `throws MojoExecutionException` and only catches `IOException` around the call to `verifySafeHtml()`. However, `verifySafeHtml()` wraps any IOException it encounters (e.g. missing English file, line 70 and 78-79) in an unchecked `RuntimeException`, which is not caught by the `catch (IOException e)` in `verify()`. As a result, any failure while reading the referenced English file propagates out of `verify()` as a raw RuntimeException, bypassing the plugin's intended error-reporting path and surfacing as an unhandled exception in the Maven build instead of a clean, actionable error message.

title: Hard-coded, non-extensible whitelist for MessageFormat choice/placeholder exceptions
body: normalizeValue() special-cases only four specific keys (`templateHelp`, `optimizeLookupHelp`, keys starting with `linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit`, and `error-invalid-multivalued-size`) to strip angle-bracket placeholders or MessageFormat `{n,choice,...}` syntax that would otherwise be mistaken for HTML by the sanitizer. Any future message key that introduces similar `{n,choice,...}` syntax or literal `<...>` placeholder text (as several locale files in this very PR needed, e.g. `error-invalid-multivalued-size` in multiple languages) will not be covered by this list and will cause false 'Illegal HTML' failures until someone manually extends this hard-coded list. There is no generic handling of MessageFormat choice syntax across all keys, only for the enumerated ones.

title: No positive-path tests for the new HTML/anchor sanitizer
body:
All four new/updated tests (`verifyIllegalHtmlTagDetected`, `verifyNoHtmlAllowed`, `verifyNoChangedAnchors`, and the duplicate-key test) only assert that violations are correctly detected. There is no test confirming that a translation containing legitimate HTML matching the English source (e.g. matching ``/``/`

` tags in both English and translation) passes verification without any findings. Given the complexity of the anchor-matching and choice-format normalization logic in `VerifyMessageProperties`, lacking a 'happy path' regression test risks silently breaking valid translations in the future without any test failing.

title: New dependency versions hard-coded instead of using property placeholders
body: The newly added `owasp-java-html-sanitizer` (20240325.1) and `commons-text` (1.13.0) dependencies have their versions hard-coded inline, while every other dependency in this pom (maven-plugin-api, maven-plugin-tools, etc.) uses a `<properties>`-defined version variable. This is inconsistent with the existing convention in the file and makes future version bumps/dependency management (e.g. via a BOM) harder to track centrally.

title: i18next placeholder syntax broken by Java-style MessageFormat/ChoiceFormat substitution
body: This file is consumed by the React account-ui app via react-i18next, which requires double-curly-brace interpolation syntax (`{{0}}`). The change replaces `Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).` with `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.`, which uses single braces and Java's MessageFormat ChoiceFormat syntax. i18next will not interpret `{0}` as a variable and has no understanding of `{2,choice,...}`, so this message will render literally/unsubstituted (or broken) in the Account Console UI instead of being correctly interpolated. The same regression is applied to the admin-ui translation file.

title: i18next placeholder syntax broken in admin-ui translations
body: Same issue as in account-ui: `error-invalid-multivalued-size=Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).` was changed to `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.`. This file is consumed by the React admin-ui through react-i18next, which uses `{{var}}` double-brace syntax, not Java MessageFormat/ChoiceFormat. The new text will not be correctly interpolated in the Admin Console, showing raw/unsubstituted template text to users.

title: Lithuanian translation replaced with Italian text
body: The key `totpStep1` for the Lithuanian locale was changed from a valid (if HTML-containing) Lithuanian sentence to `Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:`, which is Italian, not Lithuanian. This appears to be a copy/paste mistake made while stripping disallowed anchor tags from the translation, resulting in Lithuanian users seeing Italian text instead of their own language.

title: Lithuanian login translation replaced with Italian text
body: The key `loginTotpStep1` for the Lithuanian login theme was changed to `Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:`, which is Italian text, not a Lithuanian translation. This is the same mistake as in the account theme's `messages_lt.properties` and will show Lithuanian users an Italian sentence on the TOTP setup screen.

title: verifySafeHtml throws unchecked RuntimeException instead of the declared MojoExecutionException
body: verify() declares `throws MojoExecutionException` and only catches IOException from the duplicate-key check, but verifySafeHtml() wraps its own IOExceptions (reading the file or the derived English reference file) in `RuntimeException`. These RuntimeExceptions are not caught anywhere in verify(), so they propagate uncaught out of the public API, producing an unhandled exception/raw stack trace during the Maven build instead of the clean MojoExecutionException the method contract promises, and aborting the whole verification run rather than reporting it as a verification failure for that file.

title: Fragile, unguarded derivation of the English reference file path
body: The English counterpart file path is derived purely via two chained `String.replaceAll` calls on the absolute path (`resources-community`->`resources`, and the locale suffix ->`_en.properties`). If this heuristic fails to produce an existing file (e.g. non-standard directory layouts, or a locale file whose English source doesn't live where the heuristic expects), the subsequent `new FileInputStream(englishFile)` throws an IOException that is converted into an uncaught RuntimeException (see other finding), crashing the whole verification run instead of reporting a specific, actionable error for that file.

title: Anchor-tag comparison assumes identical ordering between translation and English source
body: santizeAnchors() walks through ``/`` matches in the translated value and the English value in lockstep (sequential `find()` calls), requiring the Nth anchor tag in the translation to equal the Nth anchor tag in English. Translations that legitimately reorder anchor tags (common due to different grammar/word order) will trigger a false 'Didn't find anchor tag' verification failure even though the same tags are present, just in a different order, causing legitimate translations to fail CI/build verification.

title: HTML detection regex misses uppercase and closing tags
body: `HTML_TAGS = Pattern.compile("<[a-z]+[^>]*>")` only matches lowercase opening tags. English source strings whose only HTML markers are closing tags (e.g. ``) or use uppercase tag names will be judged as not containing HTML by containsHtml(), causing the stricter POLICY_NO_HTML to be applied to translations even when the English source itself is HTML-bearing, which can produce confusing or incorrect verification results.

title: No tests for normalizeValue special-case branches or the happy-path (valid translation) scenario
body: normalizeValue() contains several non-trivial special-case branches (templateHelp's `CLAIM.<NAME>` allowance, optimizeLookupHelp's `<Extensions>` allowance, linkExpirationFormatter/error-invalid-multivalued-size ChoiceFormat stripping, and email RTL style stripping), none of which are covered by any test. There is also no test confirming that a well-formed translation containing legitimate allowed HTML/anchors passes verification without reporting any messages, so regressions in these code paths (e.g. the i18next-breaking change found in account-ui/admin-ui files) would not be caught by this test suite.

title: ICU MessageFormat choice syntax injected into i18next (double-brace) translation file
body: The value for 'error-invalid-multivalued-size' was changed from 'Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).' to 'Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.'. Every other key in this file (and the whole account-ui/admin-ui message bundle) uses i18next's double-curly-brace interpolation syntax ({{0}}) and i18next pluralization suffixes (e.g. resourceSharedWith_one/_zero/_other), not Java's single-brace MessageFormat/ChoiceFormat. react-i18next does not interpret '{0,choice,...}' syntax, so the UI will render the literal unprocessed string instead of a correctly pluralized sentence. This appears to be the Java-theme fix (which is appropriate for FreeMarker/MessageFormat-based themes) mistakenly applied to the JS UI translation bundle as well.

title: Same ICU choice-format regression applied to Admin UI i18next messages
body: error-invalid-multivalued-size was changed from the i18next double-brace form 'Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).' to a Java ChoiceFormat string 'Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.'. This file feeds the React admin console (i18next), which uses {{var}} interpolation and _one/_other plural key suffixes, not inline ChoiceFormat syntax. The new string will be displayed verbatim to admins instead of being properly interpolated/pluralized, breaking this specific validation error message in the Admin Console UI.

title: Lithuanian translation replaced with Italian text
body: The fix for the illegal-HTML content in 'totpStep1' replaced the Lithuanian sentence with 'Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:', which is Italian, not Lithuanian. Lithuanian-locale users will now see Italian text for this instruction. The same incorrect replacement text appears in themes/src/main/resources-community/theme/base/login/messages/messages_lt.properties for 'loginTotpStep1'.

title: Lithuanian login translation replaced with Italian text
body: loginTotpStep1 was changed to 'Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:' which is Italian, not Lithuanian, when removing the disallowed anchor tags. This is a content/locale regression introduced while fixing the HTML sanitization issue; the replacement text should be a correct Lithuanian translation.

title: Simplified Chinese (zh_CN) file populated with Traditional Chinese text
body: totpStep1 was changed to '在您的手機上安裝以下應用程式之一：', which uses Traditional Chinese characters (手機, 安裝, 應用程式) inappropriate for a zh_CN (Simplified Chinese) locale file. Users of the Simplified Chinese locale will see Traditional Chinese characters mixed into otherwise Simplified Chinese text.

title: Missing/unreadable English reference file crashes the whole build instead of reporting a validation error
body: verifySafeHtml() computes the path of the English reference file via a brittle string-replace heuristic (replacing "resources-community" with "resources" and the locale suffix with "_en.properties"), then wraps any IOException from reading it in an unchecked RuntimeException (lines 76-80). Because verify() only catches IOException, this RuntimeException propagates uncaught out of verify(), aborting the whole Maven build with a raw stack trace instead of producing a MojoExecutionException or an entry in the returned messages list. Since theme-verifier-maven-plugin is packaged as a general-purpose plugin, any theme/module whose directory layout doesn't match this exact convention (or that lacks an '_en' counterpart) will crash the build rather than fail gracefully with an actionable message.

title: No tests cover the hardcoded per-key normalization exceptions
body: normalizeValue() hardcodes special handling for specific keys ('templateHelp', 'optimizeLookupHelp', and keys starting with 'linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit' or equal to 'error-invalid-multivalued-size') to avoid false-positive HTML/illegal-tag detections caused by legitimate '<NAME>'/'<Extensions>'/ChoiceFormat syntax. None of the added tests exercise these branches, so regressions in this fragile, key-name-based allowlist (e.g. a new key using '{0,choice,...}' syntax not added to the list) would silently be flagged as illegal HTML with no test coverage to catch it.

title: HTML sanitizer policies rebuilt for every file instance
body: POLICY_SOME_HTML and POLICY_NO_HTML are non-static instance fields rebuilt via HtmlPolicyBuilder().toFactory() every time a VerifyMessageProperties object is constructed (i.e., once per properties file being verified). Since these policies are stateless and identical across all files, they should be static final fields shared across instances, avoiding unnecessary object construction for every theme message file scanned.

title: ANCHOR_PATTERN overly broad, matches tags other than anchors
body: ANCHOR_PATTERN = Pattern.compile("</?a[^>]*>") matches any tag whose name starts with the letter 'a' (e.g. '<address>', '<abbr>'), not just '<a>' anchor tags, because '[^>]*' allows any following characters. This can cause santizeAnchors() to mislabel and process non-anchor tags as if they were anchors, producing a misleading 'Didn't find anchor tag' message for tags that are not actually anchors.

title: isAccessTokenId matcher never actually validates the grant-type shortcut
body: In `isAccessTokenId(String expectedGrantShortcut)`, the grant shortcut is supposed to occupy characters at index 4-5 of the 6-char context prefix (2 chars session type + 2 chars token type + 2 chars grant type), but the code extracts `items[0].substring(3, 5)` instead of `substring(4, 6)`, picking the wrong characters. On top of that, the boolean logic is inverted: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` returns false (no match) when the (wrong) substring equals the expected shortcut, and otherwise falls through to only check the UUID portion. Combining the wrong substring with the inverted condition means the comparison practically never triggers a failure based on the expected grant shortcut — the matcher effectively validates only the UUID suffix and silently ignores the grant-type encoding it claims to check. All the `expectCodeToToken`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, and `expectAuthReqIdToToken` assertions that rely on `isAccessTokenId(...)` therefore do not actually verify that the correct grant-type shortcut was encoded into the access token id, defeating the purpose of this test helper and of the related integration tests.

title: Constructor validates grantType twice and never validates rawTokenId for null
body: In the `AccessTokenContext` constructor, `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null grantType not allowed")` is called twice (lines 72 and 73); the second call reuses `grantType` instead of `rawTokenId`, despite the message claiming to check `rawTokenId`. As a result, a null `rawTokenId` is never actually rejected. If `rawTokenId` is ever null (e.g., due to a caller bug), it will silently flow into `encodeTokenId()` and produce a malformed token id (`...:null`) instead of failing fast with a clear error.

title: Access token id format changed from plain UUID to a prefixed, colon-delimited string
body: `initToken()` previously set the token id (`jti`) to a plain UUID via `KeycloakModelUtils.generateId()`. Now the id is produced by `encoder.encodeTokenId(tokenCtx)`, which prepends a 6-character context prefix and a colon (e.g. `onrtac:1f65761e-...`) before the UUID. This is a visible change to the structure/length of the standard `jti` claim for every access token issued going forward. Any external system, client library, logging/SIEM tooling, or custom Keycloak extension that parses or validates the access token id as a bare UUID (length 36, dash positions, etc.) will break. The PR does not appear to document this as a breaking change or provide an opt-out/compatibility mode for consumers relying on the previous format.

title: Removal of public copy constructor breaks binary/source compatibility for OAuth2GrantType.Context
body: The previously public `Context(Context context)` copy constructor has been removed entirely from `OAuth2GrantType.Context`, which lives in `server-spi-private` and is part of the SPI surface used by custom/extension `OAuth2GrantType` implementations. Any third-party code (or future in-tree code) that relied on this copy constructor to clone/extend a `Context` instance will fail to compile after this change. Since this is an SPI-facing class, its public constructors should be treated as part of the public contract and removing one without deprecation is a breaking API change.

title: Non-atomic two-map update when lazily resolving unknown grant shortcuts
body: `getShortcutByGrantType` and `getGrantTypeByShortcut` update the two `ConcurrentHashMap`s (`grantsByShortcuts` and `grantsToShortcuts`) with separate, non-atomic `put` calls when a grant type is not found in the initially populated maps (e.g., a provider deployed after `postInit`). Under concurrent requests triggering the same lazy-resolution path, one thread could observe one map updated but not the other, leading to a transient inconsistency between the two maps. While the code recovers on subsequent calls, this is a minor race that could be avoided by computing both updates together (e.g., with `computeIfAbsent` or a lock) rather than as two sequential, independently-visible writes.

title: Duplicate null-check bug: rawTokenId is never validated
body: In the AccessTokenContext constructor, line 73 reads `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed");` which checks `grantType` twice (once on line 72) instead of checking `rawTokenId`. As a result, a null `rawTokenId` is silently accepted. Later, `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId()` concatenates `':' + tokenContext.getRawTokenId()`, so a null rawTokenId would simply produce the literal string "null" appended to the token id instead of failing fast, risking malformed/duplicate access-token IDs rather than an early, clear error.

title: isAccessTokenId() matcher has inverted logic and wrong substring offset, so it never actually validates the grant shortcut
body: `isAccessTokenId(String expectedGrantShortcut)` is supposed to assert that the 4th/5th characters of the encoded token-id context equal the expected grant-type shortcut (as the comment above states, chars 4-5, i.e. `substring(4, 6)`). Instead: (1) it uses `substring(3, 5)` which is the wrong character range (off-by-one, grabs the last char of the token-type shortcut plus the first char of the grant-type shortcut), and (2) the condition is inverted: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` returns false (no match) precisely when the substring equals the expected value, and otherwise falls through to only check that the raw id portion is a UUID, effectively ignoring the grant-type shortcut entirely. This means `expectCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken`, and `expectAuthReqIdToToken` (all of which rely on this matcher) will fail when the grant shortcut is actually correct, and will incorrectly pass when it is wrong, defeating the purpose of the added assertion and potentially causing spurious CI failures or false-positive test passes.

title: New abstract method getShortcut() breaks existing OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations
body: OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is a public extension SPI (used to plug in custom OAuth2 grant types). This PR adds a new abstract method `String getShortcut();` with no default implementation. Any existing third-party/custom implementation of this SPI will fail to compile or fail provider loading until it implements this new method, which is a backward-incompatible API change for an SPI explicitly intended to be extensible (as mentioned in the PR description itself). A default method (e.g. returning a generated/fallback shortcut) would avoid breaking existing providers.

title: getShortcutByGrantType/getGrantTypeByShortcut dereference sessionFactory without a null check, causing NPE instead of a clear error
body: `getShortcutByGrantType()` (line 110) and `getGrantTypeByShortcut()` (line 125) use `sessionFactory` to refresh the shortcut maps when a lookup misses, but `sessionFactory` is only assigned in `postInit()`. If these methods are invoked on an instance where `postInit()` has not run (e.g. unusual initialization ordering, or direct instantiation as done in the accompanying unit test), a NullPointerException is thrown instead of the intended, user-facing `IllegalArgumentException`/`IllegalStateException` for unknown shortcuts/grant types. This makes failure diagnosis harder in edge cases and indicates the methods should defensively check for a null `sessionFactory`.

title: testIncorrectGrantType masks a NullPointerException instead of verifying the intended error
body: `testIncorrectGrantType()` never calls `factory.postInit(...)`, so `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.sessionFactory` remains null. When `getTokenContextFromTokenId("ofrtac:5678")` looks up the unknown shortcut "ac", `getGrantTypeByShortcut()` falls through to `sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream(...)`, which throws a NullPointerException rather than the intended `IllegalArgumentException` for 'Unknown value ... for grant type'. The test's `catch (RuntimeException iae)` is broad enough to swallow this NPE, so the test passes without actually verifying that unknown grant shortcuts produce the expected, well-formed error message; it only proves that *some* RuntimeException is thrown, which hides the underlying defect described separately in DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.java.

title: Access token 'jti' is no longer an opaque random UUID; no backward-compatibility note or opt-out
body: `initToken()` now builds the access token id via `encoder.encodeTokenId(tokenCtx)`, producing ids like `onrtac:1f65761e-...` instead of a plain UUID as before. External tooling, log parsers, audit systems, or custom code relying on the `jti` claim being a canonical UUID (fixed length/format) will break after upgrading. The PR introduces no migration notes, deprecation warning, or configuration flag to retain the previous plain-UUID behavior for users who depend on the old format, which is a user-facing behavioral/API change for a widely consumed token claim.

title: Decoding logic unconditionally treats any colon-containing token id as encoded context, risking false failures for unrelated legacy ids
body: `getTokenContextFromTokenId()` treats the presence of a ':' anywhere in the token id as indicating the new context-encoded format, then requires the prefix to be exactly 6 characters matching known shortcuts, throwing `IllegalArgumentException` otherwise. If any pre-existing or externally generated token id (not produced by this encoder) happens to contain a ':' for unrelated reasons, this method will throw a hard error instead of gracefully treating the whole string as a raw/legacy id (as is done for ids without a colon). This is a stricter contract than the previous 'any string is a valid token id' assumption, and has no fallback path for ids that incidentally contain a colon but aren't 6-char-shortcut encoded.

title: isAccessTokenId() matcher has wrong substring offset and inverted comparison logic
body:
In `isAccessTokenId(String expectedGrantShortcut)`, the matcher does:
```
if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;
```
Two separate bugs here:
1. The grant-type shortcut occupies characters 4-6 of the 6-character context prefix (positions `[4,6)`), not `[3,5)`. For a token id like `onrtac:...`, `substring(3,5)` yields `"ta"`, not the grant shortcut `"ac"`.
2. Even ignoring the offset bug, the condition is inverted: the method should return `false` (fail the match) when the shortcut does NOT equal the expected value, but it currently returns `false` only when it DOES equal it.

As a result, this matcher almost never fails regardless of which grant type is actually encoded in the token id (since `substring(3,5)` virtually never matches `expectedGrantShortcut`, the `if` never triggers and the method falls through to `isUUID()` on the raw id, effectively ignoring the grant-type check entirely). All tests using `expectCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken`, `expectAuthReqIdToToken`, etc. that rely on this matcher do not actually verify the new token-id encoding feature, defeating the purpose of the added assertions and potentially masking real encoding bugs.

title: Duplicate null-check validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId
Javadoc for getShortcut() contradicts the fixed 2-character format enforced by the encoder
body: The javadoc states: "@return usually like 3-letters shortcut of specific grants ... Shortcut should be unique across grants." However, `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider`/`DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory` hard-code a fixed 2-character length for the grant-type segment (e.g. `encodedContext.substring(4, 6)` and the overall length check `encodedContext.length() != 6`). All built-in grant factories indeed return exactly 2 characters, which contradicts the "3-letters" documentation. If a developer follows the javadoc and implements a 3-character shortcut for a custom grant type, the fixed-length assumptions in the encoder will break (the encoder will produce malformed ids, and decoding of its own just-generated token ids will throw IllegalArgumentException due to the length-6 check).

title: No validation that OAuth2GrantTypeFactory shortcuts are exactly 2 characters, risking self-generated tokens becoming undecodable
body: `postInit()` collects grant-type shortcuts from all `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` implementations without verifying their length. `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId()` simply concatenates the session/token/grant shortcuts assuming each is exactly 2 characters, and `getTokenContextFromTokenId()` enforces a strict 6-character total length for decoding. If any (built-in or third-party) `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` implementation returns a shortcut that isn't exactly 2 characters (which the javadoc actually suggests is acceptable, e.g. 3 characters), tokens generated with that grant type will fail decoding later (e.g. in introspection or revocation code paths that call `getTokenContextFromTokenId`), throwing `IllegalArgumentException("Incorrect token id ... Expected length of 6")` for tokens the server itself just issued.

title: New abstract method added to existing provider factory interface without a default implementation
body: `getShortcut()` is added as a new abstract method on `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory`, which extends `ProviderFactory`. Any existing custom/third-party implementation of this SPI (e.g. a custom grant type extension) will now fail to compile/deploy until it implements this new method, since no default implementation is provided. Given this is meant to be an extensible SPI (the PR description explicitly states "provider adds ability for someone to introduce his own provider"), this is a breaking change for existing extensions without a deprecation/default-method migration path.

title: Access token jti format change is an unannounced/unflagged contract change with no opt-out
body: `initToken()` now always runs the generated token id through `TokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId()`, changing the shape of the `jti` claim for every access token from a plain UUID to a prefixed value like `onrtac:<uuid>`. Any external tooling, logging/correlation systems, or internal code (admin REST API, introspection consumers, custom SPI implementations) that assumes the access token id is a canonical UUID (e.g. checks length 36, applies UUID regex, or compares it against other UUID-shaped identifiers) will now break. There is no configuration flag/toggle shown to disable this new encoding for backward-compatibility, and no migration note is provided for deployments relying on the previous token id format.

title: Recovery codes stored unhashed when delegated to a UserStorageProvider
body: createRecoveryCodesCredential() builds the UserCredentialModel passed to user.credentialManager().updateCredential() from the raw, un-hashed `generatedCodes` list (JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes), line 119/123) and hands that straight to the federated storage provider's updateCredential(). This bypasses the hashing mechanism that RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode()/verifyRecoveryCodeInput() implement for the local (DB) path, where only hashed codes are ever persisted via RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel. If a UserStorageProvider accepts the credential (returns true), the plaintext one-time recovery codes end up stored verbatim in the external store, unlike the hashed representation used for Keycloak's own storage. This is a security regression: anyone with read access to the external store (or its logs/backups) can recover valid one-time codes, defeating the purpose of hashing recovery codes in the first place.

title: Javadoc does not document the plaintext-vs-hashed storage discrepancy
body: The method's Javadoc ("Create RecoveryCodes credential either in userStorage or local storage") gives no indication that the two branches store fundamentally different representations: the user-storage branch persists raw, unhashed codes while the local-storage fallback persists hashed codes via credentialModel. This is a crucial behavioral detail for anyone implementing or reviewing a custom UserStorageProvider for this credential type, and its omission can easily lead integrators to assume codes are hashed everywhere.

title: Reference test provider validates recovery codes by plaintext comparison, codifying insecure pattern
body: isValid() for RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE deserializes the stored credential data and compares the raw input challenge response directly against the stored list with `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))`. Since this reference/test implementation (meant to illustrate correct SPI usage) stores and compares plaintext codes, it reinforces the plaintext-storage pattern introduced in CredentialHelper rather than demonstrating a secure implementation (e.g., hashing the codes itself before persisting), which real third-party storage implementers may copy.

title: getCredentials() returns a live mutable reference to internal state
body: credentialModels.add(myUser.getOtp()) adds the stored CredentialModel object directly (same reference held in the shared `users` map) instead of a defensive copy. Any caller that mutates the returned CredentialModel (e.g., through generic credential-management code that edits fields in place) would silently corrupt the provider's internal state for that user, since there is no copy-on-read protection. The same applies to the newly added recoveryCodes exposure path.

title: New recovery-codes test does not verify stored data format/security, only functional login
body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin() only exercises the happy-path (setup codes, log in with one). It never asserts what is actually persisted in the federated storage (e.g., whether codes are stored hashed or in plaintext), nor does it cover negative cases such as entering an invalid/used code, disabling the credential through admin/account REST, or re-authenticating after all codes are consumed when backed by a UserStorageProvider. Given the security-sensitive change to how/where codes are stored (see CredentialHelper), a test asserting the persisted representation would be valuable to catch regressions like plaintext storage.

title: User label and creation time are lost when recovery codes are created in user storage
body: createRecoveryCodesCredential() builds the UserCredentialModel passed to user.credentialManager().updateCredential() from only the raw generatedCodes list (`new UserCredentialModel("", credentialModel.getType(), recoveryCodesJson)`). The RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel passed in (which carries the userLabel entered by the user in RecoveryAuthnCodesAction and the original generatedAt timestamp) is only used in the local-storage fallback branch (`recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(...)`). When the credential is actually created in a user storage provider (the success path), the userLabel and createdAt metadata are silently dropped – the storage provider only ever receives the raw code list. Any UserStorageProvider implementation that tries to preserve the user-chosen label (as the updated BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials() attempts to read back via getUserLabel()) will always get null, so the recovery-codes label feature is effectively broken for storage-backed users.

title: Recovery-codes provider id is now a magic string instead of a constant
body: createRecoveryCodesCredential() looks up the provider with the hard-coded literal "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes" instead of using RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID (whose import was removed from RecoveryAuthnCodesAction.java in this same PR). If the provider id ever changes, this string will silently diverge from the real constant and the fallback-to-local-storage path will fail without a compile error to catch it.

title: Recovery codes are stored and validated in plaintext with no single-use enforcement
body: updateCredential() stores the raw challengeResponse (the JSON array of plaintext recovery codes) directly into CredentialModel.credentialData, and isValid() simply checks `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))`. There is no hashing step (unlike passwords, which go through PasswordHashProvider) and no mechanism to mark a matched code as used/remove it from the stored list, so the same recovery code can be reused indefinitely once validated. Since this file is the reference/compatibility example for implementing recovery codes in custom user storage providers, it demonstrates an insecure pattern that defeats the single-use guarantee that recovery codes are supposed to provide; no test in this PR exercises reuse of an already-used code to catch this.

title: getCredentials() does not null-check myUser, unlike sibling methods
body: The new getCredentials(RealmModel, UserModel) override calls `var myUser = getMyUser(user);` and then directly dereferences `myUser.recoveryCodes` / passes myUser to credentialModels.add(myUser.getOtp()), without checking for null. Other methods in this class (isConfiguredFor, getDisableableCredentialTypesStream) explicitly guard against `myUser == null`. If this method is ever invoked for a user not present in the in-memory map, it will throw a NullPointerException instead of failing gracefully like the other methods.

title: New test does not verify recovery-code single-use behavior or label persistence
body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin() only exercises generating recovery codes in the user-storage provider and logging in once with one code; it never attempts to reuse the same code a second time (which should fail) and never sets/verifies a user label for the generated credential. Given that the credential metadata handling (userLabel/createdAt) and single-use enforcement are both affected by this change, the added test does not catch either regression.

title: Recovery codes stored in user storage have no one-time-use tracking
body: isValid() for RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE only checks whether the submitted code exists in the stored raw list (`generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(...)`) and never removes/marks the matching code as used, nor is there any subsequent call anywhere in the authentication flow (RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.action) that writes back a 'used' state to the user-storage provider after a successful login. Since getCredentials()/isValid() always reconstruct the credential model from the same unchanged raw code list stored in credentialData, every recovery code remains valid forever for users whose recovery codes live in this storage provider, defeating the single-use guarantee that recovery codes are supposed to provide. This is a real security/data-integrity regression introduced together with the feature that lets recovery codes be created in user storage, and the reference provider shipped in this PR demonstrates the gap without addressing it.

title: getCredentials() can NPE when user is not found in the backing map
body: getCredentials(RealmModel, UserModel) calls `var myUser = getMyUser(user);` and then immediately dereferences `myUser.recoveryCodes` without a null check. Every other method in this class that uses getMyUser() (e.g. getDisableableCredentialTypesStream, isConfiguredFor) explicitly guards against `myUser == null` before accessing its fields. If getMyUser returns null here (user removed concurrently, race, or lookup inconsistency), this will throw a NullPointerException instead of returning an empty/partial credential stream.

title: Raw (unhashed) recovery codes are forwarded to the user-storage provider
body: createRecoveryCodesCredential builds `UserCredentialModel recoveryCodesCredential` from `recoveryCodesJson`, which is the plain JSON serialization of the raw generated codes (`generatedCodes`), not the hashed representation used by `credentialModel` for local storage. This value is passed verbatim to `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)`, which the companion test provider (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage) stores and compares as-is, i.e. in plaintext. Unlike the local-DB path where RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel stores hashed codes, any user-storage implementation that persists the UserCredentialModel's challenge response directly (as the shipped reference implementation does) will store one-time recovery codes unhashed at rest, weakening the security of the feature for federated users.

title: removeStoredCredentialById likely cannot remove a user-storage-backed recovery codes credential
body: When all recovery codes have been used, the code calls `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())`. For credentials that are now newly supported to live in user storage (per this PR), the id returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() comes from the federated provider (e.g. a synthetic id generated by the test storage provider), not from the local credential store. removeStoredCredentialById is historically scoped to credentials persisted in the local DB store; it is not guaranteed to propagate removal to an external UserStorageProvider. Consequently the exhausted recovery-codes credential may silently remain configured in the user-storage provider even though the authenticator believes it removed it, leaving a stale/exhausted credential rather than cleanly forcing re-setup.

title: No test coverage for recovery-code exhaustion/removal or disabling when stored in user storage
body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only exercises generating recovery codes and performing a single successful login with one code against the new user-storage-backed credential path. There is no test verifying that codes become single-use (cannot be reused), that the credential is properly removed/replaced once all codes are consumed, or that admin/account REST credential disable operations behave correctly for a recovery-codes credential stored in user storage (unlike the analogous OTP tests testDisableCredentialsInUserStorage / testOTPSetupAndRemoveThroughAccountMgmtAndLogin). Given the new behavior this PR introduces, these scenarios should be covered to catch regressions like unlimited code reuse.

title: Reader thread is never joined, making the regression test unreliable
body: The new test `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti` starts a background thread that repeatedly calls `managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(...)` while the main thread deletes groups, but it never calls `Thread.join()` (or any other synchronization) on that thread before asserting `caughtExceptions` is empty. Because `deletedAll.set(true)` is set immediately after the delete loop finishes and the assertion runs right after, the reader thread may still be mid-request (or may not have started at all) when the check executes. Any exception thrown by the reader thread after the assertion point is silently lost, so the test can pass even though the concurrency bug this PR is meant to fix still exists. In addition, the thread is not guaranteed to terminate before the test method returns, leaking a running thread into subsequent tests.

title: getSubGroupsCount() silently returns null instead of surfacing the stale-group condition
body: The fix changes `getSubGroupsCount()` to return `null` when the underlying group can no longer be loaded from the delegate (e.g. because it was concurrently deleted), instead of throwing an NPE. While this avoids the crash, it changes the contract of `GroupModel#getSubGroupsCount()`, which elsewhere in the codebase (and in other GroupModel implementations) is expected to return a non-null `Long`. Callers such as `GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount` (`representation.setSubGroupCount(group.getSubGroupsCount())`) now may propagate a `null` subgroup count into REST responses or downstream logic that may not expect `null`, potentially moving the NPE to a different, less obvious location instead of truly fixing the root cause (stale cached group reference being used after the entity was deleted).

title: No direct/unit-level regression test for the fixed NPE in GroupAdapter.getSubGroupsCount
body: The only test added for this bug fix is a broad integration test with background concurrent HTTP calls and group deletion, which is inherently timing-dependent and does not deterministically exercise the exact code path that was fixed (`GroupAdapter.getSubGroupsCount()` being called after the cached group's backing entity was deleted). There is no focused test (e.g., at model/cache level) that directly triggers `GroupAdapter.getSubGroupsCount()` on a GroupAdapter whose underlying group has been removed, to verify the method now returns `null` instead of throwing an NPE.

title: Same NPE pattern left unfixed in sibling getSubGroupsStream overloads
body: getSubGroupsCount() was fixed to null-check the result of modelSupplier.get() before calling getSubGroupsCount() on it, to avoid the NPE reported in #40368. However, the three overloaded getSubGroupsStream(...) methods just below it (lines ~255-268) use the exact same pattern: `return modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` without checking whether modelSupplier.get() returned null. Since modelSupplier resolves the underlying GroupModel via cacheSession.getGroupDelegate().getGroupById(...), it can legitimately return null if the group was concurrently deleted — the very race this PR claims to fix. These methods will still throw an NPE under the same concurrent-deletion scenario, so the fix is incomplete.

title: getSubGroupsCount() can now silently return null
body: The fix changes getSubGroupsCount() to return null when the backing GroupModel can't be resolved (e.g. group deleted concurrently), instead of throwing an NPE. This is a behavior/contract change: previously the method either returned a count or threw; now callers that unconditionally unbox/use the Long result (e.g. GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount -> representation.setSubGroupCount(group.getSubGroupsCount())) may propagate a null count into the REST representation without it being documented as a possible value, or could NPE themselves if they ever assume a non-null Long. There's no test verifying the null-returning behavior itself or how downstream consumers are expected to treat it.

title: Background thread in new test is never joined, causing a race in the assertion and a potential thread leak
body: In createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti(), a background Thread is started to repeatedly call managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(...) while the main thread deletes groups. After setting deletedAll.set(true), the test immediately asserts caughtExceptions is empty without calling thread.join(). Because the background thread only checks deletedAll at the top of its loop, an exception thrown during the in-flight iteration (the one started just before the flag flip) may be added to caughtExceptions after the assertion already ran, making the test non-deterministically pass even when the bug it targets reproduces (false negative).
