Additionally, the thread is not joined or marked as a daemon, so it can keep running past the end of the test method, potentially interacting with a realm/session that is being torn down by other tests.

title: Fix for NPE is incomplete: sibling getSubGroupsStream overloads still dereference a possibly-null model
body: getSubGroupsCount() was changed to guard against modelSupplier.get() returning null (line 274-275), but the three overloaded getSubGroupsStream methods right above it (lines 255-256, 261-262, 267-268) still call `modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` directly without checking for null. Since modelSupplier.get() can legitimately return null when the backing group was concurrently deleted (which is exactly the scenario this PR is fixing), these methods remain susceptible to the same NullPointerException the PR claims to fix. The fix should be applied consistently to all call sites that dereference modelSupplier.get().

title: getSubGroupsCount() now silently returns null instead of failing or throwing, changing the method contract
body: Previously getSubGroupsCount() delegated to getGroupModel().getSubGroupsCount() which threw an NPE on concurrent deletion. The fix now returns null when the model can't be resolved. GroupModel#getSubGroupsCount() is used elsewhere (e.g. GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount, which calls representation.setSubGroupCount(group.getSubGroupsCount())) without a null check; depending on how callers consume this boxed Long (e.g. unboxing to a primitive, or serializing to a non-nullable representation field), this could introduce a new NPE downstream or silently report an incorrect/misleading subgroup count instead of surfacing the real condition (the group was deleted mid-operation).

title: New concurrency test does not wait for background thread before asserting, making the test unreliable
body: In createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti(), a background Thread is started to repeatedly call groups().groups(...) while the main thread deletes groups. After setting deletedAll.set(true) at line 155, the test immediately asserts caughtExceptions is empty at line 157 without joining the background thread. The background thread may still be mid-iteration (e.g. in the middle of an HTTP call) when the assertion runs, so an exception that occurs just after the check will never be observed, and the test can pass even though the bug it's meant to catch actually occurred. The test should join() the thread (with a timeout) before asserting on caughtExceptions.

title: New regression test may not exercise the fixed getSubGroupsCount()/getSubGroupsStream() code paths
body: The new test calls managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(null, 0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, true) with briefRepresentation=true. Brief representations typically skip populating subGroupCount/attributes, so this call may never invoke GroupAdapter.getSubGroupsCount() or the other getSubGroupsStream overloads that are the actual subject of the NPE fix. As written, the test may pass regardless of whether the underlying bug is fixed, providing false confidence in the regression coverage.

title: Unrelated dead-code removal bundled into an NPE bugfix PR
body: This PR removes the private helper method groupMatchesSearchOrIsPathElement from GroupUtils, which is unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (fixing an NPE on concurrent group access). Mixing unrelated cleanup with a targeted bug fix makes the change harder to review and bisect, and there's no explanation in the PR description for why this method is being removed or confirmation that it isn't still needed/referenced elsewhere.

title: Negative offset slicing on Django QuerySet will raise ValueError/AssertionError
body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is True and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset` directly. Django's QuerySet slicing explicitly rejects negative start/stop indices (raises `ValueError`/`AssertionError`, 'Negative indexing is not supported.'). The surrounding comment claims 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically,' which is incorrect. Any authorized caller (superuser or org member with global access) who sets `optimized_pagination=true` and supplies a cursor with a negative offset will get an unhandled exception/500 error instead of a page of results.

title: Behavior change in shared BasePaginator silently clamps negative offsets for all paginator subclasses
body: The change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` was made directly in `BasePaginator.get_result`, which is the shared base class used by `Paginator`, `DateTimePaginator`, and other paginators across the entire codebase — not just the new audit-log-specific `OptimizedCursorPaginator`. Previously a negative offset (e.g. from a malformed/tampered cursor string) would raise an error from the underlying queryset slice. Now, for non-prev cursors, a negative offset is silently clamped to 0, changing the result set returned (restarting from the first page) instead of surfacing an error. This is a behavior change affecting every endpoint that uses these paginators, introduced to support a single endpoint's opt-in feature, and risks unintended regressions elsewhere. The `is_prev` branch is left unclamped and will still raise on negative offsets, so the fix is also inconsistent.

title: Potential AttributeError if organization_context.member is None
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` accesses `organization_context.member.has_global_access` without checking that `member` is not None. If `request.user.is_superuser` is False and `organization_context.member` is None (e.g. a staff/non-member user who is nonetheless authorized by `OrganizationAuditPermission`), this will raise an `AttributeError` and return a 500 instead of a handled 403/empty result. Elsewhere in the codebase this pattern is typically guarded as `organization_context.member and organization_context.member.has_global_access`.

title: No tests added for new optimized pagination branch or permission gating
body: This PR introduces a new conditional code path (`optimized_pagination=true` query param combined with superuser/global-access gating, routed to `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `enable_advanced_features=True`) but does not add or update any tests for the endpoint. Given this path has a concrete bug (negative offset slicing crashes, see paginator.py), and changes authorization-sensitive behavior, the lack of test coverage is a significant gap that would have caught the crash before merge.

title: New OptimizedCursorPaginator class has no unit tests
body: The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` class (101 lines of new pagination logic, including the negative-offset code path) has no accompanying unit tests in the diff. Core pagination logic like this is exactly the kind of code that needs direct test coverage for boundary conditions (empty cursor, prev cursor, negative offset, hits counting), none of which are exercised here.

title: Misleading comment about negative offset support
body: The added comment states this enables 'efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets' via negative offsets, but `Cursor` itself does nothing to validate or support negative offsets safely — the actual slicing logic in `paginator.py` that consumes `cursor.offset` will raise an error when given a negative value (Django disallows negative slice bounds). The comment implies functionality that does not actually work end-to-end.

title: Negative offset queryset slicing will raise an exception, not provide pagination
body: When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ explicitly disallows negative indices in slices and raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` (it does not fall back to Python list-style negative indexing). Any authorized caller (superuser or org member with global access) that supplies a cursor with a negative offset (e.g. by crafting `cursor=0:-1:0`) while passing `optimized_pagination=true` will cause the endpoint to raise an unhandled exception and return a 500, rather than the 'efficient reverse pagination' described in the comments. The advertised 'advanced feature' is non-functional and introduces a crash vector that is trivially triggerable by any user who qualifies for `enable_advanced` access.

title: Misleading comments claim negative-offset pagination is handled safely by the ORM
body: The comments above the negative-offset branch state 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' and 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level.' Both claims are incorrect: Django raises an exception on negative slice bounds (see the related bug finding), and the comment about permissions is irrelevant to the actual failure mode. These comments will mislead future maintainers into believing the negative-offset code path is tested/working when it is not.

title: Possible AttributeError if organization_context.member is None
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` will raise `AttributeError` if `organization_context.member` is `None` and `request.user.is_superuser` is False (e.g. a non-superuser context where member lookup failed/is absent). There is no null-check before accessing `.has_global_access`, so a legitimate request from a user without `is_superuser` but with a falsy/missing `member` will crash the endpoint instead of falling back to the standard DateTimePaginator path.

title: Comment describes a change that was not made
body: The added comment claims 'Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios' but the line below (`self.offset = int(offset)`) is unchanged from before this PR and already allowed negative integers. The comment implies new functionality was added here when nothing functionally changed, which is confusing and inaccurate documentation that could mislead future readers into thinking this file enables/validates the new negative-offset feature.

title: No tests added for new OptimizedCursorPaginator or the new endpoint branch
body: This PR adds a new ~100-line paginator class (OptimizedCursorPaginator) with a distinct code path (including the broken negative-offset handling) and new branching logic in OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint.get (optimized_pagination query param, enable_advanced permission check), but no test files were added or modified. Given the duplicated/complex logic and the permission-gated behavior, the lack of tests means the negative-offset crash bug (and the permission-gating logic in the endpoint) would not be caught by CI.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator.get_result with no real optimization
body: Aside from the broken negative-offset branch, OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result is a near-exact copy of BasePaginator.get_result (same query building, extra/offset handling, cursor building). This duplicates logic that will now need to be kept in sync in two places, while providing no actual performance benefit described in the PR title ('Enhanced Pagination Performance') — the only behavioral delta is the non-functional negative offset path. This increases maintenance risk without delivering the claimed performance improvement.

title: Negative-offset slicing on Django QuerySet will raise AssertionError, breaking the 'advanced pagination' feature
body: When `enable_advanced_features` is True and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ explicitly disallows negative start indices (`assert k.start >= 0` / 'Negative indexing is not supported.'), so this will raise an AssertionError at runtime rather than return results. This means the entire advertised 'negative offset for bidirectional pagination' feature will crash with an unhandled exception for any client that actually exercises it, resulting in a 500 error for superusers/org admins using `optimized_pagination=true` with a negative-offset cursor. The feature as implemented does not work and was apparently never exercised against a real QuerySet.

title: Misleading/incorrect comment about Django ORM negative-slice support
body: The comment states 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' and 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level.' Neither claim is accurate: Django does not support negative slicing on querysets (it raises an assertion error), and the comment about permission-safety is irrelevant to the actual bug (the crash described above). Leaving this comment in will mislead future maintainers into believing the negative-offset code path is functional and reviewed, when it is not.

title: Audit-log-specific pagination change applied to shared BasePaginator used by all other endpoints
body: The offset-clamping change (`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`) was added directly to `BasePaginator.get_result`, which is the base class used by `Paginator` and `DateTimePaginator` across the entire codebase (issues, projects, teams, etc.), not just the audit log endpoint this PR targets. Modifying shared pagination infrastructure for a feature scoped to one experimental endpoint increases blast radius: any subtle behavior change here affects every consumer of `Paginator`/`DateTimePaginator`. The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` subclass already exists for isolating this behavior; the shared `BasePaginator` should not need to change for this feature.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates ~90 lines of BasePaginator.get_result instead of extending it
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` copies almost the entirety of `BasePaginator.get_result` logic (cursor handling, hits counting, result trimming, cursor building) with only a small branch added for negative offsets. This duplication means any future bug fix or behavior change made to `BasePaginator.get_result` (e.g., the prev-cursor edge-case handling) will silently diverge from this subclass unless manually kept in sync, creating a maintenance and correctness risk going forward.

title: Direct use of request.user.is_superuser instead of the project's active-superuser check
body: The code gates the 'advanced pagination' feature with `request.user.is_superuser`, which reflects whether the user account has the superuser flag set, not whether the user currently has an active, elevated superuser session. Sentry's security model elsewhere requires verifying active superuser status (e.g. via `is_active_superuser(request)`) before granting elevated behavior, specifically to prevent a superuser-flagged account from getting superuser-level access/features without explicitly entering superuser mode. Using the raw flag here bypasses that intended control for an administrative audit-log feature.

title: Potential AttributeError if organization_context.member is None
body: `organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated whenever `request.user.is_superuser` is False. If `organization_context.member` can be `None` for some caller allowed through `OrganizationAuditPermission` (e.g., certain service/API-key or cross-silo contexts), this line will raise an AttributeError resulting in an unhandled 500 instead of a graceful permission denial.

title: No tests added for new OptimizedCursorPaginator or advanced pagination code path
body: This PR introduces a new paginator class (`OptimizedCursorPaginator`) with a non-trivial new negative-offset code path, plus new endpoint logic gating access to it by permission, but no tests were added or updated for either file. Given the negative-offset path is actually broken (see other finding), test coverage would have caught this before merge. Missing tests for the new `optimized_pagination` query parameter branch in `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint.get` as well.

title: Comment added without corresponding functional change, is misleading
body: The added comment claims 'Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios... enables efficient reverse pagination,' but no functional change was made in this file — `self.offset = int(offset)` behaves exactly as before and does not newly 'allow' negative offsets (it always accepted any int, including negative, same as before). The comment implies a capability change that didn't happen here, which can confuse future readers trying to find where 'negative offset support' is actually implemented.

title: Negative offset slicing crashes Django querysets
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result special-cases `cursor.offset < 0` and slices the queryset directly with `queryset[start_offset:stop]` where `start_offset` can be negative. Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ explicitly raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` for negative slice bounds. The comment claims 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' and 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level', but this is incorrect — any request using `enable_advanced_features=True` (now wired up in organization_auditlogs.py) with a crafted cursor containing a negative offset will raise an unhandled exception and return a 500 to the client.

title: Inconsistent/incomplete clamping of negative offsets in BasePaginator
body: The new line `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` only clamps the offset to be non-negative for the forward-paging branch; for `cursor.is_prev=True` the raw (potentially negative) `offset` is passed straight into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Since `Cursor.offset` can be set to a negative integer via `Cursor.from_string` (e.g. a crafted `cursor` query param like `0:-5:1`), this reaches the ORM with a negative slice bound and raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported`, affecting every endpoint using `BasePaginator`/`DateTimePaginator`/`Paginator`, not just the new optimized paginator.

title: Misleading comment about negative offset support with no validation added
body: The added comment claims negative offsets are an intentional 'performance optimization' enabling 'efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions', but no validation was added to `Cursor.__init__` or `Cursor.from_string` to bound the offset, and downstream consumers (BasePaginator, OptimizedCursorPaginator) do not safely handle negative offsets against Django querysets (see other findings). This comment documents behavior that is not actually safe or supported, which will mislead future maintainers.

title: Potential AttributeError when organization_context.member is None
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` accesses `organization_context.member.has_global_access` unconditionally. For a superuser who is not an actual member of the organization, `organization_context.member` can be `None`, and Python's `or` still evaluates/accesses `.has_global_access` on the right-hand side only if the left side is falsy — but even for non-superuser staff with no org membership this attribute access will raise `AttributeError` instead of returning a controlled 403/400, turning what should be a permission check into an unhandled 500 error.

title: Eviction can silently remove the segment's root span without updating the has-root-span flag
body: When `span_count > 1000`, `zpopmin` removes the lowest-scored members from `set_key`, where the score is `end_timestamp_precise`. There is no protection to keep the span whose `span_id` equals the segment key (the root/segment span) from being evicted. Meanwhile `has_root_span_key` is set independently as a separate boolean flag and is not affected by eviction. If the actual root span payload is evicted, `flush_segments` in buffer.py (which derives `is_segment` by comparing each remaining payload's `span_id` to the segment key) will never find a span with `is_segment=True`, even though the segment is still flushed as if it has a root span. This produces inconsistent/incorrect output for consumers relying on the root span marker.

title: No test coverage for the new per-insert eviction logic
body: This PR's stated purpose is 'eviction during insert' via `zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua when a segment exceeds 1000 spans, but no test in tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py exercises this path (e.g., inserting >1000 spans into one segment and asserting that only the most recent 1000 remain, or that a root span is preserved). The core new behavior introduced by this PR is therefore untested.

title: max_segment_spans constructor parameter is now dead code with a mismatched hardcoded limit in Lua
body: `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans: int = 1001`, but the only code that used to enforce it (the span-count check in `_load_segment_data` that logged `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and dropped oversized segments) has been removed. The actual limit enforcement moved into `add-buffer.lua` as a hardcoded `1000` constant, which is not driven by `self.max_segment_spans` at all. This leaves a misleading, unused constructor parameter (callers may believe they can tune this value, but it no longer has any effect) and a silent off-by-one mismatch (1001 vs 1000) between the old config default and the new hardcoded behavior.

title: Loss of observability for oversized segments after moving limit enforcement into Redis
body: Previously, segments exceeding `max_segment_spans` were fully dropped with an `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` error metric and log line, giving operators visibility into data loss. That code path was removed in this diff. The replacement eviction logic in add-buffer.lua silently pops the lowest-scored members with no metric or log emitted, so operators lose visibility into how often/how much span data is being evicted due to the 1000-span cap.

title: Redirect depth limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 without updated justification
body: The loop bound for resolving redirect chains was reduced from 10000 to 1000 and the explanatory comment ('theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly') was deleted entirely rather than updated. This is a behavioral change (traces with redirect/segment depth between 1000 and 10000 will now fail to join correctly) with no comment or changelog explaining why the threshold was lowered or whether it's intentionally aligned with the new 1000-span cap.

title: No tests added for the new OptimizedCursorPaginator
body: The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` class (and the `enable_advanced_features`/negative-offset code path it introduces) has no corresponding unit tests anywhere in the diff, despite being wired into a user-facing endpoint (`OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`) and gated by a permission check that itself has a bug (see organization_auditlogs.py finding). Given this class diverges from BasePaginator's slicing behavior specifically around boundary conditions, it should have dedicated tests, including for negative-offset inputs that currently crash.

title: Negative-offset slicing on Django QuerySet always raises, contradicting the advertised feature
body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is true and cursor.offset < 0, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start_offset. Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ explicitly rejects negative start/stop values in slices (it raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.`), so this code path cannot work as described. The accompanying comment claims 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' which is factually incorrect. As soon as a client supplies a negative cursor offset with `enable_advanced_features=True` (reachable from OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint via `optimized_pagination=true`), the request will raise an unhandled exception (500) instead of the intended 'advanced pagination'.

title: Potential AttributeError when organization_context.member is None
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` will evaluate `organization_context.member.has_global_access` whenever the requesting user is not a superuser. If `organization_context.member` can be None (e.g., edge cases where a user has org access without a direct member record, which RpcUserOrganizationContext explicitly supports as an optional field), this raises an AttributeError and turns a valid, permitted request into an unhandled 500 error.

title: Unrelated, under-specified feature introduced in a PR about spans buffer
body: This endpoint change (adding an `optimized_pagination` query parameter that swaps in OptimizedCursorPaginator with 'advanced features' for superusers/global-access members) is unrelated to the PR's stated purpose ('Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert'). It introduces new user-facing API behavior gated by a client-supplied flag with no validation of cursor offsets, no tests, and depends on the broken negative-offset handling in OptimizedCursorPaginator (see paginator.py finding). This should either be reverted from this PR or properly scoped, tested, and reviewed on its own merits.

title: Redirect traversal depth silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 with explanatory comment removed
body: The loop bound for following span-id redirects was lowered from `0, 10000` to `0, 1000`, and the comment that explained the implication of this limit ('theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly') was deleted entirely instead of being updated. This silently reduces the maximum depth of a span tree that can be correctly merged via redirects, and removes the only documentation of this known limitation, making it harder for future maintainers to understand why extremely deep traces might not merge correctly.

title: max_segment_spans parameter is now dead/unenforced in Python, duplicating an inconsistent hardcoded cap in Lua
body: `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans: int = 1001`, but the corresponding enforcement code in `_load_segment_data` (which used to skip/log segments exceeding this span count) was removed in this PR. The only remaining cap on segment size is the hardcoded `1000` threshold inside `add-buffer.lua`'s `zpopmin` eviction logic, which is off-by-one from the Python-side `max_segment_spans=1001` and not configurable from Python anymore. This leaves a now-meaningless constructor parameter and removes a defense-in-depth check that previously protected the flush path if the Lua-side cap were ever bypassed (e.g., due to script version skew during a rolling deploy).

title: No test coverage for the new eviction-on-insert behavior
body: This PR's stated purpose is to add eviction during span insertion (capping a segment at 1000 spans via `zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua). None of the tests added or modified in this PR (test_buffer.py, test_consumer.py, test_flusher.py) exercise a scenario with more than 1000 spans in a single segment to verify that the oldest spans are correctly evicted and that `flush_segments`/`done_flush_segments` behave correctly on an evicted segment. The core feature being shipped is untested.

title: Misleading comment added without any corresponding functional change
body: A comment claiming 'Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios' was added above `self.offset = int(offset)`, but no actual behavior changed here (the line is identical to before). This creates the false impression that negative-offset support was added/validated at the Cursor level, when in fact no validation or handling of negative offsets exists anywhere in this class, and downstream consumers (e.g., Django querysets) do not support negative slicing at all.

title: Negative offset slicing on Django QuerySet will raise an exception, not work as claimed
body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0, the code slices the queryset directly with a negative start_offset (`queryset[start_offset:stop]`). Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ explicitly disallows negative indices/slices and raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` The comment above this block claims 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' which is false. Since Cursor.from_string (sentry/utils/cursors.py) does not validate that offset is non-negative, any caller can supply a cursor string with a negative offset (e.g. `0:-5:0`) together with `optimized_pagination=true` and trigger an unhandled 500 error on this endpoint — a denial-of-service style bug for a code path meant to be a performance optimization.

title: Potential AttributeError when organization_context.member is None
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` will raise AttributeError if `organization_context.member` is None for any non-superuser request reaching this line (e.g. users accessing the org via a path that does not populate `member`). There is no None-check before accessing `.has_global_access`, so a non-superuser request could 500 instead of simply falling back to the default paginator.

title: New pagination code path has no test coverage
body: This PR introduces a brand-new conditional branch (triggered via the `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter) that switches to `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `enable_advanced_features=True` for superusers / org admins with global access. No tests were added for this branch, nor for the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` class in paginator.py (~100 new lines), despite it introducing new behavior (negative-offset handling) that can crash requests (see related finding). This is a significant test gap for security- and stability-sensitive code.

title: max_segment_spans parameter is now dead/misleading configuration
body: The `max_segment_spans` constructor parameter (default 1001) is no longer referenced anywhere in buffer.py after this change — the span-count limiting logic that previously used it in `_load_segment_data` (checking `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans`) has been removed and replaced by a hardcoded cutoff of 1000 inside `add-buffer.lua` (`zpopmin` when `span_count > 1000`). Any caller setting a custom `max_segment_spans` value now has zero effect, and the hardcoded Lua threshold (1000) is inconsistent with the old default (1001), making the parameter dead and misleading.

title: Silent span eviction with no metrics/logging, changing failure mode from 'drop whole segment' to 'silently truncate'
body: Previously (in Python, `_load_segment_data`), when a segment exceeded `max_segment_spans`, the whole segment was dropped and a metric (`spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded`) plus an error log were emitted, making this clearly observable. Now the eviction happens inside the Lua script via `zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)`, silently discarding the oldest-scored (earliest end_timestamp) spans whenever a segment exceeds 1000 entries, with no corresponding metric or log anywhere in the codebase. This is a data-integrity/observability regression: oversized segments are now silently truncated instead of being flagged, and operators have no way to detect how often or how severely this occurs.

title: Redirect lookup depth limit reduced from 10000 to 1000 without updated rationale
body: The loop bound for following redirect chains was reduced from 10000 to 1000, and the explanatory comment ('theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly') was deleted entirely rather than updated. The same correctness caveat still applies at the new, much smaller bound, meaning very deep segment/span trees (depth > 1000) are now substantially more likely to fail to be joined correctly than before, and there is no comment documenting this trade-off for future maintainers.

title: Unrelated, under-reviewed feature bundled into a PR about span-buffer eviction
body: This PR's title/description describe an optimization to span buffer insertion/eviction, yet the bulk of the diff (OptimizedCursorPaginator, the new `optimized_pagination` endpoint branch, and the Cursor negative-offset comment) is an unrelated pagination feature exposed to privileged users with dubious safety claims ('This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level') that does not actually prevent the negative-offset crash described in another finding. Bundling a large, untested, security-adjacent feature into a PR ostensibly about Redis Lua script changes makes this hard to review properly and should be split out or justified separately.

title: Accidental git submodule added pointing at base commit
body: This PR adds a new file `sentry-repo` as a git submodule (gitlink) pointing to commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a, which is the base commit of this very PR. This looks like an accidental artifact from running `git submodule add` against the repo itself rather than an intentional change. Merging this will add a broken/self-referential submodule entry to the repository, which can break clone/checkout tooling, CI, and confuse contributors. This should be removed before merge.

title: Upsampling eligibility check uses outer `dataset` instead of the per-call `scoped_dataset`
body: Inside `_get_event_stats`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` is called with the closure variable `dataset` (computed once in `get()`), not the `scoped_dataset` parameter that is actually passed into this specific invocation. The dashboard-widget-split logic in `get_event_stats_factory` calls `_get_event_stats` multiple times with different `scoped_dataset` values (e.g. `discover` for `errors_only_query`, `discover` for `transactions_only_query`, or the original scoped dataset for the main query), but the upsampling eligibility/transform decision is always made against the single outer `dataset`. This means, for split queries, the eligibility check can use the wrong dataset (e.g. `metrics_performance` instead of `discover`), causing upsampling to incorrectly be skipped or applied for sub-queries whose actual dataset differs from the top-level dataset, producing silently wrong counts for error vs transaction split queries.

title: Cache key built from Python's built-in hash(), risking collisions
body: `cache_key = f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))}"` uses the built-in `hash()` over a tuple of project ids to build part of the cache key. Hash collisions (different project id sets producing the same hash value) are possible, which would make two different project-id sets share the same cache entry, causing one project group to be served a stale/incorrect eligibility decision cached for a completely different project set. A stable, collision-free key (e.g. joining sorted ids with a delimiter) should be used instead of `hash()`.

title: invalidate_upsampling_cache is defined but never called
body: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is intended to keep the 60-second eligibility cache in sync when the allowlist option changes, but nothing in this PR (or the shown diff) calls it from the option-update path. As a result the function is dead code and the cache will simply rely on its 60s TTL to expire, meaning there is no actual mechanism wired up to proactively invalidate on allowlist changes despite the function's docstring implying it should be invoked 'when the allowlist configuration changes'.

title: Unused `organization` parameter in allowlist check suggests missing org scoping
body: `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled(project_ids, organization)` accepts an `organization` argument but never references it in the function body; the allowlist check (`options.get("issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist")`) is purely global, keyed only on project ids. This is either dead code or indicates the allowlist was intended to be organization-scoped and that scoping was never implemented, which could allow unrelated organizations sharing a project id namespace collision or make per-org rollout of this option impossible even though the option name/semantics suggest per-org control.

title: upsampled_count() only registered for discover dataset, but eligibility logic treats errors dataset as always eligible
body: The new `upsampled_count` SnQL function is added only to `discover.py`'s `function_converter`. However, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` in `error_upsampling.py` unconditionally returns True for `dataset == errors` (the errors dataset module), meaning queries routed through `errors.py`'s dataset config will have their `count()` column rewritten to `upsampled_count() as count` by `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`. If the `errors` dataset's own function converter does not also define/inherit `upsampled_count`, those queries will fail at query-build time with an unknown-function error.

title: Column transform only matches the exact literal 'count()'
body: `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only transforms a column when, after lower-casing and stripping, it equals exactly `"count()"`. Any other common equivalent forms — e.g. `count() as total`, equations referencing `count()`, or whitespace inside the parentheses — are left untouched and silently fall through to regular `count()`, meaning the upsampling feature will not kick in for those forms even though the surrounding eligibility check indicated the query should be upsampled. This limited coverage is not documented as a known limitation and could cause inconsistent results depending on how the caller phrases the column.

title: No tests cover the caching behavior that is central to the PR's performance claim
body: The PR title advertises 'performance optimizations' via caching in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` (60s TTL cache of allowlist eligibility), but none of the added tests exercise the caching path: there is no test for a cache hit returning a previously cached value, no test for cache expiry, and no test for `invalidate_upsampling_cache`. The existing tests only cover `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`, `_is_error_focused_query`, and `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` directly, bypassing the caching wrapper entirely.

title: Broad exception swallowing hides malformed error_sampling context data
body: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` wraps both the dict traversal and the float conversion in bare `except Exception: pass` blocks. Any malformed `contexts.error_sampling` structure (e.g. `contexts` present but not a dict, or a non-numeric `client_sample_rate`) will be silently ignored rather than surfaced, which can mask test setup bugs and make failures using this factory helper hard to diagnose since the event will just not get the expected `sample_rate` without any warning.

title: Upsampling eligibility check uses wrong dataset variable
body: Inside `_get_event_stats`, the eligibility check `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` is called with the outer closure variable `dataset` instead of the function's own `scoped_dataset` parameter, which is the dataset actually used to execute the query (`scoped_dataset.timeseries_query(...)`, `scoped_dataset.top_events_timeseries(...)`, etc.). In the dashboard-widget discover-split code path (`get_event_stats_factory`), `_get_event_stats` is invoked with `scoped_dataset` values such as `discover` for error-only/transaction-only sub-queries while the outer `dataset` variable remains something else (e.g. `metrics_performance`/`metrics_enhanced_performance`). Because `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` branches on the dataset argument passed in, this mismatch causes upsampling to be incorrectly enabled/disabled for these split sub-queries, producing wrong (un-upsampled or incorrectly-upsampled) counts for dashboard widgets.

title: upsampled_count() changes result meta type for the same field name
body: The new `upsampled_count` SnQL function is aliased as `count` by `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` ("upsampled_count() as count") but declares `default_result_type="number"`, whereas the standard `count()` function used elsewhere returns `default_result_type="integer"`. Since the field name exposed to API consumers is identical (`count`), clients that rely on a stable meta type for this field will now see different types depending on whether the querying org/projects happen to be on the error-upsampling allowlist, which is a silent, data-dependent API contract change that can break strict type-based response parsing.

title: Option key used but registration not shown in this PR
body: `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` calls `options.get("issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist", [])`. Nowhere in this PR's changed files is this option registered (e.g. via `options.register(...)` in options defaults). If this option is not already registered elsewhere in the codebase, calling `options.get()` on an unregistered key will raise at runtime and break every call to `get_event_stats` (since this check now runs unconditionally for every event-stats request). This should be verified/confirmed before merge.

title: Cache key built from Python's built-in hash() of project id tuple
body: The cache key `f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))}"` relies on the built-in `hash()` of a tuple to disambiguate different project-id sets. This is fragile: hash collisions between different project-id tuples (however unlikely) would cause one project set's eligibility result to be served for a different project set under the same organization, silently enabling/disabling upsampling incorrectly. A deterministic, collision-free key (e.g. a stable string built directly from the sorted ids) would be safer than relying on `hash()`.

title: invalidate_upsampling_cache is never called anywhere
body: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined to keep the 60-second eligibility cache consistent with allowlist option changes, but nothing in this PR (or apparently the rest of the codebase, based on the changed files) calls it when the `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` option is updated. As written, the cache will always rely purely on the 60-second TTL for consistency, making this function dead code that implies a staleness-mitigation mechanism that doesn't actually exist yet.

title: Docstring contradicts the caching behavior added in the same PR
body: The docstring of `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` states "This function reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time, which means it can return different results between calls if the configuration changes during request processing." This is misleading: the caller (`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`) wraps this function behind a 60-second cache specifically to avoid calling it on every request, so the claim of per-call freshness no longer holds once cached.

title: Transform only matches exact 'count()' string, silently skips other forms
body: `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only transforms a column when `column.lower().strip() == "count()"`. Any aliased form (e.g. `count() as total`) or equation referencing count is left untouched with no warning or logging, so users querying with a slightly different but semantically equivalent column string will silently get un-upsampled results while believing upsampling is enabled for their allowlisted project, with no indication of the mismatch.

title: Shared store_event() test factory now silently mutates sample_rate for all callers
body: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` is unconditionally invoked on every call to `Factories.store_event`, and if `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` is present in the event payload for any reason, it overwrites `normalized_data["sample_rate"]`. This is a broad, implicit behavior change to a widely-used test helper; any existing or future test that sets this context field for unrelated purposes will now have its `sample_rate` silently altered. Errors during lookup/conversion are caught with a bare `except Exception: pass`, which will mask bugs (e.g. malformed contexts) rather than surfacing them in tests.

title: Stray git submodule reference committed
body: A new file `sentry-repo` was added containing only a subproject commit reference (`Subproject commit a5d290951def84...`), which looks like an accidental git submodule addition rather than an intentional change. This is unrelated to the feature being implemented and could break checkouts/CI for other contributors or indicate a broken local repository state that should not be merged.

title: No tests for the caching entry point or cache invalidation
body: The tests cover the private helper functions (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`) but never test the main public entry point `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, which contains the new caching logic (cache hit/miss, TTL behavior) that this PR's description specifically calls out as a 'performance optimization.' There is also no test for `invalidate_upsampling_cache`. Given the caching logic is the novel/riskiest part of this change, its absence from the test suite is a significant gap.

title: Substring match for error-focused query misclassifies negated queries
body: `_is_error_focused_query` determines whether a discover query is error-focused by checking if the literal substring "event.type:error" appears anywhere in the lowercased query string. This naive check does not account for negation: a query like `!event.type:error` (which explicitly excludes error events) contains the substring "event.type:error" and will be incorrectly classified as error-focused. As a result, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` will return True and `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` will rewrite `count()` into `upsampled_count() as count` (a `sum(sample_weight)` aggregation) for a query that is explicitly NOT about errors, producing wrong/garbage counts (or query errors if `sample_weight` is absent for non-error rows) for any caller using negated error filters.

title: invalidate_upsampling_cache is never called anywhere
body: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined with a docstring stating it "should be called when the allowlist configuration changes to ensure cache consistency", but no caller of this function exists anywhere in the diff or referenced code (no signal handler, no option-update hook). The only real mitigation against a stale allowlist decision is the 60-second TTL in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`. This means that when a project is removed from (or added to) the allowlist, the previous eligibility decision can continue to be served for up to 60 seconds with no mechanism to force a refresh, contradicting the documented intent of the invalidation helper and leaving dead code that gives a false sense of correctness.

title: Unrelated nested repository/submodule reference added
body: This PR adds a file `sentry-repo` containing a git submodule-style reference ("Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a") pointing back to the base commit of this very repository. This is unrelated to the error-upsampling feature described in the PR and looks like an accidental artifact (e.g., a nested git clone or submodule added by mistake). It should be removed before merge since it can confuse git tooling, bloat the repository, or break CI checkout steps that don't expect a submodule here.

title: No tests for the public caching entry point or cache invalidation helper
body: The test file exercises the private helpers `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, and `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`, but never tests the actual public function `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, which contains the new caching logic (cache hit/miss paths, TTL, and the AND-combination with `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`). `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is also completely untested. Since the caching behavior is the core 'performance optimization' being introduced by this PR, and is the most likely place for subtle bugs (e.g., stale cache across allowlist changes), this is a significant gap in test coverage.

title: Unrelated user-facing error message text changed in an upsampling PR
body: The validation error message for `topEvents <= 0` was changed from "If topEvents needs to be at least 1" to "topEvents needs to be at least 1". This wording change is unrelated to the error-upsampling feature this PR claims to implement, is not covered by any added/updated test asserting the new message, and silently changes an API error response that external clients or existing tests might depend on verbatim.

title: Column transformation only matches an exact 'count()' string, missing aliased/equation variants
body: `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only rewrites a column when, after lowering and stripping, it equals exactly `"count()"`. Any variant such as an already-aliased column (`"count() as total"`), an equation wrapping count (`"equation|count() / 2"`), or extra internal whitespace (`"count( )"`) will not match and will silently fall through unmodified, meaning the upsampling transform silently fails to apply for these forms while the caller believes upsampling is enabled. This can produce inconsistent results between different query shapes (e.g., top-events queries that generate aliased column strings) without any error or log indicating the transform was skipped.

title: upsampled_count() assumes sample_weight is populated for all events, risking undercounting
body: The new `upsampled_count` SnQL function computes `toInt64(sum(Column("sample_weight")))` and is used as a drop-in replacement for `count()` whenever upsampling is enabled for a project. If `sample_weight` is NULL/absent for any error events that predate this feature or were ingested without the `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` field (i.e., normal, non-client-sampled errors), ClickHouse's `sum()` will not count those rows as 1 (as plain `count()` would), but will effectively contribute 0, causing the upsampled count to be lower than the true event count for projects/time ranges with mixed sampled and non-sampled events. The code comments explicitly assume 'the database schema ensures sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects' without any validation or test covering historical/non-sampled events, making this a real data-correctness risk if that assumption doesn't hold.

title: TableWidgetVisualization rendered with hardcoded empty data instead of actual query results
body: When organization feature 'use-table-widget-visualization' is enabled, tableResultComponent renders <TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} /> with hardcoded empty values, completely ignoring the `tableResults`/`result` variable that was fetched for the widget. Any dashboard widget table rendered under this feature flag will always display as empty regardless of the actual query results, which is a functional regression for anyone on this flag.

title: Mutually-exclusive age/timestamp validation uses truthiness instead of presence checks
body: validate_timestamp/validate_age check `self.initial_data.get("age")` and `self.initial_data.get("timestamp")` to enforce that age and timestamp are mutually exclusive. Since `timestamp` has min_value=0 and age could legitimately be 0, a falsy-but-present value of 0 for either field will not be detected as 'present', so a payload containing both `age: 0` and `timestamp: <n>` (or vice versa) will incorrectly pass validation instead of being rejected.

title: Broad exception swallowing and non-serializable value passed to logger.extra in get_environment_info
body: get_environment_info catches bare `Exception` around `issue.get_recommended_event()`/`get_environment()` and only logs at info level, silently hiding any underlying bug (e.g. nodestore errors) rather than surfacing it to Sentry. Additionally it logs `extra={"issue_id": issue.id, "error": e}` passing the raw exception object (not `str(e)`) into the logging extra dict, which can fail or lose information depending on the logging formatter/handler used downstream.

title: MERGED_PR_SINGLE_ISSUE_TEMPLATE trailing newline plus join('\n') produces double blank lines between issues
body: `MERGED_PR_SINGLE_ISSUE_TEMPLATE = "* ‼️ [**{title}**]({url}){environment}\n"` already ends with a newline, but github/gitlab integration.py build the issue_list via `"\n".join([...])`, adding an additional newline between each entry. This produces a blank line between every bullet (and multiple trailing blank lines before the footer), which breaks the intended tight bullet list formatting in the rendered PR/MR comment (confirmed by the updated test expectations which now show blank lines between bullets).

title: Global default for autofix automation tuning silently changed from 'low' to 'off'
body: DEFAULT_AUTOFIX_AUTOMATION_TUNING_DEFAULT (and the corresponding project option default in projectoptions/defaults.py) was changed from "low" to "off", which changes the default automated-autofix behavior for every project that hasn't explicitly configured this option. This is a production-wide behavior change bundled into a PR that is nominally about the Replays bulk-delete system; it should be confirmed this is an intentional, reviewed change and not an accidental revert/leftover from another branch.

title: Refactor to useQuery drops staleTime/retry/refetchOnWindowFocus settings used by previous useApiQuery call
body: The previous implementation used `useApiQuery` with `staleTime: 0, refetchOnWindowFocus: false, retry: false`. The refactored version uses a bare `useQuery` call without reproducing these options, so the hook now inherits the client's default caching/retry/refetch-on-focus behavior. This silently changes request frequency and retry semantics for trace item attribute key fetching (e.g. it may now retry failed requests and refetch on window focus, which was explicitly disabled before).

title: Analytics event recorded before feature-flag gate, polluting metrics for disabled orgs
body: `analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` is called unconditionally at the top of `post()`, before the `features.has("organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble", ...)` check that can return a 404. This means every call to this endpoint — including from organizations without the feature enabled — generates an analytics event, even though the request is ultimately rejected, skewing usage metrics for this feature.

title: Feature-flagged table widget renders hardcoded empty data instead of real results
body: In `tableResultComponent`, when the organization has the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature flag enabled, the code renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />` instead of passing the actual fetched `result.data` / `result.meta` that are available in scope (and are used by the `StyledSimpleTableChart` branch). Any organization with this flag enabled will see an always-empty table widget regardless of the underlying query results, a functional regression for dashboard table widgets.

title: Mixing millisecond and second timestamps when interleaving errors with breadcrumbs
body: `gen_request_data` compares `error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"]` (populated from `ErrorEvent`, sourced from the Sentry event's `data.get("timestamp")`, which is a Unix timestamp in seconds) against `event.get("timestamp", 0)` from rrweb-style breadcrumb/recording events, whose `timestamp` field is conventionally in epoch milliseconds. Comparing these directly (seconds vs. milliseconds, differing by ~1000x) will produce an incorrect chronological merge of errors and breadcrumbs in the generated log stream sent to Seer for summarization — errors will systematically sort far earlier (or later) than their true position relative to breadcrumbs. The added tests use the same unit for both values and do not exercise this mismatch, so the bug is untested.

title: Fragile positional zip between error_ids and nodestore results
body: `fetch_error_details` builds `node_ids` from `error_ids`, then does `events = nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` and zips `error_ids` with `events.values()`. This assumes `events` is a dict that preserves the exact order of `node_ids` and contains one entry (even if None) for every requested id. If the backend's `get_multi` implementation ever omits missing keys rather than mapping them to `None`, the zip will silently misalign `error_id`s with the wrong event data for all entries after the first missing one, corrupting the summary (wrong title/message attributed to an error). Using `events.get(node_id)` per id would be safer than relying on positional correspondence via `.values()`.

title: Analytics event recorded before feature-flag check and request validation
body: `analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` is called at the very top of `post()`, before the `features.has(...)` check and before the request body is validated. This means the analytics event fires even for requests from organizations without the feature enabled, and even for malformed/invalid requests that will ultimately be rejected with a 400/404, polluting usage analytics with non-successful or unauthorized attempts.

title: Broad exception swallowed and logged with a raw exception object in `extra`
body: `get_environment_info` catches bare `Exception` and logs via `logger.info("get_environment_info.no-environment", extra={"issue_id": issue.id, "error": e})`, passing the exception instance itself as a value in `extra`. Depending on the logging/serialization pipeline, non-serializable values in `extra` can cause logging failures or be silently dropped; `str(e)` or `exc_info=True` should be used instead. The overly broad except also means genuine bugs in this code path (e.g., AttributeError from a code change) will be silently swallowed rather than surfaced.

title: Static method references a differently-named class instead of itself/cls
body: `CommitContextIntegration.get_merged_pr_single_issue_template` is a `@staticmethod` that calls `PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title(title)` instead of `CommitContextIntegration._truncate_title(title)` (or using `cls`). This only works if `PRCommentWorkflow` happens to inherit `_truncate_title` from `CommitContextIntegration`; hard-coding a differently named class inside a base-class method is fragile and will break (AttributeError) if that inheritance relationship ever changes or if this method is reused from a context where `PRCommentWorkflow` isn't in the MRO.

title: fetch_error_details misaligns error IDs with nodestore results via positional zip
body: In fetch_error_details, `events = nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a dict that typically only contains entries for nodes that were actually found (missing/expired nodes are simply absent). The code then does `zip(error_ids, events.values())` to pair each error_id with its fetched data. If any single error_id's node is missing from nodestore, `events` will have fewer entries than `error_ids`, and zip() pairs the remaining items positionally rather than by key — causing every subsequent error_id to be paired with the wrong event's title/message. The fix is to look up each error_id's data by its generated node_id (e.g. `events.get(node_id)`), not rely on positional correspondence.

title: Error event timestamps (seconds) are compared against breadcrumb timestamps (milliseconds)
body: In gen_request_data, `error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)` compares the error event's timestamp (sourced from the Sentry Event model via fetch_error_details, which is a float number of seconds since epoch) directly against the breadcrumb/rrweb event's `timestamp` field, which for recording segment events is conventionally milliseconds since epoch. Because these two values differ in scale by a factor of ~1000, the chronological interleaving logic will be wrong in production: error timestamps (~1e9) will almost always appear smaller than breadcrumb timestamps (~1e12), so errors will be emitted far earlier in the generated log than they actually occurred. The included tests use artificially small, homogeneous-unit timestamps for both error and breadcrumb events, which hides this unit mismatch.

title: get_merged_pr_single_issue_template references PRCommentWorkflow instead of the defining class
body: The new `get_merged_pr_single_issue_template` static method is added to `CommitContextIntegration`, and it calls `PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title(title)` rather than calling the sibling static method on the class it's actually defined in. `_truncate_title` is defined on `CommitContextIntegration`, not on `PRCommentWorkflow`. Unless `PRCommentWorkflow` happens to inherit from `CommitContextIntegration`, this cross-class reference will raise an AttributeError at runtime when GitHub/GitLab's `GitHubPRCommentWorkflow`/`GitlabPRCommentWorkflow` (both subclasses of `PRCommentWorkflow`) call `self.get_merged_pr_single_issue_template(...)` to build suspect-issue PR comments, which would break that comment feature entirely. Even if it happens to resolve today, it is a fragile, incorrect reference that should use the class itself (e.g. `CommitContextIntegration._truncate_title` or just `_truncate_title`) rather than an unrelated class name.

title: TableWidgetVisualization is rendered with hardcoded empty data behind a feature flag
body: When `organization.features.includes('use-table-widget-visualization')` is true, the table widget now renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />` with hardcoded empty arrays instead of passing through the actual `eventView`/`result.data` that the existing `StyledSimpleTableChart` branch uses. Any organization with this flag enabled will see an always-empty table regardless of the underlying query results, which is a functional regression/incomplete wiring if the flag is or becomes active.

title: Undocumented default behavior change for autofix automation tuning
body: DEFAULT_AUTOFIX_AUTOMATION_TUNING_DEFAULT is changed from "low" to "off" (mirrored in src/sentry/projectoptions/defaults.py), meaning Seer Autofix will no longer run automatically by default for projects that rely on the default. This is a meaningful behavior change affecting all projects without an explicit setting, but it's unrelated to the stated PR title/description ("Replays Self-Serve Bulk Delete System" / "Test 5") and has no explanation, making it hard for reviewers to assess intent or impact.

title: Sender/installer validation is skipped entirely when the local Integration record does not yet exist
body: When Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id) raises DoesNotExist, GitHubInstallation.dispatch() immediately returns pipeline.next_step() (line 482) without ever checking the authenticated GitHub user against the installer. The Integration row (and its metadata['sender']) is only created/updated via an asynchronous GitHub webhook delivered independently of the OAuth redirect that brings the user back to Sentry. If the webhook has not yet been processed when the browser redirect reaches this view (a realistic race given both happen concurrently after installation), the exact cross-account hijack this PR is meant to prevent (attaching someone else's GitHub installation_id to an attacker-controlled Sentry org) is not blocked, because there is no local record yet to compare against.

title: Unsafe dict access can raise uncaught KeyError instead of producing the error page
body: `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes the `sender` key always exists in `metadata`. However `build_integration()` only sets `metadata['sender']` conditionally (`if state.get('sender')`), so integrations created without that state value (e.g. legacy installs, or installs where the webhook hasn't populated sender yet) will have no `sender` key. Accessing it directly will raise an unhandled KeyError, producing a 500 error instead of the intended graceful 'Invalid installation request.' response.

title: Non-constant-time comparison for pipeline signature/state
body: The OAuth `state` parameter is compared to `pipeline.signature` using plain `!=` rather than a constant-time comparison (e.g. `hmac.compare_digest`). For a PR specifically hardening the installation flow against forged state/signature values, using a non-constant-time string comparison leaves a (minor) timing side channel that a stricter implementation would avoid.

title: Overly broad exception handling hides real token-exchange failures
body: The `try/except Exception: payload = {}` block around parsing the GitHub token response silently swallows any error (malformed body, encoding issues, library/network bugs), not just malformed/erroneous OAuth responses. This makes it impossible to distinguish a genuine attacker/error scenario from an unrelated bug in parsing, and it will always present the same generic 'Invalid installation request.' message, potentially masking a legitimate internal error.

title: No error handling around get_user_info call
body: `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` is called without any try/except. If the GitHub `/user` API call fails (network error, rate limiting, ApiError), this will raise an unhandled exception and surface as a 500 error rather than the controlled installation-failed page used elsewhere in this view for comparable failure modes.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the 404 'installation not found' code path
body: The test now sends `state="ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"`, which does not match the pipeline signature used elsewhere in these tests (`9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`). Because of the new state-mismatch check added in OAuthLoginView, the request now fails before ever reaching GitHubInstallation/build_integration, so the test only verifies the generic 'Invalid installation request.' message from the state check, not the intended scenario where GitHub's installation-info API returns 404 and build_integration raises IntegrationError('The GitHub installation could not be found.'). The original code path (404 handling in build_integration) is now untested, and a regression there would not be caught.

title: Unguarded dict access on integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] can raise uncaught KeyError
body: In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, when an Integration record already exists but no OrganizationIntegration is linked, the code does `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`. The `sender` key in metadata is only populated when pipeline state happens to include it during build_integration (via `state.get("sender")`), which this PR never binds anywhere in the pipeline; in practice this field appears to rely on an out-of-band webhook updating the integration's metadata after the fact. Any Integration row that was created before this logic existed, or where the corresponding webhook has not yet been processed (a realistic race given webhooks are typically processed asynchronously), will not have a `sender` key in its metadata. Accessing `integration.metadata["sender"]` in that case raises an unhandled KeyError, producing a 500 error for the user instead of the intended graceful 'invalid installation request' page. The code should defensively use `.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and treat a missing sender as a failed/ambiguous match (returning `error()`), not crash.

title: Overly broad exception swallowing hides real errors during token exchange
body: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, the code wraps the token-exchange response parsing in a bare `except Exception: payload = {}` with no logging. Any failure here (network error inside safe_urlread, decode error, malformed response, etc.) is silently converted into an empty payload and surfaces only as the generic 'Invalid installation request' error page, with no logged diagnostic information. This makes it difficult to distinguish genuine security failures (bad/reused code, state mismatch) from transient/operational failures (GitHub API outages, encoding issues), hampering debugging and incident response.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the 404 'installation not found' code path
body: The test still mocks a 404 response for `/app/installations/{installation_id}` (used by build_integration to detect a missing GitHub installation), but now sends a 'state' value ('ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05') that does not match the new pipeline.signature check added in OAuthLoginView. As a result, the request now fails earlier at the state-mismatch check in OAuthLoginView.dispatch and never reaches build_integration or the mocked 404 endpoint at all. The assertion was changed from checking 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' to the generic 'Invalid installation request.', meaning the original 404/'installation not found' behavior in build_integration is no longer covered by any test, despite the test name implying it still is.

title: Missing dedicated tests for access_token exchange failure and missing 'login' in user info
body: The PR description explicitly calls out two new failure conditions it intends to guard against: (1) GitHub failing to return a valid access_token (e.g. invalid/reused code) and (2) the authenticated user info lacking a 'login' field. The added test suite (test_github_user_mismatch, test_installation_not_found, etc.) does not directly exercise either of these two branches (lines ~431 and ~435 in integration.py) by mocking a token-exchange response without 'access_token' or a /user response without 'login'. These are core new security-relevant code paths introduced by the PR and should have explicit regression tests.

title: Sender/user validation is bypassed when Integration record doesn't exist yet (webhook race)
body: In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, when Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id) raises DoesNotExist, the code immediately returns pipeline.next_step() (line 482), completely skipping the newly added 'github_authenticated_user' vs 'sender.login' check that appears later (lines 500-505). Since the Integration row is normally created asynchronously by GitHub's webhook, there's a race window where the webhook hasn't been processed yet when the user's browser redirect reaches this view. In that window, the entire point of this PR (preventing a mismatch between the OAuth-authenticated GitHub user and the user who actually installed the app) is bypassed, allowing an attacker to complete installation under a different GitHub identity than the one that performed the OAuth authorize step.

title: KeyError if integration.metadata lacks 'sender' key
body: The check `integration.metadata['sender']['login']` assumes 'sender' is always present in metadata. However, build_integration() only sets metadata['sender'] conditionally (`if state.get('sender')`), so there are legitimate code paths where an Integration can exist without a 'sender' key in its metadata. If that happens, this line raises a KeyError, producing an unhandled 500 error instead of the intended graceful 'invalid installation request' error page.

title: safe_urlopen call for OAuth token exchange is not wrapped in error handling
body: `req = safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` can raise an exception (e.g. ApiError, network failure) but only the subsequent safe_urlread/parse_qsl call is wrapped in try/except (lines 425-429). Any failure from safe_urlopen itself (GitHub API down, network error, etc.) will propagate as an unhandled exception, resulting in a 500 error for the user instead of the intended friendly 'invalid installation request' error page.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the 'installation not found' code path
body: The rewritten test now sends a mismatched `state` value ("ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05") that does not match the pipeline signature used elsewhere in the suite ("9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3"). As a result, the request is rejected early by the new state-check in OAuthLoginView.dispatch, before ever reaching build_integration()/get_installation_info(), which is where the 404-handling logic ('The GitHub installation could not be found.') lives. The assertion was changed to match the generic 'Invalid installation request.' message, so the original 404 'installation not found' behavior added in build_integration is no longer covered by any test, while the test name/intent remains misleading.

title: New OAuth failure branches lack test coverage
body: The new OAuthLoginView introduces several failure branches: 'access_token' missing from the token exchange response (line 431-432), and 'login' missing from get_user_info's response (lines 435-436). None of these branches are exercised by the added tests, so regressions in this new security-critical logic (e.g. incorrectly treating a failed token exchange as success) would not be caught.

title: Authorize URL built via string interpolation instead of proper URL encoding
body: The GitHub OAuth authorize URL is built with f-string interpolation (`f"{...}?client_id={github_client_id}&state={state}&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}"`) rather than urlencode(). The redirect_uri value itself contains characters ('://') that are not percent-encoded as a query value, and github_client_id/state are also inserted unescaped. If any of these values ever contain reserved query characters, the resulting URL could be mis-parsed by GitHub, breaking the install flow silently.

title: AssignmentSource.queued default is evaluated once at import time, not per-instance
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a dataclass field default. Field defaults (unlike `default_factory`) are evaluated exactly once, at class-definition time (i.e. at module import / process startup), and that same datetime object is reused for every `AssignmentSource` instance that doesn't explicitly pass `queued`. This means `AssignmentSource.from_integration(...)` (used on every inbound assignment) always produces the same stale timestamp (process start time) rather than the actual time the assignment was queued. Should use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead.

title: AssignmentSource.queued type is not preserved across serialize/deserialize round trip
body: `to_dict()`/`from_dict()` are used to pass an `AssignmentSource` through a Celery task's kwargs (`sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(..., assignment_source_dict=...)`). The `queued` field is a `datetime` object; once it is serialized to the task broker (JSON) and deserialized on the worker side, `queued` will come back as a string (ISO-formatted) rather than a `datetime`. `from_dict` does not convert it back, so `AssignmentSource.queued` silently becomes a string after the round trip, inconsistent with its declared type and potentially breaking any future code that treats `queued` as a datetime (e.g. arithmetic, timezone comparisons).

title: assignment_source added to sync_status_outbound signature but never wired into loop-prevention logic
body: The abstract `sync_status_outbound` now accepts an `assignment_source` parameter, mirroring the assignee flow, but unlike `should_sync` for `outbound_assignee`, there is no corresponding check that compares `assignment_source.integration_id` against the target integration for status syncing. This leaves the same inbound/outbound sync-cycle bug this PR is meant to fix still possible for status syncs, and adds a parameter that currently has no behavioral effect (dead parameter) unless callers and subclasses are updated to actually use it.

title: No test exercises assignment_source_dict through an actual serialized Celery round trip
body: All new tests call `GroupAssignee.objects.assign/deassign` and rely on `self.tasks()` to execute the dispatched task in-process, which keeps the `AssignmentSource.to_dict()` output as native Python objects (including a real `datetime` for `queued`). There is no test that serializes the task kwargs through an actual message broker/JSON encoder, so the datetime round-trip inconsistency described above (queued becoming a string after real serialization) is not caught by the test suite.

title: Typo in test method name
body: `test_from_dict_inalid_data` should be `test_from_dict_invalid_data`. Minor, but reduces discoverability/readability of the test and indicates it wasn't proofread.

title: `queued` field default is evaluated once at import time, not per-instance
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a dataclass field default. Like default arguments in ordinary functions, this expression is evaluated exactly once, when the class body executes at module import time, not each time an `AssignmentSource` is constructed. As a result, every `AssignmentSource` created without explicitly passing `queued` (e.g. via `AssignmentSource.from_integration(...)`, which is the only way instances are produced in this PR) will carry the same stale timestamp — the moment the module was first imported in the process — instead of the actual time the assignment context was created. This defeats the purpose of having a `queued` timestamp at all and would silently produce incorrect audit/debug data if this field is ever relied on (e.g., for staleness checks or ordering). Should use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead.

title: `sync_status_outbound` gained an `assignment_source` parameter that is never populated by any caller
body: The abstract method `sync_status_outbound` was updated to accept `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`, mirroring the anti-cycle mechanism added for `sync_assignee_outbound`/`should_sync`. However, none of the changed files in this PR (nor the task that dispatches status sync, which is untouched) actually construct and pass an `AssignmentSource` into this call path. The parameter is therefore dead on arrival: status-sync-triggered webhooks can still create the same kind of sync loop this PR is meant to fix (an assignee loop is fixed, but an equivalent status loop remains unaddressed), while the API surface misleadingly suggests the cycle-prevention feature now covers status sync as well.

title: `AssignmentSource.to_dict()` embeds a raw `datetime` object into task kwargs without serialization safety
body: `assignment_source.to_dict()` returns a dict containing a live `datetime` object for the `queued` field, which is placed directly into the Celery task kwargs (`assignment_source_dict`).
