Depending on the task serializer configured for this queue, a `datetime` may be converted to an ISO-formatted string during transport. `AssignmentSource.from_dict` on the receiving side (`src/sentry/integrations/tasks/sync_assignee_outbound.py`) does not convert this back to a `datetime`, so the reconstructed `AssignmentSource.queued` attribute can end up holding a plain string instead of a `datetime`, silently violating the declared type and causing downstream type errors if that field is ever consumed.

title: No test exercises type-invalid or round-tripped-through-serialization input for `AssignmentSource.from_dict`
body: The added tests only check an empty dict, a dict with an unrelated key, and a fully well-typed dict. There is no test covering a dict with correctly-named keys but wrong value types (e.g. `integration_id` as a non-int, or `queued` as an ISO string as would occur after JSON serialization through Celery), nor a full round trip via `to_dict()` -> celery-style JSON encode/decode -> `from_dict()`. Given `from_dict` only catches `ValueError`/`TypeError` from the constructor call and dataclasses do not validate field types at runtime, bad/mismatched data would pass through silently; this gap means such issues would not be caught by tests.

title: Dataclass default `queued` is evaluated once at class definition, not per-instance
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a dataclass field with a plain default value, which Python evaluates exactly once when the class body is executed (at import time), not each time an `AssignmentSource` instance is constructed. Every `AssignmentSource` created without explicitly passing `queued` (e.g. via `from_integration()`, which is the only construction path used in production code) will therefore share the exact same stale timestamp from process start, instead of reflecting when the assignment was actually queued. This should use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead. As written, any logic that later relies on `queued` to reason about staleness/ordering will be silently wrong.

title: Raw datetime embedded in task kwargs may not survive Celery serialization
body: `assignment_source.to_dict()` (via `dataclasses.asdict`) includes the raw `queued: datetime` field, and this dict is passed directly as a kwarg to `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs={...})`. Depending on the task's serializer, a native `datetime` object inside a dict may not be JSON-serializable, which could cause the task enqueue to fail (or require a custom encoder) in production. Because tests use `self.tasks()` (synchronous/eager execution), this potential serialization failure would not be exercised by the current test suite, so there's no coverage proving the AssignmentSource survives real task queuing.

title: No test exercising the "different integration" propagation path
body: The new `should_sync` logic in `mixins/issues.py` is explicitly designed to still propagate outbound sync when the `AssignmentSource` originates from a *different* integration than the one being evaluated (per the inline comment: "This should still allow other integrations to propagate changes outward"). The only new test (`test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration`) covers the same-integration (blocked) case; there is no test asserting that a non-matching `AssignmentSource` (e.g. assignment source from Integration A, sync check on Integration B) still results in `sync_assignee_outbound` being called. This is the core multi-integration guarantee of the fix and is currently unverified.

title: `assignment_source` added to `sync_status_outbound` abstract signature but never wired up
body: The abstract method `sync_status_outbound` now accepts an `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None` parameter, matching the pattern used for assignee sync, but no caller in this PR (or in the shown diffs) actually constructs/passes an `AssignmentSource` into `sync_status_outbound`. The status-sync task/pipeline isn't touched, so the parameter is dead for now. If the intent was to also prevent status sync cycles, this is incomplete; if not, the signature change is premature and may confuse implementers of `IssueSyncIntegration` subclasses who now need to accept a parameter that's never populated.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is abstract and cannot be instantiated
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler (an abc.ABC) via `class MetricAlertDetectorHandler(StatefulDetectorHandler[QuerySubscriptionUpdate]): pass`, but does not implement the required abstract members `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, or `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. Previously this class was concrete because it implemented a stub `evaluate()`. Now, any code path that resolves `Detector.detector_handler` for a detector of type `metric_alert_fire` (e.g. via `group_type.detector_handler(self)` in `src/sentry/workflow_engine/models/detector.py`) will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract methods ...` at runtime instead of returning a usable (even if no-op) handler. This is a regression from a working no-op handler to a handler that crashes on instantiation.

title: Stale docstring says evaluate returns a list
body: The docstring of `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` still states 'Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`', but the method signature and implementation were changed in this PR to return `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`. The abstract `DetectorHandler.evaluate` also still implies list semantics in neighboring comments. This is misleading for implementers of custom detector handlers.

title: Removed duplicate-group-key test with no replacement coverage
body: The previous test `test_state_results_multi_group_dupe`, which verified that `process_detectors` logged an error when a detector handler returned duplicate group keys, was deleted and not replaced with an equivalent test for the new dict-based `evaluate()` contract. Since `evaluate()` now returns a dict, a handler that computes the same group_key twice (e.g. due to a bug in `get_group_key_values` or a custom `DetectorHandler.evaluate` implementation) will silently have one result overwritten with no error/log, losing the previous diagnostic signal. There's no test asserting this new silent-overwrite behavior is acceptable, nor any safeguard reproduced for it.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler cannot be instantiated: abstract methods not implemented
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler (abstract) but only contains `pass`. StatefulDetectorHandler declares several abstract members that must be implemented: `counter_names` (abstract property), `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the newly-added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. Since none of these are overridden, attempting to instantiate this handler (e.g. via `Detector.detector_handler` -> `group_type.detector_handler(self)`) will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract methods ...`. Previously this class had a concrete (stub) `evaluate` method and worked fine when instantiated; this change silently breaks that contract. Any code path that resolves a Detector of type `metric_alert_fire` and tries to use its handler will crash.

title: Stale comment after switching base class
body: The comment `# TODO: This will be a stateful detector when we build that abstraction` is left in place even though the class now already inherits from `StatefulDetectorHandler`. The comment is now inaccurate/misleading and should be removed or updated to reflect that the handler is stateful but still unimplemented.

title: Unused logger after removing duplicate-group-key error logging
body: The duplicate detection code in `process_detectors` that previously used `logger.error(...)` to report duplicate group keys was removed as part of switching `evaluate()` to return a dict. The module-level `logger` instance at line 30 is now unused anywhere in this file, which is dead code and may trip lint/static-analysis checks (unused variable).

title: No regression test covers MetricAlertDetectorHandler instantiation
body: The PR changes `StatefulDetectorHandler` to require implementing `build_occurrence_and_event_data` (and other abstract members), and updates `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` to subclass it with only `pass`. No test in this PR (or elsewhere visible) instantiates `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` or calls `Detector.detector_handler` for a detector of type `metric_alert_fire`, so the resulting `TypeError` on instantiation (due to unimplemented abstract methods) goes undetected by the test suite.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and cannot be instantiated
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains `pass` — it does not implement the abstract members `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and `build_occurrence_and_event_data` that StatefulDetectorHandler declares with @abc.abstractmethod. title: No test exercises instantiation of MetricAlertDetectorHandler after refactor
body: There is no test verifying that `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` (or any detector configured with the `metric_alert_fire` group type) can actually be constructed via `Detector.detector_handler`. Since the class is now abstract (see related finding), this would fail at runtime, but no test catches this regression.

That logging call was removed as part of switching `evaluate()` to return a dict, and there is no other use of `logger` remaining in this file, leaving dead code that linters would flag.

title: Functions renamed and moved without updating/verifying all call sites and test mocks
body: `mark_failed_threshold` and `create_issue_platform_occurrence` were renamed to `try_incident_threshold` (in `incidents.py`) and `create_incident_occurrence` (in `incident_occurrence.py`) and moved out of `mark_failed.py`. body: A module-level `logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)` is defined but never used anywhere in `incident_occurrence.py`. This is dead code carried over from the original `mark_failed.py` module and should be removed or put to use.

body: This refactor renames `mark_failed_threshold` -> `try_incident_threshold` (moved to `monitors/logic/incidents.py`) and `create_issue_platform_occurrence` -> `create_incident_occurrence` (moved to `monitors/logic/incident_occurrence.py`), along with moving helpers like `get_failure_reason`, `get_monitor_environment_context`, `HUMAN_FAILURE_STATUS_MAP`, `SINGULAR_HUMAN_FAILURE_MAP`, and `SimpleCheckIn` out of `mark_failed.py`. title: No new/updated tests accompany the extracted logic modules
body: The PR moves substantial behavior (`try_incident_threshold`, `create_incident_occurrence`, `get_failure_reason`, `get_monitor_environment_context`) into new files `incidents.py` and `incident_occurrence.py`, but no test files are included in the diff. Given the public API surface changed (function names and module paths), existing tests that exercised this logic via `mark_failed.py` need to be relocated/updated to cover the new modules directly, otherwise coverage for this logic could silently be lost or tests could break due to now-invalid import paths.

title: join() can leave later flusher processes neither waited-for nor terminated
body: In join(), the loop over self.processes.items() checks the deadline and does `break` if remaining_time <= 0 (lines 338-341) before waiting on/terminating the *current* process. Because this is now a loop over multiple per-shard processes (previously there was only a single process so this bug was latent), if the deadline is exceeded while waiting for an earlier process, the loop exits immediately and any remaining processes in the dict are never joined nor terminated. This leaks child processes (each holding a Kafka producer connection and Redis client) on shutdown/rebalance under timeout pressure, which can accumulate open connections and zombie/orphan processes over time.

title: Division by zero if flusher is configured with 0 processes
body: self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards)) can be 0 if max_processes (derived from the new --flusher-processes CLI option, default 1 but user-settable) is passed as 0. The subsequent loop `process_index = i % self.num_processes` (line 65) will then raise ZeroDivisionError, crashing the consumer with an unclear error instead of a clear validation message. There is no guard anywhere (CLI option in src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py has no min=1 validation, and SpanFlusher.__init__ does not validate max_processes > 0).

title: Inconsistent metric tag keys for shard grouping across related timers
body: The 'spans.buffer.flusher.produce' and 'spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes' metrics are tagged with key 'shard' (line 185, 193) holding a comma-joined list of shard ids, while 'spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce' uses the key 'shards' (line 199) for the same comma-joined value. This inconsistency between closely-related timers for the same logical dimension will break dashboards/alerts that expect a single consistent tag name across the flush pipeline, and conflates 'shard' as both a single shard id (used in spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy) and a joined list of shards (used here) under the same tag key, which is confusing and can lead to incorrect aggregation.

title: Dead code: _create_process_for_shard is never called
body: The newly added method `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` (singular) that restarts the process owning a specific shard is never invoked anywhere in the class; `_ensure_processes_alive` calls `_create_process_for_shards` (plural) directly with the full shard list for a process index. This leftover method is dead code and suggests an incomplete implementation of per-shard-granularity restart logic that was intended but not wired up.

title: Added synchronization sleep is a no-op due to global time.sleep monkeypatch
body: At line 15, `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` patches the `time` module's `sleep` attribute globally for the test process. The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` at line 62 (intended, per the comment, 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change') looks up `time.sleep` at call time via the module-level `import time`, so it also resolves to the patched no-op lambda and does not actually wait. This makes the added synchronization ineffective; the test's correctness for picking up the message after `current_drift` changes effectively relies on thread scheduling/GIL timing rather than any deterministic wait, making the test more likely to be flaky rather than fixed.

title: New max_processes parameter not documented in docstring
body: The class docstring for SpanFlusher (lines 29-41) documents `topic` and `produce_to_pipe` parameters but was not updated to describe the newly added `max_processes` parameter, even though the whole point of this PR is to introduce configurable per-shard multiprocessing. This makes the new, most important parameter undocumented for future maintainers.

title: New isinstance guard can silently skip killing unhealthy multiprocessing flusher processes
body: In `_ensure_processes_alive()` the new code guards `process.kill()` with `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process):`. The processes are actually created via `self.mp_context = multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")`, so they are instances of `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`. On platforms/configurations where the *default* multiprocessing context is not spawn (e.g. fork on Linux, which is Sentry's typical deployment target), `multiprocessing.Process` resolves to a different class (e.g. `ForkProcess`), and `isinstance(spawn_process, multiprocessing.Process)` evaluates to False. Previously (pre-PR) `kill()` was called unconditionally, so this guard is new and can silently prevent an unhealthy/hung child process from ever being killed before a replacement process is spawned for the same shards. The result is two processes concurrently flushing/producing the same shard's segments, risking duplicate production to the buffered-segments topic (data integrity) and leaked/zombie OS processes.

title: join() aborts terminating remaining flusher processes once a deadline is hit mid-loop
body: In `join(timeout)`, the loop over `self.processes.items()` breaks out entirely as soon as the deadline is exceeded for the process currently being iterated (`if remaining_time <= 0: break`). This skips the `process.terminate()` call for all subsequent process indexes in the dict, not just the one that timed out. With a single flusher process (pre-PR behavior) this was not an issue, but with multiple flusher processes per shard group, hitting the timeout while waiting on an early process means later processes are never explicitly terminated during this shutdown path (e.g. during a strategy teardown/rebalance where the whole interpreter does not exit), leaving them running as orphaned subprocesses.

title: Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op due to earlier global monkeypatch, so it doesn't actually fix the intended race
body: The test patches `time.sleep` globally at line 15 (`monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`), which replaces the `sleep` attribute on the actual `time` module for the duration of the test. The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` at line 62, intended to "give flusher threads time to process after drift change," therefore does nothing — it resolves to the same monkeypatched no-op. The test's reliability against the race between updating `current_drift` and the background flusher thread observing it relies solely on incidental GIL/thread scheduling from the extra `step.poll()` call, not on any real wait, so the fix may not reliably prevent flakiness it was meant to address.

title: Inconsistent metric tag key between related timers ("shard" vs "shards")
body: The `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` metrics use tag key `"shard"` (lines 185, 195), while the `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer at line 199 uses tag key `"shards"` (plural). This inconsistency means dashboards/alerts built around one tag name won't match the other metric, making it harder to correlate produce time with wait-for-produce time per shard.

title: Docstring overstates that one process is created per shard
body: The class docstring states "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing," but the implementation actually creates `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` processes and distributes shards round-robin across them via `process_to_shards_map`, so multiple shards commonly share a single process (as also demonstrated by `test_flusher_processes_limit`). The docstring should clarify that shards are distributed across up to `max_processes` processes, not necessarily one process per shard.

title: join() aborts terminating remaining flusher processes once the deadline is hit for one process
body: In join(), the for-loop over self.processes.items() does `break` when the join deadline has passed for the *current* process index. Because break exits the entire for-loop (not just the inner while), any processes that come later in the dict are never waited on nor have .terminate() called on them. Previously there was only a single process and .terminate() was always reached after the wait loop; now, with multiple flusher processes, a timed-out shutdown can leave one or more real subprocesses running un-terminated after join() returns, leaking Kafka producer connections and Redis clients/orphaned processes.

title: isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) guard likely never true for spawn-context processes, so .kill() is silently skipped
body: _ensure_processes_alive() now only calls process.kill() when isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is true. Processes here are created via self.mp_context.Process where self.mp_context = multiprocessing.get_context('spawn'); such a call returns an instance of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which is a sibling of (not a subclass of) the generic multiprocessing.context.Process class that multiprocessing.Process refers to. Consequently this isinstance check evaluates to False for real spawned subprocesses, meaning the unhealthy process is never killed before _create_process_for_shards spawns its replacement. Previously .kill() was called unconditionally (only ValueError was swallowed), so this is a regression: hung/unhealthy processes may now keep running alongside their replacements, consuming Redis connections and potentially double-producing flushed segments to Kafka.

title: Memory usage may be double-counted across per-process shard buffers when computing backpressure threshold
body: submit() now sums buffer.get_memory_info() across self.buffers.values(), where each buffer is a SpansBuffer scoped only to the shards owned by one flusher process. Previously a single SpansBuffer covering all assigned shards computed memory info once per distinct Redis node/cluster. If multiple shards (now split across different per-process buffers) map to the same underlying Redis node, that node's ServiceMemory will be reported and summed multiple times, inflating 'used'/'available' totals used to decide spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage backpressure. This can skew the used/available ratio and trigger (or fail to trigger) hard backpressure incorrectly depending on how shards are distributed across nodes and processes.

title: Inconsistent metric tag key between related timers ('shard' vs 'shards')
body: The produce timer uses tags={"shard": shard_tag} while the wait_produce timer right below it uses tags={"shards": shard_tag} for the same shard_tag value. This inconsistency means the two related metrics (spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) cannot be correlated/filtered by the same tag key in dashboards or alerts, undermining the observability improvement this change is meant to add.

title: Docstring overstates default flusher behavior
body: The class docstring states SpanFlusher 'Creates one process per shard for parallel processing,' but the actual process count is capped by max_processes (the --flusher-processes CLI option), whose default in src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py is 1. By default this still runs as a single flusher process handling all shards, identical to pre-PR behavior, unless operators explicitly raise --flusher-processes. The docstring should clarify that one-process-per-shard only happens when max_processes is unset/None or >= number of assigned shards.

title: New multiprocess-flusher test only checks internal bookkeeping, not actual multi-process flush behavior
body: test_flusher_processes_limit only asserts len(flusher.processes), max_processes, num_processes and the total shard count in process_to_shards_map; it never submits spans, advances the clock, and verifies that segments for shards handled by different processes are actually flushed/produced correctly, nor does it exercise the per-process restart path added in this PR. Given the PR's core change is spawning one process per shard group, there is no test exercising end-to-end correctness of flushing across multiple flusher processes.

title: close()/terminate() tear down the shared, persistent FixedQueuePool, breaking processing after any rebalance
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (line 335-338) and terminate() (line 340-342) both call self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which permanently stops all worker threads and shuts down all underlying queue.Queue objects. However, queue_pool is the SAME object that lives on ResultsStrategyFactory (created once in __init__, see result_consumer.py) and is intended to persist across the whole lifetime of the consumer process - it is only supposed to be torn down once via ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown(). In Arroyo, create_with_partitions() is invoked on every partition assignment change (rebalance), and the previous strategy instance's close()/join() are called first. That means on the very first rebalance, the shared queue_pool's workers/queues are shut down for good, while factory.queue_pool still points at this now-dead pool. The next strategy created by create_thread_queue_parallel_worker() reuses this dead queue_pool. When submit() then calls work_queue.put(work_item) on a queue that has been shut down, queue.ShutDown is raised, caught by the broad except Exception in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit(), which force-marks the offset as added+completed without ever having it processed. The net effect: after the first rebalance, uptime results stop being processed entirely while Kafka offsets keep advancing normally (silent data loss, no lag/alerting signal).

title: Sequential worker joins in shutdown() can block for minutes
body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown() (lines 231-243) iterates over all workers sequentially and calls worker.join(timeout=5.0) for each one. With the default num_queues=20, if several workers are slow to exit (e.g. stuck in a long-running result_processor call), the overall shutdown can block for up to num_queues * 5 seconds (100s by default) before returning. Combined with the fact that this shutdown path is invoked from strategy close()/terminate() on every rebalance (see related finding), this can cause the whole consumer to stall far beyond typical graceful-shutdown/rebalance timeouts, risking forced kills by orchestration and loss of the ability to commit final offsets.

title: Queues are unbounded, contradicting the documented backpressure guarantee
body: FixedQueuePool creates each worker queue as queue.Queue() with no maxsize (line 185), yet the class docstring (around line 253, 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up') and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's docstring both claim backpressure is provided. Because the queues are unbounded, a single slow/stuck group can cause its queue to grow without limit while submit() keeps accepting and enqueuing new items, risking unbounded memory growth instead of the advertised backpressure. This undermines the stated goal of isolating a slow item's impact.

title: Relies on Python 3.13-only queue.Queue.shutdown()/queue.ShutDown API
body: queue.Queue.shutdown() and the queue.ShutDown exception were only added in Python 3.13. OrderedQueueWorker.run() catches queue.ShutDown (lines 132-133, 142-143) and FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) (line 238) to unblock worker threads. If the project's supported/runtime Python version is older than 3.13, q.shutdown() will raise AttributeError (caught and merely logged at line 238-240), but the workers will then never receive a ShutDown signal and will remain blocked forever on work_queue.get(), so worker.join(timeout=5.0) will always time out without the thread actually stopping. This silently defeats the entire graceful-shutdown mechanism on any Python version prior to 3.13.

title: join(timeout) ignores the caller-supplied timeout
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(timeout) (lines 344-345) ignores the timeout parameter entirely and always calls self.close(), which itself uses hardcoded internal timeouts (5.0s for the commit thread plus up to 5.0s per worker in queue_pool.shutdown()). Callers (e.g. Arroyo's StreamProcessor, which is configured with join_timeout) expect join() to respect the requested deadline for bounding shutdown time; ignoring it can make the strategy's shutdown take substantially longer than what was configured, breaking the ProcessingStrategy contract.

title: get_committable_offsets does an O(n) scan under a lock on every tick, scaling with backlog size
body: get_committable_offsets() (lines 67-98) iterates offset-by-offset from last_committed+1 to max_offset while holding the per-partition lock, and this runs every second from the commit loop. If one group backlogs its queue (the exact scenario this PR intends to tolerate), the gap between last_committed and max_offset for that partition grows large, making this scan increasingly expensive and holding the partition lock longer each tick - which blocks add_offset()/complete_offset() calls from worker threads processing unrelated groups on the same partition, partially reintroducing the contention the queue-based design was meant to avoid.

title: No test exercises strategy close()/recreate across a simulated rebalance
body: All of the new thread-queue-parallel tests (test_thread_queue_parallel, test_thread_queue_parallel_preserves_order, etc.) build a single strategy via factory.create_with_partitions() and only ever call factory.shutdown() at the end; none of them call consumer.close() (or terminate()) and then call factory.create_with_partitions() again to simulate a Kafka rebalance and continue processing more messages. This is exactly the scenario where the shared FixedQueuePool gets torn down by SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() (see related finding), so the test suite does not catch that the thread-queue-parallel mode becomes non-functional after the first rebalance.

title: Use of queue.Queue.shutdown()/queue.ShutDown requires Python 3.13+
body: OrderedQueueWorker.run() catches `queue.ShutDown` (lines 132, 143) and FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` (line 238). Both `queue.Queue.shutdown()` and the `queue.ShutDown` exception were only added in Python 3.13. If Sentry's runtime is on an earlier Python version (3.11/3.12, which is common for this codebase), `q.shutdown()` will raise `AttributeError: 'Queue' object has no attribute 'shutdown'`, which is silently swallowed by the broad `except Exception: logger.exception(...)` in `shutdown()`. As a result, worker threads will never receive a shutdown signal and will hang forever blocked on `work_queue.get()`, making graceful shutdown completely non-functional and leaking daemon threads for the life of the process.

title: Queues are unbounded, contradicting the documented backpressure guarantee
body: `work_queue: queue.Queue[WorkItem[T]] = queue.Queue()` is created without a `maxsize`, and `FixedQueuePool.submit()`/`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` never block on a full queue. The class docstrings claim 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up,' but since the queue is unbounded, a single slow group assigned to a queue will cause that queue (and thus memory usage) to grow without limit while the main consumer thread keeps consuming and submitting new items. This defeats the stated goal of this PR (avoiding unbounded backlog from slow items) and risks unbounded memory growth under sustained slow processing.

title: Sequential worker joins on shutdown can take far longer than expected
body: In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()`, `for worker in self.workers: worker.join(timeout=5.0)` joins each worker thread sequentially with a 5 second timeout. With the default `num_queues=20`, a slow shutdown could take up to 20 * 5 = 100 seconds in the worst case. This can exceed typical process termination grace periods (e.g. Kubernetes `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`), resulting in SIGKILL before threads finish, undermining the goal of a graceful shutdown and risking lost/duplicated in-flight work.

title: queue_pool is permanently nulled on shutdown, breaking subsequent create_with_partitions calls
body: `ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown()` sets `self.queue_pool = None` after calling `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, but `self.thread_queue_parallel` stays `True` and the pool is never recreated. If `create_with_partitions()` is invoked again on this factory instance after `shutdown()` is called (e.g. during a partition rebalance or any lifecycle path where the strategy factory outlives individual strategy instances), `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker()` will hit `assert self.queue_pool is not None` and raise an AssertionError, crashing the consumer. The other modes (`parallel`, `batched-parallel`) don't exhibit this exact null-out pattern on their pools/executors.

title: Kafka offset commit invoked from a background thread, not the main poll loop
body: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop` runs on a dedicated daemon thread (`self.commit_thread`) and periodically calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which ultimately drives the arroyo `Commit` callback tied to the underlying Kafka consumer. The underlying confluent-kafka-python/librdkafka client is documented as not safe for concurrent calls across threads (e.g. concurrent `poll()` from the main stream processor loop and `commit()`-related calls from this background thread). Introducing a separate thread that periodically triggers commits concurrently with the main consumer loop's polling is a new concurrency risk that did not exist for the other (serial/batched-parallel/parallel) modes, which all perform commits from the strategy pipeline on the main processing thread.

title: WorkItem retains the full Kafka Message object though it is never used
body: `WorkItem` stores the entire `message: Message[KafkaPayload | FilteredPayload]` (set in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()`), but neither `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` nor any other code path reads `work_item.message` — only `partition`, `offset`, and `result` are used. Keeping a reference to the full raw Kafka message for every queued item unnecessarily increases memory retained by backlogged queues, especially since the queues are unbounded (see related finding), compounding potential memory pressure under backlog.

title: New thread-queue-parallel tests are tightly coupled to the 1-second commit loop timing
body: Tests such as `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_commit` and `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps` poll for up to ~2 seconds (20 iterations of `time.sleep(0.1)`) waiting for a commit to appear, while `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop` only attempts a commit once per second (`self.shutdown_event.wait(1.0)`). This leaves very little margin under CI load or thread scheduling delays, making these tests prone to intermittent flakiness rather than deterministically synchronizing on the commit event.

title: Shared FixedQueuePool is permanently destroyed by per-rebalance strategy close()/terminate()
body: ResultsStrategyFactory creates a single `FixedQueuePool` instance once in `__init__` (result_consumer.py, inside `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__`, `self.queue_pool = FixedQueuePool(...)`), intended to live for the lifetime of the consumer process and be reused across partition rebalances. However, `create_with_partitions` builds a brand-new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` every time it is called (e.g. on every rebalance), and that strategy's `close()`/`terminate()` methods (queue_consumer.py lines 335-342) call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets every worker thread's `shutdown` flag and shuts down every underlying `queue.Queue`. Arroyo calls `close()`/`terminate()` on the active strategy whenever partitions are revoked (which happens on every consumer group rebalance), and then calls `create_with_partitions` again for the new assignment. Because the factory still holds the same (now permanently dead) `queue_pool` object, the new strategy submits work items into queues whose worker threads have already exited, so no further messages are ever processed after the first rebalance - the consumer silently stalls without raising any error, with no new offsets being committed from that point forward.

title: Work queues are unbounded, so claimed back-pressure does not exist
body: `FixedQueuePool.__init__` creates each `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize` (line 185), and `submit()` (`work_queue.put(work_item)`) never blocks or applies any limit. The class docstrings for `FixedQueuePool` and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` explicitly claim 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up,' but since the queues are unbounded, a single slow/stuck group (which this PR's description cites as the motivating problem) will cause its queue to grow without bound while the main consumer thread keeps accepting and enqueuing new messages. This can lead to unbounded memory growth (queued `WorkItem`s also retain the original `Message` object) and an ever-growing `OffsetTracker.all_offsets`/`outstanding` set, defeating the stated goal of avoiding backlog/parallelism problems.

title: Unsynchronized dict mutation/iteration race in OffsetTracker
body: `OffsetTracker` protects each partition's offset *set* with a per-partition lock, but the outer dictionaries (`all_offsets`, `outstanding`, `last_committed`, `partition_locks`) have no lock guarding structural changes. `get_committable_offsets()` does `for partition in list(self.all_offsets.keys())` (line 74) while `add_offset()` (called from the consumer thread) can concurrently insert a brand-new partition key into the same defaultdict via `self.all_offsets[partition]`. Mutating a dict's size while another thread is iterating/snapshotting its keys can intermittently raise `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration` in CPython, since `add_offset` and `get_committable_offsets`/`mark_committed` run on different threads (main consumer thread vs. the dedicated commit thread) without a shared lock around the top-level containers.

title: No test coverage for partition revocation/reassignment (rebalance)
body: None of the new tests in test_queue_consumer.py or the thread-queue-parallel tests added to tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py exercise calling `create_with_partitions` more than once on the same `ResultsStrategyFactory`/`queue_pool`, or calling `close()`/`terminate()` on the returned `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` followed by a second `create_with_partitions` call (which is what happens on a real Kafka consumer group rebalance). This leaves the critical bug where `strategy.close()` kills the shared `FixedQueuePool` permanently (see queue_consumer.py close()/terminate()) completely uncovered by tests, even though rebalances are a normal and frequent occurrence in production Kafka consumers.

title: Misleading docstring claiming backpressure that doesn't exist
body: The docstring of `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` (and similarly `FixedQueuePool`) states 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' as a guaranteed property, but the underlying `queue.Queue` objects are created with no `maxsize`, so they never 'fill up' and no backpressure is ever applied to the Kafka consumer. This documentation is inaccurate and could mislead future maintainers into believing memory/backlog growth is bounded when it is not.

title: Backup codes not invalidated after use on disable endpoint
body: In disable.ts, when a backup code successfully matches, the code just proceeds (comment says 'we delete all stored backup codes at the end'). But the matched index is never nulled nor is a single-use check performed - this is fine because the whole backupCodes field is cleared when 2FA is disabled. However, if the TOTP/backup code check fails validation elsewhere (e.g., only disabling but code is reused across multiple requests before 2FA is actually disabled, e.g. concurrent requests), the same backup code could be reused multiple times before the user update commits, since there's no atomic consumption. This is a minor race but worth flagging as a correctness gap relative to the login flow in next-auth-options.ts which explicitly consumes (nulls) the backup code.

title: Backup code lookup does not skip already-used (null) codes correctly and allows case/format mismatches
body: backupCodes.indexOf(credentials.backupCode.replaceAll('-', '')) finds the first matching code, but used codes are set to null (line 148), so there's no issue with reuse of consumed codes. However, there's no normalization (e.g. lowercase) of user input before comparison, while codes are generated via crypto.randomBytes(...).toString('hex') which is lowercase hex. If a user copies/pastes with different casing (e.g., auto-caps on mobile), the backup code will incorrectly fail even though it is valid, causing legitimate lockout. This should normalize case before comparing.

title: Exported component named TwoFactor instead of BackupCode
body: The default export function is named `TwoFactor` even though the file is BackupCode.tsx and it's imported elsewhere as `BackupCode`. This is misleading/confusing for maintainers and could cause confusion when debugging (e.g., in React DevTools component names will show 'TwoFactor' for the backup code input).

title: backupCodes state typed as never[] due to missing generic
body: `const [backupCodes, setBackupCodes] = useState([]);` has no type annotation, so TypeScript infers `never[]`, which may cause type errors (or implicit any) when later calling `.map((code) => ...)` with `code` typed as `never`, and prevents compile-time safety for the backup codes array of strings returned by the API.

title: resetForm clears password on reset after successful disable, but lostAccess toggle keeps password typed, risk of stale state
body: resetForm(false) called from the 'lost access'/'go back' toggle does not clear password, which is fine, but after a successful disable, resetForm() (default clearPassword=true) clears password and codes, yet modal is not necessarily closed/unmounted before onDisable() runs; if the modal remains mounted and reopened, previous errorMessage state is cleared, but twoFactorLostAccess flag was already reset separately - this is a minor state management inconsistency without an actual bug but worth checking the modal fully resets between opens, as there's no reset tied to `open` prop toggling via useEffect.

title: Backup codes regenerated and overwritten on repeated setup calls without 2FA actually being enabled
body: The setup endpoint generates new backupCodes and stores them, but twoFactorEnabled is explicitly set to false here. If a user calls /setup multiple times before completing /enable, previous unused backup codes are silently discarded and replaced, and any codes already shown/downloaded from a prior incomplete setup become invalid without any indication. There's also no check that an in-progress setup isn't overwritten mid-flow (e.g. a race between two tabs).

title: Backup code consumption not atomic — race condition allows multi-use of a single backup code
body: The code reads user.backupCodes, decrypts, checks index, then performs a separate prisma.user.update to null out the used code and re-encrypt. Between the read and the update there is no locking/transaction, so concurrent requests with the same backup code could both pass the index check before either write completes, allowing a single backup code to be used more than once (defeating the one-time-use guarantee).

title: Disable endpoint allows backup-code based disable without consuming/invalidating the code
body: In the backup-code branch, the code validates index !== -1 but does not mark the backup code as used (no update to backupCodes before the final update). While the final update nulls all backupCodes as part of disabling 2FA entirely, if a future change short-circuits that final step, the same backup code could be reused. More importantly, unlike next-auth-options.ts, there's no single-code invalidation step, so behavior around backup codes differs inconsistently between login and disable flows.

title: Backup codes and secret kept in component state without clearing on modal close/cancel
body: backupCodes, secret, and the generated backupCodesUrl (an object URL referencing sensitive backup codes) are stored in React state but resetState() (called on cancel) does not clear backupCodes, secret, or revoke the backupCodesUrl via URL.revokeObjectURL. This leaves sensitive 2FA backup codes resident in memory/DOM (download link) after the user cancels, and the object URL leaks until the component unmounts or setup is run again overwriting it.

title: backupCodes state typed as never[] due to missing generic/type annotation
body: useState([]) for backupCodes has no type annotation, so TypeScript infers never[]; code calling backupCodes.map(formatBackupCode) and backupCodes.indexOf elsewhere relies on this being string[]. This will likely cause TS errors or require implicit any, and signals a missing type-safety fix (should be useState<string[]>([])).

title: Backup codes stored in plaintext array without hashing/removal consistency
body: Backup codes are generated and encrypted as a blob, but each code remains a plaintext secret within that blob. When one code is used (next-auth-options.ts), it is replaced with null but the array length/order persists; there's no indication other than null to users which codes remain used. More importantly, codes are never hashed before storage—only the whole JSON array is symmetrically encrypted. If CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY is ever compromised, all backup codes are exposed in plaintext, unlike typical implementations where backup codes are hashed individually (similar to passwords). This is a weaker security posture than TOTP secret handling for sensitive, one-time credentials.

title: backupCodes state typed as never[] causes implicit any/missing type safety
body: `const [backupCodes, setBackupCodes] = useState([]);` infers backupCodes as never[], relying on implicit any assignment from setBackupCodes(body.backupCodes) where body is untyped JSON. There's no runtime validation that body.backupCodes is actually a string array, so a malformed/missing response could cause .map() to throw or silently render nothing without clear error handling.

title: Setup endpoint regenerates and overwrites backup codes even if 2FA setup is abandoned
body: Calling /setup regenerates backupCodes and persists them to the DB immediately (before the user confirms via /enable). If a user starts setup but never completes it (abandons at QR step), stale backup codes remain stored on the user record while twoFactorEnabled is false. These codes could later be reactivated by just calling /enable without ever being re-shown to the user, since enable.ts (not shown) presumably doesn't regenerate backup codes. This creates a risk of a backup code set associated with a now-stale/forgotten secret being usable without the owner's current knowledge of them, and multiple incomplete setup attempts quietly overwrite previous codes with no audit trail.

title: Backup code match doesn't invalidate/remove the used code
body: In disable.ts, after finding `index` for the supplied backup code, the comment says "we delete all stored backup codes at the end, no need to do this here" — this is true for disable flow since all backupCodes/twoFactorSecret are nulled below. However the index variable is computed but never used otherwise; this works accidentally only because disable always wipes everything. If this logic is ever reused elsewhere (e.g. refactored into a shared helper for other backup-code consuming endpoints), failing to invalidate the specific used code would allow reuse of the same backup code multiple times. There's no shared single-use enforcement abstraction, raising future reuse risk.

title: No E2E coverage for backup-code login or disable-via-backup-code flow
body: The PR description states backup codes can be used for login (clicking 'Lost access') and for disabling 2FA, but the only test changes added are around the backup-codes-download/copy/close UI during setup. The TODO comment explicitly acknowledges missing tests: 'add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup'. This leaves the core new login-with-backup-code and disable-with-backup-code logic (including single-use invalidation) completely untested, despite being significant new auth-critical code paths.

title: Possible crash on undefined destructure when destinationCalendar is empty
body: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` followed by `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"` will throw a TypeError if destinationCalendar is empty/undefined, since mainHostDestinationCalendar will be undefined and `.integration` access throws. This happens whenever MeetLocationType is used without any destinationCalendar set, breaking booking creation.

title: Looping over multiple destinationCalendar entries can create duplicate calendar events per credential
body: createAllCalendarEvents now iterates over every destinationCalendar entry and, when no credentialId is set, creates an event for every matching credential of that integration type. If multiple destinationCalendar entries share the same integration type (e.g., several hosts using google_calendar without credentialId), this results in duplicate event creation for the same credential across iterations, since there's no dedupe logic tracking which credentials have already been used.

title: Team destination calendars collected only from non-first users but based on isTeamEventType/collective check happening after push
body: teamDestinationCalendars is populated inside teamMemberPromises map (over users.slice(1)) regardless of whether isTeamEventType is COLLECTIVE at the time of iteration, relying on the outer `isTeamEventType && eventType.schedulingType === "COLLECTIVE"` check inside the callback. This is correct logically, but the subsequent push after evt creation (`evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`) mutates the array only if eventType.destinationCalendar or organizerUser.destinationCalendar existed to seed the initial array; if both are null, `evt.destinationCalendar` is `null` and `?.push` silently no-ops, meaning team hosts' destination calendars for a collective event are silently dropped when the organizer and event type have no destination calendar configured — which defeats the purpose of this PR (handling collective multi-host destinationCalendar).

title: credential.id passed as externalId-like second positional arg but used as credentialId in createEvent signature mismatch risk
body: createEvent now accepts credentialId as the second parameter in CalendarManager.createEvent, but the exported function `createEvent(credential, calEvent, externalId?)` passes `credential.id` to `calendar.createEvent(calEvent, credential.id)` while naming its own third param `externalId` (unused for that purpose) — the externalId parameter added to the outer createEvent signature is only used for the returned EventResult.externalId field, not forwarded to the calendar.createEvent call, which may cause confusion/maintenance bugs since externalId used for the per-calendar event isn't actually threaded through to the lower level createEvent engines (e.g., Google uses credentialId to find calendar id instead of using passed externalId).

title: updateEvent selectedCalendar lookup compares externalId to itself making filter useless
body: `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` — since externalCalendarId is already truthy-checked in the ternary's other branch, this fallback branch only executes when externalCalendarId is falsy, meaning the `find` predicate `cal.externalId === externalCalendarId` compares against undefined/empty, which will basically never match any destinationCalendar entry. This logic appears broken: it can never find the right calendar as a fallback, so updateEvent calendarId resolution silently fails back to undefined for all cases where externalCalendarId isn't passed in directly, same for deleteEvent (line 317) and CalendarService.ts's listCalendars via similar logic in packages/lib/CalendarService.ts and larkcalendar's code.

title: Unsafe access of mainHostDestinationCalendar when destinationCalendar array is empty
body: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` can yield `undefined` when the array is empty, yet the next line does `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"` without an optional chain, which will throw a TypeError if destinationCalendar is an empty array (a valid state introduced by this PR). This will crash event creation for any booking where no destination calendar resolves.

title: Mutating evt.destinationCalendar via push creates possible undefined access and side effects on shared array
body: `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is only guarded by optional chaining on `destinationCalendar` but when it's `null` (the fallback branch sets it to `null`), the push silently no-ops instead of including team members' calendars, defeating the purpose of this PR (multi-host destinationCalendar support) for the common case where neither eventType nor organizer has a destinationCalendar set but team hosts do with COLLECTIVE scheduling.

title: Booking.destinationCalendar relation only connects first calendar, losing multi-host information
body: When persisting the booking, `destinationCalendar: { connect: { id: evt.destinationCalendar[0].id } }` only connects the first calendar in the array to the Booking model (which still has a single destinationCalendar relation). For collective events with multiple hosts' destination calendars, only the first host's calendar reference is persisted on the booking record, so later reads of booking.destinationCalendar (e.g. in handleCancelBooking) will not reflect all hosts' calendars, breaking cancellation/reschedule for non-first hosts.

title: N+1 credential fetch inside loop over destinationCalendar entries
body: `createAllCalendarEvents` and `updateAllCalendarEvents` now loop over all destination calendars/calendar references and, for every entry whose credential isn't already cached, issue a separate `prisma.credential.findUnique` call. For events with many hosts this results in multiple sequential DB round-trips per event creation/update instead of a single batched query, which could meaningfully slow down booking creation for larger collective/round-robin events.

title: Inconsistent destinationCalendar assertions across webhook e2e tests
body: The BOOKING_CREATED and BOOKING_REQUESTED tests still assert `destinationCalendar: null` while BOOKING_REJECTED was updated to `destinationCalendar: []`. Since destinationCalendar is now always an array (or null when truly undefined per handleNewBooking), these inconsistent expectations suggest the other two test blocks were not updated to match the new array-based contract, risking either silent pass due to loose matchObject or future breakage once the underlying code is fully normalized.

title: loadUsers no longer selects organization.slug, used downstream
body: The rewritten loadUsers() for the eventTypeId path (hosts/eventType.users branch) drops the `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` field that was previously fetched for all users in the non-dynamic case. If any downstream code (e.g. booking links, redirect logic) relies on `user.organization.slug` for users loaded via the eventType.hosts/users path, it will now be undefined, since that field is only fetched in the dynamicUserList branch now.

title: Unsafe access to possibly undefined destinationCalendar element
body: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` can yield `undefined` if the array is empty, but the next line accesses `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without an optional chain or null check, causing a TypeError ("Cannot read properties of undefined") whenever no destination calendar exists for the event (e.g., falling back to default calendar). This will throw at runtime for the common case of a user without a destination calendar set.

title: createEvent passes credential.id as externalId-unrelated 3rd param inconsistently
body: createEvent in CalendarManager now accepts an optional `externalId` parameter and passes `credential.id` as the calendar's createEvent `credentialId` parameter, but the resulting `externalId` field in the EventResult is just whatever was passed in by the caller (often undefined when called without it, e.g. for non-traditional/other_calendar paths and the fallback path). This means `referencesToCreate` built from `result.externalId` in EventManager.ts will often be `undefined`, silently losing the destination calendar's externalId in those paths which previously worked via `evt.destinationCalendar.externalId`. This could cause the correct calendar to not be updated when later referencing it.

title: N+1 DB queries fetching credentials per destination calendar
body: Inside createAllCalendarEvents, for every `destination` in `event.destinationCalendar` with a `credentialId` not already present in `this.calendarCredentials`, a separate `prisma.credential.findUnique` call is issued inside the loop. For events with many hosts/destination calendars, this results in many sequential DB round trips instead of batching with `findMany`, significantly increasing booking creation/update latency. The same pattern is repeated in updateAllCalendarEvents (lines ~516-541).

title: loadUsers organization slug field dropped for dynamic bookings
body: The original query for dynamic event bookings selected `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` on top of userSelect.select. The rewritten loadUsers function in the `!eventTypeId` branch omits `organization` from the select entirely, so `users[].organization` will be undefined downstream (e.g. when building org-aware links or redirects for dynamic bookings), silently breaking that feature path.

title: loadUsers falls back incorrectly when eventType.hosts is empty for non-dynamic events
body: When eventTypeId is set and `eventType.hosts` is empty/undefined, the function returns `eventType.users` directly without mapping in `isFixed`, unlike the hosts branch which always sets `isFixed`. Downstream code (e.g., ensureAvailableUsers) relies on `isFixed` property; falling back silently without it may cause assumptions elsewhere (`isFixed` undefined) to behave differently than before, where `eventType.users || []` was used but callers may expect isFixed consistently set after this refactor given the surrounding logic changes with COLLECTIVE host handling.

title: teamMemberPromises destinationCalendar collection happens as a side effect inside map, order not guaranteed with Promise.all
body: teamDestinationCalendars.push(...) is performed as a side effect within the async map callback passed to users.slice(1).map, then awaited via Promise.all. Because the push happens synchronously before the async getTranslation resolves, order is fine, but if any promise in the array rejects, partially mutated teamDestinationCalendars will already contain some calendars leading to inconsistent state on partial failure. More importantly, destination calendars for non-collective team events are silently dropped (not pushed) but every team member's email/name truthfully still gets added as an attendee — review whether skipping calendar aggregation for ROUND_ROBIN was intentional, since those hosts' destination calendars won't receive the event either, which seems to defeat part of the PR's purpose of supporting multiple hosts generally.

title: destinationCalendar connect only uses first calendar when booking multiple hosts' calendars
body: After building `evt.destinationCalendar` as an array (potentially containing several hosts' destination calendars for collective events), the Prisma booking creation only connects `evt.destinationCalendar[0].id` to the booking's single `destinationCalendar` relation. This means only the first host's destination calendar reference is persisted on the Booking record, even though createAllCalendarEvents will create events on all hosts' calendars. Subsequent updates/cancellations relying on `booking.destinationCalendar` (a single relation) will only ever see one calendar, breaking calendar sync during reschedule/cancel for the other hosts, since those flows build `destinationCalendar` as `[booking.destinationCalendar]` (single) throughout other files (handleCancelBooking.ts, confirm.handler.ts, etc.).

title: updateEvent calendar lookup logic is broken: compares externalId to itself
body: `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` is only reached when `externalCalendarId` is falsy (due to the ternary), meaning this find will always compare each `cal.externalId` against a falsy `externalCalendarId`, which will never match any valid calendar externalId. Effectively, when no externalCalendarId is explicitly passed, `selectedCalendar` always resolves to `undefined`, silently breaking calendar id resolution rather than falling back to the destination calendar's externalId as likely intended (e.g., previously `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`). Same issue appears in deleteEvent (line ~317).

title: Error swallowed silently without logging in updateAllCalendarEvents catch block
body: The removed `console.error(message)` call in the catch block of updateAllCalendarEvents means errors during calendar update are no longer logged anywhere before being converted into a resolved (non-throwing) promise, making failures harder to diagnose in production.

title: Non-constant-time secret comparison and header lookup allows timing/array edge cases
body: The webhook secret check uses `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. Header values can be arrays (e.g., duplicate headers), in which case the comparison will always be false/true in unexpected ways, and more importantly a plain `!==` string compare is vulnerable to timing attacks on the secret. A constant-time comparison (e.g., crypto.timingSafeEqual) should be used instead, and the header value should be normalized to a string before comparison.

title: No rate limiting or method check on credential sync webhook
body: The handler does not verify req.method (so GET/PUT/etc. are all accepted) and has no rate limiting. Combined with the weak secret comparison, this endpoint that creates/updates user credentials is more exposed to brute force or misuse than it should be for a sensitive, cross-tenant credential-writing endpoint.

title: appId lookup mismatches credential.appId (slug vs appMetadata.slug) potentially inconsistent, and type cast assumptions
body: `appMetadata.slug` is used for both `appId` filter and create, and `appMetadata.type` for `type`, but there is no validation that these fields exist/match the expected shape of app store metadata beyond a loose JS object check. If `appMetadata.type` is undefined (some metadata entries may lack `type`), the credential will be created with type `undefined`, silently breaking later type-based lookups used by CalendarService/VideoApiAdapter constructors (which key off `credential.type`).

title: symmetricDecrypt called with empty key fallback can throw unclear errors or decrypt incorrectly
body: `process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY || ""` silently falls back to an empty string key if the env var is unset, even though APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED already requires both CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET and CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY to be set per constants.ts. If somehow unset at runtime (race/misconfiguration), this produces either a cryptic crypto error or a wrong decryption rather than a clear validation error at the top of the handler.

title: Missing prisma import causes runtime ReferenceError
body: The new code in `getClient` calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` but `prisma` is never imported in this file (no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`). This will throw `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined` at runtime whenever Salesforce credentials are refreshed, breaking the Salesforce calendar refresh flow entirely.

title: Token refresh now happens unconditionally on every client creation, ignoring expiry/validity
body: Previously `getClient` likely only refreshed when needed; now it unconditionally calls the Salesforce OAuth refresh endpoint every time a `SalesforceCalendarService` is constructed, for every API call (create/update/delete event, availability). This causes excessive refresh-token usage, potential rate limiting/token invalidation by Salesforce (refresh tokens can become single-use leading to race conditions on concurrent requests), and performance overhead on every operation.

title: Removed error logging when refresh token response fails validation
body: The original code logged `tokenResponse.error` and the raw MS response via console.error when `refreshTokenResponseSchema.safeParse` failed. This diagnostic logging was removed when switching to `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, and `parseRefreshTokenResponse` only throws a generic "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" error without surfacing the actual Zod error or API response, making production debugging of OAuth refresh failures much harder.

title: Refresh token response mutated to literal string "refresh_token" when missing, risking credential corruption
body: When `refresh_token` is absent from the response, `parseRefreshTokenResponse` sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` — a literal placeholder string rather than preserving the existing refresh token or leaving it undefined. If this value is persisted to the credential record (as several call sites do, e.g. salesforce/zoho CalendarService), it will overwrite a valid refresh token with the literal string "refresh_token", breaking future refresh attempts and effectively invalidating the credential silently.

title: External credential-sync endpoint response shape not validated against call site expectations
body: When app credential syncing is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw fetch `Response` from `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` instead of invoking `refreshFunction`. Call sites generally assume either a `Response`-like object (then call `.json()`/`handleErrorsJson`) or a provider SDK response object (e.g., HubSpot's `createToken()`, axios responses with `.data`). Because the self-hosted endpoint returns a plain fetch Response while the provider SDK calls (e.g., hubspotClient.oauth.tokensApi.createToken, axios) return different shapes, mixing these paths behind one generic function silently breaks providers whose refresh path expects a non-fetch response shape (e.g., HubSpot, Zoho, Salesforce axios-based calls use `.data`, but the synced response is a raw Response with no `.data`).

title: Non-constant-time secret comparison and header injection risk
body: The webhook secret check uses `!==` for comparison instead of a constant-time comparison function, which can leak timing information to attackers attempting to brute-force the secret. Additionally there's no rate limiting on this endpoint, making brute-force attacks on the webhook secret more feasible.

title: Unhandled zod parse errors returns 500 instead of 400
body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws if validation fails, but there's no try/catch or error handler around it, so malformed requests will cause an unhandled exception / 500 error rather than a clean 400 response.

title: Decryption failures and malformed JSON not handled
body: `symmetricDecrypt` and `JSON.parse` can both throw (e.g., wrong encryption key, corrupted payload, or no payload). There is no try/catch, so these errors will crash the handler and leak a generic 500 instead of a controlled error response. Also, if `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is unset, decryption proceeds with an empty string key silently.

title: Credential uniqueness query doesn't guard against multiple user credentials for same app
body: `findFirst` is used to locate an existing credential by `userId` and `appId`, but since a user can have multiple credentials for the same app type (as seen in other parts of this PR, e.g. office365video/zoom explicitly deleting duplicates), this could silently update the wrong credential, especially when a user has installed the same app more than once (e.g., team credentials vs personal).

title: Minimum token schema always resolves to the last defined computed property
body: `minimumTokenResponseSchema` defines two computed properties both using `z.string()`-based keys (`[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`), which because they are not literal strings evaluate to object keys like `"ZodString"`; this makes the intended "any numeric property is the expiry" and "other properties optional" catch-alls non-functional. The schema effectively never validates arbitrary extra keys as intended, so when `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` is set, almost any response other than access_token-only objects will fail parsing, breaking refresh for self-hosted syncing.

title: Credential sync endpoint called without authentication/secret
body: The call to `process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` in a POST body but includes no authentication header, API key, or shared secret, even though a `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`/`CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` env var exists for the reverse direction (self-hoster → Cal.com). This endpoint can be impersonated or man-in-the-middled by anyone who knows (or guesses) the self-hoster's sync URL, allowing an attacker to retrieve access tokens for arbitrary `calcomUserId` values if the self-hosted endpoint doesn't do its own strict validation.

title: Removed error logging path for invalid refreshed token responses
body: The diff removes the `console.error` logging that reported the zodError and MS response when the refreshed token failed validation. Now failures silently fall through, making it much harder to diagnose refresh token failures in production, especially newly introduced via `parseRefreshTokenResponse` which can throw instead but the surrounding try/catch (if any) isn't shown here to handle that thrown error gracefully, risking an unhandled rejection and losing diagnostic context.

title: Missing prisma import for new credential update call
body: `CalendarService.ts` now calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` inside `getClient`, but the diff/file shown does not import `prisma` anywhere in this file (no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`). This will cause a reference error / fail to compile at runtime, breaking the Salesforce calendar refresh flow entirely.

title: Salesforce token now refreshed on every service instantiation, ignoring expiry
body: `getClient` previously likely used existing stored tokens unless expired; now it unconditionally calls the Salesforce OAuth refresh-token endpoint every time `SalesforceCalendarService` is constructed, regardless of whether the current token is still valid. This causes unnecessary API calls per request/booking and could hit Salesforce rate limits, and discards the previously valid access token even when unnecessary refresh happens, which is a behavior change not called out in the PR description.

title: Missing `prisma` import causes compile/runtime failure
body: The new refresh-token logic calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` (and reads `response.json()`), but the file never imports `prisma` from `@calcom/prisma`. Only `getAppKeysFromSlug` and `parseRefreshTokenResponse` were added as imports. This will fail TypeScript compilation (or throw `prisma is not defined` at runtime if type-checking is bypassed), breaking the Salesforce calendar integration entirely.

title: refreshOAuthTokens returns a raw unparsed fetch Response, inconsistent with refreshFunction's return shape
body: When credential syncing is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw `fetch()` Response object directly without calling `.json()`. However, callers assume the shape returned by `refreshFunction()`, which varies per app (e.g. Google Calendar's refreshFunction resolves to `fetchTokens.res`, an object with a `.data` property, not a Response). Code such as `const res = await refreshOAuthTokens(...); const token = res?.data;` will get `undefined` when the self-hosted sync endpoint is used, since a Response object has no `.data` field, breaking token refresh silently when CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT is configured. Similarly in HubSpot's CalendarService the sync-path response is used directly as if it were the already-parsed HubspotToken object (accessing `.expiresIn`), which won't exist on an unparsed fetch Response.

title: minimumTokenResponseSchema's computed keys don't do what's intended
body: The schema uses `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()` as object keys. Calling `.toString()` on a Zod schema instance does not produce a dynamic/generic key matching any string field name; it produces a fixed literal string (e.g. "[object Object]"), so these computed properties define a single, meaningless property name rather than validating 'any additional numeric/unknown fields'. Combined with Zod's default behavior of stripping unrecognized keys from a parsed object, this means that when APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is on, the parsed/stored token data will silently drop fields like `expiry_date`/`refresh_token` that aren't explicitly `access_token`, defeating the purpose of this schema and corrupting stored credentials for self-hosters using credential sync.

title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time `!==`
body: The webhook secret validation uses a direct string comparison (`!==`), which is vulnerable to timing attacks that could let an attacker incrementally guess the shared secret. A constant-time comparison (e.g. `crypto.timingSafeEqual`) should be used for comparing secrets, especially since this endpoint can create/overwrite OAuth credentials for any user.

title: Unhandled exceptions from decryption/parsing produce generic 500 with no safeguards
body: `symmetricDecrypt` and the subsequent `JSON.parse` are not wrapped in try/catch. A malformed or incorrectly-encrypted `keys` payload will throw an unhandled exception, resulting in an unstructured 500 error instead of a clear 400 'invalid payload' response, making debugging harder for self-hosters integrating with this endpoint.

title: Hardcoded redirect URI slug diverges from config-driven value used elsewhere
body: This change replaced the dynamic `${appConfig.slug}` with a hardcoded `zoho-bigin` string in the redirect URI, while `callback.ts` for the same app still builds its redirect URI from `appConfig.slug`. Although currently equivalent, this introduces an inconsistency: if `config.json`'s slug ever changes, the OAuth add and callback URIs would mismatch, breaking the integration flow.

title: No automated tests for new credential-sync webhook endpoint
body: The PR description explicitly states no tests were added ('I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective'). This endpoint performs sensitive operations (creating/updating OAuth credentials for arbitrary users based on an externally supplied userId and a secret header) with no unit/integration test coverage, increasing risk of regressions or security gaps going unnoticed.

title: Incorrect permission check: AND instead of OR for team admin/owner
body: `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`, requiring the user to be BOTH admin and owner simultaneously. This is logically wrong — a team admin who is not the owner (or vice versa) will be denied, defeating the purpose of the variable name. This likely blocks legitimate team admins from adding guests unless they also happen to be the owner.

title: Blacklist filtering is case-sensitive mismatch
body: Blacklisted emails are lowercased (`blacklistedGuestEmails`), but `guests` input emails are compared as-is without lowercasing (`!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`). If a user submits an email in a different case than the blacklist entry, the blacklist check silently fails to filter it out.

title: EventManager built with wrong user credentials
body: `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` fetches credentials for the requesting user, but the booking's calendar should be updated using the organizer's (booking owner's) credentials, not necessarily the current ctx user (who could be an attendee or team admin per the earlier permission check). This can cause calendar updates to fail silently or use wrong calendar accounts when the acting user differs from the booking owner.

title: New guest attendees created with empty name
body: Guests added via this flow get `name: ""` persisted to the attendees table, unlike organically-booked attendees which typically have proper names. This could break UI elements and emails that rely on attendee.name (e.g., `FirstAttendee`/`Attendee` components fall back to email when name is falsy, but other consumers of attendee data may not handle empty string gracefully).

title: Email send failures silently swallowed without proper logging
body: The catch block only does `console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails")` without logging the actual error (`err`) or using the structured logger used elsewhere in the codebase (`@calcom/lib/logger`). This makes debugging failed guest-notification emails difficult in production.

title: Zod schema recreated on every render
body: `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` is created inside the component body on every render instead of being hoisted to module scope. This is a minor but unnecessary recomputation on every re-render of the dialog.

title: Empty string guest input passes validation incorrectly
body: `multiEmailValue` is initialized as `[""]` and the dialog allows submitting with default state. `z.array(z.string().email())` will reject an empty string, so this particular case would fail, but if a user removes rows down to zero entries the `handleAdd` early-returns only on `length === 0`; however there's no guard preventing submission with duplicate/trimmed whitespace-only entries which may pass or fail inconsistently with server-side validation (`z.string().email()` in addGuests.schema.ts), causing inconsistent UX between client validation message and server error.

title: Permission check is incorrectly ANDed, locking out legitimate team admins/owners
body: `isTeamAdminOrOwner` uses `&&` between `isTeamAdmin` and `isTeamOwner`, meaning a user must be BOTH admin AND owner simultaneously to pass. In practice a user is normally either an admin or an owner, not both, so this condition will almost always evaluate false, breaking the intended authorization path for team admins/owners who aren't the booking organizer or an attendee. This should be `||`.

title: Blacklist/duplicate filtering is case-sensitive, inconsistent with blacklist lowercasing
body: `blacklistedGuestEmails` are lowercased, but `uniqueGuests` comparisons against `attendee.email` and `blacklistedGuestEmails` use the raw, non-lowercased `guest` value. An email entered with different casing (e.g. `John@Example.com`) will not match an already-existing attendee with the same address in lowercase, nor match a blacklisted entry, allowing duplicates or bypassing blacklist checks.

title: EventManager instantiated with wrong user context for credentials
body: `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` fetches credentials for the currently logged-in user (who could be an attendee adding guests), not for the booking organizer. Then `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials })` uses the requesting user's identity/credentials for calendar updates, which is likely wrong when an attendee (not the organizer) is the one calling this endpoint — calendar events should be updated via the organizer's calendar credentials, not the attendee's. This can lead to calendar updates failing silently or being made with incorrect account context.

title: New attendee name hardcoded to empty string
body: `guestsFullDetails` sets `name: ""` for every new guest with no way to supply one. This means added guests will show with blank names everywhere in the UI (emails, attendee lists) instead of at least falling back to the email or omitting name display gracefully.
