title: containsHtml regex may false-negative for self-closing or uppercase tags
body:
HTML_TAGS pattern `<[a-z]+[^>]*>` only matches lowercase tag names and does not account for self-closing tags like `
` without a space, or tags with uppercase letters. If the English source uses a tag not matching this pattern (e.g., `
` or malformed markup), containsHtml returns false, causing the stricter POLICY_NO_HTML to be applied even though English technically contains HTML-like markup, potentially producing false-positive 'Illegal HTML' errors in translations that mirror the English content.

title: santizeAnchors mutates value incrementally during find() iteration, risking IndexOutOfBounds/incorrect removal with duplicate anchors
body: The loop calls `matcher.find()` on the original `value` string, but `value` itself is updated inside the loop body via replaceFirst. Because `matcher` keeps iterating over the original string snapshot (Matcher is bound to the original CharSequence, not the mutated `value` variable), find() positions and group() text no longer correspond to the current state of `value` once replacements have happened, especially when the same anchor tag occurs multiple times. This can produce incorrect sanitization results for messages with repeated or multiple anchor tags, though it won't throw since Matcher operates on the original immutable string, but results are quietly wrong for multi-anchor messages.

title: isAccessTokenId matcher logic inverted
body: The matchesSafely method returns false when the actual grant shortcut equals the expected shortcut: `if (items[0].substring(3,5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`. This inverts the intended check — it should return false (fail) when the shortcut does NOT match, but as written it fails precisely when it matches and otherwise falls through to return true even for wrong shortcuts. This means tests using isAccessTokenId effectively never properly validate the grant type shortcut and will reject the correct token IDs, causing false test failures or false negatives (letting incorrect token IDs pass undetected).

title: Wrong variable null-checked for rawTokenId
body: In the constructor, `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` checks `grantType` again instead of `rawTokenId`. As a result, a null `rawTokenId` will not be caught here, potentially leading to NPEs later when `rawTokenId` is used (e.g., string concatenation producing "null" instead of failing fast).

title: Hardcoded refresh grant type note set unconditionally on token refresh/validation path
body: In validateToken, `clientSessionCtx.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, OAuth2Constants.REFRESH_TOKEN);` is set unconditionally whenever a token is being recreated/validated. This overwrites whatever grant type was originally used to create the client session context (e.g., authorization_code, device_code, ciba), even when this path is invoked for scenarios other than classic refresh-token grant (e.g. offline token refresh paths reused elsewhere), causing the encoded token ID's grant-type shortcut to incorrectly always read as 'rt' instead of the actual originating grant, undermining the stated purpose of the feature (correctly identifying grant type from the token ID).

title: Non-atomic cache refresh for grant type shortcuts can race under concurrent token issuance
body: getShortcutByGrantType and getGrantTypeByShortcut perform read-then-conditionally-write operations on ConcurrentHashMap without synchronization across the two maps (grantsByShortcuts/grantsToShortcuts). Although ConcurrentHashMap operations are individually thread-safe, the two maps can become inconsistent between each other under concurrent provider deployment/refresh scenarios, and the duplicate-shortcut validation done once in postInit is not re-run during runtime cache refresh, so a newly deployed grant type with a shortcut colliding with an existing one would silently overwrite entries without the earlier safety check that aborts startup.

title: Access token ID format changed, breaking consumers that assume raw UUID token IDs
body: Token IDs are now encoded with a 6-character context prefix followed by ':' and the raw UUID (e.g. `onrtac:1f65761e-...`). Any external or internal code/tests that previously assumed access token 'jti'/id is a plain UUID (e.g. length 36, UUID format validations, log parsing, DB lookups keyed by token id) will break. The PR already needed to update AssertEvents' isUUID-based matchers for this reason, indicating this is a breaking format change that should be clearly called out as such for downstream integrations relying on jti format.

title: isAccessTokenId matcher logic inverted
body: In isAccessTokenId(), the condition `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` returns false when the shortcut MATCHES the expected value, and implicitly returns true (falls through to isUUID check) when it does NOT match. This is backwards: the matcher should fail (return false) when the shortcut does not equal the expected grant shortcut, and succeed when it does. As written, tests using this matcher will pass when the grant type encoding is wrong and fail when it's correct, defeating the purpose of the assertion and potentially masking real encoding bugs.

title: Refresh grant type hardcoded instead of using actual context grant type
body: In validateToken (used when refreshing tokens), `clientSessionCtx.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, OAuth2Constants.REFRESH_TOKEN)` unconditionally sets the grant type to refresh_token. However this method can be invoked in different token-refresh contexts (e.g., token-exchange or other flows reusing validateToken), so hardcoding REFRESH_TOKEN may encode an incorrect grant-type shortcut into the new access token ID, misleading consumers who rely on the encoded context for optimization decisions.

title: Lazy-refresh of grant maps has race/DoS potential and no synchronization
body: getShortcutByGrantType/getGrantTypeByShortcut fall back to scanning all OAuth2GrantType factories and mutating the shared ConcurrentHashMap when a grant type/shortcut is unknown. If an attacker repeatedly sends access tokens with bogus/invalid grant shortcuts, each lookup triggers a full stream scan of all grant type factories (via sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream) on every call without caching the negative result, which can be used for a minor CPU-amplification/DoS vector, and there's no synchronization protecting concurrent writes to the two maps, which could leave them transiently inconsistent under concurrent access.

title: Wrong variable null-checked in constructor
body: In the AccessTokenContext constructor, the null check `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` checks `grantType` again instead of `rawTokenId`. As a result, passing a null rawTokenId will not throw the intended NPE with a correct message, and a null rawTokenId can slip through into token ID encoding, producing a malformed token ID (e.g., 'xxxxx:null').

title: isAccessTokenId matcher logic inverted
body: In `isAccessTokenId`, the condition `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` returns false when the shortcut MATCHES the expected value, which is backwards — it should return false when it does NOT match. As written, the matcher will fail for the correct grant shortcut and pass for any other shortcut, making this test helper assert the wrong thing (effectively testing that the grant shortcut is NOT the expected one).

title: Overwriting GRANT_TYPE on refresh may be incorrect for offline tokens
body: In validateToken, `clientSessionCtx.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, OAuth2Constants.REFRESH_TOKEN)` is unconditionally set when refreshing a token. This loses the original grant type context (e.g., device flow, CIBA) that produced the original token, and conflicts with session restored by `clientSessionCtx` built from stored client session, potentially producing inconsistent/incorrect token id encoding for subsequent refreshes of offline/CIBA/device sessions, which the PR explicitly aims to make visible for optimization.

title: Potential race in lazy-refresh of grant maps
body: getShortcutByGrantType/getGrantTypeByShortcut lazily refresh grantsByShortcuts/grantsToShortcuts maps using ConcurrentHashMap, but updates are not atomic across both maps (two separate put calls), so concurrent threads could observe a `grantsByShortcuts` entry without the corresponding `grantsToShortcuts` entry (or vice versa), risking inconsistent round-trip encode/decode under concurrent load right after a new grant type provider is deployed.

title: Wrong variable null-checked in constructor
body: The constructor checks `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` twice instead of checking `rawTokenId`. This means a null `rawTokenId` will not be caught here and will later throw a NullPointerException elsewhere (or silently produce a malformed token id), with a misleading error message if the check were ever triggered.

title: Backward-compat token ids without ':' prefix accepted silently
body: getTokenContextFromTokenId treats any token id without a ':' delimiter as an old/unencoded token id and returns UNKNOWN context without validation. This is a reasonable compatibility fallback, but there's no test or doc describing what happens for malformed ids that happen to contain a ':' but aren't actually encoded by this scheme (e.g., from a different IdP-issued string reused as a token id), which could throw unexpected IllegalArgumentException during introspection/userinfo instead of gracefully falling back as 'unknown'.

title: updateCredential return value used ambiguously to detect userStorage success
body: createRecoveryCodesCredential relies on user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...) returning true to mean 'created in user storage'. However updateCredential's contract is generic (used for updating any credential type) and some storage providers may return true for reasons unrelated to actually persisting a new recovery-codes credential (e.g. no-op success), or false even though partially processed. This mirrors the same questionable pattern already used for OTP but duplicates the ambiguity for a new credential type without additional safety checks (e.g. verifying supportsCredentialType first), risking silently creating duplicate or no credential in edge-case federated providers.

title: Missing null checks on required form parameters before use
body: generatedCodesString, generatedAtTimeString, and generatedUserLabel are read from form parameters without null checks before being used in generatedAtTimeString.equals(...) and Long.valueOf(generatedAtTimeString). If an attacker/misbehaving client submits the required action without these hidden fields, this throws NPE/NumberFormatException instead of being handled gracefully, which existed before but is still unaddressed by this change that otherwise reworks the flow.

title: getCredentials does not use JsonSerialization generics safely
body: JsonSerialization.readValue(myUser.recoveryCodes.getCredentialData(), List.class) uses a raw List type (unchecked generic cast), risking a ClassCastException at runtime if the stored JSON isn't a List<String>, and losing compile-time type safety. This is minor but inconsistent with the typed usage pattern used elsewhere (e.g., CredentialHelper uses List<String> directly).

title: New test only covers single recovery code usage, not exhaustion/removal flow
body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only validates login with the first recovery code (index 0) stored in the federated/user-storage provider. It does not test the removeStoredCredentialById or RequiredAction re-trigger path from RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator when allCodesUsed() is true for a user-storage-backed credential, which is directly relevant to the PR's goal of supporting recovery codes in user storage and could hide bugs in that specific interaction (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById may not be supported for federated storage credentials).

title: No fallback/error handling if neither user storage nor local credential provider accept the credential
body: createRecoveryCodesCredential relies on user.credentialManager().updateCredential returning false to fall back to the local provider, but it doesn't check whether recoveryCodeCredentialProvider itself is null (e.g. if the 'keycloak-recovery-authn-codes' provider isn't registered) or handle the case where createCredential fails. Unlike createOTPCredential, there's no return value or validation step, so callers cannot detect failures, potentially leaving the user without a recovery credential silently.

title: getCredentials ignores password credential and uses raw List type
body: The newly added getCredentials() method only returns OTP and recovery-code credentials, omitting the password credential entirely, which may be inconsistent with how getCredentials is expected to enumerate all credentials for a user. Also, JsonSerialization.readValue(..., List.class) with no generic type parameter produces unchecked raw List<Object>, which could cause ClassCastException issues downstream when code expects List<String>.

title: No null/format validation on required action form parameters
body: generatedCodesString, generatedAtTimeString are used directly (e.g. generatedAtTimeString.equals(...), Long.valueOf(generatedAtTimeString), generatedCodesString.split(",")) without null checks. If these hidden fields are missing from the form submission (e.g. due to a malformed request), this will throw an NPE or NumberFormatException instead of being handled gracefully, which was already a pre-existing issue but is now exercised via the new createRecoveryCodesCredential flow without added safety.

title: No fallback/error handling when both userStorage and local credential provider fail
body: createRecoveryCodesCredential() calls user.credentialManager().updateCredential() and if that returns false, falls back to recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(). However there is no check of the return value of createCredential nor any indication to the caller whether credential creation succeeded (unlike createOTPCredential which returns a boolean). If both the user storage update and local creation fail silently (e.g. provider returns null), the required action (RecoveryAuthnCodesAction) will still call reqActionContext.success() unconditionally, leading to users believing recovery codes were saved when they were not.

title: Unchecked raw List type used for recovery code comparisons
body: In isValid(), generatedKeys is declared as a raw List (no generic type), and compared with input.getChallengeResponse() via key.equals(...). Since JsonSerialization.readValue deserializes JSON array elements that could be any type, this raises an unchecked-cast/type-safety concern and makes it brittle if the recovery code data format changes. This should use List<String> and verify hashed comparisons, consistent with RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.verifyRecoveryCodeInput used elsewhere, rather than ad hoc plain-text equality checking against raw codes (potential inconsistency with how codes are hashed/stored in the real implementation).

title: generatedCodes passed to createRecoveryCodesCredential are raw strings, not re-validated against credentialModel hashed codes
body: The credentialModel already contains hashed recovery codes constructed via createFromValues, but generatedCodes (raw, unhashed) is passed separately into createRecoveryCodesCredential, which re-serializes the raw codes into JSON for the user-storage case. This duplicates data between credentialModel and generatedCodes and could get out of sync if createFromValues logic changes (e.g., different hash algorithm or code transformation), silently storing different codes in user storage vs local DB storage.

title: getSubGroupsCount contract change may break callers expecting non-null
body: getSubGroupsCount() now returns null when the underlying group model cannot be loaded (modelSupplier.get() returns null), whereas previously it would throw an NPE calling getGroupModel().getSubGroupsCount(). Callers of GroupModel#getSubGroupsCount() (e.g. GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount which does representation.setSubGroupCount(group.getSubGroupsCount())) may not expect a null Long and could behave unexpectedly (e.g. silently showing no count, or NPE if later code unboxes the value). This silently changes the method's contract without updating callers or documenting the new null-return semantics.

title: Test spawns thread with no join/cleanup and busy-loops without any delay or timeout
body: The new createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti test starts a background thread that tightly loops calling groups() until deletedAll is set, but never joins the thread or verifies it has actually finished before the test method returns. If the background thread throws an exception after the main thread exits (e.g., during the final iteration), it's recorded into caughtExceptions but the assertion may run before the thread observes deletedAll and exits, causing flakiness. There's also no timeout/retry bound, so a stuck condition could hang resources indefinitely across test runs sharing the JVM. The lack of thread.join() means the test can finish while the reader thread is still running, polluting subsequent tests or causing non-deterministic failures.

title: getSubGroupsCount can now return null, breaking Long contract and callers expecting a count
body: getSubGroupsCount() now returns null when modelSupplier.get() returns null (group not found). GroupModel.getSubGroupsCount() is declared to return a count; callers (e.g. GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount, which does representation.setSubGroupCount(group.getSubGroupsCount())) may not expect null and could NPE on unboxing or produce inconsistent representations elsewhere. This silently changes the method's contract without updating callers or interface docs.

title: New concurrency test lacks join/synchronization, making it potentially flaky
body: The new test starts a background thread that polls groups() while the main thread deletes groups, but never joins the thread or waits for it to actually stop reading after deletedAll is set. The reader thread could still be in the middle of a request when the test method returns, and any exception thrown after the final deletedAll check won't be captured, making the test non-deterministic (could pass despite races, or fail due to unrelated flakiness since there's no timeout/join).

title: getSubGroupsCount can now return null, breaking primitive callers
body: getSubGroupsCount() previously always delegated to a non-null model via getGroupModel(); now when modelSupplier.get() returns null (group deleted concurrently), the method returns null instead of throwing. GroupModel.getSubGroupsCount() is declared to return Long, but any caller treating this as always non-null (e.g. unboxing to long, or GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount which calls representation.setSubGroupCount(group.getSubGroupsCount())) may now NPE downstream or silently store a null subgroup count where previously an exception made the failure obvious. This changes the contract silently without updating callers/docs.

title: New concurrency test can leave a stray background thread and swallow failures
body: The new test starts a raw Thread that loops until deletedAll is set, but there is no join() after `deletedAll.set(true)`, so the test may finish and assert before the thread observes the flag and before any trailing exception is recorded; the thread could also still be running when the test process exits. The lack of join() makes the assertion on caughtExceptions racy and the test potentially flaky or not actually exercising the fixed race before assertions run.

title: Client-controlled query param bypasses intended pagination restrictions and permission check is insufficient
body: The endpoint lets any authenticated user toggle `optimized_pagination=true` and relies on `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` to gate access. However, the `enable_advanced_features` path in OptimizedCursorPaginator allows arbitrary negative offsets supplied directly by the client cursor (`cursor.offset`), which is attacker-controlled input independent of this permission check. A user with global access (which is not necessarily a superuser, e.g. any org owner) can craft cursors with large negative offsets to access rows outside the normal paginated window, since the comment in paginator.py asserts "permissions are checked at the queryset level" but no actual queryset-level restriction is added — it's just a slice offset trick. This could allow reading unintended rows or causing unexpected DB query costs.

title: Negative offset slicing produces invalid/undefined queryset behavior
body: When `self.enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing/slicing (unlike Python lists) and will raise `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` at runtime. This means any client passing a negative-offset cursor to this paginator will cause a 500 error instead of being handled gracefully, contradicting the PR's claim of 'enhanced' pagination support.

title: Incorrect result-trimming condition when negative offset is used
body: The check `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` assumes `offset` is always non-negative (consistent with the original BasePaginator). When `enable_advanced_features` allows negative offsets, this arithmetic becomes incorrect, potentially leaving an extra row in `results` or stripping a valid row off the end, producing incorrect pagination boundaries/cursors even if the earlier negative-slice crash were fixed.

title: No tests added for new OptimizedCursorPaginator
body: The PR adds an entirely new paginator class (OptimizedCursorPaginator) with non-trivial new behavior (negative offset handling, enable_advanced_features flag) but includes no unit tests. Given the negative-offset slicing bug and altered trimming logic, this lack of test coverage means the regression would not be caught before release.

title: Undocumented/experimental query parameter with no validation or documentation
body: `optimized_pagination` is read directly from `request.GET` without being part of `AuditLogQueryParamSerializer`, so it's unvalidated and undocumented. There's no changelog, API doc update, or test added demonstrating the new behavior, making it hard for consumers or reviewers to know this flag exists and is intentional versus leftover debug/test code (the PR description just says "Test 1").

title: Negative offset bypasses pagination boundaries, allowing unauthorized data access
body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0, the code uses queryset[start_offset:stop] with a negative start_offset directly. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing/slicing (unlike Python lists) - this will raise an AssertionError/ValueError at runtime ("Negative indexing is not supported"), not perform any 'advanced bidirectional pagination' as the comment claims. This makes the advertised feature non-functional and will crash the endpoint whenever a client sends a negative offset. Additionally the comment claiming 'this is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level' is misleading since offset manipulation doesn't bypass the WHERE filters, but the crash itself is a real bug.

title: enable_advanced_features flag doesn't actually change behavior safely due to paginator bug
body: The endpoint allows superusers/global-access members to opt into OptimizedCursorPaginator with enable_advanced_features=True via a GET query param. Since this triggers the broken negative-offset code path in paginator.py (which fails on real Django querysets), any client-controlled request with a crafted negative offset cursor will cause a server error rather than yielding any actual performance benefit. There's also no test coverage demonstrating this new code path works correctly against a real queryset-backed paginator rather than the in-memory SequencePaginator used elsewhere in tests.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator.get_result with no added safety checks
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator re-implements get_result almost verbatim from BasePaginator, with the sole addition of the broken negative offset branch. This duplication increases maintenance burden and risk of divergence (e.g., bug fixes to BasePaginator.get_result won't propagate here). No tests were added for this new paginator class despite it introducing new, security-sensitive behavior (bypassing standard pagination offset clamping).

title: Misleading comment about negative offset support
body: The comment states this change 'enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets', but no actual behavior changed here (self.offset = int(offset) was unchanged) and nothing in this file validates or specially handles negative offsets. The comment is misleading documentation suggesting a feature that isn't implemented at this layer, and combined with the broken paginator.py negative-offset code, could lead maintainers to believe negative offsets are a supported, tested feature when they are not.

title: Authorization bypass via client-controlled flag using global_access
body: `enable_advanced` grants advanced pagination (which allows negative offsets, bypassing normal result boundaries) to any user with `is_superuser` or `organization_context.member.has_global_access`. `has_global_access` is a broad flag not necessarily tied to audit log read permissions, and combined with the client-controlled `optimized_pagination=true` query param, this allows a wider set of users than intended to trigger a different, less-tested code path that manipulates raw SQL slicing (negative offsets). This is a privilege-escalation-adjacent risk: a feature flag toggled entirely by request parameters controls which pagination/query logic runs, with no audit or rate limiting around it.

title: Negative offset slicing produces invalid/undefined SQL querysets
body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing/slicing (unlike Python lists) and will raise `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` or similar errors. This will crash the endpoint rather than provide any 'efficient reverse pagination', directly contradicting the claimed functionality and causing 500 errors whenever a negative offset cursor is supplied (which is also client-controlled via the cursor cookie/param).

title: Dead/misleading advanced-features code with no real optimization
body: The class docstring and comments claim 'negative offset support', 'streamlined boundary condition handling', and 'optimized query path for large datasets', but the actual implementation is nearly identical to BasePaginator.get_result except for the broken negative-offset branch. There is no genuine performance optimization (e.g., no index-based seek optimization, no changed query plan) despite the PR title and description promising enhanced pagination performance. This is misleading to future maintainers and reviewers evaluating the actual behavior change.

title: Incorrect extra-row trimming when negative offset branch taken
body: The trimming logic `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` uses the original (pre-negative-offset) `offset` variable, but when the negative-offset branch is used, `start_offset` differs from `offset`. This inconsistency means the extra-row removal check can be wrong, causing an extra row to leak into cursor results or a valid row to be dropped, depending on the sign/magnitude of the offset the queryset lookup actually used.

title: No tests added for new optimized pagination branch
body: The PR introduces an entirely new code path (`OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `enable_advanced_features`) gated by a request parameter and permission check, but no test files are included in the diff. Given the branch changes query semantics (negative offsets) and gates access by permission, there should be tests covering: unauthorized access attempts, negative offset cursors, and equivalence with the standard paginator for typical cases.

title: Comment describes unimplemented feature in Cursor class
body: The added comment claims `self.offset = int(offset)` 'enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets' via negative offsets, but `Cursor` itself does no bounds checking and the actual consumer (`OptimizedCursorPaginator`) mishandles negative offsets (crashes on Django querysets). The comment overstates functionality that is broken elsewhere in the PR, which is confusing for maintainers trying to understand supported Cursor semantics.

title: Insecure/undocumented pagination bypass gated by client-controlled query param
body: `use_optimized = request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"` lets any authenticated caller opt into `OptimizedCursorPaginator` merely by passing a query string, combined with a permission check (`is_superuser or has_global_access`) that is evaluated per-request with no audit trail. This introduces an undocumented, non-reviewed pagination mode in a security-sensitive audit log endpoint. Combined with the negative-offset feature in OptimizedCursorPaginator, it enables bypassing normal page-boundary semantics to query negative offsets directly against the DB-backed queryset, which is unvetted and not covered by any tests added in this PR.

title: Negative offset slicing can throw or produce confusing results
body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` and `cursor.offset < 0`, `start_offset = cursor.offset` is used directly as the slice start on a Django queryset: `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing in slices (raises `AssertionError`/`ValueError` for negative start in slicing), so this will throw at runtime rather than doing what the comment claims ("Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically"). This is untested and will blow up as soon as a negative offset cursor is supplied in combination with `enable_advanced_features=True`.

title: Clamping offset to 0 silently changes pagination semantics for non-prev cursors
body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` was newly introduced in `BasePaginator.get_result`. Previously `offset` (which could theoretically be negative from a malformed/garbage cursor) was used directly; this silently clamps negative offsets to 0 without raising `BadPaginationError`, unlike other paginators in this file (e.g., `OffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`) which explicitly raise `BadPaginationError('Pagination offset cannot be negative')`. This creates inconsistent behavior across paginators and can mask bugs/bad input instead of surfacing an explicit error.

title: Redirect-depth loop bound reduced from 10000 to 1000 without justification
body: The loop bound for following redirect chains was reduced from 10000 to 1000, and the explanatory comment about segment trees of depth up to that limit possibly not joining correctly was removed. For deep span trees exceeding 1000 redirects, segments may silently fail to merge correctly, and there is no comment warning future maintainers of this truncation behavior.

title: zpopmin eviction can discard the segment's root span before flush
body: When `span_count > 1000`, `redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)` evicts the lowest-scored (earliest `end_timestamp_precise`) spans without regard for whether any evicted span is the root/segment span. Since segments are scored by `end_timestamp_precise`, the root span (often the first span to start but potentially not the first to end) could be evicted, silently corrupting flushed segments with missing root-span data and no detection/logging of this data loss. There is no test covering span buffer eviction behavior at the 1000-span boundary.

title: max_segment_spans config no longer enforced
body: The constructor still accepts `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` but the code path in `_load_segment_data` that previously checked `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans` and skipped/logged oversized segments has been removed. Enforcement is now solely delegated to the Lua script's `zpopmin` eviction (capped at 1000), making the `max_segment_spans` parameter dead/misleading code, and removing the previous safety net against oversized segments being loaded into memory on the Python side if eviction is skipped or miscounted (e.g., due to script errors).

title: Unauthenticated-style privilege escalation via query param plus misleading comments
body: `use_optimized`/`enable_advanced` gates the OptimizedCursorPaginator on `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`, triggered purely by a client-supplied query param `optimized_pagination=true`. Combined with OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset handling, this allows a privileged (but not necessarily organization-owner) user with global access to request negative offsets, bypassing normal pagination boundary protections. The comments ("Enable advanced pagination features for authorized administrators") assert safety without any actual validation that negative offsets can't be abused to view out-of-range/deleted data. This needs a security review and either removal or stronger justification/tests.

title: Negative offset slicing can produce incorrect/duplicate results or wrap around
body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when `enable_advanced_features` is True and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start_offset. Django querysets do not support negative indexing the way Python lists do (negative slice indices on QuerySet raise ValueError or behave unexpectedly depending on Django version), so this will either throw at runtime or silently return wrong results. There's no test covering this path (test files for buffer/spans don't test this paginator at all), so this bug is not caught in CI.

title: Clamping offset to 0 silently changes paging semantics for BasePaginator
body: The change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` alters behavior from the previous unconditional `offset`. If `offset` was ever meant to be used as negative in some legitimate codepath (e.g. computed from cursor math elsewhere), clamping silently to 0 changes results without raising an error, making debugging harder. This introduces an undocumented behavior change to the widely-used BasePaginator affecting all paginator consumers (DateTimePaginator, Paginator), not just the new optimized one, with no accompanying tests validating offset-clamping behavior under normal and edge/negative-offset cursor values.

title: Reduced redirect-depth traversal limit from 10000 to 1000 silently breaks deep segment merging
body: The loop limit for following redirect chains was reduced from 10000 to 1000 with no comment explaining why, dropping the original comment noting "segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly." This means segment trees deeper than 1000 spans will now have redirects silently truncated/broken at a much lower threshold than before, a regression for very deep traces, without any test coverage for this specific boundary case.

title: zpopmin eviction count can exceed available members and doesn't account for merges correctly
body: After zunionstore calls, `span_count` is set to the returned cardinality of the unioned set, but if both branches (span_key and parent_key unions) execute, `span_count` is overwritten by the second zunionstore's result rather than reflecting the final cumulative count correctly if logic changes; also when `span_count` is 0 initially (both unions skipped) it falls back to `zcard` which is correct, but if only one union happens and leaves stale state, eviction via `zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)` could evict legitimate spans that were just added before the current span is even added to `set_key`, since this script runs per-span before the current span's own zadd into `set_key` occurs. This can cause newly-ingested spans belonging to the same segment but processed in a later pipeline step to be evicted or the oldest-timestamp spans (by zscore, i.e. end_timestamp_precise) to be dropped even though the real intent is likely to cap by count irrespective of order, which may silently drop arbitrary spans from large segments without a corresponding test added for span-buffer.lua's eviction logic.

title: Insecure feature gating via unauthenticated query parameter
body: `use_optimized` is derived from a plain client-supplied query parameter (`request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"`) with no CSRF/signing protection, and `enable_advanced` relies on `is_superuser` or `has_global_access`. Combined with `OptimizedCursorPaginator`'s negative-offset feature (see paginator.py), this lets any user who happens to have global org access (not necessarily a true superuser) opt into bypassing normal offset bounds. There's no rate limiting or validation that negative offsets stay within sane bounds, so this could be used to scan/exfiltrate audit log entries outside the intended paginated window or cause excessive DB load. At minimum this is an unvetted, security-sensitive code path that should not be toggled by a public query string.

title: Negative offset slicing can return no results or wrap incorrectly, breaking pagination contract
body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start_offset. Django querysets do not support negative indices in slicing (unlike Python lists) — this will raise `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` at runtime for a real QuerySet, immediately crashing the request instead of gracefully handling pagination. This is also inconsistent with the base `BasePaginator.get_result`, which explicitly clamps `offset` to 0 to avoid this exact issue, suggesting the 'advanced' negative-offset branch was never actually run against a real queryset in testing.

title: Redirect loop depth reduced from 10000 to 1000, lost comment about correctness implications
body: The redirect-chasing loop bound was reduced from 10000 to 1000 without adjusting (or re-validating) the previously documented caveat: 'this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly.' Reducing the bound to 1000 makes incorrect joins now possible for segment trees of depth >1000 instead of >10000, a significant regression in correctness for deep span trees, and the explanatory comment was deleted so future maintainers won't know why/how this limit interacts with correctness.

title: Changed from a Redis set to sorted set (zset) with eviction, but zunionstore semantics change payload scoring and silently drop spans
body: The script switched from `sadd`/`sunionstore` (plain set semantics, union does not merge/overwrite values) to `zunionstore` using span payloads as members and timestamps as scores. `zunionstore` aggregates scores by default via SUM when the same member exists in both sets, which is likely never intended here (payloads should be unique per span so this may not trigger immediately, but is semantically fragile). More importantly, this change introduces eviction logic in lines 62-64 (`zpopmin` when span_count > 1000) that silently discards the lowest-scored (oldest timestamp) spans once a segment exceeds 1000 members. This is a data-loss change: spans that overflow the limit are silently dropped from the segment rather than being flagged/logged, which will corrupt or truncate large segments without any observability (contrast with the Python-side `_load_segment_data`, which explicitly logs and metrics when max_segment_bytes is exceeded, but the max_segment_spans python-side guard was removed in this PR, see buffer.py diff removing the span-count-exceeded check).

title: Removed max_segment_spans enforcement and error logging on the Python side
body: The diff removes the block that checked `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans` and logged/metriced 'segment_span_count_exceeded', deleting the segment from processing with visibility. This safety net is now solely delegated to the new Lua-side zpopmin eviction (add-buffer.lua), which silently drops data with no logging/metrics at all. This is a loss of observability for an already risky operation (truncating a segment), and the `max_segment_spans` constructor parameter is now effectively dead/unused in this file (still accepted as a constructor arg but never enforced), which is misleading to future readers of the code.

title: No test coverage added for new 1000-span eviction behavior
body: The PR title and lua changes introduce span eviction when count exceeds 1000, but no test in test_buffer.py exercises this path (e.g., processing >1000 spans in a segment and asserting that only the most recent 1000 are kept, or that evicted spans are dropped as expected). Given this is a data-dropping behavior change, it should have explicit test coverage verifying the eviction count and which spans are retained/dropped.

title: Cache key leaks across org/project combos insecurely and uses hash() non-deterministically across process restarts
body: Using Python's built-in hash() on a tuple of project ids for cache keys is risky: hash() for tuples is stable within a process but PYTHONHASHSEED can randomize hashes for strings in other contexts; more importantly, hash collisions are possible, meaning two different project-id sets could map to the same cache key and return a stale/wrong upsampling decision for an unrelated project set, causing wrong query behavior (either applying or skipping upsampling incorrectly). Should use a stable encoding (e.g. a sorted comma-joined string) instead of hash().

title: Cached boolean conflated with None causes cache to never be effectively used when eligibility is False
body: cache.get(cache_key) returning None is used to detect cache miss, but the cached value is itself a boolean that is False when the project set is not eligible. Depending on the cache backend, False may be stored/retrieved fine distinct from None, but this pattern is fragile — if the cache backend ever returns None for a falsy stored boolean (e.g. after serialization quirks or if cache.get default differs), the eligibility check will silently recompute every time, negating the intended performance optimization. More importantly, this means ineligible results are cached as `False` for 60s causing stale negative decisions if the allowlist is updated during that window, which combined with no cache invalidation call ever being wired in (see invalidate_upsampling_cache, which doesn't appear to be called anywhere) means allowlist updates take up to 60s to take effect — acceptable per docstring, but worth flagging since the invalidation function is dead code since nothing calls it in this PR, making it misleading/complete only on paper.

title: upsampled_count() aliasing to 'count' only works for simple yAxis=count(), breaks for multiple metrics or custom aliases
body: transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling replaces 'count()' with the literal string 'upsampled_count() as count', hardcoding the alias. If query_columns contains multiple aggregates or if downstream code expects the original alias format matching 'count()' (not aliased), this can conflict with existing alias logic in the query builder, produce duplicate alias errors when count() appears multiple times (e.g. in top events with multiple yAxis entries), or silently break non-count-only queries since only exact-match 'count()' survives transformation while equations/other representations of count referencing it won't be transformed consistently with the renamed alias.

title: New upsampled_count() function unconditionally reads sample_weight column which may not exist
body: The new SnQLFunction 'upsampled_count' directly references Column('sample_weight') without any guard. This function is reachable any time a query column is transformed via transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling, which is gated only by the allowlist/dataset heuristics in error_upsampling.py — not by verification that the underlying table/dataset actually has a sample_weight column. If this function is invoked against a dataset/table without that column (e.g. due to a bug in the eligibility heuristic, or future reuse of this function elsewhere), the query will fail with a column-not-found error at Snuba, surfacing as a 500 to users rather than a graceful fallback.

title: is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects called repeatedly per widget-split sub-query re-reading cache/options each time
body: _get_event_stats calls is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects on every invocation (including the up to 4 sub-queries performed for dashboard widget split-detection: error_results, original_results, transaction_results, and retry on exception). Although there's a 60s cache, this still does Redis/cache round trips multiple times per single HTTP request and recomputes `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` each time without caching, undermining the stated 'performance optimization' goal in the comments and adding unnecessary latency per request compared to computing it once outside the closure.

title: Broad except Exception silently swallows malformed error_sampling context
body: _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling uses bare 'except Exception: pass' twice, which will silently swallow bugs such as AttributeError from malformed contexts (e.g. contexts.error_sampling being a non-dict) or ValueError from float conversion, making test setup failures silently produce no sample_rate instead of surfacing a clear error, potentially masking real bugs in tests that rely on this helper.

title: Test asserts upsampled count of 10 without verifying client_sample_rate-to-weight calculation logic
body: test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects asserts count == 10 for events stored with client_sample_rate=0.1, implicitly assuming sample_weight = 1/client_sample_rate = 10. However there is no test anywhere in this PR for the actual sample_weight calculation/ingestion pathway (e.g., in event processing or factories) that sets the sample_weight column from client_sample_rate; the factories.py change only sets 'sample_rate' on normalized_data, not 'sample_weight'. This leaves a gap: the test may pass only if some other untouched part of the pipeline computes sample_weight = 1/sample_rate, which isn't verified or documented in this PR, making the test's correctness assumption unverified for reviewers.

title: Accidental submodule/subproject commit added
body: The diff adds a file `sentry-repo` containing `Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a`, which looks like an accidental git submodule reference committed into the repo. This is almost certainly not intentional, can break checkouts/CI (missing .gitmodules, broken submodule pointer), and should be removed before merge.

title: Cache key ignores dataset/request context but cached value is reused across different datasets/queries
body: The cache key is only `error_upsampling_eligible:{org_id}:{hash(project_ids)}`, keyed solely on allowlist eligibility, but then on a cache hit the code calls `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform(dataset, request)` fresh each time anyway (line 32), so this is fine for correctness. However when caching only is_eligible, the `is_eligible` result derived from `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` doesn't vary with dataset — so this isn't actually a bug, but it's confusing: the comment says 'Cache allowlist eligibility' and that's what's stored, yet the public function conflates caching rationale with the per-request dataset check in a way that's easy to misread as caching the full decision. This should be clarified or restructured for maintainability, since a future refactor could easily introduce a stale-decision bug by caching `is_eligible and _should_apply_sample_weight_transform(...)` instead of just `is_eligible`.

title: hash() of a tuple used as cache key is not stable across processes
body: `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))` is used to build a cache key. Python's built-in `hash()` for tuples of ints is stable within a run, but if `PYTHONHASHSEED` is not fixed, it's fine for ints (int hashes are consistent since hash(int)==int generally), so this specific case is mostly safe. But using `hash()` instead of a deterministic key (e.g. joining ids with a separator) increases risk of collisions across different project_id sets and makes cache keys unnecessarily opaque/undebuggable in production (e.g., in cache inspection or logs). Prefer deterministic string formatting for cache keys.

title: count() transformation does not handle count(column) or other count variants
body: `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only matches the exact string `count()` (after lowercasing/stripping). Any other valid discover count-like usage, aliasing, or whitespace inside the parens (e.g. `count( )`) or `count() as count` would not be transformed, silently falling back to normal, non-upsampled `count()`. This creates inconsistent behavior where some equivalent queries get upsampled counts and others silently don't, with no error or warning raised to the caller.

title: Error-upsampling eligibility for discover dataset relies on fragile raw substring match on query text
body: `_is_error_focused_query` just checks if the literal substring `event.type:error` appears in the lowercased raw query string. This fails for equivalent but differently formatted queries (e.g. `event.type: error`, `!event.type:transaction`, parenthesized boolean combinations, or use of `is:unresolved event.type:error`). As a result, discover dataset queries that are effectively error-only but don't contain this exact substring will not get upsampled counts, producing inconsistent/incorrect aggregate counts compared to functionally identical queries phrased differently. This is a correctness/data-integrity risk since the resulting count values differ substantially (upsampled vs raw) depending on exact query text matching, not actual semantics of the query, and there's no validation or logging to detect such mismatches.

title: upsampled_count() silently assumes sample_weight column always exists
body: The new SnQL function `upsampled_count` performs `sum(sample_weight)` without any guard for missing/null `sample_weight` values. The comment acknowledges this assumption ('assumes sample_weight exists ... per schema design') but there is no validation anywhere in the call chain (endpoint, helper, or here) that enforces this invariant beyond the allowlist. If any allowlisted project has events without `sample_weight` populated (e.g., due to ingestion lag, backfill gaps, or schema migration order), the resulting aggregate will silently return incorrect (lower) counts rather than erroring, which is a data-integrity concern with no test coverage for this failure mode.

title: No test coverage for is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects caching behavior
body: The new public function `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` in error_upsampling.py, which contains the actual caching logic (cache hit/miss, 60s TTL) and is the main integration point used by the endpoint, is not tested at all. Only its private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, `_is_error_focused_query`) are tested directly. This leaves the caching logic — including correctness of cache keys, TTL behavior, and the interaction between cached eligibility and the dataset/request check — completely unverified.

title: Overly broad bare except clauses swallow all errors silently
body: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` uses two separate bare `except Exception: pass` blocks that silently swallow any error, including programming errors unrelated to malformed input (e.g., AttributeError from `.get` on a non-dict value, or unexpected TypeError). This can mask real bugs in test setups without any indication, making test failures confusing to debug when sample_rate silently fails to be set.

title: Cross-org cache key collision risk from using hash()
body: The cache key uses `hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))`. Python's built-in `hash()` for ints is stable per-process but PYTHONHASHSEED randomization affects strings/some types; more importantly hash() is not guaranteed collision-free, and across different processes/workers hashing may differ (not an issue here since ints hash to themselves), but combining org id with a non-cryptographic hash of a short list has real collision risk is low but using str(project_ids) would be simpler and safer. More critically, the cache value is a simple boolean with no versioning: if `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` changes, cached entries for up to 60s will serve stale eligibility, silently flipping which aggregation (count vs sum(sample_weight)) is applied — causing incorrect counts returned to users with no error during the window.

title: Fragile string-based detection of count() usage breaks aliasing and other call forms
body: `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only matches the exact string `count()` (after lowering/stripping). Any aliased form like `count() as total`, `count(id)`, or columns with extra whitespace inside parentheses won't be transformed, silently leaving regular (non-upsampled) counts for queries that should be upsampled. This is a brittle approach compared to parsing the actual function AST already used elsewhere in the codebase (event_search parsing).

title: Error-focused detection relies only on raw query string containment
body: _is_error_focused_query does a naive substring check for "event.type:error" in the lowercased query string. This will produce false positives/negatives for queries like `!event.type:error` (negation) or `message:"event.type:error"` as literal text, or when combined with OR logic in different environments. This can cause upsampling to be wrongly applied/not applied for the discover dataset, directly affecting event counts shown to users.

title: Upsampling eligibility recomputed/cached per-call despite inline comment claiming otherwise
body: The comment states "This cached result ensures consistent behavior across query execution," but `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` is called separately in `_get_event_stats` for every closure invocation (top events, rpc, standard), including repeated calls in `get_event_stats_factory` for split-decision requests (errors_only_query, transactions_only_query, original query) which use different `query` strings each time. Since `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` depends on `request.GET` query content, not the varied `query` argument passed to `_get_event_stats`, this can lead to inconsistent upsampling decisions between the split sub-queries (e.g. error-only vs full query) even though the comment implies a single consistent decision was cached for the whole request.

title: Silently swallows all exceptions when extracting client_sample_rate
body: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` catches bare `Exception` twice and silently ignores failures, including type errors from malformed `contexts` structures. This can mask bugs in test setup where sample_rate is silently not set, making test failures confusing to debug, and is overly broad for test utility code that should fail loudly on unexpected input.

title: Test for upsampled count asserts implausible fixed values without verifying actual sample_weight derivation
body: `test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects` asserts `data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10` based on a single stored event with `client_sample_rate: 0.1`, assuming sample_weight = 1/0.1 = 10. This test doesn't verify that `sample_rate`/`sample_weight` is actually computed and stored correctly end-to-end (depends on `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` in factories.py and the `sample_weight` column population), so if that chain breaks the test might still pass with coincidental values 1 or fail with an unrelated error, not clearly diagnosing the upsampling math itself.

title: Null segment_ids silently skip video deletion for non-javascript platforms
body: When max_segment_id is None, the function returns [] early, skipping deletion of any recordings. This is correct for replays with no segments. But this change also means that if max_segment_id is None but the replay still has orphaned data in storage (e.g., partial write), nothing is cleaned up — not flagged as an error, just silently a no-op. This may be intentional but there's no logging/metric to track how often this happens, making it hard to detect data retention issues.

title: get_environment_info swallows all exceptions broadly
body: The except Exception as e clause catches all exceptions including unexpected ones (e.g., AttributeError due to API misuse), silently absorbing them as 'no environment info' and only logging at info level. This could mask real bugs in production without any alerting, since this is on a non-critical path (comment formatting) but still worth tracking more carefully (e.g. with sentry_sdk.capture_exception) rather than just a logger.info call.

title: GitHub PR comment workflow lost subtitle/culprit information without replacement
body: The old MERGED_PR_SINGLE_ISSUE_TEMPLATE included `subtitle` (culprit) in the per-issue line. The new implementation via get_merged_pr_single_issue_template replaces subtitle with environment info, but these aren't equivalent — culprit information is dropped entirely from the comment body, which is a regression in information shown to developers reviewing the PR comment, unless this was an intentional design decision not stated in the PR description.

title: Detector update() does not persist owner changes atomically with other updates
body: In update(), owner_user_id/owner_team_id are set directly on the instance before instance.save() is called later in the method, but there's no transaction wrapping (unlike create() which wraps everything in transaction.atomic). If an exception occurs after setting the owner fields but before save(), partial state could leak, though in practice this is unlikely since it's all in-memory until save(). More importantly, there's no validation that the new owner (if a team) belongs to the same organization/project, unlike in create() where validate_owner presumably handles this; this inconsistency allows setting an invalid owner during update that would be rejected during create (per test test_owner_not_in_organization only tested for POST not PUT).

title: get_slow_conditions_for_groups called once but still queries potentially large/duplicate dcg_ids
body: The refactor moves get_slow_conditions_for_groups to be computed once in process_delayed_workflows and passed down, which is good for the duplicate call that existed before. However, the function is called with list(event_data.dcg_ids) which may contain duplicate entries if event_data.dcg_ids are not deduplicated; this was pre-existing but worth checking since this is now a single more consequential call feeding both get_condition_query_groups and get_groups_to_fire -- any inconsistency in this shared data now affects both functions instead of being isolated.

title: Removed option 'grouping.experiments.parameterization.traceparent' may break usages still referencing it
body: The traceparent parameterization experiment option registration was removed, but it's unclear if any code paths still reference this option key via options.get(). If so, this would raise an UnknownOption error or silently fail. Given parameterization.py's traceparent regex is still part of DEFAULT_PARAMETERIZATION_REGEXES, verify no remaining references to this option exist before removing its registration.

title: Removed ParameterizationRegexExperiment and related dead branch without replacement
body: ParameterizationRegexExperiment class and the isinstance-based branching in parametrize_w_experiments were removed, along with the exported name in __all__. This removes support for pure-regex experiments distinct from callable experiments. If any external/future code relied on this type (e.g. the removed traceparent experiment option), it is now unsupported. This is a breaking API change for the parameterization module with no reported deprecation path.

title: get_environment_info can throw during logging if issue.id used inside except with partial failure
body: In get_environment_info, if get_recommended_event() or get_environment() raises, the exception is caught generically and logged, but if issue.id itself is unavailable (unlikely) or the exception message `e` is not serializable this could cause secondary issues. More importantly, catching bare Exception here silently swallows errors (including potential programming errors) without re-raising, which could mask real bugs when environment data fails to be retrieved for valid reasons unrelated to missing environment info.

title: Visualize no longer supports multiple yAxes per overlay; breaking change condensing feature
body: The Visualize class and UI were changed from supporting multiple yAxes per visualize (chart) to a single yAxis. This removes the ability to overlay multiple series within one chart entry, changing established UX/API behavior (toolbarVisualize.tsx, visualizes.tsx). Any saved queries, URLs, or state relying on multiple yAxes per Visualize may lose data fidelity, since Visualize.fromJSON now expands multiple yAxes into multiple separate Visualize instances instead of preserving them as one grouped chart. This is a significant behavior change but doesn't appear well guarded with migration logic for existing saved searches containing multi-yAxis visualizes beyond simple fan-out, potentially altering labels/semantics for users with existing saved queries.

title: updateLocationWithAggregateFields flattens visualizes, which changes semantic grouping and label assignment
body: The change from mapping each aggregateField to one yAxes-based BaseVisualize to flatMapping multiple Visualize instances from Visualize.fromJSON means grouped overlays (previously one Visualize with multiple yAxes) are now split into multiple separate serialized entries. This can alter chart label numbering/order (`label: String.fromCharCode(65+i)`) when round-tripping through location state, inconsistent with the previous grouped behavior, and could break saved query comparisons that expect one BaseVisualize per original grouping.

title: Added noise_config without accompanying tests
body: A new noise_config = NoiseConfig(ignore_limit=5) was added to DBQueryInjectionVulnerabilityGroupType, but there's no test coverage verifying this new noise suppression behavior takes effect for this specific group type, risking silent misconfiguration if ignore_limit semantics change.

title: Null max_segment_id check uses wrong semantics
body: `_make_recording_filenames` returns [] when `row["max_segment_id"]` is None, but previously the test fixture used `max_segment_id: 0` to represent 'no segments'. Now a replay with a single segment (max_segment_id=0) would also be misinterpreted: `range(0+1)` still correctly includes segment 0, so that case is fine, but the change silently assumes None means no ingested segments without validating this assumption against production data where segment_id could legitimately be absent from Snuba aggregation (e.g. due to Function('max', ...) returning NULL for an empty group), potentially masking real deletions of orphaned recordings when the aggregation subtly differs from expectations. This should be verified against the exact Snuba NULL-max behavior to ensure deletions aren't silently skipped for replays with ingested but unlinked segment metadata.

title: get_environment_info swallows all exceptions broadly
body: The newly added `get_environment_info` catches a bare `Exception` and logs at `info` level, which could hide real bugs (e.g. AttributeError due to API misuse) as benign 'no environment' cases, making future regressions harder to detect in PR comment generation.

title: Default behavior change for autofix automation tuning
body: Changing `DEFAULT_AUTOFIX_AUTOMATION_TUNING_DEFAULT` from "low" to "off" silently changes default behavior for all projects/orgs relying on this default, without an accompanying migration or changelog note found in the diff. This could unexpectedly disable autofix automation for existing users who had not explicitly set the option, since `sentry:autofix_automation_tuning` project option default was also changed to "off" in projectoptions/defaults.py.

title: Removed grouping option without migration/cleanup for existing stored values
body: The option `grouping.experiments.parameterization.traceparent` was removed from registration, but if this option was previously set to a nonzero value in production (via admin), removing the registration could cause runtime errors or unexpected fallback behavior when the system tries to read an option that's no longer registered. No cleanup/migration is shown for existing stored option values.

title: TableWidgetVisualization rendered with hardcoded empty data behind new feature flag
body: When `organization.features.includes('use-table-widget-visualization')` is true, the code renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />` with completely empty hardcoded data instead of the actual `result`/`eventView` data used by `StyledSimpleTableChart`. This means any organization with this feature flag enabled will see an always-empty table widget in dashboards, a significant regression that silently discards real data.

title: updateLocationWithAggregateFields silently drops non-BaseVisualize/Visualize items
body: The function assumes every non-BaseVisualize aggregateField is a plain GroupBy JSON-serializable object, but if a `Visualize` instance (not BaseVisualize) is passed directly (as hinted by other code paths using `Visualize` class instances interchangeably with BaseVisualize), `JSON.stringify(aggregateField)` on a class instance may not serialize as expected (methods are dropped, but internal fields like `selectedChartType` could leak unexpectedly into the URL), given the Visualize class has private fields and getters not meant for direct JSON serialization in this flattened path.

title: Analytics event name changed without checking consistency with existing event key definitions
body: The event name was changed from `replay.view_html` to `replay.view-html`, matching the type definition in `replayAnalyticsEvents.tsx`. This appears intentional and consistent, but renaming the actual Amplitude/analytics event key for an existing feature breaks continuity of previously collected analytics data under the old event key, which could affect historical reporting/dashboards unless this was already broken (i.e., events never actually fired due to the mismatch) prior to this fix. No dashboard migration or backward compatibility handling is mentioned.

title: CSRF/replay: state reused from pipeline.signature without binding to session nonce
body: The state check compares `request.GET.get('state')` directly to `pipeline.signature`, which is a deterministic value derived from pipeline state rather than a per-session random nonce. If an attacker can predict or capture this signature (e.g., via logs, referrer leakage, or by initiating their own pipeline with similar session state), they could craft a matching callback to replay or cross-link an OAuth flow. Typically CSRF-state tokens should be freshly generated random values stored server-side and compared, not a reproducible signature of pipeline data.

title: No validation of error/exception responses from token exchange and user info calls
body: `safe_urlopen`/`safe_urlread` and `get_user_info` calls are wrapped only loosely: body parsing failures fall back to an empty dict silently (bare except swallowing all exceptions), and `get_user_info` is called without any try/except — if GitHub returns a non-200 or malformed response, `get_user_info` could raise an unhandled exception (e.g., ApiError) instead of being caught and converted to a friendly `error()` response, resulting in a raw 500 to the user instead of the intended integration-failed page.

title: KeyError risk if integration.metadata lacks 'sender'
body: `integration.metadata['sender']['login']` is accessed directly without checking existence. If an installation's metadata doesn't contain a 'sender' key (e.g., legacy integrations installed before this feature, or integrations created via other paths), this raises a KeyError instead of gracefully failing with the intended `error()` response, causing an unhandled 500 instead of a user-friendly error page.

title: Hardcoded provider_id check reduces extensibility without clear doc
body: Replacing the list-based `FORWARD_INSTALL_FOR` constant with an inline string literal check (`provider_id == 'github'`) removes the previous extension point for other providers needing the same install-redirect behavior; if another provider needs similar handling in the future, this requires modifying this file directly rather than extending a configurable list, which was arguably better practice given multiple pipeline-based integrations exist.

title: OAuth token exchange request not validated/logged on failure
body: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, safe_urlopen response is not checked for HTTP status before parsing; if GitHub returns an error page/body, parse_qsl silently produces an empty dict and the code falls into generic error() without any logging of the failure reason (e.g., invalid_grant, rate limiting). This makes debugging GitHub-side failures (expired code, revoked app, API outages) difficult and could mask abuse attempts (e.g., repeated invalid code use) since there's no logging/metrics around failed exchanges.

title: github_authenticated_user validation only triggers when Integration already exists
body: The check comparing pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") to integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] only runs when `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` succeeds (i.e., integration already created by webhook) and OrganizationIntegration does not yet exist. If the Integration record does not exist yet at this point in the pipeline (e.g., webhook delivery is delayed/race), the code returns pipeline.next_step() at the `except Integration.DoesNotExist` branch without ever validating github_authenticated_user, bypassing the newly added security check. This creates a race condition where a malicious actor could complete installation before the webhook-created Integration record propagates, bypassing user validation entirely.

title: No validation that get_user_info succeeded with a 200 response
body: get_user_info(payload["access_token"]) is called without checking that the underlying request succeeded (e.g. GitHub API outage, rate limiting, or revoked token could cause errors). If get_user_info raises an exception (e.g., ApiError) this is not caught here, so an unhandled exception could propagate and produce a 500 error instead of the intended user-facing error page, which is inconsistent with the rest of the flow's error handling pattern reflected elsewhere in this method (try/except around token parsing).

title: installation_id bound to pipeline state in OAuthLoginView redirects to GitHub before validating organization context
body: self.determine_active_organization(request) is called, but if the user is not authenticated or has no valid organization, nothing prevents proceeding to the OAuth redirect; this doesn't match prior behavior where organization context was established before any installation steps. This may be intentional but is not covered by tests validating unauthenticated/invalid org access during this new OAuth hop.

title: No null-check on integration.metadata['sender']
body: integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] assumes the integration metadata always contains a 'sender' key. build_integration only sets metadata['sender'] if state.get('sender') is truthy, so integrations created without that state field will raise KeyError here instead of failing gracefully with the intended error() response. This can turn an auth-mismatch case into an unhandled 500.

title: safe_urlopen response not checked for errors before reading
body: req = safe_urlopen(...) is used without verifying the HTTP status code succeeded. If GitHub returns a non-200/error response (e.g., invalid client credentials), the code still attempts safe_urlread/parse_qsl which may not raise, silently falling into the generic 'access_token not in payload' error path, but earlier failures (5xx, connection reset) are only caught by the broad except Exception around parsing, which could mask legitimate operational issues instead of surfacing a clearer failure mode in logs.

title: Overly broad bare except swallows parsing errors silently
body: The except Exception: payload = {} catches all exceptions from safe_urlread/parse_qsl without logging, making it hard to diagnose failures (e.g., network errors, decode errors) in production. At minimum this should log the exception for observability.

title: installation_id from query bound to pipeline state without validation
body: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, installation_id from request.GET is bound directly to pipeline state before any OAuth validation occurs. Since this happens prior to verifying state/signature or exchanging the code, an attacker could manipulate the installation_id value on the initial request if it influences later authorization flow, since the binding happens unconditionally on every dispatch call (including the first redirect leg).

title: Changed error message not clearly justified by test name
body: test_installation_not_found now expects 'Invalid installation request.' instead of the previous specific 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' message. This generic message change reduces the clarity of error feedback to users when the installation lookup fails for unrelated reasons (e.g., state mismatch here), and the test doesn't verify that build_integration's IntegrationError path is actually exercised anymore -- the failure in this test is actually due to signature mismatch, not the installation-not-found code path, so the test name is now misleading.

title: Default datetime evaluated once at class definition time
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a dataclass default evaluated once when the module is loaded, not per-instance. All AssignmentSource instances created without explicitly passing `queued` will share the same stale timestamp (the time the module was imported), not the time the instance was created. This should use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead.

title: where_should_sync does not pass sync_source to should_sync
body: In `where_should_sync`, `installation.should_sync(key)` is called without a `sync_source` argument, so this path never benefits from the new assignment-source cycle-breaking logic. If this function is used anywhere relevant to assignment sync, cycles could still occur through this code path.

title: Sync-cycle check compares integration_id to org_integration.integration_id but AssignmentSource is built from models.Integration without currently-synced-integration disambiguation
body: `should_sync` only guards against the same integration that originated the change; it does not persist/propagate the assignment_source through intermediate inbound sync tasks (e.g. `sync_status_inbound`), so chains of different sync types between the same integration are not fully protected, and other call sites (e.g. status sync inbound task) are not shown to pass assignment_source consistently, risking partial fixes for the described loop.

title: Mutable/stale default evaluated once at class definition time
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once when the class is defined (module import time), not per-instance. All AssignmentSource instances created without explicitly passing `queued` will share the same timestamp (the time the module was imported), not the actual time the instance was created. This should use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead.

title: to_dict/from_dict round-trip may fail on datetime serialization
body: to_dict() uses dataclasses.asdict which keeps `queued` as a native datetime object. This dict is passed as `assignment_source_dict` through Celery task kwargs (sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async), which typically require JSON-serializable arguments depending on the serializer configured. If the task broker uses JSON serialization, a raw datetime will fail to serialize, breaking the outbound sync task entirely.

title: where_should_sync doesn't pass sync_source to should_sync
body: where_should_sync calls `.should_sync(key)` without threading through any AssignmentSource, so inbound-related sync checks here (e.g. inbound_assignee) can't filter cycles consistently with the new sync_source mechanism added elsewhere. This is inconsistent with the rest of the PR's goal and could still allow cycles for code paths going through this function with a source context ignored (not used anywhere currently, but is a latent inconsistency with the new API).

title: Mutable default evaluated once at class definition time
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated a single time when the dataclass is defined (at module import), not per-instance. All AssignmentSource instances that don't explicitly pass `queued` will share the same timestamp (the time the module was imported), not the actual time the assignment occurred. This should use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead.

title: where_should_sync does not pass sync_source to should_sync
body: `where_should_sync` calls `integration.get_installation(...).should_sync(key)` without passing an `AssignmentSource`, so this path never applies cycle-breaking logic. This is only used for inbound sync currently, but if later reused with sync_source context it would silently ignore the loop-prevention check.

title: remove_old_assignees runs even when outbound sync is skipped due to source
body: The `assign`/`deassign` logic still records activity, history, and calls remove_old_assignees regardless of whether sync_group_assignee_outbound actually propagates (it's guarded only by the feature flag, not by whether should_sync will reject due to matching assignment_source). This isn't itself wrong, but the outbound skip logic is only enforced deep in task/installation code, meaning multiple analytics/activity records could still be generated per cycle even though the external sync is suppressed - worth confirming this is intended for the cycle-breaking goal of this PR, since activity/history records could still loop-generate even if the direct Jira sync does not.

title: evaluate_group_key_value calls build_occurrence_and_event_data with raw value, not necessarily matching group_key's current value semantics
