body: In evaluate_group_key_value, build_occurrence_and_event_data is called with 'value' (the raw metric value for this evaluation), but the abstract method's signature/docstring doesn't clarify units or validate correctness. If a subclass's new_status is e.g. OK transitioning to non-OK, the value passed may not correspond to what caused the status change if multiple conditions were evaluated across different value representations. This is minor but could confuse implementers producing occurrence evidence.

title: Removed duplicate group_key detection without replacement safeguard
body: The previous process_detectors logic explicitly checked for duplicate group_keys from detector_results and logged an error, skipping duplicates. Now that evaluate returns a dict keyed by group_key, duplicates are implicitly deduped by dict insertion order, silently overwriting the first result without any logging or metric. This removes an existing data-integrity safeguard/signal that previously surfaced bugs in detector implementations producing colliding group keys; now such bugs will fail silently (lost occurrence) instead of being logged.

title: New abstractmethod build_occurrence_and_event_data breaks existing non-stateful DetectorHandler subclasses only partially
body: Adding @abc.abstractmethod build_occurrence_and_event_data to StatefulDetectorHandler is a breaking API change for all existing subclasses of StatefulDetectorHandler that don't implement this method; they will fail to instantiate. The PR only updates grouptype.py's MetricAlertDetectorHandler (which doesn't implement it either, so it will raise TypeError when instantiated), and the test's MockDetectorStateHandler. Any other subclasses in the codebase not shown here (or added later) will break without a clear error message tied to this specific hook; the TODO comment in grouptype.py doesn't mention this requirement for implementers.

title: value and group_key passed to build_occurrence_and_event_data are not the actual triggering values
body: In evaluate_group_key_value, `build_occurrence_and_event_data(group_key, value, ...)` is called with `value` being the raw metric value passed into evaluate_group_key_value, but there's no validation that this is semantically correct for all condition evaluations (e.g. multiple conditions could evaluate differently, but only the final new_status is used while the raw value is reused). This isn't inherently wrong given current single-condition tests, but as more conditions are added this could misrepresent the occurrence data. No test covers multiple conditions contributing different priorities for the same group key.

title: Removed duplicate group-key detection logging without equivalent safety at the dict level
body: Previously process_detectors explicitly detected and logged duplicate group keys from handler.evaluate() results via a list, which was a safety check against buggy handler implementations silently dropping or merging results silently. Now that evaluate returns a dict, duplicate keys are silently overwritten by the handler without any observability (last write wins) since dict construction in evaluate() (`results[result.group_key] = result`) can't detect duplicates either. If a custom handler implementation has a bug producing duplicate group keys, this failure will be silent instead of logged, making bugs harder to detect in production.

title: New abstract method breaks existing non-stateful subclasses silently only at instantiation
body: Adding abc.abstractmethod build_occurrence_and_event_data to StatefulDetectorHandler is correct in intent, but since Python abstractmethod checks only happen at instantiation time, any other production StatefulDetectorHandler subclasses not updated in this PR (if any exist elsewhere) will fail only when instantiated, not at import time, risking a runtime failure instead of a type-checking failure caught earlier in CI with mypy strict settings disabled for this file.

title: value passed to build_occurrence_and_event_data is not the actual triggering value
body: In evaluate_group_key_value, `value` is the raw group value passed into the method, but build_occurrence_and_event_data is called with this same `value` regardless of which condition triggered the status change. If multiple group keys/conditions are evaluated, this is fine per-call, but the occurrence creation logic has no access to which specific condition/threshold triggered `new_status`, making it hard for subclasses to build accurate occurrence data (e.g. evidence_data) that reflects the triggering comparison. This is a design limitation that silently loses information needed for a correct occurrence.

title: Removed duplicate detector_group_key validation without replacement safeguard
body: The previous code detected and logged duplicate group_key results returned from handler.evaluate() to catch handler bugs producing duplicate state entries. Now that evaluate returns a dict, duplicates are structurally impossible from a single handler call, which is reasonable, but the removal means any pre-existing/legacy handler returning overlapping keys across multiple invocations/retries silently overwrites prior results with no logging, losing visibility into misbehaving handlers that was previously present via logger.error. This could hide real duplication bugs if a handler indirectly produces colliding keys via other code paths before conversion to a dict occurs upstream.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now inherits abstract StatefulDetectorHandler without implementing abstract methods
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler but provides no implementation for the abstract methods counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and build_occurrence_and_event_data (all declared via @abc.abstractmethod in detector.py). Since the class body is just `pass`, instantiating MetricAlertDetectorHandler will raise a TypeError at runtime (Python enforces abstract method implementation), breaking any code path that calls `detector.detector_handler` for a Detector of type metric_alert_fire. This is a functional regression compared to the previous version, which at least implemented a concrete (if stubbed) evaluate method via DetectorHandler.

title: Each sub-flusher process creates its own separate SpansBuffer and Redis connections
body: _create_process_for_shards creates a new SpansBuffer(shards) per process and multiple processes now share the same backing Redis, but each gets its own connection pool / client. With many processes per consumer (num_processes shards split across up to flusher_processes), this multiplies Redis connections significantly beyond what one buffer-per-consumer used before, which can exhaust Redis maxclients under scale-up scenarios the PR is explicitly targeting (scaling down consumers but relying on more flusher processes).

title: join() deadline handling can let a process be killed/skipped silently without raising
body: In join(), the loop `for process_index, process in self.processes.items(): if deadline is not None: remaining_time = deadline - time.time(); if remaining_time <= 0: break` just breaks out of the whole loop once the deadline is exceeded for any single process, leaving the remaining processes neither waited-on nor terminated. Previously there was only one process so this corner case didn't exist; now, with multiple processes, some may be left running (not terminated) if the deadline is hit partway through, leaking subprocesses after shutdown of the strategy pipeline step and continuing to write to Kafka/Redis after the main process intends to be done with this instance's lifecycle (e.g. during rebalance restarts) causing duplicate/zombie flusher activity until the whole consumer process exits.

title: max_processes default silently falls back to shard count causing non-deterministic process count across runs with varying partitions
body: `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` means if `max_processes=0` is passed, it is treated as falsy and replaced by shard count, which could be surprising/undocumented behavior (0 should probably mean "zero processes" or raise, not fall back silently). This isn't tested and could mask configuration bugs where `flusher_processes=0` is passed unintentionally via CLI defaulting weirdly.

title: process.kill() only guarded for multiprocessing.Process, silently no-ops for Thread
body: In _ensure_processes_alive, `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.kill()` means that when running in testing mode where processes are threading.Thread (produce_to_pipe set), an unhealthy/dead thread is never killed (threads can't be killed) but also _create_process_for_shards is still called to spawn a replacement, potentially leaving the old hung thread running indefinitely alongside the new one, leading to duplicate flush activity in tests using produce_to_pipe mode if a thread were ever detected unhealthy.

title: Each flusher process creates its own SpansBuffer for shared Redis keys, duplicating memory metrics and buffer views
body: Previously there was a single SpansBuffer shared across the whole flusher; now `_create_process_for_shards` creates a separate `SpansBuffer(shards)` per process, and `self.buffers` holds one buffer per process. In `submit()`, `get_memory_info()` is now summed across these per-process buffers instead of a single buffer covering all assigned shards. If `SpansBuffer.get_memory_info()` returns info per-Redis-cluster-node (not per-shard), this can double count memory usage from shared Redis nodes across multiple shard subsets, causing incorrect backpressure decisions (false positives for max-memory backpressure) once more than one process is used.

title: join() does not kill processes that fail to stop before deadline per-process
body: In the new join loop, if the first process doesn't terminate within the deadline, the while loop exits due to deadline but `process.terminate()` is still called unconditionally afterward only for that process; however, for subsequent processes in the dict iteration, `remaining_time <= 0` immediately breaks the outer for-loop, skipping termination entirely for any processes not yet checked. This could leave live child processes without being terminated when timeout is tight and there are multiple flusher processes, causing dangling processes/resource leaks.

title: max_processes can be None-derived shard-count larger than available shards silently clipped without validation of flusher_processes=0 or negative
body: `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats a passed `max_processes=0` the same as `None` (falls back to shard count) due to Python truthiness, which may be surprising/undesired behavior if a caller intends zero flusher processes (though zero wouldn't make sense, the silent coercion from invalid config to default behavior could mask a configuration bug).

title: Test changed to require transactional DB without justification
body: test_basic was changed from `@pytest.mark.django_db` to `@pytest.mark.django_db(transaction=True)`. This increases test cost/slowness and signals a new reliance on real transactions (likely due to multiprocessing in the flusher), but there's no comment explaining why, which can confuse future maintainers running into flaky/slow tests.

title: process.kill() now gated behind a broken isinstance check, preventing restart of hung/crashed processes
body: In `_ensure_processes_alive`, the call to `process.kill()` is now wrapped in `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process):`. However, processes are created via `self.mp_context.Process` with a 'spawn' context (`multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process`), which returns a `SpawnProcess` instance. `SpawnProcess` does NOT subclass `multiprocessing.Process` (the default context's Process class) — both only share a common base `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`. Therefore `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is always False for the actual spawned worker processes, and `kill()` is silently skipped. Previously (pre-PR) `process.kill()` was called unconditionally (wrapped only in try/except ValueError), so it worked correctly. With this change, hung or crashed flusher processes are never actually killed before a replacement process is spawned to handle the same shards, leading to zombie/leaked processes that may still be alive and could continue producing to Kafka or interacting with Redis concurrently with the new process for the same shards — risking duplicate segment production and resource leaks.

title: Dead code: unused `_create_process_for_shard` method
body: `_create_process_for_shard` (singular) is defined but never called anywhere in the class; `_create_process_for_shards` (plural) is used instead throughout. This leftover method should be removed to avoid confusion.

title: Inconsistent metrics tag key between related timers
body: The `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` timer uses tag key `"shard"` while the nearly-identical `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer uses tag key `"shards"` (plural) for the same value (a comma-joined shard list). This inconsistency fragments metrics dashboards/queries that expect a single consistent tag name across these two closely related timers.

title: Use of queue.ShutDown / Queue.shutdown() requires Python 3.13+
body: The code relies on `queue.ShutDown` (as an exception type) and `queue.Queue.shutdown()` (lines 132, 142, 238), both of which were only added to the stdlib `queue` module in Python 3.13. Sentry currently targets Python 3.11/3.12, so `queue.Queue` instances will not have a `shutdown()` method and `queue.ShutDown` will raise `AttributeError` when referenced. In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` (line 238) the `AttributeError` is swallowed by the broad `except Exception` and merely logged, meaning the queue is never actually shut down and the worker threads remain blocked forever on `work_queue.get()` since they have no timeout and no sentinel value to unblock them. This leaves daemon threads running indefinitely (though daemon threads won't block process exit, `join(timeout=5.0)` will always time out and `thread-queue-parallel` mode will never cleanly release workers), and the whole feature is effectively broken/untested on the Python version this repo runs.

title: Worker threads block forever on queue.get() with no way to interrupt on unsupported Python versions
body: `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` calls `self.work_queue.get()` with no timeout, relying entirely on `queue.ShutDown` being raised by `Queue.shutdown()` to break out of the loop during shutdown. Since this stdlib behavior doesn't exist before Python 3.13 (see above), setting `self.shutdown = True` has no effect on an already-blocked `.get()` call — the thread will never notice the shutdown flag unless a new item arrives. This means on consumer shutdown, worker threads can hang, and `strategy.close()`/`terminate()` won't actually stop in-flight work promptly, risking data loss or delayed shutdown during deploys.

title: OffsetTracker.all_offsets dict grows unbounded for low-traffic partitions
body: `get_committable_offsets()` iterates `self.all_offsets.keys()` but never removes a partition's entry when its offset set becomes empty (it is only pruned in `mark_committed`, which filters by offset value, not deleting the partition key entirely when offsets are completed without any commit happening, e.g. for FilteredPayload offsets added+completed immediately). Over the life of a long-running consumer process this results in slow unbounded growth of `all_offsets`/`outstanding`/`partition_locks` dictionaries, particularly for partitions that get reassigned/rebalanced repeatedly, since partition keys are never fully removed.

title: Per-message metrics.gauge call on queue depth may add significant overhead
body: `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` emits a `metrics.gauge` call for every processed item (line 150-156), tagged by identifier. For high-throughput queues (e.g. uptime results) this adds a statsd/metrics emission per message per worker, which may become a non-trivial source of overhead/metrics volume at scale, especially compared to the previous batch-based processing which could emit stats per batch rather than per item.

title: num_queues defaults to max_workers but worker count semantics changed silently
body: In `thread-queue-parallel` mode, `max_workers` (previously documented as thread pool size for `batched-parallel`) is reused to mean "number of fixed queues" (`num_queues=max_workers or 20`). Each queue spawns exactly one dedicated worker thread for its lifetime (in `FixedQueuePool.__init__`), so unlike `batched-parallel`'s ThreadPoolExecutor (which dynamically allocates threads bounded by max_workers), this always creates `num_queues` persistent threads regardless of actual load. This is a meaningful behavior change for the same CLI option across modes, worth documenting more clearly, especially since the click help text for `--max-workers` was only updated to "maximum amount of parallelism" without noting the always-on persistent threads per queue in this mode.

title: hash() is not stable across process restarts/instances, breaking consistent group-to-queue assignment guarantee claimed in docstring
body: get_queue_for_group uses Python's built-in hash() on group_key (a str). Python randomizes string hash seeds per-process (PYTHONHASHSEED) unless explicitly disabled, so the same group_key can map to different queue indices across different consumer processes or restarts. The FixedQueuePool docstring and comments claim 'Each group is consistently assigned to the same queue' - this is only true within a single process's lifetime, not across restarts. While ordering is still preserved within one process (which is likely the actual requirement, since each partition is handled by one process), the comment is misleading, and if any code or operator assumption relies on cross-process group->queue determinism (e.g., comparing queue assignment for debugging) it will be wrong. Should use a stable hash (e.g., hashlib) or document this limitation.

title: get_committable_offsets scans from last_committed+1 every time -- O(n) per call, called every 1s in commit loop, could become costly with large backlogs
body: get_committable_offsets iterates from `start` to `max_offset` every time it's called (every 1 second via _commit_loop). If a queue backs up significantly (e.g., thousands of outstanding offsets due to a slow consumer in one queue), this loop becomes expensive and runs under a per-partition lock, blocking add_offset/complete_offset calls from worker threads for that partition. This could cause lock contention and slow down the whole pipeline when backlog grows, defeating part of the purpose of this PR (handling slow items without clogging).

title: shutdown() doesn't drain/join queues before stopping workers, risking item loss or offsets never completed
body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown=True and calls queue.shutdown(immediate=False) then joins with a 5s timeout. If a queue still has many items and the single worker is slow, items remain un-processed when join times out; those offsets are left 'outstanding' and never committed, and in-flight items are simply dropped (no attempt to drain before closing). This could cause messages to be silently skipped on shutdown/rebalance, which is a correctness risk for an at-least-once pipeline relying on this component for commit safety.

title: get_committable_offsets copies/uses live sets without full isolation; potential iteration-while-mutating under lock release points
body: Inside the per-partition lock block, `outstanding = self.outstanding[partition]` is a reference to the live set, and the loop checks membership against it while iterating `all_offsets`. This is read-only within the lock so it's safe here, but `list(self.all_offsets.keys())` taken outside any lock before the per-partition locking could race with a new partition_lock being created concurrently in `_get_partition_lock`, since `partition_locks` dict itself isn't guarded by a single lock (setdefault is not atomic against concurrent reads elsewhere). This is a subtle concurrency hazard worth flagging even if currently unlikely to manifest.

title: max_workers=None silently defaults to 20 queues with no metric tag differentiation
body: For thread-queue-parallel mode, `num_queues=max_workers or 20` is used, but unlike the batched-parallel mode's metric_tags handling (which distinguishes 'default' vs explicit worker count), there is no equivalent tracking of whether queue count was explicitly set or defaulted for thread-queue-parallel mode. This makes it harder to debug/monitor the chosen parallelism from metrics tags, an inconsistency with the existing batched-parallel code path directly above.

title: queue.Queue.shutdown() does not exist before Python 3.13
body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` and OrderedQueueWorker.run() catches `queue.ShutDown`. Both `Queue.shutdown()` and the `queue.ShutDown` exception were only added in Python 3.13 (PEP 578 / bpo-... added in 3.13). Sentry currently targets Python 3.11/3.12 in production, so this call will raise `AttributeError`/`AttributeError: 'Queue' object has no attribute 'shutdown'` at runtime. Because the call is wrapped in a bare `except Exception: logger.exception(...)`, the error is swallowed, but the net effect is that worker threads are never actually signaled to stop (they remain blocked in `work_queue.get()`), causing `worker.join(timeout=5.0)` to time out on every shutdown and the daemon threads to leak for the life of the process.

title: Workers can block forever on shutdown since queue has no sentinel/unblock mechanism
body: Since `queue.Queue.shutdown()` isn't available on the Python version in use (see above), there is no fallback mechanism (e.g. a sentinel value or `put_nowait`) to unblock worker threads doing a blocking `get()` on an empty queue. As a result, `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` cannot reliably stop workers that are idle-waiting, leading to resource leaks (threads never terminate) and `ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown()` effectively not fully cleaning up, which could keep stale state (open sentry_sdk transactions, DB connections, etc.) running after the strategy is supposedly closed.

title: get_committable_offsets does an O(gap) linear scan every second
body: `get_committable_offsets` iterates `range(start, max_offset + 1)` for every partition on every tick of the 1-second commit loop. If a message is delayed/stuck (e.g. a slow group) while many offsets pile up behind it, this becomes a large linear scan repeated every second, consuming CPU proportional to the gap size. Given the stated motivation of the PR is to avoid slow items blocking the pipeline, a slow item can still cause this scan to balloon, partially offsetting the perf benefit this PR intends to deliver.

title: WorkItem retains full Message object unnecessarily, inflating queue memory
body: `WorkItem` stores the entire original `message` (including the raw Kafka payload) even though only `partition`, `offset`, and the decoded `result` are ever used by `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`. For a backlog of thousands of queued items (which this feature expects to build up when a group is slow), this needless retention of the raw message/payload bytes in every work item increases memory pressure substantially.

title: max_workers=0 silently falls back to default num_queues
body: `num_queues=max_workers or 20` treats `max_workers=0` the same as `None`, falling back to the default of 20 queues instead of raising an error or honoring an explicit (if nonsensical) value of 0. This could mask a configuration mistake silently.

title: Queue assignment uses Python's randomized hash() for consistent routing
body: `get_queue_for_group` uses the builtin `hash(group_key)` to pick a queue index. Python's string hashing is randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED) by default, so while this is consistent for the lifetime of a single process (satisfying in-process ordering guarantees), it is non-deterministic across process restarts/rebalances. This isn't a functional bug given the stated invariants, but is worth calling out as fragile/surprising if used anywhere assuming cross-process determinism (e.g. tests asserting fixed indices, or future features relying on sticky partitioning across restarts).

title: Backup code validation has a read-then-write race condition allowing double use
body: In the credentials authorize() handler, a backup code is validated by decrypting `user.backupCodes`, finding the matching index (`backupCodes.indexOf(...)`), and only afterwards persisting the invalidated code back to the DB (`backupCodes[index] = null` followed by `prisma.user.update`). There is no transaction, row lock, or atomic conditional update between the read and the write. Two concurrent login attempts (or an attacker replaying a captured request) using the same backup code can both read the un-invalidated code, both pass validation, and both succeed in logging in before either write completes — violating the single-use guarantee that backup codes are supposed to provide. This should use an atomic update (e.g. a conditional update keyed on the still-encrypted blob, or a per-code DB row with a unique/used flag) instead of decrypt → compute in memory → re-encrypt → write.

title: Backup code comparison is case sensitive but codes are generated lowercase
body: Backup codes are generated in apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts via `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")`, which always produces lowercase hex characters (0-9a-f). However, when matching the user-supplied code here (`credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")`) and in apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts (`req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")`), no case normalization (e.g. `.toLowerCase()`) is applied before the `indexOf` comparison. Mobile keyboards/autocapitalize, copy-paste from a capitalized rendering, or a user simply typing uppercase hex letters will cause a valid backup code to be rejected as `IncorrectBackupCode`, producing confusing lockouts for legitimate users.

title: Backup codes are stored with reversible encryption instead of a one-way hash
body: Backup codes only ever need an equality check to be verified (unlike the TOTP secret, which must be decrypted repeatedly to compute codes). Storing them with `symmetricEncrypt` means that anyone who obtains both the database and `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY` can recover all ten plaintext backup codes for every user, rather than being limited to verifying a guess as with a proper one-way hash (e.g. bcrypt/sha256 with per-code comparison). Using a one-way hash would reduce the blast radius of a database/key compromise for this specific secret.

title: Misleading "missing_backup_codes" message tells users to regenerate codes in settings, but no such feature exists
body: The new string `"missing_backup_codes": "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings."` is shown when a user's `backupCodes` column is null but 2FA is otherwise enabled. However, there is no settings UI or API endpoint added in this PR (or elsewhere) that lets a user regenerate backup codes without fully disabling and re-enabling two-factor authentication (which also resets the TOTP secret). The message gives users incorrect instructions and no actionable path to resolve the error.

title: No automated test covers logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code
body: The PR's own TODO (`// TODO: add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup`) acknowledges that the actual backup-code authentication paths are untested. The added test only exercises the backup-codes *display* step (download button, copy button, close button) during setup; it never submits a backup code through the login form (apps/web/pages/auth/login.tsx) nor through the "Lost access" flow in DisableTwoFactorModal. Since this is the core new functionality (bypassing 2FA with a backup code) and touches authentication/security-sensitive code, shipping without end-to-end coverage of the actual login/disable-with-backup-code flow is a significant gap.

title: New BackupCode component exported under the wrong function name (copy-paste leftover)
body: `apps/web/components/auth/BackupCode.tsx` is clearly adapted from `TwoFactor.tsx`, but the component function itself is still declared as `export default function TwoFactor({ center = true })` instead of `BackupCode`. This is cosmetic for the default export, but it means React DevTools, error stack traces, and any code that inspects `Component.name` or `displayName` will show "TwoFactor" for two completely different components, making debugging and future refactors confusing.

title: Backup-codes download Blob URL is never revoked when the modal is cancelled, leaking memory
body: `handleSetup` creates a Blob URL via `URL.createObjectURL(textBlob)` and stores it in `backupCodesUrl`. The only place the previous URL is revoked is right before creating a new one inside `handleSetup` (`if (backupCodesUrl) URL.revokeObjectURL(backupCodesUrl)`). `resetState()` (used when the user cancels the modal or closes it after setup) resets `password`, `errorMessage`, and `step`, but does not revoke `backupCodesUrl` nor reset it to an empty string. If a user completes/cancels the 2FA setup flow without triggering another `handleSetup` call, the created Blob URL is never released for the lifetime of the page, leaking memory.

title: Backup code request field is used without type/presence validation before calling string methods
body: `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` assumes `req.body.backupCode` is always a string whenever it is truthy, but request bodies from an API endpoint are not type-checked. If a client (or an attacker probing the endpoint) sends a non-string value for `backupCode` (e.g. an object or number), `.replaceAll` will throw a runtime TypeError that is not caught anywhere in the handler, resulting in an unhandled exception/500 instead of a clean 400 validation error.

title: Backup code validation/consumption has a check-then-update race (TOCTOU)
body: The backup-code login path reads `user.backupCodes`, decrypts it, checks `indexOf` for a match, then later re-encrypts and writes back the array with the used code nulled out (lines 139-156). There is no transaction, row lock, or optimistic version check between the read and the write. If two requests for the same user run concurrently (e.g. a double-submitted login or two tabs), both can read the same pre-update state, both pass the `index !== -1` check, and whichever update runs last overwrites the other's change — meaning the single-use guarantee promised by the UI text ('Each backup code can be used exactly once') can be violated: a single code can authenticate more than once, or one of two different codes used concurrently can end up still marked as unused.

title: Backup codes are stored with reversible symmetric encryption instead of being hashed
body: Backup codes are encrypted with `symmetricEncrypt`/`symmetricDecrypt` using `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (setup.ts line 68, next-auth-options.ts lines 140/154) rather than hashed. Unlike TOTP secrets, backup codes never need to be redisplayed after generation, so they should be hashed (similar to passwords) rather than stored reversibly. Anyone who obtains the DB plus the single symmetric encryption key (which protects many other secrets) can recover every user's plaintext backup codes, which is a stronger blast radius than necessary for a one-time-use credential.

title: Backup code input has no normalization, but generated codes are lowercase hex only
body: `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")` (setup.ts) always produces lowercase hex characters, but the `TextField` used to collect the backup code here has no `autoCapitalize="off"`/lowercasing/trim applied, and the server-side comparison (`backupCodes.indexOf(credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""))` in next-auth-options.ts and disable.ts) is an exact, case-sensitive string match. Many mobile browsers auto-capitalize the first character of a plain text input by default, and hex codes contain letters a-f roughly 37% of the time as the first character. A user who manually types a valid backup code on a mobile device can have it silently mismatched and rejected as 'incorrect', even though the code is correct.

title: BackupCode component's internal function is misnamed "TwoFactor"
body: This new file exports a component for displaying/collecting the backup code, but the function is declared as `export default function TwoFactor({ center = true })`, an apparent copy-paste leftover from TwoFactor.tsx. While the default export still works because callers alias the import (`import BackupCode from "@components/auth/BackupCode"`), the component will show up as "TwoFactor" in React DevTools/stack traces alongside the actual TwoFactor component, which is confusing for debugging and future maintenance.

title: "missing_backup_codes" message points to a non-existent settings feature
body: The new string `"missing_backup_codes": "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings."` is shown to users on login/disable when no backup codes exist, but this PR provides no settings UI or endpoint to regenerate backup codes after 2FA has been enabled — the only way to get new backup codes is to disable and re-enable 2FA entirely (which re-runs the setup flow). Telling users to 'generate them in your settings' is misleading and will create support confusion since no such control exists.

title: onEnable() is no longer called immediately after 2FA is actually enabled server-side
body: Previously, a successful TOTP verification called `onEnable()` immediately, letting the parent page refresh its 2FA-enabled state. Now, on success the code only does `setStep(SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes)` (line 135); `onEnable()` is deferred until the user explicitly clicks the new 'Close' button on the backup-codes screen (around line 267). At this point 2FA is already enabled on the server (the enable API call already succeeded). If the user dismisses the dialog any other way (Escape key, clicking the overlay, closing the tab) before clicking 'Close', the parent component's `onEnable` callback never fires, leaving the UI out of sync with the backend (e.g. a toggle/switch that still shows 2FA as disabled even though it is enabled) until the page is reloaded.

title: No e2e coverage added for logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code
body: This PR implements an entirely new authentication path (logging in via backup code) and a new disable path (disabling 2FA via backup code), but the only test addition related to these flows is a `// TODO: add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup` comment. The existing tests only exercise download/copy/close of the backup-codes dialog during setup; the actual consumption of a backup code to log in or to disable 2FA (including the single-use/invalidation behavior) is left completely untested, despite being the core new feature of this PR.

title: FIXME comment added but the broken assertion is left unfixed
body: A new comment at line 50-51 explicitly documents that `await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=two-factor-switch]').isChecked()).toBeTruthy()` passes even when the switch is not checked (because `.isChecked()` returns an unawaited Promise, which is always truthy). The PR acknowledges this is broken but ships it unfixed, so the 'Enable 2FA' step in this test does not actually verify that the switch became checked, reducing confidence in the enable-2FA regression coverage that this PR also modifies.

title: Backup-codes download Blob URL can leak if setup is cancelled before completion
body: `handleSetup` creates a Blob URL via `URL.createObjectURL` for the backup codes (lines 94-99) and only revokes the previous URL the next time `handleSetup` succeeds (`if (backupCodesUrl) URL.revokeObjectURL(backupCodesUrl)`). `resetState()` (line 71-75), which runs when the user clicks 'Cancel' at any step or 'Close' after viewing backup codes, does not revoke `backupCodesUrl`. If the user cancels after the password step succeeded (so a Blob URL was created) but before starting setup again, or simply finishes the flow, the object URL is never revoked and the Blob remains referenced for the lifetime of the page, which is a minor memory leak that is easy to avoid by revoking in `resetState`.

title: Backup code check-and-invalidate is not atomic, allowing reuse via race condition
body: In the credentials authorize() callback, a backup code is validated by decrypting the stored backupCodes array, finding the matching index, then issuing a separate prisma.user.update() to persist the code as used (lines ~137-156). Between the read and the write there is no transaction/lock, so two concurrent login attempts using the same backup code can both pass the `indexOf` check before either write completes, letting a single-use backup code be consumed more than once. Since backup codes are meant to grant exactly one use (per the UI copy 'Each backup code can be used exactly once'), this undermines the single-use guarantee and is a legitimate security/data-integrity issue for a security-sensitive code path.

title: Backup code comparison is case sensitive while generated codes are lowercase hex
body: `backupCodes.indexOf(credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""))` compares the raw user input against stored codes without normalizing case. Codes are generated with `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString('hex')` which is always lowercase, but the BackupCode input field has no autoCapitalize/autoCorrect restrictions, so mobile keyboards or manual re-typing from a printed copy can introduce uppercase characters, causing a valid backup code to be rejected as incorrect. The same issue exists in `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts` line 61.

title: Backup codes are stored with reversible symmetric encryption instead of one-way hashing
body: In `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts` line 68, backup codes are stored using `symmetricEncrypt`, the same reversible scheme used for the TOTP secret. Unlike the TOTP secret (which must be decrypted to compute codes), backup codes only need equality comparison and should be hashed (e.g. bcrypt/sha256) so that leaking CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY does not also reveal every user's plaintext backup codes. Storing them reversibly increases the blast radius of a key compromise.

title: BackupCode component function is misnamed "TwoFactor"
body: The exported default function in BackupCode.tsx is declared as `function TwoFactor({ center = true })`, apparently copy-pasted from TwoFactor.tsx and never renamed. This doesn't break runtime behavior since it's a default export, but it causes React DevTools/profiler and stack traces to show the wrong component name (identical to the actual TwoFactor component), making debugging and future maintenance confusing.

title: No e2e test actually exercises logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code
body: The PR's stated purpose includes 'enable their use during 2fa login flow', but the only backup-code-related additions to the e2e suite are clicking the download/copy/close buttons on the backup codes screen during setup (lines 110-125). There is no test that logs in using a backup code, no test that disables 2FA via the new 'Lost access' backup-code path, and no test for the IncorrectBackupCode/MissingBackupCodes error paths. This gap is explicitly acknowledged by the added comment '// TODO: add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup' but is never addressed, leaving the core new functionality (backup code login, which has the race-condition and case-sensitivity issues noted elsewhere) completely untested.

title: Backup code recovery is unreachable for SSO/magic-link forced-TOTP login flow
body: When a user is routed to the login page via `loginWithTotp` (SSO/email identity providers requiring 2FA, surfaced via the `totpEmail` prop), the footer renders `ExternalTotpFooter` (lines 135-143), which only offers a 'Cancel' button. The 'Lost access' button that toggles `twoFactorLostAccess` (enabling the BackupCode input) only exists in `TwoFactorFooter`, used when `!totpEmail`. As a result, users signing in through Google/SAML/magic-link flows with 2FA enabled have no UI path to use a backup code if they lose access to their authenticator, even though the backend `authorize()` callback supports a `backupCode` credential for exactly this scenario. These users are locked out despite the feature nominally covering the login flow.

title: 2FA is enabled server-side before the UI confirms it, and dismissing the backup-codes screen skips onEnable()
body: After the OTP is verified, `handleEnable` sets `step` to `SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes` instead of calling `onEnable()` immediately (as it did before this PR). `onEnable()` is now only invoked when the user clicks the explicit 'Close' button (lines 263-272). If the user dismisses the dialog any other way (Escape key, clicking outside, or the dialog's native close affordance via `onOpenChange`), 2FA is already enabled in the database but the parent component is never notified via `onEnable()`, leaving the parent's UI (e.g. the two-factor switch) potentially stale until a manual refresh. Previously this race did not exist because `onEnable()` fired as soon as the server confirmed success.

title: backupCodesUrl Blob object URL is never revoked when the modal is cancelled/closed
body: `setBackupCodesUrl(URL.createObjectURL(textBlob))` (line 99) creates a Blob URL for the downloadable backup codes file. It is only revoked on a subsequent call to `handleSetup` (`if (backupCodesUrl) URL.revokeObjectURL(backupCodesUrl)`, line 98). `resetState()` (lines 71-75), used when the user cancels or closes the modal, does not revoke the URL, so every completed 2FA setup leaks one Blob URL for the lifetime of the page/tab.

title: "missing_backup_codes" message implies a settings action that doesn't exist
body: The string `"missing_backup_codes": "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings."` tells users to regenerate backup codes in settings, but no such explicit 'regenerate backup codes' action was added in this PR — the only way to get new backup codes is to fully disable and re-enable two-factor authentication. The message is misleading and may confuse users trying to find a non-existent settings option.

title: Known-broken test assertion acknowledged via comment but left unfixed
body: A new comment was added: '// FIXME: this passes even when switch is not checked, compare to test below which checks for data-state="checked" and works as expected', directly above `await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=two-factor-switch]').isChecked()).toBeTruthy();` (line 53). The `.isChecked()` call returns a Promise that is never awaited before being wrapped in `expect(...).toBeTruthy()`, so the assertion always passes regardless of actual switch state. The PR author identifies this defect but does not fix it, leaving the first 2FA-enable test unable to actually verify that the switch became checked.

title: Missing optional chaining causes crash when no destinationCalendar exists
body: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` followed by `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"` will throw a TypeError ("Cannot read properties of undefined") whenever `evt.destinationCalendar` is empty/null and the booking location is Google Meet. This is a very common scenario (organizer/host has no connected calendar), and since this code runs inside `EventManager.create()`, which is invoked on every booking, this will crash booking creation for any Google-Meet booking without a destination calendar. The old code used `evt.destinationCalendar?.integration !== "google_calendar"`, which was safe; the refactor to an array dropped the optional chaining on the destructured element.

title: Inverted condition for setting organization slug breaks org creation
body: The condition for assigning `slug` was changed from `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`, inverting the logic. Combined with the unchanged `requestedSlug` assignment (`...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { requestedSlug: slug } : {})`), when billing is disabled the newly created organization now gets neither `slug` nor `requestedSlug`, so the org has no usable slug at all; when billing is enabled it gets both `slug` and a pending `requestedSlug`, which is contradictory. This change is unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (destinationCalendar handling) and looks like an accidental regression from a bad merge/rebase that will break organization creation, particularly for self-hosted instances where billing is disabled.

title: Dead fallback logic in updateEvent leaves calendarId undefined
body: `const selectedCalendar = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;` searches for a destinationCalendar entry whose `externalId` equals `externalCalendarId` — but this branch is only reached when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so the comparison `cal.externalId === externalCalendarId` can essentially never match. The fallback therefore always resolves to `undefined`, and `calendar.events.update({ calendarId: undefined, ... })` is called, which will fail against the Google Calendar API. This breaks calendar updates whenever `externalCalendarId` isn't already known/stored (e.g. missing/legacy booking references), a case this PR's multi-calendar support is supposed to handle correctly.

title: Same dead fallback logic duplicated in deleteEvent
body: `const calendarId = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;` has the identical self-referential bug as in updateEvent: the `.find` predicate compares against the already-known-falsy `externalCalendarId`, so it never matches and always yields `undefined`. Unlike updateEvent, this one is masked by the subsequent `calendarId ? calendarId : defaultCalendarId` fallback to `"primary"`, but it means the code silently falls back to deleting from the primary calendar instead of the correct destination calendar whenever `externalCalendarId` is not supplied, which can delete the wrong event or fail to delete the intended one for secondary host calendars.

title: Hangout link patch call omits the "primary" fallback used for insert
body: In `createEvent`, the `calendar.events.insert` call uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"`, but the subsequent `calendar.events.patch` call (to attach the hangout link in the description) uses the raw `calendarId: selectedCalendar` without the same fallback. If no destinationCalendar entry matches the current `credentialId` (so `selectedCalendar` is `undefined`), the insert succeeds against "primary" but the patch call is made with an undefined calendarId, which will fail to update the description with the hangout link.

title: Organizer email override always uses the first destinationCalendar regardless of which host's credential is creating the event
body: `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is destructured as the first element of `calEventRaw.destinationCalendar` and used to override the organizer attendee's email (`email: mainHostDestinationCalendar?.externalId ? mainHostDestinationCalendar.externalId : calEventRaw.organizer.email`). When `createAllCalendarEvents` loops over multiple destination calendars/hosts and calls `createEvent` once per host credential, every call still uses the same first-array-entry override instead of the entry matching the `credentialId` actually creating the event (which is correctly looked up a few lines later via `calEventRaw.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.credentialId === credentialId)`). As a result, for collective events with multiple hosts, every secondary host's calendar event will show the first host's calendar email as the "organizer" attendee instead of their own, undermining the core fix this PR is meant to deliver. The same bug exists in `updateEvent` (lines 198-230) with `mainHostDestinationCalendar`.

title: Pushing team destination calendars onto evt.destinationCalendar is a no-op when it is null
body: `destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` exists (see the ternary ending in `: null,`). Later, `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars);` uses optional chaining, which silently does nothing when `evt.destinationCalendar` is `null`. Consequently, for a COLLECTIVE event where the organizer has no personal destination calendar but other hosts do, all the collected `teamDestinationCalendars` are discarded and only the organizer is considered (incorrectly, with none at all), so secondary hosts never get their calendar invites created — defeating the main goal of this PR in exactly the scenario it is meant to fix.

title: organization.slug selection dropped from loadUsers query for dynamic bookings
body: In the refactored `loadUsers` function, the Prisma `select` used for the dynamic/group booking branch (`!eventTypeId`) no longer includes `organization: { select: { slug: true } }`, which was present before this change. If any downstream code in this handler (or in dynamic booking flows generally) relies on `organizerUser.organization?.slug` (e.g., for organization-aware booking links), it will now silently receive `undefined`, changing behavior for dynamic/group bookings tied to an organization without any related test coverage added.

title: Error logging removed from updateAllCalendarEvents failure path
body: The previous `console.error(message)` call in the catch block of `updateAllCalendarEvents` was removed when converting the single-reference return to the multi-reference `.map()` version. Errors that occur while updating calendar events (e.g. missing credentials) are now silently swallowed without any log output, making production issues in this path much harder to diagnose.

title: Inconsistent null vs empty-array representation of "no destination calendar" across code paths
body: This test now expects `destinationCalendar: []` for the BOOKING_REJECTED webhook payload (produced via confirm.handler.ts, which always falls back to `[]`), while the BOOKING_CREATED and BOOKING_REQUESTED tests in the same file still expect `destinationCalendar: null` (produced via handleNewBooking.ts, which falls back to `null`). Both represent the same "no calendar connected" state but surface differently depending on which code path produced the CalendarEvent. Since `destinationCalendar` is now a public/typed field consumed by webhooks and third-party integrations, this inconsistency (`null` in some flows, `[]` in others) is a fragile and confusing contract that should be normalized to one representation.

title: No tests cover multi-host destinationCalendar behavior introduced by this PR
body: This PR converts `destinationCalendar` from a single object to an array across 22 files and rewrites significant parts of EventManager.ts, CalendarManager.ts, and handleNewBooking.ts's collective-event calendar logic (including the host-list building at this line and the `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...)` call), but the author's checklist explicitly states no tests were added, and the only test file touched (webhook.e2e.ts) merely adjusts one assertion to match the new shape rather than verifying the multi-host calendar invite behavior described as the purpose of the PR. Given the number of latent bugs this refactor introduces (e.g. the no-op push when destinationCalendar is null, and the Google Calendar organizer-override/fallback bugs), the lack of any automated test for the actual collective multi-host calendar scenario is a significant gap for a change of this risk level.

title: Unsafe destructuring can crash booking creation when no destination calendar exists
body: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` followed by `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"` accesses `.integration` without an optional chain. If `evt.destinationCalendar` is `null`/`undefined`/`[]` (e.g. the booking organizer has no destination calendar configured) and the chosen location is Google Meet, `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined`, and the comparison throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'integration')`, crashing `EventManager.create()`. Previously this used optional chaining (`evt.destinationCalendar?.integration !== ...`), which safely evaluated to true. This regression can break every new booking that selects Google Meet without a connected Google Calendar.

title: Broken fallback calendar lookup in updateEvent/deleteEvent always resolves to undefined
body: In both `updateEvent` (line 256) and `deleteEvent` (line 317) the fallback branch computes `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` — but this code only executes when `externalCalendarId` is falsy (the ternary's else branch), so the `.find` predicate compares `cal.externalId` against the same falsy value that triggered the fallback. This will essentially never match a real destination calendar entry, so `selectedCalendar`/`calendarId` resolves to `undefined` whenever no `externalCalendarId` is supplied (e.g. for older booking references without a stored externalCalendarId). Previously the fallback correctly used `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. This breaks updating/deleting Google Calendar events for any booking reference lacking an externalCalendarId.

title: Only Google Calendar filters destinationCalendar by credentialId; other calendar apps always use the first host's calendar
body: `createAllCalendarEvents` iterates `event.destinationCalendar` (which now contains one entry per host for collective events) and calls `createEvent(credential, event, destination.externalId)` for each host's credential, but the full, unfiltered `event` object (with the complete destinationCalendar array for all hosts) is passed to every calendar provider's `createEvent`. Only `GoogleCalendarService.createEvent` (packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts) actually uses the `credentialId` argument to pick the matching destination calendar entry. Office365 (`packages/app-store/office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` lines 72-77), Lark (`packages/app-store/larkcalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` lines 125-129), and the CalDAV-based `packages/lib/CalendarService.ts` (lines 156-166) all just destructure `event.destinationCalendar[0]` as the 'main host' regardless of which host's credential is currently creating the event. As a result, for collective events where the second (or later) host uses Office365/Lark/CalDAV, the event will be created against the first host's calendar externalId using the second host's credentials — the wrong calendar, or an inaccessible one — defeating the PR's stated purpose for every non-Google calendar integration.

title: Inverted condition for assigning organization slug vs requiring billing
body: The condition for setting the `slug` field was changed from `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`, inverting the original intent. Previously the subdomain `slug` was only assigned directly when team billing was NOT required (so no payment gate was needed); when billing was enabled, only `metadata.requestedSlug` was set pending payment. With this change, `slug` is now set immediately when billing IS enabled (potentially letting an org claim a subdomain before completing required payment) and is never set when billing is disabled (orgs created in that mode end up with no slug at all). This change is unrelated to the PR's stated destinationCalendar fix and appears to be an accidental regression carried in from elsewhere.

title: Recurring-event calendar deletion logic runs once per calendar reference, duplicating deletes
body: The outer loop over `bookingCalendarReference` was changed from a single `.find()` result to `.filter()` plus a `for` loop to support multiple hosts/credentials. However, the nested recurring-event branch (lines 444-468) that deletes every remaining recurring booking instance from `bookingToDelete.user.credentials` and `updatedBookings` is executed on every iteration of the outer loop. For a collective booking with N calendar references (N hosts with credentialId set), this recurring-deletion pass — which already iterates all organizer calendar credentials and all updatedBookings internally — now runs N times, issuing duplicate `deleteEvent` calls for the same bookings/credentials. This is wasteful, risks extra/duplicate calendar API calls, and can surface spurious errors.

title: Team destination calendars silently dropped when evt.destinationCalendar is null
body: After building `evt`, the code does `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars);` guarded only for COLLECTIVE events. `evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` exists. In that case the optional chaining makes `push` a no-op, so the destination calendars collected for the other (non-organizer) hosts in `teamDestinationCalendars` are silently discarded and those hosts never receive calendar invites for a collective event. This is exactly the multi-host scenario the PR claims to fix, so the fix fails for organizers without a configured destination calendar.

title: organization.slug dropped from the dynamic-booking user select without apparent replacement
body: In the rewritten `loadUsers` function, the `prisma.user.findMany` select for the dynamic (no-eventTypeId) booking path used to include `organization: { select: { slug: true } }`, but this field was removed in the rewrite (only `...userSelect.select, credentials: true, metadata: true` remain). If any downstream logic in the dynamic booking flow (e.g. building org-aware links or multi-tenant routing) relies on `user.organization.slug`, it will now silently be `undefined`. This field removal is unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (destinationCalendar array support) and looks like an unintentional regression.

title: No test coverage added for the actual multi-host destinationCalendar behavior
body: The PR converts `destinationCalendar` to an array across ~20 files and changes behavior for collective events with multiple hosts, but the only test changes are updates to expected JSON shape (`destinationCalendar: null` -> `destinationCalendar: []`) in existing single-host webhook e2e tests. The PR description itself states 'I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective or that my feature works.' There is no test verifying that a collective event with two hosts using different calendar credentials actually results in calendar invites being created in each host's correct calendar — the exact scenario this PR is meant to fix, and the area where several of the above bugs (e.g. non-Google calendar providers always using host #1's calendar) would have been caught.

title: Inconsistent empty-value representation for destinationCalendar across handlers
body: Different handlers normalize a missing destination calendar differently now that the field is an array: `confirm.handler.ts` (line 179), `webhook.ts`, `paypal-webhook.ts`, and `deleteCredential.handler.ts` fall back to `[]`, while `handleNewBooking.ts` falls back to `null`. Consumers of the webhook payload (and any other code reading `evt.destinationCalendar`) now observe different representations (`null` vs `[]`) for the logically identical 'no destination calendar' state depending on which code path produced the event, which is an inconsistent contract that can break strict-equality checks or type assumptions downstream.

title: Hangout-link patch call can target an undefined calendarId
body: In `createEvent`, the initial `calendar.events.insert` call uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"`, defaulting to `"primary"` when no destination calendar matches the current `credentialId`. However, the follow-up `calendar.events.patch(...)` call made when a hangout link is present (line 168) uses the raw `calendarId: selectedCalendar` without the same `|| "primary"` fallback. If no destination calendar entry matches the credential (so `selectedCalendar` is `undefined`), the event is inserted into `"primary"` but the subsequent patch to add the hangout link to the description targets an undefined calendar id, which will likely fail silently or error out, leaving the event without the hangout link update.

title: Inverted condition sets org slug immediately even when billing is required, bypassing the pending-approval flow
body: The condition for setting `slug` directly on org creation was inverted. Previously `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` meant the real `slug` was only set immediately when billing was NOT required, while `metadata.requestedSlug` (a staged/pending value) was set when billing WAS required (`...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { requestedSlug: slug })`), so a team billing flow could later confirm and activate the slug. The new code does `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})` and `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { requestedSlug: slug } : {})`, which sets BOTH the final `slug` and `requestedSlug` immediately whenever team billing is enabled. This activates/publishes the organization's slug before payment/approval is completed, bypassing the intended billing gate for organization creation. This change is unrelated to the PR's destinationCalendar purpose and looks like an accidental regression that should be reverted.

title: Unguarded property access on possibly-undefined destinationCalendar entry causes a crash
body: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` followed by `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"` will throw a TypeError ("Cannot read properties of undefined") whenever `evt.destinationCalendar` is null, undefined, or an empty array, because destructuring an empty array yields `undefined` for `mainHostDestinationCalendar`. The previous code used optional chaining (`evt.destinationCalendar?.integration !== "google_calendar"`), which correctly fell back to Cal Video when no destination calendar existed. Now, any booking with Google Meet selected as location but no destination calendar (e.g. `handleNewBooking.ts` can set `destinationCalendar: null`) will crash the booking-creation flow instead of gracefully falling back to Cal Video.

title: Broken calendar lookup fallback in updateEvent/deleteEvent always resolves to undefined/primary
body: In `updateEvent` (line 254-256) and `deleteEvent` (line 315-317), the fallback branch is `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`, but this code only executes when `externalCalendarId` is already falsy (the ternary's true-branch already handles the truthy case). This means it searches the destinationCalendar array for an entry whose `externalId` equals the already-known falsy value, which will essentially never match a real calendar entry. As a result, `updateEvent` ends up calling the Google API with `calendarId: undefined` (likely causing API errors), and `deleteEvent` silently falls back to the hardcoded `"primary"` calendar instead of the correct host-specific calendar. This defeats the multi-host destinationCalendar support this PR is meant to add for update/delete flows whenever a booking reference lacks a stored externalCalendarId (e.g. legacy bookings or non-primary calendars).

title: updateEvent() never returns externalId/credentialId, dropping calendar reference tracking on location change
body: `EventResult` now has an `externalId` field and `EventManager.updateLocation()` builds `referencesToCreate` using `externalCalendarId: result.externalId` and `credentialId: result.credentialId ?? undefined` (previously it fell back to `evt.destinationCalendar?.externalId`/`?.credentialId`). However, `CalendarManager.updateEvent()`'s returned object (lines 313-322) never sets `externalId` or `credentialId` - only `createEvent()` does. Consequently, after a booking's location is edited (`updateLocation()`), the newly created booking reference will always have `externalCalendarId: undefined` and `credentialId: undefined`, losing the information needed to target the correct calendar for future updates/deletes of that booking, especially important for multi-host bookings where picking the wrong credential/calendar is now possible.

title: Organizer attendee email override uses the first destinationCalendar entry regardless of which host's credential is creating/updating the event
body: In both `createEvent` (lines 100-124) and `updateEvent` (lines 198-230), `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is simply the first entry of `event.destinationCalendar` (an array now containing every host's destination calendar). This value is used to override the organizer attendee's `email` field. Since `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents`/`updateAllCalendarEvents` invoke this service once per host/credential while passing the same shared `event` object (with the full array), every host's calendar-event creation/update will use the FIRST host's calendar externalId for the organizer attendee email instead of the calendar belonging to the credential actually performing the call (which is already correctly resolved via `selectedCalendar`/`credentialId` elsewhere in the same function). This can produce incorrect organizer attendee identities in secondary hosts' calendar events.

title: Team hosts' destination calendars silently dropped when evt.destinationCalendar resolves to null
body: `destinationCalendar` on `evt` is set to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` exist. Later, `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is used to append other hosts' destination calendars for collective events. Because `evt.destinationCalendar` can be `null`, the optional chaining makes this push a no-op in that case, silently discarding all other hosts' destination calendars. This is precisely the scenario this PR is meant to fix (collective event with multiple hosts having calendars), so bookings where the organizer has no destination calendar but other hosts do will still fail to deliver calendar invites to those hosts.

title: Dropped organization.slug selection in rewritten loadUsers() for dynamic bookings
body: The rewritten `loadUsers()` function's dynamic-user-list branch (`!eventTypeId`) queries `prisma.user.findMany` with `select: { ...userSelect.select, credentials: true, metadata: true }`, but the previous implementation also selected `organization: { select: { slug: true } }`. This field is no longer fetched for dynamic bookings. If any downstream logic in this handler or in email/booking link generation for dynamic events relies on `user.organization.slug`, it will now be undefined, which is an unrelated regression introduced while refactoring this function for the destinationCalendar changes.

title: Calendar event creation for multiple hosts is now sequential instead of parallel
body: In `createAllCalendarEvents`, the new `for (const destination of event.destinationCalendar) { ... await createEvent(credential, event, destination.externalId) ... }` loop awaits each host's calendar event creation sequentially. For a collective event with N hosts, this results in N sequential network calls to external calendar providers instead of running them concurrently (as the credential-type branch below it still does via `Promise.all`). This can noticeably increase booking latency for collective events with several hosts that each have a calendar connected.

title: No new/updated tests cover the multi-host destinationCalendar array behavior
body: The PR converts `destinationCalendar` to an array across the whole booking/calendar pipeline (EventManager, CalendarManager, multiple calendar app services) but the only test change is updating one expected value from `null` to `[]` in an existing webhook e2e test. The PR description explicitly acknowledges no tests were added to prove the fix works. Given the number of subtle correctness issues identified in the array-handling logic (e.g. in GoogleCalendarService update/delete calendar resolution, and the dropped team destinationCalendar push), this feature lacks test coverage for the core multi-host invite scenario the PR claims to fix.

title: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses broken computed property keys, stripping all fields except access_token
body: The schema is built with `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()`. Calling `.toString()` on a Zod schema instance does not produce a dynamic/catch-all key based on the input data - it returns a fixed literal string (effectively the default `Object.prototype.toString()` output, the same value for both computed keys). The resulting zod object schema therefore only actually validates `access_token` plus one bogus, never-matching literal key. Because `z.object()` strips unknown keys by default (no `.passthrough()`), every other field in the token response (`expiry_date`, `refresh_token`, `expires_in`, etc.) is silently dropped from the parsed result whenever the minimum schema is used (i.e. whenever `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` are set). This corrupts the stored credential object (fields are lost) and, combined with the refresh_token fallback a few lines below, actively destroys real refresh tokens, breaking the very feature this PR implements.

title: Fallback overwrites real refresh_token with the literal string "refresh_token"
body: When `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token` is falsy (e.g. because the schema stripped it, or because the provider legitimately omits refresh_token on refresh responses - several providers, including Office365 whose schema marks `refresh_token` as optional, do not always return a new refresh_token), this code assigns the literal string `"refresh_token"` as the refresh token value. That bogus placeholder then gets persisted to the credential's `key` in the database, permanently destroying the real refresh token and breaking all subsequent token refreshes for that credential until the user re-authenticates. This can happen even without the new credential-sync feature enabled, as a regression for any provider whose refresh endpoint omits refresh_token.

title: Sync-endpoint response shape does not match what several callers expect, causing runtime failures
body: When credential sync is enabled, this function returns the raw, un-parsed `fetch` `Response` object from `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`. However several callers assume a different shape depending on their normal (non-sync) refresh implementation: GoogleCalendarService reads `res?.data` (expecting an axios/googleapis-style response), HubspotCalendarService reads properties like `.expiresIn`/`.accessToken` directly off the return value (expecting an already-parsed `HubspotToken` object), and the Zoho-Bigin/ZohoCRM CalendarServices read `tokenInfo.data` (expecting an axios response). None of these properties exist on a raw fetch `Response`, so when sync mode is enabled these integrations will silently receive `undefined` values (NaN expiry dates, undefined access tokens) or throw, and then typically fail to persist anything useful, breaking token refresh for these providers under the very feature this PR adds.

title: Outgoing credential-sync request has no HTTP status check and no built-in authentication
body: The POST request made to `process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` carries no authentication header/secret from Cal.com's side (only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` in the body), and the response is returned and used regardless of `response.ok`. A failing or malicious response at this endpoint (e.g. a 4xx/5xx or an endpoint that answers unauthenticated) would be treated as a successful token refresh, and the self-hosted receiving endpoint has no way to verify the request actually originated from the paired Cal.com deployment, since no shared secret is sent.

title: appStoreMetadata is looked up by app.slug, but the generated metadata map is keyed by app directory name, not slug
body: `appStoreMetadata` is generated by scanning app-store directories and is keyed by each app's folder/dirName (e.g. `office365video`, `googlecalendar`, `zoomvideo`, `larkcalendar`), while `app.slug` (and `reqBody.appSlug`) is the user-facing slug stored on the `App` model, which frequently differs from the directory name (e.g. slug `msteams` for dir `office365video`, slug `google-calendar` for dir `googlecalendar`, slug `zoom` for dir `zoomvideo`, slug `lark-calendar` for dir `larkcalendar`). Indexing `appStoreMetadata` with `app.slug` will return `undefined` for most of these apps, causing the handler to incorrectly respond with 404 "App not found" even though the app and slug are valid, breaking credential sync for the majority of the apps this PR claims to support.

title: Webhook secret comparison is not constant-time
body: The webhook secret check uses plain `!==` string comparison between the request header and `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. This is vulnerable to timing attacks that could help an attacker brute-force the secret byte-by-byte. Given that a correct secret grants the ability to create/overwrite arbitrary users' third-party credentials (full account/app takeover), this comparison should use a constant-time equality check (e.g. `crypto.timingSafeEqual`).

title: Unvalidated request body/decryption can throw unhandled exceptions
body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` uses `.parse` (which throws on invalid input) instead of `.safeParse`, and there is no try/catch around it or around `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` further down. A malformed request body or payload that fails decryption/JSON parsing will throw an uncaught exception inside the handler instead of returning a controlled 400 response, and the handler also never checks `req.method`, so non-POST requests are processed the same way.

title: Credential lookup via findFirst can target the wrong credential when multiple exist for the same app/user
body: The handler finds an existing credential with `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` and, if found, overwrites its `key`. Several apps (e.g. Google Calendar) support installing multiple credentials of the same type for one user. `findFirst` with no explicit ordering can return any one of them non-deterministically, so this sync could silently overwrite the wrong one of a user's multiple connected accounts for the same app.

title: Salesforce token refresh was not wired up to the new credential-sync mechanism
body: Unlike every other provider touched by this PR (Google Calendar, Office365, Hubspot, Zoom, Webex, Lark, Zoho CRM/Bigin), the newly added Salesforce refresh-token logic calls `fetch("https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token", ...)` directly instead of going through `refreshOAuthTokens`. As a result, enabling `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED`/`CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` has no effect for Salesforce credentials; they will always be refreshed against Salesforce directly, contradicting the PR's stated goal of letting self-hosters' app store be the source of truth for all apps, and nothing in the PR description calls out this exclusion.

title: Unrelated change replaces dynamic redirect URI with a hardcoded slug
body: This line was changed from `WEBAPP_URL + \`/api/integrations/${appConfig.slug}/callback\`` to the hardcoded `WEBAPP_URL + \`/api/integrations/zoho-bigin/callback\``. This is unrelated to the credential-sync feature described in the PR, and it introduces maintenance drift risk: if `appConfig.slug` in `config.json` is ever updated, this redirect URI will silently stop matching the app's configured slug, instead of automatically staying in sync.

title: Dynamic zod keys via .toString() don't validate anything meaningful
body: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses computed property keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` intending (per the comment) to allow any numeric property to pass as the expiry and allow other properties through. However, calling `.toString()` on a Zod schema instance does not produce a wildcard matcher — it produces a fixed, identical string literal for both expressions (Zod schemas don't override toString()), so both computed keys collapse onto the same literal key, and the second (optional/unknown) overwrites the first. The resulting schema is effectively just `{ access_token: string }`. Because Zod objects strip unrecognized keys from the parsed result by default, every other field returned by a self-hosted credential-sync endpoint (expiry, refresh_token, etc.) is silently discarded whenever APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set. This defeats the entire purpose of the sync feature: expiry/refresh data never survives the parse.

title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token"
body: When the parsed refresh response has no `refresh_token` field, the code sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` — a hardcoded placeholder string, not the previously stored refresh token. This path runs for both sync and non-sync refresh flows (e.g. office365calendar and zoomvideo call parseRefreshTokenResponse with the raw refresh-response object as the schema input). Many OAuth providers do not re-issue a new refresh_token on every access-token refresh, so this code will silently overwrite a user's valid refresh token with the garbage string "refresh_token" in the database, permanently breaking that calendar/video integration until the user reconnects the app. There is no fallback to the existing credential's refresh_token value.

title: refreshOAuthTokens returns an un-parsed fetch Response, but many callers expect `.data` or a final token object
body: When app credential sync is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw, unread `fetch` Response object from CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT. Callers are inconsistent in what they expect: googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts does `const token = res?.data;` (expects an axios-like object with `.data`), hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts assigns the return value directly to a `HubspotToken` (expects a parsed token object, not a Response), and zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts & zohocrm/lib/CalendarService.ts both do `tokenInfo.data.error`/`tokenInfo.data.expiryDate` (expect an axios response shape). A plain fetch Response has none of these, so when sync is enabled these call sites will throw TypeErrors (reading properties of undefined) or silently store corrupted/empty credential keys. Only providers that explicitly call `.json()`/`handleErrorsJson` on the result (office365calendar, office365video, zoomvideo, webex, lark) work correctly with this return shape.

title: `prisma` is used without being imported, breaking compilation/runtime
