body: The new refresh-token logic in getClient() calls `await prisma.credential.update(...)`, but this file never imports `prisma` (no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` was added despite the new usage). This will fail TypeScript type-checking ("Cannot find name 'prisma'") and, if it somehow passes a build, will throw a ReferenceError at runtime the first time a Salesforce credential needs a token refresh, breaking the Salesforce integration entirely.

title: Salesforce token refresh bypasses refreshOAuthTokens, so credential sync never applies to Salesforce
body: Unlike every other updated provider (google, hubspot, office365, zoho-bigin, zohocrm, zoom, webex), the Salesforce CalendarService calls `fetch("https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token", ...)` directly instead of going through `refreshOAuthTokens`. As a result, even when APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are configured, Salesforce token refresh will always hit Salesforce directly and never use the self-hoster's sync endpoint, silently excluding Salesforce from the feature this PR advertises.

title: Fragile success check using response.statusText instead of response.ok
body: `if (response.statusText !== "OK") throw new HttpError(...)` relies on the HTTP reason phrase being exactly the string "OK". Depending on the runtime/fetch implementation (e.g. HTTP/2 responses or certain fetch polyfills), statusText can be empty or differ even for a successful 200 response, causing valid refresh responses to be incorrectly treated as errors. `response.ok` (or checking `response.status`) is the standard, reliable way to detect failures.

title: Webhook secret comparison is not constant-time
body: The shared-secret check `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` uses a plain string inequality comparison. This is vulnerable to timing attacks that can let an attacker incrementally guess the secret by measuring response-time differences. A constant-time comparison (e.g. `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on buffers of equal length) should be used for secret/token verification on a publicly reachable endpoint.

title: Ambiguous credential lookup can overwrite the wrong credential
body: `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` does not disambiguate between multiple credentials a user may have for the same app (e.g. multiple Google Calendar or Office365 accounts connected under the same appId). If more than one credential row matches, `findFirst` picks an arbitrary one and the subsequent `update` will overwrite that record's `key`, potentially corrupting an unrelated, working connection for a different account than the one the self-hoster intended to sync. The request schema has no way to target a specific credential (e.g. an external account id), making this unsafe for any app that supports multiple accounts per user.

title: No HTTP method restriction on the webhook handler
body: The handler does not check `req.method`, so GET/PUT/DELETE requests are processed identically to POST. For non-POST requests the body will typically be empty/invalid, causing the unguarded `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` call to throw, which is not caught anywhere in the handler and will surface as an unhandled exception/500 instead of a clean 405 Method Not Allowed response.

title: Redirect URI hardcoded instead of derived from appConfig.slug
body: This change replaces `WEBAPP_URL + \`/api/integrations/${appConfig.slug}/callback\`` with a hardcoded `WEBAPP_URL + \`/api/integrations/zoho-bigin/callback\``, while `zoho-bigin/api/callback.ts` still builds its redirect URI dynamically from `appConfig.slug`. This introduces an inconsistency: if `appConfig.slug` ever changes, the authorize URL and the token-exchange redirect URI will diverge, breaking the OAuth flow (redirect_uri mismatch errors from the provider). This change is unrelated to the credential-sync feature and appears to be an unintended regression.

title: No automated tests for the new credential-sync webhook or token-refresh helpers
body: This PR introduces a new externally reachable webhook endpoint that decrypts and writes arbitrary third-party OAuth credentials into the database, plus shared helpers (parseRefreshTokenResponse, refreshOAuthTokens) used across nine app integrations. None of this new, security- and data-integrity-sensitive logic has accompanying unit/integration tests (the PR description explicitly states no tests were added), despite the bugs identified in parseRefreshTokenResponse/refreshOAuthTokens that tests would likely have caught.

title: Google Calendar refresh persists the safeParse wrapper object instead of the parsed data
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse()` returns a Zod safeParse-style object `{ success, data }`. Here the whole return value is assigned to `key` and stored directly as `data: { key }` in `prisma.credential.update`. Every other integration in this PR (Office365, Zoom, Webex, Salesforce) correctly destructures `.data` before persisting, but Google does not. As a result, every time a Google Calendar access token is refreshed (which happens routinely as tokens expire), `credential.key` in the DB becomes `{ success: true, data: { access_token, refresh_token, ... } }` instead of the flat object expected by `googleCredentialSchema`. The next call to `googleAuth()` does `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)`, which will throw because the stored object no longer has the required top-level fields. This permanently breaks the Google Calendar integration for the account after the first refresh, for all users (not just self-hosters using the new sync feature).

title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token" instead of a real value
body: When the parsed token response lacks a `refresh_token` field, the code sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` — a hardcoded placeholder string, not a variable. This path runs unconditionally (both in the sync and non-sync branches). For integrations whose schema marks `refresh_token` optional (e.g. Office365's `refreshTokenResponseSchema`), if the provider's refresh response omits a new refresh_token, this garbage string gets merged into the credential object and persisted to the DB (e.g. `o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }`), silently destroying the previously valid refresh_token. Subsequent refresh attempts will send the literal string "refresh_token" to the OAuth provider and fail, permanently breaking the calendar connection until the user reconnects.

title: minimumTokenResponseSchema's computed property keys collapse to the same literal key, defeating the intended schema
body: The schema uses computed property names `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`. Calling `.toString()` on a Zod type instance does not return the string "any string"; it returns the default `Object.prototype.toString()` result, i.e. the literal string `"[object Object]"`, for both expressions. The two computed keys collide into one key named `"[object Object]"`, which never matches any real response property. The comments ("Assume that any property with a number is the expiry", "Allow other properties") indicate the intent was to keep arbitrary/expiry fields, but because `z.object()` strips unrecognized keys by default, the parsed result of `minimumTokenResponseSchema.safeParse()` only ever retains `access_token` (plus the refresh_token fallback). This means when credential syncing is enabled, fields like `expiry_date`/`expires_in` are silently stripped from the refreshed credential before being persisted, breaking expiry tracking for every app that relies on this schema (Google Calendar in particular).

title: refreshOAuthTokens returns a different response shape depending on branch, breaking several consumers when credential sync is enabled
body: When the sync feature is active, this function returns the raw Fetch API `Response` object from `fetch(CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, ...)`. When it is not active, it returns whatever `refreshFunction()` resolves to. For Google Calendar, `refreshFunction` resolves to a gaxios-style object exposing `.data` (via `fetchTokens.res`), and the caller does `const token = res?.data; token.access_token`. A raw Fetch `Response` has no `.data` property, so when the sync endpoint is configured this throws/returns `undefined.access_token`. The same mismatch exists for Hubspot (caller expects `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` from the Hubspot SDK's token object, not a Fetch Response), and for Zoho Bigin/Zoho CRM (caller expects `tokenInfo.data` as returned by axios, not a Fetch Response). This means the exact feature this PR introduces (syncing credentials via `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`) will throw or silently break for Google Calendar, Hubspot, Zoho Bigin and Zoho CRM as soon as it is enabled.

title: Outbound credential-sync request carries no authentication/secret header
body: When calling out to the self-hoster's `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, the request is a plain POST with only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` in the body — no signature, bearer token, or shared secret (e.g. `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`) is sent. The self-hosted endpoint therefore has no built-in way to verify that the request genuinely originated from this Cal.com instance, unlike the inbound `/api/webhook/app-credential` endpoint, which does require a shared secret. This is a one-sided trust model: any party that can reach the configured endpoint URL can impersonate Cal.com's refresh requests unless the self-hoster independently reinvents authentication, which is not documented anywhere in `.env.example`.

title: credential.id is passed to refreshOAuthTokens where credential.userId is expected
body: `refreshAccessToken(credentialId: number, credentialKey: BiginToken)` only has access to `credentialId` (`credential.id`), not `credential.userId`; there is no `userId` variable in scope. The call `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` therefore passes the credential's primary key as the third argument, which `refreshOAuthTokens` treats as `userId` and sends to the self-hosted sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. When credential syncing is enabled for Zoho Bigin, the self-hoster's endpoint will receive the wrong identifier and will be unable to correctly map the request to the Cal.com user, breaking token refresh for this app specifically.

title: Salesforce access token is unconditionally refreshed on every service instantiation, without an expiry check or the new sync mechanism
body: `getClient()` is invoked from the constructor on every `SalesforceCalendarService` instantiation (i.e. on essentially every booking/calendar operation for a Salesforce credential), and it unconditionally POSTs to `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` to refresh the access token — there is no check of token expiry before doing so, unlike every other integration in this codebase (which gate refreshing behind an `isExpired`/`isTokenValid` check). This wastes Salesforce API quota on every call and, since Salesforce issues/may rotate refresh tokens, repeated unnecessary refreshes under concurrent requests can race and invalidate tokens still in use elsewhere. Additionally, unlike all the other apps touched in this PR, this refresh call is not routed through the new `refreshOAuthTokens` helper, so the self-hosted credential-sync feature this PR introduces does not work for Salesforce at all, despite the PR's stated goal of broad app support.

title: Webhook secret verified with non-constant-time string comparison and no HTTP method restriction
body: The webhook secret check uses plain `!==` comparison between the incoming header value and `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. This is vulnerable to timing side-channel attacks that can be used to guess the secret byte-by-byte, especially since the endpoint has no rate limiting. A constant-time comparison (e.g. `crypto.timingSafeEqual`) should be used instead. Additionally, the handler does not check `req.method`, so non-POST requests are processed the same way; a GET/other request without a JSON body will fail the zod `.parse()` with an unhandled exception rather than a clean 405, leaking a generic error instead of a well-defined API contract.

title: Decrypted credential payload is persisted without any schema validation
body: After `symmetricDecrypt` + `JSON.parse`, the resulting `keys` object is written straight into `prisma.credential.create/update` as the `key` field, with no validation that it matches the shape expected by the corresponding app's CalendarService/VideoApiAdapter (e.g. `googleCredentialSchema`, `zoomTokenSchema`, etc.). A malformed or incomplete payload from the self-hosted sync source (missing `refresh_token`, wrong types, etc.) will be accepted and stored, and will only fail later — at booking/availability time — when the relevant integration tries to `schema.parse(credential.key)`, causing a runtime exception far removed from the original cause. There is also no try/catch around the decrypt/JSON.parse calls, so a bad payload or wrong encryption key results in an unhandled exception rather than a clear 4xx response.

title: Redirect URI hardcoded, diverging from appConfig.slug used in callback.ts
body: This change replaces `WEBAPP_URL + \`/api/integrations/${appConfig.slug}/callback\`` with a hardcoded `WEBAPP_URL + "/api/integrations/zoho-bigin/callback"`. `packages/app-store/zoho-bigin/api/callback.ts` still builds its redirect URI from `appConfig.slug`. The two files are now inconsistent: if `appConfig.slug` in `config.json` ever changes, the authorize URL and the token-exchange redirect URI would silently diverge, breaking the OAuth flow for this app. This change appears unrelated to the credential-sync feature and looks like an unintended regression introduced by the refactor.

title: No automated tests for the new credential-sync webhook or OAuth refresh-sync code paths
body: This PR adds a new unauthenticated-by-default webhook endpoint that decrypts and writes arbitrary third-party OAuth credentials into the database, plus new shared helpers (`refreshOAuthTokens`, `parseRefreshTokenResponse`) that are wired into nearly a dozen app integrations' token-refresh logic. None of this is covered by unit or integration tests (the PR description explicitly states no tests were added). Given the security sensitivity (webhook secret, symmetric encryption/decryption) and the data-integrity risk (credential corruption as seen in the bugs above), this is a significant gap that would have caught the shape-mismatch and placeholder-value bugs before merge.

title: Team admin/owner permission check uses AND instead of OR
body: `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`. Since `isTeamOwner` is a strict subset of `isTeamAdmin` (an OWNER role satisfies both, but an ADMIN-only role satisfies only `isTeamAdmin`), this expression is effectively equivalent to just `isTeamOwner`. As a result, a team ADMIN who is not also the OWNER, and who is neither the booking organizer nor an attendee, will be incorrectly denied with FORBIDDEN when trying to add guests to a team member's booking, even though team admins should normally have this privilege (as elsewhere in the codebase, e.g. reassign). This should be `||`.

title: EventManager built with requesting user's credentials instead of the booking organizer's
body: `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` fetches credentials for the user making the request, and `EventManager` is instantiated with `{ ...user, credentials }` where `user` is `ctx.user`. Because the permission check above allows an attendee (not just the organizer) to add guests, when an attendee triggers this flow the calendar sync in `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` will run with the attendee's own (likely absent or unrelated) calendar credentials rather than the organizer's. The booking already fetched `user: { include: { destinationCalendar: true, credentials: true } }` (the organizer), but those credentials are never used. This can silently fail to update the organizer's actual calendar event with the new guests.

title: Guest email blacklist comparison is case-sensitive, allowing trivial bypass
body: `blacklistedGuestEmails` is built by lower-casing every entry from `BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS`, but the comparison `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)` uses the raw, non-lowercased `guest` value. A blocked email such as `spam@example.com` can bypass the blacklist simply by submitting `Spam@Example.com` or `SPAM@EXAMPLE.COM`, since the exact-case string will never match the lowercased blacklist entries.

title: Duplicate-guest detection is case-sensitive
body: `uniqueGuests` is derived by checking `guest === attendee.email` without normalizing case. Combined with the client-side uniqueness check in AddGuestsDialog.tsx (which also does a case-sensitive `Set` comparison), a guest can be added twice with differing email casing (e.g. `John@Example.com` vs `john@example.com`), creating duplicate Attendee rows that represent the same real email address and causing duplicate notifications/calendar invites for what is effectively the same guest.

title: Wrong attendee email template sent when a resubmitted guest email is not actually new
body: `sendAddGuestsEmails(calEvent, newGuests)` decides which template to send an attendee based on `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)`. The caller (`addGuests.handler.ts`, line 168) passes the raw, unfiltered `guests` array from the request rather than `uniqueGuests` (the guests that were actually inserted after filtering out existing attendees and blacklisted emails). If a user resubmits an email that is already an existing attendee (so it gets filtered out of `uniqueGuests` and not re-added to the DB), that existing attendee's email is still present in `guests`, causing them to incorrectly receive the full `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (meant for brand-new attendees) instead of `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail`, which is confusing and semantically wrong.

title: Email-send failure is swallowed with a bare console.log, losing error details
body: The `catch (err)` block around `sendAddGuestsEmails` only logs the static string `"Error sending AddGuestsEmails"` via `console.log`, discarding the actual `err` object and bypassing the project's structured logger (`@calcom/lib/logger`) used elsewhere in this same file's imports. This makes it impossible to diagnose production email failures for this flow, and `console.log` (rather than `console.error`/the logger) is inconsistent with how errors are handled elsewhere in the codebase.

title: No check on booking status before adding guests
body: The handler fetches the booking and immediately proceeds to add attendees, sync the calendar and send notification emails without verifying `booking.status`. Guests can therefore be added to CANCELLED or REJECTED bookings, resulting in calendar invites and "guests added" notification emails being sent for an event that is not actually happening, confusing invitees and polluting calendars with stale events.

title: Fallback toast message in onError is dead code
body: `showToast(message || t("unable_to_add_guests"), "error")` uses `message` which is built from a template literal (`` `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}` ``) and is therefore always a non-empty, truthy string even when `err.data` or `err.message` are undefined (yielding something like "undefined: undefined"). The `|| t("unable_to_add_guests")` fallback can never actually trigger, so users may see a raw/unhelpful "undefined: ..." message instead of the intended friendly error text for unexpected error shapes.

title: isInvalidEmail state is never reset after a successful submission or new attempt
body: `isInvalidEmail` is only reset to `false` in the Cancel button handler. If a user triggers the "emails must be unique and valid" error once, then fixes the input and successfully submits (via `handleAdd`'s success branch or the mutation's `onSuccess`), `isInvalidEmail` remains `true`. Since the dialog closes on success but the flag is never cleared, reopening the dialog afterward will immediately show the stale invalid-email warning banner even though no new validation error has occurred.

title: Hardcoded, non-localized tooltip text
body: The remove-email tooltip uses a hardcoded English string `<Tooltip content="Remove email">` instead of going through the `t()` translation function that is already imported and used elsewhere in this same component (e.g. for "add_another" and the field label). This breaks localization for non-English users of this new shared UI component.

title: No automated tests for the new add-guests feature
body: This PR introduces a new tRPC mutation with non-trivial authorization logic (organizer/attendee/team-admin checks), guest deduplication/blacklist filtering, calendar sync, and dual email notifications, plus new UI components (`AddGuestsDialog`, `MultiEmail`). No unit, integration, or component tests are included for any of `addGuests.handler.ts`, `addGuests.schema.ts`, `AddGuestsDialog.tsx`, or `MultiEmail.tsx`, despite the permission-check bug and case-sensitivity issues that tests would likely have caught.

title: Team admin permission check uses AND instead of OR, excluding team admins
body: `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`. Since `isTeamAdmin` already returns true for both ADMIN and OWNER roles while `isTeamOwner` only returns true for OWNER, the AND combination collapses to 'owner only'. As a result, team members with the ADMIN role (but not OWNER) are denied permission to add guests even though the variable name and intended UX (editBookingActions menu item shown to all users regardless of exact role) imply admins should be allowed. This should be `||` (or just use `isTeamAdmin` alone), otherwise legitimate team admins will get a FORBIDDEN error when trying to use this feature.

title: EventManager is built with the acting user's credentials instead of the booking organizer's
body: `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` and `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials: [...credentials] })` use `ctx.user` (the person triggering the mutation), not the booking's organizer (`booking.user`). The handler explicitly allows team admins/owners and attendees (not just the organizer) to add guests, so in those cases the EventManager will be instantiated with the wrong account's calendar/video credentials. This can cause `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` to silently fail, update the wrong calendar, or throw, because the acting user may have no credentials at all or different ones than the organizer who actually owns the calendar event.

title: Blacklisted guest email filter is bypassed by case variation
body: `blacklistedGuestEmails` is lower-cased (`.map((email) => email.toLowerCase())`), but the incoming `guest` strings are compared against it without being lower-cased (`!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`). An attacker/user can bypass the blacklist simply by submitting the email with different casing (e.g. `Blocked@Example.com` instead of `blocked@example.com`), defeating the purpose of `BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS`.

title: Duplicate-attendee check is case sensitive, allowing duplicate attendees with different email casing
body: `!booking.attendees.some((attendee) => guest === attendee.email)` performs an exact, case-sensitive string comparison. If an existing attendee's email is stored as `Jane@Example.com` and a new guest is submitted as `jane@example.com`, the guest will not be recognized as a duplicate and a second attendee record with the 'same' email (different case) will be created, leading to duplicate emails sent and inconsistent attendee lists.

title: Email send failure is silently swallowed with no error detail logged
body: The catch block only does `console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails")`, discarding the actual `err` object and using `console.log` instead of the project's structured logger (`@calcom/lib/logger`) used elsewhere. This makes it impossible to diagnose production email failures (e.g. SMTP errors, template rendering errors) from logs, and the handler still returns a success message to the client even though guest notification emails may not have been sent.

title: Fallback error toast message is unreachable dead code
body: `showToast(message || t("unable_to_add_guests"), "error")` where `message` is built as a template literal `` `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}` ``. A template literal always produces a non-empty string (even `"undefined: ..."` if `err.data?.code` is undefined), so the `|| t("unable_to_add_guests")` fallback can never execute. This also means users will see a raw, unlocalized error such as `undefined: emails_must_be_unique_valid` or `BAD_REQUEST: booking_not_found` instead of a friendly translated message in edge cases where `err.message` is not a recognized i18n key.

title: Unsafe array access on calEvent.attendees[0] can throw if attendees list is empty
body: `name: this.calEvent.attendees[0].name` assumes `calEvent.attendees` always has at least one element. If this email class is ever invoked for an event with zero attendees (e.g. due to a filtering bug upstream or future reuse of this class), this will throw a runtime TypeError instead of degrading gracefully, breaking the whole email send flow (including the `Promise.all` in `sendAddGuestsEmails`).

title: No automated tests added for the new add-guests feature
body: This PR introduces a new tRPC handler/schema, a new dialog component, a new MultiEmail form component, and two new email templates, but no unit or integration tests were added (no tests for addGuests.handler.ts permission logic, duplicate/blacklist filtering, AddGuestsDialog validation, or MultiEmail behavior). Given the permission-check bug and case-sensitivity issues identified above, test coverage would have caught these regressions before merge.

title: Team-admin permission check uses AND instead of OR, locking out plain team admins
body: `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`. `isTeamOwner` only returns true for the OWNER role while `isTeamAdmin` returns true for ADMIN or OWNER. Combining them with `&&` means the variable is effectively only true for OWNERs - a plain team ADMIN (who is not also the OWNER) will fail `isTeamOwner` and therefore be denied permission to add guests, even though the variable name and apparent intent ("AdminOrOwner") indicate admins should be allowed. This should be `||`. Consequence: legitimate team admins cannot add guests and will get a FORBIDDEN error.

title: Calendar update uses requesting user's credentials instead of the booking organizer's
body: The handler fetches `booking.user` with `destinationCalendar` and `credentials` included (lines 35-40), but never uses them. Instead it calls `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` and builds `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials: [...credentials] })` using `ctx.user` - the person making the request (which per the permission logic above can be a team admin or even just an attendee, not necessarily the booking organizer). When the caller is not the organizer, the EventManager will attempt to update the organizer's external calendar event using the caller's own calendar credentials (or lack thereof), which will either silently fail to update the calendar, update the wrong calendar, or throw, since the caller may not have access to the organizer's calendar integration at all.

title: Email classification uses unfiltered guest list instead of the deduplicated list actually added
body: `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` is called with the raw `guests` input, not `uniqueGuests` (the list after filtering out emails that already belong to existing attendees or are blacklisted). Inside `sendAddGuestsEmails` (packages/emails/email-manager.ts), each existing attendee is sent `AttendeeScheduledEmail` if their email is in this list, or `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail` otherwise. If a caller re-submits an email that already belongs to an existing attendee (so it's filtered out and not actually added), that pre-existing attendee is nonetheless treated as "new" and will incorrectly receive a full `AttendeeScheduledEmail` invite instead of (or in addition to) the lighter `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail` notification - a case that can legitimately occur any time the submitted guest list overlaps with current attendees.

title: Blacklist comparison is case-sensitive while the blacklist itself is lowercased
body: `blacklistedGuestEmails` is built by lowercasing every entry from `BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS`, but the comparison `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)` compares against the raw, non-lowercased `guest` string. An email that differs only in case from a blacklisted address (e.g. `Spam@Example.com` vs `spam@example.com`) will bypass the blacklist filter entirely, defeating the intended restriction.

title: Server-side schema does not enforce unique guest emails, allowing duplicate attendee rows
body: `ZAddGuestsInputSchema.guests` is just `z.array(z.string().email())`, with no refinement against duplicate entries within the array. The client-side dialog adds its own uniqueness check via a local zod refine, but that is easily bypassed by calling the tRPC mutation directly (or via any other client). The handler's `uniqueGuests` filter only removes emails that match *existing* attendees - it does not deduplicate entries within the submitted `guests` array itself - so a payload with the same email repeated multiple times will create multiple attendee rows with an identical email via `createMany`, corrupting booking attendee data.

title: No upper bound on number of guests that can be added per request
body: Any attendee of a booking (not just the organizer/team admin) is permitted to add guests, per the permission check a few lines below, but there is no limit on the size of the `guests` array. A single attendee could submit a very large list of guest emails in one request, causing unbounded attendee record creation, unbounded calendar-attendee updates, and unbounded email sends (invite spam) for a booking they do not own.

title: Email send failures are silently swallowed with console.log and no error detail
body: The `catch (err)` block only does `console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails")`; the actual `err` object is discarded, and this bypasses the project's logger (e.g. `@calcom/lib/logger` used elsewhere in email-manager.ts) used for structured error reporting. This makes it impossible to diagnose production email failures for this feature, and the user is given no indication that guest-notification emails failed even though the booking mutation itself succeeded.

title: Error toast fallback is unreachable code
body: `const message = `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}`;` always produces a non-empty string (a template literal with at least ": "), so `showToast(message || t("unable_to_add_guests"), "error")` never falls back to the friendlier `unable_to_add_guests` message. If `err.data?.code` or `err.message` is undefined, or `err.message` is not a valid translation key, the user will see a raw/garbled string like `undefined: you_do_not_have_permission` instead of a clean fallback message.

title: Label htmlFor references a non-existent id, breaking label association
body: `<label htmlFor="emails" ...>{label}</label>` targets an element with `id="emails"`, but none of the rendered `EmailField` inputs are given `id="emails"` (or any matching id per field). This breaks the label-to-input association for assistive technology and for click-to-focus behavior, since with multiple emails the label can only ever point at most to one field and in practice points at none.

title: No automated tests for new addGuests permission, email, and calendar-update logic
body: This PR introduces a new tRPC mutation with non-trivial permission logic (organizer/team-admin/attendee checks), a new UI dialog, new email templates, and calendar-attendee update logic, but no unit or integration tests are included anywhere in the diff. Given the permission-check bug and credential-mismatch bug identified in this handler, test coverage (e.g. verifying who can/cannot add guests, that duplicate/blacklisted emails are rejected, and that the correct calendar credentials are used) would have caught these issues before merge.

title: deleteMany retryCount branch is not scoped to method: SMS
body: In the deleteMany() call (lines 29-45), the OR clause's second condition `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` constraint, unlike the first condition which explicitly filters `method: SMS`. Since `retryCount` was added as a shared column on the `WorkflowReminder` model (used by all methods: EMAIL, SMS, WHATSAPP), this query will delete ANY workflow reminder (regardless of method) whose retryCount happens to exceed 1, not just SMS reminders. Today only this file increments retryCount so it only affects SMS reminders in practice, but the query itself is inconsistent with the stated purpose (cleaning up SMS reminders) and is a latent bug waiting to silently delete Email/WhatsApp reminders if retryCount is ever incremented elsewhere.

title: New retryCount update inside catch block can throw and abort processing of remaining reminders
body: The catch block (lines 189-199) now performs an additional `await prisma.workflowReminder.update(...)` with no surrounding try/catch. If this update itself fails (e.g., the record was concurrently deleted by the deleteMany cleanup on a parallel/overlapping cron invocation, a transient DB error, etc.), the exception propagates out of the `for` loop entirely since nothing catches it there. This means a single failure updating one reminder's retryCount aborts processing of all subsequent reminders in the batch for that cron invocation, and likely results in an unhandled promise rejection / 500 response instead of the previous behavior where errors were only logged and the loop continued. This is a regression in robustness for a cron job meant to process many independent reminders.

title: retryCount increment is not atomic, risking lost updates under overlapping cron runs
body: Both the failure branch (lines 178-187) and the catch block (lines 190-197) compute the new retryCount as `reminder.retryCount + 1` using the value fetched once at the start of the request, then write it back. If the cron endpoint is invoked again before the previous invocation finishes (e.g., due to a slow run or concurrent triggers), two overlapping runs could both read the same stale retryCount and write the same incremented value, effectively losing an increment. Using Prisma's atomic `{ retryCount: { increment: 1 } }` would avoid this race and guarantee failures are counted correctly regardless of overlap.

title: Reminders with no sendTo/message never get retryCount incremented, leaving them stuck indefinitely
body: The retryCount increment logic only runs inside the `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)` block (success/failure) or inside the catch block. If `sendTo` is empty/undefined or `message` resolves to an empty string (e.g., attendee has no SMS number, or reminderBody/template produced no text), this whole block is skipped silently — no error is thrown, no retryCount increment happens. Such reminders will remain `scheduled: false` and keep getting re-selected and reprocessed by every cron run until their `scheduledDate` passes, without ever reaching the retryCount threshold that this PR introduces to stop infinite retries. This defeats the stated goal of the PR for one of the most common real failure causes (missing/invalid phone number resulting in an empty sendTo rather than a thrown error).

title: No test coverage added for new retryCount/deletion behavior
body: This PR introduces non-trivial new logic (incrementing retryCount on failure, and deleting reminders after retryCount exceeds the threshold) but adds no unit or integration tests to verify: (1) retryCount is incremented correctly on twilio.scheduleSMS failure and on thrown errors, (2) reminders are deleted once retryCount surpasses the threshold, and (3) the deleteMany query only targets the intended records. Given the subtlety of the query logic (see the unscoped retryCount deletion condition), tests would have caught at least one of the issues introduced here.

title: retryCount deletion branch is not scoped to SMS method
body: The new OR clause `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` in the deleteMany call has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, unlike the sibling condition. The function is documented/intended to operate only on SMS reminders, but as written it will delete ANY WorkflowReminder row (EMAIL, WHATSAPP, SMS) whose retryCount happens to exceed 1, regardless of method. Since `retryCount` is a shared column on the WorkflowReminder model (not SMS-specific), any future code path that increments retryCount for non-SMS reminders (or any data migration/bug that sets retryCount>1) will cause this cron job to silently delete unrelated email/whatsapp reminders. This should be `{ method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` to keep the deletion scoped correctly.

title: Non-atomic retryCount increment can race across concurrent cron invocations
body: Both the success-path failure branch (line ~184) and the catch block (line ~195) update retryCount by computing `reminder.retryCount + 1` in application code from a value fetched earlier in the same request, rather than using Prisma's atomic `{ increment: 1 }`. If the cron endpoint is invoked more than once concurrently (e.g. duplicate cron triggers, retried HTTP calls, multiple instances), two processes can read the same stale retryCount and write the same incremented value, losing an update. This means a reminder could fail many more than twice yet never reach retryCount > 1, defeating the intended cleanup logic and leaving broken reminders stuck in the scheduling loop indefinitely.

title: Transient errors are treated the same as permanent failures, causing premature deletion of valid reminders
body: Any error thrown while scheduling the SMS (network blip, Twilio rate limiting/outage, temporary API failure, etc.) increments retryCount exactly the same way as a permanent failure like an invalid phone number. Because the cron runs repeatedly and only allows 2 failures before the reminder is deleted (deleteMany with retryCount > 1), a short period of transient Twilio/network issues across two consecutive cron runs will cause legitimate, otherwise-valid workflow reminders to be permanently deleted before the scheduled date, even though the underlying booking/reminder was fine. There is no distinction between retryable and non-retryable errors, so the fix can silently drop reminders that should have eventually succeeded.

title: Stale comment does not describe the new retryCount-based deletion
body: The comment above the deleteMany call still reads "delete all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date", but the query now also deletes any reminder (regardless of method, see related finding) whose retryCount exceeds 1. The comment was not updated to describe this second deletion condition, which will mislead future maintainers reading only the comment about what rows are removed.

title: No tests added for new retry/deletion behavior
body: This PR introduces a behavioral change (failed SMS reminders are now deleted after two failures) that affects data integrity (permanent deletion of WorkflowReminder rows). No unit/integration tests were added to verify that retryCount increments correctly on failure, that reminders are deleted only after exceeding the retry threshold, or that successful sends are unaffected. Given the destructive nature of the deleteMany query, this logic should have test coverage to prevent regressions (e.g., accidental deletion of valid reminders or failure to ever clean up broken ones).

title: retryCount deletion branch not scoped to SMS method, risking deletion of unrelated WorkflowReminder rows
body: The new `OR` clause in the `deleteMany` call adds `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` with no `method: SMS` constraint, while the original/sibling branch explicitly filters `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`. Since `retryCount` is a column on the shared `WorkflowReminder` model used by EMAIL, SMS and WHATSAPP reminders alike, any reminder of any method that ends up with `retryCount > 1` (now or in a future change that reuses this column for other channels) will be silently deleted by this SMS-only cron endpoint. This conflates concerns and creates a latent data-integrity hazard: a future feature that increments `retryCount` for email/whatsapp reminders would have those reminders deleted by the SMS cron job. The condition should be `AND: [{ method: WorkflowMethods.SMS }, { retryCount: { gt: 1 } }]` to match the stated intent of only removing failed SMS reminders.

title: Non-atomic retryCount increment can lose updates under concurrent/overlapping cron runs
body: retryCount is incremented via `data: { retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 }`, using the value read earlier in the same request (from the initial `findMany`). If the cron job is triggered more than once concurrently (e.g., overlapping invocations due to a slow run or manual trigger plus scheduled trigger), two processes could read the same stale `retryCount` and both write the same incremented value, causing a lost update. This undermines the 'delete after two failures' guarantee the PR aims to provide. Using Prisma's atomic increment (`data: { retryCount: { increment: 1 } }`) would avoid the race entirely and is low-cost to apply here and in the catch block below (line ~195).

title: Overly broad catch block increments retryCount for unrelated failures, risking premature deletion of valid reminders
body: The try block wraps not only the actual SMS-sending call (`twilio.scheduleSMS`) but also unrelated DB/network operations such as `prisma.profile.findFirst` and `getBookerBaseUrl`, and template rendering. Any transient failure in these unrelated steps (e.g., a brief DB hiccup or an external API blip while resolving the booker URL) increments `retryCount` exactly the same as a genuine SMS-provider failure such as an invalid phone number. Because the reminder is deleted once `retryCount > 1`, two unrelated/transient errors (not actual SMS failures) could cause a legitimate, sendable reminder to be permanently deleted before it ever had a real chance to be delivered. The retry/delete logic should be scoped specifically to the SMS send failure path rather than the entire per-reminder processing block.

title: No automated tests added for new retry/deletion behavior
body: This PR introduces non-trivial new behavior (incrementing retryCount on failure, and deleting reminders once retryCount exceeds the threshold) but no tests were added or updated to cover: (1) a failed `twilio.scheduleSMS` call incrementing retryCount, (2) an exception during processing incrementing retryCount, and (3) the deleteMany query correctly removing reminders once retryCount surpasses 1 while not catching reminders of other methods/states. Given this logic directly controls whether reminders are permanently deleted, lack of test coverage increases the risk of silent regressions.

title: Public findMany() method removed and return types changed without updating/verifying callers
body: The service previously exposed `findMany(findManyArgs)` which executed a Prisma ORM query and returned typed rows, and `getAuthorizationConditions()/getFilterConditions()` returned `Prisma.BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedWhereInput` objects. In this PR `findMany` is removed entirely and those methods now return `Prisma.Sql` fragments instead, replaced only by `getBaseConditions()` which returns a raw SQL fragment that the caller must manually embed in a `$queryRaw` call. The 2-file diff in this PR contains no updates to any consumer of `InsightsBookingService` (e.g. tRPC routers or other services that likely call `.findMany()` or rely on the old where-object return type). If any such caller exists outside this diff, it will fail to compile/run after this change. This is a breaking API change that should be verified against all current consumers before merge.

title: Caching behavior tests were deleted instead of updated
body: The previous test suite included a `describe("Caching", ...)` block with two tests ("should cache authorization conditions" and "should cache filter conditions") that verified `cachedAuthConditions`/`cachedFilterConditions` caching logic. This PR removes that entire block rather than updating the assertions to the new `Prisma.Sql` comparison style. The caching implementation (`getAuthorizationConditions`/`getFilterConditions` memoization) still exists in `insightsBooking.ts`, but there is now no test coverage verifying that repeated calls reuse the cached SQL fragment instead of rebuilding them (which would re-run DB membership/team lookups). This leaves a regression gap for future changes to the caching logic.

title: PR description misrepresents scope of changes to production service code
body: The PR description states the Prisma.sql conversion "was previously converted in the service implementation" and that this PR "updates... integration tests" only, implying `insightsBooking.ts` is unchanged production code being re-verified. However the diff shows `insightsBooking.ts` itself undergoes a full rewrite in this PR: changing the import of `Prisma` from type-only to value import, replacing the `findMany` method with `getBaseConditions`, changing `getAuthorizationConditions`/`getFilterConditions` return types from Prisma where-objects to `Prisma.Sql`, and changing the constructor's accepted options type. This mismatch between the stated scope (test-only) and the actual scope (significant production logic + API changes) risks reviewers under-scrutinizing the new authorization/filter SQL-building logic, despite the PR's own checklist flagging it as "HIGH RISK".

title: Unreachable fallback branches in getBaseConditions due to buildAuthorizationConditions never returning falsy
body: `getBaseConditions()` branches on `if (authConditions && filterConditions) ... else if (authConditions) ... else if (filterConditions) ... else return NOTHING_CONDITION`. However `buildAuthorizationConditions()` (and thus `getAuthorizationConditions()`) always returns a `Prisma.Sql` object (never null/undefined), so `authConditions` is always truthy. The `else if (filterConditions)` and final `else` branches are therefore dead code that can mask a future contract change (e.g. if `getAuthorizationConditions` is later made to return null in some case, the fallback behavior silently differs from what a reader would expect).

title: Public `findMany()` method removed with no visible update to callers
body: The diff removes the previously-existing `async findMany(findManyArgs: Prisma.BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedFindManyArgs)` method (visible as deleted lines in the diff) and replaces it with `getBaseConditions()`, which only returns the combined SQL `WHERE` fragment instead of performing a query. This PR only touches this service file and its test file; no other files are shown being updated to account for the removal/renaming of this method. If any production code (trpc routers, insights handlers, etc.) still calls `.findMany()` on `InsightsBookingService`, it will fail to compile or throw at runtime after this merges. This is a breaking API change that the PR description frames merely as a 'test update'.

title: Constructor's options type no longer enforces required teamId for team scope
body: The constructor parameter type was changed from the strict discriminated union `InsightsBookingServiceOptions` (where `teamId: number` is required when `scope === "team"`) to the new, looser `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions`, where `teamId?: number` is optional regardless of scope. Previously, omitting `teamId` for a team-scoped call was a compile-time TypeScript error. Now it compiles fine, and an incorrect call is only caught by the internal Zod validation at runtime, silently falling back to `NOTHING_CONDITION` (i.e., the query returns zero rows) rather than surfacing an explicit error. This can mask integration bugs as 'no data' instead of a clear failure.

title: Caching behavior test coverage removed without replacement
body: The previous `describe("Caching", ...)` block, which verified that `getAuthorizationConditions()` and `getFilterConditions()` return cached results on repeated calls, has been deleted entirely in this PR and not replaced with an equivalent test using the new `Prisma.Sql` return types. The service still implements `cachedAuthConditions`/`cachedFilterConditions` caching (lines 49-50, 84-95), but after this change there is no test asserting that caching still works correctly (e.g. that a second call doesn't re-run repository/database lookups) with the new SQL-fragment return type.

title: PR explicitly admits the rewritten integration tests were never actually run
body: The PR description states: "I encountered test runner configuration issues, so please verify the tests actually pass" and "The test runner had configuration issues during development, so manual verification of test execution is critical." This means the substantially rewritten authorization/filter-condition test suite for a security-sensitive code path (org/team/user scoping of booking data) was never confirmed to pass before submission. Given the high-risk nature of this change (authorization logic), merging without actually executing `TZ=UTC yarn test packages/lib/server/service/__tests__/insightsBooking.integration-test.ts` risks landing tests that don't actually validate the intended behavior (false confidence) or that fail outright.

title: PR's own diagram misrepresents insightsBooking.ts as unchanged context
body: The PR's mermaid diagram classifies `packages/lib/server/service/insightsBooking.ts` as "context" (no-edit, white) while the changed-files table and the actual diff show 73 insertions / 82 deletions to this file, including removal of the `findMany` method and changing the return types of `getAuthorizationConditions`/`getFilterConditions`/`buildAuthorizationConditions` from Prisma object where-clauses to raw `Prisma.Sql` fragments. This mislabeling, combined with the description framing this as purely a test update, could cause reviewers to under-scrutinize a substantial production authorization-logic change.

title: Public findMany() method removed with no replacement for ORM-based consumers
body: The previous `findMany(findManyArgs)` method, which returned real Prisma-typed `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` rows via Prisma's ORM query builder, has been removed entirely and replaced by `getBaseConditions()`, which only returns a `Prisma.Sql` fragment. Any other code in the repository that called `InsightsBookingService.findMany(...)` (outside the two files touched by this PR) will now fail to compile/run, since that method no longer exists and callers must switch to writing their own `$queryRaw`/`$queryRawUnsafe` calls. This PR's file list does not include any other call sites being updated, so if production code outside these two files relied on `findMany`, this change silently breaks that integration. This should be verified against all current callers of `InsightsBookingService` before merging.

title: Org-scope authorization condition skips org members when the org has no sub-teams
body: In `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition`, `userIdsFromOrg` is only queried when `teamsFromOrg.length > 0`, even though `teamIds` always includes `options.orgId` itself. If an organization has no sub-teams yet (a realistic state for a newly created org), `teamsFromOrg.length` is 0, so `userIdsFromOrg` is forced to `[]` and the membership lookup (which would include direct org members via `teamId = orgId`) is never executed. As a result, org owners/admins viewing insights for an org with zero sub-teams will see no personal (non-team) bookings for any org member, even though they are authorized to see them. This pre-existing logic is unexercised by the new tests (no test covers an org with zero sub-teams), so the bug remains uncaught despite the PR's stated goal of testing 'org scope' authorization thoroughly.

title: Caching behavior tests removed without replacement
body: The previous test suite included a 'Caching' describe block that verified `getAuthorizationConditions()` and `getFilterConditions()` correctly cache and reuse computed conditions (`cachedAuthConditions`/`cachedFilterConditions`). This PR deletes that entire block and does not add any equivalent coverage for the Prisma.sql-based implementation. The caching fields/logic still exist in `insightsBooking.ts` (`cachedAuthConditions`, `cachedFilterConditions`), but there is now no test verifying that repeated calls reuse the cached `Prisma.Sql` value rather than rebuilding (and re-querying the database) on every call, which is a meaningful regression in test coverage for a performance-sensitive code path.

title: Constructor options type weakened, loses compile-time validation of discriminated union
body: The constructor parameter type changed from `InsightsBookingServiceOptions` (the zod-inferred discriminated union, which requires `teamId` only for `scope: "team"`) to the looser `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions`, where `teamId` is always optional regardless of `scope`. This means TypeScript no longer catches a caller constructing the service with `scope: "team"` but omitting `teamId` at compile time; it now silently fails zod validation at runtime and falls back to `NOTHING_CONDITION`, hiding the mistake until it is observed as unexpectedly empty insights data rather than a type error during development.

title: PR description misstates scope of changes, downplaying risk in reviewed service file
body: The PR description states the service (`insightsBooking.ts`) was 'previously converted' to Prisma.sql and that this PR only updates the integration tests to match. However, the actual diff shows the service file itself undergoing the Prisma.sql conversion in this same PR (removing `findMany`, changing the constructor's option type, rewriting all authorization/filter condition builders from ORM objects to raw SQL). This mismatch between the stated scope and the real diff could cause reviewers to under-scrutinize the higher-risk service-layer SQL/authorization logic, assuming it was already reviewed and merged separately.

title: deleteCache mutation does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query, leaving stale cache status in UI
body: The `deleteCacheMutation`'s `onSuccess` handler only shows a toast and calls the optional `onSuccess` prop; unlike `disconnectMutation`, it never calls `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate()`. Since `cacheUpdatedAt` shown in the dropdown comes from the `connectedCalendars` query result, after a user deletes the cache the UI will keep showing the old 'Cache Status'/timestamp until an unrelated refetch happens. This defeats the core purpose of the feature (showing accurate cache status) and matches the review checklist item 'Confirm cache deletion works and UI updates appropriately', which this implementation does not satisfy.

title: deleteCache handler throws a plain Error instead of TRPCError
body: `deleteCacheHandler` throws `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")` instead of a `TRPCError` with a proper code (e.g. `NOT_FOUND`/`FORBIDDEN`) as is the convention elsewhere in the tRPC routers in this codebase. This results in a generic 500 Internal Server Error being surfaced to the client/monitoring instead of a meaningful 4xx error, which complicates error tracking/alerting and is inconsistent with how access-denied/not-found cases are handled by other handlers.

title: Credential existence check fetches full credential row including secrets
body: `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { id: credentialId, userId: user.id } })` has no `select` clause, so it loads the entire Credential record into memory, including the `key` field which typically stores OAuth tokens/secrets. Since only an existence/ownership check is needed here, this unnecessarily pulls sensitive data into the handler's memory/log context (e.g. via error reporting middleware) when a `select: { id: true }` would suffice.

title: dev:cron script switched to npx tsx without declaring tsx as a dependency
body: The `dev:cron` script was changed from `ts-node cron-tester.ts` to `npx tsx cron-tester.ts`, but `tsx` is not added to `devDependencies` (only `ts-node` remains listed). Using `npx` will attempt to fetch/install `tsx` on demand, which can fail in offline/CI/Yarn PnP environments and is inconsistent with the rest of the monorepo's tooling (other scripts in the same file still use `ts-node` directly). The dependency should be added explicitly and invoked via the existing package manager instead of `npx`.

title: New helper script uses macOS-only sed syntax, will fail on Linux
body: `sed -i '' -E "s|^GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=.*|GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=$TUNNEL_URL|" "$ENV_FILE"` uses the BSD/macOS form of `sed -i` which requires an empty string argument for in-place editing without backup. On GNU/Linux (the typical CI/dev container OS), this syntax is invalid and will either error out or behave unexpectedly, making this new developer utility script non-portable despite being added to a cross-platform repo.

title: Handler bypasses the CalendarCache factory/feature-flag pattern used elsewhere
body: `connectedCalendarsHandler` directly instantiates `new CalendarCacheRepository()` to call `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`, instead of going through `CalendarCache.init(...)`, which is the established factory used throughout the codebase to decide between the real repository and `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` (e.g. based on the 'calendar-cache' feature flag/license gating). As a result, cache status is always read directly from the database regardless of whether calendar caching is enabled for the user's team/org, which is inconsistent with how caching is gated everywhere else and could surface stale/irrelevant cache status data for users whose org has calendar caching disabled.

title: Unconditional broad SelectedCalendar.updatedAt update with no consumer, flagged by the PR author as unresolved
body: After every `fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache` call, `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` updates `updatedAt` for ALL selected calendars under the credential, not just the subset that was actually refreshed in that call (the per-event-type grouping is bypassed). The PR description itself notes this field is not currently surfaced in the UI (the feature uses `CalendarCache.updatedAt` instead) and asks whether this update should be removed. Shipping this as-is adds extra, seemingly unused database writes on every cache refresh cycle and risks future confusion/misuse of a timestamp that doesn't actually reflect per-calendar freshness.

title: Backfilled updatedAt for existing CalendarCache rows will misrepresent cache freshness
body: The migration adds `updatedAt` as `NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()`, which backfills all pre-existing CalendarCache rows with the migration deployment timestamp rather than their actual last-updated time. Once deployed, the new 'Cache Status'/'Last updated' UI will show every pre-existing cache entry as having been refreshed at the exact moment of deployment, which is misleading to users trying to judge actual cache freshness until those rows are naturally re-upserted.

title: No tests added for new deleteCache handler, cache status repository method, or UI component
body: This PR introduces several new pieces of logic (`deleteCacheHandler`, `CalendarCacheRepository.getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`, and the `CredentialActionsDropdown` component) with user-facing destructive actions (cache deletion) and access-control checks, but no unit or integration tests were added for any of them. The PR's own review checklist calls out multiple untested behaviors (authorization, cache status mapping, conditional rendering) as high priority items needing manual verification, which should instead be covered by automated tests before merge.

title: Cache deletion does not invalidate connectedCalendars query, leaving stale cache status in UI
body: The `deleteCacheMutation` only calls `onSuccess?.()` on success, unlike `disconnectMutation` which explicitly invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` and `utils.viewer.apps.integrations` in its `onSettled`. If the parent component's `onChanged`/`onSuccess` prop doesn't itself trigger a refetch of the connectedCalendars query (it is optional and may be undefined), the dropdown will continue to show the old `cacheUpdatedAt` timestamp and cache-status UI after the cache has actually been deleted, giving the user incorrect information about cache state.

title: Plain Error thrown instead of TRPCError with proper code
body: When the credential isn't found or doesn't belong to the user, the handler throws a plain `Error("Credential not found or access denied")` instead of a `TRPCError` with a code like `NOT_FOUND` or `FORBIDDEN`. tRPC will surface this as an `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR` (HTTP 500), which is misleading for monitoring/alerting and prevents the client from distinguishing an authorization failure from an actual server error, unlike the convention typically used in sibling handlers.

title: Directly instantiates CalendarCacheRepository, bypassing the CalendarCache factory/mock abstraction
body: Elsewhere in the codebase (e.g. GoogleCalendarService) calendar cache access goes through `CalendarCache.init(...)`, which is the abstraction responsible for choosing between the real `CalendarCacheRepository` and the `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` (presumably gated by license/feature flag, given the mock exists specifically to disable calendar-cache behavior). Here, `new CalendarCacheRepository()` is instantiated directly, bypassing that selection logic. This means cache-status lookups run unconditionally regardless of whether the calendar-cache feature is actually enabled/licensed for the deployment, which is inconsistent with how the rest of the codebase gates this functionality.

title: getCacheStatusByCredentialIds ignores cache expiry, showing stale timestamps as if cache is active
body: `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups by `credentialId` and returns `_max(updatedAt)` without filtering on `expiresAt >= now()`. As a result, a credential whose cache rows have long expired will still report a 'last updated' timestamp, and the UI (CredentialActionsDropdown) will present it as current cache status. This misleads users into believing cached data is still being served when in fact the next read will be a cache miss and hit the live API.

title: Cache timestamp is formatted with a hardcoded en-US locale
body: The cache-updated timestamp is formatted using `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", {...})`, ignoring the user's actual locale/timezone preference used elsewhere in the app via `useLocale`/dayjs. For non-English locales this produces an inconsistent date format compared to the rest of the UI.

title: dev:cron now relies on npx tsx without adding tsx as a dependency
body: The `dev:cron` script was changed from `ts-node cron-tester.ts` (using the already-declared `ts-node` devDependency) to `npx tsx cron-tester.ts`, but `tsx` is not added to `devDependencies`. Using `npx` will attempt to fetch the package from the npm registry at invocation time (or use a globally cached version), which can produce version drift across environments and fails in network-restricted/offline CI or dev setups, unlike the project's convention of relying on locked workspace dependencies via yarn.

title: updateManyByCredentialId incorrectly bumps updatedAt for all selected calendars of the credential, not just the ones actually refreshed
body: `fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache` operates on the `selectedCalendars` parameter it is given (which can be a subset of all selected calendars for a credential, e.g. the `remainingCalendars` passed in from `unwatchCalendar`). After updating the cache only for that subset, it calls `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})`, which updates the `updatedAt` field for *every* SelectedCalendar row tied to that credential, including ones that were not part of the `selectedCalendars` argument and were not actually refreshed in this call. This causes `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` to misrepresent when a specific calendar's data was last cached, which is a data integrity issue even though the field isn't yet surfaced in the frontend (the PR author's own notes flag uncertainty about whether this update is needed at all).

title: Ownership check excludes team/organization-owned credentials
body: The authorization check `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { id: credentialId, userId: user.id } })` only matches credentials with a direct `userId`. Team- or organization-managed Google Calendar credentials (where `userId` may be null and access is granted via team membership) will fail this check and the user will be unable to delete cache for those credentials even if they are legitimately authorized to manage them, despite the feature targeting calendar integrations broadly.

title: No automated tests for the new deleteCache mutation, cache-status repository method, or UI dropdown
body: This PR introduces a new tRPC mutation (`deleteCache`), a new repository method (`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`), and a new UI component (`CredentialActionsDropdown`) that handles destructive actions (cache deletion, app disconnection) behind confirmation dialogs, but no unit, integration, or e2e tests were added for any of this logic. The PR's own review checklist acknowledges testing was manual-only and limited due to lack of a connected Google Calendar integration, leaving the deletion authorization logic, cache-status mapping, and dropdown rendering conditions unverified by CI.

title: deleteCacheHandler throws a plain Error instead of TRPCError
body: When the credential lookup fails, the handler does `throw new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. tRPC handlers elsewhere in the codebase throw `TRPCError` with an explicit code (e.g. NOT_FOUND/FORBIDDEN) so the client can distinguish error types and so tRPC doesn't log/report it as an unexpected internal error. A plain `Error` will be surfaced to tRPC as an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, meaning routine 'wrong credentialId / not owner' cases get logged/alerted as server errors and the client-side `onError` handler (which just shows a generic toast) can't differentiate an authorization failure from any other failure.

title: deleteCache mutation never invalidates the connectedCalendars query
body: The `disconnectMutation` explicitly invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` and `utils.viewer.apps.integrations` in its `onSettled`, but `deleteCacheMutation` only calls `onSuccess?.()` with no query invalidation of its own. Since `cacheUpdatedAt` (which drives the 'Cache Status' section and whether it is shown at all) comes from the `connectedCalendars` query, after a successful cache deletion the dropdown will keep showing the stale 'Last updated' timestamp and the cache section won't disappear unless the external `onChanged` callback happens to invalidate exactly that query. This is inconsistent with the disconnect flow and can leave the UI showing outdated cache information right after the user is told 'Cache deleted successfully'.

title: Cache status lookup bypasses the CalendarCache factory/feature-flag abstraction
body: `connectedCalendarsHandler` instantiates `new CalendarCacheRepository()` directly instead of going through `CalendarCache.init(...)`, which is the pattern used elsewhere in this same PR (e.g. `CalendarService.ts`) to decide between the real repository and the mock based on whether calendar caching is enabled. Bypassing that abstraction means every call to the `connectedCalendars` query (used on every visit to calendar settings pages) now issues an additional `groupBy` query against the CalendarCache table even for users/teams for which calendar caching is disabled, and it diverges from the established DI pattern used by the rest of the cache feature.

title: Unconditional bulk SelectedCalendar.updatedAt update appears unused by the new feature
body: `fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache` now calls `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` on every invocation (which runs per Google webhook ping / sync), issuing a write against every SelectedCalendar row for the credential just to bump `updatedAt`. The PR's own notes state the frontend uses `cacheUpdatedAt` from `CalendarCache`, not `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt`, and explicitly ask whether this update should be removed. As shipped, this adds unnecessary database write load on a hot path with no consumer of the resulting value.

title: UserWithCalendars type now requires fields not guaranteed by all producers
body: `allSelectedCalendars`/`userLevelSelectedCalendars` were widened from `Pick<SelectedCalendar, "externalId" | "integration" | "eventTypeId">` to also require `updatedAt` and `googleChannelId`. Only one producer of this shape (`UserRepository.findUnlockedUserForSession` in `packages/lib/server/repository/user.ts`) was updated in this PR to select those extra fields, and neither field is actually consumed anywhere in this file's logic (the new cache-status feature reads `cacheUpdatedAt` from `CalendarCacheRepository`, not from these fields). Any other caller in the codebase that builds a `UserWithCalendars`-shaped object without selecting `updatedAt`/`googleChannelId` will fail to type-check against this widened contract, for no functional benefit tied to this feature.

title: No automated tests for the new data-deleting deleteCache mutation
body: The new `deleteCacheHandler` (and the related `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` repository method and mock) ship with no unit or integration tests, despite this being a mutation that deletes user data (calendar cache rows) based on an access-control check. The PR's own review checklist flags 'Confirm repository pattern correctness' and credential-access validation as untested high-priority items; without tests, a regression in the ownership check (`credential.userId === user.id`) or in the deletion scope could silently allow deleting another user's cache or fail to delete the intended one.

title: Ownership check fetches the full Credential row including secret key material
body: `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { id: credentialId, userId: user.id } })` is called without a `select`, so it loads every column of the Credential row — including the `key` field, which stores the (encrypted) OAuth tokens/secrets — purely to verify that the credential exists and belongs to the user. This is unnecessary exposure of sensitive data in application memory/logs; the check should use `select: { id: true }` (or similar) to avoid pulling credential secrets into memory when they are never used.

title: Cache timestamp is formatted with a hardcoded 'en-US' locale
body: The 'Last updated' timestamp is formatted via `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" })`, ignoring the user's actual locale even though the component already imports and uses `useLocale()` for translations. Non-English users will see dates/times formatted in US English conventions while the rest of the UI (including this same dropdown's strings) is localized, which is an inconsistent and incomplete localization of the new feature.

title: dev:cron now invokes `npx tsx` without tsx being a declared dependency
body: The `dev:cron` script was changed from `ts-node cron-tester.ts` to `npx tsx cron-tester.ts`, but `tsx` does not appear anywhere in this package's `dependencies` or `devDependencies` (only `ts-node` remains, still used by other scripts). Using `npx` for a package that isn't pinned in the manifest means the command will fetch whatever version of `tsx` is available on the registry (or fail without network access), which is a reproducibility/supply-chain concern and is unrelated to this PR's calendar-cache feature.

title: Leftover auto-generated warning comment contradicts the actual migration
body: The migration's header comment states 'Added the required column `updatedAt` to the `CalendarCache` table without a default value. This is not possible if the table is not empty.' immediately followed by SQL that adds the column WITH a `DEFAULT NOW()` specifically to handle non-empty tables. This is leftover boilerplate from Prisma's migration generator that was not cleaned up and is misleading/contradictory to anyone reading the migration history to understand why a default was used.

title: sed syntax is macOS-only and will fail on Linux
body: `sed -i '' -E "s|...|...|" "$ENV_FILE"` uses BSD sed's syntax (`-i ''`), which is required on macOS but is invalid on GNU sed used by most Linux distributions/CI images (GNU sed would try to treat the empty string as the input file). Since this script is added to the shared `scripts/` directory for contributors to use, it will error out for any Linux-based developer who tries to run it to update `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL`.

title: Stale-reminder cleanup runs before cancellation and doesn't exclude cancelled reminders
body: The first step in this cron handler deletes every EMAIL WorkflowReminder whose scheduledDate is already in the past, without excluding rows that have `cancelled: true` but have not yet been processed by the subsequent SendGrid-cancel step (e.g. because a prior cron run failed to reach them, see the for-loop issue below). Since this deletion runs before the `remindersToCancel` query/cancel loop, any cancelled reminder whose scheduledDate has already slipped into the past gets silently purged from the DB without ever calling SendGrid's cancel endpoint. If SendGrid has not already sent the email by that point, it will still be sent, reproducing exactly the bug this PR is meant to fix.

title: Single try/catch around the whole cancellation loop aborts remaining cancellations and drops already-queued deletes
body: The for-loop that cancels scheduled SendGrid sends is wrapped in one try/catch for the entire loop instead of per-iteration. If `client.request` throws for one reminder (e.g. an invalid/expired batch id or a transient SendGrid error), the exception propagates out of the loop, so all remaining reminders in `remindersToCancel` for that cron run are never attempted. Additionally, Prisma delete calls are lazy (`PrismaPromise`); the `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` calls queued into `workflowRemindersToDelete` for reminders processed before the failing one are never executed because `await Promise.all(workflowRemindersToDelete)` is skipped when the exception is thrown. The net effect is that successfully-cancelled reminders can remain in the DB forever as `cancelled: true` (getting re-processed, and re-sent to SendGrid's cancel endpoint, on every subsequent run) and reminders after the failing one in the batch are not cancelled at all during that run, increasing the risk that they later fall into the stale-delete bug above and get purged without ever being cancelled.

title: remindersToCancel query is missing a method filter
body: The `remindersToCancel` query only filters by `cancelled: true` and `scheduledDate`, without restricting `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL`. This file is specifically the email-reminder cron job and calls SendGrid's `/v3/user/scheduled_sends` cancel endpoint with `reminder.referenceId`, which for SMS reminders would be a Twilio SID rather than a SendGrid batch id. Currently no code path sets `cancelled: true` for SMS reminders, so this is latent rather than actively triggered, but the missing filter makes the handler fragile to future changes in SMS cancellation logic and is inconsistent with the deleteMany query above it which does filter by method.

title: deleteScheduledEmailReminder with immediateDelete=true never removes or marks the WorkflowReminder row
body: When `immediateDelete` is true and a `referenceId` exists, the function calls SendGrid to cancel the scheduled send and then simply returns — it never deletes the WorkflowReminder row nor sets `cancelled: true`. This is inconsistent with `deleteScheduledSMSReminder`, which always deletes the row after cancelling. Callers that pass `immediateDelete=true` (e.g. handleNewBooking.ts when cancelling reminders of the original booking on reschedule, and the workflow/step-deletion flows in workflows.tsx) rely on this to clean up, but for the reschedule flow in handleNewBooking.ts the original booking row is not deleted, so there is no cascading delete to clean up the orphaned WorkflowReminder record. It will linger in the DB (potentially for days, matching the original scheduledDate) until the cron job's stale-date cleanup eventually removes it, rather than being cleaned up immediately.

title: Guaranteed synchronous reminder cleanup replaced with unawaited fire-and-forget calls
body: Previously, cancelling a booking performed a synchronous `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany` for every workflow reminder, included in the awaited `prismaPromises` array, guaranteeing DB consistency regardless of whether the remote SendGrid/Twilio cancellation succeeded. The new code only calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` inside a `forEach` without awaiting them, and the handler returns its HTTP response before these promises resolve. In serverless/edge execution environments, the request lifecycle can be torn down right after the response is sent, which can prevent these in-flight `update`/`delete` Prisma calls from completing, leaving WorkflowReminder rows neither marked cancelled nor deleted for a booking that was just cancelled.

title: File header comment not updated to reflect new cancellation responsibility
body: The top-of-file comment still reads "Schedule any workflow reminder that falls within 72 hours for email", but this handler now also performs cleanup of stale reminders and cancellation of scheduled SendGrid sends for cancelled/rescheduled bookings (the core fix of this PR). The comment should be updated so maintainers understand the full, and now more safety-critical, responsibilities of this cron endpoint.

title: No automated tests added for the new cancellation/cron logic
body: This PR introduces a new `cancelled` field, a deferred-cancellation design split across booking handlers and a cron job, and changes to multiple delete/cancel reminder functions, specifically to fix a subtle production bug (reminders still sent after cancellation/reschedule). No unit or integration tests were added to cover the new cancellation flow (e.g. verifying that a cancelled reminder is actually cancelled via SendGrid before its DB row is purged, or that the cron job doesn't delete unprocessed cancelled reminders). Given the bug class being fixed is timing/ordering-sensitive, the lack of tests makes similar regressions (such as the ordering issue noted above) likely to go undetected.

title: Unused Prisma import after refactor
body: `Prisma` is imported from `@prisma/client` (previously used for `PrismaPromise<Prisma.BatchPayload>` typings that were removed in this refactor), but after the change there is no remaining usage of `Prisma.` in this file.
