Depending on the project's ESLint/TypeScript strictness (`no-unused-vars`), this can fail CI/build linting.

title: Reschedule flow cancels old EMAIL reminders immediately via SendGrid, reintroducing the exact limit bug this PR fixes
body: When rescheduling a booking, the old booking's EMAIL workflow reminders are cancelled with `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)` — the `immediateDelete=true` flag causes an immediate SendGrid 'cancel' API call. According to the PR description, calling this SendGrid endpoint immediately is exactly what caused the original bug: SendGrid only allows up to 100 pending cancellations, and once that limit is hit, new cancellations fail silently and reminder emails keep being sent. The fix elsewhere (handleCancelBooking.ts, bookings.tsx `requestReschedule`) correctly avoids this by calling `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` without the immediate flag, deferring the actual SendGrid cancellation to the new CRON job that only cancels within the last hour before send. This reschedule code path is the one explicitly named in the PR title ('...and rescheduled bookings...') yet still uses the broken immediate-cancel strategy, so under moderate reschedule volume the same SendGrid pending-cancellation limit can be hit again and reminder emails for rescheduled bookings can still be sent.

title: A single failed SendGrid cancellation aborts cancellation of all other reminders in the same cron run
body: The new cancellation loop wraps the entire `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop (including the SendGrid `client.request` call for every reminder and the final `Promise.all`) in one try/catch. If the SendGrid cancel request throws for one reminder (e.g. transient network error, stale/invalid batch id), the loop stops immediately and none of the remaining reminders in that batch get their cancellation request sent during this cron invocation, nor are their WorkflowReminder rows deleted. Because the cron only runs every 15 minutes and only reminders due within the next hour are considered, a persistently-failing single entry can repeatedly block processing of the rest of the batch on every subsequent run (since the same failing item is encountered again before reaching later items), risking that otherwise-cancellable reminders are still sent by SendGrid because the cancel call never reaches them in time. Cancellation and deletion should be handled per-item with its own try/catch so one failure doesn't block the others.

title: Immediate cancellation path never deletes or updates the WorkflowReminder DB row
body: In `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`, when `immediateDelete` is true, the function calls SendGrid to cancel the scheduled send and then simply `return`s — it never deletes the WorkflowReminder row nor sets `cancelled: true`. This leaves a stale row in the database that still looks 'scheduled' (scheduled=true, cancelled=null/false) even though the underlying email was cancelled. The row only gets cleaned up later by the unrelated generic cleanup in scheduleEmailReminders.ts (`deleteMany` where `scheduledDate <= now`), once its original scheduledDate passes, potentially leaving inconsistent/stale state in the table for a long time and making this data unreliable for any other logic or UI that inspects WorkflowReminder rows in the meantime.

title: Old booking's workflow reminders are cancelled before confirming the reschedule actually succeeded
body: The cancellation of `originalRescheduledBooking.workflowReminders` happens unconditionally right before calling `eventManager.reschedule(...)`, regardless of whether that reschedule call later succeeds. Further down, the code explicitly checks `if (results.length > 0 && results.some((res) => !res.success))` and merely logs an error without rolling back — the booking's calendar/video integrations may fail, but the original booking's reminders have already been cancelled irreversibly (for EMAIL, moved to immediate-SendGrid-cancel / for SMS, outright deleted from Twilio and the DB). This can leave a booking that effectively did not get successfully rescheduled with no reminders scheduled at all.

title: Defense-in-depth ownership check dropped from WorkflowReminder cancel/delete mutations
body: Previously (e.g. in workflows.tsx update mutation) the WorkflowReminder deletion query included an ownership guard directly in the Prisma `where` clause (`booking: { userId: ctx.user.id }`), so even if an upstream bug allowed another user's reminder id to reach this code, the mutation itself would affect 0 rows. The new shared helpers `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` (used from multiple callers including trpc routers) perform `update`/`delete` solely by `id`, with no ownership check baked into the query. This removes a layer of protection against reminder ids leaking across callers/users and now relies entirely on each caller's upstream query having correctly scoped the reminder list.

title: Generic past-due cleanup can delete a cancelled reminder before its SendGrid cancellation request is ever sent
body: The handler first runs an unconditional cleanup: `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany({ where: { method: EMAIL, scheduledDate: { lte: now } } })`, deleting any EMAIL reminder whose scheduledDate has passed, regardless of its `cancelled` flag. This runs before the new cancellation block that queries `cancelled: true` reminders due within the next hour. Because the cron runs every 15 minutes, if a reminder is marked `cancelled: true` less than one cron interval before its `scheduledDate`, the next cron execution may find `scheduledDate <= now` already true by the time it runs and delete the row in the first cleanup step — without ever having issued the SendGrid 'cancel' request for it. If SendGrid had not yet actually sent the email at that instant, it will still go out as originally scheduled, since it was never told to cancel. This narrow but real race window undermines the PR's goal for reminders cancelled close to their send time.

title: No automated tests for the new cancellation logic despite history of a broken prior fix
body: The PR description states that the previous fix (PR #6991) for this exact issue 'was wrong and didn't work as expected.' This PR introduces new, non-trivial logic (the `cancelled` flag lifecycle across emailReminderManager.ts, smsReminderManager.ts, and the new cron cancellation block in scheduleEmailReminders.ts) that is central to actually fixing the reported bug, yet no unit/integration tests are added to verify that cancelled/rescheduled bookings' scheduled reminders are correctly prevented from sending. Given the history of this exact feature being silently broken in production, the lack of test coverage is a significant risk for a repeat regression.

title: Workflow reminder cancellation (and the new `cancelled` DB write the whole fix depends on) is fire-and-forget
body: In the `forEach` loop that replaced the old explicit `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany` logic, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...)` are called without being awaited or collected into the `prismaPromises` array that is later awaited via `Promise.all`. Previously the handler explicitly awaited the DB deletion of each `workflowReminder` row before returning, guaranteeing durability. Now, for EMAIL reminders, the critical write (`cancelled: true`) that the entire PR's fix relies on happens inside an un-awaited async call. If the Next.js API route/serverless function finishes and the response is returned before that promise resolves, the write may never complete, silently defeating the fix and allowing the reminder to still be sent.

title: Reschedule-cancellation of workflow reminders is fire-and-forget, no longer awaited
body: In `requestReschedule`, the previous code collected `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany` promises into `remindersToDelete` and awaited them with `Promise.all` before continuing. That collection/await has been removed; now `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...)` are invoked inside a `forEach` with no awaiting at all. The DB write that marks the reminder as `cancelled` (for EMAIL) is therefore not guaranteed to complete before the trpc mutation resolves and the request lifecycle ends, risking the reminder remaining un-flagged and still being sent by SendGrid.

title: A single failed SendGrid cancel request aborts processing of all remaining pending cancellations for the run
body: The `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop and the subsequent `Promise.all(workflowRemindersToDelete)` are wrapped in one try/catch. If `client.request` throws for any single reminder (e.g. invalid/null `referenceId`, SendGrid rate limiting, or a batch already cancelled), execution jumps straight to the catch block: every reminder later in the array that hasn't been iterated yet is skipped entirely for that run, and even reminders already successfully cancelled earlier in the loop never get their `workflowReminder.delete` committed because `Promise.all` is never reached. Since this cron is the mechanism the whole PR relies on to actually cancel reminders before they're sent, one bad row can block cancellation of every other pending reminder in that run (and potentially every subsequent run if the same row keeps failing), reintroducing the risk the PR set out to fix.

title: `remindersToCancel` query is missing a `method: EMAIL` filter
body: The query `prisma.workflowReminder.findMany({ where: { cancelled: true, scheduledDate: {...} } })` has no `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` filter, even though this cron endpoint and the subsequent code treat `reminder.referenceId` as a SendGrid batch id. Today this works only because SMS cancellation (`deleteScheduledSMSReminder`) never sets `cancelled: true`. This is an implicit, undocumented invariant across two separate files; if any future code path sets `cancelled: true` on a non-EMAIL reminder, this cron will send a Twilio SID (or other non-SendGrid id) to the SendGrid cancel endpoint as `batch_id`, causing spurious API errors (which, per the loop-abort issue, could also block other cancellations).

title: Reschedule flow still cancels SendGrid email reminders immediately instead of using the new deferred-cancellation strategy
body: For the cancel flow, this PR defers actual SendGrid cancellation to the `scheduleEmailReminders` cron (only cancelling within 1 hour of send time) specifically to avoid hitting SendGrid's ~100 pending-cancellation limit that caused the original bug. However, the reschedule flow calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)` with `immediateDelete = true`, which cancels at SendGrid synchronously regardless of how far in the future the original `scheduledDate` is. Since rescheduling can happen for reminders scheduled well in the future (up to 72 hours), a burst of reschedules can still accumulate many pending SendGrid cancellations exactly as before, partially reintroducing the root cause for the "rescheduled bookings" case the PR title explicitly calls out.

title: `immediateDelete` branch leaves a stale `WorkflowReminder` row in the database
body: When `immediateDelete` is true, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` only calls the SendGrid cancel endpoint and returns; it neither deletes the `WorkflowReminder` row nor sets `cancelled: true` on it. For the reschedule path (`handleNewBooking.ts`), the original booking is not deleted, so this row is never cleaned up by cascade; it will sit in the table (with `scheduled: true`, `cancelled` unset) until the unrelated 'delete all EMAIL reminders past their scheduledDate' cleanup in `scheduleEmailReminders.ts` eventually removes it — which can take up to 72 hours. This is a data-hygiene gap left over from the refactor.

title: Unused `Prisma` import after removing `Prisma.BatchPayload`-typed deletion arrays
body: `Prisma` is imported from `@prisma/client` (line 9) but the only place it was previously used — `PrismaPromise<Prisma.BatchPayload>[]` arrays for `remindersToDelete`/`deleteReminderPromise` — has been removed as part of this refactor. No other usage of the `Prisma` namespace remains in the file, so this import is now dead code, which will trigger `no-unused-vars`/unused-import lint errors in a codebase that appears to enforce strict linting, and should be removed.

title: No tests added for the new cancellation flow or the `cancelled` flag semantics
body: This PR introduces a new `cancelled` field, changes the signatures of `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder`, and adds a new cancellation branch to the `scheduleEmailReminders` cron that is the core mechanism fixing the reported bug (reminders still sent after cancel/reschedule). No unit or integration tests are included to verify that: cancelling/rescheduling a booking marks the reminder `cancelled`; the cron correctly cancels and removes reminders whose scheduledDate falls within the next hour; or that a failure for one reminder doesn't silently drop others. Given this is explicitly a bug-fix PR for a subtle, hard-to-notice regression (emails silently still sending), the lack of regression tests is a significant gap.

title: async forEach callback breaks the enclosing try/catch, silently swallowing calendar/video cleanup errors
body: The `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(...)` call (line 125) is wrapped in a `try { ... } catch (error) { logger.error(error.message) }` (lines 124-139). The PR makes the forEach callback `async` so it can `await getCalendar(...)`. `Array.prototype.forEach` never waits for or propagates the promises returned by its callback, so if `getCalendar` or the subsequent `calendar.deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` call rejects, that rejection now escapes as an unhandled promise rejection instead of being caught by the surrounding try/catch. Before this change, `getCalendar` was synchronous, so a thrown error propagated synchronously through `forEach` straight into this same catch block and was logged. After this change, failures during reschedule cleanup of calendar/video events are silently lost (no log, potential unhandled-rejection crash) rather than being handled as before.

title: async forEach callback breaks the enclosing try/catch, silently swallowing calendar/video cleanup errors
body: Identical issue as in vital/lib/reschedule.ts: the `forEach` callback at line 125 was made `async` to accommodate the now-async `getCalendar`, but `forEach` does not await or propagate the callback's promise, so errors thrown inside (e.g. from `getCalendar` or `calendar.deleteEvent`) now become unhandled promise rejections instead of being caught by the `try/catch` at lines 124-139 that previously caught them when `getCalendar` was synchronous. This is a regression in error visibility for reschedule cleanup of stale calendar/video events.

title: forEach(async ...) fire-and-forgets calendar/video cleanup with no error handling in requestReschedule
body: Line 553 changes `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach((bookingRef) => {...})` into `forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` to allow the now-async `getCalendar` call on line 556 to be awaited. There is no try/catch around this block. Previously, since `getCalendar` was synchronous, a thrown error would propagate out of `forEach` and reject the enclosing async tRPC mutation, surfacing a failure to the client. Now, any rejection from `getCalendar`/`calendar.deleteEvent` inside the async callback is an unhandled promise rejection that never reaches the mutation's caller: the reschedule request can report success even though the old booking's calendar/video event was never actually cleaned up, and no error is logged anywhere.

title: Object literal with eager `import()` calls does not provide lazy loading, yet forces async access everywhere
body: `appStore` is defined as an object literal whose property values are `import("./app")` expressions. Because object literals are evaluated immediately, every one of the ~28 `import()` calls fires as soon as any file does `import appStore from "@calcom/app-store"` (or `@calcom/core/videoClient`, etc.) — exactly as eager as the previous static imports. This gives none of the deferred/on-demand loading benefits typically associated with dynamic import (e.g. `() => import(...)` invoked only when a specific app is actually needed), yet it forces every call site across the codebase (CalendarManager, EventManager, videoClient, handleCancelBooking, handleNewBooking, bookings.tsx, payment handlers, getCalendar) to become `await`-based, adding overhead and the error-handling regressions noted elsewhere in this review, without delivering the stated goal.

title: No tests added for a cross-cutting async refactor of appStore access
body: This PR changes the type of every `appStore[key]` access from a directly-usable module object to a `Promise`, forcing `await` in a dozen call sites spanning booking cancellation, rescheduling, calendar, video and payment flows. None of the 12 changed files are tests, and no new/updated tests accompany this refactor. The forEach/async regressions identified in vital/wipemycalother reschedule.ts and bookings.tsx (where error handling silently breaks) would likely have been caught by tests exercising calendar/video deletion failure paths during cancellation/reschedule.

title: Possible incomplete migration: other appStore consumers outside this diff may still assume synchronous access
body: The exported shape of `appStore` changed from directly usable namespace objects to `Promise`s that must be awaited before use. Only 12 files are updated in this PR, but `@calcom/app-store` is referenced throughout the monorepo (app installation/configuration flows, OAuth callback routes, admin app pages, event-type app settings, etc.) that are not part of this change set. Any such file that still does `appStore[key].lib...` without `await` will now receive a pending `Promise` instead of the resolved module, which will either fail type-checking (if strongly typed) or silently misbehave at runtime wherever indexing bypasses the type system (e.g. via `any`/loose casts). The PR description and diff don't show that every usage of `appStore` in the repo was audited/updated.

title: getVideoAdapters now resolves app modules sequentially instead of concurrently
body: `getVideoAdapters` was converted from a synchronous `reduce` into a `for...of` loop that does `await appStore[appName...]` once per credential (lines 24-33). Since each `appStore[appName]` is a module-level promise, awaiting them sequentially inside the loop adds one microtask tick per credential instead of resolving all of them concurrently with `Promise.all`. For call sites with many credentials (e.g. `getBusyVideoTimes`), this introduces unnecessary sequential latency compared to a `Promise.all(withCredentials.map(...))` approach.

title: Dynamic imports are evaluated eagerly, defeating the purpose of lazy loading
body: All entries of the appStore object are built with `import("./appname")` calls placed directly inside an object literal. Because this literal is evaluated once, synchronously, as soon as the module is first loaded, every one of the ~26 dynamic import() calls fires immediately and in parallel, exactly like the previous static imports. None of them is deferred until the specific app is actually needed. As a result, every consumer (getCalendar, videoClient, handleCancelBooking, etc.) still triggers loading of all app packages up front, but now each access additionally requires an `await`, adding complexity and promise-resolution overhead without achieving true on-demand/lazy loading. To actually defer loading, each entry would need to be a function returning the import (e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`), invoked only when that specific app is required.

title: Example comment references a non-existent module path
body: The comment `// example: import("./example"),` doesn't match the actual folder name. The previous code's commented-out import referenced `"./_example"` (with a leading underscore), which is the real folder used to keep the example app excluded from the registry. If a developer later copies this comment to register a new app, it will point at a module that doesn't exist.

title: forEach with async callback no longer reliably initiates calendar deletion before later steps run
body: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` now calls `await getCalendar(...)` inside the callback (previously `getCalendar` was synchronous). Array.prototype.forEach never waits for promises returned by its callback, so once getCalendar became async, the loop body suspends at the `await` and the surrounding `forEach` call returns before any of the calendar deletion requests are even issued. Execution then proceeds to `await sendRequestRescheduleEmail(...)` and the function returns `true`, with no guarantee that the calendar/video deletion calls have started, let alone completed. Previously, since getCalendar was synchronous, the deletion request was synchronously kicked off inside the loop before any later code executed. Additionally, the enclosing try/catch (lines 124-139) cannot catch errors thrown inside these detached async callbacks, so failures become unhandled promise rejections instead of being logged. Net effect: a reschedule can report success and send the reschedule email while the old calendar/video events are still pending deletion or were never actually requested to be deleted in time.

title: forEach with async callback no longer reliably initiates calendar deletion before later steps run
body: Same issue as in vital/lib/reschedule.ts: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` now awaits the newly-async `getCalendar(...)` inside the callback, but forEach does not wait for the returned promises. The loop no longer guarantees the calendar/video deletion requests are even started before the function continues to send the reschedule email and returns. The surrounding try/catch also cannot catch rejections raised inside these detached async callbacks.

title: requestReschedule forEach no longer waits for (or even reliably starts) calendar/video deletion before sending the reschedule email and webhooks
body: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` was previously a synchronous callback that called `getCalendar` synchronously, so the deletion request was always issued inside the loop before the mutation continued. Now `getCalendar` is awaited inside the async callback, and since forEach ignores the promises returned by async callbacks, the deletion requests may not even be initiated before the code proceeds to `await sendRequestRescheduleEmail(...)` and subsequently dispatches BOOKING_CANCELLED webhooks. This changes the ordering guarantees of the reschedule flow and can leave stale calendar/video events behind while users are already notified of the reschedule.

title: Nested forEach(async) race widened by newly-async getCalendar, risking dropped deletions from final Promise.all
body: In the recurring-event branch, `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })` is not awaited by the surrounding code. `apiDeletes` is only consolidated and awaited much later via `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` (line ~652), relying on other intervening awaits in the function to give these detached async callbacks enough time to push their results. Converting the previously-synchronous `getCalendar` call to `await getCalendar(credential)` adds an extra asynchronous hop before each callback even starts its inner loop, widening the race window during which `apiDeletes` may not yet contain the recurring-booking's calendar deletion promises when the final Promise.all executes, risking recurring-booking calendar events that are never actually deleted on cancellation.

title: getVideoAdapters resolves credentials sequentially instead of in parallel
body: The rewritten `getVideoAdapters` uses a `for...of` loop with `await appStore[appName as keyof typeof appStore]` inside, resolving each credential's app module one at a time rather than concurrently (e.g. via `Promise.all`). For bookings with multiple video credentials this unnecessarily serializes independent promise resolutions on every call to createMeeting/updateMeeting/deleteMeeting/getBusyVideoTimes, adding avoidable latency compared to a parallelized implementation.

title: No tests cover the new async appStore / getCalendar / getVideoAdapters behavior
body: This PR converts appStore's values to Promises and makes getCalendar, getVideoAdapters, and getCalendarCredentials asynchronous, touching booking cancellation, rescheduling, calendar/video event creation, and payment flows across many files. Several of these changes introduce race conditions around unresolved promises inside `Array.prototype.forEach` callbacks (see findings on vital/wipemycalother reschedule.ts, bookings.tsx, and handleCancelBooking.ts). No unit or integration tests were added or updated to verify that calendar/video events are still correctly created, updated, and deleted during these flows after the conversion, so these regressions would not be caught by CI.

title: forEach callback made async but not awaited, breaking error handling and ordering
body: The callback passed to `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(...)` was changed from a synchronous function to an `async` function so that `getCalendar` can be awaited inside it. However, `Array.prototype.forEach` never awaits the promises returned by its callback, so the surrounding `try { ... } catch (error) { logger.error(...) }` block (lines 124-139) no longer catches errors that occur inside the async callback (e.g. from `getCalendar` or `calendar.deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting`) — they become unhandled promise rejections instead. In addition, execution proceeds to the subsequent 'Send emails' step and the function's return without waiting for the calendar/video deletions to actually finish, so cancellations can race with (or occur after) the reschedule email being sent, and failures are silently swallowed instead of logged. Previously (sync callback + sync getCalendar) the try/catch correctly caught thrown errors synchronously. This should use `for (const bookingRef of bookingRefsFiltered)` with awaited iterations, or `Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => {...}))` awaited before continuing.

title: forEach callback made async but not awaited, breaking error handling and ordering
body: Identical issue to vital/lib/reschedule.ts: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach((bookingRef) => ...)` was changed to `forEach(async (bookingRef) => ...)` to allow `await getCalendar(...)`. Since `forEach` does not await the returned promises, the enclosing try/catch (lines 124-139) can no longer catch errors thrown inside the callback, they become unhandled rejections. The function also proceeds to send the reschedule email and return before the calendar/video deletions have resolved, introducing a race condition where the booking is reported as rescheduled/cancelled while the actual calendar/video cleanup may not have completed or may fail without being logged.

title: forEach callback made async but not awaited in requestReschedule mutation
body: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach((bookingRef) => {...})` was changed to `forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` to allow `await getCalendar(...)`. `Array.prototype.forEach` ignores the promises returned by async callbacks, so this code fires off calendar/video deletion calls without waiting for them. The mutation then immediately proceeds to call `sendRequestRescheduleEmail` and send webhooks (lines 570-618) without any guarantee that the previous calendar event/video meeting has actually been deleted/updated, and any thrown error inside the callback becomes an unhandled promise rejection rather than being surfaced to the caller. This should use a for...of loop or `Promise.all` with `.map` so the async work is properly awaited before continuing.

title: Dynamic import() calls execute eagerly at module load, not lazily on access
body: `appStore` is an object literal whose property values are `import("./X")` calls. These dynamic import expressions are evaluated immediately when the object literal itself is evaluated (i.e. as soon as this module is loaded), not when a specific key such as `appStore.googlecalendar` is actually accessed. As a result, every consumer that imports `appStore` (getCalendar, videoClient, payment handlers, etc.) still triggers loading of all ~27 app sub-packages concurrently on every module load, rather than only the app that is actually needed for a given credential/booking. This does not provide selective/lazy loading of individual apps — it only converts previously-synchronous property access into asynchronous access (via `await appStore[key]`) while still eagerly fetching every app module. This may fail to deliver the performance/bundle-size benefit implied by the PR, while adding `await` boilerplate throughout many call sites.

title: getCalendarCredentials now returns an unresolved Promise for `calendar`, risking silent breakage for other callers
body: `getCalendarCredentials` calls `getCalendar(credential)` (now async) without awaiting it, so the `calendar` field in its returned objects changed from a resolved `Calendar | null` value to an un-awaited `Promise<Calendar | null>`. Within this file, `getConnectedCalendars` was updated to `await item.calendar` correctly, but `getCalendarCredentials` is an exported utility and this PR's file list does not show every consumer of it being updated. Any other caller that destructures `calendar` and does a truthiness check (e.g. `if (calendar) {...}`) will now always treat it as truthy because a Promise object is always truthy, silently breaking null-handling logic for credentials whose calendar service failed to initialize. This contract change should be verified against all call sites of `getCalendarCredentials`, not just the one touched in this diff.

title: getVideoAdapters now resolves app lookups sequentially instead of in parallel
body: The previous implementation built the adapters array synchronously via `Array.reduce`. The new implementation uses a `for...of` loop with `await appStore[appName]` inside, resolving each credential's app module one at a time instead of concurrently (e.g. via `Promise.all`). For callers that pass multiple credentials (e.g. `getBusyVideoTimes`), this serializes N dynamic-import resolutions where they could be run in parallel, adding unnecessary latency proportional to the number of credentials.

title: No tests added for the new async appStore resolution / concurrency behavior
body: This PR converts many previously-synchronous app-store lookups (getCalendar, getVideoAdapters, payment app resolution) into asynchronous ones and changes several forEach loops to async callbacks. None of the changed files include test updates verifying that calendar/video deletions during booking cancellation/reschedule actually complete before the function returns, or that errors from the now-async app lookups are still surfaced/logged correctly. Given the concurrency regressions introduced by the `forEach(async ...)` pattern in this PR, a regression test exercising cancellation/reschedule with a failing or slow calendar/video provider would have caught the issue.

title: Dead-code `===` comparison for zero-length date overrides never evaluates true
body: `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` compares two separately-created Dayjs object instances with reference equality. Two different `dayjs()` calls never return the same object reference, so this condition is always `false`, even when the override truly has start === end (the common representation of a date override that blocks an entire day). Because this branch is unreachable, a date override meant to mark a whole day unavailable for a fixed host/organizer will not be detected here, and the slot can still be considered available — directly undermining the goal of this PR (respecting fixed-host date overrides).

title: Working-hours check never flags a day the host has no entries for at all
body: The `workingHours.find((workingHour) => { if (workingHour.days.includes(slotStartTime.day())) {...} })` guard at lines 139-148 only evaluates the out-of-range condition for workingHours entries whose `days` already include the slot's weekday. If a fixed host has no workingHours entry at all for that weekday (i.e. a day off with zero availability rows), none of the entries ever return `true`, `.find()` returns `undefined`, and the surrounding `if` is skipped entirely — the function falls through to the busy-time check instead of returning `false`. As a result, a fixed host who simply does not work on a given day is still treated as available for that day as long as there is no conflicting busy time. This is exactly the scenario this PR claims to fix for round-robin events (slots should not be offered when the fixed host is unavailable), so this logic gap leaves the core bug only partially fixed.

title: `end` variable duplicates `start`, so slot end time is never checked against working-hours close time
body: `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` is computed identically to the `start` variable on the preceding line, instead of being derived from the slot's end time (e.g. using `slotEndTime`/`eventLength`). Consequently `end > workingHour.endTime` is equivalent to re-checking `start > workingHour.endTime`, so a slot that starts within business hours but whose duration would push it past the host's configured closing time is never flagged as out of bounds. This can let round-robin/collective bookings be offered that run past a fixed host's working hours.

title: `dateOverrides.find()` short-circuits on the first same-day override, breaking multi-range overrides
body: The availability decision for date overrides (lines 106-131) is based on the first override entry whose date matches the slot's date, via `Array.prototype.find`. If a user has more than one override time range configured for the same calendar date (e.g. a split day with a morning and an afternoon range), and the slot falls within the second range but not the first, the first entry's callback already sets `dateOverrideExist = true` and returns `true` (since `slotStartTime.isAfter(dayjs(date.end)...)` for the earlier range), causing `.find()` to stop and the outer `if` to return `false` (unavailable) for a slot that is actually covered by the later range. This produces incorrect 'unavailable' results whenever a date has multiple override ranges.

title: No automated test for the headline round-robin fixed-host date-override fix
body: The PR description states its primary goal is to ensure round-robin events respect a fixed host's date overrides so slots aren't offered when the fixed host is unavailable. The only tests added ('Check for Date overrides' and its new timezone variant) use a single-user event type with `hosts: []` and no `schedulingType`, so they never exercise the `fixedHosts`/`isFixed` branch together with a `ROUND_ROBIN` schedulingType and a date override. There is no regression test creating a round-robin event with a fixed host that has a date override, verifying that slots outside that override are excluded while the round-robin (non-fixed) host's own availability does not override it — the exact scenario this PR claims to fix.

title: `timeZone` added as optional but is now functionally required for correct override math
body: `TimeRange.timeZone` was added as an optional field, yet `packages/lib/slots.ts` now relies on it (`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)`) to compute the organizer's UTC offset for a date override. Nothing in the type enforces that every caller supplies it; if a `DateOverride`/`TimeRange` is constructed without `timeZone` (e.g. by another call site not updated in this PR), `dayjs(...).tz(undefined)` silently falls back to the dayjs-timezone plugin's 'guess' (the server process's local timezone) instead of erroring, which would silently produce incorrect slot times rather than surfacing the missing data.

title: Working-hours boundary check never evaluates the slot's end time
body: In the new working-hours check added to `checkIfIsAvailable`, both `start` and `end` are computed from `slotStartTime` (`const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();`). `end` should be derived from `slotEndTime` (i.e. slot start + event length) to verify the whole booking fits before the organizer's/fixed host's working hours end. Because `end` duplicates `start`, the check `end > workingHour.endTime` is equivalent to `start > workingHour.endTime`, so a slot whose start is inside the window but whose end (after adding eventLength) extends past the working-hours end time is not flagged as unavailable. This directly undermines the PR's stated goal of correctly respecting a fixed host's hours for round-robin events, allowing bookings that run past a fixed host's actual availability window.

title: Dead code: dayjs instances compared with strict equality always evaluate false
body: `if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares two freshly created dayjs objects with `===`, which is always false regardless of their represented time, since they are different object references. This branch, apparently intended to detect a zero-duration date override (e.g. representing a fully blocked day), can never trigger. As written this is unreachable/dead logic, and any scenario relying on detecting start === end for an override silently falls through to the later branches instead of being handled as intended.

title: Date-override day matching depends on implicit server-local timezone
body: The date-override day match (`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD") === slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")`) builds `dayjs(date.start)` without `.utc()`, so its displayed date/format depends on the Node process's local timezone. `slotStartTime`, however, is explicitly `.utc()`. If the server (or a developer's machine, or CI) is not running with TZ=UTC, this comparison can disagree with the rest of the file, which consistently uses explicit `.utc()`/`.tz()` conversions elsewhere, causing date overrides to be matched to the wrong day or missed entirely depending on deployment environment.

title: No test covers the primary fix: fixed-host date overrides blocking round-robin slots
body: The PR description states its main purpose is to make date overrides of fixed hosts taken into account for round-robin events so slots aren't offered when a fixed host is unavailable. The only test changes add a second timezone assertion to the existing single-user 'Check for Date overrides' test (no scheduling type / no hosts). There is no new test combining a ROUND_ROBIN event with a fixed host that has a date override and a non-fixed round-robin host that is available, to verify that the slot is excluded. Given the newly added/changed availability logic in `checkIfIsAvailable` (working hours and date-override checks per fixed host) contains at least one concrete bug (see other findings), this is exactly the scenario that should have automated coverage but does not.

title: Override timezone offset computed from a field that is typed optional without a fallback
body: `const organizerUtcOffset = dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset();` passes `override.timeZone` directly to `.tz()`. `TimeRange.timeZone` (packages/types/schedule.d.ts) is declared optional (`timeZone?: string`), so nothing in the type system guarantees it is set. If any caller of `getSlots`/`getTimeSlots` supplies `dateOverrides` without a `timeZone` (the field was only newly introduced and is only populated by the one call site touched in this PR), `.tz(undefined)` will silently fall back to some default/local timezone behavior rather than failing, producing incorrect offsets and therefore incorrect override slot times instead of a clear error.

title: Override offset adjustment can cross midnight but only the time-of-day is kept
body: The new override start/end computation shifts `override.start`/`override.end` by `offset` minutes (the difference between invitee and organizer UTC offsets) and then extracts only `.hour() * 60 + .minute()`. When the offset difference between organizer and invitee pushes the adjusted time across a day boundary (common for large timezone differences, e.g. near the International Date Line), the date portion is discarded and only the wrapped time-of-day is kept, which can make the override appear to apply on the wrong day or produce an incorrect time window instead of being excluded/moved to the adjacent day.

title: Dayjs objects compared with `===`, condition is always false
body: In `checkIfIsAvailable`, the check `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` compares two freshly-created Dayjs object instances with strict equality. Dayjs objects are never `===` equal to each other even when they represent the same instant, so this branch can never evaluate to true. This branch appears intended to detect a zero-length date override (start == end), which should make the whole day unavailable for the fixed host; because the comparison is dead code, such overrides silently fall through to the subsequent `isBefore`/`isSame`/`isAfter` checks instead, which may not correctly block all slots for that day, risking round-robin/fixed-host bookings being allowed when the host should be fully unavailable.

title: Working-hours bound check computes `end` from the slot start time, not the slot end time
body: In the new working-hours validation inside `checkIfIsAvailable`, both `start` and `end` are computed from `slotStartTime` (`const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();`), so `start` and `end` are always identical. The intent is clearly to check that the slot's end (accounting for event length) does not exceed `workingHour.endTime`, but since `end` is actually just the slot start again, the check degenerates to only validating the start time twice. As a result, a slot that starts inside working hours but would run past the organizer's working-hours end (e.g. due to event length) is not correctly flagged as out-of-bounds by this check.

title: Date parsed via `.toString()` before dayjs parsing is dependent on server local timezone
body: `organizerUtcOffset` and `inviteeUtcOffset` are computed as `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(...).utcOffset()`. Calling `.toString()` on a JS `Date` renders it using the running process's local timezone (influenced by `process.env.TZ`), and that string is then re-parsed by dayjs. This indirection is unnecessary (dayjs can accept the `Date` object directly, e.g. `dayjs(override.start)`), and if the server process's timezone isn't fixed to UTC, this round-trip can shift the instant being parsed and produce an incorrect UTC offset for the override, undermining the very timezone fix this PR is making.

title: No fallback when `override.timeZone` is undefined, unlike the equivalent code in slots.ts (trpc router)
body: `TimeRange.timeZone` (packages/types/schedule.d.ts) is declared optional, yet `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)` here uses it directly without any guard. If any override lacks a `timeZone` (whether from another caller of `getSlots`, or any upstream data path that doesn't populate this newly-added field), `.tz(undefined)` will silently resolve to some default/guessed timezone instead of throwing, producing a silently wrong offset. Note that the companion logic added in `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/slots.ts` (`organizerTimeZone ? dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone).utcOffset() * -1 : 0`) does defensively guard against a missing timezone, making this omission inconsistent and a latent correctness risk.

title: No regression test added for the PR's headline fix: fixed-host date overrides in round-robin events
body: The PR description states the primary fix is that date overrides of fixed hosts are now taken into account for round-robin events, preventing round-robin bookings when a fixed host is unavailable (fixes #8207/#8329/#8273). However, the only test added in this file (around line 788) covers a personal, non-team event with a date override across two timezones — it does not exercise a ROUND_ROBIN event type with a fixed host plus a round-robin host where the fixed host has a date override. The existing round-robin test at this location (line 1032) was not extended to cover date overrides either. Without such a test, the main behavioral fix claimed by the PR has no automated regression coverage.

title: Date-override day matching does not account for invitee timezone, and isn't tested across larger offsets
body: The `activeOverrides` filter compares `dayjs.utc(override.start)` (which encodes the organizer's local override time as raw UTC digits) against `startOfInviteeDay`/`endOf('day')` computed in the invitee's timezone, without adjusting for the difference between organizer and invitee timezones before deciding which day's override applies. The only added test uses a 30-minute timezone difference (IST vs Dhaka), which is too small to expose day-boundary issues. For larger timezone differences (e.g. organizer and invitee many hours apart), this day-matching could select the wrong day's override, or miss an override entirely, since the comparison is done before the organizer/invitee offset adjustment is applied to determine the true instant.

title: Migration crashes when embed_category/uncategorized_category_id were never overridden
body: The migration does `execute("SELECT c.id FROM categories ... WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id'].to_i` and later `execute("SELECT value FROM site_settings WHERE name = 'uncategorized_category_id'")[0]['value'].to_i`. In Discourse, a site_setting only has a row in the `site_settings` table if it was explicitly changed from its default. Both `embed_category` (default '') and `uncategorized_category_id` (default -1) are typically never explicitly set, so both queries will return zero rows. `result[0]` is then `nil`, and calling `['id']`/`['value']` on `nil` raises `NoMethodError`, which will fail the migration for the vast majority of installations, blocking deployment entirely.

title: Unescaped string interpolation into INSERT statement (SQL injection / syntax errors)
body: `execute "INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, category_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES ('#{h}', #{category_id}, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)"` interpolates `h` (a value read from the old `embeddable_hosts` site setting) directly into the SQL string without escaping/quoting. If that legacy value contains a single quote or other SQL metacharacters, the migration will fail with a syntax error or could execute unintended SQL. This should use parameterized SQL or `ActiveRecord::Base.connection.quote`.

title: before_validation crashes with NoMethodError when host is nil
body: The `before_validation` block calls `self.host.sub!(/^https?:\/\//, '')` and `self.host.sub!(/\/.*$/, '')` unconditionally. If `host` is nil (e.g. the admin submits the create/update form without a `host` value, which the controller does not guard against), this raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'sub!' for nil:NilClass` before validation even runs, resulting in an unhandled 500 error instead of a normal validation failure message.

title: update/destroy actions crash with NoMethodError for a missing id
body: In both `update` (`host = EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first`) and `destroy`, the controller does not check whether `host` is nil before calling `save_host(host)` or `host.destroy`. If `params[:id]` does not match any record (e.g., stale client state, race with another delete), this raises `NoMethodError` on `nil`, producing an unhandled 500 instead of a clean 404/error response.

title: Fabricator file contents swapped with embeddable_host_fabricator.rb
body: After this change, `spec/fabricators/category_fabricator.rb` contains only the `:embeddable_host` Fabricator definition, while the newly added `spec/fabricators/embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` contains the `:category`, `:diff_category`, `:happy_category`, and `:private_category` Fabricators (the content that used to live in category_fabricator.rb). The file names no longer match their contents, which will mislead future maintainers looking for category or embeddable_host fabricators and increases the risk that one of these files gets incorrectly deleted/edited based on its name alone.

title: New admin controllers lack behavioral test coverage
body: Both `spec/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller_spec.rb` and `spec/controllers/admin/embedding_controller_spec.rb` only assert that the controller is a subclass of `Admin::AdminController`. Neither exercises the actual `create`, `update`, or `destroy` actions (success paths, validation failures, missing-record handling, serialization format), despite this PR introducing the entire embeddable-host CRUD surface. Real regressions in these new endpoints (e.g., the nil-record crashes in update/destroy, or the nil-host crash in the model) would not be caught by this test suite.

title: saveChanges action is defined but never invoked
body: The `saveChanges` action calls `this.get('embedding').update({})`, which performs a PUT to `/admin/customize/embedding`. However, `app/assets/javascripts/admin/templates/embedding.hbs` only renders an "addHost" button and the per-host edit/delete controls; nothing in the template triggers the `saveChanges` action. This is dead code, and the corresponding `Admin::EmbeddingController#update` action is a no-op (it just re-serializes the current DB state), so this part of the exposed API has no real purpose as wired up.

title: Host validation regex rejects valid modern TLDs
body: `validates_format_of :host, :with => /\A[a-z0-9]+([\-\.]{1}[a-z0-9]+)*\.[a-z]{2,5}(:[0-9]{1,5})?(\/.*)?\Z/i` restricts the TLD portion to 2-5 characters. Many legitimate modern gTLDs (e.g. `.london`, `.company`, `.photography`) exceed 5 characters and would be rejected by this validation, preventing admins from registering otherwise valid embeddable hosts using those domains.

title: Migration crashes when embed_category/uncategorized_category_id were never explicitly saved to site_settings
body: The migration does `category_id = execute("SELECT c.id FROM categories AS c INNER JOIN site_settings AS s ON s.value = c.name WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id'].to_i`. SiteSetting rows are only persisted to the `site_settings` table when an admin explicitly changes a value away from its default; on virtually every installation that never customized `embed_category` (default '') there is no matching row, so the query returns zero rows and `result[0]` is nil. Calling `nil['id']` raises NoMethodError, aborting the migration. The same problem exists for the fallback query at lines 14-16 for `uncategorized_category_id` (default -1, also usually unset). Since both guards are missing (unlike the properly-guarded `embeddable_hosts` query a few lines below), this migration will fail to run on most real databases, blocking deploy of this feature entirely.

title: update/destroy raise NoMethodError instead of 404 for unknown id
body: `update` does `host = EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first; save_host(host)` and `destroy` does `host = EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first; host.destroy`. If no record matches `params[:id]` (e.g. stale client state, double-submission, or a race with another admin deleting the host), `host` is nil and the subsequent `host.host = ...` or `host.destroy` call raises NoMethodError, resulting in an unhandled 500 error instead of a clean 404/error response.

title: before_validation crashes with NoMethodError when host is nil/blank
body: The `before_validation` callback unconditionally calls `self.host.sub!(...)` twice. If `host` is nil (e.g. the `embeddable_host` param is missing or explicitly blank when creating/updating a host via the admin controller, which assigns `host.host = params[:embeddable_host][:host]` directly), `nil.sub!` raises NoMethodError before the format validation ever runs, turning what should be a normal validation failure into an unhandled 500 error.

title: Host lookup is only half case-insensitive, can fail to match
body: `record_for_host` does `where("lower(host) = ?", host).first`, lower-casing only the database column but not the `host` variable used for comparison (`host = uri.host`, which preserves whatever case the referer/embed URL used, e.g. 'MySite.com'). If the stored host or the inbound host differs only in case, the match fails even though the intent is clearly to be case-insensitive. This can cause legitimate embeds to be rejected with 'invalid referer host'. Existing tests only use all-lowercase hosts, so this gap is not covered.

title: Fabricator file contents were swapped with embeddable_host_fabricator.rb
body: `category_fabricator.rb` now defines only the `:embeddable_host` fabricator, while the category fabricators (`:category`, `:diff_category`, `:happy_category`, `:private_category`) that used to live here were moved into the newly added `spec/fabricators/embeddable_host_fabricator.rb`. The file names no longer match their contents (the Fabrication gem loads all files regardless of name, so tests still pass, but this is clearly an accidental swap that will confuse anyone looking for category or embeddable_host fabricators by filename) and should be corrected before merge.

title: Host format validation rejects many legitimate modern TLDs
body: `validates_format_of :host, :with => /\A[a-z0-9]+([\-\.]{1}[a-z0-9]+)*\.[a-z]{2,5}(:[0-9]{1,5})?(\/.*)?\Z/i` restricts the TLD portion to 2-5 letters. Many valid gTLDs in use since well before 2015 are longer than 5 characters (e.g. `.company`, `.technology`, `.community`), so hosts using them will be rejected as invalid even though they are perfectly legitimate domains, limiting the usability of this new admin feature.

title: Migration builds INSERT via unescaped string interpolation
body: `execute "INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, category_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES ('#{h}', #{category_id}, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)"` interpolates the previous `embeddable_hosts` setting value directly into raw SQL without quoting/escaping. If any historical value contains a single quote or other SQL-significant character, the migration will fail with a syntax error (or, in the worst case, execute unintended SQL). `connection.quote(h)` (or a parameterized execute) should be used instead.

title: No uniqueness validation on host allows duplicate records
body: `EmbeddableHost` has no `validates_uniqueness_of :host` (case-insensitive). The admin UI and controller allow creating multiple `EmbeddableHost` rows with the same host value pointing at different categories; `record_for_host`/`host_allowed?` will silently pick whichever one happens to be returned first by the DB, giving inconsistent/undefined category routing for topic embeds without any error or warning to the admin.

title: find embedded test does not actually exercise the requested id
body: The 'find embedded' test was changed from `store.find('fruit', 1)` to `store.find('fruit', 2)`, asserting that the result's `colors` are ids `[1, 2]`. However, the `/fruits/:id` pretender route in create-pretender.js.es6 is unchanged and always returns `fruits[0]` (the apple record with color_ids `[1,2]`) regardless of the requested id. Fruit id 2 (banana) actually only has `color_ids: [3]` in the fixture data. The test therefore passes only because the mock server ignores the id parameter, not because the embedded-ids hydration logic was verified against the record it claims to fetch; a real regression in id-based lookups would go undetected by this test.

title: embeddable_hosts resource routes lack matching controller actions
body: `resources :embeddable_hosts, constraints: AdminConstraint.new` generates the full set of RESTful routes (index, new, show, edit, in addition to create/update/destroy), but `Admin::EmbeddableHostsController` only implements `create`, `update`, and `destroy`. Requests to the unimplemented routes (index/show/new/edit) will raise `AbstractController::ActionNotFound` rather than a clean 404, which is unnecessary attack surface/noise for routes that are never used by the UI; `resources :embeddable_hosts, only: [:create, :update, :destroy]` would be more correct.

title: Migration crashes when no 'embed_category' site_setting row exists
body: `execute("SELECT c.id FROM categories AS c INNER JOIN site_settings AS s ON s.value = c.name WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id'].to_i` assumes the query returns at least one row. Since `embed_category` was historically a setting that is only persisted in `site_settings` when an admin explicitly changed it from its default, most installations will have zero matching rows, making `execute(...)[0]` return `nil`. Calling `['id']` on `nil` raises `NoMethodError`, which will abort the migration for the common case of a site that never customized `embed_category`. The fallback lookup on the next line (`uncategorized_category_id`) has the same unguarded-indexing problem if that setting was never persisted either.

title: Unescaped string interpolation into SQL INSERT in migration
body: `execute "INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, category_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES ('#{h}', ...)"` interpolates the raw `host` value (read from the previous `embeddable_hosts` site setting) directly into a SQL string without escaping/quoting. Any host string containing a single quote will break the SQL statement or allow arbitrary SQL to run during migration. It should use `ActiveRecord::Base.connection.quote(h)` or parameterized execution.

title: update/destroy actions crash with NoMethodError when id is not found
body: In both `update` (line 10) and `destroy` (line 15), `EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` can return `nil` if the id doesn't exist (e.g. already deleted, race condition, or a bad id). `destroy` then calls `host.destroy` on `nil`, and `update`'s `save_host(nil)` calls `host.host = ...` on `nil`, both raising `NoMethodError` and resulting in an unhandled 500 error instead of a proper 404/error response.

title: before_validation callback raises NoMethodError when host is nil
body: `self.host.sub!(/^https?:\/\//, '')` and the following line assume `host` is always a String. If `host` is `nil` (e.g. a client sends a create/update request without the `host` param, or a new EmbeddableHost record is saved before the field is populated), this raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'sub!' for nil:NilClass` instead of surfacing a normal validation error, causing a 500 response rather than a controlled 422/validation failure.

title: has_many association missing include: true, embeddable_hosts likely omitted from JSON response
body: `has_many :embeddable_hosts, serializer: EmbeddableHostSerializer, embed: :ids` only emits an `embeddable_host_ids` array on the `embedding` object; without `include: true` the actual host records are not embedded at the root of the payload. The client-side `store.js` `_hydrateEmbedded` logic for `_id(s?)$` keys expects a sibling root-level `embeddable_hosts` collection to resolve each id against (`root[this.pluralize(subType)]`). Without that sibling collection, hydration will produce an array of `undefined` entries, breaking `embedding.embeddable_hosts` on the client and causing the admin embedding page (table rendering, addHost/deleteHost actions) to fail or render incorrectly.

title: expandable_first_post? no longer checks whether any embeddable host is configured
body: Previously `expandable_first_post?` required `SiteSetting.embeddable_hosts.present?` in addition to `embed_truncate?` and `has_topic_embed?`. The new implementation (`SiteSetting.embed_truncate? && has_topic_embed?`) drops the check for whether any `EmbeddableHost` exists, so the 'expand' affordance for truncated embedded posts can now be shown even when no embeddable host is configured (feature effectively disabled). The accompanying spec in spec/models/topic_spec.rb ("is false if embeddable_host is blank") still passes, but only because `embed_truncate` defaults to false, not because the embeddable-host condition is actually exercised — so this behavior is both a quiet regression and untested.

title: Fabricator file contents swapped between category_fabricator.rb and embeddable_host_fabricator.rb
body: `spec/fabricators/category_fabricator.rb` now only defines `Fabricator(:embeddable_host)`, while the newly added `spec/fabricators/embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` contains all the `:category`, `:diff_category`, `:happy_category`, and `:private_category` fabricators. The file names no longer match their contents, which is misleading for anyone maintaining these fabricators later (Fabrication itself doesn't care about filenames, so tests still pass, but this is a clear naming/organization mistake that should be corrected).

title: New admin controllers have no functional test coverage
body: Both `spec/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller_spec.rb` and `spec/controllers/admin/embedding_controller_spec.rb` only assert that the controller class is a subclass of `Admin::AdminController`. There is no test coverage for `create`, `update`, `destroy`, or `show` actions, including important edge cases such as updating/destroying a non-existent id (which, per the related finding, currently raises an unhandled `NoMethodError`), invalid host formats, or the embedding/`embeddable_hosts` payload shape returned to the client. This leaves the new admin embedding feature essentially untested at the controller level.

title: String#replace without global flag only replaces the first underscore
body: `type.replace('_', '-')` uses a plain string argument (not a regex with the `g` flag), so only the first underscore in `type` is replaced. This works for `embeddable_host` (single underscore) but will silently fail to fully convert any future model/type name containing more than one underscore, causing `ADMIN_MODELS.indexOf(...)` to miss a match and route requests to the wrong base path.

title: Max upload size hardcoded, ignoring site settings
body: The client-side file size check previously read `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, honoring the admin-configured per-type (image/attachment) limits. It is now hardcoded to `10 * 1024` KB for every upload type. This removes admin configurability: sites configured with a smaller (or larger) `max_image_size_kb`/`max_attachment_size_kb` will now get an incorrect client-side limit that no longer matches the server-side setting used elsewhere (e.g. `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` in `uploads_controller.rb`). This can let users attempt uploads the server will reject (bad UX) or block uploads the admin actually wants to allow.

title: 413 error message now reports a hardcoded size instead of actual configured limit
body: In `displayErrorForUpload`, the max size shown to the user for HTTP 413 (entity too large) responses was previously `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb`, reflecting the real server-configured limit. It is now hardcoded to `10 * 1024`. If the admin has configured a different `max_image_size_kb`, the error message shown to users will state an incorrect maximum size, causing confusion.

title: URL-based upload download limit hardcoded, bypassing configured max image size
body: `FileHelper.download(url, SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes, ...)` was changed to `FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)`. This decouples the API-driven URL download size cap from the admin-configured `max_image_size_kb` setting, allowing downloads up to 10MB regardless of what the admin has configured (potentially larger than intended), and is inconsistent with the rest of the method which still checks `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` for the downsizing loop.

title: Downsize failures are silently ignored in the retry loop
body: The new retry loop calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...)` without checking its return value. `OptimizedImage.convert_with` (invoked under the hood) returns `false` and logs an error when the `convert`/`gifsicle` shell command fails or raises, but here that failure is never checked. If the command fails partway (e.g. ImageMagick not installed, corrupt source, unsupported format) while writing to the same path as the source (`from == to`), the loop will still decrement `attempt` and continue, and ultimately the method proceeds to create the Upload from whatever is left in `tempfile.path`, which could be a corrupted, zero-byte, or unmodified oversized file — with no error surfaced to the caller.

title: No fallback when image cannot be downsized under the max size within 5 attempts
body: After the `while attempt > 0 ...` loop exits, there is no check whether `tempfile.size` is still over `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes`. If 5 rounds of 80% downsizing are not enough to bring the file under the configured limit (e.g. for certain image types that don't compress well), the code silently proceeds to create the Upload with a file that still exceeds the configured maximum, defeating the purpose of the size check and potentially bypassing storage constraints.

title: Duplicate `self.downsize` definition silently shadows the original method, breaking its public signature
body: Two class methods named `downsize` are now defined: one at line 145 with signature `(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` and a new one at line 149 with signature `(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`. In Ruby, the second definition completely replaces the first — the `(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` version becomes dead, unreachable code. Any existing caller elsewhere in the codebase that invokes `OptimizedImage.downsize(from, to, width, height, opts)` with width and height as separate arguments (the previously documented/public signature) will now raise an `ArgumentError` (wrong number of arguments) because the surviving method only accepts a single `dimensions` string plus 3 positional args. This is a breaking API change for any code that wasn't updated alongside this PR, and the leftover dead method should be removed rather than shadowed.

title: Missing tests for changed downsize/optimize behavior and new auto-downsizing feature
body: The PR changes the public signature of `OptimizedImage.downsize`/`optimize` (switching from separate width/height args to a `dimensions` string) and adds a new auto-downsizing retry loop in `UploadsController#create_upload`, but no test changes are included. Given the signature collision bug and the silent-failure risk in the retry loop, this change is particularly risky to ship without unit/controller tests covering: successful downsizing under the limit, failure to downsize within 5 attempts, and compatibility of any other callers of `OptimizedImage.downsize`.

title: Duplicate `self.downsize` definition silently discards the original method
body: Two `def self.downsize` methods are now defined (lines 145-147 and 149-151) with different arities: `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` and `downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`. In Ruby, the second definition overwrites the first at load time (Ruby emits a 'method redefined' warning), so the original 4-argument signature becomes permanently unreachable. Any existing caller elsewhere in the codebase that calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(from, to, width, height, opts)` with four positional arguments will now raise an ArgumentError (wrong number of arguments) or silently misinterpret `height` as part of the options hash. This is dead/conflicting code that should be removed/merged rather than left as two definitions.

title: Percentage dimension string is invalid for gifsicle-based animated downsizing
body: `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails)` passes a percentage string as the resize dimension. When `allow_animation` is true and the file is a GIF, this routes to `downsize_instructions_animated` → `resize_instructions_animated`, which runs `gifsicle --resize-fit 80%`. Gifsicle's `--resize-fit`/`--resize` options require an explicit `WxH` pair and do not accept percentage syntax, so the command will fail. Consequence: animated GIFs larger than `max_image_size_kb` will never actually be downsized (the shell command errors out every iteration), the while loop will exhaust all 5 attempts without reducing the file, and the oversized/animated original will still be uploaded, defeating the stated purpose of the feature for this file type.

title: Downsizing an oversized animated GIF can permanently strip its animation
body: When `SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails` is false (the typical default), the downsizing call falls back to `downsize_instructions`, whose ImageMagick command reads `#{from}[0]` — i.e. only the first frame of the source. Because this logic is now applied directly to the user's original uploaded file (not just to a generated thumbnail), any animated GIF that exceeds `max_image_size_kb` will be silently converted into a static single-frame image before it is ever stored. This is a destructive, user-visible content change with no warning, caused purely by reusing thumbnail-oriented resize instructions on the original upload.

title: In-place resize uses the same path for input and output
body: `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, ...)` uses the identical path for both the source and destination of the external `convert`/`gifsicle` command. Tools that open the output file for writing (truncating it) before fully reading/processing the input (gifsicle in particular, via `--output`) risk truncating or corrupting the source file before processing completes, resulting in a zero-byte or corrupted temp file being uploaded. A safer pattern is to write to a distinct temporary path and then replace the original once the conversion succeeds.

title: No handling for failed downsize attempts or files still over the limit after 5 tries
body: The loop `while attempt > 0 && tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` calls `OptimizedImage.downsize` and decrements `attempt`, but never checks the boolean return value of `downsize` (which is false on shell-command failure) nor reports anything if, after 5 attempts, the file is still larger than `max_image_size_kb`. In both cases (repeated failures, or diminishing returns from 80% scaling not reaching the target), the code proceeds to call `Upload.create_for` with a file that may still exceed the configured size limit or may be corrupted, with no user-facing error or log entry indicating the size restriction was not honored.

title: Hardcoded 10MB cap replaces configurable max_image_size_kb for URL-based uploads
body: The API URL download limit changed from `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` to a hardcoded `10.megabytes`. This removes admin configurability: sites that configure `max_image_size_kb` smaller than 10MB will now allow larger downloads than intended before any downsizing occurs, and sites that configure it larger than 10MB can no longer fetch URLs beyond 10MB even though their own size policy would otherwise permit it. This also applies uniformly regardless of upload `type` (image vs. attachment), losing any type-specific limit that existed before.

title: Client-side upload size validation no longer respects per-type site settings
body: `maxSizeKB` in `validateUploadedFile` was changed from `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']` to a hardcoded `10 * 1024`. This removes the distinction between image and attachment size limits and ignores whatever the admin has actually configured (e.g. `max_image_size_kb`, `max_attachment_size_kb`). As a result, client-side validation can now accept files that the server would reject (if the configured limit is lower than 10MB) or reject files the server would accept (if the configured limit is higher), and the error message shown to users will state an incorrect maximum size relative to the server's actual configuration.

title: 413 error message now shows a hardcoded size instead of the configured max_image_size_kb
body: In `displayErrorForUpload`, the 413 (entity too large) handler replaced `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` with a hardcoded `10 * 1024`. If the site's actual configured `max_image_size_kb` (or webserver/proxy upload limit) differs from 10MB, the error message presented to the user will state the wrong maximum allowed size, which is misleading and inconsistent with the rest of the validation logic.

title: No tests added for new image auto-downsizing behavior
body: This PR introduces non-trivial new logic (a bounded retry loop invoking external image-processing commands on the original uploaded file, with different code paths for animated vs. static images) but includes no new or updated specs covering it. Given the identified risks (gifsicle percentage argument failure, animation stripped from GIFs, in-place file corruption potential, and the changed `OptimizedImage.downsize` method signature), the lack of test coverage leaves these regressions and edge cases unverified before merge.

title: Duplicate `self.downsize` definition silently discards the original 4-arg method
body: The pre-existing method `def self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` (lines 145-147) is immediately redefined by a new `def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` (lines 149-151). In Ruby, the second definition silently replaces the first in the method table (producing a 'method redefined' warning), so any existing caller that invokes `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, max_width, max_height, opts)` with separate width/height arguments (e.g. thumbnail-creation code elsewhere in the app that previously relied on this 4-positional-argument signature) will now raise `ArgumentError: wrong number of arguments` at runtime, because the surviving method only accepts 3 positional arguments plus an options hash. This breaks any existing thumbnail/downsize call site that isn't in this diff, not just the new feature path.

title: Animated GIF detection never triggers because tempfile paths have no extension
body: `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails)` passes `tempfile.path` as the `from` argument. Inside `OptimizedImage.optimize`, the check `from =~ /\.GIF$/i` (optimized_image.rb line 155) decides whether to use the gifsicle-based animated instructions. Rack/ActionDispatch tempfiles typically have no file extension (e.g. `/tmp/RackMultipart...`), so this regex will never match for uploads coming through this new code path. As a result, large animated GIFs that need downsizing will always go through the regular ImageMagick `downsize_instructions`, which selects only the first frame (`#{from}[0]`), silently stripping the animation from any animated GIF that exceeds `max_image_size_kb`.

title: Downsizing loop ignores failure and may silently upload an oversized image
body: The loop at lines 64-70 calls `OptimizedImage.downsize` up to 5 times but never checks its boolean return value. `convert_with` (and therefore `downsize`) returns `false` on any ImageMagick/gifsicle failure (e.g. missing binary, malformed input, unsupported geometry string). If downsizing fails on every attempt, the loop exits solely because `attempt` reaches 0, and the code proceeds to call `Upload.create_for` with the original oversized `tempfile` and no error is surfaced to the caller or the user. This defeats the purpose of the size check and can let files larger than the configured `max_image_size_kb` through unnoticed.

title: API URL download size limit hardcoded to 10MB regardless of site settings
body: `FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, "discourse-upload-#{type}")` replaces the previous `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` limit with a fixed 10MB constant. Since `type` can represent non-image attachments as well as images, this removes any admin-configurable control over how large a file the server will fetch via the API URL path (e.g. `max_attachment_size_kb`), silently allowing downloads up to 10MB even on sites configured with a much smaller limit, and wasting bandwidth/memory for attachments that cannot later be downsized.

title: Client-side max upload size hardcoded to 10MB, ignoring configured site settings
body: `validateUploadedFile` previously read `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, honoring separate admin-configured limits for images (`max_image_size_kb`) and attachments (`max_attachment_size_kb`). It is now hardcoded to `10 * 1024` KB for both types. Attachments cannot be downsized server-side the way images can, so an admin who configured a smaller `max_attachment_size_kb` will no longer have that limit enforced client-side; uploads up to 10MB will be attempted and only fail (if at all) after the fact, producing a confusing UX and bypassing the admin's intended restriction. The same hardcoding is repeated for the 413 (entity too large) error message at line 246, which previously reported `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` and can now show an incorrect max size to users if the server's actual limit differs from 10MB.

title: No test coverage for the new automatic downsizing feature
body: The PR adds a new downsize-on-upload code path (lines 63-70) plus corresponding API changes in `optimized_image.rb` (collapsing `downsize` to a 3-arg/percent-based signature), but no tests were added or updated to cover: downsizing being triggered when `max_image_size_kb` is exceeded, the loop giving up after 5 attempts, or the behavior change to `OptimizedImage.downsize`'s signature. Given this changes both a public model API and upload behavior, the lack of tests makes it easy for the regressions noted above (duplicate method definition, lost GIF animation, silent oversized uploads) to go unnoticed before release.

title: unsubscribe action crashes with NoMethodError when no TopicUser record exists
body: `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil (e.g. a logged-in user navigating directly to `/t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe` for a topic they have never visited or been notified about). The very next line calls `tu.notification_level` on this possibly-nil value, which raises `NoMethodError` and results in a 500 error instead of a handled response. The code should use `TopicUser.change`/`TopicUser.find_or_create_by` or otherwise guard against a missing record.

title: unsubscribe bypasses TopicUser.change, losing MessageBus publish and reason/changed_at bookkeeping
body: Instead of calling the existing `TopicUser.change` class method (used everywhere else notification_level is modified, e.g. in `set_notifications`), this action mutates the `TopicUser` record directly and calls `tu.save!`.
