title: Missing documentation of required middleware ordering for context propagation
body: The previous InstrumentationMiddleware had a doc comment explicitly stating it "should live at the top of the middleware stack" because it both instrumented metrics and enriched the context with a contextual logger. That constraint has now shifted to require ContextualLoggerMiddleware to sit immediately before LoggerMiddleware in CreateMiddlewares (so the enriched context created by ContextualLoggerMiddleware reaches LoggerMiddleware's `FromContext` call). No comment documents this ordering requirement in either contextual_logger_middleware.go or the CreateMiddlewares slice, so a future reorder of middlewares (e.g. moving NewLoggerMiddleware before NewContextualLoggerMiddleware) would silently drop contextual log fields (pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName/dsUID) with no indication of why.

title: Adding FromContext to the Logger interface is a breaking change for all implementers
body: The exported `plugins/log.Logger` interface gained a new method `FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger`. Any other implementation of this interface in the codebase (mocks, adapters, etc.) that isn't updated in this PR will fail to compile. Only `grafanaInfraLogWrapper` (logger.go) and `TestLogger` (fake.go) were updated here; it should be verified that no other implementers of plugins/log.Logger exist elsewhere in the repository (or in downstream consumers of this package) that would be broken by this interface extension.

title: traceID no longer included in 'Plugin Request Completed' log line
body: The previous implementation of logRequest explicitly extracted the trace ID via `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` and appended it as a `traceID` log field. This PR removes that logic entirely (the `tracing` import was dropped from this file) and the new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware.instrumentContext` that replaces the removed context-enrichment code only adds `endpoint`, `pluginId`, `dsName`, `dsUID` and `uname` - it does not add `traceID`. Unless the underlying infra logger automatically injects trace IDs from the context (not evidenced anywhere in this diff), this change silently drops trace correlation information from the 'Plugin Request Completed' log entries, which is a regression for anyone correlating logs with traces.

title: New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no unit tests
body: This PR introduces a brand-new middleware, `ContextualLoggerMiddleware`, which is responsible for enriching the context with plugin/request attributes used by downstream logging (notably `LoggerMiddleware`, which now relies on `FromContext(ctx)` to pick up these attributes). No test file (e.g. contextual_logger_middleware_test.go) was added to verify that QueryData/CallResource/CheckHealth/CollectMetrics correctly attach the expected contextual attributes, or that SubscribeStream/PublishStream/RunStream intentionally do not. Given that this logic was previously covered indirectly inside the (deleted) instrumentation middleware tests, extracting it into its own middleware without dedicated tests leaves this behavior unverified.

title: Missing documentation of required middleware ordering
body: The previous `InstrumentationMiddleware` had an explicit comment stating it must be placed at the top of the middleware stack because it both records metrics and enriches the context with a contextual logger. After this refactor, `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` must still be placed before `LoggerMiddleware` (and any other middleware that wants the enriched contextual logger) in the stack for the logging to pick up the attributes via `FromContext`. This ordering constraint is no longer documented anywhere (neither on `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` nor on `LoggerMiddleware`), making it easy for a future change to reorder middlewares (e.g. in pluginsintegration.go) and silently lose the contextual log attributes without any test or compiler error to catch the regression.

title: TestLogger.FromContext discards state, making contextual logging unverifiable in tests
body: `TestLogger.FromContext` always returns a brand-new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()`, rather than returning the receiver `f` (or otherwise preserving the recorded `InfoLogs`/`WarnLogs`/etc. fields). Since `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` now calls `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)` instead of logging directly on `m.logger`, any test that uses `TestLogger` to assert on the 'Plugin Request Completed' log output (e.g. checking `InfoLogs.Calls`/`Message`) will observe no change on the original logger instance, because the actual `Info` call lands on a disposable, unreferenced `TestLogger` returned by `FromContext`. This effectively makes `TestLogger` unusable for verifying any code path that logs via `FromContext`, which is now the primary logging path for plugin client middlewares.

title: Test function name not updated after Instrumentation→Metrics rename
body: The file was renamed from instrumentation_middleware_test.go to metrics_middleware_test.go and the helper `newInstrumentationMiddleware` call site was updated to `newMetricsMiddleware`, but the test function itself is still named `TestInstrumentationMiddleware`. This is inconsistent with the stated goal of the PR ('Renamed instrumentation middleware to metrics middleware') and leaves stale naming that should have been updated to `TestMetricsMiddleware` for consistency with the rest of the rename.

title: Device limit enforcement is bypassed after the first rejection due to caching before persistence succeeds
body: In tagDeviceUI, `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})` is executed BEFORE the call to `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice(ctx, device)`. When the device limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, which TagDevice now propagates and client.go's Authenticate turns into an authentication failure for that request. However, the cache entry for that device ID was already set during this failed attempt. On the very next request from the same (blocked) device, within the ~29 minute cache TTL, tagDeviceUI short-circuits on `a.localCache.Get(key)` and returns nil without ever calling CreateOrUpdateDevice again. TagDevice then returns nil, and Authenticate proceeds to return a valid anonymous Identity. So after the single first rejection, the same over-the-limit device is silently let through for the remainder of the cache TTL, completely defeating the device limit feature for any device that retries (e.g. a browser reload).

title: TOCTOU race between CountDevices and insert allows exceeding the configured device limit
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice first calls CountDevices to check whether the active-device count is >= deviceLimit, and only falls back to updateDevice (reject new devices) when the limit is already reached; otherwise it proceeds with a plain INSERT/UPSERT. There is no transaction, locking, or atomic constraint tying the count check to the subsequent insert. Multiple concurrent requests for different new device IDs can all read a count below the limit and then all insert successfully, letting the active device count exceed deviceLimit. Under any real concurrent anonymous traffic this race defeats the purpose of the configurable device limit.

title: Anonymous authentication now blocks synchronously on a DB call with no timeout, removing previous async/timeout/panic-recovery protections
body: Previously TagDevice was invoked in a goroutine with its own context.WithTimeout(2*time.Minute) and a recover() to guard against panics, so a slow or failing device-tagging write never affected the latency or stability of the anonymous authentication response. This change removes the goroutine, the timeout, and the panic recovery, and calls `a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, httpReqCopy, anonymous.AnonDeviceUI)` synchronously using the request context. Every anonymous authentication for a not-yet-cached device now blocks on a DB upsert (and, when a device limit is configured, an additional COUNT query) with no bounded timeout of its own, and an unrecovered panic in this path would now propagate into the request-handling goroutine. This is a latency and availability regression on the anonymous auth hot path, especially under DB slowness or load.

title: Changed constructor signature may leave generated DI (Wire) code out of sync
body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService's signature changed from accepting `anonStore anonstore.AnonStore` (previously resolved elsewhere, presumably via a Wire provider calling anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore) to accepting `sqlStore db.DB` directly and building the AnonDBStore internally with `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore(sqlStore, cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit)`. anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore's own signature also changed (added deviceLimit int64 parameter). The PR's file list does not include any update to generated wire_gen.go (or equivalent DI wiring) that would reference these constructors; if such generated code exists and still calls the old signatures, the build will fail to compile or Wire codegen will fail due to an unused/missing provider. This should be verified and, if needed, regenerated before merge.

title: New auth.anonymous device_limit setting is undocumented
body: A new ini key `device_limit` under `[auth.anonymous]` is introduced and parsed into `cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit`, but the PR does not update conf/defaults.ini (sample config) or the configuration documentation to describe this new setting, its default (0 = unlimited), or its effect. Without this, administrators have no way to discover or understand how to configure the new device limit feature.

title: 30-day anonymous-device window duplicated as separate constants across three files
body: The 30-day 'active device' window is now hardcoded independently in three places: `thirtyDays` in pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/impl.go (used for usage stats), `anonymousDeviceExpiration` in pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database.go (used for the device-limit count window and the update-match window), and `anonymousDeviceExpiration` in pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/api/api.go (used for listing devices). These must stay numerically identical for the device-limit feature, usage stats, and the devices API to remain consistent; having three independent literals increases the risk that a future change to one location silently desynchronizes the others.

title: No test coverage for cache-bypass or concurrent device-limit races
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a single new device is rejected once the limit is reached; it does not cover (a) that an already-known device can still refresh its timestamp when the limit is reached, (b) concurrent CreateOrUpdateDevice calls for distinct new devices that could race past the limit (see the CountDevices/insert TOCTOU issue), or (c) the interaction between the local cache in impl.go and repeated calls for a device that was previously rejected, which currently lets a rejected device through on retry. These are exactly the scenarios where the new feature is most likely to fail silently.

title: Device limit is trivially bypassable by omitting the device-id header
body: In TagDevice, if the client does not send the `X-Grafana-Device-Id` header, the function immediately returns nil without ever calling CreateOrUpdateDevice/CountDevices: `deviceID := httpReq.Header.Get(deviceIDHeader); if deviceID == "" { return nil }`. Since the new device-limit enforcement lives entirely inside CreateOrUpdateDevice, any client that omits this client-supplied, unauthenticated header (or sends a fresh random value each request) never triggers the limit check and is never denied. This means the newly added `AnonymousDeviceLimit` feature can be completely circumvented by non-browser clients or by simply not sending/rotating this header, defeating the purpose of capping anonymous devices.

title: TOCTOU race condition lets device count exceed the configured limit
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice first runs CountDevices to check if the limit has been reached, and only if `count >= s.deviceLimit` falls back to update-only mode; otherwise it proceeds to INSERT a new device row. This check-then-act sequence is not wrapped in a transaction or any locking mechanism. Under concurrent anonymous requests (which is exactly the scenario the device limit is meant to guard against, e.g. traffic spikes or multiple server instances in HA), multiple goroutines/requests can all read a count below the limit simultaneously and then all insert new devices, allowing the actual number of active devices to exceed `deviceLimit`. This undermines the correctness guarantee the feature is supposed to provide.

title: Tagging call made synchronous in the authentication hot path, removing prior async/timeout/panic protections
body: Previously, TagDevice was invoked from a separate goroutine with its own timeout context and panic recovery, so a slow or failing DB write never blocked or crashed the Authenticate() call. This change removes that wrapper and awaits TagDevice directly on the request context. Now every anonymous authentication request whose local device cache entry is cold (new device or every ~29 minutes per returning device) blocks on a synchronous DB write (plus, when the limit feature is enabled, an extra COUNT query) before the auth flow can complete. It also removes the recover() that previously guarded against panics inside the tagging logic, so an unexpected panic there can now propagate up through the authentication path instead of being safely contained.

title: No test exercises Authenticate() denying access when the device limit is reached
body: The new `errors.Is(err, anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached)` branch in Authenticate() causes anonymous authentication to fail entirely once the device limit is hit, which is the primary user-facing behavior of this feature. Only the low-level anonstore.CreateOrUpdateDevice function is covered by a test (TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit in anonstore/database_test.go); there is no test validating that the Anonymous client's Authenticate() method actually returns an error (and thus denies anonymous access) once the configured limit is exceeded, nor any test for the new ProvideAnonymousDeviceService wiring with a non-zero AnonymousDeviceLimit.

title: New auth.anonymous.device_limit setting is undocumented
body: A new configuration key `device_limit` under `[auth.anonymous]` (mapped to `Cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit`) is introduced here, but no accompanying documentation was added: there is no update to the sample/defaults ini files or to the configuration reference docs describing the setting, its default (0 = unlimited), or its effect. Administrators have no way to discover or understand this new setting, and the Cfg struct field itself has no doc comment explaining the 0-means-unlimited semantics implemented in anonstore.go.

title: AnonymousDeviceLimit type/semantics mismatch between backend DTO and frontend type
body: The Go DTO field `AnonymousDeviceLimit int64` has no `omitempty` and is always serialized (defaulting to 0 when unset), whereas the corresponding TypeScript declarations (`packages/grafana-data/src/types/config.ts` and `packages/grafana-runtime/src/config.ts`) type it as `number | undefined` and default the client-side value to `undefined`. In practice the frontend will always receive a concrete number (0 when not configured) rather than `undefined`, so any frontend code that checks for `undefined` to detect the "no limit configured" state will never see that condition and must instead treat 0 specially — a subtle mismatch between the documented type and actual runtime contract.

title: TOCTOU race allows exceeding the configured device limit
body: In CreateOrUpdateDevice, the device count is read via CountDevices and then, based on that snapshot, the code decides whether to insert a new device or fall back to update-only. These two steps (count check and insert) are not executed in a single transaction/lock. Under concurrent anonymous requests from different new devices arriving close together, multiple goroutines/requests can all observe count < deviceLimit and all proceed to insert, allowing the actual number of devices to exceed the configured limit. Since the feature's entire purpose is to cap the number of anonymous devices, this race undermines the guarantee the limit is supposed to provide.

title: Local cache is set before the DB write succeeds, letting a device bypass the device limit on retry
body: tagDeviceUI calls a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{}) immediately, before calling anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. If CreateOrUpdateDevice returns anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached (new behavior added by this PR), tagDeviceUI still leaves the cache entry set. On the next request from the same device (within the ~29 minute cache TTL), the early 'if _, ok := a.localCache.Get(key); ok { return nil }' check short-circuits and returns nil without ever calling CreateOrUpdateDevice again. As a result TagDevice returns nil, client.Anonymous.Authenticate() sees no error, and the device is authenticated successfully even though it was never persisted to anon_device and the device limit was exceeded on its first attempt. This defeats the device limit: a rejected device only needs to retry once to be let in, and will never actually be counted/limited again until the cache entry expires.

title: Anonymous device tagging changed from fire-and-forget to synchronous, blocking authentication on a DB round-trip
body: Previously TagDevice was invoked in a background goroutine with its own timeout, so a failure or latency in anon_device writes never affected the anonymous request itself (errors were only logged). Now TagDevice is awaited synchronously inside Authenticate, so every first-seen device for every anonymous request blocks on a DB count+insert/update before the request can proceed, and any DB error/latency now directly affects anonymous authentication latency and availability (not just the tagging feature). This is a meaningful behavior/availability change for the anonymous auth path that should be called out and load-tested, since anonymous access is often used for public/embedded dashboards with high request volume.

title: New auth.anonymous device_limit setting is not documented
body: A new configuration key `device_limit` under `[auth.anonymous]` is introduced (parsed via anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0)) and exposed through Cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit, but no corresponding entries were added to conf/defaults.ini, conf/sample.ini, or the configuration reference docs in this PR. Administrators have no documented way to discover or configure this new limit.

title: No test coverage for Authenticate() rejecting anonymous auth when the device limit is reached
body: client.go now returns an error from Authenticate when anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached, which is a new, security/availability relevant behavior (anonymous users can be denied access). No unit test (e.g. in a client_test.go) exercises this path to confirm Authenticate correctly propagates the error, nor is there a test validating the setting.go parsing of the new `device_limit` ini key (e.g. in setting_test.go). This leaves the core new behavior of the feature unverified by automated tests.

title: Cleanup job interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute without explanation
body: The background cleanup ticker was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This affects the entire `clean()` routine, which runs all cleanup jobs (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, user invites, short URLs, query history), not just the annotation cleanup this PR is about. Running every cleanup job 10x more frequently is a significant behavioral/performance change that is not mentioned in the PR description, is unrelated to the stated goal of avoiding MySQL deadlocks (and could actually increase contention since jobs now run far more often), and has no corresponding test coverage or justification. This looks like it may be a leftover debugging change that should be reverted or explicitly justified before merge.

title: Error-level logging used for normal/successful cleanup batches, including full ID lists
body: In CleanAnnotations (lines 534, 537, 554, 557) and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags (lines 576, 579), `r.log.Error(...)` is called on every batch iteration even when there is no error. The `err`/`y` values logged at line 534/554/576 are guaranteed nil at that point because the function already returned early on error, so these statements always report a bogus 'error' for a success case. Since these calls run on every batch of every cleanup cycle (now potentially every minute, with batch sizes that can be in the tens of thousands as exercised by the new test), this will flood error-level logs/alerting systems with non-error noise and also logs the entire fetched ID slice (up to the configured batch size) on every iteration, adding unnecessary log volume/overhead. These should be at Debug/Info level and should not include an always-nil error field.

title: Error-level logging used for routine, non-error cleanup events, including full ID list dumps
body: In CleanAnnotations/CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags, r.log.Error(...) is called unconditionally on every successful batch iteration (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579), even though the preceding error checks already returned on actual errors (so `err` logged here is always nil). This mislabels normal operation as an error, which will pollute error logs/alerts and error-rate metrics/dashboards that key off log severity. Additionally, the full `ids` slice (which can be tens of thousands of entries given AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize can be configured up to 32767+ as shown in the new test) is serialized into every log line, which is expensive and will bloat log storage/throughput when cleanup runs frequently (especially now that the cleanup job interval was reduced to 1 minute). These should be Debug level and should not dump entire ID arrays.

title: Unexplained change of cleanup job ticker interval from 10 minutes to 1 minute affects all cleanup jobs, not just annotations
body: The ticker driving CleanUpService.Run was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This is a 10x increase in the frequency of the entire cleanup job list (temp file cleanup, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, old annotations, user invites, stale short URLs, stale query history) — not just the annotation cleanup logic that this PR is meant to fix. This change is not mentioned in the PR description, has no accompanying rationale, and no test coverage. Running all of these jobs 10x more often increases database load system-wide and could introduce new contention/performance issues, which seems inconsistent with a PR whose stated goal is reducing lock contention.

title: O(n^2) string concatenation when building literal ID list for SQLite large-batch delete
body: In deleteByIDs, when running on SQLite with a batch size over 999, the code builds the IN(...) literal values by repeatedly doing `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside a loop (lines ~609-612). Each iteration reallocates and copies the growing string, making this O(n^2) in the number of IDs. With batch sizes in the tens of thousands (as exercised by the new test with batch size 32767), this results in unnecessary CPU and memory overhead compared to using a strings.Builder or similar amortized approach.

title: Test name references SQLite >= 3.32.0 behavior but code uses the conservative pre-3.32.0 parameter limit
body: The new test case is named "should not fail if batch size is larger than SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER for SQLite >= 3.32.0", implying it targets SQLite's newer default limit of 32766. However, the production code's sqliteParameterLimit constant (xorm_store.go) is hardcoded to 999 — the pre-3.32.0 default — so the literal-value workaround is triggered for any batch size above 999, regardless of SQLite version. The test therefore does not actually validate behavior specific to the 3.32.0 threshold; it only exercises the already-conservative workaround path, making the test name misleading about what scenario is being verified.

title: No test demonstrates or guards against the MySQL deadlock the PR is intended to fix
body: The PR's entire motivation is a MySQL-specific deadlock between annotation cleanup and concurrent inserts (grafana/grafana#64979), caused by a single DELETE-with-subquery statement. The added/changed tests (cleanup_test.go) only run against the test DB (typically SQLite) and verify functional correctness of batched deletion, not the concurrency/deadlock behavior that motivated the change. There is no test (e.g., a concurrent-insert-during-cleanup scenario) that would catch a regression back to the deadlocking pattern or validate that the fix actually avoids it under contention.

title: Cleanup loop ticker interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute without justification
body: The ticker driving `CleanUpService.Run` was changed from `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)` to `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)`. This is unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (splitting annotation cleanup queries to avoid MySQL deadlocks) and is not mentioned anywhere in the PR description. This change affects every job scheduled through `clean()` - temp file cleanup, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, old annotations, user invites, stale short URLs, and stale query history - making all of them run up to 10x more often. Since `clean()` still has a 9-minute timeout (`const timeout = 9 * time.Minute`), a slow run can overlap with or immediately follow the next tick, effectively causing near-continuous execution of these maintenance jobs. This risks substantially increased DB/file-system load and could ironically reintroduce lock contention similar to the deadlock this PR is trying to fix. This looks like an accidental leftover from local testing and should be reverted or explicitly justified and tested.

title: Routine, successful batch cleanup progress logged at Error level with full ID list dumps
body: In `CleanAnnotations` (lines 534, 537, 554, 557) and `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` (lines 576, 579), every successful batch iteration logs via `r.log.Error(...)` even though no error occurred (the `err` field logged is always nil at that point, since the function already returned early on error). These log calls also include the full `ids` slice, which can contain up to `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` entries (the added test exercises a batch size of 32767). Because this loop runs until no more rows match and may run every minute now (see the ticker change in cleanup.go), this will flood logs with large ID dumps at Error severity on every normal run, which both degrades logging performance/storage and can trigger false-positive error alerting in production monitoring that treats Error-level logs as incidents. These should be downgraded to Debug/Info and should avoid dumping entire ID slices.

title: Quadratic string concatenation when building SQLite literal ID list
body: In `deleteByIDs`, when running on SQLite with a configured batch size greater than the 999 parameter limit, the code builds the literal `IN (...)` clause by repeatedly doing `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside a loop over `ids`. This recreates and copies the growing string on every iteration, giving O(n^2) time/memory behavior. The PR's own test uses a batch size of 32767, meaning this path is exercised with tens of thousands of iterations, which is unnecessarily expensive compared to using a `strings.Builder` or the `strconv.AppendInt`-into-byte-slice pattern already used elsewhere in this same file (e.g., `getAccessControlFilter`).

title: Async legacy-write goroutines derive their timeout from a request-scoped context that is likely already canceled
body: In Create (line 51), Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163), the fire-and-forget goroutine does `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10*time.Second, ...)` using the *incoming request* ctx as parent. In the real apiserver, `http.Request.Context()` (and the context threaded through REST handlers) is canceled as soon as the handler that invoked Create/Update/Delete returns and the response is written - which happens essentially immediately after the goroutine is spawned, often before the goroutine even runs. Because `context.WithTimeout`/`WithTimeoutCause` on an already-canceled parent returns an already-canceled context, the asynchronous Legacy write will frequently fail immediately with a 'context canceled' error, defeating the entire purpose of mode 3's 'write to legacy as a safety net' feature. This bug is masked in the unit tests because they call the dual writer with `context.Background()`, which never cancels. The goroutines should detach from request cancellation (e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` plus a fresh timeout, or `context.Background()` carrying only the needed values) instead of inheriting the request's cancellation.

title: Update no longer wraps the Legacy update with the already-resolved object, risking resourceVersion/precondition failures on every legacy write
body: The previous Mode3 implementation (removed by this diff) called `d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, &updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}, ...)`, deliberately feeding Legacy the already-resolved object produced by Storage.Update instead of letting Legacy re-derive it. The new code instead passes the raw `objInfo` straight to `d.Legacy.Update` (line 139). Internally, Legacy.Update will fetch its own 'old' object and call `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, legacyOld)`/check preconditions again, but the resourceVersion embedded in the request (and any client-supplied preconditions) reflects Storage's state, not Legacy's independently-versioned object. Since reads in mode 3 only go through Storage, Legacy's resourceVersion will generally not match, which is very likely to cause every asynchronous legacy update to fail with a conflict error, silently breaking the legacy-sync safety net for Update that this PR is supposed to provide.

title: Delete success path records the storage-duration metric with the object name instead of the resource kind
body: On the success path of Delete, `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the per-object `name` as the metric label, whereas the error path two lines above (and every other method in this file) passes `options.Kind`. Using the object's name as a Prometheus label value creates one time series per distinct object name, leading to unbounded metric cardinality and potential monitoring/storage issues in production, in addition to making the metric inconsistent with the error path and with every other method's labeling.

title: Storage.Create failure is recorded via recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration
body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the error path calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` (line 45), mislabeling a Storage failure as a Legacy failure. The success path two lines below correctly uses `recordStorageDuration`. This corrupts the error-rate metrics used to distinguish Storage vs Legacy problems, which is particularly important for a mode whose purpose is to monitor divergence/failures between the two stores.

title: Storage.Update failure is recorded via recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration
body: Same issue as in Create: on the error path of Update, `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` is invoked for a failure that occurred in `d.Storage.Update`, not in Legacy. This mislabels the metric and makes it impossible to reliably distinguish storage failures from legacy failures via metrics.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection duration/error is recorded under the storage metric
body: Inside the async goroutine of DeleteCollection, after calling `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection`, the result is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration`. Every other method (Create, Delete, Update) correctly calls `recordLegacyDuration` for the legacy-side async call; this inconsistency mislabels the Legacy DeleteCollection outcome as a Storage outcome in metrics.

title: Delete attaches the wrong logger to the context, losing structured fields
body: In Delete, `log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method)` builds a logger with contextual fields, but the very next line does `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`, attaching the base `d.Log` (without the added fields) to the context instead of the local `log` variable. Any code downstream that retrieves the logger via `klog.FromContext(ctx)` (e.g. inside Storage.Delete/Legacy.Delete) will not see the name/kind/method fields, unlike in Create, Update and DeleteCollection which correctly propagate their local `log`.

title: Unrecovered panics inside the async legacy-write goroutines will crash the whole process
body: Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection each spawn a bare `go func() { ... }()` that calls into `d.Legacy.*` with no `recover()`. Any panic raised inside these goroutines (e.g. a nil-pointer dereference or type assertion failure in the legacy storage implementation) is not caught by the HTTP server's per-request panic-recovery middleware, because it runs on a goroutine that outlives the request handler. An unrecovered panic in a goroutine terminates the entire Go process, so a single bad legacy write could take down the whole apiserver instead of merely failing one request, which is a significant regression in robustness compared to the previous synchronous implementation.

title: Tests never verify the asynchronous legacy write actually happens
body: TestMode3_Create, TestMode3_Delete, TestMode3_Update and TestMode3_DeleteCollection configure mock expectations on the Legacy storage (`setupLegacyFn`) but the dual writer now calls Legacy asynchronously in a goroutine launched just before Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection return. The tests return immediately after asserting on the result of the synchronous Storage call, without any synchronization (no WaitGroup, channel, or sleep) and without calling `m.AssertExpectations(t)`/`AssertCalled`. As a result, these tests do not actually verify that the legacy write occurs, and would still pass even if the async legacy call were removed entirely or always failed, leaving the core 'dual write' behavior of mode 3 effectively untested.

title: Fire-and-forget legacy writes derive their context from the request context, which is cancelled when the request completes
body: In Create (and similarly in Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) the async goroutine does `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10*time.Second, ...)` using the `ctx` that was passed into the method, which is ultimately the HTTP request context. Go's net/http cancels the request context as soon as the handler (i.e. this Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection call and the rest of the request pipeline) returns and the response has been written. Since the goroutine is launched right before the function returns, in practice the derived context is cancelled almost immediately, well before the intended 10s timeout elapses, so the asynchronous write to legacy storage is very likely to be aborted mid-flight. This defeats the entire purpose of Mode 3's "write to legacy as a safety net" behavior: legacy will frequently fall out of sync without any visible error to the caller (errors are only logged/metriced inside the goroutine). The context used for the detached write should not inherit cancellation from the request (e.g. use `context.Background()` or `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` plus the desired timeout).

title: Storage create failure is recorded as a legacy-duration metric
body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration`. Legacy was never invoked on this path (the function returns before the async legacy call), so this mislabels a Storage failure as a Legacy failure, corrupting the dual-writer metrics used for monitoring/alerting.

title: Storage update failure is recorded as a legacy-duration metric
body: In `Update`, when `d.Storage.Update` fails, `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` is called instead of `d.recordStorageDuration`. As with Create, Legacy.Update is never reached on this path, so the error is incorrectly attributed to the legacy backend instead of storage, making the dual-writer metrics misleading.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection result recorded under storage-duration metric
body: Inside the async goroutine in `DeleteCollection`, after calling `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection`, the result is recorded via `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration`. This mislabels the legacy call's duration/error as a storage metric, which is inconsistent with the equivalent code in Create/Delete/Update (which correctly use `recordLegacyDuration` for the legacy call) and corrupts observability data.

title: Delete records the per-request object name as a Prometheus metric label instead of the resource kind
body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object's `name` as the metric label where every other call site (Create, Get, List, Update, DeleteCollection, and the error branch just above at line 103) passes `options.Kind`. Using an effectively unbounded, per-object value (the resource name) as a Prometheus label value causes label cardinality to grow unboundedly with the number of distinct objects deleted, which can blow up memory/storage in the metrics backend and degrade or break querying. This is also inconsistent with every other metric label in this mode, making dashboards/alerts based on `kind` silently miss delete-success events.

title: Delete puts the un-enriched base logger into the context instead of the locally built logger
body: `log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method)` is built but then `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` stores `d.Log` (without the added values) into the context, not the local `log` variable. Every other method in this file (Create, Get, List, Update, DeleteCollection) correctly stores the enriched `log`. As a result, any code downstream of `Delete` that retrieves the logger via `klog.FromContext(ctx)` loses the name/kind/method fields, making it harder to correlate logs for delete operations.

title: Async legacy Update no longer uses the object actually written to Storage, risking divergence between stores
body: The previous Mode3 implementation fetched the current object from Storage, computed the `updated` object once via `objInfo.UpdatedObject`, and explicitly wrapped that same computed object for both `Storage.Update` and `Legacy.Update` so both backends ended up with an identical payload. The new implementation calls `d.Storage.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...)` and then, in the detached goroutine, calls `d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...)` with the same raw `objInfo`. Since `objInfo.UpdatedObject` is invoked independently by each store (each using its own view of the "old" object), Legacy and Storage can end up computing and persisting different final objects, especially for patch-style updates. This undermines the stated goal of Mode 3 ("write to unified storage and then asynchronously write to legacy as a safety measure") because the legacy copy may not actually mirror what was stored in unified storage.

title: No panic recovery in detached goroutines performing legacy writes
body: The goroutines spawned in Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection (lines 50, 108, 134, 161) call into `d.Legacy.*` with no `recover()`. An unrecovered panic in any of these detached goroutines (e.g. triggered by a bug or unexpected state in a legacy store implementation) will crash the entire Grafana process, since Go terminates the program on an unhandled panic in any goroutine, not just the one serving the HTTP request. Fire-and-forget background work like this should guard against panics to avoid turning a legacy-storage bug into a full server crash.

title: Mode3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy writes actually occur
body: The Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection tests configure `setupLegacyFn` mock expectations but the dual writer now performs the corresponding legacy write in a background goroutine. The tests return immediately after asserting on the synchronous result and never wait for the goroutine (no sync.WaitGroup, channel, or `require.Eventually`) nor call `m.AssertExpectations`/`AssertCalled` on the legacy mock. Consequently these tests would pass even if the goroutine were never launched, called the legacy store with wrong arguments, or if any of the metric-mislabeling bugs introduced in this PR regressed further — the new asynchronous behavior added by this PR is effectively untested.

title: Duplicate checksum entry added for grafana/pkg/apimachinery go.mod
body: The line `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod h1:DkxMin+qOh1Fgkxfbt+CUfBqqsCQJMG9op8Os/irBPA=` already existed in the file and is added again by this diff, producing a duplicate entry. This indicates `go.work.sum` was not regenerated cleanly (e.g. via `go mod tidy`/`go work sync`) and the unrelated dependency churn in this file (azure-sdk-go, prometheus-alertmanager, otel packages, etc.) seems unrelated to the Mode 3 dual-writer feature described in the PR, suggesting it was accidentally bundled in from a different branch/rebase.

title: Storage.Create failure recorded under legacy metrics instead of storage metrics
body: In DualWriterMode3.Create, when d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` (line 45) instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. This mislabels a Storage (unified store) failure as a Legacy failure in the dual-writer metrics, corrupting the error-rate dashboards/alerts that distinguish unified-storage health from legacy-storage health. The same mistake is repeated in Update (line 129).

title: Storage.Update failure recorded under legacy metrics instead of storage metrics
body: In DualWriterMode3.Update, when d.Storage.Update fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. This duplicates the same mislabeling bug found in Create (line 45): a Storage failure is reported as a Legacy failure, which will skew metrics used to monitor the health of each backend independently.

title: Wrong label value (object name instead of resource kind) passed to storage duration metric
body: In DualWriterMode3.Delete, the successful-path metric call is `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` (line 106), passing the individual object's `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind` (the resource kind, e.g. "playlists"). Since `name` varies per deleted object, this will create a distinct Prometheus label value per object name, causing unbounded metric cardinality and breaking any dashboards that group by resource kind for delete operations. The failure path on line 103 correctly uses `options.Kind`, confirming this is an inconsistency/bug rather than intentional.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection duration recorded as storage metric
body: Inside the async goroutine of DeleteCollection, after calling `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection(...)`, the result is recorded via `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` (line 166) instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`, which is what Create, Delete, and Update use for their analogous legacy-write goroutines. This mislabels legacy-store latency/error metrics as unified-storage metrics for the delete-collection operation.

title: Delete attaches the wrong logger to the context
body: In DualWriterMode3.Delete, a richer logger is built with `log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method)` but the context is populated with the plain `d.Log` instead: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` (line 97). Every other method in this file (Create, Get, List, Update, DeleteCollection) correctly injects the enriched `log` variable into the context. As a result, any downstream code that pulls the logger via `klog.FromContext(ctx)` during a Delete call loses the name/kind/method structured fields, reducing traceability specifically for delete operations.

title: Async legacy writes derive their timeout context from the request context, which is canceled once the handler returns
body: Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection (lines 51, 110, 135, 163) each spawn a goroutine that does `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, ...)` using the inbound request `ctx` as the parent. For an HTTP server, the request context is canceled once the handler (ServeHTTP) returns; since these methods return the Storage result to the caller immediately after launching the goroutine (without waiting), the apiserver handler will typically finish and the request context will be canceled shortly afterward — well before the 10 second timeout and often before the legacy write even completes. Because cancellation propagates to the derived timeout context, the "safety measure" asynchronous write to legacy storage can be silently aborted on effectively every request, defeating the purpose of mode 3's async legacy write. The goroutine should detach from request cancellation (e.g. use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` or a fresh context carrying only the needed values) before applying its own timeout.

title: Legacy write errors are silently swallowed (no logging) in async goroutines
body: In the async legacy-write goroutines for Create (line 56), Delete (line 113), Update (line 140), and DeleteCollection (line 166), the only outcome recorded on failure is a boolean passed into the duration metric (`d.recordLegacyDuration(errObjectSt != nil, ...)`); none of them call `log.Error(...)` the way the previous Mode3 implementation did (e.g. "could not update object in legacy store"). Operators now have no way to see which object/resource failed to replicate to legacy storage except by correlating metrics, substantially reducing observability for a feature explicitly intended as a safety net against unified-storage/legacy divergence.

title: Update no longer guarantees the same resolved object is written to both stores
body: The previous Mode3.Update implementation fetched the current object from Storage, resolved `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old)` once, and wrapped the already-resolved object so that both Storage.Update and Legacy.Update applied the exact same final object. The new implementation instead calls `d.Storage.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...)` and then, in the async goroutine, calls `d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...)` with the same unresolved `objInfo` (line 139). Each backend will internally invoke `objInfo.UpdatedObject` against its own "old" object; for patch-style updates (merge patch, strategic merge patch, JSON patch) this can produce two different resulting objects if the legacy store's and unified store's current state differ even slightly, causing silent divergence between the two stores — the exact problem dual-writing is meant to prevent. Additionally, invoking `UpdatedObject` a second time may not be safe/idempotent for all `rest.UpdatedObjectInfo` implementations.

title: TestMode3_Delete never mocks Legacy.Delete even though it is always invoked
body: DualWriterMode3.Delete unconditionally spawns a goroutine that calls `d.Legacy.Delete(...)` after a successful Storage.Delete. The `testCase` struct in TestMode3_Delete only has a `setupStorageFn` field (no `setupLegacyFn`), so for the "deleting an object in the unified store" success case the legacy mock (`m := &mock.Mock{}`, never associated with `t` via `.Test(t)`) has no registered expectation for `Delete`. Calling an unmocked method on a `testify` mock without `.Test(t)` set panics; since this call happens in a background goroutine, an unrecovered panic there crashes the entire test binary non-deterministically, rather than failing just this test. The test needs to register a Legacy.Delete expectation (and ideally await/verify the call) for success cases.

title: TestMode3_DeleteCollection never mocks Legacy.DeleteCollection even though it is always invoked
body: Same issue as in TestMode3_Delete: DualWriterMode3.DeleteCollection always spawns a goroutine calling `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection(...)` after a successful Storage.DeleteCollection, but the `testCase` struct here only defines `setupStorageFn`; there is no `setupLegacyFn` and no `m.On("DeleteCollection", ...)` registered on the legacy mock for the success case. The unmocked call made from the background goroutine will panic in testify's mock (since the mock is not bound to `t`), risking an unrecovered panic that crashes the test process.

title: No test waits for or verifies the asynchronous legacy write actually occurs
body: None of the Mode3 tests (Create, Delete, Update, DeleteCollection) synchronize with the goroutine that performs the async legacy write, nor do they call `m.AssertExpectations`/`AssertCalled` to confirm `Legacy.*` was actually invoked. Since the goroutine may run after the subtest has already returned, the tests effectively never verify the core new behavior this PR introduces (asynchronous write-through to legacy storage as a safety measure); a regression that removed the legacy write entirely would not be caught by this test suite.

title: Duplicate entry added to go.work.sum
body: The diff adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod h1:DkxMin+qOh1Fgkxfbt+CUfBqqsCQJMG9op8Os/irBPA=` as a new line even though an identical entry already exists a few lines above (unchanged). Having a duplicate checksum line suggests the file was not cleanly regenerated via `go work sync`/tooling, which can mask inconsistencies in a manually-edited lock file.

title: Missing double-check after acquiring write lock causes redundant work
body: After acquiring the write lock (line 48-49), the code does not re-check whether entryPointAssetsCache is already populated and the environment is non-Dev before redoing the (potentially expensive) file/CDN read. Multiple goroutines that pass the initial RLock check with ret == nil (e.g. at startup, before the cache has been populated) will each serialize on the write lock and redundantly re-read the manifest file or re-fetch from the CDN, overwriting the cache with the same result each time. This defeats much of the purpose of caching for concurrent initial requests and can add unnecessary I/O latency under load. The fix should re-check `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` right after acquiring the write lock and return early if so.

title: No test added to verify the data race fix
body: This PR's stated purpose is fixing a data race in GetWebAssets, but no test (e.g. a concurrent-call test runnable with `go test -race`) was added to verify that the race is actually fixed or to guard against regressions. Without such a test, a future refactor could silently reintroduce the race on the shared entryPointAssetsCache global.

title: Missing double-check after acquiring write lock causes redundant work
body: After taking the RLock and finding entryPointAssetsCache == nil, the code unconditionally acquires the write lock and recomputes the assets without re-checking whether another goroutine already populated the cache while waiting for the lock. If multiple goroutines call GetWebAssets concurrently on a cold cache (e.g. right after startup), each one that was blocked on entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock() will redundantly re-read the manifest file (or hit the CDN) and overwrite entryPointAssetsCache again, instead of returning the value the first goroutine just computed. This does not reintroduce the data race, but it defeats part of the purpose of caching and can cause unnecessary file/network I/O under concurrent load.

title: No regression test added for the fixed data race
body: The PR fixes a data race on the entryPointAssetsCache global by adding a mutex, but no test (e.g. a -race enabled test that calls GetWebAssets concurrently from multiple goroutines) was added to verify the fix or to prevent regressions if the locking is refactored later. Without such a test, a future change could silently reintroduce the race without being caught by CI.

title: Missing double-check of cache after acquiring write lock
body: After the first (read-locked) check of entryPointAssetsCache fails (e.g., cache not yet populated or cfg.Env == Dev), the code acquires the write lock at line 48 but never re-checks whether another goroutine already populated the cache while waiting for the lock. As a result, under concurrent initial requests (common right after startup), multiple goroutines can all proceed past the first check, serialize on the write lock, and each redundantly re-read and re-parse assets-manifest.json (or hit the CDN) even though the first goroutine already finished and stored a valid result. This doesn't reintroduce the data race, but it defeats part of the purpose of caching and wastes I/O/CPU under load. A standard fix is to re-check `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` immediately after acquiring the write lock and return early if so.

title: No regression test added for the data race fix
body: The PR fixes a data race on the global entryPointAssetsCache variable in GetWebAssets, but no test was added (e.g., a test that calls GetWebAssets concurrently from multiple goroutines, intended to be run with `go test -race`) to guard against regressions. Without such a test, a future refactor could silently reintroduce the race with no automated signal.

title: enableSqlExpressions() contains dead/confusing logic that always returns false
body: The helper computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then has `if enabled { return false }` followed by an unconditional `return false`. Both branches return false, so the function always disables SQL expressions regardless of the `FlagSqlExpressions` toggle state. While the intended effect (permanently disabling the vulnerable feature) matches the goal of this security PR, the code reads as though the feature flag controls the outcome when it actually has no effect at all. There is no comment explaining this is a deliberate kill-switch for CVE-2024-9264. A future maintainer could easily 'simplify' this apparent dead code (e.g. by returning `h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(...)` directly) and unknowingly re-enable the vulnerable SQL expression code path, since nothing in the code documents why it must always be false.

title: Misleading error message for a feature that is deliberately disabled, not unimplemented
body: When a SQL expression query is submitted, `ReadQuery` now returns the error "sqlExpressions is not implemented". This is inaccurate: the feature was previously implemented and working, and is being force-disabled here as an emergency security mitigation (CVE-2024-9264), not because it was never built. Users/admins who had the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle enabled before upgrading will see a confusing message that doesn't reflect the real reason the feature stopped working, making it harder to diagnose the regression after upgrade.

title: No tests added or updated to verify the SQL-expressions disablement, likely breaking existing coverage
body: This PR replaces the DuckDB-backed `DB` implementation with a stub whose `TablesList`, `RunCommands`, and `QueryFramesInto` methods unconditionally return `errors.New("not implemented")`, and pairs it with a reader.go change that unconditionally rejects QueryTypeSQL. No test files are included in the diff, yet pkg/expr/sql/parser.go (table extraction via DuckDB AST parsing) and pkg/expr/sql_command.go (SQL command execution) are exactly the kind of logic that would normally have unit tests asserting successful parsing/execution against a real DuckDB instance. Those pre-existing tests, if they exist, would now fail since every call into the stub returns an error instead of real results, and this PR does not update or remove them. Additionally, for a PR whose explicit purpose is to close an RCE/LFI vulnerability, there is no new regression test asserting that `ReadQuery` rejects SQL expression queries regardless of the `FlagSqlExpressions` toggle state, or that the stub DB always errors. Without such tests, there is no CI safety net to catch an accidental future re-enablement of the vulnerable path.

title: enableSqlExpressions contains dead/misleading logic that always returns false
body: The new helper always returns false regardless of the feature flag value: `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`; `if enabled { return false }`; `return false`. Both branches return the same literal, so the computed `enabled` value (and the feature-flag lookup itself) is completely unused/irrelevant, and the variable name `enabled` is also inverted relative to what it actually measures (it is true when the flag is NOT enabled). This makes the code highly misleading: a future maintainer could easily believe toggling `FlagSqlExpressions` re-enables SQL expressions, when in fact it never will with this implementation, and there's no comment explaining that this is an intentional, hard-coded kill-switch for a security fix (CVE-2024-9264). This should be simplified to an explicit `return false` with a clear comment, to avoid confusion and accidental 'fixes' that re-enable the vulnerable code path.

title: No test coverage added for disabling SQL expressions
body: This PR's core behavior change is that QueryTypeSQL now always errors out with "sqlExpressions is not implemented" via enableSqlExpressions(), which is the security-relevant fix. No test changes are included in the diff to verify this behavior (e.g., a test that ReadQuery returns an error for QueryTypeSQL regardless of feature flag state), nor are there tests for the new pkg/expr/sql/db.go stub (DB.TablesList/RunCommands/QueryFramesInto) to confirm they always fail safely. Given the severity of the vulnerability being fixed, a regression test preventing silent re-enablement of SQL expression execution is important and currently missing.

title: Misleading public error message when SQL expressions are effectively disabled
body: NewSQLCommand calls sql.TablesList(rawSQL), which now always fails because pkg/expr/sql/db.go's DB.RunCommands is a stub that unconditionally returns errors.New("not implemented"). When this happens, NewSQLCommand returns errutil.BadRequest("sql-invalid-sql", errutil.WithPublicMessage("error reading SQL command")), which tells the user their SQL is invalid, when the real reason is that the feature has been completely disabled/stubbed out. Any code path that reaches NewSQLCommand without going through ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery's explicit "sqlExpressions is not implemented" check (e.g. UnmarshalSQLCommand, used for raw-node parsing) will surface this confusing message instead of a clear explanation, making it harder for users/admins to diagnose why previously working SQL expressions now fail.

title: Leftover DuckDB-specific code/naming contradicts stated PR goal of removing DuckDB references
body: The PR description states the intent is to "Remove reference to DuckDB", but TablesList still names its local variable `duckDB` (`duckDB := NewInMemoryDB()`) and still constructs a DuckDB-specific SQL command (`SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')`) to pass to RunCommands, even though the underlying DB is now a stub that always returns "not implemented" and has nothing to do with DuckDB. This leftover naming/logic is confusing: it implies the code still talks to a DuckDB engine with a real SQL dialect, when in fact it is now dead code whose output is always discarded due to the stub's unconditional error. This should be cleaned up or at minimum commented to reflect that the underlying engine has been removed.

title: enableSqlExpressions() contains dead, misleading logic that always returns false
body: The new helper `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then both the `if enabled` branch and the fallthrough path return `false`. The computed `enabled` value is never actually used to decide the return value — the function unconditionally returns `false` no matter what the feature toggle is set to. While the net effect (always disabling SQL expressions) matches the PR's stated goal, the code reads as if it is checking the feature flag when it is not, and there is no comment explaining that this is an intentional, permanent kill-switch. A future contributor who 'simplifies' this apparent dead code (e.g. by returning `enabled` directly) could unknowingly re-enable the vulnerable code path review intended to permanently disable. This should either be a plain `return false` with an explanatory comment referencing the CVE, or the SQL query type should be removed from the switch entirely.

title: No tests added for the new SQL-expressions kill switch, and existing tests likely broken
body: This PR fundamentally changes SQL expression behavior (TablesList/RunCommands/QueryFramesInto now always return "not implemented", and ReadQuery now always errors for QueryTypeSQL), but none of the changed files are tests. Given there must be pre-existing tests exercising pkg/expr/sql/parser.go (TablesList) and pkg/expr/sql_command.go (NewSQLCommand/Execute) that previously asserted correct DuckDB-based behavior (e.g. extracting table names, running real queries), those tests would now fail against the stubbed-out DB that always returns errors, since they are not included/updated in this diff. Conversely, no new test verifies that SQL expressions are now reliably blocked regardless of the FlagSqlExpressions toggle value (i.e., a regression test for the security fix itself is missing). For a PR whose entire purpose is to close an RCE/LFI vulnerability, lacking a test asserting the vulnerable path is unreachable is a significant gap that risks silent regression in future refactors.

title: Error message "sqlExpressions is not implemented" is misleading
body: When QueryTypeSQL is requested, ReadQuery now returns the error "sqlExpressions is not implemented". This is factually incorrect — SQL Expressions were implemented and are being deliberately disabled for security reasons (RCE/LFI, per CVE-2024-9264), not because the feature was never built. Users/administrators who previously had FlagSqlExpressions enabled and relied on it will see a confusing message implying the feature never existed, rather than a clear message indicating it has been disabled. This can misdirect support/debugging efforts and should be reworded (and ideally referenced in release notes/changelog, since this is a breaking change for anyone who had the toggle on).

title: Leftover "duckDB" variable name contradicts stated PR goal of removing DuckDB references
body: The PR description states the goal is to "Remove reference to DuckDB", yet the local variable in TablesList is still named `duckDB` (`duckDB := NewInMemoryDB()`) even though it now constructs the stub `sql.DB`, not a DuckDB instance. This is purely cosmetic but is inconsistent with the PR's own stated intent and could confuse future readers into thinking real DuckDB code still exists here.

title: Removing the coarse BuildIndex lock allows concurrent builds of the same index key to race
body: The previous code held `b.cacheMu.Lock()` for the entire `BuildIndex` function, which incidentally serialized all builds for the same NamespacedResource key (even though it hurt cross-namespace concurrency). This PR removes that lock and only takes `cacheMu` around the final `b.cache[key] = idx` write (lines 137-139). However, nothing now prevents two goroutines from concurrently calling `BuildIndex` for the *same* key - this happens in practice via `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` (resource/search.go), which is called on every `Search` RPC and on every watch event, and performs an unlocked `GetIndex` read followed by a `build` call on cache miss. If two concurrent requests for a newly-seen (or not-yet-indexed, e.g. small/skipped-at-startup) namespace both see a nil index, they will both call `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` against the same on-disk directory concurrently (line 98), which can fail or corrupt the index, and will both finish and overwrite `b.cache[key]`, wasting work and potentially leaving an index object whose underlying bleve.Index was already closed/overwritten. This is a regression introduced by the finer-grained locking change, not just a perf improvement.

title: Shared `err` and counter variables mutated unsynchronized across the errgroup goroutines in searchSupport.init
body: In `searchSupport.init`, `err` (declared from `stats, err := s.storage.GetResourceStats(...)`) and `totalBatchesIndexed` are captured by every goroutine launched in `group.Go(...)` (lines 186-193) and written concurrently without any synchronization (`totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(...)`), then `err` is read back and returned from each goroutine, and `totalBatchesIndexed` is read after `group.Wait()` for a trace attribute. This is a data race: one goroutine's error result can be clobbered by another before it reads it back to return to the errgroup, meaning `group.Wait()`/`s.initErr` can reflect the wrong build's error (masking a real failure or spuriously failing because of an unrelated goroutine's transient error), and `totalBatchesIndexed` can under-count due to lost updates. Because `NewResourceServer` now calls this `init` synchronously at startup (previously it only ran lazily on the first gRPC call), this race is exercised on every process startup instead of occasionally, increasing the chance that a single namespace's indexing error incorrectly fails (or incorrectly succeeds) server construction for all tenants.

title: Resource server construction now blocks indefinitely on full search index build with no timeout
body: `NewResourceServer` now calls `s.Init(ctx)` synchronously before returning the constructed server. `Init` calls `s.search.init(ctx)`, which performs a full index build across every namespace returned by `GetResourceStats` using a background context with no deadline. For installations with many/large namespaces this can take a long time (this is literally called out in the PR description as the reason gRPC calls were timing out). Moving this work into the constructor removes the context-cancellation symptom but replaces it with an unbounded blocking call during process/module startup, which can now cause the whole module server (not just a single RPC) to hang past readiness/liveness probe timeouts or deployment rollout windows, with no partial availability and no circuit breaker. This tradeoff (named explicitly as an open question by the PR author: 'What could this break?') should be called out/resolved before merging, e.g. by bounding the startup init with a timeout or making it async with a readiness gate.

title: Removing per-RPC Init() guards removes the only safety net if initialization wasn't performed
body: Every RPC method (`Create`, `Update`, `Delete`, `Read`, `List`, `Watch`, `Search`, `History`, `Origin`, `IsHealthy`, `PutBlob`, `GetBlob`) previously called `s.Init(ctx)` defensively before doing any work, which both lazily initialized the server and acted as a guard against using an uninitialized `server` (e.g. `s.broadcaster` being nil, which would be used at `s.broadcaster.Subscribe(ctx)` in `Watch`). These guards are all removed on the assumption that `NewResourceServer` always performs `Init` before returning the server. Any code path that constructs a `server` value without going through `NewResourceServer` (e.g. test helpers within the `resource` package) will now hit a nil-pointer dereference on `s.broadcaster` (or other uninitialized fields) in `Watch`, rather than the previous lazy fallback. The PR description itself raises this exact risk ('Does anything else depend on initializing US lazily?') and it isn't verified or addressed in the diff.

title: Trace context propagation fix applied inconsistently - only one of several call sites updated
body: The PR fixes `GetResourceStats` (line 126) to reassign `ctx, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)` so the derived span context is propagated into the subsequent `b.db.WithTx(ctx, ...)` call, matching the PR's stated goal of 'fixing trace propagation by passing span contexts down'. However, the same pattern (`_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)` discarding the new ctx) remains unfixed in other methods in this same file, e.g. `WriteEvent` (line 158), `ReadResource` (line 353), and `ListIterator` (line 388). In each of these, child operations (`dbutil.Exec`, `dbutil.QueryRow`, `dbutil.QueryRows`, nested `WithTx` calls) continue to use the original, non-span context, so trace propagation remains broken for most of the SQL backend despite the PR claiming to address it. This is misleading for anyone reviewing the trace-fix claim and leaves most of the intended fix undone.

title: Postgres integration test silently skipped with no tracking issue
body: The test now unconditionally skips when `GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres` with the comment 'skipping - test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally.' This removes postgres coverage for `TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer` from CI without a linked tracking issue or explanation of what is failing, making it easy for this gap to be forgotten and for a real postgres-specific regression to go undetected going forward.

title: No test added for the new fine-grained locking behavior in BuildIndex
body: The change to `BuildIndex` narrows the locked section from the whole function to just the final cache-map write, explicitly to improve concurrency when building indexes for many namespaces at once. This is a concurrency-sensitive change (see related finding about same-key concurrent builds), yet no test was added to exercise concurrent `BuildIndex`/`GetOrCreateIndex` calls (e.g. with `-race`) to confirm the new locking scheme is safe for repeated/parallel calls for the same key, or that cross-key builds genuinely run in parallel as intended.

title: TotalDocs() reads the index cache map without holding cacheMu, racing with concurrent writes
body: bleveBackend.TotalDocs() iterates over b.cache without acquiring cacheMu (neither RLock nor Lock), while BuildIndex() now writes to the same map under a lock that only protects the final cache assignment (b.cache[key] = idx). This PR adds a new call site for TotalDocs() in resource/search.go's searchSupport.init(), invoked immediately after the background watch-event goroutine is started (which can trigger new BuildIndex calls via getOrCreateIndex). This creates a genuine unsynchronized concurrent map read/write, which in Go can panic at runtime ("fatal error: concurrent map read and map write") or produce corrupted/garbage results. TotalDocs should take cacheMu.RLock()/RUnlock() like GetIndex does.

title: Shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` variables are written concurrently by multiple goroutines in searchSupport.init
body: In searchSupport.init(), the errgroup with SetLimit(s.initWorkers) launches one goroutine per namespace that does `totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(...)` followed by `return err`, where both `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` are variables shared across all goroutines without any synchronization (mutex/atomic). Previously this race was largely masked because bleve.BuildIndex held a single mutex across its entire body, effectively serializing the actual work done inside s.build() for different namespaces. This PR's locking change in bleve.go (lock now only guards the final cache write) removes that serialization, so multiple goroutines can now genuinely run s.build() concurrently, widening the race window. The consequence is real: one goroutine's error can be overwritten by another's success (or vice versa) before its own `return err` executes, so group.Wait() may incorrectly report success even though a particular namespace failed to build its index (or report a failure for a namespace that actually succeeded), and totalBatchesIndexed can lose increments. Given this path now runs synchronously at every server startup and failures are supposed to block startup, silently losing an error here is a data-integrity risk (a namespace could end up with a stale/missing index with no error surfaced).

title: NewResourceServer now blocks indefinitely on search index build with no timeout or cancellation path
body: NewResourceServer calls s.Init(ctx) synchronously before returning, and Init in turn calls searchSupport.init which builds the full search index for every namespace returned by GetResourceStats. The context used is derived from context.Background() with no deadline, so there is no bound on how long server construction can take for large installations with many/large namespaces. Previously this cost was paid lazily on the first gRPC call (which had its own problems per the PR description), but now any process that constructs a ResourceServer (app startup, tests, other callers) will block for however long index building takes, with no way to time out, report partial progress, or fail fast. This can turn into very long or hanging startups in production without any visible health/readiness signal during that window.

title: Init() is now a no-op if called again after construction, which may silently break other callers relying on it
body: Init() still uses sync.Once and is now invoked internally during NewResourceServer. Any other code path in the codebase that calls ResourceServer.Init(ctx) later (e.g. as part of a module/service lifecycle contract, with a different context carrying its own cancellation/tracing) will be a silent no-op because the Once has already fired during construction with an internally-created background context. The PR description itself raises this exact concern ("Does anything else depend on initializing US lazily? What could this break?") but the diff does not show any audit or update of such callers. If any lifecycle manager expects Init(ctx) to perform the actual initialization work tied to its own context, that expectation is now silently violated.

title: Trace-context propagation fix is incomplete — several spans still discard the updated context
body: The PR fixes span-context propagation in resource/search.go and in sql/backend.go's GetResourceStats (ctx, span := ...), but other methods in the same file still discard the span-carrying context with `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)` and then pass the original (un-updated) ctx to nested calls, e.g. WriteEvent (line 158, passing ctx to b.create/b.update/b.delete), ReadResource (line 353), and ListIterator (line 388, passing ctx to listAtRevision/listLatest). As a result, spans created inside create/update/delete, dbutil.QueryRow calls in ReadResource, and listAtRevision/listLatest will not be properly parented under the WriteEvent/Read/List spans, leaving the exact trace-propagation bug the PR claims to fix still present in several high-traffic code paths.

title: Postgres integration test skipped rather than fixed, potentially masking a startup regression from the new synchronous Init
body: This test exercises ResourceServer/module startup (waiting only 500ms for the HTTP server to become available) and is now skipped for postgres with the comment "test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally." Given this PR moves ResourceServer initialization (including search index building) to be synchronous at construction time, it is plausible that the added latency is exactly what causes this test to fail intermittently under Drone's resource constraints for postgres. Skipping the test instead of investigating removes coverage for the very scenario (server startup timing) that this PR changes, and may hide a real regression rather than fixing it.

title: NewResourceServer now blocks synchronously on full index build
body: NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) before returning, and Init() runs the full search index build for every namespace (searchSupport.init). Previously NewResourceServer returned immediately and Init() was deferred to the first gRPC call. Index building can take a long time (this is exactly the problem the PR is trying to avoid inside gRPC request contexts), so now the constructor itself can block for an arbitrarily long time, and will fail outright (returning nil, err) if anything in Init fails. Any caller of NewResourceServer that expects a cheap/fast constructor (process startup with readiness/liveness timeouts, module startup sequencing, tests) can now time out or fail to start. The PR description itself asks 'what could this break?' which indicates this tradeoff was not fully evaluated; no caller-side timeout/async handling was added to accommodate the new blocking behavior.

title: BuildIndex no longer serializes concurrent builds for the same key
body: The previous implementation locked cacheMu for the entire BuildIndex call, which (while slow) also serialized concurrent build attempts for the same NamespacedResource key. Now the lock only protects the final `b.cache[key] = idx` write. getOrCreateIndex() in search.go has no locking either (it just checks GetIndex() for nil and calls build() if so), so two concurrent calls for the same cold key (e.g. two simultaneous Search requests, or a Search racing with a watch event) can both perform a full BuildIndex, each creating its own bleve.Index (including on-disk files for file-backed indexes), and whichever finishes last silently overwrites b.cache[key]; the loser's index/resources are never closed or cleaned up, leaking file handles/disk usage and duplicating work.

title: TotalDocs() reads cache map without holding cacheMu, racing with BuildIndex writes
body: TotalDocs() iterates over b.cache with `for _, v := range b.cache` without acquiring cacheMu (neither RLock nor Lock), while BuildIndex now writes to the same map under cacheMu.Lock() after doing the (now unlocked) expensive build work concurrently. Since BuildIndex calls can run concurrently for different keys (that is the whole point of this PR's locking change) and TotalDocs can be invoked at the same time (e.g. the search.go init() logging call right after group.Wait(), or any external caller/metrics path), this is an unsynchronized concurrent map read/write. Go maps are not safe for concurrent read/write; this can produce a 'fatal error: concurrent map read and map write' crash, not just a benign race. GetIndex already correctly uses RLock for cache reads; TotalDocs should do the same.

title: Parallel index build goroutines race on shared err and counter variables
