body: The loop that follows redirect pointers (`for i = 0, 1000 do ... end`) was previously bounded at 10000 with a comment explaining that 'segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly.' The bound was cut to 1000 and the comment was deleted entirely. This makes it 10x more likely that deep redirect/segment trees fail to be joined correctly, and removes the only documentation warning future maintainers about this trade-off, with no corresponding test for deep trees near/above the new limit.

title: max_segment_spans constructor parameter is now dead code; segment size cap is a hardcoded magic number in Lua, decoupled from configuration
body: `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans: int = 1001`, but the Python-side enforcement of this limit in `_load_segment_data` was removed entirely in this PR. The new eviction cap is hardcoded as the literal `1000` inside `add-buffer.lua` (`if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', ...)`), completely independent of `self.max_segment_spans`. Callers who construct `SpansBuffer` with a custom `max_segment_spans` value will silently get no effect from that setting, which is a misleading public API and an operational trap for anyone trying to tune this value.

title: Unconditional dict indexing on end_timestamp_precise can crash the consumer on payloads missing the field
body: `process_batch` now does `end_timestamp_precise=val['end_timestamp_precise']` via direct key access with no fallback, where `val` is the raw span payload deserialized from Kafka. If any ingested message lacks this field (e.g. during a rollout where Relay has not yet started populating it everywhere, replay of older backlog messages, or a malformed/older-schema payload), this raises `KeyError` and will crash/raise inside the batch-processing task, taking down the whole consumer batch rather than degrading gracefully. Given this is a critical ingestion pipeline, a schema-evolution-safe default (e.g. `.get('end_timestamp_precise', ...)`) or explicit validation should be used instead of hard failure.

title: No test coverage for the new eviction behavior, including the risk of evicting the root span's payload
body: The new eviction logic (`if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', set_key, span_count - 1000) end`) removes the lowest-scored (earliest `end_timestamp_precise`) spans once a segment exceeds 1000 members. Since the root/segment span can legitimately have an earlier end timestamp than some of its children, it can be evicted by this logic while the separate `has_root_span` flag key still persists, causing `flush_segments` to report a segment as having a root span even though the root span's actual payload was dropped. No test in `tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py` exercises a segment exceeding 1000 spans or validates eviction/root-span-retention behavior, so this edge case is unverified.

title: Unconditional access to organization_context.member attribute can crash the endpoint
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated on every GET request to this endpoint, regardless of the `optimized_pagination` query parameter. If the requesting user is not a superuser, `organization_context.member` is accessed; for callers where `member` is `None` (e.g. a non-member caller permitted through some other path) this raises an `AttributeError`. Additionally, `has_global_access` does not appear to be an existing attribute on the organization member RPC model used elsewhere in the codebase, which would make this crash on every non-superuser request to the audit log endpoint, not just when the new optimized-pagination feature is requested. This turns what should be an opt-in feature into a potential 500 error for normal customer use of the audit log API.

title: Unrelated, untested, privilege-gated pagination feature bundled into audit log endpoint
body: This endpoint now branches into a brand-new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` code path based on a client-supplied `optimized_pagination` query parameter, gated only by `is_superuser`/`has_global_access`. This change is unrelated to the PR's stated purpose (spans buffer eviction), has no new tests covering the branch, and (per the related finding in paginator.py) the underlying negative-offset logic it enables is broken and will raise an exception at runtime. Shipping an untested, privilege-gated alternate code path with vague comments like "this is safe" inside an unrelated PR is risky and should be reviewed/tested on its own, or removed if unintentional.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch will raise an exception, not optimize anything
body: When `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset` (and potentially negative `stop`). Django QuerySets explicitly disallow negative slice indices and raise an exception (`AssertionError`/`ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported`) in `QuerySet.__getitem__`. This means the newly-added "advanced" negative-offset pagination path is non-functional and will crash any request that reaches it (e.g. a superuser manually crafting a cursor string with a negative offset), rather than providing the described performance optimization.

title: Shared BasePaginator.get_result silently changed offset-clamping behavior for all paginated endpoints
body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` modifies `BasePaginator.get_result`, which is the base class used by `Paginator`, `DateTimePaginator`, and other widely-used paginators across the whole codebase, not just the spans-buffer feature this PR is about. Previously, a negative cursor offset (e.g. from a tampered/corrupted cursor string) would fail loudly via Django's queryset slicing restriction; now it is silently clamped to 0 for forward cursors, changing pagination semantics without any accompanying tests or documentation of the new contract, and leaving the `is_prev` branch still able to pass a negative offset straight into queryset slicing (same crash risk as before, just for a different code path).

title: Misleading comment claims negative-offset support with no corresponding behavior change
body: The added comment states "Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios... This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions" directly above `self.offset = int(offset)`, which is unchanged code. No validation or new behavior was actually added here; the comment implies a capability that doesn't exist in this file and is misleading to future readers trying to understand where negative-offset support is implemented or guarded.

title: Redirect-depth loop limit reduced 10x with explanatory comment removed
body: The loop bound for walking the redirect chain was reduced from `0, 10000` to `0, 1000`, and the comment explaining the known correctness limitation ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted entirely rather than updated. This makes it 10x more likely in practice for deeply-nested span trees to hit the redirect-depth cutoff and be incorrectly merged/split, and removes the only documentation warning maintainers about this risk, with no explanation given for why the limit was lowered.

title: zpopmin eviction can remove the segment's root span, corrupting flushed output
body: When a segment's span count exceeds 1000, `redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)` evicts the lowest-scored (oldest `end_timestamp_precise`) entries with no protection for the span that is the segment's root (`is_segment_span`). If the root span's end timestamp happens to be lower than one or more of its children's (e.g. due to clock skew or async child spans finishing later), the root span's payload can be evicted from the sorted set while the separate `has_root_span` boolean flag remains true. Later, `flush_segments` in buffer.py determines `is_segment` by comparing `segment_span_id == val["span_id"]` only over the spans actually present in the set; if the root span was evicted, no span in the flushed output will have `is_segment: true`, even though the segment was flushed via the root-span timeout path. This silently produces segments lacking a root span marker, which downstream consumers expecting exactly one root span per segment may not handle correctly.

title: max_segment_spans parameter is now dead/disconnected from the actual eviction threshold
body: `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans: int = 1001`, but nothing in the class uses this value anymore (the only prior usage, in `_load_segment_data`, was removed). The actual span-count cap enforced during insertion is now hardcoded as `1000` inside `add-buffer.lua` and is not derived from or passed through this configuration value. This leaves a misleading, non-functional configuration knob: changing `max_segment_spans` has no effect on behavior, and the real cap (1000) is off-by-one from the stated default (1001) and only discoverable by reading the Lua script.

title: Removed oversized-segment safety check and metric with no replacement observability
body: The previous check in `_load_segment_data` that dropped and logged (via `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded")` and `logger.error`) segments whose span count exceeded `max_segment_spans` was removed without any replacement. The new insertion-time eviction in `add-buffer.lua` silently trims excess spans via `zpopmin` and does not report whether/how many spans were evicted (the script's return tuple `{redirect_depth, span_key, set_key, has_root_span}` carries no eviction count), so there is no metric or log anywhere indicating that spans are being dropped from an oversized segment. This is a loss of operational visibility into data loss that previously existed.

title: No test exercises the new insert-time span eviction behavior
body: The PR's stated purpose is to add eviction during insert for the spans buffer (capping segments at 1000 spans via `zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua), but the only changes to this test file are adding the new required `end_timestamp_precise` field to existing `Span(...)` constructions. No test inserts more than 1000 spans into a single segment to verify that old spans are correctly evicted, that the segment is capped at the expected size, or that the root span survives eviction. The core new behavior introduced by this PR is therefore untested.

title: No tests added for new OptimizedCursorPaginator class
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` is a substantial new class (~90 lines) with a non-trivial negative-offset code path, but no test file changes accompany it in this PR. Given that the negative-offset branch appears to be broken (see related finding on queryset negative slicing), the absence of any unit test means this bug would not be caught before merging or in CI.

title: Negative-offset "advanced pagination" branch is fundamentally broken with Django querysets
body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is True and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `start_offset = cursor.offset` and then `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly disallows negative slice indices and raises an exception (`Negative indexing is not supported.`) rather than handling it the way list slicing would. The comment claiming "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is incorrect. As soon as this code path is reached (any authorized user supplies a cursor string with a negative offset while `enable_advanced_features=True`), the request will raise an unhandled exception and return a 500 instead of paginated results, making the entire 'advanced pagination' feature non-functional and a self-inflicted DoS vector for whoever can trigger it.

title: Overly broad authorization gate for a pagination path that crashes
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` allows any organization member with "global access" (not just superusers/admins) to opt into `OptimizedCursorPaginator` via the `optimized_pagination=true` query param. The in-code comments describe this as being for "authorized administrators" only, but `has_global_access` is a much weaker bar than superuser. Combined with the broken negative-offset handling in `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (see paginator.py finding), this means a relatively large set of non-admin users can trigger unhandled 500s on this endpoint just by crafting a cursor string, and the intended admin-only restriction is not actually enforced as described.

title: Negative-offset clamp only applied for forward pagination, not for prev-cursors
body: In `BasePaginator.get_result`, the new code clamps `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. This only guards the forward-pagination case; when `cursor.is_prev` is True, the raw (potentially negative, since `Cursor.offset` is parsed directly from user-supplied cursor strings via `int(bits[1])`) offset is passed straight into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, which will raise an exception on Django querysets. The fix is incomplete/inconsistent: it protects one pagination direction but leaves the other exposed to the same crash.

title: zunionstore uses default SUM aggregate, corrupting timestamp scores on overlapping members
body: After switching the span buffer from Redis sets (`sadd`/`sunionstore`) to sorted sets (`zadd`/`zunionstore`) keyed by `end_timestamp_precise`, the `zunionstore` calls at lines 47 and 53 do not specify `AGGREGATE MIN`, so Redis defaults to `AGGREGATE SUM`. If the same member (identical span payload) exists in both sets being merged — e.g. in the edge case where `parent_span_id == span_id` causes `span_key` to equal `set_key`, or if a span payload is present under more than one bucket due to redirect processing/retries — its score (meant to represent an end timestamp used for both flush-timeout tracking and the new `zpopmin` eviction) gets summed with itself, producing a corrupted, non-timestamp value. This can cause spans to be evicted/retained in the wrong order or to never expire as intended, silently defeating the new eviction logic this PR introduces.

title: Redirect-depth safety limit cut 10x without justification or test coverage
body: The loop bound for resolving the redirect chain was reduced from `0, 10000` to `0, 1000`, and the previous explanatory comment ("theoretically this limit means segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was removed entirely rather than updated. This silently lowers the maximum depth of a redirect/parent chain that can be correctly resolved before the script gives up, risking incorrect segment joining for deeply-nested span trees that previously worked. No test exercises this changed limit, and the change is unrelated to and undocumented in the PR description, which only discusses buffer eviction.

title: max_segment_spans parameter is now dead code, and its prior observability was removed without replacement
body: `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans` (default 1001), but after this change nothing in `buffer.py` reads `self.max_segment_spans` anymore. Previously, `_load_segment_data` used this value to detect and skip (with `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded")` and an error log) segments whose span count exceeded the limit. That enforcement and its metric were removed in favor of the Lua script's hard-coded eviction at `span_count > 1000`, but no equivalent metric/log was added for the new eviction path, and the now-unused constructor parameter is misleading to callers/tests who may still pass it expecting enforcement.

title: Eviction cap hardcoded to 1000, decoupled from the Python-configurable (and now-unused) max_segment_spans=1001
body: The eviction threshold `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000) end` is a magic number baked into the Lua script, no longer driven by the `max_segment_spans` setting on `SpansBuffer` (which is unused after this change, see buffer.py finding). The two numbers (1000 here vs. 1001 previously configured in Python) are also off-by-one from each other, making it easy for future maintainers to believe changing `max_segment_spans` has any effect, when it no longer does.

title: New hard-required field `end_timestamp_precise` with no fallback risks consumer crash on rollout/old messages
body: `process_batch` now does `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` using direct dict indexing (unlike the optional `val.get("parent_span_id")` pattern used elsewhere). If any in-flight or backlog Kafka message lacks this field (e.g. during a mixed-version rollout where Relay/producers haven't yet guaranteed this field, or on topic replay of older messages), this raises a `KeyError` that is not handled anywhere in this path, which will fail the whole batch and likely crash/stall the consumer. This is a behavior change from the previous code which did not require this key at all.

title: No test coverage for the new >1000-span eviction behavior added by this PR
body: The PR's stated purpose is "Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert," implemented via `zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua when a segment's sorted set exceeds 1000 members. None of the changes in this test file add a case that inserts more than 1000 spans into a single segment to verify that the oldest entries are correctly evicted, that the retained spans are the newest ones, or that `flush_segments` behaves correctly afterward. The only changes here are adding the new required `end_timestamp_precise` field to existing unrelated test spans, so the core new behavior of this PR is entirely untested.

title: New OptimizedCursorPaginator and the audit log endpoint's optimized_pagination flag have no tests
body: This PR adds a new paginator class (`OptimizedCursorPaginator`) with a security-relevant negative-offset code path, and wires it into `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` behind a new query parameter and an authorization check. No tests were added for either the paginator class or the new endpoint branch (e.g. verifying authorized vs. unauthorized access, or correct/incorrect handling of negative offsets). Given the broken negative-offset handling identified separately, tests would have caught this before merge.

title: Misleading comment implies a functional change that doesn't exist in this file
body: The added comment states "Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios... This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets," but the code on the next line (`self.offset = int(offset)`) is unchanged from before — `int()` already accepted negative numbers. No validation or enablement logic was added here. The comment is misleading: it suggests this file deliberately sanctions negative offsets as a safe, supported feature, while the actual consumers of `Cursor.offset` (in paginator.py) do not safely support negative values and will raise exceptions when given one. This can mislead future maintainers into believing negative offsets are a vetted, working feature.

title: Unrelated, security-sensitive pagination feature bundled into a PR described as a spans-buffer optimization
body: This PR's title/description describe an optimization to the spans Redis buffer (add-buffer.lua, buffer.py), but it also introduces and wires up an entirely new, broken pagination mechanism (`OptimizedCursorPaginator`, negative-offset cursor handling, and a new `optimized_pagination` endpoint flag in the audit log API) that is unrelated to spans buffering. This combination of an unrelated, under-tested, and crash-prone authorization-adjacent feature with a narrowly-described infra change is the kind of change that should be split into its own PR with explicit review of its authorization model and failure modes; as bundled, it is easy for reviewers focused on the stated spans-buffer change to miss the new attack surface in the pagination code.

title: Accidental git submodule added, pointing back at the PR's own base commit
body: This PR adds a new file `sentry-repo` with mode/content indicating a git submodule pinned to commit `a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a`, which is exactly the base commit of this same PR. This looks like an accidental artifact (e.g. from a bad `git submodule add` or tooling mistake) rather than an intentional change, has no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry shown, and is unrelated to the stated feature. Merging it risks broken clones/checkouts, confusing repo tooling, and bloats the diff with no functional purpose. It should be removed before merge.

title: Upsampling eligibility check uses the outer closure `dataset` instead of the function's own `scoped_dataset` parameter
body: Inside `_get_event_stats(scoped_dataset, ...)`, the call `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` passes `dataset` — the module-level variable computed once in `get()` — instead of the function parameter `scoped_dataset`, which represents the actual dataset being queried for this specific call. In the dashboard-widget-split code path, `_get_event_stats` is invoked multiple times with different `scoped_dataset` values (e.g. `discover` for `errors_only_query`/`transactions_only_query`, or the original `scoped_dataset` for the main query) while the outer `dataset` stays fixed. As a result, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` evaluates against the wrong dataset module for these sub-calls, causing upsampling to be incorrectly enabled or disabled depending on which dataset was resolved at the top of `get()`, producing inconsistent/incorrect counts for dashboard widgets using the discover-split logic.

title: `_is_error_focused_query` inspects the raw request query string, not the effective query used for the specific sub-call
body: `_is_error_focused_query` (used by `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` for the discover dataset) always reads `request.GET.get("query", "")`, i.e. the original top-level request query. However, `_get_event_stats` is called with different, dynamically-constructed `query` strings in the dashboard-widget split flow (e.g. `errors_only_query = f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction"`, `transactions_only_query`). The eligibility check never looks at these per-call query strings, so it can make the wrong upsampling decision (e.g. deciding not to upsample an errors-only sub-query because the raw request query didn't literally contain `event.type:error`, or vice versa).

title: New `upsampled_count()` SnQL function is not marked `private`, bypassing the allowlist gating entirely
body: The newly added `upsampled_count` `SnQLFunction` omits `private=True`, unlike the function immediately preceding it in the same list which does set `private=True`. Because it is registered in `function_converter`'s public function map without the private flag, any caller can directly request `upsampled_count()` via the public events/events-stats API (e.g. as `yAxis=upsampled_count()` or in `field`), for any project — not just those in `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`. This completely bypasses the allowlist/eligibility checks implemented in `error_upsampling.py`, which were supposed to be the only gate controlling access to `sum(sample_weight)`-based counts.

title: Cache key derived from Python's built-in `hash()` risks collisions across unrelated project sets
body: `cache_key = f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))}"` uses the built-in `hash()` to fold the sorted project id tuple into the cache key. Distinct sets of project ids can map to the same hash value (hash collisions), which would cause the eligibility decision computed for one set of projects to be served from cache for a different, unrelated set of projects sharing the same organization id, within the 60s TTL. A deterministic, collision-resistant encoding (e.g. a delimited string of sorted ids) should be used instead of relying on `hash()`, which is also not part of any stable contract for this purpose.

title: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is unused dead code — no mechanism actually invalidates the 60s eligibility cache
body: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined to clear the cached allowlist-eligibility decision "when the allowlist configuration changes," but nothing in this diff calls it (no options-change hook, signal, or admin action wiring it up). Combined with the 60-second cache TTL in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, this means allowlist changes can silently take up to 60 seconds to propagate with no active invalidation path, and the presence of this function creates a false impression that cache consistency is actively managed.

title: Bare `except Exception: pass` silently swallows all errors when deriving `sample_rate` from event contexts
body: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` wraps both the dict traversal (`normalized_data.get("contexts", {}).get("error_sampling", {}).get("client_sample_rate")`) and the `float()` conversion in bare `except Exception: pass` blocks. If `contexts` is explicitly `None` (a valid value some code paths may set), `.get(...)` on `None` raises `AttributeError`, which is silently discarded. This means malformed or unexpected test fixture data will silently fail to populate `sample_rate` with no error or warning, making it hard to diagnose test failures or regressions that rely on this helper (used directly by `store_event`, a widely used test utility).

title: No tests exercise the caching behavior of `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`
body: The PR title advertises "performance optimizations" via caching, implemented in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` (cache hit/miss paths, 60s TTL) and `invalidate_upsampling_cache`. None of these are covered: the unit tests only exercise `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`, `_is_error_focused_query`, and `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` directly, bypassing the caching wrapper entirely. There is no test verifying that a cached `True`/`False` eligibility value is actually reused on a subsequent call, that it expires correctly, or that `invalidate_upsampling_cache` has any effect.

title: `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only matches the exact literal `count()`, missing aliased or spaced variants
body: The transform does `if column_lower == "count()":` after lowercasing and stripping, so it only matches an exact `count()` token. Common query shapes like `count() as my_count`, `count(id)`, or any alias form will not be transformed, silently falling back to the regular (non-upsampled) count for those columns while other `count()` columns in the same request get upsampled. This produces inconsistent upsampling behavior across a single request/query without any error or indication to the caller.

title: Upsampling eligibility check uses the wrong dataset variable
body: Inside `_get_event_stats`, the function parameter is named `scoped_dataset` (the dataset actually being queried for this specific call), but the eligibility check calls `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` using the outer closed-over `dataset` variable from `get()` instead of the local `scoped_dataset` parameter. In the simple path these happen to be equal, but `get_event_stats_factory`'s `fn` calls `_get_event_stats` with different dataset values (e.g. `discover` for the errors-only/transactions-only split queries, or `split_dataset`) when handling dashboard-widget discover splitting. In those calls, the upsampling decision is computed against the wrong dataset, so the `count()`→`upsampled_count()` transform can be incorrectly applied or skipped for the dataset that is actually executed, producing inconsistent/incorrect counts for dashboard widgets using the discover-split code path.

title: invalidate_upsampling_cache is never called anywhere
body: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is introduced with a docstring stating it 'should be called when the allowlist configuration changes to ensure cache consistency', but nothing in this PR (or apparently the rest of the codebase) calls it. As written, it is dead code, and the 60-second eligibility cache set in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` has no actual invalidation path wired to allowlist option changes. This either means the function is unused dead code that should be removed, or an integration point (e.g. an options-changed signal handler) is missing, leaving stale upsampling decisions for up to 60 seconds with no way to force a refresh.

title: Cache key built from hash() of project id tuple risks collisions
body: The cache key `f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))}"` relies on Python's built-in `hash()` of an integer tuple to disambiguate different project-id sets within the same organization. Hash collisions between distinct tuples are possible (hash() truncates to a fixed-width integer), which could cause one set of projects to incorrectly reuse another set's cached eligibility result for up to 60 seconds, silently enabling or disabling upsampling for the wrong query. A deterministic string key built from the sorted ids directly (e.g. joined by commas) would avoid this risk entirely and is no more expensive.

title: New upsampled_count() function is public, bypassing allowlist gating
body: The new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is registered without `private=True`, unlike other internal-only aggregate functions in the same converter. This means any user can directly type `upsampled_count()` in a Discover/Events query, bypassing the allowlist check in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`/`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` entirely. Depending on how `sample_weight` is populated for non-allowlisted projects (NULL vs default value), this could either return misleading data or raise a SQL error (e.g. converting NULL to a non-nullable Int64), since the function assumes sample_weight is always present 'per our data model requirements' — an assumption the public API doesn't enforce.

title: Stray gitlink/submodule artifact added to the repository
body: A new top-level entry `sentry-repo` is added that is a gitlink pointing to commit `a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a` (the PR's own base commit), with no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry shown in the diff. This looks like an accidental artifact from a bad rebase/squash or local tooling leftover rather than an intentional change. Committing a dangling gitlink with no submodule registration can confuse `git status`/`git submodule` tooling and CI checkout steps, and should be removed before merge.

title: No tests for the public cached entry point or cache invalidation
body: The test file only exercises the private helpers `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, and `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`. The PR's headline feature — the 60-second caching behavior in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` (cache hit/miss paths, correct bool-vs-None handling) — and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` are never directly unit tested. Given the PR title explicitly calls out 'performance optimizations' via caching, the caching logic itself (the riskiest new behavior) has no dedicated test coverage.

title: Misleading/contradictory docstring about cache freshness
body: The docstring of `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` states the function 'reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time... This is intentional to ensure we always have the latest configuration state.' In reality, its caller `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` wraps this function's result in a 60-second cache, so the configuration is not read fresh on every call — only on cache misses. This contradicts the stated intent and could mislead future maintainers into believing allowlist changes take effect immediately, when in fact they can be delayed up to 60 seconds.

title: Test helper overloads generic 'sample_rate' field and silently swallows all errors
body: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` writes into the generic top-level `normalized_data["sample_rate"]` key whenever `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` is present, for any event type processed by `store_event` (not just errors). This repurposes a field name that is also used elsewhere in Sentry for transaction/dynamic sampling semantics, risking ambiguity if both mechanisms ever intersect on the same event. Additionally, both exception-handling blocks use bare `except Exception: pass`, silently discarding malformed `client_sample_rate` values or unexpected `contexts` shapes, which can mask bugs in tests relying on this helper instead of surfacing a clear failure.

title: Transform only matches exact 'count()' string, silently ignoring aliased forms
body: `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only rewrites a column when its lowercased/stripped value equals exactly `"count()"`. Any other valid representation of the same aggregate — e.g. `"count() as total"`, or `count()` embedded in an equation — is left untouched with no warning or fallback, so the request silently uses the raw (non-upsampled) count. There is no test covering this partial-match limitation, and callers have no way to know the transform was skipped for their specific column form.

title: New `upsampled_count()` aggregate is not marked private, bypassing the allowlist gate
body: The new SnQLFunction `upsampled_count` (computing `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`) is registered in the public function converter without `private=True`, unlike the function defined immediately above it which does set `private=True`. Because this function is publicly resolvable, any user/org can request it directly (e.g. `yAxis=upsampled_count()` or in `field`), completely bypassing the `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` gate implemented in `error_upsampling.py`. For non-allowlisted projects where `sample_weight` is not meaningfully populated, this returns incorrect/misleading aggregate values, and more importantly it exposes an internal column (`sample_weight`) and computation path outside the intended governance of the feature flag/allowlist mechanism.

title: Upsampling eligibility check uses outer `dataset` instead of the `scoped_dataset` parameter actually being queried
body: Inside `_get_event_stats(scoped_dataset, query_columns, query, snuba_params, ...)`, the call `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` references the enclosing `dataset` variable computed once in `get()`, not the `scoped_dataset` parameter that is actually used to execute the query (`scoped_dataset.run_top_events_timeseries_query`, `scoped_dataset.top_events_timeseries`, `scoped_dataset.timeseries_query`). In the dashboard-widget discover-split logic (`get_event_stats_factory`), `_get_event_stats` is invoked with varying first arguments (`discover`, `split_dataset`, `scoped_dataset`) that can differ from the outer `dataset`. As a result, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` can make its decision based on the wrong dataset (e.g. outer dataset is `metrics_enhanced_performance` while the actual sub-query runs against `discover` with an error-focused query), causing upsampling to be incorrectly skipped or applied for that sub-query.

title: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined but never called anywhere
body: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is documented as something that "should be called when the allowlist configuration changes to ensure cache consistency", but no code in this PR (or evidently elsewhere) calls it when the `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` option changes. This leaves the 60-second TTL as the only consistency mechanism, so removing a project from the allowlist (e.g. to fix an incident or stop a misconfiguration) will continue to serve stale, upsampled/scaled counts for up to 60 seconds with no way to force immediate invalidation, despite the function's docstring implying such a mechanism exists.

title: Cache key derived from Python's built-in `hash()` on project id tuples risks collisions across different project sets
body: `cache_key` is built as `f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))}"`. Using the generic `hash()` of a tuple (rather than a stable, collision-free encoding like a joined string of ids) means two different project-id sets within the same organization could theoretically hash-collide, causing the eligibility result computed for one project combination to be served for a different, unrelated combination for up to 60 seconds — i.e. a non-allowlisted project set could incorrectly inherit `True` (or vice versa), producing incorrect (scaled or unscaled) error counts for users.

title: No fallback/null handling for `sample_weight`, risking silent undercount for pre-upsampling or non-sampled events
body: `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` rewrites `count()` to `upsampled_count() as count` (i.e. `sum(sample_weight)`) for any allowlisted project, with the comment "no additional null checks are needed here" because sample_weight is assumed to exist for all events. If historical events ingested before this feature (or events not going through the client-sampling code path) have `sample_weight` as NULL or unset, `sum()` over those rows effectively treats them as 0 rather than 1, silently undercounting legitimate error events the moment a project is added to the allowlist, with no defensive `coalesce`/default applied in the SnQL (`sum(Column("sample_weight"))` in discover.py).

title: Docstrings contradict each other regarding cache freshness
body: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` documents caching the allowlist eligibility result for 60 seconds ("Cache allowlist eligibility for 60 seconds ... eventual consistency is acceptable"), while the helper it calls on a cache miss, `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, states "This function reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time... This is intentional to ensure we always have the latest configuration state." In practice, due to the 60-second cache wrapping it, the configuration is NOT read fresh on every call, contradicting the inner function's documented intent and potentially misleading future maintainers about the actual consistency guarantees.

title: Unrelated/accidental file (looks like a git submodule reference) added to the PR
body: The PR adds a file named `sentry-repo` whose only content is `Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a`, which is characteristic of an accidentally committed git submodule/embedded repository reference rather than an intentional source change. This is unrelated to the stated feature, is not referenced by any other changed file, and risks causing checkout/tooling issues (e.g. "adding embedded git repository" warnings, or broken clones if the referenced commit isn't fetchable as a submodule) for anyone who clones or rebases on top of this commit. It should be removed before merge.

title: No tests for the public caching entry point or cache invalidation
body: The test suite only exercises private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`) but never calls `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` itself — the function that actually implements the caching behavior described as the PR's core "performance optimization". There is no test validating cache-hit vs cache-miss paths, TTL behavior, or that `invalidate_upsampling_cache` actually clears the correct key. Given the caching logic introduces real correctness risk (stale allowlist decisions, hash-based key collisions), this is the part of the change most in need of direct test coverage, and it currently has none.

title: Broad silent exception swallowing in new test helper
body: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` wraps both the dict traversal (`normalized_data.get("contexts", {}).get("error_sampling", {}).get("client_sample_rate")`) and the float conversion in bare `except Exception: pass` blocks. Any malformed or unexpected shape of `contexts`/`error_sampling` (e.g. `contexts` explicitly set to `None`) will silently skip setting `sample_rate` with no logging or error surfaced, making it harder to diagnose why upsampling-related fixtures in tests produce unexpected counts if the test data doesn't match the expected shape exactly.

title: TableWidgetVisualization is rendered with hardcoded empty data instead of the actual query results
body: In `tableResultComponent`, when the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature flag is enabled, the new `<TableWidgetVisualization>` is rendered with `columns={[]}` and `tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}}` — these are hardcoded literals, not derived from `result`/`tableResults` (the actual query results used by the `StyledSimpleTableChart` branch). As a result, any dashboard/table widget rendered with this flag enabled will always show an empty table regardless of the underlying data, while the legacy branch (flag disabled) continues to show real data. This looks like an unfinished wiring of the new table visualization component into the widget card. There is also no test exercising this new conditional branch in chart.tsx.

title: get_merged_pr_single_issue_template references the wrong class for _truncate_title
body: `get_merged_pr_single_issue_template` is a `@staticmethod` defined on `CommitContextIntegration`, and it calls `PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title(title)`. However `_truncate_title` is defined as a staticmethod on `CommitContextIntegration` itself, not on `PRCommentWorkflow`. `GitHubPRCommentWorkflow`/`GitlabPRCommentWorkflow` (subclasses of `PRCommentWorkflow`) call `self.get_merged_pr_single_issue_template(...)` in `get_comment_body`. Unless `PRCommentWorkflow` happens to inherit from `CommitContextIntegration` (which is not indicated by the sibling `OpenPRCommentWorkflow(ABC)` pattern that takes `integration: CommitContextIntegration` as a composed attribute rather than a base class), this call will raise `AttributeError: type object 'PRCommentWorkflow' has no attribute '_truncate_title'` at runtime, breaking the merged-PR suspect-issue comment feature for both GitHub and GitLab integrations.

title: fetch_error_details pairs error_ids with get_multi results purely by positional zip
body: `fetch_error_details` builds `node_ids` from `error_ids` and calls `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)`, then does `zip(error_ids, events.values())` to reconstruct each `ErrorEvent`. This assumes the dict returned by `get_multi` preserves the same ordering as the input `node_ids`/`error_ids` list. If the backend returns results in a different order (e.g. due to internal batching, concurrent fetches, or sorting), this will silently associate the wrong title/message/timestamp with an error id, corrupting the generated AI summary input. A keyed lookup (`events.get(node_id)`) would be safer than relying on dict insertion order matching input order.

title: Likely timestamp unit mismatch when interleaving error events with breadcrumb events
body: `gen_request_data` interleaves `error_events` (whose `timestamp` comes from the stored event's `data.get("timestamp", 0.0)`, which is Unix epoch seconds) with breadcrumb/recording events read from segment data, comparing `error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)`. Recording/rrweb events conventionally carry `timestamp` in milliseconds since epoch, not seconds. If that holds here, comparing a seconds-based error timestamp against millisecond-based event timestamps will produce badly out-of-order interleaving (errors will appear to occur either far before or far after all breadcrumbs). The accompanying test (`test_get_with_error`) constructs both the breadcrumb and error timestamps from the same `now.timestamp()` (seconds) value, which masks this potential unit mismatch rather than verifying correct behavior against realistic millisecond-based breadcrumb timestamps.

title: Environment filter silently dropped when fetching trace item attribute keys
body: `makeTraceItemAttributeKeysQueryOptions` builds the query options for the trace-items attributes endpoint but no longer includes `environment`, with a comment stating it's "left out intentionally as it's not supported". The previous implementation in `useTraceItemAttributeKeys` sent `environment: selection.environments` to the same endpoint. If the endpoint does use this parameter, consumers of the new shared hook (`useGetTraceItemAttributeKeys`/`useTraceItemAttributeKeys`) will now fetch attribute keys across all environments instead of the selected one, silently changing results for any caller that previously relied on environment scoping.

title: Undocumented default-behavior change for autofix automation tuning, unrelated to stated PR scope
body: `sentry:autofix_automation_tuning` default is changed from `"low"` to `"off"` (mirrored in `src/sentry/constants.py`'s `DEFAULT_AUTOFIX_AUTOMATION_TUNING_DEFAULT`). This silently changes behavior for every project that has not explicitly set this option, turning off automatic Seer autofix runs on new issues by default. The PR description ("Test 5") gives no rationale for this change, and it is unrelated to the stated "Replays Self-Serve Bulk Delete System" scope, making it hard for reviewers to assess whether this regression/intentional change is safe to ship alongside the rest of the PR.

title: Analytics event recorded before feature-flag and input validation checks
body: In `ProjectPreprodArtifactAssembleEndpoint.post`, `analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` is called unconditionally at the very top of the handler, before the `features.has("organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble", ...)` check and before the request body is validated. As a result, an analytics event is recorded for every POST to this endpoint even when the organization does not have the feature enabled (which returns a 404) or when the payload is malformed (which returns a 400). This pollutes the `preprod_artifact.api.assemble` analytics stream with events for requests that never actually assembled anything, making the metric unreliable for its intended purpose. The call should be moved after the feature check (and ideally after successful validation).

title: Static method on CommitContextIntegration references unrelated class PRCommentWorkflow
body: The new staticmethod `CommitContextIntegration.get_merged_pr_single_issue_template` calls `PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title(title)` instead of `CommitContextIntegration._truncate_title(title)` (or just calling the sibling staticmethod directly), even though `_truncate_title` is defined on `CommitContextIntegration` itself a few lines above. This only works if `PRCommentWorkflow` happens to inherit from `CommitContextIntegration`; if that class hierarchy changes, or if this method is ever reused from a context where `PRCommentWorkflow` is not in scope/does not inherit the helper, this will raise an AttributeError. Referencing a specific subclass by name from a base-class method is a fragile and confusing design that should instead reference the class that actually owns the method.

title: Exception object passed directly into logger extra, failure silently swallowed at info level
body: In `CommitContextIntegration.get_environment_info`, the except block logs `extra={"issue_id": issue.id, "error": e}` where `e` is the raw exception instance rather than `str(e)`. Passing non-serializable objects (like exceptions) into logging `extra` can break log processors/formatters that try to JSON-serialize log records (e.g. structured logging pipelines), and since this is logged at `logger.info` level with a broad `except Exception`, any real bug in `get_recommended_event()`/`get_environment()` (e.g., a programming error, not just "no environment") will be silently absorbed without being captured by Sentry or surfaced at a visible log level.

title: TableWidgetVisualization wired with hardcoded empty data instead of actual query results
body: In `WidgetCardChart.tableResultComponent`, when `organization.features.includes('use-table-widget-visualization')` is true, the new `<TableWidgetVisualization>` component is rendered with `columns={[]}` and `tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}}` — completely hardcoded empty values — instead of being derived from `result`/`fields`/`eventView` like the `StyledSimpleTableChart` branch it replaces. Any organization with this feature flag enabled will see a permanently blank table widget regardless of the actual query results, since none of the real `tableResults` data is passed through.

title: fetch_error_details misaligns error ids with event data when ids repeat or are missing
body: `fetch_error_details` builds `node_ids` from `error_ids` (which may contain duplicates, e.g. if the same error occurred multiple times in a replay) and fetches them via `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)`, then zips `error_ids` with `events.values()`. Because dict keys must be unique, duplicate node ids collapse into a single entry in the `events` dict, making `events.values()` shorter than `error_ids`. `zip()` silently truncates to the shorter sequence, so after the first duplicate (or any backend behavior that omits missing keys rather than returning them with `None`), every subsequent `(event_id, data)` pair is shifted and misattributed to the wrong `error_id`, producing incorrect titles/timestamps/messages in the generated AI summary log. A safer implementation would look up each entry explicitly via `events.get(node_id)` keyed by the corresponding node id rather than relying on positional correspondence between two independently constructed sequences.

title: No test coverage for duplicate or missing error ids in fetch_error_details/get_request_data
body: The new tests (test_get_with_error, test_get_with_error_context_disabled, test_get_request_data) only cover the straightforward case of a single, successfully-found error event. There is no test exercising `fetch_error_details` with duplicate `error_ids` or with an `error_id` that is absent from nodestore, which is exactly the scenario where the `zip(error_ids, events.values())` pairing in `fetch_error_details` can misattribute error data to the wrong id (see related finding on project_replay_summarize_breadcrumbs.py).

title: Environment filter silently dropped when fetching trace item attribute keys
body: The previous implementation in useTraceItemAttributeKeys.tsx sent `environment: selection.environments` as part of the query to the trace-items attributes endpoint. The new shared `makeTraceItemAttributeKeysQueryOptions` helper omits this parameter entirely, with only a comment stating '// environment left out intentionally as it's not supported'. This removes previously-existing environment-scoped filtering of attribute/tag keys without any test asserting the new (or old) behavior, so if the backend does support environment filtering, this is a silent regression that will surface irrelevant attribute keys from other environments in the Explore UI.

title: TableWidgetVisualization branch renders hard-coded empty data instead of query results
body: In tableResultComponent, when organization.features.includes('use-table-widget-visualization') is true, the code renders <TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} /> instead of passing the actual `result`/`fields`/`metadata` that are available in this scope (and which are passed to the StyledSimpleTableChart in the other branch). As written, enabling this feature flag will always render an empty table regardless of the real query results, making table widgets effectively broken for any organization with the flag on.

title: validate_timestamp/validate_age use truthy checks instead of presence checks
body: BrowserReportSerializer.validate_timestamp checks `self.initial_data.get("age")` and validate_age checks `self.initial_data.get("timestamp")` to enforce that exactly one of the two fields is present. Since both checks rely on truthiness rather than key presence, a report containing `timestamp=0` together with `age=0` (or vice versa) will bypass the mutual-exclusivity validation entirely, because `0` is falsy. This silently accepts malformed/ambiguous reports that the validators are supposed to reject, and there is no test covering the zero-value edge case.

title: Overly broad exception handling and non-serializable value in log extra
body: get_environment_info wraps the whole body in `except Exception as e` and logs at `logger.info` with `extra={"issue_id": issue.id, "error": e}`. Catching all exceptions this broadly (not just the expected Environment.DoesNotExist / missing-event cases) will silently swallow genuine bugs (e.g. AttributeError from a code defect, DB errors) and mislabel them as the benign 'no environment' case at info level, making real failures hard to notice. Additionally, putting the raw exception object `e` (rather than str(e) or using exc_info) into the `extra` dict can fail to serialize cleanly depending on the logging backend/formatter in use.

title: Caching/retry safeguards lost when switching from useApiQuery to raw useQuery
body: The previous implementation called useApiQuery with explicit `staleTime: 0, refetchOnWindowFocus: false, retry: false`. The refactor replaces this with a bare `useQuery({enabled, queryKey, queryFn})` that omits all three options, so the hook now falls back to the QueryClient's global defaults for staleness, window-focus refetching, and retries. This can introduce unwanted retries on failed attribute-key fetches and extra refetches whenever the browser tab regains focus, which the original code explicitly avoided — a behavior regression for a hook used in interactive search/typeahead UI.

title: Migration gutted to a no-op without a corresponding test update
body: convert_org_saved_searches_to_views in 0920 (like 0917) is reduced to a no-op because "this migration had an error and was never run". For 0917, the matching test file (tests/sentry/migrations/test_0917_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views.py) was removed in this same PR since it asserted the old behavior. No corresponding test file for migration 0920 appears anywhere in this changeset. If such a test exists elsewhere in the repo asserting that running 0920 creates GroupSearchView rows, it will now fail (or pass vacuously) since the migration body no longer performs the transformation — this should be verified/cleaned up the same way 0917's test was.

title: 60s processing deadline may be too tight for a 100-identity chunk doing network calls
body: check_auth_identities now has `processing_deadline_duration=60` while it is invoked with `chunk_size=100` (the default) and loops over each auth identity calling `check_single_auth_identity`, which in turn calls `provider.refresh_identity(auth_identity)` — a network-bound call to the external SSO/auth provider for each identity. Giving only 60 seconds total to refresh up to 100 identities (effectively ~0.6s per identity including request overhead) risks the task being killed mid-batch under normal network latency, which would abort remaining identity refreshes in that chunk without obvious indication which ones were processed.

title: Environment filter silently dropped from trace-item attribute key requests
body: The previous implementation (in useTraceItemAttributeKeys.tsx) explicitly sent `environment: selection.environments` as part of the query to `/organizations/.../trace-items/attributes/`. The new shared `makeTraceItemAttributeKeysQueryOptions` omits the environment parameter entirely, with only a comment stating it's 'left out intentionally as it's not supported'. If the backend endpoint does in fact filter by environment, this is a behavior regression that will cause attribute-key suggestions to no longer respect the user's selected environment(s); this should be confirmed against the backend endpoint's actual support for the parameter.

title: Analytics event recorded before feature flag and input validation
body: analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...) is called unconditionally at the very start of post(), before the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` feature check and before any request validation. This means analytics will record an 'assemble' event even for requests that are ultimately rejected with 404 (feature disabled) or 400 (invalid payload), inflating/skewing usage metrics for this event rather than reflecting actual successful or attempted assemble operations.

title: Unsafe dict access can crash the install pipeline instead of failing gracefully
body: The new user-mismatch check does `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` using direct dict indexing instead of `.get()`. If an existing `Integration` row (reached via the 'OrganizationIntegration does not exist, but Integration does exist' branch, e.g. a re-install of a previously uninstalled/legacy integration, or one created without full sender data) has a `metadata` dict that lacks the `sender` key or the `sender` dict lacks `login`, this raises an unhandled `KeyError`. That turns what should be a controlled 'Invalid installation request.' error page into an uncaught 500, which directly contradicts the goal of this PR (gracefully rejecting mismatched installs). This should use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and compare, falling back to the error response when missing.

title: Unhandled exception from get_user_info() on GitHub API failure
body: In `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`, the call `authenticated_user_info = get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` is not wrapped in a try/except, unlike the token-exchange response parsing just above it (which explicitly catches `Exception` when decoding/parsing the token response). If GitHub's `/user` endpoint returns an error (rate limiting, network failure, invalid/expired token edge cases, etc.), `get_user_info` can raise (e.g. `ApiError`), which will propagate out of the pipeline view as an unhandled exception and produce a generic 500 error instead of the intended friendly 'github-integration-failed.html' error page that the rest of this flow is designed to show.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the scenario it is named for
body: `test_installation_not_found` stubs a 404 response for `/app/installations/{installation_id}` to simulate GitHub reporting that the app installation cannot be found (originally asserting 'The GitHub installation could not be found.'). After this change, the second request uses `state="ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"`, which does not match `pipeline.signature` (the correct value used elsewhere in these tests is `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`). Because `OAuthLoginView.dispatch` checks `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature` and returns the generic error immediately on mismatch, the request never reaches the code path that calls `get_installation_info`/`build_integration`, so the stubbed 404 response is never exercised. The test now only verifies the unrelated 'state mismatch' error path while the mocked 404 scenario (and its original purpose) goes untested, and the test's name/setup is misleading about what it actually checks.

title: KeyError risk when comparing authenticated user against missing 'sender' metadata
body: In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch()`, the new check `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` accesses `integration.metadata["sender"]` with direct dict indexing instead of `.get()`. Elsewhere in the same file (`build_integration`), `sender` is explicitly treated as an optional field (`if state.get("sender"): integration["metadata"]["sender"] = state["sender"]`), implying integrations can legitimately exist without a `sender` key in metadata (e.g. integrations created before this feature shipped, or if the installation webhook that populates `sender` was never received/processed). For any such integration, this line will raise an unhandled `KeyError`, crashing the reinstall flow with a 500 error instead of showing the graceful 'Invalid installation request' page that the rest of this pipeline is designed to show.

title: New user-mismatch check can be bypassed when Integration row does not yet exist
body: When `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `DoesNotExist`, the code immediately returns `pipeline.next_step()` (line 482), completely skipping the newly added `github_authenticated_user` vs `sender` comparison further down. Since `sender` metadata appears to be populated by the asynchronous GitHub installation webhook rather than by this OAuth pipeline itself, if that webhook has not yet been processed when the user completes the OAuth dance (e.g. due to webhook delivery delay), the Integration row will not exist yet, this branch will be taken, and the newly-added authenticated-user validation will never run for that installation — defeating the security check this PR is meant to add for that race window.

title: Unhandled exceptions from OAuth token exchange and user-info calls
body: `safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` (line 423) and `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` (line 434) are called without any exception handling. Only the subsequent `safe_urlread`/`parse_qsl` step is wrapped in a `try/except`. If GitHub's token endpoint is unreachable, times out, or `get_user_info` raises `ApiError` (e.g. GitHub API hiccup or rate limiting), the exception propagates unhandled and the user sees a generic 500 error instead of the intended 'could not verify installation' error page that this PR is supposed to guarantee for all failure cases.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the scenario it is named for
body: The test was changed to add a second request using a hardcoded, deliberately different `state` value (`"ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"`) than the one the pipeline actually signs (`"9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3"`, used everywhere else in this file). Because of the newly added `OAuthLoginView`, this mismatched state now causes the request to fail at the `state != pipeline.signature` check inside `OAuthLoginView.dispatch()`, never reaching `GitHubInstallation`/`build_integration()`, which is what actually raises the 'GitHub installation could not be found' error this test is supposed to validate (the GH `/app/installations/{id}` 404 stub set up at the top of the test is now never hit). The test now only re-validates the generic state-mismatch path (duplicating coverage already implied elsewhere) while silently dropping coverage for the original 404-from-GitHub scenario.

title: No test coverage for failed OAuth token exchange
body: The PR description explicitly calls out a third failure mode — GitHub failing to return a valid `access_token` for the supplied `code` (e.g. invalid or reused code) — handled by the `if "access_token" not in payload: return error(...)` branch. No test in the diff stubs a failing/empty token-exchange response to verify this path actually produces the expected error page, so this behavior is unverified.

title: Unsafe dict access on integration.metadata['sender']['login'] can raise KeyError
body: In GitHubInstallation.dispatch(), the new user-validation check does `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` using direct dict indexing instead of `.get()`. The "sender" key in metadata is only ever set conditionally (via `state.get("sender")` in build_integration, or asynchronously by the webhook handler) and is not guaranteed to exist for every Integration row (e.g. legacy integrations created before this field existed, or installations where the webhook hasn't arrived/failed). If "sender" (or its "login" sub-key) is missing, this line raises an unhandled KeyError, producing a generic 500 error instead of the intended friendly 'Invalid installation request' page, defeating the purpose of this security-focused PR's graceful error handling.

title: External GitHub API calls in OAuthLoginView are not exception-guarded
body: `safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` (line 423) and `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` (line 434) are called without try/except, unlike the subsequent response-parsing code which is wrapped in a broad `try/except Exception`. If GitHub's token endpoint or user endpoint fails due to network errors, timeouts, or returns an error status that causes the underlying client to raise (e.g. ApiError), the exception propagates unhandled, producing a generic 500 error instead of the intended 'Invalid installation request' error page that the rest of this view carefully produces for every other failure mode.

title: Identity check relies on mutable GitHub username instead of immutable user ID
body: `pipeline.bind_state("github_authenticated_user", authenticated_user_info["login"])` stores the GitHub "login" (username) which is mutable and can be renamed/reused by a different account over time. The later comparison in GitHubInstallation.dispatch (`!= integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`) also compares usernames rather than GitHub's immutable numeric user id. For a security-hardening change meant to prevent user-mismatch attacks, relying on a renamable/reusable identifier is weaker than comparing the stable account id that GitHub also provides in both the OAuth user info response and the webhook sender payload.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the 'installation not found' code path
body: The second request in `test_installation_not_found` now sends `state="ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"`, which does not match the pipeline signature used everywhere else in this test file (`"9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3"`). This causes the request to fail the new `OAuthLoginView` state-mismatch check (`request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature`) and return the generic 'Invalid installation request.' error before the code ever reaches `build_integration`'s GitHub-installation-404 handling that this test was originally written to verify. As a result, the originally intended scenario (GitHub API returning 404 when fetching installation info) is no longer actually covered by any test, even though the test name and the previous assertion ('The GitHub installation could not be found.') implied it was.

title: No test for OAuth access_token exchange failure (invalid/reused code)
body: The PR description explicitly calls out a third failure mode: 'If GitHub could not generate correct access_token from the code (wrong or attempt of re-use of code).' This path is implemented in OAuthLoginView (`if "access_token" not in payload: return error(...)`), but no test in this file simulates the `/login/oauth/access_token` endpoint returning a response without an access_token (e.g. an error/invalid_grant response) to confirm the pipeline correctly surfaces the failure page for this scenario.

title: `queued` default is evaluated once at class definition time, not per-instance
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a dataclass field default. Field/parameter defaults in Python are evaluated exactly once, when the class body executes at module import time — not each time an `AssignmentSource` is instantiated. As a result, every `AssignmentSource` created without explicitly passing `queued=` (e.g. via `AssignmentSource.from_integration()`, used throughout `sync.py`) will carry the same frozen timestamp: the moment the module was first imported (e.g. worker startup), not the actual time the assignment was queued. This silently defeats the purpose of the `queued` field for any logging/debugging/TTL use and is a classic Python footgun that should use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead.

title: `queued` datetime is not safely round-tripped through task serialization
body: `to_dict()` returns `asdict(self)`, which keeps `queued` as a raw `datetime` object. This dict is passed verbatim as Celery task kwargs (`assignment_source_dict`) in `sync_group_assignee_outbound` (`src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py`). If the task broker uses JSON serialization, the `datetime` will be converted to an ISO string on the wire, but `AssignmentSource.from_dict()` (line 30-35) does not convert it back into a `datetime` when reconstructing the object — it just passes the raw dict through `cls(**input_dict)`. This leaves `queued` as a `str` on the consumer side instead of the declared `datetime` type, which can raise exceptions or silently misbehave wherever `queued` is later treated as a datetime. No test exercises the actual serialize/deserialize round trip through the task boundary, so this discrepancy is not caught.

title: No test verifying cross-integration assignment sources still sync outward
body: The new test `test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration` only verifies that outbound sync is suppressed when the `assignment_source` integration matches the target integration. There is no corresponding test confirming the stated complementary behavior — that when `assignment_source` refers to a *different* integration than the one being synced to, the outbound sync still fires (per the comment in `issues.py`: "This should still allow other integrations to propagate changes outward"). Without this test, a regression that accidentally suppresses all outbound syncs whenever any `assignment_source` is present would go undetected.

title: `assignment_source` parameter added to `sync_status_outbound` abstract method is unused
body: The abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature now accepts `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`, mirroring the assignee-sync fix, but nothing in this PR actually threads an `AssignmentSource` into a `should_sync` cycle-break check for status syncing (unlike `sync_assignee_outbound`, where `should_sync('outbound_assignee', parsed_assignment_source)` is called). No caller in the diff passes a real value for this parameter, so it is effectively dead/unused, and the status-sync equivalent of the issue this PR claims to fix (repeated inbound/outbound status webhooks causing sync loops) is not actually addressed despite the API surface suggesting it is.

title: Typo in test method name
body: `test_from_dict_inalid_data` misspells "invalid", which can make the test harder to find/search for and reads as unintentional sloppiness in new test code; should be `test_from_dict_invalid_data`.

title: Dataclass default for `queued` is evaluated once at import time, not per-instance
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a plain default expression, which in Python is evaluated exactly once when the class is defined (i.e., at module import time), not each time an `AssignmentSource` is constructed. Every `AssignmentSource` created via the default (e.g. `AssignmentSource.from_integration(...)` or direct construction without passing `queued`) will share the same stale timestamp - the process start time - rather than the actual time the assignment source was created. This silently defeats the purpose of the field (tracking when the source was 'queued') and will mislead any future logic or monitoring/debugging that relies on it to detect staleness or measure timing between inbound/outbound sync events. The fix is to use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead of a bare default value.

title: `AssignmentSource.queued` (a `datetime`) is embedded in task kwargs and will not round-trip correctly
body: `assignment_source.to_dict()` is placed directly into the `kwargs` of `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(...)`, including the raw `datetime` value of `queued`. When this crosses the task broker's serialization boundary (Celery/kombu JSON serializer), the `datetime` gets converted to an ISO string on encode but is not restored to a `datetime` on decode. `AssignmentSource.from_dict()` (sync_assignee_outbound.py) then constructs the dataclass with `queued` as a plain string even though the field is typed `datetime`, silently violating the declared type. Nothing in this PR crashes because of it today, but any future code that calls datetime methods or performs datetime comparisons on `queued` after a task round-trip will raise `AttributeError`/`TypeError`. This should either drop `queued` from the serialized payload, or explicitly serialize/deserialize it (e.g. via `isoformat()`/`datetime.fromisoformat()`).

title: `assignment_source` parameter added to `sync_status_outbound` abstract method is never populated by any caller
body: The abstract method `sync_status_outbound` was changed to accept a new `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None` parameter, but no caller in this PR (or shown in the diff) actually passes a non-default value for it - unlike `sync_assignee_outbound`, which is wired through `sync_group_assignee_outbound`/`sync_assignee_outbound` task with a real `assignment_source`. This makes the parameter effectively dead code that implies status-sync loop prevention exists when it does not, which can mislead future maintainers who assume the anti-loop protection already covers status sync as well as assignee sync.

title: No test verifies outbound sync still proceeds when the assignment source is a *different* integration
body: The new test `test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration` only asserts that sync is blocked when `assignment_source` matches the target integration. The code comment in `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync` explicitly states the intent is to 'still allow other integrations to propagate changes outward', but there is no test exercising that path (i.e., `assignment_source` referencing a *different* integration than the target `ExternalIssue`'s integration, confirming `sync_assignee_outbound` is still called). Without this test, a regression that accidentally blocks all outbound sync whenever any `assignment_source` is present would not be caught.

title: New task kwarg has no forward/backward compatibility guard for rolling deploys
body: `sync_assignee_outbound` gained a new keyword parameter `assignment_source_dict` with no corresponding `**kwargs` catch-all. During a rolling deploy, producers running the new code (e.g. `sync_group_assignee_outbound` in `src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py`) will enqueue tasks with this extra kwarg while older worker processes still running the previous task signature will reject the call with `TypeError: sync_assignee_outbound() got an unexpected keyword argument 'assignment_source_dict'`, causing outbound assignee sync to fail (and retry/exhaust retries) until all workers are upgraded. Consider adding a `**kwargs` fallback or deploying the worker-side change ahead of enabling the new kwarg producer-side.

title: Dataclass field default `timezone.now()` is evaluated once at import time, not per-instance
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a plain field default, which in Python is evaluated exactly once, when the class body is executed at module import. Every `AssignmentSource` created afterwards without explicitly passing `queued` (including every call to `AssignmentSource.from_integration(...)`, which is the only constructor used throughout the PR) will get the exact same frozen timestamp -- the time the module was first imported (e.g. process/worker startup) -- rather than the actual time the assignment source was created. This silently produces incorrect/misleading `queued` values for the lifetime of the process. It should use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead of a bare default expression.

title: test_to_dict does not catch the stale/shared default timestamp bug
body: `test_to_dict` only asserts `result.get("queued") is not None`, which passes trivially even with the eager-default-evaluation bug in `AssignmentSource.queued` (see finding in assignment_source.py). No test verifies that two different `AssignmentSource` instances created at different times actually get different `queued` values, so the bug goes undetected.

title: New `assignment_source` parameter added to abstract sync_status_outbound is never populated by any caller
body: The abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature was extended with `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`, mirroring the loop-prevention mechanism added for assignee sync. However, nothing in this PR (or shown in the diff) ever passes a non-None value for this parameter from any inbound status-sync code path, nor does `should_sync` for the `outbound_status` attribute get checked against it anywhere. As written, this is dead/unused scaffolding: the status-sync cycle (resolve/unresolve flapping analogous to the assignee flapping this PR fixes) is not actually addressed, despite the interface now suggesting support for it. This risks misleading future maintainers into thinking status-sync loops are already handled.

title: Loop-prevention check is scoped to integration, not to the specific external issue that triggered the change
body: `should_sync` suppresses outbound sync whenever `sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id`, matching only on integration id. `sync_group_assignee_outbound` iterates over every `GroupLink`/`ExternalIssue` tied to the group and invokes `sync_assignee_outbound` for each one. If a single Group happens to be linked to more than one `ExternalIssue` under the same integration (e.g. multiple linked issues within the same Jira/GitHub instance), an inbound change originating from one of those external issues will also suppress the outbound sync to the other, unrelated external issue tracked by the same integration, even though that other issue was not the source of the loop and should still receive the update.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is abstract and cannot be instantiated
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler[QuerySubscriptionUpdate] with just `pass`, but StatefulDetectorHandler declares several abstract members that are not implemented here: `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the newly-added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. Because none of these are overridden, MetricAlertDetectorHandler remains an abstract class (ABCMeta keeps it in `__abstractmethods__`), so calling `MetricAlertDetectorHandler(detector)` (e.g. via `Detector.detector_handler` -> `group_type.detector_handler(self)`) will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract methods ...`. Previously this class directly implemented `evaluate` and was a valid concrete class; the refactor silently turned it into a non-functional stub that will crash any code path that tries to use a Detector of type `metric_alert_fire` (including `process_detectors`, which does not guard against an exception here, only against `None`).

title: Stale docstring says evaluate returns a list
