body: The docstring for `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` still reads "Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`", but this PR changed the return type to `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`. The docstring was not updated to reflect the new dict-based contract, which is misleading for future readers/implementers of this hook.

title: No test coverage exercising MetricAlertDetectorHandler / detector_handler instantiation for example group types
body: The test suite was rewritten extensively to cover StatefulDetectorHandler behavior through a local MockDetectorStateHandler, but there is no test that instantiates or evaluates MetricAlertDetectorHandler (the real example subclass changed in src/sentry/incidents/grouptype.py in this same PR). Because of that, the fact that MetricAlertDetectorHandler is left abstract (missing required overrides) and will raise TypeError on instantiation was not caught by any test in this PR.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler cannot be instantiated: abstract methods not implemented
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler with only `pass` as its body. StatefulDetectorHandler (and its parent DetectorHandler) declare several abc.abstractmethod members that are not implemented here: the `counter_names` property, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the newly-added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. Because both DetectorHandler and StatefulDetectorHandler inherit from abc.ABC, Python will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract methods ...` the moment anything tries to construct this handler (e.g. `Detector.detector_handler` property calling `group_type.detector_handler(self)`). Previously this class subclassed the non-abstract-in-practice DetectorHandler with a concrete (if stub) `evaluate` method, so it could be instantiated; this change silently breaks that. Any processing path that reaches a detector of type `metric_alert_fire` will now crash.

title: Stale docstring still describes evaluate() as returning a list
body: The docstring for StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate() still says "Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`", but the method (and the whole point of this PR) now returns a `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`. The stale wording is misleading to future readers/maintainers about the actual contract.

title: No test exercises MetricAlertDetectorHandler after it was changed to subclass StatefulDetectorHandler
body: The PR changes `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` in src/sentry/incidents/grouptype.py to subclass the abstract `StatefulDetectorHandler` with an empty body, which makes the class impossible to instantiate (missing implementations for `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, `build_occurrence_and_event_data`). No test in this PR (or elsewhere in the diff) attempts to construct or evaluate a detector of type `metric_alert_fire`, so this regression is not caught by the test suite. A simple test instantiating `Detector.detector_handler` for this grouptype would have caught the abstract-class instantiation failure before merge.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now an uninstantiable abstract class
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains `pass`. StatefulDetectorHandler declares `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values` as abstract (pre-existing) and this PR adds a new abstract method `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. None of these are implemented by MetricAlertDetectorHandler. Since StatefulDetectorHandler is an abc.ABC with these as @abc.abstractmethod, attempting to instantiate MetricAlertDetectorHandler (e.g. via `Detector.detector_handler` -> `group_type.detector_handler(self)` for any Detector whose type is `metric_alert_fire`) will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract methods ...`. Previously this class was a concrete (if no-op) DetectorHandler subclass that worked fine; this change silently turns it into a landmine that crashes at runtime the moment it's used.

title: evaluate() docstring not updated for new dict return type
body: The docstring for StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate() still says 'Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`', but the method signature and implementation now return a `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, not a list. This is left over from before the API change described in the PR and is now inaccurate, which can mislead future readers/maintainers about the actual return type/shape.

title: No test exercises instantiation of the changed MetricAlertDetectorHandler
body: This PR changes MetricAlertDetectorHandler to subclass StatefulDetectorHandler (previously DetectorHandler) without providing the newly-required abstract method implementations. No test in this PR (or referenced in the diff) instantiates MetricAlertDetectorHandler or exercises `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler(detector)` / `Detector.detector_handler` for a detector of type `metric_alert_fire`. Such a test would have caught the TypeError raised when trying to instantiate this now-abstract class, so this regression was not caught by the test suite included in the PR.

title: Public function renamed/relocated without visible update of call sites or tests
body: `mark_failed_threshold` (previously defined in `sentry/monitors/logic/mark_failed.py`) has been renamed to `try_incident_threshold` and moved into a new module `sentry/monitors/logic/incidents.py`. The PR only touches 4 files, with no accompanying changes to any test files. Sentry's existing unit tests for monitor failure handling commonly import and/or `mock.patch` these internal functions directly (e.g. `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed.mark_failed_threshold`). Since the symbol no longer exists under the old module path/name, any such import or patch target will now raise `ImportError`/`AttributeError`, breaking the test suite. If no test updates exist elsewhere in this change set, CI will fail.

title: create_issue_platform_occurrence renamed to create_incident_occurrence and moved, along with helper symbols, without compatibility shim
body: `create_issue_platform_occurrence`, `get_failure_reason`, `HUMAN_FAILURE_STATUS_MAP`, `SINGULAR_HUMAN_FAILURE_MAP`, and `get_monitor_environment_context` were all removed from `sentry/monitors/logic/mark_failed.py` and relocated/renamed in the new `incident_occurrence.py` module. These were previously public (non-underscore-prefixed) names in `mark_failed.py` and are the kind of symbols that get imported directly or mocked in tests (e.g. `mock.patch('sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed.create_issue_platform_occurrence')`). No test files are included in this change, so any existing references to the old module path/names will fail at import/patch time, constituting an unannounced API break for internal consumers and tests.

title: SimpleCheckIn moved to types.py without checking for other importers
body: `SimpleCheckIn` was previously defined in `sentry/monitors/logic/mark_failed.py` and is now defined in `sentry/monitors/types.py`, with `mark_failed.py` no longer exposing it. Any other module or test that imported `SimpleCheckIn` from its old location (`sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed`) will break with an `ImportError` since it is not re-exported from the old path for backward compatibility.

title: Public functions renamed and relocated without verifying/updating other references
body: `mark_failed_threshold` (now `try_incident_threshold` in incidents.py) and `create_issue_platform_occurrence` (now `create_incident_occurrence` in incident_occurrence.py), along with `get_failure_reason`, `get_monitor_environment_context`, `HUMAN_FAILURE_STATUS_MAP`, and `SINGULAR_HUMAN_FAILURE_MAP`, were moved out of `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` into new modules and in some cases renamed. The PR only touches 4 files and does not show any update to test files or other call sites that may reference these symbols by their original module path or name (e.g. via `mock.patch('sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed.create_issue_platform_occurrence', ...)` or direct imports in unit tests exercising threshold/occurrence logic). If any such references exist elsewhere in the codebase, they will now fail with ImportError/AttributeError or silently stop patching the intended code path, since the old names no longer exist in `mark_failed.py`.

title: Typo carried over in get_failure_reason docstring
body: The docstring for `get_failure_reason` reads "Builds a humam readible string from a list of failed check-ins." (should be "human readable"). This typo was simply relocated from the old `mark_failed.py` file into the new module; since this code is being actively reorganized, it would be a good time to fix the wording.

title: Moved/renamed internal functions without updating or adding corresponding tests
body: This PR removes `mark_failed_threshold`, `create_issue_platform_occurrence`, `get_failure_reason`, `get_monitor_environment_context`, `HUMAN_FAILURE_STATUS_MAP`, `SINGULAR_HUMAN_FAILURE_MAP`, and the local `SimpleCheckIn` TypedDict from `src/sentry/monitors/logic/mark_failed.py`, moving/renaming them into the new `incidents.py` (as `try_incident_threshold`) and `incident_occurrence.py` (as `create_incident_occurrence`) modules. The changed-file list contains no test updates. Any existing tests that import these symbols directly (e.g. `from sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed import get_failure_reason`) or that use `mock.patch("sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed.create_issue_platform_occurrence", ...)` to avoid hitting Kafka during `mark_failed` tests will now either fail to import or have their patch silently become a no-op (since the patched module/symbol no longer exists at that path), which can cause real occurrence/Kafka production calls to run unmocked during tests, or outright ImportError failures in CI.

title: No new unit tests added for the newly split-out logic modules
body: The refactor introduces two new logic modules, `incidents.py` and `incident_occurrence.py`, each containing previously-tested business logic (threshold detection, occurrence payload construction, failure-reason text generation). No corresponding test files (e.g. `test_incidents.py`, `test_incident_occurrence.py`) were added or referenced in this PR to validate the functions at their new locations, leaving the reorganized code without direct test coverage tied to its new module paths.

title: join() can skip terminate() for multiple flusher subprocesses on timeout
body: In join(), the per-process loop does `if deadline is not None: remaining_time = deadline - time.time(); if remaining_time <= 0: break`. Once the overall deadline has elapsed (e.g. because an earlier process took a while to die, or next_step.join(timeout) already consumed most of the timeout), the loop breaks immediately for that process and all subsequent processes in `self.processes`, so `process.terminate()` (line 346-347) is never called for them. In the old single-process implementation, terminate() was called unconditionally after the wait loop regardless of the deadline. Now, with multiple flusher processes, a timed-out join() can leave one or more child processes running and un-terminated after join() returns (e.g. during partition rebalance), potentially continuing to read Redis and produce segments for shards the consumer no longer owns, which can cause duplicate/late segment production to Kafka and resource leaks.

title: Inconsistent metric tag key ('shard' vs 'shards') fragments flusher metrics
body: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` are tagged with `tags={"shard": shard_tag}` (lines 185, 195), but `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is tagged with `tags={"shards": shard_tag}` (line 199). This inconsistent tag key means the two related timers will produce separate, inconsistently-named tag dimensions in the metrics backend, breaking dashboards/alerts that expect a uniform 'shard' tag across these flusher metrics, especially important now that this PR is specifically introducing per-shard-process observability.

title: `max_processes or len(...)` silently discards an explicit 0, and CLI option allows invalid values
body: `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` uses `or`, so an explicitly passed `max_processes=0` is treated the same as `None` and silently replaced by one-process-per-shard instead of being honored or rejected. Additionally, the new `--flusher-processes` click option in src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py (around lines 432-437) has no `min=1` validation, so a negative value causes `self.num_processes = min(max_processes, len(shards))` to become negative; `range(negative_number)` yields an empty dict for `process_to_shards_map`, and the subsequent `self.process_to_shards_map[process_index].append(shard)` assignment then raises an unhandled `KeyError` at consumer startup rather than a clear configuration error.

title: Unused dead code: `_create_process_for_shard`
body: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` (singular) is defined but never called anywhere in the class; all restart paths (`_ensure_processes_alive`) call `_create_process_for_shards` (plural) directly with the process_index and full shard list. This leftover method suggests an incomplete refactor (e.g. an intended per-shard-only restart path that was dropped) and should either be wired up or removed to avoid confusing maintainers.

title: Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op due to earlier global monkeypatch, defeating its purpose
body: The test patches the global `time.sleep` with `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at the top of the test. The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` call (with comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change') therefore also resolves to the same no-op lambda, since monkeypatch replaces the attribute on the shared `time` module used by both the test and the flusher's background thread. The intended 100ms wall-clock wait never happens, so the test's correctness now relies on incidental GIL/thread-scheduling timing rather than a deterministic wait, which can make the test flaky under CI load despite the comment implying a real wait was added to fix flakiness.

title: New multiprocess test only checks shard→process bookkeeping, not actual flush behavior
body: `test_flusher_processes_limit` only asserts on `flusher.processes`, `flusher.max_processes`, `flusher.num_processes`, and `flusher.process_to_shards_map` sizes; it never submits any spans and never asserts that segments assigned to different shards (handled by different threads/processes) are actually flushed and produced correctly. This leaves the core new feature of this PR — correct end-to-end flushing when more than one flusher process/thread is active — without a test that exercises actual data flow and verifies correctness across multiple processes.

title: join() aborts cleanup of remaining flusher processes once the timeout budget is exhausted on an earlier process
body: In join() the per-process wait/terminate loop (lines 337-347) uses `break` once `remaining_time <= 0` while iterating `self.processes.items()`. `break` exits the entire for-loop, not just the current iteration, so every flusher process that has not yet been visited in the dict is skipped completely: it is never waited on and `process.terminate()` is never called for it. Before this PR there was only one flusher process, so this had no visible effect. Now that there is one process per shard group (up to `max_processes`), if the deadline is exhausted while waiting on the first process(es) in the dict, the remaining per-shard flusher processes are left running un-terminated. Because they are daemon processes they will eventually die with the parent, but during controlled shutdown/rebalance they can keep producing to Kafka / polling Redis for shards that may already belong to another consumer instance, risking duplicate segment production and resource leaks.

title: New isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) guard likely disables kill() for real flusher subprocesses
body: _ensure_processes_alive() now wraps the restart kill with `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.kill()` (lines 253-257). Previously this call was unconditional (`self.process.kill()`). Processes are spawned via `self.mp_context.Process` where `self.mp_context = multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")` (line 53), producing instances of `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`. `multiprocessing.Process` (the bare module attribute used here) resolves to the *default* context's process class, which on platforms whose default start method is not 'spawn' (e.g. Linux defaults to 'fork') is a sibling class of `SpawnProcess`, not its superclass. In that case `isinstance(spawn_process_instance, multiprocessing.Process)` is False, so the new guard silently prevents `process.kill()` from ever running on real flusher subprocesses in production. A hung/unresponsive flusher process detected by the health check would then never actually be killed, while a brand-new replacement process is started for the same shards right away — leaving two processes concurrently operating on the same Redis shard/segment data, which can cause duplicate flush/production or resource exhaustion.

title: Inconsistent metric tag key "shards" vs "shard" for related flusher timers
body: In SpanFlusher.main, the `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` timer and the `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` metric are tagged with `{"shard": shard_tag}` (lines 185 and 192-196), but the `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer right below uses `{"shards": shard_tag}` (line 199) for the exact same value. This tag-name typo means these two logically related metrics cannot be grouped or filtered consistently on the same tag in dashboards/alerts.

title: Unused dead method _create_process_for_shard
body: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` (singular) is defined but never invoked. `_ensure_processes_alive` restarts crashed processes by directly calling `_create_process_for_shards` (plural) with the already-known `process_index`/`shards`, bypassing this helper entirely. This leftover method is unreachable dead code and should be removed or wired up if it was meant to be used.

title: No validation of max_processes/flusher_processes allows silent fallback or a crash on invalid values
body: `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats `0` as falsy and silently substitutes the shard count, so passing `--flusher-processes 0` does not do what the operator asked. A negative value is not filtered out by `or` and flows into `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))`, which can become negative; `range(num_processes)` then produces an empty `process_to_shards_map`, and the subsequent `process_index = i % self.num_processes; self.process_to_shards_map[process_index].append(shard)` loop raises a `KeyError` because no entries exist. Neither the CLI option in src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py (plain `type=int`, no bounds) nor `SpanFlusher.__init__` validates for these cases.

title: Docstring claims one process per shard, but shards can share a process when max_processes < shard count
body: The updated class docstring states "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing," but the implementation caps processes at `max_processes` (the `flusher_processes` CLI option) and distributes shards round-robin across that smaller process count via `process_to_shards_map`. When `max_processes < len(assigned_shards)`, multiple shards share a single process/thread, contradicting the stated guarantee and potentially misleading operators tuning `--flusher-processes`.

title: No test coverage for multi-process restart or multi-process join() timeout behavior
body: The new test `test_flusher_processes_limit` only asserts that shards are distributed into the expected number of `process_to_shards_map` entries. It does not exercise `_ensure_processes_alive()` for the multi-process case (e.g. confirming that a crashed/hung process in one shard-group is restarted without disturbing other groups, or that kill()/restart actually works), nor does it exercise `join()` with a timeout while multiple processes are tracked (the path affected by the break-on-timeout issue in join()). Given this PR changes the flusher from a single background process to N per-shard-group processes, these newly introduced multi-process code paths are untested.

title: Unrelated documentation change bundled into this PR
body: The diff to CLAUDE.md adds an isinstance-vs-hasattr anti-pattern example that is unrelated to the span-buffer multiprocessed flusher feature this PR is about. Bundling unrelated doc changes into a feature PR increases review noise and makes it harder to bisect history for the actual feature change.

title: Inconsistent metric tag key between related flusher timers
body: In `SpanFlusher.main`, the "spans.buffer.flusher.produce" timer and the "spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes" timing both use the tag key `{"shard": shard_tag}` (lines ~185-196), but the "spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce" timer uses `{"shards": shard_tag}` (plural) at line 199. This inconsistency means dashboards/alerts that filter or group by the `shard` tag will not pick up the `wait_produce` metric, breaking correlation between produce time and wait-for-produce time per shard group.

title: New SpansBuffer instance created on every process restart without cleaning up the old one
body: `_create_process_for_shards` (called both on initial startup and from `_ensure_processes_alive` on every restart, e.g. line 259) always constructs a brand-new `SpansBuffer(shards)` and overwrites `self.buffers[process_index]` (line 125). Previously, a single buffer object was created once in `__init__` and reused across restarts. Now, every unhealthy-process restart creates a fresh buffer/Redis client without explicitly closing the previous one, which can leak Redis connections over the lifetime of a long-running consumer that experiences repeated flusher process restarts.

title: Memory backpressure check now aggregates memory info across per-process sub-buffers, risking double counting
body: `submit()` now iterates `self.buffers.values()` (one `SpansBuffer` per flusher-process shard group, each created independently via `SpansBuffer(shards)`) and sums `get_memory_info()` results across them (lines 299-303), instead of calling `get_memory_info()` once on a single buffer covering all assigned shards as before. If `get_memory_info()` reports memory per underlying Redis host rather than per shard, and two different process groups contain shards that map to the same physical Redis host, that host's memory will be counted multiple times in the aggregated `used`/`available` sum. This directly feeds the `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` hard-backpressure check used to avoid Redis OOM, so an incorrect aggregation could cause the check to behave incorrectly (false positive or negative backpressure).

title: Dead/unused method `_create_process_for_shard`
body: `_create_process_for_shard` (singular, lines 127-132) is defined to look up the process group for a single shard and restart it, but it is never called anywhere in the class — `_ensure_processes_alive` calls `_create_process_for_shards` (plural) directly with the already-known shard list. This leaves dead code in place, suggesting either an incomplete refactor or a helper that should have been used instead of duplicating the lookup logic.

title: Added synchronization sleep is a no-op due to an earlier global monkeypatch
body: In `test_basic`, `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` (line 15) patches the `time` module's `sleep` attribute globally for the whole test. The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` call at line 62, whose comment states it is meant to "give flusher threads time to process after drift change", therefore does nothing — it resolves to the same patched no-op function. The test's reliability for catching the flushed segment thus still depends entirely on uncontrolled thread scheduling rather than an actual wait, so the intended fix for test flakiness is ineffective and the test can still be flaky.

title: New --flusher-processes option defaults to 1, disabling the new multi-process-per-shard behavior by default
body: The new `--flusher-processes` CLI option defaults to `1`. Combined with `SpanFlusher.__init__`'s `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` logic, passing `1` (a truthy value) overrides the "one process per shard" default that would otherwise kick in when `max_processes` is `None`. As a result, the headline feature of this PR (spawning one flusher process per Redis shard) is not enabled unless operators explicitly override this CLI flag in deployment configuration — worth calling out since the PR description implies this is the new default behavior.

title: Unrelated documentation change bundled into the multiprocessed-flusher PR
body: The diff adds an unrelated "hasattr vs isinstance" anti-pattern snippet to CLAUDE.md (lines 449-458). This has no connection to the span-buffer flusher feature described in the PR and appears to be scope creep or an accidental inclusion, which makes the PR harder to review and could be better split into its own change.

title: No test coverage for per-shard-group process restart/failure isolation
body: The new tests only verify that shards are distributed across a limited number of processes (`test_flusher_processes_limit`); there is no test exercising `_ensure_processes_alive`/`_create_process_for_shards` restart path for the multi-process case — e.g. verifying that killing one shard-group's process only restarts that group's shards and leaves other groups' processes/buffers untouched, or that `process_restarts`/`process_healthy_since` are tracked independently per group. Given this PR substantially rewrote the restart logic to be per-process-group instead of global, this is an important gap in test coverage for a concurrency-sensitive code path.

title: close()/terminate() permanently destroy the factory-level shared FixedQueuePool, breaking subsequent Kafka rebalances
body: `FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` (result_consumer.py lines 131-137) and is meant to live for the lifetime of the factory, the same way `self.multiprocessing_pool` and `self.parallel_executor` do (those are only torn down in `ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown()`, never by a per-assignment strategy). However, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` (line 338) and `.terminate()` (line 342) call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` directly, which permanently calls `Queue.shutdown()` on every internal queue and stops every worker thread in the shared pool. Arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the currently active strategy and then calls `create_with_partitions()` again on the *same factory instance* on every partition rebalance (not just final consumer shutdown). After the very first rebalance, the shared `queue_pool` is dead: its queues are shut down and its worker threads have exited, but `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker()` in result_consumer.py (lines 244-259) just reuses `self.queue_pool` without recreating it. Any subsequent `submit()` call on the new strategy will raise `queue.ShutDown` from `work_queue.put()`, which is caught by the generic `except Exception` in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()`; that handler then marks the offset as added+completed as if it were processed, even though the message was never passed to `result_processor`. This causes silent data loss for every message after the first rebalance while still advancing committed offsets, defeating the purpose of the feature and corrupting data integrity guarantees.

title: Use of queue.ShutDown / Queue.shutdown() requires Python 3.13+
body: This module relies on `queue.ShutDown` (lines 132, 142) and `queue.Queue.shutdown()` (line 238, called from FixedQueuePool.shutdown at lines 231-243), both of which were only added to the standard library in Python 3.13. If Sentry's runtime is on an earlier Python version (3.11/3.12, which has been the case historically for this codebase), referencing `queue.ShutDown` or calling `.shutdown()` on a `queue.Queue` instance will raise `AttributeError` at runtime, crashing the consumer during normal strategy shutdown/rebalance/termination paths (i.e. the thread-queue-parallel mode would be completely non-functional, not just degraded).

title: Internal queues have no maxsize, so the advertised "natural backpressure" does not exist
body: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`'s docstring (around line 253) claims the strategy provides "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but each per-group queue is constructed as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize` (line 185), which defaults to an unbounded queue. `put()` therefore never blocks, so there is no backpressure mechanism at all: if one hashed queue backs up (exactly the scenario this PR is meant to mitigate), the consumer will keep reading from Kafka and enqueueing work indefinitely, growing memory without bound instead of slowing down. This contradicts the documented guarantee and creates an OOM risk under the very failure mode the PR targets.

title: join(timeout) ignores the timeout argument and duplicates close() shutdown logic
body: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(self, timeout=None)` (line 345) simply calls `self.close()`, discarding the caller-provided `timeout`. Arroyo's `ProcessingStrategy.join(timeout)` contract is expected to block up to the given timeout waiting for outstanding work to flush before shutdown completes; here the actual draining/joining logic in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` (lines 231-243) hardcodes a fixed 5.0 second timeout for both queue draining and worker-thread joins, regardless of what timeout the stream processor configured for graceful shutdown (e.g. `join_timeout` passed through `get_stream_processor`). This can cause premature strategy teardown if more time was actually available, and if `close()` is invoked followed by `join()` (both call the same shutdown path), the second invocation triggers `queue_pool.shutdown()` again on already-shutdown queues, causing extra "Error shutting down queue" exception logs on every normal shutdown.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling assertion is racy and contradicts the test's stated intent
body: The test's docstring states it verifies "errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages," implying the successfully-processed message's offset should still get committed. However the final assertion is `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, which actually asserts that NO commit happened. Since `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` completes (and thus makes committable) an offset in its `finally` block regardless of whether `result_processor` raised, both offsets (100 and 101) should become contiguous and committable once both items are processed, and the asynchronous commit loop (`_commit_loop`, firing every 1 second) will eventually commit offset 102. The test's wait loop (max ~0.2-2.2s) races against that 1-second commit cycle: on a fast run the assertion passes merely because the periodic commit hasn't fired yet, not because the intended behavior holds, and on a slower CI run (where the loop takes closer to its 2s budget) the commit may already have happened, making the test flaky/liable to fail intermittently. The assertion does not reliably validate the described behavior either way.

title: CLI help text for --mode not updated to describe the new thread-queue-parallel mode
body: The `--mode` option's choices were extended to include `thread-queue-parallel` (line 121), but the help string still reads "The mode to process results in. Parallel uses multithreading." (line 123), which does not mention or explain the new mode's semantics (fixed queue pool with per-group ordering guarantees). Operators using `--help` to choose a processing mode have no way to understand what thread-queue-parallel does or how it differs from parallel/batched-parallel.

title: close()/terminate() permanently destroy the shared queue pool, breaking processing after any rebalance
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (and terminate()) calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which stops all OrderedQueueWorker threads and shuts down every internal queue.Queue permanently. The FixedQueuePool instance, however, is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and reused across every subsequent call to create_with_partitions (e.g. after Kafka partition rebalances) — exactly like parallel_executor/multiprocessing_pool in result_consumer.py, which are intentionally only torn down in ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() at final process exit, never per-strategy-close. Because arroyo calls close()/terminate() on the current strategy whenever it is being replaced (which happens on every rebalance, not just final shutdown), the first rebalance kills the workers and shuts down the queues. Any create_with_partitions call afterwards reuses the now-dead queue_pool: submit() pushes items into shut-down queues (raising queue.ShutDown, silently caught and the offset marked 'complete' without any real processing), so messages after the first rebalance are effectively dropped while the consumer appears healthy.

title: Uses Python 3.13-only queue.Queue.shutdown()/queue.ShutDown API
body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls q.shutdown(immediate=False), and OrderedQueueWorker.run() catches queue.ShutDown. Both queue.Queue.shutdown() and the queue.ShutDown exception were introduced in Python 3.13. On earlier Python runtimes, q.shutdown() raises AttributeError; since that call is wrapped in a bare 'except Exception', the failure is silently logged rather than propagated, meaning the queue is never actually put into a shutdown state. Worker threads blocked in work_queue.get() are consequently never woken and will hang indefinitely instead of shutting down, defeating the entire purpose of FixedQueuePool.shutdown()/close().

title: Offsets are marked complete (and committed) even when processing raises an exception
body: In OrderedQueueWorker.run(), the finally block always calls self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...) regardless of whether result_processor succeeded or raised an exception caught by the preceding 'except Exception' clause. This contradicts the guarantee stated in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's docstring ('Only commits offsets after successful processing'): a message whose processing failed is treated identically to a successfully processed one, so its offset becomes eligible for commit and will never be retried or reprocessed — a processing failure silently advances the committed offset past the failed message.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts behavior inconsistent with the implementation
body: This test mocks the result processor to raise on the first call and succeed on the second, then asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, implying a processing failure should block the offset commit. But per OrderedQueueWorker.run()'s finally block, offsets are always marked complete regardless of exceptions, so the commit loop should still compute and commit an offset for test_partition once both items complete (which happens almost immediately since the mocked calls return synchronously). This makes the assertion likely to fail or flake against the real implementation, or indicates the test does not actually validate any failure-handling guarantee.

title: Per-queue queue.Queue() has no maxsize, so the claimed backpressure doesn't exist
body: Each internal queue created in FixedQueuePool.__init__ (queue.Queue()) is unbounded, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() never raises arroyo's MessageRejected to signal backpressure regardless of queue depth. Despite the docstrings on FixedQueuePool and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy explicitly claiming 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', no bound is enforced anywhere, so a slow or stuck group (or an overall slow downstream) can grow its queue without limit while the consumer keeps reading from Kafka, risking unbounded memory growth instead of the intended backpressure.

title: get_committable_offsets iterates the offsets dict without a lock protecting its structure
body: get_committable_offsets() takes list(self.all_offsets.keys()) and then separately locks per-partition to read self.all_offsets[partition]. The all_offsets defaultdict's key set can be mutated from another thread calling add_offset for a partition never seen before (defaultdict.__missing__ inserting a new key) without any lock protecting the dict's structure itself — only the per-partition lock (created lazily, after the key may already need to be inserted) guards the inner set contents. Enumerating dict.keys() into a list while another thread inserts a new key concurrently can race, and in CPython can even raise RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration, which would crash the background commit loop thread.

title: Offset commits are issued from a dedicated background thread instead of the main strategy thread
body: _commit_loop runs on its own daemon thread started in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.__init__ and calls self.commit_function(committable), which ultimately invokes the arroyo `commit` callback passed into create_with_partitions. Arroyo processing strategies are designed to be driven single-threadedly by the StreamProcessor's main loop (submit/poll/join); none of the other modes in this same file (serial, parallel, batched-parallel) invoke the commit callback from a separate thread. Calling `commit` concurrently with the main thread's own poll()/submit() activity deviates from that contract and risks races in whatever internal bookkeeping the Commit implementation performs, since it is not documented/guaranteed to be safe for concurrent use from worker threads.

title: close() shuts down the queue pool without draining it first
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() immediately calls self.queue_pool.shutdown() without first calling the already-implemented FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty() helper. FixedQueuePool.shutdown() only gives each worker a 5 second join() timeout; if there is still a backlog when close() runs, items may not finish processing within that window (a timed-out join() does not stop the thread, it just stops waiting), so close() can return while unprocessed/uncommitted work is still in flight, risking those messages being left in an inconsistent processed/committed state depending on what happens after close() returns.

title: close()/terminate() destroy the factory-level shared queue pool, breaking processing after every rebalance
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() and terminate() call self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which shuts down every worker thread and all underlying queues. However, FixedQueuePool is created exactly once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ (result_consumer.py) and is reused unchanged across every subsequent create_with_partitions() call (create_thread_queue_parallel_worker just returns a new SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy wrapping the same self.queue_pool). Arroyo's StreamProcessor calls close()/join() on the current strategy on every partition revoke (which happens on every consumer-group rebalance, e.g. deploys/scaling) before calling create_with_partitions() again for the new assignment. Since the pool is never recreated, the new strategy instance submits work into queues that have already been shut down. In FixedQueuePool.submit(), add_offset() runs before work_queue.put(); when put() then fails against the shut-down queue, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()'s except branch calls add_offset()+complete_offset() again, marking the offset as processed even though the message was never handed to a worker. The periodic commit loop then commits these offsets. The net effect is that after the very first rebalance, the consumer silently stops doing any real work while continuing to advance/commit offsets, i.e. permanent, hard-to-notice data loss until logs are inspected.

title: Worker queues are unbounded, so there is no actual backpressure
body: Each per-queue work_queue is created with queue.Queue() (no maxsize), so put() never blocks. The class docstring for SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy explicitly claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but there is nothing enforcing that: submit() is always non-blocking regardless of how backlogged a given group's queue is. Combined with WorkItem retaining the full original Message (including raw payload), a single slow group under sustained load will cause unbounded memory growth in that queue instead of applying backpressure, which is exactly the scenario (a slow item clogging processing) this PR claims to address — here it manifests as a potential OOM rather than a batch stall.

title: Reliance on queue.Queue.shutdown()/queue.ShutDown, which require Python 3.13+
body: queue.Queue.shutdown() and the queue.ShutDown exception were only added to the standard library in Python 3.13. If the deployed runtime is on an older Python version, q.shutdown(immediate=False) raises AttributeError, which is swallowed by the surrounding `except Exception: logger.exception(...)` in FixedQueuePool.shutdown() (lines 236-240). Because this is the only mechanism used to interrupt the blocking self.work_queue.get() call in OrderedQueueWorker.run() (lines 131-133), the worker threads never actually unblock when the AttributeError path is hit, so they keep running (or block forever) despite shutdown() ostensibly having completed. This needs to be verified against Sentry's supported Python version; if unsupported, graceful shutdown silently never happens (thread leak and no real teardown).

title: Worker shutdown joins threads sequentially, so shutdown time scales with num_queues
body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown() joins each worker thread sequentially with a 5 second timeout per worker (`for worker in self.workers: worker.join(timeout=5.0)`). With the default of 20 queues/workers, if workers are stuck (e.g. due to the queue.Queue.shutdown compatibility issue noted elsewhere, or simply slow in-flight processing), this loop can take up to num_queues * 5 seconds (100s by default) to return, rather than a bounded ~5s. This can make consumer shutdown unexpectedly slow and risks the process being force-killed by orchestration before a graceful stop completes.

title: decode_payload asserts against FilteredPayload, but the queue strategy's decoder contract requires handling it
body: decode_payload has `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)`. create_thread_queue_parallel_worker passes `partial(self.decode_payload, self.topic_for_codec)` as the `decoder` for SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy, whose declared type is `Callable[[KafkaPayload | FilteredPayload], T | None]` — i.e. it is expected to tolerate FilteredPayload inputs and return None. Instead, any FilteredPayload reaching submit() causes decode_payload to raise AssertionError, which is caught by the generic `except Exception` in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() and logged as 'Error submitting message to queue' even though a filtered payload is an expected, non-error condition. This produces misleading error-level log noise for a normal case and masks real decode errors among the noise.

title: join(timeout) ignores the supplied timeout and re-runs close() with hard-coded internal timeouts
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(self, timeout=None) simply calls self.close() again, discarding the caller-supplied timeout entirely. close() internally uses fixed 5.0s timeouts for the commit thread join and (via FixedQueuePool.shutdown) for each worker join. This means any operator-configured join timeout (e.g. via the consumer's --join-timeout / join_timeout plumbing in sentry/consumers/__init__.py) has no effect for the thread-queue-parallel mode, and shutdown duration is not actually controlled by the configured value, which can surprise operators expecting a bounded, configurable shutdown.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts an invariant the implementation does not provide
body: This test expects that when the first of two same-group messages raises during processing, offsets are not committed (`assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`). However OrderedQueueWorker.run() unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset() in a `finally` block regardless of whether result_processor raised, so both submitted offsets (100 and 101) become 'complete' and thus committable as soon as the periodic (1s-interval) commit loop runs. Given the test waits up to ~2 seconds for processing/queue-draining before asserting, the commit loop is very likely to have already run and committed by the time the assertion executes, making the assertion either reliably false or flaky depending on timing, rather than verifying a real guarantee.

title: Test decoder diverges from production decode_payload, masking the FilteredPayload assertion bug
body: TestSimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.setUp defines a custom `decoder` function that explicitly checks `isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)` and returns None, unlike the actual production decoder (ResultsStrategyFactory.decode_payload) which asserts the payload is NOT a FilteredPayload and raises otherwise (see the separate finding on result_consumer.py). Because none of the added tests exercise SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy with the real decode_payload function against a FilteredPayload input, the mismatch between the declared decoder contract and the actual production implementation is not caught by this test suite.

title: Backup code login bypasses password check
body: The password check is guarded by `user.password && !credentials.totpCode`, so when a backupCode is supplied with no totpCode the password is verified. But a request with `totpCode` set (any value) skips the password check entirely, and the same applies to the new backup-code branch. An attacker who submits email + a valid backup code and a dummy totpCode would skip the password. Even without a dummy totpCode, the check must be restructured so password is always required for CAL users; with this change a backup code is only effective as a second factor if the first factor is enforced independently of totpCode.

title: Backup code comparison and handling are fragile (null codes, non-string input)
body: Used codes are set to null in the array and re-saved. `indexOf(credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""))` is a plain non-constant-time comparison, fine in practice, but the lookup is not atomic: two concurrent logins with the same code can both read the array before either writes back, so a single-use code can be reused (read-modify-write race). There is also no per-attempt rate limit specific to backup codes beyond the generic limiter.

title: Unvalidated backupCode type can crash the endpoint
body: `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll` is called on user-controlled JSON; if backupCode is a non-string truthy value (number, object) this throws a TypeError and returns a 500 rather than a 400. Also JSON.parse of the decrypted codes isn't guarded. Validate that backupCode is a string first.

title: Throwing errors in API handler instead of returning a response
body: Missing encryption key in the backup-code branch does `throw new Error(...)`, producing an unhandled 500 with no JSON body, while the modal expects `body.error` from `response.json()`. This can cause a JSON parse failure in the client; the setup endpoint returns a proper 500 JSON for the same condition.

title: Backup codes overwritten on each setup call and returned before 2FA confirmed
body: Backup codes are generated and persisted at setup time, before the user has verified the TOTP code, and are regenerated whenever setup is re-run (e.g. cancel and retry). The stored codes are only shown after enable succeeds, and the state is not reset on cancel except password/step; if the user cancels, backupCodes remain in DB with twoFactorEnabled=false. This is mostly harmless but stale codes linger.

title: Modal can be dismissed without ever showing/saving backup codes; state not reset
body: After enable succeeds the step moves to DisplayBackupCodes, but the Dialog's onOpenChange (outside click/Esc) closes the dialog without calling resetState/onEnable. The parent's switch state then isn't updated and the modal re-opens at the backup-codes step with the old codes; also the onEnable callback (which refreshes 2FA status) is only called through the Close button. Additionally the blob URL is never revoked on unmount, and `useState([])` is typed as never[].

title: Component misnamed TwoFactor
body: The default export of BackupCode.tsx is named `TwoFactor`, duplicating the other component's name and confusing stack traces and devtools.

title: Toggle button defaults to submit and BackupCode `required` interferes with form
body: The 'Lost access' Button has no `type="button"`; depending on Button's default it may submit the form inside the Form. In addition, `required` on the BackupCode field plus switching modes with `resetForm` leaves the hidden TwoFactor input registered with no value, and `required` was newly added to PasswordField even when the user is passwordless-protected.

title: No tests for backup code login or disable flows
body: The core new behavior (logging in with a backup code, single-use enforcement, disabling with a backup code, invalid code errors) has no test coverage; the PR only adds download/copy/close checks and leaves a TODO. The PR checklist admits no tests were added.

title: Backup code login does not verify password in the 2FA step (password check is skipped when only backupCode is provided? / used-code reuse)
body: Used backup codes are set to null in the array, but the check `backupCodes.indexOf(code)` is a non-atomic read-modify-write. Two concurrent logins with the same code can both succeed before the update lands, so a single-use code can be used more than once. Also, when all codes are consumed the array stays full of nulls and nothing tells the user.

title: Backup code comparison is non-constant-time and user input is not type/length validated
body: `indexOf` on plaintext codes is a non-constant-time compare. `credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` also assumes a string. Only the shared generic rate limit applies, which is weak protection for a 40-bit code. Codes are never validated against format before comparison.

title: Disable endpoint crashes on non-string backupCode and null-valued entries are not handled
body: `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll` throws a 500 if backupCode is not a string (e.g. a number or object in the JSON body). Unlike login, no rate limiting is applied to this endpoint, so backup codes can be guessed by an authenticated session holder. Also, `symmetricDecrypt` and `JSON.parse` are not guarded.

title: Backup codes regenerated and returned on every setup call, and stored/validated without being consumed on the null entries
body: Each call to setup (including abandoned setups) overwrites existing backupCodes and returns them in plaintext. The codes are persisted before the user confirms TOTP, so an abandoned setup leaves codes in the DB while twoFactorEnabled is false. Combined with the login check, any user whose setup was abandoned has stale codes if they later enable 2FA via another route.

title: Blob URL leaks and cancel/close do not clear sensitive backup codes from state
body: `backupCodesUrl` in the handler closure is stale (revokes only the value from the render), and the object URL is never revoked when the modal closes. Backup codes remain in component state after `resetState`, which does not clear `backupCodes`, `dataUri`, `secret` or `backupCodesUrl`. Closing via the dialog's onOpenChange also bypasses resetState, so reopening the modal could resume at the backup-codes step.

title: Lost-access toggle button lacks type="button" and resetForm clears values rather than unregistering
body: The 'lost access' Button is inside a form and has no explicit `type="button"`; depending on the Button default it may submit the form. Also when switching to the BackupCode input, `required` and minLength validation on the hidden TOTP vs backup field combine with `setValue` resets, and a stale `totpCode`/`backupCode` can be sent together; the server prefers backupCode if truthy.

title: Component misnamed TwoFactor
body: The default export in BackupCode.tsx is named `TwoFactor`, duplicating the name of the other component and making stack traces/devtools confusing.

title: Backup code errors surfaced but lost-access state not reset on 2FA return, and email-login totp path not handled
body: For the external TOTP flow (`totpEmail`), the lost-access footer is not shown (ExternalTotpFooter), so users who authenticated via Google/SAML cannot use backup codes. Additionally, the authorize path skips password verification only when `totpCode` is present; for a backup-code submission with password the flow works, but for IdP users `!credentials.totpCode` is true and they get ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled.

title: No tests for backup code login or disable with backup code
body: The security-sensitive backup code paths (login, single-use enforcement, disable) are untested; the PR only adds UI download/copy checks and leaves a TODO. The PR description acknowledges no tests were added.

title: Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write
body: The user row is read at the start of authorize(). The code is then nulled out in memory, and the whole re-encrypted array is written back with an unconditional update. Two concurrent logins with the same backup code both read the unconsumed array and both succeed, which breaks the 'can be used exactly once' guarantee. Whichever write lands last also overwrites the other's changes, so a code consumed by one request can be restored by the other. Use a transaction or an optimistic check, for example update where backupCodes equals the value that was read, and fail if no row matched.

title: Message tells users to generate backup codes in settings, but no such feature exists
body: The `missing_backup_codes` string says "Please generate them in your settings". Backup codes are only generated inside the `/totp/setup` flow, and there is no regenerate option in settings. Existing users who already had 2FA enabled before this migration have `backupCodes = NULL`. They will see this message on 'Lost access' login or disable, with no way to act on it. If they have also lost their authenticator, they are locked out. Either add a regeneration path or change the message.

title: Backup codes are lost if the dialog is dismissed on the codes step
body: By the DisplayBackupCodes step, 2FA is already enabled on the server. The Dialog's `onOpenChange` is passed straight through and does not call `resetState()` or `onEnable()`. Pressing Esc or clicking the overlay therefore closes the modal without the user ever saving the codes, and the codes can never be shown again. It also leaves the step stuck at DisplayBackupCodes, so reopening the modal shows the old codes instead of restarting. Dismissal on this step should be blocked, or routed through the same close handler as the 'Close' button.

title: E2E tests do not cover backup code login/disable; first test not updated for new step
body: The PR says it fixes the 2FA setup test for the new backup-code screen. Only the 'disable' test was updated to close the backup-codes dialog. The 'enable and login' test never dismisses that dialog and works around it with a FIXME assertion that passes even when the switch is unchecked. The core new behaviours are untested: login with a backup code, single-use enforcement, and disabling with a backup code. Only a TODO comment mentions them.

title: Clipboard write not awaited; success toast shown unconditionally
body: `navigator.clipboard.writeText` returns a promise that can reject, for example without permission or on a non-secure context. The code ignores it and always shows 'Backup codes copied!'. A user may believe the codes were saved when they were not, and these are one-time-display secrets. Await the promise and show an error on failure.

title: Password visibility toggle removed from keyboard tab order
body: Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the shared PasswordField toggle button makes it unreachable by keyboard. This regresses accessibility in every place PasswordField is used, not just the 2FA screens, and is unrelated to the feature.

title: Unvalidated backupCode type can cause a 500
body: `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll(...)` assumes a string. A non-string truthy value, such as a number or object, throws a TypeError and returns a 500 instead of a 400 IncorrectBackupCode. There is also no rate limiting on guesses against this endpoint, unlike the login path.

title: Null/empty destinationCalendar crashes Google Meet fallback
body: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` yields `undefined` when destinationCalendar is null or an empty array. The next line then reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining. This throws a TypeError for any Google Meet booking where the organizer has no destination calendar. handleNewBooking can pass `null`, and many handlers now pass `[]`. Previously `evt.destinationCalendar?.integration` was safe. It should be `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.

title: Pushing team calendars mutates the event type's destinationCalendar
body: When the event type has a destinationCalendar, evt.destinationCalendar is built as `[eventType.destinationCalendar]`. That fresh array is then mutated with `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`. Separately, `destinationCalendar` is `null` when neither the event type nor the organizer has one, so `?.push` silently does nothing and the collective hosts' calendars are dropped. This is the exact multi-host scenario the PR targets. The team members' calendars should be collected into the array unconditionally.

title: Event-type destinationCalendar takes precedence, losing organizer calendar for collective events
body: For collective events, the organizer's own destination calendar is only included when the event type has none. If the event type has one, the host calendars are appended after it. If it has none and the organizer has none, the array is null. The organizer's calendar is therefore inconsistently included. Since teamDestinationCalendars is built from `users.slice(1)`, the first (organizer) user's personal calendar may never get the event.

title: loadUsers rewrite drops organization select and throws for dynamic groups
body: The dynamic-user branch no longer selects `organization: { select: { slug } }`, which the old query included, so downstream code that reads `user.organization` will break or lose data. It also throws if dynamicUserList is empty, and the catch converts every non-HTTP error into a generic 500 'Unable to load users'. This is an unrelated behavioral rewrite inside a calendar fix, with a regression risk for dynamic group bookings.

title: Inconsistent e2e expectations for destinationCalendar
body: Only the BOOKING_REJECTED test was changed to expect `[]`. BOOKING_CREATED and BOOKING_REQUESTED still expect `destinationCalendar: null`. The confirm handler now yields `[]`, while handleNewBooking can yield null. The payload shape is now inconsistent across events, and there are no unit tests for multi-host behavior.

title: No-op destinationCalendar lookup in updateEvent and deleteEvent
body: `externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` is only reached when externalCalendarId is falsy. The find predicate then compares against a falsy value, so it can never match a real calendar and always returns undefined. The old fallback to destinationCalendar.externalId is silently lost. Update therefore passes an undefined calendarId, and delete falls back to 'primary'. The fallback should use the first destination calendar, or match by credential.

title: Patch after insert uses selectedCalendar without the 'primary' fallback
body: The insert uses `selectedCalendar || "primary"`, but the follow-up `calendar.events.patch` uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar`, which can now be undefined. This happens when no destination calendar matches the credentialId (previously it defaulted to 'primary'). The hangout-link description patch then fails or targets the wrong calendar.

title: Missing credentialId/externalId on fallback event creation; duplicate events possible
body: The `else` branch creates events via `createEvent(c, event)` without passing `destination.externalId`, so the resulting reference gets no externalCalendarId. Reference creation previously used evt.destinationCalendar's values. The loop over every destination calendar plus the 'other_calendar' pass can also create multiple events for the same credential. Each host's destination calendar with the same credential is handled separately, but Google's createEvent picks the calendar by credentialId only, so two destinations sharing a credential produce duplicate events in one calendar.

title: updateEvent called with undefined credential when lookup fails
body: If reference.credentialId is set but neither this.calendarCredentials nor the DB lookup (which also requires `app.slug`) yields a credential, `credential` stays undefined. `updateEvent(credential, ...)` is still called and will throw on `credential.appName`, aborting all remaining references via the catch. The result is that every reference is reported as failed. Skip the reference or push a failure result instead.

title: Recurring cancellation now repeats the delete for every calendar reference
body: The recurring-event branch deletes events for all updatedBookings across all calendar credentials. Previously it ran once because only the first calendar reference was handled. Now it sits inside `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)`. With N calendar references it runs N times, which makes redundant delete calls that return 404/410 and pushes the already-resolved results into apiDeletes.

title: User-facing note string changed unrelatedly
body: 'Notes have been hidden by the organiser' was changed to 'organizer'. Any tests or snapshots matching the old text will break. The change is unrelated to the PR.

title: Inverted slug logic in organization creation changes behavior
body: The original code set `slug` when `!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED` and `requestedSlug` when billing is enabled. The new code sets `slug` only when billing IS enabled, which reverses the semantics. This is unrelated to the PR's stated purpose. With billing enabled, orgs are now created with a live slug before payment or verification. With billing disabled, no slug is set at all.

title: Possible TypeError when destinationCalendar is empty and location is Google Meet
body: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` yields `undefined` when the array is empty or null. The next line reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` with no optional chaining. Several callers now pass `[]` (cron, webhook, confirm and others), and handleNewBooking can pass `null`. Any Google Meet booking with no destination calendar will throw instead of falling back to Cal Video. The old code used `?.`. It needs `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.

title: Pushing team destination calendars onto a null array, and wrong main destination
body: `evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar. `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is then a no-op, so collective team members' calendars are silently dropped. This is the exact scenario the PR is meant to fix. Also, when the event type has a destinationCalendar it is placed first, which is correct. But the organizer's own calendar is then never added in that case, so the organizer is not invited. The array should be built explicitly, e.g. `[]` plus organizer plus team members.

title: loadUsers rewrite drops organization select and changes behavior
body: The rewritten `loadUsers` removes the `organization: { select: { slug } }` from the dynamic user query, so downstream code that reads `user.organization` may break or silently lose data. It also now throws 'dynamicUserList is not properly defined or empty' for any request without an eventTypeId and an empty list. Other errors are wrapped as a generic HTTP 500. This refactor is unrelated to the PR and risks regressions.

title: Same event created on every team member's credential with the same event object; the else branch lacks externalId
body: In the no-credentialId branch, `createEvent(c, event)` is called without `destination.externalId`. The resulting references therefore carry `externalCalendarId` undefined. On reschedule or cancel, the update/delete then falls back to the default calendar instead of the intended one. Also, because `calEvent.additionalNotes` is mutated in `createEvent` when hideCalendarNotes is set, and the same `event` is shared across all iterations, there are side-effect risks.

title: Organizer attendee email and calendar selection use the first destination for all hosts
body: `createEvent` sets the organizer attendee email from `destinationCalendar[0].externalId` regardless of which credential/calendar is being written. For a second host's calendar the event is created with the first host's calendar email as the organizer. The selected calendar is looked up by `credentialId` only, so if two destinations share a credential the first match always wins.

title: Nonsensical fallback lookup in updateEvent/deleteEvent
body: `externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` is dead logic. In the else branch `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so the find compares externalId to a falsy value and will essentially never match. Previously the code fell back to the destination calendar's externalId. Now it falls back to undefined/primary, which is a regression for the fallback case.

title: Recurring cancellation repeats deletes inside the per-reference loop
body: The recurring-events branch iterates over all user calendar credentials and deletes all updated bookings' first calendar reference. This runs once per calendar reference of the booking, which is now several for collective events. That causes duplicate delete calls and wasted API requests, and the single `bookingRef` lookup via `find` still only handles the first calendar reference per updated booking, so multi-host recurring events are not fully cleaned up.

title: Booking only connects to the first destination calendar
body: The booking's `destinationCalendar` relation connects only `evt.destinationCalendar[0]`. That is acceptable for the schema. But when the event type has no destination calendar and the array holds only team members' calendars, the connected one will be wrong. Ordering is not guaranteed to put the organizer first.

title: CalDAV createEvent ignores the credentialId and always filters by the first destination
body: The CalDAV base service takes `event.destinationCalendar[0]` and filters calendars by its externalId. For a collective event with multiple hosts on CalDAV credentials, each host's credential filters by the main host's calendar URL, so events are created in the wrong or no calendar. The `credentialId` argument is ignored, unlike the Google service.

title: Office365 and Lark services ignore credentialId and use the first destination
body: Both services pick the first destination calendar regardless of which credential is creating the event. For multi-host collective events, a second host's O365/Lark credential will attempt to write into the first host's calendar id, which fails or creates the event in the wrong place.

title: E2E expectations inconsistent and no tests added
body: Only the BOOKING_REJECTED expectation was updated to `[]`. BOOKING_CREATED and BOOKING_REQUESTED still expect `destinationCalendar: null`. This works only because handleNewBooking can emit null, but it is inconsistent with the other handlers. The PR also adds no unit tests for the new multi-destination logic in EventManager, which is the core behavior change.

title: Possible TypeError when destinationCalendar is empty and location is Google Meet
body: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` yields `undefined` when the array is empty or null. The next line then reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining. Many callers now pass `[]` (cancel, confirm, payment webhooks, bookingReminder), and handleNewBooking may pass `null`. A Meet-located event with no destination calendar will therefore throw instead of falling back to Cal Video. It needs `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.

title: evt.destinationCalendar can be null so team calendars are silently dropped, and the array can be mutated
body: `destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar. `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is then a no-op, so teammates' calendars are never added for a COLLECTIVE event. In that case the organizer gets the fallback calendar while the team members' calendars are skipped. The array literal also only holds one element, and pushing mutates it after the event has been built. Initialise to `[]` and concatenate instead.

title: If the event type has its own destinationCalendar, the organizer's calendar is ignored
body: When `eventType.destinationCalendar` is set, the array becomes `[eventType.destinationCalendar]` and the organizer's own destination calendar is never included. Team members' calendars are then appended after it. The fallback semantics are confusing and may leave the organizer's own calendar un-invited for collective events.

title: createEvent picks the destination calendar by credentialId only, falling back to 'primary'
body: `calEventRaw.destinationCalendar?.find(cal => cal.credentialId === credentialId)?.externalId` falls back to `"primary"` when no match is found. EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents also calls `createEvent` for entries that have no credentialId (matched by integration type) and for the fallback and other_calendar paths. In those cases Google can create the event on the credential's primary calendar rather than the intended destination. Previously the single destination calendar's externalId was always used. This is a behaviour regression for destination calendars without a credentialId. In addition, the later `calendar.events.patch` uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar`, which is undefined when only the 'primary' fallback was used, so the hangout-link patch fails.

title: No-op find on externalCalendarId in updateEvent/deleteEvent
body: `externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find(cal => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` only evaluates the `find` when `externalCalendarId` is falsy. It then searches for a calendar whose externalId equals that falsy value, so it never matches. The fallback is dead code and `calendarId` becomes undefined in `updateEvent`, whereas it previously fell back to the destination calendar's externalId.

title: Duplicate events created: createEvent runs per destination with the full event
body: When a destination has no credentialId, `createEvent` is called for every credential of that integration type for each destination. If several destinations share an integration type, the same credentials receive multiple creates, which produces duplicate events. The result list also mixes references with `externalId` undefined, so saved references lose their calendar id and updates and deletes may target the wrong calendar.

title: updateEvent called with an undefined credential
body: If `reference.credentialId` is set but neither the in-memory credentials nor the DB lookup yield a credential, `credential` stays `undefined` (or keeps the previous loop value). `updateEvent(credential, ...)` is called anyway, which throws inside CalendarManager. The outer catch then discards every result. The old code had a similar shape, but a missing credential is now more likely because other hosts' credentials are referenced. Skip the reference when no credential is found.

title: Error log removed in the catch block of updateAllCalendarEvents
body: The `console.error(message)` call was deleted, but `message` is still built. Failures in updateAllCalendarEvents are now swallowed with no logging, which makes debugging harder, and the `message` variable is left unused.

title: Multi-host destination calendars not handled by Office365/Lark/CalDAV
body: These services take only the first destinationCalendar (`mainHostDestinationCalendar`) and ignore `credentialId`. EventManager calls `createEvent` once per destination with the same full event. With a collective event where several hosts use the same provider, each credential's service creates the event in the main host's calendar id, which is wrong for the other hosts. The Office365 `deleteEvent` and `updateEvent` are also unchanged.

title: Unrelated rewrite of loadUsers changes behaviour and drops the organization select
body: The `loadUsers` rewrite removes the `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` select for dynamic users, which later code may rely on. It also throws when `dynamicUserList` is empty and wraps any error into a 500 'Unable to load users'. This is an out-of-scope behaviour change that is hard to review in a PR about destination calendars.

title: Unrelated inversion of org slug logic
body: The old code set `slug` when `!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED` and `requestedSlug` when billing was enabled. The new code sets `slug` when `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED` is true, which flips the behaviour. With billing enabled the org slug is now set immediately, before payment or verification, and without billing no slug is set at all. This is unrelated to the PR and looks like a bug.

title: Only the first destination calendar is used for the broken calendar name
body: Only the first element of `destinationCalendar` is used, so a failure on another host's calendar would report the wrong integration name. This is also an arguably acceptable fallback, but it is undocumented.

title: updateLocation references lose externalCalendarId for results without it
body: `externalCalendarId: result.externalId` is now taken from the result. `updateEvent` in CalendarManager does not set `externalId` or `credentialId` on its result, so references created via `updateLocation` (calendar updates) get an undefined externalCalendarId where they previously got the destination calendar's externalId. Stored references lose their calendar id.

title: E2E expectations inconsistent and no tests added for the new multi-destination behaviour
body: Only BOOKING_REJECTED was changed to expect `[]`, while the other webhook tests still expect `destinationCalendar: null`. No unit or e2e tests cover the new multi-host collective flow, even though the PR says no tests were added.

title: Salesforce: `prisma` is used but never imported
body: The new code calls `prisma.credential.update(...)`, but this file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. It fails type-check, and at runtime throws a ReferenceError on every Salesforce client construction.

title: Salesforce refresh bypasses credential sync and runs on every construction
body: The new token refresh is a direct fetch to login.salesforce.com. It does not use `refreshOAuthTokens`, so it never calls the sync endpoint. It also runs unconditionally in every service constructor, not only when the token has expired. This adds a network call and a DB write per instantiation. The resulting connection still uses the old `credentialKey.access_token` instead of the freshly fetched one, so the refresh has no effect on the connection it builds. The refresh also needs the actual refresh_token, but with credential sync enabled the fallback `refresh_token = "refresh_token"` placeholder would be stored.

title: Broken computed-key zod schema
body: `[z.string().toString()]` evaluates to a literal string such as "[object Object]" or "ZodString", not a catch-all key. The schema therefore requires a property with that literal name, and `safeParse` fails for any real token response. When sync is enabled, every refresh throws "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". The intended pattern is `.passthrough()` or `.catchall()`.

title: Dummy refresh_token written into the data, and the non-sync path is changed
body: A missing refresh_token is replaced with the string "refresh_token", and this runs even when credential sync is disabled. For schemas without `refresh_token` this also mutates the parsed data, adding a bogus field. The placeholder could later be stored and used as a real token. In Google's CalendarService the result of this function (a SafeParse object `{success, data}`) is saved as `key`, so the DB credential becomes `{success:true,data:{...}}` and loses its token fields.

title: Credential key stored as a safeParse result object
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the zod safeParse result, not the parsed data. Storing it as `key` corrupts the credential, since Google would later fail to read access_token or refresh_token. Previously `googleCredentialSchema.parse` returned the data directly. Also, with sync enabled, `res?.data` is undefined for a fetch `Response`, which makes `token.access_token` throw.

title: Sync endpoint response has different shape than callers expect, and no auth or error check
body: The function returns a raw fetch `Response` in the sync case, but the non-sync paths return different shapes. Examples: Google `fetchTokens.res` with `.data`, hubspot a token object, zohocrm/bigin an axios response with `.data`. Hubspot, Google, Zoho CRM and Zoho Bigin read `.expiresIn`, `.data` or similar directly off the result, so with sync enabled those properties are undefined and these paths break. There is also no `response.ok` check and no authentication header on the POST to the sync endpoint.

title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time `!==`; unvalidated body and decrypt
body: The secret is compared with a plain `!==`, which is timing-attackable. Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual`. `schema.parse` throws on a bad body, which becomes a 500 instead of a 400. `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` can also throw on bad ciphertext and is not caught. There is no method check, so any HTTP method is accepted.

title: Credential lookup/update can collide with teams and existing credentials; keys not validated
body: `findFirst` on userId + appId may match a different credential than intended when a user has several for the app, and a race can create duplicates because there is no unique constraint. Decrypted keys are written to the DB without schema validation per app.

title: Zoho refresh passes userId but synced response will not have `.data` shape
