body: The original value was `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%)`. The new rule is `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 70%))`. The light branch moved from 70% to 30%, so light themes get a much darker hint text than before. The desktop counterpart in `desktop/modal.scss` correctly uses 70%/30%. The mobile rule should be `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 30%))`.

title: topic-map h3 color changed from 20% to 50%/50%
body: The original color was `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%)`. The new rule uses `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%)` for the light branch, which silently lightens the heading on light themes. The dark branch is `$secondary` at 50%, which is also wrong. It should be 20%/80%, as in the desktop `.topic-map h3` and the mobile `.number, i` rules.

title: group-member-info .name lightness changed from 30% to 50% in both branches
body: The original color was `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)`. The new rule is 50%/50%, which alters the light-theme appearance and makes `.name` identical to `.title`. It should be `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 70%))`.

title: Remaining raw scale-color($primary) not converted
body: `.topic-list.categories .category .badge-notification` still uses `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%)` directly. On dark themes it gets the same low-contrast color this PR is meant to fix. It should use `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 50%))` like the rest.

title: Light-theme value silently changed from 30% to 70% for topic-meta-data h5 a
body: The original rule was `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)`. The new rule is `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 30%))`. The light-theme arm now uses 70% instead of the original 30%, so embedded-post author links become much lighter on light themes. This is a regression in the very theme the PR is not meant to affect. The light arm should stay at 30%, and the dark arm should then be 70% to match the pattern.

title: Light-theme lightness for .group-member-info .name changed from 30% to 50%
body: The original color was `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)`. The new rule uses `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 50%))`. This changes the light-theme appearance by making the name lighter and giving it the same color as `.title`, which removes the visual distinction between name and title. The light arm should be 30% and the dark arm `$secondary` 70%, consistent with `.user-small .name` elsewhere in this PR.

title: Light-theme lightness for mobile .group-member-info .name changed from 30% to 50%
body: The original color was `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)`. The new rule uses 50%/50%, which alters the light-theme look and makes `.name` identical to `.title`. This is a copy/paste error. It should be `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 70%))`.

title: Light-theme value for .custom-message-length changed from 70% to 30%
body: The original rule was `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%)`. The new rule is `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 70%))`. The light arm was swapped from 70% to 30% and the dark arm uses 70%, so the pair is inverted. On light themes the text is much darker than before, and on dark themes it is brighter than the desktop equivalent. The desktop version of the same rule correctly uses 70% / 30%. This should be `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 30%))`.

title: Light-theme value for .topic-map h3 changed from 20% to 50%
body: The original color was `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%)`. The new rule uses 50%/50%, which makes the topic-map heading as faint as the h4 below it on light themes. This is a regression in the light theme and loses the heading/subheading hierarchy. It should be `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 80%))`, matching the `.number, i` rule in the same file.

title: totalPages overcounts when user_count is an exact multiple of limit
body: `totalPages` is `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`. With 50 members and a limit of 50 it reports 2 pages, and with 100 members it reports 3. `showingLast` compares `currentPage` to `totalPages`, so on the real last page it is false and "next" stays enabled. Clicking "next" sets offset to `min(offset + limit, user_count)`, which equals `user_count`, and loads an empty page. The calculation should be `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)`.

title: Unbounded and unvalidated limit/offset on the public members endpoint
body: `limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i` and `offset = params[:offset].to_i` are used without clamping. A client can pass `limit=1000000` and force the whole group, which may be tens of thousands of users, to be loaded and serialized in one request. Negative values are passed straight to SQL `LIMIT`/`OFFSET`, which makes PostgreSQL raise an error and the request returns a 500. The old code only applied pagination to automatic groups. This should cap the limit at a sane maximum and floor both values at 0.

title: Breaking change to the response shape of /groups/:id/members, with no test
body: The endpoint used to return a bare JSON array of users. It now returns `{members: [...], meta: {...}}`. Any other consumer of the old shape, such as plugins or external API clients, will break. There is also no spec for `GroupsController#members` covering the new shape or the limit/offset behaviour. The only spec changes are in the admin controller spec.

title: `{{#if model}}` is now always truthy
body: The route now sets the controller model to the Group object instead of an array of members, so `{{#if model}}` is always true. The members table, including its header row, renders even before members load or when the group is empty. The condition should check `members`.

title: Spec uses the wrong HTTP verb for remove_member
body: The route for `remove_member` is `delete`, but the automatic-group test calls `xhr :put, :remove_member`. It passes only because controller specs do not check the verb. The test therefore does not reflect the real route and would hide a verb constraint regression. It should use `xhr :delete`.

title: remove_member bypasses Group#remove and ignores unknown user ids
body: Membership is removed with `group.users.delete(user_id)` rather than `group.remove(user)`, which the old incremental-delete code used. This is inconsistent with `add_members`, which uses `group.add`, and it skips any logic in the model's remove path. There is also no handling for a user_id that does not belong to the group, so the controller reports success for a no-op.

title: Pagination params are unbounded and unvalidated
body: `limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i` has no upper bound. A client can send `limit=10000000` and force the server to load and serialize every member of a large group. A negative `limit` or `offset` is passed straight to SQL, and PostgreSQL errors on a negative LIMIT or OFFSET, which returns a 500. The old code at least limited the result for automatic groups. Clamp `limit` to a maximum (e.g. 1..200) and `offset` to >= 0.

title: Public members endpoint changes its response shape and default size
body: `GET /groups/:name/members` used to return a bare JSON array, unpaginated for non-automatic groups. It now returns `{members: [...], meta: {...}}` and silently caps results at 50 for every group. Any other client of this endpoint, such as plugins, other JS code or API users, will break or silently see a truncated list. The change is not documented, and no spec covers the new `members` action's shape, limit, offset or meta.

title: totalPages is off by one when user_count is a multiple of limit
body: `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` gives 2 pages for exactly 50 members at limit 50, and 3 for 100. The last page is therefore empty. `showingLast` stays false on the real last page, so "next" is still enabled. `next` then sets `offset = min(offset+limit, user_count)`, which equals `user_count`, and loads an empty page. It should be `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)`.

title: Username input is never cleared and is not reset between groups
body: After `addMembers`, `usernames` stays set. Clicking Add again re-sends the same users, and the old value can persist when the controller is reused for another group. The code has a TODO acknowledging this but ships it. The result of `addMembers` is also not handled, so a failed request gives the user no feedback.

title: Reload after removal can leave the user on an empty page
body: `removeMember` and `addMembers` call `findMembers()` with the current offset. If the last member of the last page is removed, `offset` still points past the end (the clamp is only against `user_count`, which is stale until the response arrives). The admin sees an empty list and a wrong page indicator. Neither method has an error handler.

title: Spec uses the wrong HTTP verb and misses key cases
body: The route for `remove_member` is DELETE, but the automatic-group test uses `xhr :put, :remove_member`. It passes only because controller specs do not enforce the verb. There are also no tests for removing a non-member, adding non-existent usernames, or the new paginated `GroupsController#members` response. The old tests for those cases (silent success on unknown users) were deleted without replacement.

title: Client-controlled `limit` is unbounded and `offset` is not validated
body: `limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i` is passed straight to `.limit(...)` with no upper cap. Any user who can see the group can request `limit=10000000` and force a full-group serialization, which is a cheap DoS on large groups. A negative `limit` or `offset` from the client can also raise a DB error and a 500. The previous code at least had a default cap for automatic groups. Clamp `limit` to a sane range (for example 1..200) and `offset` to >= 0.

title: Public group members page now silently shows only the first 50 members
body: `GroupsController#members` now returns at most 50 users by default for every group. Before, non-automatic groups were returned in full. The public `group/members.hbs` template was only changed to iterate `members`. It has no paging controls and never advances `offset`, so any group with more than 50 members shows a truncated list with no way to see the rest. Pagination was added only in the admin UI.

title: totalPages is off by one when user_count is an exact multiple of limit
body: `totalPages` is `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`. With 50 users and a limit of 50 it reports 2 pages, so the pager shows "1/2" and the next arrow is enabled. Clicking it moves to offset 50 and shows an empty page. It should be `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)`.

title: addMembers never clears the input and has no error handling
body: `addMembers` does not reset `usernames` after the add, and the model's `addMembers` promise has no failure handler (the in-code TODO acknowledges the missing clear). Clicking Add twice re-submits the same names. An error response, such as the 422 for automatic groups, is swallowed with no feedback to the admin.

title: Reloading after removeMember can leave the pager on an empty page
body: After a remove, `findMembers()` reuses the existing `offset`. When the removed member was the only one on the last page, the new page is requested at an offset equal to the new total. The server returns an empty list and the view shows a blank page. The offset should be re-clamped after the removal, for example by stepping back one page.

title: Members are no longer loaded before render, so stale or empty list shows briefly
body: `afterModel` previously waited for the member load. Now `setupController` fires `findMembers()` without waiting. The cached Group object keeps its old `members`, `offset` and `user_count` from an earlier visit, so the previous page or members are displayed until the request returns. The error is not handled either.

title: No test for the new paginated members endpoint or its edge cases
body: `GroupsController#members` changed its response shape to `{members, meta}` and gained limit/offset pagination, but no spec covers it. Nothing tests the meta values, offset/limit behaviour, or bounds. The add/remove-member specs also never check that a nonexistent username or user id is handled. Removing the old patch specs without replacement leaves those edge cases untested.

title: Fallback locales are only loaded in ApplicationController#set_locale
body: Locale files are loaded lazily, and `translate` only calls `load_locale(config.locale)`. The new `ensure_loaded!` is called only from `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Any code that sets the locale elsewhere (Sidekiq jobs, mailers, `I18n.with_locale`, rake tasks, other entry points) will never load the site-default or `:en` fallback locales. A key missing in the user's locale will then still come back as 'translation missing' because the fallback backend finds nothing in the unloaded fallback locales. The loading should happen inside `translate` or `load_locale`, not just one controller filter.

title: LRU cache key ignores the fallback chain
body: The cached key is `key + config.locale + backend.object_id`. With the new fallback list, the result for a locale now depends on `SiteSetting.default_locale`. If an admin changes the default locale, cached translations that were resolved through the old fallback (or cached as 'translation missing') stay stale until the cache is reset. The key or cache invalidation should account for the fallback chain, or the cache should be cleared when `default_locale` changes.

title: ensure_loaded! mutates @loaded_locales outside the mutex
body: `@loaded_locales ||= []` and the `include?` check run outside `LOAD_MUTEX`, while `load_locale` mutates the array under the mutex and `reload!` resets it to a new array. Concurrent requests can race with a reload, or read the array while another thread appends to it. The check is repeated inside `load_locale`, so the outer unsynchronized check and initialization are a thread-safety smell, and `@loaded_locales` is still nil if `load_locale` is called before `ensure_loaded!`.

title: No tests for the new fallback behavior
body: The PR replaces `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` (previously production-only) with a custom global fallback list that applies in every environment, including test and development. It adds no specs covering the fallback order (user locale, then site default, then en), the lazy loading of fallback locales, or the interaction with the translate cache. Behavior changes in all environments without any coverage.

title: Fallback locales are only loaded in the web request path
body: Translations load lazily, and `translate` only calls `load_locale(config.locale)`. Fallback locales (site default and `:en`) are loaded only by `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` here in `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Sidekiq jobs, mailers, rake tasks and any code that sets `I18n.locale` or uses `I18n.with_locale` outside a controller never load them. A missing key there will not fall back to the site default or English, so the user gets 'translation missing' output. This is most likely in emails sent in a user's locale. Loading the fallback locales should happen inside the I18n layer (e.g. in `translate`/`load_locale`), not only in a controller filter.

title: Fallback list reads SiteSetting (DB-backed) on every lookup and can fail or return stale results
body: `Fallbacks#translate` calls `I18n.fallbacks[locale]` on each translation, so `SiteSetting.default_locale` runs on every lookup. Early in boot, during migrations or asset precompile, or before the settings table exists, `SiteSetting` may not be usable. If `default_locale` returns nil, `.to_sym` raises NoMethodError before `.compact` can help, and the `.compact` is useless where it sits. The translate accelerator's LRU cache key is `key + config.locale + backend.object_id`, which ignores the site default locale. A cached fallback-resolved string can therefore stay stale after an admin changes the default locale. Guard against a nil or unavailable setting and include the fallback chain in the cache key, or clear the cache when the setting changes.

title: ensure_loaded! initializes and checks @loaded_locales outside the mutex
body: `@loaded_locales ||= []` and the `include?` check run without `LOAD_MUTEX`, while `reload!` reassigns `@loaded_locales = []` and `load_locale` mutates it under the mutex. Concurrent requests can race on the unsynchronized initialization or read. A fully safe approach would take the lock, or simply delegate to `load_locale`, which already rechecks under the lock.

title: No tests for the new fallback behaviour
body: The PR replaces the Rails `config.i18n.fallbacks` setting with a custom fallback list, lazy loading of fallback locales, and a new `ensure_loaded!` method. It adds no specs. Nothing covers the fallback order (user, site default, en), a missing key falling back correctly, or the interaction with the lazy locale loader and LRU cache. A regression in any of these would not be caught.

title: Translation cache key ignores the fallback chain
body: `translate` caches no-arg lookups under `key + config.locale + backend.object_id`. With fallbacks, the result for a locale now also depends on `SiteSetting.default_locale`, which is not part of the key. If a key is missing in the user's locale, the cached value is the site-default or English text. When an admin changes `default_locale`, or the fallback locale is loaded later, the stale fallback string stays in the 300-entry LRU cache until it is evicted or the backend reloads.

title: Fallback locales are only loaded in controller requests
body: The translate accelerator loads translations lazily, per locale, and only for `config.locale`. `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` is called only in `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Sidekiq jobs, mailers and rake tasks that use `I18n.with_locale` or set `I18n.locale` never load the fallback locales (site default and `:en`). In those contexts a missing translation will not fall back and renders as a 'translation missing' string. The loading should happen inside the I18n layer, for example in `translate`, rather than only in one controller filter.

title: Fallback lookup hits SiteSetting on every translate and can fail without a database
body: `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks#translate` calls `I18n.fallbacks[locale]` on every lookup, including cache misses and calls with arguments. Each call runs `SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym` and allocates new arrays. If the DB or SiteSetting is not ready (assets precompile, migrations, early boot) or the setting is nil, any translation call raises. The fallbacks hash also now applies in development and test, because the per-environment `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` lines were removed and replaced by a global initializer. Consider guarding against a nil setting and caching the chain.

title: Fallbacks module included into whatever backend class is active at load time
body: `I18n.backend.class.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks)` includes the module into whichever class the backend happens to be at initializer time. If the backend is a Chain or a plugin-provided class, fallbacks are silently not applied to `Simple`. The pluralization include targets `Simple` explicitly, so the two are inconsistent. Include into `I18n::Backend::Simple` explicitly.

title: No tests for the new fallback behaviour
body: The PR adds a custom fallback order (user locale, site locale, English), lazy loading of fallback locales, and `ensure_loaded!`. None of this has specs, for example a missing key in a non-English locale falling back to the site default or English, or `ensure_loaded!` loading the fallback locales.

title: Stale folder-tree cache is reused after the DB requery, so the new denial is cached wrongly
body: When cached permissions don't allow the request, `Check` requeries permissions from the DB and calls `checkPermission` again. For resources with folder support, that call goes through `checkInheritedPermissions` and `buildFolderTree`, which reads `folderCache` with its 30s TTL. Only the permission map is refreshed. If a user creates a child folder under a parent they have inherited access to, the cached tree doesn't contain the new folder. The check fails again and the result is stored in `permDenialCache` for another 30s. That is the same "can't access what I just created" bug this PR targets, now sticky for nested folders and for dashboards inside them. The fallback should also bypass or refresh the folder cache, or the denial should not be cached when the tree may be stale.

title: Denial cache can hide a resource that becomes accessible right after a denied check
body: Every denial is cached for 30s under (namespace, user, action, name, parent). Any check issued before the permission exists is remembered as a denial. Examples are an existence or read probe before creation completes, or a permission granted moments after a check. Subsequent checks short-circuit and never reach the DB requery that this PR adds. So the newly created dashboard or folder can still be inaccessible for up to 30s. The denial entry is not invalidated when permissions are refreshed or changed.

title: Denial cache key is ambiguous and shares the `perm_` prefix with the permission cache
body: The key is `ns.perm_<uid>_<action>_<name>_<parent>`, built by plain concatenation with `_` and sharing the same underlying cache and the `perm_` prefix with `userPermCacheKey`. Names or UIDs containing `_` can make distinct tuples map to the same key. For example, name `a_b` with parent `c` collides with name `a` and parent `b_c`. The key can also overlap with `userPermCacheKey` for a user whose UID contains underscores. A collision would wrongly deny an unrelated resource. The key should use a distinct prefix such as `perm_denial_` and an unambiguous separator or encoding.

title: No test that a DB-confirmed denial is written to the denial cache
body: `TestService_CacheCheck` only pre-populates `permDenialCache` and checks that it is honored. Nothing verifies the write path, where a deny from the DB fallback populates the denial cache. Nothing verifies that the DB is not hit again on a repeat check. Nothing covers the anonymous or render identity paths through the new `getCachedIdentityPermissions`, or the folder-inheritance fallback. The `Check`-level tests also never assert how many DB calls the fallback makes.

title: `TestService_getUserPermissions` still has a dead `cacheHit` branch after the cached case was removed
body: The cache-hit test case was deleted because `getUserPermissions` no longer reads the cache. The `cacheHit` field and the branches that set the cache and expect `store.calls == 1` are now unreachable. They are misleading leftovers, and the new cache-first behavior now lives only in `Check` and `List`.

title: Per-resource denial cache means every distinct denied resource triggers a DB permission requery
body: When cached permissions don't allow the request, Check falls through to getIdentityPermissions, which always queries the DB because the cache lookup was removed from getUserPermissions. The denial cache is keyed by (user, action, name, parent), so it only suppresses repeats of the identical resource. A user who checks many different resources they cannot access, such as filtering a large list item by item, causes one permission-store query per distinct resource within the TTL. The singleflight key is per user and action, so it only collapses concurrent calls, not sequential ones. This can put a lot of load on the DB for exactly the denied-heavy workloads the cache is meant to protect.

title: Denial cache can keep denying a user right after permissions are granted or a resource is created
body: A denial is cached for 30s under (ns, user, action, name, folder), and nothing invalidates it. This includes name-less checks such as folders:create, where name and parent are empty. If a check for a resource runs before the user's permission exists (an existence probe before creation, or a permission granted moments later), the user is denied for up to 30s even after the DB is correct. That partly defeats the PR goal that creators can immediately access what they just created.

title: Requery on cache miss refreshes permissions but not the folder tree
body: On a cached-permission denial the code re-fetches permissions from the DB, but checkPermission then calls buildFolderTree, which uses the folder cache with a 30s TTL. A user who creates a new folder, or a dashboard in a newly created folder, can still be denied inherited access until the folder cache expires. This is because the new folder is not in the cached tree, so the requery does not fully fix the new-folder case.

title: Deny-cache test does not prove the permission cache is bypassed; denial write path is untested
body: The comment says the permCache entry 'allows access to prove this is not checked', but the value is set to false (`"dashboards:uid:dash1": false`). A map entry with false already means not allowed, so the test would pass even if the denial cache were ignored. Nothing tests that a denied Check actually writes the denial entry, that the entry is keyed correctly, or that an allowed check does not write one.

title: getUserPermissions test left with dead cacheHit branches after the cache-hit case was removed
body: The 'from cache' test case was deleted, so cacheHit is always false and the cacheHit branches (the s.permCache.Set and the `store.calls == 1` assertion) are dead code. The remaining case named 'should return error if store fails' expects no error. Together these make the test misleading, and the change that moved the cache lookup out of getUserPermissions has no direct test.

title: Requery after a cache miss still uses the stale cached folder tree
body: When cached perms don't allow the request, Check refetches permissions from the DB and calls checkPermission again. For resources with folder support, checkPermission calls checkInheritedPermissions, which goes through buildFolderTree and reads the cached folder tree (30s TTL). If a user creates a folder, then a subfolder or dashboard inside it, the refreshed permissions include the new parent folder scope. The cached tree does not contain the new folder, so tree.Ancestors does not find the ancestor. The check is denied, and the denial is then cached for another 30s. The PR's stated goal (creators can access what they just created) is therefore only partly met for nested resources. The folder tree should be refreshed on the requery path as well.

title: Negative cache entries are written for resources that may not exist yet
body: Every deny is cached for 30s under a key of user, action, name and parent folder. If a check for a dashboard or folder runs before its permissions exist (for example a pre-creation or race check by the creator), the denial is cached. The creator then gets denied for up to 30s after creation, because the denial check at line 117 runs before any DB requery. This reintroduces the bug the PR is meant to fix. Nothing invalidates the entry on permission or resource creation.

title: Denial cache key is ambiguous and shares the permission cache key prefix
body: The denial key is namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent. It reuses the `.perm_<uid>_<action>` prefix of userPermCacheKey, so the two entry types live in the same keyspace. Because name and parent are joined with a plain `_` and UIDs can contain underscores, different (name, parent) pairs can produce the same key, for example ("a_b","c") and ("a","b_c"). A denial for one resource could then wrongly deny another. A distinct prefix such as `.perm_denial_` and an unambiguous separator would avoid this.

title: Deny-cache test does not prove the denial entry short-circuits the check
body: The test comment says the permCache entry is set to "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked", but the value is `false`. A false scope would produce a deny even if the denial cache were ignored. The test also falls through to the fake store, which has no permissions, so it would pass without the feature. No test covers the denial cache being populated after a DB-confirmed deny, or a denial entry expiring and permissions being requeried. The value should be `true`, and a populate-on-deny test should be added.

title: Missing React key on GrafanaRuleListItem in list map
body: The old `GrafanaRuleLoader` was rendered with `key={key}`. The replacement `GrafanaRuleListItem` in the `case 'grafana'` branch has no key at all. The other branches (`DataSourceRuleLoader`, `UnknownRuleListItem`) still set one. React will warn about missing keys. Because `rules` is appended to as pages load, it will also reconcile items by index, which can mix up the per-item state held in `RuleActionsButtons` (delete modal, silence drawer) between rules.

title: Delete menu item never renders in the ruler-less list view
body: The Delete item is gated on `canDelete && rulerRule`. `GrafanaRuleListItem` now passes only `promRule` and no `rulerRule`, so Delete is never shown in the list view even when the user has permission. `handleDelete` also takes a `RulerRuleDTO`. The new `GrafanaGroupLoader` test confirms this: it grants delete permission yet asserts exactly 4 menu items, with Delete not among them. This is a functional regression for the list view, and the new prom-based `canDelete` ability is effectively dead code.

title: Silence drawer cannot open for prom-only rules
body: The `SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer` is rendered only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true, but `rule` is undefined in the new list view. `AlertRuleMenu` now shows 'Silence notifications' based on `promRule` abilities, and the new test asserts it is present. Clicking it only sets `showSilenceDrawer`, and nothing is rendered, so the menu entry silently does nothing.

title: Pause item hidden for prom-only rules while canPause is still true
body: `MenuItemPauseRule` is rendered only if `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`. With no ruler rule in the list view, pause is never shown even though `canPause` is true from the prom abilities. `canPause` still feeds `showDivider`, so the menu can end up with a divider that is not justified by any visible item.

title: Federated rule group check dropped for all callers
body: `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` used to call `isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` to mark federated Mimir groups as immutable. The refactor delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, which hardcodes `isFederated = false` (with only a TODO). Federated data-source rule groups can now show edit, delete and pause as supported in every existing view that uses the deprecated hook, which is a behavioural regression.

title: returnTo parameter dropped from the rule view link
body: The previous implementation built the href with `createRelativeUrl(..., { returnTo: createReturnTo() })`. The new one builds `/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view` with no `returnTo`. The rule details page therefore loses its 'back to list with the current filters' navigation when opened from the list.

title: Tests for removed behaviour deleted without replacement; no Delete/Silence coverage
body: The tests for the creating and deleting operation states and for `matchRules` were removed together with the feature, which is fine. The new tests, though, only check that the menu contains 4 items. They do not exercise Delete, Silence or Pause from the list view, which is why the dead-end behaviour in `AlertRuleMenu` and `RuleActionsButtons` goes unnoticed.

title: Missing React key on GrafanaRuleListItem in the filtered rule list
body: The old `<GrafanaRuleLoader key={key} .../>` became `<GrafanaRuleListItem .../>` with no `key`. It is returned from `rules.map(...)`, so the Grafana branch now has no stable key, unlike the datasource and unknown branches. React will warn and fall back to index-based reconciliation. As rules stream in or filters change, per-item state (delete modal, silence drawer, menu state) can attach to the wrong rule. Add `key={key}`.

title: Silence menu item does nothing in the list view because the drawer requires a ruler rule
body: In the list view `RuleActionsButtons` is now called with only `promRule`, so `rule` is undefined. `AlertRuleMenu` shows 'Silence notifications' based on the prom-rule ability, and the click calls `setShowSilenceDrawer(true)`. The drawer only renders when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) && showSilenceDrawer`, which is false without a ruler rule. The user clicks Silence and nothing happens. The drawer needs to work from the prom rule, or the item should be hidden.

title: Delete and Pause actions are unreachable in the list view (permission computed from promRule, rendering needs rulerRule)
body: The new code computes `canDelete` and `canPause` from `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`. Rendering still requires a ruler rule: `canDelete && rulerRule` and `canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`. In the list view `rulerRule` is undefined, so Delete and Pause never appear for Grafana rules, even for users with permission. This silently removes functionality, and the added tests only assert 4 items (no delete or pause) so they do not catch it. Either the handlers must work from the prom rule and identifier, or the abilities should not claim support.

title: Federated rule group check dropped for legacy CombinedRule abilities
body: `useAllAlertRuleAbilities(rule: CombinedRule)` previously used `isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` to mark federated groups as immutable. It now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, which hard-codes `isFederated = false` with a TODO. The legacy list (`RulesTable`) therefore treats federated data-source rule groups as editable and deletable, a behavior regression. The group is still available via `rule.group`, so the check can be preserved for the legacy path.

title: View link no longer includes returnTo
body: The removed `GrafanaRuleListItem` built the href with `createRelativeUrl(..., { returnTo: createReturnTo() })`. The new one links to `/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view` with no `returnTo`, so the 'back' navigation from the rule view to the list/filter state is lost. This is unmentioned in the PR and looks accidental.

title: Stale comment/variable names reference ruler preload that was removed
body: The ruler prefetch was removed, but the comment ('This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules...') and the variable `cacheAndRulerPreload` still describe ruler preloading. This is misleading and should be updated.

title: Tests for creating/deleting operation states were removed without replacement
body: The 'creating' (ruler-only) and 'deleting' (prom-only) list item tests and the `matchRules` tests were deleted. The new tests cover only the happy path and permissions. `GrafanaRuleListItem` still accepts an `operation` prop that nothing passes now. No test covers the recording-rule or unknown-rule branches of the new item, or the Delete and Pause menu behavior.

title: Missing React key on GrafanaRuleListItem in filtered list
body: The old `GrafanaRuleLoader` element had `key={key}`. The replacement `<GrafanaRuleListItem ...>` in the `rules.map` has no key, even though the artificial `key` is still computed for every rule. React will warn about missing keys. The list is appended to incrementally and each item holds local state (delete modal, silence drawer, clone redirect), so reconciliation without keys can mix up item state. `DataSourceRuleLoader` and `UnknownRuleListItem` in the same switch still pass `key`.

title: Silence drawer can never open for list-view rules (promRule only)
body: The list view now passes only `promRule`, so `rule` is undefined. The drawer renders only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) && showSilenceDrawer`. `AlertRuleMenu` shows "Silence notifications" via the new prom-based ability check, and clicking it calls `setShowSilenceDrawer(true)`. The drawer never renders, so the menu item appears but does nothing. The drawer needs a path that works from `promRule`, or the item must be hidden when there is no ruler rule.

title: Delete and Pause actions silently disappear in the new list view
body: `canDelete` and `canPause` are now computed from the prom-based abilities, but rendering still requires a ruler rule. Delete needs `canDelete && rulerRule`, and Pause needs `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`. In the list view only `promRule` is passed, so neither item is ever shown, even for users with permission. The new test expects exactly 4 menu items and so codifies this. Delete and pause are regressions in the list menu, and the ability computation for them is dead code. This needs either an explicit decision and comment, or a delete and pause path that works from the prom rule.

title: Federated rule group check dropped in the deprecated useAllAlertRuleAbilities
body: `useAllAlertRuleAbilities(rule: CombinedRule)` used to compute `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`. It now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, which hardcodes `isFederated = false` with a TODO. Existing consumers that pass a CombinedRule from a federated (Mimir) group will now see update, delete and pause as supported where they were previously blocked. This is a behavior regression outside the list view that this PR targets.

title: returnTo dropped from rule view link
body: The removed `GrafanaRuleListItem` built the href with `createRelativeUrl(..., { returnTo: createReturnTo() })`. The new one links to `/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view` with no `returnTo`. Navigating from the list to a rule and using the back or return affordance no longer returns the user to their filtered list. This is not mentioned as intentional.

title: Stale comment and variable name after ruler prefetch removal
body: The ruler prefetch was removed, but the comment still says "This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules..." and the variable is still named `cacheAndRulerPreload`. Both now describe behavior that no longer exists.

title: Queries are interpolated twice in the sharding path (here and again in runSplitQuery)
body: runShardSplitQuery now calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables on every target, including request.filters. Each shard sub-request then goes through runSplitQuery, which this PR also changed to call applyTemplateVariables on every target. So each target is interpolated once up front and again per shard group. The updated test confirms this: it expects 5 calls where the old code made 1. applyTemplateVariables is not idempotent in general. Ad hoc filters may be injected into the expression a second time, producing duplicate label matchers or line filters. Template variable values that contain `$` or `[[...]]` get re-expanded. The extra work is repeated for every shard group and every time chunk. The fix is to interpolate in only one place, for example by having the shard path pass already-interpolated targets to an inner function that skips interpolation, or by dropping interpolation from the shard path now that runSplitQuery does it. If interpolation stays in the shard path, the shard code must still interpolate before it calls getSelectorForShardValues, because it needs the final selector.

title: Test asserts the redundant interpolation count instead of guarding against it
body: The test 'Interpolates queries before running' now expects applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times. That is 1 call in runShardSplitQuery plus 4 from the sub-requests going through runSplitQuery. The test hard-codes the double interpolation as correct behaviour and depends on the shard count. It will break whenever the shard grouping changes, and it would make it harder to remove the duplicate interpolation later. The mock of applyTemplateVariables also mutates the query in place, so it hides any non-idempotence problem when a query is interpolated twice.

title: Shard splitting now interpolates every query twice, and ad-hoc filters may be added twice
body: runShardSplitQuery already calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables (passing request.filters) on every target. Each shard sub-request then goes through runSplitQuery, which now calls applyTemplateVariables again on the same, already-interpolated targets. The backend path then interpolates a third time. The second pass can re-apply ad-hoc filters to an expression that already contains them, which duplicates the filter clauses. It can also re-process interpolated variable values that contain `$` or regex characters. It also wastes work once per shard group and per time chunk. The updated shard test now expects 5 applyTemplateVariables calls instead of 1, which confirms the repeated work. Interpolation should happen once: either skip it in runSplitQuery when the caller has already interpolated, or stop interpolating in runShardSplitQuery.

title: Test asserts an implementation-detail call count that bakes in double interpolation
body: `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` ties the test to the exact number of shard groups and sub-requests (1 initial call plus 4 inside runSplitQuery). It breaks whenever grouping changes, and it asserts the redundant double interpolation as expected behaviour. The mock also mutates the passed query in place, unlike the real implementation, which returns a new object, so in-place mutation masks any problem with repeated application.

title: Queries are interpolated twice on the sharding path, which can duplicate ad-hoc filters
body: `runSplitQuery` now calls `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)` on every target. `runShardSplitQuery` already does the same interpolation and then passes each shard sub-request, whose targets are already interpolated, to `runSplitQuery`. The same query is therefore interpolated twice, and the passed `request.filters` are applied to the expression twice. `applyTemplateVariables` is not idempotent. Ad-hoc filters can be injected into the expression a second time. Interpolated values that contain `$` or `[[ ]]` sequences can be re-expanded. The updated shard test asserts `applyTemplateVariables` is called 5 times, which locks in the double work instead of catching it. Interpolation should happen once, either in `runSplitQuery` only, or the already-interpolated queries should be marked and skipped.

title: Assertion hard-codes 5 calls, which encodes redundant double interpolation
body: `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` replaces the previous `toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)` check on `interpolateVariablesInQueries`. The count of 5 is one initial interpolation plus one per sub-request. It is a brittle number that confirms queries are re-interpolated per shard request, rather than verifying that interpolation happens once at the start. The mock also mutates the query in place, so it cannot reveal non-idempotent behaviour such as duplicated filters.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, so recorded logs are lost
body: `FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()`. `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` now logs through `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`. With this fake, the "Plugin Request Completed" call lands on a throwaway instance. The original `TestLogger`'s `InfoLogs` therefore stays at zero calls, and any test that asserts on those logs will fail or silently stop checking anything. `FromContext` should return the receiver (or a logger that shares its state). No test for `LoggerMiddleware` or the new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` is added in this PR.

title: New middleware has no tests and does not guard against nil requests
body: `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` takes over the contextual-logger behaviour that used to live in the instrumentation middleware, but no test covers it. That includes the endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID and uname attributes it puts on the context. It also dereferences `req.PluginContext` without a nil check, whereas `LoggerMiddleware` explicitly guards `req == nil`. A nil request now panics here, in the new middleware, instead of passing through.

title: traceID and request attributes now depend on middleware ordering and context-provider behaviour
body: `logRequest` used to add `pluginId`, `endpoint`, `uname`, `dsName`, `dsUID` and `traceID` explicitly. It now relies entirely on `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)` picking up attributes set by `ContextualLoggerMiddleware`, plus traceID from the context. If `FromContext` fails the type assertion to `*log.ConcreteLogger`, the wrapper falls back to `d.New()`. That fallback is a plain logger, so the request log silently loses all of these fields. `LoggerMiddleware` depends on `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` running earlier, and nothing enforces that ordering; the dependency is only implicit in the middleware list in `CreateMiddlewares`. No test verifies that the emitted log still carries the same fields as before.

title: Adding FromContext to the exported Logger interface breaks other implementers
body: `FromContext` is a new required method on the public `plog.Logger` interface. Any other implementation of this interface (mocks or logger wrappers in other packages or enterprise code) will stop compiling. The PR only updates `TestLogger` and the infra wrapper. The change is also not mentioned in the PR description.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, so recorded calls are lost
body: LoggerMiddleware now logs through `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`. `TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()`, a new instance, so the `Info` call is recorded on a throwaway logger and never on the original. Any test that injects a `TestLogger` into `NewLoggerMiddleware` and checks `InfoLogs.Calls` or `Ctx` would see nothing. `New` has the same limitation. The fake should return the receiver, or share its state.

title: No tests for the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware or the reworked LoggerMiddleware
body: Plugin ID, endpoint, datasource name/UID, user, and traceID used to be logged explicitly by LoggerMiddleware. They now depend on ContextualLoggerMiddleware putting them into the context and on `FromContext` picking them up. Nothing tests either part. The renamed metrics test only checks metrics. A regression, such as a middleware ordering change or `grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext` hitting its fallback, would silently drop these fields from the "Plugin Request Completed" log line.

title: FromContext silently drops context when the type assertion fails
body: If `d.l.FromContext(ctx)` does not return a `*log.ConcreteLogger`, the code falls back to `d.New()`. The returned logger then has none of the contextual attributes (plugin ID, endpoint, datasource, traceID). The request log line would lose these fields with no error or warning. Before this PR they were added explicitly by LoggerMiddleware, so this is a quiet regression risk.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, so recorded calls are lost
body: LoggerMiddleware.logRequest now logs through `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`. `TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()`, a new instance, so the `InfoLogs` call count, message and context are recorded on a throwaway object. Any test that injects a TestLogger into NewLoggerMiddleware and asserts on `InfoLogs` will see zero calls. The fake should return `f` so the middleware's output stays observable.

title: New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no tests
body: The contextual-logger behaviour (endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID and uname attributes) moved into a new middleware with no unit test. Nothing verifies that the context is enriched per endpoint, or that the stream methods are passed through unchanged. Previously this was covered only indirectly through the instrumentation middleware.

title: Logger middleware drops its explicit traceID/plugin fields and relies on the context logger
body: The log line used to add pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName/dsUID and traceID explicitly. It now gets them only from `FromContext(ctx)`. The wrapper's `FromContext` silently falls back to `d.New()`, which carries no request context, when the type assertion to `*ConcreteLogger` fails. In that case, or if ContextualLoggerMiddleware is not earlier in the chain, the 'Plugin Request Completed' log loses all identifying fields without any error. The traceID is no longer added explicitly, so its presence now depends on the infra logger's context providers.

title: Incomplete rename: test and logger names still say 'instrumentation'
body: `TestInstrumentationMiddleware` was not renamed to match the file and type. The logger is still named `plugin.instrumentation` in pluginsintegration.go, and the helper `instrumentContext` now lives in the contextual logger middleware. This leaves the 'consistent naming' goal of the PR only partly done.

title: Local cache is set before the DB write, so a rejected device bypasses the limit afterward
body: `tagDeviceUI` calls `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, ...)` before `CreateOrUpdateDevice`. When the device limit is reached, `CreateOrUpdateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` and the first request is rejected. The cache key is already set, so for the next ~29 minutes every request from that device hits the early `return nil` and is admitted anonymously without any DB record. The limit is therefore enforced only once per device per cache TTL. The cache entry should be set only after a successful write, or removed when the write fails.

title: Limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert, so concurrent requests can exceed the limit
body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs `CountDevices` in one session and then does the upsert in another, with no transaction or lock. Concurrent requests from many new devices (and multiple Grafana instances) can all see `count < limit` and all insert, so the configured limit can be overshot. An insert guarded by the count (for example `INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < ?`) or a transaction would make it enforceable. At the least the limit should be documented as best-effort.

title: Device tagging moved from a background goroutine to the synchronous auth path
body: The anonymous device tag used to run in a goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout and panic recovery. It now runs inline in `Authenticate` with the request context. Every anonymous request from a device not in the local cache now waits on a COUNT query plus an upsert (or update) before authentication completes. A slow or locked DB therefore adds latency to, or fails, anonymous requests. The panic recovery was also dropped. When the limit is not enabled there is no need to make this synchronous.

title: Limit error returned raw from Authenticate with no user-facing handling or test
body: When the limit is reached, `Authenticate` returns the bare `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. It is not wrapped as an authn error with a meaningful status or message, so the client likely sees a generic 401 or 500 and the server logs may be noisy. There are no tests for this client path or for `TagDevice` propagating the error, and the only new test is at the store level.

title: Provider signature changed to take db.DB, which may break DI wiring
body: `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` now takes `db.DB` and builds the store itself. `ProvideAnonDBStore` also now requires an `int64`, which wire cannot inject. If the wire set still binds `ProvideAnonDBStore`/`AnonStore`, wire generation or compilation fails. The diff shows no wire.go/wire_gen.go changes. Also, no `device_limit` entry was added to defaults.ini/sample.ini or the docs, so the new setting is undiscoverable.

title: anonymousDeviceLimit typed as undefined but backend always sends a number
body: The backend DTO sends `anonymousDeviceLimit` as a non-omitempty int64, so it is `0` when unconfigured. The TS side declares `number | undefined` and defaults the field to `undefined`; the class field then infers type `undefined`. The type does not match the payload, and consumers must treat `0` as unlimited, which is not documented.

title: Device limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert (TOCTOU)
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice first runs CountDevices and then does a separate INSERT. Concurrent requests from many new devices can all see count < limit and all insert, so the limit is exceeded. Under load, which is when the limit matters, it is not enforced. The count and insert need to be atomic, for example one conditional INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*)) < limit, or a transaction.

title: Device tagging moved from async goroutine to synchronous DB work on the auth path
body: The previous implementation tagged the device in a background goroutine with a timeout and panic recovery. TagDevice now runs inline in Authenticate with the request context. Every anonymous request that misses the local cache now blocks on a COUNT query plus an INSERT or UPDATE, which adds latency. A DB slowdown or an expired request context also stalls or fails anonymous auth. The panic recovery was dropped as well.

title: Local cache is populated before the DB write, so rejected devices are cached as tagged
body: tagDeviceUI calls localCache.SetDefault(key) before CreateOrUpdateDevice. If the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached or any other DB error, the key stays cached for 29 minutes. Subsequent requests from that device return nil from the cache and are authenticated as anonymous. The limit is therefore bypassed after the first rejection: only the first request is denied and later ones are let through. The key should be cached only after a successful write.

title: updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached for any zero-rows-affected result
body: A zero-row result is reported as limit reached. On MySQL, RowsAffected returns 0 when the row values are unchanged, because the default driver does not use CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS. An existing device that is re-tagged at the limit with an identical client_ip, user_agent and updated_at second would then be wrongly rejected. The WHERE clause also excludes devices older than 30 days, so a known device that has been idle is rejected as new.

title: Args slice mutated inside the session callback
body: In updateDevice and CreateOrUpdateDevice, `args = append([]any{query}, args...)` reassigns the outer variable inside the closure. If WithDbSession retries the callback, the query gets prepended twice and the Exec call is malformed. Building a local slice inside the closure would avoid this.

title: Limited test coverage for device limit
body: The test only covers a new device being rejected at the limit. It does not cover an existing device still being updatable at the limit, a device older than 30 days being rejected, or the limit disabled with 0 (apart from the incidental use in other tests). There is also no test for the client.go path that now returns the error from Authenticate, and no test for the setting parsing.

title: New device_limit setting is undocumented
body: The new `[auth.anonymous] device_limit` option is not added to conf/defaults.ini, conf/sample.ini or the docs. The PR description is also an empty template. Users cannot discover the option or its semantics, such as 0 meaning unlimited.

title: Local cache is populated before the DB write, so a rejected device bypasses the limit on its next request
body: `tagDeviceUI` calls `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, ...)` before `CreateOrUpdateDevice`. When the store returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the key stays cached (TTL about 29 minutes). The device's next request hits the cache, returns nil from `tagDeviceUI`, and `Authenticate` succeeds. A device over the limit is therefore rejected only once, then allowed for the cache window without being recorded. The cache entry should be set only after a successful write, or removed on error.

title: Device-limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert
body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs `CountDevices` in one session, then performs the upsert in a separate one, with no transaction or lock. Concurrent requests from different new devices can all see `count < limit` and all insert, so the limit can be exceeded, especially under bursts when many new anonymous devices arrive at once. A conditional insert (INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE count < limit) or a transaction would enforce it.

title: Device tagging moved from background goroutine into the request path
body: The previous code tagged the device asynchronously with a detached 2-minute context and panic recovery. It now runs synchronously on the request context. Every uncached anonymous request pays for a COUNT query plus a write when the limit is enabled, and a cancelled request context aborts tagging. The panic recovery was also removed. This is needed to return the limit error, but it adds latency and DB load, and nothing in the PR acknowledges or mitigates it.

title: Frontend type and default disagree with the backend payload
body: The Go DTO always sends `anonymousDeviceLimit` as an `int64` (0 when unset). The frontend types it as `number | undefined`, and `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined` infers the property type as `undefined` in the class. The typing is inconsistent, and the frontend cannot distinguish 'no limit' (0) from unset.

title: New `device_limit` option is undocumented
body: The new `[auth.anonymous] device_limit` setting is read here but not added to `conf/defaults.ini`, `conf/sample.ini` or the docs. The PR description is also an empty template. Operators have no way to discover the option or learn its semantics (0 = unlimited, 30-day window, rejection behaviour).

title: Limit tests are thin
body: The only new test checks that a second new device is rejected at limit 1. There is no test that an existing device can still update at the limit, that expired devices stop counting toward the limit, or that `Anonymous.Authenticate` returns the error. The cache-bypass bug on rejected devices would also be caught by a service-level test.

title: Cleanup ticker interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The cleanup loop now runs every minute instead of every 10 minutes. This looks like a leftover debug change and is unrelated to the PR's purpose. Every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, annotations, query history, etc.) will run 10x more often, adding DB load and increasing lock contention. The job timeout is 9 minutes, so overlapping runs are also more likely. It should be reverted.

title: Debug logging at Error level with full ID lists on every batch
body: Each batch logs at Error level, including the full list of IDs and the condition string. The batch size is configurable and can be thousands of IDs, so this floods the logs and produces false error-level alerts on every successful cleanup. The same pattern is repeated for the after-delete logs and for the count and tag cleanup paths (lines 537, 554, 557, 576, 579). These look like leftover debug statements. Remove them, or use Debug level without the ID list.

title: SQLite parameter limit check uses configured batch size, not the actual ID count, and the 999 limit is outdated
body: The inline-ID path is chosen when the batch size is above 999, otherwise placeholders are used. SQLite 3.32+ allows 32766 variables, so the code is overly conservative. The test name also says the batch size is larger than SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER for SQLite >= 3.32.0. The inlined path is untested for older limits. This is not a bug in itself, but the comment is misleading. Building the string with repeated fmt.Sprintf concatenation is O(n²) for large batches, and a strings.Builder would avoid that.

title: Max-count cleanup relies on offset query; the loop can end early or run under concurrent changes
body: The batch loop terminates only when a batch deletes 0 rows. If `affected` is less than `len(ids)` because rows were deleted concurrently, the loop continues, which is fine. However, `fetchIDs` for annotation_tag with `NOT EXISTS ... LIMIT` and for annotations with `ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT/OFFSET` re-scans the table on each batch. This is the same as before, so it is not a regression, but the tag condition is built without a table alias: `annotation_id = a.id` is evaluated inside the subquery against annotation_tag, which is fine only because of name resolution. The key point is that errors from the fetch and delete are not distinguished from partial progress, and the loop's `x, y` results are returned with ignored context cancellation between fetch and delete.

title: Large-batch test only exercises SQLite's inline-ID path, and the MySQL deadlock fix is untested
body: The new 40003-annotation test covers the SQLite inlined-ID branch. Nothing tests the concurrent-insert deadlock scenario that motivates the PR. Test records are also created with explicit IDs (`ID: i+1`), which changes the previous behaviour of autoincrement IDs and may conflict across subtests if cleanup is incomplete. Cleanup deletes all rows, so this is fine in practice.

title: Cleanup ticker interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The ticker is reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute with no mention in the PR description. It looks like a debugging leftover. All cleanup jobs (snapshots, dashboard versions, annotations, query history, and others) will now run 10x more often. That adds database load, and the annotation cleanup now issues many more round trips per run. clean() also has a 9-minute timeout, so runs can overlap or queue up. Revert to 10 minutes.

title: Debug logging at Error level, logging full ID lists every batch
body: Every batch calls r.log.Error(...) with the full `ids` slice and the SQL condition, both before and after the delete. This happens in the time-based and count-based annotation paths and in CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags (lines 554, 557, 576, 579). Healthy cleanup runs will emit Error-level log lines, which triggers alerting and pollutes logs. With large batch sizes (e.g. 32767), each line contains tens of thousands of IDs. This is clearly leftover debug output and should be removed or lowered to Debug, without dumping the ID list.

title: SQLite parameter-limit check uses configured batch size and a stale 999 limit
body: The inline-ID branch is chosen from the configured batch size, not from len(ids). When the batch size is above 999 it inlines IDs. Otherwise it uses placeholders, and those are limited only by the batch size, so this part is fine. However, the 999 limit is the pre-3.32 default, so newer SQLite builds pay for building a huge string for no reason. The inline path also builds the string with repeated fmt.Sprintf concatenation, which is O(n^2) for 32k IDs. Use strings.Builder, or chunk by len(ids).

title: Orphan tag query: unqualified annotation_id and LIMIT inside the NOT EXISTS condition
body: The condition is `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM annotation a WHERE annotation_id = a.id) LIMIT n`. It is appended as `SELECT id FROM annotation_tag WHERE ... LIMIT n`. That works syntactically, but the unqualified `annotation_id` relies on name resolution to the outer table. If the batch always returns the same orphan IDs and the delete affects 0 rows, the loop ends, which is fine. A real concern: annotation_tag may have no `id` column in some schemas (the original query also used `id`), so the behaviour is the same as before. Mainly, the unqualified column should be `annotation_tag.annotation_id` for clarity and safety.

title: Raw string-concatenated condition passed to fetchIDs relies on annotationType being a trusted fragment
body: fetchIDs interpolates an arbitrary SQL condition into the query and also inserts the table name. The callers pass in annotationType, which is an SQL fragment, via Sprintf. This was already the case before, but it is now a generic helper that accepts unvalidated SQL strings. The empty-condition check is the only guard. This is fragile, though currently inputs are internal constants.

title: Large test creates 40k annotations, which is slow, and the test name claims a SQLite version condition that is not enforced
body: The new case inserts 40003 annotations and 80k tag rows, and the shared fakeSQL runs on whichever DB is configured. The name refers to 'SQLite >= 3.32.0', but nothing is checked. It also does not cover the non-SQLite placeholder path with a large batch (e.g. MySQL or Postgres parameter limits of 65535). Batch 32767 with placeholders is fine, but a batch above 65535 is untested.

title: Cleanup ticker interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The global cleanup job interval was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This looks like a leftover debugging change. It makes every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, short URLs, query history) run 10x more often. The annotation cleanup is the one that contends with inserts, so this raises the chance of the deadlock the PR is meant to fix. It is also unrelated to the PR description and should be reverted.

title: Debug logging at Error level that dumps all IDs on every batch
body: Each batch calls `r.log.Error(...)` with the full `ids` slice (up to the batch size, which may be tens of thousands), the condition and the result. The same pattern appears at lines 537, 554, 557, 576 and 579. These are routine events, not errors, so the log will fill with error-level entries. Dumping huge ID lists on every batch bloats logs and falsely triggers error alerting. Remove them or use Debug without the ID list. The `err` logged right after the `err != nil` check is also always nil.

title: SQLite parameter-limit workaround keyed on batch size config instead of len(ids)
body: The inline-IDs path is chosen from `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999` rather than from the number of IDs actually being deleted. It also hardcodes 999, although newer SQLite builds allow 32766. This is functionally safe, but it builds SQL by string-concatenating the IDs, which is quadratic via repeated `fmt.Sprintf` for tens of thousands of IDs. Use a `strings.Builder`, or chunk the deletes into groups under the limit and always use placeholders. Other drivers also have limits: MySQL allows 65535 placeholders and Postgres allows 65535 bind parameters. A batch size above those would fail on those databases.

title: Orphaned tag cleanup fetches IDs in a way that can loop forever or stay slow
body: In `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags`, `fetchIDs` selects `id` from `annotation_tag` with `NOT EXISTS (... WHERE annotation_id = a.id)` and no ORDER BY. The condition is built as `WHERE NOT EXISTS (...) LIMIT n`. That is valid, but the subquery's unqualified `annotation_id` and `a.id` rely on scoping, so it is fragile. More importantly, the delete count now depends on `RowsAffected` from a separate statement. If the loop's only termination is `affected == 0`, a delete that affects fewer rows than fetched (concurrent deletion) is fine, but a delete that persistently affects zero while IDs are still returned ends the loop early. This leaves orphans, but they are cleaned next cycle, so it is low impact.

title: Condition string built with raw annotationType and ORDER BY/LIMIT concatenation; MaxCount path semantic
body: `fetchIDs` appends the condition as a raw string (`WHERE %s`). The callers embed `annotationType` and the ORDER BY/LIMIT clause into it. `fetchIDs` therefore isn't a reusable, safe helper: any condition lacking the right structure produces broken SQL. `LimitOffset` with a changing offset is correct only because deleted rows shift the window. If a delete partially fails to affect rows, the same IDs are re-fetched on each pass.

title: Large-batch test inserts 40k rows with explicit IDs into a shared DB and does not exercise MySQL/non-SQLite paths
body: The new case sets explicit `ID: int64(i+1)` on annotations, which in this test conflicts with prior leftover rows only if cleanup is incomplete. It also only verifies the SQLite large-batch path. There is no test for the actual deadlock scenario (concurrent inserts during cleanup), nor for `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` with large batches. The test names say SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER, but the fallback threshold used in code is 999, so the 32767 case only checks the inline-ID path.

title: Storage failure is recorded in the legacy duration metric
body: In Create (line 45) and Update (line 129), a failure in `d.Storage.Create` / `d.Storage.Update` is recorded with `recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `recordStorageDuration`. Storage errors are therefore attributed to the legacy histogram, which skews the metrics that are meant to be compared when migrating between modes.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection duration recorded as storage metric
body: In the async goroutine of DeleteCollection, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded with `recordStorageDuration` rather than `recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy latency and errors are mixed into the storage series and the legacy series gets no data for delete-collection.

title: Delete success metric uses `name` as the kind label
body: `recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object name where every other call passes `options.Kind`. This creates a metric label per object name, which is high cardinality, and splits the success series from the error series for the same method.

title: Delete stores the wrong logger in the context
body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` ignores the `log` built with name, kind and method values on the previous line. Downstream storage logging loses that context, unlike every other method in the file, which uses `log`.

title: Async legacy writes reuse the request context and are not detached from it
body: The goroutines derive their timeout context from the request `ctx`. Once the HTTP handler returns, that context is cancelled, so the legacy write is typically cancelled before or during execution, and the failure is only recorded as a metric. The same applies in Update, Delete and DeleteCollection. The "safe measure" legacy write is therefore unreliable. The code needs `context.WithoutCancel` or a fresh background context, with the values it needs copied over.

title: Async legacy Update/Create reuse objects and objInfo after the request returns
body: The goroutine calls `d.Legacy.Update` with the original `objInfo`, and Create passes the original `obj`. Both were already used or mutated by the storage write, and `objInfo.UpdatedObject` is re-evaluated against the legacy object concurrently with the request path. The previous code wrapped `objInfo` in `updateWrapper` so legacy received the exact object stored in unified storage. Now legacy may compute a different result, and there is a data race on the shared request objects. The legacy write is also not ordered across consecutive updates, so older writes can land after newer ones.

title: Redundant `return created, err` after the err != nil check
body: After the early return on error, `err` is always nil. Returning `created, err` (also in Update and Delete) is misleading, and `return created, nil` is clearer.

title: Tests don't verify the async legacy write and race with mock use
body: The tests never assert that the legacy store is called after a successful storage write, and they don't wait for the goroutines. Legacy mock calls can happen after the test ends, and `mock.Mock` is shared between the storage and legacy mocks. Legacy expectations are set up but never verified, so a regression where legacy is never written would pass. The error cases for Create set a legacy expectation that is never used.

title: Redundant per-test registry shadows the package-level one
body: TestMode3_Get creates a new `prometheus.NewRegistry()` that shadows the package-level `p`, while the other tests use `p`. This is inconsistent. The Mode1 test had the same line removed in this PR.

title: Storage create failure recorded with the legacy duration metric
body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the error path calls `recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)`. The failure was in unified storage, so this inflates legacy error metrics and hides storage errors. The same mix-up is in Update at line 129. It should be `recordStorageDuration`.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection duration recorded as storage metric
body: The async legacy DeleteCollection goroutine calls `recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)`. Legacy timings and errors are therefore attributed to storage, which corrupts both series. It should be `recordLegacyDuration`.

title: Delete success metric uses the object name as the kind label
body: The success path calls `recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, ...)`, while the error path and the legacy path use `options.Kind`. Passing the object name as a label adds a high-cardinality, inconsistent label value.

title: Delete stores d.Log in context instead of the enriched logger
body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` drops the `log` with name, kind and method values that was just built. Downstream logging loses that context. It should be `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`.

title: Async legacy writes reuse the request context, which is cancelled when the request ends
body: The goroutines derive their timeout context from the request `ctx`. That context is cancelled as soon as the HTTP request completes, so the legacy write is often cancelled mid-flight or never runs. Request-scoped values such as user identity and namespace are also still needed. The goroutines need a detached context, for example `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)`, plus the 10s timeout. The same issue is in Delete (110), Update (135) and DeleteCollection (163). The legacy copy is meant as a safety net, and this makes it unreliable.

title: Legacy writes are fire-and-forget and the objects are shared with the request
body: The goroutines share `obj`, `objInfo` and `options` with the request after it returns, which risks data races if these are mutated or reused. Legacy errors are only recorded in a metric and never logged. Create passes the original `obj` to legacy rather than the stored object, so server-generated fields such as the name from generateName, the UID and the resource version are missing. Legacy can then get a different identity than unified storage. Update passes the original `objInfo` to Legacy, which can compute a different result than Storage did. The old code wrapped it in `updateWrapper` to apply the stored result.

title: Tests do not verify async legacy writes
body: The tests never assert that Legacy Create, Update, Delete or DeleteCollection were called. Delete and DeleteCollection have no legacy mock set up, so the goroutine calls into an unconfigured testify mock and panics or races after the test finishes. The async path is also not synchronised. In the create failure case, the legacy mock is set up but should never be called, and nothing asserts that.

title: Update error path records legacy duration instead of storage duration
body: When `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)`. The failure comes from the unified store, so this should be `recordStorageDuration`. The same slip is in Create at line 45. The metrics misattribute storage failures to legacy, and storage error metrics are never recorded.

title: DeleteCollection legacy goroutine records storage metric instead of legacy
body: After the async `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection`, the code calls `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)`. It should call `recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy latency and errors get folded into the storage metrics, which corrupts both series. Legacy delete-collection is never recorded as legacy.

title: Delete uses d.Log instead of the enriched log for the context
body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` drops the `name`, `kind` and `method` values built into `log`. Downstream logging then lacks that context. Every other method uses `log`.

title: Delete success metric uses `name` as the kind label
body: `recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object name where every other call passes `options.Kind`. This creates a Prometheus label value per object, which means unbounded cardinality, and it splits the series between success and error.

title: Async goroutines reuse the request context and objects after the request returns
body: The legacy write goroutines derive their context from the request `ctx`, which is cancelled once the HTTP request completes. The legacy write then races with the cancellation, so the 'safety' write to legacy can be cancelled and silently fail. Update also reuses `objInfo`, `createValidation` and `updateValidation` closures after the request has returned. These may capture request state, and the legacy update recomputes the object from the legacy store rather than using the updated result. The result is a non-deterministic legacy copy. A detached context (`context.WithoutCancel`) is needed. Create and Delete have the same problem.

title: Redundant `return created, err`; legacy failures are never logged
body: After the error check, `err` is always nil, so `return created, err` is misleading. In the goroutines (Create, Delete, Update, DeleteCollection), legacy errors are only recorded in metrics and never logged. That makes the asynchronous legacy write hard to debug when it fails.

title: Tests don't synchronize with or verify the async legacy writes
body: The code launches goroutines that call the legacy mock. Tests neither wait for them nor assert that legacy was called or not called. The goroutines can run after the test finishes and race on the shared `mock.Mock`, which is not safe under `-race`. In the Delete and DeleteCollection tests no legacy mock is set up, so the goroutine calls an unmocked method, which panics in testify and can crash the test binary. The async behavior this PR introduces is effectively untested.

title: No re-check of cache after acquiring write lock (thundering herd)
body: After the RLock check misses, every concurrent caller takes the write lock in turn and re-reads and parses the manifest from disk (and from the CDN if enabled). The cache is not re-checked once the write lock is held. On startup, or any time the cache is nil, N concurrent requests each do the full file read and JSON decode serially. Add a second check of `entryPointAssetsCache != nil && cfg.Env != setting.Dev` after `Lock()`.

title: Cache overwritten with nil result when loading fails
body: `entryPointAssetsCache = result` runs even when `err != nil`, so `result` is nil. A transient failure, for example a missing manifest, replaces a previously valid cache with nil. In non-dev mode this discards good assets and forces a reload on every call. Callers get `(nil, err)`. The cache should only be updated when `err == nil`. The fix to the data race did not address this.

title: No test covering the race fix
body: The PR fixes a data race but adds no test, such as a concurrent `GetWebAssets` run under `-race`, to guard against regression. Nothing exercises the new locking.

title: No re-check of cache after taking the write lock (thundering herd)
body: After the read-lock fast path misses, every concurrent caller that saw a nil cache serializes on `Lock()` and then re-reads the manifest file (and possibly makes an HTTP call) one by one.
