With a JSON serializer the datetime is either rejected or turned into a string. The task then calls `from_dict`, which does `cls(**input_dict)`, so `queued` is a string rather than a datetime. Nothing checks this, and the type is silently wrong. `to_dict` should serialize the timestamp explicitly and `from_dict` should parse it.

title: `from_dict` does not validate field types
body: `from_dict` only catches `ValueError` and `TypeError`. A dict with correct keys but a wrong `integration_id` type is accepted without complaint. A malformed source then fails the equality check in `should_sync` quietly, and the cycle protection is skipped.

title: `assignment_source` kwarg is passed to every integration's `sync_assignee_outbound`
body: The task now always calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=...)`. The abstract `sync_assignee_outbound` signature accepts `**kwargs`, but other implementations (Jira, VSTS, GitHub and others) may not. Any that don't will raise `TypeError` and the outbound assignee sync will fail. Every implementation needs to be checked or updated. The PR also changes the `sync_status_outbound` abstract signature without touching its implementations.

title: Inbound sync still not covered for other callers of `where_should_sync`
body: `where_should_sync` calls `should_sync(key)` without a source. That is fine for this path. But `sync_group_assignee_inbound` builds the `AssignmentSource` from the `integration` argument, so the cycle break depends on `integration.id` matching `org_integration.integration_id`. If other assign paths do not pass an `assignment_source`, such as the Jira webhook handling or `sync_status_inbound`, the loop is still possible. The PR gives no evidence these are covered.

title: No test for deassign with a matching source, or for another integration
body: Only the `assign` path is tested with a matching-source integration. There is no test that `deassign` with a matching source skips the outbound sync. There is also no test that a different integration still syncs. The task-level serialization round trip through `to_dict`/`from_dict` is not covered by an assertion either.

title: `queued` default is evaluated once at import time
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once, when the module is imported, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit value gets the same stale timestamp (process start time). The field is meant to record when the assignment was queued. It should use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. The test only checks that `queued` is not None, so it does not catch this.

title: `to_dict` puts a raw datetime into Celery task kwargs
body: `asdict(self)` returns `queued` as a `datetime`. `sync_group_assignee_outbound` passes this dict to `apply_async` as kwargs. With the JSON serializer the datetime may fail to serialize or may come back as a string. After the round trip, `from_dict` would build the dataclass with `queued` as a string, which is the wrong type. It is also possible that `from_dict` raises for unexpected types, since it only catches ValueError and TypeError. `queued` should be serialized explicitly, for example as an ISO string, and parsed back in `from_dict`.

title: `where_should_sync` calls `should_sync` without `sync_source`
body: The sync-cycle check is only applied in the outbound task. Other callers of `should_sync` ignore the source, which is fine for inbound. However, `sync_status_outbound` gained an `assignment_source` parameter in the abstract signature that no caller ever passes. This is dead plumbing and implies a status-cycle guard that does not exist.

title: New `assignment_source` kwarg is passed to every integration's `sync_assignee_outbound`
body: The task now always passes `assignment_source=...` to `installation.sync_assignee_outbound`. The abstract signature accepts `**kwargs`, but the diff does not update the concrete implementations. Any integration whose `sync_assignee_outbound` lacks `**kwargs` will raise a TypeError on every outbound sync, and the retry decorator will retry that error. Concrete implementations (Jira, VSTS, etc.) should be verified or updated.

title: Cycle-prevention test covers only the assign path, not deassign or other-integration cases
body: The only new test checks `assign` with a matching source. Missing cases: `deassign` with a source (which the inbound path uses), and the case where a different integration is the source and outbound sync must still happen. The `sync_group_assignee_inbound` tests also don't verify that an AssignmentSource is passed through.

title: `queued` default is evaluated once at import time
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated when the class body runs, so every `AssignmentSource` created without an explicit `queued` gets the same process-start timestamp. The field is meant to record when the assignment was queued. It should use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

title: `to_dict()` puts a datetime into Celery task kwargs and `from_dict` can't round-trip it
body: `asdict(self)` keeps `queued` as a `datetime`. `sync_group_assignee_outbound` passes this dict as `apply_async` kwargs. If the broker serializer is JSON, the datetime is either rejected or turned into a string. On the receiving side, `from_dict` then builds `queued` as a string rather than a datetime. The dict is not a safe serialization format. The test only checks that `queued` is not None. Serialize `queued` to ISO format explicitly, or drop the field.

title: Passing `assignment_source` kwarg to `sync_assignee_outbound` breaks integrations that don't accept it
body: The task now always calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)`. Implementations that lack `**kwargs`, or that reject unexpected arguments, will raise `TypeError`. The abstract signature has `**kwargs`, but the diff doesn't show that every concrete integration (Jira, VSTS, GitHub, etc.) accepts it. The PR also changes only the abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature. That change is unrelated to this fix.

title: Inbound sync check does not use the source, and other call sites of `should_sync` are unverified
body: `where_should_sync` still calls `should_sync(key)` without a source. That is fine for inbound. But `should_sync` gained a new parameter in a base class and a subclass, and the PR does not show that every override (for example, integrations that override `should_sync`) was updated. An override with the old signature would raise `TypeError` when the task passes the second positional argument.

title: Runtime import of the integrations package from the models layer
body: `AssignmentSource` is imported at module level and used only as a type annotation. The import adds a runtime dependency from `sentry.models` on `sentry.integrations.services`, and `from __future__ import annotations` is already in effect. It should go under `TYPE_CHECKING` to avoid the import-cycle risk.

title: No test covers the end-to-end inbound webhook path or deassign with a source
body: The new tests cover only `assign` with a matching source. There is no test that `sync_group_assignee_inbound` passes the source through to outbound sync. There is also none for `deassign` with a matching source, or for a non-matching source (another integration) still syncing. The task-level `from_dict` round-trip through Celery is not tested either, which is where the serialization problem would show up.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now an uninstantiable abstract class
body: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` now subclasses `StatefulDetectorHandler` with an empty body. That base class has abstract members: `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the newly added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. Calling `group_type.detector_handler(self)` in `Detector.detector_handler` for a `metric_alert_fire` detector will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class`. `process_detectors` does not catch it. Before this change the handler was concrete and returned an empty result. A detector of this type would now crash processing instead of being a harmless no-op. Keep the stub concrete (return `{}` from `evaluate`), or implement the abstract methods.

title: evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: The docstring of `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` says it "returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`". The method now returns a dict keyed by group key, which is the point of this PR's signature change. The docstring should be updated.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now an abstract class and cannot be instantiated
body: The handler was changed from a concrete `DetectorHandler` with a stub `evaluate` to `StatefulDetectorHandler` with an empty body. `StatefulDetectorHandler` has abstract members: `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the newly added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. None are implemented here. `MetricAlertFire` is registered with this class as its `detector_handler`, so `Detector.detector_handler` raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class` for any detector of type `metric_alert_fire`. `process_detectors` would then crash instead of returning an empty result as it did before. Either keep the previous no-op handler or implement the abstract methods. The leftover `TODO: This will be a stateful detector` comment is also misleading now.

title: evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: The `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` docstring still says it 'returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`'. The signature now returns a `dict` keyed by group key, so the documentation contradicts the contract this PR changed.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now an abstract class that cannot be instantiated
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler with an empty body. That base class has abstract members that the subclass does not implement: counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values and the newly added build_occurrence_and_event_data. MetricAlertFire.detector_handler points at this class. Detector.detector_handler calls group_type.detector_handler(self), so any detector of type metric_alert_fire will raise TypeError ("Can't instantiate abstract class") inside process_detectors. Before this change the handler had a stub evaluate that returned [], so this is a regression. Keep the old stub behaviour or implement the abstract methods.

title: evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: The signature of StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate now returns dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult], but the docstring still says it "returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`".

title: Public functions renamed and moved with no caller or test updates in this PR
body: `mark_failed_threshold` became `try_incident_threshold` in `incidents.py`. `create_issue_platform_occurrence` became `create_incident_occurrence` in `incident_occurrence.py`. `get_failure_reason`, `get_monitor_environment_context`, the `*_HUMAN_FAILURE*` maps and `SimpleCheckIn` were also removed from `mark_failed.py`. The PR changes only these four source files. Any remaining import or `mock.patch('sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed.<old name>')` elsewhere, such as the existing mark_failed tests, will now fail with ImportError or AttributeError. The reorganization also adds no tests for the new modules, so `get_failure_reason` and the threshold logic are not covered at their new locations. The author should grep for and update every reference to the old names, and move or add tests alongside the new modules.

title: Display-friendly schedule_type is computed but never used
body: `get_monitor_environment_context` copies the config and replaces `schedule_type` with its display value. The returned dict then uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config`, the original, instead of the local `config` copy. The copy is dead code, and the event context carries the raw `schedule_type`. The bug existed before the move, but this PR touches the code and could fix it by returning `config`.

title: Unused logger in new module
body: `logger` is defined but never used in `incident_occurrence.py`. The same applies to `incidents.py` at line 11.

title: Public functions renamed and moved without updating other importers or tests
body: `mark_failed_threshold` became `try_incident_threshold`, and `create_issue_platform_occurrence` became `create_incident_occurrence`. `get_failure_reason`, `get_monitor_environment_context`, the `*_HUMAN_FAILURE_*` maps and `SimpleCheckIn` also moved out of `mark_failed.py`. The PR changes only four files and touches no tests. Any remaining import or `mock.patch` of the old names in `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` (for example in monitor tests, or in tasks that import `get_failure_reason`) will now fail with ImportError or AttributeError. I could not check this from the diff alone. Update those callers and tests, or re-export the old names, and add tests for the new modules.

title: Copied config is built but the original config is returned
body: `get_monitor_environment_context` copies `monitor.config` and replaces `schedule_type` with its display value. It then returns `monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead of the modified copy, so the conversion is dead code and the raw numeric `schedule_type` goes into the event context. This behaviour came from the old code, but the function is being moved into a new module, so it is a good time to return `config` and fix it.

title: Public functions renamed and moved with no compatibility aliases or test updates
body: `mark_failed_threshold` is now `try_incident_threshold` in a new module. `create_issue_platform_occurrence` is now `create_incident_occurrence`. `get_failure_reason`, `get_monitor_environment_context`, `HUMAN_FAILURE_STATUS_MAP` and `SINGULAR_HUMAN_FAILURE_MAP` moved to `incident_occurrence`, and `SimpleCheckIn` moved to `types`. All of these are gone from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed`, and the PR touches only four files with no test changes. Any other importer or `mock.patch('sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed.<name>')` target, including existing mark_failed tests, will fail with ImportError or AttributeError. Update the remaining callers and tests, or re-export the old names.

title: Copied config with display schedule_type is computed but never used
body: `get_monitor_environment_context` builds `config = monitor.config.copy()` and swaps in the human-readable `schedule_type`. The returned dict then uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead of `config`, so the substitution is dead code and the raw value is sent. This bug was carried over unchanged in the move; the refactor is a chance to fix it.

title: isinstance check against multiprocessing.Process never matches SpawnProcess, so hung flushers are never killed
body: Processes come from `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which is `SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` subclasses `BaseProcess`, not `multiprocessing.Process` (that is `context.Process`), so `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is always False. The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. The new guard means a hung process (cause="hang") is never killed before `_create_process_for_shards` starts a replacement. The old process keeps running against the same Redis shards alongside the new one, and the `ValueError` handling no longer matters. The same broken check in `join()` (line 346) means `terminate()` is never called either. Use `hasattr(process, 'kill')` / `isinstance(process, threading.Thread)` negated, or check against `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`.

title: time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
body: The test starts with `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, so the newly added `time.sleep(0.1)`, meant to "give flusher threads time to process after drift change", does nothing. The flusher thread has no guaranteed time to flush before `step.join()` sets `stopped`. `assert (msg,) = messages` can then fail intermittently. Wait with a real sleep (capture the original `time.sleep` before patching), or poll until `messages` is non-empty with a timeout.

title: join() stops terminating remaining processes once the deadline is hit
body: When the deadline expires the loop `break`s. The remaining processes are neither waited on nor terminated, because `terminate()` sits inside the loop body after the wait. With several processes, the later ones are left running (or killed only by daemon semantics). Terminate all processes after the wait phase regardless of the deadline.

title: Inconsistent metric tag name `shards` vs `shard`
body: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `segment_size_bytes` use the tag `shard`, while `wait_produce` uses `shards`. `flusher_unhealthy` uses `shard` with a single int. The value is a comma-joined list of shards when a process owns several. This makes dashboards and aggregations inconsistent and produces high-cardinality tag values. Use one tag name and consistent semantics.

title: Unused `_create_process_for_shard` method
body: `_create_process_for_shard` is never called. Remove the dead code.

title: Hung flusher process is never killed because the isinstance check never matches SpawnProcess
body: `process.kill()` is now guarded by `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. The processes come from `mp_context.Process` on a spawn context, which are `SpawnProcess` objects. `SpawnProcess` subclasses `BaseProcess`, not `multiprocessing.context.Process`, so the isinstance check is False. When a flusher is declared hung (`cause == "hang"`), it is not killed and a replacement is started for the same shards. Two flushers then run on the same shards and the old one leaks. Repeated restarts accumulate orphaned processes, and duplicate segments can be flushed. The same wrong check in `join()` (line 346) means `terminate()` is never called either. Check against `threading.Thread` instead, or use `hasattr(process, 'kill')`.

title: The added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
body: `test_basic` patches `time.sleep` to a no-op at the top, so the `time.sleep(0.1)` added to "give flusher threads time to process" does not wait. The test still depends on thread scheduling to get the flushed message before `join()`, so it can be flaky. Use a real wait (poll until `messages` is non-empty, with a timeout), or capture the real sleep before patching.

title: Inconsistent metric tag name and comma-joined shard values
body: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `segment_size_bytes` are tagged `shard`, but `wait_produce` is tagged `shards`. This makes the metrics hard to correlate and aggregate. The tag value is a comma-joined list of shards, which creates a new tag value for every distinct shard grouping. `flusher_unhealthy` uses a per-shard tag instead, so the conventions also differ across metrics.

title: Unused method _create_process_for_shard
body: `_create_process_for_shard` is not called anywhere. It would also restart a process without the kill or restart-count handling that `_ensure_processes_alive` does. Remove it.

title: Hung flusher process is never killed because the isinstance check is always False
body: The new code guards the kill with `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. Processes come from `mp_context.Process`, which is `SpawnProcess`. That class derives from `BaseProcess`, not from `multiprocessing.context.Process`, so the check is always False. The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally, so this is a regression. When a flusher is detected as hung (`cause == "hang"`), it stays alive and a replacement is started for the same shards. Two flushers then run on the same shards, which can produce duplicate segments and leak processes. The same wrong check in `join()` means `terminate()` is also never called. Use `hasattr(process, 'kill')`, check `isinstance(process, threading.Thread)` and invert it, or check `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`.

title: join() skips terminating remaining processes when the deadline passes
body: In the `join()` loop, `break` fires when the deadline has passed. This skips the `terminate()` call for every process not yet visited. With several flusher processes, one slow process can use up the whole timeout, and the others are left running until the interpreter exits. The loop should terminate all processes regardless of the deadline, or the deadline check should only skip the waiting.

title: time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
body: The test sets `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at the top. The added `time.sleep(0.1)`, commented as giving flusher threads time to process, therefore does nothing. `step.join()` then races against the flusher thread picking up the new drift. The `(msg,) = messages` assertion can be flaky. Use the real sleep, for example by saving a reference before patching, or poll until `messages` is non-empty with a timeout.

title: Inconsistent metric tag name: "shards" vs "shard"
body: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` use the tag `shard`. `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` uses `shards`. The value is a comma-joined list in all three. Dashboards that group by tag will not line up. In `spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy` the `shard` tag is a single int, which is a third meaning for the same tag name.

title: Unused dead method _create_process_for_shard
body: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is never called. `_ensure_processes_alive` calls `_create_process_for_shards` directly. Remove it.

title: Strategy close()/terminate() shuts down the factory-owned queue pool, which is reused after a rebalance
body: The FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and handed to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy built by create_with_partitions. Arroyo closes and joins the old strategy on every rebalance, and close()/join()/terminate() call queue_pool.shutdown(). That sets the worker flags and shuts down the queues permanently. The next strategy created by the factory then reuses a dead pool: workers have exited and queue.put() raises ShutDown. The exception is caught in submit(), where the offset is marked complete, so after the first rebalance messages are silently dropped and their offsets are committed. The pool's lifetime should belong to the factory (shutdown() in the factory), not to the per-assignment strategy.

title: Submit failure marks the offset as completed, so the message is lost and its offset committed
body: If anything in submit() raises (grouping function error, queue.put failure, and so on), the except block calls add_offset followed by complete_offset. The message was never processed, but the offset becomes committable and is committed, so it is permanently skipped. Combined with the shut-down-pool issue, every message after a rebalance is dropped this way. The error should propagate or retry rather than be treated as success.

title: Unbounded queues and no backpressure despite the docstring claiming it
body: The queues are created with queue.Queue() and no maxsize, and submit()/poll() never raise MessageRejected or pause. The strategy docstring says 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', which is false. If workers are slower than Kafka ingestion, which is the exact scenario this PR targets, the consumer keeps pulling messages. Memory grows without bound and uncommitted lag piles up in process.

title: Committable-offset computation requires strictly contiguous Kafka offsets
body: The loop only advances while every integer offset is present in all_offsets. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be contiguous: transaction markers, compaction and skipped records all leave gaps. Once such a gap is hit, start = last_committed+1 points at an offset that will never be added, so the loop breaks forever. Commits for that partition stall permanently and all_offsets grows without bound. Tracking should be based on the ordered offsets actually seen (commit up to the largest offset below the smallest outstanding one), not on integer contiguity.

title: Commit called from a background thread; offset state is never reset across rebalances
body: The Arroyo commit callable is invoked from a separate daemon thread rather than the consumer thread that polls. StreamProcessor's commit is not designed for cross-thread use. The shared OffsetTracker also keeps last_committed/outstanding state for partitions that have since been revoked. Stale entries can then be committed for partitions this consumer no longer owns, and a re-assigned partition inherits an old last_committed. No clean-up is done in the strategy lifecycle.

title: Worker shutdown flag defeats the graceful drain
body: shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False). The worker loop checks `while not self.shutdown` after each item, so it exits after its current item even though queued items remain. The docstring says 'gracefully' and the shutdown(immediate=False) call intends to drain. The remaining items are abandoned, and the join timeout of 5s per worker can also serially block shutdown for up to 100s with 20 workers.

title: Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its docstring and passes only due to timing
body: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling says errors 'don't block offset commits', but it asserts that no offset was committed. In the implementation a failed item is completed in `finally`, so offsets 100/101 are committable and would be committed on the next 1s commit-loop tick. The test passes only because it checks about 0.2s after processing, before the commit loop fires. The assertion is both wrong in intent and flaky, and it does not verify the real behaviour.

title: Distribution test depends on randomized string hashing
body: test_different_groups_distributed asserts that 20 string keys hit all 3 queues, but the queue is chosen with Python's per-process randomized hash(). The test is therefore non-deterministic. It fails with small but real probability, roughly 0.1%, and it asserts a property that nothing in the code guarantees.

title: Strategy close() shuts down the factory-shared queue pool; the next rebalance silently drops and commits messages
body: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`, `terminate()` and `join()` call `queue_pool.shutdown()`. That pool is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and reused by every strategy from `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker`. Arroyo closes the strategy and calls `create_with_partitions` again on every partition rebalance. After the first rebalance the new strategy therefore gets a pool whose workers have exited and whose queues are shut down. `queue.put` then raises `queue.ShutDown`. `submit()` catches that with its generic `except Exception`, calls `add_offset` and `complete_offset`, and the offset becomes committable. The result is that every message after a rebalance is dropped and its offset committed, which is data loss. The pool should be created per strategy, or the strategy should not own the shared pool's lifecycle. The `OffsetTracker` is also shared across rebalances, so stale offsets and `last_committed` for revoked partitions persist.

title: Any failure while enqueuing is treated as 'processed' and the offset is committed
body: The broad `except Exception` in `submit()` logs the error, then registers and immediately completes the offset. That includes failures of `queue_pool.submit` (for example `queue.ShutDown`) and of `grouping_fn`. The offset becomes committable and the message is permanently skipped. Only decode failures (result is None) should be skipped this way. Infrastructure errors should be raised or retried so the message is not lost.

title: Claimed backpressure does not exist; queues and offset tracker are unbounded
body: The docstring promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up'. The queues are `queue.Queue()` with no maxsize, `submit()` never blocks, and `poll()` never raises `MessageRejected`. If one queue is slow, which is the scenario this PR targets, the consumer keeps reading from Kafka. Messages accumulate in memory without bound. `all_offsets` grows with them, and so does the per-commit `range()` scan. The consumer can run out of memory, and the offset stuck at the slow item can never advance. Use bounded queues and reject or block when full.

title: Kafka commit callback is invoked from a background thread
body: `commit_function` (arroyo's `commit`) is called from `_commit_loop`, a separate daemon thread, while the StreamProcessor main thread is polling and managing the consumer. Arroyo's commit callback and the Kafka consumer state are designed to be used from the processing thread. Calling them concurrently risks races and corrupted offset state. The commit is also not tied to partition ownership, so offsets can be committed for partitions already revoked during a rebalance. Commits should be issued from `poll()`/`submit()` in the main thread.

title: Non-contiguous Kafka offsets stall commits forever
body: Commit advancement requires every integer offset in the range to be present in `all_offsets`. Offsets that are never delivered to the strategy (transaction control markers, compacted or skipped offsets) look like a permanent gap. Commits for that partition then stall indefinitely and `all_offsets` and `outstanding` grow without bound. The gap test encodes this as intended behaviour. A tracker keyed on submitted offsets (commit up to the lowest outstanding offset minus one) would avoid it.

title: Error-handling test contradicts the implementation and its own docstring
body: The test docstring says errors in processing 'don't block offset commits'. The implementation completes the offset in a `finally` block even when processing fails, so offsets 100 and 101 are committed (as 102). The assertion `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` expects no commit. It passes only because the wait loop ends before the 1-second commit loop fires, so it is timing-dependent. It verifies nothing about the intended behaviour and will fail or flake as timing changes.

title: Distribution test depends on randomized string hashing
body: `test_different_groups_distributed` asserts that 20 group keys cover all 3 queues. The queue index comes from `hash(str)`, which is randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED). There is a small but non-zero chance (about 0.1%) that a queue is missed, so the test can fail occasionally.

title: Strategy close() shuts down the factory-wide shared queue pool, so after a rebalance new strategies get dead queues and drop messages
body: `FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and passed to every strategy from `create_with_partitions`. Arroyo calls `close()` or `join()` on the strategy at every rebalance, and that calls `queue_pool.shutdown()`. This sets `worker.shutdown = True`, calls `q.shutdown()` on every queue, and joins the workers. The next `create_with_partitions` reuses the same pool: the workers are dead and the queues are shut down. `queue_pool.submit` then raises `queue.ShutDown` on `put`. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` catches this as a generic Exception, marks the offset added and completed, and the commit loop commits it. Every message after the first rebalance is silently dropped and its offset committed, which is data loss. The pool lifetime must be tied to the factory, not to individual strategies, or the pool must be created per strategy.

title: Arroyo commit callback is called from a background thread and may commit revoked partitions
body: `_commit_loop` runs in its own daemon thread and calls the arroyo `commit` callable directly. Arroyo's commit function mutates `StreamProcessor` state and is meant to be called from the consumer's main thread, so this is a data race. The `OffsetTracker` also keeps state for partitions after they are revoked. The commit thread may therefore try to commit offsets for partitions no longer assigned, which errors or conflicts with the new owner. On `close()` there is no final commit after the queues drain, and the tracker is never cleared per assignment.

title: Commit requires strictly contiguous offsets; any real Kafka offset gap stalls commits forever
body: `get_committable_offsets` stops at the first offset that is not in `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be dense: transaction markers, compaction and skipped offsets all create gaps. The first such gap permanently blocks commits for that partition. `all_offsets` and the per-second scan range then grow without bound, and consumer lag grows with no error. The tracker should treat consecutive submitted offsets as contiguous rather than requiring every integer in between.

title: Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure despite the docstring
body: The docstring claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but `queue.Queue()` is created with no maxsize, `submit` never blocks, and `poll` never signals backpressure (it raises no `MessageRejected`). If the workers are slower than the topic, or one queue is clogged by a slow item, the consumer keeps reading and buffers all messages in memory. Memory grows unbounded and the commit lag is never surfaced to arroyo. This undermines the stated goal of handling slow items.

title: "Graceful" shutdown drops queued items instead of draining them
body: `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before shutting down the queues. The worker loop checks `while not self.shutdown`, so each worker exits after its current item and never drains the rest of its queue. Remaining items are neither processed nor committed. They are redelivered, which is at-least-once but contradicts the docstring and `immediate=False`. Workers also block forever in `get()` if the queue is never shut down.

title: Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its stated behavior and is timing-dependent
body: `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` says errors must not block offset commits, yet it asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`. The worker's `finally` completes the offset even on exception, so the offsets are committable. The assertion only passes because the test finishes before the 1-second commit loop fires. The test is racy and does not verify the intended behavior. It should wait for a commit and assert that offset 102 is committed.

title: Distribution test depends on randomized string hashing
body: `test_different_groups_distributed` asserts that 20 string keys hit all 3 queues. `get_queue_for_group` uses Python's built-in `hash()`, which is randomized per process via PYTHONHASHSEED. There is a small but nonzero probability (roughly 0.1%) that a queue is unused, which makes the test flaky. It also shows the assignment is not stable across processes.

title: Backup codes are overwritten and returned before 2FA is enabled
body: The setup endpoint generates new backup codes, persists them and returns them in plaintext, all before the TOTP code is verified. If a user cancels setup, the stored codes remain on the account. Because twoFactorEnabled is false, they are unused for now, but they stay valid secrets. If 2FA is later enabled by another path, they apply. Codes should be generated at enable time, or cleared when setup is cancelled.

title: Disable endpoint does not guard against non-string backupCode or malformed data
body: `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll(...)` throws a 500 if backupCode is not a string, for example a number or an object sent in the JSON body. `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` is also unguarded. Validate that the input is a string first. In addition, consumed codes are nulled in the login flow, and `indexOf` on user input could match a null or empty entry if the input is odd.

title: Backup code check has no format validation and a non-atomic consume
body: `credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` is compared with plain `indexOf`. This is not constant-time, though that is minor. More importantly, consuming the code is a read-modify-write, so two concurrent requests with the same code can both succeed. Also, the existing condition `user.password && !credentials.totpCode` skips the password check whenever totpCode is empty. Passing a backupCode with no totpCode therefore works, but a TOTP code with a wrong password still skips the password check. This pre-existing behavior is now extended by the backup path.

title: Modal state and the blob URL are not cleaned up after the backup codes are shown
body: resetState does not clear backupCodes, the blob URL, the secret or dataUri. The object URL is never revoked on close or unmount, so a leak remains. The plaintext codes also stay in component state after the dialog closes. Also, onOpenChange (clicking the overlay or pressing Esc) closes the dialog on the backup codes step without calling resetState, so the next open may resume at the backup codes step.

title: Component is misnamed TwoFactor
body: The default export in BackupCode.tsx is named `TwoFactor`, which duplicates the name of the other component and is confusing in stack traces and devtools.

title: Lost access toggle button lacks type="button"
body: The Button defaults to type submit inside the Form, so clicking 'Lost access' or 'Go back' may submit the form. The submit would carry validation of the required fields, such as the backup code, and could trigger an unwanted disable request. Set type="button". The same applies to the Cancel button.

title: Backup-code login can bypass the password check
body: The password check is skipped whenever `credentials.totpCode` is set (line 121). The backup-code branch only checks `twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode`. The password check is conditioned only on `totpCode` being absent, so it still runs when a backupCode is sent without a totpCode. But an attacker who sends both `totpCode` (any value) and a valid `backupCode` skips the password check and logs in with only a backup code. With no totpCode, backup-code login would need the password, which is the intended behavior. The skip condition should not be satisfiable by an arbitrary `totpCode` string.

title: Non-constant-time backup code comparison with no single-use check for nulls
body: `indexOf` on the decrypted array compares codes with plain equality. Used codes are replaced with `null`, which is fine. Rate limiting on this path is only the generic per-email limit. The read-modify-write of the encrypted array is not atomic, so two concurrent logins with the same code can both succeed before the update lands and the code is consumed twice.

title: Backup code type not validated and not consumed
body: `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll` throws a 500 if backupCode is not a string, for example a number or object. There is no rate limit on this endpoint, so a session holder with the password can brute-force the codes. If a backupCode is sent with a stale `code`, the backup branch takes precedence, which can be confusing.

title: Backup codes overwritten on every setup call
body: Setup regenerates and overwrites backup codes each time it is called while 2FA is not yet enabled. If the user abandons the flow, stale codes remain stored. Codes are returned before the TOTP is verified, so the client holds codes for a not-yet-enabled 2FA. The codes are shown only after enabling, so a user who closes the modal early or reloads loses them with no regenerate option.

title: Backup codes dialog can be dismissed, and state is not fully reset
body: After enabling, the close button calls `onEnable` and `resetState`, but `backupCodes` and the blob URL are never cleared or revoked after close. The codes stay in React state, and the object URL leaks. Clicking outside the dialog (`onOpenChange`) bypasses the codes screen, so the user may never see their codes.

title: Component misnamed TwoFactor
body: The default export in BackupCode.tsx is named `TwoFactor`, which duplicates the name of the other component and is misleading.

title: No tests for backup code login or disable
body: Backup-code login and disable are untested, as the TODO admits. The copy and download assertions do not check content. The new security-sensitive logic has no coverage.

title: Backup-code login skips password verification and 2FA bypass is possible
body: The password check is skipped whenever `credentials.totpCode` is set (existing logic). The backup-code branch is reached with `credentials.backupCode` and no `totpCode`, so the password is verified there. However, a request carrying both a bogus `totpCode` and a `backupCode` skips the password check and then passes the backup-code branch, logging in with only a backup code and no password. The password-skip condition must also account for `backupCode`, or the backup-code branch must require the password.

title: Backup code comparison is non-constant-time and codes are never invalidated reliably
body: `indexOf` on the plaintext codes is a non-constant-time comparison. Used codes are set to `null` and re-encrypted via read-modify-write, so two concurrent logins with the same code can both succeed. The rate limit is keyed per email only, so there is limited protection against guessing.

title: Backup code input not validated or normalized
body: `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll` throws a 500 if backupCode is not a string (e.g. a number or object). Used codes are stored as null, but the lookup does not guard against this. Add type validation. The same applies to credentials.backupCode in next-auth-options.

title: Backup codes regenerated on every setup call
body: Setup writes fresh backup codes each time it runs, before 2FA is confirmed. The codes are returned to the client before the user has verified TOTP. If the user abandons setup, stale codes remain stored. Codes are shown only after enable succeeds, but they are held in client state and the old URL object is never revoked on close.

title: Modal state not reset after enabling; codes persist
body: After the user closes the backup-code step, backupCodes, backupCodesUrl and the form totpCode remain. The blob URL is never revoked on close. The form totpCode value is not cleared, so reopening can auto-submit the old 6-digit code via the watch effect. Dismissing the dialog via onOpenChange (outside click or Esc) bypasses resetState and onEnable, leaving the UI inconsistent with 2FA already enabled.

title: BackupCode field is required, but TOTP is not, and the lost-access toggle button lacks type
body: The toggle Button has no `type="button"`, so it may submit the form depending on the Button default. A submit would trigger validation and a disable request when the user only meant to switch modes.

title: Null deref when destinationCalendar is empty and location is Google Meet
body: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` yields `undefined` when the array is empty or null, but the next line reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining. Bookings with a Meet location and no destination calendar will throw a TypeError instead of falling back to Cal Video. Use `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.

title: Team destination calendars lost when the organizer has none
body: `evt.destinationCalendar` is set to null when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar. `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is then a no-op, so collective team members' calendars are silently dropped. It also mutates the array that was just built. Initialise to `[]` and push into it.

title: Event type destination calendar overrides the organizer's, and the first item is persisted as the booking's
body: When the event type has a destination calendar, the organizer's own calendar is not added. For a collective event whose first calendar is a team member's or the event type's, the booking record connects only `destinationCalendar[0]`, which may not be the organizer's. Reschedule and cancel flows that fall back to booking.destinationCalendar then point at the wrong calendar.

title: loadUsers rewrite drops organization select and throws for dynamic groups
body: The `organization: { select: { slug } }` selection was removed from the dynamic-user query, which may break code that reads `user.organization`. A new throw was added when `dynamicUserList` is empty, and errors are mapped to a generic 500 "Unable to load users". This is an unrelated behavioural change to user loading that is not described in the PR.

title: Fallback lookup is a no-op
body: In updateEvent and deleteEvent the fallback is `destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. It runs only when externalCalendarId is falsy and compares against that same falsy value, so it can never find anything meaningful. The fallback to a destination calendar is effectively removed. In updateEvent this leaves calendarId undefined.

title: Unrelated inversion of slug logic
body: The change flips `!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug }` to `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {}`. The slug is now set on the org only when team billing is enabled, where before it was set only when billing was disabled. This reverses behaviour and is unrelated to destination calendars.

title: Inconsistent e2e expectations for destinationCalendar
body: Only the BOOKING_REJECTED expectation was changed to `[]`. The BOOKING_CREATED and BOOKING_REQUESTED tests still expect `destinationCalendar: null`. No tests cover the new multi-host behaviour.

title: Possible TypeError when destinationCalendar is empty
body: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` yields `undefined` when the array is empty or null. The next line then reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining. For a Google Meet location with no destination calendar, `create()` throws instead of falling back to Cal Video. Use `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.

title: Selected calendar lookup depends on credentialId, with a fallback that can write to the wrong calendar
body: createEvent now picks the target calendar by matching `cal.credentialId === credentialId`. EventManager calls `createEvent(c, event)` with no externalId when the destination has no credentialId. A destination that lacks credentialId never matches, so the event goes to "primary", which can be wrong. Also, the patch call uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar`, which is undefined when there is no match, instead of the "primary" fallback used for insert. The hangout-link patch then fails.

title: Dead and tautological destination lookup in updateEvent and deleteEvent
body: The code is `externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find(cal => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. In the else branch externalCalendarId is falsy, so the find compares against a falsy value and returns nothing useful. The original fallback to the destination calendar's externalId was lost, so updates and deletes without an explicit id no longer reach the destination calendar. This also affects `deleteEvent` at line 317.

title: Mutating a shared array, and an array that may be null, when adding team destination calendars
body: `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is a no-op when the organizer has no calendar, because destinationCalendar is then `null`. In that case the team members' calendars are silently dropped. teamDestinationCalendars is filled inside async map callbacks, which run synchronously up to the first await, so the ordering works only by accident. Also, a collective host whose destination calendar duplicates the organizer's will get duplicate events.

title: loadUsers rewrite changes behavior
body: The rewrite drops `organization: { select: { slug } }` from the dynamic user query. It also now throws for an empty dynamicUserList and wraps every error as an HttpError 400 or 500. These changes are unrelated to the fix and can break dynamic group bookings and anything that reads `user.organization`.

title: Inverted slug logic with no explanation
body: The change from `!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug }` to `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {}` flips behavior. The org slug is now set only when team billing is enabled, and requestedSlug is unchanged. This is unrelated to the PR and looks like a regression for self-hosted instances without billing, because the org is created with no slug.

title: Unrelated user-visible string change
body: The string "Notes have been hidden by the organiser" was changed to "organizer" in an unrelated edit. Any tests or consumers that match the old text will break.

title: Null dereference when destinationCalendar is empty and location is Google Meet
body: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` yields `undefined` when the array is empty or null. The next line then reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining and throws a TypeError. This happens for any booking with a Meet location and no destination calendar, which is exactly the case the Cal Video fallback is meant to handle. handleNewBooking can also set destinationCalendar to null. Use `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.

title: Patch of hangout link uses undefined calendarId
body: `selectedCalendar` can now be undefined, because it is resolved by `find` on credentialId. The insert falls back to "primary", but the follow-up `calendar.events.patch` passes `calendarId: selectedCalendar` with no fallback. When the event is created on the primary calendar and has a hangout link, the patch call fails or targets the wrong calendar, so the description never gets the Meet link. Use the same `selectedCalendar || "primary"` for the patch.

title: Meaningless fallback lookup in updateEvent/deleteEvent
body: `externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` runs its `find` only when `externalCalendarId` is falsy. It then looks for a calendar whose externalId equals that falsy value, so it almost never matches. The destination-calendar fallback therefore no longer works the way it did before the array conversion (previously `destinationCalendar.externalId`). The same pattern is in deleteEvent.

title: teamDestinationCalendars is read before the async map is awaited, and it mutates a shared array
body: `teamDestinationCalendars` is filled inside `teamMemberPromises` callbacks. Those callbacks run synchronously inside `.map`, so the array is populated before the push, which works. However, `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...)` mutates the array that holds `eventType.destinationCalendar`, and when the event type has no destination calendar and the organizer has none, destinationCalendar is null so the push is skipped and the team members' calendars are silently dropped. This also breaks collective events where the organizer has no calendar.

title: loadUsers rewrite drops organization select and changes behavior
body: The rewritten `loadUsers` removes the `organization: { select: { slug } }` selection for dynamic users, so downstream code that reads it breaks. It also throws when `dynamicUserList` is empty and wraps all errors into generic 400/500 responses. These changes are unrelated to this PR and risk regressions.

title: Inverted slug condition changes org creation behavior
body: The old code set `slug` when `!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED` and `requestedSlug` when billing was enabled. The new code sets `slug` when billing is enabled. This reverses the logic and is unrelated to the PR. Orgs will get a slug immediately under billing, bypassing the payment/verification flow, and will have no slug when billing is disabled.

title: updateEvent called with undefined credential
body: If the credential is not found in `this.calendarCredentials` or in the DB, or the DB credential lacks an app slug, `credential` stays undefined. It is still passed to `updateEvent(credential, ...)`, which then dereferences it (for example `credential.appName`) and throws. The outer catch then marks all references as failed. Skip the reference when no credential is found.

title: Salesforce: undeclared prisma, and token refresh runs on every client construction
body:
`prisma` is used at line 96 but never imported in this file, so this fails to compile or throws at runtime. The new refresh block also runs on every client construction, without checking expiry. It never calls `refreshOAuthTokens`, so credential sync is bypassed here. The jsforce Connection at lines 101-108 is still built from the old `credentialKey.access_token`, so the freshly fetched token is discarded.

A failed refresh now breaks the whole service, and a successful one adds a network call to every instantiation.

title: Computed zod keys are bogus, so the minimal schema is wrong
body: `[z.string().toString()]` evaluates to the string "[object Object]" or similar. The schema therefore requires a numeric property with that literal name, so `safeParse` fails on real token responses whenever credential sync is on. Zod objects strip unknown keys by default, so data such as `expiry_date` or `refresh_token` is dropped. The intended 'any number is the expiry' logic does not exist; it needs `.passthrough()` or `catchall`.

title: Placeholder refresh_token written for schemas that don't define it
body: Setting `refresh_token = "refresh_token"` as a fake value mutates the parsed data for every caller, even with sharing disabled. For Google, Office365 and Salesforce it injects a bogus refresh token into stored credentials. This is also a TypeScript error, because `data.refresh_token` does not exist on the type for schemas that lack it.

title: parseRefreshTokenResponse result stored as the key
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns a safeParse result object (`{success, data}`), not the data. It is saved directly as `key`, so the stored credential becomes `{success:true,data:{...}}`. This corrupts Google credentials and breaks all subsequent auth. It should use `.data`.

title: Sync endpoint call is unauthenticated and unchecked
body: The POST to the credential-sync endpoint sends no secret or auth header, so the endpoint cannot verify the caller. The response status is never checked before callers parse it. Callers expect different shapes (axios `.data`, a fetch Response, or Google `.res`) from the sync endpoint's plain fetch Response. For example, zoho `tokenInfo.data` and the Google `res?.data` access are undefined on a fetch Response.

title: Secret compared non-constant-time; unvalidated input and decrypt errors
body: The header secret is compared with `!==`, which is not timing-safe. `parse` throws a ZodError (500) on a bad body instead of a 400. The JSON.parse and decrypt calls are also unguarded, so malformed payloads return 500s. The route accepts any method.

title: Non-boolean flag exported
body: `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` is a `string | undefined` (the secret itself) rather than a boolean. It is easy to misuse or leak, so wrap it in `!!(...)`.

title: Synced response not normalized
body: With sync enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw fetch Response. It is treated as a HubspotToken, so `expiresIn` and `accessToken` are undefined. `setAccessToken(undefined)` is then called and garbage is saved to the credential. The same pattern applies to the zoho-bigin and zohocrm `.data` accesses.

title: Salesforce: `prisma` is used but never imported
body: `prisma.credential.update` is called, but the file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. This fails type-check, and at runtime it throws a ReferenceError every time a Salesforce client is created.

title: Salesforce refresh bypasses credential sync and runs on every client construction
body: The new refresh `fetch` calls Salesforce directly and does not go through `refreshOAuthTokens`, so credential syncing is ignored for this app. It also fires on every service construction, not only when the token is expired. The refreshed `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token` is then discarded: the Connection is built from the stale `credentialKey.access_token`.

title: Computed zod keys produce a broken schema
body: `[z.string().toString()]` evaluates to the string "[object Object]" (or similar), not a wildcard. The resulting schema only requires `access_token` plus a literal junk key. Because `z.number()` is required on that junk key, every sync-mode response fails validation, and extra properties are not allowed through as intended.

title: Fake refresh_token is injected into all parsed responses
body: If `refresh_token` is missing, it is set to the literal string "refresh_token", even in the normal non-sync path. That bogus value can then be saved over a real refresh token in the DB. The type of `data` is also not guaranteed to have this property.

title: Parse result object saved as the credential key
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns a safeParse result (`{success, data}`), but it is stored directly as `key`. The credential key becomes `{success:true,data:{...}}` and the stored Google credentials are corrupted. The old code stored the parsed data.

title: Sync response is a fetch Response, but code reads `.data`
body: In sync mode `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw fetch `Response`, so `res?.data` is undefined and `token.access_token` throws. The Google path only works when sync is disabled. The same mismatch affects the hubspot, zoho-bigin and zohocrm callers, which expect a JSON or axios-shaped result.

title: Sync endpoint call is unauthenticated and has no error handling
body: The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends no secret or auth header, and the response status is not checked. The caller will try to parse an error body as tokens.

title: Webhook secret compared with `!==` and body errors unhandled
body: The secret is compared with a non-constant-time `!==`. `schema.parse` throws on a bad body, which gives a 500 instead of a 400. `JSON.parse` of the decrypted keys, or decryption itself, can also throw unhandled. There is no method check either.

title: Bigin passes credentialId as userId
body: `refreshOAuthTokens` expects `userId`, but `credentialId` is passed. The sync endpoint will receive the wrong id for `calcomUserId`.

title: Salesforce: `prisma` is never imported and a token refresh is always forced
body:
The new code calls `prisma.credential.update`, but this file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. That fails type-check and throws a ReferenceError at runtime. The refresh also runs on every client construction and bypasses `refreshOAuthTokens`, so credential sync is never used for Salesforce. It then builds the Connection from the old `credentialKey.access_token` instead of the refreshed one, so the refresh has no effect on the connection. The stored `refresh_token` is fine, but the parsed object's other fields come from a token response.

The parsed schema lacks `refresh_token` in the Salesforce response, and `parseRefreshTokenResponse` then mutates `data.refresh_token` to a placeholder string. The code overwrites it afterwards, which is fragile.

title: Computed zod keys make the minimum schema meaningless
body: `[z.string().toString()]` evaluates to the string "[object Object]" (or similar), not a catch-all key. The schema therefore requires a property literally named that, so the sync-mode schema either always fails or never checks expiry. The intent is `z.object({access_token}).passthrough()` or a similar construct. Also, `refresh_token` is silently set to the literal string "refresh_token" when missing, and that fake value can then be persisted as the real refresh token.

title: Google: stores the wrong value as the credential key
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns a zod SafeParse result (`{success, data}`), not the parsed data. `key` is that wrapper object, and it is written to `prisma.credential.update`. The credential is corrupted as `{success:true, data:{...}}`, and the next read fails `googleCredentialSchema.parse`. It should store `.data`.

title: Sync endpoint response is not checked and callers expect different shapes
body: The `fetch` response is returned without checking `response.ok`, and no auth header is sent to the sync endpoint. Callers expect axios responses (`.data`), jsforce results or Google `res.data`, but a raw fetch `Response` is returned in sync mode. Zoho/Bigin `tokenInfo.data` and Google `res?.data` and similar accesses break because they are undefined on a fetch Response.

title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time `!==` and bad-input handling
body: The secret is compared with `!==`, which is not timing-safe. `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` is only truthy when both env vars are set, but `req.headers[...]` may be an array. `schema.parse` throws on invalid bodies, so the endpoint returns a 500 instead of a 400. `JSON.parse` and decryption errors are also unhandled. There is no method check, so any HTTP method is accepted.

title: Credential lookup by userId and appId can pick the wrong or a team credential
body: `findFirst` filters by `userId` and `appId` only. If a user has several credentials for the app, an arbitrary one is overwritten. The lookup is also non-atomic, so concurrent webhooks can create duplicates.

title: Passes credentialId instead of userId to refreshOAuthTokens
body: The third parameter is `userId`, but the code passes `credentialId`. In sync mode the endpoint is asked for tokens of the wrong user (the credential ID reinterpreted as a user ID).

title: Authorization check for team admin uses AND instead of OR
body: `isTeamAdmin && isTeamOwner` requires the user to be both admin and owner, which is wrong. Legitimate team admins who are not owners are denied. Separately, `isAttendee` lets any attendee, matched only by email, add arbitrary guests to someone else's booking. Authorization is also unchecked against booking status, so cancelled or past bookings can be modified.

title: Blacklist and duplicate checks are case-sensitive and the input is not deduplicated
body: The blacklist is lowercased, but the guest email is compared without lowercasing, so `Foo@x.com` bypasses the blacklist. Comparison against existing attendees is also case-sensitive. Duplicates within `guests` are not removed server-side, because the uniqueness check exists only in the client. Direct API calls can create duplicate attendees.

title: Calendar update failure is unhandled after the DB write, and the guest list is sent unfiltered to emails
body: The attendees are already persisted when `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` runs. If it throws, the mutation fails with the DB already changed and no emails are sent, so retrying yields a 'must be unique' error. Also, `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` passes the raw input rather than `uniqueGuests`. Guests who were already attendees therefore get the 'scheduled' email again. Errors in the catch block are swallowed with only a console.log.

title: EventManager built from the caller's credentials rather than the organizer's
body: Credentials and user come from `ctx.user`, but the calendar events belong to the booking organizer. When an attendee or team admin adds guests, the update targets the wrong credentials and the organizer's calendar event is not updated.

title: Add-guests emails ignore the disable-standard-emails metadata and send to all attendees
body: Unlike the sibling senders, `sendAddGuestsEmails` does not honor `eventTypeDisableHostEmail` or `eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail`. New guests also receive `AttendeeScheduledEmail`, which sends the email to the whole attendee list.

title: Error toast message is built unconditionally, so the fallback never applies
body: The template string is always truthy, so `|| t("unable_to_add_guests")` is dead code. The toast shows 'CODE: message', for example 'BAD_REQUEST: ...'. The `isInvalidEmail` error is also never cleared once the input is corrected.

title: Subject uses attendees[0] name
body: The subject uses `attendees[0].name`, which is correct for the original booker. The newly added guests have an empty name, so the guest-add emails lose useful context. The `name` default of "" may also render badly in the `to:` address as ` <email>`.

title: Team admin/owner check uses AND instead of OR
body: `isTeamAdmin && isTeamOwner` is true only for users who are both, so a plain admin, or an owner whose membership is not also flagged as admin, is denied. Separately, `teamId ?? 0` is queried for non-team events. The intent is clearly admin OR owner. This is a permissions bug.

title: Any attendee can add guests to the booking
body: Authorization passes if the caller's email matches any attendee, including a guest who was added earlier. Guests can then invite further people, and the organizer's calendar event and emails are triggered. The email comparison is also case-sensitive, and the handler does not check that the user's email is verified.

title: Guest dedup and blacklist comparisons are case-sensitive; no limit on guests
body: Blacklisted emails are lowercased, but the guest value is compared as-is, so `Foo@x.com` bypasses the blacklist. The comparison against existing attendees is also case-sensitive. The duplicates inside the `guests` input are not removed server-side, and the array has no max length, so a single call can create an unbounded number of attendees and emails.

title: Emails are sent using the raw `guests` input rather than the filtered `uniqueGuests`
body: `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` receives the unfiltered list. Existing attendees or blacklisted addresses in the input are treated as new guests and receive the scheduled email again. Pass `uniqueGuests` instead.

title: Calendar update is unguarded and runs after the DB write
body: The DB update has already committed when `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` runs, and the call is not in a try/catch. A calendar failure makes the mutation error out even though the guests were saved, and the emails are never sent. The EventManager is also built from `ctx.user` credentials, not the organizer's, which is wrong when the caller is an attendee or admin.

title: New guests get the standard scheduled email, ignoring the event type's disabled-email settings
body: `sendAddGuestsEmails` neither checks `eventTypeDisableHostEmail`/`eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail` nor accepts event type metadata, unlike the other senders. Emails are sent even when the event type disables them.

title: Error toast message is built incorrectly
body: The message is always a non-empty template string, so the `|| t("unable_to_add_guests")` fallback never applies. The raw `err.data?.code` is also shown to the user, and `t(err.message)` is applied to arbitrary server messages. Also, `isInvalidEmail` is never reset after a successful retry.

title: Add guests action is offered on all bookings, including past ones
body: The item is placed in the shared `editBookingActions`, so it appears for past bookings, and for seated and recurring events, where adding attendees may be inappropriate. The label also reuses `additional_guests`, and the action id is named `add_members`.

title: Authorization check uses AND for team admin and owner, and allows any attendee
body: `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `isTeamAdmin && isTeamOwner`. That is too strict for admins who are not owners, and the name says "or". Separately, any attendee of the booking can add guests, and the organizer is never notified for approval. Since the new guest list is unbounded, attendees can inject arbitrary emails into the organizer's event and calendar, and the host's mailer sends them invitations. Restrict to the organizer and team admins (use OR), and drop the attendee permission or document it.

title: Case-sensitive dedupe and blacklist comparison
body: The blacklist is lowercased, but `guest` is compared as-is, so `Foo@x.com` bypasses the blacklist. The existing-attendee check is also case-sensitive, so the same address can be added twice with a different case. Normalize guests to lowercase before comparing and storing.

title: Calendar update runs unguarded after the DB write, with the wrong credentials and user
body: Attendees are persisted before `updateCalendarAttendees`. If the calendar update throws, the guests are already saved, the mutation fails, and no emails are sent; a retry then hits the "unique" error. The EventManager is also built from `ctx.user` and `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)`. When an attendee or team admin performs the action, the organizer's calendar credentials are not used, so the calendar event is not updated.

title: New-guest detection by exact email match, and no honoring of disabled-email settings
body: `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)` receives the raw `guests` input, not the filtered `uniqueGuests`. Existing attendees whose addresses appear in the input (for example blacklisted ones that were filtered out) get the wrong email, and case differences cause the same problem. In addition, `sendAddGuestsEmails` ignores the event type's `disableStandardEmails` metadata that sibling functions respect.

title: Email failure swallowed with no error detail
body: The catch block logs a generic string and drops the error object, making email failures impossible to debug. Use the logger and include `err`.

title: Error toast built from the raw code and a translated message
body: The message is always a non-empty template string, so the `unable_to_add_guests` fallback is never used. The user sees text like "BAD_REQUEST: ...". Zod validation errors from the server would also be passed through `t()` as raw JSON.

title: Add guests action shown for all bookings in the edit menu
body: The action is shown regardless of event-type settings such as seated events or the user's role, and regardless of whether the user is allowed. For non-permitted users the call just fails with FORBIDDEN.

title: Array index used as React key
body: Using the index as the key while rows can be removed from the middle makes inputs keep stale state and focus when one is deleted.

title: Retry-count delete clause is not restricted to SMS reminders
body: The second OR branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` condition. Previously the whole delete was scoped to SMS. Now any WorkflowReminder with retryCount > 1 is deleted, regardless of method. Other cron jobs (email, WhatsApp) may start using retryCount, and their reminders would then be deleted by the SMS cron. Add `method: SMS` to that branch.

title: Catch-block update can throw and abort the whole cron run
body: The `prisma.workflowReminder.update` inside the catch is not guarded. If it fails (for example the row was deleted concurrently, or the DB is unavailable), the exception escapes the for-loop. The remaining reminders are then not processed and the handler returns a 500. Wrap the update in its own try/catch.

title: Threshold `gt: 1` does not match the description and is delayed by a run
body: The PR says reminders are deleted after two failed attempts. The deletion runs at the start of the next cron run, and only for retryCount > 1. A reminder that fails twice reaches retryCount 2 and is deleted on the third run. Reminders that never reach the send branch (no message or no sendTo) never increment the count and are retried until the scheduled date, which is the behaviour the PR aims to remove.

title: retryCount delete clause is not restricted to SMS reminders
body: The new OR branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` has no `method: SMS` condition. It applies to every WorkflowReminder, including EMAIL and WHATSAPP ones. Any reminder of another method that later gets a retryCount above 1 would be deleted by this SMS cron. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` to that branch.

title: Retry threshold deletes only after a third attempt, contradicting the stated behaviour
body: The PR says the reminder is deleted after scheduling failed twice. With `gt: 1`, deletion happens at the start of the next cron run once retryCount is 2, which is after two failures. That matches. However, the unscheduled query does not filter on retryCount, so the reminder is not excluded until the next run's delete. Deletion therefore depends on cron ordering. This is fragile, and the query should also filter `retryCount < 2`.

title: Retry update in the catch block can throw and abort the whole loop
body: The `prisma.workflowReminder.update` inside the catch is not guarded. If it fails, for example because the reminder was deleted concurrently, the exception escapes the loop. The remaining reminders are skipped and the request returns a 500. Wrap the update in its own try/catch.

title: Reminders with no sendTo or empty message never count as a retry
body: When `message` is empty or `sendTo` is missing, for example an invalid or absent phone number, the code neither schedules nor increments retryCount. Those reminders are retried on every cron run until their date passes, which is the exact problem the PR aims to fix.

title: Retry-count delete clause is not restricted to SMS reminders
body: The second OR branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` condition. Before this change the deleteMany was scoped to SMS. Now it deletes any WorkflowReminder row with retryCount > 1, including EMAIL and WHATSAPP rows. Those rows currently default to 0, but other code paths or later features that use retryCount would be silently deleted by this SMS cron. The condition should be `method: SMS AND (scheduledDate <= now OR retryCount > 1)`.

title: Reminders with missing message or recipient never increment retryCount
body: The retry increment only happens inside `if (message?.length && sendTo)`. If sendTo is missing (e.g. invalid or absent phone number) or the message is empty, nothing is updated and no retry is counted. Those reminders are rescheduled on every cron run until the date passes, which is the exact problem the PR aims to fix.

title: Update inside catch can throw and abort the whole batch
body: The `prisma.workflowReminder.update` in the catch block is not guarded. If it fails (for example the row was deleted concurrently, or a DB error), the exception escapes the loop and the handler returns 500. The remaining reminders are skipped for that run. Wrap it in its own try/catch.

title: Threshold gt:1 gives a retry limit that is easy to misread
body: A reminder is deleted only after retryCount reaches 2. That means two failed attempts, matching the description. However, deletion happens at the start of the next cron run, so the logic is off-by-one-prone and untested. No tests were added for the new retry behavior.

title: Unparenthesized OR in filter condition can break AND composition when used as the sole filter
body: The eventTypeId filter returns `("eventTypeId" = x) OR ("eventParentId" = x)` with no outer parentheses. When it is the only filter, getBaseConditions wraps it as `(${filterConditions})`, which is safe. But getFilterConditions/getFilterConditions().reduce consumers, or any caller that embeds the filter or authorization condition directly (e.g. `WHERE ${cond} AND other`), will get wrong precedence and leak rows. The same applies to the auth conditions, which are top-level ORs (lines 164-174, 196-207). Wrap each composite condition in parentheses at construction.

title: Removed findMany public method and changed constructor type without updating callers
body: findMany was removed and replaced by getBaseConditions, and the constructor's options type was changed. Any existing callers of findMany would now fail to compile or run. The diff does not show callers being updated, so confirm that none remain.

title: Caching tests removed and no coverage for empty-user/team edge cases
body: The caching tests for authorization and filter conditions were deleted rather than converted, even though the caching logic remains in the service. There are also no tests for the new branches where the user list is empty, or for a team scope whose team is not a child of the org.

title: Unparenthesized OR can be combined into broken AND logic
body: The eventTypeId condition is an unwrapped `(a) OR (b)`. `getBaseConditions` wraps both parts as `(${auth}) AND (${filter})`, so that path is safe. But `getFilterConditions` output is meant to be reused, and in the reducer the first element is returned bare. If a caller interpolates it without parentheses next to other AND terms, precedence silently breaks the filter and widens results. The same applies to auth conditions: org/team conditions are bare `A OR B`, and user scope is `A AND B`. Wrap each returned condition in parentheses.

title: Org-scope user condition skipped when org has no child teams
body: `userIdsFromOrg` is `[]` when `teamsFromOrg.length` is 0, so only the team-booking condition is produced. Personal bookings (isTeamBooking=false) of the org's own members are therefore excluded. This is pre-existing behavior, but it is now an observable authorization gap. In addition, the team scope now omits the user condition when the team has no members, whereas the old code always included it. That is harmless but is a behavior change that is untested.

title: Removed caching tests and the only end-to-end query test is narrow
body: The caching tests were deleted without replacement, although the service still caches auth and filter conditions. The only DB-executed test is the user scope with an eventType filter. The org and team ANY(array) SQL is never run against Postgres, only compared as Sql objects, so syntax or type errors (for example ANY with an int array parameter) would go undetected. The BookingTimeStatusDenormalized view is also queried right after inserts, with no check that the view is populated.

title: Removed findMany public method breaks callers
body: `findMany` was removed and replaced by `getBaseConditions`. Any existing consumer of `InsightsBookingService.findMany` would break. The PR does not show that the callers were updated or searched for. The constructor option type was also changed to a new public type.

title: Unparenthesized OR in filter condition when nested in AND combinations
body: A single eventTypeId filter produces `("eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)` with no outer parentheses. If a caller embeds this condition without wrapping it, for example `WHERE ${filter} AND other`, the OR binds incorrectly and the filter is bypassed. The `getBaseConditions` and reduce paths happen to wrap it, but `getFilterConditions` is public and returns the bare OR. Wrap the whole expression in parentheses.

title: Team and org scope auth conditions are returned unwrapped
body: The reduce in both the team and org auth builders yields `(A) OR (B)` with no outer parentheses. `getAuthorizationConditions` returns it directly, so a caller appending `AND ...` gets wrong precedence. That could leak bookings outside the authorized scope. `getBaseConditions` wraps it correctly, but the public method is unsafe. Wrap the result in parentheses.

title: Raw SQL test queries a denormalized view whose rows may not exist or may be stale
body: The test selects from "BookingTimeStatusDenormalized" and asserts exact equality on the results. Other bookings from parallel tests could match, and the denormalized data may not reflect new rows if it is a view or is populated asynchronously. Test coverage of the empty-user branch (userIdsFromOrg empty) and the team branch against real data is also missing, so the new conditional-push logic is untested.

title: Plain Error instead of TRPCError for auth failure
