title: Public members endpoint response shape changed, breaking existing consumers
body: `GET /groups/:id/members` used to return a bare array of users. It now returns `{members: [...], meta: {...}}` and defaults to 50 results. Any other client of this endpoint (plugins, other JS callers, API users) will break. The old automatic-group-only limit workaround is also gone, so non-automatic groups are now silently capped at 50 for callers that don't paginate. No controller spec covers the new response shape or pagination.

title: Unvalidated limit and offset parameters
body: `limit` comes straight from `params[:limit].to_i` with no upper bound, so a client can request an arbitrarily large page and load the whole group. A negative limit or offset can also cause a database error (negative OFFSET raises in Postgres), resulting in a 500.

title: remove_member deletes via the association with a raw id and skips group-level cleanup
body: `group.users.delete(user_id)` is passed an integer. This works for has_many :through, but it bypasses `Group#remove`, and any callbacks or counters tied to it. Elsewhere in the code `group.add` is used for adds, so removal is inconsistent. A non-member id is also silently ignored. The spec for this path only checks the simple case.

title: totalPages overcounts when user_count is an exact multiple of limit
body: `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` gives an extra empty page when user_count is a multiple of limit (e.g. 50 users gives 2 pages). `next` can then navigate to an offset equal to user_count and show an empty list. This should use `Math.ceil`.

title: Spec uses wrong HTTP verb and routes
body: The remove_member spec for automatic groups uses `xhr :put` although the route is DELETE. It passes only because controller specs bypass routing verbs. There are also no specs for the new paginated `GroupsController#members` response.

title: addMembers never clears the input and ignores errors
body: After `addMembers`, the usernames field is not cleared (there is a TODO), so clicking Add twice re-sends the same names. The returned promise has no failure handler, so server errors such as the 422 for automatic groups are silent.

title: remove_member passes an integer to the has_many collection delete
body: `group.users.delete(user_id)` is given an integer id. Depending on the Rails version, `CollectionProxy#delete` with an id may not remove the join row correctly, or it may raise `AssociationTypeMismatch`. The spec only covers the happy path through the controller. It is safer to load the user (`User.find`) or use `delete_all`/`where` on the join table, and to return a proper error when the user is not a member.

title: Unbounded and unvalidated limit/offset on public members endpoint
body: `limit` comes straight from `params[:limit].to_i` with no upper cap, and negative values are not rejected. A client can request an arbitrarily large page, which removes the old protection and is a DoS risk. A negative offset or limit can also cause a database error. Clamp the values, for example `limit` to 1..200 and `offset` to >= 0.

title: Response format change breaks existing consumers of /groups/:name/members
body: The endpoint used to return a bare array of users and now returns `{members, meta}`. Any other client or plugin using the old shape will break. The old default of 200 users for automatic groups also changed to 50 for every group. Only the group members view was updated to the new shape.

title: totalPages is off by one when user_count is an exact multiple of limit
body: `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` gives one extra, empty page when the count divides evenly. For 50 users with a limit of 50 it reports 2 pages. The next button then navigates to an empty page. Use `Math.ceil`.

title: addMembers never clears the usernames input and ignores failures
body: After a successful add, `usernames` stays populated (the code has a TODO acknowledging this). A repeated click re-submits the same names. There is no error handling if the PUT fails, so the user gets no feedback.

title: findMembers returns undefined for an unnamed group
body: The old code returned a resolved promise. Now it returns `undefined`, so any caller that chains `.then` on it will throw.

title: Public members endpoint changes response shape, breaking other consumers
body: The `/groups/:name/members` response changed from a bare array to `{members, meta}`. Any other client that reads this endpoint as an array (plugins, or other JS such as the group members page and mention/autocomplete code) will break. Existing specs for GroupsController#members are not updated or added to cover the new shape. The previous behavior of returning all members for non-automatic groups is also gone.

title: Unbounded, unvalidated limit/offset parameters
body: `limit` and `offset` come straight from params with `.to_i` and no upper cap. A client can request an arbitrarily large limit and dump the whole group in one call. A negative limit or offset is passed to the query unchecked, which can raise a database error or give odd results.

title: remove_member deletes via association with a raw id, skipping group bookkeeping
body: `group.users.delete(user_id)` is passed an Integer, and has_many through delete expects records. It may delete the join row without the logic `Group#remove` provides. `add_members` uses `group.add`, so this is inconsistent. A nonexistent user_id is silently accepted. Using `User.find` and `group.remove(user)` would be safer.

title: totalPages is off by one when user_count is an exact multiple of limit
body: `Math.floor(user_count/limit)+1` gives 2 pages for exactly 50 users at limit 50. The UI shows a non-existent empty last page. `next` can then request an offset equal to user_count and return an empty list. Use Math.ceil.

title: usernames not cleared after addMembers
body: After adding members, the `usernames` input keeps its value (a TODO admits this). Clicking Add again resubmits the same names. The TODO is left unresolved.

title: create no longer accepts the nested group params
body: The create and update actions now read top-level params instead of `params[:group]`. The old nested format is silently ignored. Group visibility is also set from `params[:visible] == "true"`, so an omitted param resets visible to false on update.

title: ensure_loaded! reads @loaded_locales before the mutex, and the cache key ignores fallbacks
body: `ensure_loaded!` reads and initializes `@loaded_locales` outside LOAD_MUTEX, and `load_locale` does the same. Another thread's `reload!` can reset the array to `[]` mid-call, and a concurrent request can race on it. Separately, `translate` caches by `key+locale+backend`. With fallbacks, a cached result may have come from the fallback locale, or the cache may be stale after the site default locale changes. The cache is never invalidated when `SiteSetting.default_locale` changes.

title: ensure_loaded! races with load_locale on @loaded_locales
body: `ensure_loaded!` does `@loaded_locales ||= []` outside LOAD_MUTEX. Concurrent requests can each create a new array, and one thread can replace an array that another is appending to, so a locale load can be lost or repeated. `reload!` also sets `@loaded_locales = []` without the lock. Initialize and check inside the mutex.

title: Fallback list evaluated against SiteSetting.default_locale, which may be unavailable at boot or invalid
body: `FallbackLocaleList#[]` calls `SiteSetting.default_locale` on every lookup. During early boot, migrations or asset precompile, the DB or SiteSetting may not be ready, so any I18n lookup that consults fallbacks can raise. Also, `default_locale` can be nil or blank, and `.to_sym` on nil raises NoMethodError. `.compact` runs after `.to_sym`, so it cannot protect against that.

title: Fallbacks included into the backend class at initializer time
body: `I18n.backend.class.send(:include, ...)` depends on the backend class at initializer time and on initializer ordering. The comment says it must run after 02-freedom_patches.rb, but the filename `i18n.rb` sorts alphabetically before `pluralization.rb` and the numbered files. This is fragile, and the file may load before the freedom patch.

title: ensure_loaded! on every request
body: `set_locale` runs for every request. It builds a fresh array and calls `SiteSetting.default_locale` each time, then loads up to three locales' translations. The first request for each locale pays a large synchronous load while holding a global mutex. Non-English locales also load the English and default-locale files.

title: ensure_loaded! can crash or return early on nil @loaded_locales
body: `ensure_loaded!` sets `@loaded_locales ||= []`, but `load_locale` returns early if the locale is already loaded and loads the `.rb` files only `if @loaded_locales.empty?`. Loading fallback locales first (e.g. :en before the current locale) is fine, but `translate` calls `@loaded_locales.include?` without initializing it. If `translate` runs before any `ensure_loaded!`, it raises NoMethodError on nil. Initialization should happen in one place, not only in the new method.

title: Fallback list uses SiteSetting at lookup time and may fail when invoked early
body: `FallbackLocaleList#[]` calls `SiteSetting.default_locale` on every lookup. During boot, migrations or the asset precompile, the DB or settings may not be available, so any I18n lookup that consults fallbacks can raise. The `locale` argument can also be a string, which then fails to dedupe against the symbol `default_locale`, giving duplicate entries.

title: Fallbacks included on I18n.backend.class at initializer time
body: `I18n.backend.class` is included before the translate_accelerator patch is guaranteed to have run (relying on a file-ordering comment). It also silently depends on the backend being Simple. If the backend is later replaced, fallbacks are lost. The `config.i18n.fallbacks` removal also means the Rails-level setup is gone, so the behaviour is now enabled in every environment, including test and development, without a test.

title: ensure_loaded! on every request
body: `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` runs on each request and calls `SiteSetting.default_locale` and builds arrays each time. It is cheap after the first call, but the global `I18n.fallbacks` is only a custom Hash subclass. Anything that expects normal Hash behavior (such as `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks` methods like `map`) will not work.

title: Denial cache key collides with the permission cache key
body: userPermDenialCacheKey is namespace+".perm_"+userUID+"_"+action+"_"+name+"_"+parent. userPermCacheKey is namespace+".perm_"+userUID+"_"+action. The prefixes are the same, and both are stored in the same underlying cache. Underscore-joined fields with no separator escaping are also ambiguous: names containing underscores could collide with other users' or actions' keys. Use a distinct prefix such as ".perm_denied_" and an unambiguous separator.

title: Denial cache blocks newly granted access for the TTL, defeating the PR goal
body: A denial is cached for 30s per (user, action, name, folder). If a check runs just before a resource is created or permissions are granted, for example a creator checking a dashboard before the permission row is visible, access stays denied for the full TTL even though the permission now exists in the DB. The fallback requery is skipped on every denial-cache hit. Nothing invalidates the entry when permissions change.

title: Denied checks on cached permissions requery the DB each time
body: When the cached permissions do not allow the request, the code always calls getIdentityPermissions, which hits the DB. The denial cache is only populated after that call succeeds, so a burst of concurrent denied checks for different resources causes a DB query per distinct resource. Distinct names also each get their own denial key, so the cache gives little protection against scanning patterns. Metrics also count a cache miss in this case.

title: Errors from the cached-permission lookup are ignored
body: getCachedIdentityPermissions can return a real error, such as a failure in GetUserIdentifiers. Check treats every error as a cache miss and falls through, which is acceptable. However, the err variable is shadowed inside the if block, and List does the same. The resulting double lookup of identifiers is a minor inefficiency.

title: Missing test that a denial is cached after a DB-checked deny
body: The tests never verify that Check populates permDenialCache after a denial, or that a repeat call avoids the DB. The 'should return permissions from cache' case in getUserPermissions was removed without equivalent coverage of the singleflight and DB paths.

title: Denial cache key collides with permission cache key
body: userPermDenialCacheKey is `ns.perm_<uid>_<action>_<name>_<parent>`, while userPermCacheKey is `ns.perm_<uid>_<action>`. Both are stored in the same underlying cache, and the key spaces overlap. The key is also ambiguous because the parts are joined with '_' and names or actions may contain underscores. A denial entry could therefore collide with a permission entry, or with another user/resource combination. Fix by using a distinct prefix such as `.perm_denial_` and an unambiguous separator.

title: Denial cache defeats the fix for newly created resources
body: After a denial, the entry is cached for 30s under (user, action, name, parent). A user who checks a resource just before it is created, or before their permission is granted, stays denied for 30s even though the DB now allows access. Nothing invalidates the denial entry when permissions change. This undermines the stated goal of letting creators access resources they just created. Negative caching of denials for the same user and resource should be shorter or be invalidated on creation.

title: Errors from the cached lookup are swallowed and metrics are skewed
body: An error from getCachedIdentityPermissions is silently ignored, and the code falls through to the DB path. That path then repeats GetUserIdentifiers, so the same failure is hit twice. Separately, the permissionCacheUsage metric is incremented as a cache miss whenever the cached permissions are present but do not grant access, and also when the cache simply misses. The two cases are conflated. On a cache miss the DB path is always taken even when the miss is only a not-found result.

title: Removed cache-hit test and unverified single-flight behavior
body: The test case for returning permissions from the cache in getUserPermissions was deleted. The `cacheHit` field and its branch in that test are now dead code. There is also no test that a denial is written to the denial cache after a DB-confirmed deny, nor that List falls back to the DB on a cache miss.

title: Denial cache key collides with the permission cache key
body: userPermDenialCacheKey produces namespace.perm_<uid>_<action>_<name>_<parent>, which shares the namespace.perm_ prefix with userPermCacheKey (namespace.perm_<uid>_<action>). Both caches wrap the same underlying cache.Cache. Because the denial key is longer, an exact collision is unlikely in practice, but the shared prefix is fragile. The unescaped '_' separators also let different (name, parent) pairs map to the same key, for example name 'a_b' with parent 'c' versus name 'a' with parent 'b_c'. Use a distinct prefix such as '.perm_denial_' and an unambiguous separator.

title: Denial cache blocks access for 30s after a permission is granted
body: A denial is cached for shortCacheTTL (30s). If the same user is denied on a resource and then gets access (for example, creating a dashboard or folder), every Check for that (action, name, parent) returns denied from the denial cache until it expires. The cache is checked before the DB requery, so this can reintroduce the stale-permission problem the PR is meant to fix. It matters most for a Check issued just before creation, for example an existence probe. The denial entry is never invalidated.

title: Cache lookup errors abort or skew the fallback path and metrics
body: getCachedIdentityPermissions calls GetUserIdentifiers, which can hit the DB. Any error from it is silently swallowed and the code falls through to getIdentityPermissions, which repeats the same lookup. The permission-cache metric is also double counted: it is incremented 'true' on denial-cache hits and 'false' on every non-allowed cached result. A cache hit that results in a deny, followed by a DB requery, is counted as a miss, which makes the metric misleading.

title: Cache-hit test case removed and cacheHit field left unused
body: The cache-hit case was removed from TestService_getUserPermissions, but the cacheHit field and its branches remain as dead code. The new tests do not assert that the DB is not called on a cache hit, or that a denial is stored after a DB deny. There is no test that a denial is written to permDenialCache.

title: Queries are interpolated twice in the shard path
body: runShardSplitQuery now interpolates each target with applyTemplateVariables. It then passes the already-interpolated targets, via runSplitQuery at line 163, into code that applies applyTemplateVariables to each target again. Double interpolation can corrupt values that contain `$` or escaped characters after the first pass, and it duplicates ad-hoc filter injection. Adhoc filters may be added twice to the expression. It also costs extra work for every shard sub-request. The test change that expects applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times shows the repeated calls. Interpolate once at the top level and skip it in the inner runSplitQuery, for example with an option.

title: applyTemplateVariables may mutate the original request targets
body: The map result replaces the targets, but the tests' mocks of applyTemplateVariables mutate and return the input query. If the real implementation returns shared objects, request.targets gets modified. Later retries and sub-requests would then see interpolated expressions. trackGroupedQueries receives the original request, which could end up inconsistent. Callers may also depend on the un-interpolated targets.

title: Assertion on call count 5 is brittle and encodes the double interpolation
body: toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5) hard-codes the number of redundant applyTemplateVariables calls (1 outer, then 4 inner, one per sub-request). It makes the double interpolation look intentional, and it will break when the group sizing changes.

title: Queries are interpolated twice in the sharding path and the ad hoc filters get duplicated
body: runSplitQuery now calls applyTemplateVariables on every target. runShardSplitQuery already interpolated the targets and then calls runSplitQuery for each sub-request, so each query goes through applyTemplateVariables twice. applyTemplateVariables also applies ad hoc filters (request.filters), so they can be added to the expression twice. Re-running interpolation on an already-interpolated expression can also mangle it, for example by double-escaping or expanding things like `$__auto` or `$__range` a second time. The fix is to interpolate once, at the top-level entry point only.

title: Test asserts a brittle call count that encodes double interpolation
body: The assertion `applyTemplateVariables` toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5) only holds because each sub-request is interpolated again inside runSplitQuery. That is 1 call in runShardSplitQuery plus 4 in the sub-requests. The test therefore locks in the redundant interpolation and will break when it is removed.

title: Queries are interpolated a second time via runSplitQuery
body: runShardSplitQuery interpolates targets with applyTemplateVariables. Each shard sub-request is then passed to runSplitQuery, which now calls applyTemplateVariables on every target again. Interpolation is not idempotent. Ad-hoc filters are injected into the expression twice, and `$` or `\` characters that appear in already-expanded values get re-expanded or re-escaped. Both layers also need to interpolate in the same order, which this change does not guarantee. This is the reason the test now expects applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times. The call count is a symptom of the double work.

title: Interpolation happens before grouping, but the request keeps raw targets
body: Only the derived group requests carry interpolated targets. trackGroupedQueries still receives the original `request`, so tracking sees uninterpolated queries. This may be fine, but the existing tests that compare the tracked request now depend on the mock's applyTemplateVariables returning the same object. Separately, the new `.map` can mutate the input targets, because the test mocks mutate and return the query. If the real implementation shares references, a retry or re-run could see already-interpolated targets.

title: Test asserts a brittle call count that encodes the double interpolation
body: `toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` locks in the redundant applyTemplateVariables calls (1 up front plus 4 inside runSplitQuery). It would fail if the double interpolation were fixed, and it does not verify correctness.

title: Plugin request log loses traceID
body: The old logRequest explicitly added a traceID (via tracing.TraceIDFromContext) to the log params, and that code was removed. The new code relies on m.logger.FromContext(ctx). That only adds traceID if the infra logger's context hooks inject it, and the diff does not show that they do. If they don't, the 'Plugin Request Completed' logs silently lose their trace correlation. The PR does not mention or test this change.

title: Stale function name and no tests for the new middleware
body: The helper is still called instrumentContext even though it now lives in the contextual logger middleware, which the rename was meant to clean up. The new ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no tests, and the moved behavior (logger attributes added to the context, and logging order relative to the other middlewares) is not covered anywhere.

title: FromContext fallback drops context attributes
body: If the type assertion fails, the code returns d.New(), which silently discards the context-derived attributes. The failure is not logged, so the logger has no endpoint or plugin fields and the loss is invisible.

title: Logger no longer emits traceID and relies on FromContext
body: The explicit traceID field was removed from logParams, as were pluginId, endpoint, dsName, dsUID and uname. These now come only from the contextual attributes via `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)`. The traceID is only emitted if the infra logger's FromContext adds it, which was not verified. If it does not, the 'Plugin Request Completed' log silently loses trace correlation. In addition, the wrapper's FromContext falls back to `d.New()` when the type assertion fails, which drops contextual attributes without any signal. There is no test covering the new logging output.

title: Stale function name and no tests for the new middleware
body: `instrumentContext` keeps the old 'instrumentation' naming even though this PR renames things for consistency. The new ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no unit test, and the metrics test no longer verifies that the contextual logger is set.

title: Logger name still references instrumentation
body: The logger is still named "plugin.instrumentation" even though the middleware was renamed to metrics. This is inconsistent with the stated goal of the rename, and changing the name would alter existing log filters.

title: traceID dropped from request log; contextual logger may not add it
body: The old logRequest explicitly appended traceID from tracing.TraceIDFromContext, and also pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName and dsUID. The new code relies on m.logger.FromContext(ctx) to supply these. The contextual attributes cover only endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID and uname. traceID is not added by the ContextualLoggerMiddleware. It is only present if the infra logger's FromContext adds it, which is not shown here. If it does not, the 'Plugin Request Completed' logs lose traceID, which breaks log-to-trace correlation. No test covers this.

title: FromContext fallback discards the context
body: If the type assertion fails, the code returns d.New(), which drops the contextual attributes and does not contain the requested context. The failure is silent. Callers such as the logger middleware then lose pluginId, endpoint and the other attributes without any signal. It would be better to fall back to d, or to wrap the returned logger.

title: Logger name still says instrumentation
body: The PR renames instrumentation to metrics, but the logger is still created as log.New("plugin.instrumentation"). The name is now inconsistent with the new middleware names. It is also unclear whether it was intentionally left unchanged to keep the log name stable.

title: No tests for new ContextualLoggerMiddleware
body: The new middleware moves behavior that previously lived in the instrumentation middleware: context enrichment with the contextual logger. No test verifies that it sets the attributes, or that the LoggerMiddleware picks them up. The helper is also still named instrumentContext despite the rename.

title: Device limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert (TOCTOU)
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts devices and then inserts in separate statements with no transaction or lock. Concurrent requests from new devices can all see count < limit and all insert, so the limit can be exceeded. It also issues a COUNT query on every uncached tag when a limit is set.

title: Cache entry set before the DB write, so a rejected device is cached as tagged
body: tagDeviceUI calls localCache.SetDefault(key) before CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached (or any DB error), the key stays cached for 29 minutes. The next request from that device then returns nil and is silently allowed through. The limit is therefore enforced only on the first request per device per cache window, and transient DB errors also cause skipped tagging.

title: Tagging moved from an async goroutine to the synchronous auth path
body: TagDevice, which does DB reads and writes, now runs inline in Authenticate. Every anonymous request that misses the cache pays that latency. A slow or failing database now delays or blocks anonymous page loads, which previously completed independently of tagging. The request context is also now used, so a client cancellation aborts the tagging.

title: updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached for any zero-row update
body: A zero-row update does not necessarily mean the limit was reached for a new device. It can also happen for a device last updated more than 30 days ago or just outside the time window. A returning-but-expired device is rejected, and Authenticate then fails with a generic error rather than a clear limit message.

title: Limit test covers only the rejection of a new device
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit checks only that a second new device is rejected. It does not check that an existing device can still update at the limit, that the limit=0 path is unlimited, or the client.go behaviour of returning the error. impl_test and the client tests were not extended.

title: Device limit check is racy (count then insert)
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts devices and then inserts in separate statements with no transaction or lock. Concurrent requests from new devices can all see count < limit and all insert, so the limit is exceeded. Across multiple Grafana instances the overshoot can be larger. The limit is not strictly enforced.

title: Cache is set before the DB write, so a rejected device is cached as tagged
body: tagDeviceUI sets the local cache entry before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the call fails with ErrDeviceLimitReached (or a transient DB error), the key stays cached for about 29 minutes. Later requests from that device return nil with no error and are admitted as anonymous even though the limit is reached. Only the first request is rejected, so the limit is effectively bypassed. The cache entry should be set only after success.

title: Tagging moved from async goroutine to the synchronous auth path
body: TagDevice used to run in a goroutine with its own timeout. It now runs inline in Authenticate with the request context. Every uncached anonymous request therefore waits on a COUNT query plus a write, which adds latency. If the request context is cancelled, the tagging DB operation is aborted too. Tagging failures also now sit on the critical path.

title: Count window uses two separate time.Now() calls and does not match the update window
body: The count uses a window of now-30d to now+1m. The update path uses device.UpdatedAt-30d to UpdatedAt+1m. updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached for a device that does not exist, which is the intended meaning. It returns the same error for a device that exists but is older than 30 days. This hides the real reason and adds inconsistency.

title: args is mutated inside the session closure
body: In updateDevice, `args = append([]interface{}{query}, args...)` runs inside the WithDbSession closure and reassigns the captured variable. If the session helper retries the closure, for example on a SQLite busy error, the query is prepended twice and the Exec call breaks. CreateOrUpdateDevice has the same pattern.

title: Device limit check is racy (count then insert)
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts devices and then inserts in separate statements with no transaction or lock. Concurrent requests from new devices can all see count < limit and all insert, exceeding the limit. In a multi-instance deployment the overshoot can be large. The limit is only approximately enforced.

title: Cache is set before DB write and not cleared on failure
body: tagDeviceUI puts the device key in the local cache before CreateOrUpdateDevice runs. If the call fails with ErrDeviceLimitReached, the key stays cached. Subsequent requests from the rejected device return nil and are authenticated as anonymous, bypassing the limit for about 29 minutes. Only the first request is rejected, so the limit is effectively unenforced for that device. The key should be set only after a successful write.

title: Tagging moved from async goroutine to synchronous request path
body: TagDevice now runs inline on the request context, so every uncached anonymous request pays for the extra DB count and write. The previous 2-minute timeout and panic recovery are gone. A slow DB now delays authentication, and a cancelled request context aborts tagging.

title: Misleading ErrDeviceLimitReached for non-existent or expired devices
body: updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached whenever zero rows are updated. The update is restricted to updated_at within the last 30 days, so a device that exists but is older also gets this error. The error is accurate for those cases, but the 'between the given times' comment is misleading.

title: Limit test is narrow
body: The test covers only the rejection of a new device at the limit. It does not test that an existing device can still be updated at the limit, or that expired devices are excluded from the count. There is also no test that Anonymous.Authenticate rejects when the limit is reached.

title: Cleanup ticker interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The ticker was reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This looks like a leftover debugging change unrelated to the deadlock fix. All cleanup jobs (snapshots, dashboard versions, annotations, query history and others) will run 10x more often. Each run can last up to the 9 minute timeout, so runs may nearly back to back and add DB load. Revert it to 10 minutes.

title: Debug logging at Error level that dumps all IDs on every batch
body: Each batch logs at Error level, including the full `ids` slice (up to the batch size, which may be tens of thousands of IDs) and the condition. This also happens when nothing was found. The same pattern appears at lines 537, 554, 557, 576 and 579. It floods error logs and triggers alerting on error logs during normal operation. Use Debug level and drop the ID list. Also, the 'err' value logged is always nil at that point.

title: SQLite parameter-limit check uses configured batch size and misses the placeholder cap
body: The inline-ID branch triggers only when the configured batch size is above 999. The decision should be based on len(ids). With a small configured value the placeholders path is fine, but the check depends on config rather than on the actual number of parameters. Also, for MaxCount cleanup, LimitOffset may return up to the batch size, so the logic is consistent only by coincidence. Prefer checking len(ids).

title: Orphan tag cleanup condition is ambiguous inside fetchIDs
body: The condition `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM annotation a WHERE annotation_id = a.id)` is now used in `SELECT id FROM annotation_tag WHERE ...`. The unqualified `annotation_id` resolves to annotation_tag only because annotation has no such column, which is fragile. More importantly, the `id` column of annotation_tag is used for the delete. That is correct only if the table has an id column, so verify that it does.

title: Cleanup ticker interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The cleanup loop now runs every minute instead of every 10 minutes. The PR description does not mention this. It looks like a debugging leftover. All cleanup jobs (snapshots, dashboard versions, annotations, query history) will hit the database 10x more often. Combined with a 9-minute job timeout, runs can overlap with the ticker. Revert to 10 minutes.

title: Debug logging at Error level with full ID lists
body: Each batch logs at Error level, including the whole ids slice (up to batch size, potentially tens of thousands of IDs), the condition and a nil err. This runs on every batch of every cleanup cycle. It floods error logs and triggers false alerts. It also logs 'cleaned ...' at error level even on success. The same pattern repeats at lines 537, 554, 557, 576 and 579. Remove these logs or use Debug without the ID list.

title: SQLite parameter limit check uses configured batch size, not the actual id count
body: The 999-parameter limit is checked against the configured batch size, but the real concern is how many IDs are in the batch. This is only a heuristic. Also, the MaxCount path uses LimitOffset, which can return fewer IDs. A batch size of 999 or less is fine, but the inlined-ID branch depends on configuration rather than on len(ids). Use len(ids) for robustness.

title: Orphan tag condition: unqualified annotation_id and no ORDER BY in fetch
body: The condition `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM annotation a WHERE annotation_id = a.id)` sits in a query on annotation_tag. The column resolves via the outer scope, so it works, but it is fragile. More importantly, the whole orphan scan is re-run for every batch, as before. The semantics are unchanged, but the unbounded LIMIT is appended after the NOT EXISTS clause without ORDER BY, so batch selection is nondeterministic.

title: Large test inserts 40k rows per backend with a 32767 batch
body: The batch-size test creates 40003 annotations and 80k tags. With the SQLite inline branch this covers the limit. However, no test exercises the non-SQLite placeholder path with large batches or the concurrent-insert scenario that motivated the change, so the deadlock fix is untested.

title: Cleanup ticker interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. It looks like a leftover debugging change and is unrelated to the deadlock fix. All cleanup jobs (snapshots, dashboard versions, annotations, query history) now run 10x as often. The job timeout is 9 minutes, so runs can overlap with load. It should be reverted.

title: Debug logging at Error level, including full ID lists
body: Each batch logs at Error level, in both the time-based and count-based cleanup and in orphaned-tag cleanup. The log lines include the full slice of IDs, which can be tens of thousands of entries, and they are emitted even when nothing happened or no error occurred. This floods the error logs, inflates log volume and misleads alerting. These look like debug leftovers and should be removed, or reduced to Debug without the ID list.

title: Orphaned tag cleanup condition is fragile and likely mis-scoped
body: fetchIDs builds `SELECT id FROM annotation_tag WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM annotation a WHERE annotation_id = a.id) LIMIT n`. The unqualified `annotation_id` and `id` in the select list depend on name resolution. The subquery is still a correlated read on annotation, so the original MySQL lock interaction may remain. The condition string is also assembled by concatenation, which makes it brittle.

title: SQLite parameter-limit check uses configured batch size rather than actual ID count
body: The check compares the configured batch size to 999 instead of len(ids). Beyond that, the placeholder path is also used for non-SQLite databases with large batches. Postgres allows at most 65535 bind parameters, and MySQL limits placeholders to 65535 in prepared statements. A large configured batch size can therefore make the delete fail. Branching on len(ids) and chunking the deletes would be more robust.

title: Loop termination depends on affected rows, which can cause an endless loop
body: The loop stops only when affected==0. If the IDs fetched in a batch are deleted concurrently by another process, affected is 0 and cleanup stops early even though more rows remain. Stopping when no IDs were fetched would be more accurate.

title: Storage failures recorded as legacy duration metrics
body: When Storage.Create fails (line 45) and when Storage.Update fails (line 129), the code calls recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration. Unified-storage errors are therefore attributed to the legacy metrics, and the storage error metrics miss them.

title: Async legacy DeleteCollection recorded as storage duration
body: The goroutine that calls Legacy.DeleteCollection records its outcome with recordStorageDuration. It should use recordLegacyDuration, so the legacy metric is never emitted for delete-collection and the storage metric is polluted.

title: Delete success metric uses name as the kind label
body: On successful delete, recordStorageDuration is passed `name` where every other call passes options.Kind. This creates a high-cardinality label series per object name and splits the metrics for this method.

title: Delete stores the wrong logger in the context
body: klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) is used instead of the enriched `log`. The method, name and kind values are lost for downstream logging, and the async legacy goroutine inherits this context.

title: Async legacy write reuses the request context
body: The goroutines derive their context from the request ctx. Once the HTTP request completes, that ctx is cancelled, so the legacy create/update/delete may be cancelled mid-flight or fail immediately. The legacy write is not reliable. Use context.WithoutCancel(ctx), or a background context that carries the logger, for the legacy write. Update's goroutine also reuses objInfo and the validation closures after the request has returned, and legacy failures are only recorded in metrics, not logged.

title: Tests don't verify async legacy writes
body: The tests never wait for or assert that the legacy mock is called after the unified write. The legacy mocks are set up but unverified, and the goroutines may outlive the test or race with mock state. The error case sets up a Legacy Create expectation that is never used.

title: Storage failures recorded as legacy duration metrics
body: When Storage.Create fails, the code calls recordLegacyDuration even though the failed call was against Storage. The same mistake occurs in Update at line 129. This pollutes the legacy-store error metrics and hides storage failures from the storage metrics.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection duration recorded as storage metric
body: The goroutine that calls Legacy.DeleteCollection records its result with recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration. Legacy timings and errors are attributed to the storage metrics, so legacy deletecollection metrics are never emitted.

title: Delete success metric uses name instead of kind
body: recordStorageDuration on the success path passes `name` where every other call passes `options.Kind`. This creates a high-cardinality label (one per object name) and splits the delete metric inconsistently from the error path.

title: Context built from d.Log instead of the enriched log
body: In Delete, `klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` is used rather than `log`, so the name, kind and method values are dropped from the context passed to storage and to the async legacy call.

title: Async legacy write reuses the request context
body: The goroutine derives its context from the request ctx, which is cancelled once the HTTP request returns. The legacy write is therefore often cancelled, especially under the 10s timeout, so the legacy store silently drifts. The same applies in Update, Delete and DeleteCollection. Use a context detached from the request, e.g. context.WithoutCancel. In addition, errors from the legacy writes are never logged, only counted in metrics, and the objInfo and obj are shared across goroutines.

title: Tests do not verify async legacy writes and race with the mock
body: The tests never wait for or assert that the legacy goroutines ran. In the failing-create case the legacy mock is set up for a call that never happens. The goroutines share a testify mock without synchronization, which risks data races and leaked goroutines after the test ends. The tests should use a sync mechanism and AssertCalled for the legacy calls.

title: Storage failure recorded as a legacy duration
body: In Create (line 45) and Update (line 129), a failure of the Storage call is recorded with recordLegacyDuration. The call that failed is the unified-storage one, so storage error metrics are missed and legacy error metrics are inflated. Both should use recordStorageDuration(true, ...).

title: Legacy DeleteCollection duration recorded as storage metric
body: The goroutine that calls Legacy.DeleteCollection records its result with recordStorageDuration. That should be recordLegacyDuration. As written, the legacy outcome is counted under storage and the legacy metric is never emitted for this method.

title: Delete uses d.Log instead of the enriched logger
body: ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) discards the `log` built just above with name, kind and method values. Downstream log lines therefore lack that context. It should be klog.NewContext(ctx, log).

title: Delete success metric labelled with name instead of kind
body: The success path passes `name` (the object name) where every other call passes options.Kind. This creates one metric label value per object, which is a high-cardinality leak, and splits the series from the error path.

title: Async legacy write reuses request context and objInfo after the request returns
body: The goroutines derive their context from the request ctx, which is cancelled when the HTTP request finishes. The legacy write can then be cancelled before it runs. In Update, objInfo is also reused after Storage.Update has already applied it, and it is not rebased on the stored result. Create and Update also reuse the same obj or objInfo, which the storage layer may have mutated, so this can race and send inconsistent data to legacy. The goroutine should use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) and a copy of the stored result.

title: Tests do not verify async legacy writes and can race with mock use
body: The tests never wait for or assert the goroutine's legacy call. In the error-case Create test, setupLegacyFn registers a legacy mock, but Create returns before it is used. The unsynchronised testify mock is shared between the goroutine and the test, which can trigger the race detector or panics for unexpected calls. The Update/Create legacy calls therefore have no real coverage.

title: No re-check of cache after taking write lock (thundering herd)
body: After the RLock check misses, every concurrent caller takes the write lock and then reloads the manifest from disk. The cache is not re-checked under the write lock. On a cold start, N concurrent requests will each read and parse assets-manifest.json serially. Re-check `entryPointAssetsCache != nil && cfg.Env != setting.Dev` after `Lock()` to avoid the duplicate work.

title: Cache overwritten with nil result on error
body: `entryPointAssetsCache = result` runs even when `err != nil`, in which case result is nil. A transient read failure therefore wipes a previously valid cache, which matters in Dev mode, where the code reloads on every call. Callers also receive a nil assets pointer alongside the error. The cache should only be assigned when err == nil.

title: No re-check of cache after acquiring write lock
body: After the read-locked check fails, every concurrent caller blocks on Lock() and then reloads the manifest from disk. On a cold start, N concurrent requests each re-read and re-parse the manifest (and possibly fetch from the CDN), because the cache is not re-checked once the write lock is held. This is the classic double-checked locking omission. Re-check `entryPointAssetsCache != nil && cfg.Env != setting.Dev` after Lock() to avoid redundant work.

title: Cache overwritten with nil result when loading fails
body: `entryPointAssetsCache = result` is assigned even when err != nil, so result is nil. A transient failure (e.g. a missing manifest) wipes a previously valid cache entry. The function then returns (nil, err), which callers may dereference. Only store the result when err == nil.

title: No re-check of cache after acquiring write lock
body: After the RLock is released and the write Lock is taken, the cache is not checked again. When the cache is cold in non-dev mode, N concurrent callers all pass the nil check and then serialize on the write lock. Each one re-reads the manifest file and rebuilds the assets, and each one overwrites the cache. Add a double-checked `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return ... }` after Lock().

title: Cache is overwritten even when loading fails
body: `entryPointAssetsCache = result` runs unconditionally. If the read fails, result is nil and the cache is set to nil, which discards a previously good value. This is mainly a problem in dev mode. The error is still returned alongside a nil pointer. Only assign the cache when err == nil.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false, with confusing dead logic
body: The function computes `enabled := !IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns false on both branches. It is unconditionally disabled regardless of the feature flag. That is the intended security fix, but the inverted flag check and the redundant branches look like a bug and mislead readers into thinking the flag still controls the feature. It should be a plain `return false` with a comment explaining why. The error message 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' also gives users no hint that the feature was deliberately disabled.

title: SQL expressions are still reachable through the non-reader path
body: Only ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery is gated. UnmarshalSQLCommand in sql_command.go (used by the legacy node-building path) still calls NewSQLCommand, and nothing in that path checks the flag or the disabled state. Because the stub DB returns 'not implemented' from TablesList, those queries fail rather than execute. Still, the disabling is incidental to the stub and not enforced at the entry point. Add an explicit guard in NewSQLCommand or UnmarshalSQLCommand.

title: No tests cover the disabled behaviour
body: The PR changes SQL expression behaviour to always fail but adds no test asserting that QueryTypeSQL returns an error and that the stub DB errors. Any existing SQL expression tests that expect success will now fail or silently go stale.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false, with confusing dead logic
body: The function computes `enabled := !IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions)` and returns false on both branches, so the result never depends on the flag. The inverted flag check and the redundant branches suggest a mistake or a half-finished edit. If SQL expressions are meant to be disabled outright, the function should be `return false`, or the check should be removed. The flag is also now meaningless, and the error 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' hides the real reason (disabled for security).

title: SQL command construction paths outside the reader still reachable
body: Only ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery blocks SQL. UnmarshalSQLCommand (the legacy path that calls NewSQLCommand) has no guard and is not gated. It now fails with a generic 'error reading SQL command' because TablesList returns 'not implemented', hiding the real reason. The disabling is incomplete and inconsistent: it relies on stubs rather than an explicit check at all entry points.

title: No tests for the disabled behavior
body: No test verifies that SQL query types are rejected by the reader or that the stub DB returns errors. Existing SQL expression tests that relied on DuckDB will likely fail or remain unadjusted, and the security-critical behavior is left unprotected against regressions.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false, with confusing dead logic
body: The function computes `enabled := !IsEnabledGlobally(...)`, then returns false in both branches. SQL expressions are therefore disabled unconditionally, even with the feature flag on. That matches the security intent, but the inverted `enabled` variable and the redundant branches suggest a bug and make the code hard to review. It should be a plain `return false`, or the call site should return the error directly, with a comment explaining the intentional hard-disable.

title: Disabling is only enforced in ReadQuery; other construction paths are not guarded
body: Only the ExpressionQueryReader path rejects SQL queries. UnmarshalSQLCommand and NewSQLCommand are still reachable, for example through the legacy node-building path in the pipeline. They call sql.TablesList, which now returns a 'not implemented' error and surfaces as a generic 'error reading SQL command'. The behavior is inconsistent, and the user-facing message differs by path. The disabling should be applied centrally, for example in NewSQLCommand.

title: No tests cover the disabled behavior
body: The PR adds stub DB methods and a hard-disable but no tests asserting that SQL expression queries are rejected. Existing SQL command/parser tests that depended on DuckDB may now fail or be silently stale. A regression test is needed to guard against re-enabling the vulnerable path.

title: Data race on shared err and counter in init workers
body: The errgroup closures run concurrently. They all assign to the outer `err` with `_, _, err = s.build(...)`, and they all do `totalBatchesIndexed++` without synchronization. This is a data race, and it is now on the startup path. The reported `namespaced_indexed` count can also be wrong. Use a local error variable and an atomic counter.

title: Blocking Init in constructor with a cancelable background ctx; stale/hanging failure modes
body: NewResourceServer now runs the full search index build synchronously, so construction blocks until every namespace is indexed. If anything fails, the whole server fails to construct. Previously this failure only surfaced on the first request. The lifecycle `Init` also runs here with the server's own context. Startup time and failure semantics change significantly, and the PR's own question about lazy-init dependents remains unanswered. The `Init` call to `lifecycle.Init` can also run before the SQL backend has been set up by other callers.

title: Concurrent builds of same key can race and leak/overwrite index
body: Removing the lock around the whole of BuildIndex means two concurrent builds for the same key can both run. For file-backed indexes, `bleve.New(dir)` fails for the second caller because the directory already exists. For memory indexes, the second build silently overwrites the first in the cache and leaks it. `getOrCreateIndex` is a check-then-build with no dedup. Previously the lock serialized this.

title: TotalDocs iterates cache without lock
body: `TotalDocs` reads `b.cache` without taking `cacheMu`. Builds can now write to the map concurrently, and `init` calls `TotalDocs` in a new log line. A concurrent map read and write can cause a fatal runtime error.

title: Test skipped for postgres instead of fixed
body: The integration test is now skipped for postgres to work around a failure that is probably caused by the eager init change. This reduces coverage rather than addressing the cause.

title: Concurrent BuildIndex for the same key can clobber file index / leak
body: The whole-function lock was removed. Two concurrent builds for the same key (for example getOrCreateIndex racing with init) now both call bleve.New on the same directory. The second call fails with an 'already exists' error, or one index overwrites the other in the cache and the loser is never closed. Nothing deduplicates builds per key, so a concurrent build can fail or leak an index.

title: TotalDocs iterates cache without lock
body: TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without taking cacheMu. The map is now written under a fine-grained lock from concurrent BuildIndex calls, and TotalDocs is also called from search.init's new log line. Reading the map without the lock is a data race and can cause a fatal 'concurrent map iteration and map write'.

title: Data race on shared err and counter in init workers
body: Inside group.Go closures running concurrently, `totalBatchesIndexed++` is an unsynchronized increment and `_, _, err = s.build(...)` assigns to the outer shared `err` variable. Both are data races, and the recorded batch count may be wrong. Use a local err and an atomic counter.

title: Eager Init uses the long-lived server context and blocks construction
body: NewResourceServer now runs the full index build synchronously with s.ctx, which is cancelled on Stop. Constructor failure now aborts startup entirely when the index build or lifecycle init fails. Previously the error only surfaced per request. Startup time scales with the index size, and the backend/DB must be ready at construction. The PR also skips the postgres integration test rather than fixing it.

title: Data race on shared err and counter in init worker goroutines
body: Inside group.Go closures, `totalBatchesIndexed++` is an unsynchronized increment from multiple goroutines, and `_, _, err = s.build(...)` assigns to the outer `err` shared by all workers. These are data races. Init now runs at startup, with many namespaces and high concurrency, so the race is more likely to bite. The event count may also be wrong. Use an atomic counter and a local err.

title: Init at construction runs before DB backend lifecycle and uses a cancelable server ctx
body: NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) synchronously, so the constructor blocks until all indexes are built, and any failure makes server creation fail outright. Also, the ctx passed to Init is the server-lifetime ctx (cancelled by Stop). It is also used for the search.init Watch goroutine; this is fine. But lifecycle.Init previously ran lazily after DI wiring, so the SQL backend now has to be fully usable at construction time. Callers constructing servers in tests or in non-storage targets will now eagerly hit the DB and may fail. The PR itself skips a postgres test because of this.

title: TotalDocs iterates cache without lock
body: BuildIndex now writes to b.cache under cacheMu only briefly, and concurrent builds are now possible. TotalDocs reads the map without taking cacheMu.RLock. This is a concurrent map read/write race and can panic. search.init now calls TotalDocs right after the concurrent builds, and the new logging call makes it more likely.

title: Concurrent BuildIndex for same key can create duplicate/overwritten indexes
body: Removing the function-wide lock means two concurrent builds for the same key (for example getOrCreateIndex from a search request racing with init or a watch event) both build and the last one silently overwrites the cache entry. For file-backed indexes, bleve.New on the same directory fails for the second builder, or leaks the earlier index, which is never closed.

title: Trace context still not propagated in other methods
body: Only GetResourceStats was fixed. WriteEvent, ReadResource and ListIterator still discard the span context with `_, span :=`, so child spans are not parented correctly. The same applies to bleve BuildIndex, which still uses `_, span`.

title: Passkey form attributes are set on a form that is not used for the username-only login page
body: The branch around line 115 now calls webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) when a user is already set. fillContextForm sets a new challenge auth note and sets attributes on context.form(). UsernameForm now skips its success shortcut and falls through to super.authenticate in that case. That is the intended re-authentication path. However, this means the challenge note is overwritten on every re-render, including after a failed password attempt. A passkey page left open in another tab then fails challenge validation. This is a minor robustness issue.

title: Missing @Override on overriding method
body: shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators overrides the parent method but has no @Override annotation. If the parent signature changes, the override silently stops working.

title: Catch of a generic Exception swallows the test's own failure
body: The try block calls fail(...) when the webauth form is found. fail() throws AssertionError, which is an Error, so it is not caught by catch(Exception). The nullValue() assertion on a findElement result would also throw NoSuchElementException, so the check is convoluted. If an element is present, the nullValue assertion throws AssertionError, which propagates correctly. The real concern is the catch of all Exceptions, which hides unrelated driver errors. Use findElements().isEmpty() instead.

title: UsernameForm re-auth with passkeys but no passkey registered shows the username form
body: When conditional passkeys are enabled for the realm and context.getUser() != null, the auto-skip is bypassed for every user, not just those who have a passkey. A re-authenticating user with no passkey is forced through the username form again. Because USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH is not set in this path, the form may offer a different username instead of re-authenticating the current user. The previous behaviour (skip the form) is lost for non-passkey users. The existing tests do not cover this case for UsernameForm.

title: Conditional passkey UI enabled in re-authentication even if the user has no passkey
body: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(user) only checks that passkeys are enabled and the user is non-null. During re-authentication, the webauthn form and conditional UI are therefore rendered for users with no registered passkey. The WebAuthn authenticator list is deliberately hidden (shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators returns false), so nothing narrows the prompt to this user's credentials. Discoverable credentials of a different user could be offered. A later mismatch is rejected only by the different-user check, which gives a confusing error.

title: Negative assertion wrapped in try/catch(Exception) is ineffective
body: fail(...) throws AssertionError, which is an Error and not an Exception, so it is not swallowed. The real flaw is that findElement throws NoSuchElementException, so the assertThat(..., nullValue()) line is never reached when the element is absent. Any other Exception, such as a driver or timeout error, also silently passes the test. Use Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, ...) or findElements(...).isEmpty() instead.

title: UsernameForm re-auth with passkeys enabled shows a username input for an already-known user
body: When a user is already set and conditional passkeys are enabled, the shortcut that skips the form is bypassed. super.authenticate then renders createLoginUsername() via the overridden createLoginForm/challenge. That form is a username-only form for a user who is already identified, and USERNAME_HIDDEN is set only in UsernamePasswordForm.authenticate. In the UsernameForm+PasswordForm flow, the user may be asked to type a username during re-authentication. A mismatched username then clears or conflicts with the user, so the flow is confusing or broken.

title: Conditional passkeys are now set up only when a user is already set
body: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(user) requires user != null. The old code filled the webauthn context form exactly when the user was NULL, which is the normal first-time login case. Now authenticate() (line 115) and challenge() (line 137) skip fillContextForm when no user is set, so the passkey/conditional UI would not be set up on a fresh login. The tests that expect passkeys on a fresh login (e.g. webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey) would fail. The condition looks inverted, or the user check should be dropped; if the flow was intentionally changed, the helper name and semantics are misleading.

title: Test still asserts passkeys are absent after username step
body: passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey asserts that the webauthn form is absent on the password page. The same scenario in PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest was changed to expect it present, so the two are inconsistent. The new re-authentication tests do not cover the UsernameForm re-auth path with a password-less user in a way that exercises the changed condition.

title: Org-filter searchKey does not capture the cached result's dependence on the organizationId
body: The cache key is only realm+mode, and the searchKey is the organizationId. IdentityProviderListQuery stores one entry per searchKey. When an org changes membership of an IDP, only the three login keys are invalidated, which is fine. However, the query is built per search key and an IDP's enabled/org state may change via organization enable/disable or removal of an org, with no login invalidation. Org-bound IDPs are wrapped for isEnabled, but removing an org or unlinking an IDP through the organization provider can leave stale lists. getById invalidation of the IDP id does not invalidate the list query.

title: Update invalidation relies on a possibly stale or null original model
body: update() calls getById(model.getInternalId()), which may return the cached model. The login predicate is evaluated on that. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate calls getLoginPredicate on `original` and `updated`. The predicate reads idp.getConfig().get(...), which could NPE if the config is null. Also, if the model is returned wrapped, the enabled state reflects the organization's state, so the original's enabled state is misjudged (an org-disabled IDP looks disabled), which can skip a needed invalidation.

title: remove() now fetches the IDP unconditionally and may NPE
body: storedIdp = idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias) can be null for a nonexistent alias. registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp) is safe because the predicate checks nonNull, but the isInvalid branch still calls registerIDPInvalidation(storedIdp), which throws an NPE on null (previous behavior was the same). The added DB query on every remove is also needless when the cache branch is taken.

title: getLoginPredicate semantics changed without matching the search options
body: The predicate now also requires org-linked IDPs to have BROKER_PUBLIC=true. getLoginSearchOptions is unchanged, and other callers of getLoginPredicate get new filtering behavior. Also, idp.getConfig() may be null, causing an NPE.

title: Cleanup registered with the literal alias "alias"
body: getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove) uses the literal string "alias" instead of the created alias, so the IDPs are never cleaned up. This can leak state into other tests. The same bug appears for idp-alias-20.

title: Cached IDP list is not safe when organization membership changes or an org is invalidated
body: The login cache key contains only realm and fetch mode, so each search (per organizationId) is stored in a single IdentityProviderListQuery. Invalidation happens only when an IDP's login status or organization link changes. getByOrganization also checks isInvalid(orgId), but getForLogin does not. Org-level changes such as deleting an org or removing its IDPs can therefore leave stale results. The wrapped enabled state is also not part of the cached ids. Deleting an org or unlinking an IDP through the organization API may not hit the registerIDPLoginInvalidation path, depending on whether it goes through update().

title: remove() may NPE or change behavior for a missing alias
body: storedIdp = idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias) is now fetched unconditionally. If the alias does not exist it is null. When isInvalid(cacheKey) is true, registerIDPInvalidation(storedIdp) dereferences it and throws a NullPointerException. This path previously only ran in the invalid case. registerIDPLoginInvalidation tolerates null via the predicate's nonNull check, but the first call does not. remove() on a nonexistent alias should return false. The extra DB query on every removal is also unnecessary when the cache already holds the IDP.

title: Set-based result loses ordering and may return disabled IDPs
body: Results are collected into a HashSet and the cached ids are a Set, so any ordering from the delegate is lost. getById returns org-aware wrappers whose isEnabled depends on the organization's state. Callers that don't re-check isEnabled would get disabled IDPs, because the cache holds IDs computed with the original enabled state. Only OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean was patched, and not the REALM_ONLY path.

title: getLoginPredicate semantics changed for non-cache users
body: The added clause makes an org-linked IDP count as a login IDP only if BROKER_PUBLIC is true. This changes a shared SPI predicate. It also calls idp.getConfig().get(...), which NPEs if the config is null. The change is only justified for cache invalidation, but it alters public behaviour for any other user of the predicate.

title: Cleanup registered for the wrong alias
body: getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove) uses the literal "alias" instead of the created alias. The created IDPs are never cleaned up and may leak into other tests. The same bug exists at line 303 and is copied here.

title: Cached login IDP set is keyed by organizationId but ignores org-scoped invalidation
body: The login query is cached per realm and FetchMode, with the organizationId as the searchKey. Invalidation only fires from IDP create/update/remove. Changes that alter results without touching the IDP, such as disabling an organization, deleting one, or changing org membership, do not invalidate the entry. The code relies on the isEnabled wrapper for the disabled-org case, but a deleted org or an IDP unlinked through the organization API may leave stale entries. In getByOrganization the code also checks isInvalid(orgId), and that check is missing here.

title: update() invalidation uses the cached original, which may be stale or wrapped
body: registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate compares the original (from getById, an org-aware wrapper whose isEnabled() depends on org state) with the updated model. The predicate is evaluated on the wrapper, so a disabled organization makes the original look like it is not a login IDP. As a result invalidation can be skipped or triggered wrongly. The comparison should use the raw stored model.

title: remove() may NPE when the IDP does not exist
body: storedIdp is now fetched unconditionally via idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias). When the alias is unknown it is null. registerIDPLoginInvalidation tolerates null through the predicate's nonNull check. However, in the isInvalid branch registerIDPInvalidation(storedIdp) dereferences it, which is the same as the old behavior. The unconditional extra DB lookup on every remove is also new.

title: Per-id getById calls on every cached login lookup
body: On a cache hit, each cached id is resolved via session.identityProviders().getById(id). Each miss there costs a DB query, so the cache gives limited benefit after an IDP invalidation. The resulting set is also an unordered HashSet, so result order is not preserved.

title: getLoginPredicate dereferences idp.getConfig() and changes semantics
body: The new condition treats an org-linked IDP as a login IDP only if BROKER_PUBLIC is true. This is used for cache invalidation decisions. The ORG_ONLY fetch with a specific organizationId includes the public filter, so it is consistent, but any other consumer of the predicate now behaves differently. Linking or unlinking an IDP to an org through the organization API changes the org id without going through this check unless update() is called.

title: readSequence loop mishandles indefinite length and can loop forever
body: readLength() returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding, so the `while (length > 0)` loop is skipped and an empty list is returned without any error. Separately, if readNext() returns a zero-length array, `length` never decreases and the loop does not terminate. Truncated or malformed signatures are therefore not rejected cleanly.

title: Incorrect length bound check
body: The out-of-bounds check is only done for long-form lengths, and the comparison `length >= limit` is against the whole input rather than the remaining bytes. Short-form lengths are never checked. The subsequent `new byte[length]` in read() can therefore be sized by malformed input, with failure only at EOF. Inside nested decoders, `limit` is the size of the sub-array, which makes the check inconsistent.

title: Dead code: redundant ASN1 encodings
body: The two `ASN1Encoder.create().write(...)` calls at lines 114-115 discard their results and do nothing. They are leftovers and should be removed.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default KeyStore's provider
body: The method returns the provider of the default KeyStore type, which is SUN, not BouncyCastle. Callers that use `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER` can end up with a mismatched provider name. This is misleading and is likely to break when other CryptoProvider methods are invoked in the authz-client.

title: New abstract method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: `order()` is added as an abstract interface method without a default. Any third-party or other-module CryptoProvider implementation will fail to compile. Providing `default int order() { return 0; }` would avoid the break.

title: Ties between providers resolved silently and nondeterministically
body: The check that rejected multiple providers was removed. Providers with equal order (e.g. Default, Elytron and FIPS are all 200) are now chosen by ServiceLoader order, so a misconfigured classpath no longer fails fast. The ignored providers are logged only at debug level.

title: readSequence loops forever or misbehaves on indefinite-length or truncated input
body: readLength() returns -1 for the indefinite-length form (0x80). readSequence() then skips the `while (length > 0)` loop and returns an empty list without reading anything. For malformed input the loop depends on readNext() consuming data. A zero-length element can make no progress. The caller only checks `seq.size() != 2`, so malformed signatures yield confusing errors instead of a clear rejection. Short-form lengths are also not validated against the remaining stream size.

title: Dead duplicate ASN1 encoding calls
body: Lines 114-115 create encoders and write r and s, then discard the result. The same values are encoded again in the return statement. This is leftover code that does useless work.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns a non-BC provider
body: The method returns the provider of the default KeyStore type, which is SUN. It is not BouncyCastle. Callers such as BouncyIntegration use the returned provider's name for `Provider`-based lookups. They would then request algorithms by the SUN provider name, or fail in unexpected ways. The result also depends on the default keystore type.

title: New abstract method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: Adding the abstract `order()` method to a public SPI interface breaks any third-party CryptoProvider implementation at compile time and at runtime (AbstractMethodError). A `default` method returning a neutral value would avoid this.

title: Duplicate providers with equal order are silently resolved
body: The previous check that threw on multiple providers is removed. Two real providers on the classpath that both have order 200, for example default plus fips, now pick one arbitrarily, depending on classpath order, with only a debug log. A misconfigured deployment would then run with the wrong crypto provider and no error.

title: readSequence loops forever or misbehaves on indefinite length (-1)
body: readLength() returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding. The loop `while (length > 0)` then skips parsing and returns an empty list. A sequence whose declared length exceeds the available data fails with an IOException from read(). The error handling is lenient or inconsistent on malformed input. Trailing bytes are not checked, and a truncated element is only caught indirectly.

title: Dead code in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
body: The two statements `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` build encoders and discard the results. They have no effect and should be removed.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns an unrelated JDK provider
body: The method returns the provider of the default KeyStore type, which is a Sun provider and not BouncyCastle. Callers that use BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER (derived from this provider's name) would then request algorithms by that provider name. Many of those lookups, such as getKeyFactory, are unsupported here anyway, so this can fail confusingly.

title: Abstract order() added to a public SPI breaks existing implementations
body: Adding the abstract method `order()` breaks every third-party CryptoProvider implementation at compile time and load time (AbstractMethodError in detectProvider). It should be a default method, for example returning 100, to stay compatible.

title: Providers with equal order are silently chosen arbitrarily
body: The previous check that failed on multiple providers is gone. Two providers with the same order, such as default and elytron (both 200), are now resolved by classpath order, and the loser is logged only at debug level. A misconfigured classpath is no longer detected.

title: Possible NPE when the Clients type resource is missing
body: In hasPermission(client, scope), when the per-client resource is null, getResourceTypeResource(...) is called. It can return null (for example when authz schema support is off, or the resource was not created). The result is passed straight to findByResource(server, resource) and later to resource.getScopes(), so a null causes a NullPointerException instead of returning false. Add a null check.

title: Fallback to all-clients can grant permission when the per-client resource exists
body: If a client-specific resource exists, evaluation uses only that resource. The evaluation of a specific resource with permissions defined only on the type resource may therefore not fall back to the all-clients permission. In addition, when no specific resource exists, the all-clients resource is evaluated with all of its scopes, which is okay. The two paths are inconsistent and the first path can deny access that the all-clients permission should grant.

title: canMapRoles/composite/clientScope ignore all-clients permission
body: canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles and canMapClientScopeRoles only call hasPermission(client, ...). The Javadoc in ClientPermissionEvaluator says the all-clients scope also applies, but the resource type path is used only when no per-client resource exists. A client with its own resource therefore loses the all-clients grant. The check for CONFIGURE also does not imply MANAGE semantics consistently.

title: Dead code and unused imports
body: The private getEvaluationContext method, the logger, the TOKEN_EXCHANGE static import, and the Scope import are all unused. This is dead code that should be removed.

title: Role/client/group removal listener gated on feature flag changes behavior
body: The listener body is now wrapped in Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ). This is an unrelated behavior change, and it is also a risk: with V2 enabled and the V1 feature off, no cleanup runs. Meanwhile ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException, so if both are enabled, deleting a client or role would throw from the listener. The change is neither described nor tested.

title: Possible NPE when the Clients type resource is missing
body: In hasPermission(client, scope), if the per-client resource is not found, the code loads the "Clients" type resource via getResourceTypeResource. That method returns null when the schema is unsupported or the resource is absent. The result is passed straight to policyStore.findByResource(server, resource) and later to resource.getScopes(), which causes a NullPointerException and a 500 instead of a clean deny.

title: Per-client resource lookup does not fall back to the all-clients permission
body: If a per-client resource exists (for example one with only a CONFIGURE permission), evaluation uses only that resource. A MANAGE or VIEW permission granted on all clients is never consulted for that client. The users flow handles this fallback, so a client with its own resource can be denied despite an all-clients grant. The negative-permission semantics also differ from users.

title: Dead code and unused imports
body: getEvaluationContext is never used. The imports Scope, TOKEN_EXCHANGE, the Logger field, ClientModelIdentity and DefaultEvaluationContext are also unused. Remove them.

title: isPermissionsEnabled/setPermissionsEnabled throw UnsupportedOperationException
body: The ClientRemovedEvent listener in AdminPermissions calls clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false). With V2 this now throws UnsupportedOperationException, because AdminPermissions.management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2. The event listener is gated only by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ feature check, which is true when V2 is enabled. Deleting a client or role can therefore fail. Other callers, such as the client representation's authorization-permissions-enabled handling, would hit the same exception.

title: getClientsWithPermission returns resource names, which are client internal IDs, and may miss per-client resources
body: findByType is applied to the type "Clients", and the resource name is added to the result. The all-clients resource itself may match that type, so the name "Clients" can end up in the result set. A client that is covered only by an all-clients permission and has no per-client resource is not listed. This weakens list and search for clients.

title: NPE when the all-clients resource is missing
body: In hasPermission(client, scope), if no per-client resource exists, getResourceTypeResource() is used. It returns null when the schema is not supported or the resource is absent. The next line, findByResource(server, resource), is then called with null, which can throw an NPE or give wrong results.
