Also, `operation` is no longer passed by any caller, and the redundant `rule && rule.type === PromRuleType.Alerting` re-check after the type guard is dead code.

title: Stale comments still describe Ruler loading
body: The component doc says it 'Loads an evaluation group from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints', and the `expectedRulesCount` doc refers to the 'Ruler response'. The component now only queries Prometheus. A similar leftover is in `prometheusGroupsGenerator.ts`, where the comment about preloading ruler rules and the `cacheAndRulerPreload` variable name remain after the ruler prefetch was removed. These are misleading for maintainers.

title: GrafanaRuleListItem rendered in .map() without a `key`
body: The previous `<GrafanaRuleLoader key={key} .../>` became `<GrafanaRuleListItem .../>` and the `key` prop was dropped. The `datasource` and default branches still pass `key={key}`. Siblings without keys in a mapped list trigger React's missing-key warning. They also break reconciliation as the list grows via infinite scroll and `startTransition` updates, so per-item state can attach to the wrong row. That state includes the delete modal, silence drawer and clone redirect held in `RuleActionsButtons`. Add `key={key}`.

title: Delete and Pause menu items can never appear in the ruler-less list view
body: The new list view passes only `promRule` and no `rulerRule`. `canPause` and `canDelete` are computed from the prom abilities, but rendering is still gated on the ruler rule. Pause requires `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` (line 123). Delete requires `canDelete && rulerRule` (line 165). With only a prom rule, both items are silently hidden even when the user holds the permissions. The new `GrafanaGroupLoader` test grants `AlertingRuleDelete` yet asserts only four menu items (silence, copy link, duplicate, export), which confirms delete is gone. Users lose the ability to delete or pause Grafana rules from the list. `handleDelete` and `MenuItemPauseRule` need to work from a prom rule or identifier, or the gating needs to be reworked.

title: 'Silence notifications' menu item does nothing in the list view
body: The silence drawer is only mounted when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) && showSilenceDrawer`. In the list view `rule` is undefined because only `promRule` is passed. `AlertRuleMenu` still shows 'Silence notifications' via `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` and its `onClick` sets `showSilenceDrawer` to true. Nothing renders, so the menu action silently does nothing. The drawer needs to be supported with a prom rule, or the menu item hidden when no ruler rule is available.

title: Federated rule group check dropped from the legacy useAllAlertRuleAbilities path
body: `useAllAlertRuleAbilities(rule: CombinedRule)` previously computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`. It now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, which hardcodes `isFederated = false` with a TODO. The legacy list, RulesTable and `RuleActionsButtons` v1 still use this hook. Rules in federated (`source_tenants`) groups are therefore no longer treated as immutable, and Edit/Delete/Pause become available for them. The deprecated wrapper should keep the federation check, or the `CombinedRule.group` should be passed through.

title: Grafana recording rules lose Export (and Pause/Restore) abilities in the prom-based path
body: The ruler-based hook uses `isGrafanaManagedAlertRule`, which is true for both alerting and recording Grafana rules, for `ModifyExport`, `Pause`, `Restore` and `DeletePermanently`. The new prom-based hook uses `prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` for these. Recording rules lose Export in the new list view, and Pause/Restore/DeletePermanently are inconsistent with the ruler path. The comment says all rules are Grafana-managed 'by definition', which suggests a `grafana.rule` check was intended. Only Silence should be restricted to alerting rules.

title: returnTo parameter dropped from the rule view link
body: The old `GrafanaRuleListItem` built the href with `createRelativeUrl(..., { returnTo: createReturnTo() })`. The new component links to `/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view` with no `returnTo`. After opening a rule from the list, the view page can no longer navigate back to the current list or filter state. It is also inconsistent with the other list item types. This looks accidental, since the rest of the change is about removing ruler requests.

title: Tests encode the missing Delete item and miss the broken Silence flow
body: The test grants `AlertingRuleDelete` and `AlertingRuleUpdate` but asserts exactly four menu items with no Delete. That locks in the regression where Delete and Pause are unreachable from the list view. No test clicks 'Silence notifications' and checks that the drawer opens, which would have caught the dead action. The old creating/deleting-state tests and `matchRules` tests were removed with the feature. The RulesTable RBAC tests still use rules that carry both `rulerRule` and `promRule`, so they do not exercise a prom-only rule.

title: Stale doc comments still mention the Ruler endpoint
body: The component doc says it 'Loads an evaluation group from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints', and the `expectedRulesCount` doc says 'Ruler response might contain different number of rules'. The component no longer calls the Ruler API. Update both comments to avoid misleading future readers.

title: Comment and variable name still refer to ruler preload that was removed
body: The ruler-group prefetch was deleted, but the comment 'This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules, but it improves the UX' and the variable name `cacheAndRulerPreload` remain. The block now only upserts the Prometheus cache. Rename the variable and fix the comment.

title: Shard path now interpolates the same queries repeatedly (once up front, again per sub-request)
body: runShardSplitQuery now calls applyTemplateVariables on every target. Each shard-group sub-request is then passed to runSplitQuery, which this PR also changed to call applyTemplateVariables on every target. DataSourceWithBackend.query() interpolates once more when runQuery executes. So each query is interpolated 1 + N + N times, where N is the number of shard groups and time chunks. Each pass re-runs addAdHocFilters, which does a Loki AST parse and rewrite. Ad-hoc filters are re-applied to already-filtered expressions, and text that is already interpolated is run through the template engine again. The result is wasted CPU on every sub-request, plus a risk of re-substituting `$…` text that was produced by a first-pass variable value. Interpolate once at the top-level entry point, or have the shard path tell runSplitQuery to skip re-interpolation.

title: Test hard-codes the redundant interpolation count (5 calls)
body: The assertion changed from `interpolateVariablesInQueries` being called once to `applyTemplateVariables` being called 5 times. That is 1 call from runShardSplitQuery plus 4 from runSplitQuery, one per sub-request. The test pins the double interpolation as expected behaviour. It will break whenever the number of shards or groups changes, and it will fail if the redundancy is later fixed. It should assert that interpolation happened and that the final queries are correct, not the exact call count.

title: Empty-expression filter runs before interpolation
body: Targets are filtered with `.filter((query) => query.expr)` before `applyTemplateVariables`. A query whose expression is only a variable that resolves to an empty string, such as `$myQuery`, therefore survives as an empty expr after interpolation. It then flows into `isLogsQuery`, `querySupportsSplitting`, `calculateStep` and the request, instead of being dropped as an empty query. The same ordering is used in shardQuerySplitting.ts (hide and expr filters before the map). The old shard code filtered after interpolation, so this is a behaviour change there. Run the empty-expression filter after the interpolation map.

title: New interpolation tests do not cover scopedVars or ad-hoc filter forwarding
body: The new 'Interpolates queries before execution' tests only exercise the mocked `replace` on `$__auto` and `$step`. Nothing verifies that `request.scopedVars` and `request.filters` are forwarded to `applyTemplateVariables`, which is the new contract in both runSplitQuery and runShardSplitQuery. Nothing verifies that ad-hoc filters end up in the executed sub-queries. There is also no test that the interpolated step is what feeds `calculateStep` for grouping, which is the point of the fix. A regression that drops the filters argument would pass these tests.

title: Sharded path interpolates the same targets at least three times
body: `runShardSplitQuery` now calls `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, scopedVars, filters)` on every target. Each shard sub-request is then passed to `runSplitQuery`, which this PR also changed to call `applyTemplateVariables` on every target. `DataSourceWithBackend.query`, reached through `datasource.runQuery`, applies it a third time. Ad hoc filters (`request.filters`) are now added to the expression at every layer, so the stream selector can pick up the same label filter several times. Already-substituted variable values are also re-scanned, so a value containing `$name` or `${name}` text can be expanded a second time. The updated shard test even asserts `applyTemplateVariables` is called 5 times for one query (1 + 4 sub-requests). Interpolate once at the top, or give the inner `runSplitQuery` a way to skip interpolation when it is called from the shard splitter.

title: Interpolated targets are still re-interpolated downstream, and filters are applied pre-split and again later
body: `runSplitQuery` now applies `applyTemplateVariables` with `request.scopedVars` and `request.filters` to the targets before building the sub-requests. Those interpolated targets are then sent to `datasource.runQuery`, which goes through `DataSourceWithBackend.query` and interpolates them again, adding ad hoc filters a second time. The change is needed so that `isLogsQuery`, `calculateStep` and `querySupportsSplitting` see resolved text. The non-idempotent steps (ad hoc filter injection, regex escaping of multi-value variables) now run on already-processed expressions. Nothing in the PR checks that a second pass is a no-op, for example with several ad hoc filters or a multi-value variable inside a regex matcher.

title: Brittle call-count assertion locks in redundant interpolation; duplicate test name
body: `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` depends on 1 initial interpolation plus 4 sub-requests, each re-interpolating inside `runSplitQuery`. The assertion breaks whenever the shard count changes, and it enshrines the double interpolation as expected behaviour. It does not show that interpolation happens before execution, which is what the test title claims. This test is also named 'Interpolates queries before running', almost identical to the new 'Interpolates queries before execution' test a few lines above, which makes the two hard to tell apart. The new test only checks the first `runQuery` call and does not check ad hoc filters passed via `request.filters`, the main new input to `applyTemplateVariables`.

title: Queries are now interpolated repeatedly (shard path 3x, normal split path 2x)
body: `runSplitQuery` now calls `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, scopedVars, filters)` on every target. `runShardSplitQuery` already interpolates its targets (shardQuerySplitting.ts line 52). It then calls `runSplitQuery` once per shard group, which interpolates the already-interpolated targets again. Each sub-request then goes through `datasource.runQuery`, which (as `DataSourceWithBackend.query`) interpolates a third time. On the plain split path interpolation also happens twice, where before it happened once. `applyTemplateVariables` is not idempotent. Ad-hoc filters (`request.filters`) can be injected into the expression more than once. Variable values that were already substituted and contain `$name`-like text get re-interpolated. Interpolation should happen once at the entry point. The shard path should hand already-interpolated targets to an inner function that skips interpolation, or `runSplitQuery` should skip it when called from the shard path.

title: Test locks in redundant repeated interpolation as expected behaviour
body: `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` (1 call from the shard entry plus 4 from the per-shard `runSplitQuery` sub-requests) asserts the double interpolation as correct. The count depends on the number of shard groups, so it breaks whenever the shard grouping changes. If interpolation is later de-duplicated, this test fails for the wrong reason. The test should assert that the interpolated query reaches `runQuery`, or that interpolation happens once per user query, not an exact call count. The `applyTemplateVariables` mocks also mutate and return the input query in place, which hides any bugs from repeated application on the same object.

title: New ContextualLoggerMiddleware and the reworked LoggerMiddleware have no tests
body: The PR moves the contextual-logger enrichment (endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, uname) out of the metrics middleware into a new ContextualLoggerMiddleware. It also changes LoggerMiddleware to log through `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)` and drops the explicit pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName, dsUID and traceID params. The only test change is renaming a constructor call in the metrics test. Nothing checks that the context ends up carrying the attributes, or that the 'Plugin Request Completed' log still contains the same fields. A regression in the middleware ordering or in `FromContext` would silently drop fields from the data-egress log.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger and discards recorded calls
body: `TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()`, a new instance that does not share state with the receiver. LoggerMiddleware now calls `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`. A test that injects a `TestLogger` and asserts on `InfoLogs` will see zero calls, because the log goes to a throwaway instance. The fake cannot be used to verify the middleware's output. It should return the receiver, or share the log state.

title: Ordering requirement for the contextual logger middleware was dropped from the docs
body: The old InstrumentationMiddleware doc said it enriches the context with a contextual logger and therefore 'should live at the top of the middleware stack'. That responsibility now lives in ContextualLoggerMiddleware, but its doc comment has no ordering note. Its correctness still depends on running before LoggerMiddleware and any other downstream code that calls `logger.FromContext(ctx)`. A future reorder in `CreateMiddlewares` could silently drop the plugin and request fields from logs.

title: Stale 'instrumentation' naming left after the rename
body: The logger is still created as `log.New("plugin.instrumentation")`, so log output keeps the old 'instrumentation' name even though the middleware concept was renamed to metrics and contextual logger. In `metrics_middleware_test.go` the test function is still called `TestInstrumentationMiddleware`, and the local variable in `NewMetricsMiddleware` is still `imw`. This undercuts the stated goal of naming consistency. If the logger name is kept deliberately for log-query compatibility, say so.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, discarding recorded log calls
body: LoggerMiddleware now logs through `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`. `TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()`, a new instance, instead of the receiver. The `Info` call lands on a throwaway object, so `InfoLogs.Calls`, `Message` and `Ctx` on the logger a test injected stay empty. Any test that injects a `TestLogger` into `NewLoggerMiddleware` and asserts on its logs will see nothing. The fake should return `f` (or share its log state) so that assertions on the injected logger work.

title: No tests for the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware or the changed LoggerMiddleware
body: The contextual-logger logic moved out of the metrics middleware into this new middleware, and LoggerMiddleware dropped its manual pluginId/endpoint/dsName/dsUID/uname/traceID params in favour of `logger.FromContext(ctx)`. The only test change is a rename in the metrics test. Nothing verifies that `instrumentContext` attaches the expected attributes for each endpoint. Nothing verifies that the logger middleware still emits those fields, including the traceID it used to add explicitly, or that the middleware ordering works. A regression in the log fields of 'Plugin Request Completed' would go unnoticed.

title: Adding FromContext to the exported Logger interface breaks other implementers
body: `FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger` is added to the exported `plog.Logger` interface. Any other implementation of this interface outside the two updated here (`grafanaInfraLogWrapper` and `TestLogger`), such as test fakes in other packages or downstream/enterprise code, will fail to compile. This is a breaking contract change that the PR description (a rename and move) does not mention.

title: FromContext silently drops contextual attributes if the assertion fails
body: If `d.l.FromContext(ctx)` returns anything other than `*log.ConcreteLogger`, the code falls back to `d.New()`. That logger has none of the request's contextual attributes (pluginId, endpoint, dsUID, traceID, etc.), and nothing signals that they were lost. The middleware would then emit 'Plugin Request Completed' without the fields that were previously always added explicitly. The wrapper holds a `*ConcreteLogger` and relies on a type assertion on an interface return, which is fragile. The fallback at least deserves a comment or a test.

title: LoggerMiddleware now silently depends on ContextualLoggerMiddleware being earlier in the chain
body: The explicit pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName, dsUID and traceID log params were removed. The log line now only carries them if `FromContext(ctx)` finds contextual attributes set by `ContextualLoggerMiddleware`. That coupling is implicit: `NewLoggerMiddleware` can be wired without the contextual middleware, for example by enterprise or other callers of `CreateMiddlewares`, or after a reorder. In that case the "Plugin Request Completed" / grafana-data-egress log lines lose the plugin and datasource identity, which makes them much less useful. Nothing documents or enforces the ordering. The old doc comment saying the instrumentation middleware must be at the top was deleted and not replaced on the new middleware.

title: No tests for the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware or the refactored LoggerMiddleware
body: Logic that used to be inside the instrumentation middleware (building contextual attributes from the plugin context, including the optional datasource and user fields) now lives in a new middleware with no test. The `LoggerMiddleware` change to `FromContext(ctx).Info(...)` is also untested. The only test touched is the renamed metrics test. A regression where the contextual attributes are not attached, or are attached to the wrong endpoint, would go unnoticed. Add tests that run a request through the contextual middleware and assert on the attributes the logger sees.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, so recorded calls are lost
body: `TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()`, a new instance, instead of the receiver. `LoggerMiddleware` now logs via `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`. Any test that injects a `TestLogger` into `NewLoggerMiddleware` and asserts on `InfoLogs` will see zero calls, because the call is recorded on a throwaway instance. Return `f` (or a logger sharing the same `Logs` state) so the fake is usable for asserting on logs.

title: FromContext silently drops context when the type assertion fails
body: If `d.l.FromContext(ctx)` does not return a `*log.ConcreteLogger`, the code falls back to `d.New()`. That is the original logger without any context attributes, and nothing is logged about the fallback. The caller then emits log lines without the contextual plugin and request attributes. The path is silent and untested, so a change in the infra logger's return type would quietly degrade logging.

title: Adding FromContext to the exported plugins Logger interface is a breaking change
body: `FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger` was added to the public `log.Logger` interface. Any other implementation of this interface, such as fakes, wrappers or enterprise or out-of-tree code, no longer compiles. This is reasonable for the feature, but it is a contract break, and the PR description does not call it out. The same file also converts `interface{}` to `any` across unrelated signatures, which adds diff noise.

title: Test function and leftovers still use the old Instrumentation naming
body: The file was renamed to `metrics_middleware_test.go`, but the test is still named `TestInstrumentationMiddleware`. Leftovers of the old name remain elsewhere: the `imw` variable in `NewMetricsMiddleware`, the `instrumentContext` helper that now lives in the contextual logger middleware, and the `plugin.instrumentation` logger name in `pluginsintegration.go`. This contradicts the stated goal of naming consistency and makes `go test -run TestMetricsMiddleware` miss the test.

title: Rejected device is cached before the store call, so a retry bypasses the limit
body: `tagDeviceUI` calls `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, ...)` before `CreateOrUpdateDevice`. If the store returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the key stays cached for 29 minutes. The next request from the same rejected device hits the cache at line 83, returns nil, and `Anonymous.Authenticate` lets the request through as an anonymous user. A rejected device is therefore blocked once and then allowed for the rest of the cache TTL, which defeats the feature. The cache key should only be set after a successful store call, or removed when the store returns an error.

title: Count-then-insert limit check is not atomic and can overshoot under concurrency
body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs `CountDevices`, compares it with `deviceLimit`, and then does a separate upsert, with no transaction or lock. Concurrent first requests from many new devices, or from several Grafana instances in HA, can all see `count < limit` and all insert. The configured limit can then be exceeded by roughly the request concurrency. If the limit is meant to be hard, the check and insert need to be atomic (for example a conditional INSERT ... SELECT with the count in the same statement, or a transaction/lock). If it is meant to be soft, the docs should say so.

title: Limit error is a plain error, so rejected users get an unhelpful generic auth failure
body: When the limit is hit, `Authenticate` returns the bare `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached`, which is created with `fmt.Errorf` and carries no HTTP status or public message. The authn layer treats it as a generic authentication failure, so the user sees an opaque 401 or a redirect to login rather than a message that the anonymous device limit was reached. Using a typed error such as an `errutil` Unauthorized or Forbidden with a public message would give a deterministic status code and a useful message.

title: Device tagging is now synchronous on the request path and uses the request context
body: The previous fire-and-forget goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout context is replaced by a blocking `TagDevice(ctx, ...)` call. Every anonymous request that misses the local cache now waits on a COUNT query plus an upsert before authentication completes. If the request context is cancelled, the tagging fails. Synchronous behaviour is needed to enforce the limit, but it adds DB latency and a DB dependency to the auth path. Reviewers should be aware of this, and the tradeoff should be applied only when `AnonymousDeviceLimit > 0`.

title: No test covers the limit-reached path through the service or client
body: The only new test is the store-level `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit`. Nothing tests `AnonDeviceService.TagDevice` or `Anonymous.Authenticate` with a limit set. That means nothing exercises that the error propagates, that a rejected device is not cached, or that other tag errors are still only logged. A test of this kind would have caught the cache-before-store bug in `tagDeviceUI`.

title: New `device_limit` option under [auth.anonymous] is undocumented
body: `auth.anonymous.device_limit` is read here, but `conf/defaults.ini`, `conf/sample.ini` and the configuration docs are not updated. Operators cannot discover the option, nor that 0 means unlimited. The PR description is also left as the unfilled template.

title: Local cache entry is set before the store call, so a rejected device bypasses the limit on its next request
body: `tagDeviceUI` calls `localCache.SetDefault(key, ...)` before `CreateOrUpdateDevice`. When the store returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the cache key is already set. The first request from that device is rejected. Every later request within the cache TTL (29 minutes) hits `localCache.Get(key)`, returns nil and is authenticated as anonymous without being recorded. The limit is therefore only enforced once per device per TTL, so any over-limit device gets through on retry or page reload. The same ordering also means a transient DB error suppresses retries for 29 minutes. Fix: set the cache entry only after `CreateOrUpdateDevice` succeeds, or delete it on error.

title: Check-then-insert on the device limit is racy and can exceed the configured limit
body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs `CountDevices` in one session and then does the `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` in a separate session, with no transaction or lock. N concurrent requests from N new devices can all read `count < deviceLimit` and all insert, so the table can overshoot the limit, and more so with several Grafana instances. Fix: do the count and insert atomically, for example `INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < limit`, or use a serialized transaction. At minimum, document the limit as approximate.

title: Device tagging moved from a background goroutine into the authentication path
body: `TagDevice` used to run in a goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout and panic recovery. It now runs synchronously on the request context. Every anonymous request from an uncached device now waits for DB work: a `COUNT(*)` when a limit is set, plus a write. A slow or locked DB therefore slows or fails anonymous requests. Request cancellation also aborts the tagging write. The panic recovery that guarded this code is gone as well. Only the limit-reached error needs to be synchronous. Consider keeping the non-limit path async, or at least a bounded timeout.

title: Device limit behavior is only minimally tested
body: Only one test covers the limit: a new device is rejected once the limit is reached. Nothing tests that an existing device within the 30-day window can still be updated at the limit, or that a device older than 30 days is rejected. Nothing covers the `Anonymous.Authenticate` change that now returns an error on `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. Nothing covers the local-cache interaction, which is where the real bug in this change sits. A test for repeated requests from a rejected device would have caught it.

title: New `device_limit` option is undocumented
body: The new `[auth.anonymous] device_limit` setting is read here, but it is not added to `conf/defaults.ini`, `conf/sample.ini` or the docs. The PR description is also an empty template. It is not documented that 0 (or any non-positive value) means unlimited, that the limit counts devices seen in the last 30 days, or that over-limit new devices are rejected with an authentication error. Operators cannot discover or safely use the setting.

title: Local cache is set before the DB write, so a rejected device bypasses the limit on its next request
body: `tagDeviceUI` calls `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, ...)` before `CreateOrUpdateDevice`. When the store returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the key stays cached for about 29 minutes. The device's next request hits the cache, `tagDeviceUI` returns nil, `TagDevice` returns nil, and `Anonymous.Authenticate` lets it through. A device that was rejected once is therefore admitted on retry without ever being stored, and the limit is not enforced. The same ordering means any transient DB error or cancelled request context (now that tagging is synchronous on the request context) leaves the device untagged for the cache TTL. The key should be cached only after the write succeeds, or removed when it fails.

title: Check-then-insert on the device limit is not atomic
body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs `CountDevices`, compares the result to `deviceLimit`, and then does a separate upsert, with no transaction, lock, or conditional insert. Concurrent requests from many new devices can all read `count < limit` and all insert, so the limit can be exceeded by roughly the request concurrency. A burst of new anonymous visitors, which is when the limit matters most, makes this likely. The limit check should be folded into the insert statement (for example `INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < limit`) or done under a lock or transaction. At a minimum the code should document that the limit is approximate.

title: Device tagging moved onto the synchronous auth path, and the limit error is returned untyped
body: The goroutine, its background context with timeout, and its panic recovery were removed. Every anonymous request that carries an uncached device ID now blocks on DB writes before authentication completes: `COUNT(*)` when a limit is set, then the upsert. A slow or failing DB therefore adds latency to, or stalls, anonymous requests. A cancelled request context also aborts the tag. A panic in `TagDevice` is no longer recovered. On limit reached, the raw `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached` (a plain `fmt.Errorf`) is returned from `Authenticate`. It carries no HTTP status or user-facing message, so what the user sees depends on how the authn layer maps unknown errors. A typed error with a proper status (such as 403 or 429) and message would make the behaviour deterministic.

title: Device-limit tests only cover rejecting a new device
body: `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` covers only the case where a second, new device is rejected at limit 1. It does not test that an already-registered device can still be updated once the limit is reached, which is the main purpose of `updateDevice`. It does not test that devices older than 30 days are excluded from the count, or that the limit is not enforced when it is 0. There is also no test for `Anonymous.Authenticate` returning the error on `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, or for the local-cache interaction after a rejection (which is currently buggy).

title: anonymousDeviceLimit typed as `undefined` although the backend always sends a number
body: `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` makes the class field type `undefined`, and `GrafanaConfig` declares it `number | undefined`. The Go DTO field is `int64` with no `omitempty`, so the frontend always receives a number, with 0 meaning unlimited. The `undefined` default and type are inconsistent with the wire contract and force consumers to handle a state that cannot occur. Use `number` with a default of 0.

title: New `device_limit` setting is undocumented
body: A new user-facing option, `[auth.anonymous] device_limit`, is read here. `conf/defaults.ini`, `conf/sample.ini` and the docs are not updated, so admins cannot discover it or learn that 0 means unlimited or what happens when the limit is hit. The PR description is also left as an unfilled template.

title: Cleanup ticker interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute (unrelated to the fix)
body: `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)` became `time.Minute * 1`. This is unrelated to the deadlock fix and looks like a leftover debugging change. Every cleanup job now runs 10x more often: snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, short URLs and query history. The annotation cleanup is the job that contends with inserts on MySQL, so more frequent runs raise the chance of hitting the deadlock this PR tries to avoid. The per-run timeout is 9 minutes, so a slow run can also overlap the next tick. Revert to 10 minutes.

title: Debug logging at Error level, including the full ID list, on every batch
body: Each batch logs `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", ..., "ids", ids, ...)` plus a second Error line after the delete. The same pattern is at lines 537, 554, 557, 576 and 579. Successful, routine cleanup therefore emits Error-level logs on every batch, on every run, even when zero rows are found. These lines dump the entire slice of IDs, which can be thousands of entries for large `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` values such as the 32767 used in the new test. This pollutes error monitoring and alerting and bloats log volume. The `"err", err` field is always nil at that point. Remove these lines or downgrade them to Debug without the full ID list.

title: Quadratic string concatenation when inlining IDs for large SQLite batches
body: In the inline-ID branch, `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` re-copies the whole accumulated string for every ID. With a batch of 32767 IDs the string reaches about 250KB, so this performs gigabytes of copying and allocation per batch, and the test with 40003 rows runs it repeatedly. Use a `strings.Builder` (or `strings.Join` over formatted values) to make this linear.

title: Placeholder-based IN list breaks for large batch sizes on MySQL/Postgres
body: The old code deleted via a subquery with no bind parameters, so any `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` worked. The new code binds one `?` per ID, and only SQLite with batch size >999 gets the inline path. MySQL and Postgres have a hard limit of 65535 bind parameters per statement. A configured batch size above that now makes every cleanup fail with a 'too many placeholders' error, which is a regression for such configurations. The inline-literal fallback should also apply to other dialects, or the IDs should be chunked into sub-batches below the limit.

title: Test case name no longer matches what it tests
body: The case 'running the max count delete again should not remove any annotations' relied on state left by the previous sub-test, so it really was a second run. The refactor now creates fresh data (9 annotations, 3 per type) and runs cleanup once. It only checks that nothing is deleted when the count is already at the limit, not idempotence of a repeated run. Rename it, or actually run the cleaner twice.

title: Debug logging left in at Error level, dumping every ID list on each batch
body: Six `r.log.Error(...)` calls (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579) run unconditionally in the cleanup loop. They log the full `ids` slice, the SQL condition, and an `err` value that is always nil at that point. Each batch emits two Error-level lines, including the final empty batch when there is nothing to clean. With the batch size configurable, the ID list can reach tens of thousands of entries per line. Together with the 1-minute ticker, this floods the error logs and trips alerting on error-level logs even when nothing went wrong. These look like debugging leftovers. Remove them, or log only counts at Debug level.

title: Cleanup ticker interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The cleanup service ticker is changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This is unrelated to the deadlock fix and is not mentioned in the PR description. It looks like a local-testing leftover. It makes every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, short URLs, query history) run 10x more often. The annotation cleanup now runs a SELECT plus a DELETE per batch, so this raises load and contention on the annotation table, the very thing this PR is meant to reduce. It also multiplies the log noise from the Error-level logging. Revert to 10 minutes.

title: Bound-parameter IN list can exceed driver placeholder limits on Postgres/MySQL for large batch sizes
body: Outside SQLite, `deleteByIDs` builds `DELETE ... WHERE id IN (?,?,...)` with one placeholder per ID, so the number of placeholders equals `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize`. Postgres and MySQL prepared statements cap placeholders at 65535. The old query embedded the limit in SQL and used no parameters, so any batch size worked. With this change, a deployment that configures a batch size above that cap will fail every cleanup run with a driver error. The special case only handles SQLite (threshold 999). Chunk the IDs, or inline the integer IDs for all dialects (they are int64, so this is safe).

title: Cleanup ticker interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, unrelated to this fix
body: The change from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1` is not mentioned in the PR and looks like a leftover from debugging. It makes every cleanup job run ten times as often. That includes snapshot, dashboard version, image, short URL and query history cleanup, and the annotation cleanup this PR is meant to make safe. Each run can take up to the 9-minute timeout, so runs can now start back to back. That means more DB load and more chances of the lock contention the PR is trying to remove. Revert it to 10 minutes.

title: Debug logging at Error level that dumps every ID, on every batch
body: The new cleanup code logs each batch at `r.log.Error` (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579). Each log line includes the full `ids` slice, the SQL condition and an `err` that is always nil at that point. The messages are not errors, so Error level pollutes error logs and may trigger alerting on every cleanup cycle. With `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` up to tens of thousands (the test uses 32767), each line can contain tens of thousands of IDs. This runs every cycle until the table is drained and will flood the logs. Remove these lines, or use Debug level and log only counts.

title: Quadratic string building when inlining IDs for SQLite
body: The SQLite path builds the ID list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` in a loop. Every iteration copies the whole accumulated string, so the cost is O(n²). For the 32767-ID batch the test uses, the final string is about 230KB, so this copies on the order of GBs of memory and creates tens of thousands of large temporary strings. Use a `strings.Builder` (or `strconv.AppendInt` into a byte slice) instead.

title: Bound-parameter delete can exceed the MySQL/Postgres placeholder limit for large batch sizes
body: Outside SQLite, the delete always uses one `?` per ID. MySQL prepared statements and Postgres both cap bind parameters at 65535. `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` is user-configurable with no upper bound enforced here. The old single-statement subquery had no such limit, so this is a new failure mode on large batch sizes. The SQLite branch got a workaround, but other dialects did not. Either chunk the `DELETE ... IN (...)` into sub-batches, or inline the int64 IDs for all dialects, as is already done for SQLite.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled when the request returns
body: The goroutines in Create (line 51), Delete (110), Update (135) and DeleteCollection (163) derive their timeout context from the handler's `ctx`. That context is cancelled as soon as the HTTP request finishes, and Create/Update/Delete return right after spawning the goroutine. The legacy call then runs with an already-cancelled or soon-cancelled context. SQL-backed legacy storage will usually fail with `context canceled`, so the 'safe measure' legacy write silently does not happen. Detach cancellation with `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (or a fresh context carrying the needed values) before applying the 10s timeout. The unit tests use `context.Background()`, so they cannot catch this.

title: Storage create failure is recorded as a legacy duration
body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)`. The failure came from Storage, so it should call `recordStorageDuration`. As written, unified-storage failures are counted under the legacy metric, and the storage error metric for create is never incremented. The same mistake is in Update at line 129.

title: Storage update failure is recorded as a legacy duration
body: On `d.Storage.Update` error the code calls `recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. Storage update errors are therefore attributed to the legacy backend and storage metrics undercount failures.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection duration is recorded with the storage metric
body: In the async goroutine, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ..., startLegacy)`. It should be `recordLegacyDuration`. The legacy latency and errors get mixed into the storage series, which already has an entry for this call, and the legacy metric never sees delete-collection.

title: Delete builds a contextual logger but stores the unenriched d.Log in the context
body: `log` is created with name, kind and method, but `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` stores the base logger. The downstream Storage and Legacy deletes therefore lose those values. Every other method uses `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`. Line 106 has a related inconsistency: the success path passes `name` as the kind label to `recordStorageDuration`, while the error path and the legacy goroutine pass `options.Kind`. That produces a high-cardinality, inconsistent metric label.

title: Legacy update re-applies the original objInfo instead of the object written to storage
body: The previous implementation wrapped the storage result in `updateWrapper` so legacy received the exact object that was persisted. Now the raw `objInfo` is passed to `Legacy.Update` in a goroutine. For patch/apply requests, `UpdatedObject` is recomputed against the legacy store's own copy. That copy can differ from unified storage, including its resourceVersion, which risks conflicts or divergent data. The same `objInfo` is also used concurrently with the request handler after the function returns.

title: Errors from async legacy writes are neither logged nor surfaced
body: The old code logged legacy failures with the object context. In the new goroutines (Create 55-56, Update 139-140, Delete 112-113, DeleteCollection 165-166) the error is only turned into a boolean for a metric and then discarded. When legacy diverges from unified storage there is no log line saying which object or why, which makes the 'safe measure' write effectively unobservable. Log the error with the name/kind logger in each goroutine.

title: Tests never verify the async legacy write, which is the core of mode 3
body: None of the Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection tests assert that the legacy store is called after a successful storage write (for example `assert.Eventually` plus `m.AssertCalled`). They also do not assert that it is not called when storage fails. The legacy goroutines run unsynchronized and may outlive the test. The mock is shared between the legacy and storage stores, so the 'legacy' mock setups are satisfied by whichever side calls first. All tests use `context.Background()`, so the request-context cancellation problem cannot be detected. The tests would pass even if the legacy write were removed.

title: Unrelated go.work.sum churn including a duplicated entry
body: The PR adds 16 unrelated checksum lines (azure sdk, otel, alertmanager and others). One of them, `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod`, duplicates the line directly above it. These look like accidental output from a local `go work sync` and add noise to a PR about dual-writer mode 3.

title: Async legacy writes derive their context from the request context, which is cancelled when the handler returns
body: Each goroutine (Create l.51, Delete l.110, Update l.135, DeleteCollection l.163) does `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` on the request-scoped `ctx`. The API server cancels that context as soon as the HTTP handler returns, and the goroutine intentionally outlives the handler. The legacy write will therefore usually run with an already-cancelled context and fail or abort. The legacy store silently drifts from unified storage, which is the opposite of the 'safe measure' described in the PR. Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (or a fresh background context carrying the logger) as the parent of the timeout context.

title: Legacy write errors are no longer logged; failures in the goroutines are invisible
body: The old code logged legacy failures (`unable to create object in legacy storage`, `could not delete from legacy store`, `could not update object in legacy store`). In the new goroutines the error is only used as a boolean for `recordLegacyDuration`, and never logged. Combined with the cancelled-context problem, legacy writes can fail with no log trace. That makes legacy/unified divergence hard to diagnose. Log the error inside each goroutine.

title: Storage create failure is recorded as a legacy duration metric
body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)`. The failure came from unified storage, so it should be `recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. As written, storage errors pollute the legacy error and latency series and the storage error series stays empty, which misleads dashboards and alerts during the mode 3 rollout.

title: Storage update failure is recorded with recordLegacyDuration
body: On `d.Storage.Update` error the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with `startStorage`. This is the same copy/paste mistake as in Create. Unified-storage failures get attributed to the legacy metric. It should be `recordStorageDuration`.

title: Delete success metric uses `name` instead of `options.Kind` as the label
body: Every other metric call passes `options.Kind` as the name/kind label. The success path of Delete passes `name` (the object name). This produces one label value per deleted object, which is a high-cardinality metric. It also splits the success series from the error series, which uses `options.Kind`. It should be `options.Kind`.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection duration is recorded as a storage duration
body: Inside the goroutine that calls `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection`, the result is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ..., startLegacy)`. It should be `recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy latency and errors are attributed to the storage metrics, which double-counts storage and hides legacy failures.

title: Delete puts the un-annotated logger into the context instead of the enriched one
body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` discards the per-call `log` (name, kind, method) that was just built. All other methods use `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`. Logs emitted downstream from the context lose the request attributes. It should use `log`.

title: Legacy update re-applies the original objInfo instead of the object written to storage
body: The previous implementation wrapped the result in `updateWrapper` so legacy stored exactly the object that unified storage persisted. Now the goroutine calls `d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...)` with the raw `objInfo`. For patch/apply requests the update is re-computed against whatever legacy currently holds, and it runs after the response has gone out. If legacy state differs, or `forceAllowCreate` or validation behave differently, legacy ends up with a different object than unified storage. This divergence is not detected or logged.

title: Same `obj` is handed to the async legacy Create while the handler may still serialize `created`
body: The goroutine passes the original `obj` to `d.Legacy.Create` after `Storage.Create` has returned. `created` is often the same pointer or shares its internals with `obj`. Legacy Create commonly mutates the object (UID, resourceVersion, metadata), while the request handler concurrently encodes `created` for the response. This is an unsynchronized read/write on the same object (a data race). Deep-copy the object before launching the goroutine.

title: Unit tests never verify the asynchronous legacy writes
body: The Mode 3 tests only check the return values from unified storage. The legacy write runs in an un-awaited goroutine, and nothing asserts that Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection are called, or that the legacy error path is handled. Because legacy and storage mocks share one `mock.Mock`, the legacy goroutine silently consumes the storage expectation. The tests would still pass if the goroutines were removed, or if they received a cancelled context. The tests need a sync mechanism (channel/WaitGroup or `Eventually`) with `AssertCalled`, and separate legacy and storage mocks.

title: Mode 3 integration runs reuse tests that read legacy immediately after k8s writes, but legacy writes are async
body: `doPlaylistTests` creates, updates and deletes through the k8s API and then immediately reads the legacy `/api/playlists` endpoint (`searchResponse`, `getFromBothAPIs`). In mode 3 the legacy write is fire-and-forget, so those assertions race with the goroutine. They are flaky, or they pass only by accident of timing. Mode 3 needs its own assertions, or the legacy checks should poll with `Eventually`.

title: Unrelated and duplicated go.work.sum entries
body: The go.work.sum changes (azure sdk, otel, alertmanager, genproto, etc.) are unrelated to the dual-writer change. The line for `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod` is added twice, directly under the identical existing line. This looks like an accidental `go work sync` artifact and should be dropped from the PR.

title: Async legacy writes derive from the request context, which is cancelled when the handler returns
body: The goroutines in Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection call `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` on the incoming request `ctx`. The request context is cancelled as soon as the HTTP handler returns, which happens right after `Create` returns the response. The goroutine then runs the legacy SQL write with an already-cancelled context, so the 10s timeout never applies and the write can fail with `context canceled`. The failure is only recorded as a legacy error metric. This defeats the stated purpose of keeping legacy in sync. Detach cancellation while keeping values (user identity, namespace) with `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` before applying the timeout.

title: Storage failure in Create is recorded as a legacy duration
body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)`. The failed call was to unified storage, so the error is attributed to the legacy metric. Storage error rates are under-reported and legacy error rates are inflated. It should be `recordStorageDuration`.

title: Storage failure in Update is recorded as a legacy duration
body: The error path after `d.Storage.Update` calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with `startStorage`. This is the same wrong-metric mistake as in Create: unified-storage update failures show up as legacy failures. It should be `recordStorageDuration`.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection duration recorded with the storage metric
body: Inside the async goroutine, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ..., startLegacy)`. The legacy timing and errors are therefore mixed into the storage metrics, and the legacy metric is never emitted for this method. It should be `recordLegacyDuration`.

title: Delete success metric uses the object name as the kind label
body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` where every other call passes `options.Kind`. Successful deletes are therefore labelled with the resource name. This creates one label value per deleted object (unbounded cardinality) and splits success and error series for the same operation.

title: Delete stores the base logger in the context instead of the enriched one
body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` should use the `log` variable built one line earlier. As written, the name, kind and method values are dropped from logs emitted by the storage layer and by the async legacy delete. Every other method uses `log`.

title: Legacy Update re-applies the original objInfo instead of the object written to storage
body: The previous implementation computed the updated object and wrapped it with `updateWrapper`, so legacy received the exact object that unified storage persisted. The new code passes the raw `objInfo` to `d.Legacy.Update` in a goroutine. For PATCH and PUT with a resourceVersion, `UpdatedObject` is evaluated again against the legacy store's own current object. Legacy and unified resourceVersions differ, so this can fail with a conflict or produce a different result. The two stores can then silently diverge, and the only trace is a legacy error metric.

title: Tests never verify the async legacy write or its failure behavior
body: Every Mode3 test asserts only the storage result. None waits for the goroutine or asserts that Legacy was called with the expected arguments. Nothing checks that a legacy error leaves the response unaffected. The legacy and storage mocks share one `mock.Mock`, so a storage expectation silently satisfies the legacy call. The legacy mock set up in the 'error' Create case is never used. A goroutine can also touch the mock after the test returns. As a result the core feature of this PR (async legacy write after a unified-storage write) is untested, and the bugs in the goroutines (context cancellation, wrong metrics) go undetected.

title: Mode 3 integration tests read legacy state right after k8s writes, but legacy is written asynchronously
body: `doPlaylistTests` creates and updates playlists through the k8s API and immediately compares them with the legacy `/api/playlists` endpoints via `getFromBothAPIs` and the legacy list. In mode 3 the legacy write is fire-and-forget, and with the request-context cancellation issue it may not happen at all. These new mode 3 subtests (file and unified) are therefore timing-dependent and can be flaky. They do not actually verify that legacy was updated.

title: Unrelated go.work.sum churn including a duplicated entry
body: The diff adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod` directly after an identical existing line, so it now appears twice. Together with the other added otel, genproto and alertmanager hashes, these changes are unrelated to the dual-writer feature and look like accidental output from a local `go work sync`. They should be dropped or regenerated cleanly.

title: No re-check of the cache after taking the write lock
body: The cache is read under RLock, the lock is released, and the write Lock is taken afterwards without checking the cache again. On a cold start in non-dev mode, N concurrent requests all see nil. They then queue on Lock(), and each one in turn reads and parses assets-manifest.json and re-applies the CDN URL, even though the first one already filled the cache. The result is correct but the work is redundant, and every request waits behind that serialized I/O. Re-checking `entryPointAssetsCache != nil && cfg.Env != setting.Dev` right after acquiring the write lock avoids this.

title: No regression test for the race being fixed
body: The PR fixes a data race but adds no test. A test that calls GetWebAssets from several goroutines and is run with `-race` would show the race is gone and keep it from coming back. It could also check that the cache is populated once in non-dev mode.

title: No re-check of the cache after taking the write lock
body: The cache is read under RLock, the lock is released, and then the write lock is taken without checking the cache again. At startup, or whenever the cache is nil, every concurrent caller sees nil. Each one then queues on `Lock()` and re-reads and re-parses assets-manifest.json one after another, even though the first caller has already filled the cache. In Dev mode every request takes the exclusive lock and does file I/O while holding it (and potentially an HTTP fetch if the CDN branch is enabled), which serializes all callers. A second check of `entryPointAssetsCache != nil && cfg.Env != setting.Dev` right after `Lock()` would avoid the redundant reloads.

title: No regression test for the data race
body: The PR fixes a data race but adds no test. A test that calls `GetWebAssets` from many goroutines, run under `go test -race`, would show the race is fixed and stop it coming back. The package has no such coverage, so a later change to the cache logic could silently reintroduce the race.

title: No re-check of the cache after taking the write lock, so concurrent cold-start callers each reload the manifest
body: The cache is read under RLock, the lock is released, and the write lock is taken without re-checking `entryPointAssetsCache`. Several requests can arrive while the cache is still nil, for example right after startup. Each one sees nil, then queues on `Lock()`. Each then re-reads and re-parses `assets-manifest.json` serially, and overwrites the cache with an equivalent value. This is the standard double-checked-locking gap. After acquiring the lock, re-check `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }`. That way only the first caller does the work.

title: File and network I/O is done while holding the exclusive lock
body: `defer Unlock()` keeps the write lock held for the whole function, including `os.Open` and JSON decoding, and the CDN HTTP fetch if that branch is enabled. In Dev mode the early return never fires, so every call takes the exclusive lock and does disk I/O, and all concurrent page renders are serialized behind it. Only the final assignment to the cache needs the lock. The manifest could be loaded without it, then the lock taken briefly to publish the result.

title: No regression test for the data race
body: The PR fixes a data race but adds no test. A test that calls `GetWebAssets` from many goroutines, run under `go test -race`, would show the race is fixed and stop it coming back. It could also check that the cache is populated only once in non-dev mode.

title: enableSqlExpressions is convoluted, always returns false, and ignores the feature flag
body: `enabled := !IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions)` followed by `if enabled { return false }; return false` returns false on every path. The `sqlExpressions` toggle therefore has no effect, and the function reads as if it gates on the flag. The inverted `!` and the identical branches will confuse the next maintainer and invite a mistaken 'fix' that re-enables the path. The call also dereferences `h.features`, which the SQL branch did not do before, so a reader built with nil features would now panic on any SQL query. If the intent is to hard-disable SQL expressions, return the error unconditionally with a clear comment and drop the helper and the feature-toggle lookup.

title: Misleading error and stale flag semantics when SQL expressions are disabled
body: A user who enables the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle gets `sqlExpressions is not implemented` for any SQL expression. The toggle's registry description and docs still say it enables SQL expressions, and the frontend can still offer the option. The behavior (deliberately disabled for a security fix) and the user-facing message are inconsistent. The flag's description or docs should be updated to say it is disabled, or the message should say SQL expressions are disabled.

title: No tests added or updated for the disabled SQL expression behavior
body: The PR touches no test files. `sql.TablesList` and `NewSQLCommand` now always fail because the stub `RunCommands` returns 'not implemented'. Any existing test that expects a successful `TablesList` or `NewSQLCommand` (for example `parser_test.go` or `sql_command_test.go`) will fail or must be removed, and none are updated here. There is also no test that `ReadQuery` rejects `QueryTypeSQL`, or that the `UnmarshalSQLCommand` path fails closed. For a security fix, a regression test that SQL expressions cannot be created or executed is warranted.

title: Legacy UnmarshalSQLCommand path gives a generic, misleading error
body: The `UnmarshalSQLCommand` -> `NewSQLCommand` path has no explicit check for SQL being disabled. It fails closed only because the stub `RunCommands` errors inside `TablesList`. The caller then sees `error reading SQL command` (a bad-request about invalid SQL), and the real reason is only in server logs at Warn/Error level. Security depends on a side effect of the stub rather than an explicit guard. Users will think their query is malformed, and the log noise from the failing `json_serialize_sql` call is repeated on every attempt.

title: Dead DuckDB-specific parsing code left behind
body: `TablesList` still builds a DuckDB-specific `SELECT json_serialize_sql('...')` command and parses the AST JSON, and `SQLCommand.Execute` is still wired to the stub DB. All of this is unreachable now that `RunCommands` and `QueryFramesInto` always return 'not implemented'. It keeps the string-concatenated SQL construction around, which was part of the vulnerable pattern, and implies a working feature to readers. The unused paths, and the `jeremywohl/flatten` dependency that supports them, should be removed or clearly marked as disabled.

title: enableSqlExpressions is a hard-coded `false` that ignores the feature flag
body: `enabled := !IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions); if enabled { return false }; return false` returns false on every path. The `sqlExpressions` toggle is now a no-op: enabling it changes nothing. The double negation and duplicated `return false` suggest the logic was gutted from a real flag check, so a future reader may think the flag still gates something. It also dereferences `h.features` for no effect, so a reader built with nil features would panic on an SQL query. Since the feature is intentionally off, return the error directly and drop the pointless flag lookup. Alternatively, document that the flag is now inert and fix its registry description.

title: User-facing error text "sqlExpressions is not implemented" is misleading
body: SQL expressions were deliberately disabled for a security fix, and the feature flag still exists and is documented. Users who enable the flag now get "sqlExpressions is not implemented", which looks like a missing feature or a bug. The message should say the feature is disabled, preferably with a pointer to the CVE or advisory. The flag's registry description and docs still advertise SQL expressions and should be updated or marked as non-functional.

title: Other SQL entry point reports a misleading error and is only blocked by the stub
body: The disable check lives only in `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery`. `UnmarshalSQLCommand` and `NewSQLCommand` have no gate, so the legacy node-building path is blocked only because the stubbed `TablesList` returns "not implemented". That path then logs a Warn "invalid sql query", including the full user SQL, and returns "error reading SQL command" (`sql-invalid-sql`). Callers are told their SQL is invalid when the feature is disabled. Failing closed here is good, but the two entry points give inconsistent errors, and the security property depends on the stub rather than an explicit check. Put the disabled check in `NewSQLCommand` too, so all paths behave the same.

title: No tests cover the new disabled behavior; existing SQL tests need updating
body: The PR replaces the DuckDB-backed implementation with stubs that always return "not implemented", and adds a reader gate that always rejects SQL queries, with no tests. Nothing asserts that `QueryTypeSQL` is rejected, or that `NewSQLCommand`, `TablesList` and `Execute` fail closed. Any existing tests (for example in `pkg/expr/sql` and `pkg/expr`) that exercise successful SQL parsing or execution can no longer pass. They should be skipped or removed explicitly rather than left failing or silently untouched. A regression test for the security-relevant gate is also missing.

title: enableSqlExpressions ignores the feature flag and always returns false
body: The function computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions)`, returns false if that is true, and otherwise also returns false. Every path returns false, so the flag has no effect. The inverted, redundant logic obscures that this is an unconditional kill switch. If someone later fixes the apparent inversion, or the flag is meant to re-enable the feature, the behaviour changes unpredictably. It also dereferences `h.features` for every SQL query, which panics if the reader was built with nil toggles. If the intent is to hard-disable SQL expressions, the case should return the error directly with a comment explaining why, and not consult a flag it then ignores.

title: Misleading error and a still-advertised feature flag that now does nothing
body: Users get `sqlExpressions is not implemented` even when they have explicitly enabled the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle. The PR description says the flag and its docs are intentionally left in place. Operators will therefore enable a documented flag and get a confusing error with no hint that the feature was deliberately disabled for security reasons. The message, and the flag's description or docs, should say the feature is disabled.

title: Legacy UnmarshalSQLCommand path is disabled only as a side effect of the stub failing, with a misleading error
body: Only the `ExpressionQueryReader` path gets an explicit guard. `UnmarshalSQLCommand` -> `NewSQLCommand` -> `sql.TablesList` is not gated. It is blocked only because the stub `DB.RunCommands` returns an error. `NewSQLCommand` then logs a warning about an invalid sql query and returns a BadRequest `sql-invalid-sql` / 'error reading SQL command'. Users see a bad-query error instead of 'feature disabled', and the logs say the SQL was invalid. The security posture also depends on the stub never being implemented or partially restored. A single explicit gate inside `NewSQLCommand` / `Execute` would be more robust.

title: Dead DuckDB-specific code left behind
body: `TablesList` still builds a DuckDB `json_serialize_sql` command and parses its JSON AST, and the variable is still named `duckDB`. Against the stub it always returns an error. `tablesFromAST` and its helpers are therefore unreachable from production code. This leftover code makes the disabling look incomplete and invites someone to wire a real backend back in without a security review. It should be removed or clearly marked as disabled.

title: No tests cover the new disabled behaviour; existing SQL tests are not updated
body: This security fix adds no test asserting that a `sql` query type is rejected by `ReadQuery`. It also adds none asserting that `NewSQLCommand`/`Execute` fail with the stub. Existing tests that exercise `sql.TablesList` or SQL command execution against a real DuckDB are not touched in this diff. They will either fail or silently test nothing now that `TablesList` and `QueryFramesInto` always return 'not implemented'. A regression test is especially valuable here so the guard is not accidentally removed.

title: TotalDocs iterates the cache map without cacheMu, and this PR adds a startup caller
body: `TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` without taking `cacheMu`, while `BuildIndex` writes to the same map under `cacheMu.Lock()`. The PR now calls `s.search.TotalDocs()` from `searchSupport.init` for the new log line. That call runs right after the goroutine consuming `WatchWriteEvents` is started, and that goroutine calls `handleEvent`, then `getOrCreateIndex`, then `BuildIndex`, which writes to the map. The first event for a resource that was skipped by `InitMinCount` therefore races with the unlocked read. Go can abort the process with 'fatal error: concurrent map iteration and map write'. `TotalDocs` should take `cacheMu.RLock()`.

title: Removing the BuildIndex lock allows duplicate concurrent builds, and the overwritten index is never closed
body: The old whole-function lock serialized builds, and it also made `GetIndex` (which takes `RLock`) block until a build finished. With the lock removed, `GetIndex` returns nil while a build is in flight. Two concurrent callers of `getOrCreateIndex` for the same key (for example two searches, or a search plus a watch event, for a resource under `InitMinCount`) then both run a full `BuildIndex`. The work is duplicated and `IndexTenants` is incremented twice. For file-backed indexes the second `bleve.New(dir)` fails on the existing directory. For in-memory indexes the second build silently replaces the first in `b.cache` without closing it, which leaks the old bleve index. `BuildIndex` needs per-key de-duplication (singleflight or a per-key lock), or at least a re-check and close of any existing cache entry when inserting.

title: Stop() sets initErr but nothing reads it any more, so requests are no longer rejected during shutdown
body: Every handler used to call `s.Init(ctx)`, which returned `s.initErr`. `Stop` set `initErr` to 'service is stopping' or 'service is stopped', so requests arriving during or after shutdown failed fast. This PR removes all of those calls and `Init` is now only called from the constructor. `Stop` still writes `initErr`, but nothing consumes it. Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch and the rest now run against a stopped backend or a closed DB and fail with confusing errors. There is also an unsynchronized write to `initErr`. A cheap stopped-state check should be restored in the handlers, or the dead state removed.

title: Failed Init in the constructor leaves the context, lifecycle and backend resources un-cleaned
body: When `s.Init(ctx)` fails in `NewResourceServer`, the function returns `nil, err` without calling `cancel()` and without calling `lifecycle.Stop`. Init may already have run the lifecycle `Init` (opening the DB), run the search `init` (which starts an event-consuming goroutine on `context.Background()`), or started the broadcaster, so those leak. Because Init is now eager in the constructor, this error path is reachable at startup. `cancel` (and ideally the lifecycle Stop) should be invoked before returning the error. `Init` also already logs the same error, so it is logged twice.

title: Test is skipped for postgres instead of fixing a likely regression from eager init
body: The PR adds a skip with 'test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally' to the only test that exercises the storage-server module. That test now starts the resource server through `InitializeModuleServer`, which runs the eagerly-initialized resource server. A failure appearing in CI right after moving initialization into the constructor suggests the change breaks something in that startup path (for example the DB or lifecycle init order, or timing). Skipping hides this, and postgres coverage for the module server is lost. The root cause should be investigated, or at least tracked in an issue rather than a bare TODO.

title: Trace-context propagation fix is incomplete: other spans still discard the derived context
body: The PR is described as fixing trace propagation, but only `GetResourceStats` was changed to `ctx, span := ...`. `ListIterator` (this line, which is on the index-build path), `ReadResource` and `WriteEvent` in this file still use `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)`. `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` in bleve.go does the same. The child DB and `listLatest` work in those functions therefore attaches to the caller's span rather than the new span, and the spans are not nested as intended.

title: Data race on shared err and totalBatchesIndexed in the parallel init workers
body: Inside `group.Go`, each worker does `totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(...)`. Both variables are shared across goroutines without synchronization, and `err` is the outer variable also used by `GetResourceStats` and `Wait`. This is a data race under `-race`. A worker can also return another worker's `err`, so a failed build can be masked as nil. The `namespaced_indexed` span attribute can be wrong too. With `init` now run at construction time, with potentially many workers, each closure should use a local `err` and an atomic counter.

title: Removing the BuildIndex lock allows duplicate concurrent builds of the same index
body: The old `cacheMu.Lock()` held for the whole of `BuildIndex` did more than serialize writes. `GetIndex` takes `RLock`, so it blocked while any build was running, and a second caller then found the freshly cached index. After this change `GetIndex` returns nil while a build is in progress. `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` (Search requests and the watch-event handler) can therefore start a second `BuildIndex` for the same key, and the search code has only a TODO about this. For file-backed indexes the second `bleve.New(dir, ...)` hits an existing path and fails, so the search errors or the watch event is dropped. For memory indexes the work is duplicated, the `IndexTenants` and `IndexedKinds` metrics are double-counted, and the first index is overwritten in the cache without being closed. A per-key singleflight or in-progress map is needed once the global lock is gone.

title: TotalDocs iterates the cache map without taking cacheMu
body: `TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` without `RLock`, while `BuildIndex` now writes to the map under `Lock` from many goroutines with no other serialization. This PR adds a `TotalDocs()` call at the end of `searchSupport.init`, after the watch goroutine has already started. A watch event that triggers a lazy build of another index can therefore write the map while it is being iterated. Go's runtime treats that as a fatal 'concurrent map iteration and map write', which kills the process. `TotalDocs` should take `cacheMu.RLock()`.

title: Data race on shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` in parallel index init
body: The errgroup goroutines in `init` increment the captured `totalBatchesIndexed` and assign to the outer `err` (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) with no synchronization. With `WorkerThreads > 1`, which is the case this PR optimizes, this is a data race. A worker can also `return err` after another worker has overwritten the shared variable. A failed build can then be reported as nil, so startup init silently succeeds with a missing index, or it reports another goroutine's error. Now that init runs at startup this path always executes. Use a local `err` inside the closure and `atomic.Int64` for the counter.

title: Test skipped for postgres instead of investigating the startup-init regression
body: The test is skipped for postgres with 'not working with postgres in Drone'. It exercises the storage-server target, which now runs `ResourceServer.Init` synchronously at construction: backend DB init, index build and watcher start. A test that starts failing in CI right after eager init was introduced is a strong sign of a startup ordering or DB-readiness problem, such as tables or migrations not being ready when the server is built. Skipping it hides that signal, and the 'works locally' claim is unverified. No new test covers the changed behaviors: `NewResourceServer` failing on an init error, the index being built before the server is returned, or the lifecycle/search/watcher ordering.

title: Requests are no longer rejected after Stop or a failed init
body: `Stop` sets `s.initErr` to 'service is stopping' or 'service is stopped'. This worked because every handler called `s.Init(ctx)`, which returns `s.initErr` after the `sync.Once`. With those calls removed, nothing reads `initErr` any more. After `Stop`, Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search and the blob endpoints keep running against a stopped backend and a cancelled server context. `IsHealthy` also no longer reports an unhealthy state when the server is stopping. Either keep a cheap stopped check in the handlers or drop the dead `initErr` writes in `Stop`.

title: Failed eager Init leaks the cancelable context and any started goroutines
body: When `s.Init(ctx)` fails, `NewResourceServer` returns `nil, err` without calling `cancel()` or `lifecycle.Stop`. By then `lifecycle.Init` may have succeeded and `search.init` may have started its event-watching goroutine, so those resources leak. Previously the server object stayed reachable and could be stopped. Call `cancel()` and best-effort `lifecycle.Stop` on the error path. The error is also logged twice, once inside `Init` and once here.

title: Trace context propagation fix is incomplete
body: The PR is described as fixing trace propagation, but only `GetResourceStats` was changed to keep the span context. `WriteEvent` here still does `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)`. The same applies to `ReadResource` and `ListIterator` in this file and to `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` in bleve.go. The child spans (create/update/delete, the list queries, the bleve index writes) are parented to the caller's span instead of the new one, so traces are still flattened or mis-parented. Use `ctx, span :=` in these places as well.

title: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without holding cacheMu; new init log call makes the race reachable
body: `TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` without taking `cacheMu.RLock()`, while `BuildIndex` writes `b.cache[key]` under `cacheMu.Lock()`. This PR adds `s.search.TotalDocs()` to the 'search index initialized' log line in `searchSupport.init`. That call runs right after the goroutine consuming `WatchWriteEvents` has been started. `handleEvent` can call `getOrCreateIndex`, then `build`, then `BuildIndex` and write the map at the same moment. Go treats concurrent map iteration and write as an unrecoverable fatal error, so the process can crash at startup. Because the lock around the whole of `BuildIndex` was removed, builds now overlap more, which widens the window. `TotalDocs` should take `cacheMu.RLock()`.

title: Data race on shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` in errgroup workers
body: Inside `group.Go`, each worker does `totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(...)`. Both write to variables shared by all workers (the outer `err`, which is also assigned from `GetResourceStats`) with no synchronization. Previously `BuildIndex` was serialized by the bleve-wide mutex, which hid this. Now that the lock is removed so builds run truly in parallel (the stated goal), the races are real. `go test -race` would flag them. They can also lose a build error: one worker's `err` can be overwritten by another's `nil` result, and `group.Wait()` returns the goroutine's returned value, not the shared one. Use a local `err :=` per worker and an `atomic.Int64` (or mutex) for the counter.

title: Unlocked BuildIndex allows concurrent duplicate builds and silently overwrites/leaks the previous index
body: With the whole-function lock gone, two concurrent `getOrCreateIndex` calls for the same key (for example a search request and a watch event) both see `GetIndex == nil` and both run a full build. The last writer replaces `b.cache[key]`, and the replaced `bleveIndex` is never closed, so bleve resources are leaked. For file-backed indexes the second `bleve.New(dir, ...)` fails because the directory already exists, so the caller gets an error. The existing TODO in `getOrCreateIndex` acknowledges there is no per-key dedupe. Removing the lock without adding per-key singleflight or a recheck-under-lock before storing makes this worse.
