body: To remove the anchor tags, the Lithuanian `totpStep1` was replaced with `Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:`. That is Italian, not Lithuanian. Lithuanian users will see an untranslated Italian sentence in the account console. The old Lithuanian text should be reduced to a proper translation of 'Install one of the following applications on your mobile:' instead.

title: Italian text inserted as the Lithuanian translation of loginTotpStep1
body: `loginTotpStep1` now reads `Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:`, which is Italian. The Lithuanian login OTP setup page will show an Italian instruction instead of Lithuanian. The previous Lithuanian sentence was replaced with the wrong language.

title: Traditional Chinese text placed in the Simplified Chinese (zh_CN) bundle
body: `totpStep1` was replaced with `在您的手機上安裝以下應用程式之一：`, which uses Traditional characters (手機, 安裝, 應用程式). The same bundle and the zh_CN login bundle use Simplified Chinese (手机, 安装, 应用). This looks copied from zh_TW and gives zh_CN users the wrong script and wording.

title: i18next placeholders replaced with Java MessageFormat syntax in a JS-consumed bundle
body: Every other `error-*` key in this account-ui bundle uses i18next interpolation (`'{{0}}'`, `{{1}}`, `{{2}}`). `error-invalid-multivalued-size` was changed to MessageFormat style (`{0}`, `{1}`, `{2}`, `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}`). i18next does not interpolate `{0}` and does not evaluate `choice` expressions, so the UI is likely to show the raw placeholders. The change is also unnecessary for adding the HTML verifier, because the verifier already tolerates `{{n}}`.

title: admin-ui bundle: i18next `{{n}}` placeholders replaced by MessageFormat `{n}` and `choice`
body: This file is consumed by the admin UI through i18next, and its other `error-*` messages use `{{0}}`-style interpolation. `error-invalid-multivalued-size` is changed to `Attribute {0} ... {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}`. i18next will not substitute `{0}`/`{1}`/`{2}` or evaluate the choice, so the validation error would display literal placeholders. This is a functional change unrelated to HTML sanitizing.

title: Choice-format expressions are blanked out before sanitizing, so HTML inside them is never checked
body: For keys starting with `linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit` and for `error-invalid-multivalued-size`, `normalizeValue` replaces `\{[0-9]+,choice,[^}]*}` with `...` before sanitizing. Any markup inside a choice branch (for example `{0,choice,0#|1#minute}`) is never seen by the sanitizer. The `linkExpirationFormatter` values are inserted into HTML email bodies, so the verifier silently passes a translation that can inject HTML. The exemption should be limited to the `<` in the choice operator, or the branches should be sanitized separately.

title: Diff-context computation can throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException when the common prefix and suffix overlap
body: `start` and `end` are computed independently and can overlap. If a translation has an unclosed tag at the very end, such as `text `, the sanitizer closes it as `text `. Then `start == value.length()` and `end == 1`, so `value.substring(start, value.length() - end)` is called with begin greater than end and throws. The build then fails with an unhelpful runtime exception instead of reporting 'Illegal HTML in key ...'. `end` should be capped at `min(len) - start`.

title: Anchor-tag error message names neither the key nor the file
body: `santizeAnchors` receives `key` but never uses it. It reports only `Didn't find anchor tag <a ...> in original string`. With hundreds of translation files checked per build, the maintainer cannot tell which file or key has the unexpected anchor. The 'Illegal HTML' message includes both, and this message should too.

title: English reference file is derived by regex over the whole absolute path and failures surface as raw RuntimeException
body: The English file path comes from `replaceAll` on the entire absolute path (`resources-community` anywhere, then the first `_xx.properties` suffix). If no `_en` counterpart exists at the derived location, an unchecked `RuntimeException` is thrown instead of a `MojoExecutionException` or a clear message. A single translation bundle without a sibling English file would then abort the whole verification with a stack trace.

title: No positive test cases; duplicate-key assertion weakened
body:
All new tests check only that an error is reported. There is no test where a translation legitimately contains the allowed HTML (``, `

`, `
`, an identical anchor, `{{0}}`, or choice formats) and the result must be empty, so false-positive regressions in the sanitizer comparison would go unnoticed. The duplicate-key test was also weakened from `contains` to `hasItem`, so it no longer fails if the verifier starts emitting unrelated messages for that file.

title: isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted condition and wrong substring offsets, so it never checks the grant type
body: The token id format is `<st:2><tt:2><gt:2>:<uuid>`, so the grant shortcut is at indices 4..6, i.e. `substring(4, 6)`. The matcher uses `substring(3, 5)`, which returns the last char of the token type plus the first char of the grant (e.g. "ta" for "onrtac"). The condition is also inverted: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` rejects a match instead of a mismatch. The two bugs together mean the grant shortcut is never verified, and the check can only fail by accident (e.g. if the shifted substring happens to equal the shortcut). Every event assertion built on it (`expectCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken`, `expectAuthReqIdToToken`) only checks the `xxx:uuid` shape, not the encoded grant. It should be `!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)`, and the length of `items[0]` should be checked first. The comment saying "4th char" is also misleading.

title: Null check for rawTokenId actually checks grantType
body: `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed");` re-checks `grantType` (already checked on the line above) instead of `rawTokenId`. A null `rawTokenId` is therefore accepted and the constructor builds a context with a null raw id. `encodeTokenId` would then produce an id ending in the string "null" (e.g. `onrtac:null`).

title: testIncorrectGrantType passes because of an NPE, not the intended validation
body: In `before()` only `factory.init(null)` is called, so `sessionFactory` stays null. For the unknown shortcut "ac", `getGrantTypeByShortcut` misses in the map and falls into the fallback path `sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream(...)`, which throws a NullPointerException. The test's `catch (RuntimeException iae)` swallows it, so the test passes without ever reaching the `IllegalArgumentException("Unknown value ... for grant type")` branch. The catch should be narrowed to `IllegalArgumentException`, and the factory given a mock or real session factory. There is also no test for `getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext` (session-type detection, default "na" grant), nor for malformed ids such as a wrong context length or unknown session type.

title: Grant shortcut length is not validated, and the OAuth2GrantTypeFactory javadoc says '3-letters'
body: The decoder requires the encoded context to be exactly 6 chars and slices the grant shortcut as chars 4..6, so every shortcut must be exactly 2 characters. `postInit` only checks for duplicates and never validates length or null. A custom or future grant factory returning e.g. a 3-letter shortcut (which the new javadoc on `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut` says is the usual form: "usually like 3-letters shortcut") produces ids such as `onrtabc:uuid`. These ids cannot be decoded ("Expected length of 6" error). A null shortcut makes `ConcurrentHashMap.put` throw an NPE and fail startup with an unhelpful error. Validate `shortcut != null && shortcut.length() == 2` in `postInit` (and in the lazy-refresh paths) and fix the javadoc to state the 2-character requirement.

title: New abstract getShortcut() breaks existing custom OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations
body: `getShortcut()` is added as an abstract method with no default. Any third-party `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` fails to compile, or fails at startup with `AbstractMethodError` from `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit`. That takes down the whole server rather than just the new feature. A default implementation (or a graceful fallback in the encoder for factories without a shortcut) would avoid the break.

title: Access token issued together with a new offline session is tagged as ONLINE
body: The session type is derived from `userSession.isOffline()` at access-token creation time. For a code or password flow with the `offline_access` scope, `createTokenResponse` / the ROPC grant creates the access token from the online user session first. The offline session is only created later, in `generateRefreshToken`, and the online session may then be removed (`FIRST_OFFLINE_ACCESS` / direct grant). The access token id therefore says `on...`, while only the offline session exists afterwards. The stated purpose is to let later endpoints look up only the correct session type, so such tokens would send consumers to a session that no longer exists. The offline-ness should be derived from the requested scope / refresh token type, not only from the session used at issue time.

title: Client credentials grant never sets the GRANT_TYPE attribute, so its tokens get 'na'
body: Grant type is recorded explicitly in `createTokenResponse` (used by the auth-code, device and CIBA grants), in ROPC, pre-authorized code, refresh and standard token exchange. The client credentials grant is not touched by this PR, and neither are the UMA/permission grant or the legacy (V1) token exchange paths. Their access tokens are therefore always encoded with the `na` grant, although the factories were given shortcuts (`cc`, `pg`, ...) and the unit test treats `trltcc:` ids as normal. The grant-type information promised by the PR is silently missing for these flows.

title: Access token jti format change (non-UUID) is user-visible but undocumented
body: Access token `jti` was previously a plain UUID and is now `<6 chars>:<uuid>` (e.g. `onrtac:1f65...`). Clients, resource servers, log pipelines or custom providers that assume `jti` is a UUID will break, and this is not mentioned in the upgrading or release notes. Token id parsing (`getTokenContextFromTokenId`) also throws `IllegalArgumentException` for any id containing `:` that does not match the 6-char format, so callers must handle that.

title: isAccessTokenId matcher never checks the grant shortcut (wrong offset and inverted condition)
body: The encoded ID is `ssttgg:uuid`, so the grant shortcut is at indexes 4..6 (`substring(4, 6)`). The matcher uses `substring(3, 5)`, which spans the last char of the token type and the first char of the grant. It then does `if (...equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`, which rejects a match instead of a mismatch. The two mistakes cancel out: the check can never fail, so `expectCodeToToken`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh` and `expectAuthReqIdToToken` only verify the `xxxx:<uuid>` shape. If a grant type put the wrong shortcut in the token ID, the tests would still pass. Fix by comparing `items[0].substring(4, 6)` and returning false when it does NOT equal the expected shortcut. The failure message in `describeTo` is also not meaningful.

title: Null check for rawTokenId actually checks grantType
body: `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` repeats the grantType check, so `rawTokenId` is never validated. A null `rawTokenId` is accepted silently, and `encodeTokenId` would then emit a token ID ending in the literal string "null" (e.g. `onrtac:null`) instead of failing fast. It should be `requireNonNull(rawTokenId, ...)`.

title: testIncorrectGrantType passes because of a NullPointerException, not the intended validation
body: In `before()`, the factory's `sessionFactory` is never set (it stays null). Decoding `ofrtac:5678` misses "ac" in `grantsByShortcuts`. `getGrantTypeByShortcut` then falls into the 'refresh maps' branch and calls `sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream(...)`, which throws an NPE. The test catches any `RuntimeException`, so it passes on that NPE rather than on the `IllegalArgumentException` the decoder is supposed to throw for an unknown grant type. The test does not verify the real behavior. It should catch `IllegalArgumentException` specifically and provide a usable session factory, or the refresh fallback should be made testable.

title: Access token is tagged ONLINE even when the session is converted to offline right after
body: The session type is derived from `userSession.isOffline()` at access-token creation time. In authorization-code and ROPC flows with `offline_access`, the access token is created first from the online user session. Only afterwards does `generateRefreshToken()` create the offline session, and the online session is then removed (`FIRST_OFFLINE_ACCESS` and ROPC handling in `OAuth2GrantTypeBase`/`ResourceOwnerPasswordCredentialsGrantType`). That access token gets an `on` prefix, but its `sid` points to a session that no longer exists as online, and only the offline session remains. The stated purpose of the PR is to let endpoints look up only the correct session type. For these tokens the encoded session type would point at the wrong (non-existent) session type. The offline_access case should be considered when computing the session type, or the limitation should at least be documented.

title: Grant shortcuts are not validated (null or length != 2)
body: `postInit` inserts `gtf.getShortcut()` into a `ConcurrentHashMap` without validating it. A third-party `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` returning null causes an NPE during server startup. A shortcut that is not exactly 2 chars makes tokens encode fine, but `getTokenContextFromTokenId` then throws `IllegalArgumentException` because it requires the context part to be exactly 6 chars. The existing duplicate check only covers collisions, and the lazy refresh paths in `getShortcutByGrantType`/`getGrantTypeByShortcut` skip validation too. Add an explicit startup check that every shortcut is non-null and exactly 2 characters, with a clear error message.

title: New abstract method breaks existing OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations
body: `getShortcut()` is added as an abstract method to a provider SPI interface. Any custom grant type factory compiled against the previous version fails to compile and, if already built, throws `AbstractMethodError` when `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit` calls it. Since the encoder already has an 'na' fallback, a default implementation would keep existing extensions working. If it is intentionally mandatory, this breaking change should be called out in the upgrade notes.

title: Javadoc says 3-letter shortcut, but implementation requires exactly 2 characters
body: The Javadoc says the shortcut is 'usually like 3-letters', yet all factories use 2-letter shortcuts and the decoder (`encodedContext.length() != 6`, fixed 2-char slices) only works with exactly 2 characters. Someone implementing a custom grant following the Javadoc and using 3 letters would produce token IDs that cannot be parsed. The contract should state 'exactly 2 characters'.

title: Access token `jti` format change is user-visible but undocumented
body: Access token IDs (`jti`, also logged in the `token_id` event detail) change from a plain UUID to `<6-char context>:<uuid>`. Clients, log pipelines, or custom extensions that assume the `jti` is a UUID will behave differently. This PR adds no release/upgrade note or documentation for the new format or the new `tokenContextEncoder` SPI, so operators have no notice of the change.

title: isAccessTokenId matcher compares the wrong substring and the condition is inverted
body: The token id format is `<st:2><tt:2><gt:2>:<uuid>`, so the grant shortcut is at indices 4..6 (`substring(4, 6)`). The matcher reads `substring(3, 5)`, which is the last char of the token type plus the first char of the grant. It also returns false when the values are equal (`if (...equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false`). For `onrtac` it compares `ta` with `ac`, never matches, and so never fails. The helper therefore only checks the `x:uuid` shape. Every `expectCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken` and `expectAuthReqIdToToken` call passes `isAccessTokenId(<shortcut>)` and implies the grant is verified, but it is not. Wrong grant encodings would go undetected. Use `!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)`.

title: rawTokenId null check validates grantType instead of rawTokenId
body: The fourth `Objects.requireNonNull` is `requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")`. It re-checks `grantType` and never checks `rawTokenId`, so a null raw id is accepted. `encodeTokenId` would then silently produce `…:null` as the access token `jti`. Pass `rawTokenId` to the check.

title: Grant shortcut length is never validated and the SPI Javadoc says 3 letters while the decoder requires exactly 2
body: `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` is documented as "usually like 3-letters shortcut". The encoder just concatenates whatever the factory returns. The decoder (`DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId`) requires the prefix to be exactly 6 chars and slices the grant at fixed offsets 4..6. A custom or future grant factory that follows the Javadoc and returns 3 characters, or returns 1 character or an empty string, produces tokens whose own id is later rejected with `IllegalArgumentException('Expected length of 6')`, or is mis-parsed. `postInit` only checks for duplicate shortcuts, not length or null. Validate that every shortcut is exactly 2 characters at startup, and fix the Javadoc to say so.

title: Client credentials grant never records its grant type, so its tokens are encoded with "na"
body: The PR registers a `cc` shortcut and the unit test uses `trltcc:…`. The grant type is only put into the ClientSessionContext in `OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse`, the password grant, the pre-authorized-code grant, the refresh path and standard token exchange. `ClientCredentialsGrantType` is not modified, and, as far as I recall, it builds its response via `tokenManager.responseBuilder(...).generateAccessToken()` rather than `createTokenResponse`. Its access tokens would therefore carry `na` as the grant type (`trrtna:…`). The same applies to the legacy token exchange, permission (UMA) and implicit/hybrid flows. The stated purpose of the encoding (grant-type-aware logic, e.g. #37117) does not work for these grants. Set `Constants.GRANT_TYPE` in each flow that creates access tokens, or document that these grants are unknown.

title: Session type is derived from the session at issuance time, so first offline-token issuance is tagged "online"
body: The session type comes from `userSession.isOffline()` when the access token is built. For an initial login or direct grant with `offline_access`, the access token is created from the online user session. The offline session is only created afterwards, when the refresh token is generated. In the password grant the online session is even removed right after. The access token is therefore tagged `on…` although its session exists only as an offline session. The PR's stated goal is to look up only the session type the token came from (#37662), so such tokens would be looked up in the wrong store and fail. Take the requested `offline_access` scope into account, or otherwise derive the type from what the refresh token will use.

title: testIncorrectGrantType passes because of a NullPointerException, not the intended validation
body: The test only calls `factory.init(null)` and fills the grant maps by hand, so `sessionFactory` stays null. For `ofrtac:5678` the shortcut `ac` is not in the map, so `getGrantTypeByShortcut` takes its refresh branch and calls `sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream(...)`, which throws NPE. The test catches `RuntimeException` and passes on that NPE instead of the intended `IllegalArgumentException('Unknown value … for grant type')`. The test does not verify the behaviour it claims to. Catch `IllegalArgumentException` specifically and provide a mock session factory. There is also no test for `getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext` (session type, lightweight, grant attribute) and no integration test checking real issued token ids. `assertEquals` arguments are also reversed (actual first).

title: New abstract SPI method and removed public constructor break existing custom grant implementations
body: `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` is added with no default implementation. Every existing third-party `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` stops compiling, and nothing is said about a migration path. The PR also deletes the public copy constructor `OAuth2GrantType.Context(Context)`, which is another source-incompatible change for any extension that used it. Provide a default (or make the shortcut optional) or call out the breaking change. In the same SPI change, add an upgrade note: the access token `jti` changes from a bare UUID to `<6 chars>:<uuid>`, which affects consumers that assume a UUID. No documentation or migration note is included.

title: Raw recovery codes are handed to the user-storage provider; the user label is dropped
body: On the local path only hashes are persisted, via `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues`. The new user-storage path serializes the unhashed `generatedCodes` to JSON and passes them in a `UserCredentialModel` to `updateCredential`. The external provider (and anything it logs or stores) therefore receives usable one-time bypass credentials in clear text. The user-supplied label (`generatedUserLabel`) is also silently discarded on this path. This difference from local storage should at least be documented, and ideally the provider should receive the hashed credential data rather than raw codes.

title: Existing local recovery codes are not removed when the user storage accepts the new codes
body: When `updateCredential` returns true, the method only logs and never touches an existing locally stored recovery-codes credential. `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` prefers the federated credential, but a user who previously had local codes keeps a stale hashed credential in the Keycloak DB. That credential still counts for `isConfiguredFor` and credential listings. It also becomes active again if the storage provider later stops supporting the type. The local credential should be removed or replaced when the storage takes over.

title: Exhausted-code cleanup and next-code lookup do not work for federated credentials
body: `getCredential` can now return a credential that came from user storage. The code that follows was written for locally stored credentials. When `allCodesUsed()` is true it calls `removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())`, but a federated credential may have a null or non-local id (the test storage's `getCredentials` returns a model with no id). That call does not remove the credential from the storage, so the exhausted credential stays and is still returned first on the next login. `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` then calls `getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get()` on an empty Optional and throws `NoSuchElementException`, which breaks the login page. There is also no step that records a used code in the federated store, so single-use semantics depend entirely on the provider. None of this is handled or tested.

title: getCredentials dereferences a possibly null MyUser
body: `getMyUser(user)` returns null when the user is not in the map, for example after `removeUser`. `getCredentials` then does `myUser.recoveryCodes` and throws an NPE. The neighbouring methods `isConfiguredFor` and `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream` guard against null. Since `getFederatedCredentialsStream` now routes through this method, a missing user should yield an empty stream. In addition, the returned recovery-codes model has no id, so account credential listings and any `removeStoredCredentialById` call would see a null id.

title: Recovery-keys test covers only the happy path and hides that codes are never consumed
body: `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` only logs in once with code index 0. It has no negative case (wrong code rejected), no check that a used code is consumed or that the next login asks for index 1, and no check that a user with local credentials still works through the fallback. The test storage's `isValid` never marks codes as used, so the same code is accepted forever, and the prompted index would stay 0. The test therefore passes without exercising the single-use behaviour. The extra `delayed-authenticator` sub-flow, with a typo'd alias "delayed-suthenticator-config" and a delay of 0, adds nothing to what is being tested.

title: User-storage recovery codes are never consumed, so they can be replayed and the same code is always requested
body: `isValid` for recovery codes only checks that the submitted code is in the stored JSON list and never marks it used. `getCredentials` (line ~237) rebuilds a fresh `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...)` from the full list on every call, so every code always looks unused. `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` therefore always asks for the same code number (index 0). Any code stays valid indefinitely, which breaks the one-time semantics of the local provider. The `allCodesUsed()` cleanup in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` can never trigger for federated credentials. The new model also has no id, because `createFromValues` does not carry over `recoveryCodes.getId()`, so `removeStoredCredentialById(model.getId())` would be called with a null id if it were ever reached. The new `getCredential()` path is exercised against a provider whose behavior diverges from the local provider on a core security property, and the test cannot detect that.

title: getCredentials dereferences a possibly-null MyUser
body: `getMyUser(user)` returns null when the username is not in the `users` map, for example after `removeUser` or for a user from another provider instance. `getCredentials` then calls `myUser.recoveryCodes` immediately and throws an NPE. Every other method in this class (`isConfiguredFor`, `isValid`, `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream`) guards against null. Since `getFederatedCredentialsStream()` is now called from the login path via `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential`, this can turn a missing user into a 500.

title: Recovery codes can be created and validated in user storage but not disabled or removed
body: `supportsCredentialType`, `updateCredential`, `isConfiguredFor` and `isValid` now handle recovery codes. `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream` and `disableCredentialType` still only handle OTP. An admin therefore cannot see recovery codes as a disableable credential, and `disableCredentialType` logs "Unsupported to disable credential" and does nothing. Once recovery codes are written to the user storage they can never be removed through the admin API, which is inconsistent with the OTP handling next to it.

title: Creating codes in user storage leaves stale local recovery codes valid (and vice versa)
body: When `updateCredential` succeeds, the method returns without touching any existing recovery-codes credential in the local DB. The local `createCredential` path likewise ignores federated codes. If a user already has local recovery codes and the storage later accepts the type, regenerating codes in the storage does not invalidate the old local ones. `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` prefers the federated credential while `isValid` can still accept the old local codes. The user then holds two live recovery-code sets, and regenerating codes does not revoke the previous set.

title: Undocumented SPI contract: plaintext JSON list of codes handed to user storage
body: `createRecoveryCodesCredential` serializes the raw (unhashed) recovery codes to a JSON array and passes them as the value of a `UserCredentialModel`. The local provider stores only hashes. The javadoc says nothing about this format, that the storage receives plaintext codes, or how the storage should report used/unused codes through `getCredentials` (see the replay problem above). Third-party `CredentialInputUpdater` implementations have to guess the contract, and storing plaintext codes is a security-relevant decision that should be stated. The provider id is also hard-coded as `"keycloak-recovery-authn-codes"` instead of using the factory constant.

title: Recovery-key test covers only one happy-path login
body: `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` sets up codes and logs in once with code index 0. It does not test a wrong code being rejected, a second login that should ask for the next code index, reuse of an already-used code, or the exhausted-codes path (`allCodesUsed` removal and re-adding the required action). The first two would have exposed that user-storage codes are never consumed. The flow also includes a pointless `delayed-authenticator` with a constant `delay` of 0 and a misspelled alias (`delayed-suthenticator-config`), which looks copy-pasted from another test.

title: Undocumented SPI contract: raw recovery codes go to user storage as a JSON string, and label/created date are dropped
body: For user-storage users, `createRecoveryCodesCredential` calls `updateCredential` with a `UserCredentialModel` whose value is a JSON array of the plaintext (unhashed) codes. The local path stores only hashed codes. The `credentialModel` built by the caller carries the creation time and user label, but neither reaches the storage provider. Nothing in the Javadoc or SPI documents that format. Provider authors must guess it, and the test stub only works because it hard-codes `JsonSerialization.readValue(..., List.class)`. The storage also has to implement one-time-use tracking on its own, because the form authenticator never marks a federated code as used. Document the expected contract (value format, plaintext codes, one-time use) in the Javadoc and the SPI docs, or pass the metadata through.

title: Unguarded Optional.get() will 500 the login page when a federated provider is configured but returns no credential
body: `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user)` now looks up federated credentials first and falls back to local ones. The bean still calls `credentialModelOpt.get()` and then `getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get()` with no guard. The authenticator's `configuredFor` uses `isConfiguredFor`, which the provider answers separately from `getCredentials`. A storage provider that reports the type as configured but does not return a matching model from `getCredentials` therefore throws `NoSuchElementException` while rendering the recovery-code input form. The same happens if every code is already used. The feature now depends on providers implementing four methods consistently (`updateCredential`, `isValid`, `isConfiguredFor`, `getCredentials`). A misbehaving provider produces an unhandled exception instead of a clean error or a fall-back to reconfiguration.

title: getCredentials dereferences a possibly-null MyUser and returns a recovery model without the stored ID
body: `getMyUser(user)` returns null for a user not in the map, for example after `removeUser`. `getCredentials` then does `myUser.recoveryCodes` without a null check, so it throws an NPE. The other methods (`isConfiguredFor`, `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream`) do check for null. The recovery model returned is rebuilt with `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues`, which sets no ID. This discards the ID generated in `updateCredential`, so the credential Keycloak sees has a null ID. `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` passes `getId()` to `removeStoredCredentialById` when all codes are used, and a null ID would break that. The user label is also read from a model that never sets it. The IOException handler logs without the exception. Add a null guard, and carry over the ID and metadata from the stored model.

title: New test only covers the happy path; the stub does not model one-time codes or code progression
body: `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` sets up codes and logs in once with code #0. The stub's `isValid` accepts any stored code any number of times, and its `getCredentials` rebuilds the model from the original list. Every code therefore always looks unused and the form always asks for code 0. The test never exercises recovery codes being consumed, `getNextRecoveryAuthnCode` advancing, `allCodesUsed` triggering re-registration, or a wrong code being rejected. It also does not cover regenerating codes in user storage or the account REST/console view of the credential. Regressions in the user-storage path for these cases would go unnoticed.

title: Same NPE remains in the other getSubGroupsStream overloads
body: The PR fixes only getSubGroupsCount(). The three getSubGroupsStream(...) overloads (lines 256, 262, 268) still call `modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` with no null check. `modelSupplier.get()` returns null when the group was deleted concurrently, which is the exact condition behind #40368. Concurrent deletion of a group that is being listed or expanded can therefore still throw an NPE on these paths. A related path, `isUpdated()` (lines 73-74), throws IllegalStateException when the group disappears after invalidation. The fix is therefore partial, and the new null-tolerance applies to one method only.

title: getSubGroupsCount() now silently returns null for a deleted group
body: When the underlying group no longer exists, getSubGroupsCount() returns null instead of signalling that the group is gone. The JPA implementation of GroupModel never returns null here. Callers that unbox the Long, or that treat a missing count as 0, will still fail or misreport. In `GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount` the deleted group is still emitted in the response with a null subGroupCount, rather than being skipped. This hides the race instead of handling it, and the nullable return is not documented in the GroupModel contract.

title: Concurrency test starts an unjoined reader thread and may not detect the failure
body: The reader thread is started with `new Thread(...).start()` and is never joined or awaited. After `deletedAll.set(true)` the test immediately asserts on `caughtExceptions`. The reader may be mid-request at that point, so an exception it throws afterwards is lost, and the thread can outlive the test while still hitting the server. The test also does not wait for the reader to start before deleting, and it has no timeout or deterministic ordering. It is probabilistic: it may pass on unfixed code if deletion finishes before the reader overlaps, and it can leak a thread into later tests. Use an ExecutorService or a joined thread with a start latch, and assert only after the reader has fully stopped.

title: Other sub-group methods still NPE when the group is deleted concurrently
body: Only `getSubGroupsCount()` gets the null guard. The three `getSubGroupsStream(...)` overloads (lines 256, 262, 268) still call `modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` with no null check. `modelSupplier` returns null when the group was deleted by another transaction after the cached entry was read, which is exactly the race this PR targets. A concurrent delete plus a sub-group listing through the cache adapter will therefore still throw the same NPE. Apply the same null handling (or a consistent not-found behaviour) to all delegating methods so the fix is not partial.

title: getSubGroupsCount() now silently returns null for a deleted group
body: When the backing group no longer exists, `getSubGroupsCount()` returns `null` instead of failing. The `GroupModel` contract does not document a null result. Any caller that unboxes the `Long` (for example `getSubGroupsCount() > 0`) will now NPE somewhere else, and callers that only copy it into a representation will emit a null count that looks like valid data. The null return and the reasoning behind it should be documented, or the caller (`GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount`) should handle it explicitly. The null return also differs from the other adapter methods, which throw `IllegalStateException("Not found in database")` for a missing group.

title: Concurrency test leaves reader thread unjoined, so results are racy and the thread can outlive the test
body: The reader thread is started with `new Thread(...).start()` and never joined. After `deletedAll.set(true)` the test immediately asserts `caughtExceptions` is empty. The thread may be mid-request at that point, so an exception from the last iteration can be added after the assertion has already passed, which makes the test unreliable. The thread can also keep calling the admin client after the test ends and the realm is cleaned up. Keep a reference to the thread and `join()` it (with a timeout) before asserting. The loop also has no pacing, so it hammers the server with `Integer.MAX_VALUE` page sizes. Nothing guarantees the read overlaps the deletes, so the test may pass without ever exercising the race.

title: Other getSubGroupsStream overloads still NPE when the group is deleted concurrently
body: Only `getSubGroupsCount()` got a null check on `modelSupplier.get()`. The three `getSubGroupsStream(...)` overloads (lines 256, 262, 268) still call `modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` unguarded. `modelSupplier` resolves to `getGroupModel()`, which returns null when the group was removed after the cached entry was loaded. That is the same race this PR fixes for the count, so those paths will throw the same NPE. Anything that lists subgroups of a group being deleted concurrently, such as the subgroups endpoint or tree loading, remains exposed. The fix should be applied consistently, for example by returning `Stream.empty()` when the model is null.

title: Returning null for subgroup count silently leaks a null into the representation
body: When the group vanished, `getSubGroupsCount()` now returns null instead of a number. `GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount` passes it straight to `representation.setSubGroupCount(...)`, so a deleted group can still be returned to the client with a null `subGroupCount`. Clients and any other caller that unboxes the Long may not expect null. A count of 0, or dropping the vanished group from the result, would be a safer contract. At minimum the Javadoc/contract for null should be documented.

title: Concurrency test starts an unjoined thread and asserts before it has finished
body: The reader thread is started with `new Thread(...).start()` and is never joined. After `deletedAll.set(true)` the test immediately asserts that `caughtExceptions` is empty. The reader may be mid-request at that point and add its exception after the assertion has already passed, so a regression can go undetected. The thread is also non-daemon and untracked, so it can outlive the test. The test also depends on timing: nothing forces a reader call to overlap a delete, so it may pass even without the fix. It should join the thread (or use an ExecutorService/Future) before asserting, and ideally create overlap deterministically.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot paginate datetime keys, so the audit-log endpoint fails on every non-empty page
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` is a copy of `Paginator.get_item_key`: it calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly on `getattr(item, self.key)`. The audit-log endpoint orders by `-datetime`, so the value is a `datetime` and `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError`. `build_cursor` calls the key function on the first result, so any request with `optimized_pagination=true` that returns at least one row will 500. `value_from_cursor` (line 842) also returns the raw integer cursor value instead of converting the millisecond timestamp back to a `datetime` as `DateTimePaginator` does. Any follow-up cursor would therefore compare a datetime column against a raw integer. The new class should subclass or reuse `DateTimePaginator` semantics.

title: Negative cursor offsets are passed straight into queryset slicing, based on a false claim about the ORM
body: The comment says the ORM "properly handles negative slicing automatically". It does not: Django querysets raise `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported` for a negative start or stop. Cursor offsets come from the user-supplied `cursor` query param (`Cursor.from_string` accepts any `int` for the offset, including negatives, with no validation). A request with `optimized_pagination=true` and a cursor like `0:-5:0` therefore reaches `queryset[start_offset:stop]` and returns a 500. The comments ("access to data beyond normal pagination bounds", "safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level") suggest the intent is to bypass pagination bounds. If negative indexing did work, it would let a caller read from the end of the dataset and sidestep the offset checks that other paginators enforce with `BadPaginationError`. The right fix is to reject negative offsets, not to enable them.

title: Shared BasePaginator behaviour changed for all endpoints with a misleading comment and an inconsistent clamp
body: This edit changes `BasePaginator.get_result`, which every endpoint using it shares, not just the audit-log endpoint. For forward cursors, a negative offset is now silently clamped to 0, where it used to fail loudly. That hides malformed or tampered cursors and can return a wrong page or loop. For `is_prev` cursors the negative offset is still passed through unchanged, so Django still raises on negative slicing, and the comment claiming negative offsets are now allowed and "safe" is false. The later check `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` also still uses the unclamped `offset`. Invalid offsets should be rejected explicitly, and this global change is unrelated to the PR's stated scope.

title: organization_context.member can be None, causing AttributeError
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences `member` without a None check. For callers authenticated without an org membership (for example an API token or key with `org:write`, or a non-member user), `member` is `None`. Evaluating this line then raises `AttributeError` and returns a 500. The line runs on every request, even when `optimized_pagination` isn't set, so it can break the previously working default path. The `use_optimized` check should come first, and `member` should be guarded. The condition also reads as a security gate, but `has_global_access` is not a meaningful authorization check for an experimental pagination mode.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator.get_result wholesale
body: The new class copies about 70 lines of `BasePaginator.get_result`. The only differences are the negative-offset branch and a duplicated `start_offset` branch that is identical to the base behaviour. Any future fix to the base cursor logic must now be applied twice, and the two copies will drift. The "optimized query path" described in the docstring does not exist: there is no query optimization, just a different slicing path. The code should be an override of the one differing step or should not exist.

title: Comment claims negative offsets are supported but nothing validates or implements this
body: The added comment says negative offsets are allowed for "efficient reverse pagination", but no code changed. `Cursor` accepts any integer offset, and nothing downstream (Django slicing) supports negative values. The comment misleads maintainers into thinking negative offsets are a supported feature of the cursor contract. It also lets unvalidated user input flow into the paginators. The comment should be removed, or `Cursor` should validate non-negative offsets.

title: No tests for the new paginator, the optimized_pagination flag, or negative-offset handling
body: The PR adds a new paginator class, a new query parameter with a permission-dependent code path, changes to the shared `BasePaginator` slicing, and negative-offset cursor handling, but includes no tests. A single test that hit the endpoint with `optimized_pagination=true` would have exposed the `TypeError` on datetime keys. Tests are also needed for admin versus non-admin gating, negative cursor offsets, and prev/next cursor round-trips. The description is also just 'Test 1' and gives no rationale or benchmark for the claimed performance gains.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key copies the integer Paginator logic and crashes on datetime ordering
body: The audit log endpoint orders by `-datetime`, but `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly on `getattr(item, 'datetime')`, which is a `datetime`. That raises `TypeError`. `build_cursor` calls the key function on the first result, so any `?optimized_pagination=true` request with at least one row returns a 500. `value_from_cursor` also returns the raw cursor value instead of converting the timestamp back to a datetime, as `DateTimePaginator` does. On later pages the WHERE clause would then compare the datetime column to a raw integer. The new path has to reuse `DateTimePaginator`'s conversion (`strftime('%s.%f') * multiplier`) to work at all.

title: Negative offset slicing is not supported by Django QuerySets; the 'advanced feature' only produces errors
body: When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code runs `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` rejects negative indexes ("Negative indexing is not supported"), so this raises and returns a 500. The comment 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' and 'enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds' are wrong. A very negative offset also makes `stop` negative, which fails the same way. Cursor strings are user-controlled (`Cursor.from_string` accepts `int(bits[1])`), so any caller who can pass the gate can trigger this on demand. If a backend ever did accept it, the feature would let callers read rows outside the intended page window. Nothing validates or bounds the offset.

title: Permission expression is evaluated on every request and can raise when member is None
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` runs unconditionally, even when `optimized_pagination` is not requested. `organization_context.member` can be `None` for non-members, for example a non-member caller authenticated via a token or API key. For a non-superuser in that case it raises `AttributeError`, which turns previously working audit log requests on the default path into 500s. The check should be evaluated lazily, only when `use_optimized` is true, and should guard against `member is None`.

title: Behavior change in shared BasePaginator.get_result with a misleading comment
body: `BasePaginator.get_result` is used by many endpoints, and this edit changes it. Non-prev cursors with a negative offset are now silently clamped to 0, so a malformed cursor returns the first page instead of failing. Prev cursors still pass the negative offset straight to the queryset, which fails, so the claim that this 'allows negative offsets' and that the queryset 'will handle boundary conditions' is false. `offset` and `start_offset` now differ in the non-prev case, but the later `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` check still uses `offset`. The change is unrelated to the audit log feature, risks regressions elsewhere, and should be reverted or properly validated (reject negative offsets with a `BadPaginationError`).

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator.get_result wholesale; the 'else' branch is identical to the base
body: The class copy-pastes the whole of `get_result`. Only the negative-offset branch differs, and that branch cannot work (see the negative-slicing finding). The `else` branch is identical to the modified base logic. The result is two parallel implementations that can drift apart. The docstring's claims of 'optimized query path' and 'streamlined boundary condition handling' are not backed by any code, since the query is the same as the base class's.

title: Comment claims negative offsets are supported but no code change backs it
body: The added comment says the `Cursor` constructor now 'allows negative offsets ... for efficient reverse pagination'. The constructor is unchanged (`int(offset)` already accepted negatives) and nothing downstream supports negative offsets. The comment misleads future maintainers about a capability that does not exist.

title: No tests for the new paginator or the new endpoint branch
body: The PR adds a new paginator, a new query-param-gated code path and a change to the shared `BasePaginator`, with no tests. A basic test of `?optimized_pagination=true` would have exposed the datetime `get_item_key` crash, and a negative-offset cursor test would have exposed the slicing error. There is also no coverage of the permission gating (superuser, global access, no member).

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator uses numeric key handling for a datetime sort key, so the optimized path crashes
body: The endpoint passes `order_by="-datetime"` to `OptimizedCursorPaginator`. Its `get_item_key` copies `Paginator.get_item_key` (`math.floor(getattr(item, self.key))`), not `DateTimePaginator`'s. For `AuditLogEntry.datetime` this calls `math.floor` on a `datetime` and raises `TypeError` as soon as `build_cursor` computes the key for the first result. `value_from_cursor` (lines 842-843) also returns the raw integer cursor value instead of converting milliseconds to a timezone-aware datetime, so `build_queryset` would compare the datetime column to an integer on any follow-up page. Every `?optimized_pagination=true` request that returns rows fails with a 500, or with a SQL error on later pages.

title: Negative-offset slicing is unsupported by the Django ORM and the comment claiming otherwise is wrong
body: When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code runs `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start. Django querysets do not support negative indexing and raise (`ValueError`/`AssertionError`: "Negative indexing is not supported"). The comment "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false. A client who supplies a cursor such as `0:-5:1` (`Cursor.from_string` accepts negative offsets) triggers an unhandled exception and a 500. `stop = start_offset + limit + extra` can also go negative. The branch cannot deliver the advertised "access to data beyond normal pagination bounds", and it adds a user-controlled error path to an admin endpoint. If negative offsets are meant to be supported, they need real handling, or an explicit `BadPaginationError`.

title: Change to shared BasePaginator silently alters behavior for every paginator and contradicts its own comment
body: The edit to `BasePaginator.get_result`, which every `Paginator`/`DateTimePaginator` consumer in Sentry uses, claims to "allow negative offsets". In reality `max(0, offset)` clamps negative offsets to 0 for forward cursors, so a malformed or tampered cursor now silently returns the first page instead of failing. For `is_prev` cursors the negative offset is still passed straight to the queryset and raises. The behavior is inconsistent, changes a global code path for an unrelated feature, and the "safe because the queryset handles boundary conditions" comment is incorrect. This hunk should be reverted or replaced with explicit validation (`BadPaginationError` for offset < 0).

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator.get_result and delivers no actual optimization
body: The class copies about 60 lines of `BasePaginator.get_result`, differing only in the negative-offset branch. Both branches build the same queryset and the same slice, so the "optimized query path" and "streamlined boundary condition handling" in the docstring do not exist. It also copies `Paginator.get_item_key`/`value_from_cursor` rather than subclassing the correct `DateTimePaginator`, which is how the datetime bug above arose. Any future fix to `BasePaginator.get_result` will have to be mirrored here by hand. The docstring and PR title are misleading, since there is no performance change.

title: `organization_context.member` may be None and the check is evaluated on every request
body: `enable_advanced` is computed eagerly, before checking `use_optimized`. For a non-superuser, `organization_context.member` can be `None` (for example, non-member or token-based access), so `.has_global_access` raises `AttributeError`. This would break the default audit-log listing for requests that never asked for optimized pagination. Compute the flag only when `use_optimized` is true, and guard against `member is None`.

title: New query parameter, paginator and endpoint branch have no tests
body: The PR adds an undocumented `optimized_pagination` query parameter, a new paginator class and a privileged code path with no tests. No test exercises the optimized path, the authorization gate (superuser / global access vs. regular admin), or negative-offset cursors. A basic test of the optimized path would have caught the `math.floor(datetime)` crash, so the new behavior is currently unverified.

title: Comment claims Cursor allows negative offsets, but nothing supports them downstream
body: The added comment says negative offsets are allowed for advanced pagination and enable efficient reverse pagination. `Cursor` already accepted negative ints, and no logic was added. The downstream consumers (Django slicing) reject negative indices, so the comment is misleading documentation of a non-working feature.

title: Trailing whitespace and stray blank lines will fail lint
body: Lines 72 and 89 in the endpoint have trailing whitespace. The paginator docstring also has trailing-whitespace lines and three consecutive blank lines before `OptimizedCursorPaginator`, and a stray trailing blank line at the end of the file. These will trip the repo's pre-commit/flake8/black checks.

title: `organization_context.member` can be None, so every audit-log GET can raise AttributeError
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` runs on every request, not only when `optimized_pagination=true`. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is None when the caller is not an org member, for example an org auth token or API key. For any non-superuser caller in that situation, `None.has_global_access` raises AttributeError and the endpoint returns a 500, even on the default path. This regresses an endpoint that worked before. Compute it lazily and guard for None, for example `member and member.has_global_access`, only when `use_optimized` is set.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key cannot handle the datetime key the audit-log endpoint uses
body: The endpoint pairs `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `order_by="-datetime"`. `get_item_key` copies `Paginator`'s numeric logic and calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` on `item.datetime`, which raises TypeError for a `datetime`. `DateTimePaginator` avoids this by converting to epoch milliseconds. `value_from_cursor` also returns the raw integer cursor value instead of converting it back to a datetime, so the `datetime >= <int>` filter built in `build_queryset` would be wrong. As a result the optimized path fails with a 500 whenever there are results, and it would paginate incorrectly even if it didn't crash.

title: Negative-offset slicing is not supported by Django; comments claiming otherwise are wrong
body: The comments say "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" and that negative offsets give "access to data beyond normal pagination bounds". Django querysets raise `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` for `queryset[-n:m]`. Any client-supplied cursor with a negative offset, which `Cursor.from_string` accepts, produces a 500 on this path. The `cursors.py` comment, which says negative offsets are allowed for "efficient reverse pagination", is equally misleading, since nothing changes there. The `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` check further down also assumes the unclamped offset. Remove the negative-offset path, or implement it explicitly and validate it. The 'safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level' justification should not be relied on for user-controlled offsets.

title: Unrelated behavior change in shared BasePaginator.get_result
body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes the core paginator used by many endpoints. For forward cursors, a negative offset is now silently clamped to 0 instead of being rejected, so a malformed cursor returns the first page. For `is_prev` cursors the negative offset is still passed straight to the queryset, which fails exactly as before. The comment claims this enables 'efficient bidirectional pagination', but it does neither. It is unrelated to the spans-buffer change in this PR and has no tests.

title: Redirect-following depth limit reduced 10x without justification
body: The loop bound was changed from `0, 10000` to `0, 1000`, and the comment explaining the limit was deleted. The PR is about eviction and does not mention this. Segment trees with parent chains deeper than 1000 now stop following redirects early, so they can be split into multiple segments, a data-correctness regression for deep traces. Revert it, or document and test the new limit.

title: Hard-coded 1000-span cap conflicts with `max_segment_spans` and evicts silently
body: The script evicts down to a hard-coded 1000 members with `zpopmin`. `SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans` still defaults to 1001 and is no longer used anywhere, because the Python-side check in `_load_segment_data` was removed. The configured limit and the real limit now disagree and the parameter is dead. Previously an oversized segment logged an error and emitted `segment_span_count_exceeded`. Now spans are dropped silently, with no metric or log for how many were evicted. Pass the limit into the script as an ARGV value from `max_segment_spans`, and have the script or caller emit a metric when it evicts.

title: ZUNIONSTORE defaults to SUM aggregation, which corrupts timestamp scores for duplicates
body: Scores are now span end timestamps, and eviction relies on `zpopmin` removing the oldest. `zunionstore` defaults to `AGGREGATE SUM`. If the same payload is present in both sets being merged, for example after a Kafka redelivery, its score is added to itself and becomes roughly 2×timestamp. That span is then treated as the newest and survives eviction ahead of genuinely newer spans. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or `MIN`). The same applies to the second union on line 53.

title: Switching segment keys from SET to ZSET under the same key names breaks rolling deploys
body: The `span-buf:s:*` keys keep the same names but change type from SET (`sadd`/`scard`/`sunionstore`/`sscan`) to ZSET (`zadd`/`zcard`/`zunionstore`/`zscan`). Keys written by the old version live for up to `redis_ttl` (1h). During or after deployment, any existing set-typed key hit by `zadd`, `zcard`, `zunionstore` or `zscan` fails with WRONGTYPE. That fails the batch or the flush and crashes or loops the consumer. Old and new consumers running side by side will also conflict. Use a new key prefix, or flush or drain the buffer before rollout.

title: No test covers the new eviction behavior
body: The PR is titled 'eviction during insert', but the tests only add `end_timestamp_precise` to existing fixtures. Nothing exercises inserting more than 1000 spans into a segment, checking that the oldest-by-end-timestamp spans are the ones evicted, or checking that eviction works across merged sets and with root-span flags. There is also no test for the new ZSET scoring or the removed span-count check. Likewise, `OptimizedCursorPaginator` and the new `optimized_pagination` endpoint path have no tests, which is how the datetime and negative-offset failures went unnoticed.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot paginate the datetime key used by the audit log endpoint
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `math.floor(getattr(item, self.key))`, and `value_from_cursor` returns the raw `cursor.value`. The audit log endpoint orders by `-datetime`, so `getattr` returns a `datetime` and `math.floor` raises `TypeError`. `DateTimePaginator` avoids this by converting through `strftime` with a multiplier and rebuilding a datetime from the cursor. Even if the key function worked, `build_queryset` would compare the `datetime` column to a raw millisecond integer. Any request with `optimized_pagination=true` that returns at least one row will therefore 500, or produce an invalid SQL comparison on the next page.

title: Negative-offset slicing is unsupported by Django and the comments claim otherwise
body: The code does `queryset[cursor.offset : stop]` with a negative `cursor.offset`, and the comment says "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically". Django querysets raise on negative indexing ("Negative indexing is not supported"), so a client-supplied cursor such as `value:-5:0` produces a 500. The comments ("access data beyond normal pagination bounds", "safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level") describe a capability that does not exist. They also invite a future change to bypass offset validation. Nothing validates or bounds the user-controlled offset.

title: Shared BasePaginator behavior changed for every consumer with a misleading rationale
body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` silently changes `BasePaginator.get_result`, which is used by many endpoints. A negative offset on a forward cursor used to fail; it is now silently clamped to 0, so a malformed cursor returns the first page instead of an error. For `is_prev`, negative offsets still reach `queryset[...]` and still crash. The later trim logic (`len(results) == offset + limit + extra`) still uses the unclamped `offset`, so it is inconsistent with the actual slice. The comment says the queryset "will handle boundary conditions", which is false. This change is unrelated to the spans buffer work in the PR title.

title: Eager evaluation of `organization_context.member.has_global_access` can crash every request
body: `enable_advanced` is computed on every request, even when `optimized_pagination` is not set, as `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` can be `None` (for example for org auth tokens or API keys with org:write that are not tied to a member). For such callers the existing audit-log endpoint now raises `AttributeError` and returns a 500, even though they never asked for the new feature. The check also uses `is_superuser` rather than `is_active_superuser`, so it ignores whether the superuser session is actually active. The new option should be evaluated lazily and `None`-safely, or not added at all.

title: Redirect-chain depth limit silently cut from 10000 to 1000
body: The loop bound changed from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000`, and the comment documenting the limitation was deleted. This is unrelated to the eviction work and is not mentioned in the PR. Span trees with redirect chains deeper than 1000 will now stop resolving early. The span is then attached to an intermediate set instead of the real segment, which fragments segments. The reduction should be justified or reverted.

title: Eviction silently drops spans with a hard-coded limit and no signal
body: When a segment has more than 1000 spans, `zpopmin` silently discards the earliest-ending ones. The old behavior logged an error and bumped the `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric. The new path emits nothing, so truncated segments are invisible. The limit 1000 is hard-coded in Lua while `SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans` (default 1001) is still a constructor argument that is no longer used anywhere, so configuration and behavior have diverged. Also, `zunionstore` defaults to `AGGREGATE SUM`, so a payload present in both sets (for example after a redelivery) gets its score added together. That distorts the eviction ordering, and `AGGREGATE MAX` or `MIN` would be correct.

title: Switching key type from SET to ZSET breaks in-flight segments during deploy
body: Segment keys (`span-buf:s:*`) change from sets (`sadd`/`sscan`/`scard`/`sunionstore`) to sorted sets (`zadd`/`zscan`/`zcard`/`zunionstore`) with no migration or versioned key prefix. Keys written by old consumers live up to `redis_ttl` (1h). Any new consumer touching an existing set-typed key, in `zadd`, in the Lua `zcard`/`zunionstore`, or in `zscan` on flush, gets a `WRONGTYPE` error. That fails the batch or the flusher and can crash-loop the consumer until the old keys expire or are flushed. A new key prefix, or a drain-before-deploy step, is needed.

title: Comment claims Cursor allows negative offsets for 'efficient reverse pagination', but nothing changed
body: The added comment says negative offsets are allowed for advanced pagination and enable efficient reverse pagination. `Cursor.__init__` still does `int(offset)` exactly as before, and downstream code cannot execute negative offsets (Django rejects negative slicing). The comment is misleading and documents a feature that is not implemented.

title: No test covers the new eviction behavior or the new paginator/endpoint path
body: The tests only add the `end_timestamp_precise` argument to existing Span constructions. There is no test that inserts more than 1000 spans and checks that the lowest-score spans are evicted. There is none for eviction after a merge via `zunionstore` either, and none for the removal of the `max_segment_spans` check in `_load_segment_data`. There are also no tests for `OptimizedCursorPaginator`, for the `optimized_pagination=true` branch of the audit-log endpoint, or for the paginator offset-clamping change. The new paginator and endpoint code would fail on first use (datetime key handling, negative slicing).

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot paginate by a datetime key, which is the only way the audit-log endpoint uses it
body: The audit-log endpoint passes `order_by="-datetime"`. `get_item_key` calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` on `getattr(item, "datetime")`, which is a `datetime`, so it raises `TypeError` as soon as `build_cursor` computes the next/prev cursor. `value_from_cursor` also returns `cursor.value` as a raw integer instead of converting it back to a datetime, as `DateTimePaginator` does. Any request with a non-zero cursor would therefore compare the `datetime` column to an integer in SQL. The `?optimized_pagination=true` path is broken on the first page and on every later page. The class apparently copies `Paginator` instead of `DateTimePaginator` and was never exercised.

title: Negative-offset slice on a Django QuerySet raises instead of paginating; justifying comments are wrong
body: When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code runs `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing and raise `AssertionError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`. A user-supplied cursor such as `0:-5:0` (`Cursor.from_string` accepts negative offsets) therefore produces a 500. The comments are wrong on two counts. "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing" is false. "This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level" does not apply, because the slice does not become a valid read of earlier rows. This feature is exposed to superusers and global-access members, so it is a crash path in new code, not an optimization.

title: `organization_context.member` dereferenced eagerly for every request, can raise AttributeError on the default path
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated for every request, even when `optimized_pagination` is not set. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is Optional. It is `None` for non-member access, such as org-auth-token requests where `request.user` is anonymous and `is_superuser` is False. Those requests now fail with `AttributeError` (500) on an endpoint that previously worked. The check should be computed only when `use_optimized` is true, and it should guard against `member is None`.

title: Clamping negative offsets in the shared BasePaginator makes cursors inconsistent for all paginators
body: `BasePaginator.get_result` is inherited by many endpoints. The change silently clamps a negative offset to 0 for the query, but `build_cursor` still receives the original cursor with the negative offset. `_build_next_values` and `_build_prev_values` compute `next_offset = offset + limit` from that negative value. The returned page therefore does not match the cursors that follow it, causing skipped or duplicated rows. Previously a negative offset failed loudly in Django. The comment "the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions" is incorrect, and `is_prev` cursors still pass the negative offset straight through to the slice. This behavior change to a shared class has nothing to do with the spans buffer.

title: Redirect-chain depth limit silently reduced 10x and explanatory comment removed
body: The loop bound changes from `0, 10000` to `0, 1000`, and the comment explaining the limit is deleted. This is unrelated to the eviction work in the PR. Span trees whose redirect chains are deeper than 1000 will now stop resolving early and fail to merge into the correct segment. That produces split segments, and it is not mentioned in the title or description.

title: Switching segment storage from Redis SET to ZSET with no migration will hit WRONGTYPE on existing keys
body: Segment keys `span-buf:s:*` change from sets (`SADD`/`SSCAN`/`SCARD`/`SUNIONSTORE`) to sorted sets (`ZADD`/`ZSCAN`/`ZCARD`/`ZUNIONSTORE`). On deploy, buffers already in Redis are still plain sets, with TTL up to `redis_ttl` (1h). `ZADD`, `ZCARD`, `ZUNIONSTORE` and `ZSCAN` on them will return WRONGTYPE. This causes consumer errors, and flushes of in-flight segments will fail. Nothing handles or documents the transition, such as a new key prefix or draining first.

title: ZUNIONSTORE uses default SUM aggregation, corrupting scores of duplicate members
body: Scores are `end_timestamp_precise`, and the eviction via `zpopmin` relies on them as an ordering. `ZUNIONSTORE` defaults to `AGGREGATE SUM`, so a payload that exists in both `set_key` and `span_key` (or `parent_key`) gets its score doubled. A span redelivered after a consumer restart is one such case. The span then looks far newer than it is, so ordering is wrong and the wrong spans are evicted. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or `MIN`).

title: max_segment_spans is now dead config and the cap is hard-coded to a different value in Lua
body: The span-count check in `_load_segment_data` was removed, but `max_segment_spans` (default 1001) is still a constructor argument and attribute and is now unused. The real cap is the hard-coded `1000` in `add-buffer.lua`, which does not match the 1001 default and cannot be configured. Eviction also discards the oldest spans without emitting any metric or log, so operators can no longer see that segments are being truncated. The old `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric is gone.

title: No test covers the new eviction behavior or the new paginator/endpoint code
body: The PR's headline feature is evicting spans beyond 1000 per segment inside the Lua script (`zpopmin` on lowest score), and its correctness depends on the score ordering and the union count logic. The tests only add `end_timestamp_precise` to existing fixtures. There is no test that inserts more than 1000 spans and checks which ones survive, or that eviction works across merged sub-segments. There are also no tests for `OptimizedCursorPaginator`, the `optimized_pagination` endpoint path, or the BasePaginator offset clamping. The datetime-key bug and the member-None bug would have been caught by even a basic test.

title: Comment claims Cursor allows negative offsets for reverse pagination, but nothing implements or supports that
body: The added comment says negative offsets are allowed for "efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions", yet no code changed. `int(offset)` already accepted negatives, and downstream consumers (Django slicing, `build_cursor`) do not support them. The comment misleads future readers into thinking negative offsets are a supported, safe feature.

title: 60s eligibility cache is stale, never invalidated, and runs before the cheap dataset check
body: The allowlist result is cached for 60s per (org, hash of project ids). `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined but never called, so removing a project from `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` keeps returning upsampled counts for up to a minute. `options.get` is already served from an in-process cache, so the extra cache round trip buys little. The cache lookup and write also happen before `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`. Every stats request on transactions, spans or metrics therefore pays a cache get and set for a decision that can never be True. The key also uses `hash(tuple(...))` instead of the ids themselves, so two different project sets can collide and share a wrong cached result. Do the dataset check first, and either drop the cache or invalidate it from the option-change path with an explicit id-based key.

title: Substring match on raw request query misclassifies negated and mixed queries as error-only
body: `_is_error_focused_query` returns True if the lowercased `query` GET param contains the substring `event.type:error`. That also matches `!event.type:error`, `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`, and any value that merely starts with `error`. Queries that exclude errors or include transactions are then upsampled. `sum(sample_weight)` is meaningless or zero for transactions, so those counts come out wrong. A proper parse of the search filters is needed instead of a substring test.

title: Upsampling check uses outer `dataset` and raw request query instead of the scoped dataset and actual query
body: `_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` and a possibly rewritten `query`, but the eligibility check passes the closure variable `dataset` and reads `request.GET['query']` inside the helper. In the dashboard-widget split flow the function is called with `discover` and `(query) AND !event.type:transaction`, or with `scoped_dataset` for the transaction-like split. The decision is then made against the original dataset and query, not the ones actually executed. The error-only split query on a metrics-enhanced request is never upsampled, so the counts differ from the same query run directly. The helper should take the scoped dataset and the query actually being run.

title: upsampled_count uses sum(sample_weight) with no fallback for missing weights
body: `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` returns 0 or undercounts for any error row where `sample_weight` is NULL, 0 or absent. That includes events ingested before the column was populated and events from allowlisted projects whose SDK sends no client sample rate. The code comment says the column is assumed to exist for all events, but nothing enforces it. For those rows the chart count becomes lower than the real `count()`, so it is a silent regression. Use something like `sum(coalesce(sample_weight, 1))`, or keep `count()` when weights are missing.

title: upsampled_count is a public query function but references a column absent from non-error datasets
body: Unlike the neighbouring function marked `private=True`, `upsampled_count` is publicly selectable by users. It depends on the `sample_weight` column, which the transactions dataset does not have, as the PR's own helper docstring says. A user calling `upsampled_count()` against transactions through the shared discover config will get a Snuba error. It should be private, or restricted to the errors dataset.

title: RPC upsampling branches are dead code
body: `use_rpc` is only true for `spans_rpc` and `ourlogs`. `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns False for every dataset other than errors and discover. The `upsampling_enabled` branches in the RPC and RPC top-events paths can therefore never run. The `upsampled_count() as count` string is also not a valid RPC y-axis. The branches add misleading code and should be removed.

title: Docstrings and comments contradict the actual caching behaviour
body: `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` says it reads the allowlist fresh each time to always have the latest configuration. Its only caller caches the result for 60s, so the statement is false. The endpoint comments ("This cached result ensures consistent behavior", "most current schema assumptions", "better query optimization and caching") describe nothing the code does and mislead maintainers.

title: Trailing whitespace in new code
body: Whitespace-only lines with trailing spaces were added in the endpoint (around lines 223, 234, 278) and throughout `error_upsampling.py` docstrings and blank lines. This will fail the repo's formatting and lint hooks (black, flake8 W291/W293).

title: Stray submodule pointer committed
body: A `sentry-repo` gitlink pointing at the base commit is added. It has nothing to do with the feature and looks like an accidental artifact of the working setup. It should be removed from the PR.

title: Core eligibility function, cache behaviour and edge cases are untested
body: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` is not unit-tested, including its cache hit, miss and invalidation paths. Nothing covers `!event.type:error` or mixed queries, the top_events path, or the dashboard-split path. `self.snuba_params` is built in `setUp` but never used. The endpoint tests rely on freshly created project ids to avoid cache pollution rather than clearing the cache.

title: Test helper swallows all exceptions and skips a zero rate
body: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` wraps lookups in bare `except Exception: pass`, which hides malformed contexts (for example `contexts: None`) and bad rates. `if client_sample_rate:` also ignores a legitimate value of 0. It runs on every `store_event` call and mutates the normalized payload for all tests that set `contexts.error_sampling`, which is a broad side effect for a fixture helper.

title: upsampled_count uses sum(sample_weight) with no NULL handling
body: The new aggregate is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. Events stored before `sample_weight` was populated, or without a client sample rate, have NULL in that column. `sum` skips NULLs, so those events are counted as 0, or the whole bucket becomes NULL and `toInt64` then yields 0 or an error. Allowlisted projects therefore show undercounted or zeroed error charts as soon as their data contains any unweighted events. The comment says the schema guarantees the column exists, but a nullable column existing does not mean it is populated. It should be `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))` so unweighted events count as 1. Also, the function is registered as a public (non-private) discover function. Users can call `upsampled_count()` directly, including on datasets or event types where `sample_weight` does not exist.
