title: Upsampling check uses the outer `dataset` and request query instead of the scoped dataset and actual query
body: `_get_event_stats` takes `scoped_dataset` and `query`, but the eligibility check passes the closed-over endpoint-level `dataset`. The check also reads `request.GET['query']` instead of the `query` argument. In the dashboard-widget split path, the code calls `_get_event_stats(discover, ..., f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction")` or `scoped_dataset` with a modified query. The decision is still based on the original dataset (for example `metrics_enhanced_performance`, which returns False) and the original request string. The same widget can then get upsampled counts in one branch and raw counts in another. The split-decision logic compares `error_results` against `original_results`, which can come out inconsistent. The decision should be computed from `scoped_dataset` and the `query` actually being executed.

title: Substring match on 'event.type:error' misclassifies negated and compound queries
body: `_is_error_focused_query` returns True if the raw lowercase query string contains `event.type:error`. That matches `!event.type:error` (the opposite intent), `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`, and any query where the text appears inside a longer token or value. In those cases `count()` is rewritten to `sum(sample_weight)` over transaction or other non-error rows, which have no sample weight. The result is wrong counts or Snuba errors. The docstring claims this errs on the side of caution, but a substring match does the opposite. It needs to parse the query, or at least check token boundaries and negation.

title: Cache layer is unnecessary, collision-prone, and never invalidated
body: The allowlist check is an in-process `options.get` followed by an `in` scan. Wrapping it in `cache.get`/`cache.set` (a network round-trip to memcached or redis) is likely slower than the lookup it replaces. It also adds staleness: option changes take up to 60s to apply, and the module's own `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is never called anywhere. The key is built from `hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))`, a 64-bit non-cryptographic hash, so two different project sets can collide and share an eligibility result. It is also not independent of the organization's data beyond org id. Joining the sorted ids, or dropping the cache entirely, would be safer.

title: Docstring contradicts the caching behavior
body: The NOTE on `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` says it reads the allowlist fresh each time so the latest configuration is always used. The caller wraps it in a 60-second cache, so results can be up to a minute stale. Comments in the endpoint make similar claims ("cached result ensures consistent behavior", "most current schema assumptions", "better query optimization and caching") that are not true of the code. They will mislead maintainers about when the allowlist takes effect.

title: Upsampling transform applied in RPC branches that can never be eligible
body: `use_rpc` is only true for `spans_rpc` and `ourlogs`. `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns False for every dataset other than errors and discover, so `upsampling_enabled` is always False in the two RPC branches (top-events and timeseries). The `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` calls there are dead code. They also suggest to readers that RPC datasets are supported, and they would feed a non-RPC `upsampled_count() as count` column into the RPC `y_axes` if the gating ever changed.

title: Endpoint tests miss top_events, negated queries, the cache path and the dashboard split path
body: The new tests only cover plain timeseries with `count()`. They do not cover the `topEvents` branch where the transform is also applied. They do not cover `!event.type:error` or compound queries, which the substring check mishandles. They do not cover events with NULL `sample_weight`, the likely failure for `sum(sample_weight)`. They do not cover the dashboard split path, where the outer `dataset` is used instead of the scoped one. The tests also mock `options` while using the real cache, and `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` have no direct unit tests. The 60s cache and the unused invalidation are therefore untested.

title: Blanket exception swallowing in test factory helper hides malformed fixtures
body: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` wraps both the context lookup and the float conversion in `except Exception: pass`. A malformed `client_sample_rate` (for example a string) is silently ignored and the event is stored without `sample_rate`. The upsampling tests then fail on count assertions rather than at the real cause. The `if client_sample_rate:` check also skips a legitimate rate of 0. Narrow the exceptions or let invalid fixtures fail loudly.

title: Stray submodule gitlink committed to the repository
body: A new `sentry-repo` entry is added as a git submodule pointer (`Subproject commit a5d2909...`, the base commit). It is unrelated to the feature and has no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry, so it looks like an accidental commit of a local checkout. It can break `git submodule` operations and should be removed from the PR.

title: Upsampled count ignores NULL sample_weight, so events without a sample rate count as 0
body: `count()` is rewritten to `upsampled_count()`, which is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. Only events that carry a client sample rate get a `sample_weight`. Events in allowlisted projects that predate rollout, or come from SDKs that don't send `client_sample_rate`, have NULL there. `sum` skips NULLs, so those events add 0 and the chart undercounts, possibly showing 0 for projects that do have errors. The comments ("rely on the database schema to ensure sample_weight exists") assert a guarantee nothing in the PR enforces. The aggregate should treat missing weights as 1, for example `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))`.

title: Eligibility cache is stale for 60s and its invalidation function is never called
body: The result of the allowlist check is cached for 60s under a key built only from org id and project ids, not from the allowlist contents. After an operator changes `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`, queries keep using the old decision for up to a minute. `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is documented as the fix but has no callers, so it is dead code. The `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` docstring says the config is read "fresh each time" to have the latest state, which contradicts the cache. The key also uses `hash(tuple(...))`, so two project sets can collide and get each other's cached answer; joining the sorted ids would be collision-free.

title: The "performance" cache adds a cache round trip for something that is already cheap
body: `options.get` is served from Sentry's local option cache, and the allowlist check is a few integer lookups. Wrapping it in `cache.get`/`cache.set` adds a network round trip (memcached/redis) on every `_get_event_stats` call, and the dashboard split path calls that function several times per request. The dataset and query check, which is the cheap part, runs after the cache access, so even spans, transactions and metrics requests pay for the lookup. The cache costs more than it saves. Evaluating `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` first and dropping the cache would be simpler and faster.

title: Upsampling decision uses the outer `dataset` and the raw request query, not the dataset and query actually being executed
body: `_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` and `query`, but the eligibility check passes the closure variable `dataset` and `_is_error_focused_query` re-reads `request.GET['query']`. In the dashboard-widget split flow the function is called with `discover` and a derived query such as `(q) AND !event.type:transaction`, and also with the original dataset and query. The decision then reflects neither the dataset nor the query of the call being made. Error-only split queries are not upsampled unless the user's raw query happens to contain `event.type:error`. A transactions or metrics query can be judged eligible because of the outer dataset. The decision should be based on `scoped_dataset` and the `query` argument.

title: Substring match on `event.type:error` misclassifies queries
body: `"event.type:error" in query` is a raw substring test on the lowercased query string. It is also true for `!event.type:error` (errors excluded), for `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` (transactions have no `sample_weight`), and for values like `event.type:error_foo`. Those queries get `count()` rewritten to `sum(sample_weight)`, producing wrong numbers or failing on transaction rows. Parse the query, or at least check for the negation and OR cases.

title: `upsampled_count` is a public discover function not restricted to error data
body: The new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is registered without `private=True`, so any caller of the events or stats API can request `upsampled_count()` directly. On transactions, spans or any non-error query this references a `sample_weight` column that does not exist, so users get Snuba errors or a 500 instead of a validation error. It is also not gated on the allowlist. The function is an internal rewrite target and should be private, like the neighbouring internal function.

title: Comments claim caching, separation and "current schema assumptions" that the code does not implement
body: The comments say "This cached result ensures consistent behavior across query execution", "This separation allows for better query optimization and caching" and "ensure we use the most current schema assumptions". The check runs on every call, `upsampling_enabled = should_upsample` is a pure alias, and the "late transformation" is just a list rewrite. The same transform block is also copy-pasted into three branches. The comments mislead readers about the behavior and should be removed, and the transform done once.

title: No tests for the eligibility entry point, the cache, or invalidation
body: The unit tests cover only the private helpers. `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, the cache hit/miss paths and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` are never exercised, and nothing checks that an allowlist change is picked up. Negated or OR-combined `event.type` queries and the topEvents path are not tested either. The `snuba_params` built in `setUp` is never used. The endpoint tests mock `options` but not the cache, so they depend on cache state between runs.

title: Stray submodule gitlink committed
body: The PR adds a `sentry-repo` entry as a gitlink (`Subproject commit a5d29095...`, the base commit of this very repo) with no matching `.gitmodules`. It is unrelated to the feature and almost certainly an accident. It leaves a dangling submodule entry that makes `git submodule` commands error and confuses checkouts and CI. It should be removed from the PR.

title: Error timestamps (seconds) compared against replay event timestamps (milliseconds)
body: `fetch_error_details` copies the nodestore event `timestamp`, which is float epoch seconds, into `ErrorEvent`. `gen_request_data` compares it with `event.get("timestamp", 0)` from the rrweb recording segments, which are epoch milliseconds. Every error therefore compares as earlier than the first replay event. All errors are emitted at the top of the log instead of interleaved chronologically, and the 'at <ts>' text mixes units. The tests hide this because they use the same small or second-scale values on both sides. Convert one side (for example multiply the error timestamp by 1000) so the units match.

title: zip(error_ids, events.values()) can pair event IDs with the wrong nodestore payloads
body: `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a dict keyed by node ID. It is not guaranteed to preserve input order, and missing nodes may be omitted. Zipping `error_ids` with `events.values()` therefore misaligns IDs and data whenever any node is missing or the order differs. The `id` field of the resulting `ErrorEvent` can then be attached to the wrong error. Look each event up with `events.get(node_id)` while iterating `zip(error_ids, node_ids)`.

title: Snuba replay query runs even when error context is disabled
body: `query_replay_instance` and `process_raw_response` always run, and `enable_error_context=false` is only checked afterwards. When the caller opts out of error context, the extra Snuba round trip is wasted and adds latency to every summarize request. Check the flag first and skip the query entirely when it is false.

title: age/timestamp exclusivity validation is incomplete and truthiness-based
body: `validate_timestamp` and `validate_age` only run when their own field is present. A report with neither `age` nor `timestamp` therefore passes validation, although the spec requires one of them. The cross-check uses `self.initial_data.get("age")` / `.get("timestamp")` truthiness, so a value of `0` (valid for `timestamp`, allowed for `age`) is treated as absent. A report containing both `age: 0` and `timestamp` is accepted. Use `"age" in self.initial_data` and add an object-level `validate()` requiring exactly one of the two fields.

title: Feature-flagged TableWidgetVisualization renders hardcoded empty data
body: When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, the widget renders `TableWidgetVisualization` with `columns={[]}` and a hardcoded empty `tableData`. It ignores `result.data`, `result.meta`, `fieldAliases`, the custom field renderers, the `loading` handling and the title. Every table widget for an org with the flag on would show an empty table. Either wire the real result data and metadata through or do not ship this branch.

title: Analytics event recorded before the feature-flag check
body: `analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` fires before the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` check. Requests from orgs without the feature, which are answered with 404, are still counted as assemble API usage. This inflates the metric and records events for a disabled feature. Move the call after the feature gate.

title: Query key omits organization slug
body: The react-query key is `['use-trace-item-attribute-keys', queryOptions]`, and `queryOptions` contains only itemType, attributeType, project IDs, search and date params. The organization is not part of the key. Switching organizations with the same page filters and project IDs can serve cached attribute keys from the previous org. Include `organization.slug` in the key, as the previous `useApiQuery` path-based key did.

title: Error timestamps (seconds) compared against replay event timestamps (milliseconds)
body: `gen_request_data` interleaves errors with breadcrumbs by checking `error_events[idx]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)`. The error timestamp comes from the nodestore event payload, which is epoch seconds. The `event["timestamp"]` from an rrweb replay segment is normally epoch milliseconds. With real data every error then compares as 'earlier' than the first replay event, so all errors are emitted at the start of the log instead of in chronological order. The Seer summary receives a wrong timeline. The tests use the same unit for both sides (`now.timestamp()` for both, and small numbers in `test_get_request_data`), so they cannot catch this. Normalise the units, for example by multiplying the error timestamp by 1000, and add a test that uses millisecond replay timestamps.

title: Per-issue get_recommended_event() lookup when building PR comments
body: `get_environment_info` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` for every issue in the comment (up to 5). That performs an event lookup (Snuba plus nodestore) per issue, synchronously in the comment-building path, just to show an environment name. Failures are swallowed and logged only at `info`, so persistent lookup problems will go unnoticed and the comment silently loses the environment. Consider a single batched lookup, or reading the environment from data already available on the group or query.

title: Issue title placed unescaped inside markdown link text and truncated mid-token
body: `MERGED_PR_SINGLE_ISSUE_TEMPLATE` puts the raw (user-controlled) issue title inside `[**{title}**]({url})`. A title containing `]`, `[`, `**` or `](...)` breaks the link or lets the title alter the rendered link in the PR comment. `_truncate_title` cuts at 50 characters without regard to markdown, so it can also leave an unbalanced `**` or bracket and mangle the rest of the comment. The title should be escaped, or have markdown-significant characters stripped, before it is interpolated.

title: Unknown report types reject the whole batch with 422
body: `type` is a `ChoiceField` limited to 8 values, and a single invalid report makes the endpoint return 422 for the entire array. The Reporting API can deliver other report types to a collector (e.g. `network-error` or newer types), and browsers batch reports. One report of an unlisted type discards all valid reports in the same request. The previous code only used the types as hints and accepted everything. For a data-collection endpoint it is safer to skip or tag unknown types than to fail the batch.

title: age/timestamp mutual-exclusion check uses truthiness and is not enforced when both are missing
body: `validate_timestamp` and `validate_age` use `self.initial_data.get(...)` truthiness, so a value of `0` (valid for both `age` and `timestamp`) is treated as absent. A report with `age: 0` and `timestamp: 5` therefore passes. Field-level validators also only run when the field is present, so a report containing neither `age` nor `timestamp` is accepted, although the comments say exactly one spec format is required. Use `is not None` / `in initial_data` checks and add an object-level `validate()` requiring exactly one of the two.

title: TableWidgetVisualization rendered with hardcoded empty columns and data
body: When the `use-table-widget-visualization` flag is on, every table widget renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />`. The real `result.data` / `result.meta`, field aliases, loading state and custom field renderers are all ignored. Any org with the flag enabled sees every dashboard table widget as an empty table. If this is intentional scaffolding, it should be marked clearly. Otherwise pass `result.data`/`result.meta` (converted to `TabularData`) and the columns.

title: Default autofix automation tuning silently changed from 'low' to 'off'
body: `DEFAULT_AUTOFIX_AUTOMATION_TUNING_DEFAULT` and the `sentry:autofix_automation_tuning` project option default both change from `"low"` to `"off"`. Every project that never set the option explicitly changes behaviour on deploy: autofix automation turns off, and the API/serializer now reports `off`. This has nothing to do with the PR title (replay bulk delete), and the PR description is just 'Test 5'. It should be a separate, clearly described change, with a decision on whether existing projects need a migration to preserve their effective setting.

title: Analytics event recorded before the feature-flag check
body: `analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` runs before the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` feature check. Requests from orgs without the feature (which get a 404) are still counted as assemble API usage, which skews the metric. Also, `request.user.id` is None for org-auth-token requests, so those events carry no user. Move the call after the feature check unless counting rejected requests is intended.

title: New max_segment_id=None handling is not actually exercised
body: The test now feeds `max_segment_id: None`, but it patches `delete_matched_rows`, so the real `_make_recording_filenames` / `delete_replay_recordings` code that gained the `None` early-return is never run. A regression back to `range(None + 1)` would still pass. Add a direct unit test of `_make_recording_filenames` with a `None` segment id, or an unmocked `delete_matched_rows` test.

title: 60s processing deadline for a batch of up to 100 external identity refreshes
body: `check_auth_identities` loops over up to `chunk_size=100` auth identities. Each `check_single_auth_identity` makes a network call to the SSO provider's `refresh_identity`. A fixed `processing_deadline_duration=60` allows only about 0.6s per identity, so a slow provider can hit the deadline. `check_auth` has already bumped `last_synced` for the whole chunk, so the identities that were not reached will not be re-selected until the next interval (about a day). The final `check_auth.apply_async` reschedule is also skipped. Size the deadline to the chunk, or reduce the chunk size.

title: Query key omits organization; isLoading/attributes semantics changed
body: The react-query key is `['use-trace-item-attribute-keys', queryOptions]`, but `queryOptions` contains no organization slug, and the fetch URL does depend on `organization.slug`. Cached attribute keys can be reused across organizations within a session. The hook also now returns `isLoading: isFetching`, which is true on every background refetch rather than only the initial load. `attributes` can now be `undefined` (it was previously always a `TagCollection`). Callers that gate UI on `isLoading` or assume a defined object may flicker or break. The old `staleTime: 0`, `refetchOnWindowFocus: false` and `retry: false` options were also dropped.

title: Saved queries with multi-yAxis visualizes will always look modified
body: A Visualize now holds a single yAxis. A saved query stored in the old format `{yAxes: [a, b]}` is parsed into two Visualizes, which `toJSON()` serialises as `[{yAxes:[a]},{yAxes:[b]}]`. `valueIsEqual(visualizes.map(v => v.toJSON()), singleQuery?.visualize, true)` then never matches the stored value. The Save button is permanently highlighted as 'has changes', and the saved overlay is split into separate charts. There is no migration or normalisation of the stored `visualize` shape on load.

title: HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES only applied when a search query is entered
body: `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` (`is_segment`, `project_id`, `received`) is checked only in the `.filter()` that runs after the `if (!searchQuery.trim()) return sorted;` early return. With an empty search box, which is the default, the hidden attributes are still shown. They disappear as soon as the user types something, so the list changes inconsistently. The hidden-attribute filter needs to run before the early return so it applies in both cases.

title: Error timestamps (seconds) are compared against replay event timestamps (milliseconds)
body: `gen_request_data` compares `error_events[i]["timestamp"]` with `event.get("timestamp", 0)`. Error timestamps come from the nodestore event payload and are float seconds (~1.7e9). Replay recording events (rrweb) carry millisecond timestamps (~1.7e12). Every error is therefore treated as earlier than the first replay event, and all errors are emitted at the start of the log instead of interleaved chronologically. The unit tests hide this because they use seconds for both sides (`now.timestamp()`, 1.5/3.0). The error timestamp should be converted to ms, or the replay timestamp to seconds, before comparing and before formatting the log line.

title: Snuba replay query runs even when error context is disabled
body: `query_replay_instance` and `process_raw_response` are executed unconditionally to obtain `error_ids`. The `enable_error_context=false` check is only evaluated afterwards, so the result is discarded. A disabled request still pays for an extra Snuba query. Check the flag first and skip the query.

title: zip(error_ids, events.values()) can pair IDs with the wrong events
body: `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a dict keyed by node id. Depending on the backend, it may omit missing keys or not preserve request order. Zipping `error_ids` with `events.values()` can then attach the wrong event id to an event, or shift the pairing after a missing node. Iterate over the `node_ids` and look each one up in the returned dict, or build the id mapping explicitly.

title: Analytics event recorded before the feature-flag check
body: `analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` fires before the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` feature check and before any payload validation. Requests from organizations without the feature, which get a 404, still emit the event. That inflates usage numbers for a feature that is not enabled. Move the call after the feature gate, or after validation, so only real attempts are counted.

title: age/timestamp exclusivity check uses truthiness and does not require either field
body: `validate_timestamp` and `validate_age` test `self.initial_data.get("age")` and `get("timestamp")` for truthiness. A report with `age: 0` or `timestamp: 0` (both valid) passes alongside the other field, so the 'mixed' check is bypassed. Both fields are also `required=False`, and field-level validators only run when the field is present. A report with neither `age` nor `timestamp` is accepted even though one of them is mandatory. The docstrings also describe the opposite of what the code checks. Use `is not None` checks and add object-level validation that exactly one of the two is present.

title: Strict ChoiceField for report type rejects the whole batch with 422
body: The old dataclass did not enforce the `Literal` type at runtime. `type = ChoiceField(choices=BROWSER_REPORT_TYPES)` now returns 422 for the entire request if any report has a type outside the eight hard-coded values, such as other Reporting API types browsers may send. The endpoint is explicitly meant to collect real-world data on what browsers send. One unknown report therefore drops every valid report in the same POST and discards the data the experiment is trying to observe. Consider accepting unknown types (tagging them as 'unknown' in the metric) and validating per report rather than failing the whole batch.

title: Flagged TableWidgetVisualization renders hard-coded empty data
body: When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, the table widget passes `columns={[]}` and `tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}}`. The real `result.data`, `result.meta`, loading state and custom renderers are all ignored. Any org with the flag on sees every dashboard table widget render as an empty grid. Either wire the real query results into the new component or do not ship the branch until it is ready.

title: Query key omits organization slug
body: The key is `['use-trace-item-attribute-keys', queryOptions]`, but `queryFn` fetches `/organizations/${organization.slug}/trace-items/attributes/` via `useGetTraceItemAttributeKeys`. The org slug is not part of the key. Switching organizations with otherwise identical page filters, project ids and item type can serve cached attributes from the wrong org. Include `organization.slug` in the key.

title: get_environment_info does a per-issue event lookup and logs failures as info
body: For each issue in the PR comment, `get_environment_info` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()`, which can hit Snuba and nodestore. That is up to five extra lookups, executed serially in the list comprehension while building the comment. Any exception is swallowed and logged at `info` under the name `no-environment`. Real failures such as Snuba errors are indistinguishable from 'issue has no environment' and will not alert. Consider batching or using data already available from the query, and log failures at a higher level.

title: Default autofix automation tuning silently changed from 'low' to 'off'
body: `DEFAULT_AUTOFIX_AUTOMATION_TUNING_DEFAULT` and the `sentry:autofix_automation_tuning` project option default (src/sentry/projectoptions/defaults.py) both flip from `low` to `off`. Every project that never set the option changes behavior on deploy: automatic autofix on new issues stops. The change is unrelated to the PR's stated purpose (replay bulk delete) and has no description or migration plan. Confirm it is intended and split it out so it can be rolled out and reverted independently.

title: 60s processing deadline may be too short for a 100-identity chunk
body: `check_auth_identities` loops over up to `chunk_size=100` identities. Each one runs `check_single_auth_identity`, which can call the SSO provider's `refresh_identity` over the network. A 60s deadline can be exceeded when providers are slow. Those identities already had `last_synced` bumped in `check_auth` before scheduling, so a timed-out chunk is not rechecked until the next interval. The follow-up `check_auth.apply_async` at the end of the task also never runs for that chunk.

title: None max_segment_id handling is not exercised by any test
body: The new early return for `max_segment_id is None` in `_make_recording_filenames` is only reached through `test_run_bulk_replay_delete_job_completion`, which patches `delete_matched_rows`. The real filename generation and deletion therefore never runs with a null segment id. Add a direct unit test for `_make_recording_filenames` / `delete_matched_rows` with a `None` row so a regression would be caught.

title: GitHub user check is skipped whenever no Integration row exists yet
body: The authenticated-user comparison (lines 500-505) only runs after `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` succeeds. The `except Integration.DoesNotExist` branch at 481-482 returns `pipeline.next_step()` without comparing `github_authenticated_user` to anyone. `installation_id` comes from the query string and takes precedence over the bound state (line 448). If the installation webhook has not been processed yet (the user is redirected at the same time the webhook fires) or was never delivered, anyone who supplies that installation_id gets it linked to their org. `build_integration` then fetches the installation with the app JWT. `test_basic_flow` exercises exactly this path with no webhook, so the PR's stated guarantee that the pipeline fails on a user mismatch does not hold. A failed or late webhook should be treated as a failure or verified some other way, not as success.

title: KeyError/500 when existing Integration has no `sender` metadata
body: `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes `sender` is always present. `build_integration` only stores it when `state.get("sender")` is truthy, so integrations created through the pipeline flow without a prior webhook, or created before sender tracking, have no `sender`. For such an Integration that has no OrganizationIntegration (for example, a re-install after the org integration was removed), the lookup raises KeyError and the user gets a 500 instead of the friendly error page. Use `.get` and treat missing data as a validation failure or handle it explicitly.

title: OAuth `state` is a deterministic pipeline signature, not a per-session nonce
body: The `state` sent to GitHub and later compared (line 412) is `pipeline.signature`. It is derived from the pipeline's views and is the same for every user and org; the tests reuse the same hard-coded value for two different orgs and users. It is therefore guessable and gives no CSRF or session binding for the OAuth authorize round trip. Anyone can craft a callback URL with their own `code` and the known `state`. The comparison is also a plain `!=` rather than a constant-time compare. For a security fix whose description lists the state check as a protection, use a random, session-bound value.

title: Network/HTTP failures in the token exchange and user lookup are not handled
body: `safe_urlopen(...)` at line 423 is outside the `try`, so connection errors or timeouts raise and produce a 500. `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` at line 434 also performs an HTTP request and can raise on non-2xx responses or network errors; only the missing-`login` case is handled. These GitHub-side failures should yield the same friendly `error(...)` response as the other failure modes the PR describes.

title: Authorize URL query string is built by string interpolation without encoding
body: `client_id`, `state` and `redirect_uri` are interpolated directly into the authorize URL. `redirect_uri` is a full URL containing `:` and `/`, and it is not percent-encoded. It works with GitHub today, but it is fragile, for example with a customized `url-prefix`, and `urlencode` should be used.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer tests the installation-not-found path
body: The test still stubs the installation lookup with a 404. It now sends a bogus `state` (`ddd023d8...`), so the flow ends in the state-mismatch error and asserts the generic "Invalid installation request." message. The `IntegrationError("The GitHub installation could not be found.")` branch in `build_integration` is therefore no longer covered, and the old assertion was silently replaced. The test now passes for a reason unrelated to its name.

title: Only one of the new failure modes (and no success case for an existing Integration) is tested
body: The PR lists three failure causes: user mismatch, state mismatch, and a failed `code` exchange. Only the user mismatch is tested. Nothing covers a wrong `state`, an `access_token` exchange failure, a `/user` response with no `login`, or an Integration that exists with no `sender` metadata. There is also no positive test where the authenticated GitHub user matches `metadata["sender"]["login"]` for a pre-existing Integration. Without these, the new validation can regress, or crash as in the KeyError case, unnoticed.

title: KeyError when the existing Integration has no `sender` metadata
body: `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes every pre-existing Integration carries webhook-provided `sender` metadata. `build_integration` only sets `sender` from `state.get("sender")`, and nothing in this pipeline ever binds that key. The updated `test_basic_flow` also shows an Integration created through the pipeline with no `sender` in its metadata. If such an Integration remains without an OrganizationIntegration, for example after one org is uninstalled, a legacy record, or an install created through the pipeline, this lookup raises `KeyError`. The user gets a 500 instead of the friendly error page, and the install is blocked. Use `.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and treat a missing sender as a controlled failure, or define explicit behaviour for it.

title: Authenticated-user check is skipped whenever the Integration row doesn't exist yet
body: The new `github_authenticated_user` vs `sender.login` comparison only runs when an Integration with that `external_id` already exists. It is created by the `installation` webhook. When `Integration.DoesNotExist` is raised, the code calls `pipeline.next_step()` without checking that the OAuth-authenticated user is the one who installed the app. Anyone who learns an installation_id can therefore finish the pipeline before the webhook has been processed, or if it was delayed or lost, and bind someone else's installation to their org. The check depends on a webhook race. A robust fix would verify against GitHub directly, for example by confirming the installation appears in `GET /user/installations` for the user token. The OAuth user token is already available at that point but is discarded after reading `login`.

title: OAuth `state` is a static, guessable value, so it gives no CSRF protection
body: `state` is `pipeline.signature`, which the tests pin to the constant `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`. That is a deterministic hash of the pipeline view classes, not a per-flow random nonce. Every user and session therefore gets the same value, and an attacker can craft `/extensions/github/setup/?code=...&state=<known>` links that pass the check. An OAuth `state` must be unpredictable and tied to the user's session. Also, `!=` is a non-constant-time comparison; use `constant_time_compare`. As written, the PR's claim that a mismatching `state` is rejected adds little real protection.

title: Network and HTTP errors in the token exchange and user lookup are not handled
body: Only `safe_urlread` and decoding are inside the `try`. `safe_urlopen(...)` on line 423 can raise connection, timeout or SSL errors, and `get_user_info(...)` on line 434 calls `raise_for_status()`, so an invalid or expired token raises `HTTPError`. Either failure surfaces as an unhandled 500 in the middle of the install dialog, not the 'Invalid installation request' page the PR describes for these cases. The existing `OAuth2CallbackView.exchange_token`, which this code is modelled on, wraps the whole exchange in exception handling. The failure paths also log nothing, so a failed exchange gives support and debugging no signal.

title: `test_installation_not_found` no longer exercises the installation-not-found path
body: The test now sends `state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`, which differs from the pipeline signature `9cae5e...`. The request is therefore rejected by the `state` mismatch check in `OAuthLoginView` before the 404 from `/app/installations/...` is ever reached. It asserts the generic 'Invalid installation request.' text. So it now covers state mismatch under a misleading name, and the `The GitHub installation could not be found.` branch in `build_integration` has lost its coverage. Use the valid state for this test, and add a separate test for state mismatch.

title: New failure and success paths of the validation are untested
body: Only the user-mismatch case is covered, and only incidentally the state mismatch. There are no tests for: a failed token exchange (no `access_token` in the response); a `/user` response without `login`; or the positive case where an Integration with webhook-provided `sender` already exists, has no OrganizationIntegration, and the authenticated user matches. That last case is the main new success path of `GitHubInstallation`. There is also no test for an existing Integration lacking `sender` metadata, which would currently raise `KeyError`. `assert_setup_flow` additionally hard-codes `responses.calls[2]`, which silently breaks whenever the number of HTTP calls in the flow changes.

title: GitHub user check is skipped when no Integration row exists yet
body: The authenticated-user check only runs when an `Integration` already exists without an `OrganizationIntegration`. If `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `DoesNotExist`, the code returns `pipeline.next_step()` without comparing `github_authenticated_user` to anything. The `Integration` row is normally created by the `installation` webhook, so until that webhook is processed (or if it is delayed or lost) any user who completes the OAuth step can claim any `installation_id`. `build_integration` then fetches the installation with the app JWT and creates the integration, and `state['sender']` is never set. This is the attack the PR is meant to stop, and the validation does not cover it. A stronger check would verify with GitHub, using the user's OAuth token, that the user can access that installation.

title: KeyError (HTTP 500) when stored Integration has no `sender` metadata
body: `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes the key always exists. `build_integration` only sets `metadata['sender']` when `state.get('sender')` is truthy, and nothing in this pipeline sets it. Integrations created through the pipeline, or before the webhook started recording the sender, have no `sender` key. If such an Integration exists without an OrganizationIntegration, the lookup raises `KeyError` and the user gets a 500 instead of the friendly error. Use `.get()` chains and treat a missing sender as a failed validation.

title: Network failures in token exchange and user lookup are not handled
body: `safe_urlopen(...)` is called outside the `try` block, so connection errors, SSL errors and timeouts reach the user as a 500. `OAuth2CallbackView.exchange_token`, which this code copies, wraps the request in a `try`. Likewise `get_user_info` (line 434) is not guarded and, as far as I recall, calls `raise_for_status()`, so a GitHub 4xx/5xx raises instead of reaching the `'login' not in ...` check. These failures should produce the same 'could not verify the installation request' error as the other failure paths.

title: OAuth authorize URL is built without URL-encoding its parameters
body: The authorize URL is built with an f-string, so `client_id`, `state` and `redirect_uri` are not percent-encoded. The existing `OAuth2LoginView` uses `urlencode`. An unencoded `redirect_uri` that contains a port, query or special characters can be mangled or rejected by GitHub. The test asserts the unencoded form, which locks in this behaviour. Build the query with `urlencode`.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer tests the 404 path
body: The test stubs a 404 for `/app/installations/{id}`, but it now sends `state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`. The pipeline signature in the other tests is `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`, so this request fails the new state check in `OAuthLoginView`. The installation lookup is never reached. The assertion was changed from 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' to the generic 'Invalid installation request.', which hides the fact that the original behaviour is no longer covered. The 404 handling in `build_integration` has no test, and the state-mismatch case is only tested by accident under a misleading name. Use the correct state in this test so it reaches `build_integration`, and add a separate state-mismatch test.

title: Missing tests for the success path and the new OAuth failure modes
body: Only the user-mismatch rejection is tested. There is no test where an Integration already exists (created by the webhook) with `sender.login` matching the authenticated user and the install succeeds. There are also no deliberate tests for a wrong `state`, a failed `access_token` exchange (for example `error=bad_verification_code`), a `/user` response without `login`, or an Integration whose metadata lacks `sender`. These are the behaviours listed in the PR description, and the last case would currently hit the `KeyError`.

title: `queued` default is evaluated once at import time, not per instance
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` calls `timezone.now()` once, when the class body executes at module import. Every `AssignmentSource` that doesn't pass `queued` explicitly gets that same timestamp, which is the process start time. `from_integration` never passes it, so the field in the serialized `assignment_source_dict` is stale and useless for debugging or ordering. This is the classic dataclass mutable/dynamic default mistake. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. The existing `test_to_dict` only checks `queued is not None`, so it passes with the bug.

title: `assignment_source` added to `sync_status_outbound` signature but never used
body: The abstract `sync_status_outbound` gains an `assignment_source` parameter. Nothing in the PR passes it, reads it, or uses it for status sync, and concrete integrations are not updated. This widens the contract for no behavioural gain and suggests status sync is cycle-protected when it is not. Remove it, or implement and test the status-sync behaviour.

title: Cycle-breaking tests cover only the assign path with a matching source
body: Only `assign()` with a matching source integration is tested. Nothing covers `deassign(..., assignment_source=...)`, which is the path `sync_group_assignee_inbound` takes when `assign=False`. Nothing covers an `AssignmentSource` from a different integration still propagating outbound, which the comment in `should_sync` says must keep working. Nothing checks that `sync_group_assignee_inbound` attaches the source when it calls `assign`/`deassign`. The existing inbound tests don't mock outbound sync, so a regression in the wiring (the actual loop fix) would go unnoticed.

title: `queued` default is evaluated once at import time, not per instance
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` calls `timezone.now()` once, when the class body executes at module import. Every `AssignmentSource` created without an explicit `queued` therefore gets the same process-start timestamp, not the time the assignment was queued. The field exists to record when the source was queued, so any later use for ordering, staleness checks or logging will see wrong data. The fix is `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. `test_to_dict` only asserts `queued is not None`, so it passes despite this bug.

title: Cycle-breaking is not tested on the deassign path or end-to-end through inbound sync
body: The only new test of the suppression behaviour covers `GroupAssignee.objects.assign` with an `AssignmentSource` that matches the integration. Three paths are untested. First, `deassign(..., assignment_source=...)` never has its suppression asserted. Second, `sync_group_assignee_inbound` (the actual webhook entry point that builds the source, for both assign and deassign) is never checked for skipping the outbound call. The existing inbound tests don't assert that `sync_assignee_outbound` is not called. Third, there is no test that a different integration's source still propagates outward, which the `should_sync` comment says is intended. A regression in any of these would reintroduce the sync loop unnoticed.

title: Unused `assignment_source` parameter added to abstract `sync_status_outbound`
body: The abstract `sync_status_outbound` now declares `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`. Nothing in this PR passes it, and status sync is not part of the assignee-cycle fix. It widens the contract for all subclasses with an argument that is never populated. This is misleading, and it suggests status sync is cycle-protected when it is not. Either remove it or wire it through.

title: `queued` default is evaluated once at import time, not per instance
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a plain dataclass default, so `timezone.now()` runs once when the module is imported. Every `AssignmentSource` created without an explicit `queued` gets that same stale timestamp, so the field does not record when the assignment was queued. If anything later uses `queued` for ordering, staleness or debugging, it will see wrong data. It should be `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. The `test_to_dict` test only asserts `queued is not None`, so it passes despite this bug.

title: `to_dict` puts a raw `datetime` into Celery task kwargs; `from_dict` does not validate it
body: `asdict(self)` leaves `queued` as a `datetime`, and `sync_group_assignee_outbound` passes the result straight into `apply_async` kwargs. This only works while the broker serializer can handle datetimes, such as pickle. With a JSON serializer it would fail at enqueue time. `from_dict` also accepts any value for `queued` (for example an ISO string after a JSON round trip) and returns a source whose field has the wrong type. The cycle-breaking check only needs `integration_id`, so `queued` adds a serialization risk for no current use.

title: Unused `assignment_source` parameter added to abstract `sync_status_outbound`
body: The abstract `sync_status_outbound` gains an `assignment_source` parameter, but nothing in this PR passes it and no implementation uses it. The PR only deals with assignee sync, so this widens the abstract contract with dead API surface. It also suggests status-sync cycles are handled when they are not. It should be removed, or actually wired up and tested.

title: No test covers the inbound path that supplies the `AssignmentSource`
body: The cycle fix depends on `sync_group_assignee_inbound` passing `AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration)` to `assign`/`deassign`. The added tests only call `GroupAssignee.objects.assign` with a hand-built source. The existing inbound tests (`test_assignee_sync_inbound_assign` and `_deassign`) do not assert that outbound sync is suppressed. Removing the `assignment_source=` argument in `sync.py` would therefore break the fix without failing any test. There is also no test that an assignment from integration A is still propagated to integration B, and none for the deassign-with-source case or the task-level parsing of `assignment_source_dict`.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now an uninstantiable abstract class
body: The class was changed from a concrete `DetectorHandler` whose `evaluate` returned `[]` into `StatefulDetectorHandler[...]` with only `pass`. `StatefulDetectorHandler` has abstract members `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and now `build_occurrence_and_event_data`, and this class implements none of them. `Detector.detector_handler` calls `group_type.detector_handler(self)`, so any detector of type `metric_alert_fire` raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class` instead of evaluating to nothing. `process_detectors` has no guard around that property, so one such detector aborts processing of the whole detector list. The `# TODO: This will be a stateful detector when we build that abstraction` comment is also stale, since the class now claims to be stateful. Either keep the no-op `DetectorHandler` (returning `{}`) until the real implementation exists, or implement the abstract methods.

title: evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: The `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` docstring says it "returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`". The return type is now `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, keyed by group key. The new abstract `build_occurrence_and_event_data` hook has no docstring either. A subclass author has nothing saying what `event_data` must contain (event_id, project_id, timestamp, and so on) or how the hook is called.

title: Expected occurrences are built with a value that differs from the evaluated value, so value passthrough is untested
body: The mock `build_occurrence_and_event_data` ignores `value`. The tests build expected occurrences with a hard-coded `6` even when the evaluated value is different: group_2 is 10 here, `test_results_on_change` uses 100, and `test_dedupe` uses 8. The tests would still pass if `evaluate_group_key_value` passed the wrong value, the wrong group key, or the wrong priority to the hook. Nothing asserts the arguments the hook receives. Either have the mock encode `value` in the occurrence, for example in `evidence_data`, or add a test that asserts the hook's call arguments.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler subclasses an abstract class without implementing its abstract methods
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler with an empty body (`pass`). StatefulDetectorHandler declares abstract members `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values` and the newly added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. `Detector.detector_handler` calls `group_type.detector_handler(self)`. For any detector with type `metric_alert_fire`, this now raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler`. Before this change the handler instantiated fine and returned `[]`. The exception propagates out of `process_detectors` and aborts processing for every detector in the batch. Either keep it a plain `DetectorHandler` with a no-op `evaluate` returning `{}`, or implement all the abstract methods. The `TODO: This will be a stateful detector` comment above the class is also stale or misleading now.

title: evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: The `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` signature now returns `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, but the docstring still says "returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`". The new abstract `build_occurrence_and_event_data` also has no docstring explaining the contract: what `value` is, and that the returned event_data must be valid for `produce_occurrence_to_kafka`. Both are needed by subclass implementers.

title: Mock hook ignores `value`, so tests cannot catch wrong arguments being passed to the new hook
body: `MockDetectorStateHandler.build_occurrence_and_event_data` delegates to `build_mock_occurrence_and_event`, which ignores `value` and builds output only from `group_key` and `new_status`. Several tests pass a hard-coded `6` for the expected occurrence while the real value is 8, 10 or 100 (for example `test_dedupe`, `test_results_on_change`, and `test_state_results_multi_group` with group_2=10). Expected and actual values therefore match whatever the real value is. If `evaluate_group_key_value` passed the wrong value to the hook, no test would fail. A test using a mock or spy that asserts the hook's call arguments would close this gap. There is also no test for the `DetectorPriorityLevel` to `PriorityLevel` conversion beyond HIGH.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now an abstract class and cannot be instantiated
body: The handler was changed from a concrete `DetectorHandler` with a stub `evaluate` to `StatefulDetectorHandler` with only `pass`. `StatefulDetectorHandler` is an `abc.ABC` with abstract members `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values` and the new `build_occurrence_and_event_data`, and none are implemented here. `Detector.detector_handler` does `group_type.detector_handler(self)`, so any detector of type `metric_alert_fire` now raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class` instead of returning an empty result. Because `process_detectors` iterates detectors without a try/except, one such detector would abort processing for the whole list. Either keep the previous concrete stub, or implement the abstract methods. The TODO comment above the class is also stale, since it says this will become stateful later.

title: evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: The PR changes the return type of `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` to `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, but the docstring still says it "returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`". This is misleading, since the dict keying is the point of the change (to prevent duplicate results per group key).

title: New abstract hook has no docstring or contract
body: `build_occurrence_and_event_data` is a new public extension point for subclasses, but it has no docstring. Implementers get no guidance on what `value` is, that `new_status` is never OK (OK produces a StatusChangeMessage instead), or what `event_data` must contain. The `event_data` requirements for `produce_occurrence_to_kafka` are non-obvious, such as `project_id`, `event_id`, `timestamp` and `platform`.

title: Mock occurrence builder ignores `value`, so tests cannot detect a wrongly passed value
body: `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` accepts `value` but never uses it. The tests then build expectations with a hardcoded `6` even when the evaluated value is 100, 8 or 10 (for example `test_results_on_change`, `test_dedupe` and `test_state_results_multi_group` for group_2). If `evaluate_group_key_value` passed the wrong value to the hook, these tests would still pass. The tests only verify `group_key` (via the fingerprint) and `new_status`. Encoding `value` into the mock occurrence, for example in `evidence_data`, and using the real value in expectations would give the hook argument real coverage.

title: get_monitor_environment_context discards its prepared config copy and returns the raw config
body: The function copies `monitor.config` and replaces `schedule_type` with its display string. It then returns `"config": monitor_environment.monitor.config`, the original dict, so the copy is never used. The occurrence event context therefore carries the raw numeric `schedule_type` instead of the readable value the code meant to send. The bug was carried over unchanged from `mark_failed.py`. Since the function is being moved into a new module anyway, it should return `config` (the copy).

title: get_failure_reason produces a malformed message when no failed statuses match
body: `status_counts` only counts statuses in `HUMAN_FAILURE_STATUS_MAP` (ERROR, MISSED, TIMEOUT). If none match, for example when the check-in list is empty or holds only other statuses, the sum is 0. The singular branch is skipped, `get_text_list([])` returns an empty string, and the result is " check-ins detected" with a leading space and no count. The evidence 'Failure reason' would then show a meaningless string. A fallback message is needed for the zero case. Separately, the docstring promises "were detected" phrasing and "A failed check-in was detected", but the code never produces them.

title: get_monitor_environment_context builds a display-friendly config copy but returns the original
body: The function copies `monitor.config` and replaces `schedule_type` with `get_schedule_type_display()`. It then returns `monitor_environment.monitor.config` (the uncopied original) under "config", so the copy is dead code. The event's `contexts.monitor.config` therefore carries the raw numeric `schedule_type` instead of the human-readable value. The bug came over with the move. Since the code now lives in a new module, it is a good moment to return `config` instead.

title: get_failure_reason produces a malformed message when no statuses match the map
body: `status_counts` only counts check-ins whose status is in `HUMAN_FAILURE_STATUS_MAP` (ERROR, MISSED, TIMEOUT). If none match, `sum(...)` is 0 and the singular branch is skipped. `get_text_list([])` then returns an empty string, and the result is " check-ins detected" with a leading space and no count. This can happen when `previous_checkins` contains only other statuses. That list comes from the last N check-ins ordered by `date_added`, so for example an in-progress check-in is not filtered out. The evidence value shown to users would then be garbage. A fallback message for the empty case would avoid it.

title: Copied config with display schedule_type is built but never used
body: `get_monitor_environment_context` copies `monitor.config` into `config` and replaces `schedule_type` with its display value. The returned dict then uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` (the original) instead of `config`. The copy is dead code, so the occurrence's monitor context carries the raw numeric `schedule_type` instead of the human-readable one the code intends. The bug was already in `mark_failed.py`, but this PR moves the function into a new module, so it is a good time to fix it by using `config` in the returned dict or removing the copy.

title: isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is False for SpawnProcess, so hung flushers are never killed
body: The flusher processes come from `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which is `SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` derives from `BaseProcess`, not from `multiprocessing.context.Process`, which is what `multiprocessing.Process` names. The `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` guard is therefore always False for real processes, and `process.kill()` is never called. The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. In the `cause == "hang"` case the old process is left running and `_create_process_for_shards` starts a second flusher for the same shards. Two flushers then compete over the same Redis keys, which can cause duplicate or fragmented segments and leaked processes. Fix this by checking `hasattr(process, 'kill')`, by checking `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`, or by using `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`. The same wrong check in `join()` means `terminate()` is also never called.

title: time.sleep(0.1) added to fix a race is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
body: `test_basic` begins with `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`. The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)`, commented "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change", calls that patched function and does nothing. The flusher thread therefore still races with `step.join()`, which sets `stopped` right after the drift change, so `(msg,) = messages` can fail intermittently. Wait explicitly instead, for example by polling until `messages` is non-empty with a deadline, or capture the real `time.sleep` before patching.

title: Docstring says one process per shard, but shards are capped and shared
body: The class docstring says "Creates one process per shard". That is wrong, because `max_processes` caps the process count and shards are distributed round-robin across processes, so one process can serve several shards. The CLI default `--flusher-processes=1` runs a single process for all shards. The `:param topic:` entry is also stale, since no such parameter exists, and `max_processes` is undocumented.

title: Inconsistent metric tag names (`shard` vs `shards`) for the same shard_tag
body: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` are tagged with `shard`, while `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` uses `shards`. Both carry the same comma-joined value. Dashboards that group or filter by tag will miss one of the two. Pick one name. Also note that the comma-joined list becomes a tag value whose cardinality depends on the shard-to-process assignment.

title: Memory check queries Redis once per flusher buffer on every submit
body: The memory-pressure check in `submit()` used to call `get_memory_info()` on a single buffer. It now calls it on every per-process buffer in `self.buffers`. Assuming `get_memory_info()` reports on the whole Redis cluster rather than only the buffer's assigned shards (not checked here), each call repeats the same `INFO` queries. `submit()` then does up to N times more Redis round trips per batch, and the used/available sums are inflated N-fold, which cancels out in the ratio. Query one buffer, or deduplicate by node, instead.

title: join() breaks out of the loop on deadline without terminating remaining processes
body: When the deadline expires, `join()` does `break`, so the `process.terminate()` call at the bottom of the loop never runs for the remaining processes. They are only reaped as daemons at interpreter exit. Terminating should happen for every process even if the wait budget is exhausted, and the unused `process_index` loop variable can be dropped.

title: No validation of max_processes; negative values crash with KeyError
body: `max_processes or len(assigned_shards)` treats 0 as "one per shard", but a negative value from `--flusher-processes -1` (click `type=int` accepts it) is kept. `num_processes = min(-1, n)` is -1, so `process_to_shards_map` is empty and `i % self.num_processes` yields an index that is not in the map, which raises a KeyError at consumer startup. Validate `>= 1`, for example with `click.IntRange(min=1)` on the option.

title: Unused helper _create_process_for_shard
body: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is never called; the restart path uses `_create_process_for_shards` directly. It is dead code that adds API surface and a second way to restart processes.

title: New test only checks process bookkeeping, not multi-process flushing or restarts
body: `test_flusher_processes_limit` checks only the process count and the shard-to-process map. It never submits spans on multiple shards and checks that segments are flushed, and it never covers the restart, hang or crash paths in `_ensure_processes_alive`, nor the per-process backpressure aggregation. The restart path is where the `isinstance`/`kill` regression lives, and nothing exercises it.

title: isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is False for spawn processes, so hung flushers are never killed
body: The processes are created with `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which is `SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` subclasses `BaseProcess` directly and is not a subclass of `multiprocessing.Process` (that is `context.Process`). The new `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` guard around `process.kill()` is therefore always False in production, and the kill never runs. The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. When the cause is `hang`, the stuck process is now left running and `_create_process_for_shards` starts a second flusher for the same shards. Two flushers then consume and produce the same segments concurrently, and every further restart leaks one more process. Use `hasattr(process, 'kill')` or check `multiprocessing.context.BaseProcess`/`SpawnProcess` instead.

title: join() never terminates spawned processes, and its deadline break skips cleanup for the rest
body: Two problems in `join()`. First, `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is False for `SpawnProcess`, so `process.terminate()` never runs for real flusher processes. Second, the new `if remaining_time <= 0: break` leaves the loop before reaching terminate for the current and all remaining processes. If the deadline expires while waiting on an early process, the later processes are neither waited on nor terminated. Terminate should run for every process regardless of the deadline, and the type check needs to match `SpawnProcess`.

title: time.sleep(0.1) added to de-flake test_basic is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
body: The test starts with `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, which replaces `time.sleep` globally. The new `time.sleep(0.1)`, commented "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change", therefore does nothing. `step.join()` sets `stopped` immediately, and the flusher thread can exit its `while not stopped.value` loop before it flushes. The `(msg,) = messages` assertion can then fail intermittently. Wait on a condition (poll until `messages` is non-empty, with a timeout) or use the real sleep (`monkeypatch.undo()` or a saved reference) for this wait.

title: Inconsistent metric tag name `shards` vs `shard`
body: `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is tagged with `shards`, while `spans.buffer.flusher.produce`, `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` and the unhealthy metric all use `shard`. This makes dashboards and queries that group by shard inconsistent. In addition, `shard` carries a comma-joined list of shards in `main` but a single shard id in `_ensure_processes_alive`, so one tag key has two different value shapes.

title: Memory info is polled once per per-process buffer on every submit
body: `submit()` now loops over every per-process `SpansBuffer` and extends `memory_infos` with `buffer.get_memory_info()` for each one. That method appears to report on the whole Redis cluster rather than just the buffer's shards. If so, each submit issues N times the INFO calls, and `used` and `available` are both inflated by N. The ratio stays the same, so the result is correct but wasteful. The same applies to `record_stored_segments` per buffer. Query memory once, from a single buffer.

title: isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is False for spawn-context processes, so hung flushers are never killed
body: Processes are created with `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which is `SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` subclasses `BaseProcess`, not `multiprocessing.context.Process`, which is what `multiprocessing.Process` refers to. So `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is always False for real flusher processes. The original code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally; this PR guards it with that isinstance check, so `kill()` is now dead code. When a flusher is detected as hung, the old process keeps running while `_create_process_for_shards` starts a replacement on the same shards. The result is duplicate flushers on one shard (possible duplicate segments to Kafka), leaked processes, and eventually the MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS crash. The same check in `join()` (around line 346) means `terminate()` is never called either. Check against `multiprocessing.context.BaseProcess`, or use `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`.

title: Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
body: `test_basic` begins with `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`. The new `time.sleep(0.1)` ("Give flusher threads time to process after drift change") calls the patched function and does nothing. The test therefore still races: `step.join()` sets `stopped` immediately after the drift change, and the flusher thread may exit before flushing, making `(msg,) = messages` flaky. The extra `step.poll()` doesn't help either. Capture the real sleep before patching, or poll/wait until `messages` is non-empty with a timeout.

title: join() can break out of the loop and skip waiting for or terminating the remaining processes
body: In the new per-process join loop, once the deadline expires the code does `break`. This skips the wait and the `terminate()` for all remaining processes. The original code always attempted `terminate()` after the wait. With multiple processes, one slow process can consume the whole timeout and leave the others neither awaited nor terminated. They are only cleaned up if they are daemons and the parent exits. Iterate over all processes and terminate stragglers after the deadline instead of breaking.

title: Docstring claims one process per shard, but the number of processes is capped by max_processes
body: The class docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing." Actually `num_processes = min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` and shards are distributed round-robin, so processes can serve several shards. The CLI option `--flusher-processes` defaults to 1, so by default a single process handles all shards. The docstring misleads readers and operators about the default behavior.

title: Inconsistent metric tag keys (`shard` vs `shards`) and comma-joined shard lists as tag values
body: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `segment_size_bytes` are tagged with `shard`, but `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` uses `shards`. Dashboards and queries that group on one key will silently miss the other. The tag value is also a comma-joined list of shards (e.g. `0,4,8`), which changes with the process/shard mapping and creates new tag values on every assignment change. `flusher_unhealthy` uses a single-shard `shard` tag, so the same key now has different value formats across metrics.

title: submit() now makes per-process Redis calls on every message, with redundant memory-info queries
body: Before, `submit` called `record_stored_segments()` and `get_memory_info()` once on one buffer. Now it iterates all per-process buffers. Each buffer is built over a subset of shards but points at the same Redis cluster(s), so cluster-wide `get_memory_info()` is repeated N times and the results summed. The used/available ratio is unchanged, but Redis INFO round-trips on the consumer's main thread scale with the flusher process count, which defeats the goal of keeping the main thread minimal. Query memory once (e.g. via the main buffer) instead.

title: Unused `_create_process_for_shard` helper
body: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is never called. `_ensure_processes_alive` calls `_create_process_for_shards` directly. This is dead code and should be removed.

title: No validation of --flusher-processes; negative values crash SpanFlusher
body: `--flusher-processes` is a plain `int` with no lower bound. `0` silently falls back to one process per shard because of `max_processes or len(shards)`. A negative value makes `num_processes` negative, so `process_to_shards_map` is empty. The distribution loop then does `i % self.num_processes`, which is 0 for `-1` and raises `KeyError` on the empty map. Use `click.IntRange(min=1)`.

title: New test only checks process counts, not distribution, flush behavior or restart logic
body: `test_flusher_processes_limit` asserts `len(processes)==2` and that the total shard count is 4. It does not check that each shard appears in exactly one process or that spans from different shards are flushed. It also doesn't exercise `_ensure_processes_alive` (restart/kill) or the real spawn path, since it uses the threaded `produce_to_pipe` mode. The restart/kill regression (spawn `Process` not matching the `isinstance` check) therefore goes untested.

title: Strategy close() shuts down the factory-shared queue pool, which is reused after the first rebalance
body: `FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and passed to every `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` that `create_with_partitions` builds. Arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the current strategy on every partition revocation and then calls `create_with_partitions` again. `close()` and `join()` both call `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets `worker.shutdown = True`, calls `q.shutdown()` on every queue and joins the workers. After the first rebalance the replacement strategy is handed the same dead pool: the worker threads have exited and `queue.put` raises `ShutDown`. Combined with the broad `except` in `submit`, every later message is dropped and its offset is committed (see the next finding). The `OffsetTracker` is also shared across rebalances, so leftover offsets for revoked partitions can be committed later and rewind the group's progress. The pool needs to be owned by the factory and only shut down in `factory.shutdown()`, or be created per strategy instance, and the tracker should be reset for revoked partitions.

title: Any exception in submit() marks the offset completed, so failed enqueues are silently dropped and committed
body: The `except Exception` branch in `submit` calls `add_offset` and `complete_offset` for the message, which makes it immediately committable. That is fine for an undecodable payload. It is data loss when the failure is in `queue_pool.submit`, for example `queue.ShutDown` from a shut-down queue, or an error in `grouping_fn`. The message is never processed, its offset is committed past, and the only trace is a log line. Infrastructure failures should propagate, or the offset should not be completed, so the message is retried after a restart.

title: Queues are unbounded and poll() applies no backpressure, contrary to the class docstring
body: The strategy docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but each queue is `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `poll()` only emits a gauge. `submit` never raises `MessageRejected`, so the consumer keeps pulling from Kafka at full speed. If one queue is slow or stuck, committed offsets stall at the first outstanding offset, which is exactly the case the PR describes. Meanwhile every later message is decoded and held in memory, each with both the decoded result and the original message in `WorkItem`. A stuck worker therefore leads to unbounded memory growth and a large reprocessing burst on restart. Use bounded queues and reject or pause submission when the target queue is full.

title: Commit logic treats any gap in offsets as unprocessed and stalls commits permanently
body: `get_committable_offsets` walks `range(start, max_offset + 1)` and stops at the first offset that is not in `all_offsets`. Kafka partitions can legitimately have non-contiguous offsets (transaction markers, compacted topics, retention). The tracker only knows offsets it was given, so it cannot tell "never delivered" from "in flight". After such a gap, `highest_committable` never advances. Commits stop for that partition, and `all_offsets` and `outstanding` grow without bound. The tests (`test_offset_gaps_block_commits`, `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps`) enshrine this behaviour. Commit decisions should rely on the lowest outstanding offset (commit everything below it), not on contiguity of submitted offsets.

title: Kafka commit is invoked from a background thread while the main thread polls
body: `_commit_loop` runs in its own daemon thread and calls `commit_function`, which wraps the arroyo `commit` callable. That callable is wired to the `StreamProcessor` and its Kafka consumer, which stages and commits offsets and are not thread-safe. They are normally used only from the processor's run loop, the same thread that polls and handles assignment and revocation callbacks. Calling them concurrently from the commit thread risks racing with `poll`, assignment and revocation state, and committing partitions that were just revoked. The strategy should hand the committable offsets back to the main thread (for example, compute them in `poll()` and call `commit` there) instead of committing from a separate thread.

title: "Graceful" shutdown discards items still queued
body: `shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before calling `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. The worker loop checks `self.shutdown` at the top of each iteration, so each worker finishes only its current item and exits, leaving the rest of its queue unprocessed. `close()` also joins the commit thread before shutting down the pool, so work finished during shutdown is never committed. This does not lose offsets, because they simply stay uncommitted, but it contradicts the docstring and causes avoidable reprocessing. Either drain the queues (let `queue.ShutDown` end the workers) or fix the docstring.

title: Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its stated intent and is timing dependent
body: `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` is documented as "errors in processing don't block offset commits". The worker's `finally` completes the offset even when the processor raises, so both offsets 100 and 101 become committable at the next 1s commit tick. The assertion `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` requires that nothing was committed. It passes only if the test finishes before the commit thread's next tick, and fails if the loop straddles a tick. It therefore does not verify the documented behaviour and can flake. It should wait for the commit and assert that offset 102 (the next offset to read) is committed.

title: Probabilistic assertions in queue tests can flake
body: `test_stats_reporting` asserts `stats["total_items"] > 0` immediately after submitting, but three live workers may already have drained all 10 trivial items. `test_different_groups_distributed` (line 106) asserts that 20 string keys hit all 3 queues. Python's string hash is randomized per process, so there is a small chance (about 0.1%) that some queue is missed. Both tests should use deterministic setup, such as blocking the workers or choosing keys by computed queue index.

title: Strategy close()/terminate() shuts down the factory-owned queue pool, so messages are silently dropped and committed after the first rebalance
body: The `FixedQueuePool` and its `OffsetTracker` are created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and shared by every strategy from `create_with_partitions`. Arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the strategy at every rebalance, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`. That permanently shuts down all queues and workers. The factory still holds the dead pool (`queue_pool` is only set to None in `factory.shutdown()`), so the next strategy gets the same pool. Every `work_queue.put()` then raises `queue.ShutDown`. `submit()` catches `Exception`, marks the offset as added and completed, and moves on. The result is that after the first rebalance every message is dropped without being processed, and its offset is still committed. The tracker also keeps `last_committed`, `all_offsets` and `outstanding` for partitions that were revoked or reassigned. The strategy should not own the shared pool's lifecycle. Either build the pool and tracker per strategy, or leave them running in `close()` and only stop them from `factory.shutdown()`.

title: Offsets are committed from a background thread, but arroyo's commit callback and KafkaConsumer are not thread-safe
body: `_commit_loop` runs on its own daemon thread and calls `self.commit_function(...)`, which wraps arroyo's `commit` callback.
