body: The new null check was only added to getSubGroupsCount(), but getSubGroupsStream(String, Integer, Integer) at line 256, getSubGroupsStream(Integer, Integer) at line 262, and getSubGroupsStream(String, Boolean, Integer, Integer) at line 268 still call modelSupplier.get() and dereference the result. When a cached group is deleted concurrently, getGroupModel() returns null and these methods throw the same NPE. The fix should handle a null delegate consistently for all delegating methods or make the supplier throw a controlled exception.

title: Concurrency test asserts before reader thread finishes
body: The test starts the reader thread at line 139, deletes groups, sets deletedAll=true, and then immediately asserts that caughtExceptions is empty without joining the reader thread. The reader can still be inside the groups(...) call and can add an exception after the assertion, so an NPE regression can pass unnoticed. If a deletion throws before deletedAll is set, the non-daemon thread also keeps looping forever. Join the thread (or use an ExecutorService and shut it down in a finally block) before asserting.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator is not datetime-compatible but is used with order_by="-datetime"
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator overrides get_item_key/value_from_cursor with the integer-key logic from Paginator. The new endpoint path in src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_auditlogs.py (line 80) instantiates it with order_by="-datetime", so self.key is "datetime" and each item's value is a Python datetime. get_item_key then calls math.floor(datetime), which raises TypeError. Additionally, value_from_cursor returns the raw integer cursor value instead of converting it to a datetime like DateTimePaginator does, so any cursor with a value will compare a timestamp column to an integer in SQL and can fail with a Postgres operator error. The result is that any non-empty request with optimized_pagination=true by an eligible admin returns HTTP 500.

title: Negative-offset path relies on unsupported negative Django QuerySet slicing
body: When enable_advanced_features is true and cursor.offset is negative, the code sets start_offset = cursor.offset and then evaluates queryset[start_offset:stop] with a negative start. Django QuerySet slicing explicitly does not support negative indexing/slicing and raises ValueError/AssertionError (or otherwise generates invalid SQL OFFSET), so a crafted or generated negative cursor causes a 500. The adjacent comment claiming Django ORM handles negative slicing automatically is false. Additionally, the prev-page cleanup condition at line 891 compares len(results) to offset + limit + extra rather than to the number of rows actually fetched when start_offset differs from offset, so it would not correctly drop the extra row for negative offsets.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle datetime ordering used by audit logs
body: get_item_key() calls math.floor() or math.ceil() on the value of self.key. When OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint uses OptimizedCursorPaginator with order_by="-datetime", this value is a datetime, so math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError: must be real number, not datetime. Any non-empty audit-log page requested with optimized_pagination=true by an allowed user will return a 500 instead of results. Additionally, value_from_cursor() returns cursor.value directly rather than converting it to a datetime like DateTimePaginator does, so cursor comparisons are not correct for datetime keys.

title: Negative offset pagination slices a Django QuerySet with a negative start
body: When enable_advanced_features is true and cursor.offset < 0, start_offset is set to the negative cursor offset and the code executes queryset[start_offset:stop]. Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative indexes and raises ValueError ("Negative indexing is not supported."), so the advertised negative-offset reverse pagination cannot work. A request such as cursor=0:-1:0&optimized_pagination=true from an authorized user will produce a server error instead of a page or a clean 400.

title: No tests cover the new OptimizedCursorPaginator or the endpoint opt-in path
body: The PR adds a new paginator with custom slicing and offset behavior and a new endpoint feature flag but does not change any tests. This leaves both the datetime ordering failure and the negative slice failure uncovered, so CI would not catch a broken optimized-pagination flow.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot paginate the datetime field used by audit logs
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `int(math.floor(value) if self._is_asc(for_prev) else math.ceil(value))`, but OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint constructs it with `order_by="-datetime"`. For AuditLogEntry rows, `getattr(item, self.key)` is a datetime, and `math.floor`/`math.ceil` cannot convert a datetime to a number, so even the first page raises TypeError inside build_cursor. Any admin request with `optimized_pagination=true` will return HTTP 500. Additionally, value_from_cursor returns the raw integer cursor value instead of converting it back to a datetime for build_queryset, so subsequent pages would also be broken. The paginator must either be restricted to numeric keys or implement DateTimePaginator-style epoch conversion and reverse conversion.

title: Negative offset path passes a negative slice start to Django QuerySet
body: When `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code sets `start_offset = cursor.offset` (negative) and then evaluates `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative offsets and raises an exception. A privileged user can trigger this with a crafted cursor such as `cursor=0:-1:0` plus `optimized_pagination=true`, causing an unhandled 500. Offset should be validated as non-negative before building the slice.

title: No tests cover OptimizedCursorPaginator or the new endpoint flag
body: The PR adds a new paginator class and a new `optimized_pagination` request path but no tests. A basic test for the first page with `order_by="-datetime"` would catch the datetime conversion crash, and a crafted negative-offset cursor test would catch the negative slicing crash. Add paginator unit tests and endpoint tests for both the enabled and fallback paths.

title: Misleading comment about negative offset support
body: The added comment says the change allows negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios, but `self.offset = int(offset)` already accepted negative integers and this file adds no negative-aware behavior or validation. The comment describes behavior that is not implemented here and may mislead maintainers into believing negative offsets are safely supported.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot paginate datetime fields
body: The audit log endpoint uses this paginator with `order_by=-datetime`, so `self.key` is `datetime` and `get_item_key` receives a `datetime` object. It then calls `math.floor` or `math.ceil` on that datetime, which raises `TypeError` because datetime is not a real number. `DateTimePaginator` handles this by converting to a timestamp with `strftime('%s.%f') * multiplier`, but this class does not. Even if the key conversion were fixed, `value_from_cursor` returns the raw cursor value instead of converting it back to a datetime, so `build_queryset` would compare the datetime column with an integer. Consequence: any non-empty audit log request with `optimized_pagination=true` fails with a 500.

title: Negative offset slicing is not supported by Django QuerySet
body: When `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code sets `start_offset = cursor.offset` and evaluates `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative indices; the SQL compiler raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported`. The comment claims the ORM handles negative slicing automatically, but it does not. Since `Cursor.from_string` accepts negative offsets from API cursor strings, an authorized request with a crafted negative cursor and `optimized_pagination=true` will produce a 500, so the advertised negative-offset feature is broken.

title: Eviction can remove the root/segment span from a segment
body: The script trims the sorted set to 1000 members with `zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)`. `zpopmin` removes members with the smallest `end_timestamp_precise` scores and makes no exception for the segment root span. A root span can have one of the smallest end timestamps, for example when async child spans outlive the root span or multiple spans share the same timestamp. The current root span can also be inserted and immediately popped in the same script call. If the root span is dropped, the buffered segment is later flushed without its root span, yet the `has_root_span` flag may still be set because it is based on the HRS key or current `is_root_span` and is not cleared when the root payload is removed. Downstream receives a malformed segment whose `segment_id` no longer appears as a span.

title: ZUNIONSTORE default SUM corrupts scores on duplicate payloads
body: Both `zunionstore` calls use Redis's default aggregate SUM. If the same payload member already exists in the destination and source, for example when Kafka at-least-once delivery reprocesses the same span, its score is added to itself and `end_timestamp_precise` becomes roughly doubled. The score no longer represents the span's end time, which breaks the eviction order used by `zpopmin` and can cause the wrong spans to be evicted. The operation should be made idempotent for score preservation, such as using `AGGREGATE MIN` or another strategy.

title: Redirect traversal limit reduced from 10000 to 1000
body: The script now follows parent redirects only through `i = 0..1000`. If a segment tree has more than 1000 redirect levels, the loop exits without reaching the canonical root, but the script still writes `hset(main_redirect_key, span_id, set_span_id)` using the last intermediate ID. This can join the span to the wrong segment or split a segment that the previous 10000-iteration limit would have handled. If the limit is intentional for performance, the truncation case should be handled explicitly rather than writing a potentially incorrect redirect.

title: No test covers the new eviction behavior
body: The new insertion-time eviction logic in `add-buffer.lua` is not covered by tests. Existing buffer tests insert only a handful of spans, so they cannot catch regressions where `zpopmin` drops the root span, evicts the wrong spans, or the hardcoded limit diverges from `max_segment_spans`. A test that inserts more than 1000 spans and asserts the root span is preserved and the segment is capped correctly is needed.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot paginate datetime fields
body: OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint now allows OptimizedCursorPaginator with order_by="-datetime". That paginator is a copy of the numeric Paginator: get_item_key does math.floor/math.ceil on the attribute, and value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor number. AuditLogEntry.datetime is a datetime, so after fetching rows build_cursor calls math.floor(datetime) and raises TypeError; if a numeric cursor value is provided, build_queryset also compares a timestamp column to a number, causing a SQL operator error. The optimized audit-log pagination path is therefore broken for admins.

title: Negative offset slicing on Django QuerySet raises ValueError
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result takes the enable_advanced_features branch when cursor.offset < 0 and slices queryset[cursor.offset:stop]. Django QuerySets do not support negative slicing; this raises ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported. The audit log endpoint enables this flag, and cursor offsets are user-controlled strings parsed by Cursor.from_string, so a request with a negative cursor offset will produce a 500 instead of paginating.

title: Buffer storage changes from Redis set to sorted set without migration
body: process_spans now executes ZADD against span-buf:s:*, and _load_segment_data/add-buffer.lua now use ZSCAN/ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE. The previous version stored these keys as Redis sets with SADD/SUNIONSTORE. During a rolling deploy, keys written by the old code before the deploy still have type set; the first ZADD or ZCARD on those keys returns WRONGTYPE, failing span processing and causing retries until the old keys expire. There is no migration, key-format versioning, or cleanup for existing set-typed keys.

title: Eviction can remove the segment root span producing invalid segments
body: After merging, the script does zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000) to keep only 1000 spans. The lowest score is the oldest end_timestamp_precise, and the segment/root span is frequently the oldest member. If the root span is popped, the remaining set can contain child spans whose parent_span_id/segment_id refers to the removed root, but no span with span_id == segment_key; the flush path then emits a segment with segment_id set and no is_segment=True span. This silently corrupts/incompletes the segment. The cap is also hardcoded to 1000 while SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans defaults to 1001 and is now unused, so configuration cannot control this behavior.

title: No tests cover insertion-time eviction or sorted-set migration
body: The tests were updated to pass end_timestamp_precise, but no test exercises the new sorted-set eviction path: inserting >1000 spans, verifying the cap is applied, checking that the root span is not evicted, or verifying that old set-typed keys are migrated/handled. Given the data-integrity risks in this change, this behavior should be covered.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator does not support datetime ordering used by audit logs
body: The optimized path uses `OrderedCursorPaginator` with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `self.key` is the `datetime` field. However `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` in `src/sentry/api/paginator.py` does `math.floor(value)` / `math.ceil(value)` on the raw `datetime` object, which raises `TypeError`. Its `value_from_cursor` also returns the raw numeric cursor value instead of converting it to a datetime as `DateTimePaginator` does. As a result, any request with `optimized_pagination=true` will 500, making the new pagination path unusable.

title: Negative offset slicing is unsupported by Django QuerySet
body: When `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, this code sets `start_offset` to a negative number and executes `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django QuerySets do not support negative slicing and raise `TypeError: Negative indexing is not supported`. The comment above says Django handles negative slicing automatically, which is incorrect. A crafted cursor with a negative offset can therefore produce a 500 for users allowed to use the optimized paginator.

title: In-place change from Redis sets to sorted sets breaks existing span buffer keys
body: The span buffer previously stored `span-buf:s:*` keys as Redis sets via `SADD`, `SUNIONSTORE`, and `SSCAN`. This PR changes the same key space to sorted sets using `ZADD` here and `ZSCAN`/`ZUNIONSTORE` later. Existing keys created by the old code are Redis set values and have a TTL of up to `redis_ttl` (default 3600s). During a rolling deploy, new code will issue Z* commands against those set keys and Redis will return WRONGTYPE, causing ingestion/flushing failures and potential span loss until all old keys expire. A migration to a versioned key format, a drain step, or some compatibility handling is needed.

title: Redirect chain resolution limit reduced from 10000 to 1000
body: The loop resolving redirects via `HGET` now stops after 1000 iterations instead of 10000. The previous code explicitly noted that deeper segment trees may not be joined correctly when the limit is hit. Lowering the limit makes this failure reachable for traces with parent redirect chains deeper than 1000, causing spans to be associated with the wrong `set_key` and emitted in incorrect segments. If the reduction is intentional for performance or DoS protection, that tradeoff should be documented; otherwise this is a silent data-integrity regression for deep traces.

title: Error-focused query check uses substring matching and can transform transaction queries
body: `_is_error_focused_query` only checks whether `event.type:error` appears anywhere in the lowercased `query` URL parameter. This matches queries such as `!event.type:error` (selects non-error events) or `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` (mixed errors and transactions). When it returns true, `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` replaces `count()` with `upsampled_count()`, which emits `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. `sample_weight` is only valid for error events, so these queries can fail in Snuba or return incorrect counts. Parse the actual query filter structure instead of using a substring.

title: Upsampling decision is based on the URL query, not the actual query being executed
body: `_get_event_stats` has a `query` argument but calls `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` without passing it; the helper instead reads `request.GET['query']`. The dashboard split path calls `_get_event_stats` with derived queries such as `({query}) AND !event.type:transaction` and `({query}) AND event.type:transaction`. Therefore the upsampling transformation can be applied to a transaction-only derived query or skipped for an errors-only derived query based on the original URL query, causing `sum(sample_weight)` to run against an inappropriate event set. The decision should use the same query string passed to the dataset query builder.

title: Top events are ordered by raw count, not upsampled count
body: In the `top_events > 0` branch, only `timeseries_columns`/`y_axes` are transformed to `upsampled_count()`; `selected_columns` and `orderby` are still obtained from the original request, typically `-count()`. The top groups are therefore selected and ranked by raw event counts while their timeseries values are upsampled. If the allowlisted projects or events have different `sample_rate` values, the top-N groups can be the wrong groups. The orderby and count fields used for top-event selection should be transformed consistently.

title: Allowlist cache invalidation is never called
body: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined but no caller is added in this PR. Eligibility is cached for 60 seconds in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`. If a project is removed from `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`, existing cache entries can remain `True` for up to 60 seconds, causing queries for no-longer-allowlisted projects to be transformed to `sum(sample_weight)` even though `sample_weight` may not be valid for them. Wire this invalidation into the allowlist update path or remove the cache.

title: upsampled_count is exposed as a public SnQL function and bypasses allowlist/dataset checks
body: `upsampled_count` is added to `function_converter` without `private=True`. A client can therefore request `yAxis=upsampled_count()` directly; the endpoint will pass it to Snuba without going through `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` or the error-only query check. On a transaction query or a project that is not allowlisted, this still builds `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`, which can fail or produce invalid data. Mark it private/internal so only the server-side transformation can emit it.

title: Accidental submodule/gitlink file committed
body: The PR adds a file named `sentry-repo` containing `Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a`, i.e. a gitlink/submodule entry. This appears unrelated to the feature and can break clones or CI because there is no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry. Remove this accidental repository link before merging.

title: Error-focused query check uses naive substring matching
body: `_is_error_focused_query` returns True whenever the lowercased query string contains `event.type:error`. A negated query (`!event.type:error`), a mixed query (`event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`), or a quoted literal (`message:"event.type:error"`) all satisfy this check. For Discover, that makes `count()` get rewritten to `upsampled_count()`/`sum(sample_weight)` for rows that are not error events; transaction rows may not have meaningful sample_weight, leading to incorrect counts or Snuba errors. Parse the actual query terms (and handle negation/quotes) instead of substring matching.

title: Upsampling eligibility uses request query rather than executed query
body: `_get_event_stats` receives the actual `query` being executed, but `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` only inspects `request.GET["query"]` inside `_is_error_focused_query` for the Discover dataset. In `get_event_stats_factory`, dashboard widget discover-split paths call `_get_event_stats` with rewritten queries such as `errors_only_query` (`... AND !event.type:transaction`) or `transactions_only_query` (`... AND event.type:transaction`). The helper can therefore decide an error-only split is not error-focused (undercounting) or decide a transaction-only split is error-focused (applying sample_weight to transactions). Pass the actual `query` string to the eligibility helper or derive the dataset/event type from the query being executed.

title: Accidental submodule/gitlink committed
body: The PR adds a `sentry-repo` gitlink/submodule entry pointing at commit `a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a`. There is no related `.gitmodules` change and no code uses it; this looks accidental. Committing a submodule tracking the base commit can make clones fail or leave the working tree dirty and should be removed before merge.

title: Transaction event not flushed before Snuba query
body: In `test_error_upsampling_with_transaction_events`, a transaction is stored via `self.store_event(...)` after the setUp wait calls, but no `wait_for_event_count` is issued for it before the API request. Snuba indexing is asynchronous, so `data[0][1][0]["count"] == 1` can race and fail. Wait for the transaction to be indexed (for example `self.wait_for_event_count(self.project.id, 2)`) before querying.

title: Substring check misclassifies negated and mixed event.type queries
body: `_is_error_focused_query` lowercases the raw query string and checks for substring `'event.type:error'`. A discover query such as `!event.type:error` still contains that substring, so `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns true and the endpoint transforms `count()` into `upsampled_count()` for non-error/transaction data. Mixed queries that include both error and transaction predicates are also treated as error-only. This can silently produce wrong counts or invalid `sample_weight` references for non-error rows. The query should be parsed/tokenized or the check should use the actual event-type condition.

title: Upsampling decision is based on the original request, not the query actually executed
body: `_get_event_stats` computes `should_upsample` from `request.GET` via `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(...)`, but the dashboard-split factory later calls `_get_event_stats` with derived query strings such as `errors_only_query = f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction"` and `transactions_only_query = f"({query}) AND event.type:transaction"`. The helper never sees those synthetic query strings. An error-only split query can therefore run without upsampling when the original query did not explicitly contain `event.type:error`, and a transaction-only split query can be upsampled when the original query did. This produces inconsistent or incorrect counts in the split path. The eligibility check should receive the actual query string being executed.

title: upsampled_count is exposed as a public SnQL function
body: The new `SnQLFunction` for `upsampled_count` is added without `private=True`, unlike the adjacent private function. With Sentry's default `SnQLFunction` visibility, users can write `upsampled_count()` directly in searches, bypassing the `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` allowlist/dataset gate and applying a `sample_weight` aggregation on transactions, non-allowlisted projects, or other datasets. It should be marked `private=True` so it is only usable by the internal transform.

title: Accidental submodule gitlink added
body: The PR adds a new `sentry-repo` gitlink (`Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a`), which points back to the base commit. This looks like an unintended submodule addition and will change the repository's submodule state. It should be removed unless intentionally adding this submodule.

title: Error event data is paired with the wrong error IDs when nodestore omits missing events
body: `fetch_error_details` zips `error_ids` with `events.values()`. If any requested node is missing from nodestore, `get_multi` omits it, so subsequent values shift and are paired with the wrong error IDs. This can attach an error's title/message/timestamp to a different error ID in the generated summary request. Look up each event by the generated node ID instead, or zip against the node IDs/keys so missing entries preserve position.

title: Feature-flagged dashboard table path renders empty data and ignores query results
body: When `organization.features.includes('use-table-widget-visualization')` is true, this branch always renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{ data: [], meta: { fields: {}, units: {} } }} />` instead of passing the actual `result.data`, `result.meta`, `fields`, and field aliases. Any organization with this flag enabled will see blank table widgets, losing dashboard data. The feature branch should use the actual table results or remain disabled until implemented.

title: Mutual-exclusion validation for age/timestamp uses truthiness, so zero values bypass it
body: `validate_timestamp` checks `if self.initial_data.get("age")`, and `validate_age` checks `if self.initial_data.get("timestamp")`. Because `0` is falsy, a report with both `age=0` and `timestamp=0` is not rejected even though the field contract says age and timestamp must be mutually exclusive. Use an explicit presence check such as `if "age" in self.initial_data` / `if "timestamp" in self.initial_data` (or `is not None`).

title: Span samples analytics sends `Visualize` class instances while other effects send serialized objects
body: In the `queryType === 'samples'` effect, `trackAnalytics` is called with `visualizes: visualizes` instead of `visualizes.map(visualize => visualize.toJSON())`. The aggregate and traces effects in the same file serialize these objects before sending. Passing class instances can send non-plain objects or private fields to analytics instead of the expected `BaseVisualize` JSON shape, producing inconsistent or unusable analytics data for span samples.

title: Feature-flagged table visualization renders hardcoded empty data
body: In tableResultComponent, when organization.features includes 'use-table-widget-visualization', TableWidgetVisualization is rendered with columns={[]} and tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} instead of the actual result.data, result.meta, and fields. Any dashboard table widget for an organization with this feature enabled will show an empty table and ignore the query results.

title: Error details can be paired with the wrong error ID
body: fetch_error_details builds node_ids from error_ids and then zips error_ids with events.values(). Nodestore get_multi returns a mapping keyed by node id and may omit missing events or not preserve input order; zip pairs by position, so if a replay references an expired/deleted error, subsequent titles/messages/timestamps are attached to the wrong error_id and sent to the summarization endpoint. Use the returned mapping (for example iterate node_ids and look up events.get(node_id)) instead of positional zip.

title: Mutual-exclusivity validation uses truthiness instead of key presence
body: validate_timestamp checks `self.initial_data.get("age")`, and validate_age checks `self.initial_data.get("timestamp")`. age=0 is a valid report age but is falsy, so a report with age=0 and a timestamp is not rejected. Similarly, timestamp=0 with age is not rejected. Presence should be checked with `in self.initial_data` or `is not None`. Also both age and timestamp are currently optional, so reports with neither are accepted; if exactly one is required by the Reporting API specs this endpoint claims to support, add that validation.

title: Analytics event is recorded before feature-flag enforcement
body: analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...) runs before the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` feature check later in the endpoint. Requests that are not allowed and will return 404 are still counted as preprod artifact assemble events, inflating analytics and reporting usage from disabled organizations. Move the record call after the feature check or record a separate denied event.

title: Feature-flagged table widget path renders an empty table
body: When organization.features includes 'use-table-widget-visualization', tableResultComponent renders TableWidgetVisualization with hard-coded empty columns and tableData instead of the already-available fields, result.meta, and result.data (and the existing custom field renderers/header map). Any organization with this flag enabled gets blank dashboard table widgets regardless of the query results, so the flag cannot be safely enabled until this is wired to the real result.

title: Timestamp/age validation uses truthiness and never requires either field
body: Both age and timestamp are declared optional, and the mutual-exclusion checks use if self.initial_data.get("age") and if self.initial_data.get("timestamp"). If both are present with value 0, which is a valid timestamp under min_value=0, both checks are skipped and the report is accepted. Additionally, a report with neither field is accepted because no validate() enforces that one of age or timestamp is present. This allows malformed reports to be ingested and counted, and the existing tests only cover age=1 while timestamp is present.

title: Error IDs are paired with nodestore values by position
body: fetch_error_details builds node_ids from error_ids, calls nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids), then does zip(error_ids, events.values()). If get_multi omits missing nodes or returns values in a different order, the list is shifted and an error ID can be paired with another error's title/message, so the AI summary is built from incorrect error context. Look each node_id up in the returned mapping, for example events.get(node_id), instead of relying on positional alignment.

title: KeyError when installation metadata lacks sender
body: The user mismatch check dereferences integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] unconditionally. Integrations created by build_integration without state["sender"] (or existing rows from before sender was recorded) will have no "sender" key in metadata. On the reinstallation path where the Integration exists but no OrganizationIntegration exists, this raises KeyError and returns a 500/Internal Error instead of the GitHub integration failure page. Use integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login") and fail closed if it is missing.

title: GitHub user validation skipped when Integration does not exist yet
body: In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, when Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id) raises DoesNotExist, the code returns pipeline.next_step() before comparing pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") to the installation's sender. For a first-time installation (or if the installation webhook has not yet created the Integration row), pipeline.next_step() proceeds to build_integration and creates the integration without any sender-vs-OAuth-user check. An attacker who can reach the setup URL with a valid installation_id and complete OAuth as a different GitHub user can attach that installation to their Sentry organization. The check should not be conditional on the Integration row already existing; the sender must be obtained elsewhere or installation should fail closed.

title: get_user_info exceptions escape OAuthLoginView
body: The token-response parsing around safe_urlread is wrapped in try/except, but get_user_info(payload["access_token"]) is not. get_user_info makes an HTTP request to GitHub and can raise on network failures, timeouts, non-JSON bodies, or HTTP errors that it does not convert to a plain missing-login dict. Because dispatch does not catch these exceptions, a valid pipeline can return a 500 instead of rendering the installation failure page. Wrap get_user_info in an error-handling block and return error(request, self.active_organization) when the user cannot be fetched.

title: OAuth access token exchange omits redirect_uri
body: The authorization redirect includes redirect_uri (line 408), but the access token request only sends code, client_id, and client_secret. GitHub requires the same redirect_uri in the token request whenever it was supplied to /authorize. As written, GitHub will reject the exchange with bad_verification_code or redirect_uri_mismatch, causing real installations to fail. The test stub returns success without checking this parameter, so it is not caught.

title: GitHub identity is verified by mutable login instead of immutable user id
body: The pipeline binds only 'login' from get_user_info (lines 434-438) and later compares it to integration.metadata['sender']['login']. GitHub logins are mutable and may be released/reused after a rename, so a different account holding the old login could pass this validation. The sender payload also contains GitHub's immutable user id; compare ids (or at least bind and compare id) to ensure the OAuth-authorized user is actually the installer.

title: Existing integrations without sender metadata cause KeyError
body: The check directly accesses integration.metadata['sender']['login'] without guarding for missing or malformed sender data. build_integration only adds metadata['sender'] when state.get('sender') exists, and older integrations or integrations created through paths without sender will not have it. On re-install, GitHubInstallation raises KeyError and returns a 500 instead of rendering the installation error page.

title: Installation-not-found test no longer reaches the 404 path
body: The test uses state 'ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05', while the pipeline signature in these tests is '9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3'. With the new OAuthLoginView, this fails the state check before GitHubInstallation/build_integration runs, so the 404 response configured for /app/installations/{id} is never exercised. The test should use the valid pipeline state to actually cover the 'installation not found' behavior.

title: GitHub installer validation is skipped when Integration row does not exist yet
body: In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the first `except Integration.DoesNotExist` immediately returns `pipeline.next_step()`. This means if the GitHub installation webhook has not yet created the `Integration` row when the browser completes the Sentry setup pipeline (or if it never does), the sender check is bypassed completely. The pipeline then proceeds to `build_integration`, which uses the app JWT to fetch the installation by user-supplied `installation_id` and creates the Integration without `metadata.sender`. An attacker with a Sentry session and a known/guessed `installation_id` can therefore link a GitHub installation to their Sentry organization without being the GitHub user who installed it. The check should fail closed in this path, or `build_integration` should require/derive and store the installer and validate it.

title: Direct metadata indexing can raise KeyError for integrations without sender
body: `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes every active Integration has a `sender` dict with `login`. However `build_integration` only sets `metadata["sender"]` when `state.get("sender")` is truthy, and the pipeline state does not populate `sender`, so integrations created through this fallback (and older rows) may lack it. When this branch is reached for such an Integration, the request raises KeyError and returns a 500 instead of the intended installation error page. Use `.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and handle a missing value explicitly.

title: queued timestamp is evaluated once at import time
body: In a dataclass, default values are evaluated when the class is defined, not per instance. `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` stamps every `AssignmentSource` created without an explicit `queued` with the module import time. `from_integration` does not pass `queued`, so all sources created via inbound sync share a stale creation/queue timestamp; any future use for ordering, TTL, or queue delay will be wrong. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` after importing `field`.

title: Source guard suppresses outbound sync for all issues on the same integration
body: `should_sync` returns `False` whenever `sync_source.integration_id` matches the target integration. The outbound path enumerates every `ExternalIssue` linked to the group (`sync_group_assignee_outbound`), and a group can be linked to multiple issues in the same integration or across org integrations. An inbound assignment from one external issue will therefore skip outbound assignment to every other linked issue in that integration, not just the originating issue; those linked issue trackers silently remain out of sync. The source should carry a more specific identifier (for example, org integration id and external issue id) and the guard should compare narrowly.

title: Outbound task always passes new arguments to overridable integration methods
body: The task now calls `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)` and later `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)`, even when no source exists (the argument is `None`). The base `should_sync` signature was updated, but concrete integration subclasses that override the old one-argument `should_sync` or define `sync_assignee_outbound` without `assignment_source`/`**kwargs` were valid before and will now raise `TypeError`. This can break assignee outbound sync for those integrations on every task, not just the new inbound source path. All concrete overrides need to be updated or call sites made backward-compatible.

title: AssignmentSource queued default is evaluated at import time
body: The dataclass uses `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` as a default. Dataclass defaults are evaluated once when the class is defined, so every `AssignmentSource` created without an explicit `queued` value, including via `from_integration`, gets the module import timestamp rather than the time the assignment source was actually created. Any logic that later reads `queued` for ordering, expiry, or burst detection will see all sources with the same stale timestamp. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead.

title: New should_sync argument can break subclass overrides
body: The task now calls `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)` with a second positional argument. The base classes were updated to accept this argument, but `should_sync` is a polymorphic method that integrations commonly override with the previous one-argument signature to customize per-direction sync behavior. Any such override now raises `TypeError` on this line, causing assignee-sync tasks to crash instead of running. The same contract concern applies to the new `assignment_source` kwarg passed to `installation.sync_assignee_outbound` for overrides that do not accept `**kwargs`. All existing subclasses/overrides need to be audited and updated, or the call must be made backward-compatible.

title: Missing test for propagation to a different integration
body: The new suppression test only covers an assignment source whose integration matches the outbound target and asserts that outbound sync is not called. There is no test for the other required branch: when an inbound assignment comes from integration A and the group also has a linked issue for integration B, the outbound sync to B should still be scheduled. The same gap exists for inbound deassignment with a matching source. Without this coverage, an over-broad suppression would not be caught.

title: Same-integration suppression is overbroad for groups linked to multiple external issues
body: should_sync now returns False whenever the assignment source's integration_id matches the target organization integration. AssignmentSource only carries integration_id, not the specific external issue that triggered the inbound change. sync_assignee_outbound uses the same assignment_source_dict for every GroupLink for the group, so if a group is linked to multiple external issues in the same integration, an inbound assignment from one of those issues suppresses outbound sync to all of them. The other linked issues in that integration will remain on the old assignee. The source should include the originating external issue key and the check should suppress only that external issue, or otherwise avoid suppressing unrelated linked issues.

title: should_sync is now called with an extra argument that existing overrides may not accept
body: The task now calls installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source). Previously should_sync was defined and overridden as should_sync(self, attribute). Any integration subclass that still overrides should_sync with the old single-argument signature will raise TypeError when outbound assignee sync runs, causing the task to fail and retry for that integration. All overrides must be updated or the task must call this without a second positional argument unless it knows the installation can accept it.

title: AssignmentSource.queued uses import-time default instead of creation time
body: queued: datetime = timezone.now() is evaluated once when the module is imported. Every AssignmentSource constructed without an explicit queued argument, including from_integration, therefore gets the module import time rather than the time the source was created. If queued is intended to track when the assignment source was queued or generated, use field(default_factory=timezone.now) from dataclasses so each instance is stamped at construction time.

title: No regression test for same-source deassign suppression
body: There is a test for assign with a matching source integration, but the inbound deassign path also passes AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration) in sync_group_assignee_inbound and should be suppressed by the same should_sync check. A Jira unassign webhook would still echo back to Jira if this path regresses or fails to propagate the source. Add a test where GroupAssignee.objects.deassign is called with a matching AssignmentSource and assert sync_assignee_outbound is not called.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is abstract and cannot be instantiated
body: StatefulDetectorHandler declares abstract methods such as counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and the new build_occurrence_and_event_data. MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits it with only `pass` and implements none of them, so Python treats it as an abstract class. MetricAlertFire.detector_handler is set to this class, and Detector.detector_handler does `group_type.detector_handler(self)`; for a detector of this type, that will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler ...`. Implement the required methods or keep this handler as a concrete non-stateful stub that returns an empty dict.

title: Expected occurrence built with the wrong group key in TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe
body: `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, ...)` creates an occurrence whose fingerprint is `[<detector_id>:val1]`, but the evaluated call uses `expected_result.group_key`, which is `"group_key"` (and value 10). The actual result's occurrence will have fingerprint `[<detector_id>:group_key]`. Since IssueOccurrence is a dataclass and equality includes fingerprint, the assertion comparing the handler result to `expected_result` will fail. Build the expected occurrence with the same group_key/value that will be evaluated.

title: Occurrence produced before detector state is committed; retries can duplicate issues
body: `process_detectors` calls `create_issue_occurrence_from_result` for each result and only afterwards calls `handler.commit_state_updates()` (line 68). If the process crashes or the DB/Redis state commit fails after Kafka production, the dedupe/status state is not advanced. A retry of the same data packet will evaluate the same transition again and emit another occurrence/status change. This is now a real path because stateful detectors return non-None occurrence results. Commit state before producing, or make occurrence production idempotent/transactional.

title: Expected occurrences are built with wrong evaluated values
body: In `test_state_results_multi_group`, `group_2` is evaluated with value 10 from the data packet, but the expected occurrence is built with value 6. The mock `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` currently ignores `value`, so the test passes and does not verify that the hook receives the actual group value. Similar mismatches occur in `test_results_on_change` (evaluates 100, expects 6) and `test_dedupe` (evaluates 8, expects 6). Use the same value as the evaluation so the hook's value argument is covered.

title: evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: The docstring for `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` says it returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`, but the method now returns `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`. This can mislead implementers and callers about the contract.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is abstract and cannot be instantiated as a detector handler
body: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` now subclasses `StatefulDetectorHandler` but does not implement the abstract methods `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. It therefore remains an abstract class. `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler` references this class, and `Detector.detector_handler` will do `group_type.detector_handler(self)`. For any detector whose type is `metric_alert_fire`, processing will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler ...` instead of evaluating. Either implement the required methods or avoid registering this unsupported handler until it is implemented.

title: Evaluation crashes for stateful detectors with no counters
body: `get_state_data` only populates `counter_updates` inside `if self.counter_names:`. When a concrete `StatefulDetectorHandler` defines `counter_names = []` (a valid stateful detector with no Redis counters), `counter_updates` remains `{}`. The `DetectorStateData` construction then accesses `counter_updates[gk]` for each group key and raises `KeyError`, so evaluating any data packet with group values fails. Use `counter_updates.get(gk, {})` or default each group key to `{}`.

title: Evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: The docstring on `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` still says it returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`, but the method now returns a dict keyed by `DetectorGroupKey`. This is misleading for implementers and callers after the signature change.

title: Mock occurrence builder ignores `value`, so the new hook's value argument is not verified
body: `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` accepts `value: int` but never uses it when constructing the expected `IssueOccurrence` or `event_data`. Because expected results in tests such as `test_state_results`, `test_results_on_change`, and `test_dedupe` are built through this helper, those tests would pass even if `evaluate_group_key_value` passed the wrong value to `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. The helper should incorporate `value` into the expected occurrence/event data, or tests should assert the hook call received the correct value.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is abstract and cannot be instantiated
body: StatefulDetectorHandler declares abstract methods counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and build_occurrence_and_event_data. MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from it with pass and implements none of them, so it remains an abstract class. MetricAlertFire.detector_handler points to this abstract class, and Detector.detector_handler does group_type.detector_handler(self), so processing any Detector with type 'metric_alert_fire' will raise TypeError when trying to instantiate it. Either implement the stateful detector methods or keep this as a plain DetectorHandler stub until the stateful implementation exists.

title: StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: The evaluate method now returns dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult], but its docstring still says it returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult. This is misleading for implementers and callers and should be updated to match the new contract.

title: Test builds expected occurrence with the wrong group key
body: In TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe, the expected occurrence is built with group key 'val1', but the evaluate_group_key_value call under test uses group key 'group_key'. The handler's build_occurrence_and_event_data uses the group key it receives to build the fingerprint, so the actual occurrence fingerprint will be '<detector_id>:group_key' while the expected occurrence fingerprint is '<detector_id>:val1'. DetectorEvaluationResult equality compares the result field, so this assertion will fail. Build the expected occurrence with 'group_key' or change the evaluation to use 'val1' consistently.

title: get_monitor_environment_context returns the unmodified config, discarding schedule_type display value
body: The function creates `config = monitor_environment.monitor.config.copy()` and conditionally replaces `config["schedule_type"]` with `get_schedule_type_display()`, but the returned dict uses `"config": monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead of the modified `config`. The copy and mutation are therefore dead, and issue occurrence contexts will contain the raw `schedule_type` choice/enum value rather than the human-readable display value. This defeats the only reason for making the copy and gives consumers incorrect monitor config data.

title: Moved module-level symbols removed from mark_failed without re-export
body: This refactor removes `SimpleCheckIn`, `mark_failed_threshold`, `create_issue_platform_occurrence`, `get_failure_reason`, and `get_monitor_environment_context` from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` and moves them to other modules without leaving backwards-compatible re-exports in `mark_failed.py`. Any existing code or tests that import these names from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` will now fail with ImportError. All importers should be updated, or the old module should re-export the moved names.

title: Failure threshold can be reached without enough failed check-ins
body: When `failure_issue_threshold` is greater than 1, the code slices the most recent check-ins to that threshold length and only bails out when one of them is OK. If the monitor environment has fewer than `failure_issue_threshold` check-ins and none is OK (for example, the first check-in of a new monitor fails), `previous_checkins` can contain a single failure, the OK check is false, and the monitor is marked ERROR with an incident created. This defeats the configured consecutive-failure threshold and produces false incidents for new/sparse monitors. The code should require that the window contains the configured number of check-ins or explicitly count consecutive non-OK statuses before creating the incident.

title: Monitor context returns original config instead of adjusted copy
body: `get_monitor_environment_context()` creates `config = monitor_environment.monitor.config.copy()` and updates `config["schedule_type"]` to the schedule-type display value, but the returned dict uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` rather than `config`. The modified copy is never used, so the `schedule_type` display transformation is discarded and the original mutable config is passed into the occurrence context.

title: Monitor context returns original config instead of the modified copy
body: `get_monitor_environment_context` copies `monitor_environment.monitor.config` into `config` and, when `schedule_type` is present, replaces it with the display value. However the returned dict uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` on line 168, not the modified `config`. The copy and display conversion are dead code, so `schedule_type` is emitted as the raw stored value (for example an int/enum) instead of the intended display string in the occurrence context.

title: Incident can be triggered before reaching failure_issue_threshold
body: For `failure_issue_threshold > 1`, the code slices the latest `failure_issue_threshold` check-ins but does not verify that there actually are that many. On a new or sparse monitor, after the first failed check-in `previous_checkins` contains only that one failure; the `any(... == CheckInStatus.OK)` check is false, so the monitor is set to ERROR and an incident is created even though the configured consecutive-failure threshold has not been met. This defeats the user-configured threshold and can cause premature monitor alerts.

title: Spawned flusher processes are not killed before replacement
body: `self.mp_context` is `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")`, so the entries in `self.processes` are `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` objects. The top-level `multiprocessing.Process` is a different class on systems where the default context is not spawn, so `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` can be false for these spawned processes. In `_ensure_processes_alive`, a hung process is therefore not killed, but `_create_process_for_shards` still starts a replacement for the same shards. This leaves the old flusher alive and can cause two processes to flush/produce the same segments concurrently, leading to duplicate spans in Kafka. The same incorrect check in `join()` (line 346) also prevents spawned processes from being terminated on timeout. Check against `self.mp_context.Process` or `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` instead.

title: join() skips termination of remaining processes once timeout expires
body: In `join`, the loop checks `remaining_time <= 0` and then `break`s out of the entire process loop. If `next_step.join(timeout)` or waiting for an earlier flusher process consumes the whole deadline, later flusher processes are never waited on and never reach `process.terminate()`. Because `stopped` only requests a graceful shutdown, a stuck child can keep running after `join()` returns, leaking resources or continuing to produce during shutdown/rebalance. The loop should still terminate all remaining processes after the deadline expires, or calculate per-process timeouts differently.

title: Multi-process flusher test only checks process mapping, not flushing behavior
body: `test_flusher_processes_limit` verifies that `SpanFlusher` creates the expected number of processes and distributes shards, but it never submits spans, polls the pipeline, or asserts produced Kafka payloads. The actual behavior of multiple flusher processes sharing shards—flushing segments from Redis, producing to Kafka, and completing `done_flush_segments`—is not exercised, so a regression in the multiprocess flushing path would not be caught by this test. Add a functional test with spans on multiple partitions and assert the produced messages.

title: SpanFlusher.join can leave remaining flusher processes running after timeout
body: When `deadline` is not None and `remaining_time <= 0`, the loop breaks before calling `process.terminate()` on any later processes. Since `self.next_step.join(timeout)` may consume the entire timeout, this commonly skips all flusher processes. If a process is hung and does not observe `self.stopped`, it is never terminated, so old flusher processes can continue flushing and producing Kafka messages after the consumer has moved on. The timeout path should continue terminating all processes even after the deadline expires instead of breaking out of the loop.

title: Negative --flusher-processes crashes SpanFlusher initialization
body: The new `--flusher-processes` option is accepted as any int and `SpanFlusher` does not validate that `max_processes` is positive. If a negative value is supplied, `self.num_processes` becomes negative, so `range(self.num_processes)` is empty and `process_to_shards_map` has no keys. The shard distribution loop then computes `process_index = i % self.num_processes` and indexes the empty map, raising `KeyError` and preventing the consumer from starting. Add `click.IntRange(min=1)` or an explicit constructor check.

title: record_stored_segments is called on unused per-flusher buffers
body: `submit()` now calls `buffer.record_stored_segments()` on each `SpansBuffer` in `self.buffers`. Those buffers are created by `_create_process_for_shards` for the flusher processes and are never passed to `process_batch`/`process_spans`; spans are actually written through the original ingest-side buffer created in `ProcessSpansStrategyFactory.create_with_partitions`. The previous code recorded on that ingest-side buffer. Any segment counters or state accumulated by `process_spans` are no longer recorded, so stored-segment metrics can silently underreport or zero out.

title: New flusher_processes parameter inserted before produce_to_pipe breaks positional callers
body: `ProcessSpansStrategyFactory.__init__` now has `flusher_processes` as the sixth positional argument with `produce_to_pipe` seventh. Any existing caller that passed `produce_to_pipe` as the sixth positional argument will now bind that callable to `flusher_processes` and leave `produce_to_pipe` as `None`, silently disabling the pipe/test path or causing type/value errors. `SpanFlusher.__init__` has the same issue with `max_processes`. Prefer keyword-only for the new parameters or append them after existing parameters.

title: Negative flusher_processes disables flushing and backpressure silently
body: `max_processes` comes from the new `--flusher-processes` click option with `type=int` and no range validation. `SpanFlusher` first does `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, so `0` becomes "all shards", but a negative value survives to line 60 where `min(negative, len(shards))` returns a negative number. `range(negative)` then produces an empty `process_to_shards_map`, so no flusher processes or per-process buffers are created. `submit()` still accepts messages: the backpressure and Redis-memory checks iterate over empty `process_backpressure_since` and `self.buffers` collections, so spans continue to be written to Redis while nothing flushes them. This can fill Redis and lead to data loss/consumer failure. Add validation such as `click.IntRange(min=1)` and handle `0` explicitly.

title: join(timeout) can return while later flusher processes are still running
body: In `join`, after `next_step.join(timeout)` consumes the deadline, the loop over `self.processes` sees `remaining_time <= 0` and executes `break`, skipping termination for the current and all remaining processes. Only processes iterated before the deadline expires are terminated. Because `close()` intentionally leaves flusher processes running until `join()`, this can leave an old generation of flusher processes alive after rebalance, concurrently flushing shards that may now be assigned to a new consumer and producing duplicate buffered segments.

title: Inserting flusher_processes before produce_to_pipe breaks positional callers
body: `ProcessSpansStrategyFactory.__init__` previously accepted `produce_to_pipe` as the sixth positional argument. The new `flusher_processes` parameter is inserted before it, so any existing caller that constructs the factory with `produce_to_pipe` positionally now binds it to `flusher_processes`. The factory then passes the callable to `SpanFlusher` as `max_processes`, where `min(callable, int)` raises a `TypeError` during process count calculation. New parameters should be added after existing ones, or made keyword-only, to preserve the existing call contract.

title: Production multiprocessing flusher path is not tested
body: Both tests pass `produce_to_pipe=messages.append`, which makes `SpanFlusher._create_process_for_shards` create `threading.Thread` instances instead of the production `mp_context.Process` path with `run_with_initialized_sentry(SpanFlusher.main, shard_buffer)`. The new test only asserts that two thread objects are created and that shards are distributed; it does not submit spans or verify that flushing works across processes. As a result, multiprocess-specific behavior such as pickling the per-shard buffer, process restart/health handling, and `join`/terminate behavior in real spawned processes is not exercised.

title: OffsetTracker can commit past an offset gap after the prior offset is committed
body: In get_committable_offsets, start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset) treats every offset below min_offset as already accounted for. If a gap exists before min_offset, it is forgotten after the first commit because mark_committed removes all offsets <= the committed offset from all_offsets. For example, with completed offsets 100, 102, and 103, the first call commits 100 and removes it; the next call sees min_offset=102 and last_committed=100, so start=102, and it returns 103, committing past missing offset 101. This violates the class's gap-handling contract and can cause Kafka offsets to be skipped if such a gap ever occurs.

title: Unbounded queues provide no backpressure
body: Each work_queue is created as queue.Queue() with no maxsize. Since submit never blocks, a slow group or worker can accumulate an unbounded number of queued WorkItems and offset-tracking entries. The class docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but these queues never fill. Under sustained slowdown this can exhaust memory and take down the consumer instead of slowing Kafka consumption.

title: Shutdown exits workers before queued items are drained
body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True while work is still queued, then calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) and joins. OrderedQueueWorker.run checks self.shutdown at the top of its loop, so a worker that is between items exits immediately without draining queued WorkItems. A worker blocked on get() may also not be woken by Queue.shutdown(immediate=False), causing join(timeout=5.0) to return while the daemon thread remains blocked. The result is queued messages not processed on shutdown and leaked worker threads; those offsets will be reprocessed after restart, causing duplicate work.

title: Unbounded per-group queues remove backpressure and can exhaust memory
body: FixedQueuePool creates `queue.Queue()` without a maxsize, so each per-group queue is unbounded, and FixedQueuePool.submit uses a non-blocking `put`. A single slow subscription will keep all of its messages accumulating in that worker's queue while the main Arroyo loop continues polling and submitting. Contrary to the class docstring's 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', there is no backpressure; memory and OffsetTracker's all_offsets/outstanding sets grow without bound, risking OOM and a stalled consumer. Bound the queue or use blocking put with a timeout, and expose pressure metrics/backpressure.

title: Worker failure still marks offsets complete and commits them
body: In OrderedQueueWorker.run, exceptions from result_processor are caught and logged, then the finally block at line 149 unconditionally calls complete_offset. The commit loop later commits completed offsets, so a failed result is treated as processed and will not be retried or sent to DLQ. This violates the strategy's stated guarantee 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and can silently drop results when result_processor raises. Complete offsets only in the success path; failures should leave the offset outstanding or be explicitly routed to a retry/DLQ path.

title: Shutdown flag can leave queued work unprocessed
body: OrderedQueueWorker.run checks `while not self.shutdown` at the top of the loop. FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets `worker.shutdown = True` before draining queues. If a worker finishes an item and returns to the top while its queue still has items, it exits without calling get() again, so queued WorkItems and their offsets are never processed by this pool. This contradicts the graceful drain implied by `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` and can cause in-flight backlog to be dropped until the consumer is restarted. The shutdown flag should not be set before queue drain, or the worker should drain until queue.ShutDown before exiting.

title: Negative max_workers creates an empty queue pool that crashes on submit
body: `num_queues=max_workers or 20` passes negative values through (e.g. `--max-workers=-1`). FixedQueuePool.__init__ then `range(-1)` creates no queues/workers, and the first `submit` does `self.queues[hash(group_key) % -1]`, which indexes 0 and raises IndexError. Validate `max_workers > 0` or normalize non-positive values.

title: Shutdown stops workers before queued work is drained
body: `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` sets each worker's `shutdown` flag before calling `Queue.shutdown(immediate=False)`. `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` checks `while not self.shutdown` at the top of every loop, so a worker that finishes its current item will exit immediately instead of dequeuing the remaining items already in its queue. Since there is exactly one worker per queue, queued work is left unprocessed. This makes the advertised graceful shutdown incorrect and can cause those messages to be delayed or reprocessed after restart/rebalance.

title: Result processor exceptions still mark offsets complete and get committed
body: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run()`, exceptions from `self.result_processor` are caught and logged, but the `finally` block unconditionally calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)`. The commit loop only checks whether offsets are outstanding, so an offset whose processing raised will later be committed as successfully processed. This contradicts the class guarantee that only successful work is committed and can silently drop a message if a result processor ever raises transiently.

title: Shared FixedQueuePool becomes unusable after strategy close and can drop messages on rebalance
body: `ResultsStrategyFactory` creates one `FixedQueuePool` in `__init__`, and each `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` receives that same pool. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which shuts down the queues and workers, but `factory.queue_pool` remains non-None. If Arroyo creates a new strategy from the same factory after a rebalance, the new strategy reuses the shut-down pool. `Queue.put()` on a shut-down queue raises `queue.ShutDown`; `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` catches all exceptions and marks the offset complete, so messages for the new assignment can be silently dropped.

title: Unbounded queues provide no backpressure and can exhaust memory
body: `FixedQueuePool.__init__` creates each work queue with `queue.Queue()` using the default `maxsize=0`, meaning queues are unbounded. The class doc says there is "natural backpressure when queues fill up," but these queues never fill. If workers process more slowly than the consumer submits, both the queues and the offset-tracking sets grow without bound, eventually risking memory exhaustion or very large commit-lag.

title: OffsetTracker forgets missing offsets after earlier prefix is committed
body: After `mark_committed()` removes offsets <= the committed offset, `get_committable_offsets()` uses `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)`. If offsets 100, 102, and 103 are recorded and 100 is committed, `all_offsets` becomes `{102, 103}`. The next scan starts at 102, so it can commit 103 after 102 and 103 complete even though 101 was never added or processed. This violates the stated rule that all prior offsets must be processed and can skip a genuinely missing message if a real offset gap exists.

title: Concurrent partition insertion can race with commit-loop key iteration
body: `get_committable_offsets()` iterates over `list(self.all_offsets.keys())` without a global lock. `add_offset()` can concurrently insert a new partition key into the same defaultdict. Mutating a dict while iterating over its keys can raise `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration` (or otherwise produce an inconsistent snapshot), which would interrupt that commit-loop pass. Per-partition locks do not protect the outer key set.

title: One-time backup code can be replayed in concurrent login attempts
body: The backup code verification and invalidation are not atomic. Two concurrent login requests using the same backup code can both pass the `indexOf` check (line 144) before either updates the database (line 149). Both would then set the same index to null and update the user record, effectively allowing the same one-time code to authenticate multiple sessions. An attacker who obtains a valid backup code (e.g., via shoulder surfing) could exploit this race to gain multiple valid sessions.

title: `onEnable` callback is not fired immediately after enabling 2FA
body: In `handleEnable`, after a successful enable API call (response.status === 200), the code only sets the step to `DisplayBackupCodes` and does not call `onEnable`. Previously, `onEnable` was invoked immediately to notify the parent that 2FA was enabled. Now `onEnable` is only called when the user clicks the 'close' button on the backup codes screen. If the user dismisses the dialog by clicking outside, pressing Escape, or using any other close mechanism (which triggers `onOpenChange`), `onEnable` is never called, leaving the parent component (e.g., the settings page) in a stale state where 2FA appears disabled until a refresh.

title: Object URL from Blob is not revoked on modal reset or unmount
body: In `handleSetup`, a Blob URL is created with `URL.createObjectURL(textBlob)` and stored in `backupCodesUrl`. While the code revokes the previous URL before creating a new one, it never revokes the URL when the component is unmounted or when `resetState` is called (e.g., on cancel or close). This causes a memory leak of the object URL, especially if a user repeatedly starts and cancels the 2FA setup flow.

title: Component is named `TwoFactor` instead of `BackupCode`
body: The default export function is named `TwoFactor`, but the file and its purpose are for entering a backup code. This is likely a copy-paste error that will cause confusion during imports and debugging, and it violates the principle of least surprise for maintainers.

title: No tests for backup code login or disabling 2FA with backup code
body: The PR introduces backup code functionality for both login and disabling 2FA, but the only added tests cover displaying, downloading, and copying the codes during setup. There are no tests that verify a backup code can be used to log in, that it is invalidated after use, or that it can be used to disable 2FA. Given the security-sensitive nature of one-time backup codes, missing tests for the core flows increase the risk of regressions.

title: Backup code reuse race condition
body: In the authorize callback, backup code consumption is not atomic. The code reads the user's backupCodes, finds the code, sets it to null, and updates the DB. Two concurrent login requests using the same valid backup code can both read the same backupCodes array before either update commits, so both will pass the `indexOf` check and both log in. This defeats the one-time use guarantee of backup codes. Use a conditional update (e.g., updateMany with a filter on the backupCodes value, or a transaction with row lock) to ensure each code is consumed exactly once.

title: Download button triggers form submission
body: The download button is rendered inside the form as ``. The Button's default type is "submit" and there is no `onClick` handler that calls `preventDefault`. Clicking it will submit the surrounding form (which calls `handleEnable` with the still-registered `totpCode`), in addition to the anchor's download navigation. This can cause a second `/enable` API request after 2FA has already been enabled, producing an error or unintended side effects. The Button should have `type="button"` or an `onClick={(e) => e.preventDefault()}`.

title: Backup code option not available for OAuth/SSO 2FA flow
body: When `totpEmail` is present (i.e., the user is in the 2FA challenge after an OAuth/SSO login), the footer renders `ExternalTotpFooter`, which only contains a cancel button. There is no "Lost access" button to switch to the backup code input, even though the `authorize` callback in `next-auth-options.ts` supports backup codes for any user with `twoFactorEnabled`. Users who log in via Google/SAML and have 2FA enabled cannot use their backup codes if they lose access to their authenticator. The backup code option should be available in this flow as well.

title: Component name is wrong
body: The exported component is named `TwoFactor` although this file implements the backup code input field. This is misleading and may confuse maintainers. Rename it to `BackupCode` to match the file and usage.

title: Backup code can be replayed due to non-atomic update
body: In the backup code login branch, the code decrypts the stored backupCodes array, finds the matched code with indexOf, sets backupCodes[index] = null, and then updates the user record with the modified array. Because there is no transaction or conditional update (e.g., checking that the code is still present before writing), two concurrent login attempts using the same backup code can both pass the indexOf check and both write the modified array. This allows a single-use backup code to be used more than once, defeating its security purpose.

title: onEnable not called if modal closed after successful enable
body: After the TOTP code is verified, handleEnable sets the step to DisplayBackupCodes instead of calling onEnable. The onEnable callback is only invoked when the user clicks the 'Close' button in the backup codes step. If the user dismisses the modal by clicking outside, pressing Escape, or via the close X, the Dialog's onOpenChange fires but onEnable is never called. As a result, the parent component's state (e.g., the 2FA toggle switch) remains out of sync with the server, showing 2FA as disabled even though it has been successfully enabled.

title: No end-to-end test for backup code login or disable
body: The PR adds backup code functionality but the only e2e tests added verify the download, copy, and close actions on the backup codes screen. There is no test that actually logs in using a backup code or disables 2FA via a backup code, despite the PR description claiming these are supported. The TODO comment in the test file acknowledges this gap. Core authentication behavior with backup codes remains unverified by automated tests.

title: Exported component is misnamed TwoFactor
body: The default export of BackupCode.tsx is declared as `function TwoFactor({ center = true })`, which is a copy-paste error from the TOTP component. While it does not affect functionality, it is misleading and may cause confusion during maintenance or debugging.

title: Meet fallback dereferences undefined destinationCalendar
body: `evt.destinationCalendar` is now `DestinationCalendar[] | null | undefined`. Here `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is undefined when no destination calendar exists, but the condition immediately reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration`. Any booking with `location === MeetLocationType` and no destination calendar throws a TypeError instead of falling back to daily video.

title: Team destination calendars are not added when organizer destination is null
body: `evt.destinationCalendar` is initialized to `null` when neither the event type nor organizer has a destination calendar. The later `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is a no-op for `null`, so in a collective event where the organizer has no selected destination but hosts do, all host `teamDestinationCalendars` are dropped. EventManager then falls back to the organizer's first connected calendar and host calendars never get the event. Initialize to an array or handle null explicitly.

title: Update/delete fallback can never find destination calendar
body: In the fallback expression `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`, `externalCalendarId` is only falsy when the else branch runs, so the predicate always compares against null/undefined and the find returns undefined. The previous implementation used `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. As a result, updating (and similarly deleting, line 317) an existing event without an `externalCalendarId` reference passes `undefined` as the Google calendar ID instead of the stored destination calendar, causing API failures or the wrong calendar (delete falls back to primary).

title: Hangout link patch uses undefined calendarId after primary fallback
body: `calendar.events.insert` uses `selectedCalendar || "primary"`, but the follow-up `calendar.events.patch` uses `selectedCalendar` directly. When no destination matches the credential and creation succeeded on the primary calendar, `selectedCalendar` is undefined, so the patch to add the hangout link is made with an undefined calendarId and fails.

title: Collective calendar events use first host's calendar as organizer for every credential
body: In `createEvent` (and `updateEvent` line 228), `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is always the first element of `calEventRaw.destinationCalendar`, even though `selectedCalendar` is correctly looked up by `credentialId`. For a collective event, when the manager creates an event in a non-first host's Google calendar, the organizer attendee email is still set to the first host's `externalId`. The event can be owned by/attributed to the wrong Google account. It should look up the destination whose `credentialId` matches the current credential.

title: Required credentialId contract is not honored by most calendar services
body: The `Calendar` interface now requires `createEvent(event, credentialId)`, and EventManager will call each destination with its credential. However the calendar services changed in this PR (Office365, Lark, BaseCalendarService/CalDAV, and likely other app-store calendars) still choose `[mainHostDestinationCalendar]` and ignore `credentialId`. They will always create/update in the first destination in the array, so multi-host collective bookings still send non-first hosts' calendar events to the wrong calendar. Making the new argument mandatory without updating all implementations masks the broken behavior.

title: Recurring cancellation deletes only first calendar reference for every host
body: In the recurring branch, for each `reference` in `bookingCalendarReference`, the code loops over all calendar credentials but inside each updated booking it always uses `updBooking.references.find((ref) => ref.type.includes("_calendar"))`.
