The code treats any non-nil error as a cache miss and proceeds to getIdentityPermissions, which will perform the same DB/identity lookup again. On transient DB errors this doubles load and can hide the underlying failure from logs. Distinguish errors.Is(err, cache.ErrNotFound) from other errors and return immediately for real errors.

title: Delete action missing from alert list view
body: The condition `{canDelete && rulerRule && (` requires `rulerRule` to be truthy. In the new alert list view, `GrafanaRuleListItem` passes only `promRule` to `RuleActionsButtons`, so `rulerRule` is always `undefined`. Even though `canDelete` is correctly computed as true using `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`, the Delete menu item will never render, making it impossible for users to delete Grafana-managed rules from the alert list. This is a regression from the previous behavior where the ruler rule was always available.

title: Pause action missing from alert list view
body: The condition `{canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) && groupIdentifier.groupOrigin === 'grafana' && (` depends on `rulerRule`. In the new alert list view, `rulerRule` is `undefined` because only `promRule` is provided. Consequently, even when `canPause` is true via `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`, the Pause menu item is never shown, preventing users from pausing/unpausing Grafana-managed rules from the list.

title: Federated rule groups become editable/deletable
body: The deprecated `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities` and no longer checks `isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`. The new implementation sets `isFederated = false` unconditionally (line 244). This means for external (e.g., Mimir) federated rule groups, actions like Update and Delete will be reported as supported and allowed, potentially allowing users to edit or delete federated rules that should be immutable. This is a security/authorization regression for components that still use `useAlertRuleAbility`.

title: List view still invokes ruler ability hook with undefined rule
body: `RuleActionsButtons` always calls `useRulerRuleAbility(rule, groupIdentifier, AlertRuleAction.Update)` even when `rule` (RulerRuleDTO) is `undefined` in the new list view. This hook eventually calls `useIsRuleEditable(rulesSourceName, undefined)`, which may still trigger ruler API requests (e.g., to determine ruler availability). Since the PR aims to remove all ruler API requests from the alert list, this undermines the performance improvement. Consider using a skip mechanism for the ruler hook when only `promRule` is available.

title: Missing `key` prop on list items can cause React state leakage between rules
body: In the `rules.map` call, the `<GrafanaRuleListItem>` is rendered without a `key` prop. This component contains stateful children (`RuleActionsButtons` with delete modal and silence drawer). Without a stable key, React may reuse component instances when the list changes (filtering, pagination, re-fetch), leading to state (e.g., an open delete confirmation) showing for the wrong rule or being lost. This is a regression from the previous version where `key={key}` was provided.

title: Delete menu item won't appear for Grafana rules in list view
body: The condition `{canDelete && rulerRule && (...)}` requires `rulerRule` to be present. In the new list view, `rulerRule` is `undefined` because ruler API calls have been removed. Even though `canDelete` may be true based on `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`, the delete option will never render, preventing users from deleting Grafana managed rules from the list. The `handleDelete` callbacks no longer use `rulerRule`, so the condition should be changed to `canDelete && (...)`.

title: Pause menu item won't appear for Grafana rules in list view
body: The pause menu item is gated by `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`, but in the list view `rulerRule` is undefined. Although `canPause` may be true from `grafanaPauseAbility`, the item is not rendered, making pause unavailable from the list. This is likely an oversight given the PR's goal to remove ruler dependencies from the list view; either the pause component needs to accept a `GrafanaPromRuleDTO`, or the condition should be revisited.

title: Missing React key on GrafanaRuleListItem
body: In the rules.map, the GrafanaRuleListItem branch does not receive the `key` prop that is computed for each rule. The `key` variable is passed to DataSourceRuleLoader and UnknownRuleListItem, but omitted here. This causes React to warn about missing keys and can lead to incorrect DOM reuse and state loss when the list updates or reorders.

title: Delete action hidden for Grafana rules in list view
body: The condition for rendering the Delete menu item is `{canDelete && rulerRule && (` but in the alert list view the `rulerRule` prop is undefined because ruler API requests have been removed. `canDelete` may be true based on the new `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`, but the `rulerRule &&` check prevents the Delete item from ever appearing. As a result, users cannot delete Grafana-managed rules from the alert list view, which is a regression from the previous behavior.

title: Pause action hidden for Grafana rules in list view
body: The pause menu item is only rendered when `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` is true. In the alert list view, `rulerRule` is undefined, so even if `canPause` is true via the Grafana Prometheus rule abilities, the pause item is never shown. Users lose the ability to pause/unpause Grafana-managed rules from the list view.

title: Silence drawer never opens for Grafana rules in list view
body: The SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer is only rendered when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true, but in the alert list view the `rule` prop (rulerRule) is undefined. Clicking "Silence notifications" sets `showSilenceDrawer` to true, but the drawer component does not mount because the condition is false. Therefore, the silence action is broken for Grafana-managed rules in the new list view.

title: Transient Creating/Deleting states are no longer shown
body: The component previously fetched both ruler and Prometheus rule groups and displayed rules that existed in only one of the sources as "Creating" or "Deleting" operation items. After this change, only rules present in the Prometheus response are rendered. Rules in the process of being created (exist only in ruler) or deleted (exist only in Prometheus) disappear from the list entirely, causing a brief but user-visible gap and lack of feedback during rule lifecycle transitions.

title: Lost returnTo query parameter in rule detail link
body: The previous GrafanaRuleListItem included a `returnTo` query parameter built with `createReturnTo()` when creating the view link (`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view?returnTo=...`). The new component constructs the href with only the path, omitting `returnTo`. This means that when a user navigates from a filtered alert list to a rule detail view and then uses the back navigation, they may lose the filter and pagination state they came from.

title: Labels may be undefined and cause rendering issues
body: The component destructures `labels` from the Prometheus rule DTO and passes it to `commonProps.labels` without a fallback. In the old implementation, `labels` defaulted to `{}`. If a rule has no labels (the field is optional in `GrafanaPromRuleDTO`), `labels` will be `undefined`, and downstream components that expect a `Labels` object may throw or render incorrectly. This can happen for rules without labels.

title: Double interpolation of queries in shard splitting path
body: runShardSplitQuery now calls applyTemplateVariables on each query at line 52, but later, when it invokes runSplitQuery (line 163), runSplitQuery also applies applyTemplateVariables (querySplitting.ts line 299). This causes every query to be interpolated twice. In particular, ad hoc filters (request.filters) are applied twice, leading to duplicated filter matchers and invalid Loki expressions. This also affects any non-idempotent interpolation. The fix is to interpolate only once: either remove interpolation from runShardSplitQuery and rely on runSplitQuery, or add a flag to runSplitQuery to skip interpolation when targets are already interpolated.

title: Interpolation before querySupportsSplitting bypasses $__range detection
body: The new .map() call interpolates each query before partition(queries, ...) on line 300. querySupportsSplitting (line 282) uses isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) to identify queries containing $__range and avoid splitting them. After interpolation, $__range is replaced with a concrete duration (e.g., 2d), so isQueryWithRangeVariable no longer detects it, and such queries are split despite the explicit comment explaining why they should not be. This produces incorrect subqueries with the full range baked into each split interval. The check should be performed on the original query.expr before interpolation, or the raw expr must be preserved for this decision.

title: RequestSupportsSharding check bypassed for $__range due to early interpolation
body: Like in querySplitting, runShardSplitQuery now interpolates queries at line 52 before splitQueriesByStreamShard is called on line 54. Inside splitQueriesByStreamShard, groupTargetsByQueryType calls requestSupportsSharding (line 243), which likely checks for $__range via isQueryWithRangeVariable. Because the expression has been interpolated, $__range is no longer present, so queries that should not be sharded are incorrectly considered shardable. This can lead to shard splitting of queries with range variables, producing wrong results. The raw expression must be used for the sharding eligibility check.

title: Missing tests for double interpolation and range variable bypass
body: The new interpolation tests use mock replace functions that are idempotent for the specific variables, so they do not reveal double interpolation (especially duplicate ad hoc filters) or the fact that $__range detection is bypassed after interpolation. Tests should cover a query with $__range to ensure it is not split, and a query with ad hoc filters to verify filters are applied only once. Without these, the regressions introduced by this PR may go unnoticed.

title: Interpolation before $__range check causes incorrect splitting
body: The queries are interpolated with `applyTemplateVariables` before `querySupportsSplitting` is evaluated. `querySupportsSplitting` checks `!isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)`, but after interpolation, `$__range` is replaced with a concrete value, so the check no longer detects it and the query is incorrectly split. This can yield wrong results because the original comment states that such queries must not be split since `$__range` is interpolated on the backend with the split time range.

title: Redundant interpolation of already-interpolated queries
body: In `runShardSplitQuery`, queries are interpolated at lines 49-52 and then passed to `splitQueriesByStreamShard`. Inside that function, for each shard group, `runSplitQuery` is called (line 163) which will again interpolate the targets (querySplitting.ts line 299). This double interpolation is redundant and may cause performance overhead, especially with many shards, and could lead to unexpected behavior if interpolation is not idempotent or has side effects.

title: Possible mutation of request targets if applyTemplateVariables mutates in place
body: The `.map((query) => datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, ...))` passes the original query objects. If `applyTemplateVariables` mutates the query (as the mocks in tests do), the original `request.targets` are mutated, which can affect other consumers of the request object, including tracking (`trackGroupedQueries`) or subsequent calls. The implementation should ensure a new object is returned, or the mapping should clone the query before interpolation.

title: Interpolating before split-support check defeats $__range split protection
body: `applyTemplateVariables` is called before `partition(queries, ... querySupportsSplitting)`. `querySupportsSplitting` deliberately excludes queries containing `$__range` via `isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)` because split sub-requests would otherwise use the full range duration rather than the sub-range. After frontend interpolation, any `$__range` token in the expression is replaced with the full request range duration, so `isQueryWithRangeVariable` no longer sees it and the query is split, producing incorrect results for each sub-request. The check must use the original (pre-interpolation) expression or preserve the raw expression for this test.

title: Sharded queries are template-interpolated twice
body: `runShardSplitQuery` now interpolates each target via `applyTemplateVariables` and passes the already interpolated `queries` to `splitQueriesByStreamShard`. Inside that function, each shard group is executed via `runSplitQuery`, which on line 299 of querySplitting.ts again applies `applyTemplateVariables` to its targets. This double interpolation is redundant and can produce incorrect expressions if a template variable resolves to a string containing another variable placeholder. The test change to expect `applyTemplateVariables` to be called 5 times for a single target confirms this behavior. Interpolation should happen only once or `runSplitQuery` should skip interpolation when targets are already interpolated.

title: Filtering by expr before interpolation can include queries that become empty
body: Previously `interpolateVariablesInQueries` was called before `.filter((query) => query.expr)`, so a query whose expression contained a template variable that resolved to an empty string was filtered out. Now filtering occurs before `applyTemplateVariables`; if interpolation yields an empty `expr`, the query remains in the target list and will be sent to Loki as an empty expression, likely causing a query error. The filter should be applied after interpolation or additionally check the interpolated expression.

title: Adding FromContext to Logger interface breaks all implementations not updated
body: The Logger interface gains a new method, FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger. This is a breaking change for any type implementing this interface. The PR updates only grafanaInfraLogWrapper and TestLogger. If the repository contains other implementations (e.g., additional test fakes or alternative loggers), they will fail to compile. All implementations must be updated, or a default adapter should be provided.

title: FromContext type assertion can silently drop contextual attributes
body: The method asserts that d.l.FromContext(ctx) returns a *log.ConcreteLogger. If the underlying FromContext returns a different concrete type (e.g., a wrapper or decorated logger), the assertion fails and the code falls back to d.New(), which discards all context attributes. Consequently, log entries produced by LoggerMiddleware that rely on FromContext may lose pluginId, endpoint, dsName, etc. A more robust approach should preserve attributes even if the returned logger type differs.

title: New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no unit tests
body: The newly added ContextualLoggerMiddleware is responsible for enriching the request context with plugin and request details for several endpoints. There are no tests verifying that the context passed to the next middleware contains the expected attributes, or that the middleware correctly passes through unchanged for stream endpoints. This leaves a significant behavior change untested.

title: LoggerMiddleware change to use FromContext is not covered by tests
body: LoggerMiddleware now uses m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...) instead of directly logging with m.logger and manually appended fields such as pluginId, endpoint, uname, traceID, dsName, and dsUID. No tests were updated or added to verify that these fields are still present when the ContextualLoggerMiddleware is in the chain, nor that logging still works when the middleware is used without the contextual logger.

title: Logger name still says 'plugin.instrumentation' after rename
body: The logger passed to NewLoggerMiddleware is still created with log.New("plugin.instrumentation"). Since the PR renames instrumentation to metrics and separates contextual logging, this logger name is now misleading. Consider renaming it to something like "plugin.logger" or "plugin.request" to reflect its actual purpose.

title: Test function name not updated after middleware rename
body: The test function is still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware, while the middleware type and constructor have been renamed to MetricsMiddleware. Renaming the test function to TestMetricsMiddleware would improve consistency and avoid confusion.

title: Adding FromContext to Logger interface is a breaking change
body: The Logger interface now requires a FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger method. Any type implementing this interface (outside the two modified implementations) will fail to compile until updated. This includes potential internal implementations not shown in the diff, as well as external packages that may rely on this interface. The PR should update all implementations in the repository or provide a compatibility path.

title: traceID is no longer logged in plugin request logs
body: The previous version of logRequest included traceID in logParams when traceID was non-empty (via tracing.TraceIDFromContext). After moving contextual logging to a separate middleware, the traceID block was removed and is not re-added by ContextualLoggerMiddleware. This loses trace correlation in the 'Plugin Request Completed' log lines, which may be a regression for users relying on traceID to connect logs with traces.

title: FromContext fallback may silently discard contextual attributes
body: The FromContext method performs a type assertion to *log.ConcreteLogger. If d.l.FromContext(ctx) returns a different type (e.g., a different logger implementation or a non-ConcreteLogger wrapper), the assertion fails and the fallback d.New() is returned. This fallback logger does not contain the contextual attributes set by ContextualLoggerMiddleware (or any other context enrichment). As a result, logs produced by LoggerMiddleware would miss pluginId, endpoint, and other fields. Even if current infra/log always returns ConcreteLogger, this is fragile and could break silently if logging internals change.

title: No tests for the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware
body: The new ContextualLoggerMiddleware is untested. It should have unit tests verifying that instrumentContext adds the expected contextual attributes (endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, uname) for QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, and CollectMetrics, and that these attributes are not added for stream methods (SubscribeStream, PublishStream, RunStream). Additionally, test that LoggerMiddleware (when configured) receives the enriched context and logs correctly.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh instance, losing accumulated state
body: TestLogger.FromContext always returns NewTestLogger(), which creates a new TestLogger with zeroed Logs. If a test uses the same TestLogger instance across multiple requests and expects logs to accumulate, this will break. It also means that any context-specific logger attributes cannot be inspected later. While it's a test fake, it may cause confusing test failures if not used carefully.

title: Test function name not updated after file rename
body: The test function is still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware even though the file was renamed to metrics_middleware_test.go and the middleware is now MetricsMiddleware. This is inconsistent and may confuse readers searching for tests by middleware name. Rename to TestMetricsMiddleware for clarity.

title: traceID removed from plugin request completed log entries
body: The refactoring removes the addition of traceID to logParams in logRequest. Previously, the logger middleware included the tracing trace ID in the 'Plugin Request Completed' log line, but this PR deletes that logic (along with the tracing import). As a result, plugin request logs will no longer contain traceID, reducing correlation between logs and traces. This change is not mentioned in the PR description and appears unintentional.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a new logger without shared log state
body: The newly added FromContext method on TestLogger returns a fresh NewTestLogger() instead of returning the receiver or a logger that shares the same Logs fields. Any code that obtains a contextual logger via FromContext and then logs will write to a separate TestLogger instance, causing the original TestLogger's Logs to remain empty. This will break existing tests (e.g., for LoggerMiddleware) that pass a TestLogger and assert on its recorded log messages after invoking middleware methods.

title: Logger name still references deprecated 'instrumentation'
body: The logger is created with log.New("plugin.instrumentation"). Since the middleware has been renamed from InstrumentationMiddleware to MetricsMiddleware and the contextual logging moved to a separate middleware, this logger name is outdated and may cause confusion. Consider renaming it to something like "plugin.requests" or "plugin.client" to align with the new naming convention.

title: No tests for the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware
body: The new ContextualLoggerMiddleware is not covered by any tests. Given that it is responsible for injecting contextual attributes into the request context that LoggerMiddleware relies on, a regression here could break logging or context propagation. At minimum, tests should verify that instrumentContext correctly adds endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname to the context for the relevant client methods.

title: Device limit can be bypassed by retrying after a rejected device because the local cache is populated before the limit check succeeds
body: In tagDeviceUI, the device key is added to localCache before a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice is called. When CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, TagDevice propagates the error and the anonymous authentication fails, but the cache entry remains valid for 29 minutes. A subsequent request from the same device ID hits the cached value at the top of tagDeviceUI and returns nil without consulting the device limit, so authentication succeeds. A client can intentionally send two requests: the first triggers the limit and the second is allowed, defeating the configurable device limit. Cache the device only after CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds, or delete the cache entry on error.

title: Device limit can be exceeded under concurrent requests because count and insert/update are not atomic
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice first calls CountDevices to check whether the current count is below deviceLimit, then performs a later INSERT/UPDATE outside any transaction or lock. Concurrent authentication attempts for different new device IDs can all observe count < deviceLimit and all proceed to insert, pushing the total above the configured limit. In a multi-instance Grafana deployment this race is realistic. The count-and-insert/update pair should be performed in a transaction with appropriate locking, or otherwise made atomic, to actually enforce the limit.

title: Anonymous authentication now synchronously performs database work for device tagging
body: The previous implementation tagged anonymous devices in a goroutine with a separate timeout, keeping the authentication hot path independent of the anon_device database table. This change moves TagDevice into the synchronous Authenticate path. On a local-cache miss, tagDeviceUI executes a COUNT query on anon_device followed by an INSERT/UPDATE before authentication completes. A burst of first-time device IDs, a large anon_device table, or a slow/unavailable database will add latency to anonymous sign-in, and the request context will be consumed by that database work. If the limit must be enforced synchronously, consider a cheaper or transactional enforcement mechanism that does not couple every new anonymous session to a multi-query database round trip.

title: Device limit can be bypassed after first rejection because local cache is set before validation
body: tagDeviceUI sets the local cache entry before calling anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. When that call returns ErrDeviceLimitReached for an unknown device, the cache entry is not removed. On the next request for the same device ID within the cache TTL (29 minutes), tagDeviceUI returns nil from the cache and Authenticate proceeds without checking the limit. As a result, a rejected anonymous device can immediately retry and authenticate, defeating the configured device limit. Cache should only be populated after CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds, or the entry should be invalidated on error.

title: Device limit check is not atomic with insert
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice performs a separate CountDevices query and then, if count < deviceLimit, executes an INSERT/UPDATE without any transaction or locking. Concurrent anonymous authentication requests can all observe count < limit and all insert new devices, allowing the configured anonymousDeviceLimit to be exceeded. Use a transaction with appropriate locking or an atomic conditional insert to enforce the limit.

title: MySQL zero affected rows can falsely trigger ErrDeviceLimitReached for an existing device
body: updateDevice treats rowsAffected == 0 as ErrDeviceLimitReached. On MySQL, an UPDATE that matches an existing row but does not change any column values (or only changes values within timestamp precision) returns 0 affected rows by default because the server reports changed rows rather than matched rows. When a device is already stored with the same client_ip and user_agent and the updated_at value resolves to the same stored value (for example, within the same second), updateDevice may return ErrDeviceLimitReached even though the device is within the active window and should be allowed. This causes intermittent authentication failures for existing devices under the limit, especially in multi-instance deployments that do not share the local cache.

title: Anonymous authentication now blocks on a database write for every new device
body: Authenticate changed from fire-and-forget TagDevice in a goroutine with a timeout to a synchronous call using the request context. Even when AnonymousDeviceLimit is 0 (the default), every first request for a device on each Grafana instance performs a synchronous DB INSERT/UPDATE in CreateOrUpdateDevice before authentication returns. This adds database latency to anonymous login and reintroduces the DB as a dependency on the auth hot path that the previous async timeout was designed to avoid. Consider keeping the write asynchronous when no limit is configured, or otherwise constrain the synchronous path to only the operations needed to enforce a limit.

title: No test for an existing device when limit is reached or cache failure bypass
body: The new test only covers two distinct new devices exceeding the limit. It does not cover updating an existing active device when the limit is already reached (which should succeed), nor does it exercise the local-cache path in impl.go where a limit rejection leaves the cache populated and permits the next attempt. These cases are important because both are places where the current implementation has edge cases.

title: Device limit can be bypassed because cache is set before persistence
body: In `tagDeviceUI`, the device key is inserted into `localCache` before `CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs. When the configured device limit is reached, `CreateOrUpdateDevice` returns `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached`, which makes `Anonymous.Authenticate` fail for that request; however, the cache entry remains. A retry with the same device ID hits the cache at line 83 and returns nil without checking the store, so authentication then succeeds and the limit is bypassed for the cache TTL (29 minutes). Move `SetDefault` after a successful store, or remove the cache entry on error.

title: Device count check and insert are not atomic, so limit can be exceeded under concurrency
body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` first calls `CountDevices` and then, if `count < deviceLimit`, proceeds to the INSERT/upsert. The count and insert are separate statements with no transaction or lock preventing concurrent inserts. When multiple new anonymous devices arrive while the count is just below the limit, several goroutines can all observe `count < deviceLimit` and insert, exceeding the configured `device_limit`. The limit should be enforced atomically, for example with a transaction, row lock, or an `INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(...)) < ?` approach.

title: Anonymous device tagging is now synchronous even when device limit is disabled
body: The previous implementation tagged devices in a background goroutine with a timeout. This PR moves `TagDevice` into the authentication path unconditionally. With the default `AnonymousDeviceLimit = 0`, no limit enforcement is needed, but every uncached anonymous request still synchronously performs the DB write/upsert before authentication can complete. This adds latency and database load to anonymous/public dashboard traffic for installations that did not enable the new limit. Consider keeping the old asynchronous path when `deviceLimit <= 0` or gating synchronous enforcement behind `deviceLimit > 0`.

title: Cleanup interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The global cleanup ticker is changed from time.Minute * 10 to time.Minute * 1. This is unrelated to the annotation deadlock fix and runs every cleanup job (expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history) ten times as often, significantly increasing database and CPU load. If a full cleanup pass takes longer than one minute, the ticker can also cause back-to-back cleanup passes. This looks like an accidental debug change and should be reverted or explicitly justified before merging.

title: Cleanup logs at Error level with full ID lists on every batch
body: The new cleanup path calls r.log.Error for 'Annotations to clean by time/count', 'cleaned annotations by ...', 'Tags to clean', and 'cleaned tags' on every batch, passing the complete 'ids' slice. With a batch size such as the newly tested 32767, every successful cleanup cycle emits multiple error-level log records containing tens of thousands of IDs. This creates noisy error logs, can make error monitoring misleading, and can produce very large log payloads. These are normal debug/info events, not errors, and the full ID lists should not be logged at this level.

title: DELETE placeholders can exceed database parameter limits except on SQLite
body: deleteByIDs only special-cases SQLite when building the DELETE statement with an IN clause. For other supported databases with parameter limits, such as SQL Server (2100 parameters) and depending on batch size PostgreSQL, setting AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize above that limit will generate DELETE FROM ... WHERE id IN (?,?,...) with too many bind parameters and fail. The previous subquery-based DELETE did not bind one parameter per ID. The ID list should be batched for deletion across all dialects, or equivalent dialect-specific limits should be applied.

title: Global cleanup ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: This line changes the main cleanup loop from every 10 minutes to every 1 minute. It affects every job registered in clean(), including dashboard versions, snapshots, expired images, query history, and annotation cleanup. The PR is aimed at reducing MySQL lock contention in annotation cleanup, but running all cleanup work 10x more often can significantly increase database load and may worsen lock contention. This unrelated behavior change should be reverted or explicitly justified.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged at error level with full ID lists
body: r.log.Error is used after fetchIDs succeeds (and similarly after deleteByIDs at lines 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579), even though err is nil on every successful path and the code logs the entire ids slice plus the generated condition. Cleanup runs on a schedule and can process many batches, so this floods logs with error-level entries and large ID lists during normal operation. These should be Debug-level logs, or the ID lists should be omitted.

title: deleteByIDs can exceed bind-parameter limits on non-SQLite databases
body: The new delete-by-ID query builds one placeholder per row ("?" + strings.Repeat(",?", len(ids)-1)) and only special-cases SQLite. If AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is configured above the database bind-parameter limit (for example 65535 on PostgreSQL/MySQL), every cleanup batch will fail with a SQL error. The previous subquery-based DELETE did not have a per-batch placeholder limit. The IDs should be chunked on all dialects according to their dialect limits, not only for SQLite.

title: SQLite IN-list construction is quadratic in batch size
body: The SQLite branch builds the IN-list by repeatedly calling values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v), which copies the entire accumulated string for each ID. With a batch size over 999 (the test uses 32767), this causes O(n²) string copying and many large allocations on a hot cleanup path. Use strings.Builder or strings.Join to construct the literal list in linear time.

title: Normal cleanup batches are logged at error level, including full ID lists
body: These are expected per-batch status messages, but they use r.log.Error even when err is nil and log the full ids slice. The same pattern repeats at lines 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579. With the cleanup job running every minute, this will flood error logs and can trigger alerts, and large batch sizes may produce very large log entries listing tens of thousands of IDs. These should be debug/info logs, and full ID lists should not be logged on success.

title: Cleanup job ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute without explanation
body: The cleanup loop now runs every minute instead of every 10 minutes, applying to all cleanup jobs: temporary files, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, and query history. This change is unrelated to the annotation cleanup deadlock fix and is not mentioned in the PR description. It increases database load and lock contention and may make the deadlock being fixed more likely. If this was a debug leftover, it should be reverted to 10 minutes.

title: deleteByIDs can exceed SQL Server's 2100-parameter limit for large batch sizes
body: deleteByIDs only special-cases SQLite for parameter limits and otherwise builds an IN clause with one placeholder per ID. Microsoft SQL Server supports a maximum of 2100 parameters per statement, so configuring AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize above 2100 will cause every cleanup batch on SQL Server to fail with a 'too many parameters' error. The old subquery-based delete did not bind IDs this way. The new test covers only SQLite, so this cross-database regression is not caught. The delete should be chunked or use a dialect-specific literal strategy for parameter-limited non-SQLite databases.

title: Async legacy writes use request-scoped context and will be canceled
body: In Create, the goroutine derives its context from the method's ctx parameter, which is typically the HTTP request context. Once the handler returns, this context is canceled, causing the legacy write (Legacy.Create) to fail or be interrupted before completion. The same pattern is used in Delete (line 110), Update (line 135), and DeleteCollection (line 163). The intended async 'safe measure' write to legacy will almost always be aborted because the request context is canceled when the response is sent. The goroutine should use a context detached from the request, such as context.Background() or a context with a timeout but no request cancellation.

title: Create error path records legacy duration instead of storage duration
body: When d.Storage.Create returns an error, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage). This records the failed unified storage operation as a legacy operation, polluting metrics used to monitor legacy write behavior. It should call d.recordStorageDuration instead.

title: Update error path records legacy duration instead of storage duration
body: When d.Storage.Update returns an error, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage). This mislabels the failed unified storage update as a legacy operation. Metrics for storage failures will be missing, and legacy metrics will be incorrectly incremented. It should record storage duration.

title: DeleteCollection legacy write records storage duration instead of legacy duration
body: Inside the goroutine that writes to Legacy.DeleteCollection, the code calls d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). This records the legacy operation as if it were a unified storage operation, corrupting both storage and legacy metrics. It should call d.recordLegacyDuration.

title: Delete success storage duration uses object name as kind label
body: In the success path of Delete, the call d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) passes the object name as the 'kind' argument. Other methods pass options.Kind. This will cause storage duration metrics to be split by object name, creating a high-cardinality label and making the metric useless for aggregation by kind. It should use options.Kind like other paths.

title: Integration test checks legacy API immediately after async legacy write
body: In doPlaylistTests, after creating playlists via the Kubernetes API (which in mode 3 triggers an asynchronous legacy write), the test immediately performs a legacy API list request and expects the newly created playlists to be present. Because the legacy write is asynchronous and may not have completed, the test is prone to flakiness. A wait mechanism or retry loop should be added to ensure the legacy write has propagated before asserting.

title: Unit tests for mode 3 do not wait for async legacy writes
body: The unit tests for Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection call the dual writer and then return without waiting for the asynchronous goroutine that writes to legacy storage to complete. This can lead to: (1) the legacy mock not being called before the test ends, so the test does not actually verify that legacy write happens; (2) a potential data race if the mock is used by the goroutine after the test has finished or while other tests are using the shared mock; (3) leaked goroutines that may run after test completion. The tests should synchronize with the goroutine (e.g., using a sync.WaitGroup or a channel) before asserting on the mock or returning.

title: Async legacy writes inherit request context and will be canceled prematurely
body: The goroutines started for legacy writes (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) use the same `ctx` that was derived from the incoming HTTP request. When the HTTP handler returns, the request context is canceled by the server, causing the legacy write to be aborted before it completes. This defeats the purpose of the asynchronous safe write and will likely cause legacy data loss. Use a context detached from the request (e.g., `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` or a new background context) for these goroutines.

title: Legacy Update reuses the same UpdatedObjectInfo causing a second invocation
body: The legacy update goroutine passes the same `objInfo` that was already used by `d.Storage.Update`. This causes `objInfo.UpdatedObject` to be invoked a second time, possibly against a different old object (the legacy store's current state), leading to incorrect data or side effects. The previous implementation wrapped the already updated object to reuse it for legacy; that behavior was lost. This can produce updates inconsistent with what was written to unified storage.

title: Wrong metric function used on storage error in Create
body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration`. This records the storage failure as a legacy operation and pollutes the legacy latency metrics, making monitoring misleading. Similar mislabels occur in Update (line 129) and in the DeleteCollection goroutine (line 166).

title: Storage duration metric for Delete uses object name as kind
body: After a successful storage delete, the call `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` as the `kind` argument. The metric label will be incorrectly populated with resource names instead of resource kinds, breaking dashboard queries and alerts based on the `kind` label.

title: Delete uses wrong logger when updating context
body: In `Delete`, the code sets `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` instead of using the per-call `log` variable that includes method, name, and kind. As a result, subsequent log entries from this context will lack the per-request fields, reducing log usefulness.

title: Mode 3 unit tests do not wait for or assert async legacy writes
body: The tests set up legacy store mocks but never call `m.AssertExpectations(t)` nor synchronize with the goroutines performing the legacy writes. The async operations may still be running when the test ends, and failures in legacy writes are not detected. This leaves the mode 3 legacy write path essentially untested. The tests should use a channel or wait group to ensure the goroutine completes and then verify the legacy mock was called and metrics recorded correctly.

title: Integration tests for mode 3 may be flaky due to asynchronous legacy writes
body: The `doPlaylistTests` function checks that legacy API endpoints reflect changes made through the Kubernetes API immediately after operations. In mode 3, legacy writes are asynchronous and not awaited, so the legacy API may not have the latest data when the test queries it. This can cause intermittent failures in the newly added mode 3 test cases. The tests need a synchronization mechanism (or the implementation must guarantee completion before returning) to be reliable.

title: Async legacy writes use the request-scoped context and will be canceled immediately
body: In Create (lines 50-56), Delete (108-113), Update (134-140), and DeleteCollection (161-166), the goroutine creates a timeout context from the request context (ctx). When the HTTP handler returns, its context is typically canceled. The goroutine's legacy write then inherits this canceled context and is aborted before completing. This defeats the purpose of asynchronous fallback writes: the legacy store will almost never receive the write. The code should use a context detached from the request (e.g., context.Background() with timeout) while preserving any necessary values (like authentication).

title: Legacy update uses the original objInfo instead of the object updated in unified storage
body: In Update, after d.Storage.Update succeeds, the goroutine calls d.Legacy.Update with the same objInfo that was passed to the unified storage call. The previous implementation used an updateWrapper to reuse the already computed updated object. Without it, Legacy.Update will invoke objInfo.UpdatedObject against the legacy store's own old object, which may differ (e.g., missing new fields, different resourceVersion). This can cause the legacy write to produce a different object or fail validation, breaking the dual-write guarantee. The code should pass a wrapper or the object returned by Storage.Update to ensure both stores persist the same data.

title: Multiple metrics are recorded under the wrong name or store
body: Several metric calls are incorrect: in Create error path (line 45) records legacy duration instead of storage; in Update error path (line 129) records legacy duration instead of storage; in Delete success path (line 106) passes the resource name as the 'kind' label instead of options.Kind; in DeleteCollection goroutine (line 166) records storage duration for the legacy operation instead of legacy duration. These errors cause Prometheus metrics to be mislabeled or attributed to the wrong store, leading to incorrect monitoring and alerting. All timing and label arguments must be corrected to reflect the actual operation being measured.

title: Delete uses the base logger instead of the request-scoped logger
body: In Delete, ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) is used, discarding the enriched log variable (log) that includes name, kind, and method fields. Consequently, subsequent logs in the Delete method (including errors from Storage.Delete) will lack these contextual fields, making debugging harder. It should be ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, log).

title: Legacy Create receives the original input object, not the object persisted in unified storage
body: In Create, the goroutine passes `obj` (the original input) to Legacy.Create, ignoring the `created` object returned by Storage.Create. Unified storage typically applies defaulting, assigns UID, resourceVersion, and creationTimestamp. The legacy store will therefore receive an object missing these modifications, leading to data inconsistency between the two stores. The code should pass `created` (or a sanitized copy) to the legacy write to ensure both stores reflect the same final state.

title: Removal of local prometheus registry causes duplicate metric registration panic
body: The diff removes `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` from TestMode1_Get, causing it to use the package-level global `p` (var p = prometheus.NewRegistry()). If NewDualWriter registers metrics on the provided registry (as dualWriterMetrics likely does using promauto), then the first test that uses the global registry (e.g., TestMode1_Create) will register metrics, and any subsequent test using the same global registry will panic with duplicate metric registration. This will break the entire test package. Each test should create and use its own fresh prometheus registry, or the global registry must be reset between tests.

title: Tests for asynchronous legacy writes do not wait for completion and ignore mock expectations
body: Multiple tests (e.g., TestMode3_Create, TestMode3_Delete, TestMode3_Update) set up legacy mock expectations but never call m.AssertExpectations() and do not wait for the goroutine to finish. The test may pass even if the legacy write is never called or fails, and the mock call may occur after the test completes, causing race conditions or panics if the legacy method is not stubbed. This prevents any verification of the asynchronous dual-write behavior and can lead to flaky or silently failing tests. The tests must synchronize with the goroutine (e.g., using a WaitGroup or a done channel) and assert expectations before finishing.

title: Integration tests for mode 3 may be flaky due to asynchronous legacy writes
body: The added subtests for mode 3 (file and unified storage) run the same doPlaylistTests which immediately checks legacy API results after k8s API operations. Since mode 3 writes to legacy asynchronously, there is no guarantee that the legacy write has completed before the test queries the legacy endpoint. This can cause intermittent failures (e.g., legacy list missing the just-created playlist). The test needs a synchronization mechanism or a polling wait to ensure the async write has propagated before asserting on the legacy API.

title: Missing cache recheck after acquiring write lock causes thundering herd
body: The fast path checks `entryPointAssetsCache` under `RLock`, then releases the lock. If it is nil, the function takes the write lock at line 48 but never re-reads `entryPointAssetsCache`. When several goroutines call `GetWebAssets` concurrently before the cache is populated, they all pass the nil check and then serialize on the write lock; each one repeats the expensive manifest load (file or CDN) and overwrites the cache. Add a second cache check immediately after acquiring the write lock and return the cached value if it is now non-nil.

title: No regression test for the data race fix
body: This change fixes a data race on the global `entryPointAssetsCache`, but no test exercises concurrent calls to `GetWebAssets`. A test that invokes `GetWebAssets` from multiple goroutines concurrently, ideally run under `go test -race`, would verify that the mutex protects the cache and would prevent the original race from being reintroduced.

title: Missing re-check after acquiring write lock causes redundant asset loading
body: After acquiring the write lock at line 48, the code does not re-check whether entryPointAssetsCache has been populated by another goroutine. In a non-Dev environment, if multiple requests arrive concurrently when the cache is nil, the first goroutine acquires the lock and begins loading. The others block on RLock until the first releases, then one of them acquires the write lock (since ret is still nil from their earlier RLock snapshot) and repeats the full loading process. This can lead to unnecessary file reads or CDN requests under startup concurrency. Adding a re-check inside the write lock (e.g., `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }`) would prevent redundant work.

title: Typo in error message
body: The error message says "asssets-manifest" instead of "assets-manifest". This is a pre-existing typo but it appears in an error string that could be shown to users; correcting it improves clarity.

title: Double-checked locking missing re-check after acquiring write lock
body: GetWebAssets releases the read lock at line 43 and later acquires the write lock at line 48, but after acquiring the write lock it does not re-read entryPointAssetsCache before doing the expensive load. If many goroutines call concurrently when the cache is nil (e.g. the first requests in production), all of them will see nil under RLock, block on Lock, and then sequentially reload the manifest from file/CDN and overwrite the cache. The cache is not single-flight; this can cause a thundering herd of disk/network reads and JSON parsing at startup. Add a second cache check immediately after acquiring the write lock (e.g. if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }) before loading.

title: No test for concurrent access or caching behavior
body: This change modifies only webassets.go and adds synchronization around the global cache, but no test is added that exercises concurrent calls to GetWebAssets (e.g. under -race) or verifies that non-Dev callers reuse the cached value and that concurrent startup loads are handled correctly. A regression test would help confirm the data race is actually fixed and would reveal the duplicate-load issue described above.

title: SQL expression feature flag is now a no-op
body: `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` but then returns `false` in both branches, so SQL expressions are rejected even when the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle is enabled. Operators who had enabled the flag to use the SQL expression feature will see all such queries fail with "sqlExpressions is not implemented", while the flag remains present and documented. Either remove/deprecate the flag and its documentation, or make this function honor it; as written the flag is misleading dead configuration and the helper name does not match its behavior.

title: No regression tests for the disabled SQL expression path
body: This PR disables SQL expressions by making `sql.TablesList` always fail through the stubbed `DB.RunCommands`, so `NewSQLCommand` should always return an error. However, no test was added to lock in that behavior for `QueryTypeSQL`/`NewSQLCommand` regardless of the feature flag, and none verifies that the DuckDB-based path cannot be re-enabled accidentally. A regression test would prevent a future change from reintroducing the vulnerable dependency or execution path unnoticed.

title: Security fix has no regression test
body: This PR disables SQL expressions by returning an error before query parsing and by stubbing the SQL DB methods. No test files are changed in this PR, so there is no automated verification that a QueryTypeSQL query is rejected or that NewSQLCommand/TablesList never executes SQL. Given this is a critical security fix, a regression test should be added asserting the error path and that the SQL execution path remains unreachable.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false
body: The helper computes enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions) and then returns false in both branches, making the feature toggle ineffective and leaving dead code. Operators who enable the sqlExpressions feature flag will still get 'sqlExpressions is not implemented'. If unconditional disable is intended, the code should return false directly with a comment; otherwise it should honor the toggle so the documented flag has the expected effect.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false and contains dead code
body: The function `enableSqlExpressions` is misleading: it checks the `sqlExpressions` feature flag but ignores the result and always returns `false`. The logic `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(...); if enabled { return false } return false` is equivalent to `return false`. This dead code suggests the flag can enable the feature, which is not the case after this security fix. It should be simplified to `return false` with a comment explaining the feature is permanently disabled, or the function removed entirely.

title: No tests for disabled SQL expressions or stub DB
body: This PR disables SQL expressions for security reasons and replaces the DuckDB-backed implementation with a stub that always returns "not implemented". However, no unit tests were added or updated to verify that (1) `ReadQuery` returns an error for `QueryTypeSQL` regardless of the feature flag, and (2) the stub DB methods (`TablesList`, `RunCommands`, `QueryFramesInto`) always return the expected error. For a security-critical change, test coverage is important to prevent accidental regression that could re-enable the vulnerable feature.

title: TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding the read lock
body: TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without acquiring b.cacheMu.RLock(). In searchSupport.init, the watch goroutine is started immediately before s.search.TotalDocs() is called, and that goroutine can call getOrCreateIndex -> BuildIndex, which writes to b.cache under cacheMu. Concurrent map iteration and write can trigger a runtime panic ("concurrent map iteration and map write"). TotalDocs must take the read lock or operate on a stable snapshot.

title: Index startup can permanently miss writes that occur during the build
body: In searchSupport.init, the resource version returned by s.build is discarded (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`), and WatchWriteEvents is started only after all indexes are built. A write that occurs after a namespace has been listed but before WatchWriteEvents captures the latest RV is neither in the initial index nor emitted by the watcher, because the watcher starts from that latest RV. The index can remain stale until another write for that resource occurs or the server restarts. The watcher must be started before/during the build with replay, or the last-read RV from each build must be used to seed the watcher.

title: Fine-grained cache locking allows duplicate index builds for the same key
body: getOrCreateIndex checks GetIndex before calling BuildIndex, but with the cacheMu lock now held only at the end of BuildIndex, two concurrent callers for the same key can both see nil, build separate indexes, and both insert into b.cache; the last write wins. The losing caller can still return the discarded index, and file-based builds may concurrently open/create the same directory and fail. This violates the intended single-index-per-key behavior and can cause inconsistent search results or build errors under concurrent access.

title: Index event goroutine panics when the watch channel closes
body: The goroutine reads `v := <-events` forever and passes the result directly to s.handleEvent. WatchWriteEvents implementations, such as the SQL backend's poller, close the channel when they stop. A receive from a closed channel returns a nil *WrittenEvent, and handleEvent immediately dereferences evt.Type/evt.Key, causing a panic during shutdown. The loop should check `v, ok := <-events` and return when the channel is closed. It should also use a cancellable context instead of context.Background() so shutdown can stop it cleanly.

title: Non-atomic increment in concurrent index initialization
body: `totalBatchesIndexed++` runs inside group.Go without synchronization while errgroup runs up to s.initWorkers goroutines concurrently. This is a data race, can produce an incorrect count in the trace span, and will be flagged by the race detector. Use an atomic counter or compute the count safely after group.Wait returns.

title: Stop flag is no longer checked by RPC methods
body: The PR removes the `s.Init(ctx)` guard from every RPC entrypoint. Stop sets s.initErr to "service is stopping"/"service is stopped", but after this change no method reads s.initErr, so requests accepted after Stop can still execute against a stopped backend. A separate readiness/stopping check, or ensuring the gRPC server is fully drained before Stop, is needed to preserve the previous shutdown behavior.

title: Postgres integration test is skipped instead of fixed
body: The new eager initialization makes this integration test fail on Postgres in CI, and the PR adds a skip with a TODO rather than diagnosing the failure. This removes Postgres coverage for the storage server startup path and may hide a regression in the new initialization ordering. If this is a known environmental issue it should be tracked separately, but skipping the test means the new eager-init path is not verified on Postgres.

title: BuildIndex now allows duplicate concurrent builds for the same index
body: The previous global cacheMu lock around the entire BuildIndex call has been reduced to locking only the final cache write. However, getOrCreateIndex in resource/search.go has no per-key synchronization and checks GetIndex only once before building. Two concurrent callers that miss the same NamespacedResource can both enter BuildIndex. With file-backed indexes, both will call bleve.New on the same directory, which can fail or conflict; one index is then leaked and the cache is overwritten. Add per-key singleflight/locking, or re-check the cache under the lock before building.

title: Data races on shared counters and error variable during parallel index initialization
body: In searchSupport.init, errgroup runs one goroutine per resource. Every goroutine increments the plain int totalBatchesIndexed and assigns the shared outer err variable via `_, _, err = s.build(...)`. These are unsynchronized concurrent writes, so the race detector will flag them and the namespace count metric can be lost. Use atomic operations for the counter and a local error variable inside each goroutine.

title: Search event watcher uses an uncancellable background context and panics on close
body: searchSupport.init starts WatchWriteEvents with `watchctx := context.Background()` instead of the supplied ctx, then launches a goroutine that does `v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v)` in an infinite loop. This goroutine cannot be stopped by server.Stop/s.cancel. When the backend closes the events channel during shutdown, the receive returns a nil *WrittenEvent and handleEvent dereferences evt.Type, panicking and crashing the process. Because Init is now eager, this watcher is created during NewResourceServer for every process rather than only after a request.

title: Starting search index build before watchers creates a write-event gap during startup
body: Init now runs s.search.init to completion before s.initWatcher is called. The SQL backend's WatchWriteEvents snapshots the latest resource versions when it is called and only emits later events. Because the initial index build can take a long time and runs before either the search or server watcher starts, any writes committed during the build are not indexed and are not broadcast to Watch clients, leaving both stale until a subsequent write. The last RV returned by the build is discarded, and there is no backfill from that point.

title: Postgres storage server integration test is newly skipped without a fix
body: The test is now explicitly skipped for Postgres with a TODO, and the diff does not add equivalent coverage. Since the storage server is the target affected by eager initialization and watcher ordering changes, losing this integration test removes protection against regressions on Postgres.

title: Concurrent BuildIndex for the same key can cause file index creation errors
body: Removing the global cacheMu.Lock from BuildIndex means two goroutines can now concurrently build an index for the same NamespacedResource. getOrCreateIndex does not provide per-key mutual exclusion (see TODO at resource/search.go lines 288-290), so concurrent search requests for the same resource will both see a nil index and call BuildIndex. For file-based indexes (size > FileThreshold), both goroutines will call bleve.New on the same directory path, which is not safe and can fail with an error such as 'index already exists' or corrupt the index. For memory indexes, both will build identical indexes and the last insertion wins, wasting work. Need per-key locking or singleflight to prevent duplicate concurrent builds.

title: TotalDocs reads the cache map without holding RLock
body: TotalDocs iterates over b.cache without acquiring b.cacheMu.RLock. With the reduced locking in BuildIndex, cache is now written concurrently by any call to BuildIndex (e.g., from getOrCreateIndex on search requests) while TotalDocs may be called (for example, in searchSupport.init at resource/search.go line 216 or externally). This constitutes a concurrent map read/write and will cause a runtime panic or map corruption. TotalDocs must take cacheMu.RLock, or the cache must be otherwise synchronized.

title: Cancel function not called when Init fails during NewResourceServer
body: NewResourceServer creates a cancellable context and stores its cancel function in the server struct. If s.Init(ctx) returns an error, the function logs and returns nil, err without calling s.cancel(). Any goroutines started during Init (e.g., from lifecycle.Init or WatchWriteEvents in search.init) may continue running with no way to be stopped, leaking resources. The cancel should be invoked before returning the error.

title: Data race on totalBatchesIndexed in concurrent errgroup goroutines
body: Inside s.init, totalBatchesIndexed++ is executed by multiple goroutines running under an errgroup with SetLimit(s.initWorkers). The variable is not protected by a mutex or atomic operation and is later read after group.Wait() to add a span event. This is a data race and can produce incorrect counts or be flagged by the race detector.

title: Search watcher goroutine uses background context and does not handle closed channel
body: The searchSupport.init function starts WatchWriteEvents with watchctx := context.Background() rather than the cancellable ctx passed to init. This watcher goroutine will never be cancelled when the server stops, causing a goroutine leak. Additionally, the goroutine reads from the events channel without checking for closure; if the channel is closed (e.g., due to backend termination), the receive yields a nil *WrittenEvent, and handleEvent will dereference it in the slices.Contains call, causing a panic. The context should be tied to the server and the channel closure should be handled safely.

title: Gap between index build and watch start can miss write events
body: In searchSupport.init, the index is built from a snapshot using ListIterator (lines 181-193), and only afterwards is WatchWriteEvents called to start the watcher (line 203). Any writes that occur between the snapshot read and the watcher's initialization will not be reflected in the newly built index, because the watcher starts after the build and does not replay missed events. This can lead to stale search results until the next event for that resource. The watcher should ideally be started before or atomically with the snapshot, or the backend should provide a mechanism to replay missed events.

title: Call to undefined no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() breaks compilation
body: The changed condition invokes isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments. The only method defined in UsernamePasswordForm is isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel), so this call cannot be resolved and the module fails to compile. The call probably should pass context.getUser(), or a no-arg overload must be added.

title: Passkey conditional UI is no longer filled when no user is set
body: authenticate() now calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()), which returns false when context.getUser() is null. On the normal first-factor username/password page, the user is not set yet, so webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) is skipped and the WebAuthn/passkey form is absent. Previously this code filled the passkey form for that case. The challenge(...) override at line 137 has the same condition, so passkeys also disappear after an invalid username or password submission. Existing passkey tests such as passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey and passwordLoginWithExternalKey expect the webauth form at these stages.

title: Re-authentication enables passkey UI regardless of whether the user has a passkey
body: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) only checks that passkeys are enabled for the realm and that user is non-null. During re-authentication it causes fillContextForm to be called even for a user with no WebAuthn passwordless credential. Such users get a passkey option that cannot succeed and may produce WebAuthn errors. The check should also verify the user has a configured passwordless credential, for example via user.credentialManager().isConfiguredFor(WebAuthnCredentialModel.TYPE_PASSWORDLESS).

title: Passkey conditional UI is not set up when user is null, breaking passwordless login
body: In authenticate(), the call to webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) is now guarded by isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()). This method returns false when context.getUser() is null (its condition includes user != null). Previously, fillContextForm was performed when user == null (inside the else block). As a result, on the normal login page with no pre-selected user, passkey conditional UI is never set up, so users cannot use passkeys for passwordless login. Existing tests for initial login (e.g., passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey) will fail. The guard should not require user != null; it should be `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()`.

title: Passkey conditional UI no longer added on error challenges when user is null
body: In the challenge() override, the condition changed from `context.getUser() == null && webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()` to `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`, which requires user != null. This means when an error occurs during initial authentication (user not set), passkeys will not be filled into the challenge response, so the conditional UI disappears on error pages. The original intent was to fill passkeys when user is null; the new condition reverses that. This breaks the error flow for passwordless login.

title: Passkeys are no longer populated for initial username/password login
body: `authenticate()` now calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`, but that helper includes `user != null`. In the normal initial login flow `context.getUser()` is null, so this block is skipped and `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` is never called. Previously the code filled the WebAuthn context whenever passkeys were enabled and no user had been selected. As a result conditional passkeys/autofill are disabled on the first factor page, discoverable-key auto-login stops working, and tests that assert the `form[@id='webauth']` element on the initial page or after an invalid username will fail. The same helper is also used in the error `challenge(...)` method, so passkey data is lost on initial-login errors as well.

title: Re-authentication shortcut is disabled for users without passkeys
body: The shortcut is now disabled whenever `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` is true, but that method only checks that passkeys are enabled for the realm and that the user is non-null; it does not check whether this user actually has a passwordless WebAuthn credential. Therefore a user with only a password who is re-authenticating in a realm with passkeys enabled will no longer proceed directly to the password step via `context.success()`, and will instead be shown an extra username/passkey form they cannot use. The feature should verify that the known user has a configured passkey before disabling this shortcut.

title: Login IDP cache not invalidated when organization enabled or public broker status changes
body: The new cache for getForLogin stores the set of IDP internal IDs based only on the IDP model's own fields (enabled, linkOnly, hideOnLogin, organizationId, and BROKER_PUBLIC config). However, the actual login availability of an organization-linked IDP also depends on the organization's enabled state and potentially on organization-level public broker settings. The invalidation logic (registerIDPLoginInvalidation and registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate) only reacts to IdentityProviderStorageProvider CRUD operations and does not invalidate the login cache when an organization is disabled/enabled or its public broker flag changes. As a result, after such an organization change, the cached list will still contain the affected IDPs, causing getForLogin to return IDPs that are no longer suitable for login. Downstream consumers that rely on the returned stream without re-checking isEnabled() will present stale login options.

title: Cleanup attempts to remove a hardcoded 'alias' instead of the actual IDP alias
body: In testCacheIDPForLogin, the cleanup call `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove);` uses the literal string "alias" instead of the variable `alias` holding the actual IDP alias. This means the cleanup will try to delete an identity provider with alias "alias" (which does not exist), leaving the created IDPs in the realm after the test. This can pollute subsequent tests or cause cleanup failures. The same mistake appears on line 425 as well.

title: Test cleanup uses wrong alias literal, causing NPE and test pollution
body: In multiple places (lines 303, 381, 425), the cleanup registration uses `testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")` instead of the actual alias variable. The literal string "alias" does not correspond to any created identity provider, so `get("alias")` returns null and calling `.remove()` on it will throw a NullPointerException during cleanup. Moreover, the actual created IDPs will not be removed, leading to cross-test contamination and potentially making other tests fail. This affects both `testCacheIDPByOrg` and `testCacheIDPForLogin`.

title: Potential NullPointerException in remove() when alias does not exist
body: In `remove(String alias)`, `storedIdp` is assigned from `idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)` which may return null if the alias does not exist. If `isInvalid(cacheKey)` is true, the code calls `registerIDPInvalidation(storedIdp)` which dereferences `storedIdp.getInternalId()` and `storedIdp.getAlias()`, causing a NullPointerException. While this path is unlikely in normal flows (the caller usually confirms existence), the method is part of the public storage provider API and should handle null gracefully. The previous code also had this issue, but the refactoring makes it more explicit and still unresolved.

title: Login cache is not invalidated when an organization is enabled or disabled
body: The getForLogin cache key is invalidated only in registerIDPLoginInvalidation and registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate, which are triggered by IDP create/update/remove. However, the login eligibility also depends on the organization's enabled state (enforced by the organization-aware wrapper added elsewhere). If an organization is disabled after the cache is populated, the cached login list still includes IDPs from that organization, potentially showing them on the login page or allowing them to be used for authentication by consumers that do not re-check isEnabled(). The cache should be invalidated when an organization's enabled state changes, but there is currently no mechanism to register such invalidation. This leads to stale, security-relevant data.

title: Test cleanup uses literal "alias" instead of the actual alias variable
body: In both testCacheIDPByOrg and testCacheIDPForLogin, the cleanup registration `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove);` passes the string "alias" instead of the loop variable `alias`. This means the created identity providers are not cleaned up after the test, leaving leftover data that can affect subsequent tests. It should be `testRealm().identityProviders().get(alias)::remove`.

title: Non-deterministic provider selection when order values are equal
body: detectProvider sorts providers by order descending and picks the first. If two or more providers have the same order (e.g., DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all have order 200), the selection depends on the unspecified iteration order of ServiceLoader. Previously, the code threw an IllegalStateException when multiple providers were found, preventing this ambiguity. Now, a misconfigured classpath could silently select the wrong crypto provider, leading to runtime failures or security issues (e.g., using non-FIPS provider in a FIPS-required environment). The selection should either require unique order values or handle ties explicitly (e.g., throw if multiple providers share the highest order).

title: Dead code: encoders created and discarded
body: Lines 114-115 create new ASN1Encoder instances, write BigInteger values to them, and discard the results. This is dead code and should be removed. It does not affect correctness but is confusing and wasteful.

title: Indefinite-length ASN.1 sequences are silently accepted as empty
body: readLength() returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding (tag 0x80). readSequence() then loops while length > 0, so a sequence with indefinite length will yield an empty list without consuming any content. This is incorrect and can lead to parsing failures or silent misinterpretation of input. For DER-encoded ECDSA signatures (which must be definite-length), the decoder should throw an IOException or support indefinite-length properly.

title: Length validation uses total buffer size instead of remaining bytes
body: The check `if (length >= limit)` compares the declared length against the total byte array length, not against the number of bytes remaining to be read. If a length is smaller than the total buffer but larger than the remaining unread bytes, the check passes and the subsequent read will eventually hit EOF and throw IOException. While not a security issue, the validation is not accurate and may allow malformed input to be processed further than necessary.

title: Test uses a single EC key pair for all three curves
body: The test generates one KeyPair using the default EC curve (likely secp256r1) and uses it to sign data for ES256, ES384, and ES512. The signature length passed to asn1derToConcatenatedRS/concatenatedRSToASN1DER depends on the curve, but the actual key does not match the algorithm's curve. The test only verifies round-trip conversion, which may pass even if the conversion is incorrect for certain curves (e.g., handling of leading zeros). The test should generate a proper key pair for each algorithm to ensure the conversion functions work correctly across different key sizes.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default keystore provider, not BouncyCastle
body: The method getBouncyCastleProvider returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which is typically the SUN or SunJCE provider, not BouncyCastle. Other CryptoProvider implementations return an actual BouncyCastle provider. This may mislead callers that expect BC-specific behavior or cause unexpected failures if BC algorithms are requested. The method name is misleading and the implementation may not fulfill the contract.

title: Default authz-client crypto provider throws UnsupportedOperationException for standard operations
body: The service file registers AuthzClientCryptoProvider, and CryptoIntegration now selects providers automatically, so a standalone authz-client classpath with only this provider will use it as the active CryptoProvider. However many methods required by Keycloak JOSE/client-credential flows are implemented as `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet.")`, including getSignature() at line 218. For example, signed-JWT client authentication uses JWSBuilder, which calls CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getSignature(...), so it will fail at runtime. This breaks existing authz-client functionality for private_key_jwt/signed client assertions.

title: Removing the multiple-provider error can silently bypass FIPS provider selection
body: detectProvider() now sorts providers by order instead of throwing when more than one provider is present. But DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return the same order value (200). If a FIPS distribution accidentally also contains keycloak-crypto-default, the first provider among equal order values will be chosen based on undefined ServiceLoader/resource ordering rather than an explicit FIPS decision. This can silently select the non-FIPS DefaultCryptoProvider and violate FIPS mode.

title: Adding abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: CryptoProvider is a public interface, but this change adds a new abstract method `int order()` without a default implementation. Existing third-party or downstream implementations of CryptoProvider will fail to compile against this version, and already-compiled implementations will fail at runtime with AbstractMethodError when loaded through ServiceLoader. A default method with a predictable default order would preserve compatibility.

title: ES384/ES512 tests reuse the same default EC key pair and do not verify signatures
body: The constructor generates a single EC key pair with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")`, which normally uses the default curve (secp256r1/P-256). The same key pair is then used for testES256(), testES384(), and testES512(). The test only round-trips DER<->concatenated R/S encoding using the requested signLength and never verifies a signature, so ES384 and ES512 conversions are not actually validated against an appropriate P-384/P-521 key and incorrect curve-specific behavior can pass unnoticed.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default KeyStore provider, not BouncyCastle
