Enforce the limit in a transaction with an appropriate lock/serialization, or use an atomic insert-and-check mechanism.

title: RowsAffected()==0 is treated as a limit hit, but MySQL reports changed rows, not matched rows
body: updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached whenever RowsAffected() is zero. On MySQL (unless clientFoundRows=true is configured), UPDATE returns the number of rows actually changed, not matched. If an existing device at the limit sends a request with the same client_ip/user_agent and the same second-precision updated_at as the stored row, the UPDATE is a no-op, RowsAffected() is 0, and a legitimate existing device is rejected. This can happen when multiple Grafana instances handle the same device in the same second because the in-process cache does not coordinate replicas. Check existence separately or use a driver-independent matched-row approach.

title: Device-limit tests only cover the store's rejection path
body: The new test only calls ProvideAnonDBStore directly and checks that a second new device ID returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. It does not cover (a) an existing device still updating when the limit is reached, (b) the Anonymous auth client rejecting an over-limit device, or (c) the local-cache interaction that currently allows the device after the first rejection. Add a service/auth-level integration test with a nonzero AnonymousDeviceLimit.

title: New device_limit setting is not documented or added to defaults.ini
body: The PR adds a user-facing auth.anonymous device_limit option, but no sample/default config or documentation is updated. Users cannot discover the new setting from defaults.ini or the configuration reference. Add it to conf/defaults.ini and the anonymous auth configuration docs.

title: Cleanup progress logged at Error level with full ID list
body: All the new progress/success log statements use `r.log.Error` instead of `r.log.Debug`/`Info`: 'Annotations to clean by time' (line 534), 'cleaned annotations by time' (537), 'Annotations to clean by count' (554), 'cleaned annotations by count' (557), 'Tags to clean' (576) and 'cleaned tags' (579). These fire on every successful batch of every cleanup cycle (and the cycle now runs every minute), so normal operation will continuously emit error-level logs that trigger alerting/noise. Worse, each call logs the entire `ids` slice, which can contain up to `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` IDs (the new test uses a batch size of 32767), producing enormous log lines and substantial log-storage pressure. These should log at Debug level and log only `len(ids)`, not the full slice. This looks like debugging output left in by accident.

title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The cleanup job interval was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`, making the entire cleanup suite (temporary files, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, old annotations, user invites, short URLs, query history) run ten times more often. This change is unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (avoiding annotation cleanup deadlocks), is not mentioned in the description, and does the opposite of helping: running the annotation deletes far more frequently increases write/lock contention on the annotation tables rather than reducing it. It should be reverted (or, if intentional, justified and validated separately), otherwise production DB load and contention increase by an order of magnitude.

title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, likely a test leftover
body: The cleanup loop's ticker was reduced from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. Nothing in the PR description or the annotations-cleanup change requires this; it looks like a debug leftover used while testing. This makes every cleanup job run 10x more often (temp files, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, temp users, short URLs, and the query-history row-limit enforcement of 200k/150k rows), sharply increasing DB and IO load on large deployments. If the intent was to compensate for possible under-deletion in the annotations job, that should be scoped to annotations only and documented, not applied to the global ticker.

title: Routine cleanup progress is logged at Error level with full ID slices and a nil err
body: All six new log lines (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579) use `r.log.Error(...)` for normal per-batch progress, and each logs the entire `ids` slice (up to the configured batch size) plus `"err", err`. The first log of each pair always passes `err` from `fetchIDs` after it has already been nil-checked, so it emits an ERROR line with `err=nil`; the second logs the delete error, which is also returned to the caller. Consequences: cleanup now floods the error log on every cycle (and with the ticker change, every minute), formatting potentially tens of thousands of IDs per line, which wastes CPU/memory and produces false ERROR signals that will trigger alerting. These should be Debug-level messages and should not dump the full ID list or log a nil error.

title: SQLite inline-ID branch builds the value list in O(n^2) time
body: In the SQLite path of `deleteByIDs`, the ID list is built incrementally with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)`. Each iteration allocates and copies the entire growing string, so building a list of n IDs is O(n^2) in bytes copied. The newly added test deliberately exercises batch size 32767, where this copies on the order of gigabytes per delete and dominates the runtime; with large configured batch sizes it also burns real CPU in production. Use a `strings.Builder` (or `strconv.AppendInt` into a byte slice) to build the list in linear time.

title: Only SQLite's bind-parameter limit is handled; large batches on MySQL/Postgres can exceed the placeholder limit
body: `deleteByIDs` special-cases SQLite (over 999 parameters are inlined) but otherwise emits `len(ids)` `?` placeholders. `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` is a configurable value and `fetchIDs` can return up to that many IDs, so with a large configured batch size on MySQL or Postgres the generated DELETE can exceed the driver/server placeholder limit (commonly 65535) and fail with "too many placeholders"/"bind message has N parameter formats". Either cap/validate the batch size or apply the same inline / chunking strategy for all dialects.

title: Annotation cleanup tests are now skipped under -short, removing short-mode coverage
body: `TestAnnotationCleanUp` and `TestOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst` were renamed to `TestIntegration...` and now `t.Skip` when `testing.Short()` is set. Previously these DB-backed tests ran in short mode (they use the in-memory/test DB via `db.InitTestDB`), so they were the only coverage for the batched cleanup logic. After this change, short-mode CI runs no longer exercise `CleanAnnotations`, `fetchIDs`, `deleteByIDs`, or `untilDoneOrCancelled` at all. If the intent is to move them to integration CI, that is fine, but it should be confirmed that a non-short job actually runs this package, otherwise the rewritten cleanup path is effectively untested in most CI runs.

title: Cleanup scheduler interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute for every cleanup job
body: Changing the ticker from time.Minute*10 to time.Minute*1 makes the whole CleanUpService run all cleanup jobs ten times as often. This PR is about annotation deadlocks, and this change is neither mentioned nor justified. Because clean() is synchronous and has a 9-minute timeout, a 1-minute ticker will queue a tick while a long cleanup is running and then immediately start another run, so cleanup can execute back-to-back and increase database and CPU load. Revert to 10 minutes unless this operational change is deliberate and justified.

title: Successful annotation cleanup batches are logged at Error level with the full ID list
body: The new fetch/delete loop logs 'Annotations to clean by time', 'cleaned annotations by time', and the equivalent orphan-tag messages via r.log.Error unconditionally, including when err is nil and when the batch is empty. The callback always runs once, so an idle cleanup still emits ERROR entries, and for large batches the ids value can contain thousands of IDs. This floods error logs and alerting and makes real failures hard to find. Normal progress should be logged at Debug, with Error reserved for actual failures; all new r.log.Error calls at lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579 need this treatment.

title: High batch sizes can exceed MySQL/PostgreSQL bind-parameter limits
body: deleteByIDs only special-cases SQLite. For MySQL/PostgreSQL it builds one ? placeholder per fetched ID (line 615), and those servers reject statements with more than 65535 bind parameters. If AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is configured above that limit, every batch DELETE fails with a parameter-count error and annotation cleanup stops; the previous single DELETE with a subquery had no such parameter limit. The code should also chunk or inline for non-SQLite dialects, or clamp the configured batch size.

title: Async legacy writes use the request context and get cancelled when the handler returns
body: Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection launch the legacy write in a goroutine that derives its context from the request-scoped `ctx` (line 51 `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, ...)`; same pattern at lines 110, 135, 163). The apiserver cancels that context as soon as the handler returns, which is immediately after the goroutine is spawned. The legacy backup write is therefore usually aborted with `context canceled` before it runs, so mode 3's safety-net write to legacy silently does not happen and the legacy-store metrics record spurious failures/timeouts. Detach the goroutine's context from the request (e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` to keep values, or a fresh background context) so it survives handler completion.

title: Storage failures are recorded into the legacy metric and legacy writes into the storage metric
body: On the Storage error-return path, Create calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ..., startStorage)` (line 45) and Update does the same (line 129) instead of `recordStorageDuration`. Conversely the DeleteCollection legacy goroutine records its result via `d.recordStorageDuration(...)` (line 166). As a result storage errors/latency are attributed to the legacy store and legacy-write errors to unified storage, making the per-backend error and latency metrics/dashboards wrong. Use `recordStorageDuration` for the Storage call and `recordLegacyDuration` for the Legacy call on every path.

title: Delete records the object name as the resource `kind` metric label
body: In the Delete success path the storage duration is recorded with the object name passed as the `kind` argument: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` (line 106). The third parameter of `recordStorageDuration` is the resource kind, so every deleted object adds a new label value, exploding metric cardinality and mislabeling the series. It should pass `options.Kind`, as all the other calls do.

title: Async legacy-write failures are never logged
body: The legacy-write goroutines capture the legacy error but only feed it to a metric and never log it (e.g. Create lines 55-56 `_, errObjectSt := d.Legacy.Create(...)` then `d.recordLegacyDuration(errObjectSt != nil, ...)`; same in Delete, Update and DeleteCollection). The previous synchronous implementation logged these failures with `log.Error`. Now a failed legacy backup write is invisible in logs, so operators cannot diagnose why the legacy copy is missing. Log the error inside the goroutine (using a logger not tied to the soon-to-be-cancelled request context).

title: mode 3 integration tests race the asynchronous legacy write
body: The new mode 3 subtests reuse `doPlaylistTests`, which after writing through the k8s API immediately reads the legacy `/api/playlists` endpoint and asserts the same UIDs are present (line 529), and `getFromBothAPIs` does a legacy GET right after each k8s write. Mode 3 writes to legacy asynchronously, so these assertions race the background write and can fail intermittently (and will fail deterministically while the request-context cancellation bug exists). The test needs to wait/poll for the legacy copy to appear (e.g. `require.Eventually`) rather than asserting immediately.

title: Unit tests never assert the legacy (async) write and don't wait for the goroutine
body: TestMode3_Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection set up expectations on the legacy store but never verify the legacy write occurred (no `AssertCalled`/`AssertExpectations`) and never wait for the goroutine. Because the legacy write is fire-and-forget, the tests pass even if the legacy path never runs, so the defining behavior of mode 3 (dual write to legacy) is not actually tested. The goroutine can also still be invoking the shared `*mock.Mock` and metrics registry after the subtest returns, which can cause data races/flaky failures under `-race`. Wait for the goroutine (channel/WaitGroup) and assert the legacy call was made.

title: Delete stores the wrong logger in the context
body: Delete does `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` (line 97) using the base logger instead of the per-request `log` that carries name/kind/method fields, unlike Create/Get/List/Update/DeleteCollection. Downstream storage.Delete error logs therefore lose the request-scoped fields, making them harder to correlate. Use `log` here as the other methods do.

title: Async legacy writes use the request context, which is cancelled when the handler returns
body: All four async goroutines (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) derive their context via `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` from the handler's request `ctx`. In the Kubernetes apiserver (net/http) the request context is cancelled as soon as the handler returns, which happens immediately after these goroutines are spawned. The legacy call therefore usually receives an already-cancelled context and aborts before writing. The whole point of mode 3 (best-effort async replication to legacy as a safety net) will silently not happen. Detach first, e.g. `context.WithTimeoutCause(context.WithoutCancel(ctx), ...)`, so the goroutine is not tied to the request lifetime.

title: Unified-storage errors are recorded on the legacy metric (and storage errors not counted)
body: In Create the error branch after `d.Storage.Create` records `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` using `startStorage`; it should record a storage-failure metric (`recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`). The same mistake exists in Update at line 129. As a result a failed unified-storage write is reported as a legacy-write failure, the unified-storage error rate is under-reported, and the legacy error rate is inflated, making the metrics misleading for exactly the failure everyone cares about.

title: Delete success path passes the object name as the `kind` label
body: On the success path of Delete, `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` where the metric expects the resource `kind` (every other call site passes `options.Kind`). This mislabels the metric and, worse, makes the `kind` label take on every individual object name, causing unbounded label cardinality in the Prometheus metric. Use `options.Kind`.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection result recorded with the storage metric
body: Inside the DeleteCollection goroutine the legacy call's outcome is recorded via `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)`. It should be `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`, consistent with the other legacy branches. As written, legacy delete-collection failures/successes are attributed to the unified-storage metric and the legacy metric never sees them.

title: Delete stores the unfielded logger in the context
body: Delete builds `log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method)` but then does `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` instead of `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`. The context passed to `d.Storage.Delete` and to the async legacy goroutine therefore lacks the name/kind/method fields, so log lines from these operations cannot be correlated as intended. Should use `log`.

title: Async legacy write failures are no longer logged
body: The previous synchronous implementation logged errors from the legacy write (`unwrap...Error(err, "unable to create object in legacy storage")`, etc.). The new goroutines (Create line 55, Delete line 112, Update line 139, DeleteCollection line 165) only increment a metric and never log `errObjectSt`/`err`. Combined with the context-cancellation issue above, legacy writes can fail completely invisibly; operators have no log line to diagnose drift between unified and legacy storage. Log the error (with kind/name) inside the goroutine.

title: Tests do not verify or synchronize the async legacy writes
body: The new unit tests set up legacy mock expectations but never assert them (no `m.AssertExpectations` on the legacy calls) and provide no synchronization (channel / `require.Eventually`) to wait for the spawned goroutines. Because the legacy write happens in a goroutine that may run after the subtest returns, the tests pass even if the legacy write never occurs, so the central new behavior of mode 3 (async dual write) is effectively untested. Add a wait/assertion that each legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection is actually invoked with the expected object.

title: Mode 3 integration runs assume immediate legacy consistency but legacy writes are async
body: The newly added mode 3 subtests (file at line 132, unified storage at line 191) reuse `doPlaylistTests`, which after a k8s create/update immediately asserts the same object is visible through the legacy API (the `/api/playlists` list compare and `getFromBothAPIs` legacy GET). In mode 3 the write to the legacy/SQL store happens asynchronously in a goroutine, so those assertions can observe stale data and fail intermittently. Either wait for eventual consistency (e.g. poll the legacy API) for mode 3, or don't run the synchronous legacy-consistency assertions under mode 3.

title: Async legacy writes are derived from the request context and get canceled when the request returns
body: In Create (line 51), Update (line 135), Delete (line 110) and DeleteCollection (line 163), the background goroutine derives its context via context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...) from the ctx passed into the handler, which is the request-scoped context. The API server cancels the request context as soon as the response is written and the handler returns, so these goroutines will usually see context.Canceled almost immediately and the LegacyStorage call will abort before writing. This defeats the entire purpose of mode 3 (mirroring writes to the legacy store as a safety net): most legacy writes will silently never happen. Fix by detaching from cancellation, e.g. context.WithTimeoutCause(context.WithoutCancel(ctx), ...), while still carrying the logger values.

title: Delete records the object name as the metric 'kind' label, creating unbounded label cardinality
body: On success Delete calls d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage). The third argument of recordStorageDuration is the kind label (every other call passes options.Kind), so here the object's metadata.name is used as the kind label. Object names are request/user-controlled and unbounded (generated names, arbitrary names), so this turns the storage-duration metric into a high-cardinality metric and can cause memory growth / scrape slowdowns. It should pass options.Kind.

title: Storage failures are recorded as legacy durations
body: In Create the error branch calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) even though the operation that just failed was the synchronous Storage.Create (and startStorage measures the storage call), so storage errors are attributed to the legacy-store metric. The same mistake exists in Update at line 129. Both should call recordStorageDuration with the storage timing. As-is, the storage error-rate/latency dashboards will be wrong and legacy error metrics will be inflated.

title: DeleteCollection records the legacy operation as a storage duration
body: Inside the DeleteCollection goroutine the legacy store's DeleteCollection result is recorded with d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). Since startLegacy and the operation are both the legacy store, this should be recordLegacyDuration. Otherwise legacy latency/errors are counted as unified-storage metrics and the storage metric is polluted with legacy timings.

title: Async legacy write failures are never logged, so legacy drift is invisible
body: After writing to storage, the goroutines call the legacy store and only feed the error into d.recordLegacyDuration(...) (Create line 56, Update line 140, Delete line 113, DeleteCollection line 166). There is no log statement on failure, unlike the previous implementation which logged 'unable to create/update/delete ... in legacy storage'. Because the legacy write is the safety net for mode 3, a persistent failure (e.g. the context cancellation above, or a real legacy error) would silently cause the legacy store to diverge from unified storage with only a boolean counter to show it. Log the error, including the object name/kind, so operators can detect and repair drift.

title: Dual-write tests never wait for or assert the async legacy write, and share one mock for both stores
body: TestMode3_Create (line 65) and TestMode3_Update (line 345) return as soon as the synchronous storage call completes; the background legacy goroutine is not awaited and no assertion verifies LegacyStorage was actually called. Moreover the same *mock.Mock instance is used for both legacyStoreMock and storageMock, so even AssertCalled/AssertNotCalled cannot distinguish storage calls from legacy calls. The test therefore does not exercise the core behavior of mode 3 (async mirroring to the legacy store). The leaked goroutine can also touch the shared, non-thread-safe testify mock and the shared package-level prometheus registry after the subtest has finished, producing data races under -race. Use separate mocks and synchronize on the goroutine (e.g. a channel/WaitGroup injected for tests) before asserting.

title: Mode 3 playlist integration tests read the legacy API immediately after k8s writes and will be flaky
body: The added 'with dual write (... mode 3)' subtests (lines 132-144, 191-204, 287-312) run doPlaylistTests, which performs k8s CRUD and then immediately reads back via the legacy /api/playlists endpoints (e.g. the legacy list at line 523 and getFromBothAPIs at line 623) and asserts identical results. Under mode 3 the legacy write happens asynchronously, so the legacy store may not yet reflect the k8s create/update/delete when the legacy read runs, making require.Equal on the UID/field values intermittently fail. The tests need to wait/poll for the legacy mirror (or the shared helper must account for mode 3's asynchronous write semantics).

title: Delete puts the bare d.Log into the context instead of the enriched logger
body: Delete builds log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method) but then calls ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log), discarding the per-request values. Every other method stores the enriched logger in the context. Downstream Storage.Delete/Legacy.Delete and their logs therefore lose the kind/method/name context that was intended. Use klog.NewContext(ctx, log).

title: Missing double-check after acquiring the write lock causes duplicate manifest loads
body: After reading the cache under RLock and releasing it, the function takes the write lock at line 48 but never re-checks whether the cache was filled by another goroutine in the meantime. On a cold start (or any time the cache is nil in non-Dev env), N concurrent callers all observe `ret == nil` at line 45 and then queue on the write lock; each one runs the full read path (lines 51-67, including reading and JSON-decoding assets-manifest.json, and its error paths) and overwrites the cache. The final value is still correct, but N concurrent requests produce N serialized disk reads/parses instead of one, and every queued request is blocked for the whole duration of the I/O. This is the classic double-checked-locking omission: re-check `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` after `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` and return the cached value early.

title: No test exercises concurrent GetWebAssets calls
body: The PR's sole purpose is to eliminate a data race on the global entryPointAssetsCache, but it adds no test. A race like this is only reliably caught by running concurrent GetWebAssets invocations under `go test -race`; without such a test, a future refactor could reintroduce an unguarded read/write without CI noticing. Add a test that spawns multiple goroutines calling GetWebAssets against a temp manifest and asserts they all get a non-nil, consistent result (run with -race).

title: Missing cache re-check after acquiring write lock causes redundant manifest reads
body: GetWebAssets snapshots the cache under RLock (line 41-43), and if it is nil acquires the exclusive Lock (line 48) but never re-checks entryPointAssetsCache after taking the lock. When the cache is cold (e.g. at startup) or always in Dev mode, every goroutine that saw nil in the read-lock phase queues on the write lock and each one independently performs the manifest file read/JSON decode (and, in Dev, potentially the CDN fetch) while holding the exclusive lock. The result is serialized, repeated I/O for N concurrent requests instead of a single load, and each late arrival overwrites the cache written by the previous one. A double-checked-locking pattern (re-test `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` immediately after `Lock()` and return the cached value) is needed to avoid the thundering-herd recompute.

title: No test verifying the race fix
body: The PR claims to fix a data race on the shared entryPointAssetsCache global, but no test is added that exercises GetWebAssets concurrently (e.g. many goroutines calling it in non-Dev mode with a fixed manifest) and run under `-race`. Without such a test, a future refactor that drops or narrows the locking would silently reintroduce the race without CI detecting it. A concurrency test should be added to lock in the fix.

title: Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock
body: GetWebAssets checks entryPointAssetsCache before taking the write lock but never checks it again after `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()`. If several goroutines observe an empty cache at the same time, each one will acquire the write lock in turn and perform a full manifest read (and, if CDN loading is enabled, an HTTP request) before replacing the global cache. This serializes all late callers behind slow I/O and defeats the cache. It also means a later reload that fails can overwrite an already-populated valid cache with nil, since `entryPointAssetsCache = result` is executed even on error. Re-check `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` immediately after taking the write lock (or use singleflight/double-checked locking) so only the first loader performs the work.

title: No concurrent regression test for the data-race fix
body: This PR exists specifically to fix concurrent access to the global web-assets cache, but no test exercises multiple goroutines calling GetWebAssets while the cache is initially empty and being populated. A race-detector regression test that starts several goroutines against a temporary assets-manifest.json and runs under `go test -race` would verify the synchronization and would also make the missing post-lock cache re-check visible.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false and ignores the feature flag
body: enableSqlExpressions always returns false: if the flag is enabled, the !flag expression yields false so the if is skipped and it returns false; if the flag is disabled, the if is entered and it also returns false. The feature flag FlagSqlExpressions therefore has no effect, and SQL expressions are rejected even for operators who explicitly enable the flag. The enabled := !IsEnabledGlobally(...) computation plus the branch is dead code, and the function name and flag read imply the flag is supposed to control availability. If the flag is intended to keep an opt-in path (the PR description says the flag still exists), the final statement should return true; otherwise it should simply return false and drop the flag read so it is not mistaken for a working security control. As written it is a latent trap: restoring the DB implementation later would still leave the feature permanently disabled.

title: Behavior change disabling SQL expressions is untested; existing SQL tests likely break
body: The change makes TablesList, NewSQLCommand, SQLCommand.Execute and the QueryTypeSQL branch of ReadQuery always fail, but no test files are included in the diff. The new pkg/expr/sql/db.go stubs return errors from RunCommands/QueryFramesInto, so existing tests that call TablesList/NewSQLCommand (for example pkg/expr/sql/parser_test.go and pkg/expr/sql_command_test.go) or that exercise the SQL branch of ReadQuery will now fail with 'not implemented'. There is also no new regression test asserting that a SQL expression is rejected. Add or update tests for the reader rejecting QueryTypeSQL and for the stub behavior so the security fix is covered and CI stays green.

title: Misleading error message: 'sqlExpressions is not implemented'
body: When SQL is disabled the reader returns fmt.Errorf('sqlExpressions is not implemented'). The feature is not unimplemented - it is deliberately disabled for security - so this user-facing error is misleading. Likewise the new stubs in pkg/expr/sql/db.go make TablesList fail, and NewSQLCommand maps that failure to 'error reading SQL command', hiding the real reason a query is rejected. Use a message that states SQL expressions are disabled/unsupported.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false; FlagSqlExpressions is a dead no-op
body: `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` but then returns `false` from both the `if` branch and the fallthrough, so the computed value is never used and SQL expressions are disabled unconditionally. The PR description says the `FlagSqlExpressions` toggle is intentionally kept, yet this code makes it a no-op: turning the flag on will not re-enable the feature, and the dead `enabled` computation plus the negated flag read make the code look like a mistake or a polarity bug. Either return `false` directly (dropping the flag reference) if this is a permanent hard-disable, or use the flag value if the toggle is supposed to remain functional. Leaving it as-is invites a future maintainer to 'fix' the polarity and re-open the vulnerability.

title: No regression test proving SQL expressions are rejected
body: This is a security fix that disables the SQL expression query type, but no test is added or updated to assert that a `type: sql` expression is now rejected by `ReadQuery` (and by `NewSQLCommand`). Additionally, the new `pkg/expr/sql` DB stub makes `TablesList`/`RunCommands`/`QueryFramesInto` unconditionally return 'not implemented', so any existing tests in `pkg/expr` that build or execute SQL expressions will fail unless they are updated. Without a dedicated test, a later change that re-enables the SQL query type or restores a real in-memory DB would not be caught by CI. Add a test that an SQL expression query is rejected.

title: Misleading error text 'sqlExpressions is not implemented'
body: When the SQL query type is encountered, the code returns `fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")`. The feature is not unimplemented; it is intentionally disabled to close CVE-2024-9264. Users with saved SQL-expression panels (and anyone debugging support cases) will read 'not implemented' as a bug or an unfinished feature rather than a deliberate security removal. Use a message that states the feature is disabled, e.g. `"SQL expressions are disabled"`.

title: sqlExpressions feature flag is ignored because the helper always returns false
body: `enableSqlExpressions` sets `enabled` to the negation of `FlagSqlExpressions` and then returns `false` in both branches. The `sqlExpressions` feature toggle therefore has no effect: enabling the documented flag still makes SQL queries fail with `sqlExpressions is not implemented`, and disabling it does the same. If permanent disable is intended, remove or explicitly deprecate the flag and update its documentation; if the flag is supposed to control the feature, this helper must return the flag value. As written the documented toggle is dead and the code hides the intended condition.

title: No regression test verifies SQL expressions are disabled
body: This security fix changes behavior for `QueryTypeSQL`, but no test was added or changed. There is no assertion that a query with `type: sql` is rejected even when `FlagSqlExpressions` is enabled, nor that the disabled path cannot construct or execute an `SQLCommand`. Without such a test, a later change to the helper or the stub DB could silently re-enable the vulnerable path.

title: Stub DB makes SQL command construction fail with a misleading invalid-SQL error
body: `RunCommands` is a stub that always returns an error. `sql.TablesList` calls it, and `NewSQLCommand` calls `TablesList`, so SQL command construction now always fails. Because `NewSQLCommand` converts this into `errutil.BadRequest("sql-invalid-sql", "error reading SQL command")`, users with existing SQL expressions are told their SQL is invalid rather than that SQL expressions have been disabled. The reader path reports a different message. Short-circuit the SQL paths with one consistent disabled-feature error instead of invoking the parser.

title: Eager Init turns any search/DB failure into a fatal Grafana startup failure
body: NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) and returns an error if it fails. Init runs the lifecycle hook (the SQL backend opens the resource DB) and searchSupport.init, which synchronously rebuilds every search index with no timeout. Any failure — a temporarily unreachable resource DB, a single namespace failing to build, a bleve error — now aborts construction of the ResourceServer and therefore Grafana startup, whereas before the server was constructed and only the affected requests failed. Because Init is guarded by sync.Once and the constructed server is discarded on error, there is no retry path: a transient failure requires a process restart. Consider making init failure non-fatal (mark unhealthy instead of failing construction) or bounding the index build with a timeout.

title: Init error path leaks the cancel func, the DB pool, and the search watcher goroutine
body: When s.Init(ctx) returns an error, NewResourceServer returns nil but never calls the cancel func created at line 229 and never invokes s.lifecycle.Stop (which is what calls backend.Stop and closes the resource DB pool opened by lifecycle.Init). Additionally, searchSupport.init has already started its WatchWriteEvents consumer goroutine with context.Background() (search.go:202), which polls the SQL backend every 100ms and is not tied to the server context, so it keeps running forever against a server that was never returned. Clean up (cancel()/Stop) before returning nil, err.

title: Data race on shared err and totalBatchesIndexed inside search index init errgroup
body: In searchSupport.init, every goroutine launched into the errgroup does `totalBatchesIndexed++` and assigns its result to the outer `err` variable (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`; return err). With WorkerThreads > 1 (group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers)) these are unsynchronized writes to the same variables from multiple goroutines: a data race that can make group.Wait() return a nil or unrelated error and corrupt the reported count of indexed namespaces. This is now on the startup path, where a returned error makes the whole server fail to start, so use per-goroutine locals and an atomic counter.

title: TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu
body: bleveBackend.TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without taking cacheMu.RLock, while BuildIndex now writes to the same map from multiple concurrent goroutines (the coarse lock that previously serialized all builds is gone and only the final `b.cache[key] = idx` is locked). A concurrent TotalDocs call — e.g. from a metric collector or while the index for another namespace is being built — can trigger the unrecoverable runtime error "concurrent map iteration and map write" and crash the process. Guard the loop with RLock.

title: No longer serialized: concurrent BuildIndex for the same key races and leaks the losing index
body: Removing the function-wide cacheMu means two BuildIndex calls for the same NamespacedResource can now run simultaneously (e.g. two Search RPCs that both miss the cache for a key, which is exactly the case the TODO in getOrCreateIndex warns about). Both build a full index, both assign to b.cache[key], and the index that loses the assignment is never closed, leaking file handles/disk (bleve file-backed indexes) or memory. The old coarse lock at least serialized the two builds; if per-key concurrency is now intended, add per-key single-flight and close the replaced index before overwriting the cache entry.

title: Postgres variant of the storage-server integration test is skipped, hiding a startup regression
body: This test validates that the storage-server target starts and serves the instrumentation endpoint. Skipping it for GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres (with a TODO saying it only fails in Drone) removes the only coverage for the storage target against Postgres exactly in the PR that makes initialization eager and therefore makes construction depend on the resource_api DB being reachable. If the test now fails because NewResourceServer can no longer be constructed with that configuration, that is the regression the PR should address rather than skip.

title: Concurrent builds for the same index key are no longer serialized
body: BuildIndex used to hold cacheMu for the entire build; now it only locks around the final map write. Two goroutines can call BuildIndex for the same NamespacedResource at the same time because getOrCreateIndex has no per-key lock and both Search and watch-event handling can call it. For file-backed indexes both call bleve.New on the same directory, which can fail or corrupt the index; for memory indexes they create two separate indexes, the last one wins in the cache, and callers may keep using a different instance. Add a per-key mutex or singleflight and re-check the cache under it before building.

title: TotalDocs ranges over the cache without locking
body: TotalDocs iterates b.cache with no cacheMu, while BuildIndex now writes to the same map under cacheMu. The new log line in searchSupport.init (resource/search.go:216) calls TotalDocs after starting the watch goroutine, so an event can trigger getOrCreateIndex/BuildIndex and mutate the map while TotalDocs iterates, causing a fatal concurrent map iteration and map write. Hold cacheMu.RLock in TotalDocs and around all cache iterations.

title: init shares one err variable across errgroup workers
body: Each errgroup goroutine assigns to the outer err via `_, _, err = s.build(...)` and also increments totalBatchesIndexed without synchronization. With multiple workers these are data races; one successful build can overwrite another build's error before it is returned, so errgroup.Wait may see nil and startup can continue with a missing index. Use local per-goroutine error variables (`_, _, buildErr := s.build(...); return buildErr`) and an atomic or mutex-protected counter.

title: Watch loop dereferences nil when the event channel is closed
body: The goroutine receives from events without checking the closed-channel ok value, then passes nil to handleEvent, which dereferences evt.Type. The SQL backend closes its WatchWriteEvents channel when the backend is stopped (defer close(stream) in sql/backend.go:572), so stopping a search-enabled server will panic the process. Receive with `v, ok := <-events` and return when !ok, and tie the watcher to a cancelable lifecycle context. The same closed-channel pattern exists in server.initWatcher.

title: Constructor leaks initialized resources when Init fails
body: NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) and returns nil on failure, but never calls s.cancel() or lifecycle.Stop. If lifecycle.Init and search.init succeeded and a later step such as initWatcher fails, the search watch goroutine and open DB resources are left running with a context that is never canceled. Clean up on the error path before returning.

title: Postgres integration test is skipped, hiding startup regressions
body: This PR changes when unified storage is initialized (constructor instead of first RPC) and the only integration test exercising the storage-server target is now skipped for Postgres. That removes CI coverage for exactly the startup path being changed and can hide failures. Fix the test or add equivalent Postgres coverage instead of skipping.

title: Removing the BuildIndex lock allows concurrent duplicate builds of the same key and concurrent opens of the same on-disk index
body: BuildIndex no longer holds cacheMu while it creates/flushes the bleve index; the mutex is now only taken to assign b.cache[key] = idx at the end. Nothing else serializes builds per key: searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex calls GetIndex (returns nil), then both callers independently call s.build -> BuildIndex (this is also reached from handleEvent). Two concurrent callers therefore both create a bleve index, both run the full storage scan, and the later assignment silently overwrites the earlier cache entry, whose index is never closed (leak for mem-only indexes). For keys above FileThreshold both goroutines call bleve.New on the same directory concurrently, which bleve/bolt does not support and can fail or corrupt the on-disk index. The previous global lock serialized these builds; if it is removed, a per-key lock/singleflight is required (the TODO in getOrCreateIndex explicitly notes this is missing).

title: Data race on err and totalBatchesIndexed inside the errgroup in searchSupport.init
body: The errgroup closures write to function-scoped shared state: `_, _, err = s.build(...)` assigns the outer `err`, and `totalBatchesIndexed++` mutates a shared counter. With group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers) and WorkerThreads > 1 these closures run concurrently, so this is a data race (will be reported by -race). Consequences: the error returned by a closure can be a value written by another goroutine (wrong error propagation), and the 'namespaced_indexed' span attribute is racy/incorrect. Use a closure-local error (`_, _, buildErr := ...; return buildErr`) and an atomic (or per-goroutine) counter.

title: Watch-event consumer dereferences a nil event when the events channel is closed, panicking on shutdown
body: The goroutine started by searchSupport.init does `v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v)` without checking the receive ok flag and without ever exiting. When the storage backend is stopped, the SQL backend's poller closes this channel (defer close(stream) in sql/backend.go), the receive yields a nil *WrittenEvent, and handleEvent immediately dereferences evt.Type -> nil-pointer panic that crashes the process; if the channel were not closed the loop would spin. Additionally the goroutine uses context.Background() and has no way to be stopped. Because this PR makes searchSupport.init run unconditionally during construction, this goroutine (and the shutdown panic) is now always started. Check the comma-ok receive and return when the channel is closed.

title: Writes committed between index build and watch subscription are dropped permanently by searchSupport.init
body: init builds each index from storage and then calls s.storage.WatchWriteEvents, which for the SQL backend starts polling from the *latest* resource versions at subscription time. The per-index RV returned by s.build (the last RV read during the build) is discarded (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`), so any ADDED/MODIFIED/DELETED committed between the build snapshot and the watcher subscription is never applied to the index. The search index is then permanently stale for those resources (deleted documents keep matching, new documents are missing) until that resource is written again. The window is the whole startup index-build duration, so moving init to startup makes this easy to hit. The watch must start before/at the build RV (or events since that RV must be replayed) instead of from the current latest version.

title: Skipping the postgres variant of the storage-server integration test removes the only DB-backed coverage of the new startup path
body: This PR makes NewResourceServer run Init (lifecycle init, search index build via GetResourceStats/ListIterator, and WatchWriteEvents) synchronously during construction. That is exactly the path the storage-server-target integration test exercises, and postgres is the only real database variant left after sqlite is already skipped. Adding a skip with a TODO hides whatever failure the change introduces (e.g. unified-storage tables/migrations not being available when the resource server is constructed, or a startup error/hang) and leaves zero postgres coverage for the storage server target. The underlying failure should be fixed, or at minimum tracked by an issue referenced from the TODO, rather than silently skipping.

title: Call to undefined isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() breaks compilation
body: UsernameForm.authenticate calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments, but UsernameForm, UsernamePasswordForm, and AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator do not define a no-argument method with that name. The only method added by this PR is UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel). This is a compile error, so the services module cannot build. The call should pass context.getUser() or use a correctly defined passkeys-enabled helper.

title: Conditional passkeys are no longer rendered when the user is unidentified
body: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel) returns false when user is null (line 161), but fillContextForm() is now gated on this helper both in authenticate() at line 115 and in the error challenge override at line 137. Before this change, authenticate() filled conditional WebAuthn when context.getUser() was null and challenge(error, field) explicitly filled only when context.getUser() == null. On the first username/password page, after a username-only submission, and after a failed password while the user is still unidentified, fillContextForm() is therefore not called, so the WebAuthn challenge, RP ID, and ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI attributes are absent. Discoverable passkeys will not auto-fill/one-tap and the webauth form is missing, breaking first-login passkey flows and tests that expect //form[@id='webauth'] on those pages. The fill condition must remain true for passkeys-enabled realms even when no user is identified, while also running for known re-authenticating users.

title: UsernameForm calls a no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() that does not exist
body: Line 47 calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments. The only method with that name is `UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel)` (UsernamePasswordForm.java line 160); neither UsernameForm nor any superclass in the changed files defines a no-arg overload, so this class does not compile. If a no-arg overload is added, it must return whether passkeys are enabled independently of the current user, otherwise the initial login page stays broken (see the UsernamePasswordForm finding).

title: Null-user guard disables conditional passkey UI on the initial login page
body: `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel)` (line 161) returns false when `user == null`, and it is used at lines 115 and 137 to decide whether to call `fillContextForm`. `fillContextForm` is what sets `ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI`, the WebAuthn challenge, RP ID, user-verification, etc. Since `context.getUser()` is null on the initial username/password page and on invalid-username errors, the conditional passkey autofill/`#webauth` form is no longer rendered there. Previously `fillContextForm` was called exactly in the `user == null` branch, so this swap inverts the behavior. Consequence: the username field loses `autocomplete="username webauthn"`, discoverable-key automatic login on the first page stops working, and unchanged tests fail (e.g. PasskeysUsernameFormTest.passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey lines 183-190, PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest lines 145-146, PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest lines 192-194). `fillContextForm` should run whenever passkeys are enabled, regardless of whether a user is already set.

title: Unused NoSuchElementException import after replacing assertThrows
body: The diff removes the only two usages of `NoSuchElementException` (the `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, ...)` calls) but leaves the import on line 51. Keycloak's checkstyle rejects unused imports, so the build will fail unless the import is removed.

title: Unused PasswordCredentialModel import
body: `PasswordCredentialModel` is imported on line 35 but never referenced in the file (the tests use `WebAuthnCredentialModel` and `getPassword`). This would be flagged/failed by checkstyle as an unused import.

title: reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey does not test a user without a passkey
body: The test name and intent say it covers a user who has no passkey, but `setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(Boolean.FALSE)` disables passkeys for the whole realm, which is a different code path (`WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator.isPasskeysEnabled` returns false and `fillContextForm` is never invoked). The new code only checks the realm policy, not whether the re-authenticating user actually has a passkey, so a user with only a password would still be shown the passkey UI during re-authentication. Add a case that keeps passkeys enabled for the realm and re-authenticates a user that has no passkey credential, to verify the expected fallback to password (especially for the UsernameForm flow).

title: Call to non-existent isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() does not compile
body: UsernameForm.authenticate now calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments, but the only method of that name is UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) (declared at UsernamePasswordForm.java:160). Neither UsernamePasswordForm, AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator nor the Authenticator interface defines a no-arg overload, so this class will not compile. Either pass the user (isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())) or add the intended no-arg overload.

title: Conditional passkey UI is no longer enabled for unauthenticated (user == null) logins
body: The new helper returns false whenever user is null because of the trailing `&& user != null`. Both new call sites in this file, authenticate() at line 115 and challenge(context, error, field) at line 137, pass context.getUser(). Before this change fillContextForm() was deliberately called when the user was NOT yet identified (the original code was inside the `user == null` branch and guarded with `context.getUser() == null`). As a result the initial/anonymous login page will no longer render the conditional passkey UI (the `#webauth` form and `autocomplete="username webauth"`), so discoverable-key/passkey autofill login stops working and the feature regresses. This directly contradicts unchanged assertions such as PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest.passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey (lines 145-146) and PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest.passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey (lines 192-194), which expect the `#webauth` form on the anonymous page. The guard should not depend on user being non-null (fill for both null and non-null users), otherwise re-authentication cannot be fixed without breaking first-time passkey login.

title: reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey does not exercise a user without a passkey
body: The test name promises to cover re-authentication of a user who has no passkey, but the body only disables passkeys for the whole realm via setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(Boolean.FALSE). Since UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(user) checks only the realm passwordless policy plus `user != null` and never consults the user's credentials, the actually interesting case - passkeys enabled for the realm, user has no registered passkey, re-authentication page is rendered - is never tested. In that case the passkey control would be offered even though it cannot succeed. Add a test that leaves passkeys enabled and uses an account with no WebAuthn/Passkey credential.

title: Cleanup registers the literal alias "alias" instead of the created provider alias
body: In the new testCacheIDPForLogin, cleanup is registered as `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove);` using the string literal "alias" rather than the alias of the provider just created (`"idp-alias-" + i`; the same mistake is repeated on line 425 for `idp-alias-20`). At teardown this invokes remove() on a non-existent provider (typically a 404/WebApplicationException, which can fail the test teardown), and none of the 20+ `idp-alias-*` providers the test creates are ever deleted. They leak into the realm and can break later tests in the class that assume a clean IDP set or re-create the same aliases. It should use `idpRep.getAlias()` (or `"idp-alias-" + i`) in the cleanup.

title: Login-cache invalidation on update computes the 'original' state from an org-aware wrapper, so disabling an IDP of a disabled org is not invalidated
body: In update(), `original` is obtained via `getById(model.getInternalId())`, which returns `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(...)` whose `isEnabled()` returns false when the linked organization is disabled (see line 141 and 436-443). However the login cache is populated from the raw `enabled` column (the delegate's `getForLogin`/`getAllStream` ignores organization enabled state), so an IDP linked to a currently-disabled organization is present in the cached login list while `getLoginPredicate().test(original)` evaluates to false for it. `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate` then hits the `!predicate(original) && !predicate(updated)` early-return at line 405 and skips invalidation when that IDP's own `enabled` flag is set to false, leaving a now-disabled IDP in the cached list returned by `getForLogin` (violating the method contract that it returns login-eligible IDPs). create()/remove() use raw (un-wrapped) models, so update() is inconsistent with them. The original state used for the login predicate should be the raw model (e.g. from `idpDelegate`), not the organization-aware wrapper.

title: New remove() login invalidation path is only tested with a non-login IDP
body: The test removes `idp-alias-1`, which was created disabled (`enabled = (i % 2) == 0`), so it only exercises the negative branch of the newly added remove() logic (`registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp)` where the provider is not login-eligible and therefore must not invalidate the caches). No test removes an enabled, public IDP and asserts that the login caches ARE cleared, so the positive invalidation path added to remove() is untested; a regression there (or an NPE/pruning of the newly introduced `storedIdp` lookup) would go unnoticed.

title: Login cache invalidation can be skipped when the original IDP is org-disabled
body: registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate evaluates getLoginPredicate() against the original model returned by getById(), which is wrapped by createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(). That wrapper's isEnabled() returns false whenever the associated organization (or the organization provider) is disabled, even though the raw IDP is enabled and may already be present in the login cache populated from the delegate. If an admin then updates that IDP while the organization is disabled, e.g. sets hideOnLogin=true, linkOnly=true, or enabled=false, the updated raw model also fails the predicate because of the changed login field. The method therefore returns at this guard without invalidating any cacheKeyForLogin entry, leaving the stale internal id in the login cache. After the organization is re-enabled, getForLogin() returns that IDP even though it is hidden/link-only/disabled; the new OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean only rechecks isEnabled(), so hidden or link-only IDPs can still be displayed. Cache membership must be compared using the same raw IDP state used to populate the delegate query, not the organization-aware wrapper.

title: Cleanup removes literal alias 'alias' instead of the created alias
body: The cleanup action is bound to testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove, so the receiver is resolved immediately for an IDP whose alias is literally 'alias'. The IDPs just created as idp-alias-N are never removed, and the cleanup may also fail with a 404. The same mistake appears at line 425. This leaks up to 20 IDPs into the test realm and can make count-based assertions in this test class order-dependent. Use get(alias)::remove for the actual alias, or remove the created IDPs in @After.

title: Positive create/remove invalidation paths for login IDPs are not tested
body: The new test only creates and removes IDPs that do not qualify for login (disabled or hideOnLogin=true) and asserts that the login caches remain. The new registerIDPLoginInvalidation calls in create() and remove() are never exercised for a login-qualified IDP, so a regression where creating or removing a visible enabled IDP fails to invalidate the login caches would still pass this test. Add steps that populate the caches, then create and remove an enabled, visible IDP and assert all login caches are invalidated.

title: Login-cache invalidation can be skipped for IDPs in a disabled organization
body: registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate evaluates getLoginPredicate() against original, which is obtained via getById(). getById() returns createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(), whose isEnabled() returns false when the IDP's organization is disabled (or the organization provider is disabled). The login cache, however, is populated from idpDelegate.getForLogin(), which filters the raw stored IDP and does not consider organization enabled state, so an org-linked IDP can still be present in the cached list while original tests as not login-eligible. If an update changes hideOnLogin, enabled, or BROKER_PUBLIC while the organization is disabled, both original and updated predicates can evaluate false and the method returns without invalidating any login cache. After the organization is re-enabled, the stale cached ID remains and a hidden/non-public IDP can be returned to login pages. The predicate should be evaluated against the raw stored model rather than the organization-aware wrapper, or org enabled state must be part of the invalidation decision.

title: Test cleanup registers removal for literal alias "alias", leaking created IDPs
body: The cleanup registered here (and again at line 425) is testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove, using the literal string "alias" instead of the loop's alias variable. It therefore tries to remove a non-existent IDP rather than the IDPs created by the test. The created IDPs, including ones linked to the shared test-realm organization, remain after the test and can change counts/assertions in other OrganizationCacheTest methods or later tests, making the suite order-dependent. Use the actual alias and avoid double-removal for idp-alias-1, which is removed inline.

title: New test does not cover create/remove invalidation for login-eligible IDPs
body: testCacheIDPForLogin only exercises the non-invalidating create/remove paths: it creates a hidden IDP and removes a disabled IDP, then verifies the login caches remain. It never verifies that creating or removing an IDP that does qualify for login invalidates the per-mode login caches. A regression in the registerIDPLoginInvalidation() calls from create() or remove() would therefore not be caught by this test.

title: Provider selection is nondeterministic when highest order is tied
body: detectProvider now sorts all discovered providers by order and returns the first, only logging the rest at debug. All existing built-in providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, WildFlyElytronProvider) still return order 200, so when more than one is visible there is no unique winner and selection depends on ServiceLoader/JAR order. In a FIPS deployment this can silently select the non-FIPS provider, or at minimum construct/register both providers' global security state before ignoring one, defeating FIPS compliance. The previous code failed fast on multiple providers. The selection should fail on a tie for the highest order or the built-in providers need distinct orders.

title: Adding abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: order() was added to the public CryptoProvider SPI as an abstract method. Third-party implementations compiled against the previous version do not implement it, so ServiceLoader can instantiate them but CryptoIntegration.detectProvider's call to CryptoProvider::order throws AbstractMethodError, breaking all crypto initialization. Make order() a default method with a defined fallback order, or otherwise preserve compatibility with legacy providers.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JVM default KeyStore provider
body: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the provider of the JVM default KeyStore type, which is normally SUN, not BouncyCastle. The CryptoProvider contract documents this method as returning the BouncyCastle security provider, and callers may use the returned provider to resolve BC-specific algorithms or to obtain a provider name. Returning SUN silently gives such callers the wrong provider. Since this minimal authz-client provider has no BouncyCastle dependency, it should return null or throw UnsupportedOperationException rather than return an unrelated provider.

title: ES384/ES512 tests do not use P-384/P-521 keys
body: The test class creates one default EC key pair (typically P-256) and reuses it for testES256, testES384 and testES512. The ES384 and ES512 cases therefore only exercise padding a P-256 signature to 96/132 bytes; they never exercise real P-384/P-521-sized r and s values, nor verify the produced ASN.1 DER against the key. A regression that mishandles full-size ES384/ES512 signatures could pass. Generate the matching curve key pair per algorithm, or use fixed vectors and verify the result.

title: Removing the multi-provider failure and relying on order() allows non-deterministic/unsafe provider selection
body: Before this change, loading more than one CryptoProvider threw an IllegalStateException, which was a deliberate fail-fast guard against ambiguous crypto configuration. The code now silently keeps the highest-order provider and only debug-logs the others. However DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order() == 200 (see the other files in this PR), so when two of them are on the classpath (for example a FIPS deployment that also pulls in keycloak-crypto-default) the sort leaves their relative order unchanged and the winner is the ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order, which is undefined. The result is that a FIPS deployment can silently select the non-FIPS DefaultCryptoProvider instead of failing, i.e. it silently weakens crypto/compliance guarantee. Equal orders should be detected and rejected (or at minimum given distinct, guaranteed values) rather than resolved by an arbitrary tie-break.

title: Adding order() as an abstract method breaks existing third-party CryptoProvider implementations
body: CryptoProvider is a public interface in keycloak-common that external/extension code implements (custom FIPS variants, etc.). Adding `int order();` as a non-default abstract method is a source- and binary-incompatible change: existing implementations will no longer compile, and prebuilt implementations will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when CryptoIntegration.detectProvider sorts by CryptoProvider::order. Since the interface already uses default methods (getSupportedKeyStoreTypes, getSupportedRsaKeySizes), order() should be declared `default int order() { return 0; }` so existing providers keep working and get a sane default priority.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default KeyStore provider instead of a BouncyCastle provider
body: The method contract (see the interface Javadoc) is to return the BouncyCastle security provider (non-FIPS or FIPS). This implementation returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which is normally SunJSSE/SUN, not BouncyCastle. Any consumer that calls CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getBouncyCastleProvider() and then uses it as a provider argument to Signature.getInstance(..., provider) or similar will get the wrong provider and fail or behave incorrectly. If no BC provider is available, returning null (as WildFlyElytronProvider does) is safer than returning an unrelated provider.

title: Dead/unused encoder calls in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
body: The two statements `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` create encoders, write into them, and immediately discard the result. They have no effect on the returned value (the actual sequence is built in the following writeDerSeq block) and are leftover code that will confuse maintainers and inflate the method. They should be removed.

title: Test uses a default (P-256) key for all ES256/ES384/ES512, so ES384/ES512 are not exercised realistically
body: The key pair is generated with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, which on standard JDKs defaults to a P-256 key regardless of the algorithm under test. ES384 and ES512 are still run over this P-256 key, so the produced r/s values are only 32 bytes and `integerToBytes(..., len)` just pads them to 48/66 bytes; the real P-384/P-521 cases (where r/s can be 48/66 bytes with leading high bits) are never tested. The round-trip assertion still passes, so the test gives a false sense that the 96- and 132-byte signature paths are validated. Generate a curve-specific key (e.g. `ECGenParameterSpec("secp384r1"/"secp521r1")`) per algorithm.

title: No test covers the new multi-provider ordering/selection logic
body: The core behavioral change of this PR is that detectProvider now sorts providers by order() and picks the highest instead of failing on multiple providers, but there is no test asserting which provider is selected when several are present, nor that the ignored providers are logged. The only added test (ECDSAAlgorithmTest) instantiates AuthzClientCryptoProvider directly and never goes through CryptoIntegration. A test with two registered providers of different order (and ideally an equal-order case) would protect this logic from regressions.

title: Adding abstract `order()` breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: `order()` is added as an abstract method to the public `CryptoProvider` SPI. Existing third-party or downstream `CryptoProvider` implementations compiled against the previous `keycloak-common` do not implement it, and `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider()` now invokes `CryptoProvider::order` on every provider discovered via `ServiceLoader`. Those implementations will fail with `AbstractMethodError` during initialization, turning a previously valid provider into a startup failure. Make `order()` a default method with a sensible default priority, or explicitly handle providers that do not implement it.

title: Provider selection is nondeterministic when real providers have equal priority
body: `detectProvider()` now silently chooses the highest-priority provider, but all existing real providers added in this PR (`DefaultCryptoProvider`, `FIPS1402Provider`, and `WildFlyElytronProvider`) return the same `order()` value of 200. If more than one of them is present on the classpath, the winner depends on `ServiceLoader` iteration/classpath order. In particular, a FIPS deployment that also sees the default provider can silently fall back to non-FIPS crypto instead of failing closed as the old multi-provider check did. Assign distinct priorities to the real security providers, or reject ties involving security-sensitive providers.

title: `getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns the default KeyStore provider, not BouncyCastle
body: The `CryptoProvider` contract says `getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns the non-FIPS or FIPS BouncyCastle security provider. This implementation instead creates a default `KeyStore` and returns its provider, which is normally `SUN`/`SunJSSE`, not BC or BCFIPS. Any caller relying on this method to obtain BouncyCastle will receive an unrelated provider and may fail cryptically or make incorrect security assumptions. Return the actual BC provider if one is available, or throw `UnsupportedOperationException` rather than returning a different provider.

title: New provider-selection behavior is not tested
body: The added test only round-trips ASN.1 ECDSA signatures through the new encoder/decoder. It does not test the central new behavior: loading `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` via `META-INF/services`, or verifying that `CryptoIntegration` chooses the higher-priority `DefaultCryptoProvider` when both providers are on the classpath. A regression in the sorting/selection logic could therefore pass CI. Additionally, the ES384/ES512 cases use the default 256-bit EC key, so they do not actually exercise P-384/P-521 keys.

title: Existing admin-permissions clients never receive the new Clients scopes/resources
body: init() returns as soon as realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is non-null. Realms that already had the V2 admin-permissions client before this change will therefore never get the newly added Clients scopes (configure, map-roles-client-scope, map-roles-composite) or the 'Clients' all-resource. Creating a client permission later fails in AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource when those new scopes are not found ('No scopes found.'), and ClientPermissionsV2 can then fall back to a null resource and NPE in policyStore.findByResource. Initialization needs to be idempotent and upgrade an existing admin-permissions resource server by adding missing scopes/resources.

title: Client-specific resources are looked up with the wrong owner id
body: The third argument to ResourceStore.findByName is the resource owner. V2 per-resource authorization resources are created with owner resourceServer.getClientId() in AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource (line 104), but this lookup passes server.getId(), which is the Keycloak client UUID (see AdminPermissionsSchema.isAdminPermissionClient). The lookup therefore misses the per-client resource and falls back to the 'Clients' all-resource, ignoring per-client grants/denials: per-client MANAGE/VIEW grants do not work, and a per-client negative permission can be bypassed by a global allow. The same owner mistake exists at line 244 for the 'Clients' all-resource lookup. Use the same owner as creation or the two-argument findByName.

title: Client removal event breaks when V2 permissions are enabled
body: The new listener guard checks only Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ, but management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled. If both features are enabled, ClientRemovedEvent reaches clients().setPermissionsEnabled(...), which ClientPermissionsV2 overrides to throw UnsupportedOperationException, so deleting a client can fail. If only V2 is enabled, the listener is skipped entirely and the deleted client's V2 permission resource/policies are never cleaned up. The guard needs to handle V2 explicitly (skip it or provide a no-op/cleanup implementation).

title: canExchangeTo now throws UnsupportedOperationException under V2
body: With ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 enabled, MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() returns ClientPermissionsV2, whose canExchangeTo throws UnsupportedOperationException. Token exchange invokes this evaluator, so token exchange requests will return a 500 instead of a normal authorization decision. Implement the check or return a denial; the other overrides that throw UnsupportedOperationException are similarly reachable from management endpoints and should not leak 500s.

title: getResourceName does not handle the new Clients resource type
body: getResourceName only special-cases USERS. For the newly added CLIENTS resource type it falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), which is not set for resources created by getOrCreateResource. Client permission resources will therefore be shown with null/empty names instead of the client id or 'All clients' in APIs/UI. Add a CLIENTS branch analogous to the USERS branch.

title: requireView/requireViewClientScopes Javadoc incorrectly describes return values
body: The Javadoc for requireView() says 'Returns true if canView() returns true', but the method is void and throws ForbiddenException. The same wrong text is repeated for requireViewClientScopes() at line 101. This contradicts the actual contract and will mislead implementors; document both as throwing ForbiddenException when the corresponding can* check is false.

title: Specific client deny permissions are bypassed when a broad VIEW permission exists
body: canView(ClientModel) first calls no-arg canView(), which returns true whenever the caller has a VIEW permission on the all-clients resource. That short-circuits the method before hasPermission(client, VIEW), which is the only path that evaluates the client-specific resource. As a result, a negative VIEW permission on an individual client is ignored for any admin who also has all-clients VIEW; the admin can still view the denied client. This differs from the intended FGAP behavior exercised by the user-resource tests, where a specific resource overrides the all-resource. The no-arg canView()/all-clients shortcut should not be used here (or must only short-circuit on legacy admin roles), and a test should cover all-clients VIEW plus a client-specific negative VIEW.

title: Client role mapping checks no longer honor MANAGE_CLIENTS
body: canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles and canMapClientScopeRoles return only hasPermission(client, scope). They do not delegate to the V1 implementation or otherwise check root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS), unlike the other overrides in this class. With V2 enabled, an administrator who only has the standard manage-clients role can no longer add client roles, add composites, or map client-scope roles; those endpoints will reject the request. The new tests grant explicit MAP_ROLES/MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE permissions, so they do not catch this regression. At minimum these methods need the MANAGE_CLIENTS check (and should consider a MANAGE grant if MANAGE is meant to be inclusive).

title: Existing admin-permissions clients never receive the new Clients scopes/resources
body: init() returns immediately when the realm already has an admin permissions client. Adding the CLIENTS resource type to SCHEMA only affects realms initialized after this change. After upgrading a realm that already has the admin-permissions client, the Clients scopes (configure, map-roles-client-scope, map-roles-composite, etc.) and the 'Clients' all-resource do not exist. Creating Clients permissions then fails scope validation, and client permission evaluation can fall through to a missing all-clients resource. The existing admin permissions client must be reconciled/updated to add missing scopes and type resources, or a migration is required.

title: Null all-clients resource is dereferenced during client permission checks
body: When no specific client resource exists, hasPermission(ClientModel, scope) obtains the Clients all-resource and immediately calls authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) without checking resource for null. getResourceTypeResource returns null when the resource cannot be found (for example a realm initialized before the Clients resource type was added, or a partially initialized admin permissions client). The authorization check then throws NPE/500 instead of denying. The no-arg hasPermission(String) already handles a missing resource; this method should do the same before calling findByResource.

title: Client resources are not resolved to client IDs for permission representations
body: getResourceName only handles the USERS resource type. Client-specific resources are stored under the internal client UUID, so for CLIENTS the method falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), producing a UUID/null instead of the clientId, and the all-clients resource is not displayed as 'All clients'. This makes permission/resource REST output for the new Clients resource type unreadable or inconsistent with the Users implementation. Add a CLIENTS branch analogous to USERS, including the all-clients case.

title: Client removal handling is skipped for V2 and still throws when both features are enabled
body: The listener body is now guarded only by ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1). When only V2 is enabled, deleting a client no longer triggers any cleanup for V2 client-specific resources/permissions, so those can remain as orphans. When both V1 and V2 are enabled, management(...) returns MgmtPermissionsV2 and clients() returns ClientPermissionsV2, whose setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException, so client deletion can fail. Handle the V2 case explicitly (cleanup or no-op) instead of relying only on the V1 feature flag.

title: New MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE scope is not exercised
body: The PR adds MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE to the Clients scopes and implements canMapClientScopeRoles, but the new test only grants MAP_ROLES, MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE and CONFIGURE and never tests mapping roles to a client scope. A regression in the new client-scope role authorization path would not be detected. Add a test that grants MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE and exercises the corresponding client-scope role operation.

title: Existing admin-permissions clients are not migrated to the new Clients resource type
body: `init` returns immediately when `realm.getAdminPermissionsClient()` already exists. Realms that already enabled ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 before this change therefore never get the newly added `Clients` resource or the new scopes (`configure`, `map-roles-client-scope`, `map-roles-composite`). On such realms, creating a `Clients` scope permission later fails in `getOrCreateResource` because `scopeStore.findByName` returns null for the new scopes and throws `ModelException("No scopes found.")`. Code paths that look up the `Clients` all-resource also receive null. `init` must reconcile an existing admin-permissions client with the current schema instead of only creating it when absent.

title: Per-client resources hide global all-clients permissions
body: `hasPermission(ClientModel, scope)` looks up the client-specific resource and, when one exists, evaluates only that resource. It never evaluates the all-clients `Clients` resource in that case.
