This occurs routinely with at-least-once duplicate/reprocessed spans: a duplicate child is re-added under its parent key and then merged into the destination where the first copy already exists. Since `ZPOPMIN` later uses the score to decide which spans to evict, duplicated spans can be moved to the wrong end of the ordering and be kept or evicted incorrectly. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` or otherwise define duplicate-score handling.

title: No test exercises the new ZPOPMIN eviction path
body: All buffer tests still use only a handful of spans, so the new >1000-span eviction path is completely untested. There is no coverage for the cap being enforced, eviction ordering by `end_timestamp_precise`, retention of a root/segment span, or cleanup/redirect behavior for evicted spans. A regression here silently drops span data, so a test with more than 1000 spans should verify the resulting segment contents and Redis key cleanup.

title: New OptimizedCursorPaginator and audit-log branch have no tests
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` is a new ~90-line paginator used by the audit-log endpoint, but no test instantiates it or calls the endpoint with `optimized_pagination=true`. Basic coverage would have caught both the datetime `TypeError` and the negative-offset `ValueError`. Add tests for first/next/prev pages, forged negative offsets, and the audit-log optimized path.

title: Redirect-chain traversal limit reduced from 10,000 to 1,000
body: The loop that resolves parent redirects was changed from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000`, removing the comment that documented the old limit. If a trace's span-buffer redirect chain is deeper than 1000, the loop stops at an intermediate span id, so the current span is attached to the wrong buffer and segments can be split or duplicated. This is an abrupt behavior change unrelated to the eviction work and has no test; either restore the old bound or justify and test the new one.

title: Switching span-buffer keys from sets to sorted sets breaks existing Redis data and rolling deploys
body: The buffer still uses the existing `span-buf:s:...` key namespace, but now writes with `zadd` and reads with `zscan`/`zcard`. Any keys created by the previous version are Redis sets, not sorted sets. During an upgrade or rolling deploy, processing a batch that touches an existing set key raises a Redis `WRONGTYPE` error at this `p.zadd` or in `add-buffer.lua`; batches then fail and in-flight segments can be lost until those keys expire. The key type change needs a new key namespace/version or an explicit drain/migration before deployment.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot paginate datetime fields used by audit logs
body: `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` now uses `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `order_by="-datetime"`, but `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` applies `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly to the model value and `value_from_cursor` returns the raw cursor value. `AuditLogEntry.datetime` is a `datetime`, so the first non-empty page raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`; even if that were fixed, `build_queryset` would compare a datetime column to an integer. The paginator needs the same timestamp conversion as `DateTimePaginator` or should subclass it.

title: Negative offsets in OptimizedCursorPaginator are passed to Django querysets and raise ValueError
body: The advanced branch accepts a client-supplied negative cursor offset and slices the queryset with it. Django querysets reject negative indexes (`Negative indexing is not supported`), and `Cursor.from_string` accepts negative offsets, so a request with a cursor containing `:-1:0` reaches this line and returns a 500 instead of performing reverse pagination. The same problem remains in the `cursor.is_prev` path at line 182. Negative offsets should be validated/rejected or implemented without negative ORM slicing.

title: max_segment_spans is no longer enforced; eviction cap is hardcoded in Lua
body: The previous `_load_segment_data` check that skipped a segment once it exceeded `self.max_segment_spans` was removed and is not replaced on the Python side. The only cap is now the literal `1000` in `add-buffer.lua`, so `SpansBuffer(max_segment_spans=...)` has no effect, and deployments that configured a different limit silently keep/evict up to 1000 spans without the old `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric. Either pass the configurable limit into the Lua path or remove the parameter and update callers/tests.

title: Redirect depth limit was silently reduced from 10000 to 1000
body: The loop resolving parent redirects now stops after 1000 hops. For a segment tree deeper than 1000, the script writes a redirect to that truncated ancestor and merges spans into a non-root buffer, causing incorrectly split/merged segments. The previous limit was 10000 and had an explanatory comment; this behavior change is unrelated to eviction and has no covering test.

title: No test covers the new zset eviction behavior
body: The changed tests only add the required `end_timestamp_precise` argument to existing `Span` constructions. They never ingest more than 1000 spans into a segment or assert which spans are evicted, so the new `zpopmin` cap, eviction ordering, and root-span retention are untested. Add a case with more than 1000 spans and explicitly verify the cap and evicted members.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle datetime order keys
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` treats every order key as numeric by calling `math.floor`/`math.ceil`. The audit-log endpoint selects this paginator with `order_by="-datetime"`, so any non-empty optimized page calls `math.floor(datetime)` and raises `TypeError`, returning 500. `value_from_cursor` also returns the raw integer cursor value instead of a datetime, so subsequent pages would compare a timestamp column to an integer. The optimized audit-log path is unusable.

title: Negative-offset pagination slices a Django QuerySet with a negative index
body: When `enable_advanced_features` is set and the cursor offset is negative, this branch passes a negative start index to a Django QuerySet slice. Django rejects negative slicing with `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported`; the comment claiming the ORM handles negative slicing is incorrect. `stop = start_offset + limit + extra` also becomes a nonsensical bound when `start_offset` is negative. A caller can therefore trigger a 500 simply by supplying a cursor with a negative offset.

title: Changing span-buffer keys from sets to sorted sets breaks rolling deploys
body: Existing `span-buf:s:*` keys in Redis were written as sets by the previous `SADD`/`SSCAN` implementation. After a rolling deploy those keys can remain for the Redis TTL (default 3600s) and are still referenced by the flush queue, but the new code performs `ZADD` here and `ZSCAN`/`ZCARD`/`ZUNIONSTORE` elsewhere on them. Redis raises `WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value`, so consumers and flushers fail and buffered spans can be lost. This needs a versioned key prefix, backward-compatible handling, or draining the buffer before deploy.

title: ZUNIONSTORE default SUM corrupts eviction scores for duplicate spans
body: `ZUNIONSTORE` without an aggregate uses `SUM`. Span processing is at-least-once, so after a span has been merged into a parent set, a retry can re-add the same payload to the source key; when the sets are merged again the member exists in both destination and source and its score is doubled. The score is `end_timestamp_precise`, so the `ZPOPMIN` eviction ordering is corrupted (an old span can look newer and survive eviction). The merge should preserve the original timestamp, e.g. with `AGGREGATE MAX`.

title: Eviction cap hardcodes 1000 and ignores max_segment_spans
body: The new eviction limit is hard-coded to 1000, while `SpansBuffer` still accepts `max_segment_spans` (default 1001) but no longer uses it. Deployments that configure a different limit are silently ignored, and spans beyond 1000 are dropped without any metric or log because the previous `segment_span_count_exceeded` signal was removed. This changes the configured data-loss boundary without visibility.

title: Redirect loop cap lowered to 1000 can misroute deep traces
body: The redirect-resolution loop was reduced from 10000 to 1000 iterations and the comment documenting the depth limitation was removed. For a project/trace chain longer than 1000 parent links, the loop stops at an intermediate span and writes the redirect to the wrong set, so spans can be merged into the wrong segment or split across segments. The redirect hash is not bounded by the 1000-span eviction cap until flush.

title: No test exercises the new eviction behavior
body: All test changes only add the new required `end_timestamp_precise` field to existing fixtures. There is no test that inserts more than 1000 spans to exercise the new `ZPOPMIN` cap, verifies that the oldest spans are evicted, or checks sorted-set merge behavior for duplicate payloads/scores. The main behavior added by this PR is therefore untested.

title: Accidental gitlink submodule added without .gitmodules
body: This PR adds a gitlink entry at the repository root named `sentry-repo`, pointing at the base commit. No `.gitmodules` entry is added, so `git submodule update --init` will fail with a missing-URL error in CI or normal clone workflows, and the entry is unrelated to the feature. Remove this file from the PR.

title: Tests assign to read-only DRF Request.GET and fail during setup
body: `self.request` is a `rest_framework.request.Request`, whose `GET` attribute is a read-only property. `self.request.GET = QueryDict("")` and the later assignments at lines 79, 83, 87, 97, and 100 raise `AttributeError: can't set attribute`, so the new helper tests never run. Build the query string through `RequestFactory().get("/", data=...)` or set the underlying `_request.GET` instead.

title: Discover eligibility uses a naive substring of request.GET instead of the actual query
body: `_is_error_focused_query` returns True for any raw request query containing `event.type:error`, so it also matches negated or mixed queries such as `!event.type:error` and `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`. It also ignores the actual `query` argument passed to `_get_event_stats`; dashboard split calls with derived `errors_only_query`/`transactions_only_query` are judged against the original request query instead. This can apply `upsampled_count()` to transaction rows where `sample_weight` is absent, or skip upsampling for an error-only derived query, producing incorrect counts.

title: Upsampling check uses the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset
body: `_get_event_stats` receives the actual dataset as `scoped_dataset`, but the upsampling check passes the closure variable `dataset` from `get()`. In the dashboard split path, `_get_event_stats(discover, errors_only_query, ...)` is called while the outer dataset is a metrics dataset, so the helper sees metrics and never applies upsampling to the error split. If the scoped dataset differs in the other direction, the transform can be applied to the wrong dataset. Pass `scoped_dataset` to the helper.

title: Cache key uses Python hash and can collide across project sets
body: The eligibility cache key is `error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))}`. Different project sets can produce the same Python hash, so a cached allowlist result for one set can be reused for another set in the same organization, causing `upsampled_count()` to run for non-allowlisted projects and inflating counts. Use the serialized sorted project IDs (or a cryptographic digest) as the key instead.

title: Internal upsampled_count function is exposed to user queries
body: The new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction does not set `private=True`, unlike neighboring internal functions such as `count_if`. User-supplied queries can therefore request `yAxis=upsampled_count()` directly, bypassing the allowlist/dataset/query checks in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` and obtaining sample-weighted counts for arbitrary projects. Mark it private if it is only intended to be emitted internally.

title: Top-events ordering and equations still use unsampled count()
body: Only `timeseries_columns` is transformed to `upsampled_count()`; `orderby=self.get_orderby(request)` and `equations=self.get_equation_list(...)` still use raw `count()`. For topEvents requests, the top-N groups are selected and ranked by unsampled counts while the returned series shows upsampled counts, and equations containing `count()` remain unsampled. Apply the transform to orderby/equations or reject those combinations.

title: Upsampling transform applied even when the discover query uses the metrics layer
body: The endpoint can route a discover query through the metrics layer via `use_metrics_layer` (line 311), but `upsampled_count` was only registered in `DiscoverDataset`. The transform at line 296 is applied based solely on dataset/request and does not check `forceMetricsLayer` or the `organizations:use-metrics-layer` feature, so in that configuration the generated metrics-layer query can reference an unknown `upsampled_count()` function. Gate the transform on the metrics-layer setting or register the function there.

title: Accidental git submodule entry added to repository
body: The PR adds a file `sentry-repo` containing `Subproject commit a5d290951...`, i.e. a gitlink to the base Sentry commit. No `.gitmodules` entry is included and the change is unrelated to the feature. This will leave a broken/empty submodule in checkouts and can break CI or tooling that recursively updates submodules. Remove the gitlink from the PR.

title: Tests assign to read-only DRF Request.GET and fail in setUp
body: `rest_framework.request.Request.GET` is a read-only property proxying the underlying Django request. Assigning `self.request.GET = QueryDict('')` in `setUp` (and later in the test methods) raises `AttributeError`, so the whole new test module fails before any assertion. Build requests with query strings via `RequestFactory().get('/?query=...')` or mutate `self.request._request.GET` instead.

title: Naive query substring check applies upsampling to non-error queries
body: `_is_error_focused_query` treats the presence of the literal substring `event.type:error` as proof that the query is error-only. Negated filters such as `!event.type:error`, mixed filters such as `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`, or quoted text containing that substring all match. When the dataset is `discover`, this makes the endpoint replace `count()` with `sum(sample_weight)` for queries that also contain transactions or are transaction-only; transactions have no sample weight, so results are wrong or the query fails. Parse the query conditions (or at least handle negation/mixed event.type filters) instead of using `in`.

title: New upsampled_count function is publicly exposed without gating
body: `upsampled_count` is registered in the discover dataset's function converter without `private=True` (unlike neighboring internal functions). This makes it available to user-supplied `yAxis`/query strings even when the project is not allowlisted or the dataset is transactions. In those cases `sample_weight` is absent/meaningless, so users can get ClickHouse errors or counts that bypass the eligibility logic that the helper is supposed to enforce. Mark the function private or otherwise restrict it to the transformed internal path.

title: Upsampling eligibility ignores the scoped dataset and rewritten query
body: `_get_event_stats` computes eligibility with the closure's original `dataset` and with `request.GET['query']`, not with the `scoped_dataset` and `query` parameters that are actually executed. In the dashboard-widget split path, `_get_event_stats` is called with `scoped_dataset=discover` and a rewritten query (e.g. `errors_only_query`), but the check still sees the original dataset (such as `metrics_enhanced_performance`) and original user query. As a result, error-only split queries are not upsampled, and internal query rewrites cannot alter the decision. Pass the actual dataset/query into the eligibility check.

title: Top events ordering still uses raw count while displayed counts are upsampled
body: Only `timeseries_columns`/`y_axes` are transformed to `upsampled_count()`; `orderby=self.get_orderby(request)` is passed through unchanged. For a `topEvents` query ordered by `-count()`, the top N groups are therefore selected by raw event count while the returned series shows upsampled counts. If sample rates differ between groups, the API can return the wrong groups/order. Transform the orderby (and any count references in equations) consistently for top events.

title: Accidental submodule/gitlink `sentry-repo` committed at PR base commit
body: The PR adds a file `sentry-repo` whose only content is `Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a` (the PR base SHA), with no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry in the change. This is a gitlink to a nested repository checkout, almost certainly committed by accident. Checking it in makes the tree contain a broken/uninitialized submodule reference that can confuse CI, `git submodule` tooling, and clean checkouts. It is unrelated to the feature and should be removed before merge.

title: Upsampling decision uses outer `dataset`/`request.GET` instead of the actual `scoped_dataset`/`query`
body: `_get_event_stats` computes `should_upsample` with `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` using the closure variable `dataset` (the originally requested dataset from `get_dataset`) and re-reading `request.GET['query']`. But the actual query built below uses the first parameter `scoped_dataset` and the `query` argument, which in the dashboard discover-split path (lines ~345-452) differ: `_get_event_stats` is called with `discover` and query strings like `(<query>) AND !event.type:transaction` or `(<query>) AND event.type:transaction`. In those calls the eligibility decision is evaluated against the wrong dataset and the wrong query string, so upsampling is either silently skipped for an error sub-query or applied to a transaction sub-query (where `sample_weight` is null), yielding wrong counts. The eligibility check should receive `scoped_dataset` and the actual `query` being executed.

title: `_is_error_focused_query` substring match matches negated and mixed queries
body: `_is_error_focused_query` returns True whenever the raw query string contains the substring `event.type:error`, using `'event.type:error' in query`. That is true for negated filters such as `!event.type:error` (which selects transactions) and for mixed clauses such as `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`. In those cases upsampling is enabled and `count()` is rewritten to `upsampled_count()` even though the query includes/excludes transactions, so `sum(sample_weight)` runs over events that have no sample weight and the reported count is wrong. The check needs to parse the filter rather than do a substring search (or at least exclude negated occurrences).

title: `errors` dataset enables `upsampled_count` but function is only registered in DiscoverDataset
body: `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns True for `sentry.snuba.errors`, so `count()` is rewritten to `upsampled_count()` for `dataset=errors` requests. However the new `upsampled_count` SnQL function is only added to `DiscoverDataset.function_converter` (src/sentry/search/events/datasets/discover.py). If `ErrorsQueryBuilder`/the errors dataset resolves functions through a different converter that does not know `upsampled_count`, every errors-dataset stats request for an allowlisted org will fail with an unknown-function error at query time. Verify the errors dataset shares DiscoverDataset's function converter, or register `upsampled_count` there as well.

title: `sum(sample_weight)` silently drops events with NULL sample_weight
body: `upsampled_count` is defined as `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. ClickHouse `sum` ignores NULL inputs, so any event whose `sample_weight` is NULL is excluded from the count. The helper claims the schema guarantees `sample_weight` for all events (error_upsampling.py:85), but the only code populating it in this PR is gated on `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` (factories.py), i.e. only explicitly sampled events appear to have a weight. Events in an allowlisted project that were ingested without a client sample rate would have NULL `sample_weight` and vanish from the upsampled count, undercounting. Confirm the ingest pipeline writes a default weight of 1 for unsampled events, or use `sum(coalesce(sample_weight, 1))`.

title: Cache lookup and option read run for every stats request regardless of dataset
body: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` builds the cache key and performs `cache.get` before checking whether the dataset is even relevant, and then still calls `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` on a cache hit. `organization_events_stats` is a high-volume endpoint used for transactions/spans/logs, where the result is always discarded, so this adds a cache round-trip (and, on miss, an option read plus `cache.set`) to requests that can never use upsampling. Evaluate `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform(dataset, request)` first and only do the allowlist cache lookup when it is True.

title: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is never called; stale eligibility after allowlist changes
body: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` documents that it must be called when the allowlist configuration changes, but nothing in this PR calls or wires it up. Changing `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` therefore leaves stale eligibility cached for up to 60s per org/project-set, so a newly allowlisted (or de-allowlisted) project keeps the old behavior until the TTL expires. Also note the contradictory documentation: `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` says it always reads the allowlist fresh, while its caller caches the result for 60s. Either wire invalidation into the option-update path or remove the function and correct the docstrings.

title: Empty-allowlist branch is not actually tested
body: Under the comment 'Test when no projects are allowlisted' the test sets `mock_options.get.return_value = []` but then calls `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled([], self.organization)` with an empty project list. That returns False via the earlier `if not project_ids` guard, never reaching the `if not allowlist: return False` branch. The intended case (non-empty project ids with an empty allowlist) is therefore untested; pass `self.project_ids` instead of `[]` to exercise it.

title: New TableWidgetVisualization branch ignores query results and renders an empty table
body: Inside tableResultComponent, when the organization has the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature, the code renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}}/>` instead of passing the actual `result` (its `data`/`meta`) that was fetched and used by the `StyledSimpleTableChart` path. This means any organization with the flag enabled will see completely blank table widgets on dashboards — columns and rows are hard-coded empty and the fetched `tableResults[i]` is discarded. The non-flag path still works, so this is a functional regression gated behind the flag; the new visualization should be fed `result.data`/`result.meta` (and the dataset's custom field renderers) rather than stub values.

title: get_merged_pr_single_issue_template references PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title from the wrong class
body: `_truncate_title` and `get_merged_pr_single_issue_template` were both added as members of `CommitContextIntegration`, but the new staticmethod calls `PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title(title)`. `_truncate_title` is defined on `CommitContextIntegration`, not on `PRCommentWorkflow` (a separate ABC that the GitHub/GitLab comment workflows derive from). Class-level access to `PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title` will raise `AttributeError` at runtime when a merged-PR comment body is generated (the call is unconditional, even for short titles). It should reference the class the method lives on, e.g. `CommitContextIntegration._truncate_title(title)`.

title: Null max_segment_id fix in _make_recording_filenames is not actually exercised
body: The production fix in `src/sentry/replays/usecases/delete.py` adds an early `return []` in `_make_recording_filenames` when `row["max_segment_id"] is None`. The only test change here sets `"max_segment_id": None` in a mocked row, but `delete_matched_rows` (and therefore `delete_replay_recordings`/`_make_recording_filenames`) is fully patched out with `@patch("sentry.replays.tasks.delete_matched_rows")`, so the new null branch is never executed and there is no regression coverage for it. A direct unit test of `_make_recording_filenames` (returning `[]` for a None `max_segment_id`) is needed to validate the fix and catch future regressions.

title: Feature-flagged table widget renders empty data for every table
body: When the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature is enabled, this branch replaces the populated `SimpleTableChart` with `TableWidgetVisualization` initialized with `columns={[]}` and a hard-coded `tableData` containing no rows and empty meta. It never passes `result.data`, `result.meta`, the result title, loading state, or custom field renderers, so every dashboard table widget becomes blank for organizations with the flag on. The new visualization needs to receive the actual `result` data, or the branch must remain disabled until that integration is implemented.

title: Error details can be paired with the wrong replay error IDs
body: `fetch_error_details` builds `node_ids` from `error_ids` and then does `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. `nodestore.backend.get_multi` returns a mapping keyed by node ID and can omit missing nodes; its value ordering is also not guaranteed to match the input list. If any event is missing or the backend returns a different order, the `zip` shifts entries: an error ID is paired with another event's title/message/timestamp, causing incorrect error context in the replay AI summary. Iterate `events.items()` and derive the event ID from the node key, or build a `node_id -> event_id` mapping and look up each result explicitly.

title: Timestamp/age mutual exclusion ignores zero values and neither is required
body: `validate_timestamp` and `validate_age` check the other field via truthiness (`self.initial_data.get("age")` / `get("timestamp")`). Since zero is a valid value for these integer fields, a report containing `timestamp` and `age: 0` (or `age` and `timestamp: 0`) passes validation even though the two fields are supposed to be mutually exclusive. Both fields are also optional, so a report with neither timestamp nor age is accepted, whereas the old structure required a timestamp. Use key-presence checks and enforce that exactly one of the two fields is supplied.

title: PR comment helpers are placed on CommitContextIntegration but used from PRCommentWorkflow
body: `get_merged_pr_single_issue_template` calls `PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title(title)`, but `_truncate_title` is defined on `CommitContextIntegration`. The new helpers are invoked from `GitHubPRCommentWorkflow`/`GitlabPRCommentWorkflow` via `self.get_environment_info` and `self.get_merged_pr_single_issue_template`; those workflows derive from `PRCommentWorkflow`, not from `CommitContextIntegration`, so these methods are not available on `self`. This will raise `AttributeError` when building a merged PR comment. Move the helpers onto `PRCommentWorkflow` (or call them through the integration object) and reference the defining class consistently.

title: Hook can return undefined attributes when the query is disabled or has no data
body: The new `useQuery` return path exposes `data` directly as `attributes`. When `enabled` is false, or before a successful fetch, `data` is `undefined`; the previous implementation always built and returned a `TagCollection` object (falling back to `{}` over `result.data ?? []`). Consumers that spread or iterate `attributes` can now throw. Return a safe default such as `attributes: isFetching ? previous ?? {} : data ?? {}`.

title: New None max_segment_id handling is not actually exercised by this test
body: This test changes the mocked row to `max_segment_id: None`, but `delete_matched_rows` is mocked, so the new `_make_recording_filenames` branch (`if row["max_segment_id"] is None: return []`) is never called. The production fix in `src/sentry/replays/usecases/delete.py` remains untested. Add a test that calls `delete_matched_rows` with a real row or directly calls `_make_recording_filenames` and asserts it returns no filenames for a null segment ID.

title: PR comment template helpers are added to the wrong class
body: The new `get_merged_pr_single_issue_template` and `get_environment_info` helpers are added to `CommitContextIntegration`, but `GitHubPRCommentWorkflow` and `GitlabPRCommentWorkflow` call them on `self` and extend `PRCommentWorkflow`, not `CommitContextIntegration`. `PRCommentWorkflow` has neither method, and this line also calls `PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title`, which does not exist because `_truncate_title` is defined on `CommitContextIntegration`. Generating or updating a suspect-PR comment will raise `AttributeError` instead of posting the comment.

title: Feature flag replaces table data with hard-coded empty table
body: When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, this branch passes `columns={[]}` and an empty `tableData` object to `TableWidgetVisualization` instead of the `fields`, `result.data`, and `result.meta` already computed above. Every dashboard table widget will render as an empty grid under the flag, and the existing loading, metadata, and custom field renderer behavior is lost. It should pass the same table data/columns that the legacy `StyledSimpleTableChart` path uses.

title: Age/timestamp mutual exclusion is bypassed when either value is zero
body: The validators use truthiness (`if self.initial_data.get("age")` and similarly for `timestamp`) to detect the other field. A report containing `age=0` plus `timestamp`, or `timestamp=0` plus `age`, passes validation even though the two fields are supposed to be mutually exclusive. `age=0` is a legitimate value for a fresh report. Use key presence such as `"age" in self.initial_data` and validate exactly one of the spec fields.

title: Attribute key query cache key omits organization slug
body: The React Query key is only `['use-trace-item-attribute-keys', queryOptions]`, while `getTraceItemAttributeKeys` fetches `/organizations/${organization.slug}/trace-items/attributes/`. If the active organization changes while the query options hash to the same value (especially with no selected projects), React Query can serve attribute keys cached from the previous organization. Include `organization.slug` in the query key/options.

title: Hidden span attributes are only filtered during search
body: `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` is applied only after the `searchQuery.trim()` early return. With no search text, the function returns all `sorted` attributes, so `is_segment`, `project_id`, and `received` remain visible in the default attributes tree; they disappear only when the user searches. Apply the hidden-attribute filter unconditionally before the early return if these attributes are meant to be hidden.

title: Custom cell renderers returning falsy ReactNodes are treated as absent
body: The documented contract says the fallback runs when a custom renderer returns `undefined`, but the code checks `if (cell)` (and `renderDefaultHeadCell` does the same). Valid `ReactNode` return values such as `0`, `''`, `false`, or `null` are treated as no override and replaced by the default renderer, so a custom renderer cannot intentionally render an empty or zero-valued cell. Check `cell !== undefined` instead.

title: User/installer verification is skipped whenever the Integration row does not already exist
body: In GitHubInstallation.dispatch the new check that the OAuth-authenticated GitHub user matches the installer is reached only after `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` succeeds. When that lookup raises `Integration.DoesNotExist`, the code returns `pipeline.next_step()` immediately, and `build_integration` then creates the Integration. This is exactly the first-install path (it is also what happens whenever the GitHub `installation` webhook that populates `metadata["sender"]` has not been processed yet, since webhook delivery is not ordered relative to the browser redirect). Consequently the authenticated GitHub user is never compared to the installer on the primary flow; the check only runs on later re-install attempts. An attacker who starts an install with their own installation_id while the victim completes OAuth as a different GitHub account is not caught, which defeats the stated security fix. The verification needs to run (or fail closed) even when the Integration row is absent / the sender is not yet known.

title: Unchecked metadata["sender"] access raises KeyError instead of showing the error page
body: `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes `metadata` contains a `sender` dict with a `login` key. `GitHubIntegrationProvider.build_integration` only adds `sender` when `state.get("sender")` is set, and `test_basic_flow` asserts that pipeline-created integrations have metadata without `sender`. Any Integration whose metadata lacks `sender` (e.g. created by the pipeline itself, created by an older version, or whose metadata was overwritten by `build_integration`) will raise `KeyError` here, returning a 500 rather than the intended `github-integration-failed.html` error. Use `.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and treat a missing value as a verification failure.

title: Token exchange and user-info fetch are not guarded, so upstream failures produce a 500
body: `safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` is outside the try/except; the except only wraps `safe_urlread`. `safe_urlopen` raises on connection errors and non-2xx responses, and `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` (line 434) can raise `ApiError` as well. Those exceptions propagate and render a 500, not the friendly `github-integration-failed.html` page, contradicting the PR's claim that an invalid/reused code or failed token exchange always shows that error. Wrap the exchange and the user-info call in error handling and return `error(...)` on failure.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer covers the 404 installation-not-found path
body: The test still stubs a 404 for `/app/installations/{id}`, but the requests it issues never reach `get_installation_info`/`build_integration`: the second GET uses a bogus `state` ("ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05") and the changed assertion now checks the generic "Invalid installation request." message emitted by OAuthLoginView's state-mismatch branch. The original assertion (`The GitHub installation could not be found.`) was removed, so the `ApiError` 404 → `IntegrationError` code path in `build_integration` is no longer tested by any test. Either keep a test that drives the pipeline to completion with a 404 or rename/repurpose this test and add coverage for the 404 branch.

title: Runtime _() on error_short prevents these messages from being extracted for translation
body: The refactor passes the user-facing strings as plain `error_short` arguments (`"GitHub installation pending deletion."`, `"Github installed on another Sentry organization."`, and the `"Invalid installation request."` default), then calls `_()` on the runtime variable inside `error()`. `gettext`/`makemessages` only extracts literals passed directly to `_()`, so these strings will no longer appear in the message catalog and will be shown untranslated (previously they were `_("...")` literals). Pass lazy literals at the call sites (or make the arguments default to `_()` literals) so they remain extractable.

title: Installer-vs-authenticated-user check is skipped when the Integration row does not exist yet
body: The new user-identity check is only reached when an `Integration` row with this `external_id` already exists: the first lookup `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `Integration.DoesNotExist` in the normal case where the `installation` webhook has not yet created the Integration, and that branch returns `pipeline.next_step()` immediately (line 481-482). Execution then goes straight to `build_integration`, which builds/creates the Integration from `get_installation_info` without ever comparing `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user")` against anything. `build_integration` also only sets `metadata["sender"]` when `state.get("sender")` is truthy, and no view in this pipeline binds a `sender` state. Consequently the PR's stated guarantee — the pipeline fails on a mismatch between the authenticated GitHub user and the user who installed the app — does not hold in the window before the installation webhook is processed (or if that webhook is delayed/lost). Anyone with the `installation_id` who can complete the pipeline during that window can attach the installation, which defeats the cross-tenant protection this PR is meant to add. The path should fail closed when the installer identity cannot be determined.

title: KeyError on integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] yields a 500 instead of the failure page
body: The comparison reads `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` directly. `sender` is only present in metadata when the Integration was created by the GitHub `installation` webhook; Integrations created through this pipeline (the `DoesNotExist` branch), Integrations created before `sender` started being recorded, or any Integration whose metadata lacks `sender` will raise `KeyError` here. That turns an expected rejection into an unhandled 500 error page, and it is reachable for example when an Integration exists with no `OrganizationIntegration` (e.g. orphaned/reinstalled integration) and metadata has no `sender`. Use `(integration.metadata.get("sender") or {}).get("login")` and treat a missing login as a failed validation (error page), not an exception.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the installation 404 path
body: The second request passes `state="ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"`, which is not the pipeline signature, so `OAuthLoginView` returns the generic "Invalid installation request." before the pipeline ever reaches `GitHubInstallation`/`build_integration`. The stubbed 404 for `/app/installations/{id}` is therefore never hit, and the previous assertion for "The GitHub installation could not be found." was replaced with the generic message. The test name no longer matches what it verifies and the 404 handling in `build_integration` is now untested. It should use the correct signature and assert the intended installation-not-found error.

title: Token exchange and /user calls are unguarded and can surface as 500 errors
body: `safe_urlopen` at line 423 and `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` at line 434 are outside any try/except; only the decoding of the token response body is wrapped. A network/connection failure during the access-token exchange, or a non-2xx response from GitHub's `/user` endpoint (invalid/expired token, rate limit, GitHub outage) will raise out of `dispatch`, producing a 500 rather than the intended `error()` failure page that the PR describes for all failure modes. These calls should be wrapped and mapped to the same failure response.

title: Installer/OAuth-user check is skipped when no Integration row exists
body: In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, when Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id) raises DoesNotExist, the view calls pipeline.next_step() without comparing the OAuth-authenticated user to the installation sender. This is the fresh-install path and is reachable before/asynchronously to the GitHub installation webhook that records metadata['sender']; build_integration then creates the integration from the API. A user who supplies another installation_id can therefore finish the pipeline without the new check ever running, so the advertised security fix can be bypassed. This branch should fail closed or obtain a trusted installer identity when no Integration/sender is available.

title: Sender metadata is assumed to exist and can cause a 500 on reinstall
body: The comparison dereferences integration.metadata['sender']['login']. Not every Integration has this structure: build_integration only adds metadata['sender'] when pipeline state contains a sender, and integrations created through the pipeline fallback (as exercised by assert_setup_flow) or older integrations can lack it. On a reinstall where the Integration exists but its OrganizationIntegration is gone, this raises KeyError and returns a 500 instead of the intended invalid-request page. Use .get('sender', {}).get('login') and reject with ERR_INTEGRATION_INVALID_INSTALLATION_REQUEST when it is missing.

title: User-mismatch test can pass via state validation, not the new security check
body: test_github_user_mismatch switches to user_2, starts a new pipeline with init_path_2, then calls the callback with the hardcoded state from the first user's pipeline. Pipeline signatures are tied to the pipeline/session, so the request will normally fail OAuthLoginView's state check before GitHubInstallation reaches the sender comparison. Since the test only asserts the generic 'Invalid installation request.' message used for both failures, it can pass without exercising the new mismatch check. Capture/follow the redirect from init_path_2 to get the correct state, and assert that the failure came from the user comparison.

title: Installation-not-found test no longer exercises the 404 path
body: test_installation_not_found now sends state=ddd023... which is not the signature for the pipeline it just started, so OAuthLoginView rejects the request before build_integration calls /app/installations/{id}. The assertion was also changed from 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' to the generic invalid-request text. As a result, the 404 installation-not-found path is no longer covered; use the actual pipeline state and keep the specific assertion.

title: queued default is evaluated once at import, not per instance
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated a single time when the module is imported, not when each instance is created. Dataclasses only reject clearly mutable defaults (list/dict/set), so a datetime default is accepted, but every AssignmentSource constructed without an explicit `queued` — including every call to `from_integration()` — will share the exact same timestamp equal to the process/module import time. The field therefore never records when an assignment was actually queued, so any future staleness, debounce, or ordering logic reading it will be wrong. It should be `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. The accompanying `test_to_dict` only asserts `queued is not None`, so it does not catch this.

title: Raw datetime is put into Celery task kwargs via to_dict()
body: `assignment_source.to_dict()` returns `asdict(self)`, which contains a raw `datetime` for `queued`, and that dict is placed directly into `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs=...)`. Raw datetimes in Celery kwargs are only safe if the task serializer is pickle or a datetime-aware encoder; with a JSON serializer (Celery's default) publishing the task raises a serialization error inside `sync_group_assignee_outbound`, which is called from `GroupAssignee.assign`/`deassign` and would surface as a failure of the assignment itself. Even if a serializer round-trips it, `AssignmentSource.from_dict` does `cls(**input_dict)` without converting `queued` back to a datetime, so after a JSON round-trip the frozen dataclass holds a `str` where `datetime` is annotated, violating its type contract. The new tests run under `self.tasks()` (eager), which never serializes, so they cannot detect this.

title: Loop-prevention tests only cover assign with a matching source
body: The new test only covers `assign()` when the source integration matches. There is no test for `deassign()` with a matching source (even though `deassign` was given an `assignment_source` parameter and forwards it to `sync_group_assignee_outbound`), and no test verifying the stated behavior that a different integration still receives the outbound sync. The inbound tests (`test_assignee_sync_inbound_assign`/`_deassign`) call `sync_group_assignee_inbound` without `self.tasks()`, so they never execute or assert on the enqueued outbound tasks end-to-end. A regression in the source comparison for the deassign path or for non-matching integrations would pass the suite.

title: from_dict fails open, silently disabling loop prevention
body: `from_dict` catches `ValueError`/`TypeError` and returns `None`. In `sync_assignee_outbound`, a `None` source simply means `should_sync` runs without the source comparison, i.e. the cycle-prevention guard is silently disabled and the outbound sync proceeds — the exact loop this PR is meant to stop. If a payload is ever malformed (e.g. an unexpected/renamed key during a partial deploy), the protection degrades silently rather than being logged or surfaced.

title: sync_status_outbound gains an assignment_source parameter that is never supplied
body: The abstract `sync_status_outbound` now declares an `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None` argument, but no caller passes it and no status-sync path constructs an `AssignmentSource`, so the parameter is dead. It advertises a source-context contract to implementers that is never provided, and it does not actually prevent the analogous status-change sync cycle.

title: New task kwarg breaks task signature during a rolling deploy
body: `sync_assignee_outbound` now accepts `assignment_source_dict`. During a rolling deploy, tasks published by already-updated web/API code (which include this kwarg) can be consumed by not-yet-updated workers whose function signature does not accept it, raising `TypeError`; the `@retry` wrapper will exhaust retries and drop the task, so outbound assignee propagation to other integrations is silently lost for the duration of the deploy.

title: `queued` timestamp is evaluated once at import
body: `queued` is assigned a default of `timezone.now()`, which Python evaluates once when the module is imported. Every `AssignmentSource` created without an explicit `queued` value therefore carries the process start time instead of the time the assignment was queued. The field is serialized into the Celery task payload, so the value is misleading and any freshness/dedup logic based on it would be wrong. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. Relatedly, `from_dict` passes a supplied `queued` value through unchanged, so an ISO string produced by JSON serialization remains a string despite the `datetime` annotation.

title: Cycle guard suppresses outbound sync for all links in the source integration
body: `AssignmentSource` stores only `integration_id`, and `should_sync` returns False whenever the target external issue's integration matches the source. `sync_group_assignee_outbound` iterates every `GroupLink` for the group, so if one Sentry group is linked to multiple external issues in the same Jira/GitHub integration, an inbound assignment on one issue will not propagate to the other linked issues (for example, Jira A unassigns, Sentry unassigns, but Jira B stays assigned). The loop that needs breaking is the echo back to the triggering external issue; carry the external issue key in `AssignmentSource` and compare that, or explicitly document that all links in the source integration are intentionally skipped.

title: New cycle-prevention tests cover only assign with one integration
body: The added matching-source test exercises only `GroupAssignee.objects.assign` and only a single linked external issue. It does not cover the `deassign` path, which was also changed to forward `assignment_source`, nor does it verify the claimed behavior that other linked integrations still receive the outbound update. A regression that skips all outbound sync whenever any source is present, or that fails to propagate the source on deassign, would pass these tests. Add a deassign matching-source test and a two-integration test asserting the non-source integration is still called.

title: Datetime in Celery task kwargs will fail JSON serialization
body: `sync_group_assignee_outbound` now puts `assignment_source.to_dict()` into the kwargs of `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async`. `AssignmentSource.to_dict()` (assignment_source.py:27-28) returns `asdict(self)`, which includes the `queued` field as a `datetime` object. Celery serializes task kwargs, and Sentry's Celery configuration uses the JSON serializer, which cannot encode a `datetime`; enqueueing the task therefore raises an `EncodeError` ("Object of type datetime is not JSON serializable") for every outbound assignee sync. All previously passed kwargs were JSON-safe primitives (int/str/bool/None). The tests run tasks under `self.tasks()` (eager mode), which bypasses serialization, so this is not caught. Serialize `queued` as an ISO string/timestamp or drop it from the payload.

title: `queued` default is bound once at import time instead of per instance
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated a single time when the module is imported, not when an `AssignmentSource` is constructed. Every source created without an explicit `queued` (including all `from_integration` calls) therefore reports the process start time rather than the time the assignment was queued. This is the classic mutable/static default pitfall and will produce wrong data for any future use of `queued` (e.g. latency or ordering). Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so each instance gets its own timestamp.

title: Tests do not catch the shared `queued` default or payload serialization
body: `test_to_dict` only asserts `result.get("queued") is not None`, so the module-level default (always non-None) passes even though every instance shares the same stale timestamp. Additionally, the outbound sync tests run under `self.tasks()` (eager), which skips Celery serialization, so nothing verifies that the `assignment_source_dict` task payload can actually cross the queue. Add a test asserting `queued` reflects construction time and a test that the produced dict is JSON-serializable / that `apply_async` succeeds without eager mode.

title: New required-on-the-wire task kwarg breaks in-flight messages during a rolling deploy
body: `sync_assignee_outbound` gains a new `assignment_source_dict` kwarg, and callers now always send it (even when `None`). During a rolling deploy, tasks enqueued by new workers can be consumed by workers still running the previous `(external_issue_id, user_id, assign)` signature, which will raise `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'assignment_source_dict'`. The `@retry` decorator will retry these, but since the signature mismatch is not transient the retries are exhausted and the assignee syncs are dropped. Consider versioning the task or otherwise ensuring old consumers tolerate the new payload.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is abstract and cannot be instantiated
body: Changing `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` to subclass `StatefulDetectorHandler` with only `pass` leaves it abstract because it does not implement `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, or the new `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. Python will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler...` when `Detector.detector_handler` tries to instantiate `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler`, so processing any detector of this type now crashes instead of yielding no results. Implement the required abstract methods or keep this handler on `DetectorHandler` until it is ready. The TODO comment above is also stale now.

title: Expected occurrence in TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe uses the wrong group key
body: The expected occurrence is built for group key `val1`, but the call under test uses `group_key` (`expected_result.group_key`). `build_occurrence_and_event_data` derives the fingerprint from the group key, so the actual occurrence has fingerprint `[id:group_key]` while the expected occurrence has `[id:val1]`. The equality assertion in this test will fail; build the expected occurrence with `group_key` instead.

title: StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate docstring still documents a list return
body: The method now returns `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, but its docstring still says it returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`. This is misleading for callers and subclass implementers.

title: Mock occurrence helper ignores the value argument
body: `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` accepts `value` but never uses it, so the tests do not verify that `evaluate_group_key_value` passes the per-group value into the new occurrence hook. For example, `test_state_results_multi_group` builds group_2's expected occurrence with value 6 even though the packet contains 10, and the test still passes. A regression that passed the wrong value to `build_occurrence_and_event_data` would not be caught; use the value in the expected occurrence or assert the call explicitly.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now an abstract class and cannot be instantiated
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler but implements none of its abstract members (`counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the newly added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`). Because StatefulDetectorHandler uses abc.ABC/abc.abstractmethod, this class remains abstract, so `Detector.detector_handler`'s `group_type.detector_handler(self)` will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler` for any Detector whose type is `metric_alert_fire`. Previously the class was instantiable and simply returned an empty list. Implement the required methods (even if stubs), or don't wire this abstract class as the group type's detector handler. The adjacent comment `# TODO: This will be a stateful detector when we build that abstraction` is also now stale.

title: test_dedupe builds the expected occurrence with the wrong group key and will fail
body: In `TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe`, the expected occurrence is built with `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)`, but the call under test is `handler.evaluate_group_key_value("group_key", ...)` (the expected result's group_key is "group_key"). The mock helper derives the occurrence fingerprint from the supplied group key, so the expected occurrence gets fingerprint `[f"{id}:val1"]` while the actual occurrence produced by `evaluate_group_key_value` gets `[f"{id}:group_key"]`. Since `IssueOccurrence`/`DetectorEvaluationResult` equality compares the fingerprint (and in any case the objects differ), the assertion `handler.evaluate_group_key_value(...) == expected_result` will not pass. The expected occurrence must be built with "group_key".

title: evaluate docstring still documents a list return value
body: `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` was changed to return `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, but its docstring still says it 'returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`' and that there is 'one result for each group key result'. This is misleading for implementers of the new `build_occurrence_and_event_data` hook and for callers; update the docstring to describe the returned dict.

title: New hook's value argument is never asserted by the tests
body: `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` accepts `value` but never uses it, so none of the tests verify that the correct group value is passed into the new `build_occurrence_and_event_data` hook. This is visible in `test_state_results_multi_group`, which builds the expected occurrence for `group_2` with value `6` even though the packet value for `group_2` is `10`, and in `TestEvaluate.test_dedupe`, which passes `6` while the evaluated value is `8`. A regression where `evaluate_group_key_value` passed the wrong value would go undetected; the mock should incorporate `value` into the occurrence or event data.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and cannot be instantiated
body: The class was changed from `DetectorHandler` (where it implemented the only abstract method, `evaluate`) to `StatefulDetectorHandler`, but it does not implement any of the new abstract members (`counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, `build_occurrence_and_event_data`). Because it still inherits `abc.ABC` through the base, `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` remains abstract. `Detector.detector_handler` instantiates it via `group_type.detector_handler(self)` (src/sentry/workflow_engine/models/detector.py:86), so for any Detector whose type is `metric_alert_fire`, that property now raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class` instead of returning a handler that yields an empty evaluation as it did before. Stub implementations or a concrete handler are needed.

title: Expected occurrence in TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe uses the wrong group key
body: The expected occurrence is built with `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)`, but the value actually evaluated is `expected_result.group_key`, which is `"group_key"`. `build_fingerprint` embeds the group key, so the expected `IssueOccurrence` has fingerprint `[<detector_id>:val1]` while the handler produces `[<detector_id>:group_key]`. Since `DetectorEvaluationResult` (and presumably `IssueOccurrence`) is compared field-by-field, the first assertion compares unequal and the test fails; even if equality ignored the fingerprint, the test would not be validating the occurrence it claims to. Build the expected occurrence with `"group_key"`.

title: evaluate docstring still documents a list return value
body: The return type of `evaluate` was changed to `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, but the docstring still says it "returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`". Anyone implementing or calling the (now changed) handler contract will be misled about the return shape, which is exactly the part of the API this PR is changing.

title: Occurrence helper ignores `value`, so the new hook's value argument is never verified
body: `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` accepts `value` but never uses it, and several call sites pass an unrelated value (`test_results_on_change` evaluates 100 but builds the expected occurrence with 6; `TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe` evaluates 10 but builds with 6; `test_state_results_multi_group` evaluates 10 for group_2 but builds with 6). As a result no test verifies that `evaluate_group_key_value` forwards the evaluated group value to `build_occurrence_and_event_data`, even though that value is a required input of the newly added hook. Include `value` in the generated occurrence/event data and use matching values in the expectations.

title: Removed mark_failed helpers without updating imports/mocks that target that module path
body: This module previously defined `mark_failed_threshold`, `create_issue_platform_occurrence`, `get_failure_reason`, `get_monitor_environment_context`, and `SimpleCheckIn`. The refactor deletes all of them and does not re-export the new names, which now live in `sentry.monitors.logic.incidents` (`try_incident_threshold`), `sentry.monitors.logic.incident_occurrence` (`create_incident_occurrence`), and `sentry.monitors.types` (`SimpleCheckIn`). Any test that imports one of these from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` (for example a `get_failure_reason` unit test) will now raise ImportError, and any `patch("sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed.create_issue_platform_occurrence")` no longer intercepts the production code path because the call site moved to `sentry.monitors.logic.incidents`, so occurrence-production assertions would silently stop exercising the real path. No test files are updated in this PR, so references must be migrated to the new module locations.

title: Monitor context returns raw config instead of the computed display config
body: `get_monitor_environment_context` copies `monitor_environment.monitor.config` into a local `config` and replaces `config["schedule_type"]` with `get_schedule_type_display()`, but the returned dict sets `"config": monitor_environment.monitor.config` rather than the local `config`. The human-readable schedule type substitution is therefore dead code, and the occurrence's monitor context contains the raw internal `schedule_type` value instead of the display string, producing incorrect data in the issue occurrence payload. Return the mutated `config` (or remove the dead copy/conversion).

title: Modified config copy is discarded in monitor environment context
body: get_monitor_environment_context copies monitor_environment.monitor.config into `config` and replaces `schedule_type` with the human-readable `get_schedule_type_display()` value, but the returned dict uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead of `config`. As a result, issue occurrence event context still contains the raw schedule_type value and the intended display conversion is never used. Return `config` here (or stop creating the unused modified copy).

title: Monitor context returns the unmodified config instead of the prepared config
body: `get_monitor_environment_context` copies `monitor_environment.monitor.config` and replaces `schedule_type` with `get_schedule_type_display()`, but the returned context uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead of the local `config`. The schedule type conversion is therefore discarded, and the occurrence's monitor context contains the raw `schedule_type` value rather than the human-readable display value. Return `config` instead.

title: Join timeout exits loop before terminating flusher processes
body: In `SpanFlusher.join`, when the deadline expires the loop breaks before reaching `process.terminate()` at line 346. Since `next_step.join(timeout)` is called first and can consume the whole timeout, this can leave all spawned flusher processes alive after a rebalance or shutdown. Those daemon processes keep flushing and producing from their old shard assignments, and a new flusher for the same shards may then produce duplicate segments and leak processes. Remaining processes must be terminated even when the wait deadline is exceeded.

title: Invalid flusher process count can disable flushing entirely
body: `--flusher-processes` is an unvalidated integer. If a negative value is supplied, `self.max_processes = max_processes or ...` keeps it and `num_processes = min(...)` becomes negative. `range(self.num_processes)` is then empty, so no flusher processes or per-process buffers are created; spans are written to Redis but never flushed. A value of 0 is also silently treated as "all shards" rather than rejected. The process count should be validated to be at least 1.

title: New multiprocess flusher path is not exercised by tests
body: `test_flusher_processes_limit` passes `produce_to_pipe`, which makes `SpanFlusher._create_process_for_shards` use the `threading.Thread` branch instead of `mp_context.Process`. The assertions therefore only verify shard-to-thread mapping; they never exercise spawning real child processes, the per-process `SpansBuffer` in a child, process death/restart detection, or shutdown of `multiprocessing.Process` objects. Since the core change is the multiprocess flusher, regressions in the actual production path would not be caught.

title: Added synchronization sleep is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
body: The test replaces `time.sleep` with `lambda _: None` at line 15, so the new `time.sleep(0.1)` at line 62 does not actually wait despite the comment saying it gives flusher threads time to process after the drift change. The test relies on incidental thread scheduling and can be flaky; use the original sleep function or an explicit synchronization primitive instead.

title: wait_produce metric uses inconsistent shard tag key
body: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and the unhealthy metric use the tag key `shard`, but `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` at line 199 uses `shards`. Dashboards or alerts filtering by the `shard` tag will not include producer wait time, so this metric becomes effectively invisible in existing shard-level queries.

title: Docstring incorrectly says one process per shard
body: The class docstring says the flusher "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing," but `max_processes` caps the number of processes and the CLI default is 1, so multiple shards can be handled by a single process. The documentation should describe the capped/process-sharing behavior to avoid misleading operators about resource usage and concurrency.

title: SpanFlusher.join breaks out of the loop on timeout, leaving later flusher processes un-terminated
body: join() sets `stopped`, computes a single `deadline`, calls `self.next_step.join(timeout)`, and then iterates processes. For every process it first checks `if remaining_time <= 0: break`, which exits the whole loop before the `while ... is_alive()` wait and before `process.terminate()` for that and all remaining processes. Because `next_step.join(timeout)` is called on the line above with the same full timeout, it can consume the entire budget on its own, so in the worst case *no* worker process is ever terminated. The per-process `terminate()` was the only safety net for a worker that is hung inside `flush_segments`/`produce` and therefore never observes the shared `stopped` flag; with this break, such hung spawn processes keep running (holding Redis/Kafka connections, and potentially still producing) after the consumer has moved on via rebalance. Use `continue`/per-process termination instead of `break`, and terminate all processes that exceed the deadline rather than skipping them.

title: Added `time.sleep(0.1)` is a no-op because `time.sleep` is monkeypatched, so the flusher race is not actually fixed
body: test_basic begins with `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, which replaces `time.sleep` on the `time` module. The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` (with the comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change') therefore calls the patched lambda and sleeps for zero seconds, so it provides no delay or yield. The line was clearly intended to let the background flusher thread observe `current_drift.value = 9000` before `step.join()` sets `stopped` and the thread exits; since no real waiting happens, the race remains and the test can intermittently observe an empty `messages` list. Restore real sleeping for this call (e.g. keep a reference to the original `time.sleep` and use it, or synchronize explicitly on the flusher having flushed) or the extra line gives false confidence.

title: Restarting a hung flusher in thread mode leaves the old thread running
body: In `_ensure_processes_alive`, a process detected as dead/hung is only killed when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. When `produce_to_pipe` is set (the code uses `threading.Thread` instead of a spawn process, as done by the tests), the old thread is neither stopped nor joined before `_create_process_for_shards` overwrites `self.processes[process_index]` with a brand-new thread. Both threads then run `SpanFlusher.main` for the same shards concurrently, producing the same flushed segments twice and racing on `done_flush_segments`/Redis key deletion. This is limited to the thread path, but that path is what the test suite relies on, and a hang-triggered restart there would corrupt results.

title: Non-positive `max_processes` silently disables the flusher or spawns one process per shard
body: `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` (and `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(...))`) does no validation. Passing `--flusher-processes 0` is treated as falsy and becomes `len(assigned_shards)` (i.e. 'max 0' spawns one process per shard), while a negative value makes `num_processes = min(negative, n)` negative, so `range(self.num_processes)` is empty, `process_to_shards_map`/`processes`/`buffers` are all empty, and no flusher worker is ever created. In that state `submit()` still inserts spans into Redis and forwards to `next_step`, but nothing ever calls `flush_segments`, so segments are never expired or produced and Redis grows without bound — with no error or warning. Validate that `max_processes >= 1` (or explicitly define the meaning of 0) rather than relying on `or`.

title: `_create_process_for_shard` is dead code and never called
body: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is defined but no caller exists; the restart path in `_ensure_processes_alive` calls `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly. This unused method adds confusion about whether a single-shard restart path is supposed to exist (it would also break the assumption that a process owns a fixed set of shards) and should be removed.

title: New multiprocess flusher is only checked structurally, not for actual flushing or restart behavior
body: test_flusher_processes_limit only asserts the sizes of `processes`/`process_to_shards_map` and then calls `step.join()`; it runs in thread mode (`produce_to_pipe`) and never submits spans, so it never verifies that spans for different partitions are actually flushed/produced by the correct per-shard processes, nor does it exercise `_ensure_processes_alive` (dead/hung restart) or the per-process backpressure accounting. The core new behavior (each process flushing its own shards and restarting independently) has no functional test coverage.

title: isinstance guard prevents killing spawn-context flusher processes
body: In `_ensure_processes_alive` the call `process.kill()` is now guarded by `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. On Linux, `multiprocessing.Process` resolves to the default (fork) class `ForkProcess`, while these flusher workers are created with `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, i.e. `SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` is a sibling of `ForkProcess` (both subclass `BaseProcess`), not a subclass of it, so this check is False and `kill()` never runs. As a result a dead or hung worker is never terminated before a replacement is spawned: dead children become zombies (never reaped) and hung children keep running and flushing the same shards concurrently with the new worker, leading to duplicate/partial writes to `buffered-segments`. The pre-PR code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally (with a `ValueError` catch), so this is a regression. The same guard at line 346 also means `terminate()` in `join()` never fires for spawn processes. Use `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)` or `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)` (and keep the added `AttributeError` guard for the thread case).

title: join() skips waiting for and terminating remaining workers once the shared deadline is reached
body: `join()` iterates the worker processes and does `break` whenever `deadline - time.time() <= 0`. If the timeout is exhausted while waiting on an earlier worker (or already consumed by `next_step.join(timeout)`), all remaining workers are neither waited on nor terminated, so shutdown returns while they are still running and producing to Kafka. The previous single-process implementation always executed `terminate()` after the wait loop regardless of whether the deadline had passed. With multiple workers this needs to attempt termination of every worker even after the deadline, otherwise a hung worker keeps flushing after a rebalance/shutdown.

title: Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
body: The test sets `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at line 14, which patches the global `time.sleep`, so the newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` on line 62 does nothing and the comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change' is false. `step.poll()` also does not drive the flusher's background loop (SpanFlusher.poll only polls `next_step`). Nothing therefore guarantees the flusher thread completes a `flush_segments` iteration after `current_drift` is set and before `step.join()` sets `stopped`, so the test races with thread scheduling and can be flaky. Use a real sleep (e.g. only patch the flusher's sleep) or synchronize deterministically on an event/message.

title: New test only exercises the thread path and does not cover the real multiprocessing behavior
body: `test_flusher_processes_limit` passes `produce_to_pipe`, which makes `SpanFlusher` use `threading.Thread` instead of spawn processes. The actual production path (`mp_context.Process`, pickling the per-shard buffer, `kill`/`terminate`, worker restart) is never exercised, and the assertions only check process count and the trivial sum of shard-list lengths. Consequently the spawn-process bugs in this PR (e.g. the `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` kill/terminate issue) are invisible to CI. Add coverage that uses spawn processes and/or verifies the restart path and that each process actually flushes its assigned shards.

title: Shard metric tag uses inconsistent key and a comma-joined shard list as its value
body: The produce timer uses tag key `shard` (line 185) while the wait_produce timer uses `shards` (line 199), and both pass `shard_tag` — the comma-joined list of all shards owned by the process (e.g. `"0,1,2,3"`) — as the value. This mislabels the metric (the value is a combination of shards, not a single shard), makes the tag cardinality the set of distinct shard groupings, and the differing key means dashboards/alerts querying `shard` versus `shards` will not line up. Use one consistent key and emit one data point per shard, or a fixed process-index tag.

title: `_create_process_for_shard` is dead code
body: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is never called; restarts are performed by `_ensure_processes_alive` via `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`. The unused helper is dead code and suggests an intended per-shard restart API that was never wired up. Remove it or use it.

title: Class docstring claims one process per shard, but shards are shared across at most max_processes workers
body: The docstring now says 'Creates one process per shard for parallel processing', but the implementation computes `num_processes = min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` and distributes shards round-robin across that many processes, so each process may own several shards (and fewer processes than shards are run when the limit applies). The docstring should describe 'up to max_processes workers, each handling a subset of shards' so the documented behavior matches the code.

title: Uses Python 3.13-only queue shutdown APIs
body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown calls q.shutdown(immediate=False), and OrderedQueueWorker catches queue.ShutDown. Both APIs were added in Python 3.13. On the Python versions Sentry currently runs, q.shutdown raises AttributeError, which the broad except swallows, so blocked worker threads are never woken. Each worker.join(timeout=5.0) then waits the full 5 seconds, meaning shutdown takes 100 seconds with the default 20 queues and leaves the threads alive. Separately, if a worker ever hits the except queue.ShutDown clause, evaluating the missing attribute raises another AttributeError and kills that worker. Use an Event/sentinel-based shutdown compatible with the supported Python version.

title: Shared queue pool is permanently shut down and then reused
body: ResultsStrategyFactory creates one FixedQueuePool in __init__ and reuses it for every create_with_partitions call, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() and terminate() call queue_pool.shutdown(), which permanently shuts down all queues and workers. On a Kafka rebalance Arroyo closes the old strategy and calls create_with_partitions again with the same factory, so the new strategy gets an already shut-down pool. With queue shutdown available, put() raises ShutDown, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches it, marks the offset complete, and the background commit loop commits it, silently dropping messages. Without queue shutdown, the workers are gone and the offsets may never complete. The pool should be owned by the strategy or recreated for each strategy instance, not shut down from close() while the factory still holds it.

title: Queues are unbounded, so submit applies no backpressure
body: Each queue is created as queue.Queue() with the default maxsize of 0, which is infinite, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit always enqueues immediately. poll() only emits a metric and never blocks or rejects based on queue depth. A single slow subscription can therefore grow its queue without bound while the consumer keeps polling and decoding messages, increasing memory use and accumulating an uncommitted Kafka backlog until the process is OOM-killed. This contradicts the class docstring's claim of natural backpressure; use a bounded queue and block or apply another explicit backpressure policy.

title: Failed work items are still marked offset-complete
body: OrderedQueueWorker.run has a finally block that unconditionally calls complete_offset(), including when result_processor raises and the exception is merely logged by the generic except. Once the offset is removed from outstanding, OffsetTracker will treat it as processed and the commit loop will commit past it, so the failed result is acknowledged to Kafka and will not be retried. This also contradicts the strategy docstring that offsets are committed only after successful processing. Failed offsets should remain outstanding or be sent through an explicit retry/DLQ path, not completed as if the work succeeded.

title: Shutdown stops workers before draining queued items
body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False), but each worker checks while not self.shutdown before calling get() again. A worker that finishes its current item therefore exits immediately, leaving any remaining items in the queue even though immediate=False was requested. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close also joins the commit thread before shutting the pool down, so work processed during shutdown is not committed. The net effect is that graceful shutdown abandons buffered results and relies on Kafka redelivery, contrary to the graceful-drain behavior implied by the code and docstrings.

title: Error-handling test is timing-dependent and asserts the wrong outcome
body: The test makes the first result processor call raise and the second succeed, then asserts that no offset was committed for the partition. In the implementation, OrderedQueueWorker completes the offset in its finally block even when processing raised, so both offsets become complete and the background commit loop should eventually commit the partition. The test only sleeps 0.2 seconds after processing finishes, while the commit loop wakes every 1 second, so it usually passes before the commit happens and will flake when setup or processing takes slightly longer. It therefore does not reliably verify the intended error semantics; it should either assert the actual expected commit behavior or the production code should keep failed offsets outstanding.
