title: Uses queue.Queue.shutdown/queue.ShutDown, which require Python 3.13+
body: `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` and the worker catches `queue.ShutDown`. Both APIs were added in Python 3.13. On older supported runtimes the shutdown path raises AttributeError for every queue and workers blocked in `get()` are never released; the worker exception handler also cannot resolve `queue.ShutDown`, so an unexpected processing exception can kill the worker thread. This makes the new consumer unable to shut down correctly unless the whole repository is already on Python 3.13.

title: Broad submit exception handler commits offsets for messages that were never enqueued
body: If `grouping_fn(result)` raises, or if `queue_pool.submit` fails (for example `work_queue.put` raises `ShutDown` during shutdown), the `except Exception` block calls `add_offset` plus `complete_offset` for the message. The commit thread then sees the offset as complete and commits past it even though the message was never processed or even queued. Only an intentional decode failure returning `None` should be skipped; unexpected failures must propagate, retry, or go to a DLQ rather than silently advancing the Kafka offset.

title: Worker marks an offset complete even when result processing raised
body: `OrderedQueueWorker.run` catches `Exception` from `result_processor`, logs it, and then unconditionally calls `complete_offset` in `finally`. Any exception that escapes processing (a bug, tracing failure, unexpected DB error, etc.) therefore makes the offset committable and permanently skips that message. This contradicts the class contract that offsets are only committed after successful processing and turns transient failures into silent data loss.

title: Commit callback is invoked from a background thread concurrently with the stream processor
body: `_commit_loop` runs on its own thread and calls the arroyo `Commit` callback, which ultimately commits the Kafka consumer used by the main `StreamProcessor` polling thread. The Confluent Kafka consumer and arroyo commit path are not thread-safe, and existing strategies only call `commit` from the processing thread. This can race with `poll`/rebalance and cause undefined behavior, failed commits, or duplicate processing. Commit requests should be handed back to the processing thread or otherwise serialized.

title: Work queues are unbounded, so the strategy has no backpressure
body: `queue.Queue()` is created with the default `maxsize=0`, so `put()` never blocks. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` continues accepting messages as fast as Kafka delivers them even if one or more queues cannot keep up; each queued `WorkItem` retains both the decoded result and the full original `Message`. A single slow subscription can therefore grow memory without bound and eventually OOM the consumer. The class docstring claiming `Natural backpressure when queues fill up` is false unless a bounded queue and blocking submission are added.

title: Shutdown stops workers before draining queued work
body: `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets every worker's `shutdown` flag before shutting down the queues. Workers check that flag only at the top of the loop, so a worker that is processing an item exits immediately afterwards even if more items remain in its queue. The existing `wait_until_empty` helper is never used. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close`/`join` therefore can abandon messages that were already accepted by `submit`, causing avoidable reprocessing on restart and making the `graceful shutdown` behavior misleading. Shutdown should stop accepting new work, drain queued and in-flight items, and only then stop workers.

title: Error-handling test asserts no commit even though failed offsets are marked complete
body: The test patches `result_processor.__call__` to raise for offset 100 and succeed for offset 101. In the implementation, the worker catches the exception and `finally` calls `complete_offset`, so both offsets become committable and the commit loop will normally commit past offset 100. The assertion `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` can only pass if the 1-second commit thread happens not to run during the 0.2-second sleep, so the test is timing-dependent and also does not encode the intended error semantics. It should explicitly define whether failed messages are retried, sent to a DLQ, or committed, and assert that contract deterministically.

title: Stats test races with live queue workers
body: `test_stats_reporting` submits ten items to a live pool and immediately asserts `stats['total_items'] > 0`. The three worker threads can dequeue and process all ten items before `get_stats()` is called, making `total_items` zero and causing an intermittent failure. The test should synchronize with the workers (for example by pausing them or using a barrier) instead of assuming queue depth remains non-zero after submission.

title: Queues are unbounded and poll() provides no backpressure
body: Each work queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll()` (line 327) only emits metrics; neither `submit()` nor `poll()` ever blocks. Arroyo's StreamProcessor pulls from Kafka and calls `submit()` as fast as it can, relying on the strategy to push back, so there is nothing limiting how many WorkItems can accumulate in memory. If one group (the exact slow-subscription case this PR is meant to address) backs up, its queue grows without bound while the consumer keeps reading, leading to unbounded memory growth / OOM. The class docstring's claim 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' is false because the queues never fill and submit never blocks. Use a bounded queue with a blocking put (or make submit/poll block once total in-flight exceeds a limit).

title: submit() swallows exceptions and commits the offset, silently dropping messages
body: The broad `except Exception` in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` wraps the decoder, the grouping function, and the enqueue. On any exception it calls `add_offset` + `complete_offset`, which marks the offset as processed so the commit thread will commit it, even though the message was never handled. The most realistic trigger is `grouping_fn` (i.e. `ResultsStrategyFactory.build_payload_grouping_key`) raising on a malformed/partial result: that message is then discarded with only a log line and its offset is committed, bypassing any DLQ or retry. This differs from the batched/serial modes where a grouping failure propagates. The message should not be treated as successfully processed (e.g. add to DLQ / let the error propagate) rather than being committed away.

title: Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its intent and passes only vacuously
body: `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` is documented as 'errors in processing don't block offset commits', but it asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, i.e. that commits are blocked. That contradicts the implementation: `OrderedQueueWorker.run` calls `complete_offset` in a `finally` block even when `result_processor` raises, so both offsets (100 and 101) become committable and WILL be committed. The test only passes because it breaks out after ~0.2s while the commit loop (`_commit_loop`) fires every 1.0s, so `len(committed_offsets) == 0` happens to hold — it is both flaky (slow CI where >1s elapses before the assertion makes it fail) and does not actually test error handling. It should wait deterministically for a commit (like the other tests) and assert the correct behavior.

title: FilteredPayload reaches a decoder that asserts against it; the skip path is only reached via exception
body: `decode_payload` starts with `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)`, but the new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` passes every message's payload (`self.decoder(message.payload)`) to it unconditionally. When a `FilteredPayload` message arrives, the assertion raises `AssertionError`, which is only 'handled' by the new catch-all in `submit` (logging an error per message); the intended `if result is None: complete and return` skip path is never used for filtered messages because `decode_payload` never returns for them. Under `python -O` the assert is stripped and `payload.value` on a FilteredPayload raises `AttributeError` instead (also swallowed). The test `test_handles_invalid_messages` exercises this by sending a FilteredPayload, so it is validating the exception-swallowing fallback rather than the intended skip logic. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` should check for `FilteredPayload` explicitly (or `decode_payload` should return None for it) before calling the codec.

title: 2FA users without backup codes have no way to obtain them
body: Any user who enabled 2FA before this PR has `backupCodes = NULL`. If they click "Lost access" and try to log in with a backup code, `authorize` throws `ErrorCode.MissingBackupCodes`, and the login UI shows the message "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." However there is no way to (re)generate backup codes once 2FA is already enabled: `/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup` returns `TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled` when `user.twoFactorEnabled` is true. These existing users therefore hit a permanent dead end, and the guidance in the message is false. A regeneration path (or disabling/re-enabling) is needed before this is safe to ship.

title: Dismissing dialog after enable skips onEnable()
body: Previously `handleEnable` called `onEnable()` immediately on success. Now it only advances to `SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes`, and `onEnable()` is called solely from the "Close" button. If the user enables 2FA and then dismisses the dialog via the X button, overlay click, or Escape (`onOpenChange`), `onEnable()` is never invoked and `resetState()` never runs. The parent settings page is not notified that 2FA is now enabled, so the two-factor switch stays visually off while the account actually has 2FA active. The `onOpenChange` handler should invoke `onEnable()` when the flow had reached the post-enable backup-code step (and reset state).

title: Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write
body: Consuming a backup code does `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes))`, finds the index, sets `backupCodes[index] = null`, then writes the whole re-encrypted array back. Two concurrent login requests using the same backup code can both read the pre-consumption array, both find the code, and both write — resulting in the code being accepted twice (and the two writes clobbering each other). Since the guaranteed single-use property is the core security promise of backup codes, this should be made atomic (e.g., a conditional update / transaction) rather than a read-then-write.

title: No test coverage for backup code login or one-time consumption
body: The added e2e work only asserts that the download/copy/close buttons appear on the backup-code screen (with `// TODO: check file content` and `// TODO: check clipboard content`), and the header even notes `// TODO: add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup`. The core new behavior — logging in with a backup code via "Lost access", the one-time deletion of the consumed code, `MissingBackupCodes`/`IncorrectBackupCode` handling, and disabling 2FA with a backup code — is entirely untested. The PR checklist itself states "I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective." The most bug-prone logic (code consumption/concurrency) is unverified.

title: Copy success toast shown without awaiting clipboard write
body: `navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` returns a promise that is neither awaited nor caught, and the "backup codes copied!" success toast is fired unconditionally. In non-secure contexts or when clipboard permission is denied the write rejects silently while the user is told the copy succeeded — dangerous here because backup codes are shown once. The toast (and the e2e assertion on `toast-success`) should only fire after the write resolves.

title: Backup-codes object URL is never revoked on unmount
body: `setBackupCodesUrl(URL.createObjectURL(textBlob))` creates an object URL that is only revoked on a subsequent `handleSetup` call. If the user closes the dialog (or the component unmounts) the blob URL leaks. The URL should be revoked in a cleanup effect on unmount.

title: tabIndex={-1} makes password visibility toggle keyboard-inaccessible for all PasswordFields
body: Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the show/hide-password button removes it from the tab order for every `PasswordField` in the app, not just the two-factor modals this PR targets. Keyboard-only users can no longer reach the toggle, which is an accessibility regression. If the intent was only to prevent a specific form-submit issue, it should be scoped rather than applied to the shared component.

title: Backup-code login can bypass password verification when a totpCode is also sent
body: Password verification is gated on `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)` (line 121), while the backup-code branch is entered whenever `user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode` is truthy (line 131), regardless of whether a `totpCode` was supplied. Because these two conditions are independent, a request that contains a valid backup code AND any non-empty `totpCode` value skips password checking but still goes through the backup-code validation path. The consequence is that anyone holding a single leaked backup code can log in with just that code plus a garbage totpCode, without knowing the account password — the backup code ceases to be a second factor and becomes a single factor. The UI happens to set `totpCode` to an empty string in backup mode, so this is only reachable by calling the credentials provider directly, but it is a real authentication bypass of the password requirement. The backup-code branch should also require the password (or the password check should not be skipped merely because `totpCode` is present when `backupCode` is being used).

title: Backup code single-use enforcement is a non-atomic read-modify-write
body: Backup-code consumption is implemented as: decrypt the stored array, set `backupCodes[index] = null`, then `prisma.user.update` with a re-encrypted copy. This is a classic TOCTOU read-modify-write with no locking or conditional update. Two concurrent login requests that present the same backup code can both read the pre-update value, both find the code valid, and both succeed — so a single backup code can be used more than once under concurrency. Since backup codes are a recovery/second-factor credential, being able to replay one defeats the 'used exactly once' guarantee stated in the UI copy. A conditional/atomic update (e.g. compare-and-set on the ciphertext, or a DB transaction with row lock) is needed.

title: Dismissing the dialog after enabling 2FA never calls onEnable, leaving the toggle out of sync
body: Previously `handleEnable` called `onEnable()` immediately on success. Now it transitions to `SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes`, and `onEnable()` is only invoked from the explicit 'Close' button (line 269). The `Dialog`'s `onOpenChange` (line 166) is still wired straight to the parent, so a user who dismisses the modal via Escape, backdrop click, or the close (X) button after the TOTP code was accepted leaves the server-side 2FA enabled (the enable endpoint already set `twoFactorEnabled: true`) while the parent never runs `onEnable()` / refetch, so the settings switch and related state can continue to display 2FA as disabled. The finalization should happen on any close path (or the parent should refetch on close), not only on the dedicated Close button.

title: No test covers the core feature: logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code
body: The PR description's checklist explicitly states no tests were added, and the added e2e steps only click the download and copy buttons and then close the dialog; both content assertions are left as `// TODO` and nothing exercises the actual backup-code path. The two security-sensitive behaviors this PR introduces — consuming a backup code during login (single-use invalidation) and disabling 2FA via a backup code — have zero automated coverage. Given the password-bypass and single-use race described elsewhere, the absence of a test that actually signs in with a backup code and asserts that the same code is then rejected leaves these regressions undetected. At minimum, a login-with-backup-code test (and the already-flagged 'TODO' file-content check) should be added.

title: Existing 2FA users have no backup codes and no way to generate them, making 'Lost access' a dead end
body: `backupCodes` is a new nullable column, so every user who enabled 2FA before this migration has `user.backupCodes === null`. When such a user uses 'Lost access' and submits anything, they hit `if (!user.backupCodes) throw new Error(ErrorCode.MissingBackupCodes)`, which renders `t("missing_backup_codes")` = 'No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings.' That instruction is impossible to follow: the only endpoint that creates backup codes is `setup.ts`, which returns `TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled` for users who already have 2FA on, and this PR adds no 'regenerate backup codes' UI. These users are therefore permanently locked out of the recovery path (they must disable and re-enable 2FA, which is exactly what the feature is meant to avoid). Either the message should not tell users to do something the product does not offer, or a way to generate/regenerate backup codes for already-enabled 2FA should be provided.

title: Exhausting all backup codes reports 'incorrect code' instead of 'no backup codes'
body: After codes are consumed they are set to `null` but the array (and therefore the encrypted string) is never emptied, so `user.backupCodes` remains a truthy JSON string of nulls. The guard on line 137 (`if (!user.backupCodes) throw new Error(ErrorCode.MissingBackupCodes)`) never fires once all codes are used; instead `backupCodes.indexOf(...)` returns -1 and the user is told `incorrect_backup_code` forever. A user with zero remaining codes should be told they have none left (the `MissingBackupCodes` path) rather than being told each retry that their code is wrong.

title: Backup-code login can bypass the password when any totpCode is sent
body: The new branch accepts `credentials.backupCode` as sufficient to validate the second factor, but the password check above only runs when `!credentials.totpCode`. A request with a valid backup code plus any non-empty dummy `totpCode` therefore skips password verification and logs in using only the backup code. Since backup codes are often printed or exported, this defeats the password factor. Password verification must also be required when `credentials.backupCode` is present, or the TOTP-only bypass must be scoped to the trusted `totp` flow.

title: Backup-code consumption is a non-atomic read/modify/write
body: The code decrypts the whole backup-code list, mutates one element to null, and writes the whole encrypted list back. Two concurrent logins with the same backup code can both read the original array and both succeed, violating single-use. Two concurrent logins with different codes can each null a different index, and the last write wins, resurrecting the other already-used code. Use a DB transaction/conditional update or a row per code so consumption is atomic.

title: Backup-code recovery is unreachable for `?totp=` logins
body: When `totpEmail` is present (the `/auth/login?totp=...` flow used after OAuth/SAML sign-in), `footerText` renders `ExternalTotpFooter`, which only has Cancel. The new Lost access button that sets `twoFactorLostAccess` exists only in `TwoFactorFooter`, so the `BackupCode` form can never be shown. A 2FA-enabled user who reaches login through this path cannot use their backup codes if the authenticator is lost.

title: onEnable is skipped if the backup-code dialog is dismissed via Escape/outside click
body: After `handleEnable` succeeds, 2FA is already enabled server-side and the modal switches to DisplayBackupCodes, but `onEnable()` is only called by the Close button at line 269. The `Dialog` still receives the parent's `onOpenChange`, so pressing Escape or clicking outside closes it without notifying the parent or resetting state. The settings page can remain showing 2FA as disabled, and the user may not have saved the codes. Handle `onOpenChange` or call `onEnable` when entering the backup-code step.

title: Core backup-code login/disable paths are untested
body: The added e2e coverage only verifies that the backup-code screen appears and that download/copy/close controls work. It never submits a backup code to `next-auth-options` or the disable endpoint, so the new password/backup-code logic (including the password-bypass and single-use behavior above) is not exercised. Add tests for successful backup-code login, rejection/reuse of a consumed code, and disabling 2FA with a backup code.

title: Password visibility toggle removed from keyboard tab order
body: Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the show/hide password button makes it unreachable by keyboard for every PasswordField in the app. Keyboard-only users can no longer toggle password visibility; this is an accessibility regression unrelated to the 2FA feature. Remove the tabIndex or provide an accessible alternative.

title: Google Meet fallback dereferences undefined destination calendar
body: After destinationCalendar became an array, `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` yields undefined when the event has no destination calendar. The next line still reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` whenever the location is MeetLocationType. Any Google Meet event without a destination calendar now throws a TypeError instead of falling back to Cal Video. Guard the access or use optional chaining.

title: Video booking references lose credentialId
body: In create(), referencesToCreate now sets `credentialId` only for calendar results (`isCalendarType ? result.credentialId : undefined`). Video results previously kept `result.credentialId`. Without a credentialId on the video booking reference, handleCancelBooking's video cancellation branch (`if (bookingVideoReference && bookingVideoReference.credentialId)`) is skipped, so the video meeting is not deleted when the booking is cancelled. Preserve `result.credentialId` for non-calendar results.

title: externalId is dropped before creating calendar events
body: createEvent now accepts an externalId argument, and EventManager passes `destination.externalId` so each destination should create its event on that calendar. But this call still invokes `calendar.createEvent(calEvent, credential.id)` and never forwards externalId; it only copies externalId into the returned result. Google uses credentialId to pick the right destination, but Office365, Lark and BaseCalendarService all read `event.destinationCalendar[0]`. For a collective event with multiple hosts, every service call therefore uses the first host's calendar: the second Office365/Lark event fails or is created in the wrong calendar, and CalDAV silently creates nothing. Pass the destination externalId or make every service select by credentialId.

title: Team destination calendars dropped when organizer destination is null
body: `evt.destinationCalendar` is set to null when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar. The following `if (COLLECTIVE) evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` silently does nothing in that case, so destination calendars collected from other hosts are discarded. A collective event whose organizer has no destination calendar but whose other hosts do will not invite those hosts. Initialize the array before pushing.

title: Organization slug condition flipped
body: The spread condition for `slug` was changed from `!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED` to `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED`. With team billing disabled (the self-hosted/default case), organizations are now created without a slug, breaking organization URLs. With billing enabled, the code now writes both `slug` and `requestedSlug`, changing the deferred-slug flow. This unrelated change should be reverted or explicitly justified.

title: Google update/delete fallback matches externalId against null
body: When externalCalendarId is null/empty, updateEvent and deleteEvent fall back to `event.destinationCalendar?.find(cal => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. Since externalCalendarId is falsy, this searches for a destination with a null/empty externalId and normally returns undefined. updateEvent then calls Google without a calendarId, and deleteEvent falls back to deleting from `primary`. Previously the code used `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. Use the first destination calendar or select by credential as the fallback.

title: Only first old calendar event deleted when merging bookings
body: The method now processes all calendar references for the new booking, but the `newBookingId` merge cleanup still calls `booking.references.find(...)` and deletes a single old calendar event. For collective bookings with multiple calendar references, the remaining hosts' old events are left on their calendars after reschedule/merge. Loop over all old calendar references and delete each one.

title: Recurring collective cancellation still only uses booking owner credentials
body: In the recurring/allRemainingBookings branch, the code still iterates `bookingToDelete.user.credentials` and picks the first calendar reference from each updated booking, rather than using the current reference's credentialId/externalCalendarId. For collective recurring bookings, calendar events belonging to other hosts are not deleted. The new outer loop over bookingCalendarReference also re-runs this same deletion for every reference, causing duplicate delete attempts. Use the current reference to delete the matching event for each updated booking.

title: updateLocation references lose calendar external id and credential id
body: referencesToCreate in updateLocation now reads `result.externalId` and `result.credentialId`, but CalendarManager.updateEvent's returned EventResult never populates either field. For calendar update results these values are undefined, so editLocation creates booking references without externalCalendarId/credentialId; later updates or cancellations must fall back to primary/all credentials. The old code used evt.destinationCalendar for these values. Either populate them in CalendarManager.updateEvent or keep the destination fallback.

title: Crash when Google Meet is selected without a destination calendar
body: `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is the first element of `evt.destinationCalendar ?? []`, so it is undefined when the event has no destination calendar. The next condition dereferences `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` whenever `evt.location === MeetLocationType`. Previously optional chaining made this safe. Any Google Meet booking without a destination calendar now throws inside EventManager.create instead of falling back to Cal Video.

title: Stale credential reused when a reference credential cannot be loaded
body: In `updateAllCalendarEvents` the loop reuses the outer `credential` variable. If `this.calendarCredentials` has no match and the DB lookup fails or returns a credential without `app.slug`, `credential` still holds the previous iteration's credential or remains undefined. The code then calls `updateEvent(credential, ...)`, potentially updating the wrong calendar or failing. It should skip that reference when no credential is resolved and scope the variable per iteration.

title: Updated calendar references lose credentialId and externalCalendarId
body: `referencesToCreate` for `updateLocation` now reads `result.externalId` and `result.credentialId`, but `CalendarManager.updateEvent` never puts those fields on its returned EventResult. Editing a booking location therefore creates BookingReference rows with both fields undefined. Previously the `evt.destinationCalendar` fallback populated them. Later updates/cancellations may then target the wrong calendar or fail to find the external event.

title: Collective hosts' destination calendars are dropped when the organizer has none
body: `evt.destinationCalendar` is explicitly set to `null` when neither the event type nor organizer has a destination calendar. The optional push then silently does nothing, so `teamDestinationCalendars` collected from the other collective hosts is discarded. In that case EventManager never receives those hosts' destination calendars and collective hosts do not get calendar invites. The array should be initialised to `[]` before collecting/pushing team destinations.

title: Organization slug creation is inverted for self-hosted billing settings
body: This PR changes `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`. When team billing is disabled, which is the normal self-hosted path, the organization is now created without a slug, whereas previously it always received one. This is unrelated to the destination-calendar fix and will break organization URLs on instances without team billing.

title: Hangout-link patch uses undefined calendarId when destination is absent
body: `selectedCalendar` can be undefined when no destination calendar matches the credential, and insert correctly falls back to `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"`. The follow-up `events.patch` still passes `calendarId: selectedCalendar`, so in the fallback case the patch is sent with an undefined calendar id and the generated hangoutLink is not written into the event description. Use the same `selectedCalendar || "primary"` fallback in the patch.

title: Google update/delete fallback compares externalId with the null externalCalendarId
body: When `externalCalendarId` is not provided, the fallback is `event.destinationCalendar?.find(cal => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. Because `externalCalendarId` is null/undefined, this almost always returns undefined. Previously it fell back to `event.destinationCalendar.externalId`. Updates may now fail because calendarId is undefined, and deletes fall back to `primary` instead of the event's destination calendar, leaving events behind. The same broken pattern exists in `deleteEvent` at line 317.

title: Office365 createEvent writes to the first host's calendar for every credential
body: `createEvent` ignores the new `credentialId` argument and always chooses `event.destinationCalendar[0].externalId`. When EventManager iterates collective hosts, the second host's Office365 credential is used against the first host's calendar id, causing 403/404 errors or creating the event in the wrong calendar. It needs to select the destination whose `credentialId` matches the credential passed to `createEvent`.

title: Lark createEvent also ignores credentialId and uses the first destination
body: The Lark implementation now takes the first element of `event.destinationCalendar` for every credential. For a collective booking, the second host's Lark credential will attempt to use the first host's calendarId, likely failing or writing to the wrong calendar. `createEvent` needs to choose the destination entry matching the credential it was called with.

title: Base CalDAV service ignores credentialId when selecting destination calendars
body: With multiple destination calendars, `createEvent` filters the credential's calendars by the first destination's externalId. For the second host's credential that externalId belongs to another account, so the filter produces no calendars and the method returns success without creating anything. The selection must be made using the `credentialId` passed to `createEvent` or another identifier that belongs to the current credential.

title: Recurring collective cancellation only uses organizer credentials and repeats deletes
body: When cancelling all remaining recurring bookings, the loop over the new multiple calendar references re-enters the same block for every reference, but inside it ignores the current reference and only iterates `bookingToDelete.user.credentials`, deleting the first calendar reference of every updated booking. For a collective booking, second-host references/credentials are never used, so those external events remain, and the same organizer deletions are issued once per reference.

title: No test for collective multi-host destination calendars
body: The only test change updates the expected webhook shape for BOOKING_REJECTED. There is no test covering collective events with multiple destination calendars or the new create/update/delete paths, despite many calendar services and EventManager being changed. This leaves the primary regression and the calendar-service credential-selection bugs untested.

title: Crash when Meet location has no destination calendar
body: `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is undefined when `evt.destinationCalendar` is null or an empty array, but the code dereferences `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration`. Any Google Meet event whose organizer has no destination calendar will throw before the Cal Video fallback can run. The previous code used optional chaining, so this is a regression; guard with `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration` or equivalent.

title: Video references lose credentialId
body: `referencesToCreate` now sets `credentialId` only for calendar results (`isCalendarType ? result.credentialId : undefined`). Non-calendar results are video meetings, and their `result.credentialId` is what lets later cancellation/update code find the video credential. With this change new video references have no `credentialId`, so deletion paths such as `handleCancelBooking` skip `deleteMeeting` and leave orphaned video meetings.

title: Location updates create references without externalCalendarId or credentialId
body: `updateLocation` now builds `referencesToCreate` using `result.externalId` and `result.credentialId`, but `CalendarManager.updateEvent` never returns either field. As a result, after editing a location the newly created booking references omit `externalCalendarId` and `credentialId`, breaking future calendar updates/deletes and forcing legacy fallback behavior. The reference data must be taken from the update result/credential or from the event destination calendar.

title: Google updateEvent loses destination-calendar fallback
body: When `externalCalendarId` is not supplied, the `find` callback compares `cal.externalId === externalCalendarId`, which is `undefined` and therefore never matches a real destination calendar. The previous fallback used `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. Updates for booking references that lack an external calendar id now send `calendarId: undefined` and fail instead of updating the selected destination calendar.

title: Collective team destination calendars dropped when organizer has none
body: `evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar. In that case `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is a no-op, so destination calendars collected from the other collective hosts are discarded. This means an organizer without a connected calendar prevents other hosts from receiving calendar invites, which is one of the cases this PR is meant to fix. Initialize the array and push unconditionally when team destinations exist.

title: Office365 creates all events in the first host's destination calendar
body: `createEvent` always uses the first element of `event.destinationCalendar` as the target calendar. `EventManager` now invokes `createEvent` once per destination with that host's credential, so the second Office365 host's credential is used against the first host's `externalId`. That creates the event in the wrong calendar or gets a Graph 404, and the second host is not properly invited. The target destination must be matched to the credential being used (or passed explicitly).

title: Lark creates all events in the first host's destination calendar
body: `createEvent` takes the first destination calendar from the array and ignores which credential called it. With multiple collective hosts, the second host's Lark credential will try to create the event in the first host's calendar id, so the event either fails or lands in the wrong calendar and the second host does not receive the expected invite. The service needs to select the destination corresponding to the credential used.

title: CalDAV/BaseCalendar silently skips additional hosts
body: `createEvent` filters available calendars down to the first destination calendar's `externalId`. When EventManager calls this service for the second host's destination, that externalId belongs to the first host's calendar and does not match any calendar for the second credential, so the filter returns an empty list and no event is created. Because empty responses are treated as success, the missing host event is silent. The filter should target the destination for the current credential rather than always the first array element.

title: Recurring collective cancellations delete only one calendar reference
body: The recurring cancellation branch still uses `updatedBooking.references.find(...)` and deletes only the first `_calendar` reference for each booking. With multi-host bookings there are now multiple calendar references, so only one host's recurring events are cancelled while the others remain on calendars. It also runs this work once per outer calendar reference, duplicating calls. It should iterate all calendar references for each updated booking.

title: Organization slug condition appears inverted
body: This unrelated change reverses the existing condition: previously `slug` was included only when `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED` was false, now it is included only when it is true. For self-hosted/no-billing installs, organizations will be created without a slug; for billing-enabled installs, they now get both a direct `slug` and `requestedSlug`, potentially assigning an unverified subdomain before the billing flow. Revert this or document why the condition should flip.

title: Google Calendar sharing path reads .data off a fetch Response
body: In credential-sharing mode refreshOAuthTokens (packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts) returns the raw fetch Response when CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT is set, but this code treats the result like Google's refreshToken() return value and reads res?.data. A Response has no data property, so token is undefined and token.access_token throws. The surrounding catch (message !== invalid_grant) swallows it and returns myGoogleAuth still holding the expired token, so subsequent Google Calendar API calls fail with 401. The feature silently never refreshes Google tokens.

title: HubSpot sharing path stores a raw Response as the credential key
body: refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response when credential sharing is enabled, but here the result is used as a HubspotToken object: hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn is undefined so expiryDate becomes NaN, and the Response is passed directly to prisma.credential.update({ data: { key: hubspotRefreshToken } }). A Response serializes to {} in JSON, so the stored credential key is destroyed and all HubSpot calls fail. In the non-sharing path the refresh function returned a parsed HubspotToken, so the two return types are incompatible.

title: Zoho Bigin sharing path crashes reading .data on a Response
body: When credential sharing is enabled refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response; in the non-sharing path it returns the axios response that has .data. This code then evaluates tokenInfo.data.error, so in sharing mode tokenInfo.data is undefined and the property access throws a TypeError, breaking token refresh entirely. The two branches return incompatible types and the feature does not work for Bigin.

title: Zoho CRM sharing path crashes reading .data on a Response
body: With credential sharing enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response, but this code expects the axios result and reads zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error. In sharing mode .data is undefined, so the property access throws a TypeError and token refresh is broken. Non-sharing returns the axios response (with .data), so the two paths are type-incompatible.

title: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses computed keys that collapse to [object Object] and strips all fields
body: The schema builds keys via [z.string().toString()]. Zod does not override toString, so z.string().toString() evaluates to the literal string [object Object]; both computed keys collapse to the same name and the last one wins. The schema is effectively { access_token: z.string(), '[object Object]': z.unknown().optional() }, which is not the intended 'any numeric property is expiry' validation. Because Zod strips unknown keys by default, the parsed output contains only access_token, so in sharing mode every caller loses expiry_date/expires_in/refresh_token and ends up storing credentials with NaN expiry or missing fields, causing repeated refreshes or stalled tokens.

title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string 'refresh_token' and persisted
body: When the parsed response has no refresh_token (exactly the sharing case, where the sync endpoint is documented to return only the access token and expiry), this assigns the literal string 'refresh_token'. Callers such as Office365 and Zoom then write the parsed object back to the credential, overwriting the real stored refresh token with this placeholder. The next time a real refresh is attempted against the provider it fails because the stored refresh token is now the string 'refresh_token'. This silently corrupts credential data.

title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time !==
body: The incoming CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET header is compared to process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET with !==. String inequality short-circuits at the first differing byte, leaking timing information about the expected secret and enabling a timing side-channel to guess it. Use a constant-time comparison (e.g. crypto.timingSafeEqual on equal-length buffers). Also note the header name is looked up case-sensitively from process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME; since Node lowercases incoming header names, a non-lowercase value makes every request fail with 403.

title: Malformed body or bad ciphertext returns 500 instead of 400
body: appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body) throws a ZodError on invalid input, and JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...)) at line 57 throws on bad ciphertext or a wrong/missing encryption key. Neither is caught, so the handler returns a 500 with a stack trace instead of a 400. This makes misconfiguration and attacker probing hard to distinguish and leaks internals. Wrap request parsing, decryption and JSON parsing and return a 400 on failure.

title: findFirst-then-create race can create duplicate credentials
body: The findFirst followed by create/update is not atomic. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same (userId, appId) can both observe no existing credential and both insert one, producing duplicate Credential rows (the schema does not enforce uniqueness on userId+appId). Use a unique constraint with upsert, or otherwise serialize per user/app.

title: Updating credentials does not reset the invalid flag
body: When updating an existing credential only key is written; the invalid flag is left untouched. Services such as GoogleCalendarService mark a credential invalid: true on invalid_grant, so a credential that was previously invalidated stays invalid even after fresh synced keys are written, and the app remains disabled. Reset invalid: false in the update.

title: No tests for the new webhook or refresh routing
body: The author states no tests were added and local tests were not run. This PR introduces a new authenticated endpoint that decrypts and writes credentials, plus a refresh-routing layer whose return type is inconsistent across callers. There is no coverage for: rejecting disabled sharing or a bad secret, decrypting and upserting credentials, and verifying that refresh flows hit the sync endpoint and still persist valid tokens. A single test exercising the sharing path would have caught the Response-vs-parsed-object mismatches in the Google/HubSpot/Zoho services.

title: Dynamic Zod keys collapse and strip token fields
body: The computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` in `minimumTokenResponseSchema` both evaluate to the same static key such as `[object Object]`, so the schema is effectively only `{ access_token: z.string(), "[object Object]": ... }`. It does not validate any numeric expiry field as the comment claims, and because `z.object` strips unknown fields, every other field returned by the sync endpoint (`expiry_date`, `expires_in`, `refresh_token`, etc.) is discarded. In sync mode callers persist incomplete tokens.

title: Missing refresh_token is overwritten with the literal string `refresh_token`
body: When the provider or sync endpoint does not return a new refresh token, this code writes the literal value `"refresh_token"` into the parsed data. For O365, where `refresh_token` is optional in the schema, this replaces the existing valid refresh token during the merge in `Office365CalendarService`, so the next refresh fails. It also guarantees corruption in sync mode for any callers that store `refresh_token`.

title: Google Calendar stores the safeParse wrapper instead of credential data
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns a `SafeParseReturnType` object (`{ success, data }`), not the parsed data itself. Assigning it to `key` and then writing `key` to `prisma.credential.update` changes the database credential to `{ success: true, data: {...} }`. On the next use, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` no longer sees top-level `access_token`, so Google Calendar stops working after the first token refresh. The code should store `parsed.data` or the helper should return data consistently.

title: Sync mode returns a raw fetch Response but callers expect token objects
body: When credential sharing is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `Response` from `fetch`. Several callers assume provider-specific objects instead: `GoogleCalendarService` reads `res?.data`, `HubspotCalendarService` treats it as a `HubspotToken` and mutates `expiresIn`, and Zoho Bigin/CRM read `tokenInfo.data.error`. These paths throw TypeErrors or persist invalid credentials whenever sync is enabled. The helper needs a consistent parsed contract, or each caller must explicitly handle `Response`.

title: Zoho Bigin sends credential ID as calcomUserId
body: `refreshOAuthTokens` expects the third argument to be the Cal.com user ID and sends it as `calcomUserId` to the sync endpoint. `BiginCalendarService.refreshAccessToken` passes `credentialId`, which is the internal `Credential` primary key, not `credential.userId`. The parent app will look up the wrong user and may return tokens for a different user, which are then written to this credential.

title: Synced credentials do not clear the invalid flag
body: When an existing credential is found, the webhook only updates `key`. If the credential had been marked invalid (Google, Webex, Zoom, etc.), it remains invalid after fresh credentials are synced, so Cal.com continues to reject the newly provided valid credentials. The update should also reset `invalid` to false when new keys are supplied.

title: Salesforce refresh bypasses the credential sync endpoint
body: The new Salesforce refresh path calls `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` directly instead of going through `refreshOAuthTokens`. With `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` configured, Salesforce never asks the parent application to refresh, so the credential-sync feature does not apply to Salesforce and self-hosters relying on the parent app as source of truth still depend on local Salesforce secrets. It should use the same sync helper as the other apps or document that Salesforce is unsupported.

title: No tests cover the new credential-sync endpoint or refresh helpers
body: This PR adds a security-sensitive webhook and rewrites token refresh behavior across multiple apps without tests. Basic tests for `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, the sync-enabled `refreshOAuthTokens` path, and the webhook update/create flow would have caught the malformed Zod schema, literal `refresh_token` injection, wrong user ID, and raw `Response` handling issues.

title: Uses prisma without importing it
body: The new token-refresh block in getClient calls `await prisma.credential.update({...})` but the module never imports `prisma` (imports are jsforce, rrule, zod, getLocation, WEBAPP_URL, HttpError, logger, calendar types, CredentialPayload, getAppKeysFromSlug, parseRefreshTokenResponse). This will fail type-check and throw `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined` at runtime whenever a Salesforce credential is used, breaking the Salesforce integration entirely.

title: Defaults missing refresh_token to literal string and persists it
body: When the response has no `refresh_token`, the function sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. Callers spread/save the parsed data back into the credential (e.g. zoomvideo sets `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token`; office365calendar spreads tokenResponse.data over the stored key). This overwrites a real refresh token with the literal string `"refresh_token"`, permanently breaking future refreshes. The fallback should preserve the existing stored refresh token, not fabricate one.

title: Passes credentialId as the userId argument to refreshOAuthTokens
body: `refreshOAuthTokens(fn, appSlug, userId)` expects a Cal.com user id as its third argument. zoho-bigin passes `credentialId`. When credential sharing is enabled this sends `calcomUserId=<credentialId>` to the self-hoster endpoint, so the wrong user is looked up and the wrong credentials are returned/synced.

title: Sharing-mode returns a raw fetch Response incompatible with most callers' expected shapes
body: In the sharing branch this returns a `fetch` Response whose body (per its own comment) only contains an access token and expiry. Several adapters pass provider-specific parsing over the result and will fail/misbehave in sharing mode: hubspot reads `.expiresIn`/`.accessToken` off the raw Response (both undefined → NaN expiry, no access token set); zoho-bigin and zohocrm read `.data.error` (Response has no `.data` → TypeError); lark expects a `RefreshTokenResp` from handleLarkError but gets the minimal body; webex parses with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema` which requires literal `scope`/`token_type` that the minimal response lacks → rejection. Only callers that use parseRefreshTokenResponse tolerate the minimal shape.

title: Connection is created with stale access token after refresh
body: getClient always refreshes and writes the new token to the DB, but then constructs the jsforce.Connection with `accessToken: credentialKey.access_token`, where `credentialKey` is the pre-refresh credential. The newly obtained `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token` is never used, so all API calls use the old (likely expired) token. Additionally getClient now performs a network refresh on every instantiation instead of using the stored token, adding an extra token round-trip per calendar operation.

title: Computed-key schema is broken and does not validate expiry numbers
body: The object literal uses `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` as keys. These stringify the Zod schema objects (both evaluate to the same fixed string, e.g. "[object Object]"), so the second definition simply overrides the first and the intended "match any property whose value is a number (the expiry)" behavior never happens. The resulting schema only requires `access_token` and ignores expiry entirely, so the minimum-validity check in sharing mode is silently weaker than documented.

title: Credential-sync request is sent with no authentication
body: The POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT includes only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` and no shared secret/authorization, so the self-hoster cannot verify the request actually came from the configured Cal.com instance. Anyone who can reach the endpoint can request credential refreshes for arbitrary user ids/app slugs. It should send an authenticated header derived from a shared secret (analogous to the webhook secret).

title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time equality
body: `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` compares the shared secret with `!==`, leaking timing information that can be exploited to recover the secret over many requests. Use a constant-time comparison (e.g. crypto.timingSafeEqual on Buffers of equal length).

title: No HTTP method check and unhandled zod parse errors
body: The handler never inspects `req.method`, so any verb (GET/PUT/DELETE/...) is accepted as long as the header matches, and `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throwing on an invalid payload surfaces as a 500 instead of a 400. A method guard plus wrapping parse in try/catch (returning 400) would give correct, predictable behavior.

title: Team admin/owner permission check uses AND instead of OR
body: `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`. This means a user must be both admin and owner to pass, so a normal team admin who is not an owner receives a 403 when trying to add guests. The permission should be `isTeamAdmin(...) || isTeamOwner(...)`, or a single helper should be used.

title: Any booking attendee can add guests and trigger invites
body: The handler grants access to any user whose email appears in `booking.attendees`. An attendee can call the mutation with arbitrary email addresses, which adds those addresses to the booking, updates the organizer's calendar through EventManager, and sends emails to the organizer and all attendees. This is an authorization expansion beyond the organizer/team-admin dashboard flow and enables attendee-driven invite/spam abuse. The permission should be restricted to the organizer and authorized team admins/owners unless attendee self-service is explicitly intended and protected.

title: Guest email filtering is case-sensitive and does not dedupe input
body: `uniqueGuests` compares raw guest emails against existing attendee emails and against `blacklistedGuestEmails`, which are lowercased. Because guest emails are not normalized/lowercased and the `guests` array itself is not deduped, an uppercase form of a blacklisted address bypasses the blacklist, and duplicate addresses in one request create duplicate attendee rows. The server must trim/lowercase and dedupe before filtering and inserting, independent of the client-side Zod uniqueness check.

title: Email logic receives all requested guests instead of actually added guests
body: `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` is called with the original request array, not `uniqueGuests`. If the request contains a new guest plus an already-existing attendee, `uniqueGuests` excludes the existing attendee from insertion, but the email manager still sees that address in `newGuests` and sends that existing attendee `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (a full booking confirmation) instead of `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail`. Pass `uniqueGuests` to the email sender.

title: Calendar update uses the current session user's credentials, not the organizer's
body: The handler builds `EventManager` from `ctx.user` via `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` and `{ ...user, credentials }`. When a team admin/owner or attendee invokes the mutation, this attempts to update the organizer's calendar using the caller's credentials. That can fail or update the wrong account even though the guests have already been persisted in the database. It should load and use the booking organizer's credentials for the calendar operation.

title: Guests are persisted before external calendar update can fail
body: The Prisma update inserts the new attendees before `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` runs. If the calendar update throws, the mutation fails and the caller sees an error, but the guest rows remain in the booking without the corresponding calendar update (and before any emails). This leaves booking data and external calendars inconsistent. The operation needs failure handling or a rollback path.

title: New guest emails bypass disableStandardEmails settings
body: `sendAddGuestsEmails` unconditionally sends organizer/team-member and attendee emails and does not accept or check `EventTypeMetadata`. Unlike other send functions, event types configured with `disableStandardEmails.all.host` or `disableStandardEmails.all.attendee` still receive these guest-added emails. The function should accept event type metadata and respect the same host/attendee email-disable guards as the existing email flows.

title: Invalid email state is not cleared on success or non-cancel close
body: After a failed validation, `isInvalidEmail` is set to true, but the success handler closes the dialog and only resets `multiEmailValue`; it never calls `setIsInvalidEmail(false)`. Closing via the dialog's X/overlay also does not reset either state. Reopening the dialog can therefore show a stale validation error and stale email values. Reset the dialog state on both success and any close path.

title: No tests cover the new add-guests mutation
body: This adds a security-sensitive mutation with authorization, deduplication, blacklist filtering, calendar update, and email behavior, but no tests are included. At minimum, tests should cover organizer vs team admin vs attendee permissions, duplicate/blacklisted email filtering, passing only actually-added guests to the email sender, and the error path when the calendar update fails.

title: Team admin/owner permission check uses AND instead of OR
body: `isTeamAdminOrOwner` requires the caller to satisfy both `isTeamAdmin` and `isTeamOwner`. A normal team admin is not a team owner, so the computed value is false and the mutation returns FORBIDDEN even though the UI and variable name treat team admins as allowed. Depending on whether `isTeamAdmin` also returns true for owners, owners may fail as well. This should use OR semantics, or a helper that checks either role.

title: Guest filtering is case-sensitive and does not dedupe requests
body: `blacklistedGuestEmails` is lowercased but `guest` is not, so a blacklisted address such as `evil@example.com` can be bypassed as `Evil@Example.com`. Existing-attendee checks are also case-sensitive (`guest === attendee.email`), so mixed-case duplicates can be inserted. The request schema allows duplicate emails and the handler only compares each guest to existing attendees, not to other guests in the same request, so `guests: ["a@x.com", "a@x.com"]` creates duplicate Attendee rows and can send duplicate invitations. Normalize/lowercase addresses and dedupe both against existing attendees and within the request.

title: Any booking attendee can add arbitrary guests
body: The authorization check explicitly permits `isAttendee` callers to add guests. An external invitee who knows or guesses the numeric booking id can therefore append arbitrary email addresses, cause calendar invites to be sent, and trigger emails to all attendees that contain meeting details. Unless the product intentionally allows guests to invite further guests, this should be restricted to the organizer and authorized team admins/owners.

title: Calendar update uses the caller's credentials, not the organizer's
body: The EventManager is constructed from `ctx.user` credentials. When the caller is a team admin/owner or attendee rather than the booking organizer, the calendar update runs with the wrong account and may fail or modify the organizer's calendar event under a different user's credentials. The handler already loads `booking.user` with credentials, so the organizer's credentials should be used for the booking's calendar update.

title: Guests are persisted before the external calendar update
body: `prisma.booking.update` inserts the new attendees before `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` runs. If the calendar update throws, the API returns an error but the guest rows remain in the database. The user sees failure and retries, but the retry then reports `emails_must_be_unique_valid` because the guests already exist. This leaves the operation in an ambiguous state; calendar sync failures should be handled without committing an unreported partial update.

title: Emails are sent using the original guests list instead of the filtered list
body: `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` passes the raw request array, not `uniqueGuests`. If a request contains both an already-existing attendee and a new guest, the existing attendee is treated as newly added by the email manager and receives `AttendeeScheduledEmail` instead of the add-guests notification. The email manager should receive only the guests that were actually inserted (`uniqueGuests`).

title: addGuests emails ignore event type standard-email settings
body: `sendAddGuestsEmails` unconditionally sends organizer and attendee emails and does not accept or check `eventTypeMetadata`, unlike the surrounding `sendScheduledEmails`, `sendCancelledEmails`, etc. As a result, event types configured with `disableStandardEmails.all.host` or `disableStandardEmails.all.attendee` will still notify those users when guests are added. The handler has the event type and should pass metadata through so these settings are honored.

title: No tests for the new addGuests mutation
body: The new endpoint has no tests covering authorization (organizer, team admin/owner, attendee), duplicate or mixed-case email handling, blacklist filtering, or email recipient selection. These are exactly the areas where the current implementation has defects, so endpoint-level tests would both catch regressions and document the intended permissions.

title: Calendar update uses actor credentials instead of booking owner credentials
body: The handler fetches booking.user with destinationCalendar and credentials, but then builds EventManager from ctx.user and calls getUsersCredentials(ctx.user). For any actor other than the organizer—especially the team-admin and attendee cases allowed by the permission check—this tries to update the organizer's calendar event using the actor's calendar credentials. If the actor has no matching calendar credentials, the mutation can fail after attendees have already been written; otherwise the organizer's calendar event is not updated correctly. Use the booking owner/organizer credentials for this booking.

title: Team admin/owner check requires both admin and owner
body: `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed with `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`, so a team admin who is not also an owner is denied access. Depending on the helper semantics, an owner who is not also an admin may also be denied. This makes the new endpoint return FORBIDDEN for legitimate team admins. This should be an OR check, and the team permission check should only be used when the booking has a team event type.

title: Guest filtering is case-sensitive and does not dedupe submitted emails
body: `uniqueGuests` only excludes exact-case matches against existing attendee emails, and compares non-normalized guest emails against a lower-cased BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS list. An attacker can bypass the blacklist by changing case and can create duplicate attendees whose emails differ only by case. The filter also only checks against the pre-update attendee list, so duplicate emails inside the submitted `guests` array all pass and are inserted. Emails should be normalized to lower case and deduped both within the input and against existing attendees server-side.

title: Emails use raw guests list instead of filtered uniqueGuests
body: `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` passes the original client input, while only `uniqueGuests` were inserted. If a caller includes an existing attendee's email, that attendee is still present in `newGuests`, so sendAddGuestsEmails classifies them as a newly added guest and sends them AttendeeScheduledEmail instead of the guest-added notification. It also bypasses the filtering done above. Pass `uniqueGuests` to the email function.

title: New guest email path ignores disabled standard email settings
body: Unlike sendScheduledEmails and sendLocationChangeEmails, sendAddGuestsEmails has no eventTypeMetadata parameter and unconditionally sends OrganizerAddGuestsEmail and attendee emails. Users who configured eventType.metadata.disableStandardEmails for host or attendee emails will still receive these guest-added emails, breaking the existing opt-out contract. Accept metadata and guard host/attendee sends with eventTypeDisableHostEmail and eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail.

title: No limit on guest count or invite rate
body: The only validation is that each array item looks like an email; there is no maximum guest count or per-booking/rate limit. Any authorized attendee or organizer can submit an arbitrarily large list, causing a large createMany, calendar fan-out, and mass emails to arbitrary addresses from Cal.com. Add a reasonable max and enforce rate limiting on this mutation.

title: Error toast can show 'undefined:' instead of fallback message
body: `const message = `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}`` always produces a non-empty string, so the `|| t('unable_to_add_guests')` fallback is unreachable. When err.data is absent, users see `undefined: <message>` rather than the intended fallback. Build the message conditionally and use the fallback when no usable error text exists.

title: Retry cleanup deletes non-SMS and already-scheduled workflow reminders
body: The new OR branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` and no `scheduled: false` condition. The surrounding `deleteMany` therefore deletes every WorkflowReminder row with `retryCount > 1`, including EMAIL/WHATSAPP reminders, and it can delete a reminder that is already successfully scheduled. The retry limit is intended only for failed SMS scheduling, so this can silently remove unrelated reminders. Scope the retry-count branch to SMS (and typically unscheduled) reminders.

title: retryCount is incremented via non-atomic read-modify-write
body: Both failure paths update the row with `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1`, where `reminder.retryCount` was read at the start of the cron run. If two cron invocations overlap, both can read the same value and write the same increment, losing failures. A reminder can then remain unscheduled for the entire 7-day window without ever reaching the deletion threshold, and overlapping runs can still send duplicate SMS. Use an atomic increment such as Prisma's `{ increment: 1 }`.

title: Errors in the catch-block update abort the whole cron run
body: The new `await prisma.workflowReminder.update(...)` inside the `catch` is not itself protected. If the row has been deleted by another concurrent cron run (the new `deleteMany` can delete rows with `retryCount > 1`) or the database update fails, this rejection escapes the per-reminder catch, stops the loop, prevents all remaining reminders from being processed, and makes the cron endpoint fail. Wrap the recovery update or use `updateMany` so one bad row cannot abort the run.

title: Missing sendTo or empty message never increments retryCount
body: The retry increment only happens when `twilio.scheduleSMS` is called and returns falsy or throws. If `sendTo` is missing or `message` is empty, the `if (message?.length && sendTo)` block is skipped entirely, so `retryCount` stays at 0 and the reminder is re-fetched on every cron run until its scheduled date passes. These are exactly the kinds of unschedulable reminders the retry limit is meant to stop retrying, so they should also be counted/deleted or otherwise marked as failed.

title: retryCount cleanup has no supporting index
body: The new `deleteMany` predicate `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` is not covered by any index on WorkflowReminder. Because this cleanup runs on every cron invocation and the OR includes an unindexed predicate, the database may scan the entire WorkflowReminder table repeatedly. Add an index on `retryCount` (or a partial index for the rows the cron needs) to keep the cron cheap as the table grows.

title: No tests cover the retry-count lifecycle or deletion scope
body: The PR changes failure handling and adds destructive cleanup logic but adds no automated tests. There should be coverage for: incrementing on scheduling failure, deleting only after the intended number of failures, not deleting non-SMS reminders, not deleting successfully scheduled reminders, and handling missing `sendTo`/empty `message` failures. Without these, regressions in the retry threshold or accidental cross-method deletion will not be caught.

title: Retry cleanup deletes non-SMS and already-scheduled reminders
body: The second branch of the cleanup `deleteMany` has only `retryCount: { gt: 1 }`. It is not scoped to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` or `scheduled: false`, so this SMS cron will delete any `WorkflowReminder` with `retryCount > 1`, including non-SMS reminders if the field is used elsewhere, and including rows that are already marked as scheduled. Deleting a scheduled row drops its provider reference (for example the Twilio SID) while the provider-side message may still be queued, and it can no longer be cancelled through the normal workflow path. Add the method and unscheduled predicates to this branch.

title: retryCount increment is a lost-update race under overlapping cron runs
body: On failure, both paths write `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1`, using the value read before the network call. The cron endpoint has no lock or claim preventing overlapping invocations. Two runs can process the same unscheduled reminder, both call Twilio (causing duplicate SMS), and both write the same incremented value. As a result, two failures can leave `retryCount` at 1 instead of 2, so the reminder is retried more often than intended and may never reach the deletion threshold. Use an atomic update such as `{ increment: 1 }` and claim the row (e.g. conditional update or `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) before sending.

title: Retry update failure can abort the whole reminder batch
body: The new `retryCount` update inside the `catch` block is not itself protected. If it fails, for example because another cron invocation already deleted the row or because of a transient database error, the exception escapes the catch, aborts the `for` loop, and prevents every remaining due reminder from being processed. The endpoint then returns 500 instead of continuing with the rest of the batch. Perform this update in its own try/catch or use `updateMany` so one stale row cannot break processing of other reminders.

title: Post-send database errors cause duplicate SMS sends
body: The `try` block wraps both `twilio.scheduleSMS` and the subsequent database update. If Twilio successfully schedules the SMS but the database update fails, execution enters this catch, increments `retryCount`, and leaves `scheduled` false without persisting `scheduledSMS.sid`. On the next cron run the same reminder is still considered unscheduled and the SMS is sent again, producing a duplicate message to the recipient. Persist the provider SID independently of the update failure, or mark the reminder as scheduled once Twilio confirms the send.

title: retryCount delete branch is not scoped to SMS or scheduled:false
body: The new OR branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` in the deleteMany has no `method` and no `scheduled` filter, so on every cron run it deletes any WorkflowReminder row whose retryCount exceeds 1 regardless of method (EMAIL/WHATSAPP too) or whether it was already successfully scheduled (`scheduled: true`, `referenceId` set). Today only this file increments retryCount, but the branch is clearly meant to target failed, unscheduled SMS reminders. If another reminder path ever increments retryCount, or a reminder reaches retryCount >= 2 and is then successfully scheduled, this deletes a reminder that still has a live Twilio message scheduled — leaving an orphaned SMS that will still be delivered. Scope the branch to `{ method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, scheduled: false, retryCount: { gt: 1 } }`.

title: retryCount increment uses a stale in-memory value, causing lost updates
body: Both the else-branch and the catch-branch increment with `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1`, where `reminder.retryCount` was read once at the start of the batch by `findMany`. If two cron executions overlap (or the row is updated between read and write), both compute the same value from the same stale snapshot and the second write silently overwrites the first, so retryCount can fail to advance and the retry limit is never reached. Use an atomic increment (`{ increment: 1 }`) instead of read-then-write.

title: Error handler performs a DB write that can itself throw and abort the whole batch
body: The `catch (error)` block now performs `prisma.workflowReminder.update(...)` before logging. If that update throws — e.g. the reminder was concurrently deleted by another cron run, or a transient DB error — the exception is thrown from inside the catch, escapes the loop, and the handler returns a 500 without processing the remaining reminders in the batch. Previously the catch only logged and continued. Wrap the increment so a failure there cannot abort the loop.

title: Reminders skipped for empty message or missing sendTo never increment retryCount
body: Both the success and failure branches live inside `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)`. When a reminder has no rendered message or no destination number, neither the success nor the else-branch executes, so retryCount is never incremented and the reminder is re-selected on every run indefinitely. That is exactly the infinite-rescheduling problem this PR is meant to fix, and it persists for these rows. Those rows should also bump retryCount (or be deleted) when they cannot be scheduled.

title: No index supports the new retryCount filter in deleteMany
body: The added `retryCount: { gt: 1 }` predicate in the global deleteMany has no index (the existing indexes are on bookingUid, workflowStepId, seatReferenceId, method/scheduled/scheduledDate, cancelled/scheduledDate). Because the OR includes this unindexed condition, the cron will scan the WorkflowReminder table on every invocation. Consider adding an index for the retry sweep or restructuring the predicate so it can use an existing index.

title: No tests cover the new retry-count behavior
body: The PR changes scheduling semantics (delete after N failures, increment on failure/error) but adds no tests for the new retryCount logic — neither for the delete threshold (`gt: 1`), nor for the increment on the falsy-schedule path, nor for the catch path. Add unit/integration coverage for the retry lifecycle, including deleting at the right count and not deleting successfully scheduled reminders.

title: Removing public `findMany` breaks service consumers
body: The public `findMany(findManyArgs)` entry point is deleted and replaced by `getBaseConditions()`, which only returns a SQL fragment. No consumer is updated in this PR. Any caller that currently constructs `InsightsBookingService` and calls `findMany` (including passing `select`, `orderBy`, or extra `where` clauses) will fail to compile or throw at runtime. The conversion also removes the service's ability to execute/select data at all; callers must be migrated to call `$queryRaw` with `getBaseConditions()` or the old API must be preserved.

title: Org-scope test is sensitive to unspecified repository ordering
body: This assertion compares the exact order of IDs stored inside `Prisma.sql` values for `ANY(...)`. The service builds `teamIds` from `teamsFromOrg.map(...)` and `userIdsFromOrg` from `findAllByTeamIds(...)`, then de-duplicates with a `Set` without sorting. Unless those repository calls have an explicit ORDER BY (not shown or guaranteed), Postgres can return teams/members in a different order, so the test can fail nondeterministically even though `ANY` is order-insensitive. Sort IDs before building the SQL or compare normalized values.

title: Caching tests were removed while caching logic remains
body: The diff deletes the entire `Caching` describe block, but `cachedAuthConditions` and `cachedFilterConditions` are still part of the service. There is now no test that `getAuthorizationConditions`/`getFilterConditions` reuse the cached SQL fragment on subsequent calls, so a regression that drops caching (extra membership/team queries per request) would go undetected.

title: Public findMany method removed without updating consumers
body: This PR deletes the public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method from `InsightsBookingService` and replaces it with `getBaseConditions()`, which only returns a `Prisma.Sql` fragment. The diff updates only this service and its tests; no other call sites are migrated. Any code that invokes `service.findMany({...})` will fail to compile (method no longer exists), and any caller that relied on the previous behavior (merging caller-supplied `where`/`select`/pagination with the authorization and filter conditions) must now build and execute its own `$queryRaw`. If such consumers exist, this is a breaking change that is not covered by the PR.

title: Only user-scope conditions are actually executed against the database
body: The single test that runs the generated SQL (`prisma.$queryRaw ... WHERE ${baseConditions}`) uses `scope: "user"`, whose authorization condition contains no array parameter. The security-critical org/team paths, which build `"teamId" = ANY(${teamIds})` and `"userId" = ANY(${userIds})`, are only checked structurally via `toEqual(Prisma.sql...)` and never executed. Prisma array binding into `ANY($1)` has known type-inference pitfalls (e.g. requiring a cast such as `::int[]`, or failing when the array is empty). A broken/empty array binding would therefore pass this suite but throw or silently return no rows in production, which is precisely the parameter-binding risk the PR description flags.

title: Org-scope assertion depends on DB row ordering of team/user IDs
body: The org-scope test compares the service's `Prisma.Sql` to a literal with `teamIds` ordered `[org.id, team.id, team2.id, team3.id]` and `userIds` ordered `[user.id, user2.id, user3.id]`. The service builds those arrays from `teamRepo.findAllByParentId` and `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds`, neither of which is shown to enforce an `ORDER BY`. `toEqual` on `Prisma.Sql` compares the interpolated value arrays element-by-element, so if Postgres returns the rows in a different order the arrays differ and the test fails even though the generated SQL is semantically identical (`ANY(...)` is order-insensitive). This makes the test flaky/order-dependent rather than validating behavior; either sort the arrays before comparison or assert the query result instead.

title: getFilterConditions can return an unparenthesized OR fragment
