Because `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` was changed to `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info("Plugin Request Completed", ...)`, a test that injects a `*TestLogger` and asserts on `logger.InfoLogs.Calls`/`Message` will now observe zero calls, and the middleware's log output can no longer be asserted on the injected logger at all. The fake should return the receiver (or share the `Logs` state) so callers can inspect what was logged; otherwise this double silently hides regressions in the newly refactored logging path.

title: New ContextualLoggerMiddleware and infra FromContext have no tests
body: The entire refactor now depends on the new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware`/`instrumentContext` to reproduce the log fields that `LoggerMiddleware` used to add explicitly (endpoint, pluginId, and the conditional dsName/dsUID when `DataSourceInstanceSettings` is set and uname when `User` is set), plus the new `grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext` in pkg/plugins/log/logger.go (including its `*log.ConcreteLogger` type assertion and `!ok` fallback). None of these are covered by tests; the only test change in the PR is a one-line rename in metrics_middleware_test.go. A regression here (e.g. attributes not being applied or the type assertion failing) would silently drop pluginId/endpoint/uname/dsName/dsUID/traceID from the "Plugin Request Completed" log without any failing test. Add tests asserting the produced contextual attributes.

title: FromContext fallback silently drops traceID and all contextual attributes
body: `grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext` type-asserts `d.l.FromContext(ctx)` to `*log.ConcreteLogger` and, on failure, returns `d.New()`. `d.New()` is a base logger with no traceID and no contextual attributes, so if the infra logger ever returns a different implementation (e.g. a context-aware wrapper type), every request-completed log emitted via `LoggerMiddleware` would silently lose pluginId/endpoint/uname/dsName/dsUID/traceID with no error or fallback signal. The fallback masks the failure rather than degrading gracefully. Storing the infra `log.Logger` interface (which exposes Debug/Info/etc.) instead of `*log.ConcreteLogger` would avoid the assertion entirely.

title: Adding FromContext to the Logger interface is a breaking change for implementers
body: Adding the `FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger` method to the exported `plugins/log.Logger` interface breaks every implementation. This PR only updates `grafanaInfraLogWrapper` and `TestLogger`. Verify there are no other implementations (in particular generated mocks, e.g. via mockery, or test doubles in other packages) that now fail to satisfy the interface and break the build; if any exist they must be regenerated/updated in this PR.

title: Test function still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware after rename
body: The file and middleware were renamed from Instrumentation to Metrics, but the test function is still `TestInstrumentationMiddleware`. This is a leftover from an incomplete rename and is misleading now that `InstrumentationMiddleware` no longer exists. Rename it to `TestMetricsMiddleware` for consistency.

title: Refactor moves pluginId/endpoint/uname/ds labels from explicit log params to FromContext with no test
body: Before this PR the "Plugin Request Completed" log line explicitly added pluginId, endpoint, uname (dsName/dsUID) and traceID from the request's PluginContext. Those explicit params were deleted; the line now depends entirely on the contextual attributes added by the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware being read back through m.logger.FromContext(ctx). If the middleware ordering, the WithContextualAttributes plumbing, or the grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext type-assertion ever fails, these labels silently disappear from the log line and nothing detects it. No test covers this path (the renamed metrics test only checks Prometheus metrics), so this behavior change is unverified. At minimum a test should wrap the logger middleware with a logger that records FromContext output and assert pluginId/endpoint/labels are present.

title: TestLogger.FromContext discards context, making the new FromContext-based logging path untestable
body: TestLogger.FromContext ignores its context.Context argument and returns a brand-new empty TestLogger. The refactored LoggerMiddleware now obtains contextual attributes exclusively via FromContext, so any test using this fake can never observe whether the attributes were actually propagated. The fake silently masks exactly the behavior this PR introduces. It should copy/record the contextual attributes from the context (or the log call should include them) so tests can assert the merged output.

title: Test function still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware after rename
body: The file and symbol were renamed from Instrumentation to Metrics, but the test function is still `func TestInstrumentationMiddleware`. This leaves the rename inconsistent and makes the test hard to locate by name; it should be renamed to TestMetricsMiddleware.

title: Rejected over-limit devices are cached before the DB call and bypass the limit afterward
body: In tagDeviceUI the device's cache key is written with localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{}) *before* calling anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. Now that TagDevice propagates the DB error (line 147) and client.go turns ErrDeviceLimitReached into a failed Authenticate, the failure happens after the cache is already populated. The local cache (localcache.New(29*time.Minute, ...)) therefore still holds the entry, so the next request from that same device hits the cache short-circuit at line 83, tagDeviceUI returns nil, TagDevice returns nil, and Authenticate succeeds. Result: a device that is over the configured limit is rejected only once per ~29-minute window and is otherwise granted anonymous access, defeating the feature. The cache key must only be set after a successful CreateOrUpdateDevice, or removed when the write fails.

title: Device limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert and can be exceeded under concurrency
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice performs a separate CountDevices query and then, if count < deviceLimit, does an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT/ON DUPLICATE KEY. These are two independent statements with no transaction or locking, so N concurrent requests for new device IDs all observe count == limit-1 and all insert, leaving the table with limit-1+N devices. The configured device_limit is therefore not a hard cap under bursty anonymous traffic. Enforcing the limit needs the count check and the insert to be atomic (e.g. a single conditional/transactional statement or a locking advisory lock).

title: Device tagging is now synchronous on the anonymous auth path
body: The previous code ran TagDevice in a detached goroutine with its own timeout so anonymous authentication did not block on the device store. It is now called synchronously with the request context inside Authenticate. For every anonymous request that misses the per-device cache this adds a database round trip to authentication: when device_limit > 0 it is at least a COUNT over anon_device plus an INSERT/UPDATE. On instances serving many distinct anonymous devices (public dashboards), this makes the login/auth path DB-bound and couples anonymous auth latency (and availability) to the anon_device table. The change should preserve the non-blocking behavior while still being able to enforce the limit (e.g. only reject after a synchronous existence/limit check that is cheap, or move the enforcement off the hot path).

title: New auth.anonymous device_limit option is not documented
body: A new config key device_limit is read from the [auth.anonymous] section (cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit = anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0)), but no sample configuration (conf/defaults.ini / conf/sample.ini) or reference documentation for this option is added in this PR. Operators have no way to discover the setting, its default of 0 (unlimited), or its interaction with the 30-day device window. Add the option to the config sample and the authentication configuration docs.

title: No test covers the limit enforcement through the service/cache path
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only exercises AnonDBStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice directly and asserts the second insert returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. There is no test that drives TagDevice/Authenticate for an over-limit device, which is exactly where the localCache ordering bug (cache set before write) makes the limit unenforced on subsequent requests. Add a test that goes through the Anonymous/AnonDeviceService path and verifies a rejected device stays rejected, and that a device under the limit still succeeds.

title: Failed device-limit write leaves a positive cache entry, allowing retry bypass
body: In `tagDeviceUI`, the local cache entry is written before `CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs. If `CreateOrUpdateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, `TagDevice` now returns the error and the unauthenticated request is rejected, but the cache entry remains. The next request from the same device hits the cache check and returns nil without touching the database, so `Anonymous.Authenticate` succeeds even though the device was never stored and the limit is still reached. A user can bypass the new device limit by retrying the request. Set the cache only after a successful write, or delete the key on error.

title: Device limit check and insert are not atomic
body: The limit is enforced with a non-atomic check-then-act: `CountDevices` runs at line 110 and the INSERT/UPSERT runs later at line 120+ without a transaction or lock. Concurrent requests from different new devices can all read `count < deviceLimit` and then all insert, so the configured limit can be exceeded. The local cache only deduplicates the same device ID and does not prevent this. Use an atomic insert conditioned on the current count, a transaction with appropriate locking, or another mechanism that makes the count and insert serialization atomic.

title: Zero affected rows is incorrectly always treated as device limit reached
body: `updateDevice` treats `RowsAffected() == 0` as `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, but zero affected rows does not only mean the device is missing. MySQL by default reports changed rows, not matched rows, so an UPDATE that leaves `client_ip`, `user_agent`, and `updated_at` unchanged can return 0 even though the device exists and is within the limit. This can happen with coarse timestamp precision or with multiple Grafana instances whose local caches are independent. The result is that a legitimate existing device is incorrectly rejected as over the limit. Distinguish 'device not found/stale' from 'matched but unchanged' by checking existence or using found-rows semantics.

title: Device is cached before DB write, so a rejected device is let through on retry
body: tagDeviceUI inserts the device key into localCache (line 87) and only afterwards calls anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice (line 93). When the device limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, which is now propagated (line 147) and by client.go aborts authentication. However the cache entry is never removed on this failure. Any subsequent request from the same device within the 29-minute cache TTL hits the early `localCache.Get` return (line 83) and succeeds without touching the DB. The net effect is that the device limit only blocks the first request of a device (per instance) and then silently allows it, the device is never recorded in the DB/count, and because the cache is per-process the behavior also differs across HA instances. The cache must be populated only after a successful DB write (or deleted on error).

title: Count-then-insert check is not atomic, so the device limit can be exceeded
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice reads CountDevices (line 110) and then, if under the limit, performs a separate INSERT/ON CONFLICT (line 149) in a different DB session with no transaction or lock between them. Under concurrent anonymous requests two or more new devices can all observe count < deviceLimit and all insert, pushing the table past the configured limit. The limit is therefore only approximately enforced under load. Consider counting and inserting in one transaction/locking, or enforcing the cap in SQL.

title: Returning the raw limit error from Authenticate fails anonymous requests instead of denying gracefully
body: When TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, Authenticate returns `nil, err`. Because this is the anonymous authn client, a returned error aborts authentication for the whole request rather than yielding a successful anonymous identity, so a device that is over the limit gets an authentication failure (generic error/401-500) on the requests where the DB path runs. Combined with the localCache being primed before the DB call, this produces intermittent failures: the first request fails and later ones (cache hit) succeed. There is no user-facing handling for 'device limit reached'; the decision to hard-fail the request (vs. logging and continuing, or mapping to a controlled response) should be made explicit.

title: anonymousDeviceLimit typed as number | undefined but backend always sends a number
body: FrontendSettingsDTO.AnonymousDeviceLimit is an int64 without omitempty, so the API always serializes a number (0 when unset / unlimited). The TS type `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined` and the GrafanaBootConfig default `undefined` therefore misrepresent the wire contract: consumers checking for `undefined` to mean 'unset' will never see it, they always get 0. The type should be `number` (with 0 documented as unlimited) to match the backend.

title: Limit test only covers rejection of a new device; no coverage that existing devices still update
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit verifies only that a brand-new device is rejected when the limit is reached. It does not assert the complementary and important behavior that an already-registered, active device continues to update successfully at the limit (the updateDevice path returning rowsAffected > 0), nor does it cover the localCache-before-DB-write interaction that lets a rejected device through on retry. Without these cases the bypass and the 'existing devices keep working' contract are untested.

title: Cleanup interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: This PR changes the global cleanup ticker from 10 minutes to 1 minute. The cleanup loop runs every cleanup job, including temporary file cleanup, snapshot deletion, dashboard-version deletion, image cleanup, short URL cleanup, query-history cleanup, and annotation cleanup. This makes all of those jobs run 10x more often on every instance, unrelated to the annotation deadlock fix and with potentially significant DB/IO load. It may also increase the frequency of the annotation cleanup that is reported to deadlock. Revert this change or make the interval configurable and justify it separately.

title: Normal cleanup progress is logged at Error level, including full ID lists
body: The new batch-cleanup code logs every batch at error level, including the complete list of IDs and the SQL condition (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579). These calls happen on every cleanup cycle and every batch, even when there is nothing to delete. With cleanup scheduled every minute and a configurable batch size that can be as large as 32767 in the tests, this can emit very large error-level log entries in normal operation and make real errors hard to spot. Use debug/info for normal progress, and avoid logging unbounded ID lists.

title: MaxCount cleanup can delete beyond the configured retention count under concurrent deletes
body: In the MaxCount branch, the IDs to delete are selected with LIMIT/OFFSET in one statement and deleted by ID in a separate, non-transactional statement. If annotations among the newest cfg.MaxCount rows are deleted between the SELECT and DELETE (for example by a user deleting an annotation or by another cleanup process), the OFFSET window shifts. IDs that were outside the protected set at SELECT time can then be inside the newest MaxCount rows, but the DELETE still removes them, leaving fewer than MaxCount annotations and losing data beyond the configured retention policy. The previous DELETE-with-subquery made the selection and deletion atomic for this purpose. Revalidate the offset in the DELETE or otherwise make the two steps atomic/guarded.

title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: Run now ticks every minute instead of every 10 minutes, so every cleanup job in the slice (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, query history, short URLs, temp files, etc.) runs ten times more often. This is an unrelated global scheduling change not described by the PR and increases database and logging load across the application. Restore the 10-minute interval unless the frequency change is intentional and validated.

title: Normal cleanup progress is logged with Error and full ID lists
body: The cleanup path logs expected normal progress with r.log.Error and includes the entire ids slice. These calls occur for every batch at lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576 and 579, so a successful cleanup can emit large error-level log entries containing up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize IDs. Combined with the one-minute cleanup ticker this can flood error logs and add significant I/O. Use debug/info level and avoid dumping full ID lists, and do not include the fetch error in a success-path log message.

title: MaxCount cleanup can delete annotations that should be retained under concurrent deletes
body: The MaxCount cleanup is split into a SELECT that loads excess IDs at OFFSET MaxCount and a later DELETE by those IDs, with no transaction between them. If newer annotations are deleted in that window, rows selected as excess can become part of the newest MaxCount annotations but are still deleted. For example, with MaxCount=1 and annotations id=1 and id=2, cleanup selects id=1 as excess; if a user deletes id=2 before the DELETE runs, cleanup deletes id=1 and leaves zero annotations even though one should have been retained. The PR comment only acknowledges under-deletion from concurrent inserts, not this over-deletion/data-loss case from concurrent deletes.

title: SQLite parameter-limit test does not actually exceed the modern limit
body: The new test creates 40003 annotations but splits them across alert, dashboard and API annotation types, so each per-type cleanup batch fetches at most about 13335 IDs. The configured batch size is 32767, but the actual DELETE statement never contains more than about 13335 IDs. On SQLite >= 3.32.0 the variable limit is 32766, so this test would still pass even if deleteByIDs used placeholders instead of inlining the IDs. It therefore does not exercise the >32767-ID case named by the test; create more than 32767 annotations of a single type or test deleteByIDs directly.

title: Cleanup interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The cleanup loop ticker is changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`, so every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, query history, etc.) runs ten times as often. `clean` is synchronous and can take up to the 9-minute timeout; because ticker events are buffered as one pending tick, a long-running cleanup can be followed immediately by another, effectively running cleanup continuously and increasing database load/contention. Unless a tenfold increase in global cleanup frequency is intended and coordinated, this change should be reverted.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged at error level with full ID lists
body: The new batch code logs normal, successful cleanup work with `r.log.Error` and includes the entire `ids` slice and generated `cond`. This occurs in `CleanAnnotations` (by age and count) and `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579). On a table with many matching rows a single log line can contain tens of thousands of IDs, every cleanup cycle, even when `err` is nil. This floods error logs/alerting and can slow the cleanup job itself. Use Debug/Trace and log counts or errors, not full ID lists.

title: New SQLite batch-size test does not actually exceed SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER
body: The new test case creates 40,003 annotations, but cleanup is run per annotation type and each type has only about 13,334 rows. Therefore no DELETE statement ever contains more than about 13,334 IDs, which is below SQLite >=3.32's 32,766 parameter limit. The test would still pass if the large-batch/inlining fallback were removed, so it does not verify the boundary it claims to cover. It needs more than 32,766 annotations of a single type (or an equivalent setup producing a single batch above the limit).

title: SQLite large-batch ID list is built in quadratic time
body: In the SQLite fallback, the ID list is materialized with repeated `fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)`, which copies the entire growing string on every iteration. This makes construction O(n^2) in the number of IDs; a batch in the tens of thousands can copy gigabytes and create GC pressure during cleanup. Use `strings.Builder`, a byte slice, or `strings.Join` to build the list in linear time.

title: Storage failures recorded as legacy metric
body: In Create, when d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage). No legacy call has happened, so this records the storage failure and storage duration under the legacy metric. Update has the same bug at line 129. These should call recordStorageDuration instead; otherwise storage error/latency dashboards are wrong and legacy failure counts are inflated.

title: Delete metric uses object name as kind label
body: Delete records a successful storage duration with d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage), passing the object name where the kind label belongs. This mislabels every successful delete metric and creates unbounded cardinailty/corrupted kind grouping. It should pass options.Kind like the other metric calls.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection recorded as storage metric
body: The asynchronous DeleteCollection goroutine times the legacy call into startLegacy but then calls d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). Legacy latency/failures are therefore attributed to unified storage, and the legacy metric is never updated. It should call recordLegacyDuration.

title: Async legacy writes can be canceled by request context
body: All write methods start their background legacy call with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...) where ctx is the original HTTP request context. The server cancels that context when the request handler returns, which can happen immediately after the method returns while the goroutine is still starting. The derived context is canceled too, so the legacy fallback write can be skipped or fail spuriously. The same pattern occurs in Delete (line 110), Update (line 135), and DeleteCollection (line 163). Use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or a fresh background context with only the needed values.

title: Independent async writes can reorder legacy state
body: Each write launches an independent goroutine with no per-object sequencing. A rapid create/update/delete sequence for the same object can reach LegacyStorage out of order, e.g. a delete may complete before an earlier update and leave the object deleted in unified but still present in legacy, or an older update may overwrite a newer one in legacy. Because reads only use unified storage, this divergence goes unnoticed until fallback is needed. Legacy writes need serialization per object (queue/worker) or another ordering guarantee.

title: Legacy Update no longer uses the object produced by unified storage
body: The old implementation wrapped objInfo so LegacyStorage.Update received the exact object returned by Storage.Update. The new implementation passes the original objInfo to Legacy.Update, so LegacyStorage recomputes UpdatedObject against its own copy. If that copy is stale because prior asynchronous writes have not landed, or if unified storage defaulted/mutated fields, legacy can store a different object than unified storage, defeating the fallback guarantee. Capture res from Storage.Update and pass a wrapper using that object to Legacy.Update.

title: Legacy write failures are no longer logged
body: The background legacy Create path records only a metric and does not log errObjectSt. The same is true for Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection. Previously legacy failures were logged with object and error details. Now a failed fallback write is invisible in logs, making production diagnosis much harder.

title: Delete tests do not mock or wait for async legacy call
body: TestMode3_Delete success configures only Storage.Delete, but Mode3.Delete now asynchronously invokes Legacy.Delete. There is no legacy mock expectation, so testify's mock panics with an unexpected call if the goroutine runs. TestMode3_DeleteCollection has the same issue at line 284. More generally, none of the Mode3 unit tests wait for the background goroutine, so they can pass without exercising the legacy write path and can panic or race nondeterministically. The tests should set up the legacy mock, synchronize on the goroutine, and assert the legacy call.

title: Mode 3 playlist tests assume synchronous legacy writes
body: The new file and unified-storage mode 3 subtests reuse doPlaylistTests, which immediately reads /api/playlists after k8s create/update/delete and asserts the legacy API already reflects the change. Mode 3 performs those legacy writes asynchronously, so the legacy request can race ahead of the background write and make these tests flaky. The mode 3 cases need an eventually/retry check for legacy consistency or should not assert immediate legacy state.

title: Async legacy writes inherit request context and are canceled when the request ends
body: Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection start legacy writes in goroutines using the handler's request context. Go's HTTP server cancels that context as soon as ServeHTTP returns, so these goroutines will frequently begin with an already-canceled context and the legacy write will fail immediately. The 10-second timeout added inside the goroutine does not help because its parent is already canceled. Use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) (to preserve values such as user/tenant) or a writer-scoped background context before spawning the goroutine.

title: Async legacy writes are unordered and can overwrite newer state
body: Each write spawns an independent goroutine with no sequencing. Two successive updates to the same object can reach legacy storage out of order, and an update can run before the create that preceded it. Legacy storage can therefore end up with older data than unified storage even when both operations succeed, which defeats the purpose of the safety copy. This needs ordered delivery (for example a per-object or per-resource queue) or a different fallback strategy.

title: Legacy update recomputes the update from the legacy object instead of using the stored result
body: Storage.Update computes the new object by calling objInfo.UpdatedObject against the unified-storage old object. The async legacy path then passes the original objInfo again, so Legacy.Update calls UpdatedObject against the legacy store's old object. For patches/applies or any UpdatedObjectInfo that depends on the current object, the two stores can produce different results and diverge. The previous implementation explicitly wrapped objInfo with the object returned from unified storage; this path should pass a wrapper carrying the storage result (res) instead of the raw objInfo.

title: Mode 3 records several metrics with the wrong recorder or arguments
body: On Storage.Create failure, line 45 calls recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration, so unified-storage failures are reported as legacy failures and no storage failure metric is emitted. Update has the same bug at line 129. Delete at line 106 passes the object name as the kind label, producing incorrect and potentially high-cardinality kind values. DeleteCollection at line 166 records the legacy goroutine's result with recordStorageDuration, double-counting storage metrics. These make the dual-writer metrics unreliable for diagnosing mode-3 behavior.

title: Async legacy write failures are silently dropped
body: The async Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection goroutines only feed legacy errors into a metric; no log is emitted. If legacy writes fail because of context cancellation, validation, conflicts, or storage errors, operators get no explicit indication that unified and legacy storage have diverged. At least log the error with kind/name and the fact that it occurred on the async legacy path.

title: Mode 3 Create error test mocks legacy instead of unified storage
body: The error case for TestMode3_Create configures setupLegacyFn to return an error, but mode 3 calls Storage.Create first. There is no expectation set for the storage mock, so the test will panic on an unexpected mock call instead of exercising the intended storage-error path. This case needs setupStorageFn returning the error (and should leave legacy unconfigured because it should not be called).

title: Delete and DeleteCollection tests spawn async legacy calls that are neither mocked nor awaited
body: TestMode3_Delete and TestMode3_DeleteCollection only configure storage expectations. On success, mode 3 launches a goroutine that calls d.Legacy.Delete or d.Legacy.DeleteCollection, but the legacy mock has no matching expectation and the test does not wait for the goroutine. That leads to a panic from testify's mock (often asynchronously) and the assertions do not verify that the legacy write happened at all. The tests need legacy mock expectations plus a synchronization mechanism (or an injectable executor) for the async operation.

title: Mode 3 playlist integration test assumes synchronous legacy propagation
body: The new mode-3 cases run the shared doPlaylistTests helper, which creates/updates via the Kubernetes API and then immediately lists or gets the same data through the legacy API and requires exact equality. Mode 3 intentionally writes to legacy asynchronously, so legacy may not have caught up yet and the test will be flaky or fail. These checks need eventual-consistency polling or should not assert immediate legacy visibility for mode 3.

title: Async legacy writes use the request context, which is canceled when the handler returns
body: Mode 3 launches the legacy write in a goroutine using the incoming request context: `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`. In Go's HTTP server, the request context is canceled as soon as the handler returns, and these methods return the unified-storage result immediately after starting the goroutine. The legacy `Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection` calls (also at lines 110, 135 and 163) therefore commonly run with an already-canceled context, so the shadow write to legacy fails and the safety copy is never made. Derive the goroutine context from `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (preserving request values) or a fresh context with an explicit timeout.

title: Fire-and-forget legacy writes can be applied out of order
body: All mode 3 legacy writes are independent goroutines with no per-object serialization. Two sequential updates to the same object can complete their legacy writes in reverse order, leaving legacy with the older state; a delete followed by a re-create can likewise leave the shadow store missing or containing an object after the unified store already reflects the opposite operation. Because the legacy write is meant as a safety copy, this silently makes the two stores diverge. A per-key queue/worker or version/order check is needed if legacy is expected to remain consistent.

title: Mode 3 records several operations under the wrong metric or label
body: The metrics in this file are mis-attributed. A unified-storage create failure is recorded with `recordLegacyDuration` (line 45), and a unified-storage update failure is also recorded with `recordLegacyDuration` (line 129), even though no legacy call has happened. Delete success passes the object `name` as the `kind` argument to `recordStorageDuration` (line 106), which both mislabels the series and creates unbounded `kind` label cardinality. DeleteCollection's async legacy call records `recordStorageDuration` instead of `recordLegacyDuration` (line 166). These produce incorrect dashboards/alerts and misleading legacy vs. storage latency/error rates.

title: Legacy write failures in async mode are never logged
body: Every async goroutine discards the legacy error and only calls a metrics recording function, e.g. `_, errObjectSt := d.Legacy.Create(...)` followed by `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`. There is no `log.Error`, unlike the previous synchronous implementation. Since these writes are fire-and-forget, operators have no log evidence when the shadow write fails, making the safety mechanism effectively undiagnosable. Log the error (including object identity and method) in each async legacy path.

title: Create error test configures the wrong store and will hit an unexpected mock call
body: The case named "error when creating object in the unified store fails" sets `setupLegacyFn` to return an error and never sets a `Storage.Create` expectation. Mode 3's `Create` calls `Storage.Create` first, so this test invokes the storage mock without an expectation and fails with a testify panic rather than exercising a unified-storage failure. Configure `setupStorageFn` for the error and, if the legacy path is to be covered, set the legacy expectation separately.

title: Delete/DeleteCollection success tests do not account for the async legacy mock call
body: The success cases for `TestMode3_Delete` and `TestMode3_DeleteCollection` only set up the Storage mock. Mode 3 always launches a goroutine that calls `Legacy.Delete`/`Legacy.DeleteCollection`, but there is no legacy expectation and the tests do not wait for the goroutine. With testify's bare `mock.Mock`, the unexpected call panics; even if it did not, the test returns before the legacy write happens and never asserts that the shadow delete occurred. Add legacy expectations and a synchronization mechanism (or refactor to inject a synchronous executor) to verify the async write.

title: Mode 3 integration subtests read legacy before the async shadow write can complete
body: The new mode 3 subtests reuse `doPlaylistTests`, which assumes writes made through the k8s API are immediately visible through the legacy `/api/playlists` API (for example the list comparison around lines 516-531 and `getFromBothAPIs` after k8s create/update/delete). Mode 3 writes to legacy asynchronously, so the legacy read can race ahead of the shadow write and see stale or missing data. These mode 3 subtests will be flaky/failing even if the implementation is correct; they need to poll/wait for legacy convergence or use a synchronous test mode for immediate-visibility assertions.

title: Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock
body: After the read-lock fast path misses, the function takes the write lock and unconditionally re-reads/re-parses the manifest (readWebAssetsFromFile) and republishes the cache, without re-checking entryPointAssetsCache. On a cold start, N goroutines can all observe the cache as nil under RLock, then serialize on the write lock and each perform a full file open + JSON decode of assets-manifest.json even though the first one already populated the cache. The consequence is redundant sequential I/O and CPU per waiter (a thundering herd) right at startup. Re-check `if entryPointAssetsCache != nil` (for non-dev env) immediately after acquiring the write lock to avoid this.

title: Write lock is held during blocking I/O
body: The exclusive lock (taken at line 48 and held via defer until return) covers the entire manifest read, including readWebAssetsFromFile (file open + JSON decode) and, when the CDN path is enabled, readWebAssetsFromCDN (an HTTP GET with the request context). While the writer holds the lock, all other GetWebAssets callers block on RLock, so slow disk or a slow/hanging CDN response stalls every concurrent request. In dev mode this happens on every call. A better structure is to build the result outside the lock and only hold the write lock briefly to publish it, or use sync.Once for the non-dev path.

title: Write lock acquired without re-checking the cache, so concurrent cold-start requests each re-read the manifest
body: GetWebAssets checks `ret != nil` under the read lock (lines 41-47) and, if empty, unconditionally takes the write lock at line 48 and recomputes the assets without re-checking `entryPointAssetsCache` after acquiring the lock. Two (or N) concurrent requests arriving while the cache is empty all observe `ret == nil`, then serialize on the write mutex, and each in turn performs a full `readWebAssetsFromFile` (or CDN fetch) and overwrites the cache. On a cold cache under load this means N sequential disk reads/JSON decodes instead of one, and each request's latency is multiplied by the number of queued callers because the lock is held for the entire IO. The standard fix is to re-check the shared state under the write lock (and return it if already populated) before doing the work, or to only compute outside the lock and swap under it, so exactly one goroutine populates the cache.

title: In Dev mode every request holds the exclusive write lock during file IO, serializing all callers
body: When `cfg.Env == setting.Dev` the early return at line 45 is skipped, so every call now takes the exclusive `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` and holds it for the whole `os.Open` + JSON decode (and potentially the HTTP round-trip to the CDN if the `cdn` branch is ever enabled). Previously concurrent dev requests read the manifest in parallel. Since dev mode intentionally re-reads on every request, a page load issuing several asset requests will now serialize them on this mutex, and a slow/failed read stalls all other callers. If the intent is to always refresh in dev, read/build the result before taking the lock and only swap the pointer (and/or use singleflight to collapse concurrent refresh work) so the critical section contains only the assignment rather than blocking IO.

title: Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock
body: After the fast-path read finds `entryPointAssetsCache == nil` and the goroutine acquires `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()`, the cache is never checked again. With two concurrent requests in a non-dev environment, both can observe nil, then serialize on the lock and each call `readWebAssetsFromFile`. The second goroutine performs redundant I/O and, worse, overwrites the cache populated by the first goroutine; if its own read fails, it clobbers a valid cache with nil and reports an error. Re-check `entryPointAssetsCache` while holding the write lock and return the cached value if it has been populated by another goroutine.

title: No regression test for concurrent GetWebAssets calls
body: This PR specifically fixes a data race, but no test exercises concurrent calls to `GetWebAssets`. Without a test that starts multiple goroutines against an uninitialized cache and runs under `-race`, a future regression could reintroduce the race or the missing double-check behavior without being detected.

title: SQL expression feature flag is ignored; helper always returns false
body: In `enableSqlExpressions`, `enabled` is assigned `!h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(...)`, but both the `if` branch and the fall-through return `false`. The function therefore always returns false regardless of `featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions`. As a result `ReadQuery` rejects every SQL expression with `sqlExpressions is not implemented`, and enabling the documented `sqlExpressions` feature flag has no effect. If hard-disabling is intended, remove the flag check and update the flag documentation; otherwise return `h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`.

title: Stub DB makes TablesList/NewSQLCommand fail with misleading invalid-SQL error
body: All methods on the new in-memory DB return `not implemented`, but `pkg/expr/sql/parser.go` still calls `RunCommands` from `TablesList`. Thus `TablesList` can never parse any SQL and `NewSQLCommand` always returns `sql-invalid-sql` with the public message `error reading SQL command` for any non-empty SQL expression. That also affects the legacy `UnmarshalSQLCommand` path, which is not guarded by the new reader check, and produces a misleading 400 rather than a clear feature-disabled error. Either remove the SQL command/parser code path entirely or make the disabled state explicit at command construction.

title: No test covers disabled SQL expressions even when the feature flag is enabled
body: The security fix relies on the new `enableSqlExpressions` gate, but no test is added to assert that a `QueryTypeSQL` query is rejected and that the feature flag cannot re-enable it. A test with `FlagSqlExpressions` enabled would have caught the helper's always-false behavior and will help prevent a future regression that reopens the RCE/LFI path.

title: SQL expression feature flag is read but ignored
body: `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns `false` in both branches. As a result, the SQL expression kill switch always rejects `QueryTypeSQL`, even when the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle is enabled. That leaves the documented feature flag dead and causes users who enable it to still get the internal-looking error `sqlExpressions is not implemented`. If the intent is a permanent hard disable, the flag check should be removed and the documentation/message updated; otherwise this function should return the actual flag value.

title: No regression test for disabled SQL expressions
body: This security fix changes the SQL expression path to reject all SQL, but no test was added or updated to cover the new behavior. A regression test should assert that `QueryTypeSQL` is rejected both when `FlagSqlExpressions` is disabled and when it is enabled, otherwise a future change to `enableSqlExpressions` or the SQL stubs could silently re-enable the vulnerable path.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false and ignores the feature flag
body: `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled` from `FlagSqlExpressions`, then returns `false` in both branches. As a result the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle has no effect: SQL expressions are permanently disabled even when the flag is enabled. If permanent disable is intended, the flag lookup is dead code and should be removed; if the flag is supposed to control availability, this is a logic error that makes the toggle ineffective and prevents safely re-enabling the feature through the existing flag.

title: Legacy SQL command path is disabled only via the stub DB, not an explicit gate
body: `NewSQLCommand` (used by `UnmarshalSQLCommand` for the legacy query path) has no explicit SQL-disabled check. It currently fails only because the new `pkg/expr/sql.DB` methods return `not implemented`, which makes `sql.TablesList` error out. If the DB implementation is later restored or replaced, this path will execute SQL without consulting `FlagSqlExpressions` or the new `ExpressionQueryReader` guard, re-enabling the vulnerable feature. The disable should be enforced at command creation or execution rather than relying on the stub error.

title: No regression test for disabled SQL expressions
body: The security gate for `QueryTypeSQL` was added without any test. There is no regression test asserting that a SQL expression query is rejected even when `FlagSqlExpressions` is enabled, nor that non-SQL expression types still parse. Without such a test, a later change to the guard or the stub DB could silently restore the RCE/LFI-capable SQL expression path.

title: User-facing error incorrectly says SQL expressions are not implemented
body: When a SQL expression is submitted, the new error is `sqlExpressions is not implemented`. The feature was implemented and is being intentionally disabled for security, so this message misrepresents the state and can lead users to believe their Grafana build lacks the feature rather than that SQL expressions are blocked. Return a clear disabled/unsupported message instead.

title: Shared error variable races in index build errgroup
body: In searchSupport.init every goroutine in the errgroup assigns to the same outer err variable with `_, _, err = s.build(...)` and increments totalBatchesIndexed without synchronization. Concurrent builds race: one goroutine can overwrite another goroutine's error with nil before it is returned, so errgroup.Wait can report success even though an index failed to build. The batch counter is also unreliable. Use a local err inside each goroutine and protect the counter.

title: Removing the full BuildIndex lock leaves same-key builds unprotected
body: BuildIndex now only takes cacheMu around the final map write. getOrCreateIndex still performs an unsynchronized check-then-build, so two concurrent searches or watch events for the same NamespacedResource can both enter BuildIndex. For file-backed indexes both calls can try to create/open the same Bleve directory, and for all indexes the later cache write can overwrite an index that has already received events, leaving the cache pointing at a stale snapshot. A per-key singleflight or build lock is needed, not just locking the map write.

title: TotalDocs iterates the cache without the cache lock
body: bleveBackend.TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without taking cacheMu. The new log call `s.log.Info(..., s.search.TotalDocs())` in searchSupport.init runs immediately after the watch goroutine is started, and that goroutine can call getOrCreateIndex -> BuildIndex and write b.cache[key] under cacheMu. Concurrent map iteration and map write can panic or race. TotalDocs should take cacheMu.RLock, or the cache access should be restructured.

title: Search event watcher panics on closed event channel during shutdown
body: The watcher started in searchSupport.init uses context.Background() and never checks whether the events channel was closed. On server.Stop the SQL backend cancels its poller and closes the events channel; this loop then receives nil and calls handleEvent(nil), which dereferences evt.Type and panics. Because this PR now initializes search at startup, this watcher is always running. Use the server's cancellable context and handle the channel-close case by returning.

title: Constructor leaks startup resources when Init fails
body: NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) before returning, but on failure it returns nil without calling s.cancel() or s.lifecycle.Stop(). By that point searchSupport.init may already have started its background watcher, and lifecycle.Init may have acquired database or other resources. Since the caller receives nil, it cannot call Stop, so those resources and goroutines leak. The constructor should clean up/cancel on initialization failure.

title: Postgres storage-server startup coverage is skipped
body: The integration test now skips Postgres entirely. This is the test that exercises storage-server startup, which is exactly the behavior changed by moving unified-storage initialization into NewResourceServer. Without a replacement test, a Postgres startup regression, including failure of the eager index build, will not be caught. The test or environment should be fixed instead of skipping the backend.

title: New TotalDocs log races with index cache writes
body: The newly added log calls s.search.TotalDocs() after the watch goroutine at lines 207-213 has already been started. bleveBackend.TotalDocs iterates b.cache without taking cacheMu, while handleEvent -> getOrCreateIndex -> BuildIndex can write b.cache under cacheMu. This is a data race and can panic at startup with 'concurrent map iteration and map write'. Either make TotalDocs lock cacheMu or evaluate total docs before starting the watcher.

title: Shared err and counter are mutated by concurrent init goroutines
body: Inside searchSupport.init, every errgroup goroutine assigns to the captured outer err variable (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and returns that same variable, and they also increment totalBatchesIndexed concurrently. These are data races. In particular, another goroutine can overwrite err with nil just before a failing goroutine returns it, so group.Wait can miss a build failure and startup proceeds with a partially built index. Use per-goroutine local errors (or return s.build(...) directly) and an atomic/collected counter.

title: Removing the build lock allows concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key
body: BuildIndex no longer holds cacheMu for the duration of the build. getOrCreateIndex performs an unlocked check-then-build, so two callers can both see no index for the same NamespacedResource and enter BuildIndex concurrently. For file-backed indexes both calls use the same directory and call bleve.New on it at the same time; for memory indexes the later `b.cache[key] = idx` overwrites the first. This can cause index creation failures/corruption and can drop watch updates applied to the overwritten index. Add a per-key lock/singleflight, or re-check and serialize index creation for the same key before creating the bleve index.

title: Postgres coverage removed from storage-server startup test
body: The test now unconditionally skips Postgres, removing coverage for a production database at exactly the startup path changed by this PR (resource server initialization moved into the constructor). Because the skip is global rather than CI-specific, a Postgres-specific regression in startup initialization will not be caught. Fix the underlying Postgres issue or scope any temporary skip to CI only.

title: Concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key can race and overwrite each other
body: Removing the lock around the whole BuildIndex function leaves no per-key serialization: getOrCreateIndex does GetIndex and then BuildIndex without any lock, and BuildIndex does not re-check the cache before building. Two concurrent searches/watch events for the same NamespacedResource can therefore build two indexes. For file-backed indexes both call bleve.New on the same directory concurrently, which can fail or corrupt the index; for in-memory indexes the second build overwrites the first in the cache, so a search/watch that already got the first index keeps writing to an index the cache will never return again. Add a per-key singleflight/build lock and re-check the cache under that lock before starting a build.

title: Index build goroutines race on shared err and totalBatchesIndexed
body: Inside init, every errgroup goroutine assigns to the shared outer err variable and increments totalBatchesIndexed without synchronization. One goroutine can overwrite the error from another before it returns, so group.Wait may report success even when an index build failed; the count used for the span/event is also racy. Use a local err in each goroutine and an atomic or mutex-protected counter.

title: Stop no longer prevents requests because handlers no longer observe initErr
body: Stop sets s.initErr to a stopping/stopped error, and the per-RPC s.Init(ctx) calls used to return that error so requests arriving after shutdown failed fast. Those calls were removed without adding an equivalent stopped-state check, so Create/Update/Delete/List/Watch/Search/etc. can still execute after Stop and after lifecycle.Stop has begun closing or canceling the backend. Add an explicit stopped flag/check in the handlers or in an interceptor.

title: Postgres integration test is skipped instead of fixing startup init failure
body: The PR adds a skip for postgres to the storage-server integration test, with a TODO that it fails in Drone. This PR changes unified storage initialization to happen synchronously during server construction, so disabling the postgres case hides a possible regression in the new startup behavior and leaves the storage-server target without postgres integration coverage. Fix the underlying failure or add equivalent coverage before merging.

title: TotalDocs reads the index cache without holding cacheMu
body: BuildIndex now mutates b.cache under cacheMu, but TotalDocs ranges over the same map without any lock. If TotalDocs is called while an index build stores its result, this is a Go map concurrent read/write race and can panic. Take cacheMu.RLock while iterating.

title: Call to non-existent isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() breaks compilation
body: UsernameForm extends UsernamePasswordForm, but the only overload defined (in UsernamePasswordForm) is isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel). The new guard `if (context.getUser() != null && !isConditionalPasskeysEnabled())` calls a no-argument method that does not exist anywhere in the hierarchy, so this will not compile and the whole services module (and therefore the build) fails. It was almost certainly meant to be `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`.

title: Conditional passkey form only populated when context user is set, breaking initial page / error re-render
body: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel) returns false whenever `user == null`. It is used in authenticate() and challenge() to decide whether to call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context), which is what renders the `#webauth` form and the `autocomplete="username webauthn"` conditional-UI element. On a fresh login context.getUser() is null, and on the empty/invalid-password re-render the user was only identified from the form (validateUserAndPassword short-circuits before validateUser() calls context.setUser), so context.getUser() is still null. In both cases the conditional passkey UI is no longer populated. This regresses the primary passkey-autofill experience and breaks existing/new tests that assert `username webauthn` and the `#webauth` form on the first page (e.g. PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest.passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey lines 145-146, passwordLoginWithExternalKey lines 195-196, webauthnLoginWithExternalKey_reauthentication line 238; PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest.passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey lines 192-194). The gate should depend only on whether passkeys are enabled for the realm, not on `user != null`.

title: Broad catch(Exception) around findElement can swallow real failures and dead fail() call
body: In reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey both "webauth not present" checks are written as `try { assertThat(driver.findElement(...), nullValue()); fail(...); } catch (Exception nsee) { /* expected */ }`. findElement never returns null (it throws NoSuchElementException), so the assertThat(nullValue()) and the fail() are effectively dead code. More importantly, the catch(Exception) also swallows unrelated failures such as WebDriverException from a page that failed to load, causing the test to pass even when the login page is broken. Using Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, ...) (as the sibling PasskeysUsernameFormTest does) expresses the intent without hiding real errors.

title: Call to undefined isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() fails compilation
body: UsernameForm.authenticate now calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments, but no such method exists anywhere in its hierarchy. UsernameForm extends UsernamePasswordForm, which only defines `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` (UsernamePasswordForm.java:161); AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator and WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator define neither. The full contents of all these files at head confirm there is no no-arg variant (WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator only has `isPasskeysEnabled()`). This makes the services module fail to compile, so the whole PR cannot build. Either add the no-arg helper (e.g. `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()`) or call the correct existing method.

title: Conditional passkey UI no longer set up when no user is identified
body: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel) returns false whenever `user == null`. It is used in authenticate() (line 115) to decide whether to call `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm`, and in the error challenge() (lines 137-140). Because the previous `context.getUser() == null` branch that called fillContextForm was removed, on the initial login page (no user selected) and after failures where the user is cleared/unknown, `context.getUser()` is null and fillContextForm is never called. That means the WebAuthn challenge/AUTH_CHALLENGE_NOTE and ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI attribute are not placed on the form, so the passkey autofill (`username webauthn` autocomplete, `#webauth` form) disappears from exactly the pages where conditional UI is needed. This regresses existing behavior and contradicts the PR's own assertions that expect `//form[@id='webauth']` on the initial page and after a failed password (e.g. PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest.passwordLoginWithExternalKey line 196 and PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest.passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey line 211). The gate should depend only on `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()`, not on `user != null`.

title: Unused NoSuchElementException import will fail the unused-import check
body: This PR replaces both `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, ...)` usages in passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey with `MatcherAssert.assertThat(driver.findElement(...), notNullValue())`, so `org.openqa.selenium.NoSuchElementException` is no longer referenced anywhere in the file. The import remains, which trips Keycloak's checkstyle UnusedImports rule and fails the build. Remove the import.

title: Call to undefined no-argument isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() will not compile
body: UsernameForm.authenticate now calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments. The only method with that name introduced by this PR is `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` in UsernamePasswordForm (line 160), and neither UsernameForm nor AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator defines a no-argument overload. As written the services module fails to compile (cannot find symbol). The guard should most likely call `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`, or a no-arg overload must be added to the superclass.

title: Passkeys data no longer populated on the initial (user not yet selected) login page
body: The condition that drives `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` was inverted: previously it ran inside the `context.getUser() == null` branch (initial page), now it runs outside the branch and only when `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())` is true, which requires a non-null user (line 161). Consequently the conditional-passkeys/WebAuthn attributes (challenge, rpId, ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI, etc.) are no longer set on the first page rendered before a username is entered. The same inversion was applied to the `challenge(error, field)` override (line 137). This regresses first-page passkey login: existing tests that are unchanged by this PR still assert the `//form[@id='webauth']` element is present and click the WebAuthn 'Authenticate' button on the very first page (e.g. PasskeysUsernameFormTest.passwordLoginWithExternalKey and passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey, and PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest.passwordLoginWithExternalKey). Unless a separate passkeys execution renders that page, those flows will fail. Conditional UI is specifically meant to work before a user is identified, so gating on `user != null` is suspect.

title: Unused import of NoSuchElementException after assertions were replaced
body: The two `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, ...)` checks in passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey were replaced with `MatcherAssert.assertThat(..., notNullValue())`, but `org.openqa.selenium.NoSuchElementException` is still imported (line 51) and no longer referenced anywhere in the file (`Assert` is still used at line 134). Keycloak's build enforces checkstyle UnusedImports, so this will fail the build/verify of the testsuite module.

title: Login cache invalidation can compare the original IDP model with itself
body: registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate detects changes by comparing the model returned from getById(model.getInternalId()) with the caller-supplied model. When the ORGANIZATION feature is disabled, createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel returns the cached IdentityProviderModel directly. If a caller uses the normal getById -> mutate -> update pattern, the cached model is mutated in place, so getById inside update returns the same object as model. In that case both comparisons see identical predicate state and identical organizationId, and login caches are not invalidated even when enabled/hideOnLogin/linkOnly/organization link changed. The stale getForLogin cache can continue returning the old login IDP set. The original state must be fetched from the delegate or copied before mutation.

title: getForLogin does not check organization invalidation
body: The new getForLogin cache only checks isInvalid(cacheKey). The analogous getByOrganization method checks both isInvalid(cacheKey) and isInvalid(orgId) because organization changes can affect the cached IDP result. For getForLogin(ORG_ONLY/ALL, organizationId), a cached per-organization IDP list can survive organization invalidation/removal. If the organization change unlinks or removes an IDP without going through IdentityProviderStorageProvider.update/remove, login pages for that organization keep using stale IDP IDs. The method should also fall back when organizationId is non-null and isInvalid(organizationId) is true.

title: remove can throw NPE for missing alias when cache key is invalid
body: remove(alias) now always loads storedIdp and then, when the alias cache key is invalid, calls registerIDPInvalidation(storedIdp). If the alias does not exist, storedIdp is null and registerIDPInvalidation dereferences it, throwing NPE. The method contract says remove should return false when no IDP is found, so this path must null-check storedIdp before invalidating.

title: Test cleanup removes alias "alias" instead of the created IDPs
body: The cleanup registered at lines 381 and 425 uses testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove, but the test creates IDPs named "idp-alias-0" through "idp-alias-20". The cleanup therefore never removes the created providers and may also fail with a not-found error, leaking IDPs into the test realm and making subsequent tests order-dependent.

title: Test cleanup removes hardcoded alias "alias" instead of the created IDPs
body: In testCacheIDPForLogin the cleanup is registered as `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)`, but the IDPs created by the test have aliases like `idp-alias-N` (and an extra `idp-alias-20`). The literal "alias" matches no created provider, so none of the 20+ IDPs are actually deleted and the cleanup issues DELETE requests against a non-existent provider. Consequences: if the realm is not fully reset between tests (or cleanup is strict about 404s) this leaks enabled/public IDPs into the realm and can break the count assertions of later tests in the class (e.g. the `getForLogin(ORG_ONLY/ALL, orgaId)` sizes), and at minimum produces useless/erroneous cleanup calls. The same wrong-alias pattern is repeated at line 425 (and the pre-existing testCacheIDPByOrg line 303). Fix by capturing the created alias in the loop and removing that, e.g. `String alias = "idp-alias-" + i; ... getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get(alias)::remove);`.

title: New login cache test does not cover unlinking/removing organization brokers or deleting an organization
body: testCacheIDPForLogin exercises create/update/remove of IDPs and adding a broker to an organization, but never removes a broker from an organization nor deletes an organization. These org-level mutations are exactly the paths that can change which providers appear in the cached ORG_ONLY/ALL login lists, and the cache is only refreshed if those operations route through IdentityProviderStorageProvider.update()/remove() and register the login-cache invalidation. Without a test asserting that unlinking a broker (organizationId goes non-null -> null) and deleting an organization clear the login caches and update the returned list, a regression in that invalidation (e.g. an org mutation that bypasses the storage provider, leaving deleted/unlinked providers cached) would go unnoticed. Add assertions that the login caches are cleared and the resulting lists are correct after `organizations().get(orgId).identityProviders().removeIdentityProvider(alias)` / organization removal.

title: Login-cache invalidation uses organization-aware original model
body: update() obtains the original IDP through getById(), which returns createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(...). For an IDP linked to a disabled organization (or when the organization provider is unavailable), that wrapper's isEnabled() is false even though the raw persisted IDP is enabled and was therefore cached in the login list. If such an IDP is subsequently updated from enabled=true to enabled=false, registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate sees both the wrapped original and the raw updated model as non-login IDPs and returns without invalidating the login caches. The cached getForLogin result then continues to contain an IDP that is no longer login-eligible until another invalidation happens. The invalidation predicate should be evaluated against the raw stored model, not the organization-aware wrapper.

title: New IDP cleanup uses wrong alias and leaks all created providers
body: testCacheIDPForLogin registers cleanup with testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias") instead of the actual aliases it creates ("idp-alias-" + i, and "idp-alias-20" at line 425). Consequently none of the 21 IDPs created by this test are removed, and cleanup also attempts to delete a provider named "alias" that does not exist. The leaked IDPs can change exact-count assertions in later tests in this class and make reruns order-dependent. Register cleanup with the real alias for each created provider.

title: Create/remove invalidation for login IDPs is not tested
body: The new test only creates an IDP with hideOnLogin=true and removes a disabled IDP, i.e. both operations are for non-login IDPs, and asserts that the login caches remain. It never verifies that creating a login-eligible IDP or removing one actually invalidates the getForLogin caches. The create() and remove() invalidation branches added in this PR could be removed or broken and this test would still pass. Add cases that create an enabled/login-visible IDP and remove one, asserting that all login cache entries are cleared.

title: Provider selection is non-deterministic when order() ties; fail-fast on duplicates removed
body: detectProvider now sorts discovered providers by CryptoProvider.order() descending and silently returns the first, removing the previous IllegalStateException thrown when more than one provider is on the classpath. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order() == 200, so whenever two of them are present (e.g. default crypto plus FIPS) the winner is decided solely by the non-deterministic ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order (the sort is stable), not by the order() value. In a FIPS deployment that can silently select the non-FIPS provider and downgrade cryptography, and genuine duplicate-provider misconfigurations that used to abort at startup now go unnoticed. The built-in providers need distinct deterministic order values, and equal-order duplicates should still fail rather than silently pick one.

title: Adding order() as an abstract method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: Adding `int order();` as an abstract method to the public CryptoProvider interface is a source- and binary-incompatible change for every third-party CryptoProvider implementation (custom providers, and the keycloak-client repo this code is later synced to). Such classes will no longer compile, and classes already compiled against an older version will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when CryptoIntegration.detectProvider invokes order(). It should be declared as a default method (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) so existing implementations continue to work.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK keystore provider, not a BouncyCastle provider
body: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), i.e. the JDK provider for the default keystore type (e.g. SUN for pkcs12/jks), not a BouncyCastle provider as the CryptoProvider contract documents ("@return BouncyCastle security provider"). Any caller that trusts the contract—for example registering the result with Security.addProvider or using it for certificate/signature operations—will get the wrong provider and fail or behave unexpectedly. Since the authz-client has no BouncyCastle on its classpath, this method should return null (as WildFlyElytronProvider does) or a genuine BC provider.

title: AuthzClient.create now throws if no CryptoProvider is discoverable by its classloader
body: AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now unconditionally calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()). CryptoIntegration.init throws IllegalStateException("Not able to load any cryptoProvider with the classLoader ...") when no CryptoProvider SPI file is discoverable by that specific classloader. As a result, creating an AuthzClient now fails outright in environments where META-INF/services is not visible to AuthzClient's classloader (shaded/relocated jars, OSGi, custom classloaders), even though building the client does not otherwise need crypto. Previously create() worked without any crypto provider. This also adds an unexpected global static side effect to a simple factory method and should be made resilient to a missing provider.

title: Core provider-selection change is untested
body: ECDSAAlgorithmTest only round-trips a signature through the new ASN1 encoder/decoder; it never exercises the feature this PR introduces. There is no test that places two CryptoProvider service implementations on the classpath and asserts the highest-order provider is selected, no test that the previous duplicate-provider failure is (or is not) still raised for equal orders, and no test that an authz client obtains a usable crypto provider through CryptoIntegration after ServiceLoader discovery. Given the detectProvider behavior change, the selection logic—the main risk of the PR—has no coverage.

title: getKeyStore ignores provider and cannot load non-JDK keystore formats
body: getKeyStore(format) uses KeyStore.getInstance(format.name()) against the default JVM security providers instead of going through a specific provider. For formats the JDK does not ship (e.g. BCFKS, BKS, PEM) this throws KeyStoreException, so CryptoProvider.getSupportedKeyStoreTypes()/getKeyStore() will claim formats this provider cannot actually load, since the authz-client has no BouncyCastle on the classpath. It should throw UnsupportedOperationException for unsupported formats or otherwise limit to JDK-supported types.

title: Adding abstract order() breaks external CryptoProvider implementations
body: CryptoProvider is a public SPI discovered via ServiceLoader. Adding the abstract method `int order()` (without a body) is a source- and binary-incompatible change for every implementation that lives outside this PR. Any existing implementation (e.g. the copy in the keycloak-client repository that this PR says will be synced later, or a third-party provider jar) that was compiled against the previous interface has no `order()` method, so `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider()` will now throw `AbstractMethodError` when it calls `CryptoProvider::order` on it; recompiling such a provider also fails until it is changed. Providing a `default int order() { return 100; }` would preserve compatibility and let new providers opt into a higher precedence only when needed.

title: Removing the multiple-providers fail-fast allows silent non-deterministic (possibly non-FIPS) selection
body: Previously `detectProvider` threw `IllegalStateException` when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath, forcing an explicit single-provider configuration. The new code only logs the others at debug level and returns `foundProviders.get(0)`. This is dangerous because `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return `order() == 200`, so they tie. The `reversed()` sort is stable, so the winner among tied providers is decided by ServiceLoader/classpath order, which is non-deterministic. A misconfigured FIPS or Elytron deployment that accidentally has both the FIPS/Elytron provider and the default BC provider present would previously fail fast; now it may silently pick the non-FIPS `DefaultCryptoProvider` and run with non-FIPS crypto (or pick the wrong provider on EAP). Consider keeping a hard error when multiple providers share the top order, or at minimum logging at warn/error.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JVM default keystore provider, not a BouncyCastle provider
body: `getBouncyCastleProvider()` is documented by the `CryptoProvider` interface as returning the (non-FIPS or FIPS) BouncyCastle security provider, but this implementation returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which on a stock JVM is the platform provider (e.g. `SUN`). Any caller that relies on the contract — for example code that registers it as the BC provider or uses BouncyCastle-specific behavior — will receive the wrong provider and fail or silently behave differently. If the intent is to have no BC dependency, the method should either be documented/typed accordingly or the provider should be obtained in a way consistent with the contract.

title: ECDSA test only round-trips conversions and uses a default P-256 key for ES384/ES512
body: The test generates a single default `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` key (typically P-256) and reuses it for ES256, ES384 and ES512. It never checks that the reconstructed DER signature actually verifies against the public key, nor that the code handles a curve whose field size matches the algorithm's `getSignatureLength()`. Because `asn1derToConcatenatedRS`/`concatenatedRSToASN1DER` symmetric padding makes the DER→RS→DER→RS round-trip succeed even when `signLength` (66 for ES512) does not match the real 32-byte r/s, the test would pass even if the conversion were wrong for real P-384/P-521 keys. Use a curve matching each algorithm and assert the round-tripped/re-encoded signature verifies against the public key.

title: readSequence silently returns an empty list for indefinite-length encoding
body: `readLength()` returns -1 for the indefinite-length form (0x80), but `readSequence()` uses that value directly in `while (length > 0)`, so an indefinite-length sequence produces an empty list instead of a clear error. A caller that reads it (e.g. `asn1derToConcatenatedRS`) then fails later with the misleading message "Invalid sequence with size different to 2". Since only DER (definite length) is valid here, reject `length == -1` with an explicit error.

title: Multi-provider selection is nondeterministic and removes fail-fast FIPS guard
body: This change removes the previous guard that threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was found, and instead silently picks the highest-order provider. However DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order() == 200, so the only provider that is actually disambiguated is AuthzClientCryptoProvider (100). If two of the real providers land on the classpath together (e.g. a FIPS deployment that also has the default provider), selection among the equal-order providers falls back to the ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order, which is not guaranteed stable across filesystems/containers. The result is that a non-FIPS provider can be chosen silently in a deployment that previously failed fast at startup, disabling FIPS without any error. FIPS should have a strictly higher order than the non-FIPS providers (or the removed guard should be retained for genuinely conflicting providers).

title: Adding abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: CryptoProvider is a public interface in keycloak-common, and order() is added as an abstract method rather than a default method. Every existing implementation (including third-party providers and the keycloak-client code the PR description says will be synced later) must now add this method; old implementations that do not will fail to compile / fail at link time. Making it a default method (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) would preserve compatibility while still letting providers opt into precedence.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default KeyStore provider, not BouncyCastle
body: getBouncyCastleProvider() is documented/contractually expected to return a BouncyCastle security provider, but this implementation returns the Provider of `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType())` (typically the JDK SUN provider, or whatever the default keystore type resolves to). Any consumer that calls CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getBouncyCastleProvider() expecting BouncyCastle algorithm registration/lookup will get the wrong provider and may fail with NoSuchAlgorithm/NoSuchProvider or silently use different crypto. All other unsupported methods in this class throw UnsupportedOperationException; this one should do the same unless it genuinely provides a BouncyCastle provider.

title: Dead ASN1Encoder calls whose results are discarded
body: Lines 114-115 build two ASN1Encoder instances (write(rBigInteger) and write(sBigInteger)) and throw the results away; the returned value is produced separately by the chained writeDerSeq(...) call. These two statements have no effect and only allocate objects. They are leftover code and should be removed, since they can mislead a reader into thinking the sequence is built from them.

title: ECDSA round-trip test uses one default-curve key and never verifies the signature
body: The test generates a single `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` (default curve, normally P-256) and reuses it for ES256/384/512. It only checks that asn1derToConcatenatedRS -> concatenatedRSToASN1DER -> asn1derToConcatenatedRS is idempotent; it never verifies the produced signature with the public key and never exercises the actual 521-bit curve. Because the padding to `signLength` is symmetric, a wrong per-curve length/endianness/truncation would still round-trip and the test would pass. Generating a key per algorithm's curve and asserting Signature.verify would actually validate curve-specific behavior.

title: New provider-ordering selection logic is not covered by tests
body: detectProvider now sorts multiple providers by order() and ignores the lower-ordered ones, but there is no test that loads multiple CryptoProviders and asserts the highest-order one is selected (or that ties behave sanely). Given this ordering is the central mechanism of the PR, a test using a custom ServiceLoader/classloader with two known-order providers would guard the selection logic against regressions and would have surfaced the equal-order ambiguity noted for the real providers.
