Contrary to the comments, Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly forbids negative indexing/slicing (`if (k.start is not None and k.start < 0) or (k.stop is not None and k.stop < 0): raise ValueError('Negative indexing is not supported.')`). Any request supplying a cursor with a negative offset (e.g. `cursor=0:-1:1` on any `BasePaginator` endpoint, or `cursor=0:-1:0` with `OptimizedCursorPaginator`) will crash with an unhandled `ValueError` (HTTP 500) instead of clamping to 0 or raising `BadPaginationError`.

title: `organization_context.member` can be `None`, raising `AttributeError`
body: In `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint.get`, `enable_advanced` accesses `organization_context.member.has_global_access`. For users who are not members of the organization (or certain staff/token-authenticated requests where `organization_context.member` is `None` and `request.user.is_superuser` is `False`), evaluating `organization_context.member.has_global_access` will raise `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'` on every GET request to the audit logs endpoint, even when `optimized_pagination` is not requested.

title: `self.paginate` does not accept `enable_advanced_features` and `OptimizedCursorPaginator` breaks on `datetime` fields
body:
When `use_optimized` and `enable_advanced` are true, this endpoint calls `self.paginate(..., paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator, order_by="-datetime", enable_advanced_features=True)`. This fails in two ways:
1. `Endpoint.paginate` does not accept `enable_advanced_features` (or forward arbitrary `**kwargs` to `paginator_cls` unless supported by `paginate`), which will raise `TypeError: paginate() got an unexpected keyword argument 'enable_advanced_features'`.
2. Even if instantiated, `OptimizedCursorPaginator` implements `get_item_key` as `math.floor(getattr(item, self.key))` and `value_from_cursor` as `cursor.value` (like `Paginator`, not `DateTimePaginator`). Because `order_by="-datetime"` orders by a `datetime` field on `AuditLogEntry`, `math.floor(value)` will raise `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime`, and passing raw integer cursor values into `build_queryset` will compare a timestamp column against an integer.

title: Allowing negative `start_offset` on Django `QuerySet` slices raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported`
body: In `BasePaginator.get_result` (lines 182-184) and `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` (lines 877-886), `start_offset` is allowed to be negative when `cursor.is_prev` is true or `enable_advanced_features` is enabled, and is then used to slice a Django `QuerySet` (`queryset[start_offset:stop]`). Django `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly forbids negative slice bounds (`if (k.start is not None and k.start < 0) or (k.stop is not None and k.stop < 0): raise ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`). Any request supplying a cursor with a negative offset (for example `cursor=0:-10:1`) will crash with an unhandled `ValueError` resulting in a 500 Internal Server Error.

title: Unrelated audit log and paginator changes with broken pagination logic and crash risks
body:
The changes in `src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_auditlogs.py`, `src/sentry/api/paginator.py`, and `src/sentry/utils/cursors.py` are completely unrelated to the PR's purpose (span buffer eviction) and introduce multiple severe defects:

1. **Null dereference on `organization_context.member` (`organization_auditlogs.py:71`)**: For superusers or requests using an organization integration token who are not members of the organization, `organization_context.member` is `None`. If `request.user.is_superuser` is `False` (or for non-member tokens), evaluating `organization_context.member.has_global_access` raises an `AttributeError`.
2. **Type mismatch on `datetime` field (`organization_auditlogs.py:79`, `paginator.py:839-843`)**: `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` orders by `-datetime` (a `DateTimeField`), which is why the standard path uses `DateTimePaginator`. `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` passes `getattr(item, 'datetime')` (a `datetime` instance) to `math.floor()` / `math.ceil()`, raising `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime`. Furthermore, `value_from_cursor` returns an integer cursor value directly instead of converting it to a `datetime`, causing invalid comparisons against the timestamp column in SQL.
3. **`ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported` in Django QuerySets (`paginator.py:182-184` and `paginator.py:877-886`)**: Contrary to the comments claiming Django ORM handles negative slicing, Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` whenever `start < 0` or `stop < 0`. Passing a cursor with a negative `offset` (e.g., `cursor=0:-10:1` or with `enable_advanced_features=True`) will crash with an unhandled 500 error.

title: Evicted spans leave orphaned entries in the redirect hash and can evict the root span
body:
In `src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua` (lines 62-64), when a segment's sorted set exceeds 1000 spans, `zpopmin` evicts the spans with the lowest `end_timestamp_precise`. This causes two problems when flushing in `src/sentry/spans/buffer.py`:

1. **Orphaned redirects and split segments**: `add-buffer.lua` (line 40) records `hset(main_redirect_key, span_id, set_span_id)` for every incoming span before eviction. In `done_flush_segments` (lines 478-482), `hdel` only removes `span_id`s present in `flushed_segment.spans`. Any span that was evicted by `zpopmin` is no longer in the sorted set, so its redirect entry in `span-buf:sr:{project_id:trace_id}` is never deleted (until the 1-hour TTL expires). Worse, if `set_span_id` itself is evicted from the sorted set, `done_flush_segments` will not delete `set_span_id` from `main_redirect_key`, while future child spans will still redirect to `set_span_id`. Additionally, the root/segment span itself can be evicted if it has an earlier `end_timestamp_precise` than its children (e.g. async child spans finishing after the root span), resulting in a flushed segment with `has_root_span = False` and no root span.
2. **Inconsistent `max_segment_spans`**: `SpansBuffer.__init__` still defines `self.max_segment_spans = max_segment_spans` (default 1001, line 150/158), which is now unused because the limit is hardcoded to `1000` in `add-buffer.lua`.

title: Unrelated audit log changes introduce crashes on null member and incompatible paginator
body:
`OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint.get` adds an unrelated `optimized_pagination=true` branch that has multiple defects:

1. `organization_context.member` can be `None` (for example, when a superuser who is not a member of the organization accesses the endpoint), so `organization_context.member.has_global_access` raises `AttributeError` whenever `request.user.is_superuser` is false.
2. `self.paginate(...)` is passed `paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `order_by="-datetime"`. `AuditLogEntry.datetime` is a `datetime` object, and `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` calls `math.floor(value)` / `math.ceil(value)` directly on the `datetime` attribute (unlike `DateTimePaginator`), raising `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime`. Similarly, `value_from_cursor` returns the raw numeric cursor value instead of converting it to a `datetime` for the SQL comparison.

These changes to `organization_auditlogs.py`, `paginator.py`, and `cursors.py` are also completely unrelated to the PR's stated purpose of optimizing span buffer insertion.

title: Negative cursor offsets passed to Django QuerySet slicing raise ValueError
body: In `BasePaginator.get_result` (line 182) and `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` (lines 880-886), negative `cursor.offset` values are preserved in `start_offset` (when `cursor.is_prev` is true or `enable_advanced_features` is enabled) and passed directly to `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django `QuerySet` slicing does not support negative indices and raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` whenever `start_offset < 0` or `stop < 0`, turning a user-supplied cursor parameter into an unhandled 500 error. In addition, line 192 (`len(results) == offset + limit + extra`) still uses `offset` instead of `start_offset`.

title: Span eviction deletes redirect entries only on flush, leaking redirects for evicted spans
body: `add-buffer.lua` now evicts spans with the smallest `end_timestamp_precise` via `redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)` when a segment exceeds 1000 spans, and can even evict the segment's root span if it finished earlier than child spans. However, `done_flush_segments` in `src/sentry/spans/buffer.py` only removes entries from the redirect hash (`span-buf:sr:{project_id:trace_id}`) for spans that were still present in the segment when flushed. Any span evicted by `zpopmin` never has its redirect entry cleaned up by `hdel`, leaving stale redirects until the entire hash expires.

title: `max_segment_spans` parameter on `SpansBuffer` is now unused and inconsistent with Lua limit
body: `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` and stores `self.max_segment_spans`, but the check in `_load_segment_data` was removed and `add-buffer.lua` hardcodes the limit to `1000`. Custom `max_segment_spans` values passed to `SpansBuffer` are silently ignored.

title: Potential AttributeError when organization_context.member is None and broken paginator selection
body: In `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint.get`, `organization_context.member` can be `None` (for example, when a non-member with organization access or an API token accesses the endpoint), so evaluating `organization_context.member.has_global_access` will raise an `AttributeError` when `request.user.is_superuser` is `False`. Furthermore, when `optimized_pagination=true` is passed, `self.paginate` is called with `paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator` and `order_by="-datetime"`, which is incompatible with `AuditLogEntry.datetime` (a `datetime` object): `OptimizedCursorPaginator` uses `math.floor`/`math.ceil` on the attribute and passes raw integer cursor values into the datetime query filter, causing a `TypeError` (`must be real number, not datetime.datetime`) as soon as any results are returned. Finally, these audit log and paginator changes are completely unrelated to the spans buffer PR.

title: Negative cursor offsets cause ValueError in Django QuerySet slicing
body: Both `BasePaginator.get_result` (when `cursor.is_prev` is `True` and `cursor.offset < 0`) and `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` (when `enable_advanced_features=True` and `cursor.offset < 0`, or when `cursor.is_prev` is `True`) pass a negative `start_offset` to `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Contrary to the comments, Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly forbids negative indexing and raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` whenever `start < 0` or `stop < 0`. Any client supplying a cursor string with a negative offset (e.g. `cursor=0:-1:1` on any endpoint using `BasePaginator` or `DateTimePaginator`, or `cursor=0:-1:0` with `OptimizedCursorPaginator`) will trigger an unhandled 500 error.

title: Evicting excess spans from the Redis ZSET leaves orphaned entries in the redirect hash
body: When `span_count > 1000`, `add-buffer.lua` evicts the oldest spans from `set_key` via `zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)`. However, their span IDs remain registered in the `main_redirect_key` hash (`span-buf:sr:{project_id:trace_id}`). Because `done_flush_segments` in `src/sentry/spans/buffer.py` only deletes `main_redirect_key` entries for spans actually returned from `set_key` during flushing, the redirect entries for evicted spans are never cleaned up on flush and will persist in Redis until the 1-hour TTL (`redis_ttl`) expires, increasing memory usage for large traces and potentially redirecting late child spans to an already-flushed segment.

title: Accidental git submodule `sentry-repo` committed to the repository
body: The commit adds a gitlink/subproject file `sentry-repo` pointing to commit `a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a` without a `.gitmodules` entry. This looks like an accidentally staged nested checkout of the repository and will break `git submodule` commands or confuse tooling that clones the repository.

title: Using Python's `hash()` in shared cache keys is non-deterministic across processes
body: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` (line 27) and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (line 73) build cache keys using `hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))`. In Python 3, `hash()` is salted per-process via `PYTHONHASHSEED` (although tuples of ints alone don't use the string salt, `hash()` is not guaranteed to be stable across Python versions, architectures, or interpreter invocations, and can also collide). More importantly, if `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is called from a different worker or environment than the one that populated the cache, or if two different project sets collide on their 64-bit hash, either invalidation will miss or an unrelated project set will inherit another project set's upsampling eligibility. Use a deterministic serialization (e.g., `,`.join(map(str, sorted(project_ids))) or a cryptographic digest like SHA-256) instead of `hash()`.

title: Upsampling check uses outer `dataset` and `request` instead of `scoped_dataset` and `query`
body: In `_get_event_stats`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` is called with the outer `dataset` and `request` rather than the `scoped_dataset` and `query` passed into `_get_event_stats`. During dashboard widget splitting (`get_event_stats_factory`), `_get_event_stats` is invoked with `scoped_dataset = discover` and modified queries such as `f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction"` or `f"({query}) AND event.type:transaction"` while the outer `dataset` is `metrics_performance` / `metrics_enhanced_performance` and `request.GET["query"]` is unchanged. Because `dataset` is not `discover` or `errors`, upsampling will never be applied to split error widget queries, and even if `scoped_dataset` were passed, `_is_error_focused_query` inspects `request.GET.get("query")` rather than the `query` argument, so a transaction-split probe on a query containing `event.type:error` would still be treated as an error query.

title: Substring check `"event.type:error" in query` misclassifies negated or compound queries
body: `_is_error_focused_query` checks `if "event.type:error" in query:` on the raw query string. This matches queries that are not restricted to error events—for example `!event.type:error`, `(event.type:error OR event.type:transaction)`, or a free-text search containing the literal `"event.type:error"`. When those queries run against the `discover` dataset for allowlisted projects, `count()` will be rewritten to `upsampled_count() as count` (`sum(sample_weight)`), producing wrong counts for non-error events (such as transactions, where `sample_weight` does not apply).

title: `upsampled_count` sums `sample_weight` without handling NULL/0 defaults for unsampled events
body: `upsampled_count` is defined as `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`, assuming `sample_weight` is populated for every event in an allowlisted project. In Snuba's errors/discover schema, events ingested before client error sampling was enabled or events sent without `client_sample_rate` have `sample_weight` unset (`NULL` or `0` depending on the table). Summing `sample_weight` directly instead of falling back to `1` per event (e.g., `if(greater(sample_weight, 0), sample_weight, 1)` or ` coalesce(sample_weight, 1)`) causes unsampled events in allowlisted projects to contribute `0` to `count()`, undercounting or returning `0`.

title: Rewriting `count()` to `upsampled_count() as count` breaks alias resolution and `topEvents` / `transformAliasToInputFormat`
body: `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` replaces `"count()"` with `"upsampled_count() as count"`. However, the discover/errors query builder and `organization_events_stats` expect selected column expressions in Snuba/Discover syntax (e.g. `count()`), not SQL `AS` alias syntax, and when `transform_alias_to_input_format` is enabled (or in `top_events_timeseries`, where `orderby` or series keys look up the requested y-axis name `count()`), the returned alias or column parser will either fail to parse `upsampled_count() as count` or return results keyed under a different name than the requested `count()` y-axis.

title: Accidental git submodule `sentry-repo` committed
body: The PR adds a git submodule entry `sentry-repo` pointing to commit `a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a` without a corresponding `.gitmodules` configuration. This looks like an accidentally committed nested git checkout and will break `git submodule` commands for anyone cloning the repository.

title: Non-deterministic Python `hash()` used in shared cache key
body: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` build a shared cache key using `hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))`. In Python 3, `hash()` is randomized per process via `PYTHONHASHSEED` (and can also produce collisions across different project ID tuples). Different worker processes will compute different cache keys for the same `(organization_id, project_ids)`, reducing cache hit rate across workers and making `invalidate_upsampling_cache` unable to reliably invalidate entries written by other processes. Use a deterministic representation (e.g., `','.join(map(str, sorted(project_ids)))` or a hashlib digest) instead.

title: `_get_event_stats` checks outer `dataset` and `request.GET` instead of `scoped_dataset` and `query`
body: Inside `_get_event_stats`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` is called with the outer `dataset` and `request` rather than the `scoped_dataset` and `query` parameters passed to `_get_event_stats`. During dashboard widget discover-splitting (`get_event_stats_factory`), `_get_event_stats` is invoked with `scoped_dataset = discover` and modified queries such as `f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction"` or `f"({query}) AND event.type:transaction"` while the outer `dataset` is `metrics_enhanced_performance` / `metrics_performance`. Because `dataset` is not `discover` or `errors` (and `_is_error_focused_query` inspects `request.GET['query']` instead of the `query` argument), upsampling is either skipped on split error queries or could be misapplied if `request.GET['query']` contains `event.type:error` while executing the `event.type:transaction` split check.

title: Substring check `"event.type:error" in query` matches negated or non-error queries
body: `_is_error_focused_query` checks `"event.type:error" in query` via a plain substring match on the raw query string. Queries such as `!event.type:error`, `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`, or a message/tag search containing the literal text `event.type:error` will match and cause `count()` to be rewritten to `upsampled_count() as count` (`sum(sample_weight)`) even though the query includes transaction or default events that do not have error `sample_weight`, producing incorrect counts.

title: `upsampled_count` sums `sample_weight` without handling `NULL` or `0` weights for non-sampled events
body: `upsampled_count` is defined as `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` with the comment that `sample_weight` exists for all events in allowlisted projects. Even for an allowlisted project, historical events ingested before client error sampling was enabled, events from SDKs/clients that do not set `client_sample_rate`, or events where `sample_weight` is `NULL`/`0` will contribute `0` to `sum(sample_weight)` instead of `1` (e.g. `if(greater(sample_weight, 0), sample_weight, 1)` or ` coalesce(sample_weight, 1)`), causing `count()` to undercount or return `0` for unsampled events in allowlisted projects.

title: Accidental git submodule `sentry-repo` committed
body: A git submodule entry `sentry-repo` pointing to commit `a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a` (without a corresponding `.gitmodules` entry) was added to the repository root. This appears to be an accidental nested clone of the repository and will break `git submodule` operations or confuse tooling.

title: `_get_event_stats` passes outer `dataset` and `request` instead of `scoped_dataset` and `query` to upsampling check
body: Inside `_get_event_stats`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` is called with the outer `dataset` variable and `request` (from which `_is_error_focused_query` reads `request.GET.get("query")`), instead of the function parameters `scoped_dataset` and `query`. When `get_event_stats_factory` splits a dashboard widget query (lines 362-452), it calls `_get_event_stats` with `scoped_dataset=discover` and modified queries such as `f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction"` or `f"({query}) AND event.type:transaction"`, while the outer `dataset` is `metrics_enhanced_performance` or `metrics_performance`. Because `dataset` is not `discover` or `errors`, upsampling is never applied to split error widget queries; conversely, if `scoped_dataset` were `errors` or `discover`, checking `request.GET['query']` instead of the passed `query` would ignore query rewrites (or even upsample the `event.type:transaction` split check if the original query string contained `event.type:error`).

title: Using Python's `hash()` in shared cache key causes cross-process cache misses and collisions
body: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` build a shared cache key using `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. In Python 3, `hash()` on tuples is salted with a random per-process `PYTHONHASHSEED` (and tuple hash mixing can also vary), and 64-bit hashes can collide. Different worker processes will compute different cache keys for the same `project_ids`, making `invalidate_upsampling_cache` unable to reliably invalidate entries written by other processes and reducing cache hit rates across workers. Use a deterministic representation (e.g., `,`.join(map(str, sorted(set(project_ids)))) or a `hashlib` digest) for the cache key.

title: Substring check `"event.type:error" in query` misclassifies negated or compound queries
body: `_is_error_focused_query` checks `"event.type:error" in query` on the raw query string. This matches negated filters like `!event.type:error`, `OR` expressions that include transactions (e.g. `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`), or string literals containing `event.type:error` (e.g. `message:"event.type:error"`). In those cases on the `discover` dataset, `count()` will be replaced with `upsampled_count()`, summing `sample_weight` across non-error events (where `sample_weight` is unset/0 or not applicable) and returning incorrect counts.

title: `upsampled_count` sums `sample_weight` without handling `NULL` or `0` for unsampled events
body: `upsampled_count` is defined as `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. In Snuba's errors/discover schema, events that were ingested without client error sampling (or before sampling was enabled for the project) have `sample_weight` as `NULL` or `0` rather than `1`. Summing `sample_weight` directly without coalescing/defaulting unset values to `1` (e.g. `if(greater(sample_weight, 1), sample_weight, 1)` or ` coalesce(sample_weight, 1)`) causes unsampled events in an allowlisted project to contribute `0` to the count instead of `1`.

title: Transforming `count()` to `upsampled_count() as count` breaks `top_events_timeseries` and `transformAliasToInputFormat`
body: `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` rewrites `"count()"` into `"upsampled_count() as count"` (which is not valid Discover query syntax when parsed by `resolve_function` / `top_events_timeseries`, as column aliases use `AS` only in SnQL or are generated automatically from function names). In `top_events_timeseries`, `orderby` (frequently `count()` or `-count()`) is validated against `timeseries_columns` and `selected_columns`; replacing `count()` in `timeseries_columns` while leaving `orderby` as `count()` causes `top_events_timeseries` to fail validation or mismatch the orderby column. In addition, when `transform_alias_to_input_format=True`, the response keys are mapped back to the selected column string (`"upsampled_count() as count"` instead of `"count()"`), breaking callers expecting `count()`.

title: `BrowserReportSerializer` neither requires `age` nor `timestamp`, and mishandles `0` values
body:
`BrowserReportSerializer` defines both `age` and `timestamp` with `required=False` and validates mutual exclusivity in `validate_timestamp` and `validate_age` using truthiness checks (`if self.initial_data.get("age"):` and `if self.initial_data.get("timestamp"):`). This has two bugs:
1. If a report omits both `age` and `timestamp`, neither field validator runs and the serializer accepts the report even though both W3C Reporting specs require one of them.
2. If a report has `age: 0` (very common for newly generated reports) along with `timestamp`, `self.initial_data.get("age")` is `0` (falsy), so `validate_timestamp` will not reject the mixed report (and likewise for `timestamp: 0`, which is explicitly allowed by `min_value=0`).

Check `"age" in self.initial_data` / `"timestamp" in self.initial_data` (or `is not None`) and add an object-level `validate` method ensuring exactly one of `age` or `timestamp` is provided.

title: `zip(error_ids, events.values())` mispairs or drops events when nodestore misses or reorders keys
body: In `fetch_error_details`, `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a dict keyed by `node_id` (and some backends only include found keys or do not guarantee key order matching `node_ids`). Iterating with `zip(error_ids, events.values())` pairs `error_ids` positionally with `events.values()` instead of looking up each `node_id` in `events`. If any event is missing from nodestore or returned in a different order, `event_id` will be associated with the wrong event's payload or events will be silently dropped. Iterate over `zip(error_ids, node_ids)` and look up `events.get(node_id)` instead.

title: `CommitContextIntegration.get_merged_pr_single_issue_template` references undefined `PRCommentWorkflow`
body: `get_merged_pr_single_issue_template` is defined on `CommitContextIntegration`, and calls `PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title(title)`, while `_truncate_title` was defined on `CommitContextIntegration` (not `PRCommentWorkflow`, which isn't even imported or defined in `commit_context.py`). Calling `self.get_merged_pr_single_issue_template(...)` from `GitHubPRCommentWorkflow.get_comment_body` or `GitlabPRCommentWorkflow.get_comment_body` will either raise `NameError: name 'PRCommentWorkflow' is not defined` (if `PRCommentWorkflow` is not in module scope) or `AttributeError` if `PRCommentWorkflow` does not inherit from `CommitContextIntegration`. Call `CommitContextIntegration._truncate_title(title)` (or make it a `@classmethod` and call `cls._truncate_title(title)`).

title: `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` are only filtered out when a search query is entered
body: In `Attributes`, when `searchQuery.trim()` is empty (lines 61-63), `sortedAndFilteredAttributes` returns `sorted` directly without filtering out `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` (`['is_segment', 'project_id', 'received']`). The `!HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES.includes(attribute.name)` check is only applied in the non-empty search branch (lines 65-69), so `is_segment`, `project_id`, and `received` remain visible by default and only disappear once the user types into the search box. Filter out `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` before checking `searchQuery.trim()`.

title: Unused local helper `_handle_regex_match` left behind in `parametrize_w_experiments`
body: In `Parameterizer.parametrize_w_experiments`, removing `ParameterizationRegexExperiment` deleted the only call to the nested `_handle_regex_match` helper, leaving `_handle_regex_match` (lines 335-343) defined on every call to `parametrize_w_experiments` but never referenced.

title: `validate_timestamp` and `validate_age` fail when `age=0` or `timestamp=0`
body: `BrowserReportSerializer.validate_timestamp` checks `if self.initial_data.get("age"):` and `validate_age` checks `if self.initial_data.get("timestamp"):`. Because `0` is falsy in Python and `0` is a valid non-negative value for both `age` (a report delivered immediately has `age: 0` per the Reporting API spec) and `timestamp` (`min_value=0`), a payload containing both `timestamp` and `age: 0` (or `age` and `timestamp: 0`) bypasses the mutual-exclusion check. Additionally, neither `age` nor `timestamp` is required, so a report with neither field set is accepted. Check `"age" in self.initial_data` / `self.initial_data.get("age") is not None` (and similarly for `timestamp`), or validate mutual exclusion and presence in `validate()`.

title: `fetch_error_details` pairs `error_ids` with `events.values()` instead of matching by `node_id`
body: `fetch_error_details` builds `node_ids = [Event.generate_node_id(project_id, event_id=id) for id in error_ids]`, calls `events = nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)`, and then iterates `for event_id, data in zip(error_ids, events.values())`. `nodestore.get_multi` returns a dict mapping `node_id -> data` whose keys are not guaranteed to be in the same order as `node_ids` or to include missing keys (depending on the nodestore backend implementation). Zipping `error_ids` with `events.values()` can therefore associate an `event_id` with the wrong event's payload or drop/shift entries when some nodes are missing or when `error_ids` contains duplicates. Look up each node via `events.get(node_id)` while iterating `(error_id, node_id)` pairs.

title: `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` are only filtered out when a search query is entered
body: In `Attributes`, `sortedAndFilteredAttributes` returns `sorted` directly when `!searchQuery.trim()` (lines 61-63), and only applies `!HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES.includes(attribute.name)` inside the `filter` branch when `searchQuery` is non-empty (lines 65-69). As a result, `is_segment`, `project_id`, and `received` are displayed in the attributes tree by default and only disappear once the user types into the search box. Filter out `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` before checking `searchQuery`.

title: Replacing `FlexBox` with `<Flex direction="column" flex={1}>` drops `height: 100%` on waterfall container
body: `TraceWaterfall` previously rendered `<FlexBox>` which had `display: flex; flex-grow: 1; flex-direction: column; height: 100%;`. It was replaced with `<Flex direction="column" flex={1}>`, which does not set `height: 100%` (and sets `flex: 1` instead of `flex-grow: 1`). When `TraceWaterfall`'s parent is not a flex column container, losing `height: 100%` causes the waterfall container to collapse instead of filling its parent's height.

title: Mutual exclusion check for `age` and `timestamp` fails when either value is `0`
body: In `BrowserReportSerializer.validate_timestamp` and `validate_age`, the check uses `if self.initial_data.get("age"):` and `if self.initial_data.get("timestamp"):` (truthiness) instead of checking `is not None` (or key presence). Because `0` is a valid value for both `age` (a report delivered immediately) and `timestamp` (`min_value=0`), a report containing both `"age": 0` and a non-zero `"timestamp"` (or vice versa) will only fail validation on one of the two fields or pass `validate_timestamp` when `age == 0`. In addition, if neither `age` nor `timestamp` is provided, neither field validator runs and the report is accepted without either field. Check `self.initial_data.get("age") is not None` and `self.initial_data.get("timestamp") is not None`.

title: Non-dict element in report list causes unhandled `TypeError` (HTTP 500) instead of 422
body: In `BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint.post`, `raw_data` is verified to be a `list`, and then each element `report` is passed to `BrowserReportSerializer(data=report)`. If a client sends a list containing a primitive such as `[0]` or `["foo"]`, `serializer.is_valid()` populates `serializer.errors` with `{"non_field_errors": [...]}` but when `validate_timestamp` or `validate_age` (or any code touching `self.initial_data.get(...)`) runs, or if `report` is not a mapping, DRF's serializer validation works only up to `run_validation`, yet if `report` is a dict with `None` or if `self.initial_data` is accessed when not a dict, `AttributeError` can be raised. More importantly, `TestBrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint` has no check for non-object items in the list.

title: `zip(error_ids, events.values())` pairs event IDs with the wrong nodestore payloads when any event is missing
body: `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a dict mapping only the found `node_id`s to their data (or in an order/subset not guaranteed to match `error_ids` 1-to-1 when some keys are missing). Zipping `error_ids` with `events.values()` in `fetch_error_details` shifts all subsequent `event_id`s whenever a node is missing from nodestore, associating each `event_id` with a different event's `title`, `timestamp`, and `message`. Look up each node via `events.get(node_id)` while iterating over `zip(error_ids, node_ids)` instead.

title: `request.user.id` raises `AttributeError` when authenticated with an OrgAuthToken or ProjectKey
body: `ProjectPreprodArtifactAssembleEndpoint.post` now records analytics with `user_id=request.user.id` before checking anything else. This endpoint uses `ProjectReleasePermission` and explicitly supports org auth tokens (see lines 137-138: `if is_org_auth_token_auth(request.auth):`). When a request is authenticated via an `OrgAuthToken` (or `AnonymousUser`), `request.user` is an `AnonymousUser` whose `.id` is `None` in Django, or in Sentry's custom `AnonymousUser` may not have `.id` or may be `None`. Verify `request.user.id if request.user.is_authenticated else None` is used so token-authenticated CI uploads do not fail.

title: `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` are only filtered out when a search query is entered
body: In `Attributes`, when `searchQuery.trim()` is empty (lines 61-63), `sortedAndFilteredAttributes` returns `sorted` directly without filtering out `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` (`['is_segment', 'project_id', 'received']`). Those hidden attributes are only excluded inside the `filter` callback on lines 65-69 when `searchQuery` is non-empty, which means `is_segment`, `project_id`, and `received` are visible by default and only disappear once the user types into the search box. Filter out `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` before checking `!searchQuery.trim()`.

title: Replacing `FlexBox` with `<Flex direction="column" flex={1}>` drops `height: 100%` on the waterfall container
body: `FlexBox` previously had `height: 100%; flex-grow: 1; display: flex; flex-direction: column;`. Replacing it with `<Flex direction="column" flex={1}>` omits `height: 100%` (since `Flex` only sets `display: flex`, `flex-direction`, and `flex`). In parent containers that size children via percentage height rather than flex layout, the trace waterfall container will no longer fill the available height.

title: GitHub user validation is bypassed when Integration record does not yet exist in the database
body: In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, when `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `Integration.DoesNotExist` (lines 475-482), the view immediately returns `pipeline.next_step()`, completely skipping the `github_authenticated_user` check at lines 501-505. If a victim installs the GitHub App and the `installation` webhook is delayed, fails, or is not processed before an attacker (or the normal setup flow) hits `GitHubInstallation` with the `installation_id`, the `Integration` record won't exist in the DB yet and `build_integration()` will create it directly from GitHub's `/app/installations/{installation_id}` endpoint without ever verifying who installed the app. Additionally, even if `Integration` does exist, `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` at line 503 will raise a `KeyError` if `sender` was not populated on the `Integration` metadata (for example, if the `Integration` was previously created via `build_integration` without a `sender` in pipeline state).

title: `test_installation_not_found` fails due to OAuth state mismatch instead of testing a 404 installation lookup
body: In `test_installation_not_found`, the first request is made to `self.setup_path` instead of `self.init_path`, and the second request passes a hardcoded `state` (`ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`) that does not match `pipeline.signature` (`9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`). As a result, `OAuthLoginView` rejects the request at the `state != pipeline.signature` check and returns `"Invalid installation request."`, never advancing the pipeline to `GitHubInstallation` or `build_integration` where the mocked 404 response on `/app/installations/{self.installation_id}` would actually be exercised.

title: GitHub user validation is bypassed when `Integration` record does not yet exist
body: In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, when `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `Integration.DoesNotExist` (lines 475-482), the view immediately returns `pipeline.next_step()`, which finishes the pipeline and calls `build_integration(state)` without ever comparing `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user")` against the user who installed the GitHub App. This happens whenever the `installation.created` webhook has not yet been processed (a race condition) or failed, or when an existing `Integration` record was deleted after uninstallation from Sentry while the GitHub App installation itself remains active on GitHub (as demonstrated by `test_github_installed_on_another_org` at line 365, where `sender` is never set at all and the test still succeeds). An attacker who knows or guesses a target's `installation_id` in this state can bind that GitHub installation to their own Sentry organization despite authenticating as a different GitHub user.

title: Direct access to `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` can raise `KeyError`
body: In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` is indexed directly without checking whether `"sender"` exists in `integration.metadata`. `build_integration` (line 376) only sets `integration["metadata"]["sender"]` when `state.get("sender")` is truthy, so any `Integration` record created outside the webhook flow (or before `sender` was recorded) will not have `"sender"` in `metadata`. If its `OrganizationIntegration` is removed and a user attempts to re-link the installation, this line will raise an unhandled `KeyError` (HTTP 500) instead of handling the missing sender gracefully.

title: `test_installation_not_found` no longer tests a missing GitHub installation
body: In `test_installation_not_found`, the second request passes `state="ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"`, which does not match the pipeline signature (`9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`), and `self.init_path` is never called to initialize the pipeline with `self.installation_id`. As a result, `OAuthLoginView` fails early on the OAuth `state` mismatch check (line 412 of `integration.py`) and returns `"Invalid installation request."`, never reaching `GitHubInstallation` or `build_integration` where the mocked 404 from `/app/installations/{installation_id}` would be hit. The 404 handling in `build_integration` is therefore no longer exercised by this test.

title: GitHub user verification is bypassed when Integration record does not yet exist
body: In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, if `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `Integration.DoesNotExist` (lines 481-482), the view immediately calls `pipeline.next_step()`, skipping the `github_authenticated_user == integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` check on lines 501-505. Because the `Integration` record is only created either asynchronously via the GitHub `installation.created` webhook or at the end of the pipeline in `finish_pipeline()` -> `build_integration()`, two problems occur: (1) during a normal in-app installation flow where the redirect from GitHub arrives before the webhook is processed (or if webhooks are delayed), the `Integration` row does not exist yet and no user validation is performed at all; and (2) an attacker who learns or guesses a victim's `installation_id` before the webhook is processed—or for an installation whose `Integration` record was deleted or never created via webhook—can bind that `installation_id` to their own Sentry organization without being the user who installed the GitHub App.

title: Querying Integration by external_id without provider filter can raise MultipleObjectsReturned or match another provider
body: `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` on line 478 (and again on line 494) does not filter by `provider=GitHubIntegrationProvider.key` (i.e. `"github"`). `Integration` uniqueness is defined on `(provider, external_id)`, not `external_id` alone. If another integration provider (such as `github_enterprise` or any other provider using numeric IDs) has an `Integration` with the same `external_id`, `get()` will either raise `Integration.MultipleObjectsReturned` (causing an unhandled 500 error) or match the wrong provider's integration.

title: KeyError when existing Integration metadata does not contain 'sender'
body: Line 503 accesses `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` directly. However, `build_integration` (lines 376-377) only sets `metadata["sender"]` if `state.get("sender")` is truthy, which is only populated when the integration is created via the installation webhook. Any `Integration` record created previously via the setup pipeline (or whose `sender` key is missing) will not have `"sender"` in `integration.metadata`, causing an unhandled `KeyError` when `GitHubInstallation.dispatch` runs.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer tests a 404 from GitHub's installation endpoint
body: In `test_installation_not_found`, the test starts by requesting `self.setup_path` instead of `self.init_path` (line 386) and then passes a hardcoded `state` (`ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`) on line 392 that does not match the pipeline signature (`9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`). As a result, `OAuthLoginView` fails early on the OAuth `state` mismatch check (line 412 of `integration.py`) and returns `"Invalid installation request."`, never advancing to `GitHubInstallation` or `build_integration` where the mocked 404 response for `/app/installations/{installation_id}` would actually be hit.

title: `AssignmentSource.queued` is evaluated once at class definition time instead of per instance
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` in the `@dataclass` definition evaluates `timezone.now()` once when the module is imported, so every `AssignmentSource` instance created without an explicit `queued` argument receives the exact same timestamp (the worker's import time). Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` from `dataclasses` so that `queued` captures the time each `AssignmentSource` instance is created.

title: `assignment_source` was added to `sync_status_outbound` instead of `sync_assignee_outbound`
body: `IssueSyncIntegration.sync_status_outbound` (line 416) was updated to accept `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`, even though status syncing never passes `assignment_source`. Meanwhile, `src/sentry/integrations/tasks/sync_assignee_outbound.py` (line 60) passes `assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source` to `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(...)`, whose abstract signature on line 397 was not updated to include `assignment_source` (and concrete `sync_assignee_outbound` implementations that don't accept `**kwargs` will raise `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'assignment_source'`).

title: Default `queued` timestamp is evaluated once at class definition time
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` on `AssignmentSource` evaluates `timezone.now()` once when the module is imported, so every `AssignmentSource` instance created without an explicit `queued` argument will receive the module import timestamp rather than the time the instance was created. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` from `dataclasses` so that a fresh timestamp is generated per instance.

title: Passing `assignment_source` to `installation.sync_assignee_outbound` breaks concrete integrations
body: `sync_assignee_outbound` now calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(external_issue, user, assign=assign, assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)`. However, in `src/sentry/integrations/mixins/issues.py`, `assignment_source` was added to the abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature (line 416) instead of `sync_assignee_outbound` (line 397), and concrete `IssueSyncIntegration` implementations (such as Jira, Jira Server, GitHub, GitLab, VSTS, etc.) define `def sync_assignee_outbound(self, external_issue, user, assign=True, **kwargs)` or without `**kwargs`. Any integration whose `sync_assignee_outbound` does not accept `**kwargs` or `assignment_source` will raise `TypeError: sync_assignee_outbound() got an unexpected keyword argument 'assignment_source'` whenever an issue is assigned in Sentry (when `assignment_source` is `None`) or synced from another integration.

title: Default value `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at import time
body: In `AssignmentSource`, `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once when the module is imported rather than when each `AssignmentSource` instance is created. Every instance constructed without an explicit `queued` argument will share the exact timestamp of module import. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` from `dataclasses` so `timezone.now()` is called per instance.

title: Passing `assignment_source` to `installation.sync_assignee_outbound` breaks concrete implementations
body: `sync_assignee_outbound` task now calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(external_issue, user, assign=assign, assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)`. However, in `IssueSyncIntegration` (`src/sentry/integrations/mixins/issues.py`), `assignment_source` was added to `sync_status_outbound` (line 416) instead of `sync_assignee_outbound` (line 397), and concrete `IssueSyncIntegration` subclasses (e.g. Jira, Jira Server, GitHub, GitLab, VSTS) define `def sync_assignee_outbound(self, external_issue, user, assign=True, **kwargs)` or without `**kwargs` (only `ExampleIntegration` or classes accepting `**kwargs` tolerate extra keyword arguments). Any integration implementation of `sync_assignee_outbound` that does not accept `**kwargs` or `assignment_source` will raise `TypeError: sync_assignee_outbound() got an unexpected keyword argument 'assignment_source'` when syncing outbound to a different integration than the source.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler without implementing abstract methods
body: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` was changed to subclass `StatefulDetectorHandler` with only `pass` in its body, without implementing the abstract methods `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. Previously it implemented `evaluate` on `DetectorHandler` so it could be instantiated. Now, accessing `detector.detector_handler` for a detector with `type="metric_alert_fire"` will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract methods ...` at runtime.

title: get_group_key_values return type annotation does not allow None group keys
body: `StatefulDetectorHandler.get_group_key_values` is annotated as returning `dict[str, int]`, whereas group keys throughout the module (including `evaluate`, `get_state_data`, `evaluate_group_key_value`, and the tests in `test_detector.py` line 148) can be `None` (i.e., `DetectorGroupKey`). The return type should be `dict[DetectorGroupKey, int]`.

title: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` is now an uninstantiable abstract class
body: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` was changed to subclass `StatefulDetectorHandler` with only `pass` as its body, removing the concrete `evaluate` implementation it previously had. Because `StatefulDetectorHandler` defines abstract methods (`counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and `build_occurrence_and_event_data`), `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` remains an abstract class. Accessing `detector.detector_handler` (at `src/sentry/workflow_engine/models/detector.py:86`) for any detector of type `MetricAlertFire` (`metric_alert_fire`) will now raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract methods ...` instead of returning a no-op handler.

title: `get_group_key_values` return type annotation excludes `None` group keys
body: `StatefulDetectorHandler.get_group_key_values` is typed as returning `dict[str, int]`, whereas the rest of `StatefulDetectorHandler` (`get_state_data`, `evaluate`, `evaluate_group_key_value`, `build_occurrence_and_event_data`, and tests such as `test_state_results` with `{"group_vals": {None: 6}}`) uses `DetectorGroupKey` (`str | None`) as the dictionary key. The return type annotation should be `dict[DetectorGroupKey, int]` so subclasses returning `None` keys match the type contract.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler without implementing its abstract methods
body: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` was changed to subclass `StatefulDetectorHandler` with a `pass` body, leaving the `@abc.abstractmethod` members `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and `build_occurrence_and_event_data` unimplemented. Previously it implemented `DetectorHandler.evaluate` as a no-op stub returning `[]`. Now, accessing `detector.detector_handler` for a `MetricAlertFire` detector (in `Detector.detector_handler` at `src/sentry/workflow_engine/models/detector.py:86`) will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract methods ...` at runtime.

title: get_group_key_values return type annotation disallows None group keys
body: `StatefulDetectorHandler.get_group_key_values` is annotated to return `dict[str, int]`, whereas group keys throughout the module are typed as `DetectorGroupKey` (which allows `None`, as seen in `build_dedupe_value_key`, `bulk_get_detector_state`, and tests passing `{None: 6}`). `evaluate()` passes `list(group_values.keys())` directly to `get_state_data(group_keys: list[DetectorGroupKey])` and `evaluate_group_key_value(group_key: DetectorGroupKey, ...)`. The return annotation on `get_group_key_values` should be `dict[DetectorGroupKey, int]`.

title: build_mock_occurrence_and_event ignores the value argument and tests pass mismatched arguments
body: `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` does not include `value` in the returned `IssueOccurrence` or `event_data`, and `IssueOccurrence.__eq__` only compares a subset of fields (not including `fingerprint`). As a result, several tests pass wrong arguments when constructing the expected occurrence without failing: e.g., `test_state_results_multi_group` (line 191) passes `value=6` instead of `10` for `group_2`, `TestEvaluate.test_results_on_change` (line 490) and `test_dedupe` (line 510) pass `6` instead of `100` and `8`, and `TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe` (line 537) passes `group_key="val1", value=6` when evaluating `"group_key"` with value `10`. Including `value` in `evidence_data` (and asserting `fingerprint` or `to_dict()`) would ensure the tests actually verify the arguments passed to `build_occurrence_and_event_data`.

title: `get_monitor_environment_context` returns original `monitor.config` instead of modified `config` copy
body: `get_monitor_environment_context` copies `monitor_environment.monitor.config` into `config` (line 160) and converts `config["schedule_type"]` to its display string (line 162), but line 168 returns `"config": monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead of `"config": config`. As a result, the `config` copy and `schedule_type` display conversion are dead code and the raw integer `schedule_type` value is emitted in the monitor context.

title: Incident created before `failure_issue_threshold` failed check-ins have occurred
body: When `failure_issue_threshold > 1`, `previous_checkins` is sliced with `[:failure_issue_threshold]` (line 48), and line 52 only checks whether any returned check-in has `CheckInStatus.OK`. It does not check `len(previous_checkins) < failure_issue_threshold` (or that all `failure_issue_threshold` check-ins are actually in a failed status, as opposed to `IN_PROGRESS`). On a newly created monitor environment with fewer than `failure_issue_threshold` total check-ins, the very first failed check-in will transition the environment to `MonitorStatus.ERROR` and open an incident despite not meeting the configured threshold.

title: Redundant Redis memory info queries across per-process SpansBuffer instances
body: In `SpanFlusher.submit`, `buffer.get_memory_info()` is now called in a loop over `self.buffers.values()` (one `SpansBuffer` per flusher process) instead of once on the main `SpansBuffer`. If `SpansBuffer.get_memory_info()` queries the underlying Redis cluster hosts (rather than strictly the assigned shard keys) or if multiple shard subsets map to the same Redis nodes, iterating over every `shard_buffer` issues N times as many `INFO memory` calls to Redis on every batch submission and sums duplicate `ServiceMemory` entries. Using a single `SpansBuffer` (or deduplicating by host) avoids multiplying Redis round-trips by `num_processes`.

title: `join()` fails to terminate remaining flusher processes when the timeout expires
body: In `SpanFlusher.join()`, the loop over `self.processes` checks `if remaining_time <= 0: break` before reaching `process.terminate()`. When a `timeout` is provided and the first process (or `self.next_step.join(timeout)`) consumes the entire timeout budget, the loop breaks early and any subsequent flusher processes in `self.processes` are never terminated, leaving orphaned background processes running after `join()` returns. Instead of `break`, the loop should skip the `while process.is_alive()` wait and still call `process.terminate()` on all remaining alive processes.

title: Inconsistent metric tag key (`shards` vs `shard`) in `SpanFlusher.main`
body: Lines 185 and 195 tag `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` with `tags={"shard": shard_tag}`, whereas line 199 tags `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` with `tags={"shards": shard_tag}` (plural). Additionally, When a flusher process handles multiple shards, `shard_tag` is a comma-separated string like `"0,2"`, while `spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy` at line 244 emits individual integer shard tags. Using different tag keys (`shard` vs `shards`) and formats makes dashboarding and filtering across flusher metrics inconsistent.

title: Calling get_memory_info() across all shard buffers redundantly queries every Redis cluster node per process
body: In `SpanFlusher.submit`, the code iterates over `self.buffers.values()` and calls `buffer.get_memory_info()` on each `SpansBuffer` instance (lines 300-303). Unlike `record_stored_segments()` which is scoped to `assigned_shards`, `SpansBuffer.get_memory_info()` queries `iter_Hosts()` across the entire Redis cluster (`self.client`), not just the shards assigned to that buffer. When `num_processes > 1`, calling `get_memory_info()` on every buffer in `self.buffers` performs `num_processes` times as many `INFO MEMORY` network calls to Redis on every batch submission, adding unnecessary latency and load to Redis. Calling `get_memory_info()` on a single buffer instance (or keeping `self.buffer`) is sufficient and avoids the N-fold duplication.

title: join() fails to terminate remaining flusher processes if deadline expires mid-loop
body: In `SpanFlusher.join()`, the loop over `self.processes.items()` checks if `remaining_time <= 0` and executes `break` (lines 338-341) before reaching `process.terminate()` (lines 346-347). If a timeout is provided and the first process takes until the deadline to exit (or `next_step.join(timeout)` consumes the entire timeout), the loop breaks early and never calls `process.terminate()` on any of the subsequent flusher processes, leaving them running in the background after `join()` returns.

title: Inconsistent metric tag name 'shards' vs 'shard' and potential high tag cardinality
body: In `SpanFlusher.main`, `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` (line 185) and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` (line 195) use the tag key `"shard": shard_tag`, whereas `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` (line 199) uses the plural key `"shards": shard_tag`. In addition to the inconsistent tag naming across sibling metrics, when a process handles multiple shards (e.g. with the default `--flusher-processes=1`), `shard_tag` is a comma-joined list of all assigned partition indices (such as `"0,1,2,3,..."`), which changes across consumer rebalances and can create high-cardinality metric tags.

title: Querying `get_memory_info()` per process buffer double-counts Redis cluster memory and repeats `INFO` calls
body: In `SpanFlusher.submit`, the code now iterates over `self.buffers.values()` and extends `memory_infos` with `buffer.get_memory_info()` from each `SpansBuffer` instance. Because `SpansBuffer.get_memory_info()` queries memory across all hosts in the Redis cluster (`self.client.hosts`), calling it once per flusher process repeats the same Redis `INFO` network calls `num_processes` times on every `submit()` and duplicates the `ServiceMemory` entries in `memory_infos`. While `used / available` remains mathematically identical if all hosts are weighted equally, it causes `N` times as many Redis `INFO` calls on the main consumer thread. `get_memory_info()` only needs to be called on a single buffer instance (or the parent `buffer`).

title: `join()` leaves remaining flusher processes running if the timeout expires on an earlier process
body: In `SpanFlusher.join()`, the loop over `self.processes.items()` checks `if remaining_time <= 0: break` before reaching `process.terminate()`. If the first process takes the full timeout (or `next_step.join(timeout)` already consumed it), the loop breaks early and never calls `process.terminate()` on the remaining processes in `self.processes`, leaving orphan background flusher processes running after consumer shutdown/rebalance. Instead of breaking out of the loop, it should skip the `while process.is_alive()` wait and still terminate every remaining `multiprocessing.Process`.

title: Inconsistent metric tag name `shards` vs `shard` on `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce`
body: Lines 185 and 195 tag `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` with `tags={"shard": shard_tag}`, whereas line 199 tags `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` with `tags={"shards": shard_tag}` (plural). This makes the tag key inconsistent across the flusher metrics.

title: Committing offsets from a background thread violates KafkaConsumer thread-safety and can lose offsets on rebalance
body: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` spawns a background thread (`self.commit_thread`) that periodically calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which invokes Arroyo's `commit` callback (`KafkaConsumer.stage_positions` / `commit_positions`). In Arroyo, `StreamProcessor` is single-threaded and the `KafkaConsumer` (and its underlying `confluent_kafka.Consumer` and staged offsets dict) is not thread-safe for concurrent calls from a separate thread while the main thread is polling or rebalancing. Additionally, because commits happen outside `poll()` / `join()`, any offsets completed while the strategy is closing or rebalancing may be committed after partitions have been revoked or may never be flushed on `join()`. Offset commits should be triggered from `poll()` and `join()` on the strategy thread (matching Arroyo's `CommitOffsets` strategy) rather than from a background thread.

title: Rebalance permanently kills worker threads because FixedQueuePool is instantiated once on the factory
body: `FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and reused across `create_with_partitions` calls. However, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`, `terminate()`, and `join()` all call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`. In Arroyo, whenever a consumer group rebalance occurs, the active `ProcessingStrategy` is closed (`close()` + `join()`) or terminated (`terminate()`), and `factory.create_with_partitions` is then called to build a new strategy for the new assignment. After the first rebalance, `self.queue_pool` has all of its queues shut down (`queue.ShutDown`) and all worker threads exited, so subsequent `submit()` calls on the new strategy will raise `queue.ShutDown` (caught and logged as an error in `submit`, while marking every message's offset as completed without processing it).

title: `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before draining queues, dropping all queued items
body: In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()`, `worker.shutdown = True` is set on every worker before calling `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. Because `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` checks `while not self.shutdown:`, each worker will finish at most the single item it is currently executing and then immediately exit the loop without draining the remaining items in `work_queue` (even though `immediate=False` was passed to `q.shutdown`). Furthermore, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` stops `commit_thread` *before* calling `queue_pool.shutdown()`, so even the in-flight items that complete during shutdown never have their offsets committed. To drain gracefully, rely on `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` raising `queue.ShutDown` when the queue is empty to terminate the worker loop, and perform a final offset commit after `queue_pool.shutdown()` completes.

title: Unbounded queues provide no backpressure and can exhaust memory
body: Each queue in `FixedQueuePool` is created with `queue.Queue()` (maxsize=0, i.e., unbounded), and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` never raises `MessageRejected` or blocks. Despite the class docstring claiming "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", the main consumer thread will read from Kafka at full speed and buffer an arbitrary number of decoded payloads and `Message` objects in memory if worker threads fall behind, risking OOM kills and large uncommitted backlogs.

title: Log compacted topics or transactional markers with offset gaps will permanently stall offset commits
body: `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets` iterates `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1):` and breaks as soon as an integer offset is not in `all_offsets`. In Kafka, offsets within a partition are not guaranteed to be strictly contiguous integers (e.g., due to log compaction, control batches/transactional markers, or after a partition reassignment where `last_committed` from a prior assignment is lower than the newly assigned starting offset). If any single offset number is not delivered to `submit()`, `highest_committable` will never advance past that gap, permanently halting commits for that partition and causing `all_offsets` to grow without bound. Instead of iterating over every integer in `range(start, max_offset + 1)`, the tracker can simply commit up to `min(outstanding) - 1` (or `max(all_offsets)` when `outstanding` is empty).

title: `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` asserts the opposite of its docstring and only passes due to a timing race
body: The docstring for `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` states "Test that errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages", and `OrderedQueueWorker` indeed calls `complete_offset` in its `finally` block even when `result_processor` raises. However, line 1922 asserts `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, which only passes because the test exits after ~0.3s while `_commit_loop` sleeps for 1.0s before committing. If `_commit_loop` runs before the assertion (or when `factory.shutdown()` wakes the `shutdown_event`), offsets 100 and 101 are committed and this assertion fails.

title: `queue.Queue.shutdown()` requires Python 3.13+ and will raise `AttributeError` on Python 3.11/3.12
body: `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` (line 238) and `OrderedQueueWorker.run` catches `queue.ShutDown` (lines 132 and 142). `queue.Queue.shutdown` and `queue.ShutDown` were added in Python 3.13. On earlier Python versions (such as 3.11 or 3.12), `q.shutdown` raises `AttributeError`, which is caught and logged, leaving workers blocked indefinitely on `self.work_queue.get()` (line 131) when the queue is empty and causing `OrderedQueueWorker.run` to fail with `AttributeError: module 'queue' has no attribute 'ShutDown'` whenever an exception occurs or `get()` unblocks.

title: `FixedQueuePool` is shared across partition rebalances and permanently killed on strategy `close()`
body: `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` creates a single `self.queue_pool = FixedQueuePool(...)` instance (lines 133-137) and passes it to every `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` created in `create_with_partitions` (line 255). When Arroyo rebalances partitions, it calls `close()` and `join()` (or `terminate()`) on the current strategy before calling `create_with_partitions` for the new assignment. Because `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` and `terminate()` call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` (lines 338, 342 of `queue_consumer.py`), the shared `FixedQueuePool`'s worker threads are stopped and its queues are shut down on the first rebalance. Furthermore, its `OffsetTracker` retains stale partition/offset state across rebalances. Any subsequent strategy created by the factory will submit messages to dead queues/workers. The pool lifecycle should either be tied to each `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` instance (created in `create_with_partitions`) or `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` must not shut down a factory-owned pool without recreating it and resetting offset state.

title: Calling `commit_function` from a background thread violates Arroyo's single-threaded consumer contract
body: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` spawns a background thread (`self.commit_thread`, line 270) that calls `self.commit_function(committable)` (line 287). In Arroyo, the `commit` callback passed to `create_with_partitions` calls into the underlying `KafkaConsumer.commit` / `StreamProcessor` state, which is not thread-safe and is designed to be invoked only from the processor's main polling thread (i.e., during `poll()`, `submit()`, `close()`, or `join()`). Calling `commit_function` directly from `poll()` (and once more in `close()`/`join()` after workers drain) avoids concurrent access to the Kafka consumer and eliminates the need for a separate commit thread.

title: Unbounded `queue.Queue()` provides no backpressure and can exhaust memory
body: `FixedQueuePool.__init__` initializes each `work_queue` with `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize` (line 185), and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` never raises `MessageRejected` or blocks. Despite the class docstring claiming 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' (line 253), the main Arroyo loop will read from Kafka at full speed and buffer an unbounded number of decoded payloads and `Message` objects in memory if any worker falls behind, which will also prevent offsets on that partition from advancing and cause `OffsetTracker.all_offsets` to grow without bound.

title: `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` drop queued items and skip final offset commit
body: In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` (lines 233-234), `worker.shutdown = True` is set on every worker before draining the queues. Because `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` checks `while not self.shutdown:` on each iteration (line 129), a worker will exit after finishing its current item and leave all remaining queued items unprocessed. In addition, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` stops `commit_thread` (lines 336-337) *before* shutting down `queue_pool` (line 338), so any offsets completed while workers finish during shutdown are never committed to Kafka.

title: `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` asserts the opposite of its docstring and only passes due to commit timing
body: `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` states that 'errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages' (line 1876), and `OrderedQueueWorker` indeed calls `complete_offset` in its `finally` block even when `result_processor` raises. However, the test only waits ~0.2s after processing completes—before the 1.0s `_commit_loop` timer fires—and then asserts `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` (line 1922). If the commit loop happens to run in time, this test will fail; as written it is testing that no commit happened within 200ms rather than verifying that offset 102 is committed despite the exception at offset 100.

title: Consumer crashes or drops all messages after a Kafka rebalance in thread-queue-parallel mode
body: `ResultsStrategyFactory` creates a single `FixedQueuePool` in `__init__` (line 133), and when Arroyo closes the active strategy during a partition rebalance (`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close` / `terminate` at `queue_consumer.py` lines 338/342), that shared `self.queue_pool` is shut down (stopping its worker threads and calling `q.shutdown()` on every `queue.Queue`). On the next `create_with_partitions` call after rebalance, `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` reuses the already-shut-down `self.queue_pool`. Subsequent `submit` calls raise `queue.ShutDown` inside `work_queue.put(work_item)`, which `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` catches and immediately marks the offset as completed without processing the message — silently dropping all messages and committing their offsets. Additionally, `self.queue_pool.offset_tracker` retains stale partition offsets across rebalances. Either instantiate a fresh `FixedQueuePool` per `create_with_partitions` call (and have `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close/terminate` own its lifecycle), or avoid shutting down the factory-level pool inside the per-assignment strategy.

title: Commit callback is invoked from a background thread, violating Arroyo's single-threaded consumer contract
body: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` spawns `self.commit_thread` to call `self.commit_function(committable)` once per second. In Arroyo, the `commit` callback passed to `create_with_partitions` calls `consumer.stage_positions(...)` and `consumer.commit(...)` on the underlying `KafkaConsumer`, which is also being polled on the main `StreamProcessor` thread and is not thread-safe (for example, `KafkaConsumer.stage_positions` mutates `self.__offsets` without a lock and checks consumer state concurrently with `poll` / rebalance callbacks). Committing should happen on the main processor thread inside `poll()` and `join()` (similar to Arroyo's `CommitOffsets` strategy) rather than from a separate background thread.

title: Queues are unbounded and never raise MessageRejected, providing no backpressure
body: The docstring on `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` states "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but `FixedQueuePool.__init__` creates unbounded `queue.Queue()` instances (`maxsize=0`). `work_queue.put(work_item)` never blocks or raises Arroyo's `MessageRejected`, so the main `StreamProcessor` loop will read from Kafka as fast as possible and buffer an arbitrary number of decoded payloads and `Message` objects in memory if workers fall behind, risking OOM and long rebalance stalls.

title: Graceful shutdown discards queued items and skips committing offsets drained during shutdown
body:
There are two issues in the shutdown path:
1. In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` (lines 233-238), `worker.shutdown = True` is set before calling `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. Because `OrderedQueueWorker.run` loops on `while not self.shutdown:`, each worker exits as soon as it finishes its current item instead of draining the remaining items in `work_queue`.
2. In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close` (lines 335-338), `self.shutdown_event.set()` and `self.commit_thread.join()` run *before* `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, and no final commit is performed after the workers finish. Any offsets completed while workers finish in-flight items are never committed.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the opposite of its docstring and passes only due to a timing race
body: The docstring for `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` says "Test that errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages", and `OrderedQueueWorker.run` indeed marks failed offsets as completed in its `finally` block so that commits proceed. However, line 1922 asserts `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`. That assertion only passes because `_commit_loop` sleeps for 1.0s before its first commit while the test loop exits after ~0.2s once the queue is empty. If the commit thread happens to run before the assertion, the test will fail.

title: Password verification can be bypassed when logging in with a backup code
body: On line 121, password verification is guarded by `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)`, while line 131 checks `if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode)` before the `else if (user.twoFactorEnabled)` TOTP branch. If a request to the credentials provider includes both a `backupCode` and any non-empty `totpCode` string (e.g. `totpCode: "1"`), line 121 is skipped so `verifyPassword` is never executed, and line 131 enters the backup-code branch so `totpCode` is never validated either. This allows an attacker who obtains or brute-forces a backup code to log in as a user (or probe whether backup codes exist/match) without knowing the user's password. Additionally, lines 113 and 117 only check `!credentials.totpCode` (and `apps/web/pages/auth/login.tsx` line 180 renders `ExternalTotpFooter` instead of `TwoFactorFooter` when `totpEmail` is set), so third-party IdP users with 2FA enabled cannot use backup codes at all.

title: Dismissing the modal on the backup codes step leaves UI state out of sync and does not reset form state
body: In `handleEnable`, `onEnable()` was replaced with `setStep(SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes)`, and `onEnable()` + `resetState()` are now only invoked when the user clicks the `[data-testid="backup-codes-close"]` button (lines 266-270). If the user closes the modal on the backup codes screen via the dialog's `X` button, clicking the backdrop, or pressing `Escape` (which triggers `onOpenChange` on line 166), neither `onEnable()` nor `resetState()` is called—leaving the 2FA switch in the parent settings page unchecked even though 2FA is already enabled in the database, and leaving `step` stuck on `DisplayBackupCodes` if the modal is reopened. In addition, `resetState()` (lines 71-75) does not call `form.reset()` (or clear `totpCode`), so `totpCode` retains the previous 6-digit value if the modal is used again in the same session.

title: First 2FA E2E test does not complete the backup-codes step and passes due to an unawaited Promise assertion
body: In the first test (`"should allow a user to enable 2FA and login using 2FA"`), after `fillOtp` enters the TOTP digits, the modal now transitions to the backup codes step (`SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes`) rather than immediately calling `onEnable()`. Unlike the second test (lines 110-127), this test never waits for the backup codes step or clicks `backup-codes-close`. Line 53 (`await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=two-factor-switch]').isChecked()).toBeTruthy()`) only passes because `isChecked()` returns a `Promise<boolean>` and `expect(promise).toBeTruthy()` checks that the `Promise` object itself is truthy without awaiting it. Because neither the enable API response nor the backup codes modal is awaited after `fillOtp`'s async auto-submit, the test immediately navigates to `/auth/logout` on line 59, racing with the in-flight `/api/auth/two-factor/totp/enable` request.

title: Submitting an empty backup code on the login page fails silently with no error message
body: The login `<form>` on line 188 sets `noValidate`, which disables native HTML validation for the `required` and `minLength={10}` attributes on `<BackupCode />`, and `formSchema` (lines 57-66) uses `.passthrough()` without validating `backupCode`. If a user on the backup code step submits the form with an empty backup code, `next-auth-options.ts` skips `if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode)` (since `backupCode` is `""`) and throws `ErrorCode.SecondFactorRequired`. On line 156, `res.error === ErrorCode.SecondFactorRequired` only calls `setTwoFactorRequired(true)` (which is already `true`) and sets no error message, so the submission fails silently with no feedback to the user.

title: Closing the modal without clicking the Close button leaves 2FA UI state out of sync and does not reset form state
body:
In `handleEnable`, once `TwoFactorAuthAPI.enable(totpCode)` returns HTTP 200, 2FA is already enabled on the server, but the component now transitions to `SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes` (line 135) and defers calling `onEnable()` and `resetState()` until the user clicks the `backup-codes-close` button (lines 266–270).

1. If the user dismisses the dialog on the `DisplayBackupCodes` step via Escape, clicking the backdrop, or the dialog close button (`onOpenChange` on line 166), `onEnable()` is never called. The parent page never updates its state, leaving the 2FA toggle switch unchecked even though 2FA is active on the account.
2. `resetState()` (lines 71–75) does not clear the `totpCode` field in `form` (`form.reset()` / `form.setValue("totpCode", "")`). If the user disables 2FA and opens the modal again without reloading the page (or cancels after entering a code), `form.watch("totpCode")` retains the previous 6-digit value, which triggers the auto-submit `useEffect` on lines 157–161.

title: First 2FA E2E test leaves the backup codes modal open and relies on an unawaited Promise assertion
body: In the first test (`"should allow a user to enable 2FA and login using 2FA"`), after `fillOtp` submits the valid TOTP code on line 44, the modal now advances to the backup codes screen (`SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes`) rather than closing and calling `onEnable()`. Because this test does not click `[data-testid="backup-codes-close"]` (unlike the second test at line 125), `onEnable()` is never called and `[data-testid=two-factor-switch]` remains unchecked, as noted in the `FIXME` comment. Line 53 (`await expect(page.locator("[data-testid=two-factor-switch]").isChecked()).toBeTruthy()`) only passes because `isChecked()` returns a `Promise<boolean>` that is not awaited before being passed to `expect()`, and a `Promise` object is always truthy. The step should close the backup codes modal (or `onEnable` should be called when the enable API succeeds) and assert `[data-testid=two-factor-switch][data-state="checked"]`.

title: Backup code login is blocked for accounts using a third-party identity provider with 2FA enabled
Providing any non-empty totpCode with a backupCode bypasses password verification
body: In `authorize`, password verification on line 121 is guarded by `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)`, while the new backup code branch on line 131 (`if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode)`) executes before the `else if (user.twoFactorEnabled)` TOTP verification branch and never validates `credentials.totpCode`.
