Queries that negate the condition (such as `!event.type:error` to specifically query non-error events) or combine types with `OR` (`event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`) will match this substring and erroneously apply `upsampled_count()` (`sum(sample_weight)`) across transaction/non-error events in the `discover` dataset.

title: Rewriting `count()` to `upsampled_count() as count` breaks `topEvents` and `transformAliasToInputFormat=1`
body:
Rewriting `"count()"` to `"upsampled_count() as count"` in `query_columns` before calling the dataset methods breaks two code paths in `OrganizationEventsStatsEndpoint`:
1. When `transformAliasToInputFormat=1` is passed, `OrganizationEventsV2EndpointBase.get_event_stats_data` serializes results by looking up the original y-axis name `"count()"`, but `QueryBuilder` aliases `"upsampled_count() as count"` as `"count"` (not `"count()"`), causing the serializer to miss the column.
2. When `topEvents > 0`, `discover.top_events_timeseries` translates `timeseries_columns` via `get_field_alias(column)` (which returns `"upsampled_count"` rather than `"count"` because `get_field_alias` ignores the `AS` clause), and neither `selected_columns` (`field`) nor `orderby` are transformed, causing alias mismatches or duplicate `count` column aliases when `field=count()` or `orderby=-count()` is used.

title: Accidental `sentry-repo` git submodule gitlink committed
body: The commit adds a `sentry-repo` gitlink (`Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a`) without a `.gitmodules` entry, which appears to be a nested checkout of the repository committed by mistake and will cause `git submodule` operations to fail.

title: upsampled_count does not default missing or zero sample_weight to 1
body: `upsampled_count` is defined as `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. In Snuba, `sample_weight` is only populated for events ingested with a `sample_rate`; for unsampled error events, events ingested before client error sampling was enabled on the project, or events from SDKs that do not send `client_sample_rate`, `sample_weight` is `NULL` or `0`. Summing `sample_weight` directly without defaulting unset values to `1` (e.g., `if(sample_weight > 0, sample_weight, 1)` or `greatest(ifNull(sample_weight, 1), 1)`) causes unsampled events in allowlisted projects to contribute `0` instead of `1` to the total error count.

title: Allowlist cache uses process-salted hash() and serves stale results when options change
body: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches the allowlist check in `sentry.utils.cache.cache` for 60 seconds using `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))` in the cache key. In Python 3, `hash()` is randomized per process via `PYTHONHASHSEED`, so different worker processes compute different cache keys for the same `project_ids` and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` cannot invalidate entries written by other processes. Moreover, `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is never called when `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` is updated, `sentry.options.get` already caches option lookups, and this cache causes stale results in production as well as test pollution when `options.get` is mocked with different values for the same organization and project IDs.

title: _get_event_stats passes outer dataset and request instead of scoped_dataset and query
body: Inside `_get_event_stats(scoped_dataset, query_columns, query, ...)`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` is called with the outer `dataset` variable and `request` instead of `scoped_dataset` and `query`. When `get_event_stats_factory` splits a dashboard widget query from `metrics_enhanced_performance` or `metrics_performance` into `discover` with a modified `query` (such as `f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction"` or `f"({query}) AND event.type:transaction"`), the upsampling check evaluates the original outer `dataset` and `request.GET["query"]` rather than the actual dataset and query being executed.

title: _is_error_focused_query matches negated and mixed event.type queries
body: `_is_error_focused_query` checks `"event.type:error" in query` via a plain substring check. This returns `True` for negated queries like `!event.type:error` (which explicitly exclude errors to query transactions) and mixed queries like `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`, causing `count()` to be replaced with `upsampled_count()` on non-error events.

title: Accidental git submodule/gitlink sentry-repo committed to repository root
body: The PR adds a `sentry-repo` gitlink (`Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a`) without a corresponding `.gitmodules` entry. This appears to be an accidentally committed nested git repository and will cause `git submodule` commands in CI and developer checkouts to fail.

title: Unrelated change to topEvents validation error message
body: The validation error message for `top_events <= 0` was changed from `"If topEvents needs to be at least 1"` to `"topEvents needs to be at least 1"`, which is unrelated to error upsampling and can break existing tests or clients expecting the previous message.

title: Mutual-exclusion validation between `age` and `timestamp` fails on `0` or when both are omitted
body: `BrowserReportSerializer` marks both `age` and `timestamp` as `required=False` and uses field-level validators (`validate_timestamp` and `validate_age`) that check `if self.initial_data.get("age"):` and `if self.initial_data.get("timestamp"):`. This has two bugs: (1) `0` is a valid value for both `age` (a report delivered immediately has `age: 0`) and `timestamp` (`min_value=0`), but `0` is falsy in Python, so a payload containing both fields where one is `0` bypasses the validator; (2) in DRF, field-level `validate_<field>` methods are not called when a field is omitted, so a report missing both `age` and `timestamp` passes validation. This check should be performed in an object-level `validate(self, attrs)` method checking `"age" in attrs` vs `"timestamp" in attrs`.

title: `fetch_error_details` pairs `error_ids` with `events.values()` positionally instead of by `node_id`
body: `fetch_error_details` calls `events = nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` and then iterates over `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. `get_multi` returns a `dict` keyed by `node_id` whose key order is not guaranteed to match `node_ids` (for example when some keys are served from cache or returned in storage order, or if missing keys are omitted). Iterating with `zip(error_ids, events.values())` can associate an `event_id` with the wrong event's data; each `node_id` should be looked up via `events.get(node_id)`.

title: `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` are only filtered out when a search query is entered
body: In `Attributes`, `sortedAndFilteredAttributes` returns `sorted` early when `!searchQuery.trim()`, and only applies `!HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES.includes(attribute.name)` inside the `sorted.filter(...)` call when `searchQuery` is non-empty. Consequently, `is_segment`, `project_id`, and `received` remain visible by default and are only hidden after the user types into the search bar.

title: `renderDefaultHeadCell` computes alignment from display `column.name` instead of `column.key` and `tableData.meta.fields`
body: `renderDefaultHeadCell` calls `fieldAlignment(column.name, column.type as ColumnValueType)`. When custom `columns` are passed with a human-readable `name` (e.g. `'Count of Span Duration'`) and the optional `type` field on `TabularColumn` is omitted, `fieldAlignment` cannot recognize the aggregate/field from the display label and defaults the header alignment to `'left'`, whereas `renderDefaultBodyCell` resolves the renderer using `column.key` and `tableData.meta.fields` and right-aligns numeric cells. `fieldAlignment` should be called with `String(column.key)` and fall back to `tableData?.meta.fields`.

title: HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES are not filtered out when the search query is empty
body: In `Attributes`, `sortedAndFilteredAttributes` returns `sorted` early on line 62 when `!searchQuery.trim()`, before applying the `!HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES.includes(attribute.name)` filter on line 67. As a result, `is_segment`, `project_id`, and `received` are still displayed by default when the search bar is empty and are only hidden after the user types a search query.

title: BrowserReportSerializer age/timestamp validation fails on 0 values and when both fields are omitted
body:
`BrowserReportSerializer` has two validation bugs for `age` and `timestamp`:
1. `validate_timestamp` and `validate_age` check `if self.initial_data.get("age"):` and `if self.initial_data.get("timestamp"):`, which evaluate to `False` when `age` or `timestamp` is `0` (a common valid value for `age` when a browser report is delivered immediately). A report containing `{"age": 0, "timestamp": 1640995200000}` will bypass `validate_timestamp`'s mutual-exclusivity check.
2. Both `age` and `timestamp` are declared with `required=False` and no object-level `validate()` check ensures that at least one of them is provided, so reports missing both fields are accepted as valid.

title: fetch_error_details pairs error_ids with nodestore results positionally via events.values()
body: In `fetch_error_details`, `events = nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a dictionary mapping `node_id` to event data whose iteration order is not guaranteed to match `node_ids` (for example, `DjangoNodeStorage.get_multi` builds the dict from an unordered `WHERE id IN (...)` query and omits missing keys, and caching layers return cache hits before backend fetches). Iterating with `zip(error_ids, events.values())` can pair an `event_id` with another event's payload or misalign entries when a node is missing. Look up each event by its generated `node_id` in `events` instead.

title: renderDefaultHeadCell passes display label column.name instead of column.key to fieldAlignment
body: `renderDefaultHeadCell` computes header alignment via `fieldAlignment(column.name, column.type as ColumnValueType)`. When custom `columns` are provided, `column.name` is the display label (e.g. `'Count of Span Duration'`) while `column.key` is the actual query field/function (e.g. `'count(span.duration)'`), and `column.type` is optional on `TabularColumn` (and not populated from `tableData.meta.fields[column.key]` when `columns` is passed). Passing `column.name` instead of `column.key` prevents `fieldAlignment` from recognizing aggregate/numeric fields when `column.type` is omitted, causing numeric headers to be left-aligned instead of right-aligned.

title: HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES are not filtered out when the search query is empty
body: In `Attributes`, `sortedAndFilteredAttributes` returns `sorted` early when `!searchQuery.trim()` (lines 61-63) before applying the `!HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES.includes(attribute.name)` filter on line 67. As a result, `is_segment`, `project_id`, and `received` are still displayed in the span attributes list whenever the search input is empty, and are only hidden once the user types a non-empty search query.

title: Zipping error_ids with nodestore get_multi().values() mismatches IDs and payloads
body: In `fetch_error_details`, `events = nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a dictionary keyed by `node_id` whose iteration order is not guaranteed to match `node_ids` and, in backends such as `DjangoNodeStorage`, omits keys that were not found in the database. Iterating via `zip(error_ids, events.values())` pairs `error_ids` by position with `events.values()`, associating `event_id`s with the wrong event data whenever the backend returns rows out of order or omits missing nodes. Look up each event by its `node_id` (e.g. `for event_id, node_id in zip(error_ids, node_ids)` with `data = events.get(node_id)`).

title: Truthiness check on age and timestamp allows 0 when both fields are present
body: `BrowserReportSerializer.validate_timestamp` and `validate_age` check `if self.initial_data.get("age"):` and `if self.initial_data.get("timestamp"):`. Because `0` is falsy in Python and `0` is a valid non-negative value for both `age` (0ms elapsed since report generation in the W3C Reporting API) and `timestamp`, a report containing `age: 0` alongside `timestamp` (or `timestamp: 0` alongside `age`) bypasses the mutual-exclusion check. Check `self.initial_data.get("age") is not None` and `self.initial_data.get("timestamp") is not None` instead.

title: Direct dictionary access on `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` can raise `KeyError`
body: `build_integration` (lines 376-377) only populates `integration.metadata["sender"]` when `state.get("sender")` is present (i.e. when the `Integration` was created from a GitHub installation webhook). If an `Integration` record was originally created through the pipeline before the webhook arrived, or before `sender` was recorded in metadata, and its `OrganizationIntegration` was later deleted, reinstalling it will find the active `Integration` without a `"sender"` key in `metadata` and raise an unhandled `KeyError` at `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` instead of returning the error page. Use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` (and filter `Integration.objects.get` by `provider=GitHubIntegrationProvider.key` on lines 478 and 494 since `external_id` is only unique per provider).

title: `test_installation_not_found` fails on OAuth `state` mismatch instead of testing a 404 installation lookup
body: Adding `OAuthLoginView` to the pipeline changed the deterministic `pipeline.signature` in tests from `ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05` to `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`. `test_installation_not_found` still passes `"state": "ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"`, which causes `OAuthLoginView` to abort early at `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature` with `"Invalid installation request."`. As a result, the mocked 404 on `GET /app/installations/{self.installation_id}` and the `IntegrationError("The GitHub installation could not be found.")` path in `build_integration` are never exercised. Update `state` to `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3` and restore the assertion for `b"The GitHub installation could not be found."`.

title: OAuth `state` parameter uses static `pipeline.signature` instead of a per-session random token
body: `OAuthLoginView.dispatch` uses `pipeline.signature` as the OAuth2 `state` parameter (line 402) and validates `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature` on callback (line 412). However, `pipeline.signature` is computed only from the module and class names of the pipeline views (`"9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3"`), so it is a static constant across all users, organizations, and sessions. Because `state` is not bound to the user's session, an attacker can start the OAuth flow with their own GitHub account, capture the callback URL with their `code` and the constant `state`, and via login CSRF bind their own GitHub login as `github_authenticated_user` in a victim's pipeline.

title: Unchecked `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` access raises `KeyError` when `sender` is missing
body: In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes `"sender"` is always present in `integration.metadata`. However, `"sender"` is only added to `metadata` by the `installation` webhook, and when a pipeline completes, `finish_pipeline()` calls `build_integration(self.state)` (where `self.state` does not contain `"sender"`) and `ensure_integration()` overwrites `integration.metadata` without `"sender"`. If an organization later uninstalls the integration in Sentry (which deletes the `OrganizationIntegration` but leaves the `Integration` record active) and attempts to reinstall it, or if the `Integration` was created before this change, `integration.metadata["sender"]` will raise an unhandled `KeyError` (HTTP 500).

title: `Integration.objects.get` queries by `external_id` without filtering by `provider`
body: Lines 478 and 494 call `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id, ...)` without filtering by `provider=GitHubIntegrationProvider.key`. The `Integration` model is only unique on `(provider, external_id)`, not on `external_id` alone. If another integration provider has an `Integration` with the same `external_id`, `Integration.objects.get` will either return the wrong provider's integration or raise an unhandled `Integration.MultipleObjectsReturned` exception.

title: `test_installation_not_found` uses a stale pipeline `state` signature and no longer tests 404 handling
body: Adding `OAuthLoginView` to `get_pipeline_views()` changed the pipeline signature from `ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05` to `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`. `test_installation_not_found` still sends `"state": "ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"`, which causes `OAuthLoginView` to fail early on the `state != pipeline.signature` check and return `"Invalid installation request."` before `GitHubInstallation` or `build_integration` is ever reached. As a result, the mocked 404 on `GET /app/installations/{self.installation_id}` is never called in this test.

title: Non-canonical `installation_id` triggers `Integration.DoesNotExist` and bypasses user and org checks
body:
In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, `installation_id` is read from `request.GET` as a raw string and queried via `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)`. When `Integration.DoesNotExist` is raised, `dispatch` immediately returns `pipeline.next_step()`, skipping both the `installations_exist` check and the new `github_authenticated_user != integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` check.

An attacker can pass a non-canonical `installation_id` such as `"12345678?"` or `"/12345678"`. Because the database stores `external_id` as `"12345678"`, `Integration.objects.get(external_id="12345678?")` raises `Integration.DoesNotExist` and jumps straight to `finish_pipeline()`. `build_integration()` then requests `GET /app/installations/12345678?` from GitHub, which resolves to installation `12345678` and returns the canonical `installation["id"] = 12345678`. `ensure_integration()` then links the victim's GitHub installation to the attacker's Sentry organization, bypassing both the single-organization restriction and the GitHub user verification.

title: `finish_pipeline` overwrites `integration.metadata` without `sender`, causing `KeyError` on reinstall
body:
Line 503 accesses `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` directly, assuming `"sender"` is always present on an active `Integration`. However, when `pipeline.next_step()` completes the pipeline, `IntegrationPipeline.finish_pipeline()` calls `build_integration(self.state)` and updates the existing `Integration` record via `ensure_integration()`. Because `"sender"` is never bound to `pipeline.state`, `state.get("sender")` in `build_integration()` (line 376) is `None`, which overwrites `integration.metadata` and erases `"sender"`.

If an organization later uninstalls the integration in Sentry (which deletes the `OrganizationIntegration` row while leaving the `Integration` row active) and attempts to reinstall it, or if the `Integration` was created before `sender` was recorded, `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` will raise an unhandled `KeyError: 'sender'` (500 error). `pipeline` should preserve `sender` in state (or `build_integration` should not clobber it) and line 503 should safely use `.get("sender", {}).get("login")`.

title: `test_installation_not_found` fails on OAuth `state` mismatch and never exercises the 404 path
body: `test_installation_not_found` mocks a 404 on `GET /app/installations/{self.installation_id}` to verify how `build_integration` handles a missing installation. However, the second request passes `"state": "ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"` instead of the pipeline's actual signature `"9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3"`. Because the state does not match `pipeline.signature`, `OAuthLoginView` aborts early with `"Invalid installation request."` and the mocked 404 endpoint in `build_integration` is never called.

title: `AssignmentSource.queued` default is evaluated once at import time
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` on the `AssignmentSource` dataclass evaluates `timezone.now()` once when the module is imported rather than when each instance is created. As a result, every `AssignmentSource` instantiated without an explicit `queued` argument will carry the timestamp of when the worker process started. Use `dataclasses.field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so the timestamp is generated per instance.

title: `assignment_source` added to `sync_status_outbound` instead of `sync_assignee_outbound`
body: `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None` was added to `IssueSyncIntegration.sync_status_outbound`, which syncs resolution status and is never called with an `assignment_source`. Meanwhile, `src/sentry/integrations/tasks/sync_assignee_outbound.py` (line 60) passes `assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source` to `installation.sync_assignee_outbound`, whose signature on `IssueSyncIntegration` was not updated (and any subclass implementation of `sync_assignee_outbound` that does not accept `**kwargs` will raise `TypeError`). Either move the parameter to `sync_assignee_outbound` or omit it from the `installation.sync_assignee_outbound` call since the cycle check already happens in `installation.should_sync`.

title: Default `queued` timestamp on `AssignmentSource` is evaluated once at import time
body: In `AssignmentSource`, `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` calls `timezone.now()` once when the module is imported rather than when each `AssignmentSource` instance is created. As a result, every `AssignmentSource` created without an explicit `queued` value will share the worker's module-import timestamp instead of recording when the assignment was actually queued. Use `dataclasses.field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so the timestamp is generated per instance.

title: `assignment_source` parameter added to `sync_status_outbound` instead of `sync_assignee_outbound`
body: `IssueSyncIntegration.sync_status_outbound` was updated to accept `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`, whereas the task in `src/sentry/integrations/tasks/sync_assignee_outbound.py` (line 60) passes `assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source` to `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(...)`. `sync_status_outbound` handles resolution status changes and never receives `assignment_source`, while `IssueSyncIntegration.sync_assignee_outbound` was left without the parameter in its signature (only accepting it via `**kwargs`).

title: Default value `timezone.now()` on dataclass field is evaluated only once at import time
body: In `AssignmentSource`, `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` evaluates `timezone.now()` once when the class is defined at module import time. Every `AssignmentSource` instance created without an explicit `queued` argument will receive the same stale timestamp from process startup rather than the time the instance was created. Use `dataclasses.field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead.

title: `assignment_source` parameter was added to `sync_status_outbound` instead of `sync_assignee_outbound`
body: `IssueSyncIntegration.sync_status_outbound` was updated to take `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`, but status syncing never uses or passes `assignment_source`. Meanwhile, `src/sentry/integrations/tasks/sync_assignee_outbound.py` passes `assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source` to `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(...)`, whose abstract signature on `IssueSyncIntegration` (line 397) was left without the `assignment_source` parameter.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is an uninstantiable abstract class
body: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` now inherits from `StatefulDetectorHandler[QuerySubscriptionUpdate]` with `pass`, without implementing its abstract methods (`counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and `build_occurrence_and_event_data`). Because `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler` is set to `MetricAlertDetectorHandler`, accessing `detector.detector_handler` on a `MetricAlertFire` detector calls `MetricAlertDetectorHandler(self)` and raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract methods ...` (and fails mypy's `[type-abstract]` check on `GroupType.detector_handler`).

title: Mismatched group_key in TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe causes test failure
body: In `TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe`, `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` is called with `group_key="val1"`, whereas `expected_result` and `handler.evaluate_group_key_value` use `"group_key"`. Because `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` builds the `IssueOccurrence.fingerprint` from `group_key`, the expected occurrence's fingerprint is derived from `"val1"` while the actual occurrence returned by `evaluate_group_key_value` has a fingerprint derived from `"group_key"`, causing the equality assertion at line 546 to fail.

title: Mock IssueOccurrence hardcodes ID and ignores value, masking mismatched test expectations
body: `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` hardcodes `id="eb4b0acffadb4d098d48cb14165ab578"` and `event_id="43878ab4419f4ab181f6379ac376d5aa"` and never uses the `value` parameter. Because `IssueOccurrence` equality only compares `id` (and `event_data` only contains fields derived from those constants and the frozen timestamp), any two `(occurrence, event_data)` pairs produced during a test compare equal regardless of `group_key`, `value`, or `new_status`. This already hides several mismatches in this test file: in `TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe` (lines 536-559), `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` is called with `group_key="val1", value=6` while `evaluate_group_key_value` is called with `group_key="group_key", value=10`; and in `test_state_results_multi_group` (line 191), `test_results_on_change` (line 490), and `TestEvaluate.test_dedupe` (line 510), `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` is called with `value=6` when the evaluated packet values are `10`, `100`, and `8`.

title: `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is always False for `SpawnProcess`, preventing process kill/terminate
body:
Processes are created via `self.mp_context.Process` where `self.mp_context = multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")`, which produces `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` instances. In Python's `multiprocessing` module, `SpawnProcess` inherits from `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, not `multiprocessing.Process` (`multiprocessing.context.Process`), so `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` always evaluates to `False` at runtime.

As a consequence:
1. In `_ensure_processes_alive` (line 254), `process.kill()` is never called when a flusher process hangs, leaking the hung process while spawning a replacement process for the same shards (which can also cause concurrent flushing of the same shards if the hung process recovers).
2. In `join` (line 346), `process.terminate()` is never called when shutting down.

Use `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)` (or `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`) instead.

title: `join()` breaks out of the loop on timeout without terminating remaining processes
body: In `join()`, `deadline` is shared across all processes in `self.processes`. If the first process takes the full timeout to exit (or hangs until `deadline`), then on the next iteration `remaining_time = deadline - time.time()` is `<= 0` and line 341 executes `break`, exiting the loop immediately without terminating any of the remaining alive processes in `self.processes`.

title: `get_memory_info()` is called redundantly for every flusher process on each `submit()`
body: `SpansBuffer.get_memory_info()` queries memory usage across the Redis cluster nodes independent of which shard subset a `SpansBuffer` instance is assigned. Calling `buffer.get_memory_info()` in a loop over `self.buffers.values()` queries every Redis cluster node `num_processes` times on each `submit()` call instead of once using the main `buffer` instance.

title: Inconsistent `shards` vs `shard` metric tag key and high-cardinality tag values
body: Lines 185 and 195 emit metrics with `tags={"shard": shard_tag}`, whereas line 199 emits `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` with `tags={"shards": shard_tag}`. Additionally, when multiple shards share a process (such as with the default `--flusher-processes=1`), `shard_tag = ",".join(map(str, shards))` produces a comma-joined list of all partitions assigned to the consumer, which changes across consumer rebalances and creates high-cardinality tag values.

title: `time.sleep(0.1)` in `test_basic` is a no-op because `time.sleep` is monkeypatched
body: Line 15 monkeypatches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None`, so calling `time.sleep(0.1)` on line 62 does not actually sleep or wait for the background flusher thread to run after `current_drift` is updated. `step.join()` then immediately sets `stopped.value = True`, which can race with the background thread and cause it to exit before flushing the segment.

title: `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is always False for `SpawnProcess`, skipping `kill()` and `terminate()`
body: Processes are created via `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which instantiates `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`. In Python's `multiprocessing` module, `SpawnProcess` and `multiprocessing.Process` (`multiprocessing.context.Process`) are sibling subclasses of `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, so `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` always evaluates to `False`. Wrapping `process.kill()` in `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process):` means hung flusher processes are never killed before spawning a replacement in `_ensure_processes_alive` (and `process.terminate()` at line 346 is likewise never called in `join()`). Use `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)` or `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess)` instead.

title: `join()` breaks out of the loop on timeout without terminating remaining processes
body: In `join()`, if `deadline` expires during `self.next_step.join(timeout)` or while waiting for an earlier process in `self.processes` to exit, `if remaining_time <= 0: break` exits the `for` loop immediately. Any subsequent processes in `self.processes` never reach the termination step at the end of the loop body and will keep running in the background (for example, across consumer partition rebalances when Arroyo closes and joins the strategy). The `while process.is_alive() and (deadline is None or deadline > time.time()):` condition already skips waiting once the deadline has passed, so the early `break` should be removed so all remaining live processes are terminated.

title: `submit()` queries cluster-wide Redis memory `num_processes` times per batch
body: `SpansBuffer.get_memory_info()` queries `INFO memory` across the Redis cluster nodes rather than only for a specific shard key. Calling `buffer.get_memory_info()` in a loop over `self.buffers.values()` on every `submit()` performs `num_processes` redundant synchronous Redis queries on the main consumer thread and maintains `num_processes` extra `SpansBuffer` instances in the parent process. Retaining `self.buffer = buffer` (which already holds all `assigned_shards`) and calling `self.buffer.record_stored_segments()` and `self.buffer.get_memory_info()` once avoids the duplicate Redis round-trips.

title: Inconsistent metric tag key `shards` vs `shard` in `SpanFlusher.main`
body: `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is emitted with `tags={"shards": shard_tag}`, whereas `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` (line 185), `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` (line 195), and `spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy` (line 244) all use the singular tag key `"shard"`.

title: isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is always False for SpawnProcess
body: `self.mp_context` is created with `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")`, so `self.mp_context.Process(...)` returns a `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` instance. In CPython's `multiprocessing` module, `SpawnProcess` subclasses `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, not `multiprocessing.Process` (they are sibling classes). As a result, `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` on lines 254 and 346 always evaluates to `False` at runtime. When a flusher process hangs (`cause == "hang"`), `_ensure_processes_alive()` never kills the hung process before spawning a replacement, leaving duplicate processes flushing the same shards concurrently; similarly, `join()` never terminates still-running processes on shutdown. Check `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess)` or `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)` instead.

title: join() breaks out of the loop on timeout without terminating remaining processes
body: In `SpanFlusher.join()`, if `deadline` is reached while waiting in `self.next_step.join(timeout)` or while waiting for an earlier process in `self.processes`, the check `if remaining_time <= 0: break` exits the `for` loop immediately. Any subsequent processes in `self.processes` are skipped and never terminated. The `while process.is_alive() and (deadline is None or deadline > time.time()):` loop on line 343 already avoids sleeping once the deadline has passed, so removing the early `break` (and only calling `process.terminate()` when `process.is_alive()`) ensures all remaining processes are cleaned up when the timeout expires.

title: submit() queries cluster-wide Redis memory info once per flusher process and creates duplicate Redis clients
body: `SpansBuffer.get_memory_info()` queries `INFO memory` across all nodes in the Redis cluster and is not scoped to `assigned_shards`. By storing each child's `shard_buffer` in `self.buffers` and calling `buffer.get_memory_info()` for every entry in `self.buffers.values()` on each `submit()`, the main consumer process opens `num_processes` extra Redis connection pools and executes `INFO memory` against the entire Redis cluster `num_processes` times per batch instead of once. Keeping `self.buffer = buffer` from `__init__` (which already covers all assigned shards) and calling `self.buffer.record_stored_segments()` and `self.buffer.get_memory_info()` once avoids the redundant network calls and extra client pools in the parent process.

title: Inconsistent metric tag key ('shards' vs 'shard') and high-cardinality tag values when sharing processes
body: Lines 185 and 195 tag `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` with `tags={"shard": shard_tag}`, whereas line 199 tags `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` with `tags={"shards": shard_tag}`. In addition, when multiple shards share a process (which is the default since `--flusher-processes` defaults to 1), `shard_tag = ",".join(map(str, shards))` concatenates the consumer's assigned partition subset into a single tag value that changes across Kafka rebalances, creating high-cardinality metric tags.

title: Shutting down shared FixedQueuePool on strategy close breaks consumer after partition rebalance
body: `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` creates a single `self.queue_pool = FixedQueuePool(...)` instance (line 133) and reuses it across `create_with_partitions` calls (line 255). In Arroyo, whenever a Kafka consumer group rebalance occurs, `StreamProcessor` revokes partitions by calling `strategy.close()` and `strategy.join()` on the current strategy, and then calls `factory.create_with_partitions(...)` for the new assignment. Because `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` (line 338 of `queue_consumer.py`), all worker threads in `self.queue_pool` exit and all `queue.Queue` instances are permanently shut down. After the rebalance, the new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` receives the already-shut-down `queue_pool`; every subsequent `submit()` call hits `work_queue.put()`, which raises `queue.ShutDown`. Because `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` catches `Exception` and marks the offset completed (lines 317-325 of `queue_consumer.py`), the consumer will silently drop all messages after any rebalance while still committing their offsets to Kafka.

title: Graceful shutdown abandons queued items and stops commit thread before workers drain
body:
There are two issues in the shutdown sequence across `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` (lines 335-339) and `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` (lines 231-244):
1. `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` on all workers before calling `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. While `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` is intended to let workers drain remaining queued items until `q.get()` raises `queue.ShutDown`, `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` checks `while not self.shutdown:` on each iteration (line 129). As a result, each worker exits immediately after finishing at most one in-flight item, dropping all other items still queued.
2. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` stops and joins `self.commit_thread` *before* calling `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` and does not perform a final commit afterward. Offsets completed since the last 1-second commit tick or during queue draining are never committed.

title: OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets skips over uncommitted offset gaps after a commit
body: In `OffsetTracker.mark_committed()`, all offsets `<= offset` are removed from `self.all_offsets[partition]` (line 105). In `get_committable_offsets()`, the scan starts at `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)` where `min_offset = min(all_offsets)` (lines 83-86). If offset 100 is committed and pruned from `all_offsets`, and offsets 102 and 103 are completed while offset 101 has not yet been added, `min_offset` is `102`, so `start = max(101, 102) = 102`. The loop then starts at 102, completely skips the missing offset 101, and reports 103 as committable. Once `partition in self.last_committed`, the contiguous check must start at `last_committed + 1`, not `max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)`.

title: Background commit_thread invokes Arroyo's non-thread-safe commit callback concurrently
body: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` spawns a background `commit_thread` that periodically calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which invokes the Arroyo `commit` callback passed to `create_with_partitions`. In Arroyo, `StreamProcessor`'s commit callback (`KafkaConsumer.stage_positions` and `KafkaConsumer.commit_offsets`) is not thread-safe and mutates internal offset dictionaries and consumer state without locks on the assumption that it is only called from the main `StreamProcessor` thread (e.g., inside `submit()` or `poll()`). Calling `commit` from a background thread races with `StreamProcessor._run_once()` polling and committing on the main thread. Performing the periodic commit check inside `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll()` (and once at shutdown after workers drain) keeps all consumer operations on the main thread.

title: Queues in FixedQueuePool are unbounded, providing no backpressure to StreamProcessor
body: Although `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`'s docstring states that it provides "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", `FixedQueuePool` initializes each `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize` (unbounded). In Arroyo, `StreamProcessor` polls Kafka and calls `strategy.submit(message)` as fast as messages arrive until `submit` raises `MessageRejected`. Because `submit()` only decodes the payload in memory and pushes a `WorkItem` (including the full raw `Message`) onto an unbounded queue without ever raising `MessageRejected`, any slowdown in downstream worker processing will cause the consumer to buffer an unbounded number of messages and offsets in memory.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the opposite of actual behavior due to commit timing
body: `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` states that "errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages", and `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` unconditionally marks offsets completed in its `finally` block (line 149 of `queue_consumer.py`) even when `result_processor` raises an exception. However, the test only waits `0.2s` after both items are processed (line 1917), while `_commit_loop` waits `1.0s` before committing (`self.shutdown_event.wait(1.0)`). Because the 1-second commit interval has not elapsed yet, `committed_offsets` is still empty and line 1922 asserts `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`—the opposite of what happens once the commit loop runs (and if the test takes >= 1.0s on CI, the commit will fire and fail this assertion). Also note that calling `factory.shutdown()` without `consumer.close()` in these tests leaves `consumer.commit_thread` running in the background.

title: Reusing shut-down FixedQueuePool across rebalances silently drops all messages and commits their offsets
body: `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` creates a single `self.queue_pool = FixedQueuePool(...)` instance, which `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` passes to `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`. When Arroyo's `StreamProcessor` rebalances partitions, it calls ` close()`/`join()` (or `terminate()`) on the active strategy and then calls `factory.create_with_partitions(...)` for the new assignment. Because `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` and `terminate()` call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, all queues in `self.queue_pool` are permanently shut down (`q.shutdown()`) and all worker threads exit. On the subsequent `create_with_partitions` call, the factory reuses the same shut-down `self.queue_pool` (along with its stale `OffsetTracker` state). From that point on, every `work_queue.put(work_item)` call in `submit()` raises `queue.ShutDown` (a subclass of `Exception`), which `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` catches in `except Exception:` (lines 317-325 of `queue_consumer.py`), logs, and marks as completed via `add_offset` + `complete_offset`—causing all messages after a rebalance to be dropped while their offsets are committed to Kafka.

title: OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets commits past offset gaps on the cycle after mark_committed
body: In `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets()`, `start` is computed as `max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)`. Meanwhile, `mark_committed()` removes all offsets `<= offset` from `self.all_offsets[partition]`. If offsets `100`, `102`, and `103` finish while `101` has not been seen yet, the first call to `get_committable_offsets()` returns `100` (because `100` is in `all_offsets`, so `min_offset == 100`) and `mark_committed(partition, 100)` removes `100`, leaving `all_offsets = {102, 103}`. On the very next commit tick (1 second later, with `101` still missing), `min_offset` is now `102`, so `start = max(101, 102) = 102`, and the loop commits offset `103`, skipping right past the uncommitted gap at `101`. Once a partition has a `last_committed` value, `start` must be `last_committed + 1` rather than `max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)`.

title: Shutdown drops queued items without draining and stops the commit thread before workers finish
body:
There are two ordering bugs in the shutdown sequence:

1. `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` on all workers before calling `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. Because `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` checks `while not self.shutdown:` on each loop iteration, workers exit as soon as they finish their current in-flight item instead of draining remaining queued items until `work_queue.get()` raises `queue.ShutDown`.
2. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` sets `self.shutdown_event` and joins `self.commit_thread` *before* calling `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, and never performs a final commit afterwards. Any offsets completed while workers finish in-flight items during shutdown (or after the last commit loop iteration) are never committed.

title: Queues are unbounded and never apply backpressure to the Kafka consumer
body: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`'s docstring states that it provides "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but `FixedQueuePool.__init__` creates each queue with `queue.Queue()` (`maxsize=0`, i.e. unbounded) and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` never raises Arroyo's `MessageRejected`. If worker threads fall behind Kafka polling (e.g. due to slow database/network calls), the consumer thread will buffer an unbounded number of work items—including the unused raw `WorkItem.message` payload—in memory.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts that offsets were not committed and leaks commit threads
body: `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` states in its docstring: "Test that errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages." Because `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` calls `complete_offset` in its `finally` block, both offset 100 (which raised an exception) and offset 101 (which succeeded) are marked complete and are committable. However, the test exits its wait loop after ~0.2s (before `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop`'s 1.0s sleep elapses) and asserts `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`—the opposite of the intended behavior, and flaky if the test takes >= 1s. Additionally, all of the `test_thread_queue_parallel*` tests in this file only call `factory.shutdown()` and never call `consumer.close()`, leaving `consumer.commit_thread` running in the background for the rest of the test process.

title: Race condition in test_stats_reporting when workers drain items before get_stats() runs
body: In `TestFixedQueuePool.test_stats_reporting`, 3 worker threads are already running a fast in-memory callback (`result_processor` only appends to a list) while the test loop submits 10 items. If the worker threads dequeue all 10 items before `stats = self.pool.get_stats()` executes on line 199, `stats["total_items"]` will be `0` and `assert stats["total_items"] > 0` will fail intermittently.

title: Consumer group rebalance shuts down the shared FixedQueuePool and causes all subsequent messages to be dropped and committed
body: `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` creates a single `self.queue_pool = FixedQueuePool(...)` instance for the lifetime of the factory, and `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker()` passes that shared `self.queue_pool` into each `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` created by `create_with_partitions()`. In Arroyo, whenever a Kafka partition rebalance occurs, `StreamProcessor` closes or terminates the active `ProcessingStrategy` (`strategy.close()` / `strategy.join()` / `strategy.terminate()`) and then calls `factory.create_with_partitions()` for the new assignment. Because `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` and `terminate()` both call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, the first rebalance permanently shuts down all queues (`q.shutdown()`) and exits all worker threads on `self.queue_pool`. On the new strategy created after the rebalance, every `submit()` call hits `work_queue.put()` on a shut-down queue, raising `queue.ShutDown`. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` catches `Exception`, logs it, and calls `add_offset()` + `complete_offset()`, so the consumer will silently drop 100% of messages after any rebalance while committing their offsets to Kafka. In addition, `self.queue_pool.offset_tracker` retains state from revoked partitions across rebalances, causing the commit thread to commit offsets for partitions the consumer may no longer own.

title: OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets skips over offset gaps after mark_committed prunes all_offsets
body: In `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets()`, the contiguous scan starts at `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)`. However, `mark_committed(partition, offset)` removes all offsets `<= offset` from `self.all_offsets[partition]`. As a result, once an offset has been committed, every remaining entry in `all_offsets` is strictly greater than `last_committed`, making `min_offset >= last_committed + 1` always true for monotonically increasing offsets. If there is a gap (e.g. offsets 100, 102, 103 are completed while 101 is still missing), the first call to `get_committable_offsets()` returns 100 and `mark_committed(partition, 100)` leaves `all_offsets = {102, 103}` and `last_committed = 100`. On the very next commit loop iteration, `min_offset` is 102, so `start = max(101, 102) = 102`, causing the tracker to jump over the missing offset 101 and commit 103. When `partition in self.last_committed`, `start` must be `self.last_committed[partition] + 1`, only using `min_offset` when no offset has been committed for that partition yet.

title: Graceful shutdown abandons queued items and stops the commit thread before workers finish
body:
There are two ordering defects in shutdown handling:
1. `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` on all `OrderedQueueWorker` instances before calling `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. Because `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` loops on `while not self.shutdown:`, each worker exits immediately after finishing its current item instead of draining the remaining items in `self.work_queue` until `queue.ShutDown` is raised. Any queued items are abandoned with their offsets still in `offset_tracker.outstanding`.
2. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` sets `self.shutdown_event` and joins `self.commit_thread` *before* calling `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, with no final commit afterward. Offsets completed by workers while `queue_pool.shutdown()` is draining/joining are never committed to Kafka. (`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.terminate()` also does not join `self.commit_thread`, and `ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown()` shuts down `queue_pool` without stopping `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.commit_thread`.)

title: Worker queues are unbounded and provide no backpressure to Arroyo StreamProcessor
body: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`'s docstring states that it provides "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but `FixedQueuePool.__init__` creates each `queue.Queue()` with the default `maxsize=0` (unbounded). Arroyo's `StreamProcessor` polls Kafka and calls `strategy.submit(message)` in a tight loop until `MessageRejected` is raised. Because `work_queue.put()` never blocks or rejects, if worker processing falls behind Kafka consumption, the consumer will buffer an unbounded number of `WorkItem` and `Message` objects in memory. Furthermore, if a bounded queue were used, the broad `except Exception:` handler in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` (lines 317-325) would catch `queue.Full` / `MessageRejected` and immediately mark the unqueued message's offset as completed instead of propagating `MessageRejected` to Arroyo.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the opposite of its docstring due to commit timer timing and leaks commit_thread
body: `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` states "Test that errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages", and `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` calls `offset_tracker.complete_offset()` in its `finally` block even when `result_processor` raises an exception. However, the test exits its wait loop ~0.2s after the 2 items are processed (before `_commit_loop`'s 1.0s `shutdown_event.wait(1.0)` elapses) and asserts `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`—which asserts that offsets were *not* committed and will fail flakily if the test takes >1s on CI. In addition, the `test_thread_queue_parallel*` unit tests in `test_results_consumer.py` only call `factory.shutdown()` and never `consumer.close()`, leaving `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.commit_thread` running in the background after the tests finish.

title: Backup code single-use enforcement is not atomic (read-modify-write race)
body: In the credentials authorize() handler, the backup-code check does a read of the decrypted backupCodes array, an indexOf lookup, and then a separate prisma.user.update that writes back the whole array. Two concurrent sign-in requests using the same backup code can both pass the indexOf check before either write lands, so one single-use code authenticates twice; likewise two concurrent logins with different codes will each write their own copy of the array and the last write wins, resurrecting a code the other request already consumed. The code is also consumed (nulled and persisted) before next-auth finishes creating the session, so any later failure (JWT encode error, network drop mid-request) burns the code without a successful login. Single-use consumption should be made atomic/transactional and only committed once authentication has succeeded.

title: onEnable is only invoked via the "Close" button; dismissing the dialog any other way leaves the 2FA switch out of sync
body: After a successful enable, the modal moves to the DisplayBackupCodes step and onEnable() (which updates the settings page state, e.g. the two-factor switch) is only called from the "Close" button's onClick. If the user closes the dialog via ESC, the dialog's built-in close affordance, or onOpenChange (all wired directly to the onOpenChange prop), neither onEnable nor onCancel fires and the modal state is not reset. The security settings page will continue to show 2FA as disabled even though it is actually enabled in the database, and the dialog's internal step state persists for the next open. Previously onEnable was called directly on the successful enable response, so this is a regression introduced by deferring it to a user click.

title: Existing 2FA users can never obtain backup codes, and the error message tells them to do the impossible
body: Backup codes are only generated in the setup endpoint, which returns 400 TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled for any user who already has 2FA enabled. Users who enabled 2FA before this deploy have backupCodes = null, so the "Lost access" login path and the backup-code disable path always fail for them with MissingBackupCodes. The accompanying message ("No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." in common.json) is misleading because there is no settings flow that generates codes while 2FA is enabled — the only path is to disable 2FA (using the TOTP they may have lost) and re-enable it. Either a regeneration endpoint is needed or the message must tell the user their actual recovery option.

title: No tests for the core new functionality: logging in and disabling 2FA with a backup code
body: The e2e changes only exercise the backup-codes display step (download filename, copy toast, close button). None of the actually risky new code paths are tested: signing in with a backup code, a backup code being consumed (single-use), the incorrect-backup-code error path, the missing-backup-codes error path, or disabling 2FA with a backup code. The file itself contains a TODO acknowledging this, and the PR checklist states no tests were added for the feature. These server-side flows (including the code-consumption logic in next-auth-options.ts) can regress silently.

title: tabIndex={-1} on the password visibility toggle removes keyboard access
body: The show/hide password toggle button in PasswordField now has tabIndex={-1}, making it unreachable by keyboard in every password field across the app (login, 2FA setup/disable, etc.). Keyboard-only users can no longer verify what they typed into a password field. If the goal was to stop Enter on the toggle from submitting the surrounding form, the button already has type="button"; excluding it from tab order is an accessibility regression rather than a fix.

title: Password verification can be bypassed when logging in with a backup code
body: In the credentials `authorize()` handler, the user's password is only verified when `credentials.totpCode` is falsy (`if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)`). The new backup-code branch (`if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode)`) runs after this check and never validates `totpCode`. So a request that includes any non-empty `totpCode` (e.g. "1") together with a valid `backupCode` skips password verification entirely and authenticates successfully. The intended design (and the UI, which keeps the password field filled in the backup-code flow) is that a backup code is used together with the password; a crafted request defeats that. The backup-code branch should be gated on the password having been verified, or the password check should not depend on `totpCode` being empty when a backupCode is supplied.

title: Existing 2FA users can never obtain backup codes, but the UI tells them to generate them in settings
body: The setup endpoint rejects any user with `twoFactorAlreadyEnabled` (line 42-44), and it is the only place backup codes are generated. All users who enabled 2FA before this PR have `backupCodes = null`. When such a user clicks "Lost access" at login (or in the disable modal) and submits a backup code, they get `missing_backup_codes` — "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." — but there is no settings flow that generates codes for an already-enabled account. These users are permanently locked out of the backup-code recovery path with an error message pointing to a nonexistent feature. Either the setup endpoint needs to allow regenerating backup codes for enabled accounts (after password + TOTP verification), or the message must not instruct users to do something impossible.

title: Closing the backup-codes dialog via onOpenChange/ESC skips onEnable and resetState
body: After 2FA is enabled, the modal advances to `SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes`, and `onEnable()` plus `resetState()` are only invoked from the explicit "Close" button (`data-testid="backup-codes-close"`). If the user dismisses the dialog through `onOpenChange` (the dialog's X / ESC / outside-click path), neither callback runs: the parent's `onEnable` handler never fires so the settings switch state will not reflect that 2FA is now enabled, and the component's internal `step` stays on `DisplayBackupCodes`, so reopening the modal shows the stale backup-codes screen instead of the password step (while the server now rejects a new setup with TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled). The `onOpenChange` handler on the Dialog should also route through resetState/onEnable (distinguishing the already-enabled case).

title: Backup-code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write, allowing single-use codes to be reused
body: When a backup code is used, the code decrypts the stored array, finds the matching index, sets it to `null`, and writes the re-encrypted array back with `prisma.user.update`. Two concurrent login requests using the same code can both read the original array, both find the code at the same index, and both succeed before either write lands — the single-use guarantee ("Each backup code can be used exactly once") is broken under a race. The verification and consumption should be atomic (e.g. a transactional update or a compare-and-swap on the encrypted value).

title: "Missing backup codes" never fires once all codes are used; users get a misleading "incorrect code" error
body: Used backup codes are replaced with `null` inside the stored array rather than removing them or clearing the column. After all 10 codes are consumed, `user.backupCodes` is the string `"[null,null,...]"`, which is truthy, so the `if (!user.backupCodes) throw MissingBackupCodes` check never triggers; `indexOf` then returns -1 and the user sees "Backup code is incorrect." A user who has exhausted all codes is told their code is wrong instead of being told they have no backup codes left, leaving them without any indication of the actual state. The same pattern exists in `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts` line 54.

title: No tests for the core feature: logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code
body: The PR's headline functionality is using backup codes during login ("Lost access" flow) and the disable modal, but the only test coverage added is for the backup-codes display screen (download filename, copy toast, close button). The e2e file itself carries a TODO acknowledging this: "add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup". The single-use semantics, incorrect-code error paths, and the MissingBackupCodes path (existing 2FA users with null codes) are all untested, and the PR checklist confirms no tests proving the feature works. At minimum one e2e test should log in with a stored backup code and verify the code cannot be reused.

title: Valid backup code alone can authenticate without the account password
body: In the credentials authorize() the password check is guarded by `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)` (line 121), i.e. the password is skipped whenever any non-empty totpCode is supplied. The new backup-code branch at line 131 then runs when `credentials.backupCode` is set, without ever verifying the password. So a request containing email, an arbitrary junk totpCode (e.g. "000000"), and a valid backupCode signs the user in with no password knowledge. Backup codes are single-use 40-bit hex strings typically saved in plaintext files or on paper; they are intended as a second factor, not a password substitute. The server should require a verified password (or otherwise ensure the first-factor step actually happened) before accepting a backup code.

title: Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write; codes can be replayed or burned
body: The backup code is consumed by reading `user.backupCodes`, decrypting, nulling the matched index, and writing the whole array back with an unconditional `prisma.user.update`. There is no transaction or conditional update, so two concurrent login requests presenting the same code can both pass `indexOf` and both succeed — the code is effectively reusable within the race window. Additionally, the code is burned inside authorize() before the rest of the sign-in pipeline completes; if anything fails downstream or the client never receives the success response (network drop), the user's code is permanently consumed and their retry with the same code returns IncorrectBackupCode. Consumption should be atomic (e.g. a conditional update filtered on the code being present, or a transaction with a re-check) and ideally only committed once sign-in is assured.

title: Backup code comparison is case- and whitespace-sensitive, but codes are lowercase hex
body: Backup codes are generated with `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")` (lowercase a-f0-9), and verification does `backupCodes.indexOf(credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""))` with no lowercasing or trimming (same in apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts line 61). Codes can contain the letters a–f, so a user who types or saves the code in uppercase (the UI placeholder "XXXXX-XXXXX" actively suggests uppercase), or pastes it with leading/trailing whitespace, will be told the code is incorrect even though it is valid. Given each failed attempt is a dead end for the user, the input should be normalized (trim + toLowerCase) before comparison.

title: "Generate backup codes in your settings" is impossible — no regeneration path exists, and pre-PR 2FA users have none
body: The new `missing_backup_codes` message says "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings.", but this PR adds no endpoint or UI to generate/regenerate backup codes — they are only created once, during initial 2FA setup (setup.ts), and only shown once. Users who enabled 2FA before this PR have `backupCodes = null`, so if they lose their authenticator the "Lost access" flow is a dead end, and users who dismiss the backup-codes dialog without saving can never retrieve their codes again. The error message instructs them to do something that cannot be done, on both the login page and the disable-2FA modal.

title: resetState() does not clear the totpCode form field, leaving stale code from a previous setup
body: resetState() clears password, errorMessage, and step, but never resets the react-hook-form `totpCode` field. After a completed (or abandoned) setup, the form still holds the previously entered 6-digit code. When the user later re-opens the modal and reaches the EnterTotpCode step, the registered hidden `totpCode` input still contains the old value while the digit boxes render empty; submitting (or any change that retriggers the auto-submit effect watching `totpCode`) can send the stale, now-invalid code, producing a confusing "code is incorrect" error before the user has typed anything. resetState should also call form.setValue("totpCode", "").

title: onEnable is only fired from the "Close" button; dismissing the dialog via X/Escape skips it and resetState
body: The prop contract says onEnable is "Called when the user enables two-factor auth", and previously it was invoked as soon as enable succeeded. Now it is only called from the backup-codes "Close" button click handler. If the user dismisses the dialog through the built-in close affordances (X button, Escape key, overlay click — all routed to onOpenChange), onEnable never fires, so any parent that refreshes its state in onEnable (e.g. the two-factor switch on the security settings page) will keep showing 2FA as disabled even though it is enabled. resetState is also skipped, leaving the modal on the DisplayBackupCodes step with the codes still in memory if reopened.

title: Backup codes stored with reversible encryption instead of a one-way hash
body: Backup codes are persisted as AES-encrypted plaintext (`symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes))`) using the shared CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY, and returned in plaintext in the API response. Unlike the TOTP secret (which must be recoverable to validate codes), backup codes can be validated by hashing the user input and comparing digests, which is the industry standard (GitHub, Google, etc.). As stored, anyone with database access plus the encryption key — a key already used for many other secrets — recovers all unused backup codes, which per the finding above can even be replayed as a standalone credential.

title: No test covers actually using a backup code to log in or disable 2FA
body: The PR's headline feature — authenticating with a backup code — has zero test coverage. The updated e2e tests only exercise the backup-codes screen's download/copy/close buttons; the TODO at the top of the file ("add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup") acknowledges this. Neither the happy path (correct code logs in and is consumed), nor wrong-code rejection, nor code-single-use behavior is verified anywhere, leaving the new authorize() and disable.ts branches untested.

title: tabIndex={-1} on the password visibility toggle removes keyboard access
body: The change adds `tabIndex={-1}` to the show/hide password button inside PasswordField. This makes the toggle unreachable via keyboard (Tab/Synth events), so keyboard-only and screen-reader users can no longer reveal their password on the login page, the 2FA setup modal, or anywhere else PasswordField is used. If this was added to keep e2e selectors stable, it should be scoped differently rather than disabling focus for all users.

title: Users on the external TOTP login path (totpEmail) have no way to use a backup code
body: When a user arrives at /auth/login via a `totp` JWT (SSO/Google users with 2FA who were redirected by loginWithTotp), the footer rendered is ExternalTotpFooter, which only offers a "cancel" button — the "Lost access" button that switches to the BackupCode input exists only in TwoFactorFooter. Such users have backup codes generated by this feature but no UI to enter them, so if they lose their authenticator they are locked out despite the feature existing. The lost-access toggle should also be offered in the external TOTP flow.

title: updateEvent/deleteEvent destination-calendar fallback is dead code and resolves to undefined
body: In `updateEvent` (and identically in `deleteEvent` at line 315) the new fallback is `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. This expression is only evaluated when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so the `find` predicate compares each calendar's externalId against a falsy value and never matches. The result is always `undefined`, whereas the old code fell back to `event.destinationCalendar.externalId`. Consequence: when a booking reference has no `externalCalendarId` (e.g. bookings whose destination calendar has no externalId, or older references), Google updates are sent with `calendarId: undefined` and deletes fall through to `"primary"`, meaning updates fail and deletes can target the wrong calendar. The fallback should look up the destination calendar matching the current credential (e.g. by `credentialId`) instead of comparing against the falsy `externalCalendarId`.

title: Crash when destinationCalendar is empty and location is Google Meet
body: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` followed by `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"` accesses `.integration` without optional chaining. When `destinationCalendar` is an empty array (which all the new fallback code paths in this PR now produce, e.g. `selectedDestinationCalendar ? [selectedDestinationCalendar] : []` in confirm.handler, handleCancelBooking, webhooks, etc.), destructuring yields `undefined` and `undefined.integration` throws a TypeError, breaking booking creation for Google-Meet-located events for users without a destination calendar. The old code used `evt.destinationCalendar?.integration` which was null-safe. It must be `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.

title: Slug condition inverted: orgs now get a slug exactly when team billing is enabled
body: The change `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` → `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})` inverts the original behavior while the adjacent `requestedSlug` line keeps the same condition as before. Previously the org Team record stored `slug` when billing was disabled and `requestedSlug` when billing was enabled; now `slug` is set when billing is enabled and nothing is set when it is disabled. This is unrelated to the PR's stated purpose and will break organization subdomain creation on instances where `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED` is false (no slug persisted) and double-set slug/requestedSlug when it is true.

title: Reschedule merge deletes only the first calendar reference, leaving stale events on other hosts' calendars
body: `updateAllCalendarEvents` was extended to loop over all `_calendar` references (to support multiple destination calendars for collective events), but the merge branch that deletes the old booking's calendar events still uses `booking.references.find((reference) => reference.type.includes("_calendar"))`, deleting only the first calendar reference. For a collective booking with events on two hosts' calendars, rescheduling to a new booking leaves the old event on the second host's calendar. The deletion should iterate all old `_calendar` references (using each reference's `credentialId`/`externalCalendarId`).

title: Team members' destination calendars are silently dropped when the organizer has none
body: `evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` exists, and afterwards `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is a no-op on `null`. So for a collective event whose organizer has no destination calendar but whose co-hosts do, all team destination calendars are discarded and no calendar events are created on any host's calendar (EventManager falls back to the organizer's first connected credential). The fallback should be `[]` (matching every other call site in this PR) or the team calendars should be assigned as the initial value.

title: CalDAV BaseCalendarService ignores per-credential destination calendars, breaking multi-host collective events
body: `createEvent` filters the calendar list using only the first destination calendar's externalId (`mainHostDestinationCalendar?.externalId`). The `Calendar` interface was changed in this PR to pass `credentialId` to `createEvent` specifically so services can pick the destination matching the credential being used (as the Google service now does), but the CalDAV base class was not updated: its `createEvent(event)` signature doesn't accept `credentialId`, and when `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents` invokes it once per host destination, every invocation still targets the first host's calendar. For a collective event with two CalDAV hosts, the second host's credentials are used to write into the first host's calendar URL (failing or creating the event in the wrong place) and the second host's calendar never receives the event. The same single-first-destination pattern also remains in the office365 and lark services, so multi-destination support effectively only works for Google Calendar.

title: Cancel-all-recurring branch deletes only the first calendar reference per booking using the organizer's credentials
body: In the `recurringEvent && allRemainingBookings` path, deletion iterates `bookingToDelete.user.credentials` (the organizer's credentials only) and, for each updated booking, deletes only `updBooking.references.find((ref) => ref.type.includes("_calendar"))` — the first calendar reference. With the new multi-reference support this PR introduces for collective events, co-hosts' calendar events are never deleted when cancelling all remaining recurring bookings, and the outer loop over `bookingCalendarReference` re-runs the same deletion for every reference, duplicating work. Deletion should use each reference's own `credentialId` and iterate all `_calendar` references per updated booking.

title: No automated tests cover the new multi-destination-calendar behavior, and payload expectations are inconsistent
body: The PR checklist states no tests were added, yet it changes a core type (`CalendarEvent.destinationCalendar`) consumed by every booking flow. The only test change is updating one expected webhook payload from `destinationCalendar: null` to `[]` (BOOKING_REJECTED) while BOOKING_CREATED and BOOKING_REQUESTED still expect `null` — reflecting inconsistent fallbacks (`handleNewBooking` uses `null`, `confirm.handler` uses `[]`). There is no test exercising a collective event with multiple hosts each having a calendar app (create/reschedule/cancel across two destination calendars), which is exactly the scenario the PR claims to fix; regressions like the Google update/delete fallback bug and the empty-array crash in EventManager.create would not be caught.

title: Crash when destinationCalendar is null/empty and location is Google Meet
body: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` followed by `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` throws a TypeError when `destinationCalendar` is null or an empty array. handleNewBooking.ts sets `destinationCalendar` to `null` (not `[]`) when neither the event type nor the organizer has one, and several webhook handlers set `[]`. The previous code used optional chaining (`evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`) and safely fell back to Cal Video in that case. Booking a Google Meet event type for a user without a destination calendar will now crash event creation instead of falling back to the daily video integration.

title: updateEvent fallback is dead code, causing undefined calendarId for legacy bookings
body: `const selectedCalendar = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;` — in the else branch `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so `find` compares `cal.externalId === undefined/null` and can never match; the fallback always evaluates to `undefined`. The old code fell back to `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. For any booking whose reference lacks `externalCalendarId` (all bookings created before this PR, and new ones where the destination fell back to "primary"), `calendar.events.update` is called with `calendarId: undefined`, so rescheduling/updating those bookings fails against the Google API.

title: deleteEvent fallback silently deletes from "primary", orphaning events on real destination calendars
body: `const calendarId = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;` — since `externalCalendarId` is falsy in the fallback branch, the `find` predicate can never match and the result is always `undefined`. The code then falls back to `defaultCalendarId` ("primary"). For bookings created before this PR whose references have no `externalCalendarId`, cancelling now attempts deletion from the user's primary calendar; Google returns 404, which the error handler treats as success (`if (err.code === 404) return resolve()`), so the actual event on the configured destination calendar is silently left behind. The previous code deleted from `event.destinationCalendar.externalId`.

title: Post-insert patch uses possibly-undefined selectedCalendar
body: After `calendar.events.insert` succeeds, the follow-up `calendar.events.patch` (which adds the hangout link to the description) passes `calendarId: selectedCalendar`, but `selectedCalendar` is the result of `calEventRaw.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.credentialId === credentialId)?.externalId` and is `undefined` whenever no destination calendar matches the credential — the insert call itself guards this with `selectedCalendar || "primary"`, the patch does not. When the event was created on "primary" because no destination matched, the patch is issued with an undefined calendarId and fails, so the video link never gets added to the event description for those bookings.

title: Organizer attendee email taken from first destination calendar even when creating on another host's calendar
body: In `createEvent`, the organizer attendee's email is set to `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.externalId` (the first entry of `destinationCalendar`), while the event is actually created on `selectedCalendar`, the calendar whose `credentialId` matches the credential being used. For a collective event with multiple hosts, when creating the event on the second host's Google calendar, the organizer is still recorded with the first host's calendar address. The event on the non-primary host's calendar gets a wrong/mismatched organizer, which can misattribute the event and misroute organizer responses. The email should correspond to the destination calendar selected for that credential (i.e. `selectedCalendar`).

title: Office365 createEvent always targets the first destination calendar regardless of credential
body: `createEvent` derives the events URL from `event.destinationCalendar[0].externalId` (`/me/calendars/${mainHostDestinationCalendar?.externalId}/events`). With the new multi-destination support, EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents invokes this service once per host's credential, but the service always writes to the first host's calendar externalId while authenticating with whichever host's credential was passed. For a collective event where a non-first host uses Office365, the Graph API call targets another user's calendar id with the wrong token, failing (or writing to the wrong calendar). The service needs to select the destination calendar matching the active credential, like the Google service does with `credentialId`.

title: CalDAV base service filters by first destination calendar, silently creating no event for other hosts
body: In `BaseCalendarService.createEvent`, calendars are filtered by `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.externalId` — the first entry of `event.destinationCalendar`.
