Either the action should process and persist the submitted parameters, or the route/action and the client `saveChanges` code should be removed so nobody is led to believe saving works.

title: New admin controllers have no behavioral tests (create/update/destroy, validation, permissions)
body: Both `Admin::EmbeddableHostsController` and `Admin::EmbeddingController` specs only assert that the class is a subclass of `Admin::AdminController`. There is no test covering create/update/destroy of embeddable hosts, the host normalization/validation rules, the category_id fallback to uncategorized, error rendering for invalid hosts, or access control (e.g. that a non-admin is rejected). Given this controller writes data that gates which external sites can embed content, at least CRUD and authorization request specs should be added; as written, the nil-id and bad-param failures described elsewhere would not be caught.

title: create_table uses force: true in a production migration
body: `create_table :embeddable_hosts, force: true` will drop the table (and all host/category data) if it already exists when the migration runs. Using `force: true` is appropriate in schema definitions for test convenience, not in a shipped migration; if the table pre-exists on any install (e.g. from a partially applied migration or a plugin), this migration silently destroys the data instead of failing loudly.

title: Hardcoded 10MB limit ignores admin-configured max upload sizes
body: validateUploadedFile now uses a hardcoded `10 * 1024` KB instead of `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, and the 413 handler at line 246 similarly hardcodes 10 MB instead of `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb`. This silently disables the `max_image_size_kb` and `max_attachment_size_kb` site settings on the client: admins who set a lower limit will see users attempting uploads up to 10 MB (which then fail server-side with a confusing error for attachments), and admins who set a higher limit will get an incorrect 'file too large' rejection in the browser. This looks like leftover debug/test code (the PR description is 'Test 1') and should be reverted to read the settings.

title: Duplicate `self.downsize` definition silently overrides the width/height variant
body: The file now defines `self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at line 145 and a second `self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` at line 149. In Ruby the second definition completely replaces the first, so the width/height variant is dead code. Any existing caller that invokes `downsize(from, to, width, height)` will now have its `height` argument bound to the `opts` parameter; when `optimize` evaluates `opts[:allow_animation]` on an Integer it raises `TypeError (no implicit conversion of Integer into Hash-like)`. Either remove the old signature entirely or rename/merge the two methods so the four-argument form still works.

title: Downsize loop can never bring very large images under the limit and ignores downsize failures
body: The retry loop runs at most 5 iterations, each downsizing to '80%', so the best possible reduction is to 0.8^5 ≈ 33% of the original size. An image more than ~3x `max_image_size_kb` will still exceed the limit when the loop exits, and the oversized file is then passed to `Upload.create_for`, which will reject it — the user waits through 5 ImageMagim/ImageOptim passes only to get the same failure the feature was supposed to prevent. Additionally, the return value of `OptimizedImage.downsize` is never checked: if conversion fails (e.g. unsupported/corrupt image or ImageMagick policy limits), the loop blindly retries five times and may hand a truncated/corrupted tempfile to `Upload.create_for`. The loop should either compute the exact target percentage needed in one pass or check the downsize result and bail out with a clear error.

title: allow_animation option never applies to uploads because animated-GIF detection relies on the file extension
body: The controller passes `allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails` to `OptimizedImage.downsize`, but `OptimizedImage.optimize` (optimized_image.rb line 155) only chooses the animated code path when `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`. The `from` path here is an uploaded/action-dispatched tempfile (RackMultipart-* or discourse-upload-*), which never ends in `.gif`, so animated GIFs are always processed through `convert #{from}[0]`, which takes only the first frame. Even on sites with `allow_animated_thumbnails` enabled, every oversized animated GIF upload is silently stripped down to a single static frame — permanent loss of the original animation since the tempfile is downsized in place.

title: Hardcoded 10MB download cap regresses API uploads for sites with larger configured limits
body: The API URL-download path changed `FileHelper.download(url, SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes, ...)` to a hardcoded `10.megabytes`. On sites where an admin has raised `max_image_size_kb` above 10240 KB, remote images larger than 10 MB can no longer be fetched via the API at all (the download silently returns nil due to `rescue nil`, leading to a confusing failure downstream), even though such uploads were previously allowed. The cap should be derived from the setting (e.g. `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` plus some headroom to allow downsizing), not hardcoded.

title: Duplicate definition of self.downsize shadows the width/height variant and breaks its call signature
body: The file now defines `self.downsize` twice (lines 145 and 149). In Ruby the second definition silently replaces the first, so the four-argument version `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts)` is dead code. Worse, any existing caller invoking the old 4-argument form `downsize(from, to, w, h)` now hits the new signature `downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`, which binds `dimensions = w` and `opts = h` (an Integer). `optimize` then calls `opts[:allow_animation]` on an Integer and raises, and the dimensions string becomes just the width with no height. Either delete the old definition or rename/reorder so both signatures work.

title: Downsizing runs ImageMagick in-place on the uploaded tempfile, corrupting or mis-formatting the image
body: `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...)` passes the same path as both the convert input and output, and that path is a Rack multipart tempfile with no file extension. ImageMagick's `convert` is documented as unsafe for reading and writing the same file (it can truncate/corrupt the source when pixels are cached to disk for large images), and writing to a filename with no recognized suffix makes ImageMagick default to an unexpected format (typically MIFF) rather than PNG/JPEG. The result can be a corrupted or wrongly-formatted file that is then stored as the upload under the original filename/extension. The downsize should write to a second tempfile (with a matching extension) and the result should replace the original only after a successful conversion.

title: Client-side upload size limits hardcoded to 10MB, ignoring site settings
body: The check previously used `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, so admins could configure separate `max_image_size_kb` and `max_attachment_size_kb`. It is now hardcoded to 10MB for both images and attachments. Consequences: (1) on sites with a limit below 10MB, users are no longer warned client-side and uploads up to 10MB are submitted only to be rejected server-side; (2) on sites with a limit above 10MB, valid uploads are now blocked in the browser; (3) attachments have no relation to the new server-side image downsizing, yet their limit was also changed. If the intent was only to relax the client check for images (since the server now downsizes them), the attachment path should still honor `max_attachment_size_kb`.

title: 413 error handler reports a hardcoded 10MB limit that may not match the server
body: The 413 branch previously read `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` to tell the user the actual server limit; it now always says 10MB. If the web server rejects at a different threshold (nginx `client_max_body_size` or a site setting above/below 10MB), the user gets a wrong limit in the error message and will keep retrying files that can never succeed, or wrongly believe larger files are allowed.

title: API URL download limit hardcoded to 10MB, bypassing and capping the site setting
body: `FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)` replaces `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes`. This breaks in both directions: a site that configured a smaller `max_image_size_kb` now has API users downloading arbitrarily larger remote files (which are then run through up to five ImageMagick conversions, a CPU cost), and a site that configured a limit above 10MB can no longer pull images larger than 10MB via the API. The download cap should be a fixed ceiling (e.g. `MAX_IMAGE_SIZE` constant larger than any allowed setting) or remain derived from the setting, not an unexplained magic 10MB that silently diverges from configuration.

title: Downsize loop ignores conversion failures and may loop on a corrupted file
body: The `while attempt > 0 && tempfile.size > ...` loop never checks the return value of `OptimizedImage.downsize`, which returns false when the convert command fails. If conversion fails (e.g. unsupported/corrupt image, or the in-place issue noted separately), the code runs the same failing conversion four more times and then passes the possibly truncated/unchanged file to `Upload.create_for`. Each failed iteration also invokes `ImageOptim.new.optimize_image!` inside `convert_with`, multiplying wasted CPU. The loop should break out immediately when `downsize` returns false and surface an error to the user.

title: Animated-GIF branch can never trigger for uploaded files, flattening animated images to one frame
body: `OptimizedImage.optimize` selects the animated (gifsicle) code path only when `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`, but the path passed here is the uploaded Rack tempfile, which never ends in `.gif`. So for an animated GIF upload, `convert` is used with `#{from}[0]`, which takes only the first frame: the stored upload silently loses its animation even when `allow_animated_thumbnails` is enabled. The animation check needs to work off the filename/extension of the upload, not the tempfile path (or the tempfile should be created with the original extension).

title: Up to five sequential convert + ImageOptim passes on 10MB images in the request/defer path
body: Each downsize attempt runs a full ImageMagick convert plus an `ImageOptim.new.optimize_image!` pass on a file that can now be up to 10MB (previously capped at `max_image_size_kb`). In the async path this happens inside `Scheduler::Defer.later`, and in the synchronous API path it happens inline in the request, blocking a web worker for potentially tens of seconds. Five iterations of 80% only reduce to ~33% of the original, so a badly compressible image will do all five passes. Consider a single conversion computed from the target size, and skip ImageOptim on intermediate passes.

title: No tests for the new automatic downsizing behavior
body: The PR adds a meaningful behavior change (oversized images being silently resized on upload, animated handling, the 5-attempt loop) but includes no controller or model tests covering it: e.g. an image above `max_image_size_kb` gets downsized and accepted, a non-image file above the limit is still rejected, a failed conversion does not produce a corrupt upload, and an animated GIF preserves animation when allowed. Given the in-place and format-detection pitfalls above, this code path needs coverage before merge.

title: Duplicate definition of OptimizedImage.downsize silently overrides the width/height variant
body: The file now defines `self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at line 145 and a second `self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` at line 149. In Ruby the later definition wins, so any existing caller that passes width and height separately (the signature kept at line 145 implies such callers exist, e.g. avatar/import paths) will actually hit the second method: `dimensions` receives the width and `opts` receives the height (an Integer). Inside `optimize`, `opts[:allow_animation]` is then called on an Integer, which raises `TypeError: no implicit conversion of Symbol into Integer`, breaking every width/height-style downsize call at runtime. The first definition is dead code and the width/height calling convention is broken; either remove the old method and update all callers, or give the dimensions variant a different name.

title: Hard-coded 10MB client limit ignores max_image_size_kb and max_attachment_size_kb site settings
body: `validateUploadedFile` previously enforced `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, i.e. the admin-configured per-type limit (images vs attachments). It now always allows 10MB. For attachments there is no server-side downsizing, so on sites where `max_attachment_size_kb` is set below 10MB the client-side guard no longer rejects oversized files with the friendly size message; the upload is sent in full and then fails server-side with a generic error. It also ignores admins who raised limits above 10MB. Only image downsizing was added server-side; the attachment check should keep reading the site setting.

title: Animated GIFs are flattened to a single frame when downsized because the extension check never matches tempfile paths
body: `OptimizedImage.optimize` selects the animated (gifsicle) pipeline only when `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`, but the paths passed from `create_upload` are Rack multipart tempfiles or `FileHelper.download` tempfiles, whose names have no `.gif` extension. Consequently any animated GIF larger than `max_image_size_kb` is processed by ImageMagick `convert from[0]`, which keeps only the first frame: the user's animated upload is silently converted to a still image even when `SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails` is enabled. The animation-detection should be based on the original filename/content, not the tempfile path.

title: 413 error message always claims the limit is 10 MB
body: `displayErrorForUpload` reports a hard-coded "10 MB" maximum when the server returns 413, but the actual limit is `max_image_size_kb`/`max_attachment_size_kb`, which the admin can set to anything. On sites with a different limit the message shown to users is factually wrong and confusing. The previous code read `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` here.

title: API URL download cap hard-coded to 10MB regresses sites with higher max_image_size_kb
body: The remote-download size limit for API uploads was changed from `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` to a hard-coded `10.megabytes`. Sites that configured `max_image_size_kb` above 10MB can no longer pull images via URL larger than 10MB (they now silently fail with `rescue nil`, producing a confusing `tempfile`-nil path), while the client-facing intent of the PR is to allow large images that are then downsized. The cap should be derived from the setting (or at least max(setting, 10MB)).

title: Downsizing loop runs up to 5 full ImageMagick + ImageOptim passes per upload and can still not converge
body: Each iteration applies `-resize 80%`, which reduces area to ~64%, so five iterations shrink the image at most ~10x; an image far above the limit (e.g. 50MB against a 1MB setting) still exceeds it after the loop and then fails in `Upload.create_for` with a generic error. Additionally, when `downsize` returns false (convert failure), the return value is ignored, so the loop burns all 5 attempts doing nothing on the same file. Each pass also invokes ImageOptim, making this expensive CPU work on the request path for synchronous API uploads. The loop should stop early on failure and compute a resize percentage that reaches the target in one pass.

title: TopicsController#unsubscribe crashes with NoMethodError when the user has no TopicUser record
body: In the new `unsubscribe` action, `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil (any logged-in user can visit /t/<any topic>/unsubscribe for a topic they have never viewed, posted in, or been emailed about — the URL is trivially guessable since it is just the topic URL plus /unsubscribe). The code then calls `tu.notification_level` on nil, raising NoMethodError and returning a 500. The action should create/normalize the record via `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, params[:topic_id], notification_level: ...)` like `set_notifications` does, which also correctly sets `notifications_changed_at`/`notifications_reason_id` and publishes the MessageBus `notification_level_change` event that the direct `tu.save!` path skips.

title: State-changing GET endpoint is vulnerable to CSRF and accidental triggering
body: The new `unsubscribe` action mutates the user's notification level on a GET request. A logged-in user's browser can be made to hit this URL cross-site (e.g. an `` on an attacker page sends session cookies), silently muting or un-muting topics for the victim. Additionally, because the handler *toggles* state (watching/tracking -> regular, otherwise -> muted), any repeated visit — a page refresh, browser pre-render/prefetch of the email link, or a scanner following links in an open session — flips the user's notification level again, potentially re-subscribing someone who just unsubscribed. State changes should be made via a POST endpoint (the email link can go to a page with a button, or use a per-user token), not on GET.

title: unsubscribe_link locale now requires %{unsubscribe_url}, breaking any email builder caller that doesn't pass it
body: The `unsubscribe_link` translation was changed to interpolate `%{unsubscribe_url}`. `Email::MessageBuilder` merges its opts into template_args, so any caller using `add_unsubscribe_link: true` without also passing `unsubscribe_url` will now raise `I18n::MissingInterpolationData` when building the body (`body << I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)`) or the HTML part, and the email will fail to send. This is an undocumented new contract on the MessageBuilder API — nothing enforces or documents that `unsubscribe_url` must accompany `add_unsubscribe_link`, so plugins or future mailers that only pass `add_unsubscribe_link` will break. The builder should default `unsubscribe_url` (e.g. fall back to the preferences URL) or omit that sentence when it is absent, and this requirement needs a test.

title: Unsubscribe toggle does not actually unsubscribe watching/tracking users, contradicting the email text
body: The controller demotes watching/tracking users only to `regular` on the first click. At the `regular` notification level the user still receives notifications when they are replied to, mentioned, or quoted, yet the email footer added in this PR says "To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, click here" and the client page says "You will stop receiving notifications for <title>". A watching user who clicks the unsubscribe link in the email will keep getting reply/mention emails for that topic. If the intent is a toggle, the messaging is wrong; if the intent is unsubscribe, the level should go to `muted` (or the UI should make the choice explicit before mutating).

title: No tests for the new TopicsController#unsubscribe behavior
body: The new `unsubscribe` action implements toggle semantics, slug-mismatch 301 redirects, permission handling, and TopicUser mutation, but no request/controller specs were added for any of it (the only test touched in the PR is the message_builder spec, which merely adds an `unsubscribe_url` option without asserting the topic link appears in the body or List-Unsubscribe header). Given the reachable nil crash and the CSRF-prone GET noted above, this endpoint needs specs covering: user with no TopicUser record, watching vs regular vs muted starting levels, wrong-slug redirect, and inaccessible topic.

title: topics#unsubscribe crashes with NoMethodError when the user has no TopicUser record
body: In the new `unsubscribe` action, `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil — for example a user who received a notification email for a topic they have never opened or been tracked on (invited-to-topic, invited-to-PM, or watched-category emails where no topic_users row exists yet). The very next line calls `tu.notification_level`, raising NoMethodError on nil and returning a 500 to anyone who clicks the new email unsubscribe link in that situation. The code must handle a missing record (e.g. create one via TopicUser.change) before reading the level.

title: Unsubscribe is a state-changing GET request, enabling cross-site request forgery
body: The new routes `get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` and `get "t/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` mutate the logged-in user's topic notification level via GET. Rails' CSRF protection only covers non-GET requests, so any third-party page can embed `` and silently change notification levels (muting topics, or downgrading watching/tracking to regular) for every logged-in user who views it. State changes like this should be made resistant to cross-site GETs (e.g. require a POST/PUT with an authenticity token, or a per-user token in the URL as done for email unsubscribe keys).

title: unsubscribe bypasses TopicUser.change, so notifications_reason_id is not set and auto-track can silently undo the unsubscribe
body: The action assigns `tu.notification_level` and calls `tu.save!` directly instead of using `TopicUser.change`. TopicUser.change is what normally sets `notifications_changed_at` and `notifications_reason_id = user_changed` when the level changes. Because those columns are left untouched here, any topic_users row whose `notifications_reason_id` is still null (records created by track_visit!/update_last_read) will have its level automatically bumped back to `tracking` by the auto-track logic in `TopicUser.update_last_read` the next time the user reads the topic — silently re-subscribing the user after they explicitly unsubscribed. The direct save also skips the MessageBus `notification_level_change` publish that other clients rely on.

title: Shared unsubscribe_link translation now requires %{unsubscribe_url}, breaking any email built with add_unsubscribe_link but without that option
body: config/locales/server.en.yml changes the shared `unsubscribe_link` string to interpolate `%{unsubscribe_url}`. `Email::MessageBuilder#body` (line 90) and `#html_part` (line 67) call `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` whenever `add_unsubscribe_link` is true, and `unsubscribe_url` is only added to template_args if the caller passes it as an opt — MessageBuilder provides no default. Ruby I18n raises `I18n::MissingInterpolationData` for missing interpolation arguments, so any mailer (including plugins or future core mailers) that sets `add_unsubscribe_link: true` without passing `unsubscribe_url` will now raise instead of sending. The spec had to be amended to pass `unsubscribe_url: "/t/1234/unsubscribe"` to keep passing, which demonstrates the new hard requirement. MessageBuilder should default `unsubscribe_url` (or the translation should be split) so the option remains optional.

title: No controller specs for the new topics#unsubscribe action
body: The new `unsubscribe` action implements non-trivial behavior — a 301 redirect when the slug is missing/mismatched, a notification-level toggle (watching/tracking → regular, otherwise → muted), and HTML/JSON responses via perform_show_response — but no request specs were added for it. Combined with the nil TopicUser crash and the GET-mutation concerns above, the action ships completely untested; at minimum there should be specs covering the redirect, each starting notification level, and the case where no topic_users record exists.

title: Email/page copy promises notifications will stop, but the action only downgrades tracking/watching users to regular
body: The new email footer text says "To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, click here" and the unsubscribe page says "You will stop receiving notifications for ...". However, the toggle logic sets users at `tracking` or `watching` to `regular` (only `muted` truly stops notifications). At the `regular` level Discourse still sends notifications (e.g. replies to the user's own posts, PMs), so users who click the link believing they will receive nothing further will keep getting emails, which is both a UX trap and can push recipients toward marking the site's mail as spam. Either the copy should be softened or the action should set `muted` for all levels.

title: unsubscribe action crashes when the user has no TopicUser record
body: In TopicsController#unsubscribe, `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil, and the next line immediately calls `tu.notification_level`. A TopicUser row is only created once a user has visited/interacted with a topic, yet the unsubscribe link is included in every notification email — e.g. a user who was mentioned or invited to a topic but never opened it will have no row. Clicking the emailed 'stop receiving notifications' link then raises NoMethodError on nil and returns a 500 instead of unsubscribing them. The code should fall back to TopicUser.change(...)/create the row with the desired level.

title: Notification state is mutated by an unauthenticated-CSRF-able GET request, and refresh re-toggles it
body: The `/t/:topic_id/unsubscribe` route is a GET that flips the user's notification_level (watching/tracking -> regular, regular/muted -> muted) with no CSRF token or confirmation. Because it is a plain GET with session cookies, any logged-in user can have their topic notification settings silently changed just by loading a URL — e.g. an attacker can embed `` in a post or external page and the victim's browser will hit the endpoint and mute/unwatch the topic. Additionally, since the same GET both performs the toggle and renders the unsubscribe page, every page refresh or link re-visit toggles the level again (watching -> regular -> muted), so the user's final state depends on how many times the URL was loaded. State changes should not happen on GET (or should be idempotent, e.g. always mute).

title: Email copy promises to stop notifications but the endpoint only downgrades to regular
body: The new unsubscribe_link text says 'To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, click here', but TopicsController#unsubscribe only sets watching/tracking users to `regular` — a level that still emails the user when someone replies to them or @mentions them. A user who clicks the link believing they will no longer receive emails for that topic will keep getting reply/mention notifications, which is a trust/warranty problem for the feature. Either the endpoint should set the level to muted, or the message should accurately describe what will still be received.

title: Unsubscribe link now requires %{unsubscribe_url} and raises for callers that don't supply it
body: The `unsubscribe_link` locale now contains `%{unsubscribe_url}`, and both `html_part` (line 67) and `body` (line 90) call `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)`. I18n raises `MissingInterpolationArgument` when an interpolation key in the translation has no value, so any caller that builds an email with `add_unsubscribe_link: true` but without passing `unsubscribe_url` will now fail to render and the email send will blow up. The only in-repo caller was updated (and the message_builder spec had to be amended to pass `unsubscribe_url`), but MessageBuilder is a reusable API used by plugins and mailers that set `add_unsubscribe_link` on its own; the builder should default `unsubscribe_url` (e.g. to the user preferences URL) or use `I18n.t(..., unsubscribe_url: ... )` with a fallback so missing values degrade gracefully.

title: No request specs for the new unsubscribe endpoint
body: The TopicsController#unsubscribe action introduces new routing, access control (ensure_logged_in), a toggle rule based on the current notification level, and a 301 redirect for slug mismatch, but no controller/request specs were added for it — the only test change in the PR is unrelated (adding unsubscribe_url to a message_builder spec). Notably, the nil-TopicUser case and the watching->regular vs regular->muted toggle behavior are completely untested, which is how the nil crash above ships unnoticed.

title: should_block? performs database writes during model validation
body: BlockedEmail.should_block? increments match_count and saves the record, and it is invoked from EmailValidator#validate_each, i.e. from inside User's validation chain. Validation must be side-effect free: UsersController#create calls user.valid? (line 168) and then user.save, so every signup attempt runs validation twice and match_count/last_match_at are incremented twice per attempt. Any other code path that calls valid? on a User (e.g. User#change_username calls valid?) also performs an unexpected UPDATE on the blocked_emails table during what should be a read-only check. The collected statistics are therefore inflated and unreliable, and writes occur at times no caller expects them. Move the counter update out of the query path (e.g. record the hit only when a signup is actually rejected, or use a separate logging step).

title: Non-atomic match_count increment loses updates under concurrency
body: should_block? does a read-modify-write: it loads the record, does record.match_count += 1 in Ruby, then record.save. Two concurrent requests for the same blocked email both read the same count and both write count+1, so one increment is silently lost. Since this counter is the mechanism for tracking how often a blocked email attempts to register, it will undercount. Use an atomic update such as BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now]).

title: Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive, allowing trivial bypass
body: should_block? looks up BlockedEmail.where(email: email) with an exact string match. The rest of the codebase normalizes emails (Email.downcase is used in UsersController#change_email and User.find_by_username_or_email), but nothing downcases the value here, and User#email is stored as submitted. A blocked address like 'spammer@example.com' can be re-used by signing up with 'Spammer@Example.com' or 'SPAMMER@example.com', defeating the entire blocklist feature. The lookup (and ideally the stored value) should compare downcased emails.

title: Any server email error permanently marks the email invalid with a misleading message
body: After a failed createAccount, the controller adds the email to rejectedEmails whenever the server response contains errors.email. This includes errors that are not about validity, such as 'Email has already been taken' or the whitelist/blacklist 'not allowed from that email provider' message. Once added, emailValidation shows the generic I18n.t('user.email.invalid') reason for that address with no way to distinguish causes, so a returning user who already has an account is told their email is simply invalid. Only add to rejectedEmails when the error is actually a blocked/invalid-email error (e.g. have the server send a distinguishable error code), or surface the server's real error message in the validation reason.

title: No tests for the whitelist/blacklist logic moved into EmailValidator
body: The EmailValidator spec only exercises the BlockedEmail branch, and it stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? entirely. The domain whitelist/blacklist logic (email_in_restriction_setting? and both setting branches) was moved verbatim from User#email_validator into this new class but has no direct tests here, and no integration test covers that creating a User with an email present in blocked_emails actually fails. There is also no test for the case-sensitivity behavior of the blocked lookup. The core behavior of this PR (blocked emails reject signups end-to-end) is untested.

title: Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive, so the block is trivially bypassed
body: BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact, case-sensitive match: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`. Emails elsewhere in the codebase are matched case-insensitively (e.g., User.find_by_username_or_email uses Email.downcase). A user can register as 'Spammer@Bad.com' and bypass a blocklist row stored as 'spammer@bad.com', defeating the entire purpose of this feature. The email should be normalized (downcased/stripped) before the lookup, and the blocked_emails.email uniqueness validation/index should be case-insensitive to match.

title: match_count increment is a non-atomic read-modify-write, losing counts under concurrency
body: should_block? updates statistics with `record.match_count += 1; record.save`, which is a Ruby-side read-modify-write followed by a full-row save. Two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email will both read the same match_count and one increment will be lost. Since this method runs on every validation of a User with a changed email, it is called from concurrent web requests routinely. The increment should be atomic in SQL (e.g., `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now])`) rather than a model save that also re-runs validations.

title: User is validated twice in create, double-counting blocked-email match statistics
body: UsersController#create calls `user.valid?` (line 168) and then `user.save` (line 172), each of which runs the new email validation, and the email validation now has a side effect: BlockedEmail.should_block? increments match_count and updates last_match_at on every invocation. Every blocked signup attempt therefore inflates match_count by 2 and issues an extra write, corrupting the tracking data the BlockedEmail model exists to collect. The counter update should be idempotent per attempt or moved out of the validation path.

title: Any server-side email error permanently marks the address as 'invalid' in the client
body: In createAccount, `result.errors.email` is true for every email error the server can return — including 'email already in use' (uniqueness) and 'not allowed from that email provider' (domain restrictions) — but the code unconditionally pushes the address into rejectedEmails, which makes emailValidation show the generic I18n 'user.email.invalid' message for it. A user whose email was merely already registered, or whose domain was rejected, is told the address is syntactically invalid, and cannot resubmit it even after the underlying condition changes. The client should only blacklist the email when the error is the specific blocked-email failure, or surface the server's actual error message.

title: action_type is NOT NULL with no database default, breaking the documented manual-load workflow
body: The blocked_emails table is created with `t.integer :action_type, null: false` and no default. The BlockedEmail spec comment states the intended workflow is to 'manually load the table with some emails', i.e., admins inserting rows directly via SQL. Any INSERT that omits action_type (the natural thing when bulk-loading a list of addresses) will fail with a NOT NULL violation. A database default of 1 (the :block action value set by the model's set_defaults callback) would make manual loads work.

title: No tests for the whitelist/blacklist logic moved into EmailValidator, and BlockedEmail is only ever stubbed
body: EmailValidator now owns the email_domains_whitelist / email_domains_blacklist logic that was previously in User, but the new spec only exercises the BlockedEmail path with `BlockedEmail.stubs(:should_block?)`. There are no tests for the domain-restriction branches, for the `record.errors[attribute].blank?` guard that skips the blocked check when a restriction error was already added, nor any integration spec that the validator is actually wired onto User via `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`. A regression in any of these (including the conditional not firing when the email is unchanged) would go undetected. There is also no controller spec for the new `errors`/`values` fields in the create response that the JavaScript depends on.

title: Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive and can be bypassed
body: BlockedEmail.should_block? does `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` with the raw email string, and there is a unique index on the email column as-is. User emails are not normalized to lowercase on assignment (UsersController#create passes params[:email] straight into the model, and mixed-case emails can exist since email uniqueness is also case-sensitive here). A user whose address was blocked as 'spammer@example.com' can register as 'Spammer@Example.com' and the lookup returns no row, completely bypassing the block. The lookup (and the unique index) should compare downcased emails.

title: change_email flow bypasses the blocked-email check entirely
body: The new EmailValidator only runs on the User model when `email_changed?`. The change_email action never assigns user.email; it creates an email_token with the new address (`user.email_tokens.create(email: lower_email)`) and the address is later attached to the user when the token is confirmed (EmailToken.confirm), which typically uses update_attribute/save paths that skip validations. As a result, an existing user can switch their account email to any blocked address and receive mail there, defeating the purpose of the blocked-email feature. The blocked/whitelist/blacklist check must also be applied in change_email (and at token creation/confirmation), not only in the model's email-changed validation.

title: should_block? performs a DB write inside model validation and double-counts attempts
body: BlockedEmail.should_block? increments match_count and saves the record, and it is invoked from EmailValidator.validate_each, i.e. from inside User's validation. In UsersController#create, `user.valid?` is called at line 168 and then `user.save` runs the same validations again, so every blocked signup attempt increments match_count twice (or more if valid? is called elsewhere, e.g. change_username also calls valid?). Side-effectful writes during validation are also surprising: any code calling valid? on a user with a changed email mutates the blocked_emails table. The statistics update should happen once, outside the validation path (e.g. in the controller when the error is actually returned), or use a guard so it only runs once per attempt.

title: Read-modify-write race on match_count loses increments under concurrency
body: `record.match_count += 1; record.save` reads the counter in Ruby and writes it back. Two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email will both read the same value and both write value+1, losing one increment (and clobbering last_match_at updates with a stale AR object). Use an atomic update such as `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now])` instead.

title: Any server-side email error permanently marks the email invalid with the wrong message
body: On a failed account creation, the controller pushes `result.values.email` into rejectedEmails whenever the response contains any `errors.email` key. That includes errors unrelated to the email being unacceptable, e.g. 'Email has already been taken' or the whitelist 'not allowed' error. The emailValidation computed property then shows I18n.t('user.email.invalid') ('invalid email address') for that address, which is misleading for a taken or blocked address (the server message is 'is not allowed.' / 'has already been taken'). The client should key off the specific error type, or at least surface a message matching the server's reason. The email also stays rejected for the lifetime of the controller even if the underlying condition changes.

title: Validator spec stubs out the behavior under test; no integration coverage for users or the controller contract
body: The only spec for EmailValidator stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, so the actual model wiring (User's `validates :email, email: true`, the migration, and the BlockedEmail lookup) is never exercised end-to-end: nothing proves that a user with a blocked email fails validation and cannot be created. There is also no spec for the new UsersController#create failure payload (`errors` hash and `values` hash) that the new frontend code in create_account_controller.js depends on, so a rename or shape change of that JSON would not be caught. Add a spec that fabricates a blocked email, builds/creates a User with it, and asserts the validation error, plus a controller spec asserting the errors/values keys on failed create.

title: `<%- end if %>` is a Ruby syntax error; the embed view can never render
body: The ERb at line 6 reads `<%- end if %>` with no condition following the `if` modifier. When ERb compiles the template the generated Ruby ends with `end if`, which is a syntax error (unexpected end-of-input). Any request to /embed/best for which a TopicEmbed exists (the main success path of this feature) will raise ActionView::Template::Error instead of rendering the comments. The controller specs never render views (TopicView is mocked, no render_views), so CI does not catch this — a view-rendering test is needed.

title: Stored XSS: embed URL interpolated unescaped into raw HTML footer
body: TopicEmbed.import builds the "Imported from" footer with `"#{url}"` — the URL is interpolated into HTML with no escaping, and the resulting post is stored with cook_method raw_html (cooked = raw, bypassing the sanitizing Markdown pipeline) and rendered in app/views/embed/best.html.erb with `raw post.cooked`. The only validation is `url =~ /^https?:///`, which permits quotes, `>`, and attribute-breaking characters. An attacker can hit /embed/best with a crafted embed_url whose host matches embeddable_host (e.g. `http:///?'>

title: RSS item content imported as raw_html with no sanitization — stored XSS from feed content
body: poll_feed passes `i.content` (the raw HTML from the feed's content:encoded/body) straight into TopicEmbed.import, which creates the post with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. Post#cook then returns the raw string untouched, skipping the normal cooking/sanitizing pipeline, and best.html.erb renders it with `raw post.cooked`. Anyone who can influence the feed's HTML (compromised or malicious feed source at the admin-configured feed_polling_url) gets arbitrary JavaScript executed on the Discourse origin for every viewer, including logged-in staff. The readability path at least whitelists tags/attributes; the feed path has no equivalent. The imported HTML should be run through a sanitizer (e.g. Sanitize with a whitelist) before being stored as raw_html.

title: absolutize_urls raises URI::InvalidURIError for URLs that pass the http(s) regex
body: TopicEmbed.import only gates on `url =~ /^https?:///`, but absolutize_urls then calls `URI(url)` which raises URI::InvalidURIError for URLs containing spaces or other invalid characters (e.g. `http://exa mple.com/post` or an unencoded `%zz`). Unlike TopicRetriever#invalid_host?, there is no rescue here, so a single malformed feed link (or a crafted embed_url) raises an unhandled exception. In PollFeed this aborts the remaining feed items; in RetrieveTopic the job fails. The URI parse should be guarded or the URL rejected up front with a full URI parse.

title: Nil or failing feed item aborts the entire feed import with no per-item error handling
body: `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` assumes every RSS/Atom item has content; for plain RSS 2.0 feeds without content:encoded, simple-rss returns nil for `i.content`, so this line raises NoMethodError on the first such item and the whole poll is aborted. Similarly, any exception raised while importing one item (bad URL, PostCreator failure — note that if the post fails to save, TopicEmbed.import still calls TopicEmbed.create! with a nil topic_id, raising RecordInvalid inside the transaction) prevents all subsequent items from being imported. Each item should be processed with its own error handling (and nil content handled, e.g. falling back to i.description).

title: request.referer interpolated into a JS string literal without escape_javascript
body: The layout does `parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')`. The referer is only validated to have a host equal to embeddable_host; its path/query can contain arbitrary characters (an attacker can send a request with a crafted Referer header directly — no control of a page on the host is needed). The value is placed in a single-quoted JavaScript string with no `j`/escape_javascript; it currently survives only because Rails' HTML escaping converts quotes to `'`, which then appears literally inside the script block, producing an invalid targetOrigin that makes postMessage throw a SyntaxError and breaks iframe resizing for such referers. It should be escaped with escape_javascript (and ideally the exact origin, not the full referer, used as targetOrigin).

title: Feed and page fetches use open() with no timeout; a slow source hangs the job and the hourly schedule
body: `open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` (and `open(url)` in TopicEmbed.import_remote) use Kernel#open with no read/open timeout. The scheduled job has `retry: false` and is also invoked synchronously from TopicRetriever#perform_retrieve on a user-triggered retrieve, so a hanging or very slow feed server blocks a Sidekiq worker indefinitely and stalls subsequent scheduled runs. open-uri should be given `open_timeout`/`read_timeout` (or a job-level timeout).

title: setnx/expire are not atomic; a crash between them permanently disables retrieval for a URL
body: retrieved_recently? performs `$redis.setnx(key, "1")` followed by a separate `$redis.expire(key, 60)`. If the process dies between the two calls (or the expire fails), the key exists with no TTL and the URL is considered 'recently retrieved' forever — the embed will never be fetched again through the throttled path, leaving the loading page reloading every 30 seconds indefinitely. A single SET key 1 EX 60 NX (or a Lua script) should be used instead.

title: embed_url column is varchar(255); real URLs (plus the appended footer) can exceed it
body: The embed_url column is a Rails `string`, i.e. varchar(255) on PostgreSQL, with a NOT NULL constraint. Web page URLs frequently exceed 255 characters, and TopicEmbed.import additionally embeds the URL twice (href and text) into the post body; an over-long feed link will make the INSERT fail with 'value too long for type character varying(255)', aborting the import. The column should be text (or a larger limit) to match how URLs are stored elsewhere.

title: postMessage origin check uses substring matching instead of exact origin comparison
body: The resize handler accepts messages when `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1` is false, i.e. when the message origin appears anywhere as a substring of discourseUrl. That is not an equality check: any origin that happens to occur inside the discourseUrl string (e.g. as part of a path, or a shorter scheme/host prefix in some configurations) is accepted, and e.data.height is used unvalidated. The consequence is limited to resizing the iframe, but the check should compare `e.origin` against the exact expected origin (e.g. the parsed origin of discourseUrl) and the height coerced to a positive integer.

title: `force: true` added to an existing migration will drop an already-created top_topics table
body: This PR changes the previously shipped CreateTopTopics migration to `create_table :top_topics, force: true`. With force: true, create_table drops the table if it already exists; any environment that already ran the original migration and then re-runs it (db:migrate:redo, rebuilding from migrations rather than schema.rb) will silently lose all top_topics data. If the change was needed for test databases, it should be made in a separate migration or the test schema rebuilt, not by editing a released migration.

title: Only Gemfile_rails4.lock was updated; the default (Rails 3) lockfile is missing the new gems
body: The PR adds ruby-readability and simple-rss to the Gemfile and updates Gemfile_rails4.lock, but the repository's dual-boot setup (see the Bundler monkey patch at the top of the Gemfile) uses the default Gemfile.lock when booting in Rails 3 mode (`RAILS3` set), which per the diff was not regenerated. Any Rails 3-mode CI run or deployment will fail to resolve the new dependencies (TopicEmbed/poll_feed require them at runtime), so the Rails 3 lockfile needs the corresponding entries.

title: Stored XSS: remotely fetched HTML is rendered unescaped in the embed view
body: The view renders posts with `<%= raw post.cooked %>`, and TopicEmbed.import (app/models/topic_embed.rb:22) creates those posts with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`, which makes Post#cook return the raw string verbatim, skipping Discourse's entire sanitization/whitelist pipeline. The content originates from a remote page or RSS feed fetched by TopicEmbed.import_remote / Jobs::PollFeed. Any HTML on the embedded site (including user-generated comments on a blog, or a compromised/attacker-controlled page on the allowed host) — `<script>`, inline event handlers, etc. — is therefore stored and served as-is from the Discourse origin inside the /embed/best iframe. Because the iframe is same-origin with the forum, injected JavaScript runs with full access to the viewer's Discourse session (cookie theft, posting as the user, admin actions if a staff member views the embed). The remote content must be sanitized (e.g. with Sanitize/Nokogiri whitelist) before being stored, or rendered on a separate origin.

title: embed_url is interpolated unescaped into an HTML anchor in imported posts
body:
`contents << "
#{I18n.t('embed.imported_from', link: "#{url}")} "` interpolates the URL directly into an HTML attribute delimited by single quotes. The only validation is `url =~ /^https?://` (line 11), which does not exclude quotes. A URL such as `http://host/' onmouseover='alert(1)` (URL-encoded appropriately in the feed item or embed_url param) passes the regex, breaks out of the href attribute, and injects arbitrary attributes/HTML. Since the post is cooked with cook_method raw_html and rendered via `raw`, this is a stored XSS on the Discourse origin. The URL must be HTML-escaped (or the anchor built with Nokogiri) before insertion.

title: request.referer interpolated unescaped into inline JavaScript
body: `parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')` inserts the raw Referer header into a `<script>` block with no JavaScript or HTML escaping. The Referer header is fully attacker-controlled; the only gate is that `URI(request.referer).host` must equal `SiteSetting.embeddable_host` (EmbedController#ensure_embeddable). Ruby's URI parser accepts single quotes and other characters in the path, so a Referer like `http://embeddable.host/');alert(1);//` passes the host check and terminates the string literal in the generated script, allowing arbitrary JavaScript injection into the embed page (which is same-origin with the forum). The value must be JSON-escaped (e.g. `to_json`) or passed via a data attribute.

title: A background job is enqueued on every embed request for an unknown URL, with throttling only inside the job
body: When no TopicEmbed exists for the requested embed_url, `best` enqueues a `Jobs::RetrieveTopic` job on every (uncached) request. The 60-second Redis throttle lives inside TopicRetriever#retrieved_recently?, i.e. inside the job — it does nothing to limit enqueue volume. A busy site embedding comments (or any client that spoofs the Referer) will enqueue one Sidekiq job per page view for the same URL, flooding the queue and the Redis setnx key space (`retrieved:<url>` keys are never cleaned beyond the 60s expire, and the URL is unbounded user input). The throttle should be applied before enqueueing (e.g. in the controller, checking the Redis key), or the job should be deduplicated.

title: RetrieveTopic job runs the entire PollFeed import synchronously inline
body: `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` invokes the full feed polling job inline within the RetrieveTopic worker, rather than enqueuing it. This means a single embed page view for an unknown URL triggers a synchronous fetch and import of the entire RSS/ATOM feed inside that job: it can run for a long time, can run concurrently with the hourly scheduled PollFeed (both checking `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url:)` before either commits, leading to duplicate topic creation attempts that blow up on the unique index), and bypasses the job's sidekiq_options (retry: false). PollFeed should be enqueued as a job, or a shared lock should serialize feed imports.

title: PollFeed crashes on feed items without content, and failures are swallowed by retry: false
body: `content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` assumes every feed item responds to `content` with a non-nil value. SimpleRSS returns nil for missing elements (many RSS feeds have no `content`/`content:encoded` element), so `nil.scrub` raises NoMethodError, aborting the whole poll loop — items after the offending one are never imported. Combined with `sidekiq_options retry: false` (line 12), a single malformed item permanently breaks feed importing each hour with no retry. Guard for nil content, and rescue per-item errors so one bad entry doesn't halt the entire poll. Also note `feed_key` (line 20) is dead code — it is never used, so the intended modified-since/conditional-fetch logic is not implemented.

title: `<%- end if %>` is invalid ERB — the template fails or behaves unpredictably when rendered
body: Line 6 closes the header's if/else with `<%- end if %>`. The trailing `if` is not valid: it generates `end if` in the compiled Ruby with no condition on the tag, which depending on how ERB lays out the generated source either raises a SyntaxError at render time or consumes the next emitted statement as a bogus modifier-if condition, scrambling output order. No test renders this template (the controller specs stub TopicView.new and never render the view), so the breakage is invisible to CI. The tag should be `<%- end %>`, and a request/view spec that actually renders the embed response is needed.

title: `create_table ... force: true` silently drops an existing table during migration
body: `create_table :topic_embeds, force: true` drops any pre-existing `topic_embeds` table without warning before recreating it. In production (e.g. re-running migrations, restoring a partial schema, or a table left from a prior deploy) this silently destroys data. The same `force: true` was also added to the already-shipped migration `db/migrate/20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb:3`, which is additionally a no-op/divergence risk: installations that already ran that migration will never see the change, so the codebase's migration history no longer matches what exists in those databases. Drop `force: true` from both migrations.

title: Non-atomic setnx/expire can leave a permanent throttle key, blocking future retrievals
body: `retrieved_recently?` performs `$redis.setnx(key, '1')` and then, only if it succeeded, `$redis.expire(key, 60)` in a separate round trip. If the process dies (or the Redis connection drops) between the two calls, the key is set with no TTL and persists forever — from then on `retrieved_recently?` returns true for that embed_url and the topic is never retrieved again, permanently showing the loading view. Use a single atomic command (`$redis.set(key, '1', nx: true, ex: 60)` or setex-based pattern).

title: Origin check uses substring indexOf instead of exact origin match
body: `if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }` accepts a message from any origin that merely appears as a substring of the configured discourseUrl. For example, with `discourseUrl = 'http://forum.example.com'`, an attacker origin `http://forum.example.com.attacker.com` (or any URL containing that string) passes the check and can drive `iframe.height`. The impact is limited to resizing the embed iframe, but the check should compare origins exactly: `e.origin === discourseUrl` (normalized, e.g. trailing slash stripped).

title: X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL is not a valid header value
body: "ALLOWALL" is not part of the X-Frame-Options specification (valid values are DENY, SAMEORIGIN, and ALLOW-FROM in some browsers). Browsers that don't recognize the value ignore the header, which happens to permit framing here, but other browsers/proxies may treat the malformed header conservatively and block the embed, and the intent is unclear to anyone maintaining the code. Use `X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM <host>` (with its caveats) or, better, a CSP `frame-ancestors` policy listing the embeddable host.

title: Unescaped request.referer interpolated into inline JavaScript allows XSS on the Discourse origin
body: The embed layout renders `parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')` with the raw Referer header inserted into a JavaScript string literal without escape_javascript/html escaping. The `ensure_embeddable` before_filter only validates that the referer's *host* equals SiteSetting.embeddable_host, so an attacker making a direct HTTP request (where the Referer header is fully attacker-controlled, e.g. `http://<embeddable_host>/', alert(document.cookie), '`) can break out of the string literal and execute arbitrary script in a page served from the Discourse origin. This is a reflected XSS; the value must be escaped with `j()`/escape_javascript before interpolation.

title: Imported RSS content is stored as raw HTML with skip_validations and rendered with `raw`, enabling stored XSS
body: `TopicEmbed.import` creates posts with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` and `skip_validations: true`, which makes `Post#cook` return the raw content verbatim (no markdown/sanitization pipeline). The RSS path in `Jobs::PollFeed` passes `i.content` (fully controlled by whatever the feed at feed_polling_url contains) straight into import — unlike `import_remote`, which at least runs the content through ruby-readability's tag/attribute whitelist. `app/views/embed/best.html.erb` then renders it with `<%= raw post.cooked %>`. A compromised or malicious feed entry containing `<script>` or `onerror=` handlers is stored and executed on the Discourse forum and on every page that embeds the comments iframe. The feed content needs sanitization (e.g., Sanitize/Nokogiri whitelist) before being stored as raw HTML.

title: URL interpolated unescaped into an HTML attribute in the 'imported from' footer
body: `contents << "...#{url}..."` interpolates the embed URL directly into HTML that is later stored via the raw_html cook method and rendered with `raw`. The `^https?://` regex check on line 11 does not exclude single quotes, `>` or other markup characters that can appear in a URL's path/query (e.g. `http://embeddable-host/?x='>`). This allows attribute breakout and markup injection into the stored post. The URL should be HTML-escaped (and the href properly quoted) before interpolation.

title: `<%- end if %>` is a Ruby syntax error; the embed view fails to render
body: Line 6 closes the header if/else with `<%- end if %>`, which ERB compiles to the Ruby fragment `end if ` — a modifier `if` with no condition, a syntax error. Every render of the embed view (the success path when a topic exists) will raise ActionView::Template::Error / SyntaxError and return a 500 to the embedding site, making the whole feature non-functional in the topic-found case. It should be `<%- end %>`. The controller specs don't catch this because `TopicView` is stubbed with a mock, so the template never renders against a real topic view.

title: Referer-based authorization is trivially spoofable, allowing unbounded job enqueueing and forced fetching
body: Access control for /embed/best relies solely on the Referer header matching SiteSetting.embeddable_host. Any non-browser client can set an arbitrary Referer header, so anyone on the internet can hit the endpoint and cause `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)` for arbitrary embed_url values. The TopicRetriever throttle is only 60 seconds per exact URL string, so an attacker can vary the URL (query strings, paths) to enqueue an unbounded number of jobs, each of which causes the Discourse server to make an HTTP request to the embeddable host (a limited but real SSRF/abuse vector) and, when feed polling is enabled, synchronously executes the entire Jobs::PollFeed run inside the job. Rate limiting at the controller level and/or a global cap on retrieve jobs is needed.

title: Discussion replies rendered with `raw post.cooked` include any HTML users managed to post
body: The embed view renders each post with `<%= raw post.cooked %>`. While normal posts go through the cooking/sanitization pipeline, this view bypasses all of the markup filtering Discourse normally applies when displaying cooked content (e.g., the whitelist applied elsewhere), so any HTML that survives into `cooked` for any post in the topic — including raw_html posts created by other import paths or plugins — is executed verbatim in a frame that is served from the Discourse origin with `X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL`. Combined with the raw_html import path this widens the XSS surface; cooked output should be passed through the same sanitization used by the main topic renderer.

title: Non-atomic SETNX/EXPIRE can leave the throttle key without a TTL, permanently blocking retrieval
body: `retrieved_recently?` does `$redis.setnx(key, "1")` followed by a separate `$redis.expire(key, 60)`. If the process dies (or the Redis connection drops) between the two calls, the key exists with no TTL and never expires, so that embed_url is throttled forever — the topic is never retrieved and the embed shows the loading page indefinitely. Use a single atomic command (e.g., `SET key 1 EX 60 NX` available via the redis gem, or a Lua script) so the expiry is always set.

title: PostCreator jobs are enqueued inside the wrapping transaction, before the TopicEmbed row commits
body: `TopicEmbed.import` wraps `creator.create` in `Topic.transaction` and only creates the `TopicEmbed` record *after* the post is created. PostCreator's `enqueue_jobs` (process_post, feature_topic_users) runs while still inside this outer transaction. If the subsequent `TopicEmbed.create!` fails — most plausibly in the race where two concurrent retrieve jobs for the same embed_url both pass the `where(embed_url: url).first` check and the second hits the unique index — the whole transaction rolls back, but the already-enqueued Sidekiq jobs referencing the rolled-back post/topic are not un-enqueued, and `TopicTrackingState.publish_new` messages have already been published on MessageBus for a topic that never committed. The unique-index race should also be handled (rescue RecordNotUnique / create the embed first or use find-or-create).

title: Nil `i.content` (or a feed error) crashes the whole poll, and retry is disabled
body: `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` assumes every feed item has `content`; RSS feeds that only provide `description` (or ATOM entries with only a summary) will raise NoMethodError on nil, aborting the entire `poll_feed` run partway through — items after the offending one are never imported. Since the job has `sidekiq_options retry: false`, the failure is silent until the next hourly run, which will fail at the same item. `open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` is likewise unguarded, so a transient network error kills the run. Guard for missing content (fall back to `i.description`) and rescue per-item/feed-level errors.

title: `feed_key` is dead code — the modified/ETag check it hints at was never implemented
body: The `feed_key` method builds a Redis key (`feed-modified:<sha1 of feed url>`) but nothing in the class ever reads or writes it. Either the conditional-fetch logic was dropped accidentally, in which case the key is misleading dead code, or the intent was to skip polling when the feed is unchanged — either way it should be removed or wired up. As it stands every poll re-parses and re-imports the full feed each hour.

title: `force: true` added to an already-shipped migration can silently drop the top_topics table
body: This PR modifies the existing CreateTopTopics migration (2013-12-23) to add `force: true`, which makes `create_table` DROP the table if it exists. For any database that already ran this migration and then re-runs it (e.g., `rake db:migrate:redo`, or environments that replay migrations), all top_topics data would be destroyed. Editing historical migrations also means schema state diverges between deployments that ran the old version and the new one. The `force: true` should be reverted here (it belongs only in brand-new migrations, if anywhere).

title: Origin check via `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin)` is a weak substring match
body: The postMessage handler validates the sender with `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1`, i.e. it accepts any message whose origin string appears anywhere in the configured discourseUrl. Because it is a substring (not prefix/exact) match, an origin that happens to be contained in the URL string passes; e.g. a discourseUrl of `http://discourse.example.com` accepts an event from origin `http://d` (host `d`) or any origin that is a substring of the URL. The consequence is limited to setting the iframe height today, but the correct check is an exact/parsed comparison (e.g. compare `e.origin` against the URL's `protocol + '//' + host`), since future message types would inherit the flaw.

title: Making .small-action a flex container silently disables float: right on its button
body: The PR adds `@include flexbox()` to `.small-action`, but the rule later in the same block still styles its `button { background: transparent; border: 0; float: right; }` (line 309). Children of a flex container become flex items and the `float` property is ignored on them, so the button (e.g. the banner/small-action close button) is no longer pushed to the right edge of the row. It will now render immediately after the `.small-action-desc` text, leaving a gap on the right and misplacing the control. The button needs `margin-left: auto` (or the container needs `justify-content: space-between`) to restore right alignment, as was done for `.panel` in header.scss. The same applies to `.topic-avatar { float: left; }` (line 270), though there the flex row layout coincidentally produces a similar result.

title: .panel right-alignment relies on margin-left: auto, which IE10 flexbox does not honor
body: The new flexbox mixins explicitly target IE10 by emitting `display: -ms-flexbox` / `-ms-flex-align`, but the header's right-hand `.panel` is positioned purely via `margin-left: auto` (the old `float: right` was removed). IE10's flexbox implementation does not support auto margins for main-axis alignment (alignment there must be done with `-ms-flex-pack`), so on IE10 the search/hamburger/user panel will not be pushed to the right edge of the header and will instead sit directly next to the title. Since the whole point of the `-ms-` prefixes in the mixins is to support that browser, `.contents` needs an `-ms-flex-pack: end`-style fallback (or the panel needs a different mechanism) for the layout to hold there.

title: -ms-align-items is not a real CSS property
body: The `align-items()` mixin emits `-ms-align-items: $alignment;`. No such property exists — the Microsoft-prefixed old-syntax property is `-ms-flex-align`, which the mixin already emits on the previous line. The `-ms-align-items` declaration is invalid and will be dropped by every browser; it also fails CSS linting and can mislead future readers into thinking it does something. It should be removed.

title: align-items() mixin omits the -moz-box-align counterpart that flexbox()/order() imply
body: `flexbox()` emits `display: -moz-box` and `order()` emits `-moz-box-ordinal-group`, so the mixin set explicitly claims to support old-Gecko flexbox; but `align-items()` has no `-moz-box-align` line. Any browser that ends up using the `-moz-box` code path (the only one it is given) will get a flex container with no vertical alignment, so `.d-header .contents`, `.small-action`, and the `.badge-wrapper.bullet` would be laid out with the old default (stretch/start) instead of centered/baseline as intended. Either add `-moz-box-align` for symmetry or drop the `-moz-box` / `-moz-box-ordinal-group` output, since the two halves of the vendor story currently contradict each other.

title: .small-action button's float:right is inert now that .small-action is a flex container
body: The PR adds `@include flexbox()` to `.small-action`, which makes its direct children (`.topic-avatar`, `.small-action-desc`, and the `button`) flex items. Per the flexbox spec, `float` is ignored on flex items, so the existing `button { float: right; }` no longer has any effect, and nothing replaces it (no `margin-left: auto` on the button, no `justify-content: space-between` on the container). The button that used to be pushed to the right edge of the row will now sit immediately next to the description text. The same applies to the now-dead `float: left` on `.topic-avatar` and the `clear: both` on `.small-action`. Either drop the obsolete float/clear declarations and add an explicit right-alignment mechanism (e.g. `margin-left: auto` on the button), or verify the new compact alignment is intended.

title: Legacy flexbox fallbacks don't reproduce the new layout; non-flexbox browsers get a stacked header
body: The new `flexbox()` mixin emits 2009-spec `display: -webkit-box` / `-moz-box`, but the layouts built on it rely on mechanisms that the 2009 box model does not support. Specifically, `.d-header .panel`'s right-alignment now depends on `margin-left: auto`, which is a no-op in the old `-webkit-box` model (that spec uses `-webkit-box-pack`), so Safari 6- and old-Gecko browsers will render the panel hugging the title instead of right-aligned. Worse, the PR removes the `float: left` on `.d-header .title` and `float: right` on `.panel` with no float fallback, and `.small-action`'s children lose their floats too; in any browser with no flexbox support at all (IE9, older Android stock browser) the header contents and small-action rows collapse into vertically stacked blocks. If those browsers are still in the support matrix, a float-based fallback or `@supports` guard is needed; if not, the dead old-spec declarations only add output CSS weight.

title: -ms-align-items is not a real CSS property
body: The `align-items()` mixin emits `-ms-align-items: $alignment`, but no browser has ever implemented a property with that name; Microsoft's IE10 flexbox property is `-ms-flex-align`, which the mixin already emits on the previous line. The `-ms-align-items` declaration is dead code that ships in every compiled stylesheet that uses the mixin. It should be removed so future readers don't assume it does something.

title: order(2) on .extra-info-wrapper only works if it is a direct child of the header flex container
body: `@include order(2)` emits flexbox `order` properties, which only apply to direct children of a flex container. The only flex container introduced in the header is `.d-header .contents`, whose direct children are `.title` and `.panel`. If `.extra-info-wrapper` is rendered inside `.title` (as the header template structures it), the `order(2)` declaration is inert and the reordering it is meant to provide never happens — while the removed `&.bullet { margin-top: 5px; }` alignment fix is genuinely lost. Confirm the element's position in the DOM; if it is nested inside `.title`, either move the flex context to `.title` or drop the order include.

title: .small-action button { float: right } is ignored now that .small-action is a flex container
body: This change makes `.small-action` a flex container (`@include flexbox()` at the top of the rule), but the nested `button { float: right; }` at line 309 was left unchanged. Floats on flex items are ignored by the flexbox spec, so the float has no effect. Previously the button (e.g. the small-action buttons in the topic stream) was pushed to the far right edge of the row; now it will sit immediately after the `.small-action-desc` text with default spacing, since no `margin-left: auto` was added to replace the float. The trailing `clear: both` on `.small-action` (line 312) is likewise dead. The button needs `margin-left: auto` (or the container needs `justify-content: space-between`) to restore right-edge alignment.

title: -ms-align-items is not a real vendor-prefixed property
body: The new `align-items` mixin emits `-ms-align-items: $alignment;`. No browser has ever implemented a property with that name; Microsoft's flexbox prefixes are `-ms-flex-align` (already emitted on the line above) and, for the modern syntax, the unprefixed `align-items` (also already emitted). This declaration is always invalid and silently dropped, adding dead code to the generated stylesheet for every flex-aligned rule. It should be removed.

title: margin-left: auto on .panel does not right-align in the legacy flexbox implementations the mixins target
body: The new `flexbox()` mixin deliberately emits the 2009 syntax (`display: -webkit-box`, `display: -moz-box`) and the IE10 syntax (`display: -ms-flexbox`), but the right-alignment of the header panel relies solely on `margin-left: auto` on `.panel`. Auto-margin packing in flex containers is a feature of the final flexbox spec: IE10's `-ms-flexbox` implementation notoriously ignores auto margins for alignment, and the 2009 `-webkit-box`/`-moz-box` spec provides `box-pack` instead. So in exactly the older browsers these prefixes were added for, the search/hamburger/user panel will not be pushed to the right edge and will sit next to the site title, breaking the header layout. Either add a `box-pack: end`-based fallback or accept dropping the ancient-prefix output.

title: website_name bypasses untrusted-attribute hiding for TL0 profiles
body: The serializer registers :website as an untrusted attribute (untrusted_attributes list, lines 105-111), so when a TL0 user's profile is restricted from anonymous viewers (scope.restrict_user_fields?), the raw :website value is omitted from the JSON. The new :website_name attribute, however, is only listed in the plain `attributes` call (line 43) and its guard `include_website_name` (line 153) only checks `website.present?`. As a result, for restricted TL0 profiles the website host plus path (e.g. 'example.com/private-page') is still serialized and rendered on the profile, leaking exactly the information the hide-profiles setting is meant to conceal. It also breaks the template: since :website is omitted, user.hbs renders `<a href="">` (empty href pointing at the current page) with the leaked website_name as the link text. website_name must be added to untrusted_attributes (or its include method must check restrict_user_fields?).

title: include_website_name is missing the trailing '?' and is therefore dead code
body: The guard is defined as `def include_website_name` but ActiveModel::Serializers only invokes include methods named `include_#{attribute}?` — every other guard in this file (include_email?, include_stats?, include_card_image_badge?, etc.) follows that convention. Because of the missing '?', this method is never called, so the intended condition (only serialize website_name when the website is present) never takes effect. When a user has no website, the JSON will still contain a `website_name: null` key, and any future restriction logic added to this guard would silently not run.

title: Untrusted-attributes spec not updated for the new website_name attribute
body: The test at line 11 asserts that a fixed list of untrusted attributes (bio_raw, bio_cooked, bio_excerpt, location, website, profile_background, card_background) is omitted for TL0 users viewed anonymously, but :website_name was not added to that list. Because of this gap the suite passes even though website_name leaks the website host/path for exactly the profiles the setting protects. The spec should assert `expect(json).not_to have_key(:website_name)` in that context, which would have caught the privacy regression introduced by this change.

title: include_website_name is missing the trailing '?', so the guard is never invoked by AMS
body: The conditional-inclusion hook is defined as `def include_website_name` (line 153), but ActiveModel::Serializers dispatches guards by the exact name `include_#{attribute}?` — every other guard in this same file (include_email?, include_stats?, include_suspend_reason?, include_card_image_badge?, and the ones generated by the untrusted_attributes macro at lines 26-32) ends with a question mark. Because the dispatcher looks up `include_website_name?` and does not find it, it falls back to "always include", so the intended `website.present?` check is dead code and `website_name` is serialized for every user — including a `website_name: null` entry for users with no website at all. Rename the method to `include_website_name?` and add a test asserting `website_name` is absent from the JSON when the website is blank.

title: website_name is not registered as an untrusted attribute, leaking hidden website data for TL0 profiles
body: `website` is listed in `untrusted_attributes` (lines 105-111), which suppresses it when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` is true (e.g. a TL0 user's profile viewed by an anonymous visitor — an anti-scraping/privacy measure). The new `website_name` attribute is declared as a plain attribute and its include guard only checks `website.present?`, so for a restricted TL0 profile the serializer omits `website` but still emits `website_name`, which contains the very data that was supposed to be hidden — the website's host, and even the full path when the domain matches the instance. This partially defeats the untrusted-attributes protection. `website_name` should be added to the `untrusted_attributes` list (replacing the hand-written guard), and the spec's `untrusted_attributes` list at spec/serializers/user_serializer_spec.rb:11 should include `:website_name` so the regression is caught — currently the TL0/anonymous test passes while the leak exists.

title: Same-domain check is asymmetric: instance apex + website 'www.' subdomain does not show the path
body: The final branch only tests `discourse_host.ends_with?("." << website_host)`, i.e. whether the WEBSITE host is a parent domain of the instance host. It never checks the reverse direction. Concretely: on an instance at `example.com`, a user whose website is `http://www.example.com/my-page` gets only `www.example.com` displayed (path hidden), while on an instance at `www.example.com` a website of `http://example.com/my-page` gets the full `example.com/my-page` displayed. Since the PR's intent is to show the full path when the website lives on the same domain as the forum, and the code explicitly treats sibling subdomains (`www.example.com` vs `forum.example.com`, line 144-146) as same-domain, the apex-instance case is an inconsistency that will produce confusingly different behavior for equivalent setups. The check should also cover `website_host.ends_with?("." << discourse_host)`.

title: website_name is not registered as an untrusted attribute, leaking TL0 users' website info to anonymous visitors
