title: Adding FromContext to the exported Logger interface is a breaking change for external implementers
body: The `Logger` interface in the importable package pkg/plugins/log gains a required `FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger` method. Any out-of-tree implementation of this interface (e.g., in Grafana Enterprise or external code that constructs its own logger to pass into NewLoggerMiddleware / plugin services) will fail to compile after this change. Since the PR is described as a pure rename/refactor, the interface break should be called out, or a default provided, so downstream consumers can prepare.

title: Rename is incomplete: test function still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware and logger still named "plugin.instrumentation"
body: The PR's stated purpose is renaming instrumentation to metrics/logging, but the test function is still `TestInstrumentationMiddleware` (metrics_middleware_test.go:21), and the logger passed to NewLoggerMiddleware is still created as `log.New("plugin.instrumentation")` (pluginsintegration.go:161). Since these identifiers surface in test output and in actual log records (the logger name appears in every "Plugin Request Completed" line), the stale names are user-visible and should be updated for consistency with the rename.

title: traceID is dropped from the 'grafana-data-egress' log events
body: The old LoggerMiddleware.logRequest explicitly appended `traceID` (from tracing.TraceIDFromContext) to the log params for the "Plugin Request Completed" / "grafana-data-egress" event. The new version removed that code and now relies on `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)` picking up contextual attributes, but the only attributes anyone adds to the context are `endpoint`, `pluginId`, `dsName`, `dsUID`, and `uname` (see ContextualLoggerMiddleware.instrumentContext). Nothing in this change adds the trace ID as a contextual attribute, so unless some other middleware injects it into the contextual logger, the data-egress audit log lines lose trace correlation with the request's span. If the intent was that FromContext supplies the trace ID automatically, that should be verified and covered by a test; otherwise the traceID field should be added in instrumentContext.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a throwaway logger, hiding logs from tests
body: `TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()`, a brand-new instance that is discarded. LoggerMiddleware now always logs via `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)` (logger_middleware.go line 58), so any test that injects a `*TestLogger` and asserts on `logger.InfoLogs` (Calls/Message/Ctx) will never see the "Plugin Request Completed" event — assertions will fail, or worse, tests will pass vacuously while the logging is broken. FromContext on the fake should return the receiver `f` (or otherwise record into `f`) so the existing fake remains usable to verify the middleware's new logging path.

title: No tests for the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware or for log-field parity
body: The new ContextualLoggerMiddleware (69 lines of new behavior) ships with no test file, and no test verifies that the LoggerMiddleware's output still contains the fields it used to log directly (pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName, dsUID, traceID). Since this refactor moved those fields from explicit log params to context attributes flowing between two middlewares, a regression in either the attribute injection or the middleware ordering would silently strip identifying fields from the grafana-data-egress audit log. A test asserting the full set of attributes on the resulting log line would catch this.

title: LoggerMiddleware output now silently depends on ContextualLoggerMiddleware being earlier in the chain
body: LoggerMiddleware no longer includes pluginId/endpoint/uname/dsName/dsUID in its log output; those fields only appear if a ContextualLoggerMiddleware wrapped the client earlier in the stack (as done in pluginsintegration.CreateMiddlewares). Both `NewLoggerMiddleware` and `NewContextualLoggerMiddleware` are exported, so any caller that constructs the LoggerMiddleware on its own (e.g., Enterprise code or other middleware stacks built outside CreateMiddlewares) will emit 'grafana-data-egress' events with no plugin identification or endpoint. This ordering requirement is not documented on either constructor; at minimum a comment on NewLoggerMiddleware (and/or a debug safeguard) should state the dependency.

title: traceID no longer explicitly included in 'Plugin Request Completed' (grafana-data-egress) log lines
body: The old LoggerMiddleware.logRequest explicitly appended a "traceID" field extracted via tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false). The rewrite drops this and relies on whatever the contextual logger injects. If the infra logger's FromContext does not attach a trace id to this log line (or emits it under a different key such as "trace_id"), the data-egress log events lose trace correlation or change field naming, breaking any dashboards, alerts, or log parsers that key on the "traceID" field of these events. This should be verified and, if the field is gone, restored explicitly or the field-name change documented.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a brand-new logger, silently discarding logs written through the contextual path
body: TestLogger.FromContext returns NewTestLogger() instead of the receiver, so any log emitted via logger.FromContext(ctx) is written to a throwaway object that no test can inspect. Since LoggerMiddleware.logRequest was changed to call m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), existing and future tests using TestLogger can no longer assert on the 'Plugin Request Completed' log at all — assertions on InfoLogs will show zero calls while the code under test may be logging correctly, incorrectly, or with missing fields. The fake should return the receiver (f) so tests can actually verify the log output, including whether pluginId/endpoint/uname/dsName/dsUID still appear after this refactor.

title: No tests for the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware or for the contextual log fields of LoggerMiddleware
body: This PR moves responsibility for the pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName and dsUID log fields from LoggerMiddleware's explicit logParams into a new ContextualLoggerMiddleware that enriches the context. There is no test covering ContextualLoggerMiddleware (e.g., that the context actually carries the expected attributes per endpoint and that stream endpoints are not enriched), nor any test asserting that LoggerMiddleware's output still contains those fields when routed through FromContext. A regression here — wrong middleware ordering in CreateMiddlewares, a dropped attribute, or the grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext type-assertion fallback silently discarding attributes — would go completely unnoticed.

title: Adding FromContext to the exported Logger interface is a compile-time breaking change for external implementers
body: The exported plugins/log.Logger interface gained a required FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger method. Any implementer of this interface outside this PR (e.g., Grafana Enterprise or other downstream consumers of the public grafana repo, which already had to track the interface for New/Debug/Info/Warn/Error) will now fail to compile until they add the method. If the intent is only internal consumption, consider keeping the base interface unchanged and defining a separate ContextualLogger interface (Logger + FromContext) accepted by LoggerMiddleware, or provide an embedding helper, so existing implementations keep working.

title: Local cache is populated before the device write, so the device limit is bypassed on retry
body: In tagDeviceUI, the device's cache key is inserted into the local cache (localCache.SetDefault at line 87) BEFORE calling anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. With the new device-limit feature, an unknown device beyond the limit makes CreateOrUpdateDevice return ErrDeviceLimitReached, so the request is rejected — but its cache entry has already been set. The very next request from the same device hits the cache, tagDeviceUI returns nil without touching the database, TagDevice returns nil, and Authenticate succeeds. Consequence: an over-limit device (or an attacker generating new device IDs) gets anonymous access simply by retrying once, and the device is never recorded or counted. The cache entry must only be written after a successful store write (or removed on error). There is also no test covering the retry scenario, which would have caught this.

title: Device tagging moved from background goroutine to the synchronous auth path
body: Authenticate previously ran TagDevice in a fire-and-forget goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout and panic recovery. It is now called synchronously on the request context, so every anonymous request with a cache miss blocks on one or two database round trips (a COUNT(*) over anon_device when a device limit is configured, plus the upsert/update) before the identity is returned. This adds database latency to anonymous page loads and makes anonymous auth fail whenever the device store is slow or unavailable (previously a store outage only logged a warning). The panic recovery that protected the request handler was also removed, so a panic inside TagDevice now propagates into the request. Only the limit-exceeded case needs to be synchronous; the common path (limit not reached or no limit configured) could remain asynchronous.

title: Device limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by running CountDevices and then, if count < deviceLimit, performing the insert as two separate statements with no transaction or locking. Concurrent requests from different new devices (or requests hitting different Grafana instances behind a load balancer) can all read a count below the limit and all insert, exceeding the configured device limit by however many requests race in the window. If the limit is meant to be a hard cap (it is now used to deny authentication), the count and insert need to be atomic, e.g. a single conditional upsert or a transaction with a locking read.

title: updateDevice treats 'row not updated' as 'device limit reached', locking out existing devices
body: When the limit is reached, updateDevice runs an UPDATE ... WHERE device_id = ? AND updated_at BETWEEN (now-30d) AND (now+1min) and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached whenever rowsAffected == 0. rowsAffected can be 0 for an existing, legitimate device in at least two cases: (1) on MySQL, if none of the SET columns change (updated_at has second precision, so two updates within the same second with same IP/UA report 0 affected rows unless CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS is set), and (2) a device whose last update is older than 30 days falls outside the BETWEEN window. In both cases an existing device that should be allowed (or refreshed) is instead denied authentication with 'device limit reached'. The not-found condition should be distinguished from value-unchanged (e.g., use a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or check matched rows), and the stale-device case should be handled explicitly.

title: Provider signatures changed without any DI/wire registration updates in this PR
body: ProvideAnonDBStore gained a new `deviceLimit int64` parameter and ProvideAnonymousDeviceService changed its parameter from `anonstore.AnonStore` to `db.DB`, but the PR contains no changes to any dependency-injection registration files. If ProvideAnonDBStore is still listed in an fx/wire provider set (it was previously the provider of the anonstore.AnonStore interface), the container will fail at startup because nothing provides a bare `int64`. This needs verification against the registration sites before merge.

title: anonymousDeviceLimit is always serialized as 0 when unset, but the frontend type is `number | undefined`
body: The DTO field is `AnonymousDeviceLimit int64 json:"anonymousDeviceLimit"` with no omitempty, so when no device_limit is configured the frontend always receives 0, while the TypeScript type added in packages/grafana-data/src/types/config.ts is `number | undefined` and the runtime default is `undefined`. Frontend consumers distinguishing 'no limit configured' (undefined) from 'limit of 0' will see 0 and can misinterpret the configuration. Either add omitempty (and use a pointer) on the Go side so unset stays undefined, or change the TS type to `number` to match what is actually sent.

title: No tests for the allowed paths of the device limit, only the rejection path
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only covers the case where a second, unknown device is rejected when the limit is 1. Missing coverage: (1) an existing device within the 30-day window can still be updated when the limit is reached (the updateDevice success path, which is where the MySQL rowsAffected and stale-window bugs would surface), (2) a device whose updated_at is older than 30 days, and (3) an end-to-end test through Anonymous.Authenticate / AnonDeviceService.TagDevice that a rejected device stays rejected on retry — which would have caught the local-cache bypass where the cache entry is set before the store write succeeds.

title: New auth.anonymous device_limit setting is undocumented
body: The PR adds a new configuration option `[auth.anonymous] device_limit` (MustInt64(0)) that changes anonymous-access behavior — when exceeded, anonymous authentication is rejected — but no documentation, config example, or comment describing the option (units, 0-means-unlimited semantics, interaction with the 30-day expiration window) is included, despite the PR checklist requiring doc updates. Operators configuring anonymous auth have no way to discover or correctly interpret this setting.

title: Device tagging moved onto the synchronous anonymous auth path with no timeout or panic recovery
body: Authenticate previously ran TagDevice in a background goroutine with a dedicated 2-minute timeout and a recover() around panics. This change calls a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, ...) inline, so every anonymous request now performs database work (a COUNT over anon_device plus an INSERT/UPDATE for cache misses) on the authentication critical path, with no independent timeout; a slow or saturated database directly delays or fails anonymous page loads. Additionally, a panic inside TagDevice or the store is no longer contained (the recover() was removed along with the goroutine), so it now surfaces in the request handler instead of being logged. If the synchronous behavior is required to propagate ErrDeviceLimitReached, at minimum keep panic recovery and a bounded timeout, and make sure the count/write can be skipped cheaply when the limit is 0.

title: Device limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert (TOCTOU)
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by calling CountDevices and then, if count < deviceLimit, executing a separate INSERT ... ON CONFLICT statement. These are two independent database operations with no transaction or locking, so concurrent requests (especially from multiple Grafana instances, since the local cache in impl.go is per-process) can all observe a count below the limit and all insert, exceeding the configured device_limit. The limit is therefore only advisory under load. To enforce it strictly the count and insert need to be combined atomically (e.g., a single conditional upsert or a transaction with appropriate isolation).

title: Unauthenticated users can exhaust the device limit and deny anonymous access to everyone
body: When the limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached and Authenticate returns it, failing authentication for any device not already in the 30-day window. The device ID is taken verbatim from the client-controlled X-Grafana-Device-Id header with no authentication or rate limiting, so any anonymous visitor can send requests with random device IDs until count >= device_limit, after which every new anonymous device (i.e., every new browser) is rejected from the whole instance. This turns a licensing/limiting feature into a trivial remote denial-of-service for anonymous access. Consider capping inserts per client IP, or rate-limiting new device registrations, before enforcing a hard authentication failure.

title: MySQL RowsAffected semantics can cause spurious ErrDeviceLimitReached for an existing device
body: updateDevice treats rowsAffected == 0 as 'device limit reached', but on MySQL (without CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS, which Grafana's DSN does not set) RowsAffected reports changed rows, not matched rows. If a device row exists and the update writes identical client_ip, user_agent, and the same updated_at second (possible when two Grafana instances handle the same device within one second, since the dedupe localCache in impl.go is per-process), MySQL reports 0 affected rows and a legitimate existing device is rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached, failing that user's anonymous authentication. The check should distinguish 'row matched' from 'row changed' (e.g., check existence separately or use a dialect-aware affected-rows mode), and ErrDeviceLimitReached should not be used to mean 'device not found or unchanged'.

title: No test for the main success path: an existing device refreshing itself once the limit is reached
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only covers the rejection case (a second, new device gets ErrDeviceLimitReached). The core behavior of the feature—that a device already registered within the 30-day window can still be updated (last-seen refreshed) when the limit is reached, i.e., updateDevice returning nil—is untested, and neither is the end-to-end behavior of the authn client (what HTTP status/body an anonymous user receives once the limit is hit, and that a repeat visitor is not locked out). These are the paths most likely to regress.

title: Frontend type says anonymousDeviceLimit may be undefined, but backend always serializes it (default 0)
body: The TypeScript GrafanaConfig declares `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined`, but the Go DTO (pkg/api/dtos/frontend_settings.go, AnonymousDeviceLimit int64 with no omitempty) always emits the field, sending 0 when no limit is configured. Consumers therefore can never rely on undefined to mean 'no limit' and must special-case 0, which the type does not communicate. Either make the Go field `*int64` with omitempty to match the optional contract, or type the frontend field as a plain number and document that 0 means unlimited.

title: device_limit accepts negative values that silently disable the limit
body: cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit is read with MustInt64(0) and the store only applies the limit when deviceLimit > 0, so a negative value (e.g., device_limit = -1, a plausible typo for 'unlimited' or a mistake) is silently treated the same as 0 with no warning logged, unlike other Grafana settings that log when values are invalid. Additionally, the new auth.anonymous device_limit option is not documented anywhere in this PR (no docs or config reference update), so the semantics of 0/negative values and the blocking behavior when the limit is reached are undocumented.

title: Local cache is populated before the DB write, breaking device-limit enforcement
body: In tagDeviceUI, `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})` is executed before `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice` is called. When the device limit is reached, a brand-new device gets ErrDeviceLimitReached from the store (its row doesn't exist, so updateDevice affects 0 rows), and client.Authenticate rejects that one request. However, the cache entry has already been set, so every subsequent request from that same device within the 29-minute cache TTL hits the cache, tagDeviceUI returns nil immediately, and the user is authenticated normally. The result is that an over-limit device is blocked only ~1 request per 29 minutes and then granted access, making the configurable limit ineffective and producing flapping auth failures for users. The cache entry must only be set after a successful CreateOrUpdateDevice (or the 'blocked' state must also be cached so the rejection is consistent).

title: Anonymous authentication is now blocked on a synchronous DB write using the request context
body: The previous code ran TagDevice asynchronously in a goroutine with a detached context and a 2-minute timeout, deliberately keeping the DB write off the request path. This change calls `a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, ...)` synchronously in Authenticate. On every local-cache miss (once per device per ~29 minutes per instance), anonymous requests now pay a COUNT(*) query plus an INSERT/UPDATE against anon_device before the identity is returned, adding DB latency and DB availability coupling to the anonymous login path. Additionally, the request context is now used, so if the client disconnects mid-request the tagging write is cancelled — the old detached context existed precisely to avoid this. If synchronous enforcement is required, consider a short timeout or a background write with a blocking decision made only from already-cached state.

title: Device limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert, so the limit can be exceeded
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice first runs CountDevices and only falls back to updateDevice when `count >= s.deviceLimit`. This is a time-of-check-to-time-of-use race: two concurrent requests from different new devices can both observe count < limit and both perform the upsert insert path, inserting two devices even when the limit allows one. The same applies across multiple Grafana instances sharing a database. There is no unique constraint-based or transactional guard enforcing the cap, so the configured limit is only advisory under concurrency.

title: ErrDeviceLimitReached fails authentication but its effect on the HTTP response is undefined and untested
body: When TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, Authenticate returns the raw error `fmt.Errorf("device limit reached")`. How this surfaces to the client depends on the authn broker's generic error handling for the anonymous client (likely a 401 with the bare internal error string). There is no mapping to a dedicated status code or user-facing message, no error wrapping with context, and no logging at this site. Combined with the local-cache issue, users hitting the limit will see intermittent, unexplained 401s. The intended HTTP behavior (status code and message for a device over the anonymous device limit) should be defined and covered by a test.

title: No tests for the service/authn layer behavior when the device limit is reached
body: The only new test (TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit) exercises the store directly. Missing coverage: (1) that an existing, within-30-days device can still be updated and thus authenticate when the limit is reached (the updateDevice success path at the limit is untested), (2) that Anonymous.Authenticate rejects/accepts appropriately when the limit is hit (which would have caught the local-cache hole where a rejected device succeeds on its next request), and (3) that deviceLimit=0 keeps the previous unlimited behavior. The tests in impl_test.go all construct the service with the default cfg (limit 0), so none of the new limit logic is exercised end-to-end.

title: Service now hard-codes construction of the concrete AnonDBStore, removing AnonStore injection
body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService changed from accepting an `anonstore.AnonStore` to accepting `db.DB` and constructing `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore(sqlStore, cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit)` internally. Although the service field and the API layer still use the AnonStore interface, no implementation can be injected anymore (e.g., a fake or an alternative store), which is why the tests had to be rewritten to reach into `anonService.anonStore`. Passing the configured store (or the limit) in via the existing provider would preserve the seam the interface was created for.

title: New auth.anonymous device_limit setting is undocumented
body: The PR adds a new configuration key `device_limit` under `[auth.anonymous]` (default 0) but includes no documentation update for configure-grafana/configure-security/configure-authentication, and the PR description itself is an unfilled template (no problem statement, no linked issue). Operators have no way to discover the option, its semantics (0 = unlimited, counts unique devices seen in the last 30 days), or the consequence of hitting the limit (new anonymous devices are rejected).

title: Leftover debug logging at Error level dumps full ID lists every batch
body: In CleanAnnotations, CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579) routine progress information is logged with r.log.Error, e.g. r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, ...). These are clearly leftover debug statements: (1) they run at Error level for normal, successful operation, which pollutes error-level logs, dashboards and any alerting on error logs; (2) they log the entire `ids` slice, which can be up to annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size (the test uses 32767) IDs per line, per batch, repeated until the table is clean — megabytes of log spam on a large backlog; (3) the "err" field is always nil at that point because the error was already returned above, so the logs are misleading. These should be removed or downgraded to Debug level without the full ID list.

title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute without documentation or rationale
body: The cleanup service ticker was changed from time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10) to time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1). This is not mentioned in the PR description, which only describes the annotation delete restructuring. The consequence is that ALL cleanup jobs (expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, user invites, short URLs, query history row-limit enforcement, annotation cleanup) now run 10x more often on every Grafana instance, increasing background database load — ironically increasing lock contention with foreground writes, which is the problem this PR is meant to reduce. Combined with the 9-minute per-run timeout in clean(), cleanup work can now effectively run back-to-back. Either this change is unintentional and should be reverted, or it needs to be called out in the PR description and release notes with justification.

title: Placeholder-limit workaround only guards SQLite and keys off config, not actual ID count
body: deleteByIDs special-cases only SQLite (r.db.GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite && r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999) to inline IDs into the SQL, on the assumption that a DELETE with N `?` placeholders is otherwise safe. Other backends have their own placeholder/statement-size limits (e.g. MySQL prepared statements cap at 65,535 placeholders); with annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size configured above such a limit, every batch of the cleanup job will now fail permanently, whereas the previous subquery-based DELETE worked for any batch size. The guard should be based on len(ids) against per-dialect limits rather than the configured batch size on SQLite only. Also, the comment claims "SQLite has a parameter limit of 999" while the new test name states the limit is 32767 for SQLite >= 3.32.0 — the comment and code disagree with the test's stated rationale.

title: Deadlock fix is only exercised on SQLite; no MySQL/Postgres coverage
body: The PR fixes a MySQL-specific deadlock (grafana/grafana#64979), but all tests in this file use db.InitTestDB(t), which defaults to SQLite. The new code paths (fetchIDs + deleteByIDs, the SQLite ID-inlining branch, the batched untilDoneOrCancelled loop) are only validated against SQLite semantics; in particular the inline-ID branch at deleteByIDs is exercised only via the SQLite test, and no test verifies that the split statements actually avoid the deadlock under concurrent inserts on MySQL. There is also no test for the non-SQLite placeholder path with a large batch size. A MySQL integration test (or at least a concurrency test simulating interleaved inserts during cleanup) is needed to validate the fix the PR claims to deliver.

title: Leftover debug logging at Error level dumps full ID batches on every cleanup cycle
body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags call r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err) (and the analogous 'cleaned annotations by time/by count', 'Tags to clean', 'cleaned tags' calls at lines 537, 554, 557, 576, 579) unconditionally, even when the operation succeeded and even when len(ids) == 0. These are clearly leftover debug statements: the 'err' field is logged after it was already checked to be nil, and the level is Error for routine successful work. Combined with the cleanup interval being reduced to every minute (see cleanup.go change), every Grafana instance will now emit error-level log lines for all three annotation types plus orphaned tags on every cycle, including the entire batch of IDs (up to annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size, e.g. 32767 values per line). This pollutes error logs, defeats log-based alerting on errors, and can produce enormous log lines. These should be removed or downgraded to Debug level without the raw ID slice.

title: Undocumented 10x increase of the global cleanup job frequency
body: The ticker in CleanUpService.Run was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This is not mentioned in the PR description, which only describes the annotation-deadlock fix, and it affects all cleanup jobs, not just annotations: expired snapshot deletion, dashboard version deletion, expired image deletion, user invite expiry, stale short URL deletion, and the query_history row-limit enforcement (which performs counts and deletes across large tables). Since a clean() run is allowed up to 9 minutes and a pending tick is buffered by the ticker, a deployment whose cleanup cycle takes a minute or more will effectively run cleanup continuously, multiplying database load. If the intent was only to make the (now smaller-batched) annotation cleanup run more often, the frequency change should be scoped to that job or at minimum documented and justified in the PR.

title: deleteByIDs exceeds MySQL/Postgres placeholder limits for large batch sizes
body: deleteByIDs builds one '?' placeholder per ID and only special-cases SQLite (999-parameter limit) by inlining the IDs into the SQL string. MySQL has a hard limit of 65,535 placeholders per prepared statement (PostgreSQL's protocol limit is also 65,535). annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size is user-configurable, so any configuration above 65,535 on MySQL or PostgreSQL will now make every cleanup batch fail with a parameter-count error, whereas the previous subquery-based DELETE (which used no placeholders) worked at any batch size. The workaround should either inline values or chunk the DELETE when len(ids) approaches the dialect's placeholder limit, not just for SQLite.

title: Routine cleanup progress is logged at Error level with full ID slices
body: The new batch logging in CleanAnnotations (lines 534, 537, 554, 557) and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags (lines 576, 579) uses r.log.Error for normal, successful operation (e.g. `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, ...)`, where `err` is provably nil because it was already checked above). Since the cleanup job now runs every minute (see cleanup.go change) and each batch can contain up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize IDs (the test exercises 32,767), this will emit error-level log lines containing potentially tens of thousands of IDs per batch, on every cycle, even when nothing is deleted (count 0). This floods logs, pollutes error metrics/alerting, and looks like a production failure. These should be Debug-level and should not include the full ID slice.

title: Ticker change from 10 minutes to 1 minute multiplies frequency of ALL cleanup jobs, not just annotations
body: Changing `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)` to `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)` in CleanUpService.Run increases the run frequency of every job in `clean()` (expired snapshots, dashboard version deletion, expired image deletion, user invite expiry, short URL deletion, query history row-limit enforcement) by 10x, not just the annotation cleanup this PR targets. Additionally, `clean()` has a 9-minute timeout, so under load (e.g. the annotation cleanup processing many batches) a run can exceed the 1-minute tick interval; Go tickers buffer one tick, so the next cleanup starts immediately after the previous finishes, meaning cleanup jobs can effectively run back-to-back continuously against the database. This behavioral change is not mentioned in the PR description and should either be scoped to the annotation job or justified and documented.

title: Only SQLite's parameter limit is special-cased; large batch sizes will fail on SQL Server and MySQL
body: deleteByIDs generates one `?` placeholder per ID and only falls back to inlining literal values when the dialect is SQLite and AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999. Other supported databases have their own prepared-statement parameter limits (SQL Server: 2100, MySQL: 65,535). A user who configures `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` above those limits (the test itself uses 32,767, which would exceed SQL Server's 2100 limit) will get hard failures from the DELETE on every cleanup cycle. The old single-statement DELETE with a subquery had no such parameter count. The guard should key off the actual dialect's parameter limit (or the actual len(ids)) rather than only SQLite's 999.

title: O(n²) string building when inlining IDs for SQLite
body: In the SQLite large-batch branch of deleteByIDs, the ID list is built with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside a loop, which copies the accumulated string on every iteration. For a batch of 32,767 IDs this allocates roughly megabytes of intermediate strings and is quadratic in the batch size. Use a strings.Builder (or a single fmt.Sprint of the slice) instead.

title: Async legacy writes are canceled as soon as the request context ends
body: The goroutines that write to LegacyStorage (in Create at line 50-57, Delete at line 108-114, Update at line 134-141, and DeleteCollection at line 161-167) derive their timeout context from the incoming request context: `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`. The request-scoped `ctx` is canceled by the apiserver as soon as the HTTP handler returns, which for these fire-and-forget goroutines is typically before the legacy write even starts. The legacy write will then fail almost immediately with 'context canceled' (or the custom timeout cause), so mode 3 effectively never replicates writes to legacy storage in production. The timeout context must be derived from a non-cancelable context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or context.Background()), otherwise the whole point of dual-writing to legacy as a 'safe measure' is defeated.

title: Legacy Update now receives raw objInfo, causing resourceVersion conflicts and store divergence
body: The previous implementation wrapped the object before passing it to `d.Legacy.Update` (via `updateWrapper`), so legacy received the already-computed updated object. The new code passes the original `objInfo` to the legacy store. `objInfo.UpdatedObject` typically carries the resourceVersion/preconditions from the client request, which was read from unified storage. The legacy store has its own, different resourceVersion for the object, so the legacy update will frequently fail with a conflict (or apply a stale base object), leaving the legacy copy silently divergent from unified storage. Since legacy write errors are swallowed (only a metric bool), operators have no way to notice this drift. If raw objInfo is intentional, the conflict handling at least needs to be addressed.

title: Storage failures are recorded as legacy-storage metrics
body: In `Create` (line 45) and `Update` (line 129), when the write to unified Storage fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` — recording a *legacy* duration using the *storage* start time. This pollutes the legacy-write-duration metric with storage failures and makes the storage error rate invisible (the storage duration for the failed call is never recorded in these paths). The calls should be `recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

title: DeleteCollection records the legacy write under the storage metric
body: The async goroutine in `DeleteCollection` calls `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` for the legacy write. It should call `recordLegacyDuration`, as the other write methods do. As written, legacy delete-collection latency and errors are attributed to the unified storage metric, and the legacy metric silently shows nothing, which will mislead anyone monitoring dual-write health during migration.

title: Delete success path records the object name as the 'kind' metric label
body: In `Delete`, the success path calls `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`, passing the object's `name` where every other call in the file passes `options.Kind`. This creates high-cardinality metric labels (one per object name) on this one code path and makes the 'kind' label inconsistent between success and failure (`options.Kind`) for the same method, breaking dashboards/alerts that aggregate by kind.

title: Delete puts the base logger into the context instead of the enriched one
body: In `Delete`, the enriched logger `log` (with name, kind and method values) is built at line 96, but line 97 does `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` — inserting the *base* `d.Log` instead of `log`. All log statements inside Delete therefore lose the name/kind/method fields, and any logger already present in the incoming request context is replaced. Every other method in this file correctly uses `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`.

title: Legacy write errors in the async goroutines are never logged
body: In all four write paths, the error returned by the legacy store (e.g. `errObjectSt` at line 55, `err` at lines 112, 139, 165) is reduced to a boolean for the metric and then discarded — there is no `log.Error(...)` call in any of the goroutines. Because mode 3 intentionally treats legacy as a safety net, silent failures mean operators cannot distinguish 'legacy is in sync' from 'every legacy write is failing' without scraping metric internals. The error should be logged with the object name/kind so divergence can be investigated.

title: Mode 3 tests never assert that the async legacy write happens
body: The defining new behavior of mode 3 is 'write to unified storage, then asynchronously write to legacy'. None of the mode 3 tests assert that `Legacy.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection` are actually invoked after a successful storage write — there is no `m.AssertExpectations`, no wait/poll for the goroutine, and no assertion like `ls.AssertCalled(t, "Create", ...)`. The legacy mock expectations that are set up (e.g. lines 30-32, 313-315) are never verified. Additionally, because the legacy calls run in unmanaged goroutines, a testify mock may be invoked concurrently with (or after) the test body, which is a latent data race / flake. The core contract of this PR is therefore untested at the unit level.

title: Mode 3 integration subtests will be flaky: legacy API is checked immediately after async legacy writes
body: The new mode 3 subtests (lines 132 and 191) reuse `doPlaylistTests`, which asserts immediately after k8s writes that the legacy API returns the same data (e.g. `getFromBothAPIs` at lines 547 and 565, including `require.Equal(t, updated.GetResourceVersion(), out.GetResourceVersion())`, and the legacy list comparison at lines 523-531). In mode 3 the legacy write is asynchronous with no synchronization, so these assertions race the background goroutine and will intermittently fail (stale interval/title, missing item, or not-found from the legacy endpoint). These subtests need a retry/poll helper for the legacy-side checks, or the assertions must tolerate eventual consistency.

title: Async legacy writes derive from the request context and will be cancelled when the request finishes
body: In Create (line 51), Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163), the goroutine that performs the legacy write builds its 10-second timeout context as a child of the incoming request context (`ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). Request contexts in the apiserver are cancelled as soon as the HTTP handler returns, and in these methods the goroutine is started right before `return`, i.e. typically before the response is fully flushed. This means the legacy write can be aborted mid-flight (context cancelled) on virtually every request, silently leaving legacy storage stale. The timeout context should be derived from `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (or a background context carrying only the logger) so the derived deadline is independent of the request lifecycle.

title: Delete records the object name where the metric kind label is expected
body: On the success path of DualWriterMode3.Delete, the code calls `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`, passing the object `name` in the position of the `kind` label (compare with the error path on line 103 which correctly passes `options.Kind`). Every successful delete will emit a metric labeled with the deleted object's name instead of the resource kind, polluting metric label cardinality (one label value per object name) and making per-kind delete latency dashboards wrong.

title: Storage failures in Create and Update are recorded as legacy-storage metric failures
body: In Create (line 45) and Update (line 129), when the write to the unified Storage fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. These are the primary-store failures of mode 3, so recording them under the legacy-writer metric means unified-storage error rates are invisible and legacy-storage error metrics over-report, defeating the purpose of the dual-writer metrics for monitoring the migration.

title: DeleteCollection records the async legacy result with recordStorageDuration
body: In the DeleteCollection goroutine, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection(...)` is recorded via `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)`. It should be `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`, as done in Create/Delete/Update. Legacy delete-collection latency and errors will be attributed to the unified storage metric, corrupting both series.

title: Delete injects d.Log into the context instead of the enriched per-request logger
body: In Delete, the enriched logger `log` (built with name, kind and method values) is created on line 96, but line 97 does `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`, injecting the base logger instead of `log`. Every other method injects the enriched `log`. The consequence is that any log lines emitted from the request context in Delete (and the error log on line 102) are missing the name/kind/method fields that all other mode 3 methods provide, producing inconsistent structured logs.

title: Legacy Update re-runs objInfo.UpdatedObject against the legacy store's (possibly stale) object, dropping the previous updateWrapper protection
body: The previous mode 3 Update wrapped objInfo in `updateWrapper` so the legacy store wrote the exact object produced by the unified-store update. The new code passes the raw `objInfo` to `d.Legacy.Update` in the background goroutine (line 139). The legacy store will call `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old)` again with its own copy of the old object; if the legacy copy has a different resource version or the object info closure is tied to the (now possibly cancelled) request, the legacy update can fail conflict validation or produce a different value, causing the two stores to diverge. This is a regression relative to the replaced implementation and undermines mode 3's purpose of keeping legacy in sync as a safety measure.

title: Errors from asynchronous legacy writes are never logged
body: In the background goroutines of Create (line 55), Delete (line 112), Update (line 139) and DeleteCollection (line 165), the error returned by the legacy store is only fed into `recordLegacyDuration` and then discarded; no `log.Error` call is made. Since these writes are asynchronous, the caller never sees the failure either. If the legacy write fails or times out after 10 seconds, the two stores silently diverge with no log trace, making it impossible to diagnose why legacy data is missing or stale when rolling back from mode 3. Each goroutine should log the error (using the request-scoped logger already put in ctx).

title: Mode 3 unit tests neither wait for nor assert the asynchronous legacy writes, making them racy and non-verifying
body: The Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection happy-path tests trigger the legacy write inside a fire-and-forget goroutine, but the test never waits for the goroutine (no WaitGroup/channel/`m.AssertCalled`) before finishing. Two consequences: (1) testify's mock is invoked from another goroutine racing with test teardown, which can produce data races or 'mock: I don't know what to return' panics depending on timing — i.e. flaky CI; (2) the core contract of mode 3 (writes go to unified storage *and then* to legacy) is never actually verified — a regression that removed the legacy write entirely would still pass these tests. The tests should synchronize on completion of the async write (e.g. a done channel the mock closes) and assert the legacy mock was called.

title: Mode 3 playlist integration tests assert legacy API state immediately after async k8s writes, which is inherently flaky
body: The new `with dual write (file, mode 3)` and `with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)` subtests reuse `doPlaylistTests`, which immediately reads the legacy `/api/playlists` endpoints right after k8s API writes (e.g. the legacy list at line ~523 and `getFromBothAPIs` after the k8s PUT/Apply). In mode 3, legacy writes are asynchronous with no synchronization, so the legacy store may not yet reflect the create/update when these assertions run, causing intermittent failures (or, worse, passing while the write is silently dropped). The test needs to poll/retry for the legacy state to converge, or the mode 3 runs need dedicated assertions that accept eventual consistency.

title: Delete no longer falls back to legacy storage when the unified store returns NotFound
body: The replaced implementation explicitly tolerated `apierrors.IsNotFound` from the unified store and still deleted the object from legacy storage. The new Delete returns immediately on any storage error (lines 101-105), so if an object exists only in legacy storage (e.g. incompletely migrated), a mode 3 delete returns NotFound to the client and the orphaned legacy row is never removed. If mode 3 is meant to be a 'safe measure' that keeps legacy in sync, the NotFound-tolerant fallback for the legacy delete should be preserved; otherwise this behavior change should be documented as intentional.

title: Async legacy writes use the request context, so they are canceled as soon as the request completes
body: In Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection, the goroutine that writes to LegacyStorage derives its context from the incoming request context (`ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). The handler returns immediately after the unified-storage write, and the apiserver cancels the request context when the request finishes. Because the legacy write runs asynchronously, it will frequently observe an already-canceled parent context and fail with 'context canceled' (or the 10s timeout never even matters). The result is that the legacy store is silently not written for many (potentially most) operations, which defeats the stated purpose of mode 3 ('write to legacy as a safe measure') and leaves the two stores divergent. The goroutines should use a detached context, e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (plus the timeout), or a background context carrying only the logger.

title: Create records storage failures under the legacy metric
body: In DualWriterMode3.Create, when `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. This records a legacy-storage duration/latency observation for a failure that happened in the unified storage, corrupting the dual-writer metrics: legacy dashboards will show errors and latencies that never touched legacy storage, and no storage-side failure is recorded for the failing call. It should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`, as done in Delete/DeleteCollection.

title: Update records storage failures under the legacy metric
body: In DualWriterMode3.Update, the error path after `d.Storage.Update` fails calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. Same defect as in Create: a unified-storage failure is attributed to the legacy store in the metrics (wrong metric name, wrong latency sample, wrong error count). It should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

title: DeleteCollection records the async legacy write under the storage metric
body: In the DeleteCollection goroutine, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)`. The legacy write outcome is attributed to the unified-storage metric instead of `recordLegacyDuration`, so legacy delete-collection failures/errors never show up in legacy metrics and pollute storage metrics. Compare with Delete (line 113) and Update (line 140), which correctly use recordLegacyDuration.

title: Delete passes the object name as the 'kind' label on the success path
body: On the successful-delete path, `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes `name` (the deleted object's name) where every other call in this file passes `options.Kind` as the kind label. This creates unbounded metric label cardinality (one label value per deleted object name) and makes the delete metric rows inconsistent with all other methods. It should be `options.Kind`.

title: Delete puts the base logger into the context instead of the enriched one
body: In Delete, `log` is built with name/kind/method values, but the context is set with `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` instead of `log`. Unlike every other method in this file, the request-scoped and derived contexts (including the async legacy-delete goroutine) lose the name/kind/method log fields, so any logs emitted downstream from the legacy delete carry no identifying information.

title: Failures of the asynchronous legacy writes are never logged
body: The previous implementation logged an error when the legacy write failed ('unable to create object in legacy storage', etc.). The new goroutines only record a Prometheus metric (`recordLegacyDuration(errObjectSt != nil, ...)`) and discard the error entirely; nothing is ever written to the log. Operators investigating a divergence between unified and legacy storage will have no log evidence of when or why the legacy write failed (timeout, conflict, validation error). The goroutines should at minimum log the returned error, e.g. `if err != nil { log.Error(err, "legacy write failed") }` (using a detached context for the logger).

title: Async legacy Create mutates the request object concurrently with response serialization
body: In Create, the goroutine passes the caller's `obj` (the same runtime.Object that `d.Storage.Create` was called with and whose result the handler serializes to the client) to `d.Legacy.Create`. Storage Create implementations commonly mutate the passed object in place (setting UID, resourceVersion, creation timestamp, generation). While the apiserver is serializing the response from the unified write, the legacy write goroutine can be mutating the same object concurrently — a data race that can produce corrupted response bodies or runtime panics under `-race`. The object passed to the legacy goroutine should be a deep copy, and the same consideration applies to `objInfo` in Update (the legacy Update runs objInfo.UpdatedObject against shared state while the handler may still be using it).

title: Create error test never mocks Storage.Create, so the test exercises a mock panic instead of the error path
body: The test case 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' (input failingObj) only sets up a legacy `Create` expectation via setupLegacyFn and leaves setupStorageFn nil. Mode3's Create calls `d.Storage.Create` first; the storageMock has no expectation for it, so the mock will panic ('mock: I don't know what to return because the method call was unexpected') rather than return an error. The test therefore does not verify the intended error path (and looks like the legacy/storage mock setups were swapped relative to the other tests, e.g. TestMode3_Delete which mocks storage only).

title: Tests never assert that the asynchronous legacy write actually happens, and the shared mock is used from untracked goroutines
body: Mode 3's defining behavior is that writes go to unified storage synchronously and to legacy storage asynchronously. None of the new tests assert that Legacy.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection were invoked (e.g. via m.AssertExpectations or eventually-style waiting), so a regression that drops the legacy write entirely would still pass. Additionally, the legacy calls happen in fire-and-forget goroutines sharing the same non-thread-safe testify `mock.Mock` with the test goroutine, and the test returns without waiting for them — this is both a potential data race under -race and a source of flaky panics when the goroutine calls the mock after the test has finished. The tests should wait for the async write (e.g. a channel/signaled mock or polling on mock call counts) and then assert the legacy call happened.

title: TestMode3_Get shadows the shared prometheus registry with a local one
body: TestMode3_Get declares `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` locally, shadowing the package-level `p` used by all other tests in the file (the PR even removed exactly this pattern from dualwriter_mode1_test.go). This is inconsistent and means the metrics registered for this test are silently different from every other mode-3 test; if the intent was to share one registry, this test diverges from it and a future reader can't tell whether it is intentional.

title: Mutex guards only the cache pointer, not the shared EntryPointAssets object handed to callers
body: The new RWMutex protects reads/writes of the `entryPointAssetsCache` variable, but in non-Dev mode `GetWebAssets` still returns the *same* `*dtos.EntryPointAssets` instance to every concurrent request. That type is mutable: it has exported fields (`JSFiles`, `Dark`, `Light`) and a mutating method `SetContentDeliveryURL`. If any caller (now or in the future) mutates the returned value — e.g. calls `SetContentDeliveryURL` or appends to `JSFiles` — that write races with all other goroutines reading the same object, reproducing exactly the class of bug this PR is meant to fix. To fully close the race, return a copy of the cached value, or make the DTO immutable.

title: No cache re-check after acquiring the write lock; lock held across file I/O and JSON parsing
body: Once a goroutine that observed a nil cache acquires the exclusive lock, it never re-checks whether another goroutine has already populated the cache. At startup (or after a failed read, when the cache stays nil), N concurrent requests each perform the full manifest read and JSON decode sequentially while holding the write lock, instead of one goroutine doing it and the rest reusing the result. Additionally, the lock is held across `os.Open` + `json.Decode` and, in Dev mode, this happens on every single request, serializing all index-page requests behind each other's disk I/O. Doing the expensive computation first and only taking the lock to publish the result (double-checked locking) would avoid the redundant work and shrink the critical section.

title: No regression test for the fixed data race
body: The PR fixes a data race on shared global state but adds no test that would have caught it, so a future refactor could silently reintroduce it. A small test calling `GetWebAssets` concurrently from several goroutines (run under `go test -race`) would lock the fix in, and would also fail on the pre-PR code, demonstrating the bug.

title: Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock, causing redundant serialized rebuilds
body: GetWebAssets uses a check-lock pattern without a second check: multiple concurrent callers in non-Dev mode that all observe a nil cache (e.g. a burst of requests at server startup, before the first successful load) will each acquire the write lock in turn and each re-read and re-parse assets-manifest.json from disk, even though an earlier holder of the lock already populated entryPointAssetsCache. The work is serialized by the exclusive lock, so the first N concurrent requests queue behind each other. After taking entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock() at line 48, the function should re-read entryPointAssetsCache and return it immediately if non-nil and cfg.Env != setting.Dev.

title: Exclusive lock is held across file/network I/O on every call in Dev mode
body: In Dev mode the early-return at line 45 never triggers, so every call to GetWebAssets acquires the exclusive lock (line 48) and holds it via defer for the entire duration of reading and JSON-decoding assets-manifest.json (line 60) — and, if the CDN branch is ever enabled, an outbound HTTP request (line 90). Before this change those loads ran concurrently; now all GetWebAssets calls in Dev mode are fully serialized behind one mutex, so a slow or failed manifest read stalls every concurrent caller, including the RLock readers. Computing the result into a local variable and only taking the lock briefly to publish it into entryPointAssetsCache would preserve the race fix without serializing the I/O.

title: Double-checked locking is incomplete: no re-check of the cache after acquiring the write lock
body: GetWebAssets reads the cache under RLock, and if empty, acquires the write lock and unconditionally re-reads the manifest without re-checking whether another goroutine already populated the cache in the meantime. Two consequences in non-Dev mode: (1) redundant duplicate file reads on a cold start, and more importantly (2) goroutine A succeeds and caches a valid *dtos.EntryPointAssets; goroutine B, waiting behind A, then re-reads the file and if that read fails transiently, line 69 (`entryPointAssetsCache = result`) overwrites the good cached value with nil and B returns an error — a user-visible failure even though a valid cached result existed. The fix is to re-read `entryPointAssetsCache` after taking the write lock (or before assigning at line 69) and return the cached value if it is now non-nil in non-Dev mode.

title: Write lock is held across file/network I/O, serializing all GetWebAssets callers
body: The deferred-unlocked write lock at lines 48-49 is held while `readWebAssetsFromFile` performs disk I/O (and, if the `cdn` variable is ever set, `readWebAssetsFromCDN` performs an HTTP request via `http.DefaultClient`, which has no timeout — a hang there would block every GetWebAssets caller indefinitely). In Dev mode the cache check is skipped entirely, so every request re-reads the manifest file while holding the write lock, serializing all concurrent requests that touch this path. Computing `result` outside the lock and taking the write lock only to publish the cache assignment would avoid blocking all readers for the duration of the I/O.

title: The mutex guards the cache pointer but not the shared EntryPointAssets struct it returns
body: The fix prevents races on the `entryPointAssetsCache` variable itself, but all callers still receive the same shared `*dtos.EntryPointAssets` instance. Any caller that mutates the returned struct — for example via its `SetContentDeliveryURL` method, which the code itself calls on the result at line 64 — would race with concurrent readers of that same pointer. To fully close the race, the cached value must be treated as immutable after publication (and any mutation, such as SetContentDeliveryURL, must happen before it is stored), or a copy returned per call.

title: enableSqlExpressions() is dead logic that always returns false regardless of the feature toggle
body: The function `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` but then returns `false` in both branches of the following `if`, so the flag check has no effect whatsoever. While the net effect (always disabled) is the security intent of this PR, the code reads as if the feature flag were consulted, which will mislead future maintainers who may 'fix' or extend it. If SQL expressions are meant to be permanently disabled, the function should simply be removed and the call site should unconditionally reject the query; if the flag is meant to matter, the logic is wrong. As written, the `FlagSqlExpressions` feature toggle silently no-ops, and the only user-visible signal is the confusing error at the call site.

title: Error message "sqlExpressions is not implemented" is wrong/misleading and is not a proper bad-request error
body: When a user submits a SQL expression query, they now get `"sqlExpressions is not implemented"`. This message is inaccurate: the feature was implemented and has now been deliberately removed/disabled for security reasons (CVE-2024-9264). Users who had the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle enabled will get a message that sounds like a transient bug rather than an intentional removal, generating support noise. Additionally, unlike other invalid-query errors in this file's sibling commands (e.g. `errutil.BadRequest("sql-missing-query", ...)` in sql_command.go), this is a bare `fmt.Errorf`, so the API will likely surface it as a 500 internal server error instead of a 400 for what is invalid user input. The message should clearly state that SQL expressions are no longer available and be returned as a bad-request error.

title: UnmarshalSQLCommand path is not guarded by the same disable check as ReadQuery
body: The disable logic was only added to the new `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` path (reader.go, QueryTypeSQL case). The older `UnmarshalSQLCommand` entry point (used when raw nodes are unmarshalled from the legacy query format) still constructs a `SQLCommand` without checking whether SQL expressions are disabled. It currently fails anyway, but only as a side effect: `NewSQLCommand` calls `sql.TablesList`, which calls the stub `DB.RunCommands` that returns "not implemented", and that error is surfaced to the user as `errutil.BadRequest("sql-invalid-sql", "error reading SQL command")` — an error code and message that misrepresent the real cause (feature disabled, not invalid SQL). If the stub DB is ever given a real implementation, this unguarded path would silently re-enable SQL expressions. Both entry points should share a single explicit guard.

title: NoData branch in Execute is dead code — TableData assignment unconditionally overwrites it
body: In `SQLCommand.Execute`, when `frame.Rows() == 0` the code sets `rsp.Values` to a `mathexp.NoData` value, but immediately after the `if` block, `rsp.Values` is unconditionally reassigned to `mathexp.Values{mathexp.TableData{Frame: frame}}`. The NoData result can therefore never be observed, so downstream consumers that distinguish empty frames from NoData (e.g. alerting) get a TableData with zero rows instead. This is a pre-existing bug in a function this PR modifies, and it is worth fixing or removing the dead branch while the function is being touched (it also becomes entirely unreachable now that `QueryFramesInto` always returns an error).

title: No tests added or updated to cover the new "SQL expressions disabled" behavior
body: This PR changes user-visible behavior for the `sql` query type (it now always fails, both via the reader path with the new error and via `UnmarshalSQLCommand` which now fails in `sql.TablesList`), yet no test files are included in the change set. There is no test asserting that a SQL expression query returns an error, that the error is a bad-request rather than a 500, or that the legacy `UnmarshalSQLCommand` path is also blocked. Any existing tests covering SQL expression parsing/execution (in pkg/expr and pkg/expr/sql) would exercise the new stub DB and either fail or need updating — none are modified here. Given this is a security fix for CVE-2024-9264, regression tests proving both entry points reject SQL expressions are important to prevent accidental re-enablement.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false; the feature flag check is dead, misleading code
body: The function `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns `false` on both branches, so it always returns false and the flag lookup has no effect. While the unconditional `false` is the intended security fix for CVE-2024-9264, the leftover conditional makes the code look like it still honors `FlagSqlExpressions`. A future maintainer who 'fixes' the apparently inverted logic (e.g. changing a `return false` to `return true` or removing the negation) would silently re-enable the vulnerable SQL expression path. The flag is also now a silent no-op for operators who enable it. The function should simply return false (or be removed) with a comment referencing the CVE, so the intent is unambiguous.

title: Error message "sqlExpressions is not implemented" is wrong and misleading
body: When a user submits a SQL expression, the reader now returns the error "sqlExpressions is not implemented". The feature was implemented and has been deliberately disabled for security reasons (CVE-2024-9264); it has not been 'not implemented'. Users who explicitly enable the `sqlExpressions` feature flag (which the docs still advertise) will receive a message suggesting a missing implementation rather than that the feature is unavailable/disabled, generating confusion and support load. The message should state that SQL expressions are not supported/disabled, and the feature-flag documentation referenced in the PR description should be updated to say the flag no longer does anything.

title: Legacy SQL expression path (UnmarshalSQLCommand) is only disabled implicitly via the stub DB, with no explicit guard
body: The explicit disable check (`enableSqlExpressions`) exists only in `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery`. The legacy unmarshal path `UnmarshalSQLCommand` -> `NewSQLCommand` -> `sql.TablesList` -> `NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands` is blocked only because the stub DB in pkg/expr/sql/db.go returns "not implemented". There is no feature-flag or security guard anywhere on this path, and the resulting user-facing error is an opaque "error reading SQL command". If anyone later replaces the stub DB implementation (e.g. reintroducing an in-process SQL engine, which the code structure in pkg/expr/sql/db.go invites), the legacy path re-enables SQL expressions without passing through the reader guard, reintroducing the vulnerability. The disable should be enforced explicitly at the command-construction entry points (or the legacy unmarshal path removed), not left as a side effect of a stub.

title: No regression tests that SQL expressions are rejected on all entry points
body: This PR is the fix for a critical RCE/LFI vulnerability (CVE-2024-9264), yet it adds no tests. There is no test asserting that a query of type `sql` returns an error from `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` regardless of the `FlagSqlExpressions` toggle state, and no test that the legacy `UnmarshalSQLCommand`/`NewSQLCommand` path also fails. Without such tests, a future refactor (e.g. someone 'fixing' the inverted logic in `enableSqlExpressions` or restoring the DB implementation in pkg/expr/sql/db.go) could silently re-enable the vulnerable code path with no CI failure. Existing SQL expression tests, if any remain, would also be failing or had to be deleted; either way the disable behavior is untested.

title: enableSqlExpressions contains inverted, dead feature-flag logic that invites accidental re-enabling
body: The new helper `enableSqlExpressions` reads `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns `false` in both branches, so the function always returns false regardless of the flag. Besides being dead code, the logic is inverted relative to its name (when the flag is ON, `enabled` is false; when the flag is OFF, `enabled` is true), and the result is never used. A future maintainer 'fixing' the seemingly-wrong inversion (e.g. changing the first branch to `return true`) would silently re-enable the SQL expression code path that this PR deliberately disables for CVE-2024-9264. Since the intent is to unconditionally reject SQL expressions, the flag lookup and helper should be removed entirely and the case body should just return an error directly, making the security intent explicit and unambiguous.

title: Error message "sqlExpressions is not implemented" misleads users about why the query was rejected
body: When a user submits a SQL expression query, they now get `"sqlExpressions is not implemented"`. The feature is implemented but intentionally disabled for security reasons; additionally, the message references the internal feature-toggle name (`sqlExpressions`) which still exists in featuremgmt and can be enabled by admins, yet enabling it has no effect. An admin who enables the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle per the existing documented behavior will still get this error with no indication that the flag is now a no-op. The message should state that SQL expressions are disabled/unavailable (and ideally the flag should be removed or documented as non-functional).

title: No tests verify that SQL expression queries are rejected, and existing SQL tests are not updated
body: This PR changes the behavior of the SQL expression query type from executing (behind the `sqlExpressions` feature flag) to always failing, but adds no test asserting the new behavior (e.g. that ReadQuery with QueryTypeSQL returns an error, and that the go-duck-backed TablesList/QueryFramesInto paths are never reachable). Existing tests covering SQL expressions in pkg/expr (e.g. tests constructing SQLCommand or calling sql.TablesList) would now fail against the 'not implemented' stubs if they exercise the removed functionality, and no updated tests are included in the changed files. A regression test is needed so that a future refactor cannot silently re-enable this path without a test failure.

title: Stub DB methods keep unreachable code paths in SQLCommand.Execute alive with silent failure semantics
body: The new `DB` stub makes every method return `errors.New("not implemented")`. Because `NewSQLCommand` calls `sql.TablesList` (which now always fails) the command can never be constructed, so `SQLCommand.Execute` is dead code — yet it still contains a live call to `db.QueryFramesInto` whose error is swallowed into `rsp.Error` and returned as a successful (nil-error) result. If the construction-time guard is ever relaxed (e.g. by re-enabling the flag), queries would fail at execute time with a generic 'not implemented' error surfaced as query data rather than a clear server-side rejection. Consider deleting or clearly deprecating the unreachable Execute body, or failing fast, so the disabled state is enforced in one place only.

title: Removing the coarse BuildIndex lock allows concurrent duplicate builds of the same index key
body: BuildIndex previously held b.cacheMu for the entire function, which (coarsely) guaranteed that only one build per key could run at a time and that GetIndex would block rather than return nil mid-build. Now the lock is only taken around the final `b.cache[key] = idx` write. The caller, searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex (pkg/storage/unified/resource/search.go:287), does a check-then-build with no per-key synchronization (its own TODO comment admits this: "We want to block while building the index and return the same index for the key... simple mutex not great"). With the lock removed, two concurrent Search requests (or a Search request racing a watch-event-triggered build in handleEvent) for a namespace whose index doesn't exist yet will both see GetIndex return nil and both invoke BuildIndex for the same key. For file-backed indexes (size > FileThreshold) both goroutines call bleve.New on the same directory, which fails or corrupts the on-disk index; for in-memory indexes the build runs twice, IndexedKinds/IndexTenants metrics are double-counted, and the index object that loses the cache-map race is the one that handleEvent may keep writing watch events into, so those updates silently disappear from searches. A per-key singleflight/mutex is needed to preserve the exclusion the old lock provided.

title: Reordering Init so the watcher starts after index build silently drops all writes made during indexing
body: Init previously called s.initWatcher() before s.search.init(); it now runs the search index build first and only starts the event watcher afterwards. The SQL backend's WatchWriteEvents (pkg/storage/unified/sql/backend.go:558) initializes its poller's `since` watermark from the *current* latest resource versions at the moment it is called, so every write that occurs while the (potentially long) index build is running is never picked up: it is neither broadcast to Watch subscribers (the Broadcaster/mostRecentRV only see post-start events) nor reflected anywhere. Before this change the watcher was running during index construction, so those events were streamed to clients. The consequence is that any write landing in the startup-indexing window is silently lost from watch streams. The build path already computes the last-read resource version (comment in search.go:375: "when watching, we must add all events since that time"), but nothing uses it; the watcher should be started before or seeded from the index build's RV rather than from latest.

title: Data race on shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` in init's errgroup workers
body: In searchSupport.init, the errgroup closures assign to the captured outer variables `err` (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`, line 190) and increment `totalBatchesIndexed` (line 189) from multiple concurrent goroutines with no synchronization. This is a data race under the Go memory model. It was mostly latent before because bleveBackend.BuildIndex serialized workers behind its whole-function cacheMu lock, but this PR removes that lock specifically to let builds run concurrently, making the race real. Consequences range from torn counters in the "namespaces indexed" span attribute to one goroutine's error return value being overwritten/observed inconsistently by another. Capture local variables inside the closure and use an atomic counter for the total.

title: Failed Init in NewResourceServer leaks the context and partially started goroutines
body: NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) and returns `nil, err` on failure, but never calls s.cancel() on the error path. If any stage of Init fails partway (e.g., lifecycle hooks succeed, search init starts its event-consumer goroutine, then initWatcher fails), the server object is discarded while the cancelable context and any goroutines spawned during partial initialization keep running. Notably, the searchSupport watch goroutine (search.go:207-213) consumes from the events channel on a context.Background() with no shutdown path at all, so it polls and processes events forever for a server that was never returned to the caller. Call s.cancel() (and ideally give the search watch goroutine a stop mechanism) before returning the error.

title: TotalDocs reads b.cache without acquiring cacheMu
body: bleveBackend.TotalDocs iterates b.cache with no lock while BuildIndex mutates the map under cacheMu. TotalDocs is invoked at the end of searchSupport.init (search.go:216), which now overlaps with the just-started watch goroutine: handleEvent can trigger getOrCreateIndex -> BuildIndex -> cache write for a namespace not covered at startup, concurrently with the TotalDocs read. That is an unsynchronized map read/write and can panic (concurrent map iteration and map write). Take b.cacheMu.RLock in TotalDocs.

title: Postgres path of the storage-server integration test is now skipped entirely
body: The test now skips unconditionally for GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres ("test not working with postgres in Drone"), which means the storage server target and the addStorageServerToConfig postgres branch (db_host/db_name/db_user/db_pass keys, lines 75-79) get no CI coverage at all — that configuration code can silently rot. Since the PR also changes startup behavior of this exact target, losing the postgres coverage increases the risk of merging a startup regression undetected. Preferably fix the Drone environment issue; otherwise at least track it so the skip is temporary.

title: Data race on shared 'err' and 'totalBatchesIndexed' now that index builds run concurrently
body: In searchSupport.init, the errgroup worker closure does `totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(ctx, ...)` where both `totalBatchesIndexed` and `err` are variables captured from the enclosing function scope. Previously the whole-body cacheMu lock in bleveBackend.BuildIndex serialized the build calls (and therefore the `err` assignments), but this PR removes that lock while init still runs up to `initWorkers` goroutines concurrently. Multiple goroutines now write the same `err` variable (and increment the counter) simultaneously, which is a data race (Go race detector will flag it, and a lost/overwritten error can be returned as the init result even when another namespace failed, or vice versa). Each goroutine should use its own local error variable and the counter should be atomic or aggregated after group.Wait().

title: Removing the coarse BuildIndex lock allows concurrent builds of the same index key
body: BuildIndex previously held cacheMu for the entire function, which (among other things) serialized builds of the same NamespacedResource. Now only the final cache write is locked. getOrCreateIndex in resource/search.go has a check-then-build pattern with no per-key synchronization (its own TODO admits this): both the watch-event goroutine (handleEvent) and a Search RPC can observe `GetIndex == nil` for the same key and invoke BuildIndex concurrently. Consequences: two in-memory indexes are built for the same key and the last writer wins in the cache, so documents written via handleEvent into the losing index are silently dropped from search results; for file-based indexes (size > FileThreshold) both calls run bleve.New against the same directory path, where the second call fails with 'index path already exists' (or worse, races on the same on-disk files). A per-key lock or singleflight is needed to make the cache write safe.

title: TotalDocs reads the cache map without holding cacheMu and can panic
body: bleveBackend.TotalDocs iterates b.cache without acquiring b.cacheMu, unlike GetIndex which takes the RLock. This PR adds a call to TotalDocs in searchSupport.init (the new 'search index initialized' log line) after the watch-event goroutine has already been started (the goroutine is launched before the log line). That goroutine can concurrently call handleEvent -> getOrCreateIndex -> BuildIndex, which takes the write lock and mutates b.cache.
