body: The endpoint orders by "-datetime" but OptimizedCursorPaginator inherits Paginator's key handling: get_item_key (src/sentry/api/paginator.py:838-840) computes int(math.floor(value)) on a datetime, which raises TypeError, and value_from_cursor (line 842) returns the raw millisecond integer from the cursor and passes it into a WHERE clause comparing a timestamp column to a bigint ("datetime <= 1234567890123"), which Postgres rejects with an operator-does-not-exist error. Unlike DateTimePaginator, this class never converts between datetimes and the ms-epoch cursor representation. Consequently, any request with optimized_pagination=true from a superuser or globally-access member against a non-empty audit log will raise an unhandled exception and return a 500 instead of a page of results.

title: Negative-offset slicing of a Django QuerySet raises AssertionError; the 'advanced feature' can never work
body: The negative-offset path in OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result (lines 877-882) slices the queryset as queryset[start_offset:stop] with a negative start_offset. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing — the ORM raises "AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported" — so this branch always errors instead of returning results. The code comment claiming "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is factually wrong. Since the cursor string ("value:offset:is_prev") is client-controlled and Cursor.from_string happily parses negative offsets, any client hitting this endpoint with optimized_pagination=true and a crafted cursor such as "0:-5:0" triggers an unhandled exception / 500. There is no valid input for which this feature works.

title: BasePaginator change claims to support negative offsets but still crashes for is_prev cursors, and silently changes behavior otherwise
body: The new line `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` only clamps negative offsets for forward cursors; for previous-page cursors a negative client-supplied offset still flows into queryset[start_offset:stop] and raises Django's "Negative indexing is not supported" AssertionError, contradicting the comment that negative offsets are now allowed. For forward cursors, the clamp silently changes existing behavior: a malformed cursor like "0:-50:0" that previously errored now returns the first page, and the unclamped negative offset is still passed into build_cursor via the original cursor object, so the generated next/prev cursors can carry bogus negative offsets forward. Either validate the offset (reject negatives) or handle both directions consistently.

title: Client-toggled paginator class breaks cursor portability between requests
body: The paginator implementation now depends on a per-request query parameter (optimized_pagination) plus who is calling, so the same endpoint issues cursors with different semantics depending on the request. A cursor produced by DateTimePaginator encodes a ms-epoch value that DateTimePaginator converts back to a datetime for its WHERE clause; if the same cursor is replayed against OptimizedCursorPaginator (same user toggles the flag, or a superuser shares a link with a non-superuser), the raw integer is compared against the timestamp column and the request errors or returns wrong rows. Pagination cursors are supposed to be opaque tokens valid for the endpoint; making their interpretation depend on a mutable flag violates that contract and will produce intermittent 500s/incorrect pages for clients.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator's non-negative path is a verbatim copy of BasePaginator.get_result and provides no performance benefit
body: Apart from the broken negative-offset branch, OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result duplicates BasePaginator.get_result line for line (same build_queryset, same slicing, same cursor building). The PR is titled 'Enhanced Pagination Performance for High-Volume Audit Logs', but for every working request the query plan and workload are identical to the existing DateTimePaginator path — no index hints, no query reduction, nothing. The class adds ~100 lines of duplicated pagination logic (which will drift from the base implementation, as it already has with the misleading comments) with no measurable gain, while the only genuinely new behavior (negative offsets) is a guaranteed exception. The feature should either be justified with a real optimization or removed.

title: Admin-gated 'advanced features' flag is security theater with a misleading safety comment
body: The gating `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` combined with the comment "This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level" implies the advanced path exposes something extra that permissions must guard. It does not: pagination offsets never bypass queryset filters, and the only 'advanced' capability (negative offsets) is an error path in the ORM. Meanwhile, the flag does create a real inconsistency: a superuser and a regular owner hitting the same URL with the same cursor get different paginator semantics (and, per the other findings, a 500 vs. working results). If there is no concrete capability being gated, remove the flag and the misleading comments rather than implying there is a privileged pagination mode.

title: No tests for the new paginator, the negative-offset path, or the endpoint's optimized branch
body: The PR adds a new paginator class, modifies the shared BasePaginator.get_result used by many endpoints, and adds a new request-parameter-driven branch on a production endpoint, but includes no tests. At minimum it needs: (1) a regression test that BasePaginator.get_result behavior is unchanged for existing cursors (including the new max(0, offset) clamp), (2) tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator covering forward/prev cursors, which would have immediately caught the datetime TypeError and the Django negative-slicing AssertionError, and (3) endpoint tests covering the optimized_pagination flag for both authorized and unauthorized users.

title: Comment-only change documents behavior that does not exist
body: The only change in cursors.py is a comment asserting "Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios" above `self.offset = int(offset)`. The line of code is unchanged — Cursor has always accepted any int, and nothing in this file enables or handles negative offsets. Worse, downstream consumers (build_cursor's _build_next_values/_build_prev_values) compute new offsets via `offset + limit` / `offset - limit` with no lower bound, so negative offsets propagate into emitted cursors. The comment misleads readers into thinking negative-offset support was added and validated here; it should be removed or replaced with a note that offsets are unvalidated.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes when used with a datetime sort key, which is how the audit logs endpoint uses it
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key copies Paginator's numeric implementation: `value = getattr(item, self.key); return int(math.floor(value) ...)`. The endpoint that instantiates it (organization_auditlogs.py) passes `order_by="-datetime"`, so `value` is a `datetime` object and `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`. build_cursor/_build_next_values call get_item_key on the first result of every page that has results, so every request to the audit logs endpoint with `optimized_pagination=true` (by a superuser or org member with global access) will fail with a 500. DateTimePaginator exists precisely because datetimes need the strftime conversion; OptimizedCursorPaginator omits it. Its value_from_cursor has the matching defect (returns the raw cursor value instead of converting millis back to a datetime like DateTimePaginator does), so the cursor comparison in build_queryset would also be broken.

title: Negative-offset "advanced" slicing raises AssertionError on Django QuerySets; the feature is non-functional
body: When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start. Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative indices and raises `AssertionError: Negative indices are not allowed` when the queryset is not already evaluated, because there is no SQL equivalent of a negative OFFSET. The comment claiming "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is simply false. Any client that sends a crafted cursor with a negative offset (Cursor.from_string parses user-supplied strings like `0:-5:0` without validation) to an endpoint using this paginator gets a 500 instead of results. The whole 'advanced features' branch either crashes (negative offset) or is a byte-for-byte copy of BasePaginator.get_result with no behavioral difference (normal offsets), so it provides no optimization at all.

title: New `optimized_pagination` query-parameter code path is undocumented and completely untested
body: This PR adds a new, undocumented request parameter (`optimized_pagination=true`) that switches a public (albeit EXPERIMENTAL) endpoint to a different paginator and enables an 'advanced features' mode, gated on `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`. There are no tests for this path anywhere in the PR, no API documentation for the new parameter, and no explanation of what it actually optimizes (the paginator is functionally identical to the default except for a negative-offset branch that crashes — see other findings). The PR description is just 'Test 2', which suggests this change was not reviewed as a deliberate feature. Given the path is broken for its only configured sort key (datetime), the lack of tests is why that was not caught.

title: zunionstore merges use the default AGGREGATE SUM, corrupting scores of payloads present in both keys
body: Both merge operations (`redis.call("zunionstore", set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` at lines 47 and 53) omit an AGGREGATE argument, so Redis defaults to SUM. When the same span payload exists in both source keys — which happens under Kafka's at-least-once delivery, e.g. a span delivered in one batch lands in the set keyed by its parent while a duplicate delivery in a later batch lands in the merged set — the resulting member's score is the sum of the two end_timestamp_precise values. Since the score is the span's end timestamp used to order the zset, this silently doubles the timestamp. The consequences are that zpopmin eviction (which pops the lowest scores) evicts the wrong spans, and the flush-time iteration order no longer reflects chronological order. The previous sunionstore-based code had no score semantics so this was not an issue; the fix is to pass `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) to both zunionstore calls.

title: New span eviction (zpopmin at 1000) silently drops span data with no metric or log, and can evict the segment's root span
body: The script now evicts the lowest-scored (oldest end_timestamp) members whenever a segment exceeds 1000 spans. Unlike the previous behavior — where oversized segments were skipped at flush time with `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded")` and an error log — this eviction is completely silent: there is no metric, no log, and no marker on the flushed segment, so the ongoing data loss is invisible to operators. Additionally, if the segment/root span is among the evicted members (possible whenever its end_timestamp is not the maximum, e.g. async traces), the segment is flushed without any root span, so no span gets `is_segment=True`, while the `span-buf:hrs:` key still reads "1" and forces the shorter root timeout. The limit is also hardcoded to 1000 in Lua, diverging from the Python-side `max_segment_spans` config (default 1001), which this PR leaves as a dead, unused parameter in SpansBuffer.__init__ (buffer.py line 150) — so the two limits can drift and the config can no longer be tuned from Python at all.

title: Redirect-following loop reduced from 10000 to 1000 iterations with no justification, silently breaking deep segment trees
body: The loop bound was reduced tenfold and the explanatory comment ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. If a redirect chain in `span-buf:sr:{...}` exceeds 1000 hops, the loop exits with a stale `set_span_id`, and line 40 then writes an incorrect redirect mapping for the incoming span — the span is attached to the wrong segment and the trace is silently assembled incorrectly. There is no error signal when the cap is hit (redirect_depth is returned but nothing distinguishes 'resolved' from 'gave up'). Reducing the guarantee 10x needs at least a metric/alert on `redirect_depth == 1000` or a comment explaining why 1000 is safe; neither is present, and the diff gives no reason for the change.

title: Direct `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` access will crash the consumer on messages that lack the field
body: process_batch now reads `end_timestamp_precise` with direct dict indexing. The existing consumer test message did not contain this field until this PR added it, which is evidence that messages without the field are representable in the topic (older producers or schema versions, plus any backlog present at deploy time). A KeyError raised inside process_batch propagates out of the RunTask/multiprocessing strategy and kills the consumer, stalling the whole partition — a much worse failure mode than defaulting the score (e.g. `val.get("end_timestamp_precise") or 0` or falling back to the message timestamp). If the field is guaranteed by the current schema, that guarantee should at least be stated; the current code makes any pre-upgrade buffered message fatal.

title: BasePaginator now silently clamps negative non-prev offsets to 0 instead of erroring
body: The base-class change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` alters behavior for any client that sends a cursor with a negative offset: previously `queryset[offset:stop]` would raise Django's negative-index AssertionError (a clear failure), while now a non-prev cursor with offset < 0 silently returns the first page of results again. A paging client that somehow ends up with a negative offset (or a maliciously crafted cursor) will re-receive page one and can loop over the same data indefinitely instead of surfacing an error. The is_prev branch is left unclamped, so the two paths are inconsistent: prev cursors with negative offsets still crash while next cursors silently reset. If negative offsets are meant to be invalid, both branches should reject them the way OffsetPaginator does with BadPaginationError.

title: Comment claims negative offsets 'enable efficient reverse pagination' but they break the offset arithmetic in this module
body: The new comment on Cursor.offset states that negative offsets enable "efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets". That is not how the module works: _build_next_values and _build_prev_values compute offsets by adding/subtracting the page limit from the current offset, and consumers of these cursors slice querysets where negative offsets are unsupported (raising errors) or silently misbehave. The comment documents a capability that does not exist anywhere in the codebase and will mislead future maintainers into relying on it.

title: paginate() called with unsupported enable_advanced_features kwarg
body: The optimized branch calls self.paginate(..., enable_advanced_features=True). The base endpoint's paginate() helper has an explicit parameter list (request, queryset, paginator_cls, order_by, on_results, cursor_serializer, max_limit, etc.) and does not forward arbitrary **kwargs to the paginator constructor, so this call raises a TypeError. Any superuser (or user with global access) hitting GET /api/0/organizations/<org>/audit-logs/?optimized_pagination=true will get a 500 instead of a paginated response. The flag also needs to be plumbed through properly or the feature removed.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator negative-offset path crashes: Django ORM does not support negative slicing
body: The new 'advanced feature' branch slices the queryset with a negative start (queryset[start_offset:stop] where start_offset = cursor.offset < 0), and both the code comment and the class docstring claim 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. That is false: Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ raises AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported.') for any negative slice bound. So whenever enable_advanced_features=True and a client supplies a cursor with a negative offset, the request fails with an unhandled AssertionError instead of returning a page. The entire advertised feature is broken as written.

title: BasePaginator.get_result now silently clamps negative offsets, changing behavior for all existing paginators
body: The shared BasePaginator.get_result was changed from `stop = offset + limit + extra; queryset[offset:stop]` to `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. For a forward cursor with a negative offset, the ORM previously raised (negative slicing is unsupported), which surfaced malformed/crafted cursors; now it silently rewinds to offset 0 and returns the first page while build_cursor still carries the negative offset into the next cursor (next_offset = offset + limit in _build_next_values), producing corrupt pagination state. For is_prev cursors the negative offset is still passed through and crashes. This is an unrelated behavior change to a base class used by many endpoints, made in a PR whose stated purpose is the spans buffer.

title: Span-count guard removed; eviction is silent and max_segment_spans config is now dead
body: This PR removes the `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans` check from _load_segment_data and replaces it with zpopmin eviction inside the Lua script (add-buffer.lua, `if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin(...)`). Consequences: (1) spans are now silently dropped from segments at insert time with no metric and no log line — previously oversized segments emitted the `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric and an error log, giving operators visibility; (2) the SpansBuffer `max_segment_spans` constructor parameter (default 1001) no longer has any effect, so operators tuning it will see no change, and it disagrees with the hardcoded 1000 in the Lua script. At minimum, the eviction should emit a metric (e.g. spans evicted per segment) and the hardcoded 1000 should be tied to the configurable max_segment_spans.

title: zpopmin eviction can drop the root/segment span while the has-root-span flag stays set
body: Eviction removes the members with the lowest end_timestamp_precise scores. If the root/segment span of a segment has the oldest end timestamp (common when a parent starts before its children), zpopmin will delete it, yet the script still sets the span-buf:hrs:* key to "1" and the segment continues to be flushed on the short root timeout. The flushed segment then contains no span whose span_id equals the segment id, so `is_segment` is false for every span in the output and downstream consumers that rely on a segment span get a headerless segment. There is no guard preventing eviction of the span that defines the set key.

title: Redirect-following loop cap silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 with the explanatory comment deleted
body: The loop bound was changed from `for i = 0, 10000 do` to `for i = 0, 1000 do` and the comment explaining the tradeoff ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was removed. If a trace's redirect chain in span-buf:sr:* exceeds 1000 hops, the loop exits without resolving the final set key, and the script writes the span and the new redirect into an intermediate key, permanently splitting the segment (spans land in two different segment sets that flush separately). This is a silent, unexplained 10x reduction of a documented correctness bound; either restore the bound or justify and document the new limit.

title: end_timestamp_precise accessed with [] although the field is optional in the schema
body: process_batch now reads val["end_timestamp_precise"] on every message. In the ingest-spans v1 schema the *_timestamp_precise fields are optional (they were added later for newer SDKs/Relay versions), so messages produced by older producers or replayed from spillover topics that lack the field will raise KeyError inside the processing strategy, which halts the consumer for that partition rather than skipping or defaulting the message. Use val.get("end_timestamp_precise") with a fallback (e.g. the required end_timestamp or 0) so one old message cannot wedge ingestion.

title: No tests for the new eviction behavior or for any of the pagination changes
body: The PR's headline feature — evicting the oldest spans once a segment exceeds 1000 members — has no test anywhere: test_buffer.py only gained end_timestamp_precise fields on existing fixtures. There is no test that a >1000-span segment is truncated to 1000, that eviction prefers the oldest end_timestamp_precise, or that the segment/root span survives. Separately, the large pagination half of this PR (OptimizedCursorPaginator, the negative-offset paths in BasePaginator/Cursor, and the optimized_pagination branch of the audit-logs endpoint) ships with zero tests, and it is entirely unrelated to the PR's stated purpose of span buffer insertion, which makes it impossible to validate intent from the diff.

title: Comments claim negative offsets are a supported performance optimization
body: The only change to Cursor is two comments asserting that negative offsets are an allowed 'performance optimization' enabling 'efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets'. Nothing in Cursor enforces or implements this, and as noted for the paginator changes, Django-backed paginators cannot slice with negative bounds at all. These comments document behavior that does not exist and will mislead future readers into relying on it.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key crashes on datetime sort keys
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator copies Paginator.get_item_key, which does `int(math.floor(value))` on the item's sort-key attribute. The only caller of this class (organization_auditlogs.py) paginates with order_by="-datetime", so `value` is a `datetime` and `math.floor(datetime)` raises TypeError. DateTimePaginator exists precisely to convert datetimes to epoch-ms; the optimized class also lacks DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor's ms-to-datetime conversion, so a page-2 cursor would compare a timestamp column against a raw float in SQL. Net effect: any request with `optimized_pagination=true` will 500 (page 1 in get_item_key via build_cursor, page 2+ in the where clause).

title: Negative-offset slicing of a Django QuerySet raises AssertionError
body: When `enable_advanced_features` is on and cursor.offset < 0, the code slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start. Django QuerySet slicing explicitly rejects negative indices ("AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported"), so this path raises instead of paginating. The inline comments ("The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically", "safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level") are factually wrong: negative slicing does not work on querysets, and permissions have nothing to do with slicing. The advertised core feature of this paginator cannot function as written.

title: enable_advanced_features kwarg is not accepted by Endpoint.paginate
body: The endpoint calls `self.paginate(..., enable_advanced_features=True)`, but `Endpoint.paginate` in sentry/api/base.py has a fixed keyword signature (paginator_cls, order_by, on_results, max_limit, desc, count_hits, known_hits, max_hits) and constructs the paginator with only those arguments — it does not forward arbitrary kwargs to `paginator_cls`. Unless the base method was also changed (it is not in this PR), this call raises `TypeError: paginate() got an unexpected keyword argument 'enable_advanced_features'`, 500-ing every request that passes `optimized_pagination=true` with the required privileges. Even if the intent is for the flag to reach the paginator, `BasePaginator.__init__` would then need to receive it.

title: No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the endpoint's optimized branch
body: The PR adds ~100 lines of new paginator code (OptimizedCursorPaginator), modifies BasePaginator.get_result's offset handling for every existing paginator, and adds a new request-driven code path to the audit logs endpoint, yet includes zero tests: no unit tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator (including its negative-offset branch), no tests that BasePaginator behavior is unchanged for existing paginators, and no endpoint tests for the `optimized_pagination` parameter (including the authorization gate). Any of the crash modes described in the other findings would have been caught by a single basic test invoking the new code path.

title: Unrelated audit-log pagination feature mixed into a span-buffer PR with no rationale
body: This PR is titled "Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert" and its description is just "Test 2", yet roughly half the diff introduces an unrelated, undocumented API behavior (`optimized_pagination=true` query param enabling a different paginator for superusers/global-access members) to the audit logs endpoint. This makes the change unreviewable as a unit and unrollbackable independently: a revert of the span-buffer work would either take the API change with it or require manual surgery. The audit-log changes should be split into their own PR with a real description, and if kept, the new query param should be documented/validated rather than read ad-hoc from request.GET.

title: Redirect-chain limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000, splitting deep segments
body: The redirect-following loop was reduced from 10000 to 1000 iterations, and the comment explaining the tradeoff ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. If a trace's redirect chain in `span-buf:sr:*` exceeds 1000 hops, the loop now exits without resolving the root, `set_span_id` stays at the 1000th intermediate node, and the span is buffered under a partial key — silently splitting one segment into multiple flushed segments. This is a 10x reduction in the supported chain depth with no accompanying metric, log, or test, so the failure mode is invisible in production.

title: zpopmin eviction can drop the root span, producing segments with no is_segment span
body: Eviction removes the spans with the smallest end_timestamp_precise scores whenever a set exceeds 1000 members. Nothing protects the root/segment span from eviction: if the root span's end timestamp is among the 1000 smallest (possible for out-of-order or async spans), its payload is popped while the `span-buf:hrs:*` flag is still set and the segment is still flushed under the root's key. The flushed segment then contains no span with `is_segment=true`, and every remaining span is stamped with a `segment_id` referring to a span that isn't in the payload — breaking the segment contract for downstream consumers. Evicted spans are also silently dropped with no metric, so the data loss is unobservable.

title: max_segment_spans parameter is now dead and disagrees with the hardcoded Lua limit
body: The Python-side enforcement of `max_segment_spans` (the check in `_load_segment_data` with its `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric and error log) was removed in favor of eviction inside the Lua script, but the `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` constructor parameter was left in place and is now never read. Meanwhile the Lua script hardcodes its own limit of 1000. Consequence: any deployment that configures `max_segment_spans` via options gets silently ignored behavior, and the off-by-one (1001 vs 1000) plus the dead parameter will confuse future readers. The limit should be passed to the script (e.g., as an ARGV) or the parameter removed.

title: Substring match treats negated 'event.type:error' queries as error-focused, applying upsampling to non-error results
body: _is_error_focused_query checks `if "event.type:error" in query` on the raw query string. The Sentry search syntax negation `!event.type:error` contains that substring, so a query explicitly EXCLUDING errors (matching transactions/default events) is classified as error-focused. For the discover dataset, count() is then replaced with sum(sample_weight), producing wrong counts for a query that returns transactions (where sample_weight either doesn't exist or has different semantics). The check needs to parse the query (e.g. via the event_search parser) rather than doing substring matching.

title: Upsampling eligibility is computed from the closure `dataset` and request query, not the dataset/query actually being executed
body: Inside `_get_event_stats(scoped_dataset, query_columns, query, ...)`, the eligibility check calls `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` using the outer `dataset` variable instead of `scoped_dataset`, and the helper inspects `request.GET['query']` instead of the `query` argument. In the dashboard-widget split flow (`get_event_stats_factory`), `_get_event_stats` is invoked with different datasets (e.g. `discover`) and modified queries (e.g. `({query}) AND !event.type:transaction`). The upsampling decision can therefore be made against the wrong dataset/query than the one actually executed, yielding inconsistent counts between the split and non-split paths for the same widget.

title: Accidental 'sentry-repo' git submodule added to the repository
body: The PR adds a file `sentry-repo` containing 'Subproject commit a5d2909...' plus (implicitly) a .gitmodules entry, creating a submodule that points back at the base commit of this same repository. This looks like a local debugging artifact committed by mistake. It will clone an extra copy of the repo for every developer/CI checkout and pollutes the repository layout; it should be removed before merge.

title: invalidate_upsampling_cache is dead code — allowlist changes are never propagated to the cache
body: The PR introduces a 60-second cache of the allowlist eligibility decision and provides `invalidate_upsampling_cache(organization_id, project_ids)` with a docstring saying it 'should be called when the allowlist configuration changes', but nothing in the codebase calls it (no signal receiver on option changes, no hook where the `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` option is updated). Removing a project from the allowlist will leave stale `True` entries for up to 60s, during which queries against it use sum(sample_weight). If prompt invalidation is intended, the wiring is missing; if not, the function is dead code and should be removed.

title: upsampled_count declares result type 'number' while replacing count() whose result type is 'integer'
body: The new SnQLFunction 'upsampled_count' wraps its aggregate in toInt64 but sets `default_result_type="number"`, whereas the count() function it transparently replaces (via the alias `upsampled_count() as count`) is declared `integer`. Downstream consumers that key off the function's result type (zerofill, meta/serialization, response typing) may treat the aliased 'count' field differently than a normal count() query on the same endpoint, changing the API response shape for the same yAxis input. The result type should be 'integer' to match count().

title: _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling swallows all exceptions with bare 'except Exception: pass'
body: The new factory helper wraps both the context lookup and the float conversion in blanket `except Exception: pass`. If `contexts` has an unexpected shape (e.g. a list) or `client_sample_rate` is malformed, the failure is silently hidden, and the event is stored without a sample_rate — leading to tests that quietly exercise the non-upsampling path instead of failing loudly. The guard should be narrow (e.g. isinstance checks) rather than a bare except, and should at minimum surface unexpected error types.

title: The main entry point is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects, including its cache logic, is never tested
body: The unit tests cover only the private helpers (_are_all_projects_error_upsampled with mocked options, transform_query_columns..., _is_error_focused_query, _should_apply_sample_weight_transform). The public function that the endpoint actually calls — which composes the allowlist check, the 60s cache get/set, and the dataset check, and whose cache-hit branch (`cached_result and _should_apply_sample_weight_transform(...)`) is distinct logic — has no coverage. The SnubaParams built in setUp is never used. Cache-related regressions (e.g. caching the composite result instead of eligibility, or the invalidation helper) would not be caught.

title: Substring match misclassifies negated error queries as error-focused, inflating counts
body: _is_error_focused_query checks `"event.type:error" in query`, a raw substring test on the lowercased query string. A discover query that explicitly EXCLUDES errors, e.g. `!event.type:error`, still contains the substring, so the function returns True and `count()` gets rewritten to `sum(sample_weight)`. The query then runs against events with no/NULL sample_weight, producing wrong (likely near-zero or otherwise incorrect) counts. The check must parse the query's filters rather than substring-match, or at minimum not match negated (`!`/`-` prefixed) conditions.

title: Upsampling decision is computed from the closure dataset and raw request query, not the query actually executed
body: Inside `_get_event_stats`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` uses the outer `dataset` module and `request.GET['query']`. But `_get_event_stats` is invoked by the dashboard-split path (`get_event_stats_factory.fn`) with a different `scoped_dataset` (e.g. `discover`) and a rewritten query string such as `({query}) AND !event.type:transaction`. For example, when the request dataset is `metrics_enhanced_performance` and the widget split re-routes an errors-only query to `discover`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` evaluates the metrics dataset and returns False, so an errors-only query is NOT upsampled even though the same query on the errors dataset would be. The eligibility check should receive `scoped_dataset` and the actual `query` argument being executed, not the closure variables.

title: sum(sample_weight) has no NULL fallback; events lacking sample_weight silently count as zero
body: The `upsampled_count` SnQL aggregate is `toInt64(sum(Column("sample_weight")))`. In ClickHouse, `sum` ignores NULLs, so any event in an allowlisted project whose `sample_weight` is not populated (events ingested before this feature rolled out, or events where the `error_sampling` context was absent) contributes 0 to the count. Once a project is added to the allowlist, its historical/unmarked events vanish from counts. There is no `coalesce(sample_weight, 1)` fallback, and the PR contains no production ingestion change that populates `sample_weight` — the only code that derives it is a test factory hack (`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` in sentry/testutils/factories.py), suggesting the column may be NULL for real data. This silently undercounts errors.

title: Global store_event factory change made solely to support this feature's tests, with dead exception handling
body: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` now runs for every `store_event` call in the entire test suite, mutating `sample_rate` on normalized data whenever an `error_sampling` context is present. This changes shared factory behavior for all other tests to support one feature's endpoint tests. Additionally, the `try/except Exception` around chained `.get()` calls is dead code (dict.get does not raise), and the try/except around `float()` silently swallows bad values. The fact that a factory hack is needed also indicates the production ingestion path that should populate `sample_weight` is not part of this PR, so the endpoint tests validate test-injected data rather than the real pipeline.

title: invalidate_upsampling_cache is dead code with no caller, so allowlist changes lag up to 60 seconds
body: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined and documented as the mechanism to keep the 60-second eligibility cache consistent when the `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` option changes, but nothing in this PR calls it (no option-update signal, receiver, or task wiring). Removing a project from the allowlist therefore leaves the endpoint serving inflated upsampled counts for up to 60 seconds after the configuration change. Either wire the invalidation into the option-change path or remove the unused function.

title: Accidental nested repo/submodule committed at repository root
body: This PR adds a `sentry-repo` gitlink pointing at the base commit (a5d2909), which looks like an accidentally committed nested clone of the repository itself. It is unrelated to the feature, will confuse tooling (git treats it as a submodule with no .gitmodules entry), and should not be merged.

title: Top-events ordering and selected columns are not transformed, only the timeseries columns
body: When upsampling is enabled, only `y_axes`/`timeseries_columns` are rewritten to `upsampled_count() as count`, but `orderby=self.get_orderby(request)` and `selected_columns=self.get_field_list(organization, request)` are passed through untouched. If the client orders by `count()` (the common case for top events), the top-N series selection is ranked on the un-upsampled raw count while the displayed series values are upsampled, so the chosen top events and their relative magnitudes can disagree with the charted values.

title: upsampled_count declares result type "number" while count() is "integer"
body: The `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is registered with `default_result_type="number"`, whereas `count()` uses "integer". The SnQL expression is wrapped in `toInt64`, so the actual values are integers, but downstream consumers (zerofill defaults, chart rendering, response meta result types) key off the declared result type and may treat the aliased `count` column as a float, producing inconsistent behavior compared to every other count-like aggregate. It should be "integer" for parity with count().

title: Main entry point is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects and its caching are untested
body: The test class covers only the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`) and the column transform. The public function `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` — including the cache-hit path, cache-miss population, the 60-second TTL, and the combination of the cached allowlist result with the dataset/query check — has no test coverage, despite `setUp` constructing `self.snuba_params` and `self.request` specifically for it (both are then unused). `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is also untested. Since caching is the riskiest part of this change, it needs direct tests.

title: Test comments contradict the asserted values in the upsampling tests
body: In `test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects`, the assertions read `assert data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10  # First bucket has 1 event` and the same for the second bucket. The comments say the bucket has 1 event while the assertion checks the upsampled value of 10 (1 event at client_sample_rate 0.1). A reader will misread the expected behavior; the comments should state that each bucket has 1 stored event upsampled to a weighted count of 10.

title: upsampled_count() is only registered in DiscoverDataset but is enabled for the errors dataset
body: The new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is added only to DiscoverDataset's function_converter, yet `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` in error_upsampling.py returns True whenever the request's dataset is `sentry.snuba.errors`, causing `_get_event_stats` to rewrite `count()` into `upsampled_count() as count` for errors-dataset requests. If the errors dataset's query builder does not include `upsampled_count` in its own function converter (the errors dataset is a separate dataset class and only discover.py was modified), those requests will fail with an invalid/unknown function error for every allowlisted project. Either register the function in the errors dataset's converter as well, or restrict the transform to datasets where the function is actually defined. This path is also untested — all new endpoint tests exercise the default (discover) dataset.

title: Upsampling eligibility is computed against the closure `dataset` and original request query, not the scoped dataset/query actually executed
body: Inside `_get_event_stats(scoped_dataset, ...)`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` uses the outer `dataset` variable and the raw `request.GET["query"]`, ignoring the `scoped_dataset` and `query` arguments. In the dashboard widget discover-split flow (`get_event_stats_factory`), `_get_event_stats` is invoked with `scoped_dataset=discover` and a rewritten query such as `(<query>) AND !event.type:transaction` (errors-only). When the outer dataset is e.g. metrics_enhanced_performance, or the original query string lacks `event.type:error`, the transform is skipped even though the executed query is an error-only discover query that should be upsampled — dashboards on allowlisted projects will show under-sampled counts. The decision must be made from `scoped_dataset` and the actual `query` string passed in.

title: Substring check treats negated `!event.type:error` filters as error-focused queries
body: `_is_error_focused_query` does a raw substring test `"event.type:error" in query`. A discover query like `!event.type:error` (excluding errors, i.e. returning transactions/other events) contains the substring, so `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns True and `count()` is rewritten to `sum(sample_weight)`. For non-error events `sample_weight` is not populated (the helper itself documents that sample_weight doesn't exist for transactions), so the returned count will be wrong (typically 0) instead of the real event count. The check needs to parse the query's filter conditions rather than substring-match, or at least reject negated terms.

title: Endpoint tests don't isolate the 60s eligibility cache, making them order-dependent
body: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches its result under `error_upsampling_eligible:{org_id}:{hash(project_ids)}` for 60 seconds in the shared cache, and nothing in the new test class clears it. Django test transactions roll back org/project id sequences, so consecutive test methods in this class reuse the same org id and project ids. `test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects` caches `True` for that key; if `test_error_upsampling_with_partial_allowlist` (which mocks a partial allowlist and asserts un-upsampled counts of 1) runs afterwards in the same process with a real (non-dummy) cache backend, it reads the cached `True`, applies upsampling, and asserts against counts of 10 — failing. setUp should delete the cache keys (or the helper should be patched), and there are no tests at all for `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` itself, its caching, or `invalidate_upsampling_cache`.

title: invalidate_upsampling_cache is dead code — nothing calls it when the allowlist option changes
body: The docstring of `invalidate_upsampling_cache` says it "should be called when the allowlist configuration changes to ensure cache consistency across the system", but no code in this PR (option update handler, signal, or task) invokes it. In practice the only consistency mechanism is the 60-second TTL, so the function is misleading dead code; either wire it into the option-change path or remove it and document that only the TTL bounds staleness.

title: Equations referencing count() are not transformed, mixing sampled and upsampled values in one response
body: `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only rewrites y-axis columns; `equations=self.get_equation_list(organization, request)` is passed through untouched. A widget using yAxis `count()` plus an equation such as `equation(count() / count_unique(user))` on an allowlisted error query will get an upsampled `count()` series next to an equation computed from the raw sampled `count()`, producing internally inconsistent numbers (e.g. an "events per user" ratio computed from a count 10x smaller than the displayed count). Either rewrite count() inside equations or reject/skip upsampling when equations are present.

title: _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling silently swallows all errors and drops client_sample_rate of 0
body: The new factory helper wraps its logic in two bare `except Exception: pass` blocks, so any structural problem with `contexts` (or an invalid sample rate value) is silently ignored and the event is stored without a sample rate, making downstream upsampled-count assertions pass or fail for the wrong reason. Additionally, `if client_sample_rate:` treats a legitimate value of `0` as absent, so a client_sample_rate of 0 never sets sample_rate. At minimum, narrow the exception handling and compare against None explicitly.

title: Feature-flagged TableWidgetVisualization renders hardcoded empty data
body: In `tableResultComponent`, when the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature flag is on, the new branch renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />` instead of the real result. All of the actual widget data is discarded: `result.data`, `result.meta`, `eventView`, `fields`, `fieldAliases`, loading state, title, custom field renderers, and min column width are simply not passed. Any organization (or dogfooding/staff account) with that flag enabled will see completely empty dashboard/insights table widgets. The flag branch must either be wired to the real table data or not ship until it is; as written it silently breaks every table widget the moment the flag is flipped.

title: fetch_error_details zips error_ids against nodestore dict values, misaligning ids with data
body: `fetch_error_details` builds `node_ids` from `error_ids`, calls `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)`, and then pairs them with `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. `get_multi` returns a dict keyed by node id, and missing nodes are simply absent from the result, so `events.values()` is not guaranteed to be in the same order as `error_ids` and is shorter whenever any lookup misses. When one error event is missing (e.g. expired from nodestore), every subsequent pairing shifts, so an `ErrorEvent` gets the wrong `id`, `title`, `message`, and `timestamp`. Downstream, `gen_request_data` uses these timestamps to interleave error messages chronologically with replay breadcrumbs, so the Seer summary will report the wrong errors at the wrong times. The correct approach is to look up each id individually from the returned mapping (e.g. `data = events.get(node_id)`), not to zip two independently ordered sequences.

title: HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES are only filtered when a search query is active
body: The new `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` filter for `is_segment`, `project_id`, and `received` is applied only inside the branch that runs when `searchQuery.trim()` is non-empty; the early `return sorted;` for an empty search bypasses it. That means these internal noise attributes are shown in the span attributes panel in the normal (no-search) case and only disappear once the user types a search — the opposite of what a constant named HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES implies. The filter should be applied to `sorted` before the empty-search early return.

title: Analytics event recorded before the feature gate and request validation
body: The `analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` call was placed at the very top of `post`, before the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` feature check and before schema validation. As a result the event fires for every request, including ones that are rejected with 404 (feature disabled) and 400 (invalid payload), so the metric counts denied and malformed requests as assemble attempts and cannot be used to measure actual usage of the endpoint. Additionally, for org-auth-token requests `request.user` may not be a real user, so `user_id` can be `None` for a large share of recorded events. Record the event after the feature check (and ideally after the body validates) so the analytics reflect real assemble attempts.

title: UseTraceItemAttributeBaseProps doc comment says only LOGS is supported, but SPANS is now used
body: The doc comment on `UseTraceItemAttributeBaseProps.traceItemType` (moved into `explore/types.tsx` in this PR) states "The trace item type supported by the endpoint, currently only supports LOGS." However this same PR wires the hook family up for spans: `TransactionNameSearchBar` and `TraceItemSearchQueryBuilder` now pass `traceItemType: TraceItemDataset.SPANS` to `useGetTraceItemAttributeValues`/`useGetTraceItemAttributeKeys`. The comment is now wrong and will mislead future callers into avoiding the spans path.

title: Feature-flagged TableWidgetVisualization branch renders hardcoded empty data
body: In tableResultComponent, when the 'use-table-widget-visualization' feature flag is enabled, the code renders <TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} /> instead of the actual table results. The new component is never wired to `result.data`, `result.meta`, `fields`, `fieldAliases`, or the loading state, so any organization with the flag enabled will see a completely blank table widget in dashboards (real query results are discarded). The real data mapping only exists in the non-flagged StyledSimpleTableChart path. Either pass the actual data/columns to TableWidgetVisualization or don't ship the flag branch until it's wired up.

title: get_merged_pr_single_issue_template calls PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title, but _truncate_title is defined on CommitContextIntegration
body: In this diff, `_truncate_title` is added as a staticmethod on `CommitContextIntegration`, but `get_merged_pr_single_issue_template` invokes it as `PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title(title)`. PRCommentWorkflow is the workflow class used by the GitHub/GitLab integrations and is not a subclass of CommitContextIntegration, so this lookup raises AttributeError at runtime whenever a merged-PR comment is generated, breaking PR comment posting for GitHub and GitLab. The call should reference `CommitContextIntegration._truncate_title` (or be inlined).

title: fetch_error_details zips error_ids against events.values(), mispairing IDs with data
body: fetch_error_details builds `node_ids` from `error_ids`, fetches them via `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)`, then pairs results with `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. get_multi returns a dict keyed by node_id containing only the nodes that were found (and not necessarily in the input order). If any node is missing, or the dict iteration order differs from the input order, each error_id gets paired with the wrong event's data, producing incorrect titles/messages and attributing errors to the wrong event IDs in the Seer summary. It should iterate over the node_id->data mapping (e.g. zip(node_ids, ...) with lookups per id, or `events.get(node_id)`) so IDs and payloads stay aligned.

title: Nodestore event timestamps are strings but are compared against numeric breadcrumb timestamps
body: fetch_error_details reads `timestamp=data.get("timestamp", 0.0)` straight from the nodestore payload, where event timestamps are stored as ISO-8601 strings (not numbers). gen_request_data then compares `error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)`, i.e. str < float, which raises TypeError in Python 3 as soon as there is at least one error event and one breadcrumb event, turning the summarize endpoint into a 500. The nodestore timestamp needs to be parsed to a numeric epoch value (and note the default of 0.0 is also inconsistent with the string type) before sorting/interleaving.

title: HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES are only filtered out while a search query is active
body: The new HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES list ('is_segment', 'project_id', 'received') is only applied inside the branch that runs when `searchQuery.trim()` is non-empty; when the search box is empty the code returns `sorted` unfiltered. That means these internal attributes are visible in the default span-attributes view but disappear as soon as the user types anything, which is inconsistent and almost certainly not the intent of a constant named HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES. The filter should be applied to the sorted list regardless of whether a search query is present.

title: Shipped migrations 0917/0920 replaced with no-ops and their test deleted; conversion now depends entirely on 0921
body: Both 0917 and 0920 convert_org_saved_searches_to_views migrations are gutted to `return` with a comment pointing at 0921_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views_rerevised.py, and the migration test for 0917 is deleted. These migrations are marked is_post_deployment and dated months ago, so some environments (self-hosted installs, staging) may have already recorded them as applied; more importantly, if migration 0921 is not present in this branch's migration chain, organization-level saved searches will silently never be converted to group search views and the data migration coverage is gone. This should be verified (and ideally kept as an explicit no-op with a linked ticket) before merging.

title: Feedback summary endpoint (backed by an LLM call) is fetched on every feedback list page view with only a 5s staleTime
body: useFeedbackSummary fires a request to /organizations/<slug>/feedback-summary/ whenever the feedback list mounts for orgs with 'user-feedback-ai-summaries', with staleTime of only 5 seconds and no other caching or debouncing. The backend usecase (generate_summary) performs an LLM completion, so navigating to or refreshing the feedback list can trigger a new LLM generation per visit per user, which is both slow (the UI shows a placeholder) and expensive. Consider a much longer staleTime/cache, or generating the summary server-side with caching keyed on the query/window.

title: Tests no longer exercise the application/reports+json custom parser
body: The rewritten tests post all reports with the default JSON content type; the previous versions used content_type="application/reports+json" to cover BrowserReportsJSONParser, which is the media type real browsers use for the Reporting API. Since the endpoint's parser_classes list is the only thing making that content type work, a regression there (e.g. parser removed or media_type typo) would no longer be caught. Add at least one test that posts with the reports+json content type.

title: fetch_error_details misaligns error IDs with nodestore results via zip on dict values
body: In fetch_error_details, `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a dict keyed by node id, and the code builds ErrorEvent objects with `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. Dict values are not guaranteed to be in the same order as the requested node ids, and any node that is missing (deleted/expired event) is simply absent from the dict, which shifts every subsequent pairing. The result is that error titles, messages, and timestamps can be attributed to the wrong event id (the `id` field of ErrorEvent), and the filtering `if data is not None` does not fix the offset. The code should look up each event by its node id (e.g. `events.get(node_id)`) instead of zipping positional lists.

title: Error event timestamps read from nodestore are ISO strings, causing TypeError when compared with float breadcrumb timestamps
body: fetch_error_details builds ErrorEvent objects with `timestamp=data.get("timestamp", 0.0)` from raw nodestore event data. Nodestore event payloads store `timestamp` as an ISO-8601 string (and the 0.0 fallback is a float), while breadcrumb events from replay segments carry float timestamps. Downstream, `get_request_data` sorts error_events by timestamp (`error_events.sort(key=lambda x: x["timestamp"])`) and `gen_request_data` compares `error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)`, which mixes str and float operands and raises TypeError in Python 3 (both in the sort when a defaulted 0.0 is present, and in every comparison against a float breadcrumb timestamp). This will make the summarize-breadcrumbs endpoint raise a 500 for any replay that has associated error events. Timestamps should be parsed to floats (e.g. via `datetime.fromisoformat` / `Event.timestamp`) before use.

title: Feature-flagged table widget renders an empty table, discarding the actual query results
body: In tableResultComponent, when `organization.features.includes('use-table-widget-visualization')` is true, the code renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />` and completely ignores `result.data`, `result.meta`, `fields`, `loading`, and `fieldAliases` that the non-flagged `StyledSimpleTableChart` branch uses. Any organization with the `use-table-widget-visualization` flag enabled will see empty dashboard table widgets (no headers, no rows) regardless of the underlying data. Either the flag branch should be removed until real data wiring is implemented, or the actual result data should be passed to TableWidgetVisualization.

title: get_merged_pr_single_issue_template references PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title, but _truncate_title is defined on CommitContextIntegration
body: The new helpers `_truncate_title`, `get_environment_info`, and `get_merged_pr_single_issue_template` were all added to the `CommitContextIntegration` class (the diff hunk places them at the end of that class, immediately before `class OpenPRCommentWorkflow`). However, `get_merged_pr_single_issue_template` calls `PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title(title)`, and the GitHub/GitLab integration subclasses call `self.get_environment_info(issue)` and `self.get_merged_pr_single_issue_template(...)` from within `GitHubPRCommentWorkflow`/`GitlabPRCommentWorkflow` (which derive from `PRCommentWorkflow`, the OpenPRCommentWorkflow-based class, not from CommitContextIntegration). Unless PRCommentWorkflow also inherits from CommitContextIntegration, these lookups raise AttributeError whenever a merged-PR suspect-issue comment is generated, breaking the PR comment workflow. The helpers should live on (or be reached through) the workflow class, e.g. via `self.integration._truncate_title(...)`.

title: Analytics event recorded before the feature-flag check and request validation
body: The `preprod_artifact.api.assemble` analytics event is recorded at the top of `post()`, before the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` feature check (which returns 404) and before `validate_preprod_artifact_schema` (which returns 400). This means the event fires for every request to the endpoint, including requests from organizations without the feature and requests with malformed bodies that never reach assembly. The analytics data will overcount usage and include unauthenticated-shape/invalid traffic, defeating its purpose as a usage metric. Record the event after the feature gate and schema validation succeed.

title: Mutual-exclusion validation of age/timestamp uses truthiness, so age=0 or timestamp=0 bypasses it
body: `validate_timestamp` rejects the report when `self.initial_data.get("age")` is truthy, and `validate_age` rejects when `self.initial_data.get("timestamp")` is truthy. Per the Reporting API, `age` is a millisecond count that can legitimately be 0 (report generated immediately), and timestamp 0 is permitted by the field's `min_value=0`. When age=0 and a timestamp is also present (or vice versa), the falsy check passes and the report is accepted with both fields, violating the intended either-or invariant between the Working Draft and Editor's Draft formats. Use `"age" in self.initial_data` / `"timestamp" in self.initial_data` instead of truthiness.

title: query() mutates the caller's selected_columns list in place
body: In `ourlogs.query`, when orderby is `[-timestamp]` or `[timestamp]`, the function appends `tags[sentry.timestamp_precise,number]` to `selected_columns` directly. This mutates the list passed in by the caller, so the hidden tie-breaking column leaks into any downstream use of that same list (response meta/fields, caching of the field list, or repeated calls that would append the column again on the same list). Build a new list (e.g. `selected_columns = [*selected_columns, precise_timestamp]`) instead of appending to the input parameter.

title: Failed feedback summaries render as an empty summary panel instead of being hidden
body: `tooFewFeedbacks` is computed as `data.numFeedbacksUsed === 0 && !data.success`, so when the summary generation fails with feedbacks present (numFeedbacksUsed > 0, success: false, summary: null), the hook reports tooFewFeedbacks=false and isError=false. FeedbackSummary then falls through to rendering the 'Feedback Summary' box with `summary` of null, showing users a permanently empty summary card rather than hiding it or surfacing an error state. The success/failure distinction should be based on `data.success` (or the summary being non-null), not just on the feedback count.

title: KeyError when Integration has no 'sender' in metadata during install check
body: GitHubInstallation.dispatch accesses `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` unconditionally on the path where an Integration row exists but no OrganizationIntegration does. The `sender` key is only written when the integration was created from the installation webhook (or when `state.get("sender")` was set, which nothing in this pipeline does). Integrations created through the pipeline itself (e.g. when the installation webhook was delayed, lost, or raced with the pipeline finish), or legacy Integration rows created before sender tracking, have no `sender` in metadata. When such an installation is later added to another organization (Integration exists, OrganizationIntegration deleted after uninstall, Integration still ACTIVE), this line raises KeyError and the user gets a 500 instead of the intended error/success page. Additionally, `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user")` returns None for pipelines created before this step existed, silently failing the comparison. Use `.get()` chains with sensible defaults for both lookups.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer tests the 404/'installation could not be found' branch
body: The test previously verified that a 404 from GitHub's `/app/installations/{id}` endpoint surfaces the message "The GitHub installation could not be found." (raised by GitHubIntegrationProvider.build_integration). After this change, the test sends a deliberately wrong `state` value ('ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05') and only asserts the state-mismatch message "Invalid installation request."; the 404 stub added via `responses.replace` is never exercised because the pipeline errors out at the OAuth step before build_integration runs. The `IntegrationError("The GitHub installation could not be found.")` branch now has zero test coverage, and the test name no longer describes what it tests. Add a test that completes the OAuth step with a valid state and a 404 installation lookup.

title: No positive test for the sender-match path (OAuth user == installer)
body: test_github_user_mismatch only covers the failure case (webhook sender 'attacker' vs OAuth user 'octocat'). There is no test where the webhook-created Integration's `metadata["sender"]["login"]` matches the OAuth-authenticated user and the install proceeds successfully through the new check in GitHubInstallation.dispatch. Since no existing test drives the flow through an existing webhook-created Integration with a matching sender, a regression that inverts or breaks the comparison (e.g. always erroring, or a KeyError-style crash being masked) would not be caught by the suite.

title: OAuth `code` is not bound to the pipeline, allowing replay against a different pipeline
body: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, the `state` is validated against `pipeline.signature` and the `code` is exchanged for a token, but nothing verifies that the `code` was issued for *this* pipeline's authorize request. The tests show `pipeline.signature` is deterministic and identical across different organizations and users (the same value '9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3' works for org 1, org 2, and different users), so `state` is not an instance-specific secret. Because the token exchange uses the global GitHub app client credentials, an attacker who intercepts a victim's authorization `code` (e.g. via Referer leakage or logs from the callback URL `.../extensions/github/setup/?code=...&state=...`) can replay it on their own valid pipeline before the victim does: the state check passes (it is their own pipeline), the token exchange succeeds (single-use code, first exchange wins), and `github_authenticated_user` is then bound to the *victim's* GitHub login — satisfying the new sender-match check and allowing the attacker's Sentry organization to link an installation installed by the victim. Consider binding a per-pipeline nonce into the authorize request/state and validating it, and/or verifying that the code was issued with the same state value on exchange.

title: KeyError crash when Integration metadata has no 'sender'
body: GitHubInstallation.dispatch accesses `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` directly. Any Integration row whose metadata lacks a 'sender' key will raise an unhandled KeyError and return a 500 to the user instead of the error page. This is reachable in at least two ways: (1) GitHub integrations created before this change (or by any path that didn't record a sender, e.g. a missed/partial installation webhook) have no 'sender' in metadata; (2) both Integration lookups (`Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` at line 477 and the second lookup at line 494) are not filtered by provider, so an ACTIVE integration from a different provider whose external_id happens to collide with the GitHub installation id will be fetched and its metadata (which never contains 'sender') will be dereferenced. The lookup should filter on provider='github' and use metadata.get('sender', {}).get('login') with a defined failure policy.

title: User verification is skipped when the Integration row doesn't exist yet
body: The installer-identity check (comparing the OAuth-authenticated GitHub user with metadata['sender']['login']) only runs on the branch where an Integration row already exists (i.e. the installation webhook has already been processed). When `Integration.DoesNotExist` is raised, dispatch goes straight to `pipeline.next_step()`, and the pipeline later creates the integration via build_integration with no sender and no verification at all. Since webhook delivery is asynchronous and not guaranteed, there is a race window (or a permanent gap, if the webhook is dropped) in which anyone who knows an installation_id can complete the Sentry-side setup for a GitHub installation they did not perform — exactly the scenario this PR is meant to prevent. The verification should not depend on the webhook having already created the Integration row.

title: Unhandled exceptions from token exchange and get_user_info cause 500s
body: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, `safe_urlopen(...)` (line 423) and `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` (line 434) are called without try/except. Network errors from safe_urlopen, non-2xx responses, or an ApiError raised by get_user_info when GitHub rejects the token will propagate and produce an unhandled 500 on a user-facing, attacker-influenceable endpoint (an attacker controls whether the `code` is valid or replayed). Only the happy-path failures (missing access_token in body, missing 'login' key) are handled; exceptions should be caught and routed to the same error() page.

title: GitHub App install flow now hard-depends on GitHub OAuth app credentials being configured
body: OAuthLoginView unconditionally calls `ghip.get_oauth_client_id()` / `get_oauth_client_secret()` and redirects to the OAuth authorize URL. Previously, installing the GitHub App did not require the separate GitHub OAuth App options to be set. On deployments (notably self-hosted) where the GitHub App is configured but the OAuth client id/secret options are empty, the installation flow will now redirect users to a GitHub authorize URL with a blank client_id (GitHub shows an error page) or fail when the provider raises on missing credentials, breaking all new GitHub integration installs. There is no feature flag or fallback for this new dependency.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the installation-not-found (404) path
body: The rewritten test uses a hardcoded state of 'ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05', which differs from the pipeline signature '9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3' used by every other test with an equivalent flow. The request therefore fails at the state-mismatch check in OAuthLoginView and renders the generic 'Invalid installation request.' error, so the assertion passes without ever reaching build_integration. The `responses.replace(..., status=404)` stub for /app/installations/{id} is now dead code, and the specific 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' error message from the 404 branch (which the old test asserted) is no longer covered by any test.

title: KeyError/500 when existing Integration has no 'sender' in metadata
body: GitHubInstallation.dispatch accesses `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` unconditionally when an Integration exists but no OrganizationIntegration does. However, `build_integration` only stores `metadata["sender"]` when `state.get("sender")` is set, so Integrations can legitimately exist without a "sender" key (e.g. created through the pipeline when the installation webhook never supplied a sender, or legacy rows). For such installations this line raises KeyError and the user gets a 500 instead of a graceful error page. The lookup should use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and treat a missing sender as a failed verification.

title: Installer verification is skipped when the installation webhook has not yet created the Integration
body: The new user-identity check (comparing `github_authenticated_user` against `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`) only runs on the branch where the Integration row already exists. That row is created by the GitHub `installation` webhook; if the webhook is delayed or lost, `Integration.objects.get` raises DoesNotExist and dispatch calls `pipeline.next_step()` with no verification at all, and `build_integration` later creates the Integration without a sender. This means the security control this PR is meant to add can be bypassed by simply racing the webhook (or by webhook delivery failure), which is a common condition in practice. The verification (or an explicit 'installation not yet registered, retry' failure) should also apply on the DoesNotExist path, or the pipeline should wait/retry until the webhook-created Integration is visible.

title: OAuth 'state' is a static per-provider value, so the CSRF/state check provides no real protection
body: OAuthLoginView uses `pipeline.signature` as the OAuth2 `state` and validates the callback with `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature`. `Pipeline.signature` is a deterministic value derived from the pipeline/provider name (the tests hard-code the same state, `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`, across different users, organizations, and sessions), so it is identical for every user of the deployment. Any user who starts their own GitHub install flow sees this value in the authorize redirect URL and can therefore forge a valid callback for any other user's pipeline. Concretely: an attacker obtains their own OAuth `code` (authenticating as themselves), then gets a victim's browser to hit the setup URL with that code plus the known state; the token exchange succeeds in the victim's pipeline and binds the attacker's GitHub login as `github_authenticated_user`, after which the installer-identity check passes and the integration is linked. The state must be a per-pipeline/per-session random nonce (stored in pipeline state and compared on callback), not a shared constant, for the check described in the PR description to be meaningful.

title: Unhandled exceptions from get_user_info and token exchange produce a 500 instead of the error page
body: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` is not wrapped in error handling. `get_user_info` performs an HTTP call to GitHub's /user endpoint and raises ApiError on any non-2xx response (e.g. revoked token, GitHub 5xx, secondary rate limit); `safe_urlopen` for the token exchange can likewise raise on connection errors. These exceptions propagate out of the pipeline view and result in an unhandled 500 error rather than the intended `github-integration-failed.html` error page shown for the other failure modes. The calls should be inside the try/except (or a separate one) that falls back to `error(request, self.active_organization)`.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the 404 / 'installation could not be found' path
body: The test previously asserted `b"The GitHub installation could not be found."`, i.e. that build_integration's IntegrationError on a GitHub 404 is surfaced. After the change it asserts `b"Invalid installation request."` because the second request uses a state (`ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`) that does not match the pipeline signature, so the flow fails at the state check and the `responses.replace(..., status=404)` stub for `/app/installations/<id>` is never exercised. The renamed test now effectively duplicates a state-mismatch test, and the 'installation could not be found' regression path (IntegrationError raised in build_integration on GitHub 404) has no coverage. A separate test with a valid state and a 404 stub should be added, along with a dedicated test for the state-mismatch case.

title: `queued` default is evaluated once at import time, not per instance
body: The dataclass field `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` captures the timestamp at module import time, so every `AssignmentSource` created via `from_integration()` or `from_dict()` without an explicit `queued` value gets the same process-start timestamp instead of the time the assignment change actually occurred. The field is serialized via `to_dict()` into the `sync_assignee_outbound` task kwargs, so any use of `queued` for observability, debugging, or staleness checks will be silently wrong. The fix is `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. The new unit test (`test_to_dict`) only asserts `queued is not None`, so it passes despite the bug.

title: Base `should_sync` signature widened positionally but no provider subclasses were updated
body: `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync` now takes a second positional argument `sync_source`, and `sync_assignee_outbound` (the task) calls `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)` with two positional arguments. The PR changes no provider integration files (Jira, VSTS, GitLab, etc.). Any integration subclass that overrides `should_sync(self, attribute)` with the old single-parameter signature (the pattern this PR itself uses for the base-class override pair in this file) will raise `TypeError: should_sync() takes 2 positional arguments but 3 were given` inside the task, causing the assignee sync task to fail and retry for that provider. Every override in the codebase must be updated or verified to accept the extra argument before merging.

title: `assignment_source` plumbed into `sync_status_outbound` signature but never passed by any caller
body: The abstract method `sync_status_outbound` gained an `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None` parameter, but no call site anywhere in this PR (or the changed task) passes `assignment_source` to `sync_status_outbound`, and no implementation was updated to consume it. Since the PR is titled "Breaks issue sync cycles" and status sync is part of the same inbound-webhook/outbound-update loop described in the issue, this is incomplete plumbing: status sync cycles are not actually prevented, and the parameter is dead code that suggests protection that does not exist.

title: Cycle suppression is per-integration, dropping syncs to sibling linked issues of the same integration
body: In `sync_group_assignee_outbound`, the `AssignmentSource` only carries `integration_id`, and `should_sync` suppresses the outbound sync for every external issue belonging to the source integration. When a Sentry group is linked to multiple external issues from the same integration (multiple GroupLink rows referencing different ExternalIssues of one integration), an inbound webhook from one of those issues now silently prevents the assignee change from propagating to the other linked issues of that integration — a behavior regression from before, where each linked issue was updated. Carrying the triggering external issue id in `AssignmentSource` would scope the suppression correctly.

title: `from_dict` fails open and does not validate the `queued` type
body: `from_dict` returns `None` on `ValueError`/`TypeError`, and `sync_assignee_outbound` then proceeds with `assignment_source=None`, which re-enables the outbound sync — i.e., the exact sync-cycle bug this PR fixes silently returns if the dict is malformed. Additionally, a dict where `queued` is a string (e.g., after a JSON round-trip through the broker, since `to_dict()` emits a `datetime`) is accepted without complaint, producing an `AssignmentSource` whose `queued` field holds a string rather than a datetime. At minimum the `queued` value should be parsed/validated, and the fail-open behavior should be logged so operators can detect when cycle protection is being bypassed.

title: No test that other integrations still receive the outbound sync when a source is set
body: The PR's stated goal is that suppressing the sync to the originating integration "should still allow other integrations to propagate changes outward," but there is no test for that path. `test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration` only covers the suppression case (single integration, `assert_not_called`). A test with two linked integrations (source = integration A, asserting integration B's `sync_assignee_outbound` is still called with the assignment source) is needed to lock in the cross-integration propagation behavior and to catch regressions where the suppression is over-broad. There is also no end-to-end test of `sync_group_assignee_inbound` producing an `AssignmentSource` that suppresses the echo through the real task path.

title: AssignmentSource.to_dict() puts a raw datetime into Celery task kwargs, which breaks under JSON task serialization
body: sync_group_assignee_outbound calls sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async with kwargs containing assignment_source.to_dict(), and to_dict() (via dataclasses.asdict) includes the 'queued' field as a datetime object.
