If the Celery broker/worker uses JSON task serialization, serializing these kwargs raises TypeError, which propagates up through GroupAssignee.objects.assign/deassign and fails the entire inbound webhook assignment (including the DB-side effects if inside a transaction). Even when pickle is used, the round-trip through from_dict is inconsistent: a JSON-serialized 'queued' comes back as a string that is never validated or coerced. Since 'queued' is never read anywhere, the simplest fix is to remove the field, or serialize it as an ISO string.

title: Dataclass default 'queued: datetime = timezone.now()' is evaluated once at import time
body: The default value for the 'queued' field is computed when the class definition is executed (module import time), not when an instance is created. Every AssignmentSource created without an explicit 'queued' therefore carries the same import-time timestamp, making the field misleading if it is ever used for staleness/observability. It should be declared with dataclasses.field(default_factory=timezone.now). The added test (assert result.get('queued') is not None) passes either way and does not catch this.

title: sync_status_outbound abstract signature gains an unused 'assignment_source' parameter with inconsistent naming
body: The abstract sync_status_outbound now accepts assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None, but no caller in this PR ever passes it, no implementation is updated to use it, and status syncing has no assignment-source cycle-breaking logic (should_sync is never called with a source for status keys). It also uses a different parameter name ('assignment_source') than the sibling should_sync method ('sync_source') for the same concept. This is dead, misleading API surface: either wire status sync through the same source-checking path or drop the parameter until it is implemented.

title: No test that a different integration still receives outbound assignee sync when an assignment_source is set
body: The new test only covers the suppression case (assignment_source matching the target integration blocks sync). The core guarantee stated in the should_sync comment — 'This should still allow other integrations to propagate changes outward' — is untested: there is no test where a group is linked to external issues from two integrations, an inbound change sourced from integration A is applied, and the outbound sync to integration B still fires. A regression that over-suppresses (e.g., comparing against the wrong id or dropping the source check entirely for non-matching cases) would not be caught by the current test suite.

title: AssignmentSource.queued default is evaluated once at import time, not per instance
body: The dataclass field `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` evaluates `timezone.now()` when the module is imported, so every `AssignmentSource` created via `from_integration` (which never passes `queued`) gets the process-start timestamp instead of the time the change was actually queued. The field should be declared with `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. Any future logic that relies on `queued` (e.g. expiring stale assignment sources to break long-running sync cycles, or logging latency) will be silently wrong, and the new test `test_to_dict` only asserts `queued is not None`, which masks the defect. Additionally, embedding a `datetime` in `assignment_source_dict` (via `to_dict()` in `sync_group_assignee_outbound.apply_async` kwargs) makes the task kwargs non-JSON-serializable; if the deployment's Celery task serializer is JSON, `apply_async` will raise, breaking all outbound assignee sync. Since `queued` is never consumed, either drop it or serialize it explicitly.

title: from_dict performs no type validation, so malformed data silently disables cycle protection
body: `AssignmentSource.from_dict` only catches `ValueError`/`TypeError` from the constructor, but the dataclass constructor performs no type checking. A dict like `{"source_name": "x", "integration_id": "123"}` (string id) or one where `queued` is a string (which is exactly what a JSON round-trip of `to_dict()` produces, since `datetime` serializes to a string) is accepted without error and yields an `AssignmentSource` whose `integration_id` is a `str`. In `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync`, `sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id` then compares `str` to `int`, always evaluates False, and the same-integration outbound sync is NOT suppressed — reintroducing the sync loop this PR is meant to fix, with no error or log. `from_dict` should validate/coerce the types (or at minimum compare with `int(sync_source.integration_id)` at the check site).

title: Abstract sync_assignee_outbound signature not updated for the new assignment_source kwarg
body: The task `sync_assignee_outbound` now calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(external_issue, user, assign=assign, assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)`, and the abstract method `sync_status_outbound` in the same class was explicitly updated to declare `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`. However, the abstract `sync_assignee_outbound` (line 397) was NOT updated — it only tolerates the new kwarg through `**kwargs: Any`. Any provider implementation that shadows this method without `**kwargs` (or without an `assignment_source` parameter) will raise `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'assignment_source'` at runtime inside the Celery task; because `TypeError` is not in the task's retry exclude list, it will be retried 5 times before failing, generating noise and never syncing. The abstract signature should declare the parameter explicitly so implementers are forced to accept it.

title: No test covers the actual inbound-webhook suppression path or cross-integration propagation
body: The only suppression test (`test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration`) constructs the `AssignmentSource` by hand and passes it directly to `GroupAssignee.objects.assign`, bypassing the real webhook plumbing. The end-to-end path the PR claims to fix — `sync_group_assignee_inbound` building the source from the integration, passing it through `GroupAssignee.objects.assign`, through `sync_group_assignee_outbound.apply_async` (including the dict serialization/deserialization via `AssignmentSource.to_dict`/`from_dict`), and finally the `should_sync` suppression in the task — is never exercised. This is exactly where the `from_dict` type/serialization defects would surface. Additionally, there is no test that a *different* integration's external issue still receives the outbound sync when an `assignment_source` is present (the "should still allow other integrations to propagate changes outward" behavior), so a regression that over-blocks propagation would go undetected.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler no longer implements required abstract methods and will fail on instantiation
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler was changed from subclassing DetectorHandler (where it implemented `evaluate`) to subclassing StatefulDetectorHandler with just `pass`. StatefulDetectorHandler declares four abstract members that must be overridden: `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the newly added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. Since none of them are implemented, calling `group_type.detector_handler(self)` in `Detector.detector_handler` (triggered from `process_detectors` for any Detector whose type is "metric_alert_fire") will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class`. There is no try/except around handler construction or evaluation in `process_detectors`, so a single metric-alert detector in the input list will crash processing of the whole data packet. Either implement the abstract methods, or keep this handler on the non-stateful base until the abstraction is built.

title: TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe builds the expected occurrence with the wrong group key
body: In TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe, the expected occurrence is built via `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)`, but the handler is then evaluated with group_key "group_key". `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` sets `fingerprint=handler.build_fingerprint(group_key)`, so the expected occurrence's fingerprint is `["<detector_id>:val1"]` while the actual result produced by `evaluate_group_key_value("group_key", ...)` will have fingerprint `["<detector_id>:group_key"]`. Since IssueOccurrence is a dataclass compared field-by-field, the `== expected_result` assertion on the DetectorEvaluationResult should fail (or, if it somehow passes, the occurrence payload is not actually being validated). The expected occurrence must be built with group_key "group_key" (and ideally the actual value passed to the evaluation, 10, instead of 6). The same pattern appears in test_state_results_multi_group, where the expected occurrence for "group_2" is built with value 6 although the packet contains 10 — this only passes because `value` is ignored by the mock builder, which means the tests don't actually verify the value is propagated to `build_occurrence_and_event_data`.

title: Stale docstring: evaluate still documented as returning a list
body: The docstring of StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate says "Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`", but this PR changed the return type to `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`. The docstring should be updated so callers/subclass implementers are not misled about the contract (in particular that results are keyed by group key and duplicates are silently collapsed rather than logged, which was the previous behavior in process_detectors).

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler cannot be instantiated: abstract methods not implemented
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler with a bare `pass`, but StatefulDetectorHandler declares four abstract members (`counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, `build_occurrence_and_event_data`), none of which are implemented. Because MetricAlertFire.detector_handler is set to this class and `Detector.detector_handler` (src/sentry/workflow_engine/models/detector.py:86) does `group_type.detector_handler(self)`, any Detector row whose `type` slug resolves to `metric_alert_fire` will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class ...` inside process_detectors, and the exception is not caught anywhere in that path. The old code returned a working (if stubbed) DetectorHandler; the new code turns a previously-valid detector type into an unhandled crash. Either implement the abstract members or don't register the class as a detector_handler yet.

title: TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe builds the expected occurrence with the wrong group key
body: In `TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe`, the expected occurrence/event_data are built via `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)`, but `evaluate_group_key_value` is then called with group key `"group_key"`. The handler's `build_occurrence_and_event_data` will therefore produce an occurrence whose fingerprint is `"<detector_id>:group_key"`, while the expected occurrence's fingerprint is `"<detector_id>:val1"` (the fingerprint is derived from the group key in `build_mock_occurrence_and_event`). Unless IssueOccurrence equality is trivially true, this assertion fails; if it does pass, it means occurrence equality is not actually being verified, so the test asserts nothing meaningful about the produced occurrence. The expected occurrence should be built with `"group_key"` to match the group key being evaluated.

title: Unguarded cross-enum conversion PriorityLevel(new_status) from DetectorPriorityLevel
body: `evaluate_group_key_value` converts the internal `DetectorPriorityLevel` to the issue `PriorityLevel` via `PriorityLevel(new_status)`, relying on the two unrelated enums having identical integer values. If `DetectorPriorityLevel` ever gains or changes a value that has no `PriorityLevel` counterpart, this raises an uncaught `ValueError` at evaluation time, breaking the detector. Consider an explicit mapping between the two enums (or guarding the conversion) so the failure mode is intentional rather than incidental.

title: Stale docstring: evaluate still documented as returning a list
body: The docstring on `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` says "Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`", but the signature and implementation were changed in this PR to return `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`. The docstring should be updated so callers reading it aren't misled about the return type and the duplicate-group-key dedupe semantics.

title: Tests never verify the value passed to build_occurrence_and_event_data; wrong value used in multi-group test
body: `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` ignores its `value` argument entirely, so no test asserts that the correct group value is forwarded to the new `build_occurrence_and_event_data` hook. This is evidenced by `test_state_results_multi_group`, which builds the expected occurrence for group_2 with `value=6` even though the data packet contains `{"group_2": 10}` — the test passes only because the builder discards the value. If a real handler includes the value in evidence/subtitle, this gap would hide a wrong-value bug. The mock builder should incorporate `value` (e.g. into `evidence_data` or `subtitle`) so the forwarded value is actually asserted.

title: evaluate() docstring still says it returns a list after the signature changed to a dict
body: In src/sentry/workflow_engine/processors/detector.py, the docstring of StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate (around line 229-233) reads "Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`." This PR changed the return type of evaluate to dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult] (both on the abstract DetectorHandler and the stateful implementation), but the docstring was not updated. Anyone implementing the abstract hook based on the docstring would build and return a list, which would break process_detectors (it iterates detector_results.values() and keys results by group_key) and fail type checks. Update the docstring to describe the dict keyed by group key.

title: get_monitor_environment_context builds a modified config copy but returns the unmodified monitor.config
body: In `get_monitor_environment_context` (new file incident_occurrence.py), line 160 copies the monitor config and line 161-162 replaces `schedule_type` with its human-readable display value, but line 168 returns `monitor_environment.monitor.config` — the original, unmodified dict — instead of the local `config` variable. The local `config` is dead code and the monitor context attached to the produced occurrence event always contains the raw schedule type value. This bug was carried over from the previous location in mark_failed.py; since this PR touches and moves the function, it should be fixed by returning `config` instead.

title: Public functions removed from mark_failed module with no compatibility aliases or test updates in this PR
body: This PR deletes the module-level functions `mark_failed_threshold`, `create_issue_platform_occurrence`, `get_failure_reason`, `get_monitor_environment_context`, and the `SimpleCheckIn` TypedDict from `sentry/monitors/logic/mark_failed.py`, moving them to `sentry/monitors/logic/incidents.py` (renamed to `try_incident_threshold`) and `sentry/monitors/logic/incident_occurrence.py`. The changed-files list contains no test updates and no other callers were touched, so any existing tests or code that import these names from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` (e.g. `from sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed import mark_failed_threshold`) will now fail at import time with ImportError/AttributeError. The PR should either include the corresponding test/import updates or verify no other references to the old paths exist.

title: get_monitor_environment_context builds a display-friendly config copy but then returns the raw config
body: In `get_monitor_environment_context`, line 160 copies `monitor_environment.monitor.config` and replaces `schedule_type` with its human-readable display value (lines 161-162), but the returned dict at line 168 uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` (the unmodified original) instead of the local `config` variable. The `schedule_type` translation is therefore computed and silently discarded, and the monitor context embedded in the occurrence event always contains the raw schedule type. This is carried over from the previous location in `mark_failed.py`, but since the module is being split out now is a good time to fix it (either return `config` or drop the dead copy).

title: Public functions were renamed/moved but the PR contains no test updates
body: This PR renames `mark_failed_threshold` to `try_incident_threshold` (now in `sentry.monitors.logic.incidents`) and `create_issue_platform_occurrence` to `create_incident_occurrence` (now in `sentry.monitors.logic.incident_occurrence`), and moves the `SimpleCheckIn` TypedDict from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` to `sentry.monitors.types`. No test files are changed in this PR. Any existing tests or callers that import these names from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` (e.g. the monitors logic tests that exercise `mark_failed_threshold`/`get_failure_reason`/`get_monitor_environment_context`) will now fail with ImportError, and the moved logic loses test coverage attribution. Before merging, the PR should either update the imports in the affected tests/callers or add `mark_failed_threshold = try_incident_threshold`-style aliases, and move/extend the corresponding tests alongside the moved code.

title: get_failure_reason docstring examples do not match the produced strings and contain typos
body: The docstring for `get_failure_reason` says it builds strings like "2 missed check-ins, 1 timeout check-in and 1 error check-in were detected" and "3 missed check-ins detected", but the code actually produces "2 missed check-ins, 1 timeout check-in and 1 error check-in check-ins detected" (the template appends "check-ins detected" to a list whose items already end in "check-in"), and the "3 missed check-ins detected" example cannot be produced at all since a single-status count yields "3 missed check-ins check-ins detected". The docstring also reads "humam readible" instead of "human readable". Since the function is being moved into its own module as a public helper (part of GH-80527 work), the docstring should be corrected to describe the actual output.

title: get_monitor_environment_context builds a display-friendly config but returns the raw model config
body: In get_monitor_environment_context, the local variable `config` is computed as a copy of monitor.config with `schedule_type` replaced by its human-readable display value (`monitor.get_schedule_type_display()`), but the returned dict at line 168 uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead of `config`. The local `config` is therefore dead code, and the monitor context emitted in the occurrence's event data always contains the raw numeric `schedule_type` rather than the display string. The transformation the function clearly intends to apply is silently never used. This was carried over from the old mark_failed.py code, but since it is being re-homed now is a good time to fix it: either return `config` in the dict or remove the dead computation.

title: get_failure_reason docstring examples don't match the actual return values
body: The docstring for get_failure_reason claims outputs like "3 missed check-ins detected" and "A failed check-in was detected", but the code actually produces "3 missed check-ins check-ins detected"-style strings (the format string is "%(problem_checkins)s check-ins detected", so the human status list is followed by a second "check-ins detected" suffix), and the singular case returns "An error check-in was detected" / "A missed check-in was detected" / "A timeout check-in was detected", never "A failed check-in was detected". The docstring also contains the typo "humam readible". Anyone using the docstring to understand the user-facing evidence text will be misled; update the examples (e.g. "3 missed check-ins check-ins detected" or better, restructure the sentence) to match reality.

title: time.sleep(0.1) in test_basic is a no-op due to the time.sleep monkeypatch, leaving the test racy
body: test_basic monkeypatches `time.sleep` to a no-op at the top of the test (line 15), so the newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` at line 62 — added specifically to 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change' — does nothing. The test therefore still races: `step.join()` immediately sets the shared `stopped` flag, and if the flusher thread observes `stopped` before it has read the new `current_drift` (set at line 58) and flushed the segment, it exits its loop without producing, and `(msg,) = messages` at line 66 raises. The test only passes because the patched-out sleep makes the flusher thread busy-spin; any change that removes the monkeypatch or slows the thread will make this flaky. Replace the no-op sleep with a real wait (e.g. an unpatched wait primitive or polling for `messages` with a timeout).

title: Per-process SpansBuffer memory info double-counts Redis clusters, skewing the hard-backpressure ratio
body: In `submit()` (lines 297-304) the code now aggregates `get_memory_info()` across one SpansBuffer per flusher process. Each shard-group buffer returns memory stats for every Redis cluster its shards live on, so a cluster that hosts shards in several process groups is counted once per group. The `used / available` ratio is then weighted by how the shards happen to be distributed across processes rather than by actual cluster memory: a nearly-full cluster whose shards fall into only one process group can be diluted below `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` by other, emptier clusters, delaying the 'Pausing consumer due to Redis being full' backpressure until Redis actually evicts data. The per-cluster ServiceMemory results should be deduplicated (e.g. keyed by cluster/service) before summing.

title: Restarted flusher processes are killed but never joined, accumulating zombies
body: In `_ensure_processes_alive()` the unhealthy process is `kill()`ed and a replacement is immediately spawned via `_create_process_for_shards()`, but the killed process is never `join()`ed or waited on. A SIGKILLed child becomes a zombie until the parent reaps it; since `process_restarts` is never reset, up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS (10) killed processes per process slot can accumulate as zombies over the consumer's lifetime, each also holding an unreaped Kafka producer / Redis connection context. Call `process.join(timeout)` (or at least `process.join()` after kill) before spawning the replacement.

title: Docstring says 'one process per shard' but default configuration spawns a single process
body: The class docstring (line 32) states 'Creates one process per shard for parallel processing', but the new `max_processes` parameter and the CLI option `--flusher-processes` default to 1 (see src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py, default=1), in which case exactly one process handles all shards. The constructor default (`None` -> len(assigned_shards), i.e. per-shard) also disagrees with the CLI default of 1, so behavior differs depending on whether the factory is built via the click command or programmatically. Update the docstring and align the defaults so operators reading either the code or the `--help` text get the same story.

title: _create_process_for_shard is dead code and would double-spawn if ever called
body: `_create_process_for_shard()` (lines 127-132) is never called anywhere — the restart path goes through `_ensure_processes_alive` -> `_create_process_for_shards` directly. Worse, if someone did call it, it would start a brand-new process for the shard's group without killing or removing the existing process for that group, leaving two processes simultaneously flushing the same shards (duplicate segment production to buffered-segments) and orphaning the old entry in `self.processes`. Remove the method or make it delegate to the kill-and-restart logic in `_ensure_processes_alive`.

title: Inconsistent metric tag key: 'shards' vs 'shard' on flusher timers
body: The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer uses tag key `"shards"` (line 199) while `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` (line 185) and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` (line 195) use `"shard"`. Since both carry the same comma-joined shard-list value, anyone building dashboards/queries on the flusher metrics has to handle two different tag names for the same dimension. Use `"shard"` consistently.

title: time.sleep(0.1) in test_basic is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched away
body: The test patches `time.sleep` to a no-op with `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, which patches the attribute on the `time` module for the whole process. The later `time.sleep(0.1)` (added to 'give flusher threads time to process after drift change') therefore does nothing. The test then immediately calls `step.join()`, which sets the flusher's `stopped` flag. The flusher thread reads `current_drift` only at the top of its loop, so if it is mid-iteration (e.g. inside a Redis round-trip) when the drift is set, it will see `stopped` before ever flushing with the advanced clock and exit without producing anything, leaving `messages` empty. The intended delay needs to use an unpatched sleep (e.g. `from time import sleep` imported before patching, or a dedicated event/condition) or the test will be flaky.

title: Aggregated shard_tag metric tags create huge tag values and unbounded cardinality on rebalance
body: `SpanFlusher.main` builds `shard_tag = ",".join(map(str, shards))` and attaches it to `spans.buffer.flusher.produce`, `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes`, and `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce`. With the shipped default (`--flusher-processes` default 1), a single flusher process owns *all* assigned shards, so the tag value becomes a comma-joined list of every partition index (potentially dozens), which is unusable for grouping. Worse, the shard set assigned to a consumer changes on every Kafka rebalance, so each rebalance produces a brand-new tag value, creating unbounded time-series cardinality in the metrics backend. Tagging per shard individually (as `flusher_unhealthy` does) or not tagging these timers when multiple shards share a process would avoid this.

title: wait_produce timer uses tag key "shards" while sibling metrics use "shard"
body: The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer is tagged with `tags={"shards": shard_tag}` (plural) while `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` in the same loop use `tags={"shard": shard_tag}` (singular). Any dashboard or query grouping flusher metrics by the `shard` tag will silently miss the wait_produce series. The tag key should be `shard` for consistency.

title: get_memory_info() is queried once per shard buffer but memory info is cluster-level
body: In `SpanFlusher.submit`, the Redis memory check now loops over `self.buffers` (one SpansBuffer per flusher process) and calls `buffer.get_memory_info()` on each, summing the results. `get_memory_info()` reports memory for the Redis cluster/nodes, not for the logical shards the buffer is constructed with — all shard buffers point at the same Redis. With N flusher processes this issues N identical INFO queries (potentially to every cluster node) on every submit, instead of the single query the old code made. One call on any single buffer (or caching the result) would be sufficient.

title: Restart of a hung worker cannot kill thread-mode workers, leaking threads and duplicating production
body: In `_ensure_processes_alive`, when a worker is deemed hung (`cause == "hang"`), the code only calls `process.kill()` if it is a `multiprocessing.Process`. When `produce_to_pipe` is set (the thread mode used by all tests and any embedded usage), the hung `threading.Thread` cannot be killed and is simply leaked while `_create_process_for_shards` starts a replacement thread with a fresh `SpansBuffer` for the same shards. Both the hung thread and the new thread then run concurrently against the same shard keys and the same `produce_to_pipe`, which can produce duplicate or interleaved segment messages and makes the restart counter meaningless in this mode. At minimum, thread mode should skip or assert on the hang-restart path rather than spawning overlapping workers.

title: _create_process_for_shard is dead code
body: The method `_create_process_for_shard` (lines 127-132) is never called anywhere in the codebase or tests; restarts go through `_ensure_processes_alive` -> `_create_process_for_shards` directly. It should be removed to avoid confusion about which restart path is authoritative.

title: No test exercises the multiprocess (spawn) flusher path introduced by this PR
body: The core change of this PR — spawning real `multiprocessing` processes with per-shard `SpansBuffer` instances, pickling them via `run_with_initialized_sentry`, and restarting crashed/hung processes — is only ever exercised through the `produce_to_pipe` code path, which forces `threading.Thread` instead of a spawned process. The new `test_flusher_processes_limit` only asserts dictionary lengths (`len(flusher.processes) == 2`), never submits a message, and never verifies that shards sharing a process are actually flushed or that the `_ensure_processes_alive` restart logic works with multiple workers. The production configuration (spawn processes, Kafka producer, shard-to-process round-robin actually flushing segments end-to-end) has zero coverage.

title: join() skips terminate() for remaining flusher processes when the deadline expires
body: In SpanFlusher.join(), the loop over self.processes does `break` when `remaining_time <= 0`, which exits the for-loop before reaching the `process.terminate()` call for all processes that come after the one being waited on. With the old single-process code, terminate was always reached; now a timeout while waiting on the first process leaves every other flusher process unterminated. If any of those processes is hung (e.g. blocked in a Redis call) it keeps running after join() returns, continuing to flush and produce segments for shards that may have been reassigned to another consumer during the rebalance, risking duplicate segment production. The `break` should be a `continue` (skip the wait but still terminate), or terminate should be called for all remaining processes.

title: Restarted flusher processes are killed but never joined, leaking zombies and IPC resources
body: In _ensure_processes_alive(), an unhealthy process is killed via process.kill() and then immediately replaced by _create_process_for_shards(), which overwrites self.processes[process_index] with the new Process. The old Process object is never join()ed or otherwise reaped, and nothing else references it, so each restart leaves a zombie child and leaks its sentinel pipe/file descriptors on Linux. For a long-running consumer that recovers flusher processes periodically (the restart logic exists precisely for that), these accumulate over the process lifetime. The old process should be joined (with a small timeout) after kill before spawning the replacement.

title: Redis memory usage is summed across per-shard-group buffers, potentially double-counting clusters
body: submit() now computes Redis backpressure by extending memory_infos from every buffer in self.buffers and summing used/available across all entries. Previously a single SpansBuffer covering all assigned shards produced the memory info. If a Redis cluster is reachable from more than one shard-group buffer (shards mapping to the same cluster can be split across processes by the round-robin assignment in __init__), that cluster's ServiceMemory is counted once per buffer that touches it. This weights the used/available ratio by how many buffers reference each cluster rather than by actual memory, so the `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` threshold can trigger too early or too late. The per-cluster results should be deduplicated (e.g. keyed by cluster) before summing.

title: Metric tag typo: wait_produce timer uses "shards" while sibling metrics use "shard"
body: The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer is tagged `tags={"shards": shard_tag}` while `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` in the same function use `tags={"shard": shard_tag}`. Dashboards and queries that slice these metrics by the shard tag will silently miss the wait_produce series (it lands under a different tag name), fragmenting the flusher observability this PR is meant to add.

title: Per-process restart counters are never reset, so lifetime restarts eventually crash the consumer
body: self.process_restarts[process_index] is only ever incremented in _ensure_processes_alive() and never reset, even after a process runs healthily for a long time. The guard `> MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` (10) therefore counts restarts over the entire consumer lifetime rather than within a failure window. A long-running consumer that legitimately recovers a flusher process a handful of times per quarter will eventually hit the limit and raise RuntimeError, forcing a full consumer restart and Kafka rebalance. The counter should decay or reset after the process has been healthy for some period.

title: _create_process_for_shard (singular) is dead code
body: The method _create_process_for_shard(shard) is never called anywhere; restarts go through _ensure_processes_alive() -> _create_process_for_shards() directly. Dead code with a misleading name that suggests per-shard restarts exist; it should be removed to avoid confusion.

title: Docstring says "one process per shard" but the shipped default is one process total
body: The class docstring states "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but the new --flusher-processes CLI option in sentry/consumers/__init__.py defaults to 1, so the default (and typical) deployment runs a single process handling all shards in round-robin groups. The docstring misrepresents the actual behavior and will mislead operators reasoning about parallelism and failure blast radius (one hung process stalls all shards by default).

title: The added time.sleep(0.1) in test_basic is a no-op due to the test's own monkeypatch
body: test_basic monkeypatches `time.sleep` to a lambda returning None at the top of the test, which patches the time module globally. The later `time.sleep(0.1)` added "to give flusher threads time to process after drift change" therefore sleeps for zero time, so the comment is wrong and the intended wait never happens. The assertion `(msg,) = messages` still depends on a race: the flusher thread must observe the new current_drift and complete producing before step.join() sets the stopped flag and the thread exits its `while not stopped.value` loop. The test can flake or silently stop covering the flush path; it should use an unpatched sleep (e.g. `monkeypatch.setattr` scoped to the flusher module, or a real sleep via a saved reference).

title: Strategy close() permanently kills the factory-owned queue pool; any Kafka rebalance silently drops all subsequent messages
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (and terminate()) call self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which stops all worker threads and calls queue.shutdown() on every work queue. However, the queue_pool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and shared by every strategy the factory builds. Arroyo's StreamProcessor tears down the old strategy and calls create_with_partitions() again on every rebalance/partition reassignment, which is routine in production. After the first rebalance, the new SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy wraps a pool whose queues are shut down: FixedQueuePool.submit() -> work_queue.put() raises ValueError, which is swallowed by the except block in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() (line 317), which marks the offset complete so it gets committed. The result is that after any rebalance, every message is silently dropped while offsets advance, i.e. total silent data loss. The pool's lifecycle must be owned by the factory (only shut down in factory.shutdown()), not by each strategy instance.

title: Failed messages are marked complete and committed, contradicting the documented 'only commits offsets after successful processing' guarantee
body: OrderedQueueWorker.run() completes the offset in a finally block even when self.result_processor(...) raises, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() (lines 317-325) does the same when decoding or grouping_fn raises. The class docstring claims 'No item is lost' and 'Only commits offsets after successful processing', but the implementation is at-most-once: a message whose handling fails is logged and its offset committed, so it is never retried or DLQ'd. This is a different failure semantic from other arroyo strategies (RunTask/BatchStep propagate errors so the processor can retry), so operators switching modes will silently lose data that used to be retried. Either the docstring/guarantees must be corrected or failures should keep the offset outstanding (or route to a DLQ).

title: Graceful shutdown does not drain queued items and the commit thread is stopped before draining, so shutdown loses in-flight work boundaries
body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False). A worker's loop condition ('while not self.shutdown') is checked after each item, so a worker with a backlog exits after its current item, leaving the remaining queued items unprocessed even though q.shutdown(immediate=False) was specifically chosen to allow draining. Additionally, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (line 335) stops and joins the commit thread before queue_pool.shutdown() drains remaining items, so offsets for items completed during the drain are never committed and those messages are re-consumed (and re-processed, possibly non-idempotently) after restart. The shutdown path should let workers drain the queues first (the queue.ShutDown from q.shutdown(immediate=False) already terminates them), and run a final commit pass after draining.

title: OffsetTracker stalls forever on permanent offset gaps and does an O(offset-range) scan every second
body: get_committable_offsets() breaks at the first offset not present in all_offsets and only ever commits up to that point, assuming any gap will eventually be filled by a message passed to submit(). But offsets can be permanently absent from the consumer's view - e.g. Kafka transactional control records that librdkafka filters out, or offsets skipped after consumer-group offset expiry - so a gap that never fills blocks all commits for that partition for the life of the process, causing unbounded offset lag and rebalance risk. Additionally, the scan iterates range(start, max_offset + 1) every second; with such a permanent gap the range grows unboundedly (min to max of ever-seen offsets), making each commit tick progressively more expensive. A safer design is to track only the set of outstanding offsets and commit min(outstanding)-1, rather than requiring contiguity.

title: Unbounded work queues provide no backpressure despite the documented claim
body: FixedQueuePool creates plain queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() returns immediately after put(), so the arroyo consumer thread keeps fetching and enqueueing messages as fast as Kafka delivers them. If workers fall behind (the exact 'one slow item clogs a queue' scenario the PR is meant to mitigate, now per-queue instead of per-batch), memory grows without bound and consumer lag accumulates invisibly. The class docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', which is false. The queues should be constructed with a bounded maxsize (queue.put then blocks the arroyo thread, applying real backpressure), or another bound on in-flight messages is needed.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling is racy and asserts behavior opposite to the implementation
body: The test asserts that no commit happens for a partition after a processing failure ('assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets'). But OrderedQueueWorker completes the offset in a finally block even when result_processor raises, so once the 1-second commit tick fires the strategy will commit offset 102 for the partition. The test only passes if it finishes its wait/sleep before the commit thread's next tick, making it timing-dependent and flaky. It also masks the at-most-once data-loss behavior of the finally-block completion (see the worker implementation); either the implementation or the test's expectation needs to be fixed so they agree deterministically.

title: test_stats_reporting races on queue depth and test_different_groups_distributed can flake under hash randomization
body: In test_stats_reporting, 10 items are submitted to a pool whose workers are already running a trivially fast result_processor, and the test immediately asserts stats['total_items'] > 0; if the workers drain the queue before get_stats() is called, the assertion fails intermittently. Similarly, test_different_groups_distributed asserts all 3 queue indices are hit by 20 hashed group keys; since string hashes are randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), the mapping is effectively random each run and there is a small but real chance (~0.1%) that only 2 of 3 buckets are used, causing an intermittent failure. These assertions should be made deterministic (e.g., block the workers, or assert the index is within range rather than full coverage).

title: 'offsets_committed' metric counts partitions, not offsets
body: In _commit_loop, the metric 'remote_subscriptions.queue_pool.offsets_committed' is incremented by len(committable), which is the number of partitions in the commit dict, not the number of Kafka offsets advanced. For a busy consumer committing thousands of offsets per tick across a few partitions, the metric dramatically undercounts and its name misleads anyone dashboarding it. It should report the sum of offset deltas (or be renamed to partitions_committed).

title: Strategy close() kills the factory-wide queue pool, so any consumer group rebalance silently drops all subsequent messages
body: The `FixedQueuePool` (and its 20 worker threads) is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and shared across every `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` the factory produces. Arroyo tears down and recreates the strategy via `create_with_partitions` on every partition reassignment (any consumer-group rebalance, e.g. a rolling deploy or a peer dying). The old strategy's `close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets every worker's shutdown flag and calls `queue.shutdown()` on all queues. The new strategy created after the rebalance then reuses the same dead pool: every `queue_pool.submit()` raises ValueError from `queue.put`, which `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` catches, logs, and marks the offset as complete. The new strategy's commit thread then commits those offsets, so all messages after a rebalance are silently dropped while appearing fully consumed. The pool needs to be per-strategy (or `close()` must not destroy a pool the factory will reuse).

title: Unbounded work queues provide no backpressure despite the strategy's stated guarantee
body: `FixedQueuePool` builds plain `queue.Queue()` objects with no maxsize, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`/`poll` never block or apply throttle. The class docstring claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing can fill up: arroyo will keep polling and fetching messages as fast as the broker allows while the workers drain slowly, so a slow or backlogged subscriber causes unbounded growth of in-memory `WorkItem`s (each retaining the full Kafka payload via `WorkItem.message`) and eventual OOM. The queues should be bounded (with the submit path blocking, or poll gating fetch on total queue depth) so memory is capped.

title: Failed messages are still marked complete and committed, contradicting the "only commits offsets after successful processing" guarantee
body: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, the `finally` block calls `offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` even when `result_processor` raised, so a processing failure is treated identically to success: the offset becomes committable and the message is dropped with no retry. The `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` docstring explicitly promises "Only commits offsets after successful processing", and the new test `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` (tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py) asserts that a failed message blocks commits — which the implementation does not do. That test only passes because of a timing race: it sleeps 0.2s after processing finishes, while the commit loop only fires every 1.0s, so the commit it should be catching usually hasn't happened yet. Either the worker must keep failed offsets outstanding (at-least-once) or the docstring and test must be changed to document the at-most-once drop behavior; as written, the code drops failed messages while the tests claim otherwise.

title: get_committable_offsets iterates all_offsets without a lock while other threads insert new partition keys
body: `get_committable_offsets` does `list(self.all_offsets.keys())` with no lock held. `add_offset` (called from the arroyo submit thread) inserts new keys into this defaultdict, and per-partition locks don't protect the dict itself. A key insertion concurrent with the key iteration can raise `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration`, which aborts that whole commit tick (it's caught and logged in `_commit_loop`, delaying all offset commits by a cycle). This happens whenever a partition is seen for the first time while the commit thread is scanning — e.g. right after a rebalance. The key list should be snapshotted under a dedicated lock that also guards key insertion.

title: Per-message Sentry transaction and per-message gauge emit excessive telemetry, and the queue-depth gauge is meaningless without a worker tag
body: Each work item processed by `OrderedQueueWorker` opens a `sentry_sdk.start_transaction` (on top of the transaction already opened inside `ResultProcessor.__call__`, so there are two transactions per message) and emits a `metrics.gauge` for queue depth. Under production throughput this is one transaction and one gauge per Kafka message, which is significant overhead and metric flooding. Additionally, the gauge is tagged only with `identifier`, not `worker_id`, so the 20 workers each report their own queue's depth into the same series and the last write wins — the reported depth is a random worker's depth rather than the pool's.

title: test_stats_reporting asserts the queue is non-empty immediately after submit, a race with the worker threads
body: In `test_stats_reporting`, 10 items are submitted and the test immediately asserts `stats["total_items"] > 0`. The three worker threads are free to fully drain the queues before `get_stats()` is called (nothing synchronizes them), in which case the assertion fails. This makes the test flaky on fast machines or under load. The assertion should either block processing until stats are captured or drop the non-emptiness check in favor of the post-drain assertions.

title: Strategy close() permanently kills the shared queue pool, causing silent message loss after any Kafka rebalance
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which stops all worker threads and shuts down every queue.Queue. But the FixedQueuePool is owned by the ResultsStrategyFactory and shared across strategy instances. Arroyo's StreamProcessor rebuilds the processing strategy on every rebalance (it calls close() on the old strategy, then create_with_partitions again on the same factory). After the first rebalance, the new strategy is constructed around the already-shut-down pool: queue_pool.submit() calls work_queue.put() which raises queue.ShutDown, that exception is caught by the except block in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() (lines 317-325), which marks the offset as completed. The commit loop then advances the committed offsets past those messages. Result: after any routine consumer-group rebalance (deploys, consumer joins/leaves), every subsequent message on that consumer is silently dropped while offsets are committed as if processed. The strategy must not tear down factory-scoped resources (e.g. the pool shutdown should only happen from ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown(), or the pool should be recreated per strategy).

title: Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure and memory grows without limit under backlog
body: FixedQueuePool creates each queue via queue.Queue() with no maxsize, so submit() never blocks. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() returns immediately to Arroyo, which keeps polling and handing over messages, so if the worker threads fall behind, both the in-memory queues and the OffsetTracker's all_offsets/outstanding sets grow without bound (offsets can't be pruned until they're committed, and commits can't advance past the backlog). This is a memory leak / OOM risk exactly in the slow-consumer scenario this PR is meant to address. It also contradicts the class docstring at line 253 ('Natural backpressure when queues fill up') — no backpressure exists. Pass maxsize to queue.Queue (or bound the number of in-flight messages) so put() blocks the Arroyo thread when queues fill.

title: A sentry_sdk transaction is started per message in each worker, nested inside ResultProcessor's own transaction
body: OrderedQueueWorker.run() wraps every single work item in sentry_sdk.start_transaction(). This creates one Sentry transaction per consumed message (per worker), which at uptime-results throughput means a very large transaction ingestion volume and per-message tracing overhead. It is also redundant: ResultProcessor.__call__ (result_consumer.py line 48) already starts its own transaction per result, so every message now produces nested/duplicate transactions. Existing modes (serial/parallel) only instrument the processor, not one transaction per message. The per-item transaction should be removed or sampled.

title: Claim 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' is false: failures are still marked complete and committed
body: The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring (line 254) guarantees offsets are only committed after successful processing, but OrderedQueueWorker.run() completes the offset in a finally block even when result_processor raises (lines 144-149), and ResultProcessor.__call__ additionally swallows all exceptions itself. A message whose processing fails is therefore treated as done, its offset becomes committable, and after the commit it is permanently skipped — a silent drop of failed messages with no retry and no DLQ. This is the opposite of what the docstring (and the PR's own error-handling test, see separate finding) states. Either the guarantee should be implemented (e.g. don't complete the offset, or route to a DLQ/retry) or the docstring must be corrected to state that failed messages are skipped.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the opposite of the implemented behavior and only passes by racing the 1s commit loop
body: The test asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, i.e. that no commit happens after a processing failure. But the implementation completes offsets even when result_processor raises (the worker's finally block), so once both messages finish the commit loop will commit offset 102 for the partition on its next 1-second tick. The test only passes because it breaks out of its wait loop as soon as queues are empty (within ~0.3s) and asserts before the commit thread's 1.0s wait elapses; on a slow CI machine or if the commit interval fires earlier, the assertion fails. The test should either assert the real behavior (failed messages' offsets are committed) or the implementation should be changed to match the intended behavior.

title: queue_depth gauge is missing a worker/queue tag, so workers overwrite each other's values
body: OrderedQueueWorker emits metrics.gauge('remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth', self.work_queue.qsize()) with only an 'identifier' tag — no worker_id or queue index. Every worker reports the same metric name and tags with a different value (its own queue's depth), so the last writer wins and the gauge reflects an arbitrary single queue rather than per-queue depths. Since it's emitted after every processed item, the value is also effectively random. Add a worker_id/queue tag or drop this gauge in favor of the aggregate total_queued gauge emitted in poll().

title: FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown before draining, so queued messages are abandoned
body: In shutdown(), worker.shutdown = True is set for all workers before q.shutdown(immediate=False). A worker that is mid-item will check `while not self.shutdown` after finishing and exit, leaving any remaining items in its queue unprocessed; queue.shutdown(immediate=False) does not block until the queue is drained in this construction (and task_done() is never called anyway). The docstring says 'Gracefully shutdown all workers', but in-flight backlog is discarded. Because those offsets were added but never completed they won't be committed, so the messages are replayed on restart (at-least-once), but the shutdown is not actually graceful: to drain, only the queue shutdown should signal termination and workers should keep processing until get() raises ShutDown.

title: test_stats_reporting asserts total_items > 0 immediately after submit, racing the workers
body: The test submits 10 items and immediately asserts stats['total_items'] > 0. The three worker threads can process all items within microseconds (the result processor just appends to a list), so by the time get_stats() is called the queues may already be empty, making the assertion flaky. The assertion should either be removed, or the pool should be paused/verified deterministically (e.g. block the result processor on an event until stats are captured).

title: Code requires Python 3.13+ (queue.Queue.shutdown / queue.ShutDown) with no guard
body: The implementation uses queue.Queue.shutdown() and the queue.ShutDown exception, both of which were only added in Python 3.13. On any earlier interpreter, q.shutdown() raises AttributeError (breaking close()/terminate() and therefore consumer shutdown), and queue.ShutDown does not exist so the except clauses in the worker would themselves fail. If the repository still supports Python < 3.13 in CI or deployment targets, this breaks at runtime; if 3.13 is now the minimum, this is fine, but it's worth confirming since nothing in the PR documents or enforces the requirement.

title: Backup code consumption is not atomic (read-modify-write race)
body: The authorize callback decrypts the backup code list, checks membership with indexOf, then nulls the used entry and writes the whole list back with prisma.user.update. Two concurrent login requests using the same backup code can both read the list before either writes, both pass the indexOf check, and both be accepted — a single backup code can be replayed. The update should be conditioned on the code still being present (e.g. compare-and-swap or a transaction with a where guard) so a code can only be redeemed once.

title: "missing_backup_codes" message tells users to regenerate codes in settings, but no such feature exists
body: The new error string is "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." This PR adds no UI or API to view or regenerate backup codes after setup — codes are generated once during initial 2FA setup and (after use of one) can never be replenished. A user who exhausts or loses their codes is told to do something impossible. Either a regenerate feature must be added or the message must be corrected.

title: Backup codes are generated and persisted before 2FA is actually enabled
body: The setup endpoint (which only requires the account password) writes encrypted backupCodes to the user row and returns the plaintext codes in the response, even though twoFactorEnabled is still false at this point. If the user abandons the wizard after the password step (or the QR/secret display step) and never calls enable, valid backup codes remain stored and were transmitted to the client. Any later flow that treats the presence of backupCodes as meaningful (e.g. the MissingBackupCodes vs. present-codes distinction in login) operates on codes the user may never have seen or saved. Generating codes only on successful enable (or clearing them if setup is abandoned) would be safer.

title: Dismissing the modal at the DisplayBackupCodes step never calls onEnable, leaving the UI switch stale
body: After enable succeeds the modal moves to SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes, and only the explicit Close button calls onEnable(). If the user closes the dialog via the X button, Escape, or the overlay (all handled by onOpenChange, not resetState/onEnable), two-factor is now actually enabled server-side but the parent's onEnable callback never fires, so the settings page keeps showing 2FA as disabled until reload. resetState() is also skipped, so stale backup codes/blob URL remain in component state.

title: No test covers actually logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code
body: The PR's core feature — authenticating with a backup code — has zero test coverage. The e2e additions only exercise the download/copy/close buttons on the backup-code display screen; the file even carries a TODO ("add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup") and the download-content/clipboard checks are TODOs. The server-side redemption logic in next-auth-options.ts and disable.ts (dash stripping, single-use invalidation, MissingBackupCodes/IncorrectBackupCode paths) is untested, so a regression in the only code path that verifies backup codes would go unnoticed.

title: Backup code is consumed even if login subsequently fails
body: The used backup code is nulled and persisted in the database immediately after the indexOf match, before the rest of the authorize function runs (team checks, password-policy role validation, JWT/session creation). If anything after that point throws or the sign-in callback redirects (e.g. an INACTIVE_ADMIN downgrade or an error during token issuance), the user has permanently lost a backup code without gaining access. The invalidation should be tied to successful sign-in, not to passing the code check.

title: minLength/maxLength/required on the backup code input are not enforced on the login form
body: The login form in apps/web/pages/auth/login.tsx is rendered with noValidate, so the native minLength={10}/maxLength={11}/required attributes on the BackupCode TextField never trigger. The zod schema also does not include backupCode (the object is .passthrough()), so a user can submit an empty or malformed backup code; the empty string is falsy on the server, so the request silently falls into the TOTP branch and returns a confusing "second factor required" error instead of a validation message telling the user to enter the code.

title: Backup code consumption is a read-modify-write race (TOCTOU)
body: In the credentials authorize() handler, the backup code is validated with `backupCodes.indexOf(...)` and then consumed by re-encrypting and writing the whole array back via prisma.user.update. Two concurrent login requests using the same backup code can both pass the indexOf check before either write lands, so a single-use code can be redeemed twice. The update should be conditional/atomic (or use a transaction/optimistic check) to guarantee one-time use, since 'each backup code can be used exactly once' is the stated security contract.

title: Empty backup code submission silently does nothing on login
body: The login form has `noValidate`, so the `required`/`minLength` attributes on the BackupCode TextField are never enforced, and there is no zod/react-hook-form validation for `backupCode`. If a user in the 'lost access' flow submits without typing a code, `credentials.backupCode` is empty/falsy, so the authorize() branch `user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode` is skipped, the totpCode branch throws SecondFactorRequired, and the client just re-sets twoFactorRequired(true) — no error message is shown and nothing happens. The user gets no feedback.

title: Backup code is consumed before the login is guaranteed to succeed
body: The verified backup code is marked used (set to null and persisted) inside authorize(), before next-auth finishes signing the user in (JWT encoding, signIn callback, session creation). If any later step fails, the user has permanently lost a backup code without gaining access. The consumption should only happen once the sign-in is committed, or be idempotent/retryable.

title: req.body.backupCode is used without type/shape validation
body: The disable endpoint calls `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` without validating that it is a string. A client POSTing `backupCode` as an object/array/null-as-object (Next.js body parsing can produce nested JSON) causes `replaceAll is not a function`, throwing a 500. The login authorize() path in next-auth-options.ts (line 144) has the same unvalidated `credentials.backupCode.replaceAll(...)`. Inputs should be validated (e.g. zod string) before use.

title: No test actually exercises backup-code login or backup-code 2FA disable
body: The PR adds backup codes as the core feature but the e2e suite only tests downloading/copying/closing the backup-code dialog. There is no test that logs in with a backup code (the primary new auth path in next-auth-options.ts), verifies a code is single-use, or disables 2FA with a backup code (the new branch in disable.ts). These are security-critical code paths; a regression would go unnoticed.

title: Backup codes compared with indexOf (non-constant-time)
body: Backup codes are compared using `Array.prototype.indexOf`, which uses non-constant-time string comparison on a secret. For consistency with how passwords/TOTP are verified, a timing-safe comparison is preferable, though the practical exploitability is low given network jitter. Low priority hardening.

title: Backup code consumption is not atomic (read-modify-write race)
body: In the credentials authorize() handler, the backup code list is read from the DB, matched, set to null, and written back with prisma.user.update. Two concurrent login attempts using the same backup code can both pass the indexOf check before either write lands, so a single-use code can be replayed and used twice (or more). The update should be conditional/atomic (e.g., compare-and-set in a transaction, or store per-code hash and delete with a WHERE clause that asserts the code still exists).

title: Backup code is consumed before the login flow completes
body: The verified backup code is deleted and the DB updated inside authorize(), before next-auth issues the session/JWT and before the signIn callback runs. If anything downstream fails (signIn callback error, network failure on the client, next-auth internal error), the user's backup code is permanently burned without a successful login, reducing their remaining recovery codes through no fault of their own. Ideally consumption should happen only once login is certain to succeed.

title: Backup codes unusable for third-party identity provider (SAML/Google) 2FA users
body: The check `if (user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode) throw ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled` runs before the backup code branch. Users whose accounts use SAML/Google identity but have 2FA enabled (the totp-link login path) can never authenticate with a backup code: submitting a backupCode without a totpCode always throws, and the login page's 'Lost access' backup-code UI is not offered on the totpEmail path either. These users have no recovery option if they lose their authenticator, despite the feature claiming to provide one.

title: No test for the core feature: logging in with a backup code
body: The PR adds backup-code login and backup-code-based 2FA disable, but the only new test coverage clicks the download/copy/close buttons on the setup screen (and even that doesn't verify file or clipboard content). There is no test that a user can actually log in with a backup code, that a used code is rejected on reuse, that an incorrect code shows the right error, or that disabling 2FA with a backup code works — all explicitly deferred as TODOs. The primary security-relevant code path ships untested.

title: Both totpCode and backupCode can be submitted; backup code silently takes precedence
body: When switching between the TOTP and 'Lost access' backup-code views, only one field is cleared in some transitions, and onSubmit spreads all form values into signIn(). The authorize() handler checks backupCode first, so a user who has a stale backupCode value in the form while trying to log in with a TOTP code will get an 'incorrect backup code' error (or worse, succeed via a leftover backup code) even though they typed a valid TOTP. The submit should send only the code relevant to the currently active mode.

title: Backup codes are generated and persisted before 2FA is actually enabled
body: The setup endpoint writes encrypted backupCodes to the user row on every call, even if the user never completes the enable step. A user who starts setup, sees/saves codes, then restarts setup later and completes only the second attempt will have the first set of saved codes silently invalidated (overwritten). Also, codes exist on the DB for users who never enabled 2FA. Generating/persisting codes only on successful enable (or returning them from enable) would make the displayed codes authoritative.

title: Crash when Google Meet selected and destinationCalendar is empty
body: In `create()`: `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` followed by `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"`. When `destinationCalendar` is `[]` (the new fallback used everywhere in this PR, e.g. handleCancelBooking/paypal webhook set `[]`), `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined` and `.integration` throws a TypeError, whereas the old code used `evt.destinationCalendar?.integration` and safely fell through. Any booking with Google Meet as location and no destination calendar will fail during event creation.

title: updateEvent/deleteEvent fallback for calendarId can never match
body: `const selectedCalendar = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;` — in the fallback branch `externalCalendarId` is falsy (null/undefined/empty), so `find(cal => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)` can never match and always returns `undefined`. Previously the fallback was `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. Result: when a booking reference has no externalCalendarId, updates are sent with `calendarId: undefined` and deletes fall back to `"primary"`, so events created on a secondary destination calendar are never updated/deleted (Google returns 404 on delete, which is silently resolved), leaving stale events for cancelled/rescheduled bookings. The identical broken pattern exists in `deleteEvent` (line 315-317).

title: Unrelated inversion of slug/requestedSlug logic in org creation
body: The change `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` → `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})` (and the matching `requestedSlug` change) inverts the previous behavior: before, `slug` was set on the team when team billing was NOT enabled and `requestedSlug` when it was; now `slug` is set when billing IS enabled. This is unrelated to the PR's purpose and flips which deployments get the slug persisted on organization creation, likely breaking org subdomain resolution for those environments.

title: Webhook payload contract break: destinationCalendar type changed
body: `CalendarEvent.destinationCalendar` in webhook payloads changes from `DestinationCalendar | null` to `DestinationCalendar[]` (e.g. `null` → `[]`, and for collective events an array of multiple calendars). External webhook subscribers that parse `payload.destinationCalendar` as an object or null will break. This is a public API contract change shipped as a 'bug fix' with no changelog/migration note or versioning; consumers should be notified or the field kept backwards compatible.

title: Only first destinationCalendar persisted on booking; team calendars lost on rebuild
body: For collective events, `evt.destinationCalendar` is built with all hosts' destination calendars, but the booking is created with `destinationCalendar: { connect: { id: evt.destinationCalendar[0].id } }` — only the organizer's calendar is stored. Any later flow that reconstructs the CalendarEvent from the DB (cancel, reschedule, bookingReminder, confirm handler) sets `destinationCalendar: [booking.destinationCalendar]`, dropping the other hosts' calendars. The multi-host support therefore only works on the initial create; the deletion/update paths rely solely on references, and any path that re-derives behavior from `evt.destinationCalendar` (e.g. the Meet fallback in EventManager) will behave differently after a reload.

title: Team member/destination calendar collection depends on users order and mutates shared array
body: `teamDestinationCalendars` is populated inside the `users.slice(1).map(...)` callback with `if (isTeamEventType && eventType.schedulingType === "COLLECTIVE" && user.destinationCalendar)`. If the same user's calendar is also the eventType/organizer destinationCalendar it gets duplicated in `evt.destinationCalendar`, causing `createAllCalendarEvents` to attempt creating the event twice on the same calendar (two Google events / duplicate references). No de-duplication by credentialId/externalId is performed before `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`.

title: Hangout-link patch uses possibly-undefined selectedCalendar
body: In `createEvent`, the insert uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"` but the follow-up `calendar.events.patch` (to add the hangout link to the description) uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar` without the `|| "primary"` fallback. When the event was created on the primary calendar because no destination matched the credentialId, the patch targets `calendarId: undefined` and fails silently, so the Meet link is never added to the event description.

title: No tests for the multi-destination-calendar behavior
body: The PR checklist explicitly states no tests were added. This is a large behavioral change (destinationCalendar becomes an array, create/update/delete fan out over multiple calendar references and credentials, new DB fallback for credentials) touching ~20 files including payment webhooks and cancellation. At minimum, unit tests for `createAllCalendarEvents`/`updateAllCalendarEvents` with multiple destination calendars and mixed credential availability, plus a regression test for the Google Meet empty-destinationCalendar case, are needed before merging.

title: Crash when destinationCalendar is empty/undefined and location is Google Meet
body: In EventManager.create, `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` followed by `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"` dereferences without optional chaining. When a booking has no destination calendars (evt.destinationCalendar is null or an empty array — which is now the normal case for users without a destination calendar, e.g. handleNewBooking sets null), mainHostDestinationCalendar is undefined and this line throws a TypeError, failing the whole booking creation whenever Google Meet is selected as location. The old code used `evt.destinationCalendar?.integration` and was null-safe.

title: Patch after insert uses possibly-undefined calendarId
body: In createEvent, the insert call falls back to `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"`, but the subsequent events.patch (used to add the hangout link to the description) passes `calendarId: selectedCalendar` without the fallback. When no destinationCalendar matches the credentialId, selectedCalendar is undefined and the patch request is sent with calendarId undefined, so the description/hangoutLink update silently fails (or errors) for every event created on the primary calendar.

title: updateEvent/deleteEvent lose destination calendar fallback for legacy bookings
body: In updateEvent the new code is `externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. When externalCalendarId is null/undefined (all bookings created before the externalCalendarId reference refactor, and any reference where it wasn't stored), the `.find(cal => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)` compares against null/undefined and never matches, so selectedCalendar is undefined. The old code fell back to `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. The same broken pattern exists in deleteEvent (line 315-317). Result: updating or cancelling legacy Google bookings calls the API with calendarId undefined, which fails or hits the wrong calendar, so events on a non-primary destination calendar are never updated/deleted.

title: Organizer attendee email always set from first destination calendar, even when creating on another host's calendar
body: createEvent always uses `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.externalId` (the first entry of destinationCalendar) as the organizer attendee email. In the multi-host collective scenario this PR targets, the same event is created once per destination calendar with different credentials; for the second host's calendar the organizer email will still be the first host's externalId, producing a wrong organizer on that event and potentially bouncing attendee invites. The email should be derived from the destination matching the current credentialId (the `selectedCalendar`), not unconditionally from the first array entry.

title: Unrelated inversion of IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED slug condition
body: The diff changes `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`. This inverts when the org team gets a slug: previously the slug was set when team billing was NOT enabled and requestedSlug when it WAS; now slug is set when billing IS enabled. This is unrelated to the destinationCalendar work and silently changes organization subdomain creation behavior for self-hosted (non-billing) instances, which will now never get a slug set on team creation.

title: Lark/CalDav/Office365 services ignore per-destination calendars for multi-host events
body: LarkCalendarService.createEvent (and BaseCalendarService in packages/lib/CalendarService.ts line 156, and Office365CalendarService line 73) still only read the first entry of `event.destinationCalendar` (`const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = event.destinationCalendar ?? []`). EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents now iterates all destinations and calls createEvent per credential, but these services always create the event on the first host's calendar regardless of which destination/credential is being processed, so secondary hosts on Lark/CalDav/Office365 will either get duplicate events on the wrong calendar or no event on their own calendar — the exact bug this PR claims to fix, only fixed for Google Calendar.

title: credentialId dropped from video references in create()
body: In `referencesToCreate` inside create(), `credentialId: isCalendarType ? result.credentialId : undefined` discards the credentialId for video results. Previously it fell back to `evt.destinationCalendar?.credentialId` for non-calendar results. While the old fallback was also wrong (it used the calendar's credential for video), the new code stores no credentialId at all for video references, which handleCancelBooking relies on (`bookingVideoReference.credentialId`) to find the video credential and delete the meeting on cancellation — cancelled bookings with video meetings will now leak the video meeting. createMeeting's EventResult should carry and propagate the video credential's id.

title: Only the first destination calendar is persisted on the booking
body: When creating the booking, `destinationCalendar: evt.destinationCalendar && evt.destinationCalendar.length > 0 ? { connect: { id: evt.destinationCalendar[0].id } } : undefined` connects only the first destination calendar (the DB relation is single). For collective events, secondary hosts' destination calendars are only recoverable via the created bookingReferences; any code path that rebuilds a CalendarEvent from the booking (cancel, reschedule, requestReschedule, payment webhooks — all updated in this PR to `[booking.destinationCalendar]`) will only include the organizer's calendar. If reference creation fails or a reference lacks externalCalendarId, secondary hosts' calendar events become orphaned. Consider persisting all destinations or ensuring the fallback paths reconstruct the full list.

title: Error message in updateAllCalendarEvents catch no longer logged
body: The catch block previously did `console.error(message)`; the new code builds the same detailed message (including which credential/book failed) but never logs or reports it — it's only used in a template that is discarded. Failures inside updateAllCalendarEvents are now silent apart from the synthesized failure results, making production debugging of calendar update failures harder.

title: Crash when destinationCalendar is null: mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration on undefined
body: In EventManager.create(), `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` yields undefined when destinationCalendar is null/undefined, and the next line accesses `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining (`evt.location === MeetLocationType && mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"`). The old code used `evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`, which was null-safe. Any booking where destinationCalendar is null and location is Google Meet (e.g. handleNewBooking now explicitly sets destinationCalendar to null when neither eventType nor organizer has one) will throw a TypeError and abort booking creation.

title: updateEvent/deleteEvent externalCalendarId fallback is dead code (find by externalCalendarId === null/undefined)
body: In updateEvent: `const selectedCalendar = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;` — in the fallback branch externalCalendarId is falsy (null/undefined), so `find(cal => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)` can never match, and selectedCalendar is undefined. The same broken pattern is repeated in deleteEvent (line 315-317). The previous code fell back to `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`; now update/delete are always sent with calendarId undefined, which for update sends an invalid request to the Google API and for delete silently falls back to "primary" (line 314/322), deleting from the wrong calendar when the event lives on a non-primary destination calendar.
