However, the SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer is only rendered when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is truthy, where `rule` is the RulerRuleDTO prop. In the new list view (FilterView -> GrafanaRuleListItem -> RuleActionsButtons), only `promRule` is passed and `rule` is undefined, so the drawer is never rendered: clicking 'Silence notifications' silently does nothing. The silence action is broken for all Grafana-managed rules in the alert list.

title: Delete menu item is never rendered in the new alert list view
body: The Delete item is gated on `canDelete && rulerRule`, and its click handler requires a RulerRuleDTO (`handleDelete(rulerRule, groupIdentifier)`). In the new list view GrafanaRuleListItem passes only promRule (no ruler rule is fetched anymore), so rulerRule is undefined and users with delete permission lose the Delete action entirely for Grafana-managed rules in the list. The delete-ability checks via useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities become dead code. If deletion is meant to remain available, the menu must construct the deletion from the identifier/promRule; if it is intentionally removed, the tests asserting delete presence for Grafana rules (RulesTable.test.tsx 'Should render Delete button for users with the delete permission') contradict this behavior.

title: Pause action is never rendered in the new alert list view
body: The pause menu item requires `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` to be truthy in addition to canPause. Since the list view no longer fetches ruler rules, rulerRule is undefined and the Pause action is missing from the menu for Grafana-managed rules, even though the code computes a grafana pause ability (grafanaPauseSupported/grafanaPauseAllowed) specifically for this view. The new pause-ability path is dead code and users lose the ability to pause/unpause rules from the list.

title: GrafanaRuleListItem is rendered without a React key in the rules list
body: In the rules.map switch, the 'grafana' case renders <GrafanaRuleListItem> without a `key` prop (the old code used `key={key}`), while the 'datasource' and default cases still pass keys. Rendering list children without keys causes React reconciliation problems (element re-use across filter updates/infinite scroll, full re-mounts, state loss in menus/drawers) and React key warnings. The `key={key}` should be restored on the GrafanaRuleListItem element.

title: Federated rule group support silently dropped from ruler abilities
body: The refactored useAllRulerRuleAbilities hardcodes `const isFederated = false;` with only a TODO comment, whereas the previous useAllAlertRuleAbilities computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`. For Mimir/Metrics Enterprise data sources with federated rule groups (source_tenants set), immutableRule is now false, so the Update/Delete/Pause/Restore abilities will report these rules as editable/deletable when they are not. This is a behavior regression for cloud rules (rules in federated groups get edit/delete UI they previously did not).

title: Missing React key on GrafanaRuleListItem in list rendering
body: In FilterViewResults, the 'grafana' switch branch renders <GrafanaRuleListItem> without the `key` prop (the old <GrafanaRuleLoader key={key} ...> had it, and every other branch still passes key). Since these items are rendered inside rules.map() and the list grows via infinite scroll, React cannot stably identify items; adding/removing rules can reuse component state (open dropdown menus, silence drawer state, redirect state) across different rules and can cause incorrect DOM reuse. The key must be restored, e.g. key={key}.

title: Silence drawer never opens for Grafana rules without rulerRule (list view)
body: The 'Silence notifications' menu item is now shown based on grafanaPromRuleAbilities when only a promRule is available (AlertRuleMenu line 126 checks canSilence, which ORs the prom-based ability). However, the drawer rendering is still gated on `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)`, which is false when no RulerRuleDTO was passed. In the alert list view (where the ruler API is no longer called and only promRule is supplied), clicking 'Silence notifications' sets showSilenceDrawer=true but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer is never rendered — the action silently does nothing. The drawer needs to be constructible from the prom rule / GrafanaPromRuleDTO as well.

title: Pause menu item requires rulerRule, so pause is unavailable in the list view
body: canPause is computed as an OR of ruler-based and prom-based abilities, so in the alert list view (promRule only, no rulerRule) the menu can report pause as supported/allowed. But the actual menu item is additionally gated on `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) && groupIdentifier.groupOrigin === 'grafana'`, which is false when rulerRule is undefined. Result: users with permission see no way to pause Grafana-managed rules from the list view, a functional regression versus the previous list implementation. MenuItemPauseRule needs a prom-rule/GrafanaPromRuleDTO variant.

title: Delete menu item requires rulerRule, so delete is unavailable in the list view
body: canDelete now ORs in the prom-based ability so the menu logic considers delete permitted when only promRule is available, but the Delete item rendering is gated on `canDelete && rulerRule` and the click handler `handleDelete(rulerRule, ...)` requires a RulerRuleDTO. In the alert list view, where the ruler API is no longer fetched, users with delete permission will never see the Delete action for Grafana rules — a regression from the previous behavior where each rule's ruler data was loaded. handleDelete should be adapted to work from the rule identifier/prom rule.

title: Creating/deleting rule states no longer rendered and tests deleted without replacement
body: Removing the ruler group query means rules that exist in the Ruler but not yet in Prometheus (newly created, previously shown with a 'Creating' state) are never displayed, and rules deleted from the Ruler but still present in Prometheus (previously shown as non-actionable 'Deleting' items) now render as fully normal, actionable list items. The tests covering both behaviors ('should render rule with url and creating state when only ruler rule exists', 'should render delete rule operation list item when only prom rule exists') and the matchRules unit tests were deleted rather than replaced. If eventual-consistency handling is intentionally dropped, the PR should state so; otherwise rules will appear stale/actionable during the propagation window.

title: isProvisionedPromRule depends on `provenance` field that the Prometheus API may not return
body: The client-side change adds `provenance?: string` to GrafanaPromRuleDTOBase and uses `isProvisionedPromRule` (checking promRule.provenance) to decide immutability (edit/delete/pause) for Grafana rules in the list view. If the backend /api/v1/rules (Grafana Prometheus endpoint) does not actually include provenance in its response, provisioned (file-based) Grafana rules will be treated as mutable and users will be shown Edit/Delete/Pause actions that will fail on save. This should be verified against the API contract (or covered by an MSW mock that omits provenance) before merging.

title: Silence ability for GrafanaPromRule ignores loading state of folder/permissions
body: In useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities, [AlertRuleAction.Silence] is [silenceSupported, canSilenceInFolder && isAlertingRule]. Unlike the ruler-based useCanSilence (which returns [false,false] while folder is loading or missing), canSilenceInFolder evaluates immediately: while the folder is still loading, hasFolderSilencePermission is false, so a user whose only silence permission is the folder-scoped AlertingSilenceCreate will see the Silence item flicker (hidden, then appear) — and worse, useFolderPermissions returns {} for a rule whose folder cannot be resolved, so such rules rely solely on the global permission. Consider gating on folder loading for consistency.

title: Each Grafana list item now triggers per-rule folder fetches via hooks
body: GrafanaRuleListItem renders RuleActionsButtons which calls useGrafanaPromRuleAbility, and AlertRuleMenu calls useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities; each useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities invocation runs useFolder(folderUid) and useGetGrafanaAlertingConfigurationStatusQuery. With the old ruler-based flow these were partially memoized via useAllAlertRuleAbilities; now every rule in a large list (e.g. 80+ rules) issues hook-driven folder lookups (once per unique folder, but the ability memo/object is per-rule) — verify that the folder query is deduplicated by RTKQ caching and that the double evaluation (ruler hook + prom hook both running in AlertRuleMenu/RuleActionsButtons for every rule) doesn't measurably regress list rendering.

title: GrafanaRuleListItem rendered without a React key in the filtered rule list
body: When rendering rules of origin 'grafana', the previous code passed `key={key}` to GrafanaRuleLoader; the new GrafanaRuleListItem call omits the key entirely (the `datasource` and `default` branches still pass keys). In a list that grows via infinite scroll and re-renders, React cannot stably identify these items, which can cause incorrect DOM reuse/state reuse (e.g. open dropdowns or drawers attaching to the wrong rule) and wasted re-renders. The key should be restored.

title: Delete (and Pause) menu actions never render in the alert list view
body: In the new ruler-less list view, AlertRuleMenu is invoked with rulerRule undefined (GrafanaRuleListItem passes only promRule). The Delete item is gated on `canDelete && rulerRule` (line 165) and the Pause item on `canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` (line 123), so even though the new promRule-based abilities (`grafanaDeleteAbility`, `grafanaPauseAbility`) are computed and can be true, the menu items are never rendered. Users lose the ability to delete or pause Grafana-managed rules from the list view — a functional regression the new promRule ability code was meant to enable. Delete also needs a new identifier-based flow since handleDelete currently requires a RulerRuleDTO.

title: Silence drawer never opens when only promRule is provided
body: In the list view path only `promRule` is passed (rule/rulerRule undefined). The 'Silence notifications' menu item does render because `canSilence` can now be satisfied via useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities, but the drawer is gated on `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) && showSilenceDrawer`, and `rule` is undefined here. Clicking 'Silence notifications' sets state that has no effect — the silence drawer silently never appears. The condition needs to also handle the GrafanaPromRuleDTO case (and SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer needs a prom-rule-based invocation).

title: Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable in useAllRulerRuleAbilities
body: The refactored useAllRulerRuleAbilities hardcodes `const isFederated = false` with a TODO. The previous useAllAlertRuleAbilities computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` and used it to mark federated rules as immutable (no edit/delete/pause/duplicate). Since useAllAlertRuleAbilities now delegates to this hook and no longer receives the rule group, federated Mimir rule groups will incorrectly be reported as editable/deletable, allowing users to attempt unsupported mutations on federated rules.

title: Rule view link lost the returnTo parameter
body: The deleted GrafanaRuleLoader built the list-item href with `createRelativeUrl('/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view', { returnTo })` so navigating to a rule from the list and back preserved the list context. The new GrafanaRuleListItem creates the URL without returnTo, so users clicking a rule from the filtered list lose their filter/list context when returning. Confirm this drop is intentional; if not, restore the returnTo parameter.

title: showDivider expression wraps single values in arrays and is misleading
body: `[canPause, canSilence, shouldShowDeclareIncidentButton, canDuplicate].some(Boolean) && [canExport].some(Boolean)` — the second clause is equivalent to plain `canExport`. Beyond style, this makes the divider logic hard to verify and suggests an intended condition that was never written (e.g. shareUrl should probably also gate the divider, otherwise 'Copy link' can appear directly above/below a divider inconsistently when canExport is false). Simplify to an explicit expression.

title: getGrafanaRuleKey emits a stray '}' in the generated key
body: The template literal ends with `${rule.uid}}`, adding a literal closing brace to every grafana rule key. Harmless for uniqueness today but it is a typo that will confuse anyone extending the key format, and since this key mechanism was just re-wired (and is the key that should be passed to GrafanaRuleListItem per the missing-key finding), fix the stray character.

title: Tests mock runQuery, so double interpolation of already-interpolated queries is unverified
body: runSplitQuery now interpolates each target with datasource.applyTemplateVariables before building the sub-requests, and those interpolated targets are then handed to datasource.runQuery, which itself performs template-variable interpolation as part of the normal query path. If that second pass is not a no-op on an already-interpolated expression (e.g. a variable value that itself contains `$`, escaped characters, or format-dependent multi-value expansion), the executed query would be double-interpolated and incorrect. All new tests ('Interpolates queries before execution' in both querySplitting.test.ts and shardQuerySplitting.test.ts) replace runQuery with a jest mock, so they only assert that the pre-interpolation happened and cannot detect that the real runQuery interpolates again. A test that spies on the real interpolation path (or a check that runQuery skips interpolation) is needed before this can be trusted.

title: $__range guard in querySupportsSplitting now runs against the interpolated expression
body: querySupportsSplitting explicitly refuses to split queries containing a range variable because $__range must be interpolated on the backend against the split time range. This PR changes the order so that datasource.applyTemplateVariables runs before the partition into splitting/non-splitting queries (line 299 precedes the partition on line 300). The guard isQueryWithRangeVariable now inspects the interpolated expr: in any context where the frontend template service resolves $__range (for example when scopedVars carries a range variable, or via a dashboard variable whose value is '$__range'), the literal '$__range' no longer appears in the expr, the query is misclassified as splittable, and it gets executed with a per-chunk $__range baked in from the wrong (already-replaced) range, producing wrong data. Previously the check ran on the raw expression. The guard should be evaluated on the pre-interpolation expression, or interpolation must demonstrably preserve $__range.

title: Interpolating before querySupportsSplitting() can break the $__range guard and split queries with a baked-in full range
body: querySupportsSplitting() (line 282-289) relies on isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) to detect `$__range` and exclude those queries from time splitting, with an explicit comment saying `$__range` must be interpolated on the backend with the split time range. This PR now calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables() on every target before that check runs. If template interpolation resolves a `$__range` reference (e.g. scopedVars carries the range variables, so `$__range` becomes a fixed duration of the *original* full range), isQueryWithRangeVariable() no longer matches: the query is no longer excluded, and it gets split into day-long chunks while the expression still contains the full-range duration. Each sub-request then computes over the whole original range instead of the split range, producing wrong results — exactly the failure mode the existing comment warns about. Either applyTemplateVariables must be guaranteed not to resolve range variables, or the range-variable check must be done on the pre-interpolation expr.

title: Queries are interpolated twice in the shard-splitting path
body: runShardSplitQuery() now maps targets through datasource.applyTemplateVariables() (line 52), but it then delegates execution to runSplitQuery() (line 163), which in this same PR was changed to call datasource.applyTemplateVariables() again on every target of the request it receives (querySplitting.ts line 299). Every query is therefore interpolated twice (the updated shard test even asserts 5 calls for a single target). Template interpolation is not guaranteed idempotent: if a variable's value itself contains `$`-like syntax (e.g. a label value or regex with `$`), or if the interpolation of step/expr is not a pure function of the input, the second pass can mangle the expression or step. The duplicated interpolation should be removed from one of the two layers, or runSplitQuery should be given a way to skip interpolation for already-interpolated targets.

title: Interpolating before the $__range guard defeats the no-split check for range-variable queries
body: runSplitQuery now calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables() on each target before the partition step. The subsequent querySupportsSplitting() check relies on isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) detecting a literal $__range/$__range_s variables in the expression (see the comment at querySplitting.ts:285-287: queries with $__range must not be split because the backend interpolates $__range against the split sub-range). After applyTemplateVariables runs, $__range has already been replaced with the full original time range, so isQueryWithRangeVariable never matches and such queries are now split into per-day chunks with the full-range value baked into the expr. Every sub-request then aggregates over the whole range instead of its chunk, producing duplicated/incorrect data for any query using $__range. The interpolation must happen after the range-variable check, or the check must run on the pre-interpolation expression.

title: Double template interpolation in the shard-splitting path
body: runShardSplitQuery now interpolates every target via datasource.applyTemplateVariables(), but the resulting queries are then passed to runSplitQuery(), which (after this PR) calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables() again on the same targets (querySplitting.ts:299). Template interpolation is not idempotent in general: if a variable's value itself contains text that looks like a variable reference or a `$` character (common in label-filter values, regex patterns, or chained variables), the second pass will re-interpolate the already-substituted value and corrupt the expression or step. Either runShardSplitQuery should skip interpolation and let runSplitQuery do it once, or runSplitQuery needs a way to know the targets are already interpolated. There is also no test covering this double-interpolation scenario.

title: $__auto and other interval macros are frozen to the full-range value across all split chunks
body: By interpolating with datasource.applyTemplateVariables before splitting, built-in macros like $__auto (and any interval-derived variable) are resolved once against the original request's range/interval and then reused verbatim in every sub-request's narrower time range. Previously the backend resolved these per sub-request, allowing each chunk to use a range-appropriate value. The new test in querySplitting.test.ts ('Interpolates queries before execution') hard-codes the expectation that $__auto becomes 5m for all three daily chunks, which codifies the behavior change; for range-sensitive macros this can change results (e.g., count_over_time windows no longer adapting per chunk). This should be confirmed as intended and, if so, documented, since it silently changes query semantics for existing dashboards.

title: FromContext fallback silently drops contextual attributes
body: In grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext, if the underlying infra logger's FromContext does not return a *log.ConcreteLogger, the code falls back to d.New(), which returns a logger with only the original logger's context and none of the contextual attributes (endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, uname) that ContextualLoggerMiddleware put into the request context. Since the data-egress log line in LoggerMiddleware.logRequest now depends entirely on these contextual attributes for plugin identification, this fallback would produce 'Plugin Request Completed' logs with no pluginId/endpoint, breaking log-based data egress auditing without any error or warning. Consider logging or handling the type-assertion failure explicitly.

title: traceID field removed from grafana-data-egress log line
body: The refactor removes the explicit "traceID" key/value pair that LoggerMiddleware previously appended to every 'Plugin Request Completed' (grafana-data-egress) log entry (tracing.TraceIDFromContext is no longer called there). Any consumer or dashboard relying on the traceID field in these data-egress logs will lose the ability to correlate egress events with traces, unless the infra logger's contextual attributes happen to include it. This is a behavioral/contract change for existing log consumers and is not called out in the PR description.

title: Test and its name not updated after rename, and no tests for new middleware
body: The test function is still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware even though the middleware was renamed to MetricsMiddleware, leaving misleading test output. More importantly, the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware (contextual_logger_middleware.go) has no test coverage at all: nothing verifies that endpoint/pluginId/dsName/dsUID/uname attributes are injected into the context for each of QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth and CollectMetrics, nor that the logger-middleware integration produces the expected log fields. Given the PR claims behavior parity (contextual logging moved rather than removed), this is a test gap.

title: Comment and helper name (instrumentContext) contradict the middleware's purpose
body: The comment on instrumentContext says it 'adds a contextual logger with plugin and request details to the given context', and the function retains the 'instrument' naming from the old InstrumentationMiddleware, but the function actually stores contextual log attributes via log.WithContextualAttributes, not a logger. This misleading naming/doc invites misuse; the function should be renamed (e.g. contextWithLogAttributes) and the comment corrected.

title: Log fields now depend on middleware ordering, which is unenforced
body: After this change, the pluginId, endpoint, dsName, dsUID and uname fields in the 'Plugin Request Completed' logs are supplied only by ContextualLoggerMiddleware, which must wrap (appear before) LoggerMiddleware in the middleware stack. Previously InstrumentationMiddleware was documented as 'should live at the top of the middleware stack' and the LoggerMiddleware computed these fields itself from the request. Now nothing prevents CreateMiddlewares callers or future refactors from ordering LoggerMiddleware before ContextualLoggerMiddleware, which would silently emit egress logs missing all identifying fields. The old comment about the required stack position was dropped instead of being moved to the new middleware, so the ordering constraint is now undocumented.

title: traceID and request-scoped fields dropped from 'grafana-data-egress' log event
body: The refactored logRequest no longer emits the traceID field (previously extracted via tracing.TraceIDFromContext and appended explicitly). It now relies on m.logger.FromContext(ctx) picking up contextual attributes set by the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware, but nothing in the new chain re-adds traceID, and whether infra/log's FromContext injects the current span's trace ID depends on internals not guaranteed here. Any dashboards, alerts, or log pipelines consuming the 'grafana-data-egress' event's traceID (and, if the contextual attributes are missing, pluginId/endpoint/dsName/dsUID/uname) fields will silently lose them. Either restore the traceID field explicitly or add a test asserting the full log line content.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, hiding log assertions
body: The new TestLogger.FromContext implementation returns NewTestLogger(), a brand-new logger whose Info/Warn/Error calls are recorded on the new instance and never visible to the test holding the original TestLogger. Since LoggerMiddleware.logRequest now logs via m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), any test that wires in a TestLogger and asserts on f.InfoLogs (message, status, duration, etc.) will see zero calls and silently pass trivially. FromContext should return f itself (or record into f) so assertions on the middleware's log output actually work.

title: FromContext fallback silently discards contextual attributes
body: In grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext, when the underlying infra logger's FromContext does not return a *log.ConcreteLogger, the code falls back to d.New(), which returns a logger without any of the request-scoped contextual attributes that log.WithContextualAttributes placed in the context. All endpoint/pluginId/dsName/uname attributes added by ContextualLoggerMiddleware would be silently dropped from log output in that case. A safer fallback would attempt to re-apply the contextual attributes from the context.

title: Adding FromContext to the Logger interface is a breaking change for implementers
body: Adding a new method FromContext(context.Context) Logger to the exported plugins/log.Logger interface breaks compilation for any external package that implements Logger (the PR itself had to patch the in-repo fake in fake.go, confirming this). If pkg/plugins/log is consumed outside the repository or by plugins/tests in other modules, this needs a note or a versioning consideration.

title: Test name and coverage not updated for the rename/refactor
body: The test is still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware although the middleware is now MetricsMiddleware, and no test was added for the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware or for the LoggerMiddleware's new FromContext-based logging. The contextual-logger behavior (endpoint/pluginId/dsName/dsUID/uname attributes appearing in 'Plugin Request Completed' logs) is completely untested, so regressions in attribute propagation would go unnoticed.

title: LoggerMiddleware silently loses pluginId/endpoint/traceID unless ContextualLoggerMiddleware is composed first
body: The "Plugin Request Completed" log line (the grafana-data-egress audit event) previously included pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName, dsUID and traceID explicitly. It now relies entirely on `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)` picking up contextual attributes that were injected by the separate ContextualLoggerMiddleware. Nothing enforces that composition: if LoggerMiddleware is used without ContextualLoggerMiddleware earlier in the chain (e.g. in tests, alternative wire setups, or future reordering of CreateMiddlewares), the audit logs will silently contain no pluginId, endpoint, user or datasource identifiers and no traceID. There is no test covering the LoggerMiddleware output fields after this change to catch such a regression.

title: traceID no longer guaranteed in data-egress log event
body: The old code explicitly appended `traceID` from `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` to the "Plugin Request Completed" log parameters. The new code drops that and relies on the contextual logger (`FromContext`) to surface a trace ID. Unless `log.WithContextualAttributes`/`ConcreteLogger.FromContext` is guaranteed to attach the trace ID from the context, this removes the traceID field from the grafana-data-egress event, breaking correlation between plugin egress logs and traces. This should be verified or the traceID explicitly re-added.

title: Stream endpoints are not enriched with the contextual logger
body: SubscribeStream, PublishStream and RunStream are passed through without calling instrumentContext, so any downstream logging for streaming requests will lack pluginId/endpoint/dsName/uname. RunStream is a long-lived request where such context is especially valuable. This matches the old behavior for the logger, but since the PR introduces a dedicated middleware whose sole purpose is contextual logging, the omission is now more conspicuous.

title: No tests for the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware
body: A new middleware with non-trivial behavior (attribute selection, nil checks on DataSourceInstanceSettings and User) is added without any test coverage. There is also no test verifying that the LoggerMiddleware's output actually contains the previously-present fields (pluginId, endpoint, traceID, uname, dsName) after the refactor, which is the main behavioral risk of this PR.

title: Test still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware after rename to MetricsMiddleware
body: The middleware was renamed from InstrumentationMiddleware to MetricsMiddleware, but the test function is still called TestInstrumentationMiddleware, which is confusing for anyone searching for tests of the renamed component.

title: Anonymous auth now performs a blocking DB write on the request path
body: The previous code tagged anonymous devices in a background goroutine with a 2-minute timeout, decoupling it from request latency. This change makes `Authenticate` call `TagDevice` synchronously on the request context, so every anonymous request from a device not in the 29-minute local cache adds a database roundtrip (and a COUNT query plus INSERT/UPDATE when a device limit is configured) to login/authn latency. Under load on anonymous-enabled instances this measurably slows requests and adds DB pressure; the original async design existed for this reason and no replacement (e.g. async with error propagation for the limit case only) was provided.

title: ErrDeviceLimitReached returned raw to authn produces an opaque auth failure
body: When the device limit is reached, `Authenticate` returns `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached` directly as the authentication error. There is no mapping to an HTTP status or user-facing message, so a user exceeding the device limit will get a generic internal auth error (likely 500) with only "device limit reached" in logs, instead of a clear 4xx with an explanatory message. The error should be wrapped/mapped to a proper authn error type before being returned.

title: Device limit check is not atomic (count-then-insert race)
body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` first runs a COUNT query and then a separate INSERT/UPSERT, without a transaction or lock. Concurrent requests from multiple new devices can all observe a count below the limit and all insert, overshooting `device_limit` arbitrarily under load. The check and insert (or the update fallback) need to be done atomically (e.g. in a transaction with a row lock, or by enforcing the limit inside the upsert statement) for the limit to actually hold.

title: Local cache marker set before the store call masks the device-limit error for 29 minutes
body: In `tagDeviceUI`, `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})` is executed before `CreateOrUpdateDevice`. If the store call then fails — including with `ErrDeviceLimitReached` or any transient DB error — the cache still holds the device key for up to 29 minutes, so all subsequent requests for that device return nil early from the cache. This means the limit error is reported only on the first request per device per cache window (inconsistent enforcement), and transient DB failures are silently swallowed after the first attempt. The cache entry should be set only after a successful store write, or rolled back on error.

title: anonymousDeviceLimit always serialized, contradicting the optional TS type
body: The Go DTO field `AnonymousDeviceLimit int64` has no `omitempty`, so the frontend settings JSON always contains `anonymousDeviceLimit: 0` when unlimited, while the TypeScript type declares it as `number | undefined`. Code distinguishing "no limit" via `undefined` (e.g. `if (config.anonymousDeviceLimit)`) works, but code using `=== undefined` or relying on the key's absence will misbehave. The Go field should be a pointer with `omitempty` (like `TokenExpirationDayLimit`-style optional fields) to match the declared contract.

title: New device_limit setting is undocumented and the PR description is a template
body: A new `device_limit` key is added under `[auth.anonymous]`, but the configuration documentation (configure-security/configure-authentication docs in grafana/grafana) is not updated in this PR, and the PR description still contains unfilled template placeholders ("[Add a description...]", "Fixes #"). Users cannot discover or correctly use the setting, and the intended semantics (0 = unlimited, expiry window of 30 days) are only visible in code.

title: Device tagging now runs synchronously on the anonymous auth hot path
body: Previously TagDevice ran in a background goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout; this PR makes it a blocking call inside Anonymous.Authenticate using the request context. Every anonymous request now performs at least one (and when a device limit is configured, two: COUNT + INSERT/UPDATE) synchronous database round trips before the request is authenticated. This adds DB latency to every anonymous page load/API call and, if the DB is slow or the request context is cancelled mid-write, anonymous authentication itself fails. The device-limit enforcement could have stayed asynchronous, or only the limit-exceeded path made synchronous.

title: Device limit check is a TOCTOU race (COUNT then INSERT, no transaction or unique constraint logic)
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice first runs CountDevices and then, if count < limit, executes an upsert in a separate session. Under concurrent requests from distinct devices, many goroutines can observe count < limit simultaneously and all insert, exceeding the configured device limit by an arbitrary amount. There is no transaction, no locking, and no conditional insert. If the limit is meant to be a hard cap (e.g., for licensing), it can be materially exceeded under load.

title: Changed constructor/provider signatures with no visible update to DI registration
body: ProvideAnonDBStore gained a `deviceLimit int64` parameter and ProvideAnonymousDeviceService changed its third parameter from `anonstore.AnonStore` to `db.DB`. The PR contains no changes to the fx/wire registration (e.g., pkg/server) that supplies these providers. If the registration still lists `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` in a provider set, fx cannot satisfy the new `int64` argument and startup will fail; if it passed an AnonStore value to ProvideAnonymousDeviceService, the build breaks. The wiring change should be included in the PR (and the removed injection of an AnonStore also breaks any test doubles/Enterprise consumers of that provider signature).

title: anonymousDeviceLimit always serialized (0 when unset), conflicting with frontend type `number | undefined`
body: The DTO field is `int64` with no `omitempty`, so the frontend always receives `anonymousDeviceLimit: 0` even when no limit is configured. The TS type declares `number | undefined`, and GrafanaBootConfig defaults it to `undefined`, so consumers distinguishing 'no limit' from 'limit of 0' will see inconsistent values depending on whether backend or frontend defaults won the merge. Either use a pointer with omitempty, or make the frontend type `number` with a documented 0-means-unlimited semantic.

title: updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached for devices that exist but expired
body: When the limit is reached, updateDevice only updates rows whose updated_at is within [UpdatedAt-30d, UpdatedAt+1min]. A returning device whose row is older than 30 days (but younger than the 61-day cleanup retention) matches zero rows, so the caller gets ErrDeviceLimitReached and the user is denied anonymous access — the same error as an entirely new device. More importantly, the error name is misleading for this case and, in client.go, any ErrDeviceLimitReached from Authenticate is surfaced as an auth failure to the user with no differentiation; consider whether an expired-device renewal should evict/replace rather than hard-fail.

title: No test that an existing device is successfully updated when the limit is reached
body: The new test only covers the rejection path (second distinct device fails with ErrDeviceLimitReached). There is no test asserting the intended behavior that a *known* device can still refresh (update) its row when count >= limit, nor a test with deviceLimit=0 confirming the limit is disabled. The updateDevice path (rowsAffected > 0) has no coverage at all.

title: Query string passed as first Exec argument via args slice is fragile
body: updateDevice (and the existing upsert) prepend the query into the args slice and call dbSession.Exec(args...). This works only if the session's Exec signature is (query, args...); passing the query through an `[]interface{}` is unusual and breaks if the Exec implementation type-checks or logs parameters, and it obscures intent. Additionally, `args` is captured and mutated inside the WithDbSession closure while also being the outer variable; a retry of the session callback (xorm retries transactions in some configurations) would re-prepend the query to an already-prepended slice on a second invocation, producing an invalid call.

title: Device limit is bypassed after the first rejected request due to localCache set before the DB call
body: In tagDeviceUI, localCache.SetDefault(key, ...) is executed before calling anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. If CreateOrUpdateDevice fails with ErrDeviceLimitReached, the device ID is still marked as tagged in the 29-minute local cache. On the user's next request, the cache hit makes tagDeviceUI return nil without touching the database, so Anonymous.Authenticate succeeds. The net effect is that the device limit only rejects each new device once per ~29 minutes; every subsequent request from that device authenticates successfully. The cache entry must only be set after a successful CreateOrUpdateDevice (and any error path should invalidate it).

title: Count-then-insert race allows the device limit to be exceeded
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice first runs CountDevices in one session and, if the count is below deviceLimit, performs the insert in a separate session/transaction. Two (or many) concurrent requests from different new devices can each observe count < limit and all insert, exceeding the configured limit. The check-and-insert must be atomic (e.g. a single conditional insert/transaction with a lock, or a unique count constraint) to actually enforce the limit under load, which is exactly the scenario (burst of anonymous requests) this feature targets.

title: TagDevice moved onto the synchronous request path, removing the previous timeout/async isolation
body: The old code ran TagDevice in a goroutine with a 2-minute context.WithTimeout, so database slowness in the anon_device table never delayed or failed anonymous authentication. The new code calls a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, ...) synchronously inside Authenticate using the request context. Now every anonymous request performs up to two extra DB round trips (COUNT + INSERT/UPDATE) before the identity is returned; a slow or locked anon_device table will hang or fail all anonymous access. If the synchronous behavior is required to surface the limit error, consider at minimum retaining a timeout so DB issues cannot degrade anonymous auth.

title: ErrDeviceLimitReached returned raw from Authenticate produces an opaque 500-style auth failure
body: When TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, Authenticate returns that error directly. The authn layer will treat this as an internal authentication error rather than an expected 'too many devices' condition, so users over the limit will get a generic error (likely 500 Internal Server Error on every request) with no indication of the cause. There is no mapping of this sentinel error to an appropriate HTTP status (e.g. 403/429) or user-facing message anywhere in this PR, making the feature effectively brick anonymous access without explanation once the limit is hit (combined with the cache bug, intermittently).

title: MySQL rowsAffected==0 misinterpreted as device-limit-reached
body: updateDevice treats result.RowsAffected() == 0 as ErrDeviceLimitReached. With MySQL's default behavior (rows affected = rows *changed*, not rows matched), an UPDATE that sets identical values reports 0 affected rows. updated_at has second precision in MySQL, so an update of an existing device within the same second (or with unchanged values) can yield 0 rows affected and wrongly return ErrDeviceLimitReached, rejecting a legitimate existing device. The code should distinguish 'device row not found/not active' from 'no values changed' (e.g. check for existence separately or use CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS semantics).

title: Expiry window logic: a device that exists but is older than 30 days can never be updated when limit is reached, and error semantics conflate cases
body: updateDevice's WHERE clause requires updated_at BETWEEN (UpdatedAt-30d) and (UpdatedAt+1m). If the count of active devices has reached the limit but the requesting device's row exists yet falls outside that window (e.g. clock skew or a device idle just past 30 days before cleanup runs), the UPDATE affects 0 rows and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached even though this device is one of the 'expired' rows that shouldn't count toward the limit. The store then neither updates nor deletes the stale row, so the device stays locked out until the 61-day cleanup job removes it.

title: AnonymousDeviceLimit exposed to all frontend clients including anonymous users
body: AnonymousDeviceLimit is included in the frontend settings DTO served to every requester, including unauthenticated/anonymous visitors. This leaks an instance's configured capacity limit (useful reconnaissance for abuse: an attacker knows exactly how many spoofed X-Grafana-Device-Id values are needed to lock out legitimate anonymous users, since the limit is enforced per arbitrary client-supplied device IDs). Consider only exposing it to signed-in admins, or not exposing it at all if no frontend code consumes it — no frontend usage is added in this PR, only the type declarations.

title: New device_limit setting is undocumented and lacks validation
body: The new auth.anonymous device_limit setting is parsed with MustInt64(0) but has no documentation (configure docs/conf defaults), and negative values are not rejected. A negative value behaves like 0 (limit disabled) due to the `deviceLimit > 0` check, silently ignoring the user's intent; a validation error for negative values would be clearer. Also note that device_limit interacts with the 61-day retention (keepFor) in impl.go while the limit counts only devices active in the last 30 days — this asymmetry is nowhere documented for operators.

title: Debug/progress logging emitted at Error level with always-nil error field
body: The new batch loops call r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", ...) (and similarly at lines 537, 554, 557, 576, 579) unconditionally, even on the success path. These are informational/progress messages about normal cleanup batches, but they log at Error level, which will fire alerting and pollute error-level logs on every cleanup run for every Grafana instance with annotation cleanup enabled. Additionally, the "err" key is logged after the `if err != nil` early-return, so it is always nil. These should be Debug-level logs and the nil err fields removed.

title: Cleanup job frequency changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute without description or release note
body: The ticker driving all background cleanup jobs (snapshots, dashboard versions, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history) was changed from every 10 minutes to every 1 minute. This is a significant, unrelated behavioral change that is not mentioned in the PR description or tied to the deadlock fix, and it multiplies the background DB load of all cleanup jobs by ~10x. If the 1-minute cadence is intentionally needed for the new batched annotation cleanup, it should be documented in the PR/What's New; otherwise it should be reverted or made configurable.

title: untilDoneOrCancelled can loop forever when fetched IDs delete zero rows
body: The batching loop terminates only when a batch reports zero affected rows (or errors/context cancel). There is now a divergence between the SELECT (fetchIDs) and the DELETE (deleteByIDs) since they run in separate sessions: if fetchIDs keeps returning the same IDs but the DELETE affects 0 rows (e.g., rows concurrently deleted by another process, or RowsAffected misreporting on some drivers), the loop never terminates and spins on the same query forever. Previously the delete affected-rows and selection were one statement so this could not happen. A safer termination condition is len(ids) == 0, not affected == 0.

title: Cleanup uses r.log.Error for routine per-batch logging of full ID lists
body: In CleanAnnotations, CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags and the batch callbacks, every batch logs 'Annotations to clean by time/count', 'Tags to clean' and 'cleaned ...' via r.log.Error, including the entire slice of IDs. These are normal operational/debug messages, not errors (the err field is often even nil at that point). Since the cleanup service now runs every minute, this will flood Grafana logs with error-level entries on every instance, including potentially thousands of IDs per line, polluting error dashboards and alerting. These should be Debug/Info level and should not log the full ID slices.

title: Placeholder-based DELETE ... IN breaks on SQL Server when batch size exceeds ~2100 parameters
body: deleteByIDs builds a DELETE with one '?' placeholder per ID and only special-cases SQLite's 999-parameter limit. SQL Server (a supported Grafana database) has a limit of 2100 parameters per statement. With AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize configured above 2100 (the PR's own test uses 32767), every batch DELETE will fail on SQL Server with a parameter-count error, breaking annotation cleanup entirely on that backend. The previous single-statement LIMIT-based approach had no such limit. The inlining fallback should also apply to (or otherwise handle) SQL Server, or the batch should be chunked to the dialect's parameter limit.

title: Cleanup ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute without mention in PR description
body: The Run loop ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, a 10x increase in frequency of all cleanup jobs (snapshots, dashboard versions, query history, annotations, etc.), but the PR description only discusses the deadlock fix. This behavior change is undocumented, increases background DB load, and combined with the new per-batch Error-level logging will multiply log volume tenfold. It should either be justified/reverted or documented, and the reviewer checklist ('notable improvement' docs) addressed.

title: Log statements include a stale/always-nil err field
body: The 'Annotations to clean by time'/'by count' and 'Tags to clean' log calls include an "err" key that is always nil at that point (the error case returns earlier), and the 'cleaned ...' calls log the error after already returning it upstream. This is misleading in log output and will confuse anyone investigating issues from logs; the err fields should be removed or the error handling restructured so errors are logged once, at the appropriate level.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged at Error level
body: In CleanAnnotations, CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags the new code calls r.log.Error(...) for every batch, including fully successful ones (e.g. `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, ...)` and the matching "cleaned annotations" / "Tags to clean" / "cleaned tags" calls at lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579). This is debug/diagnostic output, and now every annotation cleanup job run on every Grafana instance will emit Error-level log lines with the full list of deleted annotation IDs, polluting logs, potentially triggering alerting on error logs, and leaking annotation IDs. These should be Debug level (and drop the always-nil "err" field and the huge "ids" slice).

title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute without mention in PR description
body: The cleanup loop ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, but the PR description only discusses the annotation deadlock fix. This makes all cleanup jobs (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history) run 10x more often, which increases recurring database load for all users and is a behavior change that should be documented in the PR description / changelog. Note also that the per-run timeout in clean() remains 9 minutes, so the intended cadence is unclear; if a cleanup cycle takes several minutes, jobs effectively run back-to-back.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled when the request finishes
body: In Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection, the goroutine that writes to the legacy store derives its 10-second-timeout context from the incoming request context (`context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). The parent `ctx` is cancelled as soon as the HTTP request that triggered the write completes, so the legacy write is very likely aborted immediately rather than running for the intended 10 seconds. This defeats the purpose of the 'safe measure' write to legacy: legacy storage will silently miss writes whenever the client disconnects or the request handler returns quickly, leaving the two stores permanently divergent with no error surfaced. The goroutine should use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (or a background context) as the parent.

title: DeleteCollection async legacy call records metric as 'storage' duration
body: In the DeleteCollection goroutine, the legacy delete result is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `recordLegacyDuration`. This pollutes the `unified_storage_write_duration`/legacy metric series with legacy-store latencies and error counts, making the dual-writer metrics wrong and misleading for anyone monitoring migration progress.

title: Storage failures recorded under the legacy metric in Create and Update
body: In `Create` (line 45) and `Update` (line 129), the error path when the unified Storage call fails calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with the storage start time. This records a failed, zero-length 'legacy' operation that never happened, corrupting legacy-store error-rate and duration metrics. It should be `recordStorageDuration(true, ...)` to match the Delete and DeleteCollection error paths.

title: Delete success metric uses object name instead of kind as label
body: On the Delete success path, `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the resource `name` where every other call passes `options.Kind` as the label. Since object names are unbounded user-controlled values, this creates unbounded label cardinality in Prometheus (one metric series per deleted object name) and inconsistent labeling versus the failure path on line 103. It should pass `options.Kind`.

title: Delete puts the base logger into the context instead of the enriched one
body: In `Delete`, `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` uses the base `d.Log` rather than the locally built `log` (with name/kind/method values) that every other method uses. Any logger retrieved from the context downstream (including in the async legacy goroutine, which inherits this ctx) will be missing the name and kind fields, making log correlation for deletes inconsistent.

title: Tests spawn unmocked async legacy calls that can panic or race in goroutines
body: Mode 3 now performs the legacy write in a background goroutine, but the tests never wait for it and in several success cases never stub it: TestMode3_Delete and TestMode3_DeleteCollection set up no `Legacy.Delete`/`Legacy.DeleteCollection` mock expectations, and TestMode3_Create's second case stubs only the legacy mock. testify's `mock.Mock` panics on calls to methods with no expected call, so these goroutines can panic non-deterministically after the subtest finishes, causing flaky suite crashes. Additionally, since the goroutine's error is never returned or awaited, no test actually verifies that the legacy write happens, times out, or that legacy failures are correctly logged/metriced — the core behavior of this PR is untested.

title: No retry, queue, or error surfacing for failed legacy writes
body: All legacy writes are fire-and-forget goroutines: if `d.Legacy.Create/Update/Delete` fails (or the derived context is cancelled per the context issue), the error is only swallowed into a metric — there is no logging of the failure, no retry, and no reconciliation mechanism. Once mode 3 is the default, any transient legacy failure leaves the legacy database permanently out of sync, which matters because legacy Grafana APIs and other code paths still read from legacy storage. At minimum the goroutines should log the legacy error, and the team should confirm a backfill/reconciliation job exists before enabling mode 3.

title: Async legacy writes derived from the request context may be cancelled
body: In Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection, the fire-and-forget goroutine calls `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the incoming HTTP request context. That context is cancelled as soon as the API handler returns, which happens immediately after the unified-storage write succeeds. The legacy write can therefore be aborted with 'context canceled' before it even starts, so legacy storage silently diverges from unified storage. The legacy call should use a detached/background context (with only the logger carried over), not the request context.

title: Update goroutine shares objInfo with the request, causing races and non-idempotent updates
body: The previous implementation wrapped objInfo with `updateWrapper` to force both stores to write the same computed object. Now `d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...)` is invoked asynchronously with the same `objInfo` that unified storage already consumed. `rest.UpdatedObjectInfo` implementations are not required to be thread-safe or idempotent (they can run arbitrary mutate funcs, and often the returned object is mutated in place by storage layers). The legacy goroutine re-invokes `objInfo.UpdatedObject` concurrently with the caller continuing to use the result, which is a data race and can produce a different object in legacy than in unified storage, breaking the dual-write guarantee.

title: Create failure records the wrong metric (legacy instead of storage)
body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with the storage start time. This counts unified-storage failures/errors against the legacy-storage metric, corrupting the dualwriter duration/error metrics used to monitor migration health. It should call `recordStorageDuration`.

title: Update failure records the wrong metric (legacy instead of storage)
body: When `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`, attributing the storage error and its latency to the legacy-storage metric. Same class of mislabeling as the Create path; should be `recordStorageDuration`.

title: DeleteCollection goroutine records legacy write under the storage metric
body: In the DeleteCollection goroutine, the legacy call duration is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)`. The async legacy delete-collection latency and error status are therefore reported as unified-storage metrics, making both series wrong. It should call `recordLegacyDuration`.

title: Delete success passes `name` where the `kind` label is expected
body: On successful unified-storage delete, the metric is recorded as `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` — every other call passes `options.Kind` as that argument. The `kind` metric label will instead contain the object name, producing unbounded label cardinality and inconsistent data for the delete method.

title: Delete builds a context with the wrong logger, dropping name/kind/method fields
body: In Delete, after building `log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method)`, the code does `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` (the bare logger) instead of `log`. The contexted logger used downstream loses the name/kind/method attributes, so error logs from Delete lack the identifying fields present in all other methods.

title: Async legacy write failures are only counted in metrics, never logged or retried
body: In all four write paths the result of the asynchronous legacy write (`errObjectSt` / `err`) is passed only to `recordLegacyDuration` and discarded; there is no `log.Error` and no retry/queue mechanism. The PR description calls the legacy write 'a safe measure', but a silent failure leaves the two stores permanently divergent with only a Prometheus counter as evidence. At minimum the error should be logged (as the previous implementation did with log.Error), otherwise operators have no way to discover divergence.

title: Tests never assert that the async legacy write actually happens
body: Mode 3 now writes to legacy storage in an un-awaited goroutine. The new tests (e.g. TestMode3_Create, TestMode3_Update, TestMode3_Delete, TestMode3_DeleteCollection) set up legacy mock expectations but never call `m.AssertExpectations(t)` or otherwise wait for/sync the goroutine, and `wantErr` cases return before the goroutine's mock call is checked. So the tests can pass even if the legacy write never executes or executes after the test finishes, and the error-path cases (e.g. 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' only sets up a legacy mock that should not be called) actually verify the wrong store. Use mock.AssertExpectations with a channel/waitgroup or testify's assert.Eventually to make the async behavior deterministic.

title: TestMode3_Get shadows the shared prometheus registry with a local one
body: TestMode3_Get declares `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` inside the subtest, shadowing the package-level `p` used by all other tests in the file. This looks like an accidental leftover from moving the registry to package scope (the corresponding line was removed from dualwriter_mode1_test.go in this same PR). While harmless functionally, it makes the test inconsistent with the rest of the file and can hide future refactoring mistakes; the local declaration should be removed.

title: Async legacy writes are canceled when the request context ends
body: In Create, Update, Delete and DeleteCollection, the goroutine that writes to legacy storage derives its 10s-timeout context from the incoming request context (`ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). As soon as the API request returns, the request context is canceled, so the deferred legacy write/delete is aborted with 'context canceled' rather than running for its timeout. This defeats the stated purpose of the mode ('write to legacy as a safe measure') and silently leaves the two stores divergent. The goroutines should use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) (or background) as the parent.

title: DeleteCollection records legacy result with the storage metrics recorder
body: In DeleteCollection's goroutine, the outcome of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded via `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy delete-collection latencies and failures are therefore attributed to unified storage, corrupting the dual-writer metrics used to monitor migration progress.

title: Delete records 'name' where the resource 'kind' label is expected
body: On success, Delete calls `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passing the object name as the label where every other call passes `options.Kind`. This produces unbounded/high-cardinality metric label values (one per object name) and inconsistent series compared to the failure path on line 103 which uses options.Kind.

title: Storage failures in Create and Update are recorded as legacy metrics
body: When d.Storage.Create fails (line 45) or d.Storage.Update fails (line 129), the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` even though the legacy store was never contacted. These failures and their durations are attributed to legacy storage, skewing the dual-writer observability data. Both should be recordStorageDuration.

title: Legacy write failures are swallowed with no logging or reconciliation
body: Previously, errors from the legacy store were at least logged. In the new goroutines, the error from d.Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection is only converted into a boolean for a metric; it is never logged and no reconciliation/retry is queued. Since mode 3 is the last dual-write stage before cutting over to unified storage, silent legacy failures mean data loss in the legacy store with no operator-visible signal beyond an aggregate counter and no way to recover the missed write.

title: Legacy Update reuses the request's objInfo, so legacy can write different data than storage
body: The previous implementation wrapped objInfo so the legacy store received exactly the object that unified storage wrote (via updateWrapper). The new code passes the original objInfo to d.Legacy.Update in a goroutine, so the legacy store re-computes the updated object from its own (possibly stale) current state. If legacy and unified have diverged (e.g., an earlier async legacy write was canceled or failed), the legacy copy can end up with different content than the authoritative unified copy. The updateWrapper mechanism was removed without a replacement guarantee.

title: Legacy Delete failures on NotFound are treated as errors
body: The old Delete tolerated apierrors.IsNotFound from the legacy store (expected when an object exists only in unified storage, which is the common case in mode 3 after migration backfill gaps). The new code records any legacy Delete error, including NotFound, as a failure metric. In mode 3, objects created before backfill will routinely 404 in legacy, producing persistent false failure signals.

title: Delete logs with the bare logger, dropping name/kind context
body: In Delete, `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` is used instead of the `log` variable built two lines above (which includes name, kind and method). Any error logged in Delete will lack the identifying fields, unlike every other method in this file. Likely a copy-paste oversight.

title: Unit tests never verify that the async legacy write actually happens
body: Mode 3's defining behavior is 'write to unified, then asynchronously write to legacy', but none of the tests assert that Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection are invoked (e.g., via m.AssertExpectations or waiting on the goroutine with mock.AssertEventually). The tests return immediately after the unified call, so the goroutines may not have run; a regression that drops the legacy write entirely (or is canceled immediately, as in the context bug) would still pass. Also the error-path test cases set up legacy mock expectations that are never exercised or verified.

title: TestMode3_Get creates its own registry instead of the shared one
body: TestMode3_Get declares a local `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` while every other mode-3 test uses the package-level `p`. This is inconsistent and, if the dual writer registers metrics in NewDualWriter, would panic on double registration in other tests or mask registration issues; the unrelated change to TestMode1_Get that moved `p` to package scope suggests this local declaration is an oversight.

title: Failed reload overwrites a previously valid cache entry with nil
body: When GetWebAssets fails to load the manifest (result == nil, err != nil), line 69 unconditionally assigns entryPointAssetsCache = result (nil). In Dev mode, where reloads are attempted on every call, a transient read failure of assets-manifest.json discards a previously cached, still-valid *dtos.EntryPointAssets, so subsequent requests also fail until the file loads again. Consider only overwriting the cache when err == nil.

title: Non-nil result can be returned together with a non-nil error
body: In the CDN branch, readWebAssetsFromCDN can return both a non-nil dto and a non-nil error (e.g. if the HTTP request succeeds but SetContentDeliveryURL or a later step fails, or if the decoder returns partial data and an error). In that case the file-read fallback at line 59 is skipped (result != nil), and GetWebAssets returns a valid-looking result alongside an error. Callers that check err first will treat this as a failure, while callers that check the pointer will use a possibly malformed asset list. The code should decide on a single source of truth (either result or err) before caching and returning.

title: Cached *dtos.EntryPointAssets is shared unsafely across callers
body: The mutex only protects the cache pointer itself. GetWebAssets returns the same *dtos.EntryPointAssets instance to every caller, and in Dev mode a new instance is built (including a call to SetContentDeliveryURL on line 64) while other goroutines may still be reading the previously returned instance. If any caller ever mutates the returned DTO (or if Dev-mode rebuilds race with concurrent readers of the old value in ways that touch shared inner slices), the race persists. At minimum the code relies on the undocumented assumption that EntryPointAssets is never mutated after being returned; consider documenting that contract or returning a copy.

title: CDN read error is silently discarded when file fallback succeeds
body: When cdn is non-empty and readWebAssetsFromCDN fails (line 56), err holds the CDN error, but line 60 overwrites err with the result of the file read. If the file read then succeeds, the CDN failure is completely lost with no log or trace, making it impossible to diagnose why assets are being served from disk instead of the CDN. The error should be logged or wrapped before falling back.

title: No test covers the race being fixed
body: The PR's stated purpose is fixing a data race on entryPointAssetsCache, but no test is added. Running the existing code under `go test -race` with concurrent GetWebAssets calls (Dev and non-Dev) should be added to prevent regression; otherwise the lock could be removed again without detection.

title: No cache recheck after acquiring the write lock (missing double-checked locking)
body: After the RLock fast path fails, GetWebAssets acquires the exclusive lock and unconditionally re-reads the manifest from disk/CDN and overwrites entryPointAssetsCache. If N concurrent requests arrive before the cache is populated (e.g. at startup in non-Dev mode), every one of them performs the file read serially instead of one goroutine populating the cache and the rest reusing it. The fix is incomplete double-checked locking: after taking the write lock, the function should re-read entryPointAssetsCache and return it if non-nil (for the non-Dev case).

title: Exclusive lock held across file I/O and CDN HTTP request
body: GetWebAssets holds entryPointAssetsCacheMu (write lock) for the entire duration of readWebAssetsFromFile and, if a CDN URL is ever set, the blocking HTTP request in readWebAssetsFromCDN (currently the cdn variable is hardcoded to "", but that is an existing call path). In Dev mode this happens on every call. A slow or hanging CDN request would block every other caller of GetWebAssets, including the RLock fast-path readers, stalling request handling. Consider loading the result outside the lock and only taking the lock briefly to publish it.

title: enableSqlExpressions has dead/misleading logic and ignores the feature flag entirely
body: The function reads `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns false in both branches, so it always returns false regardless of the flag. If intentionally disabling the feature, the function should simply return false (or be removed and the check inlined); as written it implies the flag is consulted when it is not, which will confuse future maintainers re-enabling the feature (they will flip the flag expecting it to work).

title: Error message "sqlExpressions is not implemented" is wrong and unhelpful
body: When a user submits a SQL expression (even one that was previously working with the feature toggle enabled), they get "sqlExpressions is not implemented". The feature is implemented but disabled; a message like "SQL expressions are disabled" would be accurate and actionable. As written, users and support will misdiagnose the cause.

title: Legacy UnmarshalSQLCommand path is not gated by the disable check
body: ReadQuery now returns early for QueryTypeSQL, but the rawNode-based UnmarshalSQLCommand path still constructs a SQLCommand without any feature check. Since sql.TablesList now calls the stub DB which always returns "not implemented", users going through that path get an opaque "error reading SQL command" bad-request error instead of a clear 'feature disabled' message. The gating is inconsistent between the two parsing paths; both should be disabled the same way.

title: TablesList is now guaranteed to fail and still contains the SQL-string-formatting code
body: TablesList calls NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, which now always returns errors.New("not implemented"), so TablesList can never succeed. The function (including the `fmt.Sprintf` SQL string interpolation it was built around) is effectively dead code reached only via UnmarshalSQLCommand to produce a generic error. It should either be removed or its callers short-circuited so users get a meaningful error.

title: No tests cover the new disabled-SQL behavior
body: The PR changes the behavior of SQL expressions (they now always error) and adds an enableSqlExpressions helper whose return value must stay false for the CVE fix to hold, yet no test is added asserting that a SQL expression query returns an error regardless of the FlagSqlExpressions toggle state. Without a regression test, a future refactor of this confusing helper could silently re-enable the vulnerable code path.

title: enableSqlExpressions has inverted, dead logic and always returns false
body: The new enableSqlExpressions helper computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` — so `enabled` is true when the flag is DISABLED — then returns false in both branches, making the function unconditionally false and the flag check pointless. The variable name/logic is inverted and misleading. Consequence: the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle now has no effect at all, and any future maintainer who 'fixes' the obvious inversion (returning `enabled`) would re-enable the vulnerable code path. The function should either be deleted entirely (the stub DB already blocks execution) or written to explicitly and permanently return false with a comment referencing CVE-2024-9264.

title: Error message "sqlExpressions is not implemented" is wrong and misleading
body: When a user submits a SQL expression query, they get `sqlExpressions is not implemented`. The feature was implemented and then deliberately disabled for security reasons (CVE-2024-9264). The message misleads users into thinking it's a temporary gap, and doesn't mention the feature flag. A message like "SQL expressions have been disabled" (ideally referencing the flag/CVE) would be accurate and actionable.

title: Legacy UnmarshalSQLCommand path is not gated by the new reader check
body: The feature-flag/disabled check was only added to the new `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` path (reader.go), but `UnmarshalSQLCommand` (used for the legacy/rawNode query format) still constructs and executes `SQLCommand` without any check. Execution is only prevented because the stub DB in pkg/expr/sql/db.go always returns "not implemented". This means the disable logic is inconsistent across entry points, and if the stub DB is ever re-implemented (or the enableSqlExpressions inversion fixed), the legacy path would silently re-enable the vulnerable feature. The guard should live in NewSQLCommand (or both paths) so all construction sites are covered.

title: Stub DB returns generic "not implemented" errors that surface as confusing 400s
body: All DB methods return `errors.New("not implemented")`. Via NewSQLCommand -> sql.TablesList, a user query now fails with a generic BadRequest "error reading SQL command" (or a raw "not implemented" from Execute) with no indication that SQL expressions were intentionally disabled. Since these stubs exist purely to neutralize the DuckDB dependency, the errors should state that SQL expressions are disabled so users and support can diagnose it.

title: TablesList is now unreachable dead code with SQL-string building logic retained
body: TablesList builds a DuckDB command via fmt.Sprintf with escaped quotes and calls RunCommands, which now always returns "not implemented", so TablesList can never succeed. Keeping the string-interpolation code that talks to a (removed) DuckDB API is dead weight and a hazard if someone wires a real implementation back in (the naive quote-escaping was part of the injection surface). Either delete parser.go's command-building path along with the dependency, or leave a clear comment that this is intentionally disabled.

title: No tests added or updated for the disabled SQL expression behavior
body: This PR removes a whole feature (SQL expressions) and changes the behavior of the QueryTypeSQL path, but includes no test changes: there is no test asserting that SQL expression queries now return an error regardless of the feature toggle, no test covering the legacy UnmarshalSQLCommand path, and any existing tests of sql expressions (e.g. around sql_command.go / sql parser) appear untouched and will either fail or silently no longer exercise the real behavior. A regression test pinning the 'always disabled' behavior would prevent someone from accidentally re-enabling it.

title: enableSqlExpressions is dead logic and always returns false
body: The function `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns `false` in both branches, making the feature-toggle check meaningless dead code. Since the intent of the PR is to disable SQL expressions entirely, this is misleading: readers and linters will assume the flag still has an effect. Either remove the function and the toggle check entirely (and return an unconditional error), or actually honor the flag if that was intended. As written it also guarantees the QueryTypeSQL path can never be enabled, which should be stated clearly in the code rather than hidden behind dead branches.

title: Feature-disable check not applied to UnmarshalSQLCommand / legacy path
body: The new disable check was only added to `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` (pkg/expr/reader.go, QueryTypeSQL case). However `UnmarshalSQLCommand` (pkg/expr/sql_command.go) also constructs `SQLCommand` from user-supplied query JSON (`rn.Query["expression"]`) and does not perform any feature-toggle or disable check. If any code path (e.g. older frontend payloads handled through the raw-node unmarshal route in transform.go/parse.go) still dispatches to `UnmarshalSQLCommand` for `type: "sql"`, a user can still create SQL commands; while the stub DB now fails at Execute time, the parsing/validation code is still reachable and the intended hard disable is inconsistent. The disable should be enforced at command-construction level (or both entry points), not only one reader.

title: Error message 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' is wrong/misleading
body: When a user submits a SQL expression, they get `"sqlExpressions is not implemented"`. The feature is implemented but disabled for security reasons (CVE-2024-9264). The message should say something like "SQL expressions are disabled" so users understand this is a deliberate state and can find the associated documentation/flag. The current wording will generate confusion and unnecessary support issues.

title: Execute overwrites NoData result with empty TableData
body: In `SQLCommand.Execute`, when `frame.Rows() == 0` the code sets `rsp.Values` to a `NoData` value, but then unconditionally overwrites `rsp.Values` with `TableData{Frame: frame}` on the next statement (lines 116-118). The NoData branch is dead code and downstream consumers will see an empty table instead of a NoData result. This is pre-existing, but since this PR touches Execute and leaves it in place, it is worth fixing while here.

title: No tests updated for disabled SQL expressions; existing tests will fail or are now meaningless
body: The PR replaces the DuckDB-backed implementation with stubs that always return "not implemented", and removes the go-duck dependency, but includes no test changes. Any existing tests in pkg/expr/sql (TablesList) or SQL-command integration/e2e tests will now fail because RunCommands/QueryFramesInto always error. Additionally there are no new tests asserting that a QueryTypeSQL expression is rejected with the expected error from ReadQuery, nor that the legacy UnmarshalSQLCommand path is blocked. A security-disable change should come with regression tests proving the CVE vector is closed.

title: SQL injection-prone string interpolation left in TablesList
body: `TablesList` still builds a DuckDB command via `fmt.Sprintf("SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')", rawSQL)` after only escaping single quotes. Although the stub DB now makes this unreachable-at-runtime, the unsafe interpolation pattern remains in the codebase and will be silently revived when a real implementation replaces the stub. The method should either be removed along with the DuckDB dependency, or rewritten to use parameterized command execution. Also note `ast[0]` in tablesFromAST panics on an empty AST slice.

title: Removing the whole-function lock allows concurrent duplicate index builds for the same key
body: BuildIndex previously held b.cacheMu for its entire duration, which (coarsely) serialized index creation. With the lock now only taken around the final map write, two concurrent callers (e.g. two gRPC Search requests hitting getOrCreateIndex for the same NamespacedResource, or a watch event arriving during a first search) can both observe GetIndex()==nil and both run BuildIndex for the same key. For file-based indexes both will call bleve.New with the same directory (filepath.Join(Root, namespace, resource.group)); the second call fails or clobbers the first, and the cache ends up with one index while the other caller holds a stale index object that will never receive watch updates. getOrCreateIndex in resource/search.go already has a TODO acknowledging the per-key blocking need; the lock removal makes this a live bug rather than a theoretical one. A per-key singleflight/mutex is needed.

title: TotalDocs reads b.cache without the cache lock while BuildIndex writes it
body: TotalDocs iterates b.cache with no cacheMu protection. BuildIndex now writes to b.cache (b.cache[key] = idx) concurrently with index builds running in parallel from init's errgroup workers. Previously the coarse lock at least serialized map writes across all builds; now an unsynchronized map read concurrent with a map write can panic the process with 'concurrent map read and map write' or return inconsistent totals. Take b.cacheMu.RLock() in TotalDocs.
