title: Hardcoded per-key exceptions make the sanitizer brittle for future message content
body: normalizeValue() special-cases exactly the keys 'templateHelp', 'optimizeLookupHelp', 'linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit*' and 'error-invalid-multivalued-size' to strip pseudo-HTML/MessageFormat fragments before sanitizing. Any new or existing message that legitimately contains a '<...>' fragment (such as docs examples or another choice-format key) will fail the build, and the only fix is to add another hardcoded key to this private method. A more general mechanism (e.g. an allowlist file or normalizing all {n,choice,...} patterns regardless of key) would avoid repeatedly patching the verifier.

title: isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted comparison and wrong index
body: The new matcher returns false when the grant shortcut MATCHES the expected value: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`. This inverts the logic, so a correctly encoded token ID (e.g. 'onrtac:<uuid>') will fail the matcher while wrong grant types pass (as long as the UUID part is valid). Additionally the comment and the encoding format say the grant shortcut occupies characters 4-5 (substring(4,6)), but the code reads substring(3,5), which is the second char of token type plus first char of grant shortcut. Every test using expectCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectDeviceCodeToToken, expectAuthReqIdToToken will assert against the wrong characters with inverted semantics.

title: rawTokenId null check is missing (duplicated grantType check)
body: The constructor contains `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, ...)` twice; the second occurrence was meant to be `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")`. As a result a null rawTokenId is silently accepted and will later produce a token ID like 'onrtac:null' when encoded, instead of failing fast.

title: Public copy constructor Context(Context) removed, breaking API for custom grants
body: The PR removes the public `Context(Context context)` copy constructor from the non-internal `OAuth2GrantType.Context` class (server-spi-private is part of Keycloak's provider API). Any existing third-party OAuth2GrantType implementation that used this constructor to clone the context (e.g. to override formParams) will fail to compile/deploy after upgrade. This is an API/contract break that should either be deprecated instead of removed, or noted as an intentional incompatible change with migration documentation.

title: Duplicate-shortcut validation is bypassed by lazy map refresh
body: postInit validates that no two grant types share a shortcut by comparing map sizes, but getShortcutByGrantType/getGrantTypeByShortcut later lazily insert entries into the ConcurrentHashMaps without any collision check. If a custom grant deployed at runtime has the same shortcut as a built-in grant (e.g. 'ac'), its mapping silently overwrites the built-in one in grantsByShortcuts, causing decode of existing token IDs to resolve the wrong grant type. The lazy path should detect that the shortcut is already mapped to a different grant and fail (or refuse to register), preserving the invariant enforced at startup.

title: Grant type attribute on refresh overwrites original grant context permanently for the client session
body: validateToken sets `clientSessionCtx.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, REFRESH_TOKEN)` on the (reused) client session context before recreating the token. If the same client session is later used to mint another token through a different path that does not set the attribute (e.g. another grant implementation or token exchange path that relies on the original value), it will now incorrectly encode 'refresh_token' as the grant. Every token minted after the first refresh will report grant type 'refresh_token' instead of the grant that originally authenticated the session, losing the information this PR intends to preserve. If that is intended semantics it should be documented; otherwise the original grant should be retained and only the refresh-time token flagged.

title: decode error message says 'Expected length of 6' but refers to encoded context length
body: When the prefix before ':' is not exactly 6 chars the code throws "Incorrect token id: '...'. Expected length of 6." — ambiguous/wrong message since it is the encoded context part, not the token id, that must be 6 characters. A caller reading the message with a 43-char token ID will be confused. Minor but worth fixing while the format is new.

title: isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted condition and wrong substring offsets
body: In AssertEvents.isAccessTokenId, `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` is inverted (it rejects the token when the grant shortcut matches) and also uses the wrong offsets: the encoded 6-char prefix is sessionType (chars 0-2), tokenType (chars 2-4), grantType (chars 4-6), so the grant shortcut is `substring(4, 6)`, not `substring(3, 5)`. As written the matcher fails for valid tokens with the expected grant and passes for tokens with the wrong grant, so none of the TOKEN_ID assertions in expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectDeviceCodeToToken/expectAuthReqIdToToken actually verify the new encoding.

title: rawTokenId null check checks grantType instead of rawTokenId
body: The constructor calls `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` a second time instead of `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, ...)`. A null rawTokenId is silently accepted, which will later produce an encoded token ID like "onrtac:null" (or an NPE during string concatenation in encodeTokenId), corrupting the token ID.

title: getShortcut() added to OAuth2GrantTypeFactory without a default implementation
body: Adding the abstract method `String getShortcut()` to the public SPI interface OAuth2GrantTypeFactory breaks binary/source compatibility for any third-party OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations (custom grant type extensions): they will fail to load with AbstractMethodError at runtime or fail to compile. A `default` implementation (e.g. returning getId()) would preserve compatibility.

title: Public copy constructor OAuth2GrantType.Context(Context) removed
body: The PR deletes the public `Context(Context)` copy constructor from the SPI class OAuth2GrantType.Context. Any external code (custom grant types or extensions) relying on that constructor will break at compile time or with NoSuchMethodError at runtime. Note also that the new main constructor now captures grantType from formParams, so setFormParams() after construction leaves a stale grantType — a behavior change for anyone using setFormParams.

title: Decoder assumes exactly 6-char context prefix but encoder accepts arbitrary-length grant shortcuts
body: getTokenContextFromTokenId throws IllegalArgumentException when the prefix before ':' is not exactly 6 chars, while encodeTokenId happily concatenates whatever getShortcut() returns (the SPI javadoc even says "usually like 3-letters shortcut"). A custom OAuth2GrantTypeFactory returning a shortcut of length != 2 will produce token IDs that this provider itself cannot decode — any endpoint later calling getTokenContextFromTokenId on such a token will throw IllegalArgumentException. The factory should validate shortcut length (and charset) at startup, or the decoder should be tolerant.

title: getTokenContextFromTokenId throws on malformed legacy/foreign token IDs instead of degrading to UNKNOWN
body: Token IDs without ':' are gracefully mapped to UNKNOWN context, but an ID containing ':' with a prefix that is 6 chars yet uses an unknown session/token/grant shortcut throws IllegalArgumentException. Since token IDs are attacker-influenced input at endpoints like introspection, any future caller of this method must be prepared for exceptions; returning UNKNOWN context (as done for legacy IDs) would be a safer, consistent contract. Also note OAuth2GrantType IDs like the pre-authorized-code URN contain ':' — if a grant ID were ever used as an ID component this parsing would misbehave, so the contract 'throws on anything not self-encoded' should be documented on the SPI interface.

title: Duplicate-shortcut detection via map size comparison is fragile
body: The duplicate detection only compares map sizes; it detects a shared shortcut only indirectly and its error message is confusing. It also does not detect the case where a grant uses the reserved shortcut "na" (which would silently overwrite the UNKNOWN mapping in both maps, keeping sizes equal and passing validation), after which tokens with unknown grant type would decode as that grant type. An explicit duplicate check while populating would be correct and give a clear error.

title: userSession may be null when deriving session type
body: getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext calls clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getUserSession() and immediately dereferences it. For client-credentials grants the client session may not be attached to a user session in all paths (UserSessionModel can be null in some service-account implementations); if any caller invokes this with a detached client session, an NPE is thrown during token creation. The code should null-check and fall back to UNKNOWN/transient.

title: Inverted comparison and wrong substring index in isAccessTokenId matcher
body: In isAccessTokenId the check `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` is inverted: it rejects the token when the shortcut MATCHES the expected grant, so tests will fail on correct token IDs and pass on wrong ones. Additionally the index is wrong: the grant-type shortcut occupies characters 4-5 of the 6-char prefix, so it should be `substring(4, 6)`, not `substring(3, 5)` which grabs the last char of the token-type shortcut plus the first char of the grant shortcut. Every event assertion using this matcher (expectCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectDeviceCodeToToken, expectAuthReqIdToToken) is broken.

title: rawTokenId null check checks grantType instead of rawTokenId
body: The constructor contains `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` twice; the second occurrence should check `rawTokenId`. As a result a null rawTokenId is silently accepted and the "rawTokenId" error message is never produced for an actual null rawTokenId, weakening the intended precondition.

title: Decoding malformed/unrecognized token IDs throws instead of degrading gracefully
body: getTokenContextFromTokenId throws IllegalArgumentException when the prefix before ':' is not exactly 6 chars, or when the session-type/token-type/grant shortcuts are unknown. This method is intended to be called on arbitrary incoming access tokens (e.g. tokens issued by another Keycloak version, a custom TokenContextEncoderProvider, or a custom grant with unregistered shortcut). A token with a colon but unexpected prefix format will cause an unhandled exception (500) in whatever endpoint later consumes this (introspection, userinfo, admin REST per the PR description). It should return UNKNOWN context rather than throwing, matching the no-colon fallback path.

title: getShortcut() added to SPI interface without default method breaks third-party implementations
body: OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is a public SPI (server-spi-private) that third-party grant-type providers implement. Adding the abstract method `String getShortcut()` without a default implementation makes every existing custom OAuth2GrantTypeFactory fail to compile/load at runtime after upgrade. A `default String getShortcut() { return getId(); }` (or similar) would preserve compatibility.

title: Removal of public Context(Context) copy constructor is a source/behavioral break
body: The public copy constructor `Context(Context context)` was deleted and its behavior folded into the main constructor (which now reads grantType from formParams). Any external code subclassing or copying OAuth2GrantType.Context will no longer compile. Additionally, the grantType is now only captured at construction time from formParams; if setFormParams(...) is called afterwards (an existing public mutator), context.grantType becomes stale and will be encoded incorrectly into tokens issued via OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse.

title: Lazy cache refresh can silently corrupt bidirectional grant shortcut maps with duplicates
body: The duplicate-shortcut validation only runs once in postInit. getShortcutByGrantType/getGrantTypeByShortcut later mutate grantsByShortcuts/grantsToShortcuts for newly deployed providers without re-validating uniqueness: if a hot-deployed grant reuses an existing shortcut, grantsByShortcuts is overwritten so two grant types map to one shortcut while grantsToShortcuts keeps both, permanently desynchronizing encode/decode and producing tokens whose grant type decodes to the wrong grant.

title: Unused import TokenExchangeGrantTypeFactory
body: The import org.keycloak.protocol.oidc.grants.TokenExchangeGrantTypeFactory was added but the code uses the string constant OAuth2Constants.TOKEN_EXCHANGE_GRANT_TYPE instead; the import is unused and should be removed.

title: Exhausted federated recovery-code credential cannot be removed via removeStoredCredentialById
body: After switching to RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(), the credential found may now be a federated (user-storage) credential rather than a locally stored one. When all codes are used, the code calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()), but removeStoredCredentialById only removes credentials stored in the Keycloak DB; for a federated credential (id prefixed with the storage provider, or an id generated by the storage) this call silently does nothing. The exhausted credential stays active in the user storage, so the user is forced into the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action on every login while the dead credential remains listed/valid. The removal needs to go through the storage provider's disable/update path, or be skipped for federated credentials.

title: Creating recovery codes in user storage leaves a pre-existing local recovery credential active
body: createRecoveryCodesCredential() first tries user.credentialManager().updateCredential(); if the user storage accepts the recovery-codes type it stores the credential there and returns, never removing any previously stored local (Keycloak DB) recovery-code credential for that user. The local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential() path replaces the existing credential, so the previous behavior guaranteed a single active credential. With this change a user who already had a local recovery credential and whose storage now supports the type ends up with two simultaneously valid recovery-code credentials (one local, one federated), and the old one is never invalidated. The user-storage branch should also remove any stored local credential of the same type (or the check should be skipped when a local credential exists).

title: User label and generatedAt are not propagated to user storage when creating recovery codes
body: When delegating to the user storage via updateCredential(), the UserCredentialModel carries only the JSON list of raw codes (challengeResponse). The userLabel and generatedAt timestamp that are part of the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel are dropped, so a user storage that wants to persist them cannot (the test provider's stored CredentialModel never has a user label). If the UserCredentialModel cannot carry them, this limitation should at least be documented on the method, since storages implementing CredentialInputUpdater for this type receive an input with no way to reconstruct the full credential.

title: getCredentials() returns a freshly generated credential id on every call and drops the stored one; NPE for unknown user
body: In getCredentials(), the recovery-codes CredentialModel is rebuilt via RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...), which generates a new random id each call instead of returning myUser.recoveryCodes with its stored id. Consequently the credential id reported to Keycloak is unstable (changes between calls), so operations like deleting the credential by id via the account REST endpoint (as the existing OTP test does) cannot work for recovery codes, and the stored id set in updateCredential() is effectively unused. Also, getMyUser(user) may return null for an unknown user and myUser.recoveryCodes would throw an NPE instead of returning an empty stream. Additionally, disableCredentialType() does not handle RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE even though supportsCredentialType() advertises it, so disabling recovery codes through the admin REST API silently logs 'unsupported' and leaves the credential in place — none of these paths are covered by the new test.

title: removeStoredCredentialById cannot delete a federated recovery-codes credential
body: When all recovery codes have been used, the authenticator calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()). With this PR the credential may now live in an external user storage (obtained via getFederatedCredentialsStream in RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential), and removeStoredCredentialById only operates on locally stored credentials in the Keycloak DB. The removal silently does nothing for federated credentials, so the exhausted credential stays in the user storage and is never cleaned up (only the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is added as a fallback). The delete path for federated credentials needs to go through the storage provider (e.g. disableCredentialType or an equivalent update) rather than the local stored-credential API.

title: Federated recovery codes are never consumed, so they are infinitely reusable
body: For local (Keycloak DB) recovery-code credentials, a successful authentication marks the used code as consumed (the recovery-codes credential provider updates the model on isValid). For credentials living in user storage, the validation path only calls the storage provider's isValid(); nothing notifies the storage that a code was used, and this reference storage implementation's isValid() for RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel just checks membership in the stored list without removing the used code. The result is that recovery codes stored in user storage are single-use in name only and can be replayed indefinitely, defeating the purpose of recovery codes. There is no test asserting that a used code is rejected on a second login, so this regression is invisible in the test suite. Either the framework must drive consumption (e.g. via updateCredential on use) or the contract/test provider must implement and verify consumption.

title: Raw (unhashed) recovery codes are passed to user storage via updateCredential
body: createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generated codes to JSON and passes them as the UserCredentialModel value to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(). For the local-storage branch, the credential provider stores only hashes of the codes (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues hashes them). A user storage that follows the pattern demonstrated by this PR's test provider will persist the plaintext codes (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.updateCredential stores input.getChallengeResponse() directly as credentialData), which means recoverable plaintext secrets at rest in the external store and a weaker security posture than the equivalent local credential. At minimum the contract should be documented and the example/test provider should hash the codes on store; better, pass the pre-built credentialModel (with hashed secretData) instead of the raw codes.

title: getCredentials NPEs when user is not present in the storage map
body: The new getCredentials() implementation calls getMyUser(user) and immediately dereferences myUser.recoveryCodes without a null check. getMyUser can return null (users.get returns null), and every other method in this provider (isConfiguredFor, getDisableableCredentialTypesStream) guards against a null MyUser. Any Keycloak code path that calls getCredentials for a user not backed by this provider (or looked up by a mismatched username) will throw a NullPointerException instead of returning an empty stream.

title: disableCredentialType does not handle recovery codes, leaving no way to remove the federated credential
body: supportsCredentialType and updateCredential were extended to handle RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE, but disableCredentialType still only clears the OTP credential. Combined with the fact that removeStoredCredentialById does not work for federated credentials, there is no code path demonstrated that removes a recovery-codes credential from the user storage (admin REST disableCredentialType or account-console deletion will silently do nothing for this type). The test suite also never exercises removal/regeneration of federated recovery codes, so this gap is untested.

title: Typo in authenticator config alias "delayed-suthenticator-config"
body: The delayed-authenticator execution config is created with alias "delayed-suthenticator-config" (missing the 'a' in "authenticator"). This is copy-pasted from the existing pattern used in other tests; it works only because the delayed-authenticator provider apparently doesn't rely on the alias name, but it produces a confusingly named config object in the test realm and propagates the typo if copied further.

title: Federated recovery-code credential is never removed and codes are never consumed
body: When the recovery-codes credential lives in a user storage (federated), the code-consumption logic breaks in two ways. First, line 86 calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(...) with the ID of the federated credential returned by getFederatedCredentialsStream(); that ID does not exist in Keycloak's local credential store, so the call is a silent no-op and the exhausted credential is never deleted from the user storage. Second, unlike the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider (whose isValid() updates the credential to mark a code as used), there is no mechanism that consumes a code in the user storage after successful validation: the framework only calls the storage's isValid(), and nothing updates the stored credential. The net effect is that recovery codes created in user storage are single static secrets that remain valid indefinitely and can be replayed by an attacker who observed one, defeating the one-time property that recovery codes are supposed to have.

title: Raw (unhashed) recovery codes are sent to user storage via updateCredential
body: createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the plaintext generated codes to JSON and passes them as the challengeResponse of a UserCredentialModel to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(). Whatever a user-storage provider receives it may persist as-is (as the test provider in this PR does: it stores input.getChallengeResponse() directly as credentialData). This means the security of the codes (hashing vs. plaintext storage) is delegated entirely to third-party storage implementations, whereas the local provider always stores only hashes. Additionally, the fully-populated credentialModel with hashed codes that the caller built is discarded in this branch, so the provider loses the createdDate/userLabel metadata. At minimum this contract should be documented on the method so storage implementers know they are responsible for hashing, or the hashed model should be transferred.

title: getCredentials NPEs when the user is not present in the storage map
body: In the new getCredentials() override, getMyUser(user) can return null (users.get(...) of an unknown username), but the code dereferences myUser.recoveryCodes without a null check. Every other method that calls getMyUser (getDisableableCredentialTypesStream, isConfiguredFor) guards for null. A credential listing for a user that has been removed from the map will throw a NullPointerException instead of returning an empty stream, which can break unrelated credential queries.

title: Test does not verify that a used federated recovery code cannot be replayed
body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only performs a single successful login with one recovery code and never asserts that the same code is consumed (i.e., a second login with the same code should fail, and after 12 uses the credential should be exhausted and the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action re-triggered). Since the production code has no path that consumes federated recovery codes (see the finding on RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator), the test as written passes while leaving the one-time-code property untested and broken. Add a replay/exhaustion assertion so this gap is caught.

title: NPE still possible in getSubGroupsStream overloads for deleted groups
body: The fix adds a null check only in getSubGroupsCount(), but the three getSubGroupsStream(...) overloads (lines 254-269) call modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...) with no null guard. When a group is concurrently deleted, modelSupplier.get() (cacheSession.getGroupDelegate().getGroupById) returns null and these methods will throw a NullPointerException — the exact class of failure this PR is meant to fix. The same concurrent-delete scenario exercised by the new test (listing groups while deleting them) can hit these paths via other admin endpoints, so the NPE is only partially fixed.

title: getSubGroupsCount now returns null for a deleted group, inconsistent with other methods
body: When the underlying group no longer exists, getSubGroupsCount() returns null, whereas other adapter methods (e.g. isUpdated(), getDelegateForUpdate()) throw IllegalStateException("Not found in database") and the GroupModel contract otherwise returns a Long count. Callers such as GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount will silently put a null subGroupCount into the GroupRepresentation, producing JSON with a null field instead of an error or 0, which may surprise API clients. Consider throwing the same IllegalStateException or returning 0 for consistency.

title: Reader thread is never joined; assertion can pass before concurrent reads finish
body: In createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti(), the background reader thread is started but never joined. After deletedAll.set(true), the test immediately asserts caughtExceptions is empty while the reader may still be mid-request or not yet have observed the flag. The test can pass even if an exception would be thrown one iteration later, making it flaky/ineffective at reproducing the race it targets. The thread reference should be kept and joined (with a timeout) before asserting. Also, the non-daemon thread risks leaking if the busy loop ever blocks.

title: Unbounded busy-loop hammering the admin endpoint in test
body: The reader thread loops without any sleep, issuing groups(null, 0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, true) requests back-to-back until all 100 deletes complete. This creates heavy load and log noise in CI and can slow the deleting thread, arbitrarily extending test duration. A small pause between iterations (and a bounded max iteration count) would make the test more deterministic and less wasteful.

title: Null guard applied only to getSubGroupsCount; other getSubGroupsStream overloads still NPE
body: The fix makes getSubGroupsCount() tolerate modelSupplier.get() returning null (group deleted concurrently), but getSubGroupsStream(String, Integer, Integer) at line 256, getSubGroupsStream(Integer, Integer) at line 262, and getSubGroupsStream(String, Boolean, Integer, Integer) at line 268 all still call modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...) without a null check. The same concurrent delete/read scenario (issue #40368) will still throw a NullPointerException through these code paths, e.g. when a group listing is served with pagination or search while the group is being deleted. The fix should be applied consistently (delegate to an empty stream, or the cached subgroups set, when the underlying model is gone).

title: Reader thread is never joined; test is racy and can hang indefinitely
body: In createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti, the background reader thread is started but never joined: the test sets deletedAll=true and immediately asserts that caughtExceptions is empty. If the thread has not yet observed the flag, or is in the middle of a request that fails, the final assertion can run before the exception is recorded, producing a flaky false-pass. Additionally, the while(!deletedAll.get()) loop has no iteration cap or timeout, so if a single admin call blocks (e.g. server-side deadlock), the test hangs forever instead of failing. Use a CountDownLatch/ExecutorService with awaitTermination(timeout) and join the thread before asserting.

title: getSubGroupsCount can now return null, changing the method contract
body: Previously getSubGroupsCount() either returned a Long from the delegate or threw (NPE). Now it can return null when the group was deleted concurrently. Callers such as GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount blindly call representation.setSubGroupCount(group.getSubGroupsCount()), so a deleted group's representation will serialize subGroupCount: null instead of throwing or being treated as deleted. If returning null is the intended semantic for 'group no longer exists', callers and the REST layer should handle it; otherwise prefer 0L or skip the group.

title: Concurrent-reader test does not join the reader thread, making it racy and ineffective
body: In createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti, the background reader thread is started but never joined. The main thread sets deletedAll=true and immediately asserts that caughtExceptions is empty, so the test can pass while the reader thread is still mid-request or has not yet had a chance to hit the deleted-group window; any exception thrown after the assertion (or on the final iteration) is silently lost. The reader loop may also loop zero times if the deletes finish before the thread schedules, in which case the test exercises nothing. The test should join the thread (e.g., set a done flag, interrupt/join, then assert) to reliably reproduce the race it is meant to cover.

title: LazyModel supplier caches a previously-resolved delegate, so a later concurrent delete still returns a stale model
body: getSubGroupsCount now guards against modelSupplier.get() returning null, but modelSupplier is a LazyModel that caches the delegate once resolved. If the underlying group was already resolved through this adapter (e.g., via getSubGroupsStream(search, ...) at lines 254-268, which use the same supplier) and is then deleted by another thread, modelSupplier.get() returns the cached non-null GroupModel and getSubGroupsCount() is invoked on a deleted group, which can still fail. The null guard only covers the case where the model was never resolved before the delete; the fix is incomplete for repeated access through the same cached adapter.

title: populateSubGroupCount can now propagate a null subGroupCount into GroupRepresentation
body: With GroupAdapter.getSubGroupsCount() changed to return null when the group has been concurrently deleted, GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount stores that null via representation.setSubGroupCount(null). Consumers that unbox getSubGroupCount() (the representation field is Long, and Admin UI / REST clients commonly treat it as a required count when populateSubGroupCount is requested) will see the field disappear from the JSON or risk NullPointerException on unboxing. Either the deleted-group case should be skipped (not emit/merge the representation) or the null contract should be documented and handled at this call site, rather than silently producing a representation with a missing subgroup count.

title: Negative-offset queryset slicing raises an exception, so the 'advanced pagination' path always fails
body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is true and cursor.offset < 0, the code executes `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start_offset. Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative indices: it raises `AssertionError` ("Negative indexing is not supported") unless a negative step is used, and with a step it's not valid SQL OFFSET semantics. The comment claiming 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. Any client that sends a cursor with a negative offset while using optimized_pagination=true will get a 500 error; the feature can never return data.

title: BasePaginator silently clamps negative forward-cursor offsets to 0 instead of rejecting them
body: The change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` alters behavior for all existing paginators (Paginator, DateTimePaginator, etc.). Previously, a malformed/corrupted cursor with a negative offset on a forward page would surface as an error from queryset slicing; now it is silently clamped to 0 and the client receives the first page of results while believing it is on a later page. This masks cursor corruption and can produce silently wrong data (e.g., duplicate rows already seen). For is_prev cursors the negative offset is still passed through, so it will raise an exception from the ORM — inconsistent behavior between the two directions. The correct fix is to validate and reject negative offsets (as OffsetPaginator and ChainPaginator do with BadPaginationError).

title: New undocumented 'optimized_pagination' query parameter and superuser-gated paginator add no functionality and can 500
body: The endpoint adds an undocumented, EXPERIMENTAL-status query parameter `optimized_pagination` that switches to OptimizedCursorPaginator with enable_advanced_features=True for superusers/global-access users. Since the advanced path only activates for negative cursor offsets and that path always raises an exception when slicing the queryset, this flag is a purely additive way for privileged clients to trigger server errors. There is no test coverage for the new parameter or the new paginator, and no documentation of the parameter's contract. Additionally, the gating on is_superuser/has_global_access suggests a security boundary, but the comment in the paginator ('safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level') reveals the queryset is already org-scoped — the permission gate provides no actual protection and is misleading.

title: is_prev length check uses raw (possibly negative) offset, so the trailing-row trim never fires for advanced cursors
body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when a previous-page cursor with a value is used together with a negative offset (the advanced path), the check `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` compares against the original (negative) offset, while the results were fetched using `start_offset = cursor.offset` and `stop = start_offset + limit + extra`. The length of the fetched slice can never equal a negative-plus-limit sum in the intended way, so the extra boundary row is never trimmed, resulting in off-by-one duplicate/missing rows at page boundaries for previous-page navigation.

title: Comment in Cursor implies negative offsets are a supported general feature
body: The added comment on Cursor.offset states that negative offsets are allowed for 'advanced pagination scenarios', but nothing in Cursor.from_string or anywhere else validates or supports them coherently: other paginators (SequencePaginator, OffsetPaginator, ChainPaginator) explicitly assert or raise on negative offsets, while BasePaginator-based ones now either clamp them silently or crash depending on is_prev. The comment documents behavior that does not exist and will mislead maintainers.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key crashes on datetime keys
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator copies Paginator.get_item_key, which does `int(math.floor(value))` on the sort-key attribute. The endpoint uses it with order_by="-datetime", so `value` is a datetime, and `math.floor(datetime)` raises TypeError. Every paginated request to the audit-log endpoint with optimized_pagination=true will fail with a 500. It needed the DateTimePaginator-style conversion (strftime-based ms conversion) like DateTimePaginator.get_item_key/value_from_cursor.

title: Negative-offset slicing of a Django QuerySet raises an error
body: The 'advanced feature' path slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start_offset. Django QuerySet slicing explicitly does not support negative indices and raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.` (in newer Django, ValueError). So the advertised negative-offset pagination never works; any client sending a cursor with a negative offset to the optimized path gets a 500, not 'efficient reverse pagination'. The comment claiming the ORM 'properly handles negative slicing automatically' is factually wrong.

title: value_from_cursor is incompatible with the DateTimePaginator cursors used by this endpoint
body: DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor converts the millisecond cursor value back into a UTC datetime before it is injected into the SQL where-clause in build_queryset. OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor value (an int/float). When used with the '-datetime' ordering in the audit-log endpoint, a client-supplied cursor value (e.g. 1718000000000) is compared directly against a timestamp column, so results are wrong or the query errors depending on the database. Cursours produced by one paginator are also silently consumed by the other depending on the caller's permissions, so paging behavior differs per user for the same cursor.

title: Undocumented query param silently changes pagination semantics per user
body: The new `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter is not part of the documented API (publish status EXPERIMENTAL aside) and switches the endpoint to a paginator with a different cursor value encoding, and only for superusers or users with global access. The same `cursor` string therefore yields different (or broken) results depending on who sends it, and clients cannot rely on the cursor format being stable across pages if a user's permissions change. There is no serialization/test coverage for this alternate response path.

title: BasePaginator change silently rewrites invalid cursors to page 1 for non-prev cursors
body: The rewritten slicing logic `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` clamps negative offsets to 0 for forward cursors. Previously a malformed cursor with a negative offset produced a (wrong but detectable) slice; now it silently returns the first page while the next/prev cursor computation in build_cursor still uses the original negative offset (e.g. `_build_next_values` computes `next_offset = offset + limit` from the raw offset), producing cursors that are internally inconsistent with the rows actually returned. For is_prev cursors the negative offset is still passed through, where Django raises on negative slicing. The change also alters behavior for all existing endpoints using BasePaginator, not just audit logs.

title: Comment claims negative offsets are supported but no validation or support was added
body: The added comment in Cursor.__init__ says negative offsets are now allowed as a 'performance optimization', but the code is unchanged: Cursor.from_string already accepted any int, and nothing in this file handles negative offsets. The comment misleads readers into thinking negative-offset cursors are a supported, working feature; downstream, Django queryset slicing will actually reject them. Comments-only changes that assert unsupported behavior should not be merged.

title: No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the modified BasePaginator slicing
body: The PR adds a new paginator class, a new constructor flag (enable_advanced_features), and modifies the core slicing logic of BasePaginator.get_result used by many endpoints, but includes no tests. At minimum there should be tests covering: datetime keys, negative offsets (which would have caught the math.floor(TypeError) and Django negative-slice failures), prev/next cursor round-trips, and the audit-log endpoint's two code paths.

title: Negative-offset slicing of a Django QuerySet raises an exception
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result slices the queryset with a negative start index (`queryset[start_offset:stop]` where `start_offset = cursor.offset < 0`). Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing — `QuerySet.__getitem__` raises ValueError ("Negative indexing is not supported"). So whenever a client supplies a cursor with a negative offset while `enable_advanced_features` is on, the request will fail with a 500 error rather than returning a page. The comment claiming "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is incorrect.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key crashes on datetime sort keys
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator copies Paginator.get_item_key, which does `int(math.floor(value) ...)` on `getattr(item, self.key)`. The audit-log endpoint uses this paginator with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `value` is a `datetime`, and `math.floor(datetime)` raises TypeError. The paginator should have derived from DateTimePaginator (which converts datetimes to a millisecond integer key) or overridden get_item_key/value_from_cursor accordingly; as written, the optimized path will error as soon as build_cursor calls get_item_key on a result.

title: BasePaginator silently clamps negative offsets, changing existing behavior for all endpoints
body: The change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` alters BasePaginator.get_result, which is shared by every cursor-paginated endpoint. Previously a non-prev cursor with a negative offset would surface an error from the ORM; now it is silently clamped to 0, so the client receives the first page again while believing it has paginated forward. This can produce infinite pagination loops (the returned next cursor recomputes from page 1) for any client that constructs a malformed negative offset. There is no explanation of why non-prev negative offsets must be clamped while prev negative offsets are passed through unchanged.

title: Undocumented, permission-gated query parameter changes endpoint behavior with no API contract or tests
body: A new `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter switches the endpoint to a different paginator with different cursor semantics (negative offsets allowed, different key encoding) for superusers/global-access members. This is undocumented in the API surface (no serializer field, no publish-status note), and cursors produced by one paginator may not be interpretable by the other if a client toggles the parameter between requests, causing skipped/duplicated rows. No tests are added for the new paginator class, the negative-offset path, or the endpoint's gating logic.

title: Comment-only change claims a capability the code does not implement
body: The only change in cursors.py is a comment saying "Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios", but the code (`self.offset = int(offset)`) is unchanged — Cursor already accepted any integer offset. The comment implies this PR enabled something in Cursor when it did not, which will mislead future maintainers about where the negative-offset behavior is actually implemented (and whether it is validated).

title: Negative-offset slicing in OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes on Django querysets
body: The 'advanced features' branch does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django ORM querysets do not support negative indexing — slicing with a negative start raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported in querysets`. The comment claims 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically', which is false. Any request that reaches this branch (cursor with negative offset, `optimized_pagination=true`, privileged user) will produce a 500 instead of a page of results. Since cursors are client-supplied strings parsed by `Cursor.from_string`, a negative offset is trivially craftable, making this a denial-of-service on the endpoint.

title: BasePaginator now slices with unclamped negative offsets for prev cursors
body: The original code did `queryset[offset:stop]` and the new code does `start_offset = ... if not cursor.is_prev else offset`, then slices. For non-prev cursors the `max(0, offset)` clamp prevents negative offsets, but for prev cursors the raw (possibly negative) offset is passed straight to queryset slicing. Combined with `Cursor.from_string` accepting any integer offset from the client, a malicious cursor such as `0:-5:1` on any endpoint using BasePaginator subclasses will hit Django's negative-slicing AssertionError (or, for list-backed paginators, silently return wrong rows). This changes behavior of every existing BasePaginator consumer, not just the new 'optimized' path, and is unrelated to the PR's stated purpose.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot paginate by datetime
body: The audit log endpoint sorts by `-datetime` and previously used `DateTimePaginator`, which converts datetimes to epoch-millis ints for cursor keys. `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` is copied from the plain `Paginator` and does `int(math.floor(value) if ... else math.ceil(value))` on the raw attribute; when the attribute is a `datetime`, `math.floor`/`int()` raise `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware...`/`type error`. So the optimized path crashes whenever it needs to compute an item key (any request with results). Additionally, `value_from_cursor` returns the raw cursor value, whereas `DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor` converts the millis value back into a timezone-aware datetime for the SQL comparison — the optimized path would compare a float against a datetime column and break the query. The paginator is simply not usable for this endpoint's data type.

title: zpopmin eviction silently drops buffered spans with no metric or cap configurability
body: The new eviction block pops `span_count - 1000` members off the set whenever a segment exceeds 1000 spans, permanently dropping those span payloads before they are ever flushed to the `buffered-spans` topic. The Python-side `max_segment_spans` guard (which skipped the segment and logged an error) was removed from `_load_segment_data` without replacement. The 1000 limit is hardcoded in Lua, is inconsistent with the Python `max_segment_spans = 1001` default, and there is no metric increment, log, or counter when eviction occurs — segments above 1000 spans will be silently truncated, making the data loss invisible in monitoring. Eviction also uses `zpopmin` (lowest end timestamp), meaning the oldest spans of a segment vanish, potentially including the root/segment span that later code (`is_segment` detection, redirect handling) depends on.

title: Redis structure changed from sets to sorted sets without migration handling
body: The script now calls `zcard`/`zunionstore` where it previously called `scard`/`sunionstore`. During a rolling deploy, old-version processes still write span payloads via `sadd`/`sunionstore` while new-version processes read them with `zcard`, so existing set-typed keys are invisible to the new logic (`zcard` on a set key returns a WRONGTYPE error in Redis, actually failing the EVALSHA call entirely). There is no migration or versioning strategy, so deploying this will produce errors/data loss for any in-flight traces buffered before the deploy. `buffer.py` also changed `sadd`→`zadd` and `sscan`→`zscan` symmetrically, but mixed-version operation during rollout is not handled.

title: Redirect traversal limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000
body: The redirect-following loop bound was cut from 10000 to 1000 with no explanation in the PR description and no constant shared with Python. The original comment noted the limit means segment trees of depth 10k may not join correctly; reducing to 1000 tightens that failure mode. If a redirect chain exceeds 1000 hops, the loop exits with `set_span_id` pointing at an intermediate node and the span is written to the wrong buffer key, splitting a segment — silently, since the returned `redirect_depth` metric is the only signal. If this reduction was intentional (e.g. to bound Redis script runtime), it should be documented and covered by a test; neither exists.

title: Undocumented, untested query-parameter-gated paginator switch on a control-silo endpoint
body: A new `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter changes which paginator implementation and behavior (including negative-offset support) the audit log endpoint uses, but it is not documented in the API schema, not covered by any endpoint test, and the behavior difference is invisible to clients. The permission gate uses `organization_context.member.has_global_access` (owner/manager) or superuser, but audit logs are sensitive security data and the 'advanced' path offers no clear benefit while introducing the crash bugs above. This change is also entirely unrelated to the PR's stated purpose (span buffer optimization), making it easy to miss in review.

title: paginate() may not forward enable_advanced_features to the paginator constructor
body: The call passes `enable_advanced_features=True` to `self.paginate(...)`. Whether this kwarg reaches `OptimizedCursorPaginator.__init__` depends on the endpoint base class's `paginate` implementation forwarding arbitrary kwargs to `paginator_cls`; the standard `paginate` in sentry's API base constructs the paginator with a fixed set of arguments (queryset, order_by, etc.). If it does not forward the kwarg, this raises a TypeError (500) on every optimized request; if it does forward it, the default `enable_advanced_features=False` still enables the negative-offset branch only for this flag combination, which no test exercises. Either way there is no test covering this endpoint's new code path.

title: No tests for eviction, oversized segments, or the new sorted-set behavior
body: The core behavioral changes of this PR — segments exceeding 1000 spans being truncated via `zpopmin`, the removal of the `max_segment_spans` guard in `_load_segment_data`, and the set→sorted-set conversion — have no test coverage. All existing tests use tiny traces (4-5 spans) with identical timestamps, so they cannot catch wrong sort scores, eviction of the wrong members, or eviction of the root span. A test that builds a segment of >1000 spans with distinct `end_timestamp_precise` values and asserts which spans survive is needed before this data-lossy change can be merged.

title: Pre-existing typo `order_b` means ASC conversion of descending order_by never applies
body: In `build_queryset`, the branch that converts an existing `-{key}` ordering back to ascending assigns to `queryset.query.order_b` instead of `queryset.query.order_by`. While pre-existing, the new negative-offset/OptimizedCursorPaginator work sits directly on top of this path and the diff touches the surrounding function, so the bug now affects the new paginator too: a prev-cursor request on a queryset already ordered by `-datetime` will not have its ordering flipped to ASC, producing incorrectly ordered (and thus incorrectly paginated) results. Worth fixing while this code is being modified.

title: Negative-offset slicing on a Django QuerySet raises an error / is unsupported
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result intentionally allows `cursor.offset < 0` when `enable_advanced_features` is set, slicing with `queryset[start_offset:stop]` where start_offset is negative. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing: `QuerySet[-5:...]` raises AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported'). The comment claiming 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is simply wrong, so this 'advanced' path will crash (or, for sequence-like backends, silently return semantically wrong rows) whenever a client sends a cursor with a negative offset. Since Cursor.from_string accepts any int from the client-supplied cursor string, any authorized user of the audit logs endpoint can trigger this by hand-crafting a cursor.

title: Undocumented, untested query-parameter-driven paginator switch on a public endpoint
body: The endpoint now branches on an undocumented `optimized_pagination=true` request parameter and a new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with an `enable_advanced_features` flag. This changes pagination behavior for API consumers (cursor format/semantics, result boundaries) based on a hidden flag, has no test coverage anywhere in the diff, and is not mentioned in API docs. The 'permissions are checked at the queryset level' justification in paginator.py is also misleading: the flag gates behavior, not authorization, and the paginator change itself is the risky part. Either remove this path or add tests and document the parameter.

title: zpopmin eviction silently drops span payloads, including possibly the root span
body: When a segment exceeds 1000 spans, the script calls `zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)`, permanently deleting span payloads from the buffer. The evicted spans (those with the earliest end timestamps — which typically includes the root/segment span, since it starts first) are never flushed to the buffered-spans topic; they are silently lost with no metric or log. The previous behavior (skipping oversized segments with an error log and a `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric) at least made the loss observable. Additionally, evicting the root span while still setting the `span-buf:hrs:` key means the flushed segment will have `has_root_span` set but no span with `is_segment: true`, producing malformed segments downstream.

title: Hardcoded eviction limit of 1000 conflicts with configurable max_segment_spans=1001
body: The eviction threshold is hardcoded to 1000 in Lua, while SpansBuffer still exposes `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` as a constructor parameter (now unused after the Python-side span-count check was removed from _load_segment_data). The off-by-one mismatch and the dead configuration parameter mean operators who tune `max_segment_spans` (e.g. via options) will have no effect, and the previously-enforced byte-size-only limit no longer matches the documented behavior. The limit should be passed as an ARGV so it stays configurable, or the stale parameter removed.

title: Redirect-follow loop limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000
body: The redirect resolution loop was reduced from 10000 to 1000 iterations with no explanation and the explanatory comment removed. For traces whose redirect chains exceed depth 1000, the loop exits without resolving to the final set key; the script then writes `hset(main_redirect_key, span_id, set_span_id)` with a non-final `set_span_id`, permanently corrupting the redirect map and causing the trace's spans to be split across multiple segments (data fragmentation) with no error or metric. If the reduction was intentional (e.g. Lua execution time), the failure mode should at least be detectable, and the redirect_depth metric already returned makes the old limit observable — reducing it silently is a behavioral regression.

title: max_segment_spans parameter is now dead after removing the span-count check in _load_segment_data
body: _load_segment_data no longer enforces `max_segment_spans` (the check and its `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric were deleted in favor of Lua-side eviction), but the constructor still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans=1001`. This is misleading configuration: changing it has no effect, and the docstring/comment contract ('Segments exceeding a certain size are skipped') is now only true for byte size. Remove the parameter or wire it into the Lua script.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator negative-offset slicing crashes on Django querysets
body: When `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django ORM querysets do not support negative slicing and raise `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported`. So the advertised 'advanced' negative-offset pagination path will 500 on the first request that uses a negative-offset cursor, rather than return data. The comment claiming 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is factually wrong.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator get_item_key breaks on datetime sort keys used by the audit logs endpoint
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(value))` on the attribute named by `self.key`, which is a copy of the numeric `Paginator` implementation. However, `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` (organization_auditlogs.py line 79) instantiates it with `order_by="-datetime"` where `AuditLogEntry.datetime` is a datetime. `math.floor(datetime)` raises TypeError, and `value_from_cursor` returns the raw cursor value (an epoch-ms int) which is then compared against the datetime column in `build_queryset`. This is exactly why `DateTimePaginator` exists (strftime conversion and multiplier-based `value_from_cursor`). Any request with `optimized_pagination=true` will fail with a 500.

title: BasePaginator silently clamps negative forward-cursor offsets to 0, returning wrong page
body: The change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` means a client-supplied next cursor with a negative offset (e.g. the string `0:-5:0`) is silently clamped to 0 and returns the first page instead of erroring. Combined with the new comment in cursors.py claiming negative offsets are a supported 'performance optimization', this creates an undocumented, unvalidated path where malformed/hostile cursors produce incorrect pagination results without any error. Offsets should be validated (rejected) rather than silently clamped, and the `is_prev` branch still passes negative offsets straight into queryset slicing, which raises Django's negative-indexing AssertionError.

title: Redirect-follow loop depth silently reduced from 10000 to 1000
body: The redirect loop bound was cut from 10000 to 1000 with the explanatory comment ('theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly') removed. For traces whose redirect chains exceed 1000 hops, the loop exits without finding the terminal set key; the script then writes `hset(main_redirect_key, span_id, set_span_id)` with the non-final `set_span_id`, permanently corrupting the redirect map and causing those spans to be buffered (and later flushed) under the wrong segment, splitting traces. If the reduction is intentional it needs justification and a metric/alarm; the original comment documenting the failure mode was deleted.

title: Hardcoded eviction cap of 1000 inconsistent with SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans and not configurable
body: The Lua script hardcodes `if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin(...)` while the Python `SpansBuffer` still exposes `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` (buffer.py line 150), and the Python-side enforcement in `_load_segment_data` was removed. The two limits disagree by one and the Lua value cannot be changed without redeploying the script; any config change to `max_segment_spans` in Python now has no effect. The cap should be passed in via ARGV (like `set_timeout`) so both sides stay consistent, and the unused/dead `max_segment_spans` parameter should be reconciled.

title: Eviction via zpopmin can silently drop the root span while hrs flag persists
body: When a set exceeds 1000 members, `zpopmin` removes the spans with the smallest `end_timestamp_precise` scores. If the root/segment span happens to be among the evicted spans, it is silently dropped, but the `span-buf:hrs:` flag for the set remains set (and is refreshed at line 69). The segment will then be flushed after the shorter root timeout with no root span present, producing a segment whose `is_segment` marker is never set for any span — downstream consumers that rely on exactly one segment span per segment will see malformed output. There is no guard to keep the root span (e.g. by score or by member check) during eviction.

title: Undocumented public query parameter switches paginator implementation
body: A new `optimized_pagination=true` request parameter silently changes the pagination behavior (cursor semantics, response cursor format) of an experimental but public API endpoint, with no documentation, no test coverage, and no serialization/schema change. Because `OptimizedCursorPaginator` has different cursor value encoding than `DateTimePaginator`, cursors obtained from one mode are invalid in the other, so a client toggling the flag mid-pagination will get wrong results. The feature flag should be documented and the parameter validated, or the paginator choice should be made server-side only.

title: No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the negative-offset path
body: The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` class and the modified offset handling in `BasePaginator.get_result` (line 182) have zero test coverage in this PR. Both contain the crash-producing paths described above (negative slicing assertion, datetime key TypeError), which any basic unit test exercising them would have caught. Tests should cover: normal forward/backward paging, negative offsets with and without `enable_advanced_features`, and datetime sort keys.

title: Upsampling eligibility check uses outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`
body: Inside `_get_event_stats`, the call to `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` uses the closure variable `dataset` (the request's top-level dataset), not `scoped_dataset` (the dataset actually being queried). The dashboard-widget discover-split logic calls `_get_event_stats` with `discover` as the scoped dataset and an error-only query (`AND !event.type:transaction`), but the eligibility check still evaluates against the original dataset (often metrics-enhanced performance), which `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns False for. Result: error-only split queries silently skip upsampling and return downsampled counts, producing inconsistent numbers between the split view and the direct errors view.

title: `_is_error_focused_query` uses naive substring match on raw query string
body: `if "event.type:error" in query` matches any occurrence of the substring, including negated filters like `!event.type:error` or `event.type:errorhabc`-style token prefixes, and it also ignores that the effective query can be rewritten by the caller (e.g. the endpoint's `(query) AND !event.type:transaction` split). A query that explicitly excludes errors (`!event.type:error`) will be treated as error-focused and have `count()` rewritten to `upsampled_count()`, which sums a `sample_weight` column that may not exist/apply, returning wrong counts or failing the query. The check should parse the actual filter AST rather than substring-match the raw string.

title: `upsampled_count` SnQL function only registered on the discover dataset
body: `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns True unconditionally when `dataset == errors`, and the endpoint then rewrites `count()` to `upsampled_count() as count`. But the `upsampled_count` function is only added to the discover dataset's `function_converter`. If the query actually runs against the errors dataset, the function is unregistered and the query builder will reject the column, breaking all errors-dataset stats queries for allowlisted projects. Either register the function on the errors dataset too, or never rewrite columns for that dataset.

title: `upsampled_count` declares result type "number" while `count()` is "integer"
body: The new function uses `default_result_type="number"` (a float) whereas the `count()` it replaces is `integer`. After the alias `as count`, API consumers (dashboards, alert thresholds, comparisons) receive floats like 10.0 instead of integers, and any downstream integer assertions/serialization of the `count` field changes shape. It should be `integer`, consistent with the alias it replaces (and with the `toInt64` wrapper already applied in the SnQL aggregate).

title: Cache key uses Python `hash()` and per-combination project sets, making invalidation impossible
body: The cache key is built from `hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))`. Beyond being needlessly opaque, the eligibility is cached per exact set of project IDs, so `invalidate_upsampling_cache(org, project_ids)` can only clear the one combination it is handed — removing a project from the allowlist leaves every other project-set combination stale for up to 60 seconds with no way to invalidate them. Additionally, `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is never called anywhere in the codebase, so allowlist changes never proactively invalidate anything. If a project is removed from the allowlist, its events (which may now lack valid `sample_weight`) will continue to be summed via `upsampled_count()` for the TTL, producing wrong counts. A versioned key or a short shared per-org key would make invalidation tractable.

title: Tests mock `options` but not the eligibility cache, causing cross-test contamination
body: The new tests patch `sentry.api.helpers.error_upsampling.options` but the real `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` also consults the shared Django cache keyed on org id + project ids with a 60s TTL. `test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects` caches eligibility=True for that org/project set; subsequent tests in the same run that mock `options.get` to a partial or empty allowlist will still read the cached True and take the upsampling path, inverting the assertions (e.g. `test_error_upsampling_with_partial_allowlist` and `test_error_upsampling_with_no_allowlisted_projects` expecting count==1 could see 10). The cache must be cleared or mocked per test, and the caching behavior itself is untested.

title: Accidental nested `sentry-repo` gitlink/submodule committed
body: The PR adds a `sentry-repo` gitlink pinning commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a. This appears to be an accidentally nested repository reference (likely from running tooling inside a checkout), not an intended submodule — there is no `.gitmodules` entry or description mention. It will confuse CI/checkout and should be removed from the commit.

title: `store_event` factory unconditionally copies `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` into top-level `sample_rate`
body: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` runs for every `store_event` call, mutating `normalized_data["sample_rate"]` whenever the context is present. This changes event-processing behavior for all existing tests that (even accidentally) include an `error_sampling` context, and it silently swallows all exceptions with bare `except Exception: pass`, masking real shape errors (e.g. `contexts` being None yields AttributeError that is hidden). If this is only needed for the upsampling tests, it should be opt-in (a `store_event` kwarg) rather than a global side effect.

title: Cache key uses Python hash(), which is not stable across processes
body: The cache key is built with `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. Python's built-in `hash()` for tuples of ints is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so the same project-id set produces different keys in different workers/processes. Consequence: cache entries written by one worker can never be read by another (cache hit rate collapses, defeating the stated performance goal), and worse, `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (line 73) computes the key in whichever process handles the config change, so it will almost never delete the keys other workers are reading — stale eligibility can persist well beyond 60s. Use a deterministic encoding such as a sorted, joined string of project ids.

title: Upsampling eligibility is checked against the outer dataset, not the scoped dataset actually queried
body: In `_get_event_stats`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` uses the closed-over `dataset` variable, but the query is executed against `scoped_dataset`. In the dashboard-widget split path (`get_event_stats_factory`), `_get_event_stats` is invoked with `split_dataset` = `discover` or `metrics_enhanced_performance` while the outer `dataset` may be different, so the decision to substitute `upsampled_count()` is made against the wrong dataset. This can either apply a `sample_weight`-based aggregation to a dataset that has no such column (query error) or skip it for an errors-only split query where it should apply. Pass `scoped_dataset` instead.

title: Only exact 'count()' is transformed, producing inconsistent mixed-scaled results
body: `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` rewrites only the literal string `count()` and leaves every other aggregation untouched. A request like `yAxis=count(),count_unique(user),p95(transaction.duration)` on an allowlisted errors query will return an upsampled (scaled) count alongside unsampled-based unique/percentile values in the same response, giving internally inconsistent data (e.g. unique users can exceed total count). Aliased forms such as `count() as total` are also missed. Either transform the other supported aggregations or restrict the rewrite to requests whose entire column list can be upsampled.

title: Error-focus check inspects the raw request query, not the effective query
body: `_is_error_focused_query` reads `request.GET['query']`, but the actual query executed by `_get_event_stats` can be a rewritten one (e.g. the dashboard split path builds `f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction"`, and other callers pass scoped queries). A discover query that filters errors via the rewritten query but whose original request query lacks `event.type:error` will silently skip upsampling, while an equivalent query phrased differently gets it. The decision should be derived from the query string actually being executed, not the raw request parameter.

title: No caller for invalidate_upsampling_cache and no cache-invalidation on option change
body: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined but never invoked anywhere in this PR, and nothing hooks it to changes of the `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` option. Combined with the 60s cache and the broken (hash-based) key, removing a project from the allowlist may not take effect for an unbounded time. Either wire invalidation into the option-update path or drop the cache.

title: Snuba endpoint upsampling tests are order-dependent due to shared cache state
body: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` writes its result to the shared cache under a key derived from organization id and project ids. The four tests in `OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest` use the same org/projects but different mocked allowlists, and nothing clears the cache between them. `test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects` caches `True`, so the later `test_error_upsampling_with_partial_allowlist` / `..._with_no_allowlisted_projects` can read the stale cached value and fail (or pass only due to run order). The tests must flush the cache in setUp, and the new unit tests never exercise `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` (including its cache branch) at all.

title: Accidental nested git repository / submodule entry committed
body: The PR adds a `sentry-repo` file containing 'Subproject commit ...', which indicates a nested git checkout was committed to the repository root. This pollutes the repo and should be removed (and gitignored) before merge.

title: Comments claim caching/consistency behavior the code does not provide
body: The comments in `_get_event_stats` say the eligibility check is 'cached' and ensures 'consistent behavior across query execution', and `upsampling_enabled = should_upsample` is a pointless alias. The helper's own docstring also claims the allowlist is read 'fresh each time', directly contradicting the 60-second cache in the same function. These misleading comments should be corrected or removed since they describe guarantees (freshness, consistency) the implementation explicitly does not have.

title: Error-focused query detection is a substring match that misfires on negations and near-matches
body: _is_error_focused_query does `"event.type:error" in query`, so any query containing that substring returns True — including a negated `!event.type:error` (which queries transactions/other event types) or unrelated tokens containing the substring. In those cases count() is replaced with sum(sample_weight) over non-error rows, where sample_weight is not populated, producing wrong or null counts. The check should parse the query filter (e.g. via EventSearch/parse_query) and verify event.type:error is an actual positive filter.

title: 60s eligibility cache is never invalidated and causes stale/incorrect allowlist decisions
body: The eligibility result is cached for 60 seconds keyed only by org + project ids, but invalidate_upsampling_cache is never called anywhere in the codebase, and the option value read at line 58 is mocked in tests anyway. When an operator adds or removes a project from `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`, existing cached entries keep serving the old decision for up to 60s — and since the cached True result also skips nothing dataset-specific (dataset/request are still checked, but the project allowlist decision is stale), counts can silently use (or skip) upsampling incorrectly. Worse, the cache makes the endpoint test suite order-dependent (see test gap finding).

title: Upsampling decision uses the outer `dataset` closure instead of `scoped_dataset` and the request query instead of the actual query
body: Inside _get_event_stats, is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects is called with the outer `dataset` variable, not the `scoped_dataset` argument that will actually execute the query. In the dashboard discover-split path, _get_event_stats is invoked with `discover` as scoped_dataset (and with modified queries like `... AND !event.type:transaction`), but the eligibility check still evaluates the original dataset and the original request.GET query string. This means split queries against discover can be mis-classified (e.g. the errors-only split query will only be upsampled if the user's original query contained 'event.type:error', and a transaction-like split could get the transform if the original dataset was errors). The check must use scoped_dataset and the `query` argument actually being executed.

title: upsampled_count registered only on the discover dataset, but the transform is also applied for the errors dataset
body: _should_apply_sample_weight_transform returns True unconditionally when dataset == sentry.snuba.errors, and the endpoint then rewrites count() to upsampled_count(). However the SnQLFunction `upsampled_count` is only added to the discover dataset's function_converter. If the errors dataset resolves functions through a different dataset/builder (which it does — errors uses its own dataset class), queries against the errors endpoint will fail with an unknown-function error whenever all queried projects are allowlisted, i.e. the feature breaks the errors dataset path entirely. The function must be registered on every dataset where the transform can be applied, or the errors dataset path must be verified/covered by tests.

title: count() inside aliases or equations is silently not transformed, producing inconsistent upsampling
body: transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling only matches the exact string 'count()' (case/whitespace-insensitive). Columns like 'count() as total_events', count() used inside yAxis equations, or 'count()' embedded in other aggregate forms pass through unchanged, so a chart mixing 'count()' and 'count() as total' would show one upsampled and one raw series on the same chart. At minimum the alias form should be handled or the mismatch documented, and equations containing count() are a known gap.

title: No handling of events lacking sample_weight in allowlisted projects
body: The docstring asserts the schema guarantees sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects, but the factory change in testutils/factories.py shows sample_rate is only set when contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate is present. Historical events ingested before the feature rolled out (or from SDKs without error sampling) have no sample_weight; sum(sample_weight) over those rows will yield null/0 rather than a count, undercounting errors dramatically. There is no fallback (e.g. coalesce(sample_weight, 1)) or date-boundary guard restricting the transform to post-rollout periods.

title: Endpoint upsampling tests are order-dependent and will fail spuriously due to the shared 60s cache
body: The tests mock options.get but not the cache. The first test (full allowlist) caches eligible=True under the key for org+sorted project ids; the subsequent 'partial allowlist' test runs with the same org and same project set, so it will read the cached True and expect count==1 while the code path actually upsamples to 10 — the assertion at 'Should use regular count()' would fail depending on test execution order. The tests must clear the cache between cases (or mock cache.get to return None); as written they prove the caching behavior is untested and the suite is flaky.

title: Accidental submodule/placeholder file 'sentry-repo' committed
body: The PR adds a one-line file `sentry-repo` containing 'Subproject commit a5d290...'. This looks like an accidentally created git submodule/gitlink entry pointing at the base commit, unrelated to the feature. It should be removed before merging.

title: Allowlist membership check is O(n*m) on every cache miss
body: `all(project_id in allowlist for project_id in project_ids)` performs a linear scan of the allowlist list for every project. With a large allowlist option and many projects this is quadratic-ish per request. Converting the allowlist to a set before the check is a trivial fix; also worth noting the option lookup is described as 'expensive' but options.get is an in-memory cached lookup, so the 60s cache adds staleness risk for little benefit.

title: upsampled_count declares default_result_type 'number' though it emits toInt64
body: The SnQLFunction wraps the aggregate in toInt64(...) but declares default_result_type="number" (float), while plain count() uses "integer". This can make downstream consumers (zerofill, response formatting, chart interpolation) treat the column as a float series and format/interpolate it differently from count(), an inconsistency for a function intended to be a drop-in replacement.

title: Feature-flagged table widget renders empty placeholder instead of real data
body: In `tableResultComponent`, when the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature flag is on, the code renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />` — hardcoded empty columns and empty data — instead of passing the actual `result.data`, `result.meta`, and `fields` that the existing `StyledSimpleTableChart` uses. Any organization with this flag enabled will see completely blank dashboard table widgets (no rows, no headers), losing all data currently displayed. The real table data must be mapped into the new component's `TabularData`/`TabularColumn` shape before this branch can ship.

title: fetch_error_details mispairs error IDs with node data and mixes string/float timestamps
body: `fetch_error_details` does `zip(error_ids, events.values())` where `events = nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a dict keyed by node_id.
