If any requested node is missing, `events.values()` is shorter and shifted, so each `event_id` gets paired with the wrong event's data (wrong title/message/timestamp attributed to the wrong error), and the `id` field on the resulting ErrorEvent is wrong. Additionally, nodestore event data stores `timestamp` as an ISO-8601 string, but the code defaults it to `0.0` and later compares/sorts it against breadcrumb float timestamps (`error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)` in `gen_request_data`), which raises `TypeError` when comparing str to float in Python 3. The endpoint should iterate `zip(error_ids, (events.get(n) for n in node_ids))` and parse the timestamp to a float (e.g. `datetime.fromisoformat`).

title: HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES filter only applied when a search query is present
body: The new `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` exclusion (`is_segment`, `project_id`, `received`) is only applied inside the `if (searchQuery.trim())` branch of `sortedAndFilteredAttributes`. When the search box is empty, the full sorted list is returned unchanged, so these internal attributes are still displayed. Worse, the behavior is inconsistent: a user who types a query matching e.g. `project_id` will see the attribute disappear from the results. The filter should be applied before the search filter (i.e., always), not only when searching.

title: Enabled guard `Boolean(normalizedDateRange)` is always true and data can be undefined
body: `normalizeDateTimeParams(selection.datetime)` always returns an object, so `Boolean(normalizedDateRange)` is always true — the guard does nothing. More importantly, on the success path the hook does `data.numFeedbacksUsed` without checking `data` is defined; if the query resolves without data (e.g. disabled then re-enabled states, or a 204/empty body), `data` can be `undefined` and the hook will throw a TypeError, crashing the feedback list page since the component only guards `isPending`/`isError`. Add a defined check on `data` before accessing its fields.

title: New table widget renders hardcoded empty data, breaking dashboards under the feature flag
body: In `tableResultComponent`, when the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature flag is on, the code renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />` instead of the existing `StyledSimpleTableChart`. Both `columns` and `tableData` are hardcoded to empty values, so the actual query results (`result.data`, `result.meta`, `fields`, `fieldAliases`) are discarded entirely. Any organization with this flag enabled will see empty table widgets in dashboards regardless of the data returned by the API. The wiring of real data into the new component is missing.

title: fetch_error_details zips error_ids with dict values(), misaligning events when any node is missing
body: `fetch_error_details` builds `node_ids` from `error_ids`, fetches them via `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` (which returns a dict that omits missing nodes and whose `.values()` ordering is not guaranteed to match the requested key order), then constructs ErrorEvents with `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. If any error event node is missing from nodestore, or the returned dict order differs, the wrong `event_id` is paired with the wrong event data, and the `if data is not None` filter can drop the wrong entries. This produces incorrect error titles/messages/timestamps sent to Seer for the replay summary. Iterate over `events` items keyed by node_id (or use `get_multi`'s mapping back to event ids) instead of `zip`.

title: Full unauthenticated request bodies logged at info level
body: The endpoint logs `logger.info("browser_report_received", extra={"request_body": request.data})` for every request. This is an unauthenticated, CORS-enabled public endpoint (permission_classes = ()) that accepts arbitrary JSON payloads from browsers, including report `body` contents, URLs, and user agents (potential PII). Logging the entire body at info level in production will also produce unbounded log volume for large or malicious payloads. The request body should be omitted or logged at debug with size limits.

title: Editing bodies of already-shipped data migrations
body: Migrations 0917 and 0920 have had their data-conversion logic replaced with a no-op and a comment claiming they "had an error and was never run". These migrations have already shipped in releases, and self-hosted installations (or any environment where they did run, e.g. the 0917 migration before the 0920 revision was cut) have them recorded as applied. Mutating applied migrations creates divergence: environments where 0917 ran and inserted GroupSearchView rows will also run 0921 ("rerevised"), which may duplicate or conflict with rows created by 0917, since 0917 can no longer be inspected for what it did. The corresponding test for 0917 was also deleted. The safe pattern is a new corrective migration, not rewriting history; at minimum this needs a clear statement that no environment (including self-hosted) executed these.

title: Refactor swaps useApiQuery options for useQuery defaults, enabling retries and refetch-on-focus
body: The previous implementation used `useApiQuery` with `{staleTime: 0, refetchOnWindowFocus: false, retry: false}`. The new `useQuery` call passes only `enabled`, `queryKey`, and `queryFn`, so react-query defaults now apply: up to 3 retries with exponential backoff on failure and refetch on window focus. Since this hook drives search-bar attribute-key suggestions (called per keystroke/interaction), failed requests will now be retried 3 times and refetch when the user refocuses the window, increasing load on the trace-items attributes endpoint and changing observed latency/error behavior. Preserve the original query options (retry: false, refetchOnWindowFocus: false) or set them explicitly.

title: HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES only filtered when a search query is present
body: `sortedAndFilteredAttributes` returns the unfiltered sorted list when `searchQuery` is empty, and only applies the `!HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES.includes(...)` filter inside the search branch. So `is_segment`, `project_id`, and `received` are still shown when the user has not typed anything, but disappear as soon as they type — inconsistent behavior. The hidden-attribute filter should be applied unconditionally, before the search-substring filter.

title: Table widget renders hardcoded empty data behind feature flag
body: In `tableResultComponent`, when the organization has the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature flag, the new `TableWidgetVisualization` is rendered with `columns={[]}` and `tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}}` instead of the actual `tableResults`, `fields`, `eventView`, and `location` that the existing `StyledSimpleTableChart` uses. Any org enrolled in the flag will see a completely empty dashboard table (no rows, no columns) regardless of the query results. This looks like placeholder/wiring code that was merged prematurely; the real data is never passed to the new component.

title: fetch_error_details misaligns error IDs with nodestore data via zip on dict values
body: `fetch_error_details` builds `node_ids` from `error_ids`, calls `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)`, then zips `error_ids` with `events.values()`. `get_multi` returns a dict, and per its contract keys with no result may be absent from the dict. When any node is missing (or dict ordering differs from insertion order), `zip` pairs the wrong `event_id` with the wrong `data`, producing ErrorEvents whose id/title/message/timestamp belong to a different error. It should iterate the returned mapping by node_id (e.g. `zip(node_ids, (events.get(n) for n in node_ids))`) and skip None values, so each event_id maps to its own node data.

title: query() mutates the caller's selected_columns list
body: In `ourlogs.query`, when ordering by timestamp the function appends `tags[sentry.timestamp_precise,number]` directly to the `selected_columns` argument (`selected_columns.append(precise_timestamp)`). This mutates a list owned by the caller. If the same list object is reused across calls (common when a request handler builds fields once and retries, or caches them), the precise-timestamp column is appended repeatedly and leaks into responses/other query paths, potentially causing duplicate columns or unexpected `field` validation errors. The function should copy the list (`selected_columns = [*selected_columns, precise_timestamp]`) before appending.

title: Frontend queries /organizations/<slug>/feedback-summary/ endpoint that has no backend in this PR
body: The new `useFeedbackSummary` hook (and the `FeedbackSummary` component rendered on the feedback list page) issues GET requests to `/organizations/${organization.slug}/feedback-summary/`. No such endpoint, URL registration, or handler appears anywhere in this pull request, so for any organization with the `user-feedback-ai-summaries` feature flag enabled, the feedback list page will fire a request that 404s on every load. Either the backend endpoint needs to be part of this change or the hook/component must not ship enabled.

title: ErrorEvent title/message read keys that raw nodestore payloads don't contain
body: `fetch_error_details` reads `data.get("title", "")` and `data.get("message", "")` from raw nodestore event payloads. Raw event data stored in nodestore contains structured entries (e.g. `exception.values[].type/value`), not precomputed `title`/`message` fields, so the generated error log messages (`generate_error_log_message`) will typically render as `User experienced an error: ': ' at <timestamp>` with no error type or message, defeating the purpose of including error context in the Seer summary prompt. The fields should be derived (e.g. from the exception entry) via the event model rather than read directly from the node dict.

title: timestamp/age mutual-exclusion validation is bypassed for falsy values
body: `validate_timestamp` checks `self.initial_data.get("age")` and `validate_age` checks `self.initial_data.get("timestamp")`, so the exclusion only triggers when the value is truthy. A report with `age: 0` plus a `timestamp`, or `timestamp: 0` plus an `age`, passes validation even though the specs require the two fields to be mutually exclusive. Use `"age" in self.initial_data` / `"timestamp" in self.initial_data` instead of truthiness checks.

title: KeyError/TypeError on integrations whose metadata lacks 'sender'
body: GitHubInstallation.dispatch compares `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`. Integrations created through paths that don't set the sender metadata (e.g. created by the pipeline itself via build_integration, where `state.get("sender")` may be absent, or older integrations installed before sender tracking) have no `sender` key in metadata, so this raises KeyError (or TypeError if sender is not a dict), producing a 500 error page instead of the intended error response. Use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and treat missing sender explicitly.

title: User verification is skipped when the Integration does not exist yet
body: The authenticated-user-vs-installer check only executes in the branch where the Integration already exists but has no OrganizationIntegration (line 500-505). If the Integration.DoesNotExist branch is taken (line 481-482) — e.g. the installation webhook hasn't been processed yet, or the integration was deleted — the pipeline proceeds with `pipeline.next_step()` without any verification that the currently authenticated GitHub user is the one who installed the app, and the integration is then built with unverified state. This is a race/bypass of the very control this PR adds; the check (or a sender-present requirement) should also apply on the fresh-install path.

title: get_user_info / token exchange failures raise unhandled exceptions
body: `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` (and the `safe_urlopen` call at line 423) are not wrapped in error handling. If GitHub's /user endpoint returns an error, rate limits, or the HTTP layer raises (timeout/connection error), the exception propagates and the user gets a 500 instead of the intended "Invalid installation request." error page. The code only guards against a missing `login` key, not against the call failing.

title: installation_id may be None in the direct-from-GitHub redirect
body: When a request arrives with `setup_action=install` and no pipeline, `request.GET.get("installation_id")` can be None (GitHub can send other setup_action values or the parameter may be stripped), and `reverse("integration-installation", args=[provider_id, None])` will render a URL like `.../github/None`, sending the user to a broken page. Guard for a missing installation_id and fall through to the "Invalid request." handling.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer tests the 404 installation path
body: The rewritten test asserts on "Invalid installation request." but the second request uses a hardcoded state (`ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`) that does not match the pipeline signature, so the response comes from the state-mismatch branch, not from `get_installation_info` returning 404 ("The GitHub installation could not be found." path in build_integration). The original scenario — a valid OAuth flow where the installation lookup 404s — is no longer covered; add a test that drives the flow with a valid signature and a 404 stubbed installation endpoint.

title: Disabled (non-ACTIVE) integrations produce a misleading generic error
body: In the 'Integration exists without OrganizationIntegration' branch, `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id, status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE)` fails for integrations whose status is DISABLED/PENDING_DELETION but whose OrganizationIntegration was already removed, yielding the generic "Invalid installation request." error instead of the pending-deletion message, and preventing reinstallation of a legitimately removable integration. The pending-deletion check above only inspects OrganizationIntegration rows, so a deactivated integration row with no OI rows hits this path.

title: KeyError when existing Integration metadata lacks 'sender'
body: In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the user-mismatch check does `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` with no guards. `metadata["sender"]` is only populated when the installation webhook fired before build_integration ran (see build_integration, which only adds `sender` if `state.get("sender")` is set). An existing Integration created without a preceding webhook (e.g. created through the pipeline directly, or older rows predating this flow) has no `sender` key, so this line raises KeyError and the user gets a 500 instead of a graceful error page. Same for a `sender` dict without a `login` key. Use `.get()` with explicit handling (e.g. fail closed with the error page) instead.

title: Unhandled exceptions from token exchange and get_user_info
body: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, `safe_urlopen(...)` and `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` are not wrapped in error handling. `get_user_info` performs an API call that can raise ApiError (rate limit, 401 for revoked tokens, network errors), and safe_urlopen can raise on connection failures. Any of these will propagate and produce a 500 error page mid-installation instead of the intended 'Invalid installation request.' response, degrading the UX the PR is meant to fix and generating noise in Sentry. The existing try/except only covers the response body parsing, not the requests themselves.

title: Reverse URL built with None installation_id
body: When GitHub redirects to the setup endpoint with setup_action=install but without an installation_id query parameter (malformed or crafted request), `request.GET.get("installation_id")` returns None and `reverse("integration-installation", args=[provider_id, None])` renders a URL ending in '/github/None'. The user is then redirected to an org-picker URL containing the literal string 'None', which will fail downstream when the pipeline tries to use it. The None case should be handled explicitly (redirect to the app install page or an error) rather than passed into reverse.

title: State signature compared with non-constant-time equality
body: The CSRF/anti-replay `state` parameter is validated with `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature`, a plain string comparison. Since this check is the core of the request-authenticity guarantee introduced by this PR, use `hmac.compare_digest` (or `secrets.compare_digest`) so the comparison is constant-time, matching how other OAuth state validations are typically hardened. Practical exploitability is low, but it is a trivial hardening for a security-focused change.

title: Authorize URL query parameters are not URL-encoded
body: The redirect URL is built by string interpolation: `f"{...}?client_id={github_client_id}&state={state}&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}"`. The `redirect_uri` value (containing '://' and '/'), `client_id`, and `state` are not URL-encoded. This currently works because the values happen to contain no '&' or '=' characters, but any change to the redirect path or a client_id containing reserved characters would silently corrupt the OAuth request. Use `urlencode` to construct the query string.

title: KeyError crash when integration metadata lacks 'sender'
body: GitHubInstallation.dispatch accesses `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` unconditionally when an active Integration exists. `sender` is only added to metadata when the installation webhook (or build_integration) recorded it; an Integration created through other paths (older records predating this field, or where the webhook payload had no sender) will not have the key. The result is an unhandled KeyError/TypeError that surfaces as a 500 error instead of the intended error page. Use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and decide how to treat a missing sender.

title: Sender-verification is skipped when the Integration row does not yet exist
body: The authenticated-user check only runs in the branch where an Integration with a matching external_id already exists. On a brand-new GitHub App installation, the Integration row is created asynchronously by the installation webhook; if the webhook has not been processed yet when the user (or an attacker who knows the installation_id) completes the pipeline, `Integration.DoesNotExist` is raised and `pipeline.next_step()` is returned with no sender comparison at all. This is a race that bypasses exactly the mismatch check this PR is meant to add: an attacker who learns a victim's installation_id and reaches the pipeline before the webhook lands can link the integration without ever being verified as the installer.

title: get_user_info and token-exchange network failures are unhandled
body: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, `safe_urlopen` (line 423) and `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` (line 434) can raise on network/API errors (timeouts, 5xx from GitHub). Only the body-parsing is wrapped in try/except. An exception here propagates and yields a 500 to the user instead of the friendly 'Invalid installation request' error page shown for the other failure modes described in the PR. Wrap the token exchange and user-info call so failures return the same error response.

title: State parameter compared with non-constant-time equality
body: `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature` uses ordinary string comparison. The pipeline signature is a secret-derived CSRF token; using `hmac.compare_digest` (as done in other OAuth flows in the codebase) avoids leaking signature bytes via timing. Low practical risk over the network, but it is the standard hardening for this exact check.

title: `queued` default is evaluated once at import time
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` on the dataclass captures the timestamp when the module is imported, not when an `AssignmentSource` is constructed. Every instance created without an explicit `queued` value (e.g. via `from_integration`) will carry the same stale process-start time, defeating the field's apparent purpose of recording when the assignment change was queued. It should be `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

title: Task now passes `assignment_source` kwarg to provider `sync_assignee_outbound` implementations that were not updated
body: The task calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(external_issue, user, assign=assign, assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)`, but none of the concrete provider implementations (Jira, VSTS/GitHub, etc. — none are in this PR's changed files) declare an `assignment_source` parameter; the abstract method in `IssueSyncIntegration.sync_assignee_outbound` also still has signature `(external_issue, user, assign=True, **kwargs)`. For implementations that don't accept `**kwargs`, every outbound assignee sync for an issue-sync-enabled org will now raise `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'assignment_source'`, breaking assignee sync entirely. The abstract `sync_assignee_outbound` signature (issues.py line ~397) was not updated to include the parameter, unlike `sync_status_outbound`.

title: `from_dict` silently returns None on malformed input, disabling cycle prevention
body: `AssignmentSource.from_dict` returns `None` if the dict doesn't match the constructor (e.g. unknown keys from a stale producer, or a `queued` value of the wrong shape). When that happens in `sync_assignee_outbound` (task line 53-55), `should_sync("outbound_assignee", None)` returns True and the outbound sync proceeds — i.e. exactly the sync-loop this PR is meant to prevent is silently re-enabled for any malformed payload, with no logging to surface the parse failure. At minimum the failure should be logged.

title: Round-trip through dict does not preserve `queued` as a datetime
body: `to_dict()` serializes `queued` via `asdict` into a `datetime`, and `from_dict()` reconstructs it via `cls(**input_dict)`. Since dataclasses do not validate types, a payload where `queued` arrives as a string (e.g. after JSON serialization through Celery/Redis in some configurations) will be accepted silently, leaving `queued` as a `str`. Any future consumer relying on `queued` being a `datetime` (ordering, comparisons) will fail or behave incorrectly; there is no coercion or rejection in `from_dict`.

title: Inbound assignee sync ignores organization scoping for the assignment source check
body: In `sync_group_assignee_inbound`, `where_should_sync(integration, "inbound_assignee")` is called without an `organization_id`, so groups from all orgs with the integration are affected and assigned an `AssignmentSource` for the integration. That part is fine, but note the companion outbound path in `where_should_sync` (line 48) calls `should_sync(key)` with no sync source; this is the status path so it is currently correct, but if `AssignmentSource` propagation is later extended to status sync, this call site will need updating — worth confirming intent, since the `sync_status_outbound` abstract signature was changed in this PR to accept `assignment_source` yet no caller passes one, leaving dead API surface that is untested.

title: Default `queued` timestamp is evaluated once at class-definition time
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` calls `timezone.now()` when the module is imported, not when an `AssignmentSource` is constructed. Every instance created via `from_integration` (which never passes `queued`) will therefore carry the process start time rather than the actual time the assignment was queued. Since the field is named `queued` and is meant to record when the inbound change happened, its value will be wrong/stale (constant per process). Fix by using `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

title: Datetime in task kwargs is not JSON-serializable by Celery
body: `assignment_source.to_dict()` includes the `queued` datetime field, and the resulting dict is passed directly as a Celery task kwarg in `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async`. Sentry's Celery defaults use the JSON serializer, which cannot encode `datetime` objects, so enqueueing the task will raise a `EncodeError` and the outbound sync will silently never run for any inbound-triggered assignment (the exact path this PR is meant to fix). The dict should serialize the datetime (e.g. `isoformat()`), and `from_dict` should parse it back.

title: Inbound sync ignores `organization_id` scope when assigning
body: `sync_group_assignee_inbound` calls `where_should_sync(integration, "inbound_assignee")` without the optional `organization_id`, and `where_should_sync` itself never threads the assignment source through to `should_sync` (line 48 calls it with one argument). Any future/other caller relying on `where_should_sync` to respect the source integration will not get cycle protection; more importantly the `should_sync` signature change means the inbound/outbound gating in `where_should_sync` cannot participate in the new cycle-prevention mechanism at all, so the fix only covers the direct `sync_assignee_outbound` task path. If status sync or other `should_sync` callers were intended to be covered (the abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature was changed to accept `assignment_source`), that wiring is missing.

title: No test that a different integration still receives the outbound sync
body: The new test only covers the case where the assignment source matches the target integration (asserting `assert_not_called`). The stated design intent — "This should still allow other integrations to propagate changes outward" — is not tested anywhere. A regression that suppresses all outbound assignee syncs whenever any assignment source is present would pass the current test suite. Add a test with two integrations linked to the group where the source is integration A and assert integration B's `sync_assignee_outbound` is still called.

title: `from_dict` accepts unvalidated/extra fields silently or returns None on type mismatch
body: `cls(**input_dict)` will happily construct an `AssignmentSource` with `integration_id` set to a string or arbitrary values without validation, and any extra key causes a `TypeError` swallowed into `None`, which then disables cycle protection entirely (parsed source becomes None and the outbound sync proceeds). Because this dict crosses a Celery boundary from potentially old/new producer versions, a mismatched payload silently reverts to the looping behavior the PR is fixing rather than surfacing an error. Consider logging when parsing fails and validating types.

title: AssignmentSource.queued default is evaluated once at import time
body: The dataclass field `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` calls `timezone.now()` at class-definition (import) time, so every instance created without an explicit `queued` gets the same stale timestamp from when the module was first imported (e.g. worker process start), not the time the assignment was queued. Since this PR's stated purpose is to use `queued` as context for breaking sync cycles, any logic relying on it being accurate will be wrong. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

title: Task passes new assignment_source kwarg to provider sync_assignee_outbound implementations that don't accept it
body: The task now calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(external_issue, user, assign=assign, assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)`. The abstract method in IssueSyncIntegration.sync_assignee_outbound (mixins/issues.py line 397) was NOT updated to include `assignment_source` — only sync_status_outbound was — and none of the provider implementations (Jira, VSTS, GitHub, etc.) are changed in this PR. Any provider implementation whose signature doesn't accept `assignment_source` will raise TypeError at runtime, breaking assignee outbound sync entirely for those integrations. The abstract signature and all implementations must be updated (or the kwarg not forwarded).

title: from_dict does not deserialize the queued datetime
body: `from_dict` does `cls(**input_dict)` directly. After a round trip through the Celery task (to_dict → JSON kwargs → from_dict), the `queued` value arrives as an ISO string, so the reconstructed AssignmentSource has `queued: str` instead of `datetime`. Any downstream code that formats, compares, or does arithmetic on `queued` will fail or behave incorrectly. `to_dict` should serialize to an ISO string explicitly and `from_dict` should parse it back with `datetime.fromisoformat` (or `parse`), and `from_dict` should also not silently swallow a string that fails later.

title: sync_status_outbound gained an assignment_source parameter that is never propagated or used
body: The abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature was changed to accept `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`, but no caller in this PR passes it and no provider implementation is shown being updated to use it. This is dead API surface that will drift from actual provider implementations (which still have the old signature), and misleads readers into thinking status outbound sync is also cycle-protected when it is not. Either wire it through the status outbound path or drop the parameter.

title: No test covering cross-integration propagation or inbound-triggered cycle break
body: The new test only verifies that the same integration is skipped when AssignmentSource is passed explicitly. There is no end-to-end test of the actual scenario the PR fixes: an inbound webhook (sync_group_assignee_inbound) producing an assignment_source that suppresses outbound sync back to the originating integration, and — critically — that outbound sync still fires for a *different* linked integration (the code comment in should_sync promises this). A regression in the comparison logic (e.g. suppressing all integrations, or none) would not be caught.

title: Circular import risk between incidents.grouptype and workflow_engine.processors.detector
body: src/sentry/incidents/grouptype.py now imports `StatefulDetectorHandler` from `sentry.workflow_engine.processors.detector`. That processor module imports `sentry.workflow_engine.models`, which in turn imports `sentry.issues.grouptype`. If the group-type registry (sentry.issues.grouptype) imports or is extended to import sentry.incidents.grouptype (as it does for other handler modules), this creates an import cycle: workflow_engine.processors.detector -> workflow_engine.models -> sentry.issues.grouptype -> sentry.incidents.grouptype -> workflow_engine.processors.detector. Depending on import order this will raise ImportError at startup or in first-request imports. The handler dependency should be inverted (e.g. lazy import or registration) to avoid coupling the issues/grouptype layer to the workflow_engine processor layer.

title: Multi-group test builds expected occurrence for group_2 with wrong value (6 instead of 10)
body: In test_state_results_multi_group, the data packet sets group_vals to {"group_1": 6, "group_2": 10}, but the expected occurrence for group_2 is built via `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(..., "group_2", 6, ...)` using value 6. The test only passes because the mock's build_occurrence_and_event_data ignores the `value` argument. This means the test does not actually verify that the correct per-group value is passed to build_occurrence_and_event_data; a bug that swapped values between group keys would go undetected. The mock should incorporate `value` into the occurrence (e.g. subtitle/evidence) so the assertion is meaningful.

title: Removed duplicate-group-key coverage is not replaced
body: The PR removes test_state_results_multi_group_dupe, which asserted behavior when the same group key appears twice. The rationale (dict keyed by group key) makes silent overwrite the new behavior, but there is no test asserting that a duplicate group key in the input results in exactly one produced occurrence rather than two. Since the old code explicitly logged an error and skipped duplicates, the new silent last-write-wins semantics (and the loss of the error signal) should be covered by a test to lock in the intended contract.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler does not implement the new abstract methods
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler, which declares four abstract members (counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, build_occurrence_and_event_data). None of them are implemented, so the class is still abstract; Detector.detector_handler (which calls `group_type.detector_handler(self)`) will raise TypeError at instantiation for any detector of type "metric_alert_fire". Previously the class implemented `evaluate` and was instantiable. Either implement the methods or leave a concrete placeholder implementation.

title: evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: The docstring of StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate says "Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`", but the method's signature and the PR's contract change it to return a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. The docstring was not updated and now misdescribes the API.

title: Multi-group test constructs expected occurrence with wrong value
body: In test_state_results_multi_group, the data packet has group_vals {"group_1": 6, "group_2": 10}, but the expected occurrence for group_2 is built via build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "group_2", 6, ...) using 6 instead of 10. The test passes only because the mock builder ignores `value`; if the builder or implementation starts using the value, this expectation is wrong and would silently mask a value-propagation bug between evaluate_group_key_value and build_occurrence_and_event_data. The expected value should be 10, and ideally the mock builder should include `value` in evidence_data so the propagation is actually asserted.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is abstract and can no longer be instantiated
body: `StatefulDetectorHandler` declares abstract methods (`counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the newly added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`). `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` implements none of them and is just `pass`. Previously it subclassed `DetectorHandler` and only had to implement `evaluate`, which it did. Now, when `Detector.detector_handler` (src/sentry/workflow_engine/models/detector.py line 86) calls `group_type.detector_handler(self)`, instantiating this class will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class` for any Detector whose type is `metric_alert_fire`. Since `process_detectors` does not catch exceptions, this would crash the whole data-packet processing loop. If this handler is intentionally unimplemented, it should not be registered on the group type yet.

title: KeyError in get_state_data when a detector defines no counter_names
body: In `get_state_data`, `counter_updates` is only populated when `self.counter_names` is non-empty (line 196 `if self.counter_names:`). For any handler that returns an empty `counter_names` list (which the abstract API permits), line 222 `counter_updates[gk]` raises `KeyError` for every group key. Initialize `counter_updates` as `{gk: {} for gk in group_keys}` or use `counter_updates.get(gk, {})` so handlers with no counters work.

title: Stale docstring: evaluate still documented as returning a list
body: The docstring of `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` says it "returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`", but the signature and implementation were changed in this PR to return a dict keyed by group key. The docstring should be updated to match, otherwise it misleads implementers of the abstract interface.

title: Multi-group test builds expected occurrence with wrong value, masking value-passing bugs
body: In `test_state_results_multi_group`, `group_vals` is `{"group_1": 6, "group_2": 10}`, but the expected occurrence for `group_2` is built with `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(..., "group_2", 6, ...)`. Because `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` ignores the `value` parameter entirely, this test would pass even if `evaluate_group_key_value` passed the wrong value (or a hardcoded value) to `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. There is no test anywhere that verifies the actual group value is forwarded to the occurrence hook; the helper should incorporate `value` (e.g. into the subtitle/evidence) so the contract is verified.

title: get_monitor_environment_context copies config but returns the unmodified original
body: In get_monitor_environment_context, a local `config = monitor_environment.monitor.config.copy()` is built and its `schedule_type` is replaced with the human-readable display value (lines 160-162), but the returned dict uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` (line 168) instead of the local `config`. The intent of mapping schedule_type to a display string is silently dropped, so the monitor context published in the issue event always contains the raw schedule type. This was carried over from mark_failed.py, but since the code is being reorganized into its own module it should be fixed: return `"config": config`.

title: mark_failed_threshold and create_issue_platform_occurrence removed without aliases or test updates shown
body: The refactor deletes `mark_failed_threshold` and `create_issue_platform_occurrence` from sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed and replaces them with `try_incident_threshold` in sentry.monitors.logic.incidents and `create_incident_occurrence` in sentry.monitors.logic.incident_occurrence. Any code (tasks, scripts, tests, or external consumers) importing these public module-level functions from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` will now fail with ImportError. The PR shows no changes to callers or tests, so if tests or other modules referenced the old names, they were not updated in this diff; verify no remaining references exist before merging.

title: Docstring typos: "humam readible" and stale examples
body: The docstring for get_failure_reason says "Builds a humam readible string" (should be "human readable"), and its example outputs do not match the actual format: the function returns e.g. "A missed check-in was detected" for the singular case and "N status check-ins detected" for the plural, not the free-form examples listed ("3 missed check-ins detected", "A failed check-in was detected"). Misleading docs in a freshly extracted module should be corrected.

title: get_monitor_environment_context computes a modified config copy but returns the original config
body: In get_monitor_environment_context, line 160 builds `config = monitor_environment.monitor.config.copy()` and replaces `schedule_type` with its human-readable display value (lines 161-162), but the returned dict at line 168 uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` (the raw, unmodified config) instead of the local `config` variable. As a result the schedule_type translation/display logic is dead code and the monitor context sent in the issue occurrence event always contains the raw schedule type value. This bug was carried over from the old mark_failed.py during the move, but this is a good opportunity to fix it.

title: Public helpers mark_failed_threshold and create_issue_platform_occurrence were removed without deprecation aliases
body: The refactor removes `mark_failed_threshold`, `create_issue_platform_occurrence`, `get_failure_reason`, and `get_monitor_environment_context` from mark_failed.py entirely. Any external callers, tests, or downstream code that import these names from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` (e.g. tests that patch `mark_failed.create_issue_platform_occurrence` to assert occurrence creation) will now fail with ImportError/AttributeError. The PR contains no test updates or deprecation shims, so if any test or consumer still references the old module paths, CI or production code will break. Verify all usages were updated or add temporary re-export aliases.

title: cast mislabels a ValuesQuerySet as list[SimpleCheckIn] before it is materialized
body: `cast(list[SimpleCheckIn], MonitorCheckIn.objects...values(...))` claims the queryset is a list when it is not; the code happens to work because it slices (`previous_checkins[:failure_issue_threshold]`) and wraps in list() afterwards, but any code path that used `previous_checkins` directly as a list (e.g. indexing before line 48, or type-checking) would fail. The cast is misleading and should be applied after `list(...)` materialization, or the queryset should be converted to a list before the cast. Carried over from the previous implementation.

title: active_incident may be stale relative to status, causing occurrences with no incident
body: In the MonitorStatus.ERROR branch, `incident = monitor_env.active_incident` may be None (e.g. data inconsistency, or the incident was resolved between status update and this read). The code still falls through to line 102 and sends the `monitor_environment_failed` signal and returns True even when no occurrence was produced and no incident exists. If incident is None the function reports success (True) to mark_failed callers, which may rely on that to mean an incident/occurrence was handled. Consider returning False or logging when there is no active incident in the ERROR state.

title: get_monitor_environment_context computes a modified config copy but returns the unmodified config
body: In get_monitor_environment_context, a copy of monitor.config is made and 'schedule_type' is replaced with its display value (lines 160-162), but the returned dict at line 168 uses 'monitor_environment.monitor.config' (the original, unmodified config) instead of the local 'config' variable. The human-readable schedule type is therefore never included in the monitor context emitted with the occurrence. The local 'config' variable is dead code. This was carried over from the old mark_failed module, but since this PR is specifically splitting this logic out, it should be fixed while moving it.

title: Public helper functions (mark_failed_threshold, create_issue_platform_occurrence, get_failure_reason, get_monitor_environment_context, SimpleCheckIn) removed from mark_failed with no compatibility shims
body: This PR deletes mark_failed_threshold, create_issue_platform_occurrence, get_failure_reason, get_monitor_environment_context, HUMAN_FAILURE_STATUS_MAP, SINGULAR_HUMAN_FAILURE_MAP, and the SimpleCheckIn TypedDict from sentry/monitors/logic/mark_failed.py. Any external code or tests importing these from mark_failed (e.g. tests of failure-reason formatting, or other monitor consumers) will now fail with ImportError. The PR contains no test changes showing these imports were updated repo-wide; verify all call sites/tests were migrated, or add temporary re-exports from mark_failed pointing at the new modules.

title: Refactor moves ~270 lines of incident/occurrence logic with no accompanying tests
body: The PR relocates the entire incident-threshold and occurrence-creation logic into new modules (sentry/monitors/logic/incidents.py and incident_occurrence.py) but adds no tests for the new module boundaries (e.g. try_incident_threshold behavior, create_incident_occurrence, get_failure_reason). If the existing test suite only covers these paths via mark_failed, the module-level contract is untested; adding direct tests for the new public functions would protect the new module boundary that GH-80527 plans to build on.

title: Restarted flusher processes are killed but never joined, leaking zombies and resources
body: In `_ensure_processes_alive`, an unhealthy process is `process.kill()`-ed and a replacement is immediately started via `_create_process_for_shards`, but the old process object is never `join()`-ed. In production (spawn mode) each killed process becomes a zombie until the parent exits, and its `SpansBuffer` (with its Redis connection pool) is dropped from `self.buffers[process_index]` without being closed, leaking connections. Since restarts can happen repeatedly (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per process index), a consumer running for a long time can accumulate zombies and leaked Redis connections. The old process should be joined/cleaned up before or after starting the replacement.

title: _create_process_for_shard is dead code
body: `_create_process_for_shard(shard)` is defined but never called anywhere; the restart path uses `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly. Dead code invites confusion about which restart entrypoint to use and should be removed.

title: Per-process restart counters never reset, so cumulative restarts eventually crash the consumer
body: `self.process_restarts[process_index]` is only ever incremented and never reset, even after a process has been running healthily for a long time. With `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS = 10`, a process that legitimately crashed 11 times over months of uptime (e.g. transient Redis outages) will cause `_ensure_processes_alive` to raise RuntimeError and take down the whole consumer. The counter should be reset once the replacement process has been observed healthy for some period. This was a pre-existing flaw for the single process, but multiplying the number of processes multiplies the probability of hitting it.

title: Tests only cover the threading (produce_to_pipe) path, never the multiprocessing path
body: Both consumer tests and test_flusher.py inject `produce_to_pipe`, which makes `SpanFlusher` use `threading.Thread` and `partial` instead of the spawn-based `multiprocessing.Process` with `run_with_initialized_sentry`. None of the new multi-process behavior (process-per-shard spawn, argument pickling of per-shard SpansBuffer and shared Values, process restart in `_ensure_processes_alive`, join/terminate of real processes) is exercised. The new `test_flusher_processes_limit` test only asserts on dicts/counts, not that processes actually work. A regression in the spawn path (e.g. a pickling error in the new per-shard buffer or the new `shards` argument) would not be caught.

title: test_basic relies on a fixed 0.1s sleep for the flusher thread to observe the drift change
body: `test_basic` sets `current_drift` and then sleeps for 0.1s before `step.join()`, expecting the background flusher thread to have picked up the new drift and flushed the segment. There is no synchronization guaranteeing the thread reached the read of `current_drift` or completed the flush/produce within 100ms, so the `(msg,) = messages` unpacking can flake on slow/loaded CI. A poll-until-assertion loop (with timeout) would make this deterministic.

title: max_processes default of None means one process per shard, contradicting documented default of 1
body: `SpanFlusher.__init__` treats `max_processes=None` as `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, i.e. one process per shard. The `--flusher-processes` CLI option documents "Defaults to 1", and its click default is 1, so CLI-driven deployments get 1; but any other instantiation path that omits the argument (as all existing direct callers in tests and code do) silently spawns one process per assigned partition, each of which re-imports sentry/Django under spawn. This is a significant behavioral/memory difference depending on call path, and the docstring does not mention it. The default should be consistent (e.g. 1) or the behavior documented.

title: test_basic's time.sleep(0.1) is patched away, making the test racy
body: The test monkeypatches `time.sleep` to a no-op at the top (`monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`), so the later `time.sleep(0.1)` intended to 'give flusher threads time to process after drift change' actually does nothing. The flusher thread only picks up the new `current_drift` value on its next loop iteration; if it hasn't run between setting the drift and `step.join()`, the segment is never flushed and `(msg,) = messages` will fail. The test now depends on thread scheduling luck and will be flaky (or silently not exercising the flush path). Use an unpatched sleep (e.g. `from time import sleep` bound before patching, or a real eventfd/condition) instead.

title: Killed flusher processes are never joined, leaking zombies on repeated restarts
body: In `_ensure_processes_alive`, a hung/crashed process is `kill()`ed and immediately replaced via `_create_process_for_shards`, but `join()` is never called on the old process object (it is simply dropped from `self.processes`). With the spawn start method, killed child processes remain zombies until reaped by the parent. Under a scenario where a process repeatedly hangs (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS=10 times), each restart leaks a zombie process (and its pipe/socket resources for the shared `Value` handles). Call `process.join(timeout)` after kill, or otherwise reap the old process before replacing it.

title: join(timeout) skips terminate() for remaining processes once the deadline passes
body: In `join`, once `remaining_time <= 0` the code `break`s out of the outer loop entirely, so any processes not yet waited on are never sent `terminate()`. They are only released via the `stopped` flag, which the child checks at most once per ~1s iteration (and only after completing any in-flight produce/flush work). If a child is stuck producing to Kafka, it can hold the join open well past the requested timeout. The loop should still attempt `terminate()` on all remaining processes even after the deadline expires.

title: Docstring claims 'one process per shard' but default is one process total
body: The class docstring says 'Creates one process per shard for parallel processing', but the CLI option `--flusher-processes` defaults to 1 (see src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py), so in the default configuration a single process handles all assigned shards. The docstring should describe the actual behavior (one process per shard-group, capped by max_processes).

title: max_processes=0 silently means 'all shards' instead of being rejected
body: `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` uses `or`, so a falsy value of 0 falls back to one process per shard. An operator passing `--flusher-processes 0` (a plausible typo or misconfiguration) will unexpectedly spawn one process per shard rather than getting an error. Use `max_processes if max_processes is not None else len(...)` and/or validate the CLI option is >= 1.

title: Memory backpressure aggregation across per-process buffers may double-count Redis clusters
body: `submit()` now aggregates `get_memory_info()` from each per-shard-group buffer. If `get_memory_info()` reports at the Redis cluster/connection level (rather than strictly per shard), clusters whose shards are split across multiple process groups will be counted multiple times in both `used` and `available`, weighting those clusters by how many buffers touch them and skewing the `used/available` ratio used to trigger hard backpressure (pausing the whole consumer). Verify that per-buffer aggregation yields the same totals as the previous single-buffer call for the same shard set; if not, deduplicate by cluster before summing.

title: Restarting a 'hung' process can run two flushers on the same shards, producing duplicate segments
body: In `_ensure_processes_alive`, when a process is deemed hung (`cause == "hang"`), `process.kill()` is called and a replacement is immediately spawned via `_create_process_for_shards`. `kill()` is asynchronous — the old process can still be inside its flush loop while the new process starts flushing the same shards. Both processes can call `buffer.flush_segments()` and produce the same segments to Kafka before either calls `done_flush_segments`, resulting in duplicate segments in the buffered-segments topic (duplicate span data downstream). The old process is also never joined, so it is never confirmed dead before the replacement starts. The replacement should only be started after the old process has actually exited (join with timeout), and ideally after verifying no in-flight flush.

title: Thread-based flusher (produce_to_pipe path) is never killed on restart, so restarts stack threads
body: When `produce_to_pipe` is set, the flusher 'process' is a `threading.Thread`. On an unhealthy restart, the kill is guarded by `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`, so the old thread is left running and a new one is spawned for the same shards. A hung thread never recovers, so every restart adds another thread; if the hang is caused by a stuck `produce` (as in the backpressure test, where append sleeps), multiple threads will flush the same shards concurrently, duplicating messages. This mostly affects the test path today, but the code claims Thread support, so it should either kill/stop the old thread cooperatively (e.g. per-process stop flag) or refuse to restart thread-based flushers.

title: Metric tag key inconsistency: 'shards' vs 'shard'
body: The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer uses `tags={"shards": shard_tag}` while `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` use `tags={"shard": shard_tag}`. The tag name typo means the wait_produce timer cannot be grouped/joined with the other flusher metrics by shard, and produces a second tag key in the metrics namespace for the same dimension.

title: Restart counter never resets, so cumulative restarts eventually crash the consumer even if each process is healthy
body: `process_restarts[process_index]` is only ever incremented; there is no reset after a process proves itself healthy. With MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS = 10, a shard-group that legitimately restarts 11 times over the entire lifetime of a long-running consumer (e.g. due to transient Redis/Kafka failures hours apart) will trigger `RuntimeError` and crash the whole consumer, taking down all shard flushers. The counter should reset (or decay) after a period of healthy operation, as was the case before this change for the single process — but this PR now makes it much more likely since a single misbehaving shard-group among many takes the consumer down.

title: _create_process_for_shard is dead code
body: The method `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is never called anywhere (the restart path calls `_create_process_for_shards` with a process index directly). It also has a bug if it were used: it would overwrite `self.processes[process_index]` without killing the previous process. It should be removed.

title: No test that multiple flusher processes actually flush their shards end-to-end
body: The new `test_flusher_processes_limit` test only asserts process/shard bookkeeping (counts and map sizes); it never submits a span or asserts that a segment is produced. There is no test covering the core new behavior: that with multiple flusher processes, spans on shards assigned to different processes are all flushed exactly once, nor a test for the restart path (`_ensure_processes_alive` with multiple processes), which is where the trickiest new logic lives. A regression in shard-to-process mapping or in restart handling would pass the current test suite.

title: submit() iterates self.buffers while restarts mutate it
body: `submit()` and `_ensure_processes_alive()` run on the main thread, so the dict mutation itself is not racy in-process. However `_create_process_for_shards` replaces `self.buffers[process_index]` with a brand new `SpansBuffer(shards)` each restart. If a restart happens between the `record_stored_segments()` loop and the memory-info loop within a single `submit()` call, some shards' buffers get recorded twice and some not at all within that call; more importantly each restart allocates a new SpansBuffer (with new Redis clients) while old ones are never closed, leaking Redis connections over repeated restarts.

title: queue.Queue.shutdown / queue.ShutDown require Python 3.13
body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) and OrderedQueueWorker catches queue.ShutDown, but Queue.shutdown() and the ShutDown exception were only added to the stdlib in Python 3.13. On the Python versions Sentry currently runs (3.11/3.12) this raises AttributeError at shutdown time (silently swallowed by the try/except, so workers are never told to stop and blocked worker threads never exit), and the `except queue.ShutDown` handlers would fail to even import-resolve at runtime. The graceful shutdown path is broken on supported Python versions; use a sentinel/Event-based approach instead.

title: Failed messages are marked completed and their offsets committed, silently dropping them
body: OrderedQueueWorker.run() calls offset_tracker.complete_offset in a `finally` block, so when result_processor raises, the offset is still considered complete and the commit loop will commit past it. Combined with the fact that ResultProcessor.__call__ also swallows all exceptions (logs only), any message that fails processing (e.g. DB error, bad subscription data) is permanently lost with no retry and no DLQ — the offset is committed so it will never be redelivered. The existing test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling even asserts this drop-on-failure behavior. There should be a retry/DLQ path or the offset should remain outstanding (blocking commit) on failure so the message is redelivered.

title: Queues are unbounded — no backpressure despite docstring claim, risk of unbounded memory growth
body: FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() returns immediately after enqueueing, so the arroyo consumer thread will keep polling Kafka and enqueueing as fast as it can. If processing (DB-backed result handling) is slower than consumption, queues grow without limit, holding decoded messages and their Message objects in memory until OOM. The class docstring's 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' guarantee is false as implemented. Either set maxsize and block/propagate backpressure in submit(), or bound total in-flight items.

title: close() stops the commit loop before workers drain, losing final offset commits
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread *before* calling queue_pool.shutdown(), which is what drains the worker queues. Any messages processed after the last commit-loop iteration (up to the entire remaining queue contents at shutdown) will be processed but never committed. On restart/rebalance those messages are redelivered and reprocessed, which for non-idempotent result handling means duplicate side effects. The correct order is: stop accepting new work, drain queues, do a final get_committable_offsets/commit, then stop the commit thread.

title: join() unconditionally calls close(), causing double shutdown and ignoring its timeout
body: Arroyo's StreamProcessor calls close() then join() on strategies. Here join() calls close() again: shutdown_event.set() and commit_thread.join() are harmless, but queue_pool.shutdown() runs a second time — each Queue.shutdown() (on 3.13) raises ValueError on already-shutdown queues (swallowed by the broad except, hiding errors), and worker.join() is called again. Additionally the `timeout` parameter of join() is accepted but never used, so a stuck worker blocks shutdown for the full 5s join regardless. join() should simply wait (using its timeout) for work to drain, not re-run shutdown.

title: Worker thread death permanently stalls offset commits for its queue
body: If an OrderedQueueWorker thread exits for any reason other than a clean shutdown — e.g. an exception raised by metrics.gauge or the sentry_sdk transaction wrapper inside the finally block, or a non-Exception BaseException from result_processor — the thread dies, but all offsets of items still sitting in its queue remain in OffsetTracker.outstanding forever. get_committable_offsets will never advance past the smallest such offset, so commits for that partition stop entirely, backpressure-free consumption continues enqueueing into a queue nobody reads, and memory grows until the process is killed. There is no liveness check or worker restart.

title: Arroyo Commit callable invoked from a background thread concurrently with the consumer thread
body: The commit loop thread calls the arroyo Commit function (which ends up calling consumer commit / interacting with consumer state) once per second, while the StreamProcessor's main thread concurrently polls the consumer and may itself commit or rebalance. Arroyo strategies normally call commit from the processing (main) thread; calling it from an unsynchronized background thread risks racing with the consumer during rebalances/shutdown and can produce errors or commits of stale offsets. This needs verification against arroyo's thread-safety contract, or the commit should be marshalled back to the strategy thread (e.g. via poll()).

title: test_different_groups_distributed is flaky due to salted string hashing
body: The test asserts that 20 arbitrary group keys hashed with Python's builtin hash() (which is salted per process for str) land on exactly all 3 queues. With random salt it is possible (though unlikely) that fewer than 3 distinct indices are hit, making the test flaky across runs. Asserting `>= 2` or using fixed deterministic keys would be robust.

title: A sentry_sdk transaction is started for every single message in every worker
body: OrderedQueueWorker wraps each individual result_processor call in sentry_sdk.start_transaction. At production uptime-result volumes this creates and discards a transaction object per message (20 queues × full throughput), adding significant per-message overhead and, if any transaction sampling is enabled, flooding Sentry with events. The batched-parallel mode wraps batches, not items; this should be a span or sampled/omitted entirely.

title: Unbounded queues: no backpressure despite docstring claim
body: FixedQueuePool creates `queue.Queue()` with no maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit never blocks or signals arroyo to pause (poll() only emits a gauge). The class docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but nothing fills up. If processing falls behind (the exact scenario this PR is meant to handle — a slow item backlogging a queue), arroyo will keep polling and submitting, and in-memory WorkItems accumulate without bound, risking OOM in the consumer process. Either bound the queues and block/reject submit, or expose a pause/resume mechanism to arroyo.

title: Rebalance permanently kills the shared queue pool, silently dropping messages
body: The FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and reused for every create_with_partitions call. But SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/join() (queue_consumer.py lines 335-345) calls queue_pool.shutdown(), which stops all worker threads and calls queue.shutdown() on every queue. Arroyo calls join()/close() on the old strategy on every rebalance, then calls create_with_partitions again — the new strategy gets the same, now-dead pool. Subsequent submits will raise queue.ShutDown when putting items; that exception is caught by the generic except in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit, which marks the offset as complete, so the message is silently dropped and its offset committed. The pool must either be created per-strategy, or the strategy must not shut down the shared pool.

title: Processing failures are swallowed and offsets still committed (silent data loss)
body: OrderedQueueWorker.run catches all exceptions from result_processor, logs them, and unconditionally marks the offset complete in the finally block. The commit loop then commits that offset. A permanently failing result (e.g. a bug triggered by a particular payload) is therefore dropped with no retry, no DLQ, and no metric — only a log line. At minimum this should increment a failure metric so operators can detect silent loss; ideally it should integrate with the existing DLQ policy or a retry path.

title: Offset gaps permanently block commits for a partition
body: get_committable_offsets stops at the first offset not present in all_offsets and never commits past it. Any offset that is never add_offset'ed for a partition (e.g. messages filtered/dropped upstream of this strategy, or offsets below the initial start after a rebalance where another instance committed some and the tracker's last_committed is stale or -1) creates a permanent gap: all later offsets in that partition become uncommittable, all_offsets grows without bound for the life of the process, and the consumer group's committed lag grows indefinitely, triggering rebalances/max-poll-interval expiry on restart. There is no mechanism to advance past a gap or reset state on partition reassignment.

title: OffsetTracker state is not reset on partition reassignment/rebalance
body: The OffsetTracker lives on the shared FixedQueuePool and retains last_committed, all_offsets, and outstanding across rebalances. After a rebalance, create_with_partitions may be invoked with a different partition assignment and the consumer may resume from offsets previously committed by another instance (which can be lower or unrelated to last_committed). If a new message's offset is <= last_committed for that partition, get_committable_offsets returns nothing for it (start = last_committed+1 skips it) and the offset is never committed, stalling that partition's commits. State should be scoped to a strategy/partition assignment lifecycle.

title: hash(str) is randomized across processes
body: get_queue_for_group uses Python's built-in hash() on a string, which is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED). This is fine for ordering within a single process, but any future design where multiple processes (or a restart mid-flight with different assignment) rely on consistent group→queue mapping would silently break ordering assumptions. Using a stable hash (e.g. zlib.crc32 or hashlib) would make the mapping deterministic and document the intent. Low priority since current usage is per-process.

title: A Sentry transaction is started per message in every worker
body: OrderedQueueWorker wraps every single result_processor call in sentry_sdk.start_transaction(). At uptime-results throughput this creates an enormous number of transactions (one per Kafka message per worker), which both adds per-message overhead in the hot path and can flood Sentry. The existing code path (ResultProcessor.__call__) already starts a transaction per result, so this doubles transactions per message. Consider a span or sampling.

title: submit() swallows decoder/assert errors and commits offsets for undecodable messages
body: In submit(), any exception (including the `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` failure and decode_payload exceptions) is caught and the offset is immediately marked complete, so the offset is committed even though the message was never processed and no DLQ is involved. This differs from other modes where a decode failure is at least logged with the payload. Combined with the generic ResultProcessor exception swallowing, there are three separate layers of silent-drop with no metric distinguishing 'dropped at decode' from 'dropped at process'.

title: Failed messages are still marked complete and committed, giving at-most-once semantics
body: In OrderedQueueWorker.run, exceptions from result_processor are caught and only logged (line 144-147), and the finally block at line 149 always calls offset_tracker.complete_offset. The offset is then treated as processed and will be committed by the commit loop. Combined with ResultProcessor.__call__ (result_consumer.py line 53-54) which also swallows all exceptions, any transient failure (e.g. a DB error while handling a result) silently drops the message and advances the committed offset past it, so the message is never retried. This contradicts the class docstring's guarantee 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and turns the consumer into an at-most-once pipeline with silent data loss.

title: close() permanently kills the shared queue pool, breaking rebalance recovery
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which sets the shutdown flag on every worker, shuts down every queue.Queue, and joins the threads. The queue_pool is owned by the ResultsStrategyFactory and shared across strategies. Arroyo closes the current strategy and calls create_with_partitions again on partition rebalance/reassignment (e.g. when partitions are revoked and later reassigned, or when running multiple strategies per process). After the first close(), all worker threads have exited, but the factory keeps the same (now dead) pool and creates a new SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy on top of it. All subsequently submitted items pile up in the dead queues with nothing consuming them: no processing, no offset commits, unbounded memory growth, and the consumer stalls. close() should only stop the strategy's commit thread and drain, leaving pool lifecycle to the factory.

title: Uses queue.Queue.shutdown / queue.ShutDown which only exist on Python 3.13+
body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) and OrderedQueueWorker.run catches queue.ShutDown (lines 132, 142). Queue.shutdown and the queue.ShutDown exception were only added to the stdlib in Python 3.13. On any older supported interpreter, importing is fine but calling shutdown() raises AttributeError (caught and logged at line 239-240, leaving workers blocked forever on q.get()) and the except clause referencing queue.ShutDown raises AttributeError inside run, killing the worker thread. Verify the project's minimum Python version or use a sentinel-based shutdown.

title: Docstring claims backpressure but queues are unbounded
body: The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring states 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' (and FixedQueuePool has no maxsize), but each queue.Queue is created with no maxsize (line 185), and submit() never blocks. The arroyo consumer can therefore poll and enqueue messages far faster than workers process them, with the only limit being process memory. Under a slow-consumer backlog this leads to unbounded memory growth and, since processing lags arbitrarily behind, offsets are held back indefinitely while messages accumulate. Either give queues a maxsize so submit blocks, or remove the backpressure claim and add a depth-based guard/metric alert.

title: Background commit thread commits without regard to partition ownership
body: The commit loop runs every second and calls commit_function(committable) for all partitions ever seen by the OffsetTracker, including partitions that may have been revoked during a rebalance. Committing offsets for partitions the consumer no longer owns violates Kafka consumer-group protocol (the commit is rejected or, worse, races with the new owner). There is no cancellation of in-flight work or clearing of tracker state on partition revocation, and commit also proceeds concurrently with close()/terminate(): shutdown_event is set, but the loop can already be past the wait(1.0) and issue a commit while the pool is shutting down. The strategy needs to stop committing for revoked partitions (e.g. filter against currently assigned partitions passed to create_with_partitions) and re-check shutdown_event before committing.

title: --max-workers help text/semantics conflate worker threads and queue count
body: In thread-queue-parallel mode, max_workers sets num_queues (the number of queues, each with one worker thread), and the default when max_workers is None is 20 — whereas in batched-parallel mode the default is ThreadPoolExecutor's default. The shared click option's help ('The maximum amount of parallelism to use when in a parallel mode') hides that for this mode the value also caps per-key parallelism at exactly one thread per queue and that a deploy changing max_workers remaps every group to a different queue (hash(group_key) % num_queues), which can momentarily reorder processing relative to items still in old queues. Consider documenting the remapping caveat and the differing default.

title: Backup-code requests can bypass the password check by including a dummy TOTP value
body: The password verification earlier in `authorize` runs only when `credentials.totpCode` is empty, while this new branch accepts a backup code whenever `credentials.backupCode` is set and does not validate the TOTP value. A caller can submit a valid backup code plus any non-empty `totpCode` value and an arbitrary or absent password; this skips password verification and the backup-code branch succeeds. The UI retains the password during the normal flow, but the credentials callback is directly callable. Require password verification independently of whether a TOTP field is present (or otherwise bind completion of the password step to the second-factor request) before accepting a backup code.

title: Backup codes are consumed with a non-atomic read-modify-write
body: The code list is read from the user record, checked in memory, and then written back after replacing the matched entry with `null`. Two concurrent login requests using the same code can both read the old encrypted list before either update occurs, both pass `indexOf`, and both create sessions; the last write merely overwrites the same resulting list. This violates the advertised one-time-use property. Consume the code atomically, for example by using a transaction/row lock or a conditional update that verifies the stored value has not changed and rejects the request when no row was updated.

title: The new backup-code authentication and consumption behavior is not tested
body: The added test coverage only verifies that the setup screen has downloadable/copyable controls; it does not submit a backup code through login or the disable-2FA flow, verify that a valid code succeeds, verify invalid-code handling, or verify that a used code cannot be reused. The test itself leaves these core feature paths as TODOs, so regressions in the newly added authentication branch and one-time-code behavior will not be caught.

title: Consume backup codes atomically
body: The backup code is read and validated from the initially fetched user record, then a separate unconditional update writes the modified array. Two credential requests using the same code can both read the unconsumed value before either update executes, both pass validation, and both receive sessions. This violates the stated exactly-once property and can let an attacker who races a legitimate user reuse a stolen code. Consume the code through a transaction/row lock or a conditional update that verifies the stored value has not changed, and reject the request when that update affects no rows.

title: Backup codes cannot be used in the external-provider 2FA flow
body: The new backup-code branch is unreachable for users entering the `/auth/login?totp=...` flow used after Google/SAML authentication. Before this branch, line 113 rejects every non-CAL identity provider when `credentials.totpCode` is absent; a backup-code submission intentionally has no TOTP code. The login UI also renders `ExternalTotpFooter` for this flow, which provides no "Lost access" option. Consequently, users with external-provider accounts protected by 2FA cannot use their backup codes to recover access.

title: The backup-code authentication and one-time-use behavior is untested
body: The added test coverage only verifies that the backup-code screen can copy/download data. It never submits a backup code through login or the disable-2FA recovery flow, and never verifies that a successfully used code is rejected on a subsequent attempt. These are the primary new authentication and security semantics, so regressions such as codes not being passed to NextAuth or not being consumed would pass the current suite.

title: Backup-code authentication can bypass the account password
body: The password verification at lines 121-129 is skipped whenever `credentials.totpCode` is non-empty, while the new backup-code branch takes precedence whenever `backupCode` is supplied. A caller can therefore submit a valid backup code plus any arbitrary non-empty `totpCode` and authenticate without providing the user's password. Backup codes are intended to replace the authenticator factor, not the primary password; this turns a stolen backup code into a standalone login credential. Require password verification whenever this is a CAL password login, independent of which second-factor field is used.

title: Backup codes are not consumed atomically
body: The code is looked up from an earlier user read and then consumed with an unconditional update. Two concurrent credential callbacks using the same backup code can both find the code before either update commits, and both will successfully authenticate; each writes the same remaining-code list afterward. This violates the advertised exactly-once property and can issue multiple sessions from one recovery code. Consume the code in a transaction/conditional update tied to the previously read encrypted value (or store codes in individually deletable rows) and reject the request if the conditional update affects no row.

title: Users in the external TOTP login flow cannot use backup codes
body: When `totpEmail` is present (the signed redirect used after Google/SAML 2FA), the page renders `ExternalTotpFooter` rather than `TwoFactorFooter`. That footer only has Cancel, so it does not expose the new Lost access action and there is no way to render or submit `BackupCode` for these users. This leaves accounts that already use the external-provider 2FA flow unable to use the advertised recovery mechanism; expose the backup-code switch in this flow as well and ensure the credentials authorization path accepts it.

title: Existing 2FA users have no way to obtain backup codes
body: The migration adds `backupCodes` as NULL for every existing user, but this endpoint rejects every user who already has 2FA enabled with `TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled`. Consequently, pre-existing 2FA users receive `MissingBackupCodes` if they choose Lost access and cannot follow the UI instruction to generate codes in settings without first disabling and re-enabling 2FA (which itself requires the unavailable authenticator). Provide a secure backup-code generation/recovery action for already-enabled users, or avoid offering the recovery path until codes have been provisioned.

title: Google Meet fallback dereferences an absent destination calendar
body: `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined` when an event has no destination calendar, but this condition immediately reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration`. This replaces the previous optional-chain-safe check, so creating any Google Meet event without a configured destination calendar throws a TypeError before calendar/video creation can proceed.

title: Non-Google collective host events are still created against the first host calendar
body: The loop creates one event per destination and supplies `destination.externalId` only to the CalendarManager result metadata. CalendarManager passes only `credential.id` to the provider, while the Office365, Lark, and CalDAV `createEvent` implementations ignore that argument and select `event.destinationCalendar[0]`. Consequently, when a collective event has multiple destination calendars, creation using a later host's credential targets the first host's calendar (or fails due to lacking access), while the stored reference claims the later host calendar. Subsequent updates/deletes will then address the wrong event/calendar.

title: Recurring cancellation deletes only the first calendar reference for every host
body: For each calendar reference, the recurring-cancellation branch iterates every calendar credential but selects `updBooking.references.find(...)`, which always returns only the first calendar reference.
