Any site can cause a logged-in user's browser to request a known public topic unsubscribe URL (for example with an image or redirect), changing that user's per-topic notification state without consent. State changes should require a CSRF-protected non-GET request, with the email link leading to a confirmation page or a signed one-time action token.

title: Manual unsubscribe URLs fail with a nil TopicUser record
body: `TopicUser.find_by` can return nil when a logged-in user visits an unsubscribe URL for a topic they have not previously viewed or otherwise received a topic-user row for. The following access to `tu.notification_level` then raises a 500 error. The route is publicly reachable and the new client route makes such navigation possible, so the action must create/update the association via `TopicUser.change` or handle a missing record before reading it.

title: Blocked addresses can be bypassed by changing email capitalization
body: The lookup uses exact string equality, while signup assigns the raw `params[:email]` to the user and this model does not normalize blocked-email records. On the case-sensitive database used by the application, a block for `bad@example.com` will not match a signup using `Bad@example.com` (or capitalization changes in the local part), allowing a blocked address to register. Normalize both stored and checked addresses with the application's email canonicalization, or use a case-insensitive lookup/index.

title: Match counters are inflated because validation has side effects
body: `should_block?` increments and saves on every validation invocation. The signup action calls `user.valid?` before the hub registration check and then calls `user.save`, which runs validations again; consequently one blocked signup request increments `match_count` twice. Other callers that validate a record repeatedly will similarly alter the metric. Record a blocked signup attempt outside validation or otherwise ensure the statistic is updated once per request.

title: Concurrent blocked-email checks lose match-count updates
body: The read-modify-write sequence (`record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save`) is not atomic. Concurrent signup attempts for the same blocked address can both read the same count and save the same incremented value, dropping one or more matches (and potentially overwriting `last_match_at`). Use an atomic database update such as `update_all`/`increment_counter` with a timestamp, or locking, when recording matches.

title: Blocked-email lookup can be bypassed by changing email case
body: `should_block?` performs an exact database lookup using the supplied value, but signup assigns `params[:email]` directly to the user and does not normalize it. Consequently, a block for `blocked@example.com` does not match variants such as `Blocked@Example.com`, even though these are ordinarily delivered to the same mailbox and the rest of the domain restriction validation is case-insensitive. Normalize emails consistently when creating blocked records and when looking them up (and migrate existing entries) so the block cannot be evaded by case changes.

title: Concurrent blocked-email checks lose match-count increments
body: The code reads `match_count` into an ActiveRecord instance, increments it in Ruby, and saves it back. Two simultaneous validations of the same blocked address can both read the same count and overwrite each other, so `match_count` underreports attempted registrations. Use an atomic SQL increment/update (including `last_match_at`) or locking if these statistics are expected to be reliable under concurrent signup traffic.

title: Email-change requests bypass blocked-email validation before sending mail
body: The `change_email` action only checks whether the address is already in use, then creates an email token and queues an authorization email. It never assigns the address to the user or invokes the new `email` validator, so a blocked address can still be submitted through this endpoint and receives an authorization message. Validate the proposed normalized address here before creating the token/queueing mail; otherwise the blocked-email policy is not enforced for email changes (and may be bypassed entirely if token confirmation updates the email without validation).

title: Blocked-address matching is case-sensitive and can be trivially bypassed
body: `should_block?` compares the submitted value directly against the stored string. The signup path assigns `params[:email]` directly to `User#email`, so a row for `bad@spamclub.com` does not match a signup using `bad@SPAMCLUB.COM` (or other casing variants) on a case-sensitive database. This differs from the domain restrictions, which use a case-insensitive regexp, and allows a blocked address to register simply by changing case. Normalize both blocked-email records and values being checked with the application's canonical email normalization (for example `Email.downcase(...).strip`), and ensure lookup/indexing uses that normalized form.

title: Match-count updates lose increments under concurrent validation
body: The counter is updated with a read-modify-write sequence (`record.match_count += 1` followed by `save`). Two concurrent signup attempts for the same blocked address can both read the same count and save the same incremented value, causing one or more matches to be lost. Since this table explicitly records match statistics, use an atomic database update such as `update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ...')` or locking/counter updates so concurrent attempts are counted correctly.

title: Imported feed/article HTML is persisted without sanitization
body: `import` creates posts with `cook_method: raw_html`, and `Post#cook` returns this content verbatim. `contents` comes directly from RSS/Atom feeds or a remotely fetched page and is neither sanitized nor escaped before becoming `post.cooked`; it also interpolates the unescaped source URL into an HTML attribute on line 13. A malicious article/feed item can therefore store script/event-handler HTML that executes for users viewing the imported topic (and in the embed view, which renders `raw post.cooked`). Sanitize imported HTML and URLs with the normal allowlist before storing/rendering it rather than bypassing the cooking pipeline.

title: Remote import follows redirects without enforcing the allowed host
body: The retriever validates only the host of the initial `embed_url`, but `open(url)` follows HTTP redirects and this method does not validate each redirect target or block private/reserved addresses. An unauthenticated caller can request an allowed-host URL that redirects to an internal service (for example via an open redirect on the configured site), causing the Discourse server to fetch internal endpoints. Enforce the host/address policy on every redirect hop (and reject private/link-local targets), or use an HTTP client configured not to follow redirects.

title: Relative links without a leading slash are not converted to source URLs
body: Despite the method's contract to convert relative URLs, it only rewrites `href` and `src` values beginning with `/`. Common document-relative URLs such as `images/photo.jpg`, `../article`, or `?page=2` remain unchanged. Once the content is displayed on Discourse, browsers resolve those URLs relative to the forum/embed URL rather than the original article, producing broken or incorrectly directed links and images. Resolve all non-absolute URLs against the full source URL (for example with `URI.join`).

title: The success-path spec expects a retriever call that the controller no longer makes
body: This example sets an expectation that `TopicRetriever.new(...).retrieve` is invoked, but `EmbedController#best` now calls `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)` instead. The expectation is unsatisfied whenever this example runs, so the newly added controller spec fails rather than testing the asynchronous behavior. Update it to assert the queued job and its arguments.

title: External feed/article HTML is persisted and rendered without sanitization
body: `import` marks externally supplied `contents` as `raw_html`, and `Post#cook` consequently returns it unchanged. The embed view renders `post.cooked` with `raw`, so scripts, event-handler attributes, iframes, and other active markup from an RSS item or remotely retrieved article execute under the Discourse origin. Feed and article content must be sanitized with the same trusted HTML policy used for normal posts before it is stored/rendered; the URL interpolated into the appended `imported_from` anchor must also be attribute-escaped.

title: Host validation does not protect the remote fetch after redirects
body: The only validation compares the initial URL host to `embeddable_host`, but `TopicEmbed.import_remote` follows that URL with `open(url)`. An allowed-host URL which redirects to an internal address (for example through an open redirect on the embedded site) causes the Discourse server to fetch the internal resource; its response can then be imported into a public topic. Validate every redirect target and resolved connection address against an allowlist, and reject private/link-local destinations.

title: Feed polling uses String#scrub despite the application's Ruby 1.9 compatibility
body: `String#scrub` was introduced in Ruby 2.1. This codebase still documents/supports Ruby 1.9-era execution, so enabling feed polling on those deployments raises `NoMethodError` on the first item and prevents all feed imports. Use a compatible encoding-cleanup implementation or explicitly raise the supported Ruby version before relying on `scrub`.

title: The new controller spec contradicts the asynchronous implementation
body: This example expects `TopicRetriever.new(...).retrieve` to be called during the request, but `EmbedController#best` now calls `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)` instead. The expectation is never satisfied, so the added spec suite fails. Update the test to assert the enqueue arguments (and retain separate job tests for retrieval), otherwise CI cannot pass and the intended asynchronous contract is untested.

title: Imported feed HTML is stored and served without sanitization
body: `import` creates posts with `cook_method: :raw_html` and `Post#cook` returns that raw HTML unchanged. Feed items are passed directly to this method by `PollFeed`, so a `<script>`, event handler, iframe, or other active markup in an RSS/Atom item is persisted and rendered with `raw post.cooked` in the embed and normal topic views. A compromised feed or untrusted content included by a feed can therefore execute JavaScript under the Discourse origin, including in an administrator's session. Sanitize imported HTML with the normal allowlist/cooking pipeline (or a strict dedicated sanitizer) before storing it, rather than bypassing cooking.

title: Direct article retrieval does not load open-uri before calling open
body: `import_remote` calls `open(url)` but this file does not require `open-uri`. The only new `require 'open-uri'` is in `Jobs::PollFeed`, which is not loaded on the normal embed retrieval path when feed polling is disabled. In a normal process where nothing else happened to load it, Kernel#open treats the HTTP URL as a file path and raises `Errno::ENOENT`, so requested embeds can never be imported. Require `open-uri` in this dependency's own file (or use an explicit HTTP client).

title: Remote retrieval follows redirects without validating the final destination
body: The host check in `TopicRetriever` only validates the original embed URL, but `open(url)` follows HTTP redirects. An allowed embed host with an open redirect (or a compromised allowed host) can redirect the worker to localhost, cloud metadata addresses, or other internal services; their response is then imported into a public topic. Validate every redirect target against an allowlist and block private/reserved IP ranges, or disable redirects and fetch only the validated origin.

title: Controller success spec expects a synchronous retriever that the controller never invokes
body: This example sets an expectation on `TopicRetriever.new` and `retrieve`, but `EmbedController#best` enqueues `:retrieve_topic` instead of constructing a `TopicRetriever`. The expectation is therefore unsatisfied and the added controller spec fails whenever it runs. Update the test to assert the `Jobs.enqueue` call (and cover execution in the retrieve-job spec), or change the implementation if synchronous retrieval was intended.

title: Flex conversion disables the action button's right float
body: Making `.small-action` a flex container turns its direct `button` children into flex items. Flex items do not honor `float: right`, so the existing rule at line 306 no longer places action buttons on the right; with no `margin-left: auto` or flex growth on the description, buttons will appear immediately after `.small-action-desc` instead. This regresses the layout of small-action controls such as undo/action buttons. Add an explicit flex alignment rule (for example, `margin-left: auto` on the button) if the controls should remain right-aligned.

title: Flex layout disables the small-action button's right float
body: `.small-action` is now a flex container, so its direct `button` child is a flex item and its existing `float: right` declaration (line 309) no longer controls its placement. The button will be laid out immediately after `.small-action-desc` instead of at the right edge, regressing the alignment of small-action controls. Add an explicit flex alignment rule such as `margin-left: auto` to the button (and remove reliance on the float).

title: Flex layout disables the action button's right float
body: `.small-action` is now a flex container, so its direct `button` child is a flex item. Per the flexbox layout rules, the existing `float: right` on that item computes to `none`; without `margin-left: auto`, `justify-content`, or another positioning rule, the button is laid out immediately after `.small-action-desc` instead of at the right edge. This regresses the placement of small-action controls and can push them off the row when the description is wide. Add an explicit flex alignment rule (for example `margin-left: auto` on the button, with appropriate shrinking/growth for the description).

title: The flex alignment mixin omits the Mozilla legacy box property
body: `flexbox()` and `inline-flex()` deliberately emit `-moz-box` / `-moz-inline-box`, but `align-items()` does not emit the corresponding `-moz-box-align`. Firefox versions using the legacy box implementation will therefore ignore every `@include align-items(...)` call and use the legacy default alignment (stretch), including the newly centered header contents and baseline-aligned bullet badges. Add `-moz-box-align: $alignment` alongside the other legacy declarations, or remove the unsupported legacy display mode if that browser family is no longer supported.

title: `website_name` bypasses TL0 profile-field restrictions
body: `website_name` is serialized independently of `website`, but it is not included in `untrusted_attributes`. For anonymous views of a TL0 user, `include_website?` suppresses the actual website while this new attribute still exposes its hostname and, for matching instance domains, its full path. This defeats the existing privacy restriction for the website profile field. Apply the same restriction to `website_name` (or make its inclusion depend on `include_website?`) and add coverage for an anonymous TL0 serialization.

title: Website-name inclusion predicate has the wrong serializer method name
body: The serializer convention used throughout this class is `include_<attribute>?` (for example `include_card_image_badge_id?`). This method is named `include_website_name` without the trailing `?`, so ActiveModel serialization will not use it as the inclusion predicate. Consequently `website_name` is treated as an unconditional attribute and can be emitted as null for present-but-unparseable website values; more importantly, the intended guard is not actually enforcing any visibility policy. Rename it to `include_website_name?` and make that predicate honor the website visibility restriction.

title: website_name bypasses the anonymous TL0 profile-field restriction
body: `website_name` is serialized as a normal attribute but is not included in `untrusted_attributes`. For an anonymous viewer of a TL0 user, `website` is correctly omitted by `scope.restrict_user_fields?`, yet the new attribute still derives and returns its hostname (and, for matching domains, its path) from the hidden website value. This exposes information that the existing restriction deliberately withholds. Add `website_name` to the restricted attributes and make its inclusion use the same guard as `website`.

title: The website-name inclusion predicate has the wrong serializer method name
body: The serializer inclusion convention used throughout this class is `include_<attribute>?` (for example `include_email?` and `include_card_image_badge?`), but this method is named `include_website_name` without the trailing `?`. It therefore will not be consulted as the inclusion predicate, so `website_name` can be emitted as `null` for users without a website rather than being omitted as intended. Rename it to `include_website_name?` (and apply the appropriate visibility restriction there).

title: website_name bypasses the existing anonymous TL0 privacy restriction
body: `website` is explicitly listed in `untrusted_attributes`, so an anonymous viewer of a TL0 profile does not receive it. The newly added `website_name` attribute is not subject to that restriction, but is derived directly from the hidden website and can include both its host and path. As a result, anonymous clients receive profile URL information that the serializer intentionally withholds (for example, `example.com/private-profile`) even though `website` itself is absent. Add `website_name` to the same conditional visibility policy as `website` (and ensure its include predicate follows that policy).

title: Sibling hostnames are treated as the same domain using an unsafe label-count heuristic
body: For any two hostnames with more than two labels, this compares everything except the first label. That incorrectly treats unrelated registrable domains under multi-part public suffixes as the same domain: with an instance at `forum.github.io`, a website at `alice.github.io/private` will display `alice.github.io/private`, despite being a different site; the same occurs for hosts under `co.uk` and other public suffixes. The decision to expose the full path should use a public-suffix-aware registrable-domain comparison (or restrict it to exact hostname/known instance-domain relationships), rather than dropping the first DNS label.

title: The website_name inclusion predicate is not named according to serializer convention
body: Serializer conditional methods in this class use the `include_<attribute>?` form (for example, `include_email?` and `include_card_image_badge?`). This method is named `include_website_name` without the trailing `?`, so the serializer will not invoke it as the condition for `:website_name`; profiles without a website can therefore receive a `website_name: null` field instead of omitting it as intended. Rename it to `include_website_name?` and apply the same visibility condition as `website`.

title: Embedded post author link uses inverted lightness values
body: The light-theme branch was changed from `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)` to `70%`, while the dark-theme branch uses `$secondary` at `30%`. This is the inverse of the required dark-theme mapping (30% on primary should become 70% on secondary) and also changes the established light-theme color. Embedded-post author links will become overly faint in light themes and too dark/low-contrast in dark themes.

title: Mobile custom-message counter reverses its intended lightness mapping
body: This rule previously used `$primary` at 70% but now uses `$primary` at 30% and `$secondary` at 70%. The light-theme appearance is therefore changed unexpectedly, and the dark-theme value is the opposite of the complementary mapping used elsewhere (`primary 70%` should map to `secondary 30%`). The message-length counter can be substantially less legible than before, particularly in dark themes.

title: Topic-map heading loses its intended high-contrast lightness
body: The `.topic-map h3` light-theme value was changed from `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%)` to 50%, rather than preserving 20% and adding the complementary dark-theme value `scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 80%)`. This changes the heading color in light themes and makes the dark-theme heading much dimmer than the corresponding desktop topic-map heading.

title: Group member names no longer preserve the original light-theme color
body: `.group-member-info .name` originally used `$primary` at 30%, but this change replaces it with a 50%/50% pair. The correct dark-theme counterpart for the existing 30% primary value is 70% secondary. This both alters the light-theme hierarchy between member names and titles and gives dark themes a weaker/inconsistent name color.

title: Mobile group member names use the wrong dark-theme counterpart
body: The mobile `.group-member-info .name` rule has the same regression as desktop: the previous 30% primary value was replaced by 50% primary / 50% secondary. It should retain 30% for light themes and use 70% secondary for dark themes, otherwise mobile member names lose their intended visual hierarchy and do not match desktop.

title: Category-list notification text remains unadapted for dark themes
body: ` .topic-list.categories .category .badge-notification` still uses `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%)` directly. In a dark color scheme this continues to derive the muted text color from the foreground `$primary` rather than `$secondary`, which is the issue this change set is intended to address. It should use `dark-light-choose(...$primary..., ...$secondary...)` like the other topic-list text rules.

title: Embedded post author links use the wrong lightness in both themes
body: The existing light-theme color was `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)`, but this replacement uses `$primary` at 70% and `$secondary` at 30%. This reverses the intended emphasis rather than merely adding the dark-theme alternative: light themes become substantially lighter, while dark themes receive the value that should correspond to the light theme. Preserve the original primary 30% value and use the matching secondary 70% value for dark themes.

title: Mobile topic-map heading no longer preserves its intended contrast
body: This heading previously used `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%)`. The new `dark-light-choose` expression changes the light-theme branch to 50% and uses 50% for dark themes, instead of retaining primary 20% and selecting the corresponding secondary 80% in dark mode. As a result topic-map headings lose their stronger contrast in light themes and have incorrect contrast in dark themes.

title: Mobile custom-message length hint has inverted theme lightness
body: The original mobile hint color was primary at 70% lightness. The replacement changes it to primary 30% for light themes and secondary 70% for dark themes, the reverse of the required mapping. This makes the hint unexpectedly dark in light themes and too light in dark themes; it should retain primary 70% as the first branch and use secondary 30% as the dark-theme branch.

title: Desktop group member names were changed from the original lightness
body: `.group-member-info .name` originally used primary at 30% lightness, but the new expression uses 50% in both branches. This does not preserve the light-theme rendering and does not provide the corresponding secondary 70% dark-theme color, reducing the intended visual distinction of member names.

title: Mobile group member names were changed from the original lightness
body: The mobile `.group-member-info .name` had a primary 30% color before this change. Replacing it with primary/secondary 50% alters the light-theme color and selects the wrong dark-theme counterpart. It should keep primary 30% for light themes and use secondary 70% for dark themes, matching the intended inverse lightness mapping.

title: Embedded post author link uses the wrong light-theme shade
body: The original author-link color was `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)`, but this changes the light-theme branch to 70% while using 30% for the dark branch. This reverses the intended shades and alters the existing light theme rather than only adding the corresponding dark-theme color. Preserve the 30% primary value and use `scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 70%)` for dark themes.

title: Mobile custom-message length hint reverses the intended theme shades
body: This hint previously used a 70% lightness adjustment of `$primary`, but the new light-theme branch is 30%, so the light-theme appearance regresses. It is also inconsistent with the desktop modal rule for the same hint. The dark-theme alternative should be the complementary `scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 30%)` while retaining `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%)` as the first argument.

title: Mobile topic-map heading no longer preserves its original light-theme color
body: The topic-map `h3` originally used `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%)`; this replacement changes it to 50% in the light branch. Thus the PR modifies light-theme contrast instead of solely providing the dark-theme equivalent, and it no longer matches the desktop topic-map heading. Use primary at 20% and secondary at 80%.

title: Group member name loses its original emphasized color
body: The `.group-member-info .name` color was `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)`, but the change uses 50% for both branches. This makes the name dimmer in light themes and removes its distinction from the title. Retain the 30% primary color and add the complementary 70% secondary color for dark themes.

title: Mobile group member name uses an incorrect lightness mapping
body: This is the mobile counterpart of the group-member name styling and likewise changes the existing primary lightness from 30% to 50%. Consequently light-theme styling regresses and diverges from the intended emphasis. It should choose primary at 30% for light themes and secondary at 70% for dark themes.

title: Pagination creates a phantom page when the member count is an exact multiple of the limit
body: `totalPages` uses `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`, so a group with exactly 50 members and the default limit reports two pages. The Next control is enabled, requests offset 50, and renders an empty member page. The same issue occurs after deleting the sole member on a final partial page when the remaining count becomes an exact multiple. Use a ceiling division (and clamp offsets after a reload) so only pages containing members are reachable.

title: Membership pagination accepts an unbounded client-controlled limit
body: The public members endpoint passes `params[:limit].to_i` directly to ActiveRecord without enforcing a positive maximum. Any user allowed to view a group can request an arbitrarily large limit, causing the server to load and serialize the entire membership in one response; zero or negative values can also produce database-specific invalid/unbounded query behavior. Clamp `limit` to a reasonable maximum and normalize invalid offsets/limits before querying.

title: Automatic-group removal test exercises the wrong HTTP verb
body: The remove-member route added by this change is DELETE `/admin/groups/:group_id/members`, and the client sends DELETE, but this automatic-group test invokes the controller action with PUT. Direct controller action tests do not validate route/verb wiring, so this does not cover the actual request used in production. Change it to DELETE and preferably add a route/request-level assertion for the members endpoint.

title: Pagination computes an extra page for exact page-size member counts
body: `totalPages` uses `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`, which produces one extra page whenever the member count is an exact multiple of the page size. For example, a group with 50 members and a limit of 50 displays page 1/2 and enables Next; clicking it requests offset 50 and displays an empty page. Use a ceiling calculation (for example, `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)`) instead.

title: Public group member pages now silently truncate groups to 50 members
body: The route now calls the paginated `Group#findMembers`, whose default limit is 50, but the public `group/members` template has no pagination controls or mechanism to request later offsets. Consequently, visiting the members page for any group with more than 50 users only shows the first 50 users. Previously non-automatic groups returned their complete membership list (and automatic groups used a 200-member limit). Add public pagination/infinite loading or preserve a complete list for this view.

title: Exact multiples of the page size produce an extra empty page
body: `totalPages` uses `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`, which is one too high whenever `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`. For example, a group with 50 members and a limit of 50 displays two pages; clicking Next requests offset 50 and displays an empty member list. Use a ceiling division (for example `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)`) while retaining the explicit zero-member case.

title: Out-of-order membership requests can replace the currently selected page
body: Every `findMembers` completion unconditionally writes `offset`, `members`, and pagination metadata to the shared group model. A user can click Next and then Previous before the first request returns; if the Previous request completes first and the older Next request completes afterward, the stale Next response overwrites the first-page result and changes the displayed page back to the stale offset. Track/request-cancel the latest fetch (or verify the response offset/request token before applying it) so only the current request updates the model.

title: The existing members endpoint response contract is changed incompatibly
body: `GET /groups/:group_id/members` previously returned a serialized JSON array of users, but now returns an object containing `members` and `meta`. The in-repository Ember consumer was updated, but any other client, plugin, or API integration using this established endpoint will now fail when it attempts to iterate the top-level response. Preserve the array contract or introduce/version a metadata-aware endpoint before changing this response shape.

title: Fallback locale files are not loaded outside ApplicationController requests
body: The fallback backend can only resolve keys from locales whose YAML files have been loaded, but the new fallback locales are explicitly loaded only by ApplicationController#set_locale. Workers, mailers, rake tasks, and any direct I18n.t call do not run that callback; on a fresh process the translation accelerator loads only I18n.locale, then the fallback backend searches the default/en locale before their files have been loaded. As a result, server-side calls can return missing translations instead of falling back, and behavior can vary based on whether an unrelated web request previously loaded those locales. Ensure the complete fallback chain is loaded as part of translation/fallback resolution rather than only in the controller.

title: Changing the site default locale leaves cached fallback translations in the old language
body: The fallback chain now depends dynamically on SiteSetting.default_locale, but the translation accelerator caches no-argument translations using only the requested locale, key, and backend object (lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb lines 71-76). A key requested in a partially translated user locale is cached with the current site-default fallback; after an administrator changes the default locale, the same cache key continues returning the old fallback value until it is evicted or I18n.reload! happens. Invalidate the translation cache when default_locale changes or include the effective fallback configuration in the cache key.

title: Fallback locale files are only loaded for controller requests
body: The new fallback chain depends on `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` to load the site-default and English locale files, but this call is made only from `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Mailers, background jobs, console scripts, and any other non-controller use of `I18n.t` still have the translate accelerator load only `I18n.locale`. When a key is absent in that locale, the fallback backend searches an unloaded fallback locale and returns a missing translation even when the translation exists in its YAML file. The fallback locales need to be loaded as part of the fallback lookup/translation path (or otherwise for every I18n locale context), rather than only during HTTP controller setup.

title: Fallback translations are only loaded for controller requests
body: The lazy translation loader only loads the current locale during `I18n.translate`; a fallback lookup performed by `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` reads the fallback locale directly from the backend and does not invoke `I18n.translate` again. This callback preloads fallback locales only for requests that pass through `ApplicationController`. Mailers, background jobs, model/service code, and any other `I18n.t` call outside that controller will therefore load (for example) `fr` but not the configured site locale or `en`, so missing French strings still resolve as missing translations on a cold process. Fallback locale loading needs to happen as part of translation/fallback resolution rather than only in this controller filter.

title: Translation cache does not include the dynamic fallback chain
body: A no-options translation is cached only by key, current locale, and backend object. The new fallback result also depends on `SiteSetting.default_locale`, which can be changed at runtime, but this change adds no cache invalidation for that setting. After changing the site default locale, keys absent from a user's locale can continue returning the old default locale's cached text until the entry is evicted or I18n is reloaded, producing stale and inconsistent server-rendered translations.

title: Denial-cache key is ambiguous for valid resource and folder UIDs
body: The key concatenates `name` and `parent` with `_` without escaping or length-prefixing them. Since dashboard/folder UIDs can contain underscores, distinct checks such as name `a_b` in parent `c` and name `a` in parent `b_c` produce the same key. A denial cached for the first resource is consulted before permission evaluation and will incorrectly deny the second resource for the full cache TTL, even when it has a direct or inherited grant. Use an unambiguous structured encoding (or hash/length-prefix each component) for cache-key fields.

title: Denial-cache keys collide for valid resource and folder UIDs
body: The key concatenates `name` and `parent` using an unescaped `_` delimiter, so distinct checks can produce the same key when UIDs contain underscores. For example, a denial for name `a_b` in parent `c` has the same key as a denial for name `a` in parent `b_c` for the same namespace, user, and action. Dashboard and folder UIDs may contain underscores, so a cached denial for one resource/folder combination can incorrectly deny access to another combination for the cache TTL. Encode each component unambiguously (for example, length-prefix/JSON/hash structured fields) before constructing the key.

title: Denial-cache hit prevents newly granted permissions from being observed
body: A denial entry is returned before consulting either the permission cache or the database, and there is no invalidation when a role, team membership, or resource permission is granted. Consequently, if a Check is denied just before or during creation of a dashboard/folder or an IAM permission update, subsequent checks for that exact resource remain denied for `shortCacheTTL` (30 seconds), even though the DB would now authorize them. This defeats the new stale-cache fallback for the case it is intended to solve. Either invalidate denial keys on permission/resource changes or do not use a denial entry to bypass the DB recheck for newly mutable permissions.

title: Denial-cache key is ambiguous for UIDs containing underscores
body: The key concatenates `name` and `parent` with an unescaped underscore, so distinct resource/folder pairs can produce the same cache key (for example name `a_b` with parent `c`, and name `a` with parent `b_c`). Since dashboard and folder UIDs can contain underscores, a denial for one pair can incorrectly deny another pair for 30 seconds. Encode the fields unambiguously (for example length-prefixing or structured encoding) before using them in the cache key.

title: Prometheus-only Grafana rule actions are not wired to their handlers
body: GrafanaRuleListItem now renders RuleActionsButtons with only promRule, but the menu can enable Grafana-prometheus abilities. The silence menu item is therefore shown and sets showSilenceDrawer, while the drawer is only rendered when a ruler rule exists on line 104, so clicking Silence notifications does nothing. The same prom-only path also cannot expose Pause because AlertRuleMenu requires rulerRule for its pause item, and cannot expose Delete because its delete item is gated by `canDelete && rulerRule`. As a result, Grafana-managed rules in the list lose these actions after ruler loading was removed even when the user has the corresponding permissions.

title: Federated rules are no longer treated as immutable
body: useAllAlertRuleAbilities previously had access to the CombinedRule group and used isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) to disable mutable actions. It now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, where federation is hard-coded to false. Consequently federated data-source rules can receive enabled edit, delete, pause, restore, and permanent-delete UI actions despite the explicit invariant that federated rules must not be edited or removed. This can expose unsupported or cross-tenant rule mutations to users; retain the group federation check or pass the federation state into the lower-level ability hook.

title: Grafana rule view links no longer preserve the originating list URL
body: The replacement list item constructs its view href without the returnTo parameter. The removed GrafanaRuleListItem used createReturnTo() and supplied it to createRelativeUrl, allowing the view/edit flow to return to the same filtered or paginated rule-list URL. Opening a Grafana rule from the new list now loses that context, so returning from the rule view routes users to the default list rather than their prior search/filter state.

title: Silence action is rendered but cannot open its drawer for Prometheus-only Grafana rules
body: The new list supplies only `promRule` for Grafana-managed rules. `AlertRuleMenu` now correctly enables “Silence notifications” from the Prometheus-rule ability, and clicking it sets `showSilenceDrawer`, but the drawer is rendered only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true. With no `rule`/ruler payload this condition is always false, so the visible silence menu item is a no-op.

title: Delete is unavailable for Grafana rules in the ruler-free list
body: For list entries loaded solely from the Grafana Prometheus endpoint, `canDelete` can be true through `grafanaDeleteAbility`, but the delete item additionally requires `rulerRule`. Since the new `GrafanaRuleListItem` passes no ruler rule, users with delete permission never receive a Delete action. The supplied `handleDelete` already closes over the identifier and does not require the ruler object, so this gate prevents an otherwise authorized operation.

title: Pause capability from the Prometheus rule cannot produce a pause action
body: `canPause` is calculated as an OR of ruler and Grafana Prometheus abilities, but the only rendered pause control still requires a Grafana ruler rule. In the new ruler-free Grafana list, a rule can be reported as pausable from its Prometheus representation while no Pause/Resume menu item is rendered, removing pause control from the list.

title: Skip-token Grafana ability checks grant duplicate support to non-Grafana rules
body: Passing `skipToken` calls `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined)`. That path treats the missing rule as supported (`MaybeSupported` is `AlwaysSupported`) and returns Duplicate allowed based on Grafana rule-create permission. `AlertRuleMenu` invokes this path for non-Grafana Prometheus rules and ORs its result with the source-specific ability, so a user who can create Grafana rules but lacks permission to duplicate an external rule can still be shown the Duplicate action for that external rule. The skip-token path must return unsupported/denied abilities rather than evaluating Grafana permissions for an undefined rule.

title: Federated rules are no longer treated as immutable
body: The previous combined-rule ability calculation could determine federation from the rule group. The refactor passes only the ruler rule and group identifier into `useAllRulerRuleAbilities` and hard-codes `isFederated = false`. Consequently federated external rule groups can now receive update, delete, pause, restore, and permanent-delete capabilities when their permissions otherwise allow them, despite the prior explicit restriction for federated rules.

title: Grafana rule list entries lost their React keys
body: The Grafana branch maps over `rules` without assigning the computed `key` to `GrafanaRuleListItem`, unlike the datasource and unknown branches and unlike the previous `GrafanaRuleLoader` rendering. React will reconcile these entries by position while pages are appended or updated, which can retain action/dropdown component state on the wrong rule and emits missing-key warnings. Pass `key={key}` to this component.

title: Silence menu action cannot open a drawer for Prometheus-only Grafana rules
body: The new list supplies only `promRule`, so `AlertRuleMenu` can expose “Silence notifications” based on `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` and clicking it sets `showSilenceDrawer` to true. However, the drawer is rendered only when a Ruler alerting rule is present (`rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)`), which is false when `rule` is undefined. Consequently the menu item is visible and clickable but produces no UI or action in the alert list.

title: Delete is unavailable for Grafana rules rendered without a Ruler payload
body: Although `canDelete` now includes the Grafana Prometheus-rule ability, the delete menu item still additionally requires `rulerRule`. `GrafanaRuleListItem` only passes a `promRule`, so users with delete permission never see Delete in the new Grafana alert list. The delete handler passed by `RuleActionsButtons` only needs the already computed identifier, so retaining this payload guard removes an existing rule-management operation.

title: Pause action is hidden for Prometheus-only Grafana list entries
body: `canPause` now correctly considers the Grafana Prometheus-rule ability, but rendering the pause item still requires a Grafana Ruler rule. Since the new list intentionally no longer loads or passes that Ruler rule, the pause/unpause operation disappears from the list even for editable Grafana-managed alerting rules. The pause action needs to be migrated to operate from the Prometheus representation/identifier or omitted from the advertised supported abilities.

title: Federated rules are no longer treated as immutable
body: The previous implementation determined federation from `rule.group` via `isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`. This replacement unconditionally sets `isFederated` to false, including when called through `useAllAlertRuleAbilities`, which still receives the complete `CombinedRule`. Federated datasource rules can therefore be presented as editable, deletable, pausable, or restorable when the prior behavior intentionally disabled those operations, risking invalid or unintended changes to federated rule groups.

title: Grafana rule view links no longer preserve the current list location
body: The removed `GrafanaRuleListItem` built its view URL with `createReturnTo()`, allowing the rule view to navigate back to the current filtered/paginated alert list. The replacement creates a bare view URL, so opening a Grafana rule from the list loses the filter/search return target and returns users to the default alerting location instead of their current result set.

title: Filter targets after, not before, template interpolation
body: The code tests `query.expr` before calling `applyTemplateVariables`. A target whose expression is a template variable that resolves to an empty string therefore remains in `queries` and is subsequently classified, partitioned, and sent to Loki as an empty query. Empty expressions are normally intentionally skipped (as the existing `filter((query) => query.expr)` indicates). Interpolate first and then discard targets with an empty interpolated `expr`; the sharding entry point has the same ordering issue.

title: Shard-split requests interpolate the same target repeatedly
body: `runShardSplitQuery` applies template variables here, but every generated shard request is then passed to `runSplitQuery` at line 163, which now calls `applyTemplateVariables` again for every subrequest. This is not a harmless call-count increase: `applyTemplateVariables` also receives `request.filters`, so ad-hoc filters can be added repeatedly to the generated selector, and a template value containing another `$...` sequence can be interpreted on a later pass. The initial interpolation result should be treated as final when delegating to time splitting (or the lower-level split path should accept already-interpolated targets) rather than reapplying interpolation for each shard.

title: Interpolated empty shard targets are executed instead of skipped
body: The expression-presence filter runs before `applyTemplateVariables`. Consequently, a target such as an optional query variable that expands to an empty expression survives the filter and is passed into sharding and ultimately to `runSplitQuery`. This can issue invalid empty Loki queries instead of following the intended empty-query behavior. Apply interpolation before checking `query.expr` and remove targets whose interpolated expression is empty.

title: Shard-split queries apply ad hoc filters twice
body: This interpolates each target with `request.filters` before shard discovery, but every generated shard request is then passed to `runSplitQuery`, which calls `applyTemplateVariables` again with the same `request.filters` (querySplitting.ts:299). `applyTemplateVariables` adds ad hoc filters to the LogQL selector, so shard-split requests end up with duplicated filter matchers (for example `{app="api", env="prod", __stream_shard__=~"...", env="prod"}`). This can produce invalid or unnecessarily different LogQL selectors and prevents equivalent requests from sharing query-cache entries. Interpolate/filter only once for the generated shard target, or distinguish initial template expansion needed for shard discovery from the final filter application.

title: Interpolating before the $__range split guard makes range-variable queries split incorrectly
body: `querySupportsSplitting` intentionally excludes expressions containing range variables because their value must correspond to the unsplit request range. This change applies template variables before that check, so an expression such as `rate({app="api"}[$__range])` becomes a literal duration before `isQueryWithRangeVariable` runs and is no longer recognized as exempt. It will then be split into daily requests while retaining the duration calculated from the original full range, producing incorrect query windows and potentially duplicated or missing metric results. Preserve the pre-interpolation range-variable decision (or carry that metadata through interpolation) before partitioning.

title: Queries that interpolate to an empty expression are no longer filtered out
body: The previous flow interpolated all targets and only then filtered out empty `expr` values. The new flow filters before `applyTemplateVariables`, so a target whose expression is a variable that resolves to an empty string is retained and passed into shard grouping and eventually query execution. This can send an invalid empty LogQL query instead of ignoring it; if it is the only target, it can also create a group where none should exist. Filter the interpolated `queries` collection for `query.expr` after mapping (and apply the same post-interpolation filtering in the time-splitting path).

title: Plugin request completion logs no longer include trace IDs
body: The previous logger middleware explicitly extracted `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` and emitted it as the `traceID` log field. This was removed, while the new contextual logger middleware only adds endpoint, plugin, datasource, and user attributes; it does not add the trace ID. `Logger.FromContext` consumes those contextual log attributes but does not derive a trace ID from the tracing span. Consequently, completed plugin request logs cannot be correlated with their traces anymore. Add the trace ID to the contextual attributes or retain the explicit traceID field, and cover this with a logging middleware test.

title: Plugin completion logs no longer include the trace ID
body: The previous implementation explicitly extracted `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` and added it as the `traceID` log field. That extraction was removed, while the new contextual logger middleware only adds endpoint/plugin/data-source/user fields and does not add a trace ID. `FromContext` is therefore only being used to recover those contextual attributes, so completion logs for traced plugin calls lose the trace-to-log correlation field that was previously emitted. Preserve the explicit trace field or add the trace ID to the contextual attributes, and cover this with a traced-request logging test.

title: Adding FromContext to the exported Logger interface breaks existing implementations
body: `Logger` is an exported interface, and adding a required `FromContext(context.Context)` method is a source-compatible break for every external implementation, wrapper, fake, or mock that previously satisfied it. Those consumers will fail to compile even if they do not need contextual logging. Since this PR is described as a rename/chore, provide a backward-compatible path (for example, keep the original interface and use a separate optional contextual-logger interface/type assertion in the middleware) or explicitly handle the API-versioning/migration impact.

title: Plugin completion logs no longer include the trace ID
body: The previous implementation explicitly extracted `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` and appended it as the `traceID` structured log field. The new contextual logger middleware only adds endpoint/plugin/datasource/user fields, and this call now logs only `logParams` obtained from `FromContext`, so no trace ID is added. As a result, backend plugin request completion logs cannot be correlated with traces anymore, regressing the existing observability contract. Add the trace ID to the contextual attributes or retain it in `logParams`.

title: Adding FromContext to the exported Logger interface breaks downstream implementations
body: `Logger` is an exported interface, and adding a required `FromContext(context.Context)` method means every existing custom implementation outside this change no longer satisfies it and will fail to compile when upgrading. This is a source-incompatible API change in addition to the middleware rename. Preserve compatibility by using a separate optional contextual-logger interface/type assertion at the call site, or provide an adapter/migration path rather than extending the existing interface.

title: Cache entries are retained when device-limit admission fails
body: `tagDeviceUI` adds the device ID to the local cache before calling `CreateOrUpdateDevice`, but does not remove it when that call returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. The first request from a new device at capacity is rejected, but its ID remains cached for 29 minutes; a retry then exits at the cache hit on line 83 without checking the store and authentication succeeds. This makes the configured device limit bypassable after one failed attempt per device ID.

title: Device-limit check and insertion are not atomic
body: The active-device count is read in one database session and the subsequent insert/upsert is performed later in another session. Multiple requests for distinct devices can all observe a count below `deviceLimit` and then all insert successfully, exceeding the configured limit. The limit needs to be enforced transactionally/with suitable locking or a database-side admission mechanism; the current count-then-insert sequence is inherently racy under concurrent anonymous requests.

title: Anonymous clients can bypass the limit by omitting the device header
body: Authentication only rejects when `TagDevice` returns the limit error, but `TagDevice` returns success without recording anything when `X-Grafana-Device-Id` is absent. Since this header is entirely supplied by the anonymous client, requests without it are authenticated even after the configured limit has been reached. A device cap intended to restrict anonymous access cannot be enforced through an optional client-controlled identifier.

title: Rejected devices are cached before the device-limit decision succeeds
body: `tagDeviceUI` inserts the device ID into the local cache before `CreateOrUpdateDevice` checks/enforces the limit. For a new device at capacity, the first authentication attempt correctly receives `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, but the cache entry remains. A subsequent request from the same device ID hits lines 83-85 and returns success without contacting the store, so `Authenticate` admits it. This bypasses the configured limit for the cache lifetime (29 minutes) and can be repeated whenever the entry expires. Only cache the ID after the database operation has succeeded, or remove the cache entry when it returns an error.

title: The count-and-insert limit check is not atomic
body: Each request independently counts active devices and then, if the count is below the limit, performs an upsert in a later database session. Concurrent requests for different new device IDs can all observe the same count below `deviceLimit` and all insert successfully, permanently exceeding the configured limit. Enforce the admission decision atomically, for example with a transaction and appropriate locking/serialization or a database-side conditional operation.

title: An existing device can be rejected when MySQL reports a no-op update
body: At capacity, existing devices are admitted by `updateDevice`, but it treats `RowsAffected() == 0` as proof that the device does not exist. MySQL normally reports zero affected rows when all assigned values are unchanged. In particular, Grafana already documents MySQL timestamp precision as seconds, so a request routed to another instance/restart in the same second with the same IP and user agent can assign the same stored `updated_at` value and be falsely returned as `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. This denies a device that should be allowed to refresh its existing record. Determine existence separately or use an update/result mode that distinguishes a matched row from a changed row.

title: Rejected devices are cached and allowed on their next request
body: `tagDeviceUI` adds the device ID to the local cache before calling `CreateOrUpdateDevice`. When that call returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, this new return rejects the current authentication, but the cache entry remains. A subsequent request from the same new device ID hits the cache and returns success without consulting the store, so `Authenticate` creates an anonymous identity despite the configured limit. Since the cache default TTL is 29 minutes, a device can bypass the limit simply by retrying after its first rejected request. Only cache the ID after a successful store update, or evict it when tagging fails.

title: Count-then-insert does not enforce the limit under concurrent requests
body: The limit check performs `CountDevices` in one database session and then performs the insert/upsert in a separate session. Multiple concurrent requests for distinct device IDs can all observe a count below `deviceLimit` and all insert successfully, exceeding the configured limit. This also occurs across Grafana instances sharing the same database. The check and admission need to be made atomic, for example with a transaction and suitable locking or a database-side conditional/admission mechanism.

title: The independent max-count test has an impossible affected-row expectation
body: Each table-driven subtest now creates and cleans up its own annotations, but this case creates 9 annotations with MaxCount=3 and still expects zero affected annotations. The cleanup should delete 6 rows in this isolated subtest, so the assertion at line 135 will fail (or, if altered to pass, no longer tests the intended second invocation behavior). Preserve state across two cleanup invocations in this case, or change the expected result and add a real repeat-run test.

title: The change increases the frequency of every cleanup job by 10x
body: Changing the shared cleanup ticker from 10 minutes to 1 minute does not only affect annotation cleanup: it also runs temporary-file cleanup, snapshot/version/image deletion, invite expiry, short-URL deletion, and query-history retention/enforcement ten times as often. These jobs include potentially expensive database scans/deletes and filesystem operations, so this materially increases background load and changes their established scheduling behavior. Keep the existing global interval or schedule only the annotation cleanup at the higher frequency if that is required.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors with the full ID list
body: Every successful batch emits an Error-level log entry containing the complete slice of selected IDs, and the corresponding completion entry does the same for each cleanup path. Batch size is configurable and the new test explicitly uses 32,767 IDs, so this can generate very large error log records and substantial logging overhead on normal cleanup runs, while also making monitoring report failures despite err being nil. Log only counts at Debug/Info level (and reserve Error for actual failures).

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors and include entire ID lists
body: The new cleanup path emits `Error` logs even when `fetchIDs` and deletion succeeded (`err` is nil), including for the terminating empty batch. It also attaches every selected ID to the log entry. With the configured batch size this can serialize and write tens of thousands of IDs per batch (the added test explicitly uses 32,767), producing very large error logs, false error alerts, and avoidable CPU/I/O on every cleanup run. Use an appropriate non-error level and log a bounded summary such as count (and only log the actual error when present). The equivalent calls in `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` have the same issue.

title: The unrelated ticker change runs every cleanup job ten times more often
body: Changing the cleanup ticker from ten minutes to one minute affects all jobs in `clean`, not only annotation cleanup: snapshot/version/image deletion, invite expiration, short-URL cleanup, and query-history retention and row-limit enforcement will now execute up to ten times as often. This can substantially increase database and filesystem load, and long-running cleanup cycles can become nearly continuous because another tick is already pending when a cycle completes. The PR does not scope or justify this behavioral change; retain the existing interval or make any desired annotation-specific scheduling change separately.

title: The new per-ID delete can exceed supported parameter counts on non-SQLite databases
body: `deleteByIDs` creates one bound parameter for every selected ID except for SQLite. `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` is configurable and the added test explicitly exercises 32,767 IDs; this exceeds SQL Server's 2,100-parameter limit (and sufficiently large configured values can exceed limits on other supported dialects). The previous DELETE used no per-ID bind list, so such configurations worked. On those deployments cleanup will fail each batch and old annotations/tags will accumulate. Split the delete into dialect-safe chunks or apply the same safe literal/chunking strategy for every dialect with a parameter limit.

title: Cleanup scheduling is changed from every ten minutes to every minute for all cleanup jobs
body: This unrelated change makes the entire cleanup suite run ten times as often, not just annotation cleanup. It increases database scans/deletes and filesystem work for snapshots, dashboard versions, images, short URLs, query history, and annotations, and can cause a long-running cleanup to be re-run immediately after it completes because the ticker has already fired. There is no corresponding configuration or PR rationale for this broad scheduling change; retain the ten-minute interval unless this load increase is explicitly intended and validated.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors and dump every selected ID
body: Every batch logs at Error level before and after deletion even when `err` is nil, and includes the complete `ids` slice. A configured large batch (the added test uses 32,767 IDs) produces very large error log entries for normal operation, pollutes error monitoring, and can materially increase logging/storage load during cleanup. Log only actual errors at Error level and use a non-error level with counts rather than the full ID list for successful batches.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request cancellation context
body: The goroutine derives its timeout context from `ctx`, which is the HTTP/API request context. That context is normally canceled as soon as the handler returns the successful unified-storage response, so the asynchronously scheduled legacy `Create` can be canceled before or during execution. The same pattern is used for Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection (lines 110, 135, and 163). This makes the intended legacy safety copy unreliable in normal request handling. Derive the background replication context with `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (while retaining relevant values) before applying the timeout.

title: Independent replication goroutines can apply writes to legacy out of order
body: Each successful unified write starts an independent goroutine, with no per-resource serialization or ordering. For example, a client can create an object and immediately update or delete it; the legacy update/delete goroutine may run before the legacy create goroutine, causing the update/delete to fail and then leaving the subsequently created legacy object stale. The same issue applies to successive updates. Since errors are ignored, this can permanently leave legacy storage inconsistent even though all unified writes succeeded. Replication needs ordered processing (at least per object/collection) or a mechanism to reconcile/retry failed operations.

title: Update recomputes the request's updated object separately for legacy storage
body: After `Storage.Update` has consumed `objInfo`, the async legacy update receives the original `objInfo` again rather than a wrapper around the object produced by unified storage. `UpdatedObjectInfo.UpdatedObject` can be stateful or depend on the old object (notably patch/apply semantics, generated fields, and managed fields), so it is now evaluated twice against potentially different old objects. Consequently unified and legacy can receive different updates, or the second evaluation can fail. The previous implementation computed the updated object once and passed an `updateWrapper` containing that result to both stores; preserve that single computed result for the legacy replication.

title: Several mode-3 metrics are recorded against the wrong backend or label
body: A unified-storage Create failure is recorded with `recordLegacyDuration` here, and the equivalent Update failure does the same at line 129, so storage failures are attributed to legacy. Delete success at line 106 uses `name` as the kind label rather than `options.Kind`, creating unbounded/high-cardinality per-object metric labels. DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine at line 166 calls `recordStorageDuration`, so legacy replication duration/errors are reported as storage metrics. These errors make the new mode's operational telemetry misleading and can create excessive metric cardinality.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request cancellation context
body: The goroutine derives its 10-second context from the original request context. HTTP/API-server request contexts are normally canceled as soon as the handler returns, which happens immediately after this goroutine is started, so the legacy Create will usually receive an already-canceled context rather than up to 10 seconds to complete. The same pattern is used by Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection (lines 110, 135, and 163), making the asynchronous replication unreliable or effectively skipped for normal completed requests. Detach cancellation (while preserving required context values/logging) before applying the timeout.

title: Independent replication goroutines can apply mutations out of order
body: Each successful write starts an independent goroutine with no per-resource ordering or serialization. For example, a successful unified Create followed immediately by Delete can run the legacy Delete first and the legacy Create second, leaving an object in legacy that no longer exists in unified storage. Consecutive updates can similarly overwrite newer legacy state with an older update. Since legacy APIs remain available as the stated safety measure, this produces persistent cross-store divergence; replication needs an ordered queue/keyed serialization or another ordering mechanism.

title: Legacy Update re-executes the original UpdatedObjectInfo instead of replaying the unified result
body: After Storage.Update has already evaluated objInfo against the unified object, the asynchronous legacy update receives the original objInfo and evaluates it again against legacy state. This regresses the prior implementation, which evaluated the update once and wrapped the resulting object for each store. UpdatedObjectInfo can represent a PATCH/apply operation and can depend on the old object, resource version, managed fields, or request-specific state; evaluating it again can yield a different object or fail due to the legacy object's version. As a result, successful unified updates may not be mirrored correctly to legacy. Capture and replay the object produced by the unified update (using an appropriate wrapper) rather than reusing objInfo.

title: Delete metrics use object names as the kind label
body: The successful Delete metric passes `name` where the metric helper's kind/resource label is expected, unlike the error path and all other methods which pass `options.Kind`. Every distinct object name will create a separate Prometheus time series, causing unbounded metric cardinality on deletes and making the kind dimension incorrect. Pass `options.Kind` here.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection duration is recorded as a storage duration
body: The asynchronous legacy DeleteCollection call records its result through `recordStorageDuration`, so storage metrics are double-counted and no legacy duration/error metric is emitted for this operation. This makes monitoring of replication failures and latency inaccurate; call `recordLegacyDuration` instead.

title: Create storage failures are attributed to legacy metrics
body: When Storage.Create fails, the code calls `recordLegacyDuration` rather than `recordStorageDuration`. The analogous Update error path at line 129 has the same issue. Storage write failures in mode 3 will therefore be missing from storage error metrics and falsely inflate legacy errors, obscuring which backend failed.

title: Mode 3 tests do not verify asynchronous legacy replication
body: The tests return immediately after the unified operation and never wait for or assert the background legacy call. Moreover, both `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` share one testify Mock and define identical method expectations, so an expectation configured as a storage call can also satisfy the legacy call; there is no `AssertExpectations` call to establish that either occurred. Consequently these tests would pass if replication never runs (including when the caller context is canceled), and they do not detect the ordering or Update replay regressions. Use distinct backend mocks and synchronization (for example a channel/WaitGroup) to assert the legacy call and its arguments.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request cancellation context
body: The goroutine derives its timeout context from the request context. Once the API handler returns its successful unified-storage response, Kubernetes/Grafana can cancel that request context, which immediately cancels the legacy Create call (and the same pattern is used for Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection). Consequently, many or all best-effort legacy writes can be aborted before they run, especially under normal request teardown. Derive the async context from a cancellation-detached context (while preserving required values) and apply the 10-second timeout to that context.

title: Independent async goroutines can apply legacy mutations out of order
body: Each successful unified write launches an independent goroutine, with no per-resource serialization or ordering. For example, a create followed immediately by an update or delete can execute in legacy as update/delete before create, or create after delete, leaving legacy with a stale or incorrect object even though unified storage is correct. Since mode 3 is intended to retain legacy as a safe copy, writes need an ordered queue/worker mechanism (at least per resource) rather than unconstrained concurrent goroutines.

title: Legacy update recomputes the update instead of mirroring the unified result
body: The legacy async call receives the original UpdatedObjectInfo after Storage.Update has completed. UpdatedObjectInfo is evaluated against the store's current/old object, so evaluating it again against potentially stale legacy state can generate a different payload, apply a stale resource version, or fail differently. The previous implementation explicitly evaluated the update and wrapped the unified result before passing it to legacy, ensuring both stores received the same object. Preserve that behavior by passing a wrapper containing the successful unified result to the legacy write.

title: Legacy outages can create an unbounded number of blocked goroutines
body: Every successful write creates a new goroutine that may remain blocked for up to ten seconds (or longer if a legacy implementation does not honor context cancellation). There is no queue capacity, worker limit, or backpressure. During a legacy outage and sustained write traffic this grows goroutine count and outstanding requests proportionally to traffic, risking memory exhaustion and scheduler degradation in the API server. Use bounded workers/queueing and define an overflow policy.

title: Delete metric uses resource name as the kind label
body: The successful delete metric passes `name` where all other calls pass `options.Kind`. Object names are effectively unbounded and often user-controlled, so each deleted object creates a distinct Prometheus label value/time series that is never reclaimed by the metric vector. This can cause unbounded metric memory/cardinality growth. Pass `options.Kind` instead.

title: Unified-storage failures are recorded as legacy durations
body: When Storage.Create fails, the code calls recordLegacyDuration using the unified-storage timing even though no legacy write was attempted. The same error exists in Update at line 129, and DeleteCollection records the async legacy duration as storage duration at line 166. This makes backend/error metrics and alerts report the wrong failing system; use recordStorageDuration for unified operations and recordLegacyDuration for the async legacy operation.

title: Mode 3 tests do not actually verify asynchronous legacy mirroring
body: Both the legacy and unified mock wrappers share one mock and use the same method names and argument matchers. For example, the legacy Create expectation at line 31 also matches the unified Storage.Create invocation, so the tests cannot identify which backend was called; the storage-failure case similarly configures only a purported legacy expectation. The tests also neither wait for the goroutine nor assert mock expectations. As a result, they pass without proving that legacy writes happen asynchronously, are skipped after unified failure, or receive the expected payload. Use separate mocks (or backend-identifying expectations), synchronize completion, and assert expectations.

title: Recheck the cache after acquiring the write lock
body: Requests that arrive while the cache is empty all pass the initial read-lock check before the first request publishes a value. They then serialize on this write lock, but every waiter unconditionally rereads and reparses the manifest instead of using the value populated by the first request. A burst of startup requests therefore causes O(n) sequential filesystem reads/parses and delays each request. After acquiring the write lock, check `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` again and return the cached value before performing I/O.

title: Concurrent cold-cache callers all reload the manifest serially
body: The cache is checked before acquiring the write lock, but it is not checked again after the lock is acquired. If several non-dev requests arrive while the cache is empty, each observes `nil`, waits for the previous caller to finish reading/parsing the manifest, and then performs its own file/CDN load while holding the exclusive lock. This turns one initialization load into one serialized load per concurrent request and blocks cache readers for the duration of each load. Recheck `entryPointAssetsCache` after acquiring the lock (for non-dev mode) and return it if another goroutine populated it.

title: No regression test verifies SQL expressions are rejected with the feature flag enabled
body: This change is the security boundary that disables SQL expressions, but no test is added for `ReadQuery` receiving `QueryTypeSQL` while `FlagSqlExpressions` is enabled. The implementation intentionally returns false regardless of toggle state; without a test covering the enabled-toggle case, a future cleanup that restores the usual feature-toggle logic could silently re-enable the vulnerable SQL execution path.

title: No automated regression test verifies SQL expressions remain disabled
body: This security fix adds no test covering the SQL query type with `sqlExpressions` both enabled and disabled. The behavior is intentionally independent of the feature toggle, so a regression that restores parsing/execution when the toggle is enabled would reintroduce the RCE/LFI attack surface without being caught by the test suite. Add a reader/query execution test that asserts SQL expressions are rejected for both feature-toggle states.

title: No automated regression test verifies SQL expressions remain disabled
body: This security-sensitive behavior is implemented without accompanying tests. Add coverage that submits a QueryTypeSQL expression with FlagSqlExpressions both enabled and disabled and asserts that it is rejected, plus coverage for the legacy SQL command construction path if it remains reachable. Without this, a future refactor of the feature-toggle logic or command wiring can silently re-enable SQL execution and reintroduce the RCE/LFI exposure.

title: Concurrent builds for the same namespace/resource are no longer serialized
body: Moving the cache lock to only the final map assignment permits two callers that both observe a cache miss to build the same key concurrently. There is no per-key singleflight in `getOrCreateIndex`. For file-backed indexes, concurrent `bleve.New` calls target the same directory and one build can fail; for memory-backed indexes, whichever build finishes last overwrites the cache regardless of which snapshot is newer, potentially discarding indexed documents or writes incorporated by the other build. Retain keyed build coordination (and recheck the cache after acquiring it) while allowing unrelated keys to build concurrently.

title: Bleve build span context is still not propagated to the index builder
body: `BuildIndex` starts a span but discards the returned context. The supplied `builder` callback performs the list/index work using the caller's context, so that work is not a descendant of `unified_search.bleve.BuildIndex`. This leaves the trace propagation fix incomplete for the Bleve build path; assign the returned context and invoke downstream work with it.

title: The storage-server integration test is disabled for all PostgreSQL runs
body: This change unconditionally skips the test whenever `GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres`, including CI environments. PostgreSQL is a supported non-SQLite storage-server backend, so the startup behavior changed by this PR will no longer have integration coverage there. Fix the test/environment issue rather than permanently skipping that backend.

title: Watcher goroutine panics when its backend event stream is closed
body: `initWatcher` receives from `events` without checking the receive `ok` value and immediately dereferences `v`. When the backend is stopped, the SQL backend closes its event stream; receiving from that closed channel returns a nil `*WrittenEvent`, so `v.Type` panics (and subsequent loop iterations would continue receiving nil). Eager initialization now guarantees this watcher is started for every ResourceServer, including servers that never receive an RPC, so normal shutdown can crash the process. Exit the goroutine when the channel is closed and also honor `s.ctx.Done()` while sending to `out`.

title: Per-key index builds can now concurrently create the same Bleve index
body: Moving the cache lock to only the final map assignment permits two callers that both observed a missing index to execute `BuildIndex` for the same `NamespacedResource` concurrently. For file-backed indexes they both call `bleve.New` on the same directory, which can fail due to Bleve's directory lock; for memory-backed indexes, both callers can receive distinct indexes and the last assignment silently replaces the cache entry, leaving one caller searching an index that will no longer receive watch updates. The previous broad lock at least prevented simultaneous directory creation. Use a per-resource singleflight/keyed lock and recheck the cache before creating and publishing an index.

title: Search index watch goroutine also dereferences nil after stream closure
body: The search initialization goroutine reads `v := <-events` forever and passes it to `handleEvent` without checking whether the event channel was closed. On backend shutdown, `WatchWriteEvents` closes the SQL stream, after which `v` is nil and `handleEvent` dereferences `evt.Type`, causing a panic.
