During rebalances or shutdowns with a timeout, orphaned workers can continue polling and producing buffered segments while a replacement strategy is started, leading to duplicate producers and leaked Redis/Kafka connections. The timeout should stop waiting for each remaining worker but still terminate/clean up every worker.

title: Negative --flusher-processes values crash strategy construction
body: The new CLI option accepts any integer, but a negative `max_processes` is truthy and produces a negative `num_processes`. The process map is then empty, and assigning the first shard at line 66 raises a KeyError because `i % self.num_processes` has no corresponding map entry. An invalid deployment argument can therefore prevent the consumer from starting. Validate that the option is positive before constructing the map (and define or reject zero explicitly, rather than silently treating it as the default).

title: The new process-limit test does not exercise multiprocessing
body: Passing `produce_to_pipe=messages.append` makes `SpanFlusher` create `threading.Thread` workers instead of spawned processes. Consequently this test only checks the in-memory shard mapping and cannot detect failures in the new production path, including spawn-time serialization/initialization, per-process Redis access, worker shutdown, or producer behavior. Add a test that runs without `produce_to_pipe` and mocks the producer at a process-safe boundary, or otherwise explicitly tests the spawned-worker path.

title: Validate the flusher process count as a positive integer
body: `--flusher-processes` accepts zero and negative values. Zero is silently converted to the number of assigned shards by `max_processes or len(...)`, violating the documented maximum, while a negative value reaches `range(self.num_processes)` with a negative count and then raises `KeyError` when shard assignment indexes a nonexistent process entry. A bad deployment/config value can therefore either unexpectedly spawn one worker per shard or prevent the span consumer from starting. Use a Click integer range with a minimum of 1 (and defensively validate the constructor argument).

title: The new flusher-process test never exercises multiprocessing
body: Supplying `produce_to_pipe=messages.append` intentionally makes `SpanFlusher` create `threading.Thread` workers rather than spawned processes. This test only verifies the in-memory shard-to-worker mapping; it cannot catch failures in the production path such as spawning, pickling `SpansBuffer`/synchronization values, Sentry initialization, or process lifecycle behavior. Add an integration-style test that uses the normal producer setup (mocking Kafka as needed) and verifies multiple spawned workers can flush assigned shards.

title: The process-spans command still defaults the flusher to one worker
body: `flusher_processes` is always supplied by Click with a default of `1`, so `ProcessSpansStrategyFactory` passes `max_processes=1` and `SpanFlusher` assigns every Redis shard to a single flusher process. Consequently, normal `process-spans` deployments do not get the per-shard parallelism described by this change unless every deployment is separately updated to pass `--flusher-processes`; the new multiprocess flusher provides no throughput scaling by default. Default this option to the shard-derived behavior (for example `None`) or update the deployment configuration as part of this change.

title: Negative flusher process counts are accepted and crash flusher initialization
body: The new option uses `type=int` without a positive lower bound. Passing `--flusher-processes=-1` reaches `SpanFlusher`, which computes a negative `num_processes`, creates no entries in `process_to_shards_map`, and then raises a `KeyError` while assigning the first shard. This turns an invalid command-line value into an unhelpful consumer startup crash. Validate this option as an integer greater than zero (and define the intended behavior for zero).

title: The queue shutdown API is unavailable on supported Python versions
body: `queue.ShutDown` and `Queue.shutdown()` were introduced in Python 3.13. On earlier supported Python versions, an exception raised by `result_processor` causes evaluation of `queue.ShutDown` in this handler to raise `AttributeError`, terminating the worker thread; and shutdown cannot wake workers blocked in `Queue.get()` because `q.shutdown()` raises `AttributeError` and is only logged. This makes the new mode leave daemon workers behind on shutdown and permanently stop processing a queue after its first processing exception. Use a version-compatible sentinel/wakeup mechanism (or require and enforce Python 3.13) instead.

title: Failed result processing is acknowledged and committed
body: The worker catches every exception from `result_processor` but unconditionally calls `complete_offset` in `finally`. The commit thread will then advance the Kafka offset past the failed message, so transient database/API failures lose the result instead of allowing it to be retried. This also contradicts the strategy's stated guarantee that offsets are committed only after successful processing. Only complete an offset after a successful processor return, or explicitly route failures through the consumer's retry/DLQ policy.

title: Worker queues are unbounded, so slow processing has no backpressure
body: Each queue is created with `queue.Queue()` without a `maxsize`. Consequently the Kafka consumer can continue accepting records while a slow queue is backlogged, accumulating an unbounded number of decoded messages and retained payloads in memory. Under the slow-item condition this feature is intended to handle, this can exhaust process memory rather than applying the documented natural backpressure. Configure a bounded queue size and integrate full-queue behavior with upstream polling/backpressure.

title: Invalid negative max-workers silently drops every queued message
body: The CLI accepts arbitrary integers for `--max-workers`, and a negative value is truthy here, so `FixedQueuePool` is created with zero queues. Every subsequent submit then raises a modulo-by-zero error in `get_queue_for_group`; `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` catches that error and marks the Kafka offset complete, causing all messages to be committed without processing. Validate `max_workers > 0` before constructing the pool (and do not silently substitute 20 for an explicitly supplied zero value).

title: Uses Queue shutdown APIs unavailable on supported Python versions
body: `queue.Queue.shutdown()` and `queue.ShutDown` were introduced in Python 3.13. On earlier supported runtimes, `shutdown()` raises `AttributeError` (which is only logged here), leaving idle worker threads permanently blocked in `get()`. Moreover, if a worker handles any exception, evaluating `except queue.ShutDown` at line 142 also raises `AttributeError`, terminating that worker. Use a version-compatible sentinel/condition-based shutdown mechanism, or explicitly require Python 3.13 everywhere this consumer can run.

title: Queue pool has no backpressure and can grow without bound
body: Each work queue is created with the default unbounded `queue.Queue()`, so `submit()` at line 212 never blocks when a worker or a particular queue is slow. The Kafka consumer can therefore continue accepting messages indefinitely while work accumulates in memory, eventually causing an OOM rather than applying the documented “natural backpressure when queues fill up.” Configure a bounded queue size and ensure the processing strategy/poll loop handles a full queue safely.

title: Graceful shutdown abandons queued work instead of draining it
body: `shutdown()` sets every worker's `shutdown` flag before requesting queue shutdown. A worker that finishes its current item exits on the next loop condition even when its queue still contains items, so queued offsets remain outstanding and work is not processed. `join()` then invokes this shutdown path as well, despite its expected role of waiting for in-flight work. This causes processed-but-uncommitted or partially processed results to be replayed after a normal consumer shutdown, risking duplicate side effects; drain queues before stopping workers and perform a final commit of completed offsets.

title: Processing failures are acknowledged and committed
body: The worker catches every exception from `result_processor` but unconditionally calls `complete_offset` in `finally`. The commit loop will then advance the Kafka offset past a failed result, permanently dropping it instead of retrying or routing it through the consumer's failure handling. This also contradicts the strategy's stated guarantee that offsets are committed only after successful processing. Only mark an offset complete after success, or explicitly route failures to an appropriate retry/DLQ path.

title: The work queues are unbounded, so slow processing provides no backpressure
body: `queue.Queue()` is created without a `maxsize`, and `submit` uses a non-blocking-in-practice unbounded `put`. Therefore the Kafka strategy can continue polling and enqueueing indefinitely while one or more result processors are slow or unavailable. The stated natural backpressure never occurs; memory usage grows with the Kafka backlog and can OOM the consumer during a downstream outage. Use a bounded queue and make submission block or otherwise integrate its capacity with the processing strategy's backpressure mechanism.

title: Processing failures are acknowledged and committed as successful
body: The worker calls `complete_offset` in `finally`, including when `result_processor` raises. The exception is only logged, so the commit loop can advance the Kafka offset past a result that was not processed. This permanently drops the failed result instead of allowing Kafka retry/DLQ behavior, and contradicts the strategy's stated guarantee that offsets are committed only after successful processing. Only complete an offset after successful processing, with an explicit policy for failures.

title: Queue shutdown uses APIs unavailable on supported pre-3.13 Python runtimes
body: `Queue.shutdown()` and `queue.ShutDown` were introduced in Python 3.13. On earlier Python versions, `q.shutdown(...)` raises `AttributeError`, which is caught and logged, leaving workers blocked in `get`; each subsequent `join(timeout=5)` waits out its timeout. Normal consumer shutdown consequently leaks daemon worker threads and can stall shutdown for five seconds per queue. Use a sentinel-based shutdown or a compatibility mechanism unless the project runtime is explicitly Python 3.13+.

title: The advertised graceful shutdown abandons queued work and stops commits before in-flight work finishes
body: `shutdown` immediately sets every worker's `shutdown` flag, so each worker exits after at most its currently active item rather than draining its queue. In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close`, the commit thread is stopped before this worker shutdown, so even an item that finishes during shutdown is not recorded as committed. A normal processor close can therefore abandon queued messages and replay already-processed in-flight messages after restart. Drain workers first (or explicitly terminate), then perform a final offset commit before stopping the commit loop.

title: A backup code can be used without verifying the primary credential
body: The new backup-code branch authenticates whenever a supplied backup code matches, but password verification above is skipped whenever `credentials.totpCode` is non-empty (line 121), regardless of whether that TOTP value is valid. A caller can post an email, any dummy `totpCode`, and a valid backup code directly to the credentials callback and obtain a session without the password (and can similarly bypass the identity-provider checks guarded by `!credentials.totpCode`). The UI preserves the password during the normal two-step flow, but the server must enforce this invariant itself. Require a verified primary credential before accepting either TOTP or a backup code, or use a server-bound challenge indicating that the first step was completed.

title: Backup-code consumption is not atomic, allowing reuse under concurrent logins
body: Each authorization request reads and decrypts the entire backup-code array, marks its matching entry as null locally, and then writes the full array back. Two concurrent requests using the same code can both read the original array, both validate it, and both successfully create sessions before either write occurs. Concurrent requests using different codes can also overwrite each other's consumption, restoring a code that another request already used. Consume the code with an atomic conditional database update/version check (or store individually hashed backup codes with a uniqueness/used-state condition) so only one request can claim a code.

title: The added E2E coverage does not exercise backup-code authentication or consumption
body: The test only checks that generated codes can be downloaded and copied; it never logs out and signs in with a backup code, checks an invalid code is rejected, or verifies that a successfully used code cannot be reused. Those are the feature's security-critical paths, including the new credentials-provider mutation logic, and the TODO explicitly acknowledges the omission. Add end-to-end or integration coverage for valid login, invalid login, single-use behavior, and backup-code-based 2FA disablement.

title: Backup-code consumption is not atomic, allowing code reuse under concurrent logins
body: The code reads and decrypts the complete backup-code list, validates a code, and then writes a modified copy without any conditional update, transaction isolation, or version check. Two concurrent credential requests using the same code can both read the pre-consumption list and both authenticate successfully; requests using different codes can also overwrite each other's update and restore a previously consumed code. This violates the advertised one-time-use property of backup codes and can result in multiple successful sessions from a single stolen code. Consume the code with an atomic/optimistic conditional update (or store individually hashed codes with a uniqueness/consumption state) and reject a request whose stored state changed before its update.

title: The new backup-code authentication and one-time-use behavior is not tested
body: The added tests only exercise displaying the backup-code screen and downloading/copying its UI. They never authenticate with a generated backup code, verify that a valid code works, verify rejection of an invalid code, or verify that a successfully used code cannot be reused; disabling 2FA with a backup code is also untested. These are the core security-sensitive paths introduced by this PR, so regressions such as failing backup login or non-consuming codes will ship undetected.

title: Backup-code login can bypass the account password
body: The password check is skipped whenever `credentials.totpCode` is nonempty (line 121), but the new backup-code branch takes precedence and does not validate that TOTP value at all. A request to the credentials callback containing an email, any arbitrary nonempty `totpCode`, and a valid `backupCode` therefore authenticates without the password. Backup codes are presented by the UI as a replacement for the authenticator after the primary login, not as passwordless credentials; this permits anyone with a copied/stolen backup code to sign in directly. Verify the primary credential independently of the selected second-factor method, or use a server-side first-factor challenge state before accepting either TOTP or a backup code.

title: Backup codes are not consumed atomically
body: The code is validated from a previously read `user.backupCodes` value and then consumed with an unconditional `prisma.user.update`. Two concurrent login requests using the same backup code can both decrypt and find the code before either update completes; both requests then succeed and write an equivalent array with that entry set to null. This violates the advertised single-use guarantee and can yield multiple authenticated sessions from one recovery code. Consume the code with an atomic compare-and-set/transactional update that predicates on the current encrypted value (or store individual hashed codes with a unique/conditional consumed state), and reject the request when that update affects no row.

title: Google Meet fallback dereferences a missing destination calendar
body: `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined` when an event has no destination calendar, but the condition immediately reads `.integration`. Any booking using Google Meet without a configured destination calendar will throw before the fallback to Cal Video can run (and under strict TypeScript this is also an unsafe possibly-undefined access). Guard the value with optional chaining or an explicit existence check.

title: Collective hosts' calendars are discarded when the primary host has none
body: The event starts with `destinationCalendar: null` when neither the event type nor `organizerUser` has a destination calendar. The collective-host calendars collected in `teamDestinationCalendars` are then added with `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...)`, which is a no-op for `null`. Consequently, a collective booking where only a non-primary host has a calendar integration creates no calendar event for that host, despite that being the scenario this change is intended to support. Initialize the array from the team calendars when there is no primary destination.

title: The selected destination external ID is never passed to calendar creation
body: `createEvent` accepts `externalId` and records it in the returned reference, but calls the calendar implementation with only `credential.id`. `EventManager` invokes this once for every destination calendar, all using the same full `calEvent.destinationCalendar` array. Integrations that choose the first destination (for example Office 365, Lark, and CalDAV) will therefore create every host's event in the first host's calendar; Google also cannot distinguish two selected calendars using the same credential because it finds the first matching credential. Pass the target external ID through the calendar creation contract and have each implementation use it.

title: Recurring cancellation only deletes the first calendar reference for each occurrence
body: For each calendar reference of the original booking, the recurring cancellation loop obtains `updBooking.references.find(...)`, which always selects only the first calendar reference of each recurring occurrence. With multiple host calendar references, the additional references are never selected for deletion; the loop instead repeatedly attempts deletion of the first event, including through unrelated credentials. This leaves cancelled recurring events on secondary hosts' calendars. Match each occurrence's reference by credential ID/external calendar ID and delete it using that reference's credential.

title: Rescheduling deletes multi-host calendar events with the wrong credential
body: The credential lookup map is keyed only by integration type, so multiple credentials for the same provider overwrite one another. The subsequent deletion iterates all booking references but retrieves credentials by `bookingRef.type`, not `bookingRef.credentialId`. After this change a collective event can have multiple Google (or other same-provider) references, causing all deletion attempts to use one host's credential; secondary host events will fail to be deleted and remain at the old time. Build the lookup by credential ID and use each reference's credential ID.

title: Google Meet fallback dereferences an absent destination calendar
body: `evt.destinationCalendar` is optional and is explicitly constructed as `null`/empty for bookings without a selected destination calendar. Destructuring it yields `undefined`, but the following condition reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining. Creating a Google Meet event without a destination calendar will therefore throw before any calendar/video event is created (and may also fail type checking under strict null checks). Guard this access, e.g. `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.

title: Collective host calendars are discarded when the primary organizer has no destination calendar
body: The event initializes `destinationCalendar` to `null` when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar. For a collective booking, other hosts' calendars are collected in `teamDestinationCalendars`, but `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...)` becomes a no-op when that initial value is null. Thus a collective whose organizer has no calendar configured but whose additional hosts do have calendars creates no events for those hosts, which is one of the cases this change is intended to support. Initialize this field to an empty array before appending host calendars.

title: Each destination is created with the full destination list, causing non-Google providers to target the first host's calendar
body: The loop invokes `createEvent` once per destination/credential, but passes the same unfiltered `event` each time. `CalendarManager.createEvent` only forwards the credential ID; it does not forward `destination.externalId`. Google happens to look up the matching credential, but the Office365, Lark, and CalDAV services all select `event.destinationCalendar[0]`. Consequently, when creating a collective event for a second host, those services use the second host's credential against the first host's external calendar (usually failing due to permissions, or creating in the wrong calendar). Pass the current destination to the service or provide each invocation an event whose destination list contains only that destination; providers must not infer the target from index zero.

title: Google updates lose the configured calendar when a legacy reference has no external calendar ID
body: When `externalCalendarId` is absent, the fallback now searches for a destination whose `externalId === externalCalendarId`; since that value is undefined, this always produces undefined. The previous behavior used the event's destination calendar. As a result, updating/rescheduling bookings with older references that lack `externalCalendarId` sends an undefined `calendarId` to Google instead of updating the selected destination calendar. Fall back to the destination associated with this credential (or the primary calendar) rather than searching for an undefined ID.

title: Recurring cancellation only selects the first calendar reference of each occurrence
body: For every updated recurring booking, the code uses `.find()` to obtain a single calendar reference, despite this PR now creating one reference per host destination. It then attempts that one reference with every calendar credential, while ignoring all remaining references for the occurrence. In a collective recurring booking, events created for secondary hosts are therefore not deleted on cancellation (and the primary event receives redundant deletion attempts). Iterate each updated booking's calendar references and invoke deletion using that reference's credential/calendar ID.

title: Google Meet fallback dereferences an absent destination calendar
body: When an event has Google Meet selected but no destination calendar, destructuring `evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` produces `undefined` and the subsequent `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` access throws. This used to be guarded by optional chaining. Events without a connected destination calendar can therefore no longer fall back to Cal Video and booking creation fails.

title: Non-Google calendar integrations always use the first host's destination calendar
body: `createAllCalendarEvents` invokes each host credential with the complete destination-calendar array, but Office365 selects `[0]` rather than the destination belonging to the credential currently creating the event. Thus, for a collective event whose first host uses another provider and a later host uses Office365, the Office365 call can target the first host's external ID (or fail/fall back incorrectly) instead of that Office365 host's calendar. The same first-element strategy is used by the Lark and CalDAV implementations, so multi-host events are not correctly created for mixed/non-Google calendar providers.

title: Only the first collective destination calendar is persisted on the booking
body: The event now accumulates destination calendars for every collective host, but booking creation connects only `evt.destinationCalendar[0]`. Later flows such as payment confirmation reconstruct the CalendarEvent from `booking.destinationCalendar` and the owner destination calendar, so they have no record of the other hosts' destinations. In particular, a paid collective booking that is scheduled after payment will create calendar events only for the persisted main host rather than all collective hosts.

title: Google event attendee identity is taken from the first host for every host calendar
body: Although the insertion calendar is selected by the credential at lines 147-155, the organizer attendee email is always sourced from `destinationCalendar[0]`. When creating the event for a later collective host, the payload still identifies the first host's calendar as organizer/attendee. This can cause incorrect invitations or organizer attribution for the additional hosts; the attendee identity should be selected from the destination matching `credentialId`.

title: Salesforce service references Prisma without importing it
body: The new token-refresh path calls `prisma.credential.update(...)`, but this file has no `@calcom/prisma` import. This is an unresolved identifier and prevents the app-store package from type-checking/building.

title: The sync-mode token schema strips the expiry fields needed by consumers
body: `[z.string().toString()]` does not define a Zod catch-all/index signature; it evaluates to a literal property name such as `[object Object]`. Consequently, `minimumTokenResponseSchema` only retains `access_token` (and strips arbitrary response fields). In credential-sync mode, callers such as Zoom subsequently read `newTokens.expires_in` and calculate `expiry_date` from `undefined`, producing an invalid expiry and causing the credential to remain unusable or the Prisma update to fail. The schema must explicitly accept and preserve the documented expiry field(s), e.g. via `.passthrough()`/`.catchall()` and validation of supported expiry names.

title: Credential-sync refresh returns a different response type than several integrations expect
body: When sync is enabled this helper returns the raw `fetch` `Response`, while its fallback returns whatever each supplied refresh function returns. This breaks integrations whose existing refresh functions return SDK/axios objects rather than a Fetch response. For example, HubSpot casts the result to `HubspotToken` and reads `expiresIn`/`accessToken`, while Zoho Bigin and Zoho CRM read `.data`; with a Fetch response these fields are absent, so invalid credentials are persisted or token refresh fails. Normalize the sync response to the same contract expected by each caller (or make the helper parse and return a common token payload) before replacing those calls.

title: Zoho Bigin sends a credential ID as the Cal.com user ID to the sync endpoint
body: `refreshOAuthTokens` expects its third argument to be the credential owner's user ID and serializes it as `calcomUserId`. This call passes `credentialId`, which is the database credential primary key captured at line 53, not `credential.userId`. A self-hosted credential source will therefore look up the wrong user (or potentially another user whose ID happens to equal that credential ID), making synced Bigin refreshes fail or return the wrong account's token.

title: Outbound token-sync requests contain no authentication
body: The configured credential-sync endpoint is called with only a user ID and app slug; no webhook secret, authorization header, signature, or other credential is sent. If the self-hosted endpoint follows the described contract and returns tokens for these identifiers, anyone who can reach it can request tokens for arbitrary Cal.com user IDs and apps. Require an authenticated request (for example an HMAC signature or the configured shared secret in a header) and document/verify it on the receiving service.

title: Salesforce refresh saves the new token but uses the expired token for the current request
body: The newly added refresh code updates the database with `accessTokenParsed.data`, but the `jsforce.Connection` created immediately afterward still receives `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url`, which are the pre-refresh values. Since this refresh is performed while constructing the service, the first operation after an expired token will authenticate with the expired access token and fail; only a later service instance can use the saved token. Construct the connection from the refreshed response values.

title: Credential-sync responses are returned in a shape incompatible with several refresh callers
body: The sync branch returns the raw Fetch Response, whereas the original refresh functions return provider SDK/Axios results. Google Calendar reads `res.data`, and HubSpot, Zoho CRM, and Zoho Bigin all read fields through `.data`; a Fetch Response has neither parsed data nor those token fields. With syncing enabled, token refresh for these integrations therefore reads undefined values or throws instead of using the synchronized access token. The helper must normalize the sync response to the contract expected by each caller (or all callers must explicitly parse `response.json()`).

title: The permissive sync schema strips the expiry field supplied by the credential service
body: `minimumTokenResponseSchema` is a Zod object and Zod objects strip unknown properties by default. The computed keys do not make it a catch-all schema, so a sync response such as `{ access_token, expiry_date }` is parsed down to just `access_token`; the function then injects a fake refresh token. Callers that require expiry information, notably Zoom's `newTokens.expires_in`, persist an invalid/NaN expiry and subsequently try to refresh again using the fake refresh token. Use `.passthrough()`/`z.record` as appropriate and preserve the documented expiry field, or normalize it explicitly for each provider.

title: Google credential updates store Zod's SafeParse result instead of credential keys
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the complete `safeParse` result (`{ success, data }`), but this value is written directly to `Credential.key`. Google credential loading later parses `credential.key` as the Google token object, so after the first refresh the stored wrapper no longer has top-level `access_token`, `refresh_token`, or expiry fields and the integration becomes unusable. Persist `key.data` after checking success, not the SafeParse result.

title: Zoho Bigin sends the credential ID as the Cal.com user ID to the sync endpoint
body: `refreshOAuthTokens` expects its third argument to be the credential owner user ID and sends it as `calcomUserId`, but this call passes `credentialId`, which is the database credential primary key. The self-hosted credential service will look up the wrong user (or no user), so Bigin refresh fails or can retrieve another user's token when numeric IDs happen to overlap. Pass `credential.userId` through this refresh path instead.

title: Salesforce service references Prisma without importing it
body: The newly added refresh logic calls `prisma.credential.update`, but this file has no `@calcom/prisma` import. TypeScript compilation fails with `Cannot find name 'prisma'`, blocking builds that include the app-store package.

title: Concurrent credential webhooks can create duplicate credentials
body: The endpoint implements an upsert as a `findFirst` followed by a separate create/update, but the lookup is not protected by a transaction or a unique `(userId, appId)` constraint. Two simultaneous webhook deliveries for a user without a credential can both observe no row and create separate credentials. Several integration paths use `findFirst`, so which synced credential is used becomes nondeterministic and stale credentials remain active. Use an enforced unique key with upsert, or serialize/retry this operation.

title: The fallback sync schema strips all token fields except access_token
body: `z.string().toString()` is a computed object key, not a Zod catch-all declaration; it evaluates to the same string (effectively "[object Object]") for both entries. Consequently, in credential-sync mode Zod's default object behavior strips response fields such as `expires_in`, `expiry_date`, and provider-specific fields. The helper then inserts a fake `refresh_token`. Callers persist this reduced object, losing expiry/refresh-token information and causing repeated refreshes or invalid credentials (for example, Zoom subsequently calculates expiry from an absent `expires_in`). Use a schema with `.passthrough()`/`.catchall()` and preserve the existing refresh token when the sync response intentionally omits it.

title: Google credential sync treats a Fetch Response as a parsed token payload
body: When syncing is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the native `fetch()` Response. This code still reads `res.data`, which only exists on the normal Google client response, so `token` is undefined and `token.access_token` throws. Any expired Google Calendar credential in sync mode therefore fails before it can make a calendar request. Parse and validate the sync endpoint's JSON response before accessing its token fields, while retaining the normal provider-response path.

title: Zoho Bigin sends a credential ID as the Cal.com user ID to the sync endpoint
body: `refreshOAuthTokens` expects its third argument to be the credential owner’s user ID and sends it as `calcomUserId`, but this call passes `credentialId` (the Credential primary key). The external app store will look up the wrong user and cannot return that user's refreshed Bigin credentials; IDs can also coincidentally refer to a different user. Pass `credential.userId` through this method instead.

title: HubSpot sync casts an unparsed Fetch Response into a HubSpot token
body: With credential sync enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a native `Response`, but this code casts it directly to `HubspotToken` and then reads `expiresIn` and `accessToken`. Those fields are undefined on `Response`, so it persists an invalid credential and configures HubSpot with an undefined access token. The sync response must be decoded to JSON and mapped to HubSpot's token representation before calculating expiry and updating the credential.

title: Salesforce CalendarService references prisma without importing it
body: The newly added token-refresh persistence call uses `prisma.credential.update`, but this module has no `@calcom/prisma` import. This is an unresolved identifier and prevents the app-store package from type-checking/building, blocking deployment of the PR.

title: Team admins are incorrectly denied permission to add guests
body: The authorization predicate requires a user to be both a team admin and a team owner (`isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`). These are distinct roles, so a normal team admin fails this check despite the feature/UI treating team admins or owners as authorized. Use `||` (or the existing team-admin-or-owner authorization helper) so either role can manage the booking.

title: Guest blacklist can be bypassed with email casing
body: Configured blacklist addresses are lowercased, but submitted guest addresses are compared without normalization. An address such as `Blocked@example.com` therefore does not match a `blocked@example.com` entry and is added/invited. Normalize submitted emails (and ideally existing-attendee comparisons) consistently before blacklist and duplicate checks.

title: The endpoint accepts an unbounded number of guest addresses
body: `guests` has no maximum length, while processing each address creates attendee rows, updates calendar attendees, and sends notifications to all attendees and organizers. Any authorized attendee can submit a very large array directly to this mutation and use a single booking to trigger mass email/calendar work and database writes. Impose a server-side maximum consistent with the product's guest limit before performing any writes.

title: Attendees are persisted before calendar synchronization can fail
body: The booking attendee rows are committed at lines 92-106 before `updateCalendarAttendees` is awaited. If the calendar update fails (for example due to an expired integration credential), the mutation returns an error but the guests remain in Cal.com without calendar updates or emails, leaving booking and calendar state inconsistent. Either make failure recoverable/retryable and report the persisted state, or arrange synchronization/outbox handling so the committed attendee change is eventually applied.

title: Existing attendees can receive a duplicate scheduled email
body: The notification call receives the original requested `guests` array rather than `uniqueGuests`, even though existing addresses are filtered out before insertion. `sendAddGuestsEmails` uses that list to decide who receives `AttendeeScheduledEmail`; thus a request containing one new address and an already-attending address sends the existing attendee a new-booking confirmation instead of the guest-added notification. Pass the actual inserted guest addresses (`uniqueGuests`) to the mailer.

title: Team administrators and owners are incorrectly denied access
body: The authorization flag requires `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`. Team roles are distinct, so a normal team administrator is not an owner and a normal owner is not an administrator; neither can satisfy this condition unless the helper methods deliberately overlap. This makes the advertised team-admin/owner access path unusable for bookings they do not personally organize or attend. Use an OR between the role checks.

title: Guest blacklist can be bypassed by email casing
body: Blacklist entries are normalized to lowercase, but submitted guest addresses are compared without normalization. Since valid email addresses may contain uppercase characters, submitting `Blocked@Example.com` bypasses a blacklist entry for `blocked@example.com` and creates/sends an invitation to that address. Normalize submitted addresses (and attendee duplicate comparisons) before applying policy checks.

title: The API accepts duplicate guests and can fail or create duplicate attendees
body: Duplicate validation exists only in the dialog, while the public tRPC schema and handler do not deduplicate `guests`. `uniqueGuests` only excludes attendees that existed before the request, so a direct request such as `["guest@example.com", "guest@example.com"]` retains both entries and passes both to `createMany`. Depending on the database constraint this either produces duplicate attendee rows and notifications or fails the whole mutation with a database error. Validate/deduplicate on the server before writing.

title: Guests can be added to cancelled, rejected, or pending bookings through the API
body: The handler updates any booking ID after authorization and never checks booking status or whether the event is still active. Although the list UI only exposes edit actions for accepted bookings, callers can invoke this mutation directly for cancelled/rejected/pending (and past) bookings. It then adds attendee records and sends calendar `REQUEST`/confirmed emails for an event that may no longer exist. Enforce the allowed booking state server-side before modifying attendees.

title: Existing attendees can receive a new-booking email when mixed with new guests
body: The database write correctly filters `guests` into `uniqueGuests`, but notifications are called with the original `guests` array. If a request contains both an already-attending address and a new address, `sendAddGuestsEmails` classifies the existing attendee as a newly added guest and sends it an `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (including a calendar invite) instead of the guest-added update. Pass `uniqueGuests` to the mail sender.

title: Guest list size is unbounded
body: The mutation accepts an unbounded array of email addresses. Any authorized attendee can submit a very large payload, causing an equally large database insert, calendar attendee update, and email fan-out; the latter also sends update emails to every existing attendee. This is an application-level mail/third-party API abuse vector and can exhaust request resources. Add a server-side maximum guest count (and ideally a matching UI limit).

title: Guest-add notifications ignore event-type email opt-out settings
body: `sendAddGuestsEmails` sends organizer, team-member, existing-attendee, and new-attendee emails unconditionally. Other standard booking notification paths check `disableStandardEmails.all.host` and `.attendee`, but this new path neither accepts event metadata nor performs those checks. Consequently, adding a guest overrides an event type's configured host/attendee email suppression and sends notifications users explicitly disabled.

title: Team administrators are rejected despite the UI permitting them
body: The authorization condition requires `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`. Administrator and owner are distinct team roles, so a team administrator who is not also the owner will fail this check and receive FORBIDDEN. The booking list already exposes actions based on `isUserTeamAdminOrOwner`, so team admins can open the dialog but cannot complete the mutation. This should use OR semantics (and ideally the same authorization helper/policy as the booking listing).

title: Attendees are persisted before the external calendar update succeeds
body: The booking attendee records are created before `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` is called, with no transaction, rollback, or recovery path. If the calendar update fails (particularly likely when an attendee rather than the organizer initiates the request, since the EventManager is constructed with the caller's credentials), the endpoint returns an error after the guests are already stored. A retry then sees those guests as existing and cannot repair the calendar update, leaving Cal.com, calendar providers, and notifications out of sync.

title: The mutation can add guests to cancelled or completed bookings
body: After loading the booking, the handler authorizes the caller but never verifies that the booking is accepted/upcoming (or otherwise eligible for attendee updates). A caller can invoke this tRPC endpoint directly for a cancelled or past booking and create attendees, update calendar attendees, and send a `CONFIRMED` calendar invitation. This produces misleading invitations and mutates historical/cancelled booking data; eligibility must be enforced server-side rather than relying on the dashboard action visibility.

title: Guest additions have no server-side cardinality limit
body: The public mutation schema accepts an unbounded array of email addresses, and any existing attendee is authorized to invoke it. One request can therefore create an arbitrary number of attendee rows, issue calendar updates, and send invitations/notifications to all supplied recipients (and update emails to existing attendees). This is an email-spam and resource-exhaustion vector independent of the UI; impose a reasonable maximum in the schema and enforce rate/abuse controls.

title: Guest-added notifications ignore event email-disable settings
body: Unlike the other booking notification helpers, `sendAddGuestsEmails` does not accept or check `eventTypeMetadata`, `disableStandardEmails.all.attendee`, or `disableStandardEmails.all.host`. Consequently, adding a guest sends organizer and attendee emails even for event types configured to suppress standard emails. This breaks the event-type notification preference contract and can send mail users explicitly disabled.

title: Retry cleanup deletes non-SMS workflow reminders
body: The `retryCount > 1` arm of this `OR` is not constrained to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`. This cron endpoint will therefore permanently delete any email or WhatsApp `WorkflowReminder` whose retry count exceeds one, even though this job only processes SMS reminders. Scope the retry cleanup to unscheduled SMS reminders so retry state for other delivery methods cannot cause their reminders to be removed.

title: Retry increments can be lost when cron executions overlap
body: The retry count is calculated from the value read by `findMany` and then written as `reminder.retryCount + 1`. If two cron invocations process the same unscheduled reminder concurrently, both can read (for example) zero and both write one. The failed reminder then gets more than the intended two attempts, and concurrent scheduling attempts can continue. Use a database-side atomic increment (and ideally condition it on the reminder still being unscheduled) rather than writing a stale read value.

title: Retry cleanup is not restricted to SMS reminders
body: The new `OR` branch deletes every `WorkflowReminder` with `retryCount > 1`, regardless of its method, scheduled state, or scheduled date. This cron is specifically the SMS scheduler and the previous cleanup was scoped to `method: SMS`; as written, any email/WhatsApp reminder (or another producer using this field later) with a retry count above one will be silently deleted by the SMS cron. Restrict the retry-count branch to unscheduled SMS reminders so this job cannot remove unrelated workflow work.

title: Retry count updates can be lost when cron executions overlap
body: The handler reads `retryCount` in `findMany` and later writes `reminder.retryCount + 1`. Concurrent or overlapping cron requests can select the same reminder with count 0, both fail scheduling, and both write 1. The reminder has then failed twice but is treated as having failed once and continues being retried; concurrent executions can also repeatedly attempt the same SMS. Use an atomic database increment (and ideally atomically claim/transition an unscheduled reminder) rather than a stale read-modify-write value.

title: Exception-path retry update has the same lost-update race
body: The catch path also persists a value calculated from the count captured before scheduling. Two overlapping failing invocations overwrite each other with the same value, so exceptions do not reliably advance the retry limit either. This path should use the same atomic increment/claim mechanism as the non-throwing failed-response path.

title: Retry cleanup deletes reminders for every delivery method
body: The `retryCount > 1` arm of this `OR` is not constrained to `WorkflowMethods.SMS` (or to unscheduled reminders). Consequently, any WorkflowReminder record of another method, such as email or WhatsApp, with a retryCount above one will be permanently deleted by the SMS cron. Retry cleanup must be scoped to SMS reminders so this endpoint cannot delete unrelated workflow delivery records.

title: Reminders with no usable recipient or message never consume retries
body: RetryCount is only incremented inside the `message?.length && sendTo` branch. An SMS attendee reminder without `booking.smsReminderNumber`, an SMS-number workflow with no `sendTo`, or a reminder whose generated message is empty is silently skipped and remains `scheduled: false` with retryCount 0. The cron will select it on every run until its scheduled date, which leaves a common class of unsendable SMS reminders with the behavior this change is intended to stop.

title: Retry increments can be lost between concurrent cron invocations
body: The retry value is read in `findMany` and later written as `reminder.retryCount + 1`, rather than incremented atomically or guarded by the previously read value. If two overlapping cron requests process the same unscheduled reminder, both can read 0 and both write 1 after failures. The reminder then receives additional scheduling attempts beyond the intended two-failure limit (and concurrent successful calls can also schedule duplicate SMS messages). Use an atomic increment together with a claim/conditional update of the reminder before scheduling.

title: The public `findMany` API was removed without migrating its callers
body: `InsightsBookingService.findMany`, which previously executed the authorized query and accepted Prisma find-many arguments, has been removed and replaced by `getBaseConditions`. This is an exported service contract change, but this PR only updates this service and its test; any existing production caller invoking `service.findMany(...)` will fail TypeScript compilation (or fail at runtime for untyped consumers). Migrate all callers to an equivalent parameterized `$queryRaw` query as part of this change, or retain a compatible `findMany` method.

title: Removing findMany breaks the service's existing public API
body: `findMany` was a public method on `InsightsBookingService` and was removed rather than migrated or retained. The replacement, `getBaseConditions`, only returns a SQL fragment and does not accept or apply the caller's `BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedFindManyArgs` (including select, pagination, ordering, and additional where clauses). No production call sites are updated in this PR, so existing consumers will either fail TypeScript compilation (`service.findMany is not a function`) or must be rewritten outside this change. Retain a compatible query method or update every consumer as part of the migration.

title: The public findMany API was removed without replacing its query execution contract
body: This change deletes `findMany(findManyArgs)`, which was the service's public method for applying authorization/filter conditions and executing a `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` query. The new `getBaseConditions()` only returns a SQL fragment and requires every caller to reimplement query execution, selection, pagination, ordering, and composition of caller-provided `where` clauses. Existing TypeScript callers will fail to compile and JavaScript callers will fail at runtime; no caller migrations are included in this PR.

title: Team and organization authorization SQL is never executed against the database
body: The team and org tests only compare `Prisma.Sql` objects to other `Prisma.sql` objects. The sole `$queryRaw` test below exercises only the user-scope condition, so it does not validate the new `ANY(${array})` parameter binding or the team/org `isTeamBooking` branches on the actual database. A SQL serialization or PostgreSQL array-typing issue in the primary authorization scopes would therefore pass this suite despite returning no data or failing all team/org insights requests.

title: Expired cache rows are reported as active cache
body: `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups every CalendarCache row for a credential without filtering `expiresAt`. Cache reads only use rows whose `expiresAt` is in the future, so once all rows for a credential have expired this API still returns an `updatedAt` value and the UI presents it as a current cache status and offers deletion. Filter the status query to unexpired rows (consistent with `getCachedAvailability`) so the displayed status reflects cache that can actually be served.

title: Deleting cache does not refresh the cache-status query
body: On successful `deleteCache`, this mutation only calls the optional `onSuccess` callback. Unlike the disconnect mutation below, it never invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`, which is the query supplying `cacheUpdatedAt`; `onSuccess` is optional and is not a substitute for cache invalidation. Consequently the deleted cache continues to be displayed as present (and the delete action remains available) until an unrelated refetch/reload, especially because the query disables window-focus refetching.

title: Webhook helper cannot update .env on GNU/Linux
body: The command uses BSD/macOS `sed -i ''` syntax. On GNU sed, commonly used in Linux development and CI environments, `''` is treated as an input filename and the command fails rather than updating `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL`. Use a portable replacement strategy or select the `sed -i` arguments based on the platform.

title: Deleting cache does not invalidate the displayed cache-status query
body: The delete mutation only calls the optional `onSuccess` callback and never invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. In this wrapper `onChanged` is optional, and even callers that supply it are not required to refetch this query. Consequently, after a successful deletion the card can continue displaying the old `cacheUpdatedAt` value and the "Delete cached data" action until a manual reload or another unrelated refetch. Invalidate `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` on delete settlement/success (as the disconnect mutation already does).

title: Expired cache rows are reported as an active cache status
body: `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups every CalendarCache row for a credential without filtering on `expiresAt`. Cache reads treat rows whose `expiresAt` is in the past as unusable, but this status API will still return their newest `updatedAt`, causing the UI to claim a cache exists and show a stale "Last updated" timestamp for up to however long expired rows remain in the database. The status query should restrict rows to unexpired entries, consistent with `getCachedAvailability`.

title: Webhook test script uses a macOS-only sed invocation
body: `sed -i '' -E` is BSD/macOS syntax; GNU sed (the standard on Linux development machines and CI containers) interprets the empty argument differently and fails to update the env file. The script therefore cannot perform its advertised setup on Linux. Use a portable replacement strategy or select the `sed -i` arguments based on the platform.

title: Deleting cache does not invalidate the cache-status query
body: The delete-cache mutation only calls the optional `onSuccess` callback. Unlike the credential deletion mutation below it, it never invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. Since `onSuccess` is optional and is not contractually required to refetch this query, the component can continue displaying the old `cacheUpdatedAt` and the delete action after the server has removed all cache rows. Invalidate `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` on settlement/success of this mutation (and optionally retain the caller callback).

title: Expired cache rows are reported as active cache status
body: `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups every `CalendarCache` row for the credential, without restricting results to rows whose `expiresAt` is still in the future. Cache reads explicitly reject expired rows, but this status endpoint will continue returning their `updatedAt`, so the UI reports cache data as present and offers deletion even when there is no usable cached availability. Filter the status query by `expiresAt >= now` (or otherwise clearly represent expired cache separately).

title: The new authorization and deletion behavior has no automated coverage
body: There are no tests for the newly introduced destructive tRPC handler or the cache-status enrichment. This leaves unverified that a user can delete only cache rows belonging to their own credential, that an unauthorized credential ID is rejected without deleting rows, and that cache status selects the newest timestamp per credential. Add handler/repository tests for these cases before relying on this endpoint from the UI.

title: The SendGrid client used for cancellations is never authenticated
body: This route calls `sgMail.setApiKey`, but the new cancellation logic uses the separate `@sendgrid/client` instance at line 57. Unlike `@sendgrid/mail`, that client is never given `SENDGRID_API_KEY` via `client.setApiKey`. Consequently the POST to `/v3/user/scheduled_sends` will be rejected as unauthorized, the catch block only logs the failure, and cancelled email reminders remain scheduled and are sent.

title: The one-hour cancellation window can miss reminders cancelled shortly before delivery
body: The cron only attempts a SendGrid cancellation for reminders whose scheduled date is within one hour, but it runs every 15 minutes. For example, after a run at 10:00 has processed the next hour, a booking cancelled at 10:01 with a reminder due at 10:05 is not processed until 10:15, after SendGrid has already delivered it. The implementation needs to cancel at cancellation time or maintain a safety margin greater than the cron interval so a cancelled booking cannot send a reminder before the next cron pass.

title: Rescheduling still creates unbounded pending SendGrid cancellations
body: The reschedule path passes `immediateDelete: true`, which POSTs a SendGrid `status: cancel` request and then returns without marking or deleting the local `WorkflowReminder`. The old booking remains in the database, so the cron never sees `cancelled: true` and cannot manage this record. Each reschedule therefore leaves a cancelled SendGrid scheduled-send entry until its delivery date, recreating the pending-cancellation accumulation and 100-cancellation-limit failure this PR is intended to fix; it also leaves stale workflow-reminder rows locally.

title: Reminder cancellation state updates are fired without awaiting them
body: `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` are async, but this loop does not collect or await their promises. The request can proceed to completion (and, in a serverless runtime, be torn down) before the email reminder's `cancelled` flag is persisted. If that update is lost or delayed, the cron will not cancel the SendGrid send and the cancelled booking can still receive a reminder. Await these operations, e.g. with `Promise.all`, before returning.

title: SendGrid client used for cancellation is never configured with the API key
body: This module configures `sgMail` with `SENDGRID_API_KEY`, but it never calls `client.setApiKey(...)` before using `client.request` to cancel scheduled sends at line 57. `@sendgrid/client` has separate configuration from `@sendgrid/mail`, so the new cancellation request can fail authentication and leave the SendGrid email scheduled. Configure the client in this module before making cancellation requests.

title: Expired cancelled reminders are deleted before SendGrid cancellation can be retried
body: The initial `deleteMany` removes every email reminder whose scheduled date has passed, including reminders with `cancelled: true`. If the cancellation request failed during a prior cron run (or one failed request aborted the loop at line 75), the next run deletes the only local record before attempting to cancel its SendGrid batch. The SendGrid scheduled send remains active and can still be delivered. Cancelled reminders must be excluded from this cleanup until the provider cancellation succeeds, or cancellation must be processed before cleanup with durable retry handling.

title: Cancellation does not wait for workflow reminders to be marked cancelled
body: `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` are asynchronous, but the calls inside these `forEach` loops are neither awaited nor collected into the later `Promise.all`. Previously the handler awaited the Prisma reminder deletions; now it can return successfully before email reminders have been marked `cancelled` for the cron job. In particular, in serverless/request teardown scenarios this work may not complete, and provider/database errors are detached from the cancellation request. Collect and await these operations before completing booking cancellation.

title: The SendGrid client used for cancellation is never authenticated
body: This module configures `@sendgrid/mail` with `sgMail.setApiKey`, but the cancellation request is made through the separate `@sendgrid/client` instance. Unlike `emailReminderManager`, this file never calls `client.setApiKey(sendgridAPIKey)`. Consequently the new POST to `/v3/user/scheduled_sends` will be unauthorized, the catch block only logs the error, and the cancelled reminder remains scheduled and is still delivered.

title: Rescheduling still creates unbounded pending SendGrid cancellations
body: The reschedule path passes `immediateDelete: true`, causing `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` to immediately POST a SendGrid cancellation and return without deleting the reminder row or marking it `cancelled`. These old bookings are not subsequently picked up by `scheduleEmailReminders`, so every reschedule leaves a SendGrid scheduled-send cancellation pending until its original send time. This bypasses the new deferred-cancellation design and can again hit SendGrid's 100 pending-cancellation limit, after which later reminders will not be cancelled.

title: Cancellation state updates are fired without being awaited
body: `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` is async, but these calls are made inside `forEach` and their promises are discarded; the later `Promise.all` contains neither these updates nor the SMS deletions. The handler can therefore finish successfully before the workflow reminders have been marked cancelled (and in a serverless/request lifecycle can be stopped before that happens). A cancelled booking may then retain an unmarked scheduled reminder and the cron job will not cancel the email.

title: Reschedule cancellation does not await calendar/video deletions
body: Using `forEach(async ...)` discards every callback promise. Before this change, `getCalendar()` was synchronous, so `deleteEvent()` was invoked before the callback returned; now the callback suspends on the dynamic import and the mutation proceeds to send email/webhooks and return without waiting for (or handling errors from) any external deletion. The booking is already marked CANCELLED, so a request-reschedule can leave the old calendar/video meeting active and any import/deletion failure becomes an unhandled rejection. Build an array of deletion promises and `await Promise.all` (with explicit error handling).

title: Vital reschedules fire-and-forget external resource deletion
body: The async callback passed to `forEach` is not awaited by the surrounding `try/catch`. Since `getCalendar` now awaits a dynamic import, this function can finish and send the reschedule email before it has even called `deleteEvent`; failures after the await also bypass the catch block. The booking has already been cancelled at this point, so external Vital calendar/video events can remain active. Collect the callback promises and await them, preferably with per-integration error handling.

title: WipeMyCal reschedules fire-and-forget external resource deletion
body: The async callback passed to `forEach` is not awaited by the surrounding `try/catch`. Since `getCalendar` now awaits a dynamic import, this function can finish and send the reschedule email before it has even called `deleteEvent`; failures after the await also bypass the catch block. The booking has already been cancelled at this point, so external WipeMyCal calendar/video events can remain active. Collect the callback promises and await them, preferably with per-integration error handling.

title: Recurring cancellation omits dynamically imported calendar deletions from awaited work
body: The recurring-event path starts an `async forEach` over calendar credentials, but does not await its callbacks. Each callback now waits for `getCalendar` before pushing deletion promises into `apiDeletes`; the handler subsequently reaches `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` while `apiDeletes` is still empty or incomplete. As a result, the cancellation response and database cleanup can complete before recurring external events are deleted, and import/delete failures are unhandled. Replace the `forEach` with awaited promise collection (or an awaited loop) and add the resulting deletion promises before the final `Promise.all`.

title: All integration chunks are started eagerly when appStore is imported
body: Each `import("./...")` expression is evaluated while constructing `appStore`, so importing this module immediately starts loading every app package. This does not defer loading until a particular integration is selected; it can fetch/initialize all optional integration chunks on requests that only need one (or none), undermining the intended lazy-loading benefit and increasing startup/request resource use. Store import functions (for example `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) and invoke only the selected one.

title: Recurring calendar deletions are no longer included in the awaited deletion set
body: The async `forEach` callbacks are not awaited. Before this change each callback synchronously appended the calendar deletion promise to `apiDeletes`; now it first waits for `getCalendar`, so execution reaches `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` at line 652 while `apiDeletes` is commonly still empty. The cancellation request can therefore finish and remove booking references before recurring external calendar events are deleted, and import/deletion failures become unhandled rejections. Build deletion promises with `map`/`Promise.all` (or await a `for...of` loop) before awaiting `apiDeletes`.

title: Reschedule does not await calendar imports or external deletions
body: `forEach(async ...)` discards every callback promise. As a result, this function sends the reschedule email and returns success without waiting for `getCalendar` or `deleteEvent`; an import failure is also outside the surrounding `try/catch` and becomes an unhandled rejection. This can leave the prior calendar event undeleted while the booking is already marked cancelled. Replace the `forEach` with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` (and keep it inside the error handling).

title: Reschedule does not await calendar imports or external deletions
body: `forEach(async ...)` discards every callback promise. As a result, this function sends the reschedule email and returns success without waiting for `getCalendar` or `deleteEvent`; an import failure is also outside the surrounding `try/catch` and becomes an unhandled rejection. This can leave the prior calendar event undeleted while the booking is already marked cancelled. Replace the `forEach` with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` (and keep it inside the error handling).

title: Request-reschedule returns before imported integrations are deleted
body: The async callback passed to `forEach` is not collected or awaited. Since it now awaits `getCalendar` before calling `deleteEvent`, the mutation proceeds to send email/webhooks and resolves before deletion has even started; failures while importing an app are not propagated or handled. Await a mapped set of deletion promises (or use an awaited `for...of`) so the cancellation side effect is completed or handled before reporting the reschedule request.

title: App modules are still all imported eagerly
body: Each `import("./...")` expression is evaluated while constructing `appStore`, so importing this module immediately starts loading every app package. This does not defer loading until a selected integration is used, and unused import promises can reject without any consumer. Store loader functions (for example, `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) and invoke only the selected loader at call sites to actually make integrations lazy.

title: Recurring calendar deletions are no longer included in the awaited cleanup
body: The async `forEach` callback awaits `getCalendar` before it pushes a deletion into `apiDeletes`, but `forEach` does not await its callbacks. The handler subsequently proceeds to delete booking records, send notifications, and eventually calls `Promise.all(apiDeletes)` while that array can still be empty. Consequently recurring cancellation can return successfully without deleting remote calendar events; rejected imports/deletions also become unhandled rejections. Build and await the work explicitly, e.g. with `await Promise.all(credentials.map(async credential => ...))`, rather than mutating `apiDeletes` from detached callbacks.

title: Calendar cleanup errors escape the surrounding try block
body: Changing this callback to `async` makes `getCalendar` asynchronous, but `forEach` neither waits for the callback nor propagates its rejection to the enclosing `try/catch`. The reschedule flow can send the reschedule email and return success before calendar/video deletion has started or completed, and a failed dynamic import or deletion is unhandled rather than logged. Collect these operations and `await Promise.all(...)` inside the try block.

title: Reschedule mutation returns before dynamically loaded integrations are deleted
body: The async callback passed to `forEach` is detached. Since it now awaits the app import before calling `deleteEvent`, the mutation marks the booking cancelled and sends email/webhooks before cleanup is performed, and failures while loading or deleting an integration are unhandled. Replace the `forEach(async ...)` with awaited promises so cancellation is either completed or its failure is handled before the mutation finishes.

title: Fixed-host override checks allow slots that extend outside the override window
body: The override predicate only rejects a slot when its end is at/before the override start or its start is after the override end. A slot that starts before the override and ends inside it, or starts inside it and ends after it, matches neither condition and is treated as available. For a round-robin event this can expose a slot whose fixed host is unavailable for part of the booking duration; the check needs to require the entire [slot start, slot end] interval to be contained in an override range.

title: Multiple date-override ranges on one day are treated as an intersection
body: `dateOverrides.find` returns an unavailable result as soon as any same-day override does not contain the slot. With two valid availability windows on a day (for example 09:00-10:00 and 14:00-15:00), a slot inside the first window is rejected by the second window, and vice versa. Date overrides represent alternative available ranges, so a fixed host should be available when the slot is contained in any matching override, not every override.

title: All-day date overrides are never recognized as equal start/end times
body: This compares two separately-created Dayjs objects with `===`, which is always false even when `date.start` and `date.end` represent the same instant. Consequently an all-day/unavailable override skips the intended special case and can leave a slot beginning exactly at the override timestamp available (typically the first slot at midnight). Use a value comparison such as `isSame` or compare timestamps.

title: Working-hours validation ignores the booking end time
body: `end` is calculated from `slotStartTime` exactly like `start`, rather than from `slotEndTime`. Therefore any slot that starts before a fixed/loose host's working-hours end passes this check even if the event extends beyond that host's availability. This can make round-robin slots bookable when a required fixed host cannot attend the full event.

title: The added regression test does not cover the fixed-host round-robin behavior being changed
body: The new timezone assertion uses a personal event with `hosts: []`, so it never executes the fixed-host filtering path added in `checkIfIsAvailable`. There is no test with a ROUND_ROBIN event, at least one `isFixed: true` host, and that host's date override; regressions that again expose unavailable fixed-host slots would not be caught.

title: Date-override availability does not require the whole event to fit in the override
body: The override check only rejects a slot whose end is at/before the override start or whose start is after the override end. It never rejects a slot that starts within the override but ends after its end (and also permits a slot that begins before the override and crosses its start). For example, with a 10:00-11:00 override and a 60-minute event, a 10:30 slot is considered available even though the host is only available until 11:00. This can advertise and book fixed hosts outside their date override.

title: Fixed-host working hours are compared against UTC slot clock values
body: `slotStartTime` is explicitly converted to UTC, but its UTC weekday/hour/minutes are compared directly with `workingHour.days`, `startTime`, and `endTime`, which represent the host schedule's local clock values. `organizerTimeZone` is not used for this working-hours comparison. A fixed host in a non-UTC timezone can therefore pass or fail the new fixed-host availability filter at the wrong local time; for example, a UTC+05:30 host's 18:00 local boundary is checked as 12:30 against an 18:00 local end. The check also sets `end` equal to the slot start, so it does not verify that the event duration fits before the working-hours end. This can expose round-robin slots when a fixed host is unavailable.

title: The added test does not cover fixed-host round-robin overrides
body: The stated primary regression is a round-robin event with a fixed host, but the added test is a single-user event and only exercises slot generation. It never exercises `checkIfIsAvailable` for fixed hosts, where this PR adds the override and working-hours filtering. Consequently, regressions that still offer a round-robin slot while its fixed host is outside an override are not caught.

title: Zero-length date overrides are never recognized as closed days
body: The code compares two distinct Dayjs instances with `===`, which is always false even when `date.start` and `date.end` represent the same instant. Date overrides with equal start/end are used to represent an unavailable date, but this branch is skipped; the later bounds checks can leave a slot at that instant available. Compare the timestamps (for example with `isSame`) so an all-day/unavailable override blocks every slot.

title: Fixed-host override validation accepts slots that run past the override end
body: For a matching override date, the new validation rejects slots ending before the override starts and slots starting after the override ends, but never rejects a slot whose start is inside the override and whose end is after `date.end`. A round-robin slot generated from another host can therefore be offered even though the fixed host's override ends before the meeting does, allowing bookings outside that fixed host's availability. The check must require the full `[slotStartTime, slotEndTime]` interval to be contained in the override.

title: Multiple working-hour ranges on a day make fixed hosts unavailable in valid ranges
body: The `find` callback returns true when a slot is outside any working-hour range, and the caller then rejects the slot. With split availability on the same weekday (for example 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00), a 10:00 slot is correctly inside the first range but is before the second range, so the second range causes it to be rejected. This causes round-robin events with fixed hosts and split schedules to hide otherwise valid slots; availability should be accepted when it fits at least one range for that day.

title: Working-hour validation ignores the meeting end time
body: `end` is calculated from `slotStartTime` again rather than from `slotEndTime`. Consequently, the fixed-host check only tests whether the slot starts before the end of a working-hours range and can accept a meeting that extends beyond the fixed host's normal availability. Calculate the end from `slotEndTime` (including the requested duration) before comparing it to `workingHour.endTime`.

title: Legacy host values are copied without normalization and no longer match requests
body: The migration inserts the old `embeddable_hosts` values verbatim using SQL, so entries such as `http://example.com` or `https://example.com/path` bypass `EmbeddableHost`'s normalization callback. Runtime lookup parses a request URL and compares only `uri.host` (for example, `example.com`) against the stored value, so these migrated hosts will never be allowed. The previous setting implementation explicitly supported scheme-prefixed values; upgrading such an installation can therefore disable all existing embeds until every host is manually edited.

title: Migration crashes when the legacy embed category setting has no database row
body: This dereferences `[0]['id']` from a query that returns no row when `embed_category` was never explicitly persisted or does not match a category name. A default/unused embedding configuration is a normal installation state, so the migration can abort before creating the replacement configuration. The fallback on line 14 is never reached because the exception occurs first.

title: Host authorization fails for case variants of an allowed hostname
body: The database expression lowercases the stored host but compares it to the unnormalized `host` value from `URI#host`. URI hostnames can retain input casing, while DNS hostnames are case-insensitive. Consequently, an allowed `example.com` can reject a request whose Referer or embed URL uses `EXAMPLE.COM`, breaking embeds depending on URL casing.

title: Updating or deleting an unknown host returns a server error
body: Both `update` and `destroy` use `where(...).first` and immediately call methods on the result. For an ID that does not exist, `save_host(nil)` dereferences `host.host` and `destroy` dereferences `nil.destroy`, producing a 500 instead of a not-found response. This makes stale concurrent admin edits and ordinary invalid resource requests fail as internal errors.

title: Migration interpolates legacy host configuration directly into SQL
body: Each legacy host string is concatenated into an INSERT statement without quoting or parameterization. A hostname value containing a quote will break the migration, and a maliciously crafted legacy setting can alter the SQL executed during upgrade. Values should be inserted through quoted/bound SQL or normalized `EmbeddableHost` records instead.

title: Migration crashes when no category matches the old embed_category setting
body: The category lookup dereferences `execute(...)[0]['id']` without checking whether the query returned a row. `embed_category` defaults to an empty value and may also name a deleted/nonexistent category, so a normal installation with no configured embedding category produces an empty result and raises on `nil['id']`. This prevents the entire database migration from completing; handle an empty result and fall back to the uncategorized category before dereferencing it.

title: Migrated URL-form host entries no longer match embedding requests
body: The migration inserts legacy host-list values directly into the new table, bypassing `EmbeddableHost`'s normalization callback. Existing supported values such as `http://discourse.org` or `https://example.com/1234` are therefore stored with their scheme/path, while `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host` extracts only `example.com` and queries for an exact stored host. After upgrade those migrated hosts are never allowed, disabling embeds for affected sites. Normalize each legacy value to its hostname before insertion (and avoid raw SQL interpolation).

title: Hosts configured with a port can never be allowed
body: The validation explicitly permits values such as `example.com:3000`, and the callback leaves the port intact because it only removes schemes and paths.
