However `URI(host).host` drops the port before the exact database lookup, so a request from `http://example.com:3000` searches for `example.com` and cannot match the stored `example.com:3000`. Either normalize stored values to hostname-only or consistently include and compare the port.

title: Deleting all allowed hosts no longer disables expansion of embedded posts
body: This removes the only check that embedding is configured without replacing it with `EmbeddableHost.exists?`. Consequently, if `embed_truncate` is enabled, any existing `TopicEmbed` remains expandable even after every allowed host has been removed. Host removal should disable embedding behavior; otherwise stale embed records can still expose the expansion UI and trigger remote content retrieval.

title: Migration crashes when no category matches the old embed setting
body: The query joining `site_settings.value` to `categories.name` commonly returns no rows when the old `embed_category` setting is blank (its default) or references a deleted category. Indexing `[0]['id']` then dereferences nil before the intended `category_id == 0` fallback can run, causing the migration to abort and preventing upgrades. Handle an empty result before accessing its first row and then fall back to the uncategorized category.

title: Duplicate host mappings can select an arbitrary category
body: There is no uniqueness validation or database unique index for `host`, while `record_for_host` uses `.first`. An admin can create multiple rows for the same hostname with different category IDs; subsequent imports will use whichever row the database happens to return first, so embedded topics can be filed into an unintended category. Enforce a case-insensitive unique host mapping (including a unique database index) or define deterministic conflict behavior.

title: Hosts configured with a port can never be matched
body: The validation explicitly permits values such as `example.com:8080`, and the normalization callback preserves the port, but `record_for_host` parses an incoming URL and compares only `uri.host`, which is `example.com` and never includes `:8080`. Such an allowed host saves successfully but all embed requests from it are rejected and imports receive no category. Either normalize stored hosts to hostname-only and disallow ports, or compare an appropriate host-and-port value consistently.

title: Updating a nonexistent host raises a server error
body: `EmbeddableHost.where(...).first` returns nil for an unknown ID and is passed to `save_host`, which immediately calls `host.host=`. This produces a 500 instead of a not-found response for stale or invalid admin requests. The destroy action has the same nil dereference at line 16. Fetch with a not-found-aware lookup or explicitly return 404 before updating/destroying.

title: Large animated GIF uploads are converted to a single-frame image
body: `OptimizedImage.optimize` chooses the animated GIF path by matching the `from` path against `/\.GIF$/i`, but this call passes `tempfile.path`, whose Rack/Tempfile-generated name normally has no `.gif` extension. Consequently, even when `allow_animated_thumbnails` is enabled, an oversized GIF takes `downsize_instructions`, which uses `convert #{from}[0]` and writes only the first frame. Uploading a GIF large enough to trigger downsizing therefore silently destroys its animation; pass the original filename/format through to the optimizer or select the animated path from MIME/image metadata rather than the temporary path suffix.

title: Attachment size settings are no longer enforced by the upload client
body: The maximum is now unconditionally 10 MB, even when `type` is `attachment`. This ignores `max_attachment_size_kb` (and also caps installations configured to permit image uploads larger than 10 MB), whereas the previous code used the configured per-type limit. Users can now spend time uploading attachments that the server/site policy rejects, and sites that intentionally allow files above 10 MB cannot select them at all. Keep the configured attachment limit for attachments and use a separately defined pre-downsize input limit for images.

title: API URL uploads are newly limited to 10 MB regardless of site configuration
body: Remote API uploads previously downloaded up to `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb`; replacing that with `10.megabytes` causes a configured image limit above 10 MB to be ignored before downsizing can run. An API client supplying a URL to a valid, configured-allowed 20 MB image will now receive a failed upload/download instead of the image being processed. Use a configurable source-file ceiling that is at least compatible with the site's allowed image size (or document and expose the new API limit).

title: Client-side upload limits no longer honor the configured per-type limits
body: `validateUploadedFile` now rejects every upload above 10 MB, regardless of whether it is an image or attachment and regardless of `max_image_size_kb` / `max_attachment_size_kb`. Sites configured to allow attachments larger than 10 MB will have those uploads rejected in the browser before the server sees them, and the displayed limit is incorrect. If a fixed pre-downsize ceiling is needed for images, it should be applied only to images while attachments continue to use their configured limit.

title: API URL uploads are capped at 10 MB instead of the configured upload limit
body: Remote uploads supplied through the API are now downloaded with a hard 10 MB limit. This applies before the code knows whether the URL is an image that can be downsized, and therefore also blocks remote attachment uploads that the site's `max_attachment_size_kb` permits. It also prevents configured image limits above 10 MB from being used. Preserve the configured limit for non-images (and use an explicitly documented pre-downsize image ceiling if one is required).

title: The new downsize overload replaces the existing five-argument method in Ruby
body: Ruby does not overload methods by arity: defining `downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` replaces the preceding `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})`. Any existing caller using the prior public method signature will now raise `ArgumentError` rather than resize its image. Support both forms in one method (for example with optional arguments or splatting) or update every caller and preserve compatibility for plugin callers.

title: Unbounded multipart uploads are processed by ImageMagick before validation
body: The new resizing path runs for every multipart image over the configured image limit, but there is no upper bound on `tempfile.size` before invoking `OptimizedImage.downsize`. The browser-side 10 MB check is bypassable by posting directly to this endpoint, so an attacker can submit a very large or decompression-bomb image and force up to five expensive ImageMagick conversions before `Upload.create_for` has a chance to reject it. This creates a CPU, memory, and disk denial-of-service path. Enforce a server-side input-size cap before image processing (and reject files above it) rather than relying on the client limit.

title: Image conversion uses the same path as both input and output
body: `OptimizedImage.downsize` is called with `tempfile.path` for both `from` and `to`. The generated `convert`/`gifsicle` command therefore overwrites the source while it is being read; ImageMagick conversion is intended to write to a separate output file (or use a tool explicitly designed for in-place updates). This can cause conversion failures or leave the upload tempfile truncated/corrupted, after which the controller uploads the damaged file or reports an unrelated validation error. Convert into a separate tempfile, check the conversion result and resulting size, then atomically replace the original only on success.

title: Client upload limits no longer honor configured per-type limits
body: The client previously used `max_image_size_kb` or `max_attachment_size_kb` according to `type`; it now always permits up to 10 MB. Sites configured with a smaller limit will let users select files that the server rejects, while sites configured with a larger limit will reject valid uploads in the browser. The matching 413 message is also now inaccurate for servers with non-10-MB limits. Keep the site settings for attachments and the applicable image limit, or introduce and consistently use a documented separate maximum source-image limit for the downsize feature.

title: A cross-site GET can change a logged-in user's notification preference
body: `unsubscribe` mutates `TopicUser.notification_level` on a GET endpoint, and this action is explicitly excluded from the XHR check. Since GET requests are not protected by Rails CSRF verification, any third-party page can embed or navigate to `/t/<slug>/<id>/unsubscribe` and silently alter the notification state of a visitor who is logged into the forum. The email link needs a user-specific, unguessable unsubscribe token (or a confirmation/CSRF-protected state-changing request after the GET) rather than authorizing the change solely with the ambient session cookie.

title: Unsubscribe bypasses TopicUser.change, leaving notification metadata and clients stale
body: The action writes and saves the TopicUser record directly instead of using `TopicUser.change`, which is the normal notification-level update path. As a result it does not set `notifications_changed_at` or `notifications_reason_id` to `user_changed`, and it does not publish the topic notification-level MessageBus event. A topic auto-watched due to a category can therefore continue to display its old automatic notification reason, and other open sessions/tabs for the user will not receive the state change.

title: Unsubscribe state change is exposed as a GET request
body: The new GET route invokes `TopicsController#unsubscribe`, which immediately modifies the current user's TopicUser notification level. Because GET requests are not protected by Rails CSRF verification and `check_xhr` is explicitly skipped for this action, any third-party page can cause a logged-in visitor's browser to request a known topic's unsubscribe URL (for example via an image or navigation) and silently change that user's notification preference. Render a confirmation page on GET and require a CSRF-protected POST/PUT for the state change, or use a purpose-specific signed token if one-click email unsubscribe is required.

title: Unsubscribe crashes when the user has no TopicUser row
body: `TopicUser.find_by` can return nil for a logged-in user who has permission to view a topic but has never visited it or otherwise had a topic-user record created. The route is publicly reachable by any logged-in user, not only recipients of the particular email. The subsequent `tu.notification_level` dereference raises `NoMethodError`, returning a 500 instead of allowing the notification preference to be set. Use `TopicUser.change` (which creates missing rows) or explicitly create/fetch the record before reading and saving it.

title: State-changing unsubscribe action is exposed as a GET request
body: `GET /t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe` changes a user's notification level, and this action is explicitly exempted from the XHR check. Because GET requests do not receive Rails CSRF protection, any page or email/link scanner that causes a logged-in user's browser to request this URL can change that user's topic subscription without their intent. This can also be triggered by browser prefetching or security scanners following the emailed link. Make the email link lead to a confirmation page and perform the mutation via a CSRF-protected POST/PUT request (or use a signed, single-purpose token if a one-click email unsubscribe is required).

title: Unsubscribe bypasses TopicUser.change, so automatic tracking can re-enable notifications
body: The action directly assigns and saves `notification_level` rather than using `TopicUser.change`. `TopicUser.change` records `notifications_changed_at` and, crucially, sets `notifications_reason_id` to `user_changed`. The automatic tracking logic treats a nil reason as eligible to promote a topic back to `tracking` after it is read. Thus a topic user record with no reason (the normal case for auto-tracked topics) can be muted through this endpoint and later automatically changed back to tracking when the user visits/reads it, undoing the unsubscribe. Route this update through `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, topic_id, notification_level: ...)` so the explicit user choice is persisted with the appropriate reason and timestamp.

title: Blocked-email checks can be bypassed by changing email case
body: The lookup compares the submitted value directly against `blocked_emails.email` without canonicalizing it. Email local/domain case variants (for example, a block entry for `user@example.com` and a signup using `USER@example.com`) will not match on the case-sensitive database column, allowing a blocked address to register. This is especially problematic because other user-email paths use `Email.downcase`, so the application already treats emails as canonicalized for lookup purposes. Normalize both blocked-email storage and lookup (and enforce a matching normalized unique index) before querying.

title: Match counters lose updates under concurrent signup attempts
body: `should_block?` reads a row, increments `match_count` in memory, and saves it back. Concurrent validations can read the same count and each write the same incremented value, so some blocked-email attempts are silently omitted from the statistics. Use an atomic database update such as `update_all("match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?", ...)`, or lock the row, so the tracking fields remain accurate under concurrent requests.

title: Blocked-email matching is case-sensitive and can be bypassed
body: The lookup compares the raw submitted email with the raw stored email. Email local/domain casing is commonly accepted by this application (and the domain restriction check is case-insensitive), so a blocked entry such as `spam@example.com` will not match a signup submitted as `Spam@Example.com` on the normal case-sensitive varchar comparison. Normalize emails consistently (for example with `Email.downcase(...).strip`) when storing and looking up blocked addresses, and enforce that normalization for existing/admin-created records as well.

title: Concurrent blocked-email checks lose match-count updates
body: `should_block?` reads `match_count`, increments it in Ruby, and saves the record. Multiple simultaneous signup attempts for the same blocked address can all read the same value and overwrite one another, so `match_count` and potentially the observed match state are inaccurate. Use an atomic database update such as `update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ...')` or locking/counter updates.

title: Non-matching blocked-email checks return nil instead of false
body: When no record exists, `record && ...` evaluates to `nil`, not `false`. This contradicts the included `be_false` example for this path (which will fail under RSpec's strict false matcher) and makes the predicate's return type inconsistent. Return an explicit boolean, e.g. `!!record && ...`.

title: Email-change flow bypasses the new blocked-email validation
body: `change_email` only checks uniqueness and then creates an `EmailToken` directly; it never assigns the address to the user and runs `User` validation before issuing the token. Consequently, an existing user can request and confirm a blocked address through this endpoint, bypassing `EmailValidator` and the blocked-email policy entirely. Validate the requested address (including the email validator) before creating the token, or enforce the policy in the token-confirmation path as well.

title: Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive while signup emails are not normalized
body: The lookup compares the supplied email verbatim, but signup assigns `params[:email]` directly and does not normalize it. A block entry such as `block@spamfromhome.org` can therefore be bypassed by registering `Block@spamfromhome.org` (and potentially other equivalent casing variants). Normalize both stored blocked addresses and lookup input using the application's canonical email normalization (`Email.downcase(...).strip`) and enforce uniqueness on that canonical value.

title: Match statistics are incremented once per validation pass, not once per signup attempt
body: Calling `BlockedEmail.should_block?` from the validator mutates `match_count` and `last_match_at` every time validations run. In `UsersController#create`, `user.valid?` is always called before `user.save`, and `save` validates again, so a single signup submission increments the counter twice (including for `do_nothing` records). Other callers that invoke `valid?` repeatedly have the same effect, making the recorded statistics inaccurate. Record an attempted match once at the request/policy boundary, or make validation side-effect-free.

title: Imported feed and remote HTML bypasses all post sanitization
body: `TopicEmbed.import` creates posts with `cook_method: raw_html`, and `Post#cook` returns that raw value unchanged. RSS `i.content` and readability output are external, attacker-controlled HTML, and the embed view later renders `raw post.cooked`. A malicious or compromised feed/article can therefore persist script/event-handler markup in a topic and execute it for forum and embedded-page visitors. Imported content must be sanitized with the same allowlist/sanitizer used for posts before it is stored or rendered; merely bypassing the cooking pipeline is unsafe.

title: Remote importer follows redirects to unvalidated hosts
body: The requested embed URL is host-checked before retrieval, but `open(url).read` follows HTTP redirects without revalidating the destination. An attacker can request a URL on the configured embeddable host that redirects to an internal service or cloud metadata endpoint, causing the server-side importer to fetch that resource (SSRF). Redirect destinations must be disabled or each redirect target must be parsed, host/IP validated, and restricted before fetching.

title: Resize postMessage uses the full Referer as target origin
body: `request.referer` normally includes a path and query string, but `postMessage` target origin must match the embedding window's origin. Passing a value such as `https://example.com/article?id=1` will not match the parent origin `https://example.com`, so the resize message is rejected and the iframe remains at its default height. Parse the referer and pass only its scheme/host/port origin.

title: Controller spec asserts a retrieval path the controller no longer implements
body: The test expects `TopicRetriever.new(...).retrieve`, but `EmbedController#best` actually calls `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)` when no embed exists. This expectation will fail rather than testing the implemented asynchronous behavior. The spec should assert the enqueued job and its arguments (and separately test `Jobs::RetrieveTopic` invokes `TopicRetriever`), otherwise the added test suite cannot pass and does not protect the actual contract.

title: Imported feed HTML bypasses Discourse sanitization
body: Imported content is stored with `cook_method: raw_html`, and `Post#cook` returns that raw value without running the normal cooking/sanitization pipeline. `PollFeed` passes arbitrary RSS/Atom item content directly into this method, so a feed containing `<script>`, event-handler attributes, or dangerous URLs can persist executable HTML. The embed view then renders `post.cooked` with `raw`, making this stored XSS execute for visitors of the embedding site (and the imported post may also be exposed through normal topic views). Sanitize imported HTML with the same allowlist used for posts before storing/rendering it, rather than using raw HTML as a sanitizer bypass.

title: Concurrent imports of the same URL can fail on the unique index
body: The code performs a non-locking lookup and then creates the `TopicEmbed`; two retrieve jobs for the same URL can both see no row and both create posts before one loses on the unique `embed_url` index. The losing transaction raises `ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique` and the job fails instead of returning the already-created embed. This is especially reachable because staff requests bypass throttling and scheduled feed polling can overlap retrieval. Handle the unique-conflict case (or use a locking/upsert strategy) and return/reload the winning embed.

title: Relative links without a leading slash are not converted to source URLs
body: `absolutize_urls` claims to convert relative URLs, but it only rewrites values beginning with `/`. Valid relative values such as `images/photo.jpg`, `../next.html`, and `page.html` remain relative in the stored raw HTML. When rendered by Discourse, browsers resolve them relative to the Discourse embed page rather than the source article, causing imported links and images to point to nonexistent or unintended local Discourse paths. Resolve all non-absolute HTTP(S) URLs against the source URI, while preserving fragment/mailto/etc. behavior as appropriate.

title: postMessage origin validation accepts unrelated origins that are URL substrings
body: The receiver treats an origin as trusted when it appears anywhere in `discourseUrl`. For example, if the forum URL is `https://forum.example.com/`, the distinct origin `https://forum.example.co` passes this check because it is a prefix substring. A page on such an origin can send `discourse-resize` messages and control the iframe height. Parse `discourseUrl` and compare `e.origin` for exact origin equality instead of using substring matching.

title: Unescaped Referer header is injected into executable JavaScript
body: `request.referer` is interpolated directly inside a single-quoted JavaScript string. The controller only verifies the parsed host, but an attacker can send a request with a forged Referer such as `https://<embeddable-host>/?x=';...` and cause arbitrary JavaScript to be emitted and executed under the Discourse origin. Serialize the value for JavaScript (and preferably derive and use only the validated origin) rather than interpolating the raw header.

title: Imported remote HTML bypasses Discourse's sanitizing cook pipeline
body: Posts created by `TopicEmbed.import` use `cook_method: raw_html`, and this branch returns `raw` unchanged. Feed content and readability-extracted page content are external, attacker-controlled HTML; `TopicEmbed.absolutize_urls` only rewrites relative links and does not sanitize tags, event handlers, scripts, or dangerous URL schemes. The resulting `post.cooked` is rendered with `raw post.cooked` in the embed view and can also be rendered in normal topic views, allowing a compromised feed/article source to execute script in forum visitors' browsers.

title: postMessage is sent to a full Referer URL instead of an origin
body: The second argument to `postMessage` must match the recipient's origin. `request.referer` normally includes the embedded page's path and query (for example `https://example.com/article`), so it does not equal the parent origin `https://example.com` and browsers will reject or fail to deliver the resize message. As a result, the iframe commonly remains at its default height. Build a scheme/host/port origin from the validated Referer before passing it to `postMessage`.

title: Message-origin validation accepts prefix origins
body: `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1` treats any origin string that is a substring/prefix of the configured Discourse URL as trusted. For example, with `https://forum.example.com/`, an origin such as `https://forum.example.co` passes this test. An untrusted frame can therefore send `discourse-resize` messages and set the Discourse iframe to an arbitrary height. Parse `discourseUrl` and compare `e.origin` for exact origin equality.

title: Flex layout disables the right-aligned small-action button
body: Making `.small-action` a flex container causes its direct child `button` to become a flex item. CSS floats do not apply to flex items, so the existing `float: right` on `.small-action button` is ignored. The button will now sit immediately after `.small-action-desc` rather than at the right edge, and long descriptions can leave it incorrectly positioned or squeezed. Add flex positioning such as `margin-left: auto` to the button (and appropriate sizing for the description) instead of relying on its float.

title: Header panel loses its right alignment in legacy flexbox implementations
body: The prior `float: right` was removed and replaced with `margin-left: auto` on a flex item. The legacy flexbox implementations targeted by the new `-ms-flexbox`/`-webkit-box` declarations, notably IE10's 2012 flexbox implementation, do not reliably support auto main-axis margins. In those browsers the panel will follow the title instead of being pushed to the right, potentially causing the header controls to overlap or overflow. Provide an old-flexbox-compatible alignment fallback (for example legacy box packing/flex sizing) or retain a non-flex fallback for these browsers.

title: The small-action button no longer aligns to the right after its parent becomes flex
body: `.small-action` is now a flex container, so its direct `button` is a flex item and its existing `float: right` is ignored by CSS. The button will be laid out immediately after `.small-action-desc` instead of at the right edge as before, which can visibly break the post-action row and make it overflow when the description is long. Give the button an appropriate flex alignment rule (for example `margin-left: auto`) rather than relying on float.

title: Making `.small-action` a flex container disables its right-aligned button
body: The direct `button` child still relies on `float: right` (line 309) to be placed at the right edge. Floats on flex items are ignored, so after this change the button participates in the flex flow immediately after `.small-action-desc` instead of being right-aligned. Small-action controls will therefore move beside the description (and may overflow or be poorly positioned for long descriptions) rather than retaining their existing placement.

title: `website_name` bypasses the anonymous TL0 profile-field restriction
body: The new `website_name` attribute is declared as a normal serializer attribute but is not included in `untrusted_attributes`. For an anonymous viewer of a TL0 user, `website` is intentionally omitted by `restrict_user_fields?`, but `website_name` is still serialized and reveals the host (and, for same-domain URLs, the path) from that hidden website field. Add `website_name` to `untrusted_attributes` (or implement an equivalent `include_website_name?` authorization check). The currently added `include_website_name` method also lacks the required trailing `?`, so it is not the serializer inclusion hook and does not prevent this disclosure.

title: Derived website name bypasses TL0 profile-field restrictions
body: `website_name` is serialized independently of `website` and is not included in `untrusted_attributes`. For a trust-level-0 user viewed anonymously, `include_website?` suppresses the website URL, but the new attribute is still emitted and contains the website host and, for matching instance domains, the full path. The profile page will render that value even though the underlying website field is intentionally hidden, leaking restricted profile information. Apply the same visibility predicate to `website_name` (for example by adding it to `untrusted_attributes`) and add a TL0-with-website serialization test.

title: Website-name inclusion predicate is misnamed and never used
body: ActiveModel serializer inclusion predicates use the `include_<attribute>?` method name, as elsewhere in this serializer. This defines `include_website_name` without the question mark, so it is ignored and `website_name` is serialized for every response, including as `null` when no website exists. Rename it to `include_website_name?` so the newly introduced field follows the intended optional-attribute contract.

title: `website_name` bypasses the anonymous TL0 website privacy restriction
body: `website` is an `untrusted_attribute`, so `include_website?` suppresses it when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` is true (for example, an anonymous viewer of a TL0 user). The new `website_name` attribute has no equivalent restriction and computes its value directly from `object.user_profile.website`, exposing at least the external hostname and, for same-domain URLs, the complete profile path even though the website field is intentionally hidden. Additionally, the inclusion predicate is named `include_website_name` rather than the serializer convention `include_website_name?`, so it will not be used as the attribute predicate. Define `include_website_name?` and apply the same visibility condition as `include_website?`; add an anonymous TL0 serialization test asserting that `website_name` is absent.

title: The light-theme color was changed from the original 30% to 70%
body: The embedded-post author link previously used `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)`, but the new `dark-light-choose` light-theme branch uses 70%. This changes the appearance of this link on every non-dark theme, rather than only selecting an appropriate `$secondary`-based value for dark themes. Keep the original 30% primary value and use the corresponding dark-theme secondary value (as is done for comparable username links).

title: Group member names lose their intended light-theme emphasis
body: The `.group-member-info .name` rule previously used `$primary` at 30% lightness, but the change replaces its light-theme branch with `$primary` at 50%. Consequently, group member names render differently in light themes even though this change should only correct dark-theme colors. Preserve the 30% primary branch and use the appropriate `$secondary` branch for dark themes.

title: Mobile group member names lose their intended light-theme emphasis
body: The mobile `.group-member-info .name` rule previously used `$primary` at 30% lightness, while the new light-theme branch uses 50%. This regresses the existing light-theme rendering and also makes mobile inconsistent with the intended username/name styling. The light branch should remain 30% primary, with a secondary-based dark branch.

title: Custom message length hint uses reversed lightness choices
body: This rule previously used `$primary` at 70% lightness. The replacement changes the light-theme value to 30% primary and chooses 70% secondary for dark themes, reversing the expected polarity in both modes. The desktop version of the same `.custom-message-length` rule uses 70% primary / 30% secondary; mobile should use the same values so the hint remains consistently muted and legible.

title: Mobile topic-map heading was changed to the wrong lightness level
body: `.topic-map h3` previously used `$primary` at 20% lightness, but this patch changes it to 50% for the light-theme branch and 50% secondary for dark themes. This is not a secondary substitution of the original color; it changes the heading contrast in light themes and does not match the desktop topic-map heading, which uses 20% primary / 80% secondary. Retain the 20%/80% pairing.

title: Quote author link no longer preserves the light-theme color
body: The original color was `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)`, but the light branch of the new `dark-light-choose` expression is `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%)`. This makes embedded-post author links substantially lighter in light themes, contrary to the intended dark-theme-only substitution. Keep the primary branch at 30% and use the complementary secondary value (70%) for the dark branch.

title: Mobile modal message length uses the wrong light and dark variants
body: This changes a previous `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%)` to a light branch of primary 30% and a dark branch of secondary 70%. The light-theme appearance regresses, and the dark-theme value is the inverse of the intended complementary secondary value. The light branch should remain primary 70%, with secondary 30% selected for dark themes.

title: Mobile topic-map heading loses its intended emphasis
body: The previous heading color was `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%)`, but this replacement uses 50% for both branches. As a result, topic-map headings become much more muted in light themes and do not receive the expected secondary 80% counterpart in dark themes. Preserve primary 20% in the light branch and use secondary 80% in the dark branch.

title: Desktop group member names use a different light-theme shade
body: The group-member name was previously primary at 30% lightness, but the new expression uses primary 50% in its light branch. This unnecessarily changes the light-theme styling while also selecting secondary 50% rather than the complementary secondary 70% for dark themes. Use `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 70%))`.

title: Mobile group member names use a different light-theme shade
body: The old mobile group-member name color was primary at 30% lightness, but the replacement changes it to primary 50% and secondary 50%. This regresses the existing light-theme contrast and does not apply the complementary secondary 70% needed in dark themes. Preserve the primary 30% branch and use secondary 70% for the dark branch.

title: Light-theme color for embedded post author links was changed incorrectly
body: The original light-theme value for `.embedded-posts .topic-meta-data h5 a` was `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)`, but this change uses `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%)` as the first `dark-light-choose` argument. This makes the link substantially dimmer in light themes, rather than preserving existing light-theme behavior while adding the dark-theme alternative. The first argument should remain 30% (with the appropriate secondary-based dark value).

title: Group member names no longer preserve their light-theme emphasis
body: `.group-member-info .name` previously used `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)`, but the new light-theme branch is `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%)`. This changes the appearance in light themes even though the intended change is to use `$secondary` for dark themes. Preserve the 30% primary lightness in the first branch and add the corresponding secondary-based dark branch.

title: Mobile group member names use the wrong light-theme lightness
body: The mobile `.group-member-info .name` rule had a 30% primary lightness before this PR, but now selects a 50% primary lightness in light themes. As a result, mobile light-theme member names lose their previous visual emphasis. Keep `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)` as the light branch while adding the secondary-based dark branch.

title: Modal message-length hint reverses its intended light-theme contrast
body: `.custom-message-length` originally used `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%)`, but the newly added light-theme branch is `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)`. This alters light-theme hint text rather than only fixing dark-theme rendering, and makes it much darker than before. Retain the 70% primary branch and choose the appropriate secondary-derived value for dark mode.

title: Mobile topic-map heading lost its original light-theme color
body: The `.topic-map h3` rule originally used `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%)`, but this change substitutes a 50% primary light-theme value. This is an unintended light-theme regression; the desktop counterpart preserves 20% and uses 80% secondary for dark mode. The mobile rule should likewise keep the 20% primary branch and use the secondary-based dark branch.

title: Pagination creates a phantom page for exact page-size member counts
body: `totalPages` uses `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`, which returns 2 for a group with exactly 50 members and a limit of 50 (and similarly for every exact multiple). The Next control is therefore enabled and requests offset 50, producing an empty member page. Use `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)` (while retaining the zero-member special case) so the last populated page is correctly identified.

title: Automatic groups still render a member removal control
body: This item view's context is an individual `member`, so `automatic` is looked up on that user rather than on the group being edited. It will normally be undefined, making `unless automatic` true even for automatic groups. As a result, admins see a removable-x control for automatic-group members; clicking it sends a request that the server rejects. Pass the group's automatic state into the item view or conditionally render the entire member list/control from the parent group context.

title: Members endpoint accepts an unbounded client-controlled page size
body: `limit` is taken directly from the request and passed to ActiveRecord without a maximum. A request such as `?limit=1000000` can force serialization of an entire large group's membership in one response; on PostgreSQL, a negative LIMIT may also mean no limit. This public endpoint should clamp the value to a positive, bounded page size before querying to prevent expensive queries, excessive memory use, and oversized responses.

title: Pagination creates a phantom page for exact multiples of the page size
body: `totalPages` uses `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`, so a group with exactly 50 members (or any exact multiple of `limit`) reports two pages. The Next control remains enabled, requests offset 50, and displays an empty member list. This also occurs after deleting the final member on a partially filled last page when the count becomes an exact multiple. Use `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)` (while preserving the zero-member special case) and clamp/reload the offset as needed.

title: Pagination creates an extra empty page for exact page-size totals
body: `totalPages` uses `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`, which is one too high whenever the member count is an exact multiple of the page size. For example, a group with 50 members and a limit of 50 is displayed as having two pages; clicking next requests offset 50 and renders an empty member list. Use `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)` (while retaining the zero-member special case) so the navigation and `showingLast` state match the available results.

title: Public member-list pagination accepts an unbounded client-controlled limit
body: The `members` endpoint applies `params[:limit].to_i` directly to the relation and serializes every selected user. Any user allowed to see a group (including an anonymous user for visible groups) can request an arbitrarily large limit and force loading and serializing the entire membership in one response. Clamp the limit to a reasonable maximum and normalize invalid/non-positive values; this also avoids malformed values causing database offset/limit errors.

title: Out-of-order member requests can replace the currently selected page
body: Each `findMembers` completion unconditionally writes `offset`, `members`, and pagination metadata to the shared group model. If a user clicks next and then previous before the first request finishes, the previous-page request can complete first and the stale next-page response can complete afterward, leaving the UI on the wrong page while the model offset no longer reflects the user's latest action. Cancel superseded requests or associate a request/version token with each load and ignore stale responses.

title: Fallback catalogs are only eagerly loaded for controller requests
body: The fallback locale files are loaded only through `ApplicationController#set_locale`, while the translation accelerator automatically loads only `I18n.config.locale` during a normal `I18n.t` call. The Fallbacks backend subsequently reads the default/en locale catalog directly; it does not invoke the patched top-level translator for each fallback locale. Consequently mailers, background jobs, rake tasks, model code, and any boot-time translation that run outside an ApplicationController can report a missing translation even when it exists in the configured fallback locale. Ensure fallback locales are loaded as part of the generic translation/fallback lookup path rather than relying on the controller filter.

title: Fallback locale files are not loaded for translations outside controller requests
body: The translation accelerator only loads `config.locale` before calling the backend. `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` performs fallback lookups by invoking the backend directly for the fallback locale, so it does not re-enter `I18n.translate` and therefore does not load that locale's YAML file. The new `ApplicationController#set_locale` works around this only for controller actions; jobs, mailers, models, rake tasks, and any translation performed before that callback can fall back to an unloaded default/en locale and return missing-translation errors even when the fallback translation exists. Loading every locale in `I18n.fallbacks[config.locale]` as part of translation (or otherwise ensuring this globally) is needed.

title: Fallback catalogs are not loaded for translations outside controller requests
body: The translation accelerator only lazy-loads `config.locale`. The new fallback backend then searches `SiteSetting.default_locale` and `:en` directly inside the backend, bypassing `I18n.translate` and therefore bypassing this loader. `ApplicationController#set_locale` works around this for HTTP requests by explicitly loading the whole fallback chain, but mailers, background jobs, model validations, and any other server-side `I18n.t` caller do not run that filter. In those contexts a missing translation in the active locale will still be reported as missing rather than being resolved from the configured fallback locale.

title: No tests cover the custom fallback chain with lazy-loaded translations
body: This introduces a custom fallback implementation plus explicit catalog loading, but the change contains no regression tests for resolving a key missing from a user locale through the site default and then English. Tests should exercise the translation accelerator as well as request and non-request contexts; otherwise failures caused by fallback catalogs not being loaded, incorrect fallback ordering, or locale-setting changes will not be detected.

title: Denial-cache keys are ambiguous for valid resource and folder UIDs
body: The key concatenates `action`, `name`, and `parent` using `_` without escaping or length-prefixing the variable fields. Dashboard and folder UIDs can contain underscores, so a denial for `(name="a_b", parent="c")` produces the same key as `(name="a", parent="b_c")` for the same user/action/namespace. Once the first request is denied, the second request is returned as denied directly from the cache for 30 seconds even if its database permissions allow it. Use an unambiguous encoding of the individual fields (and preferably a distinct denial-cache key prefix).

title: Per-resource denial entries allow unbounded cache growth from request input
body: Every denied `Check` inserts a distinct cache entry keyed by the caller-supplied resource name and parent folder. Unlike the permission cache, whose cardinality is bounded roughly by users and actions, this cache can be populated with arbitrary nonexistent names by repeatedly issuing authorization checks. The configured TTL only bounds retention to 30 seconds and the local cache configuration has no capacity limit here, so sufficient request volume can create a large transient memory footprint (and equivalent key churn in a shared cache). Bound this cache by size/admission policy, avoid caching arbitrary nonexistent resource names, or otherwise rate-limit/normalize these entries.

title: Denial entries prevent the intended database refresh after permissions change
body: A cached denial is returned before checking the permission cache or re-querying the database, and nothing in this change invalidates `permDenialCache` when a resource or permission is created. Consequently, if a check for a known dashboard/folder UID is denied before its permission is written, all subsequent checks for that same UID remain denied for `shortCacheTTL` (30 seconds), even though the database now grants access. This bypasses the newly added stale-cache fallback and can still prevent creators from accessing newly created resources. Denial entries need invalidation on permission/resource changes or must not be used when freshness is required.

title: Denial cache conflates anonymous and renderer identities
body: The denial key includes only `UserUID`, not `IdentityType` or the full subject. Anonymous and renderer subjects both commonly use ID `0` (as represented by `anonymous:0` and `render:0`), so an anonymous denial for a dashboard read stores the same key later used by the renderer. The renderer request will then return the cached denial instead of its built-in read-all permission for up to 30 seconds. Include the identity type/full subject in the key.

title: Delimited denial-cache key is ambiguous for resource and folder UIDs
body: `name` and `parent` are concatenated with `_` without escaping or length-prefixing. Since dashboard and folder UIDs can contain underscores, distinct pairs such as name `dash_a` with parent `folder` and name `dash` with parent `a_folder` generate the same cache key. A denial for one resource context can therefore incorrectly deny access to the other until expiry. Use an unambiguous encoding (for example JSON, escaped components, or length-prefixed fields).

title: Denial cache is shared across distinct identity types with the same identifier
body: The denial cache key contains only `UserUID`, not `IdentityType`, yet it is consulted before permissions are loaded for users, anonymous identities, and render-service identities. For example, an `anonymous:0` check denied for a dashboard stores the same key subsequently used by `render:0`; the renderer request will then be denied from cache even though `getRendererPermissions` grants renderer read access. Include the identity type in `userPermDenialCacheKey` (and update callers/tests) so a negative result for one subject class cannot poison another class's authorization decisions.

title: Silence action is displayed but cannot open a drawer for Prometheus-only list items
body: The new GrafanaRuleListItem supplies only promRule, so rule is undefined in this component. AlertRuleMenu now correctly grants the Silence menu item from the Prometheus rule ability and clicking it sets showSilenceDrawer, but the drawer is rendered only when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true. With no ruler rule this condition is always false, so selecting “Silence notifications” has no effect in the new list view.

title: Pause is unavailable for Grafana rules rendered without a ruler response
body: canPause includes the new Grafana Prometheus-rule ability, but the actual pause menu item additionally requires rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule). The new list item intentionally passes no rulerRule, so even an authorized user with a pausable Grafana Prometheus rule never sees the Pause/Resume action. This regresses rule pausing in the ruler-free list view.

title: Delete is hidden for Grafana rules in the ruler-free list view
body: canDelete now includes permissions derived from promRule, but Delete is still rendered only when rulerRule is present. GrafanaRuleListItem passes only a Prometheus rule, therefore authorized users cannot delete any Grafana-managed rule from the new alert list even though the delete modal already receives a usable identifier and group identifier.

title: Federated rules are no longer treated as immutable
body: The previous ability implementation checked isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) before enabling update/delete/pause actions. The refactored ruler-only function no longer receives the group and hard-codes isFederated to false. Consequently federated external rule groups can expose edit, delete, pause, and related controls whenever other permissions permit them, despite the prior behavior explicitly marking them immutable.

title: Grafana rule list elements no longer have React keys
body: This branch is produced inside rules.map but GrafanaRuleListItem is rendered without key={key}, unlike the datasource and unknown branches and unlike the previous GrafanaRuleLoader. React will treat these rows as unkeyed siblings, producing warnings and allowing row-local state (such as open action UI) to be associated with the wrong rule when the result list changes.

title: Silence action shown for Prometheus-only Grafana rules cannot open a drawer
body: The new list passes only `promRule` to this component. `AlertRuleMenu` now correctly enables and renders “Silence notifications” using the Prometheus-rule ability, but clicking it only sets `showSilenceDrawer`; the drawer is still rendered only when a ruler alerting rule exists. Consequently the menu item is a no-op for every Grafana rule rendered by `GrafanaRuleListItem`.

title: Delete is unavailable for Grafana rules after removing ruler data from the list
body: For the new Prometheus-only Grafana list items, `canDelete` can be true from `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`, but the Delete menu item is additionally gated on `rulerRule`. Since `GrafanaRuleListItem` never supplies a ruler rule, users with delete permission cannot delete Grafana-managed rules from either the filtered list or group list. The supplied delete handler already closes over the identifier, so this condition prevents an otherwise supported action.

title: Pause is unavailable for Prometheus-only Grafana list entries
body: The menu computes `canPause` using the new Grafana Prometheus ability, but only renders `MenuItemPauseRule` when a Grafana ruler rule is present. The new list deliberately supplies no ruler rule, so pausing/unpausing Grafana-managed rules disappears from the list even for authorized users. This leaves the newly added Prometheus pause permission path unusable.

title: Federated rules lose their immutability protection
body: `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` previously detected federated rule groups from `CombinedRule.group` and treated them as immutable. It now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, where federation is hard-coded to false because only a group identifier is available. Existing consumers of `useAlertRuleAbility`/`useAlertRuleAbilities` can therefore expose update, delete, pause, restore, and permanent-delete controls for federated external rules that were intentionally protected before this change.

title: Grafana rule links no longer preserve the originating list URL
body: The former Grafana list item added `createReturnTo()` to its view URL. The replacement constructs a bare `/alerting/grafana/<uid>/view` URL, so opening a rule from a filtered or paginated rule list no longer provides the detail page with the originating location. The detail page’s return navigation will fall back to its default list instead of restoring the user’s filters/context.

title: Silence action is rendered but cannot open its drawer for Prometheus-only list rules
body: The list now supplies only `promRule` for Grafana rules, so `AlertRuleMenu` can correctly enable and render “Silence notifications” from the new Prometheus-rule ability. Clicking it sets `showSilenceDrawer`, but the drawer is only rendered when a ruler alerting rule is present. For every Grafana rule in the new list this condition is false, making the visible silence menu item a no-op.

title: Delete is hidden for Grafana rules after removing ruler data
body: `canDelete` now includes the Prometheus-rule permission result, but the delete menu item still additionally requires `rulerRule`. `GrafanaRuleListItem` invokes this menu with only `promRule`, so users with delete permission never receive a Delete action in the alert list. The delete handler already closes over the identifier in `RuleActionsButtons`, so the ruler-rule guard prevents an otherwise available operation.

title: Pause is hidden for every Grafana rule in the ruler-free list
body: The new Grafana Prometheus ability can make `canPause` true, but rendering the pause item still requires a `rulerRule`. The new list intentionally provides no ruler rule, so pausable Grafana-managed rules no longer expose a pause/unpause action there despite the permissions calculation indicating that the action is supported and allowed.

title: Federated ruler rule groups are no longer treated as immutable
body: The previous ability implementation called `isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` and disabled mutable actions for federated groups. This replacement unconditionally sets `isFederated` to false because it no longer receives the group. Consequently edit, delete, pause, restore, and related actions can be presented for federated external rule groups that were previously intentionally immutable; attempting them may fail server-side or permit unsupported edits.

title: Grafana rule list items no longer have React keys
body: The old `GrafanaRuleLoader` received `key={key}`, but the replacement `GrafanaRuleListItem` is returned without a key. Multiple Grafana results in the `<ul>` therefore trigger React's missing-key warning and are reconciled by position, which can cause stateful child UI (such as an opened action menu) to be associated with the wrong rule when result ordering changes or additional batches are inserted.

title: Shard-split queries have template variables and ad-hoc filters applied twice
body: This interpolates targets with `applyTemplateVariables` before shard discovery, then every generated shard request is passed to `runSplitQuery`, which now calls `applyTemplateVariables` again on those already-interpolated targets. When `request.filters` contains ad-hoc filters, the filter matchers are injected both times; this can produce duplicate/conflicting label matchers or otherwise change the query sent to Loki. The previous path interpolated once. Preserve the initial interpolation needed for shard discovery, but avoid applying filters/template processing a second time when delegating the already-prepared shard request to `runSplitQuery`.

title: Queries that interpolate to an empty expression are not discarded
body: The code filters empty expressions before calling `applyTemplateVariables`, so a target such as `{ expr: "$query" }` whose variable resolves to an empty string remains in the splitting groups. It is then classified and sent as an empty LogQL expression instead of receiving the existing empty-query behavior (ignore it). Filter again after interpolation, or interpolate before the empty-expression filter, so an empty variable value does not result in a backend parse/error request.

title: An expression emptied by interpolation can leave the shard path with no runnable requests
body: As in the time-splitting path, emptiness is tested before interpolation. If interpolation turns the expression into an empty string, this target is retained in the shard group and later passed to `runSplitQuery`. `runSplitQuery` then filters that empty target out before building requests, leaving an empty request list; its grouped runner attempts to start from `requests[0]` and can fail rather than cleanly ignoring the query. Perform the empty-expression filtering after `applyTemplateVariables` in this entry point.

title: Drop queries that become empty during interpolation
body: The empty-expression filter runs before `applyTemplateVariables`. A target such as `expr: '$optionalQuery'` can therefore become `''` after its variable is resolved, but is still classified and sent to Loki as a split metric/log query. This produces unnecessary requests and can surface backend parse errors for dashboards that intentionally use an empty optional query. Filter the interpolated targets again (or interpolate before filtering).

title: Shard-split requests interpolate template filters twice
body: `runShardSplitQuery` interpolates each target here, then passes the resulting sharded `subRequest` to `runSplitQuery`, which now calls `datasource.applyTemplateVariables` again for every shard group. The second call receives the same `request.filters`; template application is not generally safe to repeat, particularly when dashboard/ad-hoc filters are injected into the LogQL selector, so filters can be duplicated or the query can be altered/invalid. Interpolate only once for a sharded execution, or ensure the nested time-splitting path does not reapply template variables to already interpolated targets.

title: Shard splitting no longer ignores targets interpolated to an empty expression
body: The previous flow interpolated targets before filtering out empty expressions, whereas this change filters `query.expr` before `applyTemplateVariables`. If a variable-backed expression resolves to an empty string, it is retained and proceeds through shard selector discovery and the nested split query, potentially issuing invalid empty LogQL requests instead of behaving as a disabled/empty target. Filter the mapped targets for a non-empty `expr` before calling `splitQueriesByStreamShard`.

title: Drop targets whose expression becomes empty during interpolation
body: The expression is filtered before `applyTemplateVariables`, but interpolation can legitimately resolve a variable-based expression to an empty string. Such a target remains in `queries` and is then classified and sent to Loki as an empty query instead of being treated like the existing empty-query filtering intends. Filter the mapped targets again (or interpolate before filtering on `expr`) so an empty variable value cannot produce an invalid backend request.

title: Shard splitting can hang or throw for expressions emptied by interpolation
body: This filters `query.expr` before template interpolation. If interpolation resolves an expression to an empty value, the empty target is passed into shard grouping and eventually delegated to `runSplitQuery`; that function filters the now-empty target out, produces an empty `requests` array, and `runSplitGroupedQueries` dereferences the nonexistent longest partition. Since this occurs from the async grouping continuation, the observable can remain unresolved with an unhandled exception. Interpolate first and discard targets whose resulting expression is empty, matching the prior shard path's effective ordering.

title: Plugin request logs no longer include the trace ID
body: The previous LoggerMiddleware explicitly added `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` as the `traceID` field on each completed plugin request log. That logic was removed, but the replacement contextual attributes contain only endpoint, plugin, datasource, and user values; `instrumentContext` does not add the trace ID. `LoggerMiddleware` now only reads these contextual attributes via `FromContext`, so requests with an active trace will lose the `traceID` log field and can no longer be correlated with traces as before. Add the trace ID to the contextual attributes (when present) or retain explicit trace-ID logging.

title: TestLogger drops logs made through FromContext
body: FromContext returns a fresh TestLogger with independent log counters instead of a contextual view of the receiver. LoggerMiddleware now always logs through `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)`, so when callers/tests provide a TestLogger, the completed-request entry is written to an unreachable temporary logger and is not observable on the logger they supplied. Return the receiver or a derived fake sharing the same backing log storage (and ideally retaining contextual fields).

title: Plugin request completion logs no longer include the trace ID
body: This change removes the explicit `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` extraction that previously appended `traceID` to every plugin request completion log. The new contextual middleware only adds endpoint/plugin/user/data-source attributes; it does not add a trace ID. Consequently, requests that have an active trace can no longer be correlated from the `Plugin Request Completed` log event to their trace, regressing existing observability behavior. Preserve the explicit trace field or ensure the contextual logger path adds the same `traceID` attribute.

title: TestLogger drops log calls made through FromContext
body: `FromContext` returns a newly allocated `TestLogger`, so a call such as `logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)` records on an unreachable logger rather than on the fake supplied by the test. `LoggerMiddleware` now logs exclusively through this path, making assertions on the original `TestLogger` silently miss request-completion logs. Make the fake retain/shared-recording state (or return itself for `FromContext`) and add coverage that verifies contextual logger middleware attributes reach the logger middleware.

title: Rejected devices are cached as successfully tagged
body: `tagDeviceUI` adds the device ID to the local cache before `CreateOrUpdateDevice` enforces the configured limit. When a new device is rejected with `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, its cache entry remains for the cache TTL; a subsequent request with the same `X-Grafana-Device-Id` returns early at line 83 without touching the store, so `Authenticate` sees no error and permits anonymous access. Set the cache entry only after a successful store write (and do not cache failed tagging attempts).

title: Device limit check and insertion are not atomic
body: The limit is enforced by a `COUNT` in one database session followed by an upsert in another session. Concurrent requests can all observe a count below `deviceLimit` and then each insert a distinct device ID, exceeding the configured limit; this also occurs across Grafana instances. The count/check/insert needs database-level serialization or an atomic conditional insert/transaction with appropriate locking.

title: Device limit check is not atomic and can be exceeded by concurrent requests
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts active devices in one database session and performs the insert/upsert later in a separate session. Multiple requests for distinct device IDs can all observe a count below deviceLimit and then all insert successfully, so the configured limit is not enforced under normal concurrent anonymous traffic (or across Grafana instances). The limit check and admission of a new device need to be made atomic, for example with a transaction/locking or a database-backed reservation scheme; a concurrent integration test should cover simultaneous new-device requests.

title: An unauthenticated caller can exhaust the global device limit with arbitrary device IDs
body: The device ID is taken from the client-controlled X-Grafana-Device-Id header and each distinct value is persisted as a new device until the global limit is reached. An attacker can send requests with generated header values to fill all slots, after which legitimate anonymous users are rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached while the attacker's known IDs remain admitted. This turns the setting into an easy anonymous denial-of-service vector; admission should not rely solely on an arbitrary caller-provided identifier, or should include protections such as a signed/server-issued identifier and appropriate abuse controls.

title: Rejected devices are cached and bypass the limit on retry
body: `tagDeviceUI` inserts the device ID into `localCache` before calling `CreateOrUpdateDevice`. When the store returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, this method now propagates that error and the first authentication is rejected, but the cache entry remains. A subsequent request using the same new device ID hits the cache at lines 83-84, skips the store and limit check entirely, and is authenticated. Set the cache entry only after a successful store write, or remove it when the write fails.

title: Device limit check is not atomic with device creation
body: The active-device count is read in one database session and the later INSERT/UPSERT is performed in another session. Concurrent requests for different device IDs can all observe a count below `deviceLimit` and then all insert successfully, exceeding the configured limit; this is especially likely during bursts or across Grafana instances. Enforce the count and insertion atomically using an appropriate transaction/locking strategy (or a database-level reservation mechanism).

title: Configured batch sizes can exceed non-SQLite parameter limits
body: The new delete path binds one SQL parameter per selected ID, but only SQLite is handled specially. Grafana also supports SQL Server, which rejects statements with more than 2100 parameters; a configured annotation cleanup batch size such as the 32767 value exercised by this PR will therefore make cleanup fail on SQL Server. MySQL/PostgreSQL also have finite prepared-statement parameter limits. The old subquery-based delete did not create one bound parameter per row. Cap/split the ID list according to the active dialect's parameter limit (or use a dialect-safe alternative) before issuing the DELETE.

title: Normal cleanup batches are logged as errors with the complete ID list
body: Each successful ID fetch and delete is logged through `r.log.Error`, including every selected annotation/tag ID. This emits false error events even when `err` is nil and can serialize tens of thousands of IDs for one batch (the added test configures 32767). With cleanup enabled this creates substantial log volume, error-alert noise, and potentially expensive formatting/storage on every cleanup cycle. Use an appropriate debug-level summary and avoid logging the full ID list; the same issue is repeated in the count and orphan-tag paths.

title: The PR increases the frequency of every cleanup job from ten minutes to one minute
body: This changes the scheduler for the entire cleanup job list, not just annotation cleanup, causing temporary-file scans and all database cleanup operations to run ten times as often. The PR description only calls for splitting annotation cleanup statements, so this unrelated change can significantly increase database/disk load and make the nine-minute cleanup window much more likely to be continuously occupied. Revert this interval change or explicitly justify and isolate a different annotation-cleanup schedule.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors with full ID lists
body: Every normal cleanup batch emits `Error` logs even when `err` is nil, and includes the complete batch of annotation IDs. The same happens for the delete and orphan-tag paths. Large configured batches can therefore generate very large error-level log entries for each batch, causing log-volume/cost spikes and potentially triggering error-based alerts despite successful cleanup. These should be debug-level progress logs (and generally avoid serializing all IDs), while actual errors should be logged only when an operation fails.

title: The PR increases the cadence of every cleanup job by 10x
body: Changing the shared cleanup ticker from ten minutes to one minute reruns not only annotation cleanup but also snapshot, dashboard-version, image, invite, short-URL, and query-history cleanup ten times as often. This materially increases database scans, delete load, and background work for all deployments, and is unrelated to splitting annotation cleanup queries. Keep the existing scheduler cadence or make a shorter annotation-specific cadence/configuration if the new cleanup behavior requires faster retries.

title: Max-count cleanup can delete annotations that should be retained after concurrent deletions
body: The IDs to remove are selected in one statement and deleted later without rechecking the max-count condition. For example, with 101 annotations and MaxCount=100, this selects the oldest annotation; if a user deletes any newer annotation before `deleteByIDs` runs, the selected annotation is now one of the 100 that should remain, but it is still deleted, leaving only 99. The former single DELETE evaluated selection and deletion atomically. Revalidate the retention condition during deletion or otherwise serialize cleanup with annotation deletes.

title: Configured batch sizes above SQL Server's parameter limit now fail cleanup
body: The new delete uses one bound parameter per selected ID. SQL Server permits at most 2,100 parameters per statement, while `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` is configurable and this change explicitly supports much larger values (the test uses 32,767). Previously the IDs were selected inside the DELETE SQL and did not consume bind parameters. On MSSQL, a batch size above the parameter limit will make cleanup fail instead of deleting annotations. Split IDs into dialect-safe chunks (or impose and validate a dialect-specific maximum).

title: Successful cleanup batches emit full ID lists as error logs
body: Every batch logs at Error level even when `err` is nil, and includes the complete list of annotation IDs. This can emit thousands or tens of thousands of IDs per batch (the configured batch size can be 32,767), creating substantial log volume and falsely signaling failures to log-based alerting. Remove the IDs and use an appropriate debug-level message, reserving Error for actual failures.

title: The change runs every cleanup job ten times more frequently
body: Changing the ticker from ten minutes to one minute affects all cleanup jobs, not only annotations: snapshot, dashboard-version, image, invite, short-URL, and query-history deletion now execute ten times as often. This materially increases database and filesystem load in every deployment, with no configuration or stated requirement for the unrelated cadence change. Keep the existing cadence or make any required annotation-specific frequency explicit and configurable.

title: Legacy writes inherit a request context that is cancelled after the response
body: The asynchronous legacy write derives its timeout context from the request context. HTTP/Kubernetes request contexts are cancelled when the handler returns, which happens immediately after the unified-storage write response is returned. Consequently the goroutine will commonly invoke Legacy.Create with an already-cancelled context (and the same applies to Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection), so the intended legacy safety copy is silently skipped or aborted. Create a detached context (for example, context.WithoutCancel(ctx)) before applying the bounded timeout, while preserving needed request metadata.

title: Asynchronous legacy writes can be applied out of unified-storage order
body: Each successful write starts an independent goroutine with no per-resource ordering or serialization. Unified storage can commit a create followed by an update/delete, while their legacy goroutines run in the opposite order: an update may fail because the create has not reached legacy yet, or a delayed create may recreate stale data after a successful legacy delete. This leaves the legacy store divergent despite both operations succeeding in unified storage. Legacy replication needs an ordered per-resource queue/retry mechanism (including handling failed predecessors), rather than one unconstrained goroutine per request.

title: Every write can retain an unbounded goroutine for ten seconds
body: A goroutine is spawned for every successful write and may remain blocked in a legacy storage call until the ten-second timeout. There is no concurrency limit, queue bound, or backpressure, so a legacy outage combined with normal or burst write traffic accumulates arbitrarily many goroutines and pending request objects, risking memory/resource exhaustion. Use a bounded worker queue or concurrency limiter and define behavior when it is full.

title: Mode 3 records several storage outcomes against the wrong metrics
body: When Create or Update fails in unified storage, the code calls recordLegacyDuration (lines 45 and 129) instead of recordStorageDuration, so unified failures are reported as legacy failures. Additionally, successful Delete uses the object name as the kind label (line 106), and the asynchronous DeleteCollection legacy operation calls recordStorageDuration (line 166). These produce misleading duration/error metrics and high-cardinality labels, preventing operators from reliably detecting which backend is failing.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request cancellation context
body: The goroutine derives its timeout context from the incoming request context. Once the REST handler returns its successful unified-storage response, the server cancels that request context, which immediately cancels the legacy operation as well (the 10-second timeout does not detach it from its parent). Consequently legacy creates, updates, deletes, and collection deletes can be aborted simply because the response was sent, defeating the intended asynchronous mirror write. Create a detached context (while preserving needed values/logging) before applying the legacy-write timeout.

title: Independent goroutines allow legacy mutations to be applied out of order
body: Every successful unified write starts an independent legacy-write goroutine with no ordering or per-object serialization. For example, a client can create an object and immediately update or delete it: unified storage observes that order, but the legacy update/delete can run before the legacy create, or the create can complete after a delete. This leaves the legacy store missing mutations or containing stale/deleted objects. The asynchronous replication path needs an ordered queue/worker (at least keyed by resource) or another mechanism that preserves mutation ordering.

title: Legacy update re-evaluates UpdatedObjectInfo instead of mirroring the unified update result
body: After Storage.Update has invoked objInfo to produce and persist the unified object, the asynchronous Legacy.Update receives the original objInfo and invokes it again against legacy state. UpdatedObjectInfo callbacks are not guaranteed to be idempotent: they may depend on the old object, apply generated values, or perform request-scoped work. Thus the two stores can receive different updates, and the callback is unexpectedly evaluated twice. The prior implementation computed the update once and used wrappers to supply the resulting object to both writes; mode 3 needs to preserve that behavior while making the legacy write asynchronous.

title: Several mode 3 metrics are recorded against the wrong operation or labels
body: The Create and Update unified-storage error paths call recordLegacyDuration (lines 45 and 129), and the legacy DeleteCollection goroutine calls recordStorageDuration (line 166). In addition, successful Delete records the resource name as the kind label (line 106). These paths make storage/legacy latency and error metrics inaccurate and can create a high-cardinality metric label from arbitrary object names, preventing reliable monitoring of replication failures.

title: Mode 3 unit tests do not verify completion of asynchronous legacy writes
body: The tests return immediately after the unified call and never synchronize with the spawned legacy goroutine or assert mock expectations. They can therefore pass when the legacy write is canceled, never runs, or fails, which misses the core mode-3 requirement. Add deterministic signaling/waiting in the mock and assertions that the legacy operation is invoked after successful unified writes; integration checks that immediately read the legacy API should similarly poll or otherwise wait for eventual replication.

title: Background legacy writes inherit the request cancellation context
body: Each asynchronous legacy operation derives its timeout context from the incoming request context. Once the API handler returns the successful unified-storage response, that parent context is normally canceled, which immediately cancels the legacy create/update/delete operation instead of allowing its intended 10-second grace period. This makes the safety copy unreliable (and often nonexistent) under normal request lifecycle timing. Start these tasks from a detached context (while retaining needed values/logging context) and apply the timeout to that context.

title: Independent goroutines can apply legacy mutations out of order
body: Every successful unified write launches an independent legacy-write goroutine with no per-resource ordering or serialization. For example, a create followed immediately by an update can run the legacy update first (and fail with NotFound) and then run the create, leaving legacy with the stale initial object; similarly, delete and update operations can be reordered. Since failures are not retried, mode 3 can permanently diverge legacy from unified storage. Queue or serialize legacy mutations in request order for a resource before making them asynchronous.

title: Legacy update recomputes the update against a different old object
body: The same `UpdatedObjectInfo` is passed first to `Storage.Update` and later to `Legacy.Update`. `UpdatedObjectInfo` is evaluated by each storage backend against that backend's current object, so the legacy write can compute a different payload from the unified write (or fail due to different resource versions), especially after prior asynchronous lag. The previous implementation computed the update once and used an `updateWrapper` to send the unified result to legacy. Preserve that single computed object/result when scheduling the legacy update so both stores receive the same mutation.

title: Mode 3 metrics attribute storage failures and legacy work to the wrong backend
body: The create storage-error path records `recordLegacyDuration` rather than `recordStorageDuration`. The same misattribution exists in the update storage-error path at line 129, and the legacy DeleteCollection goroutine records `recordStorageDuration` at line 166. In addition, the successful Delete storage metric at line 106 uses `name` as the kind label rather than `options.Kind`. These produce misleading error rates, durations, and high-cardinality per-object metric labels, preventing reliable monitoring of the migration.

title: Mode 3 unit tests do not verify asynchronous legacy writes
body: The tests return immediately after asserting the unified-storage response and never wait for the goroutine or call `AssertExpectations` on the mock. Consequently, none of the create/delete/delete-collection/update tests verifies that the legacy operation was actually invoked, received the expected object, or handled its timeout/error path. This allows broken or canceled background replication to pass the unit suite; synchronize on a channel/mock callback and assert both storage calls.

title: Exclusive cache lock is held during manifest I/O and is not followed by a cache recheck
body: After a caller observes an empty cache, it acquires the write lock and holds it while reading/parsing the manifest (and potentially performing CDN I/O if enabled). Other concurrent cold-cache callers have already passed the initial read check, so when each eventually acquires the lock it does not recheck the cache and performs another serialized manifest load. A burst of initial requests therefore causes N sequential reads rather than one load (or concurrent loads), and in development every request is serialized behind filesystem I/O. Recheck the cache after acquiring the write lock, or perform I/O outside the cache lock and lock only when publishing the result.

title: Recheck the cache after acquiring the write lock
body: A non-development caller can observe a nil cache under the read lock, release it, and then wait while another caller successfully populates the cache.
