As a result, occurrence event payloads continue to expose the raw schedule type rather than the intended display value, and the normalization code has no effect. Return `config` for the `config` field.

title: Hung spawned flusher processes are not killed before replacement
body: The workers are always created from `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")`, producing `SpawnProcess` instances. On Linux, `multiprocessing.Process` refers to the default fork-context process class, so a `SpawnProcess` is not an instance of it. Consequently, when a worker is declared hung, this guard skips `process.kill()` and immediately starts a replacement. The old hung worker can remain alive and continue using Redis/Kafka concurrently with its replacement, leaking workers and potentially causing duplicate or competing flushes. The same incorrect type test at line 346 also prevents forcibly terminating a still-running spawned worker during `join`. Check against the multiprocessing base-process type or invoke `kill`/`terminate` based on capability instead.

title: Negative flusher process counts crash initialization
body: `--flusher-processes` accepts any integer, but a negative value is passed through as `max_processes`. `min(negative_value, shard_count)` makes `num_processes` negative, creates an empty process map, and then the shard-distribution loop indexes `self.process_to_shards_map[process_index]`, raising `KeyError` for the first assigned shard. Zero is also silently converted to the default by `max_processes or ...`, rather than being rejected or honored. Validate this CLI option as a positive integer (and validate programmatic construction similarly) before computing the process map.

title: Reject non-positive flusher process counts before building the shard map
body: `--flusher-processes` accepts arbitrary integers, but negative values make `num_processes` negative. The shard-assignment loop then computes an index that is absent from `process_to_shards_map`, causing a `KeyError` during consumer startup whenever partitions are assigned. A value of `0` is also silently treated as the number of shards because of `max_processes or len(...)`, despite the option describing it as a maximum. Validate that the CLI value is positive (or explicitly define and implement zero semantics) before constructing the process map.

title: Timed joins can leave old flusher processes running
body: When `next_step.join(timeout)` consumes the timeout, `remaining_time <= 0` causes this loop to `break` before reaching the per-process `terminate()` call on line 346. The stopped flag is only observed after the worker finishes its current Redis/Kafka work, so these daemon workers can continue flushing while the consumer proceeds with rebalance/shutdown. A replacement strategy may then run workers for the same shards, causing concurrent duplicate production or continued resource use by a supposedly stopped consumer. Ensure all still-alive workers are terminated (and preferably joined) even when the join deadline has already elapsed.

title: Non-positive flusher process counts are accepted without valid behavior
body: The new `--flusher-processes` option accepts arbitrary integers. A negative value makes `num_processes` negative, produces an empty process map, and leaves the consumer writing spans to Redis with no flusher at all; Redis will eventually fill and halt ingestion. A value of zero is silently converted by `max_processes or len(...)` into one worker per shard, violating the documented maximum and potentially unexpectedly multiplying processes. Validate the CLI/configuration as at least 1 (for example with `click.IntRange(min=1)`) and avoid treating invalid values as defaults.

title: Queues are unbounded, so the consumer has no backpressure
body: Each worker queue is created as an unbounded `queue.Queue()`, while `submit` immediately returns after enqueueing. A slow group/worker can therefore accumulate every subsequently polled Kafka message in memory; increasing the configured worker count only changes the number of unbounded queues. Under sustained input or a stuck downstream dependency this can exhaust process memory rather than applying backpressure to Kafka, contrary to the strategy's stated behavior.

title: Worker exceptions are acknowledged as successfully processed
body: The worker catches every exception from `result_processor` and then unconditionally calls `complete_offset` in `finally`. The commit loop can consequently commit the failed message and all later contiguous messages, permanently dropping a result after a transient database, network, or application failure. This also contradicts the strategy's documented guarantee that offsets are committed only after successful processing; failures need to remain outstanding or be handled through an explicit retry/DLQ policy.

title: Graceful shutdown stops workers before queued work is drained
body: `shutdown` sets every worker's `shutdown` flag before attempting to shut down the queue. A worker finishes at most the item it is currently processing and then exits its `while not self.shutdown` loop, leaving all remaining queued items unprocessed. Normal consumer shutdown/rebalance therefore abandons queued work rather than draining it, causing replayed side effects on restart and preventing a graceful shutdown from completing its in-flight workload.

title: Shutdown relies on Python 3.13-only queue APIs
body: `Queue.shutdown()` and `queue.ShutDown` were introduced in Python 3.13. On Python 3.12 and earlier, `q.shutdown(...)` raises `AttributeError` (which is only logged), blocked worker threads remain stuck in `get()`, and the configured joins time out. The implementation must use a compatible sentinel/wakeup mechanism or raise the project's minimum Python version before using these APIs.

title: Queue shutdown uses Python 3.13-only APIs
body: `queue.Queue.shutdown()` and `queue.ShutDown` were introduced in Python 3.13. On earlier supported Python versions, `q.shutdown(...)` raises `AttributeError`, which is swallowed by this broad handler, leaving workers blocked indefinitely in `Queue.get()`. The subsequent joins wait up to five seconds per worker and daemon threads leak; with the default 20 workers this can turn every consumer shutdown into a long hang. Use a portable sentinel/wakeup scheme or explicitly require and enforce a Python version that provides these APIs.

title: The queue pool has no backpressure and can grow without bound
body: Each worker queue is constructed as `queue.Queue()` with its default unbounded capacity, while `submit` always returns immediately. A slow subscription or a hot group therefore accumulates an unlimited number of decoded work items and offset-tracker entries while the Kafka consumer continues polling. This contradicts the stated natural-backpressure guarantee and can exhaust process memory during a sustained slow downstream dependency. Configure a finite queue size and make submission block or otherwise apply an explicit bounded/backpressure policy.

title: Close can process results after the final offset commit
body: `close` signals and joins the commit thread before shutting down the workers. A worker already handling an item can complete it after the commit loop has exited, so its offset is never included in a final commit. On restart Kafka redelivers that successfully handled result, which can duplicate uptime result side effects. Shutdown should stop intake, drain or account for in-flight workers, and perform a final commit after their completions before terminating the commit loop.

title: Negative max-workers silently drops every queued-mode message
body: `--max-workers` accepts negative integers. In queue mode a negative value is truthy, so `FixedQueuePool` creates no queues; every submit then indexes an empty list, is caught by `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, and is marked complete for commit without invoking the result processor. Reject non-positive worker counts (or normalize them consistently) before constructing the pool.

title: Processing failures are acknowledged and committed as successful
body: The worker catches every exception from `result_processor` and then unconditionally calls `complete_offset` in `finally`. The commit loop will therefore advance Kafka offsets past a result whose handler failed, so that result is permanently skipped rather than retried or sent to a failure path. This also contradicts the strategy's stated guarantee that offsets are committed only after successful processing. Only mark the offset complete after successful processing, or explicitly route failures through the consumer's retry/DLQ behavior.

title: Queue shutdown relies on Python 3.13-only standard-library APIs
body: `queue.Queue.shutdown()` and `queue.ShutDown` were added in Python 3.13. On supported older Python runtimes, `q.shutdown(...)` raises `AttributeError` (which is merely logged), leaving workers blocked in `get()`. Moreover, the first ordinary processing exception causes evaluation of `except queue.ShutDown` and can terminate the worker because that attribute does not exist. Use a portable sentinel/timeout-based shutdown mechanism, or explicitly require and enforce Python 3.13.

title: Rebalances reuse a queue pool that the previous strategy closes
body: The queue pool is owned by `ResultsStrategyFactory`, but `create_with_partitions` creates a new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` for each partition assignment. When Arroyo closes the strategy for a rebalance, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` shuts down that shared pool. A later assignment then creates a new strategy using the same now-stopped pool, so submitted messages remain queued without workers and offsets never advance. The pool must be strategy/assignment scoped, or recreated when building a replacement strategy.

title: The queue pool has no backpressure and can grow without bound
body: Each work queue is created with `queue.Queue()` and therefore has no maximum size. `submit` consequently never blocks while a slow worker's queue accumulates arbitrary Kafka traffic, allowing memory usage and consumer lag to grow until the process is OOM-killed. This is especially likely in the slow-item scenario this mode is intended to address, and contradicts the documented "Natural backpressure when queues fill up" guarantee. Configure a finite queue size and ensure submission/polling honors it.

title: Backup-code consumption is not atomic, so codes can be reused
body: Each request decrypts and validates a snapshot of the full backup-code array, then writes a newly encrypted replacement array. Two concurrent credential requests using the same code can both pass the check before either update commits and both receive sessions. Requests using two different codes can also overwrite each other's stale array and restore a code that the other request consumed. Recovery codes are documented as one-time credentials, so consumption needs a transaction/row lock or a conditional update-and-retry that ensures the stored value has not changed before issuing the session.

title: Backup codes cannot be used for OAuth/SAML two-factor recovery
body: The external identity-provider guard rejects every credentials request that lacks `totpCode` before the backup-code branch at line 131 is reached. A backup code is intended to replace the TOTP code, so it necessarily has no `totpCode` and receives `ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled` instead. The external TOTP login page also selects `ExternalTotpFooter`, which provides no Lost access option. Consequently, users whose Google/SAML account has 2FA enabled cannot recover with the backup codes generated by this feature. Treat a backup code as a valid second-factor input in the external-provider and password-routing guards, and expose the backup-code choice in that login flow.

title: Dismissing the backup-code dialog leaves settings state reporting 2FA as disabled
body: After the enable endpoint succeeds, this only changes the modal step; `onEnable()` is deferred until the custom Close button at line 269. Normal Dialog dismissal is still wired directly through `onOpenChange` at line 166, so closing with Escape, the dialog close control, or an outside dismissal can close the modal without notifying the parent that the server has already enabled 2FA. The settings switch/local state can then remain unchecked, and attempting to enable again returns `TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled` until the page is refreshed. Route successful-dialog dismissal through the same completion handler or prevent dismissal until the explicit completion action.

title: The setup password visibility toggle cannot reveal the password
body: This new `PasswordField` call passes `type="password"`. `PasswordField` spreads its props after its internally computed visible/hidden `type`, so the supplied prop always overwrites the computed `type="text"` when the eye button is clicked. The control advertises Show password but remains masked. Remove the explicit type here or change PasswordField so its visibility state takes precedence.

title: The backup-code authentication and one-time-use paths have no automated coverage
body: The added e2e coverage only opens the backup-code screen and checks that download/copy controls exist; it never reads a generated code, logs in with it, verifies that it is consumed, or disables 2FA with it. These are the feature's security-critical server paths, and the file explicitly leaves them as TODOs. Add integration/e2e coverage for successful backup-code login, rejection on reuse, and backup-code-based disablement.

title: A backup code can be used without the account password
body: Password verification is skipped whenever the request contains any truthy `totpCode` (lines 121-129), before this new backup-code branch selects the second factor. A caller can therefore POST a valid `backupCode` together with an arbitrary nonempty `totpCode`; the bogus TOTP is never validated because the backup branch is selected, and the password is never checked. The UI normally retains the password from the first step, but the credentials endpoint is directly callable, so a stolen recovery code becomes a standalone login credential rather than a replacement only for the authenticator factor. Establish and verify the first factor independently of the user-controlled factor-selection fields, or reject simultaneous factor fields and require a password/pre-authentication proof for this flow.

title: Backup-code consumption is not atomic, allowing recovery-code replay
body: The code reads and validates the decrypted list, then later writes a separately encrypted replacement list without any conditional update, lock, or transaction. Two concurrent authorization requests can both read the same valid code before either update, both pass validation, and both return authenticated sessions. Concurrent use of different codes can also cause the last writer to overwrite the other writer's consumption, leaving an already-used code valid again. Consume the code with a compare-and-swap/conditional update on the previously read value or a transaction with appropriate row locking, and only authenticate when that update succeeds.

title: Dismissing the backup-code screen can leave enabled 2FA unreported to the parent
body: After the enable endpoint succeeds, this only switches to the backup-code step; `onEnable` is deferred until the dedicated `backup-codes-close` button is clicked. The outer controlled Dialog has a separate `onOpenChange` close path (line 166), so closing it through its normal dismiss controls such as Escape, overlay, or close button does not call `onEnable` or reset state. The server has already enabled 2FA, but the settings parent can continue showing its stale disabled state; if the modal is unmounted, the one-time display of the newly generated codes is also lost and setup cannot be rerun because 2FA is already enabled. Prevent dismissal while this step is shown or handle every post-enable close path by notifying the parent and preserving/acknowledging the codes.

title: The feature has no automated test of backup-code authentication or one-time use
body: The added coverage only verifies that the backup-code download button emits a download and that Copy shows a toast; it explicitly leaves the file/clipboard contents unchecked and never logs out and signs in through the Lost access path. Consequently the core new behavior—accepting a generated code, rejecting an invalid code, and rejecting the same code after successful use—is untested. Add an end-to-end or integration test that obtains a generated code and verifies those authentication and consumption semantics, including concurrent/conditional consumption behavior.

title: A backup code can be used without verifying the password
body: The password check above is skipped whenever `credentials.totpCode` is non-empty. The new backup-code branch then accepts a valid `backupCode` without validating that TOTP value at all. A caller can therefore post a valid backup code plus any arbitrary non-empty `totpCode` to the credentials callback and authenticate without supplying the account password (and can also bypass the external-identity gate, which uses the same `!credentials.totpCode` condition). Backup codes are presented as a replacement for the authenticator, not for the primary login factor. Verify the primary factor independently of the presence of either second-factor field, or bind the first-factor verification to a server-side challenge.

title: Backup-code redemption is not atomic, so one code can authorize concurrent logins
body: Each request reads and validates the encrypted backup-code array, then separately writes an array with the matched entry replaced by `null`. Two concurrent requests using the same code can both read the original array, both pass `indexOf`, and both return an authenticated user before either write is observed. This violates the stated one-time-use guarantee and lets a stolen code be redeemed more than once. Consume the code with a transaction or a conditional update tied to the originally-read stored value, and reject the request when that update affects no row.

title: External-provider 2FA users have no backup-code recovery path
body: When `totpEmail` is set, which is the post-Google/SAML external 2FA flow, the page selects `ExternalTotpFooter` rather than `TwoFactorFooter`. That footer only provides Cancel, so it never sets `twoFactorLostAccess`; consequently the `BackupCode` component at line 221 can never be rendered. Users already routed through this external TOTP flow cannot use backup codes after losing their authenticator, despite this feature adding backup-code login.

title: The enable-modal password visibility toggle cannot reveal the password
body: `PasswordField` sets its dynamic `type` before spreading props, so the explicit `type="password"` passed here overwrites it on every render. Clicking the eye button changes its icon/state but the underlying input remains a password input. Omit this prop at this call site or make `PasswordField` spread props before applying its controlled `type`.

title: The show-password control was removed from keyboard tab navigation
body: Adding `tabIndex={-1}` makes the interactive show/hide password button unreachable using normal keyboard navigation. This regresses keyboard-only users' ability to use the password visibility feature across every `PasswordField`, including the newly changed 2FA setup field. Keep the button focusable or provide an equivalent keyboard-accessible control.

title: The recovery authentication behavior is not covered by tests
body: The new test coverage only checks that a download has the expected filename and that clicking Copy shows a toast; it explicitly leaves backup-code login and disabling with a backup code as TODOs. It never verifies that a generated code authenticates, an invalid code is rejected, or a redeemed code cannot be reused. As a result, the central security behavior of this feature, including the one-time-use invariant, can regress without test detection.

title: Google Meet bookings without a destination calendar now throw before falling back
body: `evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` can produce an empty array, so `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined`. A booking with Google Meet selected but no destination calendar now evaluates `.integration` on `undefined` and throws instead of following the previous Cal Video fallback path. This also fails strict null checking. Use optional access or explicitly handle an empty array.

title: Collective host calendars are discarded when the primary host has no calendar
body: The event initializes `destinationCalendar` as `null` when neither the event type nor the first organizer has a destination calendar, then adds collective hosts with `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...)`. In that case the optional call does nothing, even if later collective hosts have configured calendars. Such a collective booking creates no calendar events for those hosts; initialize an empty array before appending host destinations.

title: Later destination calendars are created using the first host's target in several providers
body: The loop invokes `createEvent` with the complete destination-calendar array for every host rather than an event narrowed to the current `destination`. Office 365, Lark, and BaseCalendarService all select `event.destinationCalendar[0]`, so when processing a second host they authenticate as that host but attempt to create in the first host's calendar (usually failing with access errors or creating in a shared wrong calendar). Passing the target external ID only to `CalendarManager` does not fix this because it is not forwarded to those provider create calls. Each provider invocation must be given or select the current destination.

title: Legacy destinations without a credential ID lose their external calendar ID in references
body: The branch for a destination with no `credentialId` calls `createEvent(c, event)` without `destination.externalId`. `CalendarManager` therefore returns an `EventResult` with no `externalId`, and the new reference-building code persists that missing value rather than the selected destination ID. Subsequent update/delete operations cannot address the original calendar and may default to the primary calendar. This branch exists specifically to support destinations without credential IDs, so it must pass and preserve the current destination external ID.

title: New video references no longer retain their credential ID
body: For a non-calendar result, including every dedicated video meeting result, this now writes `credentialId: undefined`. Previously it retained `result.credentialId`. Cancellation only deletes a video meeting when its booking reference has a credential ID, so newly created Zoom/Teams/etc. meetings will be left behind on cancellation; other later operations also cannot reliably select the credential. Keep `result.credentialId` for non-calendar results.

title: Persisting only the first destination prevents delayed collective scheduling for other hosts
body: A booking stores only `evt.destinationCalendar[0]` in the scalar `Booking.destinationCalendar` relation. Required-confirmation and payment flows later reconstruct their CalendarEvent by wrapping that scalar in a one-element array (for example, `confirm.handler.ts`), with no remaining source for the other collective hosts' destinations. As a result, collective bookings scheduled after approval or payment only create the first host's calendar event. Persist all destinations or reconstruct them from the event type's hosts in every delayed scheduling path.

title: Cancelling all occurrences of a collective recurring booking leaves other host events behind
body: For each calendar reference, the recurring-cancellation branch iterates only the booking owner's calendar credentials and then calls `find` to select the first calendar reference of each updated booking. With multiple host references, every outer iteration repeatedly deletes that first reference using the owner's credentials; references belonging to the other hosts are never selected with their own credentials. Their recurring calendar events remain after the booking is marked cancelled. Iterate each updated booking reference and resolve its `credentialId` before deleting it.

title: Rescheduling deletes multi-host calendar events with an arbitrary credential
body: Credentials are stored in `credentialsMap` keyed only by integration type. A collective booking can now have multiple references of the same type, such as two `google_calendar` references owned by different hosts, but the map retains only one credential. The deletion loop then uses that one credential for every reference of the type, causing authorization failures and leaving other hosts' old events intact. Resolve credentials by each reference's `credentialId` instead of calendar type.

title: Organization slug persistence was reversed for team-billing deployments
body: This changes the previous condition from storing `slug` when team billing is disabled to storing it only when team billing is enabled. Consequently, non-billing deployments create organizations without their requested team slug even though slug collision and domain setup were performed, breaking slug-based organization routing. It also stores both `slug` and `requestedSlug` when billing is enabled, contrary to the prior deferred-slug behavior.

title: The public webhook payload changes destinationCalendar from object/null to array without compatibility handling
body: CalendarEvent is serialized in developer webhook payloads, as shown by the changed webhook E2E expectation. Existing webhook consumers that read `payload.destinationCalendar.integration` or expect `null` will now receive an array/empty array in flows rebuilt from a booking, while newly created bookings can still emit `null`. This is an externally observable schema break and also creates inconsistent shapes across lifecycle events; preserve the webhook contract or version/document the payload migration.

title: Google Meet fallback dereferences an absent destination calendar
body: `destinationCalendar` is optional/null, so destructuring `evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` can produce `undefined`. The subsequent direct access to `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` throws for a Google Meet event without a destination calendar, precisely the case this fallback is meant to handle. This prevents the booking from being created instead of falling back to Cal Video; guard the value or use optional chaining.

title: The selected destination calendar is not passed to calendar providers
body: Although `createEvent` accepts `externalId` and `EventManager` supplies each destination's ID, this call invokes the provider with only the complete `CalendarEvent` array and the credential ID. Office 365, Lark, and CalDAV currently select `destinationCalendar[0]`, so when iterating a second collective host they attempt to create the event in the first host's calendar (often with an unauthorized credential). The `externalId` is only copied into the resulting reference later and does not affect where the event is created. Pass the selected destination through to the provider, or have every provider select the entry matching the credential/target.

title: Collective host calendars are discarded when the first host has no destination calendar
body: The initial event value is `null` when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar. The collective-host calendars are then added with `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...)`, which silently does nothing for that case. A collective booking where another host has a calendar but the organizer does not therefore has no destination calendars and no host calendar event is created. Initialize this field as an empty array or assign a new array when adding host calendars.

title: Only the first collective destination is persisted on the booking
body: The booking write connects only `evt.destinationCalendar[0]`, so all secondary host destination calendars are lost once the request completes. Deferred scheduling paths such as confirmation and payment webhooks rebuild their `CalendarEvent` from the singular `booking.destinationCalendar` and consequently create an event only for the main host. Persist all destination-calendar selections (or reliably reconstruct them from the collective hosts) before supporting deferred collective bookings.

title: Video booking references lose their credential ID
body: `referencesToCreate` now sets `credentialId` to `undefined` for every non-calendar result. Dedicated video results previously retained `result.credentialId`; removing it creates video BookingReferences without the credential needed to update or delete the meeting. For example, the cancellation handler only deletes a video meeting when its reference has a credential ID, leaving these meetings orphaned. Preserve `result.credentialId` for video results.

title: Location updates create calendar references without calendar or credential identifiers
body: `updateLocation` now copies `result.externalId` and `result.credentialId` into new references, but `CalendarManager.updateEvent` does not populate either field in its returned EventResult. Every calendar reference appended by the location-update flow will therefore have no external calendar ID or credential ID. Later updates/cancellations cannot target the original event and may fall back to all connected calendars. Return the input credential/calendar identifiers from `updateEvent`, or derive them from the source reference before writing the new one.

title: Google update/delete fallback can never select a destination calendar
body: The fallback branch runs only when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, then searches for a destination whose `externalId` equals that same falsy value. Since calendar IDs are strings, it always produces `undefined`. Updates then send an undefined `calendarId`, while the analogous delete logic at line 317 falls back to `primary` instead of the configured destination calendar. Existing references without an externalCalendarId will fail updates or delete the wrong calendar event; choose an actual destination fallback, such as the entry associated with the credential.

title: Recurring collective cancellation deletes only one calendar reference per occurrence
body: For each recurring occurrence this code uses `.find(...)` to select the first calendar reference, then invokes deletion through every calendar credential. With multiple collective-host references, the remaining references are never selected with their own credential and calendar ID; the outer reference loop merely repeats the same first-reference work. Secondary host events remain on their calendars after cancelling all remaining occurrences. Iterate every occurrence reference and resolve/use that reference's credential ID.

title: Reschedule cleanup collapses multiple host credentials of the same integration
body: The cleanup map is keyed only by integration type, so multiple collective references such as two `google_calendar` host calendars are all deleted using whichever credential was last inserted for that type. A host credential normally cannot delete another host's calendar event; Google treats a 404 as a successful delete here, so the failure can be silent and leave the old event behind. Resolve the credential by each BookingReference's `credentialId` rather than by its type.

title: Organization slug creation condition was inverted
body: This changes slug persistence from `!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED` to `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED`. With team billing disabled, newly created organizations no longer receive the slug that was validated and used to create the domain, making their organization URL unavailable. With billing enabled, it also assigns the slug immediately instead of retaining it as `requestedSlug`, bypassing the previous approval behavior. This unrelated inversion should be reverted.

title: The public booking webhook payload changes destinationCalendar shape without compatibility handling
body: CalendarEvent is serialized into booking webhook payloads, as demonstrated by the webhook E2E test. Changing `destinationCalendar` from an object/null to an array changes the JSON contract for every existing webhook consumer that reads fields such as `destinationCalendar.externalId` or expects null. The PR provides no payload versioning, compatibility field, or migration documentation, so consumers will break when hosts have a destination calendar.

title: No automated test covers the multi-destination collective lifecycle
body: The PR adds creation, update, and cancellation paths for multiple destination calendars but does not test a collective booking with distinct host credentials/calendars. A test should verify that each provider receives its own selected calendar and that the resulting references allow reschedule and cancellation to update/delete every host event. The existing webhook expectation change only checks an empty-array payload and would not detect the first-destination and missing-reference regressions.

title: Video booking references now lose their credential ID
body: `credentialId` is now set to `undefined` for every non-calendar result. Video results do not satisfy `isCalendarType`, whereas the previous code persisted `result.credentialId` for them. As a result, newly created video references have no credential association; for example, `handleCancelBooking` only calls `deleteMeeting` when the video reference has a `credentialId`, so cancelling these bookings leaves the video meeting active.

title: A secondary collective host calendar is discarded when the primary host has none
body: For a collective booking, destination calendars for secondary hosts are collected, but the initial value is `null` when neither the event type nor the primary organizer has a destination calendar. The later `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is then a no-op. Thus, if only a non-primary collective host has a connected destination calendar, no destination is passed to `EventManager` and that host never receives a calendar event. Initialize this as an empty array before appending host calendars.

title: Creation does not route non-Google integrations to the destination being iterated
body: `createEvent` accepts `externalId` and later records it in the booking reference, but the actual calendar-service call receives only the full event array and a credential ID; `externalId` is never used to select the target. This happens once per destination in `EventManager`. Google was updated to match the credential ID, but Office365, Lark, and the base CalDAV service all select `destinationCalendar[0]` instead. For a collective event with different host calendars, later iterations therefore attempt to create using another host's credential against the first host's calendar (or create duplicates there), while the reference claims the event was created in the later calendar. The selected destination must be forwarded or the event must be narrowed per call, and all calendar services must select it consistently.

title: Only the first collective destination is retained for deferred event creation
body: The new multi-host destination list is reduced to `evt.destinationCalendar[0]` when the booking is persisted. This loses every other host calendar before a pending or paid booking is scheduled. The confirmation and payment handlers rebuild their `CalendarEvent` only from `booking.destinationCalendar` (or the organizer fallback), so confirming a collective booking or completing payment later creates an event only for the first host. Persist enough destination information or rebuild all collective host destinations in those deferred flows.

title: Recurring collective cancellation deletes only the first calendar reference
body: In the recurring/all-remaining path, each updated booking's calendar reference is obtained with `.find(...)`, so only its first calendar event is considered. The code then tries that one reference with every credential belonging to the booking owner, rather than using the credential attached to each reference. With multiple collective-host references, secondary host events are never deleted, and the first event is redundantly deleted once per reference (often using credentials that cannot access it). Iterate every updated booking reference and resolve/delete it with that reference's credential.

title: Google Meet bookings without a destination calendar now throw instead of falling back
body: Destructuring an empty/null destination array makes `mainHostDestinationCalendar` undefined, but the Google Meet fallback immediately reads `.integration` from it. A booking that selects Google Meet without a connected destination calendar—precisely the case this fallback is meant to handle—now throws a runtime TypeError instead of switching to Cal Video. Use optional chaining or explicitly handle an absent first destination.

title: Organization creation drops the requested slug when team billing is disabled
body: The condition was reversed: when `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED` is false, the organization now stores neither `slug` nor `metadata.requestedSlug`. The supplied slug is still collision-checked and may be registered with Vercel, but it is discarded from the created organization, leaving no persisted identifier for the requested organization URL/domain. The non-team-billing branch needs to retain the slug as before.

title: No regression test covers multiple collective destination calendars
body: The only changed end-to-end assertion adjusts a webhook payload shape; it does not create a collective event with two hosts, distinct credentials, and distinct destination calendars. There is also no coverage for confirmation/payment-delayed creation or recurring cancellation. Such tests are needed to verify that one reference and one event are created, updated, and deleted for each host calendar.

title: Salesforce refresh path references an undeclared Prisma client
body: The new refresh path calls `prisma.credential.update`, but this file does not import `prisma`. TypeScript will fail with `Cannot find name 'prisma'`, blocking the app-store type check/build before this feature can be deployed.

title: Sync mode returns an unparsed Fetch Response to handlers expecting provider data
body: When credential syncing is enabled, this function returns the native `fetch` Response directly instead of the type returned by each provider's `refreshFunction`. Google reads `res.data`, HubSpot treats the result as a `HubspotToken`, and Zoho/Bigin read Axios-style `tokenInfo.data`; a standard Response has none of those properties and its JSON body is never read. Enabling the sync endpoint therefore causes undefined-token failures or TypeErrors for those integrations.

title: The minimal sync-response schema discards expiry fields and overwrites refresh tokens
body: `z.string().toString()` is not a wildcard object key: both computed keys evaluate to `"[object Object]"`. Consequently this Zod object strips normal unknown fields such as `expiry_date`/`expires_in`, so a sync response containing the documented access token and expiry retains only `access_token`; line 26 then inserts the literal `"refresh_token"`. Consumers persist that placeholder (for example Office and Zoom), corrupting the real refresh token and losing the new expiry, so later refreshes—especially after sync is disabled—cannot authenticate correctly.

title: Google refresh stores the SafeParse wrapper instead of credential keys
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns Zod's `SafeParseReturnType` (`{ success, data }`), but this value is written directly as `Credential.key`. The next GoogleCalendarService construction parses `credential.key` as a Google credential object and instead receives the wrapper, so any Google credential refreshed through this path becomes unusable. This occurs even when credential syncing is disabled because this helper is now always used.

title: Zoho Bigin sends the credential record ID as the Cal.com user ID
body: `refreshOAuthTokens` serializes its third argument as `calcomUserId`, but this call passes `credentialId`, which is the Credential table primary key rather than `credential.userId`. The external credential source will look up the wrong user; it may return no token or, if that numeric ID belongs to another user, a token that is then saved onto the current user's credential.

title: Salesforce ignores the configured credential-sync endpoint
body: Unlike the other modified integrations, the Salesforce refresh path always calls Salesforce directly and never calls `refreshOAuthTokens` or checks `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`. Thus, even with credential syncing enabled, Salesforce continues using the locally stored refresh token rather than the self-hoster's source of truth, leaving this integration unsupported by the advertised feature.

title: Concurrent credential webhooks can create duplicate credentials
body: The handler performs `findFirst` followed by a separate `create` when no credential is found. Two simultaneous deliveries for the same user and app can both observe no row and both create one; the comment confirms there is no usable unique key for an upsert. Future syncs then update an arbitrary `findFirst` result, while duplicate credentials can lead to ambiguous or duplicate integration behavior.

title: The new credential-sync security and refresh flows have no automated coverage
body: No tests were added for this new authenticated, encrypted webhook or for the enabled/disabled refresh branches. Tests should at least cover rejecting invalid secrets, decrypting and idempotently creating/updating credentials, and consuming the sync endpoint's normal JSON response; the current unparsed-response and token-corruption regressions would have been caught by such coverage.

title: `prisma` is used without being imported
body: The new credential update references `prisma`, but this module has no `@calcom/prisma` import. Type-checking fails with `Cannot find name 'prisma'`, preventing the app-store package from building.

title: Google refresh persists the Zod safe-parse wrapper as the credential key
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns a `safeParse` result (`{ success, data }`), unlike the previous `googleCredentialSchema.parse` call which returned the credential object itself. This update stores that wrapper in `Credential.key`; on the next request `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` receives no top-level token fields and rejects the saved Google credential, breaking the integration after its first refresh.

title: The sync token schema strips expiry and provider token fields
body: The computed keys are literal `"[object Object]"` property names, not catch-all/index signatures; the second one also overwrites the first. Zod objects strip unknown fields by default, so in sync mode parsing a normal response returns only `access_token`, then line 26 adds a synthetic `refresh_token`. Expiry values, real refresh tokens, scopes, and provider-specific fields are discarded before callers persist them, producing unusable credentials (for example Zoom computes an invalid expiry and Google loses its stored refresh token).

title: Sync mode changes refresh results into an incompatible response type
body: The sync branch always returns the native Fetch `Response`, while several supplied refresh functions return an SDK response or a token object and their callers continue to consume those shapes. Google reads `res.data`, HubSpot reads `expiresIn`/`accessToken` directly, and the Zoho integrations read Axios `tokenInfo.data`; none of these callers parses the Fetch response body. Enabling `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` therefore causes undefined-token errors or writes invalid credentials for these integrations.

title: Zoho Bigin sends a credential ID as the Cal.com user ID
body: `refreshOAuthTokens` constructs its request with `calcomUserId`, but this call passes `credentialId`, which is the Credential primary key rather than the owning user's ID. Credential and user IDs are unrelated, so the remote source will generally fail to find the user and can return credentials for another user whose ID happens to match the credential ID.

title: Credential-sync refresh requests contain no authentication
body: The configured credential-sync endpoint receives only a predictable user ID and app slug. The helper does not send `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` under `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME`, nor any other authentication or signature, so an endpoint implemented according to this client cannot verify that a request came from its Cal.com instance. If that endpoint returns access tokens based on these fields, unauthenticated callers can request users' credentials.

title: Credential sync cannot identify which credential to replace
body: The payload identifies only a user and app, while the database permits multiple credentials for the same user and app (for example, the Google OAuth callback creates a credential on every connection). `findFirst` has no ordering and updates an arbitrary matching credential, leaving other stale credentials in place. Syncing one external account can therefore overwrite a different account's tokens and make bookings use the wrong calendar.

title: Salesforce bypasses the configured credential-sync endpoint
body: Unlike the other modified integrations, Salesforce performs its refresh directly against Salesforce and never calls `refreshOAuthTokens`. Consequently, when credential sharing is enabled, the configured source-of-truth endpoint is never queried for Salesforce and the implementation still depends on the locally stored refresh token.

title: Salesforce creates its client with the stale access token after refreshing
body: The new code obtains and persists `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`, but the subsequent `jsforce.Connection` is initialized with `credentialKey.access_token`, the pre-refresh token. If that old token is expired—the condition that necessitates a refresh—the immediately returned client authenticates with the expired token rather than the token just received.

title: Zoom sends a route name instead of its app slug to the sync endpoint
body: This sends `zoomvideo` as `appSlug`, but the Zoom integration's installed app ID/slug is `zoom` (as used by `zoomvideo/api/callback.ts`). A source endpoint that keys credentials by the Cal.com app slug will not find Zoom credentials for this request, so Zoom token refresh fails only when syncing is enabled.

title: Salesforce refresh path references an unimported Prisma client
body: The newly added refresh path calls `prisma.credential.update`, but this file does not import `prisma` from `@calcom/prisma`. Type-checking will fail with `Cannot find name 'prisma'`; if type-checking is skipped during deployment, every Salesforce refresh reaching this line throws a `ReferenceError`.

title: Google refresh persists the Zod SafeParse wrapper instead of credential data
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns a successful `safeParse` result (`{ success: true, data: ... }`), not the parsed token object. This line saves that wrapper as `Credential.key`, whereas `googleCredentialSchema` expects token fields such as `access_token` at the top level. After the first refresh, subsequent Google Calendar service instances cannot parse the persisted credential and the integration stops working.

title: The minimum sync-response schema does not preserve or validate expiry fields
body: The computed properties here are not Zod index signatures: both `z.string().toString()` expressions become the literal key `"[object Object]"`, with the second overwriting the first. Zod therefore accepts only `access_token` and strips normal unknown fields such as `expires_in` and `expiry_date`. When sync is enabled, a source endpoint's expiry value is discarded, causing adapters to save an already-expired or invalid token state and repeatedly refresh or fail.

title: Missing refresh tokens are replaced with a fake value and can corrupt saved credentials
body: The documented sync endpoint response contains only an access token and expiry, so this branch commonly injects the literal string `"refresh_token"`. Callers such as Zoom and Office then merge or assign that value into the stored credential, overwriting the real provider refresh token. If sync is later disabled or unavailable, direct provider refreshes will use the fake token and the user must reconnect the integration.

title: Sync refresh responses are returned as raw fetch Responses despite incompatible caller contracts
body: The sync branch returns the native `fetch` `Response`, while the original refresh functions return provider-specific objects. Existing callers are not normalized for this: Google reads `res.data`, HubSpot treats the result as a `HubspotToken`, and the Zoho adapters expect an Axios response with `.data`. A JSON response from `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` therefore yields undefined token fields or invalid persisted credentials for these integrations instead of a successful source-of-truth refresh.

title: Credential-sync token requests contain no authentication
body: The request to the configured credential source sends only a predictable numeric `calcomUserId` and an app slug. It includes neither `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, the configured header name, nor any signature or other credential. A source endpoint cannot authenticate this request using the supplied sync configuration, so anyone able to reach that endpoint can forge requests for user IDs and potentially obtain their current third-party access tokens. The request needs an authenticated header/signature and the receiver must verify it.

title: Zoho Bigin sends a credential ID as the remote Cal.com user ID
body: `refreshOAuthTokens` expects its third argument to be the credential owner's user ID and serializes it as `calcomUserId`, but this call passes `credentialId`. Credential IDs and user IDs are unrelated; normal sync requests will fail to locate the owner, and an ID that happens to match another user can fetch that user's source credential and save its access token onto the current user's credential.

title: Zoom refresh uses a non-existent app slug for credential sync
body: The helper parameter is an app slug, but this call sends `zoomvideo`. The same integration creates credentials with app ID `zoom` and uses `zoom` as its installed-app slug. A source endpoint that keys credentials by the documented app slug will not find Zoom credentials, so Zoom sync refreshes fail.

title: Salesforce refresh bypasses the configured credential-sync endpoint
body: Unlike the other modified refresh paths, Salesforce always posts directly to Salesforce's token endpoint and never calls `refreshOAuthTokens`. Consequently, enabling `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` has no effect for Salesforce: Cal.com continues to use its local refresh token rather than the self-hosted app store designated as the source of truth.

title: Concurrent webhook deliveries can create duplicate credentials
body: The lookup and create are separate operations with no transaction, uniqueness constraint, or idempotency key. Two simultaneous deliveries for a user/app with no existing credential can both observe no row and both create one. Later syncs update an arbitrary `findFirst` result, while calendar code may select a different duplicate, leaving stale credentials active and making the integration behavior nondeterministic.

title: Team admins are rejected by the authorization check
body: The code combines `isTeamAdmin` and `isTeamOwner` with `&&`. A team administrator who is not also the owner will therefore fail this check, even though the UI and variable name indicate that either role should be permitted. This prevents team admins from adding guests to bookings they are authorized to manage; use an OR check for the two roles.

title: The mutation adds attendees to bookings in invalid states
body: After verifying only that the booking exists, the handler persists new attendees without checking booking status. Although the UI hides the action for cancelled, rejected, and pending bookings, any authenticated attendee/organizer can invoke this tRPC mutation directly for those bookings. The handler then updates the calendar and sends invitations whose ICS status is CONFIRMED, effectively inviting people to an event that may be cancelled or never accepted.

title: Calendar updates use the guest's credentials rather than the booking owner's
body: Attendees are explicitly allowed to add guests, but the EventManager is initialized with credentials loaded for `ctx.user`, i.e. the attendee performing the action. The destination calendar and event references normally belong to `booking.user` (whose credentials were already loaded in the booking query). A permitted attendee generally cannot update the organizer's calendar, so the local attendee rows are created but the organizer's calendar event cannot be updated.

title: Local attendee records are committed before the external calendar update succeeds
body: `prisma.booking.update` permanently creates the attendee rows before `updateCalendarAttendees` is called. If the calendar provider update throws, the mutation fails after the database has changed, leaving Cal.com and the external event with different attendee lists. Retrying the same request then finds no `uniqueGuests` and returns BAD_REQUEST instead of retrying the calendar update. This needs compensating cleanup or a durable/outbox-based retry strategy.

title: The server accepts duplicate guest addresses in a single request
body: The tRPC input schema does not require unique guests, and this filter only compares each submitted address against attendees that existed before the update. A direct request such as `guests: ["guest@example.com", "guest@example.com"]` leaves both values in `uniqueGuests` and passes them to `createMany`, resulting in duplicate attendee records (or a database constraint failure if such a constraint is present). Client-side validation is not sufficient for this API boundary.

title: Blacklist matching can be bypassed with email capitalization
body: Configured blacklisted addresses are normalized to lowercase, but submitted guest addresses are compared without normalization. `BLOCKED@example.com` passes Zod validation and does not match a blacklist entry of `blocked@example.com`, allowing callers to bypass the explicit guest-email blocklist. Normalize/canonicalize the submitted email before checking the blacklist and existing attendees.

title: Existing attendees can receive a new-booking email when mixed with new guests
body: The database correctly filters existing addresses into `uniqueGuests`, but email classification receives the original `guests` input. For example, submitting an existing attendee plus one new address creates only the new attendee, yet `sendAddGuestsEmails` treats the existing attendee as newly added and sends them `AttendeeScheduledEmail` rather than the guest-added notification. Pass the successfully added `uniqueGuests` list to avoid false scheduling emails.

title: Add-guest notifications ignore event email-disable settings
body: `sendAddGuestsEmails` has no event metadata argument and unconditionally queues organizer and attendee emails. Other standard booking email paths check `disableStandardEmails` through `eventTypeDisableHostEmail` and `eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail`. Consequently, adding a guest sends notifications despite the event type being configured to suppress host or attendee standard emails.

title: Team members are never included in add-guest notifications
body: The constructed `CalendarEvent` never sets its `team` field. As a result, the `calendarEvent.team?.members` branch in `sendAddGuestsEmails` is always skipped, even though the mailer explicitly attempts to notify team members. For team bookings, only the assigned organizer receives the notification and the rest of the team is silently omitted.

title: Calendar updates use the guest-adder's credentials instead of the organizer's
body: The mutation explicitly authorizes any existing attendee to add guests, but it builds EventManager with credentials from ctx.user. For an attendee or a team admin who is not the booking organizer, those credentials normally cannot edit the organizer's calendar event, so updateCalendarAttendees will fail or leave the organizer's event unchanged. The booking attendee rows have already been written at this point, producing an inconsistent booking and calendar state.

title: Guest records are committed before calendar synchronization can fail
body: The attendee rows are persisted before updateCalendarAttendees is called. If the calendar provider rejects the update or a network error occurs, the mutation returns an error even though the guests remain in the database. Retrying the same request then fails because the guests are no longer considered new, leaving no way for the caller to retry calendar synchronization and no notification sent to the added guests.

title: Team admin-or-owner authorization is implemented as admin-and-owner
body: The permission check uses && between isTeamAdmin and isTeamOwner, despite the variable and intended policy being admin-or-owner. A normal team ADMIN membership does not satisfy the owner check, and an OWNER may not satisfy an admin-only check, so team users who should be allowed to manage the booking are rejected unless they also happen to be the organizer or an attendee.

title: The server accepts duplicate guest addresses in one request
body: Uniqueness is only checked by the dialog's client-side schema; this public tRPC input schema accepts repeated emails. The handler filters only against attendees that existed before the request, so repeated values are all passed to createMany and the calendar/email paths. Direct API callers can therefore create duplicate attendee rows and duplicate invitations, or cause the entire write to fail if a database uniqueness constraint is added later.

title: Guest additions have no server-side batch limit
body: The guests array is unbounded, while any authenticated attendee is authorized to invoke this endpoint. A caller can submit thousands of arbitrary addresses, causing an unbounded createMany, calendar update, translation work, and Promise.all email fan-out from the organizer's account. This enables bulk invitation spam and can exhaust request worker resources; the endpoint needs an enforced maximum or controlled batching/rate limit.

title: Cancelled and rejected bookings can still receive new guests
body: After finding and authorizing the booking, the handler never checks its status or whether the event has already ended. An authenticated attendee can call the tRPC endpoint for a CANCELLED or REJECTED booking, create attendee records, update the calendar, and send emails whose generated ICS status is CONFIRMED. This can effectively re-invite people to an event that should no longer accept attendees.

title: Add-guest notifications ignore disableStandardEmails preferences
body: Unlike the scheduled, rescheduled, cancelled, and location-change email helpers, sendAddGuestsEmails neither accepts event-type metadata nor checks eventTypeDisableHostEmail/eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail. Consequently, an event type configured to disable all standard host or attendee emails will still send organizer and attendee add-guest messages, violating the event type's notification setting.

title: Email classification uses requested guests rather than guests actually added
body: uniqueGuests filters out addresses that were already attendees, but sendAddGuestsEmails receives the original guests array. For example, submitting an existing attendee plus one new address succeeds, yet the existing attendee is treated as a new guest and receives an AttendeeScheduledEmail rather than the guest-added update. Pass uniqueGuests so notification type and recipients reflect the database change.

title: Team members are never included in add-guest notifications
body: The CalendarEvent constructed here never sets team, and the Prisma eventType include does not load its team relation or members. sendAddGuestsEmails only sends organizer updates to additional team members through calendarEvent.team.members, so that branch is always skipped for this handler. Team members other than the assigned booking user will not be notified when guests are added.

title: Blacklisted guest emails can be bypassed with casing changes
body: BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS is normalized to lowercase, but each submitted guest address is compared without lowercasing. A blacklist entry such as blocked@example.com does not match BLOCKED@example.com, allowing a caller to invite an address the deployment has explicitly blocked. Normalize submitted addresses before both blacklist and existing-attendee comparisons.

title: Team administrators are rejected by the authorization check
body: The team-role condition requires the actor to be both a team admin and a team owner. These are alternative membership roles, so ordinary team administrators (and, depending on the role query semantics, owners) receive FORBIDDEN even though they are intended to manage team bookings. This should use an OR check, consistent with the `isTeamAdminOrOwner` permission represented elsewhere in the bookings UI.

title: Guest addresses are not canonically deduplicated or compared to the blacklist
body: `uniqueGuests` compares raw email strings only against the pre-existing attendees and does not deduplicate entries within `guests`. In particular, the blacklist is lowercased at lines 70-72 while submitted addresses are not, so a blacklisted address can bypass the policy by changing case. A request containing the same new address twice also sends both rows to `createMany`, producing duplicate attendees when no database constraint exists or failing the whole batch when one does. Normalize addresses before blacklist/existing-attendee checks and deduplicate them server-side.

title: Attendees are persisted before calendar synchronization succeeds
body: The attendee records are committed before `updateCalendarAttendees` is called. If the calendar provider update fails, the mutation returns an error but the guests remain in the booking. Retrying the same request then finds those guests in `booking.attendees` and rejects it as having no unique guests, leaving the organizer calendar and the booking permanently out of sync through this workflow. Use a compensating rollback/durable retry strategy or otherwise make the external synchronization recoverable after the database write.

title: Calendar updates use the guest-adder's credentials instead of the booking owner's
body: The mutation explicitly authorizes attendees and team admins to add guests, but it builds `EventManager` with credentials fetched for `ctx.user`, the person performing the action. The booking's calendar references and destination calendar normally belong to `booking.user` (whose credentials are loaded at lines 35-40 but never used). Thus an attendee or team admin will attempt the update with an unrelated account's credentials, so the organizer's connected calendar cannot be updated reliably. Use the booking organizer/calendar owner's credentials for this update.

title: Notification classification uses requested guests rather than inserted guests
body: The database operation inserts only `uniqueGuests`, but the email call receives the original `guests` input. For example, when a request contains one already-attending address and one new address, the existing attendee is not inserted but `sendAddGuestsEmails` treats them as a new guest and sends `AttendeeScheduledEmail` with a confirmed calendar invite. Pass the actual inserted guest list (`uniqueGuests`) to avoid sending incorrect new-booking emails.

title: The mutation can add guests to cancelled or rejected bookings
body: After loading the booking, the handler checks only existence and authorization; it never validates its lifecycle status. An authorized caller can invoke this endpoint directly for a CANCELLED, REJECTED, or PENDING booking, which inserts attendees and sends calendar/email payloads hardcoded as `CONFIRMED`. This can revive a cancelled appointment in recipients' calendars or invite people to an appointment that was never accepted. Reject non-accepted bookings (and enforce the condition atomically with the update if cancellation can race).

title: Guest-addition emails bypass disabled standard-email settings
body: `sendAddGuestsEmails` unconditionally queues organizer and attendee messages and does not accept or check the event type metadata. Consequently, events configured with `disableStandardEmails` still send guest-addition notifications, unlike the adjacent location-change and scheduled-email paths. Thread the event metadata into this helper and honor the host and attendee suppression flags before enqueueing messages.

title: Team members are never included in guest-addition notifications
body: The constructed `CalendarEvent` never sets `team`, and `eventType: true` does not load Prisma's `EventType.team` relation or its members. As a result, `calendarEvent.team?.members` is always absent in `sendAddGuestsEmails`, making its team-member notification loop unreachable for this endpoint. Team booking members therefore do not receive the guest-addition update; load the team and members and include them in the calendar event.

title: Retry cleanup is not scoped to SMS reminders
body: The new delete predicate is `(SMS reminder whose date has passed) OR (retryCount > 1)`. The retry-count branch has no `method: SMS` condition, so this SMS cron endpoint will delete future EMAIL or WHATSAPP workflow reminders whenever their `retryCount` exceeds one. Keep the method restriction outside the OR (or repeat it in the retry branch) so retry cleanup cannot silently remove unrelated workflow notifications.

title: Reminders with no usable recipient never reach the retry limit
body: `retryCount` is only incremented after entering the `message?.length && sendTo` branch. An SMS attendee reminder for a booking without `smsReminderNumber`, an SMS-number step without `sendTo`, or a reminder that renders an empty message remains `scheduled: false` with `retryCount: 0`. It will therefore be selected by every cron run until its scheduled date instead of being discarded after the configured attempts. Treat an absent destination or message as a failed, terminal, or retryable scheduling outcome.

title: Retry increments lose attempts when cron executions overlap
body: The count is read by `findMany` and later written back as `reminder.retryCount + 1` (also in the catch block at line 195). Concurrent cron invocations can both read `0`, both fail, and both write `1`, so two failures are recorded as one and the reminder is attempted more than the intended two times. Use an atomic database increment and, ideally, atomically claim the unscheduled reminder before calling Twilio so overlapping jobs cannot process the same row.

title: Retry cleanup deletes reminders for every delivery method
body: The `retryCount > 1` branch is not constrained to `WorkflowMethods.SMS`. This endpoint will therefore delete any `WorkflowReminder` with more than one retry, including a future email or WhatsApp reminder, even though the retry behavior being implemented is for SMS scheduling. Keep `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` in the retry-exhaustion branch (and ensure it only targets the intended unscheduled state) so shared reminder records cannot be removed by this SMS cron.

title: Retry count updates lose failures when cron invocations overlap
body: The retry count is calculated from the value read by `findMany` and then written back. If two authorized cron invocations select the same unscheduled reminder, both can observe (for example) `retryCount = 0`, both attempt scheduling, and both write `1`; the row is then retried again despite already having failed twice. The same overlap can cause multiple scheduling attempts for one reminder. Claim the reminder/attempt atomically with a conditional update or lock, and increment in the database rather than writing a stale value.

title: Reminders with no usable destination are never counted as failed
body: Failure accounting is entirely inside the `if (message?.length && sendTo)` block. When an SMS reminder has an empty or missing recipient number (or no generated message), the loop silently skips it without setting `scheduled` or incrementing `retryCount`, so the cron continues selecting it until its scheduled date. This leaves a class of invalid SMS reminders with the exact indefinite rescheduling behavior the retry limit is intended to stop; treat an unusable destination/message as a terminal or retryable failure and update/delete the reminder accordingly.

title: Retry cleanup is not restricted to SMS reminders
body: The `retryCount > 1` branch is a separate `OR` condition, so it deletes any `WorkflowReminder` with two retries, including EMAIL and WHATSAPP reminders, regardless of its scheduled date or status. This SMS cron should scope the retry predicate to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` as well; otherwise a populated retry count on another workflow method causes that reminder to be silently deleted.

title: Retry count updates can lose concurrent failures
body: The retry value is computed from the value read by `findMany` and written back as `reminder.retryCount + 1` (with the same pattern in the catch block). Overlapping cron invocations can both read `0`, both fail scheduling, and both write `1`, even though there were two failures. The reminder then remains eligible for an additional attempt instead of being removed at the configured limit. Use an atomic Prisma increment, and condition the update on the reminder still being unscheduled so a concurrent successful scheduler cannot be counted as a failure.

title: Reminders without a recipient or message never consume retries
body: Both new retry updates are inside `if (message?.length && sendTo)`. `WorkflowStep.sendTo` and `Booking.smsReminderNumber` are optional, so an SMS reminder with no configured phone number reaches this guard, remains `scheduled: false` with `retryCount: 0`, and is selected again on every cron run until its scheduled date. This leaves the missing/invalid-recipient case the PR is intended to stop retrying; treat a missing destination or unrenderable message as a terminal failure or increment the retry count outside this guard.

title: The public `findMany` API was removed without an equivalent query API
body: This change deletes `InsightsBookingService.findMany`, which previously accepted normal Prisma findMany arguments and applied the authorization and filter conditions before reading `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized`. The replacement only returns a SQL fragment, so existing callers of this exported service will either fail TypeScript compilation or fail at runtime, and callers must now reimplement selection, pagination, ordering, and any additional where clauses themselves. Preserve a compatible query method or migrate every production consumer as part of the change.

title: Constructor type accepts an invalid team scope as valid input
body: `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions` permits `{ scope: "team", userId, orgId }` because `teamId` is optional for every scope. The constructor accepts that value at this line, but `safeParse` rejects it against the discriminated schema and the service silently returns `1=0`. Before this change, the constructor required `InsightsBookingServiceOptions`, which required `teamId` for team scope at compile time. Make the public type a discriminated union with a required `teamId` in the team variant, or accept `unknown` explicitly if invalid external input is intentionally supported.

title: No database test executes the new team or org SQL conditions
body: The only test that interpolates the generated condition into `$queryRaw` uses `scope: "user"`, which only exercises scalar `userId`/`teamId IS NULL` predicates. Team and org scopes now generate `ANY(${number[]})` raw parameters and OR-combined authorization predicates, but their tests only compare `Prisma.Sql` objects; those comparisons recreate the same template and do not validate PostgreSQL syntax, array parameter serialization, or the rows actually authorized. Add `$queryRaw` integration coverage for both scopes with included and excluded bookings.

title: The public `findMany` API was removed without a compatibility path
body: `InsightsBookingService` previously exposed `findMany(findManyArgs)`, which executed an authorized Prisma query while preserving caller-supplied selection, ordering, pagination, and `where` options. It has been removed and replaced only with `getBaseConditions()`, which is not an equivalent API and does not execute a query or accept those options. Existing consumers of this service will fail TypeScript compilation on `.findMany`, and a consumer migrated only to this fragment can easily lose its previous query constraints. Keep a compatible `findMany` implementation (using the raw-condition approach internally if necessary), or migrate every production call site and preserve each caller's query semantics in this change.

title: Removing `findMany` breaks the service's existing query API
body: The previous public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method is removed and replaced only with `getBaseConditions()`. Callers that currently use this service to retrieve booking rows will no longer type-check (or will fail at runtime if not type-checked), and the replacement does not preserve caller-supplied `select`, `where`, ordering, or pagination arguments. Migrate all consumers in the same change to execute an equivalent `$queryRaw` query, or retain a compatible `findMany` wrapper while introducing the SQL-condition API.

title: Deleting a cache does not refresh the displayed cache status
body: The delete-cache mutation only invokes the optional `onSuccess` callback. Unlike the disconnect mutation below it, it never invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. Since this callback is optional, normal usages without a callback retain the old `cacheUpdatedAt` in the React Query cache after deletion, continue showing the cache as present, and allow repeated deletes that report success even though no cached rows remain. Invalidate or refetch `connectedCalendars` when the mutation settles.

title: Every cache refresh performs an unnecessary update of every selected calendar
body: After repopulating cache entries, this unconditionally runs `updateMany` for all SelectedCalendar rows under the credential solely with an empty data object, thereby advancing their `updatedAt` values. Cache status is now read from `CalendarCache.updatedAt`, not from SelectedCalendar, so this adds a write and locks all of a credential's selected-calendar rows for every cache refresh (which can be driven frequently by calendar webhooks). It also makes SelectedCalendar.updatedAt no longer represent a selected-calendar change. Remove this update unless there is a consumer that requires this distinct timestamp.

title: The webhook setup script corrupts or fails to update env files on GNU/Linux
body: `sed -i '' -E` is BSD/macOS-specific syntax. On GNU sed, the separate empty argument is interpreted as the sed program rather than an in-place suffix, so the replacement expression is treated as an input filename; the command fails and can leave the target file empty. Because the script does not stop on that failure, it can still print that GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL was updated even though it was not. Use platform-aware in-place editing or a portable temporary-file replacement and fail on errors.

title: The new destructive cache-deletion endpoint has no automated authorization coverage
body: No test is added for this handler despite it deleting persisted availability data based on a caller-provided credential ID. Add handler/router tests that verify an owner deletes only rows for their own credential, a different user's credential is rejected without deleting rows, and deleting a credential with no cache is handled as intended. The added shell script only configures a webhook tunnel and does not exercise this endpoint or its ownership boundary.

title: Deleting cache does not refresh the displayed cache status
body: The delete-cache mutation only invokes the optional onSuccess callback. The connectedCalendars query that supplies cacheUpdatedAt is not invalidated, and this wrapper explicitly disables refetch-on-window-focus. When the wrapper is used without an onChanged callback (which its props permit), a successful deletion leaves the old timestamp and delete action visible until a full remount or reload. Invalidate viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars on successful/settled cache deletion, as the disconnect mutation already does.

title: Migration fabricates the last-updated time for every existing cache entry
body: Adding this non-null column with DEFAULT NOW() stamps every pre-existing CalendarCache row with the migration time. The new UI presents this value as "Last updated", so immediately after deployment old cache data will be reported as having been refreshed at deployment even though its value may be nearly expired. Backfill from an existing source such as expiresAt minus the cache TTL where valid, or represent legacy timestamps as unknown until the cache is refreshed.

title: Each cache warm rewrites all selected-calendar rows for the credential
body: After populating cache data for the supplied selectedCalendars, this credential-wide update touches every SelectedCalendar row with that credential, including calendars and event types that were not part of the refresh. Because SelectedCalendar has an updatedAt field, this is a bulk physical update solely to change timestamps; the new cache-status endpoint reads CalendarCache.updatedAt instead, so this write does not affect the displayed status. Cache refreshes can be triggered repeatedly by webhook/cache workflows, causing avoidable row locks, WAL/MVCC churn, and contention for credentials with many event types. Remove this touch or limit it to the rows actually refreshed if another consumer truly needs it.

title: The webhook helper cannot reliably update .env on GNU/Linux
body: `sed -i ''` is BSD/macOS syntax. On GNU sed, the separate empty argument is treated as an input file, causing sed to exit with an error; because the script does not use `set -e`, it can still print that GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL was updated. This makes the added test helper unreliable on Linux. Use a portable temporary-file replacement or select the appropriate `sed -i` form per platform and fail when the replacement fails.

title: Deleting the cache does not refresh the cache-status query
body: The delete mutation only calls the optional `onSuccess` callback. Unlike the disconnect mutation, it never invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`, which is the query supplying `cacheUpdatedAt`. Consumers that do not provide an `onChanged` callback that explicitly refetches will continue to show the old "Last updated" value and delete action after the server has deleted the rows; this is especially persistent because the query disables refetch-on-window-focus. Invalidate or refetch `connectedCalendars` when the deletion settles.

title: Legacy cache entries are stamped with the migration time rather than their update time
body: Adding this required column with `DEFAULT NOW()` gives every pre-existing CalendarCache row the time the migration runs.
