The new status query takes the maximum of this field and the UI presents it as "Last updated", so existing cache data will be reported as freshly updated at deployment even if it was fetched much earlier. Backfill from an appropriate historical value (or treat legacy rows as having unknown status) instead of presenting the schema-migration timestamp as cache freshness.

title: The cron development command executes an unpinned undeclared package
body: `tsx` is not declared in this package's dependencies or devDependencies, and `npx tsx` may download and execute the currently published version at command time (or prompt/fail in offline or noninteractive environments). This bypasses the repository lockfile and makes `dev:cron` nondeterministic. Add and pin `tsx` as a development dependency and invoke it through Yarn/the package binary.

title: Webhook setup failures exit successfully
body: `cleanup` always exits with status 0, but it is also called when Tunnelmole is rate-limited or no tunnel URL can be extracted. As a result, an automated setup/test invocation reports success even though `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` was not configured and subsequent webhook testing cannot work. Preserve a nonzero exit code for error paths.

title: The SendGrid client used by the cancellation cron is never authenticated
body: The handler only calls `sgMail.setApiKey`, which configures the mail service's internal client, not the separately imported `@sendgrid/client` instance used by `client.request` here. Consequently the new scheduled-send cancellation request can be rejected as unauthorized; the outer catch logs the error and leaves the reminder unmodified, so the SendGrid email remains queued and is sent. Configure this `client` with `client.setApiKey(sendgridAPIKey)` before making requests.

title: A cancellation shortly before send time is not processed before the email is delivered
body: Booking cancellation only marks an email reminder as cancelled, while this job performs the actual SendGrid cancellation on a 15-minute cadence. If the previous cron run has already occurred and a user cancels a booking whose reminder is due before the next run (for example, a reminder due in five minutes), SendGrid will send it before this query executes. The next run deletes the now-past database record without ever preventing the delivery. Imminent reminders need synchronous cancellation or a scheduling/worker design that guarantees cancellation before `sendAt`.

title: Rescheduling bypasses the deferred cancellation mechanism and recreates the SendGrid cancellation-cap failure
body: The reschedule path passes `immediateDelete: true`, causing `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` to POST `status: cancel` to SendGrid immediately and return without setting `WorkflowReminder.cancelled`. Therefore these records are never handled or retried by the cron job. SendGrid retains each such far-future cancellation until its scheduled date; after enough reschedules the provider's pending-cancellation limit is reached, cancellation failures are swallowed, and old reminders are sent. Reschedules should persist a retryable cancelled state and use the bounded cron cancellation path (with separate handling for imminent sends).

title: Paid booking cancellations return before any workflow reminder is cancelled
body: For a paid booking this branch refunds the payment, changes the booking to `REJECTED`, and returns at line 464. The workflow-reminder cancellation loop that marks email reminders cancelled and removes SMS reminders is below this return at lines 484-493, so it is never reached. Scheduled workflow emails for paid bookings remain active and will still be delivered after cancellation. Move reminder and scheduled-job cancellation before the paid-booking early return or execute it in that branch.

title: Reminder cancellation state updates are fire-and-forget
body: `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` are async, but the calls inside these `forEach` loops are neither awaited nor included in the later `Promise.all`. The cancellation endpoint can report success before the `cancelled` marker is persisted (or before SMS cancellation/deletion finishes); in a serverless request this work may be terminated after the response. That leaves the cron with no marker to act on and permits the queued reminder to send. Collect and await these promises, and propagate or otherwise reliably record failures.

title: The SendGrid client used for cancellation is never authenticated
body: This route only calls `sgMail.setApiKey`, but the new cancellation request at line 57 is made through the separate `@sendgrid/client` instance. `@sendgrid/mail` does not configure that client's authorization header, so the cancellation POST will be rejected by SendGrid and the error is only logged. Configure `client.setApiKey(sendgridAPIKey)` in this route before calling `client.request`; otherwise cancelled reminders remain scheduled and are sent.

title: A cancellation shortly before a reminder is due is not processed before the email sends
body: Cancellation is now deferred exclusively to a cron job that runs every 15 minutes. If a booking is cancelled after a cron invocation and its scheduled reminder is due before the next invocation (for example, a reminder due in five minutes), no SendGrid cancellation is attempted before `sendAt`, so the reminder is still delivered. The one-hour query horizon does not solve this because it is only evaluated when cron next runs. Near-term reminders need an immediate/guaranteed cancellation path or a worker cadence that completes before their send time.

title: Direct booking reschedules bypass the new durable cancellation flow
body: The normal booking reschedule flow calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(..., true)`, which performs an immediate SendGrid cancellation and returns without setting `WorkflowReminder.cancelled`. This reintroduces the exact capped-pending-cancellation failure the PR is intended to avoid: when SendGrid rejects the immediate cancellation, the helper catches the error, the reminder stays `cancelled = null`, and the cron query will never retry it. Rescheduled bookings through this endpoint can therefore still send their old reminders; use the persisted `cancelled` path (or mark it for cron retry when the immediate call fails).

title: One failed cancellation prevents all later reminders in the batch from being cancelled
body: The entire loop is enclosed by one `try` block. If `client.request` fails for any reminder, execution exits the loop immediately and skips cancellation of every remaining reminder; it also skips the accumulated database deletes for prior successful requests. A permanently invalid or transiently failing batch can consequently leave other valid, imminent cancelled reminders untouched until a later run, and can repeatedly block them. Handle failures per reminder and persist successful cancellations independently so one bad SendGrid request cannot block the rest.

title: Completed reschedules bypass the deferred SendGrid cancellation path
body: Passing `true` invokes the immediate branch of `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`, which posts `status: "cancel"` to SendGrid immediately and returns without marking or deleting the WorkflowReminder. This runs for every completed reschedule regardless of how far in the future the reminder is, so cancelled batches remain pending in SendGrid until their send time and consume the 100 pending-cancellation limit this change is intended to avoid. Reschedules that do not first pass through `requestReschedule` also leave the reminder row uncancelled and stale. Use the deferred `cancelled` state here (or only use an immediate cancellation for a near-term deadline) so the cron owns the final SendGrid request and cleanup.

title: Polling cancellation leaves reminders scheduled during the cron interval
body: A cancellation only sets `cancelled` in the database; this code does not call SendGrid until the next cron invocation. If a booking is cancelled after one 15-minute run and its reminder is due before the next run, SendGrid will send the email before this query sees it. On the next run the earlier cleanup deletes records whose scheduled date is already past, so the external scheduled send is never cancelled at all. Querying one hour ahead does not close this gap because the row was not marked cancelled at the prior run. The cancellation flow needs a safe immediate path for reminders due before the next run, or a cancellation job/timing guarantee that runs before every possible send time.

title: Reminder cancellation persistence is launched but never awaited
body: `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` are async and perform the database update/delete needed to stop or queue the reminder, but the nested `forEach` discards their promises. The later `Promise.all` does not include these operations, so this handler can return while the email's `cancelled` flag has not been written (or a serverless runtime can terminate the work). A cron run or an imminent SendGrid send can therefore observe the reminder as active and send it. Collect these promises and await them before completing the cancellation request.

title: One failed SendGrid cancellation prevents all later reminders from being cancelled
body: The single `try` covers the whole sequential loop. If `client.request` rejects for one reminder (for example, a missing or already-expired SendGrid batch), control jumps to the outer catch and every remaining `remindersToCancel` entry is skipped. Those later reminders remain scheduled and can still be sent; the bad row can also block the same batch again on subsequent cron runs. Handle errors per reminder and continue processing the remaining rows, deleting only rows whose cancellation succeeded.

title: Await calendar/video cancellation work before completing the reschedule
body: `forEach` discards the promises returned by its async callback. After the new `await getCalendar(...)`, this function proceeds to send the reschedule email and returns `true` while the integration module may still be loading and the old calendar/video event may not yet have been deleted. Rejections from either the import or deletion also bypass the surrounding `try/catch` and become unhandled. Collect these operations with `Promise.all`/`Promise.allSettled` and await them so failed or delayed external cancellations are handled deterministically.

title: Await calendar/video cancellation work before completing the reschedule
body: `forEach` ignores the async callback promises. The added `await getCalendar(...)` means cancellation is deferred beyond this block, so the function can send the reschedule email and report success before the previous calendar or video event is removed. Any module-load or deletion error is not caught by the enclosing `try/catch`, because it occurs in the detached callback. Use an awaited `Promise.all`/`Promise.allSettled` over the references instead.

title: Recurring calendar deletions are detached from the cancellation request
body: The async `forEach` callbacks are never awaited. Each callback now suspends at `await getCalendar`, while the handler continues and later snapshots `apiDeletes` in `Promise.all`; at that point the callbacks may not have added anything yet. Moreover, they add `deletedEvent` only after awaiting it, so `apiDeletes` cannot track the in-flight work. A recurring cancellation can therefore finish successfully while some or all external calendar events remain undeleted, and callback failures are unhandled. Await per-credential/per-booking deletion promises directly before completing the handler.

title: Do not detach integration deletions in requestReschedule
body: This `forEach(async ...)` is not awaited. With asynchronous app loading, the mutation continues to send email/webhooks and can resolve before `getCalendar` has loaded the integration or before `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` has run. Errors from those operations are also unhandled. Build a promise list for the booking references and await it (or await `Promise.allSettled` if deletion failures should not fail the reschedule) before returning from the mutation.

title: The dynamic imports are all started eagerly rather than on demand
body: Each `import("./...")` expression is executed while the `appStore` object is initialized. Consequently, merely importing `@calcom/app-store` starts loading and evaluating every integration module, including integrations unrelated to the request. This defeats on-demand loading and keeps cold-start CPU, memory, and chunk-loading costs coupled to the full app catalog. Store loader functions instead (for example, `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) and invoke only the selected loader at the call site.

title: Calendar and video deletion promises are discarded during rescheduling
body: `Array.prototype.forEach` does not await an async callback. The new `await getCalendar(...)` makes each calendar deletion asynchronous before `deleteEvent` is even invoked, but the surrounding `try/catch` exits immediately and the reschedule flow sends the email/returns without waiting for or observing any deletion failure. Rejections from either the import or provider call bypass this catch, and the old external event can remain active after the booking has been marked cancelled. Await a `Promise.all`/`Promise.allSettled` over `bookingRefsFiltered.map(...)`.

title: Calendar and video deletion promises are discarded during rescheduling
body: `Array.prototype.forEach` does not await an async callback. The new `await getCalendar(...)` makes each calendar deletion asynchronous before `deleteEvent` is even invoked, but the surrounding `try/catch` exits immediately and the reschedule flow sends the email/returns without waiting for or observing any deletion failure. Rejections from either the import or provider call bypass this catch, and the old external event can remain active after the booking has been marked cancelled. Await a `Promise.all`/`Promise.allSettled` over `bookingRefsFiltered.map(...)`.

title: Recurring cancellation does not wait for calendar deletions
body: The async callback passed to `forEach` is never joined. In this branch it now first awaits `getCalendar`, so the parent handler can reach its later `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` before the callbacks have populated `apiDeletes`; those callbacks push the deletion result only after the deletion has already completed. The handler can therefore remove booking references and return success while recurring external calendar events are still being deleted, and provider/import failures become unhandled. Build and await a promise per credential/booking deletion instead of using `forEach`.

title: Request-reschedule returns before integration deletions finish
body: The async callback supplied to `forEach` is discarded. Since the calendar branch now awaits `getCalendar`, neither the calendar import nor `deleteEvent` is awaited by the mutation, and there is no rejection handler for either operation. The booking is already marked cancelled and the mutation can complete while its calendar/video event remains active; a failed dynamic import or provider deletion is an unhandled rejection. Await a collected `Promise.all`/`Promise.allSettled` for these callbacks before completing the reschedule operation.

title: The app imports are all started eagerly, not on demand
body: Each `import("./...")` expression is executed while this module is initialized, so importing `@calcom/app-store` immediately starts loading and evaluating every calendar, video, CRM, and payment app. Awaiting a single entry later does not make the other entries lazy. This defeats the expected per-integration loading benefit and can create substantial startup CPU, memory, and chunk-loading contention for requests that use only one integration. Store memoized loader functions (for example, `() => import("./applecalendar")`) and invoke only the requested loader instead.

title: Calendar deletions are launched in unobserved async callbacks
body: `forEach` does not await the promises returned by its async callback. After the new `await getCalendar(...)`, this function proceeds to send the reschedule email and returns while module loading and remote calendar/video deletion are still pending. Rejections from either the dynamic import or `deleteEvent` also bypass the surrounding `try/catch`, resulting in unhandled failures and potentially leaving the old external event intact after the booking is marked cancelled. Build a `map` of deletion promises and await `Promise.all` (or `Promise.allSettled`) inside the error handling block.

title: Calendar deletions are launched in unobserved async callbacks
body: `forEach` ignores the async callback promises. The new `await getCalendar(...)` means this reschedule operation can send its email and return before the calendar module has loaded or the old external event has been deleted. Any import or deletion rejection is outside the enclosing `try/catch`, so failures are unhandled and the booking can be cancelled internally while its external calendar event remains. Await a collected set of deletion promises rather than using async `forEach`.

title: Recurring cancellation does not wait for dynamically loaded calendar deletions
body: The recurring-booking branch starts async `forEach` callbacks but never retains or awaits their promises. Since each callback now first awaits `getCalendar`, `apiDeletes` can be snapshotted by the later `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` before any remote deletion is even added to it. The handler can therefore delete local references and return success while recurring calendar events are still pending or fail with unhandled errors. Replace this loop with awaited per-credential/per-booking deletion promises and include those promises directly in the final wait.

title: Reschedule mutation returns before external deletion callbacks complete
body: The async callbacks passed to `forEach` are not awaited. With `await getCalendar(...)` added here, the mutation marks the booking cancelled, sends the reschedule email, and can complete before the calendar module resolves and before the old calendar/video event is deleted. Rejections from the dynamic import or deletion also have no error handler. Collect these operations with `map` and await them before sending the success path, with explicit error handling.

title: Override is selected for the wrong invitee date when timezone conversion crosses midnight
body: The active-override filter selects a day using the unadjusted `override.start`, but the new code later shifts that override by `inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset` (lines 212-224). That shift can change its invitee calendar date, and only the shifted hour/minute is retained. For example, a 09:00 June 10 override for an Asia/Tokyo organizer is 16:00 June 9 for an America/Los_Angeles attendee: the unshifted timestamp makes this code activate the override for June 10, then the shifted 16:00 minute value produces a June 10 slot instead of June 9. The filter must use the converted instant (and account for range overlap) before deciding which invitee day owns the override.

title: Slots inside an override bypass busy-time validation
body: When a slot is considered inside a date override, `dateOverrideExist` causes this function to return `true` before reaching the `busy.every(...)` check at line 153. `getTimeSlots` creates availability candidates but does not remove calendar or Cal.com booking conflicts, so a host with an override can be offered and booked during an existing busy event. The override should determine whether the host is scheduled to work, then the normal busy-time check must still run.

title: Date-override validation accepts partial overlaps and mishandles multiple override windows
body: The override predicate only rejects slots that are completely before or strictly after one override; it never requires the full `[slotStart, slotEnd]` interval to be contained in an override. A 60-minute slot from 09:30 to 10:30 is therefore accepted for a 10:00 to 11:00 override. In addition, using `find` means a slot in one of several override windows is rejected as soon as another same-day window does not contain it. The intended all-day/zero-length special case at line 114 also cannot work because two separately created Dayjs objects are compared with `===`. This can both expose slots outside a fixed host's override availability and hide valid override slots.

title: Fixed-host normal working hours are not checked as a containing availability range
body: This condition only looks for a working-hours entry that proves the slot invalid; it never requires that any entry for the host actually contains the slot. If a fixed host has no `workingHour` on the slot's weekday, `find` returns undefined and the host falls through as available, allowing a round-robin candidate supplied by a loose host to be booked on the fixed host's day off. Split working-hour ranges are also evaluated incorrectly because a slot valid in one range can be rejected by another, and `end` is set equal to the slot start at line 142 so the event duration is never checked. The check needs to require one host-local working interval containing the complete slot.

title: The added regression test does not cover fixed hosts in a round-robin event
body: The new test invokes an event type with only `users`; it has neither `schedulingType: "ROUND_ROBIN"` nor `hosts` with an `isFixed` host. Consequently it does not exercise the fixed-host filtering path changed in `getSchedule`, and the existing round-robin test also uses `hosts: []`. Add a scenario with a fixed host, a loose round-robin host, and fixed-host date overrides (including unavailable and busy periods) so the behavior described by this PR is actually protected.

title: Fixed-host override validation does not require a booking to fit inside an override window
body: The callback marks a slot unavailable only when it is wholly before an override or starts strictly after it; any slot overlapping either edge falls through `dateOverrideExist` and is accepted. For example, a 30-minute slot from 10:45 to 11:15 is accepted for a 10:00 to 11:00 override. The `.find` also stops on the first nonmatching range, so with 09:00-10:00 and 14:00-15:00 overrides, a valid 14:00 slot is rejected because it is after the first range. Additionally, the empty-override branch at line 114 compares two distinct Dayjs objects with `===`, so a 10:00-10:00 blackout is not detected and can admit a slot beginning at 10:00. This can book a round-robin event while its fixed host is unavailable; the code needs to require the full slot interval to be contained in at least one override range.

title: Fixed-host working-hours validation rejects split schedules and permits slots past closing time
body: `end` is calculated from `slotStartTime` rather than `slotEndTime`, so a slot that starts before the end of a host's hours but finishes after it is treated as valid. Also, using `workingHours.find` with an "outside this interval" predicate makes every slot invalid for a host with multiple windows on the same day: a 10:00 slot in a 09:00-12:00 window is rejected when the 13:00-17:00 window is inspected, and vice versa. Since this check is the new fixed-host guard after round-robin availability has been aggregated, it can both hide valid slots and allow bookings that overrun a fixed host's availability. The check should test the actual slot end and accept when any applicable working-hours range fully contains the slot.

title: Date-override end times use the start-time timezone offset across DST transitions
body: `offset` is derived only from `override.start` and is reused when converting `override.end`. An override can span a daylight-saving transition, where the endpoint has a different organizer or invitee UTC offset. For example, a New York override from 01:00 to 03:00 on the spring-forward date spans 06:00 to 07:00 UTC, but applying the start's UTC-05 offset to the 03:00 endpoint converts it to 08:00 UTC and exposes an extra unavailable hour. Resolve the organizer/invitee offset separately for each endpoint (using the override's local date/time) before calculating its local minutes.

title: The primary fixed-host round-robin behavior has no automated regression test
body: The new test exercises a personal event with one user. The existing round-robin test uses `hosts: []`, which means its round-robin users are all classified as non-fixed and never execute the new `fixedHosts.every(...)` path. There is therefore no test for the reported scenario of a round-robin event with both a fixed host and a loose host, where a loose host creates a candidate slot outside the fixed host's date override. Add that scenario and assert that slots outside the fixed host's override are absent.

title: A fixed host's date override does not require the whole slot to fit
body: Once an override date is found, this logic only rejects a slot whose start is after the override end; it never rejects a slot that starts before the override end but finishes after it. For example, a 60-minute slot from 17:30 to 18:30 is accepted for an override ending at 18:00. Such a slot can be generated from a loose round-robin host's availability and then incorrectly remain bookable even though the fixed host cannot attend. The check needs to require slotStartTime >= override start and slotEndTime <= override end using consistent half-open boundaries.

title: Working-hours validation treats no matching interval as available
body: The predicate searches for any working-hours interval that the slot is outside of, rather than requiring an interval that contains the slot. If a fixed host has no working-hours row on that weekday, find() returns undefined and the host is treated as available. It also rejects every slot for a host with split hours: a 10:00 slot in a 09:00-12:00 interval is rejected because it is outside the separate 13:00-17:00 interval. In a round-robin event, slots generated by a loose host can therefore be offered while a fixed host is unavailable, or valid fixed-host slots can all disappear. This should use a positive containment check over the host's intervals.

title: Working-hours validation ignores the booking duration
body: Both start and end are calculated from slotStartTime, so the condition only checks whether the slot starts within a fixed host's working hours. A one-hour slot beginning at 11:30 for a host working until 12:00 passes this check even though it ends at 12:30. Although getTimeSlots normally constrains the host that generated a candidate, a loose round-robin host can generate this candidate and this new fixed-host filter is then responsible for rejecting it. Calculate end from slotEndTime and require the complete slot to fit.

title: Override timezone conversion is adjusted a second time across DST
body: The override minutes are already translated using the organizer and invitee offsets at the override timestamp, but buildSlots subsequently adds organizerDSTDiff - inviteeDSTDiff based on the current date and the invitee day. This shifts date overrides by an hour whenever the override date has a different DST offset than today. For example, when evaluated in January, a 10:00 America/New_York override in July for a UTC invitee is converted here to 14:00, then buildSlots applies the -60 minute organizer DST difference and produces 13:00. Date overrides are dated absolute exceptions and must not receive the recurring-working-hours DST correction again.

title: Equal override endpoints are compared by object identity
body: Each dayjs(...).add(...) call creates a distinct Dayjs object, so strict equality is always false even when date.start and date.end represent the same instant. The special handling for a zero-length/all-day-unavailable override therefore never runs. A candidate that starts exactly at that instant can fall through to dateOverrideExist and be considered available; compare the timestamps with isSame() instead.

title: The claimed fixed-host round-robin behavior has no regression coverage
body: The added timezone assertion exercises a regular one-user event only. It does not create a ROUND_ROBIN event with a fixed host, a loose host whose availability generates the candidate slot, and a fixed-host date override. The existing round-robin test also has no fixed hosts. Consequently the new fixed-host filtering path, including the case this PR is intended to prevent, is untested and the overbooking and split-availability regressions can merge unnoticed.

title: Migration crashes when the legacy embed category has no matching category
body: The category lookup assumes the join always returns a row and immediately dereferences `...[0]['id']`. On installations where `embed_category` was left at its default blank value (or its site-setting row was never persisted), the join returns no rows, so this raises before the intended `category_id == 0` fallback can run. This blocks the entire deployment migration for the common unconfigured case.

title: Legacy URL-form host entries are copied in a form the new lookup can never match
body: The old setting accepted entries such as `http://discourse.org` and `https://example.com/path` (the previous lookup explicitly parsed these forms), but this raw INSERT stores them unchanged. The new `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host` extracts only `URI(host).host` and compares it to the stored `host`, so a row containing `http://discourse.org` or a path will never match `discourse.org`. The model normalization callback is bypassed by this SQL INSERT, causing existing configured embeds to be denied after migration.

title: Duplicate host mappings make the destination category ambiguous
body: Neither the model nor the migration enforces uniqueness of a host, while `record_for_host` resolves a match with an unordered `.first`. Administrators can create the same hostname more than once with different categories (including case variants), after which imports for that host are assigned to whichever row the database happens to return rather than to a deterministic configured relationship. Add a case-insensitive uniqueness constraint/index and validation, or define an explicit conflict policy.

title: Hosts with ports are accepted but can never be authorized
body: The validation permits values such as `example.com:8080`, and the normalization callback leaves the port in the stored value. `record_for_host` then parses a request URL and compares only `URI(...).host` (`example.com`) against the stored string (`example.com:8080`), so no referer or retrieval URL can match that saved configuration. Either reject ports or normalize/query them consistently.

title: Updating or deleting a missing host raises a server error
body: Both `update` and `destroy` use `where(...).first` but dereference the result without checking it. A request for an ID that was deleted by another admin session, or simply does not exist, calls `save_host(nil)` or `nil.destroy` and returns a 500 instead of a 404. This also leaves the admin UI without a recoverable response for concurrent edits/deletes.

title: Migration crashes when no legacy embed category is configured
body: The category lookup is indexed immediately with `[0]['id']`. On a normal installation where `embed_category` was left at its default, is absent from `site_settings`, or no longer matches a category name, the query returns no rows and this raises on nil before the fallback at lines 14-16 can run. This prevents the entire database migration from completing; both legacy-setting lookups need to handle an empty result and use the uncategorized fallback safely.

title: Legacy URL-form allowed hosts are migrated into unusable records
body: This raw INSERT copies each legacy setting value verbatim, bypassing `EmbeddableHost`'s normalization callback. The previous setting accepted entries such as `https://example.com/path`, but the new authorization lookup parses a referer to `example.com` and queries `lower(host) = 'example.com'`; it will not match the stored URL/path. Upgrading such an existing configuration silently disables embedding for every URL-form host until each row is manually edited. Normalize the legacy values before inserting them (or create records through the model).

title: Duplicate host rows make the selected category ambiguous
body: There is no uniqueness validation or database constraint on `host`, while this lookup returns only the first row matching `lower(host)`. Admins can create duplicate or case-variant entries for the same domain with different categories through the new UI; only one of those categories will be used for imports, and editing the other row has no predictable effect on routing. Canonicalize hosts and enforce a case-insensitive unique host mapping, or otherwise define deterministic multi-row behavior.

title: Hosts containing a port are accepted but can never authorize embeds
body: The validation permits values such as `example.com:3000`, and the normalization callback preserves the port. `URI(host).host` deliberately strips that port, however, so this query searches for `example.com` while the database contains `example.com:3000`. Consequently any host entered with a port is displayed as saved but all requests from it are rejected. The stored and lookup forms need to treat ports consistently (for example, strip/reject ports on save or compare URI authority).

title: Removing all allowed hosts no longer disables expansion of existing embeds
body: `expandable_first_post?` no longer checks whether any embeddable host is configured. With `embed_truncate` enabled, an old topic with a `TopicEmbed` remains expandable even after every host has been removed; expansion fetches the historical remote URL through `TopicEmbed.expanded_for`. This defeats the prior disable switch and can keep server-side remote fetches/content from a deliberately removed host available. Replace the removed setting check with an appropriate `EmbeddableHost` existence/authorization check.

title: A newly saved uncategorized host is shown without its server-assigned category
body: When a new host is saved with no category selected, the server assigns `uncategorized_category_id`, but `categoryId` is still null in this component. The success handler then explicitly replaces the host's category with `Discourse.Category.findById(null)`, discarding the category represented by the response. The row therefore shows no category until a reload and subsequent edits continue to submit a blank selection. Set `categoryId` from the returned `host.category_id` and resolve that value instead.

title: Updating or deleting an already removed host produces a server error
body: Both `update` and `destroy` use `where(...).first` and immediately dereference the result. If another administrator has deleted the row, or the client sends a stale/nonexistent id, `save_host(nil)` calls `host.host` and `destroy` calls `nil.destroy`, producing a 500 instead of a not-found response. This is a normal concurrent-admin workflow for this UI; handle a missing record explicitly before saving or destroying.

title: Migration crashes when the optional legacy category setting is unset
body: The join returns no rows when `embed_category` has its normal blank/default value, has no persisted row, or names a category that no longer exists. Indexing `[0]['id']` then raises before the fallback to `uncategorized_category_id` can run, preventing `db:migrate` on those installations. Read the first result defensively and apply the uncategorized fallback when no matching category exists.

title: Legacy URL-form host settings are migrated into values that can never match
body: This raw INSERT bypasses `EmbeddableHost`'s normalization callbacks. Existing settings such as `http://eviltrout.com` or `https://example.com/path` are stored verbatim, but `record_for_host` parses a request down to `eviltrout.com` and queries `lower(host) = ?`; it therefore cannot find these migrated rows. The previous setting implementation explicitly supported schemes and paths, so affected sites will lose embedding authorization after upgrading. Normalize each legacy value before inserting it (and preferably use the model or bound SQL).

title: Duplicate host records make the destination category ambiguous
body: There is no case-insensitive uniqueness validation or database constraint on `host`, while lookup selects an unordered `.first` matching row. The admin API permits adding the same host more than once with different categories, after which new embeds can be assigned to whichever duplicate the database happens to return rather than the category the administrator intended. Enforce normalized, case-insensitive host uniqueness with a database index as well as model validation.

title: Hosts entered with a port are accepted but cannot be authorized
body: The validation explicitly permits a port and the normalization callback retains it (for example, `example.com:8080`), but `URI(host).host` removes the port before this query. The stored value `example.com:8080` is consequently compared with `example.com` and never matches, so configured non-default-port embedding sites are always rejected. Normalize ports out of persisted host values or consistently compare host and port.

title: Host validation rejects valid modern domain names
body: The hostname expression limits the final label to two through five ASCII letters. Valid domains such as `example.museum`, `example.technology`, and other long modern TLDs cannot be added through the new admin UI and receive a validation error, even though they are valid embedding origins. Use URI/domain parsing or a TLD-length-independent hostname validation.

title: Updating or deleting a missing host returns a 500
body: Both `update` and `destroy` use `where(...).first` without handling a nil result. A stale edit after another administrator deletes the host, or a request for an unknown id, calls `save_host(nil)` or `nil.destroy` and raises `NoMethodError` instead of returning a not-found response. Explicitly fetch-or-404 before saving or destroying.

title: The data migration is not reversible despite using `change`
body: The migration performs several raw `execute` calls inside `change`; Rails cannot infer inverses for them, so `db:rollback` raises an irreversible-migration error. Even if the table were removed, the deleted `embeddable_hosts` and `embed_category` site-setting values have no restoration path. This blocks rollback deployments and permanently discards the prior configuration; implement explicit `up` and `down` paths that restore the old settings.

title: Enforce the 10 MB source limit on the server before image processing
body: The new 10 MB limit exists only in browser JavaScript and does not apply to direct multipart requests. Any image body accepted by the proxy, regardless of its source size, reaches this block and is sent through up to five ImageMagick/ImageOptim conversions before Upload.create_for can apply its normal final-size validation. An authenticated caller can bypass the client check with a very large or decompression-bomb image and consume substantial worker CPU, memory, and disk. Reject source files above the intended input limit in the controller before invoking OptimizedImage.downsize.

title: The new downsize definition replaces the existing width/height API
body: Ruby does not overload methods by argument signature, so this second def self.downsize replaces the preceding def self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={}). Existing callers using the old four-argument form bind max_height as opts and then fail when optimize evaluates opts[:allow_animation]; callers passing the optional fifth argument raise ArgumentError. Preserve both call forms in a single method or use a differently named percentage-based helper.

title: Client validation now ignores the configured per-type upload limits
body: This replaces max_image_size_kb/max_attachment_size_kb with a universal 10 MB limit for both images and attachments. Consequently, attachments larger than a site's configured attachment limit are allowed through the UI only to fail on the server, while files that a site explicitly permits above 10 MB are rejected in the browser. The image-source allowance needed for downscaling should be applied only to images; attachment validation must continue to use max_attachment_size_kb.

title: Downsizing can irreversibly turn uploaded animated GIFs into single-frame GIFs
body: When allow_animated_thumbnails is false, this call selects OptimizedImage's non-animated downsize path, whose ImageMagick input is tempfile.path[0] and therefore contains only the first GIF frame. The result is then passed to Upload.create_for as the original upload, not merely as a generated thumbnail, so an oversized animated GIF is permanently stored as a static image. Skip animated uploads when animation-preserving conversion is disabled, or always use an animation-preserving path for the original upload.

title: Five fixed resize attempts do not ensure the final upload meets the configured limit
body: The loop limits itself to five 80% dimension reductions, but file byte size is content-dependent and max_image_size_kb is configurable. For example, a 10 MB source with a low configured limit can still exceed that limit after five passes, and a re-encode can reduce less than expected. The code then submits the still-oversized tempfile to Upload.create_for, causing the upload to be rejected despite the feature promising automatic reduction. Continue until the file meets the limit or no further reduction is possible, and handle a failed downsize explicitly.

title: Multipart uploads have no server-side input limit before ImageMagick processing
body: The new 10 MB limit is only enforced by the browser and for URL downloads; a client can POST a multipart file directly with any size. Any oversized image is passed through up to five ImageMagick conversions before `Upload.create_for` gets a chance to enforce the configured stored-file limit. An upload-capable user can therefore submit very large or decompression-bomb images and consume substantial worker CPU, memory, disk, and temporary-file space. Enforce a raw byte and image-pixel limit on the server before invoking `OptimizedImage.downsize`.

title: The new downsize definition replaces, rather than overloads, the existing API
body: Ruby does not overload methods by argument count. This definition replaces the preceding `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts = {})` definition, so existing callers using the prior width/height API now either raise `ArgumentError` for five arguments or treat `max_height` as `opts` for four arguments and fail when `optimize` indexes it as a hash. Preserve both call forms in a single method or use a differently named helper.

title: Oversized animated GIF uploads lose their animation despite the setting
body: For normal multipart uploads, `tempfile.path` is Rack's generated temporary filename rather than the original `.gif` filename. `OptimizedImage.optimize` selects the animated GIF path only when `from` ends in `.GIF`; this call therefore takes the regular ImageMagick path, whose input is `#{from}[0]` and contains only the first frame. Consequently, an oversized animated GIF is converted to a static image even when `allow_animated_thumbnails` is enabled. Preserve/pass the original format when selecting the conversion path and write through a suitably typed temporary file.

title: The retry limit does not ensure the image meets the configured size limit
body: The loop stops after five 80%-dimension resizes without checking that the resulting byte size is below `max_image_size_kb`. File size is not reduced by a fixed ratio when dimensions are reduced, especially for PNGs and already-compressed images, and valid installations can configure a limit low enough that five passes are insufficient. The subsequent upload will then be rejected by the existing size validation (or stored over the intended limit), so users still cannot upload the large image the feature is meant to handle. Continue until the byte target is met or no further useful reduction is possible, and return a clear failure when it cannot be met.

title: Client-side attachment limits no longer honor site configuration
body: `validateUploadedFile` is used for both `image` and `attachment`, but this change replaces the type-specific `max_<type>_size_kb` setting with a fixed 10 MB limit for both. Non-image attachments are not downsized by the controller, so sites with a smaller attachment limit now let users upload files that the server rejects, while sites allowing attachments over 10 MB are incorrectly blocked in the browser. Keep the larger raw-file allowance limited to images being downsized and continue using `max_attachment_size_kb` for attachments.

title: The new `downsize` definition replaces the existing width/height API
body: Ruby does not overload methods by arity, so the definition at line 149 completely replaces the five-argument `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts = {})` defined immediately above it. Existing four-argument calls such as `downsize(input, output, 800, 600)` now bind `600` as `opts` and fail when `optimize` evaluates `opts[:allow_animation]`; existing five-argument calls fail with `ArgumentError`. Keep one compatible method signature (or use a differently named percentage-based helper) so existing resizing callers continue to work.

title: ImageMagick is invoked on unbounded direct uploads before server-side validation
body: The resize loop runs before `Upload.create_for` performs the normal upload validation at line 72, and there is no server-side maximum for the original multipart file before invoking `OptimizedImage.downsize`. The 10 MB check added in the JavaScript client can be bypassed with a direct request, so any logged-in user can submit a very large or highly compressed image declared by filename and make the application run ImageMagick up to five times before the upload is accepted or rejected. This creates an authenticated CPU/memory/disk denial-of-service path. Enforce a server-side source-file and image-dimension/resource limit before calling the converter.

title: Client validation no longer honors the configured image and attachment limits
body: `validateUploadedFile` receives the upload type, but this change replaces both `max_image_size_kb` and `max_attachment_size_kb` with a fixed 10 MB limit. Sites configured to permit files larger than 10 MB are now blocked in the browser despite their settings, while attachments larger than a site's configured attachment limit are sent and only fail later on the server. The automatic-downsize allowance should be applied only to image source files while retaining the configured attachment limit and respecting configurations above 10 MB.

title: Oversized animated GIF uploads are silently flattened when animated thumbnails are disabled
body: The option passed here is `allow_animated_thumbnails`, but this operation rewrites the original uploaded file rather than a thumbnail. When that setting is false, `OptimizedImage.optimize` selects `downsize_instructions`, which invokes `convert` with `#{from}[0]` and therefore writes only the first GIF frame back to the upload tempfile. Users uploading an oversized animated GIF will receive a static GIF with no warning. Preserve all frames for original uploads, or reject/warn rather than silently replacing an animation with its first frame.

title: The GET unsubscribe endpoint is vulnerable to cross-site request forgery
body: `unsubscribe` changes the current user's notification level during a GET request, and the action is explicitly exempted from `check_xhr`. The URL contains only a publicly discoverable topic slug/id, so another site can navigate an authenticated user's browser to `/t/<slug>/<id>/unsubscribe` and silently downgrade or mute that user's subscription. Keep GET non-mutating and require a CSRF-protected POST after a confirmation, or validate a user-bound signed unsubscribe token.

title: Opening an unsubscribe URL without an existing TopicUser record raises a 500
body: This action assumes every logged-in viewer has a `topic_users` row. A user can directly open the canonical unsubscribe URL for a public topic they have never visited or otherwise been associated with; `TopicUser.find_by` then returns nil and line 107 dereferences `tu.notification_level`, causing `NoMethodError`. Handle the missing row by choosing the appropriate default level and using an upsert such as `TopicUser.change`.

title: Directly saving TopicUser does not record a manual notification override
body: The action assigns and saves `notification_level` directly instead of going through `TopicUser.change`. Consequently `notifications_changed_at` and `notifications_reason_id` are not set to the manual-change values. In particular, a row with a nil reason remains eligible for the automatic tracking logic in `update_last_read`/`auto_track`, which can later promote a user who unsubscribed back to tracking and re-enable topic notifications. This also bypasses the MessageBus notification used to update other open clients. Use `TopicUser.change` (or preserve its metadata and publish behavior) for this update.

title: The added unsubscribe URL is not actually asserted in generated email content
body: The modified test supplies `unsubscribe_url` but still only checks for the pre-existing user-preferences URL. There is no assertion that the per-topic URL appears in the text or HTML email, nor a request/controller test for the notification-level transition. The primary feature can therefore regress or render a broken topic-unsubscribe link without this test failing.

title: The top-level route does not resolve the added template
body: `topicUnsubscribe` is registered as a top-level route, so Ember will look up its default template under the route name (for example `topic-unsubscribe`), not `topic/unsubscribe`. The added template is registered as `topic/unsubscribe`, which is the name for a nested `topic.unsubscribe` route. Since this route does not set `templateName` or render that template explicitly, navigating from the email link will not render the unsubscribe page and its notification-state control. Rename the template to match the top-level route or explicitly set `templateName: 'topic/unsubscribe'`.

title: A GET request changes a user's notification preference without CSRF protection
body: The new `unsubscribe` action is reached through a GET route and mutates `TopicUser` state. GET requests are not protected by Rails' normal CSRF checks, and this action is also exempted from the XHR check. A third-party page can cause a logged-in user's browser to request `/t/:topic_id/unsubscribe` and silently lower that user's notification level; mail-client/link-preview prefetching can have the same effect. Render a confirmation on GET and perform the mutation via a CSRF-protected POST/PUT (or otherwise use a recipient-bound, deliberate confirmation flow).

title: Unsubscribe bypasses TopicUser's notification-change bookkeeping
body: Saving the `TopicUser` record directly only changes `notification_level`; it does not set `notifications_changed_at`, mark `notifications_reason_id` as `user_changed`, invoke the observer path, or publish the MessageBus notification that other sessions use to refresh their state. In particular, a row whose reason remains `NULL` can later be auto-promoted from muted to tracking by `TopicUser.update_last_read`, because that method treats a NULL reason as eligible for auto-tracking. Use `TopicUser.change(current_user, topic_id, notification_level: ...)` so an explicit unsubscribe remains explicit and connected clients are notified.

title: The shared unsubscribe translation now requires an option MessageBuilder does not default
body: `unsubscribe_link` now interpolates `%{unsubscribe_url}`, but `Email::MessageBuilder` only supplies a default `user_preferences_url`; `unsubscribe_url` is optional and is only added on the notification-mail path in this change. Any existing caller using `add_unsubscribe_link: true` without the new option will raise `I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument` while building the text or HTML body, preventing delivery. Preserve the existing builder contract by defaulting `unsubscribe_url`, or use a separate translation/conditional paragraph when no per-topic URL is available.

title: The unsubscribe action changes preferences through a CSRF-able GET request
body: This GET endpoint directly changes and saves the current user's notification preference, while it is explicitly allowed outside the normal XHR path and has no signed recipient token or confirmation step. Topic URLs are predictable for public topics, so a third-party site can force an authenticated visitor to navigate to one and mute/downgrade that visitor's topic notifications; browser prefetchers or link scanners can also trigger the change. The GET should only render a confirmation, with the mutation performed by a CSRF-protected POST, or the email link should use a recipient-bound signed token with appropriate one-click semantics.

title: The endpoint crashes for users without an existing TopicUser row
body: `find_by` can return nil for a logged-in user who has never visited or otherwise interacted with the topic, which is normal for a public topic reachable through this route. The following `tu.notification_level` dereference then raises a NoMethodError and returns a 500 instead of applying the requested preference. Use a get-or-create path (such as `TopicUser.change`) and treat the absent row as the default notification level.

title: Directly saving TopicUser bypasses notification preference invariants
body: This save bypasses `TopicUser.change`, the standard path that sets `notifications_changed_at`, records `notifications_reason_id` as `user_changed`, and publishes the level change. In particular, topic-user records created only while sending an email have a nil notification reason; after this action leaves that reason nil, the auto-track logic in `TopicUser.update_last_read` is allowed to promote a muted user back to tracking when they later read the topic. Other open clients also do not receive the MessageBus update. Compute the desired level and persist it through `TopicUser.change` so the unsubscribe is recorded as an explicit user choice.

title: The added test does not verify that the per-topic unsubscribe URL is rendered
body: The test now supplies `unsubscribe_url`, but its only body assertion checks for the unchanged user-preferences URL. It never asserts that `/t/1234/unsubscribe` appears in the text or HTML email, so the suite would still pass if the new interpolation were omitted or the per-topic link were broken. Add assertions for the rendered topic-specific link, plus a request-level test for the notification-level transition.

title: Blocked-email matching is case-sensitive and uses unnormalised input
body: The lookup compares the submitted value verbatim with a case-sensitive string column. Signup assigns params[:email] directly to the User, so a blocked record for `bad@example.com` will not match a signup using `Bad@Example.com` (or whitespace variants), even though the domain portion of an email address is case-insensitive in normal use. This bypasses the block and splits the match statistics. Normalize and strip emails consistently when creating BlockedEmail records and before looking them up, or use an appropriate case-insensitive database comparison/index.

title: Validation has a persistent side effect and double-counts signup attempts
body: Calling this validator increments match_count and updates last_match_at. Validators can run more than once for one operation; specifically, UsersController#create calls `user.valid?` before the Discourse Hub check and then calls `user.save`, which runs validations again. Consequently, each blocked or do-nothing email submitted through signup is counted twice, and any caller that revalidates a record further inflates the metric. Keep validation side-effect-free and record a match once at a request/operation boundary if the counter is intended to represent attempts.

title: Concurrent matches can lose match_count increments
body: The counter is read into an ActiveRecord instance, incremented in Ruby, and saved later. Two simultaneous validations of the same blocked email can both read the same match_count and both save that value plus one, losing one of the matches; delayed saves can also overwrite a newer last_match_at with an older timestamp. Use an atomic database update such as `update_all` with `match_count = match_count + 1` and the timestamp, or locking, when updating these statistics.

title: Rejected-email additions do not invalidate emailValidation
body: The response handler adds rejected values with `rejectedEmails.pushObject`, which changes array membership. The computed-property dependency `rejectedEmails.@each` does not observe membership changes for an array of primitive strings; `@each` is for observing a named property on each item. As a result, emailValidation can remain cached as successful after the server rejects the email, and the submit button is re-enabled for the same rejected value. Depend on `rejectedEmails.[]` (or explicitly notify the property) so pushObject invalidates the validation.

title: Blocked addresses can be bypassed by changing email case
body: The lookup compares the submitted value to `blocked_emails.email` verbatim and neither this model nor `User.new_from_params` canonicalizes email addresses. On the supported case-sensitive database, a block for `person@example.com` will not match a signup using `person@EXAMPLE.COM`, even though email domains are case-insensitive and both forms deliver to the same mailbox. This also permits differently cased duplicate block-list entries with conflicting actions. Normalize and strip emails consistently when storing and querying (and enforce normalized uniqueness, ideally at the database level).

title: Match statistics are lost under concurrent validations
body: `should_block?` performs a read-modify-write of `match_count` in application memory. Two simultaneous signup validations can both read the same count, increment it, and save the same next value, so one match is lost; an older request can also overwrite a newer `last_match_at`. The feature explicitly records these statistics, so this produces inaccurate audit data under normal concurrent traffic. Update these fields atomically in SQL (for example, `match_count = match_count + 1` together with `last_match_at`) rather than incrementing a loaded record.

title: Blocked address lookup is case-sensitive and can be trivially bypassed
body: `should_block?` performs an exact database lookup using the raw submitted value. `User.new_from_params` also preserves the raw email, so a block for `user@example.com` does not match `user@EXAMPLE.COM` on the application's case-sensitive database, even though email domains are case-insensitive. An attacker can therefore evade an exact blocked-email rule simply by changing casing. Normalize emails consistently when storing and looking up blocked addresses (and enforce the same canonical form/index at the database level).

title: Each blocked signup attempt increments match statistics twice
body: The validator calls the mutating `BlockedEmail.should_block?` every time validations run. `UsersController#create` first calls `user.valid?` before the Discourse Hub check and then calls `user.save`, which validates again even when the first validation failed. Consequently one blocked registration request increments `match_count` twice and records two matches, so the statistics no longer represent blocked signup attempts. Move statistics recording out of validation or ensure it is performed only once per request.

title: Blocked-email match counter updates are not atomic
body: The counter is updated through a read-modify-write sequence on an ordinary Active Record instance. Concurrent validations of the same blocked address can both read the same `match_count` and save the same incremented value, losing matches; a delayed save can also overwrite a newer `last_match_at` with an older timestamp. Use an atomic SQL update/increment (or locking) to preserve the statistics under concurrent signup traffic.

title: Rejected-email additions do not invalidate email validation
body: `rejectedEmails` is an array of string values, but the computed property depends on `rejectedEmails.@each`. `@each` observes properties of array elements, not membership changes; pushing a rejected string at line 275 therefore does not invalidate the cached `emailValidation`. After the server rejects a blocked email, the UI can retain its previous successful validation and re-enable submission instead of showing the email as invalid. Depend on `rejectedEmails.[]` and add a client test covering the post-rejection state.

title: Feed content is stored and rendered as unsanitized same-origin HTML
body: The new raw_html cook method returns raw source without passing it through the normal cooking/sanitizing pipeline. PollFeed supplies untrusted feed entry content (and explicitly CGI-unescapes it) to TopicEmbed.import, which creates posts with this mode; script tags, event-handler attributes, and dangerous URLs can therefore be stored in cooked and rendered with raw in the embed and normal topic views. A compromised or malicious configured feed can execute JavaScript in the Discourse origin for every viewer. Sanitize imported HTML with a strict allowlist before persisting/rendering it rather than bypassing the cooker.

title: The embeddable-host check is bypassed by HTTP redirects
body: TopicRetriever validates only the hostname in the original embed URL, but open(url) follows redirects without rechecking the destination. A URL on the configured embeddable host can redirect the server to localhost, a cloud metadata endpoint, or another internal service; the fetched response is then imported into a topic and can be read through the embed endpoint. Disable redirects or validate the scheme, host, and port of every redirect target before fetching.

title: Remote retrieval depends on open-uri without requiring it
body: import_remote calls open on an HTTP URL but neither this file nor TopicRetriever requires open-uri. PollFeed requires it only if that scheduled-job class happens to be loaded; with feed polling disabled, the normal RetrieveTopic path can reach this method with Kernel#open still handling URLs as file paths and fail with ENOENT. Require open-uri in the component that performs the remote fetch.

title: Post-processing jobs are enqueued before the enclosing import transaction commits
body: TopicEmbed.import wraps PostCreator#create in an outer Topic.transaction. PostCreator enqueues its process-post and feature-topic jobs after its own nested transaction, but Rails joins that nested transaction to this still-open outer transaction. A worker can therefore run before the topic, post, and TopicEmbed are committed; if TopicEmbed.create! later loses the unique-index race, the database work is rolled back while the already-enqueued jobs remain. Enqueue these jobs after the outer transaction commits (for example via an after_commit callback).

title: A valid feed entry without content aborts the entire polling job
body: i.content is optional in both RSS and Atom feeds; many RSS feeds expose description and many Atom feeds expose summary instead. Calling scrub on a missing content value raises NoMethodError, and this job has retries disabled, so the remaining entries are skipped until a later scheduled run. Handle absent content safely and fall back to the appropriate description/summary field or skip the entry.

title: postMessage origin validation accepts prefix origins
body: The handler checks whether e.origin is a substring of discourseUrl instead of comparing origins. For example, when discourseUrl is https://forum.example.com/, a window from attacker-controlled https://forum.example.co passes this check and can send a discourse-resize message to a page it opens, forcing the embedded iframe to an arbitrary height. Parse discourseUrl and require an exact origin match, preferably also requiring e.source to be the iframe's contentWindow.

title: Only root-relative URLs are rewritten in imported HTML
body: absolutize_urls claims to convert relative URLs, but it rewrites only values beginning with /. Common relative links such as images/photo.jpg, ../photo.jpg, and ?page=2 remain unchanged and are resolved by the browser against the Discourse embed URL rather than the source article, breaking imported links and images. Resolve all relative href/src values against the article URL (for example with URI.join).

title: The Disqus import command no longer accepts its documented category option
body: Removing method_option :category makes existing invocations using --category fail as an unknown Thor switch, and there is no replacement for selecting a category for imported threads. This is a backwards-incompatible change to an administrative CLI contract and should either continue passing the category through the TopicEmbed import path or be intentionally deprecated and documented.

title: Disqus thread creation timestamps are no longer preserved
body: The previous PostCreator call passed Date.parse(t[:created_at]) when creating each imported thread. The replacement TopicEmbed.import_remote call accepts only the title here and TopicEmbed.import does not forward a created_at option, so every imported topic receives the import time instead of its original Disqus creation time. This changes topic ordering and loses migration metadata; add and pass through a created_at option.

title: Imported feed/article HTML is rendered without sanitization
body: This creates posts with the `raw_html` cook method, for which `Post#cook` returns the supplied HTML unchanged. `PollFeed` supplies external feed content directly to this method, and the embed view emits `raw post.cooked`, so a feed item containing `<script>`, event-handler attributes, or dangerous URLs executes as the Discourse origin for anyone viewing the imported topic/embed. Feed content must be sanitized with a strict HTML allowlist (and the generated source link escaped) before it is stored or rendered.

title: The host allowlist is bypassed after an HTTP redirect
body: `TopicRetriever` checks only the hostname of the initial URL, but `open(url)` follows HTTP redirects and this method does not validate the redirect destination. An attacker who can use an open redirect on the configured embeddable host can make the Discourse server request arbitrary HTTP endpoints, including internal services or cloud metadata addresses; the fetched response may then be imported into a public topic. Disable redirects or validate every redirect target, including resolved IP addresses, against the allowed destination policy.

title: Unauthenticated callers can flood the retrieval job queue
body: The only access check is the `Referer` header, which arbitrary HTTP clients can forge, and this action enqueues a job before the worker validates the URL or applies its per-URL throttle. A caller can send many GET requests with a forged allowed Referer and distinct `embed_url` values to create unbounded Sidekiq work (and, for allowed-host URLs, outbound fetches). Validate the target before enqueueing and add a server-side rate limit or signed integration token; Referer alone is not an authentication boundary.

title: The outer transaction lets post-processing jobs run before the imported post commits
body: `PostCreator#create` deliberately enqueues post-processing work after its own `Post.transaction`, but that nested transaction joins this surrounding `Topic.transaction`. Consequently `PostCreator` enqueues jobs while this outer transaction is still open, so a separate Sidekiq connection can run before it can see the post. If `TopicEmbed.create!` subsequently fails (for example, due to the unique URL index during a concurrent import), the outer transaction rolls the post back after jobs and MessageBus events have already been emitted for it. Defer those side effects with an after-commit hook or restructure the creation so the post and embed commit before jobs are enqueued.

title: Feed polling uses String#scrub on Ruby versions supported by the application
body: `String#scrub` was introduced in Ruby 2.1, while this application retains MRI 1.9 support (the Gemfile has an `mri_19` dependency path). On those supported deployments every feed item reaches this line and raises `NoMethodError`, aborting the polling run; since the job disables Sidekiq retries, later items are skipped. Use a Ruby-version-compatible encoding cleanup. This expression also needs to handle feeds without a `content` field, since `i.content` may be nil for otherwise valid RSS/Atom entries.

title: Direct embed retrieval does not load open-uri
body: This method calls `open` with an HTTP URL but does not require `open-uri`, which is what extends `Kernel#open` to handle URLs. The only new `require 'open-uri'` is in the unrelated `PollFeed` job. With feed polling disabled (the default), `retrieve_topic` reaches this method without loading `PollFeed`, so normal `Kernel#open` treats the URL as a local filename and raises instead of retrieving the article. Require `open-uri` in this model or in the retrieval component that uses it.

title: A failed worker can leave an embed URL throttled forever
body: The throttle lease is established with `SETNX` and its expiry is applied in a separate Redis command. If the process dies or the Redis connection fails after `setnx` succeeds but before `expire` succeeds, the key has no TTL. Every later non-staff retrieval for that URL sees the key and returns without importing it, leaving the embed on its loading page indefinitely. Set the value and expiration atomically (for example, Redis `SET ... NX EX 60` or a Lua script).

title: Most relative article URLs are not converted to source URLs
body: The conversion only handles `href`/`src` values beginning with `/`. Ordinary relative references such as `images/photo.jpg`, `../next-page`, and fragment links remain relative to the Discourse topic/embed URL rather than the imported article, so common images and links break. Protocol-relative URLs are also incorrectly rewritten as paths on the source host. Resolve URLs with the article URL as the base (for example via `URI.join`) instead of concatenating only root-relative paths.

title: The Disqus import command silently drops its established category option
body: The command no longer declares `--category`/`-c`, and the replacement `TopicEmbed.import_remote` call has no way to pass a category. Existing import automation using that documented Thor option now fails with an unknown switch, while invocations without it can no longer import threads into the requested category and instead use the default. Preserve the option and pass the resolved category through the embed-import creation path, or explicitly provide a compatible migration path.

title: Imported HTML and URL are stored and rendered without sanitization
body: `contents` is appended directly to a footer that interpolates `url` into an HTML attribute, then the post is created with `cook_method: raw_html`. `Post#cook` returns raw HTML unchanged and the embed view renders `post.cooked` with `raw`. `PollFeed` supplies HTML-decoded feed content, so a feed item containing `<script>` or event attributes becomes stored XSS on the Discourse origin. Even if feed content were sanitized, a valid URL containing an apostrophe (for example a query value ending `...'onmouseover='...`) breaks out of this single-quoted href and injects an attribute. Sanitize imported content and safe URL schemes/attributes, and construct the attribution link with escaped URL helpers rather than string interpolation.

title: The best embed template cannot be compiled
body: `<%- end if %>` emits the Ruby tokens `end if` with no condition, which is invalid Ruby syntax. The template is compiled when an existing embedded topic is rendered, so after retrieval succeeds requests to `embed/best` will fail with a template syntax error instead of displaying the discussion. This must be a plain `end`.

title: Remote import follows redirects outside the validated host
body: The host check in `TopicRetriever` validates only the originally supplied URL, but `open(url).read` follows HTTP redirects and no subsequent destination is checked. A requester can select a path on the configured embeddable host; if that host has an open redirect, the Discourse server can be induced to fetch an arbitrary internal URL such as a cloud metadata endpoint. The Referer check does not prevent direct clients from sending a forged Referer header. Disable redirects or validate every redirect target's scheme, host, port, and resolved IP range before fetching.

title: Embed creation is not atomic despite the unique URL index
body: The code reads the embed row and only later creates it, with no lock or unique-conflict recovery. Concurrent feed polls/retrieval jobs can both observe no row and both create a topic; the loser then raises on the unique `embed_url` index. The outer transaction rolls back that loser, but `PostCreator` has already published MessageBus events and enqueued post-processing work before this transaction commits, leaving failed jobs/phantom notifications. Use an atomic create-or-find strategy (or rescue the unique violation and reload), and avoid publishing work until the outer transaction has committed.

title: Each new embed request can trigger a complete feed import
body: For every missing embed URL, retrieval synchronously invokes `PollFeed`, which downloads and parses the entire configured feed and iterates every item before attempting the requested page. The Redis throttle is keyed by the full embed URL, so requests with distinct query strings bypass one another, and the public endpoint can queue those jobs with a forged Referer header. With feed polling enabled this permits unbounded feed downloads and import passes, exhausting workers and potentially overloading the feed source. Use a global feed-poll lock/cache (the existing `feed_key` is unused) and leave full polling to the scheduled job.

title: Feed polling uses a String method unavailable on supported Ruby versions
body: `String#scrub` was introduced in Ruby 2.1. This application still supports the Rails 3/4-era Ruby versions through its dual-boot Gemfile, including Ruby 1.9/2.0, where this line raises `NoMethodError` for every feed item and makes feed polling unusable. Use an encoding cleanup compatible with the supported Ruby versions or explicitly raise the minimum Ruby version.

title: Adding the populated posts column in one step can lock and rewrite the table
body: On the PostgreSQL versions contemporary with this application, adding a column with both a non-null default and `null: false` rewrites the entire `posts` table while holding a strong table lock. On a production forum this can block reads/writes for the duration of a large table rewrite during deployment. Add the column without a default/not-null constraint, backfill in batches, then set the default and constraint in later migrations.

title: Non-root-relative links and images resolve against the Discourse embed URL
body: `absolutize_urls` only rewrites values beginning with `/`. Common source markup such as `href="article.html"`, `href="../article"`, or `src="images/photo.jpg"` remains relative; when rendered inside the Discourse iframe, browsers resolve those URLs relative to `/embed/best` on the Discourse host rather than the imported article. This breaks links and assets for many imported pages. Resolve all relative href/src values against the source URL (for example with `URI.join`) while leaving already absolute URLs unchanged.

title: Header panel loses right alignment in IE10's flexbox implementation
body: The previous `float: right` is removed, and the only main-axis positioning now is `margin-left: auto`. IE10's `-ms-flexbox` implementation does not distribute auto margins on flex items; since a child float is ignored once `.contents` becomes a flex container, the panel will sit immediately after the title/extra-info instead of at the right edge. The new mixin explicitly emits `-ms-flexbox`, so provide a legacy-compatible spacer/flex-growth or alignment rule for that implementation.

title: The legacy Firefox flex fallback has no alignment property
body: `flexbox()` emits `display: -moz-box` for Firefox versions using the legacy box model, but `align-items()` emits only `-webkit-box-align` for legacy box alignment and omits `-moz-box-align`. Those Firefox versions therefore ignore every `@include align-items(...)` call and use the default stretch alignment, leaving the new header and small-action layouts uncentered and bullet badges unaligned. Add `-moz-box-align: $alignment` alongside the WebKit legacy declaration.

title: Flex layout disables the small-action button's right float
body: `.small-action` is now a flex container, so its direct child action button is a flex item and the existing `float: right` on line 309 has no effect. The topic-post small-action markup places this button after `.small-action-desc`, leaving it immediately after the description instead of at the right edge as before. Give the button an appropriate flex alignment rule (for example `margin-left: auto`) or otherwise preserve the previous placement.

title: Header panel has no usable non-modern-flex fallback
body: This removes the panel's `float: right` and relies on `margin-left: auto` to push it to the end of the flex row. In browsers without flexbox support, including IE9, the panel becomes a normal block instead of remaining right-aligned. The included legacy `-webkit-box`/`-moz-box` modes also do not implement modern flex auto main-axis margins, so those browsers place the panel directly after the title rather than at the right edge. Retain a fallback layout or use legacy-flex-compatible positioning if those prefixed modes are intended to be supported.

title: Making `.small-action` a flex container disables its right-aligned action button
body: The small-action row's action/undo button is positioned by the existing `float: right` rule, but a direct child of a flex container is a flex item and its float is ignored. Since neither the button nor `.small-action-desc` receives an auto margin or flex growth rule, the button will be laid out immediately after the description rather than at the right edge of the row. Replace the float-based positioning with flex positioning (for example, `margin-left: auto` on the button).

title: The header panel is no longer right aligned in legacy WebKit flexbox
body: The new flexbox mixin deliberately falls back to `display: -webkit-box` for Safari 6/older Android WebKit, but that 2009 flexbox implementation does not use `margin-left: auto` to consume main-axis free space. The previous `float: right` was removed, so in those browsers `.panel` is placed directly after the title/extra information instead of at the right side of the header, breaking the navigation layout. Provide a legacy-box-specific alignment fallback or retain a non-flex fallback for those browsers.

title: The legacy Firefox flex fallback has no matching alignment declaration
