body: `flexbox()` and `inline-flex()` enable the legacy `-moz-box`/`-moz-inline-box` layout, but `align-items()` emits only WebKit, MS, and unprefixed alignment properties. Firefox versions that select the `-moz-box` fallback ignore those properties, so the new centered header/small-action layout and baseline bullet-badge alignment fall back to stretch/default alignment. Emit `-moz-box-align: $alignment` alongside `-webkit-box-align`.

title: website_name bypasses the TL0 anonymous-profile privacy restriction
body: `website` is protected by `untrusted_attributes`, so it is omitted when an anonymous visitor views a trust-level-0 user. The new derived `website_name` attribute is not subject to that gate, and its intended inclusion method below is also not named `include_website_name?`, so the serializer still emits the hidden website's host (and, for matching domains, its path). The profile template renders this value even when `website` was withheld. Apply the same restriction to `website_name` (or implement an equivalent `include_website_name?` check) and cover anonymous TL0 serialization in the spec.

title: Hostname-label comparison mistakes unrelated public-suffix domains for one domain
body: The sibling-subdomain branch decides two hosts share a domain by dropping their first labels. For example, an instance at `forum.co.uk` and a profile website at `evil.co.uk/path` both reduce to `co.uk`, so the code displays the website path even though those are separately registrable, unrelated domains. The same problem occurs on shared suffixes such as `github.io`. Compare registrable domains using a public-suffix-aware mechanism, or avoid treating sibling hosts as equivalent.

title: `website_name` bypasses the anonymous TL0 profile-field restriction
body: `website` is explicitly treated as an untrusted attribute and is omitted when an anonymous user views a TL0 profile, but the new `website_name` attribute is not included in `untrusted_attributes`. As a result, those viewers still receive and the template displays the website hostname (and, for matching domains, its full path) even though the underlying website field is intentionally hidden. Add `website_name` to the restricted inclusion logic (and cover a TL0 anonymous profile with a website in the serializer spec) so the derived value cannot disclose the protected field.

title: The website-name inclusion callback is not recognized by the serializer
body: ActiveModel serializer inclusion callbacks use the `include_<attribute>?` form, as the other callbacks in this class do. This method is named `include_website_name` without the trailing `?`, so it is not used and `website_name` is serialized by default even for profiles with no website (or an unparsable website), producing an unexpected `website_name: null` API field. Rename it to `include_website_name?`; the predicate should also enforce the same visibility policy as `website`.

title: website_name bypasses the anonymous TL0 profile redaction
body: `website` is explicitly listed in `untrusted_attributes`, so anonymous viewers of a TL0 user do not receive it, but the newly added `website_name` attribute is not. As a result, those responses now expose the host portion of a profile website (for example an employer or personal site) despite the website field being intentionally hidden. Add `website_name` to the untrusted attributes/redaction logic and add coverage to the anonymous-TL0 serializer test.

title: The website_name inclusion predicate is named incorrectly and is ignored
body: Serializer attribute predicates in this class use the `include_<attribute>?` form (for example `include_email?`). `include_website_name` lacks the question mark, so the serializer will not use it to decide whether to emit the attribute. Consequently `website_name` is emitted by default even for profiles without a website or with an unparsable URL, producing an unintended `null` field rather than being omitted as this method attempts to specify. Rename it to `include_website_name?` (while ensuring the redaction predicate is also preserved).

title: Same-domain detection is case-sensitive for DNS hostnames
body: `URI(...).host` preserves hostname casing, while DNS hostnames are case-insensitive. A valid profile URL such as `http://EXAMPLE.COM/user` on an `example.com` instance fails the equality and suffix comparisons and is displayed as only `EXAMPLE.COM`, rather than including `/user` as required for the same domain. Normalize both parsed and instance hostnames (for example, `downcase` and ideally remove a trailing DNS dot) before comparing them.

title: The embedded-post author link reverses its intended lightness levels
body: This selector previously used `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)`, but the light-theme branch is now 70% and the dark-theme branch is 30%. This both changes the established light-theme appearance and gives dark themes the inverse of the intended secondary-derived contrast. It should retain the 30% primary branch and use the corresponding 70% secondary branch.

title: Group member names lose their intended lighter-theme emphasis
body: The `.group-member-info .name` rule previously used `$primary` at 30% lightness, but the new expression uses 50% for both branches. As a result, light themes no longer preserve the existing name color and dark themes do not get the corresponding `$secondary` 70% value. Use primary 30% and secondary 70%, as is already done for comparable user names.

title: The custom-message length hint has its contrast levels inverted
body: This hint was previously `$primary` at 70% lightness, but the change replaces it with primary 30% and secondary 70%. That makes the hint substantially darker on light themes and much brighter on dark themes instead of preserving its de-emphasized appearance. The branches should be primary 70% and secondary 30%.

title: Mobile topic-map headings no longer retain their original contrast
body: The topic-map `h3` color was `$primary` at 20% lightness, but it was changed to 50% for both theme branches. This weakens the heading on light themes and fails to use the corresponding high-lightness secondary value needed for dark backgrounds. Preserve the 20% primary branch and use secondary at 80% for dark themes.

title: Mobile group member names use the wrong lightness pair
body: The mobile `.group-member-info .name` rule had primary lightness 30%, but the new code changes it to 50% and pairs it with secondary 50%. This changes the light-theme hierarchy and does not provide the expected secondary 70% dark-theme counterpart. The rule should use primary 30% and secondary 70%, matching the intended name styling.

title: Embedded-post author links use the opposite lightness mapping
body: The original light-theme color was `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)`, but this now uses `$primary` at 70% and `$secondary` at 30%. This changes the established light-theme appearance and darkens the dark-theme counterpart instead of using the corresponding `$secondary` 70% value. Use `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 70%))` so embedded reply author links retain their intended contrast in both themes.

title: Desktop group-member names lost their intended stronger color
body: `.group-member-info .name` previously used `$primary` at 30%, while the title used 50%. The new expression changes the name to 50% in the light theme and 50% in the dark theme, making it identical to the title and failing to provide the expected dark-theme counterpart. Preserve the original 30% primary branch and use `$secondary` at 70% for dark themes.

title: Mobile custom-message length text has the light/dark lightness values reversed
body: This rule originally used `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%)`, but the new expression uses `$primary` at 30% and `$secondary` at 70%. That changes the light-theme text color and is inconsistent with the equivalent desktop modal rule. It should retain the 70% primary branch and use `$secondary` at 30% for the dark-theme branch.

title: Mobile topic-map heading no longer preserves its heading contrast
body: The topic-map `h3` originally used `$primary` at 20%, but the new expression changes both branches to 50%. This makes the h3 the same tone as the following h4 rule and removes the established visual hierarchy in light themes, while also failing to use the corresponding dark-theme value. The paired expression should be `$primary` at 20% and `$secondary` at 80%.

title: Mobile group-member names lost their intended stronger color
body: `.group-member-info .name` previously used `$primary` at 30%, distinct from the 50% title color. The replacement uses 50% for both primary and secondary, changing the light-theme color and collapsing that distinction. Use the preserved 30% primary value with `$secondary` at 70% for the dark-theme counterpart.

title: Embedded-post author link uses the inverted lightness pair
body: This rule previously used `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)`, but the new dark/light selection uses primary 70% and secondary 30%. That reverses the intended mapping in both themes: the light theme changes from the existing 30% tone, while the dark-theme link is rendered with a much darker secondary-derived color that can lack contrast against the embedded-post background. Preserve the original light branch and use the corresponding dark branch: primary 30% and secondary 70%.

title: Mobile custom-message counter reverses its intended lightness values
body: The previous color was `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%)`, but this replacement selects primary 30% in light themes and secondary 70% in dark themes. This is the opposite of the intended primary/secondary lightness pairing and changes the existing light-theme appearance. It should select primary 70% for light themes and secondary 30% for dark themes, matching the desktop modal rule.

title: Mobile topic-map heading no longer preserves its original emphasis
body: The topic-map `h3` previously used primary at 20% lightness, but the new expression changes it to 50% in light themes and uses secondary 50% in dark themes. This makes the heading substantially less emphasized on light themes and does not apply the expected secondary 80% dark-theme counterpart. Use primary 20% with secondary 80% instead.

title: Desktop group-member names were changed to the title color
body: `.group-member-info .name` previously used primary at 30% lightness, whereas this change makes it use the same 50%/50% pair as `.title`. That unnecessarily dims names in light themes and selects the wrong dark-theme tone. The name should retain primary 30% for light themes and use secondary 70% for dark themes.

title: Mobile group-member names use the wrong lightness pair
body: The mobile `.group-member-info .name` had primary at 30% lightness before this change, but it now uses a 50%/50% pair copied from the title styling. This changes the light-theme name color and gives dark themes the wrong secondary-derived tone. It should use primary 30% and secondary 70%, as required for the corresponding name style.

title: Public group member pages now silently omit members after the first 50
body: The members action applies a default limit of 50 to every group, but the public group-members route/template has no pagination controls or actions that change offset. Consequently, visiting a visible group with more than 50 members only renders the first 50 and provides no way to see the rest. Previously non-automatic groups returned their full membership list.

title: Pagination creates an extra empty page for exact multiples of the page size
body: totalPages uses Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1. When a group has exactly 50, 100, etc. members, this reports one more page than exists; for example, 50 members reports 2 pages and Next requests offset 50, which returns an empty member list. Use a ceiling calculation (while retaining the zero-member case) so the last-page guard is correct.

title: Existing PATCH membership requests now make groups invisible
body: The resource route still dispatches PATCH /admin/groups/:id to update, but this action no longer handles the former changes add/delete payload. A legacy PATCH request containing only changes therefore ignores the membership mutation and executes group.visible = (nil == "true"), setting visible to false while returning success. The previous implementation handled PATCH separately and preserved group attributes. Preserve the PATCH behavior or reject it explicitly rather than silently changing visibility.

title: Out-of-order member-list responses can overwrite the selected page
body: Each findMembers response unconditionally writes offset and members to the shared group model. The route now starts the initial request without waiting for it, and the Next/Previous actions can start another request while it is pending. If the older request finishes after the newer one, it restores the older page and offset, so an admin can click Next and end up viewing the first page again. Requests need sequencing/cancellation or the response must be ignored unless it matches the current requested offset.

title: Automatic groups display unusable remove-member controls
body: This template is rendered as an itemView for `member in members`, so its context is the member user. The unqualified `automatic` lookup therefore does not read the containing group and is normally undefined, making `unless automatic` true. Remove icons are shown for automatic groups even though the server rejects the delete request with 422. Pass/reference the parent group’s automatic flag in the item view instead.

title: Public group member lists are silently truncated to 50 users
body: The public `groups/:group_id/members` endpoint now defaults to 50 results for every group. The public group-members route calls `findMembers` only once, and `group/members.hbs` has no pagination or load-more controls, so visitors to any group with more than 50 members can never see members after the first username-ordered page. Previously non-automatic groups returned the full member list. Either retain the full response for this view or add public pagination before imposing this limit.

title: Exact page-size member counts produce a nonexistent extra page
body: `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` overcounts whenever the member count is exactly divisible by the page size. For example, a group with 50 members and a limit of 50 is shown as having two pages; clicking Next requests offset 50 and displays an empty page. Use a ceiling calculation (while preserving the zero-member case) so the final valid page is detected correctly.

title: Refreshing after removing the last member of a page can leave the UI on an empty page
body: The reload offset is clamped against the model's pre-request `user_count`, not the total after the membership mutation. For example, deleting the sole member on offset 50 of a 51-member group sends offset 50; the server then reports total 50 but returns no members at that offset, and the model retains the empty page. Normalize the offset using the returned total (and refetch if necessary), or have the endpoint clamp an out-of-range offset, so the last remaining valid page is displayed.

title: Out-of-order member-list requests can overwrite the currently selected page
body: Every `findMembers` response unconditionally replaces `offset` and `members`. The Next/Previous actions allow another request before the previous one finishes, so rapid navigation from offsets 0 to 50 to 100 can receive the offset-100 response first and then overwrite it with the late offset-50 response. The UI ends on stale data and the wrong page. Cancel prior requests or track a request/page token and ignore responses that are no longer current.

title: The public members endpoint changes its JSON response contract without compatibility
body: `GET /groups/:group_id/members(.json)` previously returned the serialized member array directly (the prior client consumed it with `result.map`). It now returns an object containing `members` and `meta`. Although the in-repository caller was updated, existing API consumers or plugins parsing this established endpoint as an array will break immediately. Preserve the old representation, introduce a versioned/paginated endpoint, or provide an explicit compatibility migration.

title: Public group member pages now truncate at 50 members with no way to continue
body: `Group#findMembers` is shared by the public group-members route and now always sends its new default `limit` of 50. The public `group/members` template has no pagination controls or offset handling, so visiting a visible group with more than 50 members permanently displays only the first 50. Either keep the public request unpaginated or add public pagination before applying this limit.

title: Legacy PATCH membership updates now silently hide groups
body: `resources :groups` still routes PATCH requests to `update`, but the previous PATCH-specific handling of `changes[:add]` and `changes[:delete]` has been removed. A previously supported request such as `PATCH /admin/groups/:id` with only `changes: { add: "user" }` now ignores the membership change and, because it has no top-level `visible` parameter, executes this line and sets `visible` to false. Existing API clients or admin automation can therefore fail to update membership while unintentionally hiding the group; preserve the PATCH behavior or explicitly reject it without changing attributes.

title: Pagination creates an empty extra page for exact page-size member counts
body: `totalPages` uses `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`. For a group with exactly 50, 100, etc. members, this reports one page too many. The enabled Next action then requests an offset equal to `user_count`, and the server correctly returns an empty member list, leaving administrators on a blank page. This calculation should use a ceiling (while retaining the zero-member special case).

title: The public group-members endpoint changes its top-level JSON contract
body: Previously `GET /groups/:group_id/members` rendered a serialized array of users. It now returns an object with `members` and `meta` keys. The bundled client was changed accordingly, but any existing API consumer that parses the endpoint as an array will break immediately. Preserve the old response on the existing endpoint or introduce/version a paginated response contract.

title: Fallback locale files are not loaded outside controller requests
body: The accelerator only lazy-loads `config.locale`. `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` then performs fallback lookups directly against the backend, so it does not re-enter this method to load the site-default or English locale files. The new preload in `ApplicationController#set_locale` masks this for normal web requests, but mailers, background jobs, rake tasks, and other non-controller code bypass that filter. In a cold worker using (for example) `:fr`, a missing French key will still be missing even if it exists in the default or English YAML because only `fr` was loaded. Load the entire fallback chain as part of translation/lazy loading rather than relying on a controller callback.

title: Changing the site default locale leaves cached fallback translations stale
body: The fallback chain is computed dynamically from `SiteSetting.default_locale`, but optionless translations are cached by the accelerator using only the key, current locale, and backend object. For example, a missing `:fr` key can be resolved from English and cached; after an administrator changes the site default locale to German, subsequent `:fr` lookups hit that cached English value instead of following the new fallback order until `I18n.reload!` happens. Include the effective fallback/default locale in the cache key or explicitly clear the translation cache when `default_locale` changes.

title: Fallback locales are only loaded for controller requests
body: `ensure_loaded!` is invoked only from the controller filter, but the translation accelerator loads only `config.locale` when `I18n.t` is called. The fallback backend probes fallback locales directly through the backend, so it does not re-enter the accelerator to load the site-default or English YAML files. As a result, translations performed outside an HTTP controller request (notably Sidekiq jobs, mailers, rake tasks, and startup code) will report a missing translation instead of falling back when the fallback locale has not already happened to be loaded in that process. Load the entire `I18n.fallbacks[config.locale]` chain in the translation/loading path, or otherwise make fallback loading global rather than controller-specific.

title: Fallback translation files are only preloaded for controller requests
body: The fallback locales are explicitly loaded only from this ApplicationController filter. The lazy-loading patch still loads only `I18n.config.locale` when `I18n.t` is called, while `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` invokes the backend directly for each fallback locale. Consequently, mailers, background jobs, console tasks, or any `I18n.with_locale` usage outside a controller can try a fallback whose YAML file was never loaded and return a missing-translation result instead of the site/default-English fallback. Load all `I18n.fallbacks[locale]` as part of the translation/lazy-loading path rather than relying on this request filter.

title: Cached translations do not vary with the configured fallback locale
body: The translation cache key contains only the requested key, current locale, and backend object id, but a missing translation now also depends on `SiteSetting.default_locale` through `FallbackLocaleList`. If an admin changes the site default locale, entries previously resolved through the old fallback remain cached for users of another locale and continue returning the old language until eviction or an `I18n.reload!`. Include fallback configuration in the cache key or clear/reload this cache when `default_locale` changes.

title: Denial-cache keys collide for distinct name/folder pairs
body: The key concatenates raw `name` and `parent` values with `_`, so distinct checks can produce the same key. For example, for the same namespace, user, and action, `name=dashboard_a,parent=folder` and `name=dashboard,parent=a_folder` both generate the same suffix. If the first check is denied, the second check will hit the entry at `Check` line 117 and be denied without evaluating its actual permissions. Dashboard and folder identifiers are not escaped or otherwise structurally encoded here. Use an unambiguous encoding (for example length-prefixed fields or a hash of a structured tuple).

title: Negative authorization results remain effective after permissions change
body: A denial-cache hit returns immediately before reading current permissions, but this cache is never invalidated when dashboard/folder permissions, roles, or folder inheritance change. Consequently, if a check is denied and the user is then granted access to that same resource (or a resource is deleted and recreated with the same UID), all checks for that tuple remain denied for `shortCacheTTL` despite the database now allowing access. This partially reintroduces the stale-denial behavior the permission requery is intended to avoid, including for newly created resources. Invalidate the negative entry on relevant writes or avoid using it when a newer permission/folder state may exist.

title: Permission refresh still evaluates inherited access using a stale folder tree
body: After a cached permission map does not authorize a resource, this path reloads permissions but calls `checkPermission` against the same `folderCache`. If the folder tree was cached before a child folder was created, a user with a scope on its parent will be denied access to a newly created dashboard in that child: `checkInheritedPermissions` cannot find the new child in the stale tree, even though the freshly loaded parent permission is sufficient. The resulting false denial is then itself placed in the denial cache. Refresh or invalidate the folder tree when retrying an inherited check after a cache-derived denial.

title: Cache misses can trigger repeated permission queries despite singleflight
body: The cache lookup was removed from `getUserPermissions`, leaving an unconditional database query inside `singleflight`. Concurrent requests can all miss `getCachedIdentityPermissions`; if one request populates `permCache` and another reaches `sf.Do` after that first singleflight call has completed, the latter starts a new database query instead of observing the newly populated cache. A burst of requests that passed the outer cache check before the first write can therefore issue multiple serial permission queries. Recheck `permCache` inside the singleflight callback (and likewise for anonymous permissions), or retain a cache check in these fetch methods.

title: The denial-cache test passes even if the denial cache is not consulted
body: The test claims to populate an allowing permission cache entry, but it stores `{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`. Without the denial-cache shortcut, `checkPermission` also denies this map and the fake store has no allowing permission, so the test still passes if the new denial-cache lookup is removed or broken. Store `true` for the dashboard scope and assert that no permission-store lookup occurs, so the test verifies that the explicit denial entry takes precedence.

title: Do not treat identity lookup failures as permission-cache misses
body: `getCachedIdentityPermissions` uses `cache.ErrNotFound` for an actual permission-cache miss, but it also propagates failures from `GetUserIdentifiers` (for example, SQL errors, unknown-user errors, or a canceled context). This code treats every non-nil error as a cache miss and immediately calls `getIdentityPermissions`, which performs the identifier lookup again. Consequently every affected Check request issues two identity-store queries during an outage or when callers send unknown subjects; List has the same pattern at line 180. Only fall back when the error is `cache.ErrNotFound`, and return other errors directly.

title: Bound the per-resource denial cache before caching arbitrary denied names
body: A denial entry is created for every denied `(user, action, name, folder)` tuple. `Name` and `Folder` are request-controlled and are not validated or restricted here, so requests for unique nonexistent dashboard/folder names continuously create distinct entries. In the in-process setup this service is backed by an in-memory `LocalCache` (constructed in `pkg/services/authz/rbac.go`), and unlike the existing permission cache this key's cardinality is not bounded by users and actions. A client can therefore grow process memory proportionally to the number of denied resource names within the cache lifetime. Use a bounded/evicting cache or avoid negative-caching arbitrary resource identifiers.

title: The denial-cache test does not prove that the denial cache is consulted
body: The test claims to put an allowing permission in `permCache` to prove that the denial entry takes precedence, but it stores `"dashboards:uid:dash1": false`. `checkPermission` treats that map as a denial, so the expected false result would also occur if `permDenialCache` were ignored entirely. Store `true` for this scope (and ideally assert that the backing store is not called) so the test actually covers the negative-cache short circuit.

title: Denial cache conflates anonymous and renderer identities
body: The denial key contains only `UserUID`, not `IdentityType`. Both `anonymous:0` and `render:0` therefore use the same key for a namespace/action/resource/folder. If an anonymous request is denied for a private dashboard, line 154 stores that denial; a subsequent renderer check for the same dashboard exits at line 117 as denied even though `getRendererPermissions` would grant dashboard reads. This permits cross-identity cache poisoning and can be used to keep renderer access denied by repeatedly causing anonymous checks. Include the identity type (or the full subject) in the denial-cache key.

title: Denial cache key encoding is ambiguous for valid resource UIDs
body: `name` and `parent` are concatenated with `_` without escaping or length-prefixing. For example, a denial for name `a_b` with parent `c` produces the same key as a check for name `a` with parent `b_c`. Dashboard and folder UIDs can contain underscores, so a denial for one resource can incorrectly short-circuit an allowed check for another resource for 30 seconds. Use an unambiguous structured encoding or a hash of separately serialized fields.

title: Per-resource denial entries allow unbounded cache cardinality
body: Every denied check writes a distinct cache entry derived from the caller-supplied resource name and folder. A caller can issue checks for continuously changing nonexistent resource IDs, causing both the database fallback and one new denial-cache entry per request. The in-process service uses a local cache without a capacity limit at construction, and expired entries may remain until its cleanup interval, so this turns arbitrary request cardinality into cache memory growth. Use a size-bounded/admission-controlled cache or avoid caching arbitrary negative resource lookups.

title: Explicit-denial-cache test does not prove the denial cache is consulted
body: The test comment says the normal permission cache should allow access if checked, but it stores `"dashboards:uid:dash1": false`. Without the new denial-cache lookup, `Check` would still return denied from that false value (and then from the empty fake store), so the test passes even if the denial cache is removed or bypassed. Store `true` for the dashboard scope and assert that no permission-store lookup occurs, so the test verifies denial-cache precedence.

title: Federated rules are no longer treated as immutable by combined-rule ability checks
body: `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, which unconditionally sets `isFederated` to `false`. The previous combined-rule implementation inspected `rule.group.source_tenants` via `isFederatedRuleGroup`, so callers of `useAlertRuleAbility`/`useAlertRuleAbilities` can now receive supported edit, delete, pause, restore, and permanent-delete abilities for federated rule groups. Federated rules must remain non-editable; retain the group federation check when adapting the combined-rule path.

title: Pause and delete actions are suppressed for prom-only Grafana list items
body: The new Grafana list passes only `promRule`, so the Grafana-prom ability checks can authorize pause and delete, but the menu still renders Pause only when a `rulerRule` is present (line 123) and Delete only when a `rulerRule` is present (line 165). Consequently, authorized users cannot pause or delete any Grafana-managed rule from the list after the ruler fetch is removed. These actions need a prom-rule-compatible implementation or must be handled by identifier rather than being gated on the absent ruler DTO.

title: Silence menu items in the prom-only list are visible but do nothing
body: For a `GrafanaRuleListItem`, `RuleActionsButtons` receives no `rule`/ruler DTO. `AlertRuleMenu` can still show “Silence notifications” from the new prom-rule ability and its handler sets `showSilenceDrawer`, but this component renders `SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer` only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true. With `rule` undefined the condition is always false, leaving the visible menu action as a no-op. Pass a supported prom-rule representation to the drawer or do not expose the action until it can be performed.

title: Grafana recording rules lose the existing modify-export capability
body: `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` uses `isAlertingRule` as the support condition for `ModifyExport`. That predicate excludes Grafana-managed recording rules, so the direct prom-only list will not show Export for those rules even for users with export permission. The prior ruler-based ability used the generic Grafana-rule predicate, which included both alerting and recording rules. Use the generic Grafana rule check for this capability unless recording-rule export is intentionally being removed and the route is changed accordingly.

title: Rule detail links no longer preserve the originating list URL
body: The previous Grafana list item built its view URL with `createReturnTo()` and supplied it as the `returnTo` query parameter. This replacement builds `/alerting/grafana/<uid>/view` without it, so opening a rule from a filtered/list view loses the return target used by the detail/edit flow and sends users back to the default alerting page rather than their current list context. Preserve the existing `returnTo` parameter when creating this link.

title: Grafana entries in filtered results are returned without the computed React key
body: `FilterViewResults` computes a unique `key` specifically for list identity, but the Grafana branch returns `GrafanaRuleListItem` without passing that key. Any filtered result containing multiple Grafana rules produces React's missing-key warning, and React cannot reliably retain item-local state if the result set is reconciled. Pass `key={key}` as is already done for datasource and unknown-rule branches.

title: GrafanaGroupLoader documentation still claims it loads the Ruler endpoint
body: The component now only calls `useGetGrafanaGroupsQuery`, but its documentation says it loads both Prometheus and Ruler endpoints. The `expectedRulesCount` documentation also refers to a Ruler response. Update these comments so future changes do not assume a ruler request or ruler/prometheus reconciliation still exists.

title: Silence action is displayed but cannot open its drawer for prom-only list rules
body: The new Grafana list items pass only `promRule`, so the menu can enable and invoke `handleSilence` using the new Prometheus-based ability. That handler sets `showSilenceDrawer`, but the drawer is rendered only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true. With no ruler rule this condition is always false, leaving users with a clickable “Silence notifications” menu item that has no effect. The drawer/action flow needs to support the Prometheus DTO or the menu item must not be exposed until it can work.

title: Pause remains unavailable for every prom-only Grafana rule in the list
body: `canPause` now incorporates the Prometheus-rule ability specifically for the ruler-free list, but rendering the pause item still requires a Grafana ruler rule. `GrafanaRuleListItem` supplies no `rulerRule`, so this condition is always false even for a user allowed to pause an unprovisioned Grafana rule. As a result, the list loses its pause/unpause action; the pause component needs a Prometheus-compatible input/operation or a separate prom-only implementation.

title: Delete is hidden for prom-only Grafana rules despite a granted delete ability
body: The menu computes `canDelete` from `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`, but still renders Delete only when `rulerRule` exists. Both new list entry points render `GrafanaRuleListItem` with only `promRule`, so users with delete permission cannot delete Grafana-managed rules from the alert list. This is avoidable here because the supplied delete handler already closes over the identifier and group identifier rather than using the ruler-rule argument.

title: Federated rules are no longer treated as immutable by combined-rule abilities
body: Before this refactor, `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` had access to `CombinedRule.group` and used `isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` in the immutable-rule check. It now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, which unconditionally sets `isFederated` to false because only a group identifier is passed. Consequently, federated rules can report update, delete, duplicate, pause, and restore as supported for users with the corresponding permissions, even though the prior UI intentionally blocked those operations. Preserve the federated-group metadata in this ability path or pass the federated status into the ruler ability hook.

title: Grafana recording rules lose export-with-modifications in the ruler-free list
body: `ModifyExport` is now supported only when `prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true. The previous ruler-based check used `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule`, which includes both Grafana alerting and recording rules. Since the new list has no ruler rule to provide the old ability as a fallback, Grafana-managed recording rules no longer show “Export with modifications” even though that action was previously available for them. The support check should cover Grafana Prometheus recording rules as well.

title: Silence action is a no-op for Grafana-only list rows
body: The new GrafanaRuleListItem supplies only promRule, so rule is undefined. The menu can still expose “Silence notifications” using the new Grafana Prometheus ability, and its handler sets showSilenceDrawer to true, but this render condition only accepts a Grafana ruler rule. Clicking the visible menu item therefore produces no drawer or feedback in the new alert list. Render a Prometheus-compatible silence drawer (or do not expose the action until one is available).

title: Pause and unpause are unavailable after removing the ruler rule
body: GrafanaRuleListItem intentionally calls this menu without rulerRule, while canPause is now allowed to be calculated from promRule. This condition still additionally requires rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule), so it is always false for the new Grafana list and users cannot pause or resume rules there despite having the displayed Prometheus-side ability. The menu needs a Prometheus-backed pause implementation or a compatible rule input.

title: Delete is hidden for every Grafana-only list row
body: The new list passes rulerRule as undefined, but this condition requires a ruler rule before rendering Delete. As a result, even users with a permitted Grafana Prometheus delete ability cannot delete a Grafana-managed rule from the list. In this caller, handleDelete ignores the ruler-rule argument and already has the identifier needed for useDeleteModal, so the stale rulerRule guard removes a previously supported operation.

title: Grafana recording rules lost the export action
body: ModifyExport is now supported only when isAlertingRule is true. GrafanaPromRuleDTO also represents Grafana-managed recording rules, and the previous ruler-based implementation used rulerRuleType.grafana.rule, which covered both alerting and recording rules. Because the new list has no ruler fallback, recording rules with export permission no longer show Export even though the existing list supported exporting them.

title: Ruler fallback can re-enable duplication of plugin-provided rules
body: For a Grafana-only list row, rulerRule is undefined. useAllRulerRuleAbilities consequently treats it as neither provisioned nor plugin-provided, so when the ruler is available and the user has create permission its duplicate ability can be allowed. This OR expression then overrides the Grafana Prometheus ability, which correctly rejects plugin-provided rules based on their labels. Plugin-provided Grafana rules can therefore regain the Duplicate action merely because the obsolete ruler-side check has no rule to inspect.

title: Federated rules are no longer treated as immutable by combined-rule abilities
body: useAllAlertRuleAbilities previously derived isFederated from rule.group. It now delegates after discarding the CombinedRule and useAllRulerRuleAbilities hard-codes isFederated to false. Any existing caller of useAlertRuleAbility/useAlertRuleAbilities with a federated datasource rule will therefore consider update, delete, pause, restore, and permanent-delete supported when permissions otherwise allow them, instead of preserving the former federated-rule protection.

title: Grafana rule view links no longer preserve the originating list route
body: The replaced GrafanaRuleLoader constructed the view URL with createReturnTo(), while the replacement omits returnTo entirely. Opening a rule from a filtered or hierarchical alert list now loses the list URL and filter state used by the rule view's in-page return navigation, sending users back to the default location rather than their originating list.

title: GrafanaGroupLoader documentation still claims it loads Ruler data
body: The component now issues only useGetGrafanaGroupsQuery and no longer reads the Ruler endpoint, but its documentation says it loads from both Prometheus and Ruler endpoints. The nearby expectedRulesCount comment also describes a Ruler response. This is misleading for future maintainers investigating the component's consistency and request behavior.

title: Sharded requests interpolate the same targets repeatedly
body: This applies template variables and request filters to each target before shard selection, but every shard subrequest is then passed to `runSplitQuery`, which now unconditionally calls `applyTemplateVariables` again with the same `scopedVars` and `filters` (and this repeats for each shard batch/retry). Template expansion is not generally idempotent: ad-hoc filters can be inserted into the selector again, and a literal `$name` produced by a variable value can be treated as another template variable on the next pass. This can send duplicated or unexpectedly rewritten LogQL selectors for sharded queries. Preserve an already-interpolated marker/targets when delegating to `runSplitQuery`, or perform interpolation in only one of these paths.

title: Shard-split queries are template-interpolated twice
body: This interpolates each target before shard grouping, but every generated shard subrequest is then passed to `runSplitQuery`, which now calls `applyTemplateVariables` again with the same `scopedVars` and `request.filters`. Template interpolation is not generally idempotent: a literal `$name` emitted as the value of one variable can be interpreted as another dashboard variable on the second pass, changing the selector and returning data for the wrong streams. In addition, ad-hoc filters supplied through `request.filters` are applied twice, producing duplicate matchers in every shard request. Pass already-interpolated targets to a split path that does not interpolate again, or ensure interpolation/filter application occurs only once for the sharded execution path.

title: Targets that interpolate to an empty expression are still executed
body: The expression-presence filter runs before applyTemplateVariables. A target such as an optional query variable whose value resolves to an empty string therefore remains in the split groups and is passed to Loki with an empty expr, which can make an otherwise valid grouped request fail. The same pre-interpolation filtering order was added to shardQuerySplitting.ts:50; both entry points should filter out empty expressions after interpolation (while still skipping hidden targets before it).

title: Sharded queries now apply template processing once per shard batch after already processing it
body: This expands each target before shard discovery, but the resulting targets are later put into subRequest while retaining request.scopedVars and request.filters. runSplitQuery then calls applyTemplateVariables again for every shard group at querySplitting.ts:299. Template replacement is not generally idempotent: a literal value produced by the first expansion that contains a variable token can be expanded on the second pass, and ad-hoc filter rewriting is also rerun on the already rewritten selector. Consequently the final query can depend on how many shard groups were created. Preserve the initially interpolated targets for the inner splitter without reapplying templates, or explicitly mark/clear the already-consumed interpolation inputs.

title: Plugin completion logs no longer include the trace ID
body: The previous implementation explicitly extracted `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` and appended it as `traceID` to every `Plugin Request Completed` record. That extraction was removed, while the new contextual middleware only adds endpoint, plugin, datasource, and user attributes. Consequently these completion logs lose their trace correlation field, making it harder to connect plugin failures and latency logs to their traces. Retain the explicit trace field or add it when constructing the contextual logger attributes.

title: TestLogger drops all log calls made through FromContext
body: `FromContext` returns a newly allocated `TestLogger` with independent, unobservable `InfoLogs`/`ErrorLogs` state. The changed LoggerMiddleware now always logs through `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)`, so a caller that supplies a `TestLogger` cannot observe the completion log on the logger it provided. This makes tests of the new behavior falsely see no log output. Return a logger sharing the original test logger's recording state (or return `f`) so derived loggers write to the same sink.

title: Plugin completion logs no longer include the trace ID
body: The prior implementation explicitly called `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` and added `traceID` to the `Plugin Request Completed` log fields. That extraction was removed, while the new contextual middleware only stores endpoint, plugin, datasource, and user attributes. As a result, these egress-completion logs can no longer be correlated with their distributed trace. Restore the explicit trace field or add it to the contextual attributes, and cover the trace-bearing request case with a test.

title: TestLogger drops logs emitted through FromContext
body: `FromContext` returns a fresh `TestLogger` with separate log storage. `LoggerMiddleware` now emits its completion event through `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`, so a test that passes a `TestLogger` to the middleware and inspects that original logger will observe no log entries; the event is recorded on an unreachable temporary fake. Return the same fake or a derived fake that shares the underlying `Logs` storage so context-derived logs remain observable.

title: Completed plugin-request logs no longer include the trace ID
body: The previous implementation explicitly extracted `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` and appended it as `traceID` to every `Plugin Request Completed` entry. That extraction was removed. The new contextual middleware only installs endpoint, plugin, datasource, and user attributes, so materializing the logger with `FromContext` does not supply the removed trace field. This breaks correlation between backend plugin request logs and distributed traces; retain the explicit trace attribute or add it when building the contextual attributes, and cover it with a logging test.

title: Adding a required method to the exported Logger interface is source-incompatible
body: `Logger` is an exported interface, and adding `FromContext` means every existing implementation, wrapper, fake, or downstream mock of `pkg/plugins/log.Logger` will no longer compile until it implements the new method. This is a breaking API change beyond the middleware rename. Preserve compatibility by keeping `Logger` unchanged and introducing a separate optional contextual-logger interface that callers can type-assert, or explicitly version/document this breaking contract change.

title: TestLogger drops log observations when LoggerMiddleware calls FromContext
body: `LoggerMiddleware` now always logs through `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)`, but this fake returns a newly allocated, unreferenced `TestLogger`. Tests that inject a `TestLogger` and inspect the original instance will observe zero log calls, and cannot verify the completed-request log or its attributes. Make `FromContext` return the same fake or a contextual clone sharing the same recorded log storage, then add coverage for the migrated contextual logging behavior.

title: A device rejected at the limit is accepted on its next request
body: tagDeviceUI adds the device ID to the 29-minute local cache before persisting it. When CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, this new return propagates the error for the first request but does not remove that cache entry. A retry for the same device then hits the cache, skips the database limit check, returns nil from TagDevice, and receives an anonymous identity even though the limit remains full. Only cache a device after a successful store operation, or invalidate the cache entry on every store error.

title: The count-and-insert limit check is not atomic
body: CountDevices is performed in one database session and the subsequent upsert is performed later in another session, without a transaction or lock. If the count is one below the limit, multiple concurrent requests with distinct device IDs can all observe available capacity and all insert successfully, exceeding the configured limit by an arbitrary number of concurrent requests. The admission check and creation need serialization/locking or a database-enforced quota mechanism.

title: Anonymous callers can bypass the device limit by omitting the device header
body: TagDevice returns success immediately when X-Grafana-Device-Id is absent, and Authenticate treats that success as permission to create an anonymous identity. Because this is a caller-controlled HTTP header, a client can simply omit it and never reach the count or limit check. Thus device_limit only restricts cooperative clients and cannot enforce a limit on anonymous access unless missing or unverifiable device identifiers are handled explicitly.

title: Anonymous authentication now waits indefinitely for device-store operations
body: Authentication now invokes TagDevice synchronously using the request context. The removed implementation ran this work asynchronously with an explicit two-minute timeout; the supplied request context need not have any deadline. On a slow database, connection-pool exhaustion, or a stalled query, each cache-miss anonymous authentication can block until the client disconnects or the database returns, causing anonymous request latency and potential request exhaustion even when device_limit is disabled. Preserve a bounded context for the store operation while retaining the synchronous limit decision.

title: A rejected device is cached and is allowed on retry
body: `tagDeviceUI` adds the device ID to the local cache before attempting the database operation. When the limit has been reached, `CreateOrUpdateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, but the cache entry is retained. The first authentication attempt is rejected, while every subsequent request with that same device ID on this server returns early from the cache and is authenticated without rechecking the limit for roughly 29 minutes. Only cache the ID after a successful write, or remove the entry when the write fails.

title: Anonymous clients can bypass the limit by omitting the device header
body: The limit is enforced only through `TagDevice`, but this method returns success when `X-Grafana-Device-Id` is absent. The anonymous authenticator then issues an anonymous identity normally. Because this is a client-controlled request header, a client can simply omit it (or use a client that never sends it) to obtain unlimited anonymous access regardless of `device_limit`. Enforcing this feature requires rejecting or otherwise accounting for anonymous requests without a server-verifiable device identifier.

title: Device count and insertion are not an atomic limit check
body: The store counts active devices in one database session and, if the result is below the limit, performs the upsert later in a separate session. Concurrent requests for different new device IDs can all observe the same count below the limit and all insert successfully, so the configured limit can be exceeded by an arbitrary number of simultaneous requests (including across Grafana instances). Use a transaction with appropriate locking/serialization or a database-enforced atomic quota operation.

title: A rejected device is cached and bypasses the limit on retry
body: `tagDeviceUI` adds the device ID to the local cache before `CreateOrUpdateDevice` determines whether it may be admitted. When the store returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the first authentication fails, but the cache entry remains. A retry with the same `X-Grafana-Device-Id` on that server returns early at line 83 without consulting the store, so `Authenticate` grants anonymous access for roughly the cache TTL. Move cache insertion until after a successful store operation, or remove the entry on every store error.

title: The count-then-insert limit check is not atomic
body: The active-device count is queried in one database session and the later upsert is performed in another, with no transaction or locking between them. Concurrent requests with different device IDs can all observe a count below `deviceLimit` and each insert successfully, permanently exceeding the configured limit for the 30-day window. The per-process local cache does not prevent this across simultaneous requests or Grafana instances. Admission needs an atomic/serialized database operation, and a concurrent test should cover the limit boundary.

title: The new anonymous device-limit setting is undocumented
body: `auth.anonymous.device_limit` is parsed here, but no defaults/configuration documentation file is updated in this PR. Administrators therefore have no discoverable configuration key or explanation that zero disables the limit and that the cap applies to devices active in the last 30 days.

title: The global cleanup cadence is increased tenfold, not just annotation cleanup
body: This ticker drives every cleanup job in the service, including dashboard-version deletion, snapshot/image cleanup, short-URL cleanup, and query-history retention/row-limit enforcement. Changing it from 10 minutes to 1 minute makes all of those database-heavy jobs run up to ten times as often; if a pass takes longer than a minute, a queued tick can also cause the next pass to start immediately. This is an unrelated operational load and lock-contention increase for a PR intended to change annotation SQL. Keep the existing cadence or schedule annotation cleanup separately/configurably.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors with every selected ID
body: `err` has already been checked and is necessarily nil before this call, but the code logs the successful ID fetch at Error level and includes the complete `ids` slice. The same Error-level success logging is repeated for the delete/count and orphan-tag paths. A normal large cleanup therefore emits multiple error records containing thousands of IDs per batch, causing false alerting and potentially substantial log volume. Log successful batch progress at Debug/Info without the full ID list, and reserve Error for actual failures.

title: SQLite literal ID list construction is quadratic for the large batches this change enables
body: Each loop iteration formats the entire previously accumulated `values` string again (`fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)`), so constructing an IN list copies an ever-growing prefix N times. This branch is used for SQLite whenever the configured batch size exceeds 999, including the newly tested 32,767-item configuration; such a batch can produce gigabytes of temporary string allocation and stall or exhaust memory during cleanup. Build the list with a pre-sized `strings.Builder` or `strconv.AppendInt` instead.

title: The PR increases the cadence of every cleanup job by tenfold
body: Changing the shared cleanup ticker from 10 minutes to 1 minute affects much more than annotation cleanup: snapshot, dashboard-version, image, temporary-file, short-URL, invite, and query-history cleanup all now run ten times as often. These jobs perform database scans/deletes and the whole cleanup run may take up to the 9-minute timeout; when a run approaches that timeout, the 1-minute ticker is already pending and the next run starts immediately. This can turn expensive cleanup into near-continuous background load. Restore the previous cadence or schedule the annotation job separately if it needs a different interval.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors with the complete ID list
body: This call, and the analogous calls at lines 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579, use Error even when err is nil and include the entire ids slice. Every normal cleanup batch therefore produces false error-level events, which can trigger error alerts and generate very large log records (especially with the newly supported 32K-sized batches). Log only aggregate counts at Debug/Info and emit Error only when the select or delete actually fails.

title: Building SQLite ID lists performs quadratic string allocation
body: For SQLite batches over 999, each iteration formats the complete accumulated values string again. The final SQL text for a 32,767-ID batch is hundreds of kilobytes, but this loop repeatedly copies all prior content and can allocate several gigabytes cumulatively. The new 40K-row test exercises this path, and orphan-tag cleanup can hit it as well. Build the list with strings.Builder or a byte slice/strconv.AppendInt so each ID is appended once.

title: Non-SQLite deletes can exceed database bind-parameter limits
body: The non-SQLite path creates one bound parameter for every fetched ID and does not cap or chunk the list. AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is configurable; values above 65,535 will fail on PostgreSQL/MySQL prepared statements (and lower limits apply to some supported dialects), causing every cleanup run to fail. The old delete subquery did not bind an ID per row. Split ids into dialect-safe chunks, or validate and enforce a conservative maximum batch size.

title: The renamed second-run test no longer performs a second cleanup run
body: This subtest now creates a fresh set of nine annotations, already exactly three per annotation type, and invokes the cleaner only once. Its zero-affected assertion only proves that an already compliant dataset is untouched; it no longer verifies the stated behavior of rerunning max-count cleanup after a preceding run has removed excess annotations. Run the cleaner twice within this subtest and assert that only the second invocation affects zero rows.

title: The new test uses a Go 1.21 builtin while the repository targets Go 1.20
body: `min` is a predeclared builtin only starting with Go 1.21. This repository's Go 1.20 language version cannot compile either this use or the equivalent use on line 286, so `go test` fails before the cleanup tests run. Replace these with a local helper or explicit end-index calculation compatible with the supported toolchain.

title: Configured batch sizes can exceed database bind-parameter limits
body: The non-SQLite path creates one bind placeholder for every fetched ID, with no chunking or limit enforcement. A configured cleanup batch above 65,535 IDs causes MySQL/PostgreSQL prepared statements to fail due to their parameter-count limits; the same cleanup then retries and fails every cycle. The previous subquery-based delete did not consume one bind parameter per row. Split deletes into backend-safe chunks or validate the configuration against the supported limit.

title: SQLite large-batch SQL construction is quadratic
body: For SQLite batches over 999, each loop iteration formats a new string containing the entire accumulated ID list. This repeatedly copies the growing list, making construction O(n²) in both allocation and copy work. The newly added test configures a 32,767-item batch, and production batches of that size can spend substantial time and memory in this loop before issuing the delete. Build the list with a strings.Builder/byte buffer or delete in bounded chunks.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors with every selected ID
body: This log statement is reached only after `fetchIDs` succeeded, so `err` is nil, yet it emits an Error log containing the complete ID slice. The same pattern occurs for the post-delete, max-count, and orphan-tag paths. Normal cleanup therefore produces error-level events and serializes up to an entire configured batch of IDs twice per batch, causing misleading alerting and potentially very large log ingestion during a backlog. Use an appropriate non-error level and log counts rather than full ID lists.

title: The change increases the cadence of every cleanup job by tenfold
body: Changing the shared cleanup ticker from ten minutes to one minute does not only retry annotation cleanup; it also runs snapshot deletion, dashboard-version deletion, image cleanup, invite expiration, short-URL cleanup, and query-history row-limit enforcement ten times as often. If a run lasts longer than a minute, the ticker also leaves a pending tick, allowing another full run to start immediately after it finishes. This substantially increases background database work for unrelated services; retain the existing global cadence and schedule any needed annotation retry separately.

title: Async legacy writes inherit a request context that is canceled when the response returns
body: Each secondary write derives its timeout context from the request context. For incoming HTTP requests, that parent context is canceled when the handler returns, which is exactly when mode 3 returns success to the caller. The legacy Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection can therefore start with, or become interrupted by, context.Canceled and silently fail after the unified write has succeeded. Detach cancellation while retaining values (for example, use context.WithoutCancel before applying the 10-second timeout) so the shadow write has its intended lifetime.

title: Independent async writes can reach legacy storage in a different order than unified storage
body: There is no ordering or serialization for the background legacy operations. For example, a successful unified Create can enqueue its legacy create, then a client can successfully Delete the same object; if the legacy delete runs first it sees NotFound and is ignored, and the delayed create then recreates the object in legacy storage. Mode 3 continues reading unified storage, so this divergence is hidden until a rollback or mode change resurrects stale data. Secondary operations need ordered, per-object delivery (and appropriate handling for collection operations), rather than one unconstrained goroutine per primary write.

title: Legacy update re-evaluates the original updater instead of replicating the primary result
body: Storage.Update has already invoked objInfo to produce res, but the asynchronous Legacy.Update receives the original objInfo and invokes it again against legacy storage's old object. UpdatedObjectInfo is a transformation over the current object and may contain patch/apply behavior, resource-version checks, or other non-idempotent logic; legacy can therefore reject the update or persist a result different from the unified result when the stores are even slightly out of sync. The secondary write should be wrapped to return the successful primary result (as the previous updateWrapper-based implementation did), rather than reapplying the client updater.

title: A primary NotFound delete no longer attempts legacy cleanup
body: Any Storage.Delete error now returns before scheduling the legacy delete, including NotFound. This leaves a stale legacy object permanently after a prior asynchronous legacy delete timed out or failed: retrying the delete returns NotFound from unified storage and never repairs legacy storage. On a rollback to legacy reads, the supposedly deleted object reappears. Preserve the prior special handling that still issues the legacy delete for an apierrors.IsNotFound primary result while returning the primary NotFound response to the caller.

title: Destroy can tear down storage while background legacy calls are still running
body: Mode 3 returns before its secondary goroutines complete, but Destroy immediately calls Legacy.Destroy and Storage.Destroy without waiting for them. During server shutdown, a goroutine can consequently call Legacy.Create/Update/Delete after Legacy.Destroy has closed its client or other resources, losing the copy and potentially racing with teardown. Track outstanding secondary work and drain or cancel-and-wait for it before destroying either backend.

title: Every successful write can create an unbounded ten-second goroutine
body: Each successful primary mutation starts a new goroutine that can remain blocked in the legacy backend for up to ten seconds (or longer if that backend does not honor context cancellation). During a legacy outage, write traffic can accumulate an unbounded number of goroutines and request objects, causing scheduler and memory pressure while the primary path continues accepting writes. Use a bounded worker queue or other admission-controlled replication mechanism; it can also provide the ordering needed for consistent legacy state.

title: Delete duration metrics use the object name as the resource label
body: The successful delete path passes name to recordStorageDuration where every other operation passes options.Kind. Object names are user-controlled and effectively unbounded, so this creates a distinct Prometheus time series for each deleted object instead of aggregating by resource kind. Besides making the metric semantically wrong, sustained deletes can cause unbounded metrics cardinality and memory use. Pass options.Kind here.

title: Several primary and legacy timings are recorded to the wrong metric family
body: A failed Storage.Create is recorded with recordLegacyDuration at line 45, and a failed Storage.Update does the same at line 129, even though no legacy operation was attempted. Conversely, the legacy DeleteCollection call records recordStorageDuration at line 166. This reports primary failures as legacy failures and double-counts storage timings while omitting legacy timing, making migration health alerts and dashboards misleading. Use the storage recorder for primary calls and the legacy recorder for secondary calls.

title: The new mode-3 integration scenario assumes legacy replication is synchronous
body: The mode-3 subtest calls doPlaylistTests, which performs K8s mutations and then immediately asserts that legacy playlist endpoints return the same data. Mode 3 intentionally returns before the legacy write completes, so a valid slow scheduler or legacy backend can make these assertions intermittently see NotFound or stale data. The test needs an eventual assertion or an explicit test-visible replication completion signal before checking legacy state; otherwise it will be flaky and cannot reliably validate asynchronous replication.

title: Async legacy writes inherit a request context that is canceled on response completion
body: The timeout context is derived from the request context captured by the handler. For normal HTTP/API-server requests that parent context is canceled when the handler returns, while this work is deliberately still running asynchronously. Consequently Legacy.Create can be canceled before or during its write even though the caller has already received a successful unified-storage response; the same issue exists in the Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection goroutines at lines 110, 135, and 163. Use a writer-owned background context (while preserving required values) with its own timeout and shutdown lifecycle rather than the request cancellation context.

title: Independent async mirror writes do not preserve write ordering
body: Every successful unified write starts an independent goroutine, with no per-resource serialization or sequencing. For example, a unified delete followed by a create of the same name can run in the opposite order in legacy storage: the create completes first and the delayed delete then removes the newly created object. Consecutive updates can similarly leave an older version as the final legacy state. This makes the legacy copy diverge permanently; queue or serialize mirror operations by resource, or apply a monotonic version/sequence check.

title: Legacy update re-evaluates the original update callback instead of mirroring the unified result
body: Storage.Update has already evaluated objInfo against the unified store's old object before this goroutine starts, but Legacy.Update is given the original objInfo and will evaluate UpdatedObject again against a potentially stale or different legacy object. UpdatedObjectInfo is explicitly old-object dependent and can perform transformations or have side effects, so the two stores can receive different payloads. The prior implementation materialized the update and wrapped the unified result for the legacy write; retain an immutable materialized result for the asynchronous mirror operation.

title: A unified NotFound delete no longer attempts legacy cleanup
body: This early return covers NotFound errors, so a resource that exists only in legacy storage is left there when it is deleted through mode 3. The previous implementation explicitly continued to Legacy.Delete for a unified NotFound while returning the unified error to the caller. Leaving the stale legacy object visible through legacy APIs also risks resurrecting it if the migration is rolled back; preserve the NotFound cleanup path, asynchronously if needed.

title: Delete metrics use resource names as the kind label
body: recordStorageDuration's third argument is the resource kind everywhere else, but this call supplies the user-controlled object name. This both misclassifies delete metrics and creates a distinct Prometheus histogram series for every deleted object name, causing unbounded metric cardinality and potentially substantial memory/scrape overhead. Pass options.Kind instead.

title: Legacy replication has no concurrency or queue bound
body: A goroutine is spawned for every successful write, and each can remain active for up to ten seconds (or longer if a legacy implementation does not honor context cancellation). A slow or unavailable legacy backend therefore lets normal unified writes accumulate an unbounded number of goroutines and backend connections with no backpressure, risking process resource exhaustion under write load. Use a bounded worker pool/queue and define behavior when it is full.

title: Duration metrics are attributed to the wrong storage backend
body: A Storage.Create failure is recorded through recordLegacyDuration even though no legacy call was made; the same mistake occurs for Storage.Update at line 129. Conversely, the async Legacy.DeleteCollection call at line 166 is recorded with recordStorageDuration after storage was already recorded at line 159. This produces false backend latency/error rates and can hide primary-storage failures during the migration rollout.

title: Mode 3 unit tests do not verify that the asynchronous legacy write occurs
body: Both storage wrappers share the same mock.Mock, their expectations have identical method signatures, and the tests never call AssertExpectations or wait for the goroutine. Thus the synchronous unified call can satisfy the configured method pattern and a regression that never invokes Legacy.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection would still pass. Use distinct backend mocks plus a channel/eventual assertion to verify exactly one legacy call after successful unified writes and no legacy call after primary failures.

title: The mode 3 integration test assumes an asynchronous legacy mirror is immediately visible
body: The newly added mode 3 subtests execute doPlaylistTests, which performs K8s writes and then immediately requires the legacy playlist list to contain those objects at this assertion (with similar immediate legacy reads later). Mode 3 intentionally returns before the legacy write completes, so scheduler or CI load can make these assertions fail nondeterministically. Poll for eventual legacy consistency with a bounded timeout, or otherwise synchronize the test with the mirror operation.

title: Legacy writes inherit a request context that is cancelled after the response
body: The background legacy write derives its timeout context from the request context. Once the REST handler returns, that parent context is normally cancelled, which immediately cancels the child context and can prevent the legacy Create from reaching storage. The same pattern is used by Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection. This makes replication scheduler-dependent and can leave legacy permanently stale even though the unified write was reported successful. Create an independent background context (while preserving required request values such as tenant identity) and track/drain it as part of shutdown.

title: Asynchronous replica writes can be applied out of order
body: Each successful primary write starts an independent goroutine, with no per-resource ordering or serialization. For example, a unified Create followed by a unified Delete can schedule a slow legacy Create and a fast legacy Delete; the delete runs first against an absent legacy object, then the delayed create leaves the object present in legacy after it is deleted in unified storage. Since mode 3 reads unified storage, this divergence is hidden until a legacy endpoint is used or a rollback occurs. Replica writes need a serialized queue or per-key ordering mechanism.

title: Every write creates an unbounded 10-second background operation
body: There is no queue, semaphore, or worker limit around the goroutine per write. If legacy storage is slow or unavailable, each incoming write can retain a goroutine, request data, and a legacy connection attempt for up to ten seconds. At normal write volume this can grow without bound and overload the API server and legacy backend. Use a bounded worker pool/queue with defined overload behavior.

title: Update replays the update transform against a different store state
body: The legacy Update receives the original UpdatedObjectInfo after Storage.Update has already consumed it. UpdatedObjectInfo produces an object from the current old object, so patches, applies, resource-version checks, and stateful transformers can produce a different result when invoked again against the legacy object's state. The previous implementation explicitly evaluated and wrapped the update before writing both stores; removing that behavior means mode 3 can report a successful unified update while applying different content, or a conflict, in legacy. Preserve a prepared update/result and the necessary resource-version translation when issuing the asynchronous replica write.

title: A primary NotFound no longer cleans up a stale legacy object
body: Delete now returns immediately for every Storage.Delete error. The prior implementation treated a unified-storage NotFound specially: it still issued Legacy.Delete while returning the primary NotFound result. If the stores have already drifted, deleting an object that is absent in unified storage now leaves the stale legacy object intact and still available through legacy paths (or after rollback). Retain the legacy cleanup attempt for primary NotFound errors.

title: Successful delete metrics use an object name as the resource label
body: The third argument to recordStorageDuration is the resource/kind label; every other mode-3 path passes options.Kind. This successful-delete path passes name instead, creating a distinct Prometheus time series for every deleted object and making success and failure metrics use incompatible labels. A workload deleting many unique names can cause avoidable metric-cardinality growth. Pass options.Kind here.

title: Several mode-3 duration measurements are recorded against the wrong store
body: When Storage.Create fails, this records a legacy duration rather than a storage duration; Update has the same error at line 129. Conversely, the asynchronous Legacy.DeleteCollection call at line 166 records a storage duration. This hides primary failures and reports legacy failures as storage failures, so dashboards and alerts cannot accurately detect replication or unified-storage health. Record each operation on its corresponding collector.

title: Unit tests do not verify the asynchronous replica calls
body: The tests return immediately after the primary operation and never wait for or assert the background legacy call. Moreover, ls and us wrap the same mock instance (lines 53-54), so an unconstrained expectation set up for Storage can also satisfy Legacy; no AssertExpectations call checks either call count or destination. Consequently these tests can pass if replication is delayed, omitted, or sent to the wrong store. Use separate mocks and a channel/WaitGroup or a deterministic replica executor to assert legacy execution, error handling, and timeout behavior.

title: The new mode-3 integration test assumes legacy replication is synchronous
body: The mode-3 subtest invokes doPlaylistTests, which immediately compares legacy API results after Kubernetes creates, updates, and deletes (for example the legacy list at line 522 and the legacy reads in getFromBothAPIs). Mode 3 intentionally performs those legacy writes asynchronously, so these assertions race the replica goroutines and will be flaky with a slow legacy backend. Wait eventually for the expected legacy state, or expose a test hook to drain the replica queue before asserting it.

title: Recheck the cache after acquiring the write lock
body: A caller that observes a nil cache under the read lock will always load and replace the manifest after it later acquires the write lock, even if another caller populated the cache while it was waiting. During a concurrent production cold start, every request that arrived before the first load completes therefore performs a separate, serialized manifest read instead of using the newly cached result. This can turn one cache miss into N sequential filesystem operations and can also allow a later transient read failure to replace an already valid cached value with nil. After acquiring the write lock, check `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` again and return the cached value before loading.

title: Recheck the cache after acquiring the write lock
body: A non-dev caller that observes a nil cache before locking does not check it again after waiting for `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()`. If several requests arrive while the cache is initially empty, every one of them will serially reload the manifest and overwrite the cache even though the first request has already populated it. Besides unnecessary blocking and I/O, a later reload failure assigns `nil` at line 69 and discards a cache value successfully produced by an earlier caller, causing requests in that burst to fail. Recheck `entryPointAssetsCache` under the write lock for non-dev calls and return it when it has been populated while waiting.

title: Recheck the cache after acquiring the writer lock
body: A caller that observes a nil cache on the read path unconditionally reloads the manifest after it eventually acquires the writer lock. If several callers observe nil before the first caller obtains that lock, they will each parse the manifest serially and overwrite an already populated cache. A burst of initial requests can therefore be delayed by N serialized disk reads rather than sharing the first initialization. Recheck `entryPointAssetsCache` under the write lock for non-development requests before loading the manifest; development mode can retain its intentional reload behavior.

title: The documented sqlExpressions feature flag is now a no-op
