body: This writes an absolute count derived from the value read earlier. If two cron invocations process the same reminder concurrently, both can read the same `retryCount` and write the same incremented value; two failed scheduling attempts can thus leave the count at 1 rather than 2, delaying or preventing cleanup under repeated overlap. Use an atomic increment or otherwise ensure only one worker processes a reminder at a time.

title: Removing `findMany` breaks existing service callers
body: This change removes the public `findMany` method and replaces it with `getBaseConditions`, but the PR does not update any callers. Existing code that calls `InsightsBookingService.findMany(...)` will fail to compile or, if reached dynamically, fail at runtime. Preserve the method with an appropriate raw-query implementation or migrate all callers in this change.

title: Removing `findMany` breaks the service query API
body: This replaces the public `findMany` method with `getBaseConditions`, which only returns a SQL condition and does not execute a query or accept the previous selection and caller-supplied filters. Existing callers of `InsightsBookingService.findMany` will fail to compile (or fail at runtime if they are not type-checked), and there is no equivalent query method in this class. Preserve the method or migrate all callers as part of this change.

title: Removing `findMany` breaks the service's existing query API
body: This replaces the public `findMany(args)` method with `getBaseConditions()`, which only returns a SQL fragment and does not execute a query or preserve `findMany` options such as selection, ordering, and pagination. Existing callers of `InsightsBookingService.findMany` will fail to compile, and this change provides no equivalent service method for them to use. Migrate those callers and provide a replacement query API as part of this change, or retain `findMany`.

title: Invalidate the connected-calendar query after deleting cache
body: The delete mutation does not invalidate `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`; it only calls the optional `onSuccess` prop, which may be undefined. After deletion, the cached query can continue returning the old `cacheUpdatedAt`, so the dropdown still reports cache data and offers deletion until the query is otherwise refreshed. Invalidate the query on successful deletion (or ensure the callback always refreshes it).

title: Exclude expired cache rows from cache status
body: This status query groups every row for the credential without filtering `expiresAt`. Expired rows are ignored by `getCachedAvailability`, but remain in the database, so they can cause the UI to show a last-updated timestamp and a delete action even when no cache entry can be served. Filter to unexpired rows if this status is meant to represent usable cached data.

title: Resolve the env file path independently of the caller's working directory
body: `ENV_FILE` is relative to the current working directory, not this script's location. Running the script from the repository root (for example, `./scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh`) reads or creates `../.env` instead of the repository's `.env`, so the app does not receive the configured webhook URL. Resolve the path from the script directory or set it explicitly.

title: Use a sed in-place-edit form that works on Linux
body: `sed -i ''` is the BSD/macOS form for an in-place edit and fails with GNU sed, commonly used in Linux development and CI environments. When `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` already exists, the script therefore cannot update the env file on those systems. Use a portable edit strategy or branch for the platform.

title: Invalidate calendar data after deleting the cache
body: The delete mutation reports success but does not invalidate `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. That query supplies `cacheUpdatedAt`, so the dropdown continues to show the old cache status and delete action after the cache has been removed unless the optional `onSuccess` callback happens to refresh it or the page is reloaded. Invalidate the query on success, as the disconnect mutation already does.

title: Expired cache rows are reported as active cache status
body: This aggregation includes cache rows regardless of `expiresAt`, but cache reads only serve rows whose expiry is still in the future. Since expired rows can remain in the table, a credential with no usable cache can still get a `cacheUpdatedAt` value and appear to have cached data in the UI. Filter the status query to unexpired rows if this status is meant to describe available cache data.

title: Resolve the environment file relative to the script
body: `ENV_FILE` is relative to the caller's working directory, not this script. Running the usual `./scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh` from the repository root points to `../.env` outside the repository, so the script creates or updates the wrong file and the app does not receive the configured webhook URL. Resolve the path from the script location or repository root.

title: Use a portable in-place sed invocation
body: `sed -i ''` is the macOS form of in-place editing and fails on GNU sed, commonly used by Linux developers. When `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` already exists, the script therefore fails to replace it; because the script does not stop on errors, it can still print that the environment file was updated. Use a portable invocation or detect the platform.

title: Expired cache rows are reported as active cache
body: This query includes cache rows regardless of `expiresAt`, but availability lookup only serves rows whose `expiresAt` is still in the future. Since expired rows remain in the table, the UI can show a cache status and offer deletion when no usable cached data exists. Filter the status query to unexpired rows, or otherwise distinguish expired data.

title: Legacy cache rows are assigned a false last-updated timestamp
body: Adding `updatedAt` with `DEFAULT NOW()` assigns the migration time to every existing cache row, even though those rows may have been created much earlier or may already be expired. The status UI then presents this migration time as the cache's last update. Backfill from a timestamp that reflects the original cache write (for example, `expiresAt` minus the cache TTL), or avoid presenting the migration default as historical update data.

title: Deleting cache leaves the connected-calendars status stale
body: The delete mutation does not invalidate `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`; it only invokes an optional `onSuccess` callback, which may be unset or may not refetch this query. After a successful deletion, the cached `cacheUpdatedAt` remains in the UI, so the status and delete action continue to indicate that cache exists until some unrelated refetch occurs.

title: The environment-file update uses BSD-only sed syntax
body: `sed -i ''` is the macOS/BSD form of in-place editing and fails with GNU sed, so running this helper on typical Linux development environments will not update `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` in the environment file. Use a portable in-place edit or handle GNU and BSD sed separately.

title: Immediate cancellation bypasses the deferred-cancellation limit fix
body: This branch sends the SendGrid cancellation request immediately and returns without setting `cancelled` or deleting the reminder. It is used for rescheduling and workflow/step deletion, so cancellations for reminders scheduled far in the future accumulate in SendGrid's pending-cancellation list until their scheduled dates. That recreates the 100-pending-cancellations limit this change is intended to avoid; once the limit is reached, later cancellations can fail and the reminder emails can still be sent. The retained reminder rows also remain unmarked and are not picked up by the cancellation cron.

title: The scheduler can schedule reminders already marked cancelled
body: This query selects unscheduled email reminders without excluding `cancelled: true`. A cancelled reminder whose scheduled date is more than an hour away is therefore submitted to SendGrid and marked scheduled, despite the cancellation marker. The cancellation cron may eventually cancel it near its scheduled date, but until then the supposedly cancelled email has been re-enqueued and can still be delivered if that later cancellation fails or does not run.

title: Immediate email cancellations still consume SendGrid’s cancellation limit
body: This branch posts `status: "cancel"` directly to SendGrid instead of marking the reminder for the cron job. SendGrid keeps these cancelled scheduled sends until their scheduled dates, so workflow deletions, step deletions, and reschedules can still accumulate pending cancellations and hit the 100-cancellation limit this change is intended to avoid. For rescheduled bookings, this branch also leaves the reminder row in the database without setting `cancelled`, so the cron job will not process it.

title: A reminder can send before the periodic cancellation job runs
body: Cancelled reminders are only sent to SendGrid for cancellation when this cron endpoint runs. With a 15-minute cron interval, a reminder scheduled less than 15 minutes away can be sent before the next run processes it, even though its booking was already cancelled or rescheduled. This leaves a window where the original reminder is still delivered.

title: Rescheduling still creates SendGrid pending cancellations immediately
body: Passing `true` takes the immediate-cancellation branch, which POSTs a cancel status to SendGrid instead of marking the reminder `cancelled` for the cron job. SendGrid retains these pending cancellations until the scheduled date, so repeated reschedules can still hit the 100-cancellation limit and cause later reminders to be sent—the failure this PR is intended to prevent.

title: A reminder can be sent before the next cancellation cron run
body: This selects cancelled reminders only when this endpoint runs; with a 15-minute cron interval, a booking cancelled just after a run can have a reminder scheduled less than 15 minutes away. The next run may occur after SendGrid has sent it, so cancellation is not guaranteed for reminders close to their scheduled time.

title: Cancellation updates are not awaited before the handler returns
body: These async cancellation calls are started without awaiting them, and the handler does not wait for them later. In particular, the email helper must persist `cancelled: true` for the cron job to cancel the SendGrid send; the booking cancellation response can complete before that write finishes, and a serverless runtime may terminate the invocation before it does, leaving the reminder eligible to be sent.

title: All app imports are still started eagerly
body: Each `import()` is evaluated while this object is initialized, so importing `app-store` immediately starts loading every app module rather than loading an app only when its entry is used. This defeats the intended lazy-loading benefit and keeps startup work and module loading for unused integrations.

title: Calendar and video cancellation is not awaited
body: The async callbacks passed to `forEach` are not awaited or collected. Since resolving the calendar now requires an asynchronous import, this function can send the reschedule email and return before calendar/video cancellations run; import or cancellation failures also escape the surrounding `try/catch`. A cancelled booking can therefore remain on an external calendar or retain its video meeting.

title: Calendar and video cancellation is not awaited
body: The async callbacks passed to `forEach` are not awaited or collected. Since resolving the calendar now requires an asynchronous import, this function can send the reschedule email and return before calendar/video cancellations run; import or cancellation failures also escape the surrounding `try/catch`. A cancelled booking can therefore remain on an external calendar or retain its video meeting.

title: Reschedule mutation does not wait for integration cancellations
body: The async callbacks passed to `forEach` are not awaited or collected. With `getCalendar` now awaiting a dynamic import, the mutation can proceed to send its email and return before calendar or video cancellation has started or completed. This can leave the old booking active in an external calendar or video service after the reschedule is reported as successful.

title: Recurring cancellation no longer waits for calendar deletions
body: This `forEach` callback now suspends at `await getCalendar`, but `forEach` does not wait for async callbacks. The handler can reach `Promise.all(apiDeletes)` at line 652 while `apiDeletes` is still empty, then return success before any recurring calendar events are deleted. If the process exits or the import/deletion fails, the external events remain even though the bookings are cancelled.

title: All app imports start eagerly when the store is loaded
body: Each `import()` is executed while this object is constructed, so loading the app-store module immediately starts imports for every integration, even when the caller needs only one app. Since common paths import the store, this still loads all provider modules and incurs their startup and memory costs rather than loading only the requested app.

title: All app imports are started eagerly
body: Each `import()` is evaluated while this object is constructed, so importing `@calcom/app-store` starts loading every app package rather than loading only the requested app. This defeats the intended on-demand loading and means consumers such as `videoClient` still incur the initialization and memory cost of the entire app store.

title: Recurring calendar deletions are not awaited or collected
body: This async `forEach` pauses at `await getCalendar()` before pushing deletions into `apiDeletes`. The handler later awaits `Promise.all(apiDeletes)`, but in this recurring-booking branch that runs before these callbacks resume, so it sees an empty array and can return without waiting for any calendar event deletion. A cancellation can therefore be reported as complete while recurring events remain on connected calendars.

title: Reschedule calendar deletions run unawaited
body: The async callbacks are not awaited by `forEach`. They pause at `await getCalendar()` before initiating `deleteEvent`, while the mutation proceeds to send the reschedule email and return. The request can finish before calendar deletion even starts, and failures from the callbacks are not propagated to the mutation.

title: Calendar deletion callbacks are not awaited
body: This async `forEach` callback waits for the dynamic calendar import, but the enclosing function does not await the callback promises. It can send the reschedule email and return before calendar deletion is initiated; callback failures also bypass the surrounding `try/catch`.

title: Calendar deletion callbacks are not awaited
body: This async `forEach` callback waits for the dynamic calendar import, but the enclosing function does not await the callback promises. It can send the reschedule email and return before calendar deletion is initiated; callback failures also bypass the surrounding `try/catch`.

title: Date overrides bypass booking and calendar conflicts
body: When a slot falls within a date override, this returns `true` before checking `busy`. Date overrides should replace the user's normal working hours, not make an already-booked or calendar-busy slot bookable. For fixed hosts in round-robin events, this can expose conflicting slots and allow double-bookings.

title: Override validation allows slots extending past the override
body: This rejects a slot only when it ends before the override starts or starts after the override ends. A slot that starts inside the override but ends after it is accepted, as is one starting exactly at the override end. For example, a 60-minute slot starting at 10:30 passes a 10:00–11:00 override. This can advertise times when a fixed host is unavailable.

title: Split working hours incorrectly reject valid slots
body: The `.find()` rejects a slot if it is outside *any* working-hours interval on that day. With separate intervals such as 09:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00, a 14:00 slot is rejected because it is outside the first interval, even though it fits the second. Check whether the slot fits at least one interval instead; otherwise users with split schedules lose valid availability.

title: Date overrides bypass busy-time checks
body: When a slot falls within a date override, this returns `true` before checking `busy`. Date overrides add availability; they do not make existing bookings or calendar events disappear. A fixed host can therefore be shown as available during an existing booking or busy calendar event, allowing a conflicting round-robin booking.

title: Working-hours validation can accept unavailable slots and reject valid ones
body: This only returns a match when a same-day interval fails the bounds check. If the host has no interval for that weekday, `.find` returns nothing and the slot is accepted; if the host has multiple intervals that day, a slot inside one can be rejected because it falls outside another. It also compares only the slot start time, so an event can extend past the host’s availability end. In round-robin availability assembled from other hosts, this can expose slots the fixed host cannot take.

title: Zero-length date overrides are never recognized as equal
body: This compares two Dayjs objects with `===`, which tests object identity rather than whether their timestamps match. For a zero-length override, the intended equality case is skipped; the subsequent range checks can then incorrectly allow a slot that spans that timestamp instead of treating the override as unavailable.

title: Date-override slots bypass busy-time checks
body: When a slot falls within a date override, this returns `true` before checking `busy`. Date overrides change a host’s working hours; they do not make existing bookings or calendar events disappear. As a result, a fixed host can be offered a slot that conflicts with a booking or calendar event during the override.

title: Working-hours validation rejects valid split shifts and misses event end times
body: This uses `find` to reject a slot if it is outside *any* working-hours interval on that weekday. For a host with separate morning and afternoon intervals, a slot inside the afternoon interval is rejected because it is outside the morning interval. Also, `end` is set to the slot start time, so a slot that starts within an interval but extends past its end is accepted. Fixed-host availability can therefore be incorrectly removed or offered.

title: Zero-length date overrides are never detected by equality
body: The two `dayjs` calls create distinct objects, so `===` is always false even when the override start and end represent the same instant. The intended zero-length-override handling is skipped; in particular, a candidate slot starting exactly at that instant can fall through to `dateOverrideExist` and be treated as available.

title: Migration crashes when no embed category is configured
body: The category lookup assumes the query returns a row, then dereferences `[0]['id']`. If `embed_category` is unset, its value does not match any category (or the setting row is absent), so the migration raises before it can finish. This is a normal configuration and will prevent the upgrade from completing.

title: SELECT row count is checked with cmd_tuples
body: `cmd_tuples` reports rows affected by commands such as INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE; for a SELECT it is typically zero. Consequently, even when the legacy `embeddable_hosts` setting contains hosts, this condition skips the inserts, and line 31 then deletes the old settings. The upgrade silently loses the allowlist and leaves embedding disabled.

title: Legacy host values are inserted without normalization
body: The old allowlist accepted host entries containing a scheme or path, but this migration copies each entry verbatim. `record_for_host` later compares the stored value to `URI(...).host`, which contains only the hostname, so migrated entries such as `https://example.com/path` will never match and those sites will lose embed access after upgrade.

title: Configured hosts with ports can never match
body: The model validation accepts hosts such as `example.com:8080`, and the normalization callback preserves the port. However, `URI(host).host` returns only `example.com`, so this query compares the stored `example.com:8080` against `example.com` and rejects the referer. Any allowed host configured with a port therefore cannot embed.

title: Migration crashes when no embed category matches
body: This indexes the first row of an inner join without checking whether the query returned anything. On installations where `embed_category` is unset, blank, or names a category that no longer exists, the result is empty and this raises before the migration can complete, blocking upgrades. Handle the missing match and fall back to the uncategorized category.

title: Legacy allowed hosts are not migrated
body: `cmd_tuples` reports rows affected by commands such as INSERT or UPDATE; for this SELECT it is zero, even when rows were returned. Consequently, the migration skips the host import and then deletes the legacy `embeddable_hosts` setting on line 31, losing the configured allowlist and disabling existing embeds. Check the result's row count instead.

title: Configured hosts with ports never match
body: The host validator accepts entries such as `example.com:8080`, but `URI#host` returns only `example.com`, so this query cannot match that stored entry. Conversely, an entry without a port matches requests on any port. Compare normalized authorities consistently or remove port support from validation if ports are intentionally ignored.

title: Migration crashes when no embed category is configured
body: This query returns no rows when `embed_category` has not been explicitly stored or does not match a category, but the next expression immediately indexes `[0]['id']`. Most installations without a configured embedding category will therefore raise during migration and be unable to upgrade. Handle the empty result before selecting the uncategorized fallback.

title: Configured hosts with ports are never recognized
body: Host values may include a port according to the validation regex and are stored with that port, but `URI(host).host` strips the port before this comparison. An entry such as `example.com:8080` therefore cannot match a referer or embed URL, so that configured host is rejected and its category mapping is not applied.

title: Migration cannot be rolled back without losing the old settings
body: This `change` migration deletes the legacy host and category settings with raw SQL, and the other raw `execute` calls have no inverse. Rails cannot automatically reverse these operations, so rolling back raises `ActiveRecord::IrreversibleMigration`; even a manual rollback cannot restore the deleted configuration unless it was separately preserved. Provide an explicit reversible migration that restores the old settings.

title: Configured attachment size limits are ignored
body: This replaces the per-type `max_image_size_kb` / `max_attachment_size_kb` limits with a fixed 10 MB limit. Attachments are not downsized, so sites that allow attachments larger than 10 MB will now reject them in the browser even though the server is configured to accept them. Preserve the configured attachment limit and apply any fixed cap only where intended.

title: Downsizing can discard animated GIF frames
body: When `allow_animated_thumbnails` is false, `OptimizedImage.optimize` selects the non-animated downsize instructions, which read only `from[0]`. Because this call overwrites the uploaded file, an oversized animated GIF is reduced to its first frame and loses its animation. Thumbnail animation preferences should not cause destructive changes to the uploaded original.

title: The new `downsize` definition breaks the existing dimensions API
body: Ruby does not overload methods by arity: this definition replaces the preceding `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` definition. Existing callers that pass separate width and height values will now pass the height as `opts` or raise an argument error, breaking downsizing. Retain support for the old call signature while accepting the new geometry-string form.

title: Oversized animated GIFs can lose all but their first frame
body: This passes `allow_animated_thumbnails` to the upload downsize operation, but that setting controls thumbnail generation, not whether an uploaded animation should be preserved. When it is false, `downsize_instructions` uses ImageMagick with `#{from}[0]`, which processes only the first frame. Any oversized animated GIF is therefore replaced by a static image when the tempfile is overwritten, causing irreversible loss of the animation.

title: The client-side limit ignores the configured attachment size
body: This replaces the type-specific `max_image_size_kb`/`max_attachment_size_kb` limit with a fixed 10 MB limit for every upload. Sites that configure attachments above 10 MB will now reject otherwise valid files in the browser before they reach the server; sites with lower limits also receive an inaccurate client-side error threshold. Keep the attachment limit configurable while allowing the intended larger image uploads.

title: Downsizing can permanently discard GIF animation
body: This resizes the upload in place and enables animated processing only when `allow_animated_thumbnails` is true. When that setting is false, `OptimizedImage.downsize` uses the non-animated ImageMagick instructions, which read only `from[0]`; an oversized animated GIF is therefore replaced by a single-frame image before it is stored. The thumbnail setting should not silently destroy animation in the uploaded original.

title: Unsubscribe does not mute watched or tracked topics
body: When the user is watching or tracking this topic, this branch changes the level to `regular`, not `muted`. Regular topics can still generate direct reply and mention notifications, so the email link's promise to stop notifications is not met for these users. Set the level to muted for this unsubscribe action.

title: Unsubscribe crashes when the user has no topic-user row
body: `find_by` can return nil for a recipient who has never visited or otherwise created a `TopicUser` row for this topic; such users can still receive mention or reply notification emails. The following access to `tu.notification_level` then raises a `NoMethodError`, so the unsubscribe link fails for them. Create or update the row through `TopicUser.change` instead of assuming it exists.

title: A GET unsubscribe link toggles state on every visit
body: This action is exposed only as GET, but it mutates the user's notification setting, and the operation toggles between muted and regular. Reopening or refreshing the email link can therefore undo the unsubscribe and resume notifications. Make the operation idempotently set muted, and avoid changing notification state on a GET request.

title: Unsubscribe crashes when the user has no topic-user row
body: `TopicUser.find_by` returns `nil` for users who have not yet created a `TopicUser` record for this topic, but the next line dereferences `tu.notification_level`. Such users receive an error instead of being unsubscribed. Handle the missing row by creating a muted preference (or use the model's change helper).

title: The unsubscribe action can resubscribe users and does not always mute
body: This endpoint toggles notification state rather than applying an unsubscribe. A second visit changes a muted topic back to regular, so refreshing or reopening the email link reverses the user's choice. Also, a watching or tracking topic is only downgraded to regular, which does not mute it. Make the operation idempotently set the topic to muted.

title: Saving the preference directly bypasses TopicUser change handling
body: Calling `save!` here bypasses `TopicUser.change`, which records `notifications_changed_at` and `notifications_reason_id` and publishes the notification-level change. In particular, if the reason remains `nil`, `TopicUser.update_last_read` can later auto-promote this preference to tracking, undoing the unsubscribe. Use the shared change path and set the reason as a user change.

title: A GET request changes the logged-in user's notification preference
body: The unsubscribe URL is a GET endpoint that mutates the current user's topic preference without a confirmation or signed per-user token. A cross-site link or embedded resource can therefore cause a logged-in user to mute a topic, and email link scanners that fetch the URL can trigger the change before the user clicks it. Avoid state changes on ordinary GET requests or require an explicit, protected confirmation.

title: The unsubscribe route cannot find its template
body: This declares `topicUnsubscribe` as a top-level route, whose template name is `topic-unsubscribe`, but the added template is `templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs`, which corresponds to a nested `topic.unsubscribe` route. No custom template mapping is provided, so navigating to the unsubscribe URL will not render the confirmation page and may fail with a missing-template error.

title: A GET request changes notification preferences
body: The unsubscribe route is a GET endpoint, and this action changes and saves the user's notification level as part of handling that request. Email security scanners, link prefetchers, or a cross-site link opened with the user's session can therefore change that user's topic preferences without an intentional confirmation. Use a non-mutating confirmation page followed by a state-changing request, or another mechanism that prevents accidental and cross-site changes.

title: The action crashes when the user has no topic-user row
body: `find_by` can return `nil` for a user who has not yet acquired a `TopicUser` row for this topic, but the next line dereferences `tu.notification_level`. Opening the unsubscribe URL in that case raises an exception instead of showing the page or changing the preference; handle the missing row or create it through the normal TopicUser API.

title: Saving directly bypasses TopicUser notification-change behavior
body: Calling `save!` directly does not apply the bookkeeping and notifications performed by `TopicUser.change`, including setting `notifications_changed_at` and `notifications_reason_id` and publishing the level change. In particular, if the reason is still nil, later reads can auto-promote this user's notification level back to tracking, undoing the unsubscribe. Update the preference through the model's change API instead.

title: Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive
body: This query compares the submitted address exactly with the stored address. User signup assigns the submitted email without normalizing it, so an address such as `BLOCK@SPAMMERS.ORG` can bypass a block entry stored as `block@spammers.org`. Normalize addresses consistently or make the lookup case-insensitive so casing cannot evade the block.

title: Concurrent matches can lose counter increments
body: The method reads `match_count`, increments the in-memory value, and saves it. If two signup validations match the same blocked address concurrently, both can read the same count and write the same incremented value, losing one match. Use an atomic database increment so the match statistics remain accurate under concurrent attempts.

title: Blocked addresses can be bypassed by changing letter case
body: This lookup compares the submitted email to the stored address exactly, but email domains are case-insensitive and the application otherwise normalizes email addresses for lookup. If `blocked@example.com` is listed, a user can sign up with `blocked@EXAMPLE.COM` and avoid the block. Normalize both the stored address and lookup value, or make the comparison case-insensitive.

title: Concurrent matches can lose statistics increments
body: The method reads `match_count`, increments it in Ruby, and saves the whole record. If two signup validations match the same blocked address concurrently, both can read the same count and write the same incremented value, so one match is lost. Use an atomic database increment (and update `last_match_at` atomically) if these statistics are expected to be accurate.

title: Blocked-email matching is case-sensitive
body: This lookup compares the submitted email string exactly with the stored value. Email addresses are commonly treated case-insensitively, but a user can submit a differently cased local part or domain (for example, `Blocked@EXAMPLE.COM`) and avoid a blocklist entry stored as `blocked@example.com`. Normalize the address consistently before lookup and when storing blocked entries.

title: Validation increments the match counter more than once per signup
body: Calling `should_block?` has a database write side effect, but Rails validations can run multiple times for one attempt. In particular, `UsersController#create` calls `user.valid?` and then `user.save`, which validates again; a blocked signup therefore increments `match_count` twice. Keep validation side-effect-free or record the match once per signup attempt.

title: Concurrent matches can lose counter increments
body: The counter is updated with a read-modify-save sequence. If two requests load the same `match_count` before either saves, both write the same incremented value, so one match is lost. This makes the blocked-email statistics undercount during concurrent attempts; use an atomic database increment or locking.

title: Imported feed HTML bypasses post sanitization
body: This creates imported posts with `raw_html`, and `Post#cook` returns that raw value without passing it through the normal sanitization/rendering pipeline. RSS/Atom item content is external and can contain executable markup such as `<script>` or event-handler attributes, so importing a malicious feed can give every reader of the topic stored XSS. Sanitize feed content with an explicit allowlist before storing it as raw HTML, or use the normal cooking pipeline.

title: Remote article retrieval can follow redirects to internal services
body: The embed URL's hostname is checked against the configured host before retrieval, but `open(url)` follows HTTP redirects without revalidating the destination. A URL on the allowed host that redirects to an internal address can therefore make the application server fetch internal resources; the URL's port is also unrestricted. Validate every redirect destination and restrict schemes, ports, and private-network addresses before fetching.

title: The Referer is interpolated unescaped into executable JavaScript
body: `request.referer` is inserted directly into a single-quoted JavaScript string. A referring page on the configured embeddable host can use a URL containing JavaScript-breaking characters to inject code that executes in the forum's origin when the embed loads. Serialize the value as a safely escaped JavaScript string and pass only a validated origin to `postMessage`.

title: Standard RSS items without a content field abort feed polling
body: RSS items commonly provide their body in `description` rather than `content`; when `i.content` is nil, calling `scrub` raises and aborts the polling job. Since retries are disabled, the feed is not imported on that run, including any later items. Fall back to the available description/content field and handle items with no body.

title: Post-processing jobs can run before the imported topic transaction commits
body: `PostCreator#create` enqueues post-processing jobs before this surrounding `Topic.transaction` commits. A worker on another connection can run immediately, fail to find the uncommitted post, and leave imported content unprocessed. Defer job enqueueing until after the outer transaction commits, or otherwise ensure the worker cannot run before commit.

title: Imported HTML is stored and rendered without sanitization
body: This marks imported content as `raw_html`, and the embed view renders `post.cooked` as raw HTML. RSS item content is external input, so a feed entry can include script or other executable markup that will be stored and run for forum visitors. The generated “Imported from” link also interpolates the feed item URL into HTML without escaping. Sanitize the content and escape generated attributes before storing it as raw HTML.

title: Standard RSS items without `content` abort the feed poll
body: This assumes every item has a non-nil `content` field, but ordinary RSS items commonly provide their body in `description` instead. Calling `scrub` on nil raises, aborting the poll; because retries are disabled, the remaining items are not imported during that run. Fall back to the available description/content field and handle items with neither.

title: A crash between setting and expiring the throttle key can block retrieval permanently
body: The Redis key is created with `SETNX` and only then given a 60-second expiry. If the worker exits between these commands, the key remains without a TTL, so future retrievals for this URL are throttled indefinitely (except for staff bypasses). Set the key and expiry atomically.

title: Imported feed HTML bypasses post sanitization
body: This sets imported posts to `raw_html`, and `Post#cook` returns their raw content without passing it through the normal rendering/sanitization pipeline. RSS item content is controlled by the remote feed, so scripts, event-handler attributes, or other active markup can be stored and executed when anyone views the topic. The imported-source link is also interpolated into that raw HTML without escaping at line 13, allowing a malicious item URL to inject markup as well.

title: RSS items without `content` abort feed polling
body: The job assumes every feed item has a non-nil `content` field and calls `scrub` on it. Standard RSS items commonly provide their body as `description` instead, and items may omit content entirely; either case raises an exception and prevents the remaining items in the feed from being imported. Fall back to the feed's available description/content fields and handle items with no body.

title: Flex layout disables the action button's right float
body: Making `.small-action` a flex container turns its direct children into flex items, and `float: right` on the button no longer positions it at the right edge. Since `.small-action-desc` also has no flex-grow or other rule to consume the remaining space, the button will sit immediately after the description instead of remaining right-aligned as before. Give the description a growing flex value or push the button with `margin-left: auto`.

title: Flex layout disables the small-action button's right float
body: Making `.small-action` a flex container causes its direct `button` child to become a flex item, so the existing `float: right` on that button no longer positions it at the far right. When the description does not fill the row, the button will sit immediately after the description instead of remaining right-aligned, changing the small-action layout.

title: The small-action button no longer floats to the right
body: Making `.small-action` a flex container causes its children to become flex items, and `float: right` on the button no longer affects its position. Since `.small-action-desc` also has no flex-grow rule, it does not consume the remaining row width, so the button sits immediately after the description instead of at the far right as before. This misaligns the action button in small-action posts.

title: Website name bypasses the untrusted-website filter
body: `website` is explicitly filtered by `untrusted_attributes` for TL0 users viewed by anonymous users, but the newly serialized `website_name` has no `include_website_name?` guard and is not included in that filter. Its value is derived from the same website URL, so anonymous responses still reveal the website host and, for matching domains, its path even when the website is supposed to be hidden.

title: Sibling-domain matching mistakes shared public suffixes for the same domain
body: This comparison treats any two hosts with the same number of labels and the same labels after the first as belonging to the same domain. For example, with the instance at `forum.example.co.uk` and a user's website at `other.co.uk`, both hosts have three labels and the compared suffixes are both `co.uk`; the serializer incorrectly appends the website path. This produces the complete-path display for unrelated domains, contrary to the same-domain behavior this change is intended to provide.

title: The new website name bypasses the untrusted-website restriction
body: `website` is gated by `untrusted_attributes`, which hides it from anonymous viewers for TL0 users, but `website_name` is added as an ordinary attribute and is computed directly from that hidden website. As a result, anonymous viewers can still learn the website host—and, when it matches the instance domain, its full path—even though the serializer intentionally withholds the website URL. Apply the same visibility check to `website_name` or omit it whenever `website` is restricted.

title: Normalize hostnames before comparing domains
body: DNS hostnames are case-insensitive, but this comparison is case-sensitive. If a user enters `https://EXAMPLE.COM/user` while the instance hostname is `example.com`, the serializer treats them as different domains and returns only `EXAMPLE.COM` instead of the complete path. Normalize both hostnames before the domain comparisons so the feature works for valid URLs with uppercase hostnames.

The corresponding dark-theme branch should use `$secondary` at 70% lightness, not 30%. As written, the author links become much lighter in light themes and too dark in dark themes.

This both darkens the text in light themes and gives it the wrong contrast in dark themes; the intended pair is primary at 70% and secondary at 30%.

title: Pass a user record when deleting through the association
body: `group.users.delete` expects associated user records, but this passes the integer `user_id`. Active Record can reject the integer as the wrong association type, causing the remove-member request to fail instead of removing the membership. Load the user or delete the matching association row by ID.

title: Group creation ignores the selected alias level
body: The admin form sends `alias_level` when creating a group, but this action only assigns `name` and `visible` before saving. A newly created group therefore keeps the model default alias level regardless of the value selected in the form.

title: Public group member pages now return only the first 50 members
body: This endpoint now applies a default limit of 50 to every group, whereas non-automatic groups previously returned all members. The public group-members route has no pagination UI, so groups with more than 50 members silently omit the rest from the page.

title: Exact page-size multiples produce an extra empty page
body: Using `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` overcounts pages when the member count is an exact multiple of the limit. For example, 50 members at a limit of 50 reports two pages, enabling Next to navigate to an empty page.

title: Pass a user record to the association delete
body: `group.users.delete` expects associated user records, but this passes the integer `user_id`. ActiveRecord can raise an association type mismatch instead of removing the membership, so the new remove-member endpoint can return a 500 and leave the member in the group. Look up the user or delete the membership by ID through an appropriate relation.

title: Exact page-size counts produce an extra page
body: Using `floor(user_count / limit) + 1` reports an extra page whenever the member count is an exact multiple of the page size. For example, 50 members at a limit of 50 shows page 1 of 2 and enables Next, which loads an empty page. Use a ceiling-based page count.

title: Removing the last member on a page can leave the list empty
body: The offset is clamped to `user_count`, but an offset equal to the new count is past the last member. If a user removes the only member on the final page, the reload requests that offset and displays an empty page even though earlier members remain. Clamp to the start of the last valid page when the count decreases.

title: Pass a user record when deleting from the association
body: `group.users.delete` expects associated user records, but this passes an integer ID. ActiveRecord may treat the integer as a record and call methods such as `id` on it, causing the removal request to fail or target the wrong ID. Look up the user or delete the join row by `user_id` explicitly; otherwise admins cannot reliably remove group members.

title: Exact page-size membership counts produce an extra page
body: This formula adds a page even when `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit` (for example, 50 members at a limit of 50 yields two pages). The Next action then requests offset 50 and displays an empty page. Use a ceiling calculation so exact multiples have no phantom final page.

title: Public group member pages now omit members beyond the first 50
body: This applies a 50-row limit to every group, whereas previously non-automatic groups returned all members. The public members template renders the returned list without pagination controls, so groups with more than 50 members silently appear incomplete. Preserve the uncapped behavior for that page or add public pagination.

title: Fallback locales are loaded only for controller requests
body: This is the only call that loads the configured fallback chain. `translate_accelerator.rb` loads only the active locale when `I18n.t` is called, so translations performed outside an `ApplicationController` request—such as in background jobs or standalone mailer execution—can try the site-default/English fallback without those locale files loaded and incorrectly return a missing translation.

title: Changing the site default locale leaves cached fallback results stale
body: The fallback chain depends on the runtime `SiteSetting.default_locale`, but the translation cache is keyed only by translation key, active locale, and backend. If the site default locale changes, cached translations for keys missing in the active locale continue returning the old fallback translation until the cache is evicted or cleared, even though lookups should now use the new default.

title: Fallback locales are loaded only for controller requests
body: This is the only call that ensures the fallback locale files are loaded, but translations are also looked up outside controller requests—for example in mailers and background jobs. The translation accelerator loads only the requested locale on its own, so a missing key in those contexts cannot be found in the site-default or English files and falls through as a missing translation.

title: Changing the site locale can leave cached fallback translations stale
body: The fallback chain depends on the mutable `SiteSetting.default_locale`, but the translation cache is keyed only by translation key and current locale. After the site default locale changes, cached translations that came from the old fallback locale can continue to be returned until evicted or the cache is reset, so users may see translations from the previous setting.

title: Fallback locales are loaded only for controller requests
body: This is the only call site that loads every locale in the fallback chain. Translations invoked outside an `ApplicationController` request—such as mailers or background jobs running under a user's locale—go through the lazy loader, which loads only the active locale. The fallback backend then cannot find translations in the site-default or English locale, so the new fallback behavior silently fails in those contexts.

title: Changing the site locale leaves cached fallback translations stale
body: The fallback chain depends on the current `SiteSetting.default_locale`, but the translation accelerator caches results using only the key, active locale, and backend. If an administrator changes the default locale, translations already cached for users with another locale can continue returning values from the old fallback locale until the cache is cleared or those entries are evicted.

title: A cached denial can block newly granted access
body: This returns a prior denial without rechecking current permissions. If a user was denied for a resource before it was created or before access was granted, the same request continues to be denied for the cache TTL (30 seconds), even though the database now allows it. This can prevent the newly created dashboards or folders this change is intended to make accessible from loading immediately.

title: Denial cache key does not distinguish identity types
body: The key identifies a principal only by its UID, but checks also support distinct identity types such as users and service accounts. If those identity namespaces contain the same UID, a denial cached for one identity will incorrectly deny the other identity's request for the same resource and action. Include the identity type in the key.

title: Unescaped key components can collide
body: The key concatenates the resource name and parent folder with underscores, so different valid name/folder pairs can produce the same key (for example, name `a_b` with parent `c` and name `a` with parent `b_c`). A denial for one resource can then incorrectly deny access to the other until the entry expires. Encode or delimit components unambiguously.

title: Cached denials mask newly granted permissions
body: A denial is retained for the full cache TTL, and `Check` consults this cache before checking even a fresh permission map. If a user is denied and then granted access to that resource, every check with the same key continues to return denied until the denial entry expires, rather than using the database fallback to observe the grant. This regresses prompt visibility of newly created resources or permission changes.

title: Denial cache key components can collide
body: The key concatenates the resource name and parent folder with `_` but does not escape or length-prefix either component. For the same namespace, user, and action, `(name="foo_bar", parent="baz")` and `(name="foo", parent="bar_baz")` produce the same key. A denial for one resource can therefore incorrectly deny a different, permitted resource for the cache TTL.

title: Cached denials can hide newly granted permissions
body: A denial-cache hit returns before checking cached permissions or querying the permission store. If a check is denied and this entry is cached, then the user is granted access to that resource, subsequent checks still deny access until the denial entry expires (30 seconds). This bypasses the new database-refresh path for stale permission-cache misses and can prevent users from accessing newly created resources promptly; invalidate denials when permissions change or otherwise avoid short-circuiting refreshed permissions.

title: Denial-cache key is ambiguous for names containing underscores
body: The name and parent are concatenated with underscores without escaping or length-prefixing, so distinct checks can share a key: for example, name `a_b` with parent `c` collides with name `a` with parent `b_c`. A denial cached for one resource/folder combination then incorrectly denies the other check until expiry. Encode the tuple unambiguously.

title: Grafana list rules lose Pause and Delete actions
body: This new list item passes only `promRule` to the action buttons, so `AlertRuleMenu` receives no `rulerRule`. The menu still gates Pause on a Grafana ruler rule and Delete on `rulerRule` being present, even though this PR now calculates abilities from `promRule` for the ruler-free list. As a result, users cannot pause or delete Grafana rules from this list.

title: Silence action does not open its drawer for Prometheus-only rules
body: The menu now derives silence permission from `promRule`, so it can display Silence for a Grafana rule loaded without a ruler rule. Clicking it sets `showSilenceDrawer`, but this condition requires `rule` to be a Grafana ruler alerting rule; in the new list path `rule` is absent, so the drawer never renders and the menu action does nothing.

title: Filtered Grafana rules are rendered without stable React keys
body: The Grafana item returned from this `rules.map` omits the `key` that is already computed for each result. React therefore warns about missing keys and may reuse the wrong item component when results are reconciled, which can associate action state with a different rule.

title: Federated rules are no longer treated as immutable
body: The previous ability check detected federated groups through `source_tenants` and disabled editing and deletion for their rules. This refactor hard-codes `isFederated` to `false`, so federated rules can now appear editable or deletable whenever the user has the corresponding permissions. Attempts to mutate these rules can fail or violate the federated-rule restrictions; preserve the group’s federated status in the ability check.

title: Silence action does nothing for Prometheus-only Grafana rules
body: The new Grafana list item supplies `promRule` without a `rule`, so `showSilenceDrawer` can become true after selecting Silence but this condition remains false. The menu can therefore offer Silence based on Prom-rule abilities, yet clicking it never renders the drawer or creates a silence. Render the drawer using the Prom rule path or avoid offering the action when it cannot be handled.

title: Pause is unavailable for Prometheus-only Grafana rules
body: The new list path supplies only `promRule`, but this menu item is gated on `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`. Consequently, even when the Prom-rule ability check says pausing is supported and allowed, the Pause item is never rendered. Adapt the pause action to the Prom rule data or otherwise retain the required ruler data for this operation.

title: Delete is hidden for Prometheus-only Grafana rules
body: The new list path does not provide `rulerRule`, so this `rulerRule` guard hides Delete even when `canDelete` is true from the Prom-rule ability check. Users viewing these rules in the list cannot delete them, although the action identifier and delete handler can be built from the Prom rule.

title: The rule detail link drops the return-to location
body: The previous Grafana rule loader included a `returnTo` URL when linking from the alert list to rule details. This replacement link omits it, so navigating back from a rule opened in the list may lose the user’s list/filter context. Preserve the return-to location when constructing the detail URL.

title: Grafana list rules lose the pause action
body: `GrafanaRuleListItem` now passes only `promRule` to `RuleActionsButtons`, so `rulerRule` is undefined for rules in the list. This condition therefore hides the pause action even when the Grafana Prometheus rule abilities allow pausing. Users can no longer pause or resume Grafana-managed rules from the list view.

title: Delete is hidden for rules rendered from Prometheus data
body: The new list item supplies `promRule` but no `rulerRule`, so this condition is always false for rules in the list. As a result, the Delete action is absent even when `canDelete` is true, removing the ability to delete Grafana-managed rules from the list view.

title: Silence action opens no drawer for list rules
body: The list now constructs `RuleActionsButtons` with only `promRule`, but the drawer is rendered only when `rule` is a Grafana ruler alerting rule. The menu can still show Silence based on the Prometheus rule abilities, so clicking it sets `showSilenceDrawer` without rendering anything; users see a working menu item that does nothing.

title: Filtered Grafana rule items are missing React keys
body: This `rules.map` branch renders `GrafanaRuleListItem` without the `key={key}` used by the neighboring branches. React will warn about missing keys and may reuse the wrong component instance when the filtered list changes, potentially carrying per-item UI state between rules.

title: Preserve range-variable detection before interpolation
body: `querySupportsSplitting` runs after this interpolation and relies on `isQueryWithRangeVariable` to keep `$__range` queries unsplit. If `applyTemplateVariables` expands `$__range` using the original request range, that check no longer sees the token and the query is split; each subrequest then uses a fixed full-range duration instead of the range for that subrequest. This produces incorrect results. Preserve the original expression for the splitting check, or otherwise keep range-variable queries unsplit.

title: Shard queries are interpolated twice
body: Shard splitting interpolates each target here, then passes it to `runSplitQuery`, which now calls `applyTemplateVariables` again before execution. The second pass can expand variable-like text introduced by the first interpolation—for example, a variable value containing `$name` or a Grafana macro—changing the query unexpectedly. Avoid re-interpolating already-prepared shard targets, or ensure interpolation happens only once.

title: Interpolating first bypasses the `$__range` splitting guard
body: `querySupportsSplitting` relies on `isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)` to keep queries containing `$__range` unsplit, because that variable must be evaluated against the original time range. Applying template variables here can replace `$__range` with a concrete value before the guard runs, so the query is then split into smaller ranges and executed with a value derived from the full range. This can change query results; preserve the original expression for this check or otherwise retain the range-variable marker.

title: Preserve range-variable detection before interpolation
body: This interpolates each expression before `querySupportsSplitting` checks it, so a query containing `$__range` (or another range variable recognized by `isQueryWithRangeVariable`) can lose the marker that prevents time splitting. The query is then executed over smaller time partitions even though its range-dependent expression was resolved for the original range, producing incorrect results. Check splitting eligibility on the original expression or otherwise preserve the range-variable information before interpolation.

title: Plugin request logs no longer include the trace ID
body: This replaces the direct `Info` call after the middleware removed its `tracing.TraceIDFromContext` handling. The new contextual logger middleware adds endpoint and plugin details, but does not add a trace ID, so completed plugin request log entries lose the `traceID` field even when the request is traced. This breaks log-to-trace correlation for these requests.

title: Completion logs no longer include the trace ID
body: This log call now relies on `FromContext` for its fields, but the new contextual-logger middleware adds endpoint, plugin, datasource, and username attributes only. The previous implementation explicitly added `traceID` from the tracing context to the completion log. As a result, backend plugin request logs lose trace correlation, making these requests harder to diagnose.

title: Context-derived test logger discards recorded calls
body: `FromContext` returns a fresh `TestLogger`, whose log calls are recorded on that new instance rather than the original fake. Since `LoggerMiddleware` now logs through `FromContext`, tests that inspect the original `TestLogger` will see no calls, so the fake cannot reliably verify this logging behavior.

title: Plugin request logs no longer include the trace ID
body: This log entry used to append `traceID` from the request context, but that extraction was removed and the new contextual logger middleware adds only endpoint, plugin, datasource, and user attributes. As a result, completed plugin request logs lose trace correlation, making it harder to connect them to traces; preserve the trace ID in the log fields or add it to the contextual attributes.

title: A rejected device is cached, so its next request bypasses the limit
body: `tagDeviceUI` inserts the device ID into the local cache before attempting the store write. When the store rejects a new device at the limit, this error is now returned here, but the cache entry is not removed. A retry from that device hits the cache and returns success without checking the limit, so the user authenticates anonymously for the cache lifetime without being recorded. Remove the cache entry when the store write fails, or only cache successful writes.

title: The count-then-insert check can exceed the configured limit
body: The device count and subsequent insert run as separate database operations with no transaction or serialization. If the count is one below the limit, concurrent requests for different devices can both observe that count and both insert, exceeding the configured limit. Enforce the check and insert atomically (or otherwise serialize limit decisions) so concurrent requests cannot overrun it.

title: A rejected device can authenticate on its next request
body: `tagDeviceUI` adds the device ID to the local cache before attempting the database write. When the limit is reached, that write fails but the cache entry remains; on the next request, the cache-hit path returns nil without checking the store, so `Authenticate` grants the anonymous identity. A client denied by the limit can therefore bypass it for the cache lifetime by retrying.

title: Concurrent registrations can exceed the configured device limit
body: The device count and subsequent insert are separate database operations with no transaction or lock protecting the check-and-insert. If the count is one below the limit, concurrent requests for different devices can both observe capacity and both insert, leaving the active device count above the configured limit. Enforce the limit atomically if it is intended to be a hard cap.

title: A rejected device can bypass the limit on its next request
body: `tagDeviceUI` caches the device ID before calling the store. When the store returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, this new return propagates the rejection but leaves that cache entry in place. On the next request from the same device, the cache hit skips the store call and returns success, so anonymous authentication is allowed despite the device limit. Only cache the ID after a successful store operation, or remove it when the operation fails.

title: Concurrent registrations can exceed the configured device limit
body: The count check and subsequent insert are separate, unprotected database operations. If the active count is one below the limit, concurrent requests for different device IDs can both observe room and both insert, exceeding the configured limit. Enforce the check and insert atomically or serialize competing registrations.

title: A no-op MySQL update can be mistaken for a device-limit rejection
body: This treats zero affected rows as proof that the device is absent. MySQL normally reports rows changed, not rows matched, so an update that leaves all stored values unchanged reports zero. In particular, `updated_at` can be stored at second precision, making a repeat update within the same second a no-op when IP and user agent are unchanged. At the limit, that valid existing device is then rejected. Distinguish absence from an unchanged update rather than relying on this affected-row check across database drivers.

title: Cleanup now runs ten times as often
body: This changes the global cleanup scheduler from every 10 minutes to every minute, although the PR only addresses annotation cleanup. Every cleanup job—not just annotation cleanup—will therefore run much more frequently, increasing database and filesystem load; if a run takes longer than a minute, a queued tick can also trigger another run immediately afterward.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors
body: This logs at error level unconditionally, including when `err` is nil and when the query finds no IDs. Normal cleanup cycles will therefore produce error-level log entries (and include potentially large ID lists), creating misleading alerts and unnecessary log volume. The other new cleanup batch logs at lines 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579 have the same issue.

title: Building the inline ID list has quadratic cost
body: Each iteration formats a new string containing the entire accumulated ID list. For a configured batch of N IDs, this repeatedly copies the growing string, giving quadratic allocation and CPU cost. Large batches take this SQLite path (the new test configures 32,767), so cleanup can incur substantial avoidable work; build the list with a builder or join instead.

title: Cleanup jobs now run ten times more often
body: This changes the interval for the entire cleanup service from 10 minutes to 1 minute, so every cleanup job—not just annotation cleanup—runs ten times as frequently. That increases recurring database and filesystem work and can create unnecessary load; keep the existing interval unless this broader scheduling change is intentional.

title: Building large ID lists repeatedly copies the growing string
body: For SQLite batches above the parameter limit, each iteration formats a new string containing the entire list accumulated so far. This is quadratic in the number of IDs and can copy hundreds of megabytes for a batch of tens of thousands, making the large-batch cleanup path—and the added large-batch integration test—needlessly slow and allocation-heavy. Build the list with a builder or join formatted values once.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged at error level with every ID
body: This logs ordinary cleanup progress as an error, including the full ID list, and the same pattern is used for count-based and orphan-tag cleanup. It can flood error monitoring and logs during normal operation, especially with large batches; use a lower log level and avoid logging every ID.

title: Build the large SQLite ID list without repeated string copies
body: When the configured batch size exceeds SQLite’s parameter limit, this loop rebuilds the entire accumulated SQL fragment for every ID. With the 32,767-ID batch covered by the new test, it copies several gigabytes of string data and creates substantial garbage for one delete. Use a builder or join the IDs so construction is linear in the batch size.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors
body: This logs at error level for every normal batch, including the full list of annotation IDs; the corresponding completion logs do the same. Routine cleanup will therefore produce error-level noise and potentially large log volume, making real failures harder to find. These messages should use an appropriate non-error level and avoid logging the full ID list.

title: Run every cleanup job ten times more frequently
body: Changing the shared cleanup ticker from ten minutes to one minute causes all cleanup jobs in this service—not just annotation cleanup—to run up to ten times as often. This increases recurring database and filesystem work; if a run takes longer than a minute, the buffered ticker can also trigger another run immediately afterward. Keep the prior interval or change the scheduling of annotation cleanup specifically if it needs a higher frequency.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context
body: The timeout context is derived from the incoming request context, which is normally canceled when the handler returns. Since the legacy operation runs after the method returns, it can receive an already-canceled context and abort instead of writing. The same pattern is used for update, delete, and delete-collection, so mode 3 can leave legacy storage stale despite successful unified writes.

title: Delete metric uses the resource name as the kind label
body: This call passes `name` where the other storage-duration calls pass `options.Kind`. If that argument is the metric's kind label, every distinct deleted object name creates a separate label value, causing unbounded Prometheus cardinality and making the metric inconsistent with other operations. Pass the resource kind instead.

title: Legacy delete-collection duration is recorded as a storage operation
body: This goroutine measures the legacy `DeleteCollection` call but records it with `recordStorageDuration`, so legacy latency and errors are attributed to unified storage and the legacy metrics omit this operation. Use the legacy duration recorder; otherwise monitoring cannot accurately show whether the asynchronous legacy write is succeeding or slowing down.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request cancellation
body: The timeout context is derived from the incoming request context, so it is canceled as soon as the API request completes; the 10-second timeout does not detach it from that cancellation. Since these legacy writes run after the unified write returns, a client disconnect or normal request completion can cancel them before they finish. The same pattern is used for update, delete, and delete-collection, so successful unified writes can routinely fail to reach legacy storage.

title: Legacy update recomputes the update against a different stored object
body: Passing the original UpdatedObjectInfo to the legacy store causes it to compute the update again using the legacy object as its base, rather than writing the object produced by the successful unified update. The stores can have different state or resource versions, so an update can fail in legacy or produce a different result there. This loses the prior behavior of forwarding the unified result and undermines the dual write's purpose of keeping the stores aligned.

title: Concurrent writes to one resource can reach legacy out of order
body: Each mutation launches an independent goroutine, with no per-resource ordering or serialization. If a create, update, and delete for the same object are handled in quick succession, the legacy calls can execute in a different order; for example, a delayed create can run after a delete and leave a deleted object in legacy storage. This can make legacy reads disagree with unified storage even when every individual legacy call succeeds.

title: Delete metrics use object names as the kind label
body: This call passes `name` where the other storage-duration calls pass the resource kind. If this argument supplies the metric's kind label, each deleted object creates a distinct label value, causing unbounded Prometheus time-series cardinality and making the delete metrics inconsistent with other operations.

title: Legacy delete-collection results are recorded as storage metrics
body: This asynchronous call records the legacy operation with `recordStorageDuration`, so legacy delete-collection latency and failures are attributed to unified storage. The same instrumentation mix-up occurs when storage create or update fails, where `recordLegacyDuration` is called instead. Monitoring will therefore misreport which backend is slow or failing.

title: The request context can cancel the asynchronous legacy write
body: The timeout context inherits the incoming request context, so it does not keep the legacy write alive after the request completes. HTTP servers cancel request contexts when handlers return; because these methods return immediately after starting the goroutine, the legacy operation can be canceled before it finishes. The 10-second timeout only limits a live parent context and cannot extend a canceled one, so mode 3 may routinely fail to mirror writes. Use a context that preserves needed values but is detached from request cancellation before applying the timeout.

title: Concurrent writes can reach legacy storage out of order
body: Each successful mutation starts an independent goroutine, with no ordering or per-object serialization. For example, a create followed quickly by a delete can have the legacy delete run first and the delayed create run afterward, leaving a deleted object in legacy storage; successive updates can likewise let an older update overwrite a newer one. This breaks the dual-write consistency the mode is intended to provide and can make legacy API results stale. Preserve mutation order when dispatching legacy writes.

title: Storage failures are recorded as legacy failures
body: This branch handles a failed unified-storage create, but records it with `recordLegacyDuration` and the storage-operation start time. The storage failure is therefore attributed to legacy metrics, while the storage metric is not updated; the update failure branch has the same mistake at line 129. Record these failures against storage so operators can correctly diagnose which backend is failing.

title: Delete metrics use the object name as the kind label
body: The successful delete path passes `name` to `recordStorageDuration` where other paths pass `options.Kind`. If this argument is used as the metric kind label, every distinct deleted object name creates a separate time series instead of grouping by resource kind, causing unbounded metric cardinality and misleading metrics. Pass the resource kind here.

title: Legacy delete-collection latency is recorded as storage latency
body: This goroutine measures the legacy `DeleteCollection` call but reports it through `recordStorageDuration`. As a result, legacy latency and failures are attributed to unified storage, and the legacy metrics omit this operation. Record the result through `recordLegacyDuration`.

title: Recheck the cache after acquiring the write lock
body: Concurrent callers can all observe a nil cache before this lock, then wait here. Once the first caller loads and stores the assets, each waiting caller still proceeds to load and overwrite the cache because the cached value is never checked again. This causes redundant serialized I/O and, if callers have different configs, can return and leave cached assets from a different config than the one that initialized the cache. Recheck the cache under the lock for non-dev callers before loading.

title: Recheck the cache after acquiring the write lock
body: Concurrent non-development calls can all observe an empty cache at lines 41–43 and then wait here. After the first call loads and caches the manifest, each waiter still proceeds to load it again because the cache is not rechecked under the lock. A burst of requests during startup therefore causes redundant manifest reads and cache replacements; recheck the cache after acquiring the lock and return it when populated.

title: Startup indexing races on shared state
body: Calling `Init` during construction runs `searchSupport.init` immediately, where multiple errgroup workers concurrently increment `totalBatchesIndexed` and assign to the shared `err` variable. This is a data race, and concurrent error assignments can cause initialization to return the wrong result. Use per-worker local errors and an atomic or synchronized counter before enabling parallel startup indexing.

title: Concurrent builds can open the same Bleve index
body: The build-wide lock has been removed, but `getOrCreateIndex` can still have multiple callers observe a cache miss for the same key and call `BuildIndex` concurrently. For file-backed indexes, both builds use the same directory, so concurrent `bleve.New` calls can fail or interfere; even if both complete, whichever stores last replaces the cached index. Serialize builds per key or recheck the cache before creating the index.

title: Starting the resource watcher after index initialization can drop events
body: `search.init` can take a long time, but the resource watcher is now started only after it completes. `WatchWriteEvents` begins polling from the latest resource version when it is opened, so writes made by other server instances during index construction are not replayed to this server's watch stream. Clients reconnecting with a `Since` version from before startup can therefore miss changes. Start the resource watcher before the long index build, or ensure the watcher replays from a durable cursor.

title: Concurrent index builds can race with TotalDocs map iteration
body: `BuildIndex` now permits concurrent builds and writes to `b.cache` under `cacheMu`, but `TotalDocs` iterates the same map without taking that lock. If a build overlaps `TotalDocs`, Go can report a concurrent map iteration/write and crash the process. This can occur during startup if a watch event triggers an index build after the watch starts but before the initialization log calls `TotalDocs`. Protect the iteration with the same lock or otherwise snapshot the cache safely.

title: Initialization failure returns without cleaning up initialized resources
body: `NewResourceServer` now runs `Init` before returning, but on an error it returns `nil` without stopping the lifecycle hooks or canceling the server context. If lifecycle initialization has opened resources, or search initialization has started its background watcher before a later initialization step fails, there is no returned server for the caller to stop and those resources can leak. Clean up partially initialized components before returning the error.

title: Clean up lifecycle resources when eager initialization fails
body: If `s.Init` fails after `s.lifecycle.Init` has succeeded—for example, while building the search index—this returns `nil` without calling `s.cancel()` or `s.lifecycle.Stop`. The caller receives no server to stop, so initialized backend resources and any background work they started can be left running, potentially interfering with retries or shutdown.

title: Do not gate conditional passkeys on an identified user
body: This helper is used to decide whether to call `fillContextForm` both when initially rendering the login form and when re-rendering it after an error. Requiring a non-null user prevents those calls for an unauthenticated login, so the form gets no WebAuthn challenge or conditional-mediation configuration and discoverable passkeys cannot log the user in. Passkey discovery must work before the user is identified.

title: Do not disable conditional passkeys when no user is selected
body: This helper returns false whenever `context.getUser()` is null, so the initial login form never calls `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm()` and does not expose conditional passkey authentication. That is the normal state before a user enters a username, and it breaks discoverable-passkey login in the username/password flow; the same guard also prevents the passkey UI from being restored after an invalid-username error clears the user.

title: Passkey UI is disabled for users who have not yet been identified
body: On a normal login, `context.getUser()` is null, so this predicate prevents `fillContextForm` from setting up conditional WebAuthn. The initial login page therefore cannot offer discoverable passkeys through this authenticator, breaking passwordless login for realms using `UsernamePasswordForm` (and its `UsernameForm` subclass). Keep conditional passkeys enabled for the unidentified-user login case as well as re-authentication.

title: Cleanup targets the literal alias `alias`
body: This registers cleanup against `identityProviders().get("alias")`, not the IDP created in the loop. The cleanup therefore leaves all generated `idp-alias-*` providers behind (and the later cleanup registration at line 425 has the same problem). The test can contaminate the shared test realm and fail on reruns or affect other tests.

title: Cleanup targets the literal alias instead of the created providers
