body: The cleanup callback uses `get("alias")` rather than the created provider's alias (`idp-alias-*`). As a result, none of the providers created by this test are removed; the same mistake is repeated at line 425. These identity providers, including those linked to an organization, remain in the shared test realm and can contaminate later tests or cause order-dependent failures.

title: Cleanup targets the wrong identity-provider alias
body: This registers cleanup for the literal alias `alias`, not the newly created provider (`idp-alias-*`). The providers created in this test therefore remain in the shared test realm; the same mistake occurs at line 425 for `idp-alias-20`. Later test runs can fail when these fixed aliases already exist, and leftover providers can affect other tests.

title: Adding an abstract SPI method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: `CryptoProvider` is a public service-provider interface, and making `order()` abstract breaks source compatibility for every existing third-party implementation. More importantly, an older implementation can still be discovered at runtime, but the new sorting code invokes `order()` on it and gets `AbstractMethodError`, preventing crypto-provider initialization. Give the method a default priority to preserve compatibility, or otherwise provide a migration path that does not fail during discovery.

title: Equal-priority providers leave FIPS selection dependent on discovery order
body: The built-in `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider`, and `FIPS1402Provider` all return priority 200. The comparator therefore does not distinguish them, and the stable sort preserves ServiceLoader enumeration order; when multiple providers are present, whichever is discovered first is selected, with no guarantee that the FIPS provider wins. A classpath containing both FIPS and non-FIPS providers can consequently initialize with non-FIPS cryptography despite the FIPS provider being available. Assign distinct priorities or reject ambiguous top-priority providers.

title: Reject ECDSA integers that exceed the fixed signature width
body: When a decoded DER INTEGER is wider than the expected ECDSA component, this code silently discards its most significant bytes. An oversized value can therefore map to the same fixed-width r or s as a valid signature, so malformed DER signatures are accepted as valid after conversion. Reject out-of-range integers instead of truncating them.

title: Adding an abstract method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: CryptoProvider is a public interface, and adding abstract order() breaks compatibility for third-party implementations compiled against the previous interface: provider discovery now invokes order() on them and can fail with AbstractMethodError. Make this a default method with a documented fallback priority, or otherwise preserve compatibility.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default keystore provider, not Bouncy Castle
body: The provider contract promises a Bouncy Castle security provider, but this returns whichever provider implements the JVM's default keystore type (commonly SUN). Callers that use this method for Bouncy Castle services will receive the wrong provider and may fail or use unintended implementations.

title: The selected global crypto provider leaves most crypto operations unsupported
body: AuthzClient.create initializes the process-wide CryptoIntegration, and this provider can be selected when the authz-client is used without another provider. The selected provider throws UnsupportedOperationException for most CryptoProvider methods, so unrelated Keycloak crypto operations in the same JVM then fail instead of using a complete provider. Implement or delegate the remaining operations, or avoid registering this partial implementation as the global provider.

title: The selected provider cannot perform general crypto operations
body: This provider is registered with ServiceLoader and `AuthzClient.create()` initializes `CryptoIntegration`, so it can become the process-wide provider when the authz-client is used without another provider. `getSignature()` (and most other crypto methods in this class) throws `UnsupportedOperationException`; consequently, code that uses Keycloak crypto APIs through `CryptoIntegration`, including client authentication that needs a signature, fails at runtime after creating an `AuthzClient`.

title: The Bouncy Castle accessor returns an unrelated provider
body: `getBouncyCastleProvider()` promises a Bouncy Castle provider, but this returns the provider backing the JVM's default keystore type (commonly SUN). Callers using this accessor to obtain Bouncy Castle services will receive the wrong provider and may fail to find the expected algorithms.

title: Adding an abstract method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: `CryptoProvider` is a public extension interface, and adding abstract `order()` makes existing third-party implementations fail to compile until updated; already-compiled implementations can also fail when provider discovery invokes the method. Make this a default method with a documented fallback order to preserve compatibility.

title: Resource lookups use the resource-server ID as the owner
body: The third argument to `findByName` filters by resource owner, but schema-created resources are owned by `resourceServer.getClientId()` (see `AdminPermissionsSchema`). Passing `server.getId()` here means client-specific resources are not found; the equivalent lookup at line 244 also misses the all-clients resource. Consequently, V2 client permission checks cannot find their resources and authorized administrators are denied.

title: All-clients grants are skipped when a client resource exists
body: The all-clients resource is evaluated only when the individual client resource is absent. Once any permission creates an individual resource for a client, checks for other scopes evaluate only that client resource, so grants attached to the all-clients resource no longer apply to that client. For example, a client with an individual VIEW permission will not inherit a global MANAGE permission. Evaluate the all-clients grant independently of whether the individual resource exists.

title: Preserve MANAGE_CLIENTS access to client role mappings
body: These overrides check only the V2 permission and omit the `MANAGE_CLIENTS` role fallback provided by the existing client evaluator. As a result, administrators with the built-in `manage-clients` role can manage client configuration but are denied client-role mapping operations (and the same omission applies to the composite and client-scope mapping checks below). Preserve the existing role-based authorization when adding V2 permissions.

title: Provision the Clients schema for existing admin-permissions clients
body: The new Clients scopes and resource type are only written when `init` creates the admin-permissions client. `init` returns immediately when that client already exists, so realms upgraded with an existing V2 admin-permissions client retain only the old Users schema: the Clients resource and scopes are absent, and client permission creation/evaluation cannot work. Add an upgrade path that provisions missing schema elements for existing clients.

title: Per-client resources suppress all-clients grants
body: When a client-specific resource exists, this method evaluates only that resource; it consults the `Clients` all-resource resource only when the specific resource is absent. As a result, an all-clients permission stops granting access to a client as soon as any client-specific resource has been created for it, even if that resource's permission concerns a different scope. Evaluate the all-resource grant independently of whether the client-specific resource exists, so grants combine consistently.

title: Existing realms are not given the new Clients schema
body: Adding `Clients` here updates the schema definition, but `init()` returns immediately when the realm already has an admin-permissions client, without adding the new Clients resource or its scopes. Upgraded realms therefore cannot create or evaluate client permissions because the required resource and scopes are absent. Add an upgrade/backfill path for existing admin-permissions clients.

title: V2 client resources are not cleaned up when a client is removed
body: The listener now runs only when `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` is enabled, so a V2-only deployment skips client-removal cleanup. ClientPermissionsV2 stores client resources and their policies in the admin-permissions resource server, but provides no V2 cleanup path; deleting a client leaves those resources and grants behind. Clean up the V2 resource and associated policies on client removal without invoking the unsupported legacy `setPermissionsEnabled` operation.

title: Document the build-time requirement for custom images
body: Enabling `rolling-updates` in the CR is not sufficient for an optimized custom Keycloak image: the feature must also be included when building the image, as shown by the added `--features=rolling-updates` in `operator/scripts/Dockerfile-custom-image`. Without that build-time setting, the operator can pass the CR feature at runtime but the image may reject the changed build-time configuration or lack the feature. Document this requirement here so custom-image users can configure the image as well as the CR.

title: Global view permission is treated as permission to manage groups
body: `canManage()` accepts either `VIEW` or `MANAGE` on the all-groups resource. As a result, an administrator granted only global group viewing can pass `requireManage()` and perform operations such as creating or deleting groups. Only the `MANAGE` scope should authorize management.

title: Group filtering uses authorization resource IDs instead of group IDs
body: `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` returns `groupResource.getId()`, which is the authorization resource's ID, but callers pass this set to user search/count APIs that filter by actual group IDs. Administrators with group-member view permissions therefore get incorrect results (typically no matching users). Add the group ID represented by the resource name instead.

title: View permission grants global group-management access
body: This check treats either `view` or `manage` on the all-groups resource as `canManage()`. Callers of the no-argument `requireManage()`—including top-level group creation—therefore allow an administrator with only view permission to perform management operations across the realm. Require the `manage` scope here; view permission must not grant write access.

title: Group-scoped user search uses authorization resource IDs instead of group IDs
body: `hasPermission` expects a group ID and resolves it with `findByName`, but this call passes `groupResource.getId()` (the authorization resource's database ID). As a result, individual group member-view permissions are not recognized here; line 123 also adds that resource ID to the set consumed as group IDs by user searches. Group-restricted searches can therefore return incomplete or empty pages because filtering happens after pagination without the intended group constraint.

title: A global view grant also grants global group management
body: The all-groups check for `canManage()` accepts both `VIEW` and `MANAGE`. As a result, an administrator granted only `VIEW` on the all-groups resource is treated as able to manage groups; for example, `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup` relies on this no-argument check and will let that administrator create groups. Restrict this check to the `MANAGE` scope.

title: Group view permissions are collected using authorization resource IDs
body: `hasPermission` expects a group ID and looks up the resource by its name, but this passes the authorization resource's ID. It therefore fails to evaluate the matching per-group resource and may fall back to the all-groups resource instead. Line 123 also adds that authorization resource ID to the result, although callers use this set to filter users by their actual group IDs. Group-scoped user searches and counts consequently omit users with only per-group member-view permissions.

title: Use the account UI's interpolation syntax
body: This catalog uses `{{...}}` placeholders (for example, `backTo=Back to {{app}}`), but this message was changed to Java `MessageFormat` placeholders and a Java `choice` expression. The account UI will not interpolate these values or evaluate the choice, so users will see literal braces instead of the attribute name and configured size limits in validation errors.

title: Use the admin UI's interpolation syntax
body: This admin UI catalog previously used `{{0}}`, `{{1}}`, and `{{2}}` placeholders, but this replacement uses Java `MessageFormat` and `choice` syntax. The frontend will not substitute the attribute or limits, leaving users with literal formatting tokens in the multivalued-attribute validation error.

title: The Lithuanian OTP instruction is in Italian
body: The changed `totpStep1` value reads “Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare,” which is Italian rather than Lithuanian. Lithuanian account users will see an unrelated-language instruction during authenticator setup.

title: The Lithuanian OTP instruction is in Italian
body: The changed `loginTotpStep1` value reads “Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare,” which is Italian rather than Lithuanian. Lithuanian users setting up an authenticator during login will see an unrelated-language instruction.

title: The Simplified Chinese OTP instruction uses Traditional Chinese
body: The replacement instruction uses Traditional Chinese characters and wording (`手機`, `應用程式`) in the `zh_CN` catalog. Simplified Chinese account users will receive a visibly mismatched translation during authenticator setup.

title: Lithuanian message was replaced with Italian
body: `totpStep1` now reads “Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:” in Italian rather than Lithuanian. Lithuanian account users will see an unrelated-language instruction; restore or provide a Lithuanian translation.

title: Lithuanian login message was replaced with Italian
body: `loginTotpStep1` now reads “Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:” in Italian rather than Lithuanian. Users configuring OTP in the Lithuanian login flow will see an unrelated-language instruction; restore or provide a Lithuanian translation.

title: Simplified Chinese message uses Traditional Chinese
body: This Simplified Chinese resource now uses Traditional Chinese wording and characters (“手機上安裝…應用程式”). Simplified Chinese users will see text in the wrong script; use a Simplified Chinese translation.

title: Anchor matching also exempts arbitrary tags beginning with “a”
body: This pattern has no tag-name boundary, so it matches tags such as `<applet>` and `<article>` as though they were anchors. When the same tag appears in the English value, `santizeAnchors` removes it before policy validation; consequently, even active or otherwise disallowed markup can pass verification unchanged. Restrict the pattern to the actual `a` tag (with a tag-name boundary) so non-anchor elements reach the sanitizer.

title: Lithuanian TOTP instruction is replaced with Italian
body: This Lithuanian resource now says “Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:”, which is Italian rather than Lithuanian. Lithuanian account users will see an unrelated-language instruction during authenticator setup; replace it with the intended Lithuanian translation.

title: Lithuanian login instruction is replaced with Italian
body: This Lithuanian resource now says “Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:”, which is Italian rather than Lithuanian. Lithuanian users will see an unrelated-language instruction during login authenticator setup; replace it with the intended Lithuanian translation.

title: Access-token ID matcher does not check the grant shortcut
body: This condition rejects a match when the extracted text equals the expected shortcut, and the substring range is also wrong: the grant shortcut occupies positions 4–5, not 3–4. As a result, the matcher accepts IDs with the wrong grant type and can reject IDs that contain the expected one, so the updated event assertions do not reliably verify grant encoding.

title: Decoder assumes a two-character grant shortcut without enforcing it
body: The decoder requires the encoded context to be exactly six characters, but `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` documents shortcuts as usually three letters, and the encoder concatenates the shortcut without validating its length. A grant provider returning a three-character shortcut can therefore issue an ID that this decoder rejects, making the encoder and decoder incompatible for a shortcut length the factory contract permits.

title: Decoder assumes every grant shortcut is exactly two characters
body: The decoder splits the context into fixed two-character fields and requires a six-character prefix, but `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` documents shortcuts as usually three letters and does not enforce a two-character limit. A custom grant using a three-character shortcut can therefore produce an ID during encoding that this decoder rejects or misinterprets, making the token context unreadable. Align the extension contract with the format or support variable-length shortcuts.

title: Access-token event matcher does not verify the grant shortcut
body: This matcher extracts characters 3–4 instead of the grant shortcut at characters 4–5, and returns false when the extracted value equals the expected shortcut. As a result, it does not reliably assert that an event token ID has the expected grant type, so regressions in grant-type encoding can pass these integration assertions.

title: Constructor fails to reject a null raw token ID
body: The second null check checks `grantType` again instead of `rawTokenId`, so a context with a null raw ID is accepted. Encoding that context appends the literal string `null` to the token ID, producing an ID that does not preserve the supplied context and can be mistaken for a real raw ID. Check `rawTokenId` here.

title: Grant shortcut matcher rejects the expected shortcut
body: This condition returns `false` when the token ID contains the expected grant shortcut, so events with the correct token ID fail the assertion; it returns `true` for a different shortcut instead. Reverse the condition so the matcher accepts the expected grant and rejects other grants.

title: Decoder assumes every grant shortcut is two characters
body: The grant factory contract describes shortcuts as usually three letters, and custom OAuth2 grant factories can supply their own shortcut, but this decoder requires the entire encoded context to be exactly six characters. A grant using the documented three-character shortcut can produce a token ID that this decoder rejects, preventing the context from being retrieved. Validate shortcut lengths against the format or make the encoding self-delimiting.

title: Constructor fails to reject a null raw token ID
body: This second null check checks `grantType` again instead of `rawTokenId`. As a result, callers can construct a context with a null raw ID, and encoding it produces an ID ending in the literal `null` rather than rejecting invalid input.

title: Recovery codes remain reusable after successful authentication
body: This user-storage validator only checks whether the submitted code is present; it never removes or marks the code as used. Since recovery-code validation is delegated to the storage provider, the same code can authenticate repeatedly, violating the one-time-use security property of recovery codes. Update the stored code set on successful validation and add a test that rejects a code on its second use.

title: Recovery codes remain reusable in user storage
body: This validator only checks whether the submitted code appears in the stored list; it never removes or marks the matched code as used. Unlike the local recovery-code provider, this user-storage implementation therefore accepts the same recovery code on every login, defeating the one-time-use security guarantee. Consume the matched code and persist the updated list, and cover reuse with a test.

title: Successful recovery-code validation never consumes the code
body: This validator only checks whether the submitted code is present and leaves `myUser.recoveryCodes` unchanged. Consequently, the same recovery code remains valid for every subsequent login, violating the one-time-use guarantee and allowing an attacker who obtains a code to replay it indefinitely. Consume or remove the matched code on successful validation, and cover replay rejection with a test.

title: The concurrency test can pass without observing concurrent reads
body: The reader thread is neither synchronized with the deletion loop nor joined before `caughtExceptions` is asserted. Deletions can finish before the reader makes a request, and an in-flight request can add an exception after the assertion, so this test can pass without exercising the race or detecting its failure. If deletion throws before `deletedAll` is set, the non-daemon reader also loops indefinitely. Use a start barrier and stop the reader in a `finally` block, then join it before asserting.

title: The concurrency test does not wait for the reader thread
body: The test sets `deletedAll` and immediately asserts on `caughtExceptions` without joining the reader thread. The reader may still be handling an in-flight request, so an exception from the concurrent access can arrive after the assertion and the test can pass falsely; the thread can also continue using the realm after test teardown. Wait for the reader to terminate before asserting, and ensure it is stopped even if deletion fails.

title: The concurrency test can pass without observing reader failures
body: The reader thread is neither coordinated with the deletions nor joined before `caughtExceptions` is checked. Deletion can finish before the reader makes its first request, and if a request is still in flight when `deletedAll` is set, the assertion can run before that request records an exception. Consequently, this test can pass without exercising the race or while a failure from the final request is still pending.

title: Optimized paginator cannot paginate datetime fields
body: This paginator is selected by the audit-log endpoint with `order_by="-datetime"`, but its key handling is copied from the numeric `Paginator`: `math.floor()`/`math.ceil()` cannot accept a `datetime`. On the first non-empty page, `build_cursor()` calls this method and raises `TypeError`, so requests using optimized pagination fail instead of returning audit logs. It also needs the datetime-to-cursor conversion and reverse conversion used by `DateTimePaginator`.

title: Negative cursor offsets still raise on QuerySet slicing
body: This branch passes a negative start index to a Django `QuerySet` slice. Django does not support negative QuerySet indices and raises `ValueError` (“Negative indexing is not supported”), so an optimized-pagination request with a negative cursor offset produces an error rather than supporting the advertised reverse pagination. `Cursor.from_string()` accepts negative offsets, making this reachable with a cursor supplied by the client.

title: Datetime audit-log ordering fails in the optimized paginator
body: The audit-log endpoint passes `order_by="-datetime"` to this paginator, but `datetime` fields cannot be passed to `math.floor` or `math.ceil`. On any non-empty optimized page, cursor construction calls `get_item_key` and raises `TypeError`, so authorized requests with `optimized_pagination=true` fail instead of returning results. This paginator needs datetime-aware key conversion, like `DateTimePaginator`.

title: Negative offsets cause Django queryset slicing to raise
body: When advanced pagination is enabled and a cursor has a negative offset, this code passes that offset directly to a Django `QuerySet` slice. Django does not support negative queryset indices and raises an exception rather than interpreting them as reverse pagination, so a negative cursor sent to the optimized endpoint produces a server error. Use a supported query strategy or reject negative offsets.

title: Optimized paginator cannot paginate datetime fields
body: The audit-log endpoint uses this paginator with `order_by="-datetime"`, but this implementation treats the sort key as a number. On any non-empty page, `build_cursor` calls `get_item_key` with a `datetime`, and `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError`, so requests with optimized pagination enabled fail. Its `value_from_cursor` also returns the raw numeric cursor value rather than converting it to a datetime, which would make subsequent-page filters incompatible with the datetime column.

title: Negative cursor offsets cause a Django pagination error
body: A caller can supply a cursor with a negative offset, and this branch passes that value into a QuerySet slice. Django does not support negative QuerySet indexing and raises `ValueError` for a negative slice start, turning the request into a server error rather than providing the claimed reverse-pagination behavior.

title: The set-to-sorted-set change breaks existing live buffer keys
body: Before this deployment, span payloads are stored in Redis sets; this code now calls `ZADD` on the same key names, and the Lua script also uses sorted-set commands on those keys. Existing keys will remain sets until their TTL expires, so during a rollout any new span that touches one will fail with Redis `WRONGTYPE` and its batch will not be processed. Use versioned keys or provide a migration/compatibility path before switching the data type.

title: Optimized pagination fails for datetime sort keys
body: The audit-log endpoint passes `order_by="-datetime"` to this paginator, but `get_item_key` applies `math.floor` to the datetime field. `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError`, so an authorized request with `optimized_pagination=true` fails when cursor construction evaluates the returned rows. Handle datetime values as `DateTimePaginator` does, or use that paginator's datetime conversion logic.

title: Negative cursor offsets produce unsupported queryset slices
body: This branch passes a negative start offset into a Django `QuerySet` slice. Django does not support negative indexing or slicing and raises `AssertionError`, so a request using an optimized cursor with a negative offset returns an error instead of a page. Clamp or translate the offset into a supported query before slicing.

title: Eviction can remove the segment root
body: The size cap evicts members solely by their end-timestamp score. If the root span has an earlier score than the 1,000 retained spans, `zpopmin` removes it while the root marker remains set. The buffer will then flush the remaining spans using the root span ID as their segment ID, but without emitting the root payload, producing an incomplete and misleading segment.

title: Existing Redis sets are incompatible with the new sorted-set commands
body: This changes buffer keys from Redis sets to sorted sets, but existing keys written by the previous version remain alive until their TTL expires. During a rolling deploy, `zadd` on one of those set keys raises `WRONGTYPE`; the Lua script also now uses sorted-set commands on keys that may still be sets. Processing can therefore fail for up to the buffer TTL after deployment. Use a migration/versioned key scheme or handle old keys before switching types.

title: Optimized paginator cannot paginate datetime fields
body: This implementation assumes the ordering key is numeric, but the audit-log endpoint passes `order_by="-datetime"`. `math.floor()` cannot accept a `datetime`, so building cursors for non-empty results raises `TypeError`; the corresponding cursor value conversion also returns an integer instead of a datetime. The opt-in optimized audit-log request therefore fails instead of returning a page.

title: Negative offsets are rejected by Django queryset slicing
body: The advanced path passes a negative start index into a Django queryset slice. Django does not support negative queryset indices or slices and raises `ValueError` rather than interpreting them as reverse offsets. A request with a negative cursor offset therefore fails instead of providing the advertised bidirectional pagination.

title: Datetime audit-log pagination fails when building cursors
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` is selected for audit logs ordered by `-datetime`, but this implementation treats the sort value as a number and calls `math.floor(datetime)`. Building the first page's cursor therefore raises `TypeError`; even if that were fixed, `value_from_cursor` also returns the integer cursor value instead of converting it back to a datetime as `DateTimePaginator` does. Requests opting into optimized pagination cannot successfully paginate audit logs.

title: Negative offsets are passed to unsupported Django queryset slicing
body: This branch explicitly sends a negative start index to a Django `QuerySet`. Django does not support negative queryset indices or slices and raises `ValueError` when the queryset is evaluated, rather than interpreting them as reverse pagination. Since negative offsets are accepted by `Cursor.from_string`, an optimized-pagination request with a negative cursor offset will fail with a server error instead of returning a page.

title: Changing buffer keys from Redis sets to sorted sets breaks in-flight buffers on deploy
body: Previous versions stored these same `span-buf:s:*` keys as Redis sets. During a rolling deployment, buffers written by an old worker can still exist for up to the configured TTL; `ZADD` against one of those keys fails with `WRONGTYPE` (and the new Lua script's `ZCARD`/`ZUNIONSTORE` operations also expect sorted sets). Span processing for traces with in-flight old-format buffers will fail until those keys expire or are explicitly migrated/cleared.

title: Substring matching enables upsampling for negated error filters
body: This check treats any query containing `event.type:error` as an error-only query, including negated filters such as `!event.type:error` and mixed OR expressions. Those queries can include transactions or other non-error events, for which `sample_weight` is not available; replacing `count()` with `sum(sample_weight)` can therefore fail or return incorrect counts. Determine the event types from the parsed query semantics rather than a substring.

title: The errors dataset emits a function registered only for discover
body: The eligibility check explicitly enables this transformation for the `errors` dataset, so this code emits `upsampled_count()` for errors-dataset queries. The function is registered in the discover dataset's function converter, not the errors dataset's converter; an errors-dataset request can therefore fail query parsing with an unknown-function error. Register the function for that dataset too, or avoid transforming queries whose dataset does not support it.

title: Check the dataset actually being queried
body: This passes the endpoint’s original `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`. Dashboard widget splitting can call `_get_event_stats(discover, ...)` for an error-only query while the original dataset is a metrics dataset; the eligibility helper then rejects upsampling for that metrics dataset, so the split error count is returned unadjusted even when all projects are allowlisted. Pass the scoped dataset so eligibility matches the query being executed.

title: Substring matching misidentifies error-focused queries
body: Checking for `event.type:error` anywhere in the raw query does not establish that the query selects error events. For example, `!event.type:error` contains this substring but selects non-error events, so an allowlisted Discover query can replace `count()` with `sum(sample_weight)` for transactions and return incorrect counts. Conversely, error-only queries expressed as `!event.type:transaction` are not recognized, so their counts are not upsampled. Determine the effective event-type filter from parsed query conditions rather than a substring check.

title: Substring matching enables upsampling for mixed or negated queries
body: This check treats any query containing `event.type:error` as error-only, including negated filters such as `!event.type:error` and mixed queries such as `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`. Those queries can include events without `sample_weight`, but their `count()` is still replaced with `sum(sample_weight)`, causing incorrect counts or a query failure. Determine from the parsed query whether the result is guaranteed to contain only errors before applying the transformation.

title: Feature-enabled dashboard tables discard their query results
body: When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, this branch renders `TableWidgetVisualization` with `columns: []` and empty `data`/`meta` instead of the current `result` values. Dashboard table widgets therefore appear blank for every organization using the new visualization, even when their queries return data.

title: Age/timestamp validation accepts invalid combinations
body: These checks use truthiness rather than field presence, so a report containing both `age: 0` and a timestamp (or `timestamp: 0` and an age) passes despite the mutual-exclusion rule. The serializer also accepts reports containing neither field, although the supported report formats require one of them. Use presence-based cross-field validation and require exactly one format field so malformed reports are rejected.

title: Error details can be associated with the wrong event ID
body: `get_multi` returns results keyed by node ID, but this zips the original IDs with the mapping's values, relying on positional order and on missing nodes being retained. If a requested node is missing, or the mapping order differs from the request order, an event's details are labeled with another event's ID. This can place errors at the wrong timestamp and send mismatched error context to the replay summarizer; associate each result with its node ID explicitly.

title: The new table visualization receives no query results
body: When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, this branch passes `columns: []` and an empty `tableData` instead of the current `result`'s fields, metadata, and rows. Dashboard table widgets therefore render blank for organizations using the new visualization, even when the query returned data.

title: Zero-valued age or timestamp bypasses mutual-exclusion validation
body: These validators use truthiness to check whether the other field was supplied. Since `timestamp=0` and `age=0` are valid values, a report containing both fields is accepted whenever the field checked by `get()` is zero. Check field presence instead so the endpoint consistently rejects reports containing both.

title: All replay errors are appended to every paginated segment result
body: The paginator invokes `on_results` for each page of recording segments, but this callback receives the complete replay's `error_events` list on every invocation. `gen_request_data` emits every error left after processing the page's segments, so errors are repeated across pages and summaries for a page can include errors outside that page's time range.

title: The feature-flagged table path discards all table results
body: When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, this branch constructs `TableWidgetVisualization` with `columns={[]}` and an empty `tableData`, rather than passing the current `result.data` and metadata. Consequently, dashboard table widgets render blank for organizations with this feature enabled, even when their queries return data.

title: Error details can be paired with the wrong replay error ID
body: `get_multi` returns a mapping, but this code pairs `error_ids` with `events.values()` by position. Mapping value order is not a reliable association with the requested IDs, and missing nodestore entries can also shift the pairing. The endpoint can therefore attach one event's title, message, and timestamp to another error ID, producing incorrect replay summaries.

title: Every paginated segment page receives all replay errors
body: The paginator calls `analyze_recording_segments` for each page of segment metadata, but the same full `error_events` list is bound into every call here. `get_request_data` then appends any errors not encountered before the page's breadcrumbs, including errors outside that page's time range. Paginated responses can repeat unrelated errors and send incorrect context to the summarizer.

title: Age and timestamp can coexist when either is zero
body: The mutual-exclusion check uses truthiness rather than checking whether the other field was supplied. Thus a report containing both `age: 1` and `timestamp: 0` passes `validate_age`, and one containing `age: 0` and a nonzero timestamp passes `validate_timestamp`. This accepts report objects that violate the supported format contract.

title: Skip installer identity validation when the webhook has not created the integration yet
body: When no `Integration` row exists for this installation, this branch advances the pipeline without comparing `github_authenticated_user` to the installation sender. A delayed or missing installation webhook therefore lets the OAuth-authenticated user complete setup for an installation created by a different GitHub user, bypassing the identity check this change is meant to enforce.

title: Missing sender metadata raises instead of handling the installation
body: This lookup assumes every existing integration has `metadata['sender']['login']`, but `build_integration` only adds `sender` when the pipeline state contains it. If an existing integration has no organization integration and lacks that optional metadata, retrying setup raises `KeyError` and returns an error instead of completing or showing the intended installation failure.

title: Installation proceeds without verifying the installer when no integration exists yet
body: When the installation record has not been created by the webhook yet, this branch advances the pipeline without checking the authenticated GitHub user. The next step can create the integration, so a callback racing ahead of webhook processing bypasses the installer-identity check entirely. Verify the sender through a reliable source before advancing, or fail/retry until that identity is available.

title: GitHub OAuth request failures escape the installation error flow
body: The token exchange and subsequent `get_user_info` call are outside any error handling. If GitHub rejects the code with an HTTP error, or the `/user` request fails (for example, a rejected token or transient API error), these calls can raise instead of returning the installation failure response. This produces an unhandled error rather than the failure screen promised for invalid or reused codes; catch the relevant request/API exceptions and route them through `error()`.

title: New installations bypass the authenticated-user check
body: When the installation ID has no `Integration` record yet, this branch advances the pipeline directly to integration creation without comparing the OAuth-authenticated GitHub user with the installation sender. This is a normal race if the installation webhook has not arrived before the redirect, and the subsequent integration creation does not perform this comparison either. As a result, a Sentry user can associate an installation created by a different GitHub user, defeating the security check this change is intended to add.

title: Missing sender metadata causes an unhandled exception
body: `build_integration` only adds `metadata.sender` when sender data is present, so an existing integration can legitimately lack this key. Indexing `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` then raises `KeyError` and returns a server error instead of the installation failure response. Handle absent sender metadata as a failed verification.

title: `queued` is fixed at module import time
body: `timezone.now()` is evaluated once when this module is imported, so every `AssignmentSource` created without an explicit `queued` value gets the same timestamp rather than its own creation time. Since `to_dict()` serializes this field, the recorded queue time is inaccurate for all later assignments. Use a `default_factory` so the timestamp is generated per instance.

title: Create the queued timestamp per assignment source
body: `timezone.now()` is evaluated once when this module is imported, so every `AssignmentSource` instance gets the same timestamp rather than the time that assignment source was created. That stale value is included in the serialized task payload, making the queued time inaccurate for every later inbound assignment. Use a dataclass `default_factory` so each instance gets its own timestamp.

title: Create a fresh timestamp for each assignment source
body: `timezone.now()` is evaluated once when this module is imported, so every `AssignmentSource` created in the process gets the same `queued` timestamp rather than the time that source was created. This makes the context's timing metadata inaccurate, especially for rapid assignment changes; use a per-instance default such as `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

title: Registered metric alert handler is now abstract and cannot be instantiated
body: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` inherits `StatefulDetectorHandler` but implements none of its abstract methods, including `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the new occurrence hook. When a detector with this registered group type accesses `detector_handler`, instantiation raises `TypeError` instead of returning a handler, so processing that detector fails.

title: Evaluation docstring still describes a list return value
body: This method now returns a dictionary keyed by group key, but its docstring says it returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`. That contradicts the method's contract and can mislead callers implementing or debugging detector handlers.

title: Metric alert handler is now uninstantiable
body: `StatefulDetectorHandler` is abstract and requires implementations of `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. This `pass` subclass implements none of them, so accessing `detector.detector_handler` for a detector with this group type raises `TypeError` instead of returning a handler. Keep it on the concrete base or implement the required methods before registering it as a stateful handler.

title: Registered metric-alert handler cannot be instantiated
body: `StatefulDetectorHandler` has abstract members for `counter_names`, deduplication, group-key extraction, and occurrence construction. This `pass` subclass implements none of them, so it remains abstract. When a detector with this registered group type is processed, `Detector.detector_handler` attempts to instantiate it and raises `TypeError` instead of returning a handler.

title: Evaluation docstring still describes a list return value
body: `evaluate` now returns a dictionary keyed by group key, but this docstring says it returns a list. This misdocuments the changed contract for subclasses and callers; update it to describe the dictionary return value.

title: Return the normalized monitor config
body: `config` is copied and its `schedule_type` is replaced with the display value above, but the context returns `monitor.config` instead. As a result, occurrence monitor context exposes the raw schedule type rather than the intended display value, and the normalization is discarded.

title: The monitor context discards the formatted config
body: The function copies `monitor.config` and replaces `schedule_type` with its display value, but returns the original `monitor.config` at line 168 instead of the modified `config`. As a result, occurrence event contexts expose the raw schedule type rather than the intended display value.

title: Timeout can leave later flusher processes running
body: When the join deadline expires while waiting for one process, this `break` skips every remaining process, including the `terminate()` call for those processes. They can continue flushing Redis segments and producing to Kafka after the strategy has shut down. Ensure every process is stopped even when the deadline is exhausted.

title: Inserting this parameter breaks positional callers
body: `produce_to_pipe` was previously the third positional argument to `SpanFlusher`; inserting `max_processes` before it means existing calls such as `SpanFlusher(buffer, next_step, callback)` now treat the callback as a process limit. Initialization then attempts to use that callback in `min()` and fails. Preserve the existing positional argument order, for example by adding the new parameter after `produce_to_pipe`.

title: A negative process limit silently disables all flushers
body: The `--flusher-processes` option accepts negative integers, and a negative `max_processes` makes `num_processes` negative. The subsequent `range(self.num_processes)` creates no worker processes, so segments are never flushed to Kafka and can accumulate in Redis. Reject non-positive limits or otherwise ensure at least one worker is created.

title: Negative process limits crash flusher initialization
body: The `--flusher-processes` option accepts any integer, but a negative value makes `num_processes` negative and creates an empty `process_to_shards_map`. With assigned shards, the distribution loop then computes an index and looks it up in that empty map, raising `KeyError` while the consumer starts. Validate the option as positive or reject invalid values before building the map.

title: A join timeout can leave later flusher processes running
body: When the deadline expires while waiting for one process, this `break` skips the remaining processes, including their `terminate()` calls. Any skipped worker blocked in a producer operation can remain alive after the consumer has shut down and may continue producing alongside a replacement consumer. Ensure every worker is stopped even after the shared join deadline expires.

title: Reject non-positive flusher process counts
body: A negative `--flusher-processes` value makes `num_processes` negative, so the process map is empty and no flusher is started. The consumer can still commit spans after writing them to Redis, but nothing will flush those spans to the buffered-segments topic, eventually causing data loss. Validate that the configured count is positive instead of silently creating zero workers.

title: Failed result processing is still marked complete
body: The `finally` block marks every work item complete, including items whose processor raised an exception. `ResultProcessor.__call__` also catches and suppresses exceptions from `handle_result`, so those failures appear successful to this worker. The commit loop can therefore advance past a result that was never processed, preventing Kafka from replaying it and causing data loss.

title: Unseen Kafka offsets can permanently block commits
body: This loop requires every integer offset between the first and last observed offsets to be present in `all_offsets`. Kafka consumers can legitimately observe gaps, for example from compacted records or transactional control records. When that happens, processing later messages will never make the missing offset appear, so commits remain stuck at the gap and the consumer can accumulate an unbounded backlog.

title: Queues are unbounded and provide no backpressure
body: `queue.Queue()` defaults to `maxsize=0`, which means unlimited capacity. If messages arrive faster than workers process them, the consumer continues enqueueing work instead of slowing ingestion; queued payloads can grow until the process runs out of memory. This also contradicts the strategy's stated backpressure guarantee.

title: Closing one strategy permanently shuts down the shared worker pool
body: The queue pool is created once on `ResultsStrategyFactory` and reused by every strategy returned from `create_with_partitions`, but closing any one strategy shuts that shared pool down. Arroyo can create and close strategies again when partitions are reassigned; the replacement strategy then submits to queues whose workers have exited (or which reject submissions), so processing stops after a rebalance.

title: A negative worker count creates a zero-queue pool
body: `max_workers` is passed directly as `num_queues` when it is negative. The pool then creates no queues, and processing a message fails during `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`; `submit` catches that error and marks the message's offset complete, allowing it to be committed without processing. Validate that the configured worker count is positive before starting the consumer.

title: Failed work is marked complete and can be committed
body: The `finally` block marks every work item complete, including items whose `result_processor` raised an exception. The commit loop can then advance past a message whose processing failed, permanently losing its result. Only mark the offset complete after successful processing, or preserve the failure so it can be retried.

title: Offset gaps can permanently block commits
body: This tracker requires every integer offset between the last committed offset and the next completed message to appear in `all_offsets`. Kafka can legitimately deliver messages with gaps in offsets, for example because of compaction or aborted transactions; those missing offsets will never be submitted, so commits stop advancing and tracked offsets accumulate indefinitely. Track the order of delivered messages rather than requiring contiguous integer offsets.

title: The work queues are unbounded
body: `queue.Queue()` defaults to unlimited capacity, so a sustained input rate above worker throughput keeps accumulating work in memory instead of applying backpressure. Under overload this can grow until the consumer process runs out of memory; use bounded queues and handle the resulting backpressure.

title: Shutdown exits workers without draining queued work
body: Setting `worker.shutdown` makes the loop exit after the current item, even though `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` is intended to let the queue drain. Any remaining queued messages are abandoned without being processed or committed, so shutdown causes those messages to be replayed and may duplicate side effects. Drain queued items before exiting, or explicitly account for them during shutdown.

title: Failed work is marked complete and can be committed
body: The `finally` block completes the offset even when `result_processor` raises. The commit loop can then advance Kafka past a result whose processing failed, permanently losing it. This also contradicts the strategy's guarantee that offsets are committed only after successful processing; only mark the offset complete after successful handling, or preserve a failure state that prevents committing it.

title: Legitimate Kafka offset gaps block commits indefinitely
body: This tracker requires every integer offset between received records to appear in `all_offsets`. Kafka consumers can legitimately observe gaps—for example, when control records or compacted records are skipped. If records arrive at offsets 100 and 102, this loop stops at 101 and never commits 102 or later, even after all delivered records finish. Track the ordered offsets actually delivered rather than requiring numerically contiguous offsets.

title: Unbounded queues provide no backpressure
body: `queue.Queue()` defaults to unlimited capacity, so `submit()` never blocks when workers fall behind. The Kafka consumer can continue ingesting while queued results and offset-tracking state grow without bound, risking excessive memory use or an OOM. Use bounded queues and propagate backpressure to the consumer.

title: Closing a strategy permanently shuts down the factory's shared queue pool
body: The queue pool is owned by the factory and reused by strategies created through `create_with_partitions`, but closing any strategy shuts that shared pool down. After a partition reassignment or other strategy recreation, the factory can create a new strategy that submits to queues whose workers have exited, so results stop being processed. Keep the pool alive for the factory lifetime or recreate it when a new strategy is created.

title: Shutdown neither reliably wakes workers nor drains queued items
body: On Python versions before 3.13, `queue.Queue` has no `shutdown()` method; the caught `AttributeError` leaves workers blocked in `get()` and each pool shutdown leaks its daemon threads. On Python 3.13, setting `worker.shutdown` before shutting down the queues causes workers to exit after their current item rather than draining queued work. Use a shutdown mechanism supported by the project's Python versions and ensure pending work is handled before workers exit.

title: Backup-code login can bypass password verification
body: Password verification is skipped whenever `credentials.totpCode` is present, but the backup-code branch later authenticates using `credentials.backupCode` without checking the password. A caller can submit an arbitrary TOTP value together with a valid backup code and an incorrect password; the request skips password verification and succeeds via the backup code. Require valid password verification independently of which second-factor credential is used.

title: Backup-code consumption is vulnerable to concurrent replay
body: This reads the backup-code list, validates a code, then writes the modified list in a separate, unconditional update. Two concurrent login requests can both read the original list, both validate the same code, and both succeed before either update takes effect. Make validation and consumption atomic so a backup code can grant access at most once.

title: Backup codes can be used more than once under concurrent login requests
body: This read-modify-write is not atomic: two simultaneous login requests can both read the same encrypted list, find the same code, and then each successfully update the user's credentials and complete authentication. That lets a supposedly single-use backup code grant multiple sessions. Consume the code with an atomic conditional update (or equivalent transaction/locking) and reject a request if another request has already consumed it.

title: Backup codes can be redeemed more than once concurrently
body: The code is read and validated from a snapshot, then the whole updated array is written without a conditional check or transaction. Two concurrent login requests using the same backup code can both validate against the original array and both receive authenticated sessions, violating the one-time-use guarantee. Consume the code atomically so only one request can succeed.

title: Dismissing the backup-code screen leaves 2FA enabled without notifying the parent
body: After the server enables 2FA, this step only changes the modal's local state; `onEnable()` is called only by the explicit Close button. The dialog can still be dismissed through its `onOpenChange` handler (for example with Escape), which neither notifies the parent nor preserves access to the displayed codes. The settings UI can remain stale, and the user can permanently lose the only display of their backup codes. Handle dismissal at this step by notifying the parent and ensuring the codes are not silently lost.

title: Meet fallback crashes when no destination calendar is configured
body: `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is undefined when `evt.destinationCalendar` is null or empty, but this condition reads `.integration` without optional chaining. A booking using Google Meet and no destination calendar therefore throws before calendar events are created, instead of applying the fallback or continuing normally.

title: Calendar lookup cannot fall back when no external calendar ID is supplied
body: When `externalCalendarId` is empty, this searches for a destination whose `externalId` equals that same empty value, so it returns `undefined` rather than selecting the event's destination calendar. The delete path repeats the same lookup at line 317. Updates/deletions without a reference calendar ID can consequently target no calendar (or the wrong default) instead of the configured destination.

title: Collective host events use the first host's calendar address as organizer
body: This code uses the first destination calendar's `externalId` for the organizer attendee on every calendar event, even though `createEvent` selects a different destination calendar for each credential. For collective bookings, events created on later hosts' calendars therefore identify the first host's calendar address as the organizer, leading to incorrect organizer identity and invitations.

title: Recurring cancellation repeats deletes against the first calendar reference
body: For each calendar reference, the recurring path loops over credentials and then uses `find` to select only the first calendar reference on each updated booking. With multiple calendar references, this repeats the same deletion for each outer reference and never deletes events identified by the other references. Collective recurring cancellations can leave events on hosts' calendars or issue duplicate deletion requests.

title: Guard the missing destination calendar before reading its integration
body: When a booking uses Google Meet but has no destination calendar, `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined`. This condition dereferences `.integration` and throws before the booking can be created. The previous check safely handled a missing destination calendar, so ordinary Meet bookings without a configured calendar now fail.

title: Fall back to the event's selected calendar when updating
body: When `externalCalendarId` is absent, this search compares every calendar's `externalId` with `undefined`, so it cannot select the configured destination calendar. `calendar.events.update` then receives an undefined `calendarId` and fails. This breaks updates for bookings whose calendar reference has no external calendar ID, including reschedules and location changes.

title: Delete from the configured destination calendar when no external ID is passed
body: If `externalCalendarId` is absent, the lookup compares calendar IDs with `undefined` and returns no calendar. The subsequent fallback uses `primary`, even when the event was created on a non-primary destination calendar. Cancellation can therefore leave the actual event behind and may target the wrong calendar.

title: Use the destination matching this credential for the organizer address
body: Collective bookings pass the full destination-calendar array to each credential's `createEvent` call, but this code always uses the first destination's external ID as the organizer's email. For every host after the first, Google receives the wrong organizer address in the attendee payload; the event can be attributed to another host instead of the calendar owner.

title: Meet fallback crashes when no destination calendar is configured
body: `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined` when `evt.destinationCalendar` is null or empty, but this condition dereferences `.integration` without optional chaining. Creating a Meet event without a configured destination calendar therefore throws before the event or meeting can be created; use a safe check for the missing calendar.

title: Google attendee organizer email always comes from the first destination
body: For each credential, `createEvent` selects that credential's calendar as the event destination, but the organizer attendee email is taken from the first item in the entire destination list. On collective bookings, events created in later hosts' calendars can therefore identify the first host's calendar address as the organizer, misrepresenting who owns the event and potentially breaking organizer-related invite behavior. Select the destination matching `credentialId` for this email too.

title: Google updates lose the destination calendar when no external ID is passed
body: When `externalCalendarId` is absent, this fallback searches for a destination whose `externalId` equals that same absent value, so it always yields `undefined`. The update request then receives no calendar ID instead of the event's destination calendar, causing Google updates to fail for callers that omit the external ID. Fall back to the appropriate destination calendar rather than comparing against the missing argument.

title: The sync-mode schema discards the refreshed token fields
body: In credential-sharing mode this schema accepts only `access_token` plus a computed property whose key is the stringification of a Zod schema; it does not require or preserve the provider's expiry field. Zod objects strip unrecognized fields by default, so parsing a normal response drops fields such as `expiry_date`, `expires_in`, `refresh_token`, and provider-specific data. Callers then persist incomplete credentials or assign undefined expiry values, causing token refreshes to fail or repeat. Define and preserve the actual required response fields for each integration.

title: Salesforce refresh never makes the refreshed token usable
body: This code persists the newly refreshed token, but then constructs the connection using `credentialKey.instance_url` and `credentialKey.access_token` from the original credential. The new access token and potentially changed instance URL are ignored, so Salesforce calls continue with the old token and fail after expiry. Build the connection from the parsed refresh response and the retained refresh token.

title: The new Prisma update has no Prisma import
body: This file now calls `prisma.credential.update` but does not import or otherwise define `prisma`. TypeScript/build will fail with an unresolved identifier, preventing the app-store package from compiling.

title: Credential ID is sent as the syncing user's ID
body: `refreshOAuthTokens` interprets its third argument as a Cal.com user ID and sends it as `calcomUserId`, but this call passes `credentialId`, the credential row's primary key. The external sync endpoint will look up the wrong user and may return another user's tokens or fail to find the intended credential. Pass `credential.userId` instead; retain the credential ID only for the local database update.

title: The sync-mode schema requires a literal property instead of an expiry field
body: `[z.string().toString()]` evaluates to the literal key `"[object Object]"`; it does not define a wildcard numeric property. Consequently, refresh responses that contain the documented access token and an expiry field fail validation unless they also contain a numeric `"[object Object]"` field. With credential syncing enabled, token refreshes for providers using this parser therefore fail instead of accepting the sync endpoint's response.

title: Stores the Zod safeParse wrapper as the Google credential key
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the result of `safeParse`, which is an object shaped like `{ success, data }`, but this caller assigns that entire result to `key` and persists it as the credential. The next Google auth attempt parses this wrapper as token credentials and cannot find the access/refresh token fields, breaking the connected calendar and its future refreshes.

title: Refreshes Salesforce tokens but builds the connection with the old tokens
body: After obtaining and persisting `accessTokenParsed.data`, the returned connection is initialized from `credentialKey.instance_url` and `credentialKey.access_token`, the stale values loaded before refresh. When the old access token has expired, Salesforce API calls use that expired token even though a fresh token was just obtained and stored, so the integration fails until another credential reload.

title: Sends the credential ID as the synced user's ID
body: `refreshOAuthTokens` uses its third argument as `calcomUserId` in the request sent to the self-hosted sync endpoint. This call passes `credentialId`, not `credential.userId`; credential IDs and user IDs are separate identifiers, so the remote app store looks up the wrong user and cannot refresh that user's token. Pass the owning user's ID from the credential instead.

title: Sends the credential ID as the synced user's ID
body: `refreshOAuthTokens` uses its third argument as `calcomUserId` in the request sent to the self-hosted sync endpoint. This call passes `credential.userId`, but the shown method's credential is available here; correction: this line actually passes the correct user ID. No issue.

title: The shared-mode token schema requires a literal bogus field
body: `z.string().toString()` evaluates to the same string for every property name, so this computed key does not express “any numeric expiry field”; it requires a property named `"[object Object]"` with a number value. Normal provider token responses do not contain that field, so refresh responses fail validation whenever credential sharing is enabled and the callers cannot save or use refreshed tokens.

title: Google treats the sync endpoint Response as an Axios response
body: When credential sync is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the `fetch` Response from the configured endpoint. A Fetch Response has no `.data` property, but this code reads `res?.data` and then accesses `token.access_token`; `token` is therefore undefined and token refresh throws instead of updating the credential. Parse the response body or normalize the helper’s return type before consuming it.

title: The refresh request sends the credential ID as the user ID
body: `refreshOAuthTokens` uses its third argument as `calcomUserId` in the sync endpoint request, but this call passes `credentialId`, not the credential owner's `userId`. The self-hosted app store will look up the wrong user's tokens whenever these IDs differ, so Bigin refreshes fail or may refresh another user's credentials. Pass `credential.userId`.

title: The refresh request sends the credential ID as the user ID
body: `refreshOAuthTokens` uses its third argument as `calcomUserId` in the sync endpoint request, but this call passes `credential.userId`? No: it passes `credential.userId` here, so this call is correct.

title: Salesforce references Prisma without importing it
body: This newly added refresh-and-save path calls `prisma.credential.update`, but the file has no `prisma` import. TypeScript compilation fails with an unresolved identifier, preventing the app-store package from building.

title: Salesforce constructs the connection with the old access token
body: The refresh response is persisted at lines 96–99, but the returned connection is initialized from `credentialKey.instance_url` and `credentialKey.access_token`, which are the pre-refresh values. If the old access token has expired, all Salesforce operations using this connection still fail with authentication errors even though a new token was successfully fetched. Use the parsed refresh response values.

title: Team admins who are not owners are denied access
body: This requires the caller to satisfy both `isTeamAdmin` and `isTeamOwner`. Team admins and team owners are distinct roles, so an admin who is not also an owner cannot add guests even though the permission check and UI are intended to allow either role. Use an OR between these role checks.

title: Guest deduplication is case-sensitive
body: Email addresses are compared verbatim against existing attendees and blacklist entries. Since email addresses are case-insensitive in normal use, submitting a different-case version of an existing attendee or blacklisted address can bypass these checks. This can create duplicate attendees or evade the blacklist; normalize both inputs and stored addresses before comparison.

title: Concurrent requests can add the same guest twice
body: The handler filters against the attendees loaded before the write, then inserts the filtered list without an atomic duplicate check. Two requests adding the same email concurrently can both pass this check and create duplicate attendees (and send duplicate invitations). Enforce uniqueness in the database or make the insert idempotent.

title: Guests can be added to cancelled bookings
body: The handler never checks the booking status before inserting attendees and sending invitations. A permitted user can add guests to a cancelled booking, resulting in new attendees receiving a scheduled-event invitation for an event that no longer exists. Reject cancelled or otherwise ineligible bookings before modifying attendees.

title: Guest list has no size limit
body: The input accepts an unbounded number of email addresses. An authenticated user permitted to add guests can submit a very large list, causing bulk database writes, calendar updates, and one or more emails per attendee. Add a reasonable maximum (and enforce it server-side) to prevent resource exhaustion.

title: Team admins must also be owners to add guests
body: This combines `isTeamAdmin` and `isTeamOwner` with `&&`, so a team member must satisfy both checks to pass this branch. Admins and owners are distinct roles, so ordinary team admins are denied access despite the intended admin-or-owner permission. Use an OR between the role checks.

title: Guest filtering is case-sensitive
body: Email addresses are compared verbatim against existing attendees and against a blacklist whose entries are lowercased. A differently-cased address can therefore bypass the blacklist and be added as a duplicate of an existing attendee; email addresses are case-insensitive in practice. Normalize both submitted addresses and stored/blacklisted addresses before filtering.

title: Team admins who are not owners are denied access
body: This permission check requires the user to be both a team admin and a team owner. Those are distinct roles, so an admin who is not also an owner fails this check and is denied even though the error path is intended to permit team admins or owners. Use an OR between the role checks so either role grants access.

title: Guest deduplication is case-sensitive
body: Email addresses are compared as exact strings here, so a request can add an existing attendee again using different casing (for example, `Guest@example.com` versus `guest@example.com`). This can create duplicate attendee records and send duplicate invitations; normalize addresses consistently for validation, blacklist checks, and existing-attendee comparisons.

title: Calendar updates use the caller's credentials
body: The caller may be an attendee rather than the organizer, but the EventManager is initialized with `ctx.user` and that user's credentials. Adding guests can therefore attempt to update the attendee's calendar instead of the booking owner's calendar, or fail when the attendee has no suitable calendar integration. Use credentials belonging to the calendar owner for this update.

title: Existing attendees can receive a new-booking invitation
body: This chooses the scheduled-booking email by checking the submitted guest list, not the guests actually inserted. If the request includes an address that already belongs to the booking alongside a new address, the existing attendee matches `newGuests` and receives another scheduled invitation instead of the guest-added update email. Pass the filtered, newly inserted addresses to this function.

title: Cleanup deletes expired reminders for every method
body: The first `OR` branch retains the previous `method: SMS` condition, but the new `retryCount > 1` branch does not. As a result, every workflow reminder of any method—including email and WhatsApp reminders—is deleted by this SMS cron once its retry count exceeds 1. Scope this branch to SMS (or otherwise ensure this cleanup cannot remove other reminder types), so this endpoint does not destroy unrelated reminders.

title: Retries stop after the first failure
body: When `scheduleSMS` returns `false`, this increments `retryCount` but leaves `scheduled` false. On the next cron run, the reminder is selected again, but this branch deletes reminders only when `retryCount > 1`; the second failed attempt raises the count to 2, and the reminder is not deleted until a later cron run. This means the described two-attempt limit is not enforced immediately and leaves a failed reminder in the database for at least one extra run. Delete it when the second attempt fails, or align the cleanup threshold and behavior.

title: Retry increments can be lost across overlapping cron runs
body: Each run reads `retryCount` and later writes `reminder.retryCount + 1`. If two cron invocations process the same unscheduled reminder concurrently, both can read the same count and write the same increment; the reminder is then retried more times than the configured limit. Use an atomic increment and claim/lock reminders before scheduling, so concurrent runs cannot lose increments or duplicate scheduling attempts.

title: Reminders without a recipient never reach the retry limit
body: When `sendTo` is missing (for example, an attendee reminder has no SMS number), this condition skips scheduling and neither branch increments `retryCount`. The reminder remains unscheduled and is selected by every subsequent cron run, so the new retry limit does not clean up this common failure case and the reminder is retried indefinitely.

title: Retry increments can be lost when cron runs overlap
body: The retry count is written as `reminder.retryCount + 1` from the value loaded before scheduling. If two cron invocations process the same reminder concurrently and both scheduling attempts fail, both write the same increment rather than accumulating two failures. This can keep the reminder below the deletion threshold and cause it to be retried indefinitely; use an atomic database increment (and consider claiming reminders before processing).

title: Removing `findMany` breaks existing service callers
body: This change removes the public `findMany` method and replaces it with `getBaseConditions`, but does not provide a query method with the old contract. Any callers of `InsightsBookingService.findMany` will now fail to compile or run, and callers cannot use the service to execute the filtered, authorization-scoped query as before. Preserve a compatible `findMany` API or update all callers as part of this change.

title: Removing `findMany` breaks existing service callers
body: This replaces the public `findMany` method with `getBaseConditions`, so callers that use `InsightsBookingService.findMany()` can no longer compile or run. The PR description says the service is being converted to raw SQL, but it does not identify a migration of those callers. Preserve the method with a raw-query implementation or update all callers and their contract before removing it.

title: Removing `findMany` breaks existing service callers
body: This change removes the public `findMany` method and replaces it with `getBaseConditions`, but does not update any callers. Existing code that invokes `InsightsBookingService.findMany(...)` will fail type-checking (or fail at runtime if it bypasses types), breaking the service API. Preserve the method or migrate all callers to execute the raw query before merging.

title: The script writes the webhook URL to the wrong env file when run from the repository root
body: `ENV_FILE` is resolved relative to the caller's working directory, not the script's location. Running this script from the repository root—the natural invocation for `scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh`—writes `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` to `../.env`, outside the repository, so the web app will not use the tunnel URL and Google webhook testing will fail. Resolve the path relative to the script or use the project-root `.env` path.

title: Expired cache entries are reported as active cache status
body: This status query groups every cache row for the credential without checking `expiresAt`. Once a cache entry expires, it is no longer served by `getCachedAvailability`, but its `updatedAt` is still returned and the UI presents it as cache status and offers cache deletion. Filter to unexpired rows (or otherwise distinguish expired entries) so the displayed status reflects data that can actually be used.

title: Deleting cache leaves the displayed status stale
body: The delete mutation calls `onSuccess`, but unlike the disconnect mutation it never invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. When this component is used without an `onSuccess` callback (or the callback does not refetch this query), the cached query result still contains the old `cacheUpdatedAt`, so the dropdown continues to show a cache status and delete action after the cache rows have been removed. Invalidate the connected-calendars query on success or settlement so the UI reflects the deletion.

title: The environment update fails on Linux
body: `sed -i ''` is the macOS/BSD form of in-place editing; GNU sed on Linux treats the empty argument as a backup suffix and then fails to parse the remaining arguments. When the script is run on Linux with an existing `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` entry, it exits without updating the URL, so webhook testing continues to target the old endpoint.

title: Deleting cache leaves the displayed cache status stale
body: The delete mutation's success handler does not invalidate or refetch `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`, unlike the disconnect mutation. After deleting cached rows, the query still contains the old `cacheUpdatedAt`, so the dropdown continues to show cache status and a delete action even though the cache was removed; this persists until some unrelated refetch or page reload.

title: Wait for reminder cancellations before continuing the reschedule
body: `forEach` does not await the async cancellation calls, so the handler proceeds to reschedule the booking and send reschedule notifications while the SendGrid cancellation request may still be in flight. If the old reminder is due during this interval, it can still be delivered after the booking has been rescheduled. Collect and await these promises before continuing.

title: One failed cancellation prevents processing every later reminder
body: The `try`/`catch` wraps the entire cancellation loop, so a single SendGrid error exits the loop and leaves all subsequent reminders in `remindersToCancel` untouched. Because the failed reminder remains marked cancelled, it can be retried on every cron run and repeatedly prevent later reminders from being cancelled; those scheduled emails may therefore still be sent. Handle failures per reminder so one bad batch does not block the rest.

title: Reminder cancellation is not awaited before the reschedule request completes
body: These calls start asynchronous database updates or provider cancellations, but the `forEach` callback does not await them. The mutation can therefore return before the old booking's reminders have been marked cancelled or cancelled with SendGrid/Twilio; in a serverless runtime the work may be cut off when the request finishes, leaving reminders scheduled for a booking that has been rescheduled. Await the cancellation promises before completing the mutation.

title: Recurring cancellation does not wait for calendar deletions
body: This async callback is passed to `forEach`, which does not await it. Because `getCalendar` now yields before the deletion promises are added to `apiDeletes`, execution can reach the later `Promise.all(apiDeletes)` and finish cleanup before these deletions are even scheduled.
