The handler can delete booking references while leaving recurring events on users' calendars; deletion errors can also become unhandled rejections. Collect and await these callback promises (or use a sequential loop) before continuing.

title: All app imports start eagerly when the store is loaded
body: Each `import()` is evaluated while this object is initialized, so importing the app store immediately starts loading every app package, even when a request needs only one integration. This retains the startup/module-loading cost the async-import change is intended to avoid and can load heavyweight apps unnecessarily. Defer each import until its app is requested, for example by storing import functions rather than their already-started promises.

title: All app imports start eagerly at module initialization
body: Each `import()` is executed while constructing `appStore`, so importing this module immediately starts loading every app package rather than loading a package only when its entry is accessed. This defeats the intended on-demand loading and can retain the startup cost and memory use of loading all app modules.

title: Recurring cancellation does not wait for calendar deletions
body: The async callbacks passed to `forEach` are not awaited. With the new async `getCalendar`, each callback pauses before scheduling its deletes, while execution proceeds to `Promise.all(apiDeletes)` before those callbacks push anything into the array. The cancellation can therefore finish and report success without deleting any recurring booking events from calendars.

title: Reschedule returns before integration cancellations complete
body: The async callbacks passed to `forEach` are not awaited. They now suspend while `getCalendar` loads the app, but the handler proceeds to send the reschedule email and return without waiting for calendar or video cancellation. The old booking can remain on external calendars or video services after a successful reschedule.

title: Reschedule returns before integration cancellations complete
body: The async callbacks passed to `forEach` are not awaited. They now suspend while `getCalendar` loads the app, but this function proceeds to send the reschedule email and return without waiting for calendar or video cancellation. The old booking can remain on external calendars or video services after a successful reschedule.

title: Reschedule returns before integration cancellations complete
body: The async callbacks passed to `forEach` are not awaited. They now suspend while `getCalendar` loads the app, but this function proceeds to send the reschedule email and return without waiting for calendar or video cancellation. The old booking can remain on external calendars or video services after a successful reschedule.

title: Recurring-event calendar deletions are not awaited
body: The async callback awaits `getCalendar` before adding deletion promises to `apiDeletes`, but `forEach` does not wait for its callbacks. Execution can reach the later `Promise.all(apiDeletes)` while the array is still empty, so cancellation returns without deleting the recurring bookings from calendars; the deletions may also continue after the request has completed.

title: All app imports are started eagerly
body: Each `import()` is evaluated as soon as this module loads, so importing the app store starts loading every app package rather than loading only the app needed by a request. This retains the startup work and dependency-loading cost the async-import change appears intended to avoid, and can increase memory and cold-start time.

title: Date overrides bypass busy-time checks
body: When a slot falls within a date override, this returns `true` immediately, before checking `busy`. Date overrides add availability; they must not make an already-booked slot or a slot conflicting with a connected calendar event bookable. Fixed-host and round-robin availability can therefore include slots that the host is busy for.

title: Working-hours check ignores the slot end time
body: `end` is calculated from the slot start rather than from `slotEndTime`. Consequently, a slot that starts before a working-hours boundary but whose event duration extends past it passes this check. When slots generated from another host's availability are evaluated for a fixed host, this can allow bookings that extend beyond that host's working hours.

title: Zero-length overrides are never recognized
body: This compares two Dayjs objects with `===`, which only checks object identity and is always false for these separately created instances. Consequently, a zero-length date override falls through to `dateOverrideExist` and returns `true`, making every generated slot on that override date available instead of applying the intended empty interval.

title: Per-host working-hours check ignores the event end time
body: `end` is computed from the slot start just like `start`, so the `end > workingHour.endTime` condition can never detect a booking that extends past a host's working-hours boundary. In round-robin events this can leave a slot available even when the assigned host cannot accommodate the full event.

title: Date overrides bypass booking and calendar busy checks
body: When a slot falls within a date override, this returns `true` before checking `busy` or `currentSeats`. Date overrides should change availability hours, not make an already-booked or calendar-busy host available. In round-robin events this can expose slots that conflict with the fixed host’s existing commitments, allowing double bookings.

title: Migration crashes when no embed category is configured
body: This query returns no rows when `embed_category` is unset, which is a normal configuration; indexing `[0]['id']` then raises before the migration can apply. The fallback to the uncategorized category is never reached, so upgrades on affected sites are blocked. Handle the missing match before reading the result.

title: Untrusted host setting is interpolated into migration SQL
body: The legacy `embeddable_hosts` setting is interpolated directly into an SQL statement. A stored host containing a quote can break the migration, and crafted setting content can alter the SQL being executed during deployment. Use a bound parameter or properly quote each value.

title: Valid hostnames with longer top-level domains are rejected
body: The validation limits the final hostname label to 2–5 letters, so valid domains such as `example.museum` and `example.technology` cannot be added. Since host registration is required for embedding, sites using these domains cannot configure them.

title: Updating a nonexistent host raises instead of returning a not-found response
body: When the requested ID does not exist, `first` returns nil and `save_host` immediately assigns fields to that nil object. A stale admin page or invalid ID therefore produces a server error instead of a handled not-found response. The destroy action has the same nil dereference pattern.

title: Migration crashes when no embed category was explicitly configured
body: This query can return no rows when `embed_category` has no persisted site-setting value or its value does not match a category. Indexing `[0]['id']` then raises, aborting the migration and preventing upgrades on those installations. Handle the missing result and use the uncategorized category as the fallback before reading the ID.

title: Migration fails when no embed category is configured
body: This query can return no rows when `embed_category` is blank or does not match a category, which is a normal state for installations that have not configured a category. Indexing `[0]['id']` then raises before the migration reaches its fallback to the uncategorized category, preventing the upgrade from completing. Handle the empty result before reading the ID.

title: Allowed hosts configured with a port never match
body: The host validator accepts entries with ports, but `record_for_host` compares the stored value against `uri.host`, which omits the port. A configured entry such as `example.com:8080` therefore cannot authorize a referer on that port, so embedding is rejected despite the host being accepted and saved. Compare the relevant port as well, or reject ports during validation.

title: The client-side upload limit ignores configured size settings
body: This hard-codes every upload type to 10 MB instead of using the configured per-type limit. Sites that allow attachments larger than 10 MB will now reject them in the browser before the server can accept them; the same applies to images when the configured limit is higher. Keep the client limit aligned with the applicable setting, or make this a deliberate independent limit that is configurable.

title: Oversized animated GIFs can be flattened during upload
body: This passes `allow_animated_thumbnails` as the switch for the GIF downsize implementation. When that setting is false, `OptimizedImage.downsize_instructions` uses ImageMagick with `#{from}[0]`, which processes only the first frame; the resulting file replaces the uploaded source, permanently discarding the GIF animation. The thumbnail setting should not determine whether the original upload's animation is preserved.

title: Animated GIFs cannot be downsized with the percentage argument
body: This call passes `"80%"` to `OptimizedImage.downsize`. When animated thumbnails are enabled, the GIF-specific path uses `gifsicle --resize-fit` with that value, but `--resize-fit` expects pixel dimensions such as `800x600`, not a percentage. Gifsicle therefore fails, the source remains oversized, and the upload is rejected after the retry loop instead of being automatically downsized.

title: The client now rejects uploads over 10 MB regardless of configured limits
body: This replaces the per-type configured limit with a fixed 10 MB limit for every upload. Sites that permit attachments or images larger than 10 MB will have those uploads rejected in the browser even though the server accepts them, so the client and server no longer honor the configured upload-size contract.

title: Large GIF uploads can lose animation during downsizing
body: When a GIF exceeds the configured size, this call preserves animation only when `allow_animated_thumbnails` is enabled. Otherwise the non-animated conversion path processes the first frame, so the saved upload can silently become a static image. Thumbnail animation policy should not determine whether the uploaded original retains its animation.

title: Unsubscribe fails when the user has no TopicUser row
body: `TopicUser.find_by` can return nil for a user who has never visited or changed notification settings for this topic, but the action immediately dereferences `tu.notification_level`. In that common case, following the email link raises an exception instead of unsubscribing. Handle the missing row by creating it with the muted notification level (or use the existing TopicUser change helper).

title: The unsubscribe action can leave the user subscribed
body: When the current level is tracking or watching, this branch changes it only to regular; regular users still receive topic notifications. Since the page and email link promise to stop notifications, following the unsubscribe link must leave the user muted regardless of their starting level.

title: A GET request mutates notification settings
body: This action changes the user's notification level as part of a GET request. Email security scanners and link-preview bots commonly follow links automatically, so merely receiving or scanning an email can unsubscribe the recipient. Render a confirmation page on GET and perform the state change only after an explicit non-GET confirmation.

title: Unsubscribing from a watching topic still leaves notifications enabled
body: When the current notification level is `watching` or `tracking`, this branch changes it to `regular`, which is not muted and continues sending ordinary topic notifications. The page and email promise to stop notifications, but the user remains subscribed; the unsubscribe action should move the topic to a level that actually suppresses those notifications.

title: The email unsubscribe link mutates state on GET
body: This action is reached through a GET link in notification emails and changes the user's topic notification level. Email security scanners commonly follow links automatically, so merely scanning an email can unsubscribe its recipient without their intent. Use a confirmation step or a state-changing request that is only submitted after explicit user action.

title: Unsubscribe does not mute users who are watching or tracking
body: This branch changes every notification level above `regular` to `regular`, but both `tracking` and `watching` are above `regular` and still receive topic notifications. Consequently, following the email unsubscribe link does not stop notifications for users with either of those settings, despite the page promising that it will. Set the level to `muted` for the unsubscribe action rather than stepping down one level.

title: The topic post-number route can capture unsubscribe URLs
body: The `/t/:slug/:id` topic resource above defines a nested `fromParamsNear` route at `/:nearPost`, which has the same URL shape as `/t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe`. Because the topic resource is declared first, the client can recognize an unsubscribe link as a topic route with `nearPost` equal to `unsubscribe` instead of entering `topicUnsubscribe`. The email link then fails to show the unsubscribe screen; ensure the unsubscribe route takes precedence over the catch-all post-number route.

title: Blocked-email lookups are case-sensitive
body: The lookup uses the submitted email verbatim, while email addresses are treated case-insensitively elsewhere in the application (for example, `change_email` lowercases them). A blocked address stored as `user@example.com` can therefore be used to register as `User@Example.com`, bypassing the block. Normalize the lookup and stored addresses consistently before comparing.

title: Concurrent matches lose statistics increments
body: This read-modify-save sequence is not atomic: simultaneous matches can both read the same `match_count` and save the same increment, losing one or more matches. Since the method is called during validation on signup, match statistics become unreliable under concurrent requests. Use an atomic database increment and update the timestamp.

title: Rejected-email list is shared between controller instances
body: `rejectedEmails` is a mutable array defined on the controller extension object, so controller instances can share it rather than each getting a fresh list. After one signup attempt rejects an address, a later account-creation modal can incorrectly mark that address invalid without contacting the server. Initialize the array per controller instance.

title: Rejected-email state is shared across controller instances
body: `rejectedEmails` is initialized on the controller definition, so its mutable array can be shared by every `CreateAccountController` instance. If one signup attempt receives an email validation error, that address may remain rejected when another user opens the signup modal, preventing that user from registering with the same address. Initialize the array per controller instance instead.

title: Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive
body: This query compares the submitted email exactly with the stored value. Email addresses with different casing, such as `Blocked@Example.com` versus `blocked@example.com`, therefore do not match on a case-sensitive database, allowing a user to bypass a block by changing capitalization. Normalize both stored and incoming addresses consistently before lookup (and when creating block records).

title: Concurrent matches can lose match-count increments
body: The method reads `match_count`, increments it in Ruby, and saves the whole record. Two concurrent validations can read the same count and both save the same incremented value, undercounting matches. Use an atomic database increment and update the timestamp atomically so the statistics remain accurate under concurrent signup attempts.

title: Rejected-email state is shared between controller instances
body: `rejectedEmails` is a mutable array created on the controller definition, so Ember can share it across `CreateAccountController` instances rather than giving each signup modal its own list. An email rejected in one signup attempt can then remain invalid in a later attempt or another user's modal in the same page session, even if the server-side reason no longer applies. Initialize this array per controller instance.

title: Concurrent matches can lose blocked-email statistics
body: This increments `match_count` by reading the current value and later saving the whole record. Concurrent signup validations for the same blocked address can both read the same count and overwrite one another, so `match_count` under-reports matches. Use an atomic database increment (and update the timestamp atomically) to preserve the statistics.

title: Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive
body: The lookup receives the submitted email unchanged, while email addresses are commonly entered with differing letter case and the blocklist's unique index also treats differently cased strings as distinct. A blocked address can therefore bypass this check simply by changing its capitalization. Normalize the address consistently when storing and looking up blocked emails.

title: Imported HTML bypasses post sanitization
body: This creates imported posts with `raw_html`, and `Post#cook` returns their raw content without passing it through the normal rendering/sanitization pipeline. Feed entries are remote, untrusted HTML, and the embed template renders `post.cooked` as raw HTML, so a malicious feed item can execute persistent JavaScript in visitors' browsers. Sanitize imported content before storing or rendering it.

title: Referer is interpolated into executable JavaScript
body: The request Referer is attacker-controlled and is inserted unescaped inside a JavaScript string. A Referer with the configured host but a crafted path can break out of the string and inject script into the forum's origin whenever the embed page is loaded. Pass a validated, serialized origin (not the full Referer) to `postMessage`.

title: Imported HTML bypasses post sanitization
body: This creates imported posts with `cook_method: raw_html`, and `Post#cook` returns their raw content without passing it through the normal rendering and sanitization pipeline. Feed item content is inserted directly into that raw content at line 13, so an RSS/Atom feed containing executable markup can create stored XSS that runs for forum visitors viewing the imported topic or embed. Sanitize the imported HTML before storing it or render it through the normal safe pipeline.

title: Resize postMessage uses a full referer as its target origin
body: `request.referer` is a full URL and commonly includes a path, but `postMessage`'s `targetOrigin` must be an origin (scheme, host, and optional port), not a URL with a path or query. The browser rejects this call with a `SyntaxError`, so the embed never sends its height and the parent iframe remains at its default height. Pass the referer's parsed origin instead.

title: Referer is interpolated into executable JavaScript without escaping
body: The request's Referer is attacker-controlled input and is inserted directly into a single-quoted JavaScript string. A crafted referer that passes the host check can break out of the string and inject script into the embed response, causing stored or reflected script execution in the forum origin for visitors loading the embed. Serialize the value with a JavaScript-safe encoder, and preferably use a parsed origin.

title: Imported feed HTML bypasses sanitization and is rendered as trusted HTML
body: This marks imported post content as `raw_html`, causing `Post#cook` to return the raw value without the normal rendering and sanitization pipeline. Feed content is only HTML-unescaped before reaching this call, and the embed view later inserts `post.cooked` as raw HTML. A feed entry containing script-capable markup can therefore execute JavaScript in the Discourse origin whenever the embed is viewed, potentially compromising forum users. Sanitize imported content before storing it or do not bypass the normal safe rendering pipeline.

title: Feed entries without `content` abort the entire polling job
body: Many valid RSS/Atom entries provide their body as `description` or omit a body entirely, leaving `i.content` nil. Calling `scrub` on nil raises, so the job stops at that entry and never imports later entries in the feed. Handle missing content (and use the appropriate description field where available) so one incomplete item does not prevent the rest of the feed from being processed.

title: The action button no longer stays at the right edge
body: Making `.small-action` a flex container turns its direct children, including the `button`, into flex items; `float: right` on the button no longer positions it at the right edge. The description also no longer has the old block-width padding that filled the available space, so the button can sit immediately after the description and leave unused space to its right. This regresses the small-action layout; give the button an explicit flex alignment such as `margin-left: auto` or otherwise preserve the right alignment.

title: The dismiss button no longer stays at the right edge
body: Making `.small-action` a flex container means the `float: right` on its `button` child is ignored. The button now sits immediately after the description instead of being pushed to the right edge, changing the small-action layout. Use a flex-compatible alignment rule, such as `margin-left: auto`, for the button.

title: Website name bypasses the TL0 anonymous-field restriction
body: `website` is explicitly treated as an untrusted attribute and omitted for anonymous viewers of TL0 users, but the newly serialized `website_name` is not. Since `website_name` is derived from that same profile URL, anonymous requests can still reveal the website host (and, for matching domains, its path) through the profile display name even when the URL itself is hidden. Add `website_name` to the untrusted attributes so it follows the same visibility policy.

title: Website details bypass the untrusted-user restriction
body: `website_name` is serialized as a public attribute but is not included in `untrusted_attributes`. For a TL0 user viewed anonymously, the serializer can therefore expose the website host and path through `website_name` even when it omits the protected `website` field. This leaks profile information despite the existing restriction; apply the same inclusion restriction to `website_name` and cover it in the anonymous-user spec.

title: Website name bypasses the untrusted-user-field restriction
body: `website_name` is added to the serialized attributes but is not included in `untrusted_attributes`. For an anonymous viewer of a TL0 user, the serializer therefore hides `website` while still calling `website_name`, which derives and returns the website host (and sometimes its path). This leaks a value from a field the serializer explicitly restricts; add `website_name` to the same restriction and cover it in the anonymous-TL0 spec.

title: Exact page-size multiples show a phantom page
body: `floor(user_count / limit) + 1` counts an extra page whenever the member count is an exact multiple of the page size. For example, a group with 50 members displays `1/2`; the next action then requests offset 50 and shows an empty page. Compute the ceiling of the page count (while preserving the zero-member case) so pagination does not expose an unusable page.

title: Exact page-size multiples show a phantom page
body: `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` reports one extra page whenever the member count is an exact multiple of the page size (for example, 50 members at a limit of 50 reports 2 pages). The UI then displays a nonexistent last page and allows navigation to an empty page. Compute the page count with ceiling division instead.

title: Member offset can remain past the last valid page
body: Clamping the offset to `user_count` still permits an offset that returns no members. For example, if a group has 51 members and its second page starts at offset 50, removing the sole member on that page leaves 50 members; the reload clamps to offset 50 and shows an empty page instead of returning to the first page. Clamp to the largest valid page-start offset (or reset the offset when it is no longer valid) before requesting members.

title: Exact page-size counts show a phantom page
body: `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` counts an extra page whenever the member count is an exact multiple of the page size. For example, with 50 members and a limit of 50, the UI reports 2 pages; Next then requests offset 50 and displays an empty page. Compute the page count with ceiling division so pagination ends on the actual last page.

title: Fallback translations can remain stale after changing the site locale
body: The fallback chain depends on `SiteSetting.default_locale`, but the translation cache in `translate_accelerator.rb` is keyed only by the requested locale and backend. If an administrator changes the default locale while the process is running, lookups already cached for a user locale continue returning translations resolved through the old default locale until those entries are evicted or the cache is reset. Include the fallback configuration in cache invalidation or otherwise clear affected entries when the setting changes.

title: Fallback locales are loaded only for controller requests
body: This is the only call site that loads the locales in the fallback chain. The translation accelerator loads only the active locale when `I18n.t` is called, while the fallback backend expects fallback locale translations to already be present. Translations invoked outside this controller filter—such as in background jobs, mailers, or other non-request code—therefore cannot fall back to the site default or English and may return missing translations. Ensure the fallback locales are loaded wherever translations can be performed, not only in this request filter.

title: Changing the site locale can leave fallback translations stale
body: The fallback chain depends on `SiteSetting.default_locale`, but the translation cache in `translate_accelerator.rb` is keyed only by translation key, current locale, and backend. If the site default locale changes while the process is running, lookups that previously fell back to the old site locale continue returning the cached result instead of using the new fallback chain. Include the fallback configuration in the cache key or clear the translation cache when the setting changes.

title: Denial cache key omits identity type
body: The denial key is built from namespace, `UserUID`, action, name, and parent folder, but not `IdentityType`. Anonymous and render identities can both use UID `0`, so a cached denial for an anonymous check can be reused for a render check of the same resource. Since render checks are otherwise granted read access, this incorrectly denies rendering until the denial entry expires. Include the identity type in the key.

title: Denial cache key collides across resource and folder boundaries
body: The denial key concatenates user, action, resource name, and parent folder with underscores but does not encode or escape component boundaries. Distinct checks can therefore produce the same key (for example, name `a_b`, parent `c` versus name `a`, parent `b_c`). Once one check is denied, the other is denied without consulting current permissions. Use an unambiguous encoding or structured hash for the key so unrelated authorization decisions cannot share a denial entry.

title: Denial cache omits identity type
body: The denial cache key uses `UserUID` but not `IdentityType`. User and service-account subjects can have the same UID while resolving to different permission sets, and anonymous/render identities can also reach this check with their own identifiers. A denial produced for one identity type will then immediately deny another identity type with the same UID, bypassing its permission evaluation. Include the identity type in the denial-cache key.

title: Denial cache omits namespace identity dimensions
body: The cache key uses the namespace string, but authorization scope can distinguish namespaces that share a value across different tenant/stack contexts if that value is not globally unique. A cached denial can consequently be reused in another authorization namespace. Key the denial by the complete parsed namespace identity (or a stable tenant identifier), consistent with the other authorization caches.

title: Permission lookup errors in the cache path are silently discarded
body: When `getCachedIdentityPermissions` returns an error other than a cache miss (for example, a database failure resolving user identifiers), this branch treats it like a miss and continues to `getIdentityPermissions`. That second lookup can mask the original failure or duplicate expensive work; if the repeated lookup succeeds inconsistently, the request proceeds despite the failed cache-path identity resolution. Only fall back on `cache.ErrNotFound`; return other errors as the previous direct lookup path did.

title: Denial cache keys collide when resource fields contain underscores
body: The key concatenates namespace, user, action, resource name, and parent folder with underscores but does not encode or delimit the fields unambiguously. For example, `(name="a_b", parent="c")` and `(name="a", parent="b_c")` produce the same key. A cached denial for one check can therefore deny a different resource check for the same user/action for up to the cache TTL. Use an unambiguous encoding or include lengths/separators that cannot occur in values.

title: Denial cache is shared across identity types
body: The denial key uses `checkReq.UserUID` but not `checkReq.IdentityType`. Different identity types can have the same UID (for example, a user and service account), while their permissions are resolved differently. A denial cached for one identity can therefore incorrectly deny another identity with the same UID, namespace, action, name, and folder. Include the identity type in the key.

title: Cached denials survive permission grants until expiry
body: A denial is cached for the full short-cache TTL, and the denial-cache lookup returns before checking current permissions. If a resource is granted to the user after a denial is cached, the user continues to be denied for up to 30 seconds even though permissions were updated. This undermines the stated goal of making newly created resources accessible and can also delay legitimate access grants; invalidate matching denial entries when permissions change or avoid caching denials where permission state can change.

title: Silence action is a no-op for Prometheus-backed Grafana rules
body: The new list items pass `promRule` without a `rulerRule`, so the menu can show Silence based on the Prometheus rule's abilities. Clicking it sets `showSilenceDrawer`, but this condition only renders the drawer when `rule` is a Grafana ruler alerting rule. In the new list view that condition is false, leaving the visible Silence action with no effect.

title: Delete action disappears when the list no longer loads ruler rules
body: The new Grafana list items provide `promRule` but no `rulerRule`. Although `canDelete` can now be determined from the Prometheus rule, this render guard still requires `rulerRule`, so Grafana rules in the list have no Delete menu item. The list-view refactor therefore removes a previously available action for users with delete permission.

title: Pause action disappears for Grafana rules in the new list view
body: The new list items provide no `rulerRule`, so this condition is false even when `canPause` is granted using `promRule`. Consequently, the list view no longer offers Pause/Resume for Grafana-managed alert rules, despite calculating the corresponding ability.

title: Grafana filtered results omit their React key
body: This branch renders `GrafanaRuleListItem` without the `key` computed for every result, unlike the datasource and unknown-rule branches. Filter results are rendered as siblings in a changing, paginated list; without stable keys React can reuse the wrong row component when results are appended or changed, and emits missing-key warnings.

title: Grafana rules cannot be deleted from the list view
body: The menu now derives delete permission from `promRule` when the list view has no `rulerRule`, but this item is still gated on `rulerRule` being present. `GrafanaRuleListItem` supplies only `promRule`, so even users with delete permission never see Delete for Grafana rules in the list view. Gate the item on an available rule identifier and pass that identifier to the delete handler instead.

title: Silence action does not open its drawer for list-view rules
body: The list view passes the rule as `promRule` and leaves `rule` undefined. Although `AlertRuleMenu` can now determine silence ability from the Prometheus DTO and invokes `handleSilence`, the drawer is rendered only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true. That condition is false for list-view rules, so clicking Silence closes the menu without opening the drawer. Render the drawer for Grafana alerting `promRule` too, using a compatible drawer input or an equivalent Prometheus-rule path.

title: Filtered Grafana items omit their React key
body: The filtered-results loop computes a unique `key` for every rule, but the Grafana branch does not pass it to `GrafanaRuleListItem`, unlike the other branches. React therefore sees unkeyed list children when filtered Grafana rules are rendered, which can reuse component state for the wrong rule as results change and produces missing-key warnings. Pass `key={key}` to this component.

title: Silence action is displayed but cannot open its drawer
body: This passes only `promRule` to `RuleActionsButtons`, so `rule` is undefined for rules rendered in the new list. The menu can still enable Silence using the Prometheus rule abilities, but `RuleActionsButtons` renders `SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer` only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true. Consequently, users can click the visible Silence notifications item and nothing happens.

title: Shard-split queries are interpolated again during execution
body: These targets are interpolated here before shard discovery and shard-selector rewriting, but each generated `subRequest` is later passed to `runSplitQuery` (line 163), which now also calls `applyTemplateVariables`. This applies template replacement twice to every shard-split query. Template values containing variable syntax or other replacement tokens can therefore be expanded a second time, changing the query sent to Loki from the value the user selected. Avoid re-interpolating already-prepared shard targets, or ensure the delegated path knows they are already interpolated.

title: Interpolation hides `$__range` from the splitting guard
body: This interpolates each expression before `querySupportsSplitting()` checks it with `isQueryWithRangeVariable()`. That check is explicitly meant to keep queries using `$__range` unsplit, because the variable must represent the full request range; after interpolation, the marker is gone, so the query is partitioned and executed with an expression containing the full-range value on each time chunk. This can produce incorrect results for range-dependent queries. Preserve the range-variable check against the original expression, or otherwise retain the non-splitting decision before interpolation.

title: Shard queries are interpolated again during execution
body: These targets are interpolated here before shard discovery, but each generated shard request is later passed to `runSplitQuery`, which also calls `applyTemplateVariables` on every target (querySplitting.ts:299). This means a value produced by interpolation can be interpreted as template syntax on the second pass, changing the query sent to Loki; for example, a variable value containing `$name` may be expanded again instead of being queried literally. Avoid applying template variables in both stages, or ensure the nested execution path knows the targets are already interpolated.

title: Completed-request logs lose the trace ID
body: This replaces the previous explicit `traceID` log parameter with a contextual logger, but `NewContextualLoggerMiddleware` only adds endpoint and plugin/user/datasource attributes; it does not add the trace ID. As a result, `Plugin Request Completed` entries are no longer correlated with their distributed trace, making requests harder to investigate. Preserve the trace ID in the log parameters or add it to the contextual attributes.

title: Request logs no longer include trace IDs
body: The previous `logRequest` implementation explicitly added `traceID` from the request context to `logParams` when one was available. Moving the plugin/request attributes into `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` does not preserve that field: `instrumentContext` adds endpoint, plugin, datasource, and user attributes, but no trace ID. As a result, completed plugin-request logs can no longer be correlated with their traces, even though the metrics middleware still records trace exemplars.

title: Failed device-limit checks are cached as successful tags
body: The cache entry is written before `CreateOrUpdateDevice` is attempted, but it is not removed when that call fails. When a device is rejected because the limit is reached, its next authentication attempt hits this cache entry and returns nil without checking the store. `Authenticate` then allows that anonymous session through, so the device limit can be bypassed by retrying.

title: Concurrent inserts can exceed the configured device limit
body: The device count and the subsequent insert/update are separate database operations with no lock or transaction protecting the limit. If multiple requests arrive while the count is below the limit, they can all observe the same count and insert distinct devices, exceeding the configured cap. Enforce the limit atomically with the insert or serialize these operations.

title: A rejected device is cached as successfully tagged
body: The cache entry is written before `CreateOrUpdateDevice` checks the device limit. If that check returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the entry remains cached; the next request from the same device returns nil at line 84 without checking the store, so anonymous authentication succeeds. This lets a device denied by the configured limit bypass the limit for the cache lifetime. Only cache the device after a successful store operation, or remove the entry on error.

title: The limit check and insert are not atomic
body: Concurrent requests can each count fewer than `deviceLimit` rows, then both insert distinct devices. Because the count and insert run in separate database sessions with no locking or constraint enforcing the cap, the active-device total can exceed the configured limit under load. Enforce the check and insert atomically (or serialize limit checks across instances).

title: Cache entries survive rejected device-limit writes
body: The device is added to the local cache before `CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs. When the database returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the cache entry remains; the next request for that device returns at the cache check without consulting the store, so `Authenticate` succeeds and the configured limit is bypassed for requests handled by this process. Only cache the device after a successful store write, or remove the entry on error.

title: Concurrent requests can exceed the configured limit
body: The device count and insert/update are separate operations with no transaction or locking. If the active count is one below the limit, concurrent requests can both observe that count and insert different devices, exceeding the configured limit. Enforce the check and insert atomically (including across Grafana instances), for example with a transaction and appropriate locking.

title: MySQL may report unchanged updates as limit failures
body: When the limit is reached, an existing device is updated and success is inferred from `RowsAffected()`. MySQL commonly reports zero affected rows when an UPDATE matches a row but all assigned values are unchanged; timestamps may also be stored only to second precision. Such a request is incorrectly returned as `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, rejecting a device that should remain allowed. Determine whether the row exists independently of changed-row count, or use a database setting/query strategy that reports matched rows.

title: Cleanup now runs ten times as often
body: Changing the ticker from 10 minutes to 1 minute causes every cleanup job to run up to ten times as often, although this PR only changes annotation cleanup. That increases recurring database and filesystem work in production and can create unnecessary load; preserve the existing interval unless the increased frequency is intentional and justified.

title: Building SQLite ID lists repeatedly copies the growing string
body: This loop uses `fmt.Sprintf` to append each ID to an immutable string, copying the entire accumulated list on every iteration. With the supported large SQLite batch sizes (the new test uses 32,767), this produces quadratic copying and can consume substantial CPU and memory during cleanup. Build the list with a `strings.Builder` or another linear-time approach.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors
body: This log call uses error severity for routine cleanup progress, and the same pattern is used for the other cleanup batches below. Every cleanup run can therefore emit error-level records even when no operation failed, including the selected IDs and query condition. This pollutes error monitoring and can generate large log volumes; use an appropriate non-error level and log IDs only when needed.

title: Cleanup jobs now run ten times more often
body: Changing the cleanup ticker from 10 minutes to 1 minute makes every cleanup job in this service run ten times as often, not just annotation cleanup. This can cause unnecessary database and filesystem load and increase contention for unrelated cleanup tasks; the interval change should be reverted or justified separately.

title: Large batches exceed SQL Server's parameter limit
body: For every non-SQLite database, this builds one placeholder per ID. SQL Server permits at most 2,100 parameters in a statement, so a configured cleanup batch size above that limit makes the delete fail (for example, the 32,767-sized batch used by the new test would fail on SQL Server). Handle the limit for supported dialects or chunk the IDs before executing the delete.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors
body: These messages use Error level even when fetching or deleting IDs succeeds, and they include every ID in the batch. Normal cleanup therefore emits error-level logs on each batch, potentially flooding error monitoring and producing very large log records for large configured batches. Log successful operations at an appropriate level and avoid logging the full ID list.

title: Cleanup interval is reduced from ten minutes to one
body: This changes the global cleanup scheduler from running every ten minutes to every minute, although the PR is addressing annotation cleanup. That makes every cleanup job—including snapshot, dashboard-version, image, invite, URL, and query-history cleanup—run up to ten times as often, increasing database and service load and potentially making cleanup work contend with normal traffic.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors
body: This `Error` log runs for every batch even when fetching IDs succeeded, and the analogous success-path logs below also use `Error`. Normal cleanup therefore produces error-level entries repeatedly, including the selected IDs, which misrepresents successful operation and can pollute alerts and error dashboards. Log successful batches at an appropriate lower level, reserving error logs for failures.

title: Async create can persist an unmodified request object to legacy storage
body: The unified store returns `created`, which may contain server-assigned fields such as the generated name, UID, and resource version, but the asynchronous legacy write receives the original `obj`. In particular, Kubernetes create requests using `generateName` may not have a concrete name in `obj`; the legacy write can therefore fail or create a different record instead of mirroring the successful unified write. Write the object returned by unified storage, or otherwise ensure the legacy write uses the exact persisted object.

title: Async update replays the request instead of the unified result
body: The legacy update receives the original `objInfo` after the unified update has completed, rather than an update wrapper containing the object returned by unified storage. The two stores can independently read different old versions and apply the request, so fields or metadata selected/assigned by unified storage can diverge in legacy storage; concurrent updates make this especially likely. Mirror the persisted unified result when writing legacy, as the previous implementation did.

title: Delete discards the per-request logger from its context
body: This constructs the operation context with `d.Log` instead of the `log` value that includes the object name, kind, and method. The asynchronous legacy delete inherits that context, so its logs lose the operation fields and cannot be reliably correlated with the request. Use `log` here, as the other operations do.

title: Delete success metric uses the object name as the kind label
body: On successful storage deletion, this call passes `name` where the other paths pass `options.Kind` to `recordStorageDuration`. The metric therefore labels successful deletes by object name instead of resource kind, creating high-cardinality labels and making delete metrics inconsistent (and potentially overwhelming the metrics backend). Pass `options.Kind`.

title: Delete-collection legacy duration is recorded as storage duration
body: The asynchronous legacy delete-collection result is recorded with `recordStorageDuration`, even though the operation ran against `d.Legacy`. This attributes legacy latency and errors to unified-storage metrics and leaves the legacy metric unreported. Record it with `recordLegacyDuration`.

title: Storage failures are recorded as legacy failures for create and update
body: When `Storage.Create` or `Storage.Update` fails, these branches call `recordLegacyDuration` even though no legacy operation was attempted. This misattributes unified-storage failures to the legacy backend and omits them from storage error metrics, undermining the metrics used to monitor migration health. Record the failure with `recordStorageDuration`.

title: Async create replays the original object instead of the unified result
body: The legacy write uses the original `obj`, not the object returned by `Storage.Create`. Storage commonly assigns server-generated metadata such as UID, resource version, timestamps, or a generated name to its returned object. In mode 3 those values are therefore absent from the asynchronously created legacy object, leaving the two stores inconsistent and potentially making later updates/deletes target different identities.

title: Async update does not apply the committed unified object to legacy
body: The mode-3 update forwards the caller's `objInfo` directly to legacy instead of ensuring legacy receives the result committed by `Storage.Update`. The unified storage may normalize the object or assign metadata, and `objInfo.UpdatedObject` may also be stateful or produce a different result on a second invocation. Consequently the legacy copy can diverge from the successful unified update, defeating the safety-copy purpose of this mode.

title: Delete loses the request logger in the context
body: This constructs the logging context with `d.Log` rather than the per-request `log` that includes the object name, kind, and method. The delete calls (including the asynchronous legacy delete) therefore lack those request-scoped fields, making failures difficult to correlate; it also drops any logger already attached to the incoming context.

title: Update storage failures are recorded as legacy failures
body: When `Storage.Update` returns an error, this records the duration through `recordLegacyDuration` even though no legacy operation ran. The storage failure is thus attributed to the legacy backend in dual-writer metrics, producing incorrect reliability and latency signals for operators.

title: Delete-collection legacy metrics are recorded as storage metrics
body: The asynchronous legacy delete-collection result is reported via `recordStorageDuration`. Failures and latency of the legacy operation are therefore counted against storage, while legacy metrics remain falsely successful or absent, obscuring the very fallback-write failures mode 3 is intended to monitor.

title: Delete duration metric uses the name as the kind label
body: On successful unified deletes this passes `name` to `recordStorageDuration` where the corresponding error path and other methods pass `options.Kind`. Per-object names will be emitted as the kind label, breaking metric consistency and potentially creating high-cardinality time series.

title: Storage update failures are recorded as legacy failures
body: This branch returns immediately when `Storage.Update` fails, but records the failure with `recordLegacyDuration` even though no legacy call was made. This misattributes unified-storage failures in dual-writer metrics, making operational monitoring of the new mode unreliable; record the storage duration instead.

title: Delete-collection legacy result is recorded as storage latency
body: The goroutine measures the legacy delete-collection call, but records it with `recordStorageDuration`. Legacy failures and latency are therefore reported as storage metrics, while legacy metrics omit them. Use the legacy duration recorder here.

title: Delete success metric uses the object name as the kind
body: On successful deletes, this passes `name` where the other paths pass `options.Kind`. The delete duration metric is consequently labeled with each object's name rather than its resource kind, producing incorrect labels and potentially unbounded metric cardinality. Pass the kind instead.

title: Async legacy writes replay the original update input after storage has committed
body: The goroutine calls `Legacy.Update` with the original `objInfo` after `Storage.Update` has already executed it. If `objInfo.UpdatedObject` is stateful or derives its result from the old object/resource version, this second invocation may produce a different update or fail; even ordinary concurrent updates can make the legacy write apply stale data. The previous implementation wrapped the already-computed unified object for legacy. Capture and replicate the committed object (and equivalent create/delete state) rather than re-executing a request against potentially changed state.

title: Background legacy writes can outlive shutdown
body: Each write launches an untracked goroutine, and `Destroy` immediately destroys both backends without waiting for in-flight legacy writes. A request can return, shutdown can close the legacy storage, and the goroutine can then fail or race against teardown, leaving the safety-copy write unapplied. Track and drain outstanding writes before destroying the legacy backend, or otherwise provide a lifecycle-safe worker.

title: Recheck the cache after acquiring the write lock
body: When concurrent non-development calls all observe an empty cache, each waits for this lock and then performs the full manifest load because the cache is not checked again after locking. This serializes redundant file/network work and can overwrite a value another caller has just populated. Recheck `entryPointAssetsCache` under the lock and return it for non-development calls before loading.

title: Recheck the cache after acquiring the write lock
body: Concurrent callers can all observe a nil cache at lines 41–43, then queue on this lock. After the first caller loads and stores the assets, every queued caller still proceeds to read the manifest because the cache is not checked again under the lock. This causes redundant serialized file or CDN reads during startup; recheck the cache after acquiring the lock for non-development environments.

title: Add regression coverage for rejecting SQL expressions
body: This change is the primary guard that rejects SQL expressions during query parsing, but no tests are added to verify that SQL queries are rejected with the feature flag both enabled and disabled, or that other expression types still parse. Without automated coverage, a later change could accidentally restore SQL expression handling and reintroduce the vulnerability without failing CI.

title: Concurrent builds can race for the same index key
body: The cache lock now protects only the final map assignment, so two callers that both observe a missing index can run `BuildIndex` for the same key concurrently. For file-backed indexes, both builds open the same Bleve directory and can fail or corrupt the build; for memory indexes, one completed index overwrites the other in the cache, leaving callers using an index that future lookups will not return. Add per-key build coordination or otherwise prevent duplicate builds.

title: Parallel startup builds race on the shared error variable
body: Each `errgroup` worker assigns to the same outer `err` while builds run concurrently. This is a data race, and the value returned by a worker can be overwritten by another worker, making initialization failures unreliable. Keep each worker's build error local and return it directly; also use an atomic or synchronized counter for `totalBatchesIndexed` at line 189.

title: Concurrent builds can replace or conflict on the same index
body: Removing the build-wide lock allows two callers building the same namespaced resource to create indexes concurrently. `getOrCreateIndex` can be reached concurrently before either build is cached; for file-backed indexes both builds target the same Bleve directory, while for memory indexes the later assignment replaces the earlier index. Callers may then write to an index that is no longer the cached one, so updates can be lost or the build can fail.

title: Concurrent builds of the same key can overwrite or fail
body: Removing the lock around the whole build allows two callers to miss `GetIndex` for the same key and both reach this cache insertion. For file-backed indexes they also call `bleve.New` on the same directory, which can fail or conflict; for in-memory indexes the later insertion replaces the earlier index, potentially discarding writes made to the other instance. Serialize builds per key (while allowing different keys to build concurrently).

title: Cache writes can race with `TotalDocs` map iteration
body: This change makes index construction and cache insertion concurrent, but `TotalDocs` iterates `b.cache` without taking `cacheMu`. A concurrent call to `TotalDocs` while a build inserts an index can cause a Go map read/write race or fatal concurrent-map iteration/write. Protect the iteration with the same mutex.

title: Initialization failure leaves the server context running
body: `NewResourceServer` now runs initialization before returning. If a lifecycle hook, index build, or watcher setup fails, this returns without calling `cancel`; initialization may already have started backend resources or background goroutines, which then remain running with no server instance available to stop them. Cancel the context and clean up initialized lifecycle resources on this error path.

title: Call to passkey helper does not compile
body: `UsernameForm` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` without arguments, but the inherited method in `UsernamePasswordForm` requires a `UserModel` argument. This prevents the services module from compiling, so the PR cannot be built or merged until the call supplies the user (or a no-argument overload is added).

title: Call to `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` does not compile
body: `UsernameForm` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments, but the method available in its superclass, `UsernamePasswordForm`, requires a `UserModel` argument, and no no-argument overload is defined in the shown class hierarchy. This causes compilation to fail; pass the context user or add the intended overload.

title: Conditional passkey UI is omitted before a user is identified
body: This condition only initializes WebAuthn form data when `context.getUser()` is non-null. On the initial login page the user is normally not identified yet, so the conditional passkey UI is never configured and passwordless/discoverable passkey login cannot start from that page. The previous code initialized WebAuthn data whenever passkeys were enabled, including for an unidentified user.

title: Call to a nonexistent overload prevents compilation
body: `UsernameForm` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments, but its superclass only declares `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel)`, and neither `UsernameForm` nor its other ancestors declare a no-argument version. This leaves the changed source uncompilable, so the PR cannot build.

title: Conditional passkeys are disabled on the initial login form
body: This predicate requires `context.getUser()` to be non-null, but the user is normally unidentified when the initial username/password form is rendered. As a result, `fillContextForm` is skipped on that form and the browser never receives the conditional WebAuthn challenge needed for passkey login. This also contradicts the added tests that expect passkeys on the initial login page.

title: Cleanup targets the literal alias instead of the created provider
body: Each created identity provider is registered for cleanup using `identityProviders().get("alias")`, but the providers created in this loop have aliases `idp-alias-0` through `idp-alias-19`. The cleanup callback therefore removes a provider named `alias` rather than the providers created by the test; the same mistake occurs for the provider added at line 425. These providers remain in the test realm after the test and can pollute later tests or make suite results order-dependent. Register cleanup using each provider's actual alias.

title: Cleanup targets the literal alias instead of each created provider
body: The loop creates providers with aliases `idp-alias-0` through `idp-alias-19`, but registers cleanup for `get("alias")` every time. That removes none of the created providers, leaving test data in the shared test realm and potentially affecting later tests. Register cleanup using the loop's `alias`; the same mistake also appears for the extra provider at line 425.

title: Adding `order()` as an abstract method breaks existing provider implementations
body: `CryptoProvider` is a public SPI, and adding this abstract method means every third-party implementation compiled against the previous interface must be updated and recompiled; old implementations can also fail at runtime when this method is invoked. Give the method a default implementation (or otherwise preserve compatibility) so existing providers remain usable.

title: JWT client credentials fail when this provider is selected
body: This provider is discovered and can become the global `CryptoIntegration` provider when the authz client runs without another provider. Its `getSignature` implementation always throws, so code paths that sign JWT client assertions—for example, JWT-based client authentication—fail with `UnsupportedOperationException` instead of producing a token. Implement the crypto operations required by supported authz-client credential flows, or avoid selecting this partial provider for those flows.

title: Adding an abstract method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: `order()` is a new abstract SPI method, so any provider implementation compiled against the previous interface must add this method before it can compile against this version. This is a source- and binary-compatibility break for third-party crypto providers; make it a default method (or otherwise preserve compatibility) if existing providers are expected to keep working.

title: Sequence parsing does not enforce the declared sequence boundary
body: The loop subtracts each child's full encoded length but never checks whether that length exceeds the remaining sequence length. A child that extends past the declared sequence boundary is therefore accepted, and parsing continues over bytes outside the sequence. Since this decoder handles ECDSA signature encodings, malformed input can be interpreted as a valid pair of integers instead of being rejected. Reject a child whose encoded length exceeds the remaining sequence bytes and verify the sequence is fully consumed.

title: Adding an abstract SPI method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: `CryptoProvider` is a public extension interface, and making `order()` abstract means implementations compiled against the previous API do not implement the new method. Such providers can fail with `AbstractMethodError` when provider discovery calls `order()`, while source implementations no longer compile. Give the method a default value to preserve compatibility, or otherwise account for existing third-party providers.

title: Providers with equal order are selected according to discovery order
body: The built-in Default, Elytron, and FIPS providers all return order `200`, but this comparator provides no tie-breaker. `ServiceLoader` discovery order depends on classpath/service-file ordering, so when more than one of these providers is present the selected implementation can change with packaging or runtime classpath order. Since the selected provider determines cryptographic and FIPS behavior, equal-priority providers need a deterministic resolution or ambiguity must remain an error.

title: Existing realms never receive the new Clients schema
body: Adding `Clients` here only affects initialization of a new admin-permissions resource server. `init()` returns immediately when the realm already has an admin-permissions client, so realms that enabled FGAP V2 before this change will not get the Clients resource or its scopes. Client permissions then cannot be created or evaluated in those realms, leaving this feature unavailable unless the admin-permissions schema is migrated for existing clients.

title: Per-client resources bypass all-clients permissions
body: When a client-specific resource already exists, this evaluates only that resource and never checks the `Clients` resource used for all-clients grants. Such resources can be created by a permission for any scope on that client; afterward, an administrator granted `manage`, `view`, or another scope on all clients can be denied access to that client. Evaluate the all-clients resource as an additional fallback even when the client-specific resource exists.

title: Per-client resources suppress all-clients grants
body: When a client-specific resource exists, permission evaluation uses only that resource and never evaluates the `Clients` type resource. A client-specific resource is created as soon as any permission references that client, so an all-clients grant (for example `manage` or `view`) then stops applying to that client. This makes authorization depend on whether an unrelated per-client permission was created and can deny intended grants across the realm; evaluate both the specific resource and the all-clients resource, or otherwise combine their grants.

title: Default-strategy cases do not enable the required feature
body: When `updateStrategy` is null, this method returns the Keycloak CR before adding `rolling-updates` to its enabled features. The updated operator documentation says the operator fails unless this preview feature is enabled, so the parameterized default-strategy tests exercise an invalid deployment and may fail before reaching their upgrade assertions. Enable the feature for these cases too, or explicitly adapt the tests if the default strategy is intended to work without it.

title: View permission grants global group management
body: This method treats either `view` or `manage` on the all-groups resource as `canManage()`. Callers use the no-argument check to authorize operations such as creating a top-level group (`requireManage()`), so an administrator granted only view access to all groups can perform management operations. Require the `manage` scope here; view-only access must not satisfy management checks.

title: Group view filtering returns authorization resource IDs instead of group IDs
body: `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` adds `groupResource.getId()`, which is the authorization resource's internal ID, to the set used by user searches to filter users by their group IDs. The group resource's name is the actual group ID. Consequently users who should be visible through a group's `view-members` or `manage-members` permission are omitted from group-restricted user searches (and user counts); add the resource name/group ID instead.

title: View permission grants global group management
body: `canManage()` accepts either `view` or `manage` on the all-groups resource. This method backs `requireManage()` for operations such as creating top-level groups, so an administrator granted only view access to all groups can perform global management operations. Require the `manage` scope here.

title: Group resource IDs are used as membership group IDs
body: `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` adds the authorization resource's internal ID, but callers pass this set to user search as group membership IDs. Authorization resource IDs are not the corresponding `GroupModel` IDs, so users granted member-view access through these groups are omitted from filtered user searches and counts. Add the resource name (which represents the group ID) instead, and evaluate the permission against that group ID.

title: Group view permission grants realm-wide management
body: `canManage()` evaluates the all-groups resource with both `VIEW` and `MANAGE` as acceptable scopes. Consequently, an administrator granted only `VIEW` on all groups is treated as having global manage permission; `canManage(GroupModel)` calls this method first and then allows updates, child creation, and other management operations on every group. Only the `MANAGE` scope should satisfy this check.

title: Group view filtering collects authorization resource IDs instead of group IDs
body: `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` iterates group resources but passes each authorization resource's internal ID to `hasPermission()` and adds that ID to the returned set. `hasPermission()` looks up resources by name, while group resources are named with the actual group ID, and user searches apply this returned set as group IDs. Thus per-group member-view grants do not correctly constrain user searches/counts: the actual group members can be omitted, and the returned authorization IDs are not valid group IDs. Use the resource name (the group ID) for evaluation and collection, and handle the all-groups resource separately.

title: Unescaping sanitized output can hide forbidden tags
body: The sanitizer escapes disallowed markup as HTML entities, but this unescapes every entity in the sanitized result before comparing it with the original. For example, a forbidden tag such as `` can be escaped by the policy and then restored to the original text, making the comparison report no violation. This lets unsafe translated HTML pass the verifier, defeating the security check.

title: Lithuanian TOTP instruction is in Italian
body: This changed message says “Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:” (Italian), while the rest of this file is Lithuanian. Lithuanian users configuring TOTP will see an unrelated-language instruction; please use a Lithuanian translation.

title: Lithuanian login instruction is in Italian
body: This changed message says “Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:” (Italian), while the rest of this file is Lithuanian. Users configuring TOTP on the login flow will see an unrelated-language instruction; please use a Lithuanian translation.

title: Lithuanian authenticator instruction was replaced with Italian text
body: This value is Italian (“Install one of the following applications on your mobile”), not Lithuanian. It is displayed during Lithuanian OTP setup, so users see an untranslated instruction; the same incorrect replacement also appears in the account-theme Lithuanian message file.

title: Lithuanian TOTP instruction is replaced with Italian
body: This value is Italian (“Install one of the following applications on your mobile”), not Lithuanian. Users selecting Lithuanian see an untranslated instruction during authenticator setup.

title: Lithuanian login instruction is replaced with Italian
body: This value is Italian (“Install one of the following applications on your mobile”), not Lithuanian. Users selecting Lithuanian see an untranslated instruction during login authenticator setup.

title: Simplified Chinese instruction is replaced with Traditional Chinese
body: This value is written in Traditional Chinese, despite being in the Simplified Chinese locale file. Simplified Chinese users will see the wrong script for this authenticator setup instruction.

title: The grant-shortcut matcher rejects the expected shortcut
body: This condition returns `false` when the token ID contains `expectedGrantShortcut`, so events with the correct grant type fail the matcher while IDs with a different shortcut can pass. Reverse the condition; as written, the updated integration assertions cannot verify the intended token IDs.

title: Grant shortcuts are parsed as exactly two characters without enforcing that contract
body: The decoder consumes exactly two characters for the grant shortcut, but `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` only documents a shortcut that is usually three letters and the factory never validates its length. A custom grant factory returning a shortcut of any other length will produce token IDs that cannot be decoded correctly, causing token-context lookup to reject valid tokens or resolve the wrong grant. Enforce the two-character contract when registering shortcuts or encode/decode a delimiter-based variable-length value.

title: The access-token ID matcher rejects the expected grant
body: This condition returns `false` when the shortcut equals `expectedGrantShortcut`, so every otherwise well-formed token ID with the expected grant fails the matcher. The updated event assertions for authorization-code, device, refresh, and CIBA flows will therefore fail on valid events; reverse the condition so it rejects mismatches.

title: Grant shortcuts are not constrained to the two-character encoding format
body: The token-ID decoder reads the grant shortcut from exactly two characters, but this API says shortcuts are usually three letters and does not require exactly two. A custom grant factory returning a three-character shortcut will issue IDs that the decoder misparses, causing context decoding to fail for its tokens. Require and validate a two-character shortcut, or make the encoding and decoding length-aware.

title: Access-token event matcher rejects the expected grant shortcut
body: The matcher returns false when `substring(3, 5)` equals the expected shortcut, so it rejects rather than accepts matching IDs. It also reads characters 3–4, but the grant shortcut is encoded at characters 4–5 (zero-based). Consequently, event assertions using this matcher fail for valid access-token IDs and do not verify the intended grant type.

title: Exhausted federated recovery credentials are never removed
body: `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` now returns federated credentials before local ones, but this path still removes the credential using `removeStoredCredentialById`, which only removes credentials from Keycloak's local storage. When the exhausted credential is in user storage, it remains there and continues to be reported as configured and exposed in credential listings until replacement succeeds. Remove it through the appropriate user-storage mechanism, or otherwise ensure the exhausted federated credential is actually cleared.

title: Recovery codes remain reusable in the user-storage test provider
body: This validator only checks whether the submitted code appears in the stored list; it never removes the matched code or persists an updated list. Since authentication delegates validation to this user-storage provider, a successfully used recovery code remains valid for subsequent logins. The new integration test exercises only one login, so it does not catch the violation of recovery codes' one-time-use behavior.

title: Exhausted federated recovery credentials are not removed
body: When the last recovery code is used, this calls `removeStoredCredentialById`, which removes only a credential from Keycloak's local store. For a credential returned by `getFederatedCredentialsStream()`, this does not remove the credential from user storage. The following required action may create a replacement, but until then the old federated credential remains configured and its consumed codes can still be accepted if the storage provider does not independently invalidate them. Remove the federated credential through the user-storage credential API, or otherwise ensure it can no longer be used.

title: The test can pass before the reader thread reports failures
body: The test sets `deletedAll` and immediately asserts the exception list without joining the reader thread. The reader may still be in an in-flight request and add an exception after this assertion, so the test can pass despite reproducing the NPE. Join the reader thread before checking the collected exceptions.

title: The concurrency test does not wait for the reader thread
body: The reader thread is started but never joined before the test checks `caughtExceptions`. The deletion loop can finish and the assertion can run while a group-list request is still in flight, so an exception caused by the race may be added only after the assertion and the test will pass. The reader may also be scheduled only after deletion has completed, meaning the test can pass without exercising concurrent access. Coordinate the reader and deleter so overlap is guaranteed, then stop and join the reader before asserting its result.

title: The test can assert success before the reader finishes
body: The reader thread is started but never joined. After the deleter sets `deletedAll`, the main thread can assert that `caughtExceptions` is empty while the reader is still handling an in-flight request; an exception from that request can therefore arrive after the assertion and the test still passes. Join the reader before asserting so the regression test reliably observes failures from the full concurrent-read interval.

title: Optimized audit-log pagination cannot build cursors from datetimes
body: The audit-log endpoint configures this paginator with `order_by="-datetime"`, but this method applies `math.floor` or `math.ceil` directly to the datetime value. Those functions require a real number, so an optimized request with results raises `TypeError` while building the cursor instead of returning a page. The datetime-specific conversion used by `DateTimePaginator` is needed here as well.

title: Negative offsets are passed to a queryset slice
body: When advanced pagination receives a cursor with a negative offset, this branch passes that offset directly to a Django queryset slice. Django does not support negative queryset indices and raises `ValueError`; it does not clamp or otherwise handle them as the comment claims. Such a cursor therefore causes the request to fail rather than paginate.

title: Optimized audit-log pagination fails when building a cursor
body: Audit-log rows have a `datetime` sort key, but this implementation passes that value directly to `math.floor`/`math.ceil`, which do not accept `datetime` objects. When an authorized administrator requests `optimized_pagination=true` and the result page is non-empty, cursor construction raises `TypeError` and the endpoint returns a 500. Convert the datetime to the same numeric timestamp representation used by `DateTimePaginator`.

title: Negative offsets are passed to unsupported Django queryset slicing
body: When advanced pagination is enabled and a cursor has a negative offset, this code evaluates a queryset slice with a negative start. Django does not support negative queryset indexing or slicing and raises `ValueError`, so such a cursor produces a server error rather than a page. Clamp or reject negative offsets before slicing; Django does not provide the claimed automatic boundary handling.

title: Optimized paginator cannot paginate datetime fields
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` is used here with `order_by="-datetime"`, but this implementation applies `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly to the model’s datetime value. Those functions require a number, so building cursors for non-empty audit-log results raises `TypeError` and the optimized request fails. It also returns the raw numeric cursor from `value_from_cursor`, rather than converting it to a datetime for the queryset filter. Reuse the datetime-specific conversion and key logic from `DateTimePaginator`.

title: Negative offsets cause an error in Django queryset slicing
body: This branch deliberately passes a negative start offset to `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, but Django querysets reject negative slice indices and raise `ValueError`; they do not interpret them as a way to paginate backwards. A request with a negative cursor offset therefore fails instead of returning a page. The non-advanced previous-page path can hit the same invalid slice when its cursor offset is negative.

title: Datetime ordering cannot be handled by the optimized paginator
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` is selected for audit-log queries ordered by `-datetime`, but this implementation applies `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly to the datetime value. Building cursors for non-empty audit-log pages will raise `TypeError` instead of returning a response. Use datetime-to-cursor conversion equivalent to `DateTimePaginator` or do not use this paginator for datetime ordering.

title: Negative QuerySet slices are not supported by Django
body: This branch passes a negative `start_offset` to a Django QuerySet slice. Django does not support negative indexing or slicing on QuerySets, so a request with a negative cursor offset reaches this branch and raises an exception rather than paginating. The comments claim Django handles these boundaries, but the ORM requires a non-negative slice offset; implement supported reverse pagination or reject the cursor.

title: Existing span-buffer keys still have the old Redis set type
body: This change switches `span-buf:s:*` keys from Redis sets to sorted sets, but buffers written by the previous version can remain alive until their TTL expires. When the new consumer encounters one of those keys, `ZCARD`/`ZUNIONSTORE` (and the Python-side `ZADD`) operate on a set and fail with `WRONGTYPE`, interrupting span ingestion during rollout.
