Migrate or version existing keys, or otherwise make the type transition safe.

title: Changing buffer keys from sets to sorted sets breaks buffers surviving deployment
body: This writes span payloads to the existing `span-buf:s:{...}` keys as sorted sets, but the previous implementation stored those same keys as Redis sets. During a rolling deploy—or for up to the one-hour TTL after an upgrade—an old buffer can still be a set. `ZADD` then fails with `WRONGTYPE`, preventing span processing; the Lua script's `ZCARD`/`ZUNIONSTORE` operations also assume sorted sets. Use a versioned key or migrate/delete legacy keys safely before using sorted-set commands.

title: Negative offsets reach a Django queryset slice, which raises
body: When advanced pagination is enabled, a cursor with a negative offset is passed directly into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django querysets do not support negative slice indices and raise `ValueError` rather than treating them as reverse-pagination offsets. Since cursor offsets can be supplied by the API caller, a negative offset can produce a server error on the optimized audit-log endpoint. Implement reverse pagination using a supported query strategy or reject negative offsets.

title: Optimized paginator cannot paginate datetime fields
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` is selected for the audit-log endpoint, whose ordering key is `datetime`, but this implementation applies `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly to the field value. Datetime objects do not support those operations, so building the response cursor raises `TypeError` and the optimized audit-log request fails. Reuse the datetime-to-timestamp conversion used by `DateTimePaginator`.

title: Changing buffer keys to sorted sets breaks existing set keys during rollout
body: Before this change, span-buffer keys were Redis sets; existing keys can remain alive for up to the configured TTL during a rolling deployment. `zcard`/`zunionstore` here, and the corresponding `zadd`/`zscan` operations in the new code, fail with `WRONGTYPE` on those old set keys. Spans already buffered under them can therefore stop processing until expiry, and a rollback has the same incompatibility in the opposite direction. Add a migration/compatibility path or otherwise ensure old-format keys are handled before switching commands.

title: Negative offsets are passed to Django queryset slicing
body: When advanced features are enabled and a cursor has a negative offset, this branch passes that offset directly to `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django querysets reject negative slice bounds rather than interpreting them as reverse-pagination offsets, so the request raises an exception instead of returning a page. Implement reverse traversal with supported query semantics or reject negative offsets explicitly.

title: Substring detection can upsample queries that exclude errors
body: This treats any occurrence of `event.type:error` as an error-focused query, including negated filters such as `!event.type:error` and queries that combine the error filter with other event types. Those queries can include transactions or other events without `sample_weight`, yet their `count()` aggregation is rewritten to sum that field. The result can be a query failure or incorrect counts; determine the event-type filter semantically instead of matching a substring.

title: Substring matching can upsample queries that include non-error events
body: Checking whether the query contains `event.type:error` does not establish that it selects only errors. For example, `!event.type:error` contains this substring but selects non-error events, and an OR query can include both errors and transactions. The caller then replaces `count()` with `sum(sample_weight)` for those events, even though transaction events may not have `sample_weight`, producing incorrect counts or a query failure. Parse the query semantics or otherwise ensure the transformation is applied only when the query is restricted to errors.

title: Substring matching can upsample mixed event queries
body: This treats any query containing `event.type:error` as error-only, including queries that also select transactions (for example, an OR between error and transaction types). The transformed aggregation sums `sample_weight`, which is not available for transaction events, so mixed queries can fail or return incorrect counts. Determine that the query is exclusively errors rather than checking for a substring.

title: Cached allowlist eligibility can apply stale weighting
body: The 60-second cache is not invalidated when the project allowlist changes, so a project removed from the allowlist can continue receiving weighted counts, and a newly allowlisted project can continue receiving ordinary counts, until the entry expires. The helper `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is not called by this change, so the cache can produce incorrect counts after configuration updates.

title: Feature-flagged table visualization discards the query results
body: When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, this branch passes `columns: []` and an empty `tableData` instead of the current `result`'s columns, metadata, and data. Dashboards using the new visualization will therefore show a blank table despite successful queries. Pass the actual result data and derived columns to the component.

title: Zero-valued age bypasses the mutually exclusive timestamp check
body: This check uses truthiness rather than field presence. A report containing both `age: 0` and `timestamp: 0` passes both validators, even though the endpoint requires exactly one field. Check whether the other key is present in the input so this invalid combination is rejected.

title: The feature-flagged table path discards the query results
body: When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, this branch constructs `TableWidgetVisualization` with `columns: []` and empty `data`/`meta` instead of passing `result.data`, `result.meta`, and the computed fields. Dashboard table widgets therefore render blank for organizations with the flag enabled, regardless of the query response.

title: Error timestamps and breadcrumb timestamps use different time bases
body: The fetched error timestamp comes from the stored event and is an absolute Unix timestamp, while replay breadcrumb timestamps are elapsed replay-relative seconds. Comparing them directly means errors will generally be treated as later than every breadcrumb and appended at the end, rather than interleaved chronologically; the emitted error log also reports the wrong time basis. Convert both values to a common timeline before sorting and comparing.

title: Age/timestamp exclusivity checks accept zero values
body: These validators use truthiness on the other field, so a report containing both `age: 0` and `timestamp: 0` passes validation even though the two formats are mutually exclusive. Check field presence instead; otherwise malformed mixed-format reports are accepted and counted as valid.

title: Feature-flagged table widgets discard their query results
body: When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, this branch passes an empty `columns` array and empty `tableData` instead of the current `result`'s fields, metadata, and rows. Consequently, every dashboard table widget for organizations with this feature enabled renders blank even when the query returned data. Pass the actual result data and columns to the new visualization.

title: Zero-valued age or timestamp bypasses the mutual-exclusion check
body: These checks use truthiness to detect whether the other field was supplied. Since `timestamp: 0` and `age: 0` are valid integer values, a report containing both `age: 0` and `timestamp: 0` passes validation, despite the Reporting API formats requiring exactly one of those fields. Check field presence instead, so mixed-format reports are rejected consistently.

title: Installation proceeds without verifying the installer when no integration exists
body: When the installation webhook has not created an `Integration` yet, this branch advances the pipeline directly. The sender comparison below only runs for an already-existing integration, so the normal pipeline can create the integration from GitHub’s installation API without ever confirming that the OAuth-authenticated user matches the installer. Webhook delivery can be delayed or fail, allowing the account-mismatch check this change is intended to enforce to be bypassed.

title: Missing sender metadata causes installation callback to crash
body: This directly indexes `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`, but integrations created before this check—or installations whose webhook did not populate `sender`—may have no `sender` key (or no `login`). In that case the callback raises `KeyError` and returns a server error instead of the intended invalid-installation response, preventing legitimate reinstalls and leaving the user without the documented failure flow. Handle absent or malformed sender metadata as a validation failure.

title: First-time installations bypass the GitHub-user check
body: When no `Integration` exists yet for this installation ID, this branch advances the pipeline without comparing `github_authenticated_user` to the installation sender. A first-time GitHub App installation commonly reaches this path if its installation webhook has not yet created the Integration, so an authenticated GitHub account different from the installer can complete setup despite the security check. Validate the installer identity on this path too, or ensure the comparison is performed against trusted installation data before completing setup.

title: Missing sender metadata causes an unhandled KeyError
body: This assumes every existing Integration has `metadata['sender']['login']`. Integrations created before this check was introduced, or integrations whose sender metadata was not recorded, can lack either key. Reinstalling such an installation reaches this line and raises `KeyError`, returning a server error instead of the intended invalid-installation response. Treat missing or malformed sender metadata as a failed validation and return the normal error response.

title: `queued` is initialized once at module import
body: `timezone.now()` is evaluated when the dataclass is defined, so every `AssignmentSource` created in the same process receives the same timestamp rather than the time that source was created. This makes the `queued` field misleading and prevents it from distinguishing assignment events; use a `default_factory` so each instance gets its own timestamp.

title: `queued` is fixed at module import time
body: `timezone.now()` is evaluated when the dataclass is defined, so every `AssignmentSource` created without an explicit `queued` value gets the same timestamp rather than its creation time. Since `to_dict()` includes this field in the task payload, the recorded queue time is misleading for every subsequent assignment. Use a `default_factory` so each instance gets its own timestamp.

title: `queued` is fixed at module import time
body: `timezone.now()` is evaluated once when this module is imported, so every `AssignmentSource` created afterward receives the same timestamp rather than its creation/queue time. The field therefore cannot identify when a particular assignment was queued, and its value may be arbitrarily stale in long-lived workers. Use a `default_factory` so the timestamp is generated for each instance.

title: Metric alert handler is now abstract and cannot be instantiated
body: `StatefulDetectorHandler` has abstract methods for `counter_names`, dedupe extraction, group-key extraction, and occurrence construction, but this subclass implements none of them. Since this handler is registered on `MetricAlertFire`, accessing `detector.detector_handler` for a metric-alert detector attempts to instantiate it and raises `TypeError` rather than returning a handler. Implement the required hooks or keep this registered handler concrete.

title: Metric alert handler is abstract and cannot be instantiated
body: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` inherits `StatefulDetectorHandler` but implements none of its abstract methods, including `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the new occurrence hook. When a detector with this registered group type accesses `detector_handler`, instantiating the handler raises `TypeError` instead of allowing detector processing to proceed. Implement the required methods or keep this handler concrete.

title: Registered metric-alert handler cannot be instantiated
body: `StatefulDetectorHandler` has abstract `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and `build_occurrence_and_event_data` members, but this subclass implements none of them. Since this handler is registered on `MetricAlertFire`, accessing `Detector.detector_handler` for a metric-alert detector attempts to instantiate an abstract class and raises `TypeError`, preventing detector processing.

title: Evaluation docstring still documents a list return value
body: This method now returns a dictionary keyed by group key, but its docstring says it returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`. That documents the old contract and can mislead callers implementing or consuming detector handlers.

title: A negative flusher process count disables flushing entirely
body: `max_processes` is supplied by the new `--flusher-processes` option, which accepts negative integers. A negative value is truthy, so this expression preserves it; `min()` then makes `num_processes` negative, causing the following `range(self.num_processes)` to create no workers. The consumer can continue writing spans to Redis, but no flusher will ever publish buffered segments, leading to an unbounded Redis backlog and missing downstream span data. Reject non-positive values or clamp them to a valid count.

title: Wait for the old flusher to exit before starting its replacement
body: `Process.kill()` only sends a termination signal; it does not wait for the process to stop. The replacement is started immediately afterward, so a hung flusher that is still executing Redis or Kafka operations can overlap with its replacement. Both may flush the same segment and produce it to Kafka, causing duplicate buffered segments. Join the killed process before starting the replacement.

title: Reject non-positive flusher process counts
body: This option accepts zero and negative values, but `SpanFlusher` uses the configured value to determine how many workers to create. With a negative value, `num_processes` is negative and the worker map is empty, so no process flushes buffered spans; with zero, the fallback currently masks the invalid value and silently creates a different worker count. Validate that `--flusher-processes` is positive so invalid configuration cannot leave spans unflushed or behave unexpectedly.

title: Reject non-positive flusher process counts
body: `--flusher-processes` accepts any integer, but this calculation can produce `num_processes == 0` for a value of zero (or a negative value). With assigned shards, the following mapping loop then evaluates `i % self.num_processes` and raises `ZeroDivisionError`, preventing the consumer from starting. Validate the option as positive or clamp/reject invalid values before building the shard map.

title: Do not require numeric Kafka offsets to be contiguous
body: Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be consecutive for records delivered to a consumer: compacted topics and control records can leave gaps even when every delivered record has been processed. This loop stops at the first missing integer, so a partition with completed records at offsets 100 and 102 will never commit past 100 unless offset 101 is delivered—which may never happen. The consumer will repeatedly replay later records after restart and can remain stuck indefinitely. Track completion of delivered records rather than requiring every numeric offset.

title: Queues are unbounded, so slow workers do not provide backpressure
body: Each worker queue is created without a maximum size, and `submit` can keep adding work while workers are slow. Consequently this mode can accumulate an unbounded backlog in memory instead of slowing consumption as the strategy documentation claims, potentially causing excessive memory growth or an out-of-memory failure during a sustained processing slowdown. Bound the queues and define how submission waits or pauses consumption when they fill.

title: Failed work is marked complete and its offset can be committed
body: When `result_processor` raises, this handler logs the exception but the `finally` block still calls `complete_offset`. The commit loop can therefore commit past a message whose processing failed, so Kafka will not redeliver it after a restart. Leave failed offsets outstanding or route them through the consumer's failure/DLQ handling before marking them complete.

title: Offset gaps can prevent commits indefinitely
body: This loop requires every integer offset between the lowest and highest observed offset to be present in `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be consecutive among delivered records: compacted records and broker/control records can leave gaps. If an offset is skipped, the tracker will refuse to commit any later completed records for that partition indefinitely, eventually causing reprocessing and stalled progress. Track delivery order/commit safety without requiring every numeric offset to have been delivered.

title: Shutdown relies on Queue.shutdown, unavailable on supported Python versions
body: `queue.Queue.shutdown()` and `queue.ShutDown` were added in Python 3.13. On runtimes without that API, the call raises `AttributeError` and is swallowed here, while workers blocked in `Queue.get()` are never woken; their joins time out and the daemon threads remain alive after shutdown. Use a compatible sentinel/event-based shutdown or ensure the project's supported Python version provides this API.

title: Queue shutdown API is unavailable on supported Python versions
body: `Queue.shutdown()` and `queue.ShutDown` were added in Python 3.13, while this service runs on older Python versions. On those versions this call raises `AttributeError` (which is swallowed here), leaving workers blocked forever in `Queue.get()`; setting `worker.shutdown` does not wake a blocked worker. Each shutdown therefore leaks worker threads, and the pool cannot drain or stop cleanly. Use a shutdown mechanism supported by the project's Python version, such as sentinels.

title: Failed processing is marked complete and its offset can be committed
body: The worker catches any exception from `result_processor` and then unconditionally calls `complete_offset` in `finally`. The commit loop treats that offset as successfully processed and can commit past it, permanently losing the message despite the strategy's stated guarantee that only successful processing is committed. Leave failed offsets outstanding or route them through the existing retry/DLQ behavior before completing them.

title: Work queues are unbounded, so they provide no backpressure
body: `queue.Queue()` defaults to `maxsize=0`, which is unbounded. If Kafka delivers faster than the workers process, submissions continue accumulating in memory rather than blocking or applying backpressure; a sustained backlog can exhaust the consumer's memory. Bound the queues or otherwise pause intake when queue capacity is reached.

title: Closing a partition strategy shuts down the shared worker pool
body: `ResultsStrategyFactory` owns one queue pool shared by the strategies it creates, but each `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` shuts that pool down. Arroyo can close and recreate a strategy when partitions are reassigned; after the first close, the factory still points to this stopped pool, so subsequent strategies submit to workers that no longer process items. Make pool lifecycle factory-scoped, or give each strategy an independently owned pool.

title: Backup code consumption is not atomic
body: This reads the user's encrypted code list, verifies a code, then writes a modified copy without checking that the stored list is unchanged. Two concurrent logins can both authenticate with the same code; concurrent use of different codes can also overwrite one another's updates and restore a consumed code. Make verification and consumption atomic so a code can authorize at most one login.

title: Backup codes cannot be used for SSO 2FA challenges
body: The third-party identity-provider guard earlier in `authorize` rejects requests without `totpCode` before this backup-code branch is reached. The login UI also omits the lost-access option for the `totpEmail` challenge. A local account that has backup codes and later switches to Google or SAML retains its 2FA state, but cannot use those codes to recover access through the resulting SSO challenge.

title: The new backup-code authentication flow is not tested
body: The added test coverage checks displaying, copying, and downloading codes, but never submits a backup code to log in or verifies that a used code is rejected on a subsequent attempt. The core authentication behavior and its one-time-use guarantee can therefore regress without failing this suite; add coverage for successful use and rejection on reuse.

title: Copy reports success even when the clipboard write fails
body: `navigator.clipboard.writeText` is asynchronous, but its promise is not awaited before the success toast is shown. If clipboard access is denied or unavailable, the user still sees “Backup codes copied!” and may believe they saved codes they do not have. Show success only after the write resolves and handle failures.

title: The password visibility toggle is no longer keyboard accessible
body: Setting the shared password-field toggle button to `tabIndex={-1}` removes it from keyboard focus order. Keyboard-only users can no longer reach or activate the show/hide control in any form using `PasswordField`; keep the control keyboard-focusable.

title: Backup codes can be redeemed concurrently more than once
body: Two login requests can both read the same stored backup-code list, find the supplied code, and then each write a copy with that slot set to null. Since the updates do not compare against the original stored value, both requests succeed and create sessions, violating the one-use guarantee. Make consumption atomic so only one request can update the list and authenticate.

title: Federated 2FA users cannot choose the backup-code flow
body: The Lost access control is added only to `TwoFactorFooter`. When `totpEmail` is present—which is how federated-login users are sent to the 2FA prompt—the page uses `ExternalTotpFooter`, which has no Lost access action. These users therefore have no UI path to enter a backup code.

title: Backup-code-only credentials are rejected for federated users
body: The new backup-code branch below this check accepts `backupCode`, but the earlier identity-provider guards require `credentials.totpCode`. A backup-code submission has no TOTP code, so federated users are rejected with `ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled` before backup-code verification runs. Update the guards to recognize backup-code credentials as an allowed second factor.

title: The password visibility toggle cannot reveal this password
body: This field is now a `PasswordField`, but it still passes `type="password"`. `PasswordField` spreads caller props after its visibility-controlled `type`, so this prop overrides the toggle and the input remains masked even after clicking the eye button.

title: Password visibility controls are no longer keyboard-accessible
body: Setting the show/hide button to `tabIndex={-1}` removes it from normal keyboard tab navigation. Keyboard-only users cannot reach the control to reveal or hide a password; keep it in the tab order.

title: The tests do not exercise backup-code authentication
body: The added test checks the download filename and that a toast appears, but never submits a generated backup code to log in or verifies that the code is rejected after use. The central authentication behavior and its one-time guarantee can therefore regress without any test failure; add coverage for backup-code login and reuse.

title: Backup-code consumption is not atomic
body: This read-modify-write can let concurrent login requests both validate the same backup code. Requests using different codes can also overwrite each other’s updates because each writes a stale copy of the entire encrypted list, restoring a code that was already consumed. This breaks the promised one-time-use guarantee and allows backup-code replay; consume codes with an atomic compare-and-swap or equivalent serialized update.

title: The setup password visibility toggle cannot reveal the password
body: This field passes `type="password"` to `PasswordField`. That component sets its visibility-dependent type before spreading the supplied props, so this fixed type overrides the component’s `text` type when the eye toggle is clicked. Remove the explicit type or change the component so the toggle can reveal the password.

title: Password visibility toggle is no longer keyboard reachable
body: Setting `tabIndex={-1}` removes the show/hide password button from the Tab order for every `PasswordField`. Keyboard-only users can no longer focus or activate this control; keep it keyboard reachable.

title: The new backup-code login flow is not covered by an end-to-end test
body: The added test exercises displaying, downloading, and copying codes, but never attempts login with a backup code or verifies that a consumed code is rejected. The central authentication behavior—and its one-time-use contract—can therefore regress while this test still passes; add coverage for successful backup-code login and reuse rejection.

title: Handle an empty destination-calendar list before checking its integration
body: When a booking uses Google Meet but has no destination calendar, destructuring produces `undefined` and this condition dereferences `.integration`, throwing before the booking can be created. Check that the calendar exists before reading its integration.

title: Select the Office 365 destination for the current credential
body: EventManager invokes calendar creation once per destination, passing the matching credential ID, but this implementation ignores that ID and always uses the first destination calendar. For every later collective host, Graph is asked to create the event in the first host's calendar, which can fail with an access error or put the event in the wrong mailbox; the later host then receives no event.

title: Select the Lark destination for the current credential
body: EventManager invokes calendar creation once per destination, but this implementation always uses `event.destinationCalendar[0]` rather than the destination belonging to the credential being used. Later collective hosts therefore try to create their event in the first host's Lark calendar, typically failing due to permissions or creating it in the wrong calendar.

title: Avoid filtering CalDAV creation to another host's calendar
body: EventManager creates an event separately for each host credential, but this implementation filters the current account's calendars using only the first destination in the shared array. For a later host, that first calendar is generally not in their CalDAV account, so no event is created; the method can still return a successful result and leave a booking reference for an event that does not exist.

title: Restore all collective destinations when confirming a booking
body: This handler rebuilds the event using only the booking's single persisted destination calendar (or the current user's calendar). Collective host calendars are assembled during initial booking creation, but only one destination is stored on the booking, and this handler does not reload the other hosts' destinations. Confirming a pending collective booking therefore creates calendar events and references for at most one host, leaving the other hosts uninivited.

title: Preserve collective destinations when creating paid-booking events
body: On payment success this event contains only the booking's single persisted destination calendar or the organizer's calendar; it does not reload the collective hosts' destinations. When this path creates the calendar events, EventManager sees only one target, so other hosts are not invited. The setup-intent path in this file and the PayPal payment-success path have the same single-destination reconstruction and need the same fix.

title: Use the destination calendar as the fallback for update and delete
body: When `externalCalendarId` is absent, this `find` compares each calendar's external ID to that absent value, so it does not fall back to the event's destination calendar. Updates then receive an undefined calendar ID; deletes instead fall back to `primary` (the same broken lookup appears at line 317), which can leave the event on its selected calendar. This breaks operations for callers or older references without an external calendar ID.

title: Delete every old calendar event when rescheduling to a new booking
body: The reschedule update path now handles multiple calendar references, but when `newBookingId` is set this cleanup still finds and deletes only the first old calendar reference. Collective bookings can have an old event on each host's calendar, so the other hosts' old events remain after rescheduling and appear as duplicate appointments.

title: Delete every host's event when cancelling a recurring collective booking
body: The recurring-cancellation branch still selects only the first calendar reference for each updated booking and iterates only the booking user's credentials, rather than deleting each reference with its own credential. For collective bookings, events on secondary hosts' calendars are therefore left behind when cancelling the recurring series.

title: Use each reference's credential when deleting events for a reschedule request
body: Collective bookings can have several calendar references of the same integration type, each with its own `credentialId`, but this handler maps credentials only by integration type and uses that one credential for every reference. It can attempt to delete another host's event with the requester’s token; providers may reject the call or silently ignore a not-found response, leaving the old event on that host's calendar.

title: Meet fallback crashes when no destination calendar is configured
body: When `evt.location` is Google Meet and `evt.destinationCalendar` is null or empty, destructuring produces no first calendar and this direct `.integration` access throws. The previous optional access handled this case, so booking creation now fails instead of falling back to Cal Video.

title: Video booking references lose their credential IDs
body: This conditional writes `credentialId` only for calendar results and sets it to `undefined` for video results, even though video creation results carry the credential ID. The booking reference then cannot identify the video credential; cancellation code that requires a reference credential ID skips deleting the meeting, leaving the external video meeting behind.

title: Lark always creates collective events in the first destination calendar
body: The event manager calls `createEvent` for each destination using that host's credential, but this adapter ignores the credential ID and always selects `destinationCalendar[0]`. For a collective event where the first destination belongs to another host or integration, Lark is sent the wrong calendar ID and the Lark host's event is not created in its intended calendar.

title: Office 365 always creates collective events in the first destination calendar
body: The event manager invokes this service once per destination credential, but this method ignores that credential and always uses the first destination's external ID. When another host's Office 365 account is being used, the ID can refer to a different account's calendar, so creation fails or targets the wrong calendar instead of notifying that host.

title: CalDAV creation filters against the first host's calendar only
body: The event manager invokes calendar creation separately for each destination credential, but this service always filters calendars using the first destination. For a later host's CalDAV account, that calendar will generally not be present in its calendar list, so the filter produces no create requests; the method then still returns success, leaving the host without an event.

title: Recurring collective cancellation deletes only the first calendar reference
body: In the recurring cancellation path, each booking can now have multiple calendar references, but this lookup chooses only the first one for every updated booking. The code then attempts deletion through the organizer's credentials rather than the credential for each matching host reference. As a result, recurring collective cancellations leave events on other hosts' calendars, while repeatedly targeting the first reference.

title: Google update and delete no longer fall back to the destination calendar
body: When `externalCalendarId` is null or undefined, this search compares calendar IDs to that nullish value, so it cannot select a configured destination calendar. Updates are sent with an undefined calendar ID, and the equivalent lookup in `deleteEvent` falls back to `primary`, leaving events on the configured calendar untouched. This breaks rescheduling or cancellation for references without a stored external calendar ID.

title: Organization slug is omitted when team billing is disabled
body: This condition is reversed from the previous behavior: when team billing is disabled it spreads an empty object instead of `{ slug }`, so newly created organizations have no slug. When billing is enabled it sets `slug` directly, whereas the existing flow records it as `requestedSlug`. This breaks the expected organization URL/slug creation behavior.

title: Destinations without a credential ID lose their external calendar ID
body: This branch supports destinations with no `credentialId`, but unlike the branch above it calls `createEvent` without `destination.externalId`. `CalendarManager.createEvent` uses that argument to populate the result's `externalId`, which is then stored as the booking reference's `externalCalendarId`. The resulting reference cannot identify the selected calendar for later updates or deletions.

title: Location updates create calendar references without calendar or credential IDs
body: `updateLocation` now builds references from `result.externalId` and `result.credentialId`, but the calendar results returned by `CalendarManager.updateEvent` do not populate either field. Consequently, location changes create calendar references with missing destination and credential identifiers, so later operations cannot reliably target the correct host calendar.

title: Rescheduling a booking with multiple calendars deletes only one old event
body: The reschedule merge path now updates all calendar references, but this lookup still selects only one old calendar reference and deletes only that event. With multiple host calendars, the remaining old events are left behind, producing duplicate or stale events after rescheduling.

title: Google Meet fallback throws when no destination calendar is configured
body: When `destinationCalendar` is null or empty, destructuring leaves `mainHostDestinationCalendar` undefined, so accessing `.integration` throws before the booking can be created. This is the very case the fallback is meant to handle: a Google Meet location with no Google Calendar should switch to Cal Video rather than fail the booking.

title: Co-host calendars are dropped when the organizer has no destination calendar
body: The event is initialized with `destinationCalendar: null` when neither the event type nor organizer has a destination calendar. Optional-chaining this push then does nothing, even when `teamDestinationCalendars` contains calendars for collective co-hosts. Event creation consequently receives no co-host destinations, so those hosts do not get calendar entries.

title: Only the first collective destination calendar is persisted for pending bookings
body: This relation stores only `evt.destinationCalendar[0]`, so the other hosts' destinations exist only in the in-memory event. For bookings awaiting confirmation or payment, later confirmation flows rebuild the event from the booking's single destination-calendar relation and the organizer's calendar; they cannot recover the co-host destinations. Those hosts therefore never receive calendar entries for these bookings.

title: Lark creates every host's event in the first destination calendar
body: `EventManager` calls calendar creation once per destination using that destination's credential, but this method always selects `event.destinationCalendar[0]` and ignores the supplied credential ID. For a collective booking with multiple Lark credentials, later calls use the first host's calendar ID with another host's credentials, causing creation to fail or target the wrong calendar.

title: Office 365 creates every host's event in the first destination calendar
body: `EventManager` invokes creation separately for each destination credential, but this method always selects the first destination and does not use the credential ID to select the matching calendar. When collective hosts have different Office 365 credentials, later calls try to create an event in the first host's calendar using another host's credentials, so that host's event is not created.

title: CalDAV silently skips host calendars other than the first destination
body: Each destination is created with its own calendar credential, but this code filters that credential's calendars against only the first destination's external ID. For another host, that ID may not exist in its CalDAV account, leaving `responses` empty; the method still returns success, so the booking records a reference to an event that was never created.

title: Google ignores configured destinations without a credential ID
body: When a destination has an external ID but no `credentialId`, the event manager still supports it by selecting credentials by integration type. This lookup then finds no match and falls back to `primary`, so creation ignores the configured destination calendar and may write to the wrong calendar.

title: Google update and delete cannot resolve a destination when the reference has no external ID
body: When `externalCalendarId` is null or undefined, this lookup compares each real calendar ID to that same nullish value and finds nothing. Updates then send no calendar ID; deletes fall back to `primary` (the same faulty lookup appears at line 317), so an event in the configured destination can remain orphaned after cancellation. This affects callers or older references without an external calendar ID.

title: Video booking references lose their credential ID
body: This now sets `credentialId` to `undefined` for every non-calendar result, discarding the video result's credential ID. Cancellation code only deletes a video meeting when its booking reference has a credential ID, so meetings created through video integrations can remain active after their booking is canceled.

title: Recurring cancellation still processes only the first calendar reference
body: In the recurring-booking path, each future booking is reduced to its first calendar reference, and the code then uses the organizer's credentials rather than the credential for each reference. Collective bookings now have multiple references, including co-host calendars, so canceling all remaining instances can leave those calendar copies in place or attempt deletion through the wrong account.

title: Organizations created without team billing no longer receive their slug
body: This reverses the previous condition: when `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED` is false, the organization is now created without a `slug`; when it is true, the slug is assigned immediately as well as recorded as `requestedSlug`. In the non-billing configuration, organizations therefore lack the slug needed for their organization URL.

title: `prisma` is not imported
body: This new `prisma.credential.update` call references `prisma`, but this file has no `prisma` import or declaration. TypeScript will report `Cannot find name 'prisma'`, preventing the app from type-checking or building.

title: The sync branch returns a Fetch Response instead of token data
body: When credential syncing is enabled, this returns the raw `fetch` Response, while the fallback returns each provider's native token result. Several callers expect token data directly or under `.data`: Google reads `res.data`, HubSpot reads `accessToken`/`expiresIn`, and Zoho Bigin/CRM read `tokenInfo.data`. A Fetch Response has none of those fields, so these integrations fail or persist malformed credentials when they use the sync endpoint. Decode and normalize the endpoint response to the contract expected by callers.

title: The computed Zod keys do not match arbitrary response fields
body: `z.string().toString()` produces a fixed property name, not a wildcard key matcher; both computed properties therefore refer to a fixed key, and the second overwrites the first. Zod strips unrecognized object properties by default, so synced responses lose fields such as `expires_in`, `expiry_date`, and `refresh_token`. For example, Zoom then receives no expiry and replaces its refresh token with the literal placeholder added below, while Office 365 retains a stale expiry and may refresh repeatedly.

title: The SafeParse wrapper is stored as the credential key
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the result of `safeParse` (`{ success, data }`), but this code treats that result as the parsed key and saves it to `credential.key`. On the next Google auth attempt, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` receives the wrapper rather than the token fields and fails, leaving the user's Google Calendar credential unusable after a refresh.

title: The connection uses the old access token after refreshing
body: The code obtains and persists `accessTokenParsed.data`, but constructs the Salesforce connection with `credentialKey.access_token`, which is the pre-refresh token. If that token expired, the connection still uses an expired token and Salesforce API calls fail despite the refresh succeeding. Use the refreshed access token when constructing the connection.

title: Salesforce refresh bypasses the credential sync endpoint
body: Unlike the other adapters, this refresh path calls Salesforce directly and never uses `refreshOAuthTokens`. When credential syncing is enabled, Salesforce therefore continues using the locally stored refresh token instead of asking the configured source-of-truth endpoint for the user's refreshed credentials, so Salesforce does not support the feature this PR adds.

title: Bigin sends a credential ID as the user ID
body: The third argument is interpreted by `refreshOAuthTokens` as the Cal.com user ID and is sent as `calcomUserId`, but this call passes `credentialId` (the credential record ID). The sync endpoint will look up the wrong user, causing refresh failures or associating credentials with a different user if IDs happen to collide. Pass the credential's user ID instead.

title: Zoom sync requests use the wrong app slug
body: This sends `zoomvideo` as `appSlug`, but Zoom credentials are registered under the app slug `zoom` (for example, the callback creates credentials with `appId: "zoom"`). A sync endpoint that looks up the app by slug will not find the Zoom app, so token refresh fails. Pass the registered slug.

title: Missing Prisma import breaks the app-store build
body: This new call references `prisma`, but this module does not import or otherwise define it. TypeScript cannot resolve the name, so the app-store build/type-check fails. Import the Prisma client before using it here.

title: The sync path returns a Fetch Response to callers expecting token objects
body: When credential syncing is enabled, this returns the raw Fetch `Response`, unlike the provider-specific object returned by the normal refresh function. Several callers treat the result as parsed token data: Google reads `res.data`, HubSpot reads token fields such as `accessToken`, and Bigin/Zoho CRM read `tokenInfo.data`. Those properties are absent on a Fetch `Response`, so refreshes fail or persist unusable credentials. Parse the response and adapt it to each caller's expected token shape.

title: The minimum schema strips the expiry and refresh-token fields
body: These computed property names are literal strings, not a wildcard for arbitrary token fields, and `z.object` strips unrecognized response properties. Thus a sync response containing `access_token` and `expiry_date` is parsed down to `access_token`; the parser then adds the literal placeholder `refresh_token`. Zoom subsequently uses the missing `expires_in` to compute a NaN expiry and persists the placeholder refresh token, leaving the credential unusable. Preserve and validate the actual expiry field and retain the existing refresh token when the sync response omits one.

title: Webex rejects the documented minimal sync response
body: The sync endpoint is documented in `refreshOAuthTokens` as returning only an access token and expiry, but Webex still validates the parsed response against `webexRefreshedTokenSchema`, which requires `scope`, `token_type`, `refresh_token`, and `refresh_token_expires_in`. A response following the documented sync contract therefore fails validation and no refreshed token is saved. Handle the minimal response while retaining the old refresh-token metadata, or define a compatible endpoint contract.

title: Salesforce refresh bypasses the configured credential-sync endpoint
body: This new refresh path calls Salesforce directly and never uses `refreshOAuthTokens`, so configuring `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` has no effect for Salesforce. Salesforce credentials therefore continue to refresh locally instead of using the external app store as the source of truth, leaving this integration outside the feature.

title: Bigin sends the credential ID as the Cal.com user ID
body: The third argument is serialized by `refreshOAuthTokens` as `calcomUserId`, but this call passes `credentialId`, which is the credential row's ID rather than the user's ID. The sync endpoint will look up the wrong user and cannot return that user's Bigin tokens. Pass `credential.userId` instead.

title: Zoom sends an integration name instead of the app slug
body: This argument becomes the sync request's `appSlug`, but Zoom credentials use app ID/slug `zoom` (the OAuth callback creates them with `appId: "zoom"`); `zoomvideo` is the integration type/name. An endpoint that looks up the app by slug will not find Zoom and cannot return the user's tokens. Pass `zoom` here.

title: Replacing a credential does not clear its invalid state
body: When an existing credential has been marked invalid, this update replaces only its key and leaves `invalid` set. The app will continue to treat the newly synced credentials as invalid, so this endpoint cannot recover a connection after the parent platform supplies valid replacement credentials. Clear the invalid flag when accepting a replacement key.

title: The minimum token schema does not capture arbitrary expiry fields
body: `z.string().toString()` is evaluated as a literal property name, not a wildcard key, and the same applies to the optional property on line 10. Consequently, normal fields such as `expires_in` or `expiry_date` are not validated or retained by this `z.object` (which strips unrecognized properties); depending on the computed keys, responses may also fail parsing. With credential syncing enabled, token refreshes across the affected apps therefore fail or lose their expiry data.

title: The SafeParse wrapper is saved as the Google credential key
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the result of `safeParse`, which has the shape `{ success, data }`, but this line stores that whole result as `credential.key` instead of its `.data`. After a token refresh, the next Google auth initialization parses this wrapper as a Google credential and fails, leaving the integration unusable.

title: The new credential update references an unimported Prisma client
body: This file does not import or otherwise declare `prisma`, but the newly added refresh code calls `prisma.credential.update`. TypeScript compilation fails with an unresolved `prisma` name, preventing the app-store package or application from building.

title: Salesforce refresh bypasses the configured credential-sync endpoint
body: This refresh path calls Salesforce directly instead of using `refreshOAuthTokens`. When credential syncing is configured, Salesforce still refreshes against Cal.com's Salesforce app rather than the self-hosted platform's source of truth, so the advertised sync behavior does not work for Salesforce.

title: The Salesforce connection uses the pre-refresh access token
body: The newly added code obtains and stores a refreshed token, but the connection is then constructed with `credentialKey.access_token`, which came from the original credential and was not updated with `accessTokenParsed.data`. When the original token is expired, Salesforce API calls therefore use the expired token despite the successful refresh.

title: Bigin sends a credential row ID as the user ID
body: The third argument to `refreshOAuthTokens` is used as `calcomUserId`, but this call passes `credentialId`, the ID of the credential row, rather than the owning user's ID. The sync endpoint will look up the wrong user (or fail to find one), so Bigin token refreshes cannot reliably retrieve the correct user's credentials.

title: Webex rejects the documented minimal sync response
body: The sync endpoint is documented to return only an access token and expiry date, but the response is passed on to `webexRefreshedTokenSchema` at line 88, which also requires `scope`, `token_type`, `refresh_token`, and `refresh_token_expires_in`. A response following the stated sync contract fails validation, so Webex refreshes fail and the integration cannot use synced credentials.

title: The synced Teams token is immediately treated as expired
body: The sync endpoint is expected to return an access token and expiry date, but the refresh handling later derives `expiry_date` solely from `expires_in` and overwrites it with `Date.now()` when `expires_in` is absent. The next `getToken` call sees that timestamp as expired and calls the sync endpoint again, causing repeated refresh requests and potentially rate-limiting the integration.

title: Zoom sync uses a different slug from the stored app credential
body: The refresh request identifies Zoom as `zoomvideo`, while Zoom credentials are stored with `appId: "zoom"` (as shown by the callback). The receiving sync endpoint uses `appSlug` to identify the app, so it cannot reliably match this request to the Zoom credential.

title: Concurrent initial webhooks can create duplicate credentials
body: The lookup at line 62 and the create here are separate, non-atomic operations. If two deliveries for the same user and app arrive before either creates its row, both observe no credential and insert one. This leaves duplicate credentials, after which consumers using `findFirst` may select an arbitrary copy.

title: Team admins and owners are checked as if they must be both
body: The permission check combines `isTeamAdmin` and `isTeamOwner` with `&&`. These are alternative team roles, so a normal admin or owner will fail this check and be denied access unless they also hold the other role. Use an OR check to allow either role.

title: Calendar updates use the caller's credentials instead of the booking owner's
body: This endpoint allows attendees and team admins to add guests, but it loads credentials for `ctx.user` and supplies them to the calendar event manager. For those callers, these are not necessarily the credentials for the booking owner's calendar, so the provider update can target the wrong account or fail; the newly added guests may then be missing from the actual calendar event.

title: Guest-add notifications ignore disabled standard-email settings
body: This email path sends organizer and attendee notifications unconditionally and does not accept or check the event type metadata used by the standard email senders to honor `disableStandardEmails.all.host` and `.attendee`. Events configured to disable standard emails will still send these notifications when guests are added, contrary to that setting.

title: Email classification uses the unfiltered guest input
body: The handler filters existing attendees out of `uniqueGuests`, but passes the original `guests` input to `sendAddGuestsEmails`. That sender treats every attendee whose email is in this list as newly invited and sends them a normal scheduled-booking email. If a request includes an existing attendee alongside a new address, the existing attendee receives the wrong email; pass the filtered list instead.

title: Guest blacklist checks can be bypassed with email casing
body: Blacklist entries are lowercased when loaded, but the submitted `guest` is compared without normalization. Submitting a blacklisted address with different casing (for example, an uppercase domain) bypasses the configured blacklist and creates the attendee. Normalize both sides before checking.

title: A calendar-sync failure leaves guests saved without notifications
body: The attendee rows are committed by the booking update before this external calendar operation runs. If `updateCalendarAttendees` rejects, the mutation returns an error and never reaches the email send, even though the guests are already saved. Retrying the same request then finds no new guests and rejects it, so the missing calendar update and notifications cannot be retried through this endpoint.

title: Team admins and owners are checked with AND
body: This requires the caller to be both a team admin and a team owner. Those are separate team roles, so an admin or owner who is not also in the other role is rejected by the permission check and cannot add guests. This should authorize either role.

title: Guest blacklist can be bypassed with uppercase addresses
body: The blacklist entries are lowercased, but `guest` is compared without normalization. Since email validation accepts uppercase addresses, a caller can submit a differently cased version of a blacklisted address and have it added as a guest. Normalize both sides before checking the blacklist.

title: The server accepts duplicate guest addresses
body: This schema validates each address but does not require the array to contain unique addresses. The uniqueness check exists only in the dialog, so a direct tRPC request can submit the same address multiple times; the handler does not deduplicate those entries before `createMany`, potentially creating duplicate attendees or causing the mutation to fail on a database constraint.

title: Email notifications use the unfiltered guest list
body: The handler filters out guests who are already attendees before inserting them, but passes the original `guests` array to the email sender. If a caller includes an existing attendee while adding a new guest, the sender classifies that existing attendee as newly added and sends them a scheduled-booking invitation instead of the existing-attendee notification. Pass the filtered list to the sender.

title: Calendar sync failure leaves attendees added but unnotified
body: The attendee rows are committed by the preceding booking update before this external calendar update runs. If calendar synchronization throws, the mutation exits before sending emails, while the new attendees remain in the database. The user sees a failure, and retrying can fail because those addresses are now already present, leaving them without invitations. Handle this partial-success case or arrange the flow so it can be retried safely.

title: Team access requires both admin and owner roles
body: This condition grants the team path only when both checks return true. Team admins who are not owners—and owners not recognized as admins—are therefore denied access, even though the intent appears to allow either role. Use an OR between the checks.

title: The server does not enforce unique guest addresses
body: The input schema checks only email syntax, and this filter checks each value only against the attendees loaded before the request. Repeated addresses in the request, or case variants of an existing address, can all pass and be sent to createMany. This can create duplicate attendee records (or make the mutation fail if a database constraint rejects them); enforce uniqueness on normalized addresses server-side.

title: Mixed-case addresses bypass the guest email blocklist
body: Blocklist entries are lowercased, but the submitted guest address is compared without normalization. A mixed- or uppercase spelling of a blocked address therefore passes the filter and is added to the booking. Normalize the submitted address before checking the blocklist.

title: Calendar updates use the caller's credentials instead of the organizer's
body: This procedure allows an existing attendee to add guests, but it constructs EventManager with credentials for ctx.user. For an attendee caller, those are not the credentials for the organizer-owned calendar, so updating that calendar's attendee list can fail or be skipped. The attendee rows are already committed before this call, and a failure also prevents the email step, leaving guests persisted without the expected calendar update or notifications.

title: Email classification uses requested guests rather than guests actually added
body: The handler filters existing attendees out of uniqueGuests, but passes the original guests array to sendAddGuestsEmails. If a request contains both an existing attendee and a new address, the existing attendee is still classified as newly added and receives an AttendeeScheduledEmail, causing a duplicate booking confirmation or calendar invite. Pass uniqueGuests so notification types reflect the attendees actually inserted.

title: The guest list has no size limit despite per-attendee fan-out
body: This array is unbounded, and each accepted address creates an attendee row and adds work for calendar synchronization and email delivery. An authorized booking participant can submit thousands of unique addresses in one request, causing large database writes and a correspondingly large email fan-out. Enforce a reasonable maximum batch size (and consider rate limiting).

title: Unprocessable reminders never accumulate retries
body: When `message` is empty or `sendTo` is missing, this condition skips the scheduling call without updating `retryCount` or deleting the reminder. Because the query selects unscheduled SMS reminders again on every cron run, these rows bypass the two-failure limit and are only removed when their scheduled date expires.

title: Retry increments can be lost by overlapping cron runs
body: The failure paths write `reminder.retryCount + 1` from the value read by `findMany`. If two cron requests process the same reminder concurrently, both can read the same count and overwrite it with the same next value, so multiple failed scheduling attempts count as one. The reminder can therefore be retried more than twice before reaching the deletion threshold; use an atomic increment and coordinate concurrent processing.

title: Retry increments can be lost when cron runs overlap
body: Both failure paths write `reminder.retryCount + 1` using the value loaded before scheduling. If two cron executions process the same reminder concurrently, they can both read the same count and write the same next value, so two failed scheduling attempts may count as only one. The `retryCount > 1` cleanup then does not enforce the intended two-failure limit. Use an atomic database increment, and guard updates against reminders that have already been scheduled.

title: Increment retryCount atomically
body: Both failure paths write `reminder.retryCount + 1` using the value loaded before the SMS call. If two cron invocations process the same reminder concurrently, they can both read the same count and overwrite it with the same next value. The failed attempts are then counted as one, so the reminder can be retried more than twice instead of being removed at the intended limit. Use Prisma's atomic `increment` update in both failure paths.

title: Removing `findMany` breaks existing service callers
body: This replaces the public `findMany` method with `getBaseConditions`, which only returns a SQL predicate and does not execute a booking query. Existing callers of `InsightsBookingService.findMany(...)` will no longer type-check, and this PR does not migrate them to a replacement API. Keep a query method or update all callers before removing it.

title: Removing `findMany` breaks the service query API
body: This replaces the public `findMany` method, which accepted Prisma query arguments and returned booking rows, with `getBaseConditions`, which only returns a SQL fragment. Existing callers of `InsightsBookingService.findMany(...)` will no longer compile, and there is no equivalent method here to execute their queries. Migrate all callers in this change or preserve a compatible query method.

title: Preserve or migrate the public `findMany` API
body: This change removes the service’s public `findMany` method and replaces it with a condition builder, but no production call sites are migrated in this PR. Any existing caller of `InsightsBookingService.findMany(...)` will no longer type-check, so the application cannot build until those callers are updated or a compatible method is retained.

title: Execute org and team authorization SQL in integration tests
body: The only database-backed query here uses user scope, which does not exercise the new `ANY(...)` array predicates. The org/team tests only compare `Prisma.Sql` fragments, so they will not catch invalid PostgreSQL array binding or incorrect authorization results when those predicates execute. Add database-backed queries covering org and team scopes.

title: Cache deletion leaves the connected-calendars query stale
body: After deleting the cache, this handler only invokes an optional callback and does not invalidate `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`, whose response supplies `cacheUpdatedAt`. When no callback invalidates that query, the dropdown continues to show the deleted cache and its delete action until the page is refreshed.

title: The environment-file update uses macOS-only sed syntax
body: On GNU/Linux, `sed -i ''` is not the macOS-compatible in-place edit syntax and fails when `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` already exists. Because the script does not stop on errors, it still prints that the URL was updated even though the environment file remains unchanged.

title: The environment-file path depends on the caller's working directory
body: `ENV_FILE` is resolved relative to the current directory, not this script's location. When invoked from the repository root as `./scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh`, `../.env` points outside the repository, so the script creates or edits the wrong file and the app does not load the webhook URL it reports setting.

title: Deleting cache leaves the connected-calendar query stale
body: The delete mutation only shows a toast and invokes an optional callback; it does not invalidate `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. Since `onSuccess` is optional, a successful deletion can leave the cached response showing the old `cacheUpdatedAt` and delete action until the page is reloaded. Invalidate the query on success so the UI reflects the deleted cache.

title: Legacy cache timestamps are set to the migration time
body: Adding this column with `DEFAULT NOW()` assigns the migration timestamp to every existing cache row, not the time that row was actually last updated. The cache-status query uses this field and the UI labels it “Last updated,” so existing credentials will appear to have refreshed at deployment even when their data is old or expired. Backfill a meaningful timestamp or avoid presenting the synthetic value as the actual update time.

title: The environment-file path depends on the caller's working directory
body: `ENV_FILE` is resolved relative to the current directory, not the script's location. Invoking this script from the repository root (for example, `scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh`) targets `../.env` outside the checkout instead of the repository's `.env`, so the application will not use the configured webhook URL. Resolve the path relative to the script or explicitly change directories.

title: The environment update uses BSD-only sed syntax
body: `sed -i ''` is the BSD/macOS form of in-place editing. On GNU/Linux, the empty argument is treated as a script or input path and the command fails, leaving `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` unchanged. Use a portable in-place update or handle the platform-specific syntax.

title: Deleting cache leaves the displayed status stale
body: The delete mutation only invokes an optional `onSuccess` callback and does not invalidate `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. When no callback is provided, the mounted query retains the deleted cache’s `cacheUpdatedAt`, so the dropdown continues to report cached data and offer deletion after the operation succeeded. Invalidate or refetch the connected-calendars query after deletion.

title: Legacy cache rows are reported as updated at migration time
body: Adding this column with `DEFAULT NOW()` assigns the migration timestamp to every existing cache row. The UI presents `updatedAt` as the cache’s last-updated time, so all pre-existing caches appear freshly updated on deployment even when their contents are older. Backfill a timestamp derived from the existing cache metadata, or avoid presenting the migration-time value as the actual update time.

title: The existing-URL update only works with BSD sed
body: `sed -i ''` uses BSD/macOS syntax. On GNU/Linux, when `.env` already contains `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL`, this command treats the empty argument as a file operand and fails to update the value; because the script does not stop on that failure, it can still print that the file was updated. Use a portable in-place edit or branch on the platform.

title: Reschedules bypass deferred email cancellation
body: Passing `true` selects the immediate-cancellation branch in `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`, which sends the SendGrid cancel request now instead of marking the reminder `cancelled` for the hourly-window cron. SendGrid keeps canceled scheduled sends pending until their scheduled date, and the cron will not find these rows because they are never marked cancelled. Reschedules far ahead can therefore consume the 100-pending-cancellation limit again, causing later cancellations to fail and reminders to be sent.

title: The cancellation marker update is not awaited
body: This call starts an async helper that marks the email reminder `cancelled` in the database, but the surrounding `forEach` discards its promise. The handler's later `Promise.all` does not include these helper calls, so it can finish before the marker is committed. If the cron runs before that update completes, it will not find the reminder and the scheduled email can still be sent. Await the reminder-cancellation operations before completing the handler.

title: One SendGrid failure aborts all remaining cancellations
body: The SendGrid request is inside a single `try` surrounding the entire loop. If any one request fails, iteration stops and the `Promise.all` that executes the queued reminder deletions is skipped, so later cancelled reminders are not attempted in this run. Since this cron runs every 15 minutes, a reminder due before the next run can still be sent, and previously processed rows will also be retried. Handle failures per reminder so one failure does not block independent cancellations.

title: Reschedules bypass deferred cancellation and retry handling
body: The reschedule path calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` with `immediateDelete=true`, so it posts the cancellation to SendGrid immediately instead of marking the reminder `cancelled` for the cron. SendGrid keeps pending cancellations until their scheduled dates, which can again exhaust the 100-cancellation limit. Also, if this request fails, the helper only logs the error and never sets `cancelled`, so the cron will not retry and the old reminder can still be sent.

title: The cancellation cron can still exceed SendGrid's 100-cancellation limit
body: The one-hour window does not cap how many cancellations this loop submits. If more than 100 cancelled reminders are due within that window, SendGrid can reject requests after the limit; the surrounding catch then stops processing the remaining reminders. Those reminders remain scheduled and can be sent before a later cron run retries them. The cron needs to defer or otherwise limit requests so it does not exceed the pending-cancellation cap.

title: Immediate cancellations still fill SendGrid's pending-cancellation limit
body: When `immediateDelete` is true, this sends the SendGrid cancel request immediately and returns without setting `cancelled=true`. Rescheduling uses this path, as do workflow/step deletion, so far-future sends remain in SendGrid's pending-cancellation queue until their scheduled dates—the limit of 100 that this PR is intended to avoid can still be reached. Once reached, later cancellations can fail and reminders may be sent. If the request fails, the error is swallowed and the cron has no `cancelled` flag to retry. These cancellations need to use the deferred cancellation flow or otherwise ensure they are cleaned up and retried.

title: One failed cancellation aborts the rest of the cron batch
body: The `try` covers the entire loop, so a single failed SendGrid request exits the loop and skips every later cancelled reminder in the batch. Those reminders remain pending at SendGrid; if one becomes due before the next cron run, the initial cleanup at lines 34–41 deletes its database row before it can be retried, and the email can be sent. Handle failures per reminder or ensure due cancelled reminders are processed before cleanup.

title: Defer app imports until an app is selected
body: Each `import()` is executed while this object is constructed, so merely importing `@calcom/app-store` starts loading every integration module. Awaiting only the selected entry later does not prevent the other integrations and their dependencies from loading. This defeats on-demand loading and retains the startup and memory cost of loading all apps; store loader functions instead and invoke only the selected one.

title: Await the calendar cancellation callbacks
body: This callback now awaits the dynamic calendar import, but `forEach` discards the callback promise. The reschedule mutation can therefore continue to send emails and webhooks, and return, before the calendar deletion has started; a failed import also becomes an unhandled rejection. Await the callbacks (for example, with `Promise.all` over `map`) so cancellation completes or its failure is handled before reporting success.

title: Await the calendar cancellation callbacks
body: This callback now awaits the dynamic calendar import, but `forEach` discards the callback promise. `Reschedule` can send the reschedule email and return success before calendar deletion has started, and failures inside the async callback are not caught by the surrounding `try/catch`. Await the callbacks and handle their failures before reporting success.

title: Await the calendar cancellation callbacks
body: This callback now awaits the dynamic calendar import, but `forEach` discards the callback promise. `Reschedule` can send the reschedule email and return success before calendar deletion has started, and failures inside the async callback are not caught by the surrounding `try/catch`. Await the callbacks and handle their failures before reporting success.

title: All app imports start when the store is initialized
body: Each `import()` is evaluated while this object is constructed, so importing the store starts loading every app module, not just the app selected later. This defeats per-app lazy loading and makes unrelated app dependencies load and initialize for every consumer of the store.

title: Reschedule does not wait for asynchronous integration cleanup
body: `forEach` discards the promises returned by its async callbacks. The function can therefore send the reschedule email and return success before `getCalendar` and the calendar/video deletion finish. Rejections from the callback also bypass the surrounding `try/catch`, so an import or cleanup failure can leave the old integration event in place while the reschedule is reported as successful.

title: Reschedule does not wait for asynchronous integration cleanup
body: `forEach` discards the promises returned by its async callbacks. The function can therefore send the reschedule email and return success before `getCalendar` and the calendar/video deletion finish. Rejections from the callback also bypass the surrounding `try/catch`, so an import or cleanup failure can leave the old integration event in place while the reschedule is reported as successful.

title: The reschedule mutation does not wait for integration cleanup
body: `forEach` discards the promises returned by its async callbacks, so the mutation does not wait for `getCalendar` or the subsequent calendar/video deletion. It can continue to send the reschedule email and finish while the import or deletion is still pending; callback failures are unhandled and the old integration event can remain after the booking is canceled.

title: All app imports are still started eagerly
body: Each `import()` is evaluated while this object is constructed, so importing the app-store barrel immediately starts loading every app module, even when the caller needs only one. This does not provide on-demand loading and means a cold request that first touches the app store can still pay for loading and evaluating all app packages.

title: Reschedule does not wait for calendar deletion
body: `forEach` discards the promises returned by its async callbacks. Since `getCalendar` now requires an asynchronous import, the callback can still be waiting for the app module when this function finishes sending the email and returns; the old calendar event can therefore remain in place after rescheduling, and callback failures will not be caught by the surrounding `try/catch`. Await the callbacks, for example with `Promise.all`.

title: Reschedule does not wait for calendar deletion
body: `forEach` discards the promises returned by its async callbacks. Since `getCalendar` now requires an asynchronous import, the callback can still be waiting for the app module when this function finishes sending the email and returns; the old calendar event can therefore remain in place after rescheduling, and callback failures will not be caught by the surrounding `try/catch`. Await the callbacks, for example with `Promise.all`.

title: Recurring cancellation can finish before calendar deletions are tracked
body: The async callback is not awaited by `forEach`. It only adds a deletion to `apiDeletes` after awaiting both `getCalendar` and `deleteEvent`, while the outer handler can reach its later `Promise.all` before either finishes. The handler may then delete booking references and report cancellation without deleting the external recurring calendar events; any later callback failure also escapes the surrounding flow.

title: Reschedule does not wait for integration deletions
body: `forEach` discards the promises returned by its async callbacks. The mutation can proceed to send the reschedule email and return while a callback is still awaiting `getCalendar`, leaving the old calendar event undeleted when the request completes. Errors from those callbacks are also not propagated. Await the callbacks, for example with `Promise.all`.

title: Date overrides bypass booking and calendar conflict checks
body: When a slot falls within a date override, this returns `true` before the later `busy.every(...)` check. A date override should replace normal working hours, not make an already-booked or calendar-busy period available. This can expose slots that overlap existing bookings and allow double-booking the host.

title: Fixed-host working hours are not checked for full-slot containment
body: This uses `find` to reject a slot if any same-day working-hours row does not contain its start, rather than checking that one row contains the whole slot. If the host has no row for that weekday, the check falls through and treats them as available; with split hours, a valid slot in a later window can be rejected because it is outside an earlier window. Also, `end` is set to the slot start, so an event that runs past the end of a window is accepted. Round-robin slots can therefore be offered when a fixed host is unavailable, or hidden when they are available.

title: Date-override validation accepts partial overlaps and rejects later windows
body: These comparisons only reject slots wholly before or after an override; they do not require the entire slot to fit inside the override. For example, a 09:30–10:30 slot passes a 10:00–11:00 override even though it starts before availability. The `find` also stops at the first disjoint override, so a slot in a later same-day window (such as 13:00–17:00 after a 09:00–12:00 window) can be rejected before that window is checked. Validate that the slot is fully contained in at least one applicable override.

title: DST offset is calculated from the encoded instant, not the override wall time
body: Override times are represented as UTC clock fields for the organizer’s local hours (for example, 14:00Z can mean 14:00 in Asia/Kolkata). Applying `.tz()` to that `Date` treats it as an actual instant, so around a DST transition it can select the offset for a different local date or time. For example, a 03:30 America/New_York override on the spring-forward date is encoded as 03:30Z, which localizes to the previous evening and uses the pre-transition offset; the generated attendee time is then shifted by an hour.

title: The new regression test does not cover fixed-host round-robin overrides
body: The added timezone assertion uses the existing personal-event scenario, whose fixture has no round-robin scheduling type or fixed host. Consequently, none of the new test coverage verifies the advertised fix that makes a fixed host’s date override constrain round-robin availability.

title: The added slot assertion can pass when expected slots are missing
body: This assertion uses `toHaveTimeSlots`, whose implementation checks each actual slot against the expected array but does not require the actual and expected arrays to have equal lengths. If only the first of the four expected slots is returned, the assertion still passes, so the new timezone test can miss regressions that drop later slots.

title: Date overrides bypass booking and calendar conflicts
body: A slot inside a date override returns here before the `busy.every` check. An override should make the host available outside their normal hours, but it should not make existing bookings or calendar events disappear. As a result, getSchedule can advertise slots that conflict with a host's existing commitments, risking double bookings.
