title: Multiple override windows on one date reject each other's slots
body: The find callback returns true when a slot is outside an individual override, and find stops at the first true result. If a user has two separate override windows on the same date, a slot in either window is outside the other one and gets rejected before the matching window can be considered. Valid slots in multi-window date overrides are therefore hidden.

title: Working-hours validation does not check that one window contains the full slot
body: The validator sets end to the slot start instead of slot start plus eventLength, so a slot can be accepted even when the event runs past a host's working-hours end. It also returns an invalid result when the slot is outside any one same-day window, rather than checking whether some window contains it; users with split working hours can have valid slots rejected. In round-robin events, candidates from another host's availability can consequently be offered even when the fixed host cannot host the full event.

title: Timezone conversion drops date changes when an override crosses midnight
body: Adding the timezone offset can move the converted override to a different calendar day, but this code keeps only its hour and minute. The active-override selection still uses the original date, so the converted time is then placed on the wrong invitee day. For example, a 00:30 override in UTC+10 converted for a UTC invitee belongs to the previous day at 14:30, but the code selects it on the original day and places it at 14:30 there.

title: The start-time offset is reused for the override end across DST changes
body: The offset is calculated once from override.start and applied to override.end as well. If the override spans a daylight-saving transition, the organizer's offset can differ at the two endpoints, shifting the end time by an hour. For example, a New York override from 01:00 to 04:00 on the spring-forward day should end at 08:00 UTC for a UTC invitee, but reusing the start offset can extend it to 09:00 UTC and expose an extra hour.

title: The added test does not cover the fixed-host round-robin behavior
body: The new test changes the timezone for a personal event, but its scenario has no round-robin scheduling type or fixed hosts. It therefore does not exercise the primary claimed fix: filtering round-robin slots using a fixed host's date override. A regression in that path would not be caught by this test.

title: Date overrides bypass busy-time checks
body: When a slot falls within a date override, this returns `true` before the subsequent `busy.every` check. Existing bookings and calendar events are still reported in `busy`, so a host can be shown as available during an override despite already being booked, allowing a double booking. An override should replace regular working hours, not ignore busy times.

title: Multiple override windows reject each other
body: The `.find` callback returns a truthy value when the slot is outside the current override window, which immediately marks the slot unavailable without checking later windows. For example, with overrides 09:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00, a slot in either window is rejected because it falls outside the other one. Check whether the slot fits any window for that date instead.

title: Slots only need to overlap an override to be accepted
body: These checks reject slots wholly before or after an override, but accept any slot that overlaps it. For example, a 09:30–10:30 slot passes a 10:00–11:00 override even though it starts outside the host's availability. This can incorrectly count a fixed host as available for a slot generated from another host; require the entire slot to fit within the override.

title: Split working-hour windows make slots unavailable
body: This rejects a slot if `.find` finds any working-hour interval that does not contain it, rather than rejecting only when no interval contains it. With 09:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00 hours, a 10:00 slot is rejected because it is outside the second interval. Hosts with multiple windows on a day can therefore lose their availability.

title: Working-hour check ignores the event end time
body: `end` is calculated identically to `start`, so the check only verifies that the slot begins within a working-hour interval. A fixed host whose hours end at 10:00 can consequently be treated as available for a 09:30 slot lasting 60 minutes, even though the event ends at 10:30. Check the slot's actual end against the interval end.

title: Timezone conversion drops date changes across midnight
body: The timezone adjustment can move an override to the previous or next day, but this code keeps only its hour and minute and later anchors those to the unshifted invitee day. The active-override filter also selects overrides using the unshifted start date. For example, an override at 00:30 in UTC+5:30 maps to 19:00 on the prior UTC day, but is selected and placed on the original date for a UTC invitee. Availability near timezone day boundaries is therefore missing or shown on the wrong day.

title: Timezone test can pass when expected slots are missing
body: This assertion uses `toHaveTimeSlots`, whose implementation iterates the actual slots and compares each with the expected slot at that index. If the result contains only a matching prefix—for example, one of the four expected slots—the matcher still passes. The new timezone regression test therefore does not ensure that all expected slots are returned.

title: Migration fails when no embed category is configured
body: If `embed_category` is blank or has no matching category, this query returns no rows and indexing `[0]['id']` raises before the fallback below can run. Since the old setting defaults to blank, upgrades without an explicitly configured embed category can fail during migration, blocking the upgrade.

title: Legacy hosts with schemes are migrated in a form that never matches
body: This inserts the old setting value verbatim, bypassing `EmbeddableHost`'s normalization callback. Existing configurations may contain entries such as `http://example.com` (which the old host check accepts), but `record_for_host` later looks up only the parsed hostname `example.com`; those migrated entries will no longer authorize embeds.

title: Configured ports are discarded during host lookup
body: The model accepts and retains entries such as `example.com:8080`, but `URI(host).host` returns only `example.com`, without the port. This query therefore cannot find a configured host with a port, so embeds from that origin are rejected despite the entry passing validation.

title: Valid domains with longer top-level domains are rejected
body: The format limits the final label to 2–5 letters, so valid domains such as `example.museum` cannot be saved. Administrators cannot allow embeds from domains using longer top-level domains.

title: A null host raises before validation can report an error
body: When a create or update request supplies `host: null`, `self.host` is nil and calling `sub!` raises `NoMethodError` in the validation callback. The request returns a server error instead of the normal validation response for a missing host.

title: Duplicate host records make category routing ambiguous
body: The model and table do not enforce host uniqueness, while this lookup returns only one matching record. Administrators can create the same hostname with different categories; imported topics then use only the first matching record's category, so the other association is silently ignored.

title: Legacy hosts are skipped and then deleted
body: `embeddable_hosts` is the result of a `SELECT`, and PostgreSQL reports zero affected rows via `cmd_tuples` for a SELECT. This condition therefore skips copying the legacy host list, but line 31 still deletes the old settings. Upgrading a site with configured hosts loses its allowlist, so previously working embeds are rejected.

title: An unset legacy embed category aborts the migration
body: `embed_category` is optional and defaults to an empty value; if it is unset or does not match a category, this join returns no rows. Indexing `[0]['id']` then raises before the migration can fall back to the uncategorized category, preventing the upgrade. Handle an empty result before accessing the row.

title: Host lookup does not normalize both sides consistently
body: The saved host is only stripped of its scheme and path, while `URI(host).host` omits any port and preserves hostname casing; the query lowercases only the stored column. Consequently, a host accepted with a port (the validation explicitly allows ports) will never match, and an uppercase hostname in a request will fail to match a lowercase stored host. Normalize both values consistently so valid hosts are not rejected.

title: Duplicate host rows can assign embeds to the wrong category
body: There is no uniqueness validation or database index on `host`, so the admin UI can create multiple rows for the same hostname with different categories. `first` selects only one row, meaning the chosen category depends on which duplicate is returned and later edits to another duplicate may have no effect; newly imported topics can be assigned to the wrong category. Enforce one mapping per host.

title: Handle an unset legacy embedding category
body: The legacy `embed_category` setting is optional, so this query can return no rows when the setting is blank, unset, or names a category that no longer exists. Indexing `[0]['id']` then raises before the fallback below can run, preventing the migration and blocking upgrades for those sites. Check for a matching row before reading it and use the uncategorized category when none exists.

title: Do not use affected-row count to test a SELECT result
body: `cmd_tuples` reports rows affected by a command, not rows returned by this SELECT, so it is zero even when the legacy host setting exists. The migration therefore skips copying the host list and then deletes the original settings at line 31, permanently losing the configured allowlist. Check the result's returned-row count instead.

title: Normalize legacy host values during migration
body: This inserts each legacy value verbatim, bypassing `EmbeddableHost`'s normalization callback. Existing allowed-host entries may include a scheme or path, both of which the old configuration supported; `record_for_host` later compares against `URI(...).host`, which contains only the bare hostname. Those migrated entries will never match, so previously allowed sites lose embedding access. Strip schemes and paths before inserting.

title: Normalize the request hostname before matching
body: The query lowercases the stored host but compares it to the request host unchanged, so a valid referer such as `http://EXAMPLE.COM` will not match a configured `example.com`. Also, `URI(host).host` omits the port, while the model accepts and stores hosts such as `example.com:8080`, so those configured entries can never match. Normalize case and handle ports consistently on both sides.

title: Accept valid domains with longer top-level domains
body: The validation restricts the final domain label to 2–5 letters, rejecting valid hostnames with longer top-level domains, such as `example.museum` or `example.photography`. Administrators cannot add these otherwise valid embedding hosts.

title: Preserve unresolved plural foreign keys
body: This branch always replaces a `*_ids` field and deletes it, even when `_lookupSubType` cannot find the corresponding embedded object and returns `undefined`. If a REST-serialized payload includes IDs but omits the plural collection or an individual referenced item, the model loses the IDs and receives a relationship array containing `undefined`. Preserve the original IDs unless the related objects were actually resolved.

title: Untrusted upload type reaches a shell command
body: `type` comes directly from the request and is included in the tempfile prefix for API URL uploads. This call passes that tempfile path to `OptimizedImage.downsize`, whose optimizer interpolates paths into a backtick shell command without escaping. An API caller can supply shell metacharacters in `type` and an oversized image URL, causing arbitrary commands to run as the application process. Restrict `type` to known values and invoke the image tool with safely escaped arguments or an argv array.

title: The new definition overwrites the existing downsize signature
body: Ruby does not overload methods, so this definition replaces the preceding `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})`. Existing callers using that width/height form now fail: five arguments raise an arity error, while four arguments bind `max_height` as `opts` and later fail when it is indexed by `:force_aspect_ratio`. Preserve the old call form in a single method or update all callers.

title: Upload validation no longer honors the attachment size setting
body: This validator handles both images and attachments, but the fixed 10 MB limit replaces the per-type site setting. Attachments above a configured lower `max_attachment_size_kb` are now sent to the server only to be rejected there, while valid attachments cannot be selected when the configured limit is above 10 MB. Keep attachment validation tied to its configured limit and use a separate raw-upload cap for images that will be downsized.

title: Five resize attempts can still leave an image over the configured limit
body: The loop stops after five 80% dimension reductions even if the file remains larger than `max_image_size_kb`; the upload then reaches `Upload.create_for` and is rejected. For example, a high-entropy 10 MB PNG reduced by 80% in each dimension retains about 64% of its size per pass, leaving roughly 1.07 MB after five passes against a 1 MB limit. Continue resizing until the limit is met or report that downsizing failed.

title: The new downsize definition replaces the existing API
body: Ruby does not overload methods, so this definition replaces the four-dimension-argument `downsize` method immediately above it. Existing calls such as `downsize(from, to, width, height)` now treat `height` as the options argument and fail while building resize instructions; calls that also pass options raise an argument error. Preserve both call forms in one method or update every caller.

title: Oversized animated GIFs can be permanently reduced to one frame
body: When an oversized GIF is uploaded while `allow_animated_thumbnails` is false, this call selects the non-animated downsize path. That path reads only the GIF's first frame, and the result is written back to the upload's original tempfile, so the stored upload becomes a still image and the remaining animation frames are lost. Thumbnail animation settings should not silently destroy animation in the original upload.

title: Upload validation no longer honors the attachment size setting
body: This applies a fixed 10 MB limit to both images and attachments, even though validation receives the upload type and previously used the corresponding site setting. Sites configured to allow attachments larger than 10 MB now block valid files in the browser; sites with a lower attachment limit let oversized files through to a server-side rejection instead of enforcing the configured limit here.

title: Downsizing can permanently discard animation frames
body: When `allow_animated_thumbnails` is false, `OptimizedImage` uses its non-animated conversion path, which reads only `from[0]`. Because this call uses the same path for input and output, an oversized animated GIF is replaced with a still image and its remaining frames are lost. Thumbnail settings should not silently destroy animation in the uploaded file.

title: The client-side limit now ignores configured attachment sizes
body: This fixed 10 MB limit is applied to both images and attachments, bypassing the configured per-type limits. For example, installations that allow attachments larger than 10 MB will have valid uploads rejected in the browser; installations with a lower attachment limit will let users submit files the server then rejects. Keep attachment validation tied to its configured limit.

title: The second method definition overwrites the width/height form
body: Ruby does not overload methods by argument list, so this definition replaces the `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` definition immediately above it. Existing callers using the previously supported width/height arguments will now pass the height as `opts` or raise an argument error, breaking those callers. Use a single method that handles both forms or update all callers.

title: The unsubscribe link does not mute watched or tracked topics
body: When the current level is `tracking` or `watching`, this branch changes it only to `regular`, which still allows notifications such as replies and mentions. The page says notifications for the topic will stop, but those users can continue receiving them. Set the topic to `muted` for an unsubscribe action.

title: Saving the topic-user row directly bypasses notification-state bookkeeping
body: `TopicUser.change` is needed when changing a notification level: it records `notifications_changed_at` and the user-change reason, and publishes the level change. Saving the row directly leaves those fields unchanged; in particular, a row with a null reason can later be auto-tracked by `update_last_read`, undoing the unsubscribe. Use the shared change method so the preference persists and other clients are notified.

title: A GET request changes the user's notification preference
body: This route exposes `TopicsController#unsubscribe` as GET, and that action writes the user's topic notification level. A cross-site navigation or an email link scanner can therefore trigger the state change without an explicit user confirmation or a CSRF-protected state-changing request. Render a confirmation page on GET and apply the change through a protected POST.

title: The unsubscribe route does not resolve to the added template
body: This declares a top-level `topicUnsubscribe` route, which Ember resolves to the `topic-unsubscribe` template name, but the added template is at `templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs` (the path for a nested `topic.unsubscribe` route). There is no template-name override, so the unsubscribe page will not render its message and notification control.

title: A single click does not fully unsubscribe watched or tracked topics
body: When the user's level is tracking or watching, this branch sets it to regular rather than muted. Regular users can still receive notifications for direct replies and mentions, so the email's promise to stop notifications is not fulfilled by one click. Set the topic to muted for this unsubscribe action, or change the feature's behavior and wording to make the partial downgrade clear.

title: Direct save bypasses notification-level change handling
body: Saving the level directly skips the invariants in `TopicUser.change`: it does not set `notifications_changed_at` or mark the reason as `user_changed`, and it does not publish the level change to other open clients. In particular, a record whose reason is still nil can be auto-tracked by `TopicUser.update_last_read` on a later visit, re-enabling notifications after the user unsubscribes. Use the established change helper or apply the same state updates here.

title: The GET unsubscribe route allows cross-site state changes
body: This GET route invokes `TopicsController#unsubscribe`, which changes the logged-in user's topic notification level. Because GET requests do not receive Rails' normal CSRF verification, a third-party page can send a logged-in user to this URL and force a notification-level change. Use a state-changing method with CSRF protection, or a suitably user-bound signed token for the email link.

title: Unsubscribe does not mute users who are tracking or watching
body: When a user's notification level is `tracking` or `watching`, this branch lowers it only to `regular`. Regular topics can still send notifications for replies and mentions, so the page's promise to stop notifications is not met. Set the level to `muted` for every unsubscribe request, regardless of the starting level.

title: Saving the level directly lets auto-tracking undo the unsubscribe
body: This direct save bypasses `TopicUser.change`, which stamps `notifications_changed_at` and sets `notifications_reason_id` to `user_changed` when a notification level is explicitly changed. Email recipients can have a topic-user row with a nil reason; `update_last_read` treats that row as eligible for automatic tracking and can raise the level back to `tracking` after the user reads enough of the topic. Use the normal notification-level update path so the user's explicit preference is preserved.

title: The GET unsubscribe endpoint changes user state
body: This action is reached through a GET route but changes the current user's notification preference before returning the page. Because GET requests do not require a CSRF token, a cross-site link or navigation can trigger the change whenever the user has an active Discourse session. Keep GET read-only and require an explicit CSRF-protected action to apply the preference.

title: The route name does not match the added template path
body: This declares a top-level `topicUnsubscribe` route, whose conventional template lookup is for `topic-unsubscribe`; the added template is `templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs`, which corresponds to a nested `topic.unsubscribe` route. There is no explicit template-name override, so visiting this route will not render the unsubscribe page. Nest the route under `topic` or provide a template matching the declared route name.

title: Blocked-email matching is case-sensitive
body: This exact equality lookup misses a blocked address when the signup uses different casing, especially in the domain, which is case-insensitive. Signup assigns the submitted email without normalizing it, so an address on the blocklist can register by changing its capitalization. The unique index on `email` also permits differently cased duplicate entries.

title: Non-blocking matches are counted twice per signup
body: `should_block?` increments `match_count`, but this validator runs as part of validation and therefore has a write side effect. `UsersController#create` calls `user.valid?` and then, when validation passes, `user.save`, which validates again. For a matching `:do_nothing` entry, a single signup consequently increments `match_count` twice, so it does not represent the number of signup attempts.

title: Concurrent matches can lose counter increments
body: The counter update is a read-modify-save sequence. If two validations load the same `match_count` concurrently, both can save the same incremented value, losing one match. Since this field is intended to track matching attempts, use an atomic database increment or otherwise serialize updates.

title: Blocked-email matching can be bypassed with case variants
body: This lookup compares the submitted address exactly with the stored address, and the registration validation path does not canonicalize it first. Since email domains are case-insensitive, a blocklist entry for `bad@example.com` will not match `bad@EXAMPLE.COM`, allowing the latter to pass validation and register. Normalize stored and submitted addresses consistently, or use a case-insensitive comparison.

title: Validation side effects double-count blocked signup attempts
body: Calling `should_block?` increments the stored match statistics during model validation. `UsersController#create` calls `user.valid?` and then calls `user.save`, which validates again; a single blocked signup attempt therefore increments `match_count` twice. Keep statistics tracking out of validation or ensure it runs once per signup attempt.

title: Concurrent matches can lose counter increments
body: This read-modify-save sequence is not atomic. If two blocked signup validations load the same `match_count` before either saves, both can write the same incremented value, so the final count increases by one instead of two. Use an atomic database increment (and update `last_match_at` atomically) to preserve the statistics under concurrent requests.

title: Exact email lookup lets casing changes bypass the blocklist
body: This lookup compares the submitted address verbatim with the stored address, and signup does not normalize the email before validation. Because email domains are case-insensitive, a user can submit the same address with different domain casing (for example, `bad@SPAMCLUB.COM` instead of `bad@spamclub.com`) and avoid the blocklist match. Normalize both stored and submitted addresses before comparing them.

title: Validation side effects count each signup attempt more than once
body: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` increments match statistics, but it is called from a validator, which can run multiple times for one operation. In particular, `UsersController#create` calls `user.valid?` and then `user.save`, which validates again; a matching address therefore increments `match_count` twice for one signup attempt. Keep validation side-effect-free and record a match once at the submission boundary.

title: Concurrent matches can lose counter increments
body: The counter is updated with a read-modify-save sequence. If two signup validations load the same row before either saves, both can write the same incremented value, losing one match from `match_count`. Use an atomic database increment (and update the timestamp atomically) or lock the row.

title: The best-embed template has invalid ERB/Ruby syntax
body: This tag ends with `end if`, leaving a postfix `if` with no condition. The generated template cannot compile, so requests that render an existing embed fail instead of displaying the discussion. Close the conditional with `end`.

title: Imported content is rendered as unsanitized HTML
body: This assigns imported content the `raw_html` cook method, and `Post#cook` returns that raw string without sanitizing it. RSS item content is externally supplied, so a feed entry containing script or event-handler markup is stored and can execute for users viewing the post or embed. Sanitize imported HTML before it is persisted or rendered.

title: Remote article fetching permits SSRF through redirects
body: The worker fetches the supplied URL with `open`, but the host check in `TopicRetriever` validates only the initial URL. `open-uri` follows redirects, so a URL on the configured host can redirect to a private or internal address; the fetched response is then imported into a public topic. Validate every redirect destination and reject private/internal addresses (and disallowed ports) before fetching.

title: Standard RSS items without a `content` field abort feed polling
body: The poller assumes every parsed item has `content` and calls `scrub` on it. Common RSS feeds provide their body in `description` instead, leaving `i.content` nil; that raises an exception and stops the poll before the remaining items are imported. Handle the RSS description field as a fallback and tolerate missing content.

title: Imported feed HTML bypasses post sanitization
body: This creates imported posts with `cook_method: raw_html`, so `Post#cook` stores the supplied HTML without the normal rendering and sanitization pipeline. RSS content is external input, and the polling code explicitly unescapes it; a feed publisher can therefore inject script-capable markup that is persisted and executed when users view the topic.

title: Remote fetches can follow redirects to internal services
body: `open(url)` follows HTTP redirects, but the embed URL is only checked against `embeddable_host` before this call. A URL on that host that redirects to a private or loopback address can make the server fetch internal resources; the response is then parsed and imported into a public topic, potentially exposing internal data.

title: The Referer check can be forged to trigger imports
body: A non-browser client can set an arbitrary `Referer` header, so this does not restrict requests to pages actually hosted on `embeddable_host`. Anyone can pass the check, request an uncached URL on that host, and cause `best` to enqueue a retrieval that may create a public topic. The per-URL throttle does not prevent abuse with distinct URLs.

title: Description-only RSS items stop feed polling
body: Standard RSS items commonly provide their body in `<description>`, not `<content>`. For an item without a `content` field, `i.content.scrub` raises instead of importing it; because the exception is not handled, it also prevents later items in the feed from being processed.

title: Message origins are checked by substring rather than exact match
body: This accepts any message origin that appears anywhere in `discourseUrl`, including a different origin that is a prefix of the configured forum hostname (for example, `https://forum.example.co` when the URL is `https://forum.example.com/`). Such a sender can post a `discourse-resize` message and manipulate the iframe height on the embedding page; compare parsed origins exactly.

title: Raw HTML imports bypass post sanitization
body: Posts imported from RSS are assigned `cook_method: raw_html`, so this branch stores the feed's HTML directly as `cooked` instead of passing it through the normal rendering and sanitization pipeline. Feed content is unescaped before import and is rendered as HTML, so a feed publisher can inject scripts or event handlers that execute on forum pages with the forum's origin and user privileges. Sanitize imported HTML before it is stored or rendered.

title: Remote fetches can follow redirects to internal addresses
body: The embed URL's hostname is checked before this fetch, but `open-uri` follows HTTP redirects without rechecking the destination. An allowed-host URL that redirects to loopback, a private network address, or cloud metadata can therefore make the server fetch internal resources; the response is then passed into the import path. Restrict redirect targets and reject private or otherwise non-public resolved addresses.

title: RSS items with only a description abort feed polling
body: A standard RSS item commonly provides its body in `<description>` rather than `content`; when SimpleRSS has no `content` value, calling `.scrub` on it raises `NoMethodError`. That aborts the poll before later items are processed, and this job has retries disabled. Fall back to the item's description (and handle items with neither field).

title: The iframe height attribute is assigned an invalid value
body: `HTMLIFrameElement.height` reflects an integer-pixel HTML attribute, but this assigns a value such as `500px`. Browsers can treat that as invalid and use the default iframe height instead, leaving the embed clipped even after receiving a resize message. Assign the numeric pixel value or set `iframe.style.height`.

title: The embed URL column truncates valid long URLs
body: A Rails `string` column defaults to `varchar(255)`, while valid embed URLs can exceed 255 characters, especially when they contain query parameters. Saving such an embed raises a database error inside the topic transaction, so the topic import is rolled back. Use a column type and index strategy that support the intended URL lengths.

title: The throttle key can be left without an expiration
body: `SETNX` and `EXPIRE` are separate Redis operations. If the process stops or the second command fails after `SETNX` succeeds, the key remains indefinitely; subsequent non-staff retrieval attempts then treat the URL as recently retrieved and never fetch it. Set the key and TTL atomically, or remove the key when expiration setup fails.

title: Flex layout disables the action button's right float
body: Making `.small-action` a flex container turns its direct children into flex items, so the `float: right` on the button at line 306 no longer positions it at the right edge. Since the description has no `flex-grow` and the button has no auto margin, short small-action descriptions leave the button immediately after the text instead of right-aligned. Add flex alignment for the button or make the description fill the available space.

title: Legacy flexbox fallback no longer right-aligns the panel
body: The new `flexbox()` mixin falls back to the legacy `-webkit-box`/`-moz-box` layout in older browsers, but `margin-left: auto` does not push an item to the far edge in that legacy box model. Since the previous `float: right` was removed, the header panel will sit beside the title instead of at the right edge in browsers that use this fallback. Add a legacy-compatible spacing rule or avoid selecting the legacy box layout without one.

title: The legacy Mozilla box fallback cannot apply item alignment
body: `flexbox()` and `inline-flex()` emit `-moz-box` and `-moz-inline-box` fallbacks, but `align-items()` does not emit the corresponding `-moz-box-align` property. In older Firefox versions that use those display fallbacks, the new header centering and badge baseline alignment are ignored, so those layouts differ from browsers using modern flexbox. Add the Mozilla legacy alignment declaration if these fallbacks are intended to work.

title: The small-action button no longer floats to the right
body: Making `.small-action` a flex container causes its button child to ignore the existing `float: right`. Since `.small-action-desc` has no flex-grow, the button can sit directly beside the message instead of at the far right, changing the placement of the action control. Give the description flexible space or push the button to the end with a flex-compatible rule.

title: The legacy flexbox fallback may not keep the panel right-aligned
body: For browsers that use the `-webkit-box` or `-moz-box` fallback but do not support modern flexbox, `margin-left: auto` does not provide the modern flex auto-margin behavior that pushes the panel to the right. The previous `float: right` has also been removed, so the panel can sit beside the title rather than at the right edge.

title: The old Firefox flexbox fallback omits its alignment property
body: `flexbox()` emits `display: -moz-box` for older Firefox, but `align-items()` does not emit the corresponding `-moz-box-align`. In browsers using that fallback, requested vertical alignment (such as the header's `center`) is ignored and the items use the old box model's default alignment. Add the matching legacy property or remove the fallback.

title: The derived website name bypasses the untrusted website restriction
body: For anonymous viewers of TL0 users, `website` is intentionally omitted by `untrusted_attributes`, but `website_name` is a separate serialized attribute and is not subject to that restriction. The `include_website_name` method does not implement the serializer's `include_website_name?` predicate, so it does not prevent serialization. As a result, the website hostname and path can still be exposed to viewers who are meant not to see the website. Apply the same restriction to `website_name` and add a regression test with a populated website.

title: Website labels drop explicit ports
body: `URI#host` excludes the port, so a website such as `http://example.com:8443/user` is labeled `example.com/user` when the instance host matches, or just `example.com` otherwise. The link still targets port 8443, but the displayed label hides that part of its destination; the previous client-side parsing preserved it. Include the port in the serialized label when one is present.

title: Derived website name bypasses TL0 privacy filtering
body: `include_website_name` is not the serializer predicate `include_website_name?`, and `website_name` is not covered by `untrusted_attributes`. The serializer therefore includes this derived value even when `include_website?` hides a TL0 user's website from anonymous viewers. Because `website_name` contains the website host and may include its path, anonymous users can still see information the website restriction is meant to hide. Apply the same restriction to `website_name` and add a regression test for an anonymous viewer.

title: Website labels drop non-default ports
body: `URI#host` excludes the port. For a profile URL such as `https://example.org:8443/user`, `website_name` becomes `example.org` (or `example.org/user` when the host matches the instance), whereas the previous display included `:8443`. The profile label can therefore misidentify the endpoint, especially when multiple services share a host. Preserve an explicitly specified port in the displayed host.

title: Website privacy restriction is bypassed by website_name
body: `website` is an untrusted attribute, so it is omitted for anonymous viewers of TL0 users when `restrict_user_fields?` applies. The newly serialized `website_name` is not in `untrusted_attributes`, and its inclusion method lacks the `?` used by the serializer's inclusion checks. It therefore still exposes the website host—and sometimes its path—in the user JSON, bypassing the existing privacy restriction.

title: Preserve the original light-theme color scaling
body: This link previously used `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)`, but the first `dark-light-choose` branch now uses 70%. Light themes select that first branch, so this change makes the link substantially lighter than before; the dark-theme branch also uses 30% of `$secondary` rather than the complementary 70%. Keep the 30% primary value and use 70% for the secondary value.

title: Custom-message length color uses reversed lightness values
body: This color previously scaled `$primary` by 70%, but the first `dark-light-choose` branch now scales it by 30%. Light themes therefore render a different, darker color than before, and the secondary branch uses 70% where the complementary value is 30%. Preserve the original 70% primary scaling and use 30% for the secondary branch.

title: Group member name color no longer preserves the light-theme value
body: The group-member name previously used `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)`, but the first `dark-light-choose` branch now uses 50%. Light themes select this branch, so the name becomes noticeably lighter than before; the corresponding dark-theme value should use 70% of `$secondary`. Restore the 30% primary value and use 70% for the secondary value.

title: Mobile group member name color no longer preserves the light-theme value
body: The group-member name previously used `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)`, but the first `dark-light-choose` branch now uses 50%. Light themes select this branch, so the name becomes noticeably lighter than before; the corresponding dark-theme value should use 70% of `$secondary`. Restore the 30% primary value and use 70% for the secondary value.

title: Topic-map heading lightness changed unintentionally
body: This heading previously used `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%)`, but the first `dark-light-choose` branch now uses 50%. Light themes select that branch, changing the existing heading color, and the complementary dark-theme branch should use 80% of `$secondary`. Preserve the 20% primary value and use 80% for the secondary value.

title: Public group pages only load the first 50 members
body: This now applies pagination to every group, whereas the previous endpoint only limited automatic groups. The public group-members route loads members once, and its template has no pagination controls, so members beyond the first 50 are inaccessible on groups with more than 50 members.

title: Exact multiples of the page size show a phantom page
body: Adding one after `Math.floor` reports an extra page whenever `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit` (for example, 50 members at a limit of 50 reports 2 pages). The Next control then requests an empty page, and the UI displays a page that does not exist.

title: Removing members from the last page can leave the list on an empty page
body: After a member is removed, `findMembers` computes the request offset using the pre-removal `user_count`. If the removal makes the current last-page offset invalid, the request returns no members and the model keeps that out-of-range offset, leaving the admin list blank until someone manually navigates back.

title: The public members endpoint changes its response shape
body: This replaces the endpoint's serialized array response with an object containing `members` and `meta`. Existing clients of `/groups/:name/members.json` that parse the response as an array will break; this is an unversioned contract change.

title: Exact page-size counts produce an extra page
body: When `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`, this formula adds an extra page: 50 members at a limit of 50 reports 2 pages, and 100 reports 3. The admin next action can then fetch at `offset == user_count`, showing an empty page that the UI treats as valid. Calculate the ceiling of `user_count / limit` (while preserving the zero-member case).

title: Public group member lists are silently truncated at 50
body: This query now limits every group's members, but the public group-members route fetches the list only once and its template has no pagination controls. Groups with more than 50 members therefore display only the first 50; previously ordinary groups returned all members, and automatic groups could return up to 200. Add pagination to the public page or preserve its ability to load the full list.

title: Exact page-sized groups show a phantom page
body: `floor(user_count / limit) + 1` overcounts whenever the member count is an exact multiple of the page size. For example, 50 members at a limit of 50 are shown as 1/2, and Next loads an empty page. Use a ceiling-based page count instead.

title: Removing the last member on a page leaves the list empty
body: After a member is removed, `removeMember` reloads the current page, but this offset is clamped using the model's pre-removal `user_count`. If the removed member was the only one on the last page, the requested offset is now at or past the new total, so the refresh returns no members and leaves the UI on an empty page. Adjust the offset after receiving the updated total, or move back a page when necessary.

title: Fallback locales are loaded only during controller requests
body: The translation accelerator loads only the active locale when `I18n.t` is called; this callback is the only new code that loads the fallback locales. Calls from Sidekiq jobs, rake tasks, or other code outside a controller request therefore try fallback lookups without having loaded those locale files, so translations that should fall back can still be missing. Load the fallback chain as part of translation lookup or initialize it for non-request processes too.

title: Changing the site locale can leave cached translations stale
body: This fallback chain depends on the mutable `SiteSetting.default_locale`, but the translation accelerator caches results by translation key, active locale, and backend—not by the fallback chain. For a logged-in user whose locale is unchanged, changing the site default can leave translations cached from the old fallback locale, so they continue seeing the old text until the cache is cleared. Include the fallback configuration in cache invalidation or otherwise invalidate translations when the setting changes.

title: Cached translations ignore changes to the site fallback locale
body: Fallback results depend on `SiteSetting.default_locale`, but the translation accelerator caches by translation key and requested locale without including the fallback locale in its cache key. If an administrator changes the site default while the process is running, translations missing in a user's locale can keep returning text from the old default indefinitely, even though the new fallback translations are loaded.

title: Fallback locales are loaded only for controller requests
body: This is the only call that preloads fallback locales, so translations outside controller requests (for example, in a background job or mailer that switches to a user's locale) do not load the site-default or English catalogs. The translation accelerator loads only the current locale, and the fallback backend cannot find translations in catalogs that have not been loaded; such calls can return missing translations instead of falling back.

title: Fallback locales are loaded only for controller requests
body: This loads the fallback chain only in the controller locale filter. The translation accelerator loads only the active locale, and translations are loaded on demand, so a mailer or background job that sets a non-default locale and calls `I18n.t` without passing through this filter cannot find missing keys in the site-default or English locale. Such calls return missing translations instead of the configured fallback.

title: Changing the site default locale can leave cached translations stale
body: The fallback chain depends on the current `SiteSetting.default_locale`, but the translation accelerator caches results using only the key, active locale, and backend identity. After the site default locale changes, a key missing from the active locale can continue returning the translation from the old default locale until its cache entry is evicted or the process restarts.

title: Cached denials prevent newly granted access from reaching the database
body: This short-circuits every check with a cached denial before checking current permissions. If a resource was denied and then created or granted to the user, subsequent checks for the same namespace, action, name, and folder continue to return false until the denial entry expires (30 seconds), even though the database now grants access. This undermines the fresh-permission fallback intended to let creators access newly created resources.

title: Denial cache keys omit the identity type
body: This key is used for users, service accounts, anonymous identities, and render services, but includes only the parsed UID. For example, `anonymous:0` and `render:0` both have UID `0`; an anonymous denial for a dashboard can therefore be reused for a renderer check that should be allowed. Include the identity type in the key to prevent one principal's denial from blocking another principal for the cache TTL.

title: Underscore-separated fields make denial keys ambiguous
body: The name and parent folder are concatenated without escaping or length delimiters. For example, `(name="a_b", parent="c")` and `(name="a", parent="b_c")` produce the same key. Since resource and folder UIDs can contain underscores, a denial for one resource can incorrectly deny access to a different, permitted resource until the entry expires. Encode the fields unambiguously.

title: Denial cache key does not distinguish identity types
body: The key uses `UserUID` but not `IdentityType`. For example, `anonymous:0` and `render:0` both produce the UID `0`; a cached denial for an anonymous dashboard read can therefore make a renderer check for the same resource return denied before the renderer’s wildcard read permission is evaluated. The reverse can also deny an anonymous user who has permission. Include the identity type in the denial key to prevent one identity’s decision from affecting another.

title: Denial key can collide for different resource and folder pairs
body: The key concatenates `name` and `parent` with an unescaped underscore. Since dashboard and folder UIDs can contain underscores, `(name="a_b", parent="c")` and `(name="a", parent="b_c")` produce the same key. A denial for the first check then short-circuits the second check even if that resource is allowed, for up to the cache TTL. Encode the components unambiguously, such as with length prefixes.

title: Federated rules are no longer treated as immutable
body: This refactor replaces the previous `isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` check with `false`. `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` now forwards only the ruler rule and a group identifier, so federated-group metadata is lost and the Update/Delete/Pause abilities can be allowed whenever ordinary permissions permit them. This regresses the prior protection for federated Mimir rules and can expose edits or deletions that the UI previously blocked.

title: Prometheus-only list items cannot expose pause or delete actions
body: The new `GrafanaRuleListItem` supplies `promRule` but no `rulerRule`. As a result, the Delete menu item is hidden by this `rulerRule` guard even when `canDelete` is true; the Pause item has the same ruler-rule requirement at line 123. This prevents users from pausing or deleting Grafana rules directly from the list, despite the new Prometheus-rule ability checks and the identifier-based delete callback.

title: Silence menu action does not open a drawer for Prometheus-only rules
body: The new Grafana list item passes its rule as `promRule` and leaves `rule` undefined. The menu can still show Silence based on that Prometheus rule, but clicking it only sets `showSilenceDrawer`; this condition prevents the drawer from rendering because it requires a Grafana ruler rule. Users therefore see a Silence action that does nothing in the new list view.

title: Rule view links no longer preserve the return destination
body: This URL omits the `returnTo` value that the removed loader added to Grafana rule view links. When a user opens a rule from a filtered or searched list and uses the detail page's return navigation, Grafana can no longer restore that list context and instead falls back to its default destination.

title: Silence action opens no drawer for list rules
body: This list item passes only `promRule` to `RuleActionsButtons`, so `rulerRule` is undefined. The menu can still show Silence based on the Prometheus rule abilities, but the silence drawer is rendered only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true. Clicking Silence therefore sets state without displaying a drawer, leaving the action unusable.

title: Pause and delete actions disappear from Grafana rule menus
body: The new list path supplies no `rulerRule`, but `AlertRuleMenu` renders both Pause and Delete only when a ruler rule is present. Consequently, Grafana rules in this list lose those actions even when the Prometheus-based ability checks say the user is allowed to perform them. This removes actions that were available in the previous list view.

title: Federated rules are no longer treated as immutable
body: The previous `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` checked `rule.group` for federated rule groups before allowing edits or deletes. It now delegates to this helper, which hardcodes `isFederated` to false and no longer has the group metadata needed for that check. As a result, rules in federated Mimir groups can be presented as editable or deletable even though those operations were previously disabled as unsupported.

title: Rule links no longer preserve the return destination
body: The previous Grafana rule list item added a `returnTo` URL when linking to a rule's details; this replacement omits it. Opening a rule from a filtered or grouped list therefore loses the originating list location, so the details page's return navigation cannot reliably restore the user's prior view and filters.

title: Prometheus-only rows break existing rule actions
body: This supplies only `promRule`, so the menu receives no `rulerRule`. The menu still requires a ruler rule to render Pause and Delete, making both actions disappear from the new Grafana list. It can also show Silence based on the Prometheus rule, but the drawer is only mounted when a ruler alert rule exists, so clicking Silence does nothing. Adapt these actions to work with the Prometheus DTO or avoid exposing a nonfunctional action.

title: Rule view links no longer preserve the originating list URL
body: The previous Grafana rule loader added a `returnTo` URL to this view link. Omitting it means opening a rule from a filtered or otherwise customized rule list loses that originating context when the user returns from the rule view. Preserve the current return URL as before.

title: Federated rules are no longer treated as immutable
body: The previous `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` checked `rule.group` for `source_tenants` and disabled editing and deletion for federated rules. This refactor drops the group information and hardcodes `isFederated` to false, so callers of the combined-rule ability hook now expose Update, Delete, and related actions for federated rules that were intentionally blocked. Preserve the federated-group check when delegating to the new hook.

title: Preserve range-variable detection before interpolation
body: This interpolates the expression before `querySupportsSplitting` checks `isQueryWithRangeVariable`. When Grafana resolves `$__range`, the guard no longer sees the variable and a query that is explicitly meant to avoid splitting is partitioned into time chunks. The chunks then use an interpolated range value rather than the original backend-per-request range behavior, changing query semantics and potentially repeating full-range scans. Determine split eligibility from the original expression, or retain its range-variable status through interpolation.

title: Avoid applying template variables twice to sharded targets
body: The shard path interpolates targets here, then passes each shard request to `runSplitQuery`, which now calls `applyTemplateVariables` again. Template interpolation is not generally idempotent: if a variable's value contains a literal `$name` sequence, the second pass can interpret it as another variable and silently change the query sent to Loki. Apply variables once in this path, or ensure the nested split call does not re-interpolate already-expanded targets.

title: Preserve range-variable checks before interpolation
body: This interpolates each expression before `querySupportsSplitting` checks it. If `applyTemplateVariables` expands `$__range`, the later `isQueryWithRangeVariable` guard can no longer recognize the query and it will be split. That guard exists because `$__range` must be evaluated against the split time range; instead, each chunk can use the full dashboard-range value, producing incorrect or overlapping results. Check split eligibility against the original expression or preserve range-variable queries as non-splitting.

title: Drop targets that become empty after interpolation
body: The empty-expression filter runs before interpolation. A nonempty expression such as `$query` can pass that filter and then resolve to an empty string, but it is still partitioned and sent to `runQuery` as an empty Loki expression. This bypasses the existing empty-query skip and can produce unnecessary backend requests and parse errors. Filter the interpolated targets for empty expressions as well.

title: Preserve the `$__range` check before interpolation
body: This interpolates each expression before `querySupportsSplitting` checks it. When `applyTemplateVariables` expands `$__range`, `isQueryWithRangeVariable` can no longer recognize the macro, so a query that the existing guard deliberately keeps unsplit is divided into time chunks. That changes the macro’s intended range semantics and can produce incorrect results. The same eager interpolation in `shardQuerySplitting.ts` also affects the sharded path; retain whether the original expression contained `$__range` when deciding whether to split.

title: Preserve trace IDs in plugin request completion logs
body: This removes the explicit `traceID` field previously added with `tracing.TraceIDFromContext`. The new contextual logger middleware adds endpoint, plugin, datasource, and user attributes, but does not add a trace ID, so completion logs for traced plugin requests can no longer be correlated with their traces.

title: Keep contextual log calls observable in TestLogger
body: `FromContext` returns a fresh `TestLogger` with separate counters and no shared recorder. `LoggerMiddleware` now logs through `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)`, so tests that inject a `TestLogger` and inspect the original instance will see no completion log and cannot reliably assert that it was emitted. Return a logger sharing the original capture state, or otherwise make derived logger calls observable.

title: Preserve trace IDs in completion logs
body: `logRequest` no longer adds the `traceID` field that it previously extracted from the request context. The new contextual logger middleware adds endpoint, plugin, datasource, and user attributes, but not the trace ID, so `grafana-data-egress` completion logs lose their direct correlation with distributed traces. Preserve the trace ID as a log field or contextual attribute.

title: Keep contextual test logs observable
body: `FromContext` returns a new `TestLogger` with separate log fields. `LoggerMiddleware` now writes through `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)`, so when a test injects a `TestLogger` and checks that instance, the completion log is recorded only on this discarded child and the test sees no call. Return the same logger or share log storage between contextual instances.

title: Plugin request logs no longer include the trace ID
body: The previous `logRequest` added `traceID` to the completion log when one was available. This log parameter list omits it, and the new contextual logger middleware does not add a trace ID to the context attributes. As a result, plugin request completion logs lose their direct trace correlation, making it harder to investigate requests that also emit tracing data.

title: FromContext discards logs recorded by the test logger
body: `FromContext` returns a fresh `TestLogger` with independent log fields. `LoggerMiddleware` now logs through the logger returned by `FromContext`, so tests that inspect the original `TestLogger` will see no calls or messages. Return the same fake or share its recorded log state so middleware logging remains observable in tests.

title: Rejected devices remain cached and can bypass the limit
body: `tagDeviceUI` caches the device ID before calling the store. When the store returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, this error is propagated but the cache entry is not removed. The next request with the same ID hits the cache, skips the store check, and authenticates successfully for the cache lifetime, bypassing the configured device limit.

title: Device count and insert are not atomic
body: The limit check counts devices in a separate operation from the subsequent insert. Concurrent requests for distinct devices can all observe a count below the limit and then all insert successfully, exceeding the configured limit; this can also happen across Grafana instances. Enforce capacity atomically rather than relying on this count-then-insert sequence.

title: A no-op MySQL update is treated as a limit rejection
body: MySQL normally reports only changed rows from `RowsAffected`. At the limit, updating an existing device can leave every field unchanged—for example, when another Grafana instance handles the same device in the same second and the IP and user agent match, given the database's second-level timestamp precision. In that case this check returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` and rejects a device that should be allowed.

title: Document the new anonymous device-limit setting
body: This adds `auth.anonymous.device_limit` as a configurable setting, but the PR does not update the default configuration or configuration documentation. Operators have no documented way to discover the setting or understand its default and behavior, making the feature difficult to configure correctly.

title: A failed device-limit check is cached, allowing the next request through
body: `tagDeviceUI` adds the device ID to the local cache before storing it. When storage returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, this return propagates the error and the first authentication is rejected, but the cache entry is not removed. The next request with the same device ID hits the cache and returns success without checking the limit, so a retry bypasses the configured cap. Remove the cache entry after a failed store or cache only successful stores.

title: Concurrent registrations can exceed the configured device limit
body: The limit check counts devices separately from the later insert, with no lock or atomic database constraint covering both operations. Concurrent requests for different device IDs can all observe a count below the limit and then insert, exceeding the configured maximum; this can also happen across Grafana instances sharing the database. Enforce the limit atomically across the count-and-insert operation.

title: Document the new anonymous device-limit setting
body: This reads `auth.anonymous.device_limit`, but the setting is not added to the shipped defaults or configuration reference. Administrators cannot discover the option or learn its default and semantics from Grafana's configuration documentation. Add a documented `device_limit` entry, including that zero disables the limit.

title: A retry bypasses the device limit after the first rejection
body: `tagDeviceUI` adds the device ID to the local cache before persisting it and does not evict the entry when persistence fails. With this new error propagation, the first request for an over-limit device is rejected, but subsequent requests with the same ID hit the cache and return successfully without checking the limit. A retry can therefore authenticate despite the configured cap for the cache TTL. Only cache the ID after a successful store operation, or remove it on failure.

title: Concurrent registrations can exceed the configured limit
body: The device count check and the subsequent insert are separate database operations with no reservation or lock. Concurrent requests for different device IDs can both observe a count below the limit and both insert, leaving the database above the configured cap. This can also happen across Grafana instances sharing the database. Enforce the cap atomically across the count-and-insert operation.

title: A no-op update can reject an existing device on MySQL
body: This treats zero affected rows as proof that the device is absent. MySQL normally reports changed rows, not matched rows, so an update that matches an existing device but changes no values can return zero. Since MySQL timestamps are stored at second precision, a request on another instance in the same second with the same IP and user agent can leave every updated column unchanged and incorrectly return `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, rejecting an already-registered device when the cap is full. Check whether the row exists independently of whether the update changed it, or otherwise handle the database's matched-row semantics.

title: The new configuration option is not documented
body: This introduces `auth.anonymous.device_limit`, but the PR does not add it to the shipped configuration reference or defaults documentation. Operators cannot discover the setting or learn its default and behavior, making the feature difficult to configure reliably.

title: Building the SQLite ID list performs quadratic copying
body: Each iteration formats the entire accumulated ID string again, so constructing a list of N IDs copies O(N²) bytes and creates O(N²) allocation pressure. With the 32,767-ID batch size used by the new test, this can copy several gigabytes of strings for one delete batch, causing substantial CPU and GC overhead. Build the list with a `strings.Builder` or an append buffer instead.

title: All cleanup jobs now run ten times more often
body: Changing the ticker from ten minutes to one minute increases the frequency of every cleanup job, not just annotation cleanup. This also increases database and filesystem work for snapshots, dashboard versions, images, query history, and other jobs; if a cleanup run takes over a minute, the buffered ticker can cause runs to start back-to-back. The PR description does not explain this broader workload change.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged at error level
body: This and the corresponding cleanup logs use `r.log.Error` for normal batch progress, including cases where `err` is nil (the same occurs at lines 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579). Every successful cleanup therefore generates error-level log records, and the records include the batch's IDs. This creates misleading error noise and can trigger log-based alerts during routine cleanup.

title: Build large SQLite ID lists without repeatedly copying them
body: When the configured batch size exceeds SQLite’s parameter limit, this loop rebuilds the entire accumulated string for every ID. Constructing a batch of tens of thousands of IDs therefore performs quadratic copying and can allocate gigabytes cumulatively, making cleanup and the large-batch test unnecessarily slow. Use a builder or join preformatted IDs instead.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors
body: This log runs after a successful ID query and uses the error level even when `err` is nil; the corresponding cleanup and orphan-tag batch logs do the same. Normal cleanup—including empty final batches—therefore produces error-level events, which can trigger false alerts and flood error logs.

title: The cleanup interval increases tenfold for every cleanup job
body: Changing the ticker from 10 minutes to 1 minute makes the entire cleanup job list run up to ten times as often, not just annotation cleanup. This increases recurring database and filesystem work for snapshots, dashboard versions, images, query history, and other jobs, despite the PR describing only a change to annotation deletion.

title: Large configured batches can exceed database bind-parameter limits
body: For every non-SQLite database, this creates one bind parameter per selected ID. PostgreSQL and MySQL support at most 65,535 parameters in a statement, so a valid batch-size configuration above that limit will make cleanup fail whenever a batch contains more than 65,535 rows. Split deletes into parameter-safe chunks or otherwise cap the number of bound IDs.

title: Max-count cleanup can delete annotations that moved into the retained set
body: The IDs are selected using the max-count offset, then deleted in a separate statement without rechecking their rank. If another request deletes a newer annotation between those statements, a selected ID can move into the set that should be retained but will still be deleted. For example, with a max count of 1, cleanup selects the older of two annotations; if a user deletes the newer one before this delete, cleanup then removes the only remaining annotation.

title: Building SQLite ID lists with repeated formatting has quadratic cost
body: Each iteration copies the entire accumulated string with `fmt.Sprintf`, so constructing the IN-list takes quadratic time and allocation in the number of IDs. The added test exercises this path with batches containing over 13,000 IDs, causing hundreds of megabytes of cumulative string allocations per list; larger configured batches can impose substantial CPU and GC pressure on cleanup.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors with every ID
body: This logs each batch at error level and includes the full ID list even when the query succeeded; the subsequent delete log does the same. Normal cleanup therefore produces error-level log entries and potentially very large log messages for every batch, creating alert noise and avoidable log-volume overhead.

title: Async legacy writes inherit request cancellation
body: `WithTimeoutCause` derives the new context from the incoming request context; it does not detach it. When the API server finishes the request, cancellation propagates to this goroutine, potentially aborting the legacy write before the 10-second timeout. The same pattern is used for delete, update, and delete-collection, so successful unified writes may not be mirrored. Use a context that preserves needed values but is independent of request cancellation, then apply the timeout.

title: Independent goroutines can reorder writes for the same object
body: Each successful request launches an independent legacy-write goroutine, with no ordering or version guard. For example, an update can reach legacy before the earlier create and fail with NotFound; if the delayed create then succeeds, legacy is left stale. A delayed delete can likewise run after a recreate and remove the newer legacy object. Since these background errors are not returned to the caller, the divergence can persist. Serialize shadow writes per resource or otherwise ensure stale operations cannot overwrite newer ones.

title: Legacy updates recompute the mutation against legacy state
body: The legacy update receives the original `objInfo` instead of the result of the unified update. For patches or other updates whose result depends on the old object, `Legacy.Update` applies the mutation to the legacy copy's potentially divergent state and can produce a different object from unified storage. Pass the unified result through an updated-object wrapper or otherwise ensure the legacy write stores that same result.

title: Unified NotFound now skips legacy deletion
body: This returns for every unified delete error, including NotFound, without attempting the legacy delete. The previous mode-3 implementation specifically continued to legacy on unified NotFound, which lets a delete clean up a legacy-only orphan during migration or after divergence. Preserve that behavior while still returning the unified NotFound response, or explicitly handle orphan cleanup another way.

title: Delete metrics use the object name as the kind label
body: This passes `name` as the third argument to `recordStorageDuration`, while the other operations pass `options.Kind` for that label. If the metric uses this argument as its kind/resource label, every distinct object name creates a new Prometheus label value, causing unbounded cardinality and potentially exposing resource names. Pass the kind instead.

title: Delete-collection shadow writes are recorded as storage metrics
body: This records the duration and error of `Legacy.DeleteCollection` with `recordStorageDuration`, even though the unified-storage duration was already recorded at line 159. As a result, legacy delete-collection failures and latency are attributed to storage. Use the legacy recorder here; storage create and update failures are also currently attributed to legacy at lines 45 and 129.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request cancellation
body: `WithTimeoutCause` adds a deadline but keeps the request context as its parent. These REST calls return immediately after starting the goroutine, and the request context is canceled when request handling completes. Any legacy operation still in progress is therefore canceled on response, so the mode's mirror writes are unreliable. Detach the background context from request cancellation before applying the timeout.

title: Independent goroutines can apply writes to legacy out of order
body: Each write starts an independent goroutine, with no per-resource ordering. For example, a legacy update can run before the legacy create for the same object, fail with NotFound, and then the later create leaves legacy with stale data; a delayed create can similarly run after a delete and resurrect an object. The errors are not retried, so the stores can remain divergent. Serialize or otherwise order mirror writes per resource.

title: Legacy updates are recomputed against the legacy copy instead of mirroring unified storage
body: The goroutine passes the original `objInfo` to `Legacy.Update` rather than applying the object returned by unified storage. For patch or apply updates, legacy recomputes the result against its own old object; if that copy is stale, fields omitted from the patch can remain stale and the mirror will differ from the authoritative unified result. Mirror the computed unified object (as the previous update wrapper did) so both stores receive the same update.

title: Mode 3 duration metrics use incorrect backend and resource values
body: This storage-duration call passes the individual object `name` where the other calls pass `options.Kind`, creating a high-cardinality metric dimension as arbitrary resource names accumulate. The attribution is also inconsistent elsewhere: Create and Update record storage failures as legacy durations (lines 45 and 129), while the asynchronous legacy DeleteCollection result is recorded as a storage duration (line 166). These errors make backend metrics misleading and can cause excessive metric series.

title: The mode 3 integration test assumes the asynchronous mirror is immediate
body: This subtest invokes `doPlaylistTests`, which checks the legacy API immediately after Kubernetes create and update operations. Mode 3 returns before its legacy-write goroutines complete, so those assertions race the mirror and can fail intermittently. Poll for eventual convergence or synchronize the test with completion of the background writes.

title: Background legacy writes inherit the request context
body: `WithTimeoutCause` creates a child of the incoming request context; it does not detach cancellation. The API server cancels that context when the request handler returns, which happens immediately after this method returns, so the legacy write can be canceled before it completes. The same pattern is used for delete, update, and delete-collection at lines 110, 135, and 163. The unified write is still reported as successful, leaving legacy storage unsynchronized.

title: Legacy updates are recomputed against a potentially divergent object
body: The legacy update receives the original `objInfo`, so it computes the update independently against the legacy object's current state. During dual writing, that state can differ from unified storage; patches, defaults, or other update logic can therefore produce a legacy object different from the object successfully written to unified storage. The previous implementation passed the unified update result to legacy through an update wrapper, avoiding this divergence.

title: Independent goroutines can apply mutations to legacy out of order
body: Every successful mutation starts an independent goroutine, with no per-resource ordering or queue. For example, a delete can reach legacy before an earlier create, return not found, and then the delayed create can leave the supposedly deleted object in legacy; an update can similarly arrive before its create. These legacy errors are not retried, so the stores can remain divergent.

title: Destroy does not wait for in-flight legacy writes
body: The asynchronous writes are not tracked, but `Destroy` immediately destroys both backends. If shutdown calls `Destroy` while a legacy write is still running, the backend can be closed underneath that write and the shadow write can be lost. Track and drain pending writes, or otherwise ensure the legacy backend remains available until they finish.

title: Write latency and error metrics are attributed to the wrong backend
body: When unified storage fails, this records a legacy duration even though legacy storage was never called; the same mistake occurs for update at line 129. Conversely, the asynchronous legacy delete-collection result at line 166 is recorded as a storage duration. This misattributes backend errors and latency, leaving the corresponding storage or legacy metrics inaccurate.

title: Delete metrics use each object name as the kind label
body: This call passes `name` where the other duration-recording calls pass the resource kind (`options.Kind`). If the value is used as the metrics kind label, every distinct deleted object creates a separate Prometheus time series, causing unbounded cardinality as objects are deleted and making per-kind metrics inaccurate.

title: Recheck the cache after acquiring the write lock
body: Concurrent callers that observe a nil cache before the first load all proceed to this lock. After the first caller loads and publishes the assets, each waiting caller still reloads and reparses the manifest because it never checks the cache again. A cold-start request burst therefore turns one cache initialization into multiple serialized loads, making every waiter pay the I/O latency. Recheck the cache under the lock and return it for non-Dev environments.

title: Recheck the cache after acquiring the write lock
body: A caller that observed an empty cache before waiting for this lock never checks it again after acquiring the lock. During a cold-start burst, each queued non-Dev caller therefore reloads and parses the manifest and overwrites the cache in turn, delaying all waiting requests with redundant serialized work. Recheck `entryPointAssetsCache` under the lock and return it when populated before loading again.

title: Recheck the cache after acquiring the write lock
body: Multiple non-development calls can all observe a nil cache before any of them acquires this lock. After the first call loads and caches the manifest, each waiting call still reloads and replaces it because the cache is not checked again under the lock. A burst of initial requests therefore serializes repeated file reads and JSON decoding; if a later read fails, it can also replace the successfully populated cache with nil. Recheck the cache under the lock for non-development calls before loading.

title: Update tests that still require SQL execution
body: This replacement makes `TablesList` and the corresponding database operations fail unconditionally. Existing SQL parser and command tests that expect successful table discovery or query execution will therefore fail, but no test files are updated in this PR. Update the tests to assert the intended disabled behavior, including coverage for both the typed reader and the legacy `UnmarshalSQLCommand` path.

title: Add a regression test for rejecting SQL expressions
body: This security change adds no automated test asserting that SQL expression requests are rejected, including when `FlagSqlExpressions` is enabled. Because the feature flag remains in the code and this check is the reader's explicit gate, a later change could restore SQL command construction without detecting that the security invariant was broken. Add coverage for both flag states and for the alternate SQL-command construction path.

title: Failed eager initialization does not clean up partial startup
body: This call can run `Lifecycle.Init` successfully and then fail during search or watcher initialization. The constructor returns `nil` without calling `s.cancel` or `Lifecycle.Stop`, and the caller cannot access the partially initialized server to stop it. Any resources or goroutines started by the lifecycle hooks can therefore survive a failed server construction. Clean up the partially initialized server before returning the error.

title: Eager initialization starts a watcher that panics when its event stream closes
body: With search configured, `s.Init` starts a goroutine in `search.init` that reads `WatchWriteEvents` using a background context and passes each received value to `handleEvent` without checking whether the channel is closed. The SQL backend closes that channel when stopped, so the goroutine receives `nil` and `handleEvent` dereferences it, causing an unrecovered panic. Eager initialization starts this watcher even before the server handles a request; stop the consumer on context cancellation or channel closure.

title: Start the server event watcher before indexing
body: The server watcher is now started only after `s.search.init`, which can take a long time. `WatchWriteEvents` establishes its polling cursor from the latest resource version when it starts, so writes committed during index construction are already behind that cursor and will never be emitted.
