A client watching from a resource version before startup can therefore miss those changes. Start the watcher before the potentially slow index build, or replay events from a durable cursor.

title: Serialize builds for the same index key
body: Removing the build-wide lock allows concurrent `BuildIndex` calls for the same key: callers can both observe a missing index in `getOrCreateIndex` before either build caches its result, and there is no per-key build coordination. For file-backed indexes, both builds can concurrently open/create the same Bleve directory; for memory-backed indexes, one build can overwrite the other's cached index while callers still hold the other instance. This can cause build failures or leave writes applied to an index that is no longer served. Preserve parallel builds for different keys while serializing builds per key.

title: Clean up resources when initialization fails
body: `NewResourceServer` now runs `s.Init` and returns `nil` on error without canceling `s.ctx` or stopping the lifecycle backend. If failure occurs after `s.search.init` starts its background event watcher—for example, if the subsequent `initWatcher` call fails—the constructor loses the server handle while the watcher and initialized backend can remain running. Clean up initialized resources before returning the error.

title: Concurrent first access can build the same index twice
body: Removing the lock around the build means `GetIndex` can return a cache miss while another `BuildIndex` for the same key is still running. Concurrent first searches for an index not built at startup can therefore open/build it twice; for file-backed indexes both builds target the same Bleve directory, and even if both succeed, one can publish an index that later gets replaced in the cache. This can cause search failures or leave an in-flight query using an index that no longer receives updates. Serialize builds per key or recheck the cache after acquiring per-key build coordination.

title: Initialization failure returns without cleaning up started resources
body: If `s.Init` fails after `s.search.init` has started its background watch, this return discards the server without calling `Stop`, `s.cancel`, or `lifecycle.Stop`. For example, `search.init` starts a watch before `initWatcher` runs, and `initWatcher` can then fail; the constructor returns an error while the search watch and backend resources may continue running. Clean up partially initialized resources before returning the error.

title: The no-argument passkey predicate does not exist
body: This call cannot compile: `UsernameForm` inherits only `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel)` from `UsernamePasswordForm`, and neither this class nor its other superclass declares a no-argument overload. The services module and its tests will fail compilation until the call supplies the user or uses a declared method.

title: Fresh logins no longer initialize conditional passkeys
body: This predicate returns false when `context.getUser()` is null, which is the normal state on the initial login page. Consequently `fillContextForm` is not called and the form is rendered without the WebAuthn challenge and conditional-UI attributes needed to start a discoverable passkey login. The previous code initialized those attributes for this no-user case; the re-authentication support should not remove that path.

title: Calls a nonexistent no-argument method
body: `UsernameForm` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments, but its superclass only declares `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel)`, and no no-argument overload exists in the hierarchy. This makes the changed source fail to compile and blocks the build.

title: Disables conditional passkeys for anonymous login
body: This helper returns false whenever no user is already selected. On a fresh login, the authentication context normally has no user, so the calls that use this helper do not populate the form with WebAuthn conditional-UI options. As a result, users cannot discover and sign in with passkeys on the normal login page; the same condition also omits those options after errors before a user is identified.

title: This call does not match the inherited method signature
body: `UsernamePasswordForm` defines `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel)`, and no zero-argument overload exists in its superclass. This invocation therefore fails Java compilation; pass the current user or add the intended overload.

title: Conditional passkeys are disabled before a user is identified
body: This helper returns false whenever `user` is null, but the initial login is precisely when a userless discoverable passkey must be offered. The calls that populate the form with WebAuthn challenge data are guarded by this helper, so normal unauthenticated logins through this form no longer get conditional passkey UI; passkey-only users cannot authenticate through this flow.

title: Clear setup events before asserting the first login
body: This test logs out after `registerDefaultUser()` but does not clear captured events before opening the login form. Setup can leave login events in the event collector, so the following `expectLogin()` may inspect a stale event instead of the passkey login. Clear the events after logout, as the neighboring tests do.

title: Use the underlying IdP state when deciding whether to invalidate login caches
body: `update()` obtains `original` through `getById()`, which returns an organization-aware model whose `isEnabled()` is false whenever its organization is disabled. If a cached, enabled public organization IdP is updated from `BROKER_PUBLIC=true` to `false` while that organization is disabled, the predicate is false for both `original` (because the organization is disabled) and `updated` (because the IdP is now private), so this code skips invalidation. Once the organization is enabled, the cached ID remains in `getForLogin()` results and its model reports enabled, exposing a broker that is no longer public. Compare the underlying IdP eligibility independently of organization enabled state, or invalidate when the public setting changes.

title: Cleanup callbacks target the literal alias instead of the created providers
body: This cleanup registration uses `get("alias")` rather than the created provider's alias. The loop creates providers named `idp-alias-0` through `idp-alias-19`, so its callbacks target the same unrelated alias instead of removing those providers; the added cleanup for `idp-alias-20` has the same problem. The test therefore leaves its created IdPs behind (and may issue deletes for a nonexistent provider), risking test contamination.

title: Disabled organizations can mask login-eligibility changes
body: `original` comes from `getById()`, which wraps organization-linked providers so `isEnabled()` is also false when their organization is disabled; `updated` is typically an unwrapped model. If the organization is disabled, changing an otherwise enabled provider from visible to `hideOnLogin=true` can make both predicates false and take this early return, leaving the cached login query unchanged. When the organization is later enabled, the stale cached ID can expose the hidden provider on the login page. Changes that make a provider newly eligible can likewise be missed, leaving it absent from the cache.

title: Use raw login eligibility when deciding whether to invalidate
body: `original` comes from `getById`, which wraps organization-linked providers so `isEnabled()` is false when their organization is disabled. If a cached provider belongs to a disabled organization and an update changes `linkOnly` or `hideOnLogin` to exclude it, both predicates here can be false, so this early return leaves the login-IDP cache intact. After the organization is enabled, the stale cached ID is returned and the login bean rechecks only `isEnabled()`, allowing the link-only or hidden provider to appear. Base invalidation on the persisted IDP login fields or otherwise invalidate when those fields change.

title: Distinguish a missing organization ID from an empty one
body: This maps both `organizationId == null` and `organizationId.equals("")` to the same search key. The provider contract treats null as no organization filter for `ORG_ONLY`/`ALL`, but treats any non-null ID—including an empty string—as a specific organization filter. If the broad query is cached first, a call with an empty ID can incorrectly receive providers associated with other organizations; the reverse order can incorrectly hide them from the broad query.

title: Cleanup uses an alias that was never created
body: The test creates providers with aliases such as `idp-alias-0` through `idp-alias-19`, but registers cleanup for the literal alias `alias` on every iteration. Those cleanup actions therefore do not remove the created providers (the later provider at alias `idp-alias-20` uses the same incorrect cleanup). If the test realm is reused, these records remain and can pollute subsequent tests.

title: JWT client credentials fail with this provider
body: When the authz-client is used without another crypto provider on the classpath, service discovery selects this provider, but `getSignature()` always throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. The authz-client documents support for JWT credentials, whose client assertions need a signing implementation; that flow therefore fails instead of obtaining a token. The other unsupported crypto operations can similarly break callers that use the selected provider.

title: ECDSA conversion silently accepts oversized signatures
body: This method copies only the first `signLength` bytes and never checks that the input has exactly that length. When used to convert an untrusted JOSE ECDSA signature for verification, a signature with arbitrary trailing bytes is converted as though those bytes were absent, so malformed, non-canonical signatures can verify as the valid prefix. Inputs shorter than the expected length instead throw `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`. Reject any input whose length differs from `signLength`.

title: Equal provider orders make FIPS selection depend on discovery order
body: The default, Elytron, and FIPS providers all return order `200`, so when more than one is visible the sort does not establish a preference; the selected implementation depends on service-resource discovery order. In particular, a classpath containing both the default and FIPS providers can silently select the default provider, undermining the configured FIPS crypto implementation. Assign distinct priorities or reject ambiguous top-ranked providers.

title: Adding an abstract method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: `CryptoProvider` is a service-provider interface, and adding an abstract `order()` method breaks implementations compiled against the previous interface. Such providers either fail to compile when rebuilt or throw `AbstractMethodError` when `CryptoIntegration` invokes `order()` during provider sorting, preventing startup. Make the method backward-compatible with a default implementation or otherwise preserve compatibility.

title: FIPS and non-FIPS providers have equal priority
body: This provider returns order 200, the same as DefaultCryptoProvider and WildFlyElytronProvider. If a classpath contains both FIPS and non-FIPS provider services, the sort does not prefer the FIPS provider; the first service discovered wins. CryptoIntegration now silently accepts that configuration, so a FIPS deployment can select the non-FIPS implementation depending on service-resource order.

title: Adding an abstract SPI method breaks existing provider implementations
body: CryptoProvider is a public service-provider interface. An implementation compiled against the previous version can still be loaded by ServiceLoader, but it has no order() implementation; invoking this method during CryptoIntegration's sort then throws AbstractMethodError and prevents crypto initialization. Make this a default method or otherwise preserve compatibility with existing providers.

title: The method returns a keystore provider instead of Bouncy Castle
body: The CryptoProvider contract requires this method to return the Bouncy Castle provider, but this returns whichever provider implements the JVM's default keystore type (commonly SUN). Because this provider is registered for CryptoIntegration, consumers that use the returned provider for Bouncy Castle algorithms will instead use a provider that does not implement them and can fail with NoSuchAlgorithmException. Return an actual Bouncy Castle provider or represent its absence consistently.

title: The selected provider makes signature operations fail unconditionally
body: This implementation is registered as a CryptoProvider and can be the only provider discovered by a standalone authz-client deployment, but getSignature() always throws UnsupportedOperationException. Any authz-client or other Keycloak core code path that obtains signatures through CryptoIntegration—for example, a signed client-credentials JWT path using this SPI—will fail instead of obtaining a JCA Signature. The other unsupported SPI methods have the same limitation.

title: Sequence parsing can read elements past the declared sequence boundary
body: The loop tracks the sequence's declared length, but readNext() checks inner element lengths only against the entire input buffer. If an element extends past the remaining sequence bytes, readNext() consumes bytes after the sequence and the subtraction makes length negative, which ends the loop successfully. This accepts malformed DER and can interpret trailing bytes as sequence contents; reject any element whose encoded length exceeds the remaining sequence length.

title: Equal-priority providers can silently select a non-FIPS implementation
body: `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider`, and `FIPS1402Provider` all return order 200, so sorting does not define which one wins when more than one is available. The first provider in ServiceLoader discovery order is silently selected; a deployment containing both FIPS and the default provider can therefore run with the default implementation instead of FIPS, whereas the previous behavior rejected multiple providers. Assign distinct priorities or reject ties.

title: Adding an abstract method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: Existing third-party `CryptoProvider` implementations compiled against the previous interface have no `order()` implementation. `CryptoIntegration` now invokes `order()` on every discovered provider while sorting, which causes `AbstractMethodError` and prevents crypto initialization for those applications. Make the method backward-compatible with a default implementation or otherwise preserve compatibility.

title: The Bouncy Castle getter returns the default keystore provider
body: This returns the provider that implements the JVM's default keystore type, not a Bouncy Castle provider. Callers using `getBouncyCastleProvider()` for provider-specific algorithms or services will receive the wrong provider and may fail to obtain those services, despite the method contract promising Bouncy Castle.

title: Existing realms do not receive the new Clients schema
body: Adding Clients to the schema map does not update an already initialized authorization server: `init()` returns early when the realm already has an admin-permissions client. Upgraded realms therefore keep the old scopes and lack the Clients resource-type resource, so client permission checks cannot evaluate the new schema and may fail when looking up that resource. Reconcile the schema for existing clients instead of only seeding it when the client is first created.

title: Role-mapping checks omit the MANAGE_CLIENTS bypass
body: These V2 overrides check only the new per-client FGAP scopes. A caller with the standard `MANAGE_CLIENTS` admin role can pass `canManage(client)` but still fail `canMapRoles`, `canMapCompositeRoles`, and `canMapClientScopeRoles` unless separately granted each scope. This removes the role’s existing ability to manage client roles when V2 is enabled; preserve the global admin-role authorization in these checks.

title: Client-permission lookup does not return individual clients
body: This query searches resources by type, but the schema marks the all-clients resource as type `Clients` while `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource()` creates individual client resources without setting that type. Consequently, client-specific grants are not found here; an all-clients grant instead returns the sentinel resource name `Clients` rather than client IDs. Callers of `getClientsWithPermission` therefore receive an incorrect set.

title: Token-exchange checks throw when V2 is enabled
body: `AdminPermissions.evaluator()` selects this V2 evaluator whenever the V2 feature is enabled, but `canExchangeTo` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. A token-exchange authorization path that consults this evaluator will therefore fail with an unhandled exception instead of making an authorization decision, breaking token-exchange requests. Implement the V2 behavior or fail closed with a handled authorization denial.

title: Resource lookups filter on the wrong owner
body: The three-argument `findByName` lookup filters by resource owner, but client resources are created with `resourceServer.getClientId()` as their owner, whereas this code passes `server.getId()`; the all-clients lookup at line 244 uses the same mismatch. As a result, per-client lookups miss their resources and the all-clients lookup misses its resource, so V2 client permissions are not recognized.

title: Existing permission clients are not upgraded with the Clients schema
body: Adding Clients to `SCHEMA` does not update realms that already have an admin-permissions client: `init` returns immediately when that client exists, without creating the new Clients resource or scopes. After upgrading, those realms cannot create or evaluate client permissions because the required schema entries are absent.

title: Role-mapping checks drop the MANAGE_CLIENTS role
body: These V2 overrides (and the composite and client-scope variants below) authorize only through the new scope permissions; they omit the existing `MANAGE_CLIENTS` role check that client-management operations retain in `canManage`. Consequently, administrators granted `MANAGE_CLIENTS` cannot map client roles or composites under V2 unless they also receive separate authorization policies.

title: Client role-mapping checks drop built-in admin-role grants
body: This override authorizes role mapping only through the V2 permission schema, unlike `canManage(ClientModel)`, which also honors `MANAGE_CLIENTS`. As a result, an administrator whose access comes from the built-in `MANAGE_CLIENTS` role can manage a client but may be denied when assigning client roles or composites through the corresponding mapping checks. The same omission appears in `canMapCompositeRoles` and `canMapClientScopeRoles`; preserve the existing built-in role grants in these overrides.

title: Client permission enumeration does not return granted client IDs
body: This scans only resources with type `Clients` and adds each matching resource's name to the result. The schema initializes that type on the aggregate all-clients resource, whose name is the literal `Clients`; per-client resources are created separately with the client ID as their name. Consequently, individual grants are not enumerated here, and an all-clients grant adds `Clients` rather than the IDs of the clients it covers. Consumers using this method to filter or enumerate accessible clients will omit authorized clients or receive a non-client identifier.

title: V2 client deletion leaves authorization resources orphaned
body: The removal-event listener now runs only when the legacy `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` feature is enabled. In a V2-only deployment, deleting a client therefore skips the `ClientRemovedEvent` branch, and this PR adds no V2 cleanup for the per-client resources and policies stored in the admin-permissions resource server. Those authorization records remain after the target client is gone; add V2-specific cleanup for deleted clients.

title: Assert the feature-disabled exit code
body: This test checks only the error text, not the exit status. Exit code 4 is part of the newly documented scripting contract for a disabled feature, so the test would not catch a regression that prints this message but returns a different status. Assert that the command exits with `CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED`.

title: Feature-disabled exit code is not verified
body: This test checks only the error text, not the exit status. Exit code 4 is now a documented automation contract for a disabled `rolling-updates` feature, so a regression that returns a generic error code would still pass this test while breaking scripts that distinguish this case.

title: A view-only all-groups grant allows group creation
body: `canManage()` accepts either `VIEW` or `MANAGE` on the all-groups resource. This method backs `requireManage()` for top-level group creation, so an administrator granted only permission to view all groups can create groups despite lacking any manage scope.

title: Group view-permission lookup uses authorization resource IDs as group IDs
body: `groupResource.getId()` is the authorization resource record ID, but `hasPermission` resolves its argument with `resourceStore.findByName`, and group resources are named with the group model ID. This therefore misses per-group resources and falls back to the all-groups resource; the subsequent addition of `groupResource.getId()` also supplies authorization IDs where user searches and counts expect group IDs. Administrators granted `VIEW_MEMBERS` or `MANAGE_MEMBERS` through group permissions can consequently get empty or incorrect user search results and counts.

title: Existing admin-permissions clients are not seeded with the Groups resource
body: This lookup assumes the `Groups` type resource exists, but `AdminPermissionsSchema.init` returns immediately when a realm already has an admin-permissions client and only seeds schema resources and scopes when creating a new client. On upgrade, existing realms therefore lack the `Groups` resource and its new scopes; all-groups permission evaluation cannot find the resource (and may dereference null at the following lookup), leaving the new group authorization unusable for those realms.

title: A view-only grant allows creating groups
body: This method treats the `VIEW` scope on the all-groups resource as `canManage()`. `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup` relies on `requireManage()`, so an administrator granted only view access to all groups can create top-level groups. Require the `MANAGE` scope for this check.

title: Evaluate impersonation grants as the requester, not the target user
body: When a requester is supplied, this context uses the impersonated target user as the authorization identity. `canClientImpersonate` delegates to this overload, so its permission check evaluates policies against the target rather than the requesting client/current administrator. This can deny valid requester grants or allow impersonation based on the target user's identity instead of the caller's authorization.

title: Return group IDs, not authorization resource IDs
body: This adds an authorization resource's database ID to the set used as `UserModel.GROUPS` search filters, but that set must contain realm group IDs. In particular, an all-groups `VIEW_MEMBERS` grant causes user searches to filter by the synthetic Groups resource ID, which matches no group and omits authorized members. Also, per-group resources created by `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` are not assigned the `Groups` type, so this `findByType` scan does not enumerate those grants.

title: A view-only all-groups grant also grants group management
body: This check accepts either the `view` or `manage` scope as proof of `canManage()`. Consequently, an administrator with only an all-groups `view` permission passes `requireManage()` for operations such as creating a top-level group. Require the `manage` scope here; a read-only grant must not authorize mutations.

title: Group visibility lookup uses authorization resource IDs as group IDs
body: `hasPermission` treats its argument as a group ID and looks up a resource by name, but this passes the generated authorization resource ID. The following line also adds that resource ID to the returned set, which callers use as actual group IDs to constrain user searches and counts. As a result, group-member visibility grants are not represented by the correct group IDs, causing user searches, pagination, or counts to omit permitted users or return incorrect results.

title: Existing realms do not receive the new Groups schema resources and scopes
body: Adding `Groups` to the schema only affects realms whose admin-permissions client is initialized after this change. `init()` returns immediately when a realm already has that client, so existing realms are not given the `Groups` resource or the new group scopes. Group permission setup or evaluation after upgrading can therefore fail because those resources and scopes are missing.

title: Preserve the account UI interpolation syntax
body: This resource is consumed by the account UI, which uses `{{...}}` interpolation (as in other messages in this file). Changing the placeholders to Java `MessageFormat` syntax means the UI will not substitute the attribute name or limits, and it will display the `{2,choice,...}` expression literally in the multivalued-size validation error.

title: Preserve the admin UI interpolation syntax
body: The admin UI uses `{{...}}` interpolation for resource messages. These single-brace placeholders and the Java `choice` expression are not interpreted by that client-side formatter, so this validation message will show literal `{0}`, `{1}`, `{2}` and the choice expression instead of the attribute name and limits.

title: Keep the Lithuanian TOTP instruction in Lithuanian
body: This change replaces the Lithuanian instruction with Italian text (“Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare”). Lithuanian users will see an unrelated-language instruction when setting up TOTP.

title: Keep the Lithuanian TOTP instruction in Lithuanian
body: This change replaces the Lithuanian login instruction with Italian text (“Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare”). Lithuanian users will see an unrelated-language instruction while setting up TOTP.

title: Use Simplified Chinese for the zh_CN resource
body: This replacement is written in Traditional Chinese (for example, “手機” and “應用程式”), while this file is the Simplified Chinese `zh_CN` resource. Simplified Chinese users will receive a visibly inconsistent instruction.

title: Preserve the account UI interpolation syntax
body: This account UI bundle uses i18next-style `{{...}}` interpolation, as in other entries such as `Back to {{app}}`. Changing this message to Java `MessageFormat` placeholders and a ChoiceFormat expression means the UI will display literal `{0}`, `{1}`, and `{2,choice,...}` instead of the attribute name and bounds when this validation error is shown.

title: Preserve the admin UI interpolation syntax
body: This admin UI bundle used i18next-style `{{0}}`, `{{1}}`, and `{{2}}` placeholders. The new Java `MessageFormat` placeholders and ChoiceFormat expression are not interpolated by that UI, so users will see the literal `{0}`, `{1}`, and `{2,choice,...}` in this validation error rather than the attribute name and limits.

title: Use Lithuanian text for the authenticator instruction
body: The `totpStep1` value is Italian (`Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:`) in the Lithuanian account theme. Lithuanian users therefore receive an instruction in the wrong language during authenticator setup.

title: Use Lithuanian text for the login authenticator instruction
body: The `loginTotpStep1` value is Italian (`Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:`) in the Lithuanian login theme. Lithuanian users therefore receive an instruction in the wrong language during authenticator setup.

title: Use Simplified Chinese in the zh_CN resource
body: This `totpStep1` translation uses Traditional Chinese characters and wording (`手機`, `應用程式`) in the Simplified Chinese `zh_CN` bundle. This makes the authenticator setup instruction inconsistent with the rest of the locale.

title: Keep the UI bundle's interpolation format
body: This React UI bundle uses i18next-style `{{0}}` interpolation; the previous value for this key used that syntax. The new Java `MessageFormat` placeholders (`{0}`, `{1}`, `{2,choice,...}`) are not expanded by the UI, so users seeing this validation error will get literal placeholders instead of the attribute name, limits, and pluralized value count.

title: Keep the admin UI bundle's interpolation format
body: This React UI bundle uses i18next-style `{{0}}` interpolation; the previous value for this key used that syntax. The new Java `MessageFormat` placeholders (`{0}`, `{1}`, `{2,choice,...}`) are not expanded by the UI, so users seeing this validation error will get literal placeholders instead of the attribute name, limits, and pluralized value count.

title: Restore Lithuanian text for TOTP setup
body: This replacement sentence is Italian (`Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:`), not Lithuanian, so Lithuanian users see an untranslated TOTP setup instruction. The corresponding `loginTotpStep1` in `themes/src/main/resources-community/theme/base/login/messages/messages_lt.properties` has the same Italian text and should be corrected as well.

title: Use Simplified Chinese in the zh_CN message
body: This replacement uses Traditional Chinese forms such as `手機`, `安裝`, and `應用程式` in the `zh_CN` resource, whose surrounding text is Simplified Chinese. The account TOTP setup flow will therefore switch scripts mid-message; use Simplified Chinese wording here.

title: Grant shortcuts are not constrained to the parser's two-character format
body: The encoder concatenates `getShortcut()` directly into the token ID, but decoding requires the context prefix to be exactly six characters. `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` does not enforce a two-character value and its documentation even describes a three-letter shortcut as typical. A custom grant using a three-character shortcut will therefore issue IDs that this provider cannot decode, causing later context lookups to fail with `IllegalArgumentException`. Either enforce and document the two-character contract or make parsing support variable-length shortcuts.

title: Access-token event matcher does not verify the grant shortcut
body: The grant shortcut occupies characters `[4,6)`, but this matcher reads `substring(3, 5)`, which overlaps the token-type prefix. It also returns `false` when that substring equals the expected shortcut. Consequently, event assertions do not detect an incorrect grant shortcut and can reject some otherwise valid IDs. Read the actual grant segment and compare it against the expected shortcut.

title: The raw token ID null check validates the grant type twice
body: This second `requireNonNull` checks `grantType` again instead of `rawTokenId`, so a context with a null raw ID is accepted. Passing it to `encodeTokenId` then produces an ID ending in the literal `null` rather than rejecting the invalid context. Validate `rawTokenId` here.

title: The grant shortcut length is not constrained to the decoder's fixed format
body: The decoder requires exactly six context characters and reads the grant shortcut from the last two, but `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` does not enforce a two-character value and its Javadoc says shortcuts are usually three characters. A custom grant factory returning a three-character shortcut will produce token IDs that this decoder rejects, so encoding and decoding do not round-trip for supported providers. Require and validate exactly two characters, or make the format support variable-length shortcuts.

title: The access-token event matcher never checks the expected grant shortcut
body: The grant shortcut occupies positions 4–5, but this matcher extracts positions 3–4 and returns false when that substring equals the expected shortcut. Consequently it accepts a well-formed UUID token ID regardless of its grant type, so event tests cannot catch incorrect grant metadata. Compare the correct two-character segment and reject IDs whose segment differs from the expected shortcut.

title: The constructor checks grantType twice and allows a null raw token ID
body: This second `requireNonNull` checks `grantType` again instead of checking `rawTokenId`. Passing a null raw ID therefore succeeds, and `encodeTokenId` concatenates it as the literal string `null`, producing an ID that no longer represents the supplied context. Validate `rawTokenId` here.

title: Grant shortcuts must be fixed at two characters
body: The parser requires the encoded context to be exactly six characters and slices the grant shortcut as two characters, but `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` documents shortcuts as “usually” three letters, without requiring a two-character value. A custom grant using a documented three-character shortcut can be encoded, but its token ID will fail to parse. Require and validate exactly two characters in the factory contract, or make the encoding and parser support variable-length shortcuts.

title: Access-token event matcher does not verify the grant shortcut
body: This condition returns false when the extracted value equals the expected shortcut, and the extraction uses `substring(3, 5)` rather than the grant shortcut's positions 4–5. For normal IDs such as `onrtac:<uuid>`, it therefore ignores the grant and accepts IDs with the wrong grant shortcut, so the updated integration assertions cannot catch mis-tagged tokens.

title: The constructor does not reject a null raw token ID
body: This second null check checks `grantType` again instead of `rawTokenId`. A context with a null raw ID is accepted, and encoding it appends the literal string `null` to the token ID rather than rejecting invalid input.

title: Remote recovery-code updates leave old local codes valid
body: If a user already has a local recovery-code credential and their user storage accepts this update, this writes the new codes to user storage without removing the local credential. The old local codes can therefore remain valid after the user has regenerated or revoked them. Remove the local credential on successful remote replacement, or otherwise ensure validation treats the remote credential as authoritative.

title: The user-storage fixture accepts recovery codes repeatedly
body: This validator only checks whether the submitted code appears in the stored list and never marks it used or removes it. As a result, the same recovery code can authenticate repeatedly in the new user-storage path, and the added test—which uses each code only once—does not detect this violation of recovery-code one-time-use semantics. Make the fixture consume a code on successful validation and test that replay is rejected.

title: The exposed federated credential loses its storage ID
body: `updateCredential` assigns an ID to the stored recovery credential, but this reconstruction creates a new model using only the codes, date, and label and never copies that ID. The credential returned by `getCredentials` therefore has no stable link to the stored entry (or may expose a different ID), so callers that address federated credentials by ID cannot reliably operate on it, including removal or account credential management. Preserve the stored credential ID on the returned model.

title: The storage fixture allows recovery codes to be reused
body: This validation only checks whether the submitted code appears in the stored list; it never removes or marks the matched code as used. The same recovery code therefore succeeds on every login, unlike the one-time behavior of recovery codes, and the new integration test's single successful login cannot detect reuse or exhaustion bugs. Consume the matched code and test that a second attempt with it is rejected.

title: Local fallback does not revoke an existing federated recovery credential
body: If a user-storage provider exposes an existing recovery credential but returns `false` from `updateCredential` (for example, because it is read-only), this branch creates a local replacement without removing or disabling the federated credential. The federated credential remains usable for authentication, and `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()` prefers it over the new local credential. Consequently, reconfiguring recovery codes does not revoke the old codes and may leave the newly generated credential masked.

title: Federated recovery codes are never consumed
body: This validator returns true for a matching recovery code but never removes or marks that code as used in `myUser.recoveryCodes`. The same code can therefore authenticate repeatedly in this user-storage implementation, unlike a one-time recovery code. The new integration test uses each code only once, so it passes without detecting this behavior; update the stored credential on successful validation and test that reuse fails.

title: The regression test does not exercise the guarded subgroup-count lookup
body: This call requests a brief group listing (`true` is `briefRepresentation`) and does not request `subGroupsCount`; the subgroup-count lookup is a separate, conditional operation. As a result, the test does not exercise the changed `GroupAdapter.getSubGroupsCount()` null guard. It also has no start barrier or join, so deletion can finish before the reader runs, or the assertion can run before an in-flight read records its exception. Request subgroup counts and synchronize with the reader so the test verifies the fix.

title: A failed deletion can leave the reader thread looping indefinitely
body: If any group deletion throws, control exits the `forEach` before `deletedAll` is set. The reader catches request exceptions and continues looping while that flag is false, so the background thread can keep issuing requests indefinitely and prevent the test JVM from shutting down. Set the flag in a `finally` block and wait for the reader thread to terminate.

title: Wait for the reader thread before asserting
body: The test sets `deletedAll` and checks `caughtExceptions` without joining the reader thread or synchronizing its start. It can therefore pass without any overlapping read, or assert before an in-flight read records an exception; the reader can also outlive the test. A deletion failure before `deletedAll.set(true)` can leave its non-daemon loop running indefinitely. Coordinate the reader's start and completion, and stop it in a `finally` block.

title: Subgroup queries can still dereference a missing delegate
body: The new null check handles `getSubGroupsCount`, but the subgroup-stream overloads at this line and lines 262 and 268 still call `modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` without checking for null. If a request obtains this cached adapter before a concurrent group deletion and resolves its delegate afterward, the supplier can return null—as this change explicitly anticipates—and a subgroup-list request still fails with an NPE and a server error.

title: The concurrency test can pass before the reader reports failures
body: The test starts the reader without waiting for it to issue a request, then sets `deletedAll` and asserts immediately without joining the thread. The reader may not run until after deletion, or an in-flight request may record its exception after the assertion, so the test can pass without detecting the regression. Also, if deletion throws before the flag is set, the non-daemon reader loops forever. Coordinate reader startup and ensure it is stopped and joined, including on failure.

title: The optimized paginator cannot paginate audit-log datetimes
body: This paginator is used with `order_by="-datetime"`, but `AuditLogEntry.datetime` is a `datetime`, and `math.floor(value)` raises `TypeError`. On the first optimized request with any results, `build_cursor` calls this method and the endpoint returns a 500. The cursor conversion is also incompatible: `value_from_cursor` returns the raw integer cursor value rather than converting it back to a datetime, so subsequent-page filtering would fail even if key generation were fixed.

title: Negative offsets still fail on Django querysets
body: Django does not support negative `QuerySet` slice indexes; evaluating `queryset[-N:stop]` raises `ValueError`. Consequently, an optimized request with a cursor containing a negative offset reaches this branch and returns a 500 instead of providing the advertised negative-offset pagination. `Cursor` accepts signed offsets, so such a cursor can be supplied.

title: Paginator option is passed to the pagination helper
body: `enable_advanced_features` is passed to `self.paginate`, rather than directly to `OptimizedCursorPaginator`. The pagination helper does not accept or forward this paginator-specific option, so requests that meet this branch fail with a `TypeError` instead of returning audit logs. Forward it as a paginator constructor option or configure the paginator directly.

title: Optimized paginator cannot build cursors for datetime fields
body: The audit-log endpoint orders by `datetime`, but this implementation applies `math.floor` or `math.ceil` to the field value. Those functions do not accept `datetime` objects, so any non-empty response using the optimized paginator raises `TypeError` while building its cursor. Use the datetime key conversion implemented by `DateTimePaginator`.

title: Negative offsets cause invalid queryset slicing
body: Django querysets reject slices with a negative start index; they do not interpret them as reverse pagination. `Cursor.from_string` accepts negative offsets, so an optimized request containing one reaches this slice and raises `ValueError` instead of returning a response. Reject or normalize negative offsets rather than passing them to queryset slicing.

title: Optimized pagination cannot handle audit-log datetimes
body: The audit-log endpoint orders by `datetime`, so each item key here is a `datetime` object. Passing it to `math.floor` raises `TypeError` on the first non-empty page when `optimized_pagination=true` is used by an authorized administrator. The cursor conversion also returns the raw integer value rather than converting it back to a datetime, so subsequent-page filtering would fail too. Use the datetime key and cursor conversions from `DateTimePaginator`.

title: Negative QuerySet offsets are not supported by Django
body: This branch passes a negative start index to a Django QuerySet slice. Django raises `ValueError` for negative slice indices rather than treating them as offsets from the end, so an authorized request using the advertised negative-offset pagination path fails instead of returning a page. Implement reverse traversal without negative slicing, or reject negative offsets explicitly.

title: Changing buffer keys from sets to sorted sets breaks in-flight buffers
body: These `span-buf:s:*` keys previously contained Redis sets, and their TTL allows them to survive for up to an hour. `ZADD` against an existing set fails with `WRONGTYPE`; during a rolling deploy, old workers also fail when they use set commands against keys created as sorted sets by new workers. Batches touching these traces will fail instead of being processed until the old keys expire or the workers are coordinated. Use a versioned key namespace or an explicit migration/drain strategy.

title: Merging overlapping sorted sets changes span eviction scores
body: Redis `ZUNIONSTORE` defaults to `AGGREGATE SUM`. If the same payload is present in both the canonical set and `parent_key`—for example, a replay recreates the payload under a parent ID that now redirects to the canonical set—the merged member's score becomes the sum of both timestamps rather than its end timestamp. Since the score determines which spans `ZPOPMIN` evicts, repeated deliveries can make old spans look newest and cause genuinely newer spans to be evicted. Preserve a single event score when merging, such as with an appropriate aggregate.

title: Optimized pagination fails for datetime ordering
body: The audit-log endpoint selects `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `order_by="-datetime"`, but this implementation assumes the ordering field is numeric and calls `math.floor` or `math.ceil` on it. On a nonempty first page, cursor construction invokes this method with a `datetime`, raising `TypeError` and making requests with optimized pagination enabled return a server error. The paginator needs datetime-aware cursor key and value handling, or the endpoint must use a compatible paginator.

title: Negative offsets are passed to unsupported Django queryset slicing
body: This branch deliberately evaluates `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django querysets reject negative slice indices and raise `ValueError` when evaluated; they do not handle negative offsets as the comment claims. A request using an advanced cursor with a negative offset therefore fails instead of paginating.

title: The configured maximum segment span count is no longer honored
body: The Lua script now always caps sets at 1000, while `SpansBuffer` still exposes `max_segment_spans` as a constructor option. The previous load-time check enforcing that option was removed, so a buffer configured with a lower limit can now retain and return more spans than its configured bound; a higher limit is also silently capped at 1000. Pass the configured limit into the script or retain enforcement of the option.

title: Use datetime-aware cursor keys for audit-log pagination
body: The audit-log endpoint passes `order_by="-datetime"`, but this implementation uses the generic numeric key conversion. On a nonempty first page, cursor construction calls `math.floor()` on a `datetime`, which raises `TypeError`; subsequent pages would also pass an integer cursor value to a datetime field filter. Requests opting into this paginator therefore fail instead of returning audit logs. Preserve the date conversion used by `DateTimePaginator`.

title: Negative offsets cause Django queryset slicing to fail
body: When advanced pagination is enabled and a cursor has a negative offset, this branch evaluates a queryset slice with a negative start. Django does not support negative queryset indexes and raises `ValueError`, turning the request into a server error. Negative offsets can be supplied in a cursor; implement reverse paging using valid slices or reject them before slicing.

title: Changing span-buffer keys from sets to sorted sets breaks live Redis data
body: This writes sorted sets under the same `span-buf:s:*` keys that previous versions stored as Redis sets. During a rolling deploy, or while old buffered segments remain, `ZADD` against an existing set fails with `WRONGTYPE`; the new Lua `ZCARD`/`ZUNIONSTORE` and flush-time `ZSCAN` operations also fail on those keys. New and old consumers cannot safely share these keys, so ingestion or flushing can stall until the old keys expire. Use versioned keys or migrate existing data before switching types.

title: The shorter redirect traversal limit can split deep segments
body: This loop now follows only about 1,000 redirect links before using the current `set_span_id` as the destination. For a deeper span hierarchy, that value may not be the segment's root, so the new span is stored under an intermediate key and can be flushed as part of the wrong segment. Redirect chains can outlive the 1,000 retained payloads because eviction does not remove their mappings. Retain a sufficient traversal bound or detect exhaustion and resolve the chain safely.

title: The max_segment_spans setting is no longer enforced
body: The load-time check against `self.max_segment_spans` has been removed, while the insertion script uses a hard-coded limit of 1,000. A caller configuring a lower limit can now receive segments up to 1,000 spans, and a caller configuring a higher limit still loses spans at 1,000. Preserve the constructor's configured limit by passing it to the script or enforcing it when loading.

title: Add coverage for the new destructive eviction behavior
body: The added buffer tests supply timestamps but do not create a segment larger than 1,000 spans or assert which spans survive eviction. Since this code intentionally removes stored payloads, add tests for the cardinality boundary, eviction ordering, and eviction while merging buffers; otherwise regressions can silently drop the wrong spans or fail to enforce the cap.

title: Changing the Redis key type breaks buffers created by the previous version
body: This changes `span-buf:s:*` keys from Redis sets to sorted sets without changing the key namespace or migrating existing keys. During a rollout, active keys written by the old version remain sets; `ZADD` here then fails with `WRONGTYPE` (and the Lua script also uses sorted-set commands on these keys). Consumers processing traces with such buffers will fail until the keys expire, stalling ingestion and potentially losing buffered spans.

title: Paginator-specific option is passed to the endpoint pagination helper
body: `enable_advanced_features` is an option on `OptimizedCursorPaginator`, but this call passes it to `self.paginate`. The endpoint pagination helper does not accept or forward this paginator-specific keyword, so an authorized administrator requesting `optimized_pagination=true` gets a `TypeError` instead of a response. Pass the option through the helper's supported mechanism or construct the paginator with it.

title: Optimized paginator cannot paginate datetime fields
body: The audit-log endpoint orders by `datetime`, but this implementation uses `math.floor`/`math.ceil` on the field value, which is a `datetime`; that raises `TypeError` when `build_cursor` processes a nonempty page. Its `value_from_cursor` also returns the raw integer cursor value instead of converting it back to a datetime, so subsequent-page filtering would fail as well. This paginator needs the datetime cursor encoding used by `DateTimePaginator`.

title: Negative cursor offsets cause unsupported Django queryset slicing
body: When advanced features are enabled, a negative cursor offset is passed directly as the start of a queryset slice. Django querysets reject negative slice indices with `ValueError`; `Cursor.from_string` accepts negative offsets, so a request containing such a cursor returns a server error rather than a pagination response or a client error.

title: The eviction limit ignores the configured segment span limit
body: Eviction is hard-coded to 1000 here, while `SpansBuffer` exposes `max_segment_spans` as a configurable limit and previously enforced that value when loading segments. The new insertion-time cap no longer honors non-default values, so configurations expecting a lower cap can retain and emit substantially more spans than allowed, while higher configured limits are silently reduced.

title: Substring matching can upsample unrelated Discover queries
body: This checks whether the raw query contains `event.type:error`, not whether that is an actual filter. A query matching that text inside a message or tag value—or a mixed query that also selects transactions—will still replace `count()` with `sum(sample_weight)`. The response then reports weighted counts for rows that are not exclusively errors. Parse the query and verify its event-type constraints before enabling the transformation.

title: Upsampling eligibility uses the original dataset during widget splits
body: For a split dashboard widget, `_get_event_stats` can be called with `scoped_dataset=discover` for the error-events query while the captured `dataset` remains the original metrics dataset. Passing that original dataset here makes the helper reject upsampling for non-Discover/non-errors datasets, so the split error count remains an unweighted `count()` and undercounts sampled errors. Check eligibility against the scoped dataset and the query actually being executed.

title: Substring matching enables upsampling for queries that exclude errors
body: This checks whether the raw query contains `event.type:error`, not whether the query selects only errors. For example, the valid discover query `!event.type:error` contains this substring but excludes errors; an `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` query also matches while including transactions. For allowlisted projects these queries are rewritten to sum `sample_weight`, so they can return incorrect counts or fail when that column is unavailable for transaction events.

title: Upsampling eligibility ignores the effective dataset and query
body: `_get_event_stats` receives the effective `scoped_dataset` and `query`, but eligibility is decided using the outer `dataset` and the original request. Dashboard split paths can call this function with a discover error split and a generated query while the original dataset is a metrics dataset and the request has no `event.type:error` filter. In that case the split's error counts are not upsampled, so the feature returns sampled rather than estimated counts.

title: Remove the unregistered nested-repository gitlink
body: This adds a gitlink to commit `a5d2909` rather than a normal source file. No `.gitmodules` entry is included, so a fresh checkout will not populate this directory and submodule initialization cannot resolve its URL. Remove this accidental repository entry unless it is an intentional, fully configured submodule.

title: Substring matching enables upsampling for non-error queries
body: This check matches `event.type:error` anywhere in the query, including negated filters such as `!event.type:error` and mixed queries such as `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`. Those queries include non-error events, but the rewritten aggregation sums `sample_weight`, which is not defined for transactions. The result can undercount events or make the query fail; determine that the query positively restricts results to errors instead of searching for a substring.

title: Error-split dashboard queries use the original dataset for eligibility
body: `_get_event_stats` receives a `scoped_dataset`, but this check passes the outer `dataset` selected for the request. For a metrics-enhanced dashboard widget split into `ERROR_EVENTS`, the caller executes the error query against `discover` while the outer dataset remains a metrics dataset, so `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` rejects it and the split error count stays unupsampled. The eligibility check needs to reflect the dataset and query actually being executed.

title: The errors dataset uses an aggregation registered only for discover
body: This branch enables transformation for the `errors` dataset, causing `count()` to become `upsampled_count()`. The new function is registered only in `DiscoverDataset.function_converter` in `src/sentry/search/events/datasets/discover.py`; the errors dataset cannot resolve that function, so allowlisted requests using that dataset fail when the rewritten query is built. Register the function for the errors query path too, or avoid rewriting that dataset.

title: PR comment workflow calls helpers on the wrong object
body: `self` here is a `GitHubPRCommentWorkflow`, but `get_merged_pr_single_issue_template` was added to `CommitContextIntegration`, so generating a merged-PR comment raises `AttributeError`. The equivalent GitLab workflow makes the same call. Moreover, the helper itself calls `PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title`, although `_truncate_title` was also added to `CommitContextIntegration`; fixing only the call site would still leave comment generation failing.

title: Feature-enabled dashboard tables are rendered with empty data
body: When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, this branch passes `columns: []` and an empty `tableData` instead of the current `result` data and fields. The new visualization therefore renders a blank table for every dashboard table widget using the feature, even when the query returned rows.

title: Error and breadcrumb timestamps use different units
body: This compares an issue event's nodestore timestamp (Unix seconds) directly with the raw replay recording event timestamp (RRWeb milliseconds). In real replays, the comparison treats errors as occurring before breadcrumbs, so the combined log sent for summarization is chronologically incorrect. Convert both timestamps to the same unit before comparing; the added test misses this because it supplies breadcrumb timestamps in seconds.

title: Reports with no age or timestamp are accepted
body: Both `age` and `timestamp` are optional, and the cross-field validators only run when their respective fields are supplied. Consequently, a report containing neither field passes validation; when both are zero, the truthiness checks also fail to reject the mutually exclusive pair. Malformed reports are then counted as valid received reports. Validate field presence explicitly and require exactly one of the two fields.

title: Hidden span attributes remain visible when the search is empty
body: The empty-search branch returns `sorted` before applying `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES`; the new exclusion runs only when a search term is entered. As a result, `is_segment`, `project_id`, and `received` are shown in the normal attributes view despite being designated as hidden.

title: Falsey custom cell output incorrectly falls back to the default renderer
body: The custom-renderer contract says fallback occurs when the callback returns `undefined`, but this truthiness check also falls back for valid outputs such as `null`, `0`, or an empty string. A renderer therefore cannot intentionally leave a cell blank or render a numeric zero. The head-cell renderer has the same truthiness check at line 31.

title: The feature-flagged table visualization always renders an empty table
body: When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, this branch passes `columns={[]}` and a `tableData` with empty `data`, `fields`, and `units` instead of the current `result`. Consequently, dashboard table widgets show no columns or rows for organizations using the new visualization. Pass the actual result data and metadata, along with the appropriate columns.

title: PR comment generation calls helpers that the workflow does not define
body: `get_comment_body` runs on a `GitHubPRCommentWorkflow` and calls `self.get_merged_pr_single_issue_template` (and `self.get_environment_info`). Those helpers were added to `CommitContextIntegration`, not the PR workflow class, so they are not available on this `self`; generating a comment raises `AttributeError` instead of returning the comment body. The GitLab workflow has the same issue. Move the helpers onto the workflow or call them through its integration.

title: Attribute-key query cache key omits the organization
body: This query key contains the filters but not the organization slug, even though the query function fetches keys from an organization-specific endpoint. When switching organizations with the same filters (especially when all projects are selected), the query client can reuse the previous organization's cached attribute keys, showing incorrect or organization-specific metadata. Include the organization slug in the query key.

title: Age and timestamp validation accepts invalid field combinations and values
body: Both temporal fields are optional, so a report with neither `age` nor `timestamp` is accepted. The cross-field validators also use truthiness, allowing both fields to be present when both are zero, and `age` has no non-negative constraint. These malformed reports receive a successful response and increment the received-report metric; require exactly one temporal field by checking presence and validate age as non-negative.

title: The feature-flagged table visualization receives no query results
body: When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, this branch passes `columns={[]}` and a `tableData` object with empty `data`, `fields`, and `units` instead of using the current `result`. Consequently, dashboard table widgets in the flagged cohort render no columns or rows even when the query returned data.

title: Reports without a valid age or timestamp pass validation
body: Both `age` and `timestamp` are optional, but there is no object-level check requiring exactly one, so a report containing neither is accepted and counted as valid. `age` also has no nonnegative minimum, and the mutual-exclusion checks use truthiness, allowing both fields to be present as zero. These invalid reports receive HTTP 200 and pollute the received-report metrics.

title: Falsy custom cell output incorrectly falls back to the default renderer
body: The renderer contract says fallback occurs when a custom renderer returns `undefined`, but this truthiness check also treats valid outputs such as `null`, `false`, `0`, and an empty string as missing. A caller cannot intentionally render a blank cell or a falsy value; the default field renderer is shown instead.

title: Tabular rows cannot represent boolean field values
body: `TabularValueType` includes `boolean`, but `TabularRow` only permits numbers, strings, string arrays, and null. Callers therefore cannot type valid table data for boolean fields without a cast, undermining the new table API's type safety.

title: The no-existing-integration path skips the identity check
body: When the installation callback arrives before a webhook has created the Integration row, this `DoesNotExist` branch advances the pipeline without comparing the OAuth-authenticated user to the installation sender. Since the comparison below only runs when an Integration already exists, the installation can complete without the validation this change is intended to enforce. Reject or defer this path until the sender identity can be verified.

title: Use a stable GitHub user ID for the identity comparison
body: This stores only the GitHub login for the later identity check, but logins are mutable and can become available to another account after a rename. If the original installer renames their account and another user claims the old login, that different user can satisfy the comparison against the stored webhook sender. Bind and compare GitHub's stable user ID instead.

title: Missing sender metadata causes an uncaught KeyError
body: This assumes every existing Integration has `metadata.sender.login`, but `build_integration` adds `sender` only when the pipeline state contains it. An existing integration without sender metadata therefore raises `KeyError` here and returns a server error instead of the intended invalid-installation response. Treat missing sender data as a failed validation.

title: The installer identity check is skipped when no Integration row exists
body: The identity comparison is reached only after the `Integration.objects.get` lookup succeeds. When the row is absent, the earlier `DoesNotExist` branch calls `pipeline.next_step()` and proceeds with installation without comparing the OAuth user to GitHub’s installer. A delayed or failed installation webhook can therefore leave this path available for connecting an installation using a different GitHub account, defeating the validation this change is intended to enforce.

title: Missing sender metadata causes an unhandled KeyError
body: This directly indexes `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`, but `build_integration` only adds `sender` when `state.get("sender")` is present, and existing integrations may not have this metadata. If an Integration exists without an OrganizationIntegration and without sender metadata, setup raises KeyError and returns a 500 instead of handling the installation.

title: Request a scope for the GitHub user lookup
body: The authorize URL requests no OAuth scopes, but the next step calls `get_user_info` to fetch the authenticated user from GitHub’s `/user` endpoint, which requires a user profile scope such as `read:user`. A token issued with no scopes can be denied by that endpoint, preventing installations from completing; the tests stub `/user` and do not catch this real API behavior.

title: New installations can bypass the installer identity check
body: This comparison runs only when an `Integration` already exists. For a new installation whose GitHub installation webhook has not yet created that row, the earlier `Integration.DoesNotExist` branch advances the pipeline and creates the integration without comparing the authenticated user to the webhook sender. Because webhook delivery is asynchronous, a user mismatch can be accepted during that race; the pipeline needs to validate the identity before proceeding even when the integration row is absent.

title: The queued timestamp is shared across all instances
body: `timezone.now()` is evaluated once when this module is imported, so every `AssignmentSource` created in the process gets the same `queued` value rather than the time that source was created. Since `to_dict()` includes this value in outbound task payloads, the serialized assignment context reports an incorrect timestamp for later assignments. Use a `default_factory` so each instance gets its own timestamp.

title: `queued` is fixed at module import time
body: `timezone.now()` is evaluated when this module is imported, so every `AssignmentSource` created in the process gets the same `queued` timestamp rather than the time that source was created. The serialized field therefore cannot represent when an assignment was queued, making any timing or freshness information derived from it incorrect. Use a `default_factory` so each instance gets its own timestamp.

title: The queued timestamp is fixed at module import
body: `timezone.now()` is evaluated when this module is imported, not each time an `AssignmentSource` is created. As a result, sources created later in the process all carry the same stale `queued` value, so the timestamp serialized with outbound sync tasks does not reflect when the assignment was queued. Use a `default_factory` to generate it per instance.

title: Metric alert handler is abstract and cannot be instantiated
body: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` inherits the abstract methods of `StatefulDetectorHandler` but implements none of them. Because `MetricAlertFire` registers this class as its detector handler, `Detector.detector_handler` will raise `TypeError` when it tries to instantiate a detector of this type, preventing that detector from being processed.

title: Evaluation docstring still promises a list
body: This method now returns a dictionary keyed by group key, but its docstring says it returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`. That contradicts the method’s return contract and can mislead callers implementing or using detector handlers.

title: Registered metric-alert handler is abstract and cannot be instantiated
body: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` now subclasses `StatefulDetectorHandler` but implements none of its abstract members, including `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. The class can be registered, but `Detector.detector_handler` will raise `TypeError` when it tries to instantiate it for a detector of this group type, preventing that detector from being processed.

title: Document the new dictionary return type
body: This docstring says `evaluate` returns a list, but the method now returns a dictionary keyed by group key. That contradicts the method’s contract and can mislead callers or handler implementers about how to consume its results; update the documentation to describe the dictionary.

title: Metric alert handler is now abstract and cannot be instantiated
body: `StatefulDetectorHandler` requires subclasses to implement abstract methods, including `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. This `pass` subclass implements none of them, so `Detector.detector_handler` raises `TypeError` when processing a detector with this registered handler. The previous handler was concrete and returned an empty result; preserve a concrete no-op handler or implement the required methods.

title: Evaluation docstring still says the method returns a list
body: `evaluate` now returns a dictionary keyed by group key, but this docstring says it returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`. That documents the old contract and can mislead subclasses and callers about the returned shape; update it to describe the dictionary.

title: Removed module-level helpers break existing imports
body: This refactor removes the `mark_failed_threshold`, `create_issue_platform_occurrence`, `get_failure_reason`, `get_monitor_environment_context`, and `SimpleCheckIn` names from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` without forwarding aliases. Any existing test or caller importing these names from that module will now fail with `ImportError`; update those importers or preserve compatibility aliases.

title: Return the normalized monitor config
body: `get_monitor_environment_context` copies `config` and replaces `schedule_type` with its display value, but returns `monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead. As a result, occurrence event contexts expose the raw stored schedule type rather than the display value this code prepares; return `config` here.

title: Do not leave later flusher processes running when the join deadline expires
body: This `break` exits the loop over all processes. If `next_step.join(timeout)` has already used the deadline, or an earlier process consumes it, later processes never reach `process.terminate()`. A worker that is hung or blocked can therefore continue using Redis and Kafka after the strategy's timed shutdown returns.

title: Reject nonpositive flusher process counts
body: The CLI accepts any integer for `--flusher-processes`. A value of `0` is treated as unset here and silently selects one process per shard, potentially creating far more workers than configured. A negative value produces a negative `num_processes`, then shard distribution indexes an empty process map and fails consumer initialization. Validate that configured counts are positive rather than interpreting or failing on them unexpectedly.

title: The process-limit test exercises threads, not multiprocessing
body: Passing `produce_to_pipe` selects the `threading.Thread` path in `SpanFlusher`; this test's process-count assertions therefore do not exercise the production spawn-process path. It cannot catch failures specific to spawning workers or sharing synchronization state across processes, so the new multiprocessing behavior remains unverified by this test.

title: Reject non-positive flusher process counts
body: The CLI accepts any integer for `--flusher-processes`, but `or` turns an explicit `0` into the number of assigned shards, defeating the configured cap and potentially spawning one process per shard. A negative value remains negative, produces an empty process map, and then raises `KeyError` when assigning a shard, crashing the consumer. Validate that the value is positive before computing the process count.

title: Terminate workers when the join deadline expires
body: When the deadline has expired, this `break` skips the termination code for the current worker and every remaining worker. The deadline may already be consumed by `next_step.join(timeout)`, so a wedged flusher process can survive strategy shutdown with access to Redis and Kafka; later workers are also left running. Ensure timed-out workers are terminated rather than breaking out before cleanup.

title: The process-limit test exercises threads, not processes
body: Passing `produce_to_pipe` makes `SpanFlusher` choose `threading.Thread`, so this test's process-count assertions only verify the shard mapping and do not exercise the new spawn-process path. It will not catch failures in process startup, argument pickling, or process cleanup. Add coverage that starts the real multiprocessing branch (with Kafka production suitably mocked).

title: Timeout can leave later flusher processes running
body: When the shared join deadline expires while waiting for an earlier process, this `break` skips the remaining processes, including the `terminate()` call below. A later worker blocked in Redis or Kafka can therefore outlive `join(timeout)` and continue producing or accessing Redis during shutdown. Continue through the workers and terminate any that remain alive after the deadline.

title: Reject non-positive flusher process limits
body: The CLI accepts any integer for `--flusher-processes`, but this expression treats `0` as unset (silently allowing one worker per shard) and leaves negative values unchanged. With a negative value, `num_processes` is negative, the process map is empty, and assigning a shard raises `KeyError` during consumer startup. Validate that the limit is positive and only use the shard count when the argument is `None`.

title: The added wait is disabled by the test's sleep monkeypatch
body: This test replaces `time.sleep` with a no-op at line 15, so this call does not give the flusher thread time to observe the updated drift. `step.join()` immediately sets the shared stop flag, and the worker can exit before flushing; the test therefore still has a race and can fail intermittently. Use synchronization that is not patched out, such as an event or a bounded wait on the expected output.

title: Failed work is still marked complete
body: The `finally` block marks every item’s offset complete, including when `result_processor` raises and the worker logs the exception. The commit loop can then commit past a result that was never processed, preventing Kafka from redelivering it. The normal `ResultProcessor` also catches handler exceptions and returns, so those failures likewise appear successful to this tracker. Only mark an offset complete when processing has actually succeeded, or explicitly define and test a skip-on-error policy.

title: The work queues are unbounded
body: `queue.Queue()` defaults to an unlimited size, so `put()` does not provide the natural backpressure claimed by this implementation. If Kafka delivers faster than the workers can process, queued `WorkItem`s accumulate in memory until the consumer process can be OOM-killed. Bound the queues and ensure a full queue appropriately slows or pauses consumption.

title: Shutdown exits workers without draining queued work
body: Setting `worker.shutdown` before shutting down the queues makes each worker exit after its current item; `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` does not override the loop condition or ensure the remaining items are processed. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close` also stops the commit thread before shutting down the pool. Pending items therefore remain unprocessed and uncommitted at shutdown, causing them to be replayed after restart and potentially duplicating side effects. Drain the queues and allow completed offsets to be committed before stopping the workers and commit thread.

title: Shutdown relies on a Python 3.13-only queue API
body: `Queue.shutdown()` and `queue.ShutDown` were added in Python 3.13. On supported runtimes below 3.13, this call raises `AttributeError`, which is swallowed here; workers blocked in `get()` are never woken, and each `join(timeout=5.0)` leaves daemon worker threads behind. Use a shutdown mechanism supported by the project’s Python versions, or explicitly require Python 3.13+.

title: A negative worker count silently drops results
body: The CLI accepts any integer for `--max-workers`, and a negative value is truthy here, so it is passed as `num_queues`. `range(num_queues)` then creates no queues or workers. Submissions fail when indexing the empty queue list, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` catches that failure and marks the message offset complete, allowing it to be committed without processing. Reject non-positive worker counts before starting the consumer.

title: Do not mark failed work as complete
body: The `finally` block completes the offset even when `result_processor` raises and the worker logs the failure. The commit loop can then advance past that result, preventing Kafka from redelivering it. The submission exception handler at lines 317–325 has the same problem: grouping or enqueue failures are marked complete even though the item was never processed. Only complete offsets after successful handling, or propagate failures for retry/DLQ processing.

title: Do not shut down the factory-owned pool when a strategy closes
body: The queue pool is created and retained by `ResultsStrategyFactory`, then shared with strategies created by that factory. Arroyo can close and recreate a strategy when partition assignments change; shutting down the shared pool here leaves the factory pointing at stopped workers or shut queues, so the replacement strategy cannot process messages. In this state submissions can remain unprocessed or fail and be acknowledged by the exception handler. Keep the pool alive until factory shutdown, or recreate it when the strategy is rebuilt.

title: Use a shutdown mechanism supported by the project's Python versions
body: `queue.Queue.shutdown()` was added in Python 3.13 and is unavailable on supported earlier Python versions. The resulting `AttributeError` is caught, but setting `worker.shutdown` does not wake workers blocked in `Queue.get()`. Each subsequent `join(timeout=5.0)` can time out; with the default 20 workers, normal shutdown can take about 100 seconds and leave daemon workers alive. Use a compatible wake-up mechanism, such as sentinels.

title: Bound the work queues to provide backpressure
body: A `Queue` with the default `maxsize=0` is unbounded, so `put()` never blocks when processing falls behind and the claimed natural backpressure does not occur. A sustained input rate above worker throughput will accumulate `WorkItem`s without limit and can exhaust process memory; each item also retains the original message payload. Set a finite queue capacity and define how the consumer handles a full queue.

title: Processing failures are marked complete and committed
body: This runs in `finally`, so an exception from `result_processor` still removes the offset from the outstanding set. The commit loop can then advance past a result that was never processed; failures swallowed by `ResultProcessor.__call__` have the same outcome. Do not mark an offset complete until processing succeeds or the message is explicitly routed to a failure-handling path.

title: Closing a strategy permanently shuts down the shared queue pool
body: `queue_pool` is owned by `ResultsStrategyFactory` and reused by each `create_with_partitions` call, but closing one strategy shuts it down. When Arroyo recreates a strategy after a partition-assignment change, the factory reuses this non-None pool with stopped workers and shut-down queues. Subsequent submissions fail, and `submit()` treats those failures as completed offsets, allowing results to be committed without processing. Keep the shared pool alive across strategy instances, or create and manage a separate pool per strategy.

title: A missing Kafka offset can permanently block commits
body: The tracker requires every integer offset between `start` and `max_offset` to have been received. Kafka consumers can legitimately observe gaps, for example when compacted or aborted records are not returned.
