For http://example.com:8080/article that value is example.com, so the saved entry can never match. The UI reports a successful save while embedding and topic retrieval remain denied. Either normalize away ports consistently or include the port in the lookup according to the intended authorization rules.

title: Prevent conflicting category mappings for the same host
body: Neither the model nor the migration's table definition enforces host uniqueness, so administrators can save two entries for the same hostname with different categories. Host lookup uses only the first matching row, silently ignoring the other mapping even though both appear as successfully configured in the UI. Enforce uniqueness on the normalized, case-insensitive hostname, including a database constraint, so each host has an unambiguous destination category.

title: The second downsize definition replaces the existing API
body: Ruby does not overload methods by argument count: this definition replaces the downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={}) method immediately above it. Existing calls with width, height, and options now raise ArgumentError; calls with just width and height bind the height to opts and fail when optimize indexes it as a hash. Keep a single method that explicitly supports both calling conventions, or give the dimensions-string variant a different name.

title: Downsizing multipart GIF uploads discards their animation
body: The resize operation receives the multipart tempfile path rather than a path carrying the original filename's extension. Such paths normally have no .gif suffix, but OptimizedImage.optimize selects its animation-preserving implementation only when the input path ends in .GIF. Consequently, even with allow_animated_thumbnails enabled, an oversized animated GIF goes through convert with the [0] frame selector. Because the output overwrites the upload itself, the stored original permanently loses every frame except the first. Determine the image format independently of the tempfile suffix and preserve animation when downsizing the original.

title: Keep the configured size limit for attachments
body: The hard-coded 10 MB limit applies to attachments as well as images, although the new server-side downsizing only handles images. Attachments larger than max_attachment_size_kb now pass client validation and are uploaded before being rejected by the server. Conversely, sites configured to allow attachments larger than 10 MB can no longer upload them through this client. Retain the configured attachment limit and apply any larger pre-downsizing limit only to images.

title: The new downsize definition replaces the existing width/height API
body: Ruby does not overload methods by argument count: this second definition of `self.downsize` replaces the definition above it. Existing calls passing width, height, and options now raise ArgumentError; calls passing just width and height treat the height as `opts` and fail when `optimize` accesses `opts[:allow_animation]`. Preserve both call forms in a single method or give the dimensions-based method a separate name so existing image-downsizing callers continue to work.

title: Oversized animated GIF uploads lose their animation even when it is allowed
body: The downsizing call passes the multipart tempfile path, which normally has no `.gif` extension. `OptimizedImage.optimize` selects its animated implementation only when the input path ends in `.GIF`, so `allow_animation: true` does not preserve animation here. The regular conversion reads only `from[0]` and overwrites the uploaded file with its first frame. Consequently, uploading an oversized animated GIF permanently discards its animation despite `allow_animated_thumbnails` being enabled. Detect the format independently of the temporary filename or use an appropriately suffixed working file.

title: Keep the configured size limit for non-image attachments
body: The unconditional 10 MB limit also applies to attachments, although the new server-side downsizing applies only to images. This removes enforcement of `max_attachment_size_kb` in the client: attachments above a smaller configured limit are submitted only to be rejected by the server, while attachments allowed by a configured limit above 10 MB can no longer be uploaded through the UI. Apply the expanded input limit only to images and retain the configured attachment limit.

title: The new downsize definition replaces the width/height API
body: Ruby does not overload methods by argument signature: this second definition of `self.downsize` replaces the definition immediately above it. Existing calls using `(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts)` now raise ArgumentError. Calls with just width and height instead treat the height as `opts`, which fails when `optimize` accesses `opts[:allow_animation]`. Preserve both calling conventions in a single method or give the dimensions-based entry point a different name.

title: Downsizing can permanently remove animation from uploaded GIFs
body: The upload's original file is overwritten using `allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails`. When animated thumbnails are disabled, the conversion reads only `from[0]`, so an oversized animated GIF becomes a single-frame image before it is stored. A setting governing thumbnails should not silently discard animation from the original upload. Preserve animation during upload downsizing, or reject an image that cannot be downsized without losing it.

title: Percentage dimensions are not supported by the animated resizing command
body: For a temporary file ending in `.gif` with `allow_animated_thumbnails` enabled, this call selects gifsicle and passes `--resize-fit 80%`. Gifsicle's resize-fit option requires pixel dimensions in WIDTHxHEIGHT form, not a percentage. Conversion therefore fails, and the loop repeats the same failing operation five times without checking its result. Oversized animated GIFs remain oversized and cannot benefit from automatic downsizing. Calculate pixel dimensions for this path or use a command that supports percentage scaling.

title: Keep attachment validation tied to the configured attachment limit
body: The hard-coded 10 MB limit applies to attachments as well as images, although only images can be downsized. Sites configured to accept attachments larger than 10 MB now have those valid uploads blocked in the browser. Conversely, attachments exceeding a smaller configured limit are uploaded unnecessarily before being rejected by the server. Apply the expanded pre-downsizing allowance only to images and continue using `max_attachment_size_kb` for attachments.

title: Do not change notification preferences through an unprotected GET
body: The new GET route immediately saves a notification-level change for the authenticated user, without a confirmation or recipient-specific token. Rails CSRF protection does not protect GET requests, so an attacker can send a logged-in user to a known topic's unsubscribe URL and silently downgrade or mute its notifications. Serve the confirmation page on GET and perform the change through a CSRF-protected request, or require an appropriately scoped signed token.

title: Record the unsubscribe as an explicit notification preference change
body: Saving the TopicUser directly bypasses TopicUser.change, which sets notifications_reason_id to user_changed and records notifications_changed_at. For records whose reason is nil, TopicUser.update_last_read can subsequently replace the unsubscribed regular or muted level with tracking once the reading threshold is reached. The unsubscribe therefore does not persist as an explicit user choice. Use the existing notification-change API rather than only assigning notification_level.

title: Handle users without an existing TopicUser record
body: TopicUser.find_by can return nil, but the next statement unconditionally calls notification_level on it. Although sending an email creates a record for its intended recipient, the URL contains no recipient identity and acts on current_user: opening a forwarded email, or opening it while signed into another account that has not visited the topic, produces a 500 response. Initialize the missing per-user topic state and apply the unsubscribe through TopicUser.change, which already supports creating records.

title: Apply the unsubscribe when entering the route client-side
body: This route only loads the ordinary topic view; it never invokes the unsubscribe action. Notification preferences are changed solely by the initial Rails GET to the unsubscribe URL. When the Ember application transitions to this route client-side, that GET is not made, yet the template tells the user they will stop receiving notifications. Ensure entering the client route performs the unsubscribe through a protected mutation request before displaying the success message.

title: Do not change notification preferences through an unauthenticated GET action
body: The new GET route immediately changes the logged-in user's notification level, using only the session cookie and a predictable topic URL. GET requests do not receive Rails' normal CSRF-token protection, and this action also skips the XHR check. An external site can therefore cause a logged-in visitor to unsubscribe from a topic by navigating them to this URL, without their consent. Serve the confirmation page on GET and perform the preference change through a CSRF-protected POST, or use an appropriately scoped signed unsubscribe token.

title: Record unsubscribe as an explicit notification preference change
body: Saving notification_level directly bypasses TopicUser.change, which sets notifications_reason_id to user_changed and records notifications_changed_at. For a topic-user record whose reason is still nil, TopicUser.update_last_read can subsequently overwrite the unsubscribed regular or muted level with tracking once the reading-time threshold is reached. Thus reading the topic after unsubscribing can undo the choice automatically. Apply the new level through the existing preference-change API so the explicit choice is preserved.

title: Handle users without an existing topic-user record
body: TopicUser.find_by can return nil, but the next statement unconditionally reads its notification_level. Although sending a notification email creates a record for its recipient, the unsubscribe URL is not bound to that recipient: someone opening a forwarded email while logged into another account, or opening the URL before interacting with the topic, may have no record. The endpoint then returns a server error instead of unsubscribing. Treat a missing record as the default notification level and create it through TopicUser.change.

title: Do not change notification settings through an unprotected GET
body: The new GET route immediately changes the logged-in user's notification level, and the unsubscribe action explicitly skips the XHR check. GET requests do not require Rails' CSRF token, so another site can navigate a logged-in user to this predictable URL and silently disable notifications for a topic. Serve a confirmation page on GET and perform the change through a CSRF-protected POST instead.

title: Handle users without a TopicUser record
body: TopicUser.find_by can return nil, but the next statement unconditionally reads its notification_level. The unsubscribe URL is not tied to the email recipient, so opening it while logged into another account that has never interacted with the topic causes a server error instead of unsubscribing. This action does not track a visit or otherwise ensure a row exists. Handle the missing record and create the preference through TopicUser.change.

title: Record unsubscribe as an explicit notification preference change
body: Saving notification_level directly bypasses TopicUser.change, which sets notifications_reason_id to user_changed. For users whose topic preference still has a nil reason, TopicUser.update_last_read automatically switches the topic back to tracking once the reading-time threshold is reached, even after this action has muted it or set it to regular. Unsubscribing must record an explicit user change so subsequent reading does not undo the preference.

title: Normalize email addresses before matching the blocklist
body: The blocklist lookup uses an exact, case-sensitive database comparison, and neither BlockedEmail nor the new validator normalizes the address. A blocked address such as `block@spamfromhome.org` can therefore register as `block@SpamFromHome.org`, even though email domains are case-insensitive and this is the same mailbox. Normalize both stored blocklist entries and incoming addresses using the application's email normalization rules before comparing them.

title: Update match statistics atomically
body: The match counter is updated with a read-modify-save sequence. If two requests match the same blocked address concurrently, both can read the same match_count and save the same incremented value, losing one match. The timestamp can also move backward when an older request saves last. Use an atomic database update or a row lock so concurrent validation attempts do not corrupt the blocklist statistics.

title: Email blocks can be bypassed by changing address casing
body: The blocked-email lookup uses case-sensitive equality, and neither BlockedEmail nor User normalizes the address before this lookup. For example, blocking `block@spamfromhome.org` still allows signup with `block@SPAMFROMHOME.ORG`, which identifies the same mailbox because domain names are case-insensitive. Normalize stored blocked addresses and lookup values consistently with the application's email handling so casing cannot bypass a block.

title: Concurrent matches lose counter increments
body: The match counter is updated by reading a record, incrementing its in-memory value, and saving it without locking. Two concurrent requests matching the same blocked address can both read a count of N and both save N+1, recording only one of the two matches. Use an atomic database increment or lock the record while updating the statistics to keep match_count accurate under concurrent signup attempts.

title: Exact-case lookup allows blocked addresses to bypass validation
body: The blocked-email lookup compares the supplied address verbatim, and neither BlockedEmail nor User.new_from_params normalizes it. With `blocked@example.com` on the blocklist, registering as `blocked@EXAMPLE.COM` does not find the record, even though email domain names are case-insensitive and this is the same destination. Canonicalize addresses consistently when storing and looking up blocked emails, using the application's email-normalization rules, and test case variants.

title: Concurrent matches lose counter increments
body: `should_block?` reads `match_count`, increments it in Ruby, and saves the result without locking. Two concurrent registration attempts for the same blocked email can both read N and save N+1, recording only one of the two matches; an older request can also overwrite a newer `last_match_at`. Update the statistics atomically in the database or serialize these updates with a row lock so the recorded blocklist activity remains accurate.

title: Invalid ERB conditional prevents rendering existing discussions
body: The conditional ends with `end if`, but the trailing `if` has no condition. ERB generates invalid Ruby for this template, so requests for an embed whose topic already exists fail with a template syntax error instead of displaying the discussion. Close the conditional with just `end`.

title: Imported feed HTML bypasses sanitization
body: Feed content is passed through Nokogiri fragment parsing and stored as a raw-HTML post, whose cooking method returns the input unchanged. Fragment parsing does not remove scripts, event-handler attributes, or dangerous link schemes. Consequently, active HTML supplied by a feed executes on the forum's origin when the post is rendered, including through the embed template's `raw post.cooked`. Sanitize the imported HTML before storing/rendering it, and escape the URL interpolated into the attribution link.

title: Feeds without a content field abort polling
body: The poller unconditionally calls `scrub` on `i.content`. Ordinary RSS feeds commonly provide article text in `description` or `content:encoded` rather than `content`, and Atom feeds can provide only a summary. A missing content value therefore raises instead of importing the entry, aborting the entire poll and preventing subsequent entries from being processed. Select the supported content fields with a fallback and handle entries with no body.

title: Remote retrieval follows redirects outside the allowed host
body: TopicRetriever validates only the host of the initial embed URL, then this `open(url)` follows HTTP redirects without checking their destinations. An allowed-host URL that redirects to another host, including a private-network address, therefore causes the background worker to fetch that destination and potentially publish its contents as a topic. Validate the scheme and destination address for every request and redirect rather than relying solely on the original URL's host.

title: URL absolutization mishandles relative and protocol-relative links
body: The converter only handles values beginning with `/` and treats all of them as paths on the article's host. Thus `images/photo.jpg` remains relative and loads from the forum rather than the source article, while `//cdn.example.com/photo.jpg` becomes a path such as `http://source.example.com/cdn.example.com/photo.jpg`. The same problem affects anchor links. Resolve references against the full source URL with URI-aware joining so imported images and links retain their intended destinations.

title: Invalid ERB Ruby prevents existing discussions from rendering
body: The opening `if` is closed with `end if`, leaving a trailing `if` without a condition. Rails cannot compile this template, so requests for an existing embedded topic fail with a template syntax error instead of displaying the discussion. Close the block with `end`.

title: Sanitize imported HTML before storing it as cooked content
body: Feed content reaches this method without HTML sanitization, and the post is created with `raw_html`, which makes `Post#cook` return the HTML unchanged. `absolutize_urls` only parses and rewrites URLs; it does not remove scripts, event handlers, or dangerous URL schemes. Consequently, malicious HTML in a feed becomes stored executable content on the forum's origin. Sanitize both initial imports and revisions before bypassing the normal cooking pipeline.

title: Validate redirect destinations before fetching embedded pages
body: The request-driven retrieval path checks only the hostname of the original embed URL, then uses `open(url)`, which follows HTTP redirects. An allowed-host URL that redirects to another host can therefore make the worker fetch internal services or attacker-controlled content despite the hostname restriction. Validate the scheme, port, resolved address, and each redirect destination before fetching rather than relying solely on the initial host check.

title: Handle RSS entries that use description or content:encoded
body: The poller assumes every item has a non-nil `content` field. Ordinary RSS feeds commonly provide the body through `description` or `content:encoded` instead, so `i.content.scrub` raises for those entries. This aborts the entire polling run, preventing the entry and all subsequent entries from importing. Select the supported body fields with a fallback and handle missing bodies explicitly.

title: Resolve relative URLs with URI joining instead of prefix concatenation
body: The URL rewriting handles only values starting with `/` and treats protocol-relative URLs as local paths. For example, `//cdn.example.com/image.jpg` becomes `http://article-host/cdn.example.com/image.jpg`, while `images/photo.jpg` remains relative to the forum rather than the source article. The same problem affects links. Resolve references against the source URL with URI joining so imported images and links continue to point to their original destinations.

title: Invalid ERB Ruby prevents existing discussions from rendering
body: The conditional is closed with `end if`, which is invalid Ruby because the trailing `if` has no condition. Rails will raise a template syntax error whenever an existing embedded topic renders this view, so the discussion iframe returns an error instead of showing comments. Close the block with `end`.

title: Imported feed HTML bypasses sanitization
body: Imported contents are stored with the `raw_html` cook method, whose implementation returns the raw text without sanitizing it. `absolutize_urls` only parses and rewrites URLs; it does not remove scripts, event-handler attributes, or dangerous link schemes. The RSS polling path passes feed contents directly into this method, so executable HTML from a feed is persisted as cooked content and rendered on the forum's origin. Sanitize imported HTML before storing it, including on updates.

title: RSS entries without a content element abort feed polling
body: The poller assumes every entry has a non-nil `content` value and calls `scrub` on it. Ordinary RSS entries can provide their body in `description` rather than an Atom-style `content` element, and entries may omit a body entirely. Such an entry raises an exception and stops the entire polling run, preventing subsequent entries from being imported. Support the RSS body fields and handle missing content explicitly.

title: Remote retrieval follows redirects outside the allowed host
body: TopicRetriever checks only the host of the initial embed URL, but `open(url).read` follows HTTP redirects without checking their destinations. An allowed-host URL that redirects to another host, including an internal HTTP service, therefore bypasses the embedding host restriction and can have its response imported into a public topic. Validate every redirect destination and restrict retrieval to permitted HTTP(S) endpoints before fetching it.

title: URL rewriting corrupts protocol-relative links and misses relative paths
body: The rewrite treats every URL beginning with `/` as a path on the article's host. For example, `//cdn.example.com/image.jpg` becomes `http://article-host/cdn.example.com/image.jpg`; the image rewrite below has the same problem. Conversely, document-relative URLs such as `images/photo.jpg` are left unchanged and resolve against the Discourse URL rather than the source article. This breaks links and images in imported articles. Resolve URLs against the complete source URL using URI joining, preserving protocol-relative hosts.

title: Preserve right alignment in the legacy flexbox fallback
body: The panel now relies on `margin-left: auto` to stay at the right edge, but the `flexbox()` mixin also enables the 2009 `-webkit-box` layout for browsers such as Safari 6. That layout does not distribute free space to auto margins, and the previous `float: right` has been removed. In those browsers the navigation panel sits immediately beside the title/topic information instead of at the right edge. Provide equivalent positioning for the legacy box layout, or retain a working non-flex fallback rather than selecting `-webkit-box`.

title: Preserve right alignment in the legacy flexbox fallback
body: The new header layout relies on `margin-left: auto` to push `.panel` to the right, but the `flexbox()` mixin also selects the legacy `display: -webkit-box` layout on browsers without modern flexbox support. That layout treats auto margins as zero, and the removed `float: right` cannot position a box-layout child. On those browsers (including older Android stock browsers), the navigation panel now sits immediately beside the logo/topic information rather than at the right edge. Provide a legacy-compatible expanding spacer or retain a working fallback instead of relying solely on the auto margin.

title: Apply the website visibility restriction to website_name
body: The new `website_name` attribute is not included in `untrusted_attributes`, so it is serialized even when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` hides a TL0 user's website from anonymous visitors. The template now displays this unrestricted value, exposing the hidden hostname (and path for matching domains) and bypassing the existing profile-field restriction. Also, `include_website_name` is missing the trailing `?`, so ActiveModel::Serializer will not use it as an inclusion predicate. Add `website_name` to the restricted attributes and cover it in the anonymous TL0 serialization test.

title: Apply the website visibility restriction to website_name
body: The new website_name attribute is not included in untrusted_attributes, and include_website_name lacks the trailing `?` required for a serializer inclusion predicate. Consequently, anonymous requests for TL0 profiles receive the website hostname (and, for matching domains, its path) even when scope.restrict_user_fields? suppresses website itself. The updated template also displays that restricted information. Add website_name to the same visibility guard as website and use a correctly named inclusion predicate.

title: Refresh the website label when saving profile changes
body: The label now comes from the server-populated website_name instead of a computed property dependent on model.website. User.save() sends the changed website but only copies bio_excerpt from the response; it never updates website_name. After changing or clearing a website on the loaded user model, the profile can therefore show the old domain with a new or empty link target, or keep a newly added website hidden, until user details are fetched again. Update website_name from the save response or otherwise recompute it when website changes.

title: Apply untrusted-field restrictions to website_name
body: The new website_name attribute is not included in untrusted_attributes, so it is serialized even when scope.restrict_user_fields?(object) suppresses website for an anonymous viewer of a TL0 user. This exposes the otherwise-hidden website hostname (and path for same-domain URLs), and the updated template displays it because it checks website_name rather than website. The include_website_name method does not prevent this: it lacks the required '?' suffix and only checks presence anyway. Apply the same restriction used for website and extend the anonymous/TL0 serializer test to cover the new field.

title: Preserve the light-theme contrast of expanded-post attribution links
body: The light-theme branch changes the expanded-post attribution link from scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%) to 70%, rather than preserving the existing value. With a #333 primary on a white background, this changes approximately #707070 to #c2c2c2, reducing contrast from about 5:1 to 1.8:1. These small attribution links become difficult to read in light themes. Keep the light branch at 30% and use the complementary 70% secondary scaling for the dark branch.

title: Keep group-member names at their existing light-theme lightness
body: The group-member name previously used 30% primary lightness, but the new light-theme branch uses 50%. The same change occurs in mobile/user.scss at line 497. For a #333 primary on white, this changes the name from approximately #707070 to #999999, dropping contrast from about 5:1 to 2.8:1 and removing its contrast distinction from the member title. Preserve the original 30% light-theme branch and use 70% secondary scaling for dark themes in both files.

title: Adjust the badge foreground when making its dark-theme background dark
body: The default notification badge now uses a dark background in dark themes, but its foreground remains $secondary, including the explicit &[href] rule. For a dark palette with black secondary, the new background is approximately #4d4d4d while the count text is black, giving only about 2.5:1 contrast for 11px text. Previously the primary-based background was light and the secondary foreground remained readable. Change the dark-theme foreground to a contrasting color, or retain a sufficiently light background; otherwise default badge counts become difficult to read.

title: Preserve the light-theme color for embedded-post author links
body: The light-theme branch changes the existing primary lightness adjustment from 30% to 70%, rather than preserving it while adding a dark-theme alternative. This makes embedded-post author links substantially fainter on light backgrounds; for example, a #333 primary becomes approximately #c2c2c2 instead of #707070. Keep 30% in the light branch and use the corresponding 70% secondary adjustment in the dark branch.

title: Preserve group-member name contrast in light themes
body: The group-member name previously used a 30% primary lightness adjustment, but the new light-theme branch uses 50%. The same unintended change occurs in mobile/user.scss at line 497. With a #333 primary and white background, this changes the name from approximately #707070 to #999999, reducing contrast from about 4.95:1 to 2.85:1. Preserve the existing 30% light-theme adjustment and add the complementary 70% secondary adjustment for dark themes.

title: Retain the existing light-theme topic-map heading color
body: The new light-theme branch changes topic-map h3 headings from a 20% primary lightness adjustment to 50%. This unnecessarily reduces heading contrast in light themes and gives headings the same color as the smaller h4 labels. With a #333 primary on a near-white topic-map background, the heading changes from approximately #5c5c5c to #999999. Keep the original 20% light-theme adjustment and use 80% for the dark-theme secondary branch.

title: Update notification-badge text when darkening its background
body: The generic notification-badge background now becomes a lightly brightened secondary color in dark themes, but its text remains the unmodified secondary color, including the explicit [href] rule. This puts dark text on a dark gray badge: with a black secondary, the new background is approximately #4d4d4d and the black text has only about 2.5:1 contrast. Previously, the primary-based background remained light and contrasted with that text. Use a contrasting dark-theme foreground, such as primary, alongside the new background.

title: Preserve the light-theme color of embedded-post author links
body: The light-theme branch changes the embedded-post author link from 30% to 70% lightness instead of preserving the existing value. This makes the author substantially paler on the light background and reduces readability (with a #222 primary and white background, the new color has roughly 1.9:1 contrast). Keep the light branch at 30% and use the complementary 70% secondary value for the dark branch.

title: Retain the distinct color for group-member names
body: The group-member name previously used 30% primary lightness, but now uses 50%, exactly like the adjacent title. This unintentionally fades names in light themes and removes the existing visual distinction between the member's name and title. The same regression appears in mobile/user.scss at line 497. Preserve 30% for the light branch and use 70% secondary lightness for the dark branch in both files.

title: Preserve the stronger light-theme color for topic-map headings
body: The mobile topic-map h3 changes from 20% primary lightness to 50% in the light-theme branch. It now has the same faded color as h4, weakening the heading hierarchy and reducing text contrast even when no dark theme is enabled. The desktop equivalent correctly retains 20%/80%; use that pair here as well so this dark-theme fix does not regress light-theme headings.

title: Public group pages cannot display members beyond the first 50
body: The members endpoint now limits every group to 50 members by default, and the public route calls findMembers only once. This template has no pagination controls or load-more mechanism. Consequently, members beyond the first 50 are inaccessible on public group pages; previously, non-automatic groups displayed their entire membership. Add public pagination alongside the new server-side limit.

title: Exact page-size multiples produce an extra empty page
body: totalPages uses floor(user_count / limit) + 1, which overcounts whenever the membership count is an exact multiple of the page size. For example, a group with 50 members reports two pages and enables Next, which requests offset 50 and displays an empty list. Use ceiling division for nonzero counts so the last populated page disables Next.

title: Member removal can leave pagination on an empty, unreachable page
body: findMembers clamps the offset to the member count rather than to the start of the last populated page, and it calculates that clamp using the count from before the request. If an administrator removes the sole member on page two of a 51-member group, the reload requests offset 50 and returns an empty list with total 50. Subsequent membership changes can clamp the offset to the count itself, still returning no members and potentially reporting page one with Previous disabled. Normalize the offset to a valid page boundary after the total changes and refetch when necessary.

title: Existing membership PATCH requests silently hide groups
body: The previous update action supported PATCH /admin/groups/:id with changes[add] and changes[delete], and the resources route still accepts PATCH. The replacement action ignores changes and unconditionally sets visible to false when visible is absent. Existing API callers therefore receive a success response without changing membership, while unintentionally making the group invisible. Preserve the PATCH behavior or explicitly reject the obsolete request before modifying the group.

title: Public group member lists are truncated with no way to fetch subsequent pages
body: The public members route now calls findMembers() with its default limit of 50, and the server applies that limit to every group. However, the public members template has no pagination controls or load-more behavior. A custom group with more than 50 members, which previously displayed all members, now permanently hides everyone after the first 50. Add pagination to the public page or preserve its complete member listing.

title: Exact multiples of the page size produce an extra empty page
body: totalPages uses floor(user_count / limit) + 1, which overcounts whenever the member count is an exact multiple of the limit. For example, a 50-member group with limit 50 displays two pages and enables Next; clicking it requests offset 50 and displays an empty member list. Use ceiling division for the number of pages.

title: Existing membership PATCH requests now silently change group visibility
body: The previous update action supported PATCH /admin/groups/:id with changes.add and changes.delete, as demonstrated by the removed incremental-update tests. The route still accepts PATCH, but this action now ignores changes and unconditionally sets visible to false when no visible parameter is supplied. Existing clients therefore receive a successful response without the requested membership change, while also unexpectedly hiding the group. Preserve the PATCH contract or explicitly reject unsupported requests without modifying the group.

title: Removing the final member on a page leaves pagination at an invalid offset
body: removeMember reloads members using the existing offset without moving back when the current page becomes empty. For example, removing the only member on page 3 of a 101-member group leaves offset 100 after the total falls to 100. Subsequent reloads still return an empty list because findMembers clamps the offset to the member count rather than to the start of the last valid page. Normalize the offset to a valid page after membership removal so the administrator sees the remaining members.

title: Existing membership PATCH requests now silently hide the group
body: The resource still exposes PATCH /admin/groups/:id, but update no longer handles the previously supported changes: {add: ..., delete: ...} payload. An existing client sending that payload now receives success without changing membership, and because it does not supply visible, this assignment also sets the group's visibility to false. Preserve the PATCH behavior or explicitly reject the obsolete payload instead of silently applying an unrelated settings change.

title: Public member lists are truncated without pagination controls
body: findMembers now requests only 50 members by default, and the server applies that limit to every group. The public group members template has no pagination controls or load-more mechanism, and this route makes only one request. Consequently, users cannot view members beyond the first 50; custom groups previously returned their complete member list. Add pagination to the public page or otherwise fetch the remaining members.

title: Exact page-size multiples produce an extra empty page
body: The total-page calculation uses floor(user_count / limit) + 1, which overcounts whenever the member count is an exact multiple of the page size. For example, a group with 50 members and a limit of 50 shows two pages and enables Next, which requests offset 50 and displays an empty member list. Use a ceiling-based calculation so the last populated page disables Next.

title: Load fallback locales for translations outside controller requests
body: Fallback translations are loaded only by this controller filter, while the translation accelerator still loads only `config.locale` when `I18n.t` is called. Background jobs, mailers, and other non-controller callers therefore do not load the site-default and English YAML files before the fallback backend searches them. In a worker where those locales have not already been loaded, missing localized keys still produce missing-translation results instead of the intended fallback. Ensure the fallback chain is loaded in the translation path itself, rather than relying on an HTTP request filter.

title: Include the site fallback locale in the translation cache key
body: The new fallback chain depends on `SiteSetting.default_locale`, but this cache key includes only the translation key, requested locale, and backend identity. If an administrator changes the site's default locale, a cached translation for a key missing from the user's locale continues returning the previous site's fallback-language text until eviction or reload. Include the effective fallback configuration in the cache key or invalidate the cache when it changes.

title: Load fallback locales for translations outside controller requests
body: Fallback translations are preloaded only by ApplicationController#set_locale. The translation accelerator still loads only the current locale, and I18n::Backend::Fallbacks searches other locales directly through the backend without invoking that loader. In a fresh worker or other non-controller context, a missing non-English translation therefore cannot fall back to English (or the site locale) because those YAML files have not been loaded. Ensure the fallback chain is loaded on the translation path itself rather than relying on a controller filter.

title: Include the site fallback locale in the translation cache key
body: The new fallback chain depends on SiteSetting.default_locale, but the translation cache key contains only the requested key, current locale, and backend identity. If the site default changes—or sites with different defaults share this process—a cached translation missing from the user's locale is reused even though it should now resolve through a different site locale. Loading the new fallback locale does not invalidate this cached result. Include the fallback configuration or site identity in the cache key, or invalidate the cache whenever that configuration changes.

title: Load fallback locales for translations outside controller requests
body: Fallback locales are loaded only when ApplicationController#set_locale calls I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!. The translation wrapper still loads only config.locale, and this backend explicitly disables automatic loading of translation files. Consequently, translations performed outside a controller request (for example, by a background job using a non-English locale) cannot find missing keys in the site locale or English unless those locales happen to have been loaded previously in that process. Ensure the applicable fallback locales are loaded on the translation path rather than relying on a controller filter.

title: Include the fallback configuration in the translation cache identity
body: The fallback chain now depends on SiteSetting.default_locale, but the translation accelerator caches optionless translations using only the key, requested locale, and backend object ID. If a missing translation is cached from the site locale and an administrator subsequently changes the default locale, the same lookup continues returning the old locale's text because the fallback chain is never consulted on a cache hit. Include the site fallback locale in the cache key or invalidate the translation cache when the default locale changes.

title: Include the identity type in denial cache keys
body: The denial key uses only the parsed subject ID, discarding IdentityType. Supported subjects such as `anonymous:0` and `render:0` therefore share a key for the same namespace, action, name and folder. If an anonymous dashboard read is denied, a subsequent renderer read hits that denial and returns false without evaluating the renderer's unconditional dashboard-read permission. Include the identity type (or full typed subject) in the key so one principal cannot poison another principal's authorization result.

title: Encode denial cache key components unambiguously
body: Concatenating the resource name and parent folder with underscores creates collisions for valid UIDs containing underscores. For the same namespace, user and action, a request for name `a_b` in folder `c` produces the same key as name `a` in folder `b_c`. A denial for the first request consequently denies the second request for 30 seconds, even if the user has direct or inherited permission on it. Use an unambiguous encoding, such as a serialized tuple or length-prefixed components, for the denial key.

title: Include the identity type in denial-cache keys
body: The denial key uses only the parsed subject ID, discarding IdentityType even though permission lookup distinguishes anonymous, renderer, and user identities. For example, `anonymous:0` and `render:0` produce the same denial key for the same dashboard request. If the anonymous request is denied first, the renderer request is also denied for 30 seconds without reaching getRendererPermissions, which would grant dashboard read access. Include the identity type in the key to prevent denials from crossing identity boundaries.

title: Encode denial-key components without delimiter collisions
body: Concatenating resource name and parent with unescaped underscores allows different requests to share a denial key. For the same namespace, subject, and action, name `foo_bar` with parent `baz` collides with name `foo` and parent `bar_baz`. Underscores are supported in legacy dashboard/folder UIDs, and request validation does not exclude them. A denial for one resource can therefore incorrectly deny access to another resource for the cache TTL. Use an unambiguous encoding of the components.

title: Seed an actual grant in the denial-precedence test
body: The test says it grants dashboard access to prove that the denial entry takes precedence, but it stores `"dashboards:uid:dash1": false`. checkPermission treats that entry as a denial, so this does not test the intended conflict between a cached grant and a cached denial. Set the entry to true so the test verifies that a denial-cache hit overrides an otherwise allowed request.

title: Include identity type in the denial-cache key
body: The denial-cache key uses only the parsed subject ID, omitting IdentityType. Distinct supported subjects such as anonymous:0 and render:0 therefore share a denial entry for the same namespace, action, name, and folder. If an anonymous dashboard read is denied, a subsequent renderer read is also denied for 30 seconds, even though getRendererPermissions grants dashboard reads unconditionally. Include the identity type (or full subject) in this key so one identity cannot poison another identity's authorization checks.

title: Encode denial-cache key components unambiguously
body: Concatenating resource name and parent folder with underscores allows distinct requests to produce the same key. For example, name=a_b with parent=c and name=a with parent=b_c both end in _a_b_c. Underscores are valid in these identifiers, so denying access to one resource can cause an unrelated, permitted resource to be denied until the cache entry expires. Use an unambiguous encoding, such as a serialized tuple or length-prefixed components.

title: Silence action does nothing for Prometheus-only Grafana rules
body: The new list items pass only promRule, and AlertRuleMenu now enables 'Silence notifications' using that rule's permissions. Clicking it only sets showSilenceDrawer, however: the drawer is still rendered only when rule is a Grafana ruler alerting rule, and requires that ruler rule as its input. Consequently, the silence option shown in both the grouped and filtered Grafana lists does nothing. Load the required rule on demand or adapt the drawer to the Prometheus-only path.

title: Pause and delete disappear from the new Grafana rule list
body: GrafanaRuleListItem now supplies promRule without rulerRule. Although this menu computes pause and delete permissions from promRule, rendering the pause item still requires a Grafana rulerRule, and rendering Delete at line 165 still requires rulerRule. Thus authorized users lose both pause/resume and delete actions from the new Grafana list. These actions need a Prometheus-only implementation or an on-demand ruler fetch rather than retaining guards that can never pass for list items.

title: Preserve federated-group immutability in the CombinedRule abilities hook
body: useAllAlertRuleAbilities previously checked isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) and disabled update/delete for federated groups. It now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes isFederated to false and has no group data. Existing consumers of the CombinedRule hook therefore enable edit and delete for Mimir federated rules that were explicitly treated as immutable before this change. Preserve the group-level check when computing these abilities.

title: Return disabled abilities when the Grafana rule hook is skipped
body: skipToken is converted to undefined, but useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined) still marks Duplicate as supported and grants it to anyone with Grafana rule-create permission. AlertRuleMenu calls this hook with skipToken for every non-Grafana rule and ORs its result with the actual ruler abilities. As a result, Grafana create permission can expose Duplicate for external rules even when their ruler does not support duplication or the external create permission is absent. The skipped hook must return disabled abilities rather than abilities for an absent Grafana rule.

title: Keep export available for Grafana recording rules
body: ModifyExport support is now restricted to isAlertingRule in the Prometheus abilities implementation. Previously, the ruler implementation supported export for any Grafana-managed rule, including recording rules. Since the new Grafana list no longer supplies a rulerRule, recording rules now lose their Export menu even for users with export permission. Use the Grafana rule predicate rather than the alerting-only predicate for this ability.

title: Pause and Delete disappear from Grafana rule list menus
body: The new list item supplies only promRule to RuleActionsButtons, but AlertRuleMenu still requires a Grafana rulerRule to render Pause and requires rulerRule to render Delete. Computing the Prometheus-based abilities does not remove those rendering guards. Consequently, even users with update and delete permissions can no longer pause, resume, or delete Grafana-managed rules from the new list. These actions need handlers and rendering paths that work with the Prometheus rule identifier.

title: Silence notifications is a no-op for Prometheus-only list items
body: GrafanaRuleListItem now calls this component without rule, and AlertRuleMenu can display Silence notifications using promRule permissions. Clicking it sets showSilenceDrawer to true, but the drawer is still rendered only when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true. With rule undefined that condition is always false, so no drawer opens. Load the required ruler data on demand or adapt the drawer to accept the Prometheus rule before exposing this action.

title: The skip token still grants Grafana duplicate abilities
body: Passing skipToken converts the rule to undefined but does not disable the returned abilities. For an undefined rule, useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities treats duplication as supported and allows it whenever the user has Grafana rule-create permission. AlertRuleMenu calls this hook with skipToken for data-source-managed rules and ORs its result with the ruler abilities. This can expose Duplicate for external rules whose ruler does not support it, or for plugin-provided external rules whose duplication was explicitly disabled. Return disabled abilities when the hook is skipped rather than evaluating an absent rule as a supported Grafana rule.

title: Preserve the immutability check for federated rule groups
body: useAllAlertRuleAbilities previously checked isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group), but it now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, where isFederated is hardcoded to false. Existing CombinedRule consumers therefore lose the protection that disables Update and Delete for Mimir federated groups with source_tenants. Users with external write permissions are now offered editing and deletion of rules that this UI previously treated as immutable. Preserve the group-level federation information when delegating rather than dropping this existing restriction.

title: Grafana recording rules lose the Export menu action
body: The Prometheus-based ModifyExport ability is supported only for alerting rules. The previous ruler-based ability used rulerRuleType.grafana.rule, which includes Grafana recording rules as well. Since the new Grafana list items no longer supply rulerRule, recording rules now have no supported export ability and their Export menu disappears even for users with read permission. Use the Grafana-rule check rather than the alerting-only check for this action to retain recording-rule export.

title: Silence notifications is a no-op for Prometheus-only list items
body: Grafana list items now pass only promRule, and the new abilities expose “Silence notifications” for those rules. Clicking it sets showSilenceDrawer, but the drawer is still guarded by rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule). Since rule is undefined in both list views, no drawer opens. Adapt the drawer to the new input or fetch the ruler rule when the action is invoked.

title: Removing the ruler input also removes Pause and Delete actions
body: Every Grafana list item now supplies RuleActionsButtons with only promRule. AlertRuleMenu still requires a Grafana rulerRule to render Pause and any rulerRule to render Delete, even when the new Prometheus abilities authorize those actions. Consequently, users with update/delete permissions lose both actions in the grouped and filtered list views. These actions need Prometheus-compatible handlers or an on-demand ruler fetch rather than disappearing when the initial ruler request is removed.

title: The ability skip token does not disable abilities
body: Passing skipToken calls useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined), which reports Duplicate as supported and allows it whenever the user has Grafana rule-create permission. AlertRuleMenu ORs this result with the ruler abilities, so a user who can create Grafana rules but cannot write external rules now sees Duplicate for an external rule despite its ruler permission check denying the action. Return disabled abilities for skipped inputs so the unused Grafana permission branch cannot authorize actions on other rule sources.

title: Preserve the federated-group restriction for combined rules
body: useAllAlertRuleAbilities previously checked isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group), but now delegates to this implementation, which hardcodes isFederated to false and discards the group metadata. Existing consumers of the combined-rule abilities therefore enable Update and Delete for Mimir rules in groups with source_tenants, although these operations were explicitly unsupported for federated groups before this change. Preserve the group-level immutability check when adapting CombinedRule to the ruler abilities.

title: Keep export available for Grafana recording rules
body: ModifyExport is now supported only when prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) succeeds. Grafana recording rules also support export, and the previous ruler-based check used rulerRuleType.grafana.rule, which included them. Because list items no longer provide the ruler fallback, recording rules lose their Export menu even for users with read permission. Use the Grafana-rule check rather than the alerting-only check for this ability.

title: Avoid interpolating shard queries a second time in runSplitQuery
body: Queries interpolated here are subsequently passed to runSplitQuery, which now calls applyTemplateVariables again for every shard batch. Template interpolation is not idempotent when a variable's value contains variable-like text. For example, if a service variable has the literal value `$other`, the first pass correctly produces a selector containing that value, but the second pass expands `$other` if that variable exists, querying a different service. Keep the early interpolation needed for shard selection, but ensure runSplitQuery can accept already-interpolated targets without applying template variables again. The updated test asserting five interpolation calls currently enshrines this double-processing rather than preventing it.

title: Avoid interpolating already-interpolated shard queries again
body: The shard-splitting path now calls applyTemplateVariables in runShardSplitQuery and then delegates each shard batch to runSplitQuery, which calls it again here. Template interpolation is not idempotent when a variable value contains another variable reference. For example, if search has the literal value '$host', `{app="x"} |= "$search"` is first expanded to a search for '$host', then expanded again to the value of host. This changes the user's query and can return incorrect results. Pass already-interpolated shard targets through without another template expansion, and add a regression test covering dollar-containing variable values.

title: Preserve recorded logs when deriving a test logger from context
body: TestLogger.FromContext returns a new, unrelated TestLogger, so calls on the returned logger are not recorded on the original test logger. LoggerMiddleware now emits every completion log through logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), which means a TestLogger supplied to that middleware no longer exposes those logs through its InfoLogs field. Return the same recorder or share recording state with the derived logger so logging assertions remain meaningful.

title: Preserve the test logger's recorder in FromContext
body: FromContext returns a fresh TestLogger with independent log storage. LoggerMiddleware now emits every request-completion log through logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so injecting a TestLogger records those calls on an inaccessible temporary instance while the supplied logger's InfoLogs remains empty. Tests inspecting the injected logger can no longer observe request logging. Return the existing fake, or share its recording state with the contextual logger.

title: Keep contextual log calls observable on the test logger
body: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh TestLogger with independent log records. LoggerMiddleware now logs every completed request through logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so an injected TestLogger no longer records those calls in its InfoLogs; they are written to a temporary logger that is immediately discarded. This breaks request-log assertions and prevents tests from observing the middleware's logging. Return the existing fake, or share its recording state with contextual children.

title: Rejected devices are cached as successfully admitted
body: TagDevice now propagates the limit error to authentication, but tagDeviceUI inserts the device into localCache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the store rejects a new device with ErrDeviceLimitReached, that cache entry remains for 29 minutes. A second request with the same device ID hits the cache and returns nil, so Authenticate grants anonymous access despite the limit. Concurrent requests can bypass the check the same way. Cache a device only after successful admission, and add a test that retries a rejected device.

title: Device admission is not atomic with the limit check
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts active devices in one database session and performs the insert in another, without serializing admission. If the count is one below deviceLimit, multiple requests for distinct new devices can all observe the available slot and then insert successfully. All of those devices subsequently qualify for updates, so the configured limit can remain exceeded. Make the count-and-admit operation atomic across requests and Grafana instances, and test concurrent admission.

title: Omitting the device header bypasses limit enforcement
body: Authenticate relies on TagDevice returning ErrDeviceLimitReached to deny anonymous access, but TagDevice immediately returns nil when X-Grafana-Device-Id is absent. Because this header is supplied by the client, an anonymous caller can omit it and continue accessing protected APIs even when the configured device limit is full; those requests are neither counted nor checked. Limit enforcement needs a defined admission path for requests without a device ID rather than treating missing identification as successful admission.

title: Rejected devices are cached as successfully admitted
body: TagDevice now propagates the limit error to authentication, but tagDeviceUI still inserts the device into localCache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, that cache entry remains for 29 minutes. A second request with the same device ID hits the cache and returns nil, so Authenticate grants anonymous access despite the limit. Concurrent requests can bypass the check even before the first store call completes. Cache only successfully admitted devices, and ensure in-flight checks cannot be treated as successful admissions.

title: Omitting the device header bypasses the configured limit
body: Authenticate enforces the limit solely through TagDevice, but TagDevice returns nil without consulting the store when X-Grafana-Device-Id is absent. Consequently, an unauthenticated client can omit that header and continue accessing anonymous APIs even when device_limit is exhausted. The configured limit needs an admission policy for requests without a device ID, rather than treating skipped tracking as successful admission.

title: Device counting and admission are not atomic
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts active devices in one database session and performs the insert in a separate session without locking or another atomic admission mechanism. If the count is one below deviceLimit, concurrent requests for different new devices can all observe the available slot and all insert successfully. This also occurs across Grafana instances sharing the database, allowing the active device count to exceed the configured limit; subsequent updates continue admitting those excess devices. Serialize the count-and-admit operation at the database level and add a concurrent admission test.

title: Rejected devices are cached as successfully admitted
body: TagDevice now propagates the device-limit error to authentication, but tagDeviceUI still inserts the device into localCache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the store rejects a new device because the limit is reached, that cache entry remains for 29 minutes. A second request with the same device ID hits the cache, returns nil, and is authenticated anonymously despite the limit. Cache a device only after a successful store operation, and add a test that retries a rejected device.

title: Device admission uses a non-atomic count-then-insert
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts active devices in one database session and performs the upsert separately, without locking or an atomic admission operation. If the count is one below the limit, concurrent requests with different new device IDs can all observe the available slot and all insert successfully. This also occurs across Grafana instances sharing the database, so the configured limit can be exceeded persistently. Serialize admission at the database level and cover concurrent admissions in a test.

title: Omitting the device header bypasses the anonymous limit
body: Authenticate enforces the limit only when TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, but TagDevice returns nil immediately when X-Grafana-Device-Id is missing. An unauthenticated client can therefore omit this client-controlled header and continue receiving an anonymous identity and accessing protected APIs even when the configured device limit is exhausted. Admission needs a server-enforced device-identification path, or equivalent enforcement for requests without this header, rather than relying on clients voluntarily supplying it.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors
body: The new cleanup logging calls use Error unconditionally, including when fetching and deleting succeed and when no rows need cleanup. The same pattern appears in count-based cleanup and orphaned-tag cleanup. Normal background maintenance will therefore continually generate false error events, potentially triggering log-based alerts, and will emit every selected ID at the default logging level. Remove these diagnostic calls or move successful-batch logging to Debug without dumping entire ID lists.

title: SQLite ID-list construction performs quadratic copying
body: For SQLite batches larger than 999, each iteration formats a new string containing the entire accumulated ID list. Building a batch of N IDs therefore copies O(N²) bytes. With batch sizes in the tens of thousands, as explicitly supported by the new test, this creates gigabytes of temporary allocations per full batch and can substantially delay cleanup and increase GC pressure. Build the list with strings.Builder or an append-based byte buffer instead.

title: The shorter ticker accelerates every cleanup job, not just annotations
body: Changing this ticker from ten minutes to one minute makes all cleanup jobs run ten times as often, including filesystem scans, dashboard-version deletion, image deletion, and query-history limit enforcement. It also leaves the nine-minute execution timeout unchanged: if a cleanup cycle takes longer than one minute, a tick will already be pending when it finishes, allowing repeated cycles to run without a pause. This unrelated scheduling change can materially increase database and filesystem load. Preserve the existing interval for this annotation-query fix, or isolate and justify a separate scheduling change.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors
body: The new cleanup paths emit Error logs for every successful SELECT and DELETE, including empty batches, with a nil error. Orphan-tag cleanup runs even when annotation retention is disabled, so normal scheduled cleanup now produces recurring false error reports. This can trigger log-based alerts and obscure actual failures; log successful operations at Debug level and reserve Error for failures.

title: Build the SQLite ID list without repeatedly copying its entire prefix
body: For SQLite batches above 999, each iteration formats the entire accumulated ID list into a new string. Building a batch of N IDs therefore takes quadratic copying and allocation rather than linear work. Configured batches containing tens of thousands of IDs can allocate gigabytes of temporary strings, causing substantial GC pressure and delaying cleanup and other work. Use strings.Builder or a byte buffer to append each ID once.

title: Bound parameterized deletes by the database parameter limit
body: The non-SQLite branch creates one bound parameter per selected ID without capping the batch. MySQL prepared statements and PostgreSQL's parameter protocol support at most 65,535 parameters, so an annotation cleanup batch configured above that limit fails whenever enough eligible rows exist. The previous subquery-based DELETE did not have this restriction. Split the selected IDs into supported-size deletes or otherwise avoid exceeding the backend's parameter limit.

title: Keep the shared cleanup cadence unchanged
body: Changing this ticker from ten minutes to one minute accelerates every cleanup job, not just annotation cleanup. Temporary-file directory scans, snapshot and dashboard-version deletion, image cleanup, invite expiration, and query-history retention now run ten times as often, increasing filesystem and database load independently of the deadlock fix. The shared cleanup timeout is still nine minutes, so slow cleanup passes can also leave a tick pending and run again immediately. Keep the existing cadence unless this broader scheduling change is separately justified.

title: Successful cleanup emits unconditional error-level logs
body: The new cleanup logging uses Error for normal batch selection and successful deletion, including empty batches with a nil error. The same issue occurs in both annotation cleanup branches. Orphan-tag cleanup therefore emits error messages even when there is nothing to clean, on every scheduled run. This creates false failure signals for log-based monitoring and logs entire ID batches at the normal production log level. Use debug-level logging for successful work and error-level logging only for actual failures.

title: SQLite ID-list construction has quadratic allocation cost
body: Each iteration formats and copies the entire accumulated ID list into a new string. For a batch of N IDs, this makes construction quadratic rather than linear and can allocate gigabytes of temporary strings for batches around the newly tested size of 32,767. This is a substantial regression from the previous database-side subquery and can make large SQLite cleanup batches consume excessive CPU and memory. Build the list with a strings.Builder or a byte buffer instead.

title: Large cleanup batches exceed MySQL and PostgreSQL parameter limits
body: The non-SQLite path now creates one bound parameter per selected ID without limiting the number of parameters. MySQL prepared statements and PostgreSQL's bind protocol have a 65,535-parameter limit, so a configured cleanup batch larger than that fails whenever enough eligible rows are present. The previous subquery-based DELETE did not have this restriction. Split deletion into parameter-limit-safe chunks or use an integer-literal strategy for these dialects as well, so previously working large batch configurations continue to clean annotations and orphaned tags.

title: Detach background writes from request cancellation
body: The legacy write's timeout context is derived from the request context. The HTTP server cancels that parent when the request handler returns, so returning the unified-storage result can immediately cancel the background legacy write rather than give it ten seconds to complete. This affects all four asynchronous write methods and can routinely leave legacy storage unchanged after successful requests. Preserve the request's context values while detaching cancellation before applying the background timeout.

title: Preserve write ordering when mirroring to legacy storage
body: Each successful write launches an independent goroutine with no ordering between operations on the same resource. A client can successfully create an object and then delete it, while the legacy delete executes before the legacy create finishes; the create then leaves an object in legacy storage that is absent from unified storage. Consecutive updates can likewise overwrite newer data with older data. Background mirroring needs ordered execution or another mechanism that prevents stale operations from being applied.

title: Mirror the resolved update rather than replaying UpdatedObjectInfo
body: The legacy update now receives the original UpdatedObjectInfo instead of a wrapper containing the object returned by unified storage. UpdatedObjectInfo can calculate a PATCH or server-side apply result from the old object supplied by the store. Replaying it against legacy storage, which may be stale because mirroring is asynchronous, can produce a different object or fail even though the unified update succeeded. Pass the resolved unified-storage result to the legacy update, as the previous implementation did, rather than independently recomputing the update against legacy state.

title: Do not use resource names as the kind metric label
body: The successful delete duration passes name in the argument position used for options.Kind by the other metric calls. This creates separate metric series for every deleted resource name rather than a bounded set of kinds, causing unbounded Prometheus cardinality and memory growth as resources are deleted. It also makes successful delete metrics inconsistent with failed delete metrics. Pass the resource kind instead.

title: Attribute duration and error metrics to the store actually called
body: The asynchronous DeleteCollection call records its legacy-store duration and failures through recordStorageDuration, so legacy failures are reported as unified-storage failures and unified-storage timings include legacy work. Conversely, the unified Create and Update error paths at lines 45 and 129 call recordLegacyDuration even though legacy storage was never invoked. Correct these store assignments so operators can distinguish primary-storage failures from failed safety copies.

title: Use distinct store mocks and wait for background assertions
body: The tests give legacy and unified storage the same mock.Mock, so expectations for identically named methods cannot distinguish which store was called. For example, the create failure case configures only setupLegacyFn but that expectation also satisfies the unified Create call. The write tests also return without waiting for or asserting the background legacy calls. As a result, they can pass when writes go to the wrong store or legacy mirroring never happens. Use separate mocks and synchronize assertions on completion of the asynchronous writes.

title: Detach background writes from request cancellation
body: The asynchronous legacy write derives its timeout context from the request context. HTTP request contexts are canceled when the handler returns, so returning the unified-storage result can cancel the legacy write before it starts or while it is running; the ten-second timeout does not prevent parent cancellation. The same problem affects Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection. Preserve the necessary context values but detach cancellation before applying the background timeout so successful requests actually replicate to legacy storage.

title: Preserve write ordering when replicating asynchronously
body: Each successful mutation launches an independent goroutine with no ordering between legacy operations. Even sequential client requests can therefore be applied out of order: a create followed by a delete can execute the legacy delete first and then leave the deleted object present in legacy, while two updates can leave the older value last. Since legacy is intended as a safety copy, replication needs an ordered mechanism for conflicting writes rather than independent goroutines.

title: Replicate the committed update result instead of replaying objInfo
body: The legacy Update now receives the original UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the updateWrapper containing the object committed by unified storage. UpdatedObjectInfo can represent a PATCH or server-side apply transformation that depends on the existing object. Re-evaluating it against legacy's potentially stale object can produce a different result—for example, preserving fields that an earlier unified update changed but that have not yet reached legacy. Pass a snapshot of the successful unified update result through the wrapper so legacy receives the same desired object rather than recomputing the request against a different base.

title: Do not use object names as the metric kind label
body: The successful Delete metric passes name where the other duration calls pass options.Kind. This creates a separate Prometheus label value for every deleted object instead of a bounded resource kind, causing unbounded metric-series growth as objects are deleted and making successful and failed delete metrics inconsistent. Pass options.Kind here.

title: Attribute operation durations to the store that was called
body: DeleteCollection records its asynchronous legacy operation with recordStorageDuration, so legacy latency and errors are reported as unified-storage observations. Conversely, the Create and Update unified-storage error paths at lines 45 and 129 call recordLegacyDuration even though legacy is not called. These mistakes hide failures in the actual store and incorrectly inflate the other store's metrics. Use recordLegacyDuration for the legacy collection deletion and recordStorageDuration for unified Create/Update failures.

title: Detach legacy writes from request cancellation
body: The background write derives its timeout context from the original request context. HTTP request contexts are canceled when the handler returns, so returning the unified-storage result can cancel the legacy write before it starts or completes; the ten-second timeout does not prevent parent cancellation. This affects Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection and can leave legacy storage permanently out of sync after successful requests. Preserve the context values but detach request cancellation before applying the background timeout.

title: Mirror the committed update rather than re-evaluating objInfo
body: Legacy.Update now receives the original UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the updateWrapper containing the object committed to unified storage. UpdatedObjectInfo can represent a PATCH or server-side apply operation whose result depends on the old object. Re-evaluating it against a divergent legacy object can preserve stale fields or produce a different result, even though the authoritative update succeeded. Pass a snapshot of the committed result through the wrapper so the legacy write mirrors that result rather than independently executing the update transformation.

title: Preserve per-object ordering of asynchronous legacy writes
body: Each successful mutation launches an independent goroutine with no ordering between writes to the same object. A client can wait for Create to succeed and then issue Delete, yet the legacy Delete can execute before the legacy Create, leaving a legacy-only object after both operations finish. Likewise, two updates can reach legacy storage in reverse order and leave stale data. Serialize or sequence the background mutations per resource identity so legacy storage converges to the authoritative state.

title: Do not use object names as the metric kind label
body: The successful Delete path passes name to recordStorageDuration where every other path passes options.Kind. This creates a separate metric label value for every deleted object instead of grouping by kind, causing unbounded Prometheus series growth for workloads with many distinct resource names and making successful and failed deletes appear under different kinds. Pass options.Kind here.

title: Attribute duration and failure metrics to the correct backend
body: The background Legacy.DeleteCollection call records its result with recordStorageDuration, so each successful collection deletion records two unified-storage observations and no legacy observation; a legacy failure is incorrectly reported as a unified-storage failure. The Create and Update unified-storage error paths have the inverse mistake at lines 45 and 129, recording storage failures as legacy failures. Correct these recorder selections so backend latency and error metrics accurately identify the failing store.

title: Recheck the cache after acquiring the write lock
body: Concurrent non-development calls that observe an empty cache all proceed to acquire the write lock. After the first call populates the cache, each queued call still reloads and parses the manifest while holding the exclusive lock instead of using the cached result. A burst of requests at startup therefore causes repeated, serialized file reads and blocks otherwise cacheable requests behind those reloads. Recheck entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the write lock and return it when populated outside development mode.

title: Keep index construction serialized for each namespace/resource key
body: The cache mutex now protects only publication, so GetIndex returns nil while an index is being built. Concurrent searches, or a search racing with the write-event handler, can therefore build separate indexes for the same key. For in-memory indexes, the last publication replaces the other index and can discard updates already applied by the event handler; for file-backed indexes, both builds attempt to create the same directory and one can fail. Use per-key locking or singleflight around the cache recheck, construction, and publication while allowing different keys to build concurrently.

title: Synchronize TotalDocs with index-cache writes
body: The new startup log calls TotalDocs after the write-event consumer has been started. TotalDocs iterates the Bleve backend's cache map without taking cacheMu, while that consumer can build and publish an index for a new namespace or one skipped by InitMinCount. This introduces an unsynchronized map read/write and can terminate the process with 'concurrent map iteration and map write' during startup. Protect TotalDocs's cache traversal with the cache read lock.

title: Preserve the stopped-service guard when removing lazy initialization
body: Removing the Init checks from request handlers also removes their shutdown guard: Stop sets initErr to 'service is stopping' or 'service is stopped', and previously Init returned that error to subsequent requests. Now Create, Update, Delete, and the other handlers continue using the backend after Stop. The SQL backend's Stop only cancels its pollers, so these writes can still succeed without being propagated to watchers or search indexes. Retain a separate lifecycle-state check even though initialization is now eager.

title: Preserve per-key serialization while building indexes
body: BuildIndex now locks only when publishing the completed index, so GetIndex returns nil throughout an in-progress build. Concurrent searches, or a search and a write-event handler, can therefore build separate indexes for the same namespace/group/resource.
