body: TopicUser.find_by can return nil, but the next statement unconditionally reads tu.notification_level. A logged-in user opening a forwarded unsubscribe link, or opening the link while signed into a different account that has never visited the topic, can see the topic without having a TopicUser row and receives a server error instead of an unsubscribe page. Create or initialize the user-topic preference when absent, as TopicUser.change does.

title: Normalize email addresses before storing and matching blocks
body: BlockedEmail stores the supplied email unchanged and matches it using an exact, case-sensitive equality query. An entry for `bad@example.com` therefore does not match `bad@EXAMPLE.COM`, although those addresses refer to the same mailbox (domain names are case-insensitive). No normalization is performed by this model or the new validator, so differently cased block entries or registration addresses can evade the block. Normalize both stored entries and lookup values consistently with the application's email handling.

title: Update match statistics atomically
body: The match counter is incremented with an unlocked read-modify-save sequence. If two registration requests match the same blocked email concurrently, both can read the same match_count and save the same incremented value, losing one match. A delayed save can also overwrite a newer last_match_at. Use an atomic database increment/update or lock the record while updating these statistics.

title: Case-sensitive lookup allows blocked addresses to register
body: BlockedEmail looks up the supplied email with an exact, case-sensitive equality comparison, and neither this model nor User.new_from_params normalizes it. A block for `block@example.com` therefore does not stop registration with `block@EXAMPLE.COM`, even though the domain refers to the same mailbox. Normalize addresses consistently when storing blocked entries and checking user emails so casing cannot bypass the block.

title: Concurrent matches lose counter increments
body: The match counter is updated using a read-modify-save sequence without locking. Two simultaneous checks for the same blocked email can both read the same match_count and save the same incremented value, recording only one match instead of two. Use an atomic database increment or a locked update to preserve the statistics under concurrent registration attempts.

title: Exact-case lookup allows blocked addresses to bypass the block
body: The blocked-email lookup uses case-sensitive equality without normalizing either address. User.new_from_params assigns the submitted email unchanged, so a block for `block@spamfromhome.org` does not prevent registration with `block@SPAMFROMHOME.ORG`, even though it is the same mailbox (domain names are case-insensitive). Normalize addresses consistently when storing blocks and checking submissions, using the application's email normalization rules.

title: Concurrent matches lose updates to match_count
body: The match counter is updated through an unlocked read-modify-save sequence. Two requests matching the same blocked address can both read the same count and save the same incremented value, recording only one match instead of two. This makes the newly introduced statistics inaccurate under concurrent registration attempts. Increment the counter atomically in the database and update last_match_at in the same operation.

title: Invalid ERB closing statement prevents rendering existing discussions
body: The template closes its conditional with `end if` without a condition after `if`. This is invalid Ruby syntax, so compiling the ERB raises a SyntaxError whenever the controller renders an existing embedded topic. Replace it with `end` and add a controller test that actually renders the view.

title: Feed imports persist unsanitized HTML as cooked posts
body: TopicEmbed.import passes externally supplied contents through Nokogiri parsing and then stores them using raw_html cooking, which returns the HTML unchanged. Nokogiri::HTML.fragment does not sanitize scripts, event handlers, or javascript URLs. PollFeed calls this method directly with feed content, so malicious feed HTML becomes stored XSS on the forum and in the embed view. Sanitize imported HTML with an explicit safe tag, attribute, and URL-scheme policy before storing it; the appended source URL also needs proper HTML escaping.

title: Redirects bypass the remote retrieval host restriction
body: TopicRetriever checks only the host of the initial embed URL, then import_remote fetches it with open-uri, which follows HTTP redirects. An endpoint on the configured embedding host can therefore redirect the worker to an internal HTTP service or another unapproved host, and the fetched content can be published as a topic. Validate each redirect destination and reject private/internal addresses before fetching, rather than relying solely on the initial URI host check.

title: Relative and protocol-relative article URLs are resolved incorrectly
body: absolutize_urls only handles values starting with `/` and treats all of them as paths on the article host. Consequently `//cdn.example.com/image.jpg` becomes `http://article-host/cdn.example.com/image.jpg`, while document-relative values such as `images/image.jpg` remain relative to the Discourse page instead of the source article. Both links and images in imported articles can therefore break or point to the wrong site. Resolve href and src values against the full source URI using URI joining, preserving protocol-relative hosts.

title: RSS items without a content element abort feed polling
body: The poller unconditionally calls scrub on i.content. RSS feeds commonly supply article text in description rather than content:encoded, leaving content nil; such an item raises NoMethodError and aborts the entire polling job before subsequent items are imported. Select the appropriate content/description field with a nil-safe fallback and test polling an actual RSS feed with description-only items.

title: Invalid Ruby prevents the discussion template from rendering
body: The conditional is closed with `end if` rather than `end`. The trailing `if` has no condition, so the generated ERB Ruby fails to compile. Every embed request that finds an existing topic will fail instead of displaying the discussion. Close the block with `end` and add a test that renders the actual view.

title: Feed imports persist unsanitized HTML as cooked posts
body: Imported contents are parsed by Nokogiri but never sanitized before being saved with the raw_html cook method, which returns the HTML unchanged. PollFeed passes feed content directly into this method, so script tags, event-handler attributes, and dangerous links from a feed become stored executable content on the forum's origin. The source URL is also interpolated into HTML without escaping. Sanitize the final imported HTML, including the attribution link, before bypassing the cooking pipeline.

title: RSS entries without a content element abort feed polling
body: The poller unconditionally calls `scrub` on `i.content`. Valid RSS feeds commonly provide article text in `description` rather than a content element; for those entries, content is nil and polling raises instead of importing the entry. Since the exception exits the loop and retries are disabled, later entries also go unprocessed. Handle missing content and use the appropriate RSS description fallback.

title: Relative URL conversion corrupts protocol-relative links
body: The URL conversion treats every href beginning with `/` as a path on the article host. A valid protocol-relative link such as `//cdn.example.com/file` is consequently rewritten to `http://article-host/cdn.example.com/file`; the image conversion below has the same problem. Path-relative links such as `images/photo.jpg` are not resolved at all and instead point at the forum when rendered there. Resolve references against the full source URI rather than concatenating the source host.

title: Remote retrieval follows redirects outside the allowed embed host
body: TopicRetriever validates only the initial URL's host, then this method fetches it with open-uri, which follows HTTP redirects. An allowed-host URL that redirects to another host can therefore cause the worker to fetch internal HTTP services and publish their extracted content as a topic, bypassing the embedding host restriction. Validate redirect destinations and resolved addresses before each request, rejecting private or otherwise disallowed targets.

title: Invalid Ruby syntax prevents rendering existing discussions
body: The template closes its conditional with `end if`, leaving a trailing `if` without a condition. This is invalid Ruby syntax in the ERB-generated code, so requests that find an existing embedded topic fail with a template compilation error instead of displaying the discussion. Close the conditional with just `end` and exercise this path with view rendering enabled.

title: Imported feed HTML is persisted without sanitization
body: Feed contents pass through Nokogiri URL rewriting, which does not sanitize HTML, and are saved with the raw_html cook method. Post#cook then returns this HTML unchanged, and the embed template renders post.cooked with `raw`. A feed entry containing a script or an event handler therefore becomes stored XSS on the forum origin. The appended source URL is also interpolated directly into HTML. Sanitize the complete imported fragment and escape the source link before persisting it.

title: RSS entries without content abort the entire poll
body: The poller unconditionally calls `scrub` on `i.content`. Ordinary RSS feeds can provide article text only in `description`, with no content element, so this value can be nil. Such an entry raises an exception and stops importing all subsequent entries; retries are disabled for this job. Support description-only entries and handle entries without either field explicitly.

title: Relative URL conversion corrupts protocol-relative links
body: Every href starting with `/` is rewritten onto the article host, including protocol-relative URLs such as `//cdn.example.com/file`. This produces `http://article-host/cdn.example.com/file` rather than preserving the CDN host. The image branch has the same problem, while path-relative references such as `images/photo.jpg` are not resolved at all and consequently load from the forum origin. Resolve references against the full source URL using URI joining instead of stripping leading slashes.

title: Redirects bypass the retrieval host restriction
body: TopicRetriever checks only the host of the initial embed URL, but `open(url)` follows HTTP redirects without checking their destinations. An allowed-host URL that redirects to another host, including an internal HTTP service, causes the background worker to fetch that service and potentially publish its response as a topic. Validate each redirect destination and enforce restrictions on resolved addresses before connecting, rather than relying on the initial hostname check.

title: Include alignment for the Mozilla box fallback
body: The flexbox mixins explicitly support older Firefox through `display: -moz-box` and `display: -moz-inline-box`, but `align-items` does not emit the corresponding `-moz-box-align` property. Firefox versions using that fallback ignore the other alignment declarations, so the newly converted header and small-action rows use the default stretch alignment instead of centering their children, and bullet badges do not receive baseline alignment. Add `-moz-box-align: $alignment` so the advertised fallback preserves the intended layout.

title: Apply the untrusted-field restriction to website_name
body: The new website_name attribute is not included in untrusted_attributes, so it is serialized even when scope.restrict_user_fields?(object) suppresses website for a TL0 user viewed anonymously. This exposes the restricted website host (and, for matching domains, its path), and the updated template displays it despite the website field being hidden. Give website_name the same restriction as website and test with a populated TL0 website.

title: Apply the website visibility restriction to website_name
body: The new website_name attribute is not included in untrusted_attributes, and include_website_name lacks the trailing '?' required for a serializer inclusion predicate. Consequently, an anonymous viewer of a TL0 user receives the website hostname (and, for matching domains, its path) even when scope.restrict_user_fields? suppresses website. The template also displays this leaked value because it now checks website_name independently. Apply the same restriction as website and add a test with a populated TL0 website.

title: Apply the website visibility restriction to website_name
body: The new website_name attribute is not included in untrusted_attributes, so it is serialized even when scope.restrict_user_fields?(object) hides website for an anonymous visitor viewing a TL0 user. It exposes the hidden website's hostname (and path for same-domain URLs), and the updated template now displays that value despite the website itself being omitted. Add website_name to the same visibility guard as website; the new include_website_name method neither follows the include_website_name? hook naming convention nor checks this restriction.

title: Refresh the server-derived website label after editing preferences
body: The template now uses the server-derived website_name instead of a computed property dependent on model.website, but User.save() only copies bio_excerpt from the update response. Editing the website in preferences therefore changes model.website without changing website_name on the existing user model. Returning to the profile can show the old hostname linked to the new URL, or no website at all if none was previously set, until the user details are fetched again. Update website_name from the save response or otherwise refresh it when the website changes.

title: Preserve the light-theme color for embedded-post author links
body: The light-theme branch changes the embedded-post author link from 30% lightness scaling to 70%, although this change is intended to fix dark themes. With a black primary color, this changes the link from approximately #4d4d4d to #b3b3b3, substantially reducing its contrast and making the author attribution harder to read. Keep the original 30% light-theme value and use the complementary 70% secondary scaling for the dark-theme branch.

title: Keep mobile topic-map headings distinct from secondary labels
body: The new light-theme branch changes topic-map h3 headings from 20% to 50% lightness scaling, making them lighter even on existing light themes. It also gives h3 headings exactly the same color as the h4 secondary labels immediately below them, removing the existing visual hierarchy and reducing heading contrast. Preserve the original 20% primary scaling and use 80% secondary scaling for dark themes, as the desktop topic-map h3 rule does.

title: Preserve the light-theme contrast of embedded-post attribution
body: The light-theme branch changes the embedded-post attribution link from 30% lightness scaling to 70%, rather than preserving the existing color. With a black primary color this changes approximately #4d4d4d to #b3b3b3, making the small attribution text substantially harder to read on a light background. Keep the light branch at 30% and use the corresponding 70% secondary scaling for the dark branch.

title: Do not dim mobile topic-map headings in light themes
body: The new light-theme branch scales the primary color by 50%, whereas the previous topic-map h3 heading used 20%. This unnecessarily reduces heading contrast in existing light themes and makes headings use the same muted color as the h4 metadata beneath them. Preserve the 20% light-theme value and use 80% secondary scaling for the dark-theme branch.

title: Preserve the light-theme contrast of expanded-post attribution links
body: The light-theme branch changes expanded-post attribution links from scaling $primary by 30% to scaling it by 70%, rather than preserving the existing color. With a black primary color this changes the text from approximately #4d4d4d to #b3b3b3 on a light background, substantially reducing readability for these small (0.929em) links. Keep the light branch at 30% and use the complementary 70% secondary scale for the dark branch.

title: Page count includes an extra empty page for exact multiples
body: The total page calculation uses floor(user_count / limit) + 1 rather than rounding up. With 50 members and a limit of 50, it reports two pages and enables Next, which requests offset 50 and displays an empty member list. Use a ceiling calculation while retaining the zero-member handling.

title: Public member list is truncated without a way to load remaining members
body: The public group-members route now calls findMembers(), which requests only 50 members by default, but the public members template has no pagination or load-more controls. Non-automatic groups previously returned all members; groups with more than 50 members now have members that cannot be viewed from this page. Add public pagination or otherwise load the remaining results.

title: Existing membership PATCH requests now silently hide groups
body: The resources route still accepts PATCH /admin/groups/:id, but update no longer handles the previously supported changes.add and changes.delete payloads. An existing client sending a membership-only PATCH now receives success without changing membership, and because its request omits visible, this assignment also sets the group's visibility to false. Preserve the PATCH contract or explicitly reject obsolete payloads without modifying the group.

title: Exact multiples of the page size produce an empty extra page
body: totalPages uses floor(user_count / limit) + 1, so a group with 50 members and a limit of 50 reports two pages. The Next action remains enabled on the actual last page and requests offset 50, displaying an empty member list. Use ceiling division for nonempty groups so the page count and showingLast match the available results.

title: Public member lists are truncated without a way to load subsequent pages
body: The shared findMembers method now requests only 50 members, and the server applies that limit to all groups. This public route fetches only once, while the public group/members template has no pagination or load-more controls. Consequently, members beyond the first 50 are inaccessible on the public group page; previously nonautomatic groups returned their complete membership. Add pagination to the public page alongside the new paginated response.

title: Existing membership PATCH requests silently hide groups
body: The resources route still accepts PATCH /admin/groups/:id, but update no longer handles the previously supported changes: {add: ... , delete: ...} payload. Such a request now ignores the membership changes and sets visible to false because it contains no visible parameter, then returns success. Existing API clients therefore silently lose their membership updates and unintentionally hide the group. Preserve the PATCH contract or explicitly reject unsupported payloads without modifying the group.

title: Public member lists are truncated with no way to fetch subsequent pages
body: The public group members route now calls findMembers(), which requests only 50 members by default, but the public members template has no pagination controls or load-more mechanism. Previously non-automatic groups returned their complete membership. For groups with more than 50 members, users can now see only the first 50 and cannot access the remaining members through this page. Add pagination to the public page alongside the newly paginated endpoint.

title: Exact multiples of the page size produce an extra empty page
body: totalPages uses floor(user_count / limit) + 1, so a group with exactly 50 members and a limit of 50 reports two pages. Next remains enabled on the only populated page and fetches offset 50, displaying an empty member list. Use ceiling division for nonzero counts so exact multiples do not create a phantom final page.

title: Existing PATCH membership requests silently hide groups instead of updating membership
body: The resources route still accepts PATCH /admin/groups/:id, but update no longer dispatches PATCH requests to the incremental membership handler. An existing client sending changes: {add: username} or changes: {delete: username} now has its membership changes ignored, while the unconditional visible assignment sets the group to false because that payload has no visible parameter. The request then returns success. Preserve the existing PATCH contract or explicitly reject obsolete membership payloads without changing group visibility.

title: Load fallback translations outside the controller request path too
body: Fallback locale files are loaded only by this controller filter, but the translation accelerator deliberately disables automatic loading and loads only the current locale in I18n.translate. Translations performed outside controller requests (for example, mailers and background jobs in a separate worker process) therefore search fallback locales whose YAML files have never been loaded. Missing localized keys will still produce missing-translation results even when the site language or English contains them. Ensure the fallback chain is loaded as part of translation lookup rather than relying on a request filter.

title: Include the site fallback locale in the translation cache context
body: The fallback result now depends on SiteSetting.default_locale, but the accelerator caches argument-free translations using only the key, current locale, and backend object ID. If the site default language changes while a user's locale stays the same, a key missing in that user's language continues returning the previously cached fallback text instead of the new site-language translation. On a shared backend this also allows sites with different defaults to reuse each other's fallback results. Include the fallback context in the cache key or invalidate the cache when that context changes.

title: Load fallback locales for translations outside controller requests
body: Fallback locales are only preloaded by ApplicationController#set_locale. The translation wrapper still loads only config.locale, and the patched backend disables automatic loading. In a background worker or mailer that has not processed a controller request, translating a missing key in a non-English locale therefore cannot find the site-locale or English translation unless those locales happen to have been loaded previously. Load the fallback chain in the translation path, rather than relying on a controller callback, so server-side fallbacks also work for jobs and mail.

title: Include the site fallback locale in translation cache identity
body: The fallback result now depends on SiteSetting.default_locale, but the accelerator caches no-argument translations using only the key, current locale, and backend object ID. If a key is missing in the user's locale, its site-language fallback is cached and remains in use after the administrator changes the site's default locale. Include the fallback configuration in the cache key or invalidate the cache when it changes; otherwise users continue receiving translations from the old fallback language.

title: Load fallback locales for translations outside controller requests
body: Fallback locale files are loaded only when ApplicationController#set_locale calls this method. The translation accelerator otherwise loads only I18n.config.locale, and its patched load_translations disables automatic loading. Consequently, a fresh background worker or other non-controller caller translating an incomplete non-English locale will search unloaded site-default/English translations and return a missing translation instead of the fallback. Ensure fallback locales are loaded on the translation path, not only in a controller filter.

title: Include the site fallback locale in translation cache invalidation
body: The fallback chain now depends on SiteSetting.default_locale, but the accelerator caches no-options translations using only the key, current locale, and backend object ID. If the site default locale changes, cached translations for keys missing in the user's locale continue returning the previous site's fallback language, while uncached keys use the new language. Include the fallback configuration in the cache key or invalidate the translation cache when the site default changes.

title: Include identity type in the denial cache key
body: The denial key uses only the parsed subject ID, not its identity type. Both `anonymous:0` and `render:0` therefore share a key for the same namespace, action, name and folder. If an anonymous dashboard read is denied, subsequent renderer reads of that dashboard are denied for 30 seconds without reaching getRendererPermissions, even though renderers are granted wildcard read access. Include the identity type (or full subject) in the denial key to isolate these permission models.

title: Encode denial key components without ambiguous separators
body: Concatenating name and parent with underscores produces identical denial keys for distinct requests: name `a_b` with parent `c` and name `a` with parent `b_c` both end in `_a_b_c`. These identifiers can contain underscores, so denying access to one resource can cause an otherwise permitted resource to be denied for the cache TTL, before its permissions are checked. Use an unambiguous encoding, such as length-prefixed components or a serialized tuple, for the denial key.

title: Include identity type in the denial-cache key
body: The denial key uses only the parsed subject ID and omits IdentityType, even though permissions differ by identity type. For example, a denied dashboards:read check for anonymous:0 caches a denial that also matches render:0 for the same namespace, dashboard and folder. The renderer is explicitly granted wildcard read permission, but the early cache return now denies it without evaluating those permissions for 30 seconds. Include the identity type (or full subject) in the key to isolate these identities.

title: Encode denial-cache components without ambiguous separators
body: Concatenating resource name and parent folder with underscores produces collisions when either identifier contains underscores. For the same namespace, user and action, name=a_b with parent=c produces the same key as name=a with parent=b_c. A denial for one resource therefore incorrectly denies access to the other, even if its permissions allow access, because Check returns immediately on a denial-cache hit. Use an unambiguous encoding of the components, such as a serialized tuple or length-prefixed values.

title: Include identity type in denial cache keys
body: The denial key uses the parsed subject ID but omits IdentityType, even though different identity types have different permission rules. For example, denying a dashboard read for `anonymous:0` caches a denial that also matches `render:0` for the same namespace, action, name and folder. The renderer is normally granted all dashboard reads, but now receives a denial until the cache entry expires. Include the identity type (or full subject) in this key to prevent one identity's denial from affecting another.

title: Encode denial key components unambiguously
body: Concatenating name and parent with underscores allows different resource checks to share a denial key. For the same namespace, user and action, name `a_b` with parent `c` produces the same key as name `a` with parent `b_c`; underscores are supported in dashboard and folder UIDs. A denial for the first resource therefore causes the second resource to be denied without checking its permissions, even if access is granted. Use an unambiguous encoding of the component tuple rather than delimiter concatenation.

title: Silence action is a no-op for Prometheus-only list items
body: GrafanaRuleListItem now passes only promRule, and the menu can expose Silence notifications using its Prometheus abilities. Clicking it only sets showSilenceDrawer, while the drawer at lines 104–105 still requires a Grafana ruler rule and receives that rule. Consequently, clicking Silence notifications in the new Grafana rule list does nothing. Load the ruler rule on demand or adapt the drawer to the Prometheus rule before exposing this action.

title: Prometheus abilities do not restore Delete and Pause menu actions
body: The new list supplies promRule without rulerRule, but the Pause menu item still requires rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) at line 123 and Delete still requires rulerRule at line 165. Thus both actions disappear from every Grafana rule in the new list even for users with the appropriate permissions, despite calculating their Prometheus abilities. These actions need Prometheus-compatible handlers or on-demand ruler loading rather than retaining the ruler-only rendering guards.

title: skipToken still grants Grafana duplicate abilities
body: Passing skipToken substitutes undefined but does not disable the returned abilities. With no rule, loading is false and duplicateSupported becomes true, so Duplicate is allowed whenever the user has Grafana rule-create permission. AlertRuleMenu calls this hook with skipToken for every data-source rule and ORs its result with the ruler ability. This can expose Duplicate for external rules whose ruler API does not support it, or plugin-provided external rules for which duplication was explicitly disabled. A skipped rule should return unsupported abilities rather than global Grafana abilities.

title: Combined-rule abilities lose the federated-group immutability check
body: useAllAlertRuleAbilities previously checked isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group), but now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes isFederated to false. Existing consumers of the combined-rule hook therefore treat federated Mimir rules as mutable and expose Update and Delete when the user has external write permission, whereas these operations were deliberately unsupported for federated groups. Preserve the group-level federation check when adapting the combined-rule hook.

title: Silence notifications is a no-op for Prometheus-only list items
body: GrafanaRuleListItem now supplies only promRule, and AlertRuleMenu exposes Silence notifications using that rule's permissions. Clicking it sets showSilenceDrawer, but the drawer is still rendered only when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true (lines 104–105). Since rule is undefined for every Grafana rule in the new list, no drawer opens. Adapt the drawer flow to load the necessary ruler data on demand or support the Prometheus rule.

title: Removing rulerRule also removes Pause and Delete actions
body: This list item now passes only promRule to RuleActionsButtons. Although AlertRuleMenu computes pause and delete abilities from promRule, its Pause item still requires a Grafana rulerRule and its Delete item still requires rulerRule to exist. Consequently authorized users can no longer pause, resume, or delete rules from either the grouped or filtered Grafana list. These actions need an identifier-based flow or on-demand ruler loading rather than silently disappearing.

title: skipToken does not actually disable Grafana abilities
body: Passing skipToken converts the rule to undefined but still returns the abilities computed by useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities. For an undefined rule, loading is false, duplicateSupported is true, and Duplicate is allowed whenever the user has Grafana rule-create permission. AlertRuleMenu calls this hook with skipToken for datasource rules and ORs its result with the datasource abilities. This exposes Duplicate for datasource rules even when their ruler is unavailable or the user lacks external rule-create/write permission. Return unsupported/disallowed abilities when the token is supplied.

title: Preserve federated-group immutability in the CombinedRule hook
body: useAllAlertRuleAbilities previously checked isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group), but now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes isFederated to false. Existing CombinedRule consumers therefore treat Mimir groups with source_tenants as ordinary editable groups and enable Update/Delete for users with external write permission. This removes the explicit protection against modifying federated rules through flows that do not support federation. Preserve the group-level federation check when adapting the legacy hook.

title: Pause and Delete remain gated on the removed ruler data
body: Grafana list rows now pass only promRule, but the Pause menu item still requires a Grafana rulerRule and Delete still requires rulerRule. Computing permissions from promRule does not remove those rendering guards, so users with update/delete permissions lose both actions in the new list. Render these actions using the Grafana identifier or load the required ruler data on demand.

title: Silence action does nothing for Prometheus-only Grafana rows
body: The new GrafanaRuleListItem supplies promRule without rule, and AlertRuleMenu now exposes Silence notifications for those rows. Clicking it sets showSilenceDrawer, but the drawer is still rendered only when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true. Since rule is undefined, no drawer opens. Adapt the drawer path to the Prometheus rule or fetch the ruler rule when the action is selected.

title: skipToken still grants Grafana duplication abilities
body: skipToken is converted to undefined, but useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined) marks Duplicate supported once loading is false and grants it to users with Grafana rule-create permission. AlertRuleMenu calls this hook with skipToken for data-source rules and ORs its result with ruler abilities. Consequently external rules can show Duplicate even when their ruler does not support it, the user lacks external write permission, or the rule is plugin-provided. Skipped rules should return disabled abilities rather than abilities for a nonexistent Grafana rule.

title: Preserve federated-group immutability in CombinedRule abilities
body: useAllAlertRuleAbilities previously checked isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group), disabling update and delete for federated Mimir groups. Delegating directly to useAllRulerRuleAbilities discards the group and uses its hard-coded isFederated=false instead. Existing consumers of the CombinedRule hook therefore expose editing and deletion for federated rules that were deliberately immutable. Preserve the group-level federation check when adapting this hook.

title: Preserve the test logger's recording state in FromContext
body: FromContext returns a fresh TestLogger with independent log buffers on every call. LoggerMiddleware now writes completion logs through logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so a TestLogger supplied to that middleware no longer records those messages in its InfoLogs; the logs are written to an inaccessible temporary instance instead. Return the same recorder, or a contextual wrapper sharing its recording state, so callers can still inspect and assert the emitted logs.

title: Preserve recorded logs when deriving a contextual test logger
body: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh TestLogger with independent log records. LoggerMiddleware now logs exclusively through logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so a TestLogger supplied to that middleware never records the completion message on its InfoLogs; the message is recorded on a temporary instance that the caller cannot access. This breaks assertions and observation of middleware logging through the provided test logger. Return the original logger or share the recording state with the contextual instance.

title: Keep contextual logging observable through the test logger
body: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh, disconnected TestLogger on every call. LoggerMiddleware now writes its completion log through logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so a TestLogger passed into the middleware never records those messages in its InfoLogs; they are recorded on an instance that is immediately discarded. Return the existing test logger or share its recording state with the contextual logger so callers and tests can still observe the logs.

title: Rejected devices are cached as successfully admitted
body: TagDevice now propagates the device-limit error to authentication, but tagDeviceUI adds the device ID to the 29-minute local cache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice and does not remove it when that call fails. When a new device is rejected because the limit is full, its next request hits that cache and returns nil without checking the store, so Anonymous.Authenticate grants access. Cache only successful admissions (and ensure concurrent requests cannot treat an in-progress admission as successful), and add a test that retries a rejected device.

title: Device-limit check and admission are not atomic
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts active devices in one database session and performs the subsequent upsert in another, without any serialization. If the count is one below the limit, concurrent requests with different device IDs can all observe that count and all insert successfully, exceeding the configured limit. This also occurs across Grafana instances sharing the database. Serialize the count-and-admit operation with a database-level mechanism or equivalent cross-instance coordination, and test concurrent admissions at the limit.

title: Rejected devices are cached as successfully admitted
body: TagDevice now propagates the device-limit error to authentication, but tagDeviceUI still inserts the device ID into its 29-minute local cache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice. When a new device is rejected because the limit is full, that cache entry remains. A second request with the same device ID hits the cache, returns nil without checking the store, and authenticates successfully. Concurrent requests can likewise use the entry before the first admission check finishes. Cache only successful admissions and ensure requests cannot treat an in-progress admission as successful; add a test that retries a rejected device.

title: Device count and admission are not atomic
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts active devices in one database session and inserts the new device in a separate session without any serialization. When the count is one below the configured limit, multiple requests with distinct device IDs can all observe the available slot and each insert successfully, exceeding the limit. This also occurs across Grafana replicas sharing the database, so a process-local lock alone would not fix it. Serialize the count-and-admission operation at the database level and test simultaneous admissions at the limit.

title: Rejected devices are cached as successfully admitted
body: tagDeviceUI sets the device's local cache entry before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice and leaves that entry in place when the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Although this change propagates the error for the first request, a second request with the same device ID hits the cache and returns nil, so Anonymous.Authenticate grants access. A rejected device can therefore bypass the configured limit simply by retrying, for the 29-minute cache lifetime. Cache only successful admissions (and ensure concurrent requests cannot treat an in-progress admission as successful).

title: Requests without a device header bypass limit enforcement
body: Authentication now relies on TagDevice returning ErrDeviceLimitReached to enforce the limit, but TagDevice returns nil immediately when X-Grafana-Device-Id is absent. An anonymous client can omit that client-controlled header and still receive an authenticated anonymous identity even when the device limit is full, without being counted. The limited authentication path needs to handle missing device IDs explicitly rather than treating an untracked request as an admitted device.

title: Device admission count and insertion are not atomic
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts active devices in one database session and subsequently inserts in another, without locking or an atomic admission mechanism. When the count is one below the limit, concurrent requests for distinct device IDs can all observe available capacity and all insert successfully. This allows the active device count to exceed the configured limit, including across Grafana instances sharing the database. Serialize the capacity check and admission using a database-coordinated mechanism and add a concurrent admission test.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors
body: The new cleanup paths unconditionally emit Error-level messages for successful queries and deletes, including the final empty batch. The same issue occurs in count-based cleanup and orphaned-tag cleanup. Consequently, a healthy background job now continually produces error logs and can trigger error-based monitoring alerts; logging every selected ID also makes these messages unnecessarily large. Use debug-level batch diagnostics and reserve error logging for actual failures.

title: Building the SQLite ID list repeatedly copies the entire accumulated string
body: For SQLite batches larger than 999, each iteration formats a new string containing all previously accumulated IDs. This makes statement construction quadratic in the batch size rather than linear. With the 32,767 batch size explicitly supported by the new test, constructing a single delete can allocate gigabytes of temporary strings, adding substantial garbage-collection and CPU overhead to cleanup. Build the list with a strings.Builder or append to a byte buffer instead.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors
body: The new cleanup paths unconditionally emit Error logs before and after every batch, including when no IDs are found and no error occurred. Orphaned-tag cleanup therefore emits errors even on an idle, healthy instance. This creates false error alerts and floods production error logs; use debug-level logging for successful work and reserve Error for actual failures.

title: SQLite ID-list construction is quadratic in batch size
body: Each iteration formats and copies the entire accumulated ID string. For large configured SQLite batches (including the 32767 batch size introduced in the tests), constructing one DELETE allocates and copies gigabytes cumulatively rather than work proportional to the number of IDs. This can cause substantial GC pressure and delay cleanup. Build the list with a strings.Builder or append into a byte buffer instead.

title: Restore the existing interval for unrelated cleanup jobs
body: Changing this ticker from ten minutes to one minute runs every cleanup job ten times as frequently, not just annotation cleanup. This includes dashboard-version deletion, snapshot cleanup, temporary-file scans, and query-history retention queries. The deadlock fix does not require this scheduling change, and it adds recurring filesystem and database load across all installations. Keep the existing interval or explicitly isolate and justify an annotation-specific scheduling change.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors
body: The new cleanup logging emits Error messages unconditionally, even when ID selection and deletion succeed or there is nothing to delete. The same pattern appears in count-based cleanup and orphaned-tag cleanup. Consequently, normal background maintenance produces error-level logs every cycle, triggering log-based alerts and obscuring genuine failures; logging every selected ID also makes these messages unnecessarily large. Use debug-level summary logging for successful work and reserve error-level logging for actual failures.

title: SQLite ID-list construction copies the entire prefix for every ID
body: For SQLite batches larger than 999, each iteration formats the accumulated values string into a new string. Building a batch of N IDs therefore requires quadratic copying and allocation rather than linear work. Large configured batches, such as the 32767 batch size introduced in the tests, can allocate gigabytes of temporary strings during cleanup, causing substantial GC and CPU overhead in the server. Build the list with a strings.Builder or an append-based buffer instead.

title: Detach background writes from request cancellation
body: All four background writes derive their timeout context from the incoming request context. HTTP request contexts are canceled when the handler returns, so returning after launching the goroutine cancels the legacy write rather than giving it ten seconds to finish. This makes successful unified writes routinely fail to reach the legacy safety copy. Preserve context values but detach cancellation before applying the background timeout.

title: Mirror the committed update instead of reapplying UpdatedObjectInfo
body: The legacy update now receives the original UpdatedObjectInfo instead of a wrapper containing the object committed to unified storage. UpdatedObjectInfo can compute a patch against the supplied old object; evaluating it again against a stale legacy object can produce different contents or fail (for example, a JSON Patch test can succeed in unified storage and fail in legacy). Restore mirroring of the committed result so both stores receive the same update.

title: Preserve write ordering for each resource
body: Each successful mutation launches an independent goroutine with no ordering relative to other mutations of the same resource. A client can create an object and then delete it after receiving the create response, yet the legacy delete can execute before the legacy create, leaving a deleted object resurrected in the safety copy. Updates can likewise overwrite newer values with older ones. Background replication needs per-resource ordering or equivalent version-aware reconciliation.

title: Do not use object names as metric kind labels
body: The successful delete duration is recorded with name in the argument used elsewhere for options.Kind. This creates a separate metric label value for every deleted resource, causing unbounded Prometheus series cardinality, and prevents successful and failed delete measurements from being aggregated under the same kind. Pass the kind rather than the resource name.

title: Record durations against the store actually called
body: The background legacy DeleteCollection call records its outcome as a storage duration, so unified storage gets two samples per successful collection deletion and is blamed for legacy failures, while legacy gets no samples. Similarly, the unified Create and Update error paths at lines 45 and 129 record legacy durations despite never calling legacy. These misclassifications make store-specific error rates and latency metrics incorrect; use the appropriate store recorder in each path.

title: Detach asynchronous writes from request cancellation
body: The legacy-write timeout is derived from the incoming request context, which is canceled when the HTTP handler returns. Since Create now returns without waiting for the goroutine, the legacy operation can receive an already-canceled context or be canceled midway through its write, regardless of the ten-second timeout. The same issue affects Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection. Preserve context values but detach request cancellation before applying the background-write timeout.

title: Replicate the committed update rather than reapplying UpdatedObjectInfo
body: Legacy.Update now receives the original UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the wrapper containing the object committed to unified storage. UpdatedObjectInfo can compute a patch or server-side apply against the old object supplied by each store; if legacy is behind, reapplying it there can produce a different object or fail despite a successful unified update. The previous implementation explicitly passed the unified result to legacy. Replicate a snapshot of res rather than evaluating the original update against legacy state again.

title: Preserve operation ordering for background replication
body: Each successful mutation launches an independent goroutine with no ordering between writes to the same resource. For example, a client can create a resource and then delete it after Create returns, while the legacy delete executes before the legacy create; the delete fails with not-found and the later create leaves a deleted resource in legacy permanently. Successive updates can likewise overwrite newer legacy data with older data. Serialize or queue replication per resource so the legacy safety copy follows committed operation order.

title: Correct storage metric attribution and resource labels
body: The successful Delete metric uses the object name as the kind label, creating a separate metric series for every deleted resource rather than the bounded kind label. Other new metric calls also attribute operations to the wrong backend: failed unified Create and Update call recordLegacyDuration (lines 45 and 129), while background legacy DeleteCollection calls recordStorageDuration (line 166). These errors both risk unbounded metric cardinality on deletes and make backend error rates and latency measurements incorrect.

title: Detach asynchronous writes from request cancellation
body: The legacy goroutines derive their timeout contexts from the incoming request context. An HTTP request context is canceled when the handler returns, so returning after the unified write cancels the legacy operation rather than allowing it ten seconds to complete. This affects Create, Update, Delete and DeleteCollection and can leave the fallback store missing successful writes. Preserve context values with a cancellation-detached context before applying the timeout.

title: Mirror the committed update instead of reapplying the original updater
body: Legacy.Update now receives the original UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the wrapper containing the unified store's committed result. UpdatedObjectInfo can compute a patch or server-side apply against the old object supplied by each store; applying it again against a stale legacy object can produce a different document or fail validation. The previous implementation explicitly mirrored the committed object. Restore that behavior so the backup receives the actual successful unified update.

title: Preserve write ordering in the legacy mirror
body: Each successful write launches an independent goroutine with no ordering mechanism. Even sequential client requests can therefore be applied in reverse order to legacy storage: a delete can execute before an earlier create, leaving the deleted object recreated, or an older update can overwrite a newer update. A per-resource ordered replication mechanism is needed for the legacy store to remain a usable fallback.

title: Do not label delete metrics with object names
body: The successful Delete path passes name as the kind argument to recordStorageDuration, while the other paths use options.Kind. This creates a distinct metric label value for every deleted resource name, causing unbounded Prometheus series cardinality and incorrectly grouping delete durations. Pass the resource kind instead.

title: Attribute operation metrics to the store actually called
body: DeleteCollection records the asynchronous legacy call through recordStorageDuration, so unified-storage metrics include legacy latency and failures and legacy metrics omit this operation. Similarly, the Create and Update unified failure paths call recordLegacyDuration even though legacy was never invoked. Correct these recorder selections so monitoring can distinguish unified failures from fallback failures.

title: Recheck the cache after acquiring the write lock
body: Concurrent production requests can all observe a nil cache under the read lock before any request finishes loading it. Each then acquires the write lock in turn and rereads and reparses the manifest, even though the first request has already populated the cache. This serializes redundant disk I/O and parsing across the initial request burst and blocks cache readers while those loads run. After acquiring the write lock, check the cache again and return it if non-nil in non-development mode.

title: Recheck the production cache after acquiring the write lock
body: Concurrent requests arriving before the cache is populated can all read a nil cache and then queue for the write lock. Each queued request subsequently reloads and parses the manifest even though the first request has already populated the cache, serializing redundant disk I/O and delaying requests during cold start. A later reload failure can also replace the successfully populated cache with nil and return an avoidable error. After acquiring the write lock, check the cache again and return it when running outside development mode.

title: Recheck the cache after acquiring the write lock
body: Concurrent production requests arriving before the cache is populated all observe a nil cache under the read lock, then queue for the write lock. Because the cache is not checked again after acquiring that lock, every queued request rereads and parses assets-manifest.json serially even after the first request has successfully populated the cache. This turns a cold-start request burst into repeated serialized disk I/O and delays all queued requests unnecessarily. After acquiring the write lock, return the populated cache when cfg.Env is not setting.Dev before loading the manifest.

title: Serialize index creation per resource key before publishing
body: The cache mutex now protects only publication, so GetIndex returns nil while an index is being built. Concurrent searches, or a search and the write-event handler, can consequently build separate indexes for the same namespace/group/resource. For memory indexes, the last builder overwrites the cached index; an event applied to the other index can then be lost from subsequent search results. For file indexes, both builders attempt bleve.New on the same directory and one fails. Add per-key synchronization and recheck the cache after acquiring it, while retaining parallel builds for different keys.

title: Preserve rejection of requests after Stop
body: Removing the Init checks also removes the stopped-state check: Stop sets initErr to a stopping/stopped error, which previously caused subsequent RPCs to be rejected by Init. Create, Update, Delete and the other handlers now continue using the backend after Stop. In particular, the SQL backend's Stop only cancels its pollers, so writes can still succeed after shutdown while watchers and search indexing are no longer running. Preserve a separate lifecycle-state guard in the handlers rather than relying on eager initialization alone.

title: Serialize index creation per key before publishing to the cache
body: The narrowed cache lock allows GetIndex to return nil while an index for that same key is being built. Concurrent searches, or a search and the write-event handler, can therefore build separate indexes for one NamespacedResource. If the event handler publishes its index and applies an update before the other builder publishes, the latter replaces the updated index with its older snapshot, losing the update from search results. Disk-backed builds can also compete to create the same directory and fail. Keep builds for different keys parallel, but coordinate creation for the same key and recheck the cache before building.

title: Retain the stopped-state check when removing lazy initialization
body: Removing the Init checks also removes the request guard against shutdown: Stop sets initErr to 'service is stopping' or 'service is stopped', and previously subsequent calls to Init returned that error without executing the operation. Create, Update, Delete and the other RPCs now continue accessing the backend after Stop. For the SQL backend, Stop only cancels polling and does not disable database writes, so requests can successfully mutate resources after the watchers have stopped. Replace the lazy-init checks with an explicit lifecycle-state guard rather than removing the shutdown protection.

title: Serialize index creation per namespaced resource
body: The cache lock now protects only publication, so GetIndex returns nil while an index is being built. Concurrent searches, or a search and the write-event handler, can consequently build separate indexes for the same key. If the event handler publishes its index and applies an update before the other build publishes an older snapshot, that second publication discards the update and leaves searches permanently stale until another event or restart. File-backed builds also compete to create the same directory and can fail. Keep builds parallel across different keys, but coordinate creation and publication for each individual key.

title: Protect TotalDocs against concurrent cache publication
body: This new TotalDocs call runs after the search write-event listener has started. That listener can build and publish an index for a resource omitted from startup indexing (for example, one below InitMinCount). bleveBackend.TotalDocs iterates its cache map without taking cacheMu, while BuildIndex writes that map under the mutex. An event arriving during this startup log can therefore cause a data race or a fatal concurrent-map-iteration-and-write crash. Add read locking to TotalDocs before invoking it concurrently with index creation.

title: Call to isConditionalPasskeysEnabled does not compile
body: UsernameForm calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() without arguments, but the only method defined in its superclass UsernamePasswordForm requires a UserModel argument. There is no zero-argument overload in the supplied inheritance hierarchy, so the services module fails compilation. Pass context.getUser() or provide the intended overload.

title: New passkey predicate disables passkeys on ordinary login
body: The new predicate requires user != null, and both authenticate() and the error challenge use it to decide whether to initialize conditional WebAuthn. On an ordinary login, context.getUser() is null because no identity has been selected yet, so the form no longer receives the conditional-UI attributes or WebAuthn challenge. This breaks the existing username-less discoverable-passkey login and removes the passkey option from initial username/password and username forms. The predicate must also allow the unidentified-user case rather than enabling passkeys exclusively after a user is selected.

title: Call to conditional-passkey helper does not compile
body: UsernameForm.authenticate() calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() without arguments, but the only method defined in its superclass is isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user). There is no zero-argument overload in the supplied inheritance chain, so the services module fails compilation. Pass the context user or provide an appropriate overload.

title: Conditional passkeys are disabled for ordinary unidentified logins
body: The new helper requires user != null, and both initial form rendering and error challenges now use it. During an ordinary login context.getUser() is null, so fillContextForm() is no longer called and the login page receives neither conditional WebAuthn UI attributes nor a WebAuthn challenge. This removes the existing username-less passkey login path (including for passkey-only users) and breaks the existing discoverable-key login tests. Passkeys must remain enabled when no user has yet been selected, as well as during re-authentication.

title: Call the passkeys helper with its required user argument
body: UsernameForm.authenticate() calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments, but the only method defined in its superclass is isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user). This does not compile, preventing the services module and the PR from building. Pass context.getUser() or provide a matching overload.

title: Preserve conditional passkeys for login before a user is identified
body: The new helper requires user != null, and both initial form rendering and error challenges now use it. On a normal login, context.getUser() is null, so fillContextForm() is no longer called and the page receives neither conditional WebAuthn UI attributes nor a WebAuthn challenge. This disables the existing username-less passkey login path (including for passkey-only users) and contradicts the existing discoverable-key login tests. Enable passkeys for unidentified users as well as for re-authentication.

title: Use stored enabled state when deciding login-cache invalidation
body: The original model passed here comes from getById(), which wraps isEnabled() to return false when the associated organization (or organization feature in the realm) is disabled. The cached login query, however, selects IDs using the stored IDP enabled flag, independently of organization enabled state. If a public IDP is cached, its organization is disabled, and the IDP is then changed to hideOnLogin=true or linkOnly=true, both predicates here are false and invalidation is skipped. After the organization is enabled again, getForLogin still returns that IDP, and the login bean's isEnabled() recheck does not exclude hidden or link-only providers. Compare unwrapped persisted models for invalidation so organization state cannot suppress necessary membership changes.

title: Register cleanup for the actual created provider alias
body: The new test creates providers named idp-alias-0 through idp-alias-19, but every cleanup callback removes the literal alias "alias" instead. The additional callback at line 425 has the same problem. Cleanup therefore requests deletion of a nonexistent provider and leaves the created providers behind, potentially causing cleanup failures and contaminating subsequent tests with enabled realm-level brokers. Capture and use each created provider's actual alias in its cleanup callback.

title: Use persisted enabled state when deciding login-cache invalidation
body: The original model passed to this method comes from getById(), which wraps isEnabled() to return false when its organization (or organization support in the realm) is disabled. The login query, however, caches IDs based on the persisted IDP fields. For example, populate the cache for a public enabled organization IDP, disable its organization, then set hideOnLogin=true on the IDP. Both predicates here return false, so the cached membership is retained. After re-enabling the organization, getForLogin still returns that hidden IDP, and OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean only rechecks isEnabled(), so it displays the provider despite hideOnLogin. Compare unwrapped persisted models for invalidation rather than organization-dependent enabled state.

title: Register cleanup for the actual created provider aliases
body: The new test creates providers named idp-alias-0 through idp-alias-19 but registers every cleanup against the literal provider name "alias"; the same mistake occurs for idp-alias-20 at line 425. Cleanup therefore attempts to delete a nonexistent provider instead of the created resources, potentially failing teardown and leaving realm-level providers behind to contaminate later tests. Register each created alias in its cleanup callback.

title: Evaluate invalidation against stored enabled state, not organization-aware state
body: The original model passed to this method comes from getById(), which wraps isEnabled() to return false when the organization or organization support is disabled. The login query, however, caches IDs using the delegate's stored enabled flag. If a public, enabled organization's IDP is cached, the organization is disabled, and the IDP is then hidden on login or made link-only, both predicates here return false and invalidation is skipped. After the organization is re-enabled, the cached ID is still returned; OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean only rechecks isEnabled(), so the hidden/link-only provider appears on the login page. Compare the original persisted login-filter fields without the organization-aware enabled override.

title: Do not republish old query results using a fresh startup revision
body: When adding an uncached organization search, this branch copies all existing searches from query and publishes them using cache.getCurrentCounter() after the database query. An IDP change can invalidate the login cache between reading query and publishing the replacement. The fresh counter allows the replacement to pass the revision check despite containing pre-invalidation search results (and potentially stale database results). This can resurrect lists that omit newly available providers or include providers that have been hidden or made private. Use a revision captured before reading/loading the results and avoid copying a query invalidated in the meantime.

title: Register cleanup for the actual created IDP aliases
body: The test creates providers named idp-alias-0 through idp-alias-19, but every cleanup callback removes the literal provider name "alias" instead. The additional callback at line 425 repeats the same mistake for idp-alias-20. Consequently these providers are not cleaned up, and cleanup may fail with a not-found response; leftover realm-level providers can also contaminate subsequent tests. Register each callback with the alias of the provider it created.

title: Reject concatenated signatures with an incorrect length
body: concatenatedRSToASN1DER copies only signLength bytes without checking signature.length. A signature containing a valid R/S pair followed by arbitrary extra bytes is therefore converted to exactly the same DER signature as the valid input and can pass verification, despite not being a valid JOSE ECDSA signature. Short inputs instead cause an unchecked array-copy exception. Require signature.length == signLength and reject mismatches with IOException before copying.

title: Exercise the actual curves and verify the converted signature
body: All three tests generate the same default EC key (typically P-256), including testES384 and testES512. Changing the digest algorithm does not change the key's curve, so these tests never exercise 384-bit R/S values or the long-form DER sequence length used by P-521 signatures. Additionally, comparing only the two concatenated outputs can pass if the first conversion corrupts or truncates the original signature. Generate keys with the corresponding explicit curve for each algorithm and verify the reconstructed DER signature against the original data and public key.

title: Reject concatenated signatures with an unexpected length
body: concatenatedRSToASN1DER copies only the first signLength bytes without checking signature.length. An otherwise valid JOSE ECDSA signature with arbitrary bytes appended therefore produces exactly the same DER signature and can still verify successfully. JOSE requires the exact fixed signature length; accepting these inputs permits token/signature malleability. Check the input length and throw IOException before copying (also avoiding unchecked array-copy exceptions for short inputs).

title: Exercise the actual ES384 and ES512 curves and verify the reconstructed signature
body: All three tests generate an EC key using the provider's default curve (normally P-256), including testES384 and testES512. Changing the hash algorithm does not change the curve, so these tests only pad P-256 integers to larger lengths and never exercise real P-384 or P-521 signatures, including the long-form DER sequence length needed for P-521. Moreover, comparing two concatenated conversions can pass when the first conversion loses data. Generate the appropriate curve for each algorithm and verify the reconstructed DER signature against the original data and public key.

title: Reject concatenated signatures whose length differs from signLength
body: concatenatedRSToASN1DER copies only the first signLength bytes without checking signature.length. An otherwise valid JOSE ECDSA signature with arbitrary bytes appended is therefore converted to the same valid DER signature and can pass verification, although JOSE requires an exact signature length. Short inputs instead produce an unchecked array-copy exception. Validate the input length and throw IOException for mismatches before copying.

title: Exercise the actual ES384 and ES512 curve sizes
body: All three tests generate an uninitialized EC key pair, which on the standard JDK defaults to P-256. Changing the hash algorithm to ES384 or ES512 does not change the curve, so those tests merely pad 256-bit r and s values and never exercise real P-384 or P-521 signatures. In particular, the ES512 test misses the long-form DER sequence length needed for P-521. Initialize the generator with the matching curve for each algorithm and verify the reconstructed DER signature with JCA, rather than only checking a round trip through the same implementation.

title: All-clients view permission bypasses client-specific denials
body: canView(ClientModel) returns immediately when canView() grants the all-clients VIEW permission, without evaluating the target client's resource. Consequently, an administrator granted VIEW on all clients can still read a client with an explicit client-specific denying VIEW policy. The per-client evaluation must take precedence over the all-clients fallback, rather than treating the global fine-grained grant like an unconditional administrative role.

title: Handle a missing Clients resource before evaluating the fallback
body: The fallback assumes getResourceTypeResource() always returns a resource, but it can return null. In particular, a realm initialized with V2 permissions before this change has only the Users resource: AdminPermissionsSchema.init() returns immediately when the admin-permissions client already exists, so it never adds Clients or the new scopes. Checking a client in such a realm passes null to findByResource() and can subsequently dereference it at resource.getScopes(), producing a server error instead of an authorization decision. Reconcile existing schemas and guard the missing-resource case.

title: Global view permission bypasses client-specific denials
body: canView(ClientModel) returns true as soon as canView() grants the all-clients VIEW permission, without evaluating permissions on the requested client. Consequently, an administrator granted VIEW on all clients can still read a client for which a client-specific VIEW permission explicitly denies access. This defeats the resource-specific override behavior used by V2 permissions (and tested for users in UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest). Keep the built-in admin-role shortcut, but evaluate fine-grained view access through the client-specific resource, falling back to the all-clients resource only when appropriate.

title: Global view permission bypasses client-specific denials
body: canView(client) returns immediately when canView() grants the caller the all-clients view permission, without evaluating the client's own resource. Consequently, an administrator granted view on all clients can still read a client for which a client-specific view policy denies access. This defeats the resource-specific override behavior already tested for Users in UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest. Keep the administrative-role shortcut, but evaluate fine-grained view access through the client-specific resource before falling back to the all-clients resource.

title: Deletion listener still invokes an unsupported V2 operation when both features are enabled
body: The listener is guarded by ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ, but management() selects MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled. If both features are enabled, deleting any client calls ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled(client, false), which unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException. The removal event therefore fails and can roll back client deletion, including deletion by a full administrator. Ensure this V1 cleanup listener does not dispatch to the V2 implementation.

title: View-only permission authorizes top-level group creation and moves
body: canManage() accepts either the VIEW or MANAGE scope on all groups. GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup() relies on requireManage(), which calls this method, so an administrator granted only VIEW can create top-level groups or move existing groups to the top level. This check must require MANAGE rather than treating read access as write access.

title: Group search restriction uses authorization resource IDs instead of group IDs
body: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() searches resources by the Groups type and passes/adds groupResource.getId(). However, AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource() creates individual authorization resources with the group ID as their name, gives them a separate generated resource ID, and does not set their type. Consequently individual group resources are not found by this scan; the typed all-groups resource can instead contribute its authorization ID, which is not a group ID. UsersResource uses this set to restrict user searches and counts by group membership, causing permitted members to disappear or counts to be incorrect. Enumerate the actual group resources/groups and evaluate and return model group IDs, not authorization resource IDs.

title: Group membership restriction excludes users authorized individually
body: When an administrator lacks global user-view permission but has both an individual user-view permission and view-members permission on a group, searchForUser sets UserModel.GROUPS to only the permitted groups. The user provider then restricts the search to those memberships before canView is evaluated. An individually authorized user outside those groups is therefore omitted even though GET by user ID succeeds. The search must include the union of individually authorized users and users authorized through groups rather than applying the group restriction to all results. The same issue affects the corresponding brute-force user search.

title: View-only group permission allows top-level group creation
body: canManage() accepts either the VIEW or MANAGE scope on all groups. GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup() calls requireManage(), which delegates to this method, so an administrator granted only read access can create groups or move an existing subgroup to the top level. Require MANAGE alone here and add a test that an all-groups VIEW permission cannot perform these mutations.

title: Authorization resource IDs are used as group model IDs
body: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() passes groupResource.getId() to hasPermission() and returns it as a group ID. Authorization resources are created with generated IDs; the corresponding GroupModel ID is stored in the resource name by AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource(). Consequently the permission lookup misses the specific resource and falls back to all-groups permissions, and the returned IDs cannot match user group memberships when UsersResource applies the search filter. Use the mapped group model ID rather than the authorization resource ID, and handle the all-groups resource separately.

title: Individual group resources are not assigned the Groups type
body: When creating an individual group authorization resource, getOrCreateResource() sets its name and scopes but never sets its type to Groups. The new GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() discovers resources exclusively through findByType(..., "Groups", ...), so individual group permissions are omitted from that discovery. This prevents group-member permissions from supplying the group filters needed by user searches and counts. Assign the resource type when creating the resource and test discovery of an individual group's member-view permission.

title: View-only group permission authorizes group creation and moves
body: canManage() accepts either VIEW or MANAGE on the all-groups resource. GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup() calls requireManage(), which delegates to this method, so an administrator granted only read access to all groups can create new groups or move an existing group to the top level. Require the MANAGE scope here and add a negative test for creation with only VIEW.

title: Group enumeration uses authorization resource types and IDs instead of group IDs
body: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() searches resources by type Groups and passes/returns their authorization resource IDs. AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource() creates individual group resources with the group ID as their name, a separately generated resource ID, and no resource type. Consequently individual group resources are not enumerated, and the all-groups resource that is enumerated contributes an authorization ID rather than a real group ID. UsersResource uses this set to restrict user searches and counts, so group-member permissions can produce empty results despite allowing access to those users individually. Enumerate the actual groups (including the all-groups case), evaluate using group IDs, and return model group IDs.

title: Group-based search restriction excludes users authorized independently
body: Whenever getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() returns a nonempty set, searchForUser() restricts the provider query to those groups before checking individual user permissions. In V2 an administrator can have both a VIEW permission on a specific user outside those groups and VIEW_MEMBERS on a group, without global user view permission. That independently authorized user is then excluded by the provider query and never reaches canView(), even though fetching the user by ID succeeds. The same restriction is applied in BruteForceUsersResource. The search must include users authorized directly as well as users authorized through groups.
