The public members template (group/members.hbs) only iterates `members` and has no next/previous controls, unlike the admin group screen. Previously this endpoint returned every member of a non-automatic group and defaulted automatic groups to 200 when no limit was sent. After this change, any group with more than 50 members (including large custom groups and automatic groups such as trust_level_0) silently hides everyone past the first page, with no way to load the rest.

title: totalPages is off by one when count is a multiple of page size
body: totalPages is Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1, which is wrong whenever user_count is greater than 0 and divisible by limit. A group of exactly 50 members with the default limit of 50 is reported as 2 pages, 100 members as 3, and so on. showingLast compares currentPage to that value, so Next stays enabled on the last real page. next() then sets offset to min(offset + limit, user_count), which equals user_count, and findMembers loads an empty page. Admins see a blank extra page and a wrong "N/M" indicator for every full page of members.

title: Removing the last member on a page leaves a blank page
body: findMembers clamps the request offset with Math.min(user_count, offset) using the in-memory user_count, which is only refreshed from the response. removeMember (and addMembers) then call findMembers() without moving offset back. Deleting the last user on the current page therefore re-requests an offset that is now past the end (the clamp still allows offset == old total). The server echoes that offset in meta and returns an empty members array, and the client stores meta.offset, so the admin UI stays on a blank page until Previous is clicked. The members action never clamps offset to the last non-empty page either.

title: Remove control ignores whether the group is automatic
body: This row is rendered by the group-member itemView, not in the admin group template's context. Ember's each+itemView sets the row context to the each keyword ({member: user}) or to the user record; neither has the group's automatic flag, and a replaced context does not fall back to the admin-group controller. {{#unless automatic}} is therefore always true, so the remove link is shown for automatic groups (admins, moderators, trust_level_*, and so on). Confirming still calls DELETE /admin/groups/:id/members, which correctly returns 422, but neither the removeMember action nor Group.removeMember handles the failure, so the admin gets a confirm dialog and then no error and no list refresh.

title: Creating a group drops the chosen alias level
body: create assigns name and visible, then saves, but never reads params[:alias_level]. The admin form shows the alias-level combo for new groups (it sits outside the {{#if id}} block), and Group.asJSON posts alias_level on create. update does apply alias_level, so editing an existing group works, but the first save always persists the default (0, nobody) no matter what was selected. The client only copies resp.basic_group.id back onto the model, so the UI keeps showing the unsaved choice until the group is reloaded. The new create spec only checks name stripping and would not catch this.

title: Members limit and offset are unbounded and can 500
body: The rewritten members action uses limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i and offset = params[:offset].to_i with no upper or lower bound. This route is available to anyone who can see the group, including public automatic groups that contain every user. A very large limit loads and serializes the entire membership in one request. A negative offset or limit is sent through to SQL; PostgreSQL rejects OFFSET/LIMIT < 0, so those query params 500 the endpoint. The old action at least defaulted automatic groups to 200; the rewrite should cap limit (and reject negative offset/limit) rather than trusting the client.

title: GET /groups/:name/members.json response shape changed
body: members used to render_serialized an array of GroupUserSerializer objects. It now returns an object {members, meta: {total, limit, offset}}. The in-repo Group.findMembers caller was updated, but this is a public route. Themes, plugins, and API clients that treated the body as an array (for example result.map or a JSON array decode) will break or show no members. There is no compat path, such as keeping the array when limit/offset are omitted, or a versioned response.

title: No coverage for alias level or the new members payload
body: The create example only posts a name and asserts stripping. Nothing asserts that alias_level from the flat params is persisted, which is the field create now ignores. There is also no spec for GroupsController#members, so the new {members, meta} contract, the default page size, and unbounded limit/offset are untested. The automatic remove example calls xhr :put, :remove_member while the route is DELETE; controller specs still invoke the action, so that mismatch does not fail CI and does not lock the route param (:group_id) either.

title: Add/remove member endpoints read group_id but routes set id
body: add_members and remove_member both load the group with params.require(:group_id). The new routes are declared inside resources :groups the same way as put "suspend" on users (config/routes.rb delete/put "members"), so Rails registers member routes PUT/DELETE /admin/groups/:id/members and sets params[:id], not params[:group_id]. The admin client calls exactly /admin/groups/:id/members.json, so every add and remove raises ParameterMissing and returns 400 before any membership change. Controller specs inject group_id directly and never go through the router (the automatic-group remove example even uses xhr :put while the route is DELETE), so they stay green while the feature is broken in the browser.

title: Public members page is stuck on the first 50 users
body: findMembers always sends limit from the model default of 50, and the public group-members route only calls findMembers. group/members.hbs then renders that single page with no next/previous controls. Before this change, non-automatic groups returned every member and automatic groups defaulted to 200. Any group larger than 50 now silently shows only the first page on the public members tab, so the rest of the membership cannot be viewed.

title: Pager invents a blank page when count divides limit evenly
body: totalPages is Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1, so exactly 50 members with limit 50 is reported as 2 pages (100 members as 3, and so on). showingLast stays false on the real last page, and next() then sets offset to min(offset + limit, user_count), which equals user_count. That request returns no rows, so the admin UI shows an empty extra page. Page count needs ceil division, and the next-page offset must be capped at the last page start, not at user_count.

title: Invalid member offset is echoed and can 500
body: members sets offset = params[:offset].to_i and limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i with no lower bound and no clamp to the last page, then returns that same offset in meta. The client copies meta.offset. Deleting the last user on the last page (51 members, limit 50, offset 50) therefore reloads an empty page and leaves offset at 50 even though total is now 50, so the admin pager stays on a blank page. A negative offset or limit is passed through to PostgreSQL, which errors with OFFSET/LIMIT must not be negative and turns the request into a 500. Both values need to be clamped to >= 0, and offset past the end should rewind to the last page before the query.

title: Remove link is shown for automatic groups
body: group_member.hbs is rendered as an {{each}} itemView, so the template context is the member user, not the group. {{#unless automatic}} therefore looks up user.automatic, which is never set, and the remove control is always rendered. The add-members block in group.hbs correctly checks the group's automatic flag; this remove link does not. The server rejects membership edits on automatic groups with 422, and removeMember does not display that error, so the member looks removable and then simply stays in the list.

title: Create ignores the alias level chosen in the form
body: The admin form shows the alias-level combo box even before the group has an id, and the client asJSON payload includes alias_level on create. Admin::GroupsController#create only assigns name and visible. Unlike update, it never sets alias_level, so the first save stores the default (0, nobody) and drops whatever the admin selected. The value is only persisted if they open the group and save a second time.

title: Membership add/remove failures are silent
body: addMembers and removeMember fire the ajax calls and never handle rejection, unlike save which parses the response and shows bootbox.alert. addMembers also never clears the username field. On the server, unknown usernames are skipped one by one and add_members still returns 200, so a typo looks like a successful add that did not change the list. A 422 (automatic group) or a network error is an unhandled rejection with no message, and the filled input makes a retry resubmit the same names.

title: Members endpoint does not cap page size
body: limit is taken from the query string with only a default of 50 and no maximum. /groups/:name/members.json is available to anyone who can see the group, including very large automatic groups such as trust_level_0. A caller can pass limit=1000000 and force the process to load and serialize every member in one response. The new pagination API should clamp limit to a small maximum.

title: Specs miss the route mismatch and the public members API
body: The new membership examples call the controller actions directly with group_id, so they never notice that the routes expose params[:id]. The automatic-group remove example uses xhr :put, :remove_member even though the route is DELETE, which a request spec would not match. There is also no coverage of GroupsController#members: the new {members, meta} shape, the 50-row default, offset past the end, or negative limit/offset. Those gaps hide both the broken admin add/remove URLs and the public list truncation.

title: Add/remove members read group_id but the route only sets id
body: add_members and remove_member load the group with params.require(:group_id). The new routes are member routes (PUT/DELETE /admin/groups/:id/members), so Rails sets params[:id], not params[:group_id]. The client calls /admin/groups/<id>/members.json and only puts usernames or user_id in the body. require(:group_id) therefore raises ParameterMissing and every add or remove returns 400. destroy and update in this same controller correctly use params[:id]. The controller specs pass group_id straight into the action and never go through the router, so they stay green.

title: Public members page only loads 50 users and cannot page
body: setupController now calls model.findMembers(), which always requests /groups/:name/members.json with the Group model's default limit of 50 and offset 0. The public members template only iterates that one page and has no next/previous or load-more control; paging was added only on the admin group screen. Non-automatic groups previously returned every member, and automatic groups returned up to 200. A group with more than 50 members now hides the rest with no way to reach them.

title: Creating a group ignores alias_level
body: create only assigns name and visible. The admin form shows the alias-level combo before the group has an id, and Group#asJSON sends alias_level on POST /admin/groups. update applies params[:alias_level], but create never reads it, so a non-default level (for example everyone/99) is not saved. The client keeps the unsaved value until the group is reloaded, so the admin thinks the setting stuck.

title: totalPages is one too high when the count divides the page size
body: totalPages uses Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1. When user_count is an exact multiple of limit (50 members, limit 50) that is 2, not 1. showingLast compares currentPage to that value, so the next guard does not fire on the real last page. next then sets offset to min(offset + limit, user_count), which equals user_count and loads an empty page. The same formula also leaves the admin on a blank last page after removing the final member of a page, because findMembers keeps the server's unclamped offset.

title: Remove link is shown for automatic groups
body: The remove control is wrapped in {{#unless automatic}} inside the group-member itemView. With {{each member in members itemView="group-member"}}, Ember sets that view's context to the item view (so {{member}} works) or to the user, not to the admin group. automatic is not the group's automatic flag there; it is missing, so the unless is always true. Automatic groups still show a remove button. The server answers 422, and removeMember has no failure handler, so the admin confirms and the member stays with no error.

title: Add/remove membership failures are silent and the add field is not cleared
body: addMembers posts usernames and on success reloads the current offset, but it never clears usernames (the TODO on the line above). The selector still holds the same names, so another click resubmits them. Neither addMembers nor removeMember handles a rejected promise. A 400, 422, or 500 leaves the list unchanged and shows no alert, which looks the same as a successful add of a user who sorts onto a different page because the reload does not reset offset to 0.

title: Membership specs never hit the router and one uses PUT
body: The automatic-group remove example calls xhr :put, :remove_member while the route is DELETE, and both add_members and remove_member examples pass group_id. Controller specs invoke the action directly, so they pass even though the router only sets params[:id] and the live requests 400. There is also no spec for the public GroupsController#members contract (limit, offset, and the {members, meta} shape) that this PR changes.

title: Translation path never loads fallback locale files
body: I18n.translate still only calls load_locale for config.locale, and the new ensure_loaded! helper is invoked only from ApplicationController#set_locale. The accelerator otherwise refuses to load YAML except for that one locale, while I18n::Backend::Fallbacks looks up SiteSetting.default_locale and :en in memory. Jobs, mailers, I18n.with_locale, and any I18n.t outside that before_filter therefore miss fallback strings (and plural rules) that exist on disk. Calls with no interpolation args then freeze the "translation missing" result in the LRU cache, so later loading the fallback locale does not repair that key until restart or eviction.

title: Cached translations ignore the fallback locale
body: The no-argument translation cache key is only the key, I18n.locale, and backend object id. FallbackLocaleList now resolves missing keys through SiteSetting.default_locale, which admins can change at runtime without I18n.reload!. A string that was filled from the old site locale stays cached under the user locale, so after a default-locale change users of incomplete locales keep seeing the previous language for hot keys until process restart or LRU eviction.

title: Fallbacks turned on in development and test
body: config.i18n.fallbacks = true was previously limited to production, profile, and the cloud66 production file, so development and test left missing keys visible. This initializer always includes I18n::Backend::Fallbacks and installs FallbackLocaleList, with no environment guard. In development and test, a key missing from the current locale now silently becomes the site-locale or English string instead of the missing-translation marker, which hides incomplete locale files and can change specs that set a non-English locale and assert on missing keys or exact untranslated output.

title: Fallback locale files are not loaded on the translation path
body: Server-side fallbacks cannot work unless the fallback YAML is actually loaded, but I18n.translate only calls load_locale for config.locale. The on-demand loader (load_translations patched to load nothing unless given filenames) will not pull in SiteSetting.default_locale or :en. The new ensure_loaded! helper is only invoked from ApplicationController#set_locale (line 159), so background jobs, mailers, rake tasks, and any I18n.with_locale / I18n.t(..., locale:) call that does not go through that before_filter look up fallback locales in an empty store and treat real English (or site-default) strings as missing. That is the main server-side path this change is for: notification emails run outside ApplicationController. It is worse with the LRU cache: getset memoizes the result of translate_no_cache under a key that does not record which locales were loaded. If a missing-translation handler returns a string (instead of raising), that miss is frozen in the cache, and a later ensure_loaded! cannot repair hot keys. Interpolated lookups (args.length > 0) skip the cache but still do not load the fallback chain. Load the fallback chain inside translate before lookup/cache fill, including an explicit locale: option, instead of relying on the controller filter.

title: Translation cache key ignores the fallback locale
body: FallbackLocaleList resolves missing keys through SiteSetting.default_locale, which admins can change at runtime without a process restart, but the accelerator cache key is only "#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}". A string resolved via the old site locale is stored under the user locale and reused after default_locale changes. Hot keys stay in the 300-entry LRU indefinitely, so users keep seeing the previous fallback language until restart. Include the fallback chain (at least SiteSetting.default_locale) in the cache key, or clear this cache when default_locale changes.

title: No tests for fallback order or fallback bundle loading
body: The new contract is locale, then SiteSetting.default_locale, then :en, and it depends on on-demand YAML loading that previously only happened for the active locale. Nothing in this change covers that order, the ApplicationController ensure_loaded! hook, or a non-request entry point such as a job or mailer. Those paths are exactly where fallback files are not loaded, so the feature can ship while still returning missing-translation results for incomplete locales outside HTTP requests.

title: Fallback locale files are never loaded from I18n.translate
body: translate in lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb only calls load_locale for config.locale (line 68), then either returns translate_no_cache immediately when arguments are present (line 69) or caches that call (line 74). The new FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded! is invoked only from ApplicationController#set_locale. Mailers, Sidekiq jobs, rails runner, and any I18n.with_locale / I18n.locale= path never hit that filter, so the lazy loader never reads the site-default or :en YAML. I18n::Backend::Fallbacks then searches empty catalogs and I18n.t becomes "translation missing: ..." for keys that exist only in a fallback locale — the main server-side case this change is for. Because the LRU cache stores that miss under key+locale+backend object id and nothing invalidates it when catalogs are loaded later, a lookup that runs before set_locale (boot, middleware, an earlier before_filter, or another thread) keeps serving the missing string for the life of the cache entry even on later web requests that do call ensure_loaded!.

title: Translation cache key ignores the fallback chain
body: The accelerator cache key is only "#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}" (lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb:72). Resolved strings now depend on SiteSetting.default_locale via FallbackLocaleList#[] and on which fallback catalogs were loaded. default_locale is a runtime admin setting and is not part of the key, and neither ensure_loaded! nor a default-locale change calls I18n.reload! (the only path that nils @cache). After an admin changes the site locale, arg-less I18n.t calls keep returning the previously cached fallback translation until that LRU slot is evicted or the process restarts, so users keep seeing the old language for missing keys.

title: No coverage for fallback order or non-request loading
body: The new fallback chain in config/initializers/i18n.rb (locale, SiteSetting.default_locale, :en) and the lazy-load hook are untested. Nothing asserts that a key missing from the user locale is served from the site locale and then :en, that pluralization still runs on the fallback locale, or that I18n.t falls back when locale is set outside ApplicationController (the mailer/job path). Without that, the broken load/cache behavior above can ship unnoticed, and a later change to FallbackLocaleList or translate_accelerator can drop fallbacks in production only.

title: Denial cache pins false denies and skips the DB re-query
body: Check returns Allowed=false as soon as permDenialCache has an entry for (namespace, subject id, action, name, parent), before reading permissions or the folder tree. That entry is written for every DB deny and kept for shortCacheTTL (30s), and nothing deletes it when permissions are granted or the folder cache is refreshed. A check that races ahead of the creator ACL insert (or any deny followed by a grant, including a new wildcard/admin role) therefore stays denied for the full TTL even though the new re-query path would now allow it. The same stickiness freezes inheritance failures caused by a stale folder tree: once denied, later requests never rebuild the tree or reload scopes. A slow in-flight query that snapshotted pre-grant rows can also Set the denial after a concurrent request already observed the grant, so retries keep failing for 30s. This recreates the 'creator cannot open what they just created' failure on the retry that the PR is meant to fix.

title: Denial cache key omits identity type and collides on id 0
body: userPermDenialCacheKey is built from checkReq.UserUID only, not the identity type or the canonical UID from GetUserIdentifiers. Anonymous checks use subject anonymous:0 and the renderer uses render:0 (both covered by tests), so both produce the same key for a given namespace, action, name, and folder. An anonymous deny of dashboards:read on a dashboard is then served to the renderer for 30s, and every anonymous retry refreshes that TTL, so image rendering/PDF of that dashboard can stay broken as long as anonymous checks keep missing. The reverse is also true for actions the renderer is denied. Numeric subjects (user:123) are likewise keyed separately from the resolved UID, so the same person does not share denial entries across id and uid forms, and a numeric id can collide with another identity whose id string matches.

title: Denial cache key joins name and folder with an underscore
body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates action, name, and parent with '_' and no escaping. Dashboard and folder UIDs may contain underscores, and parent is often empty, so distinct resources share one key. For example name=foo, parent=bar and name=foo_bar, parent="" both become ..._foo_bar_, and name=abc, parent=de_f matches name=abc_de, parent=f. A deny for one resource then returns Allowed=false for the other for 30s with no permission or folder check.

title: Every newly denied resource reloads the full permission set
body: If the permission cache hits but checkPermission is false, Check always calls getIdentityPermissions, which ignores the cache and loads every scope for that user and action from the DB, then writes the cache back. Absence in a just-refreshed complete set is treated the same as a stale cache. Denial entries only dedupe the exact same name and folder, so a sequential sweep of unauthorized resources (list filtering, many GETs) issues one full permission query per resource per 30s instead of the previous single query per user+action. Concurrent checks share one singleflight, but sequential checks do not.

title: Denial-cache test still denies if the cache is ignored
body: TestService_CacheCheck's explicit-deny case comments that the permission cache allows dash1 so a denial hit is the only way to deny, but it stores map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}. checkPermission treats a false value as no grant, and the fake permission store is empty, so a fall-through to the DB also returns Allowed=false. The test passes even if the denial-cache short-circuit is removed and does not cover deny-then-grant, renderer/anonymous key collision, or UID delimiter collisions.

title: Denial cache key omits identity type and collides on id 0
body: Check builds the denial-cache key only from namespace, raw subject id, action, name, and parent. Identity type is dropped, unlike the positive permission cache, which uses a separate anonymousPermCacheKey. In this service anonymous subjects are "anonymous:0" and the renderer is "render:0", so both have UserUID "0" and share one denial entry. A denied anonymous dashboards:read Check therefore writes a 30s denial that the next renderer Check for the same name/folder hits immediately and returns Allowed=false, never applying the renderer's static read-all grant. The reverse also holds for actions the renderer is denied. Unrelated identities can force false 403s on each other for shortCacheTTL.

title: Denial cache overrides fresher permission data for 30s
body: A denial-cache hit returns Allowed=false before the permission cache or the database is consulted, and a DB deny at the end of Check stores that denial for shortCacheTTL (30s) with no invalidation. The new fall-through reloads permissions and overwrites permCache when some other resource is missing, and List will authorize from that updated map, but a later Check of the previously denied resource still short-circuits on the denial entry. A creator Check that races the permission insert, a grant after a deny, or an inherited allow that only works once the folder tree cache refreshes therefore stays denied for up to 30s even after this process already has an allow in permCache. Denials also freeze the result of getUserPermissions, which still uses the 30s basic-role and team caches, so a role or team change can remain denied after those caches expire.

title: Denial-cache test does not actually grant the cached permission
body: "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" says the permission cache allows dash1 so the deny can only come from the denial entry, but it stores map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}. checkPermission treats a false value as no grant, and this subtest never installs a permission store result that would allow dash1, so the DB fall-through also denies. The test passes if the denial-cache short-circuit is removed. Store true for that scope (and a store grant) so the test fails unless the denial cache is what forced Allowed=false.

title: Denial cache pins false denies for 30s after access is granted
body: Check returns Allowed=false as soon as permDenialCache contains the user/action/name/folder key, before consulting either the permission cache or the database. On any deny it then stores that key for shortCacheTTL (30s) and never deletes it when a later load would allow the resource. A check that races ahead of the permission insert for a dashboard or folder the user just created (or any grant after a deny) therefore keeps failing until the denial entry expires, which is the failure this PR is meant to fix. The same pin also freezes denies caused by a stale folder tree in checkInheritedPermissions: once recorded, the denial is served even after folderCache has been rebuilt and inherited access would succeed.

title: Warm permission cache is not trusted for denies, so each new resource hits the DB
body: If cached scopes are present but do not allow the requested resource, Check always falls through to getIdentityPermissions. That path no longer returns the cached set; it singleflight-loads permissions, teams, and the basic role from the DB and overwrites permCache. A just-refreshed cache is therefore ignored for every distinct unauthorized name. The denial cache only dedupes repeats of the same name and folder, and singleflight only coalesces overlapping calls for the same user and action, so sequential Checks (or Checks that do not overlap) each issue a full permission reload. Previously one cached permission set served all checks for that action until TTL.

title: Denial-cache test does not actually grant the cached permission
body: TestService_CacheCheck's "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" comment says the permission cache allows dash1 so the test proves the denial entry is what short-circuits. The map value stored is false, so scopeMap["dashboards:uid:dash1"] is not a grant. If the denial-cache read were removed, Check would still deny via the empty fake permission store. The test would pass without the new short-circuit, and nothing covers the creator retry: deny, permission appears in the store, next Check within 30s must be allowed.

title: Pause and delete never appear without a ruler rule
body: The list view now computes canPause and canDelete from Grafana Prometheus abilities, but the menu still renders Pause only when rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) is true (line 123) and Delete only when rulerRule is set (line 165). GrafanaRuleListItem and FilterView pass only promRule, so both items stay hidden even for users who are allowed to pause or delete. Those actions are gone from the new alert list; GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx locks this in by expecting exactly four menu items and never asserting Delete or Pause.

title: Silence menu item does not open a drawer
body: AlertRuleMenu shows Silence when the Prometheus-rule ability allows it and calls handleSilence, which only sets showSilenceDrawer. The drawer is still gated on rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule). The new list never passes a ruler rule, so clicking Silence notifications does nothing. The group-loader test only checks that the menu item exists and never clicks it.

title: skipToken still grants Duplicate via Grafana create permission
body: useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(skipToken) evaluates useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined) instead of returning all-denied abilities. With no rule, loading is false, so MaybeSupported is AlwaysSupported and Duplicate is allowed whenever the user has Grafana AlertingRuleCreate. AlertRuleMenu ORs that result with the ruler result, so cloud and ruler-only rules show Duplicate for anyone who can create Grafana rules, even when the datasource ability denies it. Update and Delete do not leak because their allowed flag stays false, but Duplicate does.

title: Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable
body: useAllAlertRuleAbilities used to set isFederated from isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) and block update, delete, pause, restore, and permanent delete. It now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes isFederated to false (TODO on line 243). Every caller of useAlertRuleAbility, including the existing rules UI, will offer edit and delete on Mimir/enterprise federated groups. groupIdentifier does not carry source_tenants, so the check was dropped rather than moved.

title: Filtered Grafana rules are rendered without a list key
body: The grafana branch of the filtered-rule map used to render GrafanaRuleLoader with key={key}. The replacement GrafanaRuleListItem has no key, while the datasource and unknown branches still use key. As infinite scroll appends rows, React can reuse the wrong list-item instance, so action-menu and drawer state can attach to a different rule.

title: Rule links no longer include returnTo
body: The removed GrafanaRuleListItem built the view href with createReturnTo() so the rule detail back link returned to the current list, including filters. The new href is only /alerting/grafana/${uid}/view. Opening a rule from the list and using the in-app back control drops the user on the default alerting page instead of the filtered list.

title: Prometheus abilities treat only alerting rules as exportable
body: useAllRulerRuleAbilities allows ModifyExport, Pause, Restore, and DeletePermanently for any Grafana-managed rule (alerting or recording) via rulerRuleType.grafana.rule. useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities gates those same actions on prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule. The list view relies on the Prometheus hook, so Grafana recording rules lose Export (and would also lose pause/restore/permanent delete once those menu items no longer require a ruler rule).

title: Creating and deleting rules are no longer distinguished
body: GrafanaGroupLoader used to match ruler and Prometheus rules and render ruler-only rules as Creating and Prometheus-only rules as Deleting (without edit or more actions). It now lists only Prometheus rules. Until Prometheus catches up, a just-created rule is missing from the group, and a just-deleted rule still appears as a normal rule with edit, silence, duplicate, and export. The tests that covered those states were removed rather than replaced.

title: isProvisionedPromRule reads provenance on a type that lacks it
body: isProvisionedPromRule takes PromRuleDTO and accesses promRule.provenance after prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(promRule). That helper is not a type predicate, and PromRuleDTO (PromAlertingRuleDTO | PromRecordingRuleDTO) does not declare provenance — only GrafanaPromRuleDTOBase does. This is a TypeScript error, and RuleActionsButtons passes a Rule into this function, so provisioned detection for the clone flow may not typecheck. At runtime a non-Grafana rule short-circuits, but a Grafana rule is only treated as provisioned if the object happens to have provenance.

title: Ability checks OR ruler and Prometheus results, widening permissions
body: canPause, canDelete, canDuplicate, canSilence, and canExport are each true if either the ruler-rule ability or the Grafana Prometheus ability allows the action. Callers that still have a ruler rule (rule detail and any menu that passes both) previously trusted only the ruler check. The Prometheus path treats a rule as not provisioned when provenance is missing, and it never treats groups as federated, so a denial from the ruler check can be overridden and Edit, Delete, Pause, Duplicate, Silence, or Export can appear for provisioned or otherwise immutable rules. These flags should fall back to the Prometheus abilities only when rulerRule is absent, not be unioned.

title: Edit button uses the same permissive OR of ability checks
body: canEditRule is true when either useRulerRuleAbility or useGrafanaPromRuleAbility allows Update. Any caller that still passes a ruler rule plus a Grafana prom rule (the previous V2 contract always had a ruler rule) can now show Edit even when the ruler result says the rule is not editable, for example a provisioned rule whose Prometheus DTO has no provenance. Use the Prometheus result only as a fallback when rule is undefined.

title: Delete and Pause never render in the ruler-free list
body: The list view now passes only promRule into AlertRuleMenu, and canDelete/canPause can be true from the new Prometheus abilities. The Delete item is still gated on rulerRule (line 165) and Pause is still gated on rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) (line 123), and both handlers require a RulerRuleDTO. With no ruler payload those actions are impossible to open, so users lose Delete and Pause from the alert list even when folder permissions allow them. RuleActionsButtons already builds an identifier and delete modal from the Prometheus uid, so the menu gate is what blocks delete. GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx grants AlertingRuleDelete, defines a delete menu selector, and then asserts exactly four items (silence, copy link, duplicate, export), which locks this regression in.

title: Silence menu item is a no-op without a ruler rule
body: List rows render RuleActionsButtons with only promRule. AlertRuleMenu can still show Silence notifications because canSilence is taken from the Prometheus ability, and handleSilence only sets showSilenceDrawer. The drawer is rendered only when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true, so in the list view the click never opens SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer. Users with silence permission get a menu action that does nothing.

title: Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable
body: useAllAlertRuleAbilities used to set isFederated from isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) (source_tenants) and fold that into immutableRule, which disables update, delete, pause, restore, and permanent delete. The refactored useAllRulerRuleAbilities hardcodes isFederated to false with a TODO, and every combined-rule and ruler-rule ability check now goes through it. Federated cloud rules therefore show edit and delete actions they were previously blocked from, and the backend may reject the write or apply it in the wrong tenant scope.

title: Recording rules lose export, pause, restore, and permanent delete
body: useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities sets ModifyExport, Pause, Restore, and DeletePermanently from isAlertingRule (prometheus type alerting). The ruler implementation used isGrafanaManagedAlertRule, which includes Grafana recording rules. Silence correctly needs an alerting rule, but the other four actions were not limited that way. On the new list, which only consults this hook, Grafana recording rules no longer get Export (and will not get Pause once that item no longer requires a ruler rule), even though they are Grafana-managed and still editable.

title: Filtered Grafana rules are rendered without a React key
body: Switching the filtered list from GrafanaRuleLoader to GrafanaRuleListItem dropped key={key} on the grafana branch of the map. Datasource rows still use the stable key computed by getRuleKey. Filter results are appended as the user scrolls, so missing keys make React reuse the wrong row state (open menus, action buttons) across different rules and can show the wrong rule's actions after the next page loads.

title: Rule view links no longer include returnTo
body: The removed list item built the view href with createReturnTo() so Back from the rule page returned to the current list, including filters. The new href is createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`) with no returnTo query. From the filtered list, opening a rule and going back lands on the default alerting page instead of the filtered results.

title: Pause and Delete stay hidden without a ruler rule
body: Alert list rows now pass only a Prometheus rule into AlertRuleMenu, and canPause/canDelete are computed from those prom abilities. The Pause item is still rendered only when rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) is true (line 123), and Delete only when rulerRule is set (line 165), with onClick forwarding that ruler DTO. In the new list both are therefore never shown, even for users who have pause/delete permission. The rewritten GrafanaGroupLoader test grants AlertingRuleDelete and then expects exactly four menu items (silence, copy link, duplicate, export), so it locks this regression in instead of catching it.

title: Silence click does nothing in the ruler-less list
body: List items enable Silence from Grafana Prometheus abilities and AlertRuleMenu calls handleSilence, which only sets showSilenceDrawer. The drawer is still mounted only when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true, and SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer requires a RulerGrafanaRuleDTO. The new GrafanaRuleListItem passes promRule and no ruler rule, so the menu item appears and clicking it never opens a silence drawer.

title: Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable
body: useAllAlertRuleAbilities now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes isFederated to false (with a TODO) instead of calling isFederatedRuleGroup on the combined rule's group. Federated Mimir/GEM groups were previously immutable, so Update, Delete, Pause, Restore, and Delete permanently were not offered. Those actions are now reported as supported for every existing useAlertRuleAbility/useAllAlertRuleAbilities caller, not only the new list, and the UI can offer edits the previous guard blocked.

title: Recording rules lose export, pause, and restore
body: useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities sets isAlertingRule via prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule and uses that flag for ModifyExport, Pause, Restore, and DeletePermanently. The ruler equivalent used rulerRuleType.grafana.rule, which is true for both Grafana alerting and recording rules (only Silence excluded recording rules). Grafana recording rules in the new list therefore cannot be exported or paused even when the user can edit them, and is_paused exists on those rules.

title: Filtered Grafana rules are rendered without a list key
body: Replacing GrafanaRuleLoader dropped key={key} on the grafana branch of the filtered-rule list. Datasource and unknown rows still use key, and getRuleKey still builds a frontend id specifically to avoid duplicate keys. Without it, React reconciles Grafana rows by index as infinite scroll appends pages, so row state (open menus, silence drawer, action buttons) can attach to the wrong rule.

title: Rule view links no longer include returnTo
body: The removed GrafanaRuleListItem built the view href with createReturnTo() so the rule view could navigate back to the current list URL, including filters and search. The new item links to /alerting/grafana/${uid}/view with no returnTo query. Opening a rule from the list or filtered list drops that context, so Back/return no longer restores the list the user came from.

title: Early interpolation defeats the $__range split exclusion
body: runSplitQuery now runs every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables before querySupportsSplitting. That helper replaces Grafana range macros ($__range, $__range_s, $__range_ms) from request.scopedVars using the full request range. querySupportsSplitting then calls isQueryWithRangeVariable on the already-rewritten expr, so the $__range token is gone and the query is treated as splittable. The comment on querySupportsSplitting says these queries must not be split because the macro is meant to be interpolated on the backend against each request's own time range. After this change each chunk is executed with the full-range duration baked in (for example count_over_time({app="x"}[7d]) on every 1-day slice), so merged results overlap or over-count and Loki load grows with the selected range. The new tests only cover $__auto and $step, and the default test templateSrv does not expand $__range, so this production path is untested. Interpolate only after classifying queries on the raw expr, and leave $__range* in the expression sent to the backend.

title: Shard queries are template-interpolated twice, including ad-hoc filters
body: runShardSplitQuery now maps every target through applyTemplateVariables(query, scopedVars, request.filters), then splitQueriesByStreamShard rewrites those expressions with interpolateShardingSelector and calls runSplitQuery. runSplitQuery unconditionally applies applyTemplateVariables again on that rewritten expr, with the same request.filters still set. applyTemplateVariables is not idempotent: ad-hoc filters are inserted into the stream selector on each call, so a sharded query gets duplicate matchers (or a failed/misplaced insertion once `| drop __stream_shard__` is already in the LogQL). A second template replace can also expand `$` sequences that appeared in variable values. The updated shard test expects applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times for a single target (once here plus once per split group) and only uses an idempotent replace mock, so it locks in the double application instead of catching duplicate filters. Interpolate once, before shard selector injection, and do not run applyTemplateVariables again inside runSplitQuery for targets that are already interpolated.

title: Interpolating before the split check drops the $__range exclusion
body: runSplitQuery now runs every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables before querySupportsSplitting. That helper substitutes variables via templateSrv.replace (the new test depends on this for both expr and step), and panel/Explore requests put __range, __range_s, and __range_ms on request.scopedVars. After substitution, isQueryWithRangeVariable no longer sees [$__range] / [$__range_s] / [$__range_ms], so a query such as count_over_time({app="foo"}[$__range]) is treated as splittable. The comment on querySupportsSplitting says these must not be split because the backend interpolates $__range from the time range of the request it actually receives. Each chunk is then executed with the full dashboard duration already baked in (or, if a later pass still sees the variable, with the chunk duration), so rates and range aggregations over multi-day windows are wrong or rejected by Loki. Keep the range-variable check on the pre-interpolation expression, and add a regression test that a $__range query is not split.

title: Shard path applies template variables twice
body: runShardSplitQuery now maps every target through applyTemplateVariables(query, scopedVars, request.filters) and then splitQueriesByStreamShard always calls runSplitQuery, which applies applyTemplateVariables again on those same targets (including expressions already rewritten by interpolateShardingSelector with __stream_shard__ and `| drop __stream_shard__`). applyTemplateVariables' contract is to inject ad-hoc filters from the third argument, and that injection appends matchers into each `{}` selector; it is not idempotent. With loki shard splitting on, every request that has ad-hoc filters therefore executes LogQL with duplicate matchers, and the second rewrite runs on an already sharded selector, which can produce invalid LogQL or a selector that does not match the stream selector used to fetch shard values. The updated test expects applyTemplateVariables five times (once up front plus once per shard group) but never passes filters, so this is untested. Interpolate once, and do not pass already rewritten targets back through filter injection.

title: Empty expressions after interpolation are no longer removed
body: Previously shard splitting interpolated first and then dropped targets whose expr was empty. The new code filters on query.expr before applyTemplateVariables, so a target whose expression is only a variable (for example `$query`) that resolves to `""` is kept. That empty target is then grouped, used for shard lookup, and sent to Loki. An empty query parse error fails the shard group and stops the split instead of skipping the target as before. Filter again after interpolation, matching the old order.

title: Shard splitting applies template variables and ad-hoc filters twice
body: runSplitQuery now maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables(..., request.filters) before executing. runShardSplitQuery does the same before grouping, then builds each shard sub-request from those already interpolated targets and calls runSplitQuery. On the shard-splitting path template application therefore runs twice per target (once up front, then once per shard group inside runSplitQuery). applyTemplateVariables is not idempotent: its contract appends ad-hoc filters to the LogQL expression, so the second call inserts the same matchers again, for example {app="foo", env="prod", __stream_shard__=~"1|2", env="prod"}. Loki rejects duplicate label matchers, so dashboards with ad-hoc filters and shard splitting fail or change query meaning. A variable value that itself contains $ or ${...} is expanded again on the second pass and can be corrupted. The updated shard test expects applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times for a single target (1 initial call plus 1 per shard group), which locks in the double application. Interpolate once for sharding decisions in runShardSplitQuery, and do not call applyTemplateVariables again in runSplitQuery on targets that are already interpolated (or strip filters from the sub-request so they cannot be reapplied).

title: $__auto is not resolved before splitting; the new test only stubs it
body: The new tests claim a query such as count_over_time({a="b"}[$__auto]) is interpolated to a concrete range before split execution, but they only pass because createLokiDatasource is given a templateSrv.replace stub that string-replaces $__auto. $__auto is a Loki query macro, not a Grafana template variable, and TemplateSrv.replace does not define it. The only interpolation this PR adds is applyTemplateVariables, which leaves $__auto in the expression. It is still resolved later by the Loki backend (the same step path calculateStep says it replicates from pkg/tsdb/loki/step.go) or by runQuery, using each sub-request's split time range. Chunks therefore still get a step derived from the chunk instead of the original range, which is the failure mode early interpolation is supposed to prevent. The unit test cannot catch that because the stub removes $__auto before runQuery is observed. Substitute $__auto from the original request range before partitioning, and do not fake that substitution in templateSrv.replace.

title: Plugin request logs lose traceID
body: "Plugin Request Completed" used to include traceID from tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false), so every valid trace (sampled or not) was on the log line. That field was removed and is not added by ContextualLoggerMiddleware, which only sets endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname. The new call is logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...) and Info does not take a context.Context, so the infra logger cannot recover the span at log time. Plugin request logs can no longer be correlated with traces, including unsampled ones that metrics exemplars (requireSampled=true) never recorded.

title: TestLogger.FromContext discards recorded logs
body: LoggerMiddleware now emits the completion line via m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...). TestLogger.FromContext ignores the receiver and returns NewTestLogger(), a different object whose InfoLogs/WarnLogs/ErrorLogs are not the instance tests hold. Calls, message, and key/value pairs are silently dropped, so assertions on the injected test logger see zero logs even when a request was logged. The fake also ignores ctx, so it cannot observe the contextual attributes this change depends on.

title: No test locks the moved contextual log fields
body: Contextual attributes were moved out of the metrics middleware into instrumentContext, and completion logs now depend on a separate middleware having called log.WithContextualAttributes before LoggerMiddleware.FromContext. Nothing in this change asserts that QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, and CollectMetrics attach endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname, or that "Plugin Request Completed" still emits them (and traceID). The renamed metrics test only checks Prometheus counters. A middleware reorder, a FromContext miss, or a dropped field would ship unnoticed.

title: Plugin request logs lose traceID
body: "Plugin Request Completed" no longer includes traceID. logRequest used to call tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false) and append that value on every completion line, including unsampled traces. That extraction was deleted and not replaced: instrumentContext only sets endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname, and grafanaInfraLogWrapper.Info forwards to ConcreteLogger.Info(msg, kv...) without a context.Context, so a trace ID that exists only on the span is not read at log time. Completion logs can no longer be correlated with traces. pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName, and dsUID are also no longer written on the line itself; they appear only if ContextualLoggerMiddleware ran earlier and FromContext merged WithContextualAttributes.

title: TestLogger.FromContext discards recorded logs
body: TestLogger.FromContext ignores the receiver and returns NewTestLogger(), a different logger with empty counters. LoggerMiddleware now emits "Plugin Request Completed" via logger.FromContext(ctx).Info instead of logger.Info. Tests that hold a *TestLogger will not observe those calls, and the compile-time Logger assertion hides the broken fake. FromContext should return the same recorder (or a child that writes into the same Logs).

title: Moved log fields have no test coverage
body: Contextual attributes (endpoint, pluginId, datasource name/UID, user login) were moved out of LoggerMiddleware into ContextualLoggerMiddleware, and completion logs now depend on FromContext to surface them. The only test edit renames newInstrumentationMiddleware and still only asserts Prometheus counters. Nothing checks that instrumentContext attaches those fields, that LoggerMiddleware still emits them on "Plugin Request Completed", or that traceID is still present, so the dropped traceID and a broken FromContext merge would both pass CI.

title: Plugin request completion logs drop traceID
body: logRequest used to add traceID from tracing.TraceIDFromContext before emitting "Plugin Request Completed". That argument was removed, and ContextualLoggerMiddleware.instrumentContext does not put it back (it only sets endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname). The plugin tracing middleware does not store traceID as a log contextual attribute either, so Logger.FromContext will not restore it. Completion logs, including alerting and other non-HTTP plugin calls, can no longer be correlated with the span started for the request.

title: TestLogger.FromContext discards the logger under test
body: FromContext ignores both the receiver and the context and returns NewTestLogger(), a fresh instance whose Logs are not the caller's. LoggerMiddleware now records every completion exclusively via logger.FromContext(ctx).Info, so a test that injects *TestLogger and asserts InfoLogs, ErrorLogs, or contextual fields will see no calls even when a request was logged. The fake should return itself, or a child that writes into the same Logs and exposes contextual attributes.

title: Moved request log fields have no test coverage
body: pluginId, endpoint, datasource identity, and user were removed from LoggerMiddleware's explicit log parameters and are now supposed to arrive via ContextualLoggerMiddleware plus Logger.FromContext. Nothing in this change tests that path: there is no test for the new middleware, and metrics_middleware_test.go only renames the metrics constructor. A mis-ordered middleware stack or a FromContext implementation that drops those attributes would ship without failing CI, which is how traceID was already dropped.

title: Device-limit denial is cached as success
body: tagDeviceUI writes the device key into the 29-minute local cache before CreateOrUpdateDevice returns. On ErrDeviceLimitReached the first call correctly fails, but the cache entry is left in place and the next TagDevice for that same X-Grafana-Device-Id hits the cache and returns nil. Authenticate treats nil as success, so anonymous access is granted and the device is never recorded. A client that retries once (or any later request within the TTL) bypasses the limit entirely. The cache is also not cleared on transient DB errors, so a failed write is treated as tagged and is not retried for 29 minutes. Set the cache only after a successful write, and do not treat a limit failure as a cache hit.

title: Device limit is enforced only if the client sends a device id
body: The new auth denial depends on TagDevice, which returns nil immediately when X-Grafana-Device-Id is missing, and Authenticate then issues an anonymous identity. The header is optional and client-controlled, so omitting it never consumes a slot and never hits ErrDeviceLimitReached. A caller can also mint device_limit distinct ids to fill the quota (locking out honest frontends that do send the header) and then drop the header to keep its own anonymous access. As written, the limit cannot cap anonymous access. Enforcement needs a server-issued identifier, or requests without a tracked device must be denied once the cap is reached.

title: Provider signature change will not compile with existing wire code
body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService no longer accepts anonstore.AnonStore and now requires db.DB, and ProvideAnonDBStore gained a deviceLimit parameter. This package is constructed by the committed Wire injector (pkg/server/wire_gen.go), which is not updated in this PR and still calls the old signatures. The server build fails until wire is regenerated. Any other in-repo or enterprise caller that passed an AnonStore is also broken, and tests can no longer inject a fake store.

title: Device limit check is not atomic with the insert
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts rows in one session, then inserts in another, with no transaction, row lock, or unique cap. Concurrent anonymous logins that all observe count < deviceLimit all take the INSERT path and the table (and thus anonymous access) exceeds the configured limit. This is the common case when many new devices arrive together at the cap. The count and the insert/update need to be serialized (single transaction with a lock, or an insert that rechecks the cap) so the limit cannot be overrun.

title: Device-limit failure is returned as an unclassified error
body: When the cap is hit, Authenticate returns the raw anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached sentinel (a plain fmt.Errorf). That is not an errutil or authn error, so the auth middleware treats it as an unexpected failure and typically responds with HTTP 500 rather than a controlled 401/403 and a user-facing device-limit message. It also shows up as a server error in logs. Return a typed unauthorized/forbidden auth error so the client chain and HTTP layer handle it as an access denial.

title: Limit tests miss the allow-existing path and auth enforcement
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only inserts a second, unknown device id against the store and expects ErrDeviceLimitReached. It never checks that a device already inside the 30-day window can still be updated once the cap is reached, and nothing covers TagDevice, the local cache, or Anonymous.Authenticate. Those are the paths that actually grant or deny access, so the cache-as-success bypass and the missing-header bypass are untested and would ship green.

title: device_limit is not added to default config
body: auth.anonymous.device_limit is read with MustInt64(0), but conf/defaults.ini (and the docs generated from it) are not updated. Operators have no documented default, comment, or sample for the new cap, and 0-means-unlimited exists only in the store's if deviceLimit > 0 check. Add the key to the [auth.anonymous] section in defaults.ini with that meaning spelled out.

title: Device-limit denial is cached, so anonymous auth fails open
body: tagDeviceUI writes the device id into the 29-minute local cache before CreateOrUpdateDevice returns. When the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached (new device while at the cap), that error is returned once, but the cache entry is left in place. The next TagDevice call for the same id hits the cache and returns nil, and Anonymous.Authenticate only denies access when that error is returned, so it issues an anonymous identity. The rejected device is never inserted, so the counted total never grows and every further new device id is denied at most once per process per TTL and then allowed. The configured device limit therefore does not actually stop anonymous access.

title: Device limit check and insert are not atomic
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts recent rows in one session, then inserts in a second session with no transaction, row lock, or advisory lock. Concurrent anonymous requests (including across Grafana replicas) can all observe a count below AnonymousDeviceLimit and all insert. A burst of new device ids can overshoot the cap by an arbitrary amount, and those extra rows then match updateDevice, so they stay authorized for the 30-day window. The limit is not enforced under the concurrent load it is meant to cap.

title: MySQL zero rows-changed is treated as device limit reached
body: updateDevice maps RowsAffected == 0 to ErrDeviceLimitReached. On MySQL (the driver default is rows-changed, not rows-matched) an UPDATE that matches an existing anon_device row but does not change client_ip, user_agent, or updated_at at second precision reports 0. Parallel requests for an already counted device, which this code now runs on the auth path once the cap is hit, can therefore get a false device-limit error and be denied even though the device is registered. Postgres/SQLite report matched rows, so the same path is DB-dependent.

title: Anonymous auth now blocks on device tagging even when unlimited
body: Tagging used to run in a background goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout and panic recovery, so a slow anon_device write could not stall login. It is now synchronous on every anonymous Authenticate, including the default device_limit of 0 where the result is only logged. Every cache miss waits on a database upsert (and, when the limit is enabled, a COUNT of anon_device) before an identity is returned. A slow or locked anon_device table delays all anonymous requests for as long as the request or DB query runs, with no separate timeout.

title: Wire constructors changed but generated wiring was not updated
body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now takes db.DB instead of anonstore.AnonStore, and ProvideAnonDBStore takes an extra deviceLimit int64. This repo builds from checked-in Wire output (pkg/server/wire_gen.go) that still calls the old signatures, and that file is not in the change. The server package will not compile. Wire also cannot inject a bare int64, so if ProvideAnonDBStore stays in the provider set, regeneration fails until it is removed from the set and only called with cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit as this function now does.

title: device_limit is undocumented and 0 means unlimited
body: auth.anonymous.device_limit is read with MustInt64(0), and any value <= 0 disables enforcement (unlimited devices). Nothing in this change adds the key to conf/defaults.ini or docs, so operators have no description of the setting, its unit, or that 0 does not mean "allow zero devices". There is also no configured value that means a hard cap of zero; anonymous access with no tagged devices still has to be turned off via enabled.

title: No test that the limit keeps denying auth
body: Service tests construct the anonymous service with setting.NewCfg(), so AnonymousDeviceLimit stays 0, and they only assert TagDevice succeeds. The new store test checks a second insert returns ErrDeviceLimitReached once. Nothing repeats TagDevice or Authenticate after that error, so the cache fail-open (denial on the first call, anonymous identity on the next) is untested and would merge green.

title: Device-limit denial is cached, so a retry is allowed
body: tagDeviceUI writes the device cache key (29-minute TTL) before CreateOrUpdateDevice returns. When the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, that error is now propagated and Anonymous.Authenticate denies the request, but the cache entry is left in place. The next TagDevice call for the same X-Grafana-Device-Id hits the cache, returns nil, and anonymous authentication succeeds even though the device was never stored. After one rejection per process, the configured limit is not enforced for the rest of the TTL; the new store test never calls TagDevice twice, so it does not catch this.

title: Omitting the device ID header skips the limit and still grants anonymous access
body: The new limit is enforced only inside TagDevice, and TagDevice returns nil immediately when X-Grafana-Device-Id is missing. Authenticate then still returns an anonymous identity with the configured org role. The header is client-supplied, so any caller can keep using anonymous auth after device_limit is exhausted by simply not sending it (or by rotating IDs until the cache bypass above applies). The cap does not actually bound anonymous access.

title: Device limit check and insert are not atomic
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts rows in one session, then inserts in another, with no transaction, row lock, or advisory lock. Concurrent anonymous requests (including across HA instances, which do not share the in-process cache) can all observe count < device_limit and all insert. Nothing in the schema caps the number of rows, so the overshoot sticks: active devices refresh updated_at about every 29 minutes and never fall out of the 30-day window used by the count. The limit can be permanently exceeded until those extra devices go idle for 30 days.

title: Anonymous auth now waits on device tagging even when the limit is off
body: Tagging used to run in a background goroutine with a detached 2-minute timeout and a panic recover, so it could not stall authentication. It is now a synchronous TagDevice call on the request context for every anonymous login, including the default device_limit of 0 (unlimited), which still does a database upsert on each cache miss. A slow or stuck database delays or ties up all anonymous requests until the DB call returns or the request is cancelled; a panic in tagging is no longer isolated from the request.

title: Provider signature change is not matched by Wire
body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now takes db.DB instead of anonstore.AnonStore, and ProvideAnonDBStore gained a deviceLimit parameter. Grafana constructs these via the committed Wire graph (pkg/server/wire.go / wire_gen.go), which is not updated in this PR. wire_gen.go still calls the old signatures, so the server package will not compile until Wire is regenerated and the generated file is included.

title: Limit test never covers auth, cache, or an existing device
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only asserts that a second new device ID is rejected by the store. It does not check that a device already inside the 30-day window can still be updated when count == device_limit, and nothing in impl_test or the auth client tests asserts that a second TagDevice/Authenticate after ErrDeviceLimitReached stays denied. Those are the paths that actually decide whether anonymous users are blocked, and both currently fail open.

title: Cleanup debug logs left at Error level and dump every ID
body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log every batch with r.log.Error, including the full ID slice, the SQL condition, and a nil err (same pattern at lines 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579). These run on the normal cleanup path, including the orphan-tag pass that always executes and the empty-batch case that happens when there is nothing to delete. Each scheduled cleanup will therefore emit error-level logs even when healthy, and when retention is configured a batch can be tens of thousands of IDs. That floods logs, inflates error metrics/alerts, and can stall or OOM the cleanup job while formatting the slice. These look like leftover diagnostics and should be removed or dropped to debug without the ID list.

title: Cleanup scheduler interval accidentally reduced from 10 minutes to 1
body: CleanUpService.Run now ticks every 1 minute instead of 10, and the PR does not mention this. clean() is synchronous and its context timeout is 9 minutes, so the old interval left a gap between runs. With a 1-minute ticker, any cleanup that lasts longer than a minute (the timeout allows up to 9) finds a tick already pending and starts the next pass immediately, so temporary-file, snapshot, dashboard-version, image, annotation, invite, short-URL, and query-history cleanup can run back-to-back. That is a large unintended load increase and is unrelated to the MySQL deadlock fix; restore the 10-minute interval.

title: SQLite ID list is built with quadratic string concatenation
body: When the database is SQLite and AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is above 999, deleteByIDs inlines every ID by repeatedly doing values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v). That copies the whole growing string on each ID. The new path is specifically for large batches (the test uses 32767, and the setting can be set higher), so one DELETE builds O(n^2) bytes of temporary strings — several seconds and heavy GC at 32k IDs, and much worse if the batch size is raised further. Build the list with strings.Builder (or strings.Join of preformatted IDs) instead.

title: Cleanup schedule accidentally changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: Run now starts the background cleanup ticker at 1 minute instead of 10. This is unrelated to the annotation deadlock fix and is not mentioned in the PR. clean() still applies a 9-minute timeout, which was chosen so a cycle finishes before the next 10-minute tick. time.Ticker buffers one tick, and clean() is synchronous, so if any job (annotation cleanup of a large table, snapshot expiry, query-history enforcement, etc.) runs longer than a minute, the buffered tick fires as soon as it returns and cleanup runs back-to-back. That multiplies database load, can hold the cleanup server lock almost continuously, and increases the chance of the annotation insert/cleanup contention this PR is trying to reduce. Restore the 10-minute interval.

title: Leftover Error logs fire on every cleanup batch, including idle runs
body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log at Error after every ID fetch and every delete (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579), including when the batch is empty and err is nil. The messages are not failures; they dump the SQL condition and the entire ID slice. Annotation cleanup runs on the periodic cleanup job, so a healthy idle instance emits multiple error-level lines per cycle (age cleanup, count cleanup, and orphan-tag cleanup). Operators who alert on error logs will treat normal retention as an incident, and a large batch (the new test uses 32767 IDs) will format tens of thousands of IDs into each line, spiking memory and log volume. Remove these statements, or drop them to debug and do not log the ID list.

title: Max-count cleanup can delete annotations that should be retained
body: The max-count path selects excess IDs with ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT batch OFFSET MaxCount in one session, then deletes those IDs in a later session. Those IDs are excess only relative to rows present at SELECT time. If newer annotations (the ones inside the keep window) are deleted by a user or API between fetchIDs and deleteByIDs, some already-selected IDs now fall inside MaxCount but are still deleted. The previous single-statement DELETE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT ... OFFSET MaxCount) evaluated the window and the delete atomically, so this could not happen. The comment only accepts under-deletion from concurrent inserts; this race over-deletes, and the next cycle will not recreate the rows. With a large batch size, one interleaving can drop retention by up to that batch below MaxCount.

title: Batched ID deletes are not bounded to engine parameter limits
body: deleteByIDs issues one statement with one placeholder per ID, except when the DB is SQLite and AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is greater than 999, in which case IDs are interpolated. The old cleanup was a DELETE with a LIMIT subquery, so statement size did not grow with the batch. PostgreSQL rejects more than 65535 parameters, and other engines fail or truncate once the packet size is exceeded. Batch size is an operator setting (the new test uses 32767) and nothing chunks len(ids) to a safe bound. If the configured batch is above the engine limit and at least that many rows match, the DELETE fails every cycle after the SELECT succeeds, untilDoneOrCancelled returns the error, and that batch is never removed. The SQLite branch also keys off the configured batch size rather than len(ids), and 999 is the pre-3.32 SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER (default is 32766 since 3.32), so it does not match the limit the new test name refers to.

title: SQLite IN-list is built with quadratic string copies
body: On the SQLite inline path, deleteByIDs builds the ID list by fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) in a loop, copying the whole string on every ID. That path is taken whenever AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is above 999, which is exactly the case the new 32767-ID test exercises and the workaround operators would use to get large batches on SQLite. For n IDs the copies are O(n^2): about 32k IDs is on the order of gigabytes of temporary allocations and can stall the cleanup goroutine for seconds. Build the list with strings.Builder (or chunk the delete) so large batches do not spike memory.

title: Cleanup success path logs full ID lists at error level
body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags call r.log.Error on every batch, including when the fetch returns no rows and err is nil (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579). Each call dumps the entire ID slice and the SQL condition. These run before the empty-batch stop, so every cleanup cycle emits error logs even when nothing is deleted, and a large backlog emits two error lines per batch with tens of thousands of IDs. That floods logs, looks like a failing job to anything alerting on error level, and can stall the cleaner on log serialization. These look like leftover diagnostics and should be removed, or reduced to debug without the ID list.

title: Global cleanup interval accidentally cut from 10 minutes to 1
body: Run now uses time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1) instead of 10 minutes. This is unrelated to the annotation deadlock fix and is not described in the PR. It schedules every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history) ten times as often. clean() is synchronous with a 9-minute timeout chosen for the old 10-minute cadence; if a pass takes longer than a minute the ticker's buffered tick starts the next pass immediately, so a busy instance can run cleanup continuously and multiply DB load. Restore the 10-minute interval unless a faster schedule is an intentional, documented change.

title: SQLite ID list is built with quadratic string concatenation
body: When the DB is SQLite and AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize exceeds 999, deleteByIDs inlines every ID with values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) in a loop. Each step copies the whole string, so a batch of N IDs copies O(N^2) bytes. The new test uses batch size 32767, which is on this path and copies on the order of gigabytes of temporary strings, adding multi-second latency and GC pressure exactly when the batch is large. Build the IN list with strings.Builder (or chunks) instead.

title: Async legacy writes are cancelled with the request
body: Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection start the legacy write in a goroutine whose context is derived from the incoming request context via context.WithTimeoutCause (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163). When the apiserver handler returns, that parent context is cancelled, which cancels the child immediately. The 10s timeout never applies, and Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection observe context.Canceled instead of finishing. Mode 3's legacy copy therefore does not land on the success path, so a rollback to legacy storage loses or stale-reads every write that was acknowledged from unified storage.

title: Per-object legacy writes are unordered
body: Each successful Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection fires an independent goroutine with no per-key queue, lock, or generation check. The handler returns as soon as unified storage succeeds, so a later delete (or newer update) can be applied to legacy before the earlier create/update. Legacy can then contain a resurrected object or an older spec while unified storage, which mode 3 reads, has the new state. Rollback or any legacy reader then serves data the API already deleted or overwrote. The closure also shares the request object with the caller; if Storage.Create returns that same pointer, the caller's continued use races with Legacy.Create.

title: Legacy update no longer persists the unified result
body: Update now passes the original objInfo into Legacy.Update after Storage.Update returns. The previous implementation computed the object once from unified storage and wrote that exact result to legacy through updateWrapper. In mode 3 the client resourceVersion comes from unified storage, so legacy GuaranteedUpdate's optimistic check fails with a conflict once the two backends' resource versions differ, and the safety copy is dropped. Even if legacy ignores resourceVersion, UpdatedObject runs against legacy's own old object and can persist a different spec. objInfo is also not guaranteed to be reusable after the first Update, so the async second call can fail or write a mutated object.

title: NotFound on unified delete skips legacy cleanup
body: Delete returns on any Storage.Delete error, including NotFound, and never starts the legacy delete. The previous mode 3 delete still removed the object from legacy when unified storage returned NotFound. During migration, legacy can still hold objects that unified storage does not. Those deletes now fail to the client and leave the legacy row in place, so a fallback to legacy resurrects objects the API reported as gone.

title: Successful delete records the object name as the kind label
body: On a successful Storage.Delete, recordStorageDuration is called with the object name as the third argument. Every other call in this file passes options.Kind. If that argument is a Prometheus label, every distinct deleted name becomes a new series. That grows without bound for the process registry and any scraper, and the delete latency/error series can no longer be aggregated by kind.

title: Storage and legacy durations are recorded on the wrong series
body: When Storage.Create fails, line 45 calls recordLegacyDuration for a unified-storage failure, and Update does the same at line 129 with recordLegacyDuration. DeleteCollection's async legacy call at line 166 calls recordStorageDuration, so the legacy outcome is counted as another storage observation and legacy delete-collection latency is never recorded. Alerts and dashboards for mode 3 will attribute unified-storage failures to legacy and hide real legacy delete-collection failures.

title: Legacy write failures are not logged
body: The async Legacy.Create, Legacy.Update, Legacy.Delete, and Legacy.DeleteCollection calls only feed a boolean into the duration metric. The previous synchronous path logged the legacy error with the object identity. A timeout, conflict, or context cancellation now leaves unified storage and legacy diverged with no log line, so the safety copy can fail indefinitely without an operator-visible signal.

title: Destroy does not wait for in-flight legacy writes
body: Destroy closes Storage and Legacy immediately, but Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection do not track their goroutines. Shutdown can destroy legacy storage while a goroutine is still inside Legacy.Create/Update/Delete, which races with teardown and drops the safety copy for writes that were already acknowledged. There is no WaitGroup or drain anywhere in DualWriterMode3.

title: Mode 3 tests never wait for or assert the legacy write
body: Success-path tests install legacy On expectations (Create around line 31, Update around line 313) but return as soon as the synchronous unified call finishes, and they never call AssertExpectations or wait for the goroutine. testify will not fail if the legacy call is skipped, and the goroutine can invoke the mock after the test has finished. Both stores also share one mock.Mock, so a single Create/Update expectation cannot prove which backend ran.
