The new cases in pkg/tests/apis/playlist/playlist_test.go (file mode 3 at line 132, unified mode 3 at line 191) call doPlaylistTests, which immediately lists and gets the legacy playlist API after a k8s write. Those checks assume the legacy write is synchronous; with this mode 3 they race, and they fail outright if the request context cancels the legacy write.

title: Async legacy writes are canceled with the request
body: Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection start the legacy write in a goroutine whose context is context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s) derived from the incoming request context. WithTimeoutCause is canceled as soon as the parent is canceled, which the apiserver does as soon as the handler returns—immediately after this goroutine is spawned. The 10s timeout therefore never applies, and the legacy write is aborted with context.Canceled on almost every request. Mode 3's rollback/safety copy to legacy does not actually persist, so a later read from legacy or a rollback from unified storage drops creates, updates, and deletes that clients were already told succeeded. Derive the background work from context.WithoutCancel (or Background plus copied values) and then apply the timeout. The same pattern is at the Delete (line 110), Update (line 135), and DeleteCollection (line 163) goroutines.

title: Legacy update re-applies the request instead of the unified result
body: Update used to materialize one updated object from unified storage and pass that exact object to both stores (via updateWrapper). It now calls Legacy.Update with the original objInfo after Storage.Update returns. Legacy storage will Get its own copy and run UpdatedObject/Preconditions again. In mode 3, clients read resourceVersion from unified storage, so those preconditions do not match legacy's resourceVersion and the legacy update fails with a conflict (or, if preconditions are absent, applies the transform to a divergent legacy object). Patch goes through this same Update path. The legacy "safe measure" copy therefore does not match what was committed to unified storage. Write the object returned by Storage.Update (and clear legacy resourceVersion preconditions) rather than re-running objInfo.

title: Async legacy Create races on the caller's object
body: After Storage.Create returns, the goroutine calls Legacy.Create with the same obj pointer the caller still holds. Storage implementations commonly mutate that object in place and return it as created, and the apiserver then encodes created while Legacy.Create is still mutating resourceVersion, UID, timestamps, or unstructured maps. That is a data race: responses can be corrupted or the process can panic, and the legacy row can be written from a half-updated object. Deep-copy the object (and any options the legacy call mutates) before handing it to the goroutine. The same sharing applies to objInfo on the async Update path (line 139), which is not safe to use again after Storage.Update has consumed it.

title: Storage failures and legacy latency are recorded on the wrong metric
body: On Storage.Create failure the code calls recordLegacyDuration (line 45) with the storage start time, and on Storage.Update failure it does the same (line 129). Those paths never touched legacy, so unified-storage errors disappear from the storage metric and show up as legacy failures. DeleteCollection's async legacy call then does the opposite: line 166 calls recordStorageDuration for Legacy.DeleteCollection, so legacy delete-collection latency and errors inflate the storage series and never appear on the legacy series. Success paths for Create/Update correctly use recordStorageDuration, which shows these error-path calls are swapped. Dashboards and alerts for mode 3 will page on the wrong store and hide the safety-write failures.

title: Successful Delete records the object name as the kind label
body: The success path of Delete calls recordStorageDuration with name (the object name) as the kind label, while the error path on line 103 and every other method pass options.Kind. Every distinct deleted name becomes a new Prometheus label value. That blows up cardinality on the storage-duration metric and makes delete latency unusable for dashboards. Pass options.Kind, consistent with the error path.

title: Legacy write errors are dropped with no log
body: The previous synchronous implementation logged legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection failures. The goroutines now only feed a duration metric and discard errObjectSt (Create line 56, Update line 140, Delete line 113, DeleteCollection line 166). Combined with the mis-attributed metrics, a legacy timeout, conflict, or outage leaves unified storage and legacy permanently diverged with nothing in the logs identifying the object or the error. Log the legacy error (with name/kind) before recording the metric. Also, Delete puts d.Log into the context on line 97 instead of the enriched log, so even storage-side logs for that method lack name, kind, and method.

title: Destroy does not wait for in-flight legacy writes
body: Destroy closes Storage and Legacy immediately, but Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection fire unbounded goroutines that can still be inside Legacy.* for up to 10 seconds. Shutdown therefore either drops the safety write or calls into a store that has already been destroyed (use-after-close, errors, or panics). There is also no limit on how many of these goroutines can pile up under write load. Track in-flight legacy work and wait for it in Destroy (or cancel it explicitly), and bound concurrency.

title: Mode 3 unit tests do not match async dual-write behavior
body: The Create failure case only stubs Legacy.Create and never stubs Storage.Create, but mode 3 fails the request only when unified storage fails, so this case does not exercise the error path (and, with an unconfigured mock returning a nil error, assert.Error fails). Success cases stub legacy but return as soon as Storage.* returns, with no wait and no AssertExpectations, so they pass even if the legacy goroutine never runs. The goroutine can also call the shared testify mock after t.Run returns, which races and can panic. None of the tests cover legacy failure, timeout, or the requirement that legacy receives the object unified storage actually stored. Synchronize the goroutine (or inject a synchronous hook) and assert both stores.

title: Mode 3 playlist tests assume legacy is updated synchronously
body: The new file/unified/etcd mode 3 subtests call doPlaylistTests, whose k8s CRUD case immediately lists and gets the same playlists through the legacy /api/playlists endpoints (and getFromBothAPIs does the same after update and delete). Mode 3 returns as soon as unified storage succeeds and only then writes legacy in a goroutine that is also tied to the request context. Those assertions will fail or flake whenever the legacy copy has not landed yet, and they will fail consistently if the request context cancels the legacy write. The new mode 3 cases need to wait until the legacy copy is visible, or the test will not actually prove the safety write.

title: Async legacy writes are cancelled with the request
body: Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection start the legacy write in a goroutine whose context is derived from the incoming request context via context.WithTimeoutCause (Create line 51, Update line 135, Delete line 110, DeleteCollection line 163). When the handler returns, the apiserver cancels that request context, which cancels the child immediately. The 10s timeout never extends past the parent, so the legacy "safety" write is aborted (or races the cancel) instead of running to completion. Mode 3 will report success for unified storage while the legacy copy is systematically dropped, and a later rollback to legacy will be missing creates, updates, and deletes.

title: Async legacy Create races on the caller's object
body: After Storage.Create returns, the handler encodes the returned object while a goroutine calls Legacy.Create on the same obj pointer (line 55) with no deep copy. Storage and legacy implementations mutate metadata in place (resourceVersion, UID, timestamps). That is a data race with response serialization and can tear or overwrite the object returned to the client. Previously the legacy create finished before Create returned, so this race did not exist. Copy the object (and do not share it with the caller) before the goroutine.

title: Legacy Update reapplies objInfo instead of the stored result
body: Update now passes the original objInfo into asynchronous Legacy.Update (line 139). The previous implementation snapshotted the object already written to unified storage and passed an updateWrapper so legacy stored that same object. UpdatedObjectInfo is not guaranteed to be reusable or to return an independent object: a second UpdatedObject call can conflict because the request resourceVersion is the unified-storage version, not the legacy one, can apply a patch to a different base and diverge, or can return the same pointer the API response is still encoding while legacy mutates it. Legacy will not reliably receive the write that unified storage just acknowledged.

title: Storage failures and legacy writes recorded on the wrong metric
body: On Storage.Create failure the code calls recordLegacyDuration (line 45) with the storage start time, and Update does the same at line 129. Those paths never called legacy, so legacy failure rate is inflated and the unified-storage failure is invisible to the storage metric. DeleteCollection's async legacy path does the opposite: line 166 calls recordStorageDuration for the legacy DeleteCollection result, so legacy errors are counted as storage errors and legacy latency is not recorded. Alerts and dashboards for mode 3 will point at the wrong store.

title: Successful Delete uses object name as the metric kind label
body: The success path of Delete calls recordStorageDuration with name (the object name) as the kind argument (line 106). Every other call, including the error path two lines above, passes options.Kind. Object names are unbounded, so each deleted object creates a new Prometheus series on that label and the process (and any scraper) will grow memory without bound under normal delete traffic.

title: Legacy write failures are no longer logged
body: The async legacy Create (line 56), Update (line 140), Delete (line 113), and DeleteCollection (line 165) ignore the error except for a duration metric. The previous synchronous implementation logged these failures. Combined with the mis-labeled metrics, a legacy timeout, conflict, or outage leaves the two stores diverged with no log line an operator can alert on. The request still returns success, which is intended, but the safety write's failure must be logged.

title: Destroy does not wait for in-flight legacy writes
body: Each successful write spawns an unbounded goroutine that may block on legacy storage for up to 10s, and nothing tracks those goroutines. Destroy (line 172) immediately calls Legacy.Destroy() and Storage.Destroy(). On shutdown or storage teardown, in-flight legacy creates/updates/deletes run against a closed store (panic or error) or are dropped when the process exits, so the safety copy is lost exactly when it is needed for rollback.

title: Delete puts the unscoped logger into the context
body: Delete builds log with name, kind, and method, then calls klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) instead of klog.NewContext(ctx, log). Storage.Delete and the async Legacy.Delete therefore do not see those fields, unlike Create, Update, and DeleteCollection, which install the enriched logger. Delete failures will be missing the object identity in contextual logs.

title: Tests never wait for or assert the async legacy write
body: Mode 3 unit tests return as soon as the synchronous storage call finishes (Create at line 65, and the same pattern in Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection). They never wait for the goroutine, never AssertExpectations, and would still pass if the legacy write were removed. The success-path mocks are also invoked from a goroutine after the test can return, which races testify's mock. The new playlist integration cases (pkg/tests/apis/playlist/playlist_test.go line 132 and the unified-storage mode 3 case) call doPlaylistTests, which immediately compares the legacy HTTP API (line 529 and getFromBothAPIs) with k8s results. That assumed synchronous dual-write; under mode 3 it will flake or fail when the legacy copy has not landed yet.

title: Write lock does not re-check cache and can clobber a good value
body: GetWebAssets drops the read lock and later takes the write lock without reading entryPointAssetsCache again. Every caller that observed a nil cache (or is running in Dev) therefore reloads the manifest while holding the global mutex, then unconditionally assigns entryPointAssetsCache = result. On a cold start, N concurrent calls all pass the nil check, queue on the write lock, and each performs a full file read; a later caller whose read fails stores nil and wipes the successful cache published by an earlier caller, so subsequent non-Dev requests miss and can return an error even though a valid asset set was already loaded. Re-check the cache after acquiring the write lock (and do not overwrite a non-nil cache with a failed load). The exclusive lock is also held across the manifest read, so those redundant loads are fully serialized.

title: Write lock does not recheck cache and is held across asset I/O
body: GetWebAssets snapshots entryPointAssetsCache under RLock, drops the lock, then later takes the write lock and always reloads and assigns the global. It never re-reads the cache after Lock, so every caller that observed a nil cache (all of them at startup, and every call when cfg.Env == Dev) reloads assets-manifest.json while holding the exclusive lock. A later waiter whose load fails stores that nil result into entryPointAssetsCache and wipes a value another goroutine already published, so a successful load can be discarded and the next requests miss again. Because the exclusive lock spans the file read (and the CDN HTTP path if enabled), those redundant loads are fully serialized and also block cache hits that arrive while a load is in progress. After acquiring the write lock, return the existing cache when Env is not Dev and it is already set; only publish a non-nil successful result; and do not hold the mutex across the file or HTTP read.

title: Write lock held across manifest load and can clear a filled cache
body: GetWebAssets copies entryPointAssetsCache under a read lock, drops that lock, then at line 48 takes the exclusive lock and holds it for the whole readWebAssetsFromFile call (line 60). It never re-reads the cache after acquiring the write lock, and line 69 always stores result, including nil. Callers that all observed a nil cache therefore each load the manifest while holding the process-wide mutex, so a startup burst does N sequential disk reads and blocks every other GetWebAssets for that I/O. In Dev the fast path is skipped on purpose, so every call takes this exclusive section and asset loads are globally serialized on disk I/O. A waiter whose load fails after another caller already published a value replaces that cache with nil, so later non-dev requests miss and reload. Load outside the lock; under the lock, return the existing cache when not in Dev and it is already set, and do not store a nil result over a populated cache.

title: No concurrent test for the cache race fix
body: This change only wraps the global entryPointAssetsCache in a mutex inside GetWebAssets and adds no test. Nothing runs concurrent GetWebAssets calls under the race detector, or checks that a successful fill is reused by waiters and is not cleared by a concurrent failed load. The data race this PR is fixing can come back with no regression coverage.

title: Live SQL path still interpolates user SQL into a DuckDB statement
body: TablesList still escape-doubles single quotes only and builds SELECT json_serialize_sql('<user SQL>'), then passes that string to RunCommands. NewSQLCommand calls TablesList for every SQL expression, and SQLCommand.Execute still forwards the raw query to QueryFramesInto. The new enableSqlExpressions check in ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery does not cover that path; the reader comment says it has not replaced the existing expression pipeline in transform.go. RunCommands and QueryFramesInto currently return "not implemented", so DuckDB is not invoked and this is not an active RCE. The CVE sink is still on the request path: quote-doubling does not make that statement safe, and any change that makes those methods succeed, or a caller that ignores the TablesList error and still executes, runs attacker-controlled SQL with no feature-flag gate. Reject in NewSQLCommand and Execute before formatting or dispatching SQL, and remove the json_serialize_sql interpolation.

title: SQL disable helper inverts the feature flag and always returns false
body: enableSqlExpressions sets enabled to the negation of FlagSqlExpressions, then returns false whether that value is true or false, so the flag read does nothing. ReadQuery treats false as a hard error, so this reader disables SQL only because both branches hardcode false. The negation is the opposite of a normal allow-check, and nothing names CVE-2024-9264. The obvious edit to make the flag check meaningful (return true when the flag is on) would build SQL commands again on any instance with the still-documented sqlExpressions flag enabled. Make the disable unconditional and independent of the feature flag.

title: Disabled SQL expressions are reported as unimplemented or invalid SQL
body: When SQL expressions are refused, ReadQuery returns "sqlExpressions is not implemented". That is wrong: the feature existed and is being turned off for CVE-2024-9264, not left unimplemented. On the expression command path, NewSQLCommand still returns the public BadRequest "error reading SQL command" (sql-invalid-sql in pkg/expr/sql_command.go) for every SQL expression, because TablesList now always fails. Users and support will treat a security disable as a syntax error in their query. Return one stable message that SQL expressions are disabled.

title: No regression test that SQL expressions are rejected and not executed
body: This change is the CVE-2024-9264 fix (DuckDB removed, SQL expressions disabled) but it adds or updates no tests. Nothing asserts that a SQL expression fails closed on the production command path, that user SQL is not handed to an engine, or that turning on FlagSqlExpressions cannot restore execution. The mitigation is a stub whose methods return "not implemented"; restoring a real RunCommands/QueryFramesInto, or skipping the TablesList error and still calling Execute, would not fail CI. Add a test that builds a SQL expression through NewSQLCommand/Execute and expects a disable error without running the statement.

title: Security disable is reported as "not implemented"
body: ReadQuery rejects every SQL expression with fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented"). That message is false: SQL expressions were implemented and are being turned off because of CVE-2024-9264. enableSqlExpressions (line 194) also reads FlagSqlExpressions with inverted polarity and then returns false on both branches, so enabling the documented feature flag does not change the result and is not mentioned in the error. Clients and operators will treat a security kill-switch as a missing feature or a malformed query, and anyone following the feature-flag docs will not be able to tell why SQL expressions stopped working. Return a stable error that states SQL expressions are disabled for security, and do not consult the flag unless it can actually enable a safe path.

title: Legacy SQL path fails as bad SQL and logs every query
body: The pipeline that still builds commands through UnmarshalSQLCommand does not use the new reader kill-switch. NewSQLCommand always calls sql.TablesList, which now always errors because the stub DB refuses RunCommands. That expected failure is logged at Warn with the full user SQL (line 32) and again at Error in pkg/expr/sql/parser.go:28 (including the constructed statement), then returned as BadRequest with public message "error reading SQL command" (line 34). Alert evaluations and panel refreshes that still contain a SQL expression will therefore emit error-level logs of the raw query on every tick and show a message that blames the SQL text. That hides the security disable, floods logs, and can copy sensitive literals from expressions into error logs. Reject in NewSQLCommand/Execute with an explicit disabled error before TablesList, and do not log the query at Error for this intentional failure.

title: User SQL is still interpolated into a DuckDB statement
body: TablesList still quote-doubles apostrophes and builds SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s') from the raw user query, then passes that string to RunCommands. Apostrophe doubling is not a safe DuckDB string sanitizer (other quote forms and escapes can break out). This is the same sink class as CVE-2024-9264, and it is reached from UnmarshalSQLCommand, which never calls enableSqlExpressions. The reader comment says ExpressionQueryReader has not replaced the existing Query path in transform.go, so the historical request path is this one. Execution is stopped only because pkg/expr/sql/db.go RunCommands and QueryFramesInto return "not implemented"; Execute in sql_command.go:100 still forwards the raw user query into QueryFramesInto. Filling in those stubs, or any caller that ignores the error, reactivates injection and RCE without passing the reader gate. Delete the statement construction and fail closed before any command string is built.

title: No regression test that SQL expressions cannot execute
body: This is the in-tree fix for critical CVE-2024-9264 (DuckDB SQL expressions allowing remote code execution and local file read), but no test was added or updated. Nothing asserts that a SQL expression is rejected, that FlagSqlExpressions cannot turn it back on, or that a file-read or command-execution statement passed through NewSQLCommand, TablesList, or Execute does not succeed. Disablement is split between an always-false helper and stub methods whose errors say "not implemented", so a later cleanup can restore execution without a failing test. Add a unit test that malicious SQL is rejected and that RunCommands/QueryFramesInto cannot execute it.

title: Live SQL path still builds DuckDB commands and reports invalid SQL
body: Dashboard and alerting server-side expressions still enter through UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand, not ExpressionQueryReader. NewSQLCommand always calls sql.TablesList, which interpolates the user query into SELECT json_serialize_sql('...') and calls RunCommands. That now fails only because the new DB stub returns an error, and the failure is turned into BadRequest sql-invalid-sql with public text "error reading SQL command". Callers are told the SQL is invalid rather than that SQL expressions were disabled, and TablesList logs the raw query and the constructed command at error level on every attempt. The RCE/LFI closure on this path is entirely the stub; the old injection string is still built for every SQL expression. Reject in NewSQLCommand before TablesList, with an explicit disabled error, and do not assemble or log a DuckDB command.

title: Disabled SQL expressions are reported as not implemented
body: When QueryTypeSQL is read, the new gate always fails and returns "sqlExpressions is not implemented". The feature was implemented and is being turned off because of CVE-2024-9264; the feature flag is still present and documented as the switch for it. Clients and support will treat this as an unfinished feature rather than a security disable, and the message does not match the legacy path's "error reading SQL command" either.

title: No regression test that SQL expressions cannot run
body: This change is the in-repo fix for a critical RCE/LFI bug, but it adds no test that UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand reject SQL expressions, that ExpressionQueryReader rejects QueryTypeSQL even when FlagSqlExpressions is on, or that RunCommands/QueryFramesInto do not execute caller SQL. The only verification cited is manual. A later edit that fills in the DB stub or "fixes" enableSqlExpressions can re-open execution with nothing in CI failing.

title: BuildIndex no longer single-flights per key
body: BuildIndex used to hold cacheMu for the whole build, which also blocked GetIndex and serialized builders. The lock is now taken only to publish b.cache[key]. getOrCreateIndex is still check-then-act (GetIndex, and on nil call build/BuildIndex) and has no per-key lock or singleflight. Concurrent first searches, watch events, or init workers for the same NamespacedResource therefore build two bleve indexes. The later cache write blindly overwrites the earlier one, so one caller keeps writing and searching an index that is no longer in the cache while everyone else uses the other. The discarded index is never closed (memory and file-handle leak). For file indexes both builders use the same directory, so the second bleve.New fails and that caller gets an error even if the first build succeeded.

title: File indexes cannot be reopened, so eager init crash-loops
body: When size exceeds FileThreshold, BuildIndex always calls bleve.New on a stable path (Root/namespace/resource.group) and never bleve.Open. bleve.New fails if that directory already exists. A successful build, a killed process, or a failed init that already created the directory leaves the path on disk. Init now runs inside NewResourceServer and any BuildIndex error aborts server construction, so the next start hits the same bleve.New error and the process cannot boot until the directory is deleted by hand. The removed log was the only hint that an existing index/RV should be reused; the TODO remains unimplemented.

title: Index init workers race on shared err
body: searchSupport.init starts initWorkers goroutines that all do `_, _, err = s.build(...)` and `return err`, plus `totalBatchesIndexed++`, on variables owned by the outer function with no mutex or atomic. That is a data race. One worker can return another worker's nil and hide a failed namespace build, so startup continues after an index failed (the opposite of the comment that any init failure must block startup), or a success can be overwritten and fail startup incorrectly. The span attribute namespaced_indexed is also racy. This function is now on the blocking startup path.

title: Postgres storage-server startup test is skipped
body: TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer is the integration coverage for the storage-server target coming up and serving /metrics. This change makes NewResourceServer run unified-storage Init (stats, index build, watch) during that startup, which this test previously never reached because it never issued a storage RPC. The PR skips the test on postgres with a TODO that it fails in Drone, so the CI job that would catch a postgres-specific eager-init failure no longer runs it.

title: BuildIndex no longer single-flights a key, so concurrent builds race
body: BuildIndex used to hold cacheMu for the entire build, so GetIndex blocked until that key was published and a second caller reused the same index. The lock is now taken only to assign b.cache[key] after the build. getOrCreateIndex still does an unlocked check-then-build (GetIndex, then build if nil), and init can also call BuildIndex concurrently. Two callers for the same NamespacedResource therefore both miss the cache and both build. For file indexes both call bleve.New on the same directory (one fails or they corrupt the path); for memory indexes both succeed and the later write silently replaces b.cache[key] without closing the first index. The discarded index never receives watch updates, while the caller that kept the other pointer searches a divergent copy. Cache publication also does not check whether an entry already exists, and TotalDocs ranges b.cache with no lock, so a concurrent insert is a concurrent map read/write that can panic.

title: File index rebuild uses bleve.New and will fail every subsequent startup
body: When size exceeds FileThreshold, BuildIndex always calls bleve.New on a stable directory under Root (namespace/resource.group). bleve.New creates a new index and returns an error if that path already exists; there is no bleve.Open fallback, and neither the error paths nor shutdown delete or close the directory. A successful on-disk build therefore leaves a directory that makes the next BuildIndex fail. Init now runs inside NewResourceServer and any error aborts server construction, so the second process start cannot bring unified storage up until that directory is removed by hand. A failed or crashed build poisons the same path the same way. The removed log even noted that the last resource version is not checked before recreating the index.

title: Startup index workers share err and can swallow build failures
body: init launches one goroutine per namespace via errgroup and each one does `_, _, err = s.build(...)` then `return err`, where err is the single variable from GetResourceStats, not a per-goroutine local. Those goroutines write and read err concurrently (data race). One worker can overwrite another's error with nil between the assignment and the return, so group.Wait can return nil even though a build failed. Init is now mandatory in NewResourceServer and a swallowed error lets the process start with a partial search index and no retry (server.Init is sync.Once). totalBatchesIndexed++ in the same closure is also an unsynchronized counter, so the "namespaces indexed" span attribute is wrong under the same workers.

title: Search watch loop panics or spins after the event channel closes
body: After indexing, init always starts `for { v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v) }` on context.Background(), ignoring the server cancel context. SQL WatchWriteEvents' poller closes that channel when the backend is stopped (backend.Stop cancels b.done, poller defers close(stream)). A receive on a closed channel yields a nil *WrittenEvent, and handleEvent immediately reads evt.Type, which panics and crashes the process during shutdown. Even with a nil check the loop never exits, so it would busy-spin. This goroutine is now started for every search-enabled server at construction, not only after the first RPC, and nothing in Stop waits for it or stops it.

title: Postgres storage-server integration test is skipped instead of fixed
body: TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer is the integration coverage for bringing up the storage-server target, which now builds the unified-storage index inside InitializeModuleServer / NewResourceServer. This change skips the test entirely when GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres, with a TODO that it fails in Drone. CI no longer exercises eager init, DB stats, or index build against Postgres, so a Postgres-only startup failure caused by moving Init out of the RPC path will not be caught.

title: BuildIndex no longer excludes concurrent builds of the same key
body: BuildIndex used to hold cacheMu for the whole build, which serialized bleve.New and cache publication. The lock is now taken only to publish b.cache[key] at the end, and nothing single-flights a key. getOrCreateIndex still does GetIndex then build with no per-key lock, so two searches or watch events for a missing namespace (indexes below InitMinCount, or any key created after startup) both pass the cache miss and call BuildIndex together. For file indexes both call bleve.New on the same directory and race the index files; for memory indexes both succeed. The slower build then overwrites b.cache[key], so the cached index can be the staler one, the other index is leaked and never closed, and callers that already received the losing index keep searching a copy that will not receive later watch updates.

title: Parallel index init races on shared err and counter
body: init now actually builds many namespaces at once (errgroup plus the BuildIndex lock removal). Every worker does totalBatchesIndexed++ and err = s.build(...) on the same outer variables with no mutex or atomic. That is a data race: a failed build can return another worker's nil error, so group.Wait can succeed and the process starts with a missing index, or a successful worker can return another worker's error and fail startup. The namespaced_indexed span attribute is also racy and can be wrong. Each worker needs its own err variable, and the counter must be atomic or updated after Wait.

title: Startup index watch cursor skips writes made during the build
body: build returns the resource version of the list snapshot and documents that watchers must apply every event after that RV, but init discards both return values and only then calls WatchWriteEvents. That helper records the latest RV at call time and the SQL poller emits only history rows after that cursor. With a long startup build — the path this PR moved onto process start — and with namespaces built in parallel, an index finished early misses every write committed after its list and before the slowest build finishes. Those writes are never replayed, so the search index stays permanently stale. The watch must start from each build's returned RV (or from the RV captured before listing), not from a single cursor taken after all builds.

title: Search watch goroutine panics when the event channel closes
body: After index build, init starts a goroutine that does v := <-events and always calls handleEvent. watchctx is context.Background(), not the server's cancellable context, so server.Stop cannot stop it. SQL WatchWriteEvents closes the channel when the backend stops, and server.Stop calls lifecycle.Stop (the SQL backend implements LifecycleHooks) before cancelling the server context. A closed channel yields a nil event; handleEvent immediately reads evt.Type and panics, crashing the process. Because Init now always runs from NewResourceServer, every storage-server shutdown hits this. The loop must exit on !ok and must use the server context. The same unbounded read exists in initWatcher.

title: Failed constructor Init leaks watchers and never cancels its context
body: NewResourceServer calls s.Init and, on error, returns nil without s.cancel() or Stop. Init can already have run lifecycle.Init (opening the DB) and search.init, which starts the background WatchWriteEvents poller and the handleEvent goroutine, before a later step such as initWatcher fails. Callers only receive the error, so they have no server handle to Stop, the cancellable context is abandoned, and those goroutines run until process exit. On the search-watch path a later backend stop then panics, as described above. The error path needs to cancel and stop anything Init already started before returning.

title: Server watch now starts only after the full index build
body: Init used to call initWatcher before search.init. It now builds every search index first and only then starts the server broadcaster's WatchWriteEvents. That poller does not replay history; it starts at whatever the latest RV is when it is called. Writes committed during the startup index build (other HA replicas; WatchWriteEvents is documented to observe remote writes) are therefore never pushed to the broadcaster. A client that reconnects with Since set to the last RV it saw misses those events. Previously the broadcaster poller was already running for the whole index build, so those events were captured. Start the server watcher before the long index build, or replay from the RV observed before the build.

title: Postgres storage-server integration test is skipped instead of fixed
body: TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer is the integration test that constructs and runs the storage-server target. This PR makes NewResourceServer block on full unified-storage Init (DB plus index build) during that construction, then skips the test whenever GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres, with a TODO that it fails in Drone and works locally. CI no longer exercises storage-server startup on postgres, so a postgres-specific failure in the new eager Init path — the behavior this PR adds — will not fail the build.

title: No-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() does not exist
body: UsernameForm.authenticate() now calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments, but the only method added on UsernamePasswordForm is isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel). There is no zero-arg overload in this class or its parents, so this change does not compile and the passkey re-authentication fix cannot build. The call needs to match the actual method (for example passing context.getUser()), and that method must not require a non-null user if it is also used for the anonymous login page.

title: Passkey UI only filled when user is already set
body: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() returns true only when webauthnAuth is present, realm passkeys are enabled, and user != null. authenticate() and the error challenge() now use that helper as the only place that calls webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(), after the previous user == null setup was removed. On the initial username/password (and username-only) page the user is still null, so the conditional WebAuthn form, challenge, and autocomplete attributes are never set and passkey login cannot start. The same gate drops the passkey UI on a failed password challenge, because badPasswordHandler runs while context.getUser() is still null (the user is only attached in validateUser after the password check, and is cleared on failure). Re-authentication is the only path that still gets the WebAuthn form. The condition should be passkeys enabled regardless of whether a user is already selected, which is what the existing login tests still assert via //form[@id='webauth'] on the first page.

title: UsernameForm calls a method that does not exist
body: UsernameForm.authenticate now calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments, but the only method added on UsernamePasswordForm is isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel). There is no zero-arg overload anywhere in the hierarchy, so this class does not compile and the re-authentication skip change cannot build. The call is also in the branch where context.getUser() is already non-null, so it needs a passkeys-enabled check that does not depend on a missing overload.

title: Conditional passkeys UI is skipped when the user is not yet known
body: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires user != null, and both authenticate() (line 115) and the error challenge() override (line 137) now gate WebAuthn form setup on that helper. Previously authenticate() filled passkey/conditional-UI data precisely when no user was selected, and the error challenge did the same when context.getUser() was null. On a normal first login the user is null, so the login page and invalid-password error page no longer get the WebAuthn challenge, rpId, or ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI. Conditional passkey login (discoverable and non-discoverable) therefore regresses; only the re-authentication path, where a user is already on the context, still initializes passkeys.

title: No-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() does not exist
body: UsernameForm.authenticate now calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments, but the only method added on UsernamePasswordForm is isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel). There is no no-arg overload and no static import, so this class does not compile. The re-authentication change that is supposed to keep the username form available when passkeys are enabled cannot build or run until the call matches a real method (for example isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()), and only if that predicate does not itself require a non-null user).

title: Passkey form data is only set up when a user is already known
body: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires user != null, and both authenticate() (around the fillContextForm call) and the error challenge() use that predicate as the only gate for webauthnAuth.fillContextForm. Previously the WebAuthn challenge, rpId, conditional-UI flag, and AUTH_CHALLENGE_NOTE were written when the user was not yet selected, which is the normal passkey/conditional-UI login. They are now written only during re-authentication, when context.getUser() is already set. A fresh login therefore renders without passkey data, so discoverable-credential login and the webauth form on the first page fail, and a failed unidentified login no longer restores that data on the error page. The user != null check should not be part of “passkeys enabled”; fillContextForm needs to run whenever passkeys are enabled, including when the user is still null.

title: Login-cache invalidation uses the org-aware isEnabled wrapper
body: update() loads the previous provider with getById() and passes that object into registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate. With the organization feature on, getById() does not return the stored model: it returns an anonymous IdentityProviderModel whose isEnabled() is false when the IdP is linked to an organization that is missing, disabled, or whose OrganizationProvider is disabled, even if the IdP's own enabled flag is still true. LoginFilter.ENABLED is IdentityProviderModel::isEnabled, so getLoginPredicate() fails for that wrapper. The method then returns without registering any .idp.login.* invalidation when both sides fail the predicate. That is exactly the in-session path (getByAlias/getById, mutate, update) while the org is disabled, and it also happens for an admin update whose raw model no longer qualifies (hide-on-login, link-only, enabled=false, kc.org.broker.public cleared, or organizationId moved) if the wrapped original already fails the predicate. The cached id set keeps the old membership until expiry. After the organization is enabled again, getForLogin still serves that set, and OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean only re-checks isEnabled(), not hide-on-login, link-only, or broker-public. IdPs that were configured to stay off the login page, including non-public organization brokers, can be offered for login. Compare the delegate/raw model (and null-check it) instead of the organization-aware wrapper.

title: Login-cache test cleans up the wrong IdP alias
body: testCacheIDPForLogin creates providers with aliases idp-alias-0 through idp-alias-20, but every cleanup is registered as testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove (the loop at line 381 and idp-alias-20 at line 425). The admin-client get() receiver is bound immediately, so cleanup DELETEs the nonexistent alias "alias" and never removes the providers this test created. Those IdPs remain in the shared realm. The test asserts exact cache sizes (5, 6, 10, 11), so a rerun, or testCacheIDPByOrg running first (it has the same get("alias") cleanup and leaves public org-idp-* brokers linked to orga), changes those counts and can fail this test or later organization tests.

title: Login-cache invalidation uses org-wrapped isEnabled()
body: update() loads the pre-update IDP with getById(), which, when the ORGANIZATION feature is on, returns a wrapper whose isEnabled() is false if the linked organization is missing or disabled, even when the IDP row itself is enabled. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate then applies LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate(), whose ENABLED check calls that overridden isEnabled(). If the org is disabled, the original model fails the predicate, and the method returns immediately whenever the updated model also fails it (hide-on-login, link-only, not broker-public, or disabled) without comparing organizationId. The getForLogin cache was filled from the JPA delegate using the raw columns, so that IDP id stays in the cached list. Later getForLogin replays the cached ids and returns an IDP that no longer matches the login filters. OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean only re-checks isEnabled(), not hide-on-login, link-only, or broker-public. After the organization is enabled again, the login page can show brokers the admin hid, marked link-only, or made non-public until the realm cache entry is evicted. Decide invalidation from the unwrapped delegate model (raw isEnabled/isHideOnLogin/isLinkOnly/config and organizationId), not the organization-aware wrapper.

title: Per-org login lookups evict the shared FetchMode cache
body: getForLogin stores every organizationId under one realm+FetchMode entry (search key is the org id, cache key is only realm and mode). The login UI calls getForLogin(ALL, orgId) once per organization. The first org fills the entry; each new org misses its search key and calls cache.invalidateObject on that shared key before merging a replacement. That evicts every organization's cached login-IDP list for the mode, including on other cluster nodes, on a read path. Concurrent logins for different orgs also lose merged search keys: each request merges only its own key into the old snapshot and the last addRevisioned wins. In a multi-organization realm the cache never stays warm and the login page keeps hitting the database. Put organizationId in the cache key (with a dedicated key for null) so a lookup does not invalidate other organizations.

title: Login-cache test cleans up the wrong IDP alias
body: testCacheIDPForLogin registers cleanup as testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias") (the literal string) both in the create loop and again for idp-alias-20, instead of the alias just created. The admin client get() returns a resource proxy, so this does not remove idp-alias-0..20. Teardown can 404, and those providers stay in the shared test realm. The same literal is already used in testCacheIDPByOrg. Leftover enabled or public brokers change later getForLogin counts and can fail this class or later organization tests. Register cleanup with the actual alias (get(alias) and get("idp-alias-20")).

title: Login-cache invalidation uses the org-wrapped IdP model
body: update() loads the pre-update provider with getById(), which, when the organization feature is on, returns a wrapper whose isEnabled() is false whenever the organization is missing, disabled, or the organization provider is disabled — even if the stored IdP is enabled. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() then treats that wrapper as “not a login IdP”. getForLogin() fills its cache from the delegate query, which only checks the IdP’s own enabled/linkOnly/hideOnLogin/public flags, so that IdP can already be in the cached id set. If the update also makes the raw model ineligible (disable it, set hideOnLogin or linkOnly, or clear kc.org.broker.public) while the organization id is unchanged, both predicate checks fail and the login caches are left untouched. After the organization is enabled again, getById() returns the updated model (the per-IdP cache was invalidated) but the stale id is still in the login list. OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean only re-checks isEnabled(), so a hidden, link-only, or non-public broker is rendered on the login page, and any other getForLogin() caller is handed providers that no longer match the method contract. Decide eligibility from the unwrapped delegate model (idpDelegate.getById), not from the organization-aware wrapper.

title: Login-cache test cleanup deletes the wrong IdP alias
body: testCacheIDPForLogin registers cleanup as identityProviders().get("alias")::remove both in the loop that creates idp-alias-0..19 (line 381) and again for idp-alias-20 (line 425). Nothing removes the aliases that were actually created. On a shared test realm, those brokers remain after the test; the DELETE of the non-existent alias "alias" can also fail cleanup. Later cases in this class, including this test’s own exact cache sizes (5/10/6/11), then see extra login providers and become order-dependent. Register cleanup with the alias just created (and the same mistake at the pre-existing line 303 should be fixed the same way).

title: Equal-order crypto providers are now chosen silently
body: detectProvider used to fail fast when ServiceLoader found more than one CryptoProvider. It now sorts by order() and keeps the first, only logging the rest. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return 200, so a classpath that contains both FIPS and non-FIPS (or Elytron and default) no longer errors. ServiceLoader order is classpath order, and sorted() is stable, so which full provider wins is environment-dependent. ServiceLoader also instantiates every provider before the sort, so FIPS1402Provider still inserts BCFIPS/BCJSSE and rewrites key/trust manager security properties even if the non-FIPS provider is the one selected (and DefaultCryptoProvider still registers BouncyCastle). A FIPS deployment can therefore keep running in a mixed or non-FIPS mode instead of refusing to start. Tie at the winning order should still be a hard error, and FIPS must outrank the non-FIPS providers if silent preference is intended.

title: New abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: order() was added as an abstract interface method with no default. CryptoProvider is a public SPI in keycloak-common. Existing downstream or custom implementations (and any already-compiled class) will not have this method. ServiceLoader instantiates every provider and then calls order() during sort, so one old implementation on the classpath throws AbstractMethodError and aborts detection entirely, even if a newer provider is also present. That turns a compatible server startup into a hard failure. A default method (for example returning 0) would keep old providers loadable and still let the new order-200 providers win.

title: AuthzClient.create can permanently install the stub crypto provider
body: AuthzClient.create now calls CryptoIntegration.init with AuthzClient's own classloader, and init only selects a provider when the static cryptoProvider field is still null. That selection is process-wide and never refreshed. AuthzClientCryptoProvider is registered via META-INF/services and implements almost every CryptoProvider method by throwing UnsupportedOperationException, with order 100. If create() runs before the server calls init with a classloader that can see DefaultCryptoProvider or FIPS1402Provider (deployment/module classloader that only exposes the authz-client service file, embedded startup, or a test that builds an AuthzClient first), the stub is locked in for the JVM. Later server init is a no-op, so token signing, PEM handling, and the other crypto entry points fail or use the incomplete provider even though a real one is on the server classpath.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK keystore provider
body: The CryptoProvider contract says getBouncyCastleProvider returns the non-FIPS or FIPS BouncyCastle provider. This implementation returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is the platform provider for the default keystore type (typically SUN), not BC or BCFIPS. Callers use that Provider's name and instance for Cipher/Signature/CertificateFactory and for BouncyIntegration. Algorithms that exist only under BC (AES/CBC/PKCS7Padding, many JOSE/JWE transforms, BCFKS) will fail or silently run outside FIPS when this provider is the one CryptoIntegration selected. Elytron returns null rather than a lookalike; this should not hand back an unrelated JCA provider.

title: ECDSA test does not compile in this module
body: ECDSAAlgorithmTest imports org.keycloak.crypto.ECDSAAlgorithm and org.keycloak.crypto.JavaAlgorithm. Those types live in the server SPI (the crypto modules already import them from there), not in keycloak-core. authz/client/pom.xml only adds junit and hamcrest; its compile/test classpath is still just keycloak-core plus HTTP/Jackson. server-spi is not a dependency, and keycloak-core cannot depend on server-spi without a cycle. testCompile of keycloak-authz-client-tests therefore fails with a missing org.keycloak.crypto package, so the new coverage never runs.

title: ECDSA transcoding test never checks a real signature
body: The only assertion is that asn1derToConcatenatedRS and concatenatedRSToASN1DER round-trip each other. The key pair is generated once with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC"), which is P-256 on standard JDKs, and that same key is used for ES256, ES384, and ES512. ES384/ES512 signature lengths are 96 and 132 bytes and their DER SEQUENCEs need long-form lengths once R and S match P-384/P-521, but a P-256 signature stays short and is only zero-padded to those lengths. Nothing calls Signature.verify on the original DER or on the re-encoded DER, and there is no known-answer vector. A self-consistent but non-interoperable encoder (wrong tag, non-minimal INTEGER, broken long-form length) still passes, which is the failure mode this provider exists to prevent.

title: Equal-order crypto providers are no longer a startup failure
body: detectProvider now sorts CryptoProvider implementations by order() and, when more than one is present, logs the rest at debug and keeps foundProviders.get(0). DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so a classpath that contains more than one of them no longer hits the previous IllegalStateException. ServiceLoader order is classpath order, so a FIPS deployment that also has the default (or Elytron) provider can silently run non-FIPS crypto, or the reverse. Selection also instantiates every provider: FIPS1402Provider's constructor inserts BCFIPS/BCJSSE and may rewrite ssl.KeyManagerFactory.algorithm, and DefaultCryptoProvider registers non-FIPS BouncyCastle, and those JVM-wide side effects now remain in a running server instead of aborting startup. Tie on the highest order should still fail, and only a strictly lower order (such as AuthzClientCryptoProvider's 100) should be ignored.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK keystore provider
body: CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider is contracted to return the BouncyCastle (or BCFIPS) provider. AuthzClientCryptoProvider instead returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which on a normal JDK is SUN, not BC. This provider is a ServiceLoader CryptoProvider and becomes the process-wide provider whenever it is the only one or wins order(). Callers that do Cipher/Signature.getInstance(alg, getBouncyCastleProvider()) or that register that provider under the name they expect to be "BC"/"BCFIPS" will use SUN or fail NoSuchProviderException. PKCS7Padding, BC named curves, and FIPS algorithm lookups break, and a non-null SUN provider also skips null fallbacks. This should throw like the other unimplemented methods, or return a real BC provider; it must not impersonate one.

title: New abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: order() was added as an abstract interface method with no default. keycloak-common is a published library, and CryptoProvider is a public SPI. Implementations compiled against the previous interface (downstream distributions, the separate keycloak-client tree, test fakes) will not compile, and old binaries will throw AbstractMethodError when ServiceLoader instantiates them during CryptoIntegration.init, which now runs from AuthzClient.create as well as server startup. A default method is required for compatibility. That default must be greater than AuthzClientCryptoProvider.order() (100); a default of 0 would let the incomplete authz-client provider outrank every legacy full provider that does not override order().

title: ECDSA test never verifies signatures or curve-sized keys
body: ECDSAAlgorithmTest builds one KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC") key (SunEC default P-256) and reuses it for ES256, ES384, and ES512. It only checks that asn1derToConcatenatedRS and concatenatedRSToASN1DER round-trip to the same byte array. ES384/ES512 therefore never see 48-byte or 66-byte R/S values (including the leading-0x00 high-bit case on P-521); those components are just zero-padded 32-byte integers, so both branches can be wrong for real curve sizes and the test still passes. Nothing calls Signature.verify on the re-encoded DER, so a DER encoding that this decoder accepts but Java rejects would stay green. There is also no test that ServiceLoader ordering prefers a higher order() over AuthzClientCryptoProvider, or that two providers with the same highest order are rejected.

title: Tied CryptoProviders are chosen non-deterministically
body: detectProvider no longer throws when ServiceLoader finds more than one CryptoProvider. It sorts by order() descending and returns the first entry. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return 200, so any two of them tie, and ServiceLoader order is classpath-dependent. The loser is only mentioned in a debug log. Previously this misconfiguration aborted startup. Now a FIPS deployment that also has the non-FIPS provider can keep running with DefaultCryptoProvider even though FIPS1402Provider's constructor has already inserted BCFIPS at JCA position 1 and rewritten ssl.KeyManagerFactory.algorithm / ssl.TrustManagerFactory.algorithm. The process then mixes a non-FIPS CryptoProvider with FIPS JCA settings, or the reverse. When several providers share the highest order, startup should still fail.

title: order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: order() was added as an abstract method with no default on the public CryptoProvider interface in keycloak-common. Implementations compiled against the previous interface will not compile, and at runtime ServiceLoader detection calls order() and throws AbstractMethodError, so CryptoIntegration.init fails and the server does not start. A default such as default int order() { return 0; } would keep older providers loadable and sort them below the in-tree providers (200) and AuthzClientCryptoProvider (100).

title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK keystore provider
body: getBouncyCastleProvider() is documented to return the BouncyCastle or BCFIPS provider. This implementation returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is the platform keystore provider (typically SUN), not BouncyCastle. WildFlyElytronProvider returns null when BC is absent so callers can take a non-BC path. A non-null SUN provider fails those null checks and is then passed to Signature.getInstance or Cipher.getInstance. SUN does not provide SHA256withECDSA (that is SunEC) or BC algorithms such as AES/CBC/PKCS7Padding, so provider-pinned operations throw NoSuchAlgorithmException or use the wrong implementation. For a standalone authz-client this class is the selected CryptoProvider, so return null or throw instead of handing back the keystore provider.

title: AuthzClient.create freezes the JVM crypto provider
body: AuthzClient.create(Configuration) calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()), and init() keeps the first provider it detects forever. ServiceLoader on the authz-client classloader does not see CryptoProvider services registered only in a child deployment or server classloader. Those order-200 providers are skipped, AuthzClientCryptoProvider (order 100) is installed, and a later CryptoIntegration.init from the server is a no-op. The rest of the JVM then uses a provider that throws UnsupportedOperationException from getSignature, getPemUtils, cipher, certificate, and truststore methods. Creating a client must not permanently install this stub from the library classloader; a later init that can see a higher-order provider has to be able to replace it.

title: ECDSA integer conversion silently truncates
body: integerToBytes, used by asn1derToConcatenatedRS, copies the low-order qLength bytes whenever BigInteger.toByteArray() is longer than the coordinate size. It does not require the discarded prefix to be a single 0x00 sign octet, and it does not reject a negative INTEGER. An oversized or negative DER integer therefore becomes a different R or S instead of failing the conversion with IOException. Signature verification then runs against a value that is not the encoded integer, so malformed ECDSA input is mishandled rather than rejected. Throw unless the encoding is at most qLength+1 bytes and any extra leading byte is 0x00.

title: ECDSA test only checks a self-roundtrip on P-256
body: The only new coverage of the ASN.1 ECDSA conversion generates one key with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair(), which is the provider default curve (P-256 on standard JDKs), then runs ES256, ES384, and ES512 with that key. The sole assertion is that decoding the encoder's output matches the intermediate R||S. Signature.verify is never called, and the result is never compared with Java's original DER. A decoder/encoder pair that ignores the real R and S and inverts each other would pass. ES384 and ES512 also never see 48-byte or 66-byte coordinates, so the sign-octet padding path at those widths is untested. Each algorithm needs a key on secp256r1, secp384r1, or secp521r1, and the DER produced from the concatenated form must verify with Signature.verify.

title: Role-mapping checks ignore manage-clients admins
body: canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles, and canMapClientScopeRoles only call hasPermission and never treat AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS as sufficient. This class fully replaces ClientPermissions whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, and V1 granted those operations to holders of manage-clients (including master-realm and realm admins) before any fine-grained policy was consulted. canManage and canManageClientScopes still short-circuit on that role, so the same admin can update a client but is denied mapping client roles, composite roles, and client-scope roles. Admin console role-mapping calls fail with 403 even when no FGAP policy was meant to restrict that admin. The new tests only cover a user without manage-clients, so they do not catch this.

title: Per-client resource hides all-clients allow and deny
body: hasPermission(ClientModel, scope) loads the object resource by client id and, if that row exists, evaluates only that resource. The all-clients resource is consulted only when no object resource exists. Creating any object permission (for example VIEW on one client) therefore drops realm-wide grants such as MANAGE/CONFIGURE/MAP_ROLES on "Clients" for that client, so an admin who can manage every client loses manage on any client that also has an object-level permission. The same short-circuit skips a realm-wide negative permission, so a deny-all policy on Clients does not apply to a client that already has an object resource and a positive object permission. Authorization becomes order-dependent and can both lock out legitimate admins and bypass a type-level deny.

title: Missing Clients resource NPEs permission checks
body: When no per-client resource exists, hasPermission assigns getResourceTypeResource(...) and immediately calls PolicyStore.findByResource(server, resource) with no null check. getResourceTypeResource returns null if the "Clients" resource was never created. findByResource dereferences that resource and throws NullPointerException, so canView/canManage/canConfigure/canMapRoles return 500 instead of false. AdminPermissionsSchema.init returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is already non-null and never adds the new Clients resource type or the new scopes (configure, map-roles-client-scope, map-roles-composite). Any realm that enabled admin permissions before this schema change keeps the old resource server, so the first per-client check 500s and creating a Clients permission fails because those scopes are absent. init needs an upgrade path, and the evaluator must treat a missing type resource as deny.

title: V2 throws on token exchange and permissions API
body: MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() now always returns ClientPermissionsV2 when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is on, but canExchangeTo, exchangeToPermission, mapRolesPermission, mapRolesClientScopePermission, mapRolesCompositePermission, managePermission, configurePermission, viewPermission, isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, resource, and getPermissions all throw UnsupportedOperationException. Token exchange calls AdminPermissions.management().clients().canExchangeTo and will fail the request with a server error for every realm that has the feature enabled, even if token-exchange permissions are unused. The admin client management-permissions endpoint calls isPermissionsEnabled, then resource and getPermissions, so opening fine-grained permissions for a client 500s. These methods are still part of the live ClientPermissions contract; they need a V2 behavior (or a safe deny/empty result), not an exception. getEvaluationContext is unused dead code left from an unfinished exchange check.

title: Client permission resources have no display name
body: getResourceName only resolves Users resources to a username. Client object resources are stored under the client UUID (resolveClient returns client.getId()) and getOrCreateResource never sets a display name, so the fallback resource.getDisplayName() is null. Admin APIs that label permission resources will show a blank name for every client permission, and a deleted client is not reported as missing the way a missing user is (ModelIllegalStateException). This method needs a Clients branch that loads the client and returns its clientId, and a defined error if the client is gone.

title: getClientsWithPermission returns the type name, not client ids
body: getClientsWithPermission adds resource.getName() for every Clients-typed resource that grants the scope. The schema's all-clients resource is named "Clients" (init sets both name and type to the resource type). A user who only has a type-level grant therefore gets a set containing the literal "Clients" rather than every client id, and callers that filter with client.getId() match nothing. Object resources are only included if their type was set to Clients; getOrCreateResource creates them by name and scopes and never calls setType, so per-client grants are also omitted if no other layer sets the type. Listing and role-mapping UIs that rely on this set will hide clients the user is allowed to access. The type resource should be expanded or skipped, and returned ids must be real client ids.

title: Removal listener checks V1 but dispatches V2 clients
body: Cleanup now runs only when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) is enabled, but AdminPermissions.management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, and ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled throws. If both features are on, ClientRemovedEvent calls the throwing V2 method and client deletion fails. If only V2 is on, the listener does nothing, so the authorization resource created for that client id is never removed. There is no other V2 delete hook in this change, so object-level client permissions are left pointing at deleted clients.

title: requireView javadoc describes a boolean result
body: requireView is void and throws ForbiddenException, but its new javadoc says it returns true if canView() returns true. requireViewClientScopes (line 101) has the same error: it says it returns true if canViewClientScopes() returns true. Callers reading the interface will treat these as predicates instead of enforcing methods. The comments should match requireManage/requireList and state that they throw when the corresponding can* check is false.

title: Role-mapping checks drop the manage-clients admin role
body: canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles, and canMapClientScopeRoles only call hasPermission. Unlike canManage(ClientModel) and canView(), they never call root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS) and they do not delegate to the parent implementation that treated that role as a short-circuit. AdminPermissions.evaluator installs this class for every realm whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, including realms that have not turned on fine-grained admin permissions. A master admin or a realm admin who only has the manage-clients role therefore gets false from these methods (hasPermission also returns false when the admin is from another realm). Client role assignment and composite/client-scope role mapping that previously succeeded are denied. The new interface javadoc documents the same omission, so callers cannot rely on it either.

title: A per-client resource hides all-clients policies
body: hasPermission(ClientModel, scope) evaluates only the resource named with that client's id when one exists. The all-clients resource is consulted only when findByName returns null. Any object permission (for example VIEW on one client) therefore suppresses all-clients grants for every other scope. canManage(client), canConfigure, canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles, and canMapClientScopeRoles all go through this helper, and only canView() checks the all-clients resource independently. A policy that manages or maps roles for all clients will not apply to a client that already has any dedicated resource, so those operations are incorrectly denied. The reverse is also wrong if a realm-wide negative policy is supposed to deny a scope: once an object resource exists and grants that scope, the all-clients deny is never evaluated. This contradicts the new ClientPermissionEvaluator javadoc, which says all-clients MANAGE, CONFIGURE, VIEW, and MAP_ROLES permissions also grant the corresponding per-client checks.

title: Already-initialized admin-permissions clients never get Clients scopes
body: init still returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is non-null. That client is created the first time admin permissions are enabled, and earlier versions of this schema only seeded the Users resource type. Realms that already have the client will not get the new configure, map-roles-client-scope, or map-roles-composite scopes, nor the Clients all-resource. Creating a client permission then fails in getScope or in getOrCreateResource ("No scopes found." / scope not found), and evaluation cannot fall back to a Clients resource that was never created. There is no migration in this change to add the missing scopes and resource on startup.

title: Null all-clients resource causes a 500 on permission checks
body: When no per-client resource exists, the code loads the Clients type resource and immediately calls policyStore.findByResource(server, resource) without a null check. getResourceTypeResource returns null when admin-permissions schema support is off, when the type is unknown, or when the Clients resource was never created (the upgrade case above). The usual PolicyStore implementation dereferences resource.getId(), so the admin API throws NullPointerException instead of denying the call. The sibling hasPermission(String) path does null-check findByName and returns false; this path should do the same.

title: Existing client permission methods now throw UnsupportedOperationException
body: canExchangeTo, isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, getPermissions, resource, and the Policy accessors are overridden to throw UnsupportedOperationException. MgmtPermissionsV2 is selected solely because ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, so these overrides replace working boolean/Policy behavior for every realm. Token exchange calls canExchangeTo (and often isPermissionsEnabled first); the admin client permissions endpoints call getPermissions and setPermissionsEnabled. Those callers expect false, an empty map, or a 403, not an unchecked exception, so enabling the feature turns token exchange and the client permissions admin API into HTTP 500s even when the realm is not using Clients permissions. Returning a deny/no-op, as the V1 methods did when permissions were not enabled, is required until V2 implements them.

title: Removal cleanup is gated on the wrong feature flag
body: The client/role/group removal listener now runs only when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) is enabled. The evaluator switches to MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, regardless of the V1 flag. With neither flag on (the default), deletion no longer calls setPermissionsEnabled(false), so fine-grained permission data created while V1 was previously enabled is left behind and can break client deletion with leftover authorization rows. With both flags on, management() returns V2 and setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException, which fails the removal transaction. The guard needs to follow the same V2 switch as AdminPermissions.evaluator: skip or replace the V1 cleanup only when V2 is the active implementation.

title: Client resources are displayed as a null name
body: getResourceName resolves Users resources to the username, but the new Clients branch is missing. Per-client resources are stored with name equal to the internal client id (resolveClient) and getOrCreateResource never sets a display name, so the method returns resource.getDisplayName(), which is null. Permission list/detail APIs and the admin UI therefore show a blank resource for every client-specific permission instead of the clientId. A deleted client is also not reported, whereas a missing user throws ModelIllegalStateException.

title: requireView javadoc describes a boolean return
body: requireView and requireViewClientScopes are void and throw ForbiddenException when the matching can* method is false, which is what the other require* javadocs in this interface say. These two comments instead say "Returns true if canView()/canViewClientScopes() returns true", which is the contract of the boolean methods above them. Callers reading only the new javadoc will not know that the methods throw.

title: V2 client permission methods throw instead of degrading
body: ClientPermissionsV2 is installed for every realm whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is on (MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()), but isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, getPermissions, resource, and the Policy accessors all throw UnsupportedOperationException. Those methods are still called by the admin client management-permissions API, so opening or updating a client's permissions tab returns 500 for every realm, not only realms using FGAP. canExchangeTo (line 148) throws the same way, so token-exchange permission checks 500 instead of denying. setPermissionsEnabled must no-op or return a normal error, and the boolean/read methods must return false/empty when V2 does not use per-client authz resources.

title: Schema init does not add Clients type to existing realms
body: init() returns immediately when the realm already has an admin-permissions client. That client was created by the earlier Users-only schema, so upgraded realms never get the Clients resource, or the new configure, map-roles-client-scope, and map-roles-composite scopes. Creating or evaluating a Clients permission then fails with missing-scope or missing-resource errors, and ClientPermissionsV2 falls through to a null type resource. Init needs to add any schema resource types and scopes that are not already present.

title: Role-mapping checks ignore manage-clients and manage
body: canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles, and canMapClientScopeRoles only call hasPermission for that scope. Unlike canManage in the same class, they do not treat AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS as allowed, and they do not treat a Clients manage grant as allowed. A realm admin (or any caller who can manage the client) is therefore forbidden from mapping client roles, composite roles, or client-scope roles unless a separate FGAP map-roles policy exists. V1 granted these via the manage-clients short-circuit inside permission checks.

title: Per-client evaluation skips all-clients policies and can NPE
body: hasPermission(ClientModel, scope) loads only the per-client resource when one exists and never evaluates the Clients type resource in that case. FGAP requires both: a positive all-clients grant must still apply when the client already has a resource for another scope, and a negative all-clients policy must still deny a positive per-client grant. As written, all-clients manage/view is ignored whenever any per-client resource exists (incorrect deny), and a negative all-clients policy does not override a positive per-client policy (incorrect allow). If the per-client resource is missing and getResourceTypeResource returns null (schema not migrated, or admin permissions not enabled for this server), findByResource(server, null) on line 219 throws NullPointerException and the admin call 500s instead of returning false.

title: Per-client resources are created without a type
body: getOrCreateResource creates the client resource by name and scopes but never setType(CLIENTS). The aggregate Clients resource created in init() does set its type. ClientPermissionsV2.getClientsWithPermission then uses resourceStore.findByType(..., CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE), so it will not see per-client grants. It will see the aggregate resource and add its name "Clients" to the granted id set, which is not a client id. Callers that filter the client list or role-mapping targets with this set therefore omit clients the user was granted and never match a real client id.

title: Client resource names are not resolved for display
body: getResourceName resolves Users resources to a username (or "All users") but has no Clients branch. Per-client resources are stored under the internal client id and display name is never set, so permission listings fall through to resource.getDisplayName() and show null instead of the clientId. After a client is deleted the orphaned resource still will not be reported as missing, unlike the user path which throws ModelIllegalStateException.

title: Client-removal cleanup throws or skips V2 resources
body: The removal listener now runs only when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is enabled, but management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled. If both features are on, ClientRemovedEvent calls ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled, which throws UnsupportedOperationException and can fail client deletion. If only V2 is on, the listener is skipped entirely. Nothing deletes the FGAP resource that getOrCreateResource stored under the client id on the admin-permissions client, so deleted clients leave orphaned resources and policies.

title: Configure test rotates the shared admin client secret
body: testConfigureOnlyOneClient calls generateNewSecret() on myclient, which is the confidential client used by the injected realmAdminClient (and by other tests that log in with client secret mysecret). onAfter only deletes scope permissions and does not restore the secret, name, or default client scopes mutated by these tests. Later tests in the same realm then fail authentication or see a changed client, depending on method order. The new map-roles-client-scope scope is also never exercised.

title: requireView javadoc describes the wrong contract
body: requireView is documented as returning true when canView() is true, and requireViewClientScopes (line 101) as returning true when canViewClientScopes() is true. Both methods are void and are specified elsewhere to throw ForbiddenException. Callers reading only these comments will treat them as predicates.

title: Recreate exit code moved from 4 to 3 and 4 reused
