Both the hang-restart path (process.kill() around line 254) and join() (process.terminate() around line 346) are guarded by isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process), which is always false for these workers, so the signal is never sent. Crash recovery still works because a dead process is simply replaced, but a hang does not: a second worker is started for the same shards, and once it updates the shared healthy_since value the slot looks healthy, so MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS never fires and the original worker is leaked. That leaked worker can keep calling flush_segments/produce on the same Redis shards as the replacement, duplicating buffered-segments output and racing flush state. On shutdown, a worker blocked in Redis or Kafka produce is also never force-stopped after stopped is set, so it can still produce after those shards have been reassigned.

title: join() abandons flusher processes once the deadline has passed
body: join() gives the entire caller timeout to next_step.join(timeout) before it waits on flusher workers. If that call consumes the timeout, deadline is already in the past and the loop breaks immediately, without waiting for or terminating any remaining flusher process. The previous single-process join always called terminate() even when the deadline had already elapsed. These workers are daemon processes only in the sense that they die if the parent exits; the consumer process stays alive across rebalance. A worker still inside flush_segments or Kafka produce therefore keeps flushing shards the new assignment no longer owns, which duplicates segments onto the buffered-segments topic and conflicts with whichever consumer now owns those Redis shards.

title: Restart starts a new flusher before the old one has stopped
body: _ensure_processes_alive replaces a worker by signalling it (when the isinstance check is fixed) and then immediately calling _create_process_for_shards for the same shard list. kill()/terminate() return as soon as the signal is sent; the old process is not joined, and its handle is overwritten in self.processes so a later join cannot reap or stop it. The old worker can still be inside flush_segments, produce, or done_flush_segments while the new worker starts the same cycle. Both will publish the same segments and both will mutate the same Redis flush keys. The thread path used when produce_to_pipe is set never signals the old thread at all, so tests hit this overlap on every restart.

title: Drift wait in test_basic is patched into a no-op
body: test_basic monkeypatches time.sleep to a no-op so the flusher thread does not pause, then calls time.sleep(0.1) to let that thread observe current_drift before join(). The test looks up time.sleep at call time, so it hits the patch and does not wait. join() then sets stopped immediately. The flusher can leave its loop before flush_segments runs with the advanced drift, so the assertion on the produced segment is racy. The new poll/sleep was added to close that race and does not. Nothing in the new test_flusher_processes_limit covers actual multi-process flushing, restart, or shutdown either, so the kill/terminate and overlap bugs above are untested.

title: Flusher timers use mismatched, high-cardinality shard tags
body: spans.buffer.flusher.produce is tagged with key "shard" while spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce on the next block is tagged with key "shards", so the two timings cannot be joined in dashboards. The value is a comma-separated list of every shard on that process, not one shard. The process-spans CLI defaults --flusher-processes to 1, which puts the entire partition assignment in a single tag. Each rebalance yields a new tag value (unbounded cardinality) and the string can exceed statsd tag-length limits, dropping the timings this change needs in order to tell whether the flusher is keeping up. The unhealthy counter already emits one bounded tag per shard and should be the pattern here.

title: Shared queue pool is destroyed on rebalance and later messages are committed unprocessed
body: FixedQueuePool is created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and reused by every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy. Strategy.close() (queue_consumer.py) calls queue_pool.shutdown(), which sets each worker's shutdown flag, calls Queue.shutdown(), and joins the workers. Arroyo closes the strategy and calls create_with_partitions again on the same factory on every partition revoke/assign, so the next strategy is handed a pool whose queues reject puts and whose workers are dead. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit then hits the bare except, logs, and add_offset+complete_offset without ever running the result processor. The commit thread treats that as success and commits offset+1. After the first rebalance or consumer restart-in-process, every uptime result is acknowledged and dropped. The same except also permanently drops any message whose grouping function or enqueue raises, instead of letting the consumer retry.

title: Offsets are committed from a background thread against a non-thread-safe Kafka consumer
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy starts a daemon commit thread that calls the Arroyo commit callback (and therefore the Kafka consumer's stage/commit path) every second. The consumer thread is simultaneously in poll()/submit(). confluent-kafka Consumer objects are not thread-safe, and Arroyo's commit policy mutates shared offset state that is only used from the processing thread elsewhere. Concurrent commit and poll can crash the consumer, skip commits, or publish a torn offset map. terminate() only sets shutdown_event and does not join this thread, so it can still be inside commit_function after the processor has closed the consumer. close() joins the thread for at most 5s and then continues, so a slow commit leaves two commit threads if a new strategy is created. Commit from poll() on the consumer thread instead.

title: Queues are unbounded, so the claimed backpressure does not exist
body: Each work queue is created with queue.Queue() and no maxsize, and submit() always put()s without blocking. The class docstring says queues provide natural backpressure, but poll() only emits a gauge and never pauses the consumer. A slow subscription (the case this mode is meant to isolate) makes its queue retain every subsequent message in memory while the main thread keeps fetching. Offset commits cannot advance past that item, so the process holds the entire uncommitted backlog until it OOMs. get_committable_offsets also walks range(start, max_offset+1) under the partition lock, so a large backlog stalls every worker's complete_offset for the duration of that scan.

title: Shutdown abandons queued work and can block for num_queues * 5s
body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True before draining, and OrderedQueueWorker.run only calls get() while that flag is false. After the current item, the worker exits even if Queue.shutdown(immediate=False) would still return queued items, so those items are never processed and never completed. close() stops and joins the commit thread before joining workers, so items that do finish during shutdown are not committed either. join() ignores its timeout and calls close(). On a deploy/rebalance, in-flight uptime results are redelivered and applied twice (duplicate incidents/occurrences). Joins are also sequential with a 5s timeout each, so 20 workers stuck in slow handlers make close()/terminate() block for about 100s and still drop the work.

title: An exception in the worker finally kills the only thread for that queue forever
body: OrderedQueueWorker has no supervisor. complete_offset and metrics.gauge run in the same finally block with no handler, and run() has no outer try around the loop. If gauge (or complete_offset) raises, the thread exits. That queue is the only worker for every group hashed to it, and nothing restarts it. Any offset already queued there stays in outstanding forever, so get_committable_offsets cannot advance that partition. The consumer keeps polling, health checks still pass because poll() only records queue depth, and commits for the partition stop until the process is restarted.

title: Worker threads never reset Django DB connections, so one DB error drops later results
body: OrderedQueueWorker calls result_processor on a long-lived thread and never calls django.db.close_old_connections(). Django only runs connection health checks and obsolete-connection cleanup on the request path, which these threads do not have. After an idle timeout, failover, or OperationalError, that thread's connection stays dead. ResultProcessor.__call__ swallows the exception, and the worker's finally still complete_offset, so the failed check is committed and will not be retried. Every later message on that same queue fails the same way and is also acknowledged. One transient DB blip silently disables 1/num_queues of subscription processing until the consumer restarts.

title: Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its docstring and races the commit loop
body: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling says processing errors must not block offset commits, but the assertion requires the partition to be absent from committed_offsets. The worker always complete_offset in a finally, including when the patched processor raises, so a commit of offset 102 (101+1) is the actual behavior and the assertion fails if it happens. The test only sleeps 0.2s after the calls return, while the commit thread waits 1.0s before its first commit, so the assertion usually passes only because the commit has not run yet and fails when scheduling is slower. It neither locks the intended contract nor reliably passes.

title: Uptime --mode help still describes the wrong execution model
body: uptime_options() now accepts thread-queue-parallel, but the help text is still "The mode to process results in. Parallel uses multithreading." The parallel mode uses a multiprocessing pool, batched-parallel uses a thread pool, and thread-queue-parallel uses one thread per queue. Operators enabling the new flag get no description of what it does or that --max-workers is the queue count rather than a thread-pool size.

title: Shared queue pool is destroyed on the first strategy close
body: FixedQueuePool is created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and reused by every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy, including its OffsetTracker. Arroyo calls strategy.close()/join() on partition revocation and shutdown, and close() always calls queue_pool.shutdown(), which stops the workers and shuts the queues down. The next create_with_partitions() (every rebalance) builds a new strategy on that same dead pool, so submits no longer run and the consumer stops processing uptime results after the first assignment change. Offsets left outstanding when workers exit are also kept on the shared tracker; get_committable_offsets stops at that gap, so commits for the partition never advance. Each new strategy also starts another commit thread against the same tracker.

title: Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure
body: Each worker queue is created with queue.Queue() (maxsize unlimited) and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() returns as soon as the item is enqueued. poll() only records a gauge and never blocks. The class docstring says full queues apply natural backpressure, but the consumer thread is never stalled, so a slow result handler or one hot group key grows the queue and the process heap until the consumer is OOM-killed. Commits also cannot move past the oldest unfinished offset on a partition, so one slow subscription pins the commit point while later messages on other queues are already handled; a crash or rebalance then redelivers that whole uncommitted prefix and repeats incident/issue side effects.

title: Offsets are committed from a background thread, and shutdown drops the final commit
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy starts a daemon thread that calls the Arroyo commit callback about once a second. That callback is meant to run on the stream-processor thread and ultimately touches the Kafka consumer, which is not thread-safe. Invoking it concurrently with poll, rebalance, and processor shutdown can crash the consumer or record a bad offset. close() makes the window worse: it signals the commit thread and joins it before workers are drained, so any offset completed after the thread exits is never passed to commit(). Those messages are processed again on restart. terminate() does not join the commit thread at all, so a commit can still run after the consumer is being torn down. join() also ignores the timeout Arroyo passes in and uses its own 5s joins.

title: Shutdown flag abandons queued work instead of draining it
body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True and only then calls Queue.shutdown(immediate=False). The worker loop checks that flag before every get(), so after it finishes the item it already pulled it exits even though the queue still holds items. Those abandoned items were already recorded as outstanding offsets and will never be completed, because the thread has exited. On a shared tracker that gap blocks every later commit for the partition; even with a per-strategy tracker, a deploy or rebalance fails to drain FIFO and reprocesses the queued backlog instead of finishing it.

title: Submit failures are acknowledged and the message is dropped
body: Any exception in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() (grouping_fn, put() after the queue is shut down, or the BrokerValue assert) is logged and then the offset is both added and completed. The commit loop will commit that offset, so the payload is skipped permanently instead of crashing the consumer and being redelivered. OrderedQueueWorker.run() has the same pattern: the finally block always complete_offset, including when result_processor raises, which contradicts the strategy comment that offsets are committed only after successful processing. A transient handler error therefore drops the uptime result with no retry.

title: Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its docstring and of the code
body: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling says processing errors must not block commits for other messages, but the assertion requires that nothing was committed (len(committed_offsets) == 0 or the partition is absent). The worker completes the offset in a finally block even when the patched processor raises, so a commit of offset 102 should happen about a second later. The test only sleeps 0.2s after the queues drain, so it sometimes passes before the commit thread runs and fails when the 1s commit loop wins. It neither locks the intended behavior nor matches the implementation.

title: Queue-depth assertion races already-running workers
body: test_stats_reporting submits ten items and immediately asserts get_stats()["total_items"] > 0. Workers are started in setUp and the test processor only appends to a list, so they can drain the queues before the main thread reads stats. On a fast run the assertion fails even though the pool is working; the later wait only checks that the queue eventually hits zero.

title: Shared queue pool is destroyed on rebalance, then new messages are acked unprocessed
body: FixedQueuePool is created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and reused by every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy from create_with_partitions. close() and join() call queue_pool.shutdown(), which shuts the queues down permanently. Arroyo closes the current strategy and builds a new one on every partition revocation/assignment, so after the first rebalance the new strategy submits into already-shut-down queues. queue.Queue.put raises queue.ShutDown, submit() swallows that exception, and the handler marks the offset completed. The commit thread then commits it. Those results are never processed and will not be redelivered, so uptime checks are silently dropped for the rest of the process lifetime. The shared OffsetTracker also keeps last_committed across assignments, so a later strategy can stall or skip commits for replayed offsets. The pool and tracker must be created per strategy instance and only shut down after that instance has finished its own work.

title: Submit and worker failures are committed as successfully processed
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches every exception (grouping_fn errors, BrokerValue assert, queue shutdown, put failures), logs, and calls add_offset plus complete_offset. OrderedQueueWorker.run also completes the offset in a finally block after logging processing exceptions. get_committable_offsets then treats those offsets as safe to commit, and ResultsStrategyFactory commits offset+1 to Kafka. The class docstring says offsets are committed only after successful processing and that no item is lost, but a failed message is acknowledged and never retried. In serial and batched-parallel modes an exception from batching/grouping escapes RunTask and is not committed, so this is a data-loss regression: a bad payload or a transient queue error permanently skips the check result.

title: Queues are unbounded and poll() never applies backpressure
body: Each worker queue is created with queue.Queue() (maxsize 0, unlimited), and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll only emits a gauge. submit() never blocks. The strategy docstring claims natural backpressure when queues fill, but nothing stops the consumer thread from pulling the entire partition into memory. One slow subscription blocks only its worker, while every other message on that partition keeps being queued, and the offset watermark cannot advance past the slow item. The process RSS grows with lag until the consumer is OOM-killed; on restart the uncommitted prefix is replayed. poll() or submit() needs a bounded queue and must block when any queue is full so Arroyo stops polling.

title: Graceful shutdown does not drain queues or wait for in-flight work
body: OrderedQueueWorker stops as soon as shutdown is True, before it drains the queue. FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets that flag and only then calls Queue.shutdown(immediate=False), so the graceful drain never happens: after the current item, the worker exits and leaves the rest of the queue unprocessed and incomplete. close() also joins the commit thread (5s) before shutting workers down, so anything completed after that final commit iteration is never committed. join() ignores its timeout and calls close() again. Worker joins are 5s each and sequential, so a stuck handler (the case this mode is meant to isolate) blocks the consumer thread for about num_queues*5 seconds, then the daemon worker keeps running after join returns. Those threads can still apply uptime side effects after partitions were revoked and another owner started, duplicating incidents, while the abandoned queued messages are only redelivered if they were not already acked.

title: Offsets are committed from a background thread
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy starts a daemon commit thread that calls the Arroyo commit callback every second. That callback is invoked by every other strategy on the consumer thread, which owns the Kafka consumer and the processor's staged-offset map. librdkafka consumers are not thread-safe, and the processor iterates that map while committing. Concurrent commit() from _commit_loop can corrupt staged offsets or raise RuntimeError if the map is mutated during iteration, and close() joins this thread from the consumer thread while it may be inside commit(), which deadlocks if commit needs the processor lock (join then times out after 5s and shutdown continues with a commit still in flight). Commits should be staged in poll()/close() on the consumer thread.

title: Queue stats test races workers and order is not asserted
body: test_stats_reporting submits 10 items to a live pool and immediately asserts get_stats()['total_items'] > 0. Workers are already running and the test processor only appends to a list, so the queues can be empty before that assertion; it will flake under load. test_different_groups_distributed similarly asserts that 20 hashed keys hit all 3 queues, which is not guaranteed. test_preserves_order_within_group only checks that 5 results were processed, not that they were processed in offset order, so an ordering regression in the strategy would still pass. None of the tests revoke partitions or call close()/join() and then submit again, so they miss the shared-pool shutdown data loss.

title: Backup-code login skips the password when any totpCode is sent
body: Password verification runs only when credentials.totpCode is empty (line 121). The new branch then accepts a matching backup code and never checks the TOTP value. A caller who knows the email and one backup code can therefore sign in with no password by also sending any non-empty totpCode (for example "000000"). The UI copy and the login form still treat the backup code as a replacement for the authenticator only, after the password step, so this is an account takeover path if a backup code leaks (downloaded file, clipboard, setup response). Require a valid password for CAL users on the backup-code path, and do not let a dummy totpCode bypass that check.

title: Backup codes are compared case-sensitively
body: Codes are 10 hex characters (0-9a-f) and the login UI placeholder is "XXXXX-XXXXX", which leads users and mobile keyboards to enter uppercase. Matching uses indexOf on the raw string after only stripping dashes, so "AAAAA-AAAAA" does not match "aaaaa-aaaaa". The same check in apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts (line 61) has the same bug. Legitimate backup codes will be rejected at login and when disabling 2FA. Normalize by lowercasing (and trimming) before compare.

title: A backup code can be redeemed twice under concurrent logins
body: Consumption is a read-modify-write: decrypt the list, indexOf the code, set that slot to null, then update. Two overlapping authorize calls can both observe the same unused code and both return a session before either write lands. The product promise is that each code works exactly once. The update needs to be conditional (transaction or compare-and-swap on the stored ciphertext) so a code that was already removed cannot authorize a second session.

title: Lost-access toggle submits the disable form
body: The Lost access / Go back control is a Button inside the disable Form with no type="button" and no preventDefault. A button's default type is submit, so clicking it both flips the backup-code view and posts whatever is currently in the password/TOTP/backup fields. That can disable 2FA accidentally, or fail the request and show an incorrect-code error, instead of only switching inputs. Set type="button" (same issue on the download control in EnableTwoFactorModal, which sits inside the enable Form and will also submit handleEnable).

title: Enable-2FA login test never leaves the backup-code step
body: After a successful OTP, EnableTwoFactorModal now stays open on the backup-code step and only calls onEnable when backup-codes-close is clicked. This test still waits for the security-page switch and asserts it is checked without closing that dialog. The second test was updated to click close; this one was not, so it will fail or pass only because of the existing isChecked() quirk noted in the FIXME. It also never exercises login or disable with a backup code (the new TODO), so the feature this PR adds is untested.

title: Missing-backup-codes message points at a settings action that does not exist
body: missing_backup_codes tells the user to generate codes in settings. This PR only creates codes during 2FA setup and clears them on disable; there is no regenerate control. Users who enabled 2FA before the migration have backupCodes null and will see this error on Lost access, with no way to follow the instruction except fully disabling and re-enabling 2FA. The string should describe that actual path.

title: Backup code plus any TOTP value skips password
body: Credential login only verifies the password when totpCode is empty (the existing `user.password && !credentials.totpCode` check). The new branch then accepts a backup code whenever backupCode is non-empty and never checks the TOTP value. A caller who knows the email and one backup code can therefore sign in by also sending any non-empty totpCode (for example "000000") and omitting or faking the password. Backup codes are meant to replace the authenticator, not the password, so this is an account takeover for any CAL user who has saved a backup code.

title: Backup-code consumption is a lost-update race
body: A used backup code is cleared by reading the decrypted array, setting that index to null, and writing the whole blob back. Two overlapping logins (same code twice, or two different codes) both read the same snapshot and the later write overwrites the earlier one. The same code can therefore be redeemed twice, or a code that was just consumed is restored and can be used again. The update needs to be conditional (transaction/compare-and-swap on the stored ciphertext) and should remove the code, not leave a null slot.

title: IdP TOTP login cannot enter a backup code
body: When login is reached with the totp query param (Google/SAML users who already have 2FA), the footer is ExternalTotpFooter, which only offers Cancel, and nothing ever sets twoFactorLostAccess. The backup-code field is only rendered from the normal Lost access button, so those users cannot submit a backup code even though authorize() would accept one. Losing the authenticator locks them out of the only UI this PR adds for recovery.

title: Dismissing the dialog discards the only copy of backup codes
body: Backup codes are generated once in setup, returned only in that response, and shown only after TOTP enable succeeds. Dialog open state is still controlled by onOpenChange, and only the explicit Close button calls onEnable after reset. Escape, overlay click, or any parent close on the backup-code step dismisses the codes with no acknowledgement and no later retrieval or regeneration API. The user is left with 2FA on and no backup codes, which is exactly the lockout this feature is supposed to prevent.

title: No test that a backup code logs in or is single-use
body: The new e2e coverage only clicks download/copy/close on the setup dialog. Nothing submits a backup code at login or on disable, checks that a bad code is rejected, or checks that a used code cannot be reused. The authorize path that consumes codes (and the password-bypass case) can ship broken while these tests stay green. The enable-and-login test also never closes the new backup-code step, so it does not actually exercise the flow users hit.

title: Backup code plus any TOTP value skips the password
body: Password verification runs only when credentials.totpCode is empty (if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)). The new branch then accepts login whenever twoFactorEnabled is set and credentials.backupCode matches a stored code, and it never checks the TOTP value. A caller who knows only a backup code can send that code together with any non-empty totpCode and no password and receive a session. Backup codes are supposed to replace the authenticator, not the password, so this is a single-factor account takeover. Always verify the password on the backup-code path, and do not treat a present totpCode as proof that the password was already checked.

title: Backup code match is case-sensitive and not normalized
body: Stored codes are lowercase hex from randomBytes().toString("hex"), but the login (and the same indexOf in pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts) only strips "-" before comparing. Uppercase hex, spaces, or other separators from copy/paste or manual entry fail indexOf and are rejected as IncorrectBackupCode even when the code is correct. Normalize by removing non-alphanumerics and lowercasing before compare.

title: Backup code consumption is not atomic
body: The handler decrypts backupCodes, finds an index, then later writes the array back with that slot set to null. Two concurrent authorize calls can both read the same ciphertext, both see the code as unused, and both issue a session before either update lands. The code is therefore reusable under a race, contrary to the "exactly once" contract. Consume the code in a single conditional update (transaction or compare-and-swap on the encrypted blob) and only create the session if that update wins.

title: Download control cannot start the file download
body: The download action is a Button nested inside <a download href={backupCodesUrl}>. A click lands on the button, which does not activate the parent anchor, so the blob is never downloaded. The button also has no type="button" and no preventDefault, unlike the adjacent Close/Copy handlers, so if it sits in the enable form it will submit and call the enable API again with the previous TOTP code. Use a real anchor or a button that programmatically saves the blob, and keep it from submitting the form.

title: Error tells users to generate backup codes in settings
body: missing_backup_codes is "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." Codes are only created inside TOTP setup and there is no settings action to generate or view them later. Users who enabled 2FA before this migration, or who dismissed the one-time display, are told to do something the UI cannot do. The copy should say they must disable and re-enable 2FA (with the authenticator) to obtain codes.

title: 2FA e2e never proves a backup code can authenticate
body: After OTP confirmation the UI now stops on the backup-code screen and does not call onEnable until Close. The enable-and-login test never dismisses that screen and still asserts the switch via locator.isChecked(), which is a Promise and is always truthy. The disable test only checks that a download filename and a toast appear. Nothing submits a backup code to credentials authorize or to the disable API, so the new login and one-time-consumption paths are untested. The file's own TODO notes this gap.

title: Google Meet fallback crashes when destinationCalendar is empty
body: create() now reads mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration without a null check. If destinationCalendar is missing or [], destructuring yields undefined and this throws before any calendar or video event is created. Previously optional chaining treated a missing calendar as not Google and fell back to Cal Video. Bookings that use Google Meet with no destination calendar now fail entirely instead of falling back.

title: Collective host calendars dropped when organizer has none
body: Team destination calendars are appended with evt.destinationCalendar?.push. When neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar, the field is set to null, so the push is skipped and teamDestinationCalendars is discarded. Collective hosts who do have calendars connected never get events created, which is the case this PR is meant to fix.

title: Office 365 always writes the first host's calendar
body: createEvent ignores the credentialId now passed by EventManager and always uses destinationCalendar[0].externalId. For a collective booking, EventManager calls createEvent once per host credential, but every call targets the main host's calendar id. Secondary hosts' tokens then hit the wrong calendar (create fails) and their own calendars never receive the event. LarkCalendarService has the same [0]-only behavior in create/update/delete.

title: Organizer email is always the first destination calendar
body: createEvent inserts into the calendar matching credentialId, but the organizer attendee email is always destinationCalendar[0].externalId. On a secondary host's calendar that external id is a different Google account, so the insert can be rejected or stored with the wrong organizer. updateEvent repeats the same mistake, so reschedules rewrite every host's copy with the first host's email.

title: Update/delete calendar fallback never matches
body: When externalCalendarId is missing, updateEvent and deleteEvent search destinationCalendar for an entry whose externalId equals that same missing value, which cannot match. The old code fell back to destinationCalendar.externalId. Updates now call Google with an undefined calendarId and fail; deletes only survive because they default to "primary", which may be the wrong calendar. Any booking reference without externalCalendarId can no longer be updated.

title: Recurring cancel deletes the wrong events, repeatedly
body: The new per-reference loop still runs the recurring branch inside each reference. That branch loads every calendar credential on the booking owner and, for every remaining instance, deletes only references.find("_calendar") — the first calendar reference — not the reference currently being processed. Extra host events are never deleted, and the same first event id is deleted once per reference times every calendar credential, producing duplicate failing API calls and leaving other hosts' recurring events on their calendars.

title: Paid confirmation only creates the organizer calendar event
body: Payment success rebuilds CalendarEvent from booking.destinationCalendar or the booking owner's destination calendar only, then calls EventManager.create. Booking stores a single destinationCalendar relation (handleNewBooking connects [0]), so collective host calendars gathered at booking time are gone. Stripe's payment webhook does the same. Paid collective bookings therefore confirm with a calendar event for one host only.

title: Organization slug condition is inverted
body: Unrelated to destination calendars, the create payload changed from setting slug when team billing is disabled to setting slug only when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true. Self-hosted orgs no longer get a slug, and billing-enabled orgs now persist slug immediately instead of only requestedSlug. Organization URLs will be wrong or rejected after create.

title: Google Meet fallback crashes when destinationCalendar is empty
body: The Meet-to-Cal-Video fallback now does `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` and then reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` with no null check. If the array is missing or empty, `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is undefined and this throws before any calendar or video event is created. Bookings that use Google Meet and have no destination calendar (previously safe via optional chaining) will 500 instead of falling back to Cal Video.

title: Organizer attendee email is always the first host calendar
body: createEvent and updateEvent pick `destinationCalendar[0]` and, when that entry has an externalId, send it as the organizer attendee's email on every insert/update. EventManager now calls this once per host credential and passes the full array, while the calendarId is chosen by credentialId. Secondary hosts therefore get an event on their own calendar whose organizer email is the first host's calendar id. Google treats that field as an attendee email, so the insert can be rejected as an invalid attendee or the event is attributed to the wrong person. The organizer email must be the destination that matches this credential, or the organizer's real email.

title: Update/delete no longer fall back to a destination calendar
body: When `externalCalendarId` is missing, updateEvent and deleteEvent now do `destinationCalendar.find(cal => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)`. That comparison is against a falsy id, so it never matches, and the Google call is made with `calendarId: undefined` (delete then substitutes "primary"). Previously these methods used `destinationCalendar.externalId`. Reschedules, location edits, and cancellations that lack a stored externalCalendarId will hit the wrong calendar or fail, leaving the original event in place.

title: Outlook creates every host event on the first destination calendar
body: createEvent still ignores the credentialId CalendarManager now passes and always builds the Graph URL from `destinationCalendar[0].externalId`. For a collective booking EventManager invokes createEvent once per host credential with that host's token but the shared array. A second Outlook host therefore writes into the first host's calendar id (usually 404) or, if the first entry has no externalId, into the caller's default calendar rather than their configured destination. The same first-element-only pattern is in Lark (`CalendarService.ts` create/update/delete) and CalDAV (`packages/lib/CalendarService.ts` createEvent filter), so non-Google hosts still do not get their own events.

title: Collective host calendars dropped when organizer has none
body: Host destination calendars are appended with `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...)`. The field is set to `null` when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar, so optional chaining skips the push. Collective co-hosts who do have a calendar connected then never get an event created, which is the case this PR is meant to fix. Initialize to an array before pushing team calendars.

title: Cancelling all recurring instances drops extra host calendars
body: The new loop walks every calendar reference, but the recurring `allRemainingBookings` branch ignores that reference and, for each updated booking, does `references.find(ref => ref.type.includes("_calendar"))`. Only the first calendar reference is deleted, and the block runs once per outer reference using every calendar credential, so the first event is deleted repeatedly while other hosts' recurring events are never removed. Non-recurring cancel uses each reference's uid and credential; recurring cancel must do the same per updated booking reference.

title: Missing credential fails the entire calendar update silently
body: After the DB lookup, `updateEvent(credential, ...)` is still pushed when `credential` is undefined (deleted or no app slug). `getCalendar(undefined)` throws, the catch abandons every reference in the batch, and the previous `console.error(message)` was removed, so reschedule and location updates fail with no log. Skip a missing credential (or record that one failure) instead of failing the whole update, and keep the error log.

title: Organization slug condition was inverted
body: Unrelated to destination calendars, the create payload changed from `!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug }` to `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {}`. When team billing is off, new organizations are stored with no slug. When it is on, slug is written immediately as well as `requestedSlug`, which skips the previous "slug only after billing" behavior. This will break org URLs or billing gating and should not be in this PR.

title: Google Meet fallback crashes when destinationCalendar is empty
body: The Meet-without-Google-Calendar fallback now does `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` after destructuring `evt.destinationCalendar ?? []`. If that array is empty or missing, `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is undefined and this throws before any event is created. The previous code used optional chaining (`evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`), so bookings with no destination calendar and a Google Meet location now fail instead of falling back to Cal Video.

title: Organizer email is always the first destination calendar
body: createEvent (and updateEvent) set the Google organizer attendee email from `destinationCalendar[0]`, while the calendar written to is chosen by `credentialId`. For a collective booking EventManager calls createEvent once per host credential with the full destination array, so every host's event is created with the first host's calendar id as the organizer email. Secondary hosts can fail Google insert/update or get an event owned by the wrong identity, which is the case this PR is meant to fix.

title: Update/delete no longer fall back to a destination calendar
body: When `externalCalendarId` is missing, updateEvent and deleteEvent now do `destinationCalendar.find(cal => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)`. That comparison is against a falsy id, so it never matches, and `calendarId` becomes undefined. Previously this fell back to `destinationCalendar.externalId`. Updates and deletes for bookings that have no stored external calendar id (or a null one) are sent to Google without a calendar id and fail, leaving stale events.

title: Lark still writes only the first destination calendar
body: createEvent, createAttendees, updateEvent, and deleteEvent all take `destinationCalendar[0].externalId` and ignore the credential CalendarManager now passes in. On a collective event that array starts with the organizer, so a co-host's Lark credential tries to create or delete on the organizer's calendar id and throws "no calendar id" or a permission error. The co-host never gets their own Lark event. Office 365 createEvent and the CalDAV base service have the same first-element-only behavior, so any non-Google host is not actually supported.

title: Collective host calendars dropped when organizer has none
body: evt.destinationCalendar is set to null when neither the event type nor the organizer user has a destination calendar, and the collective branch then does `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`. Optional chaining no-ops on null, so every co-host calendar collected above is discarded. Those hosts are not invited on their calendars even though they have destination calendars configured — the exact failure this PR describes — whenever the organizer has no destination calendar.

title: Recurring cancel deletes the same event with every credential
body: The new loop walks every calendar booking reference, and the all-remaining recurring branch ignores that reference's credential. For each reference it loads every user calendar credential and, for each updated booking, deletes only the first `_calendar` reference (`find`) with that credential. One recurring series cancel therefore issues duplicate deletes of the same event id against unrelated calendars, and never targets the other hosts' references. Later instances can be left on calendars or the cancel promise set can fail.

title: updateEvent is called with an undefined credential
body: If a calendar reference has a credentialId that is not on the EventManager user and the DB lookup misses (or the credential has no app slug), `credential` stays undefined, but the code still pushes `updateEvent(credential, ...)`. getCalendar(undefined) throws, the surrounding catch returns failure for every reference, and remaining hosts' calendar events are not updated. createAllCalendarEvents guards this with `if (credential)`; the update path does not.

title: Organization slug assignment flag is inverted
body: This unrelated change flips `!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug }` to `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {}` while still writing `requestedSlug` only when billing is enabled. With billing off, the new organization is created with no slug, so its URL does not resolve. With billing on, slug is set immediately instead of only `requestedSlug`, skipping the billing gate the old condition enforced. Organization creation is broken in both configurations.

title: Webhook destinationCalendar shape is now inconsistent
body: CalendarEvent.destinationCalendar changed from a single object or null to an array, and handlers do not agree on the empty value: confirm/cancel send `[]`, while other payloads still emit `null` (the BOOKING_CREATED and BOOKING_REQUESTED webhook tests still expect null; only BOOKING_REJECTED was updated to []). Subscribers that read `payload.destinationCalendar.integration` or `externalId` will throw, and clients cannot rely on one type. The PR is marked non-breaking, but this is a webhook contract change.

title: Salesforce refresh writes credentials without importing prisma
body: getClient now always calls prisma.credential.update after refreshing the Salesforce token, but prisma is never imported in this file. The first time a Salesforce calendar service is constructed, that reference throws ReferenceError and calendar create/update/delete all fail. The refresh also runs on every client construction even when the stored access token is still valid, so a transient token-endpoint failure now breaks Salesforce for the request instead of letting jsforce refresh lazily.

title: Refreshed Salesforce token is not the one used
body: After a successful token refresh, the new access token is written to the database, but the jsforce Connection is still constructed with credentialKey.access_token (the pre-refresh value) and credentialKey.instance_url. The in-memory client therefore keeps using the expired access token for the current booking/sync operation. This path also never goes through refreshOAuthTokens, so CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT is ignored for Salesforce even when credential sharing is enabled.

title: Google refresh persists the Zod parse wrapper as the credential
body: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a safeParse result ({ success, data }), but the Google refresh path stores that whole object in credential.key. Previously googleCredentialSchema.parse returned the token object itself. After the next token refresh, the stored key no longer matches googleCredentialSchema, so later Google Calendar calls fail schema parse and the real access/refresh tokens are overwritten in the database.

title: Refresh parser injects a fake refresh token and cannot validate sync payloads
body: If the parsed payload has no refresh_token, this helper sets refresh_token to the literal string "refresh_token" and returns it for callers to persist. Office 365 (and any provider that omits refresh_token on refresh) will overwrite the real refresh token with that placeholder, so the next refresh fails with invalid_grant. The sharing-mode schema is also wrong: computed keys are z.string().toString() / z.string().optional().toString() (strings like "ZodString"), not a catchall, and z.object strips unknown keys. Real sync responses therefore either fail validation or are saved without expiry_date, expires_in, and refresh_token.

title: Sync refresh returns a raw fetch Response that callers cannot consume
body: When credential sync is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns the fetch Response and never reads JSON or checks response.ok. Callers were not updated to a single shape: Google reads res.data (axios-style), HubSpot/Zoho read .data.accessToken/.expiresIn/.error, and Lark/Webex/Zoom/Office pass the value to helpers that expect either a provider-specific JSON body or a Response whose JSON matches that provider. With sync on, token refresh throws or writes undefined tokens. The POST also sends no auth header and no Content-Type, so a typical JSON sync endpoint will not even accept the body.

title: Zoho Bigin sync sends credential id as the Cal user id
body: refreshAccessToken calls refreshOAuthTokens with credentialId as the third argument, but that argument is documented and used as calcomUserId. When CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT is set, the parent app is asked for tokens for the wrong id (or no user), so Bigin refresh returns another user's tokens or fails, and those tokens can be stored on this credential.

title: Zoom sync uses app slug zoomvideo instead of zoom
body: Credential rows and the OAuth callback use appId "zoom", but refreshOAuthTokens is called with appSlug "zoomvideo". A sync endpoint that keys off the app slug used by the webhook (appMetadata.slug / "zoom") will not find the Zoom credential and will fail or return the wrong app's tokens during meeting creation.

title: Credential webhook can create duplicate rows and has no error handling
body: The handler does findFirst then create/update with no transaction or unique constraint. Concurrent webhook deliveries for the same user and app both see no row and insert two credentials; later findFirst updates only one, so calendar code that also uses findFirst can keep using a stale token. zod parse, symmetricDecrypt, and JSON.parse are uncaught, so a bad payload becomes an unstructured 500. The secret check is a plain !== (timing-leaky, and an array header value never matches).

title: No tests for credential sync or the changed refresh paths
body: The PR adds an unauthenticated-except-for-a-shared-secret endpoint that writes OAuth secrets, and it changes token refresh for Google, Office 365, Zoom, Salesforce, and others. The author notes tests were not added. There is no coverage that the webhook rejects a bad secret, decrypts and upserts a credential, or that a normal (sync disabled) refresh still persists a provider token object rather than a Zod wrapper or the string "refresh_token".

title: OAuth helper imports decodeOAuthState from a path that does not exist
body: After the move into `_utils/oauth/`, `createOAuthAppCredential` imports `decodeOAuthState` from `../oauth/decodeOAuthState`. From this file that resolves to `_utils/oauth/oauth/decodeOAuthState`, which is not a module. Every callback that creates credentials through this helper (HubSpot, Salesforce, Stripe, Zoom, Webex, MS Teams, Zoho, Tandem, and others) will fail to load or throw at runtime, so those OAuth installs cannot complete.

title: Google token refresh persists the Zod result instead of the credential
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns a Zod safe-parse object `{ success, data }`, but Google Calendar assigns that whole object to `key` and writes it with `prisma.credential.update`. Previously the stored key was the parsed token object. On the next refresh (credential sync on or off) the credential row is replaced with that wrapper, so later `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` fails and Google Calendar stops working for that user.

title: Missing refresh tokens are replaced with the literal string "refresh_token"
body: If the parsed body has no `refresh_token`, this function sets `data.refresh_token` to the string `"refresh_token"`. Callers then persist that value. Office 365 spreads the parsed object over the saved credential (`o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }`), so a Microsoft refresh that omits `refresh_token` overwrites the real refresh token. The sync minimum schema also strips unknown fields, so a real refresh token is dropped and this dummy is written. Later refreshes send `refresh_token=refresh_token` and the integration is permanently invalidated.

title: Sync token schema does not accept an expiry field
body: The computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` are literal property names from Zod's `toString()`, not a catch-all for numeric expiry. Zod object schemas also strip unknown keys. When credential sync is enabled, a normal token body such as `{ access_token, expires_in }` parses, but `expires_in`/`expiry_date` are removed before the result is saved. Integrations then treat the token as already expired or cannot compute expiry, and refresh loops or fails.

title: Sync refresh returns a fetch Response that callers do not parse
body: When sync is enabled this returns the raw `fetch` Response. Google reads `res.data` (axios-style) and never calls `response.json()`, so `token.access_token` is undefined. HubSpot, Zoho CRM, and Zoho Bigin expect an axios response and read `.accessToken` / `.data` / `.expiresIn` on that fetch Response. Those fields are missing, so the sync path the PR adds cannot refresh tokens and will throw or write garbage credentials.

title: Zoho Bigin sync sends credential id as the Cal user id
body: `refreshAccessToken` passes `credentialId` (the credential row id) as the third argument to `refreshOAuthTokens`. That argument is posted as `calcomUserId`. The parent app therefore looks up the wrong user and returns another user's tokens or no tokens, and those tokens can be stored on this credential.

title: Zoom refresh uses app slug zoomvideo instead of zoom
body: The Zoom app id/slug used everywhere else in this change (callback `appId: "zoom"`, webhook lookup) is `zoom`, but `refreshOAuthTokens` is called with `"zoomvideo"`. A credential-sync endpoint keyed by app slug will not find the Zoom installation, so Zoom refresh fails whenever sync is enabled.

title: Salesforce refresh calls prisma without importing it and ignores the new access token
body: The new refresh block calls `prisma.credential.update`, but this file never imports `prisma`, so constructing a Salesforce client throws ReferenceError and Salesforce events fail. Even if prisma were imported, the `jsforce.Connection` is still created with `credentialKey.access_token` (the pre-refresh token) rather than `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`, so the in-memory client keeps using the expired token. This refresh also always hits `https://login.salesforce.com` and does not go through `refreshOAuthTokens`, so sandbox orgs and the new sync endpoint are both skipped.

title: Webhook secret check is bypassed when the secret env var is unset
body: The handler compares `req.headers[headerName] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. If `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` is unset, that is `undefined !== undefined` when the header is also absent, so the check passes. `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` is only a module-load snapshot of the env and is not rechecked here against the secret actually used for the comparison. An unauthenticated caller can then decrypt with an empty key fallback (`symmetricDecrypt(..., "")`) and create or overwrite a user's app credential JSON, including OAuth tokens.

title: Credential upsert races and can attach tokens to the wrong row
body: The handler does `findFirst` by `userId` + `appId` and then either updates that id or creates a new row. Concurrent webhook deliveries for the same user and app both miss and insert duplicates. `findFirst` also has no `type` or team filter and no order, so if a user already has more than one credential for that app the update can overwrite an arbitrary one and leave the credential the calendar/video adapters actually load stale or replaced with another account's tokens.

title: Google refresh persists the Zod result and corrupts credentials
body: After every Google token refresh, the code assigns `key` to the return value of `parseRefreshTokenResponse` and writes that object to `credential.key`. That helper returns the Zod safeParse result (`{ success, data }`), not the credential payload. Previously this path stored `googleCredentialSchema.parse(...)`. The next calendar use calls `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` and fails, so a normal token refresh (syncing disabled) permanently breaks that user's Google Calendar connection until the app is reconnected.

title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token"
body: If the parsed token body has no `refresh_token`, this helper sets `data.refresh_token` to the string `"refresh_token"` and returns that object. Office 365's refresh schema treats `refresh_token` as optional because Microsoft often omits it and expects the client to keep the existing one; `Office365CalendarService` then spreads `tokenResponse.data` over the stored credential and saves it. The real refresh token is overwritten with the placeholder, so the next refresh fails and the Outlook connection is dead. The same placeholder is copied onto Zoom tokens whenever the sync parser is used.

title: Sync token schema cannot accept a real token response
body: When credential sync is enabled, refresh bodies are validated with `minimumTokenResponseSchema`. The computed keys `z.string().toString()` and `z.string().optional().toString()` are the literal property names of those Zod types (e.g. "ZodString"), not a catchall, and Zod objects strip unknown keys by default. A normal `{ access_token, expires_in }` body therefore fails validation and every synced refresh throws "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". Even a passing parse would drop `expires_in`, so callers such as Zoom that do `Date.now() + expires_in * 1000` would store `NaN` and immediately treat the token as expired.

title: Sync refresh returns a raw fetch Response that callers cannot use
body: When syncing is on, this helper returns the `fetch` Response and does not check `response.ok`, set `Content-Type`, or parse JSON. Callers were not updated to that shape: Google reads `res.data` (undefined on a Response, so the refresh throws and can mark the credential invalid), HubSpot treats the Response as a token and computes `expiryDate` from `expiresIn` (NaN) before `setAccessToken(undefined)`, and Zoho Bigin/Zoho CRM read `tokenInfo.data` as if it were an axios response. Lark still runs `handleLarkError` expecting a Lark envelope, but the comment says the sync endpoint returns only an access token and expiry. Token refresh for those apps fails as soon as `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is set, which is the documented test path.

title: Salesforce client refresh calls prisma without importing it and keeps the old access token
body: `getClient` now always POSTs to `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` and then calls `prisma.credential.update`, but `prisma` is not imported in this file, so constructing a Salesforce calendar service throws ReferenceError before any event work. The new access token is also never passed into `jsforce.Connection` (`accessToken` stays `credentialKey.access_token`). This runs for every Salesforce credential, including when sync is disabled, and hardcoding `login.salesforce.com` fails sandbox and My Domain orgs that previously relied on the stored `instance_url`. It also never calls `refreshOAuthTokens`, so credential sync does not apply to Salesforce.

title: Zoho Bigin sync sends credential id as calcomUserId
body: `refreshAccessToken` calls `refreshOAuthTokens` with `credentialId` as the third argument. That argument is sent as `calcomUserId` to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`. The parent app will look up the wrong user (or none) and return another user's tokens or an error, so Bigin refresh cannot succeed in sync mode. Other adapters correctly pass `credential.userId`.

title: Zoom sync uses app slug zoomvideo instead of zoom
body: The refresh call passes `"zoomvideo"` as `appSlug`, but Zoom credentials are stored and addressed everywhere else as app id `"zoom"` (see the OAuth callback and the webhook's `appSlug` lookup). A self-hoster syncing by app slug will not find the Zoom credential and will refresh the wrong app or fail.

title: Credential webhook can duplicate or leave stale invalid credentials
body: The handler does `findFirst` by `userId` + `appId` and then create-or-update with no transaction and no `invalid: false`. Concurrent deliveries can both miss the row and insert two credentials; later reads use `findFirst` and ignore the other. An update of a credential already marked `invalid` keeps `invalid: true`, so synced tokens are never used. `schema.parse` and `symmetricDecrypt`/`JSON.parse` are also uncaught, so a bad body or ciphertext becomes an unhandled 500 instead of 4xx, and there is no method check so non-POST requests are processed the same way.

title: Team admin/owner check requires both roles
body: isTeamAdminOrOwner is computed with && between isTeamAdmin and isTeamOwner, so the caller must be both admin and owner of the event type's team. A team admin who is not an owner, or an owner who is not an admin, is treated as unauthorized and cannot add guests unless they are also the booking user or an attendee. The variable name and the intended permission are OR. When eventType.teamId is null the code also queries team id 0, which will never match a real team.

title: Any attendee can add guests; host restrictions ignored
body: Authorization succeeds for any logged-in user whose email matches an attendee on the booking, with no check that the event type allows guests (disableGuests) and no check that the booking is accepted and upcoming. A booker (or a compromised attendee account) can therefore append arbitrary emails, persist them as attendees, and have the meeting details—including videoCallData url/password—emailed to those addresses, bypassing the booker-side guest disable setting. The mutation is also unbounded: ZAddGuestsInputSchema does not cap guests.length, so one call can create and email a very large attendee list.

title: Calendar update uses the caller's credentials, not the host's
body: updateCalendarAttendees is invoked with an EventManager built from ctx.user and getUsersCredentials(ctx.user). The booking query already loads booking.user.credentials and destinationCalendar, but those are never passed to EventManager. When a team member (or attendee) adds guests, the calendar write runs as that caller. The organizer's connected calendar is not updated, and the caller's own calendar may be written instead, so the new attendees never appear on the host event (or the wrong calendar is mutated).

title: Guest dedupe and blacklist are case-sensitive
body: uniqueGuests drops an address only when guest === attendee.email exactly, and the blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing only the env list. 'Guest@x.com' is therefore not treated as a duplicate of 'guest@x.com' and is not blocked if the blacklist entry is 'guest@x.com'. createMany then inserts the mixed-case row, so the same person can be added twice and a blocklist entry can be bypassed by changing letter case. The schema also does not require unique emails, so two identical strings in one request both pass the filter and are inserted.

title: Emails use the raw guest list, not the guests actually added
body: sendAddGuestsEmails is called with the original guests array, not uniqueGuests. sendAddGuestsEmails treats any attendee whose email is in that list as a brand-new invitee and sends AttendeeScheduledEmail (a new-booking confirmation plus an ICS REQUEST) instead of AttendeeAddGuestsEmail. Re-submitting an existing attendee, or including an address that was filtered only as a duplicate, therefore sends that person a second booking confirmation and a second calendar invite. Filtered-out addresses also still influence which template existing attendees receive.

title: Add-guest mail ignores disable-standard-emails settings
body: sendAddGuestsEmails always emails the organizer, every team member, and every attendee. Unlike sendScheduledEmails, sendLocationChangeEmails, and the other booking mailers, it never consults eventType metadata disableStandardEmails for host or attendee. Hosts who turned off standard booking emails still get these messages, and attendees who were opted out still receive both the 'guests added' notice and a full scheduled-email invite for new guests.

title: Seated bookings get raw attendee rows, not seats
body: Guests are inserted with attendees.createMany and the handler copies seatsPerTimeSlot onto the calendar event but never creates BookingSeat / seat-reference rows or checks remaining capacity. On a seated event type, attendance is tracked via seats, not free-form attendees. This can overfill the slot, omit the new people from seat-based emails and cancellation, and leave attendee rows that the seats UI does not treat as booked seats.

title: Team admin/owner check requires both roles
body: isTeamAdminOrOwner is computed with && between isTeamAdmin and isTeamOwner. A team admin who is not also the owner (and an owner who is not also returned as admin) fails the check and gets FORBIDDEN unless they are the booking user or an attendee. The bookings UI treats admin and owner as alternative roles (isUserTeamAdminOrOwner), so team admins cannot add guests on bookings they are allowed to manage.

title: Calendar update uses the actor's credentials, not the organizer's
body: updateCalendarAttendees is run with EventManager built from ctx.user and getUsersCredentials(ctx.user). The booking already loads booking.user.credentials, but they are ignored. When a team admin or an attendee (both explicitly authorized) adds guests, the organizer's calendar event is updated with the wrong user's integrations, so the invite is not updated on the host calendar (or is applied to the actor's calendar). Guests are already written to the DB before this call, so a failure also leaves attendees and calendars out of sync.

title: Guest dedupe and blacklist are case-sensitive
body: BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS entries are lowercased, but each guest is compared with includes(guest) and with attendee.email using strict equality. Zod's email() does not normalize case, so a blocked address submitted with different casing bypasses the blacklist, and the same person can be inserted again as another attendee (duplicate calendar invites and emails).

title: Emails are keyed off the raw guest list, not the guests actually added
body: sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests) is passed the original input, not uniqueGuests. In sendAddGuestsEmails, any attendee whose email is in that list gets AttendeeScheduledEmail (a new-booking confirmation with a fresh invite) instead of AttendeeAddGuestsEmail. Re-submitting an existing attendee, or a case-mismatched address that was filtered out of the insert, therefore sends the wrong email and ICS to people who were already on the booking.

title: No status, seat, or capacity checks before inserting attendees
body: The handler updates any booking by id after the permission check. Cancelled, rejected, and pending bookings can gain attendees, and seated event types (seatsPerTimeSlot is only copied onto the calendar payload) get extra Attendee rows with empty names and no seat reference or capacity check. That overbooks the slot, breaks seat-based cancel/reschedule (which keys off seatsReferences), and still triggers calendar updates and emails.

title: Custom email title/subject are overwritten by props spread
body: Both AttendeeAddGuestsEmail and OrganizerAddGuestsEmail set title, subject, headerType, and (organizer) callToAction, then spread {...props} afterward. Those props are ComponentProps of the scheduled-email components, which already include title/subject/callToAction. Any caller or renderEmail default that passes those fields replaces new_guests_added / guests_added_event_type_subject / callToAction={null}, so the HTML body is a normal scheduled-event email instead of a guests-added notice. Put the overrides after the spread.

title: Team admin/owner check requires both roles
body: isTeamAdminOrOwner is computed with && between isTeamAdmin and isTeamOwner. A team admin who is not also the owner (and an owner who is not also an admin) is treated as unauthorized. Unless that user is the booking host or already an attendee, addGuests throws FORBIDDEN, so the people who manage team event types cannot add guests.

title: Calendar update uses the caller's credentials, not the host's
body: updateCalendarAttendees is invoked with an EventManager built from ctx.user and getUsersCredentials(ctx.user). The mutation also allows attendees (and is intended to allow team admins) to add guests, and the booking query already loads the host's credentials but never uses them. When the caller is not the host, the organizer's destination calendar is updated with the wrong user's integrations, so the invite is not updated or a different calendar is written.

title: Guest dedupe and blacklist are case-sensitive
body: Existing attendees are excluded with guest === attendee.email, and BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS is lowercased but the submitted guest is not. Mixed-case copies of an existing attendee are inserted again, and a blacklisted address can be added by changing letter case. Those addresses are then stored and included in calendar and email fan-out, including the meeting link.

title: Emails are keyed off the raw guest list, not the guests actually added
body: sendAddGuestsEmails is called with the original guests array after uniqueGuests has already dropped duplicates and blacklisted addresses. In sendAddGuestsEmails, any attendee whose email is in that raw list is sent AttendeeScheduledEmail (a new-booking confirmation) instead of AttendeeAddGuestsEmail. Re-submitting an existing attendee therefore sends them a fresh scheduling email and ICS REQUEST, while the database insert skipped them.

title: Attendees are committed before calendar/email, so a failed retry cannot finish the job
body: booking.update createMany runs before updateCalendarAttendees and sendAddGuestsEmails, with no transaction. If the calendar update throws, the mutation fails after the rows exist and emails never send. A retry then filters those emails out as already present, hits uniqueGuests.length === 0, and throws BAD_REQUEST, so the calendar and notifications stay permanently out of date.

title: No checks for booking status, disableGuests, or seat capacity
body: Any organizer, attendee, or (broken) team admin can add an unbounded guest list to any booking id, including cancelled, rejected, and past bookings, and event types with guests disabled. Seated event types are not checked against seatsPerTimeSlot or BookingSeat; guests are inserted as normal attendees and then emailed the video URL. That bypasses event-type policy and can overfill seated events or leak meeting links from cancelled bookings.

title: Add-guest emails ignore disableStandardEmails
body: sendAddGuestsEmails always emails the organizer, every team member, and every attendee. Sibling helpers (sendLocationChangeEmails, sendScheduledEmails, etc.) skip host or attendee mail when event type metadata sets disableStandardEmails. This path never receives that metadata, so event types that disabled standard mail still blast new-guest and full scheduled emails, including ICS attachments.

title: Retry cleanup deletes every WorkflowReminder, not just failed SMS
body: The new deleteMany OR branch matches retryCount > 1 with no method, scheduled: false, or scheduledDate constraint. WorkflowReminder is shared by EMAIL, SMS, and WHATSAPP, and this job runs as the SMS cron. Any non-SMS row that reaches retryCount > 1 (or an SMS row that is already scheduled: true with a Twilio referenceId) is deleted on the next run. That drops the record used to track or cancel the provider message, and it does not match the PR intent of deleting only SMS reminders that failed to schedule twice.

title: Missing phone or empty body never counts as a failed attempt
body: retryCount is only incremented when twilio.scheduleSMS returns a falsy value or throws. If sendTo is missing/empty or the rendered message is empty, the reminder is skipped with scheduled left false and retryCount unchanged. Those rows stay in the unscheduled query and are retried on every cron until scheduledDate is in the past, which is the infinite reschedule this PR is meant to stop (including invalid or absent phone numbers that never reach Twilio).

title: Retry update inside catch can abort the rest of the batch
body: The new workflowReminder.update in the catch is not itself guarded. If that update throws (row already removed by a concurrent cron's deleteMany, or a transient DB error), the exception leaves the catch and the handler stops. Reminders later in unscheduledReminders are never scheduled, and the route fails instead of logging and continuing, which is what the catch did before.

title: retryCount is a lost-update read-modify-write
body: Both failure paths set retryCount to the value loaded at the start of the request (reminder.retryCount + 1) instead of an atomic increment. Overlapping cron runs can both read 0 and both write 1, so the gt: 1 deletion never triggers and failed SMS reminders keep being rescheduled. Use an atomic increment so concurrent failures still reach the retry limit.

title: No test covers retry limit or the widened delete
body: The cron now deletes reminders by retryCount and mutates retryCount on Twilio failure, but nothing asserts that two failures delete only the failed unscheduled SMS row, that a successful schedule is kept, or that EMAIL/WHATSAPP rows are untouched. That deletion is easy to get wrong (the OR is already unscoped) and will not be caught before production.

title: Retry cleanup deletes every reminder type, not just SMS
body: The new deleteMany OR branch matches retryCount > 1 with no method (or scheduled) filter. WorkflowReminder is shared by EMAIL, SMS, and WHATSAPP, and this cron now deletes any of those rows once retryCount exceeds 1, including future reminders that were never part of this SMS job. That drops unrelated workflow reminders and, if a row was already handed to a provider, removes the only referenceId needed to cancel it. Scope the clause to unscheduled SMS reminders (method SMS and scheduled false), matching the comment and the PR intent.

title: Unsendable SMS reminders never increment retryCount
body: retryCount is only increased when twilio.scheduleSMS returns falsy or throws. If sendTo is missing or the message is empty, the if block is skipped and the row stays scheduled: false with retryCount 0. The cron will keep selecting that reminder on every run until scheduledDate is in the past, which is the infinite reschedule this PR is meant to stop (for example a booking with no attendee phone number). Count that path as a failed attempt, or delete it, so it cannot spin until the event date.

title: Catch treats a successful Twilio schedule as a failed retry
body: The new retryCount update sits in a catch that wraps both twilio.scheduleSMS and the following prisma update that stores scheduled and referenceId. If the provider accepts the message and the DB update then fails, the catch increments retryCount, leaves scheduled false, and never saves the SID. The next cron schedules a duplicate SMS, and after two such failures the opening deleteMany removes the row while Twilio still has the message queued and there is no referenceId left to cancel it. Only increment retryCount when scheduleSMS itself fails, and do not count a post-success persistence error as an exhausted attempt.

title: retryCount increment is a lost update
body: Both failure paths write retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 from the value read at the start of the run instead of an atomic increment. Overlapping cron invocations can each read the same count, each call Twilio, and each write the same next value, so the gt: 1 deletion never trips and duplicate SMS can be scheduled. Use Prisma's increment so concurrent failures cannot collapse to one count.

title: retryCount cleanup deletes every method, including already scheduled reminders
body: deleteMany's second OR branch matches only retryCount > 1 and does not constrain method to SMS or scheduled to false. WorkflowReminder is shared by EMAIL and WHATSAPP as well as SMS, and a row can be scheduled: true with a Twilio referenceId while still having retryCount > 1 (a later failed attempt only writes retryCount). The next cron run therefore permanently deletes those rows. Already-queued SMS can no longer be cancelled or reconciled, and any non-SMS reminder that ever exceeds one retry is removed even though this job is only supposed to drop failed SMS reminders.

title: retryCount is a lost-update read-modify-write
body: Both failure paths set retryCount to the value loaded at the start of the loop (reminder.retryCount + 1) instead of an atomic increment. Overlapping cron runs that both read the same count and both fail write the same number back, so the counter can stay at 1 forever. Those reminders are never deleted by the retryCount > 1 cleanup and are rescheduled on every run until scheduledDate passes — the leak this PR is meant to stop. The same non-atomic update in the catch block is unguarded; if a concurrent run already deleted the row, Prisma throws and the exception leaves the for-loop, so the handler 500s and skips every remaining reminder in the batch.

title: Missing number or empty body never counts as a failed attempt
body: retryCount is only increased when scheduleSMS returns falsy or throws. If sendTo is missing or the rendered message is empty, the loop neither schedules nor increments and leaves scheduled false. The next cron selects the same row again, so those reminders are retried until scheduledDate is in the past. That is the same unbounded reschedule the PR describes, and it is not covered by the new retry limit.

title: No test for retry limit or the widened delete
body: The cron now deletes workflow reminders and gives up after two scheduling failures, but the PR adds no test for the retryCount > 1 predicate, the method/scheduled scope of that delete, or the increment on a falsy scheduleSMS result versus a missing sendTo. A wrong OR (as written) silently drops live reminders and would not be caught before merge.

title: OR authorization SQL is not a single parenthesized predicate
body: buildOrgAuthorizationCondition and buildTeamAuthorizationCondition return `(team predicate) OR (user predicate)` with no outer parentheses (the reduce at lines 171-174 and 204-207). getAuthorizationConditions is now the public fragment callers interpolate after findMany was removed. `WHERE <other> AND ${auth}` parses as `(other AND teamBranch) OR userBranch` because AND binds tighter than OR, so the personal-booking branch ignores every predicate the caller ANDs on the left (date range, status, tenant, extra auth). That returns rows outside the intended scope. Wrap the whole OR (and any other returned fragment) in one parenthesis group before returning it.

title: Prisma.sql toEqual assertions do not match nested Sql objects
body: Team scope (line 295), org scope (line 332), and combined filters (line 429) expect one flat Prisma.sql template, but the service builds those strings by nesting Prisma.sql inside reduce (`(${acc}) OR/AND (${condition})`). Prisma.Sql equality is structural: nested fragments stay as child Sql values with a different `strings` array, so vitest toEqual fails even when the flattened SQL text and bound parameters are what the test author intended. These cases never execute against the database either, so a red run does not tell you whether ANY(${number[]}) is valid. Compare flattened SQL text plus values, or build the expected Sql with the same nesting, and run the team/org fragments through $queryRaw.

title: ANY() over JS arrays will fail at query time
body: Org and team authorization SQL is built as `"teamId" = ANY(${teamIds})` and `"userId" = ANY(${uniqueUserIds})` (also lines 168 and 201). Prisma.sql binds a JavaScript array as one untyped parameter; PostgreSQL then rejects `integer = ANY($1)` (typically "operator does not exist: integer = text" or a malformed-array error) instead of treating it as an int[]. The previous Prisma `in` filters did not have this problem. Team and org insights queries will throw whenever those scopes run, and no test executes them — the only `$queryRaw` case is user scope, which does not use ANY(). Use `IN (${Prisma.join(ids)})` or an explicit `int[]` cast.

title: SQL assertions do not match nested Prisma.sql the service returns
body: Team, org, and combined-filter tests (lines 295, 332, and 429) expect one flat Prisma.sql template via toEqual. The service joins fragments with reduce, so the Sql object has nested Sql values and different `strings`, not the flat parameter list the tests build. Those assertions fail even when the SQL text would be equivalent, which matches the PR note that the suite was never run. The org case is also order-sensitive: it hardcodes `[org, team, team2, team3]` and `[user, user2, user3]`, but `findAllByParentId` / `findAllByTeamIds` do not guarantee that order, so a corrected comparison would still flake. None of these cases hit the database, so the broken ANY() queries above stay untested.

title: ANY() over JS arrays will fail at query time
