This change makes the resolved string also depend on SiteSetting.default_locale, because a key missing from the current locale is filled from the site default (then English) and that resolved string is what gets stored. default_locale is an admin setting that updates in-process without a restart, and nothing here includes the fallback locale in the cache key or clears @cache when it changes (I18n.reload! would clear it, but setting updates do not call that). Hot no-arg keys stay in the 300-entry LRU indefinitely, so after the default locale changes, users missing those keys keep seeing strings from the previous default locale until the worker is restarted.

title: No coverage for fallback order or on-demand loading
body: The custom chain [requested locale, SiteSetting.default_locale, :en] and the ensure_loaded! hook ship with no specs. Nothing asserts that a missing key resolves to the site locale before English, that the fallback YAML is actually loaded before lookup, or that translations outside ApplicationController#set_locale (jobs, mailers, I18n.with_locale) fall back at all. Those non-request paths are exactly where fallback files are not loaded, so the failure would not be caught before merge.

title: Fallback locales are not loaded on the translation path
body: Fallback YAML is loaded only from ApplicationController#set_locale (I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!). I18n.translate still only calls load_locale for the current I18n.locale, and the freedom patch's load_translations no-ops unless given explicit filenames, so I18n::Backend::Fallbacks cannot load a missing fallback locale itself. Jobs, mailers, I18n.with_locale, and I18n.t(..., locale:) therefore resolve keys that are missing in the active locale as missing instead of falling back to SiteSetting.default_locale and then :en. Non-interpolated results are stored in the process-wide LRU (the getset at the cache key built just below), so a later call that does load those files still serves the cached missing or wrong string. Server-side fallbacks fail for the email and notification paths that need them, and can poison web workers that share the cache.

title: Translation cache ignores the fallback locale
body: Cached translations are keyed only by key, current locale, and backend object id. FallbackLocaleList now resolves missing keys using SiteSetting.default_locale, which can change at runtime and, on multisite, differs per site, but nothing includes that locale in the key or clears @cache (I18n.reload! is what nils the cache, and changing the site locale does not call it). After an admin changes the default locale, or when two sites with different default locales share a process, hot no-argument lookups keep returning the previous fallback language for the life of the size-300 LRU working set. Interpolated calls skip the cache, but most UI and email strings do not.

title: Negative checks reload full permissions from the DB per resource
body: Check only returns early when the cached permission set allows the request (line 131). Any cache hit that does not allow, and any cache miss, falls through to getIdentityPermissions, and the in-function cache read was removed from getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions, so that call always runs GetUserPermissions and reloads the user's full permission set. The new denial cache only suppresses a repeat of the exact same user, action, name, and parent. After that reload refreshes permCache, the next Check for a different resource this user cannot access still misses the denial cache, fails the scope check, and starts another full permission query. singleflight collapses only overlapping calls for the same user and action; once that call returns, the next distinct name queries again. Sequential authz of many dashboards or folders therefore becomes one DB permission load per denied resource per TTL instead of one load per user per action per 30s. In-proc clients now use NoopCache, so they no longer absorb repeats either. Random UIDs (including anonymous GETs) bypass the denial cache and can drive unbounded permission queries. Trust a negative result while the cached permission set is still fresh, and bypass it at most once per TTL rather than once per resource.

title: Denial cache pins non-authoritative denies for 30s and overrides later allows
body: Check returns Allowed=false immediately when permDenialCache contains the key, before consulting cached or current permissions. On any successful deny after the DB path, line 154 stores that denial for shortCacheTTL (30s) and nothing deletes it when a later permission reload would allow the same resource. The denial also wins over a positive permCache entry, so List (which uses the permission cache) can show a resource that Check still denies. This is not limited to authoritative DB denies: checkPermission returns false when the cached folder tree does not yet contain a newly created parent, so an ancestor folder grant is recorded as a denial and keeps failing after the folder cache would have allowed it. getUserPermissions is singleflighted and does not re-read after the in-flight query, so a Check that joins a permission load started before a create/grant can observe the pre-grant snapshot and then pin that stale deny for 30s. That recreates the creator-cannot-open-the-new-dashboard failure, and it extends false denies past permission-cache expiry when a grant follows an earlier deny. Do not write a denial when the result depends on a stale folder tree or a shared in-flight snapshot, and invalidate denial entries whenever permissions are reloaded.

title: Denial cache key collides for UIDs that contain underscores
body: userPermDenialCacheKey joins name and parent with '_' (namespace.perm_<user>_<action>_<name>_<parent>). Dashboard and folder UIDs may contain underscores, and those two fields sit next to each other, so different pairs encode to the same key. For example name "a_b" with parent "c" and name "a" with parent "b_c" both end in _a_b_c for the same user and action. The cache only stores negatives, so a deny for one resource is returned for the other for 30s without checking permissions, and a user who can access one of them is incorrectly denied. Use an unambiguous encoding (length prefixes, a delimiter that cannot appear in UIDs, or a hash).

title: List still serves stale permissions for newly created dashboards and folders
body: List now returns getCachedIdentityPermissions on a hit and only calls getIdentityPermissions on a miss. Check was changed so a cached set that does not include the requested resource is reloaded from the DB, but List still treats the cached set as complete for the whole shortCacheTTL (30s). A creator whose permission cache was filled before the create will not see the new dashboard or folder in list results until that entry expires, which is the failure this PR describes for any caller that fetches via List rather than Check. Use the same freshness rule as Check, or invalidate the permission cache when a dashboard or folder permission is created.

title: Denial-cache test still passes if the short-circuit is removed
body: TestService_CacheCheck subtest "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" claims the permission-cache fixture allows dash1 so that only the denial cache can explain the deny. The fixture is map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}. checkPermission treats a false or missing scope as not allowed, and setupService's fake store returns no permissions, so Check still returns Allowed=false if the permDenialCache lookup is deleted. The comment says the entry allows access, but the value is false. Set that scope to true and assert the permission store is not called, otherwise a regression of the deny short-circuit is invisible.

title: Denial cache key collides across identities
body: Check builds the new denial-cache key from the raw subject id only (namespace, user UID, action, name, folder) and never includes the identity type or the resolved user UID. Anonymous and render subjects are both "…:0", so they share one key, and a hit returns Allowed=false before renderer or anonymous permissions are evaluated. A denied anonymous dashboards:read Check therefore makes the image renderer, which is hard-coded to be allowed dashboards:read and folders:read, get Allowed=false for that same name and folder for shortCacheTTL (30s). Repeating the anonymous check keeps rendering broken. The same raw id also conflates subject forms this service otherwise treats as distinct, such as a numeric user id versus a UID string.

title: Undelimited denial key collides across resources
body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates action, name, and parent with underscores and does not escape them. Dashboard and folder UIDs may contain underscores, so different checks produce the same key: name "a_b" with an empty folder and name "a" with folder "b" both end in "_a_b_". Check treats any denial-cache hit as Allowed=false and does not consult the permission cache or the database. A deny for one pair therefore denies the other pair for 30s even when the user has that permission.

title: Denial cache hides grants already reloaded into the permission cache
body: A denial entry is consulted before the permission cache and before the database fallback added to see new creator permissions, and nothing deletes it when permissions are refreshed. getUserPermissions replaces the cached scope map on every reload but does not drop denial keys. After a grant, a Check for some other resource can reload permissions and observe the new scope, yet a follow-up Check for a resource denied earlier still returns Allowed=false until the denial TTL (30s) expires. That skips the requery this PR added. It also sticks when a Check runs before the creator permission is committed, including waiters on an in-flight singleflight permission fetch in getUserPermissions that started before the insert: those callers share the stale miss and then denial-cache the new dashboard or folder.

title: Stale folder-tree misses are cached as denials
body: When the cached scope map does not allow the resource, Check reloads permissions and calls checkPermission. Folder inheritance still uses buildFolderTree, which returns the cached tree for up to 30s and is not bypassed on this path. If the parent folder was created after that fill, the tree has no parent pointer, so an ancestor grant is not found and checkPermission returns false. Check then stores a denial for 30s. Previously, folder-cache expiry alone let the next Check rebuild the tree and allow access from the already cached ancestor scope. The denial is now served first and skips both the permission cache and a tree rebuild, so inherited access to resources in newly created folders stays denied after the folder cache is no longer stale.

title: Every distinct deny reloads the full permission set
body: If the denial cache misses and the cached scope map does not already allow the resource, Check always calls getIdentityPermissions. The cache short-circuit was removed from getUserPermissions and getAnonymousPermissions, so each of those calls queries the database (plus team and basic-role lookups) inside singleflight. The denial cache only suppresses an exact repeat of the same name and folder. Sequential Checks for one user and action against different unauthorized UIDs therefore run one full permission query per resource instead of one query per user and action per TTL. Each call also inserts a denial entry keyed by the client-supplied name and folder, so a burst of distinct names grows that cache until TTL cleanup.

title: Denial-cache test never sets up an allow
body: TestService_CacheCheck's explicit-deny case says the permission cache allows dash1 so only the denial short-circuit can explain the deny, but it stores map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}. checkPermission treats a false or missing scope as no permission, and the fake permission store is left empty, so the test still passes if the denial-cache lookup is removed. Nothing covers the anonymous/render key collision, underscore UID collisions, or a grant that stays denied after a permission reload.

title: Denial cache key drops identity type and collides anonymous with renderer
body: Check builds the denial-cache key from only the subject id (checkReq.UserUID), not the identity type. This package's own Check tests use subjects "anonymous:0" and "render:0", so both parse to UserUID "0" and share one key for the same namespace, action, name, and folder. The denial lookup at the start of Check returns Allowed:false on any hit, before getRendererPermissions or anonymous permission logic runs. Renderer is supposed to be allowed dashboards:read, folders:read, and datasources:read unconditionally, but an anonymous deny for that dashboard (or the reverse, a renderer deny for an action anonymous is allowed) sticks for shortCacheTTL (30s) and 403s the other identity. Image rendering, alert screenshots, and anonymous access can deny each other.

title: Denial cache key joins name and parent with underscore, so distinct resources collide
body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates name and parent with "_", but both values are resource UIDs and Grafana UIDs may contain underscores. A deny for dashboard "report" in folder "q1_2024" and a check for dashboard "report_q1" in folder "2024" produce the same key (namespace.perm_<user>_<action>_report_q1_2024). Check treats any hit as definitive deny and does not consult permissions, so one resource's deny is applied to the other for 30 seconds. That is a wrong authorization decision, not just a missed cache optimization.

title: Sticky denial cache skips the DB refresh and outlives a stale folder tree
body: A denial-cache hit in Check returns Allowed:false immediately and never reaches the new path that reloads permissions when the cached scope set does not allow the resource. Denials are also stored whenever the post-refresh checkPermission call is false, including when the negative answer came from the cached folder tree rather than from fresh permission rows. checkInheritedPermissions returns false if ParentFolder is missing from that tree, which is exactly the case for a dashboard just created in a new child folder whose access is inherited from an ancestor. Folder cache and denial cache are both 30s, but they are written at different times, and nothing deletes a denial when permissions are later reloaded or the folder tree is rebuilt. So a check that races permission insert, or that runs while the folder tree is stale, keeps 403ing for up to 30s even after a later reload has already cached the grant. That reintroduces the creator lockout this PR is fixing, and a refreshed perm cache cannot override the denial because the denial entry is consulted first.

title: Duplicate is authorized by the ability source that has no rule
body: canDuplicate is the OR of the ruler ability and the Grafana prom ability, and a missing rule is not treated as "no opinion". useRulerRuleAbilities(undefined) still marks Duplicate supported whenever the ruler is available, because isPluginProvidedRule(undefined) is false and allowance is only the global Grafana create permission. useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(skipToken) does the same: skipToken is turned into undefined, useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities then sets MaybeSupported to AlwaysSupported, and Duplicate is allowed for anyone with Grafana AlertingRuleCreate. The permissive side wins. In the new list, plugin-provided rules therefore show Duplicate even though the prom path correctly denies it. In any AlertRuleMenu caller that has a cloud or other non-Grafana prom rule (or no prom rule), skipToken still grants Duplicate from the Grafana create permission, including when the ruler path says duplication is unsupported or the user lacks external-rule write. The menu item does not need a ruler rule, so the click starts the clone flow for a rule that should not be offered.

title: Federated rule groups are no longer immutable
body: useAllAlertRuleAbilities now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes isFederated to false. The previous isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) check was removed, and RuleGroupIdentifierV2 does not carry source_tenants, so the TODO cannot be evaluated with the data this hook receives. immutableRule is therefore never set for Mimir/GEM federated groups. Edit, delete, pause, and restore stay enabled for those rules in every consumer of these hooks, not only the new list. Users can change or delete cross-tenant federated rules that the UI previously blocked, which can break multi-tenant evaluation or drop rules the normal editor cannot represent.

title: Delete never appears in the ruler-less list view
body: The Delete item is rendered only when canDelete && rulerRule. GrafanaRuleListItem passes only promRule into RuleActionsButtons, so rulerRule is undefined and Delete is omitted even when useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities allows it. The list handler already deletes via the prom-derived identifier and ignores the ruler-rule argument, so the guard drops a working action. Users with delete permission cannot delete Grafana-managed rules from the list.

title: Pause is unreachable without a ruler rule
body: The pause item is still rendered only when rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) is true, and MenuItemPauseRule requires that ruler payload. The list view no longer fetches or passes a ruler rule, so Pause/Resume never appears even when the new prom ability says pause is supported and allowed. Removing the guard alone would pass undefined into MenuItemPauseRule. After this change, pausing or resuming an alert from the list is impossible.

title: Silence menu item is a no-op in the list view
body: AlertRuleMenu shows "Silence notifications" from prom-rule abilities and does not require a ruler rule. handleSilence only sets showSilenceDrawer. The drawer is mounted only when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true, and the list calls RuleActionsButtons with promRule and no ruler rule, so the click never opens SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer. Users get an enabled Silence action that does nothing.

title: Recording rules lose export, pause, and restore
body: useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities gates ModifyExport, Pause, Restore, and DeletePermanently on prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule. The ruler hook it replaces uses rulerRuleType.grafana.rule, which is true for Grafana recording rules as well. Recording rules are Grafana-managed, share isPaused / is_paused with alerting rules, and previously could be exported. In the list view Export is hidden for every recording rule, and pause/restore stay unsupported even for users who can edit them.

title: Filtered Grafana rows are rendered without a key
body: FilterViewResults maps each result to a list child and previously set key={key} on GrafanaRuleLoader. The replacement GrafanaRuleListItem omits key, while the datasource and unknown branches still set it. React reconciles Grafana rows by index. RuleActionsButtons holds silence-drawer and clone redirect state on the row, so loading more results or refreshing the filtered list can attach that state to the wrong rule.

title: View links drop returnTo
body: The deleted list item built the view href with createReturnTo() so the rule detail page could link back to the current list URL, including filters and search. The new href is /alerting/grafana/${uid}/view with no returnTo query param. Opening a rule from the filtered or grouped list and using the in-app back link lands on the default list instead of restoring the user's place.

title: Menu test locks in the incomplete action set
body: The More-menu test grants AlertingRuleDelete and folder update/delete, defines a delete selector, and then expects exactly four items: silence, copy link, duplicate, and export. It never clicks Silence and never asserts Delete or Pause. That count matches the current bugs (Delete and Pause omitted, Silence not required to open a drawer) and will fail a fix that shows the missing actions, so CI freezes the incomplete menu. Nothing covers plugin-provided or cloud rules, which is what would catch Duplicate being granted by an empty ability source.

title: Delete never appears in the ruler-less list view
body: AlertRuleMenu now ORs Grafana Prometheus-rule abilities into canDelete so the list can authorize actions without a ruler fetch. The Delete item is still rendered only when rulerRule is set (`canDelete && rulerRule` at line 165). The new list (GrafanaRuleListItem → RuleActionsButtons) passes only promRule, so rulerRule is undefined and Delete is never shown, even for users with folder delete permission. The list click handler already ignores the ruler argument and opens the delete modal with the identifier built from the Prometheus rule uid, so this guard drops a primary action rather than protecting anything. GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx grants AlertingRuleDelete, defines a delete menu query, and then asserts exactly four menu items, so the regression stays green.

title: Pause/resume is unreachable without a ruler rule
body: The Pause item is still rendered only when rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) is true, and MenuItemPauseRule is given that ruler rule. The new list never loads a ruler rule, so canPause computed from useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities is ignored. Users cannot pause or resume rules from the list, including rules whose paused state is already shown from the Prometheus payload (isPaused). MenuItemPauseRule still needs a RulerGrafanaRuleDTO to call the pause API, so the prom-rule ability check cannot drive the action until pause is implemented from the rule uid or the ruler rule is loaded on demand.

title: Silence menu item is a no-op in the list view
body: AlertRuleMenu renders "Silence notifications" from prom-rule abilities and does not require a ruler rule. handleSilence only sets showSilenceDrawer. The drawer is mounted only when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true, and rule is the optional ruler rule, which the list view does not pass. Clicking Silence therefore closes the menu and does nothing. The new group-loader test asserts the menu item is present but never activates it, so the no-op is not caught. Silencing from the list needs a path that can run from the Grafana rule uid, or an on-demand ruler fetch before opening SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer.

title: Federated rules are no longer immutable
body: useAllAlertRuleAbilities used to set isFederated from isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) and fold that into immutableRule, which blocks Update, Delete, Pause, Restore, and DeletePermanently. That body now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which only receives a RulerRuleDTO and RuleGroupIdentifierV2 (neither has source_tenants) and hardcodes isFederated to false. Every existing caller of useAlertRuleAbility / useAllAlertRuleAbilities — rule detail and the old rules table, not only the new list — will offer edit and delete on federated Mimir/GEM rules. Those mutations were blocked because saving the group without source_tenants can drop cross-tenant evaluation. The CombinedRule path still has rule.group and should keep the check even if the ruler-only hook cannot.

title: skipToken still grants Duplicate via Grafana create permission
body: useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(skipToken) is meant to skip the check for non-Grafana rules, but it calls useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined). For a missing rule, useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable returns loading: false, so MaybeSupported becomes AlwaysSupported, and Duplicate is [true, user has getRulesPermissions('grafana').create]. AlertRuleMenu ORs that with the ruler result. On a cloud/datasource rule, a user who cannot duplicate external rules but can create Grafana-managed rules still sees Duplicate, and choosing it starts RedirectToCloneRule for that cloud rule. skipToken/undefined should be not-supported and not-allowed for every action. The OR also means any false allow on the prom side overrides a ruler denial.

title: Filtered Grafana rules are rendered without a React key
body: FilterViewResults maps rules and passes the computed key for datasource and unknown origins. The grafana branch previously rendered GrafanaRuleLoader with key={key} and now renders GrafanaRuleListItem with no key, even though key is still destructured specifically to avoid duplicate keys. React then reconciles Grafana rows by index. RuleActionsButtons holds silence-drawer and clone-redirect state, so load-more appends or a list update can attach that state to the wrong rule. Pass key={key} on GrafanaRuleListItem, matching the other branches.

title: Recording rules lose export and pause in prom abilities
body: useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities uses prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule as the Grafana-managed check for ModifyExport, Pause, Restore, and DeletePermanently. Recording rules are Grafana-managed too (uid, folderUid, isPaused, provenance on the shared prom DTO). The ruler abilities this replaces used rulerRuleType.grafana.rule, which is true for recording rules, so the old list offered Export and Pause. The new list will not, while Edit and Delete are not gated this way. Silence should stay alerting-only; export, pause, restore, and permanent delete should follow "is a Grafana prom rule" plus the immutability checks, not alerting type.

title: Rule view links drop returnTo
body: The removed GrafanaRuleLoader built the view href with createReturnTo() so rule detail could navigate back to the current list URL, including filters and pagination. GrafanaRuleListItem now links to /alerting/grafana/${uid}/view with no returnTo query. Opening a rule from the filtered list and going back lands on the default list instead of the filtered results.

title: skipToken still grants Grafana Duplicate on non-Grafana rules
body: useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities is called with skipToken (converted to undefined) whenever the menu has no Grafana Prometheus rule, including every datasource-managed rule. useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable(undefined) returns loading:false, so MaybeSupported becomes AlwaysSupported, and Duplicate is then [true, user has Grafana AlertingRuleCreate] via toAbility(getRulesPermissions('grafana').create). AlertRuleMenu ORs that tuple with the ruler ability (canDuplicate), so an editor who may create Grafana-managed rules but may not write external rules still sees Duplicate and the clone flow is started with the cloud rule identifier. skipToken is meant to skip the check, but it does not return [false, false]. View and Explore are the same shape (supported plus a global permission even when the rule is missing) and will leak if callers OR them the same way. Existing RBAC tests mock these hooks, so they never execute this path.

title: Delete stays hidden in the list view without a ruler rule
body: The new list passes only a Prometheus rule into RuleActionsButtons, and AlertRuleMenu now treats the Grafana prom-rule delete ability as enough for canDelete. The Delete item is still rendered only when rulerRule is truthy (canDelete && rulerRule) and the click passes that ruler rule into handleDelete. The list no longer loads ruler rules, so rulerRule is undefined and Delete never appears, even for users with folder delete permission. RuleActionsButtons already ignores the ruler argument and calls showDeleteModal with the uid identifier built from the prom rule, so the gate is leftover and removes an action that would otherwise work.

title: Pause is unreachable once ruler rules are dropped from the list
body: canPause is now true for an editable Grafana alerting rule based on useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities, but the Pause item is still rendered only when rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) is true, and it passes that ruler rule into MenuItemPauseRule. GrafanaRuleListItem never supplies a ruler rule, so Pause cannot appear in the list the PR is migrating. Dropping the rulerRule check is not sufficient: MenuItemPauseRule still requires a RulerGrafanaRuleDTO. The prom rule already has uid and isPaused, but nothing maps those into the pause action, and onPauseChange is not wired from RuleActionsButtons either.

title: Silence menu item does nothing without a ruler rule
body: The list menu shows Silence notifications because useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities allows it for Grafana alerting rules, and handleSilence only sets showSilenceDrawer. The drawer is mounted only when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true, where rule is the optional ruler-rule prop. GrafanaRuleListItem passes only promRule, so that condition is false and the click is a no-op. SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer still requires a RulerGrafanaRuleDTO; the list needs a fetch-on-demand or a drawer that can create the silence from the prom rule uid and labels. The new GrafanaGroupLoader test only asserts the menu item is present and never clicks it.

title: Federated rule groups are no longer immutable
body: useAllAlertRuleAbilities used to set isFederated from isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) (true when the group has source_tenants) and treat those rules as immutable. It now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes isFederated to false and drops the isFederatedRuleGroup import. useAlertRuleAbility still goes through this for every CombinedRule, not only the new list. Update, delete, pause, restore, and permanent delete therefore become supported for federated Mimir/GEM groups whenever the user otherwise has permission. Editing those rules through the normal form rewrites the ruler group and can strip source_tenants, breaking cross-tenant evaluation.

title: Recording rules lose export and pause in prom-rule abilities
body: useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities uses isAlertingRule (Prometheus alerting type only) as the support flag for ModifyExport, Pause, Restore, and DeletePermanently. The ruler ability path uses isGrafanaManagedAlertRule, which is true for both Grafana alerting and recording rules, and the comment here says every GrafanaPromRuleDTO is Grafana-managed by definition. Recording rules in the new list therefore lose Export, and Pause stays unsupported even after the rulerRule menu gate is fixed. Silence correctly depends on alerting type; these other actions should not. Detail views that still use ruler abilities will keep showing Export and Pause for the same recording rule, so the two UIs disagree.

title: Filtered Grafana rows are rendered without React keys
body: FilterViewResults builds a KeyedRuleWithOrigin key specifically to avoid duplicate list keys, and the previous GrafanaRuleLoader was rendered with key={key}. The replacement GrafanaRuleListItem omits that prop, while the datasource and unknown branches in the same map still set key. Grafana rows are therefore unkeyed siblings of keyed rows. As infinite scroll appends pages, React can reuse the wrong row instance (open More menu or silence-drawer state) and will warn about missing keys. getGrafanaRuleKey on line 209 also has a stray closing brace (`rule.uid}}`), so putting key={key} back without fixing that helper still yields malformed keys.

title: Rule view links drop the returnTo back-navigation target
body: The removed list item built the view href with createReturnTo() so the rule detail back link returned to the current list URL, including search filters. The new GrafanaRuleListItem always links to `/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view` with no returnTo query param. Opening a rule from the group list or the filtered list therefore loses that context, and back navigation no longer returns to the same filtered results. Group-loader tests only assert that the href contains the view path, so they do not catch the missing parameter.

title: Menu test asserts the incomplete action set
body: The new More-menu test grants AlertingRuleUpdate and AlertingRuleDelete, defines a Delete menuitem selector, and then asserts the menu contains exactly four items (silence, copy link, duplicate, export). That locks in the missing Delete and Pause actions introduced by dropping ruler rules. It also never clicks Silence, so it does not notice that the drawer does not open. A green run of this file does not cover the list-view action regressions, and RulesTable RBAC tests mock useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities entirely, so they do not execute the skipToken permission logic either.

title: Shard splitting interpolates every query twice
body:
runSplitQuery now always maps targets through datasource.applyTemplateVariables before grouping and execution. runShardSplitQuery does the same (shardQuerySplitting.ts:52) and then, for every shard group, calls runSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts:163) with targets that are already interpolated and rewritten by interpolateShardingSelector. Substitution therefore runs twice on every shard-split query. The updated shard test locks this in by expecting applyTemplateVariables 5 times for one target (once up front, once per group) and stubs an idempotent string replace, so it never fails.

applyTemplateVariables is not idempotent: it both expands variables and injects request.filters into the LogQL. The second call sees the already substituted text plus the __stream_shard__ selector. Ad hoc filters are applied again onto a selector that was not the input the injector first rewrote, so matchers are duplicated and can be attached in the wrong place, producing invalid LogQL or a selector that no longer matches the shard values fetched on the first pass. Template replacement also does not rescan substituted values within one pass, so a label or line-filter value such as team-$env is left intact the first time and then expanded on the second pass if env is a dashboard variable. The same query with shard splitting off is interpolated only once, so shard splitting silently returns different streams. Interpolate once: keep a single applyTemplateVariables step for shard grouping, and skip it inside runSplitQuery when the caller has already prepared the targets.

title: Shard path no longer pre-expands $__range, so those queries are not time-split
body:
runShardSplitQuery used to call interpolateVariablesInQueries(request.targets, request.scopedVars), which substitutes every scoped variable, including $__range, $__range_s, and $__range_ms, against the original request range. It now calls applyTemplateVariables, which deliberately strips __range, __range_s, __range_ms, __interval, and __interval_ms out of scoped vars so those macros stay in the expression for the backend.

The still-macro expressions are passed into runSplitQuery. querySupportsSplitting (querySplitting.ts:282-288) refuses to time-split any expression that still contains $__range, because the backend would otherwise interpolate it with the chunk time range. Previously the macro was already a constant full-range duration, the guard did not match, and the query was still chunked with a correct lookback. After this change, a shard-split metric query such as count_over_time({job="x"}[$__range]) over a multi-day dashboard range is sent as one unsplit request. The range value stays correct, but queries that previously completed via chunking can now hit Loki's max query duration or time out. $__interval / $__interval_ms are also no longer baked in from the original scoped vars, so the backend expands them per sub-request instead of using the dashboard interval. The new tests stub templateSrv.replace with a blind replace of $__auto and $step, so they never observe this. Expand range macros against the original scoped vars before the splitting decision (while still using applyTemplateVariables for step, legend, and ad hoc filters), or explicitly accept the no-split behavior and test it.

title: Expressions that interpolate to empty are no longer dropped before sharding
body: The previous shard entry point interpolated first and then dropped targets with a falsy expr. The new code filters on query.expr and !query.hide and only then calls applyTemplateVariables, with no second filter. A target whose expression is only a template variable that resolves to an empty string (a common optional dashboard variable) used to be removed and not executed. It is now passed into splitQueriesByStreamShard and groupTargetsByQueryType, which calls getSelectorForShardValues on that empty expression and languageProvider.fetchLabelValues for __stream_shard__. runSplitQuery later drops empty expressions, so the target is not queried, but the label lookup still runs and failures are only logged. If selector extraction throws, groupTargetsByQueryType rejects and the .then at shardQuerySplitting.ts:213 has no .catch, so the query observable never emits or completes and the panel hangs. Filter again after applyTemplateVariables, as the old interpolate-then-filter order did.

title: $__range queries are split after interpolation removes the guard
body: runSplitQuery now runs datasource.applyTemplateVariables before querySupportsSplitting. Grafana puts __range, __range_s, and __range_ms on request.scopedVars from the full dashboard/Explore range, and applyTemplateVariables sends the expression through templateSrv.replace, so those tokens are already gone when isQueryWithRangeVariable runs. The guard therefore never matches, and queries that the comment says must not be split are partitioned into day-sized chunks. Previously the raw expression still contained $__range, so the query was one request and the backend interpolated the macro against the original range. After this change a common metric such as rate({app="foo"}[$__range]) over 30 days becomes rate({app="foo"}[30d]) executed as ~30 one-day requests, each with a 30-day lookback. That multiplies bytes scanned by roughly the chunk count and turns queries that used to succeed into timeouts, limit errors, or aborted splits (shouldStop on the first failed chunk). Decide splitting from the original expression, keep $__range queries in the non-splitting group (they can still be interpolated so other variables resolve), and add a test that such a query calls runQuery once.

title: $__auto is still expanded per chunk; the new test stubs it away
body: The early interpolation only calls applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters) and does not inject an __auto value. $__auto is not a Grafana scoped macro ($__interval and $__range are); this file already notes that step handling lives in the backend (pkg/tsdb/loki/step.go) and is only replicated here for chunk boundaries. applyTemplateVariables also cannot compute it: that API receives no time range or intervalMs. Split sub-requests therefore still contain literal $__auto, and the backend substitutes a step derived from each chunk's shorter range, so chunks get different range vectors and the merged series do not match an unsplit query. The new "Interpolates queries before execution" test hides this by replacing templateSrv.replace with a function that unconditionally rewrites $__auto to 5m, which production replace will not do. Substitute $__auto from the original request range (using the same calculateStep result used to partition) before splitting, and assert the executed expression without stubbing that replacement.

title: Shard path applies template variables twice, duplicating ad-hoc filters
body: runShardSplitQuery now interpolates every target with applyTemplateVariables, then splitQueriesByStreamShard always executes those targets through runSplitQuery, which applies applyTemplateVariables again after interpolateShardingSelector has rewritten the LogQL to inject __stream_shard__. For one target and four shard groups that is five substitutions; the updated test locks this in by expecting applyTemplateVariables toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5), where it previously expected a single interpolateVariablesInQueries call. The second call is not a no-op: it is passed request.filters again, so ad-hoc matchers are inserted into an expression that already has them, and the executed query looks like {app="foo", env="prod", __stream_shard__=~"1|2", env="prod"}. A second templateSrv.replace pass can also rewrite $... text that the first substitution or the shard rewrite introduced. Interpolate once, before shard grouping and selector lookup, and skip the new interpolation inside runSplitQuery when the caller already did it.

title: Blank expressions are no longer dropped after interpolation
body: The empty-expression filter now runs on the raw target, before applyTemplateVariables. The previous shard path interpolated with interpolateVariablesInQueries and only then dropped falsy expr values. A target whose expression is only a variable, such as expr "$logql" resolving to "", used to be removed and is now kept, grouped, and sent to Loki. The parse error is not retriable, so the shard loop sets shouldStop and never runs the remaining groups — one blank interpolated target fails every other query in the request. The same order was introduced in runSplitQuery (querySplitting.ts filters on query.expr and only then maps applyTemplateVariables), with the same abort-the-batch consequence. Filter hidden targets, interpolate, then drop targets whose expression is blank.

title: $__range queries are split after early interpolation
body: runSplitQuery now passes every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables before querySupportsSplitting. applyTemplateVariables interpolates with TemplateSrv.replace, and during dashboard or Explore queries that replaces $__range, $__range_s, and $__range_ms from the active time range. querySupportsSplitting then calls isQueryWithRangeVariable on that already-substituted expr, so the macro is gone and the query is treated as splittable. The comment on querySupportsSplitting says these queries must not be split: the backend fills $__range from the time range of the request it actually receives, and a split chunk is not the range the user selected. After this change, rate({job="app"}[$__range]) over several days is rewritten to a fixed full-window duration (for example [7d]) and then executed as one-day chunks, each looking back the whole window. Merged results do not match an unsplit query. The new tests cannot catch this: they stub replace to rewrite only $__auto and $step, so $__range stays in the expression under test and the guard still looks like it works. Check isQueryWithRangeVariable on the raw expr and keep those targets in the non-splitting partition before interpolating.

title: Shard path applies template variables twice
body: runShardSplitQuery already maps each target through applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters) before sharding. For every shard group it then calls runSplitQuery with a sub-request that still carries request.filters and the already interpolated targets, and runSplitQuery maps those targets through applyTemplateVariables again. Substitution is not idempotent: the first pass turns an escaped $$ into a literal $, and the second pass treats that $ as a variable, so a label value or query text containing $name can be expanded to a different variable. Ad hoc filters are applied on both passes (the old interpolateVariablesInQueries call did not receive request.filters; both new call sites do), so matchers are inserted once before the shard selector is injected and again after. The executed LogQL ends up with duplicate label matchers, for example {job="x", env="prod", __stream_shard__=~"1|2", env="prod"}. The shard test now expects applyTemplateVariables five times (once up front plus once per shard group), which locks in the double pass instead of interpolating once.

title: Expressions that interpolate to empty hang shard splitting
body: runShardSplitQuery used to interpolate with interpolateVariablesInQueries and then drop targets with an empty expr. It now filters on the raw expr and only then calls applyTemplateVariables. A target whose whole expression is a variable, such as $query, passes the filter because the raw string is non-empty, then becomes expr: '' after substitution, and is still passed to splitQueriesByStreamShard. If that target is alone in a group (non-shardable groups are queued first, so one empty query next to shardable queries is enough), runNextRequest calls runSplitQuery, which filters the empty expr out and calls runSplitGroupedQueries with an empty request list. That function immediately evaluates requests.filter(...)[0].partition and throws TypeError. The throw is inside a .then() with no rejection handler, so the subscriber never errors or completes and the whole request hangs, including valid sibling queries. Previously the empty target was removed before grouping and the other queries ran. The same filter-before-map in runSplitQuery (line 298) also keeps an empty interpolated expr in a split group and sends it to runQuery, which fails the batch with a Loki parse error.

title: Plugin request logs drop traceID
body: LoggerMiddleware used to append traceID to every "Plugin Request Completed" line (eventName=grafana-data-egress) via tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false), which includes the ID even when the span is not sampled. That call was removed with the tracing import. The attributes now stored by ContextualLoggerMiddleware are only endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname, and the new plugins/log FromContext wrapper does not add a trace ID either. Completion logs will no longer carry traceID, so these egress events cannot be correlated with traces.

title: TestLogger.FromContext discards recorded logs
body: TestLogger.FromContext ignores the receiver and returns NewTestLogger(), a separate logger whose InfoLogs/WarnLogs/ErrorLogs/DebugLogs stay empty. LoggerMiddleware now emits "Plugin Request Completed" through m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info rather than m.logger.Info. Tests that inject a TestLogger and assert on InfoLogs will see zero calls even when the line was logged, because the write lands on the discarded child. FromContext should return the same TestLogger (or a child that records into the same Logs) so this path is observable.

title: No test locks the split logging contract
body: ContextualLoggerMiddleware is new and has no tests, and LoggerMiddleware no longer puts pluginId, endpoint, user, or datasource on the log line itself; those fields now exist only if this middleware ran first and FromContext reads them back. The renamed metrics test only checks Prometheus counters. Nothing installs the production order (contextual logger outside the request logger) and asserts that "Plugin Request Completed" still contains those fields, so a reorder or a dropped attribute would ship without a failing test.

title: Plugin request completion logs drop traceID
body: "Plugin Request Completed" (eventName grafana-data-egress) used to include traceID from tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false) whenever it was non-empty. That parameter was removed and not replaced: ContextualLoggerMiddleware only stores endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname via log.WithContextualAttributes, and plugins/log.FromContext does not add a trace id before Info. Info itself is not context-aware, so this call site no longer records the trace. Egress logs can no longer be correlated with the request trace (including unsampled traces, which the old false argument included). Put traceID back on the log params, or add the same TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false) value to the contextual attributes.

title: TestLogger.FromContext discards subsequent log records
body: FromContext ignores the receiver and returns NewTestLogger(), a new zero TestLogger. LoggerMiddleware now emits the completion log only through m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info, so every Debug/Info/Warn/Error call is recorded on that discarded instance and never increments the injected fake's InfoLogs/ErrorLogs (Calls, Message, or Ctx). Tests that inject TestLogger will not observe plugin request logs and can miss regressions, or fail if they assert on the original logger. FromContext should return the same TestLogger so records stay observable.

title: No test checks that request identity fields still reach the completion log
body: Identity fields were moved off LoggerMiddleware's explicit parameters into instrumentContext, and traceID was dropped, but nothing asserts the resulting "Plugin Request Completed" record. metrics_middleware_test.go only checks Prometheus counters and constructs MetricsMiddleware directly, so it never runs NewContextualLoggerMiddleware ahead of LoggerMiddleware. FromContext only sees endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname if that middleware runs first and enriches the same context; a reorder or a missed attribute would not fail CI. Add a test that composes both middlewares and asserts those fields, plus traceID, on the completion log for the instrumented endpoints.

title: Plugin request completion logs drop traceID
body: Plugin Request Completed (eventName grafana-data-egress) used to append traceID from tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false), which includes the ID even when the span is not sampled. That call and the tracing import were removed when the line switched to m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info. instrumentContext only stores endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname; it does not store traceID, and grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext does not add one either. Info does not take a context.Context, so the span cannot be read at log time unless it was already copied onto the logger. Nothing in this change attaches traceID, so these egress logs can no longer be joined to distributed traces, including unsampled ones.

title: FromContext fallback silently drops request context
body: grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext type-asserts infra log's FromContext result to *log.ConcreteLogger. On failure it returns d.New() and ignores ctx. New with no arguments does not read contextual attributes, so pluginId, endpoint, datasource name/UID, and user are omitted while the caller still logs. LoggerMiddleware now depends entirely on FromContext for those fields, so this branch emits Plugin Request Completed with no plugin identity and no error. It also throws away the logger infra log returned, even if that value already had the right fields. Fall back to the original wrapper (return d) or otherwise keep ctx, and do not hide the type mismatch.

title: TestLogger.FromContext discards receiver and context
body: TestLogger.FromContext ignores both the receiver and the context and returns NewTestLogger(), a blank logger. LoggerMiddleware now emits its only line via m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info, so those calls are recorded on the discarded instance. InfoLogs, WarnLogs, and ErrorLogs on the injected TestLogger stay empty, and contextual fields are never applied. That breaks the Logger contract, which says FromContext keeps this logger's context and adds attributes from the given context. Tests using this fake cannot observe plugin request completion logs and will fail if they assert that a line was written.

title: Contextual logging move is untested
body: ContextualLoggerMiddleware is new and has no tests, and the logger middleware change that stopped passing pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName, dsUID, and traceID as explicit log fields is also untested. metrics_middleware_test.go only renames the constructor and still only checks Prometheus series. Nothing asserts that QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, and CollectMetrics attach those attributes (or that stream RPCs do not), or that Plugin Request Completed still contains them and traceID after FromContext. A wrong attribute list, middleware order, or FromContext implementation would still pass CI.

title: Device-limit denials are cached as successful tags
body: tagDeviceUI stores the device key (anon-device:<deviceID>) with SetDefault before CreateOrUpdateDevice returns, and a cache hit returns nil without touching the database. The default TTL is 29 minutes and the cache is process-local. This PR only rejects anonymous access when TagDevice returns anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached, so the first over-limit request for a new device is denied and leaves that key cached; every later request within the TTL skips the limit check, is not inserted or counted, and still receives an anonymous identity. Any other tagging error (count/insert failure, context cancel) is treated as non-fatal by Authenticate, but the poisoned key turns the following attempts into successes, so one transient database error also disables enforcement for 29 minutes. After expiry a single request fails and access is allowed again. The configured cap therefore does not limit anonymous sessions. Cache only after a successful write, and a cached denial must keep returning ErrDeviceLimitReached rather than nil.

title: Device limit is skipped when the client omits the device header
body: Anonymous.Authenticate denies access only when TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. TagDevice returns nil without consulting deviceLimit when X-Grafana-Device-Id is missing, and again when network.GetIPFromAddress fails (invalid RemoteAddr or forwarded address). Those requests are not counted and still get a full anonymous identity with the configured anonymous org role. The header is optional and client-supplied; nothing in this path mints a server-side device id, and Anonymous.Test always returns true, so any unauthenticated request can use this client. A script, API client, or browser that omits the header — including one that was just denied and retries without it — bypasses the cap entirely, while UI clients that send the header are restricted. If device_limit is meant to restrict anonymous access, it has to run on every anonymous authentication, not only on requests that opt into device tagging.

title: Wire provider signatures changed without updating generated injectors
body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService no longer takes anonstore.AnonStore; it now takes db.DB and builds the store internally with cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit. ProvideAnonDBStore gained a bare int64 device-limit argument. Both are Google Wire providers. The previous signature required Wire to supply an AnonStore and pass it into ProvideAnonymousDeviceService, which is what pkg/server/wire_gen.go still does — that file is not in this diff. Those generated calls will not compile. Regenerating Wire is not enough while ProvideAnonDBStore remains in the provider set, because Wire cannot inject an unnamed int64. Remove ProvideAnonDBStore from the set (the store is already constructed inside ProvideAnonymousDeviceService) and regenerate wire_gen.go before merge.

title: Device limit check races with the insert
body: When deviceLimit > 0, CreateOrUpdateDevice counts active rows for the last 30 days in one session and, if count < deviceLimit, performs INSERT ... ON CONFLICT in a second WithDbSession. There is no shared transaction, row lock, or conditional insert, so the cap is not atomic. Concurrent new devices — many browsers opening a shared anonymous dashboard, or every instance's cold cache after a restart — can all observe a count under the limit and all insert. The extra rows stay inside the 30-day window and can keep refreshing through updateDevice, so the overshoot persists until those devices age out or are deleted on login. Nothing later reconciles the table back down to the configured limit. The count and the write need to be one atomic operation that inserts only when this device_id already exists or the active count is still below the limit.

title: Anonymous sign-in now blocks on device tagging
body: TagDevice previously ran in a background goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout, so a slow anon_device write could not delay authentication. Authenticate now calls it synchronously on the request context before returning an identity, including when AnonymousDeviceLimit is 0 (the default), where the new limit branch is skipped and the call is only an upsert. The 29-minute per-process cache hides this in steady state, but a restart or deploy clears the cache and every anonymous request then waits on the database during sign-in. With a limit configured, each of those requests also runs COUNT(*) over the 30-day window before the user is admitted. A slow anon_device table, or row locks from DeleteDevicesOlderThan, now stalls anonymous page loads and API calls instead of a background goroutine. Do the synchronous round-trip only when a configured limit must allow or deny the request.

title: Device-limit test never checks existing devices or auth enforcement
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit inserts one row under the limit and asserts that a second new device id is rejected by the store. It never checks that a device already inside the 30-day window can still be updated once count >= deviceLimit, which is the updateDevice path existing anonymous users depend on. A bad WHERE clause or a RowsAffected == 0 false negative would lock out every anonymous user at the cap and this test would still pass. It also never calls TagDevice or Anonymous.Authenticate, so the local-cache short-circuit, a missing X-Grafana-Device-Id, and the new auth denial are all untested. The test stays green even if every retry is granted anonymous access. Cover existing-device refresh at the cap, repeated denial for a new device through TagDevice, and Authenticate both with and without the device header.

title: device_limit is undocumented and 0 silently disables it
body: auth.anonymous device_limit is parsed in readAuthSettings but not added to conf/defaults.ini or the configure-grafana docs. MustInt64(0) means enforcement is off, because the store only checks the cap when deviceLimit > 0; a negative or unparseable value also becomes unlimited, with no startup error. The cap counts devices whose updated_at is inside a hardcoded 30-day window, not the 61-day cleanup retention. Operators cannot discover the key, can set 0 expecting to allow no devices and instead disable the control, and cannot tell which devices consume a slot. Add the key to conf/defaults.ini with that default and document the 30-day active-device window and the 0/negative = disabled behavior.

title: Device-limit denials are cached as successful tags
body: tagDeviceUI inserts the device ID into the process-local cache (default TTL about 29 minutes) before CreateOrUpdateDevice returns, and a cache hit returns nil without touching the database. CreateOrUpdateDevice now returns ErrDeviceLimitReached for an unknown device once the cap is hit, and Anonymous.Authenticate treats that error as an authentication failure. The cache entry is not removed on that error, so the next request with the same X-Grafana-Device-Id hits the cache, TagDevice returns success, and a full anonymous identity is issued even though the device was never stored and does not count toward the limit. A second in-flight request can also observe the cache entry while the first call is still in the database and be authenticated before the denial is known. After one rejected attempt, that device ID is allowed for the rest of the TTL, so the new cap does not stop anonymous access. Cache only a successful write, or cache the denial and keep returning ErrDeviceLimitReached.

title: Requests without a device ID skip the cap
body: The new limit is enforced only when TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached and Authenticate rejects the login. TagDevice returns nil immediately when X-Grafana-Device-Id is empty, and also returns nil when the remote address cannot be parsed as an IP, without reading AnonymousDeviceLimit. Authenticate treats that nil as success and still returns an anonymous identity with the configured org role. Any client that omits the header (API callers, the initial document request before the frontend sets the header, or a client that strips it) is never counted and never rejected. The setting therefore does not cap anonymous access; it only affects clients that voluntarily present a device ID.

title: Limit check and insert are not atomic
body: When deviceLimit > 0, CreateOrUpdateDevice runs SELECT COUNT(*) and, if the count is still below the limit, a separate INSERT/upsert on another session. There is no transaction, SELECT FOR UPDATE, advisory lock, or use of the existing server lock around the two steps. Concurrent first-time devices can all observe count < limit and all insert, so the number of rows in the 30-day window can exceed AnonymousDeviceLimit. A burst of new device IDs (restart, many anonymous browsers) will overshoot the configured cap. The count and the write need to be one atomic conditional insert, or held under a lock, so the limit cannot be passed.

title: Wire providers changed but injector was not updated
body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now takes db.DB instead of anonstore.AnonStore, and ProvideAnonDBStore gained a bare int64 deviceLimit argument. These Provide* functions are constructed by Google Wire; pkg/server/wire.go and the checked-in pkg/server/wire_gen.go are not in this PR. The generated injector still calls the old signatures, so the server package will not compile. Regeneration will also fail if ProvideAnonDBStore remains in the provider set, because Wire cannot tell which int64 should be cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit. Build the store only inside ProvideAnonymousDeviceService, drop ProvideAnonDBStore from the Wire set if nothing else injects AnonStore, and commit the regenerated wire_gen.go.

title: Anonymous login now blocks on untimed DB tagging
body: Device tagging used to run in a background goroutine with a 2-minute timeout and could not delay authentication. TagDevice is now called inline on the request context, which has no dedicated deadline, before an anonymous identity is returned. Every cache miss waits for an upsert, and when device_limit is set it also waits for COUNT(*) on anon_device (rows are retained for 61 days). A slow, locked, or unreachable database stalls anonymous authentication for those requests instead of bounding the tag. Put a short timeout around the call and define the timeout outcome so a database problem cannot hang anonymous traffic.

title: device_limit is an undocumented ini key
body: auth.anonymous.device_limit is a new operator-facing setting, defaulting to 0 via MustInt64(0). The store only enforces the cap when the value is greater than 0, so 0 means unlimited, not "allow no devices". conf/defaults.ini and the configure-grafana docs are not updated, so the key, its default, and that meaning are undiscoverable. Add it, with that comment, under [auth.anonymous] in defaults.ini and next to the other anonymous auth options.

title: Limit tests never cover allow-existing or auth
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only checks that a second new device ID returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. It does not check that a device already inside the 30-day window is still updated and allowed when the count is at the limit, which is the updateDevice path every returning user depends on. No test calls TagDevice or Anonymous.Authenticate with a non-zero limit, so a local-cache hit that turns a limit error into a successful anonymous login, or a missing X-Grafana-Device-Id that skips the cap, would not fail CI. Add a store test for the at-limit refresh of an existing device and a service test that a new device is denied on every attempt while an already-counted one still authenticates.

title: Device-limit denial is cached as success
body: tagDeviceUI calls localCache.SetDefault before CreateOrUpdateDevice, and a cache hit returns nil without touching the database. The cache TTL is 29 minutes and the entry is not removed when tagging fails. Authenticate now treats a nil TagDevice result as success and only denies access for ErrDeviceLimitReached. So the first request from a new device over the limit is rejected, but that rejection is stored as a successful cache entry. Every later request for that device id skips the limit check and is issued an anonymous identity, and the device is never inserted, so it never consumes a slot. A concurrent request can also observe the cache entry and be authenticated before the first request's limit check finishes. After one denial, the cap does not apply to that client for the rest of the TTL, on every instance that has seen it.

title: Device limit does not actually gate anonymous access
body: The new access check only denies authentication when TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. TagDevice returns nil, and Authenticate then still returns an anonymous identity, when X-Grafana-Device-Id is absent or when web.RemoteAddr cannot be parsed as an IP. Existing tests show client IP is taken from X-Forwarded-For, so a non-IP forwarded-for value forces the parse-failure path even if a device id is sent. Any other tagging error is only logged in client.go and authentication continues, so a request that makes the insert fail is granted access and is not counted. The device id is also chosen by the client, so many users can send one already-accepted id and all pass the update path while occupying a single slot. Omitting the header is enough to use anonymous access with no limit check at all. As written, device_limit does not bound anonymous access.

title: Device limit check and insert are not atomic
body: When device_limit is positive, CreateOrUpdateDevice counts rows in one WithDbSession and, if the count is under the limit, inserts in a second WithDbSession. Nothing wraps the two statements in a transaction or takes a lock, and the unique key is only on device_id, so it does not cap the number of rows. Concurrent anonymous requests that all observe count < limit will all insert. With 50 simultaneous new device ids and a limit of 10, all 50 can commit and the table stays at 50; nothing rolls the extras back. That is the multi-instance, multi-user load this cap is meant to control, so AnonymousDeviceLimit is not a hard limit.

title: Provider signature change breaks Wire startup
body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService no longer takes an anonstore.AnonStore and now requires db.DB, and ProvideAnonDBStore gained a bare int64 device-limit argument. Grafana builds the server with Google Wire and commits pkg/server/wire_gen.go; this PR does not update wire.go or wire_gen.go, and the only updated call sites are tests. The generated injector still calls the old signatures, so the server package will not compile. Regenerating Wire also cannot satisfy a raw int64, so ProvideAnonDBStore has to be dropped from the provider set (it is now called internally) or the limit must be injected via *setting.Cfg. Until that is done the binary does not build.

title: Anonymous auth now waits on the database even when the limit is off
body: Device tagging used to run in a background goroutine with its own timeout and did not block login. Authenticate now calls TagDevice on the request path for every anonymous authentication, including when device_limit is 0, which disables enforcement. A local-cache miss waits for a database write before an identity is returned; a non-zero limit adds a COUNT(*) first, and that count is not cached. The cache is per process, so each instance repeats the work. A slow database delays every new anonymous session, and because the call is synchronous an unauthenticated client can force a count-and-write per request by rotating X-Grafana-Device-Id. Previously that work could not stall the request.

title: Limit tests never cover the allow-existing or auth paths
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only inserts one device and asserts that a second new device id returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. It never checks the behavior the new branch claims: an already-registered device must still be updated and accepted once the count is at the limit. A broken updateDevice WHERE clause that rejects every device, including known ones, would still pass. Nothing at the AnonDeviceService or Anonymous.Authenticate level covers the limit either, so the 29-minute cache treating a failed tag as success, and a missing device-id header still receiving an anonymous identity, are both untested. The new test runs on SQLite only, so MySQL/Postgres placeholder or rows-affected differences in the new UPDATE are not exercised.

title: device_limit is undocumented and 0 means unlimited
body: auth.anonymous.device_limit is read with MustInt64(0) but conf/defaults.ini and the configure-grafana docs are not updated. Operators discover settings from defaults.ini, and generated config docs come from that file, so the new cap is invisible. The code treats 0 as 'do not enforce' rather than 'allow zero devices', and that is not stated anywhere a user will see it. Setting device_limit = 0 to try to disallow anonymous devices silently leaves the limit disabled.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged at Error with every ID
body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log every batch with r.log.Error (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579), including the full ID slice, the SQL condition, and an err value that is already known to be nil. These fire even when the batch is empty, so an idle instance emits error-level lines on every cleanup cycle for age, count, and orphan-tag passes. Error is always emitted at production log levels, so this will flood logs, trip error-rate alerts, and serialize up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize IDs (the new test uses 32767) on the hot path between the SELECT and the DELETE. That I/O also widens the race window of the split statements. These are leftover debug traces and should be removed; do not keep them at Error, and do not log the ID list.

title: Cleanup job interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: CleanUpService.Run now uses time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1) instead of 10 minutes. The PR is about splitting annotation cleanup statements to avoid MySQL deadlocks; this schedule change is unrelated and undocumented. clean() still applies a 9-minute timeout, which only makes sense with the old 10-minute period so a run finishes before the next tick. At 1 minute, every cleanup job (temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, and query history) runs up to 10x more often. If a run lasts longer than a minute, time.Ticker drops ticks and the next clean() starts immediately, so a slow annotation cleanup can run back-to-back with no gap and continuously load the database. Revert this to 10 minutes unless the frequency change is an intentional, documented product decision.

title: SQLite IN-list is built with quadratic string concatenation
body: When the database is SQLite and AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is above 999, deleteByIDs interpolates IDs into DELETE ... WHERE id IN (...). The list is built with values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) inside the loop, which copies the entire growing string on every iteration. That is O(n^2) allocations on the path added specifically for large batches (the new test sets the batch size to 32767, and the setting is user-configurable with no upper bound here). Tens of thousands of IDs produce gigabytes of intermediate strings, GC pauses, and a cleanup stall or OOM, which defeats a larger batch size. Build the clause with strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt into a buffer.

title: Max-count cleanup can delete annotations that should be kept
body: Count-based retention selects IDs with ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT batch OFFSET maxCount, then deleteByIDs removes those IDs in a later autocommit statement with no re-check that they are still outside the cap. The previous single-statement DELETE evaluated the OFFSET atomically with the delete, so a row that no longer fell past MaxCount could not be removed. If newer annotations (the ones the OFFSET skipped) are deleted between the SELECT and the DELETE — by a user, the API, or another instance — the already-selected IDs can now sit inside the retention window and are still deleted. Those annotations are permanently lost and the configured max count is not honored. Concurrent inserts only under-delete, which the next cycle can fix; this race over-deletes, which the next cycle cannot undo. The comment on the age path only mentions under-deletion from inserts. The Error log of the full ID list between the two statements makes the window larger. The DELETE needs to be conditional on the row still being past the cap, or the data-loss window has to be an explicit accepted risk.

title: Cleanup job interval accidentally reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: Run's ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, and nothing in the PR description, changelog, or annotation-deadlock fix calls for that. This loop drives every cleanup job (temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, and query-history row-limit enforcement), not just annotations. Each clean() call is allowed to run for up to 9 minutes, and the ticker is not drained, so once a job exceeds 1 minute the next run starts immediately and cleanup can become continuous. That is about a 10x increase in database load and works against the deadlock fix by running the annotation cleaner far more often. Restore the 10-minute interval unless a shorter schedule is an intentional, documented change.

title: Cleanup debug traces left in at Error level and log every ID
body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log at Error on every batch, including the terminating batch that finds nothing to delete: "Annotations to clean by time" (line 534), "cleaned annotations by time" (line 537), "Annotations to clean by count" (line 554), "cleaned annotations by count" (line 557), "Tags to clean" (line 576), and "cleaned tags" (line 579). These are not failures — the err field is logged after the error has already been returned, so it is always nil on the success path — but they are emitted as errors. Each line also dumps the full ID slice and the SQL condition. With a large AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize that is one enormous log record per batch, and with cleanup enabled it will fire on every cycle even when zero rows are deleted, triggering error-rate alerts and flooding log pipelines. Remove these traces, or drop them to Debug and do not log the ID list.

title: SQLite ID inlining builds the IN list with quadratic string copies
body: When the database is SQLite and AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is above 999, deleteByIDs inlines every ID into the DELETE statement by repeatedly doing values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v). Each iteration copies the whole string, so a batch of n IDs allocates O(n^2) bytes. That path exists specifically for large batches (the new test uses 32767). For n around 10k–30k this is hundreds of MB to multiple GB of temporary allocations and a multi-second pause on every batch, which can stall cleanup or OOM a small SQLite instance. Build the list with strings.Builder (or strings.Join of preformatted IDs) instead.

title: Cleanup interval accidentally reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: Run() now ticks the background cleanup loop every 1 minute instead of every 10 minutes. Nothing in the PR description or the annotation deadlock fix calls for this, and it changes every job in this service (temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, invites, short URLs, query history, and annotations), not just annotation cleanup. clean() uses a 9-minute timeout that was paired with the 10-minute interval so one pass finished before the next tick. With a 1-minute ticker, any pass longer than a minute (likely now that each annotation batch is a separate SELECT plus DELETE, and on large tables) leaves a tick buffered, so the next pass starts immediately and cleanup runs back-to-back. That multiplies database load and can increase the write contention this change is meant to reduce. Restore the 10-minute interval unless a documented, intentional schedule change is actually wanted.

title: Success-path debug logs at Error level dump every cleaned ID
body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log at Error after every ID fetch and every delete (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579), including batches that find nothing. These are leftover debug statements: the fetch log's err is always nil because a real error already returned, and the messages fire on the normal success path. Error-level lines are what most Grafana deployments alert on, so every cleanup cycle will raise false errors for alert, dashboard, and API annotations plus orphaned tags. Each line also includes the full ID slice and the SQL condition. Batch size is configurable and the new test uses 32767, so a single line can be megabytes, flooding log pipelines and risking dropped real errors. Remove these calls, or at most log a count at Debug without the ID list.

title: SQLite IN-list is built with quadratic string concatenation
body: When the database is SQLite and AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is above 999, deleteByIDs inlines IDs by repeatedly assigning values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v). Each iteration copies the whole string, so n IDs cost O(n²) allocations before the DELETE is sent. The new test sets the batch size to 32767, and orphaned-tag cleanup can emit several lists of that size; that is on the order of gigabytes of temporary strings and multi-second stalls on the cleanup goroutine, which runs the other cleanup jobs only after annotations finish. Build the list with strings.Builder (and consider chunking) so large SQLite batches stay linear.

title: Async legacy writes are canceled when the request ends
body: Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection perform the legacy write in a goroutine whose context is derived with context.WithTimeoutCause from the incoming request context (Create line 51, Update line 135, Delete line 110, DeleteCollection line 163). A child context is canceled as soon as its parent is. net/http cancels the request context when ServeHTTP returns, which is immediately after these methods return the unified-storage result, so the 10s timeout never applies and Legacy.Create/Update/Delete typically fail with context.Canceled before the DB write finishes. Mode 3 exists so legacy storage stays current enough to roll back; those safety writes will systematically fail in production, and nothing retries them. The goroutines also discard the legacy error without logging, unlike the previous synchronous implementation, so the divergence is invisible aside from a metric. Detach with context.WithoutCancel (not context.Background(), which would drop user/org/trace values) before applying a timeout, and log the legacy error.

title: Unordered goroutines can resurrect or revert legacy objects
body: Every successful Create (line 50), Update (line 134), Delete (line 108), and DeleteCollection (line 161) starts an independent goroutine with no per-resource queue, generation check, or in-flight tracking. Goroutines for the same object run in parallel and can finish out of order. A create followed quickly by a delete can delete on legacy first (NotFound) and then create, resurrecting an object that unified storage has already removed. Two updates can commit the newer spec and then the older one, rolling the safety copy backward. On rollback to legacy reads, users would see deleted or stale objects. Serialize legacy writes per resource and reject a write whose unified-storage resourceVersion/generation is older than what legacy already applied.

title: Legacy update no longer stores the object written to unified storage
body: Update passes the caller's original objInfo into Legacy.Update (line 139) after Storage.Update has already applied it. The code this PR replaces loaded the unified object, computed UpdatedObject once, and passed that exact result to both stores via updateWrapper. That snapshot is required because mode 3 reads come from unified storage, so the client's resourceVersion and any patch base belong to the unified copy, not the legacy copy.
