Legacy.Update will call UpdatedObject again against the legacy object and enforce the unified resourceVersion, which conflicts or yields a different spec whenever the stores differ. Most updates will fail to land in legacy, so the rollback copy stops tracking writes. Write the object returned by Storage.Update into legacy instead of replaying objInfo. Create has the same shape at line 55: it forwards the pre-write input obj rather than the created object, so server-side defaults present only on the returned object are not what legacy stores.

title: Successful deletes record the object name as the metric kind
body: On the delete success path, recordStorageDuration is called with the object name as its third argument (line 106). Every other call in this file, including the delete error path on line 103, passes options.Kind there, and these duration helpers are Prometheus metrics registered from the registry passed into NewDualWriter, with that argument as the kind label alongside mode and method. A distinct series per deleted object is unbounded cardinality and can exhaust Prometheus memory once mode 3 is enabled. Success and error delete series also cannot be joined. Pass options.Kind, as the error path does.

title: Storage failures and legacy delete-collection hit the wrong metric
body: When Storage.Create fails, line 45 calls recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration, and the observed interval is the failed storage call. Storage.Update's error path does the same at line 129. The async legacy DeleteCollection path at line 166 calls recordStorageDuration for a legacy operation. Unified-storage create/update failures are counted as legacy failures and omitted from storage error latency, while legacy delete-collection outcomes are attributed to unified storage. During a mode 3 migration, alerts will point at the wrong store. Use recordStorageDuration on the storage error paths and recordLegacyDuration for the legacy delete-collection goroutine.

title: NotFound from unified storage skips the legacy delete
body: Delete returns immediately on any Storage.Delete error, including NotFound (lines 101-104), and never starts the legacy delete. The previous implementation treated unified NotFound as non-fatal and still deleted from legacy. If an earlier legacy delete failed or lost the race with a later create, a client retry gets NotFound from unified storage (the source of truth) and the legacy object is left in place. After a rollback to legacy reads, that object reappears. A NotFound from unified storage should still attempt the legacy delete and ignore a legacy NotFound, since the client-facing error remains the unified result.

title: Destroy closes stores while legacy goroutines may still be writing
body: Destroy calls Storage.Destroy and Legacy.Destroy immediately and does not track the goroutines started by Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection. Apiserver shutdown can destroy legacy storage while those goroutines are still inside Legacy.Create/Update/Delete, which can panic on a closed backend or leave a half-applied safety write. Track in-flight legacy writes with a WaitGroup and wait for them in Destroy before tearing the stores down.

title: Unit tests never observe the async legacy write
body: TestMode3_Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection set legacy mock expectations but return as soon as the unified-storage call returns (Create at line 65). They never wait for the goroutine, never call AssertExpectations, and never check that legacy was invoked with the persisted object. Both mocks share one testify Mock, so the two Create expectations are interchangeable and a test passes even if the legacy call is skipped. They also use context.Background(), which is never canceled, so they cannot catch request-context cancellation. Inject a synchronous executor or wait for the goroutine, assert the legacy call and its arguments, and add a case whose parent context is already canceled.

title: Mode 3 playlist tests assume legacy is updated before the handler returns
body: The new mode 3 cases (file storage at line 133 and unified storage at line 192) call doPlaylistTests, which immediately lists and gets via the legacy /api/playlists endpoint after k8s create, update, and delete. Modes 0-2 mirror those writes synchronously, which is why that comparison works; mode 3 mirrors them only after the handler returns. The legacy read can therefore observe a missing or stale playlist and fail or flake, especially once the request context cancels the legacy write. If that endpoint no longer reads legacy storage, the new cases never check that the safety write landed at all. Wait until the legacy write is visible, or assert it through a hook, before comparing the two APIs.

title: Async legacy writes are cancelled when the request ends
body: Create derives the legacy call context with context.WithTimeoutCause on the incoming request context (same pattern in Delete at line 110, Update at line 135, and DeleteCollection at line 163). A child context is cancelled as soon as its parent is. The apiserver cancels the request context when the handler returns, which is immediately after this method returns the unified-storage result, so the 10s timeout never applies and Legacy.Create/Update/Delete fails with context.Canceled. The safety copy mode 3 exists to write never lands. Those failures are not logged, only turned into a duration metric (and some of those metrics hit the wrong histogram), so divergence is silent. Detach with context.WithoutCancel before applying the timeout so org/namespace/user values are kept but request cancellation is not, and log the legacy error.

title: Unordered fire-and-forget legacy writes can drop or resurrect data
body: Every successful unified write starts a goroutine that mutates legacy with no per-name ordering, version check, or cancellation of older in-flight writes. Delete of "foo" can commit to unified storage and start a legacy delete, then a recreate of "foo" can commit and start a legacy create; if the delete goroutine runs last, legacy no longer has the object unified storage is serving. A stale update finishing after a newer update leaves legacy on old contents. After rollback to legacy those races are user-visible data loss. Serialize legacy writes per object (or drop writes older than the latest unified resource version) and track the goroutines so they can be drained.

title: Legacy update replays the request object and its unified resourceVersion
body: After Storage.Update succeeds, the goroutine calls Legacy.Update with the original objInfo. UpdatedObjectInfo.Preconditions() carries the resourceVersion on the object the client submitted, which in mode 3 was read from unified storage, not legacy. A legacy updater that honors the standard contract will reject the write as a conflict, so the safety copy does not move. Re-running UpdatedObject against legacy's current object can also persist different contents than unified storage just stored (merge patch, generation, managed fields). The previous code forced both stores to persist the object Storage.Update returned via updateWrapper; that was removed and nothing logs the legacy failure. Pass a wrapper whose UpdatedObject returns a deep copy of the stored object and whose preconditions are empty or taken from the legacy object.

title: Successful delete metrics are labeled with the object name
body: On the Storage.Delete success path, recordStorageDuration is called with name, the object name, as the resource argument. The error path at line 103 and every other call in this file pass options.Kind. Successful deletes are therefore recorded on a different series than failed deletes and cannot be aggregated with the rest of mode 3. That argument is the resource label used for the other observations; using the object name creates one series per deleted object and the metric cardinality grows without bound.

title: Durations are recorded on the wrong histogram
body: When Storage.Create fails, the code calls recordLegacyDuration (line 45) instead of recordStorageDuration, so unified create errors never show up on the storage histogram and are counted as legacy failures. Storage.Update's error path does the same at line 129. In the DeleteCollection goroutine, the legacy outcome is recorded with recordStorageDuration (line 166) instead of recordLegacyDuration, so legacy delete-collection latency and errors are attributed to unified storage and the legacy series stays empty. Migration dashboards and alerts will be wrong in both directions.

title: NotFound from unified storage skips the legacy delete
body: Any error from Storage.Delete, including NotFound, returns immediately and never starts the legacy delete. In mode 3 an object can still exist only in legacy (written before cutover, or left behind by an earlier failed legacy write). The client then gets NotFound while the legacy row remains, and rolling back to legacy resurrects the deleted object. The implementation this replaces still deleted from legacy when unified storage returned NotFound. Treat NotFound as success for the purpose of the async legacy delete.

title: Expected NotFound results are logged as errors
body: Get logs every storage error, including NotFound, with log.Error. NotFound is a normal result for existence checks and for idempotent deletes. Delete (line 102), Update (line 128), and DeleteCollection (line 155) do the same. The code this replaces skipped apierrors.IsNotFound before logging. Once mode 3 is on, routine 404s will be emitted at error level and trip log-based alerts. Log NotFound at a lower level or not at all.

title: Legacy create shares the live request object with no copy
body: The goroutine passes the same obj pointer just given to Storage.Create into Legacy.Create, and Create returns the storage result to the handler, which encodes it concurrently. Stores commonly set resourceVersion, UID, and timestamps on the input object and return that same pointer. Legacy create then either sees a resourceVersion and fails admission ("resourceVersion may not be set on objects to be created") or mutates the object while the response encoder reads it, which is a data race. Deep-copy the incoming object before the unified write and give legacy the copy with resourceVersion cleared.

title: Destroy closes both stores while legacy goroutines may still run
body: Destroy calls Storage.Destroy and Legacy.Destroy immediately, but Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection never track the goroutines they start. On shutdown an in-flight legacy write can run against a store that has already been closed, failing the safety copy or panicking, and the process can exit before the goroutine is scheduled. Keep a WaitGroup or worker queue and wait for it in Destroy before tearing the stores down.

title: Mode 3 tests never observe the async legacy write
body: Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection return as soon as unified storage returns and write legacy in a background goroutine. These tests only assert the synchronous return value. Legacy and storage share one mock.Mock, so an On("Create") or On("Delete") cannot tell which backend was called, and nothing waits for the goroutine or calls AssertExpectations. The delete and delete-collection success cases do not register a distinct legacy expectation at all. A change that never calls legacy, or that calls it with an already-cancelled context, still passes. The background mock call can also outlive t.Run and panic if it reports a failure after the test returns. Drive the legacy path synchronously in tests and assert it runs only after unified success, on a context that is not already cancelled.

title: Async legacy writes are cancelled with the request context
body: Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection start the legacy write in a goroutine and derive its context with context.WithTimeoutCause on the incoming request context (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163). A child context is cancelled as soon as its parent is cancelled, and the apiserver cancels the request context when the handler returns — which is immediately after these methods return success. The 10s timeout therefore never keeps the legacy call alive; Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection run with an already-cancelled context and fail. Mode 3 reads only from unified storage, so the missed legacy write is invisible to API clients, but rollback to a legacy-read mode drops every write made in mode 3. The new playlist mode 3 integration tests that expect the legacy HTTP API to show k8s writes will fail or flake for the same reason.

title: Background legacy writes use the caller's objects without a copy
body: The legacy goroutines call Legacy.Create with the same obj pointer passed to Storage.Create (line 55), Legacy.Update with the same objInfo (line 139), and Legacy.DeleteCollection with the same listOptions (line 165). k8s create/update/delete-collection mutate those values in place (generated name, UID, resourceVersion, continue/resourceVersion on list options), and the caller may keep using them after the method returns. The goroutine therefore races with the storage layer and the client. Legacy create can also reject the object because resourceVersion/UID were already set by unified storage, or it can persist a different name than the one returned to the client. Deep-copy the inputs before the unified call (and clear server-assigned resourceVersion on the legacy copy) before handing them to the goroutine.

title: Legacy update no longer writes the object stored in unified storage
body: The previous Update loaded the unified object, ran objInfo.UpdatedObject once, and passed an updateWrapper so Legacy.Update received the exact object just written to unified storage. That wrapper is gone. Legacy.Update is now invoked with the original objInfo, so it loads the legacy row and re-runs UpdatedObject plus the client's preconditions against that row. Mode 3 serves reads from unified storage, so the resourceVersion on the update is the unified one and will not match legacy; a normal precondition check fails the legacy update with a conflict and the backup copy is never updated. Even if legacy ignores resourceVersion, a patch is applied to drifted legacy state instead of replacing it with the unified result, so the stores diverge. Delete has the same precondition problem: line 112 forwards the caller's DeleteOptions, including a unified-storage resourceVersion precondition, into Legacy.Delete.

title: Unified NotFound skips the legacy delete
body: Delete returns immediately on any Storage.Delete error, including NotFound, and never starts the legacy delete. The previous implementation still deleted from legacy when unified storage returned NotFound, and only treated other errors as fatal. After a failed or cancelled legacy delete, a retry sees NotFound in unified storage (the source of truth for reads) and now leaves the legacy object in place permanently. Orphans also remain for objects that exist only in legacy. NotFound should still be returned to the client, but the async legacy delete should run so the backup store is cleaned up.

title: Latencies are recorded on the wrong store's metric
body: On Storage.Create failure the code calls recordLegacyDuration (line 45) and never records a storage sample, so unified-storage create failures show up as legacy failures and storage error latency is missing. Update does the same on line 129 (recordLegacyDuration for a storage error). DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine calls recordStorageDuration (line 166) with the legacy start time, so legacy delete-collection latency and errors are added to the storage histogram and the legacy series stays empty. Dashboards and any mode-promotion checks that compare legacy vs storage success will attribute outages to the wrong store and can page or block migration incorrectly.

title: Successful delete metrics use the object name as the kind label
body: The delete success path calls recordStorageDuration with name (the object name) as the third argument, while the error path two lines above and every other method pass options.Kind. That label is the resource kind. Every successful delete therefore emits a unique series per object name, which is unbounded cardinality on a hot write path and can exhaust Prometheus memory. Success and failure also cannot be aggregated together because they do not share the same label value, so delete success rate is not measurable.

title: Legacy write failures are not logged
body: The goroutines in Create (line 56), Delete (line 113), Update (line 140), and DeleteCollection (line 166) only feed the legacy error into a duration metric and otherwise discard it. The previous synchronous implementation logged legacy create/update/delete/delete-collection failures. With writes now best-effort and easy to cancel, a broken legacy path produces no log line, so operators cannot tell which object diverged or why (conflict, timeout, cancelled context, validation). Log errObjectSt/err with the object name before recording the metric.

title: Expected NotFound responses are logged as errors
body: Get logs every Storage.Get error at Error level, including NotFound (line 71). List (line 87) and Delete (line 102) do the same, and the apierrors.IsNotFound guard that the old Delete used was removed. NotFound on get/delete is a normal client result (the playlist tests even delete twice and expect it). Those calls will flood error logs and hide real storage failures. Log NotFound at a higher verbosity, or not at all, and keep Error for unexpected failures.

title: Destroy does not wait for in-flight legacy writes
body: Destroy closes Storage and then Legacy immediately and does not track the goroutines started by Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection. Those goroutines can still be inside Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection after Legacy.Destroy returns, which races with teardown and can panic or hit a closed database. Shutdown also drops the backup writes the goroutines were supposed to finish. A WaitGroup (or similar) should be added around the legacy goroutines and waited on in Destroy before calling Legacy.Destroy.

title: Unit tests never check that the legacy write happens
body: Mode 3 success tests register legacy mock expectations but return as soon as the unified call finishes (Create at line 65, and the same pattern in Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection) and never call AssertExpectations or wait for the goroutine. The defining behavior — an asynchronous legacy write — is therefore untested, and a cancelled or skipped legacy call still passes. Legacy and unified also share one testify mock, so method names like Create cannot be attributed to a store; the "unified store fails" create case only stubs the legacy Create expectation, which the synchronous storage call consumes by accident. testify mocks are not thread-safe, so the background call can also race or panic after the test function returns.

title: Mode 3 playlist tests assume legacy is updated before the handler returns
body: The new mode 3 cases (file at line 132, unified storage at line 191, etcd at line 287) reuse doPlaylistTests. That helper creates, updates, and deletes through the k8s client and then immediately requires the legacy /api/playlists API to match (search at line 529 and getFromBothAPIs). Mode 3 returns after the unified write and only then writes legacy on another goroutine whose context is tied to the request. The legacy HTTP read therefore races the backup write and, because that context is cancelled when the request ends, will often never see the object. These new integration cases will fail or flake until the test waits for the legacy write or the dual writer detaches that work from request cancellation.

title: Write path never rechecks cache and can clear a good entry
body: In pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go, GetWebAssets drops its read lock and at line 48 takes entryPointAssetsCacheMu for the entire load (the assets-manifest file read, and readWebAssetsFromCDN if that branch runs) without reading entryPointAssetsCache again. Every caller that saw a nil cache therefore repeats that I/O while holding the write lock, so concurrent startup or dev calls serialize and the read-fast path blocks behind them. Line 69 then always stores the result, including when the load failed and result is nil. A caller that loses the race to a successful load can overwrite the published cache with nil and return an error even though assets were already loaded. After the write lock is acquired, return the existing pointer when Env is not Dev and the cache is non-nil, and only assign entryPointAssetsCache when the load succeeds.

title: Write path never rechecks the cache and can clear a good entry
body: GetWebAssets snapshots entryPointAssetsCache under a read lock, drops that lock, then later takes the write lock and always reloads. It never re-reads entryPointAssetsCache after Lock, and it always stores the load result, including a nil result when readWebAssetsFromFile fails. Every caller that observed a cold cache therefore runs the load, and a later waiter that fails (missing manifest, transient read error, bad JSON) overwrites a cache entry an earlier waiter already published. Non-dev callers then miss the cache and hit the filesystem again. The same stampede also repeats the manifest read serially while holding the exclusive lock, so startup latency stacks instead of one successful load serving the other waiters. After acquiring the write lock, return the existing pointer when cfg.Env is not Dev and the cache is already non-nil, and do not replace a populated cache with a failed nil result.

title: Process-wide exclusive lock is held across manifest I/O
body: The write lock taken at the start of the slow path is held, via defer Unlock, until GetWebAssets returns, and that section calls readWebAssetsFromFile (os.Open plus JSON decode). Lock hold time is therefore disk latency, and a slow or stuck open blocks every other GetWebAssets caller in the process, not just the request that is loading. In dev the fast path is never taken (the early return requires Env != Dev), so every call takes this exclusive lock and reads the manifest under it, serializing concurrent renders. If the load fails the cache is left nil, so later requests keep queueing on the same mutex to repeat the failed open. Read the manifest outside the lock and hold entryPointAssetsCacheMu only to publish a successful result.

title: Race fix has no concurrent regression test
body: This change only adds a mutex around the global asset cache and does not add a test that calls GetWebAssets concurrently on a cold cache, or one where one load succeeds and another fails. The missing re-check under the write lock and the nil overwrite of entryPointAssetsCache would not be caught, and the original data race can regress. A race-detector test with several goroutines, including a failing manifest read, should assert that a successful non-dev result stays cached and is what the other callers receive.

title: Write lock does not re-check cache, so waiters reload and can clear it
body: GetWebAssets copies entryPointAssetsCache under a read lock, drops that lock, and only then takes the write lock. It never looks at the cache again after Lock. Every caller that observed a nil cache—the concurrent first requests this change is meant to protect—runs the manifest load while holding the exclusive lock and then unconditionally assigns entryPointAssetsCache = result. A later waiter whose load fails stores nil and wipes an entry an earlier waiter already published, so following non-dev calls miss the cache and reload. Even when every load succeeds, the missing re-check serializes a full disk read per waiter instead of returning the value the first loader stored. After acquiring the write lock, return the existing cache when Env is not Dev and it is already set, and do not replace a populated cache with a failed nil result.

title: Live SQL path still builds DuckDB statements and fails as a parse error
body: UnmarshalSQLCommand, the existing server-side expression entry point, never applies the new disable. NewSQLCommand always calls sql.TablesList (pkg/expr/sql_command.go:30). TablesList interpolates the user expression into a DuckDB statement, SELECT json_serialize_sql('...'), after only doubling single quotes (pkg/expr/sql/parser.go:24-26) and passes that string to RunCommands. The replacement DB always returns an error (pkg/expr/sql/db.go:16), so DuckDB is not executed and CVE-2024-9264 is not currently reachable here, but that stub error is the only control on this path. Every dashboard refresh or alert evaluation then logs at Error with the full SQL and the constructed command (parser.go:28) and again at Warn (sql_command.go:32), and the public error is BadRequest 'error reading SQL command' (sql_command.go:33-35). Instances that had sqlExpressions enabled — the population exposed by the CVE — will flood error logs with query text that may contain sensitive literals and will look like a SQL parser outage rather than an intentional shutdown. enableSqlExpressions is not consulted. Reject at NewSQLCommand/UnmarshalSQLCommand with a dedicated disabled error before any DuckDB statement is built or logged; quote-doubling is not enough if RunCommands is later wired to a real engine.

title: SQL disable helper always returns false and panics if features is nil
body: enableSqlExpressions (pkg/expr/reader.go:194-200) is the only explicit gate added for SQL expressions, but it always returns false: it stores the negation of FlagSqlExpressions and then returns false from both branches. The flag has no effect, yet IsEnabledGlobally is still called before either return. If ExpressionQueryReader.features is nil, that call panics on a nil interface instead of returning a rejection, and only SQL queries hit it — math, reduce, resample, and classic parsing do not touch h.features. Callers also receive fmt.Errorf('sqlExpressions is not implemented') at line 131, which is false: the feature existed and is being turned off for CVE-2024-9264. This helper is not used by UnmarshalSQLCommand, so it does not cover the existing execution path.

title: No regression test that SQL expressions stay disabled
body: This change is the in-repo fix for critical CVE-2024-9264, but no test was added or updated. Nothing asserts that ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery rejects QueryTypeSQL even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled, that a nil FeatureToggles does not panic, that UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand fails closed without Error-logging a serialization failure, or that TablesList and QueryFramesInto cannot execute SQL. Restoring a DuckDB-backed RunCommands, or changing the inverted enableSqlExpressions helper so the flag turns the ReadQuery path back on, would not be caught. Manual checks mentioned in the PR description are not a substitute for a regression test on a patch intended to be cherry-picked across release branches.

title: Disabled SQL expressions are logged as DuckDB serialization errors
body: Classic dashboard and alerting SQL expressions do not use the new ReadQuery gate. They call NewSQLCommand, which always calls TablesList. TablesList still interpolates the raw user expression into a DuckDB statement (`SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')`, with only single quotes doubled) and passes it to RunCommands. The new stub always returns "not implemented", so the statement is not executed, but the error branch always logs both the raw expression and that command at error level. NewSQLCommand logs the raw SQL again at warn. Every panel refresh or alert evaluation of an existing SQL expression therefore emits error logs containing the full user SQL (including any literals) and looks like an outage rather than an intentional disable for CVE-2024-9264. Reject the expression before building or logging that statement.

title: Security disable is reported as an unreadable SQL command
body: Because TablesList now always fails, every non-empty SQL expression on the SSE path (dashboards and alerting) is returned as errutil.BadRequest "sql-invalid-sql" with public message "error reading SQL command". That message is wrong: the expression was not malformed, and the underlying stub error is discarded. Callers, alert error states, and users cannot tell a CVE-2024-9264 kill switch from a bad query, so they will debug or rewrite valid expressions instead of removing a disabled feature. Return a single explicit disabled error from NewSQLCommand and UnmarshalSQLCommand.

title: SQL disablement is reported as not implemented and ignores the flag
body: ReadQuery rejects every SQL expression with "sqlExpressions is not implemented". The feature existed and is being turned off for CVE-2024-9264; the text is false. enableSqlExpressions also ignores FlagSqlExpressions: it negates IsEnabledGlobally and then returns false from both branches, and it dereferences h.features before that, so a nil toggle service panics instead of returning this error. Enabling the documented sqlExpressions flag does not change the result and is not mentioned. Clients that only read the toggle still believe the feature is available, then get a message that does not explain the security disable.

title: No regression test that SQL expressions stay disabled
body: This is the CVE-2024-9264 fix, but no test was added or updated. NewSQLCommand is the dashboard and alerting entry point and now fails only because the stub's RunCommands returns an error; ReadQuery depends on enableSqlExpressions, which always returns false through an inverted flag check. Nothing asserts that both entry points reject SQL when sqlExpressions is on and when it is off, or that Execute does not run user SQL. A later change can restore DuckDB or make the helper honor the flag without CI failing, which would reintroduce the RCE/LFI. Add a regression test for both paths that expects an explicit disabled error and does not need the duckdb binary.

title: Legacy SQL path fails as invalid SQL and error-logs every query
body: The explicit reject added in ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery does not cover the frontend entry point. UnmarshalSQLCommand always calls NewSQLCommand, and NewSQLCommand still calls sql.TablesList for every non-empty expression. reader.go itself notes that ExpressionQueryReader has not replaced the existing parser, so this is the path dashboard and alert evaluation use. TablesList now always fails because the stub RunCommands returns an error, and that failure is mapped to a BadRequest whose public message is "error reading SQL command" (lines 33-35). That text is wrong: the statement was not parsed or rejected as invalid SQL; the DuckDB engine was removed to close the RCE/LFI issue. Before returning, TablesList logs the raw expression and the assembled SELECT json_serialize_sql(...) command at Error (pkg/expr/sql/parser.go:28), and NewSQLCommand logs the raw SQL again at Warn (line 32). Instances that had enabled SQL expressions will therefore show a misleading invalid-query error and emit error-level logs containing the expression text on every panel refresh and every alert evaluation. Reject the feature in NewSQLCommand/UnmarshalSQLCommand before calling TablesList, with a stable disabled-feature error, and do not log the statement at Error.

title: SQL gate is an inverted no-op that can panic and misreports the feature
body: enableSqlExpressions is the only explicit SQL-expression gate, but it is not a real flag check. It sets enabled to the negation of FlagSqlExpressions and then returns false from both branches, so the flag cannot turn the feature back on. That matches the security intent, but it hides the kill switch, and the error returned to callers (line 131) is "sqlExpressions is not implemented", which is false — the feature existed and is being disabled because of the RCE/LFI vulnerability. The flag read also panics if ExpressionQueryReader.features is nil. This case did not touch features before, so a reader built without toggles now crashes on SQL queries instead of returning a controlled error. Return false without reading the flag, and use an error that says SQL expressions are disabled.

title: No regression test that SQL expressions stay disabled
body: This change set is the in-tree fix for the SQL-expression RCE/LFI issue, but it adds or updates no tests. Nothing asserts that ReadQuery rejects SQL queries even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled, that UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand fail closed without executing a statement, or that DB.RunCommands and DB.QueryFramesInto do not run SQL or touch the filesystem. The disable is an always-false helper with inverted flag logic plus stub methods that return "not implemented". Restoring a DuckDB call inside RunCommands, or changing the helper so the feature flag reaches NewSQLCommand while a later DB implementation executes queries, would not fail CI. Add a regression test for both entry points that expects a disabled-feature error with the flag on and asserts the supplied statement is not executed.

title: Parallel index init shares err and can ignore build failures
body: searchSupport.init starts one errgroup goroutine per namespace, but every goroutine assigns the build result to the single outer err variable and returns that same variable. BuildIndex used to hold its cache mutex for the whole build, so those goroutines mostly ran one at a time; after the lock was narrowed they actually run in parallel and the unsynchronized err writes race. A goroutine whose build failed can observe nil after another goroutine's success overwrites err, return nil, and let errgroup.Wait succeed, so the server starts with that namespace missing from the index. The reverse also happens: a successful goroutine can return another goroutine's error and fail startup incorrectly. totalBatchesIndexed is incremented from the same goroutines without synchronization. Each goroutine needs its own error variable.

title: Narrowed BuildIndex lock races same-key builds and clobbers the cache
body: BuildIndex previously held cacheMu for the entire build, which serialized bleve.New and cache publication. The mutex is now taken only for b.cache[key] = idx. getOrCreateIndex in search.go is still check-then-build with no per-key lock (the TODO above it says so), so two searches, or a search and a watch event, for a namespace that was not prebuilt can both miss the cache and build at once. File-backed builds then call bleve.New on the same directory concurrently; that races inside bleve, and the loser fails with path-already-exists even though an index was created. Memory builds both succeed and the later cache write replaces the earlier index without closing it, so watch updates applied to the replaced index disappear from later searches and the orphaned index leaks. In-flight builds need to be deduplicated per NamespacedResource, and the cache insert must keep an existing entry instead of overwriting it.

title: Index watch starts at the latest RV and drops writes made during the build
body: build returns the resource version observed while listing a namespace, and the comment on that return says watchers must apply every event since that version. init discards the returned version and then calls WatchWriteEvents, which samples the latest resource version at subscription time and only delivers newer rows. Creates, updates, and deletes that commit after a namespace was listed and before that subscription — expected when another HA replica writes during the long startup index build — are neither in the listed snapshot nor replayed. Updated documents stay stale in the search index, and deletes from that window remain searchable until a full rebuild. Namespaces are listed concurrently, so each list has its own version; the watch cursor has to be the earliest of those list versions, not the global maximum after every build finishes.

title: File indexes cannot be reopened, so eager init fails every restart
body: File-backed indexes are created with bleve.New on a stable path (Root/namespace/resource.group). bleve.New fails if that directory already exists, and this code never calls bleve.Open or deletes a leftover directory. If the builder fails, BuildIndex returns without closing the index or removing the partial directory. After the first successful file-backed build, or after a failed build that created the directory, the next process calls BuildIndex again, bleve.New fails, and NewResourceServer now aborts Init and refuses to construct the server. FileThreshold's zero value is 0, so any namespace with a positive count uses disk unless the caller sets a higher threshold. Startup must reopen or replace an existing directory, and error paths must delete partial indexes, or a normal restart cannot bring the storage server up.

title: Init failure returns nil without rolling back partial startup
body: NewResourceServer now calls Init and, on error, returns nil without calling the cancel func created above, lifecycle.Stop, or closing the blob bucket opened earlier in the constructor. If lifecycle.Init already opened the SQL database, those connections leak because the caller has no server value on which to call Stop. If search indexing succeeded and only the later watcher setup failed, search.init has already started a watch goroutine on context.Background that nothing will stop. Indexes already published into the caller-owned SearchBackend stay cached, so a retry that reuses that backend treats them as complete and skips rebuilding. Failure needs to stop lifecycle hooks, cancel background work, and drop partial indexes before returning the error.

title: Search watch loop ignores shutdown and panics when the event channel closes
body: After indexing, init starts a goroutine that reads WatchWriteEvents in a bare for loop and does not check the receive ok value. The watch context is context.Background, not the server context cancelled by Stop, so server shutdown does not stop the loop. The SQL poller closes that channel when the backend stops; the next receive yields a nil event, and handleEvent immediately dereferences evt.Type and panics, crashing the process during shutdown. If the backend is never stopped, the goroutine and poller leak for the rest of the process. Init now runs inside NewResourceServer, so this goroutine is created for every search-enabled server, including ones that are constructed and shut down without serving a request. The loop should use the server lifetime context and exit when the channel closes.

title: Same-key index builds are no longer serialized
body: BuildIndex used to hold bleveBackend.cacheMu for the entire build, including bleve.New and the document scan. GetIndex takes that same lock, so a caller that arrived while a build was in progress blocked and then saw the published index instead of starting a second build. The lock is now taken only for the unconditional `b.cache[key] = idx` at the end. getOrCreateIndex is still an unlocked check-then-act (GetIndex, and if nil, build); its own comment says that is unsafe. Two searches, or a search and a watch event, for a namespace that is not cached yet can both miss and both build. Each build creates a separate bleve index; the slower one overwrites the cache entry and the first index is never closed. Callers that already hold the first index keep writing into an object that is no longer served, so later searches miss those updates and the two views diverge. If size is above FileThreshold — including the zero default, where any positive size uses a file index, and getOrCreateIndex passes a placeholder size of 10 — both builds also call bleve.New on the same directory, which can fail or corrupt the index. Different keys can still build in parallel, but each NamespacedResource must be single-flighted, and a finished build must not replace an index already published for that key.

title: Index init workers share one err and can drop failures
body: searchSupport.init launches one errgroup goroutine per namespace, and each goroutine does `_, _, err = s.build(...)` then `return err`, using the single err variable from the outer function. Those goroutines run concurrently up to initWorkers. That assignment races with the other workers and with `err = group.Wait()` after they join. A worker can return another worker's error, or nil if a successful build overwrote err before the return, so group.Wait can return nil even though a namespace failed to index. Startup then logs success and starts the watch with that namespace missing from the search index and no error. The same closure also does totalBatchesIndexed++ with no synchronization, so the "namespaces indexed" span attribute is a data race and can be wrong. Each worker needs its own error variable, and the counter should be atomic or computed after Wait.

title: Writes during index build are never applied to the search index
body: Index init lists each namespace and builds its index, discards the resource version that build/ListIterator returns, and only then calls storage.WatchWriteEvents. That subscription samples the latest resource version at subscribe time, and the SQL poller only returns history rows newer than that version. A create, update, or delete committed after a namespace was snapshotted and before the subscription — including writes from another replica while this process is still building indexes — is neither in the snapshot nor replayed. Search keeps serving the stale index until that object is written again. The gap is the full index build, which this change says is long enough to exceed a request deadline, and it is now on the startup path. The watch needs to start first (or from the minimum version captured before listing), and events newer than each snapshot version must be applied when that build finishes.

title: Search index watch panics or leaks on shutdown
body: After indexing, init starts `for { v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v) }` with watchctx set to context.Background(). The loop never checks whether the receive succeeded, and server Stop cannot cancel that context. WatchWriteEvents' poller closes the channel when the SQL backend stops (backend done / lifecycle.Stop). A receive on a closed channel returns a nil *WrittenEvent, and handleEvent immediately reads evt.Type, which nil-pointer panics and crashes the process during shutdown. If the backend is not stopped, the goroutine never exits either, because it is not tied to the server context. Init now runs inside NewResourceServer whenever search is configured, so this goroutine is always started, not only after a client triggers lazy init. The loop should use the server's cancellable context and return when that context is done or the channel is closed.

title: Failed file index build is left on disk and blocks every retry
body: BuildIndex calls bleve.New on a stable path (root/namespace/resource.group) when size > FileThreshold. If that succeeds and the builder callback or Flush then fails, the function returns the error (lines 128 and 134) without closing the index or deleting the directory. bleve.New fails if the path already exists, and this code never falls back to bleve.Open. The next build of that namespace, including the next process start, fails immediately. NewResourceServer now aborts startup when index init fails, so one document that fails to index during the startup build can leave a directory that prevents the storage server from ever starting again until it is deleted by hand. On any error after a successful bleve.New, close the index and remove a partially created on-disk index before returning.

title: Broadcaster watch goroutine panics when the event stream closes
body: initWatcher starts a goroutine that forever does `v := <-events` and then reads v.Type and v.ResourceVersion, with no check that the channel is still open. The SQL poller closes that channel when the backend stops. The next receive is a nil event, the dereference panics, and process shutdown crashes. NewResourceServer now always calls Init, which always calls initWatcher, so this goroutine is created on every storage-server start rather than only after the first RPC. The loop must exit when the receive fails or the server context is cancelled, and it must not touch the event after a closed channel.

title: RPCs no longer fail after Stop
body: Stop stores "service is stopping" and then "service is stopped" in s.initErr. Init returns that value on every later call because sync.Once has already run, which is how handlers used to reject work after shutdown. Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search, History, Origin, IsHealthy, PutBlob, and GetBlob all called Init first and therefore returned that error instead of touching storage. Those calls were removed when initialization moved into NewResourceServer, and nothing else reads initErr. After Stop, those handlers still perform reads and writes against the backend while shutdown is in progress. Each RPC needs an explicit stopped check, or it must observe the cancelled server context, so a stopped server rejects new requests.

title: Postgres storage-server startup test is skipped
body: TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer is the integration test that boots the storage-server target and checks that it actually serves /metrics. This change initializes unified storage inside server construction, which is the startup path that test covers, but the patch skips it whenever GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres, with a TODO that it fails in Drone and works locally. Postgres is a supported backend (sqlite is already excluded). CI will not catch eager-init startup failures on Postgres — SQL errors, hangs, or the HTTP server never binding — and the known failure is skipped instead of fixed.

title: Same-key index builds are no longer single-flighted
body: BuildIndex used to hold cacheMu for the whole build, so a second GetIndex blocked until the finished index was published. The mutex is now taken only around the cache insert. getOrCreateIndex still does check-then-act (GetIndex, and on a miss build) and even has a TODO that same-key builds must not run together. After startup, two Search calls, or a Search and a watch event, for a namespace that was not built during init (count at or below InitMinCount) both see a cache miss and both call BuildIndex. Memory indexes both succeed and the later cache write overwrites the earlier one without closing it, so documents already written to the discarded index disappear from search and the Bleve index is leaked. File indexes both call bleve.New on the same directory; the loser fails with a path-exists error, so the caller gets a search error even if the other build published a usable index. Parallel builds of different keys are fine, but same-key builds need a per-key lock or singleflight held from the existence check through cache publish.

title: Search index misses writes committed during startup indexing
body: init lists every namespace and only afterward calls WatchWriteEvents. That snapshot records the latest resource version and the SQL poller only returns history newer than that snapshot. The RV returned by build is discarded. Any create, update, or delete committed after a namespace was listed and before the watch snapshot, including writes from other HA replicas, is neither in the bulk index nor replayed. The watch starts only after the slowest namespace finishes, so namespaces that finished early have a gap as long as the rest of the index build, which is the long operation this change is about. Search will keep serving missing, stale, or already-deleted objects until that document is written again. Record the RV before listing, or buffer watch events first, and replay history from that RV after the bulk load.

title: Parallel index builders share err and can hide failures
body: Each errgroup worker assigns s.build's result to the outer err variable and then returns err. When WorkerThreads is greater than 1 those goroutines race on that variable. A failed build can return nil if another worker stores nil into err before the return, so group.Wait succeeds and NewResourceServer starts with some namespaces never indexed. A successful worker can also return another worker's error and fail startup. This is a real data race, not just a logic race. totalBatchesIndexed is incremented from the same goroutines with no synchronization, so the trace attribute is racy as well. Use a local error inside the closure and an atomic counter.

title: Search watch loop panics when the event channel closes
body: After indexing, init starts a goroutine that loops on v := <-events and calls handleEvent, using context.Background rather than the server context. The SQL backend poller closes that channel when the backend stops (it selects on backend done and defers close). A receive on a closed channel yields a nil event, and handleEvent immediately reads evt.Type, which panics. An unrecovered goroutine panic crashes the process during graceful shutdown, skipping the rest of cleanup. server.Stop cannot stop the loop because it only cancels s.ctx. The loop must exit when the channel is closed or the context is cancelled, and the watch must be tied to the server lifetime.

title: File-backed indexes cannot be reopened, so restart fails startup
body: When size is above FileThreshold (the zero value is 0, so any positive count takes this branch unless the option is overridden), BuildIndex calls bleve.New on a directory under Root and never bleve.Open. bleve.New fails if that path already exists, and a failed builder returns without closing the index or removing a partial directory. Init now runs inside NewResourceServer and any error aborts construction, so a restart after a successful file index, or a retry after a build that left the directory behind, cannot start the storage server. The comment that was removed even said the last RV should be checked so an unchanged index can be skipped. Open an existing index when the directory is present, and delete or uniquely name the directory if a build fails, or every file-backed namespace wedges process startup.

title: Init failure in the constructor leaks the backend and watchers
body: NewResourceServer calls Init and, on error, logs and returns nil without calling cancel or Stop. lifecycle.Init may already have opened the database. If search.init succeeded and initWatcher then failed, search.init has already started a WatchWriteEvents poller and an event goroutine on context.Background. The caller never receives the server, so it cannot Stop those resources, and the connection pool and pollers live until the process exits. On the error path, stop the lifecycle/backend and cancel the server context, while still returning the original init error.

title: Startup index build cannot be cancelled or given a deadline
body: The context now used for the full index build is created from context.Background inside NewResourceServer, which does not accept a caller context. The only cancel is Stop, and Stop cannot run until NewResourceServer returns, which is blocked on GetResourceStats and every ListIterator in the index build. A stuck database call therefore hangs process startup with no deadline, and a shutdown signal cannot abort the build. The old request context cancelled too early; this replacement needs a long but bounded startup context that process shutdown can cancel.

title: TotalDocs ranges the index cache without holding cacheMu
body: TotalDocs iterates b.cache with no RLock, while BuildIndex writes that map under cacheMu. Narrowing the lock means builds now publish into the map concurrently, during startup and for later cold namespaces. In Go, a concurrent map read and write is a fatal runtime error, not a missed update. init also calls TotalDocs immediately after starting the watch goroutine that can BuildIndex on a cache miss, and TotalDocs is part of the SearchBackend interface so any other caller can hit the same crash. Hold cacheMu.RLock for the whole iteration.

title: Storage-server integration test is skipped on Postgres
body: TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer is the integration coverage for the storage-server target, and this PR makes that target initialize unified storage and build the search index during construction. The change skips the test whenever GRAFANA_TEST_DB is postgres, with a TODO that it fails in Drone but works locally. Postgres is a primary deployment database, so CI no longer runs storage-server startup there, and a startup regression from eager init will not be caught. Fix the Postgres failure instead of skipping it.

title: No-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() does not exist
body: UsernameForm.authenticate() now calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments so the username step is not skipped on re-authentication when passkeys are on. The only new method is UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel); nothing in this class or its parents defines a no-arg overload, and there is no static import. services will not compile, so the re-authentication fix cannot build or be tested. The call has to match a real method that reports whether conditional passkeys are enabled (a no-arg check, or pass context.getUser() only if that helper does not require a non-null user).

title: Passkeys UI removed from the unidentified-user login form
body: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel) is true only when user != null, and both authenticate() (line 115) and the error challenge() override (line 137) use it before webauthnAuth.fillContextForm. That call used to run when the user was not yet selected (webauthnAuth != null && isPasskeysEnabled()), which is how conditional passkeys are rendered on the first username/password page. Moving it out of the else branch and requiring a non-null user inverts that: initial login and invalid-credential redisplay no longer get a WebAuthn challenge, RP ID, or conditional UI, because context.getUser() is still null until validateUser, which runs only after a successful password check. Discoverable-key auto-login and the passkey control on the combined form stop working; existing tests such as PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest.webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey and passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey still expect username webauthn autocomplete and //form[@id='webauth'] on that first page. Passkeys should be filled whenever webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled(), including when the user is null, and additionally when the user is already set for re-authentication.

title: No-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() does not exist
body: UsernameForm.authenticate() now calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments so re-authentication will not skip the username form when passkeys are on. The only new method is UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel), and UsernameForm does not define a no-arg overload. This does not compile, so the username-form flow (and PasskeysUsernameFormTest) cannot be built. The call needs a real method: either pass context.getUser(), or add a no-arg helper that only checks that the passkeys feature and realm policy are enabled.

title: Conditional passkey UI dropped when user is unknown
body: authenticate() and the error challenge() (line 137) now call fillContextForm only when isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()) is true. That helper (line 161) requires a non-null user, replacing the previous checks that set up WebAuthn conditional UI precisely when the user was not yet selected (webauthnAuth != null && isPasskeysEnabled(), and user == null on errors). Moving the call outside the else does not restore the anonymous case. On a normal login the user is null, so the page never gets the WebAuthn challenge, rpId, or ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI. Discoverable-credential auto-login, the webauth form, and "username webauthn" autocomplete fail on the initial page and on invalid-username/invalid-password redisplay. Only re-authentication, where a user is already on the context, still sets up passkeys. Passkeys should be filled whenever the feature is enabled, whether or not a user is already known.

title: UsernameForm calls a passkeys method that does not exist
body: UsernameForm.authenticate() now calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments so re-authentication will not skip the username form when passkeys are on. The only method added on UsernamePasswordForm is isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel); nothing in the authenticator hierarchy defines a no-arg overload, and there is no static import. This does not compile, so the services module cannot build and the username-form re-authentication change never runs. Call the real method (for example isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())) and make sure that implementation does not require a non-null user if it is also used before identity is known.

title: Conditional passkeys UI is no longer set up on the initial login page
body: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel) is true only when its user argument is non-null, and both setup sites now use that helper: authenticate() around line 115 and the error challenge() override around line 137. Previously fillContextForm ran when passkeys were enabled and the user was not yet selected (context.getUser() == null). That is what puts the WebAuthn challenge, rpId, and AUTH_CHALLENGE_NOTE on the first login page and on the invalid-username error page. The new check is the inverse, so a normal login with no user on the context never embeds passkey data. Discoverable-credential sign-in and the username webauthn autocomplete field stop working, and passkey-only users (the existing tests delete the password before expecting auto-login) cannot authenticate. Unchanged tests such as webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey and the first page of passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey still require that form. Drop the user != null requirement so passkeys are prepared both before the user is known and during re-authentication; WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator.shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators() already returns false, so fillContextForm will not abort when a known user has no registered authenticators.

title: Login-cache invalidation treats wrapped isEnabled() as the DB flag
body: update() loads the previous identity provider with getById() and passes that instance to registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate(). With the organization feature on, getById() does not return the persisted row; it returns the wrapper from createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(), whose isEnabled() is false whenever the IdP has an organization id and the organization is missing, the organization is disabled, or OrganizationProvider.isEnabled() is false, even if the IdP's own enabled flag is still true. The new login list is populated by idpDelegate.getForLogin(), which filters on the stored enabled, link-only, hide-on-login, and kc.org.broker.public values, not on that wrapper. getLoginPredicate() calls IdentityProviderModel::isEnabled, so on the wrapper it can conclude the IdP was never a login IdP. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() then returns without invalidating realmId.idp.login.* when the update model also fails the predicate — for example the update sets hideOnLogin, linkOnly, enabled=false, or clears kc.org.broker.public, which is exactly when the cached id list must be dropped. A common admin sequence hits this: organizations (or one org) are disabled, a public login IdP is edited so it should disappear from getForLogin, then organizations are turned back on. getForLogin still expands the cached internal ids and does not re-apply the login filters, so it returns an IdP the JPA query would exclude. OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean only re-checks isEnabled(), not hide-on-login, link-only, or broker-public, so the login page will show a broker the admin hid or marked non-public. Decide invalidation from the raw persisted model (idpDelegate.getById), not the organization-aware wrapper. The new OrganizationCacheTest only updates IdPs while they remain effectively enabled, so it does not catch this.

title: Login-cache test deletes the alias "alias" instead of the IdPs it creates
body: testCacheIDPForLogin registers cleanup with testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove, both in the creation loop (line 381) and again for idp-alias-20 (line 425). That is the literal alias "alias", not idp-alias-0 through idp-alias-20. Cleanup therefore issues a delete for a provider that was never created and leaves the new brokers in the shared test realm, including enabled, non-hidden realm IdPs and public organization brokers. The same mistake is already present in testCacheIDPByOrg (line 303), which creates org-idp-0..org-idp-9, sets kc.org.broker.public=true, and links them to organizations. If that method runs first, those brokers are still present when this test calls getForLogin(ORG_ONLY/ALL, orgaId), so the expected sizes 5 and 10 are wrong and the new test fails. Even if this test runs first, the leaked idp-alias-* providers remain for later organization and broker tests. Capture the real alias in a final variable and register cleanup against that resource.

title: Login-cache invalidation uses wrapped isEnabled and keeps hidden IdPs
body: update() loads the pre-update IdP with getById() and passes that object to registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate(). With the ORGANIZATION feature enabled, getById() always returns the organization-aware wrapper from createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel, whose isEnabled() is false unless the organization exists, OrganizationProvider.isEnabled() is true, and the organization itself is enabled. LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate() (used at the checks around lines 405 and 409) treats IdentityProviderModel::isEnabled as a login-eligibility flag. So a storage-enabled, public, non-hidden org IdP fails the predicate whenever its org is disabled, missing, or the realm organization switch is off, even though delegate getForLogin still selected it using the stored enabled/linkOnly/hideOnLogin/broker-public flags and its internal id is already in the login list cache. If an update then removes login eligibility (hideOnLogin, linkOnly, or kc.org.broker.public=false) — or unlinks the IdP while also making it ineligible — both the wrapped original and the raw updated model fail the predicate, and the method returns without invalidating realmId.idp.login.{REALM_ONLY,ORG_ONLY,ALL}. The cached ids are not self-healed on the next read, because getById() still finds the row. OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean only rechecks isEnabled(), not hideOnLogin, linkOnly, or broker public, so once the organization (or realm organizations switch) is turned back on, or immediately if the IdP was unlinked in the same update, that IdP is rendered on the login page. create() and remove() evaluate the predicate on the raw delegate model, so only update() is wrong. The new test only mutates realm-level IdPs and does not cover a disabled organization. Decide invalidation from the unwrapped storage model (or from config flags), not from the wrapper.

title: Login-cache test cleans up a nonexistent IdP alias
body: testCacheIDPForLogin creates providers aliased idp-alias-0 through idp-alias-20, but the cleanups at lines 381 and 425 call testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias") — the literal alias "alias", not the alias just created (the same mistake as the existing loop in testCacheIDPByOrg). The admin client proxy is non-null, so the test does not fail at registration, but cleanup never deletes idp-alias-*. Those providers stay in the shared test realm (half of them public and enabled, and several linked to orga). A rerun fails on duplicate aliases, and any later test that counts login or organization IdPs in the same realm sees extra brokers. Register cleanup with the actual alias (and unlink org brokers before remove).

title: Login-list invalidation uses wrapped isEnabled as membership
body: update() takes the pre-image from getById() (line 91) and passes it to registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate. With the organization feature on, getById() returns the organization-aware wrapper whose isEnabled() is false unless the IdP is enabled and its organization exists, the organization provider is enabled, and the organization itself is enabled. LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate() applies ENABLED via IdentityProviderModel::isEnabled, so that override runs. The login list is filled from the JPA delegate's getForLogin, which filters only stored enabled / link-only / hide-on-login plus organization id and kc.org.broker.public, not organization enabled state. If an org-linked IdP is updated while its organization is disabled or missing, the wrapped original already fails the predicate. If the update also makes the raw model ineligible (hide-on-login, link-only, disabled, or broker-public turned off), both sides fail and the method returns without invalidating the .idp.login.* keys. The id stays in the cached set. A later getForLogin expands those ids with getById and does not re-apply hide-on-login, link-only, broker-public, or organization-id checks. OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean only re-checks isEnabled(). After the organization is enabled again, that broker is shown on the login page even though it was configured as hidden, link-only, or not public, and getForLogin breaks its contract. The same skip happens when the organization feature is off if the caller mutates the instance returned by getByAlias/getById and passes it to update(): createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel then returns the cached model without copying, so the before/after comparison sees only the new state. Load the pre-image from the JPA delegate (raw flags, not the wrapper) or always invalidate the login keys, and drop resolved models that no longer match the requested mode. testCacheIDPForLogin never updates an org-linked login IdP while the org is disabled, so this is untested.

title: Cached getForLogin results have unstable order
body: getForLogin stores delegate ids with Collectors.toSet() and, on a hit, copies them into another HashSet before returning identityProviders.stream(). Set iteration order is undefined and can change between requests even when membership is unchanged. The previous implementation was the interface default, which returned the delegate getAllStream order. OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean sorts that stream with IDP_COMPARATOR_INSTANCE; List.sort is stable, so providers that compare equal (the usual case when guiOrder is unset or tied, if the comparator has no unique tiebreaker) keep this random order and can swap on the login page on every load. Callers that do not sort lose the previous query order entirely. Cache and return the ids in encounter order (List or LinkedHashSet), not a HashSet.

title: Login-cache test never removes the IdPs it creates
body: testCacheIDPForLogin registers cleanup as testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove (line 381 inside the create loop, and again at line 425) instead of the alias just created (idp-alias-N). The method reference is bound to a proxy for the literal alias "alias", so the 20 providers this test creates are never removed, and cleanup may DELETE a non-existent alias. This class does not otherwise delete those brokers: onAfter only removes a user named member. The new test links ten of them to whichever organization getAll().get(0) returns and asserts exact login-cache sizes (5, 10, 11). Leftover public enabled IdPs change those counts on another run and will also change testCacheIDPByOrg, which asserts an exact getByOrganization size of 6 for the same organization. The new test is therefore order-dependent on the pre-existing leak in testCacheIDPByOrg (same wrong "alias" cleanup). Clean up each created alias (and unlink org brokers) so the realm is isolated.

title: Tied crypto providers are chosen silently instead of failing startup
body: detectProvider used to throw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath, which stopped the server from running with an ambiguous crypto stack. It now sorts by CryptoProvider.order() descending and always returns the first entry, logging the rest only at debug. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return 200, so they tie. Stream.sorted is stable, so the winner is whichever jar ServiceLoader encounters first (classpath or module order), not an explicit preference. A deployment that accidentally contains both the default BouncyCastle provider and the FIPS provider — previously a startup error — will now boot and can run non-FIPS crypto, or drop Elytron in favor of BC, with no error and no info-level log. ServiceLoader also instantiates every provider before the sort, so the losing provider's constructor still registers JCA providers and mutates security properties, and the process continues in that mixed state. AuthzClientCryptoProvider at order 100 is correctly deprioritized, but that does not require ignoring a tie at the winning order. If several providers share the maximum order, startup should still fail and list them. Nothing in this change tests that selection.

title: order() is abstract, so existing CryptoProvider implementations crash
body: CryptoProvider is a public SPI implemented outside this interface (the default, Elytron, and FIPS artifacts, plus downstream crypto providers). order() was added as an abstract method with no default. An implementation compiled against the previous interface throws AbstractMethodError when ServiceLoader instantiates it and detectProvider sorts with CryptoProvider::order. That error aborts provider detection entirely, so Keycloak will not start even if a newer provider on the classpath would have been selected. A default method returning a low value (below AuthzClientCryptoProvider's 100 and the in-tree providers' 200) would keep existing implementations loadable and still prefer the updated providers.

title: AuthzClient.create permanently pins CryptoIntegration to its classloader
body: CryptoIntegration.init is process-global and returns immediately once a provider is set, so the first caller permanently chooses it. AuthzClient.create now calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()) as a side effect of constructing a client. ServiceLoader therefore runs only against that classloader, not the thread context classloader and not the classloader a later server or application init would pass. If this runs first in a JVM where AuthzClient's classloader can see AuthzClientCryptoProvider (order 100) but not DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, or WildFlyElytronProvider — for example keycloak-common in a parent classloader and the real crypto module only in a child — the stub provider is installed and every later CryptoIntegration.init is a no-op. PEM, signature, certificate, AES, and truststore calls then throw UnsupportedOperationException, and the server no longer uses BouncyCastle or FIPS. Before this change, creating an AuthzClient did not initialize crypto, so the server's own init still selected the intended provider. A library constructor should not freeze detection, or a later init that finds a higher-order provider must be allowed to replace the stub.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK keystore provider
body: CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider is specified to return the BouncyCastle or BCFIPS Provider. AuthzClientCryptoProvider instead returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is whichever JDK provider implements the default keystore type (typically SUN, or SunJSSE when the default type is PKCS12) and follows the keystore.type security property. Callers that pass this Provider into Signature.getInstance, Cipher.getInstance, or CertificateFactory.getInstance do not get BouncyCastle algorithms. PKCS7 padding, BCFKS, and other BC-only operations fail, or they silently run on a non-FIPS JDK provider. WildFlyElytronProvider returns null for this method and callers already null-check and fall back; a non-null SUN provider skips that fallback. This should return null or throw UnsupportedOperationException like the other unimplemented methods, not an unrelated JCA provider.

title: ECDSA test never checks JCA DER or the real curve sizes
body: ECDSAAlgorithmTest builds one KeyPair with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() and no ECGenParameterSpec, so the key is the JVM default curve (P-256 on SunEC). It then runs ES256, ES384, and ES512 against that same key and only asserts that asn1derToConcatenatedRS(concatenatedRSToASN1DER(rs)) equals rs. It never checks that the DER matches the original Signature.sign() bytes, and it never calls Signature.verify on the converted DER. A codec that is self-inverse but not valid DER still passes, and integerToBytes silently pads or truncates to algorithm.getSignatureLength(), so a P-256 signature padded out to the ES512 length of 132 also round-trips. Because R and S stay about 32 bytes, sequence and integer lengths stay under 128, so the long-form length paths in ASN1Encoder.writeLength and ASN1Decoder.readLength — required for real P-521 signatures — are never executed. Provider ordering is also untested. The test should initialize secp256r1, secp384r1, and secp521r1 explicitly, assert the DER equals the JCA signature or verifies, and cover ServiceLoader selection.

title: Tied crypto providers are picked arbitrarily and no longer fail startup
body: detectProvider now sorts CryptoProviders by order() and, if more than one is found, only debug-logs the rest and returns foundProviders.get(0). The previous hard failure for multiple providers is gone. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so any two of them tie. Stream.sorted is stable, so the winner is whichever ServiceLoader yielded first (classpath order), not a defined preference. ServiceLoader also constructs every provider before the sort, and FIPS1402Provider's constructor inserts BCFIPS/BCJSSE at the front of the JVM security providers even when that implementation is then ignored. A classpath that contains more than one real provider — previously rejected at startup — can now run with the wrong CryptoProvider (including not actually being in FIPS mode) while FIPS JCA providers may already have been installed globally. Equal top order should still be a startup error.

title: order() is abstract and breaks existing CryptoProvider implementors
body: order() was added as a new abstract method with no default. CryptoProvider is a public SPI. Any implementation not recompiled with this change (downstream forks, custom or test providers, an older provider jar still on the classpath) fails to compile, and at runtime ServiceLoader hits AbstractMethodError when detectProvider calls CryptoProvider::order while sorting. That aborts crypto init and server startup. The same interface already uses default methods for optional behavior (getSupportedKeyStoreTypes, getSupportedRsaKeySizes). order() should default (for example to 0) so older implementors still load and lose to the in-repo providers that return 200.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK keystore provider
body: CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider is specified to return the BouncyCastle or BCFIPS JCA provider. AuthzClientCryptoProvider returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is the provider of the default keystore type: SUN on Java 8 (JKS) and typically SunJSSE on later JDKs (PKCS12). Neither implements the ciphers, signatures, or BC algorithms callers request from this method. WildFlyElytronProvider returns null in the same situation. A non-null unrelated provider makes null-checks succeed, so Security.addProvider or Signature/Cipher.getInstance(alg, provider) runs against SUN/SunJSSE and throws NoSuchAlgorithmException or silently uses a non-BC implementation. This class is the provider selected for the standalone authz client, so any keycloak-core path that uses getBouncyCastleProvider() is wrong. Return null or throw; do not return the keystore provider.

title: AuthzClient.create can lock the JVM onto the stub crypto provider
body: AuthzClient.create(Configuration) unconditionally calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()). init only runs detection while the static cryptoProvider field is null; every later init is ignored for the life of the JVM. ServiceLoader is given the authz-client class loader, which always sees AuthzClientCryptoProvider (META-INF/services in this jar, order 100) but does not see providers that are only on a child or thread-context class loader. If create() runs before the server's own CryptoIntegration.init — embedded use, or a test that builds a client before server startup — the process is permanently stuck with AuthzClientCryptoProvider. That implementation throws UnsupportedOperationException for signature, PEM, certificate, cipher, and truststore operations. The new order() preference cannot correct this, because the higher-order provider was never visible to the class loader used for the first init. Creating a client should not freeze the process-wide provider on this stub.

title: ECDSA tests use a P-256 key and never check a real signature
body: The suite builds one KeyPair with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() and no ECGenParameterSpec, so the key is the JDK default curve (secp256r1). testES384 and testES512 still sign with that P-256 key while passing algorithm.getSignatureLength() (96 and 132) into the converter. ECDSA r/s width follows the curve order, not the JWS algorithm name, so those tests only round-trip 32-byte coordinates zero-padded to 48 or 66 bytes. They never hit P-384 or P-521 sizes or the long-form DER length path that real ES512 signatures need (sequence content longer than 127 bytes). The only assertion compares two outputs of the same codec (DER to RS to DER to RS). A converter that swaps r and s, or that emits DER which Signature.verify would reject, still passes. Nothing tests that CryptoIntegration prefers a provider with order 200 over AuthzClientCryptoProvider (order 100), which is the behavior this PR says keeps the testsuite on DefaultCryptoProvider. The new codec and provider selection can be wrong and CI stays green.

title: Tied crypto providers are chosen silently instead of failing startup
body: detectProvider used to abort startup with IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath. It now sorts by order() descending and keeps the first, logging the rest only at debug. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return 200, so they tie, and ServiceLoader/classpath enumeration order picks the winner. A deployment that contains both the FIPS provider and a non-FIPS provider, which previously refused to boot, now starts and can run non-FIPS algorithms with no warn or error. Constructors of every discovered provider still run before the choice, so the non-selected provider has already mutated JVM security state (provider insertion, securerandom.strongAlgorithms, KeyManagerFactory/TrustManagerFactory properties) while the process continues. Nothing in this PR tests two providers that share the top order. Fail when more than one provider shares the highest order (AuthzClientCryptoProvider at 100 can still coexist with a single order-200 provider), and if a priority is intended give FIPS a strictly higher order than Default and Elytron.

title: ECDSAAlgorithmTest cannot compile with this module's dependencies
