The new formParams.getFirst call also NPEs if formParams is null, which the previous constructor accepted.

title: Legacy token exchange still encodes grant type as unknown
body: The grant shortcut is taken from ClientSessionContext attribute Constants.GRANT_TYPE; if it was never set, the id is encoded with "na". Token exchange does not go through OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse, so each provider must set the attribute itself. Only StandardTokenExchangeProvider.exchangeClientToOIDCClient does so (line 237). TokenExchangeGrantTypeFactory still enables the legacy TOKEN_EXCHANGE feature as well as the v2 features, and the legacy V1 token-exchange provider builds access tokens in its own exchangeClientToOIDCClient path, which this PR does not change. Those tokens get grant shortcut "na" and cannot be distinguished from tokens whose grant was never recorded, so the token-exchange use case this PR is for will not see them. Any other TokenExchangeProvider that overrides exchangeClientToOIDCClient and does not call this method has the same gap. Set the attribute on the shared issuance path, not only in the standard v2 provider.

title: Bad token-id error claims the whole id must be length 6
body: When the prefix before ':' is not 6 characters, getTokenContextFromTokenId throws IllegalArgumentException saying the token id has 'Expected length of 6.' The check is only on that prefix. A valid encoded id is 6 prefix characters, a colon, and a 36-character UUID (43 characters). The message points operators at a 6-character jti and does not say which part failed. State that the context prefix before ':' must be exactly 6 characters.

title: First offline access token is encoded as an online session
body: createTokenResponse calls createClientAccessToken, which stamps the jti session-type from userSession.isOffline(), before generateRefreshToken() and before the online session may be deleted. On the first offline_access response the login session is still online at that point, so the prefix is online (on…). Lines 116-120 then issue an offline refresh token and, when the FIRST_OFFLINE_ACCESS note is set, remove that online user session. Offline sessions live in a separate store but keep the same session id, so today's validation only finds the session by falling back from online to offline. The prefix names the store that no longer holds the session. Callers that use it to pick a single store, which is the stated reason for encoding session type, will miss the session and reject the access token returned with that first offline refresh token. ResourceOwnerPasswordCredentialsGrantType has the same order and is stricter: generateAccessToken() at line 139 runs first, then any offline refresh token causes removeUserSession at lines 142-146, not only the first-offline-access case. Later refreshes are fine because the loaded session is already offline. No test issues an offline_access token and checks the session-type characters.

title: Constructor null-checks grantType instead of rawTokenId
body: The fourth Objects.requireNonNull still passes grantType, with the message Null rawTokenId not allowed. A null rawTokenId is accepted. encodeTokenId concatenates the raw id with string +, so null becomes the literal suffix :null. Every such token shares that jti suffix, so ids are no longer unique, and the constructor does not enforce the invariant it claims.

title: Access-token id matcher is inverted and reads the wrong slice
body: isAccessTokenId is what expectCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectDeviceCodeToToken, and expectAuthReqIdToToken now use to assert the new jti. The grant shortcut is characters at indexes 4 and 5 of the six-character prefix (onrtac is ac), but the matcher uses substring(3, 5), which is ta for that id. The condition is also backwards: it returns false when that slice equals the expected shortcut. For every built-in shortcut these helpers pass, the wrong slice is not equal to the expected value, so the inverted check does not fire and any id with a colon and a UUID suffix passes, including the na fallback used when GRANT_TYPE was never set. The new assertions therefore do not fail if grant encoding is missing or wrong, and they never check session type or token type. A prefix shorter than 5 characters throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException from the matcher instead of a mismatch.

title: getShortcut() has no default and breaks existing grant factories at startup
body: OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is an existing extension SPI, and getShortcut() was added as a new abstract method with no default implementation. DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit loads every OAuth2GrantTypeFactory and calls getShortcut(). A custom grant factory built against the previous interface throws AbstractMethodError there, and Keycloak fails to start. A default method that returns a stable two-character fallback would keep existing providers loading.

title: Grant shortcuts are not constrained to the two-character encoding
body: Decoding assumes every grant shortcut is exactly two characters and contains no colon, so the prefix is always six characters and the first colon separates the raw id. getShortcut() is documented as usually like a 3-letter shortcut, and postInit only checks that the two maps end up the same size. A unique shortcut of any other length is stored, encodeTokenId writes it into the jti, and getTokenContextFromTokenId then throws IllegalArgumentException because the prefix length is not 6. That exception text says the token id is expected to have length 6, but the check is only on the prefix; a valid id is six characters, a colon, and a UUID, so the message is wrong. The lazy reload in getShortcutByGrantType and getGrantTypeByShortcut, meant for grants deployed after startup, inserts the new shortcut with no length check and no collision check, so a duplicate shortcut overwrites another grant and later tokens decode as the wrong grant type.

title: setFormParams leaves the cached grant type stale
body: Context snapshots grant_type from the constructor form parameters, and getGrantType() returns that field. setFormParams replaces formParams but does not update grantType. A caller that uses this public setter to change the request parameters after construction will encode the original grant type, or na if the original map had no grant_type, rather than the grant type actually being processed. The getter should read the current form parameters, or the setter should refresh the cached value.

title: Rotating recovery codes into user storage leaves old local codes valid
body: createRecoveryCodesCredential treats a true result from user.credentialManager().updateCredential as done and returns without deleting recovery-authn-codes credentials already stored in Keycloak's local database. The local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential path is skipped in that branch, and nothing else removes those rows. Federated users who already had recovery codes locally (the only option before their user-storage provider accepted this type, or if another API wrote them locally) and then regenerate will keep the old set. UserCredentialManager.isValid accepts a code if any supporting CredentialInputValidator accepts it, and the local recovery-code provider validates local credentials independently of user storage, so the retired codes still authenticate after rotation. RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential also prefers the federated credential, so the login form can show the new code number while the old codes still work. The same gap exists in the other direction: if updateCredential returns false but user storage already holds codes, the fallback local create adds a second valid set and does not disable the user-storage one. After a successful user-storage write the helper must remove existing local recovery-authn-codes credentials, and when falling back to local storage it must disable the user-storage credential, so only one set remains valid.

title: Spent federated recovery codes are not removed and the next login crashes
body: After a recovery code is accepted, the authenticator reloads the credential through RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential, which now returns a user-storage credential ahead of a local one. If that model reports all codes used, it calls credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById. That API only deletes credentials in Keycloak's local credential store; a federated credential id is not there, so the call is a no-op and the user-storage credential stays configured. isConfiguredFor therefore remains true. CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES is added, but required actions run only after the browser flow succeeds. On the next login the recovery-code authenticator still runs and constructs RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean, which unconditionally calls getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get() (RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean.java line 21). With no unused code left that throws NoSuchElementException, the user gets an error page, and never reaches the setup action. If the browser flow requires recovery codes, they cannot sign in. Spent federated credentials have to be removed through the user-storage disable path (disableCredentialType or an equivalent federated remove), not only removeStoredCredentialById. BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.disableCredentialType (line 217) currently ignores recovery-authn-codes, so that provider must clear them as well or this path cannot be fixed end to end.

title: User-storage recovery codes are stored in cleartext and never consumed
body: updateCredential writes input.getChallengeResponse() — the JSON array of raw recovery codes from CredentialHelper — straight into credentialData (line 197). isValid deserializes that list and returns true if any entry equals the submitted code. It does not delete the matched code, mark it used, or require the next unused code. getCredentials then rebuilds the credential with RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues (line 237), which hashes the original list, marks every code unused, and does not copy the id that was stored on the saved credential. disableCredentialType (line 217) and getDisableableCredentialTypesStream (line 259) only handle OTP, so recovery codes cannot be disabled from account or admin APIs. Local recovery codes are hashed and one-time; this provider keeps plaintext codes valid for the life of the server-side user map, the login form always asks for code 0, and the authenticator's all-codes-used branch is unreachable. testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only submits the first code once, so it passes even though the same code can be replayed.

title: User-storage recovery codes are reusable and not sequential
body: BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid accepts a recovery code if any stored code equals the submitted value, and it never removes the matched code. After CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential stores the codes in user storage, login calls credentialManager().isValid, which hits this method instead of RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider (the component that consumes a locally stored code). Nothing in the authenticator updates the stored list afterward. A previously used code therefore keeps working forever, and any of the twelve codes is accepted regardless of the index RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean displays. Shoulder-surfing or replay of one code is enough to authenticate again. The new login test only submits the first code once, so it does not catch this.

title: Recovery codes stored in plaintext
body: updateCredential saves input.getChallengeResponse() straight into CredentialModel.credentialData. That value is the JSON array of raw recovery codes written by CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential, and isValid later compares those strings with String.equals. The password branch in the same method hashes the secret with PasswordHashProvider before storing it. Recovery codes are password-equivalent; anyone who can read this provider's user map, or a storage implementation that persists the challenge response the same way, can log in as the user. Hash the codes (RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode, or the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel secret format) before persisting them, and compare hashes on validation.

title: getCredentials drops id and resets usage
body: getCredentials does not return the stored recovery-code CredentialModel. On every read it deserializes the original plaintext list and passes it to RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues, which builds a new all-unused model and does not keep the id assigned in updateCredential (recoveryCodesModel.setId). The id Keycloak sees is therefore null, so account-console deletion and removeStoredCredentialById cannot target the stored credential. The next-code number shown by RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean is always the first code, even after a code has been used, and any usage state a correct isValid would persist is discarded on the next read. Login keeps prompting for code 0.

title: Recovery codes cannot be disabled
body: disableCredentialType only clears OTP. For recovery-authn-codes it logs that the type is unsupported and leaves MyUser.recoveryCodes set. getDisableableCredentialTypesStream likewise only reports OTP, so the admin API and account console will not treat recovery codes as disableable. OTP removal in this class works because both methods handle OTP; recovery codes need the same treatment. After setup, a user cannot turn recovery codes off, isConfiguredFor stays true, and a browser flow that requires them keeps challenging for a code that cannot be removed.

title: Exhausted user-storage recovery codes are not deleted
body: After a successful recovery-code login the authenticator now loads the credential with RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential, which prefers user storage, and if allCodesUsed() is true it calls removeStoredCredentialById and ignores the result. That API deletes a row in Keycloak's local credential store. A credential created when user storage's updateCredential returns true is not in that store. The model getCredentials returns also has a null id, because createFromValues does not preserve the id stored on the provider, so the remove call cannot match the federated credential either. The exhausted credential stays configured. The next login still runs this authenticator, and RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean then calls getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get() with no remaining code, which throws and fails login with a server error instead of the reconfigure required action. Cleanup needs disableCredentialType (and the storage provider must honor it); removeStoredCredentialById alone does not clear user storage.

title: Old local recovery codes survive user-storage create
body: When user.credentialManager().updateCredential returns true, createRecoveryCodesCredential logs success and does not delete recovery-authn-codes credentials already stored in Keycloak's local store. Before this change, federated users always received local recovery codes, because user storage did not accept the type. After this change, a provider that returns true (including BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage, which newly supports the type) stores the new set externally and leaves the previous local set in place. credentialManager().isValid still tries local credential providers when the user-storage check does not accept the submitted code, so the old codes remain valid after the user generates a new set. Regeneration does not revoke previously issued recovery codes. On a successful user-storage write, existing local credentials of this type must be removed.

title: Recovery-code storage test misses reuse and removal
body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin writes recovery codes, asserts they are absent from Keycloak's DB and present in the user-storage map, and logs in once with code index 0. It never reuses that code, never checks that the next login asks for the next index, never submits an out-of-order code, never regenerates codes after a local credential already exists, and never disables or deletes the credential. Those are the paths this PR gets wrong: isValid accepts any code and does not consume it, getCredentials rebuilds an unused set with a null id, disableCredentialType ignores the type, and a later user-storage create does not revoke an older local set. The test passes while recovery codes remain reusable and irremovable.

title: User-storage recovery codes are reusable and not ordered
body: isValid deserializes the stored raw code list and returns true if any entry equals the submitted value, then leaves the list unchanged. Recovery codes are one-time and must be used in order: the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider hashes the input, matches only the next remaining code, and deletes it. credentialManager().isValid stops at the user-storage validator when that provider supports and is configured for the type, so the local provider never runs for credentials accepted by CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential. RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator does not consume the code after a successful check; it only re-reads the credential. The same backup code can be replayed forever, and a code other than the one the login form requested is accepted. The new test logs in only once, so it does not catch this.

title: Recovery-code login form crashes unless storage returns Keycloak's internal model
body: The bean loads a credential via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential and immediately calls Optional.get() and RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel. That parser requires credentialData and secretData in the hashed recovery-code schema and throws NoSuchElementException or RuntimeException otherwise. When user storage's updateCredential returns true, createRecoveryCodesCredential does not persist that model; it only sends a JSON array of raw codes on a UserCredentialModel. isConfiguredFor can still be true, so the authenticator renders this bean. A provider that stores the updateCredential payload and returns it, or that implements supportsCredentialType, updateCredential, isConfiguredFor, and isValid but not getCredentials, makes recovery-code login fail with a server error before a code can be submitted. There is no fallback to a local credential or a default index. Only the test storage papers over this by rebuilding a model in getCredentials.

title: Exhausted user-storage recovery credentials are not deleted
body: After a successful check, if the credential from RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential reports allCodesUsed(), the authenticator calls removeStoredCredentialById. That API deletes only credentials in Keycloak's database. Credentials stored because user storage updateCredential returned true are not there, and the test storage's getCredentials rebuild does not copy the id assigned in updateCredential, so the id is often null and the delete is a no-op. The configure-recovery-codes required action is still added, but required actions run after the browser flow. On the next login the recovery authenticator is still configured, RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean calls getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get() on an empty list, and rendering the challenge throws. That exception aborts the authenticator instead of skipping it, so the user can be locked out even when another factor is configured.

title: Plaintext recovery codes are sent to user storage
body: createRecoveryCodesCredential JSON-encodes the raw generatedCodes list and puts that string in the UserCredentialModel passed to updateCredential. The RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel argument already contains only hashes. Local storage persists those hashes; this path gives the federation provider every unused code in cleartext and drops userLabel and generatedAt, so they cannot be stored either. BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage writes that string unchanged into credentialData and keeps it for later equality checks. A storage dump or credential-update log discloses all backup codes, which authenticate as the user. Verification only needs the existing hashRawCode/verifyRecoveryCodeInput helpers, so the hashed secret data should be what is handed off, and the reference provider should not keep reversible codes.

title: getCredentials drops the stored id and renumbers codes
body: updateCredential sets an id with KeycloakModelUtils.generateId, but getCredentials ignores that CredentialModel and returns a new one from RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues. That factory does not copy the stored id and assigns fresh indexes starting at 0 to whatever list it is given. The same method now sets an id on OTP credentials because listing and deletion need it; recovery codes are returned with a null id, so account-console delete and removeStoredCredentialById cannot target them. If used codes are removed from the stored list, the remainder is renumbered and the login page asks for code 0 instead of the next original number. The rebuilt view also cannot be written back: its credentialData is metadata JSON, not the raw list isValid reads.

title: Recovery codes cannot be disabled in the new storage support
body: disableCredentialType clears OTP and otherwise only logs that the type is unsupported. getDisableableCredentialTypesStream only reports OTP, so recovery-authn-codes is not advertised as disableable. Admin REST disableCredentialType and account-console removal therefore leave myUser.recoveryCodes set. isConfiguredFor stays true and isValid still accepts the codes, so an administrator cannot revoke recovery codes after this provider has stored them.

title: New test never checks replay, next-code index, revocation, or local fallback
body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only checks that setup writes no Keycloak DB credential, that the storage flag is set, and that the first displayed code logs in once. It never submits that code again, never asserts a later login asks for the next index, never disables or deletes the credential, and never covers a user storage that returns false from updateCredential so the helper must keep the local hashed credential. Those are the paths this change adds and the ones the new storage implementation gets wrong, so the suite stays green while replay and revocation are broken.

title: Concurrent group test never joins the reader and can false-pass or hang
body: createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti starts a non-daemon Thread at line 139 that lists groups until deletedAll is true, but the test never retains that Thread, never joins it, and never sets deletedAll in a finally block. After the deletes it sets deletedAll (line 155) and immediately asserts caughtExceptions is empty (line 157). The list call most likely to overlap the deletes can still be in flight, so a NullPointerException (or any other failure) is added to caughtExceptions only after the assertion and the test passes while the race is still broken. There is also no start latch and no check that a read ran during the deletes, so an empty list does not prove the bug was exercised. If any group remove() throws, deletedAll stays false and the non-daemon reader loops forever, which keeps the Surefire JVM alive and can hang the suite. Even on the success path the in-flight HTTP call continues after the test method returns and races with later tests that share this class's injected realm and admin client. Keep the Thread, signal stop in a finally, join with a timeout before asserting, and fail if the reader never overlapped the deletes.

title: Null delegate is memoized by modelSupplier and count is returned as null
body: getSubGroupsCount now loads the persistence delegate through modelSupplier (line 274). That supplier is a LazyModel, which invokes getGroupModel() once and then permanently returns the same result, including null. The previous code called getGroupModel() directly, so a missing row was not stuck on the adapter. After a concurrent delete the cache can still hand out this GroupAdapter while the database lookup returns null; the first count call then pins modelSupplier to null for the rest of the session. Later calls on that same adapter to getSubGroupsStream(String, Integer, Integer) (line 256), getSubGroupsStream(Integer, Integer) (line 262), and getSubGroupsStream(String, Boolean, Integer, Integer) (line 268) dereference modelSupplier.get() with no null check and throw NullPointerException without querying again. The same poisoned supplier is passed into CachedGroup's lazy loaders (getAttributes, getRoleMappings, getSubGroups); those loaders treat a null model as the empty fallback and store it on the CachedGroup instance held in the Infinispan cache, so other sessions can see empty attributes, roles, or subgroup ids until that entry is invalidated. The method also returns null rather than a count, and GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount copies that into GroupRepresentation, so a listing that used to 500 now succeeds with subGroupCount null and any caller that unboxes the Long NPEs. Call getGroupModel() directly so a null is not cached, and return 0L when the delegate is missing.

title: Paginated subgroup lookups still NPE if the cached group is gone
body: The null check added in getSubGroupsCount was not applied to the other delegate lookups in the same adapter. getSubGroupsStream(String, Integer, Integer) at line 256, getSubGroupsStream(Integer, Integer) at line 262, and getSubGroupsStream(String, Boolean, Integer, Integer) at line 268 all do modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...) with no null check. modelSupplier loads the persistence delegate and returns null when the DB row is already gone while this session still holds the cached GroupAdapter — the same cross-request race as the reported NPE. Those overloads are what paginated/search subgroup listing uses. A cache hit followed by a concurrent delete still throws NullPointerException and fails the request with HTTP 500. A missing delegate should yield an empty stream (and the stale cache entry should be invalidated) instead of being dereferenced.

title: Concurrent regression test can pass without observing the race and leaks its reader
body: createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti starts a background thread that lists groups while the test thread deletes them, then sets deletedAll and immediately asserts that caughtExceptions is empty. The reader is never gated by a latch and is never joined, so the assertion can run before any list call has started, and it always runs before the in-flight list that overlaps the last deletes has finished. A server NPE from that call is recorded only after the assertion has already passed, so a green run does not show the concurrent getSubGroupsCount failure is fixed. If a delete throws, deletedAll stays false and the non-daemon reader loops forever, still calling managedRealm.admin() during later tests and blocking JVM shutdown. That same admin client is used concurrently by the deleter; it is not safe to share across threads, so the test can also fail on unrelated client errors or corrupt the client for subsequent tests.

title: Concurrency test never joins the reader and can miss the race
body: createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti starts a non-daemon reader that calls groups() in a loop, but never waits for that thread to enter the loop or to finish. deletedAll is set true immediately after the deletes and caughtExceptions is asserted on the next line, so the assertion can run before any list call has started or before an in-flight list has recorded its exception. A regression of the original NPE can therefore pass CI. There is also no finally that stops and joins the thread: if group.remove() throws before deletedAll.set(true), the reader stays in while (!deletedAll.get()) forever, keeps issuing admin requests against the shared realm for the rest of the suite, and can hang JVM shutdown because the thread is not a daemon. The same managedRealm.admin() client is used from both threads, so a client-side concurrency failure is also treated as a product failure. Start the reader behind a latch, delete only after it has begun, and in a finally set the stop flag and join with a timeout before asserting.

title: Missing delegate makes getSubGroupsCount return null
body: When the cached group has already been deleted, getSubGroupsCount returns null instead of a count. GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount copies that value straight into GroupRepresentation.subGroupCount, so a list request that races with a delete can return 200 with a group whose subGroupCount is null. Other GroupModel implementations do not do this: a subgroup count query returns 0 when the parent row is gone, and null is also how the admin API signals that the count was not requested. Callers that unbox the Long (comparisons, arithmetic, longValue()) still NPE, so the crash is moved out of this method rather than removed. Return 0L when modelSupplier.get() is null.

title: Paged subgroup streams still NPE if the group was deleted
body: The null-delegate race is only handled in getSubGroupsCount. The paged overloads still dereference the lazy delegate unconditionally: getSubGroupsStream(String, Integer, Integer) at line 256, getSubGroupsStream(Integer, Integer) at line 262, and getSubGroupsStream(String, Boolean, Integer, Integer) at line 268 all do modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...). If the group was removed after the CachedGroup was loaded, modelSupplier.get() returns null and these methods throw NullPointerException. Those overloads back the admin children API (search and pagination), so delete-while-list still returns 500 on that endpoint. Guard the null delegate the same way and return Stream.empty() instead of chaining the call.

title: Audit-log GET 500s for every non-superuser
body: enable_advanced is evaluated on every GET, before the optimized_pagination branch, as request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access. organization_context is an RpcUserOrganizationContext, so member is an RpcOrganizationMember or None, not the Django OrganizationMember model. That RPC object has no has_global_access attribute (global access is derived from member.role via organization roles), and member is None for some callers that still pass OrganizationAuditPermission, such as org-auth tokens. Any non-superuser therefore raises AttributeError and the previously working audit-log endpoint returns 500 even when optimized_pagination is absent and the DateTimePaginator path would have run. Superusers only avoid this because is_superuser short-circuits the or. Guard member is not None and check the role (organization_roles.get(member.role).is_global) only inside the new branch.

title: Optimized paginator cannot order audit logs by datetime
body: The new branch paginates AuditLogEntry with OptimizedCursorPaginator and order_by="-datetime". That class implements get_item_key with math.floor/math.ceil on the order field and value_from_cursor by returning the raw cursor number (paginator.py around lines 839-843), which is the numeric Paginator contract, not DateTimePaginator. AuditLogEntry.datetime is a datetime, so any non-empty page raises TypeError while build_cursor computes next/prev keys. A later request that supplies a cursor also fails in SQL: build_queryset compares the timestamp column to that integer/float cursor value instead of converting with DateTimePaginator's millisecond multiplier and datetime.fromtimestamp. The optimized path cannot return a successful page or a usable Link cursor. It needs DateTimePaginator key handling (or should not replace DateTimePaginator).

title: Negative cursor offsets crash queryset slicing
body: When enable_advanced_features is true and cursor.offset < 0, OptimizedCursorPaginator slices with queryset[cursor.offset:stop]. Django querysets do not support negative indexes and raise ValueError or AssertionError ("Negative indexing is not supported."). Endpoint.paginate only maps BadPaginationError to HTTP 400, so a client-supplied cursor such as value:-5:0 becomes a 500. The audit-log endpoint always passes enable_advanced_features=True on this path, and Cursor.from_string accepts any integer offset with no lower bound. The comments that the ORM handles negative slices and that this safely reaches data beyond pagination bounds because permissions are checked on the queryset are wrong: a negative slice does not succeed, and slicing would not remove the queryset WHERE clause anyway. Reject offset < 0 with BadPaginationError, as OffsetPaginator already does.

title: Shared paginator silently rewrites negative forward offsets
body: BasePaginator.get_result backs every Paginator and DateTimePaginator list endpoint, including the unchanged audit-log path. The new start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset changes results for a forward cursor whose offset is negative. The cursor query param is client-controlled. Previously that slice failed; now the offset is forced to 0 and a page is returned, which repeats rows at that cursor value instead of rejecting the cursor. Previous-page cursors still pass a negative offset straight into the queryset slice, so those requests 500, despite the new comment saying negative offsets are a safe optimization the queryset will handle. This is not a performance improvement for valid cursors (non-negative offsets behave exactly as before). Invalid offsets should raise BadPaginationError in both directions, and this global change should be reverted.

title: No tests for the new paginator or offset behavior
body: The PR adds OptimizedCursorPaginator, switches organization audit logs onto it behind optimized_pagination, and changes BasePaginator slicing, but adds no tests. Existing audit-log and paginator tests do not cover a non-superuser GET (which now touches member.has_global_access on every request), optimized_pagination=true with a datetime order key, cursor resume, or a negative cursor offset on either paginator. Those cases 500 or return a different page and need an endpoint test plus a paginator unit test before this can merge.

title: Optimized paginator crashes on datetime audit logs
body: When optimized_pagination=true and the caller is a superuser or has global access, the audit-log GET uses OptimizedCursorPaginator with order_by=-datetime. That class copies the numeric Paginator key logic: get_item_key does math.floor/math.ceil on the attribute, and value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor number. AuditLogEntry.datetime is a datetime, so build_cursor raises TypeError as soon as a page contains any rows (it calls get_item_key on the first result to build Link cursors). A later page would also compare the timestamptz column to an integer in SQL, which PostgreSQL rejects. DateTimePaginator, which this path replaces, converts datetimes to millisecond timestamps and converts cursor values back to UTC datetimes. Any opted-in request for an org that has audit entries returns 500 instead of rows, and cursors would be incompatible with existing DateTimePaginator cursors for this endpoint.

title: Negative cursor offsets crash queryset slicing
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is true and cursor.offset < 0, evaluates queryset[negative:stop]. The audit-log endpoint always passes enable_advanced_features=True for this paginator, and Cursor.from_string accepts a negative middle field (for example 0:-1:0). Django QuerySet does not support negative indexing: __getitem__ raises AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported.'). If assertions are stripped, the SQL compiler emits a negative OFFSET, which PostgreSQL rejects. Nothing in build_cursor ever produces a negative offset, so this does not speed up reverse pagination; it only 500s on a client-supplied cursor. Comments that the ORM handles negative slicing and that this safely reaches rows beyond pagination bounds are wrong — the organization filter is unchanged, and the slice errors before any extra rows are returned.

title: Shared paginator mishandles negative offsets
body: BasePaginator.get_result now sets the slice start to max(0, offset) only for forward cursors and passes the raw offset through for previous-page cursors. The new comment says this is safe because the queryset handles boundary conditions. It does not: a negative start or stop raises AssertionError in Django, so a prev cursor such as 123:-5:1 (which Cursor.from_string will parse) 500s on every endpoint using BasePaginator, including the default DateTimePaginator audit-log path. That prev behavior is the same crash as the old queryset[offset:stop], now explicitly kept and described as an optimization. Forward cursors with a negative offset used to 500 and now silently clamp to 0 and return 200 with the offset dropped (the cursor value filter still applies), so a corrupt cursor can show a different page than requested. Valid non-negative offsets are unchanged. This is not a performance improvement and should not ship on the shared paginator.

title: Missing member None check 500s every audit-log GET
body: enable_advanced is evaluated on every GET, not only when optimized_pagination is set: request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access. RpcUserOrganizationContext.member is optional and is None when the acting principal has no OrganizationMember row. Permission is enforced by OrganizationAuditPermission via request.access, which is a different object and can succeed without member being set (org auth tokens and similar). For those non-superuser callers, this line raises AttributeError before pagination, so the previously working audit-log list returns 500 even if optimized_pagination is absent. Superusers avoid it only because or short-circuits. Null-check member, and do not touch it unless the optimized branch is actually taken.

title: No tests for new paginator or offset changes
body: This change adds OptimizedCursorPaginator, the optimized_pagination branch on the audit-log endpoint, and new offset handling in BasePaginator.get_result, with no tests. Existing pagination tests do not pass datetime rows through the new class or send negative cursor offsets, so they will not catch the TypeError on any non-empty audit-log page or the AssertionError from negative queryset slices. Coverage should lock the default DateTimePaginator path, require the optimized path to page datetime rows without skipping or 500ing, and reject negative offsets instead of slicing them.

title: Optimized paginator is incompatible with datetime ordering
body: When optimized_pagination=true, OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint pages AuditLogEntry with OptimizedCursorPaginator and order_by="-datetime". That class implements numeric cursor semantics: value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor number, and get_item_key (paginator.py around line 840) does math.floor/math.ceil on the attribute. Audit log datetime is a datetime, so any non-empty first page raises TypeError (math.floor/ceil requires a real number) inside build_cursor while deriving the next cursor, and the API turns that into a 500 rather than a pagination error. A request that already has a cursor also builds a SQL comparison of the timestamp column to that integer (datetime <= <cursor value>), which PostgreSQL rejects. The previous code used DateTimePaginator, which converts datetimes to millisecond timestamps and back via fromtimestamp. Cursors from the two paginators are not interchangeable. Superusers and members with global access who pass the new query parameter get a 500 instead of audit logs whenever the org has any entries. Keep DateTimePaginator, or subclass it so both key extraction and cursor decoding stay datetime-aware.

title: Client-controlled negative offsets are sliced into the audit-log query
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator, with enable_advanced_features=True (always set by the audit-log endpoint for this class), takes a negative cursor offset and uses it directly as the queryset slice start. Cursors are unsigned client input; Cursor.from_string accepts a negative offset with int(). Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative indexes and raises ValueError before SQL runs. That exception is not BadPaginationError, so the request 500s instead of returning 400 the way OffsetPaginator, ChainPaginator, and CallbackPaginator do for offset < 0. The comments here are false and dangerous: the ORM does not handle negative slices, a negative offset does not read past the organization_id filter, and queryset permissions do not make out-of-bounds access safe. This should be deleted, not implemented. Do not materialize the queryset to a list to "make negative indexes work" — Python would then return a different window than the cursor describes, and the prev-page trim (len(results) == offset + limit + extra) is wrong for a negative offset. Reject offset < 0 with BadPaginationError.

title: Shared paginator silently rewrites negative forward offsets to zero
body: BasePaginator.get_result backs Paginator and DateTimePaginator, so this is not limited to audit logs. For a forward cursor the new code sets start_offset = max(0, offset), so a negative offset is treated as the first page and the request returns 200. Previously queryset[negative:] raised ValueError and the request failed. Cursors are client-controlled (from_string does not sign or clamp the offset), so a forged cursor with a real sort value and a negative offset now returns the first page of an authorized queryset instead of the requested window. build_cursor still sees the original negative offset; if the page boundary key equals the cursor value, the next cursor is emitted as offset + limit and can stay negative, so clients that follow it keep getting that same first page until the offset climbs to zero. For is_prev the expression passes the negative offset through unchanged, and Django still raises ValueError — the new comment that the queryset handles negative boundary conditions is wrong. This also contradicts the new Cursor comments that advertise negative offsets as a supported performance feature. Invalid offsets should keep failing with BadPaginationError in both directions; revert this shared-path change.

title: No tests for the new paginator or the shared offset change
body: The diff adds OptimizedCursorPaginator, the optimized_pagination branch on the audit-log endpoint, and a behavior change in BasePaginator.get_result, but adds no tests. Existing paginator tests only exercise non-negative offsets, so they stay green while three regressions ship: TypeError/SQL errors when audit logs are ordered by datetime through the new paginator, ValueError when a negative cursor offset hits the advanced slice, and forward cursors with a negative offset being rewritten to the first page for every BasePaginator caller. Add regression coverage for the datetime audit-log path, for rejection of negative offsets, and for the unchanged happy path of BasePaginator before merging.

title: ZUNIONSTORE sums scores and breaks redelivery
body: The merge calls ZUNIONSTORE with no AGGREGATE, so Redis defaults to SUM. Members are the raw span payloads and scores are end_timestamp_precise. Kafka delivery is at-least-once: a retry ZADDs the same payload into the parent key and this script unions that key into the segment key that already holds the member. Each retry adds the timestamp again (T, 2T, 3T). The previous SUNIONSTORE path was idempotent. After the new 1000-span cap, ZPOPMIN keeps the inflated duplicates and drops spans that were ingested only once. Under the cap every member is still present, so the existing flush tests do not catch it. Pass AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN) so a retry keeps a real timestamp.

title: Segment keys changed from SET to ZSET with no migration
body: Span segment keys stay at span-buf:s:{project:trace}:span_id, but this write switched from SADD to ZADD, add-buffer.lua switched from SCARD/SUNIONSTORE to ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE, and _load_segment_data switched from SSCAN to ZSCAN. Redis raises WRONGTYPE when those commands hit the other type. TTL is 3600s and unflushed segments live at least until the 10s/60s flush. A rolling deploy runs both versions on the same keys, and after cutover leftover SET keys cannot be updated or scanned. process_spans then errors on every retry of that batch and can stall the partition until the key expires; flush_segments fails the same way, so those spans are never emitted. Version the key prefix or dual-handle existing sets before deploying.

title: Parent-redirect walk cap reduced from 10000 to 1000
body: The loop that follows span-buf:sr redirects used to run to 10000, with a comment that a deeper chain would not be joined onto the correct segment. It is now for i = 0, 1000 and the warning is gone. This limit is not the eviction cap: it is how many parent hops are resolved to compute set_span_id. A chain longer than 1000 spans, which the old code explicitly tolerated up to 10k and which large traces can produce when batches arrive one level at a time, stops at an intermediate parent. Those spans are merged into the wrong segment key and flushed apart from their root. Restore the previous bound unless there is a measured reason to lower it.

title: Over-cap eviction is silent, ignores config, and can drop the root
body: If the segment sorted set has more than 1000 members, ZPOPMIN deletes the lowest end_timestamp_precise scores and throws the members away. The limit is hardcoded and does not read SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans (default 1001), which is now unused: the flush path that enforced it, logged the span count, and incremented spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded was removed. Dropped spans are not metered and not marked on the flushed payload, and the consumer still commits the Kafka offset, so the loss is permanent and invisible. There is also no exception for the segment span, so a root whose timestamp is among the lowest is deleted while the has-root-span flag can still be set and a partial segment is emitted as a normal one. Equal scores, which the tests all use, make ZPOPMIN break ties by raw payload bytes, so which spans survive is arbitrary. Pass max_segment_spans into the script, record a metric and a truncation marker, and do not evict the segment span.

title: No coverage for eviction, score order, or duplicate ingest
body: The insert-time cap is the point of this change, but every buffer test still inserts four spans that share end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0 and only checks flushed span ids. Those assertions still pass if ZPOPMIN never runs, if it drops the wrong members, if a second process_spans of the same payloads inflates ZUNIONSTORE scores, or if a segment larger than 1000 spans is returned in full. Add a case with more than 1000 distinctly scored spans (lowest scores removed, segment span kept) and a case that processes the same payloads twice.

title: Optimized audit-log paginator crashes on datetime rows
body: optimized_pagination=true for a superuser or a member with has_global_access switches this endpoint from DateTimePaginator to OptimizedCursorPaginator while still ordering by -datetime. OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key (paginator.py line 840) runs math.floor/math.ceil on the order field, and value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor number. AuditLogEntry.datetime is a datetime, so any non-empty page raises TypeError while building the next cursor; a non-zero cursor would also compare a number to a timestamptz column. DateTimePaginator already converts both ways. Nothing tests this flag, and the new path cannot return a successful non-empty audit-log page. Keep DateTimePaginator, or implement the same datetime cursor conversion.

title: User-controlled negative cursor offsets are used as slice bounds
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator is turned on from the organization audit-log endpoint when the client passes optimized_pagination=true and the caller is a superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access. Cursor offsets come from the client cursor string (Cursor.from_string accepts values such as 0:-5:0). If enable_advanced_features is set and offset is negative, get_result slices the queryset with that negative start. The comments say this reads past normal pagination bounds and is safe because Django handles negative slices and the queryset is already permission-filtered. Django QuerySet.__getitem__ raises ValueError ("Negative indexing is not supported.") for a negative start or stop, so the request 500s, and an organization filter does not validate the offset or define the cursor window. Delete this branch and the audit-log switch that enables it. Do not make the slice succeed in Python or SQL; that would implement the out-of-bounds read the comments describe.

title: Every audit-log GET dereferences member without a None check
body: enable_advanced is evaluated on every GET, not only when optimized_pagination=true: request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access. RpcUserOrganizationContext.member is optional. The is_superuser check short-circuits only for superusers. Any other caller that passes OrganizationAuditPermission with member=None (org auth tokens and other non-membership auth) raises AttributeError here and the previously working audit-log endpoint returns 500 even if the new query parameter is absent. None-check member before reading has_global_access.

title: Core paginator offset change does not match its comment
body: BasePaginator.get_result backs DateTimePaginator and Paginator, so this is not limited to audit logs. start_offset clamps a negative offset to 0 only when is_prev is false, and otherwise forwards cursor.offset unchanged, including negatives. The new comment says negative offsets are allowed and that the queryset handles the boundaries. Django does not: a negative slice raises ValueError. Valid non-negative cursors behave as before, but a client forward cursor with a negative offset now silently returns the first page instead of failing, and the extra-row trim at line 192 still compares len(results) to the original negative offset, so it no longer matches the slice that was fetched. Revert this unrelated change to the shared paginator.

title: Buffer glossary still calls segment keys complete sets
body: The glossary still says span-buf:s:* keys are Redis sets containing every span payload for a segment. They are now sorted sets written with ZADD and read with ZSCAN, and ZPOPMIN drops payloads once a segment exceeds 1000 spans, so the key is neither a set nor a complete segment. The algorithm notes above still describe merging sets and never mention eviction. Following the docstring leads operators to set commands (WRONGTYPE) and to treat a flushed segment as complete.

title: SET to ZSET switch has no migration and breaks rollback
body: process_spans now ZADDs span payloads into span-buf:s:* keys, and add-buffer.lua plus _load_segment_data read those same keys with ZCARD, ZUNIONSTORE, ZPOPMIN, and ZSCAN. Existing deployments created those keys with SADD, so Redis returns WRONGTYPE for up to redis_ttl (default 3600s) after deploy. Flush of already-buffered segments fails the same way, so in-flight segments cannot be drained. Rollback is also unsafe: once this build writes a sorted set, the old SADD/SUNIONSTORE/SSCAN code cannot read it. Pipelines are transaction=False, so commands that succeed are committed even if a later command in the batch raises. A batch that touches both a new key and an old set can create sorted-set keys and then error before the Lua EXPIRE runs, leaving span payloads in Redis with no TTL and no queue entry (never flushed, never expired). There is no key-prefix change, dual-read, or conversion step.

title: ZUNIONSTORE sums scores and evicts the wrong spans on redelivery
body: Both ZUNIONSTORE calls (the span-key merge around line 47 and the parent-key merge around line 53) use Redis's default AGGREGATE SUM. Members are the raw span payload, and the score is end_timestamp_precise. Python ZADDs onto the pre-redirect parent key, then the script unions that key into the destination segment and unlinks the source. On the normal at-least-once path (crash after process_spans, before offset commit, then redelivery), the payload is ZADDed again onto the parent key while the same member still exists in the destination, so the scores are added. One redelivery doubles the timestamp; further redeliveries keep inflating it. zpopmin then treats redelivered spans as the newest and drops other spans that actually ended later. A crash between ZUNIONSTORE and UNLINK causes the same overlap on retry. The union needs AGGREGATE MIN or MAX so a member keeps a single timestamp.

title: Eviction silently drops spans and the flush-time cap was removed
body: When a segment exceeds 1000 members the script ZPOPMINs the lowest end_timestamp_precise scores down to 1000 and discards those payloads with no metric or log. The limit is hardcoded, so SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans (default 1001) no longer does anything. Nothing protects the segment root: if the root span has the lowest score (clock skew, a zero timestamp, or equal scores), it is deleted, and the script still SETEXes the has-root-span flag afterward because that flag is based on the current call, not on whether the root payload survived. Downstream then flushes a short-timeout segment with no root span and no truncation marker, and offsets are committed, so the dropped spans are gone permanently. The previous flush backstop in _load_segment_data (skip the segment and increment spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded when len(payloads) > max_segment_spans) was deleted, so a segment that slips past this cap is fully loaded and emitted instead of being rejected. zpopmin of a huge excess also runs inside the Lua script and can block the Redis shard.

title: Redirect walk limit reduced from 10000 to 1000 splits deep segments
body: The parent-redirect walk used to allow 10000 hops, with a comment that a tree deeper than that limit would not be joined correctly. The limit is now 1000 and the warning is gone. The loop still does not fail or metric when it exhausts the budget: it HSETs the span to the intermediate id it reached and merges only that far. Segment trees deeper than 1000 redirects (possible with recursive instrumentation) are flushed as separate segments, so spans are missing from the root segment or attached to the wrong segment id. The only signal left is the existing max_redirect_depth gauge sitting at the cap.

title: Optimized audit-log paginator crashes on datetime ordering
body: The new optimized_pagination=true path, used by superusers and members with global access, paginates AuditLogEntry with OptimizedCursorPaginator and order_by="-datetime". That class is a numeric Paginator clone: get_item_key does math.floor/math.ceil on the key, and value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor number. Audit log rows are ordered by a datetime, which is why this endpoint used DateTimePaginator (timestamp conversion in both directions). The first page that returns any rows calls get_item_key from build_cursor and raises TypeError (math.floor on a datetime), so the request 500s. Even if that cast were fixed, the queryset filter would compare the datetime column to an int instead of a datetime. Empty result sets happen to avoid the key callback, so the failure only shows up when there is data. There is no test for this query param. enable_advanced_features is forwarded into the paginator because paginate already forwards constructor kwargs such as order_by; it does not select a datetime-aware implementation.

title: Negative-offset slicing raises ValueError; comments falsely claim it is safe
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator, when enable_advanced_features is set and the client cursor offset is negative, slices the queryset with that negative start (queryset[cursor.offset:stop]). Django QuerySet rejects negative slices with ValueError before any SQL runs, so this path 500s instead of paginating. The comments say Django handles negative slicing and that this reaches data beyond normal pagination bounds while remaining safe because the queryset is permission-filtered. Neither is true: the call throws, and OffsetPaginator already treats a negative offset as BadPaginationError rather than something to pass through. The same mistaken change was applied to BasePaginator.get_result (line 182) for every DateTimePaginator and Paginator endpoint: a forward cursor with a negative offset is now clamped to 0 and returns the first page instead of failing, while a previous-page cursor with a negative offset is still passed through and 500s. cursors.py only adds a comment; Cursor.from_string already accepted a negative offset. This code should be removed, not papered over by evaluating the queryset to a list.

title: Missing end_timestamp_precise stalls the span consumer
body: process_batch now requires val["end_timestamp_precise"] and uses it as the Redis sorted-set score. The value is only cast to SpanEvent after rapidjson.loads; nothing validates the payload. A message that omits the field, or that has a non-numeric value, raises before any span in the batch is buffered. The previous consumer fixture did not include this field, and the old code never read it. Arroyo retries a failed batch, so one poison message stalls the partition indefinitely. A missing or non-numeric score needs an explicit drop or default plus a metric, not a KeyError.

title: No test covers eviction, score stability, or the 1000 cap
body: The buffer tests only add end_timestamp_precise so existing Span constructions still run. Every fixture is 4-5 spans with the same timestamp, then sorted by span_id before compare, so they cannot catch the new behavior: ZPOPMIN trimming to 1000, dropping the oldest scores, deleting a root span, ZUNIONSTORE doubling scores when the same payload is merged twice, or WRONGTYPE on a key that was previously a set. The insert-time cap and the removed flush-time span-count rejection can both ship while these tests stay green.

title: SET-to-ZSET change breaks in-flight segment keys on deploy
body: Segment buffers are now written with ZADD and read with ZCARD, ZUNIONSTORE, and ZSCAN (add-buffer.lua and _load_segment_data). The previous release stored the same span-buf:s:* keys as Redis SETs (SADD/SUNIONSTORE/SSCAN). There is no new key prefix, dual-read, or WRONGTYPE handling. On a rolling deploy, keys still held as SETs (redis_ttl defaults to 3600s) make ZADD and ZSCAN raise WRONGTYPE; one such error fails the whole non-transactional pipeline, so both insert and flush abort for any batch that touches an old key. Old processes still running set commands fail the same way on keys the new code has already converted to sorted sets. Segments that cannot be flushed remain until TTL and are then dropped, so in-flight spans are lost and the consumer retries until those keys expire.

title: Insert-time eviction ignores max_segment_spans and drops spans silently
body: When a segment has more than 1000 members the Lua script ZPOPMINs it down to 1000. That limit is hardcoded and is not SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans (default 1001, and a constructor argument callers can change). The flush-time backstop that skipped segments with more than max_segment_spans, logged an error, and incremented spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded was removed from _load_segment_data. A segment of 1001 spans, which the default config previously flushed intact, now loses a span with no metric, log, or truncation flag on the flushed payload. Changing max_segment_spans has no effect. The cap also only runs inside the script, which is a separate pipeline from the earlier ZADD; if the script errors after that ZADD, nothing else enforces a span count before the flusher loads and produces the segment. ZPOPMIN keeps the highest end_timestamp_precise scores, so a root span that does not have the latest end time can be deleted while the has-root-span flag stays set and the segment is still flushed on the shorter root timeout, missing its root payload.

title: ZUNIONSTORE sums timestamp scores and evicts the wrong spans
body: Both ZUNIONSTORE calls (the span-key merge and the parent-key merge) omit AGGREGATE, so Redis uses SUM. Member scores are end_timestamp_precise values, and ZPOPMIN later drops the lowest scores to enforce the cap. If the same payload is in both inputs — a retry after a partial write, or the same span stored under its own id and under the parent id — the scores are added, roughly doubling the timestamp. Those members then sort as newer than spans with a real later end time, so once the segment is over the cap the script keeps the corrupted members and drops newly ingested spans. The union needs AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN) so each member keeps an actual timestamp.

title: Optimized audit-log pagination crashes on datetime ordering
body: When optimized_pagination=true and the caller is a superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access, the audit log endpoint paginates AuditLogEntry with OptimizedCursorPaginator and order_by=-datetime. That paginator's get_item_key runs math.floor/math.ceil on the raw field, which is a datetime, so build_cursor raises TypeError as soon as a page contains any rows. value_from_cursor also returns the raw cursor number instead of converting it back to a datetime the way DateTimePaginator does, so a following page would compare the datetime column to an integer. The new path therefore 500s for every organization that has audit log rows. enable_advanced_features is passed into Endpoint.paginate, which this PR does not change; if that method does not forward unknown kwargs, the request fails even earlier with TypeError. There is no test for this path. The default DateTimePaginator branch is unchanged, but the new branch is unusable.

title: Negative cursor offsets are applied to audit-log queryset slices
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator, when enable_advanced_features is set, takes the client-supplied cursor offset and, if it is negative, slices the queryset from that negative start. OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint turns the flag on for any superuser or member with has_global_access who passes optimized_pagination=true. The comments say this is meant to read past normal pagination bounds and that queryset permission checks make it safe. Those filters only choose which rows are in the queryset; they do not validate the offset. OffsetPaginator rejects a negative offset with BadPaginationError; this path does not. Django QuerySet raises ValueError on a negative slice, so the current effect is an unhandled 500 rather than extra rows, but the bound check was removed on purpose on an audit-log API and a crafted cursor reaches the ORM. Negative offsets must be rejected before slicing. The same idea was added to BasePaginator.get_result, which now keeps a negative offset for previous-page cursors and comments that the queryset will handle it; it will not, and that helper is shared by every cursor-paginated endpoint. This is unrelated to the span-buffer change and should not be merged.

title: Redirect walk cap cut from 10000 to 1000 without a failure signal
body: The loop that follows span-buf:sr redirects to find the segment key was reduced from 10000 iterations to 1000, and the comment that this cap can fail to join a deep chain was removed. If the chain is longer than 1000, the script stops on an intermediate span id, records the new span's redirect to that intermediate node, and merges into the wrong buffer. Flush then emits a split or mis-joined trace and nothing increments a metric when the cap is hit. Typical traces are shallower than this, but the old limit was intentional and the new one fails closed only by silently attaching spans to the wrong segment.

title: No test covers eviction, score order, or the ZSET migration
body: The buffer tests only add end_timestamp_precise to existing fixtures of four or five spans that all use the timestamp 1700000000.0. Nothing builds a segment larger than 1000 spans, asserts that the lowest scores are the ones removed, checks that max_segment_spans is the cap that is actually applied, or merges two sorted sets that share a member and checks the resulting score. Insert-time eviction, wrong-span drops from summed scores, and ZSCAN of sorted-set segment keys can all regress without a failing test. The new audit-log paginator path is also untested.

title: Glossary still calls segment keys sets that hold every span
body: The SpansBuffer glossary still describes span-buf:s:* as set keys that contain all span payloads for a segment, and the insert steps above still say the payload is added to a set. Those keys are now sorted sets scored by end_timestamp_precise, and members over the cap are deleted during insert, so a flushed segment may already be missing spans. Operators following this text will run SCARD or SSCAN, which fail with WRONGTYPE on the new keys, and will not know truncation is expected.

title: Test events store the client sample rate, not an upsample weight
body: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` runs on every `store_event` and, when `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` is truthy, overwrites `normalized_data["sample_rate"]` with that raw rate. It never sets `sample_weight` and never stores `1/client_sample_rate`. The new stats test saves `client_sample_rate: 0.1` and expects `count == 10`, while `upsampled_count` in discover.py aggregates `sum(sample_weight)`. Nothing in this PR connects those: production ingest is unchanged, and this hook does not invert the rate. Unless an out-of-diff pipeline already materializes `sample_weight` as `1/sample_rate` from the event `sample_rate` field, allowlisted `count()` queries error on an unknown column or return a non-upsampled value, and the new snuba test cannot pass. The hook also swallows all exceptions, ignores a falsy rate via `if client_sample_rate`, and can clobber an existing server `sample_rate` on any other test event that includes that context.

title: Upsampled count drops events with no weight and truncates
body: `upsampled_count` is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`, and the helper comment says null checks are intentionally omitted. ClickHouse `sum` skips NULLs, so any error in an allowlisted project that has no `sample_weight` (historical events, events ingested before the column was filled, or unsampled events that should count as 1) contributes nothing. Enabling the allowlist can therefore make the series smaller than raw `count()`, including showing 0. `toInt64` truncates toward zero, so a fractional weight such as `1/0.3` is biased low on every bucket (one event at 3.333 becomes 3). If `sample_weight` is actually the rate 0.1 rather than the multiplier 10, `toInt64(sum(...))` is 0, not the 10 the new test expects. The aggregate needs a missing-weight default of 1 and rounding (for example `round(sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1)))`). With that default, mixed queries would not need the all-or-nothing allowlist gate, which today changes a project's displayed count depending on whether every other selected project is allowlisted.

title: Error-query check is a substring match and false-positives on negation
body: `_is_error_focused_query` lowercases `request.GET["query"]` and returns true when the substring `event.type:error` appears anywhere. That is true for `!event.type:error`, for `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`, and for a quoted value such as `message:"event.type:error"`. On an allowlisted project set those queries rewrite `count()` to `sum(sample_weight)`. Non-error rows do not have a usable weight, so the stats request undercounts (NULLs add nothing) or fails in Snuba. The same check misses the usual discover error filter `!event.type:transaction` and list syntax such as `event.type:[error]`, so those error queries stay at the raw sampled count. The unit tests only cover the exact strings `event.type:error` and `event.type:transaction`, so the negation false positive is untested. Parse the search query and honor negation instead of substring matching.

title: Upsampling uses the outer dataset and request query, not the query executed
body: `_get_event_stats` decides upsampling by calling `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` with the closed-over `dataset` and `request`, ignoring the `scoped_dataset` and `query` arguments it actually runs. Dashboard discover-split rewrites those arguments: error probes use discover and `({query}) AND !event.type:transaction`, transaction probes add `event.type:transaction`, and the outer dataset is often metrics-enhanced performance, which `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` always rejects. The helper only looks at `request.GET["query"]`, so every probe inherits the original request's decision. A transaction probe whose original query contains `event.type:error` is still rewritten to `sum(sample_weight)` and comes back empty or errors; `check_if_results_have_data` then reports no transactions and `save_split_decision` persists that on `DashboardWidget.discover_widget_split`. Later loads skip the check and keep the wrong split. Error-only split queries whose original request text did not contain `event.type:error` are never upsampled. Pass the executed dataset and query string into the check. The outer `except Exception` retry calls `_get_event_stats` again, so a Snuba failure from the rewrite is not avoided and surfaces as a 500 (the endpoint only catches `ValidationError`).

title: Top-events ranking, equations, and count filters are not upsampled
body: Only the y-axis list is rewritten, and `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` replaces a column only when the entire string is `count()` after strip and lower. `top_events_timeseries` still gets `selected_columns` from `get_field_list`, `equations` from `get_equation_list`, and `orderby` from `get_orderby`, plus the raw `user_query`. Top-N is therefore ranked by sampled `count()` while the series uses `upsampled_count() as count`, so a heavily sampled group can be dropped from the top N, and an orderby that still names `count()` can fail the query because that aggregate was renamed. Aggregate conditions such as `count():>10` in the user query stay raw. Equation y-axes (`equation|count() / count_unique(user)`), `count() as <alias>`, `epm()`, and `eps()` are not rewritten either, so one response can mix upsampled and sampled series. Rewrite every count-based aggregate the query will run, or refuse those shapes while upsampling is on.

title: Allowlist cache is slower than options.get and cannot be invalidated
body: Every organization events-stats request now does a default-cache get (Redis in production) under `error_upsampling_eligible:{org}:{hash(sorted(project_ids))}`, and a set on miss, to avoid `options.get("issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist")`. That option read is already process-local memory, so this adds a network round trip and a high-cardinality key (one entry per distinct project-id set) on a hot endpoint. The cached boolean does not include the allowlist version. `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is never called, and it can delete only one project-set key, so an allowlist edit cannot drop the other combinations. For up to 60 seconds after a project is removed, stats keep rewriting `count()` to `sum(sample_weight)` and can 500 or return weighted counts for projects that are no longer eligible; after a project is added, counts stay raw. The note on `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` says the allowlist is read fresh on every call so config changes apply immediately, which is false once this cache is in front. Read the option directly, or cache it in-process keyed by the allowlist contents and actually invalidate it.

title: upsampled_count is public, so the allowlist does not gate the feature
body: The new `SnQLFunction` is registered without `private=True`, unlike the internal aggregate immediately above it. The allowlist logic only rewrites a y-axis that is exactly `count()`; it does not block callers from requesting the function themselves. Any client can pass `yAxis=upsampled_count()` on discover and bypass the rollout. On datasets or projects where `sample_weight` is absent (transactions, spans, non-allowlisted projects) that same public function turns a user-controlled y-axis into a failed stats query. The aggregate should stay internal to the rewrite path so the allowlist is actually what enables it.

title: errors dataset always rewrites count() but the function is only added on discover
body: `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns true for any `sentry.snuba.errors` query, and the endpoint then sends `upsampled_count()` to that dataset's query builder. The aggregate is only inserted into discover.py's `function_converter`. `sentry.search.events.builder.errors` is not changed, and `OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest` never passes `dataset=errors` (it uses the default dataset plus `query=event.type:error`). If the errors dataset does not inherit Discover's function map, every allowlisted `dataset=errors` stats request fails with an unknown function as soon as the allowlist is non-empty. The string-level unit test does not run the query builder, so it would not catch that. Register the function on the errors dataset config and add a snuba test that uses `dataset=errors`.

title: Upsampling stats tests share one cache key and disagree on the allowlist
body: These tests patch `sentry.api.helpers.error_upsampling.options` but not `sentry.utils.cache.cache`. Eligibility is cached for 60 seconds under a key built only from organization id and the project id set. All four tests use the same projects, so they share that key, while stubbing three different allowlists (both ids, one id, and empty) and expecting different counts (10 vs 1). This class's `setUp` never calls `cache.clear()` or deletes that key, and Django's `TestCase` does not clear the cache. If an earlier test cached true, `test_error_upsampling_with_partial_allowlist` and `test_error_upsampling_with_no_allowlisted_projects` still rewrite `count()` and their `count == 1` assertions fail; the reverse order makes the allowlisted test expect 10 and get 1. Mock or clear the cache in `setUp`.

title: Transaction upsampling test queries before the event is ingested
body: `test_error_upsampling_with_transaction_events` calls `store_event` for a transaction and immediately GETs events-stats. `setUp` has to call `wait_for_event_count` before its queries, so ingestion is asynchronous here. The assertion that the first bucket `count` is 1 races the consumer and flakes at 0. Waiting for `wait_for_event_count(self.project.id, 1)` would also be wrong: `setUp` already stored an error in that project, so a count of 1 is satisfied before the transaction is written. Wait until that transaction is actually queryable (for example project event count 2, or a transaction-specific query) before asserting.

title: Upsampled count drops null weights and truncates
body: upsampled_count is defined as toInt64(sum(sample_weight)) and is substituted for count() on allowlisted error queries. There is no ifNull or if(sample_weight > 0, sample_weight, 1) fallback; the comment says null checks were removed on purpose. In ClickHouse, sum skips nulls and returns 0 when every value is null, and toInt64 truncates toward zero, so a fractional weight such as 1/0.3 becomes 3. Allowlisting a project does not backfill existing rows, and events that were not client-sampled commonly have a null or 0 sample_weight. Those events disappear from the total, so turning the feature on can collapse an error chart from the real count to 0 or a large undercount. default_result_type is also "number" rather than "integer", so the count series meta type changes for clients that requested count(). Nothing in this PR computes an upsampled weight of 1/sample_rate either, so the new stats test's expectation of 10 for a 0.1 client rate is not what this aggregate implements.

title: Test helper writes sample_rate, not sample_weight
body: _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling copies contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate into normalized_data["sample_rate"] (0.1 in the new stats test). The aggregate added in this PR sums the sample_weight column, and OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest expects each single event to contribute 10. This helper never sets sample_weight and never stores 1/client_sample_rate. It only runs inside Factories.store_event, after manager.get_data() at line 1049, so it cannot affect a weight already derived during normalize, and it is not on the production ingest path. if client_sample_rate also treats 0 as missing. The event this helper stores does not contain the value upsampled_count reads, so the allowlisted-project test cannot observe a count of 10 unless an unshown insert hook rewrites sample_rate into sample_weight.

title: Error check is a raw substring match
body: _is_error_focused_query lowercases the raw query string and returns true if it contains the substring event.type:error. That is true for queries that are not error-only, including !event.type:error, event.type:error OR event.type:transaction, and a message or tag value that merely contains that text. When it returns true and every project is allowlisted, count() is rewritten to sum(sample_weight). The helper itself says sample_weight does not exist for transactions. Those queries then either fail in ClickHouse with a missing column or count non-error events as 0 because null weights are skipped by sum. A user asking for non-error totals can get a 500 or a silently zeroed chart. The unit test only covers the exact strings event.type:error and event.type:transaction, not negation or mixed filters. Parse the search syntax and apply the rewrite only when the query is exclusively error events.

title: Eligibility cache key uses process-randomized hash()
body: The allowlist cache key is built with Python's built-in hash() of the project-id tuple. Since Python 3.3 that hash is salted per process via PYTHONHASHSEED, so it is not stable across web workers that share sentry.utils.cache. Each worker reads and writes a different Redis/memcache key for the same organization and projects, so the cache never hits across processes. invalidate_upsampling_cache (line 73) uses the same hash and is never called from allowlist updates, so it cannot invalidate other workers even if it were wired up. hash() can also collide and reuse another project set's boolean. options.get for this allowlist is already an in-process lookup; adding cache.get, and cache.set on every miss, to every organization events-stats request is a remote round trip on a hot path and is slower than the lookup it claims to optimize. Use a stable key (joined sorted ids or a digest) in an in-process cache, or just call options.get.

title: Upsampling check ignores the query actually executed
body: _get_event_stats decides upsampling from the enclosing request dataset and request.GET query, not from scoped_dataset and the query argument it actually runs. get_event_stats_factory calls this helper with scoped_dataset set to discover and with rewritten queries such as (query) AND !event.type:transaction when a metrics-enhanced dashboard widget is split. Those calls still see the outer metrics dataset, and _should_apply_sample_weight_transform returns false for metrics datasets, so the error probe and the user-visible ERROR_EVENTS result stay on raw count() even when every project is allowlisted. The upsampling decision is therefore not the decision for the dataset and query being executed. Pass scoped_dataset and the query argument into the check.

title: Top-events ranking still uses raw count()
