body: shard_tag is ','.join of every shard id on the process and is sent as the shard tag on spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes. spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce uses a different key, shards, so it will not line up with those series or with spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy, which tags a single shard id. With the CLI default --flusher-processes 1 the value is the consumer's whole partition assignment (for example 0,1,2,...,N). DogStatsD/statsd tag lists are comma-separated, so a comma inside the value is parsed as extra tags and the timer is dropped or recorded as a truncated series such as shard:0. Rebalances also mint a new series per assignment, which is unbounded cardinality. Emit one shard id per point (or omit the tag when shards are grouped) and use the same key on all three metrics.

title: Shutdown abandons flusher processes once the join deadline passes
body: SpanFlusher.join() is the only place that stops background flushers (close() deliberately leaves them running through rebalance). It spends the entire caller timeout in next_step.join(timeout) first, then walks self.processes and breaks as soon as the deadline is already past. That break skips both the wait and process.terminate() for the current process and every process after it. With the old single-process join, terminate() always ran after the wait; this loop does not. If CommitOffsets.join consumes the timeout, or one slow flusher uses up what remains, the other flushers are left alive. They are daemons, so they keep calling flush_segments and producing to buffered-segments while the consumer process stays up. Rebalance then builds a new SpanFlusher for the same partitions, and the old and new flushers flush the same Redis shards and emit duplicate segments. Even the path that does call terminate() never join()s the child, so join() can return while a just-signaled process is still producing. Under load — the case this change is meant to handle — a flush/produce longer than the join timeout is exactly when this fires.

title: Replacing a flusher does not wait for the old one to stop
body: When a flusher is dead or hung, _ensure_processes_alive kill()s it and immediately calls _create_process_for_shards for the same shards, without join()ing the old process. kill()/os.kill returns when the signal is queued, not when the process has exited; a process blocked in a syscall keeps running until the call returns, and SIGKILL does not cancel an in-flight Redis flush or Kafka produce. The old Process is then overwritten in self.processes, so nothing ever waits for it. The replacement starts flush_segments on the same shards while the old process may already have produced those segments and not yet called done_flush_segments, so the same segment is written to buffered-segments twice (or a partial delete races the new read). The kill is also skipped for threading.Thread (the produce_to_pipe path) because it is guarded by isinstance(..., multiprocessing.Process), and that check does not match the spawn-context process type this file annotates as multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess if that class is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process — in that case a hung production flusher is never killed and a second flusher is started beside it. A slow produce that exceeds spans.buffer.flusher.max-unhealthy-seconds takes this path, not only hard crashes.

title: Flusher metric shard tag is a comma-separated list
body: Each flusher process sets shard_tag to ",".join of every shard it owns and puts that string on spans.buffer.flusher.produce, spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes, and spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce. The new --flusher-processes option defaults to 1, so the default production setup runs one process for every assigned partition and the tag value is the full partition list (for example "0,1,2,5"), not a single shard. StatsD/DogStatsD frames tags as a comma-separated list, so shard:0,1,2 is parsed as shard=0 plus stray tags, the series cannot be grouped by shard, and the value changes on every rebalance (new cardinality). A long assignment can also exceed backend tag-length limits. The unhealthy metric already emits one integer shard tag per shard; these timers should do the same, or use a process index that does not contain commas.

title: wait_produce metric uses a different tag key than the other flusher timers
body: spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce is recorded with tag key "shards", while spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes in the same loop use "shard". Anything filtering or grouping the flusher timers by shard silently drops produce-ack wait time, so latency dashboards under-report the time spent blocked on Kafka and make the flusher look healthier than it is.

title: flusher_processes of 0 or negative does not do what the flag says
body: --flusher-processes is an unconstrained click int, and SpanFlusher sets max_processes with `max_processes or len(assigned_shards)`. 0 is falsy, so --flusher-processes 0 does not cap the flusher; it spawns one process per assigned shard. Each of those is a spawn-context process that imports the full Sentry app, so a config template that sets 0 (meaning unset or disabled) can start dozens of Django processes and OOM the pod. A negative value is truthy, then min(negative, shard_count) is negative, range() is empty, and no flusher process is created. self.buffers and process_backpressure_since are then empty, so neither Redis-memory hard backpressure nor flusher backpressure can fire, and the consumer keeps writing spans to Redis and never flushes them. The option needs a minimum of 1, and 0 must not be coerced into one-process-per-shard.

title: Drift wait in test_basic is a no-op, so the flush assertion is racy
body: test_basic monkeypatches time.sleep to a no-op, then after setting current_drift to 9000 calls time.sleep(0.1) with a comment that it gives the flusher time to run. That sleep is the patched no-op, so it does not wait. step.join() then sets the shared stopped flag immediately, and the flusher only produces inside `while not stopped`. If the flusher thread does not get the GIL between the drift write and that flag, it exits without flushing and `(msg,) = messages` fails. The same patch turns SpanFlusher.join's time.sleep(0.1) into a GIL-holding busy spin, so whether the test passes depends on accidental thread switches. The sleep added in this PR does not close the race it was meant to fix.

title: No test flushes spans across multiple flusher processes
body: test_flusher_processes_limit only asserts that four partitions yield two thread objects and that the shard lists sum to 4. It never submits a span or checks that each shard is flushed once. Every flush test passes produce_to_pipe, which forces threading.Thread instead of a spawn-context Process, so the production path — per-process KafkaProducer, kill/restart, and join/terminate — never runs. A bad shard split, a double-flush on restart, or the join timeout leak would not fail CI.

title: join() can return without stopping every flusher process
body: SpanFlusher.join sets stopped, then calls next_step.join(timeout) before waiting on flusher workers. The deadline is that same timeout, and the new loop breaks as soon as it has passed, skipping process.terminate() for every worker not yet visited. If next_step.join consumes the timeout, or the first stuck worker uses up the rest, the remaining shard flushers are never signaled. close() intentionally does not stop them, so join() is the only shutdown path. Those workers are daemons, but the consumer process stays up across rebalances, so a leaked flusher keeps calling flush_segments and producing to the buffered-segments topic for shards that may already have been revoked and assigned to another consumer. That races Redis flush state and emits duplicate segments. This is a regression from the previous single-process join, which always called terminate() after the wait even if the deadline had already passed. Workers that do get terminate() are never join()ed, so join() can return while they are still alive, and there is no try/finally, so an exception from next_step.join skips cleanup entirely. Always stop every worker (kill if needed) and join() it, including on the timeout and exception paths.

title: Flusher restart does not wait for the old worker to exit
body: When a flusher is unhealthy, _ensure_processes_alive calls kill() only for multiprocessing.Process, then _create_process_for_shards starts a replacement and overwrites self.processes without joining the previous worker. kill() returns before the process has actually died, and the old Process object is dropped, so the supervisor no longer tracks it and never reaps it. The thread backend used whenever produce_to_pipe is set is not interrupted at all (kill/terminate are skipped for non-Process workers). A hung thread therefore keeps flushing the same shards after a new thread is started; each hang restart adds another live flusher until MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS trips, and those threads all call flush_segments and produce, duplicating segments and racing done_flush_segments. On the process backend the replacement is spawned while the killed worker may still be inside Redis flush or Kafka produce. Join (or join-after-kill) the old worker, and do not start a second thread while the first is alive, before creating the replacement.

title: Comma-separated shard list is emitted as one metric tag
body: shard_tag is the comma-joined list of every shard that process handles, and it is sent as the shard tag on spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes, and as shards on spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce. DogStatsD encodes tags as a comma-separated key:value list and does not escape commas inside values, so a tag like shard:0,1,2 is parsed as shard:0 plus stray tags 1 and 2. Those timers and gauges will be dropped or attributed to the wrong series. With the CLI default --flusher-processes 1, every assigned partition is concatenated into that single value, so this breaks as soon as the consumer has more than one partition, not only when multiple flusher processes are enabled. The value also changes on every rebalance (high cardinality) and can exceed backend tag-length limits. wait_produce uses the key shards while the other metrics use shard, so they would not group together even after the value is fixed. The unhealthy counter already tags one shard id; the produce metrics should do the same, or use a bounded process index, and must not embed commas. The same comma-joined string is also set as the Sentry tag sentry_spans_buffer_shards.

title: test_basic wait after advancing drift is a no-op
body: test_basic monkeypatches time.sleep to a no-op so the flusher does not block, then calls time.sleep(0.1) after setting current_drift to 9000, with a comment that this gives the flusher time to process. That call uses the same patched time.sleep, so it returns immediately and does not wait. step.join() sets SpanFlusher.stopped before it waits for the worker; if the worker has not yet observed the advanced drift and produced, it leaves its loop and the (msg,) = messages assertion fails. The synchronization added to fix that race does not run. Save the original time.sleep before monkeypatching and wait on that saved function (the flusher looks up time.sleep at call time, so it will still see the no-op), and only then join.

title: Rebalance kills the shared pool, then commits unprocessed messages
body: FixedQueuePool is created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and reused by every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy, but close(), terminate(), and join() all call queue_pool.shutdown(). Arroyo handles revocation by close()+join() on the current strategy, then create_with_partitions() on the same factory. shutdown() sets each worker's shutdown flag and calls Queue.shutdown(), after which put() raises queue.ShutDown. The next strategy still uses that dead pool, so every submit fails to enqueue. submit()'s except block treats that failure as success: it add_offset/complete_offset and returns, and the new commit thread then commits those offsets (the factory wrapper adds 1, so the group offset moves past them). Results already sitting in the queue at revoke are abandoned and, on redelivery, dropped the same way. After the first rebalance, scale-in, or deploy, uptime results are never handled and will not be retried for the rest of the process. Give each assignment its own pool created in create_with_partitions, and only shut it down after that assignment has drained and committed; do not destroy a factory-owned pool from close(). Tests never close a strategy and call create_with_partitions again, so they miss this.

title: Unbounded queues provide no backpressure
body: Each worker queue is created with queue.Queue() (maxsize 0, unbounded) and FixedQueuePool.submit() always put()s without blocking. poll() only records a gauge. The strategy docstring claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing ever blocks the consumer thread. One slow subscription occupies its single worker while the consumer keeps reading that partition into memory; WorkItem also retains the full Kafka message, which the worker never reads. Commits stop at the oldest incomplete offset, so a stuck item also prevents committing every later message on the partition and those payloads cannot be released. Because poll() keeps returning, max.poll.interval is not exceeded and Kafka will not move the partition to a healthy consumer. The process can OOM and, on crash, must reprocess the entire uncommitted backlog. Bound the queues and block in submit() or poll() when a queue is full so the consumer actually applies backpressure.

title: Commit callback runs off the processing thread
body: _commit_loop is a daemon thread started from SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.__init__ and calls the Arroyo commit callback every second while the processor thread is in consumer.poll() and strategy.submit(). librdkafka consumers are not thread-safe, and Arroyo expects commit to run on the processing thread; concurrent staging/commit and poll can drop offset updates or fault the consumer. close() also joins this thread before workers finish, so the last snapshot misses offsets that complete during shutdown and those messages are redelivered. Commit contiguous offsets from poll() on the processing thread, and do one final commit at the end of join() after queued work is idle, instead of using a side thread.

title: Shutdown does not drain queues and ignores join timeout
body: OrderedQueueWorker leaves its loop as soon as self.shutdown is true, and FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets that flag before Queue.shutdown(immediate=False). A worker blocked in get() processes at most one more item and then exits, so the rest of the queue is never handled. close() has already stopped the commit thread, so those offsets are not committed. join() ignores the timeout it is given, calls close(), and never raises TimeoutError, so Arroyo treats shutdown as complete and will not call terminate(). Workers are daemon threads and are joined one after another with a 5s timeout each, so 20 stuck workers block the consumer thread inside close/join for about 100 seconds (which can exceed max.poll.interval.ms) and can then be killed mid-handler when the process exits, after partial side effects and without running finally. A second close() or ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() calls Queue.shutdown() again, which raises queue.ShutDown and is logged as an error on every clean shutdown. join() should drain (or raise TimeoutError), commit, then stop workers, using one shared deadline.

title: Error-handling test asserts that commits must not happen
body: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling says a processing error must not block commits for later messages, but the assertion requires that nothing was committed. The worker always complete_offset()s in a finally block, even when the patched processor raises, so a working consumer will commit both offsets (factory commit value 102). The wait loop returns as soon as the queue is empty, usually well under a second, while the commit thread waits 1s before its first commit. The assertion therefore passes only when the commit has not happened yet, and fails when the commit lands within the ~2s loop. It does not lock in the behavior the docstring describes, and nothing in the new tests closes a strategy and creates another one, so the rebalance data-loss path is untested.

title: Queue-pool tests race the already-running workers
body: test_stats_reporting asserts total_items > 0 immediately after submit, but the three workers are started in setUp and only append to a list, so they can drain all 10 items before get_stats() and fail the assertion on a fast run. test_offset_committing and test_offset_gaps_block_commits treat the first commit_event as proof that the final offset was committed. The commit loop fires about once a second and sets that event for whatever prefix is contiguous at that moment, so the assertion can observe a partial offset (for example 102, or 100 on the gap test) before the later commit updates it.

title: Shared queue pool is destroyed on the first rebalance, then offsets are committed without processing
body: FixedQueuePool is created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and reused by every strategy create_with_partitions returns. Arroyo closes the current strategy on partition revocation (deploy, scale, broker loss) and then creates a new one. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() always calls queue_pool.shutdown(), which permanently shuts the queues and stops the workers. factory.shutdown() is the only path that nulls queue_pool, and rebalance does not call it, so the replacement strategy submits onto those dead queues and starts another commit thread on the same OffsetTracker. Queue.put raises ShutDown; submit()'s except handler marks the offset complete without running the result processor; the new commit thread then commits it (the factory adds 1 and forwards it to the group). Those uptime results are never handled and will not be redelivered after a restart. The shared tracker also still holds the revoked assignment: the new strategy never records which partitions it owns, so a leftover committable offset can be committed for a partition this member no longer owns (skipping or rewinding the new owner) or can make commit() throw and block commits for partitions it does own. A leftover outstanding offset abandoned when workers were stopped stalls the contiguous cursor for that partition forever. Pool, workers, and offset tracker need to be per assignment and torn down only after that assignment's work is finished or explicitly abandoned. Nothing in the tests closes a strategy and creates another one.

title: Commit callback runs on a background thread and races the Kafka consumer
body: _commit_loop is a daemon thread started from SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.__init__ and calls the Arroyo commit callback about once a second. That callback is StreamProcessor's commit, which stages offsets on the KafkaConsumer and, because uptime-results is built with commit_policy=ONCE_PER_SECOND, will call KafkaConsumer.commit_offsets() into librdkafka. The confluent-kafka Consumer is not thread-safe and is polled on the processor thread; concurrent poll() and commit() is undefined and can segfault the process or corrupt the group offset. The staged-offset map is also a plain dict mutated from this thread with no lock, so it races any commit on the processor thread (including the force-commit during shutdown) and can drop or rewind staged offsets. Commit decisions have to be made from poll() or join() on the processor thread, which is the only place Arroyo strategies are allowed to commit from.

title: close() stops commits before workers finish and does not drain queues
body: close() does not match Arroyo's shutdown contract, and join() ignores the timeout it is passed (get_stream_processor defaults join_timeout to None, i.e. wait until work finishes). close() signals the commit thread and joins it (5s) before stopping workers, so the last commit snapshot is taken while items are still queued or in handlers; anything that finishes after that is never committed and will be reprocessed, duplicating uptime incident side effects. FixedQueuePool.shutdown then sets each worker's shutdown flag before queue.shutdown(immediate=False). Workers check that flag at the top of the loop and return without draining, so queued items are abandoned with offsets left outstanding (at most the one item already blocked in get() runs). join() just calls close() again and does not honor the caller's timeout; each worker is joined sequentially with a hard-coded 5s timeout, so one stuck handler blocks revocation for up to num_queues * 5 seconds (default 20 queues is 100s) and can blow the session timeout, causing another rebalance. Workers are daemon threads, so after that timeout they keep running result handlers for partitions that may already have been reassigned. terminate() shuts the same pool down and does not join the commit thread. Shutdown needs to stop intake, drain in-flight work without the early flag, then commit once from the processor thread, using a single deadline.

title: Queues are unbounded and poll() never applies backpressure
body: Each worker queue is created with queue.Queue() (maxsize 0, unbounded), and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit/poll never block or raise MessageRejected. The class docstring claims natural backpressure when queues fill, but they cannot fill. Arroyo keeps polling and submitting as long as submit() returns, so one slow subscription — the head-of-line case this mode is supposed to isolate — retains every later message for its queue in memory. Commits also cannot move past the oldest outstanding offset on that partition, so OffsetTracker retains the whole uncommitted span. get_committable_offsets holds the partition lock while scanning range(start, max_offset+1); a large span stalls the consumer thread inside add_offset and can exceed max.poll.interval.ms. The process can OOM, and a crash replays the entire uncommitted span. submit() or poll() needs a per-queue or total bound and should raise MessageRejected so the consumer pauses instead of reading unboundedly.

title: submit() acknowledges messages that were never enqueued
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit wraps decode, grouping, and enqueue in a bare except Exception. On any failure it logs and, for a BrokerValue, add_offset plus complete_offset, so the commit loop treats the message as processed. That covers queue.ShutDown after shutdown, a grouping_fn error, and any other transient enqueue failure. The result processor never runs, nothing is retried, and there is no DLQ; once the commit loop runs, the group offset moves past the message and a restart will not redeliver it. Serial and batched-parallel let unexpected exceptions propagate so the consumer resumes from the last successful commit. FixedQueuePool.submit also records the offset before put(), so a failed put is only completed by this handler — that completion is what turns a retryable failure into permanent loss. Failures before the item is on a worker should be re-raised, or left outstanding, instead of being marked complete.

title: Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its docstring and races the commit interval
body: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling claims processing errors must not block offset commits, but the assertion requires that the partition was not committed (len(committed_offsets) == 0 or the partition is absent). The worker always complete_offset's in a finally, including when the patched processor raises, so both offsets become committable and the factory would commit 102. The test also returns about 0.2s after the handlers finish, while _commit_loop waits a full second before its first commit, so the assertion usually passes only because it runs before the commit thread wakes. If that timer fires inside the wait, the test fails. It never checks that a later successful message is actually committed, which is the behavior the docstring describes, and no test covers close-then-reassign.

title: Queue-depth assertion races already-running workers
body: test_stats_reporting submits 10 items and immediately asserts get_stats()['total_items'] > 0. The pool's workers are already running and the test processor only appends to a list, so they can empty the queues before the assertion. total_items is qsize() and does not count an item a worker has already taken, so on a fast run the assert fails even though submit succeeded. The test needs a blocked processor, or it should observe a queued item before asserting depth.

title: Rebalance kills the shared pool and later results are committed unprocessed
body: FixedQueuePool is created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and shared across strategies, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close/join and ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown both call queue_pool.shutdown(). Arroyo calls close() then join(), then create_with_partitions() again on every assignment, including ordinary rebalances during deploys. shutdown() stops the workers and Queue.shutdown()s the queues, so later Queue.put raises queue.ShutDown. The new strategy still submits into that dead pool; submit()'s except block marks the offset complete without calling the result processor, and the new strategy's commit thread commits those offsets through the new commit callback. In the steady state the queues are empty, so nothing is outstanding and the commit cursor advances: those uptime results are skipped permanently. If a backlog left outstanding offsets, commits freeze and processing never resumes until the process is restarted. The OffsetTracker is also shared and never reset, so revoked partitions and the new assignment share one cursor. Recreate the pool per create_with_partitions (and tear it down only with that strategy), or do not shut the pool down on strategy close.

title: Offset commits run on a background thread against the Kafka consumer
body: _commit_loop is a daemon thread started from SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.__init__ and calls commit_function, which invokes Arroyo's commit callback (result_consumer commit_offsets). That callback stages or commits offsets on the Kafka consumer. The confluent_kafka Consumer is not thread-safe, and Arroyo runs submit/poll and its own ONCE_PER_SECOND commit on the processor thread that owns the consumer. Committing from this side thread races with poll() and can raise inside librdkafka, commit a torn offset map, or deadlock when close() joins the commit thread while it is inside the callback and the callback needs the processor thread. Perform commits from poll() and from join/close on the processor thread, and force a final commit there after in-flight work has finished.

title: Unbounded queues never apply backpressure and can OOM the consumer
body: Each work queue is queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and submit() always put()s without blocking or raising MessageRejected. The class docstring says queues provide natural backpressure, but they never fill. If handling is slower than the topic, or one item is slow, the consumer keeps polling and retains every later message in the queues, in WorkItem (full payload), and in OffsetTracker.all_offsets, because a commit cannot move past the oldest outstanding offset on that partition. get_committable_offsets then walks range(start, max_offset+1) while holding the partition lock every second, so a large backlog also stalls workers completing offsets. poll() only emits a gauge, so the healthcheck keeps succeeding until the process OOMs. This is worse than batched-parallel, which caps memory at max_batch_size, under the exact slow-item failure this mode is meant to solve. Bound the queues and signal backpressure from submit so read-ahead stays finite and the processor can still poll. A worker that exits is also never restarted, so one dead thread permanently stalls its queue and that partition's commit cursor.

title: Shutdown abandons queued work and never commits the in-flight tail
body: close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread before queue_pool.shutdown(). The commit loop then exits after at most one more pass, so offsets completed while workers finish are never committed and will be redelivered. FixedQueuePool.shutdown also sets worker.shutdown = True before Queue.shutdown(immediate=False). The worker loop checks that flag before Queue.get(), so it will not drain: it finishes at most the item already dequeued and leaves the rest outstanding. Combined with unbounded queues, a restart replays the whole buffered backlog, which can duplicate uptime incidents or notifications if handling is not idempotent. join() ignores the timeout Arroyo passes and calls close() again; Arroyo already calls close() before join(), so Queue.shutdown() runs twice and the second call raises queue.ShutDown, logged as an error for every queue on every shutdown. Drain first (do not set the worker flag until the queue is empty; let shutdown(immediate=False) unblock get), then force one final commit on the processor thread, make close() idempotent, and honor join's timeout.

title: Any submit exception is acked and the message is never retried
body: submit()'s bare except marks the BrokerValue offset complete after logging. That path runs for build_payload_grouping_key failures, Queue.put failures (including queue.ShutDown after the pool is shut down), and the decoder's AssertionError on FilteredPayload. The commit loop will then commit that offset, so the result is never retried and never sent to a DLQ. Returning None from the decoder is an intentional skip and matches serial mode; unexpected exceptions are not. Serial processing lets those exceptions fail the strategy so Arroyo can retry. A transient grouping error or a put failure therefore permanently drops an uptime result. Only complete offsets that were actually handled or deliberately filtered, and let unexpected submit failures propagate so the partition is not acked past them.

title: Graceful shutdown depends on Python 3.13-only queue APIs
body: Queue.shutdown and queue.ShutDown were added in Python 3.13. FixedQueuePool.shutdown calls q.shutdown() and the worker catches queue.ShutDown, with no fallback. On 3.11/3.12, shutdown raises AttributeError, which the bare except logs and swallows, so workers blocked in Queue.get() never wake. Each worker.join then waits out its 5 second timeout (default 20 queues is up to about 100 seconds) and in-flight DB work is abandoned when the daemon threads die at process exit. If this runtime is not guaranteed to be 3.13+, shutdown needs a compatible unblock path, such as a sentinel or get(timeout) that observes the shutdown flag.

title: Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its docstring and races the commit loop
body: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling says a processing error must not block commits for other messages, but the assertion requires that the partition was not committed (len(committed_offsets) == 0 or the partition is absent). The worker completes the offset in a finally block even when result_processor raises, so after both messages (offsets 100 and 101) the factory's commit callback should record 102 once the commit loop runs. That loop waits 1 second before its first commit, and the test breaks out as soon as both calls have run (usually a few hundred milliseconds), so it passes without ever observing a commit and will fail on a slower run once the commit arrives. Wait long enough for the commit thread and assert the offset required by the chosen retry policy.

title: Queue-depth assertion races the worker threads
body: test_stats_reporting submits 10 items and immediately asserts get_stats()["total_items"] > 0. The pool's workers are already running and the test handler only appends to a list, so they can dequeue every item before get_stats() runs. The assertion fails intermittently on a fast machine. Block the handler until after the depth check, or pause the workers before submitting.

title: --mode help misstates parallelism and omits the new mode
body: uptime_options still says "The mode to process results in. Parallel uses multithreading." Mode parallel builds a MultiprocessingPool; batched-parallel is the thread-pool mode; thread-queue-parallel, added in this change, is not described at all, nor is the fact that --max-workers becomes the queue count in that mode. Operators selecting the new mode from --help will misunderstand the concurrency model.

title: Backup-code login is rejected for users whose identityProvider is not CAL
body: The guard `if (user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode) throw new Error(ErrorCode.ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled)` runs before the new backup-code branch. A Google/SAML user with twoFactorEnabled who submits a backup code (and therefore no totpCode) gets the 'account created with identity provider' error instead of having the backup code verified — the condition was not extended to also allow `credentials.backupCode`. This user class is real: the signIn callback converts CAL accounts to Google/SAML while keeping twoFactorEnabled and backupCodes, and then routes them through the /auth/login?totp= (loginWithTotp) flow. It is compounded by apps/web/pages/auth/login.tsx, which renders ExternalTotpFooter (no 'Lost access' button) for that flow, so these users have no way to use their backup codes at all and are permanently locked out if they lose their authenticator.

title: Backup codes are shown exactly once with no recovery path, and the dialog can be dismissed at that step
body: handleEnable() enables 2FA on the server and only then moves to the DisplayBackupCodes step. At that step the dialog can still be closed without using the Close/Copy/Download buttons (dialog close control / Escape / overlay via onOpenChange), and resetState() is only wired to the Cancel and Close buttons, not to onOpenChange — so component state is also left stale (step stays DisplayBackupCodes with the old codes). The codes are never retrievable again: the totp/setup endpoint rejects users who already have twoFactorEnabled, and this PR adds no regeneration UI or API. A user who closes the wizard before saving the codes (and likewise all users who enabled 2FA before this feature and have backupCodes=null) has no way to obtain codes, and is locked out if they later lose their authenticator. Completion should be gated on an explicit confirmation and/or a regenerate-codes endpoint should exist.

title: missing_backup_codes message tells users to generate codes in settings, which is impossible
body: The string "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." is shown when a 2FA-enabled user has no stored backup codes — i.e. every user who enabled 2FA before this feature — both in the login flow and in the disable-2FA modal. No settings UI or API exists to generate backup codes after initial setup (the setup endpoint rejects already-enabled users), so the instruction cannot be followed; users who lost their authenticator are directed to a nonexistent capability instead of being told to disable/re-enable 2FA or contact support.

title: Backup-code single-use guarantee is not enforced under concurrent requests
body: Code consumption is a read-modify-write: decrypt the stored array, indexOf the supplied code, set that slot to null, re-encrypt and update the user row — with no transaction, lock, or conditional update. Two concurrent login requests presenting the same valid backup code can both read the array before either writes, both pass indexOf, and both be authenticated, violating the 'each backup code can be used exactly once' promise made in the UI copy (backup_code_instructions). A transaction or an atomic update would close the window.

title: No test exercises logging in with a backup code or disabling 2FA with one
body: The added e2e steps only verify that the backup-codes screen renders, the download filename, and the copy toast. The core behavior of the feature — a successful login with a backup code, rejection of a wrong code, single-use consumption (the code is invalidated after use in next-auth-options.ts), and disabling 2FA with a backup code — has no automated coverage, and the PR checklist explicitly states tests proving the feature works were not added. A regression in the authorize or disable logic would ship unnoticed.

title: Password visibility toggle removed from keyboard tab order in the shared PasswordField
body: Adding tabIndex={-1} to the show/hide password button removes it from the tab order in every place the shared PasswordField is used (login, password change, 2FA setup/disable, etc.). Keyboard-only users can no longer reach the control to verify what they typed, which is an accessibility regression for a security-relevant input. If the intent was to fix tab order into the 2FA digit inputs of one specific form, the change should be scoped to that form rather than the shared component.

title: Backup code login can skip password verification entirely
body: In the credentials `authorize` callback, the password check at line 121 is gated on `!credentials.totpCode`, and the new backup-code branch at line 131 verifies only the backup code. A crafted request to the credentials callback containing a valid `backupCode` together with any non-empty dummy `totpCode` therefore skips `verifyPassword` and is authenticated solely by the backup code — a static, 40-bit secret that users store in files/notes. Backup codes are meant to substitute for the authenticator as the second factor, not to replace the password, so a leaked backup code alone yields full account access. The password should be verified (when the user has one) before accepting a backup code, or the flow branching should be keyed off the presence of `backupCode` instead of piggybacking on the `totpCode` gate.

title: missing_backup_codes message directs users to a settings option that does not exist
body: The new string `missing_backup_codes` reads "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings.", but this PR adds no way to generate or regenerate backup codes outside the initial 2FA setup. Every user who enabled 2FA before this feature shipped has `backupCodes = null`; if they lose their authenticator and use the new "Lost access" link at login, they hit `MissingBackupCodes` and are told to do something impossible — they cannot log in to reach settings, and even in settings there is no regeneration option. These users are effectively locked out (admin intervention required). Either add a regeneration flow or change the message.

title: No test exercises the actual backup-code authentication behavior
body: The only test additions assert that the download/copy/close buttons render on the post-enable screen. Nothing tests the security-critical behavior of the feature: logging in with a backup code, that a redeemed code is invalidated and cannot be reused, that the password is still required alongside a backup code (see the related finding on password skipping), or disabling 2FA with a backup code. The added TODO comment ("add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup") and the unchecked PR checklist item concede this. For an authentication feature, the login-with-backup-code and single-use-invalidation paths should be covered before merge.

title: Backup code redemption is a non-atomic read-modify-write
body: The login flow decrypts the stored codes, checks `indexOf`, and then writes the updated array back in a separate `prisma.user.update`. Two concurrent sign-in requests presenting the same backup code can both decrypt and pass `indexOf` before either update commits, so a code intended to be single-use can be redeemed twice. Use a transaction with a conditional update (or a per-code consumed flag updated atomically) so only one request can consume a given code.

title: Consumed backup codes are nulled instead of removed
body: After a successful redemption the code does `backupCodes[index] = null` and re-encrypts the array, so the stored value permanently accumulates null placeholders (e.g. `[null, null, "abc123...", ...]`). Single-use still works because `indexOf` no longer matches the redeemed string, but the stored blob grows with junk entries and reveals exactly how many codes have been used. Splice the element out (or filter nulls) before re-encrypting.

title: Backup codes stored with reversible encryption instead of hashing
body: Backup codes are stored via `symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes), CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY)`. Unlike the TOTP secret, the stored codes are never read back for display — the one-time display uses the in-memory values returned by this same endpoint, and login/disable only need an equality check — so they could be stored as one-way hashes (like passwords). As implemented, anyone who obtains both the database and the encryption key recovers every user's unused backup codes in cleartext.

title: Dismissing the dialog on the backup-codes step loses the codes with no recovery path
body: The backup codes are shown exactly once on the `DisplayBackupCodes` step, and only the explicit Close button calls `onEnable()`. If the user dismisses the dialog at this step in any other way (ESC key or the dialog's close control, which fire `onOpenChange`), the modal closes without `onEnable` being called and the codes — which exist only in this component's React state — can never be displayed or regenerated again. The user's only recourse is to disable and re-enable 2FA. Consider intercepting dismissal on this step with a warning, or providing a way to regenerate codes later.

title: Copy button shows a success toast even when the clipboard write fails
body: The copy handler calls `navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` without awaiting or catching it, then immediately fires `showToast(t("backup_codes_copied"), "success")`. In non-secure contexts or when clipboard permission is denied, `writeText` rejects (an unhandled promise rejection) while the user is told the codes were copied — they may close the dialog believing they have codes they don't. Await the promise and only show the success toast on fulfillment, with an error toast on rejection.

title: Backup codes unusable in the SAML/Google TOTP login flow
body: When a user with 2FA logs in via Google/SAML they are redirected to `/auth/login?totp=<jwt>` (`totpEmail` set), and in that state the footer renders `ExternalTotpFooter`, which only offers Cancel — there is no "Lost access" option, so these users cannot enter a backup code even though the credentials provider would accept one. Accounts that enabled 2FA and later moved to an identity-provider login (e.g. after linking Google, which nulls the password) have no self-service recovery path if they lose their authenticator.

title: Password visibility toggle removed from keyboard tab order
body: Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the show/hide password button removes it from keyboard navigation in every `PasswordField` across the app, while it keeps only an sr-only label. Keyboard and screen-reader users can no longer reach the control to verify what they typed. If the goal was to streamline tab order, this trades away an accessibility affordance; consider leaving it focusable.

title: A backup code plus any arbitrary non-empty totpCode bypasses password verification
body: In the credentials authorize() flow, the password check above (lines 121-129) only runs when `!credentials.totpCode`. The new backup-code branch `if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode)` runs regardless of whether the password was ever verified. An attacker who knows a victim's email and one backup code (a static 10-hex-character secret, e.g. from the downloadable cal-backup-codes.txt) can log in by submitting email + backupCode + any dummy non-empty totpCode such as "000000": the presence of totpCode makes the password-verification condition false, and the backup-code branch then authenticates them and creates a session. Backup codes are intended as a second factor in addition to the password; this makes one static factor alone sufficient for account takeover. The skip exists to support the IdP totp redirect flow, but the backup-code branch should require successful password verification for CAL (password) users, or the password check should not be conditioned on totpCode being absent.

title: onEnable only fires from the backup-codes Close button, leaving stale state on other dismiss paths
body: Before this change, `onEnable()` (which makes the parent settings page refresh and show the 2FA switch as enabled) ran immediately when /api/auth/two-factor/totp/enable returned 200. It is now replaced with `setStep(SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes)` and only called from the "Close" button on the backup-codes screen. If the user dismisses the dialog any other way — the dialog's X button, Escape key, or overlay click, all routed through `onOpenChange` — `onEnable()` never runs, so the settings page keeps showing 2FA as disabled even though it is now on (until a manual refetch), and `resetState()` also doesn't run, so reopening the modal lands on the stale backup-codes screen displaying the old codes. The parent notification/state reset should happen on any close of the final step, not just the Close button.

title: Backup codes cannot be used by Google/SAML users in the IdP two-factor challenge
body: When a Google/SAML user with 2FA signs in, they are redirected to /auth/login?totp=<jwt>, which renders the TOTP input with `ExternalTotpFooter` — only a Cancel button, no "Lost access" option — so there is no way in the UI to enter a backup code. A backup-code-only request is also rejected server-side: in next-auth-options.ts the guards `user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode` (lines 113-121) throw ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled / IncorrectEmailPassword before the new backup-code branch is reached. Consequence: identity-provider users who lose their authenticator remain locked out despite having valid backup codes; the recovery feature only works for CAL password accounts.

title: Consumed backup codes are nulled in place instead of removed
body: After a successful backup-code login, `backupCodes[index] = null` is persisted rather than splicing the used code out of the array. The stored JSON keeps accumulating null placeholders, `user.backupCodes` stays truthy forever, and once all 10 codes have been used the user gets `IncorrectBackupCode` instead of an indication that their codes are exhausted (`MissingBackupCodes` only fires when codes were never generated). Splice the redeemed code out and treat an empty array the same as having no backup codes.

title: Backup-code verification and consumption are not atomic
body: The authorize flow decrypts the stored codes, checks `indexOf`, and then issues a separate `prisma.user.update` to persist the remaining codes. Two concurrent login requests presenting the same backup code can both pass the `indexOf` check before either update commits, so a nominally single-use code can be redeemed twice within the race window. Consider consuming the code atomically (e.g., in a transaction with a re-read/optimistic check) or documenting acceptance of the risk.

title: missing_backup_codes message instructs users to do something impossible
body: The new string "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." is shown on the login page when a user with 2FA enabled but no backup codes uses the "Lost access" flow — i.e., users who enabled 2FA before this feature existed and are now locked out of their authenticator. There is no settings UI to (re)generate backup codes for an account that already has 2FA enabled (codes are only created during initial setup), and a locked-out user cannot reach settings anyway. The recovery instruction cannot be followed and will generate support tickets.

title: First 2FA e2e test not updated for the new backup-code screen; its assertion is admittedly broken
body: In "should allow a user to enable 2FA and login using 2FA", after the OTP is accepted the modal now displays the backup-codes screen, but the test never interacts with it or closes it (unlike the second test, which was updated). The subsequent check on the switch state is annotated with a newly added FIXME stating it passes even when the switch is not checked, and since `onEnable` now only fires from the backup-codes Close button, the enabled state is never confirmed. This test would stay green even if enabling 2FA regressed. It should close the backup-code screen and assert on `data-state="checked"` like the second test does.

title: No test covers logging in with a backup code or its one-time-use guarantee
body: The security-critical behavior introduced by this PR — authenticating with a backup code, rejecting an invalid code, and consuming a code so it cannot be reused — has no automated coverage. The added test code only checks the download filename and the copy toast, and a TODO acknowledges the missing tests. A regression making backup codes reusable, unconsumed, or rejected would ship undetected.

title: navigator.clipboard used without an availability check
body: The Copy button calls `navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` directly. The Clipboard API is only exposed in secure contexts; on self-hosted instances served over plain HTTP, `navigator.clipboard` is undefined, so clicking Copy throws a TypeError and the user gets no feedback at all (the success toast is never reached). Feature-detect `navigator.clipboard` and fall back to a hidden-textarea copy, or show an error toast.

title: Crash when a Google Meet event has no destination calendar
body: In EventManager.create(), the code does `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` and then reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining. When the event has no destination calendar (null or empty array — e.g. an organizer without a connected destination calendar booking an event type whose location is Google Meet), `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined` and reading `.integration` throws a TypeError, failing the entire booking creation. The previous code (`evt.destinationCalendar?.integration !== "google_calendar"`) safely fell back to Cal Video in exactly this case. Restore the optional chain: `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration !== "google_calendar"`.

title: Unrelated change inverts IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED condition for organization slug
body: This PR changes `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`, inverting when the organization's `slug` column is written. Previously the slug was set only when team billing was disabled, and `requestedSlug` metadata was used when billing was enabled; now organizations created with billing disabled never get a `slug` (breaking their org subdomain/URL), while billing-enabled instances write `slug` directly, bypassing the requested-slug verification flow. This change is unrelated to the destinationCalendar work and appears to have been pulled in accidentally.

title: createEvent always targets the main host's calendar, breaking multi-host events on Office365
body: createEvent takes `event.destinationCalendar[0]` and posts to `/me/calendars/{externalId}/events`. With collective events, EventManager now calls createEvent once per host credential, passing the full destinationCalendar array each time. For every host other than the organizer, `destinationCalendar[0]` is still the organizer's calendar, so the Graph API call uses this host's access token against a calendar ID belonging to a different user (or a non-Office365 calendar ID if the organizer uses another provider) — the request fails and that host never receives the event on their calendar. Like GoogleCalendarService now does, this should pick the destination calendar whose `credentialId` matches the credential being used (falling back to `/me/calendar/events`).

title: createEvent uses the first destination calendar instead of the current host's calendar
body: createEvent/createAttendees derive `calendarId` from `event.destinationCalendar[0]`. For collective bookings EventManager invokes createEvent once per host credential with the full array, so for any host other than the organizer the Lark API calls are made with that host's token against the organizer's calendar ID, which belongs to a different Lark account and will fail — the non-organizer host gets no calendar event. It should select the destination calendar matching the credential in use rather than always the first element.

title: CalDAV createEvent silently creates nothing for non-organizer hosts
body: BaseCalendarService.createEvent (used by caldav/apple calendars) filters the account's calendars by `c.externalId === mainHostDestinationCalendar.externalId` where `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `event.destinationCalendar[0]`. For collective events, EventManager calls createEvent with each host's credential but the full destination array; for a non-organizer host, no calendar in their CalDAV account matches the organizer's externalId, so `responses` is empty, no error is thrown, and EventManager records a booking reference even though no event was ever written to that host's calendar. The destination calendar matching the current credential should be used.

title: Team members' destination calendars are dropped when organizer/event type has none
body: `evt.destinationCalendar` is initialized to `null` when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar, and the subsequent `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` then no-ops, silently discarding the collected team calendars. For a collective event where the organizer has no destination calendar but other hosts do, no calendar events are created for anyone (EventManager falls into its no-destination fallback path). Initialize to `[]` instead of `null` so the team hosts' calendars are always included.

title: updateEvent fallback when externalCalendarId is missing is dead code, yielding undefined calendarId
body: `const selectedCalendar = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;` — the fallback branch only runs when externalCalendarId is falsy, and then searches for a calendar whose externalId equals that falsy value, which can never match, so selectedCalendar is always undefined. Previously the fallback was `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`, which let updates for older bookings (booking references without externalCalendarId) still target the destination calendar. Now those updates call `calendar.events.update` with `calendarId: undefined` and fail (e.g. rescheduling pre-existing bookings). The same dead fallback pattern exists in deleteEvent (line ~317), where it silently degrades to the "primary" calendar.

title: Recurring cancellation deletes only the first calendar reference per booking
body: In the recurring + allRemainingBookings branch, `updBooking.references.find((ref) => ref.type.includes("_calendar"))` takes only the first calendar reference of each updated booking. Now that collective bookings store one calendar reference per host, cancelling a recurring collective booking deletes only one host's calendar event per occurrence and leaves the other hosts' events orphaned on their calendars. Additionally, because this block now sits inside the new `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)` loop, it re-runs once per calendar reference of the cancelled booking, issuing duplicate delete attempts. Iterate all calendar references of each updated booking instead.

title: Video references no longer store credentialId, so meetings are not deleted on cancel
body: In create(), referencesToCreate now sets `credentialId: isCalendarType ? result.credentialId : undefined`. Previously non-calendar (video) results used `result.credentialId`, which createMeeting populates. With credentialId now persisted as null for video references, handleCancelBooking's check `if (bookingVideoReference && bookingVideoReference.credentialId)` fails, so the video meeting (Zoom, etc.) is never deleted when the booking is cancelled — an orphaned meeting link remains valid. Keep passing `result.credentialId` for video results.

title: References created via updateLocation lose credentialId and externalCalendarId
body: updateLocation's referencesToCreate now reads `result.externalId` and `result.credentialId`, but CalendarManager.updateEvent results never populate those fields, so every booking reference created through the edit-location flow is stored with null credentialId/externalCalendarId (previously they fell back to `evt.destinationCalendar`'s values). editLocation.handler persists these via `references: { create: ... }`, and later cancel/reschedule flows can no longer map these references to the correct credential and calendar — in multi-host bookings this means those calendar events can't be updated or deleted. Either have updateEvent return the reference's credentialId/externalCalendarId or keep the previous fallback.

title: Hangout-link patch uses possibly-undefined calendarId
body: In createEvent, the insert uses `selectedCalendar || "primary"` but the follow-up `calendar.events.patch` that writes the hangout link into the event description passes `calendarId: selectedCalendar` directly. When no destination calendar matches the credential (selectedCalendar is undefined, which the new credentialId-based lookup allows), the patch is issued with an undefined calendarId and fails, so the Meet link never gets added to the event description. Use the same `|| "primary"` fallback as the insert.

title: loadUsers no longer selects organization slug for dynamic bookings
body: The rewritten loadUsers drops `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` from the dynamic-user (no eventTypeId) query that existed before this change. Any downstream logic relying on `user.organization.slug` for dynamic collective bookings (e.g. org-domain booker URLs) now receives undefined. If the removal wasn't deliberate, restore the select.

title: loadUsers masks unexpected errors and leaks Prisma messages as 400s
body: The new try/catch in loadUsers converts PrismaClientKnownRequestError into an HTTP 400 with the raw Prisma error message (exposing internal database error details to clients) and converts every other unexpected error into a generic 500 "Unable to load users", discarding the original error and making production failures undebuggable. Additionally, an empty dynamicUserList previously simply returned no users but now throws a 500. Consider letting errors propagate as before.

title: No tests cover the new multi-host calendar fan-out
body: The PR's central behavior change — createAllCalendarEvents creating one calendar event per destination calendar (including fetching other hosts' credentials from the DB) and updateAllCalendarEvents iterating multiple calendar references — has no unit or integration coverage; the only test change is an updated webhook payload expectation. Given this touches booking creation, reschedule, and cancellation for every calendar provider, at least one test exercising a collective booking with two hosts (verifying two references with correct credentialId/externalCalendarId, and that cancel/reschedule cleans up both) should be added.

title: Crash when location is Google Meet and destinationCalendar is empty
body: In `EventManager.create()` the new code does `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` and then immediately reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` in `if (evt.location === MeetLocationType && mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar")`. When the event has no destination calendar (e.g. organizer and event type both have none, which `handleNewBooking` now represents as `null`), `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined` and accessing `.integration` throws a TypeError, failing the whole booking. The previous code used optional chaining (`evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`) and safely fell back to Cal Video in exactly this scenario — this is the very fallback the comment describes ('Google Meet selected w/o a Google Cal'). Needs `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.

title: Non-Google calendar services always use the first destination calendar, so other hosts never get events
body: The PR makes EventManager create one event per host destination calendar by calling `createEvent` with each host's own credential, but the Office365, Lark and CalDAV services still only read the FIRST element of `event.destinationCalendar` (e.g. here `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = event.destinationCalendar ?? [];` then `\`/me/calendars/${mainHostDestinationCalendar?.externalId}/events\``). The first element is the organizer's calendar, whose externalId belongs to a different account than the team-member credential being used. For Office365 this posts to a calendar id that doesn't exist in the team member's account (API error, success=false); Lark (lines 128, 164, 192, 237) has the same problem; the CalDAV base service (`packages/lib/CalendarService.ts` line 156) filters its calendar list by the first destination's externalId, matches nothing, and silently returns success without creating any event. Only Google Calendar was updated to pick the destination matching `credentialId`. As a result the stated goal of this PR — every host with any calendar app receiving the event — only works for Google Calendar; Office365/Lark/CalDAV hosts get nothing.

title: Reschedule only deletes the first old calendar event, leaving stale events on other hosts' calendars
body: In `updateAllCalendarEvents`, when `newBookingId` is set (reschedule), the cleanup of the old booking's calendar events uses `booking.references.find((reference) => reference.type.includes("_calendar"))` — a single reference. Now that this PR creates one `_calendar` reference per collective-event host, the old booking can have several calendar references, and only the first host's old event is deleted; the other hosts keep the stale pre-reschedule event on their calendars. This should iterate over all old calendar references (filter) and delete each with its own credentialId/externalCalendarId.

title: Unrelated change inverts organization slug logic for team billing
body: This PR flips `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})` while keeping `requestedSlug` also set when billing is enabled. Previously, when team billing was enabled the org slug was deliberately NOT set at creation time (only `requestedSlug`, presumably until billing completed); now the slug is claimed immediately in the billing-enabled flow and never set in the billing-disabled flow. This is unrelated to the destinationCalendar change and inverts the intended behavior of the billing gate.

title: Cancelling all remaining recurring bookings only deletes the first calendar reference per booking
body: The recurring-cancel branch inside the new per-reference loop still does `const bookingRef = updBooking.references.find((ref) => ref.type.includes("_calendar"))` and deletes only that one event, and it iterates only `bookingToDelete.user.credentials` (the organizer's). With multiple hosts, each updated booking now has several `_calendar` references (one per host credential), so the other hosts' recurring instances are never deleted. Additionally, because this whole block is now nested inside `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)`, the entire delete-across-all-credentials routine runs once per reference, issuing duplicate delete calls for the same events.

title: Confirming a collective booking still builds evt with a single destination calendar
body: For bookings requiring confirmation, calendar events are created at confirmation time via `handleConfirmation`/`EventManager.create(evt)`, but the `evt` built here sets `destinationCalendar` to only `[booking.destinationCalendar]` or `[user.destinationCalendar]` — the organizer's single calendar. The per-host destination calendars of the other collective hosts are never added, so confirming a collective opt-in booking still only creates the event on the organizer's calendar — the exact bug this PR sets out to fix remains in the confirmation path. The same gap exists in the payment-success flows (`packages/features/ee/payments/api/webhook.ts` and `paypal-webhook.ts`), which also build `evt` with only the booking/organizer destination calendar before calling `eventManager.create(evt)`.

title: updateLocation creates new references without externalCalendarId/credentialId
body: In `updateLocation`, `referencesToCreate` now uses `result.externalId` and `result.credentialId`, but these results come from `updateAllCalendarEvents` → `CalendarManager.updateEvent`, whose returned `EventResult` never sets `externalId` or `credentialId`. Previously these were populated from `evt.destinationCalendar?.externalId`/`?.credentialId`. `editLocation.handler` then persists these references (`references: { create: updatedResult.referencesToCreate }`), so after a location edit the new references lack the credential/calendar ids that later update/delete flows depend on.

title: Reschedule-request deletes calendar events with the organizer's credential instead of each reference's credential
body: Calendar cleanup here builds `credentialsMap` from the requesting user's credentials keyed by type, then for every booking reference calls `getCalendar(credentialsMap.get(bookingRef.type))` and deletes `bookingRef.uid`. With this PR, collective bookings have references pointing at OTHER hosts' credentials/calendars; deleting those events with the organizer's credential of the same app type will not find the event (different account), so the other hosts' calendar events survive a reschedule request. The per-reference `credentialId` (now stored thanks to this PR) should be used to load the correct credential, as done in `handleCancelBooking`.

title: updateEvent fallback find compares against a known-falsy externalCalendarId
body: `const selectedCalendar = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;` — in the fallback branch `externalCalendarId` is falsy by definition, so the `find` predicate compares each calendar's externalId against null/undefined/'' and effectively never matches, yielding `calendarId: undefined` for the update call. The old code fell back to `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. Bookings whose reference lacks `externalCalendarId` (legacy rows) will now attempt to update `calendars/undefined/events/...` and fail, whereas before they updated the destination calendar. The same dead predicate exists in `deleteEvent` (line ~317), where it silently degrades to deleting from "primary" instead of the destination calendar.

title: Hangout-link patch uses possibly-undefined calendarId after primary fallback
body: In `createEvent`, the insert uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"`, but the follow-up `calendar.events.patch` that writes the hangout link into the description uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar` directly. When no destination calendar matches the credential (the "primary" fallback path), `selectedCalendar` is `undefined`, so the patch targets `calendars/undefined/...` and the event description never gets the Meet link. Previously `selectedCalendar` was always at least "primary".

title: loadUsers refactor drops organization.slug from dynamic booking user query
body: The rewritten `loadUsers` for the dynamic (no eventTypeId) path selects `...userSelect.select, credentials: true, metadata: true` but no longer selects `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` that the old query included. Any downstream code reading `user.organization?.slug` for dynamic collective bookings (org context/branding/URLs) will now get `undefined`. This change is also unrelated to the destinationCalendar fix.

title: destinationCalendar falls back to null here but [] everywhere else, and team calendars are silently dropped when null
body: The new evt initializer uses `: null` when neither eventType nor organizer has a destination calendar, while every other call site in this PR (confirm, cancel, payment webhooks, bookingReminder, etc.) uses `[]`. This makes the webhook payload shape inconsistent (BOOKING_CREATED/BOOKING_REQUESTED send `destinationCalendar: null`, BOOKING_REJECTED sends `[]`), which consumers must special-case — the e2e expectations updated in this PR encode exactly that inconsistency. Additionally, the subsequent `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is a no-op when the value is null, so for a collective event whose organizer has no destination calendar, the other hosts' calendars are silently discarded.

title: Google Meet fallback crashes when booking has no destination calendar
body: In `create()`, the code does `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` and then evaluates `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"` when `evt.location === MeetLocationType`. When the event has no destination calendar (`null` from handleNewBooking, or `[]` from confirm/payment flows), `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined` and reading `.integration` throws a TypeError. This is exactly the scenario this branch exists for ("Fallback to Cal Video if Google Meet is selected w/o a Google Cal"), so any booking with a Google Meet location and no destination calendar now crashes instead of falling back to Daily. The old code used optional chaining (`evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`); this needs `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.

title: IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED condition for org slug is inverted
body: This PR (which is about destination calendars) changes `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`, inverting the condition. Previously, when team billing was disabled (e.g. self-hosted), the org got its `slug` immediately, and when billing was enabled only `requestedSlug` was stored so the real slug could be set after payment. After this change, billing-enabled installs set `slug` before payment (bypassing the paid flow) and billing-disabled installs never set a slug at all, leaving the organization without a usable URL. This looks like an accidental flip during an unrelated edit and should be reverted.

title: updateEvent fallback for missing externalCalendarId is dead code; updates fail with calendarId undefined
body: In `updateEvent`, the new fallback is `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. That `.find` only runs when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so it compares each calendar's `externalId` against `null`/`""` and can never match — `selectedCalendar` is always `undefined` in that case, and `calendar.events.update` is then called with `calendarId: undefined`, which throws and leaves the Google event un-updated (caught upstream as success=false, so the booking is rescheduled in cal.com but the calendar event keeps the old time). The previous code fell back to `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. This matters more now because other changes in this PR create references with `externalCalendarId: null` (see EventManager updateLocation and the no-credentialId create branch). The same dead `.find` pattern exists in `deleteEvent` (line 315-317), where it is only masked by the later `calendarId ? calendarId : "primary"` fallback.

title: Video booking references lose credentialId, breaking meeting deletion on cancel
body: In `create()`'s `referencesToCreate`, the credentialId is now `isCalendarType ? result.credentialId : undefined`. Previously it was `isCalendarType ? evt.destinationCalendar?.credentialId : result.credentialId`, i.e. video results kept `result.credentialId` from `createMeeting`. With this change, every newly created video BookingReference is stored with `credentialId: null`. `handleCancelBooking` only deletes the video meeting when `bookingVideoReference.credentialId` is set (it looks up the credential by id to call `deleteMeeting`), so cancelling bookings created after this change will leave orphaned Zoom/Daily/etc. meetings that are never deleted. There is no reason to special-case calendar types here; use `result.credentialId` for all results.

title: updateLocation references are created without credentialId/externalCalendarId
body: `updateLocation()` now builds references with `externalCalendarId: result.externalId` and `credentialId: result.credentialId ?? undefined`, but the calendar-update results come from `updateAllCalendarEvents` → `CalendarManager.updateEvent`, whose returned EventResult never sets `externalId` or `credentialId`. Both fields are therefore always `undefined`, and `editLocation.handler` persists these references on the booking (`references: { create: updatedResult.referencesToCreate }`). The old code fell back to `evt.destinationCalendar?.externalId` / `?.credentialId`. Consequence: bookings that go through "edit location" accumulate calendar references with no credential/calendar linkage, so later updates/deletes can't find the right credential and fall into legacy paths (including the broken Google `updateEvent` fallback).

title: Office365 createEvent always targets the main host's calendar, even when creating for another host
body: `createEvent` now takes the first entry of `event.destinationCalendar` (`mainHostDestinationCalendar`) and posts to `/me/calendars/{mainHostDestinationCalendar.externalId}/events`. For collective events, `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents` calls `createEvent` once per host with that host's credential, but the full event (with all destination calendars, main host first) is passed each time. So when creating the event for a non-organizer host's Office365 account, it tries to write to the main host's calendar id using the team member's token, which fails (404/403) — the team member never gets the event. `CalendarManager.createEvent` already receives the per-destination `externalId` but doesn't forward it to `calendar.createEvent`; the credentialId-based lookup used in the Google service (or forwarding externalId) is needed here too.

title: Lark createEvent uses the first destination calendar regardless of which host's credential is used
body: Same class of bug as the Office365 service: `createEvent` derives `calendarId` from `event.destinationCalendar[0]` (the main host's calendar). For collective bookings, EventManager invokes `createEvent` separately for each host's credential, but Lark will always attempt `POST /calendar/v4/calendars/{mainHostCalendarId}/events/create_event` with the team member's token, which the member has no access to — so non-organizer hosts never get Lark calendar events. The service should select the destination calendar matching the credential being used (as the Google service now does with the credentialId parameter).

title: CalDAV createEvent silently reports success without creating anything for other hosts
body: The CalDAV base service filters `calendars` to `c.externalId === mainHostDestinationCalendar.externalId` where `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `event.destinationCalendar[0]`. When EventManager creates the event for a non-organizer host's CalDAV credential (collective events), that host's account does not contain the main host's calendar URL, so the filtered list is empty, `Promise.all([])` resolves to `[]`, `responses.some(r => !r.ok)` is false, and the method returns a successful result with a uid — but no event was created anywhere. This is a silent data-integrity failure: the booking reference is stored, but the team member's calendar has no event. It should match the destination calendar for the credential in use, like Google's credentialId lookup.

title: Team destination calendars silently dropped when organizer and event type have none
body: `evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` exists, and the collective-team calendars are added via `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`. Optional chaining means that when the base value is `null`, the push is silently skipped: for a collective event where the organizer has no connected destination calendar but team members do, none of the team members' calendars receive events (and the booking's destinationCalendar is not connected either). The array should be initialized to `[]` (or the team calendars assigned directly) so collective hosts still get their events.

title: Dynamic user query no longer selects organization
body: The `loadUsers` refactor rewrote the dynamic-group user lookup and dropped `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` from the `prisma.user.findMany` select (it was explicitly selected before, together with `metadata`). Any downstream code for dynamic collective bookings that reads `user.organization.slug` (e.g. org-subdomain/booker-url handling) will now get `undefined` and potentially throw. This removal is unrelated to the destination-calendar change and looks accidental; it should be restored.

title: Recurring-event deletion block now runs once per calendar reference
body: The recurring-cancellation branch (mapping over all of the organizer's calendar credentials × all updated recurring bookings and deleting each) lives inside the new `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)` loop. With multiple calendar references (the collective multi-host case this PR introduces, typically one per host), the entire recurring deletion pass executes once per reference, issuing duplicate `deleteEvent` calls for the same events. Google tolerates this via 404/410 handling, but other providers may log errors and it doubles the external API traffic. The recurring branch should run once, outside the per-reference loop. (Separately, that branch still only deletes the first calendar reference per updated booking, so team-member calendar events for recurring collective bookings remain stale.)

title: Hangout-link patch call uses possibly-undefined calendarId
body: In `createEvent`, the insert call uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"`, but the follow-up `calendar.events.patch` (that writes the description with the hangout link) passes the raw `selectedCalendar`, which is `undefined` whenever no destination calendar matches the credentialId. The google client will throw a missing-parameter error for that patch, so the hangout link is never written into the event description in that case. Previously `selectedCalendar` was always defined (defaulted to "primary").

title: Only the first old calendar event is deleted when merging bookings on reschedule
body: When `newBookingId` is set (reschedule/merge path), the code deletes the old booking's calendar event via `booking.references.find((reference) => reference.type.includes("_calendar"))`. Bookings can now have multiple calendar references (one per collective host), so only the first host's old event is deleted; the other hosts keep a stale event at the old time. This should iterate over all calendar references of the old booking.

title: Webhook payload sends destinationCalendar as null in some flows and [] in others
