body: The updated e2e expectations now encode that BOOKING_CREATED and BOOKING_REQUESTED payloads contain `destinationCalendar: null` while BOOKING_REJECTED contains `destinationCalendar: []` — because handleNewBooking emits `null` when there is no destination calendar while confirm.handler emits `[]`. This is an inconsistent contract for the same field across webhook triggers, and the field's shape also changed from a single object to an array, which is a breaking change for existing webhook consumers despite the PR being labelled non-breaking. Consider normalizing (always array, or always null-when-empty) across all emitters.

title: No automated tests cover the new multi-destination calendar logic
body: The PR rewrites `createAllCalendarEvents`/`updateAllCalendarEvents` and the create/update/delete paths of four calendar providers for the collective multi-host scenario, but the author explicitly checked "I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective". The only test change is a webhook payload expectation. Regressions introduced here (e.g. the Google Meet fallback TypeError, non-Google providers writing to the main host's calendar, video references losing credentialId) would be caught by even a minimal unit test around `EventManager.create` with multiple destination calendars.

title: Google Calendar credential key is overwritten with the zod SafeParse wrapper object instead of the parsed tokens
body: parseRefreshTokenResponse() returns the whole zod safeParse result ({ success: true, data: {...} }), not the parsed data. Here it is assigned to `key` and written straight into the DB via prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } }), so after the first token refresh the stored credential key becomes {"success": true, "data": {access_token: ...}}. On the next instantiation the constructor runs googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key) (line 75), which throws because access_token/refresh_token are now nested under `data`. Every Google Calendar credential breaks (availability lookups, booking creation, event updates) after its first refresh, forcing users to disconnect and reconnect. This affects all Google Calendar users regardless of whether the new credential-sync feature is enabled. The fix is to store `parseRefreshTokenResponse(...).data` (or have the util return the parsed data).

title: prisma is used but never imported, breaking the build
body: The newly added refresh block calls `await prisma.credential.update(...)` at line 96, but the file's imports (lines 1-20) do not include `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. This is a TypeScript compile error (Cannot find name 'prisma') that will fail type-check/build for the app-store package.

title: Freshly refreshed Salesforce access token is saved to the DB but the connection is built with the old, stale token
body: getClient() fetches a new access token from Salesforce and persists it (lines 75-99), but the returned jsforce.Connection is constructed with `accessToken: credentialKey.access_token` — the old token read from the credential before the refresh, which is the very token that may be expired. The refreshed token (accessTokenParsed.data.access_token) is never used for this connection, so the new code performs an extra token request on every service instantiation without actually authenticating with the fresh token. It should use accessTokenParsed.data.access_token (and instance_url from the parsed response).

title: Sync path returns a raw fetch Response, but callers expect the parsed token payload shape of their provider
body: When credential syncing is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns the unparsed fetch Response from CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT (never calls .json()). Callers, however, consume whatever their own refreshFunction returned: Google does `const token = res?.data; token.access_token` (Response has no .data → TypeError, silently swallowed by the catch so the old token is kept); HubSpot treats the result as a TokenResponseIF (`hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` is undefined → expiryDate NaN, `setAccessToken(undefined)`, and `key: hubspotRefreshToken` writes the Response object into the credential row, which serializes to `{}` and destroys the credential); zoho-bigin and zohocrm read `tokenInfo.data.error` / `.expires_in` on the Response (undefined → TypeError or wrong data). The sync branch makes the refresh flow broken for google-calendar, hubspot, zoho-bigin and zohocrm. The util needs to parse the JSON and normalize it to the shape each consumer expects, or consumers must handle the Response.

title: refreshOAuthTokens is called with the credential row id instead of the Cal.com user id
body: refreshAccessToken(credentialId, credentialKey) passes `credentialId` (the primary key of the Credential row) as the third argument to refreshOAuthTokens, whose parameter is `userId` and which posts it to the external sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. The parent platform will therefore look up and return tokens for the wrong user (or fail to find one), and the returned tokens will be stored on this user's credential — mixing up users' third-party credentials. Every other app passes `credential.userId`; this one should too.

title: minimumTokenResponseSchema drops every field except access_token, corrupting stored credentials when sync is enabled
body: The computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the literal string "[object Object]" (Zod schemas have no meaningful toString), so the intended catch-all does not exist — the second key simply overwrites the first. Combined with zod's default behaviour of stripping unknown keys, parsing any token response with this schema keeps only `access_token` and discards expires_in/expires_in-like fields, scope, instance_url, etc. Consequences when APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is on: zoom stores `expiry_date = Date.now() + undefined * 1000 = NaN` (zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts line 122) so the token can never be considered valid again; salesforce (which always uses this parser when the flag is on, even though it calls Salesforce directly) permanently loses instance_url from the stored key, breaking future connections; office365 keeps a stale expiry. Zod's .catchall()/.passthrough() or an explicit expiry field is needed.

title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token" and persisted, bricking credentials
body: When the parsed response has no refresh_token, the util sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. Callers then merge/write this into the DB: zoom does `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token` (VideoApiAdapter.ts line 120) and office365 spreads the parsed data over the stored credentials (CalendarService.ts line 264). The real refresh token is thereby overwritten with a junk literal — both in sync mode (where the endpoint returns no refresh token) and in normal mode whenever a provider omits a rotated refresh token. Any later refresh attempt (e.g. after disabling the sync feature) will fail with invalid_grant and the user must reconnect the app. The placeholder should not be written back to the stored credential.

title: appStoreMetadata is keyed by directory name, not App.slug, so the webhook 404s for most major apps
body: The lookup `appStoreMetadata[app.slug]` assumes the metadata map is keyed by the App table slug, but it is keyed by app-store directory names: `zoomvideo`, `googlecalendar`, `office365calendar`, `office365video`, `larkcalendar` — while the corresponding App slugs are `zoom`, `google-calendar`, `office365-calendar`, `msteams`, `lark-calendar` (see e.g. office365video using getAppKeysFromSlug("msteams") and createOAuthAppCredential({ appId: "zoom" }) in this PR). For those apps the metadata lookup returns undefined and the endpoint responds 404, making credential sync unusable for Google Calendar, Office 365, MS Teams, Zoom and Lark. The mapping from app slug to the metadata key needs to be resolved differently (e.g. match on metadata type/appId).

title: Webhook overwrites an arbitrary credential when a user has several for the same app, and find-then-create is racy
body: Cal.com allows a user to hold multiple credentials for the same appId (e.g. two Google accounts) and teams to hold their own. `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` picks whichever row happens to come first and overwrites its key with the pushed tokens, potentially replacing account A's tokens with account B's and silently breaking that connection; team credentials are never matched at all. Additionally the find-then-update/create sequence is not atomic and Credential has no unique constraint on (userId, appId), so two concurrent webhook deliveries for a new credential both find nothing and create duplicates. The payload should identify the exact credential (or the endpoint should enforce a uniqueness constraint and use a transaction/upsert).

title: Unhandled validation/decryption errors produce 500s, and the HTTP method is not restricted
body: appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body), JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...)) (lines 57-59) are called without try/catch — a malformed body, bad ciphertext or a mismatched CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY throws and results in an unhandled 500 (potentially with stack trace) instead of a 400. The handler also accepts any HTTP method since req.method is never checked. Use safeParse and wrap decryption/JSON.parse to return 400 responses, and reject non-POST requests.

title: Webhook secret compared with a plain !== string comparison
body: The shared secret is verified with `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, a non-constant-time comparison that is susceptible to timing attacks. For a secret that alone grants the ability to write arbitrary third-party tokens for any user, use crypto.timingSafeEqual (after length checks) instead.

title: Sync-path token refresh stores expiry_date = now and drops refresh_token/email from the credential key
body: When credential sync is enabled, the sync endpoint returns only an access token and expiry (per the contract documented in refreshOAuthTokens.ts), so `responseBody.expires_in` is undefined and `expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + (responseBody?.expires_in || 0) * 1000)` becomes the current time — the token is considered expired on the very next getToken() call, so every MS Teams API call triggers another refresh request to the sync endpoint. Additionally `key: responseBody` replaces the entire stored credential key, discarding refresh_token and email; if sync is later disabled the credential can no longer be refreshed. The refreshed fields should be merged into the existing key and the expiry read from whatever the endpoint actually returns.

title: No tests for the credential-sync webhook or the token-refresh sync path
body: The PR checklist explicitly states no tests were added. The new endpoint can overwrite any user's stored third-party tokens, and the refreshOAuthTokens/parseRefreshTokenResponse utilities sit on the critical path of every calendar/video integration — a broken response shape here corrupts credentials in the DB (several such issues exist in this PR). At minimum, tests should cover: valid/invalid webhook secret, malformed and undecryptable payloads, create vs update behaviour, apps with multiple credentials per user, and both branches (sync enabled/disabled) of the refresh helpers.

title: prisma is used but never imported in salesforce CalendarService
body: The new code in getClient() calls `await prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, ... })`, but this file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` (the import block at the top only imports jsforce, rrule, zod, CalEventParser, constants, http-error, logger, types, getAppKeysFromSlug and parseRefreshTokenResponse). This is a `Cannot find name 'prisma'` type-check failure / ReferenceError at runtime, so the build breaks and the Salesforce integration cannot work at all.

title: Credential-sync refresh path returns a raw fetch Response, but the code reads res.data and crashes
body: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `fetch` Response from the sync endpoint, which has no `.data` property and whose body is never parsed. The normal path returns GaxiosResponse (`fetchTokens.res`) which does have `.data`. So in the sync path `const token = res?.data` is `undefined` and `googleCredentials.access_token = token.access_token` throws a TypeError. The catch block treats it as a non-'invalid_grant' error and silently returns myGoogleAuth with the old, expired credentials, so every Google Calendar API call for synced users fails with 401s and the credential is never marked invalid.

title: Sync-path Response object is persisted as the HubSpot credential key, destroying the stored credential
body: `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw fetch `Response` when credential sync is enabled, but the result is typed/used as `HubspotToken`. In the sync path: `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` is undefined so `expiryDate` becomes NaN, `hubspotClient.setAccessToken(hubspotRefreshToken.accessToken)` sets undefined, and `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key: hubspotRefreshToken as any } })` JSON-serializes a Response object — i.e. the stored credential key is overwritten with `{"expiryDate": null}`. The user's HubSpot credential (including the refresh token) is permanently wiped and they must reconnect the app.

title: refreshOAuthTokens is called with credentialId instead of userId
body: `refreshOAuthTokens(refreshFunction, appSlug, userId)` is invoked as `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoho-bigin", credentialId)`. The third parameter is sent to the self-hoster's sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`, so the platform receives a credential row id instead of the Cal.com user id. Since credential ids and user ids overlap numerically, the platform can resolve this to a *different* user and return that user's third-party tokens, which would then be stored on this user's credential — a cross-user token leak. Every other app in this PR passes `credential.userId`.

title: minimumTokenResponseSchema drops expiry and refresh_token — computed keys collapse and zod strips unknown fields
body: The schema uses computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`; both evaluate to "[object Object]", so the second overwrites the first, and the schema is effectively `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), "[object Object]": z.unknown().optional() })`. Because zod strips unknown keys by default, parsing any token response returns only `{ access_token }` — the comments claiming "any property with a number is the expiry" are wrong. Consequences in the sync path: in zoomvideo `key.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + newTokens.expires_in * 1000)` becomes NaN (which then fails zoomTokenSchema's z.number() on the next read, breaking Zoom entirely), and office365calendar never updates its stored expiry.

title: Placeholder refresh_token = "refresh_token" overwrites real refresh tokens in the database
body: When a refresh response omits `refresh_token`, the code writes the literal string "refresh_token" into the result. office365calendar then merges this over the stored credential (`{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }`) and zoomvideo assigns `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token` directly, and both persist it. If the sync feature is later disabled, or a provider omits refresh_token in a normal refresh, the credential's real refresh token is permanently replaced with the placeholder and all future refreshes fail with invalid_grant, requiring the user to reconnect.

title: Zoom refresh passes app slug "zoomvideo" instead of "zoom"
body: `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoomvideo", credential.userId)` sends `appSlug=zoomvideo` to the self-hoster's sync endpoint, but Zoom's app slug everywhere else is "zoom" (see zoomvideo/api/callback.ts which stores `appId: "zoom"`, and the new webhook endpoint which looks up `prisma.app` by slug). The platform cannot resolve "zoomvideo" to the Zoom app, so token refresh via the sync endpoint will fail for Zoom. Every other app passes its real slug ("google-calendar", "msteams", "webex", etc.).

title: axios response shape assumed, but sync path returns a fetch Response
body: The normal refresh function returns an AxiosResponse (read via `tokenInfo.data`), but `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw fetch `Response` when sync is enabled, which has no `.data`. `if (!tokenInfo.data.error)` then throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`, so Zoho Bigin token refresh always crashes when credential sync is enabled. The same class of mismatch applies to zohocrm.

title: axios/fetch response mismatch breaks ZohoCRM refresh when sync is enabled
body: The wrapped refresh function returns an AxiosResponse, but the sync branch of `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw fetch `Response` with no `.data` property. `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error` therefore throws a TypeError; it is swallowed by `catch (e) { this.log.error(e); }`, leaving `this.accessToken` unset/stale. All subsequent Zoho CRM API calls go out with an empty or expired `Zoho-oauthtoken` header and fail, silently breaking the integration for synced users.

title: Webex refresh always rejects when credential sync is enabled
body: Unlike the other apps, webex kept validating with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema.safeParse(responseBody)`, which requires `refresh_token`, `refresh_token_expires_in`, and literal `scope`/`token_type` values. The documented sync-endpoint contract ("response should only contain the access token and expiry date") can never satisfy this schema, so `parsedToken.success` is always false and refresh always rejects with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" — Webex is broken whenever credential sync is on.

title: Lark refresh expects Lark's {code, data} envelope but sync endpoint returns a flat minimal payload
body: The sync-path response from `refreshOAuthTokens` is passed to `handleLarkError<RefreshTokenResp>` and then read as `data.data.refresh_token`, `data.data.refresh_expires_in`, etc. The sync endpoint returns a flat `{access_token, expiry}` payload (per the documented contract in refreshOAuthTokens), so `data.data` is undefined and the refresh throws (or stores undefined token fields into the credential key). Lark calendar refresh is broken when credential sync is enabled.

title: Salesforce refresh runs on every service instantiation and the connection is built with the stale access token
body: getClient() now performs a refresh-token exchange with Salesforce every time a CalendarService is constructed, even when the stored access token is still valid — adding a blocking network round trip (and Salesforce token-endpoint rate-limit exposure) to every calendar operation, and overwriting the DB key each time, which also fights the webhook's source-of-truth model when sync is enabled. Additionally, after refreshing and persisting the new token, the jsforce.Connection is created with the OLD `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` instead of `accessTokenParsed.data`, so the fresh token is never actually used.

title: Invalid webhook payloads throw unhandled 500s instead of 4xx responses
body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a ZodError on any malformed body, and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, ...))` (line 57) throws on a wrongly encrypted or non-JSON payload; neither is wrapped in try/catch, so callers get an unhandled 500 with a stack trace rather than a 400. The handler also never checks `req.method`, so even a GET with no body hits these throwing paths. The webhook secret comparison at line 25 is also not constant-time.

title: findFirst by userId+appId can overwrite the wrong credential for multi-account apps
body: Cal.com allows a user to connect multiple accounts for the same app (e.g. several Google or Office 365 calendars), producing multiple Credential rows with the same userId and appId. The webhook's `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` picks an arbitrary one and overwrites its key with the pushed credentials, so the platform can silently clobber the tokens of a different account than intended. The payload needs an account identifier (e.g. email/external id) to target the correct credential.

title: Outbound request to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT carries no authentication
body: The POST to the self-hoster's sync endpoint sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` in the body — no shared secret, signature, or header (CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET is only checked on the inbound webhook). The platform endpoint therefore cannot verify the request genuinely comes from its Cal.com instance; anyone who can reach that endpoint can request freshly refreshed third-party OAuth tokens for any user id / app. The implementation should include the shared secret (or an HMAC) so the platform can authenticate the caller.

title: No tests for the webhook endpoint or the sync refresh paths
body: The PR checklist explicitly states no tests were added. This change adds a new authenticated credential-writing endpoint and rewires token refresh for nine integrations with two divergent code paths (direct provider refresh vs. platform sync endpoint); the response-shape mismatches introduced here (axios vs fetch, GaxiosResponse vs fetch Response) are exactly the kind of regression a small unit/integration test per service would have caught.

title: Zod SafeParse wrapper object is stored as the credential key, corrupting Google credentials on every refresh
body: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the zod safeParse result object ({ success: true, data: {...} }), but line 97-100 stores that whole wrapper as the credential key: `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(...); await prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. Before this PR the key was the plain parsed token object. After the first access-token refresh, credential.key in the DB becomes {"success":true,"data":{...tokens...}}, and the next time GoogleCalendarService is constructed `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` (line 75) throws because the tokens are nested under `data`. This breaks Google Calendar for every user whose token refreshes, on default (non-sync) installs too. Extract `.data` (or change the helper to return parsed data) before persisting.

title: Sync-mode returns a raw fetch Response but several callers expect parsed/library-specific shapes
body: In sync mode this helper returns the unparsed fetch Response, but multiple integrations handle the return value as if it were the library-specific response: googlecalendar reads `res?.data` (a fetch Response has no `.data`, so `token.access_token` throws a TypeError that is swallowed by the catch and the expired token is silently reused); hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts treats it as HubspotToken (`expiresIn` is undefined so expiryDate becomes NaN, `setAccessToken(undefined)` is called, and the Response object itself is persisted as the credential key); zohocrm and zoho-bigin read `tokenInfo.data.error`, throwing TypeError since `.data` is undefined. Credential sync mode is therefore broken (or corrupts stored credentials) for google-calendar, hubspot, zohocrm and zoho-bigin. The helper should parse the JSON body and normalize the response shape, or callers must be adapted.

title: minimumTokenResponseSchema is not valid zod: it strips everything except access_token and forces refresh_token to the literal string "refresh_token"
body: The computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` do not create a catch-all (they evaluate to a fixed string such as "[object Object]"), and z.object strips unknown keys by default. So in sync mode the parse result contains only `access_token`; any expiry field returned by the sync endpoint is dropped, and lines 25-27 then set `refresh_token` to the literal string "refresh_token". Consequences downstream: office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts line 264 spreads this over the stored credentials, overwriting the user's real refresh token with "refresh_token" in the DB; zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts computes `expiry_date = Date.now() + newTokens.expires_in * 1000` where expires_in was stripped, storing NaN and also persisting the placeholder refresh token. Use z.catchall/passthrough for the permissive schema and preserve real expiry/refresh-token data.

title: Credential primary key passed as Cal.com userId to the credential-sync endpoint
body: refreshOAuthTokens' third parameter is the Cal.com userId, which is POSTed to the self-hoster's sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. Bigin passes `credentialId` (credential.id) instead of the user's id. The sync endpoint will look up a user whose id equals the credential id and either fail or return another user's tokens, which then get stored under this credential. Pass credential.userId (the method currently only receives credentialId and credentialKey, so it needs the credential object or userId).

title: New code uses prisma without importing it, breaking the build
body: The newly added token-refresh block calls `await prisma.credential.update(...)` but the file's imports (lines 1-20) contain no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. TypeScript compilation/type-check fails with "Cannot find name 'prisma'", so the package no longer builds.

title: appStoreMetadata is looked up by DB slug, but it is keyed by app directory name — sync 404s for most apps
body: `appStoreMetadata` is keyed by app folder names (e.g. "googlecalendar", "office365calendar", "office365video", "zoomvideo", "larkcalendar"), while `app.slug` from the App table uses the public slugs used everywhere else in this PR ("google-calendar", "office365-calendar", "msteams", "zoom", "lark-calendar"). `appStoreMetadata[app.slug]` is therefore undefined for those apps and the webhook returns 404 "App not found" — credential sync only works for the few apps whose slug equals the directory name (hubspot, zohocrm, salesforce, zoho-bigin). Look metadata up by each entry's own `slug` property or maintain a slug→metadata map.

title: Refresh runs on every service construction and the fresh token is then ignored
body: getClient (invoked from the constructor) now performs an unconditional refresh-token grant against Salesforce every time the service is instantiated — adding a blocking HTTP call and token churn to every calendar operation — but the returned jsforce.Connection is built with the old `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` instead of the freshly fetched `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`. The new token is only written to the DB, so this request is pure overhead and the connection still relies on jsforce lazily refreshing the expired token again on 401. Also note this path always talks to Salesforce directly and never uses refreshOAuthTokens, so it ignores credential-sync mode entirely (and will break once the stored refresh_token is the placeholder written by parseRefreshTokenResponse).

title: Sync-mode token response has no expires_in, so stored MS Teams token is immediately expired and loses its refresh token
body: The documented contract for the sync endpoint is that it returns only the access token and expiry date, but this code computes `expiry_date = Date.now() + (responseBody?.expires_in || 0) * 1000` and persists `responseBody` as the credential key. In sync mode expires_in is absent, so expiry_date ≈ now and `isExpired` is true on every subsequent call (a refresh request to the sync endpoint on every operation), and the stored key no longer contains refresh_token at all, breaking any later non-sync refresh.

title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time !==
body: The endpoint authenticates by comparing the secret header to process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET with `!==`, a non-constant-time string comparison that leaks prefix matches through response timing. Use a constant-time comparison (e.g. crypto.timingSafeEqual over equal-length buffers).

title: findFirst-then-create allows duplicate credentials for the same user/app
body: The lookup-then-insert sequence is not atomic and the Credential table has no unique constraint on (userId, appId). Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same user and app both take the create branch and produce duplicate credentials; later reads that use findFirst may then pick up a stale credential. Use an upsert backed by a unique constraint or a transaction with appropriate isolation.

title: Invalid payloads and decryption failures produce unhandled 500s
body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` throw on malformed bodies, bad ciphertext, or non-JSON plaintext, resulting in unhandled 500 errors (and there is no HTTP method restriction, so a plain GET also 500s). Use safeParse/try-catch and return 400 with a clear message.

title: Updating an existing credential does not clear the invalid flag
body: When a credential already exists only `key` is updated. Credentials previously flagged `invalid: true` (e.g. googlecalendar marks them on invalid_grant) stay invalid after fresh keys are synced in, so the integration remains disabled even though valid tokens were delivered. Set `invalid: false` when updating the key.

title: Team admin/owner permission check uses && instead of ||
body: isTeamAdminOrOwner is computed as `(await isTeamAdmin(user.id, teamId)) && (await isTeamOwner(user.id, teamId))`. isTeamOwner is only true for users with the OWNER membership role, so any team admin who is not also the team owner fails this check and gets a FORBIDDEN ('you_do_not_have_permission') error when calling viewer.bookings.addGuests. The variable name, and the fact that the bookings UI exposes the 'Additional guests' action to team admins, indicate the intent was OR. Consequence: team admins can open the Add Guests dialog but every submission fails.

title: Calendar update uses the requester's credentials instead of the booking organizer's
body: The handler builds EventManager from `ctx.user` and `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` — the person clicking 'add guests' — but the booking's calendar reference and destination calendar belong to `booking.user` (the organizer, whose credentials were even fetched in the booking query at lines 35-40 but go unused). When anyone other than the organizer adds guests (an attendee, or a team admin/owner managing someone else's team booking), `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` cannot find the calendar credential that owns the event, so it throws or silently skips the update. Because the attendee rows were already committed at line 92, the guests end up saved in the DB while the calendar event is never updated and the mutation returns an error; retrying then fails with 'emails_must_be_unique_valid' because the guests already exist.

title: Attendees are persisted before calendar/email side effects with no transaction or idempotency
body: `prisma.booking.update({ ..., attendees: { createMany } })` commits the new attendees first; only afterwards are the calendar event updated (line 165) and emails sent (line 168). If anything after the DB write fails (calendar API error, missing credential, process crash), the API returns an error even though the guests were added, and because the uniqueness filter at line 76 then treats them as existing attendees, the user cannot simply retry — the guests remain on the booking without calendar entries or invitation emails. The operation should be idempotent or the side effects performed in a way that can be recovered.

title: Guest email matching is case-sensitive, bypassing the blacklist and duplicate checks
body: BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS entries are lowercased (line 71) but the incoming guest is compared un-normalized (`!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`), so 'Blocked@Example.com' bypasses a blacklist entry 'blocked@example.com'. The existing-attendee dedupe (`guest === attendee.email`) and the `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)` check in sendAddGuestsEmails have the same problem, so a case-variant of an existing attendee's email creates a duplicate Attendee row, and isAttendee (line 52) can fail to recognize an attendee whose stored email case differs from their account email. Emails should be normalized (e.g. lowercased) before all comparisons. Additionally, the input array itself is never de-duplicated server-side — the uniqueness check exists only in the client dialog's zod schema — so a direct API call containing duplicate entries creates duplicate attendees.

title: Any attendee can add an unbounded number of guests to a booking
body: The permission check allows anyone whose email appears on the booking — including guests who were themselves added through this feature — to add further guests, and ZAddGuestsInputSchema places no upper bound on the guests array. A single request can therefore create hundreds of Attendee rows and trigger an email to every one of them through Cal.com's mail infrastructure (a spam/abuse vector), and it discloses the meeting location/video link to arbitrary addresses without the organizer's involvement. Consider capping the number of guests per request/booking and reconsidering whether attendees (rather than only the organizer/team admins) should have this ability.

title: No validation of booking status or time before adding guests
body: After loading the booking the handler checks only permissions; it never verifies that the booking is still active. Guests can be added to CANCELLED or REJECTED bookings, and to bookings whose endTime is in the past (the UI even offers the action on past confirmed bookings via the Edit menu in BookingListItem). In those cases the handler inserts attendees and sends emails plus an ics with status CONFIRMED and method REQUEST for an event that is cancelled or already over, leaving attendees and calendars in a misleading state. The handler should reject cancelled/rejected (and probably past) bookings.

title: Adding guests to seated bookings bypasses seat tracking
body: For event types with seatsPerTimeSlot, attendees are supposed to be backed by BookingSeat reference rows; this handler inserts plain Attendee records via createMany without creating seat references and without checking remaining seat capacity. The occupied-seat count for the slot is therefore not incremented, so the slot can be overbooked beyond seatsPerTimeSlot, and the new attendee cannot be managed through seated-booking flows (e.g. cancelling an individual seat via seatReferenceUid). Either create the seat references and enforce capacity, or reject add-guests for seated event types.

title: Raw guest input passed to sendAddGuestsEmails instead of the filtered uniqueGuests
body: sendAddGuestsEmails decides which template each attendee receives via `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)`, but the handler passes the original `guests` array rather than `uniqueGuests`. If the request includes an address that already belongs to an existing attendee (which uniqueGuests deliberately filtered out, e.g. the organizer re-submitting an existing guest), that existing attendee is treated as 'new' and receives a full booking-confirmation email (AttendeeScheduledEmail) instead of the 'new guests added' notification.

title: Team members are never notified because evt.team is never populated
body: sendAddGuestsEmails contains a loop over `calendarEvent.team?.members` to send each team member an OrganizerAddGuestsEmail, but the CalendarEvent constructed in this handler has no `team` property, so that loop is dead code and team members of collective/round-robin events never receive the guests-added notification.

title: Add-guests emails ignore the event type's disableStandardEmails settings
body: Every neighboring sender in this file (sendLocationChangeEmails, sendRescheduledEmails, sendCancelledEmails, etc.) accepts eventTypeMetadata and skips host/attendee emails via eventTypeDisableHostEmail/eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail. sendAddGuestsEmails takes no metadata and the calling handler never reads eventType.metadata, so organizers who disabled standard emails for an event type still have 'guests added' emails sent to themselves, their team, and all attendees — violating a user-facing event-type setting.

title: Untranslated 'Remove email' tooltip string
body: The remove-button tooltip uses the hardcoded English string "Remove email" instead of t(...) with a key in the locale files (the component otherwise uses useLocale), so it renders in English for every locale and is not pickable by the translation tooling.

title: No tests for the new addGuests mutation
body: The PR introduces a new authenticated mutation with non-trivial authorization logic (organizer vs team admin/owner vs attendee), dedupe/blacklist filtering, calendar updates, and email fan-out, but adds no tests. Handler tests over the permission matrix and error paths would have caught regressions such as the && / || mix-up in isTeamAdminOrOwner and the wrong-credential EventManager construction.

title: Team permission check uses && instead of ||, rejecting team admins
body: The authorization check computes `isTeamAdminOrOwner = (await isTeamAdmin(user.id, teamId)) && (await isTeamOwner(user.id, teamId))`. isTeamAdmin already matches memberships with role ADMIN or OWNER, so AND-ing it with isTeamOwner makes the whole expression equivalent to "user is team owner". Team admins — whom the variable name and the feature intend to allow — will always fail this check and hit the FORBIDDEN branch, so they cannot add guests to team bookings. The `&&` should be `||`.

title: Any attendee can add guests, triggering organizer-branded emails to arbitrary addresses
body: The handler authorizes the request when `isAttendee` is true — any person whose email happens to be on the booking can call viewer.bookings.addGuests with arbitrary addresses. Each call sends an AttendeeScheduledEmail "from" the organizer (replyTo the organizer) to the new addresses plus a notification to every existing attendee. A malicious attendee can therefore spam third parties using the organizer's identity and the booking's legitimacy, with no consent from the organizer and no cap on guests per call. If attendee-initiated guest additions are intentional, this needs rate limiting and sending from the attendee's identity; otherwise the endpoint should be restricted to the organizer and team admins/owners.

title: Calendar update uses the requester's credentials, not the organizer's, after attendees are already written
body: `eventManager` is built from `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` — the person making the request — but the calendar event being updated lives on the organizer's calendar (booking.user, which is already fetched with credentials in the booking query but never used). When a team owner/admin or an attendee adds guests, EventManager.updateCalendarAttendees searches the requester's credentials for one matching booking.references, which is either missing (throws) or belongs to the wrong user. Because prisma.booking.update has already created the Attendee rows before this call and the call is not wrapped in error handling, the mutation then returns an error even though the guests were persisted: the user sees "unable to add guests", the organizer's calendar event is never updated with the new attendees, and retrying fails with "emails_must_be_unique_valid" because the attendees already exist. Use the organizer's credentials and make the flow failure-safe (e.g., update the calendar before committing, or handle errors so the user is not told the operation failed when it half-succeeded).

title: No check on booking status or date before adding guests
body: After loading the booking, the handler never checks booking.status or the booking time, so guests can be added to CANCELLED, REJECTED, PENDING or past bookings. This is reachable from the UI for past confirmed bookings (BookingListItem renders the Edit → "Additional guests" action for `isBookingInPast && isConfirmed`) and via direct API calls for cancelled/rejected ones. Adding a guest to a cancelled booking emails them an AttendeeScheduledEmail with a CONFIRMED ics for an event that no longer exists and permanently attaches attendees to a dead booking. Reject non-ACCEPTED and past bookings before creating attendees.

title: Guest dedupe and blacklist checks are case-sensitive
body: uniqueGuests filters with `guest === attendee.email` and `blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`. The blacklist entries are lowercased but the incoming guest string is not, so `Blocked@Example.com` bypasses BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS entirely. Likewise `Existing@Email.com` is not recognized as matching an existing attendee `existing@email.com`, so a duplicate Attendee row is created (the client-side uniqueness refine has the same case-sensitivity problem). Normalize case (and trim whitespace) on the input before comparing.

title: sendAddGuestsEmails ignores event-type settings that disable standard emails
body: Every other send* function in this file accepts eventTypeMetadata and skips host/attendee emails when eventTypeDisableHostEmail/eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail is set (event types can disable standard emails, e.g. for custom workflows/platform customers). sendAddGuestsEmails takes no metadata parameter and addGuests.handler doesn't pass one, so organizers and attendees of event types with standard emails disabled will still receive "Guests Added" and booking-confirmation emails whenever a guest is added, breaking that contract. Thread eventTypeMetadata through and honor the disable flags.

title: Adding guests to seated events bypasses seat reservation logic
body: For event types with seatsPerTimeSlot, attendees are supposed to be created together with a BookingSeat record (the handleSeats flow) so that seat availability is counted and the attendee can later cancel/reschedule their seat. This handler blindly creates plain Attendee rows via createMany for any event type, so for seated events the new guests consume no seat — the slot can be overbooked through the normal booking flow afterwards — and the guests have no seat reference for seat-based operations. The handler should either reject seated event types or route through the seat-booking logic.

title: New guests are stored with the organizer's timeZone and locale
body: guestsFullDetails sets `timeZone: organizer.timeZone` and `locale: organizer.locale` for every added guest. The AttendeeScheduledEmail sent to those guests renders the meeting time in the attendee's stored timezone — which is actually the organizer's — so guests in other timezones see a wrong local time presented as theirs, and the attendee record permanently carries the wrong timezone/locale (affecting reminders and future emails too). Consider storing a neutral value or making clear whose timezone is displayed.

title: No limit on number of guests per request
body: `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` has no .max(), and each call sends an email to every existing attendee plus every new guest, and performs a calendar update. A single request can add hundreds of guests, fanning out hundreds of emails and a large calendar payload — an abuse and performance footgun even for a legitimate organizer. Add a sane .max() on the array and consider a per-booking total guest limit.

title: No tests for the new addGuests mutation
body: The PR adds a new authenticated mutation that performs a non-trivial permission matrix (organizer vs team admin vs team owner vs attendee vs stranger), dedupes against existing attendees and a blacklist, writes Attendee rows, updates calendars and sends emails, but adds no unit or integration tests. The permission matrix, duplicate/blacklist filtering, seated-event handling and cancelled-booking behavior are exactly where this implementation has defects; tests covering those cases should be added before merging.

title: EventManager is built with the caller's credentials instead of the booking organizer's
body: The handler constructs the EventManager via `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials: await getUsersCredentials(ctx.user) })`, i.e. with the session user's credentials. But the endpoint explicitly allows callers who are not the organizer (team admins/owners and attendees). For those callers the organizer's calendar credential is not present, so `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` cannot update the calendar event that lives on the organizer's calendar — it will either throw (after the attendees were already persisted, and before any emails are sent, so the user sees an error toast even though the guests were added) or silently skip the update, leaving the new guests off the calendar event. Notably, the booking query already includes `user: { include: { credentials: true } }`, i.e. the organizer's credentials were fetched but never used, which strongly suggests they were the intended source. Use the booking organizer's credentials for the EventManager.

title: Team permission check uses && instead of ||, rejecting team admins
body: `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `(await isTeamAdmin(user.id, teamId)) && (await isTeamOwner(user.id, teamId))`. A membership has a single role, so an ADMIN who is not OWNER fails this check; and if `isTeamAdmin` already includes OWNER in its role filter, the AND reduces to 'owners only'. As the variable name and the UI (which offers 'Additional guests' to team admins viewing team bookings) imply, this should be an OR. Consequence: team admins who can see the booking on /bookings get a FORBIDDEN 'you_do_not_have_permission' error when adding guests.

title: Guests are persisted before the calendar update, with no rollback or error handling
body: The attendee rows are created via `prisma.booking.update(...)` and only afterwards `await eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` runs outside any try/catch. If the calendar call throws (expired credential, provider API error, no matching credential), the mutation returns an error even though the guests are already in the database: no notification emails are sent (that call comes later), and a retry fails with BAD_REQUEST 'emails_must_be_unique_valid' because the guests now exist. The booking ends up with guests that nobody was notified about and no way to re-trigger the notifications. Wrap the calendar/email side effects so a failure there doesn't masquerade as a failed guest add, or perform them before/atomically with the DB write.

title: No validation of booking status or time before adding guests
body: After fetching the booking, the handler never checks `booking.status` or whether the booking is in the past. The UI only shows the action for upcoming confirmed bookings, but the tRPC endpoint itself can be called directly: an attendee or team admin can add guests to a CANCELLED, REJECTED, or already-past booking. The handler will then create attendee records and send `AttendeeScheduledEmail` with a CONFIRMED-status ics REQUEST to arbitrary addresses for an event that is cancelled or over. Add a guard rejecting non-confirmed or past bookings.

title: Input schema enforces neither uniqueness within guests[] nor a maximum length
body: `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` only validates email format. The client dialog checks for duplicate emails, but the tRPC endpoint can be called directly with duplicates: the handler's filter only compares against existing booking attendees, so `createMany` inserts multiple Attendee rows with the same email for one booking, and each duplicate receives its own invitation email. The array is also unbounded, so a single request can fan out invitation emails (with event details and video link) to a very large number of arbitrary addresses. Add a uniqueness refine and a reasonable `.max(...)` to the schema.

title: Guest emails are compared case-sensitively and never normalized, bypassing the blacklist and duplicate checks
body: The dedup/blacklist filter uses raw string equality: `!booking.attendees.some((attendee) => guest === attendee.email)` and `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`. The blacklist entries are lowercased (`process.env.BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS.split(',').map(e => e.toLowerCase())`) but the incoming guest is not, so `Blocked@x.com` sails past a `blocked@x.com` blacklist entry. Likewise `John@x.com` is inserted as a second attendee when `john@x.com` is already on the booking. Normalize (lowercase/trim) each guest before the duplicate check, the blacklist check, and persistence.

title: Adding guests to seated event types bypasses seat capacity and seat records
body: For event types with `seatsPerTimeSlot`, attendees normally get BookingSeat/seat references and capacity is enforced. This handler inserts the new guests as plain Attendee rows via `createMany` with no seat bookkeeping and no capacity check, so a seated booking can be overbooked beyond `seatsPerTimeSlot`, and the added guests lack the seat references that seat-based flows (attendee reschedule/cancel via seatReferenceUid) rely on. Either reject seated bookings in this mutation or create proper seat records and enforce capacity.

title: Raw `guests` input (not `uniqueGuests`) is passed to sendAddGuestsEmails
body: `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` receives the original request input rather than the filtered `uniqueGuests`. In `sendAddGuestsEmails`, any attendee whose email appears in `newGuests` gets a full `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (a brand-new 'booking confirmed' email with ics REQUEST) instead of the 'guests added' notification. So if the request redundantly included an email that was filtered out because that person is already an attendee, that existing attendee is incorrectly emailed as if they had just booked. Pass `uniqueGuests`.

title: sendAddGuestsEmails ignores the event type's disableStandardEmails settings
body: Every other send function here (sendScheduledEmails, sendLocationChangeEmails, sendCancelledEmails, etc.) accepts `eventTypeMetadata` and honors `disableStandardEmails.all.host` / `.attendee`. `sendAddGuestsEmails` takes no metadata and unconditionally emails the organizer, team members, and all attendees, so organizers who explicitly disabled standard emails for an event type will still trigger these 'guests added' and scheduling emails. Thread the event type metadata through and gate host/attendee emails like the other functions.

title: Bookings without an owner user (dynamic bookings) crash with a 500
body: `prisma.user.findFirstOrThrow({ where: { id: booking.userId || 0 } })` throws Prisma's NotFound error for bookings where `userId` is null (e.g. dynamic collective bookings), surfacing as an unhandled INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR instead of a clean client error. This path is reachable: for such bookings `isOrganizer` is false but an attendee passes the `isAttendee` check, then the handler 500s. Handle the missing-organizer case explicitly.

title: Email failures are swallowed and reported as success
body: `try { await sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests) } catch (err) { console.log('Error sending AddGuestsEmails') }` discards the actual error (it's not logged) and lets the mutation return success, so the user sees a 'Guests added' toast even when none of the notification/invitation emails were sent. At minimum log the error object via the standard logger, and consider surfacing the partial failure to the caller.

title: isInvalidEmail flag is not reset on success, so a stale error banner reappears on reopen
body: The dialog component stays mounted (visibility is toggled via the `open` prop), so its state persists between opens. `onSuccess` resets `multiEmailValue` but never calls `setIsInvalidEmail(false)`. If a user triggers the 'Emails must be unique and valid' error, then fixes the input and submits successfully, the red error banner is still set and will be visible the next time the dialog is opened, above a fresh empty input. Reset `isInvalidEmail` in `onSuccess` (and ideally whenever the dialog closes).

title: No tests for the new addGuests mutation
body: The PR adds a new authenticated mutation with non-trivial authorization (organizer vs team admin vs team owner vs attendee vs stranger), input filtering (duplicates, blacklist), and side effects (calendar update, emails), but no tests. The permission bug alone (`isTeamAdmin && isTeamOwner` instead of an OR) and the duplicate-guest handling would have been caught by even a basic permission-matrix and input-validation test.

title: Reminders that never reach the Twilio call never get their retryCount incremented
body: The retry-count increment only happens inside `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)`. When a reminder fails before reaching `twilio.scheduleSMS` — e.g. the booking has no `smsReminderNumber` so `sendTo` is null, or the resolved message is empty — the guard fails, no SMS is attempted, and no retryCount increment happens. The reminder stays `scheduled: false` with retryCount 0, so it is re-fetched and fully reprocessed (template rendering, profile lookup, etc.) on every cron run until `scheduledDate` passes. That is exactly the repeated-rescheduling behavior this PR is meant to stop, and a missing/invalid phone number is the failure mode called out in the PR description. There should be an `else` that increments retryCount (or otherwise marks the reminder) so the two-strike deletion applies to these reminders too.

title: Unawaited-safe DB write inside catch can throw and abort the entire cron run
body: The catch block now performs `await prisma.workflowReminder.update(...)` without its own error handling. The try block itself contains prisma calls (`prisma.profile.findFirst`, the update marking a reminder scheduled, and the new else-branch increment), so a database error lands in this catch where the update is likely to throw again. Additionally, if the reminder row is deleted concurrently (e.g. by a booking-cancellation flow between the findMany at the top and this update), the update raises Prisma P2025 'record not found'. In both cases the exception propagates out of the handler: the request returns 500 and the for-loop aborts, so every reminder after the failing one is skipped for the run. Before this PR the catch only logged the error, so this is a new failure mode. Wrap the increment in a nested try/catch (and consider using `retryCount: { increment: 1 }`).

title: retryCount deletion branch is not scoped to SMS reminders
body: In the cleanup `deleteMany`, the new second OR branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` has no `method` (or `scheduled`) filter, so it matches every row in WorkflowReminder with retryCount > 1 — including EMAIL and WHATSAPP reminders. The first OR branch is explicitly limited to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`, showing the SMS-only intent of this cron, but the retryCount branch is table-wide. Today only this file writes retryCount so there is no immediate data loss, but retryCount is a column on the shared WorkflowReminder model; if any other reminder type ever sets it (e.g. a similar retry mechanism for email), this SMS cron would silently delete those reminders. The condition should be `AND: [{ method: WorkflowMethods.SMS }, { retryCount: { gt: 1 } }]` (and probably `scheduled: false`).

title: No tests cover the new retry increment and deletion threshold
body: The PR adds branching logic that permanently deletes data (retryCount > 1 cleanup) and increments retryCount on two different failure paths (scheduleSMS returning falsy, and exceptions), but no tests were added or updated. A regression here either leaves users receiving duplicate SMS attempts indefinitely or silently deletes legitimate reminders. At minimum the behavior 'failure increments retryCount once per run', 'reminder is deleted on the run after the second failure', and 'successful scheduling leaves retryCount untouched' should be covered.

title: retryCount update inside the catch block can throw and abort the whole cron run
body: The catch block now performs `await prisma.workflowReminder.update({ ... retryCount ... })` with no error handling of its own. If that update fails — for example the row was concurrently deleted by an overlapping cron run's `deleteMany` (Prisma P2025), or a transient DB error — the exception escapes the handler: every remaining reminder in `unscheduledReminders` is skipped and the cron invocation fails. Before this PR the catch block only logged, so a single failing reminder could never abort the rest of the batch. Worse, if the `update` inside the try (success or else branch) throws, the catch immediately attempts the same kind of update against the same row, so a likely failure is retried once and then propagates. The retryCount update in the catch should be wrapped in its own try/catch so the loop always continues.

title: Reminders skipped before the Twilio call never accumulate retryCount and keep getting rescheduled indefinitely
body: The retry counting only happens when `twilio.scheduleSMS` is actually invoked and returns falsy, or when an exception is thrown. If the reminder never reaches that call — e.g. `sendTo` is null because the booking has no `smsReminderNumber` (common for SMS_ATTENDEE workflows where the attendee gave no phone number), or `message` is empty — the `if (message?.length && ... && sendTo)` block is skipped entirely, so retryCount stays 0. Such reminders are never deleted by the new `retryCount > 1` cleanup and are re-fetched and re-processed on every cron run until their scheduledDate passes, which is exactly the endless-rescheduling problem this PR is meant to fix. Consider incrementing retryCount (or deleting the reminder outright when there is no recipient) in the path where sending is skipped.

title: retryCount update uses read-modify-write instead of an atomic increment
body: Both failure paths write `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` using the value read at the start of the run. Because the handler loops over many reminders with awaits, two cron executions can overlap and both read the same retryCount, then both write the same incremented value, losing an increment and allowing extra retry cycles before the reminder is deleted. Using Prisma's atomic `retryCount: { increment: 1 }` avoids the lost update and also removes the need to select retryCount just for the write.

title: retryCount cleanup in deleteMany is not scoped to SMS reminders
body: The new OR branch `retryCount: { gt: 1 }` deletes WorkflowReminder rows of any method, while the sibling branch — and this entire cron job — is explicitly SMS-only (`method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`). Today only this file writes retryCount, so the practical effect is identical, but the moment the email/WhatsApp reminder paths (which share the WorkflowReminder table, e.g. scheduleEmailReminders) start using retryCount, their reminders would be silently deleted by the SMS cron. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` to the retryCount branch to keep the cleanup scoped to what this job owns.

title: deleteMany now filters on unindexed retryCount on every cron run
body: WorkflowReminder's indexes cover `[method, scheduled, scheduledDate]` and `[cancelled, scheduledDate]`, but nothing covers `retryCount`. This `deleteMany` executes on every cron invocation, and the new `OR: [ ..., { retryCount: { gt: 1 } } ]` branch cannot use the existing indexes, so on a large WorkflowReminder table each run degrades into a scan. Consider adding an index that includes retryCount (or otherwise restructuring the cleanup) along with the migration.

title: Comment above deleteMany no longer describes the query
body: The comment still says "delete all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date", but the query now also deletes reminders whose retryCount has exceeded the retry limit regardless of their scheduledDate. The comment should be updated so future readers understand that reminders are removed after two failed scheduling attempts, not only when past due.

title: retryCount update inside catch can throw and abort the whole cron run
body: The new catch block performs `await prisma.workflowReminder.update(...)` without any protection. If the original error was a database connectivity problem, this update will fail too; and if the reminder row was deleted between the initial `findMany` and this update (e.g. the booking was cancelled and its workflow reminders removed while the cron was mid-batch), `update` throws P2025 because the record no longer exists. Because this throw happens inside the catch handler, it propagates out of the loop and out of `handler`: every remaining unscheduled reminder in the batch is skipped and the endpoint returns 500 instead of continuing. Previously the catch only logged, so one bad reminder could not take down the rest of the run. The same applies to the new `else` update at line 179 (inside the try): if it throws, the catch runs and its update throws again, escaping. Wrap the increment in its own try/catch (and/or use `updateMany`, which does not throw when the row is gone).

title: retryCount incremented via read-modify-write instead of atomic increment
body: Both new updates set `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` using the value read at the start of the run (lines 184 and 195). This is a read-modify-write: if two cron executions overlap (a long run processing many Twilio calls overlapping the next scheduled run), both can read the same value and one increment is lost, so a failing reminder is retried more than the intended two times before deletion, and the delete threshold (`retryCount > 1`) is reached later than designed. Prisma supports an atomic operator for this: `data: { retryCount: { increment: 1 } }`, which also removes the need to select `retryCount` in the initial query.

title: Retry-based deletion is not scoped to SMS reminders
body: In the `deleteMany`, the new second OR branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` has no `method` filter, unlike the sibling branch which is restricted to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`. This cron job only manages SMS reminders (its query, its Twilio scheduling, and the only code that increments `retryCount` are all SMS-specific), but as written it will delete any `WorkflowReminder` row of any method — EMAIL or WHATSAPP, with any scheduledDate — as soon as its `retryCount` exceeds 1. Today `retryCount` is only ever written by this handler so nothing else can reach that state, but the column is generic on the model and the query's target set is broader than what this job owns; any future writer of `retryCount` (e.g. retries for email reminders) would have those rows silently deleted by the SMS cron. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` to the retry branch.

title: No tests for the new retry/delete behavior
body: The PR changes cron behavior in three ways — incrementing `retryCount` on failure (both on a falsy `scheduleSMS` result and on a thrown error), and deleting reminders once `retryCount > 1` — but adds no tests. The deletion threshold (`gt: 1` = exactly two attempts) and the fact that a reminder that fails twice is never attempted a third time are exactly the kind of logic that regresses silently. At minimum, tests covering: first failure increments to 1 and reminder is kept, second failure increments to 2 and the next run deletes it, and a success after a failure still marks the reminder scheduled.

title: Public findMany() method removed without migrating callers
body: The class's only query-executing public method, `findMany(findManyArgs)` (which applied the auth/filter conditions and called `this.prisma.bookingTimeStatusDenormalized.findMany`), is deleted and replaced by `getBaseConditions()`, which merely returns a raw `Prisma.Sql` fragment that callers must embed in their own `$queryRaw`. This PR only changes the service and its test file, so any existing caller of `insightsBookingService.findMany(...)` (e.g., the insights tRPC router that lists bookings) will fail type-checking/compilation after this merges. Either keep a query-executing method on the service or update all callers in the same PR.

title: Caching behavior tests removed while caching logic remains in the service
body: The entire `describe("Caching", ...)` block (which verified that repeated calls to `getAuthorizationConditions()` and `getFilterConditions()` return the cached result) was deleted rather than ported to the new `Prisma.Sql` format, yet the service still implements caching via `cachedAuthConditions`/`cachedFilterConditions` (including the subtle `undefined`-vs-`null` sentinel logic for filter conditions). Coverage for a still-active code path was dropped; the caching tests should have been converted like the others instead of removed.

title: PR description misstates the scope of the change
body: The description says 'This PR updates the InsightsBookingService integration tests to work with the new Prisma.sql format that was previously converted in the service implementation', but the diff shows the service itself is converted in this PR — including a public API change (removal of `findMany`, changed return types of `getAuthorizationConditions`/`getFilterConditions` from `BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedWhereInput` to `Prisma.Sql`). Reviewers following the description and its checklist will focus on the test file and miss the riskiest part of the change (raw SQL authorization conditions and the API break) in the service.

title: getBaseConditions returns unparenthesized top-level OR fragments that break when composed with additional AND predicates
body: For org and team scopes, buildAuthorizationConditions returns a top-level OR expression (buildOrgAuthorizationCondition, lines 171-174, produces `(A) OR (B)`; buildTeamAuthorizationCondition, lines 204-207, likewise), and when there are no filters getBaseConditions returns that fragment verbatim via `return authConditions;` at line 75. The same problem exists for a lone eventTypeId filter, which is returned as `("eventTypeId" = $1) OR ("eventParentId" = $1)` without wrapping parentheses (lines 106, 119-122). The purpose of getBaseConditions() is to be embedded as the WHERE clause of larger raw queries; as soon as a caller appends `AND <predicate>` (e.g. a date-range or status filter, which insights queries typically add), SQL precedence turns `A OR B AND C` into `A OR (B AND C)`, so rows matching A are returned regardless of the appended predicate — silently wrong result sets and potentially data outside the intended filter. The OR-reduced fragments should be wrapped in parentheses before being returned.

title: Public findMany() removed with no replacement query path or caller migration
body: The PR deletes the service's only query-execution method, `findMany(findManyArgs)` (which merged caller-supplied where/select args with the authorization and filter conditions), and replaces it with `getBaseConditions()` returning a raw SQL fragment. No other files in the repo are changed, so any existing caller of `InsightsBookingService.findMany` — the old integration test was one — will fail to compile or lose functionality. If the service is already consumed elsewhere (e.g. insights tRPC handlers), those callers must be migrated to hand-written `$queryRaw` in the same PR; if it is not consumed yet, that should be stated. Verify all callers before merging.

title: Caching tests deleted while the caching logic remains in the service
body: The 'Caching' describe block, which asserted that repeated calls to getAuthorizationConditions() and getFilterConditions() return the cached conditions, was removed in this PR, but the service still implements caching via cachedAuthConditions/cachedFilterConditions (insightsBooking.ts lines 49-50 and 84-95). The caching path is now untested: a regression that drops the cache would go unnoticed and would silently re-run the membership/team database lookups on every call to these methods.

title: PR description misdescribes the change as a tests-only update
body: The description states the PR only updates the integration tests 'to work with the new Prisma.sql format that was previously converted in the service implementation', but the diff actually performs the service conversion itself (object notation → Prisma.sql) and removes the public findMany method. A reviewer following the description could skip reviewing the new authorization SQL in the service, even though the same description flags that area as HIGH RISK. The description should be corrected to cover the service changes.

title: toEqual comparisons against flat Prisma.sql literals fail because the service composes nested Sql
body: Prisma.sql does not flatten nested templates: when the service composes conditions with `Prisma.sql`(${acc}) OR (${condition})`` (the reduces in buildTeamAuthorizationCondition, buildOrgAuthorizationCondition, and buildFilterConditions), the inner Sql objects are stored as elements of the outer Sql's `values`, producing strings like `['(', ') OR (', ')']` with Sql instances in `values`. The new assertions build the expectation as one flat template literal (e.g. `Prisma.sql`(("teamId" = ${id}) AND ("isTeamBooking" = true)) OR (...)``), whose `strings`/`values` structure is completely different (flat strings, scalar values). `toEqual` performs structural deep equality, so these assertions fail even though both would serialize to identical SQL when executed. Affected assertions: team scope (line 295), org scope (line 332), and combined filters (line 429) — the suite this PR delivers will not pass (consistent with the PR description noting the tests were never successfully run). Fix by asserting on executed query results (as the getBaseConditions test does), building the expected Sql with the same composition, or comparing a flattened serialization instead of the raw Sql object.

title: Public findMany() removed without updating any consumers
body: The PR deletes `findMany(findManyArgs)`, previously the only data-access method on InsightsBookingService, and replaces it with `getBaseConditions()`, which returns a raw Prisma.Sql fragment that callers must embed into their own `$queryRaw` against the "BookingTimeStatusDenormalized" table. Only the service and its test file are changed in this PR, so any existing caller of `service.findMany(...)` (e.g. insights tRPC/router code) will fail to compile, and consumers now each need to hand-write the raw query. Verify that all consumers are migrated — either in this PR or a clearly stacked one — before merging.

title: getBaseConditions contains unreachable branches with a fail-open shape
body: `getAuthorizationConditions()` is typed and implemented to always return a non-null Prisma.Sql (it returns NOTHING_CONDITION `1=0` at worst), so in getBaseConditions the `else if (filterConditions) { return filterConditions; }` and final `else { return NOTHING_CONDITION; }` branches are dead code, and the `authConditions &&` check is always truthy. Beyond being dead code, the structure implies a fail-open path: if authorization conditions were ever able to be null (mirroring getFilterConditions' `Prisma.Sql | null` type), the method would return the filter conditions alone and silently drop the authorization predicate. Simplify the method to always AND the never-null auth conditions with the optional filter conditions so it cannot fail open.

title: Order-sensitive ANY array assertions rely on unordered DB queries
body: The org-scope assertion expects the Sql values arrays in an exact order — teamIds `[orgId, team.id, team2.id, team3.id]` (line 333) and userIds `[user.id, user2.id, user3.id]` (line 338) — but TeamRepository.findAllByParentId and MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds issue findMany queries with no ORDER BY, so Postgres row order is not guaranteed (e.g. after autovacuum or with different plans on a busy CI database). Deep equality on the embedded arrays is order-sensitive, making this test flaky. Sort the ids deterministically in the service, or assert on unordered sets / executed query results instead.

title: Caching tests removed while the service still implements caching
body: The PR deletes the entire "Caching" describe block ("should cache authorization conditions" / "should cache filter conditions"), which was the only coverage verifying that repeated calls to getAuthorizationConditions()/getFilterConditions() reuse the cached result instead of rebuilding (including re-querying memberships). The service still implements this behavior via cachedAuthConditions/cachedFilterConditions, so the conversion silently drops coverage of existing behavior. Re-add equivalent assertions using the new Sql format (e.g. asserting a build* method is only invoked once).

title: PR description/diagram claims the service was already converted and is unedited
body: The description's summary states the tests are updated to work with "the new Prisma.sql format that was previously converted in the service implementation", and the mermaid diagram marks `insightsBooking.ts` as "Context/No Edit" — but this diff is what converts the service to Prisma.sql and removes its public `findMany` method. This misrepresents the scope of the change to reviewers (the raw-SQL authorization logic is the risky part and is presented as untouched context). Update the summary and diagram so the service conversion is reviewed explicitly.

title: deleteCache success does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query, leaving stale cache status on screen
body: The deleteCache mutation's onSuccess only shows a toast and calls the optional onSuccess prop; unlike the disconnect mutation right below it (which invalidates utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars in onSettled), it never invalidates the connectedCalendars query. The query that supplies cacheUpdatedAt is configured with refetchOnWindowFocus: false, so in any usage of SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper where the optional onChanged/onSuccess callback is not provided, the dropdown will keep showing "Cache Status / Last updated: <timestamp>" and the "Delete cached data" action for cache rows that were just deleted, until a full page reload. Add an onSettled invalidation of utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars to deleteCacheMutation so the cache status disappears after deletion.

title: Cache timestamp is hardcoded to en-US formatting, ignoring the user's locale
body: The 'cache_last_updated' timestamp is formatted with new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" }). Every user, regardless of their configured locale, will see US-style dates (e.g. 7/15/25, 3:04 PM), which is confusing for locales that use DD/MM/YYYY or 24-hour times. Use the user's locale (e.g. navigator.language or the i18n locale from useLocale) instead of the hardcoded "en-US" string.

title: Handler throws a generic Error, surfacing as HTTP 500 instead of 404/403
body: When the credential does not exist or belongs to another user, deleteCacheHandler does `throw new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. In tRPC a plain Error is reported to the client as INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (HTTP 500), which is wrong for a not-found/authorization failure and will also pollute server error monitoring. The codebase convention is to throw a TRPCError with an explicit code, e.g. `new TRPCError({ code: "NOT_FOUND", message: ... })` or FORBIDDEN, so clients get the correct status code.

title: No tests for the new deleteCache mutation or the cache-status repository method
body: This PR adds a data-deletion endpoint (viewer.calendars.deleteCache) plus CalendarCacheRepository.getCacheStatusByCredentialIds, but no automated tests. The important behavior to lock down is the authorization check: a user must not be able to delete CalendarCache rows for a credentialId owned by another user (the handler only checks prisma.credential.findFirst({ id, userId })), and the not-found path should raise the expected error. A regression here would silently let one user wipe another user's availability cache. Add handler tests covering the owner, non-owner, and missing-credential cases.

title: updateManyByCredentialId adds an extra DB write on the webhook hot path for a value nothing reads
body: fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache now ends with SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {}), which updates (and bumps @updatedAt on) every SelectedCalendar row for the credential. fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache runs on every Google Calendar webhook notification and cache repopulation, so this adds a write query per webhook event. Per the PR's own notes, SelectedCalendar.updatedAt is not displayed or consumed anywhere in the frontend — the UI uses CalendarCache.updatedAt — so this write buys nothing and, worse, makes SelectedCalendar.updatedAt meaningless as a staleness signal for any future consumer. Consider removing it until there is an actual reader.

title: sed -i '' syntax is macOS-only and fails on GNU/Linux
body: The script updates GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL with `sed -i '' -E "s|...|..." "$ENV_FILE"`. The `-i ''` form (separate empty-string argument for the backup suffix) is BSD/macOS-only; on GNU sed (Linux dev machines, CI containers) the empty string is parsed as a filename and the command fails with "sed: can't read : No such file or directory", so the .env file is never updated. Use a portable form (e.g. `sed -i.bak -E ... && rm -f "$ENV_FILE.bak"`) or detect the platform.

title: ENV_FILE="../.env" resolves relative to the caller's working directory and can write outside the repo
body: The script hardcodes ENV_FILE="../.env", which is only correct when the script is invoked from inside the scripts/ directory. A developer running `bash scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh` from the repository root (the natural way to run it) will have ../.env resolve to the parent directory of the checkout; the script then either edits an unrelated .env there or, per its own fallback, creates a brand-new .env outside the repository containing GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL. Resolve the path relative to the script's own location instead (e.g. ENV_FILE="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)/.env").

title: deleteCache mutation never invalidates connectedCalendars, leaving stale cache status in the UI
body: The `deleteCacheMutation` only calls the optional `onSuccess` prop on success. Unlike the `disconnectMutation` in the same file (which invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` and `viewer.apps.integrations` in `onSettled`), it does not invalidate `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. The `cacheUpdatedAt` value shown in this dropdown comes from that query, so after a successful cache deletion the dropdown continues to display 'Last updated: <old timestamp>' and keeps offering 'Delete cached data' until something else triggers a refetch. In usages where the parent does not pass `onChanged`/`onSuccess` (the prop is optional), the UI never refreshes at all. Fix: invalidate `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` in `onSettled`/`onSuccess` of the deleteCache mutation, mirroring the disconnect mutation.

title: Handler instantiates CalendarCacheRepository directly, bypassing the calendar-cache feature flag
body: The handler does `new CalendarCacheRepository()` and calls `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` unconditionally. The established pattern in this codebase is `CalendarCache.init(null)`, which returns `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` when the `calendar-cache` feature flag is disabled. Bypassing that means every `connectedCalendars` query (a hot settings-page query) now issues an extra `calendarCache.groupBy` against the database even when the feature is globally disabled, and it breaks the repository abstraction the mock exists for. Use `CalendarCache.init(null)` (or gate the enrichment on the feature flag) instead.
