title: getCacheStatusByCredentialIds reports status for expired cache rows that will never be served
body: `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups all `CalendarCache` rows by credentialId and returns `max(updatedAt)` with no `expiresAt` filter. `getCachedAvailability` only serves rows with `expiresAt >= now()` (30-day TTL), but expired rows are never deleted, so once a cache entry expires the UI will still show 'Cache Status / Last updated: <date>' and offer 'Delete cached data' for a cache that is effectively dead and will never be used. The status query should filter (or at least surface) expired entries, e.g. `where: { credentialId: { in: credentialIds }, expiresAt: { gte: new Date() } }`.

title: fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache now writes to SelectedCalendar on the webhook hot path for a value nothing reads
body: The added `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` runs on every Google webhook-driven cache refresh and updates every SelectedCalendar row for the credential (including calendars/event types whose cache was not part of this refresh) purely to bump `updatedAt`. Per the PR's own notes, `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` is not displayed anywhere — the frontend reads `cacheUpdatedAt` from `CalendarCache`. This is a dead database write on a high-frequency path; it should be removed rather than merged as-is.

title: Access-denied path throws a generic Error, surfacing as HTTP 500 instead of 404
body: When the credential does not exist or belongs to another user, the handler does `throw new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. tRPC converts non-`TRPCError` throws into `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR` (500), so a client requesting a foreign or nonexistent credentialId gets a server-error response (and a Sentry-eligible log) instead of a clean `NOT_FOUND`/`FORBIDDEN`. Throw `new TRPCError({ code: "NOT_FOUND", ... })` (or FORBIDDEN) as is convention elsewhere in the codebase.

title: Dev script writes GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL to the wrong env file and uses macOS-only sed syntax
body: Two portability/correctness problems in this helper script: (1) `ENV_FILE="../.env"` is resolved relative to the caller's working directory, not the script location — run from the repo root it points outside the repository, and run from `scripts/` it points at the repo-root `.env`, whereas the webapp reads `apps/web/.env`, so the webhook URL will silently not take effect; it should be derived from the script's own directory. (2) `sed -i '' -E ...` (line 68) is BSD/macOS syntax and fails on GNU sed (Linux) with "can't read : No such file or directory", so the script breaks for Linux developers.

title: Cache timestamp is always formatted with hardcoded "en-US" locale
body: The 'Last updated' timestamp uses `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" })`. Cal.com is localized into many languages and the surrounding label is translated via `t()`, but the date/time itself will always render in US format (e.g. MM/DD/YY, 12-hour clock) regardless of the viewer's locale. Use the locale from `useLocale()` (or `dayjs` with the user's locale/timezone as elsewhere in the app) instead of the hardcoded "en-US".

title: No tests for the new deleteCache mutation or the cache-status enrichment of connectedCalendars
body: The PR adds a user-facing destructive mutation (`deleteCache`, including its credential-ownership check) and changes the response shape of `connectedCalendars` (new `cacheUpdatedAt` field backed by a new repository query), but adds no automated tests. At minimum, `deleteCacheHandler` should be covered for the ownership check (cannot delete another user's cache) and the happy path, and the `connectedCalendarsHandler` enrichment should be covered (including the existing-handler unit tests, which may need the `CalendarCacheRepository` mocked now that it runs an extra `groupBy`). The PR's own checklist relies entirely on manual end-to-end testing, which the notes admit was not possible locally.

title: deleteCache mutation never invalidates the connectedCalendars query, leaving stale cache status in the UI
body: In CredentialActionsDropdown, the deleteCache mutation's onSuccess only shows a toast and calls the optional onSuccess prop; unlike the disconnect mutation in the same component (lines 61-64), it never invalidates trpc.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars. The cacheUpdatedAt value driving the 'Cache Status / Last updated' display comes from that query, so after a user deletes the cache the dropdown continues to show the old timestamp and the 'Delete cached data' option until something else happens to refetch — making it look as if the deletion failed. Add an invalidation of viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars (e.g. in onSettled) for the deleteCache mutation, as was done for disconnect.

title: Migration backfills updatedAt with NOW() for all existing rows and forces a full table rewrite
body: ALTER TABLE "CalendarCache" ADD COLUMN "updatedAt" TIMESTAMP(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW() has two problems. (1) Because NOW() is not a constant default, PostgreSQL must rewrite the entire CalendarCache table to add the column, holding an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the duration — on a large/busy cache table this can block writes during deployment. (2) Every pre-existing row gets updatedAt = migration time, so the new UI will display 'Last updated: <deploy time>' for all existing caches, which is misleading until each row is next written. Safer approach: add the column nullable (metadata-only operation), backfill in batches or leave legacy rows null, and hide the timestamp in the UI when it is null.

title: Handler throws plain Error, producing a 500 instead of a 404/403
body: When the credential doesn't exist or belongs to another user, deleteCacheHandler throws a generic `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. In tRPC, a non-TRPCError is converted to an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (HTTP 500) and is typically reported to error monitoring as a server bug, rather than a client-facing NOT_FOUND/FORBIDDEN. Throw `new TRPCError({ code: "NOT_FOUND" })` instead.

title: Handler bypasses the calendar-cache feature flag by instantiating the concrete repository
body: connectedCalendarsHandler constructs `new CalendarCacheRepository()` directly instead of using the feature-flag-aware factory (CalendarCache.init(...)), which returns CalendarCacheRepositoryMock when the calendar-cache feature is disabled. This PR even adds getCacheStatusByCredentialIds to the mock (returning []), but that path can never be reached from this handler. Consequence: users/teams without the calendar-cache feature still get cache status and delete actions surfaced (from any stale rows), and every connectedCalendars request pays the extra groupBy query even when the feature is turned off.

title: Cache status query does not exclude expired cache rows
body: getCacheStatusByCredentialIds groups over all CalendarCache rows for the given credentials without filtering on expiresAt, while the read path (getCachedAvailability) only serves rows with expiresAt >= now(). The UI can therefore show 'Cache Status: Last updated X' and offer 'Delete cached data' for a cache that has already expired and is never served; after deletion nothing visibly changes for the user. Apply the same expiresAt filter (or surface the expiry state in the UI) so status matches what is actually usable.

title: Dead write: SelectedCalendar.updatedAt is bumped on every webhook cache refresh but never read
body: fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache — which runs on every Google webhook-driven cache refresh — now executes SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {}), an UPDATE touching every SelectedCalendar row for the credential, solely to bump SelectedCalendar.updatedAt. Per the PR's own notes this value is not displayed anywhere (the frontend uses cacheUpdatedAt from CalendarCache), and nothing else in the diff reads it; the change also forced extra selected fields in UserRepository.findUnlockedUserForSession and the UserWithCalendars type to carry an unused value. This is a pure extra write on a hot webhook path and should be removed or deferred until a consumer exists.

title: sed -i '' is macOS-only; script fails on GNU/Linux
body: `sed -i '' -E "s|^GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=.*|...|"` uses BSD/macOS sed syntax. With GNU sed (Linux), `-i` does not take a separate empty suffix argument, so the command misparses the arguments and fails ('can't read s|...|'), meaning GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL is never updated on Linux dev machines. Use a portable approach (write to a temp file and mv, or detect the sed flavor).

title: ENV_FILE="../.env" is resolved relative to the caller's CWD, not the script location
body: ENV_FILE is a relative path, so its target depends on where the script is invoked from. Running it from the repo root (./scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh) writes GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL to a .env file in the repository's parent directory (creating a stray file via the touch fallback) and never updates the project's actual .env. Resolve the env file path from the script's own directory (e.g. using BASH_SOURCE) so it works regardless of the invocation directory.

title: Cache timestamp is hardcoded to en-US formatting
body: The 'Last updated' timestamp is rendered with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" })`, forcing US date/time formatting on all users regardless of their configured locale, in a product that is otherwise fully localized (the surrounding labels go through t()). Use the user's locale (e.g. navigator.language or dayjs with the user's locale) so the timestamp respects localization.

title: No tests for the new cache-status repository method or the deleteCache authorization
body: The PR adds user-facing destructive behavior with no test coverage: getCacheStatusByCredentialIds (grouping/max(updatedAt) semantics, empty credentialIds input, expired rows) and deleteCacheHandler's authorization rule (a user must not be able to delete another user's calendar cache by supplying an arbitrary credentialId). Only the mock repository was updated; the real implementation and the new tRPC handler have no tests, and the PR description itself notes end-to-end testing was not performed.

title: One failing SendGrid cancellation aborts the whole batch and silently drops the queued DB deletes
body: In the new cancellation block of the cron handler, the try/catch wraps the entire `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop, and the `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` promises collected in `workflowRemindersToDelete` are only executed by a single `await Promise.all(...)` after the loop. A PrismaPromise does not run unless it is awaited, so if `client.request(...)` throws for any reminder (e.g. SendGrid returns 404 for an unknown or already-cancelled batch_id, or a transient 5xx), then: (a) every reminder after the failing one is skipped for this run, and (b) all delete queries gathered so far are discarded — rows whose SendGrid cancellation already succeeded stay in the DB with `cancelled: true` and will be cancelled again on the next run. Worse, a persistently failing row is never deleted, so it is retried on every cron run and aborts the loop at the same point, blocking all later reminders. Because the cancellation window is only 1 hour (~4 cron runs), blocked reminders can miss their window and their emails will be sent for cancelled bookings — the exact bug this PR fixes. The try/catch should be inside the loop (per reminder), and each reminder's row should be deleted right after its own successful SendGrid cancel.

title: Marking reminders as cancelled is fire-and-forget (previously the reminder deletion was awaited)
body: The new code calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...)` inside nested `forEach` loops without awaiting the returned promises. Before this PR, the workflowReminder rows were removed via `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany(...)` promises that were awaited in `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(remindersToDelete))`. Now the entire fix depends on a DB write (`cancelled: true`) that is never awaited: in a serverless environment (Next.js API route on Vercel) the response can be sent and the invocation frozen before the update commits, so reminders intermittently never get flagged and the emails for cancelled bookings are still sent. Errors are also invisible since the inner functions swallow them. The cancel calls should be collected and awaited (e.g. `await Promise.all(...)`) before the handler returns.

title: requestReschedule marks reminders cancelled without awaiting, a regression from the previously awaited deletion
body: In the `requestReschedule` mutation the old code pushed `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany(...)` promises into `remindersToDelete` and awaited them with `await Promise.all(remindersToDelete)`. The new code calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` (which performs the critical `cancelled: true` update) and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...)` inside a `forEach` without awaiting any of the promises. In a serverless tRPC invocation the response can complete and the process freeze before these DB updates finish, so the reminders for the rescheduled booking may never be marked cancelled and the workflow emails will still go out. The calls should be awaited before the mutation continues/returns.

title: immediateDelete path cancels in SendGrid but leaves the WorkflowReminder row untouched (not deleted, not marked cancelled)
body: When `immediateDelete` is true and `referenceId` is set, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` POSTs the cancel to SendGrid and returns without deleting or updating the DB row. For the caller in `handleNewBooking.ts` (reschedule, line 968) the old booking is kept (status CANCELLED), so its reminder rows linger with `scheduled: true` and `cancelled: null` until their scheduledDate passes (only then does the cron's first deleteMany remove them). Two concrete consequences: (1) the SendGrid cancellation is issued immediately even when the email is scheduled up to 72 hours out, so the pending cancellation sits in SendGrid for days — this re-introduces the accumulation toward SendGrid's 100 pending-cancellation cap that this PR identifies as the root cause, via repeated reschedules (and via workflow/step deletions which use the same path); (2) when the `requestReschedule` tRPC flow ran first, the row still has `cancelled: true` from that flow, so the cron will POST a second cancellation for the same SendGrid batch that handleNewBooking already cancelled. After a successful immediate cancel the row should be deleted (mirroring `deleteScheduledSMSReminder`), or the reschedule path should use the `cancelled`-flag flow like the others.

title: Cancellation of the old booking's workflow reminders is fire-and-forget and the surrounding try/catch cannot catch their errors
body: The new block `originalRescheduledBooking.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(...); deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...); })` never awaits the async functions it calls, and the `try/catch` around the `forEach` can therefore never catch failures from them (it only looks protective). Since these are the only calls that cancel the previous booking's reminders on reschedule, an unawaited invocation in a serverless request can be cut short when the response is sent, meaning the SendGrid cancellation (and the DB row deletion for SMS / the eventual cleanup for email) never happens and the old booking's reminder emails are still sent — the exact issue this PR is meant to fix. The promises should be collected and awaited inside the try block.

title: One failing SendGrid cancel aborts the entire cancellation batch for the cron run
body: The new cancellation block wraps the whole for-loop in a single try/catch. If client.request throws for any one reminder (transient SendGrid error, invalid/already-cancelled batch_id, or SendGrid rejecting a cancel that is too close to the scheduled send time), execution jumps straight to the catch: (a) every remaining reminder in remindersToCancel is skipped for that run, and (b) none of the prisma.workflowReminder.delete calls collected so far actually execute, because they are only awaited after the loop via Promise.all and Prisma promises are lazy (they don't run until awaited). On the next cron run the same rows are re-fetched (still cancelled=true) and the loop aborts again at the same poisoned row, so a single bad reminder can block cancellation of all pending cancelled reminders until its own scheduledDate passes — at which point the first deleteMany in this handler silently drops the row and the email has already been sent. Each loop iteration needs its own try/catch (and each row should be deleted right after its own successful cancel) so one failure doesn't stall the queue.

title: Deferred-only cancellation still misses reminders cancelled close to their send time
body: With this PR, cancellation of scheduled emails happens exclusively in this cron job, which runs every 15 minutes and only cancels reminders whose scheduledDate is within the next hour. If a booking is cancelled shortly before a reminder's send time, the next cron run may not happen before SendGrid sends the email, and SendGrid does not allow changing the status of a scheduled send that is about to go out — so the reminder is delivered for a cancelled booking even though the cancellation was recorded in time. Consider using the immediate path (deleteScheduledEmailReminder with immediateDelete=true, already used in the reschedule flow) for reminders whose scheduledDate is near (e.g. within the next hour), and deferring only far-future cancellations to the cron. That still avoids the 100-pending-cancellations limit while closing the last-minute gap.

title: Reminder cancellation calls in booking-cancel handler are fire-and-forget
body: deleteScheduledEmailReminder / deleteScheduledSMSReminder are invoked without await inside the forEach. These calls perform the only state change that now prevents the reminders from being sent: setting cancelled=true (which the cron job relies on to cancel the SendGrid scheduled send) and, for SMS, the Twilio cancel plus DB delete. The previous version of this function collected the reminder deletions and awaited them via Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes)); now nothing reminder-related is awaited. On a serverless platform the invocation can be frozen once the response is sent, before these floating promises finish — the cancelled flag is then never persisted, the cron never cancels the SendGrid scheduled send, and the reminder email is still delivered, i.e. the exact bug this PR fixes persists intermittently. Collect the promises and await them before returning.

title: Newly added reschedule reminder-cancellation is fire-and-forget
body: In the reschedule flow, the loop that cancels the original booking's workflow reminders calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder(..., true) and deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...) without awaiting them, and the surrounding try/catch cannot observe their completion (the functions also swallow their own errors). If the serverless invocation is frozen after the response is sent before these promises finish, the original booking's SendGrid batches are never cancelled while the new booking's reminders are scheduled — so both old and new reminders fire, the duplicate-reminder bug for rescheduled bookings this PR is meant to fix. Await these calls.

title: immediateDelete path neither deletes nor flags the reminder row and has no retry on failure
body: When immediateDelete is true (used by the reschedule flow in handleNewBooking and by workflow/step deletion in the workflows router), deleteScheduledEmailReminder only posts the cancel to SendGrid and returns — it never deletes the WorkflowReminder row and never sets cancelled=true. Two consequences: (1) if the SendGrid request fails, the catch only logs and nothing retries — the row keeps scheduled=true and cancelled=null, so the old booking's reminder email is still sent (duplicates after a reschedule); (2) in the reschedule flow the stale rows (scheduled=true, referenceId set, cancelled=null) linger in the DB until the cron's past-date deleteMany removes them days later, unlike every other cancellation path which deletes or flags the row. Consider deleting the row (or marking it cancelled as a fallback) even in the immediate path, so a failed SendGrid call is retried by the cron instead of being silently lost.

title: requestReschedule: reminder cancellation no longer awaited
body: This handler previously awaited the reminder cleanup via `await Promise.all(remindersToDelete)`; the refactor removed that and now calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder / deleteScheduledSMSReminder without await inside forEach. The cancelled flag / row deletion these calls perform is the only thing preventing reminders for the cancelled booking from being sent, so for reliability they should be collected and awaited rather than left floating in a serverless handler.

title: WorkflowReminder row is leaked when Twilio cancel fails
body: In deleteScheduledSMSReminder, if twilio.cancelSMS(referenceId) throws (transient error, or the message was already sent), the catch skips the prisma.workflowReminder.delete call. The row is then left behind with scheduled=true and cancelled unset, and — unlike the email path, which flags rows for the cron to retry — nothing ever retries SMS cancellation, so the row leaks permanently and, for transient Twilio failures, the SMS is still delivered for a cancelled booking. Previously the callers deleted these rows in an awaited Promise.all regardless of the Twilio result. Delete the row even when the Twilio cancel fails (or add a retry path).

title: Prisma import is no longer used
body: The refactor removed all remaining uses of the Prisma namespace in this file (the deleted code was the last place referencing Prisma.BatchPayload), but the import was kept and even changed from `import type` to a value import. `Prisma` is now an unused import in this module (PrismaPromise is still used), which the repo's lint rules (no-unused-vars) will flag.

title: No tests for the reworked reminder-cancellation pipeline
body: This is the second attempt to fix reminders being sent for cancelled/rescheduled bookings — the first fix silently failed in production for an extended period — yet the PR adds no tests covering the new mechanism: setting cancelled=true on cancel/reschedule, the cron cancellation loop (including its all-or-nothing failure behavior when a SendGrid request fails), and the reschedule cancellation in handleNewBooking. Regression coverage around handleCancelBooking and scheduleEmailReminders would materially reduce the risk of another silent failure of this fix.

title: SendGrid client is never authenticated in the cron route, so the new cancellation calls fail silently
body: This module only calls `sgMail.setApiKey(sendgridAPIKey)` (line 19); the `@sendgrid/client` default export used by the new cancellation block (`client.request` POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends at line 57) is never given an API key here. `sgMail` uses its own internal client instance, so setting the key on sgMail does not configure the exported `client` singleton, and in a per-route/serverless deployment the `client.setApiKey()` done at module load in emailReminderManager.ts does not apply to this route's module instance. The cancellation requests will go out without a valid Authorization header and fail (401); the surrounding try/catch only logs the error, so no reminders are actually cancelled and the bug this PR fixes silently persists. (The pre-existing `/v3/mail/batch` call at line 188 in the same file has the same problem.) Add `client.setApiKey(sendgridAPIKey)` next to the sgMail one.

title: One failing SendGrid cancel aborts cancellation of all remaining reminders and poisons every future cron run
body: The new cancellation block wraps the entire `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop in a single try/catch. If `client.request` throws for any one reminder (e.g., SendGrid returns 404 for an unknown/expired batch_id, a transient 5xx, or a rate limit), every reminder after it in the list is skipped for that run, and the collected `prisma.workflowReminder.delete` promises are never executed — Prisma promises are lazy and only run when awaited, and the `await Promise.all(workflowRemindersToDelete)` after the loop is skipped when the loop throws. Because the failing row is never deleted or otherwise marked as handled, it is re-fetched on the next cron run 15 minutes later and aborts the loop again. A single persistently failing reminder can therefore block all cancellations indefinitely, so reminder emails for cancelled bookings keep being sent — the exact bug this PR is meant to fix. Each iteration (SendGrid cancel + row delete) needs its own try/catch so one failure doesn't poison the batch.

title: Reminder cancellation calls are fire-and-forget; the cancelled flag may never be written before the response is returned
body: The per-reminder cancellation calls (`deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` here and the SMS equivalent) are invoked inside `forEach` without await and their promises are never collected. The DB update that sets `cancelled: true` — the flag the cron job relies on to actually cancel the SendGrid send — is therefore not guaranteed to complete before the API handler returns; on serverless platforms the invocation can be frozen once the response is sent, the flag is never written, and the reminder email is still sent. The pre-change code awaited the reminder row deletions via `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(remindersToDelete))`; the new code awaits nothing reminder-related. The same un-awaited pattern exists in handleNewBooking.ts (reschedule path, ~line 968), trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx requestReschedule (~line 490) and trpc/server/routers/viewer/workflows.tsx (~lines 214, 378, 521, 576). Collect these promises and await them (with per-item error handling) before returning.

title: immediateDelete path cancels in SendGrid immediately and leaves stale rows, re-introducing the 100-pending-cancellations root cause
body: The new `immediateDelete` branch of `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` cancels the SendGrid scheduled send right away but neither deletes the WorkflowReminder row nor sets `cancelled`, and it is used by the reschedule flow (handleNewBooking.ts line 968) and by workflow/step deletion (workflows.tsx lines 214 and 521). Cancelling immediately re-creates the root cause described in this PR: SendGrid keeps each pending cancellation until the original send date and caps pending cancellations at 100, so a burst of reschedules or workflow edits/deletions can exhaust the quota — after which the cron's deferred cancellations also start failing and cancelled-booking reminder emails go out again. Additionally the leftover row (scheduled=true, cancelled=null) lingers until the cron's past-date cleanup removes it, and if the same booking is cancelled later the same batch_id gets cancelled a second time. These paths should either use the deferred `cancelled` flag like the cancel-booking path, or delete the row after the immediate cancel.

title: WorkflowReminder row is left behind when Twilio cancellation fails
body: In `deleteScheduledSMSReminder`, the row delete happens after `await twilio.cancelSMS(referenceId)` inside the same try block; if the Twilio call throws, execution jumps to the catch and the WorkflowReminder row is never deleted. Unlike email reminders, no cron cleanup ever deletes SMS-method rows, so the stale row (scheduled=true) stays in the database indefinitely. Previously the callers deleted reminder rows in a separate awaited deleteMany regardless of the Twilio outcome. Delete the row in a finally block (or otherwise independently of the Twilio call's success).

title: No tests cover the new cancel-flag and deferred cron cancellation flow
body: The PR reworks reminder cancellation end to end (new `cancelled` column, flag-on-cancel instead of immediate SendGrid cancellation, cron-based cancellation within a 1-hour window, immediate cancellation for the reschedule and workflow-delete paths) but adds no tests for any of it: nothing verifies that cancelling a booking flags its email reminders and removes unscheduled ones, that the cron cancels and deletes flagged reminders inside the window while leaving later ones alone, or that the reschedule path cancels the old booking's reminders. The previous fix for this same bug (#6991) was wrong and shipped to production; without regression coverage on this flow the same class of bug can ship again.

title: Dynamic imports are evaluated eagerly at module load, so nothing is actually lazy-loaded
body: Each value in the appStore map is now a promise created when this module is evaluated (e.g. `applecalendar: import("./applecalendar")`). `import()` begins loading the target module immediately, so all 28 app packages are still fetched/parsed as soon as anything imports `@calcom/app-store` — the loading is not deferred to first use, which defeats the stated purpose of the PR. To get real lazy loading the values must be thunks, e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`, with call sites doing `await appStore[key]()`. Additionally, these module-scope promises float until a caller awaits them: if one of the dynamic imports ever rejects (failed/missing chunk) and that app key is never awaited, Node raises an unhandled promise rejection, which terminates the process by default on Node >= 15.

title: requestReschedule: calendar deletions are now fire-and-forget behind an un-awaited dynamic import
body: In the `requestReschedule` mutation the PR changed the booking-reference cleanup loop from a synchronous `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach((bookingRef) => { const calendar = getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...); })` to `forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); ... })`. `forEach` does not await async callbacks and nothing else awaits them, and there is no surrounding try/catch. Before this change `calendar.deleteEvent(...)` was invoked synchronously, so the provider API calls were in flight before the mutation sent the reschedule email and returned; now each callback suspends at `await getCalendar(...)` (the dynamic import) and the deletion only starts later, possibly after the response has been sent — on serverless platforms the function can be frozen before `deleteEvent` ever runs, leaving stale events on the organizer's calendar. Failures inside the callback (import or deleteEvent rejection) become unhandled promise rejections instead of surfaced errors. Fix by awaiting the work: `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))`.

title: Recurring-cancel path: awaiting getCalendar inside fire-and-forget forEach defers deleteEvent past the end of the request
body: In the branch that cancels all remaining occurrences of a recurring event, the code does `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... await calendar?.deleteEvent(uid, evt, externalCalendarId); ... })`. The `await getCalendar(...)` added by this PR makes each callback suspend on the dynamic import before `deleteEvent` is ever invoked; previously `getCalendar` was synchronous, so every `deleteEvent` HTTP call was started synchronously while the forEach ran. Nothing awaits the forEach callbacks, and the pushes into `apiDeletes` happen only after those callbacks resume — i.e. after the handler already executed `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` (which snapshots the array) and returned success. The net effect is that deleting the calendar events for all future occurrences of a cancelled recurring booking may never start before the request completes (and may never run at all on serverless), leaving cancelled occurrences on users' calendars. Collect the promises (e.g. with `map`) and include them in the final `Promise.all`.

title: forEach made async: errors escape the surrounding try/catch and deletions are no longer started before returning
body: The PR changed `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach((bookingRef) => { const calendar = getCalendar(...); ... })` to `forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); ... })`. Because `forEach` ignores the promises returned by async callbacks, (1) the `try/catch` wrapped around this loop no longer catches anything — a rejection from `getCalendar` (dynamic import) or from `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` becomes an unhandled promise rejection (fatal by default on Node >= 15) instead of being logged by the catch block; and (2) `deleteEvent` is no longer invoked synchronously, so the function can send the reschedule email and return `true` before the calendar deletion has even started, which on serverless deployments means it may never run. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))` so the work completes and errors remain observable.

title: forEach made async: errors escape the surrounding try/catch and deletions are no longer started before returning
body: The PR changed `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach((bookingRef) => { const calendar = getCalendar(...); ... })` to `forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); ... })`. Because `forEach` ignores the promises returned by async callbacks, (1) the `try/catch` wrapped around this loop no longer catches anything — a rejection from `getCalendar` (dynamic import) or from `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` becomes an unhandled promise rejection (fatal by default on Node >= 15) instead of being logged by the catch block; and (2) `deleteEvent` is no longer invoked synchronously, so the function can send the reschedule email and return `true` before the calendar deletion has even started, which on serverless deployments means it may never run. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))` so the work completes and errors remain observable.

title: Async forEach callback makes the surrounding try/catch dead and turns deletion failures into unhandled rejections
body: The callback passed to `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach` was changed to `async` so it can `await getCalendar(...)`, but `forEach` does not collect or return the promises produced by an async callback. The `try { ... } catch` block wrapping the loop (lines 124–139) can therefore no longer catch anything: any synchronous throw that the catch previously handled (e.g. a CalendarService constructor error from `new CalendarService(credential)` inside `getCalendar`) and any rejection from the dynamic import, `calendar.deleteEvent`, or `deleteMeeting` now escapes as an unhandled promise rejection, which crashes Node ≥15 server processes by default and never reaches the `logger.error` path. Additionally, because the callback suspends at the first `await getCalendar(...)`, the `deleteEvent` calls are not even initiated before the function moves on to send the reschedule email and return `true`; in a serverless environment the function can finish (and be frozen) before the calendar/video deletions ever run, leaving stale events on users' calendars while the booking is already marked CANCELLED. Fix by replacing the forEach with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))` inside the try block.

title: Async forEach callback makes the surrounding try/catch dead and turns deletion failures into unhandled rejections
body: Same issue as in packages/app-store/vital/lib/reschedule.ts: the `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })` loop (lines 124–139) discards the promises from its async callback, so the enclosing `try/catch` can no longer catch errors that it previously caught synchronously (e.g. CalendarService constructor failures), and every failure — dynamic import rejection, `calendar.deleteEvent` rejection, `deleteMeeting` rejection — becomes an unhandled promise rejection that bypasses the `logger.error` handling and can crash the Node process. The function also proceeds to send the reschedule email and return `true` without waiting for any calendar or video deletion to complete; because the callback now suspends at `await getCalendar(...)` before `deleteEvent` is even invoked, the deletions may never start if the serverless invocation ends with the response, leaving stale events on external calendars for a booking already marked CANCELLED. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))` inside the try.

title: requestReschedule: deletions are fire-and-forget; failures are now unhandled rejections instead of thrown errors
body: In the `requestReschedule` mutation, `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) ... })` discards all async callback results. Before this change a synchronous failure in `getCalendar` (e.g. a CalendarService constructor throwing) propagated out of the mutation and produced a visible error; now it, and any dynamic-import rejection, becomes an unhandled promise rejection (a crash risk on Node ≥15). Also, since the callback suspends at `await getCalendar` before calling `deleteEvent`, the calendar/video deletions are not even started before the reschedule email is sent and the mutation returns — if the serverless function is frozen after responding, the old event is never removed from the external calendar/meeting provider even though the booking was already marked cancelled and rescheduled. The loop should be `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))` (ideally with per-item `.catch` logging) so deletions complete and errors are handled before responding.

title: getCalendarCredentials now embeds an unawaited Promise in the `calendar` field and discards promises for non-calendar variants
body: `getCalendarCredentials` is still a synchronous function but now calls the newly-async `getCalendar(credential)` without awaiting it, so the returned objects carry `calendar: Promise<Calendar | null>` where callers previously received `Calendar | null`. Only `getConnectedCalendars` (updated in this PR) awaits that field; any other consumer of this exported helper that touches `item.calendar` synchronously will now operate on a Promise instead of a Calendar and break at runtime, and the `ReturnType<typeof getCalendarCredentials>` contract changed silently. Additionally, `getCalendar(credential)` is invoked before the `app.variant === "calendar"` check, so for non-calendar-variant apps the promise is created and immediately discarded — a rejection of that dynamic import would be an unhandled rejection. Make the function async, resolve with `Promise.all`, and only call `getCalendar` for credentials that are actually returned.

title: Dynamic imports are evaluated eagerly, so all apps are still loaded on module evaluation
body: The object literal evaluates each `import("./applecalendar")` etc. immediately when `packages/app-store/index.ts` is first imported, so every consumer of `@calcom/app-store` still triggers loading all 28 app bundles — just asynchronously instead of synchronously. Any code path that needs a single app (e.g. `getCalendar` for one credential type) pays the module-loading cost for all of them, so the change adds asynchrony without delivering the lazy-loading/startup benefit the PR title implies, and on serverless cold starts everything is still fetched and evaluated. If per-app lazy loading is the goal, store thunks or use lazy getters (e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) and only invoke the one that is needed.

title: App API dispatcher still reads the appStore barrel synchronously, breaking all app OAuth callbacks and app webhooks
body: This PR changes every value of the default export of `@calcom/app-store` from the app's module namespace to a Promise of that namespace. The catch-all API route `apps/web/pages/api/integrations/[...args].ts`, which dispatches every app's API endpoints (`/api/integrations/{app}/add`, `/callback`, `/webhook`, etc. — e.g. the Google Calendar OAuth callback and the Stripe payment webhooks) looks the app up synchronously as `const app = appStore[appName as keyof typeof appStore]` and then checks `"api" in app` before calling `app.api[endpoint](req, res)`. It is not among the updated files, so after this change `app` is a Promise, the `in` check is false, and the route falls through to its error/404 path for every app. Consequence: connecting/disconnecting any integration and all payment webhooks stop working. The lookup must become `const app = await appStore[appName as keyof typeof appStore]`. It is also worth grepping the whole repo for any other remaining `appStore[...]` / `getCalendar(` consumers, since the barrel's contract changed from synchronous module to Promise and only the call sites in this PR were migrated.

title: The dynamic imports still execute eagerly — importing the barrel immediately loads all 28 app chunks
body: Each registry entry is written as `applecalendar: import("./applecalendar")`, so every `import()` expression is invoked at the moment `packages/app-store/index.ts` is evaluated. Only the *awaiting* became lazy, not the *loading*: the first import of `@calcom/app-store` still triggers fetching and evaluating all 28 app modules, so the startup/module-load cost this PR is presumably trying to reduce is essentially unchanged (only code-splitting/parallel async evaluation is gained). If the intent is to load an app only when it is actually used, the values need to be thunks (`() => import("./applecalendar")`) or a lazy getter/Proxy, with call sites adjusted accordingly. A side effect of creating all 28 promises up front is that a chunk-load failure in an app that is never used still produces an unhandled promise rejection (most entries are never awaited), which crashes Node under the default unhandled-rejections behavior.

title: Slots inside a date override return early and skip the busy-time check, allowing double bookings
body: In checkIfIsAvailable, when a host has a date override on the slot's date and the slot falls inside the override window, the new `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }` returns "available" before the `busy.every(...)` check at the bottom of the function ever runs. checkIfIsAvailable is the only place busy times (calendar events and existing bookings) are consulted — getTimeSlots never sees them. Consequence: for any host with a date override on a given day (fixed hosts via the new fixed-host filter, round-robin hosts via the loose-host filter, and single-user events since users default to isFixed), all of their existing bookings and calendar conflicts on that day are ignored, so the slot is offered and the host can be double-booked. Before this PR the busy check always ran, so this is a regression. The override-branch should fall through to the busy check instead of returning true.

title: Working-hours gate fails open when the host has no working hours on the slot's day
body: The new working-hours check treats a slot as "within working hours" whenever `workingHours.find(...)` returns undefined. The find callback only returns true when a workingHour entry matches the slot's UTC day AND the slot is outside its range; if the host has no working-hour entry at all for that weekday (their day off), the callback returns undefined for every entry, find returns undefined, the `return false` is skipped, and the host is considered available. For round-robin events, slots are generated from the union of all hosts' hours, so a slot on a fixed host's day off (generated from a round-robin host who works that day) passes the fixed-host filter and becomes bookable — exactly the kind of booking this PR is meant to prevent. The check should fail closed: if no workingHour covers the slot's day, the slot should be unavailable.

title: Copy-paste bug: `end` is computed from slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
body: In the working-hours check, `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` duplicates the `start` computation — it was clearly meant to use slotEndTime. As a result `end > workingHour.endTime` can only fire when the slot's start is already past the end of working hours, and a slot that starts within working hours but ends after the host's availability end is treated as available. Example: fixed host works until 17:00, a round-robin co-host works until 19:00, and a 60-minute slot starts at 16:45 (aligned to the co-host's schedule) — the fixed host gets booked 16:45–17:45 despite being unavailable after 17:00.

title: Date-override containment check accepts slots that only partially overlap the override
body: The new override-range logic only rejects slots that are entirely outside the override: it returns "not within" when slotEndTime <= override.start or when slotStartTime > override.end. Two cases slip through and are treated as within the override (and therefore available): (1) a slot that starts before the override start but ends inside it, because slotStartTime.isBefore(override.start) is never checked; (2) a slot that starts before the override end but ends after it, because the end-side check is the strict `slotStartTime.isAfter(override.end)` — a slot starting at 17:30 with an override ending 18:00 (and even a slot starting exactly at 18:00, since isAfter is not inclusive) passes. Hosts with non-aligned schedules (e.g., fixed host override 14:00–18:00, co-host hours starting at :30) can be booked partially or fully outside their override window. The check should require the slot to be fully contained: slotStartTime >= override.start && slotEndTime <= override.end.

title: `===` comparison between two Dayjs objects is always false (dead blocked-day branch)
body: `if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares object references, so it is never true — the author presumably meant `.isSame()`. This branch is meant to detect a fully blocked day (an override whose start equals its end, typically midnight, which is how "unavailable" date overrides are stored). Because it never fires, blocked days are only rejected incidentally via the surrounding before/after checks, and a slot starting exactly at the start==end timestamp of a blocked-day override (e.g., exactly 00:00 UTC) is reported as available on a day the host marked unavailable.

title: Timezone conversion of date overrides drops the date component; overrides land on the wrong invitee day when timezones straddle midnight
body: The new conversion shifts the stored override time by (inviteeOffset - organizerOffset) and then reads only `.hour()`/`.minute()`, discarding any day rollover, and the `activeOverrides` filter (line 207) still matches the override's stored-as-UTC date against the invitee's calendar day. When the organizer's and invitee's local dates differ, the override is applied on the wrong invitee day and never on the correct one. Concrete example: organizer in Honolulu (UTC-10) with an override Mar 10 08:00–09:00, invitee in Auckland (UTC+13). The true window is Mar 11 07:00–08:00 Auckland time, but the code offers Mar 10 07:00–08:00 Auckland (offset +1380 min rolls 08:00 to 07:00 the next day, and .hour() truncates it back onto Mar 10), while for inviteeDate Mar 11 the filter no longer matches the stored Mar 10 date so the override is missing entirely. The same happens for e.g. Tokyo organizer / Los Angeles invitee. This is the timezone-adjustment scenario the PR sets out to fix, still broken for large timezone gaps.

title: dayjs.tz(override.timeZone) silently falls back to the server's timezone when timeZone is undefined
body: TimeRange.timeZone is optional (packages/types/schedule.d.ts marks it `timeZone?: string`), and getSlots is a shared library function, but the new code calls `dayjs(...).tz(override.timeZone)` unconditionally. When timeZone is undefined, dayjs.tz does not throw — it falls back to the runtime's local timezone (typically UTC on servers/containers). The offset calculation then becomes inviteeOffset - serverOffset instead of inviteeOffset - organizerOffset, silently shifting the override's slots for any caller that passes date overrides without a timeZone. Either make the field required for date overrides or handle the undefined case explicitly.

title: No test covers the headline fix: date overrides of fixed hosts in round-robin events
body: The PR's primary change is the new fixed-host/loose-host availability enforcement in checkIfIsAvailable (packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/slots.ts), but the only added test exercises a single-user event with a date override viewed from a different invitee timezone. There is no ROUND_ROBIN scenario with an isFixed host that has a date override, and no scenario where a host with a date override also has busy times/bookings on the override day — which is why the regression where the busy check is skipped on override days (the `dateOverrideExist` early return) is not caught: the new test would pass even with that bug. Please add tests for a round-robin event with a fixed host override (including timezones where organizer/invitee dates differ) and for a host with an override plus a conflicting booking on the same day.

title: Busy times are ignored on date-override days, allowing double bookings
body: In checkIfIsAvailable, when a date override exists for the slot's date and the slot falls inside the override window, the code reaches `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }` (lines 133-135) and returns before the `busy.every(...)` check at the end of the function is ever evaluated. `busy` contains the host's existing Cal.com bookings and external calendar events, so on any day that has a date override, none of the host's actual commitments block slots. This applies to fixed hosts in round-robin/collective events, to loose hosts (the loose-host loop calls the same function), and to personal events (whose single user counts as fixed). A host who already has a booking or calendar event inside an override window can be double-booked. The early return should only skip the working-hours check; the busy check must still run.

title: Working-hours check rejects every slot for hosts with multiple windows per day
body: The new working-hours guard uses `workingHours.find(...)` and returns `false` (slot unavailable) whenever the predicate matches ANY window in which the slot does not fit. Hosts commonly define split availability on a day, e.g. 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00, which produces two WorkingHours entries with the same days. Any slot is necessarily outside at least one of those windows, so `find` always returns truthy and every slot is rejected. Because checkIfIsAvailable now runs for every fixed host (including the single user of a personal event, and both hosts of collective events), any event whose host has more than one availability window per day becomes completely unbookable on all days. The logic needs to be inverted: reject only when NO window for that day fully contains the slot (e.g. `!workingHours.some(wh => wh.days.includes(day) && start >= wh.startTime && end <= wh.endTime)`).

title: Working-hours check compares the window end against the slot start instead of the slot end
body: `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` is a copy-paste of the `start` computation; it should use `slotEndTime`. As written, `end > workingHour.endTime` only tests the slot's start time, so a slot that starts inside a window but finishes after the window closes (e.g. a 30-minute slot starting at 12:00 when the fixed host's window ends at 12:00, which can occur in round-robin/collective events where the slot originates from another host's hours) is treated as within working hours and can be booked past the host's availability.

title: Multiple date-override windows on the same date break the availability check
body: The `dateOverrides.find(...)` predicate returns true (causing the slot to be rejected with `return false`) for the first override on the matching date in which the slot is NOT contained, and find() stops iterating there. With two override windows on the same date (e.g. 10:00-11:00 and 14:00-15:00), a slot at 14:30 is rejected because it is outside the first window, and a slot at 10:30 is rejected because it is outside the second window. Only a single override window per date works correctly. The check needs 'there exists an override on this date that contains the slot' semantics rather than short-circuiting on the first non-containing override.

title: Override containment check treats partial overlap as available and misses the exact end boundary
body: The conditions used to decide that a slot is outside an override are `slotEndTime <= overrideStart` and `slotStartTime > overrideEnd` (strict isAfter). Anything else — including a slot that starts before the override and ends inside it, or starts inside and ends after it — is treated as 'within the override' and the host is considered available, even though part of the slot falls outside the override window. Additionally, a slot starting exactly at the override end fails the strict `isAfter` and is also treated as inside the override. For round-robin events where slots are generated from other hosts' working hours, this lets fixed hosts be booked outside their override window. Availability should require full containment: slotStart >= overrideStart && slotEnd <= overrideEnd.

title: Timezone-shifted date overrides that cross midnight are silently dropped
body: The override start/end are shifted by (inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset) and then reduced to hour/minute-of-day via `.hour() * 60 + .minute()`. When the shift pushes the interval across midnight — e.g. a 09:00-17:00 IST override viewed from PST (offset -810 minutes shifts start to 19:30 of the previous day and end to 03:30) — the wrapped startTime (1170) becomes greater than endTime (210) whenever only one side of the interval wraps, and buildSlots silently skips the range (`if (start >= end) continue`). Meanwhile the user's regular working hours for that day were already spliced out of computedLocalAvailability, so the invitee sees the host as fully unavailable that day. Regular working hours handle midnight spanning by splitting the range; overrides need the same treatment.

title: Zero-length override comparison uses === on dayjs objects and can never match
body: `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes') === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, 'minutes')` compares two distinct dayjs object references, which is always false. The intended detection of zero-length overrides (a 'blocked' date override where start equals end) is dead code, so such overrides fall through to the boundary conditions instead of being explicitly excluded. Use `.isSame()` for the comparison.

title: Override date matching is formatted in the server's local timezone but compared to a UTC date
body: `dayjs(date.start)` creates a dayjs in the server machine's local timezone, and `.add(utcOffset, 'minutes').format('YYYY MM DD')` is compared against `slotStartTime.format('YYYY MM DD')`, where slotStartTime is in UTC mode. On any host not running in UTC (self-hosted instances with a TZ set, dev machines), the two sides of the comparison are rendered in different zones, so an override can be matched against the wrong day near midnight. `dayjs.utc(date.start)` should be used so both sides are in UTC.

title: Override timezone conversion silently depends on the server timezone when timeZone is absent
body: `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)` is used to compute the organizer offset, but `timeZone` was added as an optional property on TimeRange, and dayjs.tz with an undefined zone falls back to the machine's local timezone. Any caller of getSlots that passes dateOverrides without a timeZone now gets results that depend on the server's timezone (and differ between UTC production servers and non-UTC dev machines), whereas the previous code did not consult a timezone at all. A deterministic fallback (e.g. `override.timeZone ?? organizerTimeZone`) should be used.

title: No tests for the round-robin fixed-host scenario or for busy blocking on override days
body: The PR adds only one test: a personal event viewed from a different timezone. The headline fix — date overrides of a fixed host constraining a round-robin event's slots — has no test. There is also no test that an existing booking or calendar busy time still blocks a slot on a date-override day (which would have caught the regression where the busy check is skipped when a date override matches), and no coverage for hosts with multiple working-hour windows in one day or multiple override windows on one date, both of which the new checkIfIsAvailable logic handles incorrectly.

title: On date-override days the busy-time check is skipped entirely, allowing double bookings
body: In checkIfIsAvailable, when a date override exists for the slot's date and the slot falls inside the override window, the code reaches `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }` (line 133) and returns 'available' before ever evaluating the `busy.every(...)` check at line 153. Since this function is now used to validate every candidate slot against each fixed host of a round-robin event (and against loose hosts), any existing booking or calendar busy time a host has on a date-override day is ignored and the slot is offered anyway, so the host can be double-booked. A matching date override should only bypass the working-hours check; the busy/busy-calendar check must still run.

title: Working-hours guard computes the slot end from the slot start time
body: In the new working-hours check, `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` is an exact copy of the `start` computation — it never adds eventLength, so the upper-bound comparison `end > workingHour.endTime` only checks the slot's start. A slot that starts inside a fixed host's working hours but ends after them (e.g. a 60-minute event starting 15 minutes before the host's day ends) passes the guard and is shown as bookable, booking the host outside their availability. `end` should be derived from the slot end time (slot start + eventLength).

title: Fixed host with no working hours at all on the slot's weekday is treated as available
body: The new working-hours guard only rejects a slot when it finds a workingHour entry whose `days` includes the slot's weekday AND the slot is outside that entry's window. If the fixed host has no availability row for that weekday (e.g. they don't work weekends), `workingHours.find(...)` returns undefined, the guard passes, and only busy times are checked. For a round-robin event, slots generated from another (non-fixed) host's schedule on the fixed host's day off are therefore still offered — exactly the kind of over-booking this PR is meant to prevent. A weekday with no matching working-hours entry should be treated as unavailable.

title: Slots inside one of several same-day override windows are rejected
body: The `dateOverrides.find(...)` at line 106 returns truthy as soon as ANY override on the slot's date does not contain the slot (slot ends at/before that override's start, or starts after its end). When a host has multiple override windows on the same day (e.g. 09:00–11:00 and 14:00–16:00), a slot at 10:00 is inside the first window but 'outside' the second, so find() returns the second override and the function returns false — the slot is hidden even though the host is available. The slot should be considered covered if it fits inside ANY of that day's override windows. Additionally the boundary is off by one: `slotStartTime.isAfter(overrideEnd)` is strict, so a slot starting exactly at an override's end is treated as inside the override and returned as available although it lies outside every window.

title: `===` between two Dayjs objects is always false, making the blocked-day branch dead code
body: `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes') === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, 'minutes')` compares two freshly created Dayjs instances by object identity, so it can never be true. The intent was evidently `.isSame()` to detect zero-length overrides (start == end, i.e. a fully blocked day). As written, blocked-day detection falls through to the other conditions, which happen to reject most slots but let a slot starting exactly at the override start pass, and the dead branch misleads anyone maintaining this logic.

title: The fixed-host date-override fix for round-robin events has no automated test
body: The PR's headline change — applying fixed hosts' date overrides and working hours in checkIfIsAvailable for round-robin events (packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/slots.ts) — is only covered by manual testing steps. The single added test exercises a personal event's slot generation with a different invitee timezone. The new checkIfIsAvailable logic has several interacting branches (override match, blocked day, working-hours bounds, busy times) and contains regressions a test would catch, e.g. a fixed host with a date override plus a conflicting existing booking is currently shown as available. A round-robin scenario with a fixed host who has a date override and a busy period on that day should be added.

title: Offset conversion of overrides discards day overflow when the shift crosses midnight
body: The invitee-local override start/end are computed as `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, 'minute').hour() * 60 + .minute()`. If applying `offset` (invitee offset minus organizer offset) pushes the time across midnight — e.g. an 00:30–02:00 override for an Asia/Kolkata host viewed by a UTC-4 invitee becomes 09:30 the previous day — `.hour()/.minute()` keep only the time-of-day and the day shift is lost. Combined with the `activeOverrides` filter, which matches overrides by the organizer-local date against the invitee's day, such overrides produce slots at the wrong time on the wrong day instead of on the adjacent invitee day.

title: Override date matching formats in server-local timezone against a UTC slot time
body: `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').format('YYYY MM DD')` creates the Dayjs in the server's local timezone (no `.utc()`), while the slot side `slotStartTime.format('YYYY MM DD')` is in UTC mode. The two date strings can therefore disagree for the same instant on any host not running in UTC, causing overrides to fail to match (or match the wrong day) depending on deployment timezone. Relatedly, when `organizerTimeZone` is undefined the offset silently falls back to 0, treating the override's wall-clock times as UTC.

title: Override conversion relies on optional timeZone with no fallback
body: `TimeRange.timeZone` was added as optional, but the conversion does `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` unconditionally and never falls back to the `organizerTimeZone` parameter that getSlots already receives. Any caller passing dateOverrides without a timeZone gets the server's own offset as 'organizer offset', silently converting override times as if they were UTC. The `override.start.toString()` round-trip also makes dayjs parse a non-ISO locale string instead of just passing the Date object, which is fragile and triggers dayjs's non-ISO parse warning.

title: Migration crashes when embed_category setting row is missing or doesn't match a category
body: The migration computes the category id via `execute("SELECT c.id FROM categories c INNER JOIN site_settings s ON s.value = c.name WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id']`. site_settings rows only exist for settings an admin actually changed, so on any site that never set embed_category (or left it blank, or where the value doesn't exactly equal a category name) the query returns zero rows, `execute(...)[0]` is nil, and `nil['id']` raises NoMethodError (PG::Result may also raise IndexError). The migration aborts, blocking the deploy — this will hit most existing sites since embedding is off by default, and fresh installs where site_settings is empty. The same unguarded `[0]['value']` pattern is used for uncategorized_category_id on line 15. Check for an empty result before indexing and fall back to the uncategorized category.

title: Migration interpolates legacy host strings directly into raw SQL
body: Legacy hosts are inserted with `execute "INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, category_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES ('#{h}', ...)"`. Any host value containing a single quote (e.g. an apostrophe someone pasted into the old free-text setting) produces malformed SQL and aborts the migration mid-run, and it is an injection vector. Use bound parameters or `ActiveRecord::Base.connection.quote(h)` when building the INSERT.

title: Migrated hosts keep http(s):// prefix and paths, so they silently stop matching
body: The old SiteSetting-based allowlist explicitly accepted entries like `http://eviltrout.com` (the removed code and its specs stripped the scheme before comparing), so real sites can have scheme-prefixed or path-bearing entries in the `embeddable_hosts` setting. The migration copies those values verbatim into the new table, but the new lookup `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host` compares the stored value against the parsed hostname (`where("lower(host) = ?", host)`), and the model's scheme/path stripping lives in `before_validation`, which raw SQL inserts bypass. After upgrading, rows like `http://discourse.org` or `https://example.com/1234` never match, so comment embedding and feed import from those previously-working sites break without any error. Normalize the values (strip scheme and path, downcase) in the migration, mirroring the model's before_validation.

title: update and destroy 500 on a nonexistent host id instead of 404
body: `update` and `destroy` fetch the record with `EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` and then use it without a nil check: `save_host(host)` immediately does `host.host = ...` and `destroy` calls `host.destroy`. If the id doesn't exist — e.g. an admin saves or deletes a row that another admin already removed in a different tab — this raises NoMethodError and returns a 500 with no meaningful feedback instead of a 404. Use `EmbeddableHost.find(params[:id])` (which renders 404 via rescuing RecordNotFound) or explicitly handle the nil case.

title: New admin endpoints have no request specs — only a subclass assertion
body: Both new controller specs (`admin/embeddable_hosts_controller_spec.rb` and `admin/embedding_controller_spec.rb`) only assert the controller is a subclass of Admin::AdminController. The feature's server API — creating, updating and deleting hosts, the uncategorized-category defaulting, validation-error responses for malformed hosts, and staff/admin permission enforcement — has no request coverage, so regressions (including the nil-host 500s in update/destroy) won't be caught. Add request specs exercising create/update/destroy with valid and invalid input and with non-admin users.

title: before_validation crashes with NoMethodError when host is nil
body: The `before_validation` callback calls `self.host.sub!` twice unconditionally. The controller assigns `host.host = params[:embeddable_host][:host]`, so a request that omits the host param leaves `self.host` nil and `nil.sub!` raises NoMethodError, turning a bad request into a 500 instead of a validation error. Guard with `if self.host.present?` or use `self.host = host.to_s.gsub(...)`, and rely on the format validation to reject blank values.

title: No uniqueness constraint on host — duplicates make category assignment ambiguous
body: `EmbeddableHost` validates only the format of `host`, and the migration adds no unique index. The new admin UI makes it easy to add the same host twice with different categories; `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host` then does `.where("lower(host) = ?", host).first`, returning an arbitrary matching row, so which category embedded topics from that host land in becomes nondeterministic. Add `validates_uniqueness_of :host, case_sensitive: false` and ideally a unique index.

title: Fabricator files' contents are swapped
body: `spec/fabricators/category_fabricator.rb` now contains `Fabricator(:embeddable_host)`, while the newly added `spec/fabricators/embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` contains the `:category`, `:diff_category`, `:happy_category` and `:private_category` fabricators. The suite still passes because Fabrication registers fabricators by name regardless of file, but the file names are misleading and break the convention that a fabricator file defines the fabricator it's named after — anyone editing or searching for these will look in the wrong place. Swap the two files' contents.

title: Plural branch of _hydrateEmbedded can leave undefined entries in the array
body: In the new `_ids` handling of `_hydrateEmbedded`, `obj[k].map(id => _lookupSubType(...))` is assigned directly to the model without any guard, whereas the singular `_id` branch only assigns `if (hydrated)`. `_lookupSubType` returns `undefined` when an id isn't present in the root payload (e.g. a sideloaded collection filtered by permissions), so the resulting property becomes `[undefined, ...]` and any later `.get()`/iteration over it will throw. Filter the mapped results (e.g. `hydrated.compact()`/`.filter(Boolean)`) or skip assignment when any id fails to resolve, matching the singular branch's behavior.

title: Migration crashes when the embed_category site setting row is missing or unmatched
body: The migration computes the default category with `execute("SELECT c.id FROM categories AS c INNER JOIN site_settings AS s ON s.value = c.name WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id'].to_i`. site_settings only contains rows for settings an admin explicitly changed, and `embed_category` defaulted to blank, so for the vast majority of installations (and every fresh install) this query returns zero rows. Indexing `[0]` on an empty result set returns nil (or raises IndexError depending on the pg adapter version), so `nil['id']` raises NoMethodError and the entire migration aborts, blocking the upgrade. The fallback for `category_id == 0` on line 15 (`... WHERE name = 'uncategorized_category_id'")[0]['value']`) has the same problem if that row is absent. Both lookups need to tolerate an empty result (e.g. `.first` with a nil check or a begin/rescue) before dereferencing.

title: Legacy host values are inserted raw and may silently stop matching after migration
body: The migration copies values from the legacy `embeddable_hosts` setting straight into the new table with `INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, ...) VALUES ('#{h}', ...)`. The old `SiteSetting.allows_embeddable_host?` stripped `http(s)://` prefixes when matching (and the old specs explicitly covered scheme-prefixed entries working), but `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host` compares the bare hostname (`uri.host`) against the stored value with `lower(host) = ?`. The model strips schemes/paths in `before_validation`, but the migration bypasses the model, so any legacy entries stored as `http://example.com`, with paths, uppercase, or trailing `\r` from Windows line endings will be inserted verbatim and will never match again — embedding silently breaks for those sites. Additionally the value is interpolated directly into the SQL string, so a host containing a single quote produces invalid SQL and fails the migration; values should be normalized and passed through quoting/bound parameters.

title: update and destroy 500 on an unknown host id instead of returning 404
body: `update` does `host = EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` and passes the result to `save_host`, which immediately calls `host.host = ...`; `destroy` calls `host.destroy`. If the id does not exist (stale page, deleted host, scripted request), `host` is nil and both actions raise NoMethodError, returning a 500. Other admin controllers in the codebase handle this by raising Discourse::NotFound (404); these actions should do the same.

title: before_validation raises NoMethodError when host is nil
body: The `before_validation` callback calls `self.host.sub!(...)` unconditionally. If a record is built without a host (for example an admin API request missing `embeddable_host[host]`, which `Admin::EmbeddableHostsController#save_host` assigns without a presence check), `sub!` is invoked on nil and raises NoMethodError, turning what should be a validation failure into a 500. Guard with `if self.host.present?` (or use non-mutating `sub` after a nil check) and add `validates_presence_of :host`.

title: Host validation accepts ports but record lookup can never match them
body: The validation regex `/\A[a-z0-9]+([\-\.]{1}[a-z0-9]+)*\.[a-z]{2,5}(:[0-9]{1,5})?(\/.*)?\Z/i` explicitly permits an optional `:port` suffix, so an admin can successfully save `example.com:3000`. However `record_for_host` compares `uri.host` — which never includes the port — against the stored value, so a host saved with a port will never match and embedding from it will always be rejected. Either strip the port in `before_validation` like the scheme/path are stripped, or disallow it in the regex.

title: Host regex rejects valid TLDs longer than 5 characters
body: The TLD portion of the validation regex is `[a-z]{2,5}`, which rejects real domains under longer TLDs such as `.museum`, `.travel`, or `.technology`. The previous free-form site setting accepted these hosts, so sites embedding from such domains can no longer add them through the new admin UI. The TLD segment should allow a more generous length (e.g. `{2,}`).

title: New host saved without choosing a category shows a blank category until reload
body: In the `save` action, after the record is created the component runs `host.set('category', Discourse.Category.findById(this.get('categoryId')))`. For a newly added host the `categoryId` property starts as null (the user is not required to pick a category; the server substitutes `SiteSetting.uncategorized_category_id`), so `findById(null)` returns undefined and the row's category badge renders blank even though the server assigned the uncategorized category. The correct category only appears after a full page reload. The component should resolve the category from the category_id returned in the save response when `categoryId` is unset.

title: Fabricator file contents were swapped
body: `spec/fabricators/category_fabricator.rb` now contains `Fabricator(:embeddable_host)`, while the category fabricators (`:category`, `:diff_category`, `:happy_category`, `:private_category`) were moved into `spec/fabricators/embeddable_host_fabricator.rb`. The suite still loads because Fabrication reads every file in the directory, but the fabricators live in files with the wrong names, which will confuse future maintainers; the contents should be swapped so each fabricator lives in its namesake file.

title: New admin controllers have no request-level specs
body: Both new controller specs (`admin/embeddable_hosts_controller_spec.rb` and `admin/embedding_controller_spec.rb`) only assert that the controller is a subclass of Admin::AdminController. There is no coverage for create/update/destroy behavior, validation errors, the category defaulting to uncategorized, or the unknown-id case — which is how the nil-host NoMethodError in `update`/`destroy` slips through. At minimum, request specs exercising the happy paths and the missing-record paths should be added.

title: Migration crashes when the embed_category site setting row is missing or matches no category
body: The migration does `execute("SELECT c.id ... WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id'].to_i`. The `embed_category` setting defaulted to an empty string and is only persisted in `site_settings` if an admin actually changed it, so on most installs (and any fresh DB) the query returns zero rows, `[0]` is nil, and `nil['id']` raises NoMethodError, aborting the migration and blocking the upgrade. It also crashes if the setting was set to a value that doesn't match a category name exactly. The same pattern at line 15 crashes if `uncategorized_category_id` has no row. Both lookups need nil-safe handling before indexing into the result.

title: Migrated hosts are inserted verbatim and will never match lookups
body: The old `embeddable_hosts` setting supported entries with scheme and path (e.g. `http://discourse.org`, `https://example.com/1234`) — the removed specs in site_setting_spec.rb and embed_controller_spec.rb prove these worked, because the old code compared against `URI(h).host`. The migration inserts the raw setting values into the new table, but `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host` looks up `where("lower(host) = ?", uri.host)`, so any migrated row containing a scheme or path will never match a referer. After upgrading, previously working embedded comments silently stop working for those sites. The migration should normalize hosts the same way the model's `before_validation` does (strip scheme and path) or insert via the model.

title: embed_category is deleted even when no host rows were created
body: If a site used feed polling with `embed_category` set but had no `embeddable_hosts` configured (feed-only embedding, which previously worked because `TopicEmbed.import` used the global `SiteSetting.embed_category`), this migration creates zero `embeddable_hosts` rows and still deletes the `embed_category` setting. From then on `TopicEmbed.import` uses `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host(url)` which finds nothing, so imported topics fall back to the uncategorized category — or fail validation entirely when `allow_uncategorized_topics` is false and the embedding user isn't staff. The previously configured category assignment is lost with no replacement.

title: Host values are interpolated into SQL without escaping
body: The INSERT interpolates the setting value directly: `VALUES ('#{h}', ...)`. A value containing a single quote (legacy/malformed data in the old free-text setting) will produce invalid SQL and abort the migration. Use `ActiveRecord::Base.sanitize`/`quote` or a parameterized insert.

title: Migration is not reversible despite using `change`
body: The migration uses `def change` but contains raw `execute` statements (data copy and `DELETE FROM site_settings`). Rolling back will raise ActiveRecord::IrreversibleMigration, and even a manual reverse can't restore the deleted `embeddable_hosts`/`embed_category` setting rows. This should be split into `up`/`down` with an explicit, safe down (or acknowledge irreversibility).

title: No foreign key or cleanup for category_id
body: `category_id` is `null: false` but has no foreign key, and the `EmbeddableHost` model has no `belongs_to` presence validation or dependent handling. Deleting a category leaves dangling `embeddable_hosts.category_id` values; `TopicEmbed.import` will then create topics pointing at a nonexistent category (PostCreator is given the stale id, and `ensure_topic_has_a_category` won't fix it since the id isn't nil), and the admin UI renders a missing category badge. Add a FK and/or handle category deletion.

title: show always renders JSON, so direct navigation/refresh to /admin/customize/embedding breaks
body: `show` unconditionally calls `render_serialized(...)`, which renders JSON for every format.
