body: The PR adds a new middleware (ContextualLoggerMiddleware) responsible for attaching endpoint/pluginId/dsName/dsUID/uname to the request context, but adds no test verifying those attributes are attached, and the renamed metrics_middleware_test.go only covers the prometheus metrics. There is also no test asserting that LoggerMiddleware's "Plugin Request Completed" output still contains the fields that were moved out of it — which is exactly why the traceID regression introduced by this PR (the explicit traceID field was removed and is no longer added anywhere in the chain) is not caught by the test suite. A small test chaining ContextualLoggerMiddleware + LoggerMiddleware and asserting the resulting log fields would lock in the intended behavior.

title: Cache is set before the limit check, so a retry bypasses the device limit entirely
body: tagDeviceUI writes the device key into the local cache (29-minute TTL) before calling anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the configured device limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached for a new device and Anonymous.Authenticate (client.go) rejects the request — but the cache entry has already been written and is never removed. Any subsequent request from the same device within 29 minutes hits the cache in tagDeviceUI, returns nil, and Authenticate succeeds, even though the device was never persisted and is never counted toward the limit. A brand-new device therefore only has to send its request twice to get anonymous access past the limit, and this is repeatable after each cache expiry (first request fails, then ~29 minutes of access). The cache key should be set only after a successful store call, or explicitly deleted when CreateOrUpdateDevice returns an error.

title: Device limit check-then-insert is not atomic; concurrent new devices can exceed the limit
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by running CountDevices and then, only if count < deviceLimit, executing the INSERT. These are two separate statements with no transaction or locking. Concurrent anonymous requests carrying distinct new device IDs — or requests landing on different Grafana replicas in an HA setup — can all observe a count below the limit and then all insert, so the stored device count can exceed deviceLimit by an arbitrary margin under a burst of new devices (e.g., bot/scraper traffic). If the limit is meant to be a hard cap, the count-and-insert must be done atomically (single transaction with locking), or the overshoot should be explicitly accepted and documented.

title: No test for the allowed path: existing device must still be updated when the limit is reached
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only asserts that a new device is rejected once the limit is reached. The complementary and more important branch — a device that already exists in anon_device must still be updated via updateDevice and allowed in while count >= deviceLimit — has no test, and neither does the propagation through Anonymous.Authenticate in client.go, which now fails authentication on ErrDeviceLimitReached. A regression in updateDevice's WHERE clause (for example a wrong updated_at window) would lock out every existing anonymous device as soon as the limit is hit, and nothing in this PR's tests would catch that.

title: New device_limit option is not documented in defaults.ini/sample.ini or the admin docs
body: readAuthSettings adds support for device_limit under [auth.anonymous], but the option is not added to conf/defaults.ini or conf/sample.ini, where every other auth.anonymous key is listed with an explanatory comment, and the configure-grafana documentation is not updated either. Operators have no discoverable way to learn the setting exists or that the default of 0 means the limit is disabled. The PR's own checklist requires docs to be updated for new configuration.

title: anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined infers the property type as undefined
body: In GrafanaBootConfig, the new field is declared as `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` with no type annotation, so TypeScript infers the class property's type as `undefined` (the `implements GrafanaConfig` clause does not widen inferred member types). Any frontend code reading config.anonymousDeviceLimit will see the type `undefined` and cannot compare or otherwise use it as a number without a cast, which defeats the purpose of exposing the value to the frontend. It should be declared as `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;`.

title: Cache is set before the DB write and never cleared on failure, so the device limit is bypassed after one rejected request
body: In tagDeviceUI, `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})` is executed before `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice(ctx, device)`, and the cache entry is not removed when the store call fails. With the new enforcement path, the first request from a new device after the limit is reached fails: CreateOrUpdateDevice returns anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached, TagDevice propagates it, and the anonymous authn client rejects authentication. But the cache key has already been written with a 29-minute TTL. Every subsequent request from that same device (the frontend sends the same X-Grafana-Device-Id each time) hits the cache, tagDeviceUI returns nil, and Authenticate succeeds — even though the device was never recorded and the limit is still exceeded. The net effect is the limit blocks only one request per device per 29 minutes, which defeats the feature. The cache entry must be deleted (e.g. a.localCache.Delete(key)) when CreateOrUpdateDevice returns an error.

title: Device-limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert and can be exceeded by concurrent requests
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by first running CountDevices and then, only if count < deviceLimit, performing the INSERT ... ON CONFLICT upsert. There is no transaction, lock, or unique-count guard spanning the check and the insert. Because tagging is now synchronous on the request path (client.go), N concurrent first-time anonymous requests (e.g. a burst of new visitors, or several HA replicas each with their own local cache) can all observe count = deviceLimit-1 and all insert, pushing the device count arbitrarily past the configured limit. If the limit is meant to be a hard cap (licensing/usage enforcement), the check and insert need to be atomic — e.g. a transaction with appropriate isolation/locking or a guarded insert.

title: Returning the bare ErrDeviceLimitReached from the authn client surfaces as a generic HTTP 500
body: When the device limit is reached, Authenticate returns `nil, err` where err is the plain sentinel anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached (created with fmt.Errorf, carrying no HTTP status). The authn service/middleware maps typed authn errors to specific status codes, but an untyped error like this is treated as an internal failure: the anonymous user gets an HTTP 500 (and an error log entry) rather than a deliberate response such as 401/429 with a meaningful message. This produces misleading monitoring/log noise and gives the frontend no way to distinguish 'limit reached' from a server malfunction. The limit-reached case should return a typed authn error with an explicit status code and user-facing message.

title: Device limit is trivially bypassed by omitting the X-Grafana-Device-Id header
body: TagDevice returns nil immediately when the X-Grafana-Device-Id header is absent, and the authn client in client.go then grants the anonymous identity without any limit check. The header is client-supplied and optional, so any client that simply does not send it is never counted and never subject to device_limit. If the intent of this feature is to cap anonymous usage, the enforcement only applies to cooperating clients (the stock frontend). Worth documenting explicitly that the limit is best-effort for honest clients, or enforcing an alternative identity when the header is missing.

title: New [auth.anonymous] device_limit option is not documented in defaults.ini / sample config / docs
body: The PR adds `cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit = anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0)` but does not add the option to conf/defaults.ini, conf/sample.ini, or the configuration documentation, despite the PR checklist requiring doc updates. Operators cannot discover the setting, its default (0), or the fact that 0 means 'unlimited'. The option (including the 0 = disabled semantics) should be added to the sample config and the auth.anonymous documentation.

title: No test for the allowed path: an existing device re-tagging while the limit is reached
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only covers rejection of a second, new device. The distinguishing behavior of this feature — that a device already present in anon_device (and updated within the 30-day window) must still be able to refresh its row via updateDevice and be allowed in when count >= deviceLimit — is untested, as is the stale-device case (row older than 30 days is rejected) and the interaction between the limit error and the local cache in tagDeviceUI (the regression where a rejected device is cached as tagged and let through). A regression in any of these paths would silently break or neuter the limit.

title: Device limit is bypassed on retry because the local cache is populated before the store write succeeds
body: In tagDeviceUI, the device cache key is set (a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{}) at line 87) BEFORE calling a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the device limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, so the first request from a new device is correctly rejected in the anonymous auth client (client.go returns the error). However, the cache entry remains for ~29 minutes (localcache.New(29*time.Minute, ...)). Any subsequent request from the same device hits the cache at line 83, tagDeviceUI returns nil without touching the store, and the anonymous authentication succeeds. The consequence is that the new configurable device limit is effectively unenforced: a blocked device only sees one failed request and then gets full anonymous access by simply retrying (e.g., refreshing the browser), with the block re-asserting only once per 29-minute cache-expiry window. The cache should only be populated after CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds (or the key must be removed when it returns an error).

title: Check-then-act race between CountDevices and the insert allows exceeding the configured device limit
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by first calling CountDevices and then, only if count < deviceLimit, executing the INSERT/upsert. The count and the insert are separate, non-transactional queries. Two concurrent anonymous requests for new devices can both observe count < deviceLimit and both insert, so the anon_device table ends up with more devices than the configured limit. Under concurrent anonymous traffic (e.g., a public dashboard link being opened by many clients at once, or multiple Grafana HA replicas), the limit is only a soft cap. Consider enforcing the limit atomically (e.g., a single statement with a subquery guard, a transaction with appropriate isolation, or an INSERT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < limit).

title: Device tagging moved from background goroutine into the synchronous auth path even when no limit is configured
body: Previously TagDevice ran in a goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout and a recover() guard, so anonymous authentication never blocked on the database write and a panic in tagging could not affect the request. This PR calls TagDevice synchronously in Authenticate for all deployments, including the default case where device_limit is unset (0) and the enforcement is not needed. On every local-cache miss (roughly once per 29 minutes per device) each anonymous request now waits for the COUNT + upsert round trips before an identity is returned, and a panic in the tagging path now propagates into request handling. Consider keeping the asynchronous path when the limit is disabled, or restoring the timeout/recover protection.

title: No test for the allowed path (existing device updated when limit is reached) or for repeated rejection
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a brand-new device is rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached once the limit is hit. Two important behaviors are untested: (1) that a device already present in anon_device is still successfully updated (updateDevice returns nil) when count >= deviceLimit — this is the intended happy path that keeps existing devices working, and a regression there would lock out legitimate users; (2) that a rejected device keeps being rejected on subsequent TagDevice/CreateOrUpdateDevice attempts — a test through AnonDeviceService.TagDevice would have caught the local-cache bypass where the second request from a blocked device succeeds.

title: New device_limit option is not documented in defaults.ini/sample.ini
body: The PR introduces cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit read from key 'device_limit' in the [auth.anonymous] section, but it does not add the option to conf/defaults.ini or conf/sample.ini, where the other auth.anonymous options (enabled, org_name, org_role, hide_version) are documented with comments. As shipped, the setting is undiscoverable for administrators and its semantics (0 = unlimited, limit counted over devices active in the last 30 days) are undocumented.

title: Routine cleanup progress logged at Error level, including full ID lists
body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags contain six r.log.Error calls (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579) that log normal, successful operation: "Annotations to clean by time", "cleaned annotations by time", "Tags to clean", "cleaned tags". These fire on every batch of every cleanup run even when nothing is wrong (the "err" kv is always nil at those points), and they log the complete slice of IDs to be deleted, which can be up to the configured AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize entries in a single line. Combined with the cleanup ticker being changed to 1 minute in this PR, this floods error-level logs during healthy operation, breaks any alerting based on error logs, and can produce enormous log lines for large batch sizes. These are leftover debug statements and should be r.log.Debug at most, and probably should not dump the raw ID list.

title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, running all cleanup jobs 10x more often
body: The Run loop ticker was changed from time.Minute * 10 to time.Minute * 1. clean() does not only run annotation cleanup — on every tick it runs the entire job list: deleting expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, old annotations, expiring user invites, deleting stale short URLs, two query-history enforcement queries, and re-scanning the temp file directories. This change therefore multiplies the database and filesystem load of all background cleanup jobs by 10, yet the PR description (about avoiding MySQL deadlocks in annotation cleanup) never mentions it. If the intent is to keep annotation cleanup batches small and frequent, that should be scoped to the annotation job or at least called out explicitly; as written this is an undocumented behavior change affecting every cleanup task.

title: SQLite literal IN-list built with O(n^2) string concatenation
body: In deleteByIDs, the SQLite fallback for batch sizes over 999 builds the ID list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside a loop over ids. Each iteration allocates and copies the entire accumulated string, so building the list is quadratic in the number of IDs. With the batch size exercised in the new test (32767 IDs) this copies on the order of gigabytes per batch, and it runs on every batch iteration of the cleanup loop. Use a strings.Builder with strconv.AppendInt (or strings.Join on pre-converted strings) to make it linear.

title: Parameter-limit guard only covers SQLite; large batch sizes break on Postgres
body: deleteByIDs only sidesteps bind-parameter limits when the dialect is SQLite and AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999; every other database gets a `DELETE FROM ... WHERE id IN (?, ?, ...)` statement with one placeholder per ID. Postgres rejects statements with more than 65535 bind parameters, and very large placeholder lists can also hit MySQL's max_allowed_packet. Since AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is operator-configurable and the PR itself tests a value of 32767, a batch size above 65535 on Postgres would make the delete fail on every cleanup cycle (the job errors out and nothing is cleaned). Consider chunking the ID list into fixed-size DELETE batches for all dialects instead of special-casing SQLite.

title: Cleanup progress logged at Error level, including full ID slices, on every batch
body: The new batched cleanup logs routine progress at Error level in six places (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579): "Annotations to clean by time", "cleaned annotations by time", "Annotations to clean by count", "cleaned annotations by count", "Tags to clean", and "cleaned tags". These fire unconditionally for every batch of every annotation type on every cleanup run — including steady-state runs where count is 0 and nothing was deleted — and each line embeds the complete "ids" slice, whose length is the configured AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize (the PR's own test uses 32767, so a single log line can contain tens of thousands of IDs). The cleanup job also now runs every minute (see cleanup.go), so this produces a constant stream of multi-kilobyte Error log lines, which will swamp error logs and trip any alerting based on error-level log volume. Lines 534/554/576 also log "err", err where err is nil by construction. These look like debugging leftovers; they should be demoted to Debug (and the ids/cond fields dropped or truncated) before merging.

title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, affecting all cleanup jobs
body: The diff changes the CleanUpService ticker from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This is unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (splitting the annotation cleanup DELETE to avoid MySQL deadlocks) and is not mentioned in the description. It makes every cleanup job run 10x more often — temp file cleanup, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, annotations, user invites, short URLs, and query history (the last of which runs several DELETE/count queries each cycle) — multiplying background database and filesystem load for all Grafana instances. If the intent was to let the batched annotation cleanup converge faster, that should be scoped to the annotation job or justified in the PR; otherwise this line looks like a local-testing leftover that should be reverted.

title: Inline ID list for SQLite built with O(n^2) string concatenation
body: In deleteByIDs, the SQLite fallback path (used when AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999) builds the IN-list string with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside a loop over all ids. Each iteration reallocates and copies the entire accumulated string, so building a list of N IDs costs O(N^2) in bytes copied — with the batch size of 32767 exercised by the new test that is on the order of several GB of copying per batch, and the tag cleanup runs the same path with even more IDs. This runs on every cleanup cycle when a large batch size is configured. Using a strings.Builder (or strings.Join on a pre-converted []string) with strconv.AppendInt would make it linear.

title: Subtest cleanup registered after data creation; a failure leaves dirty tables and cascades via PK conflicts
body: In TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp, each subtest creates its annotations and runs assertions (which use require, aborting the subtest on failure) before registering t.Cleanup at line 120. Because createTestAnnotations now inserts rows with explicit primary keys (ID: int64(i+1), line 241) and all subtests share the same fakeSQL database, any failure before the cleanup is registered leaves rows behind, and every subsequent subtest then fails with primary-key conflicts on IDs 1..N rather than its actual assertion result, making the real failure hard to diagnose. Registering the t.Cleanup before createTestAnnotations (so tables are truncated even on early failure) avoids the cascade.

title: Routine cleanup progress logged at Error level on every cycle
body: The new cleanup code logs normal, healthy operation with r.log.Error at six sites: lines 534, 537 ("Annotations to clean by time" / "cleaned annotations by time"), 554, 557 (count variants), and 576, 579 ("Tags to clean" / "cleaned tags"). These fire on every cleanup run even when there is nothing to delete (count=0), include the full ID list (up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize entries, e.g. tens of thousands), and carry a nil "err" key. Combined with the cleanup ticker being changed to every minute in cleanup.go, this produces a constant stream of ERROR log lines per Grafana instance in the healthy case, which will break error-rate-based alerting/monitoring and inflate log volume. These look like debugging leftovers and should be Debug level (and probably not log raw ID slices).

title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute for all jobs
body: The PR, which is scoped to the annotation cleanup deadlock, changes the CleanUpService ticker from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This makes every cleanup job run 10x more often on every Grafana instance: deleting expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, user invites, short URLs, query history rows (including the two EnforceRowLimit queries), scanning/removing temp files, plus the annotation cleanup itself. That is a significant, undocumented increase in background DB and disk load, and it also increases how often annotation deletes race with annotation inserts — the exact contention this PR is trying to defuse. If this is intentional it needs justification in the PR and ideally a config option; if it is a leftover from local deadlock reproduction, it should be reverted.

title: deleteByIDs only guards SQLite's parameter limit; oversized batch sizes fail on Postgres/MySQL
body: deleteByIDs builds DELETE FROM ... WHERE id IN (?, ?, ...) with one bind parameter per ID and only switches away from parameters for SQLite when AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999. On other databases the batch size is configurable and unvalidated: if it is set above the driver's bind-parameter cap (65535 for Postgres, and MySQL prepared statements have a similar 65535 placeholder limit), every cleanup batch will fail with a parameter-count error, so cleanup never makes progress. The previous subquery-based DELETE had no parameter list at all, so this is a regression for large configured batch sizes. Consider chunking the ID slice to a safe per-statement size (e.g. 1000) for all dialects.

title: SQLite inline-ID path builds SQL with quadratic string copying
body: In the SQLite branch of deleteByIDs the ID list is built with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` in a loop, which copies the entire accumulated string on every iteration — O(n^2) work. With the batch size this path is designed for (e.g. 32767 IDs, as exercised by the new test), that is on the order of gigabytes of byte copying per batch, repeated on every cleanup cycle while a backlog exists. Using a strings.Builder with strconv.AppendInt (or strings.Join on pre-formatted values) would make it linear.

title: Async legacy writes derive their context from the request context and will be canceled immediately
body: In Create (and identically in Delete at line 110, Update at line 135 and DeleteCollection at line 163), the goroutine performing the asynchronous legacy write builds its context from the incoming request context: `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, ...)`. The dual writer returns immediately after spawning the goroutine, and the HTTP request context is canceled as soon as the handler returns, so the derived context is already (or almost immediately) canceled when the legacy write actually runs. The legacy store will therefore fail with context.Canceled in the common case, silently defeating the purpose of mode 3 ("write to legacy as a safe measure") — unified storage will have the data but legacy will not. Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (keeping the log values) before applying the 10s timeout so the legacy write survives request completion.

title: Delete no longer cleans up legacy storage when unified storage returns NotFound
body: The previous Mode 3 Delete tolerated a NotFound error from unified storage (`apierrors.IsNotFound`) and still attempted the legacy delete; the new code returns immediately on any storage delete error, including NotFound. An object that exists only in legacy (e.g., written before the unified copy existed, or whose unified copy was lost during migration) can now never be deleted through the API: unified returns NotFound, the client sees a failure, and the stale legacy record is left behind, where it will resurface if the installation rolls back to a legacy-first mode. The NotFound special-case for proceeding with the legacy delete should be preserved.

title: Delete passes the object name as the kind label to recordStorageDuration
body: On a successful delete, `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object's name as the third argument, where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. That argument is the resource/kind label of the duration metric, so this both mislabels the series and creates unbounded Prometheus label cardinality — one time series per deleted object name — which can seriously degrade the metrics endpoint and Prometheus server. It should be `options.Kind`.

title: Create records a legacy-storage duration metric when unified storage fails
body: In the error path of Create, when `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` even though the legacy store was never contacted and the measured start time belongs to the unified-storage call. This should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`; as written, unified-storage create failures pollute the legacy-storage error/duration metrics and the actual storage failure is never recorded, which will mislead the dashboards this mode is meant to feed.

title: Update records a legacy-storage duration metric when unified storage fails
body: In the error path of Update, when `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. The legacy store was never called and the duration measured is the unified-storage call's, so unified-storage update errors are misreported as legacy-storage errors in the dual-writer metrics.

title: DeleteCollection records the legacy delete result as a unified-storage metric
body: Inside the async goroutine of DeleteCollection, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`. Errors and durations of the legacy delete-collection are therefore attributed to unified storage, masking real legacy failures and inflating storage timings in the metrics.

title: Delete stores the unenriched logger in the context
body: Delete builds an enriched logger (`log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method)`) but then stores the base logger in the context: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`. Anything downstream that calls `klog.FromContext(ctx)` loses the name/kind/method fields. It should pass `log`, as the other methods do.

title: No draining of in-flight async legacy writes on shutdown
body: The async legacy writes are fire-and-forget goroutines with a 10s timeout, and `Destroy()` does not wait for any of them. On pod shutdown or rollout, every legacy write still in flight is silently abandoned, so the legacy copy can diverge from unified storage exactly during deploys — the window in which the "legacy as a safe measure" guarantee matters most. Consider tracking in-flight writes with a WaitGroup and draining them in Destroy.

title: Mode 3 integration subtests assert synchronous legacy visibility of async legacy writes
body: The new subtests "with dual write (file, mode 3)" and "with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)" reuse doPlaylistTests, which asserts that objects written via the k8s API are immediately visible through the legacy REST API (the `/api/playlists` list comparison in "Do CRUD via k8s" and the legacy GET in getFromBothAPIs). In mode 3 the legacy write happens asynchronously in a goroutine with no synchronization point, so there is no guarantee the legacy store has caught up when those assertions run — these subtests will be flaky under CI load (and, given the request-context cancellation bug in the async writer, may fail consistently). The mode-3 runs need polling/eventually-style assertions against the legacy API.

title: Unit tests never wait for or assert the asynchronous legacy writes
body: None of the new mode-3 unit tests (Create, Update, Delete, DeleteCollection) synchronize with the goroutine that performs the legacy write or assert that it happened — e.g., TestMode3_Create registers a legacy Create expectation but never blocks on the goroutine nor calls `m.AssertExpectations`. The tests pass even if the legacy write is never executed, so the core behavior this PR adds (async dual write to legacy) is effectively untested at the unit level; a regression that drops the legacy call entirely would go unnoticed.

title: Create error test registers the storage failure on the legacy mock and only works via the shared mock instance
body: In TestMode3_Create's case "error when creating object in the unified store fails", the failing Create expectation is registered via `setupLegacyFn` on the legacy mock, but mode 3 calls unified storage first and the legacy expectation is never used intentionally — the test only passes because `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` wrap the same `*mock.Mock`, so the storage Create call accidentally matches the legacy-registered expectation. If the two mocks are ever given separate mock instances, the storage Create call will panic as unexpected. Register the failing expectation on the storage mock (setupStorageFn) so the test models what it claims to test.

title: Async legacy writes derive their context from the request context and are cancelled when the request completes
body: In Create (and identically in Delete at line 110, Update at line 135, and DeleteCollection at line 163) the legacy write runs in a goroutine whose context is `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10*time.Second, ...)` where `ctx` is the incoming apiserver request context. For server requests, the context is cancelled as soon as the HTTP handler returns — which happens immediately after the dual writer returns its response. The 10-second timeout therefore almost never gets to run: every legacy write races with request teardown and will frequently fail with context.Canceled. Since the failure is only recorded in a metric and never logged, mode 3 silently drops the 'safety' legacy writes it exists to perform, leaving legacy and unified storage permanently diverged with no signal. The goroutine context should be derived from `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (which preserves values like the logger and user) before applying the timeout.

title: Delete records storage duration with the object name as the resource label
body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object's name in the position where every other call site in this file passes `options.Kind`. If the third argument is the metric's resource label (as all the kind-based call sites indicate), this creates a Prometheus series per deleted object name — unbounded cardinality that grows with every object — and breaks per-kind aggregation/alerting for the delete method. Use `options.Kind` here.

title: Unified-storage failures are recorded as legacy metric errors (and vice versa in DeleteCollection)
body: In Create (line 45) and Update (line 129), when `d.Storage` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` — the failed unified-storage call is recorded as a legacy error and no storage-side failure is recorded at all. Conversely, in DeleteCollection's goroutine (line 166) the legacy delete-collection result is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(...)`. These metrics misattribute failures to the wrong backend in both directions, which will mislead the dashboards/alerting used to judge whether it is safe to advance to mode 4. The Create/Update error paths should use `recordStorageDuration`, and the DeleteCollection goroutine should use `recordLegacyDuration`.

title: Legacy goroutine reuses the request object that unified storage may have mutated and that is being serialized for the response
body: The goroutine calls `d.Legacy.Create(ctx, obj, ...)` with the same `runtime.Object` pointer that was just handed to `d.Storage.Create`. k8s-style stores mutate the object passed to Create/Update (setting UID, resourceVersion, generation, timestamps) and typically return that same pointer as `created`. If unified storage does that, the legacy goroutine and the HTTP handler then concurrently mutate and serialize the same object: the legacy store can overwrite unified's resourceVersion/UID on the object being written to the response — a data race and a potentially corrupted response body. Previously the legacy call was synchronous so mutation ordering was controlled; making it async requires passing `obj.DeepCopyObject()` to the legacy call (same concern applies to the Update path reusing request-scoped objects).

title: Unordered async legacy writes can leave legacy permanently stale (lost updates)
body: Each write spawns an independent goroutine with no ordering guarantees. Two quick successive updates to the same object (or a create immediately followed by an update) can be applied to legacy out of order: the goroutine carrying the newer update may finish before the older one, which then overwrites legacy with stale data. Because legacy errors are only counted in a metric and never logged, nothing surfaces this divergence, and the legacy copy — the stated purpose of mode 3 ('just as a safe measure') — can silently remain at an old revision indefinitely. Legacy writes need per-object serialization (e.g. a single ordered worker/queue) and/or resourceVersion-based conflict handling.

title: Delete installs the base logger into the context instead of the enriched one
body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` should pass `log` — the logger that was just built with name/kind/method values. As written, anything downstream that uses `klog.FromContext(ctx)` (including the storage and legacy delete calls in this method) logs without the identifying fields, unlike every other method in this file which passes the enriched logger.

title: Async legacy write failures are no longer logged anywhere
body: In all four write methods the error from the async legacy call is only passed to `recordLegacyDuration`; the previous implementation logged it (e.g. `log.Error(err, "unable to create object in legacy storage")`). For a mode whose purpose is keeping legacy as a safety net, a failing safety net with no log entry makes diagnosis impossible — this would also have made the request-context cancellation bug visible in logs. Log the error with object identifiers inside each goroutine.

title: Mode 3 unit tests never verify that the async legacy write actually happens
body: The legacy expectations are registered on a testify mock that is shared between the legacy and unified mocks (both `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` wrap the same `*mock.Mock`), and the tests return immediately after the dual-writer call without waiting for the legacy goroutine or calling AssertExpectations. Consequences: (a) the success cases pass even if the legacy call never runs — the request-context cancellation bug in dualwriter_mode3.go fails nothing here; (b) because both backends share one mock, the Create error case registers only a 'legacy' expectation and it is actually `Storage.Create` that matches it, so the test's name and setup do not reflect what is exercised. Use separate mocks and wait/assert on the legacy invocation (e.g. require.Eventually) so each backend's call and ordering is genuinely checked.

title: New mode-3 playlist subtests assert legacy state immediately after asynchronous legacy writes and will be flaky
body: `doPlaylistTests` performs k8s writes and then immediately reads through the legacy API (`getFromBothAPIs`, the 'Do CRUD via k8s (and check that legacy api still works)' subtest, and the `/api/playlists` list comparisons) expecting both backends to agree. Under mode 3 the legacy write is asynchronous, so these cross-backend assertions race the legacy goroutine — they pass or fail depending on goroutine scheduling (and fail outright whenever the legacy write is cancelled at request end, per the context bug in dualwriter_mode3.go). The two new mode-3 runs of this shared test need to poll for convergence on the legacy side (e.g. require.Eventually) or use relaxed expectations.

title: Async legacy writes derive their context from the request context, which is canceled when the handler returns
body: In Create (and identically in Delete at line 110, Update at line 135, and DeleteCollection at line 163) the asynchronous legacy write runs in a goroutine whose context is created with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...), deriving from the incoming request context. In the Kubernetes API server the request context is canceled as soon as the HTTP handler returns, which happens immediately after the synchronous unified-storage write completes. The detached goroutine therefore almost always executes with an already-canceled context and the legacy write fails with 'context canceled' — in mode 3 the legacy copy (the stated 'safe measure') is silently skipped, with only a metric recording the failure. The goroutine should first detach values from the request lifecycle, e.g. ctx = context.WithoutCancel(ctx), before applying the 10s timeout.

title: Update passes raw UpdatedObjectInfo to legacy, so UpdatedObject runs twice and the two stores can diverge
body: Update now hands the raw rest.UpdatedObjectInfo to both Storage.Update and the async Legacy.Update, meaning objInfo.UpdatedObject() is executed independently by each store against its own old object. The previous implementation resolved the object once (Storage.Get + UpdatedObject) and wrapped the result in updateWrapper so both stores persisted the identical object. With the new code, create-on-update paths that generate names/UIDs produce different objects in legacy vs unified storage, and any mutating logic inside UpdatedObject runs twice, so the two stores can silently hold divergent objects — exactly what dual write is meant to prevent. The object should be materialized once and the frozen result passed to the legacy update via updateWrapper, as before.

title: Delete no longer tolerates NotFound from unified storage, so legacy-only objects can never be deleted
body: Delete now returns immediately on any error from unified storage, including NotFound. The previous implementation special-cased apierrors.IsNotFound and still issued the legacy delete. With the new early return, an object that exists only in legacy storage (created before unified storage was enabled, or left behind by a failed dual write) can never be deleted in mode 3: callers receive NotFound and the stale legacy row remains forever.

title: Mode 3 integration subtests assert legacy API state synchronously, racing the async legacy write
body: The new 'with dual write (file, mode 3)' subtest (line 132) and 'with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)' subtest (line 191) run the full doPlaylistTests suite, which checks legacy API state immediately after k8s writes — e.g. listing /api/playlists right after k8s Create and getFromBothAPIs right after k8s Update. In mode 3 the legacy write is asynchronous (a goroutine with up to a 10s window), so these assertions race it and will flake: the legacy endpoint can still 404 or return the pre-update title. The mode-3 runs need eventually/polling-style assertions for legacy-side reads, or the legacy-side checks should be skipped for mode 3.

title: Delete records storage duration with the object name instead of the kind as metric label
body: On successful Delete, d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) passes the object name where every other call passes options.Kind as the metric label. Object names (e.g. playlist UIDs) are unbounded, so each deleted object creates a new Prometheus time series — a cardinality explosion — and the metric stops aggregating per kind.

title: Storage create/update failures are recorded in the legacy-duration metric
body: When the unified-storage Create fails, the error path calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage), recording a legacy failure that never happened (legacy is never called on this path) into the legacy duration metric, with the storage start time, and never recording the actual storage failure. The same bug exists in Update at line 129. Both should call d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...). This corrupts the dual-writer metrics that distinguish legacy vs unified errors.

title: DeleteCollection records the legacy operation result in the storage-duration metric
body: In DeleteCollection's async goroutine, the outcome of d.Legacy.DeleteCollection is recorded with d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy), attributing legacy latency and failures to the unified-storage metric. Every other path uses recordLegacyDuration for legacy operations; this should be d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy).

title: Delete stores the bare logger (d.Log) in the context instead of the enriched one
body: Delete builds a contextual logger with log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method) but then puts the bare logger into the context: ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log). Downstream log lines emitted from the storage layers lose the name/kind/method identifying fields. It should be klog.NewContext(ctx, log), consistent with the other methods.

title: Missing re-check of the cache after acquiring the write lock (double-checked locking)
body: After taking the exclusive lock, GetWebAssets does not re-check whether another goroutine already populated entryPointAssetsCache. At startup (or whenever the cache is empty), every concurrent request observes a nil cache under the read lock, then queues on the write lock; each one in turn re-reads and re-parses assets-manifest.json from disk (or fetches it over HTTP if the CDN path at line 56 is ever enabled) and overwrites the cache, with all but the last result discarded. This is the standard double-checked-locking pattern with the second check missing. Adding `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after acquiring the write lock avoids the redundant serialized I/O.

title: Exclusive lock held across manifest I/O serializes all callers
body: The write lock acquired at line 48 is held (via defer) for the entire recompute, including the disk read of assets-manifest.json and, if enabled, the CDN HTTP fetch. While any writer holds it, all other callers block on the initial RLock at line 41. In dev mode the cache is deliberately bypassed on every call, so every request to GetWebAssets is now serialized through this single global mutex plus a disk read. The same happens in non-dev mode whenever the manifest read persistently fails, because the cache then stays nil and every request retries under the exclusive lock, turning a missing-file misconfiguration into a global serialization point for index page loads. Consider doing the read outside the lock and taking the write lock only to publish the result (combined with the re-check from the previous point).

title: Race fix ships without a regression test exercising concurrent access
body: This PR fixes a data race on the global entryPointAssetsCache but adds no test. Nothing guards the new synchronization: if someone later removes the mutex or accesses the global without it, nothing in the test suite would catch it. A simple test that calls GetWebAssets from many goroutines (against a temp assets-manifest.json) and is run under `go test -race` would fail if the synchronization regresses and would document the concurrency contract of this function.

title: Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock
body: GetWebAssets reads entryPointAssetsCache under a read lock, releases it, and then acquires the write lock at line 48 — but never re-checks the cache once the write lock is held. When multiple requests race before the cache is first populated (e.g. at startup), each one sequentially re-opens and re-parses assets-manifest.json and overwrites the cache, defeating most of the benefit of the fix. Worse, if goroutine B populates the cache successfully and goroutine A's redundant re-read then fails (file removed during startup, transient I/O error), line 69 stores nil over the valid cache and A returns an error to its caller even though assets were already loaded. Add a second nil check after acquiring the write lock (standard double-checked locking) so only the first caller performs the load.

title: Exclusive lock held across file (and potential network) I/O
body: The write lock is taken at line 48 and held via defer for the entire remainder of GetWebAssets, which includes the assets-manifest.json read at line 60 and — if the cdn variable at line 54 is ever set to a non-empty value as the comment suggests — a CDN HTTP fetch via http.DefaultClient, which has no timeout. While one caller performs that I/O, every other goroutine calling GetWebAssets blocks on the mutex, including callers that would have been satisfied by the already-populated cache; in dev mode (where the cache is never consulted) this serializes every call. Consider performing the load outside the critical section and taking the write lock only to publish the result, combined with the double-check described above.

title: No regression test for the data race being fixed
body: This PR exists to fix a data race on the global entryPointAssetsCache, but it adds no test that would catch a regression. A test that invokes GetWebAssets concurrently from multiple goroutines (with cfg.Env != setting.Dev so the cache path is exercised) and is run under `go test -race` would fail before this change and pass after it. Without such a test, a future refactor of this function can silently reintroduce the unsynchronized access, and CI will not notice.

title: Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock (incomplete double-checked locking)
body: GetWebAssets first reads entryPointAssetsCache under a read lock (lines 41-43), then acquires the write lock at line 48 and unconditionally reloads the manifest from disk (readWebAssetsFromFile at line 60) and republishes the cache. Because there is no second check after the write lock is acquired, any requests that arrive concurrently before the cache is first populated will each perform the full manifest load sequentially and overwrite each other's cache entry. Besides duplicated disk I/O, a transient read error in a later goroutine can replace an already-populated good cache entry with nil and return an error to its caller even though a valid cached value existed. The standard fix is to re-check `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after taking the write lock.

title: Write lock is held across manifest file I/O, serializing all GetWebAssets callers
body: The deferred Unlock at line 49 keeps entryPointAssetsCacheMu held while readWebAssetsFromFile (line 60) opens, reads, and parses assets-manifest.json from disk. While the write lock is held, every other goroutine calling GetWebAssets blocks — including callers that would otherwise be served by the read-locked fast path, since RLock cannot proceed while the write lock is held. In dev mode (setting.Dev) the fast path is skipped by design, so every index page load now serializes on this disk I/O, and on a slow filesystem all such requests stall behind a single global mutex. Loading and parsing the manifest outside the lock and only taking the write lock to publish the result would avoid this.

title: No regression test for the data race this PR fixes
body: The PR adds a mutex to guard the package-level entryPointAssetsCache but adds no test. A data-race fix without a test that exercises concurrent access can silently regress. A test that calls GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines against a temporary assets-manifest.json (with cfg.Env set to a non-dev value so the cache path is exercised) and is run with the race detector enabled (`go test -race`) would have caught the original race and would verify the fix going forward.

title: Existing SQL expression tests are left in place and will now fail against the "not implemented" stub
body: This PR makes DB.RunCommands and DB.QueryFramesInto unconditionally return errors.New("not implemented"), which means sql.TablesList (pkg/expr/sql/parser.go) and NewSQLCommand (pkg/expr/sql_command.go) now fail for every input. The repository already contains tests that exercise these paths and expect them to work: pkg/expr/sql/parser_test.go calls TablesList with valid SQL and asserts on the returned table names, and pkg/expr/sql_command_test.go calls NewSQLCommand/Execute with valid SQL and asserts successful results. None of these test files are updated, skipped, or removed in this PR, so they will fail with "not implemented" / "error reading SQL command" and turn CI red. The tests should be removed or rewritten in this PR to assert the new disabled behavior.

title: Error message "sqlExpressions is not implemented" is misleading — the feature is deliberately disabled
body: When a dashboard or alert rule contains a SQL expression, the query now fails with the error "sqlExpressions is not implemented". The feature is in fact implemented but has been intentionally disabled in response to CVE-2024-9264 (RCE/LFI), which is exactly the situation users and support staff will need to understand when previously working SQL expressions start failing. The message text is wrong and will generate confusion; it should say something like "SQL expressions are disabled" (ideally referencing the security advisory) instead of claiming the feature does not exist.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false; the feature-flag check is dead, inverted code
body: The new function `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`, then returns `false` on every path (both inside the `if enabled` branch and at the final return). The flag therefore has no effect at all — which matches the PR's intent of hard-disabling SQL expressions for CVE-2024-9264, but the code is written as if it were a real flag check, with a variable named `enabled` holding the inverse of the flag state. This is a maintenance hazard: a future reader can easily misread it as flag-gated behavior, or 'simplify' it to `return enabled`, which would invert the flag (feature on when flag is off, off when flag is on). If the hard disable is intentional, the function should be reduced to an explicit `return false` (or the gate inlined) with a comment stating that SQL expressions are deliberately disabled for CVE-2024-9264, so the behavior cannot be accidentally changed.

title: No regression test pins the disabled-SQL-expression behavior
body: This security fix changes behavior in two places (ReadQuery now rejects `type: sql` queries, and the `sql.DB` stub makes `sql.TablesList`/`NewSQLCommand` always fail), but the PR adds no test asserting either behavior. There is nothing preventing a future refactor — e.g., someone 'implementing' the stub `DB` in pkg/expr/sql/db.go by reintroducing a DuckDB dependency — from silently re-enabling the vulnerable code path. A small test that ReadQuery returns an error for a SQL expression query, and that NewSQLCommand fails, would lock in the mitigation. The PR also does not touch any existing tests covering the SQL expression parser/command paths, so the impact of the always-erroring stub on the existing pkg/expr test suite should be verified before merge.

title: Stub DB has no comment explaining it intentionally disables SQL evaluation
body: The newly added `DB` type replaces the DuckDB-backed implementation with methods that all return `errors.New("not implemented")`, but neither the type, the methods, nor `NewInMemoryDB` carry any comment explaining that this is a deliberate security mitigation for CVE-2024-9264 (RCE/LFI via DuckDB) rather than an unfinished feature. Without that context, the stub looks like work-in-progress code that a contributor might helpfully 'finish' by re-adding go-duck, reintroducing the vulnerability. A short package/type comment referencing the CVE and stating that SQL expression evaluation must stay disabled would prevent that.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false, leaving dead feature-flag logic and an unreachable SQL branch
body: The new enableSqlExpressions function computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns false on every path, so the feature-flag lookup is dead code and the entire `case QueryTypeSQL` body after the gate (lines 133-138) is unreachable. As written the code looks like a logic bug (an inverted check that is then discarded) and invites a future well-meaning 'fix' that flips it and silently re-enables the CVE-2024-9264 attack surface. If the intent is permanent removal, this should be an explicit `return false` (or an unconditional error at the call site) with a comment referencing the CVE; the accompanying user-facing message 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' is also misleading, since the feature is implemented but deliberately disabled for security reasons.

title: No regression test for the CVE-2024-9264 fix
body: This PR disables SQL expressions to fix a critical RCE/LFI vulnerability but adds or updates no tests. There is no test asserting that a SQL expression query (e.g. one using read_csv/read_blob against a local file, the known exploit shape) is rejected through the ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery path, and none asserting that NewSQLCommand/sql.TablesList now fail. A future change that re-implements pkg/expr/sql.DB or touches the inverted logic in enableSqlExpressions could silently re-open the vulnerability without any test failing. Additionally, any existing unit tests that exercised sql.TablesList or SQLCommand against the real DuckDB are not touched in this PR and would now fail against the always-erroring stub, so the test suite state for this package should be verified.

title: Legacy SQL command path is blocked only implicitly via the stub DB error
body: The reader.go gate explicitly rejects QueryTypeSQL, but the legacy parsing path (UnmarshalSQLCommand -> NewSQLCommand, used by the rawNode-based query parsing) has no explicit disable check. It is blocked only as a side effect of sql.TablesList now always returning 'not implemented' from the stub DB, which surfaces to users as the confusing 400 error 'error reading SQL command' instead of a clear 'SQL expressions are disabled' message. Functionally this does close the hole today (and the DuckDB dependency is removed from go.mod), but the protection relies on the stub never being re-implemented; if pkg/expr/sql.DB is ever given a real implementation, this path would re-enable SQL expression execution with no feature-flag or security gate. An explicit check or comment here would make the security invariant robust against future refactoring.

title: Dropping the build-wide lock makes GetIndex+BuildIndex non-atomic; same key can be built concurrently
body: BuildIndex previously held cacheMu for its entire duration; it now only locks while inserting the finished index into b.cache. The check in GetIndex and the build/insert are therefore not atomic: two goroutines building the same NamespacedResource (e.g. a watch event handled via handleEvent -> getOrCreateIndex racing a concurrent Search for a namespace that was not pre-built at startup, or two concurrent Searches for a cold namespace) will both build a complete index. One result then silently overwrites the other in the cache, leaking the losing index (for file-backed indexes, an open bleve index whose handles are never closed). Worse, when size > FileThreshold both goroutines call bleve.New on the same on-disk directory, and the second open fails on the store's directory lock, so one caller gets an error even though the index is being built. Consider a per-key lock, singleflight, or an inflight-builds map so concurrent builders for the same key share one build while different keys still build in parallel.

title: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without holding cacheMu and now runs concurrently with cache writes
body: TotalDocs loops over b.cache without taking cacheMu. This PR adds a new caller: searchSupport.init now logs s.search.TotalDocs() (search.go) immediately after starting the watch-event goroutine, and that goroutine can concurrently trigger BuildIndex via handleEvent -> getOrCreateIndex, which writes to b.cache under cacheMu.Lock. An unsynchronized map iteration racing a map write causes a fatal, non-recoverable 'concurrent map read and map write' runtime panic. TotalDocs should acquire b.cacheMu.RLock() for the duration of the iteration.

title: Init failure in NewResourceServer leaks already-initialized resources
body: When s.Init(ctx) fails, NewResourceServer returns nil, err without any cleanup: the cancellable context created a few lines above is never cancelled (cancel is otherwise only invoked via Stop), the lifecycle backend initialized by lifecycle.Init (e.g. the SQL backend's open DB) is never stopped, and if the failure occurs in initWatcher after search.init succeeded, the watch goroutine started inside search.init runs on context.Background() and keeps polling forever. The error path should call s.cancel() and, when lifecycle was initialized, lifecycle.Stop (or otherwise unwind the partial initialization).

title: Stop() no longer blocks requests: handlers dropped the Init/initErr check
body: Every gRPC handler previously began with `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil { return ... }`, which surfaced s.initErr — including the 'service is stopping/stopped' values written by Stop(). With those guards removed, s.initErr is never read after construction, so Create/Update/Delete/Read/List/Search/PutBlob keep serving against the backend even after Stop() has been called; the stopped-state logic in Stop() is now dead code (and its unsynchronized writes to initErr race with any concurrent Init). Either restore a cheap initErr check in the handlers or remove the initErr mutation from Stop to avoid implying a shutdown guard that no longer exists.

title: Data race on shared err and counter in concurrent index build loop
body: In searchSupport.init, every goroutine spawned via group.Go writes to the outer err variable (`_, _, err = s.build(ctx, ...)`) and increments totalBatchesIndexed without any synchronization. With initWorkers > 1 (the whole point of this PR is concurrent namespace builds), these are concurrent reads/writes of shared variables: a Go data race that will fail under -race, the trace event count (span.AddEvent using totalBatchesIndexed) can be wrong, and worse, the closure returns the shared err — if goroutine A's build fails but goroutine B overwrites err with nil before A's `return err` is evaluated, errgroup sees nil and startup succeeds with a failed/missing index. Use a local variable inside the closure (`_, _, berr := s.build(...); return berr`) and an atomic counter (or compute the count from len(stats)).

title: Watch goroutine panics on closed events channel and uses a never-canceled context
body: The watch loop started at the end of searchSupport.init uses `watchctx := context.Background()` (so it is never canceled on server shutdown) and then does `for { v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v) }` without checking the receive's ok flag. The SQL backend's poller closes the events channel when the backend stops; receiving from a closed channel returns nil immediately, so handleEvent dereferences a nil *WrittenEvent at `evt.Type` — an unrecovered panic in this goroutine crashes the entire process during shutdown (and absent the panic the loop would spin at 100% CPU). Because this PR makes init run unconditionally at server construction, this goroutine now always starts. It should be `v, ok := <-events; if !ok { return }`, and the context should be tied to the server lifecycle. Note the same unguarded-receive pattern exists in initWatcher in server.go.

title: No guard against concurrent BuildIndex for the same key after removing the whole-function lock
body: BuildIndex now only locks cacheMu for the final cache insert, and nothing prevents two goroutines from building the same NamespacedResource concurrently: searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex checks GetIndex and then builds outside any lock (its own TODO acknowledges this), so two simultaneous Search requests, or a watch event racing a search, for a namespace that was skipped at startup (below InitMinCount) or newly created will both call BuildIndex. For file-backed indexes (size > FileThreshold) both call bleve.New on the same directory, so one fails with a store-lock/already-exists error that is surfaced to the user even though nothing is actually wrong; for in-memory indexes one fully built index is silently discarded by the last cache write and IndexTenants is double-counted. The previous whole-function mutex at least serialized these duplicate builds. A per-key lock or singleflight around check-build-cache would fix it.

title: No test coverage for the new eager-init contract
body: NewResourceServer now runs s.Init synchronously and returns an error when backend init or the index build fails, and the s.Init(ctx) guards were removed from every gRPC handler (Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search, History, Origin, IsHealthy, PutBlob, GetBlob) — but no test was added or updated to cover the new contract: that construction-time init failures propagate, or that handlers behave correctly without ever calling Init. The only test change in the PR skips the postgres variant of the one integration test that exercises the storage-server target. A unit test around NewResourceServer init success/failure (e.g., with a failing StorageBackend) would catch regressions in this new startup behavior.

title: TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu
body: TotalDocs ranges over b.cache with no lock, while BuildIndex writes to the same map under b.cacheMu.Lock() (bleve.go:137-139) and GetIndex reads it under RLock. This PR adds a new caller in searchSupport.init (pkg/storage/unified/resource/search.go) that invokes s.search.TotalDocs() in the 'search index initialized' log line immediately after starting the watch-event goroutine; that goroutine can concurrently trigger BuildIndex for a not-yet-indexed namespace (handleEvent -> getOrCreateIndex -> build). Concurrent map iteration and map insertion is a fatal, unrecoverable runtime error in Go ("concurrent map read and map write") and will crash the server. Fix: take b.cacheMu.RLock() around the iteration in TotalDocs.

title: Removing the function-wide lock allows concurrent duplicate builds of the same index
body: BuildIndex previously held cacheMu for its entire duration, which serialized builds; now nothing prevents two goroutines from building an index for the same NamespacedResource at the same time. This is reachable because getOrCreateIndex in pkg/storage/unified/resource/search.go does GetIndex-then-BuildIndex with no per-key coordination (its own TODO admits this) — e.g. two concurrent Search gRPC requests for a namespace below InitMinCount, or a search racing a watch-event-driven build. Consequences: for file-backed indexes both goroutines call bleve.New on the same directory concurrently (error or a corrupt/duplicated on-disk index), resource.IndexMetrics.IndexTenants is incremented twice, and the losing index is overwritten in b.cache without ever being closed, leaking the bleve index and its file handles. Consider a per-key mutex or singleflight so only one build per key runs and concurrent callers wait for it.

title: errgroup workers in init race on shared err and totalBatchesIndexed
body: In searchSupport.init, each group.Go closure executes `_, _, err = s.build(...)` and then `return err`, writing to the err variable declared in the outer function scope, and also does `totalBatchesIndexed++` (line 189) without synchronization. Since this PR's goal is building many namespaces with high concurrency, these goroutines race: one worker can overwrite another worker's error between the assignment and the return, so group.Wait() can report nil even though a build failed — startup then proceeds with a missing or partial index for that namespace — and the unsynchronized counter increments corrupt the span attribute and will fail the Go race detector. Fix: use a closure-local variable (`_, _, berr := s.build(...); return berr`) and replace the counter with len(stats) or an atomic.

title: Init failure in NewResourceServer leaks the search watcher goroutine
body: When s.Init(ctx) fails, NewResourceServer returns without calling s.cancel() and without stopping whatever Init already started. The reordering in Init (search.init now runs before initWatcher) makes this concrete: if s.search.init(ctx) succeeds but s.initWatcher() then fails, search.init has already spawned a goroutine consuming WatchWriteEvents using context.Background() (search.go lines 202-213), which drives a DB poller every 100ms with no cancellation path. Previously initWatcher ran first, so its failure could not strand the search watcher. Call s.cancel() on the error path, and pass the server's cancellable context into the search watcher instead of context.Background() so it can actually be stopped.

title: Removing per-request Init checks also removes request rejection after Stop
body: The deleted `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil { return ... }` guards in every handler were also the mechanism that rejected traffic after shutdown: Stop() sets s.initErr ("service is stopping"/"service is stopped"), and each handler surfaced that error via s.Init. With the guards removed, a stopped server keeps serving Create/Update/Delete/Read/List/Watch/Search normally — only the internal watch context is cancelled — and the initErr writes in Stop() no longer have any effect on requests. If rejecting requests after Stop is still intended, add an explicit stopped check to the handlers; otherwise drop the now-dead initErr bookkeeping in Stop to avoid implying a guarantee that no longer exists.

title: Storage-server startup test disabled on postgres
body: This integration test is the one place exercising the PR's core change — initializing unified storage eagerly when the ResourceServer is constructed in the storage-server target — and the PR disables the postgres variant with a TODO. That leaves the new eager-init startup path (DB access plus index build during module init) without CI coverage on postgres, one of the two supported production databases, exactly when the startup behavior changed. If the failure indicates eager init breaks under postgres in some environments, skipping hides a real regression rather than a test-only problem; this should be root-caused or tracked before relying on the new startup behavior.

title: Call to no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() does not match the one-arg method in UsernamePasswordForm — code does not compile
body: UsernameForm.authenticate() calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments, but the only method with that name in the class hierarchy is `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` declared in the parent class UsernamePasswordForm (lines 160-162). There is no no-arg overload in UsernameForm, UsernamePasswordForm, or AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator, so this is a Java compilation error and the services module will not build. The fix should either call `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())` here or make the helper no-arg (the latter is what the rest of the change actually needs, see the finding on UsernamePasswordForm).

title: Requiring a non-null user in isConditionalPasskeysEnabled disables passkey conditional UI on the initial (user-less) login page
body: The new helper `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` includes a `user != null` condition, and both call sites pass `context.getUser()` (authenticate() at line 115 and challenge(context, error, field) at line 137). On a regular, non-re-authentication login, `context.getUser()` is null when the login page is first rendered, and it is also null when the error challenge is re-rendered after a failed username/password attempt (the user is only set on the context after successful validation, and badPasswordHandler clears it). As a result `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` is skipped exactly in the cases where it ran before this PR (previously the fill was guarded by `context.getUser() == null` or was inside the user==null else-branch). The rendered login page then lacks the WebAuthn challenge, the hidden `#webauth` form, and the `username webauthn` autocomplete attribute, so passkey autofill / discoverable-key (passwordless) login stops working for normal first-time logins — the feature only works during re-authentication. This also contradicts the PR's own tests, e.g. PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest.passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey and passwordLoginWithExternalKey assert `getUsernameAutocomplete() == "username webauthn"` and the presence of `//form[@id='webauth']` on the initial login page where no user is set. The user check should be removed (make the helper depend only on `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()`).

title: No-arg call isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() does not compile
body: UsernameForm.authenticate() now calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments, but after this PR the only method with that name in the class hierarchy is `UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` (declared in UsernamePasswordForm.java at line 160). There is no zero-argument overload in UsernameForm, UsernamePasswordForm, or AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator, so this is a compilation error ("no suitable method found for isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()") and the build fails. Either restore a no-arg `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` helper in UsernamePasswordForm (e.g. `return webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled();`) or pass the user explicitly at this call site.

title: user != null check in isConditionalPasskeysEnabled removes passkeys from the initial login page
body: The new helper `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` returns true only when `user != null`. Both call sites pass `context.getUser()`: `authenticate()` at line 115 and `challenge(context, error, field)` at line 137. On a normal first-time login the user is not yet identified, so `context.getUser()` is null and `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` is never invoked. The rendered username/password page then lacks everything the passkeys conditional UI needs (the enableWebAuthnConditionalUI flag, the challenge/rpId attributes, the "username webauthn" autocomplete on the username field, and the webauth form). Previously fillContextForm ran in the user==null branch of authenticate(); the PR moved it out of that branch but gated it on the user being set, so it now runs ONLY during re-authentication — the condition was inverted instead of extended. This breaks ordinary passkey logins: the PR's own tests assert the webauthn form is present on the initial login page (e.g. PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest.passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey and passwordLoginWithExternalKey, PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest.passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey, PasskeysUsernameFormTest.passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey), so those tests would fail once the code compiles. The `&& user != null` condition should be dropped so the WebAuthn context is filled for both fresh logins and re-authentication.

title: Call to no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() does not compile
body: In UsernameForm.authenticate() the new condition calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments. The only method with that name is the one this PR adds to the superclass UsernamePasswordForm, declared as isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user). UsernameForm declares no zero-argument overload, and none exists in AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator, so this line cannot compile and the services module build fails. It presumably should be isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()).

title: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires a non-null user, so passkeys UI disappears on all fresh logins
body: The new helper returns `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null`, and both call sites pass context.getUser() (authenticate() at line 115 and challenge(context, error, field) at line 137). On a normal, non-reauthentication login context.getUser() is null, so the condition is false and webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) is never invoked for fresh logins. Previously the form was filled exactly in that case ("user is not already selected"). As a result the username/password page is rendered without the WebAuthn conditional-UI attributes (enableWebAuthnConditionalUI, challenge, rpId) for anonymous users, completely breaking passkey autofill / discoverable-key login on first-time logins — the primary scenario the passkeys feature exists for — including after a failed first login attempt (the error challenge also loses the WebAuthn markup). The PR's own tests would fail, e.g. PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest.webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey expects automatic login from a fresh login form and several tests assert //form[@id='webauth'] is present on fresh login pages. The user check should be inverted or dropped (e.g. allow a null user, and for the re-authentication case optionally verify the identified user actually has a passwordless WebAuthn credential).

title: Login cache invalidation is skipped for IDPs whose organization is disabled, leaving stale entries after the org is re-enabled
body: registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate compares getLoginPredicate() on the 'original' and 'updated' models to decide whether the .idp.login caches must be invalidated. The 'original' model comes from getById() (line 91), which returns the organization-aware wrapper whose isEnabled() returns false whenever the linked organization is disabled. The cached login ID sets, however, are built from the JPA query which only looks at the raw flags (enabled, hideOnLogin, linkOnly, BROKER_PUBLIC). So an org-linked IDP with enabled=true in a disabled org IS present in the cached login sets, yet predicate(original) is false. If an admin then updates that IDP so it no longer qualifies for login (sets hideOnLogin=true, linkOnly=true, or BROKER_PUBLIC=false, or moves it to another org), predicate(updated) is also false and no invalidation is registered (the early return at line 405-407). When the organization is later re-enabled (an org update does not invalidate these caches), the stale cached ID set is served: getById returns the fresh model whose org-aware isEnabled() is now true, and the only consumer-side re-check added in this PR (OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean) filters on isEnabled() only, so an IDP that should be hidden, link-only, or private to an org is displayed on the login page. The predicate for the 'original' state should be evaluated against the unwrapped/raw stored model (as remove() already does with idpDelegate.getByAlias) so the comparison matches what is actually in the cache.

title: Cleanup in testCacheIDPForLogin registers removal of a literal IdP named "alias" instead of the created providers
body: In testCacheIDPForLogin the creation loop does getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove) with the literal string "alias" (same again at line 425 for idp-alias-20). No identity provider with alias "alias" exists, so the 21 providers the test creates (idp-alias-0 .. idp-alias-20, ten of them linked to orga) are never cleaned up, and the deferred remove() call will hit a 404 during cleanup. Because the test realm is shared across the class, the leftover org-linked IDPs contaminate other tests that assert exact counts — e.g. testCacheIDPByOrg asserts orga's cached IDP list has exactly 6 entries, which fails if testCacheIDPForLogin ran first and left 10 more IDPs linked to orga. The cleanup should reference the actual alias created in each iteration (and "idp-alias-20" for the later one), e.g. by capturing final String alias = "idp-alias-" + i and using get(alias).

title: Login-cache invalidation on update compares org-aware (wrapped) original against raw updated model, missing invalidations
body: In update(), the "original" IdP passed to registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate is obtained via getById(...), which wraps the model with createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel when the organization feature is enabled. That wrapper overrides isEnabled() to additionally require the linked organization to be enabled. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate then evaluates LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate() (which includes isEnabled()) on this wrapped original but on the raw updated model, so the two sides are not comparable — and neither matches what defines cache membership, since the cached login lists are filled by idpDelegate.getForLogin(...), which filters on the raw persisted enabled flag. When the IdP's organization is currently disabled, the predicate on the wrapped original is always false, so any update that also makes the raw updated model fail the predicate registers no invalidation. Concretely: disable an org whose public IdP is already in the cached getForLogin lists, then set hideOnLogin=true (or linkOnly=true, or brokerPublic=false) on that IdP — original predicate is false (org disabled) and updated predicate is false, so no login-cache invalidation is registered. When the org is re-enabled (org changes do not invalidate these caches), getForLogin still returns the stale cached entry, and OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean — which only re-checks isEnabled(), not hideOnLogin/linkOnly/brokerPublic — renders the IdP on the login page even though the administrator explicitly removed it from login. Fix by basing the invalidation decision on the raw stored model (e.g. idpDelegate.getById(model.getInternalId())) instead of the org-aware wrapper, or by invalidating the login caches unconditionally on update.

title: testCacheIDPForLogin cleanup targets literal alias "alias", leaking all created identity providers
body: In testCacheIDPForLogin the cleanup is registered as getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove) — the literal string "alias" instead of the alias of the provider just created ("idp-alias-" + i in the loop at line 381, and "idp-alias-20" at line 425).
