Consequence: all updated event assertions (expectCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectDeviceCodeToToken, expectAuthReqIdToToken) pass regardless of which grant type is actually encoded in the token ID, so the integration-level verification of this PR's main feature is vacuous — a grant flow that forgets to set Constants.GRANT_TYPE (and thus encodes "na") or encodes the wrong shortcut would go completely undetected.

title: Constructor null-checks grantType twice and never validates rawTokenId
body: The AccessTokenContext constructor contains `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed");` — the third check repeats grantType instead of checking rawTokenId. As a result a null rawTokenId is silently accepted, and DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId would then produce a token ID ending in `...:null` instead of failing fast. The line should be `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed");`.

title: testIncorrectGrantType passes due to NullPointerException from uninitialized sessionFactory, not the intended validation error
body: The test's before() method calls factory.init(null) and sets the shortcut maps directly, but never calls postInit(), so DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.sessionFactory remains null. When getTokenContextFromTokenId("ofrtac:5678") encounters the unregistered "ac" shortcut, getGrantTypeByShortcut() enters its lazy-refresh branch and calls sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream(...), which throws a NullPointerException. The test catches generic RuntimeException, so it passes for the wrong reason and does not verify the intended IllegalArgumentException("Unknown value 'ac' for grant type"). If decoding stopped rejecting unknown shortcuts, this test would not necessarily catch it. It should catch IllegalArgumentException specifically (and assert the message), so the intended behavior is actually verified.

title: getShortcut() javadoc says "3-letters shortcut" but the decoder requires exactly 2 characters
body: The javadoc for the new getShortcut() method says the shortcut is "usually like 3-letters shortcut of specific grants". However, DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId assumes the grant shortcut is exactly 2 characters: it requires a 6-character context prefix and parses it as 2 (session type) + 2 (token type) + 2 (grant type). All built-in grants added in this PR return 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "ro", ...). A custom OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implemented following this javadoc with a 3-letter shortcut would emit token IDs that the decoder then rejects as malformed. The javadoc should state that the shortcut must be exactly 2 characters and unique across grants.

title: Recovery codes stored in user storage are never consumed and remain reusable
body: When the recovery-codes credential lives in a user storage provider (the new federated path introduced by this PR), a successful `credentialManager().isValid(...)` here delegates to the provider's `CredentialInputValidator.isValid`, which can only return true/false. The local `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.isValid`, by contrast, removes the used code from the stored credential as part of validation. Nothing in this authenticator (or anywhere else) marks the used code as consumed for the federated case: the subsequent `allCodesUsed()` check re-reads the credential from the user storage via `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential`, which still contains all the codes, so a used recovery code stays valid forever and can be replayed any number of times. Recovery codes are designed as one-time credentials, so this silently downgrades their security whenever they are stored in user storage, and the 'all codes used -> remove credential and force re-configuration' flow never triggers. The new test `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest.testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` only logs in once with a single code and never asserts that the same code is rejected on a second login, so the regression is not caught. Either the authenticator must consume the code through the SPI (e.g. re-write the credential without the used code) or the SPI contract must clearly require providers to consume one-time codes inside `isValid`, with test coverage for code reuse.

title: Recovery-code login 500s for user-storage users unless the provider overrides the optional getCredentials with a fully-formed hashed model
body: This bean (and `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator`) now resolve the credential via `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user)`, which for federated users relies on `CredentialInputValidator.getCredentials` — a default SPI method that returns an empty stream — and then calls `credentialModelOpt.get()` without handling the empty case. A user storage provider that opts into recovery codes the way the SPI documentation suggests for password/OTP — implementing `supportsCredentialType`, `updateCredential` (which receives a plain JSON array of the raw codes as the `UserCredentialModel` challenge response from `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential`), and `isValid` — but does not override `getCredentials` will make every recovery-code login page render throw `NoSuchElementException` (HTTP 500). If the provider instead returns the raw `CredentialModel` it stored from `updateCredential`, `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel` throws `IllegalArgumentException` because `secretData` is null and `credentialData` holds the raw JSON array rather than the hashed `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialData`/`SecretData` structures. The test provider only works because it re-builds the model through `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues`, re-hashing the raw codes on every read — a requirement that is undocumented and inconsistent with the shape handed to the provider on write. The read-side contract for `getCredentials` should be enforced or documented, and the consumers should degrade gracefully when no credential is returned.

title: Recovery codes stored in user storage are never consumed after successful use
body: When a user's recovery codes live in a user-storage provider (the capability this PR adds), a successfully used code is never invalidated. For locally stored codes, single-use semantics are enforced inside RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.isValid(), which removes the used code from the stored credential. In the federated path, RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.isRecoveryAuthnCodeInputValid() calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().isValid(...), which delegates to the storage provider's CredentialInputValidator.isValid(), and the framework performs no consumption step afterwards. The PR's own reference implementation (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid) only compares the presented code against the stored list and never removes it. Consequences: every recovery code remains valid indefinitely, breaking the one-time-use guarantee of the feature; RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.allCodesUsed() never becomes true, so the user is never forced to regenerate codes and the login form always asks for code #1; and even if a storage did consume codes itself, the cleanup call authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()) operates on Keycloak's local credential store and cannot remove a credential living in user storage. The feature needs a consumption/update mechanism for federated credentials (e.g., writing the reduced code list back through CredentialInputUpdater.updateCredential after a successful validation) or the limitation must be explicitly handled.

title: Plaintext recovery codes are pushed to user storage while local storage keeps only hashes
body: createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generated recovery codes (JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes)) and sends them to the user storage via a UserCredentialModel. When the same credential is stored locally, RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues() hashes every code via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode() so only hashes are persisted (verification is done with verifyRecoveryCodeInput against the hash). Unlike OTP secrets — which an external store genuinely needs in clear text to compute TOTP — recovery-code verification can be performed by hashing the presented code, so there is no technical need to hand the raw codes to the user storage. As implemented, any external user storage that opts into recovery codes ends up holding every user's recovery codes in clear text (and the codes transit in clear through CredentialInput.getChallengeResponse()), so a read-breach of that store, its backups, or its logs exposes all of a user's recovery codes. Consider sending hashed codes to the storage and documenting that storages should hash the presented code in isValid(), matching the local storage security posture.

title: New recovery-keys test never verifies single-use semantics
body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin performs only one successful login with one recovery code. It never attempts to reuse the same code, never checks that the remaining-code count decreases, and never exercises the all-codes-used path (credential removal and re-adding the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action). Because of this, the test passes even though recovery codes stored in user storage are currently reusable after a successful login — the core security property of the feature is unverified. The test should at minimum assert that a second login attempt with the same code fails and that a subsequent login requests a different code number.

title: Recovery codes stored in user storage are never consumed, replayable forever, and cannot be removed
body: With this PR a recovery-code credential can now live in an external user storage, but the 'single use' semantics of recovery codes are lost on that path. For locally stored codes, RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.isValid() marks the used code as consumed so it cannot be replayed and the next login asks for the next unused code. For a federated credential, validation is delegated to the storage's CredentialInputValidator.isValid() (a read-only boolean check, see BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid) and nothing ever marks a code as used, so the credential reconstructed from the storage always shows all 12 codes as unused. Consequences: (1) every recovery code of a storage-backed user stays valid indefinitely and can be replayed by anyone who observed it once; (2) the login form always asks for code #1, because RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean calls getNextRecoveryAuthnCode() on an all-unused credential, so code rotation never happens; (3) the cleanup here at lines 85-88 calls credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(id), which only removes credentials from Keycloak's own store — the CredentialInputUpdater SPI has no remove-by-id operation for external storages — so even an exhausted federated credential would silently never be deleted (likewise, admin delete/disable of such a credential is a no-op in the sample provider). The new test BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest.enterRecoveryCodes actually bakes in the always-code-#0 behavior rather than detecting it. Before merging, used-code state should be pushed back to the storage (e.g., via CredentialInputUpdater.updateCredential after a successful validation) or the limitation explicitly documented and tested.

title: Raw recovery codes are sent to and persisted in user storage as plaintext JSON
body: In CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential, when the credential is delegated to a user storage, the raw, unhashed recovery codes are serialized (JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes) at line 119) and passed to CredentialInputUpdater.updateCredential as the UserCredentialModel challenge response, so the external store persists all 12 valid codes in plaintext JSON. When the same credential is created locally (line 129), only SHA-512 hashes are stored, because RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues hashes each code via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode. Consequence: for storage-backed users, anyone with read access to the external store (database, backups, logs) immediately obtains working recovery codes that bypass the second factor entirely — a weaker protection level than Keycloak's own store provides for the identical data. The sample provider BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage mirrors this by storing the plaintext JSON and comparing the presented code in cleartext. The hashed credential data (credentialModel.getCredentialData()) could be sent to the storage instead, with validators hashing the presented code via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode before comparing, so both storage paths keep only hashes.

title: User label and original generation timestamp are dropped when recovery codes go to user storage
body: createRecoveryCodesCredential builds the UserCredentialModel sent to the user storage with only the JSON array of codes; the generatedUserLabel (collected from the setup form and applied to the locally created credential via RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues) and the generatedAt timestamp are never transmitted. The sample storage (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.updateCredential, recovery-codes branch) therefore stores createdDate = write time and userLabel = null. Consequence: the same setup flow produces different credential metadata depending on where the credential lands — the label the user assigned is silently lost for storage-backed users and createdDate no longer reflects when the codes were generated, which shows up incorrectly in the account console and breaks parity between the two paths. The label and generation time should be included in the payload sent to CredentialInputUpdater.updateCredential.

title: Paginated getSubGroupsStream overloads still NPE on the same concurrent-delete race
body: The fix null-checks the delegate model only in getSubGroupsCount(). The three paginated overloads getSubGroupsStream(String, Integer, Integer) (line 256), getSubGroupsStream(Integer, Integer) (line 262) and getSubGroupsStream(String, Boolean, Integer, Integer) (line 268) still dereference modelSupplier.get() directly. Under the exact race this PR targets — a GroupAdapter created from a still-valid cache entry whose database row was concurrently deleted — modelSupplier.get() returns null and these methods throw the same NullPointerException, e.g. when GET /admin/realms/{realm}/groups/{id}/children?first=0&max=10 is issued right after the group is removed while the cached entry is still valid. The same null handling applied to getSubGroupsCount (e.g. return Stream.empty() when the delegate is null) should be applied here so the fix is complete.

title: Reader thread is never joined, so the new regression test can pass even when the NPE still occurs
body: In createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti the main thread sets deletedAll.set(true) and immediately asserts caughtExceptions is empty, without joining the reader thread. A read iteration already in flight when the flag is set can still hit the NPE the test is meant to catch and add it to caughtExceptions after the assertion has executed, producing a false negative — the test can go green while the bug reproduces. The Thread reference is also discarded: if any group removal throws, deletedAll is never set and the non-daemon reader thread spins forever issuing requests past test teardown. The test should keep the Thread reference, set the flag in a finally block, and join() the thread before asserting on caughtExceptions.

title: Paginated getSubGroupsStream overloads still NPE when the group is deleted concurrently
body: The PR fixes getSubGroupsCount() by tolerating modelSupplier.get() returning null when the group was concurrently deleted, but the three paginated getSubGroupsStream overloads (lines 254-269: getSubGroupsStream(String, Integer, Integer), getSubGroupsStream(Integer, Integer), and getSubGroupsStream(String, Boolean, Integer, Integer)) still dereference modelSupplier.get() directly, e.g. 'return modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(search, firstResult, maxResults);'. Under the exact same race this PR targets — the cached group entry was read, then another transaction deletes the group before the call — modelSupplier.get() returns null and these methods throw a NullPointerException, surfacing as an HTTP 500 on endpoints such as GET /admin/realms/{realm}/groups/{id}/children. The same null handling should be applied there (return Stream.empty() or delegate consistently).

title: Concurrency test asserts before the reader thread finishes, so it can pass even if the NPE still occurs
body: In createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti, the reader thread is started and never joined: the main thread deletes the groups, sets deletedAll=true, and immediately asserts caughtExceptions is empty. The reader thread can be in the middle of its final groups() call when the assertion executes; an exception (such as the HTTP 500 caused by the NPE this PR fixes) can be added to caughtExceptions after the assertion has already passed, so the test reports success while the regression is still present, and conversely the timing makes it flaky. The test should keep a reference to the thread, set deletedAll, join() the thread (with a timeout), and only then assert that caughtExceptions is empty.

title: Reader thread spins forever if a group delete throws
body: deletedAll.set(true) on line 155 is only reached if all 100 remove() calls succeed. If any delete throws, the test fails but the non-daemon reader thread keeps looping and issuing list requests against the server indefinitely (until JVM exit), consuming CPU and adding load for the remainder of the test suite run. The delete loop should be wrapped in a try/finally that sets deletedAll (and, per the other finding, joins the thread) so the background thread is always stopped.

title: Reader thread is never joined, so the no-exception assertion races with in-flight requests
body: In createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti, the main thread deletes the groups, sets deletedAll, and immediately asserts that caughtExceptions is empty. The reader thread is started with new Thread(...).start() but the reference is discarded and it is never joined. When deletedAll is flipped, the reader may still be blocked inside managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(...); if that in-flight request triggers the very NPE/500 this test is meant to catch, the exception is appended to caughtExceptions after the assertion has already executed, so the test passes even though the bug reproduced. The test's outcome is therefore timing-dependent and can silently miss regressions. Keep the Thread reference, join() it (with a timeout) after deletedAll.set(true), and only then assert on caughtExceptions.

title: If a group deletion throws, the polling thread spins forever for the rest of the JVM lifetime
body: deletedAll.set(true) on line 155 is only reached if every managedRealm.admin().groups().group(groupUuid).remove() call in the preceding forEach succeeds. If any deletion throws (which is exactly the kind of failure this concurrency test is probing for), the flag is never set and the non-daemon reader thread keeps looping while (!deletedAll.get()) indefinitely, firing REST calls in a tight no-sleep loop and appending every resulting exception to the unbounded CopyOnWriteArrayList caughtExceptions. That leaked thread keeps hammering the server (and growing the list) through the remainder of the test suite, which can destabilize unrelated tests and the CI executor. Wrap the deletion loop in try/finally so the flag is always set, and join the thread.

title: Same concurrent-deletion NPE remains in the three getSubGroupsStream overloads
body: The PR fixes getSubGroupsCount() for the case where the group is concurrently deleted (modelSupplier.get() returns null), but the three getSubGroupsStream overloads directly above it (lines 256, 262, and 268) still dereference the supplier result without a null check: return modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...). Under the exact same race as issue #40368 — the group is deleted after the cached entry is loaded but before the lazy delegate lookup — modelSupplier.get() returns null and these paths throw a NullPointerException, surfacing as a 500 on endpoints such as GET /admin/realms/{realm}/groups/{id}/children. The same null handling applied in getSubGroupsCount() should be applied (or the method should consistently fall back to getDelegateForUpdate()/an empty stream) in all three overloads.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key crashes with TypeError on the datetime ordering the endpoint uses
body: OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint wires this paginator in with order_by="-datetime", but get_item_key does math.floor/math.ceil on getattr(item, "datetime"), which is a datetime object. math.floor/math.ceil raise TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime (DateTimePaginator exists precisely to convert datetimes to epoch-millis first). build_cursor calls get_item_key(results[0]) via _build_next_values/_build_prev_values, so any request to GET /organizations/{slug}/audit-logs/?optimized_pagination=true from an authorized admin 500s on the very first page as soon as the queryset returns a row. Additionally, value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor value instead of converting the epoch-ms cursor back into a datetime, so even a numeric cursor would be compared against a datetime column on subsequent pages. The entire 'optimized' path is unusable as shipped.

title: Unconditional organization_context.member.has_global_access dereferences a member that can be None
body: RpcUserOrganizationContext.member is None whenever the request is not tied to an organization membership, e.g. legacy API-key or org-token authentication against this endpoint, which previously worked. The new line computes enable_advanced on every GET request, even when optimized_pagination is not passed, and the short-circuit only protects requests where request.user.is_superuser is True. Any non-superuser request with member=None raises AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access', turning previously successful responses into 500s. The check needs to guard against member being None (e.g. organization_context.member is not None and organization_context.member.has_global_access).

title: "Advanced" negative-offset branch 500s: Django forbids negative queryset slicing
body: The new OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result branch for enable_advanced_features with cursor.offset < 0 passes the negative offset straight into queryset[start_offset:stop]. The comment claims "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically", which is false: QuerySet.__getitem__ asserts "Negative indexing is not supported". Cursor offsets come directly from the user-supplied cursor string (Cursor.from_string parses int(bits[1]) with no sign validation), so any caller who reaches the optimized path can send cursor=0:-1:0 and trigger an uncaught AssertionError -> 500. The same applies to 0:-1:1 since the branch does not check is_prev. Negative offsets must be rejected with BadPaginationError (which Endpoint.paginate converts to a 400) rather than passed to the ORM.

title: BasePaginator change makes negative cursor offsets silently return page one for forward cursors while prev cursors still 500
body: The changed slicing in BasePaginator.get_result uses start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset. A crafted forward cursor with a negative offset (e.g. 0:-5:0) is now silently clamped to 0 and returns the first page instead of being rejected, while a prev cursor with a negative offset (0:-5:1) still reaches the queryset slice and raises Django's uncaught AssertionError "Negative indexing is not supported" -> 500. The added comment ("the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions") is incorrect for the is_prev case, and the two directions now handle malformed cursors inconsistently. Negative offsets should be validated and rejected with BadPaginationError for both directions instead of clamped or passed through.

title: No tests for the new paginator, the negative-offset path, or the endpoint's optimized branch
body: The PR adds a new OptimizedCursorPaginator class, a user-reachable branch in the audit log endpoint, and a behavioral change to BasePaginator.get_result that affects all cursor-paginated endpoints, but adds no tests. Both new code paths fail on first use (the datetime TypeError in get_item_key and the negative-slice AssertionError), which a single happy-path test of GET /organizations/{slug}/audit-logs/?optimized_pagination=true would have caught, and the BasePaginator change has no coverage for prev/negative-offset cursors either.

title: New Cursor comment falsely advertises negative offsets as a supported pagination feature
body: The added comment claims negative offsets are allowed "for advanced pagination scenarios" and "enable efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets", but nothing in Cursor changed (int(offset) always accepted negatives), and the paginators that consume offsets either explicitly reject negatives (OffsetPaginator, ChainPaginator, CombinedQuerysetPaginator raise BadPaginationError on negative offsets) or crash on them (Django disallows negative queryset slicing). This documents a contract the rest of the pagination code does not support and could mislead future callers into emitting negative-offset cursors.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle datetime keys, but the audit log endpoint uses it with order_by="-datetime"
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor/math.ceil directly to getattr(item, self.key), copied from the numeric Paginator. The audit log endpoint instantiates it with order_by="-datetime", so the key value is a datetime object and math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime. get_item_key is called by build_cursor for every non-empty page (including the first page, via _build_next_values), so any request with optimized_pagination=true that returns at least one audit log row will 500. Additionally, value_from_cursor returns the raw numeric cursor value instead of converting it back to a datetime the way DateTimePaginator does, so even if get_item_key were fixed, subsequent pages would compare a timestamp column against a bare integer in the .extra(where=...) clause, causing a database error or wrong filtering. The paginator needs DateTimePaginator-style key/value handling, or the endpoint should not use it with a datetime ordering.

title: "Advanced" negative-offset branch slices the queryset with a negative index, which Django rejects with ValueError
body: When enable_advanced_features is set and the incoming cursor has a negative offset, the code evaluates queryset[cursor.offset : cursor.offset + limit + extra] with a negative slice start. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing — queryset[-10:5] raises ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported — so the request returns a 500. The inline comment claiming "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false. Negative offsets are client-controllable because Cursor.from_string accepts them (e.g. cursor=0:-10:0), while cursors produced by build_cursor never contain negative offsets, so this branch only ever triggers on hand-crafted cursors and only ever crashes. The advertised feature provides no working functionality; it should either be implemented against a real mechanism or removed, with negative offsets rejected up front.

title: organization_context.member may be None, causing AttributeError for token-authenticated requests
body: For every non-superuser request the new code evaluates organization_context.member.has_global_access, but RpcUserOrganizationContext.member is None when the caller has no membership row — for example requests authenticated with an org auth token or API key carrying org:read scope, which legitimately pass OrganizationAuditPermission. The previous code never dereferenced member, so such requests now fail with AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access' and return a 500. Guard the access (e.g. organization_context.member is not None and organization_context.member.has_global_access) and decide explicitly whether token-authenticated callers may use the optimized path.

title: No tests cover OptimizedCursorPaginator or the optimized_pagination query parameter
body: The PR adds a new ~100-line paginator class and a new endpoint branch selected via optimized_pagination=true, but adds no tests. Any test exercising the new path with actual results would have caught that it raises TypeError on datetime keys and that the negative-offset branch 500s. Add unit tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator (datetime ordering, cursor round-trips, is_prev handling) and endpoint tests covering both branches, including non-superuser members and token-authenticated callers.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator applies numeric key math to a datetime column and 500s on every non-empty page
body: The audit log endpoint invokes OptimizedCursorPaginator with order_by="-datetime", but get_item_key and value_from_cursor were copied from the numeric Paginator instead of DateTimePaginator. get_item_key executes math.ceil(getattr(item, "datetime")), which raises TypeError ("must be real number, not datetime.datetime") because datetime objects have no float conversion. build_cursor calls get_item_key whenever a page has at least one result (to compute the next/prev cursor values), so any request with optimized_pagination=true against an organization that has at least one audit log entry fails with an unhandled 500. Even if that were fixed, value_from_cursor returns the raw millisecond cursor value, which build_queryset then compares directly against the timestamp column in SQL (datetime_col <= <bigint>) instead of converting it back to a datetime the way DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor does, so page 2 and beyond would return wrong data or a database error. The class should subclass DateTimePaginator or reuse its get_item_key/value_from_cursor implementations.

title: Advanced negative-offset branch slices the queryset with a negative index, which Django rejects
body: When enable_advanced_features is set and the incoming cursor has a negative offset — trivially supplied by a client as cursor=0:-5:0, which Cursor.from_string parses without any validation — the branch at lines 877-882 executes queryset[cursor.offset : cursor.offset + limit + extra] with a negative start index. Django QuerySets explicitly reject negative indexing/slicing by raising ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported."), so the comment claiming "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false and this request crashes with an unhandled 500. The endpoint in organization_auditlogs.py enables this path for superusers/global-access members who pass optimized_pagination=true, so any such caller supplying a negative-offset cursor gets a server error instead of the advertised "efficient reverse pagination."

title: organization_context.member may be None; unconditional .has_global_access dereference can 500 every audit log request
body: RpcUserOrganizationContext.member is Optional — it is None when the caller can access the organization without holding a membership, e.g. requests authenticated with an organization auth token, where request.user is anonymous and is_superuser is False. For those callers the short-circuit on request.user.is_superuser does not protect the second operand, and evaluating organization_context.member.has_global_access raises AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'. Because this line executes unconditionally for every GET (not only when optimized_pagination=true), it turns previously working requests into 500s. It should be guarded (e.g. organization_context.member is not None and organization_context.member.has_global_access), and it should be verified that has_global_access exists on the RpcOrganizationMember pydantic model, not only on the ORM OrganizationMember.

title: New paginator and audit-log pagination path ship with no tests
body: The PR adds OptimizedCursorPaginator (about 90 lines duplicating BasePaginator.get_result) plus a new branch in the organization audit logs endpoint, but adds no tests for either. A single smoke test calling the endpoint with optimized_pagination=true against an org containing one audit log entry would have caught that get_item_key crashes on datetime values (paginator.py:840), and a negative-offset test would have caught the invalid queryset slicing (paginator.py:882). Since this paginator is documented as intended for reuse on high-traffic endpoints, it needs coverage for the first page, next/prev pages with datetime cursors, and negative offsets before merging.

title: Comment claims BasePaginator now allows negative offsets, but the code clamps them to 0
body: The added comment in BasePaginator.get_result says the change will "allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination without full dataset scanning," but the code does the opposite for forward cursors: start_offset = max(0, offset) clamps any negative offset to 0, and for previous-page cursors the behavior is identical to before (the offset is passed through unchanged). The change is therefore a behavior-preserving clamp, not the optimization described, and the misleading text (echoed by the comment added in cursors.py:26-27) may lead future callers to believe negative offsets are safely supported here, when any negative value that actually reaches a queryset slice raises ValueError.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes with TypeError when used with datetime ordering
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key is copied from the numeric Paginator and does math.floor/math.ceil on the raw attribute value. Its only caller, OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint, uses it with order_by="-datetime", so the value is a datetime and math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError. build_cursor calls get_item_key on every non-empty page, so any request with optimized_pagination=true that returns at least one audit log row will 500. Additionally, value_from_cursor returns the raw numeric cursor value, so even if the first page worked, page 2 would compare a timestamp column against a float in the extra WHERE clause and raise a database error. The class needs DateTimePaginator-style key conversion (or should subclass DateTimePaginator). No test covers this path, which is why it wasn't caught.

title: "Advanced" negative-offset pagination always 500s: Django rejects negative slices
body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is set and the client supplies a cursor with a negative offset (Cursor.from_string accepts e.g. "0:-5:0"), the code evaluates queryset[cursor.offset : cursor.offset + limit + extra]. Django's QuerySet raises ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported") for negative slice bounds, so the request errors with a 500. The comments above the branch are false: Django does not "properly handle negative slicing automatically", and the statement "This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level" is meaningless. This advertised feature cannot work as written and is reachable via a crafted cursor query parameter on the audit log endpoint.

title: SET to ZSET type change on existing span-buf:s:* keys will cause WRONGTYPE errors during rolling deploys
body: The PR changes the Redis type of the existing span-buf:s:{project_id:trace_id}:span_id keys from SET (sadd/sscan/sunionstore/scard) to ZSET (zadd/zscan/zunionstore/zcard/zpopmin) while keeping the exact same key names. Segment keys live up to redis_ttl (3600s) and consumers are upgraded in a rolling fashion, so old and new code will operate on the same keys concurrently: old consumers' SADD/SSCAN against newly created ZSET keys, and new consumers' ZADD/ZCARD/ZPOPMIN/ZSCAN against SET keys created minutes earlier, both raise redis WRONGTYPE errors. That crashes span processing and flushing and drops spans. The migration needs a new key prefix or an explicit transition plan rather than reusing the live keyspace.

title: Spans evicted by ZPOPMIN are dropped silently with no metric or log
body: When a segment exceeds 1000 spans, the script now evicts the excess with ZPOPMIN, permanently discarding span payloads from the segment. The previous behavior (skip oversized segments at flush time) emitted the metric spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded and an error log; that check is removed from _load_segment_data in this PR, and the new eviction emits nothing: the script doesn't return the evicted count and process_spans records no metric. Operators lose all visibility into truncated segments and the associated data loss. Return the evicted count from the script and emit a metric/log from Python.

title: max_segment_spans option is now dead; the cap is hardcoded to 1000 in Lua
body: SpansBuffer.__init__ still accepts and stores max_segment_spans (default 1001), but the only remaining enforcement is a hardcoded `if span_count > 1000` in add-buffer.lua. The flush-time check that used self.max_segment_spans was removed from _load_segment_data, so configuring this option now silently does nothing (and the default 1001 doesn't even match the Lua 1000). Either pass the limit into the script as an ARGV or delete the parameter.

title: Redirect resolution limit lowered 10000 to 1000; deep traces will silently split into multiple segments
body: The redirect-following loop limit was reduced from 10000 to 1000 and the comment documenting the consequence ("segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. For trace trees deeper than 1000 redirects, the loop now stops early and the span is written to whatever set the partial resolution landed on, splitting one logical segment into multiple flushed segments (partial/duplicated output downstream). This tradeoff is 10x more reachable than before; if intentional for script latency, the consequence should stay documented and a metric should be emitted when the limit is actually hit.

title: No test coverage for the eviction feature or the new paginator
body: The headline behavior of this PR — capping segments at 1000 spans via ZPOPMIN during insert — has no test: the buffer tests were only updated to add the newly required end_timestamp_precise field. A test inserting more than 1000 spans into one segment should assert which spans survive (lowest end_timestamp_precise evicted), that the segment still flushes, and that TTLs are intact. Likewise, the new OptimizedCursorPaginator / audit-log optimized_pagination path has no tests at all; even a trivial smoke test would have caught that it 500s on the first page due to the datetime TypeError.

title: Added comment falsely claims negative cursor offsets are supported
body: The new comment in Cursor.__init__ says "Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios", but no code was changed and negative offsets are not actually usable: Django querysets raise ValueError on negative slices, and BasePaginator.get_result clamps negative next-cursor offsets to 0. This misdocuments the Cursor contract for anyone building on it and should be removed or corrected.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes on datetime-ordered querysets (breaks the new audit-log path)
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `int(math.floor(getattr(item, self.key))...)`, i.e. it assumes a numeric sort key, and value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor value unchanged. The only caller added in this PR (organization_auditlogs.py) uses it with `order_by="-datetime"`, so the attribute is a `datetime`. On the very first page, `build_cursor` calls `get_item_key` on the results and `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime`, so any request with `?optimized_pagination=true` against a non-empty audit log returns a 500. Even if the key type were fixed, value_from_cursor would need to convert the millisecond cursor value back to a datetime (as DateTimePaginator does); as written the integer is compared directly against a timestamp column, which Postgres rejects. This paginator is effectively a copy of the numeric Paginator and cannot serve the endpoint it was added for.

title: "Advanced" negative-offset path passes a negative slice to the Django ORM and raises
body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when `enable_advanced_features` is on and the client supplies a cursor with a negative offset (e.g. `?cursor=0:-5:0`), the code computes `start_offset = cursor.offset` and then evaluates `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django explicitly disallows negative slicing on querysets and raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.`, so this request 500s. The inline comment ('The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically') is simply wrong. The feature gated behind `enable_advanced_features=True` — which the audit-log endpoint passes unconditionally in its optimized branch — is therefore broken for any negative-offset cursor, legitimate or malicious.

title: organization_context.member.has_global_access crashes when member is None
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated on every GET to this endpoint, even when `optimized_pagination` is not requested. `organization_context.member` is `None` for requests authenticated without an organization membership (e.g. org auth tokens or API keys carrying org:admin scope), and for any non-superuser such request the attribute access raises AttributeError, turning previously working requests into 500s. Guard for None (e.g. `member = organization_context.member; enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or (member is not None and member.has_global_access)`).

title: Set→sorted-set change will WRONGTYPE-fail on segment keys written before the deploy
body: Segment keys (`span-buf:s:*`) were previously plain Redis sets written with SADD; this PR switches all access to sorted-set commands (ZADD here, ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE in add-buffer.lua, ZSCAN in _load_segment_data). Existing keys live up to `redis_ttl` (default 3600s), so after a rolling deploy, any batch or flush touching a pre-deploy key raises `WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value` — the Lua EVALSHA aborts and `p.execute()` raises, failing the whole Kafka batch until those keys expire or are flushed. There is no migration step or type-tolerant handling; this needs an explicit rollout plan (flush the buffer cluster, or drain before enabling).

title: max_segment_spans is now dead configuration; the only enforcement is a hardcoded 1000 in Lua
body: The Python-side guard in `_load_segment_data` that skipped segments exceeding `self.max_segment_spans` (and emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded`) was deleted, but `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans` (default 1001). The only remaining enforcement is the hardcoded `if span_count > 1000` in add-buffer.lua, which neither matches the default (1001) nor any configured value — anyone tuning `max_segment_spans` now gets a silent no-op, and the span-count cap diverges from the documented setting. Either pass the limit into the script as an ARGV or remove the parameter.

title: ZUNIONSTORE default AGGREGATE SUM doubles scores of duplicated spans, skewing eviction
body: `zunionstore(set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` uses Redis's default AGGREGATE SUM, so when the same span payload exists in both source sets (e.g. a duplicate/redelivered span that was previously merged), its score becomes the sum of the two end timestamps — roughly 2× the real time. Since eviction is `zpopmin` (lowest score first), such a duplicated span is artificially protected from eviction and will survive while genuinely newer spans are dropped. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) so duplicated members keep a sane score.

title: Redirect-chain limit lowered from 10000 to 1000; over-limit chains silently mis-join segments
body: The redirect resolution loop now stops after 1000 hops instead of 10000. When the limit is hit the loop simply ends with `set_span_id` pointing at a mid-chain span, and the incoming span is merged into that mid-chain set (recreating an unlinked key as a new orphan segment) rather than the segment root — fragmenting the segment into separately flushed pieces. Redirect entries persist for `redis_ttl` (1h) for every span id ever seen, independent of the new 1000-span payload cap, so very active traces can still build chains longer than 1000. If the lower bound is intentional, at least log or metric when the loop exits without resolving (redirect_depth == 1000) so the fragmentation is observable.

title: end_timestamp_precise is used as a Redis score without validation; one bad span fails the whole batch
body: `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` is passed straight through as the ZADD score for the span payload. `rapidjson.loads` accepts NaN/Infinity, and Redis rejects non-finite ZADD scores with an error, so a single malformed span makes the entire `p.execute()` pipeline fail — failing and reprocessing the whole Kafka batch rather than just the bad span. Previously the payload went into a plain set so this value was never interpreted. Sanitize the score (e.g. skip or clamp non-finite values) before building the ZADD mapping.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes on datetime keys, breaking the new audit-log pagination path
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does math.floor/math.ceil on getattr(item, self.key), copying Paginator's numeric-key implementation. The only place it is wired up, OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint, uses it with order_by="-datetime", so self.key is 'datetime' and the attribute is a datetime.datetime; math.ceil(datetime_obj) raises TypeError. build_cursor calls get_item_key on results of every non-empty page, so every request with ?optimized_pagination=true from an eligible user (superuser or member with global access) returns a 500 as soon as the organization has any audit log rows. value_from_cursor also returns the raw numeric cursor value instead of converting epoch-millis back to a datetime like DateTimePaginator does, so even if the first page worked, subsequent pages would compare a datetime column against an integer. The 'optimized' path is completely broken as shipped; it needs DateTimePaginator-style key conversion (or should not be used on this endpoint). Note this endpoint/paginator change is also entirely unrelated to the PR's stated purpose (spans buffer eviction).

title: organization_context.member.has_global_access crashes when member is None, on every GET
body: Line 71 evaluates organization_context.member.has_global_access unconditionally for every request to the audit log endpoint. RpcUserOrganizationContext.member is None when the request is not tied to an organization member — for example API-key or org-token authentication, where request.user is anonymous and is_superuser is False, so the 'or' short-circuit does not help. Such credentials can pass OrganizationAuditPermission via org scopes, and they will now crash with AttributeError ('NoneType' has no attribute 'has_global_access'), i.e. a 500 on this endpoint even when the optimized_pagination parameter is not used. Guard the access (organization_context.member is not None and organization_context.member.has_global_access) and/or compute it lazily only when use_optimized is true.

title: 'Advanced' negative-offset pagination relies on Django negative slicing, which raises
body: The new branch in OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result (and the comments at paginator.py:179-181, 874-879 and src/sentry/utils/cursors.py:26-27) claims the Django ORM 'properly handles negative slicing automatically' and that negative offsets are a safe, supported optimization. That is false: Django's QuerySet slicing raises ('Negative indexing is not supported') for queryset[start:stop] with start < 0. Cursor offsets are client-controlled — Cursor.from_string happily parses a cursor like '0:-50:0' — so with enable_advanced_features=True any client can supply a negative offset and get an unhandled 500, and the advertised bidirectional-pagination feature cannot work at all as written. The feature should be removed or implemented explicitly (e.g. computing absolute offsets), and the misleading comments in paginator.py and cursors.py corrected.

title: SET→ZSET type change on existing span-buf:s:* keys will WRONGTYPE during rollout
body: The PR changes the value type of the existing span-buf:s:* keys from a Redis SET (SADD here, SUNIONSTORE/SCARD/SSCAN elsewhere) to a sorted set (ZADD here, ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE in add-buffer.lua, ZSCAN in _load_segment_data) without renaming the keys. Any buffer key that still exists as a SET when the new code deploys — segments not yet flushed, or orphaned keys with TTL up to redis_ttl (1h) — will cause WRONGTYPE errors in the ZADD pipeline, in the Lua script, and in the flusher's ZSCAN, making the consumer and the flusher error repeatedly on those traces until the old keys expire. Use a new versioned key prefix or otherwise migrate/flush the old keys as part of the deploy.

title: ZUNIONSTORE defaults to AGGREGATE SUM, corrupting eviction scores for duplicated spans
body: Both ZUNIONSTORE calls omit an explicit AGGREGATE, so members present in both source sets get their scores SUMMED. With at-least-once Kafka delivery, a duplicate span payload can already be merged into set_key and later be re-buffered under a recreated child/parent key; the next merge then doubles its score (~3.4e9 instead of the ~1.7e9 end_timestamp_precise). Since the score is only used for eviction ordering, duplicated spans are subsequently treated as the newest spans and are evicted last by the 1000-span cap below, skewing eviction and, with repeated duplicates, crowding out legitimate spans. Add 'AGGREGATE MAX' (or MIN) to both ZUNIONSTORE calls so scores stay idempotent.

title: Redirect-follow limit silently reduced 10000→1000 and its explanatory comment deleted
body: The redirect-chasing loop limit was lowered from 10000 to 1000, and the comment documenting the consequence ('theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly') was removed. Segment trees whose redirect chain exceeds 1000 will now silently stop resolving: the incoming span is written to its own buffer key and the trace is eventually flushed as multiple split segments with outcome 'different'. If the lower bound is an intentional tradeoff to bound Lua execution time, that decision and its correctness impact should stay documented in the script; otherwise restore the previous limit.

title: max_segment_spans is now dead configuration; Lua eviction hardcodes 1000
body: The only enforcement of the max_segment_spans constructor parameter (default 1001) — the span-count overflow check in _load_segment_data — was removed, and its replacement, the eviction in add-buffer.lua, hardcodes the threshold ('if span_count > 1000'). The configurable parameter no longer has any effect and even disagrees with the hardcoded value (1000 vs 1001). Either pass the limit into the Lua script as an argument or delete the now-misleading parameter.

title: No test covers the new 1000-span eviction during insert
body: The headline behavior of this PR — capping a segment's buffer at 1000 spans by ZPOPMIN-ing the lowest-scored (oldest) spans during insert — has no test coverage. The test changes only add the new required end_timestamp_precise field to Span constructors. Add a test that inserts more than 1000 spans into one segment (including the path where a child set is merged via ZUNIONSTORE) and asserts the buffer is capped at 1000 and that the evicted spans are the expected oldest ones.

title: Accidental git submodule (gitlink) added without .gitmodules
body: The PR adds a file `sentry-repo` containing `Subproject commit a5d290...`, i.e. a git submodule/gitlink pointing at the base commit of this same repository, but no `.gitmodules` entry is added. This is almost certainly an accidental commit of a nested checkout. It breaks any workflow that initializes submodules: `git submodule update --init` fails with `fatal: no submodule mapping found in .gitmodules for path 'sentry-repo'`, which affects CI checkouts that run with `--recurse-submodules` and fresh clones. It should be removed from the PR.

title: upsampled_count uses sum(sample_weight) without coalescing NULLs, silently undercounting unsampled errors
body: The new `upsampled_count` SnQL function is defined as `toInt64(sum(Column("sample_weight")))`. In snuba, `sample_weight` on the errors/discover storage is Nullable and is only populated for error events that carry a client sample rate; error events ingested before a project was allowlisted, from SDKs that don't sample, or server-side have NULL `sample_weight`. ClickHouse `sum()` ignores NULL rows and returns NULL if every row is NULL, so (a) any unsampled error events are silently excluded from the returned count (e.g. 10 unsampled errors + 1 error sampled at 0.1 returns 10 instead of the correct 20), and (b) a time bucket containing only unsampled events returns NULL/0 instead of the true count. The added tests never exercise events without a client_sample_rate, so this is not caught. The aggregate should treat missing weights as 1, e.g. `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))`; the code comment's assumption that sample_weight always exists for allowlisted projects is not guaranteed by the schema.

title: _is_error_focused_query substring-matches event.type:error, misfiring on negations and quoted text
body: `_is_error_focused_query` decides whether to rewrite `count()` into `sum(sample_weight)` by checking `if "event.type:error" in query.lower()`. This substring test ignores search semantics: a discover query like `!event.type:error` (the standard way to select transaction-like events) contains the substring and will be treated as error-focused, so its `count()` is rewritten to sum(sample_weight) over non-error rows that have no sample_weight — returning NULL/incorrect counts. A free-text search such as `message:"event.type:error"` also false-positives. For allowlisted projects this silently returns wrong data on common discover queries; the check should parse the query and inspect the actual event.type filter (including its negation) rather than doing a substring match.

title: Upsampling eligibility is computed from the outer `dataset` and raw request query instead of the scoped dataset and query actually executed
body: Inside `_get_event_stats(scoped_dataset, query_columns, query, ...)`, the eligibility check calls `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` using the closure variable `dataset` from `get()`, not the `scoped_dataset` argument, and `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`/`_is_error_focused_query` re-read `request.GET["query"]` instead of the `query` argument. The dashboard-widget split path calls `_get_event_stats(discover, ..., split_query, ...)` where `split_query` is rewritten to `(<query>) AND !event.type:transaction`; that error-only query is never upsampled because the decision was made against the original (metrics) dataset and the unmodified request query. The transform decision should be based on the dataset and query string actually being executed, otherwise upsampling is silently skipped (or could be misapplied) for exactly the requests the function arguments describe.

title: Cache key built with Python hash() of project ids is collision-prone
body: The eligibility cache key is `f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))}"`. Python's `hash()` is not collision-free: two different project-id sets within the same organization can produce the same hash and therefore share a cache entry, causing the wrong allowlist eligibility (and thus wrong counts) to be served for up to 60 seconds. The key should encode the ids directly (e.g. comma-joined sorted ids) rather than a hash digest of them.

title: invalidate_upsampling_cache is dead code; allowlist changes have no invalidation path
body: `invalidate_upsampling_cache(organization_id, project_ids)` is introduced with a docstring saying it "should be called when the allowlist configuration changes", but nothing in this PR (or elsewhere) calls it, and there is no signal/hook wired to the `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` option. As shipped, every allowlist change takes up to the full 60-second TTL to take effect with no supported way to invalidate. Either wire the invalidation to the option update path or remove the unused helper and rely on the documented TTL.

title: No tests for the caching behavior that is the PR's stated performance optimization
body: The unit tests only exercise the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`); the main entry point `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` — which contains the new 60-second cache, the cache key construction, and the interaction between cached eligibility and the per-request dataset/query check — is never called. Cache hit/miss behavior, the TTL, and stale-cache regressions (the headline "performance optimization" of this PR) are therefore completely unverified.

title: Accidental nested git submodule (gitlink) committed
body: This PR adds a file `sentry-repo` containing `Subproject commit a5d2909...`, i.e. a gitlink pinning a nested checkout of the sentry repository itself (at this PR's own base commit), with no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry. This is almost certainly an accidental artifact of having a local clone inside the working tree. Once merged, every checkout of the repo will contain an uninitializable submodule directory, `git status` will permanently show it, and CI/checkout tooling that recurses or validates submodules may fail. It should be removed from the PR.

title: upsampled_count uses sum(sample_weight) with no NULL fallback, silently dropping unsampled errors
body: The new `upsampled_count()` aggregate is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. ClickHouse `sum()` skips NULL values, so any error event whose `sample_weight` is NULL contributes 0 to the count. NULL weights occur for events ingested before the project was allowlisted / before the column existed, and for events the SDK/Relay sent without an `error_sampling.client_sample_rate` context (e.g. projects at sample rate 1.0 that never attach the context). The code comments assert 'sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects', but nothing enforces this: the allowlist is a mutable option applied to projects with pre-existing data. Consequence: for allowlisted projects, `count()` becomes an undercount that silently excludes exactly those events, which is worse than not upsampling at all. The aggregate should coalesce missing weights, e.g. `sum(coalesce(sample_weight, toFloat64(1)))` (or `ifNull(sample_weight, 1)`), so unsampled events count once. Note the new snuba tests only store events that carry the `error_sampling` context, so this failure mode is not covered anywhere.

title: Upsampling eligibility is checked against the request-level dataset/query instead of the scoped dataset/query actually executed
body: Inside `_get_event_stats`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` closes over `dataset` and `request` from `get()`, but `_get_event_stats` is invoked with a `scoped_dataset` and a possibly rewritten `query` argument. In the dashboard discover-split flow (`metrics_enhanced and dashboard_widget_id`), the error branch calls `_get_event_stats(discover, ..., f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction", ...)`: here `dataset` is still `metrics_performance`/`metrics_enhanced_performance`, so `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns False and the error split query is never upsampled — while the same projects queried via the errors/discover dataset would return upsampled counts, giving inconsistent numbers for allowlisted orgs depending on which path served the widget. Similarly, `_is_error_focused_query` reads `request.GET['query']`, so it never sees the augmented `!event.type:transaction` / `event.type:transaction` split queries and can misclassify them. The eligibility check should be based on `scoped_dataset` and the `query` parameter passed into `_get_event_stats`.

title: _is_error_focused_query uses substring matching on the raw query string, producing false positives
body: `_is_error_focused_query` lowercases `request.GET['query']` and checks `'event.type:error' in query`. This is not a parsed search match: a query like `message:"saw event.type:error in logs"` or a longer value such as `event.type:errortag` contains the substring and will be classified as error-focused. The `count()` → `sum(sample_weight)` transform is then applied to a query that also matches transactions/other events, whose `sample_weight` is NULL, so those events are counted as 0 and the returned counts are wrong. If the intent is to only transform queries that filter to error events, the query should be parsed (or at minimum token-boundary matched) rather than substring-matched.

title: Cache key uses built-in hash() of project ids; invalidation helper is dead code
body: The eligibility cache key is built with Python's `hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))`. Using `hash()` for a cache key is fragile: two different project-id sets in the same organization that collide would share an eligibility decision for 60 seconds, silently applying (or withholding) upsampling for the wrong project set and returning wrong counts. Use an explicit, collision-free key (e.g. the joined sorted ids). Relatedly, `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is never called from anywhere in the codebase, so despite its docstring ('should be called when the allowlist configuration changes') nothing invalidates on option changes — and the docstring on `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` ('reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time') now contradicts the 60-second caching layered on top of it, which is misleading for the next person touching this code.

title: upsampled_count registered without private=True, exposing an internal-only function in the public query API
body: The new `SnQLFunction("upsampled_count", ...)` does not set `private=True`, unlike the sibling internal helper directly above it in `function_converter`. Public functions are selectable by any API user in arbitrary discover/events queries (`upsampled_count()` in `field`/`yAxis`) and may surface in docs/function-listing surfaces. Since this function is an implementation detail of the error-upsampling feature (injected by the endpoint itself, which works regardless of visibility) and returns misleading values on non-allowlisted or unsampled data, it should be marked `private=True` to keep it out of the public query surface.

title: Accidental nested git submodule of the repo itself committed
body: This PR adds a file `sentry-repo` containing a gitlink (`Subproject commit a5d29095...` — the base commit of this same repository) with no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry. This is clearly an accidental artifact of local testing: any checkout flow that initializes submodules will fail with `fatal: No url found for submodule path 'sentry-repo' in .gitmodules`, and the stray gitlink pollutes the tree. It should be removed from the commit.

title: Upsampling eligibility check uses outer `dataset`/request query instead of the scoped dataset and effective query
body: Inside `_get_event_stats`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` passes `dataset` — the closure variable chosen once in `get()` — instead of the `scoped_dataset` argument that is actually queried, and the helper's `_is_error_focused_query` inspects `request.GET['query']` rather than the `query` argument passed into `_get_event_stats`. In the dashboard-widget split path (`get_event_stats_factory`), which only runs when the outer dataset is `metrics_performance`/`metrics_enhanced_performance`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` therefore always returns False, so the errors-only subquery (`(<query>) AND !event.type:transaction` run against the discover dataset) is never upsampled: allowlisted projects silently get raw counts instead of sample-weighted counts there. Conversely, any future caller that swaps `scoped_dataset` or rewrites `query` (the split path already does both) gets a transform decision computed against the wrong dataset and wrong query text. The check should use `scoped_dataset` and the effective `query`.

title: Substring match for 'event.type:error' also matches negations and quoted strings
body: `_is_error_focused_query` does a raw substring test: `"event.type:error" in query`. This also matches negated filters such as `!event.type:error` (a query that explicitly excludes errors) and quoted search values like `message:"event.type:error"`, and it treats mixed queries like `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` as purely error-focused. For such discover queries on fully allowlisted projects, `count()` is rewritten to `upsampled_count()` (sum of sample_weight) even though the result set contains non-error events that have no sample_weight, so the returned counts are NULL or undercounted relative to the real totals. The check should parse the query or at minimum reject matches that are negated or inside quotes.

title: upsampled_count drops rows with NULL sample_weight, silently undercounting
body: The new `upsampled_count` aggregate is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. ClickHouse `sum()` ignores NULLs, so any error row whose `sample_weight` is NULL contributes nothing at all — not even 1. That covers errors ingested before a project was added to the `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` (still inside retention) and errors stored without an `error_sampling.client_sample_rate` context — the PR's own test-factory change only sets `sample_rate` when that context is present, demonstrating such rows exist. The result is that upsampled counts for allowlisted projects can be lower than the true event count, with no indication to the user. Wrapping the column, e.g. `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))`, would make unsampled rows count as 1.

title: Cache-invalidation helper is never called, so allowlist changes are stale for up to 60s with no escape hatch
body: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is added with a docstring saying it 'should be called when the allowlist configuration changes', but nothing in this PR or elsewhere calls it — there is no hook on the `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` option. As shipped, edits to the allowlist take up to the 60-second cache TTL to take effect and there is no way to force invalidation, while the dead function implies an invalidation path that does not exist. Either wire it into the option-change path or remove it.

title: Feature-flagged TableWidgetVisualization renders hardcoded empty data
body: In `tableResultComponent`, when the `use-table-widget-visualization` organization feature is enabled, the new branch renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{ data: [], meta: { fields: {}, units: {} } }} />` — completely ignoring the actual query results (`result.data`, `fields`, `eventView`, etc.) that the existing `StyledSimpleTableChart` path uses. `columns={[]}` also means no column headers are generated (the component's fallback of deriving columns from `meta.fields` gets an empty object too). Any organization that has this feature flag turned on will see every table widget on dashboards render as an empty table with no rows and no headers, instead of their data. The new visualization needs to be wired to the real table results before the flag can be enabled, or this branch should not ship.

title: Truthy check on custom cell renderer discards valid falsy React nodes
body: In `renderDefaultBodyCell` (and identically in `renderDefaultHeadCell` at line 32), the override is applied via `const cell = renderTableBodyCell?.(...); if (cell) { return cell; }`. The documented contract (in `tableWidgetVisualization.tsx` and the stories) is that returning `undefined` from a custom renderer triggers the fallback. With a truthiness check, a custom renderer that returns other valid falsy React nodes — `null` (to intentionally render nothing), `0`, or `''` — will be silently discarded and replaced by the default field renderer. This means a custom body/head cell renderer cannot render an empty cell. The check should be `if (cell !== undefined)` to match the documented contract.

title: age/timestamp mutual-exclusion check uses truthiness and age allows negatives
body: `validate_timestamp` rejects only when `self.initial_data.get("age")` is truthy (and `validate_age` mirrors this for `timestamp`). A report containing both `timestamp` and `age: 0` passes validation even though the intent is that the two fields are mutually exclusive, because `0` is falsy. `age: 0` is a legitimate value for a report delivered immediately. Additionally, the `age` field is declared as `serializers.IntegerField(required=False)` with no `min_value`, while `timestamp` has `min_value=0`, so negative ages are accepted. Use `"age" in self.initial_data` (and add `min_value=0` to `age`) so the spec constraint is actually enforced.

title: zip(error_ids, events.values()) misaligns IDs with nodestore data when entries are missing
body: `fetch_error_details` builds pairs with `zip(error_ids, events.values())` and filters with `if data is not None`. `nodestore.backend.get_multi()` returns a dict keyed by node_id that omits entries whose data is missing (e.g., expired events). When any entry is dropped, `events.values()` is shorter than `error_ids`, so the zip shifts: an error ID gets paired with a *different* event's data, and the trailing IDs are silently dropped — the `if data is not None` filter cannot realign them. The result is `ErrorEvent` objects whose `id` does not correspond to their `title`/`message`/`timestamp`. Today `id` is not consumed downstream (only title/message/timestamp reach the Seer prompt), so the visible impact is latent, but the mapping is incorrect and any future use of `id` (and any debugging of these payloads) will be wrong. Iterate `node_ids` and look up `events.get(node_id)` instead.

title: Feature-flagged TableWidgetVisualization path renders a hardcoded empty table
body: In `tableResultComponent`, when the `use-table-widget-visualization` organization feature is enabled, the code renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />` with completely hardcoded empty data instead of the actual `result.data`/`result.meta` from the query. The flagged branch also ignores `loading` (no placeholder while loading), errors, `title`, and the `getCustomFieldRenderer`/`fieldHeaderMap` wiring that the existing `StyledSimpleTableChart` path uses. The moment anyone enables this flag for an organization, every table-type dashboard widget will render an empty table with zero columns and no loading state, silently hiding all data. Either wire the real `tableResults` data through or don't merge the flag check until the visualization actually consumes query results.

title: HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES only filtered when a search query is present
body: The new `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES = ['is_segment', 'project_id', 'received']` list is applied inside the memo like this: `if (!searchQuery.trim()) { return sorted; }` followed by `sorted.filter(attribute => !HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES.includes(attribute.name) && ...)`. Because the early return happens for the empty-search case, the hidden attributes are only excluded while the user is actively typing a search query. In the default attribute view (no search entered), `is_segment`, `project_id`, and `received` are still rendered, which defeats the purpose of the hidden list. The `!HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES.includes(attribute.name)` predicate should be applied to `sorted` regardless of whether a search query is present.

title: fetch_error_details pairs error_ids with nodestore results positionally, which is not order-safe
body: `fetch_error_details` builds `node_ids` from `error_ids`, calls `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)`, and then builds events via `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. `get_multi` returns a dict keyed by node id and does not guarantee that `.values()` comes back in the same order as the requested `node_ids` (and missing keys may be omitted or set to `None`, shifting subsequent pairs). As a result, the `id` recorded on each `ErrorEvent` can be paired with a different event's data. Today the downstream log generation only reads `title`/`message`/`timestamp` (which come from the same data object), so the user-facing impact is currently limited to the latent `id` field being wrong, but the pairing should be done by iterating the node ids and looking up `events[node_id]` instead of relying on positional zip.

title: Merged-PR comment helpers defined on CommitContextIntegration but called on PRCommentWorkflow, causing AttributeError
body: The new static method `get_merged_pr_single_issue_template` calls `PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title(title)`, but `_truncate_title` (along with `get_environment_info` and `get_merged_pr_single_issue_template` themselves) is added at the end of `CommitContextIntegration` — the diff places them immediately after `get_top_5_issues_by_count` and immediately before `class OpenPRCommentWorkflow(ABC):`. `PRCommentWorkflow` is a separate ABC that only composes an integration (`__init__(self, integration: CommitContextIntegration)`), so `PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title` does not exist and raises AttributeError the first time a merged-PR comment body is formatted. The same mismatch exists at the call sites: `GitHubPRCommentWorkflow.get_comment_body` and `GitlabPRCommentWorkflow.get_comment_body` now invoke `self.get_merged_pr_single_issue_template(...)` and `self.get_environment_info(...)` on workflow instances that do not inherit from `CommitContextIntegration`. Consequence: the merged-PR suspect-issues comment tasks for GitHub and GitLab crash instead of posting/updating the comment. Move the helpers onto `PRCommentWorkflow` (and fix the class referenced in the static call), or invoke them via `self.integration`.

title: zip(error_ids, events.values()) mis-pairs error IDs with event data from nodestore get_multi
body: `fetch_error_details` builds `ErrorEvent` objects with `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a dict keyed by node id whose value order is whatever the backend returned (the Django backend uses an unordered `id__in` query, effectively lexicographic by node id, not the input order), and it omits entries for ids that have no stored event. As a result the i-th `error_id` is not guaranteed to correspond to the i-th value: titles, messages and timestamps get attached to the wrong error ids, and any single missing event shifts every subsequent pairing. The corrupted records are then sorted by the wrong `timestamp` and sent to Seer as the error context for the replay summary, so the summary can cite the wrong errors in the wrong chronological positions. The function already computes `node_ids`; it should look up each event explicitly (e.g. `events.get(node_id)` for each `(error_id, node_id)` pair) instead of relying on `.values()` ordering.

title: Feature-flagged TableWidgetVisualization rendered with hardcoded empty columns and data
body: In `tableResultComponent`, the `organization.features.includes('use-table-widget-visualization')` branch renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{ data: [], meta: { fields: {}, units: {} } }} />` — literal empty columns and empty data — while ignoring the real query results (`result.data`, `fields`, `result.meta`, `fieldAliases`) that are computed immediately above and still feed the `StyledSimpleTableChart` fallback. As soon as the `use-table-widget-visualization` flag is turned on for an organization, every table widget on that organization's dashboards renders an empty table with no headers and no rows. This reads as an unfinished stub that slipped in: either wire the actual table results into `TableWidgetVisualization` or keep rendering `StyledSimpleTableChart` until the new path is implemented.

title: "Project not found" error flashes while projects are still loading
body: The new guard `if (replayRecord?.project_id && !project)` renders an error alert ("Project not found. Unable to load AI summary.") whenever `useProjectFromId` returns undefined. However `useProjectFromId` also returns undefined while the projects store is still loading, so on any visit where projects are not already cached the user briefly (or, on a slow load, persistently) sees a false error state instead of the loading spinner that the previous code fell through to. The error branch should be gated on the projects store having finished loading (e.g. check `initiallyLoaded` from `useProjects`) so it only fires when the project genuinely cannot be found.

title: age/timestamp mutual-exclusion validators bypassable with a 0 value
body: `validate_timestamp` and `validate_age` are meant to enforce that a report contains either `age` (Editor's Draft) or `timestamp` (Working Draft), never both, but they check presence via truthiness: `if self.initial_data.get("age")` / `if self.initial_data.get("timestamp")`. A report containing both fields passes validation whenever one of them is `0` (e.g. `age: 0` alongside a `timestamp`), because `0` is falsy, defeating the mutual-exclusion rule the endpoint explicitly documents in the serializer comments. Use a real presence check such as `"age" in self.initial_data` (or `self.initial_data.get("age") is not None`) so zero values cannot bypass the constraint.

title: KeyError crash when an existing Integration has no "sender" in metadata
body: In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, when an Integration row exists for the installation_id but has no OrganizationIntegration, the new verification does `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`. The "sender" key is only written into metadata by the installation webhook; `build_integration` adds it only when the pipeline state contains "sender", and nothing in the pipeline ever binds that key, so every integration created through the pipeline path (e.g. when the webhook was delayed or lost) lacks it, as do older rows created before the webhook recorded the sender. If such an integration later loses its OrganizationIntegration (e.g. the region-side org integration is deleted while the control-side Integration row is still ACTIVE during deletion propagation) and a user tries to install again, this line raises KeyError and returns a 500 instead of the intended failure page, blocking legitimate reinstalls. Use a guarded lookup such as `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and explicitly fail closed with the error page when the sender is unknown.

title: Unguarded GitHub API calls in OAuthLoginView can 500 the install pipeline
