body: The code exchange (`safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)`) and the profile fetch (`get_user_info(payload["access_token"])`) are not wrapped in any exception handling. safe_urlopen raises requests exceptions on connection errors/timeouts, and get_user_info can raise if GitHub returns a non-JSON error response. Any of these transient failures propagate as unhandled exceptions and the user gets a 500, which is inconsistent with the goal of this PR to show the "Invalid installation request" page whenever GitHub verification cannot be completed. Wrap both calls and render `error(request, self.active_organization)` on failure.

title: No test covers the sender-match success path of the new verification
body: test_github_user_mismatch only exercises the failure branch of the new check (authenticated GitHub user differs from the recorded installation sender). No test covers the complementary case where the Integration exists without an OrganizationIntegration and the authenticated user matches `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`, verifying that installation then proceeds. In all success-path tests the Integration row is absent at check time, so the verification code is never exercised positively. Given that this check reads nested metadata that may be missing on some rows, a success-path test with an existing sender-recorded integration would catch regressions in both directions.

title: KeyError crash when existing Integration has no "sender" metadata
body: In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the new ownership check does `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`. The "sender" key is only present for integrations created from the GitHub `installation` webhook; integrations created through the normal Sentry pipeline never get a "sender" key (build_integration only copies state["sender"], and nothing in the pipeline ever binds "sender"). If an ACTIVE integration without an OrganizationIntegration and without sender metadata is reached here — e.g., a pipeline-created integration whose Sentry organization was later deleted, or one left behind by a partially failed install — this line raises KeyError, returning a 500 instead of the intended github-integration-failed page and permanently blocking re-installation for that installation_id. Use `integration.metadata.get("sender")` and fail closed with the friendly error when it is absent.

title: OAuth token exchange and user-info fetch can raise unhandled exceptions, producing a 500
body: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, `req = safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` is outside the try/except that only wraps safe_urlread/parse_qsl. A connection error, timeout, or RestrictedIPAddress from sentry.http raises here, and there is no exception handler in the pipeline dispatch path, so a transient GitHub/network failure during installation surfaces as a 500 rather than the graceful error page this PR adds. The same applies to `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` on line 434, which performs another network call that can raise. Both calls should be wrapped so failures render the github-integration-failed page as the PR intends.

title: Ownership check compares mutable GitHub usernames instead of immutable user IDs
body: The new check compares `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user")` against `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`, i.e. it compares GitHub login names. GitHub usernames are mutable and recyclable: (a) if the user who installed the app later renames their GitHub account, the stored sender login no longer matches and that legitimate user can never link or re-link the installation; (b) conversely, if an attacker registers the abandoned old username, they satisfy this check and can attach the victim's GitHub App installation (installation IDs are sequential and guessable) to their own Sentry organization. Both the webhook sender payload and the /user API response include the immutable numeric user `id`; the check should compare IDs instead of logins.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the installation-404 path
body: test_installation_not_found stubs a 404 for GET /app/installations/{installation_id}, but it submits state "ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05", which does not match the pipeline signature used throughout these tests ("9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3"). The request is therefore rejected at OAuthLoginView's state check and the flow never reaches build_integration, so the 404 stub is never called and the "The GitHub installation could not be found." branch in build_integration is left uncovered by any test (the assertion on "Invalid installation request." passes because of the signature mismatch, not the missing installation). Either drive the flow with the correct state and a bound installation_id so the 404 path is exercised, or rename the test to reflect that it now only tests signature validation.

title: KeyError on integration.metadata["sender"] for integrations that lack sender metadata
body: In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the new check `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes every existing Integration row has `sender` in its metadata. That is not true: `build_integration` only stores `sender` when `state.get("sender")` is set, and integrations created through the normal in-Sentry pipeline never have it (the PR's own test_basic_flow asserts the final metadata contains only access_token/expires_at/icon/domain_name/account_type). Only integrations created by the installation webhook carry `sender`. This code path is reachable whenever an ACTIVE Integration exists with no OrganizationIntegration — e.g. the owning organization was deleted, orphaning the Integration row — and someone then installs the same GitHub App installation into another Sentry organization. In that case `integration.metadata["sender"]` raises KeyError and the user gets a 500 instead of the intended github-integration-failed.html page, with no way to complete the install. Use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and define explicit fail-open/fail-closed behavior for integrations without sender metadata.

title: Network/API failures during token exchange and /user fetch are unhandled and produce 500s
body: OAuthLoginView.dispatch performs two outbound HTTP calls that can raise: `req = safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` (line 423) is outside the try/except (the try only covers safe_urlread/parsing), and `authenticated_user_info = get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` (line 434) has no exception handling at all. A DNS/connection failure or timeout to github.com, or a non-JSON error body from the api.github.com/user call (resp.json() raises), will propagate out of the pipeline and return a 500 to the user, instead of the graceful github-integration-failed.html error page this PR introduces for every other verification failure. These calls should be wrapped and converted into the same error response (ideally with logging), since transient GitHub/network errors in a user-facing auth pipeline are expected.

title: Fresh-install path performs no verification that the OAuth user controls the installation
body: When `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises DoesNotExist, GitHubInstallation.dispatch goes straight to `pipeline.next_step()` and `build_integration` fetches `/app/installations/{installation_id}` using the GitHub App JWT — which can read ANY installation of the Sentry GitHub App. GitHub App installation IDs are sequential/enumerable, and the OAuth step only proves the attacker's own GitHub identity; on this path it is never compared to anything about the installation. So if the Integration row does not exist yet — the installation.created webhook is delayed, permanently failed to deliver, or webhooks aren't configured/reachable (self-hosted) — anyone who knows or guesses a victim's installation_id can attach the victim's GitHub organization installation to their own Sentry organization, exposing its repositories, commits, CODEOWNERS and source-linking data. The sender check added here only helps once the webhook-created row exists. Consider additionally verifying on the fresh path that the authenticated GitHub user belongs to / admins the installation's account (e.g. via the installation account and an org-membership check), rather than skipping verification entirely.

title: GitHub integration install now hard-requires the github-login OAuth app to be configured
body: OAuthLoginView pulls `client_id`/`client_secret` from GitHubIdentityProvider (the github-login identity OAuth app, e.g. the `github-login.client-id`/`github-login.client-secret` options), which is a separate configuration from the GitHub App (github-app.* options) that the integration previously needed. On deployments that have the GitHub App configured but never set up the github-login identity provider (a plausible self-hosted configuration), these values are None/empty: the pipeline will redirect to GitHub's authorize URL with an invalid client_id (GitHub shows an error) or the token exchange will fail, making the GitHub integration uninstallable where it previously worked. There is no feature flag, fallback, or documentation noting this new requirement. Consider gating the new step on the OAuth app being configured, or explicitly failing with a clear operator-facing error/docs update.

title: No positive-path test for the sender-match flow, and no test for integrations missing sender metadata
body: The new tests only cover the negative case (test_github_user_mismatch: webhook-created Integration whose sender does not match the OAuth user). There is no test that exercises the main protected flow end-to-end: installation webhook creates the Integration with a sender, the same GitHub user completes the OAuth step, the sender check passes, and the installation links successfully (the direct-from-GitHub install path). A regression that breaks legitimate installs from GitHub would not be caught. There is also no test with a pre-existing ACTIVE Integration whose metadata lacks `sender`, which would have exposed the KeyError in `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` reported separately.

title: `queued` default is evaluated once at module import, not per instance
body: In the `AssignmentSource` dataclass, `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` executes `timezone.now()` a single time when the class body is evaluated (at module import). Every `AssignmentSource` created without an explicit `queued` — which is all of them, since `from_integration` and the test constructors never pass it — shares the timestamp of process startup/module import rather than the time the assignment actually originated. This stale value is then serialized into every `sync_assignee_outbound` Celery payload via `to_dict()`. The field's apparent purpose (recording when the assignment was queued) is therefore defeated, and any future consumer reading `queued` would get a wrong, potentially days-old value. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so the default is computed per instance.

title: `from_dict` performs no type coercion/validation, so `queued` round-trips as a string through the task queue
body: `to_dict()` emits `queued` as a `datetime`, but the dict crosses the Celery boundary as the `assignment_source_dict` kwarg, where Sentry's JSON-based task serialization converts datetimes to ISO-8601 strings. `from_dict` then blindly splats the payload into the constructor (`cls(**input_dict)`), and dataclasses do not enforce type annotations, so after every real round trip `queued` is a `str` in a `datetime`-typed field — the class invariant is silently broken (the eager test runner does not serialize kwargs, so the tests don't catch this). The same lack of validation means a wrong-typed `integration_id` (e.g. a string after a future serialization change) would construct successfully and then never equal `org_integration.integration_id` in `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync`, failing open and re-opening the exact sync cycle this PR exists to prevent. `from_dict` should parse `queued` back into a datetime (or the field should be dropped) and coerce/validate `integration_id`.

title: No coverage that a different integration still propagates, or that deassign with a matching source is suppressed
body: The new tests cover only two cases: no `assignment_source` (outbound sync proceeds) and a matching `assignment_source` on assign (outbound sync suppressed). The explicitly stated design goal — 'This should still allow other integrations to propagate changes outward' — is untested: nothing sets up external issues on two different integrations and asserts that an assignment sourced from integration A still triggers outbound sync to integration B. Additionally, the deassign path that now threads `assignment_source` (inbound webhook deassign → `GroupAssignee.objects.deassign(..., assignment_source=...)` → `sync_group_assignee_outbound`) has no test verifying that a matching source suppresses the outbound deassign to the originating integration. A regression in either direction (over-suppressing legitimate cross-integration syncs, or failing to suppress deassign echoes) would not be caught by this suite.

title: queued defaults to the module-import time, not the instance creation time
body: In the new AssignmentSource dataclass, the field `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` evaluates `timezone.now()` exactly once, when the class body is executed at module import. Every AssignmentSource created without an explicit `queued` value (including all instances made via `AssignmentSource.from_integration(...)` in the inbound webhook path) will therefore carry the worker process's import/boot timestamp rather than the time the assignment was actually queued. This value is serialized into every `sync_assignee_outbound` Celery message via `to_dict()`. The field is not consumed by any logic in this PR, so the impact is latent today, but the field's name and inclusion make it clear it is meant to record when the assignment was queued (e.g., for future staleness/ordering checks), and any such use would silently read a wildly stale timestamp. The test `test_to_dict` only asserts `queued is not None`, so it cannot catch this. Fix: use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` from `dataclasses`.

title: No test covers outbound propagation to other integrations when a source is set
body: The new cycle-breaking logic in `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync` has two contractual halves: (1) suppress the outbound sync back to the integration that originated the assignment, and (2) still propagate the change to other linked integrations — the code comment explicitly promises "This should still allow other integrations to propagate changes outward." Only half (1) is tested: `test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration` links a single integration and asserts `sync_assignee_outbound` is not called. There is no test with a second linked integration (e.g., a different integration id) asserting that its outbound sync still fires when `assignment_source` is set, and no test for the deassign path with a matching source. A regression that suppresses all outbound syncs whenever a source is present (e.g., changing the check to `if sync_source: return False`) would pass the entire suite while silently breaking assignee propagation for multi-integration setups, and the inbound-webhook-to-outbound-suppression path via `sync_group_assignee_inbound` is likewise unexercised end to end.

title: assignment_source_dict contains a datetime, which is not JSON-serializable for Celery
body: sync_group_assignee_outbound enqueues sync_assignee_outbound with 'assignment_source_dict': assignment_source.to_dict(). AssignmentSource.to_dict() uses dataclasses.asdict(), so the dict includes the 'queued' field as a datetime.datetime instance. Sentry's Celery tasks use JSON serialization, so publishing this message raises TypeError/kombu EncodeError ('Object of type datetime is not JSON serializable') at apply_async time. This fires on exactly the path this PR adds: every inbound webhook assignment/deassignment now carries an AssignmentSource, so the first apply_async call in the loop raises, no outbound syncs are enqueued (including to other integrations, which the PR says should still propagate), and the exception propagates through GroupAssignee.assign()/deassign() back to the webhook handler, producing 500s and webhook retries. The new tests don't catch this because self.tasks() runs tasks eagerly without message serialization. Fix by removing the unused 'queued' field or serializing it (e.g., isoformat()) in to_dict and parsing it back in from_dict.

title: queued default is evaluated once at module import time
body: In the AssignmentSource dataclass, 'queued: datetime = timezone.now()' is evaluated a single time when the class is defined, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit queued value (including ones rebuilt by from_dict when the key is absent) shares the same timestamp from process start, not the time the source was actually created. The correct pattern is field(default_factory=timezone.now). Although nothing consumes 'queued' yet, any future use (e.g., ignoring stale assignments) would silently operate on wrong data, and the existing test only asserts the value is not None so it cannot catch this.

title: assignment_source added to the wrong abstract method contract
body: The abstract IssueSyncIntegration.sync_status_outbound signature now declares 'assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None', but no caller ever passes it and no inbound status flow creates an AssignmentSource, so the parameter is dead and misleading (status sync cycles are not addressed by this PR). Conversely, sync_assignee_outbound in the task now always passes assignment_source=... to installation.sync_assignee_outbound, yet the abstract sync_assignee_outbound signature was not updated to declare it — concrete implementations only receive it incidentally via **kwargs, so anyone implementing or type-checking against the documented abstract contract won't know the argument exists. Add the parameter to sync_assignee_outbound's abstract signature and drop it from sync_status_outbound until status cycle-breaking is actually implemented.

title: New task kwarg is enqueued in the same deploy it is accepted, risking TypeError on old workers
body: The PR both adds the 'assignment_source_dict' parameter to the sync_assignee_outbound task and immediately starts sending it from sync_group_assignee_outbound. During a rolling deploy, messages produced by new code can be picked up by workers still running the old three-argument signature, which raises TypeError: sync_assignee_outbound() got an unexpected keyword argument 'assignment_source_dict'. TypeError is not in the @retry exclude list, so the message retries up to 5 times at 5-minute delays and is dropped if the deploy takes longer than ~25 minutes to reach all workers. The usual mitigation is to deploy the worker signature change first and enable the enqueueing side only after all workers accept the new kwarg (or gate it behind a flag).

title: test_dedupe builds the expected occurrence with the wrong group key, so its assertion fails
body: In TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe, the expected occurrence is built via build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH), but the DetectorEvaluationResult it is compared against is produced by calling evaluate_group_key_value with group_key="group_key" (expected_result.group_key is passed in). build_mock_occurrence_and_event embeds handler.build_fingerprint(group_key) into the IssueOccurrence, so the expected occurrence has fingerprint ["<detector_id>:val1"] while the actual occurrence has ["<detector_id>:group_key"]. IssueOccurrence is a dataclass whose equality compares the fingerprint field, so the DetectorEvaluationResult equality check fails and this test errors on its first assert. The helper should be called with "group_key" (or the result built with "val1") so the fingerprints match.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler can no longer be instantiated — it doesn't implement StatefulDetectorHandler's abstract methods
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler was changed from DetectorHandler (with a working stub evaluate returning []) to StatefulDetectorHandler with a bare `pass`. StatefulDetectorHandler declares abstract members counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and the new build_occurrence_and_event_data hook, so the class remains abstract and any instantiation raises TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler. MetricAlertFire.detector_handler points at this class, and Detector.detector_handler does group_type.detector_handler(self); process_detectors only guards against a None handler, not an exception, so evaluating any Detector with type "metric_alert_fire" will now crash processing instead of returning no results as before. Either add stub implementations of the abstract methods or leave the handler non-abstract until the real implementation lands. (The TODO comment above the class — "This will be a stateful detector when we build that abstraction" — is also now stale, since it already subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler.)

title: StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: The docstring for StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate reads "Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`", but this PR changed both the abstract DetectorHandler.evaluate signature and this implementation to return a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey (dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]). The stale docstring will mislead anyone implementing a new handler; it should describe the dict return.

title: build_mock_occurrence_and_event ignores its `value` argument, so the value passed to the occurrence hook is never verified
body: The test helper build_mock_occurrence_and_event takes a `value` parameter but never uses it when constructing the IssueOccurrence/event_data. In test_state_results_multi_group the expected occurrence for "group_2" is built with value 6 even though the data packet sets "group_2" to 10, and the test still passes only because the helper discards the value. As written, no test would catch evaluate_group_key_value forwarding the wrong value into build_occurrence_and_event_data. Either include the value in the built occurrence (e.g., in evidence_data) so it is asserted, or at minimum pass the correct value (10) at this call site.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and raises TypeError when instantiated
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler with an empty `pass` body, but StatefulDetectorHandler has four abstract members it does not implement: `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the newly added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. Under ABCMeta, instantiating the class raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract methods ...`. That instantiation happens in `Detector.detector_handler` (`group_type.detector_handler(self)`) for any Detector whose type slug is `metric_alert_fire`, and the TypeError is not caught in `process_detectors`, so it would abort processing of the entire detector batch. Before this PR the class implemented `evaluate` itself and was instantiable. Either keep it on DetectorHandler until the stateful pieces exist, or implement the abstract hooks; the stale comment "This will be a stateful detector when we build that abstraction" should also be updated since the class now subclasses the stateful handler.

title: PriorityLevel(new_status) raises ValueError for DetectorPriorityLevel.CRITICAL
body: In `evaluate_group_key_value`, the new occurrence branch converts the detector status via `PriorityLevel(new_status)`. `DetectorPriorityLevel` (sentry.workflow_engine.types) includes `CRITICAL = 100`, but `sentry.types.group.PriorityLevel` only defines LOW=25, MEDIUM=50, HIGH=75. The conversion works for LOW/MEDIUM/HIGH only because DetectorPriorityLevel is an IntEnum with matching values; if a detector's DataCondition has `condition_result=DetectorPriorityLevel.CRITICAL` and it fires, `new_status` becomes CRITICAL and `PriorityLevel(...)` raises `ValueError: 100 is not a valid PriorityLevel`. The exception propagates out of `handler.evaluate` and through `process_detectors`, killing the whole detector-processing loop and discarding the enqueued dedupe/state updates for that packet. The status should be validated/mapped before conversion (or CRITICAL condition results rejected for detectors), and `PriorityLevel(new_status.value)` would make the intended int conversion explicit.

title: TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe builds the expected occurrence for the wrong group key and fails
body: In `TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe`, the expected result is built with `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)`, which embeds the fingerprint `"<detector.id>:val1"` via `build_fingerprint`. The code under test is then invoked with group key `"group_key"` (`handler.evaluate_group_key_value(expected_result.group_key, ...)`), so the occurrence actually produced by the handler has fingerprint `"<detector.id>:group_key"`. Both `DetectorEvaluationResult` and `IssueOccurrence` are dataclasses compared field by field, so the fingerprints differ and the `== expected_result` assertion fails deterministically. This worked before the PR only because the expected result had `result=None`. Build the expected occurrence with `"group_key"` (and matching value 10) instead of `"val1"`.

title: StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: The docstring on `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` reads "Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`.", but this PR changed the method (and the abstract `DetectorHandler.evaluate` signature, and `process_detectors`) to return `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`. The docstring should describe the dict keyed by group key.

title: Mock occurrence builder ignores its `value` argument, hiding value mismatches in several tests
body: `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, group_key, value, new_status)` never uses the `value` parameter when constructing the IssueOccurrence or event_data. Several updated tests depend on this: `TestEvaluate.test_dedupe` evaluates value 8 but builds the expectation with 6, `TestEvaluate.test_results_on_change` evaluates 100 but expects 6, and `test_state_results_multi_group` evaluates `group_2` with value 10 but builds the expected occurrence with 6. Because the value is silently dropped, the suite cannot catch `evaluate_group_key_value` passing the wrong `value` into `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. Include the value in the mock's evidence_data (or assert it separately) so these mismatches would fail the tests.

title: TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe builds the expected occurrence with the wrong group key, so the assertion fails
body: In test_dedupe, the expected IssueOccurrence is constructed with build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH), which embeds the fingerprint ['<detector_id>:val1'] via handler.build_fingerprint("val1"). However, evaluate_group_key_value is then invoked with group_key "group_key", so the occurrence the handler actually produces carries fingerprint ['<detector_id>:group_key']. DetectorEvaluationResult and IssueOccurrence are both frozen dataclasses whose equality compares every field (unlike StatusChangeMessage, IssueOccurrence.__eq__ is not patched in these tests), so the final `assert handler.evaluate_group_key_value(...) == expected_result` compares occurrences with different fingerprints and fails. The expected occurrence should be built with group_key "group_key" to match the key passed to evaluate_group_key_value.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and will raise TypeError when instantiated via Detector.detector_handler
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler was changed from a concrete DetectorHandler subclass (with an evaluate that returned []) to a StatefulDetectorHandler subclass with an empty body. StatefulDetectorHandler still has unimplemented abstract members: counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and the newly added build_occurrence_and_event_data. Because DetectorHandler inherits abc.ABC, calling MetricAlertDetectorHandler(detector) raises TypeError ("Can't instantiate abstract class ... with abstract methods ..."). MetricAlertFire.detector_handler points at this class, and Detector.detector_handler executes group_type.detector_handler(self), so any detector of type metric_alert_fire that flows through process_detectors will now crash instead of simply producing no results as before. Either provide stub implementations of the abstract methods or keep the class on DetectorHandler until the real stateful implementation lands. (The TODO comment above the class saying "This will be a stateful detector when we build that abstraction" is also now stale, since it already subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler.)

title: StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate docstring still documents a list return type
body: The docstring for StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate reads "Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`", but this PR changed both this method and the abstract DetectorHandler.evaluate to return a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey (dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]). The stale wording misleads anyone implementing the abstract method or consuming the results; it should describe the dict keyed by group key.

title: Modified config copy is discarded; raw monitor config returned in event context
body: In get_monitor_environment_context, the monitor's config is copied and config["schedule_type"] is rewritten to the human-readable display value, but the returned context dict uses monitor_environment.monitor.config (the original, unmodified dict) instead of the modified copy. This makes the schedule_type display conversion dead code, and every monitor incident occurrence event carries the raw integer schedule_type in its monitor context rather than the readable label. This defect was carried verbatim from the old create_issue_platform_occurrence in mark_failed.py; the fix is to return "config": config (the copy) instead of "config": monitor_environment.monitor.config.

title: get_monitor_environment_context mutates a config copy but returns the original
body: In get_monitor_environment_context, the function copies monitor_environment.monitor.config into a local variable `config` and replaces `config['schedule_type']` with the human-readable display string, but the returned dict contains `"config": monitor_environment.monitor.config` — the original, unmodified config. The copy-and-mutate code is therefore dead, and every monitor incident occurrence event still carries the raw integer `schedule_type` in its monitor context instead of the intended display value. This defect was carried over unchanged from the old mark_failed.py location, but since the code is being moved wholesale it is worth fixing now by returning the modified `config` (or deleting the dead copy if the raw value is intentional).

title: Humanized config copy is built then discarded; original raw config returned in monitor context
body: In get_monitor_environment_context (new module, carried over verbatim from the old mark_failed.py), the function copies monitor_environment.monitor.config and converts config["schedule_type"] to its human-readable display value on that copy, but the returned context dict uses "config": monitor_environment.monitor.config — the original, unmodified dict. The modified copy is never used, so the schedule_type humanization is dead code and every monitor-incident occurrence event carries the raw integer schedule_type in its monitor context instead of the display string. The return should use the copied `config`. Behavior is unchanged by this refactor (the bug predates the move), but since this PR creates the new home for this code it is the right time to fix it.

title: isinstance check against multiprocessing.Process is always False for spawn processes, so hung flushers are never killed
body: `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is never true for the processes this class creates. The flusher uses `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")`, whose `Process` class is `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` — a sibling of `multiprocessing.Process` (which is the fork-context flavor), not a subclass of it. The type annotation on `self.processes` (`SpawnProcess | threading.Thread`) even acknowledges this. Consequences: (1) In `_ensure_processes_alive`, when a flusher process is deemed unhealthy due to a hang, `process.kill()` is silently skipped before the replacement process is started — previously the kill was unconditional, so this is a regression. The hung process keeps running indefinitely: it keeps flushing the same shards as its replacement, and because the restart reuses the same shared `healthy_since` Value for that process slot, a still-looping zombie can keep refreshing `healthy_since` and permanently mask the hang from the health check. (2) The same wrong check at line 346 means `join()` never calls `terminate()` on spawn processes that outlive the deadline. Fix by checking `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)` or by calling `kill()`/`terminate()` unconditionally as before.

title: Unset max_processes defaults to one process per shard instead of preserving old single-process behavior
body: `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` makes an unset value mean "one process per shard", the most aggressive setting. The new `--flusher-processes` click option defaults to 1, which preserves the previous single-flusher-process behavior, but any construction path that does not pass the new parameter gets the aggressive behavior: for example an ops override of the `process-spans` entry in `SENTRY_KAFKA_CONSUMERS` that still uses the old `click_options` shape (the ops repo is deployed independently of this code), or any direct Python instantiation of `ProcessSpansStrategyFactory`/`SpanFlusher`. Such deployments would silently go from 1 flusher process to N spawned processes and N Kafka producers per consumer on upgrade, contrary to the PR's stated gradual-rollout intent. The default for `flusher_processes=None` should be 1, with per-shard scaling opt-in via the option.

title: --flusher-processes is not validated; 0 is silently treated as per-shard and a negative value crashes startup with KeyError
body: The new `--flusher-processes` option (and `SpanFlusher`'s `max_processes`) accepts any integer without validation. Passing 0 is silently treated as "one process per shard" because `0 or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` takes the shard count. Passing a negative number is worse: `self.num_processes = min(-1, len(shards))` is negative, so `process_to_shards_map` is built from `range(-1)` and is empty, and the very first shard assignment `self.process_to_shards_map[0].append(shard)` raises a bare `KeyError`, crashing the consumer at startup with no useful message. The option should be validated as `>= 1` (in the click callback or the constructor) and 0 should either be rejected or documented.

title: Inconsistent metrics tag keys: "shard" vs "shards", and comma-joined multi-shard tag values
body: The new per-process metrics tagging is inconsistent: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` (line 185) and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` (line 196) are tagged with key `"shard"`, while `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` (line 199) uses key `"shards"`, so dashboards or monitors grouping/filtering by `shard` will silently miss the wait_produce timer. Additionally, when `max_processes < len(assigned_shards)` a process handles multiple shards and the tag value is a comma-joined list like "0,2,4", whereas `spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy` (line 243) emits one data point per individual shard integer — two different conventions for the same dimension that cannot be correlated in metrics queries.

title: Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because the test monkeypatches time.sleep
body: `test_basic` monkeypatches `time.sleep` to a no-op at the top of the test (`monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`), so the newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` with the comment "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change" provides no synchronization whatsoever. The test still depends on the racing flusher thread observing `current_drift.value = 9000` and completing a flush+produce before `step.join()` sets `stopped.value`; if the flusher thread's next loop iteration starts after `stopped` is set, it exits without flushing and `(msg,) = messages` fails on an empty list. If the intent was to deflake the test, this doesn't do it — the flusher's completion needs to be awaited deterministically (e.g., poll `messages` with a real timeout loop, since the fake sleep also makes the flusher's own `time.sleep(1)` a hot spin).

title: Dead method _create_process_for_shard left over from per-shard design
body: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is never called anywhere: the restart path in `_ensure_processes_alive` calls `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly. This leftover single-shard helper is misleading (it suggests per-shard restarts are possible when a restart actually recreates the whole multi-shard process) and should be removed.

title: join() skips terminate() for remaining flusher processes when the deadline expires
body: In SpanFlusher.join(), the loop over self.processes breaks out entirely when the deadline is exhausted, so any processes after the one being waited on are never sent terminate(). The previous single-process implementation always called process.terminate() after the wait loop, guaranteeing the old flusher was killed at the deadline. With multiple processes, if an earlier process consumes the remaining time (e.g. it is blocked in a Kafka future.result() wait), the later processes are left running. Since close() deliberately does not stop flushers and join() is the only shutdown point, on a rebalance the leftover processes can overlap with the newly created SpanFlusher's processes for the same shards, causing two flushers to flush the same shard queues concurrently (duplicate segments produced to the buffered-segments topic), and a process hung in produce can leak indefinitely. After the while-wait, terminate() should be called for every remaining process rather than breaking.

title: max_processes=0 is silently treated as 'one process per shard', negative values disable flushing
body: self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards) conflates an explicit 0 with None: an operator passing --flusher-processes 0 (the click option accepts any int, no range validation) gets 0 or len(shards), i.e. the maximum fan-out of one process per shard instead of zero/one. Conversely a negative value survives the 'or' (truthy), making num_processes = min(negative, shards) negative, so range(num_processes) is empty and no flusher process is created at all — the consumer would keep writing spans to Redis with nothing ever flushing them, with no error surfaced. Consider explicit validation (e.g. click.IntRange(1, ...)) and treating only None as unset.

title: Inconsistent metrics tag keys: 'shard' vs 'shards', and multi-shard values under the 'shard' tag
body: In SpanFlusher.main(), the 'spans.buffer.flusher.produce' and 'spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes' metrics are tagged with 'shard' while 'spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce' is tagged with 'shards'. Additionally, when max_processes < number of shards, shard_tag is a comma-joined list like '0,2,4', so the 'shard' tag no longer contains a single shard id. This makes dashboards/alerts grouped by shard inconsistent across these related metrics and breaks any existing per-shard aggregation on the 'shard' tag for these series.

title: _create_process_for_shard is dead code left over from the refactor
body: SpanFlusher._create_process_for_shard(shard) is never called anywhere — restarts go through _ensure_processes_alive, which calls _create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards) directly. The unused method suggests a per-shard restart granularity that does not exist (restarting always recreates the whole process and all its shards), which is misleading for future maintainers. It should be removed.

title: test_basic relies on a fixed 0.1s sleep for the flusher thread to produce
body: The newly added 'step.poll(); time.sleep(0.1)' before step.join() is a timing race: the test asserts exactly one produced message, but the background flusher thread must observe current_drift, call flush_segments against real Redis, and append the message within that wall-clock window. join() sets stopped.value before waiting, so a flush that hasn't happened by then will never occur. On a loaded or slow CI runner where the thread isn't scheduled within 100ms, '(msg,) = messages' will fail intermittently. A poll/wait loop on len(messages) with a timeout would make this deterministic.

title: isinstance guard makes kill()/terminate() dead code for spawn processes, so hung flushers are never killed
body: The check `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` in `_ensure_processes_alive` is never true in practice. Flusher processes are created via `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which produces `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` instances; `SpawnProcess` is a sibling of `multiprocessing.context.Process` (both subclass `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`), not a subclass of it, and the only alternative type here is `threading.Thread`, which also fails the check. Consequences: (1) when a flusher process is detected as hung (cause == "hang"), the old process is never killed before `_create_process_for_shards` starts a replacement, so two processes end up flushing the same shards and producing the same segments to the buffered-segments topic (duplicate downstream data), and each restart leaks the previous process's Redis/Kafka connections; the old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally, so this is a regression. (2) The identical guard in `join()` (line 346) means `process.terminate()` is also never executed, so flusher processes that outlive the join timeout are not terminated. Use `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)` or invert the check to `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`.

title: The added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because the test monkeypatches time.sleep
body: Line 15 of this test does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, so the `time.sleep(0.1)` added at line 62 ("Give flusher threads time to process after drift change") never actually waits. The test therefore depends on the flusher thread being scheduled between `fac._flusher.current_drift.value = 9000` and `step.join()` setting `self.stopped.value = True`; if the thread observes `stopped` before running a flush cycle with the new drift, `messages` stays empty and `(msg,) = messages` fails. This makes the test timing-dependent/flaky. Capture the real sleep before monkeypatching (e.g. `real_sleep = time.sleep` then `real_sleep(0.1)`) or poll until `messages` is non-empty.

title: flusher_processes of 0 or negative is silently mishandled
body: `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats an explicit 0 as falsy and turns it into "one process per shard", the opposite of a limit. A negative value (the new `--flusher-processes` click option accepts any int) makes `num_processes = min(max_processes, len(shards))` negative, so `process_to_shards_map` is built as an empty dict and `self.process_to_shards_map[process_index].append(shard)` raises KeyError during consumer startup. Validate that the value is >= 1 (e.g. `click.IntRange(min=1)` on the option in `src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py` and/or an explicit check here).

title: Inconsistent metric tag key: "shards" vs "shard"
body: `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is emitted with tag key `"shards"`, while `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` (line 185) and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` (line 195) use `"shard"` for the same value. The inconsistent key prevents grouping/comparing these timers under a single tag and looks like a typo.

title: Strategy close() kills the factory-shared queue pool; after any rebalance all messages are silently dropped but their offsets are committed
body: The FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ (result_consumer.py, mode == 'thread-queue-parallel') and the same pool object is handed to every strategy built by create_with_partitions. However, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which sets worker.shutdown=True, shuts down every queue, and joins the worker threads. Arroyo's StreamProcessor closes and joins the current strategy on every partition revocation and creates a new one on the next assignment, so after the first routine consumer-group rebalance (deploy, autoscaling, another group member joining) the new strategy is built on a dead pool. From then on every submit() reaches work_queue.put(), which raises queue.ShutDown; SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() catches that with a broad 'except Exception', logs it, and then calls offset_tracker.add_offset + complete_offset for the message. The commit thread therefore commits offsets for messages that were never enqueued or processed, and since this consumer has no DLQ configured the data is silently lost until the process is restarted. Nothing recreates the pool (ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() is never invoked by the StreamProcessor). Fix by creating the pool per create_with_partitions call (or not shutting it down from the strategy), and by not marking offsets complete when the work item was never actually queued.

title: Unbounded queues and no backpressure despite docstring claiming 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up'
body: FixedQueuePool creates plain queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy never applies backpressure: submit() always enqueues immediately and poll() only emits a gauge (arroyo strategies signal backpressure by raising MessageRejected from poll/submit). The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but put() on an unbounded queue never blocks, so the Kafka consumer thread keeps polling and buffering messages in memory no matter how far behind the workers fall. A single slow group — the exact scenario this mode is built to tolerate — grows its queue without bound and the partition's entire backlog accumulates in the process heap, eventually OOM-killing the consumer pod. The queues should be bounded (maxsize) and/or poll() should raise MessageRejected when total depth exceeds a threshold.

title: Shutdown drops queued work without draining or a final offset commit, causing duplicate processing on every rebalance/deploy
body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False). OrderedQueueWorker.run loops on 'while not self.shutdown', so each worker exits immediately after its current item and never drains the remaining queued items — the immediate=False 'graceful' drain is dead code. Additionally, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/join() never waits for queued work (wait_until_empty exists but is unused) and performs no final commit after workers finish: the commit thread is joined before the pool is shut down, and its last pass races with in-flight items. The result is that on every deploy or partition revocation the queued backlog plus roughly the last commit-interval's worth of completed-but-uncommitted work is redelivered by Kafka and processed a second time. join(timeout) should drain the queues within the timeout and then stage a final commit of all completed offsets.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the opposite of the implemented behavior and races the 1s commit thread
body: The test mocks the result processor to raise on the first of two messages and then asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, i.e. that nothing is ever committed. That contradicts both the implementation and the test's own docstring ('errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages'): OrderedQueueWorker.run marks the failed item's offset complete in its finally block, so once the strategy's commit thread wakes on its 1-second tick it will commit offset 102 for the partition. The test only passes because the assertion usually runs before the commit thread's first 1s iteration; on a slow CI worker the commit fires first and the test fails nondeterministically. The test should instead wait on a commit and assert the real intended semantics — that the processing error did not prevent the partition's offsets (including the failed message's, which is skipped) from being committed.

title: test_different_groups_distributed is flaky due to per-process string hash randomization
body: The test submits 20 group keys and asserts len(queue_indices) == 3, i.e. that they cover all 3 queues. Queue assignment is hash(group_key) % num_queues, and CPython randomizes str hash values per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so each test run is effectively a random draw: the probability that 20 keys land in only 1–2 of 3 buckets is about 0.09% (3*(2/3)^20). With no code change at all, roughly 1 in 1100 CI runs will fail this assertion. Use a looser assertion (e.g. indices are within range and ordering per key is stable), pin the hash seed, or mock hash().

title: Strategy close() destroys the factory-owned shared queue pool, breaking the consumer after any rebalance
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (also reached via terminate() and join()) calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), but the FixedQueuePool is owned by ResultsStrategyFactory: it is created once in the factory's __init__ and the same instance is passed to every strategy produced by create_with_partitions(). Arroyo's StreamProcessor calls close()+join() on the strategy at every partition revocation/rebalance and then builds a new strategy from the same factory. After the first rebalance the pool's queues have been shut down (queue.Queue.shutdown()) and all worker threads have exited, so every subsequent queue_pool.submit() raises queue.ShutDown from work_queue.put(); that exception is swallowed by SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit's except clause, which marks the offset complete so it is committed even though the message was never processed. Net effect: after any routine consumer-group event (deploy, scaling, assignment change) a consumer in thread-queue-parallel mode silently drops all results until the process is restarted. The pool lifecycle should belong only to the factory (strategy.close() should stop just its own commit thread), or the factory should create a fresh pool in create_with_partitions().

title: submit()'s catch-all marks offsets complete for messages that were never processed
body: In SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit, the broad `except Exception` handler records the message's offset via add_offset + complete_offset, making it committable even though the message was never handed to a worker. Skipping is intentional for undecodable payloads, but those are already handled by decode_payload returning None; this catch-all also fires for real failures — grouping_fn raising, or work_queue.put raising queue.ShutDown once the pool has been shut down (after a rebalance, or during shutdown with in-flight submits). In those cases the offset is committed and the result is silently lost instead of being left uncommitted so it can be re-consumed. Only the intentional skip path (decoder returned None) should complete the offset; unexpected exceptions from grouping/submission should propagate or leave the offset outstanding so the message is retried.

title: Queues are unbounded, so the advertised 'natural backpressure' does not exist
body: FixedQueuePool creates plain queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize, so they are unbounded. The class and strategy docstrings advertise 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but an unbounded queue never fills: if workers fall behind on slow results (the exact problem this PR is meant to mitigate), submit() never blocks and the consumer keeps reading from Kafka and buffering WorkItem objects — each retaining the full original Kafka message — in memory without limit. Under sustained lag this grows memory unboundedly and can OOM the consumer, and it defeats the offset-based flow control since offsets are only committed after processing. Give the queues a maxsize (or otherwise cap in-flight items) so put() blocks and provides real backpressure.

title: FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker shutdown flags before draining, so queued items are abandoned
body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown() first sets worker.shutdown = True for every worker and only then calls q.shutdown(immediate=False). OrderedQueueWorker.run loops on `while not self.shutdown`, so a worker that finishes its current item after the flag is set exits its loop immediately, abandoning any items still in its queue — the immediate=False 'drain remaining items' semantics never take effect because no worker is left to read them. Those messages were already fetched from Kafka; their offsets simply never get committed and they will be reprocessed on restart, but the shutdown is not actually graceful as written. Shut the queues down first (immediate=False) so workers drain and then exit via queue.ShutDown, and only use the flag as a backstop.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the opposite of its stated behavior and is flaky
body: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, i.e. that nothing was committed. Its docstring says it verifies that 'errors in processing don't block offset commits', and the implementation under test completes the offset in the worker's finally block even when result_processor raises, so the commit thread will commit offset 102 on its next ~1s tick. The test only passes because it usually finishes before the commit thread's first 1s tick; under a slow CI worker the commit can land inside the polling window (which sleeps an extra 0.2s after processing completes) and the assertion fails intermittently, and regardless the test validates the opposite of the documented behavior. It should wait for and assert that the commit advances past both messages (offset 102) despite the processing error.

title: test_stats_reporting races with workers draining the queue
body: In test_stats_reporting, the test submits 10 items to a pool whose workers process each item in microseconds, then immediately asserts stats['total_items'] > 0. Whether anything is still queued at that point is a race between the submitting thread and the three worker threads; on a fast machine the workers can drain all 10 items before get_stats() runs, making this assertion fail intermittently. The test should hold items in the queue with an explicit blocking condition in the processor before asserting non-zero depth, or drop that assertion.

title: Shared FixedQueuePool is shut down on the first rebalance; all later messages are silently dropped but their offsets committed
body: FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and the same instance is passed to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy built by create_with_partitions. Arroyo's StreamProcessor closes and recreates the processing strategy on every partition revocation/rebalance, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() call queue_pool.shutdown(), which calls shutdown() on each internal queue.Queue. After the first rebalance the factory hands the already-shut-down pool to the new strategy: FixedQueuePool.submit's work_queue.put(...) raises queue.ShutDown, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches all exceptions and then marks the message's offset as completed, so the background commit thread commits offsets for messages that were never processed. Net effect: after any rebalance (deploy, scaling, partition movement) the consumer silently drops every subsequent message while advancing committed offsets — silent data loss plus one exception log per message — until the process is restarted. The shared OffsetTracker also retains state for revoked partitions, so the new commit thread will attempt to commit offsets for partitions this consumer no longer owns. The pool should be created per create_with_partitions call (or close() should not shut down a factory-owned pool), and a rebalance test is missing.

title: Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure and memory grows without limit when processing lags
body: FixedQueuePool creates plain queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize, so put() never blocks and queued work is unbounded. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit is called synchronously from the StreamProcessor poll loop, meaning that when processing is slower than intake — the exact scenario this PR is designed to mitigate — messages are continuously pulled from Kafka and accumulated in memory, growing consumer RSS until OOM and inflating consumer lag. The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring advertises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', which is false with unbounded queues. Use bounded queues (a blocking put naturally throttles the poll loop) or pause consumption when queue depth exceeds a threshold.

title: A single permanent offset gap wedges all future commits for a partition and the per-second scan grows unboundedly
body: OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets only advances the committable offset through a strictly contiguous integer range (for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1)). Any permanent gap in a partition's offsets blocks commits for that partition forever: Kafka topics written by transactional producers contain control-record batches that consume offsets without ever being delivered to the consumer, and compacted topics have gaps by design. Once wedged, the committed offset never advances, so every restart replays the entire post-gap backlog, and the commit loop re-scans range(start, max_offset + 1) every second, growing by one iteration per new message and burning ever-increasing CPU in the commit thread. The new tests (test_offset_gaps_block_commits) enshrine gap-blocking as intended, but it does not match Kafka offset semantics; iterating over sorted(all_offsets) and blocking only on seen-but-still-outstanding offsets would handle gaps without losing safety for submitted-but-unfinished work.

title: Shutdown stops the commit thread before workers finish; final completed offsets are never committed and queued work is dropped
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the background commit thread before calling queue_pool.shutdown(), so any offsets that workers complete after the commit thread exits (in-flight items at shutdown — common here since this mode targets slow items) are never committed and will be reprocessed on restart. Additionally, FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True before draining, so each worker exits after finishing only its current item and all remaining queued items are discarded rather than drained, despite the 'gracefully shutdown' docstring (their offsets stay uncommitted, so this is reprocessing rather than loss, but it discards the backlog on every deploy/rebalance). Finally, join(timeout) ignores its timeout argument and just calls close() again, and FixedQueuePool.shutdown() joins each of the N workers with its own 5s timeout, so strategy shutdown can take up to ~5*N seconds (default N=20 → ~100s) regardless of the join_timeout the StreamProcessor requested.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the opposite of the implementation and is timing-dependent
body: In test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling, the final assertion (assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets) contradicts the code under test: OrderedQueueWorker.run completes offsets in a finally block even when the result processor raises, so both submitted offsets (100 and 101) become committable and the background commit loop (1s cadence) will commit them. The test only passes when the assertion executes before the commit thread's first tick (~1s after create_with_partitions); on a slow or loaded CI worker it will fail intermittently. The assertion also contradicts the test's own docstring ('errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages'), which implies the successful second message's offset should eventually be committed.

title: test_stats_reporting races with live worker threads and can flake on total_items > 0
body: In TestFixedQueuePool.test_stats_reporting, the test submits 10 work items and then immediately asserts stats['total_items'] > 0 while three real worker threads (started in setUp) are actively draining the queues. If the main thread is preempted during the submit loop (e.g., on a loaded CI machine), the workers can process all 10 items before get_stats() runs, making total_items 0 and failing the assertion intermittently. The test should block processing (e.g., with a threading.Event the result processor waits on) before asserting a nonzero queue depth.

title: Backup codes cannot be used by Google/SAML users with 2FA, locking them out
body: In the credentials authorize callback, the guard `if (user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode) throw new Error(ErrorCode.ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled)` runs before the new backup-code branch. Users who log in via Google/SAML and have 2FA enabled go through the totp JWT flow (`loginWithTotp`), which submits no totpCode and no password — so if they lose their authenticator and try a backup code, they get 'third-party-identity-provider-enabled' instead of the backup-code check. Backup codes are precisely the recovery mechanism for lost authenticator access, so these users have no recovery path at all. The IdP checks should be skipped when a valid backupCode is supplied (the backup code itself is the second factor).

title: Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write, allowing code reuse under concurrency
body: The code decrypts the backup code list, checks `indexOf`, sets `backupCodes[index] = null`, and re-encrypts in a separate update. Two concurrent login requests presenting the same backup code can both read the list before either writes, both pass the `indexOf` check, and both be authenticated — defeating the single-use guarantee of backup codes (which the UI copy explicitly promises: 'Each backup code can be used exactly once'). The check-and-consume should be made atomic (e.g., a transaction with a conditional update, or a per-code row with a unique consumed marker).

title: Consumed backup codes become permanent null entries; once all 10 are used there is no recovery or regeneration path
body: Used codes are replaced with `null` inside the stored array rather than removed, and there is no endpoint or UI to regenerate backup codes. After all 10 codes are consumed, `user.backupCodes` is still non-null, so the 'MissingBackupCodes' branch never triggers; the user just gets 'incorrect-backup-code' forever. The new locale string 'missing_backup_codes' tells users to 'generate them in your settings', but no such settings UI exists in this PR, so the message directs users to a non-existent feature. Either add a regeneration flow (e.g., rerun setup) or fix the message and prune null entries.

title: Dismissing the dialog after enabling 2FA (Esc/overlay click) skips onEnable and leaves stale state
body: After `handleEnable` succeeds, the modal moves to the DisplayBackupCodes step, and `onEnable()` (which notifies the parent that 2FA is now enabled, updating the settings switch) is only called from the explicit 'Close' button. If the user dismisses the dialog via Escape or clicking the overlay, `onOpenChange` fires, `onEnable` is never called, and `resetState` is never run — the parent UI still shows 2FA as disabled even though it is enabled in the database, and reopening the modal resumes at the stale DisplayBackupCodes step. Handle cleanup in `onOpenChange` (or a useEffect on `open`) so enable notification and state reset happen on any close path.

title: No tests cover the core new behavior: logging in with a backup code or disabling 2FA with one
body: The PR's main feature is using backup codes during the 2FA login flow and in the disable-2FA flow, but the only test additions exercise the setup screen's copy/download/close buttons, and the file itself adds a TODO admitting login-with-backup and disable-with-backup tests are missing. The single-use consumption logic in the credentials provider, the dash-stripping (`replaceAll('-', '')`), and the new error paths (IncorrectBackupCode, MissingBackupCodes) are entirely untested. The PR checklist also states no tests were added proving the feature works. At minimum, an e2e test should log in with a backup code and verify the same code is rejected on a second attempt.

title: Backup code minLength/maxLength rely on native validation that is disabled on the login form
body: The input enforces the code length via native `minLength={10}`/`maxLength={11}` attributes, but the login form in `apps/web/pages/auth/login.tsx` renders with `noValidate`, so these constraints are never enforced there; any-length string is submitted as `backupCode`. Additionally the placeholder/format 'XXXXX-XXXXX' is 11 characters with the dash, so a correctly formatted code sits at the maxLength boundary and the 10-char minimum rejects a valid 10-char code entered without the dash. Move length/format validation into the zod schema or the server (the server already strips dashes, so client-side length constraints are redundant and currently misleading).

title: Backup codes unusable for Google/SAML users with 2FA
body: In the credentials authorize flow, the identity-provider guards run before the backup-code branch and only check `credentials.totpCode`: `user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode` throws ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled, and `!user.password && ... && !credentials.totpCode` throws IncorrectEmailPassword. A Google/SAML user with 2FA enabled who loses their authenticator and submits a backup code (the `/auth/login?totp=...` flow sends no totpCode) will be rejected before the backup-code check at line 131 is ever reached, and such users also have no password to fall back on. The guards should also pass when `credentials.backupCode` is present.

title: Backup code consumption is not atomic
body: The login flow decrypts the code list, checks `indexOf`, and then updates the user row in a separate, non-transactional step. Two concurrent login requests presenting the same backup code can both pass the `indexOf` check before either writes back, allowing a single-use code to be used twice. The copy in the UI explicitly promises each code "can be used exactly once". Consider an atomic update or a conditional update keyed on the stored value.

title: missing_backup_codes message instructs an impossible action
body: The new string "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." tells users to generate backup codes in settings, but this PR adds no way to (re)generate backup codes from settings — codes are only created during initial 2FA setup. A user who hits this error (e.g. 2FA enabled before this feature existed, so `backupCodes` is null) is directed to an action that does not exist.

title: No test coverage for logging in with a backup code
body: The PR's core security feature — consuming a backup code during login and enforcing single-use — has no test. The added tests only cover the download/copy buttons on the setup screen, and the file itself acknowledges this with a TODO. A regression in the authorize backup-code branch (e.g. the identity-provider guard issue) would not be caught.

title: Backup code login rejected for SAML/Google users with 2FA
body: The guard `if (user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode) throw new Error(ErrorCode.ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled)` (and the similar password check below at line 117) only exempts requests carrying a totpCode. When a user whose identity provider is Google/SAML has 2FA enabled and tries to log in with a backup code (totpCode empty, backupCode set — exactly what the new 'Lost access' flow submits via the `?totp=` JWT login page), they hit this branch first and get 'account created with identity provider' instead of reaching the new backup-code verification below. Backup codes are therefore unusable for precisely the IdP users the external-TOTP login flow serves; the checks must also allow `credentials.backupCode`.

title: Backup code consumption is a check-then-update race, allowing code reuse
body: The authorize callback decrypts the backup code list, checks `indexOf`, and then issues a separate `prisma.user.update` to mark the code used. Two concurrent login attempts with the same backup code can both pass the `indexOf` check before either update commits, so a single-use code can be redeemed twice. Since the codes are short (40 bits of entropy) and the rate limiter is the only mitigation, the consumption should be atomic (e.g., conditional update inside a transaction, or re-read-and-verify within a serializable transaction).

title: First 2FA test never closes the new backup-codes screen, so the enabled-switch assertion is unreliable
body: After the PR, successful TOTP submission shows the DisplayBackupCodes step instead of closing the modal. The first test ('should allow a user to enable 2FA and login using 2FA') was not updated: it goes straight to asserting the `two-factor-switch` state while the backup-code dialog is still open, and the PR itself adds a FIXME noting this assertion 'passes even when switch is not checked'. The test should click `backup-codes-close` (like the disable test does) and then assert on `[data-state="checked"]`; as written it no longer proves that enabling 2FA worked.

title: Unvalidated req.body.backupCode can crash the disable endpoint
body: `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` assumes the client sent a string. The request body is not validated, so a non-string value (e.g. a number or object) causes a TypeError and a 500 instead of a 400 IncorrectBackupCode. Coerce/validate the body (e.g. zod) before use, as is done elsewhere in the codebase.

title: Crash when destinationCalendar is empty and location is Google Meet
body: In `EventManager.create()`, the code destructures `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` and then immediately accesses `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining. When an event has Google Meet (`MeetLocationType`) as its location but no destination calendar (empty array or null — which this PR now produces in many places, e.g. handleNewBooking sets `null` and other handlers set `[]`), `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined` and reading `.integration` throws a TypeError, breaking booking creation. The previous code used `evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`, which was safe. This needs `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.

title: Team destination calendars silently dropped when organizer/event type has no destination calendar
body: For collective events, `evt.destinationCalendar` is initialized to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` exists, and later `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is a no-op on `null`. So if the main host has no destination calendar but other collective hosts do, those hosts' calendars are never added and they won't get calendar events — the exact scenario this PR is meant to fix. The code should initialize an array first (e.g. `evt.destinationCalendar = evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` before pushing, or use `(evt.destinationCalendar ?? []).concat(teamDestinationCalendars)`).

title: updateEvent/deleteEvent fallback find() can never match, producing undefined calendarId
body: In both `updateEvent` (line ~254-256) and `deleteEvent` (line ~315-317), the fallback branch is `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. This branch is only reached when `externalCalendarId` is falsy (null/undefined), so `cal.externalId === externalCalendarId` can never be true and the expression always evaluates to `undefined`. Previously the fallback used `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`, which resolved to the destination calendar. Now, when `updateEvent`/`deleteEvent` are called without an explicit external calendar id, `calendarId` becomes `undefined` (update) and the Google API call will fail or target the wrong calendar. The fallback should use the first destination calendar's externalId instead.

title: Recurring-event cancellation deletes are re-executed once per calendar reference
body: The recurring-event deletion block (`if (bookingToDelete.eventType?.recurringEvent && bookingToDelete.recurringEventId && allRemainingBookings)`) iterates over all of the user's calendar credentials and all updated bookings. This PR wrapped that block inside `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)`, so with multiple calendar references (now normal for multi-host collective bookings) the same full sweep of deletes runs once per reference — deleting the same events N times and pushing duplicate promises into `apiDeletes`. The recurring-cancellation sweep should be hoisted out of the per-reference loop (or guarded to run only once).

title: Hangout-link patch uses possibly undefined calendarId
body: In `createEvent`, `selectedCalendar` is computed via `destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.credentialId === credentialId)?.externalId` and falls back to `"primary"` only for the `events.insert` call. The follow-up `calendar.events.patch` that writes the hangout link description uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar` directly, without the `"primary"` fallback. When no destination calendar matches the credential, the insert succeeds on the primary calendar but the patch is sent with `calendarId: undefined`, so the description update fails silently.

title: Crash when destinationCalendar is empty/null and location is Google Meet
body: In `EventManager.create`, the new code does `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` and then immediately reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration`. When the event has no destination calendar (null or empty array — common for users with no connected calendar), `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined` and accessing `.integration` throws a TypeError. Previously this line used optional chaining (`evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`), so it was safe. Any booking with location `integrations:google:meet` and no destination calendar will now fail during event creation. The check should be `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration !== "google_calendar"`.

title: updateEvent/deleteEvent fallback lookup compares externalCalendarId to itself and can never match
body: In `updateEvent` (and the identical pattern in `deleteEvent` at line 317), the fallback when `externalCalendarId` is falsy is `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. Searching for a calendar whose externalId equals the (falsy) externalCalendarId can never succeed, so `selectedCalendar` becomes `undefined` and `calendar.events.update` is called with `calendarId: undefined`, failing the API call. Previously the fallback was `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`, which resolved to the host's calendar. The intent appears to be matching the destination calendar against the credential in use, similar to what `createEvent` now does with `credentialId`; as written, updates/deletes for bookings whose reference has no `externalCalendarId` will silently break.

title: hangoutLink patch uses undefined calendarId when fallback "primary" was used for insert
body: In `createEvent`, the insert uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"`, but the subsequent `calendar.events.patch` that adds the hangout link uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar` without the fallback. When no destination calendar matches the credentialId (selectedCalendar is undefined), the event is created on "primary" but the follow-up patch is issued with `calendarId: undefined`, so the description with the Meet link is never written (and the promise rejection is unhandled). Apply the same `|| "primary"` fallback to the patch call.

title: createEvent always uses the first destination calendar regardless of which host's credential is used
body: `Office365CalendarService.createEvent` destructures `event.destinationCalendar[0]` and posts to `/me/calendars/{firstCalendar.externalId}/events`. With this PR, `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents` now calls `createEvent` once per host credential for collective events, but the service signature was not updated to accept the credentialId/externalId being processed (unlike Google, which received a `credentialId` parameter and picks the matching calendar). For a collective booking, host B's Office365 credential will try to create the event in host A's calendar (whose externalId is meaningless to host B's account), so the call fails or creates the event in the wrong place. The same problem exists in `LarkCalendarService` and `BaseCalendarService` (caldav), which also only ever look at `destinationCalendar[0]`. The per-credential calendar must be selected the same way Google's implementation does.

title: Collective hosts' destination calendars are dropped when the organizer has none
body: The new code sets `destinationCalendar` to `null` when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar, and later does `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`. If the organizer has no destination calendar but other collective hosts do, the optional-chained push is a no-op and the hosts' calendars are silently discarded — the exact scenario this PR is meant to fix (hosts not getting invited). The collective branch should initialize the array, e.g. `evt.destinationCalendar = [...(evt.destinationCalendar ?? []), ...teamDestinationCalendars]`.

title: One unresolvable reference aborts updates for all remaining calendar references
body: In `updateAllCalendarEvents`, if a reference has a `credentialId` that is neither in `this.calendarCredentials` nor found in the DB (deleted credential, or a credential belonging to a collective host that no longer exists), `credential` stays `undefined` and `updateEvent(credential, ...)` is still pushed into `result`. `updateEvent` calls `getCalendar(undefined)`, which throws; the outer try/catch then swallows everything and returns failure results for all references — so a single stale reference prevents updating every other host's calendar event on reschedule. The loop should skip references whose credential cannot be resolved (with a logged warning) instead of pushing the update.

title: Recurring-event deletes now run once per calendar reference, causing duplicated delete calls
