body: The recurring-cancellation branch (delete all remaining bookings' events across all the user's calendar credentials) was moved inside the new `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)` loop. For a collective booking with two calendar references, the block that iterates over every user credential and every updated booking is executed once per reference, so each event is deleted N times (and `apiDeletes` collects duplicates). Besides wasted API calls, some providers error on deleting an already-deleted event. Additionally, the inner loop still only deletes `updBooking.references.find(...)` — the first calendar reference per booking — so extra hosts' references are never removed. The recurring-delete block should run once outside the per-reference loop, and should iterate over all calendar references of each updated booking.

title: Unrelated logic inversion in organization slug persistence
body: This PR about destinationCalendar arrays also changes organization creation: `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` became `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`, inverting when the org slug is stored on the team record. This is unrelated to the PR's stated purpose, untested, and changes which deployments persist `slug` vs `requestedSlug` — if unintentional it will break org subdomain resolution; if intentional it belongs in its own PR with justification.

title: No tests cover the new multi-host destinationCalendar behavior
body: The PR checklist explicitly states "I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective". This change alters the `CalendarEvent.destinationCalendar` contract from a single object to an array and rewires create/update/delete paths across Google, Office365, Lark, CalDAV, EventManager, cancellation, rescheduling, and payment webhooks — including subtle per-credential calendar selection and booking reference persistence (`referencesToCreate` now uses `result.externalId`/`result.credentialId`). Given regressions like the empty-array crash in `EventManager.create` and the Office365 first-calendar-only behavior, at minimum unit tests for `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents`/`updateAllCalendarEvents` with multiple hosts and for the no-destination-calendar case should be required before merging.

title: Crash when Google Meet is the location and destinationCalendar is empty
body: In EventManager.create(), the code does `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` and then evaluates `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"` whenever `evt.location === MeetLocationType`. If the event has Google Meet as its location but the organizer has no destination calendar (the array is empty or null), `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined` and accessing `.integration` throws a TypeError, aborting booking creation. The previous code used optional chaining (`evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`) and was safe. This needs `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration !== "google_calendar"`.

title: Team destination calendars lost when organizer has no destination calendar
body: In handleNewBooking, `evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` exists. Immediately after, for COLLECTIVE team events the code does `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` — optional chaining on `null` silently skips the push, so the co-hosts' destination calendars collected in `teamDestinationCalendars` are dropped entirely. In exactly the collective scenario this PR aims to fix, if the organizer (users[0]) has no destination calendar but co-hosts do, no calendar events will be created for the co-hosts. It should be `evt.destinationCalendar = [...(evt.destinationCalendar ?? []), ...teamDestinationCalendars]`.

title: Office365 creates every host's event in the main host's calendar
body: createEvent now always uses the first entry of `event.destinationCalendar` (`mainHostDestinationCalendar.externalId`) to build the URL `/me/calendars/{externalId}/events`. With multiple destination calendars (collective events), EventManager calls createEvent once per host credential, but this service ignores which credential it belongs to — unlike the Google service which matches `cal.credentialId === credentialId`. For a co-host's Office365 account, the main host's externalId is not valid in their account, so the API call fails (or worse, writes to an unintended calendar), and the co-host never gets the event. The same first-entry-only pattern in larkcalendar and BaseCalendarService (caldav) has the analogous problem: for non-main hosts the filter matches nothing, so no event is created at all while reporting success.

title: updateEvent/deleteEvent fallback find can never match
body: In updateEvent (and identically in deleteEvent at line ~317) the fallback is `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. This branch only executes when `externalCalendarId` is falsy (the ternary's truthy branch returns it directly), so the find compares each calendar's externalId against undefined/null and always yields undefined. The previous behavior fell back to `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. Result: when updateEvent/deleteEvent is called without an externalCalendarId, `calendarId` becomes undefined and the Google API call targets an undefined calendar. The fallback should use the first destination calendar's externalId (or match by credential) instead.

title: Hangout-link patch uses possibly undefined calendarId
body: In createEvent, the insert falls back to `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"`, but the follow-up `calendar.events.patch` that adds the hangout link to the description uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar` without the fallback. When no destination calendar matches the credentialId, the insert succeeds on "primary" but the patch is issued with `calendarId: undefined`, so the description update (containing the Meet link) silently fails.

title: Unrelated logic inversion in organization creation
body: This PR about destination calendars also flips the condition for setting `slug` on organization creation: previously `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })`, now `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`. This inverts which deployments store the slug directly on the team row vs. only as `requestedSlug` in metadata. If intentional it belongs in a separate PR with justification; as merged, self-hosted instances without team billing will stop persisting the organization slug, breaking org subdomain URLs.

title: Google Calendar stores the zod SafeParse wrapper object as the credential key
body: In refreshAccessToken, `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema)` returns a zod SafeParseReturnType ({ success, data }), and that whole object is then written to the DB via `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. Previously the code stored `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` (the parsed token). After this change the credential key becomes `{"success":true,"data":{...}}` instead of the token payload, so the next time the credential is loaded `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` fails and the Google Calendar integration breaks for every user whose token is refreshed. The fix is to use `key.data` (after checking success) as the value stored.

title: Salesforce CalendarService uses prisma without importing it
body: The newly added block in getClient calls `await prisma.credential.update(...)` but the file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma";` (check the import list — only jsforce, rrule, zod, calcom libs, types, getAppKeysFromSlug and parseRefreshTokenResponse are imported). This will fail TypeScript compilation / throw a ReferenceError at runtime whenever the Salesforce calendar service is instantiated.

title: zoho-bigin passes the credential ID as the user ID to refreshOAuthTokens
body: refreshOAuthTokens' third parameter is `userId`, and when credential sync is enabled it is sent to the sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. zoho-bigin passes `credentialId` (the Credential row id) instead of a user id — unlike every other app in this PR which passes `credential.userId`. With syncing enabled, the self-hoster's sync endpoint receives a credential id where it expects a Cal.com user id, so token refreshes for zoho-bigin will look up the wrong user (or fail) and return tokens for the wrong account.

title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time !== on a raw header value
body: The endpoint authenticates by comparing `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` with a plain string inequality. This is a timing-attackable comparison on a secret that guards writing arbitrary OAuth credentials for any userId. Use a constant-time comparison (e.g. crypto.timingSafeEqual on equal-length buffers).

title: Salesforce token is refreshed on every client construction regardless of expiry
body: getClient now performs a blocking refresh_token grant against login.salesforce.com and a DB write every time a SalesforceCalendarService is constructed — previously jsforce handled refreshing lazily only when needed. Every calendar operation (create/update/delete, and availability flows that construct services) now incurs an extra Salesforce auth round-trip plus a credential write, slowing requests and burning through Salesforce's refresh-token rotation / rate limits unnecessarily. It should check the stored token's expiry first and only refresh when needed.

title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token" and persisted
body: When the parsed response has no refresh_token, the code sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. Callers (e.g. zoom, which merges parsedToken.data over the stored key) then write this placeholder into the credential in the DB, destroying the real refresh token and permanently breaking subsequent refreshes for that credential. If the provider omits a refresh token, the existing stored one should be preserved instead of a sentinel string.

title: prisma is used but never imported in SalesforceCalendarService
body: The new getClient code calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` at line 96, but the file's imports (lines 1-20) do not include `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. This is a compile-time error (and a runtime ReferenceError if it were to build), so the Salesforce calendar service is broken by this PR.

title: Sync endpoint response is returned as a raw fetch Response without checking status or parsing the body
body: When credential sharing is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` POSTs to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT and returns the raw `Response` object. It never checks `response.ok` and never calls `response.json()`. Callers then break: for example `googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` does `const token = res?.data; googleCredentials.access_token = token.access_token;` — a fetch Response has no `.data`, so this throws TypeError whenever sync mode is on. Similarly office365video/webex call `handleErrorsJson(response)` and others call `await resp.json()`, which would consume the body of an un-checked response. Token refresh silently fails for every integration when the feature is enabled.

title: minimumTokenResponseSchema corrupts stored credentials: computed keys don't do what's intended, unknown fields are stripped, and a fake refresh_token is injected
body: In zod, computed keys in an object literal like `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` do not create a catch-all rule for 'any property that is a number'; they just produce a literal (garbage) key. So in sync mode the schema effectively becomes `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), ... })`, which (a) strips every other field from the parsed result by default — so `refreshTokenResponse.data` returned to callers contains only `access_token`, dropping `expiry_date`/`expires_in`/scope that callers then persist (e.g. Google stores the result via `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`, wiping the real refresh token and expiry from the credential), and (b) line 26 then writes the literal string `"refresh_token"` as the refresh token when none is present, permanently corrupting the stored credential so subsequent real refreshes fail with invalid_grant.

title: Passes credentialId instead of the Cal.com userId to refreshOAuthTokens
body: `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` passes the credential's database id as the third argument, but that parameter is `userId` and is sent to the sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. The parent platform will receive a credential id instead of a user id and will either 404 or refresh tokens for the wrong user. Every other integration passes `credential.userId`; this one should capture `credential.userId` in biginAuth and pass that.

title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time string equality
body: The header value is compared to `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` using `!==`. This is a timing-safe-comparison candidate: use a constant-time comparison (e.g. `crypto.timingSafeEqual`) for a shared secret guarding credential writes. Additionally the secret check does not guard against both values being empty strings in a misconfigured deployment (empty header === empty env passes), and there is no method restriction or rate limiting on an endpoint that writes OAuth credentials.

title: Zod parse and decrypt errors bubble up as unhandled 500s
body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)`, `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` throw on invalid input (malformed body, wrong encryption key, non-JSON plaintext). Since the handler has no try/catch, callers get an unhandled 500 with a stack trace instead of a 400; a misconfigured sender has no way to distinguish bad payload from server failure, and the webhook sender will likely retry forever.

title: findFirst-then-create race allows duplicate credentials for the same user/app
body: The endpoint does `findFirst` and then `create` without a transaction or unique constraint on (userId, appId). Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same user/app both miss the findFirst and both create, leaving two credentials where downstream code uses `findFirst` and silently picks one. Use `prisma.credential.upsert` on a unique compound key (add one if missing) or wrap in a transaction with serializable isolation.

title: isExpired compares expiry_date against +new Date() (milliseconds) but other services use seconds — unchanged inconsistency now matters more
body: `isExpired = (expiryDate) => expiryDate < Math.round(+new Date())` is correct here because expiry_date is stored in ms in this file, but office365calendar's own service stores `expires_in` in seconds and compares against seconds. With credentials now being pushed in from an external platform via the webhook, the expiry semantics (seconds vs ms) of the synced keys are undocumented and differ per integration, so externally-synced credentials will be treated as expired (or never expiring) depending on the app. The sync contract in the PR description only says 'access token and expiry date' without specifying units.

title: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses invalid computed zod keys, so every sync-mode refresh fails validation
body: In zod, object shape keys must be string literals. `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()` evaluate to the literal keys `"[object ZodString]"` and `"[object ZodOptional]"`, not dynamic key matchers. The resulting schema therefore requires the token response to contain a property literally named `[object ZodString]` with a number value, which no real token endpoint returns. Whenever APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, every parseRefreshTokenResponse call fails with 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned', breaking token refresh for Google Calendar, Office 365 Calendar, Zoom, and Salesforce in exactly the mode this PR introduces. Use z.record() or .passthrough()/catchall() instead.

title: Sync-mode refresh returns a fetch Response, but code reads res.data
body: refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw fetch Response when credential syncing is enabled (it only returns the googleapis `res` object in the non-sync branch). The code then does `const token = res?.data; googleCredentials.access_token = token.access_token;`. A fetch Response has no `data` property, so `token` is undefined and reading `token.access_token` throws a TypeError. It is swallowed by the catch (message isn't 'invalid_grant'), so the Google access token is silently never refreshed when credential syncing is enabled, and calendar access breaks once the stored token expires.

title: Sync-mode refresh result treated as HubspotToken but is a fetch Response
body: When credential syncing is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw fetch Response from the sync endpoint, but the code treats the result as a HubspotToken: it reads `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` (undefined, so expiryDate becomes NaN) and calls `hubspotClient.setAccessToken(hubspotRefreshToken.accessToken)` (undefined). The NaN expiry and undefined access token are then persisted to the credential row via prisma.credential.update, corrupting the stored HubSpot credentials. The Response body is never parsed.

title: Sync-mode refresh response doesn't match expected Lark RefreshTokenResp shape
body: In sync mode refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw Response from the self-hoster's endpoint, which per the PR description contains only an access token and expiry. The code then calls handleLarkError<RefreshTokenResp>(resp) and reads `data.data.refresh_token`, `data.data.refresh_expires_in`, and `data.data.expires_in`. These fields don't exist on the sync response, so `data.data` is undefined and the refresh throws, making Lark calendar refresh always fail when credential syncing is enabled. The non-Lark response shape is never mapped onto LarkAuthCredentials.

title: Sync-mode refresh response can't satisfy webexRefreshedTokenSchema (requires refresh_token)
body: When credential syncing is enabled, the sync endpoint returns only an access token and expiry, but the code still validates the response with webexRefreshedTokenSchema, which requires `refresh_token: z.string()` and `refresh_token_expires_in: z.number()`. The parse therefore always fails in sync mode and refreshAccessToken rejects with 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned', so Webex meetings stop working as soon as the access token expires. Unlike the other apps converted in this PR, Webex was not switched to parseRefreshTokenResponse.

title: Sync-mode Zoom refresh computes expiry_date as NaN and overwrites refresh_token with placeholder
body: In sync mode the endpoint returns only an access token and expiry (no `expires_in`, no `refresh_token`). parseRefreshTokenResponse fills in `refresh_token = "refresh_token"` when absent, and this code then does `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token` (the literal string "refresh_token") and `key.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + newTokens.expires_in * 1000)` where expires_in is undefined, producing NaN. Both the corrupted refresh token and NaN expiry are persisted to the credential row, permanently breaking future Zoom refreshes for that user until they reconnect.

title: Passes credentialId as the Cal.com userId to the sync endpoint
body: refreshOAuthTokens' third parameter is `userId: number | null` and is sent to the self-hoster's sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. Here the code passes `credentialId` (the credential row's primary key) instead of `credential.userId`. The sync endpoint will therefore receive a wrong user id and either fail to find the user's tokens or return tokens for the wrong user. The sibling zohocrm service correctly passes `credential.userId`.

title: Webhook updates only the first matching credential; duplicates keep stale keys
body: The webhook looks up an existing credential with findFirst({ userId, appId }) and updates only that one row. Cal.com can legitimately have multiple credentials for the same user+app (e.g., office365video/webex/zoom callbacks historically created duplicates, and users can reconnect creating additional rows, plus there is no unique constraint on (userId, appId)). Any additional rows retain the old keys and may still be picked up by findFirst-based lookups elsewhere, so the 'source of truth' sync silently leaves stale credentials active. Consider updating all matching rows or enforcing one credential per (userId, appId).

title: Secret comparison is not constant-time and handler lacks method/parse guards
body: The webhook secret is compared with a plain `!==` on header values, which is a non-constant-time comparison for a bearer-style secret; use a timing-safe comparison. Also, the handler accepts any HTTP method (GET requests will run the full credential write path), and the zod `parse` on req.body plus `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` are unguarded, so malformed payloads produce unhandled 500s instead of 4xx responses.

title: Sync-mode MS Teams refresh yields NaN expiry_date, causing refresh loop on every call
body: In sync mode the endpoint returns only an access token and expiry, with no `expires_in`. The code computes `responseBody.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + (responseBody?.expires_in || 0) * 1000)`, i.e. approximately Date.now(), and persists that to the credential. Since isExpired compares expiry_date < Date.now(), the token is immediately considered expired again, so every API call triggers another sync-endpoint refresh round-trip; and if the sync response's own expiry field is never mapped, the stored expiry is effectively meaningless. Map the sync response's expiry onto expiry_date instead of relying on expires_in.

title: Team admin OR owner check uses && instead of ||
body: `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`, so it is only true when the caller is both an admin AND an owner of the team. A team admin who is not the owner (or an owner who is not flagged admin) will be rejected with FORBIDDEN when trying to add guests to a team booking, even though the UI offers them the action. This should be `||`.

title: Any existing attendee can add arbitrary guests and trigger organizer-branded emails/calendar updates
body: The authorization check allows any existing attendee of the booking (`isAttendee`) to add new guests. An attendee can therefore add unlimited arbitrary email addresses (the schema has no upper bound on the `guests` array), which causes calendar invitations and 'AttendeeScheduledEmail' emails to be sent from the organizer's identity/calendar to anyone the attendee chooses. Additionally, when an attendee performs the action, `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` and the `EventManager` are built from the attendee's credentials rather than the organizer's, so `updateCalendarAttendees` either fails or operates on the wrong user's calendar. This should likely be restricted to the organizer/team admins, and credentials should come from the booking organizer.

title: No status check allows adding guests to cancelled/rejected/past bookings
body: The handler fetches the booking without filtering on `status` and never verifies the booking is ACCEPTED/upcoming. Guests can be added to a cancelled or rejected booking, and the emails/ICS sent by `sendAddGuestsEmails` are generated with `status: "CONFIRMED"`, so recipients receive a confirmed calendar invitation for a cancelled event.

title: Duplicate/blacklist checks are case-sensitive and racy, allowing duplicate attendees
body: Existing-attendee dedupe compares `guest === attendee.email` with exact case, while the blacklist is lowercased but the incoming guest is not. 'User@X.com' vs 'user@x.com' bypasses both checks and creates a duplicate Attendee row. There is also no unique constraint enforced transactionally, so two concurrent addGuests calls can both pass the filter and insert duplicate attendees. Normalize emails (lowercase/trim) before comparing and storing.

title: sendAddGuestsEmails ignores event-type email opt-out settings
body: Unlike neighboring functions (sendScheduledEmails, sendLocationChangeEmails, etc.), `sendAddGuestsEmails` does not accept or honor the event type metadata `disableStandardEmails` (host/attendee). Event types configured to suppress standard emails will still send organizer and attendee emails when guests are added.

title: Email failures swallowed with console.log and no error detail
body: The try/catch around `sendAddGuestsEmails` logs only the static string "Error sending AddGuestsEmails" and drops the actual error, and it runs after `updateCalendarAttendees`, which is unguarded. If calendar update throws, the mutation reports failure even though attendees were already committed to the DB, leaving the UI saying the operation failed while guests exist and no emails were sent. At minimum log the error (use the logger with safeStringify like elsewhere) and consider the ordering/partial-failure semantics.

title: No upper bound on guests array enables mass invitation/email abuse
body: `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` has no `.max()`, so a single authenticated request can add hundreds of attendees to a booking, each generating calendar invites and emails sent from the organizer's address. Add a reasonable maximum (e.g. `.max(10)`) consistent with the booking flow's guest limits.

title: New addGuests mutation has no tests
body: The PR adds a new authenticated mutation that mutates booking attendees, updates external calendars, and sends emails, with non-trivial authorization logic (organizer / team admin-owner / attendee), but includes no unit or integration tests. The broken `&&` in the admin/owner check is exactly the kind of defect a permission test would have caught.

title: Team admin/owner check uses && instead of ||, blocking team admins
body: The permission check computes `isTeamAdminOrOwner = (await isTeamAdmin(user.id, teamId)) && (await isTeamOwner(user.id, teamId))`. This only passes for a user who is simultaneously a team admin AND a team owner, so regular team admins (who are not owners) get FORBIDDEN when trying to add guests to team bookings. This should be an OR: `isTeamAdmin(...) || isTeamOwner(...)`.

title: Blacklist check is case-sensitive and easily bypassed
body: `BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS` entries are lowercased, but the incoming guest email is compared without lowercasing: `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`. A blacklisted address like `spam@example.com` can be added as `Spam@Example.com` and bypass the blacklist entirely. The guest email should be normalized (e.g. `guest.toLowerCase()`) before the comparison (and ideally before the duplicate-attendee comparison too, since email matching against existing attendees is also case-sensitive).

title: No check that the booking is in a valid state before adding guests
body: The handler fetches the booking by id but never checks `booking.status`. Guests can be added to CANCELLED or REJECTED bookings (and past bookings), and both the calendar update (`eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees`) and the emails send an ICS with `status: "CONFIRMED"` and method `REQUEST`, re-inviting people to a cancelled event. The handler should reject bookings that are cancelled/rejected (and arguably past).

title: Calendar attendee update uses the requester's credentials, not the organizer's
body: `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` builds the EventManager with the calling user's credentials. But attendees are allowed to call this endpoint (`isAttendee` passes the permission check), and an attendee typically has no credentials for the organizer's calendar, so `updateCalendarAttendees` will either no-op or update the wrong calendar. The calendar event lives on the organizer's calendar, so the organizer's credentials (already partially loaded via `booking.user.credentials`) should be used.

title: sendAddGuestsEmails ignores event-type email-disable settings
body: Every other sender in this file (sendScheduledEmails, sendLocationChangeEmails, etc.) respects `eventTypeDisableHostEmail` / `eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail` so organizers can disable standard emails via event type metadata. `sendAddGuestsEmails` takes no metadata parameter and unconditionally emails the organizer, all team members, and all attendees, so guests-added emails are sent even when the event type is configured to suppress standard emails.

title: New-guest detection can fail due to email casing mismatch
body: `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)` compares the raw user input against stored attendee emails. If the entered email differs in case from what was stored, a newly added guest receives the 'existing attendee' AttendeeAddGuestsEmail instead of the AttendeeScheduledEmail with full booking details, and conversely an existing attendee could be mis-classified. Compare case-insensitively.

title: Clicking Add with only the default empty field shows a validation error
body: `multiEmailValue` is initialized to `[""]`, so its length is 1, not 0. If the user opens the dialog and clicks Add without typing anything, `safeParse` fails on the empty string and the user sees the red 'Emails must be unique and valid' error instead of the action being a no-op. Empty strings should be filtered out before the length check and validation.

title: Team admin/owner check uses AND instead of OR, denying team admins
body: The permission variable is named `isTeamAdminOrOwner` but is computed as `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`. A user is almost never both an ADMIN and an OWNER of the same team, so this evaluates to false for ordinary team admins, and they are rejected with FORBIDDEN even though the intent (and the variable name) is to allow either role. Team admins therefore cannot add guests to their team's bookings.

title: Calendar update uses the requester's credentials instead of the booking organizer's
body: The handler builds the EventManager with `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` — the credentials of whoever called the mutation. But the handler explicitly permits attendees and team admins to add guests, in which case `ctx.user` is not the organizer and likely has no calendar/video credential connected to the event. `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` will then fail or update the wrong calendar, so guests are added to the DB (and emails are sent) while the actual calendar event is never updated. The booking organizer's credentials (already included on `booking.user.credentials` in the query) should be used.

title: No check on booking status allows adding guests to cancelled or past bookings
body: The handler fetches the booking and performs the update without checking `booking.status` or whether the booking is in the past. Guests can be added to CANCELLED or REJECTED bookings, which will create attendee records and trigger `updateCalendarAttendees` plus notification emails for an event that no longer exists, confusing recipients and potentially re-adding them to a deleted calendar event.

title: Guests array has no size limit
body: `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` accepts an unbounded array. Combined with the fact that any attendee of a booking may call this endpoint, a single request can create hundreds of Attendee rows and trigger hundreds of outgoing emails (sendAddGuestsEmails emails every existing attendee plus every new guest), enabling mail-spam amplification and DB bloat. A reasonable `.max(...)` bound should be enforced.

title: Email failures are swallowed with console.log, losing the error
body: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` call is wrapped in try/catch that only does `console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails")` without logging the actual error or surfacing anything. Guests are already persisted and calendar invites updated at that point, so if email sending fails the new guests receive no invitation and there is no trace of why. At minimum the error object should be logged via the structured logger, and ideally the caller should be informed that emails failed.

title: Duplicate-guest check is case-sensitive against existing attendees
body: `uniqueGuests` filters with `guest === attendee.email`, a case-sensitive comparison. Emails differing only in case (e.g. `User@x.com` vs `user@x.com`) bypass the check and create a duplicate Attendee row for the same person, who then receives duplicate notifications. The blacklist comparison right below lowercases entries but the submitted guests are never lowercased, so `BLACKLISTED@x.com` also bypasses the blacklist. Normalize case on both sides before comparing.

title: sendAddGuestsEmails receives the raw guest list instead of the filtered uniqueGuests
body: After computing `uniqueGuests` (excluding already-registered attendees and blacklisted emails), the handler calls `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` with the original unfiltered input. Today this happens to be harmless because the email code only uses the list for an `includes` check against existing attendee emails, but any blacklisted or duplicate email that was intentionally filtered out of the DB write is still passed to the email layer; if that logic changes (e.g. to email the list directly), invitations would go to people who were never added. Pass `uniqueGuests`.

title: retryCount increment is a read-modify-write race, not atomic
body: Both the `else` branch (line 184) and the `catch` block (line 195) compute `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` using the value fetched earlier in `findMany`. If two cron invocations overlap (this endpoint is triggered by an external cron and processing a large batch can exceed the cron interval), both runs read the same retryCount and write the same value, losing an increment. More importantly, if the row was already updated by a concurrent run, the stale value overwrites it. Use Prisma's atomic `retryCount: { increment: 1 }` so concurrent runs cannot clobber each other's counts.

title: retryCount update in catch block can throw and abort the entire cron run
body: The `catch` block performs an unguarded `prisma.workflowReminder.update`. If the original error was a database connectivity failure (a plausible cause of scheduling errors), this update will also fail, and since nothing catches it the exception propagates out of the `for` loop, aborting processing of all remaining unscheduled reminders in the batch and returning a 500. Wrap the update in its own try/catch (or use updateMany which won't throw on a missing row) so one failing reminder doesn't kill the whole run.

title: Retry-based deletion silently drops reminders that failed for transient reasons
body: The `deleteMany` with `retryCount: { gt: 1 }` deletes any reminder that failed scheduling twice, regardless of why. Failures counted include transient infrastructure problems (Twilio outage, DB errors thrown inside the try, e.g. the `prisma.profile.findFirst` lookup) since the catch block increments retryCount for any error, not just SMS provider rejections like invalid phone numbers. After two transient failures the reminder is permanently deleted and the attendee/host never receives the SMS, with no notification or logging of the deletion. Consider only incrementing for known-permanent provider errors, or at least logging deleted reminder IDs.

title: retryCount incremented via stale read-modify-write instead of atomic increment
body: Both failure paths set `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` using the value fetched at the start of the run. If two cron executions overlap (or the row is otherwise updated between the findMany and the update), one increment is lost, so a reminder that should be deleted after two failures survives for extra runs. Prisma supports `data: { retryCount: { increment: 1 } }`, which is atomic and immune to the stale read; it should be used in both the `else` branch (line ~184) and the `catch` block (line ~195).

title: Unguarded retryCount update in catch block can crash the whole cron run
body: The catch handler now performs `prisma.workflowReminder.update` before logging. If that update itself throws (e.g., the database error that caused the original exception persists, or the row was concurrently deleted), the exception propagates out of the for-loop, the handler returns a 500, and all remaining unscheduled reminders in the batch are skipped for this run. The update in the catch block should be wrapped in its own try/catch (or the failure recorded without a second awaited DB call) so one failing reminder cannot abort processing of the rest.

title: retryCount-based deletion is not scoped to SMS reminders
body: The new `OR` branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` in the deleteMany has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, unlike the sibling branch. WorkflowReminder rows are shared across EMAIL, SMS, and WHATSAPP methods, so any non-SMS reminder that ever gets retryCount > 1 (e.g., if the email cron adopts the same retry pattern, or via manual/data-fix updates) will be silently deleted by the SMS cron. The method filter should be applied to the whole OR (or duplicated in the retryCount branch) to keep this cron from touching other reminder types.

title: Reminders with empty message or missing sendTo are never counted as failures and will retry forever
body: The retry logic only increments retryCount when `twilio.scheduleSMS` returns falsy or when an exception is thrown. But if `message` is empty or `sendTo` is null (e.g., an SMS_NUMBER step with no sendTo, or a booking with no smsReminderNumber, or a template that produces an empty message), the code skips the entire `if (message?.length && ... && sendTo)` block without incrementing retryCount. Such a reminder stays `scheduled: false` with retryCount 0 and is re-fetched by the cron job on every run until its scheduledDate passes — exactly the infinite rescheduling this PR is meant to fix, and the most common cause (missing/invalid phone number often means sendTo is absent, not a Twilio failure).

title: Catch block increments retryCount even when the SMS was successfully scheduled in Twilio
body: The try block covers both the Twilio call and the follow-up `prisma.workflowReminder.update` that marks the reminder scheduled. If Twilio scheduling succeeds but the database update fails (transient DB error), the catch handler increments retryCount while leaving `scheduled: false`. The next cron run will schedule the same SMS again in Twilio (duplicate message to the attendee), and after two such occurrences the reminder is deleted while a Twilio-scheduled SMS still exists. The retry increment should only happen when the send itself failed, or the success-path update should be in its own try/catch.

title: retryCount-based deletion in deleteMany is not scoped to SMS method or unscheduled reminders
body: The new OR branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` deletes WorkflowReminder rows of any method (EMAIL, WHATSAPP) and any scheduled state, unlike the first branch which is constrained to `method: SMS`. Today only this SMS cron increments retryCount so the impact is latent, but the schema field is on the shared WorkflowReminder model — as soon as any other code path (e.g., the parallel scheduleEmailReminders cron or WhatsApp scheduling) uses retryCount, this job will silently delete those reminders, including ones already successfully scheduled with a Twilio referenceId. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` (and arguably `scheduled: false`) to the retry-count deletion clause.

title: findMany method removed without updating callers
body: The public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method on InsightsBookingService was deleted and replaced with `getBaseConditions()`, which returns a raw `Prisma.Sql` fragment. Any existing caller that invoked `service.findMany({ select: ... })` against the BookingTimeStatusDenormalized model (the previous test did exactly this, and it was the service's only query execution path) will now fail to compile or, worse, the service no longer has any method that actually executes a query — consumers must now hand-build `$queryRaw` SQL themselves and correctly interpolate the conditions into a WHERE clause. The PR only changes this file and its test, so either callers elsewhere in the repo are now broken, or the migration of callers is missing from this PR.

title: Caching behavior tests removed while caching logic remains
body: The two tests that verified `getAuthorizationConditions()` and `getFilterConditions()` return cached results on repeated calls were deleted, but the service still implements caching via `cachedAuthConditions` / `cachedFilterConditions` (insightsBooking.ts lines 49-50, 84-95). There is now no test coverage for the memoization behavior. Additionally, the PR description itself states the author could not run the test suite ('test runner had configuration issues'), so none of the rewritten SQL-expectation assertions — which are tightly coupled to exact SQL string output — have been verified to pass.

title: findMany method removed, breaking existing callers
body: The public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method on InsightsBookingService was deleted and replaced by `getBaseConditions()`, which only returns a `Prisma.Sql` fragment. Any existing caller that invoked `service.findMany({ select: ... })` to query `bookingTimeStatusDenormalized` will now fail to compile (or at runtime), and callers must now hand-write `$queryRaw` SQL against the `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` table themselves, duplicating table/column knowledge outside the service. The PR does not update or mention any call sites. Either keep a `findMany`-style query method in the service or update/migrate all consumers in this PR.

title: getBaseConditions integration test asserts exact result set without ORDER BY and without isolating other rows
body: The test runs `SELECT id FROM "BookingTimeStatusDenormalized" WHERE ${baseConditions}` and asserts `results` equals exactly `[{ id: userBooking.id }]`. The denormalized table is populated asynchronously from Booking rows in production-like setups; the test creates rows in `Booking` but never verifies/writes the denormalized rows, so the query may return zero rows (or stale rows from other test data matching the same user/eventType) making the assertion flaky. Also, without ORDER BY, any multi-row match has nondeterministic ordering for a strict toEqual on an array. The test should either write directly to the denormalized table or tolerate ordering (e.g., expect.arrayContaining / sorted comparison).

title: Caching behavior tests removed without replacement
body: The two 'Caching' describe-block tests verifying that getAuthorizationConditions and getFilterConditions return cached results on second invocation were deleted. The caching logic still exists in the service (cachedAuthConditions / cachedFilterConditions), so this regression coverage is lost; a bug that drops caching would silently cause repeated DB membership lookups per query. Re-add equivalent tests against the new Prisma.Sql return values.

title: Prisma raw queries do not support array parameters — `ANY(${teamIds})` will fail
body: The new SQL conditions pass JavaScript arrays directly as raw query parameters, e.g. `Prisma.sql`("teamId" = ANY(${teamIds}))` and `("userId" = ANY(${uniqueUserIds}))` (also used for team scope at line 201). Prisma's raw query serialization does not support array values as bind parameters — passing an array into a `Prisma.sql` placeholder throws a serialization error at runtime (the documented workaround is `Prisma.join(...)` for IN-style clauses). Any code path that executes these conditions via `$queryRaw` (as the updated integration test does) will throw instead of returning results, so the org and team scopes are broken for actual query execution.

title: `findMany` method removed — breaking change for existing callers
body: The PR deletes the public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method and replaces it with `getBaseConditions()`, changing the service's public contract from returning typed `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` rows to returning a raw `Prisma.Sql` fragment. Nothing in this PR updates callers of `InsightsBookingService.findMany`; any existing consumer will fail to compile (and would otherwise need to hand-write raw SQL against the `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` table). Either keep a query method on the service or update all call sites in the same PR.

title: Single filter condition returned unwrapped produces operator-precedence hazard when combined
body: `buildFilterConditions` returns the single condition unwrapped when only one filter is present, e.g. `("eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)` without surrounding parentheses. `getBaseConditions` wraps conditions when both auth and filters exist, but the returned filter fragment is also exposed via `getFilterConditions()` and embedded unparenthesized in the eventTypeId condition itself (line 106 lacks outer parentheses). If this fragment is ever composed with another `AND` at a level that doesn't wrap it (as `conditions.reduce` in `buildFilterConditions` does wrap, but callers composing the raw SQL themselves may not), the OR will bind incorrectly and leak rows from other event types. Add explicit parentheses around the OR clause in the eventTypeId filter, e.g. `(("eventTypeId" = ${id}) OR ("eventParentId" = ${id}))`.

title: UserWithCalendars now requires updatedAt/googleChannelId on selected calendars, breaking other callers
body: The `UserWithCalendars` type now requires every entry of `allSelectedCalendars` and `userLevelSelectedCalendars` to include `updatedAt` and `googleChannelId`. `getConnectedDestinationCalendarsAndEnsureDefaultsInDb` is called from many places besides the updated `connectedCalendars.handler` (e.g. availability/booking flows and event-type handlers) whose user queries select only `externalId`, `integration`, and `eventTypeId` for selected calendars. Those call sites no longer satisfy this type and will fail type-checking (or must be updated to select the extra fields even though they don't need them). The PR only updates `UserRepository.findUnlockedUserForSession`; the other callers were not updated.

title: deleteCache mutation does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query
body: The `deleteCacheMutation` only shows a toast and calls the optional `onSuccess` prop; unlike `disconnectMutation` right below it, it never invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. After a successful cache deletion the dropdown continues to show the old "Last updated" timestamp (because `cacheUpdatedAt` comes from that query) until something else triggers a refetch, so the UI displays stale cache status and continues offering to delete a cache that no longer exists. Add `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate()` in the mutation's onSettled/onSuccess.

title: Cache timestamp is always formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale
body: `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)` ignores the user's configured locale, so non-English users see US date/time formatting for the cache "Last updated" timestamp even though the rest of the app localizes dates. Use the user's locale (e.g. from `useLocale` / navigator.language) or dayjs with the user's locale instead of the hardcoded string.

title: getCacheStatusByCredentialIds reports expired cache entries as active cache
body: The groupBy query has no `expiresAt` filter, so rows whose `expiresAt` is in the past (no longer served by `getCachedAvailability`, which filters `expiresAt >= now`) still produce an `updatedAt` value. The UI then shows "Cache Status / Last updated" and the delete-cache action for credentials whose cache is effectively dead, which is misleading. Add `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }` to the where clause if the intent is to show only live cache.

title: dev:cron now uses tsx which is not a declared dependency
body: The script was changed to `npx tsx cron-tester.ts`, but `tsx` does not appear in dependencies or devDependencies of this package (nor is it added by this PR). `npx` will try to download tsx from the registry on every run in a fresh environment, which fails offline and can pull an unexpected version. Add `tsx` to devDependencies if the script is meant to use it.

title: Handler throws generic Error instead of TRPCError
body: When the credential is not found or belongs to another user, the handler throws a plain `Error("Credential not found or access denied")`, which tRPC converts to an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (HTTP 500). Clients cannot distinguish an authorization/not-found failure from a server crash. Throw `new TRPCError({ code: "NOT_FOUND" })` (or FORBIDDEN) as other handlers in this codebase do.

title: deleteCache mutation never invalidates connectedCalendars, leaving stale cache status in UI
body: The `deleteCacheMutation` only shows a toast and calls the optional `onSuccess` callback, but unlike `disconnectMutation` right below it, it has no `onSettled` that invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. After a user deletes the cache, the `cacheUpdatedAt` value rendered in this same dropdown still comes from the old query data, so the dropdown keeps showing 'Cache Status / Last updated' and the delete option even though the cache rows were just deleted. If the parent doesn't pass an `onChanged` that refetches (it's optional), the stale state persists indefinitely. Add `await utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate()` on success/settled for the delete-cache mutation.

title: sed -i '' syntax only works on macOS, script fails on Linux
body: Line 68 uses `sed -i '' -E ...`, which is the BSD/macOS sed syntax. On GNU sed (Linux), `-i ''` is interpreted as editing a file literally named `''` and the command fails, so GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL is never updated on Linux dev machines or containers. Use a portable form (e.g. `sed -i.bak -E ... && rm file.bak`) or detect the platform.

title: ENV_FILE relative path breaks depending on invocation directory
body: `ENV_FILE="../.env"` is resolved relative to the caller's current working directory, not the script's location. Running the script from the repo root (the natural way: `./scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh`) resolves to a `.env` one level above the repo and silently creates/updates the wrong file. Resolve the path from the script's own directory, e.g. `ENV_FILE="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)/.env"`.

title: Cache timestamp hardcoded to en-US locale, ignoring user's locale
body: The 'Last updated' timestamp is formatted with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)`, so every user sees US-style dates (M/D/YY, 12-hour time) regardless of their configured locale, unlike the rest of the app which formats dates per user preference. Pass the user's locale (available via `useLocale` / i18n language) to `Intl.DateTimeFormat` instead of the hardcoded "en-US".

title: Null credentialIds from delegation credentials break the connectedCalendars query
body: `connectedCalendars.map((cal) => cal.credentialId)` collects credential IDs and passes them straight into `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`, which runs `prisma.calendarCache.groupBy({ where: { credentialId: { in: credentialIds } } })`. For delegation credentials, connected calendar entries have `credentialId: null` (they are identified by `delegationCredentialId` instead — the UI in this same PR handles that case). Passing `null` inside the `in` array for the non-nullable Int field `credentialId` causes a PrismaClientValidationError, so the entire `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` query fails for any user who has a delegation-credential calendar connection. The IDs should be filtered (e.g. `.filter((id): id is number => typeof id === 'number')`) before querying.

title: Cache deletion does not invalidate connectedCalendars, leaving stale cache status in the UI
body: The `deleteCacheMutation` only calls `showToast` and the optional `onSuccess` prop on success, but unlike the `disconnectMutation` in the same file it never invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. After the user deletes the cache, the dropdown continues to show the old "Last updated" timestamp and keeps offering "Delete cached data" until a full refetch happens (and the query is configured with `refetchOnWindowFocus: false` in the wrapper). Add `await utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate()` (as done for the disconnect mutation) so the cache status disappears immediately after deletion.

title: Script uses macOS-only sed syntax and fails on Linux
body: `sed -i '' -E ...` is the BSD/macOS form of in-place sed; on GNU/Linux `sed -i ''` treats the empty string as a file name and the script errors out. Since this helper script is committed for the whole team, developers on Linux cannot use it to update GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL. Use a portable form (e.g. `sed -i.bak -E ... && rm file.bak`) or detect the platform. Additionally, `ENV_FILE="../.env"` is resolved relative to the caller's working directory, so running the script from anywhere other than its own directory silently creates/edits the wrong .env file.

title: One failing SendGrid cancel aborts the whole batch and skips all DB deletes
body: In the new cancellation section, all SendGrid `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` calls are awaited sequentially inside a single try/catch, and the `prisma.workflowReminder.delete` promises are only executed via `Promise.all` after the loop. If any single `client.request` throws (e.g. an invalid/expired batch_id, a reminder whose referenceId is null, or a transient SendGrid error), the catch fires and (a) all remaining reminders in `remindersToCancel` are never cancelled at SendGrid, and (b) none of the reminder rows — including the ones that were successfully cancelled — are deleted from the DB. Those rows stay `cancelled: true` and are retried every 15 minutes, permanently failing behind the one bad record; meanwhile reminders whose scheduledDate passes before a successful run are removed by the top-of-handler deleteMany without ever being cancelled at SendGrid, so the email still goes out. Each reminder should be processed independently (try/catch inside the loop) and rows should be deleted once their cancellation succeeds.

title: remindersToCancel query missing method/scheduled filters
body: The query for reminders to cancel filters only on `cancelled: true` and scheduledDate, with no `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` and no `scheduled: true` / `referenceId: { not: null }` constraint. Today only email reminders get `cancelled` set (SMS reminders are deleted immediately), but any SMS or unscheduled row that ever ends up with `cancelled: true` would be sent to SendGrid's scheduled_sends endpoint with a Twilio SID or null batch_id, which errors and — because of the shared try/catch — blocks cancellation of all legitimate email reminders in the same run. The query should restrict to scheduled email reminders with a non-null referenceId.

title: immediateDelete path cancels at SendGrid but leaves stale WorkflowReminder row
body: When `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` is called with `immediateDelete: true` (used for rescheduled bookings in handleNewBooking.ts and for deleted workflows/steps in workflows.tsx), it cancels the scheduled send at SendGrid but then returns without deleting the WorkflowReminder row or setting `cancelled`. The row remains with `scheduled: true` and a valid referenceId, so it lingers until the cron's past-date deleteMany cleans it up — for reminders scheduled close to 72h out that can be days. The row should be deleted (or marked cancelled) after the SendGrid cancellation succeeds, consistent with the SMS path in deleteScheduledSMSReminder which deletes the row.

title: One failing SendGrid cancel aborts all remaining cancellations and silently drops the queued DB deletes
body: In the new cancellation block of the cron handler, the loop awaits `client.request` for each cancelled reminder and collects `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` promises into `workflowRemindersToDelete`, awaiting them only after the loop. If any single SendGrid request throws (e.g. batch_id already gone, rate limit, network error), the loop exits immediately: (1) all remaining cancelled reminders are not cancelled at SendGrid this run, and (2) the delete promises already collected are never awaited — Prisma promises are lazy, so those rows are never deleted. The rows already cancelled at SendGrid but not deleted will be re-cancelled on the next run (harmless but noisy), while rows not yet reached keep their scheduled emails alive. Each reminder's cancel+delete should be isolated in its own try/catch, and the DB delete should be awaited per reminder.

title: Reschedule path uses immediate SendGrid cancel, re-creating the 100-pending-cancellation pile-up the PR intends to fix
body: When a booking is rescheduled, the old booking's email reminders are cancelled via `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)` with `immediateDelete=true`, which immediately POSTs `status: "cancel"` to `/v3/user/scheduled_sends`. Per the PR description, every such POST creates a pending cancellation entry in SendGrid that persists until the scheduled send date (up to 72 hours away) and SendGrid caps pending cancellations at 100 — the exact root cause of the bug being fixed. The plain-cancel path (handleCancelBooking) was changed to only set `cancelled=true` and let the cron cancel within 1 hour of the send date, which bounds pending cancellations; the reschedule path bypasses that mechanism. It also leaves the old WorkflowReminder rows in the DB with `scheduled=true, cancelled=false` (the immediateDelete branch returns without deleting or flagging the row), so they linger until their scheduledDate passes. The reschedule path should use the same `cancelled=true` flag flow as booking cancellation.

title: immediateDelete path in deleteScheduledEmailReminder never deletes or flags the WorkflowReminder row
body: `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)` (used here for workflow deletion and deleted steps, and in handleNewBooking for reschedules) cancels the send at SendGrid but then returns without deleting the WorkflowReminder row or setting `cancelled=true`. For workflow/step deletion the rows are removed by the onDelete: Cascade, but for the reschedule call site in handleNewBooking the rows survive with `scheduled=true, cancelled=false` until their scheduledDate passes and the cron's generic deleteMany removes them — meanwhile nothing in the system knows their SendGrid send is already cancelled. Either delete the row in the immediateDelete branch or set `cancelled=true` so state stays consistent.

title: Cancellation query lacks method filter and only covers a 1-hour window, so a missed cron run can leak sends
body: The `remindersToCancel` query filters only on `cancelled: true` and `scheduledDate <= now + 1h` with no `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` filter and no `referenceId` non-null check. It works today only because no other code path sets `cancelled=true` for SMS reminders; that implicit coupling is fragile. More importantly, the design relies on the cron running at least once every hour: if the cron is down or delayed beyond the 1-hour window after a reminder is flagged cancelled, the reminder's scheduledDate passes, the first `deleteMany` in the same handler removes the row without ever posting the SendGrid cancellation, and SendGrid delivers the email for a cancelled booking. Consider also cancelling already-due cancelled reminders before the deleteMany (or making the deleteMany exclude `cancelled: true` rows).

title: Reminder-cancellation DB writes are fire-and-forget and may never persist
body: The new cancellation flow relies entirely on `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` writing `cancelled: true` to the WorkflowReminder row so the cron job can cancel the SendGrid scheduled send later. But the calls are made inside `forEach` without `await` (lines 485-493), so the handler returns (and in a serverless environment the function can be frozen/terminated) before the Prisma update completes. If the `cancelled` flag is never written, the cron job will never cancel the email and the reminder is still sent — exactly the bug this PR is meant to fix. The same pattern exists in `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx` (requestReschedule, lines 488-494) and in the new reschedule block in `handleNewBooking.ts` (lines 966-972). These should be awaited (e.g. `await Promise.all(...)`).

title: Reschedule cancels SendGrid send immediately but never deletes the WorkflowReminder row
body: On reschedule, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)` is called with `immediateDelete: true`. In that branch (emailReminderManager.ts lines 213-223) the SendGrid cancellation is POSTed but the WorkflowReminder database row is neither deleted nor marked `cancelled`. The row stays in the DB with `scheduled: true` and `cancelled: null` until the cron's past-date `deleteMany` eventually removes it, and the SendGrid pending cancellation is created immediately even when the reminder's scheduled date is far in the future — re-introducing the SendGrid 100-pending-cancellations accumulation this PR is trying to avoid (a pending cancellation now sits there until the original send date passes). The row should be deleted after the immediate SendGrid cancel, as `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` does.

title: One failed SendGrid cancel aborts cancellation of all remaining reminders in the batch
body: In the cron's cancellation loop (lines 56-73), each `client.request` is awaited inside the `for` loop and the whole block is wrapped in a single try/catch. If SendGrid returns an error for one reminder (e.g. an unknown/expired batch_id), the exception breaks out of the loop, so every later reminder in `remindersToCancel` is skipped for that run. Because successfully processed reminders are deleted while the failing one is not, a persistently failing reminder at the front of the result set will block cancellation of all other cancelled reminders every run, and those emails will still be sent. Each iteration should catch its own error (or collect promises and use `Promise.allSettled`) so one failure doesn't block the rest.

title: Past-due deleteMany runs before the SendGrid cancellation pass, dropping cancelled reminders without cancelling them
body: The handler first deletes all EMAIL reminders with `scheduledDate <= now` (lines 34-41) and only afterwards processes `cancelled: true` reminders due within the next hour. A reminder marked `cancelled` whose scheduledDate has just passed is deleted by the first query without any SendGrid cancellation being issued. SendGrid's `sendAt` delivery is not instantaneous, so there is a window where the DB row is gone but the email has not yet been dispatched — it will then be sent for a cancelled booking with no way to stop it. The cancellation pass should run before (or be excluded from) the past-date cleanup, e.g. by excluding `cancelled: true` rows from the deleteMany until after they've been cancelled at SendGrid.

title: Deferred cancellation only works for reminders due within 1 hour; anything later silently stays scheduled
body: The non-immediate path only sets `cancelled: true` and relies on the cron job, which only picks up cancelled reminders with `scheduledDate <= now + 1 hour`. For any reminder scheduled further out, nothing happens at cancel time and correctness depends entirely on the cron running within the hour before the send time. If the cron endpoint is down, misconfigured, or delayed past that window (it only runs every 15 minutes and any SendGrid error aborts the run), the email is sent for a cancelled booking with no fallback. Additionally there is no alerting when the cron fails (errors are only `console.log`ed), so this failure mode is silent. At minimum the cron window should be larger than the maximum realistic cron downtime, and failures should be surfaced.

title: Recurring-event calendar deletions are never awaited and may not run before the response is sent
body: In the recurring-event cancellation branch, the code iterates calendar credentials with `.forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })`. Because `getCalendar` is now async, the `apiDeletes.push(...)` calls happen in a later microtask than the `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` at the end of the handler (line 652). `Promise.all` therefore resolves before any of these delete promises are even created, so the handler returns 'Booking successfully cancelled' and deletes booking references/attendees while the external calendar events for all remaining recurring bookings have not been deleted (and in serverless environments the pending work may be killed entirely). This leaves stale events on users' calendars for recurring bookings. Use a `for...of` loop or collect promises via `map` before awaiting.

title: async forEach defeats the surrounding try/catch and fire-and-forgets calendar/video deletions
body: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...); ... })` makes every callback an independent promise. The surrounding `try/catch` can no longer catch any failure (previously `getCalendar` was synchronous, so constructor/lookup errors were caught and logged); errors now surface as unhandled promise rejections, which can crash a Node process with default settings. Additionally the function proceeds to send the reschedule email and return without waiting for the calendar/video deletions to complete or even start. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` inside the try block.

title: async forEach defeats the surrounding try/catch and fire-and-forgets calendar/video deletions
body: Same issue as in vital/lib/reschedule.ts: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...); ... })` escapes the enclosing `try/catch` (failures become unhandled rejections instead of being logged) and the function returns/sends the reschedule email before deletions are awaited. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))`.

title: requestReschedule fire-and-forgets calendar/video deletions via async forEach
body: In the `requestReschedule` mutation, `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) ... })` is never awaited. The mutation marks the booking cancelled, sends the reschedule email and webhooks, and returns while the external calendar event and video meeting deletions are still pending; any failure is an unhandled rejection with no logging, and in serverless runtimes the deletions may never execute, leaving stale events on the organizer's calendar. Await the deletions (e.g. `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))`) before returning.

title: getCalendarCredentials now stores Promise<Calendar|null> in the `calendar` field
body: Because `getCalendar` became async, `getCalendarCredentials` silently changed the type of the `calendar` property it returns from `Calendar | null` to `Promise<Calendar | null>`. Within this diff only `getConnectedCalendars` consumes it and was updated to `await item.calendar`, but `getCalendarCredentials` is exported and any other caller (present or future) that treats `item.calendar` as a Calendar will get a truthy Promise and fail at runtime (e.g. calling `.listCalendars()` on a Promise). Consider making `getCalendarCredentials` async and resolving the calendars with `Promise.all`, so the contract stays `Calendar | null`.

title: async forEach makes calendar/video deletions fire-and-forget and defeats the try/catch
body: In `Reschedule`, the loop over `bookingRefsFiltered` was changed to `forEach(async (bookingRef) => ...)` because `getCalendar` is now async. `Array.prototype.forEach` does not await async callbacks, so all `calendar.deleteEvent` / `deleteMeeting` calls are now unawaited: the function proceeds to send the reschedule email and returns `true` before deletions finish, and any rejection inside a callback becomes an unhandled promise rejection that the surrounding `try/catch` (which only catches synchronous errors) will never see. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` (optionally with per-item catch) so failures are logged and deletions complete before the email is sent.

title: async forEach makes calendar/video deletions fire-and-forget and defeats the try/catch
body: Same issue as in vital/lib/reschedule.ts: the loop was changed to `forEach(async (bookingRef) => ...)` to await the now-async `getCalendar`, but forEach does not await async callbacks. The booking is already marked CANCELLED and the reschedule email is sent before the calendar/video event deletions complete, and any failure to delete is an unhandled rejection invisible to the surrounding try/catch. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))` with individual error handling.

title: requestReschedule no longer awaits calendar/video deletions
body: In the `requestReschedule` mutation, `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })` was introduced because `getCalendar` became async. Since forEach doesn't await its callbacks, the mutation sends the reschedule email, fires webhooks, and returns while the `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` calls are still pending; a serverless function may be frozen before they finish, leaving stale events on users' calendars, and any errors become unhandled rejections. Await the deletions with `Promise.all(...map(...))`.

title: Recurring-cancellation branch pushes into apiDeletes asynchronously after it is awaited
body: In the recurring-event cancellation path, `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })` pushes deletion promises into `apiDeletes` from async callbacks. `apiDeletes` is later consumed by `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` (and by `await apiDeletes` in the paid branch), both of which run before any of these pushes happen, so the recurring calendar event deletions are never awaited and their results/errors are lost. Cancel can return success while the recurring events remain on the calendar. Collect the deletions with `Promise.all(credentials.map(...))` and push the resulting promises synchronously.

title: appStore values are now Promises; only 6 of its consumers were updated
body: Every entry in the default-exported `appStore` map changed from a module namespace object to a `Promise` via top-level `import(...)`. This is a breaking contract change for every consumer of `@calcom/app-store`, but the PR only updates `getCalendar.ts`, `videoClient.ts`, `handleCancelBooking.ts`, `bookings.tsx`, `deletePayment.ts`, and `handlePayment.ts`. Any other file that indexes `appStore[...]` synchronously (e.g. `appStore[appName].lib` or `appStore[key].app`) will now receive a Promise and silently fail checks like `"lib" in app` or crash on property access. The change needs an audit (and ideally a type-level guarantee) that all importers of `@calcom/app-store` await the values.

title: Debug log of CalendarService constructor left in getCalendar
body: `log.info("calendarApp", calendarApp.lib.CalendarService)` logs the CalendarService class constructor on every calendar resolution. This runs on every booking/availability call, adding noisy, low-value log output (and potentially expensive serialization of a class). It looks like a debugging leftover and should be removed or downgraded.

title: Top-level import() calls execute eagerly, defeating the lazy-loading goal
body: Every value in the appStore object is `import("./applecalendar")` etc. evaluated at module evaluation time. As soon as anything imports `@calcom/app-store` (e.g. videoClient, getCalendar, payment handlers), all ~29 dynamic imports are kicked off immediately, so all app packages are still loaded up front — exactly what static imports did. The only thing gained is that the promises resolve asynchronously; the bundler still creates the chunks and the module loader still fetches/evaluates every app. To actually get lazy loading, the map must store thunks like `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")` and call sites must invoke the function. As written, the PR's stated purpose ('Async imports of all apps') is not achieved, and any app whose module has import-time side effects or heavy dependencies (e.g. stripe, exchange) still pays that cost on first touch of the index.

title: getCalendarCredentials now returns Promise-valued `calendar` without changing its contract
body: Inside getCalendarCredentials, `getCalendar(credential)` is called without await, so each entry now carries `calendar: Promise<Calendar | null>` instead of `Calendar | null`. Only getConnectedCalendars in this file was updated to `await item.calendar`; getCalendarCredentials is exported and used by other code paths (e.g. availability/connected-calendars callers) that expect a synchronous Calendar instance and call methods like `listCalendars()` directly. Those callers will now call methods on a Promise and crash or silently produce wrong results. The return type change should either be propagated to all consumers (make the function async and resolve calendars there) or all call sites must be audited and updated.

title: async forEach callback makes try/catch useless and loses errors from calendar/video deletion
body: The diff changes `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach((bookingRef) => {` to `forEach(async (bookingRef) => {` because getCalendar is now awaited inside. forEach does not await async callbacks, so the surrounding try/catch (lines 124-139) can no longer catch failures from `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` or `deleteMeeting(...)` — those rejections become unhandled promise rejections (which can crash the Node process depending on configuration) and the logged error path is dead. The same applies identically in wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` inside the try block instead.

title: requestReschedule no longer waits for calendar/video event deletions before returning
body: The loop `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) })` is now fire-and-forget: the mutation proceeds to send the reschedule email and return success while the calendar/video deletions are still in flight. Previously the forEach body was synchronous and deleteEvent promises were at least initiated with a resolved calendar; now the entire deletion (including the dynamic import + getCalendar) may never complete if the serverless function is frozen after the response is sent, leaving stale events on users' calendars. Errors are also silently swallowed as unhandled rejections. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))` (optionally with per-item .catch) before sending the email.

title: Recurring-cancellation branch uses async forEach, so apiDeletes promises pushed after Promise.all resolves are never awaited
body: In the recurring-event + allRemainingBookings branch, `credentials...forEach(async (credential) => { ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent) })` pushes deletion promises into apiDeletes asynchronously, but the code later does `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` on line 652 — by then the async forEach callbacks may not have run yet, so the pushed deletions are not included in the awaited array and may be dropped when the function returns (serverless freeze) with their errors unhandled. This existed before but is made worse because each callback now additionally awaits getCalendar. Convert the forEach to a for..of loop or collect promises with map and await them before building apiDeletes.

title: dayjs objects compared with `===` is always false
body: Inside `checkIfIsAvailable`, the new date-override branch contains `if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))`. This compares two distinct dayjs object instances by reference, so it can never be true. Whatever this branch was intended to detect (a zero-length override, presumably to skip it) is dead code; such overrides fall through to the slotEndTime/slotStartTime comparisons instead, producing whatever behavior those yield. Use `.isSame()` if a start-equals-end check was intended.

title: New working-hours check uses UTC slot time but ignores event length
body: The new working-hours guard in `checkIfIsAvailable` computes both `start` and `end` as `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()` — the two values are identical and `eventLength` is never added, so a slot that starts inside working hours but ends after `workingHour.endTime` (e.g. a 60-min slot starting 30 min before the end of availability) is incorrectly reported as available. Additionally, `slotStartTime` is `.utc()`, so `hour()`/`minute()` are in UTC, while `workingHour.startTime`/`endTime` are minutes-since-midnight in the organizer's schedule timezone; for any non-UTC organizer the comparison is off by the UTC offset and can wrongly mark valid fixed-host slots as outside working hours (making them unbookable) or vice versa.

title: Timezone conversion of date overrides depends on server local timezone
body: `const utcOffset = organizerTimeZone ? dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone).utcOffset() * -1 : 0;` followed by `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` converts the override's start into organizer-local wall time only if `dayjs(date.start)` is parsed in UTC. `dayjs(Date)` parses in the server's local timezone, so on any host not running in UTC the shifted day/hour comparison is wrong and fixed-host date overrides will match the wrong slots. Use `dayjs.utc(date.start).add(...)` (or work directly in the organizer tz via `dayjs(date.start).tz(organizerTimeZone)`) to make the conversion timezone-independent.

title: `tz(override.timeZone)` throws when override has no timezone
body: In `getSlots`, the new override handling calls `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)`. `TimeRange.timeZone` is optional (as the type change in `packages/types/schedule.d.ts` shows), and `getSlots` is a shared library function whose callers may pass date overrides without a `timeZone`. `dayjs.tz(value, undefined)` throws an "Invalid timezone" error, which would break slot computation for any such caller. Also, `override.start.toString()` converts the Date to an implementation-specific locale string and re-parses it, which is lossy/fragile; `dayjs(override.start).tz(override.timeZone ?? organizerTimeZone)` would avoid both issues.

title: Object identity comparison of two dayjs objects is always false
body: In checkIfIsAvailable, the branch `if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares two distinct dayjs object instances with `===`, which is always false. This check was presumably meant to detect a full-day blocked override (start equal to end), but it can never trigger, so that case silently falls through to the subsequent isBefore/isSame/isAfter checks. Use `.isSame()` instead.

title: Working-hours check uses the same value for slot start and end, ignoring event length
body: In the new working-hours guard inside checkIfIsAvailable, both `start` and `end` are computed identically as `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()`. The `end` should be the slot's end time (start + eventLength).
