The formula should be `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)` (with the zero case already handled).

title: Remove-member link is shown for automatic groups because `automatic` is resolved on the member
body: The item view's context is the member (a User), so `{{#unless automatic}}` looks up `automatic` on the user object, which never has that property — the condition is always true and the remove (×) link is rendered even when viewing an automatic group. The server rejects the removal with a 422, but the admin UI offers an action that can never succeed, and the failed call is silently unhandled (no error callback on `removeMember` in the model). Use `{{#unless view.parentView.automatic}}` (or pass the flag into the view) so the link is hidden for automatic groups.

title: totalPages is off by one when user_count is divisible by limit
body: totalPages is computed as Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1. For a group with exactly 100 members and limit 50, this yields 3 pages when only 2 exist. Since showingLast compares currentPage to totalPages, the user can click "next" past the real last page; the next action sets offset to min(offset + limit, user_count) (i.e. 100), and findMembers then fetches an empty page, showing a blank member list on page "3/3". The computation should use Math.ceil(user_count / limit).

title: remove_member automatic-group test uses PUT instead of DELETE
body: The test 'cannot remove members from automatic groups' issues `xhr :put, :remove_member, group_id: 1, user_id: 42`, but the route added in config/routes.rb maps remove_member to DELETE members (`delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"`); PUT members is mapped to add_members. This request therefore routes to add_members, which requires a :usernames param and will raise rather than return 422, so the test does not exercise the code path it claims to and will fail (or pass for the wrong reason) once run against the real routes.

title: add_members does not strip whitespace around usernames
body: add_members splits the usernames param on "," and passes each fragment directly to User.find_by_username without stripping whitespace. A common input like "alice, bob" (with a space after the comma) makes the lookup for " bob" fail silently, so bob is not added and the admin gets no error — the success response hides the skipped user. Each fragment should be stripped before lookup, and ideally unknown usernames should be reported back instead of being silently ignored.

title: totalPages is off by one when user_count is an exact multiple of limit
body: totalPages is computed as Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1. For a group with exactly 100 members and the default limit of 50 this yields 3 pages instead of 2. Since `showingLast` is derived from currentPage == totalPages and the `next` action clamps offset to user_count, the user can navigate to a phantom last page (offset == user_count) that renders an empty member list. The correct formula is Math.ceil(user_count / limit), or Math.floor((user_count - 1) / limit) + 1.

title: add_members does not strip whitespace around usernames
body: add_members splits the `usernames` param on commas and calls User.find_by_username(username) directly. If the submitted value contains spaces after commas (e.g. "alice, bob" — easy to produce if the input is edited manually), the lookup for " bob" silently fails and the user is not added, while the response still reports success. Each username should be stripped before the lookup, or the failure should be surfaced.

title: findMembers returns undefined instead of a promise when the group has no name
body: When the group's name is empty, findMembers now returns `undefined` (`return ;`) instead of a resolved promise as before. Callers such as the routes' setupController invoke it unconditionally; any caller that chains `.then` on the result (as the removed afterModel hooks did) will now throw a TypeError on unnamed/new groups. Return Ember.RSVP.resolve() to keep the contract consistent.

title: Fallback locales are only loaded for web requests; background jobs and mailers will emit 'translation missing'
body: The translate accelerator only loads the YAML files for `config.locale` on demand (see `translate`, which calls `load_locale(config.locale)` only). The new fallback mechanism relies on `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` to load the fallback locales (site default locale and `:en`), but that is only invoked from `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Any `I18n.t` call that happens outside a web request — Sidekiq jobs, digest/notification emails, rake tasks — with a locale whose translation only exists in the fallback locale (e.g. `:en`) will not have the fallback locale's files loaded, so the lookup returns a 'translation missing' string instead of falling back correctly. The fallback loading should happen inside the backend/translate path (or a central `with_locale`/`ensure_loaded!` hook) rather than only in the controller before_filter.

title: FallbackLocaleList#[] raises NoMethodError when SiteSetting.default_locale is blank
body: `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact` calls `.to_sym` on `SiteSetting.default_locale` before the `compact` runs. If the setting is ever nil or unset (fresh install, broken settings table, early boot before seeding), every translation lookup that goes through the fallbacks backend will raise NoMethodError. Guard with `SiteSetting.default_locale.presence&.to_sym` (or only add it when present). Also note `locale` may be a String while the other entries are Symbols, so `uniq` will not deduplicate e.g. 'en' vs :en — harmless but wasteful; normalize to symbols.

title: No tests for fallback ordering or lazy loading of fallback locales
body: This PR introduces custom fallback behavior (user locale → site default locale → :en) and a new `ensure_loaded!` code path, but adds no specs. Given that the lazy locale loader (translate_accelerator) and the fallbacks interact in non-obvious ways (e.g. fallback locale files must be explicitly loaded or lookups return 'translation missing'), a regression test covering a key that exists only in :en being resolved for a request in another locale — plus the background-job path — would catch the most likely failure modes.

title: Fallback locales are only loaded during controller requests, so fallback translations are missing in jobs/mailers
body: The new fallback mechanism depends on `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` being called to eagerly load the user's locale, `SiteSetting.default_locale`, and `:en` (because the translate accelerator only lazy-loads `config.locale`). This call was added only in `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Any code path that translates outside of a controller request — Sidekiq/scheduled jobs, email rendering (`UserNotifications`), oneboxing, rake tasks, console — will translate with only the current locale's yml loaded. When a key is missing in that locale, the fallbacks backend looks up the default locale and `:en`, finds nothing loaded, and renders 'translation missing' instead of the English fallback. `ensure_loaded!` needs to be invoked wherever `I18n.locale=` is set (e.g., in the jobs/mailer code paths), not just in the controller.

title: Custom fallback list drops parent-language fallbacks for regional locales (e.g. pt_BR no longer falls back to pt)
body: `FallbackLocaleList#[]` returns exactly `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale, :en]`. The standard `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks` behavior (which `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` provided and this PR removes) decomposes regional locales so that `pt_BR` falls back to `pt` before hitting the default. With this change, a user with locale `pt_BR` (or `zh_TW`, `nb_NO`-style tags) will see English for every key that exists in the base `pt` translation but not in `pt_BR`, which is a user-visible regression for regional locales. The TODO comment even acknowledges per-language ordering is needed; at minimum the list should insert the language-only parent (`locale.to_s.split('_').first`) between the locale and the site default.

title: @loaded_locales is read outside the load mutex and can be nil on first translate
body: In `translate`, `@loaded_locales.include?(config.locale)` is evaluated without synchronization and without the nil guard that the newly added `ensure_loaded!` has (`@loaded_locales ||= []`). `@loaded_locales` is only initialized in `reload!`; if `translate` is invoked before any `reload!` (or after a direct `load_locale` call from another thread partially completes), the first check raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'include?' for nil`. More generally the check-then-load pattern here is unsynchronized, so two threads can race through `load_locale` — the mutex inside `load_locale` makes the double-load harmless, but the nil read is not protected. `translate` should use the same `@loaded_locales ||= []` guard (or route through `ensure_loaded!`).

title: FallbackLocaleList recomputes SiteSetting.default_locale on every translation fallback lookup
body: Because `FallbackLocaleList#[]` is overridden without memoization, every translation lookup that misses the primary locale triggers a `SiteSetting.default_locale` read (which hits the site settings cache/provider) and allocates a new array. Under load this happens per missing-key translation. Consider caching the computed list per locale (e.g., storing into the Hash) and invalidating when the default locale setting changes.

title: Fallback locales are only loaded for web requests, so fallbacks silently fail in background jobs and mailers
body: The translate accelerator loads locale files lazily: only locales passed through `I18n.ensure_loaded!`/`load_locale` are ever read from disk into the backend. The new `FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded!` is only invoked from `ApplicationController#set_locale`, i.e. during HTTP requests. Any translation done outside a request cycle (Sidekiq jobs, scheduled email digests, `UserNotifications` mailers, etc.) will only have the current locale loaded; the fallback chain `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale, :en]` will be consulted by the backend but those locale files were never loaded, so lookups fall through to 'translation missing' instead of English. The fallback loading should happen wherever `I18n.locale` is set (or on first translation), not only in the controller before_filter.

title: Mixed string/symbol locales defeat uniq and loaded-locale tracking
body: `FallbackLocaleList#[]` builds `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact`. `locale` here is whatever was passed in (frequently a String such as "en" when it comes from user input or `I18n.locale` assigned from a string), while the other entries are symbols. `"en"` and `:en` are not `uniq`-equal, so the list can contain duplicates, and more importantly `ensure_loaded!` passes the string into `I18n.ensure_loaded!`, which checks `@loaded_locales.include?(locale)` in the accelerator. Since other code paths push symbols (e.g. `config.locale`) into `@loaded_locales`, a string locale will never match and `load_locale` will be taken (acquiring the global LOAD_MUTEX) on every request for that user. Normalizing `locale.to_sym` in `[]` would avoid the repeated mutex lock and duplicate work.

title: Translation LRU cache is keyed only on current locale, so fallback results go stale when the site default locale changes
body: With fallbacks now active, the result of `translate_no_cache(key)` depends not just on `config.locale` but on the whole fallback chain, which includes `SiteSetting.default_locale`. The cache key `"#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}"` does not include the fallback list, so if an admin changes the site's default locale, entries previously cached (translated via the old default locale fallback) will keep being served for users of other locales until they happen to be evicted from the 300-entry LRU or the process restarts. Including `SiteSetting.default_locale` (or the resolved fallback chain) in the cache key would make the cache correct.

title: Denial cache key omits identity type, so a denial for one identity type can deny another
body: userPermDenialCacheKey is built from namespace, UserUID, action, name, and parent folder, but not from the identity type. The UserUID is derived by stripping the type prefix from the subject (e.g. "anonymous:0" and "render:0" both yield UserUID "0", and a service account whose UID collides with a user UID is also possible). Because Check consults permDenialCache before anything else and returns Allowed=false immediately on a hit, a denial cached for an anonymous user on "dashboards:read" for some dashboard name will, for the next 30 seconds (shortCacheTTL), also deny the render service for the same action/name even though getRendererPermissions unconditionally grants render read access to dashboards/folders/datasources. The same applies to any cross-type UID collision. The identity type should be included in the denial cache key.

title: Denial cache short-circuits the DB fallback, so newly granted permissions are ignored for up to 30s
body: When a check is denied after a fresh DB lookup, the denial is stored in permDenialCache, and subsequent identical checks return Allowed=false at the top of Check without ever re-querying the permission store — even though the whole point of this PR is to re-query the DB when the cached permissions don't contain the resource. If a user's permission is granted shortly after a denial was cached (e.g. a check raced ahead of the grant write for a just-created dashboard/folder, which is the exact scenario this PR is trying to fix), the user stays denied until the 30-second denial TTL expires, whereas the non-denial path would have picked up the new grant immediately via the DB fallback. Consider skipping the denial-cache fast path when a fresh DB lookup could succeed (or at least documenting/shortening the TTL), since this partially reintroduces the stale-denial problem for creators.

title: Misleading comment in denial-cache test
body: The comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked", but the value actually seeded into permCache is map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}, which does not allow access. The test still passes because checkPermission only looks up key presence with a true value, but the comment misdescribes the setup and could confuse future maintainers into thinking cached allows are bypassed when they aren't exercised at all.

title: Denial cache is checked before the permission-allow cache, so a stale denial overrides a fresh allow
body: In Check, the permDenialCache lookup (line 117) runs before consulting permCache via getCachedIdentityPermissions. A denial entry is written whenever a fresh DB lookup denies (line 154) and lives for shortCacheTTL (30s). If a user is denied, then granted permission, and the permission cache is subsequently refreshed with the new allowing permissions (e.g. by a concurrent Check for another resource of the same action that falls through to getUserPermissions and repopulates permCache), a later Check for the originally denied resource still hits the stale denial entry first and returns Allowed=false without ever looking at the now-correct permCache. Given the stated goal of this PR is to let creators access newly created resources quickly, the allow check should take precedence over the denial cache (or the denial entry should be invalidated when fresh permissions are stored), otherwise users can be denied for up to 30s despite correct permissions being cached.

title: Test case 'should return error if store fails' never triggers a store error and asserts NoError
body: In TestService_getUserPermissions, the case named 'should return error if store fails' sets permissions to nil but never sets err: true on the fakeStore, and the test body unconditionally calls require.NoError(t, err). The test therefore exercises a successful empty-permissions lookup, not a store failure, so the error path of getIdentityPermissions is untested and the test name is misleading.

title: Denial cache takes precedence over fresh grants, extending wrongful denials after permission changes
body: In Check, the permDenialCache is consulted before anything else and short-circuits with Allowed=false. Once a denial is cached (line 154), a user who is subsequently granted the permission (e.g. an admin adds them to a team/role, or a folder permission is created) will still be denied for up to shortCacheTTL (30s), and unlike the allow path there is no DB fallback for denial hits — even a fresh DB query showing the grant is never performed. This asymmetry means the very problem this PR fixes for grants (stale allow/deny after change) now also applies to denials with no re-query escape hatch. Consider falling through to a DB re-check when a denial entry exists but the permission grant may have changed, or at least documenting/acknowledging the up-to-30s denial stickiness, and keying the TTL shorter for denials.

title: Denial cache keyed on raw subject UID while permission cache uses resolved UID, causing duplicate/inconsistent entries
body: The denial cache key is built from checkReq.UserUID, which is the raw identifier from the request subject and may be either a numeric user ID or a UID (GetUserIdentifiers explicitly handles both forms). The permission cache, by contrast, is keyed on the resolved userIdentifiers.UID. The same user queried via 'user:123' vs 'user:<uid>' will produce two independent denial entries, and a denial cached under one form will not be hit when the same user is queried under the other form, defeating the fast-deny path and making behavior inconsistent. Resolve the UID (as getCachedIdentityPermissions already does) before building the denial key.

title: Delete menu item never renders in the list view because it requires rulerRule
body: The delete menu item is guarded by `canDelete && rulerRule`. In the alert list view the whole point of this PR is that no ruler API requests are made, so consumers (RuleActionsButtons.V2 via GrafanaRuleListItem) pass only `promRule` and `rulerRule` is undefined. The new prom-based ability check will set canDelete=true, but the menu item still won't render, and `handleDelete` also requires a RulerRuleDTO. Result: users with delete permission cannot delete rules from the new list view. The pause menu item has the same problem at line 123: it is guarded by `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`, so Pause never appears in the list view even though canPause can be true via the prom rule abilities.

title: Silence action in the list view opens nothing without a rulerRule
body: The SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer is only rendered when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is truthy. In the list view only promRule is passed (rule is undefined), but AlertRuleMenu can now show the Silence menu item based on prom-rule abilities. Clicking 'Silence notifications' calls setShowSilenceDrawer(true) yet no drawer is ever rendered, so the action silently does nothing for list-view users.

title: ModifyExport ability no longer supported for Grafana recording rules
body: In useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities, AlertRuleAction.ModifyExport is `[isAlertingRule, exportAllowed]` where isAlertingRule is prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule). The ruler-based equivalent uses isGrafanaManagedAlertRule which is true for any Grafana-managed rule including recording rules. For Grafana recording rules in the list view (which now relies solely on this prom-based hook), the Export menu item disappears even though modify-export of recording rules was previously supported.

title: GrafanaRuleListItem rendered without a key in the filtered list
body: In the switch over origins, the 'datasource' and default branches pass key={key}, but the 'grafana' branch renders <GrafanaRuleListItem rule={rule} ... /> without the key prop. Every item in rules.map() needs a key; this produces React missing-key warnings and can cause incorrect reconciliation when the list updates (e.g. rule states changing between polls).

title: Rule view link lost the returnTo parameter
body: The old GrafanaRuleListItem (in deleted GrafanaRuleLoader.tsx) built the href with createReturnTo() so that navigating back from the rule view returned the user to the list. The new component uses createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`) without returnTo, regressing back-navigation behavior for users coming from the list view.

title: No unit tests for the new prom-based ability hooks
body: useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities / useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable are new permission-critical code (folder permission checks, provisioned/plugin-provided immutability, silence support) but the PR adds no direct tests for them; existing tests only mock these hooks. Edge cases like folder still loading, invalid folderUid, provisioned prom rules, and recording-rule silencing are untested, and a regression here would show/hide edit/delete/silence controls incorrectly.

title: Delete menu item can never appear for Grafana rules in the list view (rulerRule is always undefined there)
body: The Delete menu item is gated on `canDelete && rulerRule`. In the alert list view the whole point of this PR is that no ruler API calls are made, so `RuleActionsButtons.V2` is rendered with only `promRule` and `rule` (rulerRule) is `undefined`. Even though the new `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` path can set `canDelete` to true from prom-rule/folder permissions, the `rulerRule &&` guard means the Delete item is never rendered in the list view, so users can no longer delete Grafana-managed rules from the list. The pause menu item at line 123 has the same problem: `canPause` can be true via the grafana ability, but rendering requires `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`, which is false when only a promRule exists. Either the menu items need to work off the promRule (e.g. construct the delete/pause payloads from the prom rule), or the abilities should not report these actions as available.

title: Silence menu item shown in list view but clicking it does nothing (drawer requires rulerRule)
body: `AlertRuleMenu` will show 'Silence notifications' in the list view because the new `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` grants the Silence ability from the prom rule. Clicking it calls `handleSilence` which sets `showSilenceDrawer` to true, but the drawer is only rendered when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true — and `rule` (the ruler rule) is always undefined in the list view since this PR removes ruler requests there. Result: a visible menu action that silently does nothing. The silence flow needs to work from the prom rule (e.g. build the silence from promRule labels/uid) or the Silence ability should not be reported as supported when no ruler rule is available.

title: GrafanaRuleListItem rendered without a React key in the filtered results list
body: In the `origin === 'grafana'` branch the returned `<GrafanaRuleListItem>` no longer receives `key={key}` (the previous `GrafanaRuleLoader` had it). These elements are siblings of keyed `<DataSourceRuleLoader key={key}>` items inside the same `<ul>`, so React will warn about missing keys and, more importantly, reconciliation across pages of infinite-scroll results can reuse the wrong component instance for a different rule, showing stale state. Add `key={key}` to the `GrafanaRuleListItem` element.

title: ModifyExport ability for prom rules excludes recording rules, unlike the ruler-rule path
body: In `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`, `AlertRuleAction.ModifyExport` is `[isAlertingRule, exportAllowed]` where `isAlertingRule = prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)`. The equivalent ruler-based hook uses `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)`, which matches both alerting and recording Grafana rules. So a Grafana-managed recording rule shows the Export menu in the details view (ruler path) but not in the list view (prom path). If export of recording rules is intended to remain available, use `prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)` here; otherwise the two paths should be made consistent.

title: Removed coverage for creating/deleting rule states with no replacement
body: The PR deletes the tests 'should render rule with url and creating state when only ruler rule exists', 'should render delete rule operation list item when only prom rule exists', and the entire `matchRules` describe block, and the component no longer has any creating/deleting handling. The behavior change (a just-created rule now simply doesn't appear until Prometheus catches up, and a deleting rule renders fully actionable until it disappears) is a real UX regression risk that is now completely untested — there is no test asserting what the list shows during these eventual-consistency windows.

title: GrafanaRuleListItem rendered without a React key in filtered rule list
body: In the `rules.map(...)` switch, the `case 'grafana'` branch now renders `<GrafanaRuleListItem rule={...} ... />` without the `key={key}` prop that the previous `<GrafanaRuleLoader key={key} ... />` had (the `datasource` and `default` branches still pass `key`). Rendering list items without keys forces React to reconcile by position, which can mix up per-item state (open dropdowns, silence drawers, delete modals) between rules when the list updates during polling or infinite-scroll loading, and logs key warnings in development.

title: Delete menu item never appears for rules loaded without the ruler API
body: The Delete menu item is gated on `{canDelete && rulerRule && ...}`. The whole point of this PR is that the alert list view no longer fetches ruler data, so `RuleActionsButtons.V2`/`GrafanaRuleListItem` render the menu with `rulerRule` undefined and only `promRule` set. `canDelete` may be true via `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`, but the extra `rulerRule` presence check means the Delete option is always hidden in the list view, so users cannot delete Grafana-managed rules from the list even though the underlying `showDeleteModal(identifier, groupIdentifier)` handler doesn't need the ruler rule.

title: Pause menu item hidden in list view because it requires the ruler rule
body: The pause item renders only when `canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) && groupIdentifier.groupOrigin === 'grafana'`. In the list view `rulerRule` is now always undefined (ruler requests were removed), so `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` is false and Pause/Resume never appears even when `canPause` is granted through the new `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` path. The `MenuItemPauseRule` component currently needs the ruler DTO, but as implemented the prom-rule pause ability added in this PR is dead code in the UI.

title: Silence drawer cannot open from the list view without a ruler rule
body: The silence drawer is rendered as `{rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) && showSilenceDrawer && (<SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer rulerRule={rule} .../>)}`. In the list view only `promRule` is provided (`rule` is undefined), so clicking 'Silence notifications' in the menu sets `showSilenceDrawer` to true but the drawer never renders and nothing happens. The menu's Silence item can now be shown based on prom-rule abilities (`useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`), making this a user-visible no-op action.

title: Rules being created no longer appear in the group view
body: The previous implementation merged ruler rules with Prometheus rules and showed ruler-only rules with a 'Creating' state and prom-only rules with a 'Deleting' state. This PR drops the ruler fetch entirely and renders only `promResponse.data.groups.at(0)?.rules`. A newly created Grafana-managed rule is written to the ruler before it appears in the Prometheus-compatible endpoint, so during that window the rule is completely absent from the group list (and the `operation` prop on GrafanaRuleListItem is now never passed). Likewise a just-deleted rule vanishes immediately rather than showing 'Deleting'. If this temporary-inconsistency window is intentional, the removed behavior should be confirmed; otherwise users will see rules disappear/reappear with no indication.

title: Queries are interpolated twice in the shard-splitting path
body: runShardSplitQuery() now interpolates every target via datasource.applyTemplateVariables() before delegating to splitQueriesByStreamShard(), which in turn calls runSplitQuery() (shardQuerySplitting.ts:163), and runSplitQuery() now also applies datasource.applyTemplateVariables() to the same targets (querySplitting.ts:299). The updated test even encodes this: a single target results in applyTemplateVariables being called 5 times (once in runShardSplitQuery plus once per shard group's runSplitQuery call). This is harmless only if applyTemplateVariables is fully idempotent; any non-idempotent interpolation (e.g. appending ad-hoc filter matchers via the request.filters argument, or transformations that are not replace-if-present) would be applied repeatedly, producing incorrect expressions sent to Loki. It also does redundant work per shard group. The shard path should either skip re-interpolation when calling runSplitQuery (e.g. an option) or interpolate only once.

title: Template variables are now applied twice in the shard-splitting path
body: runShardSplitQuery() now maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables() before delegating to splitQueriesByStreamShard(), but each shard group is then executed via runSplitQuery() (line 163), which after this PR also calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables() on every target again. So in the sharded path every query is interpolated at least twice (once here, and once per shard group inside runSplitQuery — the updated test even asserts applyTemplateVariables was called 5 times for a single query). Beyond the wasted work, double interpolation is not guaranteed to be idempotent: if a variable's value itself contains a '$'-prefixed token (e.g. a label value like '$foo'), the second pass inside runSplitQuery will re-interpolate it and corrupt the query sent to Loki. Either the interpolation here or in runSplitQuery should be skipped when the queries were already interpolated.

title: applyTemplateVariables invoked per shard group via runSplitQuery
body: Because runSplitQuery now unconditionally calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables on all targets, the shard-splitting flow (which pre-interpolates in runShardSplitQuery and then calls runSplitQuery once per shard group) re-runs template variable interpolation on every shard sub-request, even though the expressions are already fully interpolated and only differ by the injected __stream_shard__ selector. For dashboards with many template variables this repeats the interpolation/scopedVar resolution work for every shard group; consider interpolating once and passing the results through.

title: Template variables are interpolated twice in the shard-splitting path
body: runShardSplitQuery() now interpolates every target with datasource.applyTemplateVariables() at the entry point (line 52), and each sharded sub-request is then delegated to runSplitQuery() (line 163), which this PR also changed to call datasource.applyTemplateVariables() on the same targets again (querySplitting.ts line 299). The updated test in shardQuerySplitting.test.ts confirms this: it expects applyTemplateVariables to have been called 5 times for a single-target request (once at entry, once per sub-request). For most variables the second pass is a no-op because the variable text is already gone, but if a variable's interpolated value itself contains a $-prefixed pattern (e.g. a textbox/custom variable whose value contains '$__' or another variable name, or a label value with a literal '$var' string), the second interpolation will rewrite it, corrupting the query sent to Loki. Consider skipping re-interpolation for targets that have already been interpolated (e.g. a flag on the sub-request or an option to runSplitQuery) so interpolation happens exactly once.

title: LoggerMiddleware now silently depends on ContextualLoggerMiddleware ordering for plugin context fields
body: logRequest no longer adds pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName, dsUID, or traceID to the log parameters itself; it calls m.logger.FromContext(ctx) and relies on those attributes having been injected into the context by the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware. This only works if ContextualLoggerMiddleware is placed before LoggerMiddleware in the middleware chain. The coupling is implicit and unenforced: any other wiring of middlewares (tests, alternative decorator construction such as NewClientDecorator callers that build their own middleware list, or a future reordering of CreateMiddlewares) will cause 'Plugin Request Completed' log lines to silently lose all plugin/request identifying fields. Previously the traceID was also added explicitly via tracing.TraceIDFromContext; that explicit addition was removed, so traceID inclusion now depends entirely on the infra logger's FromContext behavior. Consider either keeping the fields explicit in LoggerMiddleware or documenting/asserting the ordering requirement.

title: FromContext doc comment is inaccurate
body: The new Logger interface method FromContext is documented as 'returns a new contextual Logger that has this logger's context plus the given context', which is the same wording as New and doesn't describe what the method actually does: it derives a logger from a context.Context (extracting contextual log attributes previously stored in that context, e.g. by log.WithContextualAttributes), and the receiver's context is not necessarily preserved (the grafanaInfraLogWrapper implementation replaces the logger entirely with the one from the context, falling back to d.New() only on type-assertion failure). The comment should describe extracting a logger from the provided context.

title: No test coverage for the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware
body: The PR moves the contextual-attribute injection (endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, uname) out of the instrumentation middleware into a new ContextualLoggerMiddleware, but no test was added verifying that the middleware actually adds these attributes to the context for QueryData/CallResource/CheckHealth/CollectMetrics, including the nil-User and nil-DataSourceInstanceSettings branches. The renamed test file only updates the constructor call. A regression here would silently strip plugin-identifying fields from all downstream request logs.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh instance, so logs are not recorded
body: TestLogger.FromContext returns NewTestLogger(), a brand-new instance, rather than the receiver. All other TestLogger methods record calls into f.DebugLogs/InfoLogs/etc., which tests then assert on. With this change, LoggerMiddleware.logRequest now logs via m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so any test that constructs a TestLogger, passes it to NewLoggerMiddleware, and then inspects InfoLogs will always see zero calls and an empty message — the log entry is recorded on a throwaway logger. The fake should return the receiver itself (f) so recorded logs remain observable, matching how a contextual logger is expected to behave.

title: traceID is no longer included in the "Plugin Request Completed" log entry
body: Before this change, LoggerMiddleware.logRequest explicitly appended "traceID" (from tracing.TraceIDFromContext) to the log params, along with pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName and dsUID. Now those fields are only present if the incoming context carries the contextual attributes added by ContextualLoggerMiddleware — but that middleware never adds a traceID, and the tracing import was removed from this file. Unless pkg/infra/log's ConcreteLogger.FromContext injects traceID automatically (which the old explicit code suggests it does not), the traceID field silently disappears from the egress log line, breaking log-to-trace correlation for anyone relying on the traceID field of this event.

title: Contextual log fields now silently depend on middleware ordering
body: LoggerMiddleware no longer sets pluginId, endpoint, dsName, dsUID, or uname itself; it relies on ContextualLoggerMiddleware having already enriched the context via FromContext(ctx). In pluginsintegration.go the ordering is correct (ContextualLoggerMiddleware before LoggerMiddleware), but nothing in the code enforces or documents this dependency — if the LoggerMiddleware is ever used without the ContextualLoggerMiddleware ahead of it (or the order is swapped), the "Plugin Request Completed" log will silently lose all plugin-identifying fields. A comment on logRequest or NewLoggerMiddleware documenting this requirement would prevent a subtle observability regression.

title: traceID no longer included in "Plugin Request Completed" log line
body: Before this change, logRequest explicitly looked up the trace ID with tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false) and appended it as a "traceID" log parameter. This PR removes the tracing import and that logic, switching to m.logger.FromContext(ctx) which only picks up the attributes injected by the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware: endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname. Nothing in the new middleware chain adds the trace ID to the contextual attributes (instrumentContext in contextual_logger_middleware.go only adds the five fields listed above, and grafana's infra/log contextual logger does not add trace IDs automatically). As a result, the "Plugin Request Completed" log entries lose their traceID field, breaking log-to-trace correlation for anyone relying on this well-known egress log line (eventName=grafana-data-egress). The trace ID should be re-added, either by appending it in instrumentContext (e.g. via tracing.TraceIDFromContext) or explicitly in logRequest.

title: Local cache is populated before the device-limit check, letting rejected devices bypass the limit
body: In tagDeviceUI, `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})` runs before `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice(ctx, device)`. Now that client.go treats `ErrDeviceLimitReached` as an authentication failure, this ordering breaks enforcement: when a new device is rejected because the limit is reached, its cache key has already been set, so every subsequent request from that same device for the next ~29 minutes hits the cache branch, returns nil from TagDevice, and is allowed to authenticate anonymously. The device limit is therefore only enforced on the first request from each new device, not on ongoing usage. The cache should only be populated after the store call succeeds (or the error should clear the key).

title: Count-then-insert device limit check is not atomic and can be exceeded under concurrency
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by first running CountDevices and then, if under the limit, executing the upsert in a separate statement without a transaction or lock. Multiple concurrent anonymous requests with fresh device IDs can all observe count < deviceLimit and all insert, pushing the total above the configured limit. On a busy instance with many simultaneous first-time anonymous hits, the actual number of tracked devices can significantly exceed the configured limit. Enforcement needs to be atomic (e.g. a transaction with appropriate isolation, a conditional INSERT based on a subquery count, or a database constraint).

title: Devices idle longer than 30 days are permanently locked out when the limit is reached
body: When the limit is reached, updateDevice only updates rows whose updated_at falls between device.UpdatedAt-30d and device.UpdatedAt+1min, and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached if no row matched. However, old devices are only physically deleted after 61 days (keepFor in impl.go). A device that was tagged 31-60 days ago still exists in anon_device but is neither counted by CountDevices (which uses the same 30-day window) nor updatable by updateDevice, so on an at-limit instance that returning device gets ErrDeviceLimitReached and is denied authentication even though it already occupies a row and could simply be refreshed. The 30-day exclusion window in updateDevice should be widened (or removed) so any existing device row can be updated.

title: ErrDeviceLimitReached is returned as a raw error, producing a 500 for anonymous users
body: When the device limit is reached, Authenticate returns the plain `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached` error. The authn framework will treat this as a generic internal authentication error (HTTP 500 with 'device limit reached') rather than a deliberate access-denied response, making it indistinguishable from a server failure in monitoring and giving end users a confusing error. Consider returning a typed error (e.g. one the authn layer maps to 401/403 with a clear message) so operators and users can tell the limit was hit.

title: anonymousDeviceLimit typed as possibly-undefined but backend always sends a number
body: The Go DTO serializes `anonymousDeviceLimit` as a non-omitempty int64, so the frontend always receives a number — 0 meaning 'no limit'. The TypeScript type `number | undefined` suggests the field can be absent, which can lead frontend consumers to use undefined-checks to detect 'no limit configured' and misbehave, since the actual sentinel is 0 and the value will never be undefined. Type it as `number` and document 0 as unlimited (or make the Go field a pointer with omitempty if undefined is intended).

title: Device limit check is racy: count-then-insert is not atomic
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by running CountDevices and then conditionally inserting. Two (or more) concurrent anonymous requests for new devices can both observe count < deviceLimit and both insert, exceeding the configured limit. On a busy instance with many simultaneous first-time anonymous visitors, the limit can be breached by an arbitrary margin. Enforcement needs to be atomic (e.g., insert guarded by a transaction with a locked count, a UNIQUE/sequence-based cap, or accepting the race and documenting it).

title: Known device older than 30 days is rejected as 'device limit reached'
body: When the limit is reached, updateDevice only updates rows whose updated_at is within [now-30d, now+1m] and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when 0 rows are affected. The cleanup job (DeleteDevicesOlderThan) only deletes devices older than 61 days, so a device whose last update is between 30 and 61 days old still occupies a row (and is counted by CountDevices) but cannot be updated — its owner gets a hard 'device limit reached' auth error even though refreshing that existing device would not increase the device count. The update branch should fall back to checking whether the device row exists (and update it) before concluding the limit blocks the request.

title: ErrDeviceLimitReached aborts anonymous authentication with a raw internal error
body: TagDevice is now called synchronously in Authenticate, and ErrDeviceLimitReached is returned as the authenticate error. The authn framework will treat this as a failed authentication, so every request from a new anonymous device (once the limit is hit) fails with an unhandled internal error rather than a controlled response (e.g., a 429 or a rendered 'device limit reached' page). The error message 'device limit reached' is also a bare fmt.Errorf with no user-facing wording, and browsers will keep retrying, generating error noise. The authn error handling for this case (status code, redirect behavior, user message) should be explicitly implemented and tested.

title: Local cache is populated before the store write, so a rejected/failed tag is not retried for 29 minutes
body: tagDeviceUI calls localCache.SetDefault(key, ...) before CreateOrUpdateDevice. If CreateOrUpdateDevice fails (including ErrDeviceLimitReached or a transient DB error), the cache entry remains and subsequent requests from the same device skip the store entirely for up to 29 minutes. With the new synchronous error path this means a transient DB failure during the limit check or insert silently stops device tracking, and TagDevice returns an error to the caller on the first attempt but nil on subsequent ones, giving inconsistent auth behavior. Only populate the cache after a successful store call, or evict on error.

title: Extra COUNT query on every device tag when a limit is configured
body: When deviceLimit > 0, every CreateOrUpdateDevice call performs a full COUNT(*) over anon_device filtered by updated_at before deciding whether to insert. For known devices this count is wasted work (the upsert would have succeeded anyway), and without an index on updated_at this is a table scan per new/refreshing device. Consider only doing the count when the upsert would create a new row, or checking existence of the device_id first.

title: anonymousDeviceLimit is always serialized and typed inconsistently with the frontend
body: The Go DTO field AnonymousDeviceLimit is a plain int64 with no omitempty, so the JSON payload always contains "anonymousDeviceLimit": 0 even when no limit is configured, while the TypeScript type in packages/grafana-data declares it as `number | undefined`. Consumers cannot distinguish 'no limit configured' from 'limit of 0' except by the 0-as-unset convention, which is undocumented. Either make it a pointer/omitempty or type the frontend field as a plain number and document the 0 = unlimited convention.

title: New device_limit option is not added to sample config or docs
body: The new [auth.anonymous] device_limit setting is parsed but is not added to conf/sample.ini (or defaults.ini comments), so administrators have no discoverable documentation of the option, its default (0 = unlimited), or its semantics (limit over a rolling 30-day window). The PR description also leaves the docs checkbox unchecked.

title: Device limit check is not atomic with the insert, so the limit can be exceeded
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit with a separate CountDevices query followed by an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT. Two (or more) concurrent requests — on the same or different Grafana instances sharing a database — can both observe count < deviceLimit and both insert, exceeding the configured limit. Since anonymous auth requests are inherently concurrent, the configured device_limit is only approximate. Enforcement needs to be atomic (e.g., conditional insert in a single statement or a transaction with appropriate isolation) or the limitation should be documented.

title: Device tagging moved from async goroutine into the synchronous anonymous auth path
body: Previously TagDevice ran in a background goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout; this PR calls it synchronously in Authenticate. Every anonymous request that misses the 29-minute local cache now performs a COUNT query plus a write to the anon_device table inline before the request is authenticated. On a busy instance with many distinct devices, this adds database latency (and DB load from the extra COUNT on every uncached request) to every anonymous page load, and a slow/unavailable database now delays or breaks anonymous authentication, which was previously immune to tagging failures.

title: ErrDeviceLimitReached aborts authentication with a raw internal error
body: When the device limit is reached, Authenticate returns nil plus the raw sentinel error ErrDeviceLimitReached ("device limit reached"). This propagates through authn as a generic authentication failure, so an anonymous user hitting the limit gets an unexplained 500/internal error instead of a meaningful response. Also note the device is already cached in tagDeviceUI's localCache before the DB write fails, so the failure (and error) only surfaces on the first request per device per ~29 minutes — subsequent requests silently authenticate while the device is never recorded. If rejecting users past the limit is intended, the error should be surfaced as a deliberate user-facing message; if not, the error shouldn't fail authentication.

title: Existing devices with stale updated_at get ErrDeviceLimitReached instead of being refreshed
body: Once the limit is reached, updateDevice only updates rows whose updated_at falls within [now-30d, now+1m]. A device that exists in anon_device but hasn't been seen for over 30 days (rows are only purged after 61 days by the cleanup job) matches no rows, RowsAffected == 0, and ErrDeviceLimitReached is returned — even though that device's own stale slot could legitimately be reused. The upsert path that would have refreshed it is skipped entirely once count >= deviceLimit.

title: New device_limit option not documented in sample config
body: The new [auth.anonymous] device_limit setting is read but no corresponding entry/documentation appears to be added to conf/sample.ini or conf/defaults.ini alongside the other auth.anonymous options, so admins have no discoverable way to learn the option exists, its units, or that 0 means unlimited.

title: Routine cleanup batches are logged at Error level, including full ID lists
body: The new cleanup code logs every normal batch operation with r.log.Error (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579), e.g. r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err) where err is nil on success. Since this job runs periodically and logs every batch including the complete list of annotation IDs (which can be tens of thousands of entries with large AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize values), production error logs will be flooded with huge, non-error messages. This makes real errors hard to spot and can cause significant log ingestion cost. These should be Debug-level logs, and the full ID list should likely be omitted or truncated.

title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, affecting all cleanup jobs
body: The PR changes the main cleanup ticker from time.Minute*10 to time.Minute*1. This is not mentioned in the PR description, which is scoped to the annotation deadlock fix, and it does not only affect annotation cleanup: every job in the list (temp file cleanup, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, user invites, short URLs, query history) now runs 10x more frequently. Each run also acquires the server lock and performs database scans/deletes, so this is a meaningful load increase across the whole instance. If the intent was only to run annotation cleanup more often, this should be done separately or at least justified and called out.

title: MaxCount cleanup uses OFFSET on a moving table without a transaction, which can over-delete under concurrent inserts
body: The max-count cleanup now does SELECT id ... ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT batchSize OFFSET maxCount followed by a separate DELETE, with no shared transaction between the two (by design). Unlike the max-age cleanup, which is time-based and self-correcting, the OFFSET-based query is sensitive to concurrent inserts: rows inserted between the SELECT and DELETE shift the window, and because the loop re-runs immediately, freshly inserted annotations can be selected and deleted in a later batch even when the total count is at or below maxCount after earlier deletions. The comment acknowledges under-deletion but not over-deletion of recent rows. The old single-statement form at least evaluated the set atomically per batch. Consider bounding the delete to IDs known to be beyond the kept set (e.g. capture the ID at position maxCount once per run and delete only ids below it), or documenting/accepting this explicitly.

title: Cleanup routine logs normal operation at Error level, including full ID lists
body: The new cleanup code logs every batch at Error level: `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", ...)` (line 534), `r.log.Error("cleaned annotations by time", ...)` (line 537), and the equivalents for count-based cleanup (lines 554, 557) and orphaned tag cleanup (lines 576, 579). These are not errors — they fire on every successful batch of a job that runs on a schedule, and they include the full `ids` slice (up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize entries per line). This will flood error-level logs, trigger log-based alerting on errors that aren't errors, and produce very large log lines. They should be Debug level.

title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute for all cleanup jobs
body: This PR changes the CleanUpService ticker from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This does not just make annotation cleanup run more often — it makes every cleanup job (expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, temp user invites, short URLs, query history, tmp file deletion) run 10x more frequently. Several of these do non-trivial database deletes and filesystem scans, and query history cleanup enforces row limits over large tables. This is an undocumented, broad behavioral/performance change bundled into a PR about avoiding annotation deadlocks; if the intent was only to make annotation cleanup more responsive, the annotation job should get its own schedule rather than speeding up the entire cleanup loop.

title: MaxCount cleanup can exit early if a fetched batch is concurrently deleted
body: In the new split fetch-then-delete flow, `untilDoneOrCancelled` stops when a batch reports zero affected rows. Because the SELECT and DELETE are no longer in one statement/transaction, another process (e.g., a second Grafana instance's cleanup job, or a user delete) can delete the fetched IDs between the two statements, making `RowsAffected()` return 0 and terminating the loop even though more annotations beyond MaxCount still exist. The old single-statement form re-evaluated the subquery on each execution and only stopped when a delete genuinely matched nothing. The under-deleted rows will be cleaned on the next cycle so the impact is bounded, but it is a behavioral regression worth noting/acknowledging (e.g., loop while len(ids) == batchSize instead of affected > 0).

title: Cleanup job interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The PR changes the CleanUpService ticker from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This runs the entire cleanup suite (tmp files, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history) ten times more frequently. Nothing in the PR description mentions this, so it looks like an accidental debug leftover. If intentional it needs justification, since jobs like query-history row-limit enforcement and annotation cleanup now execute every minute against the production database.

title: Routine cleanup progress logged at Error level with full ID lists
body: CleanAnnotations, CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags now call `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", ..., "ids", ids, ...)` (and three similar calls) for normal, successful operation. These fire on every batch of every cleanup cycle, emitting error-severity log lines (which typically trigger alerting/dashboards on error counts) and dumping the full list of up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize IDs into the logs. These should be Debug level at most; as written they will spam error logs in production.

title: SQLite ID list built with quadratic string concatenation
body: In deleteByIDs, the SQLite fallback builds the IN clause via `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` in a loop, which copies the whole accumulated string each iteration — O(n²) work. The new test uses a batch size of 32767, so this builds strings totaling hundreds of thousands of bytes through ~32k reallocations. strings.Builder or bytes.Buffer would make it linear.

title: Async legacy writes use the request context and will be cancelled when the request completes
body: In Create (and identically in Delete line 110, Update line 135, and DeleteCollection line 163), the fire-and-forget goroutine derives its timeout context from the incoming request context (`ctx`). The Kubernetes apiserver cancels the request context as soon as the handler returns, and this function returns immediately after the storage write without waiting for the goroutine. As a result the legacy write will almost always run with an already-cancelled context and fail with context.Canceled, silently dropping the legacy copy that mode 3 is supposed to maintain 'as a safe measure'. The goroutine should derive from `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (or a background context carrying the logger/values) before applying the 10s timeout.

title: Storage create error is recorded as a legacy duration metric
body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` even though no legacy call was made; the failure occurred in unified storage. The same mistake exists in Update at line 129 (`recordLegacyDuration` on a `d.Storage.Update` error). This mislabels storage errors as legacy errors and records them against the storage start time, corrupting the dual-writer duration/error metrics that are presumably used to monitor the migration.

title: Delete records storage duration metric with object name instead of kind label
body: After a successful `d.Storage.Delete`, the code calls `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passing the object `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. This creates a high-cardinality, inconsistent label value (per-object names) in the storage duration metric, both breaking aggregation by kind and potentially exploding the Prometheus series cardinality.

title: DeleteCollection records legacy write duration under the storage metric
body: Inside the async goroutine in DeleteCollection, the legacy call's outcome is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy delete-collection latency and errors will be attributed to the unified storage metric, making the legacy metric silently empty and the storage metric wrong.

title: Legacy update no longer stores the object produced by the storage update
body: The previous implementation fetched the old object once, computed the updated object, ran the storage update, and then wrote the storage-produced object (`obj`) to legacy via an `updateWrapper`, guaranteeing both stores converge to the same content. The new code passes the original `objInfo` independently to both `Storage.Update` and (asynchronously) `Legacy.Update`, so `UpdatedObject` is evaluated twice against potentially different old objects, and any fields set by the storage layer during update (e.g. generated values, normalized fields) are never propagated to legacy. Legacy can silently diverge from unified storage, which defeats mode 3's purpose of keeping legacy as a consistent safety copy. Additionally the two updates race with any concurrent writer since legacy is now applied later, unordered, with no error logging.

title: Legacy write failures are no longer logged
body: The previous mode 3 implementation logged an error when a legacy Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection failed. The new async goroutines only record the failure in a metric (`recordLegacyDuration(errObjectSt != nil, ...)`) and never log it. During a migration where legacy is the fallback store, operators will have no log trail explaining why legacy drifted from unified storage; only a counter changes. The goroutine should log the error with the object/name context.

title: Delete installs the base logger into the context instead of the enriched one
body: `Delete` builds `log` with name/kind/method values but then calls `klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` with the base logger, discarding those values for anything downstream that uses `klog.FromContext(ctx)` (including the legacy delete in the goroutine). Every other method installs the enriched `log`. Use `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`.

title: Mode 3 playlist tests read from the legacy API immediately after async legacy writes, which is inherently racy
body: In mode 3, writes go to unified storage synchronously and to legacy only in a background goroutine with up to a 10s timeout. However `doPlaylistTests` (used by the new 'file, mode 3' and 'unified storage, mode 3' subtests) asserts legacy API state synchronously right after k8s writes: `/api/playlists` list must contain the just-created items (lines 523-531) and `getFromBothAPIs` does GET `/api/playlists/{uid}` immediately after create/update. Because the legacy write may not have completed yet, these assertions are timing-dependent and will flake, especially under load or CI. The tests need polling/waiting (e.g. require.Eventually) for legacy visibility in mode 3, or the dual writer needs a synchronous/blocked legacy write for testability.

title: Async legacy writes use the (soon-to-be-cancelled) request context
body: In Create (and identically in Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection), the legacy write is launched in a goroutine that derives its context from the incoming request `ctx` via `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s, ...)`. When Create returns to the caller, the API server completes the HTTP request and cancels the request context, which immediately cancels the goroutine's context as well. The 'safe measure' legacy write will therefore usually fail with context canceled before it even runs, so in mode 3 the legacy store will silently drift out of sync with unified storage. The goroutine should use a detached context (e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)`) while keeping only the values (logger, auth info) needed. This affects lines 51, 110, 135, and 163.

title: Update passes the same UpdatedObjectInfo to both stores, losing the pre-computed updated object
body: The previous implementation of mode 3 Update first did `Storage.Get`, called `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old)` once, and then wrapped the result in an `updateWrapper` so both Storage.Update and Legacy.Update received a wrapper returning the already-computed object. The new code passes the raw `objInfo` to `d.Storage.Update` and then to `d.Legacy.Update` in the async goroutine. `rest.UpdatedObjectInfo` implementations used by the API machinery generally wrap the request body and may only be consumed once (e.g. they decode the incoming object on each call, or hold the old object fetched by the first Update call). The second invocation in the legacy goroutine can fail or produce an object computed against a different 'old' state than unified storage used, so legacy can store content that differs from what was written to unified storage — the opposite of what the dual write is meant to guarantee.

title: Storage failures recorded with the legacy-duration metric
body: In Create, when `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` — recording a legacy error/duration even though the legacy store was never called. The same mistake exists in Update at line 129 (`recordLegacyDuration` on a `d.Storage.Update` failure). This corrupts the dual-writer metrics: legacy error rates and latencies will show failures that actually belong to unified storage, misleading anyone alerting on these metrics during the migration.

title: Delete records the object name as the metric 'kind' label
body: On the success path of Delete, the metric is recorded as `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`, passing the object name where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. This creates a high-cardinality metric label (one series per deleted object name) and breaks aggregation by kind for delete operations.

title: DeleteCollection async legacy call recorded with the storage metric
body: Inside the async goroutine of DeleteCollection, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy delete-collection latency/errors will be attributed to unified storage, and the actual storage call was already recorded above, so every delete-collection produces two storage-metric samples and no legacy-metric sample.

title: Delete installs the wrong logger into the context
body: Delete builds `log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method)` but then calls `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` with the base logger instead of `log`. All log lines emitted from within the storage/legacy delete calls (and the `log.Error` in this function uses `log`, but anything retrieved via klog.FromContext downstream) lose the name/kind/method values that the other methods attach.

title: Tests don't verify the async legacy write happens
body: The mode 3 write-path tests set up legacy mock expectations but then never wait for the goroutine or assert the legacy call occurred (e.g. TestMode3_Create's error case doesn't even set up a storage mock failing — the 'unified store fails' case configures only the legacy mock to fail, while the actual storage mock has no expectation, so `dw.Create` panics/fails on an unexpected call rather than exercising the intended path, and no test asserts `ls` was eventually called). As written, the tests pass even if the legacy write is dropped entirely (e.g. due to the cancelled-context bug), so they don't protect the core guarantee of mode 3.

title: Async legacy writes derive their context from the request context, which is cancelled when the request completes
body: In Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection, the goroutine that writes to legacy storage calls `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` using the incoming request `ctx`. In an HTTP/gRPC handler, that context is cancelled as soon as the handler returns — which is exactly when the goroutine starts doing its legacy write. The legacy write will therefore almost always be aborted immediately with context.Canceled, so the "write to legacy as a safe measure" silently never happens. The async write should be derived from a background/detached context (preserving trace/identity values as needed) with its own timeout.

title: Storage Create failure recorded as legacy-duration metric
body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails in Mode 3 Create, the error path calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, ...)` with `startStorage` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration`. The same mistake exists in Update's error path (line 129). This mislabels unified-storage write failures as legacy-storage failures in the dual-writer metrics, which will mislead operators monitoring the migration.

title: Async legacy DeleteCollection records storage-duration metric
body: In the async legacy branch of DeleteCollection, the legacy call's result is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration`, and uses `startLegacy` as the start time. Legacy delete-collection latencies/failures will be attributed to unified storage in the metrics.

title: Delete records storage metric with object name as the kind label
body: On successful storage delete, `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` where every other call passes `options.Kind`. The resource/kind label on the metric will contain object names, exploding label cardinality and making the per-kind dashboards useless.

title: Delete installs the wrong logger into the context
body: Delete builds an enriched `log` with name/kind/method values, but then calls `klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` — the base logger without those values — so downstream log lines from the delete path lose the contextual fields, unlike all other methods which pass `log`.

title: objInfo is invoked twice for updates; the updateWrapper caching was removed
body: The previous implementation resolved the updated object once via `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old)` and wrapped it in `updateWrapper` so legacy storage reused the same resolved object. The new code passes the original `objInfo` to both `d.Storage.Update` and, asynchronously, `d.Legacy.Update`, so `UpdatedObject` will be invoked twice — concurrently with the request handler returning. Many UpdatedObjectInfo implementations (e.g., the default one reading the request body) are single-use or not safe to invoke after the request completes, so the legacy update may fail or read inconsistent data.

title: Mode 3 integration tests read from legacy API immediately after async legacy writes
body: The mode 3 subtests reuse doPlaylistTests, which asserts that objects created/updated/deleted via k8s are immediately visible through the legacy /api/playlists endpoints (e.g., getFromBothAPIs, the legacy search listing). In mode 3 the legacy write happens asynchronously in a goroutine, so there is no happens-before guarantee between the k8s write returning and the legacy write landing. These assertions will be flaky under load; the test should poll/retry the legacy read or mode 3 should be excluded from the cross-API consistency assertions.

title: Dev mode serializes all GetWebAssets calls behind an exclusive lock
body: When cfg.Env == setting.Dev the cache is intentionally bypassed, but the new code still acquires entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock() (an exclusive write lock) around the entire manifest read, including file I/O and JSON decoding. Every request that touches web assets in a dev environment is now fully serialized, and if a future change re-enables the CDN path (the commented-out cdn variable) this would also serialize a blocking HTTP call. The lock only needs to be held while assigning entryPointAssetsCache; the read/parse could happen outside the lock (e.g., compute first, then lock and store), avoiding the convoy entirely.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false, leaving dead feature-flag logic
body: The new helper `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns false on every code path (`if enabled { return false }; return false`). This makes the feature-flag evaluation and the intermediate variable dead code that looks like an inverted-condition bug to any reader. Since the intent is to hard-disable SQL expressions regardless of the flag, the function should just be `return false` with a comment (or the call site should be a plain unconditional error), and ideally the FlagSqlExpressions feature toggle should be removed or marked disabled to avoid operators thinking they can still turn the feature on.

title: enableSqlExpressions ignores the sqlExpressions feature flag entirely
body: The new enableSqlExpressions() unconditionally returns false: it computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns false on every path, so even operators who explicitly enable the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle will get the error "sqlExpressions is not implemented" for every SQL expression query. If hard-disabling is the intent of this security fix, the convoluted always-false logic is misleading — a plain `return false` (or removing the feature flag check and the flag reference) would be honest about the behavior. As written, the feature flag documentation (which this PR explicitly says it is leaving untouched) tells users a toggle exists that silently does nothing, and the dead negation invites a future edit to mistakenly re-enable the vulnerable code path by 'fixing' what looks like a bug.

title: enableSqlExpressions reads the feature flag but always returns false
body: The new helper computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns false in every branch, so the feature-flag check is dead code and the flag's value is never actually consulted. Since the intent of this PR is to unconditionally disable SQL expressions, this is functionally correct, but the leftover flag evaluation is misleading: a future maintainer may 'fix' the inverted logic (returning `enabled`) and unknowingly re-enable the vulnerable DuckDB code path. The function should simply `return false` (or the call site should hard-code the error) with a comment referencing CVE-2024-9264 so the disable cannot be accidentally reverted.

title: User-facing error message 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' is misleading
body: When a user submits a SQL expression, the reader now returns the error "sqlExpressions is not implemented". The feature is in fact implemented but deliberately disabled due to the CVE-2024-9264 RCE/LFI vulnerability; telling users it is 'not implemented' misdirects them (they may enable the sqlExpressions feature flag expecting it to work, or file support tickets). The message should state that SQL expressions are disabled, e.g. "SQL expressions are disabled in this version of Grafana".

title: Data race on shared err variable across errgroup goroutines in init
body: In searchSupport.init, each goroutine launched via group.Go executes `_, _, err = s.build(...)`, assigning to the `err` variable declared in the outer function scope. With s.initWorkers > 1, multiple goroutines write to this shared variable concurrently while group.Wait() and the surrounding code read it, which is a data race (Go race detector will flag it). Each goroutine should use its own local error variable and return it: `_, _, berr := s.build(...); return berr`.

title: Unsynchronized increment of totalBatchesIndexed from concurrent goroutines
body: totalBatchesIndexed is incremented inside the errgroup goroutines (`totalBatchesIndexed++`) without any synchronization. With multiple init workers this is a concurrent read/write race and the final count reported in the tracing span event can be wrong. Use an atomic counter or increment outside the goroutines (e.g., from len(stats)).

title: Removing the whole-function lock allows concurrent BuildIndex for the same key
body: BuildIndex previously held b.cacheMu for its entire duration, which serialized index builds. Now the lock is only taken when inserting into the cache, so two concurrent callers can build an index for the same NamespacedResource simultaneously (e.g., getOrCreateIndex racing between a Search request and a watch event after init, since getOrCreateIndex has no per-key locking). For file-backed indexes both builds call bleve.New on the same directory, and the second one will fail because bleve locks the index directory; the loser also discards its work and one build silently overwrites the other in the cache. A per-key lock (singleflight) is needed to keep the speedup without allowing duplicate builds of the same key.

title: TotalDocs iterates b.cache map without holding cacheMu
body: TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without acquiring b.cacheMu (RLock). Now that BuildIndex writes to b.cache concurrently (during parallel init and from watch-event-driven getOrCreateIndex builds), TotalDocs can run concurrently with a map write — init itself calls s.search.TotalDocs() while other builds may still be triggered by handleEvent. Concurrent map read/write is a fatal error in Go ("concurrent map read and map write"). Take b.cacheMu.RLock() around the iteration.

title: NewResourceServer leaks the cancelable context and partially started watchers on Init failure
body: NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) and returns an error if it fails, but on that error path s.cancel() is never called. If search.init succeeded but initWatcher failed (or vice versa partially), the background watch goroutine(s) and poller started during init keep running with no way to stop them, since the constructor returned nil and the caller has no server handle to Stop. Call s.cancel() (and ideally s.Stop) before returning the error.

title: Data races on shared err and totalBatchesIndexed inside errgroup goroutines
body: In searchSupport.init, each goroutine spawned by group.Go writes to the outer shared variables: `totalBatchesIndexed++` (line 189) and `_, _, err = s.build(...)` (line 190). These run concurrently with up to initWorkers goroutines and with the main goroutine which reads/overwrites `err` at `err = group.Wait()`. This is an unsynchronized read/write race (flagged by -race) on both `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed`, and the span attribute count can be undercounted. Use an atomic counter (or collect per-goroutine) and return the build error only via the goroutine's return value instead of assigning to the shared err.

title: TotalDocs iterates the cache map without holding cacheMu
body: TotalDocs ranges over b.cache with no lock, while BuildIndex now writes b.cache[key] under cacheMu at line 138 and GetIndex reads under RLock. Previously BuildIndex held cacheMu for its whole duration, so writes only happened while no other BuildIndex was running, but TotalDocs was still unsafe — and this PR makes it worse by calling TotalDocs from searchSupport.init's new log line and by allowing concurrent builds. A concurrent map read and write panics at runtime. TotalDocs should take b.cacheMu.RLock() while iterating.

title: Removing the BuildIndex lock allows duplicate concurrent builds of the same key
body: BuildIndex previously held cacheMu for the entire function, which serialized builds. Now the lock is only taken when inserting into the cache, and getOrCreateIndex in search.go has no per-key locking (its own TODO acknowledges this). Two concurrent requests (or a request plus a watch event) for the same NamespacedResource can both see GetIndex return nil, both run a full bleve build, and both assign b.cache[key] — the loser's index is never closed (file handles/disk for file-backed indexes leak) and duplicate work is done. A per-key build mutex or singleflight is needed to keep the finer-grained locking safe.

title: Init failure in NewResourceServer leaks the cancelable context
body: NewResourceServer creates ctx/cancel, then calls s.Init(ctx) and returns nil, err on failure without calling cancel(). The background context and its goroutine resources are never released on the error path. Call cancel() before returning the error.

title: TotalDocs iterates the cache map without any lock while BuildIndex now writes concurrently
body: The PR removes the cacheMu lock that previously wrapped the entire BuildIndex, so b.cache is now written (line 138, under Lock) while TotalDocs (lines 144-154) iterates b.cache with no lock at all. searchSupport.init() calls TotalDocs right after a concurrent errgroup build, and init() is now invoked synchronously at server startup where builds run with s.initWorkers goroutines, so a concurrent map read/write here is a realistic scenario and will crash the process with 'fatal error: concurrent map read and map write'.

title: Dropping the build-wide lock allows duplicate concurrent builds of the same index
body: Previously cacheMu was held for the whole BuildIndex, guaranteeing only one build per key. Now the lock is only taken for the final map assignment, so two callers (e.g. getOrCreateIndex racing with init, or two searches for an unbuilt namespace) can both build the same NamespacedResource simultaneously. For file-based indexes both call bleve.New on the same directory path, which will fail or corrupt the on-disk index; for memory indexes one built index is silently overwritten in the cache (leaking the other and double-counting IndexTenants/IndexedKinds metrics). A per-key build lock or singleflight is needed now that the coarse lock is gone.

title: errgroup goroutines race on shared err and totalBatchesIndexed variables
body: Inside searchSupport.init(), each group.Go closure executes `_, _, err = s.build(...)` assigning to the outer `err` variable shared by all goroutines, and does `totalBatchesIndexed++` on a shared int. Both are unsynchronized concurrent accesses (a data race detectable by -race) and the write to the outer err can clobber the real error before group.Wait() returns, so a failed build could be masked. The closure should use a local error (`_, _, berr := s.build(...); return berr`) and an atomic counter.

title: Test can panic calling err.Error() on a nil error from ms.Run()
body: The goroutine does `err = ms.Run(); if err.Error() != "context canceled"`.
