The comment claims 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically', but this is false: Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing and raise `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported`. Since the audit log endpoint passes `enable_advanced_features=True` for superusers/admins, any such user supplying a negative-offset cursor gets a 500 instead of a BadPaginationError or a clamped offset.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator key handling is numeric but the endpoint orders by datetime
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `int(math.floor(value))` / `math.ceil(value)` on the sort key, which only works for numeric values. The audit logs endpoint uses it with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `getattr(item, self.key)` returns a datetime object and `math.floor(datetime)` raises a TypeError. The endpoint previously used DateTimePaginator, which converts the datetime to a millisecond timestamp. As written, the 'optimized' path will fail with a 500 on the first page that has results (build_cursor always calls get_item_key). OptimizedCursorPaginator needs the DateTimePaginator key conversion (or should subclass it).

title: organization_context.member can be None for superusers
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences `.member` unconditionally via the `or` chain — actually Python short-circuits when is_superuser is True, but a non-superuser whose RpcUserOrganizationContext has `member=None` (e.g. access via org auth token or other non-member paths that this endpoint permits through OrganizationAuditPermission) will hit `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'` and get a 500 on every request to this endpoint, even when not requesting optimized pagination. Guard with `organization_context.member is not None and organization_context.member.has_global_access`.

title: BasePaginator silently clamps negative offsets, changing prev-cursor semantics
body: The change in BasePaginator.get_result replaces `results = queryset[offset:stop]` with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. For non-prev cursors, a negative offset was previously impossible to reach successfully (Django would raise), so clamping changes behavior silently for all users of Paginator/DateTimePaginator codebase-wide: a client-supplied negative-offset cursor that used to fail loudly now returns the first page as if offset were 0, while the cursor arithmetic later (`_build_next_values` uses the raw `cursor.offset`) still computes next offsets from the original negative offset, producing inconsistent cursors. If clamping is intended, it should be applied uniformly (and probably rejected with BadPaginationError instead), not papered over only in the slice.

title: enable_advanced_features passed through self.paginate may not reach the paginator
body: The endpoint calls `self.paginate(..., paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator, ..., enable_advanced_features=True)`. Sentry's base `Endpoint.paginate` only forwards a fixed set of arguments when constructing the paginator; arbitrary extra kwargs are not passed to the paginator constructor in the standard implementation. If that is the case here, the paginator will always be constructed with `enable_advanced_features=False` (or paginate will raise TypeError for the unexpected kwarg), and the new code path is dead. This needs a test verifying the flag actually reaches OptimizedCursorPaginator.

title: No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the optimized audit log path
body: This PR adds a new paginator (~90 lines) with non-trivial boundary logic (negative offsets, prev-cursor extra-row trimming, cursor building) and a new branch in the audit logs endpoint, but includes no tests. Given that both the datetime key handling and the negative-slice behavior are broken as noted, unit tests covering first-page, next-page, prev-page, and malformed-cursor cases for OptimizedCursorPaginator, plus an endpoint test with optimized_pagination=true, are required before merging.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key crashes on datetime keys
body: The endpoint uses this paginator with order_by="-datetime", so self.key is "datetime" and getattr(item, self.key) returns a datetime object. get_item_key then calls math.floor()/math.ceil() on that datetime, which raises TypeError. Unlike DateTimePaginator (which converts via strftime to a numeric timestamp), this implementation never converts the value. Every request that takes the optimized path (optimized_pagination=true for a superuser/org admin) will 500, both when generating cursor keys in build_cursor and in the is_prev comparison. value_from_cursor has the same mismatch: it returns the raw cursor.value (an int timestamp produced by nothing, or 0), never converting it to a datetime the way DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor does, so even if the key computation were fixed the cursor filter would compare a datetime column against an integer.

title: Negative offsets are passed to queryset slicing, which Django rejects
body: When enable_advanced_features is set and cursor.offset < 0, the code does results = list(queryset[cursor.offset : cursor.offset + limit + extra]). The comment claims 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically', but Django explicitly does not support negative indexing on querysets and raises ValueError ('Negative indexing is not supported'). The cursor offset is fully attacker-controllable (Cursor.from_string parses the offset from the user-supplied cursor query parameter), so any caller who reaches this path can reliably trigger a 500. The same unclamped negative-offset hazard was introduced into BasePaginator.get_result (line 182) for is_prev cursors, where offset is no longer clamped to >= 0 before slicing.

title: organization_context.member may be None, causing AttributeError
body: The new condition request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access evaluates member.has_global_access whenever the user is not a superuser. organization_context.member is None for requests where the actor is not an org member (e.g., certain token-based or cross-org accesses that previously worked on this endpoint). The original code never touched organization_context.member, so this change introduces a new AttributeError/500 for such requests on a previously working endpoint.

title: Offset/extra length check uses unclamped offset, breaking row trimming
body: In BasePaginator.get_result (and copied into OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result at line 891), the code now slices with start_offset = max(0, offset) but the extra-row trim check still compares len(results) == offset + limit + extra. When offset is negative and gets clamped to 0, this comparison is wrong, so the extra boundary row is not dropped and the page contents/has_results cursor state are computed from an off-by-one result set, producing duplicated or skipped rows across pages.

title: New pagination path has no tests and is dead-on-arrival broken
body: The PR adds a new OptimizedCursorPaginator (~90 lines) plus a new query-parameter-controlled code path on the audit log endpoint, but includes no tests. Even a single happy-path test of optimized_pagination=true would have caught that the paginator crashes on datetime keys. The negative-offset 'advanced feature' is also entirely untested and untestable as written since Django rejects negative slices.

title: Misleading comment claims negative offsets are now supported
body: The added comment on Cursor.offset claims 'Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios', but nothing in Cursor changed (offset was always int(offset)); the only consumer that acts on negative offsets is the new paginator branch, where negative offsets actually cause a Django ValueError. The comment documents a capability that does not exist and will mislead future maintainers.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot sort by datetime; endpoint 500s
body: The audit log endpoint now routes requests with `optimized_pagination=true` to `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `order_by="-datetime"`, but `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` (src/sentry/api/paginator.py line 838) is copied from the numeric `Paginator` and calls `math.floor(value)` / `math.ceil(value)` on the key. For `AuditLogEntry.datetime` that value is a `datetime`, so `math.floor` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`. Any request that passes `optimized_pagination=true` (and satisfies the admin check) will fail with a 500 as soon as `build_cursor` computes cursor keys. The previous code path used `DateTimePaginator`, which converts datetimes to timestamps.

title: Negative-offset "advanced feature" crashes: Django does not support negative slicing
body: When `enable_advanced_features` is true and a caller supplies a cursor with a negative offset (possible now because `Cursor.from_string` happily parses a negative offset from the `value:offset:is_prev` string), the code does `queryset[cursor.offset:stop]` with a negative start. Django's ORM does not support negative indexing — `QuerySet.__getitem__` raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported`. The comment claiming "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false, so instead of crashing this will surface as a 500 for any user-supplied cursor with a negative offset. There is also no validation anywhere that a client-supplied cursor offset is non-negative, which is a security/robustness regression on a public API endpoint.

title: BasePaginator change silently drops negative offsets for forward cursors, but still passes them for prev cursors
body: The change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` alters `BasePaginator` behavior for all existing paginators: for forward cursors a negative offset is now silently clamped to 0, while for `is_prev` cursors a negative offset is still passed straight into the queryset slice, where Django raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported`. Since client-supplied cursor strings are parsed into arbitrary integer offsets (`Cursor.from_string` accepts negative values), a crafted or corrupted prev-cursor (`...: -5:1`) will now crash any endpoint using `BasePaginator`/`DateTimePaginator`/`Paginator`, not just the new optimized path. The offset should be validated/clamped in both branches.

title: Redirect resolution depth reduced from 10000 to 1000 without handling the truncated case
body: The redirect-following loop limit was lowered from 10000 to 1000. When the redirect chain exceeds 1000 hops, the loop simply ends with `set_span_id` pointing at an intermediate node rather than the true set root. The script then does `hset main_redirect_key span_id set_span_id` and merges the span into whatever set that intermediate id resolves to, so a very deep segment tree gets split into two segments that are never rejoined (the old comment explicitly documented this failure mode at depth 10k). There is no metric, error, or fallback when the limit is hit, making the split silent. If the reduction was intentional for latency, the depth-limit-exceeded case should at least be observable.

title: New hard 1000-span eviction silently drops spans, possibly including the root span
body: The script now evicts with `zpopmin` whenever a set exceeds 1000 members. ZPOPMIN removes the lowest-scored members (earliest `end_timestamp_precise`), which may include the segment's root span — evicting it does not clear the `span-buf:hrs:` flag, so the segment will still be treated as having a root but will flush without one, producing an incomplete segment. Additionally, evicted spans are dropped permanently with no metric, log, or outcome emitted, so data loss from oversized segments is invisible. The old behavior flushed oversized segments intact and only skipped them (with an error log and `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric) when reading — that check was removed in buffer.py without a replacement, so `max_segment_spans` is now a dead constructor parameter and the only guard against huge segments is this silent truncation.

title: Module docstring still describes the buffer as sets, not sorted sets
body: The module docstring (and the glossary at line 58, "span-buf:s:* -- the actual set keys, containing span payloads") still describes the segment store as Redis sets and describes step 3 as adding payloads to a "set". After this change the keys are sorted sets scored by `end_timestamp_precise`, and the redirect/merge logic in add-buffer.lua uses ZUNIONSTORE/ZPOPMIN. The stale documentation will mislead anyone reasoning about ordering, eviction, or the max-segment-size behavior.

title: Unrelated, undocumented audit-log endpoint behavior change in a spans-buffer PR
body: This PR (titled/described as a spans buffer optimization) adds a new query parameter `optimized_pagination` to the audit log endpoint that switches pagination behavior based on a client-controlled flag, gated only on `is_superuser` or `member.has_global_access`. Aside from being broken (see OptimizedCursorPaginator datetime issue), it changes a public API contract with no tests, no changelog, and no relationship to the PR's stated purpose. It should be split out or removed.

title: Negative-offset path in OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes on Django querysets
body: When `enable_advanced_features` is set and the cursor offset is negative, the code does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with a negative `start_offset`. Django's QuerySet explicitly disallows negative slicing (`Negative indexing is not supported` AssertionError), so instead of 'the ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' as the comment claims, any request that exercises this path returns a 500. Since cursor offsets are parsed from the client-supplied cursor string (`Cursor.from_string` accepts negative integers), a superuser on the audit log endpoint can trigger this with a crafted cursor. The feature is both broken and untested.

title: organization_context.member may be None, causing AttributeError
body: `organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated on every audit log request, but `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is optional (None when the request is authorized via an org auth token/integration rather than a user membership). In that case this raises AttributeError and the endpoint 500s for a class of previously working requests. The superuser check should short-circuit safely and the member access needs a None guard.

title: Redirect-follow loop limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000
body: The loop that follows span-id redirects was changed from 10000 to 1000 iterations. Segment trees deeper than 1000 redirects will now stop resolving early, so a span is attached to an intermediate set instead of the true root set, splitting one segment into multiple flushed segments (and leaving stale redirect entries). The previous code's comment explicitly warned about this failure mode at 10k; lowering the bound makes silent mis-grouping 10x more likely with no compensating metric or error when the limit is hit.

title: max_segment_spans guard removed while Lua cap is hardcoded and inconsistent
body: The `_load_segment_data` span-count safety check (`max_segment_spans`) was deleted and replaced by a hardcoded `if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua. Two problems: (1) the configurable `max_segment_spans=1001` constructor parameter is now dead code and no longer enforced anywhere; (2) eviction only happens inside the Lua script, so spans inserted via the initial `zadd` pipeline in `process_spans` (which runs before the script per batch) or races between consumers can still grow a set beyond the cap and will now be flushed unbounded, since the load-time check that previously dropped oversized segments is gone. Oversized segments can again produce multi-thousand-span Kafka messages.

title: zpopmin evicts earliest-ending spans, biasing segment contents
body: The eviction uses `zpopmin`, which removes the spans with the lowest score (earliest `end_timestamp_precise`). For a segment that exceeds 1000 spans this silently drops the oldest spans rather than the newest, which is the opposite of what one would typically want (keeping the root/earliest spans preserves segment structure), and dropped spans vanish with no metric or log, making the loss invisible in production.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot paginate by datetime but is wired to order_by="-datetime"
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `int(math.floor(value))` on the raw attribute value, and value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor value (a millisecond integer). The only caller, OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint, uses it with order_by="-datetime", so `value` is a datetime and math.floor() raises TypeError on the first page; even if that were fixed, build_queryset would compare the datetime column against a bare integer cursor value, producing wrong results or DB errors. DateTimePaginator exists precisely to handle this conversion. Any superuser/admin requesting the audit log with optimized_pagination=true will get a 500. The paginator should subclass/reuse DateTimePaginator's key conversion or the endpoint should not use it for datetime ordering.

title: Negative-offset branch slices queryset with a negative start, which Django does not support
body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is set and cursor.offset < 0 (which any caller can produce by supplying a cursor string like "<value>:-5:0", since Cursor.from_string accepts negative integers), the code executes `queryset[cursor.offset:stop]` with a negative start index. Django's QuerySet explicitly rejects negative slicing and raises AssertionError ("Negative indexing is not supported"), turning a client-supplied cursor into an unhandled 500. The comment claiming "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false. Negative offsets should be rejected with BadPaginationError like the other paginators do.

title: ZPOPMIN silently discards spans (possibly including the root span) once a segment exceeds 1000
body: The new eviction `redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)` drops the spans with the lowest end_timestamp_precise from the segment with no metric, log, or error. Previously, oversized segments were skipped at flush time with an error log and the `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` metric (code removed from _load_segment_data in buffer.py). Now spans are silently deleted from the segment, so downstream consumers receive truncated traces with no signal. Worse, because scores are end timestamps, the root span often finishes last... but a long-running root that ended early relative to children can be evicted while the span-buf:hrs flag stays set, so the segment is flushed on the fast root-timeout path with its root span missing and is_segment recomputed at flush time as false for every span. At minimum this needs a metric/log and a decision about protecting the root span.

title: Eviction threshold hardcoded to 1000, desynced from configurable max_segment_spans (default 1001)
body: The Lua script caps segment size at a hardcoded 1000, while SpansBuffer keeps the configurable `max_segment_spans` parameter (default 1001) which is now dead code after the removal of the span-count check in _load_segment_data. Operators who tuned max_segment_spans will silently get a different limit, and the two values disagree (Lua evicts down to 1000, the Python default says 1001), so a segment can be capped at 1000 spans even though configuration says 1001 are allowed. Either pass the limit into the script as an ARGV or remove the unused parameter.

title: Redirect-follow loop limit reduced from 10000 to 1000 without migration or justification
body: The redirect resolution loop was lowered from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000`. Existing segments in Redis can already have redirect chains deeper than 1000 (created while the 10k limit was in effect); for those traces, lookups now stop after 1000 hops, so new spans are written to a new span-buf:s: set keyed at the truncated chain end instead of merging with the real segment. That splits one trace into two separately flushed segments (duplicated/partial segments downstream). The removed comment explicitly acknowledged this tradeoff at 10k; the change needs either a migration/drain plan or a comment and metric for the hit-limit case.

title: organization_context.member may be None for non-superuser requests, causing AttributeError
body: The gate `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences `organization_context.member` whenever the user is not a superuser. RpcUserOrganizationContext.member is Optional (e.g., org auth tokens or certain access paths where no organization member object is attached to the context). In that case this raises AttributeError and returns a 500 instead of simply not enabling the optimized path. Use `organization_context.member and organization_context.member.has_global_access`.

title: No test covers the new zset eviction-at-1000 behavior or its interplay with flush
body: The PR changes segment storage from sets to sorted sets and adds eviction of spans beyond 1000 in add-buffer.lua, but the added test lines only thread end_timestamp_precise through existing tests. There is no test that (a) inserts more than 1000 spans into one segment and asserts which spans survive eviction, (b) verifies behavior when the evicted span is the root/is_segment span, or (c) checks that eviction interacts correctly with the queue timeout. Given the silent data loss this introduces, the eviction semantics should be pinned down by tests.

title: Accidental git submodule added at repo root
body: The PR adds a new git submodule `sentry-repo` pinned to the base commit a5d2909. This appears to be an accidental artifact of a local checkout (the PR description even says "Test 3"), and if merged it would add a nested copy of the repository as a submodule, breaking clean clones and confusing CI/tooling. It should be removed from the PR.

title: Substring match treats "!event.type:error" as an error-focused query
body: _is_error_focused_query does a naive substring check `if "event.type:error" in query`. A query like "!event.type:error" (exclude errors) or "(event.type:transaction) AND !event.type:error" also contains that substring, so it returns True. Combined with the allowlist check, count() in such queries will be silently transformed to sum(sample_weight) on the discover dataset even though the query matches non-error events, which either produces wrong counts or breaks because sample_weight doesn't exist for those rows. The query string should be parsed (or at minimum checked for negation) rather than substring-matched.

title: Cache key built with Python hash() is unstable and collision-prone
body: The cache key uses `hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))`. Python's hash() is randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so every web worker computes a different key for the same project set, making the 60-second cache largely ineffective across the fleet and causing cache entries to be orphaned. Worse, hash collisions between two different project sets would cause one set's eligibility decision to be applied to the other, flipping upsampling on/off incorrectly. Use a deterministic key such as a comma-joined sorted id list or a hash from hashlib.

title: Upsampling eligibility checked against outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset
body: Inside _get_event_stats, the eligibility check passes the closure variable `dataset` rather than the `scoped_dataset` argument that is actually queried. In the dashboard-widget discover-split path, scoped_dataset is `discover` (with an errors-only query) while the outer dataset may be metrics_performance/metrics_enhanced_performance, so the transform decision is made for the wrong dataset: the errors split query never gets upsampled, and conversely a transformation decision valid for the outer dataset could be applied to a different scoped dataset. Pass scoped_dataset to is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects.

title: Eligibility cache has no isolation; tests and allowlist changes observe stale results
body: The 60s cache keyed by (org, project set) is never invalidated when the `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` option changes (invalidate_upsampling_cache exists but nothing calls it), so flipping the allowlist takes up to 60s to take effect with no code path wiring the invalidation. Additionally, tests/snuba/api/endpoints/test_organization_events_stats.py runs multiple tests against the same org+project set with different mocked allowlists; the first test's cached True result can leak into later tests (e.g. the partial-allowlist test expecting count==1 would get the upsampled 10) if the cache is not cleared between tests, making the suite order-dependent. Tests should clear the cache in setUp, and the option-change path should call the invalidation hook.

title: Sample-rate helper swallows errors, drops valid rate 0, and runs for every stored event
body: _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling wraps dict .get() chains in bare try/except Exception (which cannot raise for the normal case but will silently mask real problems), and uses `if client_sample_rate:` so a legitimate client_sample_rate of 0 is ignored. More importantly, it is invoked unconditionally in Factories.store_event for every event stored in every test, mutating normalized_data['sample_rate'] globally — a hidden side effect that can change event processing behavior in unrelated tests that happen to include an error_sampling context. Consider gating it and using explicit None checks instead of truthiness and broad excepts.

title: Empty project list returns False, disabling upsampling for org-wide queries
body: _are_all_projects_error_upsampled returns False when project_ids is empty. Queries that target all projects in an organization (no explicit project filter) can legitimately have project_ids resolved before this call, but if snuba_params.project_ids is ever empty for an org-wide query the upsampling silently never applies with no indication why. Worth confirming the intended behavior for the all-projects case and documenting/testing it.

title: Cache key uses Python's hash(), which is randomized per process
body: The cache key is built with `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. Python's built-in `hash()` for tuples/strings is salted by PYTHONHASHSEED, so it produces different values in every process and every restart. Two workers handling the same organization/projects will compute different keys, so the 'performance optimization' cache is almost never hit across processes, and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (which recomputes the key the same way) will delete a different key than the one that was set if called in another process, making invalidation silently ineffective. Use a deterministic serialization of the sorted project IDs (e.g. join with commas or hashlib.md5).

title: Upsampling eligibility checks outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`
body: `_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` but the upsampling check calls `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` with the closure-captured outer `dataset`. In the dashboard-widget split path, `_get_event_stats` is invoked with `discover` (or the split dataset) while the outer dataset may be `metrics_performance`, and vice versa. The eligibility decision therefore reflects the wrong dataset: error-focused queries executed against `discover` for a split widget will not be upsampled (outer dataset is metrics), producing undercounted error counts in dashboard widgets, and a transactions-scoped query could incorrectly be upsampled if the outer dataset is `errors`.

title: Error detection reads request.GET instead of the actual query string, missing split/negated queries
body: `_is_error_focused_query` inspects `request.GET.get("query")` for the substring 'event.type:error'. This misses error-only queries that don't literally contain that substring — most notably the dashboard split path in organization_events_stats.py builds `errors_only_query = f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction"`, which is errors-only but never matches, so those error timeseries are not upsampled. It can also false-positive on a query like `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`. The decision should be based on the query actually being executed (and ideally on parsed search filters), not raw GET text.

title: setUp overwrites self.user after login_as, breaking the authenticated session
body: In `OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest.setUp`, `self.login_as(user=self.user)` is called first, then `self.user = self.create_user()` and `self.user2 = self.create_user()` reassign the attributes. The session is authenticated as the original user, but the events are tagged with the new (different) users, and any test behavior depending on `self.user` being the logged-in user is wrong. The new-user creation should happen before `login_as`, or the pre-existing `self.user` from the base TestCase should be reused.

title: Accidental git submodule checked in
body: The PR adds a `sentry-repo` gitlink (subproject commit a5d29095...) pointing at the repository's own base commit. This looks like an accidentally committed nested checkout/submodule; it will break clones for anyone without the submodule configured and bloat the repo. It should be removed from the PR.

title: upsampled_count truncates with toInt64 instead of rounding
body: The `upsampled_count` function wraps `sum(sample_weight)` in `toInt64`, which truncates toward zero. Sample weights derived from client sample rates are floats (e.g. 1/0.1 = 10.0 but 1/0.3 = 3.333...), so aggregated counts can be systematically under-reported whenever the summed weight lands just below an integer. Consider `toInt64(round(sum(sample_weight)))` so fractional accumulation rounds to the nearest count.

title: Cache key uses Python's unstable hash(), breaking caching and invalidation across processes
body: The cache key is built with `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. Python's built-in `hash()` for tuples/strings is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED randomization), so different gunicorn/uwsgi workers — and the same worker after a restart — produce different keys for the identical project set. Consequences: (1) the 60-second cache is almost never shared between workers, so the claimed performance optimization does not work; (2) worse, `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (line 67) computes the key the same way, so a process handling an allowlist change will delete a key that no other process ever reads, making invalidation silently useless. Additionally, `hash()` collisions across different project-id sets can cause one organization's cached eligibility to be applied to a different set of projects, which is a data-integrity risk (wrong counts served). Use a deterministic key, e.g. `':'.join(map(str, sorted(project_ids)))` or an md5/sha digest.

title: Substring match on 'event.type:error' mis-classifies negated or quoted queries as error-focused
body: `_is_error_focused_query` does `if "event.type:error" in query` on the raw lowercased query string. This returns True for queries like `!event.type:error` (explicitly excluding errors) or `message:"event.type:error"` (the string inside a quoted value). In those cases the discover query is not restricted to error events, yet `count()` will be rewritten to `sum(sample_weight)`, producing wrong (under)counts for transactions/other event types. The check should parse the query with the search grammar (or at minimum check that the token isn't negated/quoted) rather than doing a naive substring test.

title: Upsampling eligibility uses the outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`
body: Inside `_get_event_stats`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` closes over the endpoint-level `dataset`, but the query actually runs against `scoped_dataset`. In the dashboard-widget split path (`get_event_stats_factory`), `_get_event_stats` is invoked with `discover` and a synthesized query like `({query}) AND !event.type:transaction`, or with `scoped_dataset` for transaction-like widgets, while eligibility is still decided from the original request dataset. This means a widget originally on the errors dataset that is rerouted to a transaction/discover query can still get `count()` rewritten to `upsampled_count()` (wrong counts for non-error events), and conversely an errors-only discover subquery can fail the `_is_error_focused_query` check because the raw request query lacks `event.type:error`, so no upsampling is applied where it should be. The scoped dataset (and the effective query string) should be passed to the eligibility check.

title: upsampled_count registered as a public function without private=True
body: The new `SnQLFunction("upsampled_count", ...)` is added to the discover function converter without `private=True`, unlike the neighboring internal-only functions in the same mapping which are marked `private=True`. This exposes `upsampled_count()` as a user-queryable aggregate in the public Discover query API: any user can append it to a query and get `sum(sample_weight)` on arbitrary data where `sample_weight` is null or meaningless, returning misleading numbers. Since this function is only meant to be injected server-side by the error-upsampling path, it should be marked `private=True`.

title: Accidentally committed git submodule pointing at the base commit
body: The PR adds a `sentry-repo` gitlink (subproject commit a5d290951..., which is exactly the PR's base commit). This looks like a local clone of the repo that was accidentally `git add`ed. It will create a broken submodule entry (no `.gitmodules` URL) in the tree and should be removed from the PR.

title: fetch_error_details pairs error IDs with nodestore data by zip, assuming matching order
body: In fetch_error_details, `events = nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a dict, and the code does `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. There is no guarantee that `events.values()` yields entries in the same order as the input `error_ids`/`node_ids` (get_multi returns results keyed by node id, and any missing entries are absent entirely). When ordering differs or an entry is missing, an error ID gets paired with the wrong event's title/message, so the Seer summary will attribute the wrong error text to the wrong event, and timestamps used for chronological interleaving will be wrong. The lookup should be done by node id (e.g. zip(node_ids, error_ids) and use events.get(node_id)).

title: Error events are merged into every paginated segment page, duplicating error logs
body: The endpoint paginates recording segments with GenericOffsetPaginator and calls analyze_recording_segments(error_events, segments) per page. get_request_data interleaves the full error_events list into each page's logs (error_idx resets to 0 on every call), so a replay whose segments span multiple pages will have the same 'User experienced an error: ...' log lines repeated once per page in the payload sent to Seer. This inflates and distorts the summary. The error events should either be merged only once (e.g. only on the first page, or filtered to the timestamps covered by the current page's segments).

title: TableWidgetVisualization branch renders an empty table, discarding all real data
body: In tableResultComponent, when the 'use-table-widget-visualization' feature flag is on, the code renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />` — hardcoded empty columns and empty data. The actual query results (`result.data`, `result.meta`), loading state, error state, and field aliases are all ignored, so any dashboard table widget for organizations with this flag enabled will render a permanently empty table instead of its data. If this is WIP, the flag must not be enabled for anyone; otherwise the real table results need to be mapped into TabularData/TabularColumn.

title: Reports with neither timestamp nor age pass validation
body: The BrowserReportSerializer marks both `age` (Working Draft) and `timestamp` (Editor's Draft) as required=False, and the cross-field validators only reject the case where both are present. A report containing neither field is accepted and recorded, even though the Reporting API spec requires one of them and the docstring says 'Validate that age is absent, but timestamp is present' (and vice versa). Additionally, the cross-field checks use truthiness (`self.initial_data.get("age")`), so `age: 0` combined with a timestamp would slip through both validators.

title: Flex justify="right" is not a valid justify-content value
body: The delete-button wrapper was changed to `<Flex justify="right">`. `right` is not a valid CSS justify-content value (valid options include flex-end, center, space-between, etc.), so the justification silently does nothing and the Delete button will not be right-aligned as intended. Use `justify="flex-end"`.

title: TableWidgetVisualization wired up with hardcoded empty columns and empty tableData
body: In `tableResultComponent`, when the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature flag is enabled, the new `TableWidgetVisualization` is rendered with `columns={[]}` and a `tableData` object whose `data` is `[]` and whose `meta.fields`/`meta.units` are empty objects. The actual query results (`result.data`, `result.meta`, `fields`) are never passed in, so any organization with this flag enabled will see completely blank table widgets on dashboards instead of their data. This looks like scaffolding that was committed prematurely; the flag branch should either be removed from this PR or actually populated from the query result.

title: Chronological merge compares error event timestamps against segment event timestamps with a silent 0 default
body: In `gen_request_data`, the code interleaves error log messages with breadcrumb log messages by comparing `error_events[error_idx]['timestamp'] < event.get('timestamp', 0)`. Segment events that lack a `timestamp` key default to 0, which causes all remaining error messages to be flushed before those events regardless of when the errors actually occurred, silently corrupting the chronological ordering sent to Seer. Additionally, the two timestamp sources (nodestore event `timestamp` and recording-segment event `timestamp`) are assumed to be on the same clock/units; if they differ, the merged ordering will be wrong. At minimum, events without a timestamp should be handled explicitly instead of defaulting to 0.

title: Mutual-exclusion validation uses truthiness so age=0 or timestamp=0 bypasses the check
body: `validate_timestamp` checks `self.initial_data.get('age')` and `validate_age` checks `self.initial_data.get('timestamp')`. Both `age` and `timestamp` are integers where 0 is a legitimate value (age of 0 milliseconds, epoch timestamp 0). A report containing both `timestamp` and `age: 0` (or `timestamp: 0` and `age`) will pass validation even though the spec says they are mutually exclusive, because `0` is falsy. The check should test key presence (`'age' in self.initial_data`) rather than truthiness.

title: get_environment_info performs a recommended-event lookup per issue when building PR comments
body: `get_environment_info` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` for every issue in the merged-PR comment list (up to 5 issues per comment, run for each PR on each deployment). Each call hits the eventstore/nodestore, so generating one comment issues a sequence of per-issue queries inline in the PR comment task. If the recommended event lookup is expensive or times out, comment delivery is delayed (the broad `except Exception` also masks real failures by design, so problems will be invisible). Consider batching the event fetches or using a cheaper source of the environment.

title: TableWidgetVisualization branch discards all table data and renders an empty table
body: In `tableResultComponent`, when the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature flag is enabled, the code renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}}` — hardcoded empty columns and empty data. The actual query results (`result.data`, `result.meta`) and the computed `fields`/`fieldAliases` are ignored entirely. Any org with this flag enabled will see permanently empty table widgets on dashboards instead of their data. This looks like WIP scaffolding that should not merge as-is; at minimum it needs to map `result.data`/`result.meta` into `TabularData` and build columns from the widget queries.

title: Flex justify="right" is not a valid justify-content value
body: The refactor replaced a styled div using `justify-content: right` with `<Flex justify="right">`. `right` is not a valid value for the CSS `justify-content` property in most browsers (only `flex-end`, `center`, `space-between`, etc. are universally supported), so the Delete client button will no longer be right-aligned as intended. Use `justify="flex-end"` instead.

title: dcg_to_slow_conditions may be missing keys for DCGs present in dcg_to_groups
body: Previously `get_condition_query_groups` computed slow conditions for `list(event_data.dcg_to_groups.keys())`, the exact set of DCGs it iterates over. The refactor hoists the computation to the caller but builds it from `list(event_data.dcg_ids)`. If `event_data.dcg_to_groups` contains a DCG id that is not in `event_data.dcg_ids` (the two are populated from different buffer data), `dcg_to_slow_conditions[dcg.id]` in `get_condition_query_groups` (and `get_groups_to_fire`) raises KeyError, crashing delayed workflow processing. Either key the lookup off the same source the functions iterate, or use `.get(dcg.id, [])`.

title: user_id recorded before feature check and may be None for org auth tokens
body: `analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ..., user_id=request.user.id)` runs before the feature-flag 404 check, so every unauthorized call to this endpoint is recorded as an assemble event, inflating the metric. Also, when the request is authenticated via an org auth token, `request.user` is anonymous and `request.user.id` is None, so the analytics rows will have null user_id; if that distinction matters, the event should be recorded after the feature check with explicit handling for token auth.

title: KeyError when Integration metadata lacks 'sender'
body: In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the re-install path does `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`. The `sender` metadata is only populated in build_integration when the webhook-provided state contains `sender` (see `if state.get("sender")` in build_integration). Integrations created before this change, or where the installation webhook never arrived/was processed, will have no `sender` key in metadata, so any re-install/repair attempt for such an integration raises an uncaught KeyError and returns a 500 instead of the friendly error page. The lookup should use `.get("sender", {})` style access and treat a missing sender as a failed verification (or fall back gracefully).

title: Token exchange HTTP errors are not handled
body: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, `safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` is called outside the try/except that wraps safe_urlread. If GitHub's token endpoint is unreachable or returns an error status, safe_urlopen raises and the user gets a 500 rather than the intended 'Invalid installation request' error page. Similarly, `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` performs an API call that can raise ApiError (e.g. GitHub outage), which is also uncaught. Both calls should be guarded so the pipeline fails with the rendered error response instead of an exception.

title: Sender check is bypassed on fresh installs
body: The authenticated-user-vs-installer verification only runs in the branch where an Integration row already exists without an OrganizationIntegration. In the fresh-install path (`except Integration.DoesNotExist: return pipeline.next_step()`), the github_authenticated_user captured during OAuth is never compared to the account that installed the app. A user who is logged into Sentry but authenticated to GitHub as a different account can complete an installation of a GitHub App installed by someone else (e.g. an org app installed by another org member is fine, but any GitHub user who can see the installation_id can attach an app installation they don't own to their Sentry org). If the intent stated in the PR description ('fail if there is a mismatch between currently authenticated GitHub user and the user who installed the GitHub app') is to be enforced, the comparison must also be made on the fresh-install path, e.g. by comparing against the installation's account/sender from get_installation_info.

title: KeyError when Integration metadata lacks 'sender'
body: In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the re-install path does `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`. `sender` is only stored in metadata when it is present in pipeline state (`build_integration` only adds it `if state.get("sender")`), and Integrations created before sender tracking existed (or where the installation webhook was missed) will not have a `sender` key in metadata at all. For any such pre-existing Integration that has no OrganizationIntegration (the exact path this new check runs on: 'OrganizationIntegration does not exist, but Integration does exist'), this raises KeyError and the user gets a 500 instead of the failure dialog. Use a guarded lookup (e.g. `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")`) and treat a missing sender as a verification failure rather than crashing.

title: No test for the state-signature mismatch path
body: The PR description states the pipeline now fails 'If there is a mismatch between state parameter supplied by user and pipeline signature', which is a core security property of this change (CSRF protection on the OAuth callback). The added tests cover the user-mismatch and installation-not-found cases, but no test exercises `OAuthLoginView.dispatch` with a wrong/absent-but-present `state` value to assert the failure page is rendered and the flow aborts. A regression removing or weakening the signature check would not be caught by the test suite.

title: KeyError on integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] for integrations created without sender info
body: In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, when an Integration row already exists for the installation_id but has no OrganizationIntegration, the code checks `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`. The `sender` key is only written into metadata in build_integration when `state.get("sender")` is present, and many existing (legacy) GitHub Integration rows were created before sender was ever recorded. For such an orphaned integration, `integration.metadata["sender"]` raises KeyError, producing a 500 instead of the intended failure page. This path is reachable by any user who starts the install flow for an installation_id matching an existing orphaned integration. Use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and fail closed when it is absent.

title: OAuth state compared with non-constant-time == and state is the static pipeline signature
body: The OAuth `state` check in OAuthLoginView.dispatch uses `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature`, a plain string comparison rather than a constant-time compare (e.g. hmac.compare_digest), and the state value is simply the pipeline signature, which is reused as the Redis session key identifier and is not a single-use nonce. This weakens the CSRF protection the OAuth state parameter is meant to provide (timing side channel and replayability of the same state value across retries of the same pipeline). Consider generating a random one-time nonce, storing it in pipeline state, and comparing with hmac.compare_digest.

title: Default `queued` datetime is evaluated once at import and breaks JSON task serialization
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated a single time when the class is defined, so every AssignmentSource instance shares the import-time timestamp. More importantly, `to_dict()` uses `asdict()`, so the dict always contains a `datetime` object, and `sync_group_assignee_outbound` passes that dict as the `assignment_source_dict` kwarg to `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async`. Sentry's Celery tasks are serialized with JSON, which cannot encode datetime objects, so every inbound-triggered assignment will fail with an encode error when the outbound task is enqueued (or the timestamp arrives as a string and `from_dict` accepts it without parsing). Either remove the field (it is never read anywhere) or use `field(default_factory=...)` plus explicit ISO serialization/parsing in `to_dict`/`from_dict`.

title: Tests never round-trip AssignmentSource through JSON, masking the datetime serialization bug
body: `test_to_dict` only asserts that `queued` is not None on the raw dict; it never JSON-serializes the dict or verifies `from_dict(to_dict())` works, which is exactly the path taken through Celery (`apply_async` kwargs -> task -> `AssignmentSource.from_dict`). As written, the tests pass while the production path fails on the unserializable datetime, so the core new behavior of this PR is effectively untested.

title: Failed AssignmentSource parsing silently drops cycle protection
body: If `assignment_source_dict` fails to parse (e.g. the `queued` datetime arrives as a string in a slightly different shape, or the payload is malformed), `AssignmentSource.from_dict` returns None and the task proceeds to sync the assignee back to the originating integration — re-creating exactly the sync loop this PR is meant to break. There is no logging of the parse failure, so this regression would be invisible. Consider logging when parsing fails on a non-None dict, or failing closed.

title: Default value timezone.now() is evaluated once at import time
body: The dataclass field `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` calls `timezone.now()` a single time when the class is defined at module import, so every AssignmentSource constructed without an explicit `queued` value gets the same stale timestamp (the process import time) rather than the time the source was created. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` to get a per-instance timestamp.

title: datetime in AssignmentSource.to_dict() will fail Celery JSON serialization
body: sync_group_assignee_outbound passes `assignment_source.to_dict()` (which includes the `queued` datetime) as the `assignment_source_dict` kwarg to `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async`. Sentry's Celery tasks are serialized with JSON, and a raw datetime is not JSON-serializable, so enqueueing the task will raise a serialization error (or kombu EncodeError) whenever an assignment originated from an inbound integration webhook — the exact path this PR adds. The datetime should be serialized to an ISO string (and parsed back in from_dict) or the field omitted from the task payload.

title: should_sync is now always called with a second positional argument; existing overrides with the old signature will raise TypeError
body: The task now calls `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)`. Only the base classes in this PR were updated to accept the new parameter; any concrete integration installation that overrides `should_sync(self, attribute)` (a common pattern for Jira/VSTS/Azure DevOps-style integrations) will raise `TypeError: should_sync() takes 2 positional arguments but 3 were given`, and since the task retries on unexpected exceptions, this will burn retries on every assignee sync for those providers. Callers should pass the source as a keyword and overrides need to be audited/updated, or the call should be made defensively.

title: New assignment_source kwarg passed to sync_assignee_outbound implementations that don't accept it
body: The task now calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(external_issue, user, assign=assign, assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)` unconditionally. The abstract method signature in `IssueSyncIntegration.sync_assignee_outbound` was not updated (it still only declares `external_issue, user, assign=True, **kwargs` — and concrete implementations such as Jira and VSTS define `sync_assignee_outbound(self, external_issue, user, assign=True)` without `**kwargs`). For any integration whose override does not accept extra keyword arguments, every outbound assignee sync will now raise `TypeError: sync_assignee_outbound() got an unexpected keyword argument 'assignment_source'`, which will retry 5 times and permanently break assignee sync for that provider. All concrete overrides need to be updated to accept (or swallow) the new kwarg before this ships.

title: Dataclass field default `queued=timezone.now()` is evaluated once at import time
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` calls `timezone.now()` when the class body is executed, so every `AssignmentSource` instance created without an explicit `queued` value shares the same timestamp frozen at module import. The intended 'when this was queued' semantics are broken (the value can be hours or days stale in a long-running worker). Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead. The round-trip test does not catch this because it only asserts the key exists, not that it is fresh.

title: queued datetime may not survive Celery serialization of assignment_source_dict
body: `AssignmentSource.to_dict()` uses `asdict`, which leaves `queued` as a `datetime` object, and this dict is passed directly as a Celery task kwarg (`assignment_source_dict`) in `sync_group_assignee_outbound`. If the task serializer is JSON (the integrations queue commonly runs with JSON-serializable kwargs), enqueuing will fail with a non-serializable datetime, meaning no outbound assignee sync happens at all whenever an `assignment_source` is present. Either serialize `queued` to an ISO string in `to_dict` (and parse it in `from_dict`), or drop the field since nothing reads it.

title: Sync-cycle guard only applies when parsed source survives; from_dict silently returns None on malformed payloads
body: `AssignmentSource.from_dict` swallows `TypeError`/`ValueError` and returns `None`, and the task then calls `should_sync('outbound_assignee', None)`, which skips the same-integration check entirely. Any malformed or version-skewed payload in the queue (e.g. an older worker enqueued a dict without matching fields, or `queued` arrives as a string that later validation rejects) silently disables the cycle protection this PR adds, reintroducing the Jira assignment loop. At minimum a malformed payload should be logged; ideally an unparseable source should be treated conservatively rather than as 'no source'.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now has unimplemented abstract methods and will crash on instantiation
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler was changed from a DetectorHandler subclass with a stub `evaluate` to a bare `StatefulDetectorHandler` subclass with no method implementations. StatefulDetectorHandler declares four abstract members (`counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the newly added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`), so calling `MetricAlertDetectorHandler(detector)` — which is exactly what `Detector.detector_handler` does for any detector of type `metric_alert_fire` — will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class ... with abstract methods ...`. Previously this handler could be instantiated and evaluated (returning an empty list). Either implement the abstract methods with stubs/TODOs or keep the class abstract in a way that prevents it being registered as `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler`.

title: StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: The docstring for `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` reads 'Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`', but the method now returns a `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`. The stale documentation contradicts the signature change made in this PR and will mislead implementers of subclasses.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses abstract StatefulDetectorHandler without implementing its abstract methods
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler was changed from DetectorHandler (where it implemented evaluate) to StatefulDetectorHandler with just `pass`. StatefulDetectorHandler declares abstract members counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and build_occurrence_and_event_data, none of which are implemented here. Because it inherits from abc.ABC, any attempt to instantiate it (e.g., via Detector.detector_handler for a detector of type metric_alert_fire) will raise TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class. Previously it was instantiable and returned an empty result list. Either implement the abstract methods (even as stubs) or keep the class on the non-abstract base until the stateful abstraction is built.

title: StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: The docstring on StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate reads 'Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`.' but the method now returns dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]. This contradicts the signature change made in this PR and will mislead implementers of new detector handlers.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and will crash when instantiated
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler was changed from a concrete DetectorHandler subclass (with an implemented evaluate returning []) to a bare subclass of StatefulDetectorHandler. StatefulDetectorHandler declares four abstract members (counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, build_occurrence_and_event_data), none of which MetricAlertDetectorHandler implements. Detector.detector_handler (src/sentry/workflow_engine/models/detector.py line 86) calls group_type.detector_handler(self), so any attempt to process a Detector of type MetricAlertFire will now raise TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract methods ..., whereas before this PR it worked. Either implement the abstract methods or keep the class off StatefulDetectorHandler until it is ready.

title: evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: The docstring of StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate reads 'Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult', but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. This is misleading for anyone implementing or consuming the new signature introduced by this PR.

title: No validation that dict keys match each result's group_key
body: With the return type changed from a list to a dict keyed by group key, process_detectors now blindly trusts handler-provided dict keys (detector_results.values()) and dropped the old duplicate/mismatch logging entirely. A custom DetectorHandler.evaluate that returns {key_a: result_with_group_key_b} would produce occurrences whose group_key doesn't match the key under which downstream consumers (results.append((detector, detector_results))) expect to find them, silently corrupting group-keyed lookups. A cheap consistency check (or building the dict from result.group_key server-side, as StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate does) would prevent this.

title: mark_failed_threshold and helpers removed/renamed, breaking any existing importers
body: This PR deletes `mark_failed_threshold`, `create_issue_platform_occurrence`, `get_failure_reason`, `get_monitor_environment_context`, and the `SimpleCheckIn` TypedDict from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed`, moving/renaming them to new modules (`mark_failed_threshold` becomes `try_incident_threshold` in `incidents.py`, `create_issue_platform_occurrence` becomes `create_incident_occurrence` in `incident_occurrence.py`). No backwards-compatible aliases are left behind. Any module, task, or test outside this diff that imports these names from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` (e.g., timeout/missed check-in tasks or existing tests calling `mark_failed_threshold` directly) will fail with ImportError after merge. The diff shows no corresponding updates to call sites or tests, so this should be verified and all importers updated (or re-export shims added) before merging.

title: get_monitor_environment_context builds display-config but returns the raw config
body: `get_monitor_environment_context` copies `monitor_environment.monitor.config` into `config` and replaces `schedule_type` with its human-readable display value, but then returns `"config": monitor_environment.monitor.config` — the original raw config — instead of the modified copy. The display conversion is therefore dead code and the `schedule_type` in the emitted monitor context is the raw integer rather than the display string. This appears to be a pre-existing bug carried over verbatim in the move, but the refactor is a good point to fix it by returning `"config": config`.

title: Renamed/moved functions break existing importers of mark_failed helpers
body: This PR deletes `mark_failed_threshold`, `create_issue_platform_occurrence`, `get_failure_reason`, and `get_monitor_environment_context` from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` and moves/renames them (e.g. `mark_failed_threshold` is now `try_incident_threshold` in `sentry.monitors.logic.incidents`, `create_issue_platform_occurrence` is now `create_incident_occurrence` in `incident_occurrence`). Any existing code or tests that import these symbols from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` will fail with ImportError at import/collection time. Since the PR only updates the internals of `mark_failed.py` and does not add compatibility aliases or update callers, the author should verify no other modules or test files import the old names (e.g. `from sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed import mark_failed_threshold`) and update them, or keep thin re-export shims.

title: time.sleep(0.1) in test_basic is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched away
body: test_basic starts with `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, which patches the `sleep` attribute on the `time` module globally. The newly added lines `step.poll(); time.sleep(0.1)` (with the comment "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change") therefore call the no-op lambda — the test does not actually wait for the flusher thread to observe the drift change and flush. Whether the flush happens before `step.join()` depends on thread scheduling, making this test flaky: on a slow or loaded CI runner the flusher thread may not have produced the message yet, and `(msg,) = messages` will fail intermittently. Use a real wait (e.g., a threading.Event, polling loop with a deadline, or `time.sleep` from an unpatched reference saved before monkeypatching) instead.

title: max_processes=0 silently becomes one process per shard
body: `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats any falsy value as 'unset'. The new `--flusher-processes` CLI option accepts any integer, so passing `--flusher-processes 0` (or a negative number, which is also not validated) results in spawning one flusher process per shard instead of being rejected — the opposite of what an operator might intend when trying to disable extra flusher processes. Consider validating the click option (`type=click.IntRange(min=1)`) or checking `max_processes is None` explicitly instead of using truthiness.

title: isinstance check against multiprocessing.Process is always False for spawn processes, so hung/dead flusher processes are never killed
body: The flusher explicitly creates processes with multiprocessing.get_context("spawn"), so the objects are SpawnProcess instances. However, `multiprocessing.Process` resolves to the *default* context's class (ForkProcess on Linux), and SpawnProcess does not subclass it. Therefore `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` in `_ensure_processes_alive` (line 254) and in `join` (line 346) evaluates to False for every flusher process, and `process.kill()` / `process.terminate()` are silently never executed. Consequences: when a flusher process hangs, `_ensure_processes_alive` spawns a replacement without killing the hung one, leaving two processes flushing the same shards and producing duplicate segments to the buffered-segments topic; and on shutdown, processes are never terminated and linger as (daemon) zombies until interpreter exit. The old single-process code had the same latent isinstance bug in `join`, but the new restart path makes it load-bearing. Check against `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` (or just call kill/terminate unconditionally, or track which entries are threads vs processes).

title: join() breaks out of the process-wait loop on deadline, skipping terminate() for all remaining processes
body: In `join`, if the deadline is exhausted while waiting for one process, the `break` exits the for-loop over `self.processes` entirely, so none of the remaining processes get `process.terminate()` called (the terminate happens per-iteration after the wait). Previously there was only one process so this couldn't happen. With multiple flusher processes, a slow-to-stop process causes all later processes to be left running after join returns. The terminate should be applied to every remaining process even after the deadline, or the loop should continue with zero remaining time so terminate still runs.

title: Restart limit check allows MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS + 1 restarts per process
body: `if self.process_restarts[process_index] > MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` is checked before incrementing, so the RuntimeError only fires on the 12th unhealthy detection (restarts 0..10 are permitted, i.e. 11 restarts) even though the constant is named MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS = 10. This was inherited from the previous single-process code but is now duplicated per process; with N processes the consumer tolerates 11*N restarts before crashing. Use `>=` to match the constant's intent.

title: Default --flusher-processes=1 contradicts the stated goal of one flusher process per shard
body: The new CLI option defaults to 1, meaning a default deployment of process-spans gets a single flusher process shared across all shards via `flusher_processes` being passed to SpanFlusher. But the PR description says the intent is to "spawn a process per redis shard", and SpanFlusher's own default when max_processes is None is `len(buffer.assigned_shards)` (one process per shard). Because the click default (1) is always passed, the SpanFlusher default is effectively unreachable from the CLI. If per-shard processes are the intended default, the click default should be None (or omitted) so SpanFlusher falls back to one process per shard.

title: time.sleep(0.1) in test_basic is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
body: The test begins with `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` and later calls `time.sleep(0.1)` with the comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change'. Because the monkeypatch replaces `time.sleep` globally, this call returns immediately and provides no settling time. The test then relies on `step.join()` racing the flusher thread to observe the produced message, making the test timing-dependent and flaky — exactly the flakiness the added sleep was presumably meant to fix. Use a real sleep (e.g., import sleep from time before patching, or patch `sentry.spans.consumers.process.flusher.time.sleep` only) or poll until the message appears.

title: join() breaks out of the process loop on deadline expiry, leaving remaining flusher processes unterminated
body: In `join()`, if the deadline expires while waiting for an earlier process, the `break` exits the loop entirely, so all subsequent processes in `self.processes` never get `process.terminate()` called on them. With the new multi-process flusher this can leave several spawned flusher processes running past the join timeout (they are daemon processes, so they die only with the parent, but they continue flushing and producing to Kafka until then). Each process should be terminated even when the deadline has passed, rather than skipping termination for the rest.

title: max_processes=0 is silently treated as 'one process per shard'
body: `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` uses truthiness, so passing `--flusher-processes 0` (or any falsy value) does not mean zero/invalid but instead falls back to spawning one process per shard — the most expensive configuration. The CLI option added in consumers/__init__.py places no lower bound on the value, so a misconfigured deployment would silently scale the flusher to the maximum number of processes. Either validate the option (reject values < 1) or use an explicit `is None` check.

title: Queues are unbounded, so the claimed 'natural backpressure' does not exist and the consumer can OOM
body: FixedQueuePool creates plain `queue.Queue()` instances with no maxsize, and `submit()` calls `work_queue.put(work_item)` which never blocks. If processing is slower than consumption (the exact scenario this PR is designed to address — one slow item per queue), the queues grow without bound in memory, since the arroyo consumer keeps polling and submitting messages. The docstring on SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', which is false. The consumer will buffer the entire topic backlog in-process and can be OOM-killed. The queues should be bounded (maxsize) so that `put` blocks the submit thread and actually applies backpressure.

title: FixedQueuePool is shut down permanently on strategy close, breaking the consumer after any partition rebalance
body: ResultsStrategyFactory creates the FixedQueuePool once in `__init__` (result_consumer.py line 133), and every call to `create_with_partitions` builds a new SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy wrapping that same pool. When partitions are revoked (rebalance), arroyo calls `close()` on the old strategy, which calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` — and `queue.Queue.shutdown()` is irreversible, plus `worker.shutdown = True` permanently stops the worker threads. On the next `create_with_partitions` after reassignment, the new strategy submits to shut-down queues whose workers have exited: messages will be accepted by `submit` (or raise `queue.ShutDown` from `put`) but never processed, stalling the consumer indefinitely with no errors. The pool must be created per-partition-assignment (in `create_with_partitions`) or restartable.

title: close() stops the commit thread before workers finish draining, so processed offsets are never committed
body: In SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close(), the shutdown event is set and the commit thread is joined first, and only then is the queue pool shut down to drain. Any offsets completed by workers after the commit thread exits are never committed, and there is no final commit pass after the pool drains. On every shutdown/rebalance this silently reprocesses up to the last second-plus of already-handled messages; more importantly the pool's `worker.shutdown = True` flags mean items still sitting in the queues are dropped from memory entirely without their offsets ever being completed or committed. A graceful close should drain the queues, then run one final commit of get_committable_offsets() before joining the commit thread.

title: OffsetTracker retains offsets for revoked partitions forever and the commit loop may commit offsets for partitions the consumer no longer owns
body: OffsetTracker never removes entries for partitions that are revoked during a rebalance — `all_offsets`/`outstanding`/`last_committed` grow monotonically, and `_commit_loop` keeps calling `commit_function` (which is arroyo's commit callback for the current assignment) with committable offsets for partitions the consumer may no longer own. Committing offsets for unassigned partitions is rejected by Kafka (or worse, commits a stale generation's offsets) and any remaining outstanding offset in a revoked partition will cause that partition to never advance in `get_committable_offsets`, keeping the tracker data alive forever. create_with_partitions/revocation should reset or prune per-partition tracking state.

title: Factory shutdown() sets queue_pool to None while strategies still reference it, and double-shutdown of a queue.Queue raises
body: ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` and sets `self.queue_pool = None`, but any live SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy created by `create_with_partitions` still holds a reference to the pool and its `close()` will call `queue_pool.shutdown()` again. The second call invokes `queue.Queue.shutdown()` on an already-shut-down queue, which raises `queue.ShutDown`; the bare `except Exception` around `q.shutdown` in FixedQueuePool.swallows it, but the strategy's close ordering then becomes unpredictable. The factory and strategy both own pool lifecycle with no coordination — one of them should be responsible for shutdown.

title: submit() swallows all exceptions including grouping/serialization bugs and silently marks the offset complete, dropping messages
body: In SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit(), any exception from the decoder, `grouping_fn`, or `queue_pool.submit` is caught by the broad `except Exception` and the offset is added-then-completed, which makes it eligible to be committed. Unlike a decode failure (which legitimately returns None), a bug in `build_payload_grouping_key` or an internal error in pool submission now silently discards the message and commits past it with only a log line. For a Kafka consumer this converts transient/programming errors into permanent message loss rather than crashing or DLQ'ing. At minimum, non-decode failures should not mark the offset committable.

title: test_stats_reporting asserts queue is non-empty immediately after submit, which is inherently flaky
body: test_stats_reporting submits 10 items and immediately asserts `stats['total_items'] > 0`. Since the pool's worker threads start consuming as soon as items are enqueued, on a fast machine all 10 items can be processed before `get_stats()` runs, making this assertion fail nondeterministically. The same race applies to several uptime tests that poll `stats['total_items'] == 0 and call_count == N` — if a worker drains the queue before the mock records the call... actually those poll until a condition, so they are fine, but the immediate `> 0` assertion has no synchronization and will flake under load or with eager workers.

title: Worker queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure and memory can grow without limit
body: FixedQueuePool creates plain queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize. The class docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but an unbounded queue never blocks the consumer's submit path, so the Kafka consumer thread will keep polling and enqueueing WorkItems (each holding the full decoded result and original message) as fast as it can read them. If one group/queue is slow (the exact problem this PR is meant to mitigate), items pile up in memory instead of applying backpressure via the consumer, risking OOM of the consumer pod and defeating offset-based flow control. The queues should have a bounded maxsize so submit() blocks and arroyo stops polling.

title: Worker commits offsets for messages whose processing raised an exception
body: In OrderedQueueWorker.run, the broad `except Exception` only logs, and the `finally` block unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset(). That means a work item whose result_processor raised is marked complete and its offset becomes committable, so the message is silently dropped rather than redelivered or sent to a DLQ. This contradicts the strategy docstring 'Only commits offsets after successful processing'. Today ResultProcessor.__call__ swallows its own exceptions so this path is rarely hit, but any exception thrown outside that wrapper (e.g. in sentry_sdk transaction handling or a future processor) causes permanent message loss with only a log line. Failed items should either not complete the offset (forcing redelivery) or be routed to the DLQ.

title: No handling of partition revocation; stale offsets keep being committed after rebalance
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy starts a background commit thread that commits whatever OffsetTracker considers committable, but nothing in the strategy or in ResultsStrategyFactory resets state when partitions are revoked during a rebalance. After a rebalance the OffsetTracker still holds entries for partitions this consumer no longer owns, and the commit thread will happily commit those offsets to the consumer group, potentially clobbering progress made by the new owner of the partition. Additionally, if the factory's create_with_partitions is called again for a new assignment, a second commit thread is spawned while the old pool/tracker state lingers. Partition revocation should clear tracker state for revoked partitions and stop committing them.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling is flaky and its assertion contradicts the implementation
body: The test mocks the result processor to raise on the first call, then asserts no offsets were committed. But OrderedQueueWorker completes offsets in a finally block even when processing raises, so offset 100 becomes committable immediately and the 1-second commit loop will commit offset 101/102 for the partition. The test only passes because it breaks out of the wait loop after ~0.2s, racing the commit thread's 1.0s interval — under load or on a slow CI runner the commit can land before the assertion, making the test fail nondeterministically. Either the implementation should not commit failed offsets, or the test should assert the actual (committed-past-failure) behavior deterministically.

title: FixedQueuePool is created once on the factory and shared across partition assignments, breaking rebalances
body: In `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__`, the `FixedQueuePool` (with its worker threads) is created once when the factory is instantiated, and `create_with_partitions` hands that same pool to every new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`. Arroyo calls `create_with_partitions` on every assignment/rebalance and `close()`/`join()` on the old strategy when partitions are revoked. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets `shutdown=True` on every worker and shuts down every queue. After the first revoke, the shared pool is permanently dead: the next `create_with_partitions` will build a strategy around queues that raise `queue.ShutDown` on `put` and workers that have exited, so all messages either fail in submit (and get their offsets silently completed, dropping them) or are never processed. Additionally, each rebalance spawns a new commit thread while the pool is shared. The pool should be created per `create_with_partitions` call (or recreated after shutdown).

title: Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure despite the documented guarantee
body: `FixedQueuePool` creates `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, so `work_queue.put(work_item)` in `submit` never blocks.
