The class docstring for `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but messages will be read from Kafka and buffered in memory without limit; `poll()` only emits a gauge and never signals the processor to pause. If processing is slower than ingestion (exactly the slow-item scenario this PR targets), the consumer's memory grows unboundedly until OOM, and Kafka's max.poll.interval can be exceeded since submits always succeed instantly. Give the queues a bounded maxsize so `put` blocks and applies real backpressure.

title: Offsets are marked complete even when processing fails, committing failed messages with no DLQ
body: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, the `finally` block calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` regardless of whether `result_processor` raised. That means a message whose processing throws is treated as successfully processed and its offset becomes committable, so the failure is permanently skipped (the uptime consumer has no DLQ configured). This directly contradicts the strategy's documented guarantee 'Only commits offsets after successful processing'. The same happens in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`'s exception handler, which adds and immediately completes the offset on any decode/submit error. Failed items should either be retried, routed to a DLQ, or at minimum not marked complete.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling is flaky and contradicts the implementation
body: The test asserts that after one message fails processing, `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`. But the implementation completes the offset in a `finally` block even on failure, so both offsets 100 and 101 become committable and the background commit loop (1s interval) will commit offset 102. Whether the assertion passes depends purely on whether the commit thread fires within the ~2.2s polling window, making the test racy; and when it does pass, it is only because the commit thread hasn't run yet, not because failures actually prevent commits. The test should either assert the actual behavior (failed offsets are committed) or the implementation should be fixed and the test made deterministic by controlling the commit loop.

title: OffsetTracker state for revoked partitions is never cleaned up
body: `OffsetTracker` keeps `all_offsets`, `outstanding`, `last_committed`, and `partition_locks` entries for every partition forever, and the pool/tracker live as long as the factory (across rebalances). After a partition is revoked, its entries remain; worse, if the same partition is later re-assigned with the consumer continuing from a different offset, the stale `last_committed` for that partition is reused by `get_committable_offsets`, which can cause the new strategy's commit function to skip committing legitimately processed offsets (start = last_committed + 1 may be ahead of the new assignment's offsets, and `highest_committable` initialized to the old `last_committed` is never returned if lower, but a stale higher value would incorrectly suppress commits). There is no hook on partition revocation to reset per-partition state.

title: Backup code login rejected for SAML/Google (non-CAL) users
body: In the credentials authorize() flow, the guard `if (user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode) throw new Error(ErrorCode.ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled)` (and the similar check on line 117) runs before the new backup-code branch. When a SAML or Google user with 2FA enabled goes through the `/auth/login?totp=...` flow and submits a backup code, `credentials.totpCode` is empty (the UI explicitly clears it when switching to 'Lost access'), so authorize() throws ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled before ever reaching the backup-code verification. Backup codes therefore can never be used by non-CAL identity provider users — exactly the users most likely to need account recovery. The condition should also pass when `credentials.backupCode` is present.

title: Backup code single-use guarantee is racy (read-modify-write)
body: Backup code consumption decrypts the stored codes, checks indexOf, then nulls the entry and re-encrypts in a separate `prisma.user.update`. Two concurrent login requests presenting the same backup code will both read the pre-consumption state, both find the code, and both succeed before either writes back. Backup codes are documented to the user as 'can be used exactly once', but this check-then-act sequence allows parallel reuse. The consumption should be made atomic (e.g., conditional update/transaction) or the finding at least acknowledged.

title: Closing the modal via X/outside click after enabling 2FA skips onEnable
body: After a successful TOTP verification the flow now moves to DisplayBackupCodes, and `onEnable()` is only invoked from the explicit 'Close' button handler on that step. If the user instead dismisses the dialog via the dialog's close affordance or outside interaction (`onOpenChange`), `onEnable()` never runs and `resetState()` is never called. The parent settings page relies on onEnable to refresh the two-factor switch state, so the UI will show 2FA as disabled even though it was just enabled server-side (until a manual refresh). The backup-codes step should treat any dialog close as completion, or the parent should refresh on open change.

title: Password visibility toggle removed from keyboard tab order
body: The show/hide password button in PasswordField now has `tabIndex={-1}`, making it unreachable via keyboard navigation in every form that uses PasswordField (login, password change, 2FA setup, etc.). Keyboard and screen-reader users can no longer reveal their password to check for typos. If the intent was to fix tab order on a specific form, that should be solved locally rather than removing the control from the tab order globally.

title: No test covers the actual backup-code login flow
body: The PR's core feature — logging in with a backup code via 'Lost access' — has no test coverage; the file only adds a TODO comment acknowledging this. The existing tests were adjusted for the new backup-codes display step, but nothing exercises a successful backup-code login, a wrong backup code, code consumption (single use), or the third-party identity provider case where backup codes are currently broken. A login-with-backup-code e2e test would have caught the non-CAL identity provider rejection in next-auth-options.

title: Backup code plus any dummy TOTP code bypasses password verification at login
body: In the credentials authorize callback, the password check is gated on `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)` (line 121): whenever a totpCode value is present, the password is never verified. The new backup-code branch `if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode)` is evaluated before the TOTP branch, so an attacker can POST to the credentials callback with `email`, `backupCode=<valid code>`, and `totpCode=000000` (any non-empty value) and log in without knowing the account password. The web UI never sends both fields, but nothing server-side prevents it, so a backup code — intended as a second factor after the password — becomes a single-factor credential that fully bypasses the password. The fix should verify the password (when the user has one) regardless of whether totpCode or backupCode is supplied, or reject requests that contain both a backupCode and a totpCode.

title: Backup codes unusable for GOOGLE/SAML users who have 2FA enabled
body: The guard `if (user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode) throw new Error(ErrorCode.ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled)` runs before the backup-code branch. Users whose identity provider is GOOGLE or SAML but who have twoFactorEnabled — which the signIn callback itself can create by converting a CAL account with 2FA to Google/SAML (lines 693–706) — log in via the loginWithTotp flow, where the password field is empty. If such a user clicks 'Lost access' and submits a backup code, totpCode is empty, so they get ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled ('account_created_with_identity_provider') instead of the backup code being checked. These users can never use their backup codes and are locked out if they lose their authenticator. The identity-provider guards need to treat a supplied backupCode the same way as a totpCode.

title: Parent 2FA switch state stays stale if the backup-codes dialog is dismissed without clicking Close
body: Previously `onEnable()` was called immediately when the enable request succeeded; this PR replaces that with `setStep(SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes)` and only calls `onEnable()` from the 'Close' button on the backup-codes screen. If the user dismisses the dialog any other way after enabling (the dialog's X, clicking the overlay, or pressing Escape — all of which trigger onOpenChange), onEnable is never invoked, so the two-factor switch in settings remains visually unchecked even though 2FA is now enabled server-side, until a page reload. The dialog-close path should also fire onEnable (or the parent should refresh state on open change once enablement succeeded).

title: Read-modify-write race lets the same backup code authenticate concurrent requests
body: Backup code consumption is decrypt → indexOf → set slot to null → re-encrypt → save, with no locking or atomic update. Two concurrent login requests using the same backup code can both read the pre-consumption ciphertext, both find the code, and both succeed before either writes back. One-time-use of a backup code is therefore not guaranteed under concurrent requests. Consider consuming the code inside a transaction with a re-read (e.g., `prisma.$transaction` with serializable isolation) or verifying after update that the slot was still present.

title: Consumed backup codes are nulled in place instead of removed
body: After a successful backup-code login the code does `backupCodes[index] = null` and re-encrypts the array, leaving permanent `null` holes in the stored list. As a result the array never shrinks: once all ten codes are used the stored value is still truthy, so the user gets IncorrectBackupCode forever instead of MissingBackupCodes, and the stored blob accumulates dead entries. Splicing the entry out (`backupCodes.splice(index, 1)`) would keep the data clean and let the existing MissingBackupCodes error fire correctly when the list is empty.

title: No test actually exercises logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code
body: The new e2e coverage only asserts that the backup-code screen appears after enabling 2FA and that the download/copy buttons work (with TODOs for the file and clipboard contents). The core security behavior added by this PR — that a backup code logs a user in, that it works only once, that the password is still required, and that disabling 2FA with a backup code works — is entirely untested (the author also checked 'I haven't added tests that prove my feature works', and the file itself carries a TODO for it). The password-bypass and non-CAL-provider issues above would have been caught by such tests; at minimum a login-with-backup-code test and a single-use (second attempt fails) test should be added before merging.

title: missing_backup_codes message tells users to 'generate them in your settings' but no such regeneration UI exists
body: The added copy for `missing_backup_codes` reads 'No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings.' This PR adds no way to regenerate backup codes from settings — codes are only created during the 2FA setup flow, so the only way to get new ones is to disable and re-enable 2FA (which itself may require a backup code in the lost-access flow). The message directs users to an action that doesn't exist; it should be reworded (e.g., instruct them to contact support or reconfigure two-factor authentication).

title: Backup code login bypasses password verification, reducing 2FA to a single factor
body: In the credentials `authorize` callback, the password is only verified inside `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)` (line 121). Any request that includes a non-empty `totpCode` value skips password verification entirely, and the new branch `if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode)` then authenticates the user based solely on the backup code. Since requests to `/api/auth/callback/credentials` are stateless (the CSRF token is freely obtainable from `/api/auth/csrf`), an attacker can POST `email`, any dummy `totpCode`, and a valid `backupCode` and log in without knowing the account password. Backup codes are static credentials stored in downloaded text files (`cal-backup-codes.txt`), screenshots, or password managers, so a leaked backup code alone now grants full account access. Note that the new `disable.ts` endpoint does verify the password before accepting a backup code, showing the intended design. The backup-code branch should require the password to be verified as well.

title: Users with Google/SAML identity providers can never log in with a backup code
body: For users whose `identityProvider` is GOOGLE or SAML and who have 2FA enabled (they log in via the IdP and are then redirected to `/auth/login?totp=<jwt>` to enter a second factor), a backup-code submission has an empty `totpCode`. The guard `if (user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode)` at line 113 (and the similar one at line 117) throws `ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled`/`IncorrectEmailPassword` before the new backup-code branch at line 131 is ever reached. Additionally, the login page renders `ExternalTotpFooter` (only a Cancel button) for these users, so the "Lost access" backup-code UI isn't even offered. If such a user loses their authenticator device they have no recovery path and are permanently locked out, and a crafted request gets a misleading "account created with identity provider" error.

title: "missing_backup_codes" message tells users to generate codes in settings, but no such feature exists
body: The new string `missing_backup_codes` reads "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." This error is returned by both the login and disable endpoints whenever a user has 2FA enabled but `backupCodes` is null — which is the case for every user who enabled 2FA before this feature shipped, since the migration only adds a nullable column and no codes are backfilled. There is no settings UI in this PR (or elsewhere) to generate or regenerate backup codes; the only way to obtain them is to disable and re-enable 2FA. Affected users who click "Lost access" will see an instruction that leads nowhere.

title: No test coverage for the core backup-code behavior (login, single-use consumption, disable)
body: The PR's main feature — authenticating with a backup code, consuming it so it cannot be reused, and disabling 2FA with a backup code — has no test at all. The only test changes exercise the download/copy/close buttons on the setup screen, and the file itself adds a TODO acknowledging this ("add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup"), while the PR checklist explicitly states no tests were added to prove the feature works. A regression such as codes not being single-use (or being consumed but login failing) would ship undetected.

title: Closing the modal without clicking "Close" leaves parent UI stale and modal state dirty
body: Previously `onEnable()` was called immediately when 2FA was successfully enabled; now it is only called from the "Close" button on the backup-codes screen (line 269). If the user dismisses the dialog any other way (the dialog's X button, Escape, or overlay click, which go through `onOpenChange`), `onEnable()` never fires and `resetState()` never runs. Consequences: the parent page never learns 2FA was enabled, so the two-factor switch still shows as off even though `twoFactorEnabled` is now true in the database, and reopening the modal resumes at the stale DisplayBackupCodes step showing old codes instead of the password step. A user who then tries to enable 2FA again will hit the `two-factor-already-enabled` error.

title: Backup-code consumption is a read-modify-write race
body: Consuming a backup code decrypts the JSON array, finds the index, sets `backupCodes[index] = null`, and writes back the re-encrypted array in a separate `prisma.user.update`. Two concurrent login requests with the same backup code can both read the array before either writes, so both succeed — the "each code can be used exactly once" guarantee (which the UI copy promises) does not hold under concurrent requests. Similarly, two concurrent logins with two different codes can clobber each other's update, resurrecting an already-consumed code. Consider atomically updating (e.g., a transaction with re-validation, or filtering the code out and updating with a condition) or at least using `splice` instead of leaving `null` entries in the stored array.

title: tabIndex={-1} on PasswordField visibility toggle removes keyboard access everywhere
body: Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the show/hide password button changes the shared `PasswordField` component, which is used across the app (login, signup, password change, 2FA setup/disable, etc.). Keyboard and assistive-technology users can no longer tab to the toggle to reveal what they typed — the button's own `sr-only` label ("Show password") suggests it was intended to be accessible. If the goal was to fix tab order in a specific 2FA form, it should be done per-instance rather than degrading accessibility for every password field in the product.

title: Crash when destinationCalendar is empty/null and location is Google Meet
body: In EventManager.create(), the code does `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` and then immediately accesses `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` when `evt.location === MeetLocationType`. The `?? []` fallback only handles null/undefined; when destinationCalendar is an empty array (or null), the destructured `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined`, so reading `.integration` throws a TypeError. Many callers updated in this PR now pass `[]` when there is no destination calendar (e.g. confirm.handler, stripe webhook.ts, paypal-webhook.ts, editLocation.handler), and handleNewBooking passes `null`. Any booking on a Google Meet location where the organizer has no destination calendar will now crash during eventManager.create(), failing the booking/confirmation flow. The old code used optional chaining (`evt.destinationCalendar?.integration !== "google_calendar"`) and was safe. This needs `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration !== "google_calendar"`.

title: updateEvent/deleteEvent fallback computes an undefined calendarId
body: In updateEvent the fallback is `const selectedCalendar = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;`. In the branch where externalCalendarId is falsy, the `find` predicate compares each calendar's externalId against that same falsy externalCalendarId, so it can never match — selectedCalendar is always `undefined`. Previously the fallback was `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`, which actually resolved to the destination calendar. The same broken fallback was copied into deleteEvent (line ~317). Any update/delete where the booking reference has no externalCalendarId (older bookings, or references created without externalId) will now call the Google API with an undefined calendarId, so event updates and deletions silently fail, leaving stale events on users' calendars.

title: Hangout-link patch uses possibly-undefined selectedCalendar instead of the inserted calendar
body: In createEvent, the insert uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"`, but the follow-up `calendar.events.patch` that writes the description with the hangout link uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar` directly. When no destinationCalendar entry matches the credentialId, selectedCalendar is undefined: the event is created on "primary" but the patch is issued with an undefined calendarId, which the googleapis client rejects (or targets nothing), so the hangout link is never written into the event description. The patch call also has no callback/await, so the failure is an unhandled rejection.

title: updateLocation referencesToCreate loses credentialId and externalCalendarId for calendar results
body: In updateLocation, referencesToCreate now maps `externalCalendarId: result.externalId` and `credentialId: result.credentialId ?? undefined`. However, calendar results here come from updateAllCalendarEvents -> CalendarManager.updateEvent, whose returned EventResult object never sets `externalId` or `credentialId` (only createEvent in CalendarManager was updated to include them). editLocation.handler then persists these via `references: { create: updatedResult.referencesToCreate }`, creating new booking references with both fields undefined. Downstream, cancel/update flows rely on reference.credentialId and reference.externalCalendarId; losing them forces fallback paths (deleting via every user credential, or the broken undefined-calendarId fallback in the Google service). Previously externalCalendarId was taken from `evt.destinationCalendar?.externalId` and was populated.

title: References created for destinations without credentialId get no externalCalendarId
body: In createAllCalendarEvents, when a destinationCalendar entry has no credentialId, the code calls `createEvent(c, event)` without passing `destination.externalId`. CalendarManager.createEvent only puts the passed externalId onto the returned EventResult, and EventManager.create() now builds references with `externalCalendarId: result.externalId`. So for any DestinationCalendar row whose credentialId is null (the column is nullable), the stored booking reference will have externalCalendarId undefined, and later updates/deletes of that event hit the Google service with a null externalCalendarId — which (combined with the broken fallback there) targets an undefined calendar. The old code always used `evt.destinationCalendar?.externalId` for the reference.

title: Recurring cancel-all deletes duplicate per reference and only delete the first calendar reference of each booking
body: The recurring-cancellation branch (recurringEvent + allRemainingBookings) lives inside the new `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)` loop, so with the multiple calendar references this PR introduces (one per collective host), the entire 'delete across all user calendar credentials for all updatedBookings' block executes once per reference, duplicating every deletion API call. Worse, inside that block each updated booking's reference is resolved with `updBooking.references.find((ref) => ref.type.includes("_calendar"))`, which only returns the first calendar reference — so the additional hosts' calendar events for recurring collective bookings are never deleted when cancelling all remaining bookings.

title: loadUsers refactor drops organization.slug from the dynamic-user select
body: The rewritten loadUsers for dynamic bookings (no eventTypeId) selects `...userSelect.select, credentials: true, metadata: true` but no longer selects `organization: { select: { slug: true } }`, which the previous code included. Downstream booking logic (e.g. bookerUrl/organization-aware links) relies on `user.organization.slug`; for dynamic group bookings this will now be undefined, regressing organization bookings.

title: Collective team destination calendars are dropped when organizer has none
body: The evt is built with `destinationCalendar: eventType.destinationCalendar ? [...] : organizerUser.destinationCalendar ? [...] : null`, and later `if (isTeamEventType && eventType.schedulingType === "COLLECTIVE") { evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars); }`. If neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar but other collective hosts do, evt.destinationCalendar is null and the optional-chained push is a no-op — the team members' destination calendars are silently discarded and no calendar events are created for any host. It should initialize with `(evt.destinationCalendar ?? [])` before pushing.

title: Webhook payload for destinationCalendar is inconsistent across triggers (null vs [])
body: This test now expects BOOKING_REJECTED payloads to contain `destinationCalendar: []` while the BOOKING_CREATED and BOOKING_REQUESTED assertions in the same file still expect `destinationCalendar: null`. The difference comes from handleNewBooking emitting null when there is no destination calendar while confirm.handler and others emit []. Webhook consumers now see two different shapes for the same field depending on the trigger, which is a needless API inconsistency for a PR described as non-breaking.

title: Crash when destinationCalendar is null/empty and location is Google Meet
body: In `EventManager.create`, the Google Meet fallback check was changed from `evt.destinationCalendar?.integration !== "google_calendar"` (null-safe) to `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` followed by `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"`. When the event has no destination calendar (which is common — `handleNewBooking` now sets `destinationCalendar: null` when neither the event type nor the organizer has one) and the location is Meet, `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined` and reading `.integration` throws a TypeError, crashing booking creation. The optional chaining on the destructured value was lost.

title: Team destination calendars silently dropped when organizer has no destination calendar
body: `evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` exists. A few lines later, collective team members' calendars are added via `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` — the optional chaining means the push is a no-op when the value is `null`, so all collected `teamDestinationCalendars` are silently discarded. For a collective event whose organizer has no destination calendar but whose hosts do, no host receives a calendar event, which is exactly the bug this PR is meant to fix. The array should be initialized (e.g. `evt.destinationCalendar = [...(evt.destinationCalendar ?? []), ...teamDestinationCalendars]`).

title: Office365 createEvent always uses the main host's calendar ID, breaking other hosts
body: With `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents` now creating one event per destination calendar using each host's own credential, `Office365CalendarService.createEvent` still takes only the first entry of `event.destinationCalendar` (`const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = event.destinationCalendar ?? []`) and posts to `/me/calendars/${mainHostDestinationCalendar.externalId}/events`. When this service instance belongs to a non-main host, that externalId is the main host's calendar ID, which does not exist in the team member's Office365 account, so creation fails (404) and that host never gets the event. Unlike the Google service, no matching by `credentialId` was added here.

title: Lark createEvent always uses the first destination calendar regardless of credential
body: Same class of bug as Office365: `createEvent` (and `createAttendees`, `updateEvent`, `deleteEvent`) destructures only the first entry of `event.destinationCalendar`. Since `EventManager` now invokes `createEvent` once per host destination calendar with that host's credential, a Lark credential belonging to a non-main host will attempt to create the event in the main host's Lark calendar ID, which is not accessible/existent for that host's account, so the event creation fails for every non-primary host.

title: CalDAV createEvent silently creates nothing for non-main hosts
body: In `BaseCalendarService.createEvent`, the calendar list is filtered by `c.externalId === mainHostDestinationCalendar.externalId` where `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is the first entry of `event.destinationCalendar`. When this service runs with a team member's CalDAV credential (per the new per-host creation loop in EventManager), the main host's calendar URL will not match any of the member's calendars, so the filtered array is empty, `Promise.all([])` succeeds, and the method returns a success result with a uid even though no event was written anywhere. This silently reports success while creating no calendar event for that host.

title: updateEvent/deleteEvent fallback can never match, leaving calendarId undefined
body: In `updateEvent` the fallback was changed from `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId` to `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. This branch only executes when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so the find predicate compares each calendar's externalId against a falsy value and can never match — `selectedCalendar` is always `undefined`, and `calendarId: selectedCalendar` is passed to `calendar.events.update`, producing an API error and failing the update for any booking reference lacking `externalCalendarId`. The same dead fallback exists in `deleteEvent` (line ~317), where it now falls through to "primary" instead of the event's actual destination calendar, so deletes can target the wrong calendar.

title: createEvent patch uses possibly-undefined calendarId after inserting into primary
body: In `createEvent`, the insert falls back to `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"`, but the follow-up `calendar.events.patch` (used to add the hangout link to the description) still passes `calendarId: selectedCalendar` unmodified. When no destination calendar matches the credential (selectedCalendar is undefined), the event is created in the primary calendar but the patch request is issued with an undefined calendarId, so the hangout-link patch fails — and since the promise is not awaited or caught, it can also surface as an unhandled rejection.

title: Recurring-cancel deletion now runs once per calendar reference and only cleans the first reference of other bookings
body: The recurring-event deletion block (`if (bookingToDelete.eventType?.recurringEvent && ... allRemainingBookings)`) was moved inside the new `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)` loop, so for a booking with N calendar references (now normal with multiple hosts) the entire recurring-deletion routine executes N times, issuing duplicate deletes of the same events. Additionally, within that block each updated recurring booking is processed via `updBooking.references.find((ref) => ref.type.includes("_calendar"))`, which only returns the first calendar reference — the other hosts' calendar events on those recurring instances are never deleted, leaving orphaned events in their calendars after a full-series cancellation.

title: Unrelated change inverts IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED condition for org slug
body: This PR flips `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})` (and similarly for `requestedSlug`) in the organization create handler — a semantic inversion unrelated to the destinationCalendar change. With the new condition, the org's `slug` is only written when team billing is enabled and is omitted when it is disabled (previously the opposite), so organizations created on instances without team billing will be missing their slug.

title: loadUsers no longer selects organization.slug for dynamic user list
body: The rewritten `loadUsers` for dynamic group bookings drops `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` from the prisma select. Any downstream code that reads `user.organization.slug` for these users (e.g. booker URL / organization subdomain handling) will now receive `undefined`, silently changing behavior for dynamic bookings belonging to organization users. If the removal was intentional it should be verified against all consumers of the loaded users.

title: Crash when checking Google Meet fallback with empty/null destinationCalendar
body: In `EventManager.create`, the code does `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` and then immediately reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` when `evt.location === MeetLocationType`. If `destinationCalendar` is null or an empty array (which `handleNewBooking.ts` now explicitly produces via `: null` when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar), `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined` and accessing `.integration` throws a TypeError. The old code used optional chaining (`evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`) and was safe. Any booking using Google Meet as location without a destination calendar will now fail with an unhandled exception instead of falling back to Cal Video. This should be `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration !== "google_calendar"`.

title: CalDAV createEvent only ever writes to the first host's destination calendar, silently skipping other hosts
body: `BaseCalendarService.createEvent` (used by CalDAV/Apple calendar) filters the credential's calendar list with `c.externalId === mainHostDestinationCalendar.externalId`, where `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is always the FIRST element of `event.destinationCalendar` — i.e. the main host's calendar. In the new multi-host flow, `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents` iterates over every destination calendar and calls `createEvent` with each host's own credential, but this service ignores both the `credentialId` argument and the `externalId` passed to `CalendarManager.createEvent`, and keeps filtering by the main host's `externalId`. For a secondary host's CalDAV account that filter matches nothing, so `Promise.all([])` resolves, `responses.some(...)` is false, and the method returns a success result with a uid even though no event was created anywhere. A booking reference is then stored claiming the event exists on the secondary host's calendar when it does not. The service should filter by the destination calendar matching the current credential (or accept the externalId), not always the first array entry.

title: Team member destination calendars are dropped when the organizer has no destination calendar
body: For collective events the code builds `evt.destinationCalendar` as `eventType.destinationCalendar ? [...] : organizerUser.destinationCalendar ? [...] : null`, and later does `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`. When neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar, `evt.destinationCalendar` is `null`, the optional-chained push is a no-op, and all collected `teamDestinationCalendars` are silently discarded — so hosts who DO have destination calendars never receive calendar events, which is exactly the scenario this PR is meant to fix. The collective branch should initialize the array (e.g. `evt.destinationCalendar = [...(evt.destinationCalendar ?? []), ...teamDestinationCalendars]`).

title: updateEvent/deleteEvent fallback can never match, leaving calendarId undefined
body: In both `updateEvent` (lines 254-256) and `deleteEvent` (lines 315-317) the fallback when `externalCalendarId` is falsy is `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. Since this branch only runs when `externalCalendarId` is null/undefined/empty, the `find` compares each calendar's externalId against null/undefined and can never match, so `selectedCalendar`/`calendarId` becomes `undefined` and is passed as `calendarId` to the Google API call, which will fail. The previous code fell back to `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. Callers such as `CalendarManager.updateEvent`/`deleteEvent` pass `externalCalendarId: null` when the booking reference has none stored, so this path is reachable; the fallback should use the first destination calendar's externalId instead of a find that can never succeed.

title: Hangout-link patch uses possibly-undefined calendarId
body: In `createEvent`, the insert uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"`, but the follow-up `calendar.events.patch` that adds the hangout link to the description uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar` directly. When no destination calendar matches the credential (selectedCalendar is `undefined`), the event is inserted into "primary" but the patch is issued with `calendarId: undefined`, which the Google client rejects — and since the promise is not awaited or caught, this surfaces as an unhandled rejection. The patch should use the same `selectedCalendar || "primary"` fallback.

title: Video booking references no longer store credentialId
body: In `EventManager.create`, `referencesToCreate` changed from `credentialId: isCalendarType ? evt.destinationCalendar?.credentialId : result.credentialId` to `credentialId: isCalendarType ? result.credentialId : undefined`. For non-calendar (video) results, the credentialId is now always written as `undefined`, whereas before it carried `result.credentialId`. Downstream, `handleCancelBooking` only deletes a video meeting when `bookingVideoReference.credentialId` is set and resolvable to a user credential; bookings created after this change will have video references without credentialId, so cancelling them will leave orphaned video meetings (e.g. Zoom/Teams links stay alive). Unless no video adapter populates `result.credentialId` (in which case the old code was equally broken), this is a data regression for new bookings.

title: updateLocation references lose credentialId/externalCalendarId fallbacks
body: In `updateLocation`, `referencesToCreate` now uses `externalCalendarId: result.externalId` and `credentialId: result.credentialId ?? undefined`, removing the previous fallbacks to `evt.destinationCalendar?.externalId` / `evt.destinationCalendar?.credentialId`. However `CalendarManager.updateEvent` (whose results feed this) never sets `externalId` or `credentialId` on its returned `EventResult` — only `createEvent` does. So calendar references created via the edit-location flow (`editLocation.handler.ts` does `references: { create: updatedResult.referencesToCreate }`) are now always persisted with null `externalCalendarId` and null `credentialId`, whereas before they inherited them from the destination calendar. Subsequent updates/cancellations rely on these fields to target the correct calendar and credential, so location-edited bookings degrade to the legacy 'try every credential' behavior or fail to update the right event.

title: externalId not forwarded when destination has no credentialId
body: In `createAllCalendarEvents`, the branch for a destination calendar without a `credentialId` calls `createEvent(c, event)` without passing `destination.externalId`, while the credentialId branch correctly calls `createEvent(credential, event, destination.externalId)`. Since `CalendarManager.createEvent` stores that argument as `result.externalId` which becomes `externalCalendarId` on the booking reference, references created through this branch now have `externalCalendarId: undefined` even though the destination calendar's externalId is known. Pass `destination.externalId` here as well so future updates/deletes can target the right calendar.

title: loadUsers no longer selects user.organization for dynamic bookings
body: The rewritten `loadUsers` for the dynamic-user (no eventTypeId) path selects `...userSelect.select, credentials: true, metadata: true` but drops the previously selected `organization: { select: { slug: true } }`. Any downstream code that reads `user.organization?.slug` on the organizer/users (e.g. for building org-aware booker URLs) will now silently get `undefined` for dynamic group bookings. The PR description only concerns destination calendars, so this looks like an accidental omission during the refactor; re-add the `organization` select unless it is provably unused.

title: prisma is used but never imported — build-breaking error
body: The newly added token-refresh block calls `await prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, ... })` at lines 96–99, but the file's import list (lines 1–20) does not import `prisma` from `@calcom/prisma`. This is a compile-time TypeScript error (`Cannot find name 'prisma'`) and will fail the build/type-check for the whole app-store package.

title: Zod safe-parse wrapper object is stored as the credential key, corrupting the credential
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the raw `schema.safeParse(...)` result, i.e. an object of the form `{ success: true, data: {...} }`. The code then does `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema); await prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`, persisting the wrapper — not the parsed tokens — into `credential.key`. The next time a `GoogleCalendarService` is constructed, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` (line 75) fails because the stored value has shape `{success, data}` instead of the token shape, so every Google Calendar operation for that user throws after the first token refresh. Previously the code stored `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` (the data itself); the fix is to store `parseRefreshTokenResponse(...).data`.

title: Sync-mode return type (raw fetch Response) is incompatible with several callers' expectations
body: When credential sync is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `fetch` `Response` from `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, but in non-sync mode it returns whatever the provider-specific `refreshFunction` returns — and callers rely on those provider shapes. Concretely: (1) `googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` line 94 does `const token = res?.data` — a `Response` has no `.data`, so `token.access_token` throws a TypeError that is swallowed by the surrounding catch, meaning the access token is silently never refreshed in sync mode and Google calls fail with 401 once expired. (2) `hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts` lines 192–202 treat the return value as a HubspotToken: `expiryDate` becomes NaN, `hubspotClient.setAccessToken(undefined)` is called, and the `Response` object itself is serialized into `credential.key` in the DB, corrupting the credential. (3) `zohocrm/lib/CalendarService.ts` line 217 and `zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts` line 96 access `tokenInfo.data` (axios shape) — `Response.data` is undefined, so reading `.data.error`/assigning `.data.expiryDate` throws and refresh always fails in sync mode. Either `refreshOAuthTokens` must normalize the sync response (e.g. parse JSON and return it) or every call site must handle both shapes.

title: minimumTokenResponseSchema's computed keys are literal "[object Object]" and validate nothing about expiry
body: The schema uses computed property names `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`. `z.string()` returns a ZodString instance whose `toString()` yields `"[object Object]"`, so the schema is effectively `{ access_token: z.string(), "[object Object]": z.unknown().optional() }` — the intended 'any numeric property is the expiry' validation never happens. Worse, zod strips unknown keys by default, so when credential sync is enabled the parsed `data` contains only `access_token`; `expires_in`/`expiry_date` are dropped. Downstream consequences: in `zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts` line 122, `key.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + newTokens.expires_in * 1000)` becomes NaN and is persisted, after which `isTokenValid` (`NaN < Date.now()` is false) treats the token as valid forever, so Zoom stops refreshing and API calls fail once the synced token expires. In `office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` the `expires_in`→absolute-timestamp transform is also skipped in sync mode (see separate finding).

title: Credential ID is passed to refreshOAuthTokens where a user ID is expected
body: `refreshOAuthTokens(refreshFunction, appSlug, userId)` sends its third argument to the sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. Every other app passes `credential.userId`, but zoho-bigin passes `credentialId` (the credential row's primary key, from `refreshAccessToken(credentialId, credentialKey)`). With sync enabled, the self-hoster's endpoint receives `calcomUserId=<credential id>`, looks up the wrong (or no) user, and returns tokens for the wrong account or an error — so Bigin token refresh is broken/mis-attributed whenever credential sync is on.

title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token" and persisted
body: When the (sync) response has no `refresh_token`, the code sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. Callers such as `zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts` (line 120: `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token`) and `office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` then write this placeholder into `credential.key` in the database, overwriting the real OAuth refresh token. If credential sync is later disabled (or for apps like Salesforce that still hit the provider directly), the stored credential can never be refreshed again and the integration is permanently broken until the user reconnects.

title: Sync mode skips the expires_in→absolute-expiry transform, causing a token refresh on every API call
body: In non-sync mode, `refreshTokenResponseSchema` transforms `expires_in` (seconds) into an absolute epoch timestamp via `.transform()`. In sync mode, `parseRefreshTokenResponse` uses `minimumTokenResponseSchema`, which performs no transform and strips unknown keys, so `o365AuthCredentials` keeps its old, already-expired `expires_in` value. Since `getToken` decides to refresh based on `isExpired(o365AuthCredentials.expires_in)`, every single `getToken()` call triggers another POST to the sync endpoint — one extra HTTP round-trip (plus a DB write) per calendar operation, and the stored `refresh_token` is also clobbered with the placeholder string.

title: Webex refresh bypasses parseRefreshTokenResponse, so sync-mode responses always fail schema validation
body: Unlike the other apps, the Webex adapter was wrapped with `refreshOAuthTokens` but still validates the result with the strict `webexRefreshedTokenSchema.safeParse(responseBody)` instead of `parseRefreshTokenResponse`. That schema requires `scope` to be the exact literal "spark:kms meeting:schedules_read meeting:schedules_write", `token_type: "Bearer"`, `refresh_token`, and `refresh_token_expires_in`. Per the PR's own contract (comment in `refreshOAuthTokens`: 'The response should only contain the access token and expiry date'), the sync endpoint returns a minimal payload, so validation fails and every Webex token refresh rejects with 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned' whenever credential sync is enabled.

title: Salesforce now refreshes the token on every service instantiation and ignores the credential-sync endpoint
body: The new code in `getClient` unconditionally POSTs to `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` and writes to the DB every time a `SalesforceCalendarService` is constructed — previously jsforce lazily refreshed only on a 401. This adds an external HTTP call plus a DB write to every Salesforce calendar operation. Additionally, this is the only modified app that does not route through `refreshOAuthTokens`, so when credential syncing is the source of truth, the stored `refresh_token` may be the placeholder `"refresh_token"` (or absent), making this direct Salesforce refresh fail with invalid_grant and breaking the integration entirely.

title: findFirst-then-create upsert has a race that creates duplicate credentials
body: The handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst({ userId, appId })` and then either updates or creates. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same user/app (retries are typical for webhooks) can both observe no existing credential and both execute `prisma.credential.create`, leaving duplicate credential rows for the same user and app. Other parts of the codebase use `findFirst` when reading credentials, so duplicates silently shadow each other and can cause the wrong (stale) credential to be used. Since `(userId, appId)` is not unique in the schema, this should at least be serialized (e.g. transaction with locking, or a unique constraint) rather than a check-then-act.

title: Webhook secret compared with !== (non-constant-time comparison)
body: The shared-secret check `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` uses a regular string comparison, which short-circuits on the first differing byte and is susceptible to timing side-channel measurement of the secret. For a secret that gates writing arbitrary credentials into the database, `crypto.timingSafeEqual` (after length check) should be used. Additionally, `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` throw unhandled exceptions, returning a stack-trace-bearing 500 instead of a 400.

title: No tests for the credential-sync webhook or the sync-mode token refresh paths
body: The PR checklist explicitly states no tests were added. The new endpoint writes third-party credentials directly into the database and the modified refresh paths in ~10 app integrations (Google, Zoom, Office365, HubSpot, Zoho, Webex, Lark, Salesforce) now branch on `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` — several of which are broken in sync mode (shape mismatches, NaN expiry, wrapper object persisted). At minimum, tests covering the webhook (auth failure, create vs update, bad payload) and one representative sync-mode refresh per response-shape family (fetch Response vs SDK object vs axios) would have caught the regressions in this PR.

title: Missing prisma import — file will not compile
body: The newly added refresh block calls `prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, ... })` at line 96, but the file's import list (lines 1–21) never imports `prisma` from `@calcom/prisma`. This is a TypeScript compile error (`Cannot find name 'prisma'`), so the package/build fails whenever this file is type-checked.

title: Refreshed Salesforce tokens are saved but the stale access token is used
body: In `getClient`, the code fetches a fresh token set from Salesforce, validates it, and writes it to the DB (lines 75–99), but then constructs the `jsforce.Connection` with `accessToken: credentialKey.access_token` and `instanceUrl: credentialKey.instance_url` — the old, possibly-expired credential values — instead of `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`. The refresh is therefore useless for the current session: the connection is built on the stale token the refresh was meant to replace. Additionally, this refresh now runs unconditionally on every service instantiation (extra token request + DB write per operation, even when the token is still valid), and it never goes through `refreshOAuthTokens`, so when credential syncing is enabled and the stored key has no valid Salesforce refresh token, every Salesforce calendar operation throws.

title: credentialId passed as userId to refreshOAuthTokens
body: `refreshOAuthTokens(refreshFunction, appSlug, userId)` expects the Cal.com user id as its third argument, which it sends to the sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. In zoho-bigin's `refreshAccessToken`, the third argument is `credentialId` (the credential row's primary key), not `credential.userId`. With credential sync enabled, the self-hoster's endpoint receives a credential id as the user id, so it will look up and return tokens for the wrong (or no) user, and the resulting tokens get written onto this user's credential.

title: minimumTokenResponseSchema's computed keys don't work — expiry fields are silently stripped
body: `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()` do not create zod catchalls: `z.string().toString()` evaluates to a constant string ("[object Object]"), so the schema is effectively just `{ access_token: z.string() }` plus a meaningless literal key. Because zod object schemas strip unknown keys by default, parsing a sync-endpoint response like `{ access_token, expires_in }` or the mutated Google credentials object drops every property except `access_token` — including the expiry. Consequence: in sync mode the credentials written to the DB (e.g. Google at `googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:97`) lose `expiry_date`, so the token is considered expired on every subsequent call and the expiry returned by the sync endpoint is never persisted. Zod's `.catchall()`/`.passthrough()` was presumably intended.

title: Literal "refresh_token" placeholder overwrites real refresh tokens in the DB
body: When the parsed token response has no `refresh_token`, the code invents one: `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. This runs in both modes, not just sync mode. In `office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:264` the parsed data is merged over the stored credentials (`{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }`) and persisted, so if Microsoft's token endpoint omits `refresh_token` in a refresh response (which the schema explicitly allows via `.optional()`), the user's real refresh token in the database is replaced by the string "refresh_token". The next refresh then fails with invalid_grant and the user's calendar disconnects — a regression for existing Office 365 users even with credential syncing disabled.

title: Sync branch returns a raw fetch Response while callers expect provider-shaped objects
body: When credential sync is enabled this helper returns the unparsed `fetch` `Response` from `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, but the fallback branch returns whatever each provider's refresh function returns (googleapis `res` with `.data`, an axios response with `.data`, a Hubspot token object). Callers were not adapted to the Response shape: `googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:94` does `res?.data` (undefined on a Response, so `token.access_token` throws a TypeError that is swallowed by the catch and the refresh silently no-ops, leaving the expired token in use); `hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts:177` treats the Response as a `HubspotToken`, producing `expiryDate = NaN` and `setAccessToken(undefined)`; `zohocrm/lib/CalendarService.ts:217` and `zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts:96` read `.data` on a Response (TypeError, caught and logged, so the token is never refreshed). As written, enabling sync breaks token refresh for these apps.

title: Webex still enforces provider-specific token schema, rejecting sync-endpoint responses
body: Unlike zoom/google/office365calendar, the webex refresh path was not switched to `parseRefreshTokenResponse` — it still parses the response with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema`, which requires `scope` and `token_type` string literals, `refresh_token`, and `refresh_token_expires_in`. Per the PR's own contract the sync endpoint returns only an access token and an expiry, so in sync mode parsing always fails and `refreshAccessToken` rejects with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned", making Webex meetings unusable whenever credential syncing is enabled.

title: Sync response expiry is discarded, and stored key loses refresh_token
body: After the refresh call, the code computes `responseBody.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + (responseBody?.expires_in || 0) * 1000)` and then overwrites the entire stored credential key with `responseBody`. The sync endpoint contract is "access token and expiry date", not necessarily `expires_in`; if it returns anything else (e.g. `expiry_date`), that value is clobbered with ~now, so `isExpired` is always true and every `getToken()` call hits the sync endpoint again. The wholesale key replacement also drops `refresh_token` from the stored credential, so if syncing is later disabled the credential can no longer refresh.

title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time !==
body: The shared webhook secret is verified with a plain string `!==` comparison between the header value and `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. For a long-lived bearer secret protecting an endpoint that writes arbitrary credential keys for any user, this should use a constant-time comparison (e.g. `crypto.timingSafeEqual`) to avoid leaking the secret byte-by-byte through response timing.

title: Malformed input causes unhandled 500s; no HTTP method check
body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` (line 31), `symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, ...)` and the surrounding `JSON.parse` (lines 57–59) all throw on invalid input (bad body shape, wrong encryption key, non-JSON plaintext), producing an unhandled 500 with a stack trace instead of a 4xx response. The handler also accepts any HTTP method, so a GET (empty body) takes the same crash path. Wrap validation/decryption in try/catch and reject non-POST methods.

title: No tests for the credential-sync webhook or refresh-sync paths
body: The PR adds a security-sensitive endpoint that decrypts and overwrites user credentials, plus a new token-refresh code path in nine app integrations, and the author explicitly states no tests were added. Given the multiple mode-dependent behaviors (sync on/off, per-app response shapes), at minimum the webhook's auth/upsert logic and `refreshOAuthTokens`/`parseRefreshTokenResponse` need unit tests before merge.

title: SafeParse wrapper object is stored as the credential key, corrupting Google Calendar credentials
body: In refreshAccessToken, `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema)` returns the full zod SafeParse result (`{ success: true, data: {...} }`), not the parsed credentials. This object is then written to the DB via `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. The previous code stored `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` (the unwrapped data). After the very first token refresh, the credential's key in the database becomes `{"success":true,"data":{...}}`, and every subsequent construction of GoogleCalendarService fails at `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` in googleAuth, permanently breaking Google Calendar for that credential until the row is manually fixed. This affects all users, not just those with credential syncing enabled.

title: prisma is used but never imported in salesforce CalendarService
body: The newly added code calls `await prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, ... })` in getClient, but the file's import list (lines 1-20) contains no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. This is a compile-time error (Cannot find name 'prisma') and will break the type-check/build for the whole app-store package.

title: Sync branch returns a raw fetch Response while callers expect provider-specific parsed bodies
body: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw fetch `Response`. In the fallback branch it returns whatever the provider-specific refreshFunction returns (an axios response for zoho apps, a Gaxios response for Google, a token object for HubSpot, a fetch Response for office365/lark/zoom). Callers that don't expect a fetch Response break when sync is enabled: HubSpot reads `.expiresIn`/`.accessToken` off the Response and stores the Response object itself as the credential key; zoho-bigin and zohocrm dereference `tokenInfo.data.error` on the Response (`data` is undefined) and crash with a TypeError; Google reads `res?.data` which is undefined. The return-type contract of this helper is inconsistent and silently breaks most integrations in sync mode.

title: With sync enabled, HubSpot credential key is overwritten with a serialized fetch Response
body: When credential sync is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns a raw fetch Response, so `hubspotRefreshToken` is a Response object. `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` is undefined, making `expiryDate` NaN, and then `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key: hubspotRefreshToken as any } })` JSON-serializes the Response (effectively `{}`) into the credential key, permanently destroying the user's stored HubSpot tokens. `hubspotClient.setAccessToken(hubspotRefreshToken.accessToken)` also sets an undefined token, so subsequent HubSpot API calls fail. The credential row must be manually repaired afterwards.

title: credentialId is passed to the sync endpoint instead of userId
body: refreshOAuthTokens is called as `refreshOAuthTokens(fn, "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` where the third parameter is `userId: number | null` and is sent to the self-hoster's sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. Passing the credential id means the external app store will look up (and return) tokens for the wrong user — either a failure or, worse, another user's Bigin tokens stored on this user's credential. Every other integration passes `credential.userId`; this one should too.

title: Google refresh silently no-ops when credential sync is enabled
body: In sync mode refreshOAuthTokens returns a raw fetch Response, so `const token = res?.data` is undefined and `token.access_token` throws a TypeError. The catch block treats any message other than "invalid_grant" as recoverable and just returns the auth client with the stale, expired credentials. The result: with sync enabled, Google Calendar token refresh never succeeds, the new tokens are never used or stored, and the failure is completely silent — all calendar API calls then fail with expired-token errors.

title: minimumTokenResponseSchema's computed keys are nonsense — the schema only validates access_token and strips the expiry
body: `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()` do not create catch-all keys: `z.string().toString()` evaluates to the string "[object Object]", so both computed keys collapse to a single literal property named "[object Object]". The schema therefore only requires `access_token` and — because zod strips unknown keys — drops every other field, including the expiry that the comment says is being captured. Downstream consequences when sync is enabled: office365calendar never updates its stored expiry (token is re-fetched on every API call), zoom stores expiry_date NaN, and office365video sets expiry_date to Date.now() (immediately expired).

title: Placeholder string "refresh_token" overwrites real refresh tokens in the database
body: When the (sync) response has no refresh_token, the code sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. Callers then persist this: office365calendar merges tokenResponse.data into the stored key (line 264 of office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts) and zoom copies `newTokens.refresh_token` into the stored key (line 120 of zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts). The user's real OAuth refresh token is thus permanently replaced by the literal string "refresh_token", so if sync is ever disabled or the fallback path runs, the credential can no longer be refreshed and the integration is dead until re-connected.

title: Bigin token refresh crashes with TypeError when credential sync is enabled
body: In sync mode refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response, which has no `.data` property, so `if (!tokenInfo.data.error)` throws "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'error')". The same pattern exists in zohocrm/lib/CalendarService.ts line 217 (`zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error`). Token refresh for both Zoho apps is therefore guaranteed to throw whenever APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set.

title: Webex refresh rejects sync-endpoint responses because it still validates against the full Webex schema
body: Unlike the other apps, webex was not migrated to parseRefreshTokenResponse: it still runs `webexRefreshedTokenSchema.safeParse(responseBody)`, which requires scope/token_type/refresh_token/refresh_token_expires_in. When sync is enabled, the request is redirected to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, whose documented response contains only the access token and expiry, so the parse always fails and refreshAccessToken rejects with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". Webex video is therefore completely broken for any instance that enables credential sync.

title: Zoom sync path stores placeholder refresh token and NaN expiry_date
body: In sync mode, parseRefreshTokenResponse uses the minimal schema, so newTokens contains only access_token plus the placeholder `refresh_token: "refresh_token"`. The code then does `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token` (overwriting the real refresh token with the placeholder) and `key.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + newTokens.expires_in * 1000)` where expires_in is undefined, producing NaN, which is written to the Json column (JSON-serializes to null or throws depending on the Prisma version). The stored Zoom credential is corrupted after the first synced refresh.

title: MS Teams sync path stores a key without refresh_token and with an already-expired expiry_date
body: When sync is enabled, responseBody is the sync endpoint's JSON (access token + expiry only). The code then computes `expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + (responseBody?.expires_in || 0) * 1000)`, i.e. the current time, so the token is immediately considered expired and every meeting creation triggers another sync request. Worse, `key: responseBody` replaces the entire stored credential key, permanently discarding the saved refresh_token — after the next server restart the in-memory copy is gone and the credential can never be refreshed through the normal path again.

title: Office365 expiry is never updated in sync mode, causing a sync-endpoint call on every calendar operation
body: In sync mode parseRefreshTokenResponse returns only `{ access_token }` (unknown keys stripped, expiry never captured). The merge `{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }` therefore keeps the old, already-expired `expires_in` epoch value. Since getToken checks `!isExpired(o365AuthCredentials.expires_in)`, the freshly synced token is still considered expired, so every single Graph API call (availability, event create/update/delete) triggers a new POST to the sync endpoint. It also removed the previous logging of zod errors, making misconfigurations harder to diagnose.

title: Refreshed Salesforce token is stored but the client is built with the stale access token
body: getClient fetches a fresh token set and writes it to the DB, but then constructs the jsforce.Connection with `accessToken: credentialKey.access_token` — the old, possibly expired token from before the refresh. The new access token (`accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`) is never used. Additionally, this refresh fetch now runs unconditionally on every service instantiation (previously jsforce refreshed lazily only when needed), adding a blocking Salesforce round-trip to every calendar operation, and when APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is set the minimal parse schema strips fields like instance_url, so the stored key loses data needed for future connections.

title: Decrypted keys are stored without any validation against the app's expected key shape
body: The webhook decrypts `keys` and writes the parsed JSON directly into credential.key with no validation against the per-app credential schema (e.g. zoomTokenSchema, googleCredentialSchema). If the self-hoster's app sends malformed or incomplete keys (wrong field names, missing refresh token), the credential is created/updated successfully but every service that does `schema.parse(credential.key)` will throw at runtime, breaking that user's integration with no indication of why. At minimum the payload should be validated against the app's key schema before persisting.

title: findFirst-then-create/update race allows duplicate credentials
body: The handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst({ userId, appId })` and then creates a new credential if none was found. Two webhook deliveries arriving concurrently for the same user/app will both observe no existing credential and both create one, leaving duplicate credentials for the same app. Downstream code uses findFirst and silently ignores the duplicates. There is no unique constraint on (userId, appId) to back this up, so the upsert should be made atomic (e.g. a transaction with locking or a unique constraint).

title: Webhook secret compared with a non-constant-time string comparison
body: `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` uses a plain inequality check, which short-circuits on the first differing byte and is susceptible to timing analysis. Since this secret is the only thing protecting an endpoint that writes third-party OAuth credentials into the database, it should be compared with a constant-time comparison (e.g. crypto.timingSafeEqual on equal-length buffers).

title: Unhandled ZodError/decryption failures and no HTTP method check produce 500s
body: The handler doesn't restrict the HTTP method and calls `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` without a try/catch. A GET request, a malformed body, or an incorrectly encrypted `keys` payload throws an unhandled exception, returning an opaque 500 instead of a 400/401 with a useful message, which will make webhook misconfigurations hard for self-hosters to debug.

title: isTeamAdminOrOwner requires admin AND owner (&&) instead of OR
body: The check `const isTeamAdminOrOwner = (await isTeamAdmin(user.id, booking.eventType?.teamId ?? 0)) && (await isTeamOwner(user.id, booking.eventType?.teamId ?? 0));` uses `&&`, so it is only true when the user is simultaneously a team admin AND a team owner. In Cal.com's membership model a user has a single role, so this expression is effectively always false. As a result, legitimate team admins and team owners of team event types are always denied with FORBIDDEN when trying to add guests — the feature is completely broken for team bookings. This should be `||`.

title: Calendar update uses the requester's credentials instead of the organizer's
body: The handler builds `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials: [...credentials] })` from `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` — i.e. the credentials of whoever called the endpoint — even though the booking's organizer (with credentials) was already loaded via `booking.user.credentials`. When anyone other than the organizer adds guests (a team admin or an attendee, both of which the permission check explicitly allows), `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` attempts to update the organizer's calendar event using credentials that have no access to it. Worse, this call is outside any try/catch and runs after the DB update, so the attendees are already persisted but the mutation throws and the calendar event is never updated — attendees get no calendar invite on the real event and the client shows an error despite the guests having been added.

title: No validation of booking status or time — guests can be added to cancelled/rejected/past bookings
body: After fetching the booking, the handler never checks `booking.status` or whether the booking has already ended. Guests can therefore be added to CANCELLED or REJECTED bookings (receiving CONFIRMED ics invites and scheduled emails for an event that does not exist) and to bookings in the past. The UI partially hides this (the edit menu is rendered for past confirmed bookings too, via the `isBookingInPast && isConfirmed` branch in BookingListItem.tsx), and the API itself enforces nothing, so cancelled/past events can have attendees appended and calendar/email notifications sent out.

title: Any attendee can add arbitrary guests to a booking, enabling email spam through the platform
body: The permission check grants access to any existing attendee (`isAttendee`), and there is no limit on how many guests can be added or how often. Anyone who books a public event can then submit an arbitrary list of victim email addresses, and the handler will persist them as attendees and send them AttendeeScheduledEmail invitations containing the event details, organizer identity, and video meeting URL. This turns the endpoint into an unauthenticated-content email relay abusing Cal.com's sender reputation. The UI added in this PR only exposes the dialog on the organizer's bookings list, so the attendee permission appears broader than the feature requires; if attendee-added guests are intentional, they at least need rate limiting / a count cap.

title: Duplicate detection and blacklist checks are case-sensitive
body: Duplicate filtering uses `guest === attendee.email` and the blacklist uses `blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)` where the blacklist entries are lowercased but `guest` is not. Email addresses differing only in case (e.g. `Alice@x.com` vs `alice@x.com`) are treated as distinct: the blacklist can be bypassed with mixed case, and `createMany` will insert a second Attendee row for an email that is already on the booking, producing duplicate attendees who then each receive emails. The dialog-side Set-based uniqueness check has the same flaw. Compare normalized (`toLowerCase()`/`trim()`) values on both sides.

title: Guests added to seated (seatsPerTimeSlot) events get no BookingSeat reference
body: For seated events, every attendee is expected to have a BookingSeat record (seat reference) — the handler even copies `seatsPerTimeSlot`/`seatsShowAttendees` onto the CalendarEvent, but it only creates plain Attendee rows via `createMany` and never creates BookingSeat entries. Guests added to a seated booking will have no `seatReferenceUid`, won't be counted against seat availability (so the slot can be overbooked), and any flows that rely on seat references (joining, cancelling a seat, rescheduling a seat) will break or behave inconsistently for them.

title: sendAddGuestsEmails ignores the event type's disableStandardEmails settings
body: Every other sender in this file (sendScheduledEmails, sendLocationChangeEmails, sendCancelledEmails, etc.) accepts the event type metadata and skips host/attendee emails when `eventTypeDisableHostEmail`/`eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail` (metadata.disableStandardEmails) is set. `sendAddGuestsEmails` takes no `eventTypeMetadata` and unconditionally emails the organizer, all team members, and every attendee. Event types that explicitly disabled standard emails will still have emails sent whenever guests are added.

title: sendAddGuestsEmails is called with the raw `guests` input instead of the deduplicated `uniqueGuests`
body: The handler computes `uniqueGuests` (excluding emails already on the booking and blacklisted ones) but then calls `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` with the original input. In `sendAddGuestsEmails`, any attendee whose email appears in that list is sent a full AttendeeScheduledEmail as if they were a brand-new guest — so an already-existing attendee who was (re-)submitted gets a fresh 'scheduled' confirmation email rather than the 'new guests added' notice. Pass `uniqueGuests` instead.

title: Organizer email subject uses attendees[0].name, which may be an empty string
body: The subject is built with `name: this.calEvent.attendees[0].name`. The handler creates the new guests with `name: ""` and includes them in `evt.attendees`; since the ordering of `attendees` after the booking update isn't guaranteed, `attendees[0]` can be one of the new nameless guests, producing a subject like 'Guests Added: 30 min meeting with  at ...'. The scheduled-email flow this copies assumes attendees[0] is the booker with a real name.

title: isTeamAdminOrOwner uses && so it can never be true
body: In addGuests.handler.ts, `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `(await isTeamAdmin(user.id, teamId)) && (await isTeamOwner(user.id, teamId))`. A membership in Cal.com has a single role, so a user cannot simultaneously be ADMIN and OWNER of the same team — this expression is always false. As a result, team admins and team owners (whom the UI explicitly allows to manage the booking via `booking.isUserTeamAdminOrOwner` in BookingListItem) will always hit the FORBIDDEN branch and cannot add guests. The two checks should be combined with `||`.

title: Calendar update uses the caller's credentials instead of the organizer's
body: The handler builds the EventManager from `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` and `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials })`, i.e. the credentials and identity of whoever clicked "add guests". But the permission check explicitly allows attendees and team admins to call this endpoint, and the calendar event being updated belongs to the booking organizer (`booking.user`). When anyone other than the organizer adds guests, `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` runs with credentials that have no access to the organizer's calendar, so the calendar event is never updated with the new attendees (or the call fails). Note the booking query already includes `booking.user.credentials` but they are never used — the organizer's credentials/user should be used to construct the EventManager.

title: No booking status check — guests can be added to cancelled, rejected, or past bookings
body: After fetching the booking, the handler only checks permissions; it never verifies `booking.status` or `booking.endTime`. The UI only shows the action for confirmed bookings, but the tRPC mutation is directly callable, so any attendee can add guests to a CANCELLED or REJECTED booking (or one that already ended), creating Attendee rows and triggering confirmation/ICS emails with method REQUEST for a dead event. The handler should reject bookings that are not ACCEPTED (and arguably those already in the past).

title: Case-sensitive duplicate/blacklist comparison lets duplicate attendees in and breaks the blacklist
body: The dedupe filter compares `guest === attendee.email` and `blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)` with exact string equality. The blacklist entries are lowercased but `guest` is not, so `Foo@Bar.com` on the blacklist is never matched. Worse, if the booking already has attendee `foo@bar.com` and someone submits `Foo@Bar.com`, the filter passes and `createMany` inserts a second attendee row for the same person (email uniqueness in the DB is case-sensitive), producing duplicate attendees who then both receive emails and calendar updates. Emails should be normalized (trimmed/lowercased) before comparison and before insert.

title: Raw `guests` (not `uniqueGuests`) passed to sendAddGuestsEmails sends the wrong template
body: `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` is called with the raw input array, not the deduplicated `uniqueGuests`. In email-manager.ts, each attendee gets the full `AttendeeScheduledEmail` if `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)`, otherwise the "guests added" notification. So if the requester includes an email that is already an attendee (filtered out of `uniqueGuests`, not re-added), that existing attendee incorrectly receives a brand-new booking confirmation email instead of the notification. Conversely, because the matching is case-sensitive, a genuinely new guest stored with different casing than the input gets the notification template instead of the confirmation. Pass `uniqueGuests` and compare normalized emails.

title: sendAddGuestsEmails ignores event-type email opt-out settings
body: Every other send function in this file (sendScheduledEmails, sendLocationChangeEmails, sendCancelledEmails, etc.) accepts `eventTypeMetadata` and skips host/attendee emails when `disableStandardEmails.all.host/attendee` is set, and also strips `additionalNotes` when `hideCalendarNotes` is set. `sendAddGuestsEmails` takes no metadata parameter and unconditionally emails the organizer, all team members, and all attendees. Event types that disabled standard emails (a documented privacy feature, e.g. when workflows replace them) will still send these notifications, and hidden calendar notes can leak to attendees.
