title: No upper bound on guests array enables email spam abuse
body: `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` has no `.max()` and no `.min(1)`. Since the handler permits any existing attendee (not just the organizer) to call this mutation, anyone who attended a booking can submit hundreds of arbitrary email addresses, creating hundreds of Attendee rows and causing Cal.com to send organizer-branded invitation emails (with ICS attachments and reply-to set to the organizer) to all of them. Add a reasonable `.max()` (and `.min(1)`) to the schema.

title: Attendees added to seated events without BookingSeat references
body: The handler copies `seatsPerTimeSlot`/`seatsShowAttendees` into the CalendarEvent, so seated event types reach this code, but it inserts attendees with a plain `createMany` and never creates the `BookingSeat` reference rows that seated bookings require to track occupancy and to let the attendee manage/reschedule their seat. For a seated event this corrupts seat accounting (the new attendee occupies no seat) and breaks flows that rely on `seatsReferences`. The handler should either reject bookings whose event type has `seatsPerTimeSlot` set, or create proper seat references.

title: Validation error message never clears when the user edits emails
body: `isInvalidEmail` is set to true when validation fails, but nothing resets it when the user subsequently edits or removes email fields — it is only cleared on cancel or successful submit. A user who fixes the offending address still sees "Emails must be unique and valid" until they click Add again, which is confusing. Clear the flag in the `setValue` path (e.g. wrap `setMultiEmailValue` to also reset `isInvalidEmail`).

title: isTeamAdminOrOwner uses AND instead of OR, so team admins/owners can never add guests
body: The permission check computes `isTeamAdminOrOwner = (await isTeamAdmin(user.id, teamId)) && (await isTeamOwner(user.id, teamId))`. `isTeamAdmin` checks membership role ADMIN and `isTeamOwner` checks role OWNER; a single membership cannot be both, so this expression is always false. Team admins and owners who are not themselves the booking host or an attendee will always hit the FORBIDDEN branch and cannot add guests to their team's bookings. This should be `||`.

title: Calendar update uses the requester's credentials instead of the booking host's
body: `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` loads the credentials of the user making the request, and the EventManager is built from those. But the calendar event being updated lives on the booking host's (organizer's) calendar. The handler explicitly allows attendees and (intended) team admins to add guests; in those cases the requester has no credential matching the booking's destination calendar/references, so `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` silently cannot update the calendar event — new guests are never added to the actual calendar/conferencing event. The query already includes `booking.user.credentials`; the EventManager should be constructed from the booking owner's credentials (as done elsewhere, e.g. using `booking.user`), not `ctx.user`.

title: Any attendee can add an unlimited number of guests, enabling email spam through Cal.com's mailer
body: The handler authorizes anyone whose email is among the booking's attendees (`isAttendee`) to add guests, and neither the schema nor the handler caps the number of guests per request or per booking. Combined with `sendAddGuestsEmails`, which sends an `AttendeeScheduledEmail` to every new guest with the organizer's name in the From/Reply-To headers, any person who books (or is added to) a meeting can cause Cal.com to send branded invitation emails containing meeting details and links to arbitrary email addresses. This is a spam/phishing vector and can also blow up event attendee lists. Consider restricting this to the organizer/team admins, or at minimum enforcing a guest limit.

title: Email comparisons are case-sensitive: blacklist bypass and duplicate attendees
body: The filtering does `!booking.attendees.some((attendee) => guest === attendee.email)` and `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`. The blacklist entries are lowercased but `guest` is not, so `USER@BLACKLISTED.COM` bypasses `BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS`. Likewise, adding `Foo@Bar.com` when attendee `foo@bar.com` already exists passes the uniqueness check and creates a duplicate attendee row (and duplicate emails). Normalize case before both comparisons.

title: Schema does not enforce uniqueness of guests, allowing duplicate attendee rows
body: `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` accepts duplicates. The uniqueness refinement only exists client-side in AddGuestsDialog; anyone calling the tRPC mutation directly with `["a@b.com", "a@b.com"]` will pass validation, and `createMany` will insert two attendee rows for the same email (both also receiving invitation emails). Add a `.refine` for uniqueness (case-insensitive) in the schema or dedupe in the handler.

title: sendAddGuestsEmails ignores event-type settings that disable standard emails
body: Every other send function in this file (sendScheduledEmails, sendLocationChangeEmails, sendCancelledEmails, etc.) accepts `eventTypeMetadata` and honors `disableStandardEmails.all.attendee` / `.host` via `eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail`/`eventTypeDisableHostEmail`. `sendAddGuestsEmails` has no metadata parameter and unconditionally emails the organizer, team members, and all attendees. Event types that disabled standard emails (e.g. because workflows replace them) will still send these notifications, producing duplicate/unwanted emails.

title: Original (unfiltered) guest list passed to sendAddGuestsEmails
body: The handler computes `uniqueGuests` (excluding already-registered attendees and blacklisted emails) but then calls `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` with the raw input. In `sendAddGuestsEmails`, any existing attendee whose email appears in that raw list is treated as a "new guest" and receives a full `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (a fresh booking confirmation) instead of the "guests added" notification. Pass `uniqueGuests` instead.

title: No booking status/time validation: guests can be added to cancelled, rejected, or past bookings
body: The handler fetches the booking by id and only checks permissions; it never verifies `booking.status` or that the booking is in the future. The UI only exposes the action for confirmed upcoming bookings, but the mutation can be called directly to add guests to a cancelled, rejected, pending, or already-finished booking — inserting attendee rows and dispatching confirmation emails with calendar invites for an event that is cancelled or over. Reject non-ACCEPTED or past bookings.

title: Attendees are persisted before calendar update, with no transaction or compensating path
body: `prisma.booking.update(... createMany attendees ...)` commits the new attendees, then `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` runs afterwards outside any transaction. If the calendar update throws, the mutation fails but the guests remain on the booking with no calendar invite and no email — and because the uniqueness filter now sees them as existing attendees, retrying the operation throws BAD_REQUEST ("emails_must_be_unique_valid"), leaving the guests permanently without invitations. Wrap in a transaction or send/update first and handle partial failure.

title: Guests added to seated events get no seat reference, corrupting seat accounting
body: The handler copies `seatsPerTimeSlot` into the event but always creates plain `Attendee` rows. For event types with seats, attendees are expected to be booked via `SeatReference` records, and remaining-seat availability is derived from seat bookings. Adding guests this way to a seated booking inflates the attendee list without consuming seats (allowing overbooking) and the new guests won't have the seat reference data other flows rely on. Seated event types should be rejected or handled via the seats flow.

title: Initial state [""] makes Add with an untouched field show a validation error
body: `multiEmailValue` initializes to `[""]`, so the `multiEmailValue.length === 0` guard in `handleAdd` is dead code and clicking Add without typing anything runs zod validation on an empty string, failing with the red "Emails must be unique and valid" error instead of being a no-op. Also, `isInvalidEmail` is never cleared when the user edits the email fields afterward, so the error stays visible until a successful submit or cancel. Initialize to `[]` (or filter empty strings before validating) and reset the error state on change.

title: Email sending errors swallowed with console.log
body: The `try/catch` around `sendAddGuestsEmails` logs `"Error sending AddGuestsEmails"` via `console.log` and discards the actual error object, then returns success to the client. Guests will appear added with no notification sent, users see a success toast, and operators get no usable log (the rest of the codebase uses `@calcom/lib/logger` and includes the error). At minimum log the error with the structured logger; ideally surface partial failure.

title: retryCount-based deletion is not scoped to SMS reminders
body: The new deleteMany uses an OR where the second branch is just `retryCount: { gt: 1 }` with no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, unlike the first branch. `retryCount` lives on the shared `WorkflowReminder` table used by EMAIL and WHATSAPP reminders too. Today only this SMS cron increments the counter, but any other code path (e.g. the email reminder cron adopting the same column, or a backfill) that raises retryCount above 1 on a non-SMS reminder will cause those reminders to be silently deleted by the SMS cron before they are ever sent. The retryCount clause should include `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` to match the stated intent of the change.

title: retryCount update inside catch block can throw and abort the whole cron run
body: Previously the catch block only logged the error, so a failure for one reminder could never stop the loop. Now the catch block performs `prisma.workflowReminder.update` unguarded. If that update itself fails — e.g. the row was deleted concurrently by another cron execution or by a booking cancellation, or the DB connection is the very thing that failed — the exception propagates out of the catch, the for-loop terminates, all remaining unscheduled reminders are skipped for this run, and the handler returns a 500. The retry-count write in the catch should be wrapped in its own try/catch (or the loop should continue on failure) so one bad reminder cannot starve the rest.

title: retryCount incremented via read-modify-write on a stale snapshot
body: Both failure paths set `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` using the value read at the start of the run. If two cron executions overlap (possible when a run takes longer than the cron interval), both read the same retryCount and both write the same incremented value, so a failure is not counted and deletion is delayed. Using Prisma's atomic `retryCount: { increment: 1 }` avoids the lost update without changing the logic.

title: No tests covering the new retry/delete behavior
body: This PR introduces user-facing behavioral changes — reminders are deleted after two failed scheduling attempts, including via the catch-all error path — but adds no tests. There is nothing verifying that a reminder is deleted exactly after two failures (retryCount boundary `gt: 1`), that a reminder that fails once is retried and can still succeed, or that deterministic errors (e.g. template rendering throwing) also count toward deletion. A regression here silently drops customer SMS reminders, so at least the retry-count boundary and the delete query scope should be covered.

title: Retry-based deletion is not scoped to SMS reminders
body: The new second branch of the deleteMany OR ({ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }) has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, unlike the first branch which is explicitly SMS-scoped. This cron endpoint is SMS-only (the file header says so and the fetch below only selects SMS reminders), but the delete will now remove ANY WorkflowReminder row with retryCount > 1, including EMAIL or WHATSAPP reminders. It also ignores the `scheduled` flag, so even an already-scheduled reminder with retryCount > 1 would be deleted. Today only this file increments retryCount (and only for SMS rows), so the impact is latent, but the moment any other scheduler (e.g., the email reminder cron) starts using retryCount, this job will silently delete those reminders. The retryCount condition should be ANDed with `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` (and probably `scheduled: false`).

title: Unprotected prisma.update inside catch can abort the whole run
body: The catch block now performs `await prisma.workflowReminder.update({ where: { id: reminder.id }, ... })` without its own error handling. If that update itself throws — for example because the reminder row was deleted between the findMany and this update (the deleteMany at the top of a concurrent cron run can remove it), or because of a transient DB error — the exception escapes the catch, breaks out of the `for` loop entirely, and all remaining unscheduled reminders in the batch are skipped while the endpoint returns a 500. Previously the catch only logged, so one failing reminder never affected the rest of the batch. The increment in the catch should be wrapped in its own try/catch (or use updateMany which won't throw on a missing row).

title: Read-modify-write retryCount instead of atomic increment
body: Both retry updates use `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1`, computed from the value read at the start of the run. If two cron executions overlap (this endpoint is triggered by an external cron and has no locking), both can read retryCount = 0 and both write 1, losing an increment and extending the retry loop beyond the intended two attempts. Prisma supports an atomic `retryCount: { increment: 1 }` which avoids the stale-read problem entirely. Same issue at line 195 in the catch block.

title: Any transient error counts toward permanent deletion after only two attempts
body: The catch block wraps the entire per-reminder body, so retryCount is incremented for any failure — not just SMS scheduling failures. For example, a transient database hiccup in `prisma.profile.findFirst` (line 111) or `getBookerBaseUrl` (line 119) increments retryCount just the same as an invalid phone number. Combined with the hard deletion at retryCount > 1, two consecutive transient failures (e.g., a brief Twilio or DB outage spanning two cron runs) permanently delete reminders whose scheduledDate may still be days away and which would have succeeded on a later run. Consider only counting actual send failures, or using a higher threshold / not deleting reminders whose scheduledDate is still in the future.

title: Comment above deleteMany no longer matches the query
body: The comment still reads 'delete all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date', but the query now also deletes unscheduled reminders (of any method) whose retryCount exceeds 1. The stale comment misleads future readers about what this cleanup does; it should be updated to describe both deletion conditions.

title: Retry-based deletion is not scoped to SMS reminders
body: The new second branch of the deleteMany OR clause is `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` with no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, unlike the first branch. This means any WorkflowReminder of any method (EMAIL, WHATSAPP) whose retryCount ever exceeds 1 will be deleted by this SMS cron, regardless of its scheduledDate. Today only this handler increments retryCount so the blast radius is limited, but the query no longer matches its stated purpose ('delete all scheduled sms reminders...'), and as soon as any other code path (e.g. an email retry mechanism) writes retryCount, this cron will silently delete those reminders. The retryCount condition should be ANDed with `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`.

title: retryCount update inside catch block can throw and abort the entire cron run
body: The catch block now awaits `prisma.workflowReminder.update` to increment retryCount. If the original error was caused by a database problem (connection loss, timeout), this update will also fail; likewise it throws a P2025 if the reminder row was already deleted (e.g. by a concurrently running cron invocation's deleteMany). Because the await sits directly in the catch handler with no nested try/catch, the exception propagates out of the loop, aborts processing of all remaining reminders, and returns a 500. Before this PR the catch only logged, so a single failing reminder was isolated. The increment should be wrapped in its own try/catch (or use a fire-and-forget update with error handling) so one bad reminder cannot kill the whole batch.

title: retryCount incremented via stale read instead of atomic increment
body: Both failure paths set `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` using the value read at the start of the run. If two cron invocations overlap (or the same reminder is otherwise updated between read and write), one increment is lost and the reminder gets more retry attempts than the intended two. Prisma supports an atomic update via `data: { retryCount: { increment: 1 } }`, which avoids the read-modify-write race entirely.

title: Comment above deleteMany no longer describes the query
body: The comment 'delete all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date' still sits above a deleteMany that now also deletes any reminder with retryCount > 1 (of any method, any scheduledDate). The comment misleads future readers about what the query removes and should be updated to cover the retry-based deletion.

title: `ANY(${array})` with Prisma.sql renders invalid SQL — org/team scope queries will throw at runtime
body: In `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition` (line 164 and 168) and `buildTeamAuthorizationCondition` (line 201) the code writes e.g. `Prisma.sql`("teamId" = ANY(${teamIds}))``. Prisma's tagged-template helper expands an interpolated JavaScript array into a comma-separated list of bound parameters — it does NOT serialize it as a single Postgres array parameter. So with `teamIds = [10, 20, 30]` the emitted SQL is `"teamId" = ANY($1, $2, $3)`, which Postgres rejects with `syntax error at or near "$2"` (ANY requires a single array expression or subquery). Every org-scope and team-scope query will therefore fail with a raw-query error at runtime; only the user-scope path (which has no ANY) is valid. The correct pattern is `"teamId" IN (${Prisma.join(teamIds)})` or passing a single array parameter with an explicit cast. The tests don't catch this because they only structurally compare Sql objects built with the same broken pattern.

title: Public `findMany` method removed without updating callers
body: The previous implementation exposed a public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method that combined authorization/filter conditions into a `bookingTimeStatusDenormalized.findMany` call. This PR deletes that method entirely and replaces it with `getBaseConditions(): Promise<Prisma.Sql>`, shifting query execution to callers via `$queryRaw`. No caller is updated in this PR (only the service and its test are changed), so any existing consumer that invokes `insightsBookingService.findMany(...)` — e.g. the insights tRPC procedures that fetch booking events/status/hourly data — will fail TypeScript compilation and lose functionality. Either keep a compatible `findMany` wrapper or update all callers in the same change.

title: Integration tests never execute the generated SQL for org/team scopes
body: The org-scope (line 332) and team-scope (line 295) tests assert conditions via `expect(conditions).toEqual(Prisma.sql`...`)`, which only deep-compares the Sql object's internal `strings`/`values` arrays — it never runs the SQL against the database. The only test that actually executes a query (`getBaseConditions`, line 481) uses scope `"user"`, the one code path that contains no `ANY(...)` array interpolation. As a result the tests pass while the org/team SQL is syntactically invalid (Prisma expands `ANY(${ids})` into `ANY($1, $2, ...)`, a Postgres syntax error). At least one test per scope should execute the produced conditions with `$queryRaw` against the real database so invalid generated SQL is caught.

title: Org-scope expectation depends on nondeterministic row ordering for userIds
body: The org-scope test asserts exact equality with `Prisma.sql`... ("userId" = ANY(${[user.id, user2.id, user3.id]})) ...`. The service builds that array from `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds`, a `findMany` with no `orderBy`, so Postgres does not guarantee the row order (the user also has two memberships — team and org — that get deduped via `Set`, preserving whatever order rows came back in). If the membership rows are returned in a different order, the Sql `values` array order differs and the deep-equality assertion fails spuriously. The assertion should compare order-insensitively or the repository query should impose a deterministic order.

title: Public findMany() method removed without migrating or even checking callers
body: The PR deletes the service's only data-access method, `findMany(findManyArgs)`, and replaces it with `getBaseConditions()`, which just returns a raw SQL fragment. It also changes the constructor's accepted options type from `InsightsBookingServiceOptions` to the new `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions`. No other files are changed in this PR, so any existing consumer of `InsightsBookingService` (router, handler, repository, or an interface the class implements) that calls `.findMany(...)` will fail to compile, and consumers now have to hand-write `$queryRaw` queries themselves. Before merging, verify every caller of this service has been migrated (or keep a `findMany` that composes the raw query internally); if callers are migrated in a stacked PR, that dependency should be explicit, otherwise this is a breaking change.

title: Authorization/filter SQL fragments are returned unparenthesized, so ANDing extra predicates silently changes semantics
body: `getAuthorizationConditions()` for team/org scope returns a top-level `OR` expression like `("teamId" = ...) AND ("isTeamBooking" = true)) OR (("userId" = ANY(...)) AND ("isTeamBooking" = false)` with no outer parentheses, and `getBaseConditions()` returns that auth fragment bare whenever there are no filters (`return authConditions`). Likewise `getFilterConditions()` returns `("eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)` unwrapped. The old object-notation API merged conditions via Prisma `AND` arrays, so callers could safely add their own predicates; with the new raw-SQL API, any caller that writes `WHERE ${baseConditions} AND "createdAt" >= ...` (the natural way to add date-range filtering in insights) gets `A OR B AND ...` which parses as `A OR (B AND ...)`, silently broadening the result set beyond the authorized scope — a potential data-exposure bug. Wrap the final reduced auth and filter expressions in parentheses (e.g. `Prisma.sql`(${combined})``) so the fragments are safely composable.

title: Caching tests for authorization and filter conditions deleted while the caching code remains
body: The PR removes the entire "Caching" describe block ("should cache authorization conditions" and "should cache filter conditions") from the integration tests. The service still implements and relies on that behavior via `cachedAuthConditions` / `cachedFilterConditions` in `getAuthorizationConditions()` and `getFilterConditions()`. Rather than updating the two assertions to the new `Prisma.sql` format (they would only have needed the expected value changed, since the second call returning the cached object is format-agnostic), the coverage was dropped entirely, leaving the memoization logic untested. Restore equivalent tests asserting that a second call returns the identical cached `Prisma.Sql` instance.

title: findMany() removed without updating any callers
body: This PR removes the public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method from InsightsBookingService and replaces it with `getBaseConditions()`, which returns a raw `Prisma.Sql` fragment. The service no longer exposes any method that actually executes a query — consumers must now call `getBaseConditions()` and embed the result in their own `$queryRaw` (as the new test does). However, the PR only touches this service file and its test file; no consumer (e.g., the insights tRPC router or wherever this service is used to list bookings) is updated. If any existing caller still invokes `service.findMany(...)`, the TypeScript build will fail; if callers were expected to migrate, that migration is missing from this PR. Verify all consumers of InsightsBookingService are updated or confirm none exist before merging.

title: Org/team scope authorization SQL is never executed against the database
body: The tests for org-scope (line 332-343) and team-scope (line 295-299) authorization conditions only assert structural equality of the generated `Prisma.Sql` object; they never run the SQL. The only test that actually executes a query via `$queryRaw` (the `getBaseConditions` test) uses user scope, which contains only `"userId" = $1 AND "teamId" IS NULL`. As a result, the `= ANY(${array})` parameterization and the `isTeamBooking` column reference used exclusively in org/team scope are never validated — a wrong column name, bad array binding, or syntax error there would only surface at runtime in production, in the authorization-critical path. Previously the object-notation conditions were type-checked by Prisma (`BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedWhereInput`); raw SQL strings get no such checking, so execution coverage matters more. Compounding this, the PR description states the author could not run the tests at all. Add an integration test that executes the org-scope and team-scope conditions against the real database.

title: Org-scope assertion depends on row order of an unordered DB query
body: The org-scope test asserts the generated SQL equals `... "userId" = ANY(${[user.id, user2.id, user3.id]}) ...`, i.e. it requires the user IDs to appear in exactly that order inside the `Prisma.Sql` values array. That order comes from `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds`, which applies no `ORDER BY`, so Postgres is free to return membership rows in any order (e.g., after index changes or table growth). Any reordering makes `toEqual` fail even though the generated SQL is semantically identical, making this test flaky. Either sort the IDs before asserting, or compare the values order-insensitively (e.g., sort the `values` array before comparison).

title: Caching behavior tests removed while caching logic remains in the service
body: This PR deletes the entire 'Caching' describe block (the two tests verifying that repeated calls to `getAuthorizationConditions()` and `getFilterConditions()` return cached results), but the caching implementation (`cachedAuthConditions` / `cachedFilterConditions` fields and the `undefined` check in `getAuthorizationConditions`/`getFilterConditions`) is still present in the service. If the caching is intentional, its regression coverage is lost; if it is no longer needed, the fields and checks should be removed instead. Note the caching uses `undefined` as the sentinel while `cachedFilterConditions` can be `null`, so the distinction matters and is worth keeping under test.

title: PR description misrepresents the change as test-only
body: The PR description states: 'This PR updates the InsightsBookingService integration tests to work with the new Prisma.sql format that was previously converted in the service implementation.' In fact, the diff converts the service implementation itself in this PR (replacing `Prisma.BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedWhereInput` with `Prisma.sql`, removing `findMany`, adding `getBaseConditions`, changing the constructor's options type, and reworking `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition`/`buildTeamAuthorizationCondition`). Reviewers relying on the description may skip reviewing the service change, which is the higher-risk part (raw SQL in an authorization path). The description should be corrected to state that this PR performs the service conversion plus the test update.

title: deleteCache mutation never invalidates the connectedCalendars query, leaving stale cache status on screen
body: The deleteCache mutation's onSuccess only shows a toast and calls the optional onSuccess prop (onChanged). Unlike the disconnect mutation right below it (which explicitly invalidates viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars and viewer.apps.integrations in onSettled), nothing refetches connectedCalendars after a cache delete. The cacheUpdatedAt value that drives the 'Cache Status' display and the 'Delete cached data' menu item comes from that query, so after a successful deletion the UI will continue to show the old cache timestamp and offer deletion again until something else triggers a refetch — and in usages where onChanged is not provided it never updates. Add utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate() to the deleteCache mutation's onSettled.

title: getCacheStatusByCredentialIds counts expired cache rows as active cache
body: The new groupBy query aggregates over all CalendarCache rows for the given credentials with no expiresAt filter. Everywhere else the cache is read (getCachedAvailability) rows are only served when expiresAt >= now, so an expired row is functionally dead. But connectedCalendars.handler uses this method to compute cacheUpdatedAt, which the UI uses to decide whether to show 'Cache Status: Last updated ...' and the 'Delete cached data' action. A credential whose only cache rows expired weeks ago will still be presented as having an active cache with a misleading 'last updated' timestamp. The where clause should include expiresAt: { gte: new Date() } to match the read path semantics.

title: Handler throws a generic Error, surfacing as HTTP 500 instead of a proper tRPC error code
body: When the credential does not exist or belongs to another user, the handler throws `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. In tRPC a plain Error is converted into an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (500) response, which misleads clients and error monitoring into treating an expected authorization/not-found case as a server crash. The rest of the codebase uses TRPCError with code "NOT_FOUND" or "FORBIDDEN" for these cases; this should too.

title: dev:cron now uses npx tsx but tsx is not a declared dependency
body: The script was changed from `ts-node cron-tester.ts` to `npx tsx cron-tester.ts`, but tsx does not appear in dependencies or devDependencies of this package (ts-node is still declared). `npx tsx` will fetch an unpinned tsx version from the registry on each fresh machine, which fails in offline/restricted environments, is non-deterministic across developers, and can break under yarn 3 PnP setups. Add tsx as a pinned devDependency and invoke it via yarn, or keep ts-node.

title: Script uses macOS-only sed syntax and a CWD-relative .env path
body: `sed -i '' -E ...` is the BSD/macOS form of in-place edit; on GNU sed (Linux, including CI containers and most dev VMs) the empty string is interpreted as a file name and the command errors out, so the script silently fails to update GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL for Linux users. Additionally ENV_FILE="../.env" only resolves correctly if the script happens to be invoked from inside the scripts/ directory; running it from the repo root creates/updates a .env one level above the repository. Use a portable sed invocation (e.g. `sed -i.bak` plus cleanup, or detect GNU vs BSD) and resolve ENV_FILE relative to the script's own location.

title: Cache timestamp is hardcoded to en-US formatting regardless of the user's locale
body: The 'Last updated' timestamp is formatted with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)`, so every user — including those with a different app locale and different date conventions (day/month ordering, 24h clock) — sees a US-formatted date. The formatter should use the user's locale (available via useLocale / i18n.language) or the browser default by omitting the locale argument.

title: No tests for the new deleteCache mutation's ownership check or the cache-status repository method
body: This PR adds a destructive, user-facing mutation (deleteCache) whose only protection is the userId ownership check in the handler, plus a new repository aggregation (getCacheStatusByCredentialIds) that drives what the UI displays. Neither has any test coverage: there is no test that a user cannot delete another user's credential cache (the security-critical path), nor any test covering the groupBy/mapping behavior. Given this is a security-sensitive destructive endpoint, at minimum the authorization failure case and the happy path should be covered.

title: connectedCalendars handler bypasses the feature-flag/mock and queries calendarCache unconditionally
body: The handler instantiates `new CalendarCacheRepository()` directly and calls `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds()` on every `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` query. Everywhere else in the codebase the repository is obtained via `CalendarCache.init(null)`, which returns `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` when the calendar-cache feature flag is disabled. By constructing the repository directly, this handler (a) runs an extra `groupBy` query against the `CalendarCache` table on every calendar-settings page load even for instances/teams where the feature is off, and (b) makes the newly added `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds()` implementation on the mock dead code — the mock will never be consulted here. Use the same init/feature-flag path as the rest of the calendar-cache code so the query is skipped when the feature is disabled.

title: UserWithCalendars type widened to require updatedAt/googleChannelId that nothing in this module consumes
body: `UserWithCalendars` now requires `updatedAt` and `googleChannelId` on both `allSelectedCalendars` and `userLevelSelectedCalendars`, but neither field is read anywhere in `getConnectedDestinationCalendarsAndEnsureDefaultsInDb` or its helpers in this file (the only consumer of the new `updatedAt` write is the frontend reading `CalendarCache.updatedAt` instead, per the PR's own notes). Only `findUnlockedUserForSession` was updated to select the new fields; any other caller of this widely-used function (it is re-exported as `getConnectedDestinationCalendars` for `@calcom/platform-libraries`, plus tests/fixtures constructing this type) that builds the user object without these fields will now fail type-checking. Either consume the fields or revert the type widening to avoid a needless contract break.

title: deleteCache handler throws a generic Error instead of a TRPCError
body: When the credential is not found or doesn't belong to the user, the handler does `throw new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. tRPC converts a generic `Error` into an `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR` (HTTP 500), so clients see a server error for what is actually a not-found/forbidden condition, and it may get reported as an unexpected server fault. Throw a `TRPCError` with code `NOT_FOUND` (or `FORBIDDEN`) to match the convention used elsewhere in the codebase.

title: Unconditional empty updateMany write to bump SelectedCalendar.updatedAt whose value is never read
body: `fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache` now ends with `await SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})`, an `updateMany` with empty data whose only effect is to touch `updatedAt` on every SelectedCalendar row for the credential. This runs on the webhook/cache-refresh hot path, yet the PR description itself notes that `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` is not displayed or read anywhere (the UI uses `CalendarCache.updatedAt` via `cacheUpdatedAt`). This is a dead write on a hot path; either remove it or wire it to an actual consumer before merging. Additionally, the method's parameter is typed `Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateInput` while `updateMany` expects `SelectedCalendarUpdateManyMutationInput` — it only compiles because `{}` is passed; any real payload with relation fields would be a type error.

title: Dev script uses macOS-only `sed -i ''` and a cwd-relative .env path
body: Two portability/correctness issues in the new helper script: (1) `sed -i '' -E ...` is BSD/macOS syntax — on GNU/Linux `sed -i ''` treats the empty string as a filename and the script fails with "can't read : No such file or directory", so the script silently breaks for Linux developers. (2) `ENV_FILE="../.env"` is resolved relative to the caller's current working directory, not the script's location; running it from anywhere other than the `scripts/` directory will create or modify a `.env` in an unintended parent directory. Resolve the env file relative to the script's own path (e.g. via `$(dirname "$0")`).

title: Cache 'last updated' timestamp hardcoded to en-US locale
body: The cache status line formats the timestamp with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)`, ignoring the user's configured locale even though `useLocale()` is already available in the component. Non-US users will see US date/time formatting in a user-facing settings page, inconsistent with the rest of the app. Pass the user's locale (e.g. `i18n.language` from `useLocale`) or use the app's existing date-formatting helpers.

title: deleteCacheMutation never invalidates connectedCalendars, leaving stale cache status in the UI
body: The deleteCache mutation's onSuccess only shows a toast and calls the optional onSuccess prop; unlike the disconnectMutation in the same file (which explicitly invalidates viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars and viewer.apps.integrations in onSettled), it does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query. After the user deletes the cache, the dropdown will still show the 'Cache Status / Last updated' entry and the 'Delete cached data' action until some parent happens to refetch, because cacheUpdatedAt comes from the connectedCalendars query data. Add utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate() (e.g. in onSettled) so the UI reflects the deletion.

title: getCacheStatusByCredentialIds reports expired cache rows as valid cache status
body: The groupBy query that powers the 'Cache Status' display does not filter on expiresAt, while the actual cache read path (getCachedAvailability) only serves rows with expiresAt >= now. A credential whose cache entries have all expired will still show 'Last updated: <timestamp>' and offer 'Delete cached data' in the UI, even though that data will never be served as a cache hit. The where clause should include expiresAt: { gte: new Date() } so the displayed status matches what the cache actually serves.

title: ENV_FILE="../.env" is resolved relative to the caller's working directory, not the script location
body: The script sets ENV_FILE="../.env", which is evaluated relative to wherever the developer runs the script from. Running the documented path from the repo root (./scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh) would create or modify a .env file in the directory above the repository instead of the repo's .env; conversely running it from inside scripts/ targets apps' parent incorrectly unless the layout matches exactly. It should resolve the path from the script's own directory, e.g. ENV_FILE="$(dirname "$0")/../.env".

title: sed -i '' is macOS-only and fails on GNU sed (Linux)
body: The script uses `sed -i '' -E ...`, which is the BSD/macOS syntax. On Linux (GNU sed), `-i ''` is interpreted as an in-place edit with the empty string treated as a filename argument, producing 'No such file or directory' and failing to update GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL. Since this script is committed for all developers, use a portable approach (e.g. `sed -i.bak -E ... file && rm file.bak`) or detect the platform.

title: Access-denied case throws a plain Error instead of a TRPCError
body: When the credential does not exist or belongs to another user, the handler throws `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. tRPC maps plain Errors to INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (HTTP 500) rather than a meaningful NOT_FOUND/FORBIDDEN code, so clients and monitoring see a server error for what is really a client/authz failure, and error-message handling on the client can't distinguish it from an actual crash. Throw `new TRPCError({ code: "NOT_FOUND" })` (or FORBIDDEN) instead.

title: Cache timestamp is formatted with a hardcoded "en-US" locale, ignoring the user's locale
body: The 'Last updated' timestamp is formatted with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)` regardless of the user's configured locale, so non-US users see US date/time conventions (e.g. MM/DD/YYYY) in an otherwise localized UI. Use the locale from useLocale()/i18n or pass undefined to Intl.DateTimeFormat so the browser/user locale is respected.

title: No tests for the deleteCache mutation or the new repository status method
body: This PR adds a mutation that deletes CalendarCache rows based on credential ownership, and a new getCacheStatusByCredentialIds repository method feeding the UI, but includes no tests. The ownership check (a user must not be able to delete cache for a credential they don't own, including negative in-memory delegation credential IDs) and the groupBy mapping are exactly the kind of logic that should be covered; the PR description's own checklist relies on manual end-to-end testing instead. At minimum, add a handler-level test covering success, wrong-owner, and nonexistent-credential cases.

title: One failing SendGrid cancel aborts the whole cancellation batch and drops all DB deletes
body: In the new cancellation block of the cron handler, the `await client.request(...)` to SendGrid is inside the `for` loop but the whole loop is wrapped in a single try/catch. If the SendGrid request fails for any one reminder (e.g. a stale/invalid `referenceId` batch_id, which returns an error from SendGrid), the loop exits immediately: (a) all remaining `remindersToCancel` never get their SendGrid cancellation posted, so those emails will still be sent even though the bookings were cancelled — the exact bug this PR is meant to fix; and (b) the `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` promises collected in `workflowRemindersToDelete` are never awaited, and since Prisma promises are lazy, those deletes never execute. Because the failing row is never deleted, it will abort the loop again on every subsequent cron run (every 15 min), permanently blocking cancellations for all reminders that happen to sort after it (the query has no orderBy). Each reminder's SendGrid call and DB delete needs its own error handling so a single bad record can't block the batch.

title: Reschedule path cancels SendGrid sends immediately and orphans the reminder rows, re-introducing the 100-pending-cancellations problem
body: When a booking is rescheduled, the old booking's email reminders are cancelled via `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)` with `immediateDelete=true`. That path POSTs the `status: "cancel"` to SendGrid right away — for reminders that may be scheduled days in the future — which is exactly the behavior this PR identifies as the root cause of hitting SendGrid's max of 100 pending cancellations (pending cancellations accumulate until the scheduled date). Additionally, the immediateDelete path neither deletes the `WorkflowReminder` row nor sets `cancelled: true`, so the row lingers with `scheduled: true` and is invisible to the cron's `cancelled: true` cleanup; it only disappears when the generic `scheduledDate <= now` deleteMany runs after the send date. For consistency with the fix, the reschedule path should mark `cancelled: true` (like the cancel path in handleCancelBooking) and let the cron perform the SendGrid cancellation inside the final hour. Also note the whole forEach is fire-and-forget, so the surrounding try/catch can never catch errors from these async calls.

title: Reminder cancellation writes are fire-and-forget and may be lost before commit
body: Previously the cancel handler collected `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany(...)` promises into `remindersToDelete` and awaited them in `Promise.all`. The new code calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...)` inside a `forEach` without awaiting anything. The `cancelled: true` update (or row delete) therefore happens in the background after the response may already have been sent; in a serverless deployment the lambda can be frozen once the response completes, so the flag may never be written — in which case the cron never cancels the SendGrid send and the reminder email is still delivered, re-creating the bug this PR fixes. The calls should be collected and awaited (the same applies to the identical new pattern in `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx` requestReschedule and `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/workflows.tsx`).

title: Paid cancelled bookings return early and never cancel their workflow reminders
body: When a paid booking is cancelled, the handler refunds the payment, sets the booking status to REJECTED, and returns early at `return { message: "Booking successfully cancelled." }` — before reaching the new "Workflows - cancel all reminders for cancelled bookings" block further down (which calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder`). As a result, workflow reminders for refunded/cancelled paid bookings are neither flagged `cancelled` nor deleted, and SendGrid will still send the scheduled reminder emails — the exact issue this PR is meant to resolve, still reproducible for any paid event type. The reminder cancellation should happen before (or independent of) the paid-booking early return.

title: requestReschedule cancels reminders without awaiting them
body: In the `requestReschedule` mutation, the old code collected `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany` promises and awaited them via `Promise.all(remindersToDelete)`. The new code calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...)` in a `forEach` without awaiting. The mutation can complete and the serverless invocation can be torn down before the `cancelled: true` updates / deletes commit, leaving reminders active for a booking that was cancelled for rescheduling, so the cron never cancels them and emails may still be sent. The calls should be awaited.

title: Reminder-cancellation calls are fire-and-forget; the cancelled flag may never be persisted
body: In the cancellation flow, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` are invoked inside `Array.forEach` without being awaited. The whole fix depends on the `workflowReminder.update({ data: { cancelled: true } })` (or row delete) inside those async functions actually completing. The previous implementation collected the Prisma `deleteMany` promises and awaited them in `Promise.all`; now nothing is awaited, so the handler can return (and on serverless platforms like Vercel the function can be frozen) before the DB writes run, silently leaving reminders un-cancelled — the exact bug this PR fixes. The same un-awaited pattern was introduced at the other call sites: `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx` (requestReschedule, ~line 490), `packages/features/bookings/lib/handleNewBooking.ts` (~line 966) and `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/workflows.tsx` (lines 212-218, 376-382, 519-525, 574-580). These should be collected into an array of promises and awaited.

title: immediateDelete path cancels in SendGrid but leaves stale DB rows and long-lived pending cancellations
body: When `immediateDelete` is true, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` only POSTs the cancel to SendGrid and returns — it neither deletes the `WorkflowReminder` row nor sets `cancelled: true`. For the workflow-delete and step-delete callers this is masked by the DB cascade, but in the reschedule path (`packages/features/bookings/lib/handleNewBooking.ts` line 968) the old booking's reminder rows stay in the database with `scheduled=true`, `cancelled=null` until their `scheduledDate` passes and the cron's past-date `deleteMany` happens to remove them. Worse, the reschedule path still cancels immediately in SendGrid for sends up to 72h out, and per the PR description such pending cancellations sit in SendGrid's `scheduled_sends` until the scheduled date and count toward the 100-pending-cancellations limit — the exact limit whose exhaustion caused this bug. Reschedules should use the same deferred mechanism (set `cancelled=true`, let the cron cancel within the final hour, and delete/flag the row) instead of `immediateDelete`.

title: One failing SendGrid request aborts cancellation of all remaining reminders in that cron run
body: In the new cancellation block, the `for` loop awaits `client.request(...)` sequentially, and any thrown error breaks out of the loop into the outer `catch`, skipping all not-yet-processed reminders in `remindersToCancel`. Additionally, the Prisma delete promises already accumulated for successfully cancelled reminders are never awaited in that case, so those rows are not deleted either (Prisma promises are lazy and only execute when awaited). This self-heals on the next cron run only as long as the reminders' `scheduledDate` has not passed; a reminder near the end of its 1-hour window whose cancellation request repeatedly fails (or is unlucky behind a failing one) will be sent by SendGrid. Consider wrapping each reminder's cancel+delete in its own try/catch so one failure doesn't affect the rest.

title: One failing SendGrid cancel aborts cancellation of all remaining reminders, and the failure is swallowed
body: The new cancellation block wraps the entire `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop in a single try/catch. If any single `client.request` to SendGrid throws (e.g., a 404 for a batch_id that was already removed, a rate limit, or a transient network error) or any `prisma.workflowReminder.delete` rejects (e.g., the row was concurrently deleted), the loop exits immediately and every reminder after the failing one is never cancelled at SendGrid and never deleted. The catch only does `console.log` and the handler still returns 200, so there is no alerting or retry signal. A single poisoned row (e.g., a stale cancelled reminder whose batch no longer exists) will therefore block cancellation of all other cancelled reminders on every cron run until their scheduledDate passes — at which point SendGrid sends the emails anyway, re-creating the exact bug this PR is meant to fix. Error handling should be per-reminder (try/catch inside the loop) so one failure cannot starve the rest.

title: Reschedule path bypasses the new deferred-cancellation mechanism and uses the SendGrid endpoint with the 100-pending-cancellation cap
body: In the reschedule flow, old booking email reminders are cancelled via `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)` with `immediateDelete = true`. That path (emailReminderManager.ts) calls SendGrid's `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` with `status: cancel` immediately — the very endpoint whose 100 pending-cancellations limit is the documented root cause of issue #7225 — and then returns without setting `cancelled: true` or deleting the row. If the SendGrid call fails (cap reached, transient error), the error is only logged and the WorkflowReminder row is left in the DB with `cancelled = null`, so the cron job in scheduleEmailReminders (which only processes `cancelled: true` rows) will never cancel it and the reminder email will still be sent for the rescheduled booking. The PR title explicitly claims to fix reminders for rescheduled bookings, but this path has no fallback. It should use the same deferred mechanism (set `cancelled: true`, let the cron cancel within the 1-hour window) as the booking-cancellation paths.

title: Reminder cancellation calls are fire-and-forget async calls that may never complete before the response
body: The reminder-cancellation loops call the async functions `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` inside `forEach` without awaiting them (same pattern also in handleNewBooking.ts:966, trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx:488, and trpc/server/routers/viewer/workflows.tsx:212, 376, 519, 574). With this PR the critical effect of these calls is a database write — setting `cancelled: true` — because the cron job only cancels SendGrid sends for rows with that flag. In a serverless environment the function can be frozen as soon as the response is sent, so the un-awaited `prisma.workflowReminder.update` may never execute; the reminder then keeps `cancelled = null`, the cron never cancels it, and the email is still sent — silently reintroducing the bug intermittently. The old code at least awaited the reminder deletions via `Promise.all(remindersToDelete)`; that awaiting was removed in this PR. Use `for...of` with `await` or collect the promises and `await Promise.all(...)`.

title: immediateDelete path cancels at SendGrid but leaves the WorkflowReminder row in the database
body: When `immediateDelete` is true, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` issues the SendGrid cancel request and returns early without deleting the WorkflowReminder row. In the handleNewBooking reschedule path nothing else cleans those rows up (there is no cascade, since the old booking and its reminders are kept), so stale rows with `scheduled = true`, a live `referenceId`, and `cancelled = null` accumulate until the cron's past-scheduledDate cleanup eventually removes them. Besides the data hygiene issue, this also means that if the SendGrid call fails there is no marker on the row that would let the cron retry the cancellation.

title: SendGrid cancellations are awaited sequentially in the cron loop
body: Each `await client.request(...)` to SendGrid is performed sequentially inside the `for` loop over `remindersToCancel`. On a busy instance with a large backlog of cancelled reminders (which is exactly the situation that motivated this fix), hundreds of serialized HTTP calls at ~100-300ms each can exceed the serverless function timeout, terminating the run mid-loop and leaving the remaining reminders uncancelled (and, per the outer try/catch, without any failure signal). The requests should be batched/parallelized (e.g., with a concurrency limit) so the cron reliably finishes within its execution window.

title: New `cancelled` column is nullable with no default instead of `Boolean @default(false)`
body: The migration adds `"cancelled" BOOLEAN` with no default and no NOT NULL, and the schema declares `cancelled Boolean?`. This creates a tri-state field (null/false/true) where the code only ever distinguishes `true` from everything else, and all existing rows remain NULL forever. It should be a non-nullable `Boolean @default(false)` (migration: `ADD COLUMN "cancelled" BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false`) to keep the data model unambiguous and consistent with the rest of the schema's boolean flags.

title: Recurring-event calendar deletions are never awaited and may never start
body: In the recurring-event cancellation branch, the code does `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })`. Because `getCalendar` is now async (dynamic import), the entire body of the forEach callback — including the very first `calendar.deleteEvent(...)` call — is deferred until after the dynamic import resolves. Previously `getCalendar` was synchronous, so the first `deleteEvent` was at least initiated synchronously inside the callback. The handler later does `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` (line 652) using the contents of `apiDeletes` at that moment, which is still empty/partial because the async callbacks haven't run yet, and then returns the response. On serverless platforms the function can be frozen once the response is sent, so the external calendar events for all remaining recurring booking instances may never be deleted, leaving stale events on users' calendars. The pushed values are also the awaited results rather than promises, so they were never going to be awaited anyway. Use `await Promise.all(credentials.map(async ...))` and push the actual promises before awaiting.

title: requestReschedule deletes calendar/video events fire-and-forget via async forEach
body: In the `requestReschedule` mutation, `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...); })` launches async work that nothing awaits. Before this PR `getCalendar` was synchronous, so `deleteEvent` was at least invoked synchronously inside the forEach; now the await on the dynamic import defers even the initiation of the deletion past the end of the mutation, and the mutation returns its response without waiting. In a serverless environment the deletions can be dropped entirely, leaving cancelled events on attendees' calendars, and any rejection (import failure, deleteEvent failure) becomes an unhandled promise rejection instead of being logged. Collect the promises and `await Promise.all(...)` (with individual `.catch` for logging) before sending the reschedule email/returning.

title: Calendar/video deletions run un-awaited inside async forEach; surrounding try/catch is now dead
body: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) })` fires off async callbacks that nothing awaits, and the function proceeds to send the reschedule email and return immediately. Previously `getCalendar` was synchronous so `deleteEvent` was at least initiated synchronously; with the new `await getCalendar(...)` the deletion isn't even started until the dynamic import resolves, which races with the function returning (risky in serverless, where the process can freeze after the response). Additionally, errors thrown inside these async callbacks — including dynamic-import failures — reject outside the surrounding try/catch (lines 124–139), producing unhandled rejections rather than the logged errors the catch block intends. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))` inside the try block.

title: Calendar/video deletions run un-awaited inside async forEach; surrounding try/catch is now dead
body: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) })` fires off async callbacks that nothing awaits, and the function proceeds to send the reschedule email and return immediately. Previously `getCalendar` was synchronous so `deleteEvent` was at least initiated synchronously; with the new `await getCalendar(...)` the deletion isn't even started until the dynamic import resolves, which races with the function returning (risky in serverless, where the process can freeze after the response). Additionally, errors thrown inside these async callbacks — including dynamic-import failures — reject outside the surrounding try/catch (lines 124–139), producing unhandled rejections rather than the logged errors the catch block intends. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))` inside the try block.

title: Dynamic imports are evaluated eagerly at module load, so nothing is actually lazy-loaded
body: Each entry like `applecalendar: import("./applecalendar")` is evaluated when the `@calcom/app-store` module itself is first imported, which immediately kicks off loading of every app's chunk. Because the import() expressions run at object-literal evaluation time (not on property access), importing this module anywhere starts fetching all ~28 app bundles at once — there is no per-app deferral, only code splitting. If the intent of the PR is to defer loading apps until they are used, the values need to be lazy thunks (e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) with call sites adjusted. As written, the change also converts app-module load failures into rejected promises stored in this object, which will surface as unhandled rejections for any app that is never explicitly awaited.

title: async forEach makes the surrounding try/catch dead and deletions fire-and-forget
body: The change turns `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach((bookingRef) => {...})` into `forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` so `getCalendar` can be awaited. Because `forEach` never awaits async callbacks, (1) the surrounding `try/catch` (lines 124-139) can no longer catch any error thrown after the first await — a failed dynamic import or a rejected `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` now escapes as an unhandled promise rejection, which on Node's default settings can terminate the server process; (2) the function proceeds to `sendRequestRescheduleEmail` and `return true` without waiting for the calendar/video deletions, so on serverless the response may complete (and the function be frozen) before the old events are removed, leaving stale events on attendees' calendars. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` and keep the try/catch around it.

title: async forEach makes the surrounding try/catch dead and deletions fire-and-forget
body: Identical to the vital app: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` was introduced to await the now-async `getCalendar`. `forEach` does not await async callbacks, so the `try/catch` around it (lines 124-139) is now dead code for anything that happens after the first `await`, and any rejection from `getCalendar`, `calendar.deleteEvent`, or `deleteMeeting` becomes an unhandled promise rejection. Additionally the reschedule email is sent and `true` returned before the deletions finish, so a failed or incomplete cleanup is silently ignored. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))`.

title: requestReschedule deletes calendar/video events in an un-awaited async forEach
body: In the `requestReschedule` mutation, `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` now awaits `getCalendar` inside the callback. `forEach` does not wait for async callbacks, so the mutation sends the reschedule email, fires the BOOKING_CANCELLED webhooks, and returns while the calendar event deletions (`calendar.deleteEvent`) and video deletions (`deleteMeeting`) may still be in flight — and any failure (e.g. the dynamic import rejecting) surfaces as an unhandled promise rejection with no logging or error handling at all, since there is no try/catch here. Previously at least `getCalendar` was synchronous so its errors propagated to the caller. Collect the promises and `await Promise.all(...)` (ideally with per-item error handling) before returning.

title: Dynamic imports are evaluated eagerly, so all app bundles still load at startup
body: The object literal `const appStore = { applecalendar: import("./applecalendar"), ... }` evaluates every `import()` call as soon as `@calcom/app-store` itself is imported, so all ~28 app chunks begin loading immediately for any process that touches this module — the same startup cost as the previous static imports, just with extra microtask hops. If the intent of the PR is to defer loading apps until they are actually used, this does not achieve it; the values should be thunks, e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`, with call sites invoking the function. As written the change adds async complexity to every consumer without the advertised loading benefit.

title: Recurring-event calendar deletions race with Promise.all(apiDeletes)
body: In the recurring-event cancellation branch, `bookingToDelete.user.credentials...forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent) })` pushes deletion results into `apiDeletes` from an un-awaited async callback. Later at the end of the handler the code does `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` (and `await apiDeletes` in the paid branch), which snapshots the array before these callbacks have finished — the new `await getCalendar(...)` suspends the callback at least until the dynamic import resolves, guaranteeing the push happens after forEach returns. The calendar deletions for recurring bookings are therefore never awaited: the handler can return and delete the booking references from the DB before (or without) the external calendar events being removed, and in serverless environments the floating promises may be frozen/terminated after the response is sent. Any failure in these deletions is also an unhandled promise rejection. Use a `for...of` loop (like the legacy branch below it was converted to) or collect the promises and await them.

title: async forEach callback escapes the surrounding try/catch
body: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) })` is wrapped in a `try { ... } catch (error) { logger.error(...) }` block, but that block can only catch synchronous throws. Previously `getCalendar` was synchronous, so errors thrown while constructing the CalendarService (or from the lookup) were caught and logged by this handler. Now any failure — dynamic import rejection, CalendarService constructor throw, or `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` rejection — becomes an unhandled promise rejection that bypasses the catch entirely; with Node's default unhandled-rejection behavior this can crash the process, and the reschedule flow reports success while calendar/video cancellations silently failed. Iterate with `for...of` and await, or use `Promise.allSettled(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))` inside the try.

title: async forEach callback escapes the surrounding try/catch
body: Same defect as the identical vital reschedule: the `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => ...)` sits inside a `try/catch` that logs errors, but once the callback is async and `getCalendar` is awaited, errors from the dynamic import, the CalendarService constructor, or the returned `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` promises are unhandled rejections that the catch block never sees. Before this change `getCalendar` was synchronous so its throws were caught here. The booking is already marked CANCELLED and the function returns `true` while these cancellations float, so failures are invisible and may crash the Node process under default unhandled-rejection settings. Await the work with `for...of` or `Promise.allSettled`.

title: Un-awaited async forEach in requestReschedule causes unhandled rejections
body: In the `requestReschedule` mutation, `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) / deleteMeeting(...) })` is fire-and-forget. Previously the callback was synchronous and `getCalendar` was sync, so a throw (e.g., from a CalendarService constructor) propagated out of the mutation and produced a proper tRPC error. Now import or deletion failures become unhandled promise rejections (potential process crash under Node defaults), and the mutation proceeds to send the reschedule email and fire BOOKING_CANCELLED webhooks without knowing whether the old calendar event / video meeting was actually deleted, leaving stale events on attendees' calendars. Await the loop with `for...of` or `Promise.allSettled`.

title: getCalendar promise discarded for non-calendar-variant apps
body: `getCalendarCredentials` still calls `getCalendar(credential)` unconditionally and then discards the result when `app.variant !== "calendar"` (`return app.variant === "calendar" ? [{ integration, app, credential, calendar }] : []`). Since `getCalendar` is now async and returns a promise, the discarded promise triggers the dynamic import anyway and, if that import rejects (chunk load failure) or the code inside throws, nothing ever observes it — producing an unhandled promise rejection. Only call `getCalendar` after checking the variant, e.g. `return app.variant === "calendar" ? [{ integration: app, credential, calendar: getCalendar(credential) }] : []`.

title: Top-level import() calls are evaluated eagerly, so nothing is actually lazy-loaded
body: Every entry in `appStore` is `import("./<app>")` written at module top level. Dynamic import expressions execute as soon as the containing module is evaluated, so all ~28 app chunks begin loading the moment anything imports `@calcom/app-store` — the same eager-loading behavior as the static imports this PR replaces, just wrapped in promises. The PR's stated goal of async/lazy loading of app packages is therefore not achieved; consumers only defer *awaiting* the chunks, not loading them, and if any chunk fails to load and that key is never awaited, the rejection is unhandled. To get real laziness, store thunks (`applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) and invoke them at the point of use.

title: Date-override days skip the busy-time check, enabling double bookings
body: In checkIfIsAvailable, when any date override matches the slot's day, `dateOverrideExist` is set to true and, if the slot falls inside the override window (so the `find` callback never returns true), the function hits `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }` — returning 'available' before the `busy.every(...)` check at the bottom ever runs. This means that on any day where a host has a date override, that host's existing bookings and calendar busy times are completely ignored. A fixed host (or a regular solo event user, since they are also isFixed) with a date override who already has a booking/meeting inside the override window will be shown as bookable, producing double bookings — the exact problem this PR claims to fix ('prevents round-robin events being booked where the fixed hosts are unavailable'). The busy check must still run when a date override exists; only the working-hours check should be bypassed.

title: `end` in the working-hours check is a copy-paste of `start`
body: In the new working-hours block of checkIfIsAvailable: `const start = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute(); const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` — `end` should be computed from `slotEndTime` (i.e. slotStartTime + eventLength). As written, end === start, so the check `end > workingHour.endTime` only verifies that the slot *starts* before the working-hours end. A slot that starts inside the fixed host's working hours but finishes after their end time (e.g. host available 09:00–12:00, a 60-minute slot at 11:30–12:30 contributed by another round-robin host's wider availability) passes the check and is bookable, letting invitees book time the fixed host is not available.

title: dayjs objects compared with `===` — always false
body: `if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes') === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, 'minutes'))` compares two distinct dayjs object instances by reference, which is always false (`.isSame()` was presumably intended). This branch exists to detect a blocked-day override (start === end, i.e. 'unavailable the whole day'). Because it never fires, a blocked day is only rejected incidentally via the before/after checks, and a slot starting exactly at the block's start instant satisfies none of them: the callback returns undefined, `dateOverrideExist` is already true, and the function returns `true` (available) — leaking a bookable slot on a day the host explicitly marked unavailable.

title: Multiple same-day date-override windows veto each other
body: The `dateOverrides.find(...)` logic treats 'slot is outside this one override window' as grounds to return false (unavailable), but a user can have several override windows on the same date (cal.com's UI allows adding multiple time ranges to one date override, stored as separate rows). For a slot that falls inside window B, window A's callback hits `slotStartTime.isAfter(date.end)` (or `slotEndTime.isBefore(date.start)`) and returns true, so the slot is marked unavailable even though it is within window B — and vice versa. Net effect: on a day with two or more override windows, every window is rejected by the other and the host shows no availability at all. The find should only return a 'reject' verdict after confirming the slot is outside *all* same-day windows for that user.

title: Override decoding depends on the server running in UTC
body: The new code decodes the override's wall-clock-encoded Date back to a real instant with `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes')` and compares it against `slotStartTime`/`slotEndTime`, which are explicitly UTC (`time.utc()`). `dayjs(date.start)` parses the Date in the process's local timezone, so the decode math (wall time − organizer offset = real UTC instant) only holds when the Node process runs with TZ=UTC. On any non-UTC runtime (dev machines, some CI/self-hosted setups) the override window and day-matching comparisons are shifted by the server offset, making fixed-host override filtering silently wrong. Use `dayjs.utc(date.start)` for these comparisons, as the parallel code in packages/lib/slots.ts already does with `.utc()`.

title: Offset-shifted override times discard the day component
body: The invitee-timezone conversion computes `startTime`/`endTime` as `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, 'minute').hour() * 60 + ...minute()`. Taking `.hour()/.minute()` after the offset shift drops any day rollover: when the invitee/organizer offset difference pushes the override across midnight (e.g. organizer Asia/Kolkata override 01:00–02:00 = 19:30–20:30 the previous UTC day, viewed by a UTC invitee: offset = −330 min lands on the previous day, but hour() yields 1170 minutes), the slot is materialized at 19:30 on the *current* invitee day instead of the correct adjacent day. Since the activeOverrides filter keys on the unshifted date, cross-midnight overrides are placed on the wrong day — precisely the timezone-adjustment scenario this PR is fixing. The shifted value should be carried as a full timestamp (or the day delta applied to startOfInviteeDay), not reduced to minutes-since-midnight.

title: override.timeZone is optional in the type but required by the conversion
body: `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` assumes `override.timeZone` is set, but the `TimeRange` type declares `timeZone?: string` as optional and getSlots is a shared library function — nothing at the type level guarantees every caller supplies it (the slots router happens to add it in this PR). With `timeZone` undefined, dayjs's tz plugin falls back to the host system's timezone when computing `organizerUtcOffset`, so the offset correction is silently computed against the server timezone and override slots are shifted by a wrong amount. Either make the field required for date overrides passed to getSlots or guard/default it here.

title: No test coverage for the round-robin fixed-host date-override fix
body: The PR's primary purpose is making date overrides (and working hours) of *fixed hosts* apply to round-robin events via the new logic in checkIfIsAvailable, and the PR description lists a round-robin fixed-host scenario as the main test plan. However, the only test added exercises a single-user personal event with a different invitee timezone. None of the new checkIfIsAvailable behavior — fixed host availability gating, override-window filtering per host, interaction with busy times — is covered, which is how the regression where busy checks are skipped on override days (and the multi-window veto issue) went unnoticed. A round-robin scenario with one fixed host having a date override should be added, including a case where the fixed host is busy inside the override window.

title: Slots inside a date override skip the busy-time check, allowing double bookings
body: In checkIfIsAvailable, the new code returns early: if a date override exists for the slot's day and the slot falls within the override range, `dateOverrideExist` is true and the function returns `true` (available) at line 133-135 before ever reaching the `busy.every(...)` conflict check at the bottom. Since checkIfIsAvailable is the only place a fixed host's busy times/bookings are consulted, any existing booking or calendar busy time that falls inside a date-override window is ignored, and the slot is shown as bookable. Consequence: fixed hosts (and round-robin hosts via the looseHostAvailability path, which spreads the same schedule object) can be double-booked on days that have a date override. The busy check must still run when the slot is inside an override.

title: Working-hours check compares slot start against itself instead of slot end
body: In the new workingHours validation inside checkIfIsAvailable, both `start` and `end` are computed from `slotStartTime`: `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();`. This was clearly meant to be `slotEndTime` (slot start + eventLength). As written, a slot that starts inside working hours but ends after the working-hours end (e.g. a 60-minute slot starting 30 minutes before the end of a fixed host's availability) is treated as within hours and kept. Consequence: bookings can be created that extend past the fixed host's availability boundary, which is exactly the class of bug this PR is trying to fix.

title: Host with no working hours on the slot's weekday is treated as available
body: The new workingHours check in checkIfIsAvailable only returns a match (and thus rejects the slot) when a workingHour exists whose `days` includes the slot's day AND the slot is outside its times. If the host has no working hour entry at all for that weekday (e.g. a fixed host who works Mon-Fri only, while the aggregated round-robin availability still produces Saturday slots from the other host's hours), `workingHours.find(...)` returns undefined, the check is skipped, and the slot passes as long as the host isn't busy. Consequence: fixed hosts remain bookable on days they don't work at all — the new enforcement only covers days where the host has partial hours. The check should reject the slot when no working hour covers that day.

title: Multiple date overrides on the same day make all slots unavailable
body: The `dateOverrides.find(...)` callback returns `true` (meaning 'block this slot') as soon as the slot is outside the time range of the first override matching the day, and `find` short-circuits without examining the remaining overrides. If a host has two override ranges on the same date (e.g. 09:00-11:00 and 14:00-16:00, which cal.com allows as separate availability rows for one date), a slot at 15:00 is outside the 09:00-11:00 range so the callback returns true and the slot is blocked; conversely any slot inside one range is outside the other, so every slot on that day ends up blocked. Consequence: days with more than one override range incorrectly show zero availability.

title: Override day matching formats the override date in the server's local timezone but the slot in UTC
body: The day comparison uses `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').format('YYYY MM DD')` — `dayjs(Date)` is in local mode, so `format` renders in the Node server's local timezone — and compares it to `slotStartTime.format('YYYY MM DD')` where `slotStartTime` is explicitly `.utc()`. On any server not running in UTC, the override start instant shifted by the organizer offset can format to a different calendar date than its UTC date, so date overrides silently fail to match (or match the wrong day).
