This PR calls a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice synchronously inside Authenticate with no timeout and no panic guard. On every local-cache miss (at least once per ~29 minutes per device per instance) the anonymous authentication path now blocks on a COUNT plus an UPDATE/INSERT against the database, and any panic in that path will crash the request. Consider keeping the failure isolation (timeout/recover) while still propagating the limit error.

title: anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined infers property type 'undefined'
body: In GrafanaBootConfig, the new field is declared as `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;`. Under strictNullChecks this gives the class property the literal type `undefined`, so any TypeScript consumer reading config.anonymousDeviceLimit sees type `undefined` and cannot use it as a number without a cast. The neighboring fields use explicit annotations (e.g. `loginError: string | undefined = undefined;`). This should be `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;` to match the GrafanaConfig interface. Note also that the Go DTO (FrontendSettingsDTO.AnonymousDeviceLimit, an int64 without omitempty) always serializes a number, so the value is never actually undefined in boot data.

title: New device_limit option is not documented in defaults.ini/sample config or docs
body: The PR adds a new configuration key `device_limit` under [auth.anonymous] (read via anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0)) but does not add it to conf/defaults.ini, conf/sample.ini, or the administration documentation, where all other auth.anonymous options (enabled, org_name, org_role, hide_version) are documented. Admins have no way to discover the setting, its default (0 = unlimited), or its semantics without reading the source.

title: No test that an existing device can still update when the limit is reached
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only covers the rejection path (a brand-new device being refused with ErrDeviceLimitReached when the limit is reached). There is no test for the complementary updateDevice success path: an already-registered device that is at/over the limit must still be able to refresh its row (client_ip/user_agent/updated_at), otherwise legitimate returning devices would be locked out. There is also no test covering the interaction with the service-level local cache (i.e., that a rejected device is not cached and is re-checked on retry).

title: Local cache is populated before the DB write, so the device limit is only enforced once per device
body: In tagDeviceUI, the cache key is set with `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})` (line 87) before `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice` is called. When the device limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, but the cache entry was already written and stays valid for ~29 minutes. On the next request from the same device, tagDeviceUI hits the cache at line 83-84 and returns nil without touching the database, so Anonymous.Authenticate (client.go) no longer sees ErrDeviceLimitReached and the request is allowed. Result: a new device over the limit is rejected exactly once, then gets full anonymous access for the rest of the cache window (and the window renews each time the device is re-tagged after expiry fails again). This effectively defeats the configurable device limit this PR adds. The cache entry should only be set after CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds.

title: Count-then-insert limit check is racy and can exceed the configured device limit
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by calling CountDevices and then, if count < deviceLimit, running the INSERT ... ON CONFLICT upsert. These are two separate statements with no transaction or locking, so N concurrent requests with distinct new device IDs can all observe count < limit and all insert, pushing the device table past deviceLimit. Since anonymous requests are unauthenticated and arrive concurrently (and each device is only cached locally per instance for 29 minutes, so multi-instance deployments re-check often), overshooting the limit under load is realistic. If the limit is meant as a hard cap, enforcement needs to be atomic (e.g., conditional insert in a transaction or a database-level constraint).

title: updateDevice can report ErrDeviceLimitReached for an existing device on MySQL
body: updateDevice treats `rowsAffected == 0` as 'device does not exist / not in window' and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. On MySQL (grafana's DSN does not set clientFoundRows), RowsAffected counts rows actually changed, not rows matched. The UPDATE sets updated_at to the current time, but anon_device.updated_at has second precision on MySQL, so two tag refreshes for the same device within the same second with unchanged client_ip/user_agent produce no changed columns and rowsAffected == 0. An existing, in-window device then gets ErrDeviceLimitReached and its anonymous authentication fails even though it is already counted against the limit. Compare using a matched-rows semantic or restructure the check (e.g., SELECT the device first, or use CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS).

title: No test that an existing device can still be updated when the limit is reached
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a *new* device is rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached once the limit is reached. The other half of the feature — that a device already present in anon_device (and within the 30-day window) is still allowed via the updateDevice path when count >= deviceLimit — is untested. A regression that rejects existing devices at the limit (e.g., the MySQL rowsAffected issue, or a broken WHERE clause in updateDevice) would not be caught. Add a case: limit=1, create device A, then call CreateOrUpdateDevice again for device A and assert it succeeds and updates the row.

title: New device_limit option is not documented in the config files
body: The PR adds `cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit = anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0)` under [auth.anonymous], but the changed-files list does not include conf/defaults.ini or conf/sample.ini, so the new `device_limit` option is undocumented and invisible to administrators browsing or generating config. Per Grafana convention, new ini options should be added (commented, with description) to conf/defaults.ini and conf/sample.ini; otherwise the feature is undiscoverable.

title: Local cache is populated before the limit check, so rejected devices bypass the limit on their next request
body: In tagDeviceUI, the cache entry is written (a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})) before anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice is called. When the device limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, which now propagates up through TagDevice and causes the anonymous authn client to reject the request — but the cache entry for that device was already stored (default TTL ~29 minutes). On the very next request from the same device, the cache lookup hits, tagDeviceUI returns nil without touching the store, TagDevice returns nil, and the client authenticates successfully. As a result, a new device over the limit is only blocked on its first request and then gets full anonymous access, so the configurable device limit is effectively unenforced. The cache entry should only be set after CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds (or removed when it returns an error).

title: Device limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert, so concurrent requests can exceed the limit
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by running CountDevices and then, if count < deviceLimit, performing the upsert. These two statements run outside any transaction or lock, so two (or more) concurrent requests with new device IDs can both observe count < deviceLimit and both insert, pushing the device count above the configured limit. Under concurrent anonymous traffic the limit is only approximate. If exact enforcement matters, the check-and-insert needs to be atomic (e.g., a transaction with appropriate isolation, a conditional INSERT, or a database-level constraint).

title: Device tagging moved from a background goroutine into the synchronous authentication path
body: Previously TagDevice ran in a fire-and-forget goroutine with a recover() and its own 2-minute background context, so a slow or failing database never delayed or broke anonymous authentication. This PR calls TagDevice synchronously with the request context inside Authenticate. Every cache-missed anonymous request now waits on at least one DB write, and when device_limit is configured it additionally waits on a COUNT(*) query over anon_device, on the authentication hot path. A slow database will directly add latency to every anonymous request, and because the request-scoped context is used, writes can be aborted when the client disconnects. If the limit error must be returned synchronously, consider keeping the non-limit path asynchronous or bounding the DB work with a short dedicated timeout.

title: New device_limit option is not documented in conf/defaults.ini or conf/sample.ini
body: The PR adds a new configuration key device_limit under [auth.anonymous] (cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit = anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0)) but does not update conf/defaults.ini, conf/sample.ini, or the anonymous auth documentation. Operators have no way to discover the setting, its default (0 = unlimited), or its semantics from the shipped configuration samples, and the PR checklist item for docs is unchecked.

title: No test covers the update path for an existing device when the limit is reached
body: The core promise of the feature is that when the device limit is reached, existing devices keep working (updateDevice refreshes client_ip/user_agent/updated_at) while only new devices are rejected. TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only asserts that a second, new device is rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached; it never verifies that re-tagging the already-registered device succeeds once the limit is hit. A regression in updateDevice (e.g., a wrong updated_at window) that started rejecting existing devices would not be caught. There is also no test covering the cache interaction in tagDeviceUI that allows a rejected device to succeed on retry.

title: Cleanup logs every successful batch at Error level, including full ID lists
body: The new batch callbacks log at Error level during normal, successful operation: lines 534, 537, 554, 557 (CleanAnnotations) and 576, 579 (CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags) all call r.log.Error(...). These fire on every cleanup cycle and every batch, and they dump the complete slice of fetched IDs into the log line (up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize entries, potentially tens of thousands of IDs per line). This produces massive log lines and constant false error-level noise that can trip alerting on error logs and bury real errors. The 'err', err key/value pairs log a value that is always nil at those points, indicating these are leftover debug statements. They should be Debug level (or removed) and should not serialize the entire ID slice.

title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute for all cleanup jobs, undocumented
body: The PR is about splitting the annotation cleanup queries, but it also changes the CleanUpService ticker from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This makes every cleanup job run 10x more often, not just annotation cleanup: filesystem scans of the images and CSV directories (cleanUpTmpFiles), expired snapshot/dashboard-version/image deletion, user invite expiry, short URL and query history cleanup. Each minute now scans directories and issues DELETEs against many tables, and since each run has a 9-minute timeout, a slow run means cleanup work executes essentially back-to-back with no idle gap. This behavior change is not mentioned in the PR description and affects operators' DB and I/O load; if the motivation is to compensate for the new split queries under-deleting annotations, only the annotation job cadence should change.

title: SQLite inline-ID path builds the IN list with quadratic fmt.Sprintf concatenation
body: In deleteByIDs, the SQLite fallback builds the ID list via values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) inside the loop, which copies the entire accumulated string on every iteration — O(n²) byte copying. With the large batch sizes this path exists for (the new test uses a batch size of 32767), that is on the order of gigabytes of transient copying per batch on every cleanup cycle. A strings.Builder plus strconv.AppendInt would make it linear. Related minor points: the comment 'SQLite has a parameter limit of 999' is outdated for SQLite >= 3.32.0 (which supports 32766 variables, as the new test's name acknowledges), and the branch is keyed off the configured AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize rather than len(ids), so even a final 5-row batch takes the string-building path when the configured batch size exceeds 999.

title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, affecting all cleanup jobs
body: The diff changes the CleanUpService ticker from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This service runs many jobs besides annotation cleanup: deleting expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, user invites, stale short URLs, and stale query history, plus a filesystem scan of temp directories. All of these now run 10x more frequently, which increases database and filesystem load across every Grafana instance, and the change is not mentioned in the PR description (which is scoped to the annotation deadlock fix). Since the annotation cleanup itself is already batched and self-paced, this global cadence change does not appear necessary for the fix and should either be reverted or justified and called out explicitly.

title: Routine cleanup progress logged at Error level, including full ID lists
body: The new cleanup paths in CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags emit `r.log.Error(...)` for normal, successful progress (e.g. line 534 "Annotations to clean by time", plus lines 537, 554, 557, 576, 579). These are not errors; they fire on every cleanup batch, and each message includes the full `ids` slice and the raw SQL condition. With the default batch size (and especially with the new 1-minute cleanup cadence in cleanup.go), this will flood error-level logs and any error-based alerting/monitoring with noise, and with large configured batch sizes (e.g. 32767) each line logs tens of thousands of IDs. These should be Debug level and should not dump the full ID list (a count suffices).

title: Placeholder-limit workaround only applied to SQLite, not MySQL/Postgres
body: deleteByIDs special-cases SQLite's 999-parameter limit by inlining IDs into the DELETE statement, but for other dialects it always emits `len(ids)` placeholders. MySQL and Postgres both cap parameters at 65535 per statement; AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is operator-configurable, so setting it above 65535 on MySQL/Postgres makes the DELETE fail every cycle (cleanup silently broken until the config is fixed and the error noticed). Since the code already handles the same class of problem for SQLite, the limit check should be applied per dialect (or the batch size validated at startup) rather than only for SQLite.

title: Cleanup job interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute for all jobs
body: The ticker in CleanUpService.Run was changed from time.Minute*10 to time.Minute*1. This is unrelated to the annotation deadlock fix described in the PR and is not mentioned in the description. It causes every cleanup job to run 10x more frequently: deleting expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, expiring user invites, deleting stale short URLs, and two rounds of query-history deletions every minute. This is a significant increase in recurring database load across the whole system, and it also changes user-visible timing semantics (e.g., temp files and expired resources are now purged within ~1 minute instead of ~10). If this change is intentional to compensate for the cleanup now potentially under-deleting, it should be called out and justified; otherwise it should be reverted or scoped to annotations only.

title: Normal cleanup progress logged at Error level with full ID lists
body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log each batch via r.log.Error (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579), e.g. r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err). These are informational progress messages, not errors (err is nil at the points where it is logged), so every cleanup cycle now emits error-severity log lines, which will trip log-based alerting on errors. Worse, each line includes the complete ID slice, which is up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize entries — a batch size of 32767 produces ~200KB log lines, twice per batch, and with the cleanup interval now at 1 minute this happens every minute. These look like leftover debug statements and should be demoted to Debug and/or have the raw ID list removed.

title: O(n^2) string building when inlining IDs for SQLite
body: In deleteByIDs, the SQLite branch builds the IN list with values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) inside a loop over ids. Each iteration copies the entire accumulated string, so for a batch of N ids the total copied bytes grow quadratically — with the tested batch size of 32767 this is on the order of gigabytes of allocation/copying for a single DELETE. Use a strings.Builder (or strings.Join on a converted slice) to build the list in linear time.

title: Async legacy writes derive their context from the request context, so they are canceled when the request completes
body: In Create (and identically in Delete line 110, Update line 135, and DeleteCollection line 163) the background goroutine does `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the incoming request context. The request context is canceled as soon as the API handler returns, which happens immediately after the synchronous unified-storage write — so the child context used for the 'safe measure' legacy write is typically canceled before or during the legacy SQL call. The legacy write will then fail with context canceled, silently diverging legacy and unified storage (only visible as a metric). The goroutine should detach from the request lifecycle first, e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)`, before applying the 10s timeout.

title: Update passes the original objInfo to the legacy store, so UpdatedObject is invoked a second time against a different old object
body: The previous implementation fetched the old object, computed the updated object once, and wrapped it in `updateWrapper` so both stores persisted the same object. The new code passes the raw `objInfo` to both `d.Storage.Update` and, asynchronously, to `d.Legacy.Update`. This means `objInfo.UpdatedObject()` is invoked twice: the second time (in the goroutine) it runs against the old object fetched from legacy storage, which may have a different resourceVersion or may not exist yet (see the create-ordering race). `UpdatedObjectInfo` implementations are not guaranteed to be idempotent or reusable across calls, and the resulting legacy object can diverge from what was written to unified storage. The legacy call should receive a wrapper holding the object already produced by the unified update.

title: Async legacy writes are unordered, so create-then-update/delete sequences can diverge legacy storage
body: Each write method spawns an independent goroutine with its own 10s timeout and no serialization. A client that creates an object and immediately updates or deletes it will have the create's legacy write and the update/delete's legacy write racing in separate goroutines: the update can reach legacy before the create has been applied (failing with not-found, since forceAllowCreate is false), or a delete can be applied before the create lands, leaving a stale object in legacy. Because reads in mode 3 come only from unified storage, this divergence is invisible to users and only shows up as error counters. If ordering matters for the 'safe measure' copy, the legacy writes need a queue/serialization per object.

title: Delete success metric records the object name as the kind label, causing unbounded Prometheus label cardinality
body: In Delete, the success path calls `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` — passing the resource `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. This both mislabels the metric (kind label contains object names) and creates a Prometheus series per object name, which is unbounded cardinality that can blow up the metrics store. It should be `options.Kind`.

title: Create and Update record a legacy-storage error metric when unified storage fails and legacy is never called
body: In Create (line 45), when `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` even though the legacy store was never invoked — this both inflates legacy error counts and loses the unified-storage error metric. The same mistake exists in Update at line 129, which records `recordLegacyDuration` on a `d.Storage.Update` failure. Both should call `recordStorageDuration`, as the error paths in Delete and DeleteCollection correctly do.

title: DeleteCollection records the legacy delete result against the storage metric
body: In the async goroutine of DeleteCollection, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy delete-collection latency/errors will be attributed to unified storage, corrupting both metrics (all other methods use `recordLegacyDuration` in this position).

title: Delete installs the base logger into the context instead of the enriched one
body: Delete builds `log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method)` but then calls `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`, dropping the name/kind/method values for anything downstream that logs via `klog.FromContext(ctx)`. It should pass `log`, as the other methods do.

title: TestMode3_Create error case configures the failure on the legacy mock, but mode 3 calls unified storage first
body: The case 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' sets up only `setupLegacyFn` returning an error and provides no `setupStorageFn`. In mode 3, `dw.Create` calls `d.Storage.Create` first; with no expectation registered on the shared mock for that call, testify will panic with an unexpected-call failure rather than exercising the intended error path. The error expectation needs to be on the storage mock (and this worked in mode 1 only because mode 1 calls legacy first).

title: New mode-3 integration subtests read the legacy API immediately after k8s writes, racing the async legacy write
body: The added 'with dual write (file, mode 3)' and 'with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)' subtests reuse `doPlaylistTests`, which asserts legacy `/api/playlists` results immediately after k8s creates/updates/deletes (e.g. comparing `/api/playlists` list right after `client.Resource.Create`). In mode 3 the legacy write happens in a background goroutine with up to a 10s window, so these assertions race the async write and will be flaky; combined with the request-context cancellation bug in dualwriter_mode3.go they may fail consistently. The test needs polling/retry on the legacy side or the async write needs to be made deterministic for tests.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled when the HTTP handler returns
body: In Create (and identically in Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) the fire-and-forget goroutine does context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s, ...) on the incoming request ctx. The request context is cancelled as soon as the API handler finishes writing the response, which typically happens immediately after the synchronous unified-storage write returns — long before the 10s timeout matters. The legacy write will therefore be aborted with context.Canceled in the common case (any legacy call slower than handler teardown), so the 'safe measure' legacy copy silently diverges from unified storage, with the failure only visible as a metric bump. The goroutine should derive from context.WithoutCancel(ctx) (or a detached background context carrying the logger/values) so the legacy write can actually complete.

title: Delete no longer attempts legacy deletion when unified storage returns NotFound
body: The previous implementation distinguished NotFound: if d.Storage.Delete returned an IsNotFound error it still went on to delete from Legacy, so objects that exist only in the legacy store (e.g., written before mode 3 was enabled, or whose legacy write succeeded while unified failed) could still be cleaned up. The new code returns immediately on any error from unified storage, so a Get in mode 3 would 404 while the object still exists in the legacy store, and there is no way through the dual writer to delete that orphaned legacy object. This leaves permanent legacy orphans during the migration window mode 3 is designed for.

title: Delete records storage duration with the object name as the resource label
body: On the success path of Delete, d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) passes the object name where every other call site passes options.Kind as the resource label. This both mislabels the metric (deletes appear under a different 'resource' than all other operations) and turns a bounded label (kind) into an unbounded one (every individual object name becomes a label value), causing a Prometheus cardinality explosion on servers with many objects.

title: Legacy Update re-derives the object from legacy's own old object instead of mirroring what unified storage stored
body: The previous mode 3 Update fetched the old object, computed the updated object once via objInfo.UpdatedObject, and used updateWrapper so that the legacy store persisted exactly the object returned by unified storage. The new code hands the raw objInfo to d.Legacy.Update inside the goroutine, so legacy's store invokes objInfo.UpdatedObject against legacy's own (possibly stale) old object. If legacy is behind unified storage (which is expected in mode 3, since legacy writes are async), the legacy update can conflict or produce a different object than what unified storage stored, and the resulting error is only counted in a metric — never logged and never surfaced. The legacy 'safety net' copy can thus silently and permanently drift from unified storage.

title: Fire-and-forget legacy writes can be applied out of order
body: Because every mutating operation spawns an independent goroutine for the legacy write with no sequencing, two rapid operations on the same object (e.g., Update then Delete, or two Updates) can be applied to the legacy store in the opposite order — the delete goroutine can run before the update goroutine, resurrecting the object in legacy, or an older update can overwrite a newer one. Since mode 3 treats legacy as the fallback store to migrate back to, this reordering can leave the legacy copy in a state that never matched unified storage. Some ordering mechanism (per-key queue, or at minimum synchronous ordering guarantees) is needed.

title: Create storage-error path records a legacy-duration metric
body: When d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) even though no legacy call was ever made and the measured duration is the unified-storage create. It should be recordStorageDuration(true, ...). As written, unified-storage create failures are reported as legacy errors and the storage error metric is never incremented, making alerting on unified-storage failures blind to create errors.

title: Update storage-error path records a legacy-duration metric
body: When d.Storage.Update fails, d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) is called even though the failure came from unified storage and no legacy update was attempted. It should be recordStorageDuration(true, ...). Unified-storage update failures will be misattributed to legacy in the dual-writer metrics.

title: DeleteCollection legacy write records a storage-duration metric
body: Inside the DeleteCollection goroutine, the result of d.Legacy.DeleteCollection is recorded with d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...) instead of recordLegacyDuration. Legacy delete-collection latency and failures are attributed to unified storage, and the legacy metric for this method is never populated.

title: Delete installs the base logger into the context instead of the enriched one
body: Delete builds log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method) but then calls klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log), dropping all of those values. Every other method in this file installs its enriched logger. Downstream log lines emitted via klog.FromContext during a delete will lack the name/kind/method fields.

title: Mode 3 integration tests assert legacy API state synchronously while legacy writes are asynchronous
body: doPlaylistTests contains checks like 'Do CRUD via k8s (and check that legacy api still works)' that write through the k8s API and immediately read via the legacy /api/playlists endpoints (getFromBothAPIs). In mode 3 the legacy write happens in a detached goroutine after the response is returned, so these assertions race with the legacy write: on a loaded CI worker the legacy GET can observe the pre-write state and fail intermittently (and combined with the request-context cancellation in dualwriter_mode3.go, the legacy write may never land at all). The mode 3 subtests need to poll/wait for the legacy state to converge instead of asserting it immediately.

title: Async legacy writes derive their context from the request context, so they are cancelled as soon as the HTTP handler returns
body: In Create (line 51), Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163), the goroutine that performs the legacy write calls context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...) using the incoming request context as parent. In the Kubernetes API server (and net/http generally) the request context is cancelled when the handler returns. Since these goroutines are fire-and-forget and the enclosing method returns immediately after the unified-storage write, the parent context is cancelled almost immediately, and the derived 10s timeout context is cancelled with it. The legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection will therefore nearly always fail with context.Canceled, meaning the 'write to legacy as a safe measure' silently does not happen and the two stores diverge. The goroutine should detach from the request lifecycle, e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) (plus copying needed values like the logger/user), before applying the timeout.

title: Update passes the already-consumed rest.UpdatedObjectInfo to the legacy store, so the legacy update gets a wrong or failing object
body: The previous implementation fetched the old object, computed the updated object once via objInfo.UpdatedObject, and passed a pre-resolved updateWrapper to both Storage.Update and Legacy.Update. The new code calls d.Storage.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...) and then, in the async goroutine, d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...) with the same objInfo. UpdatedObjectInfo is effectively single-use: UpdatedObject is invoked once by the unified-storage update (decoding the request body / applying the mutation), and invoking it a second time inside the legacy update will either fail or recompute against different input. It also means the legacy store no longer receives the exact object that was written to unified storage (the old code wrapped the storage result with updateWrapper{updated: obj}), so generated/mutated fields (UIDs, timestamps, resource versions) can diverge between the two stores. The legacy update should receive a wrapper containing the object returned by the unified-storage update, as before.

title: Delete no longer tolerates NotFound from unified storage, so legacy copies are never deleted for unmigrated objects
body: The previous Delete implementation checked apierrors.IsNotFound on the unified-storage delete error and, for NotFound, still proceeded to delete from legacy storage. The new code returns immediately on any storage error (lines 101-105), so the async legacy delete is never started. For an object that exists only in legacy (e.g. written before unified storage was enabled, or a previous async legacy write that succeeded while the unified one failed), a delete now returns NotFound to the caller while the legacy row is left behind, permanently diverging the two stores and breaking rollback to legacy. The NotFound-tolerant fallback to legacy should be restored.

title: Storage failures are recorded as legacy-duration metrics in Create and Update
body: When d.Storage.Create fails (line 45) and when d.Storage.Update fails (line 129), the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) even though no legacy operation was attempted and the measured duration is the storage call. These should be recordStorageDuration. As written, unified-storage error rates are misreported as legacy errors, which will mislead alerting/dashboards built on these metrics.

title: DeleteCollection records the legacy result with recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration
body: In the async goroutine of DeleteCollection, the outcome of d.Legacy.DeleteCollection is recorded with d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...) while the symmetric code in Create/Update/Delete uses recordLegacyDuration for legacy operations. This double-counts legacy delete-collection results as storage metrics and leaves legacy delete-collection unobserved.

title: Delete records storage success with the object name as the 'kind' metric label
body: On the success path of Delete, d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) passes the object name where every other call passes options.Kind. This creates a high-cardinality, inconsistent label value for the storage-duration metric on deletes, breaking aggregation by kind and potentially exploding the metric cardinality.

title: Delete stores d.Log (without name/kind/method fields) into the context instead of the enriched logger
body: Delete builds log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method) but then calls klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log), discarding those fields. Downstream code logging via klog.FromContext (including the async goroutine) loses the identifying fields, unlike the other methods which pass the enriched log.

title: Mode 3 tests never verify the legacy write and race with the fire-and-forget goroutines
body: All Mode 3 write tests assert only on the synchronous unified-storage result; nothing waits for or asserts the async legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection calls, so the central behavior of mode 3 (legacy gets written) is untested — the tests would pass even if the goroutines were removed. Worse, the goroutines call the shared testify mock after the test function may have returned: testify mocks are not safe to invoke once the test is done, and the shared mock 'm' is read/written from the test goroutine and the legacy goroutine concurrently, which is a data race detectable with -race and a source of flaky panics. The tests should synchronize with the goroutines (e.g. via a WaitGroup hook or a blocking mock) and assert the legacy calls happened.

title: No re-check of cache after acquiring write lock causes duplicate loads
body: After the fast-path read returns nil, the code acquires the write lock and unconditionally reloads the assets from disk (or CDN) without re-checking `entryPointAssetsCache`. If several requests arrive before the first successful load (e.g. at startup), they will each take the write lock in turn and each perform a full file read/HTTP fetch, even though the first one already populated the cache. A simple `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after acquiring the write lock would avoid the redundant loads.

title: Write lock held across file and network I/O serializes all callers
body: The write lock acquired at line 48 is held (via defer) across `readWebAssetsFromCDN` (an outbound HTTP request) and `readWebAssetsFromFile` (disk I/O). While the load is in progress, every other goroutine calling GetWebAssets — including ones that arrive after the load has started but before the cache write at line 69 — blocks on the write lock instead of doing their own I/O in parallel, and in dev mode every single request now serializes on this mutex. This is a behavior change worth being aware of; it is not a correctness bug, but a slow or hanging CDN call will now stall all callers on the mutex.

title: Missing re-check of cache after acquiring write lock causes duplicate expensive loads
body: GetWebAssets uses a read-then-write lock pattern, but after releasing the read lock and acquiring the write lock (line 48), it never re-checks whether another goroutine populated entryPointAssetsCache in the gap. On a cold cache in non-dev mode, N concurrent requests will all pass the initial nil check, then serialize on the write lock and each re-execute the full load (parsing assets-manifest.json, calling cfg.GetContentDeliveryURL, and potentially an HTTP fetch from the CDN once the hardcoded cdn variable is enabled). Only the last result is kept, so the earlier loads are wasted work, and different concurrent callers can receive different *EntryPointAssets instances despite the cache semantics. The standard fix is to re-check `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after acquiring the write lock.

title: No regression test exercising concurrent GetWebAssets calls
body: This PR fixes a data race on the package-level entryPointAssetsCache variable, but adds no test that calls GetWebAssets concurrently (e.g., from multiple goroutines with the race detector enabled via `go test -race`). Without such a test, a future refactor that drops or weakens the mutex guarding would not be caught by CI, and the race this PR fixes would silently regress. A simple test spinning up several goroutines calling GetWebAssets against a temp manifest file in both Dev and non-Dev environments would cover the guarded paths.

title: Write lock held across file/network I/O serializes all concurrent requests
body: After the fast path misses, GetWebAssets acquires entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock() and holds it (via defer) across readWebAssetsFromFile / readWebAssetsFromCDN, i.e. across disk I/O and potentially an HTTP request using http.DefaultClient, which has no timeout. Whenever the cache is not populated — every call in Dev mode, and every call in non-Dev mode when the manifest is missing or unreadable (the error path leaves the cache nil, so the fast path never hits) — all concurrent goroutines calling GetWebAssets are serialized behind a single I/O operation. A slow or hung read blocks every HTTP request that needs web assets. The lock should only guard access to the cache variable; the load should happen outside the critical section (e.g. load first, then lock briefly to store, or use sync.Once/singleflight for the cold-start case).

title: No re-check of cache after acquiring write lock causes duplicate loads
body: The function reads the cache under RLock, releases it, then acquires the write Lock without re-checking whether entryPointAssetsCache was populated in the meantime. On a cold start in non-Dev mode, N concurrent callers all miss the fast path and each performs the full manifest read (file I/O, and CDN fetch once that path is enabled), with each one overwriting the cache. A simple `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` re-check after acquiring the write lock would avoid the redundant work.

title: Error message 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' is misleading
body: When a user submits a SQL expression query, ReadQuery now rejects it with the error "sqlExpressions is not implemented". The feature is in fact implemented but deliberately disabled as the CVE-2024-9264 mitigation, and the sqlExpressions feature flag still exists in the codebase. Users who explicitly enabled the flag will receive a message claiming the feature does not exist, which is confusing and makes support/debugging harder. The message should state that SQL expressions are disabled (e.g. "sqlExpressions is disabled") rather than not implemented.

title: No regression test covering the SQL expression disable
body: This PR disables SQL expressions as a security mitigation (CVE-2024-9264) but adds no test asserting that a query with type 'sql' is rejected by ReadQuery, nor that NewSQLCommand/SQLCommand.Execute fail with the stubbed DB now that go-duck is removed. Existing tests in pkg/expr/sql that exercised TablesList against a real DuckDB would now fail or have been silently affected, and there is no guard preventing a future change from accidentally re-enabling the execution path. A regression test verifying SQL expressions return an error would protect the security fix.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false via convoluted dead logic with no explanation
body: The new helper `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns false on every branch — the variable and the `if` are dead code and the function always returns false. That is presumably the intent (hard-disable SQL expressions for the CVE-2024-9264 fix), but nothing in the code says so. The double negative reads like a bug, and a future maintainer may 'fix' it to `return h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(...)`, silently re-enabling the SQL/DuckDB execution path that was disabled for security reasons. The function should be a plain `return false` with a comment stating the feature is intentionally disabled, or the flag should be checked with an explicit blocklist comment.

title: User-facing error says 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' although the feature exists but is deliberately disabled
body: When a user submits an SQL expression query, ReadQuery now rejects it with the error `sqlExpressions is not implemented`. This is misleading: the feature is implemented but has been disabled for security reasons (CVE-2024-9264). Users who had the sqlExpressions feature flag enabled will see a message implying their Grafana build lacks the feature rather than that it was turned off, which will generate confusing support tickets. The message should state that SQL expressions are disabled/unavailable.

title: Legacy UnmarshalSQLCommand path is only blocked implicitly by the stubbed DB erroring out
body: The explicit disable check was added only in ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery (pkg/expr/reader.go). The legacy parsing path, UnmarshalSQLCommand, has no feature-flag or disabled check; SQL execution through it is prevented only because NewSQLCommand calls sql.TablesList, which now fails because the stubbed DB.RunCommands returns 'not implemented'. If the stub in pkg/expr/sql/db.go is later replaced with a real implementation (the file keeps the full go-duck API surface, suggesting it is meant to be swapped back), the legacy path would execute SQL with no gate at all. An explicit rejection (mirroring the reader.go check, or an error in NewSQLCommand itself) should guard this path so the security fix does not depend on an incidental error from a stub.

title: No regression test verifies SQL expressions are rejected after the security fix
body: This PR disables SQL expressions to remediate an RCE/LFI vulnerability (CVE-2024-9264), but adds no test asserting the new behavior: e.g. that ReadQuery returns an error for QueryTypeSQL even when the sqlExpressions feature flag is enabled, and that NewSQLCommand/sql.TablesList fail. Without such a test, a future change that restores the go-duck dependency or 'fixes' the always-false enableSqlExpressions helper would re-open the vulnerability without any CI signal.

title: enableSqlExpressions contains dead, inverted feature-flag logic
body: The new `enableSqlExpressions` function computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` (note the negation) and then discards the result, returning `false` on both paths. The intent — SQL expressions are hard-disabled due to CVE-2024-9264 — is fine, but the leftover inverted computation is a trap: anyone later 're-enabling' the feature by changing the final `return false` to `return enabled` would invert the flag semantics, enabling SQL expressions when the flag is off and disabling them when it is on. The function should either be `return false` with a comment referencing the CVE, or correct flag logic with the feature removed.

title: Error message 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' is misleading
body: When a user submits a SQL expression, `ReadQuery` now returns `fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")`. The feature is in fact implemented but deliberately disabled for security reasons (CVE-2024-9264 RCE/LFI via DuckDB), including for users who have explicitly enabled the `sqlExpressions` feature flag. The 'not implemented' wording is wrong and gives operators no indication that the feature was disabled on purpose or where to learn why; the message should state that SQL expressions are disabled (ideally referencing the security advisory).

title: Inert stub DB leaves reachable dead code with SQL string interpolation
body: The new stub `DB` makes every method return 'not implemented', which disables the feature, but all the surrounding machinery is kept: `TablesList` in pkg/expr/sql/parser.go still builds a command via `fmt.Sprintf("SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')", rawSQL)` with hand-rolled quote escaping before calling the stub, and `SQLCommand.Execute` still calls `QueryFramesInto`. Today this is inert only because the stub never executes anything; the dangerous interpolation path remains in the codebase where a future partial revert (e.g., swapping in a real DB implementation 'just for parsing') would silently re-expose it. Consider deleting the parser/command code along with the DuckDB dependency rather than leaving it behind an error stub.

title: TotalDocs reads b.cache map without holding cacheMu
body: TotalDocs() iterates over b.cache without acquiring b.cacheMu (it never did, but it matters now). Before this PR, BuildIndex held cacheMu for its entire duration and TotalDocs was effectively only reached after all init builds completed; now the lock is only taken for the final map insertion, and this PR adds a new call to TotalDocs in searchSupport.init (search.go line 216, the "search index initialized" log) that runs right after the watch-event goroutine is started. That goroutine calls getOrCreateIndex -> BuildIndex on events for unknown namespaces, which writes b.cache concurrently with the TotalDocs iteration. Concurrent map read/write in Go is a fatal runtime error ("concurrent map read and map write"), which will crash the process. TotalDocs should take b.cacheMu.RLock() before iterating.

title: Removing the build-wide lock allows concurrent duplicate builds of the same index
body: BuildIndex previously serialized all builds with cacheMu; now two goroutines can build the same NamespacedResource concurrently (getOrCreateIndex in search.go does a check-then-build with no synchronization, and its own comment acknowledges it does not block concurrent builders of the same key). Consequences: (1) for file-backed indexes (size > FileThreshold), both builders call bleve.New on the same directory path, and the second one fails on the bleve lock file, surfacing a spurious error to a search or watch-event request; (2) for memory-backed indexes both builds succeed and the second write to b.cache silently overwrites the first, leaking an open bleve.Index that is never closed and wasting the entire duplicate build. A per-key lock (or singleflight) is needed instead of the single global lock that was removed.

title: Data race on shared err variable across errgroup goroutines in init
body: Inside searchSupport.init, every errgroup goroutine executes `_, _, err = s.build(ctx, ...)` assigning to the same outer `err` variable that is also read after group.Wait() and was previously assigned by GetResourceStats. With initWorkers > 1 (the exact scenario this PR is optimizing) these goroutines write err concurrently, which is a data race (flagged by -race) and can produce torn/ stale error values. Each goroutine should use a local error variable and return it, letting errgroup surface the first failure. The same loop also increments totalBatchesIndexed++ from multiple goroutines without synchronization (line 189), another race that can undercount the value reported in the span event.

title: NewResourceServer leaks resources when eager Init fails
body: When s.Init(ctx) fails, NewResourceServer returns nil, err but does not call s.cancel() to release the cancellable context created a few lines above, and does not close the blob bucket that may have been opened earlier in the function (OpenBlobBucket/NewCDKBlobSupport). Since Init now runs at construction time, init failures (e.g. index build errors) are a realistic path, and each failed construction leaks the context and the bucket handle. The error path should call cancel() and close any opened blob support before returning.

title: BuildIndex starts a span but drops the span context, inconsistent with the PR's trace-propagation fix
body: The PR fixes trace propagation by assigning the context returned from tracer.Start back to ctx in search.go and sql/backend.go, but bleveBackend.BuildIndex still does `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)` and discards the span-scoped context. Any operation inside BuildIndex that could use the context (e.g. passing it to the builder callback or future instrumented calls) would be detached from the BuildIndex span, so the bleve portion of index-building traces remains disconnected from its children. Use `ctx, span := b.tracer.Start(...)` for consistency with the rest of the change.

title: Removing the function-wide lock in BuildIndex allows concurrent builds of the same index
body: Previously BuildIndex held b.cacheMu for its entire duration, serializing all index builds. The PR removes that lock and only locks around the final cache write, but there is no per-key serialization anywhere else: searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex (pkg/storage/unified/resource/search.go) does GetIndex-then-build with no guard (its own TODO admits this), so two concurrent Search calls, or a Search concurrent with a watch event, for the same NamespacedResource can both enter BuildIndex. Consequences: (1) for file-backed indexes (size > FileThreshold), both goroutines call bleve.New on the same directory path, which will fail with a lock/already-exists error or risk on-disk corruption, surfacing as spurious request errors; (2) both goroutines write b.cache[key], so the loser's fully built index is overwritten without ever being closed, leaking file handles and memory. The speedup is real for distinct keys, but same-key builds need a singleflight/per-key mutex to stay safe.

title: Data races on shared err and totalBatchesIndexed in concurrent init goroutines
body: In searchSupport.init, each errgroup goroutine does `totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(...)`, where both variables are shared outer-scope variables also accessed by the main goroutine (err is reassigned by `err = group.Wait()`, totalBatchesIndexed is read for the span event). With initWorkers > 1 — which this PR explicitly promotes by moving init to startup and speeding up concurrent builds — these are genuine data races that `go test -race` will flag, and the err returned by an individual goroutine may be overwritten by a sibling goroutine's build result. Each goroutine should use a local err and the counter should be an atomic (or dropped).

title: Watch goroutine panics on nil event when the events channel closes at shutdown
body: The goroutine started at the end of searchSupport.init does `v := <-events` in a loop without checking the ok flag. The SQL backend's poller closes the stream channel when the backend is stopped (defer close(stream) in backend.poller), at which point this receive returns nil forever and s.handleEvent(watchctx, nil) immediately dereferences evt.Type, panicking the process. Because this PR moves init from the first gRPC call to server construction, this goroutine now always runs whenever search is configured, so every shutdown of a search-enabled server (including the integration test in this PR that calls ms.Shutdown) risks a process-crashing panic. The receive should be `v, ok := <-events; if !ok { return }`.

title: TotalDocs iterates the index cache map without holding cacheMu
body: bleveBackend.TotalDocs ranges over b.cache with no lock, while BuildIndex now writes to that map under a short-lived cacheMu critical section. The PR adds a new caller: searchSupport.init logs s.search.TotalDocs() (search.go line 216) immediately after starting the watch goroutine, and that goroutine can concurrently call getOrCreateIndex -> BuildIndex -> `b.cache[key] = idx` when an event arrives for a namespace that was below the initMinSize threshold and thus not pre-built. A concurrent map read and write is a fatal runtime error in Go (not a recoverable panic), so this can crash the server during or right after startup. TotalDocs should take cacheMu.RLock() before iterating.

title: Storage-server integration test is now skipped entirely on postgres
body: The PR adds a skip for GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres in TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer, so CI no longer exercises the storage-server module target (which is exactly the startup path this PR changes by moving unified-storage init into server construction) against postgres. The TODO acknowledges it only fails in Drone, but merging this means the postgres variant can silently rot; consider skipping only in CI (e.g., detecting the Drone environment) or fixing the underlying issue before relying on this test to validate the new eager init behavior.

title: Data race on shared err variable across concurrent index builds in init()
body: In searchSupport.init, each errgroup goroutine does `_, _, err = s.build(ctx, ...)` writing to the same `err` variable captured from the outer function scope, then `return err`. With this PR the bleve backend's BuildIndex no longer holds a global lock for the whole build, so these goroutines genuinely run in parallel for the first time. Concurrent writes to `err` are a data race (flagged by the race detector), and worse, a failing goroutine can have its error overwritten by another goroutine's nil before it executes `return err` — so group.Wait() can return nil even though an index failed to build, letting startup proceed with a silently missing index. Each goroutine should use a local variable: `_, _, err := s.build(...); return err`.

title: Unsynchronized totalBatchesIndexed++ inside parallel goroutines
body: In searchSupport.init, `totalBatchesIndexed++` is executed inside errgroup goroutines that now run concurrently (previously their work was effectively serialized by the bleve backend's global BuildIndex lock). This is a data race and the count reported in the span event 'namespaces indexed' will be wrong under concurrency. Use an atomic counter or aggregate after Wait().

title: Concurrent BuildIndex for the same key can corrupt file-based indexes and leak index objects
body: Removing the global cacheMu lock from BuildIndex means two goroutines can now build the same NamespacedResource simultaneously: getOrCreateIndex in search.go does GetIndex-then-build with no per-key synchronization (its own TODO acknowledges this), and it is reachable concurrently from Search and handleEvent. For indexes above FileThreshold both builds call bleve.New on the same directory concurrently, which can fail or corrupt the on-disk index; for memory indexes the work is duplicated and the second `b.cache[key] = idx` silently overwrites the first, orphaning an open bleve.Index that is never closed and double-counting the IndexTenants metric. BuildIndex should take a per-key lock (or re-check the cache under the write lock and return the existing index) now that the coarse lock is gone.

title: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without holding cacheMu
body: TotalDocs ranges over b.cache with no lock while BuildIndex now writes b.cache[key] under cacheMu (GetIndex uses RLock). This is an unsynchronized concurrent map read/write that can panic with 'fatal error: concurrent map read and map write'. The window is real: search.init starts the watch-events goroutine (whose handleEvent can trigger on-demand builds via getOrCreateIndex for namespaces/kinds skipped at startup) immediately before calling s.search.TotalDocs() in the 'search index initialized' log line. Take cacheMu.RLock() around the iteration in TotalDocs.

title: NewResourceServer error path leaks started goroutines and the cancel func
body: Now that s.Init(ctx) runs eagerly in NewResourceServer, a failure partway through init (e.g. search.init succeeded and started its watch goroutine, then initWatcher failed, or any init error) returns nil, err without calling s.cancel(). The server's internal cancellable context is never cancelled and any background goroutines already started keep running with nothing able to stop them (the search watch goroutine runs on context.Background(), independent of s.ctx). On init failure the constructor should call s.cancel() / Stop() to unwind what was started before returning the error.

title: Call to isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments does not compile
body: UsernameForm.authenticate() calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments, but the only method with that name is the one added in this PR in the superclass UsernamePasswordForm: protected boolean isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user). There is no no-arg overload anywhere in the class hierarchy, so the services module fails to compile with 'no suitable method found: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()'. The call almost certainly should be isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()), matching how the same method is invoked in UsernamePasswordForm.

title: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires a non-null user, which disables passkeys on all fresh logins
body: The new helper isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) returns webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null, and it now gates every call to webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context): in authenticate() (line 115) and in challenge(context, error, field) (line 137). On an initial login there is no user in the authentication context (context.getUser() == null), so fillContextForm is never invoked for first-time logins: the WebAuthn challenge note, the ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI form attribute, and the webauth form markup are never set. Previously fillContextForm was called precisely in the user == null branch. This inverts the behavior and removes passkey autofill/auto-login from the normal (non re-authentication) username/password page, regressing the primary passkeys scenario. The tests retained/added in this very PR confirm the expected behavior and would fail: PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest.webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey expects automatic passkey login when opening a fresh login form, and passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey (in both PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest and PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest) asserts that //form[@id='webauth'] is present on the fresh login page. The condition must also be true when the user is null (fresh login); requiring user != null makes passkeys available only during re-authentication.

title: Call to no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() does not compile
body: UsernameForm.authenticate() now calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments (`if (context.getUser() != null && !isConditionalPasskeysEnabled())`). However, the only method with that name in the class hierarchy is the one added in UsernamePasswordForm: `protected boolean isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)`, which requires a UserModel argument. UsernameForm defines no no-arg overload itself, so this code fails to compile ('required: UserModel, found: no arguments'). Either the call should pass `context.getUser()` or a no-arg overload must be added; as written, the module does not build.

title: user != null check removes conditional passkeys UI from the normal (first) login page
body: The new helper `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` returns `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null`, and it now gates `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` in both `authenticate()` (line 115) and `challenge(context, error, field)` (line 137). During a regular first login the user is not yet identified (`context.getUser() == null`), so fillContextForm is never called, the ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI attribute is never set, and the `webauth` form / passkeys autofill no longer renders on the initial login page — exactly the case the old code handled (fillContextForm was previously invoked in the user==null branch). The same regression hits the page re-rendered after a failed first-login password attempt, since the user is cleared there too. This also contradicts the PR's own tests, which assert the webauth form is present on the initial, not-yet-authenticated login page (e.g. PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest.passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey and passwordLoginWithExternalKey, PasskeysUsernameFormTest.passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey, PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest.passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey line 194), so those tests would fail. The condition should only require passkeys to be enabled, not a pre-set user.

title: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires a non-null user, so passkeys are never set up on fresh logins
body: The new helper returns `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null`, and it gates both `authenticate()` (line 115) and the error `challenge()` (line 137). On a normal first login `context.getUser()` is null, so `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` is no longer invoked — before this PR the fill happened exactly in the user==null branch. Without it, the `enableWebAuthnConditionalUI` attribute and the WebAuthn challenge/rpId are never set, so the `webauth` form and the conditional passkey autofill (including discoverable-key auto-login) disappear from the initial login page; passkey login would only work during re-authentication. The condition is inverted: it should be true when the user is not yet known, and during re-authentication when the user actually has a passwordless credential, e.g. `user == null || user.credentialManager().isConfiguredFor(WebAuthnCredentialModel.TYPE_PASSWORDLESS)`. As written, the PR's own fresh-login tests (e.g. `webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey`, which expects automatic login right after `oauth.openLoginForm()`, and the assertions that `//form[@id='webauth']` is present on the first login page in `passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey`/`passwordLoginWithExternalKey`) cannot pass.

title: Call to no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() does not compile
body: `UsernameForm.authenticate()` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments, but the only method of that name in the class hierarchy is `UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)`, added in this PR. No no-arg overload exists in `UsernameForm`, `UsernamePasswordForm`, or `AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator`, so the services module fails to compile. Presumably the call should be `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`.

title: reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey disables passkeys realm-wide instead of testing a user without a passkey
body: The test is named and commented as verifying that a re-authenticating user who has no passkey is not offered passkey login (comment at line 304: "Passkeys login should not be available on the page as this user does not have passkey"), but it actually calls `setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(Boolean.FALSE)`, disabling passkeys for the whole realm. In that setup `isPasskeysEnabled()` returns false and `fillContextForm` is skipped regardless of any per-user logic, so the test passes even though `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled` never checks whether the user has a passkey credential (it only checks `user != null`). The actual scenario — realm with passkeys enabled, re-authenticating user with only a password, who should not see the WebAuthn conditional UI — is left untested, and with the current implementation that user would incorrectly get passkey elements rendered on the re-authentication page.

title: Login-cache invalidation on update uses the org-aware wrapped model, missing invalidations while the organization is disabled
body: update() fetches the 'original' IDP via getById(), which returns the model wrapped by createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(). That wrapper overrides isEnabled() to also return false when the linked organization is disabled. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() then applies getLoginPredicate() (which includes isEnabled()) to this wrapped model. Consequence: if an organization is disabled and an admin updates one of its IDPs changing hideOnLogin or linkOnly (fields consumers of the login cache do not re-check), both 'original' (isEnabled=false due to disabled org) and 'updated' (hideOnLogin=true) fail the predicate, so no invalidation is registered. The .idp.login caches are not invalidated by organization enable/disable either, so when the organization is re-enabled, the stale cached ID list makes the IDP appear on the login page even though it is now hidden/link-only. The predicate comparison should be done against the unwrapped stored model (raw isEnabled) rather than the organization-aware wrapper.

title: Cleanup in testCacheIDPForLogin registers removal of literal alias "alias" instead of the created IDPs
body: In testCacheIDPForLogin, both cleanup registrations use getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove) with the literal string "alias" instead of the actual alias variable ("idp-alias-" + i / "idp-alias-20"). As a result none of the ~21 identity providers created by the test are removed afterwards, and the deferred remove() calls will hit a non-existent IDP (404) during cleanup, which can fail the test class teardown and pollutes the shared test realm for subsequent tests. The same literal-alias copy/paste already existed in testCacheIDPByOrg and was duplicated here.

title: update() compares against the organization-aware wrapped model, causing missed login-cache invalidations when the IDP's organization is disabled
body: In update(), the 'original' model used by registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate is obtained via getById(), which returns the model wrapped by createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel. That wrapper overrides isEnabled() to also require the linked organization to be enabled. getLoginPredicate() (LoginFilter.ENABLED) calls isEnabled(), so when an IDP's organization is currently disabled, predicate(original) evaluates to false even though the IDP itself is a valid login IDP. Now consider this sequence: (1) an org-linked public IDP is in the cached getForLogin(ORG_ONLY/ALL) ID list; (2) the organization is disabled; (3) the admin updates the IDP to make it unavailable for login — sets hideOnLogin=true, linkOnly=true, or broker_public=false — while keeping it enabled. predicate(updated) is false, and because predicate(original) is also false (due to the disabled org, not the IDP), registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate hits the first 'both false' branch and registers NO invalidation of the .idp.login.* caches. The IDP's internal id therefore stays in the cached login ID sets. (4) When the organization is re-enabled (which does not invalidate the login caches, by design), getForLogin serves the stale cached id, getById returns a wrapper whose isEnabled() is now true, and OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean only re-checks isEnabled() — it does not re-check hideOnLogin, linkOnly, or BROKER_PUBLIC in the ORG_ONLY/ALL paths — so a broker the admin explicitly hid or made private is displayed and usable on the login pages. The fix is to compute the original login-eligibility from the raw delegate model (or an unwrapped copy) rather than from the organization-aware wrapper, so org enablement does not poison the comparison.

title: Test cleanup registers removal of literal alias "alias" instead of the created IDP aliases
body: In the new testCacheIDPForLogin, the cleanup is registered as getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove) (lines 381 and 425; the same copy-paste bug exists in the pre-existing testCacheIDPByOrg at line 303). The literal string "alias" is used instead of the actual alias variable (e.g. "idp-alias-" + i). As a result the 21 identity providers created by this test (idp-alias-0 … idp-alias-20) are never removed, while teardown attempts to delete a non-existent IDP with alias "alias". The leaked, mostly enabled IDPs persist in the shared "test" realm and can pollute subsequent tests in the class and other test classes that count or render identity providers for that realm. The cleanup should reference the created alias, e.g. final String alias = "idp-alias-" + i; getCleanup().addCleanup(() -> testRealm().identityProviders().get(alias).remove()).

title: Login-cache invalidation on update compares org-aware wrapped 'original' against raw 'updated' model and can skip a needed invalidation
body: update() obtains the pre-update state via getById() (line 91), which returns the organization-aware wrapper whose isEnabled() additionally returns false when the linked organization is disabled. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate then evaluates getLoginPredicate() on this wrapped 'original' but on the raw 'updated' model. The cached getForLogin ID sets, however, are computed from the raw store filters (raw enabled/linkOnly/hideOnLogin/BROKER_PUBLIC), so the wrapper's org-dependent isEnabled() makes the comparison inconsistent: if the linked organization is currently disabled, getLoginPredicate().test(original) is false even though the IDP's ID is still present in the cached login sets. If the same update then removes the IDP from the login set (e.g. sets hideOnLogin=true, disables it, or clears BROKER_PUBLIC), test(updated) is also false, the early return at line 405 fires, and the login caches are not invalidated. The stale ID remains cached; once the organization is re-enabled (organization updates do not invalidate these caches), the now hidden/disabled/non-public IDP reappears on the login page, because OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean only re-checks isEnabled() and does not re-check hideOnLogin/linkOnly/BROKER_PUBLIC. The original state used for the comparison should be the raw model (e.g. obtained from idpDelegate.getById, or the predicate should not rely on the wrapped isEnabled()).

title: Cleanup registers removal of literal alias "alias" instead of the created identity providers
body: In testCacheIDPForLogin, cleanup after creating each identity provider is registered as getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove) (lines 381 and 425; the same copy-paste mistake already exists in testCacheIDPByOrg at line 303). The literal string "alias" is used instead of the actual provider alias ("idp-alias-" + i), so the roughly 20 identity providers created by the test are never removed and leak into the shared test realm, where they can pollute subsequent tests that enumerate or display identity providers. Additionally, the cleanup DELETE for the non-existent alias "alias" will return 404, which may surface as a cleanup failure. The real alias of each created IDP should be passed to get(...).

title: New abstract method order() breaks all existing third-party CryptoProvider implementations
body: CryptoProvider is a public SPI loaded via ServiceLoader, and this PR adds a new abstract method `int order()` without a default implementation. Any existing out-of-tree implementation of CryptoProvider (custom crypto provider extensions compiled against the previous keycloak-common) will fail to compile against the new version and, worse, will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when an old jar is used with the new keycloak-common, because CryptoIntegration.detectProvider now calls CryptoProvider::order on every ServiceLoader-discovered provider during sorting. This turns a previously working deployment into one that fails during CryptoIntegration.init. The method should be declared as `default int order() { return 0; }` (or similar) so existing implementations keep working.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default keystore provider (SUN), not BouncyCastle
body: The CryptoProvider contract states this method returns the BouncyCastle security provider. AuthzClientCryptoProvider instead returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which is the SUN provider on standard JDKs. BouncyIntegration caches the returned provider's name globally (BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER) and keycloak-core code uses that name for explicit-provider JCA lookups (e.g., KeyStore/Cipher/Signature.getInstance(alg, BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER)); pinning those lookups to "SUN" will throw NoSuchAlgorithmException/NoSuchProviderException for anything SUN does not implement (e.g., PKCS12 keystores, which live in SunJSSE), even though the algorithms are available elsewhere in the JVM. It also needlessly instantiates a KeyStore on every call. The correct behavior for an environment without BouncyCastle is to return null, as WildFlyElytronProvider does.

title: Multiple equal-order providers are now resolved silently and arbitrarily instead of failing fast
body: Previously, having more than one CryptoProvider on the classpath was a hard configuration error ("Multiple crypto providers loaded..."). Now detectProvider sorts by order() descending and silently takes the first, only logging the ignored ones at debug level. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so if two server-side providers end up on the classpath together (a real misconfiguration, e.g. both elytron and fips jars present), the winner is determined by ServiceLoader encounter order, which depends on jar/classpath ordering and is effectively arbitrary — the server may run with the wrong crypto provider with no warning above debug level. Equal-order ties should still fail fast, or at least log a warning.

title: ES384/ES512 tests sign with a P-256 key and never verify the re-encoded DER with JCA
body: The test constructor creates a single key with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, whose default curve is P-256, and reuses it for all three tests. As a result testES384 and testES512 never process real 48-byte or 66-byte r/s values, so the padding/truncation logic in integerToBytes for those sizes is untested despite the test names suggesting otherwise. Additionally, the test only asserts that decode(encode(x)) == x, which is self-consistent by construction; the re-encoded DER signature is never passed to java.security.Signature.verify(), so an encoder bug that produces DER the JCA (or the server) rejects would still pass. Each test should generate a key for the matching curve (secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) and verify the re-encoded signature with JCA.

title: New abstract order() method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: The PR adds a new abstract method `int order()` to the public `CryptoProvider` interface in keycloak-common. Any third-party or downstream CryptoProvider implementation compiled against a previous keycloak-common version does not implement this method. With the new `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` code, `Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order)` invokes `order()` on every provider found by the ServiceLoader, so an older compiled provider will throw `AbstractMethodError` during `CryptoIntegration.init`, completely failing startup instead of just being sorted differently. Making it a default method (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) would preserve binary/source compatibility for existing implementations.

title: Multiple real providers with equal order() are now silently resolved by classpath order instead of failing fast
body: Previously, `detectProvider` threw an IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath, which caught misconfigured deployments. Now providers are sorted by `order()` descending and the first is silently used, with the rest only logged at debug level. However all three 'real' providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider) return the same order value 200, so if two of their jars end up on the classpath together, the winner is decided by ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order — non-obvious and environment-dependent. This is especially risky for FIPS: if both crypto/default and crypto/fips1402 jars are present, the non-FIPS provider may silently be selected (and even when FIPS wins, merely instantiating DefaultCryptoProvider during ServiceLoader iteration registers the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider in the JVM security provider list as a constructor side effect). Equal-order ties among full providers should still be treated as a configuration error rather than silently picked.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JVM default keystore provider, not a BouncyCastle provider
body: `AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider()` is implemented as `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which returns whatever JCA provider backs the default keystore (typically the SUN provider) — not a BouncyCastle provider as the interface contract (`@return BouncyCastle security provider. Can be either non-FIPS or FIPS based provider`) documents. Any caller that obtains this provider and then requests BouncyCastle-specific algorithms or keystores (e.g. BCFKS, PKCS7Padding via BC) from it will fail at runtime, and callers that use a non-null return value as a signal that BouncyCastle is available will be misled. WildFlyElytronProvider demonstrates that returning null is an accepted implementation; if the authz-client genuinely has no BouncyCastle, this should return null (or the contract/hack should be documented) rather than returning an unrelated provider.

title: ECDSA conversion test only round-trips through the same implementation, so it cannot catch standard-noncompliant DER encoding
body: The new test verifies `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` by feeding the output of `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` back into `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` and asserting equality. Because both directions are implemented by the same new ASN1Encoder/ASN1Decoder code, any self-consistent but incorrect encoding still passes — for example, if both the encoder and decoder used a wrong tag constant for INTEGER or SEQUENCE, or mis-encoded lengths, the round-trip assertion would still succeed while real Keycloak servers would reject the produced JWS signatures.
