body: The audit log endpoint instantiates OptimizedCursorPaginator with order_by="-datetime", but OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `int(math.floor(value) if ... else math.ceil(value))` on `getattr(item, self.key)`. For the audit logs endpoint that value is a `datetime` object, and `math.floor`/`math.ceil` on a datetime raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime`. This is called from build_cursor on the very first page of results (to compute the next cursor), so every request using `optimized_pagination=true` will 500 as soon as there is at least one audit log row. The code needed the DateTimePaginator-style conversion (`value.strftime("%s.%f") * multiplier`) or should have subclassed DateTimePaginator. There is also a secondary issue: even if get_item_key were fixed to return an int, `value_from_cursor` returns the raw integer cursor value and `build_queryset` would then compare the datetime column against an integer (`datetime <= %s` with an int param), which the database will reject.

title: Negative-offset branch passes a negative index to a Django QuerySet slice, which raises AssertionError
body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[cursor.offset : cursor.offset + limit + extra]`. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing — slicing with a negative start raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported`. The inline comment claiming 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. Since cursor offsets are user-controlled (the `cursor` query string is parsed by Cursor.from_string with `int(bits[1])`, which accepts negatives), any privileged caller can supply e.g. `cursor=0:-5:0` with `optimized_pagination=true` and get a 500 AssertionError on every request. This is a reliable crash/DoS of the endpoint rather than a performance feature, and no boundary handling exists.

title: enable_advanced is computed unconditionally and dereferences organization_context.member, crashing for member-less auth
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated on every GET, even when the `optimized_pagination` query param is absent. `organization_context.member` is None for requests authenticated without an organization member (e.g., org API keys / auth tokens with the org:read scope that legitimately pass OrganizationAuditPermission). For such requests `request.user.is_superuser` is False, so the right-hand side evaluates `None.has_global_access` and raises AttributeError, returning a 500. This regresses the previously working default pagination path for those auth types. The expression should be computed lazily inside the `use_optimized` branch and guard against `member is None`.

title: Trim check compares against the raw negative offset instead of the slice actually fetched
body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, the `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra:` check uses the original `offset` variable, which in the negative-offset branch is negative. Since `queryset[negative:...]` raises before this is reached in Django, this is currently masked, but if the slicing ever 'worked' (e.g., on a list-backed queryset), the comparison would never match and the extra boundary row would not be trimmed, leaking an extra row into the page and producing wrong cursors. It should compare against the actual fetch size (`stop - start_offset` or `limit + extra`).

title: Comment claims negative offsets are a supported performance optimization, but no paginator actually supports them
body: The added comment in Cursor.__init__ states negative offsets are allowed for 'advanced pagination scenarios' and enable 'efficient reverse pagination'. No paginator actually handles negative offsets correctly — BasePaginator clamps non-prev offsets with max(0, offset), OffsetPaginator/MergingOffsetPaginator/ChainPaginator explicitly raise BadPaginationError on negative offsets, and OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset path crashes on Django's 'Negative indexing is not supported' assertion. The comment documents a capability that does not exist and is misleading to future maintainers.

title: No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the new audit-logs pagination branch
body: The PR adds ~100 lines of new pagination logic (OptimizedCursorPaginator) plus a new conditional branch in OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint gated by the `optimized_pagination` query param and superuser/global-access checks, but adds no tests. Tests would have immediately caught the two crash bugs (datetime math.floor TypeError and negative-slice AssertionError). At minimum there should be tests covering: optimized_pagination=true for a superuser with audit log rows present, a prev/next cursor round-trip, a negative-offset cursor, and a non-member token request (to cover the member-None path).

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes on datetime ordering (math.floor on datetime)
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `int(math.floor(value))` on the raw attribute value, but the only caller (OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint) uses it with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `value` is a `datetime.datetime` and `math.floor()` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime`. This is exactly why DateTimePaginator exists (it converts the datetime to a millisecond timestamp first). Every request with `optimized_pagination=true` will 500 on the first page when `build_cursor` computes the cursor key. Additionally, `value_from_cursor` returns the raw cursor value, so even past that point the datetime column would be compared against a bare integer timestamp, producing wrong filtering. The optimized path is completely broken for its intended use.

title: Negative-offset 'advanced' path crashes: Django does not support negative queryset slicing
body: The new branch `if self.enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0` slices the queryset with `queryset[start_offset:stop]` where `start_offset = cursor.offset` is negative. The comment claims 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically', which is false: Django's QuerySet slicing raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.` The cursor offset is attacker/user-controllable via the `cursor` query parameter (e.g. `?cursor=0:-100:0`), so any superuser/admin passing a negative offset with `optimized_pagination=true` gets a 500. The same crash applies in the BasePaginator change at line 182-184, where an `is_prev` cursor with a negative offset is passed through unclamped into the slice.

title: organization_context.member can be None, causing AttributeError for token-based auth
body: The gating expression `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences `organization_context.member` without a None check. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is None when the request is authenticated with an organization auth token or other non-member credentials (in which case `request.user` is anonymous and `is_superuser` is False, so short-circuiting does not save it). Such requests to the audit log endpoint will now raise AttributeError and return 500 instead of the audit log listing.

title: No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the new endpoint branch
body: The PR adds ~100 lines of new pagination logic (OptimizedCursorPaginator) plus a new conditional branch in the audit log endpoint, but adds no tests. Basic tests exercising `optimized_pagination=true` would have immediately caught the datetime math.floor TypeError and the negative-slicing AssertionError described above. At minimum, tests should cover the happy path with datetime ordering, forward/backward cursor navigation, and rejection/clamping of negative-offset cursors.

title: Misleading comments justify broken negative-offset behavior
body: New comments in cursors.py and paginator.py claim that negative offsets are a safe 'performance optimization' and that 'the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions' / 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. These statements are incorrect — Django explicitly rejects negative queryset indexing — and the comments serve to rationalize code paths that crash at runtime. The comments should be removed or corrected along with the broken code.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator is a numeric paginator but is used with order_by="-datetime", so the optimized path always 500s
body: The endpoint passes order_by="-datetime" to OptimizedCursorPaginator, but that paginator's get_item_key (src/sentry/api/paginator.py, in the new class) does `int(math.floor(value) ...)` directly on the attribute value, unlike DateTimePaginator which first converts the datetime to a numeric timestamp via strftime. Calling math.floor on a datetime raises TypeError, so on the very first page (cursor value 0, results non-empty) build_cursor will call get_item_key(results[0]) and the request will raise a 500. Additionally, value_from_cursor returns the raw numeric cursor value, so any subsequent page would feed an integer into the `datetime <= %s` comparison in build_queryset, which is also wrong. The entire optimized_pagination=true code path is non-functional for this endpoint; the paginator needs DateTimePaginator's key conversion (or should subclass it).

title: Negative-offset branch slices a Django queryset with negative indexes, which raises AssertionError — the comment claiming the ORM handles it is false
body: The new `enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0` branch does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with start_offset taken straight from the client-supplied cursor offset (cursors are parsed from the `cursor` query param as `value:offset:is_prev` in Cursor.from_string, so a negative offset like `0:-100:0` is fully client-controllable). Django querysets do not support negative slicing — queryset[-100:...] raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported`, producing a 500. The comment 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is incorrect, as is the docstring claim that this 'enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds'. The only effect of this branch is a crash for any caller who supplies a negative offset, and it is enabled on the audit logs endpoint whenever a superuser/global-access member passes optimized_pagination=true.

title: BasePaginator.get_result now silently clamps negative non-prev offsets to 0, changing shared behavior for every paginator
body: This PR modifies the shared BasePaginator.get_result: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. Since cursor.offset comes from the client-supplied cursor string, a previously invalid cursor (negative offset on a forward page) used to fail loudly (Django raises on negative queryset slicing, which is the existing signal that the cursor is malformed); it is now silently rewritten to offset 0, returning page 1 as if the cursor were valid. This affects all endpoints using Paginator/DateTimePaginator, not just the audit log endpoint, and it masks bad cursors instead of surfacing them. Meanwhile the is_prev branch still passes a negative offset straight into the slice, so the claimed 'boundary condition handling' is inconsistent. This unrelated behavioral change to shared pagination code should not ship as part of this PR.

title: organization_context.member may be None; attribute access raises AttributeError for non-member auth
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences organization_context.member unconditionally whenever the user is not a superuser. RpcUserOrganizationContext.member is optional — requests authenticated via org auth tokens or other non-member principals reach this endpoint with member=None (which is why other Sentry endpoints guard with `organization_context.member and ...`). Such requests will raise AttributeError and return a 500 instead of audit logs. Guard the access, e.g. `organization_context.member is not None and organization_context.member.has_global_access`.

title: No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the new optimized_pagination endpoint branch
body: This PR adds a new paginator class (~90 lines, mostly a copy of BasePaginator.get_result with a new negative-offset branch and an enable_advanced_features flag) plus a new conditional code path in the audit logs endpoint, but adds no tests. Tests would have caught the two hard failures introduced here: the numeric get_item_key being incompatible with the endpoint's datetime ordering (TypeError on the first page) and the negative-offset branch raising on queryset slicing. At minimum there should be unit tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator covering prev/next cursors, empty results, and negative/malformed offsets, and an endpoint test exercising optimized_pagination=true for both superuser and non-superuser requests.

title: Added comment claims a behavior change that does not exist
body: The new comment in Cursor.__init__ says 'Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios / This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets', but the code is unchanged (`self.offset = int(offset)` already accepted negatives before this PR). The comment misdocuments the code, implies a feature that Cursor itself does not provide, and — since negative offsets actually crash queryset slicing downstream — is actively misleading to future readers.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot paginate datetime-ordered querysets, breaking the audit log endpoint path that uses it
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `int(math.floor(value))` on the raw model attribute, which only works for numeric keys. The new code in organization_auditlogs.py instantiates it with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `getattr(item, "datetime")` returns a datetime and `math.floor(datetime)` raises TypeError (this is exactly why DateTimePaginator overrides get_item_key to convert via strftime). Additionally, value_from_cursor returns the raw numeric cursor value, which build_queryset then compares against a datetime column. Every request with `optimized_pagination=true` will therefore 500 on the first page when build_cursor calls the key function. The optimized branch added to OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint is non-functional as written.

title: Negative-offset 'advanced pagination' path crashes: Django does not support negative slicing
body: The new branch `if self.enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0` passes a negative start directly into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, and the comment claims 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. That is false: Django's QuerySet slicing raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` for a negative start. Cursor offsets are user-controllable (Cursor.from_string happily parses `value:-100:0`), so any caller that enables this flag — the audit log endpoint does so via `enable_advanced_features=True` — can be forced into an unhandled exception and a 500 on every such request. The misleading comment in Cursor.__init__ (src/sentry/utils/cursors.py) about negative offsets being a supported optimization compounds this.

title: organization_context.member can be None, causing AttributeError for non-member authentication
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences `organization_context.member` unconditionally whenever the user is not a superuser. RpcUserOrganizationContext.member is optional — requests authenticated with org-level auth tokens or other non-member principals have no member object — so those requests to the audit log endpoint will now raise AttributeError and return 500 instead of the audit log. This access is new in this PR; previously the endpoint never touched `.member`. Guard with `organization_context.member and organization_context.member.has_global_access`.

title: Segment keys change Redis type from SET to ZSET with no key rename or migration, causing WRONGTYPE errors during rollout
body: This PR changes the segment storage under the same key pattern `span-buf:s:{project:trace}:span_id` from a Redis SET (sadd/sscan/sunionstore) to a ZSET (zadd/zscan/zunionstore). Keys written by the old code live up to `redis_ttl` (default 3600s). After deploy, the Python `p.zadd(...)` and the new Lua script's `zcard`/`zunionstore` will hit pre-existing SET keys and Redis will raise WRONGTYPE, which propagates out of process_spans and fails the whole consumer batch (crash/retry loop) until all old keys expire. The key namespace should be versioned (e.g. `span-buf:sz:`) or a migration/compat path provided.

title: KeyError on spans missing end_timestamp_precise will fail the entire batch
body: `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` uses direct indexing on the decoded span payload. Any message from an older Relay or a producer that omits this field raises KeyError inside process_batch, which fails the whole batch and leaves the consumer stuck retrying the same poison message. The pre-existing test payload (which lacked the field and had to be updated in this PR) shows such messages exist in practice. Use `val.get("end_timestamp_precise")` with a sensible fallback (e.g. 0 or the batch timestamp) so one malformed span cannot stall processing.

title: Segment span cap is hardcoded to 1000 in Lua while SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans (1001) is now dead config
body: The eviction logic `if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)` hardcodes the limit in the Lua script instead of taking it as an ARGV, while `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` — a parameter that is no longer read anywhere after this PR removed the `max_segment_spans` check (and the `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` metric) from `_load_segment_data`. Operators tuning `max_segment_spans` will silently have no effect, and the two values (1000 vs 1001) already disagree. Either pass the limit into the script or remove the Python config.

title: Redirect-chain resolution limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000
body: The redirect-following loop was reduced from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000`, and the comment warning that segment trees deeper than the limit 'may not be joined together correctly' was deleted rather than updated. Segment trees with redirect chains deeper than 1000 will now silently fail to merge and be flushed as split/duplicated segments — a 10x tightening of a correctness-relevant limit with no mention in the PR and no remaining in-code warning. If intentional for performance, the comment should be kept (updated to 1000) and the behavior change documented; the redirect_depth metrics already emitted can verify impact.

title: Comment claims negative offsets are 'safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions' — queryset actually raises
body: The new comment above `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` says allowing negative offsets 'is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions'. In fact Django raises AssertionError on negative slice starts, which is precisely why the clamp to max(0, offset) had to be added. The comment describes the opposite of what the code does and contradicts the identical false claim in OptimizedCursorPaginator; it should be corrected so future readers don't remove the clamp believing the ORM handles it.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot paginate by -datetime; every optimized request 500s
body: The endpoint orders by `-datetime` but uses `OptimizedCursorPaginator`, whose `get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(getattr(item, self.key)))` on the `datetime` attribute — `math.floor()` on a `datetime` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime`. Even if that were fixed, `value_from_cursor` returns the raw numeric cursor value, which `build_queryset` then compares against a datetime column (`col <= %s` with a float), producing a database error. Unlike `DateTimePaginator` it has no strftime/multiplier conversion, so any request with `optimized_pagination=true` from a superuser/global-access member will return HTTP 500. The new paginator is unusable for this endpoint.

title: Negative-offset slicing crashes: Django does not support negative indexing
body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[cursor.offset:stop]` with a negative start. The comment claims 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically', but Django's QuerySet explicitly raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` for a negative slice start. Since cursor offsets are user-controlled via the cursor query parameter (`Cursor.from_string` happily parses `0:-5:0`), any admin hitting the audit log endpoint with such a cursor and `optimized_pagination=true` gets a 500. The 'advanced feature' is broken as implemented and the comment is factually wrong.

title: SET→ZSET migration breaks in-flight buffered segments with WRONGTYPE errors
body: The script and the Python producer switch segment buffer keys from Redis SETs (`sadd`/`scard`/`sunionstore`) to sorted sets (`zadd`/`zcard`/`zunionstore`), but existing keys in Redis written by the old code are still SETs. Calling `zcard`/`zunionstore` on a SET key (and likewise `p.zadd` in `SpansBuffer.process_spans`) raises a WRONGTYPE error, which aborts the Lua script and fails the whole batch of `EVALSHA` calls. During a rolling deploy — and for up to `redis_ttl` afterwards — all traces with segments buffered by the old code will cause consumer errors and those spans will not be buffered. There is no type check or migration path (e.g., probing with `type`/`object encoding`, or a key version bump).

title: Hardcoded 1000-span eviction ignores max_segment_spans and silently drops spans
body: The new eviction `if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)` hardcodes 1000, while `SpansBuffer` still accepts a configurable `max_segment_spans` (default 1001) that is now never used — the Python-side check that dropped oversized segments with a `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric and error log was removed from `_load_segment_data`. Consequences: (1) the configured limit is silently ignored, (2) spans are evicted silently instead of the segment being dropped with an error, so downstream consumers receive incomplete segments presented as complete, and (3) `zpopmin` evicts the lowest-scored (earliest `end_timestamp_precise`) spans, which can include the segment's root span, changing flush semantics. `max_segment_spans` should either be passed into the script or removed.

title: organization_context.member may be None, causing AttributeError for org-token auth
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences `organization_context.member` unconditionally for non-superusers. For requests authenticated with an organization auth token (or any non-member context), `organization_context.member` is `None`, so this raises `AttributeError` and returns 500. Previously the audit log endpoint worked for any caller passing `OrganizationAuditPermission`. The member check needs a `None` guard.

title: Redirect-follow limit reduced from 10000 to 1000 without rationale
body: The redirect-chasing loop was lowered from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000`, and the old comment documenting the consequence ('segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly') was deleted. Segment trees whose redirect chain exceeds 1000 hops will now silently stop being merged — children will stay in a separate set and be flushed as their own (incomplete) segment. If the reduction is intentional for latency, the trade-off should at least be documented; otherwise deep traces lose spans relative to the old behavior.

title: KeyError on payloads missing end_timestamp_precise crashes the batch
body: `Span(..., end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"], ...)` is a new hard dictionary access. The consumer only `cast`s the decoded JSON to `SpanEvent` and performs no schema validation, so any message lacking this field (older Relay payloads, malformed messages, spillover replays) raises `KeyError`, which fails the entire batch and causes it to be reprocessed in a crash loop. Previously this field was never read. Use `val.get(...)` with a fallback (e.g., 0 or the batch timestamp) if the field is not guaranteed to be present.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle the datetime order_by used here — every optimized request 500s
body: The endpoint passes order_by="-datetime" to OptimizedCursorPaginator, but OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `int(math.floor(value))` / `math.ceil(value)` on the raw attribute value. For a datetime attribute (AuditLogEntry.datetime) this raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime` — which is exactly why DateTimePaginator exists (it converts via strftime first). The exception is raised inside build_cursor when computing the next cursor key, so any request with `optimized_pagination=true` that returns at least one row will fail with a 500. This path is completely untested and non-functional.

title: Negative-offset slicing is not 'handled automatically' by the Django ORM — it raises AssertionError
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result explicitly enables client-supplied negative cursor offsets (`queryset[cursor.offset:stop]` when `enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0`), and the comments claim 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. That is false: Django querysets do not support negative indexing and raise `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported`, producing a 500. The offset is attacker-controllable because cursor strings are parsed from the request query string via Cursor.from_string (`int(bits[1])` accepts negatives), so any superuser/org-admin who enables `optimized_pagination` can crash the endpoint with a crafted cursor. The feature as documented cannot work; the negative-offset branch and its misleading comments should be removed.

title: organization_context.member may be None — AttributeError for token-authenticated requests
body: `organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated whenever the request is not from a superuser and `optimized_pagination=true` is passed. RpcUserOrganizationContext.member is None for requests authenticated via org auth tokens/API keys (no member object), so this raises AttributeError and returns a 500 instead of falling back to the normal paginator. Elsewhere in the codebase this is guarded as `organization_context.member and organization_context.member.has_global_access`; the same guard is needed here.

title: Redirect resolution depth cut from 10000 to 1000 silently splits deep segments
body: The redirect-chasing loop now gives up after 1000 hops (previously 10000, with a comment documenting the tradeoff, which was also deleted). When the loop exhausts its iterations, set_span_id remains an intermediate node whose set has already been merged deeper, so the incoming span and its subtree are written to a new, separate set_key and the segment is permanently split — spans that belong to one trace get flushed as two segments with different segment_ids. This failure is silent (no metric, no log). If the lower bound is intentional, the truncation case should at least be detected and emitted as a metric.

title: Eviction threshold hardcoded to 1000 while the configurable max_segment_spans enforcement was removed
body: The Lua script evicts spans whenever a set exceeds a hardcoded 1000 entries (`if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin ... end`), but the threshold is not passed in from Python. At the same time, the Python-side enforcement of the configurable `max_segment_spans` (default 1001) was deleted from SpansBuffer._load_segment_data in buffer.py, so the `max_segment_spans` constructor parameter is now dead: operators who tune it get no effect, and the effective limit is always 1000 regardless of configuration. Additionally, eviction drops the lowest-scored (earliest end_timestamp) spans with no metric or log, so data loss from over-large segments is now invisible (previously over-limit segments were skipped with an error log and the `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric).

title: zunionstore default SUM aggregate inflates scores when the same span exists in both sets
body: `zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` uses the default aggregate SUM. With at-least-once Kafka delivery, the same span payload can be present in both the parent set and the span's own set (e.g., after a consumer retry where the redirect map changed between attempts); previously `sunionstore` was idempotent for duplicate members, but now the duplicated member's score is doubled (2 * end_timestamp_precise). Since scores drive the eviction order (zpopmin evicts lowest scores first), duplicated spans are artificially protected from eviction while genuinely earlier spans are evicted instead. Pass `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) to keep merge idempotent.

title: No tests for the new eviction behavior or the reduced redirect depth
body: The PR introduces two data-affecting behaviors in add-buffer.lua — eviction of spans once a segment exceeds 1000 entries (zpopmin) and the redirect-depth reduction from 10000 to 1000 — but the test changes only add the now-required `end_timestamp_precise` field to existing fixtures. There is no test asserting which spans survive eviction (score ordering), that eviction actually caps segment size, or what happens when a redirect chain exceeds the loop limit, so a regression in either behavior (e.g., evicting the root span, off-by-one in the cap) would ship undetected.

title: Accidental git submodule of the repository itself committed
body: The PR adds a new file `sentry-repo` containing `Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a` — this is a gitlink (embedded git repository) pointing at the base commit of this very repo, almost certainly created accidentally by running git commands inside a nested checkout. There is no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry, so this will leave the working tree in a confusing state for anyone who clones or checks out this branch (uninitialized submodule, dirty status, possible CI failures). It should be removed from the PR entirely.

title: Substring match treats negated `!event.type:error` queries as error-focused and upsamples transaction counts
body: _is_error_focused_query decides whether a discover query is error-only by checking `if "event.type:error" in query` on the lowercased raw query string. A query such as `!event.type:error` (everything *except* errors, i.e. transactions on the discover dataset) contains that substring, so it is classified as error-focused and count() is rewritten to `upsampled_count()` = `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. Transaction events do not carry a meaningful `sample_weight`, so their counts come back as 0/NULL instead of the true count — silently wrong results. The same false positive occurs for any query merely mentioning the text (e.g. `message:"event.type:error"`). The check should parse the query or at least account for negation rather than doing a raw substring match.

title: Upsampling decision uses outer `dataset` instead of the `scoped_dataset` actually being queried
body: Inside `_get_event_stats`, the eligibility check calls `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` where `dataset` is the closure variable from `get()`, not the `scoped_dataset` argument that the query is actually executed against. In the dashboard-widget split path (`get_event_stats_factory`), `_get_event_stats` is invoked with `discover` as the scoped dataset and an errors-only query (`({query}) AND !event.type:transaction`) while the outer `dataset` is `metrics_performance`/`metrics_enhanced_performance`; `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` then returns False for the metrics dataset, so error counts for allowlisted (client-sampled) projects are never upsampled and are under-reported by the sampling factor. The check should use `scoped_dataset` (and ideally the actual query string being executed rather than `request.GET`).

title: Cache key built with `hash()` can collide across different project sets
body: The eligibility cache key is `f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))}"`. Python's `hash()` produces a 64-bit value with no uniqueness guarantee: two different sets of project IDs that hash to the same value share a cache entry, so one set's allowlist eligibility would be returned for a different set of projects, producing wrong (upsampled or non-upsampled) counts for up to 60 seconds. Hash values are also not guaranteed stable across Python versions, causing silent key changes on deploys. The sorted project IDs themselves (e.g. joined with commas) should be used as the key instead of a hash.

title: Docstring claims fresh allowlist reads while the caller caches results for 60 seconds
body: The docstring for `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` states: "This function reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time, which means it can return different results between calls if the configuration changes during request processing. This is intentional to ensure we always have the latest configuration state." In reality the only caller, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, caches the result for 60 seconds, so allowlist changes are explicitly *not* picked up fresh and stale eligibility is served for up to a minute. The docstring describes behavior the code does not have and contradicts the caching design documented in the caller; it should be corrected. Relatedly, `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (line 67) claims it "should be called when the allowlist configuration changes" but nothing in the codebase calls it, so there is no actual invalidation path.

title: Accidentally committed git submodule ('sentry-repo') pointing at the repo's own base commit
body: The PR adds a file `sentry-repo` containing `Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a` — a gitlink (embedded submodule) referencing the base commit of this very repository. This looks like a local checkout accidentally committed as a submodule. It adds a bogus gitlink to the tree, will break or slow down `git clone --recursive` / CI checkout steps (the submodule has no .gitmodules entry), and has nothing to do with the feature. It should be removed before merging.

title: Substring match treats negated queries like `!event.type:error` as error-focused
body: `_is_error_focused_query` returns True whenever the raw query string contains the substring "event.type:error". A query that explicitly *excludes* errors, e.g. `!event.type:error` (the standard way to query non-error/transaction events in discover), also contains that substring, so it will be classified as error-focused and `count()` will be rewritten to `sum(sample_weight)` over transaction rows, where sample_weight is absent/zero — returning wrong (likely zero) counts. Similarly, a query merely mentioning the field in another context (e.g. inside a quoted message search) triggers upsampling. The check should parse the query or at least exclude negated occurrences instead of doing a raw substring search.

title: Upsampling decision uses outer `dataset`/raw request query instead of `scoped_dataset` and the actual query string
body: Inside `_get_event_stats`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` closes over the outer `dataset` variable and the helper reads `request.GET['query']` directly, ignoring both the `scoped_dataset` parameter and the `query` argument passed to `_get_event_stats`. In the dashboard-widget split path, `_get_event_stats` is invoked with modified queries — e.g. `(<query>) AND !event.type:transaction` for the errors split (with scoped_dataset=discover) and `(<query>) AND event.type:transaction` for the transactions split — and with a scoped_dataset that can differ from the outer dataset (e.g. discover while the outer dataset is metrics_performance). As a result the upsampling transformation is applied or skipped based on the wrong dataset and the wrong query text: the transactions-only split query can get upsampled counts (wrong numbers) and the errors-only split query can fail to get upsampled counts (undercounted). The check should use `scoped_dataset` and the `query` parameter actually being executed.

title: upsampled_count sums sample_weight with no NULL fallback, zeroing out events stored without a weight
body: The new `upsampled_count` SnQL function compiles to `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` and the surrounding comments state it 'assumes sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects'. That assumption does not hold: allowlisting is per-project, but error events ingested *before* the project was allowlisted (or ingested without client sampling) have no sample_weight, and stats queries routinely cover historical time ranges. For rows where sample_weight is NULL, `sum` will either ignore them or return NULL (which `toInt64` turns into 0), so `count()` on an allowlisted project will silently undercount — showing 0 or fewer errors than actually occurred — for any time bucket containing older events. The aggregate should fall back to 1 for missing weights, e.g. `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))`.

title: upsampled_count is registered as a public function, exposing it to arbitrary user queries
body: Unlike the neighboring private SnQL functions (e.g. the one above it with `private=True`), `upsampled_count` is registered without `private=True`, making it usable by any user in arbitrary Discover queries and datasets. Against datasets/contexts where the `sample_weight` column does not exist (transactions, etc.) this produces Snuba query errors surfaced to users, and it exposes an internal implementation detail as part of the public query API. It should be marked private and explicitly allowed only where the upsampling transformation injects it.

title: invalidate_upsampling_cache is dead code; allowlist changes are stale for up to 60s with no way to invalidate, and the docstring contradicts the cache
body: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined and documented as the mechanism to call 'when the allowlist configuration changes', but nothing in the codebase calls it, so allowlist edits always take up to 60 seconds to take effect with no escape hatch. Additionally, the docstring on `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` claims it 'reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time ... to ensure we always have the latest configuration state', which is directly contradicted by the 60-second result cache in the only caller. Either wire the invalidation into the option-change path or fix the misleading documentation.

title: _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling silently swallows invalid data and drops a 0 sample rate
body: The new factory helper wraps everything in bare `except Exception: pass` blocks and only sets `normalized_data['sample_rate']` when `client_sample_rate` is truthy. A malformed or non-numeric `client_sample_rate` in a test event is silently ignored (the test then runs against unsampled data, producing confusing count assertions rather than a clear failure), and an explicit rate of 0 is dropped by the truthiness check. For test infrastructure, silently ignoring invalid fixture data makes failing tests much harder to diagnose; it should raise or at least validate explicitly.

title: Top-level eligibility function and its 60s caching behavior are never tested
body: The unit tests exercise the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`) but never call the public entry point `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`. That function contains the PR's riskiest new logic — the cache key construction, the cache-hit short-circuit, and the combination of cached eligibility with the per-request dataset check — so regressions there (e.g. caching False forever, key collisions across project sets, ignoring the dataset check on cache hits) would not be caught by these tests.

title: Accidentally committed git submodule (gitlink) of the repository itself
body: This PR adds a file named `sentry-repo` containing a gitlink entry (`Subproject commit a5d2909...`, which is the base commit of this very repository). There is no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry, so this is almost certainly an accidentally `git add`ed nested checkout rather than an intentional submodule. It pollutes the repository root, will show up as an unresolvable submodule for anyone cloning with `--recurse-submodules`, and can confuse tooling and CI. It should be removed from the PR.

title: Substring match treats negated/excluded error queries as error-focused
body: `_is_error_focused_query` does a naive substring check: `if "event.type:error" in query`. A discover query like `!event.type:error` (transactions only) still contains that substring, so the function returns True and `count()` is rewritten to `upsampled_count() as count` (sum of `sample_weight`) even though the query explicitly excludes error events and transactions don't carry `sample_weight`. The same applies to queries where `event.type:error` appears inside a quoted message or tag value, or alongside `OR event.type:transaction`. Consequence: silently wrong (under/over-counted or zeroed) results returned to users. The check should parse the search query and verify a positive `event.type:error` filter rather than substring matching.

title: Upsampling eligibility checked against outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`
body: Inside `_get_event_stats`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` uses the closure variable `dataset` (the dataset chosen for the overall request) rather than the `scoped_dataset` argument that the query is actually executed against. In the dashboard-widget split path, `_get_event_stats` is invoked with `split_dataset = discover` and an errors-only query even when the outer dataset is a metrics/performance dataset — in that case `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform(metrics_performance, ...)` returns False, so the errors-only split query never gets the upsampling transform. The result is that error counts in split dashboard widgets are reported as raw counts while the same data queried directly is upsampled, producing inconsistent numbers.

title: Eligibility inspects raw request query instead of the query actually being executed
body: `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` calls `_is_error_focused_query(request)`, which reads `request.GET.get("query")`. However, `_get_event_stats` receives a `query` string that is rewritten before execution in several paths — e.g. the dashboard-split logic builds `errors_only_query = f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction"` and `transactions_only_query = f"({query}) AND event.type:transaction"`. Because the helper ignores the effective query string, the upsampling decision is based on the original user query: the transactions-only split query can get the `count() -> sum(sample_weight)` transform applied (wrong results, since transactions have no `sample_weight`), and the errors-only split query can miss it when the original query didn't literally contain `event.type:error`. The effective query string should be threaded through to the check.

title: Python built-in `hash()` used in a shared cache key
body: The cache key is built as `f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))}"`. Using Python's built-in `hash()` for a cache key is fragile: it can collide for different project sets (a collision would make one set of projects inherit the cached allowlist decision of a different set, silently enabling or disabling upsampling for 60s), and its value is not guaranteed stable across Python builds/platforms, which defeats sharing the cache across heterogeneous deployments. A deterministic serialization (e.g. `-`.join of sorted ids, or a hashlib digest) should be used instead.

title: Docstring contradicts the caching behavior of the caller
body: The docstring of `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` states: "This function reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time... This is intentional to ensure we always have the latest configuration state." In practice the only production caller, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, wraps it in a 60-second cache and also provides `invalidate_upsampling_cache`, which is never called from anywhere in the codebase. The documented guarantee is therefore false, and allowlist changes are silently stale for up to a minute with no wired-up invalidation path. Either wire up invalidation or correct the docstring.

title: Feature-flagged table branch renders a hardcoded empty table
body: In `tableResultComponent`, when the organization has the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature, the code renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />` — completely ignoring the actual `tableResults`, `loading` state, `fields`, field aliases, and custom renderers. If this flag is ever enabled for an organization, every table widget on their dashboards will render an empty table with no columns and no data instead of the query results, with no loading or error states. If this is intentional scaffolding, the flag must remain off until real data is wired through; otherwise this branch needs to pass the actual result data before merging.

title: Custom cell renderers checked by truthiness instead of undefined, so falsy React nodes are discarded
body: In both `renderDefaultBodyCell` (line 70) and `renderDefaultHeadCell` (line 31), the custom renderer result is checked with `if (cell) { return cell; }`. The documented contract (in the component docstrings and stories) is that the fallback renderer only runs when the custom renderer returns `undefined`. A custom renderer that legitimately returns a falsy React node — e.g. `0`, `''`, or `false` — will be silently ignored and replaced by the default renderer, producing wrong cell content. The check should be `if (cell !== undefined)` (or `!= null`) to match the documented behavior.

title: fetch_error_details misaligns error IDs with nodestore results via zip
body: In fetch_error_details, the code does `for event_id, data in zip(error_ids, events.values())`. `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a dict keyed by node id whose iteration order follows the backend's query order, not the order of `error_ids`, and any missing node is simply absent from the dict. If any one error event is missing from nodestore (expired/deleted), every subsequent pairing shifts by one, so each ErrorEvent gets the wrong `id` attached to the wrong event's title/message, and the final error_ids entries are silently dropped. The result is error context injected into the Seer summary prompt with incorrect event IDs and missing errors. The lookup should map back by node id instead of relying on positional zip, e.g. iterate `zip(error_ids, node_ids)` and read `events.get(node_id)`.

title: Feature-flagged table widget path renders hardcoded empty table, discarding real query results
body: In WidgetCardChart.tableResultComponent, when the organization has the 'use-table-widget-visualization' feature, the code renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />` instead of the actual `tableResults`/`result.data`/`result.meta` that were just fetched. If this flag is ever enabled for an organization, every table widget on their dashboards will render a permanently empty table (columns is an empty array, so no headers or rows render at all), and the loading/error/fieldAlias handling in the existing SimpleTableChart path is bypassed entirely. This is clearly a placeholder that should not be merged as-is; either wire the real `result.data`/`result.meta`/fields into TableWidgetVisualization or don't branch on the flag yet.

title: Assemble analytics event recorded before feature-flag and schema validation
body: The new `analytics.record('preprod_artifact.api.assemble', ...)` call is placed at the top of `post`, before the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` feature check (which returns 404) and before `validate_preprod_artifact_schema` (which returns 400). As a result the analytics event fires for requests from orgs without the feature and for malformed requests, inflating the metric with failed/no-op calls and making it unusable as a measure of actual assemble usage. Move the record call below the feature check and schema validation (or after the task is successfully enqueued).

title: age/timestamp mutual-exclusion validation uses truthiness, so age=0 bypasses it
body: BrowserReportSerializer.validate_timestamp checks `if self.initial_data.get("age")` and validate_age checks `if self.initial_data.get("timestamp")` to enforce that the two fields are mutually exclusive. Because `age` is an IntegerField, a report containing `"age": 0` together with a `timestamp` passes both validators (0 is falsy), accepting a report that mixes the two spec formats the serializer is explicitly designed to reject. Use `"age" in self.initial_data` / `is not None` instead of truthiness.

title: Falsy check on custom cell renderer causes valid falsy renders to be discarded
body: In renderDefaultBodyCell (and the same pattern in renderDefaultHeadCell at line 32), the custom renderer result is checked with `if (cell) { return cell; }` before falling back to the default renderer. The documented contract is that returning `undefined` opts into the fallback, but a custom renderer that legitimately returns `0`, `""`, or `null` (e.g. a cell that intentionally renders an empty value) will be silently replaced by the default field renderer's output, producing incorrect cell content. Check `cell !== undefined` instead so only an explicit undefined triggers the fallback.

title: New TableWidgetVisualization is wired up with hardcoded empty data
body: In `tableResultComponent`, when the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature flag is on, the code renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />` instead of passing the actual `result.data`/`result.meta` and the widget's fields. Because `TableWidgetVisualization` derives its columns from `columns ?? Object.keys(tableData.meta.fields)`, passing an empty `columns` array and empty meta means the table renders zero columns and zero rows regardless of the query results. Any organization that gets this flag enabled will see blank table widgets on all dashboards. If the integration isn't ready, the flag-gated branch should not be merged in this state; otherwise pass the real table data through.

title: HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES are only filtered out when the user is searching
body: The new `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES = ['is_segment', 'project_id', 'received']` list is only applied inside the search-filter branch: `if (!searchQuery.trim()) { return sorted; }` returns the unfiltered attribute list whenever the search box is empty. The intent of the change is clearly to never display these internal attributes, but in the default (no search) view they are still shown in the span attributes panel. The hidden-attribute exclusion needs to be applied to the base list, not just to the search-filtered list.

title: fetch_error_details zips error_ids with events.values() positionally, which can mismatch error IDs and payloads
body: `fetch_error_details` builds the result with `zip(error_ids, events.values())` and then filters out entries whose data is None. This assumes `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a dict whose iteration order exactly matches the input `error_ids` order and that every requested key is present. If nodestore returns events in a different order, or omits missing/expired nodes entirely (which the caching backend can do), every error after the missing one gets paired with the wrong event payload: the summary sent to Seer will attach one error's title/message to another error's ID. Look up each event by its node id (e.g. iterate `zip(node_ids, error_ids)` and index into the dict, or use `events.get(node_id)`) instead of relying on positional alignment.

title: All error events are injected into every paginated segment page
body: `get` paginates over recording segments (`GenericOffsetPaginator` with `on_results=functools.partial(analyze_recording_segments, error_events)`), and `analyze_recording_segments` merges the full `error_events` list into the log stream for whichever page of segments is being processed. `get_request_data` resets `error_idx` to 0 on each call, so for replays whose segments span multiple pages, every error line ('User experienced an error...') is emitted on every page, and errors far outside the page's time range are interleaved with that page's breadcrumbs. Clients fetching multiple pages will send duplicated error context to Seer (inflating the LLM prompt with repeats) and get chronologically misleading merges. Errors should be scoped to the page's segment time range (or deduplicated across pages).

title: Flex justify="right" is not a valid justify value
body: The replaced wrapper uses `<Flex justify="right">`. `right` is not part of the justify-content value union the shared `Flex` component accepts (flex-start/flex-end/center/space-between/space-around/space-evenly), so this will either fail type checking or silently produce no justification, leaving the Delete client button left-aligned instead of right-aligned as before. Use `justify="flex-end"`.

title: get_environment_info issues a Snuba query per issue inside PR comment generation
body: `get_environment_info` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()`, which performs an eventstore/Snuba lookup, and it is invoked once per issue from the GitHub/GitLab `get_comment_body` list comprehension (up to 5 issues per merged-PR comment). That adds up to 5 sequential Snuba queries inside the PR comment celery task on top of the existing top-issues query, increasing task latency and Snuba load on every merged PR with suspect issues. Consider fetching environments for all issues in one query, or skipping environment info when the additional cost isn't justified.

title: KeyError when Integration metadata has no 'sender'
body: In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the new verification step does `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`. The `sender` key is optional: `build_integration` only adds it `if state.get("sender")`, so Integration rows created through the pipeline itself (the `Integration.DoesNotExist` branch, e.g. when the installation webhook hasn't been processed yet) never get `sender` in metadata, and older rows may lack it too. If such an integration later has no OrganizationIntegration (e.g. the org integration was deleted and the user re-runs setup, or the first org-linking happens after a pipeline-created row exists), this line raises KeyError and the user gets a 500 instead of either succeeding or seeing the new failure page. Use `integration.metadata.get("sender")` and explicitly decide whether a missing sender should fail closed or be skipped.

title: Authenticated-user check is skipped when the Integration row doesn't exist yet
body: The PR's goal is to block linking a GitHub App installation when the OAuth-authenticated GitHub user differs from the user who installed the app. However, in GitHubInstallation.dispatch the check only runs when an Integration row already exists (the webhook-created path). In the `except Integration.DoesNotExist: return pipeline.next_step()` branch, the pipeline proceeds to `build_integration`, which calls `get_installation_info(state["installation_id"])` — an app-JWT call that returns data for *any* installation of the app — with no comparison against `github_authenticated_user` at all. An attacker who learns or guesses a victim's installation_id (these are sequential integers) can still attach that installation to their own Sentry org whenever the victim's Integration row is absent (webhook delivery failed or delayed, or installation predates webhook handling), which is the same hijack this PR intends to prevent. Consider validating the authenticated user in this branch too, or refusing to proceed until the installation webhook has created the Integration row.

title: Unhandled exceptions from GitHub HTTP calls in OAuthLoginView produce 500s
body: OAuthLoginView.dispatch calls `safe_urlopen(...)` (line 423) outside any try/except, and `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` (line 434) is also unguarded — it performs an HTTP GET to api.github.com and calls `.json()` on the response. Network failures, timeouts, or a non-JSON error body from GitHub will raise and surface as a 500 during installation, even though the stated intent of this change is that all OAuth/token failures show the 'We could not verify the authenticity of the installation request' page. Only the body-parsing step is wrapped (and with a bare `except Exception`). Wrap the token exchange and user-info calls and render the error page on failure.

title: No positive test for the sender-match branch; missing-sender crash untested
body: The new test `test_github_user_mismatch` only covers the failure case. There is no test for the success path of the new check: Integration row exists (created by the installation webhook) with no OrganizationIntegration, and the OAuth-authenticated user matches `metadata["sender"]["login"]` — which is the primary real-world flow for users who install the app directly from github.com. If the comparison were inverted or `github_authenticated_user` state binding broke, the suite would still pass. There is also no test for an Integration whose metadata lacks `sender`, which currently raises KeyError (500) instead of a handled outcome.

title: Unhandled exceptions from the token exchange and get_user_info produce 500s instead of the error page
body: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, the outbound calls safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data) (line 423) and get_user_info(payload['access_token']) (line 434) are not wrapped in any error handling. If GitHub is unreachable or returns a connection/timeout error, safe_urlopen raises; if the /user API call fails, get_user_info raises ApiError. Both bubble up as unhandled 500 errors during the installation pipeline, rather than rendering the intended github-integration-failed.html page. The code only gracefully handles the case where the token response parses but lacks access_token. Since this PR's goal is to fail the pipeline cleanly with a friendly error when GitHub cannot complete the OAuth exchange, these calls should be wrapped in try/except and routed to the same error() response.

title: KeyError when Integration metadata has no 'sender' entry
body: In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the new validation reads integration.metadata['sender']['login'] directly. The 'sender' metadata key is only populated in build_integration when state contains sender info (i.e., integrations created from the GitHub installation webhook). Integrations created through the Sentry-initiated install flow, or older integrations created before sender was recorded, do not have this key. If such an Integration row exists without an OrganizationIntegration (e.g., the org link was deleted or is pending deletion) and a user tries to reinstall, this line raises KeyError and returns a 500 instead of the intended 'Invalid installation request' error page. Use .get() with a fallback (and decide the failure behavior when sender is absent) instead of direct subscripting.

title: No tests for state mismatch or failed token exchange paths
body: The PR description lists three new failure conditions: OAuth user vs installer mismatch, state parameter vs pipeline signature mismatch, and GitHub failing to return an access_token (wrong/reused code). Only the user-mismatch case is tested (test_github_user_mismatch). There is no test that supplies a wrong state parameter to the OAuth callback and asserts the error page, and no test where the access_token response lacks a token (or the /user call returns no login). These are the core security checks being added and regressions in them would currently go undetected.

title: KeyError crash when existing Integration has no 'sender' in metadata
body: In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the new user-verification check does `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`. Integration.metadata is a schemaless JSON field, and `build_integration` only writes `metadata["sender"]` when the pipeline state contains a sender (`if state.get("sender")`). Integration rows created before sender tracking existed, or created through any flow where the sender was never bound into pipeline state, will not have this key. When such an ACTIVE Integration exists without an OrganizationIntegration (exactly the branch this check runs in, e.g. re-linking after an uninstall), the check raises KeyError and the user gets a 500 instead of the intended 'Invalid installation request' page, permanently blocking that installation flow. This should use a defensive lookup such as `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and treat a missing sender as a verification failure (rendering the error page) rather than crashing.

title: OAuth token exchange and /user lookup are not wrapped in error handling
body: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, `safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` (line 423) and `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` (line 434) are called without any exception handling. Only the reading/decoding of the response body is wrapped in try/except. If GitHub is unreachable, times out, or returns a 5xx, safe_urlopen raises; if the freshly issued token is rejected, get_user_info raises ApiError. In all of these transient-failure cases the user gets an unhandled 500 rather than the friendly 'We could not verify the authenticity of the installation request' page that this PR explicitly designs for every other failure mode (bad state, missing access_token, missing login). These calls should be wrapped so network/API failures render the same error response.

title: redirect_uri omitted from the OAuth token exchange even though it was sent in the authorize request
body: OAuthLoginView builds the token-exchange payload with only code, client_id, and client_secret, but the authorize redirect a few lines above includes a `redirect_uri` parameter. RFC 6749 §4.1.3 requires that redirect_uri be included (and identical) in the token request when it was present in the authorization request, and the code comments claim this mirrors `OAuth2CallbackView.get_token_params` / `exchange_token`, which do include redirect_uri. If GitHub enforces this (it does for mismatch cases), the exchange returns an error payload with no access_token and every GitHub installation fails at this step. The test suite stubs the token endpoint without validating the request body, so it would not catch this. Add `redirect_uri` (the same absolute_uri value used in the authorize URL) to the POST data.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the installation-not-found path
body: test_installation_not_found still stubs a 404 for GET /app/installations/{id} and is named for that scenario, but it now completes the OAuth step with a deliberately wrong `state` value (`ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`, which does not match the pipeline signature `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3` used everywhere else). The request therefore fails at the state check in OAuthLoginView, before GitHubInstallation or build_integration ever run, so the stubbed 404 is never hit and the assertion on the generic 'Invalid installation request.' message would pass regardless. The 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' branch in build_integration (ApiError 404 -> IntegrationError) is now uncovered. The test should either be renamed to reflect that it tests state mismatch, or reworked to pass the correct state so it actually exercises the 404 path again.

title: AssignmentSource.to_dict() puts a non-JSON-serializable datetime into the Celery task payload
body: `sync_group_assignee_outbound` passes `assignment_source.to_dict()` as a kwarg to `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async`. `to_dict()` is `dataclasses.asdict(self)`, which includes `queued` as a raw `datetime` object. Celery's default task serializer is JSON (and Sentry's task payloads are generally expected to be JSON-safe), and a `datetime` is not JSON-serializable, so `apply_async` will raise `TypeError: Object of type datetime is not JSON serializable` at enqueue time. This failure occurs synchronously inside `GroupAssignee.objects.assign/deassign` whenever an assignment was triggered by an inbound integration webhook (which is exactly the new code path that always sets an `AssignmentSource`), so every inbound-triggered assignment would 500 the webhook handler and never enqueue any outbound sync. Even with an encoder that coerces datetimes to ISO strings, `from_dict` would then produce `queued` as a string rather than a datetime. The `queued` value should be serialized explicitly (e.g. `isoformat()` / timestamp) and parsed back in `from_dict`, or dropped from the payload. Note the new tests run tasks eagerly via `self.tasks()`, so no real serialization round-trip is exercised and this would not be caught by CI.

title: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at class definition time
body: In a dataclass, a plain default expression is evaluated once when the class body executes, not per instance. `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` therefore freezes `queued` to the module import time for every `AssignmentSource` created without an explicit value, instead of recording when the assignment was queued. Dataclasses only reject list/dict/set defaults, so this fails silently. The fix is `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. The field is currently unused, so the impact is limited to incorrect data, but it is a latent bug for any future consumer of the timestamp.

title: New task kwarg is not backward compatible with workers running the previous code
body: `sync_assignee_outbound` now accepts `assignment_source_dict`, and `sync_group_assignee_outbound` immediately starts enqueuing messages containing that kwarg. During a rolling deploy (or a rollback), a worker still running the old function signature `sync_assignee_outbound(external_issue_id, user_id, assign)` will receive these messages and raise `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'assignment_source_dict'`; after the configured retries the assignee sync is lost. The standard mitigation is to stop passing the new kwarg until the new task signature is fully deployed (or guard it behind a feature/rollout), since the parameter was given a default only on the consumer side, which doesn't protect old consumers from new messages.

title: queued default is evaluated once at module import, not per instance
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated a single time when the class body is executed at import time, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit `queued` value (e.g. via `AssignmentSource.from_integration`) shares the same stale timestamp from when the process first imported the module. Dataclass defaults must be immutable values or use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. As written, the `queued` field is always wrong (it never reflects when the source was actually queued), which makes the field useless for debugging/tracing sync cycles — the very purpose of this dataclass. Fix: `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

title: from_dict does no type coercion; queued silently round-trips as a string through the Celery task
body: `AssignmentSource.to_dict()` emits `queued` as a `datetime`, but the value is passed as a Celery task kwarg (`assignment_source_dict` in `sync_assignee_outbound`), where the JSON serializer converts it to an ISO-format string. `from_dict` then calls `cls(**input_dict)` with no validation or coercion, so the reconstructed `AssignmentSource.queued` is a `str`, not a `datetime`, despite the type annotation. Nothing consumes `queued` today so this is latent, but any future code that treats `queued` as a datetime (comparisons, arithmetic, `.isoformat()`) will fail only in the task (deserialized) path, not in tests that construct the dataclass directly. Either parse `queued` with `datetime.fromisoformat` in `from_dict`, drop the field, or store it as a string from the start.

title: assignment_source added to abstract sync_status_outbound but never wired up
body: The abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature gains an `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None` parameter, but no caller passes it (the `sync_status_outbound` Celery task is untouched) and no concrete implementation (Jira, Azure DevOps/VSTS, ExampleIntegration) accepts that parameter — several implement `sync_status_outbound(self, external_issue, is_resolved, project_id)` with no `**kwargs`, so any future caller passing the declared keyword would crash at runtime. This is dead, misleading API surface: it suggests status sync cycles are covered by this fix when only assignee sync is. Either remove the parameter from the abstract method or fully wire it through the status-sync path including the concrete implementations.

title: `queued` default is evaluated once at import time, so every AssignmentSource shares the same timestamp
body: The dataclass field is declared as `queued: datetime = timezone.now()`. Because this is a plain default value rather than `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`, `timezone.now()` is called a single time when the class body executes (i.e., at module import time). Every `AssignmentSource` constructed without an explicit `queued` value — including all instances created via `AssignmentSource.from_integration()` in the inbound sync path — will therefore carry the process's import-time timestamp instead of the time the source was created. If `queued` is ever used for staleness/freshness checks (which appears to be its intent), the value will be silently wrong. The fix is `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. The new test `test_to_dict` only asserts `queued is not None`, so it does not catch this.

title: No test coverage for deassign with a matching AssignmentSource
body: The PR adds cycle-prevention logic for both the assign and deassign outbound paths (`GroupAssignee.objects.deassign` now accepts and forwards `assignment_source`), but only the assign path gets a negative test (`test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration`). `test_assignee_sync_outbound_unassign` only verifies the no-source case (`assignment_source=None`). If the `assignment_source` forwarding in `deassign` were dropped or broken, no test would fail, and an inbound Jira unassignment would again trigger an outbound unassign back to Jira, recreating a sync loop. A test mirroring the assign case — calling `GroupAssignee.objects.deassign(group, assignment_source=AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration))` and asserting `sync_assignee_outbound` is not called — should be added.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler can no longer be instantiated after switching to StatefulDetectorHandler
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler but implements none of its abstract methods (counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, build_occurrence_and_event_data). Because StatefulDetectorHandler is an ABC with unimplemented abstractmethods, calling MetricAlertDetectorHandler(detector) raises TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class. This class is wired as MetricAlertFire.detector_handler, so any time Detector.detector_handler is accessed for a detector of type 'metric_alert_fire' (e.g. inside process_detectors, which has no exception handling around handler construction), the entire detector processing loop will crash with an unhandled TypeError. Previously the handler was instantiable and evaluate() returned an empty list. Either keep it on DetectorHandler or implement the abstract methods (even as stubs) so the class remains instantiable.

title: test_dedupe in TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue builds the expected occurrence with the wrong group key
body: In TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe, the expected occurrence is built via build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH), which sets the occurrence fingerprint to handler.build_fingerprint("val1") (i.e. ["<detector_id>:val1"]). The actual call under test is handler.evaluate_group_key_value("group_key", ...), so the occurrence the handler produces has fingerprint ["<detector_id>:group_key"]. IssueOccurrence is a frozen dataclass, so DetectorEvaluationResult equality compares the fingerprint field, and this assertion fails because the fingerprints differ. The mock occurrence should be built with "group_key" instead of "val1" for this test to pass.

title: evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: The docstring for StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate reads "Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult", but the signature was changed in this PR to return dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]. The docstring should be updated to describe the dict keyed by group key so implementers aren't misled about the return contract.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler can no longer be instantiated — it subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler without implementing any abstract methods
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now declared as `class MetricAlertDetectorHandler(StatefulDetectorHandler[QuerySubscriptionUpdate]): pass`. StatefulDetectorHandler has four abstract members: `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the new `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. Since none of these are implemented, the class remains abstract, and `Detector.detector_handler` (which calls `group_type.detector_handler(self)`) will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract methods ...` for any Detector whose type is `metric_alert_fire`. Previously this handler was concrete and evaluate() returned an empty list, so any existing code or test that resolves the handler for a MetricAlertFire detector now crashes instead of no-oping. Either implement stub versions of the abstract methods or keep it on DetectorHandler until the stateful implementation is ready.

title: test_dedupe in TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue builds the expected occurrence with group key "val1" but evaluates "group_key", so the fingerprints never match
body: In TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe the expected occurrence is built via `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)`, which sets `fingerprint=handler.build_fingerprint("val1")` (i.e. `["<detector_id>:val1"]`). However `evaluate_group_key_value` is then called with group_key `"group_key"`, so the actual result contains an occurrence whose fingerprint is `["<detector_id>:group_key"]`. IssueOccurrence equality compares the fingerprint, so `expected_result == actual` fails. The first argument to build_mock_occurrence_and_event should be `"group_key"` (matching the key passed to evaluate_group_key_value), otherwise this test fails once it runs.

title: test_state_results_multi_group builds the expected occurrence for group_2 with value 6 while the packet gives group_2 a value of 10
body: In test_state_results_multi_group the data packet is `{"dedupe": 2, "group_vals": {"group_1": 6, "group_2": 10}}`, but the expected occurrence for group_2 is built with `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(detector.detector_handler, "group_2", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)` — value 6 instead of 10. The test passes only because the mock occurrence builder currently ignores the `value` argument; if build_occurrence_and_event_data (or the mock) ever incorporates the value into the occurrence/event data, this test would silently assert the wrong expectation. Pass 10 to match the packet.

title: StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: The docstring on `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` reads "Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`", but this PR changed the signature to return `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`. The stale docstring contradicts the new contract and will mislead anyone implementing a subclass.

title: Stale TODO comment claims the handler will be a stateful detector 'when we build that abstraction'
body: The comment `# TODO: This will be a stateful detector when we build that abstraction` sits directly above MetricAlertDetectorHandler, but this PR just made it subclass StatefulDetectorHandler — so it already is a stateful detector (an unimplemented, abstract one). The comment now describes the opposite of the code and should be updated or removed.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler can no longer be instantiated — abstract methods left unimplemented
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler was changed from DetectorHandler (with a concrete `evaluate` stub) to `StatefulDetectorHandler[QuerySubscriptionUpdate]` with just `pass`. StatefulDetectorHandler declares four abstract members (`counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the new `build_occurrence_and_event_data`), none of which are implemented here. MetricAlertDetectorHandler is registered as `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler`, and `Detector.detector_handler` in src/sentry/workflow_engine/models/detector.py instantiates it via `group_type.detector_handler(self)` — that call will now raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract methods ...`. Neither `detector_handler` nor `process_detectors` guards against instantiation errors, so a single Detector of this type would raise an uncaught exception and abort processing of the entire detector batch. Previously the class was instantiable and safely returned no results. Either keep the old evaluate() stub until the stateful implementation exists, or implement the abstract methods.

title: StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: The docstring for `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` states: 'Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`.' The signature and implementation were changed in this PR to return `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, so the docstring now contradicts the actual contract and will mislead implementers of the abstract method. It should say the results are returned as a dict keyed by group key.

title: Occurrence builder mock ignores the `value` argument, so tests assert occurrences built with wrong values
body: `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` accepts `value` but never uses it, and several tests pass a value that does not match the data packet actually evaluated. For example, in `test_state_results_multi_group` the packet has `{'group_1': 6, 'group_2': 10}` but the expected occurrence for 'group_2' is built with value 6 (line 191); in `test_results_on_change`/`test_dedupe` the evaluated value is 100/8 but the expected occurrence is built with 6.
