Because the mock discards `value`, the tests pass regardless, so a regression where `evaluate_group_key_value` passes the wrong value to `build_occurrence_and_event_data` (the new hook this PR adds) would not be caught. The mock should incorporate `value` into the built occurrence/event data (or the test expectations should use the real values).

title: Module-level names removed from mark_failed without compatibility aliases
body: Before this change, `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` exposed `mark_failed_threshold`, `create_issue_platform_occurrence`, `get_failure_reason`, `get_monitor_environment_context`, `HUMAN_FAILURE_STATUS_MAP`, and the `SimpleCheckIn` TypedDict. All of these are now removed from that module (moved to the new `incidents`/`incident_occurrence` modules and `monitors.types`, and renamed, e.g. `mark_failed_threshold` -> `try_incident_threshold`) with no import aliases left behind. Any existing consumer — including test modules such as `tests/sentry/monitors/logic/test_mark_failed.py` — that imports these names from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` will now fail with an ImportError. The PR contains no test or caller updates (only 4 files changed), so this either breaks those consumers or leaves them silently stale. The refactor should either keep re-export aliases in `mark_failed.py` or update all importers in the same PR.

title: get_monitor_environment_context computes a humanized config copy but returns the original config
body: In `get_monitor_environment_context`, lines 160-162 build a modified copy of the monitor config (`config = monitor_environment.monitor.config.copy()` and replace `schedule_type` with its human-readable display value), but the returned dict's `"config"` key uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` directly instead of the local `config` variable. As a result the `schedule_type` display value is never included in the monitor context attached to the incident occurrence, and the copied/modified variable is dead code. The return should use the local `config` (e.g. `"config": config`). This was carried over verbatim from the old `mark_failed.py`, but since this PR creates the new canonical home for this logic, the dead code should be fixed here.

title: mark_failed_threshold renamed without updating any callers or tests
body: This PR renames the previously public function `mark_failed_threshold` (in `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed`) to `try_incident_threshold` in the new module `sentry.monitors.logic.incidents`, and similarly renames `create_issue_platform_occurrence` to `create_incident_occurrence`. The changed-files list contains only these four files — no test files or other callers are updated. Existing tests in `tests/sentry/monitors/logic/test_mark_failed.py` (which historically exercise `mark_failed_threshold` directly) and any other code importing `mark_failed_threshold` or `create_issue_platform_occurrence` from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` will fail with ImportError after this merges. Either keep backwards-compatible aliases in `mark_failed.py` or update the dependent tests/callers in the same PR.

title: get_monitor_environment_context discards the transformed config copy
body: In `get_monitor_environment_context`, the code copies the monitor config and replaces `schedule_type` with its human-readable display value (`config["schedule_type"] = monitor_environment.monitor.get_schedule_type_display()`), but the returned dict uses the untransformed original: `"config": monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead of `"config": config`. As a result the schedule_type display conversion is dead code and the monitor context sent with the occurrence event still contains the raw integer schedule_type. This defect was carried over verbatim from the old `mark_failed.py`, but since this PR is creating the new canonical module for this logic it should be fixed (return the modified `config` copy) rather than propagated.

title: get_monitor_environment_context discards the humanized config copy it just built
body: In `get_monitor_environment_context` the code copies `monitor.config` into a local `config` variable and replaces `schedule_type` with its human-readable display value, but the returned context dict uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` (the raw, unmodified config) instead of the local `config`. As a result the `schedule_type` humanization never takes effect in the monitor context attached to occurrence events — consumers see the raw integer schedule type. The return should use the local `config` variable. This bug was carried over verbatim from `mark_failed.py`, but since the code is being moved into a new module it should be corrected now (change `"config": monitor_environment.monitor.config` to `"config": config`).

title: Renamed/moved functions may break external imports and test patch targets
body: `mark_failed_threshold` was renamed to `try_incident_threshold` and `create_issue_platform_occurrence` to `create_incident_occurrence`, and `SimpleCheckIn`, `get_failure_reason`, and `get_monitor_environment_context` were moved out of `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` entirely, with no aliases left behind. Any code or tests outside this PR that import these names from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed`, or that patch paths such as `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed.create_issue_platform_occurrence` / `mark_failed_threshold`, will fail with ImportError/AttributeError. Confirm that no remaining references exist (e.g., in test modules or other tasks) and that the corresponding test files are updated to the new module paths in this or a companion change.

title: time.sleep(0.1) in test_basic is a no-op due to the monkeypatch, so the test is still racy
body: At the top of test_basic, `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` patches time.sleep to do nothing. The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` (with the comment "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change") therefore sleeps for zero time and provides no synchronization at all. The test still depends on the flusher thread noticing `current_drift.value = 9000` and flushing the segment before `step.join()` sets the stopped flag; if join wins the race, no message is produced and `(msg,) = messages` fails. This makes the test flaky — the added sleep gives a false impression that the race was fixed. Use a real wait (e.g., poll `messages` with a deadline using an unpatched sleep reference captured before monkeypatching) instead.

title: Restarting a hung flusher in thread mode leaves the old thread running, producing duplicate segments for the same shards
body: When `produce_to_pipe` is set, flusher workers are `threading.Thread`s. In `_ensure_processes_alive`, if such a worker is judged hung (healthy_since stale), the restart path calls `process.kill()` only when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`, so for threads nothing stops the old worker, and then `_create_process_for_shards` unconditionally starts a new thread for the same shards and overwrites `self.processes[process_index]`. The hung-but-alive thread and the replacement thread then concurrently call `buffer.flush_segments()` / `done_flush_segments()` for the same shards and both write to the same `process_backpressure_since`/`process_healthy_since` values, which can produce the same segment twice to the output and corrupts the health/backpressure bookkeeping. Either guard against restarting un-killable hung threads or document/handle the duplicate-flush window explicitly.

title: Redis memory check double-counts clusters shared by multiple per-process buffers, skewing the used/available ratio
body: Shards are assigned to processes round-robin (`process_index = i % num_processes`), so when `max_processes > 1` each per-process `SpansBuffer` typically holds shards that map to the same Redis cluster as other buffers. `submit()` now aggregates memory by calling `buffer.get_memory_info()` on every buffer and summing the results; a cluster's used/available memory is therefore counted once per covering buffer instead of once as before (previously a single buffer covered all assigned shards and could report each cluster once). If clusters are not counted a uniform number of times (e.g., cluster shard counts not divisible by the process count), the computed `used / available` ratio is skewed and `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` hard backpressure will trigger too early or too late. It also multiplies the number of Redis INFO calls made on the consumer's submit path by the number of flusher processes.

title: _create_process_for_shard is dead code and would leak a duplicate process if used
body: `_create_process_for_shard` is never called anywhere. Worse, if it ever were used, it calls `_create_process_for_shards` without killing the existing process for that shard's group and without incrementing `process_restarts`, leaving two live processes flushing the same shards (duplicate segments produced, conflicting health values). It should be removed or fixed to go through the same kill-and-track path as `_ensure_processes_alive`.

title: Inconsistent metric tag key: 'shards' vs 'shard'
body: The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer uses `tags={"shards": shard_tag}` while the sibling metrics `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` use `tags={"shard": shard_tag}`. The mismatched tag key splits the time series and makes dashboards/queries grouping by `shard` miss the wait_produce data. Pick one key and use it consistently.

title: isinstance check against multiprocessing.Process never matches spawn processes, so hung flusher processes are never killed
body: Flusher processes are created via `self.mp_context.Process`, where `mp_context = multiprocessing.get_context('spawn')`, so they are instances of `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`. On Linux, `multiprocessing.Process` resolves to the default (fork) context's `ForkProcess` class — a sibling of `SpawnProcess`, not a parent — so `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` in `_ensure_processes_alive` is always False and `process.kill()` is never executed. Previously `kill()` was called unconditionally (guarded only by try/except ValueError), so this is a regression. Consequence: when a flusher process hangs (still alive but not updating `healthy_since`), the restart path in `_ensure_processes_alive` starts a new process for those shards without killing the old one, leaving two processes flushing the same shards concurrently — producing duplicate segments to the buffered-segments topic and racing on `done_flush_segments`. The same incorrect guard at line 346 in `join()` means `process.terminate()` is also silently skipped for spawn processes, so the shutdown fallback never force-terminates them. Use `multiprocessing.context.BaseProcess` (or `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`) for the isinstance check instead.

title: The added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched, leaving the race it was meant to fix
body: In `test_basic`, `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` is applied at the top of the test, so the newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` (with the comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change') resolves to the patched no-op and does not actually wait. The race it was intended to close is still present: `step.join()` sets `stopped.value = True` immediately, so if the flusher thread has not run a loop iteration between `fac._flusher.current_drift.value = 9000` and `join()`, it exits without flushing and `(msg,) = messages` fails. The test will be flaky under thread scheduling jitter. Either capture the real `time.sleep` before monkeypatching and call that, or poll until `messages` is non-empty with a real deadline.

title: _create_process_for_shard is dead code
body: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is introduced in this PR but never called anywhere — the restart path in `_ensure_processes_alive` calls `_create_process_for_shards` directly. Worse, if it ever were used naively it would restart the entire process for a shard without updating `self.processes` consistently with the caller. It should be removed to avoid confusion about the restart API.

title: Inconsistent metric tag keys: 'shard' vs 'shards'
body: The `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` timer and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` timing are tagged with key `shard`, while `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is tagged with key `shards` (and `spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy` uses `shard`). Because the tag keys differ, the wait_produce metric cannot be grouped or filtered alongside the other flusher metrics in dashboards/monitors. Pick one tag key and use it consistently.

title: isinstance check uses the wrong Process class, so hung flusher processes are never killed
body: In `_ensure_processes_alive`, `process.kill()` is now guarded by `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. The real flusher processes are created via `self.mp_context.Process` where `mp_context = multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")`, so they are instances of `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` — a sibling class of `multiprocessing.Process` (both subclass `BaseProcess`), and `isinstance(spawn_process, multiprocessing.Process)` is always False (the file's own type annotation on `self.processes` acknowledges the type is `SpawnProcess`). Before this change the kill was unconditional; the new guard silently disables it for every production flusher process (it only 'works' to skip threads, which was its presumed intent). Consequence: when a flusher process is detected as hung (cause="hang"), the old process is left running while `_create_process_for_shards` immediately starts a replacement handling the same shards, so two (and with repeated restarts, up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS) flusher processes concurrently flush the same Redis shards and keep duplicate Kafka producers alive. The check should be inverted to exclude threads instead, e.g. `if not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`.

title: join()'s terminate() is dead code for spawn flusher processes
body: In `join()`, `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.terminate()` uses the same wrong isinstance check: spawn flusher processes are `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` instances, never instances of `multiprocessing.Process`, so `terminate()` is never executed for real flusher processes. This pattern predates the PR but is carried into the new per-process loop: any flusher process still alive after the join deadline (the loop `break`s once the deadline passes, so later processes don't even get their wait loop) is left running and only dies via the daemon flag at interpreter exit, potentially mid-produce with unflushed Kafka futures. Additionally, `remaining_time` is computed at the top of the loop and never used other than the `<= 0` check.

title: time.sleep(0.1) in test_basic is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
body: The test adds `time.sleep(0.1)` with the comment "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change", but line 15 of the same test does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, which patches the `sleep` attribute of the `time` module globally — including the call on line 62. The sleep therefore does nothing and the comment is misleading. The test only passes because `step.join()` provides the actual synchronization with the flusher thread; if a future reader relies on this sleep for timing it will be a source of flakiness confusion. Either remove the line/comment or use the real sleep (e.g. via `time.sleep` saved before patching).

title: Inconsistent metric tag keys 'shard' vs 'shards' on flusher timers
body: The new per-process metrics use `tags={"shard": shard_tag}` for `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes`, but `tags={"shards": shard_tag}` for `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` (line 199). Since these timers describe the same per-process shard grouping, the mismatched tag key means dashboards and alerts that group or filter by `shard` will silently miss the `wait_produce` series (and vice versa for `shards`). Unify the tag key across all three metrics.

title: Shared FixedQueuePool is shut down by the old strategy on rebalance, causing silent message loss
body: The `FixedQueuePool` is created once in the factory's `__init__` and shared by every `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` produced by `create_with_partitions`. Arroyo closes and re-creates the strategy on every partition revocation/rebalance: the old strategy's `close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which shuts down all queues and worker threads in the shared pool. The new strategy created after the rebalance still references the same pool. From then on, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` calls `work_queue.put()`, which raises `queue.ShutDown` on a shut-down queue; this is caught by the broad `except Exception` in `submit`, which then calls `add_offset`/`complete_offset` on the message's offset. The result: every message after a rebalance is silently dropped (never processed) while its offset is marked complete and committed to Kafka. Since consumer groups rebalance on every deploy/scale event, running this mode in production would skip uptime results without any error surfacing beyond a log line. The pool needs to be created per `create_with_partitions` call, or `close()` must not shut down a pool it doesn't own.

title: Worker queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure and memory can grow without limit
body: `FixedQueuePool` creates each work queue with `queue.Queue()` (no maxsize), so `submit`/`put` never blocks. The docstring on `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` (line ~253) claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but that never happens: the Arroyo consumer thread will keep polling Kafka and appending `WorkItem`s faster than slow workers can drain them, buffering an unbounded number of decoded results in process memory. This is exactly the failure mode the PR is meant to mitigate (one slow item/group clogging processing) — a slow group now grows its queue until the consumer OOMs. The queues should have a `maxsize` (or `submit` should otherwise block/apply backpressure) to match the documented behavior.

title: join() ignores its timeout and shutdown abandons all queued items instead of draining them
body: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(timeout)` ignores the timeout and just calls `close()`, which immediately shuts down the queue pool. In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` each worker's `shutdown` flag is set to True before `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` is called, so a worker that is woken with pending items still in its queue processes at most one more item and then exits its `while not self.shutdown` loop — everything remaining in the queues is discarded without being processed and without a final offset commit. Standard Arroyo strategies drain in-flight work and commit during `join` on graceful shutdown; here every deploy or rebalance abandons the entire in-memory backlog (which, given the unbounded queues, can be large) to be redelivered and reprocessed. At minimum `join` should wait for queues to drain up to the timeout and perform a final commit of completed offsets.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the opposite of what the implementation does and only passes by timing luck
body: The test's docstring says "errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages", but the final assertion is `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` — i.e. it asserts that nothing was committed. In the actual implementation, `OrderedQueueWorker.run` completes the offset in a `finally` block even when `result_processor` raises, so both offsets (100 and 101) become committable and the commit loop commits them on its next 1-second tick. The test only passes because it finishes (processing is mocked and instant) before the commit thread's first 1s wake-up; wait a second longer and the offsets of the "failed" message would be committed. The test should either assert that the failed message's offset *is* committed (matching the implementation and the existing at-least-once semantics of the other modes) or the implementation should be changed — as written it documents behavior that is false and is fragile to scheduling.

title: test_stats_reporting is flaky: asserts total_items > 0 after workers may have already drained the queue
body: The test submits 10 trivial work items (the processor just appends to a list under a lock) and then immediately asserts `stats["total_items"] > 0`. The three worker threads start consuming as soon as the first item is put, so on a fast machine all 10 items can be processed before the main thread reaches `get_stats()`, making `total_items` 0 and the assertion fail intermittently. The non-zero-depth assertion needs synchronization that blocks workers (e.g. an event the processor waits on) to be reliable.

title: Strategy close() permanently kills the factory-owned queue pool, breaking the consumer after any rebalance and silently dropping messages
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), but the queue_pool is owned by ResultsStrategyFactory and is reused across partition assignments. On a partition revocation, arroyo calls close()/join() on the strategy, which sets worker.shutdown = True and calls q.shutdown() on every queue, so all worker threads exit and the queues are permanently shut down. When partitions are reassigned, the factory's create_thread_queue_parallel_worker (result_consumer.py) calls create_with_partitions again; its `assert self.queue_pool is not None` passes because only factory.shutdown() sets it to None, so a new SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy is built around a dead pool. Every subsequent submit() then calls queue.put() on a shut-down queue, which raises queue.ShutDown; that exception is caught by the broad `except Exception` in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit, which marks the offset complete — so the offset gets committed even though the message was never processed. The net effect after any routine rebalance (deploy, scaling event): the consumer silently drops all messages and keeps committing offsets, appearing healthy while processing nothing. The pool should either be recreated per create_with_partitions call or its lifecycle should be decoupled from the strategy's close().

title: Worker marks offsets complete even when processing raises, so failed messages are committed and lost
body: In OrderedQueueWorker.run, the finally block unconditionally calls self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset), including when result_processor raised an exception that was caught by `except Exception`. Once the offset is marked complete, the commit loop will commit past it, and the failed message is never retried — a transient error causes permanent message loss. This also directly contradicts the new test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling in tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py, which asserts that no offset is committed when a message fails. If at-least-once semantics are intended (as the rest of the offset-tracking design suggests), complete_offset should only be called on success, and failures should either leave the offset outstanding or route to a DLQ.

title: Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure despite the docstring claiming it
body: FixedQueuePool creates each work queue with a bare queue.Queue() (maxsize=0, i.e. unbounded), and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit/poll never block or pause consumption. The class docstring for SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but submit() can never block, so if processing is slower than ingestion (the exact slow-item scenario this PR is meant to address) the consumer will read ahead without limit and buffer an unbounded number of decoded messages in process memory, risking OOM. Either give the queues a maxsize (making put block and naturally pause the consumer) or implement an explicit pause/resume in poll(), and fix the docstring if unbounded is intentional.

title: join() ignores its timeout and close() abandons queued items without draining
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(timeout) ignores the timeout parameter and just calls close(), which immediately shuts down the commit thread and the queue pool. FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True before draining, so the workers' `while not self.shutdown` loop exits even when items remain in the queues; the existing wait_until_empty() helper is never used in any production path. On graceful shutdown, in-flight queued work is simply abandoned (it will be redelivered since offsets are not committed, but the class docstring's 'No item is lost' guarantee and the arroyo join contract — wait up to timeout for in-flight work to finish — are not honored, and the final processed-but-uncommitted offsets are not flushed, causing avoidable duplicate processing on every restart).

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts behavior the implementation doesn't have and only passes due to commit-loop timing
body: The test mocks the result processor to raise on the first message and asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`. But the implementation in OrderedQueueWorker.run completes offsets in a finally block even when processing raises, so both offsets become committable and the commit loop will commit offset 102. The test only passes because the commit thread waits 1.0s before its first commit and the test finishes (including its extra time.sleep(0.2)) well before that on a fast machine; under load or with a different commit interval it becomes flaky, and worse, it encodes the exact opposite of the real behavior, masking the message-loss issue where failed items are committed.

title: test_stats_reporting races with worker threads and is flaky
body: After submitting 10 work items to a pool whose 3 worker threads are actively draining, the test immediately asserts `stats['total_items'] > 0`. If the workers process all items before get_stats() runs (likely on a fast machine since the result_processor is trivial), total_items will be 0 and the assertion fails nondeterministically. The test should block the processor (e.g. with an event) before checking queue depth, or drop the assertion.

title: Per-message metrics.gauge and per-message Sentry transaction with worker_id in the name add heavy per-message overhead
body: OrderedQueueWorker.run emits a metrics.gauge('remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth', ...) for every single processed message, and wraps every message in a sentry_sdk transaction whose name includes the worker_id (f"monitors.{identifier}.worker_{worker_id}"). On a high-throughput results topic this generates a gauge emission per message (the existing batched mode only emits per batch) and creates high-cardinality transaction names (one per worker per consumer) that won't group in Sentry Performance. Consider sampling, emitting gauges only from poll(), and removing worker_id from the transaction name.

title: Shared FixedQueuePool is permanently shut down after the first strategy close, so post-rebalance messages are silently dropped
body: The FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and shared by every strategy the factory creates. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls queue_pool.shutdown(), which calls Queue.shutdown() on every internal queue (Python 3.13 semantics: put() on a shut-down queue raises queue.ShutDown). Arroyo's StreamProcessor closes and re-creates the strategy via create_with_partitions on every partition revocation/reassignment, but create_thread_queue_parallel_worker reuses the same already-shut-down pool. After the first rebalance, FixedQueuePool.submit -> work_queue.put() raises ShutDown, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches it in its broad 'except Exception' block, logs it, and then marks the offset complete — so every message received after a rebalance is never processed while its offset is committed anyway (silent data loss). Additionally, ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() sets self.queue_pool = None, after which the assert in create_thread_queue_parallel_worker would crash on a new assignment. The pool must be created per create_with_partitions call (or recreated/restarted when shut down), and close() must not permanently kill a factory-owned resource that later strategies depend on.

title: Unbounded queues with no backpressure despite docstring claiming 'natural backpressure'
body: FixedQueuePool creates each work queue as queue.Queue() with the default maxsize=0 (unbounded), and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit never raises MessageRejected and poll() never signals the processor to pause. Arroyo only applies backpressure when a strategy rejects messages (MessageRejected) or blocks in submit; here neither happens, so if workers fall behind (the exact slow-item scenario this PR targets) the consumer keeps reading from Kafka and buffers every message in memory without limit, risking unbounded heap growth/OOM on a lag spike. The class docstring ('Natural backpressure when queues fill up') is incorrect. Either bound the queues (maxsize) so put() blocks and naturally throttles the consumer, or raise MessageRejected when total queued depth exceeds a threshold.

title: close()/join() stop the commit thread before draining and never commit final offsets; worker shutdown flag also prevents draining
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread first, then shuts down the queue pool. Any offsets completed by workers during the drain are therefore never committed, and join() (which arroyo expects to flush and commit final positions within the given timeout) just calls close() again, ignores its timeout argument, and never forces a final commit_function call. On every deploy/rebalance, all messages processed since the last 1-second commit tick are redelivered and reprocessed. Worse, FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False): OrderedQueueWorker.run checks 'while not self.shutdown' at the top of the loop, so a worker exits after at most its current item instead of draining the remaining queued items, defeating the graceful drain (those offsets simply go uncommitted). close() should drain the queues, then perform a final commit of all completed offsets, and join() should honor its timeout.

title: Offset is marked complete in a finally block even when result processing fails, committing past failed messages
body: In OrderedQueueWorker.run, the finally block unconditionally calls self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...) after catching any Exception from result_processor. That means a message whose processing raised is treated as successfully processed: the OffsetTracker will allow the commit loop to commit past it, and with no DLQ or retry the message is permanently lost. Today the concrete ResultProcessor.__call__ swallows all exceptions itself, which masks this, but this queue consumer is shared infrastructure for remote-subscription consumers (monitors, uptime, etc.) — any processor that lets an exception propagate (or any change to ResultProcessor) silently drops data and advances offsets. Failed items should either leave the offset outstanding (stalling commits so it can be retried) or be routed to a DLQ, not marked complete.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts behavior opposite of the implementation and only passes via a timing race
body: This test mocks the result processor to raise on the first message and then asserts 'len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets'. But the worker's finally block completes the offset even on failure, so after both messages are handled, offsets 100 and 101 are both committable and the 1-second commit loop WILL commit offset 102. The test only passes because it breaks out of its wait loop and checks roughly 0.2s after processing finishes, typically before the commit loop's first 1s tick fires — on a slow CI runner the commit can land first and the test fails flakily. The assertion also contradicts the test's own docstring ('errors don't block offset commits for other messages', which would imply 101 gets committed) and the real semantics (the failed message 100 is skipped and committed past). The test should either wait deterministically for a commit and assert the actual expected offset, or the implementation's error semantics should be fixed and the test updated to match.

title: Third-party identity provider users blocked from backup code login
body: The authorize callback throws `ErrorCode.ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled` for any user whose `identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL` when `credentials.totpCode` is empty. Since the backup-code submission path intentionally leaves `totpCode` empty, Google/SAML users with 2FA enabled cannot authenticate via a backup code even though the rest of the flow (decrypt codes, match, invalidate) was clearly written to support them. The guard needs `!credentials.backupCode` added (or the backup-code branch should run before this check) so non-CAL users can actually use their backup codes.

title: Lost access button hidden for external (third-party) TOTP users
body: The footer for the 2FA-required state branches on `!totpEmail`: only CAL users get `TwoFactorFooter` (which contains the new `lost_access` button that flips `twoFactorLostAccess`). External TOTP users (Google/SAML arriving via the `?totp=` JWT) get `ExternalTotpFooter` (a single Cancel button) and therefore have no way to switch the form to the `BackupCode` input. Combined with the authorize-callback bug, this means users who authenticated via an identity provider and lost their authenticator are locked out with no recovery path.

title: Continue button fires both handleSetup and handleEnable on click
body: The ConfirmPassword `Continue` button is rendered inside `<Form handleSubmit={handleEnable}>` and has both `type="submit"` and `onClick={handleSetup}`. Clicking it triggers (1) `handleSetup` directly via `onClick`, then (2) the surrounding form submission which invokes `handleEnable` via react-hook-form. Because `setIsSubmitting(true)` inside `handleSetup` is not visible to `handleEnable`'s closure until the next render, `handleEnable`'s `isSubmitting` guard does not stop the second call. The setup API and the enable API (with an empty `totpCode`, producing `IncorrectTwoFactorCode`) are both hit, which can display a spurious error and cause the TOTP enable request to race with the step transition. Remove `onClick={handleSetup}` (or change the button to `type="button"`) so only one handler runs.

title: backupCodesUrl object URL is never revoked (blob memory leak)
body: `handleSetup` calls `URL.createObjectURL(textBlob)` to build the download link for the backup codes, but neither `resetState` nor the component unmount path revokes the previously created URL. The only revocation in the file is `if (backupCodesUrl) URL.revokeObjectURL(backupCodesUrl);` inside `handleSetup`, which only runs when the user starts setup again. Closing/cancelling the modal or finishing the flow without re-entering setup leaves the blob URL pinned in memory until the page is unloaded. Revoke the URL in `resetState` and in a `useEffect` cleanup function.

title: Backup code comparison is case-sensitive but codes are lowercase hex
body: Backup codes are generated as `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")` (lowercase). The match is `backupCodes.indexOf(credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""))`, which is a strict string equality check. The login UI placeholder (`XXXXX-XXXXX`) and the format function do not normalize case, so a user typing an uppercase or mixed-case backup code (e.g. copied from a notes app that auto-capitalizes) gets `IncorrectBackupCode` even though the code is correct. Normalize both sides to lower case (or uppercase) before comparing, both here and in `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts` at line 61.

title: formatBackupCode used before its const declaration
body: `handleSetup` references `formatBackupCode` at line 95, but `formatBackupCode` is declared with `const` at line 163 (after `handleSetup`). It happens to work at runtime because the function body is only executed after the component has rendered and `const` initialization has completed, but it is order-dependent and fragile. Move the `const formatBackupCode = ...` declaration above `handleSetup` (or hoist it with a function declaration) so the dependency is explicit and the module doesn't rely on TDZ luck.

title: BackupCode component exported under the name TwoFactor
body: The new file `apps/web/components/auth/BackupCode.tsx` declares `export default function TwoFactor(...)`, so every import (`import BackupCode from "@components/auth/BackupCode"`) uses a name that does not match the function it points at. This is confusing to maintainers and also defeats React DevTools / stack-trace readability. Rename the function to `BackupCode` (and update the other call sites: `DisableTwoFactorModal.tsx` line 8, `login.tsx` line 32).

title: Object URL for backup codes download is never revoked on close
body: backupCodesUrl is created with URL.createObjectURL and only revoked when handleSetup is invoked again. There is no cleanup on modal close (onOpenChange / Cancel button), no useEffect cleanup, and resetState() does not reset backupCodesUrl. Each successful setup leaks a Blob and its object URL (containing the plaintext backup codes) for the lifetime of the page. Add a useEffect cleanup that calls URL.revokeObjectURL(backupCodesUrl) on unmount/close, and revoke inside resetState.

title: Stale internal state shown after closing the modal with the X button
body: Dialog's onOpenChange (the X / overlay close path) does not call resetState(). The component remains mounted with the previous step, dataUri, secret and backupCodes. Reopening the modal after closing it via X can show an old QR code, old TOTP secret and the previously generated backup codes. resetState should be invoked from onOpenChange (or equivalent), and the displayed data should be cleared when the modal is dismissed without completion.

title: twoFactorLostAccess not reset when disable modal is closed via X
body: The twoFactorLostAccess state is only reset after a successful disable. Closing the dialog with the X button (onOpenChange) does not reset it, so the next time the modal is opened the BackupCode input is shown instead of the TOTP input. Reset twoFactorLostAccess (and clear the form/values) when the dialog is closed without a successful submit.

title: JSON.parse of decrypted backup codes has no error handling
body: JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY)) will throw if the stored ciphertext is corrupted, the encryption key is rotated, or the data shape is unexpected. An uncaught throw here aborts the entire authorize() callback and surfaces as an InternalServerError, locking the user out. Wrap the decrypt + JSON.parse in try/catch and convert failures into a clean ErrorCode (e.g. MissingBackupCodes or InternalServerError) so authentication degrades gracefully.

title: JSON.parse of decrypted backup codes has no error handling
body: Same issue as in next-auth-options.ts: JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...)) is unguarded. A corrupt/rotated backupCodes blob will crash the disable endpoint with an uncaught exception (500), preventing the user from disabling 2FA. Catch the error and return a typed error (e.g. MissingBackupCodes) instead.

title: Backup code is not atomically consumed; concurrent logins can reuse a code
body: The backup code is looked up with backupCodes.indexOf(...) and then nulled out in a separate prisma.user.update. Between the read and the write, two concurrent signIn attempts (e.g. two browser tabs) can both observe the same code at the same index, both null it, and both be authenticated, allowing a single-use backup code to be used more than once. The same race exists in disable.ts (the indexOf succeeds but the consumed code is only later wiped by the unconditional backupCodes: null in the final update). Use a conditional update (e.g. updateMany where the code is still present, or store used codes with a unique marker) so consumption is atomic.

title: BackupCode component is exported as default function TwoFactor
body: The file apps/web/components/auth/BackupCode.tsx declares `export default function TwoFactor(...)`. Two other components in this PR are also named TwoFactor (apps/web/components/auth/TwoFactor.tsx and EnableTwoFactorModal imports it). The mismatch causes confusion in stack traces / DevTools and creates a real collision risk if anyone re-exports these modules together. Rename the function to BackupCode (or BackupCodeInput) to match the file name and the other new component.

title: formatBackupCode referenced before it is defined
body: handleSetup uses formatBackupCode at line 95, but formatBackupCode is declared as a const at line 163, below the handler. This works only because handleSetup is invoked asynchronously after render. It is fragile (moving handleSetup to a hook or memoizing it would TDZ-crash) and makes the file hard to read. Move the formatBackupCode declaration above its first use.

title: backupCodes state is implicitly typed as never[]
body: `const [backupCodes, setBackupCodes] = useState([]);` infers never[], so .map(formatBackupCode) on body.backupCodes only compiles because body.backupCodes is any. There is no compile-time guarantee that the state actually contains strings, and the explicit type <string[]>([]) (or the inferred type from body.backupCodes) would catch a future API shape change.

title: Exhausted backup codes surface as IncorrectBackupCode, not MissingBackupCodes
body: After a user has consumed all backup codes, the stored JSON array consists entirely of nulls. backupCodes.indexOf(...) still returns -1, so the user is told IncorrectBackupCode rather than MissingBackupCodes (and they cannot tell that they have no codes left). Detect the all-null case (e.g. !backupCodes.some(Boolean)) and throw ErrorCode.MissingBackupCodes before the indexOf check.

title: No end-to-end coverage for backup code login or backup code disable
body: The PR introduces an entire authentication path (login with backup code, disable 2FA with backup code, marking codes as used) that has no e2e coverage. The TODO at line 12 acknowledges this, but the new code paths are exactly where regressions are most dangerous (auth bypass, accidental single-use violation). Add at minimum: (1) login with a backup code (and confirm the code is consumed), (2) login with a previously-used backup code fails with IncorrectBackupCode, (3) disabling 2FA via the 'Lost access' button with a backup code.

title: Continue button at QR step has misleading type=submit and onClick
body: The QR step Continue button is declared `type="submit"` and `onClick={() => setStep(SetupStep.EnterTotpCode)}`. It lives inside <Form handleSubmit={handleEnable} ...>, so clicking it both fires handleEnable (which sends a request to /api/auth/two-factor/totp/enable with whatever stale totpCode is still in the form, or undefined) and changes the step. The visible behavior appears to work only because the enable endpoint errors out when 2FA is already enabled, but this is an unintended API call. Use type="button" here so clicking it does not submit the form.

title: Blob URL for backup-codes download is never revoked on close or unmount
body: When the setup step succeeds, a Blob URL is created from the backup codes and stored in `backupCodesUrl`. `URL.revokeObjectURL` is only called when a fresh URL is generated, so when the user closes the modal (which calls `resetState`, which doesn't touch `backupCodesUrl`) or the component unmounts, the previous Blob and its URL remain pinned in memory until the page reloads. This is a slow leak that accumulates each time a user opens the enable flow, and it also leaves a stale `blob:` URL reachable from the previous render. Add a useEffect cleanup (or revoke in `resetState` and on `onOpenChange(false)`) so the URL is released whenever the modal closes or the component unmounts.

title: TOCTOU race allows a single backup code to be used to log in more than once
body: The backup-code branch decrypts `user.backupCodes`, calls `indexOf`, sets `backupCodes[index] = null`, then re-encrypts and `prisma.user.update`s — but this is done as separate read/transform/write with no `WHERE backupCodes = ...` predicate or transaction. Two concurrent login attempts using the same code both find it at the same index before either write lands, both set the slot to null, and both succeed. Backup codes are explicitly documented as single-use, so reuse defeats the feature. Either wrap the read+write in a transaction with a predicate that matches the current `backupCodes` value (optimistic concurrency) or, better, persist codes as rows so consumption can be a single atomic UPDATE/DELETE on the matching row.

title: Uncaught JSON.parse on decrypted backupCodes can crash every login for affected user
body: `const backupCodes = JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY))` will throw if the stored ciphertext is ever tampered with, truncated, or encrypted under a different `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (e.g. a key rotation on a self-hosted deployment). The throw is not caught, so the NextAuth `authorize` call aborts with a generic exception and the user — including admins — is locked out of their own account with no actionable error. Wrap the decrypt+parse in try/catch and return `ErrorCode.InternalServerError` (or a clearer code) so the response is well-formed and the failure is logged with the user id, instead of an unhandled exception surfacing through NextAuth.

title: Uncaught JSON.parse on decrypted backupCodes can break 2FA disable
body: Same issue as in `next-auth-options.ts`: `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY))` is not wrapped in try/catch. If the encrypted payload is unreadable (corruption, schema drift after key rotation, partial DB write), the handler throws an uncaught error and the user is unable to disable 2FA via a backup code — which is the very path designed for 'lost access'. The handler should catch the failure, log it, and return a clear error (e.g. `ErrorCode.MissingBackupCodes` or `InternalServerError`) rather than letting it bubble to a 500.

title: Backup code comparison is case-sensitive though generated codes are lowercase hex
body: `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")` always emits lowercase, but the lookup uses `credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` with no `.toLowerCase()` and no `.trim()`. A user who pastes or types a code with caps, surrounding whitespace, or different separators (space, period) will get `IncorrectBackupCode` even though they have a valid code, which is especially painful here because the input is a long hex string with no character-class hint. Normalize the input (`replaceAll("-", "").replace(/\s+/g, "").toLowerCase()`) on both the login and the `disable` handler so users don't silently burn codes for a casing/whitespace mismatch.

title: No end-to-end coverage for backup code login or backup-code disable flow
body: The PR adds the new backup-code login branch in `next-auth-options.ts`, the new `backupCode` field in the login form, and a new disable-via-backup-code branch in `disable.ts` and `DisableTwoFactorModal.tsx`. The e2e file only exercises the post-enable display dialog (download/copy/close buttons) and does not cover the security-critical paths: logging in with a backup code, exercising the 'Lost access' toggle on the login page, or disabling 2FA via a backup code (the exact flow the feature was built for, and which is gated by `twoFactorLostAccess` and `backupCode` in `DisableTwoFactorModal`). The author explicitly flagged this as a TODO at line 12. Given that backup-code handling involves the TOCTOU race and decrypt-and-parse logic reviewed in the other findings, an e2e that signs in with a valid code and a second time with the same code (expecting rejection) is necessary before merging.

title: TypeError crash when destinationCalendar is empty/undefined
body: The code destructures `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` and then accesses `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration`. When `evt.destinationCalendar` is `undefined` or `[]`, `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined` and reading `.integration` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'integration')` at runtime. The previous code used safe optional chaining `evt.destinationCalendar?.integration !== "google_calendar"`, which silently skipped the fallback when the destination calendar was missing. Several call paths now build `evt` with `destinationCalendar: []` when no destination is set (confirm.handler.ts line 175-179, editLocation.handler.ts line 85-89, handleCancelBooking.ts lines 251-255 and 528-532, bookingReminder.ts line 130, paypal-webhook.ts line 152-156, stripe webhook.ts lines 119 and 229, requestReschedule.handler.ts line 240-242, deleteCredential.handler.ts line 290-294). For any Google Meet booking that has no destination calendar configured, EventManager.create will crash instead of falling back to Cal Video (`integrations:daily`) as intended.

title: updateEvent passes undefined calendarId when externalCalendarId is null
body: The new fallback `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` does not preserve the previous behaviour. When `externalCalendarId` is `null` or `undefined` (which is the case on the call path from `EventManager.updateAllCalendarEvents` when a booking reference lacks `externalCalendarId`), the predicate becomes `cal.externalId === undefined`, which never matches a real calendar entry, so `selectedCalendar` is `undefined`. The previous code returned `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId` (the single, primary destination calendar's externalId). The new code passes `calendarId: selectedCalendar` to `calendar.events.update`, which is now `undefined`; Google may default this to "primary" or fail, which means the wrong calendar is updated (or the update fails) for any booking whose reference does not carry an externalCalendarId.

title: deleteEvent deletes from 'primary' instead of the booking's destination calendar
body: Mirror of the updateEvent bug: the new fallback `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` returns `undefined` whenever `externalCalendarId` is `null`/`undefined`, because the predicate becomes `cal.externalId === undefined` and never matches. `calendarId` therefore becomes `undefined`, and the existing `calendarId ? calendarId : defaultCalendarId` then makes `calendar.events.delete` target the user's "primary" calendar. The previous code returned the booking's destination calendar's externalId directly. As a result, cancel/delete flows on bookings whose reference has no `externalCalendarId` will now attempt to delete from the wrong Google calendar (and only succeed if the event happens to live in "primary", or silently 404 otherwise). This is reachable via `handleCancelBooking.ts` and `EventManager.updateAllCalendarEvents`'s old-event cleanup.

title: User-facing copy changed (organiser -> organizer) in a refactor
body: The user-facing note text shown to attendees when calendar notes are hidden changed from "Notes have been hidden by the organiser" to "Notes have been hidden by the organizer". This wording change is unrelated to the destinationCalendar array refactor and is being slipped into a bug fix PR; the previous string was already shipped to end users and the rest of the codebase keeps "organise/organiser" spellings. A refactor like this should not change user-visible copy without an explicit reason.

title: updateEvent fallback to destinationCalendar never matches
body:
In `updateEvent`, `selectedCalendar` is computed as:

```ts
const selectedCalendar = externalCalendarId
  ? externalCalendarId
  : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;
```

When `externalCalendarId` is falsy (undefined/null/empty), the `find` predicate compares each calendar's `externalId` against the same falsy value, which can never be true. The function then resolves to `undefined`, and `calendarId: undefined` is sent to the Google API (the prior behavior of `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId` is gone and not replaced by something that actually works). The same defect is duplicated in `deleteEvent` at line 317. Either look up the entry by the current credential id (`cal.credentialId === credentialId`) or use the first array entry when `externalCalendarId` is absent.

title: Team destination calendars silently dropped when organizer has no destinationCalendar
createEvent ignores the new credentialId parameter required by the Calendar interface
body: `packages/types/Calendar.d.ts` now declares `createEvent(event: CalendarEvent, credentialId: number)`. The Lark implementation still has `async createEvent(event: CalendarEvent)` and uses only `event.destinationCalendar[0]` to pick a calendar. The same regression exists in `packages/app-store/office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` (`createEvent(event: CalendarEvent)`) and in `packages/lib/CalendarService.ts` (`BaseCalendarService.createEvent(event: CalendarEvent)`), which means for collective events where team members use Lark/Office 365/caldav, no credentialId-based selection is performed - only the first entry of `destinationCalendar` is ever consulted, so additional team calendars are never invited. Either implement the credentialId-aware selection in those services or update the shared `Calendar` interface so the implementers don't silently ignore the parameter.

title: createEvent silently falls back to "primary" when destination has no credentialId
body: In `createEvent` the selected calendar is `calEventRaw.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.credentialId === credentialId)?.externalId`. The `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents` integration-based branch calls `createEvent(credential, event)` without `externalId` when a destination entry has no `credentialId`, then `calendar.createEvent(calEvent, credential.id)` is invoked with only the credential id. If that credential isn't represented in `destinationCalendar` (a common case for team-added destinations), `selectedCalendar` is `undefined` and the event is created in the user's "primary" calendar instead of the team host's chosen calendar. This silently creates duplicate/wrong calendar entries for collective Google Calendar bookings.

title: Legacy reference cancel iterates every user calendar credential with the wrong uid/calendar
body: For bookings made before the references refactor, the `else` branch iterates `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter((c) => c.type.endsWith("_calendar"))` and calls `calendar.deleteEvent(uid, evt, externalCalendarId)` for *every* calendar credential the user owns, using `uid` and `externalCalendarId` taken from a single reference. With multiple Google/Lark/etc. accounts on the same user, this attempts to delete `uid` from every calendar that never had the event, producing spurious 404s (treated as success) and masking real errors. The inner `for (const credential of calendarCredentials)` should at minimum restrict to the integration type matching `reference.type` (or look up the right calendar in the user's `destinationCalendar`). The PR preserves but doesn't fix this.

title: destinationCalendar fallback to user's destinationCalendar missing
body:
Other handlers in this PR (handleNewBooking, handleCancelBooking, confirm, editLocation, deleteCredential) build `destinationCalendar` as `booking.destinationCalendar ? [booking.destinationCalendar] : user.destinationCalendar ? [user.destinationCalendar] : []`. Here it is just:

```ts
destinationCalendar: bookingToReschedule?.destinationCalendar
  ? [bookingToReschedule?.destinationCalendar]
  : [],
```

A reschedule email for a booking without a per-booking destination calendar (e.g. legacy bookings relying on the user's default) will now deliver `[]` to webhook consumers and the broken-integration email flow, instead of the user's calendar. The fallback to `bookingToReschedule.user?.destinationCalendar` is missing.

title: Crash when destinationCalendar array is empty and location is Google Meet
BaseCalendarService.createEvent signature breaks the Calendar interface contract
body: The Calendar interface in packages/types/Calendar.d.ts was changed to require `createEvent(event: CalendarEvent, credentialId: number): Promise<NewCalendarEventType>`. The BaseCalendarService (this file) is declared as `abstract class BaseCalendarService implements Calendar`, but its createEvent still has signature `createEvent(event: CalendarEvent): Promise<NewCalendarEventType>` and is not marked abstract. TypeScript will error out at build time because the implementation is not assignable to the interface (the missing required `credentialId` parameter). Additionally, concrete CalDAV-derived integrations (Apple Calendar, etc.) inherit this method, so EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents's third argument `destination.externalId` is silently dropped. The base signature must be updated to accept and forward `credentialId` (and likely ignore it where appropriate) for the project to compile and behave correctly.

title: updateEvent fallback uses a self-referential find that can never match
body: Line 256 reads `const selectedCalendar = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;`. When `externalCalendarId` is null/undefined (truthy is false), the predicate compares `cal.externalId === externalCalendarId`, i.e. `cal.externalId === undefined`. That condition is false for any real calendar (externalIds are real strings), so the find returns undefined and `selectedCalendar` becomes undefined. The previous code used a plain `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId` fallback. Net effect: updateEvent currently passes `calendarId: undefined` to `calendar.events.update` (and the subsequent `events.patch` at line 168/277) instead of either `primary` or the booking's actual destination calendar externalId. That's a regression from the single-destinationCalendar behavior and is likely to produce 400/404 errors or update the wrong calendar. The same tautological pattern is duplicated at line 317 in `deleteEvent`, where `selectedCalendar` falls back to the local `defaultCalendarId = "primary"` — meaning cancellations without a propagated externalCalendarId will try to delete from "primary" and may delete the wrong event.

title: Legacy cancellation fallback runs once per reference, producing N×M extra delete calls
body: The new code at lines 422-484 wraps both the credentialId-keyed path and the legacy fallback (no `credentialId`) inside `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)`. For any booking with multiple calendar references that lack `credentialId` (i.e. bookings created before the reference→credentialId migration), the legacy branch executes for EACH reference: it fetches ALL user calendar credentials and pushes `deleteEvent(uid, evt, externalCalendarId)` for each. That is N (legacy references) × M (user calendars) extra API calls, and each call sends that iteration's `uid`/`externalCalendarId` to every calendar — these uids correspond to different calendar providers, so the legacy branch will issue delete requests for an event ID on calendars where it never existed (and may 404). The original (pre-PR) code only invoked the legacy fallback once per cancellation. Move the legacy fallback outside of the per-reference loop and only iterate once with the original reference's uid/externalCalendarId, or guard the loop so legacy deletions only happen once per booking.

title: Booking record only stores the first host's destinationCalendar for collective events
body: When writing the new Booking row, only `evt.destinationCalendar[0].id` is used (`destinationCalendar: { connect: { id: evt.destinationCalendar[0].id } }`). For collective events the PR explicitly pushes every team member's `destinationCalendar` into the array (lines around 1074-1078), so multiple hosts each get their own calendar event via EventManager.create — but the Booking row ends up linked to only the organizer/first host's destination calendar. Later operations that read `booking.destinationCalendar` (handleCancelBooking.ts:251-255, paypal-webhook.ts:152-156, payments webhook.ts:101-119, the booking reminder cron at bookingReminder.ts:107-130, etc.) will only see one of several destinations and may therefore miss cancellations, reminders, or webhooks for other hosts. The BookingReferences table mitigates the calendar delete path, but anything keyed on `booking.destinationCalendar` (emails, webhooks, cron reminders, refund flows) silently drops the rest.

title: Read of `integration` on potentially-undefined destination calendar can throw
body: Line 119 reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without first checking if `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is defined: `if (evt.location === MeetLocationType && mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar")`. The destructure `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` yields `undefined` whenever `evt.destinationCalendar` is null/empty (which is exactly the case the Google Meet fallback is meant to handle, since non-team or no-destination flows now produce `null`). Accessing `.integration` on undefined throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'integration')` and the request fails before the location is rewritten to Cal Video. The check should be `!mainHostDestinationCalendar || mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"`.

title: Empty firstName/lastName fields added to team member objects
body: The team-member promise at lines 986-1000 now sets `firstName: ""` and `lastName: ""` in the returned object. The TeamMember/CalendarEvent.team.members TypeScript type (in packages/types/Calendar.d.ts) does not declare these keys, so they are extra/missing properties on every team attendee. They will be ignored by CalendarService implementations today, but they leak into the persisted meeting attendee list on every external calendar (e.g. ICS attendee fields, Google Meet attendee payloads generated by translateAttendees in larkcalendar/office365). The change is undocumented in the PR description and can interact with downstream consumers that expect only the documented TeamMember shape.

title: Organizer email may be overridden by undefined main destination calendar
body: Inside the attendees payload at line 122: `email: mainHostDestinationCalendar?.externalId ? mainHostDestinationCalendar.externalId : calEventRaw.organizer.email`. When the array is empty the optional chain resolves to undefined and the fallback correctly uses `organizer.email`, so this is fine for the empty-array path. However, for collective events with multiple destinations where the chosen `mainHostDestinationCalendar` lacks an `externalId` (e.g. a DestinationCalendar row created without one), the code silently falls back to the organizer's email and Google will reject/lose the organizer mapping. There's no distinction between "no destination" and "destination missing externalId".

title: createAttendees only adds attendees to the first destination calendar
body: In `createEvent` at line 128 the first host's calendar is selected for the event, then `createAttendees` (line 164) re-selects the same first element. The catch path at line 158 (`await this.deleteEvent(eventId, event, calendarId)`) cleans up by deleting from `calendarId` (the first). For a collective event whose other hosts' calendars the EventManager separately creates via createAllCalendarEvents, those other events will not have attendees attached at all (organizer + invitees included) because Lark's createAttendees only runs inside this one createEvent call. The destinationCalendar → attendee invite propagation described in the PR for collective bookings is not actually implemented for Lark.

title: destinationCalendar built from booking.destinationCalendar falls back to user.destinationCalendar unsafely
body: The expression `booking?.destinationCalendar ? [booking.destinationCalendar] : user.destinationCalendar ? [user.destinationCalendar] : []` will wrap a single `DestinationCalendar` row in an array. Downstream `EventManager.create(evt)` will then process only that one destination, ignoring the user-level `user.destinationCalendar` even when the booking actually intended to be a team/collective booking with multiple destinations. For collective events that require confirmation, the hosts that are not represented in `booking.destinationCalendar` will not be invited when the organizer confirms. Confirm `booking.eventType.schedulingType === COLLECTIVE` and append the team members' destinations (mirroring handleNewBooking.ts ~line 1074) before passing to EventManager.

title: Comment-only change: typo fix is unrelated to the PR
body: The commit changes `orginalBookingDuration` → `originalBookingDuration` in `ensureAvailableUsers`. That's a fine cleanup, but it isn't mentioned in the PR description and isn't related to the destinationCalendar-array refactor. Mixing unrelated typo fixes into a feature/bugfix PR makes bisecting and reverting harder; either split it into its own commit or document it explicitly.

title: Behavior-preserving spread refactor buried in a destinationCalendar PR
body: Two spread ternaries are rewritten (`...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` → `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})` and the matching `requestedSlug`). The results are equivalent because `false` is ignored when spreading. This isn't a bug, but the change is unrelated to the destinationCalendar refactor and should be moved to its own commit to keep the diff focused on the PR's stated purpose.

title: No tests for a sweeping CalendarEvent.destinationCalendar contract change
body: The PR converts `destinationCalendar` from a single object to an array across 22 files (every CalendarService implementation, EventManager, Booking/Cancel/Reschedule handlers, webhooks, three trpc handlers, payment webhooks, builders, types) yet adds no unit or integration tests. The author explicitly acknowledges in the checklist that tests were not added. Specific regression surfaces that are not covered: (a) collective COLLECTIVE bookings where multiple destinationCalendars are stored on the evt and propagated through handleNewBooking→EventManager.create→each CalendarService.createEvent with the correct credentialId; (b) cancellation when a booking has multiple bookingReferences with different credentials (the N×M legacy path bug); (c) the calendar-removal credentialId fallback in updateEvent/deleteEvent; (d) the BOOOKING_CREATED / BOOKING_REJECTED / BOOKING_REQUESTED webhook payload shape (only one of three test expectations was updated in webhook.e2e.ts). At minimum, a smoke test exercising collective new-booking/cancel/reschedule end-to-end on the dev stack is warranted before merge.

title: Missing `prisma` import causes ReferenceError at runtime
body: The new refresh logic in `getClient` calls `prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, data: { key: ... } })`, but the file's import block (lines 1-20) does not import `prisma`. There is no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. The function will throw `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined` the first time `getClient` is invoked, breaking all Salesforce calendar/video operations in the new code path.

title: `minimumTokenResponseSchema` is malformed and rejects expected fields
body: The schema uses computed property names `[z.string().toString()]`. Both expressions evaluate to the same string representation of the ZodString instance (e.g. `"ZodString"`), so the object literal has two duplicate keys and JavaScript silently drops the first. The resulting schema is effectively `{ access_token: z.string(), "<schema name>": z.unknown().optional() }` and does not actually declare the intended catchall/number/expiry rules. Any non-`access_token` field (`expires_in`, `refresh_token`, `scope`, `expiry_date`, etc.) is stripped by ZodObject's default stripping behavior. With sharing enabled, every caller ends up with an `access_token` only, breaking the downstream code that depends on those fields (e.g. `googleCredentials.expiry_date`, `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn`, salesforce fields).

title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token"
body: When `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token` is falsy, the code assigns the literal string `"refresh_token"` to the field and then saves it to the credential key in the DB. On the next token refresh the OAuth provider is sent `refresh_token="refresh_token"`, which it will reject (typically with `invalid_grant`), causing the credential to be marked invalid and the integration to break. The intent appears to have been to set a sentinel, but the value is being persisted and used as a real refresh token.

title: Stores the full SafeParseResult instead of `.data`
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the raw `SafeParseReturnType` object (`{ success, data }`). The Google Calendar code assigns this directly: `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema);` and then passes `key` to `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. The stored value will be `{ success: true, data: { ...googleCredentials } }` rather than the credentials object itself. On the next read, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` will fail because the top-level shape is wrong, marking the credential invalid. Other call sites (`office365calendar`, `salesforce`, `zoomvideo`) correctly use `.data`; this one does not.

title: Webhook secret compared with `!==` (timing attack)
body: The header value is compared to `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` using `!==`, which short-circuits on the first mismatching byte and leaks timing information that can be used to brute-force the secret. Use a constant-time comparison such as `crypto.timingSafeEqual` over equal-length buffers (after a length check) instead. The endpoint is unauthenticated by any other mechanism (no rate limit, no IP allowlist, no replay protection), so the secret is the only barrier.

title: Outbound call to credential sync endpoint has no authentication
body: `fetch(process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, ...)` only sends `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` in the form body, with no shared secret, signature, or HMAC. Anyone able to reach this endpoint (or to observe/intercept traffic to it) can trigger token-refresh lookups for arbitrary users. At a minimum, send the same `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` (or a dedicated HMAC) as a header so the operator's app store can authenticate the caller.

title: Inconsistent response shape breaks callers when sharing is enabled
body: When sharing is OFF, `refreshFunction` returns whatever the app's native refresh returns (a Google `GaxiosResponse` for googlecalendar, an Axios response for hubspot/zoho-bigin/zohocrm, a raw `fetch` `Response` for larkcalendar/office365calendar/office365video/webex/zoomvideo). When sharing is ON, the function instead returns a raw `fetch` `Response` from the sync endpoint. The code after the call expects the native shape — e.g. googlecalendar uses `res?.data`, hubspot uses `hubspotRefreshToken.accessToken`/`expiresIn`, zoho-bigin/zohocrm use `tokenInfo.data.error` — which are absent on a `Response`. With sharing enabled, every one of these integrations will fail on token refresh (silently for hubspot because the result is just `undefined`; loudly for the rest because they try to read properties of `undefined`). The function should either return a normalized token object in both modes or document/enforce a single shape.

title: findFirst + create/update race can produce duplicate credentials
body: The handler does `findFirst({ userId, appId })` then either `update` or `create` based on whether one was found. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same (userId, appSlug) can both find nothing and both `create`, producing duplicate `Credential` rows. The code's own comment notes that upsert can't be used because the credential id is unknown, but a `UNIQUE` constraint on `(userId, appId, type)` plus catching the unique-violation and falling back to update, or wrapping the find+create in a serializable transaction, would prevent duplicates that later cause inconsistent OAuth behavior.

title: Manually refreshed Salesforce token is never given to the returned Connection
body: `getClient` performs a manual refresh, persists the new access token, and then constructs `new jsforce.Connection({ ..., accessToken: credentialKey.access_token, refreshToken: credentialKey.refresh_token })` using the OLD `credentialKey` values that were captured before the refresh. The freshly obtained `accessToken`/`instance_url` from the refresh response is written to the DB but never used by the jsforce client, so the Connection immediately operates with a stale token and jsforce will re-refresh on first use — duplicating and racing with the manual refresh.

title: Refresh triggers on any non-OK statusText, fragile to HTTP/2
body: `if (response.statusText !== "OK") throw new HttpError({ statusCode: 400, message: response.statusText })` relies on the HTTP/1.x statusText being exactly `"OK"`. Under HTTP/2 status reason phrases are not transmitted (and many proxies/clients return lowercase or empty), so a successful Salesforce response can throw here. Use `response.ok` (or `response.status >= 200 && response.status < 300`) instead.

title: `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` does not reflect the actual sync endpoint
body: The constant is defined as `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY`. Both `parseRefreshTokenResponse` and `refreshOAuthTokens` additionally require `process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` to take the sharing branch. With only the first two variables set, the webhook will accept and store credentials but every token refresh silently falls back to the local OAuth path, which will not yield the shared token. Either include `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` in the constant or split it into two flags with clear semantics so operators see a consistent state.

title: Webhook header name is taken from env without normalization
body: `req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"]` uses the env var as an object key into `req.headers` directly. HTTP header lookup is normally case-insensitive and Node lowercases incoming headers; if the operator sets `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` in mixed/upper case the lookup silently misses and the endpoint falls through to `403` for legitimate calls (or, if unset, hardcoded). Lowercase the value before use and validate it against `/^[a-z0-9-]+$/` so it cannot be used to probe internal headers or cause lookup confusion.

title: No replay protection, rate limit, or audit trail on credential upsert
body: Anyone holding the webhook secret can repeatedly overwrite or create credentials for any `userId` in the request body. There is no timestamp/nonce check to block replays, no per-IP rate limit, no per-user limit, and no record of which credentials were written or by whom. Combined with the timing-vulnerable comparison and the unencrypted `userId` in the body, a leak or brute-force of the secret lets an attacker plant OAuth tokens for arbitrary users. Consider adding a signed timestamp window, request signing, and structured logging of (userId, appSlug, request IP) for each upsert.

title: Returns refreshed token even when the response carries an error
body: `if (!tokenInfo.data.error) { ... } else { this.log.error(tokenInfo.data); }` logs the error but then falls through to `return tokenInfo.data as BiginToken`. If the refresh response contains `{ error: "invalid_grant" }` (and `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the sync endpoint's raw `Response`, which lacks `.data.error`), the caller gets a fake/empty token and downstream calls fail opaquely. Reject on `error` or any non-2xx status instead of returning the payload.

title: Credential `appId` is taken from `appStoreMetadata` instead of the validated DB slug
body: The handler validates `reqBody.appSlug` against the `App` table but then looks the slug up in `appStoreMetadata` and stores `appId: appMetadata.slug`. If those two ever diverge, the credential row is keyed by a slug that doesn't exist in the `App` table, breaking downstream queries that join on `appId`. Use the validated `app.slug` for the stored `appId`.

title: refreshOAuthTokens returns incompatible Response vs token-object shapes
body: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the function returns the raw `fetch` Response (line 15). When disabled, it returns whatever the provider-specific refresh function returns (e.g. for googlecalendar `myGoogleAuth.refreshToken(...)` returns `{ res: { data: {...} } }`, for hubspot it returns a HubspotToken, etc.). Downstream callers were written assuming the non-sync shape. With sharing enabled the googlecalendar code at `packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:94` does `const token = res?.data;` on a Response, then `token.access_token` throws TypeError. hubspot (`hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts:192`), office365calendar (`office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` after `parseRefreshTokenResponse`), office365video (`office365video/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts:77`), zohocrm (`zohocrm/lib/CalendarService.ts:204`), zoho-bigin (`zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts:85`), webex (`webex/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts:62`) and zoomvideo (`zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts:79`) all break the same way. The function must return a normalized token object (parsed from the sync JSON plus token shape) and propagate provider-specific data on the non-sync branch, or each integration needs its own dispatcher.

title: minimumTokenResponseSchema Zod schema does not validate what the comments claim
body: Computed property keys in object literals evaluate to fixed strings at runtime: `[z.string().toString()]` yields the literal string `"ZodString"` (the ZodType's toString), not 'any string key'. The resulting schema is therefore `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), ZodString: z.number(), ZodOptional: z.unknown().optional() })`. Real token responses from the self-hoster's sync endpoint don't include a `ZodString` number field, so `safeParse` will fail (the required `ZodString` number is missing), throwing "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". The comments claim it allows any number property as expiry and any other properties, but neither is true. The correct way to express that is `.catchall(z.unknown())` on the object, or leaving the schema as-is and not adding the placeholder keys.

title: Placeholder string 'refresh_token' written into credential.key.refresh_token
body: When the parsed response has no `refresh_token`, the code sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` (a literal placeholder). That string is then persisted into `credential.key.refresh_token` via the callers (e.g. googlecalendar `CalendarService.ts` writes `key` into the DB, office365calendar writes the merged `o365AuthCredentials`, etc.).
