On the next refresh cycle the placeholder will be used as the actual `refresh_token` against Google/Microsoft/etc. and will be rejected as invalid_grant, permanently breaking the credential. If the sync endpoint does not return a `refresh_token`, refresh tokens must be left undefined and the credential marked invalid instead of being silently corrupted.

title: Webhook endpoint allows writing credentials for arbitrary user IDs with a single shared secret
body: The endpoint authenticates the caller only with a single shared header secret (lines 24-29). Once that secret is known (it is shared by every Cal.com deployment enabling this feature and there is no per-tenant signing), any caller can POST `{userId: <int>, appSlug, keys}` and overwrite that user's credentials. `userId` is a sequential integer from the users table, so attackers can iterate. There is no per-user HMAC, no per-deployment signing key bound to the user, and no proof that the caller is authorized to manage that specific user's third-party account. Concretely this lets one compromised self-host instance push attacker-controlled OAuth tokens (which can include an `access_token` issued to the attacker's account on Google/Microsoft/Zoom/etc.) into any user's Cal.com account, which the app will then use to read/insert calendar events and create meetings on behalf of the victim. Also note the header comparison `req.headers[name] !== secret` is non-constant-time and will throw/always-fail if the header is sent twice (Next.js parses duplicate headers as an array).

title: SalesforceCalendarService.refreshes access token on every getClient() call
body: Lines 75-100 unconditionally POST to Salesforce's token endpoint inside `getClient`, then overwrite `credential.key` in the database, even when the existing access token is still valid. `getClient` is called once per service instance (line 57), so a service that is held across many operations will refresh exactly once per construction - but more importantly, every API operation that constructs a new `SalesforceCalendarService` (which is the typical usage pattern in this repo, see e.g. how other CalendarService implementations are instantiated per-call) hits Salesforce for a token refresh whether or not refresh is required. This both wastes a refresh_token use (Salesforce will eventually return `invalid_grant` once the refresh token rotates out) and can trip rate limits. Refresh should be gated on token expiry, mirroring the other integrations (`isExpired` checks before calling refresh).

title: fetch() to sync endpoint has no Content-Type header and no auth
body: The body is `new URLSearchParams({...})` but no `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded` header is set, so the receiving server is not guaranteed to parse the body as a form (it will see an empty body in many frameworks, and `calcomUserId`/`appSlug` will be undefined server-side, making every refresh call effectively a no-op). Additionally, there is no authentication on this outbound call: the sync endpoint cannot distinguish a request coming from this Cal.com instance from any other HTTP client that knows the URL. The endpoint should at minimum require a shared secret / signature header that the self-hoster validates.

title: Sync endpoint HTTP errors are not detected; raw Response is returned
body: The function returns the `Response` object unconditionally (line 15) without checking `response.ok`. If the self-hoster's sync endpoint returns 401/403/429/500, the raw error response body is handed to downstream code as if it were a successful token response, then parsed with the (already broken) `minimumTokenResponseSchema` and discarded, leaving the credential unchanged on disk with no error logged. The caller has no way to know refresh failed. A `if (!response.ok) throw new Error(...)` is required, and the function should surface token refresh failures.

title: findFirst + create/update on credentials is not atomic (race condition / duplicate rows)
body: Lines 62-90 do a `findFirst` followed by either `update` or `create` on `prisma.credential` based on whether a row was found. There is no transaction or unique constraint check; if two webhook calls for the same (userId, appId) race (e.g. the self-hoster retries, or a user reinstalls while a webhook is in flight), both can observe no existing row and both `create`, producing two credential rows for the same user/app. Subsequent refresh/lookup code in this repo commonly uses `findFirst` for these (e.g. office365video callback line 79 does `findMany` and deletes duplicates by hand, but the webhook path does not), which means the duplicate row will be silently picked up by whichever path queries first and the other becomes dead weight (or causes the wrong row to be updated). The (userId, appId) pair needs a unique constraint or the write needs to use an upsert/transaction.

title: Decryption failure and bad payload not handled
body: `symmetricDecrypt` will throw if the encrypted blob is malformed or the key is wrong, and `JSON.parse` will throw if the decrypted plaintext is not valid JSON. Neither is caught, so the handler returns a 500 with the stack trace leaking to the caller instead of a 4xx with a clear message. Also, after a successful decrypt+parse, `keys` is `unknown` (since it is `JSON.parse(...)`); it is written to `credential.key` without any schema check (no zod, no type guard), so any JSON object - including something that isn't a valid OAuth token shape - will be persisted. At minimum the handler should validate `keys` is an object with the fields the downstream app actually expects, and wrap the decrypt+parse in try/catch returning 400.

title: Missing `prisma` import causes runtime ReferenceError
body: The new code added in this PR calls `prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, data: { key: ... } })` (line 96) but `prisma` is not imported in this file. The imports end at `getAppKeysFromSlug` and `parseRefreshTokenResponse`. Hitting the salesforce CalendarService code path (which happens on every salesforce CalendarService instantiation that goes through `getClient`) will throw `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined`, breaking salesforce bookings entirely for everyone — including self-hosters that never opt into credential sharing. This is an immediate runtime crash for a previously-working integration.

title: `minimumTokenResponseSchema` is invalid zod; every sharing-mode response is rejected
body: The schema uses computed object keys `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()`. `z.string().toString()` returns the schema's typeName (e.g. `"ZodString"`), so the produced keys are the literal strings `"ZodString"` and `"ZodOptional"`, not catch-all matchers. The schema therefore requires the response object to contain numeric properties literally called `"ZodString"` and `"ZodOptional"`, which no real OAuth response ever has. `parseRefreshTokenResponse` then unconditionally throws `"Invalid refreshed tokens were returned"` whenever `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is true. Consequence: every refresh-token call routed through credential sharing fails; the outer `try/catch` blocks in the integrations then return the stale, expiring auth and token refresh silently regresses. This is the central defect that breaks the new sync path.

title: Refresh token is overwritten with the literal string "refresh_token"
body: After a successful parse, the function unconditionally does `if (!refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token) { refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"; }`. Whenever the parsed payload lacks `refresh_token` (which is true for every credential-sharing response, since the broken schema above never retains one), the real refresh token is replaced in-memory with the placeholder literal `"refresh_token"`. The integrations then write this garbage value into the database (`prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`). Future refresh attempts will send the literal string `"refresh_token"` to the OAuth provider and fail with `invalid_grant`, permanently invalidating the credential. Even outside sharing mode, any integration whose schema makes `refresh_token` optional will silently corrupt its stored refresh token.

title: Sharing-mode return type incompatible with most callers
body:
When `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT && userId` is true, the function returns whatever `fetch(...)` yields — a `Response` object — and never reads its body. The signature is typed as `() => any`, and each integration expects a specific post-shape immediately after the call:

- `packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:94-96` does `const token = res?.data; ... token.access_token; token.expiry_date` — `Response` has no `.data`, so this throws and the surrounding try/catch returns the stale auth.
- `packages/app-store/hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts:192` does `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn * 1000` — `Response` has no `.expiresIn`, producing `NaN`, and the prisma update writes `NaN` into `expiryDate`.
- `packages/app-store/zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts:96` does `tokenInfo.data.error` — `Response.data` is `undefined`, so `.error` throws.
- `packages/app-store/zohocrm/lib/CalendarService.ts:217` does `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error` — same issue.
- `packages/app-store/larkcalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:84` passes the `Response` straight into `handleLarkError`, which then attempts `data.data.refresh_expires_in`. Without a documented sync-endpoint shape, Lark silently breaks the moment the response format is not exactly what the local refresh returned.

The other integrations (office365calendar, office365video, webex, zoomvideo) happen to call `handleErrorsJson`/`handleWebexResponse`/`handleZoomResponse` which accept a `Response`, but they then rely on `parseRefreshTokenResponse` (which is itself broken — see other findings), so they are still non-functional in sharing mode. Result: the feature advertises support for many apps but, in practice, breaks every app that opts in.

title: findFirst-then-create is not atomic; webhook can produce duplicate credentials
body: The handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst(...)` followed by `prisma.credential.create(...)` if no row matches, with no transaction and no unique constraint to lean on. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same `(userId, appId)` will both observe no row and both insert a new credential, leaving the user with multiple rows for the same app — a state the rest of the codebase assumes does not happen (e.g. lark's callback, webex/zoom/office365 callbacks all explicitly delete pre-existing rows). The `findFirst` lookup also doesn't filter by `type`, so when the same `appId` exists with multiple legacy `type` values, an update may be applied to the wrong row. The docstring even acknowledges this with "Can't use prisma upsert as we don't know the id of the credential", but a race-free approach (e.g. `prisma.credential.deleteMany({ userId, appId })` inside a transaction, or an upsert on a composite key) would be safer.

title: Webhook handler accepts any HTTP method and has no body-size, replay, or method check
body: The handler does not check `req.method`, so any method with the correct secret header (e.g. GET, PUT) reaches the database mutation path; only the secret comparison and `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` flag gate it. There is also no body-size limit, no timestamp/nonce, and no signature scheme beyond a static shared secret. Combined with the fact that anyone in possession of `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` can create or replace credentials for any userId in the system, an attacker who learns or leaks the secret (e.g. via logs, env backups) can rewrite every user's app tokens by replaying the request. At minimum, restrict to POST and verify a recent timestamp.

title: Uncaught zod and decryption errors produce 500 with stack trace
body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws on malformed body and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, ...))` throws on a tampered or wrong-key payload. There is no error boundary, so callers receive a default 500 plus Next.js's full error page with stack trace, leaking file paths and internals. The function should catch `ZodError`/`Error` and respond with a structured 4xx (e.g. 400 for invalid body, 422 for decryption failure) — and crucially never echo the offending key bytes.

title: Credential sync endpoint contract is undefined and inconsistent across integrations
body: The function POSTs only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` (form-urlencoded) to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` and returns the raw response unmodified. But each integration expects the response to have a different exact shape: google expects `{access_token, expiry_date}`, office365 expects `{access_token, expires_in, refresh_token?}`, hubspot expects a full `HubspotToken`, lark expects `{data:{access_token, refresh_token, expires_in, refresh_expires_in}}`, etc. Self-hosters implementing the parent endpoint have no documentation describing these required shapes (or the URL/return value must instead be customized per app — which contradicts the function being shared). Without a clear spec, the feature is unusable in practice.

title: Outbound call to sync endpoint has no authentication from Cal.com side
body: `fetch(process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, ...)` is sent with no headers, no signature, and no client identity. The receiving service has no way to verify that the call came from this Cal.com instance or that `appSlug`/`calcomUserId` weren't tampered with by a network attacker or a mis-routed proxy. Combined with the fact that `userId` is trusted blindly to look up tokens server-side, anyone who can intercept traffic to the configured endpoint can impersonate any user. The endpoint should require a Cal.com-issued signature (e.g. an HMAC of the body using a shared key) so the parent service can reject forged refresh requests.

title: No tests cover the new credential-sharing sync path
body: The PR introduces three pieces of behavior with no test coverage: the new `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` webhook (including auth/secret checking, decryption, and the find/update/create branches), `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts` (sharing vs. non-sharing branches, including what the returned value looks like to callers), and `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts` (the broken minimum-token schema and the refresh-token overwrite). The PR description explicitly states no tests were added and existing tests were not run. Given the multiple integration-affecting bugs above, merging without tests risks regressing every OAuth integration.

title: Permission check requires being both team admin AND team owner
body: `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`, which means a regular team admin who is not also the team owner is rejected by the guard, and the request falls through to `isOrganizer`/`isAttendee`. For team bookings where the booking was assigned to another host, this incorrectly denies legitimate team admins from adding guests. The two role checks should be combined with `||` (or just call `isTeamAdmin`, which typically implies owner privileges) so team admins are allowed.

title: Email comparison for dedup and blacklist is case-sensitive
body: The dedup against existing attendees (`guest === attendee.email`) and the blacklist filter (`blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`) compare raw strings. Email local parts are conventionally treated as case-insensitive, so users can submit `User@Example.com` and bypass both checks even though `user@example.com` is already an attendee or blacklisted. All comparisons should lowercase both sides (the blacklist is already lowercased on parsing, but the input `guest` and the existing `attendee.email` are not).

title: Calendar update runs with the caller's credentials, not the organizer's
body: `EventManager` is constructed with `...user` and `credentials` obtained via `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` (the logged-in user). When the caller is a team admin or an attendee (both of whom the permission check above allows), they typically don't have the host's calendar integration, so `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` either fails outright or attempts the update under the wrong account. The organizer of the booking is already fetched at line 58; the manager should be built from that user's id/credentials so the calendar invite is actually pushed to the new guests.

title: Emails are computed from the original `guests` list instead of the deduplicated one
body: `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` is called with the raw input, but the DB write only used `uniqueGuests` (deduped against existing attendees and the blacklist). In `email-manager.ts`, attendees whose email appears in `newGuests` receive a fresh `AttendeeScheduledEmail`; this causes any email that was filtered out only as a duplicate of an existing attendee (e.g. an attendee resubmits their own email) to receive a duplicate booking-confirmation email as if they were just added. Pass `uniqueGuests` so the notification logic mirrors what was actually persisted.

title: DB write is committed before calendar update with no transaction
body: `prisma.booking.update(...)` (line 92) creates the attendee rows first, then `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` is called separately, and only afterwards are the notification emails sent. If the calendar sync throws (e.g. bad credentials, see line 158) or the email send throws, the booking already has the new attendees persisted but no calendar invite went out; the client receives an error and the user is left in an inconsistent state where the API claims failure but guests are in the DB. Wrap the DB write and the external calls in a compensating/transactional pattern, or perform the calendar update first (with idempotency) and only persist attendees on success.

title: Email-send errors are silently swallowed
body: `sendAddGuestsEmails` is wrapped in `try { ... } catch (err) { console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails"); }`. The project uses a structured logger elsewhere (`logger` is already imported in this file); a plain `console.log` drops context, and swallowing the error means neither the caller nor an operator will notice that attendees were added but never notified. At minimum this should log via the project's `logger` (with `safeStringify` of the error) and ideally surface a non-fatal warning in the response.

title: replyTo header exposes every attendee's email address
body: `replyTo: [this.calEvent.organizer.email, ...this.calEvent.attendees.map(({ email }) => email)]` puts every attendee into the `Reply-To` header. Mail clients honor `Reply-To` and will deliver the response to every address listed there, so when the organizer (or any recipient) hits Reply, the message is broadcast to all attendees. The base `OrganizerScheduledEmail` only uses the organizer's email in `replyTo`; this template should do the same. Otherwise the organizer is one click away from leaking a private reply to the entire guest list.

title: Newly added guests receive a generic booking confirmation, not a guest-added notice
body: For attendees that match `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)`, the manager instantiates `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (the base class), whose subject/content is the standard 'Your booking is confirmed' wording. Existing attendees get `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail` with subject `guests_added_event_type_subject`. The newly invited guest therefore sees a confirmation email phrased as if they had booked the event themselves, with no hint that they were added by someone else. Either reuse `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail` (it already generates a `REQUEST` ICS method) or pass the `guests_added_event_type_subject`/`new_guests_added` keys down so the message matches the situation.

title: Error toast prefixes the TRPC error code in front of the translated message
body: On mutation error the toast is built as `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}`. Error codes like `BAD_REQUEST`, `FORBIDDEN`, `NOT_FOUND` are leaked to end users alongside the translated message (e.g. 'BAD_REQUEST: Emails must be unique and valid'). Codes are an internal contract; show only `t(err.message)`, falling back to `t("unable_to_add_guests")` when the key is missing or untranslatable.

title: Client-side validation reports generic 'unique and valid' even when emails clash with existing attendees
body: `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` only checks email syntax and mutual uniqueness of the typed list. It does not know about attendees already on the booking, so when the user types an email that is already a guest, the request is still sent and the server responds with `emails_must_be_unique_valid`, which the dialog surfaces verbatim even though the values were unique within the user's input. Either pre-filter the input against the booking's existing attendee emails in the dialog (the booking is already known at render time) or pick a more specific translation key on the server when the dedup against `booking.attendees` is what failed.

title: Initial state is `[""]` so the form starts in an invalid state
body: `useState<string[]>([""])` seeds the input with one empty email; pressing 'Add' immediately triggers `ZAddGuestsInputSchema.safeParse`, which fails on `z.string().email()` against `""`, surfacing the red 'emails must be unique and valid' banner before the user has typed anything. Initialize with `[]` (matching the empty-state branch of `MultiEmail`) or run validation only after the first onChange.

title: Component mutates the `value` prop
body: `value = value || []` reassigns the incoming prop before reading it. React props must be treated as immutable; this both violates React conventions and breaks if a parent passes a value of `null` vs `undefined` differently. Default-clone to a local `const` instead, e.g. `const values = value ?? [];`.

title: Schema imposes no length bounds on the `guests` array
body: `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` accepts `z.array(z.string().email())` with no `min`/`max`. A direct API caller can submit an arbitrarily large list (or an empty list that the handler then rejects with a generic error), enabling trivial abuse and unbounded cost from calendar/email fan-out on the server. Add a reasonable `.min(1).max(N)` (the existing dialog caps UI input to a small number) so the endpoint cannot be weaponised through a single request.

title: New tRPC mutation ships without tests
body: The PR adds a non-trivial mutation with a permission check, blacklist filtering, calendar sync, and email fan-out, but no test file is included. At least the following cases need coverage before merge: (1) team admin OR team owner is allowed, plain team member who is not the host is rejected; (2) emails matching an existing attendee (case-insensitively) are filtered out; (3) blacklisted emails are filtered out; (4) calendar failure does not leave the booking partially updated; (5) the new guests receive the guest-added email rather than a duplicate booking confirmation.

title: isTeamAdminOrOwner uses AND instead of OR, blocking team admins
body: Lines 46-48 compute the team permission with `await isTeamAdmin(...) && await isTeamOwner(...)`. The variable name and intent ('admin OR owner') clearly require `||`. As written, a user must be both an admin AND an owner of the team to pass the check; ordinary team admins (and owners who are not also admins) are rejected with FORBIDDEN even though the route is meant to be available to them. This silently breaks the feature for almost all legitimate team users.

title: Any existing attendee can add arbitrary guests
body: Permission is granted to the organizer, team admins/owners, OR any existing attendee (`isAttendee = !!booking.attendees.find(a => a.email === user.email)`). Any booked attendee can therefore inject new emails into the booking, mutate the underlying calendar event, and trigger calendar-invite emails to recipients of their choosing. This is a privilege escalation relative to typical calendar products where only the organizer can grow the attendee list, and it exposes a vector for spam / calendar-invite abuse. The check should be limited to the organizer (and team admins/owners), not all attendees.

title: Handler never checks booking status, event-type policy, or recurrence
body: The handler mutates booking attendees and external calendar events without verifying booking.status (ACCEPTED/PENDING/CANCELLED/REJECTED), without checking booking.endTime (past bookings), without checking eventType.disableGuests, and without handling recurringEventId (a guest added to one instance will not appear in other instances, producing a confusing state). All of these should be rejected up front.

title: Newly-added guests are sent AttendeeScheduledEmail with wrong subject/content
body: In `sendAddGuestsEmails`, every attendee whose email is in `newGuests` receives `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (subject like 'Scheduled: ...', body implying they booked the meeting), while existing attendees receive `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail` (subject 'Guests Added: ...', body 'Added - New guests added to your event'). For a brand-new guest this is the wrong template and is misleading: they did not schedule anything, they were added. Newly-added guests should receive the 'Guests Added' template (or a dedicated 'You were added' template), with a subject and body that reflect that. The current branch also uses the raw `guests` input for comparison, so an existing attendee whose email is duplicated in the input will silently get the 'Scheduled' email instead of the 'Guests Added' one.

title: EventManager is built with the requesting user's credentials, not the organizer's
body: `const credentials = await getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` and `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials })` use the caller (which may be a team admin or any attendee) instead of the booking organizer. The calendar event being updated belongs to the organizer, and `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` runs with the wrong credentials. When the caller is not the organizer (e.g., a team admin or attendee) the calendar update will silently fail or update the wrong account. Credentials and identity should come from the organizer (e.g., `getUsersCredentials(organizer)` or `new EventManager({ ...organizer, credentials })`).

title: `uniqueGuests` is not actually deduplicated and ignores case
body: The filter on lines 74-78 only removes entries that match an existing attendee's email (case-sensitive `===`) and any entry in the blacklist (lowercased). It does NOT deduplicate the input, so submitting `['a@x.com','a@x.com']` produces two `createMany` rows with identical emails (unless a unique constraint saves it, which is not visible here). It also treats email comparison as case-sensitive even though emails are case-insensitive, so `Guest@x.com` would not be detected as already present if the existing attendee is `guest@x.com`. The misleading name plus the lack of de-duplication can produce duplicate attendee rows and double calendar invites.

title: Guests schema has no min/max length and accepts unbounded input
body: `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` allows any length. With the `addGuests` mutation callable by any attendee of a booking, this is a cheap DoS / abuse vector: a single request can submit thousands of emails, triggering thousands of `createMany` rows, calendar API calls in `EventManager.updateCalendarAttendees`, and an unbounded number of emails in `Promise.all(emailsToSend)`. There is no rate limiting in the handler either. A reasonable cap (e.g., 1-50) should be added at the schema layer.

title: No transaction/locking around attendee creation; double-clicks create duplicates
body: The handler reads the booking, filters out existing emails, then `prisma.booking.update({ data: { attendees: { createMany: { data: guestsFullDetails } } } })`. Two concurrent submissions (e.g., user double-clicks, or two tabs) can both read the booking before either writes, both compute `uniqueGuests` with the same emails, and both succeed in `createMany`, producing duplicate Attendee rows. The whole flow (read -> filter -> createMany -> calendar update -> emails) is not wrapped in a transaction or guarded by any unique constraint on (bookingId, email), so this leaves the booking in an inconsistent state with duplicate attendees and duplicate external calendar invites.

title: 'Additional guests' action is shown for every booking regardless of status
body: The new `add_members` action is appended to `editBookingActions` with no gating on `isUpcoming`, `isConfirmed`, `isPending`, or non-cancelled status. Users can open the dialog for past, cancelled, or rejected bookings; the server-side handler does not block them either. The dialog should at minimum be hidden (or disabled with explanation) for non-actionable booking states, and the server should reject them.

title: `teamId ?? 0` makes isTeamAdmin/isTeamOwner query with team id 0
body: When `booking.eventType?.teamId` is null (a personal/one-on-one booking), the code calls `isTeamAdmin(user.id, 0)` and `isTeamOwner(user.id, 0)`. If any user happens to be an admin/owner of team id 0, they would satisfy this branch on a personal booking they do not own. The team-membership check should be conditional on `booking.eventType?.teamId` actually being set (e.g., `if (booking.eventType?.teamId)` then check, else skip), not fallback to 0.

title: No error handling for calendar update or emails; partial state on failure
body: `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` and `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` are the only steps that sync with external systems. `updateCalendarAttendees` is not wrapped in try/catch; a calendar provider failure throws out of the handler after the DB has already been updated with the new attendees. `sendAddGuestsEmails` is wrapped in try/catch but only `console.log`s the error. Result: attendees can exist in the DB without being on the calendar video call and without receiving any notification. Either both side-effects must be transactional/compensating, or the DB write must happen last and roll back on failure.

title: Validation only shows generic 'must be unique and valid' for any failure
body: The local schema is `z.array(z.string().email()).refine(unique)`. Initial state is `[""]`, so the very first click of 'Add' with no input typed fails on the `email()` check (empty string), but the user is shown 'Emails must be unique and valid' — which is not what is wrong. There is also no per-field error and no live validation; the error only appears after clicking submit. Either fix the message to reflect the actual problem, or run validation per row on change.

title: Mutates the `value` prop instead of using a local default
body: `value = value || [];` reassigns the destructured prop in place. With React, props are immutable from the callee's perspective; this either no-ops or, if the consumer passes a non-frozen array, mutates the caller's array on every render. It should be `const values = value ?? [];` (or default via destructuring) so that subsequent `value.map(...)`/`value.push(...)` use a local copy.

title: Organizer email subject assumes attendees[0] exists
body: `organizer-add-guests-email.ts` builds the subject with `name: this.calEvent.attendees[0].name`. If a handler ever calls `sendAddGuestsEmails` for a booking whose `attendees` array is empty (or where the recipient's distinct attendee list excludes any), this throws `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')` and the whole `Promise.all` rejects. Use optional chaining / fallback (e.g., `this.calEvent.attendees[0]?.name ?? this.calEvent.organizer.name`).

title: Emails are sent for the full original `guests` input, including duplicates and rejected entries
body: `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` passes the raw request `guests` (not `uniqueGuests`) to determine who is a 'new' guest. If the input contains an existing attendee's email (e.g., user re-submits), that attendee will be classified as 'new' and receive the 'Scheduled' email instead of the 'Guests Added' email. If duplicates appear in the input, the membership check still works on `attendees.map(...)`, so the wrong existing attendee could get the wrong template. Pass the deduped `uniqueGuests` (or a normalized Set of new emails) into the email function.

title: Permission check requires user to be both team admin AND owner
body: The variable `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed with `&&` instead of `||`: `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`. The naming and the rest of the check (`!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer && !isAttendee`) imply the intent is "admin OR owner", so that either role can add guests to a team booking. As written, only users who are both admin and owner (effectively owners only, assuming owner implies admin) are granted access, which is stricter than the variable name and likely the intended UX.

title: Duplicate-email and blacklist checks ignore email case
body: `uniqueGuests` filters new guests with case-sensitive comparisons: `guest === attendee.email` and `blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`. The blacklist list is lowercased, but the attendees list is not, and RFC 5321 mailbox names are case-insensitive. As a result a user can submit `Foo@Example.com` against an existing attendee `foo@example.com` and bypass the dedupe, or against a lowercased blacklist entry and bypass the block. Both comparisons should be case-insensitive (e.g. `.toLowerCase()` on both sides).

title: Wrong guest list passed to sendAddGuestsEmails
body: `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` is called with the original input `guests`, but `guests` can contain addresses that were filtered out (already on the booking or blacklisted) and never made it into `uniqueGuests` or the database. Inside `sendAddGuestsEmails` the branch `if (newGuests.includes(attendee.email))` is used to decide whether an attendee is "new" (gets `AttendeeScheduledEmail`) versus an existing attendee (gets `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail`). Because the input list is used instead of `uniqueGuests`, existing attendees whose email happened to also be in the input will be re-classified as "new" and receive a fresh `AttendeeScheduledEmail` instead of an `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail`. Pass `uniqueGuests` (the actually-added emails) into `sendAddGuestsEmails`.

title: Email-send errors are silently swallowed with console.log
body: The handler wraps `sendAddGuestsEmails` in a try/catch that does `console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails")`. The actual error is discarded (no `err` passed), the level is wrong (`console.error` would be appropriate), and the function returns success to the client even though the user was told guests were added but no notification emails were delivered. At minimum, log the error object via `console.error` and consider re-throwing or surfacing a partial-failure response so the UI can warn the user.

title: No transaction wraps DB update, calendar sync and email send
body: The handler commits `prisma.booking.update` first, then calls `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` and finally `sendAddGuestsEmails`. There is no surrounding transaction and no rollback if the calendar integration or email send fails partway through, the new attendees remain in the database but are missing from the underlying calendar/video meeting and from the participants' inboxes. This produces a data-integrity inconsistency between Cal.com state and the third-party calendar/video provider. Either wrap the side effects so the booking update can be rolled back, or at minimum document that a partial failure leaves the booking in this state and add a recovery path.

title: Hardcoded English message returned from handler
body: The handler returns `{ message: "Guests added" }` with a hardcoded English string. Every other booking mutation in this router uses translation keys (e.g. `booking_confirmation_success`). The frontend toast logic in `AddGuestsDialog.onSuccess` already calls `t("guests_added")` and never reads `data.message`, so the field is currently unused, but exposing a non-i18n string from the API creates a contract that downstream consumers will rely on. Either drop the field or return a translation key consistent with the rest of the codebase.

title: Subject crashes when booking has no attendees
body: `name: this.calEvent.attendees[0].name` will throw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` if `attendees` is empty. While every normal booking has at least the original booker, edge cases (data backfill, attendees deleted manually, etc.) can produce a zero-attendee booking, in which case sending this email will crash inside `getNodeMailerPayload` and abort the whole `Promise.all` batch in `sendAddGuestsEmails`. Use a safe fallback such as `this.calEvent.attendees[0]?.name ?? this.calEvent.organizer.name` (or skip the name interpolation) before accessing `.name`.

title: isInvalidEmail state not cleared after successful submission
body: In the `addGuestsMutation.onSuccess` handler, `setIsInvalidEmail(false)` is missing. The flag is set to `true` when validation fails, but if the user fixes the input and the mutation succeeds, the dialog closes without resetting the flag. Because the dialog component lives inside `BookingListItem` and stays mounted, reopening the dialog later shows the "Emails must be unique and valid" error immediately, even though the input is empty. Add `setIsInvalidEmail(false)` in `onSuccess` (and ideally on cancel too, which is already done).

title: No size limit on guests array in schema
body: ZAddGuestsInputSchema accepts `z.array(z.string().email())` with no `.min()`/`.max()`. Combined with the `MultiEmail` component, which lets the user add arbitrary rows, a malicious or accidental request can submit an enormous array that is then inserted via `createMany`, triggering a large number of calendar/email side effects in `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` and `sendAddGuestsEmails`. Add a reasonable bound (e.g. `.min(1).max(50)`).

title: Empty/whitespace entries are not stripped before validation
body: `handleAdd` runs `ZAddGuestsInputSchema.safeParse(multiEmailValue)` directly. `multiEmailValue` can contain blank rows (initial state is `[""]`, and the X control only deletes the entry but does not trim). The schema rejects the whole array as soon as one empty entry is present, so a user with one valid email plus an extra empty row is forced to manually delete the empty row. The dialog would be more forgiving if it filtered `multiEmailValue.map(s => s.trim()).filter(Boolean)` before validating and submitting.

title: Attendees can add additional guests to a booking
body: `isAttendee = !!booking.attendees.find(a => a.email === user.email)` grants any current attendee the right to add new guests to the booking. In most scheduling products only the organizer (or a team admin/owner) should be able to invite additional participants, because adding guests changes who has access to a meeting link, video room, or recording. The check should likely be `if (!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer)` (drop the `!isAttendee` branch) unless adding guests is explicitly part of the product design here.

title: No tests cover the new addGuests handler or dialog
body: This PR introduces a new public TRPC mutation, a new dialog component, two new email templates, and several new translation strings, but ships without any tests for the handler (permission rules, case-insensitive dedupe, blacklist handling, transaction/side-effect behavior), the AddGuestsDialog (validation reset, empty-row handling), or the email templates. At minimum add a handler test that covers: organizer happy path, team admin vs owner permission, attendee duplicate (case-insensitive), blacklisted email, empty guests array, and missing booking.

title: retryCount-based deleteMany is not scoped to SMS method
body: The new OR branch `retryCount: { gt: 1 }` in the cleanup deleteMany does not filter by `method`. The original deleteMany was intentionally restricted to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` because the SMS scheduling cron is the only owner of those rows; EMAIL/WHATSAPP reminders have their own cron paths. With this change, ANY WorkflowReminder row with retryCount > 1 will be deleted by this SMS handler, regardless of method. Today only this file increments retryCount, so there is no immediate data loss, but the cleanup now silently reaches across reminder types and will cause unexpected deletions the moment retryCount is reused for EMAIL or WHATSAPP elsewhere. Scope the clause to `{ method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, retryCount: { gt: 1 } }`.

title: Catch block increments retryCount after Twilio already accepted the SMS
body: The try block can throw from the success-path `prisma.workflowReminder.update({ scheduled: true, referenceId: scheduledSMS.sid })` (lines 169-177) AFTER `twilio.scheduleSMS` has already returned a truthy result and Twilio has accepted the message. The catch handler then unconditionally increments retryCount. Consequence: retryCount grows on a row whose Twilio message is already scheduled, and because `scheduled` is still false in the DB the next cron run will call `twilio.scheduleSMS` again, producing a duplicate SMS to the user. The retryCount bump must only happen when the Twilio call itself failed (or returned falsy), not when the bookkeeping update of an already-scheduled reminder fails.

title: Scheduling failures logged via console.log instead of console.error
body: The catch handler at line 198 logs the error with `console.log`, so in production this surfaces at the same severity as the routine info logs. Should be `console.error` so the failure is captured by the standard error pipeline (and the message includes the booking/reminder id, not just the raw error object).

title: Unhandled throw from catch-block update aborts the rest of the cron batch
body: The catch block performs a `prisma.workflowReminder.update` that is not itself wrapped in a try/catch. If that update fails (e.g. the row was concurrently deleted by another worker, or a transient DB error) the exception escapes the for-loop and the request returns 500 before processing the remaining reminders in `unscheduledReminders`. Wrap the catch-block update in its own try/catch (or log-and-continue) so one failed update cannot skip the rest of the batch.

title: No tests added for the new retryCount behaviour
body: The PR changes observable behaviour (WorkflowReminder rows are now deleted after 2 failed schedule attempts, and the new retryCount column drives that decision), but ships no unit or integration tests. At minimum the following cases should be covered: (1) twilio.scheduleSMS returns falsy -> retryCount incremented to 1, row preserved; (2) two consecutive falsy returns -> row deleted by the next cron run; (3) twilio.scheduleSMS throws -> retryCount incremented via the catch path; (4) twilio.scheduleSMS throws AND subsequent update throws -> loop continues for the remaining reminders. Without these the retry semantics can silently regress.

title: Lost-update race condition on retryCount increment
body: Both the else branch (line 184) and the catch block (line 195) update retryCount via a read-modify-write: `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1`. The `reminder.retryCount` value was read by the initial `findMany` at the start of the handler. If a second instance of this cron handler (or an overlapping invocation) has already updated the same row between the read and this update, the second writer will overwrite the first writer's increment using the stale value. The net retryCount will be off by at least one, causing premature (or never-triggered) deletion. The fix is to use Prisma's atomic increment: `data: { retryCount: { increment: 1 } }`, which does not require reading the current value. This is especially relevant because the cleanup at the top of the handler (line 29) will delete the row once `retryCount > 1`, so a lost update can directly cause data loss.

title: deleteMany cleanup deletes non-SMS reminders with retryCount > 1
body: The new OR branch in the cleanup deleteMany (lines 38-42) deletes any WorkflowReminder with `retryCount > 1` regardless of `method`. This handler is only responsible for SMS scheduling, so it should not be deleting EMAIL or WHATSAPP reminders. While the current codebase only increments retryCount for SMS, the column is on the shared `WorkflowReminder` model and any future code path that bumps retryCount for other methods (or pre-existing data from another env) would be silently deleted by this SMS-only cron. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` to the retryCount branch to scope the cleanup correctly.

title: Catch block increments retryCount for transient errors, not just scheduling failures
body: The catch block (lines 189-199) wraps the entire try body, which includes non-Twilio work: `prisma.profile.findFirst`, `getBookerBaseUrl`, `customTemplate`, `smsReminderTemplate`, and `bookingMetadataSchema.parse`. A transient failure in any of these (DB blip, malformed booking metadata, template variable missing) will increment retryCount exactly the same as a permanent Twilio failure like an invalid phone number. After 2 such transient errors the reminder is permanently deleted even though `twilio.scheduleSMS` was never reached or would have succeeded. The retry-counting should be scoped to the `twilio.scheduleSMS` call (and its returned falsy case), not the whole try block, or transient errors should not count toward the retry budget.

title: Else branch unreachable when message or sendTo is empty, so retryCount never advances
body: The else branch that increments retryCount (lines 178-187) is nested inside `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)`. If `message` is empty/null or `sendTo` is missing, neither the success path nor the retryCount increment runs, but `scheduled` remains false. Such reminders will never have retryCount incremented, so they will never be cleaned up by the new `retryCount > 1` branch and will sit indefinitely (only deleted when `scheduledDate <= now`). This was a pre-existing latent issue but is now more relevant because the new cleanup logic was specifically introduced to prevent indefinite retention of unprocessable reminders. The empty-message/missing-sendTo case should also bump retryCount (or be cleaned up) so the same retry budget applies.

title: No tests added for the new retry-count cleanup and increment behavior
body: The PR introduces a non-trivial state machine: a new column, a new cleanup branch (`retryCount > 1`), and two new retryCount increments (else + catch). None of these behaviors are covered by tests. At minimum, tests should cover: (1) reminders are deleted after the retryCount threshold; (2) reminders below the threshold are kept; (3) successful scheduleSMS updates `scheduled=true` and does not bump retryCount; (4) falsy return from scheduleSMS bumps retryCount; (5) thrown errors bump retryCount. Without these, future refactors can silently regress the retry budget.

title: Off-by-one between description and implementation: 2 attempts before deletion, not "twice failed"
body: The PR description says "after scheduling failed twice we delete the workflow reminder", but the implementation starts retryCount at 0 and deletes when `retryCount > 1`, meaning the row is deleted after the second failure only on the *third* cron invocation (the third invocation's cleanup deletes it because retryCount is now 2). The initial state counts as the first attempt, so the reminder is actually scheduled twice before being given up on. If the intent is "after 2 failed attempts", the description is accurate but ambiguous; if the intent is "try once, then retry once, then give up", that's what the code does. Either way, a comment near the cleanup query documenting the semantics (`retryCount > 1` means "has already been retried once") would prevent future confusion. This is also a documentation defect because the comment on line 28 ("delete all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date") was not updated to reflect the new OR branch.

title: retryCount delete branch is not scoped to SMS method
body: In the new OR clause of the deleteMany, the `retryCount > 1` branch has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, while the sibling branch is filtered to SMS. The original deleteMany only ever deleted SMS reminders. retryCount is currently only ever incremented in this SMS handler, so today no non-SMS row can reach retryCount > 1, but the schema places `retryCount` on the shared `WorkflowReminder` model (used by EMAIL/SMS/WHATSAPP). If a future change (or manual DB edit) sets retryCount > 1 on an EMAIL or WHATSAPP reminder, this cron will silently delete it. The OR branch should be wrapped under the same `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` predicate as the other branch, e.g. `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, scheduledDate: { lte: now }` OR `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, retryCount: { gt: 1 }`, or expressed as `method: SMS AND (scheduledDate <= now OR retryCount > 1)`.

title: Stale comment above deleteMany
body: The comment `//delete all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date` no longer describes the deleteMany. The query now also deletes reminders with `retryCount > 1`, and after the OR rewrite it deletes any reminder (regardless of method) that matches either branch. The comment should be updated to reflect the new semantics, otherwise future readers will misunderstand the cleanup behavior.

title: No tests cover the new retry/delete behavior
body: The PR introduces a meaningful behavior change in a cron-handler that mutates the database on every run (increment of retryCount on Twilio failure and on throw, plus deletion of reminders with retryCount > 1). There are no tests in the diff covering: (a) retryCount increments on a falsy return from twilio.scheduleSMS, (b) retryCount increments inside the catch block, (c) deleteMany removing reminders with retryCount > 1, (d) a reminder that fails twice being deleted on the subsequent run. Without tests, regressions in retry semantics (e.g. off-by-one in the threshold, double-increment under retry, or accidentally deleting scheduled rows) would go unnoticed.

title: Retries continue past scheduledDate once retryCount is < 2
body: The findMany filter is `scheduledDate: { lte: dayjs().add(7, 'day').toISOString() }`, which still includes reminders whose scheduledDate is in the past. Combined with the new retry logic, a reminder that fails twice will sit in the DB with retryCount=2 and scheduledDate in the past, then be deleted on the next cron run by the `retryCount > 1` branch. However, on the second cron run, after the first failure (retryCount=1) the reminder with a past-dated scheduledDate is not deleted by either branch (date <= now but method=SMS only matches the first OR branch, which it does — actually the date-past branch matches, so this is fine). The real concern is that between the first and second failure, the reminder whose date has passed continues to be passed to twilio.scheduleSMS in subsequent cron runs even though Twilio will obviously reject a send in the past, only to fail again and waste the second retry budget. The findMany should either skip past-dated unscheduled rows or the deleteMany should also delete past-dated + retryCount > 0 rows so a wasted retry isn't spent on an already-elapsed reminder.

title: retryCount update is non-atomic; parallel runs double-count
body: The handler reads `reminder.retryCount` from the findMany result and writes `reminder.retryCount + 1` in a separate update. If two cron invocations (or this handler and any other process touching the same row) overlap, both will read the same `retryCount` value and both will write `value + 1`, undercounting retries by 1. This matters here because the deletion threshold (`gt: 1`) is tight — a single lost increment means a perpetually-failing reminder is retried indefinitely instead of being deleted after 2 attempts. The update should use a conditional increment (`{ retryCount: { increment: 1 } }`) or be guarded by a `where: { id, retryCount: reminder.retryCount }` clause so concurrent writers can't clobber each other.

title: findMany method removed from public API; callers will break at runtime
body: The `findMany(findManyArgs: Prisma.BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedFindManyArgs)` method has been removed and replaced with `getBaseConditions(): Promise<Prisma.Sql>`. This is a breaking change to the public API of `InsightsBookingService`. Any callers in the codebase (e.g., routing layers, controller handlers, or other services) that invoke `service.findMany(...)` will fail at runtime with `TypeError: service.findMany is not a function`. The PR description frames this as a test-update PR, but the diff also rewrites the service. No callers of `findMany` are updated in this diff; if any exist they must be migrated to obtain the SQL fragment via `getBaseConditions()` and execute it with `prisma.$queryRaw` (or similar).

title: Caching describe block removed; coverage lost for cachedAuthConditions and cachedFilterConditions
body: The "Caching" describe block (which previously contained `should cache authorization conditions` and `should cache filter conditions` tests that asserted the second call returned an object structurally equal to the first) has been deleted from the test file. This drops all coverage for the `cachedAuthConditions` and `cachedFilterConditions` memoization in `getAuthorizationConditions` and `getFilterConditions`. If caching regresses (e.g., conditions are rebuilt on every call, causing an extra DB roundtrip per request, or a future change forgets to invalidate the cache when options/filters change), no test will detect it. The deleted block was located where the new `describe("getBaseConditions", ...)` (line 437) now begins.

title: Integration test relies on BookingTimeStatusDenormalized being populated synchronously by triggers
body: The "should combine authorization and filter conditions" test creates a booking directly via `prisma.booking.create(...)` and then queries `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` with `prisma.$queryRaw`, expecting exactly `[{ id: userBooking.id }]`. `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` is a denormalized table that is normally populated by PostgreSQL triggers on Booking INSERTs/UPDATEs. If those triggers are absent in the test environment, are disabled, or run asynchronously, the booking will not appear in the denormalized table and the assertion will fail with an empty array. The PR author explicitly acknowledges they could not run the integration tests due to test-runner configuration issues and asks the reviewer to verify execution manually; this specific test is the most fragile in the suite and the most likely to fail.

title: Integration test queries denormalized table that may not contain created records
body: The test creates a booking via `prisma.booking.create({...})` (lines 456-466) but the final query targets `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` (line 482). `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` is a separate denormalized table/view typically populated via triggers, materialized view refresh, or background jobs - it is not automatically populated by inserting a `Booking` row. If the sync is not configured or has not run in the test environment, the query will return `[]` and `expect(results).toEqual([{ id: userBooking.id }])` will fail for reasons unrelated to the SQL conditions under test. This makes the test unreliable as a real validation of the constructed SQL. Either insert directly into `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized`, trigger whatever sync the production code relies on, or assert against a table that reflects the data immediately. The previous `findMany`-based test had the same dependency, but converting it to `$queryRaw` made the dependency more explicit and did nothing to address it.

title: Public `findMany` method removed without updating callers in this PR
body: The service previously exposed `async findMany(findManyArgs: Prisma.BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedFindManyArgs)` and is now replaced with `getBaseConditions()` returning `Prisma.Sql`. This is a breaking change to the class's public surface. The diff does not show updates to other callers in the repo (e.g. any API route, tRPC procedure, or service consumer that imported `InsightsBookingService` and called `.findMany(...)`); those imports will fail to compile after this lands. A maintainer should grep the codebase for `InsightsBookingService` consumers and migrate them, or keep a delegating `findMany` wrapper to preserve backward compatibility.

title: Caching behavior is now untested
body: The class still caches `cachedAuthConditions` (line 49) and `cachedFilterConditions` (line 50), and the getAuthorizationConditions/getFilterConditions methods still gate their build behind `=== undefined` (lines 84-87 and 91-94). However, the entire `describe("Caching", ...)` block that previously verified (a) the first call builds conditions and (b) the second call returns the cached value with reference equality was removed by this PR. There is no remaining coverage proving the cache works, that two concurrent calls don't both populate it (a small race exists because the read-then-await-then-assign sequence is not atomic), or that the cached Prisma.Sql values are still usable as raw query fragments after the assignment. At minimum the deleted cache tests should be ported to the new `Prisma.sql` comparison style.

title: Dead branch in getBaseConditions: authConditions is always truthy
body: `buildAuthorizationConditions` always returns a `Prisma.Sql` value (either a real condition or `NOTHING_CONDITION`), never null/undefined. Therefore `authConditions` in `getBaseConditions` is always truthy, and the `else if (filterConditions)` branch on line 76 is unreachable - it can only execute if `authConditions` is falsy, which never happens. This is not a functional bug (the conditions still resolve correctly) but it indicates a misread of the type contract and leaves misleading code. Either remove the dead branch and the unreachable `else { return NOTHING_CONDITION; }`, or change `getAuthorizationConditions` to return `Prisma.Sql | null` and return `NOTHING_CONDITION` explicitly only at call sites, so the truthiness checks become meaningful.

title: toEqual comparisons of Prisma.Sql will fail for SQL built via reduce
body: Three tests assert expect(conditions).toEqual(Prisma.sql`...`) against SQL returned by the service. The service builds SQL using a reduce over a Prisma.Sql[] array (insightsBooking.ts lines 119-122, 171-174, 204-207), wrapping each inner Sql with `(${acc}) OR (${condition})` or `(${acc}) AND (${condition})`. Each wrap adds new entries to the inner strings array (one per interpolation point introduced by the wrapper). The expected SQL in the tests is written as a single tagged template literal, producing a Sql whose strings array only has entries at the original placeholders. Prisma's Sql class does not override equality, so Vitest's toEqual does structural comparison of strings and values. For example, the team scope test (line 295) expects strings of length 3, while the service produces strings of length 7 after the OR-reduce wraps the two inner Sql fragments with parens. The same mismatch affects the org scope test at line 332 (3 vs 7) and the combined filter test at line 429 (4 vs 7). The simpler tests pass (NOTHING_CONDITION, user scope, single filter eventTypeId, single filter memberUserId) because they use a single template literal in the service that matches the test literal exactly. Suggested fix: compare conditions.toString() against the expected SQL string, build the expected Sql with the same nested reduce pattern, or assert against actual database query results rather than Sql structure. The PR description already flags that tests were not run due to runner configuration issues, but the structural mismatch will cause these specific tests to fail regardless.

title: findMany method removed without documentation of caller migration
body: The findMany method previously exposed on InsightsBookingService was removed and replaced with getBaseConditions (now at line 68). External callers using service.findMany(...) will no longer compile. The PR description focuses on test updates and does not document this breaking change or describe how existing consumers should migrate to the new pattern of calling getBaseConditions() and passing the resulting Prisma.Sql into prisma.$queryRaw. Before merging, reviewers must confirm there are no remaining callers of service.findMany in the codebase, or that those callers are updated in the same change. Note also that callers using the previously removed type Prisma.BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedWhereInput will need to switch to consuming Prisma.Sql directly.

title: updateManyByCredentialId called with empty data – no-op
body: The new call `await SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {});` passes an empty object as `data`. Prisma's `updateMany` only updates fields explicitly listed in `data`, so with `{}` no columns (including the Prisma-managed `updatedAt`) are touched. The preceding comment "Update SelectedCalendar.updatedAt for all calendars under this credential" is therefore wrong – the call is a silent no-op. Either pass `updatedAt: new Date()` (or similar) to actually achieve the documented effect, or remove the call entirely. Note also that the PR description indicates `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` is only updated by the webhook handler and is not displayed in the UI, so this added line is likely dead code that obscures the actual cache-refresh flow.

title: macOS-only sed in-place edit breaks on Linux
body: Line 68 uses `sed -i '' -E ...`. The `''` after `-i` is BSD/macOS syntax (sed takes a mandatory backup-suffix argument, with empty meaning no backup). On GNU sed (Linux/CI containers), `-i` does not take an argument and the script becomes `sed: invalid option -- 'E'` / treats `''` as the script. The PR's CI runs on Linux, so the script will fail on a fresh checkout. Use `sed -i.bak` followed by `rm *.bak`, or branch on the platform (e.g., `[[ "$OSTYPE" == darwin* ]] && SED_INPLACE="sed -i ''" || SED_INPLACE="sed -i"`).

title: DropdownItem nested inside DropdownMenuItem produces invalid nested-button markup
body: Both "Delete cached data" and "Remove App" actions are written as `<DropdownMenuItem><DropdownItem .../></DropdownMenuItem>`. Since `DropdownMenuItem` (Radix) is itself an interactive `<button>`/menuitem, and `DropdownItem` is a styled `<button>` from the same dropdown module, the rendered DOM becomes a button-in-button (invalid HTML, screen-reader/AT issues) and creates competing onClick handlers with confusing focus/hover states. Typically cal.com uses either DropdownMenuItem with text, OR DropdownItem (without the wrapping DropdownMenuItem) for styled actions. Remove the wrapping `DropdownMenuItem` around `DropdownItem` (or replace DropdownItem with plain text/icon inside the item) so that exactly one button is rendered per row.

title: deleteCache mutation does not invalidate connectedCalendars – stale cache status remains in UI
body: `deleteCacheMutation` only fires a toast and the optional `onSuccess?.()` callback. Unlike `disconnectMutation` further down (which invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` and `viewer.apps.integrations` in `onSettled`), `deleteCacheMutation` does not call `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate()`. The platform-atom wrapper passes `onChanged` as the `onSuccess`, which is a consumer-defined callback that is not guaranteed to refetch the tRPC query. After a successful cache deletion the user will continue to see the previous "Last updated: <timestamp>" under "Cache Status" until a full page reload, even though the underlying rows are gone. Add an `onSettled` (or `onSuccess`) that invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` to match the disconnect flow.

title: getCacheStatusByCredentialIds ignores expiresAt – reports status for expired cache rows
body: `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` runs `groupBy` over `CalendarCache` with no `expiresAt` filter, so a credential whose only cache rows are past `expiresAt` still returns a row and the UI then renders a "Last updated: <old timestamp>" plus a "Delete cached data" entry. In contrast, `getCachedAvailability` correctly filters `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }`, so the user is told the cache exists/is recent even though no actual cache hit will ever occur. Add an `expiresAt: { gte: new Date(Date.now()) }` clause (or filter post-groupBy) so the displayed "Last updated" matches what `getCachedAvailability` would consider usable.

title: Authorization failure throws generic Error – not a TRPCError
body: When the credential isn't owned by the caller, the handler throws a plain `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. This surfaces as an opaque `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR` over tRPC, gives the client the same status as a true server bug, and merges the two failure modes (not-found vs forbidden) into one message. Use `throw new TRPCError({ code: "FORBIDDEN", message: "Credential not found or access denied" })` (or `NOT_FOUND` after a `findUnique`). That also makes the existing "Error deleting cache" toast in `CredentialActionsDropdown` distinguishable from genuine infrastructure failures if more granular handling is added later.

title: Stale generated warning comment contradicts the migration body
body: Prisma's autogenerated warning still claims: "Added the required column `updatedAt` to the `CalendarCache` table without a default value. This is not possible if the table is not empty." The actual SQL adds `DEFAULT NOW()`, so the table *is* populated safely for existing rows. Leaving the contradictory header in place is confusing for future migrations/maintenance and for anyone reading the migration file. Either drop the Prisma warning block (since the developer manually fixed it) or replace it with a short comment explaining why a `DEFAULT NOW()` was used instead of `@updatedAt` for legacy rows.

title: New deleteCache tRPC mutation and handler have no tests
body: This PR adds a brand-new destructive tRPC route (`viewer.calendars.deleteCache`) along with its handler, plus two new repository methods (`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`, `updateManyByCredentialId`) and a new UI component (`CredentialActionsDropdown`). None of these have accompanying unit/integration tests. The handler in particular performs authorization (verifying the credential belongs to the calling user) and a destructive DB op (`calendarCache.deleteMany`), and is exactly the kind of cross-cutting call most worth covering. Please add tests for: (a) another user cannot delete your cache (authorization), (b) missing/invalid credentialId is rejected by zod, (c) `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` excludes expired entries (after the fix above) and groups multiple cache rows per credential correctly, and (d) `CredentialActionsDropdown` calls `connectedCalendars.invalidate` after a successful delete (after the fix above).

title: deleteCache mutation does not invalidate connectedCalendars query
body: After a successful deleteCache mutation, the component never invalidates the trpc query that populated `cacheUpdatedAt`. Compare with the disconnectMutation further down which calls `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate()` in `onSettled`. Without an invalidation, after the user confirms cache deletion the UI continues to show the same 'Last updated' timestamp (the deleted row's data is still in the React Query cache) until some other action triggers a refetch. The proper fix is to also invalidate `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` from deleteCache's `onSettled` (or `onSuccess`) so the timestamp updates immediately.

title: updateManyByCredentialId called with empty data is a no-op
body: `await SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {});` passes an empty `data` object. Prisma's `@updatedAt` directive only fires when actual fields change, so calling `updateMany` with `{}` does nothing — no row is touched and `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` is NOT bumped, contrary to the comment immediately above it. The call either needs an explicit field set (e.g. `{ updatedAt: new Date() }`) or should be removed if there is no `@updatedAt` column on `SelectedCalendar`. As written it silently does nothing on every cache refresh.

title: getCacheStatusByCredentialIds ignores expiresAt
body: `getCachedAvailability` (line ~95) filters cache rows by `expiresAt: { gte: new Date(Date.now()) }` so only fresh entries are treated as cache hits. The new `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` does not — it just groups all rows. The UI surfaces the result as 'Cache Status / Last updated', which now reports a timestamp even for cache entries that have already expired and would never be served. This is inconsistent with the read path and will mislead users into thinking they have a fresh cache when there is none. Add an `expiresAt: { gte: new Date(Date.now()) }` filter (or document explicitly that the status is intentionally historical).

title: Existing rows get DEFAULT NOW() which misrepresents staleness
body: The migration sets `updatedAt TIMESTAMP(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()`. For every existing CalendarCache row that has not been rewritten by Prisma since the migration, the column is set to the moment the migration ran, not to the actual last cache write time. Combined with `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`, this surfaces a misleading 'Last updated: <few minutes ago>' for legacy cache that could be weeks old. Consider backfilling `updatedAt` from a closer proxy (`expiresAt - INTERVAL '30 days'` or the existing last write timestamp if available) so the UI's 'Last updated' is meaningful for legacy data.

title: sed syntax is macOS/BSD-only
body: `sed -i '' -E "s|^GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=.*|GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=$TUNNEL_URL|" "$ENV_FILE"` uses BSD sed's `sed -i ''` (empty-string backup suffix) convention, which is a no-op (or 'unknown command') on GNU sed. On Linux the script will silently fail to update `.env`, then `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` will still point at the old tunnel/port and Google webhooks will misroute. Either use `sed -i.bak ...; rm -f "$ENV_FILE.bak"` or write the file with a portable tool (printf/awk) or branch on `uname -s`.

title: Non-interactive cache status is wrapped in DropdownMenuItem
body: Lines 84-97 wrap a purely informational 'Cache Status / Last updated …' block in a `<DropdownMenuItem>`. `DropdownMenuItem` is the clickable element of a radix dropdown menu — clicking it (which users naturally do to try to focus/read it) triggers the dropdown's selection handler and closes the menu, hiding the very information they were looking at. Wrap the static text in a plain `<div>` (or a `<DropdownMenuLabel>`) so the dropdown stays open. The second `<DropdownMenuItem>` further down is the real action and is fine.

title: updateManyByCredentialId called with empty data
body: The new call `await SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` at line 1024 passes an empty `data` object. Prisma's `updateMany` requires at least one field in `data`; an empty `data` either throws (`Argument data must not be empty`) or silently no-ops, and either way it does not bump `updatedAt`. That defeats the stated intent (`// Update SelectedCalendar.updatedAt for all calendars under this credential`), so the cache-lifecycle indicator on SelectedCalendar will silently stop being updated. Pass a non-empty value such as `{ updatedAt: new Date() }`.

title: deleteCacheMutation does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query
body: The `deleteCacheMutation` defined at lines 42-50 only fires `onSuccess` (toast + `onSuccess?.()` callback) but never invalidates the `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` query. After a successful deletion the dropdown still shows the old "Cache Status: Last updated: ..." line because `cacheUpdatedAt` is not refetched. The neighbouring `disconnectMutation` (lines 53-65) correctly invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` in `onSettled`; `deleteCacheMutation` should mirror that pattern so the UI updates immediately after deletion.

title: getCacheStatusByCredentialIds ignores expiresAt
body: `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` (lines 173-188) groups all `CalendarCache` rows by `credentialId` and aggregates `_max.updatedAt` without filtering by `expiresAt >= now()`. The cache reader elsewhere (`getCachedAvailability`) only returns non-expired entries, so a credential whose only caches are expired (CACHING_TIME is 30 days) will still display a misleadingly recent "Last updated" timestamp even though the cache will never actually be served. Add a `where: { ..., expiresAt: { gte: new Date(Date.now()) } }` predicate so the status reflects cache that is actively being served.

title: Hardcoded 'en-US' locale for cache timestamp formatting
body: Line 89 instantiates `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" })`, which forces en-US date formatting regardless of the user's actual locale. The component already has `useLocale()` in scope (line 37) and uses `t()` for surrounding strings, but the formatted timestamp bypasses the user's locale. Non-US users will see US-formatted dates/times for "Cache last updated". Format with the user's locale instead of hard-coding "en-US".

title: In-place sed uses BSD-only syntax, fails on Linux
body: Line 68 runs `sed -i '' -E "..." "$ENV_FILE"`. The empty `''` argument is BSD/macOS sed syntax meaning "no backup suffix"; GNU sed (Linux) interprets `''` as the sed script and `-E` as a positional argument, so the command fails on Linux developer machines. Detect the platform or switch to a portable form (e.g. `perl -pi -E ...` or conditional `sed -i -E ...` on GNU vs `sed -i '' -E ...` on BSD) so the script works on both.

title: No tests for new deleteCache handler, repository methods, or component
body: The PR introduces the `deleteCache` tRPC mutation and `deleteCacheHandler` (this file), `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` on `CalendarCacheRepository`, `updateManyByCredentialId` on `SelectedCalendarRepository`, and the `CredentialActionsDropdown` UI component, plus an empty-data `updateMany` call in `CalendarService.fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache`. None of these additions ship with unit tests or component tests, so the empty-data `updateMany` bug and the missing-query-invalidation behavior are not regression-protected. Add at least a handler test (verifying the user/credential ownership check and the cache deletion), tests for the two new repository methods, and a component test covering the dropdown's invalidation flow.

title: deleteScheduledEmailReminder with immediateDelete=true silently swallows SendGrid errors without a DB fallback
body: When `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` is called with `immediateDelete=true` (used by `handleNewBooking.ts:969` for rescheduling and `workflows.tsx:214, 521` for workflow/step deletion), it sends a cancel request to SendGrid and returns. If that request fails (e.g., because the 100 pending-cancellation quota mentioned in the PR description is reached), the catch block at line 233 only logs the error and the function returns without writing anything to the database. The new CRON in `scheduleEmailReminders.ts:44-51` only selects reminders where `cancelled: true`, so the failed cancellation is never retried and SendGrid will still send the email. The function should set `cancelled: true` (or otherwise record that the DB row needs CRON handling) regardless of SendGrid success so the CRON can retry the cancellation.

title: Fire-and-forget pattern in workflow reminder cancellations across the codebase
body: The workflow-reminder cancellation code uses `forEach` whose async callbacks are not awaited, so the cancellation calls run in the background while the caller continues and returns its HTTP response. Affected locations: `handleCancelBooking.ts:485-493`, `handleNewBooking.ts:967-973`, `bookings.tsx:488-494`, and `workflows.tsx:212-218, 376-382, 519-525, 574-580`. In serverless deployments the function instance can be frozen right after the response is returned, which may abort in-flight SendGrid/Twilio cancellation requests. Errors from these calls are also silently swallowed; for example, the `try/catch` in `handleNewBooking.ts:965-976` cannot catch anything from an unawaited `forEach` and the error log inside `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` is the only signal. These loops should use `Promise.all(items.map(...))` so cancellations and errors are observed before the response is sent. In `workflows.tsx:212-218` the forEach is followed immediately by `workflow.deleteMany`, so the cascade can delete the reminder rows before the SendGrid/Twilio requests even fire, making the cancellations effectively lost.

title: CRON query for cancelled reminders is missing the method filter
body: The `remindersToCancel` query at lines 44-51 selects `WorkflowReminder` rows with `cancelled: true` and `scheduledDate <= now+1h`. It does not include `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL`. Today only `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` sets `cancelled: true`, so in practice the rows are email rows, but the missing filter is fragile: if a future change (or a bad data fix) ever sets the flag on an SMS row, the CRON will call `client.request` against `/v3/user/scheduled_sends` with a Twilio SID as the `batch_id`, sending SendGrid a request it cannot honor and producing a misleading error in the catch block at line 75. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` to the `where` clause.

title: Sequential SendGrid cancellation requests in the CRON
body: The `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop at lines 56-74 awaits each SendGrid `client.request` call one after another, then collects the corresponding prisma deletes. When many cancelled reminders have accumulated (e.g., after a bulk cancellation or a long CRON outage), this serial processing stretches the CRON run time and may exceed its execution budget. The SendGrid requests should be parallelised with `Promise.all(remindersToCancel.map(...))`; the prisma deletes can still be awaited together afterward.

title: No tests added for the new workflow-reminder cancellation logic
body: The PR makes several non-trivial changes to a flow that previously had a production bug (#7225): a new nullable `cancelled` field on `WorkflowReminder`, a deferred SendGrid cancellation performed by the `scheduleEmailReminders` CRON inside a 1-hour window, a new `immediateDelete` branch in `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`, and new cancellation paths added to `handleNewBooking.ts`, `handleCancelBooking.ts`, `bookings.tsx`, and `workflows.tsx`. No unit or integration tests were added to verify any of: (1) cancelling a booking actually prevents a previously scheduled workflow email from being delivered, (2) rescheduling cancels old reminders and schedules new ones without duplicates, (3) the CRON handles reminders inside and outside the 1-hour window correctly, (4) the SendGrid quota failure path falls back to the CRON, (5) workflow/step deletion truly stops email delivery for the removed workflow. For a fix to a reported production bug this leaves the regression risk unaddressed.

title: Dead try/catch around workflow reminder cancellation on reschedule
