body: The try/catch wrapping the `workflowReminders.forEach` on reschedule (lines 965–976) cannot catch any error: the inner callback only invokes `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` without awaiting them, and both callees have their own internal try/catch that swallows every error (emailReminderManager.ts line 233, smsReminderManager.ts line 187). Consequently, `log.error("Error while canceling scheduled workflow reminders", error)` is unreachable and any failure to cancel the prior booking's scheduled email/SMS is silently lost. When a SendGrid cancel fails (e.g., within the 60‑minute window, rate limit, or 100‑pending‑cancel cap), the user keeps receiving the old reminder for the rescheduled booking while the new booking proceeds.

title: Fire-and-forget reminder cancellation silently drops SendGrid/Twilio failures
body: `updatedBookings.forEach(...).forEach((reminder) => { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(...); deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...); })` (lines 485–493) calls the async helpers without awaiting them and without collecting them into `Promise.all`. Errors thrown by `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` are caught inside those helpers and only `console.log`'d, so the booking handler returns success to the user even when the cancellation against SendGrid or Twilio actually failed. This is the same failure mode the PR is trying to eliminate; consider awaiting the promises (or at minimum `Promise.allSettled`) and surfacing failures so the booking is not considered cancelled when reminders were not.

title: Fire-and-forget reminder cancellation in requestReschedule
body: `bookingToReschedule.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(...); deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...); })` (lines 489–495) does not await the async helpers, which themselves swallow errors via console.log. When the organizer requests a reschedule, the user will see the mutation succeed even if the SendGrid/Twilio cancellation actually failed, and the original booking's reminder will still fire.

title: deleteScheduledEmailReminder silently swallows all errors
body: The function wraps every code path (DB delete, SendGrid cancel, and `cancelled=true` update) in a single try/catch that only `console.log`s the error. Callers in handleCancelBooking, handleNewBooking and the requestReschedule mutation have no way to know whether cancellation succeeded, and there is no retry, monitoring hook, or persisted failure state. When SendGrid returns an error (e.g., 100 pending cancellations reached, or batch already dispatched) the only record is a console line and the email still goes out.

title: DB record leaks when Twilio cancel throws
body: `if (referenceId) { await twilio.cancelSMS(referenceId); }` followed by `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` inside a single try means that if `twilio.cancelSMS` rejects, the catch block runs and the DB row is never deleted. There is no retry path, so a stale `WorkflowReminder` with a now-orphaned Twilio SID will remain in the database. Combined with the cascade delete on the booking, this is bounded, but the row will live forever in the (rarer) case of an SMS scheduling retry or a bug elsewhere that cancels a non-existent SID.

title: CRON early-exits on first SendGrid error, stranding remaining cancellations
body: The `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop (lines 56–73) calls `await client.request(...)` and pushes the DB delete into `workflowRemindersToDelete`. The whole block is inside a single `try { ... } catch (error) { console.log(...) }`. When any SendGrid call rejects (very likely once you approach the 100‑pending‑cancel cap, which is the very issue this PR exists to mitigate), the for-of terminates, none of the remaining reminders in `remindersToCancel` are processed in this run, and the partial `workflowRemindersToDelete` is never `Promise.all`'d. The next run will only re-pick those whose `scheduledDate` is still within the next hour; everything else is silently lost and the email goes out. Consider processing each reminder in its own try/catch (or `Promise.allSettled`) so a single failure does not abort the rest.

title: Cancelled-reminder loop is fully sequential with no batching
body: `remindersToCancel` is processed one SendGrid call at a time inside a `for ... of` with no `Promise.all`/`allSettled` and no explicit batch size. If a spike of cancellations lands within the one-hour window (the case the PR is built for), the CRON's 15-minute budget can easily be exceeded; at scale it will also amplify the chance of hitting SendGrid's 100‑pending‑cancellation limit per request. Batching the SendGrid calls (or at least running them in parallel with a concurrency limit) would reduce wall time and make the CRON more predictable.

title: Unrelated UI change bundled into the bug-fix PR
body: The condition for rendering the phone-number block was changed from `(isPhoneNumberNeeded || isSenderIdNeeded)` to `isPhoneNumberNeeded`. That is a behaviour change for the SMS_ATTENDEE workflow step UI (it stops rendering the phone/verify-code panel for SMS_ATTENDEE) and is unrelated to the workflow-reminder cancellation fix. It should either be split into its own PR with a clear description or reverted, otherwise the changelog/comment history for the cancellation fix becomes misleading.

title: Email reminders are unconditionally flagged cancelled, even ones that were never scheduled
body: Previously the loop guarded with `if (reminder.scheduled && reminder.referenceId)` and otherwise just deleted the DB row. The new code calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` for every reminder. When `referenceId` is null (i.e., a not-yet-scheduled future reminder sitting in the CRON queue), `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` deletes it from the DB, which is correct, but this is now happening via a different code path with no test coverage and is invisible to anyone reading the diff. Worth a code comment, or a regression test that exercises `cancelled=true` set with `referenceId=null` (which currently falls into the `!referenceId` branch and silently deletes instead of marking cancelled).

title: Initial deleteMany strips cancelled reminders without notifying SendGrid
body: The first action of the CRON is `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany({ where: { method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL, scheduledDate: { lte: dayjs().toISOString() } } })`. It does not filter on `cancelled`. Any reminder whose `scheduledDate` has passed (including a cancelled one that the cancel branch did not get to process in time) is removed from the DB, but if the SendGrid `scheduled_sends` cancel never actually landed, the email is still in SendGrid's queue and will be delivered. Today the cancel branch runs before the deleteMany in the previous code path — verify this ordering and that the deleteMany is intentionally after the cancel pass; otherwise very-late cancellations may still leak.

title: immediateDelete path leaves reminder row without cancelled flag
body: When called with `immediateDelete=true` (handleNewBooking.ts reschedule path), the function only POSTs the cancellation to SendGrid and `return`s — it never sets `cancelled: true` and never deletes the DB row. The row is later cleaned up by the CRON's `deleteMany` once `scheduledDate` passes. That is fine for cleanup, but a developer reading the code (or grepping for `cancelled: true`) will not realize that immediate cancels do not flow through the same state as deferred cancels. Add a code comment, or also write `cancelled: true` for parity so the audit trail is consistent.

title: No automated test added for the new cancellation pipeline
body: The PR introduces a non-trivial state change (new `cancelled` column, new deferred-cancel path in the CRON, new function signatures) and rewrites cancellation in four call sites, but ships no unit or integration test for it. Specifically there is no test for: (1) the CRON processing reminders whose `scheduledDate` is within the next hour, (2) cancellation requests close to the 100 SendGrid cap, (3) handleCancelBooking/handleNewBooking/bookings.tsx correctly setting `cancelled=true` instead of deleting, or (4) the dead try/catch in handleNewBooking.ts. Given the bug the PR is fixing and that prior fixes have regressed, this is a meaningful gap.

title: Past cancelled reminders are deleted without being cancelled in SendGrid
body: The deleteMany at lines 34-41 runs BEFORE the new cancellation block at lines 44-77. It deletes ALL email reminders with scheduledDate <= now, including ones marked cancelled:true that have not yet been cancelled in SendGrid. The subsequent findMany at lines 44-51 cannot find them because they were already deleted, so the SendGrid cancellation is never sent. If a booking is cancelled while its reminder's scheduled time has already passed (e.g., when the CRON has been unavailable for an extended period), the email is still sent by SendGrid. The cancellation lookup is also written to include past reminders (lte: now+1h), so the design clearly intended them to be cancelled here. Fix: add `cancelled: { not: true }` to the deleteMany where clause, or reorder the steps so cancellation runs first.

title: Workflow deletion races with SendGrid cancellation
body: At lines 212-218, scheduledReminders.forEach calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true) without awaiting. These calls perform async SendGrid POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends cancellations. The next statement, `await ctx.prisma.workflow.deleteMany` at line 220, runs immediately and cascades through WorkflowStep.onDelete: Cascade to delete the workflowReminder rows. The SendGrid cancellation request may not have been sent, let alone processed by SendGrid, before SendGrid's scheduled send time, so the cancelled email is still delivered. Fix: await the cancellation calls (e.g., `await Promise.all(scheduledReminders.map(async (r) => { ... }))`) before issuing the workflow delete.

title: Workflow step deletion races with SendGrid cancellation
body: Same race as the workflow-deletion finding. At lines 519-525, remindersFromStep.forEach fires SendGrid cancellations via deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true) without awaiting, then `await ctx.prisma.workflowStep.delete` at line 527 cascades to delete the workflowReminder rows before the SendGrid cancellation requests may complete. Cancelled-step reminders can still be sent.

title: No tests for the new CRON cancellation flow
body: The PR introduces a new WorkflowReminder.cancelled field, a new branch in scheduleEmailReminders.ts that finds and cancels cancelled reminders in SendGrid, and significant new logic in deleteScheduledEmailReminder (new signature with reminderId and immediateDelete option, plus the soft-cancel path that only sets cancelled:true). None of these have automated test coverage. The original bug (#7225) was specifically about cancelled reminders still being sent; without tests, regressions in this code path would re-introduce the same user-visible problem and would not be caught.

title: forEach(async ...) fires calendar/video deletions without awaiting
body: The block `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })` does not wait for the async callback. `Array.prototype.forEach` ignores returned promises, so every `getCalendar(...)` and `calendar.deleteEvent(...)` / `deleteMeeting(...)` call is fire-and-forget. The surrounding `try/catch` cannot catch rejections from awaited code either, so any failure becomes an unhandled promise rejection. Consequence: the surrounding `Reschedule` function continues to `await director.buildForRescheduleEmail()`, then `await sendRequestRescheduleEmail(...)`, then returns `true` before the calendar/video deletions actually happen (or they may never finish if the request is short-lived). Bookings are reported as rescheduled while the previous calendar events and video rooms remain on the user's calendar. Fix: replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))`.

title: forEach(async ...) fires calendar/video deletions without awaiting
body: Identical pattern to packages/app-store/vital/lib/reschedule.ts: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })` does not await the async callbacks, so the calendar and video deletions start but are never waited on. The `try/catch` around the forEach only catches synchronous throws; awaited errors become unhandled rejections. The function then proceeds to `await sendRequestRescheduleEmail(...)` and returns `true`, so the caller is told the reschedule succeeded before (or even without) the previous calendar event being deleted. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))`.

title: requestReschedule returns before calendar/video deletions complete
body: Inside the `requestReschedule` mutation: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })` runs all calendar/video deletions in parallel but does not await them. The mutation then proceeds to `await sendRequestRescheduleEmail(...)` and returns. Because `forEach` ignores returned promises and the awaited `getCalendar(...)`/`deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` calls happen asynchronously, the previous calendar events may not be removed before the reschedule email is sent and the mutation returns. Errors thrown inside the async callback become unhandled promise rejections because the surrounding `try/catch` (if any) is synchronous. Fix with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))`.

title: Recurring event calendar deletions are not awaited
body: Inside the recurring-events branch the code does `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })`. `forEach` does not await async functions, so the iteration kicks off the work and returns. By the time the function reaches `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))`, the array is usually empty (or only partially populated), so the `Promise.all` resolves immediately and the response is sent. The actual calendar deletions run later (or not at all if the request lifecycle ends). For a paid/seated booking this means previously scheduled events can stay on the organizer's calendar after cancellation. Replace with `for (const credential of ...) { ... await ... apiDeletes.push(...); }` (as was done correctly in the non-recurring branch immediately below) or `await Promise.all(...)`.

title: getCalendarCredentials is sync but now returns Promises in its objects
body: `getCalendarCredentials` keeps its synchronous signature but inside it now assigns `const calendar = getCalendar(credential);` (which became async). Every returned `{ integration, credential, calendar }` object therefore has `calendar: Promise<Calendar | null>` instead of `Calendar | null`. Only `getConnectedCalendars` was updated to `await item.calendar`; any other internal or external caller of `getCalendarCredentials` that still treats `item.calendar` as a synchronous value (or whose TS type comes from `ReturnType<typeof getCalendarCredentials>`) will silently break. Either make the function `async` (and `await getCalendar(...)` inside, then re-shape the return type) or change the field name (e.g. `calendarPromise`) so callers cannot accidentally use it unsynchronized.

title: No handling when dynamic import resolves to undefined
body: After the change, `appStore[calendarType.split("_").join("") as keyof typeof appStore]` returns `Promise<... | undefined>` for unknown keys. `await` on the resulting `undefined` yields `undefined`, so `calendarApp` becomes `undefined` and falls through to the `log.warn(...)` branch. That is fine, but the type assertion `as keyof typeof appStore` lies to TypeScript: the union of awaited values is not narrowed, so the `"lib" in calendarApp` guard works at runtime but the inferred type of `calendarApp` is `Promise<typeof import("applecalendar")> | Promise<typeof import("caldavcalendar")> | ... | undefined`, and `await` does not narrow the union the way the author likely intends. There is no runtime regression here, but the type cast masks a real value coming back as `undefined` for unknown calendar types and a missing `default` / explicit 404 path. Consider an explicit `if (!app) { log.warn(...); return null; }` before the `"lib" in app` check and remove the misleading `as keyof typeof appStore` cast.

title: getCalendarCredentials now returns Promise in the calendar field, breaking its synchronous contract
body: getCalendarCredentials is an exported synchronous function. Before this PR it returned objects whose `calendar` field was a fully constructed Calendar instance. After this PR, the function still declares a synchronous signature but internally calls `getCalendar(credential)` which is now async, so the `calendar` field stored in each returned item is a `Promise<Calendar | null>`. Any external consumer that calls `getCalendarCredentials` and uses `item.calendar` directly (calling methods on it, checking truthiness, etc.) will receive a Promise object and break — for example `item.calendar.listCalendars()` would return a Promise of a Promise, or the truthiness check would always be true (a Promise is truthy). Only the in-file consumer `getConnectedCalendars` was updated (`const calendar = await item.calendar;`); any other call sites across the codebase are silently broken. Either the function must be made async (with all callers updated) or the calendar construction must happen inside the function before returning.

title: forEach(async) pushes to apiDeletes asynchronously, racing with the later Promise.all
body: In the recurring-event cancellation branch, `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })` is used. `Array.prototype.forEach` does not await async callbacks, so the synchronous execution falls through immediately after the loop is set up. The pushes of `deletedEvent` (which itself is the result of `await calendar?.deleteEvent(...)`) into `apiDeletes` happen asynchronously. Later, the code does `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes));` (line 652). Because the forEach is not awaited, some async callbacks may not have pushed their promises yet when `Promise.all` is called, so those calendar events will never be deleted. This was a pre-existing bug in the original sync version (the callback was already async), but the PR makes it strictly worse by inserting an additional `await getCalendar(credential)` before the push, widening the race window. The fix is to replace forEach with `for (const credential of ...)` and await it, matching the pattern used a few lines below at line 480.

title: await apiDeletes is a no-op and paid-booking cancellations return before integrations finish
body: At line 617 in the `if (bookingToDelete && bookingToDelete.paid)` branch, the code does `await apiDeletes;`. `apiDeletes` is an array of Promises, not a Promise itself, so `await` on a non-thenable just resolves to the array value immediately — this line does not wait for any calendar/video deletion to complete. The function then sets `req.statusCode = 200` and returns `"Booking successfully cancelled."` without having actually deleted the calendar/video events. The non-paid branch correctly uses `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes));` at line 652. This should be `await Promise.all(apiDeletes);`. This is a pre-existing bug but directly related to the async-flow changes in this PR.

title: getVideoAdapters loads apps sequentially instead of in parallel
body: After this PR, `getVideoAdapters` uses a `for (const cred of withCredentials)` loop that awaits each `appStore[appName]` dynamic import one after another. When called with multiple credentials (e.g. from `getBusyVideoTimes`), the dynamic imports run sequentially rather than concurrently. Since dynamic imports are independent I/O operations (Webpack fetches chunks in parallel), this serializes what could be parallel work. The previous synchronous reduce was effectively zero-cost per iteration, but the new version pays the full latency of each import sequentially. Using `Promise.all(withCredentials.map(...))` would allow the chunks to load concurrently, reducing total latency.

title: Async forEach swallows errors and leaves deletions fire-and-forget in vital reschedule
body: The code uses `try { bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...); await calendar?.deleteEvent(...) ... }); } catch (error) { ... }`. Two problems: (1) `Array.prototype.forEach` does not await async callbacks, so the outer `try/catch` only catches errors thrown synchronously during the forEach setup — any rejection from the awaited `getCalendar` or `deleteEvent` becomes an unhandled promise rejection. (2) Because the callbacks are not awaited, the `Reschedule` function returns `true` immediately after launching the forEach, so callers cannot rely on calendar/video cleanup having completed. The PR converts `getCalendar` to async, widening the window during which these promises are unresolved. The same pattern exists in `packages/app-store/wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts` (line 125) and `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx` (line 553), and the same caveat applies in `packages/features/bookings/lib/handleCancelBooking.ts` (line 460, already noted separately).

title: getCalendarCredentials returns Promise values from a synchronous function
body: After the async refactor, `getCalendar(credential)` now returns `Promise<Calendar | null>`, but `getCalendarCredentials` is still declared as a synchronous function and pushes that Promise into the returned objects as `calendar`. This silently changes the public contract of the exported function: callers that previously received a `Calendar | null` now receive an unawaited Promise, and any new caller (and any existing caller that does not already do `await item.calendar`) will silently treat the Promise as truthy and call methods on it, causing runtime TypeErrors. `getCalendarCredentials` should be made `async` (or the calendar should be awaited inside the flatMap) so the returned `calendar` field is always `Calendar | null`.

title: forEach(async ...) swallows errors from getCalendar in recurring cancellation path
body: Lines 457-470 use `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... })`. `Array.prototype.forEach` does not await async callbacks, and there is no try/catch around the dynamic import. If `await getCalendar(credential)` rejects (for example because one of the calendar app modules fails to load), the rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection rather than being routed to the existing `logger.error`/cancellation logic, and the corresponding calendar entries are never deleted. The booking is marked cancelled in the DB while the actual calendar event remains. The surrounding `try/catch` at lines 135-139 (in the reschedule files) gives the false impression that errors are caught — they are not, because async callback errors from forEach escape. The same pattern exists in other files modified by this PR.

title: forEach(async ...) in vital reschedule swallows getCalendar failures
body: Line 125 wraps the reference-cancellation loop in `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })` inside a `try { ... } catch` block. forEach does not await async callbacks, so a rejection from the dynamic import (`getCalendar` → `appStore[calendarType]` → `import("./...")`) propagates as an unhandled promise rejection rather than being caught by the surrounding try/catch (which only sees sync throws and the resolved values of the inner promises). The reschedule returns success even when calendar delete calls never executed, leaving stale calendar events on the user's calendars.

title: forEach(async ...) in wipemycalother reschedule swallows getCalendar failures
body: Same pattern as in `packages/app-store/vital/lib/reschedule.ts`: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })` inside a try/catch. forEach does not await async callbacks, so any rejection from `await getCalendar` (caused by a broken app module or a missing dependency) is not routed to the existing `logger.error` branch and becomes an unhandled rejection. Calendar/video deletions can silently fail.

title: forEach(async ...) in requestReschedule swallows getCalendar failures
body: Lines 553-567 fire calendar/video deletions with `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...); })` and there is no try/catch at all in this scope. Because forEach does not await the async callback, a rejection from `await getCalendar` (from the now-dynamic `appStore[...]` import) becomes an unhandled rejection. The mutation returns success while the prior calendar events on the attendee/organizer calendars may never have been deleted, leading to stale events being shown on those calendars after a reschedule.

title: getCalendar does not handle dynamic-import failures
body: Line 15 awaits the dynamic import directly: `const calendarApp = await appStore[calendarType.split("_").join("") as keyof typeof appStore];`. After the PR, `appStore` values are dynamic-import Promises that can reject if the underlying module fails to evaluate (bad syntax, missing dependency, server-side import error, etc.). There is no try/catch around the await, so any such failure propagates and aborts the whole calendar operation (booking creation, cancellation, reschedule, busy-time fetch). The existing post-await guard only handles the `undefined` / missing-`lib` case. The function should catch import errors, log them, and return `null` so that one broken app module doesn't take down operations for users who don't even use that app.

title: getCachedResults awaits all getCalendar calls sequentially inside the map
body: In `getCachedResults`, the calendars are now loaded with `await Promise.all(calendarCredentials.map((credential) => getCalendar(credential)))`, which is correctly parallelized. However the subsequent `results = calendars.map(async (c, i) => { ... })` then immediately awaits via `Promise.all`, which is fine. The new `getCalendarCredentials` function on the other hand still loads calendars sequentially (one `flatMap` callback at a time), and the `getVideoAdapters` factory in `packages/core/videoClient.ts` was also rewritten as a serial `for` loop rather than a `Promise.all` over credentials. For tenants with several credentials the first booking/cancellation pays N×(module-fetch latency) serially; parallelizing the per-credential fetches would substantially reduce tail latency of the first request after a cold start.

title: No tests added for the async app-store refactor
body: This PR converts a large surface area of calendar/video/payment loaders from synchronous to dynamic-import-based, including `getCalendar`, `getVideoAdapters`, `getCalendarCredentials`, the reschedule handlers in `vital` and `wipemycalother`, the cancellation handlers in `handleCancelBooking`, the `requestReschedule` tRPC mutation, the `confirm` mutation's refund path, and both `handlePayment` and `deletePayment`. Despite touching every booking lifecycle path, no test files are added or modified in the diff. There is no coverage that the now-dynamic imports resolve and behave identically, that error paths (missing app, broken module) return null instead of throwing, or that the new `await` placements actually preserve execution ordering. Given the scale of the refactor, this is a significant test gap.

title: dayjs objects compared with === (always false)
body: The new code compares dayjs wrapper objects with `===`: `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")`. Two distinct dayjs instances are never reference-equal even when they represent the same instant, so this branch never executes. This breaks the intended "override start === end means blocked all day" semantics and any other code that relies on this comparison. Use `.isSame()` or compare `.valueOf()` instead.

title: Copy-paste bug: `end` is identical to `start`
body: Inside the working-hours branch: `const start = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute(); const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();`. Both expressions compute the slot's start minute-of-day, so the check degenerates to `start < workingHour.startTime || start > workingHour.endTime`. The slot's end time is never considered, so any booking that crosses the end of the working window (e.g. a 60-min event ending at 18:01) is silently treated as still inside the window. Almost certainly the intent was `end = slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute()`.

title: Working-hours comparison mixes UTC with organizer's timezone
body: `slotStartTime = time.utc()`, so `slotStartTime.hour()`/`.minute()`/`.day()` return UTC values, but `workingHour.startTime`/`endTime`/`days` are documented as "minutes since midnight; serialized to UTC by using the organizer timeZone" (i.e. expressed in the organizer's local timezone). The new check at line 143 (`start < workingHour.startTime || end > workingHour.endTime`) compares UTC minutes-of-day to organizer-TZ minutes-of-day, so for any non-UTC organizer the comparison is offset by the organizer's UTC offset. Concretely, an IST organizer with hours 9:30–18:00 IST and a slot at 14:00 IST (= 08:30 UTC) yields `start = 510` vs `workingHour.startTime = 570` and the slot is incorrectly flagged as outside working hours. This is not caught by the new test because that test's slots all happen to be covered by a date override, which short-circuits before the working-hours check.

title: Override day match depends on the host machine's local timezone
body: `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD")` builds a dayjs in the system default timezone and formats it without setting `.tz(organizerTimeZone)`, while the right-hand side `slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")` is in UTC. The numeric offset shift is correct, but the format is then interpreted in whatever the server's local tz is, so the same override can match different days depending on whether the Node process is running in UTC, IST, etc. Production servers are rarely in UTC, so this introduces a flaky/cross-environment correctness bug that the test (which only runs the suite locally) cannot catch. Use `.tz(organizerTimeZone)` explicitly, or compare the day in a fixed reference (e.g. compare UTC day strings on both sides).

title: Missing null guard for `override.timeZone` will crash if undefined
body: `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` is called unconditionally, but `override.timeZone` was just added as an *optional* field on `TimeRange` (`packages/types/schedule.d.ts`). `dayjs#tz` throws on `undefined`. The corresponding call inside `checkIfIsAvailable` (`trpc/.../slots.ts:107`) defensively uses `organizerTimeZone ? ... : 0`, but `packages/lib/slots.ts` does not. Any caller (current or future) that supplies a `DateOverride` without populating `timeZone` will crash slot generation. Either default `override.timeZone` to the schedule/user tz or guard the call.

title: `find` short-circuits across multiple overrides, can wrongly mark a covered slot unavailable
body: `dateOverrides.find(...)` returns truthy as soon as *any* override for the day is encountered that does not contain the slot. If the same day has two overrides and the slot is inside override A but outside override B, the iteration visits B, returns true, and the whole function returns `false` — even though the slot is legitimately covered by A. Either iterate all overrides first, set `dateOverrideExist` only when the slot is actually inside an override, and base the final return on whether the slot is inside *any* override (or whether *all* overrides exclude it, depending on intended semantics).

title: Local type for `dateOverrides` is narrower than the data actually passed in
body: The `dateOverrides` parameter is typed as `{ start: Date; end: Date; }[]`, but the callers spread `...schedule` where `schedule.dateOverrides` comes from `getUserAvailability` and contains extra fields (`userId`, and now `timeZone` from the type change). The narrowing is benign at runtime (extra fields are ignored), but it diverges from the `TimeRange` definition and will mislead future readers.

title: First half of the PR fix (round-robin with fixed-host date overrides) is not covered by any test
body: The PR description explicitly says it fixes two bugs: (1) date overrides of fixed hosts being ignored in round-robin events, and (2) date overrides not adjusting to invitee timezones. The only added test (`scheduleForEventOnADayWithDateOverrideDifferentTimezone`) covers (2) by re-running the existing single-user scenario with a different invitee tz. There is no scenario with `schedulingType: "ROUND_ROBIN"`, a fixed host with a date override, and a non-fixed host, asserting that the slot is suppressed on the override day. Without this, the round-robin-fixed-host behaviour change is unprotected against future regressions.

title: Date-override test only covers whole-hour boundaries in a single day window
body: The new test asserts identical UTC slot times for the IST and Dhaka scenarios, but only for one whole-hour override (`14:00–18:00` IST). It does not exercise: overrides with non-zero minute components (e.g. 14:30), overrides that span midnight in either tz, half-hour offsets applied to *the override itself* rather than the invitee, DST transitions around the override day, or multiple overlapping overrides. The bug at `slots.ts:114` (`===` on dayjs objects) and the timezone-arithmetic in `packages/lib/slots.ts` are both invisible to the current matrix.

title: Stale/incorrect comments around the new date-override block
body: The comment `// slot is not within the date override` is placed above the `return false`, but `find` returning truthy here only means *at least one* override on the day didn't cover the slot — not that no override did. Likewise the trailing comment `//if no date override for slot exists check if it is within normal work hours` describes the working-hours branch, but the working-hours branch is also reached when `dateOverrideExist` is true and the slot is *inside* the override (i.e. always-true path). The comments do not match the control flow and will confuse future readers.

title: Working hours check uses identical start/end, ignoring eventLength
body: In checkIfIsAvailable the local variables `start` and `end` are both set to `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()`. The intent is clearly to compare the slot's start and end (start + eventLength) against workingHour.startTime/endTime, but because `end` is identical to `start`, the slot's duration is never checked. A slot that begins inside the working window but extends past workingHour.endTime (e.g. a 60-min event at 16:30 with working hours 9:00-17:00, ending at 17:30) will be accepted as within working hours. This directly breaks the fixed-host round-robin fix: fixed hosts can be booked for slots that run past the end of their working hours.

title: checkIfIsAvailable compares UTC slot times against organizer's timezone values
body: slotStartTime is computed as `time.utc()`, putting it in UTC mode, while workingHour.days/startTime/endTime and the override's start/end are in the organizer's timezone. The day-of-week test `workingHour.days.includes(slotStartTime.day())` therefore compares a UTC day against the organizer's days array, and `slotStartTime.hour()/minute()` return UTC values that are compared against minutes-since-midnight in the organizer's tz. For a host in IST (+5:30), a slot at 14:00 IST (08:30 UTC) is in workingHour.days for Monday in IST but slotStartTime.day() reports the UTC day, and slotStartTime.hour() returns 8 which is less than workingHour.startTime=540 (9:00 IST) - the slot is wrongly marked outside working hours. Same mismatch affects the override range check, so the date-override fix is broken for any non-UTC host.

title: Date comparison uses system local timezone, giving inconsistent results across servers
body: Both sides of the comparison `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD") === slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")` rely on the dayjs default (system local) timezone. When the server's timezone differs from organizerTimeZone, a slot that falls on the next day in the organizer's tz can still format to the same date string as the override on a UTC server, causing an incorrect match. The check should explicitly format in the organizer's timezone (e.g. `.tz(organizerTimeZone).format(...)` on both sides).

title: checkIfIsAvailable ignores dateOverride.timeZone added by the new TimeRange type
body: The PR adds `timeZone?: string` to the TimeRange type, and the router populates it from availability.timeZone (and now respects each override's own timeZone if set). But checkIfIsAvailable only takes `organizerTimeZone` into account and the `dateOverrides` parameter type is declared as `{ start: Date; end: Date; }[]` with no timeZone field, so the override's own timeZone is inaccessible. For overrides whose stored timeZone differs from the host's current timeZone (e.g. user created an override while travelling), `dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone)` will compute the wrong utcOffset and the override will be matched against the wrong time range. The type should be widened to include `timeZone?: string` and the body should prefer `date.timeZone ?? organizerTimeZone`.

title: No test for the fixed-host round-robin date override scenario the PR claims to fix
body: The PR description and the linked issues (#8207, #8329) state that the bug being fixed is that date overrides on fixed hosts were not honoured for round-robin events. The only test added in this PR extends the existing single-user test with a second timezone check; it does not create a round-robin event type with a fixed host and a non-fixed host, set a date override on the fixed host, and assert that slots are restricted to times when the fixed host is available. Without such a test the primary fix is unverified and regressions in checkIfIsAvailable (such as the UTC/organizer-tz mismatch above) will not be caught.

title: override.timeZone is dereferenced without a fallback, despite being optional in TimeRange
body: The new code calls `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()`. The TimeRange type declares `timeZone?: string`, and the only place in the codebase that supplies it is the trpc router (`timeZone: availability.timeZone`). If any other caller of `getSlots` (or legacy date-override rows that don't carry timeZone through whatever fetcher is used) supplies an override without timeZone, `.tz(undefined)` will fall back to the system timezone (or throw depending on dayjs-tz behaviour) and the conversion `offset = inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset` will be wrong for every override on that event type, silently producing bogus slots. A safe fallback like `override.timeZone ?? timeZone` or requiring callers to always provide it would prevent this. The same applies to the new `WorkingHours` import and the call signature in the router, which should document or enforce the timezone expectation.

title: Identical start/end in working hours check
body: In the new `workingHours.find((workingHour) => { ... })` callback, both `start` and `end` are computed from the same expression `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()`. This is a copy-paste error: the intent is clearly to compare the slot start time against `workingHour.startTime` and the slot end time against `workingHour.endTime` (i.e., `end` should be `slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute()`). Because both sides compare the same point, a slot starting 5 minutes before the working-hour end but lasting well past it (e.g., 60-minute event ending at 6:05 PM with hours ending 6:00 PM) is wrongly considered available.

title: Working hours day check uses UTC, not organizer timezone
body: `slotStartTime.day()` is computed from `time.utc()` and returns the UTC day-of-week, while `workingHour.days` are in the organizer's timezone (the schedule TZ). For a slot at e.g. 18:30 UTC on Tuesday, the organizer (IST, UTC+5:30) is already at 00:00 Wednesday; `workingHour.days.includes(slotStartTime.day())` will fail to match a Wednesday working-hour entry. Slots near the day boundary in the organizer's TZ will be incorrectly marked unavailable. Consequence: false double-bookings prevented, or more commonly, valid slots hidden.

title: Working hours time check uses UTC, not organizer timezone
body: `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()` is UTC minutes-since-midnight, but `workingHour.startTime` / `workingHour.endTime` are minutes-since-midnight in the organizer's timezone (per the WorkingHours type comment). Comparing UTC minutes against organizer minutes produces incorrect results for any organizer not in UTC. Even though `checkIfIsAvailable` receives `organizerTimeZone`, it never uses it for the day/time comparison, making the parameter useless for its main job.

title: Selected-slot availability check skips date overrides and working hours
body: In the selected-slots branch (lines 581-588), `checkIfIsAvailable` is called with only `time`, `busy`, `...availabilityCheckProps`, and `organizerTimeZone`. It does NOT spread `...userSchedule` (which contains `dateOverrides` and `workingHours`). Because `dateOverrides` and `workingHours` are defaulted to `[]` in the function signature, the date-override and working-hours checks are completely skipped for slots held by users with `selectedSlots`. A user that is on a date-override that closes their availability can still block / be blocked through `selectedSlots`, leading to bookings that violate the organizer's date override.

title: Date override day comparison mixes timezones
body: The override day is computed via the server's local timezone (`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').format(...)`) which is fragile and depends on the server's TZ. The slot's day is in UTC (`slotStartTime.format(...)`). For slots near midnight in either timezone, the comparison may disagree with what the organizer would consider "their" day, so slots can be mis-attributed to (or wrongly excluded from) a date override. The conversion should be done with the timezone plugin explicitly: e.g. `dayjs(date.start).tz(organizerTimeZone).format('YYYY MM DD')` compared to `slotStartTime.tz(organizerTimeZone).format('YYYY MM DD')`.

title: Identity comparison of two dayjs objects
body: `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes') === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, 'minutes')` compares dayjs instances with `===`. Dayjs objects should be compared with `.isSame()`. The strict equality only works for the same instance reference; two separately constructed dayjs objects representing the same moment are not `===`. This branch is intended to detect zero-length (start == end) overrides, and will not trigger when it should.

title: Date-override timezone offset formula is incorrect
body: The new formula is `offset = inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset`, then `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, 'minute').hour() * 60 + minute()`. Because `override.start` is a moment in time already represented in UTC, adding `organizerUtcOffset` (the organizer's offset) actively shifts the result away from the correct invitee-local minutes. The correct conversion is to add the invitee's offset only (`dayjs(override.start).utc().add(inviteeUtcOffset, 'minute').hour() * 60 + minute()`) or, cleaner, `dayjs(override.start).tz(timeZone).hour() * 60 + minute()`. With the current formula, an organizer with a non-UTC timezone paired with any invitee in a different timezone will produce override start/end values that are off by the organizer's UTC offset, causing slots to appear at the wrong hour for the invitee.

title: Unnecessary Date#toString and redundant dayjs calls
body: `dayjs(override.start.toString())` converts a Date to an ISO string and back to dayjs, which loses no information but is a code smell and risks platform-dependent string formatting. The same `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, 'minute')` is computed twice in the return expression; caching it into a local would halve the work and make the intent clearer. Not a correctness bug on its own but worth fixing alongside the offset formula.

title: New test does not actually verify the timezone fix
body: The added test reuses the IST schedule for both the IST and the BDT invitee and only asserts the same UTC strings (`08:30:00.000Z` ... `11:30:00.000Z`). Since slots are always returned in UTC and the override's UTC moment does not change, both code paths (original buggy `getUTCHours()` and the new formula) happen to land on the same UTC times for this scenario. The test would not catch the offset-formula bug above (e.g., an organizer in IST with a 14:00 IST override, plus an invitee in `Asia/Dhaka`, would yield wrong slot hours). The PR claims a timezone regression; the test must use a cross-timezone schedule (e.g., organizer in `Asia/Kolkata`, override "14:00" local, invitee in `America/New_York`) and assert the resulting invitee-local slot times to actually prove the fix works.

title: SQL injection in migration data load
body: The migration interpolates the value of `h` (a host string from `site_settings.embeddable_hosts`) directly into raw SQL: `INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, category_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES ('#{h}', #{category_id}, ...)`. Any host containing a single quote (or other SQL metacharacters) will break the statement or allow arbitrary SQL execution. Even though the input is from a trusted admin setting, the loader should sanitize/escape the value (e.g. via `ActiveRecord::Base.connection.quote` or `sanitize_sql_array`) or insert via the ActiveRecord `EmbeddableHost` model so the model's `before_validation` (http://, path stripping) is also applied consistently with how the rest of the app creates hosts.

title: NoMethodError when updating a non-existent host
body: `update` does `host = EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` and then calls `save_host(host)`. If no row matches the id, `host` is nil and `save_host` executes `host.host = ...` / `host.category_id = ...`, raising NoMethodError on nil and a 500 error to the admin. It also blindly `where().first` without scoping, which is a smaller concern. Guard the call, e.g. `head :not_found and return unless host`.

title: Strong parameters and validation not used; NoMethodError on missing params
body: `save_host` indexes straight into `params[:embeddable_host][:host]` and `[:category_id]`. A request without that key (or with non-hash input) raises NoMethodError instead of returning a 400/422. Use a permitted-parameters whitelist (`params.require(:embeddable_host).permit(:host, :category_id)`) and return proper validation errors. There's also no uniqueness validation on `host`, so two admins can create duplicate `embeddable_host` rows that will collide silently and confuse the `where('lower(host) = ?', host)` lookup in `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host`.

title: before_validation crashes on nil host
body: The `before_validation` callback calls `self.host.sub!(/^https?:\/\//, '')`. If `host` is nil (or non-string), `sub!` raises NoMethodError, blowing up validation instead of producing a clean validation error. Use `self.host = host.to_s.sub(/^https?:\/\//, '').sub(/\/.*$/, '')` (or guard with `return unless self.host.is_a?(String)` and a separate `presence` validation) so the user gets a normal validation message.

title: Host regex too narrow; valid hosts rejected and old data won't load
body: `validates_format_of :host, with: /\A[a-z0-9]+([\-\.]{1}[a-z0-9]+)*\.[a-z]{2,5}(:[0-9]{1,5})?(\/.*)?\Z/i` requires a dot plus a 2–5 letter TLD, which rejects legitimate hosts such as `localhost`, plain hostnames without TLDs, IPv4 literals, IDN/punycode-style hosts, and any host whose TLD is longer than five letters (e.g. many real-world TLDs). More importantly, the migration's raw INSERT copies values verbatim from the old `embeddable_hosts` site setting into the new table without running them through this validator, so legacy entries that don't match the regex will be silently inserted but will fail validation the moment any code tries to save them again. Add `presence` and `length` validations, broaden or replace the regex (e.g. parse with `URI`/`Addressable`), and have the migration create records through the `EmbeddableHost` model so normalization + validation are applied.

title: Migration INSERTs raw, non-normalized hosts
body: The data migration copies the old site-setting values straight into the table via raw SQL. The new model normalizes hosts (strips `http(s)://`, strips paths) in `before_validation`; skipping that means `http://example.com/foo` and `example.com/foo` end up as distinct rows in the new table that won't match the normalized values the runtime expects (because `record_for_host` queries with `uri.host` only). Use `EmbeddableHost.create!(host: h, category_id: category_id)` (or call the normalizer) inside the data-loading loop.

title: category_id may still be 0 / DB will reject null NOT NULL column
body: If both the `embed_category` site setting is missing AND the `uncategorized_category_id` row is missing or non-numeric (e.g., fresh test DBs with no settings), `category_id` stays 0 and the subsequent `INSERT ... VALUES (..., #{category_id}, ...)` writes `category_id = 0` into a `null: false` column, causing the whole migration to abort on Postgres. Also `cmd_tuples` is Postgres-specific; the migration won't run on MySQL/SQLite (it's `affected_rows`/`changes`). Guard against zero, and drop the not-null on `category_id` or default it appropriately so the migration is portable and robust.

title: category fabricator definitions moved to wrong file; will break many specs
body: The PR replaces the contents of `spec/fabricators/category_fabricator.rb` with the `embeddable_host` fabricator and puts the original category/diff_category/happy_category/private_category fabricators in a NEW file `spec/fabricators/embeddable_host_fabricator.rb`. Fabricator typically resolves `Fabricator(:category)` via the file `category_fabricator.rb`; with that file now defining `:embeddable_host` instead of `:category`, every existing test that does `Fabricate(:category)` (and the `embeddable_host` fabricator itself, which uses the bare `category` argument) will fail with `NoFabricatorDefined`. This is a broad test-suite regression. Put the category fabricators back in `category_fabricator.rb` and the embeddable_host fabricator in its own file, or rename the file to match.

title: _hydrateEmbedded does not filter undefined subtype lookups
body: The new array branch builds `const hydrated = obj[k].map(function(id) { return self._lookupSubType(subType, type, id, root); });`. `_lookupSubType` can legitimately return `undefined` (the `category` short-circuit aside, the doc lookup returns nothing for unknown ids / collection-absent). Storing those `undefined`s in the result array means embedded readers get `[undefined]` entries and `length` includes them — the new `store-test.js.es6` asserts `fruitCols.length` is exactly the number of valid ids, so this works only because the fixtures happen to contain every id. Use `.filter(Boolean)` after the map, or treat an undefined lookup as a failure to fully hydrate (delete `obj[k]`/don't populate the array), and add a test case where the embedded ids exceed the available collection to lock the behavior in.

title: type.replace('_', '-') replaces only the first underscore
body: The basePath lookup is now `type.replace('_', '-')`, but `String#replace` with a string argument only replaces the first occurrence. Any pluralized type that ends up with more than one underscore (currently none, but it's a sharp edge for future types like `foo_bar_baz`) will not match `ADMIN_MODELS`. Use `type.replace(/_/g, '-')` (regex with global flag) to be safe.

title: Embedding adapter's pathFor ignores args; breaks all REST verbs
body: `pathFor()` returns the static string `"/admin/customize/embedding"` and ignores `store`, `type`, and `findArgs`. That works for the single `embedding` model (a singleton at GET/PUT `/admin/customize/embedding`), but `rest.js#pathFor` is invoked for `find`, `findAll`, `update`, `createRecord`, and `destroyRecord`. Because the embedding adapter's `pathFor` returns the same URL for every verb, an accidental `findAll('embedding')` / `createRecord('embedding')` would issue a GET/PUT/POST/DELETE against the same endpoint and either be silently mis-handled by the controller or cause a confusing 404/route mismatch. Override only the verbs that actually exist (e.g. define a `find`/`update` that call the parent) or limit the resource surface area.

title: Discourse.Category.findById is not synchronous; assignment never updates UI
body: `host.set('category', Discourse.Category.findById(this.get('categoryId')))`. `findById` (and `find`) return a Promise; assigning the unresolved promise to `category` leaves the UI showing no category until a subsequent full reload. Use `Discourse.Category.findById(...).then(c => host.set('category', c))` or the sync store lookup. Additionally, `edit()` reads `this.get('host.category.id')` without guarding for nil — for a freshly created row whose `category` is null this throws, though the `editing || isNew` predicate normally hides that path.

title: Controller tests are placeholders; no behavior is exercised
body: The new `embeddable_hosts_controller_spec.rb` (and `embedding_controller_spec.rb`) only assert `controller_class < Admin::AdminController`, which is a trivial Ruby constant check. They don't exercise create/update/destroy, don't test the nil-host guard, don't test the category_id fallback, don't verify `before_filter` authentication, and don't check that `save_host` serializes correctly with `rest_serializer: true`. With the bugs in the controller (NoMethodError on missing params and on missing record), the absence of real specs is exactly what lets those bugs through.

title: Same placeholder-only coverage for Admin::EmbeddingController
body: Identical placeholder test as `embeddable_hosts_controller_spec.rb`. There's no coverage of `fetch_embedding` ordering/caching, of `show` vs `update` rendering shape, or that the serializer is using the rest_serializer flag — all of which the new JS code in `admin-embedding.js.es6` and `embedding.hbs` now rely on.

title: No spec for nil/blank host, or invalid hostnames
body: `EmbeddableHost`'s `before_validation` calls `sub!` on `host` without checking presence, and the format regex is strict. There are no specs asserting the behavior when `host` is nil, empty, contains only a scheme, or contains uppercase/path. Adding those would lock in intended behavior and catch the NoMethodError bug above.

title: REST PUT response no longer propagates IDs back to store
body: Pre-PR the PUT path looked like `update(...).then(function(json) { return json[typeField].id ? ... storeMap(...) : ... })` (it's gone). The new `update` adapter just returns the unwrapped payload. Combined with the changes in `store.js#update` that look up `result[type]` (note: stores now use the raw camelCase type, not `typeField`), any consumer that previously got an updated record back will now see a payload without going through the identity-map store. Not broken for this PR's editor (which sets `.category` manually) but it is an API contract change for the rest adapter.

title: Silent category fallback to nil when no EmbeddableHost matches
body: Previously an imported topic was forced into `SiteSetting.embed_category` regardless; now `eh.try(:category_id)` means a `TopicEmbed.import` for a URL that doesn't resolve to any `EmbeddableHost` record yields a topic with `category: nil`, which then gets snapped to `SiteSetting.uncategorized_category_id` by `Topic#ensure_topic_has_a_category`. That's a data-integrity change (imported topics land in Uncategorized instead of the configured embedding category), and it's worth either documenting explicitly or rejecting the import when no host matches (matching the controller-side `EmbeddableHost.host_allowed?` policy).

title: SQL injection in data migration
body: The migration interpolates the host string read from `site_settings.embeddable_hosts` directly into a raw `execute` SQL statement: `execute "INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, category_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES ('#{h}', #{category_id}, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)"`. Hosts come from admin-entered free text. A host value containing an apostrophe (e.g. `foo's.example.com`) or a multi-statement payload (e.g. `evil'); DROP TABLE users; --`) will break the migration or execute arbitrary SQL, since `execute` runs as a single connection.exec (multiple statements allowed). Use a parameterized query or, better, instantiate the model: `EmbeddableHost.create!(host: h, category_id: category_id)`.

title: before_validation crashes when host is nil
body: The `before_validation` callback calls `self.host.sub!(/^https?:\/\//, '')`. If the model is built/saved with `host: nil` (which happens when an admin submits the form with no host, or with a malformed JSON body, or when a malicious POST sends `embeddable_host[host]=`), `nil.sub!` raises `NoMethodError`, bypassing the format validator and surfacing as a 500 error instead of a clean validation failure (422). It should guard with `self.host &&` or use non-mutating assignment.

title: update/destroy crash when record not found
body: `update` and `destroy` do `host = EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` and then call methods on `host` (e.g. `save_host(host)`, `host.destroy`) without checking whether it was found. Any PUT/DELETE with a non-existent or non-numeric id (including requests where the record was concurrently removed) will raise `NoMethodError` on nil and return a 500. Should `return not_found` (or render 404) when the lookup yields nil.

title: save_host does not guard against missing embeddable_host param
body: `host.host = params[:embeddable_host][:host]` assumes `params[:embeddable_host]` is always present. A request without the `embeddable_host` key (malformed body, blank form submission, or an attacker-controlled POST) raises `NoMethodError` on nil. Guard with `return render_json_error(...)` or `params.require(:embeddable_host).permit(...)` so the controller responds with a clear 400/422 instead of a 500.

title: Host regex rejects valid long-TLD domains
body: `\A[a-z0-9]+([\-\.]{1}[a-z0-9]+)*\.[a-z]{2,5}(:[0-9]{1,5})?(\/.*)?\Z/i` caps the TLD at 5 letters. Legitimate gTLDs longer than 5 chars exist (e.g. `.museum`, `.travel`, `.coop` happens to fit, but `.technology`, `.international`, `.directory` etc. all fail). The format validator should accept TLDs of at least 2 characters, e.g. `\.[a-z]{2,}` (and case-insensitively since `/i` is used).

title: Imported topic ends up with nil category if record_for_host misses
body: Previously the imported topic was forced into `SiteSetting.embed_category`; now it is forced into `eh.try(:category_id)`. `record_for_host` returns false when no row matches, so on a race (host deleted between `TopicRetriever.invalid_host?` and `TopicEmbed.import`) the post is created with `category: nil` and falls through `Topic#ensure_topic_has_a_category` to the uncategorized category — bypassing any admin-configured per-host category and silently breaking the embed flow. Either fail loudly (return nil and let the job retry) or fall back to a clearly documented default category rather than silently degrading to uncategorized.

title: Controller spec is a stub; create/update/destroy untested
body: The new `Admin::EmbeddableHostsController` spec only asserts inheritance from `Admin::AdminController`. The real surface area — `create`, `update`, `destroy`, the `save_host` flow, and the nil-record handling — has zero coverage, which is why the bugs above (nil host in `save_host`, nil record in update/destroy) are invisible to CI. At minimum, add specs that exercise create with a valid host, update with an unknown id (expect 404), and destroy with an unknown id.

title: EmbeddingController spec is a stub
body: Same problem: the only assertion is that the class is a subclass of `Admin::AdminController`. There is no coverage for `show`, `update`, the `fetch_embedding` before-filter, or the OpenStruct payload it builds. Add at least one request spec for `GET /admin/customize/embedding` that asserts the returned JSON includes `embeddable_hosts` with the correct shape.

title: Missing model tests for nil/blank/invalid hosts
body: The new model spec only exercises three happy paths (`http://`, `https://`, path trimming) and `host_allowed?` lookups. There is no test for `EmbeddableHost.new(host: nil).valid?`, no test for invalid hosts (e.g. `not a host`, `localhost`, long-TLD hosts like `.museum`), no test that an existing record returns its hosts from `record_for_host` case-insensitively, and no test that creating two hosts with the same name is (or isn't) permitted. These would catch the nil-host crash, the TLD regex bug, and duplicate-host data integrity issues.

title: Serializer duplicates attributes via both macro and methods
body: `attributes :id, :host, :category_id` is declared at the top of the class, and then each of those three attributes is also defined as an explicit method returning `object.<attr>`. With `ApplicationSerializer` (ActiveModel::Serializer), `attributes` already wires the methods, so the explicit `def id/def host/def catbody_id` definitions are dead code that obscure the contract. Either drop the explicit methods or drop the `attributes` macro; doing both is confusing and risks subtle regressions if the serializer base class changes its convention.

title: Dead translation key admin.embedding.edit
body: The new locale block adds `edit: "edit"` under `admin.embedding`, but no template, component, or JS file references `admin.embedding.edit` (the only edit-related string is `admin.embedding.confirm_delete`). Remove the unused key to keep the locale file aligned with the UI.

title: SQL injection via interpolation in migration INSERT
body: The migration interpolates the per-line `h` value from `site_settings.embeddable_hosts` directly into a raw SQL INSERT string: `INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, category_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES ('#{h}', #{category_id}, ...)`. Any value containing a single quote in the site setting breaks the SQL and any crafted value can inject arbitrary SQL (CREATE FUNCTION, UPDATE site_settings, exfiltration, etc.). The migration must use parameterized queries (e.g. `conn.exec_params(...)` via a PG-specific helper, or sanitize/quote the value) instead of string interpolation. The same applies when `category_id` is 0 and the uncategorized fallback is used as `#{category_id}` — the assumption that this is a safe integer is asserted, not validated, and any non-integer returned by the SQL fallback would also break the query.

title: Migration will fail (or insert garbage) when uncategorized_category_id is the default -1
body: The fallback `category_id = execute(... WHERE name='uncategorized_category_id')[0]['value'].to_i` reads the raw `site_settings.value` for `uncategorized_category_id`. On a fresh install this setting is its YAML default of `-1`, so `category_id` becomes `-1` and the subsequent INSERTs write `category_id = -1`, which either violates the FK to `categories.id` (migration fails partway, leaving a half-applied state) or silently inserts invalid rows that no other code path can legitimately surface. The migration must guard against `category_id <= 0` (no valid category to assign) and either skip inserts or refuse to run with a clear error rather than blindly use whatever integer was read. Additionally, on databases where the `embed_category` lookup returns no rows, `[0]['id']` is `nil` and `[0]['value']` further on can also be `nil`, causing `nil['id']`/`nil['value']` NoMethodErrors that crash the migration.

title: before_validation crashes with NoMethodError when host is nil
body: `before_validation do; self.host.sub!(/^https?:\/\//, ''); self.host.sub!(/\/.*$/, ''); end` invokes `String#sub!` on `self.host` with no nil check. If a record is built without a `host` (e.g. via `EmbeddableHost.new`, the controller's `save_host(EmbeddableHost.new)` flow with no host supplied, or anything that ever constructs a record with `host` unset), Rails calls this `before_validation` callback first and raises `NoMethodError: undefined method `sub!` for nil:NilClass` before the format validation ever runs. Either guard with `self.host = (self.host || '').sub(...)` or move the stripping into a setter / `after_initialize` that tolerates nil.

title: No presence validation on category despite NOT NULL DB constraint
body: The migration declares `category_id` as `null: false` and the controller/admin UI relies on every embeddable host having a category, but `EmbeddableHost` only `validates_format_of :host`. The model has `belongs_to :category` but no corresponding `validates :category, presence: true`. As a result, an admin can save a host via direct API or through any future code path with `category_id: nil` and the failure surfaces only as a generic ActiveRecord `NOT NULL` DB error from the SQL adapter instead of a friendly validation error. Add `validates :category_id, presence: true` (or `validates_presence_of :category`) so the failure mode is consistent with the other validations.

title: update and destroy actions crash with NoMethodError when the host id is invalid
body: `update` does `host = EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first; save_host(host)` and `destroy` does `host = EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first; host.destroy`. If `params[:id]` does not match any record (typo, stale client, manual request), `host` is `nil` and `save_host(nil)` raises `NoMethodError` from `nil.host = ...` / `nil.category_id = ...`, and `nil.destroy` raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'destroy' for nil`. Both branches should respond with `not_found` (or render_json_error) before calling `save_host`/`destroy`, since the staff user otherwise gets a 500 for what should be a 404.

title: Fabricator file contents appear to be swapped between category_fabricator.rb and embeddable_host_fabricator.rb
body: `spec/fabricators/category_fabricator.rb` after the PR contains only `Fabricator(:embeddable_host)`, while the newly-added `spec/fabricators/embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` contains all of the `Fabricator(:category)` / `:diff_category` / `:happy_category` / `:private_category)` definitions that used to live in `category_fabricator.rb`. The fabricator gem registers by symbol so specs will still execute, but the contents are clearly the wrong way round — the file named for categories defines the embeddable_host fabricator and vice versa — which makes future maintenance (and any code that auto-loads fabricators via filename) confusing and fragile. Move `Fabricator(:embeddable_host)` into `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` and restore the category fabricators to `category_fabricator.rb`.

title: Migration performs destructive, non-reversible work inside `change`
body: The migration uses `def change` but it does irreversible things inside: it deletes `site_settings` rows for `embeddable_hosts` and `embed_category` and only inserts new `embeddable_hosts` rows. Running `rake db:rollback` will drop the `embeddable_hosts` table (the only part Rails knows how to reverse) but cannot restore the deleted site settings or the host data, so a rollback silently loses configuration. Migrations that move data should be split into explicit `up`/`down` methods, or at minimum copy the affected `site_settings` rows into a backing table before deleting so the data can be restored on rollback. There are also no tests covering the migration's data-move behavior, only the host-validation and host-allow logic.

title: Embedding PUT /admin/customize/embedding is a no-op that silently accepts writes
body: `update` only re-renders `@embedding`; it never persists anything. Combined with the front-end `saveChanges` action in `admin-embedding.js.es6` which calls `this.get('embedding').update({})`, a staff user clicking any future 'save embedding settings' button would appear to succeed (200 + refreshed JSON) while nothing was actually written. If this controller is genuinely a placeholder, it should at minimum 405 / log so it's obvious; if saving per-host records is the intended workflow (which is what the rest of the page does) then the unused `saveChanges` action and PUT route should be removed so future readers don't waste time tracing a dead path.

title: No behavioural specs for EmbeddableHostsController create/update/destroy or save_host
body: The only assertion is that the class inherits from `Admin::AdminController`. The actual behaviour — assignment of `host` and `category_id` from `params[:embeddable_host]`, the fallback to `SiteSetting.uncategorized_category_id` when category_id is blank, the JSON error render when the model is invalid, and the success response shape — has no spec. Given the SQL-injection-adjacent migration and the controller-level nil-handling bug reported elsewhere, this controller deserves at least a happy-path create spec and a 404 / not-found spec.

title: Imported embed posts will fall back to uncategorized when no EmbeddableHost record exists
body: `TopicEmbed.import` now uses `category: eh.try(:category_id)` where `eh = EmbeddableHost.record_for_host(url)`. When the referring host has no matching `embeddable_hosts` row (the previously-existing `SiteSetting.embed_category` was a simple string default), `category_id` will be `nil`, so the post is filed in the uncategorized bucket rather than the admin-configured embed category. Historically a setting ensured there was always a category; with the setting removed, the only path to a real category is registering the host. This is a behaviour change worth flagging for operators who relied on `SiteSetting.embed_category` to retroactively file old imports — it now silently does nothing for unconfigured hosts and any future import race-condition (host not yet saved) goes to uncategorized. Either restore a default-category fallback at the call site or document the new requirement explicitly in `config/locales/server.en.yml`.

title: Client-side upload size check hardcoded to 10MB
body: The client-side file size check in `validateUploadedFile` is hardcoded to `10 * 1024` KB (10MB) instead of using the configured `SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb`. This is inconsistent with the new server-side behavior in `uploads_controller.rb`, which now allows images larger than `max_image_size_kb` by automatically downsizing them (up to 5 attempts of 80% reduction). If `max_image_size_kb` is set to, e.g., 5MB, the server would accept and downsize images between 5MB and 10MB, but the client rejects them outright. Users will see a misleading 'file too large' error for images that the server would successfully process. The error message also incorrectly displays 10MB as the maximum size regardless of the actual configured limit.

title: 413 error handler hardcodes 10MB limit
body: In `displayErrorForUpload`, the 413 (entity too large) error handler is hardcoded to `10 * 1024` KB (10MB) instead of using `SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb`. When the server returns a 413 error, the client displays an incorrect maximum size to the user. This also breaks the contract with server-side configuration: if an admin configures `max_image_size_kb` to a different value, the error message shown to users will not match.

title: Duplicate `OptimizedImage.downsize` definition shadows old signature
body:
Two definitions of `self.downsize` exist in the same class:
1. `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at line 145
2. `downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` at line 149

In Ruby, redefining a method completely replaces the previous definition. The second definition shadows the first, making lines 145-147 unreachable dead code. This is an API break for any existing callers that use the old 4-positional-arg signature (e.g., `OptimizedImage.downsize("a.png", "b.png", 800, 600)`): such calls will fail because the 3rd positional argument is now interpreted as a dimensions string rather than width, and the 4th as `opts`. The dead code should be removed to avoid confusion, and callers of the old signature should be updated.

title: `OptimizedImage.optimize` signature change is a silent API break
body: The `self.optimize` method signature changed from `(operation, from, to, width, height, opts={})` to `(operation, from, to, dimensions, opts={})`. External callers (plugins, other parts of the codebase) using the old 5-positional-arg signature will silently misbehave: the 4th argument is now treated as a dimensions string (e.g., `800` instead of `"800x600"`), and the 5th argument (previously `height`) is now interpreted as `opts`. There is no deprecation or compatibility shim.

title: Removed `OptimizedImage.dimensions` helper without checking external callers
body: The `self.dimensions(width, height)` public class method was removed as part of this PR. Although it was only used internally by the old `optimize` method, it was a public class method (no `private` declaration) and could be used by plugins or external code. Its removal without a compatibility shim is a potential API break.

title: No tests for new automatic downsizing feature
body: The PR introduces a new automatic downsizing loop in `create_upload` (up to 5 attempts of 80% reduction) and modifies the `OptimizedImage.downsize` and `OptimizedImage.optimize` signatures, but no tests are included. Coverage is missing for: the downsizing loop terminating correctly when the file becomes small enough; the 5-attempt cap being respected; correct handling when `OptimizedImage.downsize` fails (e.g., unsupported format); behavior when `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` is 0 (disabled); and that the uploaded file's recorded size matches the downsized result.

title: Same path used for input and output of `OptimizedImage.downsize`
body: `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...)` is called with identical source and destination paths. While ImageMagick's `convert` typically reads the full input before writing, this is fragile: if a future implementation streams input/output, or if a tool reads the destination file as part of processing, data corruption could occur. A safer pattern is to write to a sibling temp file and then atomically replace.

title: Client-side upload validation hardcoded to 10MB, ignores site setting
body: The previous code read the per-type cap from `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`; it has been replaced with a hardcoded `10 * 1024` (10MB). This is a regression: site administrators who configure `max_image_size_kb` (or `max_attachment_size_kb`) to any value other than 10240 will see inconsistent behavior. Files between the configured limit and 10MB pass the client-side check but are rejected by the server (HTTP 413); files over 10MB are rejected by the client even though the server would accept them when the configured limit is higher. The validation must continue to honor `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`.

title: 413 error message hardcodes 10MB instead of site limit
body: The 413 handler previously displayed `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` in the `file_too_large` i18n message; it now displays a hardcoded `10 * 1024`. When an upload is rejected by the server because it exceeds the configured `max_image_size_kb`, the user sees the wrong limit (e.g. "10240 KB") rather than the actual configured limit, which is confusing and undermines the purpose of the setting.

title: Dead duplicate `downsize` method shadows real definition
body: Lines 145-147 define `self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})`, and lines 149-151 then redefine `self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`. In Ruby the second definition wins and the first is unreachable. The live signature is `(from, to, dimensions_string, opts)`, but the leftover four-arg definition is misleading to readers and any caller that still passes `width, height` positionally (matching the dead signature) will silently misbehave because Ruby will treat the fourth positional argument as the `opts` hash. The first definition must be deleted.

title: Animated GIFs cannot be downsized: gifsicle rejects percentage strings
body: The controller calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails)`. For `.gif` inputs with `allow_animation: true`, `optimize` dispatches to `downsize_instructions_animated` (lines 137-139), which forwards to `resize_instructions_animated` (lines 115-124). That helper shells out to `gifsicle --resize-fit #{dimensions}`. gifsicle's `--resize-fit` requires pixel dimensions (`WxH`) and does not accept percentage strings like `"80%"`, so the command fails. `convert_with` swallows the failure (it only logs), the return value is ignored by the controller, the file size never decreases, and after 5 iterations the oversized file is uploaded anyway. The downsize path must either pass pixel dimensions, compute an actual size target from `max_image_size_kb`, or use an ImageMagick-only path for the size-reduction loop (the thumbnail for the post can still be done with gifsicle separately).

title: Loop continues without checking whether downsize succeeded or met the target
body: After the downsize attempt, the controller neither checks the boolean returned by `OptimizedImage.downsize` nor verifies that `tempfile.size` actually shrank. A failure (e.g. animated GIF, broken image, ImageMagick error) leaves the file at its original size, so the `attempt > 0 && tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` guard is satisfied until `attempt` runs out, at which point `Upload.create_for` is called with an oversized file. The user receives no indication that automatic downsizing failed and the resulting upload will be rejected (or worse, stored over the limit) downstream. After the loop, the code must verify `tempfile.size <= SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` and return an error payload (with an i18n message) when it is not.

title: Synchronous ImageMagick downsize runs on the upload request thread
body: The downsize loop runs up to five ImageMagick invocations inline in `create_upload`, which is called from `UploadsController#create` either directly (API synchronous path) or via `Scheduler::Defer` (asynchronous path). For images up to 10MB and concurrent uploads, blocking the worker on CPU-bound image processing for many seconds per upload will back up the queue and lengthen upload latency. The resize work should be moved into a dedicated background job (`Jobs.enqueue(:downsize_upload, ...)` or similar) and the controller should merely mark the upload as `pending_optimization`.

title: URL-downloaded tempfiles are now trusted up to 10MB before validation
body: `FileHelper.download` is called with `10.megabytes` instead of the previous `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes`.
