If any caller passes a type filter that ends with OR rather than AND, the trailing 'AND created <' will silently change the operator precedence. More importantly, the MaxCount branch builds:

    cond := fmt.Sprintf(`%s ORDER BY id DESC %s`, annotationType, r.db.GetDialect().LimitOffset(...))

without any check that annotationType contains a WHERE fragment rather than a full clause. The comment in the code refers to annotationType as 'e.g. alert_id > 0 AND dashboard_id > 0', but the function silently trusts the caller. There is no validation, and an accidental empty string would produce 'SELECT id FROM annotation  ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT N', which would happily walk the entire annotation table per batch (and there is no OFFSET/limit on the SELECT itself other than what the dialect appends). A guard against empty annotationType or a small comment/contract would make this safer.

title: Integration tests now skipped under -short with no unit-level coverage added
body: TestAnnotationCleanUp and TestOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst were renamed to TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp / TestIntegrationOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst and both gained a testing.Short() skip. These were the only tests that exercised CleanAnnotations / CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags in any way. They required a real DB before too, but now they run in zero CI configurations that use -short, and the deadlock regression that this PR fixes has no unit-test coverage of its own. There should be at least one non-DB unit test that exercises the new helpers (e.g. that untilDoneOrCancelled terminates on ctx.Done() and on zero affected rows, and that deleteByIDs short-circuits on an empty id list), so the new code paths are exercised in short mode and refactoring does not silently break them.

title: Routine cleanup logs use Error level
body: The new cleanup paths emit r.log.Error for normal, expected operations: 'Annotations to clean by time', 'cleaned annotations by time', 'Annotations to clean by count', 'cleaned annotations by count', 'Tags to clean', 'cleaned tags' (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579). These are routine successful operations that will fire on every cleanup cycle. With the cleanup ticker in cleanup.go now firing every minute (a separate change in this PR), this produces a steady stream of Error-level log entries masking real errors. Severity is amplified by the same PR also logging all IDs ('ids', ids), which can be up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize entries (up to 32767) per batch, potentially producing enormous log lines. These should be Debug/Info level, not Error.

title: Cleanup ticker shortened 10x without justification
body: Ticker changed from `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)` to `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)`. The PR description is solely about fixing a MySQL deadlock via query restructuring; nothing in the description or the referenced issue (grafana/grafana#64979) justifies a 10x increase in cleanup frequency. This multiplies the database load of every cleanup job by 10x, including annotation cleanup, dashboard version cleanup, short URL cleanup, query history cleanup, etc. Combined with the noisy Error logs added in xorm_store.go, this materially changes operational behavior and should either be split into its own change or justified explicitly. Note also that `cleanUpOldAnnotations` is called inside this 1-minute loop, and the new fetch+delete implementation uses two round-trips per batch instead of one, compounding the load.

title: O(N^2) string building in SQLite IN-list inlining
SQLite parameter-limit branch checks config, not actual ID count
body: The branch `if r.db.GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite && r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit` decides whether to inline IDs into the SQL based on the configured batch size, not on `len(ids)`. The actual number of parameters needed equals `len(ids)`, which is bounded by `LIMIT AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` but usually far smaller (cleanup often finds only a handful of rows). When the operator sets a large batch size (e.g., the new test exercises 32767), the inlining path is taken on every call even if only a few rows are being deleted, building a needless literal string and skipping the (correct) parameterized path. Use `len(ids) > sqliteParameterLimit`.

title: Log fields include 'err' even when fetch succeeded
body: Each new cleanup log line passes `"err", err` as a structured field. The `err` here is the result of `fetchIDs`, which is nil on the success path. Every successful cleanup therefore emits `"err": <nil>` in its log payload, which is misleading to operators triaging errors (especially since these are emitted at Error level - see the other finding). The 'err' field should only be included when err is non-nil, or the message should be split so success and failure paths log different things.

title: Wrong metrics recorder in Mode3.Create error path
body: When Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage). The error came from d.Storage.Create and the start time (startStorage) belongs to that Storage call, so the duration should be reported as a storage metric via d.recordStorageDuration(...). As written, observability for storage errors is mis-labeled as legacy errors, and the duration bucket is attributed to the wrong store; dashboards and alerts built on these Prometheus labels will be wrong.

title: Mode3.Delete puts base logger (d.Log) in ctx instead of enriched log
body: The Delete method does log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method) but then ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log). All other methods (Create/Get/List/Update/DeleteCollection) put the enriched logger (log) into the context, but Delete discards the method/kind/name values. Downstream code that calls klog.FromContext(ctx) inside Storage.Delete will lose those structured fields, breaking log correlation and metric labels that depend on context-derived values.

title: Mode3.Delete success records 'name' as the kind metric label
body: After a successful Storage.Delete, the code records d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage). Every other storage metric in this file uses options.Kind as the 'kind' label; using 'name' here produces a metric label whose values are object names rather than Kind strings (e.g. kind="my-playlist-uid"). This breaks the cardinality and semantics of the dualwriter_*_duration metrics; dashboards filtering by kind=Playlist will miss this data.

title: Wrong metrics recorder in Mode3.Update error path
body: Same defect as in Create: when d.Storage.Update fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage). Since the error is from Storage.Update and the start time is the storage call's start, the call should be d.recordStorageDuration. As written, storage update failures are counted under legacy metrics, and the recorded duration is attributed to the wrong backend.

title: Mode3.DeleteCollection legacy goroutine records storage metric
body: Inside the async legacy DeleteCollection goroutine, after d.Legacy.DeleteCollection(...) returns, the code calls d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). The error and duration belong to the Legacy backend, so this should be d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). Result: legacy DeleteCollection failures and latencies are silently counted against the storage backend, distorting dualwriter dashboards.

title: Async legacy writes derive from request ctx and are cancelled with it
body: In Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection the async legacy goroutines do context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s, ...), deriving the legacy write's context from the incoming request context. As soon as the HTTP/RPC client disconnects (or the apiserver request finishes and cancels the request ctx), the derived context is cancelled and the legacy write aborts. The whole point of mode 3 ('write to legacy just as a safe measure') is to make legacy eventually consistent regardless of client behaviour, so legacy goroutines should detach from the request context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) in Go 1.21+) and only be bounded by the 10s timeout.

title: Mode3 unit tests do not verify that the legacy write actually happened
body: Mode3 is defined by the property that writes succeed on Storage and are then dispatched to Legacy asynchronously. In TestMode3_Create and TestMode3_Update the legacy mocks are registered, but the test returns immediately after the synchronous call without synchronising with the goroutine and never asserts that Legacy.Create/Legacy.Update was actually invoked (e.g. m.AssertCalled or a sync.WaitGroup/channel). The tests will pass even if the async legacy write is silently dropped, so they don't actually exercise the mode 3 contract. (TestMode3_Delete/DeleteCollection also lack any legacy assertion and only set up storage expectations.)

title: Doc comments for Mode3 misrepresent the write order
body: The doc on newDualWriterMode3 says 'Mode 3 represents writing to LegacyStorage and Storage and reading from Storage', and Create's comment says 'writes to LegacyStorage and Storage'. The implementation actually writes to Storage synchronously first and only then to LegacyStorage asynchronously; the comments imply a symmetric/ordered pair and don't mention that legacy is best-effort and async. This is the same issue as in the original code, but the PR was an opportunity to correct it.

title: TestMode3_Create 'unified store fails' sets up legacy mock instead of storage mock
body: The case 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' populates setupLegacyFn but leaves setupStorageFn nil. Because the test mocks share a single *mock.Mock across legacyStoreMock and storageMock, the storage call coincidentally matches the legacy expectation and the test still passes, but the intent (Storage.Create fails) and the setup (legacy mock) disagree. The test would be clearer and resilient to future refactors if the failing expectation were registered via setupStorageFn.

title: Create records storage failure as legacy duration
body: In DualWriterMode3.Create, when d.Storage.Create fails the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recording the storage duration. Because recordLegacyDuration and recordStorageDuration are distinct Prometheus metrics, a storage-side failure will be misattributed to the legacy backend. Anyone alerting or graphing on legacy failures will see storage failures, and storage failures will be invisible. Use recordStorageDuration(true, ...) here.

title: Update records storage failure as legacy duration
body: In DualWriterMode3.Update, when d.Storage.Update fails the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recordStorageDuration. Same effect as in Create: a unified-storage Update failure is reported as a legacy failure, silently corrupting the two latency/error time series. Use recordStorageDuration(true, ...).

title: DeleteCollection async legacy call recorded as storage duration
body: In the DeleteCollection async goroutine, the elapsed time of d.Legacy.DeleteCollection is fed to d.recordStorageDuration(...). Every other write path correctly uses recordLegacyDuration for the legacy leg; this one is mislabeled, so DeleteCollection legacy latency will be merged into the unified-storage histogram and the real legacy histogram will not see those calls.

title: Async legacy Create inherits request context that is cancelled when the response returns
body: The async Create goroutine derives its timeout from the inbound request context: `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, ...)`. That ctx is the apiserver request context, which is cancelled as soon as the handler writes the response and returns. The whole purpose of mode 3 is to write to legacy "as a safe measure" after the request returns; here that guarantee is broken, and the legacy write will frequently be aborted by ctx.Done() before completing. Use a detached context (e.g., context.Background()) with the klog logger still attached.

title: Async legacy Delete inherits request context
body: Same problem as the Create goroutine on line 51: the Delete goroutine derives its context from the request context with WithTimeoutCause(... 10s). The legacy Delete will be cancelled when the apiserver request finishes, so the safety-net legacy delete is not guaranteed to run to completion.

title: Async legacy Update inherits request context
body: The async Update goroutine derives its context from the request context with WithTimeoutCause(... 10s). The legacy Update will be cancelled when the apiserver request finishes, so the safety-net legacy update is not guaranteed to run. The legacy store can therefore permanently diverge from unified storage on any request that finishes inside 10s.

title: Async legacy DeleteCollection inherits request context
body: Same as above: the DeleteCollection goroutine derives its context from the request context with WithTimeoutCause(... 10s), so the legacy bulk delete will be cancelled when the handler returns and the two stores will diverge.

title: Async legacy Create uses the pre-storage object, not the stored object
body: After d.Storage.Create succeeds, the returned `created` object contains the UID, resourceVersion, creation timestamp, etc. that unified storage assigned. The async goroutine calls d.Legacy.Create with the original `obj` parameter instead, so the legacy store never sees the metadata assigned by storage (or assigns its own), producing two records with different identities for what should be the same resource. The legacy record is effectively orphaned from the unified one.

title: Async legacy Update re-evaluates UpdatedObjectInfo against legacy's current state
body: The async Update goroutine passes the original objInfo to d.Legacy.Update. UpdatedObjectInfo.UpdatedObject is called inside the legacy store against whatever it currently holds, not against the state storage just wrote. The previous implementation wrapped objInfo around the resolved object and passed the same wrapped value to both stores so they would apply identical changes; here the legacy store can compute and persist a different version, causing legacy and storage to diverge.

title: Mode3 doc comment describes the wrong write order
body: The comment on newDualWriterMode3 says "Mode 3 represents writing to LegacyStorage and Storage and reading from Storage." The actual behavior implemented below is: write synchronously to Storage, then fire-and-forget an asynchronous write to LegacyStorage, and read only from Storage. The comment therefore misleads readers about both the ordering and the async nature of mode 3.

title: Delete success path labels metric with name instead of Kind
body: On successful d.Storage.Delete, d.recordStorageDuration is called with `name` as the kind label, while every other path (and the failing branch on line 103) uses options.Kind. As a result, the storage latency histogram for Delete will be tagged with the resource name instead of the resource kind, breaking grouping with all other operations.

title: TestMode3_Create never asserts that the legacy async Create actually ran
body: TestMode3_Create registers an expectation on the legacy store mock via setupLegacyFn but the goroutine that should satisfy it is never synchronized with (no wait, no channel, no AssertExpectations). The test currently passes even if the legacy async write is removed or short-circuited, so the very behavior mode 3 introduces - the legacy safety-net write - is effectively untested.

title: TestMode3_Update never asserts the legacy async Update ran
body: TestMode3_Update registers a mock expectation for legacy Update but does not synchronize with or assert against the async goroutine. The same problem as Create: the legacy safety-net update is not actually verified.

title: TestMode3_DeleteCollection has no legacy setup or assertion at all
body: The testCase struct does not include setupLegacyFn and no mock expectation is registered for d.Legacy.DeleteCollection. The implementation runs an async legacy DeleteCollection but nothing in this test exercises it - the safety-net behavior on the bulk-delete path is entirely uncovered.

title: TestMode3_Get does not verify legacy Get is never called
body: Mode 3 reads must come from storage only, but TestMode3_Get never asserts that the legacy store is not called (the analogous TestMode1_Get uses us.AssertNotCalled on Delete). A future change that accidentally adds a legacy Get would not be caught.

title: TestMode3_Get uses a local prometheus registry while the rest of the file uses the package-level p
body: All other tests in dualwriter_mode3_test.go and dualwriter_mode1_test.go use the package-level `p`; TestMode3_Get creates its own `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` inside the test body, masking the global and being a leftover from before the global existed. Minor, but should be aligned.

title: Storage failure recorded under the legacy duration metric
body: When d.Storage.Create returns an error the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...). The metric name (legacy vs storage) is used by dashboards/alerts to distinguish the two backends, so a storage failure ends up inflating the legacy error metric and the storage success metric is never recorded for this path. The success path on line 48 correctly uses recordStorageDuration, so the error branch should mirror it: d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage). The same pattern is repeated in the Update method (line 129).

title: Delete attaches d.Log to context instead of the enriched logger
body: Every other method in this file does `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, log)` using the local `log` variable that already carries name/kind/method. Delete builds that local log on line 96 but then sets `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`, so the legacy store (and any code reading the logger from the context) only sees the bare DualWriterMode3 logger with mode=3 and loses name, kind, and method. Inconsistent with Create/Get/List/Update/DeleteCollection and reduces observability of async legacy writes.

title: Kind metric label is set to the resource name
body: The success branch of Delete calls d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage). Every other recorder in the file uses options.Kind as the kind label, but here `name` (the resource identifier) is passed instead. This (a) makes the metric inconsistent with the rest of mode 3 and (b) blows up the metric cardinality because each deleted resource name becomes a label value. Should be options.Kind.

title: Storage Update failure recorded under the legacy duration metric
body: Mirrors the bug on line 45. When d.Storage.Update fails, d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) is called, attributing the storage failure to the legacy backend in the metrics. The success branch on line 132 correctly uses recordStorageDuration, so the failure branch should be d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage).

title: Update no longer wraps objInfo for the legacy call
body: The previous implementation precomputed `updated` from the storage copy, then passed an `updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: ...}` to both Storage.Update and Legacy.Update so both backends received the exact same resolved object. The new code passes the raw objInfo to d.Legacy.Update. If Storage and Legacy disagree on the previous object (e.g. they have drifted) or if objInfo.UpdatedObject behaves differently in the two implementations, the two stores can now persist different versions of the same object, producing data drift between unified storage and legacy storage. This is a real behavioural regression, not just a refactor.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection duration recorded under storage metric
body: In the async goroutine for DeleteCollection the legacy result is timed and then d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy) is called. This is the legacy path, so it should be d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). As written, a legacy DeleteCollection failure silently inflates the storage metric, and the legacy duration histogram never receives any samples from DeleteCollection.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the cancelled request context
body: All four async goroutines (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) derive their context with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s, ...). `ctx` is the API server request context, which is cancelled as soon as the handler returns and the response is sent. In practice that means the legacy goroutines often start in an already-cancelled context and the 10-second safety net never has a chance to fire. Result: legacy writes are aborted shortly after the user sees a success response, and because the failure is only logged via metrics, the user has no visibility. For 'safe measure' dual writes this defeats the purpose. Detach from the request lifetime (e.g. context.WithoutCancel or context.Background preserving values) and rely solely on the timeout.

title: TestMode3_Create 'unified store fails' case does not set up the storage mock
body: The second test case sets up only the legacy mock and leaves setupStorageFn nil. Mode3 calls d.Storage.Create before d.Legacy.Create (see dualwriter_mode3.go line 42), so on the testify mock the Storage.Create invocation is unexpected and the test will panic/fail before reaching the legacy mock at all. The test does not exercise the intended path ('storage Create fails, no legacy call'). It needs a setupStorageFn returning an error and either no legacy expectation or an AssertNotCalled for legacy.

title: No test verifies that the async legacy write actually happens
body: TestMode3_Create, TestMode3_Update, TestMode3_Delete and TestMode3_DeleteCollection all set up the legacy mock with m.On(...) but never assert that it was called (no mock.AssertCalled for the legacy backend). The goroutine in dualwriter_mode3.go has no synchronization with the test, so on a fast machine the test function can return and t.Run can finish before the goroutine has dispatched, meaning a regression that simply removed the goroutine would still pass the tests. Add an explicit AssertCalled (and ideally a small synchronization point) to prove the async write really happened.

title: TestMode3_Get creates a local Prometheus registry instead of using the package-level `p`
body: All other tests in this file (and the matching Mode1 tests in dualwriter_mode1_test.go, which were just refactored away from this pattern in the same PR) use the shared `var p = prometheus.NewRegistry()` declared in dualwriter_mode1_test.go. TestMode3_Get introduces a local `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` on line 119. It works but is inconsistent and looks like a missed cleanup. Use the shared registry.

title: Double-checked locking is missing the second check after acquiring the write lock
body: GetWebAssets implements half of a double-checked locking pattern: it reads entryPointAssetsCache under RLock, then on miss acquires a write Lock and proceeds to read the manifest file unconditionally. After acquiring the write lock, the function never re-checks entryPointAssetsCache. As a result, in non-dev mode on a cold start, every concurrent caller that arrives while the cache is still nil will serialize on the mutex and each perform its own full file read (and any CDN read/write) and overwrite entryPointAssetsCache. The mutex prevents data corruption but does not prevent this thundering-herd I/O. The standard fix is to re-test entryPointAssetsCache under the write lock and return it early when populated (mirroring the original cfg.Env != Dev && ret != nil check).

title: No regression test for the data race fix
body: The PR's stated purpose is to fix a data race on entryPointAssetsCache, but no test is added. There is no new test invoking GetWebAssets concurrently (which would be required to actually catch the race with `go test -race`), nor any test verifying the lock semantics (e.g., that the cached pointer is observed atomically, or that concurrent cold-start calls do not corrupt the cache). Without a regression test, future refactors can silently reintroduce the race.

title: Cached pointer is shared and not protected after return
body: GetWebAssets returns the cached *dtos.EntryPointAssets pointer (entryPointAssetsCache) directly to callers. While the mutex now guards reads/writes of the cache slot itself and the initial SetContentDeliveryURL call, the returned pointer is shared with any other caller. Any caller that mutates the returned object (e.g., by calling SetContentDeliveryURL or otherwise) without holding entryPointAssetsCacheMu will race with other readers of the same object. The new locking protects the slot, not the pointee. The PR description claims the fix addresses the data race, but this residual race on the shared object is not addressed and is plausibly part of the original bug.

title: Cache is overwritten with nil on transient read failure
body: entryPointAssetsCache = result is executed unconditionally at the end of the write path, even when result is nil and err is non-nil (i.e., readWebAssetsFromFile failed). This clears the previously cached value and causes every subsequent non-dev caller to retry the file/manifest read on every request until a read succeeds, instead of continuing to serve a stale-but-valid cache during a transient failure. The assignment should be guarded by err == nil (and ideally result != nil) so a failed load does not wipe the existing cache.

title: Write lock held during I/O blocks all readers and causes redundant work
body: The write lock acquired at line 48 is held while performing I/O (readWebAssetsFromFile on line 60 and the disabled readWebAssetsFromCDN on line 56), so every concurrent reader is blocked until that I/O completes. Combined with the double-checked locking pattern (RLock at line 41, then Lock at line 48), multiple goroutines that race to populate the cache after startup will all redundantly execute the file read and overwrite each other's results. The data race itself is correctly fixed, but a more efficient pattern would use sync.Once (with a reset path for Dev mode) or release the lock around the I/O and re-acquire it only to publish the result, so only one goroutine performs the slow work and readers are never blocked by it.

title: Missing double-check after acquiring write lock
body: GetWebAssets releases the RLock before checking whether the cache is populated, then unconditionally re-reads the manifest after taking the write lock. Two concurrent callers that both observe a nil cache will both serialize on the write lock and each perform the full file read and JSON parse, instead of the second caller reusing the value just populated by the first. Adding a re-check of `entryPointAssetsCache` after the Lock() (classic double-checked locking) would eliminate the redundant I/O on the cold-start path. Not a correctness bug—safe under the mutex—but wasteful for concurrent first callers in production.

title: No regression test added for the data race fix
body: The PR's stated purpose is to fix a data race on the shared `entryPointAssetsCache` global, but no test exercising concurrent calls to GetWebAssets is included. For a race-condition fix, the maintainer should expect at least one test that invokes GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines (intended to be run with `go test -race`) to guard against the race being reintroduced. Without such a test, the fix is verified only by inspection and there is no automated guard against future regressions on this exact path.

title: enableSqlExpressions function is confusingly written and could be misread as respecting the feature flag
body: The function `enableSqlExpressions` always returns false (disabling the feature) but is written with a misleading `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` computation and two `return false` branches that suggest the flag matters when it does not. The parameter `h` is also taken but only its `features` field is consulted in a dead computation. A future maintainer trying to 'restore' the feature is likely to flip the function back to `return !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(...)` (matching the variable naming) and reintroduce CVE-2024-9264, because the current logic gives no indication that the hard-coded `false` is deliberate. The function should be reduced to a single `return false` with a clear comment, or the call site should be inlined and the function removed.

title: Error message implies SQL expressions may be implemented later
body: When SQL expressions are disabled, the code returns `fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")`. This message suggests the feature is a work in progress that may be completed later, which conflicts with the security-driven intent of this PR to keep the feature disabled. A user-facing message such as "SQL expressions are disabled" would more accurately convey the state and avoid confusing operators who read the error in logs.

title: TablesList still concatenates rawSQL into a DuckDB command but is now only safe by accident
body: `TablesList` still builds `cmd := fmt.Sprintf("SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')", rawSQL)` from user-controlled `rawSQL` (with only a naive single-quote doubling) and passes it to `RunCommands`. The current fix only neutralises this because `RunCommands` is now a stub returning an error. If the stub is ever removed or replaced to re-enable SQL expressions, this exact code path is the one that was exploited (CVE-2024-9264): the rawSQL is interpolated into a shell-style command string passed to DuckDB. The function should either be deleted outright, or hardened (e.g. reject input containing anything other than an allow-listed SQL skeleton) so that the vulnerability cannot reappear by simply swapping the stub back.

title: No automated test added for the SQL-expressions disabled behaviour
body: This is a security fix (CVE-2024-9264) that hard-codes SQL expressions to be disabled. The PR description only mentions manual testing by the author and a Slack confirmation; no automated regression test was added. A unit test in `pkg/expr` that calls `ReadQuery` (or `UnmarshalSQLCommand`) with a `QueryTypeSQL` payload and asserts the resulting error is the only thing preventing the vulnerability from being silently re-enabled in a future refactor of `enableSqlExpressions` or removal of the stub in `pkg/expr/sql/db.go`.

title: UnmarshalSQLCommand still constructs an executable SQLCommand and is not covered by the reader-level disable
body: The PR only gates SQL expressions inside `ReadQuery` in `pkg/expr/reader.go`. `UnmarshalSQLCommand` in `pkg/expr/sql_command.go` is a separate code path that calls `NewSQLCommand` directly, which in turn calls `sql.TablesList`. The function is only safe today because `sql.NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands`/`QueryFramesInto` are stubs returning errors. Any future caller of `UnmarshalSQLCommand` (e.g. another endpoint or a test harness that bypasses the reader) would not be stopped by the `enableSqlExpressions` check. The disable should be enforced at the shared `NewSQLCommand` entry point (returning the same error) so both code paths are covered by a single guard, not just the reader.

title: enableSqlExpressions has dead code and always returns false
Error message misleads users about feature status
body: The error returned to users is `fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")`. This wording is misleading: SQL expressions are implemented (the package exists, the parser, command, and DB stubs are all wired up); the feature has been deliberately disabled as a security mitigation for CVE-2024-9264. A user (or operator) reading this error would conclude the functionality was never built rather than that it is currently turned off for safety. Consider something like `"sqlExpressions are disabled for security reasons (CVE-2024-9264)"` so the situation is clear and operators can grep for the CVE in their dashboards/logs.

title: Alternate construction path for SQLCommand is not gated
body: `NewSQLCommand` and the exported `UnmarshalSQLCommand` in `pkg/expr/sql_command.go` are still publicly callable and do not consult the `enableSqlExpressions` feature check that was added in `pkg/expr/reader.go`. They rely on `sql.TablesList` failing because the new `DB` stub returns `"not implemented"`, which surfaces as the generic `errutil.BadRequest("sql-invalid-sql", ...)` with the public message `"error reading SQL command"`. This is inconsistent with the more specific `"sqlExpressions is not implemented"` produced from the reader path, and it means any caller that bypasses `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` gets a different (and less informative) error. The disablement should be enforced at a single chokepoint (or both paths should return the same clear message) so the security state is consistent regardless of entry point.

title: No tests for the security mitigation
body:
The PR is a security fix that disables the entire SQL Expressions feature, replacing the `go-duck` backend with stubs and adding a feature-gated branch in `ReadQuery`. There are no new tests verifying:
- that `ReadQuery` with `QueryTypeSQL` now returns the expected error,
- that `sql.NewInMemoryDB()` methods all return `"not implemented"`,
- that `NewSQLCommand` / `UnmarshalSQLCommand` no longer succeed.

For a CVE-driven fix, regression tests pinning the disabled behaviour are essential so that a future re-enable cannot accidentally land without an explicit test change.

title: enableSqlExpressions has dead code and misleading semantics
body: The function enableSqlExpressions always returns false because both the `if enabled` branch and the fallthrough return false, regardless of the feature flag value. The local variable `enabled` is the negation of FlagSqlExpressions, so the name reads as a double negative (`enabled := !IsEnabled(...)`). The net effect is just `return false`. This is a maintainability trap: a future developer trying to 'fix' the function to honor the feature flag will be misled by the dead branch and the variable naming, and could easily reintroduce SQL execution in a way that re-introduces CVE-2024-9264. The function should be a single explicit `return false` with a comment explaining the security reason, or the name should be changed to make the always-disabled behavior obvious.

title: Misleading 'not implemented' error message
body: The error returned when SQL expressions are rejected reads `sqlExpressions is not implemented`. SQL expressions were implemented previously; they are now intentionally disabled as the mitigation for CVE-2024-9264. The message will mislead users and operators (and make log/triage harder) into thinking the feature simply wasn't built, rather than that it was turned off for security. It should reference the security reason (e.g. 'sqlExpressions have been disabled due to CVE-2024-9264').

title: Stub DB has no comment explaining why it exists
body: The new file pkg/expr/sql/db.go replaces the vulnerable scottlepp/go-duck-backed implementation with a no-op stub. There is no package or type-level comment stating that this stub intentionally exists to neutralize CVE-2024-9264 and that the real SQL execution backend must not be re-introduced without addressing that vulnerability. Without such a comment, a future contributor is likely to delete the stub and reinstate DuckDB execution, silently re-exposing the RCE/LFI.

title: Security-fix change to SQL expressions has no test coverage
body: This PR is the public fix for CVE-2024-9264 and changes both the gating (reader.go now rejects QueryTypeSQL) and the SQL backend (db.go stub, parser.go, sql_command.go). No test file is added or updated to verify that: (1) a QueryTypeSQL request now returns the documented error from reader.go, (2) NewSQLCommand / UnmarshalSQLCommand cannot produce an executable SQLCommand, and (3) SQLCommand.Execute, if reached, returns an error instead of executing user-controlled SQL. Without regression tests it is very easy for a future change (e.g. 're-enable SQL via feature flag', or deleting the stub) to silently re-introduce the vulnerability. The PR description also leaves the feature-flag-related docs unchecked; a test asserting behavior under the flag would at least lock the mitigation down.

title: BuildIndex lost its exclusive lock; concurrent builds of the same key can race
body: The change removes `b.cacheMu.Lock()` / `defer b.cacheMu.Unlock()` that previously wrapped the entire `BuildIndex` body and replaces it with only a tiny write-lock around `b.cache[key] = idx`. With the new code, two goroutines that both see a cache miss for the same `NamespacedResource` (e.g. concurrent `getOrCreateIndex` calls for the same key, which `search.go` already flags as a TODO) will both run `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` for file-backed indexes at the same `filepath.Join(b.opts.Root, key.Namespace, fmt.Sprintf("%s.%s", key.Resource, key.Group))`, both execute the builder, and race on the final cache write. The previous global lock was, perhaps inadvertently, also serializing same-key builds. The PR's stated goal is to allow different namespaces to build concurrently, but it should have used a per-key (or RWMutex-based) strategy instead of dropping the guard entirely; otherwise bleve may error out on the duplicate directory creation or two builds will silently overwrite each other in the cache.

title: Init now starts the broadcaster after the search build, so events during build are dropped by both
body: The order inside `s.once.Do` was changed from `initWatcher()` then `s.search.init(ctx)` to `s.search.init(ctx)` then `initWatcher()`. With the new ordering, any write that occurs while the search index is being built (which can take a long time) is no longer captured by the broadcaster — `initWatcher` hasn't started yet, and `searchSupport.init` only subscribes to `s.storage.WatchWriteEvents` after all builds complete. Before the change the broadcaster was already running and would buffer those events (also bumping `mostRecentRV`), so a Watch client connecting at startup would see them via `since`. After the change both the broadcaster and the search index miss events that happen during the build, and the broadcaster can lag behind the search index's own watch for the brief window between `WatchWriteEvents` being called in search.init and `initWatcher` actually running. The PR description does not mention this reordering; it should either be reverted or called out explicitly so reviewers can verify no caller relies on the broadcaster being live during the search build.

title: Init failure is logged twice with the identical message
body: `server.Init` already calls `s.log.Error("error initializing resource server", "error", s.initErr)` on failure, but `NewResourceServer` then logs the same error again with the identical message before returning: `s.log.Error("error initializing resource server", "error", err)`. The second log line is redundant and will produce duplicate `error initializing resource server` entries in the log for every init failure; one of the two should be removed.

title: Integration test now skips postgres instead of being fixed
body: The PR adds a `t.Skip` for `dbType == "postgres"` with a TODO to "fix this test for postgres". The test was presumably failing on Drone for postgres (which is a real CI environment), so the change converts a CI failure into silently-skipped coverage: no production combination is being exercised by this test for postgres any more. Either the test should be fixed for postgres or a tracking issue should be linked so the gap is not lost.

title: BuildIndex loses per-key serialization, allowing same-key races
body: The diff removes `b.cacheMu.Lock(); defer b.cacheMu.Unlock()` from the top of `BuildIndex` and only locks around the final `b.cache[key] = idx` write. Previously, two concurrent calls to `BuildIndex` for the same `key` were serialized, so `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` (lines ~96-102) was only ever invoked once per directory. With the new finer-grained locking, two callers that race through `getOrCreateIndex` for the same key when `size > b.opts.FileThreshold` will both call `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` on the same directory. bleve's New on an already-existing directory either errors or reopens stale state; one call returns an error to a caller even though the index they wanted was successfully created and is sitting in the cache. `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` already has a TODO admitting it has no per-key mutex, so this relaxation of the backend's serialization makes a known race easier to trigger. Consider keeping the exclusive lock around the directory creation (or adding a per-key `sync.Map` / singleflight) and only using the finer-grained lock to protect the cache map mutation.

title: TotalDocs iterates the cache map without holding cacheMu
body: `bleveBackend.TotalDocs` does `for _, v := range b.cache { ... }` with no read-lock on `cacheMu`, while `BuildIndex` writes `b.cache[key] = idx` under `cacheMu`. Go map iteration concurrent with writes panics with "concurrent map iteration and map write". The new `s.log.Info(..., "total_docs", s.search.TotalDocs())` added in `search.go` happens after `group.Wait()` so it is safe today, but `TotalDocs` is part of the `SearchBackend` interface and any future caller (e.g., a metrics endpoint, health check, or test) that invokes it while index construction is in flight will crash the process. Either take `cacheMu.RLock()` for the iteration, or iterate a snapshot of the keys under the lock.

title: Two long-running WatchWriteEvents pollers run for the same backend
body: After this change, both `searchSupport.init` (lines ~202-213 in search.go) and `server.initWatcher` (line 752) each call `s.backend.WatchWriteEvents(...)`, which for the SQL backend (`pkg/storage/unified/sql/backend.go:558`) starts its own 100 ms poller goroutine. The `errgroup` already sets the search index up; now the broadcaster independently starts a second poller querying the same resource history tables. Two pollers every 100 ms doubles DB load, doubles history scans, and produces two independent `mostRecentRV` writers and two event streams. The order swap (initWatcher first vs. search.init first) does not change this — both sequences still leave the search support's watcher running alongside `initWatcher`. The author's stated goal was just to parallelize index build across distinct keys; the duplicate watcher is unrelated and should be removed (let the search support's handler pipe into the broadcaster, or use the broadcaster as the single event source).

title: Postgres integration test now silently skipped with a TODO
body: The diff adds `if dbType == "postgres" { t.Skip(...) }` to the only integration test that exercises the storage server target with a real DB. Combined with the existing `sqlite3` skip, the test is now skipped for every DB type the CI matrix runs against — it provides no coverage. The TODO comment admits the test "works locally" but not in Drone, strongly suggesting the new eager `Init()` in `NewResourceServer` exposes an init-only failure mode that the lazy initialization hid. A `t.Skip` is the wrong fix here: the test should be made to pass for both `Init()` orderings, or split so that the storage-server integration is verified separately for postgres. Otherwise a regression in the eager-init path on postgres will land unnoticed.

title: Eager Init swallows cancelation from the caller's context
body: `NewResourceServer` now passes its locally constructed `ctx` (a `context.WithCancel(context.Background(), ...)` wrapping a static service-account identity) into `s.Init(ctx)`. Inside `Init`, this `ctx` is forwarded to `search.init(ctx)`, which in turn calls `s.storage.GetResourceStats(ctx, ...)` and `s.storage.ListIterator(ctx, ...)` for every namespace being indexed. Those calls now use a context that lives for the lifetime of the server and is only cancelled when `s.Stop` runs — they never see a deadline or the caller's cancellation. That is fine for a production server, but `NewResourceServer` is also called from `InitializeModuleServer` in tests and from any tooling that builds a transient server. The previous per-handler `s.Init(ctx)` propagated the per-request deadline/cancellation, so a hung DB could be aborted by closing the test context. With the eager call, an unresponsive backend during index build will block `NewResourceServer` indefinitely, which in turn blocks module startup with no way to cancel it from outside.

title: Goroutine and resource leak when NewResourceServer init fails
body: After constructing the server struct (which creates a cancellable ctx/cancel pair stored on the struct), NewResourceServer now eagerly calls s.Init(ctx). If Init returns an error (e.g., search.init fails partway through, or s.initWatcher fails), the function logs the error and returns nil, err. Because s is nil and cancel was never invoked, any goroutines that Init started cannot be cleaned up: the s.initWatcher goroutine + SQL poller run on s.ctx and will keep polling the database; the search.init watch goroutine (see search.go) runs on context.Background() and is not tied to s.ctx at all, so it is orphaned regardless. There is no way for the caller of NewResourceServer to stop them. Before this PR Init was idempotently deferred to the first RPC, where they would only be retained on the returned server. The fix is to defer cancel() at the top of NewResourceServer (and ideally make search.init's watchctx derive from s.ctx), so a partial init always tears its goroutines down.

title: search.init's watcher uses context.Background(), preventing server.Stop from stopping it
body: In searchSupport.init the watch is set up with `watchctx := context.Background() // new context?` and the resulting events channel is consumed by `go func() { for { v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v) } }()`. The author even left a question mark in the comment. Because watchctx is background, calling server.Stop (which cancels s.ctx) does not stop this goroutine or its underlying storage backend poller; it will only exit if the storage backend itself is independently stopped. The symmetric watcher created by initWatcher in server.go uses s.ctx and so is cancelled correctly. This asymmetry is also what makes the Init failure leak above worse: even calling cancel after a failed Init cannot reach this watch. search.init should accept and use the long-lived s.ctx (or a child of it) for both WatchWriteEvents and the goroutine, so a single Stop cleans up everything.

title: Concurrent searches for the same NamespacedResource can trigger duplicate full index builds
body: getOrCreateIndex reads s.search.GetIndex (which checks a non-locked-ish cache via RWMutex) and, if nil, calls s.build, which in turn invokes SearchBackend.BuildIndex. There is no per-key synchronization. Two concurrent callers for the same key therefore both see a cache miss, both run the full document builder (potentially listing and indexing millions of rows), both flush, and the second write to b.cache[key] wins. The first caller's *ResourceIndex is still valid, but the cost of building was paid twice and the second build can also starve the watcher of resources. The pre-existing TODO right above the function (`// TODO??? // We want to block while building the index and return the same index for the key`) acknowledges this. The PR's change in bleve.go (releasing cacheMu before building) is correct for different keys but does nothing for same-key races; with the move from lazy to eager init the probability of overlapping first-request races goes up. At minimum the PR should add per-key locking around the GetIndex + BuildIndex sequence (e.g., singleflight.Group, or a sync.Map of per-key *sync.Mutex).

title: Trace propagation fix is inconsistent across the sql backend
body: The PR correctly changes GetResourceStats from `_, span := b.tracer.Start(...)` to `ctx, span := b.tracer.Start(...)` so the span context flows into the WithTx call below it. The same broken pattern is left in place in this same file for WriteEvent (line 158), create (174), update (236), delete (298), ReadResource (353), ListIterator (388), poller (580), listLatestRVs (619), poll (664) and resourceVersionAtomicInc (718). All of them discard the returned ctx, so the OpenTelemetry spans they start are not parents of the SQL calls made inside them. The fix in GetResourceStats was presumably driven by tracing the new eager index build; the same one-line fix should be applied to all the other methods that start a span and then perform work under that context, otherwise half the storage trace tree is broken.

title: Init error is logged twice
body: Init already logs `s.log.Error("error initializing resource server", "error", s.initErr)` inside the s.once.Do block, and the new caller in NewResourceServer then logs the same error again with the same message right before returning nil, err. Pick one site and drop the other to avoid the duplicate entry and to keep the error format consistent with the other NewResourceServer error paths (which only return).

title: BuildIndex still shadows the trace context with its span
body: Unlike search.go and sql/backend.go's GetResourceStats, bleve.go's BuildIndex uses `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, tracingPrexfixBleve+"BuildIndex")` and discards the returned ctx. The same trace-propagation bug the PR is trying to fix elsewhere therefore remains in this hot path: the call to `builder(idx)` (which runs the entire list-iterator + builder loop) does not see the BuildIndex span as its parent, and traces of the index build will be missing the bleve-level span. The same one-character fix (`ctx, span := ...`) should be applied here for consistency with the other files in the PR.

title: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() called without required argument — won't compile
body: The new condition `context.getUser() != null && !isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled` with no arguments, but the only definition in the hierarchy (in `UsernamePasswordForm`) is `protected boolean isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)`. No zero-arg overload exists in `AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator`, `UsernamePasswordForm`, `WebAuthnAuthenticator`, `WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator`, or `AuthenticatorUtils`. This will fail to compile. The intended call is almost certainly `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`, which would also match the surrounding logic (only skip the re-auth form when passkeys are NOT enabled, so the form is shown for passkey re-auth). As written the PR cannot build and the whole change is blocked.

title: Broker fallback path bypassed when conditional passkeys are enabled
body: With the new guard `if (context.getUser() != null && !isConditionalPasskeysEnabled())`, the `hasLinkedBrokers` short-circuit is only evaluated when passkeys are disabled. When a user has no passkey credential but DOES have a linked identity provider, and conditional passkeys are enabled at the realm level, the code falls through to `super.authenticate(context)` and the user is presented with a username-only form from which they cannot complete re-authentication (no passkey available, broker not consulted). The original `if (!this.hasLinkedBrokers(context))` skip-success path needs to remain available in that scenario, e.g. by checking broker availability independently of passkey enablement.

title: UsernamePasswordForm.authenticate now requires webauthnAuth to be non-null in the re-auth path
body: The new unconditional call `if (isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())) { webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context); }` is placed outside the `else` branch and uses the new helper that only returns true when `webauthnAuth != null`, so the NPE guard is preserved. However, the no-arg `UsernamePasswordForm()` constructor (still present in the file) leaves `webauthnAuth = null`; if any flow instantiates the authenticator via the deprecated no-arg constructor and then enters the re-auth branch (where `context.getUser() != null`), the helper short-circuits and the code works, but the dead `webauthnAuth` reference in the old `if (webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled())` block in the same method has been removed. The old guard protected against the no-arg-constructor case; the new code relies entirely on `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled` returning false when `webauthnAuth` is null, which is correct, but this invariant should be asserted or the no-arg constructor removed to avoid future regressions.

title: WebAuthn form re-rendered on every password error even when no passkey is registered
body: `challenge(AuthenticationFlowContext, String, String)` now calls `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` whenever `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())` is true, i.e. whenever a user is in context and passkeys are realm-enabled. This is invoked from `badPasswordHandler` in `AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator` for every wrong-password attempt. For users who have no WebAuthn/passwordless credential registered, the page will still render the conditional-UI WebAuthn affordance and `WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator.fillContextForm` will set `ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI=true` and issue a fresh challenge. This is confusing UX and potentially reveals feature availability. The new `PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest.reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey` only covers the case where passkeys are disabled at realm level; there is no test for the case where passkeys are realm-enabled but the specific user has no passkey credential, and the new code will incorrectly show the WebAuthn option in that scenario.

title: USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH visibility widened from protected to public
body: The constant `USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH` is changed from `protected static final` to `public static final` solely so that `AuthenticatorUtils` in a different package can read it via a static import. This expands the public API surface of the abstract authenticator for an internal coordination flag. The cleaner alternative is to keep the constant package-private (or protected) and expose a small accessor (e.g. `isUserAlreadySetBeforeUsernamePasswordAuth` is already protected and could be made public/util-style), or have `AuthenticatorUtils` accept the boolean as a parameter rather than reaching into the constant. As-is, any external code can now read and write the auth note under that key, which is an internal protocol between authenticators.

title: setupReauthenticationInUsernamePasswordFormError silently no-ops when auth note is absent
body: The new `setupReauthenticationInUsernamePasswordFormError` reads the auth note and only sets the form attributes if `Boolean.parseBoolean(...)` is true. If the note was never set, or was set to a non-boolean value (e.g. a string from a buggy caller — note that the producers in `UsernamePasswordForm` use the literal string `"true"`, which is fine, but the constant is now public so any caller can write anything), the method silently does nothing without logging. Given this is being called from error paths in both `badPasswordHandler` and `WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator.createErrorResponse`, a missing or malformed value should at minimum be logged at debug level so a maintainer can diagnose why a re-auth form is rendering with the username field visible.

title: Assertion against driver.findElement is unreachable on the success path
body: In `reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey`, the test does `MatcherAssert.assertThat(driver.findElement(By.xpath("//form[@id='webauth']")), nullValue());` followed by `fail(...)`. `Selenium WebDriver.findElement` never returns null — it throws `NoSuchElementException` when the element is absent, so the `assertThat` line is never reached in the expected case; the `fail` is also unreachable because the catch block already swallows `Exception`. The test passes only because the `catch (Exception nsee)` block catches the `NoSuchElementException`. Use `assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, () -> driver.findElement(...))` (which is the pattern used elsewhere in the same file before this PR) for clarity, and remove the dead `assertThat` + `fail`.

title: No test for re-authentication when user has passkeys disabled at user level
body: The new `reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey` covers the case where passkeys are disabled at the realm level, and `webauthnLoginWithExternalKey_reauthenticationWithPasswordOrPasskey` covers a user with both passkey and password. There is no test for the intermediate case: a realm with passkeys enabled and a user who has the passkeyless policy applied but has not actually registered a WebAuthn credential. Given the new code paths in `UsernamePasswordForm.authenticate` and `UsernamePasswordForm.challenge` will render the WebAuthn conditional UI for such a user on re-auth (because `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())` is true and the WebAuthn flow does not check whether the user actually has a WebAuthn credential at that point), this scenario should be explicitly covered to prevent a regression where the form is shown but no authenticator can satisfy it.

title: Compilation error: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() called without required UserModel argument
body: The condition `!isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` invokes the method with zero arguments, but the only method available in `UsernamePasswordForm` (the parent class) is `protected boolean isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)`. There is no no-arg overload defined anywhere in the codebase, so this line fails to compile and the PR cannot be built. The caller almost certainly meant `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`.

title: Conditional passkeys UI not initialized on initial (user-less) login
body: The new check `if (isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()))` relies on a helper that includes `user != null` in its predicate. As a result `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` is never invoked when the user has not yet been identified on the first visit to the username/password form. The pre-PR code (inside the `else` branch) unconditionally called `fillContextForm` when `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()`, which is the behavior the existing test `PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest#passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey` (and the equivalent test in `PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest`) still relies on. Both tests assert that `//form[@id='webauth']` is present and that `usernameAutocomplete` equals `"username webauthn"` on the very first login page before any user is set, so this regression will make those tests fail. The intent of the PR is to add passkey support for re-authentication (user already present), not to remove it for the initial login. The fix is to gate `fillContextForm` on `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()` only, dropping the user-presence requirement (or splitting the helper into a realm-level predicate and a user-level predicate).

title: Compile error: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() called without required argument
body: In `UsernameForm.authenticate()` the expression `!isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` invokes a zero-argument method, but the only declaration of that name in the inheritance hierarchy is `protected boolean isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` (added in this PR in UsernamePasswordForm.java at line 160). There is no no-arg overload and no static import of one, so the project will not compile and the build will fail. The intended call is almost certainly `!isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`, mirroring how the helper is used in UsernamePasswordForm.java.

title: Unreachable assertion: driver.findElement throws before the matcher can run
body: In `reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey()` the pattern `try { MatcherAssert.assertThat(driver.findElement(By.xpath("//form[@id='webauth']")), nullValue()); fail("Not expected to have webauthn button"); } catch (Exception nsee) { /* expected */ }` does not actually assert absence. Selenium's `driver.findElement` throws `NoSuchElementException` as soon as the element is missing, so the `assertThat(..., nullValue())` and `fail(...)` lines are unreachable and the catch block silently swallows the exception. The same try/catch is duplicated around line 311. The tests therefore pass regardless of whether the webauthn form is really absent. Use `driver.findElements(...)` and assert the resulting list is empty.

title: WebAuthn form data not populated for initial login (user not yet identified)
body: In `UsernamePasswordForm.authenticate()` the new guard `if (isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()))` requires `user != null`, because the helper at line 160 is `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null`. The previous code path called `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` whenever passkeys were enabled, regardless of whether a user was already in the context. The new check therefore skips `fillContextForm` for the user-null branch (initial login, no user yet identified), so the login page no longer receives the WebAuthn challenge (`AUTH_CHALLENGE_NOTE`), `CHALLENGE`, `RP_ID`, `ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI` and friends. The new tests `webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey_reauthentication` in PasskeysUsernameFormTest and `webauthnLoginWithExternalKey_reauthentication` in PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest both call `oauth.openLoginForm()` with no user yet identified and immediately expect a successful passkey login (`appPage.assertCurrent()`); without the server-side challenge the WebAuthn response cannot be verified and those tests will fail. The accompanying comment "setup webauthn data when passkeys enabled" also no longer matches the implemented condition, which additionally requires the user to be identified.

title: Broken cleanup registration uses literal 'alias' instead of actual IDP alias
body: In the new test `testCacheIDPForLogin`, each cleanup is registered as `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)`. The literal string "alias" does not match any identity provider actually created in the test (which uses aliases like "idp-alias-0" through "idp-alias-19"). `identityProviders().get("alias")` therefore returns null, and the bound method reference `null::remove` will throw a NullPointerException when the cleanup is invoked, or the cleanup will silently be a no-op. The cleanup should use the actual alias (e.g., `"idp-alias-" + i`). This is copied from the existing `testCacheIDPByOrg` test (line 303) but the new test propagates the bug to 20 more IDPs, increasing the risk of test pollution and teardown failures across the suite.

title: Inconsistent model wrapping causes login predicate to evaluate differently on original vs updated
body: In `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate(IdentityProviderModel original, IdentityProviderModel updated)`, `original` comes from `getById(model.getInternalId())` and is therefore wrapped in `OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel` (the anonymous subclass defined at line 434 that overrides `isEnabled()` to also check the linked organization's enabled status). The `updated` parameter, however, is the raw `model` passed to `update()` and is NOT wrapped. `IdentityProviderStorageProvider.LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate()` uses `IdentityProviderModel::isEnabled`, which is polymorphic: on `original` it dispatches to the overridden (organization-aware) `isEnabled()`, but on `updated` it dispatches to the raw `isEnabled()`. The predicate therefore returns different values for the same logical IDP depending on which side of the comparison is being evaluated, leading to inconsistent invalidation decisions. For example, if an IDP is linked to a currently disabled organization, `test(original)` returns false but `test(updated)` returns true, causing both early-return guards to fail and triggering a wasteful cache invalidation. In race conditions where the organization is enabled at `getById` time but disabled by the time the predicate runs (or vice versa), the asymmetry can also produce missed invalidations, leaving stale entries in the login cache. The fix is to wrap it before evaluation (e.g., `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(updated)`), or to use a non-polymorphic raw-enabled check consistently inside the invalidation helpers.

title: REALM_ONLY cache searchKey includes organizationId unnecessarily
body: In `getForLogin(FetchMode mode, String organizationId)`, the searchKey is computed as `organizationId != null ? organizationId : ""`. However, the underlying JPA implementation explicitly sets `ORGANIZATION_ID=null` in its search options for `FetchMode.REALM_ONLY` (and never consults the input `organizationId` in that branch), so the result is identical regardless of the supplied `organizationId`. By baking `organizationId` into the searchKey, callers that legitimately pass non-null values for `REALM_ONLY` (the Javadoc explicitly says `organizationId` is ignored when `mode` is `REALM_ONLY`) get a fresh, separate `IdentityProviderListQuery` entry every time, defeating the cache for any caller that does not happen to pass `null`. The searchKey should be fixed to a constant (e.g. always "") for `FetchMode.REALM_ONLY` so all REALM_ONLY lookups share one cache entry.

title: Broken IDP cleanup in testCacheIDPForLogin causes test pollution
body: In the new `testCacheIDPForLogin` test, every `create` call is followed by `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove);`. The literal string `"alias"` is not an alias of any IDP created by this test (the aliases are `idp-alias-0`..`idp-alias-19` and `idp-alias-20`), so when the cleanup runs, `get("alias")` returns `null` and `null::remove` throws a NullPointerException. None of the 21 IDPs created by this test are actually removed, so they leak into subsequent tests (and into the IDP alias cache of the test realm), which can break other organization cache tests. The same pattern is repeated in the new test on lines 381 and 425. The alias variable should be used (e.g. `idpRep.getAlias()` or a captured `final String alias = "idp-alias-" + i`).

title: Broken IDP cleanup in testCacheIDPForLogin causes test pollution (second occurrence)
body: Same issue as the finding on line 381: `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove);` uses the literal string `"alias"`, which does not match any IDP created by the test. The created `idp-alias-20` is never cleaned up, leaking into the realm's IDP store. The cleanup should reference the actual alias of the IDP just created.

title: getLoginPredicate dereferences idp.getConfig() without null check
body: The newly added clause `.and(idp -> idp.getOrganizationId() == null || Boolean.parseBoolean(idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC)))` assumes `idp.getConfig()` is never null. The `IdentityProviderModel` `config` field is mutable and can be set to `null`; `getConfig()` does not lazily initialize it in all versions, and callers using the SPI (e.g. test code, custom providers, internal `update()` flows that operate on partially populated models) may produce a model with a null `config` map, causing an NPE here. Because this predicate is invoked from `registerIDPLoginInvalidation`/`registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate` on every IDP `create`/`update`/`remove`, a single such model will crash the whole IDP write path. Either guard `getConfig()` against null (e.g. `idp.getConfig() != null && Boolean.parseBoolean(idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC))`) or normalize the field in the model.

title: remove() always queries DB for the IDP, even when the alias is already cached
body: The new line `IdentityProviderModel storedIdp = idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias);` is executed unconditionally on every `remove()` call, but in the cache-hit branch (lines 105-108) the `CachedIdentityProvider cached` is already available from the alias cache. The cached IDP could be passed to `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(...)` on line 111 (mirroring how `registerIDPInvalidation(cached.getIdentityProvider())` is already done on line 107), avoiding the extra DB round-trip in the warm-cache case. Previously, `idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)` was only invoked inside the `isInvalid(cacheKey)` branch; the hoisted fetch now runs on every remove, which is a regression for the common case where the alias cache is populated.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the wrong provider
body: The method is documented to return the BouncyCastle security provider, but the implementation returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`. On a standard JVM this is the SUN (or SUNJSSE) provider, not BouncyCastle. Any caller that relies on this method to obtain BouncyCastle (e.g. to register it with `Security.addProvider` or to pass it to JCA factories) will get a different provider and silently produce wrong crypto results (e.g. signature verification failures, or worse, signatures produced with a non-BC provider being treated as BC). Since this is the only implementation in the new `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` that is supposed to work without the full Keycloak crypto stack, it must either return a real BouncyCastleProvider (or null/throw if BC is not available), not the default-keystore provider.

title: Dead code in concatenatedRSToASN1DER wastes allocations
body: In `concatenatedRSToASN1DER`, the two calls `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` create new ASN1Encoder instances, write integers into their internal ByteArrayOutputStreams, and then discard the results without ever calling `toByteArray()`. They have no effect on the returned value. The call sites inside `writeDerSeq(...)` already create fresh encoders for the same integers. These two lines are pure dead code that allocate two extra ByteArrayOutputStreams per signature conversion. They should be removed.

title: Test constructor declares throws Exception and does shared setup
body: `ECDSAAlgorithmTest` generates the EC KeyPair in its constructor and declares `throws Exception`. JUnit 4 test class constructors should not throw checked exceptions; setup that can throw must be done in a `@Before`/`@BeforeClass` method. With the current code, if `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` ever fails (e.g. on a JVM without EC support, or under a restricted security policy), the JUnit runner will report the failure as a framework error rather than as a test failure, and the per-instance key pair means a key generated by a previous test run is never reused even when that would be desirable. Move the KeyPair generation into a `@Before` method (or a `@BeforeClass` static field) and let the test methods just do the work.

title: Dynamic string passed as format string to logger.debugf
body: The new code builds a `StringBuilder` containing the ignored providers and then calls `logger.debugf(builder.toString())`. JBoss Logger's `debugf(String, Object...)` treats the first argument as a printf-style format string. If any provider class name (or anything concatenated into the builder) ever contained a `%` character, the call would throw `IllegalFormatException` instead of logging the message, and the entire `init()` call would fail. Use `logger.debug(builder.toString())` (or `logger.debugf("%s", builder)`) so the message is logged verbatim.

title: Indefinite-length handling in ASN1Decoder.readLength is inappropriate for DER
body: The decoder returns `-1` for the BER indefinite-length form (length byte `0x80`). ECDSA signatures are required to be DER-encoded, where indefinite-length encoding is forbidden, so this branch is unreachable. More importantly, the value `-1` is then used in `readSequence()` as `while (length > 0) { ... length = length - bytes.length; }`, which is an infinite loop because `-1` is never `> 0` and `length - bytes.length` is always negative, so the loop body never executes and the method returns an empty list. While DER won't trigger this, the decoder is also fed other inputs (e.g. the inner INTEGER TLVs in `asn1derToConcatenatedRS`) and any caller that ever sends a BER-style indefinite-length value will get a silent zero-element list instead of an error. Either throw an IOException for indefinite length (DER requires definite length) or document and handle `-1` explicitly.

title: Duplicate junit and hamcrest test dependencies
body: The diff adds junit and hamcrest test dependencies at lines 61-71, but these dependencies already exist earlier in the file (visible in the full content at the same coordinates). Maven allows duplicate dependency declarations but it is a defect: it produces a confusing POM, may trigger Maven warnings on some versions, and makes future maintenance error-prone (e.g., changing scope in one place but not the other). The added junit/hamcrest block should be removed since the dependencies are already declared.

title: Dead code: discarded ASN1Encoder writes in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
body: In the anonymous ECDSACryptoProvider implementation, the two statements `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` (lines 114-115) create new ASN1Encoder instances, write a full INTEGER TLV into their internal ByteArrayOutputStream, and then discard the result. The actual DER sequence is built immediately after by the four chained `ASN1Encoder.create().write(...)` calls inside `writeDerSeq`. The discarded writes are wasted allocations and I/O and should be deleted to avoid misleading readers into thinking they are part of the encoding.

title: logger.debugf called with a non-format string, will throw on class names containing %
body: `logger.debugf(builder.toString())` passes a runtime-built string as the format argument. JBoss Logger's `debugf(String, Object...)` interprets the first argument as a `printf`-style format and expects additional varargs matching any `%` specifiers. If any class name returned by `ServiceLoader` contains a `%` (legal in JVM class names), `MissingFormatArgumentException` or similar will be thrown every time more than one provider is found, surfacing as an unexpected stack trace at debug level and, depending on JUL/LogManager configuration, potentially being promoted to a higher level. Use `logger.debug(builder.toString())` or `logger.debugf("%s", builder.toString())` instead.

title: Most CryptoProvider methods throw UnsupportedOperationException; authz-client standalone usage is broken
body: `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` is registered as the SPI provider for `org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider` in `authz/client/src/main/resources/META-INF/services/...`. However, nearly every method on the interface (`getAlgorithmProvider`, `getCertificateUtils`, `getPemUtils`, `getOCSPProver`, `getIdentityExtractorProvider`, `getEcdsaCryptoProvider().getPublicFromPrivate`, `createECParams`, `getKeyPairGen`, `getKeyFactory`, `getAesCbcCipher`, `getAesGcmCipher`, `getSecretKeyFact`, `getX509CertFactory`, `getCertStore`, `getCertPathBuilder`, `getSignature`, `wrapFactoryForTruststore`) is implemented as `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet.")`. The authz-client uses these facilities (notably `getSignature`, `getCertificateUtils`, `getPemUtils`, `getKeyPairGen`/`getKeyFactory`) when authenticating with signed-JWT client credentials and when parsing keys/certificates. When this module is used standalone (the documented intent), any such operation will throw UnsupportedOperationException at runtime, breaking client credential flows that involve private-key JWT, mutual TLS, or PEM key material. The PR should either implement these methods or document explicitly that the authz-client only supports the subset used for ECDSA R/S <-> DER conversion and fail fast at init time otherwise.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JCE default provider, not BouncyCastle
body: `getBouncyCastleProvider()` is implemented as `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`. This returns whatever JCE provider supplies the default keystore type on the host JVM (typically SUN/SunPKCS11/SunJSSE), not BouncyCastle. Callers that explicitly rely on a BC provider (e.g. to ask BC for algorithms/curves not present in the SUN provider) will silently get the SUN provider instead and may fail with `NoSuchAlgorithmException` later. Either return an actual BouncyCastleProvider (as `DefaultCryptoProvider` does) or, if BC is intentionally not bundled in the authz-client, throw UnsupportedOperationException so the failure mode is obvious.

title: readSequence silently returns empty list for indefinite-length sequences and does not check for end-of-contents
body: `readSequence` reads a length and then loops `while (length > 0)`. When `readLength()` returns `-1` for indefinite-length encoding (length byte `0x80`), the loop never executes and the method returns an empty `ArrayList`. The caller in `AuthzClientCryptoProvider.asn1derToConcatenatedRS` then fails with the misleading error "Invalid sequence with size different to 2". While DER (X.690 §10.1) forbids indefinite lengths for sequences, accepting BER signatures that use them would require consuming elements until the end-of-contents octets `0x00 0x00`. As written, any non-DER BER-encoded signature coming from another library will produce a confusing error rather than a clear one.

title: Test only covers DER -> concat -> DER -> concat, not the inverse and not the values themselves
body: The `test(ECDSAAlgorithm)` helper signs data with the JCE provider (DER output), converts to concatenated R/S, then back to DER and back to R/S, asserting the two concatenated forms are equal. It never verifies (a) the direct concatenatedRSToASN1DER round-trip with a known concatenated input, (b) that the produced DER bytes decode to the same BigInteger r,s values produced by the JCE Signature, and (c) that the produced concatenated bytes, when fed back into `Signature.verify` via `Signature.getInstance("NONEwithECDSA")` with the same algorithm, actually verify. Without (c) the test cannot catch sign-magnitude vs. two's-complement bugs, leading-zero handling bugs, or off-by-one in the `arraySize = len + 1` shift (which always prepends a 0 byte and can produce non-minimal DER).

title: getBouncyCastleProvider() does not return BouncyCastle
body: Despite its name, `getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns the Provider that backs the JVM's default keystore type (typically SUN or SunJSSE), not BouncyCastle: `return KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider();`. This is a deliberate workaround because the authz-client module does not depend on BouncyCastle, but the method name promises a BC Provider. Any caller that selects algorithms specific to BouncyCastle (e.g. certain EC curves, RSA-PSS variants, JOSE algorithms only BC exposes) will silently get the JCA default provider and may behave unexpectedly. The misleading contract should at least be renamed (e.g. `getDefaultProvider()`), or the method should throw UnsupportedOperationException to be consistent with the rest of this class.

title: Dead ASN1Encoder invocations in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
readSequence silently mishandles indefinite-length and over-long TLVs
body:
`readSequence()` does two unsafe things:
1.
