Whether user-storage credentials appear in `getFederatedCredentialsStream` is determined by the user storage provider implementing `CredentialProvider#getCredentials`; for providers that don't, this method will silently miss the federated credential. The doc should describe what `getFederatedCredentialsStream` is expected to return rather than asserting that all user storage providers will be hit.

title: Federated recovery codes not marked as used after validation
body: In `isValid()` for `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE`, the implementation returns true as soon as the input matches any raw key in `myUser.recoveryCodes.getCredentialData()` but never mutates the stored credential to remove or flag the consumed code. Recovery codes are one-time-use credentials; the local `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider` marks codes as used when validated. Here the same code can be reused indefinitely, so the security guarantee of recovery codes is lost whenever the user lives in federated storage.

title: Federated recovery-codes credential can never be removed
body: Because `isValid()` does not track per-code consumption, the `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` built by `getCredentials()` from the stored raw `credentialData` will always have `allCodesUsed() == false`. Consequently the branch in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.isRecoveryAuthnCodeInputValid` that calls `credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(...)` will never run for a federated user, so the recovery-codes credential sticks around forever, the user is never re-prompted via `CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES`, and the user storage is never asked to delete the credential.

title: Raw recovery codes persisted in federated credentialData
body: `updateCredential` saves the JSON produced by `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential` (which serializes the raw codes) straight into `credentialData` without hashing. The local `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider` hashes the codes before storage (it relies on `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode` with `NOM_ALGORITHM_TO_HASH`). Storing raw codes in `credentialData` diverges from that posture, so any path that exposes `credentialData` (DB dumps, debug logging, serialized credential model) leaks the user's recovery codes in plaintext. The model reconstructed by `getCredentials()` will also carry these raw codes through `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues`, so callers that read `RecoveryCode.getValue()` get the cleartext code.

title: Test does not verify single-use semantics or credential cleanup
body: `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` only exercises a single successful entry of one recovery code. Given that `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.isRecoveryAuthnCodeInputValid` now also targets federated credentials (via `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential`), the test should additionally assert that (a) re-entering the same recovery code is rejected by the federated validator, and (b) once the last code is consumed, the federated credential is removed and the user is asked to configure new codes. Without these assertions the two real bugs above are not caught by CI.

title: removeStoredCredentialById does not work for federated recovery codes credential
body: After switching from `getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream` (local-only) to `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` (federated-first, then local), the authenticator still calls `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())`. `removeStoredCredentialById` only removes from local Keycloak storage, so when the recovery codes credential lives in user/federated storage and all codes are used, the credential is never removed from the user storage. Result: spent codes remain valid in the user storage backend (any code still in the list can still be presented and matched by `isValid`); only the required-action fallback masks the problem. This is a regression introduced by the diff at line 80 vs. the original.

title: NPE in getCredentials when user is unknown to storage
body: The new `getCredentials` override stores the lookup in `var myUser = getMyUser(user);` and then dereferences `myUser.recoveryCodes` (and `myUser.otp`) without a null check. `getMyUser` returns `null` whenever the user is not in the in-memory map, so any call for a non-existent user (e.g., lookup paths that probe storage) throws NullPointerException. The earlier code path went through `AbstractUserAdapterFederatedStorage`'s default `getCredentials`, which tolerated missing users. Either guard with `if (myUser != null)` or match the previous null-tolerant behavior.

title: disableCredentialType silently ignores recovery-codes and leaks stale codes
body: `disableCredentialType` was extended to support OTP but not `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE`. Calling `user.disableCredentialType([RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE])` (e.g., from admin REST or `UserResource.disableCredentialType`) returns without doing anything for this storage, but the admin endpoint reports success. The recovery codes remain usable in the user storage. The parallel `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream` (line 254) was also not updated to advertise recovery-codes as a disableable type, so the admin console still lists it. Both pieces must be updated together so disabling the credential actually removes/clears it and so admins can see it as disableable.

title: NoSuchElementException when user has no recovery codes
body: The constructor calls `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user).get()` directly. If the user has no recovery codes credential (in either federated or local storage), `Optional.get()` throws `NoSuchElementException` and the login form rendering for the recovery code page fails. The bean should check `isPresent()` and render gracefully (e.g., the page should not be shown at all, or the bean should provide a default) instead of throwing. This was previously masked by `getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(...).findFirst().get()` with the same risk; the refactor was a chance to fix it.

title: Typo in authenticator config alias
body: In `configureBrowserFlowWithRecoveryAuthnCodes`, the alias is set to `"delayed-suthenticator-config"` (sic). The authenticator provider id just above is `"delayed-authenticator"`, so the alias should be `"delayed-authenticator-config"`. The typo makes the test config alias inconsistent with the provider it configures and is misleading when debugging the flow.

title: Unnecessary credential provider lookup when user storage handles recovery codes
body: `createRecoveryCodesCredential` always calls `session.getProvider(CredentialProvider.class, "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes")` at line 116, but the provider is only needed in the `else` branch when `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` returns false. When the user storage does accept the credential, this provider lookup is wasted. Move the provider lookup into the `else` branch to avoid the unnecessary work; this also matches the cleaner conditional pattern.

title: Raw recovery codes passed to user storage instead of hashed values
body: `createRecoveryCodesCredential` serializes the raw, unhashed `generatedCodes` to JSON and hands them to `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` via the third constructor argument of `UserCredentialModel`. The user storage is then expected to persist them; nothing in this helper forces or even encourages the user storage to hash them. Meanwhile, the local-storage path passes the `credentialModel` (which `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues`/the recovery-codes provider hashes internally). The new test `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage` follows this contract literally and stores raw codes as plaintext (`setCredentialData(input.getChallengeResponse())`), so any user storage that follows the same pattern will end up with raw recovery codes in their backend. Consider passing already-hashed values (the same set the local provider would persist) to the user storage so both paths store hashed values, and/or document the requirement that user storage providers must hash before persisting.

title: NPE risk when generated-codes hidden field is missing
body: `processAction` does `generatedCodesString.equals(...)`, `generatedAtTimeString.equals(...)`, and `generatedCodesString.split(",")` without null-checking `generatedCodesString` or `generatedAtTimeString`. If the form is submitted without those hidden inputs (or with empty values), `NullPointerException` is thrown and the user is bounced back via the default error path instead of the deliberate "authn codes have been tampered" branch. Guard against null/empty before calling `.equals(...)`/`.split(...)`.

title: Reader thread is never joined before the assertion
body: In createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti(), the reader thread is started with `new Thread(...).start()` but never joined. After the main thread calls `deletedAll.set(true)`, the reader thread may still be in the middle of a `managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(...)` call. Any exception thrown by that in-flight call is added to `caughtExceptions` AFTER `assertThat(caughtExceptions, Matchers.empty())` runs, so the test will pass even when the fix is missing or broken. Conversely, after the test method returns the reader thread can keep running and access the admin client / realm during teardown. The thread should be retained as a variable and `Thread.join()` should be called (e.g. after setting `deletedAll.set(true)`) before the assertion. Additionally, the thread should be marked as a daemon or otherwise prevented from outliving the test.

title: Other GroupAdapter methods still NPE when the cached group has been deleted
body: The patch only null-guards `getSubGroupsCount()`, but three `getSubGroupsStream` overloads (lines 254-257, 260-263, 266-269) still call `modelSupplier.get()` directly. In the exact same concurrent-deletion scenario that the patch targets (`cacheSession.getGroupDelegate().getGroupById(realm, cached.getId())` returning null), these methods will dereference the null and throw NPE, leaving the reported bug only partially fixed. Either apply the same null-handling pattern (and ideally also handle the symmetric case via `getDelegateForUpdate()` like `getRoleMappingsStream`/`getSubGroupsStream` do when a referenced role/subGroup is missing) or at least guard all three `modelSupplier.get()` call sites consistently.

title: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() is inconsistent with the rest of the class
body: All other paths in GroupAdapter that discover the underlying entity is gone (see `getRoleMappingsStream` at lines 206-210 and `getSubGroupsStream` at lines 242-245) react by calling `getDelegateForUpdate()`, which throws `IllegalStateException("Not found in database")`. `getSubGroupsCount()` now silently returns null instead, which is silently inconsistent with those paths and changes the contract of an existing interface method (`Long` is nullable, but no other caller handles a null count gracefully). Pick one behavior and apply it consistently across the class, otherwise concurrent code paths can produce different exception/null behavior depending on which method is invoked.

title: Test does not actually exercise the getSubGroupsCount() NPE path it claims to fix
body: The new `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti()` test only calls `managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(null, 0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, true)` with `briefRepresentation=true`. Brief group representations do not include subgroups or a subgroup count, so they do not invoke `GroupAdapter.getSubGroupsCount()` at all. As a result the test would pass even if the `getSubGroupsCount()` null-guard were reverted, so it does not actually regress-test the fix in this PR. A direct, targeted regression test (e.g. create a group, look it up so a `GroupAdapter` is cached, delete the underlying row, then call `getSubGroupsCount()` and assert it does not throw NPE) is needed to meaningfully cover the bug.

title: Reader thread is never joined before assertion
body: In createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti(), the spawned reader thread runs `managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(...)` in a loop until `deletedAll` is observed true, but the main thread never calls `Thread.join()` (or otherwise awaits the reader) before `assertThat(caughtExceptions, Matchers.empty())`. Because the REST call is synchronous but can take nontrivial time, the reader thread may still be executing a `groups()` call when the main thread performs the assertion. As a result, an NPE thrown by the reader thread can land in `caughtExceptions` only after the assertion has already passed (or, conversely, the test can pass simply because the timing race was lost on this run). Without a join (or an explicit CountDownLatch/await), the assertion does not actually prove the bug is fixed. The thread should be joined, and `deletedAll` should be set after the join is set up so the reader can observe the latch, not the main thread.

title: Null-guard added to getSubGroupsCount but not to other modelSupplier.get() call sites
body: getSubGroupsCount() was fixed to do `GroupModel model = modelSupplier.get(); return model == null ? null : model.getSubGroupsCount();` precisely because `modelSupplier.get()` (which delegates to `getGroupModel()` returning null when the underlying group is concurrently deleted) can produce a null. The same `modelSupplier.get()` is used unguarded in getSubGroupsStream(String,Integer,Integer) at line 256, getSubGroupsStream(Integer,Integer) at line 262, and getSubGroupsStream(String,Boolean,Integer,Integer) at line 268, all of the form `return modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)`. Under the same concurrent-deletion scenario these will still throw NPE. Either the fix should be applied consistently to all four methods, or `LazyModel` should be changed so that a null result is converted into a stable, non-NPE-throwing value (e.g., returning an empty stream) and the special case removed from each caller.

title: Test does not exercise the path that NPE'd (getSubGroupsCount)
body: The reader thread calls `managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(null, 0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, true)` with `briefRepresentation=true`. The NPE fixed in this PR is in GroupAdapter.getSubGroupsCount(), which is only invoked from GroupUtils.populateGroupHierarchyFromSubGroups when `subGroupsCount=true` (e.g., from the admin UI groups endpoint, not the default REST `groups` listing). If the brief-listing code path does not call getSubGroupsCount, the test will not actually reproduce the regression it claims to fix and the PR could pass CI while still shipping a broken getSubGroupsCount path. The test should either invoke the endpoint that calls populateGroupHierarchyFromSubGroups with subGroupsCount=true, or directly invoke getSubGroupsCount on a GroupAdapter that has been concurrently invalidated, so that a future regression in the fixed method is caught.

title: getSubGroupsCount can still throw IllegalStateException on concurrent deletion
body: Even after the null-guard, `if (isUpdated()) return updated.getSubGroupsCount();` is reached only after isUpdated() itself. isUpdated() (lines 70-76) calls `cacheSession.getGroupDelegate().getGroupById(...)` and throws `IllegalStateException("Not found in database")` when `invalidated` is true but the group has been deleted. So the documented scenario (a group being accessed concurrently with its deletion) still produces an exception here, just a different one. If the goal of the fix is to make concurrent delete+read not throw, the null-guard should be at the top of the method (e.g., `GroupModel m = getGroupModel(); if (m == null) return null;`) and isUpdated()'s IllegalStateException should be downgraded or guarded, otherwise callers may continue to see exceptions and the test (which catches `Exception`) might still observe a failure via the related IllegalStateException rather than via the originally reported NPE.

title: NPE fix is incomplete; sibling methods still dereference potentially-null model
body: The PR patches only `getSubGroupsCount()` to guard against a null from `modelSupplier.get()`. The three `getSubGroupsStream(...)` overloads immediately below (lines 256, 262, 268) still do `return modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` and `getGroupModel()` itself (line 299) returns `cacheSession.getGroupDelegate().getGroupById(realm, cached.getId())` which is null when the underlying group has just been deleted concurrently. After the partial fix, those code paths will still throw NPE for exactly the scenario the PR is supposed to fix, so callers that ask for the subgroup stream (e.g. UI / admin endpoints that walk the group tree) remain broken.

title: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() changes semantics and may still NPE downstream
body: `GroupModel.getSubGroupsCount()` previously either returned a count or threw. Now it silently returns `null`. The existing caller (`GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount`) forwards that to `GroupRepresentation.setSubGroupCount(group.getSubGroupsCount())`. If `setSubGroupCount` does not accept null, the NPE just moves one frame up the stack; if it does, callers of the admin REST API can now see `subGroupCount: null` where they previously got a real number. Either way this is a silent contract change that should be called out and not buried in a one-line null-check.

title: Background reader thread is never joined; the assertion races the worker
body: The test starts a reader thread that loops on `while (!deletedAll.get())` and stores any thrown exception in `caughtExceptions`. The Thread reference is discarded (no field, no `join()`). After `deletedAll.set(true)` the test immediately asserts `caughtExceptions.isEmpty()`. There is a real race: the reader may still be inside an in-flight `groups(...)` HTTP call when the flag flips, and the exception from that final call can be added to `caughtExceptions` AFTER the assertion has already evaluated. The test should keep the Thread in a field and `join()` it before asserting.

title: Test uses brief representation and may not exercise the fixed code path
body: The reproducer calls `managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(null, 0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, true)` with `briefRepresentation = true`. Brief group representations typically do not populate `subGroupCount`, so the patched `GroupAdapter.getSubGroupsCount()` (and the NPE path) may never be reached. As written the test only proves that listing groups by `groups()` does not throw; it does not prove the actual bug from #40368 is fixed. The test should call an endpoint or method that explicitly reads the subgroup count while deletion is in progress (e.g. fetch a full representation, or invoke `getSubGroupsCount()` on the cached group).

title: 100 groups are created without registering cleanup
body: `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti` creates up to 100 groups and stores their ids in a local list, but never calls `managedRealm.cleanup().add(...)` for any of them. If the test fails before the deletion loop completes (or before the thread is joined), all the created groups remain attached to the realm and pollute subsequent tests. Each successful `groups().add(group)` should be paired with `managedRealm.cleanup().add(r -> r.groups().group(uuid).remove())`.

title: Test relies on timing; the concurrent read may complete before any delete happens
body: The reader thread loops while `deletedAll` is false, but each loop iteration is a single HTTP `GET`. If the reader finishes a request just before `deletedAll` is set true, or simply iterates only a few times before the 100 deletes complete, there may be no overlap at all between read and delete and the test never exercises the concurrent path. The test would be more deterministic if it blocked deletion until the reader thread signalled that it had started, or if it performed deletes interleaved with reads inside a controlled loop rather than depending on scheduling.

title: Misleading "performance optimization" comment in BasePaginator
body: The comment block on lines 180-182 claims a "Performance optimization: For high-traffic scenarios, allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination without full dataset scanning". However, the only change made is `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`, which simply clamps a negative forward offset to zero. That is a defensive correctness change, not a performance optimization, and backward pagination is unchanged. The comment misleads reviewers about what the diff does.

title: Negative-offset branch is not a performance optimization and can regress DB cost
body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, the `enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0` branch does `start_offset = cursor.offset` and then `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`. Django cannot translate a negative lower bound on an unsliced queryset into a SQL LIMIT/OFFSET; it evaluates the queryset up to `stop` and then drops the tail in Python. This fetches strictly more rows from the database than `queryset[0:limit+extra]`, which is the opposite of the claimed "efficient bidirectional pagination without full dataset scanning". The branch should either be removed, or replaced with an actual SQL-level implementation (e.g. `(SELECT ... LIMIT N OFFSET 0)` subquery), or at minimum restricted so it cannot be triggered from network input.

title: Misleading "permissions checked at queryset level" comment
body: The comment "This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level" inside OptimizedCursorPaginator implies the paginator itself is safe to expose with negative offsets because callers will filter. The paginator class is generic and has no contract requiring callers to apply row-level filtering. Any future reuse in a different endpoint that forgets to scope the queryset would silently leak rows from outside the requested window via the negative-offset path. The comment should not assert a property the class does not enforce.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator with no added behavior
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result is a near line-for-line copy of BasePaginator.get_result (which itself was just modified in this PR). Apart from the negative-offset branch, every other step (cursor normalization, queryset build, extra row handling, post_query_filter, build_cursor) is identical. The class introduces a new public surface that callers must keep in sync with the base, but does not deliver the documented "advanced features" for any cursor whose offset is non-negative (which is every cursor produced by build_cursor). This is dead-weight API.

title: enable_advanced_features kwarg passed to self.paginate may not be accepted
body: The endpoint calls `self.paginate(..., enable_advanced_features=True)`, but `BaseEndpoint.paginate` does not declare `enable_advanced_features` as a parameter and does not forward arbitrary kwargs to the paginator constructor. If paginate uses keyword-only args (the typical pattern in this codebase), this call will raise `TypeError: paginate() got an unexpected keyword argument 'enable_advanced_features'` at runtime for every request that passes `optimized_pagination=true`. Either paginate must be extended to pass through extra kwargs, or this must be wired via the documented `paginator_kwargs` channel; otherwise the new code path is dead/broken.

title: New optimized_pagination query parameter is undocumented and unversioned
body: The endpoint introduces a `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter that switches the paginator class, but there is no API documentation, no schema, and no test coverage for it. Because the new branch is gated by `is_superuser or has_global_access`, it is effectively a privileged back-channel that admins could rely on. Without documentation or stability guarantees it can silently break clients. At minimum the parameter, its gating, and the difference in behavior should be documented or the feature removed if it provides no benefit.

title: Cursor comment claims a change that does not exist
body: The diff adds the comments "# Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios" and "# This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets" above `self.offset = int(offset)`. The line itself is unchanged and `int(offset)` already accepted negative values before this PR. The comment claims a behavioral and performance change that the diff does not make, and there is no such thing as "efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions" introduced here. This is misleading and should be removed.

title: No tests added for OptimizedCursorPaginator or new query parameter
body: The PR introduces a new paginator class OptimizedCursorPaginator (with a non-trivial negative-offset branch) and a new privileged query parameter `optimized_pagination` that selects it, but no test files are added or referenced. Existing pagination tests for DateTimePaginator do not exercise the new code path. At minimum there should be tests covering: (1) the new query parameter selects the optimized paginator, (2) gating by `is_superuser`/`has_global_access`, (3) OptimizedCursorPaginator behavior with negative and non-negative offsets, and (4) that the result content matches DateTimePaginator for non-negative offsets.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes with datetime ordering
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `value = getattr(item, self.key)` and then `int(math.floor(value) ... )`. When used with `order_by="-datetime"` (as the new audit-logs endpoint does), `value` is a `datetime` object, and `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: float argument required, not datetime.datetime`. The existing DateTimePaginator has special handling (`float(value.strftime("%s.%f")) * self.multiplier`) for exactly this reason; OptimizedCursorPaginator is essentially a copy of `Paginator` (numeric-only) and is not a drop-in replacement for DateTimePaginator. The new `?optimized_pagination=true` path on the audit logs endpoint will 500 for any superuser/global-admin caller.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor returns raw timestamp instead of datetime
body: value_from_cursor returns `cursor.value` directly. For datetime-keyed cursors that value is a Unix-timestamp integer produced by DateTimePaginator.get_item_key. The caller (BasePaginator.build_queryset) substitutes it into `WHERE <col> <= %s`, producing a comparison between a `datetime` column and an integer like `... WHERE datetime <= 1699999999000`, which PostgreSQL rejects with `operator does not exist: timestamp without time zone >= integer`. DateTimePaginator converts the integer back to a datetime; OptimizedCursorPaginator does not. Together with the get_item_key issue, the optimized audit-logs path is broken end-to-end.

title: Negative-offset path is misleadingly documented and unsafe
body: The `enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0` branch claims in its comments that 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically', that it 'enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds', and that 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level'. None of these are true: Django translates `queryset[-N:M]` into `LIMIT (M-N) OFFSET -N`, which PostgreSQL rejects as a non-positive OFFSET, so the request 500s. The framing of 'efficient bidirectional pagination' misrepresents what negative slicing does — it returns the last N rows of the queryset, not an arbitrary position. The 'safe because permissions' justification conflates row-level authorization (which the queryset already enforces) with pagination-boundary integrity; allowing a client to choose a negative offset bypasses the `offset >= 0` invariant that BasePaginator and the rest of the pagination pipeline assume. The whole branch should be removed; it adds no legitimate functionality and exists only behind a parameter that is already gated to superusers, which makes the misleading comments more concerning.

title: BasePaginator.get_result changes behavior for all subclasses, not just audit logs
body: The diff replaces `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` and `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`. This is a behavior change on a shared base class that affects every paginator inheriting from BasePaginator (DateTimePaginator, Paginator, MergingOffsetPaginator callers, etc.), not just the new OptimizedCursorPaginator. The PR title and description only mention audit logs and contain no mention of this base-class change, so reviewers of the other endpoints will not see it. The accompanying comment ('allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination') is the opposite of what the code does for non-prev cursors — it clamps negative offsets to 0, restricting rather than allowing them. This should either be reverted or split into its own PR with a real justification.

title: Query-string flag exposes broken/unsafe paginator path to admins with no test coverage
body: The new `?optimized_pagination=true` parameter routes the request through OptimizedCursorPaginator for any superuser or any member with global access. As noted above that paginator crashes on datetimes, mishandles cursor values, and contains the unsafe negative-offset branch. Gating behind `is_superuser or has_global_access` does not mitigate these issues; it just limits who sees the 500s. A security-relevant control surface (pagination of the audit log) is being routed through a new, untested code path with multiple bugs and a misleadingly-commented 'advanced' feature.

title: No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or BasePaginator change
body: The PR introduces a new paginator class with non-trivial behavior (enable_advanced_features flag, negative-offset branch, datetime-incompatible get_item_key/value_from_cursor) and modifies BasePaginator.get_result, but adds no tests. There are no tests covering: (1) the optimized audit-logs endpoint path, (2) pagination of datetime-ordered querysets through OptimizedCursorPaginator, (3) the negative-offset branch under enable_advanced_features, (4) the new max(0, offset) clamping in BasePaginator for non-prev cursors. Given that the new code is broken for datetime ordering, the lack of tests is what allowed the regressions to ship.

title: cursors.py change is comment-only and the comment is misleading
body: The diff adds two comment lines above `self.offset = int(offset)`. There is no code change — `int(offset)` was already there. The comment ('Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios / This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets') implies new functionality that was not actually added, and propagates the same misleading framing as the paginator changes. Either remove the comment or implement the documented behavior in a single place with a real test.

title: Negative-offset branch is unreachable / raises AssertionError in Django
body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0, the code does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with start_offset < 0. Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ asserts that a slice start must be non-negative (`assert (k.start is None or k.start >= 0), 'Negative indexing is not supported.'`), so this branch raises AssertionError in normal Python and produces undefined SQL offsets under python -O. Cursor.from_string happily parses a negative offset via `int(bits[1])`, so an admin who sends ?optimized_pagination=true with a crafted cursor (e.g. '0:-5:0') will crash the endpoint. The claim in the comment that 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is factually wrong; Django never supported negative slicing on querysets.

title: 'Performance optimization' comments are misleading
body: The block comment at lines 179-181 and the docstring of OptimizedCursorPaginator (lines 822-832) claim this is a 'performance optimization', provides 'efficient bidirectional pagination without full dataset scanning', 'streamlined boundary condition handling', and 'optimized query path for large datasets'. None of these are real. Compared to BasePaginator, OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result only changes behavior when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0, and even that change is broken (see the negative-offset finding). The change to BasePaginator itself (line 182-184) only clamps a negative offset to 0 in the non-prev case; that is a defensive fix, not an optimization. The repeated blank lines at lines 819-820 also suggest the class was tacked on without review.

title: has_global_access on RpcOrganizationMember is not a known attribute
body: `organization_context.member.has_global_access` accesses a Python attribute on the RpcOrganizationMember RPC type. RpcOrganizationMember typically exposes role/flags (e.g. `flags.global_access` bit) rather than a `has_global_access` property. If the attribute does not exist, this expression raises AttributeError on every request from a non-superuser, which would 500 the entire audit log endpoint for ordinary members. The reviewer needs to confirm the actual attribute name and that it represents the intended privilege (vs. e.g. `role` or a flags bit). Also, since the entire `use_optimized and enable_advanced` branch is gated to superusers or admins, exposing it via a user-controlled `?optimized_pagination=true` query parameter does not actually grant any new capability and should be questioned.

title: New paginator branch has no tests
body: No tests were added for the new optimized_pagination code path. A maintainer should at minimum cover: (1) optimized_pagination=true with a superuser hits OptimizedCursorPaginator; (2) optimized_pagination=true with a regular member falls through to DateTimePaginator; (3) OptimizedCursorPaginator with enable_advanced_features=True and a negative-offset cursor does not raise (today it will). The whole feature is unverified.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator.get_result
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result (lines 845-911) is an almost line-for-line copy of BasePaginator.get_result (lines 136-215); the only meaningful difference is the negative-offset branch. Subclassing only to flip one branch in one method duplicates ~70 lines of cursor/offset/extra/hits/post_query_filter logic. Any future fix to BasePaginator (including the pre-existing `order_b` typo on line 105) must be made in two places. A maintainer would prefer a single `enable_advanced_features` flag on BasePaginator, or an override of just the slicing step.

title: Pre-existing typo 'order_b' silently breaks ASC re-ordering
body: Pre-existing but in the file being changed and directly relevant to pagination correctness. Line 105 reads `queryset.query.order_b = tuple(new_order_by)` instead of `queryset.query.order_by = tuple(new_order_by)`. This means when the cursor's key is currently ordered DESC (`-%s` % self.key in order_by) and `asc` is True, the queryset's order_by is never actually flipped to ascending, so the descending-order rows are then compared with an ascending comparison operator, producing wrong results. Worth fixing while this file is being touched.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator negative-offset path crashes on Django QuerySet
body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result the branch for `cursor.offset < 0` does `list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with `start_offset < 0`. Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ explicitly raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.` for any negative start or stop in a slice. The comment 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is wrong; OffsetPaginator in the same file even guards against this with `raise BadPaginationError('Pagination offset cannot be negative')`. Consequence: any caller of the new endpoint that supplies a negative `cursor.offset` (the entire advertised feature) crashes instead of paginating. Since `optimized_pagination=true` is gated to superusers / `has_global_access`, this is a privilege-escalation-free DoS for admins and a broken feature for everyone else.

title: ZUNIONSTORE default SUM aggregation mangles timestamps used as eviction scores
body: The new eviction relies on scores being `end_timestamp_precise` so that `ZPOPMIN ... COUNT (span_count - 1000)` evicts the oldest spans. But the unions use `zunionstore(set_key, 2, set_key, ...)` with the default `AGGREGATE` (SUM). Whenever a payload exists in both source keys (for example when `set_span_id == span_id`, making `set_key == span_key`, or any future overlap), the resulting score is `score1 + score2` instead of the timestamp. Doubling/adding scores corrupts the relative ordering used for eviction: older spans can end up with higher scores than newer ones, and `zpopmin` will then evict the wrong (newer) spans. The script should pass `AGGREGATE MAX` (or `MIN`) so the score remains a real timestamp.

title: Redirect-chain iteration limit cut 10x without justification
body: The for-loop bound is reduced from `10000` to `1000`. The removed comment explicitly warned: 'theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly.' Now any trace whose redirect chain exceeds depth 1000 will be truncated, causing spans to be written to the wrong `set_key`. The flushed segment will then be missing spans (data loss) or span sets will never reach their root timeout (resource leak / stuck segments). The PR description does not explain why a 10x tightening of this safety limit is safe, and no test covers deep chains.

title: Unconditional dict access on end_timestamp_precise breaks older payloads
body: `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` will raise `KeyError` for any Kafka payload that lacks the field. Older ingest-spans producers / relay versions, malformed messages, or any schema drift will now crash `process_batch` instead of being logged-and-skipped, because the prior code did not require this key. Either guard with `val.get("end_timestamp_precise")` (and default to e.g. `0.0` or the message timestamp) or reject the payload explicitly with a metric. As written this is a silent backwards-compatibility break for every span that does not carry the new field.

title: max_segment_spans guard removed in Python but constructor arg retained
body: The `max_segment_spans` enforcement in `_load_segment_data` (the `if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans` block) has been deleted on the premise that Lua now evicts at insert time. The constructor parameter `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` is still accepted, still passed through `__reduce__`/`__init__`, but is no longer referenced anywhere in the module. There is no test that exercises the >1000 span eviction, and no Python-side safety net if the Lua script ever fails to load / evict (e.g. transient Redis script-cache miss or future regression). Either remove the dead parameter or keep a Python guard with a test.

title: No test for the new >1000-span zpopmin eviction path
body: test_buffer.py and test_flusher.py only add `end_timestamp_precise` to existing fixtures; nothing exercises a segment exceeding the 1000-element eviction threshold in add-buffer.lua, the `zunionstore`-score overlap case, or the new 1000-iteration redirect-chain limit. Given the eviction is the entire motivation for this PR and the only data-integrity-affecting change, the absence of a regression test means a broken eviction will not be caught by CI.

title: Django ORM does not support negative slicing, so negative offset path always crashes
body: The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` branch uses `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with `start_offset = cursor.offset` when `cursor.offset < 0`. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` asserts `k.start >= 0` and raises `AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported.')` on any slice whose `start` is negative. Therefore the only thing the 'advanced feature' does is make the request raise 500. The accompanying comment 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. The audit logs endpoint unconditionally passes `enable_advanced_features=True`, so any client that supplies a cursor with a negative offset (or any code path that constructs one) will crash.

title: Redirect-follow loop limit lowered from 10000 to 1000 silently breaks deep segment trees
body: The previous code used `for i = 0, 10000 do` and carried a comment explaining that exceeding this limit means segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly. The new code lowers the bound to `for i = 0, 1000 do` without any rationale, so any trace whose redirect chain exceeds 1000 hops will resolve to a `set_span_id` that is not the true root. The subsequent `zunionstore`/`zpopmin` will then operate on the wrong set, leaving the actual root segment orphaned and producing an incomplete or empty flushed segment. This is a silent data-integrity regression for deep traces.

title: Default SUM aggregate in ZUNIONSTORE corrupts `end_timestamp_precise` scores for duplicate payloads
body: `zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` is invoked with the implicit default `AGGREGATE SUM`. If a member (span payload) ever exists in both `set_key` and `span_key` (which can occur on Kafka retries or any path where the same payload was inserted twice with different timestamps), its score after the union becomes the arithmetic sum of the two timestamps rather than either one. Those scores drive eviction (`zpopmin`) and any downstream ordering; a corrupted score means the wrong spans get evicted and the 'oldest-first' eviction contract is broken. The script should pass an explicit `AGGREGATE MIN` (or `MAX`) to preserve a single timestamp per payload.

title: Span NamedTuple adds a required field in the middle, breaking positional construction
body: `Span` is a public NamedTuple exported from `sentry.spans.buffer`. The new `end_timestamp_precise: float` is inserted between `payload` and `is_segment_span`, has no default, and shifts `is_segment_span` to the last position. Any caller that constructs `Span(...)` positionally (the 7th argument previously implied `is_segment_span`) will silently mis-bind: a positional `True` becomes the `end_timestamp_precise` value and `is_segment_span` defaults to `False`, causing incorrect is-segment logic downstream. It also breaks unpickling of old `Span` pickles and any external code that mirrors this shape. The field should be added at the end (with a default) or supplied only via keyword to preserve positional compatibility.

title: Removed `max_segment_spans` Python guard while Lua hardcodes a different (1000) limit
body: The old `_load_segment_data` had `if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans: ... skip segment`. This guard is deleted, so the only cap on segment size is the new Lua eviction at line 62 (`if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', set_key, span_count - 1000) end`). Two issues: (1) `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_bytes`/`max_segment_spans`, so the configurable Python limit is now dead and will diverge from the Lua hardcode if anyone changes the constant. (2) The Lua limit is 1000 but `max_segment_spans` defaults to 1001, so the effective cap silently drops by 1. If the Lua eviction is bypassed (e.g., a Redis upgrade changes `ZUNIONSTORE` cardinality semantics, or a future code path skips the script), there is no Python backstop and segments can grow unbounded.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator without any actual optimization
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` is a near-verbatim copy of `BasePaginator.get_result`. The only behavioral difference is the `enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0` branch (which, per the other finding, crashes Django). There is no optimized query path, no streamlined boundary handling, and no measurable performance benefit. The docstring's claims of 'performance optimizations for high-traffic endpoints' and 'Optimized query path for large datasets' are unsubstantiated. A subclass that only adds one (broken) branch is significant duplication that will drift from the base implementation.

title: Comments and docstrings lie about safety, optimization, and Django support
body: Several new comments are misleading: (1) `paginator.py` line 179: 'Performance optimization: ... allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination' — the change actually clamps non-prev offsets to 0, it does not allow them. (2) `paginator.py` line 877: 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' — Django explicitly asserts `k.start >= 0` and raises on negative slicing. (3) `paginator.py` line 879: 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level' — permissions don't gate which rows an offset selects, only which rows the queryset can see; an admin user can still trigger a crash or expensive scan. (4) `organization_auditlogs.py` lines 68-76 repeat the same false framing about 'optimized paginator for high-performance' navigation. (5) `cursors.py` lines 26-27 add a 'Performance optimization' comment over a line that is byte-identical to the original. These comments will mislead future maintainers about the actual semantics and risks.

title: `max(0, offset)` silently changes BasePaginator behavior for callers passing negative non-prev offsets
body: The diff replaces `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. For non-prev cursors, any negative `cursor.offset` previously propagated to Django (which would raise on negative slicing); now the offset is silently clamped to 0 and the first page is returned as if no cursor were supplied. Any caller that intentionally relied on the old raise-on-bad-cursor semantics (e.g., for validation) will instead get a wrong page returned with no error. The change is presented as a 'performance optimization' rather than a behavior change; if the intent really is to silently coerce, that contract should be explicit and documented.

title: Rolling deploy will see WRONGTYPE errors until old SET data expires
body: The new code treats every `span-buf:s:*` and `span-buf:sr:*` key as a sorted set (`zcard`, `zunionstore`, `zpopmin`). The previous version stored these as plain Redis sets (`sunionstore`, `scard`). Any keys written by the old version that are still within their TTL will cause `WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value` errors on the next `EVALSHA` of this script, crashing the consumer's `process_spans` pipeline. There is no migration step in the diff, no versioned key prefix, and no defensive `TYPE` check in the Lua script. This will produce a noisy, multi-TTL-window outage during cutover in any environment with non-empty Redis state.

title: No tests for new eviction logic, score semantics, or OptimizedCursorPaginator
body: The Lua eviction block lines 58-64 (`if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin ...`) and the SUM-aggregate implication of `zunionstore` are entirely untested: no test inserts >1000 spans into a single segment to verify the eviction, no test verifies that `end_timestamp_precise` is preserved through unions, and no test exercises the off-by-one between the Lua cap (1000) and `max_segment_spans` (1001). Likewise `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (paginator.py lines 821-911) has no tests at all - not for the normal path, not for the negative-offset branch, and not for the `enable_advanced_features` flag. Without tests, the silent regressions above (redirect loop reduction, score corruption, Django crash) cannot be caught.

title: Redirect resolution loop limit silently reduced 10000 -> 1000
body: The redirect resolution loop iterates from `for i = 0, 1000 do` (line 30) but the original code used `for i = 0, 10000 do` and explicitly noted in the comment that this limit governs whether deep segment trees are joined correctly: 'theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly.' Reducing the limit to 1000 silently breaks any trace whose redirect chain has depth between 1000 and 10000 — those spans will not be merged into the same set. No tests exercise deep trees, so this regression is not caught. Consequence: traces with deep span trees (1000+) end up split across multiple buffer sets and get flushed as incomplete segments, losing parent/child relationships downstream.

title: Eviction silently drops spans from oversized segments without logging
body: Lines 62–64 add `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', set_key, span_count - 1000) end`, which silently removes the oldest (lowest `end_timestamp_precise`) spans from any set exceeding 1000 entries. The previous Python-side check at `_load_segment_data` would `metrics.incr('spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded')` and log an error before discarding the entire segment; this is now gone (see `src/sentry/spans/buffer.py`). The new behavior silently loses individual spans with no metric, no log, no error — only `zpopmin` happens. Consequence: for any segment with more than 1000 spans, downstream flushing will emit truncated segments, and operators will have no signal that data was dropped. Also note that `zpopmin` breaks ties by lexicographic member order when `end_timestamp_precise` is identical (common for sibling spans in the same transaction), making the lost-span set effectively non-deterministic.

title: `max_segment_spans` constructor parameter is now orphaned
body: `SpansBuffer.__init__` (around line 150) still defines and stores `self.max_segment_spans = max_segment_spans` with default 1001, but the consumer-side enforcement in `_load_segment_data` that read `self.max_segment_spans` was deleted in this PR. The parameter is still accepted in `__reduce__` callers and tests, but never used. Consequence: configuration knob is misleading and dead; anyone increasing `max_segment_spans` expects larger segments to be allowed, but the Lua-side eviction now silently caps segments at 1000 regardless. The Python constant and constructor argument should either be removed or actually consulted (e.g., passed to the Lua script as a configurable limit).

title: BasePaginator silently clamps negative offsets for non-prev cursors
body: The change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` (line 182) introduces a behavior change from the original `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` for cursors with `is_prev=False` and a negative `offset`. Django's queryset slicing natively supports negative offsets; the new code silently clamps them to 0. The comment ('Performance optimization: For high-traffic scenarios, allow negative offsets…') is misleading — the change actually restricts offset semantics in the base paginator. Consequence: any caller (in this repo or downstream) that previously relied on Django's negative slicing for forward cursors will silently get the first page of results instead of the tail, with no error. There is no test that exercises the negative-offset path, and the change is rolled out to all paginator subclasses (DateTimePaginator, Paginator, etc.) via inheritance.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator is a near-verbatim copy of Paginator/BasePaginator with misleading docstring
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (lines 821–911) duplicates `get_item_key` and `value_from_cursor` byte-for-byte from `Paginator` (lines 222–227) and reimplements `get_result` almost identically to `BasePaginator.get_result`, differing only in whether a negative offset passes through when `enable_advanced_features` is set. The docstring claims 'Negative offset support for efficient reverse pagination', 'Streamlined boundary condition handling', and 'Optimized query path for large datasets', but only the first is implemented (and Django natively), and the others describe no actual behavior. Consequence: dead code, false documentation, and a privileged code path ('control optimizations') that is exposed via a query parameter (see `organization_auditlogs.py`) for superusers, with no test coverage in the diff. A senior reviewer would want this consolidated into a flag on `BasePaginator` rather than a duplicate class.

title: `organization_context.member.has_global_access` may AttributeError if member is None
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` (line 71) unconditionally accesses `.member.has_global_access` whenever the requester is not a superuser. If `organization_context.member` is None for any path that reaches this endpoint (e.g., a service user or a context shape returned for non-members of the org being queried), the request will raise `AttributeError` and return a 500. The original code never touched `organization_context.member`, so this PR introduces the regression. Guard with `organization_context.member is not None and organization_context.member.has_global_access` (or equivalent), or move the check inside the `optimized_pagination` branch where it is actually consumed.

title: Privileged pagination feature is gated by a client-controlled query parameter
body: `use_optimized = request.GET.get('optimized_pagination') == 'true'` (line 70) lets any requester who is also a superuser (or has global access) flip on `enable_advanced_features=True` for that single request. Privileged behavior is typically gated by server-side configuration or user attributes, not a query parameter, because query-parameter gating leaves no audit trail and is trivially selectable. The 'feature' itself just re-enables Django's native negative-offset slicing that the BasePaginator change (line 182 in paginator.py) just removed. Either move the toggle behind a server-side feature flag/setting, or drop it — the parameter offers no functional benefit beyond Django's existing behavior.

title: No tests cover the new eviction-on-insert behavior
body: The PR adds Lua-side eviction at >1000 spans (`zpopmin`), but no test in `tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py`, `tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_buffer.py`, or `tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_flusher.py` constructs a segment with more than 1000 spans to assert (a) the cap is enforced, (b) which spans are kept vs dropped, or (c) that a metric/log is emitted. The existing parametrized tests use 4–5 spans per case. Without a test, a future change to the score semantics (e.g., switching from `end_timestamp_precise` to something else) or to the threshold could regress silently and drop arbitrary spans in production with no detection. At minimum, add a test that pushes >1000 spans into one segment and asserts the flushed result contains exactly 1000 and that the kept spans are the latest by `end_timestamp_precise`.

title: No tests cover the redirect-loop limit change (10000 -> 1000) or the new OptimizedCursorPaginator path
body: Two important behavioral changes ship without test coverage: (1) the add-buffer.lua redirect-resolution loop limit is reduced from 10000 to 1000, and (2) the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `enable_advanced_features=True` (used by `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` for superusers/global-access members) is exercised in no test in this PR. The audit-logs endpoint change should at least have a test that constructs a request as a superuser with `?optimized_pagination=true` and asserts it returns a successful paginated response, and the redirect limit should be covered by a test feeding a synthetic deep tree.

title: `cast(SpanEvent, …)` provides no runtime validation; missing `end_timestamp_precise` will KeyError
body: Line 134 does `val = cast(SpanEvent, rapidjson.loads(payload.value))`, which is purely a type-hint operation at runtime — it does not validate the payload. The very next reference, `end_timestamp_precise=val['end_timestamp_precise']` (line 141), will raise `KeyError` if any incoming payload (older producers, schema drift, malformed Kafka message) omits the field, and `TypeError` if it is `None`. Consequence: a single bad message kills the batch processing and the consumer may stall. Either validate against the schema (e.g., `sentry_kafka_schemas.codecs.decode`) before constructing the `Span`, or guard with `val.get('end_timestamp_precise', default)` and skip/log the malformed message.

title: Comment claims int(offset) enables negative offsets but it doesn't
body: Lines 26–27 add `# Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios / # This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets`, but the actual code is the unchanged `self.offset = int(offset)`. `int()` is just a numeric coercion — it does not 'allow' negatives (Python ints already accept them) and does not change pagination behavior. The comment misleads readers into believing the Cursor constructor is doing something that it is not; the actual negative-offset semantics were (re)moved in `paginator.py`. Either delete the comment or move the explanatory text to the place that actually implements the feature.

title: Cache key uses process-randomized hash()
body: The cache key is built as `f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))}"`. In CPython 3.3+, the hash of tuples and strings is randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED). Different web/worker processes will therefore generate different cache keys for the same organization/project set, so the cache will only ever hit within a single process. This defeats the stated 60-second cross-request caching optimization and causes every request in a multi-worker deployment to miss the cache and re-read the allowlist option. Replace `hash(...)` with a deterministic digest (e.g. `hashlib.md5(str(sorted_ids).encode()).hexdigest()`) or just inline the sorted ids into the key.

title: Duplicate alias when query has multiple count() columns
body: `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` always replaces `count()` with the literal string `"upsampled_count() as count"`. If `query_columns` ever contains more than one `count()` entry (e.g. `["count()", "count()"]` or `["count()", "count_unique(user)", "count()"]`), the resulting SQL has two columns aliased `count`, which ClickHouse/Snuba will reject and the endpoint will return 500. The function should uniquify the alias (e.g. `upsampled_count() as count`, `upsampled_count() as count_2`, ...) or track a counter.

title: Sample rate not range-validated and applied to all event types
body: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` blindly does `float(client_sample_rate)` and assigns it to `normalized_data["sample_rate"]` whenever the value is truthy. There is no check that the value lies in (0, 1]; out-of-range, NaN, or negative values from a malformed SDK payload will be accepted and propagated into the event's `sample_rate`, which downstream logic (including the new `upsampled_count() = sum(sample_weight)` aggregation) relies on. A negative or >1 rate will produce nonsensical or negative upsampled counts. Additionally, the helper is called from `store_event` for every event, not just errors, so a transaction that coincidentally carries an `error_sampling` context will also get `sample_rate` set. The validation should reject values outside (0, 1] and the call site should be gated on event type or at least the presence of the context.

title: Substring match for event.type:error produces false positives
body: `_is_error_focused_query` does `if "event.type:error" in query` on the lowercased raw query string. This matches `NOT event.type:error` (the user is explicitly excluding errors) and `event.type:error_handled`, both of which are not error-focused queries. In those cases `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` will return True for the discover dataset, `count()` will be rewritten to `sum(sample_weight)`, and the returned counts will be wrong (or, for the NOT case, non-zero when the user asked for non-errors). The check should at minimum look for the token as a standalone segment (e.g. whitespace-delimited) or use the existing search-query tokenizer.

title: Cache invalidation helper is defined but never called
body: `invalidate_upsampling_cache(organization_id, project_ids)` is exported and its docstring says "This should be called when the allowlist configuration changes to ensure cache consistency across the system." However, nothing in this PR (or anywhere visible in the diff) calls it - the allowlist is read via `options.get("issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist", [])` and there is no signal/listener that fires when that option changes. In practice the 60s TTL will mask allowlist edits, but the helper is dead code and its existence is misleading; either wire it up at the option-set site or remove it.

title: Public is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects is untested
body: The test file only covers the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`). The public entry point `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, which is what the endpoint actually calls and which contains the cache read/write logic, the AND-composition of allowlist eligibility with the per-call dataset/query check, and the cache-key construction (including the process-randomized `hash()` bug), is not exercised at all. Likewise `invalidate_upsampling_cache` has no test. The endpoint-level tests in `test_organization_events_stats.py` only verify the numeric output of one path and would not catch regressions in the cache logic, the substring-match false positives, or the duplicate-alias case.

title: Missing tests for duplicate count() and other aggregation functions
body: `test_transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only checks the single-`count()` case. It does not cover (a) multiple `count()` entries in the same input list (which triggers the duplicate-`as count` alias bug), (b) other aggregations that the function intentionally leaves alone such as `count_unique(user)`, `count_if(...)`, or equation columns like `equation|count()`, or (c) the case-insensitive / whitespace behavior of those non-`count()` columns. Adding these cases would have caught the duplicate-alias bug.

title: Cache key uses non-deterministic hash()
body: The cache key is built with `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. CPython randomizes the hash seed for tuples/strings per-process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so the same project set produces a different key in every web/worker process. The 60s cache therefore never shares data across processes, defeating the stated 'performance optimization during traffic spikes'. The PR description claims this cache avoids 'expensive repeated option lookups during high-traffic periods', but with N workers you still get N independent option lookups. Replace `hash(...)` with a deterministic digest (e.g. `hashlib.md5(str(tuple(sorted(project_ids))).encode()).hexdigest()`) or just stringify the tuple.

title: invalidate_upsampling_cache is dead code
body: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined and documented as 'This should be called when the allowlist configuration changes to ensure cache consistency', but nothing in the PR (or elsewhere in the diff) ever calls it. With the 60s TTL, removing a project from `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` will continue to return stale `is_eligible=True` results for up to a minute, meaning queries against that org/project will keep being rewritten to `upsampled_count()` even after the operator un-allowlisted it. Either wire up invalidation on option writes, or remove the unused helper to avoid implying a guarantee that isn't there.

title: Error-sampling context silently overwrites an existing sample_rate
body: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` runs unconditionally during `store_event` and writes `normalized_data['sample_rate'] = float(client_sample_rate)` whenever `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` is truthy, without checking whether `sample_rate` was already set. Any pre-existing `sample_rate` (e.g. set by ingest earlier in the pipeline, by a different sampling decision, or by a test fixture) is silently overwritten. The bare `except Exception` blocks also swallow any unexpected type of `contexts` value, hiding malformed payloads. The function should at most set `sample_rate` if it is currently missing, and should not catch arbitrary `Exception`.

title: Repeated lazy imports inside hot helper
body: `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` performs `from sentry.snuba import discover, errors` and later `from sentry.snuba import transactions` inside the function body on every call. Even with module caching this is avoidable per-call dict lookups, and it is invoked from the timeseries hot path of every organization events stats request. If the lazy style is only to dodge a circular import, move both imports to module scope in one statement and resolve the cycle properly.

title: Comments around upsampling block are misleading
body: The newly added comments in `_get_event_stats` make claims that don't match the code: 'Early upsampling eligibility check for performance optimization ... This cached result ensures consistent behavior across query execution' (it isn't actually cached at the call site, and the helper's cache is broken by the hash() issue), and 'Apply upsampling transformation just before query execution ... This late transformation ensures we use the most current schema assumptions' (schema does not change at runtime, and the transformation isn't late in any meaningful sense — it runs before every branch). These comments will mislead future readers about what the code does and why; either justify the comments accurately or remove them.

title: Upsampling check runs unconditionally on every stats request
body: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(...)` is invoked unconditionally on every `_get_event_stats` call, including for non-error datasets and for projects that are not allowlisted (the common case). Even with a hot cache this still does a cache key construction (with the broken `hash()`), a cache get, and a dataset/parse check per call. Move the check inside the branches where `final_columns` is actually used, or short-circuit cheaply on dataset (transactions/spans/metrics) before touching the cache.

title: Cache key built from non-deterministic hash()
body: The cache key uses `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. CPython randomizes the tuple hash seed per process via PYTHONHASHSEED, so each gunicorn/celery worker computes a different integer for the same project list, producing different cache keys. The 60-second cache claimed as a 'performance optimization' therefore never hits across workers in production and the shared Redis cache slot will be silently bypassed. Replace `hash(...)` with a stable digest such as `hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted_ids).encode()).hexdigest()` (or any non-secret, deterministic hash) before generating the key.

title: Stale cached True keeps upsampling projects that just left the allowlist
body: The allowlist check is cached for 60s, but `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined yet never wired into any option-set/management signal. If a project is removed from `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`, the cached `True` continues to be served for up to a minute, and `_get_event_stats` will then transform `count()` into `upsampled_count()` for a project whose events no longer satisfy the upsampling contract. That makes reported error counts incorrect (over-counted by the sample_weight factor). Either shorten TTL dramatically, call `invalidate_upsampling_cache` whenever the allowlist option is written, or include the allowlist version in the cache key.

title: Substring match for event.type:error causes false positives
body: `_is_error_focused_query` does `if "event.type:error" in query`, which matches any query where that substring appears anywhere. Real queries like `event.type:errorBoundary`, `tags.event.type:error`, or note-style payloads containing `event.type:error` text will all be classified as error-focused and have their counts upsampled even though they are not error events. The docstring says 'err on the side of caution', but the current implementation is the opposite — it over-applies the transform. Use proper token-based matching (split on whitespace/punctuation and check for an exact `event.type:error` token).

title: upsampled_count drops NULL sample_weight rows and truncates to Int64
body: The new `upsampled_count` aggregate is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. Two correctness issues: (1) `sum(sample_weight)` silently excludes rows where `sample_weight` is NULL (pre-upsampling or legacy events ingested before sampling rolled out on that project), so the upsampled count will be lower than the real event count and inflate/de-inflate arbitrarily as the rollout progresses; and (2) `toInt64(...)` truncates fractional sums — e.g. 10.7 becomes 10 — so reported counts can be off-by-one for any bucket whose weighted total is not integral. Wrap with `COALESCE(sample_weight, 1)` (or similar) and either keep the result as a float or round explicitly before casting.

title: _are_all_projects_error_upsampled takes organization but ignores it
body: `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled(project_ids, organization)` accepts an `Organization` argument but only reads `options.get("issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist", [])`, which is a global option. This is misleading — callers and reviewers reasonably expect the allowlist to be per-organization — and if per-org allowlists are ever introduced, this signature will silently do the wrong thing. Either drop the parameter, or actually consult an organization-scoped option.

title: setUp reassigns self.user after login_as, leaving auth against stale user
body: In `OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest.setUp`, `self.login_as(user=self.user)` is called, then `self.authed_user = self.user` saves a reference, then `self.user = self.create_user()` reassigns `self.user` to a brand-new user. Subsequent `store_event` calls use `tags={"sentry:user": self.user.email}` referring to the new (non-authenticated) user, while the request still runs as the original user. This makes the test setup brittle: any future test that depends on the authenticated user's identity vs the tagged user's identity will silently break. Move all `create_user`/`store_event` setup before `login_as`, or use distinct attribute names.

title: Upsampled-count assertion depends on unverified sample_weight semantics
body: `test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects` asserts `count == 10` after storing events with `client_sample_rate: 0.1`. This only holds if Snuba's `sample_weight` is exactly `1 / client_sample_rate` AND the factory's new `sample_rate` hook propagates through event ingest into that column — none of which is asserted in this PR. If either assumption is wrong, the test will be a false positive that masks the most important data-integrity claim of the feature. Add an explicit assertion (or a smaller unit test) that demonstrates the sample_weight value produced for a known input, e.g. assert `sample_weight == 10.0` for a stored event with sample_rate 0.1.

title: invalidate_upsampling_cache is dead code; allowlist edits have no effect for 60s
body: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined and exported, but a repo-wide search shows no caller. Combined with the 60-second TTL this means any operator change to `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` (or any future project-level toggle) cannot be observed promptly, and there is no signal that this is intentional. Either wire it into the option-set path (and any UI/admin endpoint that edits the allowlist), or delete it so callers do not assume it works.

title: Unrelated error-message change for topEvents validation
body: The diff rewrites `{"detail": "If topEvents needs to be at least 1"}` to `{"detail": "topEvents needs to be at least 1"}`. This is a user-visible API response change bundled into a feature PR for error upsampling, with no description in the PR body. Anyone parsing this message string (CI checks, docs, downstream tests) will see a silent change. Either revert the message and keep the PR scope tight, or call it out explicitly so consumers can update.

title: Empty submodule pinned to base commit with no justification
body: The PR adds a `sentry-repo` submodule entry pointing to exactly the same commit as the base (`a5d29095...`). Nothing in the diff or description references this submodule, no path within it is consumed by any of the changed Python files, and pinning a submodule to the parent commit typically only matters if downstream tooling relies on it. Remove the submodule entry, or document in the PR description what depends on it and why it must move in lock-step with the parent.

title: TableWidgetVisualization is wired up with hardcoded empty data instead of the actual table result
body: When the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature flag is enabled, `TableWidgetVisualization` is rendered with `columns={[]}` and a `tableData` whose `data` and `meta.fields/units` are all empty, instead of forwarding `result.data` / `result.meta` / the per-query field map from the surrounding `tableResults.map((result, i) => ...)` block. Consequence: any org with the flag turned on will see every dashboard table widget render with no columns and no rows, regressing table rendering for that org. The diff is replacing the `StyledSimpleTableChart` invocation that previously received `metadata={result.meta}`, `data={result.data}`, `fieldHeaderMap={datasetConfig.getFieldHeaderMap?.(widget.queries[i])}` and `getCustomFieldRenderer`; those need to be plumbed through to the new component (e.g. a `TabularData` built from `result.data` and `result.meta`) or the feature-flag branch must be removed until that plumbing exists.

title: useFeedbackSummary dereferences data.summary / data.numFeedbacksUsed without checking data is defined
body: The hook returns `{ summary: data.summary, ... tooFewFeedbacks: data.numFeedbacksUsed === 0 && !data.success }` after only guarding on `isPending` and `isError`. When `user-feedback-ai-summaries` is off (or `normalizedDateRange` is falsy), `enabled` is false so react-query never fetches and `data` is `undefined` while `isPending` is false and `isError` is false. Reaching the final return then throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'summary')` on every render of the consumer `FeedbackSummary`, which means the page crashes for any org that does not have the feature flag before the feature-flag check inside the consumer ever runs. Guard the final return on `data`, or add an explicit early-return for the `!data` branch.

title: get_environment_info swallows every exception with logger.info, hiding real errors
body: `get_environment_info` does `except Exception as e:` and then calls `logger.info("get_environment_info.no-environment", extra={"issue_id": issue.id, "error": e})`. Two issues: (1) catching bare `Exception` masks unrelated bugs (e.g. a coding error in `get_recommended_event` or `get_environment`); narrowing to `Group.DoesNotExist` / `Environment.DoesNotExist` / `Event.DoesNotExist` would still handle the documented case while letting other failures surface; (2) using `logger.info` for an error path will not show up as an error in alerting; this should be `logger.warning` or `logger.exception` so that unexpected failures are visible.

title: computeEmptyBucketsForSeries divides by zero when values array is empty
body: `computeEmptyBucketsForSeries` does `Math.floor((emptyBucketsForSeries / series.values.length) * 100)` without guarding against an empty `series.values`. When called on a `TimeSeries` with no points, this returns `NaN`, which then propagates into the `empty_buckets_percentage` analytics payload and into the confidence footer. Add an early return `if (!series.values.length) return 0;` (or similar) before the division.

title: columnOrder fallback crashes with TypeError when tableData is undefined
body: When `columns` is not provided, the fallback does `Object.keys(tableData?.meta.fields).map(...)`. Because of `?.`, `tableData?.meta.fields` evaluates to `undefined` if `tableData` is undefined, and `Object.keys(undefined)` throws `TypeError: Cannot convert undefined or null to object`. Although the prop is typed required, the optional chaining shows the author assumed `tableData` could be absent (e.g. the loading path), but the access is not actually guarded. Either short-circuit on `tableData` being undefined (`return columns ?? []`) or guard `Object.keys((tableData?.meta?.fields) ?? {})` so the component does not throw in the empty-state / loading path.

title: TableWidgetVisualization receives hardcoded empty data
body: When the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature flag is enabled, `TableWidgetVisualization` is rendered with `columns={[]}` and `tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}}` instead of the actual `fields`, `result.data`, and `result.meta` from the `tableResults.map(...)` iteration. The local variables `fields`, `result.data`, and `result.meta` are computed in the surrounding closure (used by the fallback `StyledSimpleTableChart` branch) but the new branch passes literals, so any user with the flag enabled will see empty tables in dashboards regardless of the underlying query data. This appears to be an incomplete refactor that will cause silent breakage of dashboard table widgets for opted-in users.

title: Analytics recorded before feature flag check
body: The endpoint records the `preprod_artifact.api.assemble` analytics event before checking whether the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` feature flag is enabled for the organization. Denied requests (where the feature flag is off) still record analytics, which will inflate the event count and any dashboards/metrics derived from it. If the intent is to measure usage of the feature itself, the call should be moved after the `features.has(...)` check or gated on the flag.

title: Analytics event key renamed without backward compatibility
body: The analytics event key tracked in the replay breadcrumb is renamed from `replay.view_html` to `replay.view-html`. Any existing dashboards, alerts, BI queries, or external consumers referencing `replay.view_html` will silently stop receiving data and continue to fail without error feedback. The `replayAnalyticsEvents.tsx` map is updated to the new key but the old key is not kept as an alias. If the rename is intentional, callers should be informed (e.g., a deprecation period where both keys are emitted) so dashboards do not silently break.

title: Public API `ParameterizationRegexExperiment` removed
body: The `ParameterizationRegexExperiment` class is removed from the module and from `__all__`. Any downstream code (including external Sentry forks/plugins) importing `ParameterizationRegexExperiment` from `sentry.grouping.parameterization` will fail with `ImportError`. The corresponding tests were also deleted. If this class was part of a supported extension point for grouping strategies, its removal should be documented or done behind a deprecation cycle.

title: No test for new analytics event registration
body: The new `PreprodArtifactApiAssembleEvent` analytics event is registered at module import time without any test asserting that it is registered (e.g., no equivalent of `analytics.events` containment check) or that the endpoint actually emits it.
