Combined with the fact that the endpoint records analytics before the feature flag check, this means a regression in event registration or payload shape could go undetected.

title: TableWidgetVisualization rendered with hardcoded empty data
body: In the new `use-table-widget-visualization` feature branch, `TableWidgetVisualization` is mounted with `columns={[]}` and `tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}}` — the actual `result.data` and `result.meta` produced by the dataset query (and used by the legacy `StyledSimpleTableChart` below) are discarded. Any organization that enables the `use-table-widget-visualization` flag will see fully empty tables in every dashboard table widget regardless of query results. To wire the data correctly, the component must receive the per-result columns/fields and the real `result.data`/`result.meta`, e.g. by deriving columns from `datasetConfig.getFieldHeaderMap?.(widget.queries[i])` and the fields list, and passing `tableData={{data: result.data, meta: result.meta}}`.

title: fetch_error_details pairs nodestore results assuming order preservation
body: `fetch_error_details` calls `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` and then does `for event_id, data in zip(error_ids, events.values()):`, which only produces the correct (event_id, event_data) pairs if `get_multi` returns values in the same order as the requested keys. Some nodestore backends (e.g. concurrent/Nydus-style backends) do not guarantee that, so when more than one error is fetched the AI summary can receive mismatched titles/messages/timestamps for different events. The code should key the lookup by node_id (`events[node_id]`) rather than relying on the order of `events.values()`.

title: Replays AI summary no longer honors ?project= URL override
body: The component previously obtained the project via `useLocationQuery({fields: {project: decodeScalar}})`, allowing the `?project=<id>` query parameter to choose a different project than the one stored on the replay (commonly used for cross-project replays or admin-impersonated views). The change drops that hook and now uses `useProjectFromId({project_id: replayRecord?.project_id})`, so any caller navigating to this view with `?project=...` will silently get the replay's stored project instead of the requested one, and the API call to `/projects/${slug}/replays/${id}/summarize/breadcrumbs/` may target the wrong project (404 or wrong data) or use the wrong feature flag check.

title: get_environment_info hits nodestore for every issue
body: `get_environment_info` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` for every issue included in the PR/MR comment. That helper performs a nodestore lookup (`Event.objects.get(id=...)`) per call. For a comment that lists N issues this produces N sequential nodestore round-trips on the hot path of PR comment generation, and each call is wrapped in a broad `except Exception` that swallows programming errors and only logs at info level. Consider caching the recommended event per group, batching lookups, or limiting the lookup to cases where an environment field is actually useful.

title: dcg_to_slow_conditions built from dcg_ids instead of dcg_to_groups.keys()
body: Previously `get_condition_query_groups` computed `dcg_to_slow_conditions = get_slow_conditions_for_groups(list(event_data.dcg_to_groups.keys()))` while `fetch_data_condition_groups` was fed `event_data.dcg_ids`. After the refactor both consume `event_data.dcg_ids`. If `EventRedisData.dcg_to_groups` and `dcg_ids` ever contain different sets (e.g. one includes a DCG that the other omits), `dcg_to_slow_conditions` will look up a stale or missing entry and the `KeyError` path or `slow_conditions` could be wrong. Either confirm the two sets are always equal (and add a guard) or pass the key set that actually drives `data_condition_groups`.

title: safe_urlopen for OAuth token exchange can crash view on network/transport failure
body: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, the call `req = safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` happens outside the try/except. The subsequent `try` only protects `safe_urlread(req).decode(...)` and `dict(parse_qsl(body))`. If GitHub's OAuth token endpoint is unreachable, times out, or otherwise raises (which safe_urlopen can do for connection/DNS/SSL errors), the view raises an unhandled exception and the user gets a 500 instead of the friendly 'Invalid installation request' page described in the PR. The PR claims the pipeline will fail gracefully when GitHub cannot generate an access_token, but a transport-level failure to the token endpoint bypasses that handling entirely. Wrap the safe_urlopen call (or its network I/O) in the same try/except so the failure mode is the documented one.

title: get_user_info call can crash view on GitHub /user API failure
body: `authenticated_user_info = get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` on line 434 is invoked with no exception handling. If GitHub's /user API call fails (network error, invalid/expired token causing 401, JSON parse error, etc.), get_user_info raises and the view returns a 500. This directly contradicts the PR description, which promises a graceful 'Invalid installation request' page when an access_token cannot be produced/used. The token-exchange try/except needs to extend (or a separate try/except needs to wrap get_user_info) so failures fall through to the existing `return error(...)` paths on lines 432/436.

title: KeyError when Integration.metadata lacks 'sender' field
body: The check `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` (line 504) assumes every Integration row has a `sender` dict in its metadata. That is not guaranteed: `build_integration` only adds `integration["metadata"]["sender"]` when `state.get("sender")` is truthy, and the webhook is not guaranteed to have populated pipeline state by the time build_integration runs (or sender may be absent for integrations created via other code paths). For any subsequent install attempt where an existing Integration with status=ACTIVE happens to lack `sender`, accessing `["sender"]["login"]` raises KeyError and the user gets a 500 instead of the generic 'Invalid installation request' failure. Use safe access, e.g. `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")`, and treat a missing sender as a mismatch (or as an explicit 'could not verify' failure).

title: test_installation_not_found actually exercises the state-mismatch path, not the 404 path
body: The test posts the OAuth callback with `state="ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"`, which does not match the pipeline signature `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3` used elsewhere in this file. With the new OAuthLoginView in front of GitHubInstallation, the `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature` check at line 412 fires first and returns the default `error(...)` page containing 'Invalid installation request.' The 404 stub on `/app/installations/{installation_id}` (and the `installation_id` GET that precedes it) is therefore never reached, and the assertion that replaced the original 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' check is now effectively asserting the generic-error branch. Either rename the test (e.g. test_oauth_state_mismatch) and drop the dead 404 stub + installation_id GET, or pass the matching state so the flow actually proceeds to build_integration and exercises the 404 path it claims to cover.

title: Hardcoded webhook signature is brittle to INSTALLATION_EVENT_EXAMPLE changes
body: test_github_user_mismatch posts a webhook with `HTTP_X_HUB_SIGNATURE="sha1=d184e6717f8bfbcc291ebc8c0756ee446c6c9486"`. This signature is the HMAC-SHA1 of `json.dumps(webhook_event)` (the modified INSTALLATION_EVENT_EXAMPLE) under the test GitHub webhook secret. Any change to INSTALLATION_EVENT_EXAMPLE content or formatting silently invalidates the signature: the webhook handler returns 401, no Integration is created with `sender="attacker"`, the subsequent OAuth/setup GET no longer hits the sender-mismatch branch, and the test fails at `assert resp.status_code == 204`. Compute the signature in-test from the body and the configured webhook secret (e.g. via hmac.new(secret, body, hashlib.sha1).hexdigest()) so the fixture and the signature stay in sync.

title: KeyError if integration.metadata lacks 'sender'
body: The check `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes that `sender` is always present in the integration metadata. However, `build_integration` only adds `sender` to metadata when `state.get("sender")` is truthy (line ~377). If the GitHub webhook did not include a sender (or did not run before this view), `integration.metadata["sender"]` raises KeyError, surfacing as a 500 instead of the intended graceful `error(...)` response. The code should use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` (or guard the lookup explicitly) so that a missing sender is treated like any other invalid installation request.

title: safe_urlopen not wrapped in try/except
body: The line `req = safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` performs the OAuth code-for-token exchange, but unlike the subsequent `safe_urlread`/`parse_qsl` block, it is not wrapped in a try/except. Any network failure, DNS error, TLS error, or non-2xx HTTP response will raise an uncaught exception and turn into a 500, instead of returning the generic `error(...)` page that the surrounding code clearly intends to surface for failed exchanges. This contradicts the PR's stated guarantee that 'If GitHub could not generate correct access_token from the code' the user is shown the error dialog.

title: No test for OAuth state mismatch
body: The PR description explicitly promises that the pipeline fails 'If there is a mismatch between state parameter supplied by user and pipeline signature', and the code at line 412 implements that check (`if request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature: return error(...)`). However, no test in `tests/sentry/integrations/github/test_integration.py` exercises this path by supplying a callback with a wrong `state`. Without such a test, regressions to the state check (or to how the signature is generated/compared) would go unnoticed.

title: No test for failed OAuth code exchange (wrong/reused code)
body: The PR description promises failure 'If GitHub could not generate correct access_token from the code (wrong or attempt of re-use of code)'. The branch at line 431 handles this, but no test in `test_integration.py` stubs `https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token` to return a body without `access_token` (or to return an error response) and asserts that the integration-failed template is shown. Coverage of the happy OAuth path exists, but the negative path the PR advertises is untested.

title: No test for get_user_info missing 'login'
body: The branch `if "login" not in authenticated_user_info: return error(...)` (line 435) is not covered by any test. There is no scenario in `test_integration.py` where the stub for `https://api.github.com/user` returns a payload without `login`, so a regression that, for example, accidentally trusts a different field or fails to validate the response would not be caught.

title: No test for missing 'sender' in integration metadata
body: The user-mismatch check at line 503 reads `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`. There is no test that creates an Integration record whose metadata lacks `sender` (e.g., by emulating an installation webhook that omits the sender, or by manually constructing metadata). Combined with the fact that `build_integration` only sets `sender` when `state.get("sender")` is truthy, this means the new KeyError-on-missing-sender path is completely untested.

title: test_installation_not_found may not exercise the intended code path
body: The test stubs `/app/installations/{installation_id}` with a 404 and uses a hardcoded state `ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05` for the OAuth callback. After the first GET (which binds `installation_id` to pipeline state), the actual pipeline signature is whatever Sentry's Pipeline produces for that state; it almost certainly does not equal `ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`. The test then asserts only the generic `b"Invalid installation request."` string, which is also produced by the state-mismatch branch. As a result the test passes whether the state check rejects the request or the not-found branch fires, and the 404 stub for `/app/installations/...` is never actually consumed (that endpoint is only called in `build_integration`, which never runs because the pipeline errors out first). The test should drive the OAuth callback with the real pipeline signature (or use a different setup) so it deterministically exercises the not-found branch.

title: test_github_user_mismatch ignores init_path_1 response
body: In `test_github_user_mismatch`, `self.client.get(init_path_1)` is called but its response is neither asserted nor stored. If that request fails (e.g., 500, redirect to error template), the test silently continues and the subsequent webhook/install assertions lose their meaning because the pipeline state from the first request was never established. The response should be asserted (status 302 to the OAuth authorize URL) so a regression in the initial pipeline bootstrap is caught.

title: Generic error masks real cause from logs
body: Several distinct failure modes (state mismatch, missing access_token, missing user login, sender mismatch, missing integration) all funnel into the same `error(...)` response with the user-facing message 'Invalid installation request.' and no logging of the specific reason. Because `error()` is reached from multiple call sites without any distinguishing log line, an operator triaging production failures has no way to tell from logs or user reports which branch was hit. At minimum, each `return error(...)` site should emit a `logger.info`/`warning` with the specific cause (e.g., 'oauth state mismatch', 'oauth token exchange failed', 'github user mismatch').

title: KeyError when reinstalling integrations without sender in metadata
body: In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch()`, the code accesses `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` to compare with the authenticated GitHub user. However, integrations created before this change may not have a `"sender"` key in their metadata (it is only set in `build_integration` when `state.get("sender")` is truthy). When such an existing active integration is encountered (e.g., during a reinstall flow), this line will raise `KeyError`, producing a 500 error for the user instead of the intended graceful error page. The access should use `.get()` with a safe default, e.g. `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")`.

title: Uncaught exceptions in get_user_info will produce 500 errors
body: After exchanging the OAuth code, the view calls `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` without any exception handling. If this call fails due to a network error, timeout, invalid token, or any other error, the exception will propagate up and result in a 500 error instead of the intended graceful error page. The view already catches broad exceptions when parsing the token response, so a similar try/except around `get_user_info` (and around `safe_urlopen` itself) is needed to ensure all failure paths return the `error()` page like the other validation failures do.

title: No timeout on OAuth token exchange request
body: `safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` is called without a timeout argument. If the GitHub OAuth endpoint hangs or is slow, this view will block indefinitely. Given the other `safe_urlopen` callers in the codebase typically pass an explicit `timeout=`, this call should do the same to avoid tying up worker threads on a hung OAuth handshake.

title: OAuth token exchange does not send redirect_uri or Accept header
body: The token exchange POST to GitHub sends `code`, `client_id`, and `client_secret` but omits the `redirect_uri` and an `Accept: application/json` header. While GitHub is usually lenient about `redirect_uri`, many OAuth client configurations require it to exactly match the value used at the authorize step, and on failure GitHub returns the error body as JSON (which `parse_qsl` will misparse, leading to the generic "access_token not in payload" path instead of logging the real `error_description`). Both `redirect_uri` and `Accept` should be included for correctness and debuggability.

title: test_github_user_mismatch uses hardcoded state and may pass for wrong reason
body: `test_github_user_mismatch` builds `setup_path_2` with the hardcoded state `"9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3"` (the same value asserted in `assert_setup_flow`). It then logs in as a different user (`user_2`) in a different org (`org_2`) before issuing the GETs. If `pipeline.signature` depends on the user or organization, this state will not match the pipeline started by `user_2/org_2`, and the test will pass due to state mismatch — not user mismatch. The assertion only checks for the generic `"Invalid installation request."` string, which is the same error returned for state mismatch, so the test does not actually verify the user-mismatch code path. The test should extract the actual `state` from the redirect URL returned by `init_path_2` (or otherwise obtain the correct signature) and use that in `setup_path_2`, and ideally assert a more specific error indicator.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer tests installation-not-found behavior
body: `test_installation_not_found` stubs a 404 for `/app/installations/{installation_id}` and then calls the setup path with `installation_id` and again with `code` + `state="ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"` (which deliberately does not match any pipeline signature). The first GET just bounces through `OAuthLoginView` to GitHub authorize; the second GET fails at the state check before ever reaching `build_integration`, so the 404 stub is never exercised. The test now only verifies that the generic "Invalid installation request." error is shown — the same error shown for state mismatch. Either the test should be renamed to reflect what it actually verifies, or it should be rewritten to complete the OAuth step (with a correct state) so that `build_integration` is reached and the 404 path in `get_installation_info` is actually tested.

title: AssignmentSource.queued default evaluated at class-definition time, not per-instance
body: In a dataclass, the expression on the right-hand side of a field with a default value is evaluated once at class definition, not each time the dataclass is instantiated. So `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` captures the time the module was first imported, and every `AssignmentSource` built without an explicit `queued` argument (i.e. every call to `AssignmentSource.from_integration(...)` in this PR) shares that same timestamp. The fix is `from dataclasses import field` plus `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. Consequence: the `queued` field — which is supposed to record when the assignment source was created and which is round-tripped through Celery via `to_dict()`/`from_dict()` — is wrong for every instance. It will silently break any later feature that relies on it (timeouts, staleness checks, debugging, ordering). It is also misleading to callers who read `AssignmentSource(...).queued` and assume it reflects their call.

title: Inbound sync tests do not verify the cycle-breaking behavior end-to-end
body: `test_assignee_sync_inbound_assign` and `test_assignee_sync_inbound_deassign` exercise `sync_group_assignee_inbound`, which is the entry point that the PR relies on for setting `assignment_source=AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration)` on the inbound path. Neither test mocks `ExampleIntegration.sync_assignee_outbound` (using `@mock.patch.object(ExampleIntegration, "sync_assignee_outbound")` plus `with self.tasks():`) and asserts it was NOT called. The unit test `test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration` only proves the check works when `GroupAssignee.objects.assign` is called directly with an `assignment_source`; it does not prove that `sync_group_assignee_inbound` actually propagates the source through to `GroupAssignee.objects.assign/deassign`. Without this assertion, a future refactor could silently drop the `assignment_source=...` argument in `sync_group_assignee_inbound` and re-introduce the cycle described in the PR without any test failing.

title: Test name typo: 'inalid' instead of 'invalid'
body: The method is named `test_from_dict_inalid_data(self)`. The intended word is "invalid" ("inalid" is a typo). This is purely cosmetic but is misleading to anyone searching the test suite for the case of invalid input.

title: Test name 'empty_array' describes a dict, not an array
body: `test_from_dict_empty_array` actually passes an empty dict `{}` to `AssignmentSource.from_dict`. The name suggests an empty list/array, which doesn't match the implementation under test. Rename to something like `test_from_dict_empty_dict`.

title: sync_status_outbound signature gains assignment_source but no caller/impl uses it
body: The abstract method `sync_status_outbound` was widened to accept `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`, but nothing in this PR passes it (no call site was changed to forward the source) and the generic `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync` already applies the cycle check to every attribute including `outbound_status`. So the new parameter is dead surface area: it changes the contract that every integration subclass must implement, but no implementation shown here reads it and no caller supplies it. Either remove the parameter from the abstract method or also update the implementations to forward it; leaving it as-is means downstream integrations (Jira, GitHub, etc.) will see a signature mismatch warning or be tempted to silently ignore it, undermining the whole point of plumbing the source through.

title: from_integration assumes RpcIntegration has a 'name' attribute
body: `AssignmentSource.from_integration` is declared as accepting `Integration | RpcIntegration` and accesses `integration.name`. `sync_group_assignee_inbound` (in `src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py`) declares its `integration` parameter as `RpcIntegration` and is the production caller. The existing tests in `tests/sentry/models/test_groupassignee.py` happen to pass the ORM `Integration` (which has `.name`) into `sync_group_assignee_inbound`, so they will not catch a missing attribute on `RpcIntegration`. If `RpcIntegration` exposes `provider`/something else instead of `name`, every inbound webhook will raise `AttributeError` at `AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration)`. Worth confirming against the `RpcIntegration` dataclass before merge; if `.name` is not guaranteed, the helper should fall back to `getattr(integration, 'name', None)` or use `integration.provider`.

title: AssignmentSource.queued default is a shared class-level value
body: The field default `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once when the class body is executed at module import time, not per instance. Every AssignmentSource constructed without an explicit `queued` (which is every call site in this PR, including `from_integration`) shares the exact same datetime object captured at import time. The fix is to use `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so each instance gets the timestamp of its own creation. The current `test_to_dict` only asserts the field is non-null, so this regression goes undetected.

title: sync_assignee_outbound is invoked with assignment_source kwarg that concrete subclasses may reject
body: The task now calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(external_issue, user, assign=assign, assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)`. The abstract definition in `IssueSyncIntegration` still relies on `**kwargs` to absorb extra arguments, but concrete subclasses (e.g. the Jira/GitHub/etc. integrations) typically override `sync_assignee_outbound(self, external_issue, user, assign=True)` without `**kwargs` and without an `assignment_source` parameter. Calling those overrides with the new kwarg will raise `TypeError: ... unexpected keyword argument 'assignment_source'`, breaking assignee sync for every integration. The mock-based test `test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign` does not exercise real subclass signatures and therefore does not catch this. Either add `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None` to the abstract signature (as was done for `sync_status_outbound`) and update every concrete override, or remove the kwarg from the call site until those overrides are updated.

title: from_dict silently returns None on deserialization failure, bypassing cycle protection
body: `from_dict` swallows any `ValueError`/`TypeError` and returns `None`. The only consumer (`sync_assignee_outbound`) treats `None` as 'no source' and then runs `should_sync` without the cycle guard, so any malformed or schema-drifted `assignment_source_dict` silently disables the very protection this PR introduces and re-enables the original sync loop. The dict is produced by the same code path that consumes it, so silent fallback is risky. Consider raising (so Celery retries / surfaces a metric) or at least logging a warning when reconstruction fails, and updating callers/tests accordingly.

title: sync_status_outbound signature change is unused dead code
body: `IssueSyncIntegration.sync_status_outbound` is updated to accept `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`, but no call site in this PR (or anywhere visible in the diff) ever constructs or forwards an `AssignmentSource` for the status path, and no caller of `sync_status_outbound` is modified. The parameter is dead until the status sync cycle is actually fixed, and it is inconsistent with `sync_assignee_outbound` (which still relies on `**kwargs` for the same purpose). Either thread `AssignmentSource` through the inbound status flow and add the cycle guard there, or revert the abstract signature change to avoid misleading readers.

title: No coverage for deassign path with matching AssignmentSource
body: A new test `test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration` was added to verify that `assign` skips outbound sync when the source integration matches the target. The equivalent unassign path (`GroupAssignee.objects.deassign(...)` followed by `sync_group_assignee_outbound`) is not covered — the only deassign test (`test_assignee_sync_outbound_unassign`) only asserts the no-source case. Add a parallel test that passes an `AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration)` to `deassign` and asserts `mock_sync_assignee_outbound.assert_not_called()`, since `GroupAssigneeManager.deassign` also forwards `assignment_source` to `sync_group_assignee_outbound`.

title: Mutable default value: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()`
body: In a dataclass, a default value of `timezone.now()` is evaluated once at class definition time and is then shared by every instance created without an explicit `queued` argument. Every `AssignmentSource(source_name=..., integration_id=...)` constructed in a worker will therefore have the same `queued` datetime (the import time of the module), not the time the source was actually queued. The correct pattern is `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. The field is not yet consulted in any comparison logic in this PR, so the cycle-breaking itself still works, but the field is serialized through Celery as `to_dict` / `from_dict` and any future use of `queued` for staleness, deduplication, or analytics will be incorrect. The test `test_to_dict` only asserts the key is present, so it does not catch this.

title: Test name typo: `inalid_data`
body: The test method is named `test_from_dict_inalid_data`. The intended spelling is `test_from_dict_invalid_data`. Renaming fixes a misleading test identifier that hides intent and breaks search/grep for invalid-input tests.

title: No test catches the mutable-default bug for `queued`
body: `test_to_dict` only asserts that `result.get("queued") is not None`. A test that constructs two `AssignmentSource` instances in sequence (e.g., with a short sleep between them) and asserts that `s1.queued != s2.queued` would have detected the shared-default bug in the dataclass. Add this assertion, plus a `from_dict` round-trip test, before relying on `queued` for any logic.

title: `assignment_source.to_dict()` recomputed on every loop iteration
body: In `sync_group_assignee_outbound`, the expression `assignment_source.to_dict() if assignment_source else None` is evaluated inside the `for external_issue_id in external_issue_ids` loop, so `to_dict()` (and therefore `asdict()` plus a full copy of the dataclass) is run once per linked external issue. The value does not depend on `external_issue_id`; compute it once before the loop and reuse the dict in the kwargs. The `AssignmentSource` is frozen, but the inner dict is rebuilt unnecessarily for each outbound task.

title: Missing test for cross-integration propagation (cycle break must not over-block)
body: The new `test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration` proves the loop is broken when the source equals the only target. It does not prove the other direction the PR's docstring relies on: when multiple integrations are linked to the same group, an inbound change from integration A must still propagate to integration B. Without a test that links two `ExternalIssue`s from two different provider integrations and asserts that `sync_assignee_outbound` IS called for the non-source one, the `should_sync` short-circuit could regress to blocking all outbound sync (e.g., by checking integration_id more broadly) and the suite would still pass.

title: Copy-paste error in test_state_results_multi_group mock value
body: The data packet is built with `{"group_1": 6, "group_2": 10}` but `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` is called for `group_2` with value `6` instead of `10`. This is a copy-paste from the previous line. The test passes only because `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` currently ignores its `value` parameter, so if the mock is later changed to incorporate the value (e.g., into the fingerprint or evidence), the test would fail in a confusing way rather than catching the real discrepancy.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler changed from concrete to uninstantiable abstract class
body: Previously `MetricAlertDetectorHandler(DetectorHandler[...])` defined a concrete `evaluate` that returned `[]`, so the class was instantiable and could serve as a working no-op handler referenced by `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler`. The new body is just `pass`, and since `StatefulDetectorHandler` is `abc.ABC` with abstract methods `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and `build_occurrence_and_event_data`, any code that accesses `detector.detector_handler` for a `MetricAlertFire` group type will now raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler...`. Although the inline comment says these issues are not created yet, this is a silent regression of a previously working registration.

title: DetectorHandler.evaluate return type contract break
body: The abstract method signature was changed from `-> list[DetectorEvaluationResult]` to `-> dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`. Any existing concrete subclass of `DetectorHandler` (inside or outside this repo) that returns a list will now fail at runtime with an `AttributeError` on `.values()` in `process_detectors`, or at type-check time. This is a breaking API change for a public abstract base and warrants a deprecation/migration note rather than a silent switch.

title: No coverage for build_occurrence_and_event_data raising
body: `evaluate_group_key_value` calls `self.build_occurrence_and_event_data(...)` inside the status-change branch. If the hook raises, `enqueue_state_update` and `enqueue_dedupe_update` have already mutated handler state but `commit_state_updates` will not run (exception propagates out of `evaluate` before `process_detectors` reaches the commit call). There is no test asserting the behavior in that failure path (does the dedupe get reset? are partial state updates visible on retry?), so this whole failure mode is uncharacterized.

title: Detector.group_type re-queries registry on every access
body: The new `group_type` property calls `grouptype.registry.get_by_slug(self.type)` every time it is accessed, and `detector_handler` reads it on every invocation. In `process_detectors` and any caller that does `detector.detector_handler` repeatedly (e.g., per-detector loops, tests, API serializers), this triggers an unnecessary registry lookup each time. Caching the slug→GroupType lookup on the instance would avoid the repeated calls.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now an uninstantiable abstract class registered as detector_handler
body: This change replaces `DetectorHandler` with `StatefulDetectorHandler` and removes the previously-present `def evaluate(...)` placeholder that returned `[]`. `StatefulDetectorHandler` declares four new abstract methods (`counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, `build_occurrence_and_event_data`), and `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` implements none of them. The class is therefore abstract. However, it is still referenced from `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler = MetricAlertDetectorHandler`, so any time `Detector.detector_handler` is accessed for a Detector with type `"metric_alert_fire"` (which `process_detectors` does unconditionally), `MetricAlertDetectorHandler(detector)` raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract methods ...`. This aborts the entire `process_detectors` loop, preventing any further detectors in the list from being processed. Previously the class was concrete (it had a `def evaluate` that returned `[]`), so this is a regression. To fix, either implement the four abstract methods (with sensible stubs/raises-NotImplementedError where appropriate, but the class must still be concrete), or revert to `DetectorHandler` until the abstraction is actually built.

title: build_occurrence_and_event_data exceptions leave state inconsistent (dedupe already bumped)
body: In `evaluate_group_key_value`, `self.enqueue_dedupe_update(group_key, dedupe_value)` is called (line 265) before any later logic. Once `state_data.status != new_status`, the code reaches the new `else: result, event_data = self.build_occurrence_and_event_data(...)` branch. If that subclass hook raises (network failure, invalid `value` for the detector type, missing config, etc.), the function propagates the exception out of `evaluate_group_key_value`, the dict result is never produced, but the previously-enqueued `dedupe_updates[group_key]` and `state_updates[group_key]` still get committed by `handler.commit_state_updates()` after `process_detectors` catches the failure. On retry of the same data packet, `dedupe_value <= state_data.dedupe_value` will be true, so the data packet is permanently skipped and the issue is never produced. There is no try/except around `build_occurrence_and_event_data`, and no rollback of the enqueued dedupe/state update on failure. Either swallow and log errors (mirroring the `skipping_invalid_condition_group` branch), or roll back the dedupe/state enqueue when building the occurrence fails.

title: build_occurrence_and_event_data called with PriorityLevel(new_status) but type was DetectorPriorityLevel
body: The new call is `self.build_occurrence_and_event_data(group_key, value, PriorityLevel(new_status))`. `new_status` is a `DetectorPriorityLevel` (an IntEnum defined in `sentry.workflow_engine.types`), not a `PriorityLevel`. Passing one enum's integer value to the other enum's constructor relies on the underlying integer values matching, which is true today but is a fragile coupling between two enums in different modules. If `PriorityLevel` and `DetectorPriorityLevel` ever drift (e.g., one gains a new level the other doesn't), this will raise `ValueError: ... is not a valid PriorityLevel`. Either convert via the enum's `.value`/`.name` mapping explicitly, or document and assert the invariant.

title: test_state_results_multi_group passes wrong value for group_2 to build_mock_occurrence_and_event
body: The test packet is `{"dedupe": 2, "group_vals": {"group_1": 6, "group_2": 10}}`, but the assertion builds the expected occurrence with `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(detector.detector_handler, "group_2", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)` — i.e., value 6 instead of 10. The mock currently ignores `value`, so the test passes, but as soon as a future change to `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` actually uses `value` (e.g., to embed it in evidence_data or the subtitle), the test will start asserting against a value the production code path will never produce, masking real regressions. Use the actual packet value (10) for group_2.

title: DetectorHandler.evaluate return type contract break not documented for third-party subclasses
body: The abstract `DetectorHandler.evaluate` signature changed from `list[DetectorEvaluationResult]` to `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, and all in-repo subclasses were updated. The PR description mentions this, but any out-of-tree subclass of `DetectorHandler` (e.g., downstream open-source detectors) will silently start returning the wrong shape and either crash at iteration (`.values()` on a list raises AttributeError) or behave incorrectly when keys collide. Consider a deprecation period that accepts both shapes (e.g., coerce to dict internally) or a clearer changelog note in the docstring so subclass authors are explicitly warned.

title: test_dedupe in TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue has mismatched group_keys, will fail
body: The test builds the expected `occurrence` and `event_data` with `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)`, so the occurrence's fingerprint is `[f"{handler.detector.id}:val1"]` (via `handler.build_fingerprint("val1")`). However, the test then constructs `expected_result = DetectorEvaluationResult("group_key", ...)` and passes `expected_result.group_key` (i.e. `"group_key"`) into `handler.evaluate_group_key_value(...)`. Internally that calls `self.build_occurrence_and_event_data("group_key", 10, PriorityLevel.HIGH)` -> `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "group_key", 10, ...)` producing an occurrence whose fingerprint is `[f"{handler.detector.id}:group_key"]`. Since IssueOccurrence is a dataclass with field-by-field `__eq__`, the fingerprints differ and the assertion `... == expected_result` will fail. The expected occurrence must be built with the same group_key passed into `evaluate_group_key_value`.

title: Inconsistent value passed to build_mock_occurrence_and_event in multiple tests
body: Several tests pass `value=6` to `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` even though the data packet being evaluated contains different values. For example: `test_state_results_multi_group` calls `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(detector.detector_handler, "group_2", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)` while the data packet has `group_vals: {"group_2": 10}`; `test_results_on_change` calls it with `value=6` while the packet has `val1: 100`; `test_dedupe` calls it with `value=6` while the packet has `val1: 8`; `TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe` calls it with `value=6` while `evaluate_group_key_value` is invoked with `value=10`. Currently the value isn't used inside `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` so the tests pass, but the inconsistency obscures intent and any future change that incorporates `value` into the occurrence or event_data will silently produce wrong assertions.

title: dedupe_update is enqueued before condition_group is validated
body: In `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate_group_key_value`, `self.enqueue_dedupe_update(group_key, dedupe_value)` is called immediately after the dedupe check and BEFORE the `if not self.condition_group: ... return None` early return. As a result, data packets routed to detectors that have no valid condition group are still recorded as 'processed' in Redis (the dedupe value is bumped in `commit_state_updates`). If the condition group is later attached, those prior packets will be skipped even though no evaluation actually ran for them, causing potentially missed detections. The enqueue should be moved after the condition_group check, or only enqueued on the paths that perform real evaluation.

title: Kafka produce exceptions prevent state commit, causing duplicate detections
body: `process_detectors` calls `create_issue_occurrence_from_result` (which calls `produce_occurrence_to_kafka`) BEFORE `handler.commit_state_updates()`. If Kafka is unavailable or `produce_occurrence_to_kafka` raises, the exception propagates out of the loop and `commit_state_updates()` is never executed for that detector. The Redis dedupe value is therefore not updated, so on the next processing of the same data packet the detector will re-emit the same occurrence (and re-trigger downstream workflows). This is also exposed more by the new `build_occurrence_and_event_data` path which can now raise from subclass code and have the same effect. Either wrap the produce in a try/except or commit dedupe state after successful produces.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now extends StatefulDetectorHandler without implementing required abstract methods
body: The PR changes `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` from `DetectorHandler[QuerySubscriptionUpdate]` to `StatefulDetectorHandler[QuerySubscriptionUpdate]`, but the body remains `pass`. `StatefulDetectorHandler` declares abstract members `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and now also the newly-added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. Instantiating `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler` (or any code path that constructs this handler) will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class ... with abstract methods ...`. Since `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler = MetricAlertDetectorHandler` is wired up in the same file, this will break the moment anyone references `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler`. Either leave `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` extending the non-abstract `DetectorHandler`, or implement the abstract methods (or at minimum add `detector_handler = None` until the abstraction is built).

title: get_monitor_environment_context returns original config, losing schedule_type display conversion
body: The function copies `monitor_environment.monitor.config` into a local `config` variable on line 160 and converts `schedule_type` to its display string (e.g., "crontab" instead of the raw integer choice) on lines 161-162. However, the returned dict on line 168 uses `"config": monitor_environment.monitor.config` — the un-modified original — instead of the local `config` variable. As a result, the `schedule_type` display conversion is silently discarded, and the incident event payload will show the raw integer choice value instead of the human-readable schedule type name. The fix is to change line 168 to `"config": config`.

title: Docstring typo in get_failure_reason
body: The docstring on line 132 contains "humam readible" which should be "human readable".

title: Docstring example for get_failure_reason does not match actual output
body: The docstring on line 136 shows the singular example as `"A failed check-in was detected"`, but the actual `SINGULAR_HUMAN_FAILURE_MAP` values are `"An error check-in was detected"`, `"A missed check-in was detected"`, and `"A timeout check-in was detected"`. None of the actual outputs match the documented example.

title: get_monitor_environment_context modifies a local copy but returns the original config
body: The function builds `config = monitor_environment.monitor.config.copy()` and mutates the local `config['schedule_type']` to its human-readable display value, but then the function returns `monitor_environment.monitor.config` (the original, unmodified dict) instead of the local `config`. As a result the `schedule_type` conversion is dead code, and any consumer of the `monitor` context (events produced to Kafka) will receive the raw stored value (e.g. `"crontab"`) rather than the display value (e.g. `"Crontab"`).

title: Docstring typo and inaccurate singular example in get_failure_reason
body: The docstring contains the typo "humam readible" (should be "human readable") and the third example "A failed check-in was detected" does not match what the code actually produces for a single failing check-in. The real singular messages in SINGULAR_HUMAN_FAILURE_MAP are "An error check-in was detected", "A missed check-in was detected", and "A timeout check-in was detected".

title: Public SimpleCheckIn TypedDict moved, breaking any existing import path
body: Previously `SimpleCheckIn` was defined in `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed`; it has been removed from that module and re-defined in `sentry.monitors.types`. Any external caller doing `from sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed import SimpleCheckIn` (or importing it transitively) will now hit an ImportError. Because the type is part of a function signature in the public API of this module, it should either be re-exported from `mark_failed.py` for backwards compatibility, or the rename should be called out explicitly in the PR description / changelog.

title: Renamed helper functions leave existing tests referencing the old names
body: `mark_failed_threshold` was renamed to `try_incident_threshold` and `create_issue_platform_occurrence` was renamed to `create_incident_occurrence`, but no test file was updated in this PR. Any test that imports these symbols by their previous names (or that patches them via `mock.patch`) will fail to collect/run. The refactor needs an accompanying test update (rename references, adjust patch targets) and ideally a test that exercises the new module layout end-to-end.

title: Unused module-level logger in new modules
body: Both `incidents.py` (line 11) and `incident_occurrence.py` (line 25) define `logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)` but neither file emits any log records. Either drop the unused logger or add the intended log statements; leaving it in just adds noise and a misleading signal that logging happens here.

title: monitor_env.get_environment() called twice per occurrence, in a loop
body: Inside `create_incident_occurrence`, `monitor_env.get_environment().name` is accessed on line 67 (evidence display) and again on line 90 (`event_data["environment"]`). `incidents.try_incident_threshold` then calls `create_incident_occurrence` once for every check-in in `previous_checkins`, so the environment lookup (typically a DB query on `Environment`) is performed 2 * len(previous_checkins) times per failing check-in. The environment should be resolved once at the top of `create_incident_occurrence` and reused.

title: get_monitor_environment_context discards humanized schedule_type
body: In get_monitor_environment_context (lines 159-171), a local `config` variable is created by copying `monitor_environment.monitor.config` and modifying `schedule_type` to its human-readable display value via `get_schedule_type_display()` (lines 160-162). However, the returned dict at line 168 references `monitor_environment.monitor.config` directly, so the humanized schedule_type is never included in the output. The fix is to use the local `config` variable in the returned dict instead of `monitor_environment.monitor.config`. This is a pre-existing bug carried over from mark_failed.py, but since the code is being moved to a new module, it is a good time to fix it. The humanized schedule_type would appear in the monitor context sent with issue occurrences for monitor failures.

title: Restarted process is killed but never joined, leaking zombies
body: In `_ensure_processes_alive`, when a flusher process is unhealthy the code calls `process.kill()` and then immediately calls `self._create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` to spawn a replacement. The killed process is never `join()`ed and never `close()`d. With `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS = 10` and any reasonable churn (e.g. SIGKILL exit codes, transient Redis issues during deployment), up to 10 `spawn`-context children can be left as zombies holding PIDs and OS resources until the parent exits. Repeated restarts during the consumer's lifetime will gradually leak OS resources. The fix is to `process.join(timeout=...)` (and ideally `process.close()`) after `kill()` before reassigning `self.processes[process_index]`.

title: join() breaks out of loop on deadline, leaving later processes unterminated
body: In `SpanFlusher.join`, the iteration `for process_index, process in self.processes.items():` calls `break` as soon as the supplied `timeout` is exhausted. Any processes whose entries come after the one currently being inspected are never visited and never `terminate()`d. With N flusher processes and a short join deadline, the surviving subprocesses keep running after the consumer has been declared shut down; their Kafka producers and Redis state are not cleanly closed, which can leave pending produces (`producer_futures`) unresolved and produce duplicate or partial segments on the buffered-segments topic if the broker accepts the late flush. The loop must iterate over every process and just skip the wait portion (but still call `process.terminate()`) when the deadline has passed.

title: Dead helper `_create_process_for_shard` is never invoked
body: The method `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is defined (lines 127–132) but is not called from anywhere in the module or tests. It will be flagged by static analyzers as unused and is leftover scaffolding. (Not a runtime bug, but a maintainer should remove it before merging.)

title: Docstring claims one process per shard, but implementation caps processes
body: The class docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but `__init__` actually creates `min(max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))` processes and shards are shared across processes via round-robin when `max_processes < len(shards)`. This is misleading and contradicts both the new `--flusher-processes` CLI option (which defaults to 1) and the test `test_flusher_processes_limit` that exercises sharing. The docstring should describe the actual pooling behavior.

title: Backpressure metric lost the shard/process dimension
body: Pre-refactor, the backpressure metric was emitted via `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flusher.backpressure")` from a single flusher. After the refactor, the same metric is emitted from inside a loop over `self.process_backpressure_since.values()`, but no `tags` are attached. There is now no way to tell from metrics which flusher process (or shard group) is causing the consumer to be paused. The other flusher metrics in the file (e.g. `spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy`, `spans.buffer.flusher.produce`) are correctly tagged with `{shard|shards}`. The backpressure metric should be tagged similarly, e.g. `tags={"process_index": process_index}` or `{"shards": shard_tag}`, so operators can attribute stalls.

title: Any single flusher process hitting backpressure halts the entire consumer
body: In `submit`, the backpressure check raises `MessageRejected` if **any** of `self.process_backpressure_since.values()` is non-zero past the threshold. Because shards are partitioned round-robin across processes, a single problematic shard (or hot key on one shard) can stall the whole consumer even when other processes are healthy and keeping up. The pre-refactor behavior only had a single flusher, so this regression doesn't surface there. Consider aggregating backpressure over the whole pool (e.g. require a majority of processes to be in backpressure, or check that `drift` has grown large) so a straggler doesn't take down throughput.

title: Per-process SpansBuffer in subprocesses can race with main-process writes
body: `_create_process_for_shards` constructs a brand-new `SpansBuffer(shards)` (`shard_buffer = SpansBuffer(shards)`) and pickles it into the spawned subprocess. The main consumer thread, however, was given a separate `SpansBuffer(assigned_shards=[p.index for p in partitions])` in `factory.py` and writes incoming spans via `buffer.process_spans(...)` on that object. Although both buffers are stateless wrappers over Redis, each subprocess now opens its own Redis connection pool from a different PID, and the flush logic does `buffer.flush_segments(now=now)` / `buffer.record_stored_segments()` against its private buffer. Nothing in the diff confirms this design is safe (e.g. that keys TTLs are observed the same way, or that `any_shard_at_limit`/`get_memory_info` look at the correct Redis instances consistently). The single-process version relied on one shared buffer; the refactor should validate or call out this assumption explicitly so a future change to `SpansBuffer` doesn't quietly break cross-process semantics.

title: test_flusher_processes_limit does not verify shard partitioning or end-to-end flushing
body: The new test only asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `flusher.max_processes == 2`, `flusher.num_processes == 2`, and that the shards total 4. It does not verify that (a) each shard is assigned to exactly one process (no duplicates / no missing shards), (b) the round-robin ordering is stable, (c) when `flusher_processes > len(assigned_shards)` the pool is capped, or (d) that spans sent to the consumer are actually flushed and emitted via `produce_to_pipe` for each process group. Without (d), a regression where one of the new per-process flushers silently stops emitting would not be caught. Without (a), a bug where every shard is assigned to `process_index=0` would still pass.

title: `flusher_processes` declared `int | None` but only ever set to a CLI int
body: `ProcessSpansStrategyFactory.__init__` declares `flusher_processes: int | None = None` and `SpanFlusher.__init__` declares `max_processes: int | None = None`. Both fall back to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)` via `max_processes or len(...)`, where `or` would also coerce `0` to the fallback. If an operator ever passes `--flusher-processes 0` (deliberately to disable flushers, or via a config that defaults to 0), `0 or len(shards)` evaluates to `len(shards)`, silently spawning processes anyway. Either change `or` to a strict `is None` check or document that 0 is not a valid value.

title: Dead helper `_create_process_for_shard` is never called
body: The method `SpanFlusher._create_process_for_shard(shard)` (lines 127-132) is defined but has no callers. The only restart path is in `_ensure_processes_alive`, which invokes `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly. The single-shard helper is dead code and should either be removed or wired into the restart path so callers can target a specific shard.

title: Docstring claims one process per shard, but processes shard subsets
body: The class docstring (line 32) says 'Creates one process per shard for parallel processing.' That is no longer true: `__init__` actually creates `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` processes and groups shards via `i % num_processes`. With `flusher_processes=2` and 4 shards, the docstring is misleading and the round-robin assignment also has performance implications (e.g., adjacent shards can end up in different processes and cross shard/processes). The docstring should describe the actual grouping behavior.

title: CLI help for `--flusher-processes` is misleading
body: `help="Maximum number of processes for the span flusher. Defaults to 1."` implies that passing e.g. `--flusher-processes 8` always gives 8 processes. In reality `SpanFlusher.__init__` clamps via `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))`, and the help also describes the CLI default of 1 rather than the SpanFlusher default of `len(assigned_shards)`. If a user passes a value greater than the number of assigned partitions, they will silently get fewer processes than expected. The help should note the cap.

title: `flusher_processes=0` is silently coerced to `len(assigned_shards)`
body: In `SpanFlusher.__init__`, `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats 0 as falsy and falls back to one process per shard. An operator passing `--flusher-processes 0` likely expects 'no flusher' or an error, not a default-override that spawns more processes than they asked for. Use an explicit `None` check instead of `or`, or document/validate that 0 is not accepted.

title: `test_flusher_processes_limit` never submits a message
body: The new test only asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `flusher.max_processes == 2`, `flusher.num_processes == 2` and that 4 shards are present in `process_to_shards_map`. It does not submit a payload, does not advance drift, and does not assert that any segment reaches the `produce_to_pipe`. The whole point of the multiprocess refactor is that shards split across processes are still flushed end-to-end; this test will silently pass even if the new `_create_process_for_shards` does not correctly wire shards to buffers or if the threading path is broken. Add at least one submit + flush assertion that exercises the cross-process flusher wiring.

title: `time.sleep(0.1)` is a no-op due to the monkeypatch above it
body: Lines 15-16 monkeypatch `time.sleep` to a no-op (`lambda _: None`). The comment on line 61 then says 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change' and calls `time.sleep(0.1)`, but that call is also a no-op. The comment is misleading; the test passes only because the flusher thread likewise runs `time.sleep` as a no-op and busy-loops. Either drop the call/comment, or un-monkeypatch `time.sleep` for that single line so the intent matches the code.

title: `if not process:` guard in `_ensure_processes_alive` is dead
body: `self.processes` is populated in `_create_process_for_shards` and never has `None` values, so `if not process: continue` (line 222) is unreachable. Either remove the check or, if the intent was to skip dead slots, document why None entries would ever appear (e.g., a future graceful-shutdown slot).

title: Per-submit Redis memory probe now scales with process count
body: Original code did one `self.buffer.get_memory_info()` call per submit. New code iterates `for buffer in self.buffers.values(): memory_infos.extend(buffer.get_memory_info())`, so the consumer issues N Redis probes per submit where N equals the number of flusher processes (up to one per shard). Even though `submit` is described as not hot, on every call we now do N network round-trips to gather data that conceptually represents the same underlying Redis memory. Consider caching or aggregating memory info once per flush cycle instead of once per submit.

title: `process.kill()` followed by immediate respawn can produce duplicate flushes
body: In `_ensure_processes_alive`, the unhealthy process is `kill()`-ed (non-blocking) and `_create_process_for_shards` is invoked immediately. The old subprocess may still be alive for some time (kill delivery, Redis I/O in flight), during which both the old and new flusher processes can independently call `buffer.flush_segments` and `producer.produce` on the same shard. That can produce duplicate `BUFFERED_SEGMENTS` messages on Kafka. The original code had a similar race but only one flusher existed; now that shards are shared across processes, the blast radius is wider. Consider `process.join(timeout)` before respawn, or use `terminate()` plus a join so the previous process truly exits first.

title: `process_restarts` threshold allows one more restart than the constant suggests
body: The check is `if self.process_restarts[process_index] > MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS`, followed by increment + respawn. Tracing the counter: it starts at 0, is checked then incremented. With `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS = 10` the counter reaches 11 before `11 > 10` triggers, so the consumer actually restarts the process 11 times before raising, not 10. This is an off-by-one that pre-dates this PR, but it is worth aligning either the constant (to `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS - 1`) or the comparison (`>= MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS`) so the cap matches the name.

title: Dead method `_create_process_for_shard` is never invoked
body: The new `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` method (lines 127-132) is defined to find the process that owns a given shard and restart it, but it has no caller anywhere in the codebase. The actual per-process restart logic lives in `_ensure_processes_alive`, which iterates over `self.processes.items()` directly. This method appears to be leftover from refactoring and should be removed; leaving it in is confusing because it implies a per-shard restart capability that doesn't exist and would race with the per-process restart logic if it were ever wired up.

title: Dead `if not process: continue` guard
body: Inside `_ensure_processes_alive`, the loop `for process_index, process in self.processes.items():` is immediately followed by `if not process: continue`. `process` is always a `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` or `threading.Thread` instance assigned by `_create_process_for_shards`; both are always truthy, so the guard can never trigger. The check is dead code carried over from the previous single-process implementation and should be removed for clarity.

title: Inconsistent default for flusher_processes between CLI and factory
body: The CLI option `--flusher-processes` is registered with `default=1`, but the underlying `ProcessSpansStrategyFactory.__init__` declares `flusher_processes: int | None = None`, which `SpanFlusher` then resolves to `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` (one process per shard). Consequence: production CLI runs with 1 flusher process, while any test or programmatic caller that omits `flusher_processes` silently gets N processes (e.g., the new `test_flusher_processes_limit` test deliberately passes `flusher_processes=2` precisely because the factory default would otherwise spawn 4). This divergence makes the help text (`Defaults to 1.`) and the Python signature disagree, which is a footgun for callers and obscures whether the new "process per shard" behavior is actually enabled in default deployments. Either the factory default should also be 1, or the CLI default should be None and the help text should match.

title: Added `time.sleep(0.1)` is a no-op due to earlier monkeypatch
body: `test_basic` sets `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at line 15, which replaces the `time.sleep` attribute on the imported `time` module. The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` on line 62 therefore resolves to the patched no-op lambda and waits for nothing. The accompanying comment ("Give flusher threads time to process after drift change") is misleading: the sleep does not give the thread any time. The test currently only passes because the flusher's own `time.sleep(1)` is also monkey-patched to a no-op, so the thread spins very fast and usually catches up before `step.join()` flips `stopped.value` to True; on a slow CI machine the thread can still be mid-iteration with the old drift when `stopped` is flipped, and the assertion `(msg,) = messages` will fail. The new code should either poll on `messages`, use a sleep that bypasses the monkeypatch (e.g., `time.monotonic()` busy wait), or drop the misleading line entirely.

title: Assert used for runtime type check in production code
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit contains `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` as a runtime type guard. Asserts are stripped under `python -O`, which is used by some production images and packaging tools. If the assumption is ever violated (e.g., an upstream change delivers a non-BrokerValue message.value), the code will silently fall into the broad `except Exception` block, the message will be marked complete and committed without ever being processed (data loss). Use an explicit `if not isinstance(...):` check and either drop via DLQ or raise.

title: Submit error path silently drops messages and commits their offsets
body: The broad `except Exception` in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches any failure during decoding, building the WorkItem, invoking `grouping_fn`, or calling `queue_pool.submit`. When caught, it calls `offset_tracker.add_offset(...)` followed immediately by `complete_offset(...)`. Because the offset is now present in `all_offsets` and absent from `outstanding`, the commit loop treats it as fully processed and calls `commit_function({partition: offset})`. The Kafka offset advances, the message is never queued, and the work item is permanently lost with only a `logger.exception` line as evidence. This is broader than the explicit `if result is None:` path (which mirrors existing decode-failure behavior) and will silently drop messages on any bug in user-provided code (e.g. `grouping_fn`). At minimum, the message should be routed to the DLQ, or the exception should be re-raised to crash the consumer and force investigation. Note that `uptime-results` is configured without a `dlq_topic` in `KAFKA_CONSUMERS`, so there is no DLQ to send to; this should be addressed before relying on the mode.

title: Sentry transaction name uses 'monitors.' prefix for the uptime consumer
body: OrderedQueueWorker.run names its Sentry transaction `f"monitors.{self.identifier}.worker_{self.worker_id}"`. This consumer is registered for `Topic.UPTIME_RESULTS` (see `sentry.consumers.KAFKA_CONSUMERS["uptime-results"]` and the UptimeResultsStrategyFactory subclass), so the prefix should be `uptime.` (or some neutral identifier). The same incorrect `monitors.` prefix is used by the existing code in `result_consumer.py:49`, which is why it likely got copy-pasted here; the new transaction should be fixed so traces and performance dashboards for this consumer are correctly grouped. ResultProcessor's transaction (result_consumer.py:49) has the same problem and was inherited by this PR through the new processing path.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the opposite of its docstring
body: Inside `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling`, two messages are submitted (offsets 100 and 101) and the first is configured to raise. The OrderedQueueWorker catches the exception, logs it, and still calls `complete_offset` for both, so the commit loop will commit offset 101 (last processed). However the test ends with `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, which asserts that NO commits happen for the partition. This contradicts the docstring ("errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages") and means the test passes whether or not the desired behavior is implemented. The assertion should be the opposite, e.g. `assert test_partition in committed_offsets` and `assert committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102` (101 + 1, mirroring the +1 in `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker.commit_offsets`).

title: --mode help text still describes only 'parallel uses multithreading'
body: The `uptime_options()` click choices were extended to include `thread-queue-parallel` but the help string still reads `"The mode to process results in. Parallel uses multithreading."`. Operators picking a mode from `--help` have no indication that the new option exists or what it does. Either update the help text to enumerate the modes (and describe what `thread-queue-parallel` does) or remove the now-misleading sentence about parallel using multithreading.

title: Docstring claims consistent group→queue assignment, but hash() is process-randomized
body: FixedQueuePool's docstring promises "Each group is consistently assigned to the same queue" and `get_queue_for_group` is implemented as `return hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`. CPython randomizes the string hash seed per process unless `PYTHONHASHSEED` is fixed, so two runs of the consumer can map the same group to different queues. The test `test_consistent_group_assignment` only checks within a single process, so the cross-process case is not covered. In practice ordering survives because Kafka's per-partition order pins messages to one partition and that partition's items all map to one queue within a single process — but the docstring's literal claim is false and will mislead anyone reasoning about the code. Either use a stable hash (e.g. `hashlib.blake2b(group_key, ...).digest()` mod num_queues) or correct the docstring to describe the actual guarantee.

title: WorkItem.message field is written but never read
body: `WorkItem.message` is set by `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` when constructing the work item, but no code path ever reads it (the worker only accesses `work_item.partition`, `work_item.offset`, and `work_item.result`). Either it should be used (e.g. for DLQ routing on exception, or for re-injecting on retry) or it should be removed from the dataclass to avoid carrying a dead reference to the original Message.

title: test_concurrent_processing_across_groups does not actually verify concurrency
body: The test submits 6 items split across 3 group_keys and asserts that `groups_seen` ends up with 3 distinct groups in `processed_items`. This would pass even if all 6 items were processed sequentially in a single worker (the test only checks that all groups were visited, not that they were visited in parallel). To genuinely test concurrency, the result_processor should record the timestamps (or an overlap window) at which it starts processing each item and assert that items for different groups were processed simultaneously, or use a thread-aware assertion such as verifying that processing started for at least two different groups before any single item completed.

title: Wrong assertion in test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling
body: The test 'test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling' sends two messages to the same subscription (so they end up in the same queue) and asserts `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`. However, `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` wraps `self.result_processor(...)` in `try/except Exception/finally`, and the `finally` block always calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)`. So even after the first call raises, the offset is still marked complete and the commit thread will commit it. The assertion expects no commit to happen, which is the opposite of what the code actually does. The test passes for the wrong reason and would still pass even if error handling was broken. Additionally, because both messages go to the same group/queue, the test does not exercise cross-group error isolation as its docstring claims - to actually verify that an error in one group does not block commits in another, the two results need different subscription_ids so they land in different queues.

title: Unbounded queues with no backpressure despite docstring claim
body: In `FixedQueuePool.__init__`, each work queue is created with `queue.Queue()` (no maxsize). The class docstring promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but there is no fill - the queues are infinite. If a single group is slow or backed up (e.g. one subscription id hashes to the same queue and processing of one item blocks for a long time, or that group simply gets a burst of messages), items accumulate forever. Each `WorkItem` holds a reference to the original `Message` (and therefore the decoded `result` plus `KafkaPayload`), so the memory footprint is non-trivial. An unbounded queue in front of a single-worker-per-queue setup is a straightforward OOM risk and contradicts the docstring.

title: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join ignores its timeout parameter
body: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(self, timeout: float | None = None)` accepts a timeout but does not use it - it just calls `self.close()`. The arroyo framework passes a deadline via this argument so it knows how long to wait for graceful shutdown before forcefully terminating. By ignoring the timeout the strategy can exceed the caller's deadline, causing the consumer to be killed by the orchestrator and any in-flight offsets to be left as 'outstanding' (forcing re-delivery on the next start). `join` should propagate `timeout` to `self.commit_thread.join(timeout=...)` and to `FixedQueuePool.shutdown`/worker joins, and `close()` should also respect a deadline.

title: commit_function failure leaves offsets un-committed in the tracker and is silently retried forever
body: In `_commit_loop`, `self.commit_function(committable)` is called and only on success does the loop mark the offsets via `mark_committed`. If the commit raises (Kafka unavailable, broker timeout, etc.), the whole `except Exception` just logs and the same offsets are returned by the next `get_committable_offsets()` call and retried. Two problems: (1) if the commit partially succeeded before raising, the same offsets get re-committed to Kafka (duplicate commit), and (2) there is no backoff or alerting, so a persistent failure becomes an infinite tight retry loop that floods the logs and pegs CPU. The metric `remote_subscriptions.queue_pool.offsets_committed` is also incremented before the commit call, so it counts 'attempted' rather than 'succeeded' commits, which is misleading.

title: get_committable_offsets does an O(max_offset) scan per partition
body: `get_committable_offsets` iterates `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1)` looking for the highest contiguous committed offset. If a partition has a small offset (e.g. 100) and a very large one (e.g. 1_000_000) - whether from a bug, rebalance after restart, or just a sparse stream - this allocates and walks ~1M ints per call, every second, from the commit thread. For a multi-partition topic with any sparse offsets this can dominate CPU. The check should walk the sorted `outstanding` set instead of scanning the integer range.

title: Group-to-queue assignment uses Python's randomized hash()
body: `get_queue_for_group` is `return hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`. Python's built-in `hash()` for strings is salted by `PYTHONHASHSEED` and is therefore not stable across processes. Within a single consumer lifetime the assignment is consistent (so per-group ordering is preserved), but after a restart the same subscription id may land on a different queue and worker. This is undocumented and brittle - if anything ever relies on a stable group->queue mapping across restarts (e.g. for deterministic drain order on partial shutdown, or for replay tooling), it will silently break. Use a stable hash like `hashlib.md5(group_key.encode()).digest()` or `zlib.crc32(group_key.encode())`.

title: submit() silently drops messages whose value is not a BrokerValue when an error occurs
body: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, the `except Exception` handler only marks the offset complete when `isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)`. If the message value is anything else (e.g. an `ImpulseValue` or any future arroyo value type) and either the decoder raises or the `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` itself fails, the offset is never recorded. The message disappears from the strategy but arroyo will not have been told to commit it, so on restart the same message is re-delivered. If the failure is permanent (e.g. the codec can never decode that value type) this becomes an infinite redelivery of poison messages, with no observability beyond the one log entry.

title: commit() called with one argument but arroyo's Commit requires two
body: In `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker`, the inner `commit_offsets` closure calls `commit(commit_data)` with a single argument, but arroyo's `Commit` type is `Callable[[Mapping[Partition, int], bool], None]`. At runtime this raises `TypeError: missing 1 required positional argument: 'force'`, which is swallowed by the broad `except Exception` in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop`. The result is that offsets are never committed, the offset tracker grows without bound, and on restart the consumer re-reads everything it has already processed (defeating the whole point of the commit loop and potentially causing data-integrity issues for non-idempotent result processors). The fix is `commit(commit_data, False)` (or wrap with `CommitOffsets`). The unit tests miss this because they pass a mock with a default for `force`.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps references undefined variables
body: Inside `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps` only `all_commits` and `test_partition` are defined, but the final assertion reads `committed_offsets[partition] == 103`. Neither `committed_offsets` nor `partition` exists in the test scope, so the test raises `NameError` before any assertion runs and provides no coverage of the gap-fill behavior it claims to test. The assertion should use `all_commits[-1][test_partition]` (or similar) so it actually exercises the production code path.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps asserts wrong offset value
body: After filling the gap by submitting offset 101, all of offsets 100-103 are processed, so `get_committable_offsets` returns `{test_partition: 103}`. `commit_offsets` then adds +1 (it explicitly comments "the committed offset should represent the next offset to read from") and calls `commit({test_partition: 104})`. The test asserts `committed_offsets[partition] == 103`, but the actual value should be 104. This is inconsistent with the first assertion in the same test (`actual_offset == 101` for processing up to 100) which correctly accounts for the +1.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts opposite of expected behavior
body: The test docstring claims "errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages", but the assertion `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` requires that no commits happen at all (or that the partition is absent). In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, exceptions from `result_processor` are caught by `except Exception` and the offset is still marked complete in the `finally` block, so the commit loop will eventually emit `{test_partition: 102}` for the two submitted messages. The assertion will fail and the test passes only when the implementation does the opposite of what the test name claims. The assertion should instead verify that `test_partition` is present and committed to 102.

title: get_queue_for_group uses Python's hash(), not consistent hashing
body: `get_queue_for_group` is implemented as `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues` and its docstring says "consistent hashing". Python's built-in `hash()` for strings is randomized across processes (PYTHONHASHSEED), so the same `group_key` can be assigned to a different queue on every restart. Within a single process lifetime ordering is preserved (which is what the consumer relies on, since in-flight items are lost on restart anyway), but the function does not provide the cross-process stability the docstring advertises, and it isn't true consistent hashing (e.g. it doesn't survive changes in `num_queues`). Use a stable hash like `hashlib.md5(group_key.encode()).digest()` or `zlib.crc32` and either drop the "consistent" wording or use a hash ring.

title: --mode help text does not describe thread-queue-parallel
body: `uptime_options` adds `"thread-queue-parallel"` to the choice list, but the `help` text still reads "The mode to process results in. Parallel uses multithreading." with no mention of the new mode or how its parallelism differs (queue-based, per-group ordering, etc.). Operators picking the mode have no way to know what the new option does or how it differs from the existing parallel modes.
