Initial state is `[""]`, so the dialog is invalid out of the box; the message does not indicate which entry is bad, nor does it surface the empty-string case specifically. Empty inputs should be filtered before validation, and per-field errors should be shown (or the Add button should be disabled while the list is invalid). The server's handler also does case-sensitive dedupe, so two entries differing only in case slip through here as 'unique' but cause a duplicate downstream.

title: Uses array index as React key for email fields
body: `value.map((field, index) => <li key={index}>...)`. When a user removes an item in the middle of the list, every input after it is re-bound to the wrong value (because React reuses the DOM and state by index). Use a stable key (e.g., the email value itself or a generated id) so removing index N doesn't corrupt the remaining inputs.

title: No automated tests for a new permission-sensitive mutation with email and calendar side-effects
body: The PR adds a new tRPC mutation `viewer.bookings.addGuests` that mutates the DB, calls calendar/video integrations, and dispatches emails. There are no unit tests, integration tests, or e2e tests included. Given the multiple authorization bugs (admin+owner check, attendee-as-actor, case-sensitive dedupe, wrong credentials) and side-effect ordering issues already found in this review, at minimum a test suite covering: (1) team admin can add, team member cannot; (2) attendee cannot add; (3) case-insensitive duplicate is rejected; (4) cancelled booking is rejected; (5) calendar/email failures are surfaced, must be added before merge.

title: Team admin/owner permission check uses && instead of ||
body: The `isTeamAdminOrOwner` check uses `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`. In cal.com's role model these are mutually exclusive (a user is either admin OR owner), so the conjunction always evaluates to false. The code clearly intended `||`. Effect: every team admin and every team owner is treated as unauthorized and rejected with `FORBIDDEN`; only direct organizers or existing attendees can add guests to team event bookings, defeating the entire intent of this branch.

title: Existing attendees are allowed to add arbitrary guests
body: Permission check is `!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer && !isAttendee -> FORBIDDEN`. Because `isAttendee` is satisfied by any existing attendee whose email matches the logged-in user's email, an invitee of a booking can invite unlimited additional people (including themselves under a different email) to that booking without the organizer's consent. This is a privilege escalation: an attendee can grow the meeting's attendee list and trigger calendar invites / emails on behalf of the organizer. At minimum, only the organizer / team admin / owner should be able to add guests.

title: sendAddGuestsEmails is called with unfiltered input, causing duplicate AttendeeScheduledEmail to existing attendees
body: The handler passes the original `guests` array (which may contain already-attending emails that were filtered out into `uniqueGuests`) into `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)`. In `email-manager.ts` the attendees loop then does `if (newGuests.includes(attendee.email))` and sends `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (the standard 'you have been booked' email, full calendar invite) to any existing attendee whose email happens to be in the raw input. If an organizer re-typings an existing attendee's email by mistake, that attendee will be re-issued a brand-new booking confirmation with a fresh ICS REQUEST. The function should receive the deduplicated `uniqueGuests` (or compute the post-update set) instead.

title: No booking status check: guests can be added to cancelled or past bookings
body: The handler never inspects `booking.status` (or `booking.startTime`). The action item in `BookingListItem.tsx` is reachable for past confirmed bookings and any tRPC caller can bypass the UI entirely and call the mutation for a cancelled/rejected booking. Adding attendees to a cancelled booking results in an orphan calendar invite to a meeting that will not occur and may push the meeting back into an active state on connected calendars.

title: Case-sensitive blacklist and existing-attendee filter are trivially bypassable
body: `blacklistedGuestEmails` is lowercased but `guest` is compared as-is: `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`. An email like `BOB@example.com` bypasses the env-var blacklist. The existing-attendee filter `guest === attendee.email` is also case-sensitive, so a stored `test@example.com` does not match `Test@example.com`, which leads to a duplicate attendee row in `BookingAttendee` (no unique constraint on (bookingId,email) prevents it). All email comparisons for guest handling should be lowercased before comparison.

title: Calendar sync after DB commit with no rollback: inconsistent state on failure
body: `prisma.booking.update` is executed before `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)`. The calendar update is not wrapped in try/catch, so if it throws (e.g. credentials revoked, Google 5xx) the DB rows have already been inserted but the connected calendar has not been updated. A retry will then hit `uniqueGuests.length === 0` and return a misleading `emails_must_be_unique_valid` error, leaving the meeting with attendees in the DB but not on the calendar and not notified. The handler should either perform the calendar update first (with compensation on DB failure) or wrap both in a transactional pattern.

title: EventManager is built from the caller's credentials instead of the organizer's
body: `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials: [...credentials] })` uses the currently authenticated user's spread and credentials. The booking's actual organizer is loaded into `organizer` but its credentials are not used. When the caller is a team admin or (in the corrected logic) an attendee, the calendar invite will be pushed through whichever calendar integration the caller has, not the organizer's. That causes the organizer to lose control of the event on their primary calendar and may fail entirely if the caller has no calendar credentials for the destinationCalendar.

title: No upper bound on guests array: trivially exploitable DoS / cost amplification
body: `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` has no `.max(...)`. A single authed user can submit an array of thousands of valid emails. The handler then performs N inserts, N `getTranslation` calls, one big `Promise.all` of N emails, and a calendar update with an attendees list of size N. There is no per-user / per-booking throttle. A reasonable bound (e.g. `.max(50)` or `.max(100)`) should be enforced at the schema layer to prevent abuse and keep the email/calendar blast radius small.

title: findFirst -> filter -> update pattern has a TOCTOU race that can create duplicate attendees
body: The handler reads `booking.attendees` and then issues `prisma.booking.update` with `attendees.createMany`. Between those two statements another request from the same organizer can insert the same guest; because there is no unique index on (bookingId, email) and no transactional check, both requests will succeed and produce duplicate attendee rows that share the same email on the same booking. The de-duplication should be done inside a single transaction (or use a unique constraint) to make the operation atomic.

title: New-guest check is performed after formatCalEvent, mixing raw input with formatted attendees
body: `calendarEvent.attendees` is the formatted list returned from `formatCalEvent(calEvent)`, but `newGuests` is the raw caller-supplied array. If `formatCalEvent` normalizes email casing (or trims/strips display-name suffixes), `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)` will silently mis-classify a new guest as an existing attendee (or vice-versa), causing the wrong email template to be sent. Both sides of the comparison must go through the same normalization.

title: Email To header uses empty name for newly-added guests and can crash senders
body: `to: `${this.attendee.name} <${this.attendee.email}>`` is built unconditionally. The handler inserts new attendees with `name: ""` (`addGuests.handler.ts:85`), so every new-guest email is addressed as ` <new@example.com>`, which most SMTP servers reject as malformed. New guests should have a name populated (or the formatter should fall back to the local part of the email).

title: Subject reads attendees[0].name without guarding empty array
body: `name: this.calEvent.attendees[0].name` will throw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` if `attendees` is empty (e.g. an organizer-only booking or a booking whose attendees were wiped before this code path runs). It also produces a blank name in the subject for any new-guest-led booking where the first attendee was inserted with `name: ""`.

title: Inline Zod schema diverges from the backend schema and validates case-sensitively
body: The dialog defines its own `z.array(z.string().email()).refine(... set uniqueness ...)` which is case-sensitive (`Set('A@x')` and `Set('a@x')` are different keys) and duplicates the rules from `addGuests.schema.ts`. If the two schemas drift, the user sees a confusing 'Emails must be unique and valid' error even when only one specific field is empty/invalid, and the backend may accept what the frontend rejected. The schema should live in a shared module and lower-case emails before the uniqueness check.

title: User-facing error toast prefixes the tRPC error code and raw translation key
body: `showToast(`${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}`, 'error')` exposes internal codes like `BAD_REQUEST: booking_not_found` (because `booking_not_found` is not present in the locale file, so `t()` returns the raw key) directly to end users. The fallback `t("unable_to_add_guests")` is only reached when the constructed string is falsy, which it never is. The toast should display the translated message and use the generic fallback when translation is missing.

title: Returns a hard-coded English success message instead of the i18n key
body: The handler returns `{ message: "Guests added" }`. Other handlers in this router return translation keys (e.g. `booking_confirmation_success`) that the client renders via `t()`. Returning an English string here breaks localization and the toast on success (`t("guests_added")`) is wired separately, so the API contract is inconsistent with the rest of the bookings router.

title: No tests added for a new mutating handler that touches DB, calendar and email
body: The handler introduces an end-to-end flow with multiple non-trivial branches: permission check (organizer / attendee / team admin / team owner, including the && vs || bug above), blacklist filtering, duplicate attendee detection across casing, calendar sync ordering, and email dispatch for organizer / team members / new guests / existing attendees. None of these paths are exercised by tests in this PR. Given the security-sensitive nature of the changes (any authed user can mutate a booking's attendee list), at least the permission branches, status guard (once added), and the `sendAddGuestsEmails` recipient classification must be covered.

title: Catch block increments retryCount for any error, not just SMS failures
body: The catch block increments retryCount for every exception thrown inside the try, including unrelated failures such as `prisma.profile.findFirst` (DB connection issue), `getCalEventResponses`, `getBookerBaseUrl`, `customTemplate`, and `smsReminderTemplate`. None of these have anything to do with Twilio being unable to schedule the SMS, yet each counts against the 2-retry budget. A transient infrastructure issue in any of those code paths can therefore cause a valid reminder to be auto-deleted on the next cron run before it ever gets a real second chance to reach Twilio. The retry increment should only fire when `twilio.scheduleSMS` actually returns falsy or throws — the other unrelated exceptions should bubble (or be separately handled) without poisoning the retry count.

title: retryCount increment is a non-atomic read-modify-write
body: Both the else branch (line 184) and the catch block (line 195) do `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` based on the value loaded by the earlier `findMany`. Under concurrent execution (manual cron invocations, overlapping cron schedules, retries, etc.) two invocations can both read the same stale value and both write `current+1`, losing one increment and undercounting retries. This can keep a failing reminder alive longer than intended and defeats the PR's goal of bounded retries. Use Prisma's atomic operator, e.g. `data: { retryCount: { increment: 1 } }`, and ideally combine with a WHERE clause that also requires the row to still be unscheduled / still have the expected retryCount to avoid duplicate Twilio calls.

title: No tests cover the new retry-and-delete behavior
body: The PR introduces a behavior change with real user-visible consequences (auto-deletion of workflow reminders after 2 failures), adds a new DB column, and changes the cleanup semantics of the existing `deleteMany`. No tests are added to cover: (1) `retryCount` incrementing on `twilio.scheduleSMS` returning falsy, (2) `retryCount` incrementing when the call throws, (3) the new OR-branch of `deleteMany` actually deleting rows with `retryCount > 1`, (4) the boundary case of `retryCount == 1` being retried once more before deletion, and (5) successful sends still setting `scheduled: true`/`referenceId` regardless of retryCount. Without these tests, regressions in retry accounting or the cleanup query can ship unnoticed.

title: Cleanup deleteMany uses retryCount > 1 without a method filter
body: The new branch of the cleanup `deleteMany` matches `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` with no `method` constraint, while only the SMS code path ever increments `retryCount`. This silently couples the SMS implementation to the WorkflowReminder table as a whole: any future code that starts incrementing `retryCount` for email or WhatsApp reminders will have those rows deleted by this cron. Either constrain the OR-branch with `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`, or document and enforce that retryCount is SMS-only.

title: deleteMany retryCount branch lacks method filter, can delete non-SMS reminders
body: The new OR clause in the cleanup deleteMany only filters by `retryCount: { gt: 1 }` on the second branch, with no `method` constraint. The first branch correctly restricts to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`, but the retryCount branch will match WorkflowReminder rows of any method (EMAIL, WHATSAPP) if their retryCount ever exceeds 1. While this PR only increments retryCount for SMS, this is a latent bug: any future code path (or out-of-band DB change) that pushes an EMAIL/WHATSAPP reminder's retryCount above 1 will cause it to be silently deleted by this SMS handler. The retry branch should be `{ method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` to keep the cleanup semantically consistent with the rest of the handler, which only processes SMS.

title: No guard against concurrent cron execution; duplicate SMS and lost retryCount increments possible
body: The handler reads `unscheduledReminders`, calls the external `twilio.scheduleSMS`, and then updates `workflowReminder` in separate non-transactional steps. There is no lock, advisory mutex, or single-runner coordination. If two cron instances overlap (e.g., the previous run is still in flight when a new one starts, or this cron is invoked manually while a scheduled run is active), both will fetch the same unscheduled rows, both will call `twilio.scheduleSMS` (producing duplicate SMS messages for end users), and both will perform `update` based on the same `retryCount` snapshot so one increment is effectively a no-op. The newly added retry logic amplifies this: if retryCount increments are lost due to the race, a reminder may need more than 2 actual failures before being cleaned up, or conversely may be deleted after only one observed failure. At minimum, the handler should use an advisory lock keyed on the workflow step or use an idempotent update (`update where retryCount = <stale value>`) to make the increment safe.

title: No tests cover the new retry-count / cleanup behavior
body: The change introduces new persistence logic (a new column, conditional increment in two branches, and a new cleanup predicate) but no test files were added or updated. There is no coverage verifying: (a) `retryCount` is incremented when `twilio.scheduleSMS` returns falsy, (b) `retryCount` is incremented in the catch branch, (c) reminders with `retryCount > 1` are deleted regardless of scheduledDate, (d) past-dated SMS reminders without retries are still deleted, or (e) the off-by-one threshold (2 failures -> delete) matches the PR description. Without tests, regressions in the retry threshold or in the OR-clause semantics (e.g., the missing method filter noted above) can ship undetected.

title: Error log does not identify which reminder failed
body: The catch block logs only `Error scheduling SMS with error ${error}`. It does not include the reminder id, booking uid, workflowStepId, scheduledDate, sendTo, or the prior retryCount value. When the new retry-and-delete flow drops a reminder (after retryCount > 1) there is no operator-visible trail of which reminder was deleted or why it was abandoned, which makes production debugging and audit of dropped SMS reminders very difficult. At minimum the log line should include the reminder id and the new retryCount.

title: Cleanup deletes reminders based on retryCount even when scheduledDate is still in the future
body: The new OR clause causes any WorkflowReminder with retryCount > 1 to be deleted regardless of its scheduledDate. So if SMS scheduling fails twice for a reminder that is still scheduled to fire hours or days in the future, the reminder is permanently dropped even though the event has not happened yet. This matches the PR description but is worth flagging: there is no alerting or metric when a future reminder is given up on, and no way to distinguish "transient Twilio failure" from "permanent bad phone number". Consider also classifying errors so permanent failures (e.g., invalid phone number from Twilio) are dropped immediately while transient ones use more retries, or at least log when a future-dated reminder is being dropped.

title: retryCount cleanup not scoped to SMS method
body: The new deleteMany adds an OR branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` that has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, while the sibling branch does. Today only this SMS handler ever increments `retryCount`, so only SMS rows are affected in practice — but the column is on the general `WorkflowReminder` model and the migration defaults all rows to 0. As soon as any other path (a future EMAIL/WHATSAPP scheduler, a backfill, an admin tool, manual SQL) sets `retryCount` on a non-SMS reminder, this query will silently delete those rows along with the SMS ones. The branch should be scoped to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` (or the second OR arm should be merged into the first with `AND`) so the cleanup cannot reach reminders of other methods.

title: Find-then-update is not atomic; concurrent cron ticks can double-schedule and double-count retries
body: The handler does `findMany({ scheduled: false })` and then, in a separate loop, calls `twilio.scheduleSMS` and finally updates `scheduled = true` (or `retryCount += 1`). There is no transaction, row lock, or `update ... where { scheduled: false } returning ...` guard, so if two cron invocations overlap (or the previous run is retried while still in flight) both will fetch the same `scheduled: false` row and both will call Twilio, producing two scheduled SMS messages for the same reminder. The new retryCount increment makes the failure path worse: if Twilio throws, both concurrent handlers hit the catch block and both write `retryCount: N + 1`, so retryCount can be undercounted (e.g. two simultaneous failures on a row at retryCount=0 both write 1 instead of 2) and the row may survive an extra round instead of being deleted. This should be made atomic, e.g. by doing an `updateMany` with `where: { id, scheduled: false }` returning the row, or by wrapping the scheduling call in a transaction with a `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`.

title: Permanent SMS drops after retry exhaustion are silent
body: When a reminder crosses `retryCount > 1` it is deleted by the next cron tick with no log line and no notification. The catch path only logs the underlying `twilio.scheduleSMS` error; once the row is later deleted by the `retryCount > 1` branch there is no trace that the user was supposed to receive an SMS at all. Given this is precisely the case the PR is trying to surface ("after scheduling failed twice we delete"), the deleteMany should at minimum log the reminder id, booking uid, workflowStep, and last error so that the dropped reminders are visible in logs and can be alerted on or surfaced to the organizer.

title: Caching tests removed while caching logic remains in service
body: The 'Caching' describe block (which previously verified that getAuthorizationConditions() and getFilterConditions() returned the same value on repeated calls) was removed entirely from the test file. The service still contains the caching implementation in lines 84-87 and 91-94 (`this.cachedAuthConditions` / `this.cachedFilterConditions` cache fields and the `if (this.cachedAuthConditions === undefined)` checks). Removing these tests is a regression in coverage: future refactors that silently break caching (e.g. accidentally re-fetching memberships on every call, losing the deduplication of identical `Prisma.sql` template-literal objects) would no longer be caught. The PR description also does not mention deleting caching tests, which can mislead reviewers.

title: Public findMany method removed, breaking any external consumers
body: The previous public API of `InsightsBookingService` was `findMany(findManyArgs: Prisma.BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedFindManyArgs)`. This method has been deleted and replaced with `getBaseConditions(): Promise<Prisma.Sql>`, which returns a `Prisma.Sql` fragment that callers must now embed in their own `prisma.$queryRaw` call. This is a breaking change to the service contract. The PR description does not mention updating other callers (e.g. insights API handlers or other modules that import this service). Before merging, every existing caller of `service.findMany(...)` must be migrated to use `getBaseConditions` + `$queryRaw`, otherwise the build will fail or runtime behavior will change.

title: Test redefines NOTHING_CONDITION independently from the service
body: The test file declares its own `const NOTHING_CONDITION = Prisma.sql`1=0`` (line 10) instead of importing the value from `insightsBooking.ts`, which keeps its own private copy of the same constant. If the service ever changes the definition of `NOTHING_CONDITION` (for example to `Prisma.sql`FALSE`` or some other falsy SQL expression), the assertions `expect(conditions).toEqual(NOTHING_CONDITION)` in this test file would still pass against the local copy, masking the regression. The service should export `NOTHING_CONDITION` and the tests should import it so both sides of the comparison are guaranteed to refer to the same value.

title: findMany method removed without updating callers
body: The `findMany` method that previously executed the authorization/filter query through `prisma.bookingTimeStatusDenormalized.findMany` has been removed and replaced by `getBaseConditions()` plus a `prisma.$queryRaw` interpolation. The integration test was migrated to the new shape, but no other callers are updated in this PR. If any HTTP route, tRPC procedure, scheduled job, or other service in the repository invokes `InsightsBookingService.findMany(...)`, those call sites will now fail to compile and/or at runtime. Either the call sites must be migrated in this PR or a transitional shim should be added so the change is non-breaking.

title: Org scope silently drops direct org members when there are no child teams
body: In `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition`, `userIdsFromOrg` is set to `[]` whenever `teamsFromOrg.length === 0`, so the `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds` query is skipped entirely. `teamIds` already contains `options.orgId`, but the conditional means a user who is a direct member of the organization (membership row with `teamId = orgId`) but is not a member of any sub-team is never included. Their individual bookings (and any event-type-owned bookings they make) will be invisible in org-scope insights. The query should be executed unconditionally (or fall back to a direct membership lookup on `orgId`). The bug pre-existed in the WhereInput form but is reproduced verbatim in the new SQL, and the new tests do not cover the no-sub-teams case.

title: Org-scope test depends on undefined query/Set ordering
body: The org-scope assertion compares against literal array orderings `[testData.org.id, testData.team.id, team2.id, team3.id]` and `[testData.user.id, user2.id, user3.id]`. These come from `TeamRepository.findAllByParentId`, `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds`, and `Array.from(new Set(userIdsFromOrg))`. None of those queries specify `ORDER BY`, so the order is implementation-defined and can vary across PostgreSQL versions, under concurrent load, or with different planner settings. A `toEqual` on `Prisma.sql` template literals compares the embedded `.values` arrays by deep equality, so any reorder will fail the test. Either add deterministic ordering on the repository queries, or normalize both sides of the assertion (e.g. compare by `Set` membership, or use a helper that re-sorts the array values) so the test is not order-sensitive.

title: Invalid-options test bypasses TypeScript via `null as any`
body: The constructor parameter is declared `options: InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions` (required, non-null), but the test for "invalid options" passes `options: null as any` and relies on `safeParse` returning `{ success: false }` so `this.options` ends up `null` and `NOTHING_CONDITION` is produced. This hides a real design question: invalid options silently turn the caller into an unauthorized principal instead of throwing, which means a production bug that constructs an `InsightsBookingService` with a malformed `options` object would just return no data rather than fail loudly. The constructor should either throw on invalid input, or its type should be widened to `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions | null | undefined` so callers can express intent without resorting to `as any`. The current arrangement also means the runtime contract is weaker than the type signature suggests.

title: Public findMany method removed; callers must adopt getBaseConditions + $queryRaw
body: The diff replaces the public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method with `getBaseConditions(): Promise<Prisma.Sql>`. The new method only returns a WHERE-clause SQL fragment; callers must now embed it in their own `prisma.$queryRaw` template and write the SELECT themselves. Any existing consumer of the service (e.g. insights API endpoints or other internal callers that previously did `service.findMany({ select: { ... } })`) will break: the method is gone, so those calls become a runtime TypeError, not just a behavior change. The PR description frames this as a test-only update and never mentions the contract change, nor does it list which callers were migrated, so it is unclear whether every callsite has been updated in lockstep.

title: Caching behavior of getAuthorizationConditions/getFilterConditions is no longer tested
body: The diff deletes the entire `describe("Caching", ...)` block, which previously contained `should cache authorization conditions` and `should cache filter conditions`. The service still implements caching in `getAuthorizationConditions` and `getFilterConditions` (`if (this.cachedAuthConditions === undefined) { this.cachedAuthConditions = await this.buildAuthorizationConditions(); }`), but no test now exercises that branch. A future regression that accidentally rebuilds the conditions on every call would re-run the membership/team queries on every request and degrade performance without any test catching it. The caching tests should be re-added in the new `Prisma.sql` comparison style rather than dropped entirely.

title: BSD-only sed -i '' breaks the script on Linux
body: The line `sed -i '' -E "s|^GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=.*|GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=$TUNNEL_URL|" "$ENV_FILE"` uses BSD/macOS sed syntax. On GNU/Linux, the empty string after `-i` is interpreted as the name of the file to edit in-place, so the script will not actually rewrite `$ENV_FILE` (and may create a literal file called `''`). Use a portable form such as `sed -i.bak -E ... && rm "${ENV_FILE}.bak"` or do the substitution with another tool. This script is checked in for the whole repo and any Linux user running it for local Google Calendar webhook testing will hit the bug.

title: Cache last-updated timestamp is formatted with a hardcoded en-US locale
body: The component builds the cache timestamp with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" })`. The whole rest of the component goes through `useLocale()` and `t(...)`, but the date is forced into US format regardless of the user's locale (e.g. a French user still sees `12/04/25, 3:00 PM`). It should use the locale returned by `useLocale()` (e.g. `new Intl.DateTimeFormat(locale, { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" })`) so the displayed timestamp respects the user's preference.

title: Successful cache deletion does not invalidate connectedCalendars, so UI keeps showing stale cache status
body: The `deleteCacheMutation.onSuccess` only fires `showToast(...)` and calls `onSuccess?.()`. It never invalidates `trpc.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`, which is the query that supplies `cacheUpdatedAt` in `SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper`. Compare with `disconnectMutation`, which does `await utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate()` in `onSettled`. As a result, after the user confirms "Delete cached data" the dropdown continues to render the "Cache Status" block with the old timestamp and a "Delete cached data" action until the page is refetched by some other means. Either invalidate the query here directly, or require callers to do it via `onSuccess` (and document that).

title: Empty actions wrapper div is always rendered even when CredentialActionsDropdown returns null
body:
The previous code only rendered the action area when `!connectedCalendar.delegationCredentialId && !disableConnectionModification`. The new code unconditionally renders `
` for both the AppListCard and the error Alert. When the credential is a delegation credential AND there is no cache, `CredentialActionsDropdown` returns null, but the wrapper still renders an empty 128px-wide box in the top-right of every calendar card. Either conditionally render the wrapper (`canDisconnect || hasCache`) or have `CredentialActionsDropdown` render an empty placeholder of the same size so the layout does not shift.

title: deleteCache input is not constrained to positive integers
body: The mutation uses `z.object({ credentialId: z.number() })`. `z.number()` accepts floats, negatives, NaN-passing types, and any integer range. For a database id, this should be `z.number().int().positive()` (or a dedicated `ZDeleteCacheInputSchema` similar to other inputs in this router) so the handler can't be invoked with nonsense values and so the type carries semantic meaning. As written, a negative or zero `credentialId` is silently rejected inside the handler with a generic `Credential not found or access denied`, masking bad input.

title: Migration warning text contradicts the migration body
body: The generated warning block says: `Added the required column "updatedAt" to the "CalendarCache" table without a default value. This is not possible if the table is not empty.` The actual migration below it adds the column with `DEFAULT NOW()`, so the warning is incorrect and would mislead a reviewer/operator who only reads the header. The comment should describe what the migration actually does (`Added the required column "updatedAt" with a default of NOW() to safely backfill existing rows.`).

title: findMany loses type-level validation by dropping the `satisfies` clause
body: The diff for `findMany` removes the `const args = { where, select, orderBy } satisfies Prisma.SelectedCalendarFindManyArgs;` line and inlines the call. The `satisfies` previously caught a class of type mismatches between the custom `FindManyArgs` type and the actual `Prisma.SelectedCalendarFindManyArgs` (for example an unknown orderBy key, or a where shape that Prisma doesn't support). Without it, callers like `watchCalendar` and `unwatchCalendar` that rely on `googleChannelId: { not: null }` and `orderBy: { userId: "asc" | "desc" }` are no longer type-checked at this boundary. Keep the `satisfies` (or the equivalent explicit type annotation) to preserve the previous type safety.

title: fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache bumps updatedAt for calendars that were just unwatched
body: The new line `await SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` updates `updatedAt` for *every* SelectedCalendar of the credential, not just the `remainingCalendars` that the function was actually called with. In the `unwatchCalendar` path this means the calendars whose `googleChannelId` was just cleared (and that are no longer being watched) also get their `updatedAt` stamped to NOW(), which contradicts the intent expressed in the PR notes ("SelectedCalendar.updatedAt ... only updated via Google webhook handler"). Either restrict the update to the calendars passed in, or drop this side-effect entirely if it has no consumer.

title: deleteCache handler accepts any credential the user owns, with no rate limit and no audit log
body: The handler checks `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { id: credentialId, userId: user.id } })` and then unconditionally deletes all CalendarCache rows for that credential. Issues: (1) there is no rate limiting, so a malicious or buggy client can repeatedly force cache rebuilds for any of their own Google credentials (cost + latency). (2) The mutation deletes the cache for *all* users that share this credential - the check only verifies `userId === ctx.user.id`, but in team/org setups a single credential may back multiple users' bookings, and a single user wiping it affects the whole group. At minimum, log who triggered the wipe and the credential, and consider whether org/team members should also be allowed. (3) The `credentialId` in the where clause is the only scope; selecting only cache entries that belong to the requesting user (via `CalendarCache.userId`) would be safer where applicable.

title: getCacheStatusByCredentialIds ignores expiresAt, so expired cache is reported as 'active'
body: `getCachedAvailability` (and the cache hit path) deliberately filter by `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }` so expired rows are treated as cache misses. `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` does not apply that filter and returns `_max.updatedAt` for the credential regardless of whether the latest row is expired. The UI therefore displays "Cache Status: Last updated ..." and exposes "Delete cached data" even when every cache row for the credential is already past `expiresAt` and will be ignored on the next read. Add the same `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }` filter (or an equivalent `where: { expiresAt: { gt: new Date() } }`) so the cache status reflects what would actually be served.

title: connectedCalendars now issues an extra DB round-trip on every render of the calendars settings
body: The handler now always runs `cacheRepository.getCacheStatusByCredentialIds(credentialIds)`, which executes a `prisma.calendarCache.groupBy` for every call to `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. That query is hit on every refetch (the wrapper sets `refetchOnWindowFocus: false`, but it still runs on mount, after `disconnectMutation.onSettled` invalidates it, and after onboarding). For users with many credentials this is an extra round-trip on the critical path of `/apps/installed/calendar`. Two cheap improvements: (a) only run it when there is at least one Google Calendar credential (the only consumer of `cacheUpdatedAt`), or (b) cache the result per-credentialId for a short TTL in `CalendarCacheRepository` since the value changes only when cache is written.

title: No tests for deleteCache handler, getCacheStatusByCredentialIds, or the new UI component
body: The PR introduces three new pieces of logic that each have security, data-integrity, or UX impact and none of them come with a test: (1) `deleteCache.handler.ts` performs an authz check and a destructive DB write - needs at least one test that a non-owner gets `Credential not found or access denied` and one that an owner succeeds and the cache rows are removed. (2) `CalendarCacheRepository.getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` - needs a test that credentials with no cache rows are omitted and that `updatedAt` is the MAX across keys. (3) `CredentialActionsDropdown` - needs a test that the dropdown is hidden for non-Google credentials and for Google credentials without cache, and that "Delete cached data" is only available when `cacheUpdatedAt` is present. None of these test files appear in the diff.

title: Cache status ignores expiry, marking stale rows as fresh
body: getCacheStatusByCredentialIds uses prisma.calendarCache.groupBy to find the most recent updatedAt for each credential, but it does not constrain expiresAt to be in the future. The UI displays a 'Cache Status' timestamp whenever a row exists, even when all matching rows are expired (cache TTL is 30 days, set in upsertCachedAvailability via CACHING_TIME). Because getCachedAvailability itself filters by expiresAt >= now, the user is shown what looks like valid cache data for credentials whose cache is actually invalid. Add `expiresAt: { gte: new Date(Date.now()) }` to the where clause so the UI only surfaces still-valid cache.

title: Timestamp hard-coded to en-US locale
body: Inside the cache_status dropdown, the timestamp is rendered with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" }).format(...)`. The component already has access to useLocale() for translations, but forces every user to see dates in the US format regardless of their locale, browser preference, or the locale actually in use in the rest of the app. This is a regression for non-en-US users and breaks the i18n expectations of the project. Use the locale returned by useLocale() (or navigator.language fallback) instead of the hard-coded `"en-US"`.

title: deleteCache success does not invalidate connectedCalendars
body: After deleting the cache the mutation only shows a toast and calls onSuccess?.(); it never invalidates the viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars query. The sibling disconnectMutation on lines 53-65 explicitly invalidates utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars and utils.viewer.apps.integrations on settle, which keeps the dropdown and parent list in sync. The deletion path lacks the same invalidation, so after a successful Delete cached data the dropdown continues to render the 'Cache Status' row with the previous timestamp and the 'Delete cached data' item, and the parent's ConnectedCalendarList still shows the now-stale cacheUpdatedAt. Add an invalidate of utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars (and ideally utils.viewer.apps.integrations) in onSuccess or onSettled.

title: BSD sed syntax breaks on Linux
body: The line `sed -i '' -E "s|^GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=.*|GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=$TUNNEL_URL|" "$ENV_FILE"` uses the BSD/macOS form `sed -i ''` where the empty argument is the backup-extension placeholder. On GNU sed (the default on the Linux/CI environments this repo targets), `-i ''` is parsed as `-i` followed by `''` and then `-E`, causing errors like `sed: can't read E: No such file or directory`, so the .env update silently fails and the rest of the script can't restore GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL. Detect the platform (e.g. `[[ $OSTYPE == darwin* ]] && sed_i() { sed -i '' "$@"; } || sed_i() { sed -i "$@"; }`) or use a portable alternative such as `sed -i.bak ... && rm "$ENV_FILE.bak"`.

title: updateManyByCredentialId invoked with empty data
body: `await SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {});` passes an empty data object, which only does anything because Prisma auto-bumps `@updatedAt`. Without that hidden schema behavior this would be a no-op (or even a validation error in some Prisma versions), so the intent ('bump SelectedCalendar.updatedAt for all calendars under this credential') is implicit and brittle. Pass the timestamp explicitly, e.g. `data: { updatedAt: new Date() }`, and document that the field exists at the call site.

title: deleteCache throws plain Error instead of TRPCError
body: The handler throws `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")` directly. The other handlers in this package throw `TRPCError` with appropriate codes (e.g. NOT_FOUND, UNAUTHORIZED). Throwing a bare Error here skips tRPC's code propagation: the client receives an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR with a 500 status for what is really a 404 / 403, and the toast in CredentialActionsDropdown cannot distinguish 'not found' from 'permission denied' from a transient DB error. Switch to `throw new TRPCError({ code: "NOT_FOUND", message: "Credential not found or access denied" })`.

title: Migration comment does not match SQL
body: The header comment warns: 'Added the required column `updatedAt` to the `CalendarCache` table without a default value. This is not possible if the table is not empty.' The actual SQL does add a default (`DEFAULT NOW()`), so the warning is wrong and will confuse whoever next reviews this migration or runs it against a non-empty table. Either remove the misleading warning or replace it with one that describes the actual safe approach (adding the column with a server-side default and back-filling existing rows).

title: DropdownMenuItem used for non-interactive cache info
body: The 'Cache Status' / 'Last updated' block (lines 84-97) is rendered inside a `<DropdownMenuItem className="focus:ring-muted">` even though it contains no actionable control - it is purely informational. Radix dropdown items are interactive elements that expect to be selectable, so making one that does nothing on click produces an a11y warning (role with no action/handler) and means a screen-reader user hears it as a menu choice they can activate. Use a non-interactive primitive such as a `<div>` or `<DropdownMenuLabel>` for the read-only cache status row and reserve DropdownMenuItem for the Delete cached data choice below.

title: getCacheStatusByCredentialIds ignores expiresAt and returns data for stale cache
body: The query groups by credentialId and takes the max updatedAt, but never filters by `expiresAt`. A `CalendarCache` row whose `expiresAt` is in the past will not be served by `getCachedAvailability` (which uses `expiresAt: { gte: new Date(Date.now()) }`), yet the new UI in `CredentialActionsDropdown` will still display "Cache Status: Last updated …" for that credential. Users will see a cache status indicator for cache that is effectively dead. Either add `expiresAt: { gte: new Date(Date.now()) }` to the `where` clause, or surface the cache only when not expired.

title: updateManyByCredentialId called with empty data, likely throws PrismaClientValidationError
body: `fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache` ends with `await SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {});` and the comment says it is meant to bump `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt`. The Prisma client rejects empty `data` objects for updateMany ("data must have at least one non-relation field"), so this call will throw at runtime. Because this method runs inside the `unwatchCalendar` flow (only when there are remaining calendars), the throw will leave the unwatch in a half-completed state and the `remainingCalendars` cache will be re-fetched before updatedAt is updated — or, more likely, the user receives a confusing error from the webhook flow. Either pass a real column (e.g. `data: { updatedAt: new Date() }`) or stop calling this and rely on the existing cache-write side effects.

title: No tests cover deleteCache tRPC mutation, getCacheStatusByCredentialIds, or the new component
body: The new `viewer.calendars.deleteCache` tRPC mutation, the new `CalendarCacheRepository.getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` method (including its mock), and the entire `CredentialActionsDropdown` component (including the access-control conditional rendering for delegation credentials and disabled connections) have no unit or integration tests. This PR also adds a security-relevant authorization check (`userId: user.id` in `deleteCache.handler.ts`); a regression that drops that check would be silent without a test. Add at minimum: a test that `deleteCacheHandler` rejects a credential belonging to another user, a test that `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` filters/doesn't filter expiresAt as intended, and a render test for the component's conditional dropdown rendering.

title: Removes type-check on findMany args and over-widens updateManyByCredentialId
body: Two changes to this file: (1) the change at line ~260 removes the `satisfies Prisma.SelectedCalendarFindManyArgs` so callers can now pass an object that is structurally invalid for Prisma (e.g. misspelled keys) and the compiler will no longer flag it. That weakens a type-safety net that was deliberately added with `satisfies`. (2) `updateManyByCredentialId` accepts `data: Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateInput` with no constraint enforcing non-empty `data`, which is exactly how the empty-`{}` bug at `CalendarService.ts:1024` slipped in. Tighten the parameter type to a non-empty variant (e.g. a branded `AtLeastOne<Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateInput>`) and consider restoring the `satisfies`.

title: CRON cancellation loop aborts on first SendGrid error, orphaning prior DB deletes
body: In the new `remindersToCancel` loop, the `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` calls `await client.request(...)` first, then pushes a `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` onto `workflowRemindersToDelete`. The outer `try/catch` wraps the whole loop. If SendGrid's `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` returns an error for reminder N (rate limit, already-sent batch, transient 5xx, etc.), the `await` throws and the loop is aborted. `Promise.all(workflowRemindersToDelete)` is never called, so the deletes for reminders 0..N-1 whose SendGrid cancellation already succeeded are silently dropped. Those rows stay in the DB with `cancelled: true`, so the next CRON run re-fetches them, SendGrid returns 'batch not found' for the already-cancelled ones, and the deletes keep failing forever (until the past-date deleteMany eventually clears them). The fix is either to push the delete before the SendGrid call, do the delete inside the same per-iteration try/catch so a SendGrid failure cannot abort the loop, or push both into per-reminder Promise.all blocks.

title: Reschedule workflow-reminder cleanup is fire-and-forget forEach, so errors never reach the caller
body: The block added inside `if (originalRescheduledBooking?.uid)` calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(...)` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...)` from a `forEach` callback. The async functions return promises that are never awaited, and the surrounding `try/catch` only catches synchronous throws from the iteration body (the callback itself doesn't throw synchronously). Consequence: any error thrown asynchronously by SendGrid/Twilio/Prisma is swallowed inside the helper's own try/catch, the booking is treated as successfully rescheduled, and the caller (`handleNewBooking` -> the rescheduling user) has no signal that the prior booking's reminders failed to cancel. This also means the SMS-side Twilio cancel for the old booking and the immediate SendGrid cancel for the old booking can complete after `eventManager.reschedule(...)` has already mutated external calendars and the new reminders have been scheduled, producing a race where both old and new reminders can fire. Use `await Promise.all(reminders.map(...))` or a `for..of` with `await` so the cancellation actually completes (and any error is surfaced) before the reschedule continues.

title: Cancellation response returns before workflow reminders are actually cancelled
body: The new block `updatedBookings.forEach((booking) => { booking.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { ... deleteScheduledEmailReminder(...); deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...); }); });` is invoked without awaiting the returned promises. The handler immediately proceeds to `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` and then `sendCancelledEmails(evt)` and returns the success response. For SMS reminders with `referenceId` this means Twilio cancellation may not yet have been requested by the time the user sees 'Booking successfully cancelled.', so the old SMS can still go out. Errors raised inside the helpers are also swallowed by their own try/catch. Use `await Promise.all(updatedBookings.flatMap(b => b.workflowReminders.map(async r => ...)))` (or a `for..of` with `await`) so the handler waits for cancellation to actually happen and can propagate failures.

title: immediateDelete=true path leaves `cancelled` flag unset, so failed SendGrid calls have no retry
body: When `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` is called with `immediateDelete=true` (used by reschedule in `handleNewBooking.ts` and by workflow/step deletion in `workflows.tsx`), the function only calls `client.request` and returns without updating the DB row. If SendGrid's cancel call fails (network blip, transient 5xx, batch not found, rate limit), the SendGrid scheduled-send remains active, but the `cancelled` column stays null, so the new `scheduleEmailReminders` CRON cannot pick it up and retry — the email will be sent. For comparison, the `immediateDelete=false` path correctly sets `cancelled: true`, allowing the CRON to clean it up later. The fix is to set `cancelled: true` unconditionally (or at minimum when the SendGrid call throws) so the cron-based retry is available as a fallback for the immediate path.

title: remindersToCancel query lacks defensive filters, can issue SendGrid calls with null batch_id
body: `prisma.workflowReminder.findMany({ where: { cancelled: true, scheduledDate: { lte: dayjs().add(1, 'hour').toISOString() } } })` does not restrict to `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` nor to `referenceId: { not: null }`. While the new code in `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` only sets `cancelled: true` when a `referenceId` exists, stale data from the previous (DELETE-based) bug or any future code path that sets `cancelled: true` for SMS or unscheduled reminders will be picked up here and the loop will POST `{ batch_id: null, status: 'cancel' }` to SendGrid, which SendGrid rejects. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` and `referenceId: { not: null }` to the query so it only returns rows that can actually be cancelled.

title: Sequential await client.request in CRON can cause slow runs under burst cancellations
body: The cancellation loop does `await client.request(...)` once per reminder, sequentially, before pushing the delete onto the array. With the 100-pending SendGrid cap that motivated this PR, hitting that cap means up to 100 sequential SendGrid round trips per CRON run plus their delete operations. Given the CRON runs every 15 minutes and a serverless/edge runtime typically has a hard timeout, a burst of cancellations (e.g., a mass cancellation of a recurring series) can cause the handler to be killed mid-loop, leaving `cancelled: true` rows stranded until the next run. Consider parallelism (e.g., small batches with `Promise.all`) bounded below the SendGrid limit, or chunking the work across CRON invocations.

title: Pre-existing mistakenly-unscheduled emails from PR #6991 will still be delivered
body: The PR description notes that the previous (DELETE-based) fix actually re-scheduled emails instead of cancelling them, and that those emails are still in SendGrid's queue. The migration only adds `cancelled` as nullable with no default, so existing `WorkflowReminder` rows have `cancelled = NULL` and the new CRON filter `cancelled: true` will not match them — SendGrid will deliver those legacy emails. This needs to be called out in the PR description and either accompanied by a one-off cleanup query (delete or `cancelled: true`-backfill for past reminders) or acknowledged as a known operational issue.

title: New reschedule-reminder cancellation path has no test coverage
body: The PR introduces a non-trivial new path: `getOriginalRescheduledBooking` now includes `workflowReminders`, and a new block iterates them to call `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(..., true)` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...)` before `eventManager.reschedule`. None of the existing tests in the bookings router/handler area appear to cover (a) the case where a rescheduled booking has scheduled EMAIL reminders (immediate SendGrid cancel path), (b) the case where it has scheduled SMS reminders (immediate Twilio cancel path), or (c) the case where it has unscheduled reminders. Given that PR #6991 was the bug being fixed here, a regression test that asserts the new logic actually cancels reminders on reschedule should be added.

title: New cron-driven cancellation flow has no test coverage
body: The entire new branch — finding reminders with `cancelled: true && scheduledDate <= now+1h`, calling `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` with `status: 'cancel'`, and deleting the rows — is added without any unit or integration tests. The bug that motivated this PR was a misuse of the SendGrid API, so a test that mocks the SendGrid client and asserts (a) the POST is made with `status: 'cancel'`, (b) the row is deleted only after a successful cancel, and (c) rows past `scheduledDate` get cleaned up would protect against the same class of mistake recurring.

title: deleteScheduledEmailReminder immediateDelete path leaves DB unupdated
body: When `immediateDelete` is true, the function calls the SendGrid cancel API and then returns without updating or deleting the WorkflowReminder row in the database. The two other code paths (`!referenceId` and `immediateDelete === false`) both clean up the DB row, so this branch is inconsistent. As a result, callers using `immediateDelete=true` (e.g. reschedules in `handleNewBooking.ts`) leave orphan rows in `WorkflowReminder` that will only be cleaned up once `scheduledDate` is in the past. More importantly, because the row is never marked `cancelled=true`, the CRON in `scheduleEmailReminders.ts` (which only selects `where: { cancelled: true }`) cannot retry the SendGrid cancellation if the initial API call fails, so the original SendGrid problem (failed cancellations → emails still being sent) is only partially fixed. The fix is either to also set `cancelled: true` (or delete the row) in this branch, or to stop passing `immediateDelete=true` from callers where this matters (such as the reschedule path, which unlike the workflow delete path does not rely on a cascade to remove the row).

title: Reschedule uses immediateDelete=true, bypassing the new deferred-cancel mechanism
body: When a booking is rescheduled, the workflow reminders of the original booking are cancelled by calling `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)`. This is inconsistent with the new design (which only marks `cancelled=true` and lets the CRON actually cancel in SendGrid) and with the cancellation flow in `handleCancelBooking.ts`, which calls the same function without `immediateDelete`. Because `immediateDelete=true` does not mark the row `cancelled=true`, the CRON never picks it up and there is no retry if SendGrid's `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` fails — exactly the failure mode this PR is trying to fix. Reschedules will therefore continue to send the original reminder whenever SendGrid has any transient issue. The call should drop the third argument and rely on the same deferred approach as `handleCancelBooking.ts`.

title: try/catch around forEach with awaited async work is dead code
body: `originalRescheduledBooking.workflowReminders.forEach(...)` calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(...)` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...)` without `await`, and both helpers internally wrap their work in try/catch and only log errors. No error from those calls can ever propagate into the surrounding `catch (error)` block at line 970, so the `log.error(...)` is unreachable for any real failure. This is misleading and hides the fact that the caller has no way to know whether a reminder was successfully cancelled. Either `await` each call inside a per-iteration try/catch, or have the helpers rethrow and the caller await them.

title: Catch block aborts all SendGrid cancellations on a single failure
body: The try/catch wraps the entire `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop. A single SendGrid API failure (4xx/5xx, network error, rate limit, etc.) aborts the loop and skips every subsequent cancellation in this CRON run, even though the per-iteration `await client.request(...)` and `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` are independent. There is also no partial cleanup: if the throw happens after some `workflowReminder.delete` calls have been pushed but before `await Promise.all(...)`, those prisma operations are left as fire-and-forget unhandled promises. The catch should be moved inside the loop so one failed reminder doesn't stop the rest, and the deletes should be awaited per iteration (or collected only after a successful cancel).

title: Cancellation query does not filter by method
body: `prisma.workflowReminder.findMany` selects reminders where `cancelled: true` and `scheduledDate <= now + 1h` but does not restrict to `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL`. Today only EMAIL reminders are marked `cancelled=true` (SMS reminders are deleted immediately via `deleteScheduledSMSReminder`), so this is latent, but the cron then unconditionally calls SendGrid's `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` with `batch_id: reminder.referenceId` on whatever it finds. If a future change ever marks an SMS reminder as cancelled, this code will try to cancel it via the email provider and may also `delete` it, losing the row. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` to the where clause for safety.

title: Reminder cancellation is fire-and-forget (no await)
body: The loop at lines 485-493 calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` inside `forEach` but never awaits the returned promises. The handler then continues and returns a 'Booking successfully cancelled' response while Twilio cancellation and the `cancelled: true` DB update may still be pending. A failing Twilio/SendGrid call or DB write is silently dropped, the DB may still read `scheduled: true`, and the CRON will not see the cancellation. Use `for...of` with `await`, or `Promise.all(updatedBookings.flatMap(...))`.

title: Reminder cancellation on reschedule is fire-and-forget
body: The try/catch wraps a `forEach` whose callback returns a promise that is never awaited. Any rejection from `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` will not be caught and the mutation continues. Errors are lost, and on the `immediateDelete=true` email path the DB row is never updated, so if the SendGrid cancel fails, the system has no record that cancellation was attempted.

title: Reminder cancellation in requestReschedule is fire-and-forget
body: `bookingToReschedule.workflowReminders.forEach(...)` returns promises that are never awaited. The trpc mutation then proceeds to send emails, update DB, delete refs, etc., and finally returns before the SendGrid/Twilio cancellation has completed (or even started). Failures are not propagated. Should be a `for...of` loop with `await`, or collect and `Promise.all`.

title: Reminder cancellation in workflow delete is fire-and-forget
body: `scheduledReminders.forEach(...)` returns promises that are never awaited before `ctx.prisma.workflow.deleteMany` runs. The workflow delete cascades through `WorkflowStep` and may delete the `WorkflowReminder` rows (via onDelete: Cascade) before SendGrid/Twilio cancellation completes, leaving third-party systems with still-scheduled sends and no DB record to retry. Await the cancellations before deleting the workflow.

title: Reminder cancellation for disabled event types is fire-and-forget
body: The `remindersToDelete.flat().forEach(...)` block calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` without awaiting. These are then followed by further awaits like `prisma.workflowsOnEventTypes.deleteMany`, so the mutation returns before cancellations complete and any error is silently swallowed.

title: Reminder cancellation on step edit is fire-and-forget
body: `remindersToUpdate.forEach(async (reminder) => {...})` does not await. The mutation continues and returns while SendGrid/Twilio cancellations may still be in flight. Errors are silently swallowed. Await the operations.

title: unscheduledReminders query ignores the new cancelled flag
body: The query that picks up `scheduled: false` reminders to push to SendGrid does not filter on `cancelled`. When a booking is cancelled more than 72 hours before a reminder fires, the reminder row has `cancelled: true` but `scheduled: false`. The next CRON run within 72h of `scheduledDate` will still schedule it via SendGrid. The CRON will subsequently try to cancel the resulting SendGrid send in its 1-hour window, but this is wasteful at best and creates a window in which the email is queued. Add `cancelled: { not: true }` (or `cancelled: false`) to the `where` filter on line 82-87.

title: immediateDelete path leaves DB row unchanged
body: When `immediateDelete=true`, the function only posts to SendGrid and returns without touching the database. The `WorkflowReminder` row remains with `scheduled: true` and `cancelled` unset. If the SendGrid cancel call fails (e.g. transient error or the historic 100-cancellation limit), there is no record of the attempt and the row will not be retried by the CRON (which only looks at `cancelled: true`). The row will only be cleaned up after `scheduledDate` passes. Set `cancelled: true` (or delete the row) on this path as well, so failures are recoverable.

title: Cancel loop awaits SendGrid calls sequentially
body: Inside `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` each iteration awaits a SendGrid HTTP call before moving on. With any non-trivial number of cancellations this serialises the network round-trips (CRON has a hard 15-min cadence and other tenants share it). Use `Promise.allSettled` (or chunked parallel batches) so a single failed call doesn't abort the others and so throughput is reasonable.

title: 1-hour cancel window leaves reminders scheduled in SendGrid
body: `remindersToCancel` only matches `cancelled: true` reminders with `scheduledDate <= now + 1 hour`. Reminders that were already pushed to SendGrid and whose `scheduledDate` is between 1 and 72 hours away are silently skipped: they remain as pending sends in SendGrid. If the CRON is delayed beyond the 1-hour buffer (which it can be, given that it runs every 15 minutes and can be throttled), SendGrid will deliver a reminder for a booking that was cancelled or rescheduled — the same bug this PR is meant to fix. Either cancel in SendGrid immediately on the cancel/reschedule path, or process all `cancelled: true` reminders in this loop, not just the next hour.

title: cancelled column added without default
body: `cancelled Boolean?` is added without a default value, and the migration `ALTER TABLE "WorkflowReminder" ADD COLUMN "cancelled" BOOLEAN` leaves existing rows at NULL. All call sites compare against `cancelled: true` so this is functionally safe, but it would be clearer and more index-friendly to default to `false` and add an index on `(cancelled, scheduledDate)` since the CRON scans on that pair on every 15-min run.

title: Signature change of deleteScheduledEmailReminder is inconsistent across the codebase
body: `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` now requires a `reminderId: number` as the first parameter. Existing callers were updated, but the parameter order (id before referenceId) is unusual since the function historically only needed the external reference. Consider reordering to `(referenceId, reminderId, immediateDelete)` to match `deleteScheduledSMSReminder`'s spirit (which keeps referenceId first) and to minimise future misuse.

title: SMS cancellation deletes the DB row even when Twilio cancel fails
body: `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` first calls `twilio.cancelSMS(referenceId)` and then unconditionally deletes the DB row, all inside the same `try`. If Twilio throws, the catch logs and returns, but the SMS may still be queued at Twilio and there is no record to retry. The flow for email intentionally defers cancellation to a CRON-style mechanism for resilience; the SMS path has no equivalent. Either mirror the email design (`cancelled: true` + CRON) or move the `prisma.workflowReminder.delete` outside the try so the delete only happens on Twilio success.

title: Verification-code TextField is not bound to form state
body: In the phone-number verification UI, `TextField` for the verification code uses a local `verificationCode` state via `onChange`, but is rendered with `value={verificationCode}` and no `name` registration. The field shows correctly while mounted, but loses its value if the component remounts (e.g. switching action types triggers `setNumberVerified(false)` and `setIsPhoneNumberNeeded(...)` re-renders). It also leaks `verificationCode` between steps because it is component-level state, not scoped to `step.stepNumber`. The original layout (before this PR's refactor) had the same code, but since the panel was hoisted into its own block here, multiple steps now share the same single state variable.

title: Step-deletion cancellations are fire-and-forget before prisma.workflowStep.delete
body: `remindersFromStep.forEach(reminder => deleteScheduledEmailReminder(...))` is not awaited before `prisma.workflowStep.delete({ where: { id: oldStep.id } })`. Because `WorkflowStep` has `onDelete: Cascade` on `WorkflowReminder`, the delete will remove the reminder rows from the DB before SendGrid/Twilio has had a chance to cancel them, leaving third-party queues with pending sends. Await the cancellations first.

title: Past-reminder cleanup deletes rows before SendGrid actually fires
body: The first action of the CRON deletes every `WorkflowReminder` row whose `scheduledDate <= now`. This is supposed to be housekeeping for already-sent reminders, but the only signal that an email was actually delivered is the row's existence. If SendGrid is delayed or the CRON runs late, reminders that have not been sent yet can be deleted from the DB while still being queued in SendGrid, leading to silent drops. Track delivery status (or only delete `cancelled: true` past reminders) rather than every past-scheduled row.

title: No tests added for the cancellation fix
body: This PR changes the data flow for cancelling workflow reminders on booking cancel/reschedule and adds a new DB column plus a new CRON path. There are no tests covering: (a) that `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` sets `cancelled: true` correctly, (b) that the CRON only processes `cancelled: true` rows within the window, (c) that reschedule/reschedule-via-trpc paths actually cancel, or (d) regression coverage for the bug in #7225. The previous attempt also broke things; without tests the same risk exists here.

title: Migration adds nullable column without NOT NULL or default
body: The migration is `ALTER TABLE "WorkflowReminder" ADD COLUMN "cancelled" BOOLEAN;` — no NOT NULL, no DEFAULT. For new rows the application always writes a value, so this is fine in practice, but it makes the schema's intent ambiguous. Either add `NOT NULL DEFAULT false` (preferred; all existing rows become `false`) or document that `NULL` means 'not cancelled' explicitly in the migration comment.

title: forEach(async) is not awaited, so reschedule cancellations race the reschedule email
body: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` does not await the inner async work. The control flow continues to `await sendRequestRescheduleEmail(...)` and then returns from the mutation immediately, while calendar/video deletions are still in flight. Users will receive a "please reschedule" email and the function will report success while the original booking is still present on calendars/video providers, causing double-booking and stale availability. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` or a `for...of` loop with `await`.

title: forEach(async) is not awaited in reschedule
body: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` fires off async calendar/video deletions but does not wait for them. The surrounding `try/catch` will not see rejections, and `Reschedule` returns `true` (success) before the cancellations actually complete. The previous code had the same shape but the operations were effectively fire-and-forget; now with `await getCalendar(...)` inside, the race window is larger and the lack of awaiting becomes a real correctness bug.

title: forEach(async) is not awaited in reschedule
body: Identical bug to `packages/app-store/vital/lib/reschedule.ts`: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` starts async calendar/video deletion work but never awaits it. The function returns before deletions finish and the try/catch around it cannot catch rejections.

title: forEach(async) populates apiDeletes after Promise.all already ran
Calendar deletions changed from concurrent to sequential
getCalendarCredentials returns a Promise-wrapped calendar but stays synchronous
body: `getCalendar` is now `async`, so inside `getCalendarCredentials` `const calendar = getCalendar(credential)` is a `Promise<Calendar | null>`, and the objects returned (`{ integration, credential, calendar }`) now carry a Promise where callers historically got a `Calendar`. The only in-tree caller (`getConnectedCalendars`) was patched to `await item.calendar`, but the function is exported, is not marked `async`, and the field is named `calendar` rather than `calendarPromise`. This makes it very easy for other consumers (and future code) to access `item.calendar` synchronously and silently get a Promise, leading to runtime `TypeError: calendar.deleteEvent is not a function` or undefined behavior. Either make `getCalendarCredentials` async and resolve calendars before returning, or rename the field and document the async contract.

title: Calendar credentials fetched serially in getConnectedCalendars
body: In `getConnectedCalendars`, after destructuring each item the code does `const calendar = await item.calendar;` inside `Promise.all(calendarCredentials.map(async (item) => {...}))`. Because each `.map` callback awaits the dynamic import of the calendar app before continuing, the dynamic imports for different calendar credentials run effectively serially per Promise.all branch iteration (each callback awaits before the next iterates). Although the outer `Promise.all` runs them concurrently in theory, the code path through `getCalendar` is now an extra await inside every iteration, adding latency vs. issuing all dynamic imports in parallel (e.g. `Promise.all(calendarCredentials.map(item => item.calendar))` once, then proceed).

title: forEach(async ...) does not await calendar/video deletions
body: The code wraps the bookingRef iteration in `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })`. `Array.prototype.forEach` ignores the return value of its callback and does not await Promises, so the async callbacks (which now `await getCalendar(...)` and invoke `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` / `deleteMeeting(...)`) are fire-and-forget. The outer `Reschedule` function returns as soon as the synchronous work completes, before the calendar/video integrations have been cancelled. Previously these were synchronous calls; the async refactor turned them into background tasks. The booking row is updated to CANCELLED and `sendRequestRescheduleEmail` is awaited before these deletions actually run, which is a data-integrity regression (integrations can stay in sync with the old time slot after the DB has already been flipped). Replace the `forEach` with a sequential `for...of` (or `Promise.all(refs.map(...))`) so the deletions are awaited.

title: forEach(async ...) does not await calendar/video deletions
body: Identical antipattern to vital/lib/reschedule.ts: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })`. After making the inner callback async, forEach no longer awaits any of the calendar `deleteEvent` or `deleteMeeting` Promises. The `Reschedule` function continues running and the `sendRequestRescheduleEmail` is awaited before the integration deletions actually execute. Result: the booking is updated, the reschedule email goes out, and the function returns before the previous Google/Outlook/Zoom events are cancelled. Convert to a real awaited loop.

title: forEach(async ...) drops recurring calendar deletion promises
forEach(async ...) skips calendar/video cancellations on reschedule
body: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })` does not await the async callback. Inside, the code `await`s `getCalendar(...)` and calls `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` and `deleteMeeting(...)`, but because forEach discards the returned Promise and does not block, the `requestReschedule` mutation can finish — sending `sendRequestRescheduleEmail`, webhooks, and returning to the caller — before any of the previous calendar/video entries are cancelled. Previously these calls were synchronous; the async conversion silently turned them into best-effort background work. Replace with `for (const bookingRef of bookingRefsFiltered) { ... }` or `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))`.

title: getCalendarCredentials returns Promise<Calendar> in a sync API
Sequential awaits in getVideoAdapters serialize module loads
forEach(async) fire-and-forget on calendar/video deletions
body: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })` discards the returned promises. The surrounding `try { ... } catch (error) { ... }` cannot catch rejections from inside the async callback, and the caller (reschedule API) returns to the user once the synchronous portion of the loop ends. As a result, calendar `deleteEvent` / `deleteMeeting` calls may still be in flight when the function returns `true` and the reschedule email is sent, leading to inconsistent state (booking marked rescheduled while old events are not yet deleted). This was made worse by the async conversion because both `getCalendar` and the deletion calls are now Promise-returning; before, only `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` were promise-returning. Replace with `for (const bookingRef of bookingRefsFiltered)` and `await` each step, or build an array of promises and `await Promise.all(...)`.

title: forEach(async) fire-and-forget on calendar/video deletions
body: Identical issue to `packages/app-store/vital/lib/reschedule.ts:125`. The async `forEach` callback's promises are dropped, so `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` calls may not complete (and rejections are uncaught) before this function returns `true` and the reschedule flow continues. Replace with a sequential `for ... of` loop or `Promise.all(...)` over the references.

title: forEach(async) on calendar/video deletions in requestReschedule
body: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })` does not await the returned promises. The function falls straight through to `await sendRequestRescheduleEmail(...)` and the rest of the mutation while the calendar `deleteEvent` and `deleteMeeting` calls are still pending. There is no `try/catch` around the loop either, so any rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection. With the new async `getCalendar`, the call now performs a lazy chunk download for every credential in addition to the network call to the provider, making the race more likely to be observed. Convert to `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))` or a sequential `for ... of` with awaited steps.

title: forEach(async) on recurring-event calendar deletions
body: In the recurring-event branch of cancellation, `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { ... })` discards the returned promises, so the function reaches `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` and returns the HTTP response before the per-credential calendar deletions have finished. The outer `try/catch` does not cover this loop either. Because `getCalendar` is now async, this serializes per-credential dynamic chunk loads behind an unawaited loop, widening the race window. Replace with a proper loop that collects promises and lets `Promise.all` drive completion.

title: Resolved value pushed to apiDeletes instead of the promise
body: Inside the unawaited forEach above, `const deletedEvent = await calendar?.deleteEvent(uid, evt, externalCalendarId); apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent);` pushes the already-resolved value (or `undefined`) into `apiDeletes` rather than the pending Promise. The later `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` therefore never waits for those deleteEvent calls in the recurring-event path (and even if forEach were fixed to await, the push would still capture resolved values). Push the Promise returned by `deleteEvent` directly, i.e. `apiDeletes.push(calendar?.deleteEvent(uid, evt, externalCalendarId) as Promise<unknown> | undefined);` and let `Promise.all` await it.

title: getVideoAdapters serializes dynamic imports
body: The previous `reduce` implementation ran the entire synchronous mapping in one pass; the new implementation uses a sequential `for (const cred of withCredentials) { const app = await appStore[...]; ... }`, so every credential now blocks the next on its dynamic import + module evaluation. With multiple video credentials attached (Zoom, Daily, Whereby, etc.) this turns into N sequential async chunks where it used to be one synchronous pass and could be N parallel `Promise.all(creds.map(...))` calls. Replace with `Promise.all(withCredentials.map(...))` to keep the parallel cost similar to before.

title: getCalendarCredentials is sync but leaks Promise<Calendar> in its result
body: `getCalendarCredentials` was kept synchronous, yet inside it `const calendar = getCalendar(credential);` now returns `Promise<Calendar | null>` because `getCalendar` became async. The returned objects therefore carry `calendar: Promise<Calendar | null>`, but the function signature does not advertise that and callers must remember to `await item.calendar` (which is exactly what the new `getConnectedCalendars` body now has to do). Either make `getCalendarCredentials` async and `await getCalendar`, or stop calling `getCalendar` inside it and only return `{ integration, credential }`, leaving adapter construction to the caller. As written, the public type lies about its return value and any future caller that treats `item.calendar` as a sync `Calendar` will get a rejected promise.

title: Awaiting already-resolved apiDeletes entries in seat cancellation
