body: Inside the rules.map(...) switch, the previously-rendered GrafanaRuleLoader had `key={key}` (using `key` destructured from `ruleWithOrigin` at line 152), but the new GrafanaRuleListItem element at line 157 is rendered without any key prop, and the destructured `key` is now unused. React will emit "Each child in a list should have a unique 'key' prop" warnings for every grafana rule rendered here. More importantly, without a key React cannot correctly match components across reorders or insertions, leading to incorrect component identity, lost local state in children, and unpredictable DOM/state reuse in the large rule lists this view exists for. Restore the `key={key}` prop on the GrafanaRuleListItem element.

title: Comment about ruler preload is stale after removal of ruler prefetch
body: Lines 81-82 read 'This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules, but it improves the UX / Because the user waits a bit longer for the initial load but doesn't need to wait for each group to be loaded'. The matching code, `dispatch(alertRuleApi.util.prefetch('getGrafanaRulerGroup', ...))`, was deleted in this PR, and the enclosing local variable `cacheAndRulerPreload` no longer does any ruler preload - it only upserts Prometheus groups cache entries. Both the comment and the variable name still claim to be about ruler preloading and will mislead future readers. Update the comment and rename the variable (e.g. `cachePriming`) to reflect that only Prometheus groups cache priming is happening now.

title: Delete menu item never renders in V2 list view because of stale rulerRule gate
body: The Delete menu item is gated by `canDelete && rulerRule && (...)`. In the new V2 list view paths (GrafanaGroupLoader / FilterView) `rulerRule` is always undefined, so even when `canDelete` resolves to true via the new `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` path, no Delete entry is ever rendered. Worse, the `handleDelete` prop supplied by `RuleActionsButtons.V2.tsx` does not actually need the ruler rule (it just calls `showDeleteModal(identifier, groupIdentifier)`), so the gate should be removed for Delete. With all required permissions the menu still cannot be used to delete rules from the new list, which is a user-visible functional regression.

title: Pause menu item never renders in V2 list view; Pause functionality lost
body: The Pause (`MenuItemPauseRule`) item is gated by `canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) && groupIdentifier.groupOrigin === 'grafana'`. `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(undefined)` is false, so the menu item is never rendered in the V2 list view, even when `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` reports Pause supported and allowed. Unlike Delete, Pause truly needs ruler-rule data, so this PR effectively disables pausing Grafana alerting rules from the new list. Either an alternative pause flow using only `GrafanaPromRuleDTO` data must be wired up or the action must remain available in this view; otherwise users with pause permission lose the ability to pause from this entry point.

title: Silence drawer cannot open in V2 list view because rulerRule gate
body: The `SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer` is rendered only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is truthy, where `rule` is the optional `RulerRuleDTO`. In V2 list view `rule` is always undefined, so the drawer is never rendered even though `handleSilence` can flip `showSilenceDrawer` to true. As a result, the 'Silence notifications' item opens a click handler that does nothing. The companion `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` flag `canSilence` will report the action as available, so the menu makes a promise the component cannot keep.

title: Test asserts the regression by locking the menu item count to 4
body: The new test 'should render correct menu actions when More button is clicked' grants full alerting permissions (global + folder) and then asserts `expect(menuItems.length).toBe(4)` covering only `silence`, `copyLink`, `duplicate`, and `export`. With `AlertingRuleDelete` granted, Delete should render. The test instead hard-codes the broken count, so it will silently fail or require editing whenever the Delete/Pause/Silence regressions are fixed. Either extend the assertions to cover Delete (and Pause/Silence for alerting rules) or comment that these entries are intentionally hidden behind a follow-up. As written the test acts as a regression lock-in rather than a capability check.

title: Rule details link dropped the returnTo parameter, breaking back-navigation
body: The new `GrafanaRuleListItem` builds the rule link with `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`)` and no `returnTo` query parameter. The previous `GrafanaRuleLoader` passed `{ returnTo: createReturnTo() }` for the same link, and the existing `RuleActionsButtons` and other consumers rely on `createReturnTo()` to navigate back to the originating filtered/grouped list. Removing `returnTo` traps users on the rule details page when they came from the V2 list/filter view, which is a direct UX regression for anyone drilling into a rule from a filter.

title: isProvisionedPromRule accepts PromRuleDTO but only returns true for Grafana variants
body: `isProvisionedPromRule(promRule: PromRuleDTO)` always returns false for a non-Grafana `PromRuleDTO`, but the type signature suggests it applies to any prom rule. The companion `isProvisionedRule(rulerRule: RulerRuleDTO)` narrows with `isGrafanaRulerRule`. The new function should be similarly restricted (e.g. accept `GrafanaPromRuleDTO | undefined`) or documented, otherwise downstream callers (like `getIsProvisioned` in `RuleActionsButtons.V2.tsx`) may believe they are checking provisioned state for cloud/prom rules when they will always get `false`.

title: Loss of optimistic Creating/Deleting state tests not covered elsewhere
body: The PR removes tests 'should render rule with url and creating state when only ruler rule exists' and 'should render delete rule operation list item when only prom rule exists' together with the matching optimistic UI implementation. Nothing in the new suite asserts behavior for the eventual-consistency window between Ruler and Prometheus (rules that have just been created or are being deleted). With the new design relying solely on Prometheus, the absence of either end of that optimistic state should be confirmed explicitly (e.g., a test asserting that a rule created via Ruler but not yet visible in Prometheus simply does not appear) so the contract change is intentional and visible to future maintainers.

title: useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities duplicates useCanSilence logic and may fetch folder twice
body: The new `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` hook (lines 287-337) reads `useCanSilenceInFolder(rule?.folderUid)` while the legacy `useCanSilence(rule)` (line 560) also reads `useFolder(folderUID)` internally. This means `useFolder` is fetched both directly here and via `useCanSilenceInFolder` -> `useFolderPermissions` -> `useFolder`. For every Grafana rule in the list view this triggers two redundant RTKQ/cache lookups for the folder per row. With ~80 rules on the list page this roughly doubles the folder lookups the page used to make.

title: useRulerRuleAbility still called from list view with rule=undefined
body: `RuleActionsButtons.V2` is now invoked with only `promRule` from the Grafana list view (see `GrafanaRuleListItem.tsx`, line ~47, where it is rendered with `<RuleActionsButtons promRule={rule} ...>` and no `rule` prop). However the component unconditionally invokes `useRulerRuleAbility(rule, groupIdentifier, AlertRuleAction.Update)` on line 53. With `rule === undefined` the hook falls into `useAllRulerRuleAbities -> useIsRuleEditable`, which still performs ruler availability/work per rule row even though the goal of the PR is to remove ruler from the list view. The list-view call sites should pass a sentinel (e.g. `skipToken`) or branch the call so ruler abilities are not evaluated for Grafana list items.

title: Both ruler and prom ability hooks always execute
body: `AlertRuleMenu` always invokes both `useRulerRuleAbilities(rulerRule, ...)` (line 57) and `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(... ? promRule : skipToken, ...)` (line 73), even though in the new list view `rulerRule` is undefined. `useRulerRuleAbilities` -> `useAllRulerRuleAbilities` -> `useIsRuleEditable` still performs per-group ruler availability/RBAC checks for every rule rendered by the list. For 80 rules that is 80 ruler-availability lookups, defeating the PR's stated goal of removing ruler from the list view. The component should branch on the available data source (or accept a `skipToken` for the ruler side) when invoked from the list view.

title: Stale comment about ruler preload after removing the dispatch
body: The block in `useGrafanaGroupsGenerator` (around line 82-95) previously also dispatched a `getGrafanaRulerGroup` prefetch; this PR removed that dispatch but left the comment `// This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules, but it improves the UX / Because the user waits a bit longer for the initial load but doesn't need to wait for each group to be loaded`. The comment now references behavior that no longer exists (no ruler preload) and should be updated or removed.

title: isProvisionedPromRule returns false for non-Grafana prom rules via incorrect truthy coercion
skipToken symbol conflicts with other skip-token conventions in this codebase
body: A new top-level `export const skipToken = Symbol('ability-skip-token')` is declared in this file (line 380). RTK Query already exports a `skipToken` symbol and the codebase imports it elsewhere via `@reduxjs/toolkit`. Defining a second, unrelated `skipToken` in this module is a recipe for shadowing/import-collision bugs: any code that does `import { skipToken } from '@reduxjs/toolkit/query'` near this module, or relies on the RTKQ skip semantics, will get a different value. The component-level usages here happen to compare by identity against the local symbol, but future refactors (or merging imports) will be confusing. Prefer reusing the existing RTK Query `skipToken`.

title: useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable loses memoization when rule is undefined
body: `useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable` returns the early-return object `{ isEditable: false, isRemovable: false, loading: false }` directly when `!rule || !folderUID`. Returning a fresh object on every render breaks referential equality for `loading`/`isEditable`/`isRemovable` that the parent memo `useMemo(() => ..., [..., isEditable, isRemovable, ...])` watches. Every parent render will rebuild the abilities map. Wrap the empty case in a `useMemo(() => ({...}), [])` (or hoist a module constant) so the deps array can short-circuit.

title: Redundant type narrowing for promAlertingRule
body: Inside the alerting-rule branch, `prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` has just been checked true, but the code then re-checks `rule && rule.type === PromRuleType.Alerting` to construct `promAlertingRule`. This second check is redundant (and silently nulls out valid Grafana alerting rules if their `type` field were ever different). It also means `promAlertingRule` may be `undefined` even though we are in the alerting branch, leading to a `state` of `undefined` being passed into `AlertRuleListItem`. Either drop the redundant check or rely on it exclusively.

title: mimirDataSource declared but unused after parameter change
body: `const { dataSource: mimirDs } = mimirDataSource();` is added at the top of the test file (line 37) and passed into `getCloudRule({ name: 'Cloud' }, { rulesSource: mimirDs })`. The tests do not exercise any cloud-specific behavior beyond checking that Edit/Delete buttons are absent, which is the same expected behavior regardless of datasource. The added dependency is dead - the mock provider for `mimirDs` is set up but never asserted against, so the test does not regress-protect anything that the previous signature didn't already cover.

title: Test destructures rulerRule but never asserts the new prom-rule abilities path
body: In the `creating/deleting states` describe block, the test creates `creatingRule` and `deletingRule` by destructuring `{ promRule, ...creatingRule }` and `{ rulerRule, ...deletingRule }`. After this PR, the list-view rendering path no longer reads `rulerRule` for abilities, but the tests override the abilities via `useRulerRuleAbilities` (line 172) and `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` (line 175) in such a way that everything is `[true, true]`. The 'Creating'/'Deleting' rendering path that used `RuleOperationListItem` has been removed entirely from `GrafanaGroupLoader` (it no longer fetches the ruler group), so the `deletingRule` case (where no `promRule` exists) cannot actually render through the new code path. The test now passes only because everything is mocked to `[true, true]`; it does not catch the real regression that 'pending deletion' (prom-only) UI is gone. This is a meaningful test gap introduced by the PR.

title: Delete menu item guarded only by canDelete && rulerRule
body: The Delete entry is conditioned on `canDelete && rulerRule` (line 165). With this PR, on the Grafana list view `rulerRule` is `undefined` and `canDelete` is allowed via `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` (the Grafana branch returns `true`), so Delete will not render for Grafana rules in the list view. The component should accept a Deletable identifier (the same way `RuleActionsButtons.V2.getEditableIdentifier` does) and gate Delete on having a deletable identifier (or on `canDelete` alone) - otherwise deleting a Grafana rule from the list view becomes impossible without going through a different code path.

title: Loses 'Deleting' UI for in-flight prom-only deletions
body: The previous implementation rendered `<RuleOperationListItem operation={RuleOperation.Deleting}>` for `promOnlyRules` - rules that existed in Prometheus but not in Ruler. The new implementation iterates only over `promResponse.data.groups.at(0)?.rules` and no longer considers Ruler, so rules currently being deleted (still in Prom, gone from Ruler) will simply disappear from the list view without any 'Deleting' indicator. The PR removes functionality that was documented as needed for eventual consistency between Ruler and Prometheus (see comment in `prometheusGroupsGenerator.ts`). The PR claim that 'Grafana Prometheus rules should be strongly consistent now' (former matchRules comment) is asserted in code, but the UI safety net for inconsistency is gone.

title: Declare Incident menu passes empty URL
body: `{shouldShowDeclareIncidentButton && <DeclareIncidentMenuItem title={promRule.name} url={''} />}` passes `url=''` to the menu item. With the ruler data (and presumably any annotation/labels-derived URL) no longer passed through here, the Declare Incident flow now navigates to the empty URL. This may or may not be a regression, but the URL is not the rule's view URL as one might expect; either the rule's `view` URL should be passed or this should be flagged as incomplete behavior.

title: $__range variable queries will now be incorrectly split
body: The new code interpolates queries via `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(...)` before the `querySupportsSplitting` check is evaluated. The existing check at line 287 (`!isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)`) is supposed to prevent queries containing `$__range` from being split, with a comment explaining that otherwise the interpolated `$__range` value is wrong because it gets interpolated against the split (sub-request) time range. After this change the interpolation runs first on the original full range, so `$__range` is already replaced with a literal value (e.g. `2d`) by the time `isQueryWithRangeVariable` is consulted, and the function returns `false`. As a result, queries that were previously excluded from splitting will now be split, and each sub-request will receive the same `$__range` value computed from the full time range instead of the per-chunk range. The corresponding code path is hit by `runSplitQuery` and by `runShardSplitQuery` (which calls `runSplitQuery` for each shard group), so this affects both splitting modes. The PR adds no test for a `$__range` expression to guard this behavior.

title: Stale comment about $__range interpolation
body: The comment in `querySupportsSplitting` states that `$__range` 'is interpolated on the backend with the split timeRange'. After this PR, interpolation is performed on the frontend inside `runSplitQuery` (and inside `runShardSplitQuery`) before the split happens, using the full time range from `request.range`. The comment is now misleading and contradicts the new behavior; it should be updated to describe the new interpolation point and the implication for `$__range` queries.

title: No test covers the $__range case after the interpolation change
body: The new 'Interpolates queries before execution' test only exercises `$__auto` and `$step` and uses a `replace` mock that does not touch `$__range`. There is also no existing test in either `querySplitting.test.ts` or `shardQuerySplitting.test.ts` that asserts what happens to a query containing `$__range` when it goes through `runSplitQuery` or `runShardSplitQuery`. Given that the change moves interpolation ahead of the `querySupportsSplitting` check, a regression test using `$__range` (or `__range`, `${__range}`) is needed to ensure the existing 'do not split range-variable queries' invariant still holds.

title: Queries are interpolated twice in the sharded path
body: `runShardSplitQuery` now calls `datasource.applyTemplateVariables` for every target on line 52, and then `splitQueriesByStreamShard` forwards those (already-interpolated) targets into `runSplitQuery`, which calls `applyTemplateVariables` again for each target of every sub-request (line 299 of `querySplitting.ts`). The shard test was updated to assert this redundancy: `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` for a single-target request that issues 4 sub-requests. Beyond the wasted work, the second interpolation runs over expressions that have already been mutated to add `__stream_shard__` selectors; if any of those new literal substrings happen to collide with template-variable syntax used by the templateSrv, the result is non-obvious. Either `runShardSplitQuery` should pass already-interpolated targets through and skip the re-interpolation in `runSplitQuery`, or the interpolation should be done only inside `runSplitQuery` as before.

title: New interpolation test reuses the outer `datasource` variable but bypasses beforeEach mocks
body: The 'Interpolates queries before execution' test reassigns `datasource` after the `beforeEach` has already installed `applyTemplateVariables` and `languageProvider.fetchLabelValues` mocks. The new datasource is created with a custom `replace` function and is intended to exercise the real `applyTemplateVariables`, but the previous test file conventions (see 'Interpolates queries before running' at line 110) explicitly mock `applyTemplateVariables` to control interpolation. Mixing the two approaches in the same `describe` block means the behavior under test is not really 'does querySplitting interpolate before execution?' but 'does it call applyTemplateVariables that happens to interpolate via this replace function?'. The test is also fragile to any future change in the real `applyTemplateVariables` (e.g. handling of `$__range`) because it does not stub it explicitly. Consider mocking `applyTemplateVariables` here too, or moving this case to a dedicated test that documents the use of the real implementation.

title: Redundant applyTemplateVariables calls in shard splitting flow
body: When shard splitting is active, runShardSplitQuery calls applyTemplateVariables on each target (line 52 of shardQuerySplitting.ts), then for every shard group runSplitQuery is invoked which calls applyTemplateVariables again on the same targets (line 299 of querySplitting.ts). This is confirmed by the test 'Interpolates queries before running' which expects applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times = 1 (in runShardSplitQuery) + 4 (one per shard group in runSplitQuery). For idempotent interpolation this is functionally correct but wasteful; any non-idempotent side effects in applyTemplateVariables (logging, analytics) would occur twice. The redundant call could be avoided by either skipping applyTemplateVariables in runSplitQuery when called from runShardSplitQuery, or by not re-interpolating in the inner runSplitQuery call.

title: New shard-splitting interpolation test missing direction: Scan
body: The new test 'Interpolates queries before execution' creates a query with `expr: 'count_over_time({a="b"}[$__auto])'` and `step: '$step'` but does not set `direction: LokiQueryDirection.Scan`. All other tests in this file that exercise sharding explicitly set `direction: Scan` (e.g. lines 53, 75, 173). The expected expression contains `__stream_shard__=~"20|10"` which is only added by `interpolateShardingSelector` after `requestSupportsSharding` returns true. If `requestSupportsSharding` requires the Scan direction, this query would fall into `otherQueries` instead of being sharded, the expression would not contain the shard selector, and the assertion would fail. The test should explicitly set `direction: LokiQueryDirection.Scan` to match the established convention and to ensure deterministic behavior.

title: applyTemplateVariables may mutate request.targets
body: The new code calls `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)` on items of `request.targets` directly. Standard implementations of `applyTemplateVariables` mutate the input query and return it (as evidenced by the test mock at shardQuerySplitting.test.ts lines 56-59). This means the caller's `request.targets[i]` will have its `expr` and `step` mutated to interpolated values as a side effect of running split queries. If the caller (or downstream code) inspects `request.targets` after `runSplitQuery`/`runShardSplitQuery` returns, it will see the interpolated values rather than the original template expressions. This is the same behavior as the previous `interpolateVariablesInQueries` call, but worth noting that the original request object is no longer pristine after splitting.

title: applyTemplateVariables called before $__range exclusion check
body: The new code interpolates every query via `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(...)` before `partition(...)` runs `querySupportsSplitting`, which relies on `isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)` to exclude queries whose `$__range` would be interpolated on the backend with the split time range. After `applyTemplateVariables`, `$__range` is already replaced with the literal full-range value, so `isQueryWithRangeVariable` returns false and queries with `$__range` are now placed in the splitting path. The split sub-requests are then dispatched with the full-range literal inside the expression but a per-chunk time range, so each sub-query computes its rate over the wrong window and the merged result is incorrect. Before this PR the original `$__range` token was still present when `querySupportsSplitting` ran, so the exclusion worked; this PR silently bypasses it.

title: Stale comment in querySupportsSplitting
body: The comment above the `!isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)` check says 'Queries with $__range variable should not be split because then the interpolated $__range variable is incorrect because it is interpolated on the backend with the split timeRange'. With the new `.map(applyTemplateVariables)` on line 296 running before `querySupportsSplitting`, that statement is no longer accurate: `$__range` is interpolated client-side first, so the check no longer protects against this scenario. Either the check needs to be performed before interpolation or the comment needs to be rewritten; right now the comment misleads readers about the actual control flow.

title: No test covers $__range queries after early interpolation
body: The new 'Interpolates queries before execution' test only exercises `$__auto` and `$step` and uses a `replace` mock that does not touch `$__range`. The most important behavior change in this PR is that `$__range` is now interpolated before `querySupportsSplitting` runs, but there is no test asserting that a `$__range`-bearing query is still routed to the non-splitting branch (or any test documenting the new behavior). Without such a test, the regression described in the other finding can re-occur unnoticed.

title: No $__range test for shard splitting interpolation path
body: The new 'Interpolates queries before execution' test in shardQuerySplitting.test.ts also only covers `$__auto` / `$step`. Since `runShardSplitQuery` now calls `datasource.applyTemplateVariables` once on every target before sharding, the same `$__range` interpolation that happens client-side at this layer will propagate into the sub-requests `runSplitQuery` makes. A test that uses a `$__range` expression and asserts how the shard-selector and sub-request range interact would catch any future regression here.

title: Mock for applyTemplateVariables mutates the input query
body: Both beforeEach and the 'Sends the whole stream selector to fetch values' test install `datasource.applyTemplateVariables = jest.fn().mockImplementation((query) => { query.expr = query.expr.replace(...); return query; })`. The real Loki `applyTemplateVariables` returns a new query object (via `replaceQuery` / `templateSrv.replace`). Mocking it as a mutator can hide bugs where production code relies on the original `request.targets` being left untouched, because every other test sharing this setup will see `request.targets[i].expr` already rewritten. Consider mirroring production semantics in the mock (return a new object) so test behavior matches reality.

title: Test function name not updated after rename
body: The test function is still named `TestInstrumentationMiddleware` after the file and middleware were renamed to `metrics_middleware.go`/`MetricsMiddleware`. The function name should be renamed to `TestMetricsMiddleware` to match the new naming and avoid confusion for future maintainers.

title: No test for new ContextualLoggerMiddleware
body: The new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` was extracted from the old `InstrumentationMiddleware` but no corresponding test file was added. The `instrumentContext` helper, which sets the `endpoint`, `pluginId`, `dsName`, `dsUID`, and `uname` attributes on the request context, should be covered by tests to ensure these attributes are correctly set for QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, and CollectMetrics, and that they are absent for the streaming methods (SubscribeStream, PublishStream, RunStream) which intentionally pass through.

title: FromContext doc comment does not match implementations
body: The new `FromContext` doc comment says it returns a new contextual Logger that has 'this logger's context plus the given context', but the two implementations in the diff (`grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext` in `pkg/plugins/log/logger.go` and `TestLogger.FromContext` in `pkg/plugins/log/fake.go`) only use the passed-in context and ignore the receiver's state. Either the comment should be corrected to describe the actual behavior (e.g. 'returns a Logger derived from the given context') or the implementations should be updated to also include the receiver's existing context.

title: Test function still named after old InstrumentationMiddleware type
body: The test file was renamed from instrumentation_middleware_test.go to metrics_middleware_test.go and the production identifier newInstrumentationMiddleware was renamed to newMetricsMiddleware, but the test function itself is still declared as `func TestInstrumentationMiddleware(t *testing.T)`. This is stale and misleading: the test now exercises the MetricsMiddleware, not an InstrumentationMiddleware, and the function name should be updated to TestMetricsMiddleware to match the renamed type. Leaving the old name will confuse future readers, test failure reports, and any tooling that filters by test name.

title: New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no dedicated tests
body: The new ContextualLoggerMiddleware is responsible for adding the contextual logger (endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, uname) to the request context that LoggerMiddleware later reads via FromContext. Despite being a separate middleware now, there is no contextual_logger_middleware_test.go. The new code path is not exercised by any test, and the existing TestLogger helper in pkg/plugins/log/fake.go has FromContext(ctx) implemented as `return NewTestLogger()` (ignoring ctx), so even tests that use TestLogger cannot verify that the contextual attributes are actually propagated. Without coverage, regressions in the instrumentContext helper or in the middleware ordering would not be caught.

title: grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext silently drops contextual attributes on type-assertion failure
body: The new FromContext implementation does `d.l.FromContext(ctx).(*log.ConcreteLogger)` and, if the assertion fails, silently falls back to `d.New()`. The fallback returns a wrapper around a freshly created logger that has NO contextual attributes, so pluginId/endpoint/dsName/dsUID/uname (added upstream by ContextualLoggerMiddleware) are lost and downstream code (e.g., LoggerMiddleware logging "Plugin Request Completed") will produce log lines without the expected fields. This makes debugging harder and is a behavior change versus the previous code, where the attributes were appended directly to logParams in logRequest. The implementation should either propagate the returned logger without asserting to a concrete type, or at minimum log/return an error when the assertion fails rather than silently degrading.

title: Adding FromContext to Logger interface is a breaking change for other implementations
body: The Logger interface in pkg/plugins/log is a public package and previously had five methods (New, Debug, Info, Warn, Error). This PR adds a sixth method, FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger. Any type implementing this interface elsewhere in the repository or in downstream consumers (plugin SDK helpers, test doubles in other packages, third-party Grafana plugins) will fail to compile. The PR updates grafanaInfraLogWrapper and TestLogger, but does not enumerate or update other in-repo implementers. A grep for `log.Logger` implementers should be run before merge, or the interface change should be guarded with a build tag / documented as a deliberate API break in the changelog.

title: traceID is no longer included in the Plugin Request Completed log entry
body: The previous LoggerMiddleware.logRequest explicitly extracted the OpenTelemetry traceID from the context and appended it as a 'traceID' log parameter. The new implementation relies on m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), which only auto-includes attributes injected by ContextualLoggerMiddleware.instrumentContext. The new instrumentContext (in contextual_logger_middleware.go) does not extract or add the traceID, so plugin request log entries no longer carry a traceID. This breaks the existing ability to correlate plugin request logs with distributed traces and is a regression that should be fixed by either adding the traceID inside instrumentContext or by re-introducing it in logRequest.

title: New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no test coverage
body: A new middleware file (ContextualLoggerMiddleware) is added in this PR but is not accompanied by a test file. The sibling middleware files (metrics_middleware_test.go and the existing logger_middleware_test.go) have test coverage. ContextualLoggerMiddleware has nontrivial behavior: it inspects DataSourceInstanceSettings and User, conditionally adds dsName/dsUID/uname, and is depended on by LoggerMiddleware to populate the contextual logger. It should have at least one test verifying that the contextual attributes are present on the context that reaches LoggerMiddleware (and that stream methods, which do not call instrumentContext, leave the context untouched).

title: Test function name not updated after rename
body: The test file was renamed from instrumentation_middleware_test.go to metrics_middleware_test.go and the only adjusted line updates the helper name to newMetricsMiddleware, but the top-level test function is still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware. The function name should be TestMetricsMiddleware to match the renamed type and file, otherwise test output and any -run filters will be misleading.

title: Adding FromContext to the Logger interface is a breaking change for other implementations
body: The Logger interface gained a new method: FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger. Any other type that implements log.Logger outside the two updated in this PR (grafanaInfraLogWrapper and TestLogger) will fail to compile. Within this repo there is no other implementation in the changed files, but this package is used as plog across the codebase and is the boundary type for plugin SDK consumers. This kind of additive interface change should be called out explicitly (e.g., in a changelog) or guarded so external implementers (mocks, custom plugin loggers) are not silently broken at compile time.

title: updateDevice SQL breaks on Postgres
body: The `updateDevice` function hardcodes `?` placeholders, but Grafana supports Postgres (which uses `$1, $2, ...`). `CreateOrUpdateDevice` in the same file branches on `s.sqlStore.GetDBType()` and emits `$N` placeholders for Postgres; `updateDevice` does not. When the device limit is reached and the deployment is Postgres, this UPDATE will fail to parse and the error returned to `TagDevice`/`Authenticate` is a raw SQL syntax error rather than `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. The new device-limit feature will be effectively broken on Postgres.

title: Local cache is populated before the DB call, defeating the device limit on retry
body: In `tagDeviceUI`, `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})` is executed before `CreateOrUpdateDevice` is called, and the entry is not removed on failure. The cache TTL is 29 minutes. With the new synchronous behavior, a device rejected with `ErrDeviceLimitReached` on the first request is silently allowed on any subsequent request within 29 minutes, because `tagDeviceUI` returns `nil` on a cache hit before ever consulting the DB. An attacker (or a normal user) who is denied once can simply retry and pass; after ~29 minutes the denial returns. The cache should be set only after a successful DB write, or explicitly invalidated on failure, otherwise the new `device_limit` setting is bypassable.

title: Device tagging moved to synchronous, authentication now fails on device-limit error
body: Previously the call to `anonDeviceService.TagDevice` ran in a goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout and any error was logged; authentication always succeeded. After this change, `TagDevice` runs synchronously on the request context, and `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned from `Authenticate`, causing the authn flow to deny anonymous authentication entirely. This is a significant behavior change that is not described in the PR description, has no docs/release-notes update, and offers no way for the caller to distinguish "limit reached" from any other auth failure. This should be an explicit, documented breaking change; consider a feature toggle or a dedicated error type that the authn layer can map to a friendly response (e.g., 429) rather than a generic auth failure.

title: TOCTOU race allows exceeding the configured device limit
body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` does `CountDevices(...)` and then, if below the limit, performs an unconditional INSERT. Two concurrent requests on different server instances can both observe `count < deviceLimit`, both pass the gate, and both INSERT, causing the actual device count to exceed `deviceLimit`. The PR makes no attempt to take a row-level lock, use an atomic INSERT-with-cap, or wrap the count+insert in a transaction. In multi-instance / HA deployments the limit becomes approximate and can grow without bound under load. This needs to be either documented as best-effort or enforced atomically.

title: device_limit has no validation; negative values silently disable the limit
body: `cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit = anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0)` accepts any int64 from the ini file. The store treats anything `<= 0` as "no limit" (`if s.deviceLimit > 0`). A misconfiguration such as `device_limit = -1` (or a stray negative value) silently disables the feature without any error, log line, or warning. Negative values should be rejected at startup with a clear error, or at least clamped to 0 with a warning.

title: Anonymous authentication now performs extra synchronous DB work per request
body: When the limit is enabled, every `TagDevice` call (which is now on the auth path) runs an extra `CountDevices` SELECT against `anon_device` before the INSERT/UPDATE. The local cache (`localcache.New(29*time.Minute, 15*time.Minute)`) only mitigates repeated tags of already-known devices; new devices always incur the extra query. This adds latency to the anonymous auth hot path. Consider gating the count behind the cache as well (e.g., only check the limit when the cache misses, or only enforce the limit on first-seen devices), or otherwise documenting the performance trade-off.

title: No test that an existing device can still be updated when the limit is reached
body: `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only verifies that a NEW device ID is rejected with `ErrDeviceLimitReached` once the limit is hit. It never exercises the intended happy path of `updateDevice`: tagging an already-known, still-active device when the limit is reached should succeed (the device's `updated_at` should be refreshed in place). Without that test, regressions in the `WHERE device_id = ? AND updated_at BETWEEN ?` clause (e.g., the Postgres `$N` placeholder bug) would not be caught.

title: No test for the authn flow when the device limit is reached
body: `client.go` now propagates `ErrDeviceLimitReached` out of `Authenticate`, but no test in `impl_test.go` (or a `client_test.go`) verifies that behavior. The new feature is supposed to deny authentication when the limit is hit, yet the existing `TestIntegrationDeviceService_tag` uses `deviceLimit = 0` (via `setting.NewCfg()` defaults), so it never exercises the limit code path through the auth client. At minimum, a test that sets a small `AnonymousDeviceLimit`, attempts `Authenticate` for a new device, and asserts the returned error, is required.

title: New auth.anonymous.device_limit setting is undocumented
body: A new configurable option `device_limit` is added to the `[auth.anonymous]` section and exposed to the frontend via `AnonymousDeviceLimit`. No change is made to Grafana's configuration documentation (`docs/sources/setup-grafana/configure-grafana/index.md` or equivalent), no sample/commented entry is added to `conf/defaults.ini`, and the PR description is empty (no "Why do we need this feature?", no linked issue, no release notes). Operators have no way to discover that the setting exists, what value to pick, what 0 means, or that it changes the semantics of anonymous authentication from "always allowed" to "denied when limit reached".

title: Device limit can be exceeded under concurrent load (TOCTOU)
body: In CreateOrUpdateDevice, the active device count is read with CountDevices and then, based on that single read, either an UPDATE or an INSERT path is taken. There is no row-level lock, advisory lock, or transactional serialization between the count and the subsequent write. Under concurrent requests from different device IDs, two goroutines can both observe count == limit-1, both fall through to the INSERT path, and the resulting row count exceeds the configured AnonymousDeviceLimit. The whole point of this PR is the limit; it must hold under concurrency. Fix by serializing the check+write (e.g. transaction with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on a sentinel row, an advisory lock, or pushing the limit enforcement into a single atomic SQL statement).

title: Anonymous auth now blocks on DB write and request context cancellation
body: Previously TagDevice ran in a goroutine on a fresh context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 2*time.Minute) so anonymous authentication never waited on, nor could be aborted by, the DB. The new code calls TagDevice(ctx, ...) synchronously, using the request context. Consequences: (1) every anonymous auth now incurs at least one DB round-trip (CountDevices, plus UPDATE or INSERT) before the identity is returned, (2) if the client disconnects mid-request the request context is cancelled and the tag DB write fails with context.Canceled, (3) any DB slowness or transient error directly delays/fails anonymous logins. The goroutine-and-detached-context design existed precisely to decouple auth from the side-effect DB write. The limit check needed to make auth decisions could be done as a separate read-only query while still keeping the write detached; or the limit check could run in the goroutine and short-circuit a follow-up call.

title: Panic recovery was removed from the anonymous tag path
body: The previous goroutine wrapped the TagDevice call in `defer func() { if err := recover(); err != nil { a.log.Warn(...) } }()`. The new synchronous implementation has no panic recovery, so any panic in tagDeviceUI, CreateOrUpdateDevice, or a sqlstore helper will now propagate out of Anonymous.Authenticate and into the request handler. Panics from DB drivers/serializers are not common but they do happen, and losing this safety net in the auth hot path is a regression in robustness.

title: Returning devices whose entry is expired are wrongly rejected as 'limit reached'
body: updateDevice issues `UPDATE anon_device SET ... WHERE device_id = ? AND updated_at BETWEEN ? AND ?`, where the BETWEEN range is `device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration)` to `device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(time.Minute)` (i.e. the last 30 days). CountDevices uses the same window, so any device whose updated_at is older than 30 days is NOT counted in the active device count. But the UPDATE WHERE clause filters out that exact row, returning 0 rowsAffected and surfacing ErrDeviceLimitReached. Effect: a returning user whose anon_device row is between 30 and 61 days old (the cleanup interval is 61 days) is denied authentication even though, by the counting rule, there is 'room' for them. The intent of the limit appears to be 'only NEW device_ids are limited; existing device_ids are always updatable'. Match on device_id alone, or look the device up first, before deciding to reject.

title: Race condition between count check and insert is not exercised
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit calls CreateOrUpdateDevice twice sequentially and checks the second one errors. The TOCTOU race between CountDevices and the subsequent INSERT (which can let the limit be exceeded under concurrency) is not covered. Add a test that fans out many concurrent CreateOrUpdateDevice calls with distinct DeviceIDs against a small deviceLimit and asserts the final CountDevices is <= deviceLimit.

title: Returning-device behavior at the limit and expired-device behavior are untested
body: Two important behaviors of the new limit are not covered: (1) an existing device whose ID is already in the table should still be updatable when CountDevices == deviceLimit (the happy-path 'returning user' case), and (2) a device whose updated_at is older than the 30-day window but whose row has not yet been cleaned up should still be allowed back. Case (2) currently returns ErrDeviceLimitReached (see related bug finding) and has no test to catch it. Add tests for both scenarios.

title: New auth.anonymous.device_limit option has no documentation update
body: The PR introduces a new user-facing configuration option `auth.anonymous.device_limit` (read in readAuthSettings) and surfaces it to the frontend as `anonymousDeviceLimit` / `AnonymousDeviceLimit`. The PR description leaves the docs checklist unchecked and the diff contains no documentation changes (no conf/defaults.ini updates, no What's New entry, no docs/ changes). Operators have no way to learn the option exists, its semantics, the default (0 = unlimited), or the behavior when the limit is reached.

title: Device limit bypassed on retry via local cache
body: In tagDeviceUI the local cache entry is set on line 87 with a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{}) BEFORE the CreateOrUpdateDevice DB call. When the device limit is reached and that DB call returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, the cache entry is already populated. Any subsequent request from the same client within the 29-minute cache TTL hits the cache (line 83), returns nil immediately, and Authenticate proceeds — bypassing the limit entirely. The limit is therefore only enforced on the very first request for a given device ID; a single retry lets the user through. To actually enforce it, the cache must only be populated after a successful CreateOrUpdateDevice (or the cache key must encode the limit-reached state). This regression is introduced by the new ErrDeviceLimitReached path: the cache pattern was harmless before because all errors were swallowed.

title: TOCTOU race lets device count exceed the configured limit
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice performs CountDevices and then either updateDevice or an INSERT as two separate, non-atomic steps (lines 109-118 and the switch/INSERT at 120-153). Under concurrent anonymous authentications many goroutines can each observe count < deviceLimit, all proceed to insert, and the resulting count can exceed deviceLimit by the concurrency level. This defeats the stated purpose of the feature — the limit is not a hard cap but only an approximate one, and a burst of legitimate users (or a small attacker) can inflate the table well past it. Wrap the check and write in a single transaction (or use a serializable isolation level / advisory lock) so the limit is enforced atomically.

title: Anonymous authentication now blocks synchronously on TagDevice DB writes
body: Previously TagDevice was called in a goroutine with a 2-minute context timeout, so Anonymous.Authenticate returned after one DB lookup (orgService.GetByName). The new code calls TagDevice synchronously at line 44, which internally runs CountDevices (SELECT COUNT(*)) plus an INSERT/UPDATE on anon_device on every anonymous request. Each anonymous authentication now performs 2-3 DB operations instead of 1, and any DB latency or contention is added to auth latency. For Grafana instances that expose anonymous dashboards to high traffic this is a serious performance and reliability regression. The async pattern should be kept; the limit decision can be propagated via a channel, or the CountDevices check alone can be made synchronous while the write stays async.

title: Device-limit failure surfaces as a bare sentinel error with no HTTP semantics
body: Anonymous.Authenticate returns the raw sentinel var ErrDeviceLimitReached = fmt.Errorf("device limit reached") (defined in anonstore/database.go line 18) at line 46, with no HTTP status code, no machine-readable code, and no user-facing message. The authn framework will propagate this as a generic authentication failure, almost certainly a 500/Internal-Server-Error-like response to the browser. Operators have no signal that the limit is the cause (they will see only generic auth-failure logs), and end users see no indication that they are hitting a configured cap versus a real outage. Wrap the sentinel in a typed error that carries a 429/503 status and a clear message, or convert it in the HTTP layer so the response makes the cause actionable.

title: updateDevice uses device.UpdatedAt as its time reference while CreateOrUpdateDevice uses time.Now()
body: In CreateOrUpdateDevice the 30-day window is built from time.Now().UTC() (line 110), but in updateDevice the WHERE bounds on updated_at are built from device.UpdatedAt.UTC() (lines 80-81). They happen to coincide today because TagDevice constructs the Device with UpdatedAt: time.Now() (impl.go line 141), but the two functions now disagree on what 'now' is. If a future caller passes a Device whose UpdatedAt is anything other than time.Now() (a replay, a clock-skew tolerance, a test fixture, a backfill, or simply a refactor), the updateDevice bounds will silently drift relative to the count window: a device that should be considered 'recent' by CreateOrUpdateDevice can be excluded by updateDevice and vice versa. Capture time.Now() once at the start of CreateOrUpdateDevice and pass it (or device.UpdatedAt derived from it) into updateDevice explicitly.

title: No test exercises the allowed update path of updateDevice at the limit
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a *new* device ID is rejected when the count has reached the limit. The crucial opposite case — a known device ID re-tags while the limit is reached and must be updated successfully via updateDevice — is not tested. This is the only path that uses updateDevice at all in this PR, and a regression that always returns ErrDeviceLimitReached (e.g., the WHERE bounds drifting to exclude every row, as flagged separately) would not be caught. Add a case with deviceLimit=1 that inserts device X, then calls CreateOrUpdateDevice with the same X again (optionally with a slightly different client_ip/user_agent) and asserts no error and that the row was actually updated.

title: Provider signature changes need a corresponding wire/DI regeneration
body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now takes sqlStore db.DB instead of anonstore.AnonStore (impl.go line 36), and ProvideAnonDBStore gained a new deviceLimit int64 parameter (anonstore/database.go line 52). The PR updates every direct caller it shows (impl.go and the *_test.go files) but does not include the wire-generated file(s) (e.g. wire_gen.go / providers.go / inject.go) that Grafana's wire setup regenerates from these provider signatures. Until those are regenerated the build will fail because the old ProvideAnonDBStore(store) and ProvideAnonymousDeviceService(..., anonStore, ...) calls no longer exist. Confirm the wire file is regenerated (or hand-updated) as part of this change; if it is intentionally omitted, the PR description should say so.

title: New auth.anonymous device_limit setting is not documented
body: setting.go adds cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit = anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0) under [auth.anonymous] at line 1650, but no documentation file is changed. The PR description itself leaves the 'docs are updated' checklist item unchecked. Operators have no reference for the new key, its default of 0 (= no limit), or its semantics (when the limit is reached, new anonymous device IDs are rejected while known devices can still re-tag). Add the key to the appropriate configuration reference (e.g. docs/sources/administration/configuration.md) and, if this is a notable improvement, link it from the What's New doc per the PR template.

title: Routine cleanup operations logged at Error level with nil errors
body: The new cleanup code logs every routine operation at Error level: r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err) and r.log.Error("cleaned annotations by time", "count", len(ids), "affected", x, "err", y). Cleanup runs as a background job that should never be considered an error; previously this code did not log at all. The "err" field is always nil at these sites (errors are returned early), so the messages convey no actionable signal but will spam the error log on every cycle, making real errors harder to find and tripping error-rate alerts in monitoring. The level should be Info or Debug, and the meaningless "err" field should be removed.

title: Full annotation IDs and full WHERE condition dumped into logs on every batch
body: Each batch emits "ids", ids (the entire int64 slice) and the raw SQL condition into the log. With AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize set in the tens of thousands (the new test case uses 32767), this produces extremely verbose log entries on every cycle. Logging thousands of integers is not useful and increases log volume/cost; an only the count and a truncated identifier (or none) should be logged.

title: Cleanup ticker frequency silently changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The diff changes the cleanup ticker from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`, a 10x increase in how often the entire cleanup job (including annotation cleanup, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, user invites, short URLs and query history) runs. This change is not mentioned in the PR description and is unrelated to the deadlock fix. It will significantly increase database query load and log volume (especially given the new Error-level logging above) on every Grafana instance. Either it should be reverted, made configurable, or at minimum called out in the PR description / release notes.

title: Annotation cleanup tests now skipped under -short
body: The tests `TestAnnotationCleanUp` and `TestOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst` have been renamed to `TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp` and `TestIntegrationOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst` and now call `t.Skip` when `testing.Short()` is true. Previously these tests always ran. Any developer or CI step that runs `go test -short ./pkg/services/annotations/...` will lose coverage of the new split-statement cleanup logic (including the SQLite 32767-batch path that was added). If the intent is to keep this as a required test, the skip should be removed or the package should ensure integration tests are always run in CI.

title: O(n^2) string concatenation when inlining IDs into SQLite DELETE
body: In `deleteByIDs`, when SQLite is used with a batch size greater than 999 the IDs are concatenated into a single SQL string via repeated `fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)`. This is O(n^2) in the number of IDs and, with the new default-style batch size of 32767 (and tests using batch sizes in that range), produces hundreds of thousands of intermediate string allocations per batch. Using `strings.Builder` (or `strings.Join` after pre-formatting) would be linear and cheaper.

title: Stale/incorrect "condition must be supplied" error message
body: `fetchIDs` checks `if condition == ""` and returns `fmt.Errorf("condition must be supplied; cannot fetch IDs from entire table")`, but `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` passes a non-empty condition that begins with `NOT EXISTS (...)` followed directly by the LIMIT clause with no `WHERE` keyword. The error message implies a missing WHERE clause would result in a full-table SELECT, but the guard will still fire whenever any caller forgets to prepend a WHERE. This is a minor wording/logic mismatch and could mask a real bug in future callers; the message should describe the actual invariant (e.g., "condition cannot be empty") or be removed in favor of a real precondition.

title: Routine cleanup progress logged at Error level
body:
In the new CleanAnnotations/CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags code, routine informational messages are logged with r.log.Error even on success. For example:
```
r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err)
...
r.log.Error("cleaned annotations by time", "count", len(ids), "affected", x, "err", y)
```
These messages are emitted on the happy path (the call to fetchIDs has already returned a non-nil error short-circuit before the first Error log is reached, and deleteByIDs returns success in the second). Error-level logging is reserved for actual failures, and using it for normal per-batch progress will spam production logs, trip log-based alerting, and obscure real errors. These should be r.log.Info or r.log.Debug.

title: Nil error logged as err field on success
body: Multiple new log calls include `"err", err` after the error has already been checked and returned (e.g. lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579). On the happy path err is nil, so the resulting structured log entry looks like `"err": null` for a successful batch. This is misleading to operators who scan logs for `"err":` fields and makes it look like every cleanup batch is failing. The err key should only be included when an error is actually present.

title: Undocumented 10x ticker frequency change affects all cleanup jobs
body:
The cleanup ticker is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute:
```
- ticker := time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)
+ ticker := time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)
```
This is not mentioned in the PR description and is unrelated to the MySQL deadlock fix. It increases the run frequency of *every* job in clean() (tmp files, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, annotations, user invites, short URLs, query history) by 10x, multiplying DB load and the chance of overlapping long-running cleanups against the 9-minute per-cycle timeout. If the change is intentional (e.g. to compensate for accumulation during the deadlock period), it needs its own justification, and the PR description and release notes must call it out so operators can adjust. Ideally the cleanup interval should be configurable rather than hard-coded.

title: O(n^2) string building in SQLite large-batch path
body:
The SQLite parameter-limit workaround builds the IN-list with repeated fmt.Sprintf:
```
values := fmt.Sprint(ids[0])
for _, v := range ids[1:] {
    values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)
}
```
This is O(n^2) in both time and allocations because each step copies the entire growing string. With the batch size used in the new test (32767) this is tens of millions of bytes copied. The same job can be done in O(n) with a strings.Builder and strconv.AppendInt. The path is also only triggered when batch size exceeds the SQLite parameter limit, so it is exercised by the new integration test and the cost matters.

title: fetchIDs concatenates table name and condition into SQL
body:
fetchIDs builds SQL via fmt.Sprintf with the table name and the WHERE clause as opaque strings:
```
sql := fmt.Sprintf(`SELECT id FROM %s`, table)
sql += fmt.Sprintf(` WHERE %s`, condition)
```
Today every call site passes a constant string so there is no immediate injection, but the signature invites future callers to pass user-controlled fragments. Either make the table an enumerated constant or compose the predicate through bound parameters, so the function cannot be misused.

title: Routine cleanup info logged at Error level
body: The new code in CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags uses r.log.Error for messages that describe normal operation, e.g. 'Annotations to clean by time', 'cleaned annotations by time', 'Annotations to clean by count', 'cleaned annotations by count', 'Tags to clean', 'cleaned tags'. These fire on every successful cleanup batch and are not errors. Using Error level will pollute error monitoring/dashboards (anything watching for Error-level entries will be noisy/alarmed) and may cause on-call pages. The 'err' key is also always passed in, even when err is nil. These should be r.log.Info or r.log.Debug. Logging every ID at error level also risks leaking IDs into permanent error stores.

title: annotationType interpolated into SQL without validation
body: In CleanAnnotations, the annotationType argument is interpolated directly into the WHERE clause via fmt.Sprintf: cond := fmt.Sprintf(`%s AND created < %v ORDER BY id DESC %s`, annotationType, cutoffDate, ...). annotationType is an interface-typed string parameter with no allow-list or validation in fetchIDs; any caller passing untrusted input gets a SQL injection. This pattern was inherited from the old code but is now reused via fetchIDs which itself does fmt.Sprintf(` WHERE %s`, condition). At minimum the helpers should reject table/condition values that don't match an expected allow-list or constant set (e.g. alertAnnotationType, dashboardAnnotationType, apiAnnotationType), or the SQL should be composed with bound parameters instead of string formatting.

title: O(n^2) string building in SQLite inline-id path
body: In deleteByIDs, when running on SQLite with a batch size > 999, the code builds the IN-list by repeatedly calling fmt.Sprintf('%s, %d', values, v) inside a loop. Each iteration allocates a new string of length O(i), giving O(n^2) work and O(n^2) intermediate allocations. For a batch of 32767 IDs this is on the order of a billion character copies. Use strings.Builder or a single fmt.Sprintf with a precomputed separator, or strings.Join over strconv formatted values. The new integration test exercises exactly this path with 32767 IDs, so the cost will show up in CI and any production SQLite deployment configured with a large batch size.

title: deleteByIDs chooses inlined SQL by configured batch size, not actual id count
body: deleteByIDs switches to the inlined-SQL branch when r.db.GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite && r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit. The branch should depend on len(ids), not on the configured batch size: if the operator has set a large batch size but a particular batch returns only a handful of ids (common when there are few rows left to clean), we still go down the inlined-SQL path and pay the O(n^2) cost for no benefit. Conversely, if the operator mis-configures AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize to be small (<= 999) while the actual returned ids somehow exceed that (e.g. via a future change), we would silently use the parameterized path and potentially exceed SQLite's parameter limit. Use len(ids) > sqliteParameterLimit as the gate.

title: Cleanup ticker shortened from 10 minutes to 1 minute, unrelated to deadlock fix
body: The ticker was changed from time.Minute * 10 to time.Minute * 1 with no comment and no relation to the MySQL deadlock being addressed. This is a 10x increase in how often the cleanup job runs, and combined with this PR's split-into-two-statements change each cleanup now performs roughly 2x more DB round trips per batch. On large annotation tables this can substantially increase database load, lock contention, and log volume. The 9-minute cleanup context timeout also means a single slow run (made slower by the new strategy) is much more likely to be cancelled. This belongs in its own PR with justification, or at least a comment explaining the rationale, and ideally should be configurable rather than a hard-coded 1-minute default.

title: SELECT-then-DELETE allows under-deletion with concurrent writes
body: After fetching the ids, the delete runs in a separate statement and separate session. A concurrent transaction can insert new annotations that satisfy the same cleanup predicate (MaxAge cutoff or MaxCount offset) between fetch and delete; those new rows will not be in the fetched id set and so will not be deleted this cycle. The author documented this as 'may under-delete... any such annotations will simply be cleaned on the next cycle', which is acceptable, but the test suite does not exercise this scenario (no concurrent inserter) and there is no log/instrumentation that would let an operator detect persistent under-deletion. Worth noting so it isn't quietly relied on as exact enforcement.

title: t.Cleanup uses assert.NoError, failures don't terminate subsequent subtests
body: The new per-subtest t.Cleanup deletes annotation and annotation_tag rows via session.Exec and then calls assert.NoError(t, err). assert.NoError only records t.Error and does not call t.FailNow, so if the DELETE silently fails (e.g., a SQL error in a future schema change), the next subtest will run against leftover data and produce confusing failures rather than failing at the cleanup site. Use require.NoError inside the cleanup so a failure surfaces immediately. Also, the subtests share the same fakeSQL but rely on sequential DELETE before the next subtest creates ids starting from 1; a missed cleanup causes primary-key conflicts on subsequent InsertMulti.

title: New SQLite large-batch test is slow and may run unconditionally
body: The new subtest 'should not fail if batch size is larger than SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER for SQLite >= 3.32.0' creates 40003 annotations and 80006 annotation_tags, then performs a multi-batch cleanup. createTestAnnotations uses InsertMulti in batches of 500, so this requires ~80 annotation batches and ~161 tag batches, plus several cleanup cycles. This is fine on developer laptops but will add noticeable seconds to every CI run on this package. There is no t.Skip on this case and the assertion (40000 affected) depends on the exact i%3 split working out, which is fragile if the createTestAnnotations layout changes. Consider a smaller number or guarding it behind a build tag.

title: Renamed tests now require a real database even for unit-style runs
body: The previously-in-package TestAnnotationCleanUp and TestOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst were renamed to TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp and TestIntegrationOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst and gained a t.Skip on testing.Short(). The earlier versions ran unconditionally and provided coverage of the cleanup SQL; the new versions are gated on a long mode and require the InitTestDB infra. There is no replacement test that covers the SQL composition (the cond strings, the annotationType interpolation, the MaxCount offset arithmetic) without a DB, and no test that specifically asserts the deadlock-avoidance split (id fetch + separate delete) is exercised. At minimum a table-driven unit test verifying the constructed cond strings and the Limit/LimitOffset substitution for each dialect would prevent silent regressions to the SQL the PR is trying to fix.

title: Wrong metric function in Create error path
body: When `d.Storage.Create` returns an error, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` even though the failure is on the unified storage side. This mislabels storage failures as legacy failures in the metrics, polluting dashboards/alerts built on `dual_writer_*` metrics. The call should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` to match the symmetric success branch on line 48.

title: Wrong metric function in Update error path
body: When `d.Storage.Update` returns an error, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` even though this is a storage failure, not a legacy one. The success branch on line 132 correctly uses `recordStorageDuration`. The error branch should do the same: `d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. Otherwise storage Update failures are silently misattributed to legacy.

title: Wrong metric function in DeleteCollection async legacy block
body: The async goroutine for the legacy `DeleteCollection` records the result via `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)`. This is the legacy call, so it should be `d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` (matching the corresponding calls in Create/Update/Delete). The current code will mislabel legacy failures as storage failures, breaking SLO dashboards.

title: Delete uses d.Log instead of log with structured fields
body: In `Delete`, `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` is used, while Create/Update/DeleteCollection/DeleteCollection all use `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)` where `log` includes `name`, `kind`, and `method` fields. As a result, any klog calls inside `Storage.Delete` (or inside the async legacy `Delete`) won't carry the structured `kind=`, `method=delete`, `name=` context, making it harder to filter logs by operation. Also, the async legacy `Delete` goroutine inherits this weaker logger (it references the outer `ctx`) so legacy delete errors logged downstream will be missing context too.

title: Kind label uses object name instead of options.Kind in Delete
body: The Delete success branch records `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` where the third argument is the resource `name` parameter, while every other call site uses `options.Kind`. The metric label is supposed to be the Kind, so this passes a different value into the same label, producing inconsistent time series in the dual_writer_* metrics.

title: Async legacy writes inherit cancelled request context
body: Each async legacy call derives its context from the incoming `ctx` via `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`. When the API caller cancels or times out, the parent `ctx` is already cancelled, so the child context is cancelled immediately and the legacy write never happens. The PR description frames legacy writes as a "safe measure" to keep legacy store in sync, but under request cancellation (which is common for slow upstream) the legacy side will drift from unified storage silently. The async legacy write should be derived from a non-cancelled context (e.g. `context.Background()` with timeout) so it survives caller disconnection.

title: Async legacy failures are not logged
body: Inside the goroutines that perform the asynchronous legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection, the only signal on failure is the metrics counter (`recordLegacyDuration(... true ...)`); there is no `log.Error(...)` call. If unified storage diverges from legacy (the very thing mode 3 is supposed to mitigate), operators will see no log line and no test will detect the failure because errors are swallowed. Add `log.Error(err, "async legacy ... failed")` (or equivalent) inside each goroutine after the legacy call.

title: Mode3 tests do not verify the asynchronous legacy writes
body: Mode 3's defining behaviour is that writes go to storage synchronously and then to legacy asynchronously. None of `TestMode3_Create`, `TestMode3_Update`, `TestMode3_Delete`, or `TestMode3_DeleteCollection` actually asserts the legacy mock was called. `setupLegacyFn` sets up `m.On(...)` expectations but there is no `m.AssertExpectations(t)` (and the async goroutine may run after the test function returns). The Create and Update tests register legacy expectations that may simply never be exercised, and the Delete/DeleteCollection tests don't even register them. Without synchronization (e.g. wait group, channel, or retry on the mock) plus `AssertExpectations`, a regression that removes the async legacy call entirely would still pass the test suite.

title: Mode3 read tests do not verify legacy is bypassed
body: The PR's stated semantics for mode 3 are: "reads (get, list): only use unified storage". `TestMode3_Get` and `TestMode3_List` never call `ls.AssertNotCalled(t, "Get", ...)` / `ls.AssertNotCalled(t, "List", ...)`. The Mode1 Get test does check this for storage (`us.AssertNotCalled(...)`); the analogous assertion for mode 3 (legacy must not be called) is missing. A bug that silently falls back to legacy on reads would not be caught.

title: TestMode3_Get creates a local prometheus registry
body: `TestMode3_Get` calls `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` locally even though a package-level `p` already exists (used by every other test in the file, and now exclusively by `TestMode1_Get` after this PR). The local registry is unused by the assertions in the test and just creates inconsistency. Use the package-level `p` like the rest of the suite.

title: Destroy does not wait for in-flight async legacy writes
body: `Destroy` calls `d.Storage.Destroy()` and `d.Legacy.Destroy()` immediately, but there is no synchronization with the goroutines launched by Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection. If a shutdown happens while async legacy writes are still pending (within their 10 s timeout), they will run against destroyed backends, producing confusing errors or panics. Consider tracking the goroutines with a `sync.WaitGroup` (or similar) and waiting for them in `Destroy` (with a bounded timeout).

title: DeleteCollection records storage metric for legacy call
body: In the DeleteCollection async goroutine, `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` is called after `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection(...)`. It should be `d.recordLegacyDuration` because the call is to LegacyStorage, not Storage. As written, every legacy delete-collection failure will be misattributed to Storage in metrics, defeating monitoring and SLO alerting on the legacy path.

title: Create error path records legacy metric using storage timer
body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. Two problems: (1) it records a legacy duration even though the legacy was never called; (2) the duration it computes is for Storage (startStorage), not Legacy. Should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. The same bug exists for Update on line 129. Effect: storage failures will be miscounted as legacy failures and the recorded duration will not correspond to the failing call.

title: Update error path records legacy metric using storage timer
body: When `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. Same issue as the Create error path: this should be `d.recordStorageDuration` because the error happened in Storage, and the timer being measured (`startStorage`) corresponds to Storage, not Legacy. Storage update failures will be misattributed to the legacy path in metrics.

title: Async legacy write derives context from cancelled request context
body: All four async goroutines (Create, Update, Delete, DeleteCollection) build their timeout context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the request context (`klog.NewContext(ctx, log)` from the outer function). When the originating HTTP handler returns, the request context is cancelled and the derived context is immediately cancelled as well, so the 10s timeout is effectively zero. The whole point of mode 3 is to mirror writes to legacy as a safety net; with a cancelled parent context this safety net is dropped on every request that returns before the goroutine schedules. The legacy-mirror call should be made independent of request lifetime (e.g., derive from a long-lived background context) so that the write actually completes after the response is sent.

title: Same objInfo reused for Storage and Legacy Update calls
body: `objInfo` is passed to `d.Storage.Update` and then, in the goroutine, to `d.Legacy.Update` unchanged. `rest.UpdatedObjectInfo` implementations are commonly stateful (the previous version of this file explicitly wrapped it in `updateWrapper` and supplied a fresh wrapper holding the updated object for the legacy call). Reusing objInfo risks the legacy update either re-fetching the pre-update object, returning stale data, or returning an error from the second `UpdatedObject` invocation. This is a behavioural regression from the prior implementation in this same function.

title: Async legacy goroutines have no panic recovery
body: The four `go func()` blocks (Create, Update, Delete, DeleteCollection) call into legacy storage and record metrics without any panic recovery. A panic inside the legacy storage adapter or in the metric call will crash the process because Go panics in unrecovered goroutines are fatal. Each goroutine should at minimum `defer recover()` and log the recovered value so that a single failing legacy backend cannot bring down the API server.

title: Delete records storage metric with name as kind label
body: In Delete, the success-path metric is `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`. All other methods use `options.Kind` as the third argument (the resource-kind label). Passing `name` here will produce a different label cardinality and break any dashboard or alert that aggregates by kind for delete operations. It should be `options.Kind` to be consistent with Create/Update/DeleteCollection and with the legacy-error metric on line 113.

title: Delete sets klog context with d.Log instead of enriched log
body: Create/Get/List/Update/DeleteCollection all do `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, log)` using the `log` variable enriched via `WithValues("name", ..., "kind", ..., "method", ...)`. Delete instead does `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`, so any subsequent log line (including the legacy call inside the goroutine) loses the request-scoped "name"/"kind"/"method" values, making debugging harder. It should use the enriched `log` variable.

title: defer cancel() placed after side-effecting line in Update goroutine
body: In the Update goroutine, `defer cancel()` is placed between `startLegacy := time.Now()` and the `d.Legacy.Update` call. While functionally correct (defer runs at function exit), it is stylistically inconsistent with the Create/Delete/DeleteCollection goroutines, which put `defer cancel()` immediately after the `context.WithTimeoutCause` call. Easy fix: move the deferred cancel directly under the WithTimeoutCause call.

title: Legacy mirror timeout is a hardcoded magic number
body: `time.Second*10` appears as the timeout for the legacy-mirror context in Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection. This should be a configurable constant (or a field on DualWriterMode3) so it can be tuned per resource type and tested; otherwise changing it requires editing four call sites.

title: TestMode3_Get uses local prometheus registry instead of shared one
body: Only `TestMode3_Get` creates its own registry with `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()`. Every other TestMode3_* test uses the package-level `p`. The dual-writer change in `dualwriter_mode1_test.go` removed the same leftover in mode1, but the corresponding cleanup was missed in `TestMode3_Get`. Use the shared `p` for consistency and to avoid duplicate registries across tests.

title: Tests do not verify async legacy write actually occurred
body: In TestMode3_Create, TestMode3_Update, TestMode3_Delete and TestMode3_DeleteCollection the legacy call is dispatched in a goroutine after the request returns, but the test only asserts on the synchronous return value. There is no synchronization (no WaitGroup, channel, or `m.AssertExpectations`) to ensure the legacy mock was actually invoked before the test exits. A regression where the goroutine no longer runs (e.g., refactor that accidentally makes the legacy call synchronous-but-skipped) would pass these tests silently. Add a synchronization mechanism (e.g., a `sync.WaitGroup` toggled in the goroutine, or use a channel signaled by a mock callback) and call `m.AssertExpectations(t)` to assert the legacy side effect actually happened.

title: TestMode3_Create failure case sets up the wrong store's mock
body: The second test case in TestMode3_Create is named "error when creating object in the unified store fails" and expects `wantErr: true`, but the expectation is registered via `setupLegacyFn` against the legacy store. Because the test wires both `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` to the same `mock.Mock{}`, the expectation ends up firing on whichever call runs first (the storage call), so the test happens to pass for the wrong reason. If the two mocks are ever given separate mock instances, this case will silently flip to passing on the legacy path and the error will be swallowed by the async goroutine. Either rename the case or register the expectation against the storage mock explicitly.

title: Storage error path records legacy metric instead of storage metric
body: In Create, when d.Storage.Create returns an error, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage). No legacy call has been made yet; this is the storage call that failed. The metric labels the failure as a legacy failure, polluting dualWriterMetrics and making alerts/dashboards for legacy health incorrect.
