body: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch(), `safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` is called OUTSIDE the try/except block. Network errors, DNS failures, connection timeouts, or GitHub returning 5xx will raise an exception and produce a generic 500 error page instead of the user-friendly error page rendered by the `error()` helper. The try/except block below only covers `safe_urlread`, `decode`, and `parse_qsl` failures. The same applies to `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` at line 434 — any exception there will also bubble up as a 500. Both calls should be wrapped so transient failures degrade gracefully.

title: OAuth authorize URL parameters not URL-encoded
body: The OAuth authorize URL is built via f-string interpolation: `f"{...}?client_id={github_client_id}&state={state}&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}"`. Neither `state` (currently `pipeline.signature`, an md5 hex digest, so safe today) nor `redirect_uri` is URL-encoded. If `redirect_uri` ever contains reserved characters (`&`, `?`, `=`, `#`, etc.), or if `pipeline.signature` generation changes, GitHub will parse the query string incorrectly and the OAuth callback state verification will fail or — worse — allow query parameters to bleed into `state`/`redirect_uri`. Use `urllib.parse.urlencode` for the query string.

title: test_installation_not_found doesn't exercise the 404 path
body: The test is named `test_installation_not_found` and stubs `/app/installations/{installation_id}` to return 404, but the assertion only checks for the generic "Invalid installation request." string. Tracing the flow: the first request to `setup_path` with `installation_id` triggers OAuthLoginView, which redirects to GitHub (no call to the 404 endpoint). The second request carries a hardcoded `state` of `ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05` that does NOT match the pipeline signature, so OAuthLoginView short-circuits on the state check and returns `error()` before `build_integration` is ever reached. The 404 stub is never hit. The test silently passes for the wrong reason. To actually test the 404 path, the state must match the pipeline signature (e.g., capture it from the redirect on the first request, like other tests do indirectly via `assert_setup_flow`).

title: Hardcoded HMAC signature will mismatch the modified body
body: In `test_github_user_mismatch` the webhook is posted with the hardcoded header `HTTP_X_HUB_SIGNATURE="sha1=d184e6717f8bfbcc291ebc8c0756ee446c6c9486"`, but the request body is `json.dumps(webhook_event)` after the test mutates `installation.id` and `sender.login`. That HMAC was presumably computed over the unmodified `INSTALLATION_EVENT_EXAMPLE` bytes. Standard GitHub webhook handlers verify the signature against the raw request body and reject mismatches (typically with a 401/403). When the handler rejects the webhook, no `Integration` record with `sender.login == "attacker"` is created, and the subsequent user-mismatch check in `GitHubInstallation` won't fire as intended. Either compute the signature dynamically from the mutated payload using the test webhook secret, or fix the signature for the actual bytes posted. This test should currently be failing or is silently broken.

title: No tests for the new OAuth error branches
body: OAuthLoginView introduces four new error branches that all funnel into the same `error()` helper and are therefore indistinguishable to callers: (1) `state` parameter mismatch, (2) GitHub returning no `access_token` in the token-exchange response, (3) `get_user_info` returning no `login`, and (4) the GitHubInstallation-level user mismatch (which is tested but only via the generic template assertion). Each of these is a distinct failure mode documented in the PR description ("state mismatch", "wrong or re-used code", "authenticate user mismatch") and should have a dedicated test that verifies the request reaches the expected code path and that the failure is rendered. The current `test_github_user_mismatch` only asserts `b"Invalid installation request."` and doesn't distinguish user mismatch from a state or token failure.

title: OAuth scope not requested, but no scope validation either
body: OAuthLoginView does not include a `scope` parameter when redirecting to GitHub's authorize URL. The access token returned will have only the default user:email scope (or whatever GitHub grants by default). `get_user_info` only uses `/user`, which works under the default scope, but if Sentry ever tries to use the resulting token for anything requiring an additional scope (e.g., reading private email, listing org installations), the request will silently 404/403. This is informational; consider either requesting the scopes Sentry actually needs explicitly (`scope=user:email read:org`), or documenting that only the default user-scope token is intended.

title: KeyError possible if Integration has no 'sender' in metadata
body: In GitHubInstallation.dispatch the user-mismatch check reads `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`. Existing Integration rows created before this PR shipped (or rows created via paths that don't populate `sender`, e.g., legacy migrations) will have no `sender` key in `metadata`, raising `KeyError` and surfacing a 500 instead of the intended error page. The check should be guarded — e.g., treat a missing `sender` as a failed validation (`return error(...)`) or use `.get()` with a default. Otherwise the new security check will break upgrades.

title: safe_urlopen exception not caught, 500 errors on transient GitHub OAuth failures
body: OAuthLoginView's try/except wraps safe_urlread and parse_qsl, but the preceding safe_urlopen call to GitHub's OAuth access token endpoint is outside the try block. If GitHub's endpoint is unreachable, times out, or returns a non-2xx status, safe_urlopen raises and the user receives a 500 error rather than the graceful 'Invalid installation request.' page. Move safe_urlopen inside the try block so transient GitHub outages don't break all installations.

title: KeyError risk on integration.metadata['sender'] when sender is absent
body: The user-mismatch check does integration.metadata['sender']['login'], which raises KeyError if 'sender' is missing from the metadata. build_integration only sets metadata['sender'] if state.get('sender') is truthy, so integrations created via build_integration directly (e.g., when the webhook hasn't arrived in time) lack this key. The result is a 500 error instead of the intended graceful error page. Use safe access: integration.metadata.get('sender', {}).get('login').

title: OAuth authorize URL built with raw f-string instead of URL-encoded parameters
body: The redirect URL is constructed with f-string concatenation: f'{ghip.get_oauth_authorize_url()}?client_id={github_client_id}&state={state}&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}'. If any value contains URL-special characters (&, =, %, ?, #, etc.) the URL is malformed. While current values appear URL-safe, this is fragile. Use urllib.parse.urlencode for robust URL construction.

title: TOCTOU race allows user-mismatch check to be bypassed when webhook is delayed
body: The user-mismatch check runs only if the Integration record already exists (which is created by the GitHub installation webhook). If the webhook hasn't been processed by the time the user reaches GitHubInstallation, Integration.DoesNotExist is raised and pipeline.next_step() runs without verifying the sender. build_integration then creates the Integration using only GitHub's installation API (which doesn't include the sender field), bypassing the check. The webhook typically arrives within seconds, but if delayed or skipped, an attacker who tricks a victim into completing OAuth can complete the integration in their own Sentry org using the victim's GitHub credentials.

title: test_installation_not_found never starts a pipeline, assertion cannot pass
body: The test issues two GETs to self.setup_path but never visits self.init_path to start the pipeline. PipelineAdvancerView will not find a pipeline in progress for either GET and will fall through to redirect to '/' with 'Invalid request' (added via messages.add_message), returning a 302 whose body does not contain 'Invalid installation request.'. The test as written cannot reach OAuthLoginView's state-mismatch error path. To exercise that path the test must first visit self.init_path (starting the pipeline with the default signature) before calling self.setup_path with a non-matching state.

title: Missing test coverage for several documented OAuth failure modes
body: The PR description lists three failure modes that lack explicit coverage: (1) state parameter mismatch, (2) GitHub rejecting the OAuth code (wrong or reused), (3) GitHub's /user endpoint not returning 'login'. The only failure case tested is the user mismatch. Tests for state mismatch (once test_installation_not_found is fixed), reused/invalid codes, /user error responses, and missing 'login' would help lock in the new validation behavior.

title: AssignmentSource.queued default is evaluated once at class definition, not per instance
body: The field `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a plain dataclass default, so `timezone.now()` is called exactly once at class body evaluation (i.e. at module import time) and the resulting `datetime` is reused as the default for every instance that does not override it. As a result, two `AssignmentSource` objects constructed at different times will share the same `queued` timestamp, defeating the apparent purpose of the field (recording when the source was queued/created) and producing misleading data in any log line, analytics event, or future debugging code that uses `queued`. The fix is to use a per-instance factory: `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)` (with `from dataclasses import field`). The existing `test_to_dict` only asserts `queued is not None`, so it does not catch this regression.

title: No test for deassign cycle prevention, only assign is covered
body: The PR adds `test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration` to verify that `GroupAssignee.objects.assign` does not call `sync_assignee_outbound` when the assignment source equals the target integration. The symmetric path, `GroupAssignee.objects.deassign` invoked from `sync_group_assignee_inbound(..., assign=False)`, now also accepts an `assignment_source` and propagates it through `sync_group_assignee_outbound`, but there is no test asserting `mock_sync_assignee_outbound.assert_not_called()` for the deassign case. Because both code paths were changed in this PR, both should be covered to prevent the same loop being reintroduced on unassign flows.

title: Typo in test method name: 'inalid' should be 'invalid'
body: The test is named `test_from_dict_inalid_data`, which is a misspelling of 'invalid'. This will make the test harder to discover when searching for invalid-input coverage and is a small but clear documentation defect in the test file.

title: AssignmentSource.queued default is evaluated once at class definition, not per instance
body: The field declaration `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` causes `timezone.now()` to be evaluated exactly once when the class body is executed (at module import time), not each time an `AssignmentSource` is constructed. Every instance created in the same process — including those produced by `AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration)` during inbound webhooks — will share the same `queued` timestamp (the time the module was first imported). For a long-running web server this means `queued` is effectively a process start time, not the time the assignment was queued. The field is part of the serialized payload (`to_dict`/`from_dict`) and is clearly meant to record when the change was queued, so any future logic that relies on it (staleness checks, ordering, debugging) will be wrong. The fix is to use `field(default_factory=lambda: timezone.now())` from `dataclasses`.

title: test_to_dict does not verify queued is per-instance and would not catch the mutable-default bug
body: The test only asserts `result.get("queued") is not None`, which is trivially true even when every instance shares the same timestamp (the `queued` field is never None because it was populated at class definition). A stronger assertion — e.g. creating two `AssignmentSource` instances with a small `time.sleep` between them and verifying their `queued` values differ — would catch the dataclass default-evaluation bug. As written, the test gives a false sense of coverage for the `queued` field's semantics.

title: Typo in test method name: 'inalid' should be 'invalid'
body: The test method is named `test_from_dict_inalid_data`. The word 'inalid' is a typo for 'invalid'. This makes the test harder to find by name and looks unprofessional in test reports.

title: No test for deassign cycle prevention (matching source integration)
body: The new test `test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration` only exercises the assign path when the source integration matches the target. The deassign path in `GroupAssigneeManager.deassign` also threads `assignment_source` through to `sync_group_assignee_outbound`, and the `should_sync` cycle check applies to both assign and deassign, but there is no `test_assignee_sync_outbound_unassign_with_matching_source_integration` (or equivalent) verifying that `sync_assignee_outbound` is NOT called when `deassign` is invoked with a matching source. Without this, a regression in the deassign wiring (e.g. dropping the `assignment_source` kwarg) would not be caught.

title: `AssignmentSource.queued` default is captured once at class definition, not per instance
body: The default `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated a single time when the dataclass body is executed (module import time). Every `AssignmentSource` instantiated without explicitly passing `queued` therefore shares the same stale timestamp from import. To get a per-instance timestamp, declare the field with `field(default_factory=lambda: timezone.now())`. The field is unused by current logic, so the bug is latent, but it will surface the moment `queued` is read for ordering, display, or diagnostics.

title: `from_dict` does not validate field types; type coercion can defeat the cycle check
body: `cls(**input_dict)` relies on dataclass `__init__`, which does not enforce the declared type annotations. If `assignment_source_dict` is deserialized by a JSON-based serializer (Celery or otherwise), `integration_id` will arrive as a string and be stored as a string. The downstream comparison `sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id` then compares a string to an int and is always False in Python, so the cycle-blocking guard in `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync` never trips. The `try/except (ValueError, TypeError)` only catches unexpected kwargs / bad dataclass values, not silent type coercion. Validate types (e.g. `isinstance(input_dict.get('integration_id'), int)`) before constructing the dataclass, and reject the input by returning `None` if the cast fails.

title: `test_to_dict` does not verify that `queued` is approximately the current time
body: The test only asserts `result.get('queued') is not None`, which passes even though `queued` is the module-import timestamp (because `timezone.now()` was captured once at class definition). The test should bracket `queued` between two `timezone.now()` calls (e.g. `assert before <= source.queued <= after`) so the latent default-factory bug is caught.

title: Typo in test method name: `inalid` should be `invalid`
body: The method `test_from_dict_inalid_data` has a clear spelling mistake. Rename to `test_from_dict_invalid_data` so the test reads correctly and is discoverable.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler cannot be instantiated
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now an empty `pass` body inheriting from StatefulDetectorHandler, but StatefulDetectorHandler declares `build_occurrence_and_event_data` as an @abc.abstractmethod (newly added in this PR). Because GroupType.detector_handler = MetricAlertDetectorHandler, the `detector_handler` property on the Detector model does `group_type.detector_handler(self)` and will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract method build_occurrence_and_event_data` (along with `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, and `get_group_key_values`, which are also unimplemented). This is a regression introduced by adding the abstract hook without providing any concrete implementation for the only concrete subclass in the codebase.

title: evaluate docstring still describes list return
body: The PR changed `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` to return `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]` but the docstring still reads: 'Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`. There will be one result for each group key result in the packet, unless the evaluation is skipped due to various rules.' Update the wording to describe the dict keyed by `DetectorGroupKey` so consumers reading the abstract method's contract aren't misled.

title: PriorityLevel(new_status) relies on enum values matching across modules
body: `evaluate_group_key_value` computes `new_status: DetectorPriorityLevel` and then calls `self.build_occurrence_and_event_data(group_key, value, PriorityLevel(new_status))`, converting a `sentry.workflow_engine.types.DetectorPriorityLevel` member into a `sentry.types.group.PriorityLevel` member. These are two distinct enums imported from different modules; if their integer values ever diverge, `PriorityLevel(...)` will raise `ValueError` at runtime, breaking all stateful detectors whenever a non-OK status fires. Either pass the detector-side enum directly through the hook (and let implementers convert), or assert a mapping in tests, so the conversion is explicit rather than relying on coincidental value parity.

title: test_state_results_multi_group uses wrong value for group_2
body: In `test_state_results_multi_group` the data packet is `{'dedupe': 2, 'group_vals': {'group_1': 6, 'group_2': 10}}`, but the second occurrence is built with `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(detector.detector_handler, 'group_2', 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)` — i.e. value=6 instead of 10. The test still passes because `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` ignores `value`, so it never validates that `build_occurrence_and_event_data` receives the per-group value. Use the correct 10 (or assert that the recorded mock was called with the correct value) so a regression that swaps or drops the value would be caught.

title: Stale TODO comment and silent breaking change to MetricAlertDetectorHandler
body: The TODO comment 'This will be a stateful detector when we build that abstraction' is now misleading: the class immediately below already extends StatefulDetectorHandler. More importantly, the previous implementation was a concrete class (it implemented `evaluate` returning `[]`) and could be instantiated as `MetricAlertDetectorHandler(detector)`. The new body is just `pass`, and because StatefulDetectorHandler adds new abstract methods (`get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, `counter_names`, `build_occurrence_and_event_data`), the class is now abstract. Any code path that resolves `Detector.detector_handler` for a `MetricAlertFire` detector — e.g., `Detector.detector_handler` calling `group_type.detector_handler(self)` — will now raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler` instead of returning a no-op handler. Even though the TODO claims the class 'won't be used yet', it is still wired up via `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler = MetricAlertDetectorHandler`, so the break is reachable. At minimum the stale TODO must be updated/removed; ideally the class should either remain concrete (with stub implementations of the new abstract methods) or the wiring in MetricAlertFire should be deferred.

title: test_state_results_multi_group passes wrong value to build_mock_occurrence_and_event for group_2
body: The data packet is built with `group_vals={'group_1': 6, 'group_2': 10}`, but the second call to `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` for `group_2` passes `6` as the value: `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(detector.detector_handler, 'group_2', 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)`. The value for `group_2` should be `10` to match the data packet. The test still passes today only because `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` ignores its `value` argument entirely (it never uses it when constructing the IssueOccurrence). As soon as the mock builder starts using the value (for example, putting it into evidence_data or event_data), this test will silently assert against a stale/wrong occurrence and could mask a real bug. The hard-coded `6` should be changed to `10`.

title: Behavior change to dict-keyed evaluate is not covered by tests
body: The PR description explicitly motivates the signature change: 'return a dict keyed by groupkey instead of a list. This helps avoid the chance of duplicate results for the same group key.' The previous test `test_state_results_multi_group_dupe` (which fed `group_keys=['dupe', 'dupe']` and asserted the duplicate-handling error) was deleted. However, no replacement test was added that exercises the new deduplication contract: e.g., a test where `get_group_key_values` returns a dict containing the same group_key mapped to multiple values, or where two iterations of `evaluate_group_key_value` would yield the same `result.group_key`. Without such coverage, the stated motivation of the change is not regression-protected, and any future revert to a list (or a bug where `result.group_key != input group_key`) would not be caught.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and will fail to instantiate
body: After this PR, MetricAlertDetectorHandler subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler but provides no implementations for its abstract methods (counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and the newly added build_occurrence_and_event_data). Python's ABC machinery will therefore mark MetricAlertDetectorHandler as abstract. Because MetricAlertFire declares `detector_handler = MetricAlertDetectorHandler`, and the Detector.detector_handler property invokes `group_type.detector_handler(self)`, instantiating a Detector whose GroupType is MetricAlertFire will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract methods ...`. Either implement stub abstract methods on MetricAlertDetectorHandler, or temporarily subclass DetectorHandler (or a non-abstract concrete base) until the abstraction is actually built out.

title: evaluate() docstring still describes a list return
body: The docstring on StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate says: 'Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`.' However the signature and body now produce `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`. Update the docstring to describe a dict keyed by group key, and ideally note that duplicate keys collapse to the last entry (so handlers should never emit more than one result per group_key).

title: evaluate_group_key_value() docstring omits None return path
body: The docstring states the method 'returns a `DetectorEvaluationResult` with the results and any state changes that need to be made', but the signature is `-> DetectorEvaluationResult | None` and the implementation returns None when the dedupe check fails and when `state_data.status == new_status`. The docstring should mention both early-return None cases so callers understand that a None return does not always indicate an error.

title: test_state_results_multi_group passes wrong value for group_2
body: The data packet is built with `{"group_1": 6, "group_2": 10}`, but `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(detector.detector_handler, "group_2", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)` is called with `value=6`. Because `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` ignores its `value` parameter when building the IssueOccurrence, the assertion succeeds regardless of which number is passed, and a regression that propagates an incorrect value into the occurrence would not be caught. Pass `value=10` (matching the data packet) and ideally include the value in the mock occurrence so future regressions surface.

title: Detector.group_type property is not cached
body: The new `group_type` property re-invokes `grouptype.registry.get_by_slug(self.type)` on every access. It is consumed both by the `detector_handler` property and by external callers (e.g., tests calling `handler.detector.group_type`). If `detector_handler` is read repeatedly in hot paths (e.g., once per data packet during evaluation), this adds avoidable registry lookups. Consider caching the result on the instance (e.g., via `self._group_type` populated from `self.type` at first access) so each detector instance resolves its group type at most once.

title: schedule_type display string never applied in monitor context
body: In get_monitor_environment_context, a local copy of monitor.config is built and `schedule_type` is overwritten with `get_schedule_type_display()`, but the returned dict uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` (the unmodified original) instead of the modified `config` local. The local `config` is therefore dead code and the human-readable schedule_type value never makes it into the event payload. In the Sentry UI for these monitor-incident events the schedule_type field will always show the raw enum value (e.g. "crontab") rather than the display string ("Crontab"). The returned dict should reference `config` (or simply not bother making the copy) for the override to take effect.

title: Unused logger in new module
body: `logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)` is defined at the top of incident_occurrence.py but is never referenced anywhere in the file. Since this is a newly created module, the dead import should be removed.

title: Unused logger in new module
body: `logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)` is defined at the top of incidents.py but is never referenced anywhere in the file. Since this is a newly created module, the dead import should be removed.

title: Typo in get_failure_reason docstring
body: The docstring reads "Builds a humam readible string from a list of failed check-ins." — should be "human readable". Pre-existing typo, but it was carried into the new module verbatim.

title: SimpleCheckIn moved without noting import-path break
body: The `SimpleCheckIn` TypedDict previously lived in `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` and was re-exported from there. It has been moved to `sentry.monitors.types` but the PR description does not call out the path break; any module that imports `SimpleCheckIn` from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` will fail with ImportError. The codebase should be searched for any such imports (and updated, or a re-export added in mark_failed for backward compatibility) before merging. The internal callers were updated, but nothing guarantees there are no other importers in the repo.

title: Pre-existing typo and misleading example in docstring
body: The docstring for get_failure_reason reads 'Builds a humam readible string from a list of failed check-ins.' It should be 'human readable'. Additionally, the third example 'A failed check-in was detected' does not correspond to any actual output produced by SINGULAR_HUMAN_FAILURE_MAP, which only returns 'An error check-in was detected', 'A missed check-in was detected', or 'A timeout check-in was detected'. Since this refactor moves the function into its own module (making the docstring a more prominent public surface), this is a good opportunity to fix the typo and align the example with real output.

title: Dead code: _create_process_for_shard method is never called
body: The _create_process_for_shard method (lines 127-132) is defined but never called. The _ensure_processes_alive method calls _create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards) directly, not _create_process_for_shard. This is dead code that should be removed or the call site should be updated to use it.

title: Inconsistent default for flusher_processes between CLI and factory
body: The CLI option --flusher-processes defaults to 1, but the factory parameter flusher_processes defaults to None, which becomes len(buffer.assigned_shards) in the flusher (via `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`). This means direct callers of the factory (e.g., tests) get a different default (one process per shard) than CLI users (1 process). This is a behavior change from the old code, which always created exactly 1 process regardless of shard count. Direct callers that don't pass flusher_processes and have multiple partitions will get N processes instead of 1.

title: test_flusher_processes_limit does not verify actual flushing with multiple processes
body: The test_flusher_processes_limit test only verifies the process count (len(flusher.processes) == 2) and shard distribution (total_shards == 4), but does not verify that the flusher actually works correctly with multiple processes. Since the main purpose of this PR is to introduce multiprocessed flushing, the test should submit messages to all shards, trigger flushing, and verify that all messages are correctly flushed across the multiple processes. Without this, a bug in the multi-process flushing logic could go undetected.

title: CLI help text is misleading about the default behavior
body: The help text says 'Maximum number of processes for the span flusher. Defaults to 1.' but this is only true for CLI usage. The factory parameter flusher_processes defaults to None, which results in one process per shard when called directly. The help text should clarify that the default is 1 for the CLI, and that the factory default is None (meaning one process per shard).

title: Naming inconsistency: flusher_processes vs max_processes
body: The parameter is called flusher_processes in the CLI option and factory, but max_processes in the SpanFlusher constructor. This naming inconsistency could be confusing for maintainers. Consider using the same name across all layers (e.g., flusher_processes everywhere).

title: Dead method `_create_process_for_shard` is never invoked
body: The method `_create_process_for_shard` (lines 127-132) is defined but never called anywhere in the file or by any caller. The corresponding `_create_process_for_shards` (plural) is the one used by `_create_processes` and `_ensure_processes_alive`. Either delete the dead method or wire it up — leaving it in production code is misleading and means future maintainers will assume shard-level restart is supported when it is not.

title: Inconsistent metrics tag key between `wait_produce` and surrounding timers
body: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` both use `tags={"shard": shard_tag}`, but the `wait_produce` timer right below uses `tags={"shards": shard_tag}` (plural). This will create two separate tag dimensions in the metrics backend for the same logical concept, making it impossible to filter or group these timers consistently in dashboards. Use the same key (`shard`) for all three.

title: `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` allows 11 restarts instead of the 10 the name suggests
body: The check is `if self.process_restarts[process_index] > MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS:` and the counter is incremented after the check. So the counter can take the values 0..10 with the check still False, then 11 with the check True. That means the consumer will restart an unhealthy flusher process 11 times before crashing, not 10 as the constant name and original semantics imply. Either rename the constant, change the check to `>=`, or move the increment before the check.

title: `process_restarts` counter never resets, so a long-running consumer is doomed by transient crashes
body: `self.process_restarts[process_index]` is initialized to 0 in `__init__` and only ever incremented in `_ensure_processes_alive`; it is never reset on successful operation. For a long-lived consumer that is rebalanced occasionally and where the SpanFlusher is reconstructed, this is bounded, but the per-process restart counter is shared across the lifetime of the SpanFlusher object. A single flusher that crashes 11 times over the course of days for transient reasons (deploys, brief OOM kills, broker hiccups) will permanently take down the consumer with no path to recovery short of a full restart. Consider resetting the counter once the process has been healthy for a sustained period.

title: `process_restarts` is incremented before the restart attempt, so failed restarts consume the budget
body: The order in `_ensure_processes_alive` is: check `> MAX`, increment, then `process.kill()` and `_create_process_for_shards(...)`. If `_create_process_for_shards` raises (e.g., OS resource exhaustion, pickling error), the counter has already been incremented and the next health check will be one step closer to crashing the consumer despite no successful restart ever having occurred. Move the increment to after a successful recreation, or wrap the restart in try/except and only increment on success.

title: Old flusher process is not joined before spawning its replacement
body: `_ensure_processes_alive` calls `process.kill()` and then immediately calls `_create_process_for_shards`, which spawns a new `SpawnProcess` and stores it in `self.processes[process_index]`. `kill()` only sends SIGKILL; it does not wait for the OS to actually reap the process. Until the old process is reaped it can still be inside its main loop, still flushing segments from Redis and still mutating the shared `process_healthy_since` / `process_backpressure_since` `Value`s. Once the new process is up, both processes will flush the same shards concurrently, producing duplicate Kafka payloads on `BUFFERED_SEGMENTS` (idempotency assumptions in downstream consumers are likely broken) and racing on the shared `Value`s. Call `process.join(timeout)` (with a short timeout) before spawning the replacement, or use `process.terminate()` followed by `join()` to give it a chance to exit cleanly first.

title: `max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` silently treats 0 as None
body: The `or` falls back to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)` whenever `max_processes` is falsy. Passing `max_processes=0` (e.g., to explicitly disable the flusher) will instead spin up a process per shard. Use `if max_processes is not None else len(buffer.assigned_shards)` so that 0 is honored. Additionally, with `num_processes = 0`, the subsequent `for i, shard in enumerate(...): process_index = i % 0` would raise ZeroDivisionError — there is no input validation guarding this.

title: Class docstring says 'one process per shard' but the implementation creates up to `max_processes`
body: The updated docstring states 'Creates one process per shard for parallel processing', but the constructor takes `max_processes` and defaults it to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`. A consumer configured with `--flusher-processes=2` and four shards will create 2 processes, each handling 2 shards. The docstring is therefore misleading; describe the actual semantics (e.g., 'creates up to `max_processes` worker processes, each handling one or more Redis shards').

title: `test_flusher_processes_limit` only asserts setup, not that flushing actually works
body: The new test only verifies that `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `max_processes == 2`, `num_processes == 2`, and that 4 shards are distributed. It does not submit any spans, so it cannot catch regressions where the per-process buffers route reads to the wrong Redis keys, where the multiprocessing Value objects are misbound, where restart logic corrupts `process_to_shards_map`, or where flushes are silently dropped because a process never sees data assigned to its shards. Extend the test to submit spans to at least two different shards and assert they reach the pipe, ideally with assertions that each process only flushed its assigned shards.

title: `time.sleep(0.1)` is silently neutered by the existing `time.sleep` monkeypatch
body: The test sets `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` near the top, then later adds `time.sleep(0.1)` with a comment saying it gives the flusher 'time to process'. Because `time.sleep` is already monkeypatched, this call is a no-op, so the test is silently relying on the flusher threads happening to run far enough during `step.poll()` to see the drift change. The intent (a real, brief wait) is not what the code does; either remove the misleading `time.sleep` and rely on the existing mock, or restore `time.sleep` around that specific call. The current state will hide real flakiness if the threads ever stop being fast enough.

title: join() may leave later processes alive when timeout is hit early
_create_process_for_shard is dead code
body: The method `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is defined but never called anywhere in the codebase. Restarts are done via `_ensure_processes_alive`, which calls `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly. This leftover method just adds noise and may mislead future maintainers into thinking shard-level restart is wired up when it is not.

title: Docstring claims 'one process per shard' but CLI default yields 1 process total
body: The class docstring reads: 'A background multiprocessing manager that polls Redis for new segments to flush and to produce to Kafka. Creates one process per shard for parallel processing.' However, the CLI option registered for `process-spans` defaults `--flusher-processes` to 1, and the factory forwards that value unchanged. With the production default, self.max_processes == 1, so all assigned shards end up on a single process (process_to_shards_map[0] holds every shard). The docstring is therefore misleading for any deployment that does not explicitly raise `--flusher-processes` to at least len(assigned_shards). Either update the docstring to describe the actual default ('up to N processes; default N=1 means one process handles all shards') or change the CLI default to None so the per-shard behavior is enabled out of the box.

title: CLI help for --flusher-processes contradicts PR goal
body: The new click option is documented as: 'Maximum number of processes for the span flusher. Defaults to 1.' The PR description says the goal is to 'spawn a process per redis shard'. A reader who wants per-shard processing has no hint from this help text that they must set `--flusher-processes` to a value >= the number of shards; otherwise every shard shares one process. Either rewrite the help to make the relationship to shard count explicit, or change the default so that the stated goal is achieved without operator action.

title: time.sleep(0.1) in test_basic is neutralised by monkeypatch
body: The new line `time.sleep(0.1)` was added with the comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change', but earlier in the test `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` globally replaces `time.sleep`. The 0.1s sleep is therefore a no-op, and the comment misrepresents what is happening. If the intent was to wait for the threaded flusher to observe the new drift and flush, the sleep needs to be done with a function the monkeypatch doesn't replace (e.g., a busy spin or a different module-level sleep), or the test should `time.sleep` before the monkeypatch and rely on a separate mechanism. As written, the line gives a false sense of safety.

title: test_flusher_processes_limit only asserts configuration, not behaviour
body: The new test creates the factory with flusher_processes=2 and 4 partitions, then asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `flusher.num_processes == 2`, and that the total shards across the process_to_shards_map equals 4. It never submits any Kafka message, never advances `current_drift`, never verifies that any of the two flusher threads actually flush a segment, and never asserts how the shards are split between the two processes (e.g., process 0 -> [0,2], process 1 -> [1,3]). It also does not cover the edge cases the new code introduces: flusher_processes=None, flusher_processes=0, flusher_processes >= number of shards, or an explicit per-shard assignment. Without functional coverage the multi-process path could silently regress (e.g., shards never being flushed because the buffer-per-shard mapping is wrong) without any test failing.

title: `if not process:` guard is dead code
body: Inside `_ensure_processes_alive`, the loop has `if not process: continue`, but the dict `self.processes` is only ever assigned via `_create_process_for_shards`, which stores the object returned by `make_process(...)` (either `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` or `threading.Thread`). Both are always truthy after their constructor returns, so the guard is never taken. It can be removed to avoid implying that None/False values may appear here.

title: num_processes=0 with no shards silently disables the flusher
body: `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))` evaluates to 0 when the buffer has zero assigned shards. `_create_processes()` then iterates over an empty mapping, so `self.processes`, `self.process_healthy_since`, `self.process_backpressure_since`, `process_restarts`, and `self.buffers` all stay empty. Later in `submit()` the loops over `self.process_backpressure_since.values()` and `self.buffers.values()` are also empty, so no backpressure is ever reported, no `record_stored_segments` metric is emitted, and no process liveness is enforced. If the consumer can ever be constructed with zero partitions (e.g., during a brief rebalance window or misconfiguration), the flusher silently becomes a no-op and segments can pile up in Redis with no operator-visible signal. Adding an explicit guard (e.g., skip creating the SpanFlusher, or raise) would surface this state.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the wrong behavior
body: The test docstring says "Test that errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages", but the final assertion `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` checks that NO offset is committed. The implementation in OrderedQueueWorker.run always calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` in the `finally` block, even when the result_processor raises an exception. So after both messages are processed (one with an error, one successfully), the offset WILL be committed at 102 (next to read after 101). The test contradicts the implementation: it should assert that the offset IS committed (e.g., `committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102`), demonstrating that errors don't block offset commits. Additionally, the test sleeps only 0.2 seconds after the loop break, but the commit thread runs every 1 second, making the test flaky depending on timing.

title: --mode help text does not mention thread-queue-parallel
body: The `uptime_options()` `--mode` help text reads "The mode to process results in. Parallel uses multithreading." After this PR, the choice list adds `"thread-queue-parallel"` but the help text was not updated. Users running `sentry run uptime-results --help` will see the new mode accepted but get no explanation of what it does or when to prefer it over the other modes.

title: assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue) is stripped under python -O
body: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, the line `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` is used as a runtime type guard before accessing `message.value.partition`/`offset`. Python strips `assert` statements when run with `-O` (which some production deployments use for performance). Without the assert, the code would raise `AttributeError` on non-BrokerValue messages, which is then swallowed by the generic `except Exception` that tries to recover by adding/completing the offset — but `message.value.partition`/`offset` will still AttributeError. The check should be an explicit `if not isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue): return/log/handle` rather than an assert.

title: Offsets are marked complete even when result_processor raises
body: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, the `finally` block unconditionally calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` even when the result_processor raised an exception. This silently drops processing failures: the offset is committed as if the message succeeded, and the message will not be retried. For an uptime consumer this means a failing check-in (e.g., transient DB error) is permanently lost. Either the offset should only be marked complete on success, or failures should be routed to the DLQ/stale topic, or the comment in the code should clearly call out that this is intentional at-least-once-with-loss-on-error semantics. The test `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` actually codifies the wrong expectation (see separate finding).

title: hash()-based group routing is not stable across restarts
body: `FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group` uses `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`. Python randomizes the string hash seed between processes by default (PYTHONHASHSEED), so the same group_key will map to a different queue index after a restart. The class docstring claims "Each group is consistently assigned to the same queue" and "No dynamic reassignment that could break ordering" — this is only true within a single process lifetime. Across restarts, in-flight unprocessed items from a group will not be drained in order relative to new arrivals. The docstring should clarify the lifetime guarantee, or a stable hash (e.g. hashlib) should be used.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_concurrent_subscriptions does not verify concurrency
body: The test creates two subscriptions, sends one message to each, and asserts `mock_processor_call.call_count == 2`. Nothing in the test actually verifies that the two messages were processed concurrently (e.g., by instrumenting the result_processor to hold a lock and observing that the two calls overlap in time, or by checking that they were dispatched to different workers/queues). The test name advertises a concurrency property it does not exercise.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit uses private arroyo internals
body: The Kafka integration test drives the consumer via `processor._run_once()` and `processor._shutdown()` — these are private arroyo methods whose behavior is not part of the public contract. It also creates the `UptimeResultsStrategyFactory` before the `override_settings(KAFKA_TOPIC_OVERRIDES=...)` context, and the factory's `create_with_partitions` is monkey-patched in place, so the test is not actually exercising the real consumer wiring under `override_settings`. Combined with the `mock_processor` doing nothing, the test mostly verifies that the offset-tracker/commit-loop machinery, when hand-driven, produces offset 5 — it does not validate that the production code path commits correctly. Consider using the public `processor.run()` or running the consumer in a thread with a real termination signal.

title: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.terminate has no test coverage
body: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.terminate()` (line 340-342) is not exercised by any test in `tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py` or the uptime test file. `terminate()` differs from `close()` in that it does not join the commit thread. Since arroyo's StreamProcessor may invoke `terminate()` on shutdown, a regression that double-shuts-down the queue pool or hangs the commit thread would go undetected. A simple test that calls `strategy.terminate()` after some work has been submitted would cover this path.

title: Sentry transaction name in OrderedQueueWorker is hardcoded to monitors.*
body: The transaction name in `OrderedQueueWorker.run` is `f"monitors.{self.identifier}.worker_{self.worker_id}"`. This module lives under `sentry.remote_subscriptions.consumers.queue_consumer` and is now used by the uptime consumer (`identifier="uptime"`) and potentially other consumers. Hardcoding the `monitors.` prefix will produce misleading transaction names like `monitors.uptime.worker_3` in Sentry's performance UI, making it harder to filter and group transactions correctly. The prefix should be derived from the identifier or removed.

title: Failed messages are silently lost on processing exception
body: In OrderedQueueWorker.run, the `finally` clause unconditionally calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` regardless of whether `result_processor` raised. The exception is caught and logged by the inner `except Exception`, but the offset is still marked complete, then committed to Kafka by the commit loop. The message is then gone and will not be retried on restart. This contradicts the strategy's docstring which promises "Only commits offsets after successful processing" and is a serious data integrity issue (e.g., missed uptime check results, missed monitor check-ins). Either the complete_offset must be conditional on success (e.g., a success flag set in the try), or failed messages must be routed to a DLQ. The existing batched-parallel path uses ThreadPoolExecutor.submit which silently captures exceptions, so it has the same data-loss pattern; this PR replicates and deepens the problem for the new mode.

title: hash() randomization breaks ordering guarantee across restarts
body: `FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group` returns `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`. Python's built-in `hash()` for strings is randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED). After any restart or new worker process, the same group_key can map to a different queue, violating the documented "Items for the same group are processed in order" guarantee. Example: if the consumer dies after submitting offset N to queue 5 and is restarted, offset N+1 for the same group may be hashed to queue 7 and processed in parallel/independently from any later retry of offset N, breaking in-order processing. Use a stable, cross-process hash like `int(hashlib.md5(group_key.encode()).hexdigest(), 16)` (or `hashlib.sha256(...)`) instead of `hash()`.

title: Shutdown ordering can cause workers to exit before draining queues
body: In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown`, `worker.shutdown = True` is set on all workers BEFORE `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` is called on each queue. The worker loop is `while not self.shutdown: try: work_queue.get() ...`, so a worker that just finished processing one item and is returning to the top of the loop will observe `self.shutdown == True` and exit without ever pulling the next item from its queue. Because the workers have already exited by the time `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` runs, the items left in each queue are never drained and are silently discarded (only re-read from Kafka on next start, if not yet committed). The `worker.shutdown = True` step is also redundant: `q.shutdown()` is sufficient to terminate the workers via the `queue.ShutDown` exception. Remove the `worker.shutdown = True` loop (or move it after the join), so that `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` can actually drain pending items.

title: OffsetTracker commits past unseen offsets, causing silent data loss
body: In `OffsetTracker.mark_committed` (lines 100–105), after committing offset X, all offsets ≤ X are removed from `self.all_offsets`. On the next `get_committable_offsets` call, the loop starts at `max(last_committed + 1, min(all_offsets))`, so any offset that was never submitted to the tracker is forgotten. If the consumer skips an offset (e.g., 101) but submits 100, 102, 103, the tracker will first commit 100 then, after removal, commit 103 — committing past the unseen 101 to Kafka. On restart, Kafka would begin reading from offset 104, permanently losing offset 101. The tracker assumes gaps are always due to filtering/compaction, but it has no way to distinguish that from a bug where `submit()` was never called for an offset. The test `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps` in `tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py` was clearly designed to catch this behavior (it asserts commits never exceed 101), but the implementation violates that assertion — the last commit would be 104. A safer design would either keep removed offsets to detect gaps, or require every offset in [last_committed, X] to have been at least seen.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the opposite of its docstring intent and fails
body: The test docstring says 'errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages', but the final assertion is `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, which is the opposite. With the current implementation (`OrderedQueueWorker.run` catches `Exception`, logs it, and in `finally` calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)`), both messages get their offsets marked complete regardless of the raised exception. The commit loop then commits offset 101 → Kafka offset 102. So `committed_offsets` will be `{test_partition: 102}`, both halves of the disjunction are False, and the test fails. The assertion should instead verify that the commit did happen (matching the docstring), e.g. `assert committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102`. As written, the test contradicts the implementation's actual behavior and would never pass.

title: Code depends on Python 3.13-only queue APIs
body: The file uses `queue.ShutDown` (caught in `OrderedQueueWorker.run` lines 132 and 142) and `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` (line 238). Both `queue.Queue.shutdown()` and the `queue.ShutDown` exception were introduced in Python 3.13 (October 2024). If sentry still supports Python 3.11 or 3.12, the workers will crash with `AttributeError: module 'queue' has no attribute 'ShutDown'` / `'shutdown'` the first time a shutdown is attempted or an exception is raised inside `run()`. The minimum Python version supported by sentry needs to be verified; if it is below 3.13, this module cannot be imported safely and will break the uptime-results consumer at runtime. A portable alternative is to use a sentinel object via `Queue.put` and check it in the worker, or a `threading.Event` plus a final empty marker, neither requiring Python 3.13.

title: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.terminate does not join commit thread
body: `terminate` sets `shutdown_event` and calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, but unlike `close` it never calls `self.commit_thread.join(...)`. The commit thread is daemonized, so the process exit will reap it, but during the window between `terminate` returning and the process actually exiting, the commit thread can still invoke `self.commit_function` (the arroyo `commit` callback) and mutate `OffsetTracker` state. This violates the symmetry with `close`, and means callers using `terminate` for a forced shutdown can have an arbitrary amount of background work still running against a strategy they consider terminated.

title: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join ignores its timeout argument
body: `join(self, timeout: float | None = None)` simply calls `self.close()`, dropping the `timeout` parameter. `close()` in turn calls `self.commit_thread.join(timeout=5.0)` (hard-coded 5s) and `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` (which joins workers with another hard-coded 5s). Callers that pass a smaller timeout via `join(0.5)` expecting bounded shutdown will wait up to ~10 seconds instead. The `timeout` argument should either be honored by passing it to the underlying joins or removed from the signature.

title: test_different_groups_distributed is probabilistic and can be flaky
body: The test submits 20 distinct group keys to a pool of 3 queues and asserts `len(queue_indices) == 3`. The probability of missing a queue with 20 keys and 3 buckets is 3 * (2/3)^20 - 3 * (1/3)^20 ≈ 0.00078, or about 1 in 1300. With Python's randomized string hashing (`PYTHONHASHSEED`) this is not controllable from the test. Worse, `hash()` can in principle produce collisions that bunch keys into fewer buckets than expected. The test should either use enough keys that the probability of collision is negligible (e.g. 200+), or directly assert `>= 2` rather than `== 3`, or seed/force the hash distribution.

title: Kafka integration test relies on private methods and tight timing
body: `ProcessResultThreadQueueParallelKafkaTest.test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit` reaches into `processor._run_once()` and `processor._shutdown()` (private Arroyo APIs) and only spins for 5 seconds before asserting `committed[0].offset == 5`. Under load or slow CI the consumer may not have time to fetch, decode, queue, and commit all 5 messages; the assertion then fails for timing reasons rather than correctness. Additionally, the test wraps `factory.create_with_partitions` to count commits but does not verify that all produced messages were actually decoded (`mock_processor.return_value = None` bypasses real processing). Consider using Arroyo's public `run()` loop, increasing the deadline, and asserting a lower bound (e.g. offset >= 1) rather than equality.

title: DisplayQrCode "Continue" button is type="submit" inside outer Form, fires handleEnable API call
body: The "Continue" button on the QR code step is rendered as type="submit" and lives inside the outer <Form handleSubmit={handleEnable}> (Form opens at line 209). Clicking it both runs the onClick (which advances to EnterTotpCode) AND submits the form, invoking handleEnable which immediately calls TwoFactorAuthAPI.enable() with whatever totpCode is currently in the form (empty or stale from a previous attempt). The result is a wasted API round-trip and an error toast like "code is incorrect" being briefly shown to the user before the step transitions. The button should be type="button" since its only intent is to advance the wizard step.

title: ConfirmPassword "Continue" button is type="submit" inside outer Form, fires two API calls
body: The ConfirmPassword Continue button is type="submit" and is placed inside the outer <Form handleSubmit={handleEnable}> (Form opens at line 209, the button is at line 233-240). Clicking it both runs the onClick handleSetup (which posts to /api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup) and submits the outer form which calls handleEnable, which posts to /api/auth/two-factor/totp/enable. Because totpCode is empty at this point, the second call always fails and sets an error message in state, even on a successful setup. The button should be type="button" (or moved outside the outer Form) so that only handleSetup runs.

title: Race condition allows backup code to be reused under concurrent requests
body: After a backup code is matched (line 144), the code nulls the used slot in memory and then awaits a prisma.user.update to persist (lines 148-156). Two concurrent login requests that submit the same backup code will both pass the indexOf check against the same in-memory array before either write hits the DB, and both will be authenticated. The second write then overwrites the first with the same nulled array, so the code remains "consumed" but two sessions are created. Mitigation: do the read/compare/null/write atomically (e.g. via prisma.$transaction with a conditional update that only matches if the code is still present), or perform a single UPDATE that removes the specific code rather than rewriting the whole array.

title: No rate limiting on 2FA disable endpoint, enabling brute-force of TOTP/backup code
body: The disable handler accepts a TOTP code (6 digits, ~20 bits of entropy) or a backup code (10 hex chars, 40 bits) and attempts verification on every request. Unlike the next-auth credentials authorize (which calls checkRateLimitAndThrowError), this endpoint performs no rate limiting, no lockout, and no failed-attempt counter. A user who is still logged in (or an attacker with a stolen session cookie) can submit unlimited guesses. TOTP is especially vulnerable: 10^6 / 30s is small enough that a targeted attacker can reliably find the current code. Add checkRateLimitAndThrowError (or equivalent) keyed on the user id before running code verification.

title: Object URL for backup codes download is never revoked on unmount
body: A new object URL is created (line 99) and the previous one is revoked only when another URL is created (line 98). When the modal is closed or the component unmounts, the last backupCodesUrl is never revoked, leaking the underlying Blob for the lifetime of the page. Add a cleanup useEffect that calls URL.revokeObjectURL(backupCodesUrl) on unmount, and also revoke it in resetState() / when the user navigates away from DisplayBackupCodes.

title: Returns 200 success without authenticating when 2FA is not enabled, leaking 2FA status
body: When user.twoFactorEnabled is false, the endpoint short-circuits with `return res.json({ message: "Two factor disabled" })` (line 37) without ever calling verifyPassword or checking the supplied code. Any caller who knows a valid session can use this to probe whether a given account has 2FA enabled: the response body and status differ from the "needs 2FA / needs password" branches. Either require the same authentication as the 2FA-enabled path before returning, or return a uniform response regardless of 2FA status.

title: Backup code authentication path is not exercised by any test
body: The e2e file has a TODO at line 12 ("add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup") and only verifies UI affordances (download/copy/close). The new security-critical paths added in this PR — backup-code login via next-auth-options.ts, backup-code disable via totp/disable.ts, single-use enforcement of backup codes, and the IncorrectBackupCode / MissingBackupCodes ErrorCode mappings in login.tsx — are not covered. Without these tests, regressions in single-use enforcement, race-condition fixes, or error mapping will go undetected. The author also explicitly ticked the checklist item "I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective or that my feature works".

title: formatBackupCode referenced before declaration; download Blob built on first render
body: handleSetup (line 77) references formatBackupCode (line 163) inside its body. Because formatBackupCode is a const arrow function declared after handleSetup, this works only via closure hoisting at call time — easy to break by future refactors and confusing to read. More importantly, the Blob on line 95 is built using formatBackupCode but the downloaded file content can drift from what is shown on screen if the formatter changes between setup and download (e.g. different dash placement). Define formatBackupCode before handleSetup (module scope or above the component) so both the display grid (line 204) and the Blob/copy operations (lines 95, 278) use the same definition.

title: Backup code login and disable flows have no e2e tests
body: The PR introduces backup code generation, login via backup code, and disabling 2FA via backup code across next-auth-options.ts, disable.ts, login.tsx, and DisableTwoFactorModal.tsx. The only backup-code-related test added is clicking the download/copy/close buttons in the post-enable dialog (lines 110-125). There is no e2e test that (1) logs in using a backup code, (2) verifies one-time use so a consumed code cannot log in again, (3) disables 2FA through the new 'Lost access' backup code branch, (4) verifies the IncorrectBackupCode / MissingBackupCodes error paths, or (5) inspects the downloaded file. The TODO at line 12 acknowledges the gap, but for a security-sensitive recovery flow the absence of coverage means regressions (e.g., accidental reuse of a code, broken decryption path, race between TOTP and backup branches) can ship undetected.

title: Backup-codes blob URL is never revoked on close or unmount
body: Line 99 calls URL.createObjectURL(textBlob) and stores the result in state. The only revocation is on line 98 inside handleSetup, which only runs when setup is re-invoked successfully. resetState (lines 71-75) does not revoke the URL and the Dialog's onOpenChange handler does not either, and there is no useEffect cleanup. Every successful 2FA setup that is followed by clicking Close, Cancel, X, or an outside click leaks the blob URL for the lifetime of the page. Combined with resetState not clearing backupCodesUrl (see next finding), the URL also leaks across modal open/close cycles.

title: resetState leaves backupCodes, backupCodesUrl, dataUri and secret populated
body: resetState only clears password, errorMessage and step. backupCodes (the in-memory list of plain codes), backupCodesUrl (the blob URL), dataUri (QR image) and secret (TOTP secret) remain. After Cancel/Close the next render of the dialog can therefore briefly render data that no longer matches the database, and the QR image / secret remain in the DOM and in memory until the component is remounted. The blob URL is not revoked (see companion finding), so it persists as a live object URL even after reset.

title: Making PasswordField required can break 2FA disable for non-CAL users
body: PasswordField now declares required when it is shown. The disable endpoint at apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts intentionally skips password verification for non-CAL identity providers (the guard `user.identityProvider === IdentityProvider.CAL` on line 40). If any caller of DisableTwoFactorModal renders it with disablePassword={false} (the default) for a SAML/Google user, that user will be asked for a password they do not have and will be unable to submit the form even though the API would have accepted the disable. The PR does not audit or update call sites of this modal, so this is a likely regression for non-CAL users trying to disable 2FA (including via the new 'Lost access' backup-code branch).

title: Clipboard write rejection is silently ignored
body: navigator.clipboard.writeText(backupCodes.map(formatBackupCode).join("\n")) returns a promise that can reject (insecure context, denied permission, document not focused). The handler ignores the promise and unconditionally shows the success toast `backup_codes_copied`. Users on browsers/contexts without clipboard API permission see a misleading success message while nothing was copied.

title: missing_backup_codes message is misleading and leaks account state
body: When the server returns MissingBackupCodes, the login UI shows t("missing_backup_codes") = "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." In the login flow the user has not yet authenticated, so directing them to settings is not actionable, and the message distinguishes users who have backup codes from those who do not - a small information leak about account state that is otherwise collapsed into a generic error.

title: Backup code consumption is not atomic; same code can authorize two sessions
body: After matching the code, the entry is nullified in the in-memory array and the encrypted blob is written back via a single prisma.user.update. There is no transaction or optimistic check. Two concurrent authorize() calls presenting the same backup code can both read the original array, both nullify index N, and both persist - the second call sees an apparently-valid code and authenticates. The window is small in practice (single user/device), but it directly violates the 'one-time use' guarantee that backup codes are sold on, and is worth a note.

title: Race condition allows a single backup code to authenticate multiple concurrent logins
body: In the backup code branch the lookup is `backupCodes.indexOf(...)` followed by `backupCodes[index] = null` and a plain `prisma.user.update` that re‑encrypts the array. Two concurrent requests that both submit the same valid backup code can both read the same index, both set it to null, and both `update` the row. The result is two authenticated sessions for one single‑use code. The lookup/mutation needs to be wrapped in a transaction with a row-level lock (or otherwise made atomic, e.g. by storing a hash plus a per-code marker) so that the second concurrent attempt fails with `IncorrectBackupCode`. The same race exists for any caller that re-uses a code in parallel.

title: Backup code login and backup-code disable paths have no e2e coverage
body: The PR adds the entire backup-code feature (login flow, display, copy/download, disabling 2FA via backup code) but the e2e test only exercises the TOTP login and TOTP‑based disable. The `// TODO: add more backup code tests` comment confirms the gap. There is no test that (a) re-logs in using a generated backup code via the `Lost access` button, (b) disables 2FA with a backup code, or (c) verifies that a used backup code can no longer authenticate. These are the core acceptance criteria for the issue and must be covered before merging.

title: Backup code comparison is case sensitive and can fail for valid hex codes
body: `backupCodes` is produced by `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")`, which is lowercase. The lookup compares `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` against the array with `indexOf` without normalising case, and `next-auth-options.ts` does the same. A user who copy‑pastes or types the code with uppercase letters (e.g. via autofill, or because the UI only displays a placeholder pattern `XXXXX-XXXXX` and the user assumes either case works) will be rejected with `IncorrectBackupCode` even though the code is correct. Normalise both sides to lowercase before comparing.

title: No protection against malformed/corrupted `backupCodes` ciphertext
body: The handler does `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY))` with no try/catch. If the stored ciphertext is corrupted, the JSON is invalid, or the encryption key was rotated without re-encrypting old values, the exception bubbles up as a 500 with no actionable error. The login handler in `next-auth-options.ts` has the same shape. Wrap the decrypt+parse in try/catch and return `ErrorCode.MissingBackupCodes` (or a new dedicated error) so the UI can show a sensible message and so the failure mode is not a generic 500.

title: `resetState` leaves backup codes, secret, QR data URI and the object URL in state
body: `resetState` only clears `password`, `errorMessage` and `step`. It does not clear `backupCodes`, `backupCodesUrl`, `dataUri` or `secret`. The `cancel` button at lines 224-230 calls `resetState()` then closes the modal, but because the dialog is controlled (state persists while `open` toggles), a subsequent re-open of the modal can briefly render the previous user's QR/secret/backup codes while the new password-confirm step is shown, or the `backupCodesUrl` Blob URL keeps pointing at stale data. Reset all of the 2FA-related state in `resetState` and revoke `backupCodesUrl` with `URL.revokeObjectURL` before clearing it.

title: `backupCodesUrl` Blob is never revoked when the modal is closed
body: `setBackupCodesUrl(URL.createObjectURL(textBlob))` is created on setup success and only revoked when `handleSetup` is invoked again. If the user closes the dialog without going through setup a second time, the Blob URL stays alive until the page unloads, holding the plaintext backup codes in memory. Call `URL.revokeObjectURL(backupCodesUrl)` in a cleanup effect (and in `resetState`) so the Blob is released deterministically.

title: Cancel handler invokes `onCancel` before resetting local state
body: The cancel button calls `onCancel()` and then `resetState()`. The parent is likely to hide the modal (or unmount the page) in response to `onCancel`, which can race with the second `resetState()` call and leave the component in a partially reset condition. Reverse the order: `resetState()` then `onCancel()`. The same pattern issue applies to the backup-codes close button at lines 266-269 (`onEnable()` before `resetState()`).

title: `formatBackupCode` is referenced before its declaration
body: `handleSetup` (line 77) references `formatBackupCode` inside its body, but `formatBackupCode` is declared with `const` at line 163, below the function definition. It works at runtime because `handleSetup` only runs after the component has rendered, but the order is confusing and tools that analyse temporal dead zones / eslint `no-use-before-define` will complain. Move the `formatBackupCode` definition above `handleSetup`.

title: Password field in disable modal is rendered without a label
body: The `PasswordField` is given `labelProps={{ className: "block text-sm font-medium text-default" }}` but no `label` prop, so `PasswordField` falls back to no label text and the styling from `labelProps` has nothing to attach to. Users opening the "Disable 2FA" dialog see an unlabeled text field and may not understand they must re-enter their account password. Pass `label={t("password")}` (matching what `EnableTwoFactorModal` does) so the dialog is self-explanatory.

title: `<Label>` is not associated with the input via `htmlFor`
body: The `Label` element renders the `t("backup_code")` string but has no `htmlFor` attribute, while the `TextField` declares `id="backup-code"`. Screen readers will not announce them as related and clicking the label text will not focus the input. Add `htmlFor="backup-code"` to the `Label`.

title: `TextField` length attributes ignore the dash in the middle
body: `minLength={10}` / `maxLength={11}` describe the raw character count, but the field is also visually presented as `XXXXX-XXXXX` and the server strips dashes before comparing (`replaceAll("-", "")`). Users may legitimately type 11 characters including the dash and be exactly at the limit, which is fine, but the placeholder and helper text never explain that the dash is optional. Either accept input with or without the dash consistently (currently accepted on the server but the length limits are tight against the user's expectation) or document/format the input so the count is obvious. Also, `required` plus `minLength={10}` makes the HTML5 validity message "Please lengthen this text to 10 characters or more (you are currently using X characters)" which is technically wrong for the dashed form (11 with dash, 10 without). Consider deriving the limits from the formatted length (11) and normalising before validation.

title: Backup-code branch bypasses password verification when `totpCode` is also present
body: Password verification is gated by `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)`, so any request that includes a non-empty `totpCode` skips password validation entirely. The backup-code branch then takes priority over the TOTP branch (`if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode)`). An attacker who has obtained a valid backup code (e.g. by shoulder-surfing the setup screen, by stealing the user's download, or via the race condition above) can simply include any non-empty string as `totpCode` together with the backup code, and password verification is skipped. Either verify the password whenever a password is set regardless of `totpCode`, or restrict the backup-code branch so it only runs when password has already been verified.

title: TypeError when destinationCalendar is empty array on Meet bookings
body: The new fallback that decides whether to switch the meeting location to Cal Video no longer uses optional chaining. Line 119 destructures `evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` into `mainHostDestinationCalendar`, and line 120 reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` directly. When `evt.destinationCalendar` is `null`, `undefined`, or an empty array (a normal state for many bookings), the destructured variable is `undefined` and accessing `.integration` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'integration')`. The previous code (`evt.destinationCalendar?.integration !== "google_calendar"`) safely evaluated to `true` in that case. Any booking whose `location` is Google Meet and that has no destinationCalendar configured will now crash with 500 instead of silently falling back to Cal Video.

title: Collective events silently drop all host destination calendars when organizer has none
body: `evt.destinationCalendar` is initialized as `null` when neither the event-type nor the organizer user has one (see the `evt = { ... destinationCalendar: ... ? [...] : null }` block around line 1067). The subsequent `if (isTeamEventType && eventType.schedulingType === "COLLECTIVE") { evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars); }` uses optional chaining, so the push becomes a no-op when the value is `null`. As a result, collective bookings that have no event-type-level or organizer-level destination calendar end up with an empty/null `destinationCalendar`, and `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents` falls through to the `cred.type === "calendar"` branch which never matches real credentials (`google_calendar`, etc.). The expected per-host calendar invitations for that scenario are silently lost.

title: Only the first destination calendar of a collective booking is persisted on the Booking row
body: When writing the new booking row, the change connects only `evt.destinationCalendar[0].id` to the booking's `destinationCalendar` relation: `destinationCalendar: evt.destinationCalendar && evt.destinationCalendar.length > 0 ? { connect: { id: evt.destinationCalendar[0].id } } : undefined`. For collective events the array now contains the organizer plus every host's destination calendar (built up by the `teamDestinationCalendars` push on line 1078), but the Booking schema only stores the first entry. Any later code path that consults `booking.destinationCalendar` directly (instead of `booking.references`, e.g. confirm.handler.ts, editLocation.handler.ts, handleCancelBooking.ts at line ~251, paypal-webhook.ts line 152, deleteCredential.handler.ts line 290) will only see the organizer's calendar and lose information about the other hosts. This contradicts the PR description that the booking now supports multiple destinations per host.

title: Google Calendar updateEvent passes undefined calendarId when no externalCalendarId is supplied
body: Inside `updateEvent` the new selection is `selectedCalendar = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. The `find` callback compares `cal.externalId === externalCalendarId`, but the parent ternary only enters this branch when `externalCalendarId` is falsy (typically `undefined`), so `find` matches nothing and returns `undefined`. The previous code simply used `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId` and worked for any single-destination booking. As a result, callers like `CalendarManager.updateEvent` (which always omits `externalCalendarId`) now send `calendarId: undefined` to the Google Calendar API, causing the update to 404 even though the destination calendar is present on the event.

title: Google Calendar deleteEvent always deletes from "primary" when externalCalendarId is omitted
body: `deleteEvent` uses the same `find(cal => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)` lookup as `updateEvent`. With `externalCalendarId` undefined (the only form `CalendarManager.deleteEvent` ever calls it with), the lookup never matches and the fallback `calendarId: calendarId ? calendarId : defaultCalendarId` resolves to `"primary"`. Previously it just used `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. Bookings whose host's destination calendar is not the user's Google primary calendar will now be deleted from the wrong calendar; for events that don't exist on primary, the 404/410 path silently resolves and the real calendar event is orphaned.

title: requestReschedule drops user fallback for destinationCalendar (inconsistent with other handlers)
body: The new assignment is `destinationCalendar: bookingToReschedule?.destinationCalendar ? [bookingToReschedule?.destinationCalendar] : []`.
