Any subsequent request for the same device within the cache TTL (29 minutes) hits the cache, returns nil without consulting the database, and the authentication succeeds even though the device was never registered and the limit is still exceeded. This makes the limit enforcement non-deterministic: the same new device is rejected on its first request but admitted on every subsequent request within 29 minutes, while also being absent from the database (so usage stats and the device list undercount it). The cache should only be populated after a successful insert/update, or failed attempts should not be cached.

title: TagDevice now uses the request context, so client cancellation aborts device tagging
body: Previously TagDevice was invoked from a goroutine with a fresh context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 2*time.Minute), decoupling the DB write from the caller. The new implementation calls a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, ...) directly with the incoming request context. If the HTTP request is cancelled (slow client, closed connection, timeout) before the DB write completes, ctx is cancelled and CreateOrUpdateDevice returns early without inserting the device. Anonymous devices on flaky or slow connections may therefore never be tagged even though the user authenticated. This is a regression from the previous fire-and-forget behavior.

title: No test covers the new synchronous error path in Authenticate when ErrDeviceLimitReached is returned
body: The PR changes Authenticate so that an error from TagDevice propagates and causes authentication to fail when errors.Is(err, anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached) is true. This is a significant user-visible behavior change (anonymous login now fails with an error when the limit is set and full) but is only covered at the store layer by TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit. There is no test that exercises the Anonymous.Authenticate path returning ErrDeviceLimitReached, nor any test that verifies a non-limit error from TagDevice is still logged but does not block auth. This regression-prone path needs direct coverage.

title: TOCTOU race allows the device limit to be exceeded under concurrent requests
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice performs CountDevices followed by a separate insert/update when s.deviceLimit > 0. The two operations are not atomic and are not wrapped in a transaction or row lock. With concurrent requests all observing count == limit-1, multiple new devices can pass the check and all be inserted, taking the actual count above the configured limit. If strict enforcement is desired, this needs to be made atomic (e.g., a conditional INSERT, a transaction with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or a unique-constraint-based scheme). At minimum, document that the limit is best-effort.

title: updateDevice silently rejects returning devices whose updated_at is older than the expiration window
body: updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when the WHERE clause matches zero rows. This happens not only for unknown device_ids (the intended case) but also for any device whose existing row has updated_at outside the [-30d, +1m] window relative to the new request. Because cleanup only deletes devices older than 61 days, a user who has not visited for 30-61 days has an existing row that will be treated as 'not existing' and rejected when the limit is full, even though their record is still in the table. Either remove the updated_at window from the UPDATE (use only device_id = ?) so existing devices can always re-activate, or document the 30-day activity requirement explicitly.

title: 30-day expiration constant is duplicated and inconsistently named across packages
body: The value 30 * 24 * time.Hour is defined as anonymousDeviceExpiration in both pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database.go (line 16) and pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/api/api.go (line 18), and as thirtyDays in pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/impl.go (line 25). All three must agree; if anyone updates one (e.g., to change the expiration window) the others will drift and the limit/enforcement/list/usage-stats queries will use different windows. Centralize this constant in a single package and import it from the other two.

title: Negative device_limit is silently treated as unlimited
body: MustInt64(0) returns the parsed value when it is a valid integer. A negative value (e.g., device_limit = -1) is stored as-is in cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit. The check in CreateOrUpdateDevice is `if s.deviceLimit > 0`, so a negative value disables the limit the same as 0. Operators who misconfigure the setting will believe the limit is active when it is not. Validate the value at load time and log/return an error for values < 0, or treat any value <= 0 as 'unlimited' and document it.

title: updateDevice name does not reflect that it rejects new devices when the limit is reached
body: The function is named updateDevice and its doc-comment says 'updates a device if it exists', but in CreateOrUpdateDevice it is also used as the path that rejects unknown device_ids when the limit is full (rowsAffected == 0 -> ErrDeviceLimitReached). Readers tracing the call site will be surprised that an 'update' function causes new-device rejections. Rename or split, and update the comment.

title: untagDevice logs the wrong variable when the device delete fails
body: In untagDevice the delete error is captured as errD, but the log call uses 'error', err (the post-login hook parameter, which was checked for non-nil above and is nil here). So when the DeleteDevice fails, the log message says 'Failed to untag device' with err=<nil>, providing no diagnostic value. Change the log to use errD. This is pre-existing but in a file modified by this PR and adjacent to the new error-return path.

title: TOCTOU race allows device limit to be exceeded
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice first calls CountDevices to check whether the configured deviceLimit has been reached, then, if under limit, runs an unconditional INSERT...ON CONFLICT. These two operations run in separate sessions with no locking, so under concurrent anonymous authentications several requests can all observe count < deviceLimit and proceed to insert new rows, exceeding the configured limit by however many requests race in the same window. With limit=10 a burst of new device IDs can easily push the table to 12-15 active devices. The limit cannot be safely enforced in application code in this shape; it needs either a single atomic statement (e.g. INSERT ... SELECT with a count check in a CTE, plus a database transaction), a row-level lock, or a unique constraint plus a DB trigger.

title: localCache is set before the DB call, so ErrDeviceLimitReached is silently bypassed on the next request
body: tagDeviceUI writes a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{}) before invoking CreateOrUpdateDevice and returns nil on cache hit. Combined with the new ErrDeviceLimitReached returned by the store, this means: the first request from a brand-new device when the limit is reached sets the cache and fails authentication; the very next request from the same device within the 29 minute cache TTL hits the cache, tagDeviceUI returns nil, TagDevice returns nil, and Authenticate returns a valid identity. The device limit is therefore defeated simply by retrying once. The cache entry needs to either track failure (return the cached error on subsequent hits, or only populate the cache after a successful tag) so the rejection is enforced for the full TTL.

title: Synchronous DB write and removed panic recovery in the anonymous auth path is a regression
body: The previous implementation invoked TagDevice from a goroutine with a panic recover and a 2-minute timeout, so anonymous authentication never blocked on a DB write. This PR removes the goroutine and the recover and calls TagDevice synchronously on the request context. Every anonymous request now performs an INSERT/UPDATE in the auth hot path: DB latency directly adds to login latency, a slow or unreachable DB will deny anonymous logins instead of just losing the tag, and any panic inside TagDevice now propagates to the auth handler. This is a notable behavior change that the description and reviewer checklist do not call out.

title: anonymousDeviceLimit is typed as number | undefined but the backend always emits a number
body: The Go DTO declares AnonymousDeviceLimit int64 (non-pointer, no omitempty), so the /api/frontend/settings endpoint always serializes a number, never omits the field. The TypeScript field anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined plus the runtime default anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined are inconsistent with this: the frontend will always receive a concrete number (0 for unlimited, or the configured value), and never undefined. Either change the DTO to *int64 with omitempty to truly support undefined, or fix the TS types/defaults to number with 0 default so the contract matches what the API actually sends.

title: No test exercises the concurrency path that the new check/enforce split relies on
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only runs two sequential CreateOrUpdateDevice calls. The whole correctness story of the limit hinges on the check-then-insert in CreateOrUpdateDevice being safe under concurrent load, and on the local cache correctly handling ErrDeviceLimitReached on retry. Neither is covered: there is no parallel test that fires N goroutines with unique device IDs against a small limit and asserts the resulting count, and no test that calls CreateOrUpdateDevice twice with a cache layer to assert that the second call after ErrDeviceLimitReached still returns the error. Without these, the race and the cache-bypass bugs above can regress silently.

title: New auth.anonymous.device_limit setting has no documentation or sample
body: The PR adds cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit = anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0) but does not update the configuration documentation (e.g. docs/sources/setup-grafana/configure-grafana/_index.md or the sample config under conf/defaults.ini) to describe the new key, its default (0 = unlimited), the 30-day activity window, or the new behavior that hitting the limit will reject anonymous logins. The reviewer checklist explicitly asks to confirm docs are updated and this is not done. Users will have no way to discover or understand the setting, and operators who turn it on will be surprised that anonymous access starts returning errors when the limit is hit.

title: TOCTOU race allows exceeding configured device limit
body: In CreateOrUpdateDevice the limit is enforced via a non-atomic 'SELECT COUNT(*) ... then INSERT' pattern: when s.deviceLimit > 0 the code calls CountDevices and, if count >= s.deviceLimit, routes the request to updateDevice; otherwise it falls through to the INSERT...ON CONFLICT branch. There is no row-level lock or transactional guard, so two concurrent requests for different devices (or N concurrent requests) can both observe count < limit and both succeed at INSERT, leaving the table with more than deviceLimit rows. For a feature whose stated purpose is to cap the number of devices, this race is a correctness bug: the configured limit is not actually a hard cap under concurrent traffic. Wrap the count+insert in a serializable transaction, lock a dedicated row (e.g. a 'anon_device_limit' singleton), or move the check into the database (e.g. an INSERT trigger that counts and aborts) so the check and the write are atomic.

title: Local cache set before DB call defeats ErrDeviceLimitReached lockout
body: tagDeviceUI populates a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{}) BEFORE calling a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. Previously this was harmless because CreateOrUpdateDevice errors were only logged. After this PR, ErrDeviceLimitReached propagates up and causes Authenticate to deny the user (client.go returns the error). However, once that error is returned the cache entry is still in place for ~29 minutes (the cache TTL). Any retry for the same device within that window hits the cache, returns nil, and the user is silently authenticated despite the device never having been written and the limit being reached. The lockout semantics are therefore inconsistent: same device, same DB state, allowed or denied depending on cache timing. Move the cache set to AFTER a successful CreateOrUpdateDevice, or delete the cache key on error.

title: Anonymous auth request now blocks on synchronous DB write
body: The previous implementation ran the device tagging in a goroutine with its own context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 2*time.Minute), so anonymous authentication never waited on the database. The new code calls a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, httpReqCopy, ...) inline on the auth request path and propagates the error. Every anonymous request now performs a synchronous database write (CountDevices + INSERT/UPDATE) before the auth response is returned, adding latency to every anonymous login. Worse, if the database is slow the request itself can hang because the goroutine's 2-minute timeout is gone; the request context can be canceled by the client earlier, but cannot enforce an upper bound on a hung DB. Consider keeping the tagging async (fire-and-forget or a short-lived worker) while still surfacing ErrDeviceLimitReached synchronously, or pre-computing the decision from a cached count.

title: No test that an existing device can still update when at limit
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit inserts device '32mdo31deeqwes', then tries to insert a NEW device 'keep' and asserts ErrDeviceLimitReached. The equally important branch of updateDevice - 'device already exists in the table, so the UPDATE affects 1 row and returns nil' - is not covered. The stated behavior ('if device limit is reached, only update devices') only holds if existing devices genuinely succeed; otherwise legitimate users of an already-registered device will be silently locked out when the limit is reached. Add a case where the second CreateOrUpdateDevice call uses the SAME DeviceID as the first one and assert that no error is returned.

title: anonymousDeviceExpiration constant renamed only in api package
body: The PR renames the 30-day window constant to anonymousDeviceExpiration in pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/api/api.go, and uses the same name in the new constant in pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database.go, but pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/impl.go still defines 'const thirtyDays = 30 * 24 * time.Hour' and uses it in usageStatFn. Three copies of the same magic number (30 * 24 * time.Hour) now live in the same codebase under two different names, and changing the expiration window requires touching multiple files. Consolidate to a single exported constant (e.g. in the anonstore package) and reference it from impl.go and api.go.

title: Routine cleanup logs at Error level, generating false alerts
body: The new code logs the cleanup batch with `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err)`. This is a normal/expected operational event during routine annotation cleanup, not an error. Logging it at Error level will fire false alerts on error-monitoring systems, pollute error pipelines, and dump the full list of IDs plus the constructed SQL condition into error logs every minute (after the cleanup.go ticker change). It also passes `"err", err` while `err` is always nil at that point (the function has already returned if it was non-nil). It should be `r.log.Info` or `r.log.Debug`, and the misleading `"err", err` key/value should be removed.

title: Successful cleanup batch logged as Error
body: `r.log.Error("cleaned annotations by time", "count", len(ids), "affected", x, "err", y)` is emitted on every successful cleanup batch. This logs a normal successful operation at Error level, producing repeated false-positive alerts whenever the cleanup runs. It also passes `"err", y` where `y` is always nil (since this log is reached only after a successful delete). It should be downgraded to `r.log.Info`/`Debug` and the spurious `"err"` field removed.

title: MaxCount cleanup routine logged as Error
body: `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by count", ...)` fires at Error level for routine MaxCount-based cleanup. Same problem as the MaxAge path: normal operations are reported as errors, and `"err", err` is always nil at that point. Should be `Info`/`Debug`.

title: Successful MaxCount cleanup logged as Error
body: `r.log.Error("cleaned annotations by count", ...)` is emitted on every successful MaxCount cleanup batch. Again, this is a normal success path, not an error. Downgrade to `Info`/`Debug` and remove the spurious `"err", y` field.

title: Orphan-tag cleanup routine logged as Error
body: `r.log.Error("Tags to clean", ...)` fires every time `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` is invoked by the cleanup ticker, even when there are zero orphans (`len(ids) == 0`). With the ticker now running every minute (see cleanup.go change), this floods error logs and triggers false alerts during normal operation. Should be `Info`/`Debug`.

title: Successful orphan-tag cleanup logged as Error
body: `r.log.Error("cleaned tags", ...)` is emitted on every successful orphan-tag cleanup batch. This is a normal success log, not an error. Downgrade to `Info`/`Debug` and drop the always-nil `"err", y` field.

title: Cleanup ticker frequency bumped 10x without justification
body: The PR is about fixing MySQL deadlocks in the annotation cleanup, but this change moves `ticker := time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)` to `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)`. That makes the entire cleanup routine (and the now-Err-logging annotation cleanup) run ten times as often. This is unrelated to the deadlock fix, multiplies database load unnecessarily, and combined with the Error-level logs above will multiply the false alerts accordingly. If a higher frequency is wanted, it should be a separate change with its own justification (e.g., a new config flag, defaulting to 10m).

title: O(n²) string concatenation when building the SQLite inline IN-list
body: When `r.db.GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite && r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit`, the code builds the IN-list with `values := fmt.Sprint(ids[0]); for _, v := range ids[1:] { values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) }`. Each `fmt.Sprintf` call copies the entire accumulator, so the total work is O(n²). With the newly added test case using a batch size of 32767, this is roughly a billion operations and ~hundreds of MB of garbage per cleanup batch, and it gets worse for any future larger batch sizes. Use `strings.Builder` (or `strings.Join`-style construction with a pre-sized buffer) so the build is O(n).

title: Deadlock fix has no MySQL integration test coverage
body: The new and renamed tests (`TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp`, `TestIntegrationOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst`) only exercise SQLite via `db.InitTestDB(t)`. The bug this PR fixes — annotations writes being rejected due to a deadlock with the cleanup job — is MySQL-specific (see referenced issue #64979). Without a MySQL integration test, a future regression in the locking pattern (e.g., re-introducing a subquery-based DELETE inside one transaction) would not be caught. The PR should include (or rely on an existing) MySQL integration test exercising concurrent inserts and the cleanup loop.

title: Hard-coded SQLite parameter limit (999) ignores SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER in modern SQLite
body: The condition `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit` uses `const sqliteParameterLimit = 999`. SQLite >= 3.32.0 defaults SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER to 32766, and even older builds can be recompiled with higher limits. The new test case is even named "should not fail if batch size is larger than SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER for SQLite >= 3.32.0", but the code itself still assumes 999, so for batch sizes between 1000 and 32766 the code unnecessarily takes the slow, O(n²), unsafe (no parameterization) inline path. The limit should be derived from a runtime check or configured, not hard-coded to 999.

title: Cleanup ticker frequency increased 10x without mention in PR
body: The cleanup ticker is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This is a 10x increase in the frequency of background cleanup jobs (including the annotation cleanup and other unrelated cleanup jobs that share this ticker). The PR description and linked issue only describe splitting the annotation cleanup query into two statements to avoid MySQL deadlocks; nothing explains why the global cleanup cadence is being changed. This materially increases database load and lock-contention surface, especially given that the new loop in xorm_store.go will keep running batches back-to-back with no throttle until affected==0. The change should be either justified in the PR description or removed; if it is required to compensate for early termination of `untilDoneOrCancelled` under concurrent activity, that should be stated explicitly.

title: Routine cleanup operations logged at Error level
body: The new code uses `r.log.Error(...)` for routine, expected cleanup activity. After the change, the cleanup path emits six Error-level log lines per batch (`Annotations to clean by time`, `cleaned annotations by time`, `Annotations to clean by count`, `cleaned annotations by count`, `Tags to clean`, `cleaned tags`). Even when the cleanup succeeds these will be logged at Error level and on production systems they will pollute alerting/log dashboards that key off Error severity for `annotation.test`. The success-path log lines should be Debug or Info; only the failure paths warrant Error.

title: 'cleaned annotations by time' log message printed even when deleteByIDs fails
body: The line `r.log.Error("cleaned annotations by time", "count", len(ids), "affected", x, "err", y)` is emitted unconditionally after `deleteByIDs`, including when `y != nil`. Operators reading the log will see a message saying annotations were cleaned alongside an error value, which is contradictory and makes incidents harder to diagnose. The same pattern is repeated on line 557 (`cleaned annotations by count`) and line 579 (`cleaned tags`). The log line should either branch on `err != nil` (different message/level on failure) or use Info/Debug on success and reserve Error for the failure path.

title: Log line always logs a nil error
body: Immediately before the `deleteByIDs` call, the code logs `"err", err` where `err` is the result of `fetchIDs`. Because the surrounding block already returned on `if err != nil { return 0, err }`, the value of `err` here is guaranteed to be nil. The `err` field in the structured log is therefore dead/misleading data and should be removed (or replaced with the result of the delete that follows). The same issue exists on lines 554, 557, 576 and 579.

title: sqliteParameterLimit is wrong: hardcoded 999 instead of 32766 for modern SQLite
body: The constant `sqliteParameterLimit = 999` is the SQLite compile-time default prior to 3.32, but SQLite >= 3.32 (released 2020) raises the default to 32766, and Grafana's test name explicitly acknowledges this (`should not fail if batch size is larger than SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER for SQLite >= 3.32.0`). Because of this constant, any configured batch size between 1000 and 32766 will be incorrectly routed into the unsafe string-concatenation path even though parameterized queries would work. The check should use the higher value (or be looked up via the dialect), and the comparison should ideally be against the actual `len(ids)` rather than the configured batch size — a configured batch of 1000 that returns 5 IDs should still use `?` placeholders.

title: String-concatenated SQL with IDs is fragile pattern even though IDs are int64
body: In the SQLite fast path, the delete statement is built via `fmt.Sprintf("DELETE FROM %s WHERE id IN (%s)", table, values)` where `values` is constructed by repeatedly formatting `int64` IDs with `%d`. While `%d` on an int64 is safe today, this is a regression from the prior fully-parameterized approach and is fragile: any future change that lets IDs come from a less-trusted source, or that changes the column type, breaks the SQL safety guarantee. The same pattern also bypasses query caching and makes the statement harder to read in slow-query logs. A safer workaround is to chunk the slice into batches of 999 (or 32766) and use placeholders for each chunk.

title: fetchIDs interpolates table name unescaped into SQL
body: `fetchIDs` builds `SELECT id FROM %s` and `DELETE FROM %s WHERE id IN (...)` with the `table` argument interpolated directly into the SQL string. Today every call passes the hardcoded literal `"annotation"` or `"annotation_tag"`, so there is no live vulnerability, but the helper accepts a free-form string and there is no whitelist/quoting. A future caller passing user-controlled input (e.g., a table prefix) would create an injection. The function should validate `table` against a fixed allow-list or use the dialect's identifier quoting.

title: untilDoneOrCancelled terminates early on any zero-affected batch
body: `untilDoneOrCancelled` exits when `affected == 0`. With the new two-statement design, an entire batch's IDs can be concurrently deleted (or in the MaxCount case, removed by a concurrent delete on a row that shifts the OFFSET) between `fetchIDs` and `deleteByIDs`, producing `affected == 0` while there are still annotations to clean. The comment in the code acknowledges the issue for concurrent inserts, but the same hazard exists for concurrent deletes and is more likely. The cleanup will then stop for the current cycle even though rows remain, relying entirely on the (now 1-minute) ticker to retry. A retry that re-issues the same `fetchIDs` (with fresh IDs) instead of terminating would close this gap.

title: Cleanup ticker reduced below the cleanup timeout, allows overlapping runs
body: The ticker interval was changed from time.Minute * 10 to time.Minute * 1, but srv.clean has a 9-minute timeout (const timeout = 9 * time.Minute). The original 10-minute interval was deliberately chosen to be longer than the timeout so that the next tick cannot fire while a cleanup is still in flight; with a 1-minute interval, if any single cleanup takes more than one minute - which is quite plausible now that each batch does a separate SELECT and DELETE rather than a single DELETE - the next call to srv.clean will be dispatched concurrently with the previous one. There is no mutex or re-entrancy guard around srv.clean in Run, so the only thing preventing overlap was the ticker interval itself. Two concurrent cleanups performing SELECT-then-DELETE on the same annotation tables can re-introduce the very lock-contention pattern this PR is trying to eliminate, and at minimum roughly doubles steady-state database load. Either keep the interval >= the cleanup timeout, lower the timeout below 1 minute, or add a guard (sync.Mutex / atomic flag) so srv.clean cannot overlap with itself.

title: r.log.Error used for routine informational log lines with nil error
body: In CleanAnnotations (lines 534, 537, 554, 557) and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags (lines 576, 579) every batch is logged via r.log.Error with fields such as 'count', 'ids', 'cond' and 'affected', and each line also includes an 'err' field whose value is always nil at that point (any real error has already been returned via the if err != nil blocks). Using Error level for routine progress reports - and for explicitly nil errors - means every successful cleanup batch will be surfaced as an error to any error-rate alerting (e.g. Loki / Grafana alerting, Sentry), producing noise and potentially paging on-call. These should be Debug (or Info) level. Lines to change: 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579.

title: O(n^2) string building for SQLite IN-list fallback
body: In deleteByIDs, when running on SQLite with a configured batch size > 999, the IN-list is built by fmt.Sprint(ids[0]) followed by a loop of fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) for each subsequent id. Each Sprintf allocates and copies the entire growing string, making the total work O(n^2) in len(ids). The new integration test exercises exactly this path with batch size 32767 and ~32k ids, so the construction cost dominates the batch. Use strings.Builder with strconv.AppendInt for an O(n) build.

title: SQLite IN-list branch keyed on configured batch size, not actual id count
body: deleteByIDs chooses the string-interpolated IN-list based on r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit rather than on len(ids). When an operator configures a batch size larger than 999 but a particular fetchIDs call returns fewer matching rows than that (e.g. near the end of cleanup, or whenever fewer annotations match the WHERE clause than the batch size), the code still falls into the O(n^2) string-interpolated path even though parameterized placeholders would be safe and faster. The branch should be conditioned on len(ids) > sqliteParameterLimit so the interpolation fallback is only taken when we actually have more ids than SQLite's parameter limit.

title: Storage failure metric mislabeled as legacy duration in Create
body: In DualWriterMode3.Create, when d.Storage.Create returns an error the code records the failure via d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage). The call was to Storage (not Legacy) and no Legacy call has been made yet on this error path, so the metric is being attributed to the wrong backend and the actual Storage error is not counted in the storage metrics. Should call d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) so operators see real Storage failures and do not get spurious legacy failures.

title: Delete metric uses object name as 'kind' label, causing cardinality explosion
body: After a successful Storage.Delete, the success is recorded with d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage). The third argument is the per-object name (e.g. 'foo', 'bar'), not the resource Kind. Every other method in this file (Create, Get, List, Update, DeleteCollection) passes options.Kind for this argument. Using the object name as the kind label creates a new Prometheus time series per deleted object, exploding label cardinality, breaking aggregation by kind, and risking Prometheus OOM under normal traffic. It should be options.Kind.

title: Storage failure metric mislabeled as legacy duration in Update
body: In DualWriterMode3.Update, when d.Storage.Update returns an error the code records the failure via d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage). The call was to Storage, not Legacy, and the Legacy goroutine has not been spawned yet on this error path. The metric is attributed to the wrong backend, hiding real Storage failures from the storage metrics and injecting fake legacy failures. Should be d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage).

title: Legacy DeleteCollection result recorded as storage metric
body: In the DeleteCollection legacy goroutine, after d.Legacy.DeleteCollection returns, the result is recorded via d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). The call was to the Legacy backend, so it should be recorded via d.recordLegacyDuration. As written, every legacy DeleteCollection outcome is reported against the storage metric, hiding legacy-side failures from operators and inflating the storage success/error counts.

title: Update doc comment implies sequential legacy write
body: The comment on DualWriterMode3.Update reads 'writes first to Storage and then to LegacyStorage', but the actual implementation dispatches the legacy call in a goroutine after the storage call returns, so it is asynchronous and not strictly 'then' in wall-clock order. The comment is misleading for readers trying to understand Mode 3 semantics (and the PR description explicitly calls out that the legacy write is async 'just as a safe measure').

title: Wrong metrics function on storage Create failure
body: When d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) on line 45. This records the failed storage operation's duration into the legacy histogram instead of the storage one. The error path of Create mirrors the success path on line 48 which uses recordStorageDuration, so this looks like a copy/paste mistake. Consequence: a storage outage will be reported in legacy metrics (and not in storage metrics), making on-call dashboards misleading.

title: Wrong metrics function on storage Update failure
body: When d.Storage.Update fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) on line 129. The success path on line 132 uses recordStorageDuration, so this is inconsistent. Unified-storage update failures are reported into the legacy histogram, skewing alerting/dashboards built on those metrics.

title: Delete success metric uses object name instead of kind
body: d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) passes the resource name where every other call site passes options.Kind. The error path on line 103 correctly uses options.Kind. Consequence: the storage_duration histogram gets one high-cardinality time series per deleted object name rather than one per Kind, which both breaks aggregation by Kind and risks Prometheus cardinality blow-up.

title: Async legacy DeleteCollection duration recorded as storage
body: Inside the goroutine that calls d.Legacy.DeleteCollection, the result is reported via d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). It should be d.recordLegacyDuration, like the equivalent goroutines in Create (line 56), Update (line 140), and Delete (line 113). Consequence: every DeleteCollection in mode 3 inflates the storage histogram and never appears in the legacy histogram, hiding real legacy-side latency and errors.

title: Delete uses bare logger for klog context, dropping kind/name/method
body: ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) is used in Delete, while every other verb uses ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, log) where log is enriched with kind, name and method via d.Log.WithValues(...). The local log is built on lines 95-96 but not attached to ctx. As a result, any code (including the async legacy goroutine) that pulls the logger via klog.FromContext(ctx) during a Delete will see the kind/name/method stripped, reducing observability and breaking log correlation for delete traffic specifically.

title: Update now lets legacy compute the merge independently of storage
body: The previous implementation read the current object from storage, called objInfo.UpdatedObject once, and passed the resulting 'updated' object to both Storage.Update and Legacy.Update. The new implementation passes the raw objInfo to d.Legacy.Update on line 139, so each backend will call objInfo.UpdatedObject against its own current state. If the objInfo applies a server-side merge (the normal Kubernetes pattern), the value legacy ends up with depends on what legacy already had, which in mode 3 is whatever the async legacy writes from previous operations have produced. This is a silent divergence risk between the source of truth and the 'safe measure' backup, and it is a behavior change vs. the prior mode 3 implementation that is not called out in the PR description.

title: Destroy does not wait for in-flight async legacy writes
body: Destroy calls d.Storage.Destroy() and d.Legacy.Destroy() immediately. Create (line 50), Update (line 134), Delete (line 108), and DeleteCollection (line 161) all spawn goroutines that hold references to d.Legacy and d.Storage and may still be mid-call when Destroy runs. There is no WaitGroup, channel, or context used to coordinate. Consequence: pending legacy writes can race with teardown of the legacy store, producing panics, lost writes, or partially-flushed state on shutdown.

title: Async legacy write inherits request context and is cancelled with it
body: Each async legacy goroutine derives its 10s timeout from the request ctx (e.g. line 51: context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)). If the client disconnects or the request context is cancelled, the legacy write is cancelled immediately, defeating the 'safe measure' purpose: the most common failure mode (client cancellation right after a successful response) is the one that drops the backup. Use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or context.Background() so the backup write survives request cancellation.

title: Legacy write errors are swallowed and not retried
body: In Create (line 55-57), Update (line 139-141), Delete (line 112-114), and DeleteCollection (line 165-167), an error from the legacy store is only fed into a metric and otherwise discarded. There is no log line, no retry, and no mechanism to surface or replay the failure. Consequence: if the legacy store is temporarily unavailable, every successful unified write silently leaves legacy out of sync forever, with no operator-visible signal beyond the metric counter.

title: Tests do not verify that legacy is called for any write
body: In TestMode3_Create (line 65), TestMode3_Update (line 345), TestMode3_Delete (line 230), and TestMode3_DeleteCollection (line 284) the test asserts only on the storage-side return value. None of them wait on the async goroutine or assert that the legacy mock expectation was actually hit (e.g. with m.AssertCalled or m.AssertExpectations). If a future refactor drops the async legacy call, or if the goroutine is silently cancelled by the test's context, they would still pass. The test names also describe 'unified store only', which contradicts the mode 3 contract.

title: Update goroutine measures startLegacy before defer cancel is registered
body: Inside the Update goroutine (lines 134-141) the order is: create ctx/cancel, set startLegacy := time.Now(), defer cancel(). The defer is registered AFTER startLegacy is captured, so the recorded duration excludes the cancel defer registration but the other three goroutines (Create, Delete, DeleteCollection) place defer cancel() before capturing startLegacy. The captured time now includes the WithTimeoutCause call, inflating the legacy histogram for Update specifically and being inconsistent with the other verbs.

title: Storage.Create failure is recorded as a legacy-store failure
body: When d.Storage.Create fails, the error path calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of d.recordStorageDuration. Metrics dashboards that alert on the 'legacy' failure label will be misled: every unified-storage Create error will be misattributed to the legacy backend. The same pattern is also wrong on the Update path (line 129).

title: Storage.Update failure is recorded as a legacy-store failure
body: On d.Storage.Update error, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage). It should be d.recordStorageDuration. As written, every failure to update the unified store will be reported in the legacy Prometheus bucket, breaking alerting and SLO accounting for that label.

title: Delete records the resource name where the kind label is expected
body: After a successful Storage.Delete, the success metric is recorded as d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage). The third argument is the resource name (e.g. "foo"), but every other method (Create, Update, List, DeleteCollection) passes options.Kind (e.g. "Playlist"). This is inconsistent and exposes the metric to unbounded cardinality (one new series per object name).

title: Delete strips contextual log fields before calling Storage.Delete
body: The method builds log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method) but then installs d.Log (not log) into the context: ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log). The downstream Storage.Delete will only see the base DualWriterMode3 logger and will log without the per-call name/kind/method fields, while Create/Update/List/DeleteCollection correctly install `log`.

title: Legacy Update receives the raw objInfo instead of the storage-transformed object
body: The previous implementation of Update first read the object from Storage, ran objInfo.UpdatedObject against that read, and then handed an updateWrapper carrying the already-transformed object to the Legacy store. The new code simply forwards the original objInfo to d.Legacy.Update. The legacy backend will now fetch its own old object and run UpdatedObject against a potentially different base (different RV, different UID, different defaults) than the unified store saw. The 'safe measure' requirement that the two stores stay consistent is therefore not guaranteed on Update.

title: Constructor docstring no longer matches the new write semantics
body: The comment "Mode 3 represents writing to LegacyStorage and Storage and reading from Storage" implies a synchronous write to both stores. The new implementation writes to Storage first and then asynchronously to LegacyStorage, with a 10s timeout. A reader of this file will be misled about ordering, failure semantics, and which store is the source of truth.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and get cancelled with the client
body: The goroutines in Create (line 51), Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163) all derive their context from the outer ctx via context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...). If the HTTP client disconnects mid-request, the request context is cancelled and the in-flight legacy write is aborted, defeating the entire point of an asynchronous 'safe measure' write. The async path should use a detached context (e.g. context.Background() with its own timeout) so legacy stays in sync even when the API client has gone away.

title: Background legacy writers have no panic recovery and no back-pressure
body: Each Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection spawns a bare goroutine that talks to d.Legacy. There is no recover() guard, so a panic in the legacy backend (or in the metric recorder) will crash the process. There is also no bounded worker pool, so a burst of writes can spawn an unbounded number of goroutines all holding the request's context-derived timeouts and any captured locals.

title: Update async goroutine measures legacy duration after creating the timeout context
body: In the Update async block, startLegacy := time.Now() runs after context.WithTimeoutCause(...) so the recorded legacy duration includes context-setup overhead. The Create and DeleteCollection goroutines place startLegacy := time.Now() before the context call, which is what the metric is meant to measure. The numbers reported in Prometheus will therefore be inconsistent across write methods.

title: Mode 3 write tests never verify the async legacy call happened
body: TestMode3_Create, TestMode3_Update, TestMode3_Delete and TestMode3_DeleteCollection all register mock expectations on the legacy store, but the test body returns immediately after the synchronous Storage call. Because the legacy write is dispatched in a goroutine that may not have run (or even started) before the test exits, the assertions do not actually prove the legacy backend is being written to. The very behavior the PR is supposed to guarantee ('write to unified then async to legacy') is not covered by any passing assertion. The tests also do not assert that legacy is NOT called on reads (TestMode3_Get only checks storage).

title: Shared testify mock is accessed concurrently by the async legacy goroutine
body: Each test builds a single m := &mock.Mock{} and reuses it for both legacyStoreMock and storageMock. mock.Mock is not safe for concurrent access. The async legacy goroutine that the production code dispatches will record calls on the same mock while the test goroutine is checking assertions. Even where tests are extended to verify legacy calls (as recommended in the previous finding), this sharing makes any such verification racy; the production code's async write needs to be observed via a synchronous seam or its own mock, not via the same shared mock.

title: TestMode3_Get re-introduces the local prometheus shadow the Mode1 cleanup removed
body: The Mode1 test cleanup removed a local 'p := prometheus.NewRegistry()' so that the package-level registry is reused, but TestMode3_Get still has the local shadow. This is inconsistent with the Mode1 test and obscures which registry is in use; it should be removed (or, if a per-test registry was intentionally required, the Mode1 cleanup should be reverted).

title: Per-method comments still describe the old synchronous dual-write semantics
body: The Create comment says 'writes to LegacyStorage and Storage' and the DeleteCollection comment says 'deletes from both LegacyStorage and Storage'. The implementation now performs Storage first and Legacy asynchronously, so these comments misrepresent the ordering and the failure model (a legacy error no longer surfaces to the caller). They should be aligned with the PR description.

title: Double-checked locking is incomplete; concurrent callers will redundantly re-read the manifest
body: The function checks the cache under RLock, then re-acquires a write Lock to populate it. However, it does not re-check `entryPointAssetsCache` after acquiring the write Lock. When N goroutines invoke GetWebAssets concurrently while the cache is still nil (typical at server startup), every one of them passes the RLock check, then takes the write Lock sequentially, and each independently reads `assets-manifest.json` from disk and overwrites the global. The expensive I/O — the very reason the cache exists — is repeated N times. After `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` (line 48) and before the `cdn := ""` line, add `if entryPointAssetsCache != nil && cfg.Env != setting.Dev { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` to make this a correct double-checked locking pattern. Without it, the race detector is silenced but the cache offers no benefit under cold-cache concurrency.

title: No regression test added for the data race fix
body: This PR explicitly fixes a data race on `entryPointAssetsCache`, yet no test file is added or modified. There is no existing concurrent test for GetWebAssets that would have caught the original race, and nothing here guards against reintroducing the same race (e.g. by removing the mutex or by reverting to the unlocked read in a future refactor). A short test that calls GetWebAssets from many goroutines in parallel and runs under `go test -race` would lock the fix in place and exercise the double-checked locking pattern described above.

title: Cache is overwritten with nil on read error, defeating caching for subsequent calls
body: On line 69 the code unconditionally assigns `entryPointAssetsCache = result` and on line 70 returns `entryPointAssetsCache, err`. If `readWebAssetsFromFile` returns an error (network blip, transient I/O failure), `result` is nil and the global cache is overwritten with nil. Because the write Lock is held, every concurrent caller will observe the cleared cache and will each attempt the file read again; any previously cached value is permanently lost even if it was still valid. The assignment should only happen on success, e.g. `if err == nil { entryPointAssetsCache = result }` before the return. (Note: this behavior pre-existed, but the PR is the natural place to fix it now that the variable is properly guarded.)

title: Return statement is redundant and obscures intent
body: Line 70 returns `entryPointAssetsCache, err` after having just assigned `entryPointAssetsCache = result` on line 69. Both expressions yield the same pointer, but reading the code one must verify that no other goroutine could have changed the global between the assignment and the return. While holding the write Lock this is safe, but the redundancy invites future bugs (e.g. someone removing the mutex thinking the local `result` is the returned value). Simply `return result, err` is clearer and removes the indirection.

title: Write lock held during slow HTTP and filesystem I/O
body: The write lock acquired at line 48 is held (via defer on line 49) across the potentially slow operations on lines 55-66: an HTTP request via readWebAssetsFromCDN and a filesystem read via readWebAssetsFromFile. Under concurrent requests with a cold cache, every caller will serialize on this single mutex. On a slow disk or CDN, this can cause request pile-up and latency spikes during the first requests after process start. The I/O should happen outside the critical section, with the lock held only for the pointer assignment, e.g. compute the result first, then Lock() briefly to install it.

title: Double-checked locking is incomplete; concurrent cold-cache callers all redo the I/O
body: The pattern takes RLock, snapshots the pointer, releases RLock, checks for nil, then takes Lock. After acquiring Lock, the cache is never re-checked. So if N goroutines all observe a nil cache under RLock, they all proceed to perform the file/CDN read in series (since the Lock from line 48 also serializes them) and each overwrites entryPointAssetsCache with its own result. This is functionally correct but wastes I/O and means the first N callers all pay the full initialization cost. Re-check entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the write lock and early-return if populated, or use sync.Once to gate the load so only the first caller does the work.

title: Cached pointer is shared with all callers; lock only protects the slot, not the contents
body: The mutex added in this PR only guards the entryPointAssetsCache variable itself. The function returns that exact pointer on every call (line 70), so every caller receives the same *dtos.EntryPointAssets instance, including its JSFiles slice header. Any caller that mutates the returned object (e.g. appending to JSFiles or relying on a copy-on-write assumption) will race against every other concurrent reader and against future cache reads. The PR description says it fixes a data race, but this remaining aliasing is a latent source of the same class of bug; consider returning a copy or documenting the aliasing contract.

title: Data race fix ships without a regression test
body: The PR fixes a data race on the global entryPointAssetsCache but adds no test to verify the fix or guard against future regressions. A small concurrent test (e.g. many goroutines calling GetWebAssets in a loop with t.Parallel, or any test invoking it under `go test -race`) would have caught the original race and now lock in the fix. Without it, the cache mutex can be removed in a future cleanup and the race will silently reappear.

title: Incomplete double-checked locking causes redundant manifest reads and serializes dev-mode calls
body: After taking the RLock, the code releases it and then takes the write lock without re-checking the cache. Two consequences: (1) in non-dev mode, concurrent cold-start requests each block on the write lock and then each read the manifest file from disk; the second reader does no fast-path re-check and re-does the I/O. (2) in dev mode, every call bypasses the cache and re-reads the file, but now all dev-mode calls also serialize on the write lock instead of running in parallel as before. Adding a re-check inside the critical section (e.g. `if entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }`), or replacing the RWMutex with sync.Once / atomic.Pointer[dtos.EntryPointAssets], would remove the redundant I/O and the dev-mode serialization.

title: enableSqlExpressions has dead/confusing logic that always returns false
body:
The newly added `enableSqlExpressions` function reads:

```go
func enableSqlExpressions(h *ExpressionQueryReader) bool {
    enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)
    if enabled {
        return false
    }
    return false
}
```

The function unconditionally returns `false` regardless of the feature flag's state. The `enabled` variable and the `if enabled { return false }` branch are dead code (both branches return `false`). This is confusing because:
1. The function name suggests it checks whether SQL expressions should be enabled.
2. A future maintainer is likely to interpret this as buggy logic and "fix" it (e.g. by returning `enabled` or `!enabled`), which could accidentally re-enable the vulnerable code path.
3. The `featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions` check is functionally meaningless.

For a security hardening PR, the intent should be expressed unambiguously. Either simplify to `return false` with a comment referencing CVE-2024-9264, or rename and invert the logic so the dead branches are removed.

title: Misleading error message for a security-driven disablement
body: When SQL expressions are rejected the user-visible error is `sqlExpressions is not implemented`. The feature is not merely unimplemented; it has been intentionally disabled to mitigate CVE-2024-9264 (RCE/LFI). A user reading the error or a downstream log/alert may conclude the feature was forgotten rather than turned off for security reasons. The message should clearly state that the feature is disabled (e.g. reference the CVE / security release) so that operators and users understand why a previously working dashboard now errors.

title: No tests added for the SQL-expression disablement
body: The PR introduces a new code path (`enableSqlExpressions` gating `QueryTypeSQL` in `ReadQuery`) but adds no tests. For a security fix landing in the primary repo this is a significant gap: there is nothing in the test suite that asserts a SQL expression query is rejected, and nothing that documents the expected behaviour for downstream users / release notes readers. At minimum a test exercising `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` with `QueryTypeSQL` and asserting the new error should be added; ideally also a test covering `UnmarshalSQLCommand`/`NewSQLCommand` to confirm the in-memory DB stub returns the expected errors.

title: TablesList logs a misleading "error serializing sql" for the stubbed DB
body: `TablesList` calls `duckDB.RunCommands(...)` and, on error, logs `"error serializing sql"` and returns `fmt.Errorf("error serializing sql: %s", err.Error())`. With the new `DB` stub this branch is hit on every invocation because `RunCommands` always returns `errors.New("not implemented")`. The log/return message implies a SQL serialization issue occurred, which is misleading: nothing was actually serialized or attempted against DuckDB. The wording should reflect that the SQL expression backend is disabled (or simply that the operation is not implemented).

title: UnmarshalSQLCommand bypass path may not be covered by the ReadQuery gate
body: `UnmarshalSQLCommand` is still present in `pkg/expr/sql_command.go` and still constructs a `SQLCommand` via `NewSQLCommand`. The security gate added in this PR only lives inside `ReadQuery` (the `ExpressionQueryReader` path). If `UnmarshalSQLCommand` is reachable from any other request handling code (legacy path, direct test usage, future callers), the gate in `ReadQuery` will not protect that path. It happens to be safe today only because `NewSQLCommand` -> `sql.TablesList` -> `RunCommands` returns the "not implemented" stub error, which is a fragile defense-in-depth arrangement. The PR should either verify that `UnmarshalSQLCommand` is dead code and remove it, or add the same disablement check inside it explicitly.

title: Misleading user-facing error message for disabled SQL expressions
body: The error message returned when a user submits a QueryTypeSQL is 'sqlExpressions is not implemented'. SQL expressions are in fact implemented (stubs in pkg/expr/sql/db.go); they are disabled for security reasons (CVE-2024-9264). Users who try to use the (documented) SQL Expressions feature will see a message suggesting the feature does not exist, when the actual reason is a security disable. The message should explain that SQL expressions are disabled for security, or at minimum say 'disabled' rather than 'not implemented'.

title: Misleading control flow in enableSqlExpressions risks re-introducing CVE-2024-9264
body: The newly added enableSqlExpressions function computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` but then ignores the computed value: both the `if enabled` branch and the fallthrough return false. The function therefore always returns false regardless of the feature flag. While this currently produces the desired (safe) behavior of always disabling SQL expressions, the structure suggests the gate is conditional and invites a future maintainer to 'fix' the obvious dead branch (e.g. by returning true in one of the paths) which would silently re-enable SQL expressions and re-introduce the RCE/LFI vulnerability that this PR is fixing. The function should be written as an unconditional `return false` with a comment referencing CVE-2024-9264, or the unused feature-flag check should be removed entirely.

title: NewSQLCommand/UnmarshalSQLCommand are direct entry points not gated by the new disable check
body: The disable check is only added in pkg/expr/reader.go's QueryTypeSQL case. The exported functions NewSQLCommand (line 25) and UnmarshalSQLCommand (line 51) in this file remain callable from any other caller in the codebase without going through that check. Today this is mitigated only by the fact that the new pkg/expr/sql/db.go stubs return 'not implemented' instead of executing SQL, so no DuckDB-backed SQL is run. This is a defense-in-depth concern: any code path (existing or future) that calls NewSQLCommand or UnmarshalSQLCommand directly will reach the stubbed backend, and a future change that re-implements those stubs to call real SQL would re-introduce CVE-2024-9264 without touching reader.go. The same gate (or an explicit early return with the security error) should be enforced inside NewSQLCommand so that disabling SQL expressions cannot be bypassed by callers that don't use ExpressionQueryReader.

title: New stubbed SQL backend has no tests and may break existing SQL expression tests
body: pkg/expr/sql/db.go introduces a new DB type whose three methods (TablesList, RunCommands, QueryFramesInto) all unconditionally return 'not implemented'. There are no tests added that exercise this file or that assert QueryTypeSQL now returns the expected error in pkg/expr/reader.go. Existing tests in pkg/expr that previously exercised the DuckDB-backed path (or any test that calls NewSQLCommand/UnmarshalSQLCommand or pkg/expr/sql.TablesList) will now fail with 'not implemented' instead of running the real SQL. These tests should be updated to assert the new disabled behavior, or new tests should be added covering the reader.go gating, otherwise a future regression that silently re-enables the vulnerable path could go undetected.

title: TablesList retains DuckDB-style command string even though backend is disabled
body: TablesList still constructs a DuckDB-flavoured command ('SELECT json_serialize_sql(\'%s\')', rawSQL) and calls the stub DB.RunCommands, which always returns 'not implemented'. Because pkg/expr/reader.go now blocks QueryTypeSQL before this code runs, and pkg/expr/sql/db.go stubs out the execution, there is no live vulnerability. However, the DuckDB-specific command string is now misleading dead code that documents a non-existent backend. It should either be removed (since TablesList will always error), or the function should short-circuit with a clear 'sql expressions are disabled' error before formatting any command, matching the user-facing message returned at pkg/expr/reader.go:131.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false; logic is dead/confusing and could be misread as a bug to be fixed later
body: The new function `enableSqlExpressions` reads `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns `false` in both branches of the subsequent `if`. The function is therefore equivalent to `return false`, regardless of the `FlagSqlExpressions` feature toggle. This is the correct security outcome (SQL expressions are always disabled, even if an admin re-enables the feature flag, so the flag cannot be used to bring back the vulnerable code path), but the implementation is misleading: the variable is named `enabled` but actually represents the inverted/disabled state, and the feature-flag check is effectively dead code. A future maintainer who reads this as "this is broken, the last return should be true" would silently re-introduce the CVE-2024-9264 RCE/LFI path. The function should either be a single `return false` with a comment explaining the CVE-related permanent disablement, or it should make the unconditional disablement explicit (e.g., `return false // SQL Expressions permanently disabled; see CVE-2024-9264`). As written, it is both confusing and a latent footgun for a critical security control.

title: Error string "sqlExpressions is not implemented" misleads users and operators
body: When a panel using a SQL expression is evaluated, the user now sees `sqlExpressions is not implemented`. SQL Expressions are fully implemented in this codebase — they have been deliberately disabled to mitigate CVE-2024-9264 (RCE/LFI via DuckDB). Saying "not implemented" will mislead end users into thinking it is a bug or a missing feature, and will make incident triage harder (operators will search for an unimplemented feature rather than a security disablement). The error should clearly state that SQL Expressions have been disabled for security reasons (and ideally reference the CVE / blog post so admins and users understand why).

title: No automated test asserts that SQL Expressions are disabled and return the expected error
body: This is a critical-severity security fix that introduces a new code path in `ReadQuery` (the `QueryTypeSQL` branch returning an error) and replaces the DuckDB-backed `pkg/expr/sql` implementation with stubs returning "not implemented". Despite being a security control, the PR adds no tests. At a minimum there should be a unit test in `pkg/expr` that exercises `ReadQuery` / `ExpressionQueryReader` with a `QueryTypeSQL` payload and asserts that the returned error matches the intended message, plus a test that `sql.TablesList` and `(*SQLCommand).Execute` no longer execute any SQL. Without these tests, a future refactor could silently re-enable the feature (e.g., by "fixing" the broken `enableSqlExpressions` logic or by re-introducing a real DuckDB dependency) and there would be no automated signal.

title: Dead method (*DB).TablesList is never called
body: The new stub `DB` in `pkg/expr/sql/db.go` defines a `TablesList(rawSQL string) ([]string, error)` method, but neither `parser.go` nor `sql_command.go` ever invokes `db.TablesList` — they call `RunCommands` and `QueryFramesInto` respectively. This method is unreachable dead code that adds a public-looking API surface to the stub package. It should be removed (or, if it is intended to be the replacement for the package-level `sql.TablesList`, that should actually be wired up to use it instead of going through `RunCommands`).

title: search.init goroutine panics when the events channel is closed
body: In the goroutine started by search.init, the receive `v := <-events` is not in the comma-ok form, and the loop then unconditionally calls `s.handleEvent(watchctx, v)`. The SQL backend closes the events channel via `defer close(stream)` when its poller returns (e.g., when backend.Stop calls cancel and `b.done` closes). After that, every iteration of the for loop receives nil for `v` (zero value of *WrittenEvent), and `s.handleEvent(watchctx, nil)` then dereferences `evt.Type` on a nil receiver, panicking the goroutine. Because the search watch is now started eagerly inside NewResourceServer on every startup, the lifecycle that closes this channel is reached on every shutdown. The receive should be `v, ok := <-events` with `if !ok { return }` so the goroutine terminates cleanly when the backend is torn down.

title: Finer-grain cache lock lets two callers build the same index concurrently
body: After this PR, bleveBackend.BuildIndex only takes cacheMu around the final map assignment (`b.cache[key] = idx`); the actual index creation (bleve.New/bleve.NewMemOnly and the ListIterator walk) runs unlocked. getOrCreateIndex itself has no synchronization, so two concurrent callers with the same NamespacedResource can both observe an empty cache (GetIndex returns nil), both call s.build, each constructs its own bleveIndex (running through the storage ListIterator independently), and then both contend on b.cacheMu — last writer wins. Each caller uses its own freshly built index for its Search/Origin call, so the cache may not reflect what the first caller is actually using, and the second caller's build duplicates work that was just done; if storage changes between the two walks the two indexes can diverge. Add per-key locking (e.g., a sync.Map of *sync.Mutex keyed by NamespacedResource, or use sync.Map directly) so only one goroutine builds a given index and other callers wait for it to be cached.

title: search.init watch goroutine is not bound to the server's lifecycle
body: search.init sets `watchctx := context.Background()` and passes it to `s.storage.WatchWriteEvents(watchctx)`, then spawns a goroutine that processes events with this background context. This context is completely independent of the server's cancellable context (`s.ctx`, which server.Stop cancels via s.cancel). Calling server.Stop therefore does not stop the search watch goroutine; it only terminates once the SQL backend itself is torn down (b.cancel) and the poller's defer closes the events channel. Combined with the missing comma-ok on the channel receive (related finding above), the goroutine can panic during shutdown rather than exit cleanly. The watch should be tied to a context derived from s.ctx so server.Stop halts search indexing promptly, and the backend poller should respect that context for cancellation.

title: Two independent database pollers run for WatchWriteEvents
body: Both search.init (search.go ~line 203) and server.initWatcher call s.backend.WatchWriteEvents, and the SQL backend starts a separate poller goroutine for each call. Each poller runs `listLatestRVs` plus per-resource `poll` queries against the database every defaultPollingInterval (100ms), producing essentially the same event stream. With both watchers active the backend is doing two full sets of polls for what could be a single shared source. Before this PR these two watchers were also started, but lazily on the first gRPC call; after this PR they are both started eagerly and synchronously inside NewResourceServer, so this 2x DB load is now paid on every startup. Consider having a single backend.WatchWriteEvents source that fans out to the search index and the broadcaster (e.g., a shared channel that searchSupport.handleEvent and the broadcaster both subscribe to).

title: Postgres branch is skipped instead of fixed in the integration test
body: The new lines `// TODO - fix this test for postgres` plus `t.Skip(...)` for GRAFANA_TEST_DB == "postgres" hide a real test reliability problem rather than fixing it. Now that NewResourceServer blocks on Init during module server construction, this code path is more sensitive to slow or failing init, which is plausibly contributing to the CI failure (the comment says "Works locally" but not in Drone). A skip only papers over the failure: the postgres path is no longer exercised at all in CI, so future regressions on it will go unnoticed. The TODO should be tracked and the test should actually run for postgres in CI, or the broader problem should be diagnosed (e.g., separate slow init in NewResourceServer from module server startup so the test has a chance to complete).

title: Watch goroutine never exits after backend channel close
body: In search.init(), the watch goroutine uses `for { v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v) }`. When the storage backend stops (e.g., via sql backend's `defer close(stream)` after `b.done` triggers), the channel is closed and `<-events` returns the zero value (a nil *WrittenEvent) forever. handleEvent then hits the `!slices.Contains(...)` branch and logs `ignoring watch event type 0` on every iteration, leading to unbounded log spam and a leaked goroutine for the lifetime of the process. The loop should be `for v := range events` (which exits when the channel closes) or use a `select` on a done channel. Combined with `watchctx := context.Background()` (which never cancels), there is no way to stop this goroutine. The PR's introduction of eager Init makes this more likely to be exercised during normal shutdown.

title: Trace propagation fix is incomplete for the watch loop
body: The PR description states 'Fixes trace propagation by passing span contexts down', but the long-running watch goroutine spawned in search.init() still uses `watchctx := context.Background()` (note the `// new context?` comment, suggesting this was intentionally left undone). The init() and build() functions now correctly propagate the new ctx via `ctx, span := s.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)`, but the watch loop and everything downstream of it (all handleEvent invocations) lose the trace context. Either fix this to use the parent ctx for trace propagation, or document in the commit message why watch events are intentionally not traced.

title: NewResourceServer now blocks on initialization, behavior change
body: NewResourceServer now synchronously calls `s.Init(ctx)` before returning, which performs lifecycle init, builds the entire search index across all namespaces, and starts the watch loop. Previously this was deferred to the first gRPC call. Callers that constructed the server (e.g., tests, alternate wiring code) expecting non-blocking construction, or that supplied their own timeout for init, will now block indefinitely on a potentially expensive operation with no timeout context. The PR description asks 'Does anything else depend on initializing US lazily? What could this break?' but no callers were audited in the diff. At minimum, the timeout/context contract of NewResourceServer has changed and any test or production path that wanted to construct a server without paying the init cost will be affected.

title: Search watch goroutine is leaked on partial init failure
body: Init now runs: lifecycle.Init -> search.init -> initWatcher. search.init spawns the long-running watch goroutine (the one with the closed-channel bug above). If search.init succeeds but initWatcher then fails (returning the error from NewResourceServer), the watch goroutine is never torn down and the server is returned as nil to the caller, so nothing in the caller path can cancel it. There is no rollback or cleanup if a later init step fails after an earlier one has started goroutines. This needs either an explicit cleanup step or defer-with-undo pattern to release resources on partial init failure.

title: BuildIndex span context is not propagated, inconsistent with other trace fixes
body: The PR changes `_, span := ...Start(ctx, ...)` to `ctx, span := ...Start(ctx, ...)` in search.init, search.build, and sql.GetResourceStats to propagate the new ctx to downstream calls. bleve.BuildIndex still has `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, tracingPrexfixBleve+"BuildIndex")` and never reassigns ctx, so the new ctx (with the span) is discarded. This is inconsistent with the stated goal of fixing trace propagation. Either change this to `ctx, span := ...` for consistency, or note that BuildIndex has no child spans (and the discrepancy is intentional). Note also that the surrounding `_, err := index.NewBatch()`-style code creates side effects (a batch is opened); if any future code adds tracing to those paths it would silently miss the parent context.

title: Stop writes s.initErr without synchronization
body: Stop assigns `s.initErr = fmt.Errorf("service is stopping")` outside of any mutex or sync.Once, while Init reads it under once.Do. After the PR, in practice the calls don't overlap (Init runs synchronously inside NewResourceServer and returns before Stop is reachable), but the field is still shared mutable state guarded only by `s.once` for reads in Init. A future change that calls Init externally (the once.Do machinery is still there, suggesting that was the intent) would race with Stop. Consider removing the s.initErr mutations in Stop entirely or guarding the field with a mutex.

title: Postgres skip is a workaround, not a fix
body: The diff adds `if dbType == "postgres" { t.Skip(...) }` with a TODO, but this PR directly changes the unified storage init path that the test exercises (the test boots the storage server target, which now eagerly calls Init inside NewResourceServer). The exact reason the test fails on postgres is unknown and unfixed, and the new init-at-startup behavior is not validated against postgres. The PR's main goal (fixing context-cancelled errors from lazy init) should be covered by a test that exercises the storage server target under at least one DB, not just mysql.

title: Data race on outer err variable in search.init goroutines
body: In search.init, the goroutine passed to group.Go captures the outer 'err' variable that was declared at line 181 (stats, err := s.storage.GetResourceStats(...)). Because group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers) permits multiple goroutines to run concurrently, each goroutine writes to that outer 'err' at line 190 (err = s.build(...)) and reads it at line 191 (return err). Multiple goroutines writing to and reading from the same variable without synchronization is a data race that Go's race detector would flag. With the PR moving init to run unconditionally at startup with real concurrency (initWorkers > 1), the race is now reachable in normal operation. Declare a local err inside the closure (or return the build error directly) instead of reusing the outer variable.

title: Data race on totalBatchesIndexed counter
body: totalBatchesIndexed is declared at line 177 and incremented (line 189: totalBatchesIndexed++) from inside the goroutine launched by group.Go. With group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers), multiple goroutines run in parallel and each performs a read-modify-write on the same counter without synchronization. The value reported in span.AddEvent at line 199 (and emitted via s.log.Info at line 216) is therefore non-deterministic. Use atomic.AddInt or a mutex around the increment.

title: Unsynchronized writes to s.initErr in Stop can race with Init
body: Stop (lines 320-342) writes to s.initErr (lines 321, 328, 339) without any synchronization, while Init (lines 293-318) both reads and writes s.initErr inside sync.Once. Since Init is part of the public ResourceServer interface and can be invoked by callers, a caller that calls Init and Stop concurrently will trigger a data race on s.initErr. The pre-existing lazy-init model made this easier to hit (any RPC handler could race with shutdown). Even though NewResourceServer now calls Init synchronously, the public surface still permits external concurrent use. Protect s.initErr with a mutex, or use atomic.Value/atomic.Pointer.

title: Cancel function leaks if Init fails inside NewResourceServer
body: NewResourceServer creates a cancellable background context at lines 229-235 and stores its cancel function in s.cancel. It then calls s.Init(ctx) at line 258. If Init returns an error, NewResourceServer returns nil and the error at line 261, dropping the local s. The cancel function is never invoked, so the watcher context (and the goroutines that depend on it, including the event-pump goroutine spawned in search.init at line 207 and the broadcaster goroutine in initWatcher) cannot be cancelled by the caller. Any partial init work continues to consume backend resources (a SQL poller, an indexing goroutine) until the backend is independently stopped. Call cancel() before returning nil in the error path so the caller can recover cleanly and the background goroutines terminate.

title: Postgres skip added instead of fixing the underlying test
body: The PR adds an unconditional skip for postgres (lines 36-38) along with a TODO acknowledging the test should be fixed. The integration test now runs only when GRAFANA_TEST_DB is mysql (sqlite3 is also skipped). The most common CI database (postgres) is no longer covered by TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer, reducing confidence that the storage server target still works end-to-end. The TODO should be resolved rather than carrying the skip forward.

title: Compilation error: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() called without required argument
body: The change introduces a call `!isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments in `UsernameForm.authenticate`. The only available method in the inheritance chain is `UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)`, which requires a `UserModel` argument. There is no zero-argument overload, so this code will not compile and the entire services module will fail to build. The intended call is almost certainly `!isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())` (or, more defensively, guarding against a null user). Without this fix, none of the new UsernameForm re-authentication tests (e.g. `PasskeysUsernameFormTest.webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey_reauthentication`) can be executed.

title: shouldDisplayAuthenticators not overridden alongside shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators
body: The new `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators` override in `WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator` returns `false`, ensuring no authenticators bean is set on the form. However, the related hook `shouldDisplayAuthenticators(AuthenticationFlowContext)` in the parent `WebAuthnAuthenticator` (line ~147) still returns `context.getUser() != null` and is not overridden here. During a re-authentication with `context.getUser() != null`, `fillContextForm` therefore sets `WebAuthnConstants.SHOULD_DISPLAY_AUTHENTICATORS=true` while `WebAuthnAuthenticatorsBean` is null. The login template can render an empty authenticator section or otherwise leak inconsistent UI state. `shouldDisplayAuthenticators` must also return `false` here for the conditional UI path to be consistent with the 'Do not show authenticators during login with conditional passkeys' intent stated in the comment.

title: NoSuchElementException import is now unused
body: The diff replaces `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, () -> driver.findElement(By.xpath("//form[@id='webauth']")))` with a positive `Matchers.notNullValue()` assertion, so the `org.openqa.selenium.NoSuchElementException` import is no longer referenced. Leaving the unused import can fail strict unused-import checks and adds noise; it should be removed in the same commit.

title: Compile error: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() called without required UserModel argument
body: In UsernameForm.authenticate, the new condition `!isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` is invoked with no arguments. The only matching definition in the codebase is `protected boolean isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` in UsernamePasswordForm, which requires a UserModel. As written, this file will fail to compile and the intended re-authentication change will not take effect at all. The call needs to be `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`, or a no-arg overload must be added (e.g., `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` that delegates to the user-taking version using the current AuthenticationFlowContext).

title: Regression: webauthn conditional UI no longer initialized on the initial login page (user == null)
body: The diff removes `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` from the user==null branch and replaces it with a new check `if (isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()))`.
