A shortcut of any length other than 2 will produce ids the default provider cannot decode (`IllegalArgumentException("Expected length of 6"`), and `encodeTokenId` will silently write the wrong number of characters. `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit` also does not enforce a 2-char length on `getShortcut()`, so an implementer that follows the documented 3-letter contract will only fail at runtime when an access token is issued or introspected. Either the Javadoc must be updated to "2-letter shortcut, unique across grants" or the codec must be generalised and the runtime length check removed.

title: OAuth2GrantTypeFactory adds a new abstract method (breaking SPI change with no default)
body: `String getShortcut();` was added to `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` as a fully abstract method with no default implementation. Every in-repo extension (AuthorizationCode, ClientCredentials, Refresh, ResourceOwnerPassword, TokenExchange, CIBA, Device, PreAuthorizedCode, Permission, plus any downstream implementations) is now required to implement it. Any third-party grant factory (token-exchange variants, custom grants, RAR-based extensions that Keycloak explicitly supports) that builds against the old SPI will fail to load with `AbstractMethodError` or `java.lang.Error: Unresolved compilation problem`, depending on how the SPI is loaded. The PR does not call this out as a breaking change in the description, and there is no default implementation (e.g. derived from `getId()`) to keep existing extensions working.

title: postInit shortcut-collision check is incomplete
body: The post-startup validation only asserts `grantsByShortcuts.size() != grantsToShortcuts.size()`, which detects duplicate shortcuts among grants but ignores the reserved shortcuts declared in `AccessTokenContext.SessionType` (`on`, `of`, `tr`, `un`) and `AccessTokenContext.TokenType` (`rt`, `lt`, `un`). Notably, `RefreshTokenGrantTypeFactory.GRANT_SHORTCUT = "rt"` already coincides with `AccessTokenContext.TokenType.REGULAR.getShortcut()` ("rt"), making the encoded id and the lookup maps ambiguous on inspection. The same applies to `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.UNKNOWN = "na"`: a custom grant using `"na"` as its shortcut would silently overwrite the UNKNOWN entry rather than being rejected at startup. A stronger startup assertion verifying (a) every grant shortcut has length 2, (b) no grant shortcut collides with any `SessionType`/`TokenType`/`UNKNOWN` shortcut, and (c) the maps have matching sizes would catch these classes of foot-guns before any token is issued.

title: isAccessTokenId matcher has wrong substring indices and inverted return logic
body:
Two bugs in the new isAccessTokenId matcher combined defeat its purpose of verifying the grant-type shortcut:

  1. Wrong substring indices. The encoded prefix format is sessionType(2) + tokenType(2) + grantType(2), so the grant shortcut is at indices 4..5 (substring(4, 6)). The code uses substring(3, 5), which captures the second token-type char plus the first grant-type char (e.g. for "onrtac" it returns "ta" instead of "ac").
  2. Inverted return: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` accepts any token whose (wrong) substring is not equal to the expected grant shortcut, and rejects the ones whose substring accidentally equals it. For the current shortcuts ("ac","cc","ro","rt","ci","dg") substring(3,5) never equals a 2-letter grant shortcut by accident, so the matcher silently passes for any well-formed encoded id regardless of actual grant type.

Consequence: any test using expectCodeToToken / expectDeviceCodeToToken / expectRefresh / expectAuthReqIdToToken does not actually assert the grant-type shortcut, so regressions where the encoder emits the wrong grant shortcut will not be caught.

title: Null-check parameter is wrong: checks grantType but message says rawTokenId
Public copy constructor Context(Context) was silently removed
body: The diff deletes the previously existing public copy constructor `public Context(Context context)` from `OAuth2GrantType.Context` (public static class in a public interface). Any external or subclass code that did `new Context(existingContext)` will fail to compile against this SPI after the change. The PR does not mention this as a breaking change and there is no replacement for the copy semantics that the removed constructor provided (copying all transitive state of an existing context). At a minimum the removal needs to be called out and ideally the constructor should be preserved (extended to also propagate grantType).

title: New abstract method getShortcut() is a breaking SPI change for third-party grant factories
body: The interface `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` gains the abstract method `String getShortcut();`. The PR updates every in-tree implementation, but any third-party `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` provider will fail to load after this change because it no longer implements all interface methods. Such a breaking change should at least ship with a default implementation in the interface (e.g. returning the grant id truncated or the first two letters) to preserve backward compatibility, or be announced in upgrade/migration docs.

title: requireNonNull check is on grantType, not rawTokenId
body: The fourth null-check is `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed");`. The argument is `grantType` (copied from the previous line) and the message wrongly refers to `rawTokenId`. The intended line is `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed");`. As written, a null `rawTokenId` passes silently, which later causes a "null:<uuid>" string in `encodeTokenId` or an NPE for consumers of `getRawTokenId()`.

title: isAccessTokenId matcher has wrong substring indices and inverted condition
body:
The new `isAccessTokenId` matcher does `items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut) return false;`. There are two independent bugs here:

1. The prefix is 6 chars `ST TT GG` where the grant shortcut is at indices 4..5 (0-based), so it should be `substring(4, 6)`. With the current indices the value extracted is "ta" for any well-formed token id, so it never equals any real grant shortcut (`ac`, `rt`, `dg`, `ci`, ...).
2. The condition is inverted: when the substring DOES match the expected shortcut the matcher returns `false` (fail), when it does NOT match it falls through to the UUID check and returns `true` (pass).

Net effect: the matcher enforces only the UUID format and never actually checks the encoded grant shortcut, so `expectCodeToToken`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, and `expectAuthReqIdToToken` will continue to pass even if the token ID has the wrong (or no) grant shortcut. The correct body is approximately `if (!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false; return isUUID().matches(items[1]);`.

title: Javadoc says "3-letters shortcut" but all implementations are 2-letter
body: The Javadoc on `getShortcut()` says "usually like 3-letters shortcut of specific grants" but every factory added in this PR (`ac`, `cc`, `ro`, `rt`, `dg`, `ci`, `te`, `pc`, `pg`, plus `na` for unknown) and the `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider` itself rely on a 2-character fixed width (the tokenizer even asserts `encodedContext.length() != 6`). The doc string should be corrected to "2-letters" (or simply "short") so future implementers do not accidentally introduce 3-character shortcuts that will silently fail to decode.

title: testIncorrectGrantType catches RuntimeException too broadly
body: `testIncorrectGrantType` does `catch (RuntimeException iae) { /* ignored */ }`. `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId` is documented to throw `IllegalArgumentException` for an unknown grant shortcut, but the test will also treat unrelated runtime errors (NPE, IllegalStateException, etc.) as "expected". The assertion should catch `IllegalArgumentException` (or `assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> ...)`) and the wrong-shape test data (`ofrtac:5678`) should be revisited in light of the substring bug in `AssertEvents.isAccessTokenId`.

title: Typo in authenticator alias 'delayed-suthenticator-config'
body: The alias for the 'delayed-authenticator' execution is set to 'delayed-suthenticator-config' (with the substring 'suthenticator' instead of 'authenticator'). The alias should be 'delayed-authenticator-config' to be consistent with the authenticator ID it labels. This is a naming typo and does not affect functionality, but should be corrected.

title: Recovery codes are not consumed after use; the same code can be reused indefinitely
body: In the isValid method for recovery codes (lines 326-340), the code returns true if any stored code equals the input via 'generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))' but never removes or marks the consumed code. This breaks the single-use property of recovery codes - the same code can be used to log in as many times as desired. It also breaks the downstream logic in RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.isRecoveryAuthnCodeInputValid: because the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel reconstructed from the credential data has no 'used' codes, allCodesUsed() always returns false, so the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is never triggered and the credential is never replaced. The local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider handles this correctly; the test storage provider should mirror that behavior (e.g., by removing the consumed code from the stored list or tracking a used-codes list) so that tests against a federated user storage actually exercise the production behavior.

title: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only exercises the happy path
body: The new testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only verifies that setup succeeds and that a single recovery code can be used to log in. It does not verify: (1) an invalid recovery code is rejected, (2) a recovery code cannot be reused once consumed (the single-use property), (3) when all recovery codes are consumed the user is prompted to set up new ones via the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action, (4) recovery codes can be disabled or removed via admin REST or the account console, or (5) the logoutOtherSessions=false branch of setupRecoveryKeysForUserWithRequiredAction. Given that this is the first end-to-end test for recovery codes in a federated storage, these negative and lifecycle cases should be covered.

title: Recovery codes cannot be disabled through the standard mechanism
body: disableCredentialType only handles OTP credentials; recovery codes fall through to the else branch and are simply logged as 'Unsupported to disable credential of type: ...'. Likewise, getDisableableCredentialTypesStream (lines 255-264) only adds CredentialModel.OTP. If a caller (e.g. admin REST or the account console) attempts to disable recovery codes for a user backed by this storage, the call silently does nothing while still returning success, leaving stale recovery codes in place. Recovery codes should be supported here the same way OTP is (set myUser.recoveryCodes = null and include RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE in the disableable types when present).

title: Federated recovery codes can be reused indefinitely
body: The new `isValid` implementation for `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE` only checks whether the supplied input matches any of the originally generated codes in `getCredentialData()`, but never updates the credential data or any other state to mark a code as consumed. As a result, once a recovery code is written into the federated store it can be submitted over and over and `isValid` will keep returning `true`. Recovery codes must be single-use; the local `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider` mutates its credential data on each successful `isValid` call, so the contract that the federated provider now implements must do the same (e.g. by calling `updateCredential` to remove the consumed code). Without this, the feature quietly downgrades from one-time codes to reusable passwords for any user coming from a federated storage that adopts this PR.

title: Federated recovery-code model never reports `allCodesUsed()`
body: `getCredentials` reconstructs the `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` via `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...)` from the full original code list stored in `credentialData`, and it never updates `credentialData` after `isValid` succeeds (see the other finding). Because the storage doesn't track consumption, `recoveryCodeCredentialModel.allCodesUsed()` in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` will always be `false` for federated users, so the credential is never removed and the `CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES` required action is never added even after the user has burned through every code. The credential data must be mutated on each successful validation (consumed code removed) for `allCodesUsed()` and the single-use semantics to work.

title: Federated recovery codes cannot be removed after use
body: After a successful verification, the authenticator calls `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())` whenever `allCodesUsed()` returns true. `removeStoredCredentialById` only operates on local (Keycloak DB) credentials. With this PR, `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(...)` now returns federated credentials as well, so when the federated store reports all codes consumed the call silently does nothing and the user is left with an empty/unusable credential. The code needs to use the credential-manager path appropriate for federated credentials (e.g. `removeCredential` / delegating to the user-storage provider), or branch on whether the credential is federated vs. stored.

title: `getCredentials` returns recovery-code credential with a fresh, non-matching ID
body: `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...)` is called without forwarding the stored `CredentialModel.id`. The credential returned to Keycloak therefore has a brand-new id, which means any later operation that uses that id (e.g. deletion via the account REST endpoint, or any internal code that persists the recovered model) will target a different record than what is actually stored. The `MyUser.recoveryCodes` `id` (set in `updateCredential` via `KeycloakModelUtils.generateId()`) must be propagated to the returned model so that id-based lookups and removals line up.

title: Return value of local `createCredential` is ignored
body: `createRecoveryCodesCredential` checks the boolean returned by `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` but discards the result of `recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel)`. If local creation fails (e.g. DB constraint violation, provider exception), the method returns normally and the caller in `RecoveryAuthnCodesAction.processAction` then calls `reqActionContext.success()` even though no credential was actually stored. Either propagate the failure (throw, or return a boolean) or at minimum log an error; `createOTPCredential` directly above for comparison returns a boolean for the same reason.

title: Login bean throws `NoSuchElementException` when no recovery credential exists
body: The constructor calls `credentialModelOpt.get()` without checking presence. Because `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` now consults federated storage first and then local storage, any user that legitimately has no recovery codes configured will cause this bean (and therefore the login form rendering it) to throw an unchecked `NoSuchElementException`. The pre-existing code already had the same `.get()` on `findFirst()`, but since the change introduces a new lookup path that crosses storage boundaries the failure surface expands. Guard with `ifPresent`/`orElseThrow` that produces a meaningful message, or have the template skip the prompt entirely when there is no credential.

title: Recovery-codes test never asserts codes are single-use
body: `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` only exercises a successful login with the first requested code. It does not (a) verify the same code cannot be reused on a second login, (b) verify that `allCodesUsed()` flips after consuming every code, (c) verify that the credential is removed from user storage once exhausted, or (d) verify that `CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES` becomes a required action afterwards. Given the federated-storage bugs reported above (no consumption tracking, `removeStoredCredentialById` is wrong API, id mismatch), these are exactly the cases that would catch them. The test currently passes only because it never asks the user-storage provider to mutate state.

title: `getCredential` shadows a different lookup semantic from the old call site
body: `getCredential` returns the first federated credential that matches the type, with no fallback if a local credential also exists. In the (admittedly rare) situation where both a federated and a local `recovery-authn-codes` credential coexist for the same user, the local one is silently ignored. This is a behaviour change vs. the previous code in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` and `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean`, which only ever looked at local storage. Worth either documenting the precedence rule explicitly in the javadoc or merging both sources with a deterministic ordering.

title: Raw recovery codes persisted to user storage
body: createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw (unhashed) generated recovery codes to JSON and passes them as the value of a UserCredentialModel to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...). The local DB branch goes through RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential(credentialModel) which is responsible for hashing the codes before persistence, but the user-storage branch hands the plaintext list to the user storage. Any user storage provider that does not independently hash the codes (such as the test provider introduced in this PR, which stores input.getChallengeResponse() verbatim in credentialData) will keep recovery codes in plaintext, and the credential 'value' field is left empty while 'credentialData' is misused as the secret store. Recovery codes must never be persisted in plaintext; the helper must hash them before calling updateCredential, exactly as the credential provider does on the local DB path.

title: Used recovery code is not invalidated and not removed after exhaustion
body: In the new RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE branch of isValid, the implementation only returns generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())). It never marks the consumed code as used, never rewrites the stored credential, and never triggers the credentialModel.allCodesUsed() transition that RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.action relies on. As a result, (a) the same recovery code can be reused on subsequent logins, (b) once all codes have been consumed the credential is never removed and the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is never added, leaving the user with an apparently infinite pool of one-time codes. The local DB RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider must therefore be performing this invalidation internally; the user storage provider needs to mirror that behaviour, otherwise the semantics diverge silently between local and federated storage.

title: New getCredentials does not null-check the user lookup
body: getCredentials calls getMyUser(user) and then immediately dereferences myUser.recoveryCodes and myUser.otp without checking for null. Every other method in this class that uses getMyUser (isConfiguredFor, isValid) explicitly checks `if (myUser == null) return false;` first. The new method should follow the same pattern, otherwise a user that is not in the backing map (e.g. an externally-removed user whose adapter is still being inspected) will trigger an NPE deep in the credential lookup.

title: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin does not assert one-time-use semantics
body: The new test only exercises a single successful login with one recovery code and then logs out. It never re-enters with the same code to verify it is rejected, never iterates through all codes to verify the credential is removed and CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES is added, and never verifies the codes are stored hashed. Given that the helper change introduces a plaintext-storage path and the test provider does not invalidate consumed codes, this gap means those regressions would slip through CI.

title: Hardcoded provider ID instead of constant
body: The provider id 'keycloak-recovery-authn-codes' is hardcoded as a string literal in createRecoveryCodesCredential. The companion class RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory exposes PROVIDER_ID for exactly this purpose; using the constant avoids silent breakage if the provider id is ever renamed.

title: Constructor dereferences Optional without isPresent check
body: RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean now reads the credential via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) and immediately calls credentialModelOpt.get() to feed RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel(...). If the credential is missing (e.g. the user has no recovery codes configured, or the credential was just removed because allCodesUsed() was true), this throws NoSuchElementException and the login form rendering fails. The original implementation only read from local storage and would NoSuch on the same condition, but the new code path makes the failure reachable in more scenarios (e.g. federated user whose credential expired). The bean should guard the missing-credential case.

title: Incomplete NPE fix in getSubGroupsStream(String, Integer, Integer)
body: The PR fixes getSubGroupsCount() to handle a null model from the supplier (when the underlying group is deleted concurrently), but the same `modelSupplier.get().X()` pattern that NPEs in that scenario still exists in getSubGroupsStream(String search, Integer firstResult, Integer maxResults) on line 256. The supplier (LazyModel wrapping getGroupModel -> cacheSession.getGroupDelegate().getGroupById(...)) returns null when the group no longer exists in storage, so any concurrent delete/deletion of a group being read through this method will still produce the very NPE the PR claims to fix. The fix should either be applied to this method the same way (capture the supplier result, null-check, and delegate to getDelegateForUpdate()/throw IllegalStateException as the sibling path does) or be hoisted into the supplier itself.

title: Incomplete NPE fix in getSubGroupsStream(Integer, Integer)
body: Same issue as the other getSubGroupsStream overloads: line 263 unconditionally dereferences the result of modelSupplier.get() without a null check. In the concurrent-deletion scenario this PR targets, getGroupModel() can return null and this method will still throw NPE. The fix applied to getSubGroupsCount() needs to be applied here too (capture the model, check for null, and either return Stream.empty() or route through getDelegateForUpdate()).

title: Incomplete NPE fix in getSubGroupsStream(String, Boolean, Integer, Integer)
body: Same issue as the other getSubGroupsStream overloads: line 269 unconditionally dereferences the result of modelSupplier.get() with no null guard. modelSupplier.get() can return null when the group was deleted between caching and read; calling a method on null throws the same NPE the PR is meant to eliminate. The fix for getSubGroupsCount() should be replicated here (and in the other two stream overloads).

title: Reader thread is never joined; assertion can race ahead of the worker
body: In createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti the worker thread is started with `new Thread(() -> { ... }).start();` and no reference is retained. The main thread then runs the deletion, sets `deletedAll.set(true)`, and immediately asserts that `caughtExceptions` is empty. There is no join, so a `groups(...)` call that is still in flight on the worker thread can throw (including the NPE under test) AFTER `deletedAll.set(true)` has flipped and AFTER the assertion has run; that exception is added to `caughtExceptions` too late and the test silently passes. The thread reference must be kept and `.join()`ed between `deletedAll.set(true)` and the assertion for this test to be a reliable guard against the NPE it claims to cover.

title: Reading thread is never joined before the assertion
body: The test starts a background thread that repeatedly calls `managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(...)`, then immediately proceeds to delete the groups, set `deletedAll.set(true)`, and assert on `caughtExceptions` without ever joining the thread. Two race conditions make this unreliable: (1) the thread can be in the middle of a `groups()` call when `deletedAll` flips to true; it will complete that call, potentially catch an exception, and add it to `caughtExceptions` AFTER `assertThat(caughtExceptions, Matchers.empty())` has already evaluated the list, so real NPEs are silently missed; (2) even if the thread exits before it, there is no happens-before edge between the thread's writes to `caughtExceptions` and the main thread's read (no join, no synchronization, no `volatile` semantics on the list beyond CopyOnWriteArrayList's internal ones), so the assertion is not guaranteed to observe the thread's writes. The test should capture the `Thread` reference, set `deletedAll.set(true)`, then call `thread.join()` before asserting.

title: NPE guard added only to getSubGroupsCount; same null-supplier pattern still NPEs in other methods
body: The fix changes `getSubGroupsCount()` to call `modelSupplier.get()` and return `null` if the underlying model is missing (group deleted after being cached). The same `modelSupplier` is used elsewhere in `GroupAdapter`, and those call sites will still throw NPE when a cached group is accessed after deletion: `getFirstAttribute` (line 149) calls `cached.getAttributes(keycloakSession, modelSupplier).getFirst(name)`; `getAttributeStream` (line 155) and `getAttributes` (line 163) call `cached.getAttributes(keycloakSession, modelSupplier)`; `hasDirectRole` (line 182) and `hasRole` (line 188) call `cached.getRoleMappings(keycloakSession, modelSupplier)`; `getRoleMappingsStream` (line 204) does the same; `getSubGroupsStream()` (line 240) calls `cached.getSubGroups(keycloakSession, modelSupplier)`; and the four-arg `getSubGroupsStream(...)` overloads (lines 256, 262, 268) call `modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` directly with no null check. `CachedGroup.getRoleMappings` only guards against a null supplier, not a null-resolved model, so the loader function `source -> source.getRoleMappingsStream()...` will NPE on a deleted group. Either the null-guard should be applied consistently (e.g., in `DefaultLazyLoader`/`CachedGroup` or by resolving once per method), or the test should be tightened so reviewers can see the full surface is covered.

title: NPE fix is incomplete: getSubGroupsStream variants still dereference null GroupModel
Reader thread is never joined, so the assertion can run while it is still executing
body: In createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti the background thread spawned at line 139 loops on !deletedAll.get() and is never joined before the assertion at line 157. After deletedAll.set(true) the main thread immediately runs assertThat(caughtExceptions, Matchers.empty()), but the reader thread can still be mid-call to managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(...). If that in-flight call (or the next iteration if the reader happens to be at the top of the loop) throws the NPE the PR is testing for, the exception is added to caughtExceptions only after the assertion has already evaluated, so the test passes spuriously and the bug is not caught. The test should join (or otherwise synchronize on) the reader thread after deletedAll.set(true) and before the assertion so all in-flight calls are observed.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key crashes on datetime fields
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key is copied verbatim from Paginator: it does `int(math.floor(value) if self._is_asc(for_prev) else math.ceil(value))` on `getattr(item, self.key)`. When the audit log endpoint passes `order_by="-datetime"` (and AuditLogEntry.datetime is a DateTimeField), this fetches a `datetime` object and calls `math.floor(datetime)`, which raises `TypeError: a float is required`. The class should reuse DateTimePaginator's float-conversion logic (datetime.strftime('%s.%f') * multiplier) or be parameterized by key type. As written, any request with `optimized_pagination=true` against the audit log endpoint will 500 instead of returning data.

title: enable_advanced_features kwarg is never forwarded to the paginator
body: `self.paginate(..., enable_advanced_features=True)` passes `enable_advanced_features` as a keyword argument to Endpoint.paginate. Sentry's Endpoint.paginate does not forward arbitrary kwargs to the paginator constructor; it consumes named options (per_page, cursor, etc.) itself and uses **kwargs for response wrapping, not for paginator instantiation. The OptimizedCursorPaginator instance is therefore created with `enable_advanced_features=False` (its default), so the entire `if self.enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0:` branch in paginator.py is unreachable. The user-facing `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter will appear to be honored while actually doing nothing — silently disabling the new code path. If forwarding is intended, paginate() must be changed to thread the kwarg into `paginator_cls(...)`; otherwise the call must construct the paginator directly.

title: Negative-offset pagination bypasses cursor-based paging invariants
body: When `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, OptimizedCursorPaginator slices the queryset with a negative start (`queryset[cursor.offset:stop]`). Cursor values come from the untrusted client via Cursor.from_string (cursors.py), so a caller can submit any negative integer and retrieve an arbitrary window into the queryset — e.g. `queryset[-1000000:stop]` is a valid SQL `OFFSET -1000000`. The comment "permissions are checked at the queryset level" is misleading: queryset-level filtering only restricts which organization is visible, not which row range is addressable. Combined with the fact that the cursor's `value` is also attacker-controlled, this exposes data the cursor protocol was specifically designed to forbid (the existing path in BasePaginator clamps to `max(0, offset)` for forward paging and validates offsets elsewhere). The new path must either reject negative offsets outright or bound them to a small, signed window (e.g. `max(-limit, cursor.offset)`).

title: BasePaginator offset clamping is a behavior change mislabeled as an optimization
body: BasePaginator previously did `queryset[offset:stop]` for both forward and prev pagination. The new code does `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` before slicing, which silently clamps negative offsets to 0 only for forward cursors. The inline comment calls this a "performance optimization for high-traffic scenarios" and asserts "the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions", but this is actually a behavior change, not an optimization: any existing caller that produced a negative offset on a forward (is_prev=False) cursor — including cursors built by _build_prev_values whose is_prev is later overridden, or test fixtures, or cursors from older clients — will now incorrectly restart from the beginning of the dataset instead of returning the intended page. The docstring and commit message should describe it as a behavior change, and the change should be validated against every existing caller before merging.

title: Comment claims an optimization that was not implemented
body: The diff only adds the comments "Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios" / "This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets" above the unchanged line `self.offset = int(offset)`. No code in this file was modified — Cursor.__init__ already accepted any int via `int(offset)`, and the comments are misleading the reader into believing a new capability has been introduced in this file. Either remove the comments or move the actual negative-offset handling to a place where it has an effect.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator ships with no tests and duplicates BasePaginator
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator re-implements get_result() by copy-pasting the entire BasePaginator.get_result body rather than overriding only the new branch. This duplicates ~60 lines of pagination logic that already has subtle behavior (cursor-value skipping, prev-page boundary row handling, count_hits short-circuit, post_query_filter). Combined with the fact that no tests are added in this PR (the description is literally "Test 1") and the get_item_key method is incorrect for the only caller that uses it, the change is unverified and any future fix to BasePaginator.get_result will not be reflected in OptimizedCursorPaginator. Refactor to inherit the path (e.g. override a single `_resolve_slice(cursor, limit, extra)` hook in BasePaginator and call super), and add at minimum: (a) a datetime-key test confirming correct cursor values, (b) a test confirming negative offsets raise/clampt appropriately, and (c) a regression test that the audit log endpoint returns the same rows via DateTimePaginator and OptimizedCursorPaginator for ordinary requests.

title: Typo `order_b` silently breaks ASC flip for pre-ordered querysets
body: In `BasePaginator.build_queryset`, the branch that flips a pre-existing `-(key)` ordering to `(key)` assigns to `queryset.query.order_b` instead of `queryset.query.order_by`. The typo means the in-memory queryset is never re-ordered when the key is already present in `queryset.query.order_by` (e.g. an upstream caller applied `order_by('-datetime')` before handing the queryset to the paginator). The DESC->ASC flip then silently no-ops while the surrounding code assumes ASC semantics, so backward-paginated queries can return rows that are not actually positioned before it. This file is touched by the PR, so a careful reviewer would want this fixed (or at least acknowledged) before merge.

title: Negative-offset `advanced` path returns tail of result set, not 'reverse pagination'
body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, the `enable_advanced_features` branch sets `start_offset = cursor.offset` (e.g. `-100`) and slices `queryset[-100:stop]`. With Django/Postgres this translates to `OFFSET -100 LIMIT ...`, which returns rows from the END of the result set, not the rows preceding the cursor. The surrounding comments ('efficient bidirectional pagination', 'reverse pagination from arbitrary positions', 'underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing') describe semantics that this code does not provide - it only shifts the window to the tail of the dataset. An admin who sends `cursor=<value>:-large:0` expecting 'the page before' will silently receive the last page. Either the comments should be rewritten to describe 'return a window from the tail' or the feature should be removed/renamed so callers are not misled.

title: Silent behavior change in shared `BasePaginator` for non-prev cursors
body: `BasePaginator.get_result` previously evaluated `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` for all callers; the new code sets `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. For non-prev cursors, a negative offset that previously produced a tail-of-result window now silently clamps to 0 and returns the head. `BasePaginator` powers `DateTimePaginator`, `Paginator`, and many other endpoints beyond `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`; this is an API/behavior change to a shared base class that is not justified by the PR description and could break any client (or test) that relied on negative-offset tail access. The change should either be confined to the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` or called out explicitly in the PR description.

title: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` is a near-verbatim copy of `BasePaginator.get_result`
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` duplicates `BasePaginator.get_result` almost line-for-line and only differs in the negative-offset branch. The `else` branch of `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` is the same as the modified `BasePaginator.get_result`. This duplication will rot: future fixes to `BasePaginator` (like the `order_b`/`order_by` typo on line 105) will not flow through, and the two implementations will diverge. The new paginator should subclass and override only the slice computation, or be merged into `BasePaginator` behind a feature flag rather than copy-pasting ~90 lines.

title: `optimized_pagination` query parameter is undocumented and behavior is opaque
body: The endpoint introduces `?optimized_pagination=true`, gated by `is_superuser or has_global_access`, that swaps in `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `enable_advanced_features=True`. There is no docstring, API docs entry, or schema update explaining what 'optimized pagination' does, what cursor shape to use, what negative offsets mean, or that it effectively changes how the cursor's `offset` component is interpreted (tail-of-result semantics). Admin-only internal callers will be guessing. Either add API documentation describing the cursor contract, or remove the parameter from production code until the contract is nailed down.

title: Diff claims a 'performance optimization' but changes no behavior
body: The diff for `src/sentry/utils/cursors.py` is comment-only. The new comment claims `Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios / This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets`, but `Cursor.__init__` continues to call `self.offset = int(offset)` exactly as before - negative offsets have always been representable. No validation, clamping, or any other behavior is added. The comment is misleading because it implies a deliberate relaxation that never happened. If the goal is to advertise that negatives are now first-class-supported, the constructor should at minimum assert/document a contract; otherwise the comment should be dropped.

title: New admin-gated pagination path has no test coverage
body: The PR adds a new branch in `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint.get` (and a brand-new paginator class `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with custom negative-offset handling) but ships zero test changes. There are no tests covering: the admin gating (`is_superuser` / `has_global_access`), `optimized_pagination=true` being honored, `optimized_pagination=true` being ignored for non-admins, the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` cursor round-trip, or the negative-offset slice path. Given the feature is gated only on admin status and uses an undocumented parameter, this should not merge without at least basic endpoint and paginator unit tests.

title: Negative offset to QuerySet slicing will crash at the database
body: Inside `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with `start_offset = cursor.offset` (a negative integer). The Django QuerySet `__getitem__` does not support a negative `start` in a slice: `Query.set_limits` forwards the negative value as the SQL `OFFSET`, which PostgreSQL rejects with a syntax error (e.g. `OFFSET -100`). The claim in the comment that 'the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions' is false. Any superuser / global-access caller who supplies a cursor with a negative offset through `?optimized_pagination=true` on `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` will get a 500 instead of pagination.

title: `BasePaginator.get_result` silently changes behavior for every paginator subclass
body: The diff modifies `BasePaginator.get_result` (used by `Paginator`, `DateTimePaginator`, and any other subclass) from `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` to `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` followed by `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`. This is not localized to `OptimizedCursorPaginator`; it changes the contract for every existing paginator. The 'Performance optimization' comment is misleading: this is a defensive clamp, not an optimization. The change is also inconsistent - negative offsets are only clamped for forward (`is_prev=False`) cursors; backward cursors still pass negative offsets straight to `queryset[offset:stop]`, which has the same crash potential. The behavior change should be scoped to the new paginator and either documented or rejected with a `BadPaginationError`.

title: `enable_advanced_features` is gated to admins but provides no functional benefit
body: The only behavioral difference between `OptimizedCursorPaginator` and `BasePaginator` (when `enable_advanced_features=True`) is the negative-offset branch, which crashes Django (see other finding). The endpoint hard-codes `enable_advanced_features=True` whenever `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`. So the entire feature shipped behind admin-only access is non-functional, while still adding ~100 lines of duplicated code, an `optimized_pagination` query-string toggle, and a new exported class. The PR should either implement what the comments describe or be reduced to a no-op flag until a real implementation exists.

title: No tests added for `OptimizedCursorPaginator`
body: The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` class and the modified `BasePaginator.get_result` slicing behavior have no accompanying tests. Cursor-based pagination in this file is subtle (extra row fetching, prev-direction reversal, `cursor.value` dedup, `offset + limit + extra` length check), and the PR introduces a new code path (`enable_advanced_features=True`) plus a behavioral change to the shared `BasePaginator.get_result`. At minimum, tests should cover: (1) forward pagination with the new clamp, (2) backward pagination with positive and negative offsets, (3) the `enable_advanced_features=True` branch with both negative and non-negative offsets, (4) the `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` post-filter path when `offset` is negative.

title: Pre-existing typo `queryset.query.order_b` is one line from the changed code
body: On the unchanged line 105 of `BasePaginator.build_queryset`, the assignment reads `queryset.query.order_b = tuple(new_order_by)` instead of `queryset.query.order_by = tuple(new_order_by)`. This is a typo that would raise `AttributeError: 'Query' object has no attribute 'order_b'` whenever the code path is reached (DESC ordering on a queryset that already has `-%s` in its order_by and `asc=True`). The PR is touching the very same `BasePaginator.get_result` / pagination file; the typo should be fixed in this PR while the area is being modified, since the bug is reachable and would be exercised by anything that pre-applies `-datetime` and then pages forward via `cursor.is_prev=False`.

title: Docstring and inline comments overstate and misrepresent the feature
body: The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` docstring claims 'Negative offset support for efficient reverse pagination', 'Streamlined boundary condition handling', 'Optimized query path for large datasets'. The `BasePaginator.get_result` comment claims 'the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions' and `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` claims 'permissions are checked at the queryset level'. None of these are true: Django ORM does not silently fix a negative slice (it produces `OFFSET -100` which the DB rejects), no queryset-level permission filter is added in the new code, and no query path is actually optimized. The comments also justify the negative-offset branch with 'enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds', which would be a security/authorization concern if it actually worked. The comments must be rewritten to match what the code does.

title: Redirect-follow loop limit reduced from 10000 to 1000, breaking deep segment trees
body: The loop bound was tightened from 10000 to 1000 while the explanatory comment about depth-10k trees was deleted. The redirect hash chain can still legitimately reach depths above 1000 (the data didn't change), so once `redirect_depth >= 1000` the loop exits early without resolving to a fixed point. The script then writes a `hset` mapping this span's id to an unresolved intermediate `set_span_id` and unions it into the wrong set, so subsequent children of the segment will land in a different buffer key. Result: spans get split across multiple `span-buf:s:*` keys instead of being joined into one segment — segments will be flushed incomplete or duplicated, directly causing data loss/duplication. The previous bound (and its comment) should be preserved unless the maximum possible redirect depth has been proven to be bounded below 1000.

title: Spans are silently evicted at insert time without any metric or log
body: After merging incoming spans into `set_key`, the script does `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', set_key, span_count - 1000) end`. There is no `redis.call('incrby', ...)` for a metric, no log, and the corresponding `metrics.incr('spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded')` was removed from `_load_segment_data`. Spans are silently dropped from the segment with zero observability. Worse, the eviction is by lowest `end_timestamp_precise` score, which is not necessarily the spans that are safe to drop (a parent span sent late would have a later score than its children and be kept, while a root span sent early could be evicted, leaving the segment without a root and causing it to fall through to the long `span_buffer_timeout_secs` path or be flushed incomplete). The threshold 1000 also does not match `max_segment_spans=1001` configured on `SpansBuffer`. At minimum this needs a counter (e.g. `metrics.incr('spans.buffer.evicted', n)`), a log when eviction occurs, and a guarantee that the root span (or HRS flag) is preserved.

title: Negative offset slice on Django QuerySet raises AssertionError
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with `start_offset = cursor.offset` (a negative int) when `enable_advanced_features` is True. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` asserts `k.start >= 0` and raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.` for any negative start index, so this path can never produce results. The cursor string is parsed by `Cursor.from_string` via `int(bits[1])`, which happily accepts a negative value, so any client (or a hand-crafted cursor) can trigger the crash. Combined with the `organization_auditlogs.py` change that always passes `enable_advanced_features=True` for superusers/admins, the new admin endpoint is a guaranteed `AssertionError` whenever the resulting cursor has offset < 0.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator has no working behavior beyond BasePaginator
body: The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` class duplicates almost all of `BasePaginator.get_result` and the only behavior change is the negative-offset branch. Because that branch cannot work (Django rejects negative slicing, see other finding), `OptimizedCursorPaginator` is functionally identical to `BasePaginator`. The `enable_advanced_features=True` flag exposed via `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` therefore does nothing useful in production. The PR title is 'Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert'; this entire paginator/auditlog change is unrelated and should be split out. As shipped it adds dead code, a misleading admin-only API knob, and a guaranteed crash path.

title: Required `end_timestamp_precise` field added to Span NamedTuple is a contract break
body: `Span` is a public NamedTuple. Adding `end_timestamp_precise: float` before the defaulted `is_segment_span: bool = False` makes it a required positional argument and breaks every existing `Span(...)` call site that does not supply it (TypeError). All in-repo callers in this PR are updated, but there are likely other consumers (snuba-spans ingestion, tests outside this PR, downstream internal tools) that construct `Span` instances directly. Any such caller will now crash at module/import time on first use, and any older serialized payload that doesn't carry `end_timestamp_precise` will now KeyError inside `process_batch`. This change should either default to `0.0`/`None` or have a clearly documented migration; missing-field handling in `process_batch` is not implemented.

title: No test covers the new 1000-span eviction path
body: Tests under `tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py` and `tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_consumer.py` only ever add ~4 spans per segment. The new Lua eviction kicks in at >1000 spans, which is now the actual hard cap on segment size (the Python `max_segment_spans` check was removed), yet nothing exercises it. A test that ingests >1000 spans into one segment is needed to assert: (a) eviction actually happens, (b) the root span (or HRS flag) is preserved, (c) a metric is emitted so the silent-drop path is observable. Without this, regressions in the eviction behavior would land silently.

title: Misleading 'Performance optimization' comment for a behavior change
body: The change in `BasePaginator.get_result` from `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` to `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` is a small behavioral fix, not a performance optimization. The new `max(0, offset)` call is essentially free and does not reduce query cost; it just prevents an `AssertionError` for negative non-prev cursors. The inline comment 'Performance optimization: For high-traffic scenarios, allow negative offsets...' is misleading and should describe the actual change (clamping negative non-prev offsets to 0 to avoid a crash). Also note the asymmetry: prev cursors are NOT clamped, so a negative prev cursor will still crash in Django — the two branches should behave consistently.

title: ZADD uses payload bytes as member; duplicate payloads are silently dropped
body: Switching the segment from `sadd` to `zadd` keeps the same 'member = span.payload (bytes)' model. Sorted sets require unique members, so two spans whose serialized payloads happen to be byte-identical (e.g. retries, duplicate Kafka messages, or same span replayed) will be collapsed to one entry on insertion. The Lua script's eviction then operates on this collapsed set, and the Python `_load_segment_data` will only see one copy. This is the same potential bug `sadd` had (it also dedups by member), but it is now more consequential because the score-based eviction changes ordering. Worth either documenting the assumption (that payloads are unique) or de-duplicating earlier so that eviction counts are meaningful.

title: ZUNIONSTORE used with destination equal to one of its source keys
body: `redis.call('zunionstore', set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` and the analogous `set_key, 2, set_key, parent_key` pass `set_key` as both destination and source. While this happens to behave correctly in some single-instance Redis versions (because the source data is gathered before the destination is rewritten), it is not documented as a supported pattern, can produce non-deterministic results across versions, and is a footgun in cluster mode where slot routing must already match. The safer equivalent is: gather members via ZRANGE/ZRANGEBYSCORE, then ZADD them to `set_key` (or union into a temp key and RENAME). At minimum this should be commented and pinned against a tested Redis version.

title: Admin-only pagination branch wraps a broken paginator behind an undocumented query flag
body: `use_optimized = request.GET.get('optimized_pagination') == 'true'` enables `OptimizedCursorPaginator` for superusers/org members with global access. Because the paginator's only distinguishing behavior (negative offsets) crashes Django (see paginator.py finding), the branch serves no purpose other than to expose a new failure mode. There is no test in this PR for the new branch, no documentation/changelog entry, and no consumer that actually needs negative offsets. This is dead/unsafe code shipped under an unrelated PR title; it should be reverted from this PR and either fixed properly or removed.

title: Redirect-chain depth reduced from 10000 to 1000 without rationale
body: The Lua script's redirect-following loop is reduced from `for i = 0, 10000 do` to `for i = 0, 1000 do`, and the original comment that acknowledged the limit ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") is silently deleted. With depth capped at 1000, any trace whose `span-buf:sr:` redirect chain is longer than 1000 will exit the loop before convergence, write the new span to a stale `set_span_id`, and then fail to merge subsequent spans into the real segment set. The downstream consequence is silently dropped spans (incomplete segments flushed out) - a data integrity regression. Either keep the previous limit (or document the new, lower bound), or actually change the algorithm so a depth-bounded walk is correct (e.g., iterate by current `set_span_id`, not by a fixed counter).

title: Missing `end_timestamp_precise` will raise KeyError and poison the batch
body: `process_batch` now reads `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]`. If any incoming span in the batch omits this field, the indexing raises `KeyError`, which propagates out of `RunTask` and causes the whole batch to fail repeatedly until the bad message is skipped. The existing pattern in this same function is to use `val.get(...)` for optional fields (`parent_span_id`, `is_remote`). `end_timestamp_precise` should either be sourced via `val.get("end_timestamp_precise", 0.0)` (or similar) or be guaranteed by the producer/Relay contract. Otherwise a single malformed Kafka message halts the consumer.

title: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` allows negative offsets that Django ORM does not support
body: When `enable_advanced_features=True` and `cursor.offset < 0`, the paginator computes `start_offset = cursor.offset` and slices the queryset as `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django's QuerySet slicing with negative indices is not supported and raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` (or, in some versions, produces invalid SQL `LIMIT -N`). The accompanying comment claims "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" - this is false. The new audit-log endpoint exposes this code path to any superuser or member with `has_global_access` (see `organization_auditlogs.py`), so any crafted `?cursor=...:-1:0` request against that endpoint will return a 500.

title: Audit-log "advanced pagination" gated only by `has_global_access`, with misleading justification
body: The condition `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is the only gate on `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `enable_advanced_features=True`. `has_global_access` is granted to any org member with access to all teams in the organization, not just admins who should be exposed to a brand-new, untested paginator path. The inline comment "This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level" is also incorrect: the queryset is `AuditLogEntry.objects.filter(organization_id=organization.id)` with no per-row ACL, so the new paginator gives this broader set of users arbitrary row-jumping behavior (and, given the Django-negative-slice bug above, 500s on crafted cursors). Tighten the gate (e.g., only when `request.user.is_superuser`) and add an actual permission test before enabling advanced pagination.

title: New `OptimizedCursorPaginator` is shipped with no tests
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` is a 90+ line subclass of `BasePaginator` with new behavior (negative-offset slicing, `enable_advanced_features` constructor flag, duplicate `get_item_key`/`value_from_cursor` implementations copied from `Paginator`) but no test coverage is added in this PR. The `tests/` diff only touches the spans-buffer test files. Given the endpoint in `organization_auditlogs.py` already wires this paginator into production, this needs at minimum: (1) a test that exercises `enable_advanced_features=False` parity with `BasePaginator`, (2) a test of the `enable_advanced_features=True` negative-offset path (which will currently surface the Django negative-slice bug), and (3) tests covering `get_item_key`/`value_from_cursor`/cursor-string round-trip.

title: Cursor constructor comment promises a behavior change that is not made
body: The diff adds two comment lines to `Cursor.__init__` stating that negative offsets are now allowed for "advanced pagination scenarios", but the constructor itself is unchanged (`self.offset = int(offset)` was already there). At the same time, every other paginator (`OffsetPaginator`, `MergingOffsetPaginator`, `CombinedQuerysetPaginator`, `GenericOffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`, `CallbackPaginator`) explicitly rejects negative offsets with `raise BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`. So `Cursor` accepts negative offsets but most paginators refuse them; only the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` uses them, and (per the finding above) it does so incorrectly. Either remove the misleading comment, or add the explicit validation in `Cursor.__init__` (and the new paginator) and propagate the relaxation to the other paginators consistently.

title: Redirect-follow loop bound cut 10x with no rationale; warning comment deleted
body: The Lua `for i = 0, 10000 do` bound for resolving parent redirects was reduced to `for i = 0, 1000 do`, and the comment that explicitly documented the consequence ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted in the same change. With the new bound, segment trees whose redirect chain is longer than 1000 will silently stop being joined: the loop exits while `new_set_span` is still a different key, the final `hset` then writes a wrong redirect, and subsequent spans get routed into the wrong set instead of being merged. This is a data-integrity regression that should either be reverted or come with an explicit justification for why a shallower limit is now acceptable.

title: Unrelated OptimizedCursorPaginator and audit-logs branch added to a spans-buffer PR
body: The PR is titled "Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert" and the description is just "Test 2", yet the diff also introduces an entirely new OptimizedCursorPaginator class (paginator.py:821) and a parallel branch in OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint (organization_auditlogs.py:68-83) that switches to it whenever `?optimized_pagination=true` is supplied and the caller is a superuser or has global access. Inside that branch `enable_advanced_features=True` is hardcoded, so the only gates are the new query param and the role check. None of this is related to the stated purpose of the PR, there is no justification or doc for the new endpoint flag, the new paginator has no tests, and the audit-logs branch is not tested. This should be split into a separate PR with its own description, security review, and tests.

title: Negative-offset QuerySet slicing will fail at runtime, contradicting the inline comment
body: When `enable_advanced_features` is on and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with a negative `start_offset`. The comment above asserts "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically", but Django's docs state "Negative indexing (qs[-1]) is not supported" and the compiler translates a negative low mark directly into a SQL `OFFSET -N` clause, which is invalid SQL. The very first time an admin hits the new code path the consumer will either raise `AssertionError` from the queryset machinery or produce a database error from the generated SQL. The "advanced" path needs to be reworked to actually work (e.g. reverse ordering + a positive offset, or a count-based tail query), or removed.

title: "Performance optimization" comments about negative offsets are factually wrong
body: Three comments in this PR (cursors.py:26-27, paginator.py:179-181, paginator.py:874-878) claim that allowing negative cursor offsets is a "performance optimization" that enables "efficient bidirectional pagination without full dataset scanning" and "efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets". This is incorrect: a negative offset still requires walking to that position in the result set (in SQL terms it is still an OFFSET, just expressed as a negative number). The comments advertise a benefit that the change does not deliver, which is misleading to future readers and will mislead anyone trying to reason about pagination cost.

title: Hard KeyError on Kafka messages missing end_timestamp_precise
body: process_batch now constructs `Span(..., end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"])`. The new `end_timestamp_precise` field has no default, so any incoming ingest-spans message that omits it will raise from the consumer and stall that batch. Even if the current producer always sets it, an index lookup with no `.get(..., 0.0)` fallback is fragile for a producer/consumer pipeline where the schema can evolve. Use `val.get("end_timestamp_precise", 0.0)` (or a typed default) and let the new zset score handle missing/zero values gracefully.

title: Defensive per-segment span-count cap silently removed from the flush side
body: The old `_load_segment_data` aborted and dropped a segment when `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans`, with an explicit metric/logger. That check is gone in the new version, so the only cap on segment size is now the insert-time `zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua. If the insert cap is ever bypassed (older consumer version still running, manual redis writes, or a future script change), the flusher will happily scan and ship arbitrarily large segments, with corresponding memory and downstream cost. Keep the flush-side cap (or an equivalent assertion) as a defense-in-depth bound, or add a test that exercises the case where the insert-time cap is disabled.

title: Headline eviction behavior is not covered by any test
body: The stated purpose of this PR is "eviction during insert": add-buffer.lua now does `zpopmin` once the segment set exceeds 1000 entries, and `process_spans`/`_load_segment_data` were rewritten around sorted sets (zadd with `end_timestamp_precise` as score, zscan returning `(member, score)`). None of the existing tests in tests/sentry/spans/ exercise either behavior - no test inserts >1000 spans into a single segment to verify the eviction cap and the score ordering, and no test verifies that the score passed to zadd survives through to the flusher. A regression in the score key, the cap, or the eviction order could ship undetected.

title: Aliased count() columns silently bypass upsampling transform
body: transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling matches column_lower == "count()" exactly. Any column with an explicit alias such as "count() as my_count" or even "count() as count" will not match and falls through to the else branch, which appends the original column unchanged. The endpoint code (organization_events_stats.py) now calls this transform on every y-axis column when upsampling is enabled, so a user who aliases their count column (e.g. for a chart with multiple y-axes) will silently get the raw count() while a user with no alias gets the upsampled value. The fix is to detect count() with optional "as <alias>" and replace the function name while preserving the alias, e.g. emit "upsampled_count() as my_count".

title: topEvents error message changed, breaking API contract
body: The 400 response for topEvents <= 0 was changed from {"detail": "If topEvents needs to be at least 1"} to {"detail": "topEvents needs to be at least 1"}. This is a user-visible API contract change. Any client or integration that matches the previous string (e.g. Sentry's own frontend, alert rules, or downstream tooling) will stop recognizing the error. Either keep the original wording or coordinate this with the frontend before merging.

title: Tests mock options.get but do not clear the 60s upsampling cache
body: is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects (error_upsampling.py) caches the boolean result of the allowlist check for 60 seconds using cache.get/set. The four new tests in test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects etc. patch sentry.api.helpers.error_upsampling.options, but if any earlier test in the same run (or a prior test in this class) has populated the cache for the same organization+projects, the cached True/False is returned without re-running options.get and the mock has no effect. This can cause intermittent failures or false successes. The tests should reset the cache (e.g. via cache.clear() or invalidate_upsampling_cache) in setUp/tearDown before patching options.

title: upsampled_count assumes sample_weight is non-NULL for every row
body: The new upsampled_count SnQL aggregate is implemented as toInt64(sum(sample_weight)). SQL/ClickHouse sum() ignores NULL values entirely, so any event in an allowlisted project that lacks sample_weight (e.g. older data, a partial backfill, or a schema mismatch) will be silently dropped from the count. The comment in error_upsampling.py asserts the column exists for all events, but nothing verifies it at query time, and the consequence is wrong downsampled charts that look valid. The aggregate should either coalesce NULLs (assume a weight of 1 for rows without sample_weight, or surface a null result) or the allowlist check should validate that backfill has actually completed.

title: _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling mutates all event types, not just errors
body: _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling is invoked unconditionally inside store_event right after manager.get_data() for every event, and writes normalized_data["sample_rate"] whenever contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate is present. The function does not check the event type, so any transaction, attachment, or other non-error event that happens to carry an error_sampling context (whether by a SDK bug, a test fixture, or a future feature) will have sample_rate injected, potentially affecting other code paths that read sample_rate from those events. Guard the call on the event type being an error, or move the logic into the error-specific normalization path.

title: Bare except Exception hides AttributeError/TypeError in sample rate extraction
body: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling the first try/except wraps a chain of .get() calls on dicts, which never raise. The except Exception block is dead for the intended path but will silently swallow AttributeError or TypeError caused by a malformed normalized_data (e.g. contexts not being a dict). That makes a broken event manifest look like "no sample rate" instead of failing the test loudly. Catch only the specific exception you expect, or drop the try/except entirely around the .get() chain.

title: Cache key uses Python hash() of a tuple of ints
body: The cache key is built with hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids))). While CPython's hash of a tuple of ints is deterministic within a given run, the contract relies on an internal implementation detail (the tuple hashing algorithm for nested ints) and produces a signed Python int that is concatenated into the key string. It would be safer and more portable to use an explicit deterministic digest (e.g. hashlib.md5 of the comma-joined sorted ids) so the cache key is stable across Python versions, implementations, and obvious to readers, and so cache busting via invalidate_upsampling_cache is reliable.

title: invalidate_upsampling_cache has no test coverage
body: invalidate_upsampling_cache is a public helper intended to be called when the allowlist changes, but no test in test_error_upsampling.py exercises it. Without a test, a future change to the cache key format (e.g. switching away from hash()) will silently break cache invalidation in production. Add a test that populates the cache, calls invalidate_upsampling_cache, and asserts cache.get returns None.

title: is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects is not exercised
body: The main public entry point is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects (which combines the allowlist check, the 60s cache, and the dataset/query filter) is never tested directly. The test file only covers the private helpers (_are_all_projects_error_upsampled, _is_error_focused_query, _should_apply_sample_weight_transform, transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling). The caching behavior in particular is the riskiest new logic and should have a test that verifies a cache hit short-circuits the allowlist lookup.

title: Redundant upsampling_enabled alias of should_upsample
body: Inside _get_event_stats, should_upsample = is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(...) is immediately followed by upsampling_enabled = should_upsample and the rest of the function only ever reads upsampling_enabled. The second variable adds no semantic value and makes the code look like the two could diverge. Drop one (preferably upsampling_enabled) and use should_upsample directly. (Noted as style rather than bug because there is no functional impact.)

title: Cache key uses hash() which is randomized per Python process
body: The cache key uses `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. Python's built-in `hash()` for tuples is randomized per interpreter process (PYTHONHASHSEED). In any multi-process deployment (uWSGI/gunicorn workers), each worker will compute a different hash for the same project set, so cache entries written by one worker will never be read by another. Consequences: (1) the cache provides no benefit across workers — every request is a miss; (2) `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (line 67) computes the same randomized hash in its caller, so it cannot invalidate entries created by other workers, making the invalidation function dead in practice. Use a deterministic hash (e.g., `hashlib.sha256` over the joined IDs) or simply stringify the sorted IDs.

title: invalidate_upsampling_cache is defined but never called
body: The helper `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is added but no caller exists in the diff. The function is meant to flush cache entries when the `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` option changes, but nothing in the codebase invokes it. As a result, after an admin adds/removes a project from the allowlist, stale `True`/`False` values will be served for up to 60 seconds across the whole worker pool. Either wire it up to the option change handler or remove it. Note: even if it were called, the randomized `hash()` in the key (see other finding) means it would only invalidate entries in the calling process.

title: Tests share the 60s eligibility cache and produce order-dependent results
body: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches the allowlist result in `sentry.utils.cache.cache` for 60s keyed by `hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))`. All four tests in `OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest` query the same set of project IDs and only swap `mock_options.get.return_value`. The first test that runs populates the cache (e.g., True for the full allowlist case); subsequent tests that expect the un-upsampled `count == 1` path will instead see the cached True and get upsampled counts of 10, failing. There is no `cache.clear()` in `setUp` and the helper is not patched. Add a cache reset in `setUp` (or key the cache on something that varies per test, e.g. include the option value), otherwise the suite is order-dependent and effectively does not exercise both branches.

title: Public entry point is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects has no direct test
body: The new test file exercises the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`) but never calls `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, which is the only function actually used by `OrganizationEventsStatsEndpoint._get_event_stats`. The cache hit/cache miss branches and the short-circuit behavior on the cached value are uncovered. Add at least one test that mocks `sentry.utils.cache.cache` and asserts both the cached and uncached paths.

title: _should_apply_sample_weight_transform types dataset as Any instead of ModuleType
body: `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform(dataset: Any, request: Request)` compares `dataset` against `discover`, `errors`, and `transactions` modules. The parameter is typed `Any`, but the caller (`organization_events_stats.py` line 220) passes a module from `sentry.snuba`, and the new module is in the stricter-typing `[[tool.mypy.overrides]]` block in `pyproject.toml`. Type it as `ModuleType` (matching the public `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` signature) so mypy catches accidental non-module values.

title: client_sample_rate accepted without range validation
body: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` blindly casts `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` to float and stores it as `sample_rate` if truthy. Nothing rejects values outside [0, 1], negative numbers, or NaN. A malformed client sending `client_sample_rate: 100` (or `-1`) will poison `sample_weight` for every event in that project, which then propagates into `upsampled_count()` aggregates (`sum(sample_weight)` in `discover.py`) and silently inflates or zeroes out error counts in dashboards/alerts for allowlisted projects. Add an explicit range check (or coerce/log invalid values) before writing back into `normalized_data`.

title: upsampled_count() not registered in errors dataset
body: The SnQLFunction `upsampled_count` is only registered in the discover dataset's function_converter, but `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` emits `"upsampled_count() as count"` regardless of which dataset is being queried. When the errors dataset is used (which is the primary use case for error upsampling, and is the dataset that `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns True for unconditionally), the query will fail at the Snuba layer with an unknown-function error. The function must also be registered in the errors dataset's function converter.

title: Cache invalidation function is never called
body: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined but no code anywhere calls it. Because the cache TTL is 60 seconds, when a project is removed from `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` (e.g. during a rollback), that project will continue to receive upsampled `count()` results for up to 60 seconds, producing incorrect (inflated) counts in production. The docstring acknowledges that 'allowlist changes are infrequent' but does not justify serving incorrect data after removals. The cache should be invalidated synchronously when the option changes, or the option lookup itself should not be cached.

title: _is_error_focused_query uses substring matching despite claiming caution
body: The implementation does `'event.type:error' in query` (lowercased substring), and the docstring claims it was 'Reduced to only check for event.type:error to err on the side of caution.' Substring matching is the opposite of cautious: `NOT event.type:error` matches (the query excludes errors yet upsampling will be applied), `event.type:error_handled` matches (a non-error event type is treated as an error), and `message:"event.type:error occurred"` matches. This will cause `sum(sample_weight)` upsampled counts to be returned for queries that are explicitly about non-error events, corrupting customer-facing time series. The check should tokenize and parse the query (or at minimum require word boundaries / absence of a leading `NOT`).

title: Unrelated breaking change to user-facing error text
body: The error message for `topEvents <= 0` was changed from `"If topEvents needs to be at least 1"` to `"topEvents needs to be at least 1"`. This is a user-facing 400 response that has nothing to do with the PR's stated purpose (upsampled error counts). It silently changes a documented API contract, will break any tests, alerts, or downstream consumers that pattern-match the message, and should be reverted or split into a separate PR.

title: setUp overwrites self.user after login_as uses it
body: In `OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest.setUp`, `self.login_as(user=self.user)` and `self.authed_user = self.user` are executed before `self.user = self.create_user()`. The login and stored `authed_user` reference the parent `APITestCase`'s user, then `self.user` is reassigned to a freshly created user that was never logged in. The `tags` on stored events reference this new `self.user`/`self.user2` (which are different identities than the authenticated principal), so the test fixture is internally inconsistent and any tag-based filtering or permission check against the new users will not behave as intended. Reorder setUp so users are created before login_as, or stop reassigning self.user.

title: Organization parameter unused in allowlist check
body: `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` accepts `organization: Organization` but never references it. The allowlist `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` is treated as a single global list of project IDs with no org scoping. If two organizations share a project ID space (e.g. in tests, or in any multi-tenant view of the option), a match in the allowlist could trigger upsampling for projects in the wrong organization. Either drop the unused parameter or actually verify each project_id belongs to `organization`.

title: Transform only matches literal count(), misses aliased and other count variants
body: `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only matches the exact stripped/lowercased string `count()`. It will not transform `count() as total`, `count_if(...)`, `count_unique(...)`, `count_web_vitals(...)`, etc. Any aggregation that semantically counts events but isn't literal `count()` will return non-upsampled counts in the same response, producing mixed results where some y-axes are upsampled and others are not for the same time bucket. The match should also handle aliased forms and at minimum `count_if`-style aggregates for errors, or the contract should be clearly documented.

title: Main public function and cache invalidation are untested
body: The test file covers `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`, `_is_error_focused_query`, and `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, but never exercises the main entry point `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` (cache hit/miss, cache-key determinism, interaction with `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`) and never tests `invalidate_upsampling_cache`. Given the cache-related concerns above, these are exactly the paths that need direct test coverage.

title: Hard-coded count==10 assumes undocumented sample_weight semantics
body: The assertions `assert data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10` rely on `sum(sample_weight)` producing 10 when `client_sample_rate` is 0.1. That is only true if the Snuba `sample_weight` column is precomputed as `1/sample_rate` rather than equal to `sample_rate`. The factory change only sets `normalized_data["sample_rate"] = float(client_sample_rate)`; nothing in this PR guarantees that `sample_weight` in Snuba equals `1/sample_rate`.
