If `sample_weight` is NULL or equals `sample_rate`, the test will silently produce wrong counts in CI and the assertion will fail or, worse, pass against a different column. Either add an explicit comment/schema check documenting the invariant, or compute the expected value from whatever mapping actually exists.

title: Factory silently overwrites event sample_rate with context value
body: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` unconditionally assigns `normalized_data["sample_rate"] = float(client_sample_rate)` whenever the `error_sampling` context is present. `sample_rate` is a standard SDK-provided field on events; overwriting it from a separate `error_sampling` context (which carries a different semantic — client-side reporting rate, not SDK capture rate) can corrupt downstream consumers that read `sample_rate` for ingest sampling math. It should only set the field when the event doesn't already carry a `sample_rate`, or write to a distinct field. The two bare `except Exception: pass` blocks additionally hide all errors including programming mistakes.

title: Cache returns truthy cached_result but stores strict booleans inconsistently
body: `cache.get(cache_key)` returns `cached_result` which was stored as a Python `bool` (`is_eligible`), but the return path does `return cached_result and _should_apply_sample_weight_transform(...)`. If `is_eligible` was `False`, the cached value is `False` and the short-circuit returns `False`, skipping the dataset check — this means a request whose project set is not allowlisted will never even consult the dataset/transactions filter, which is fine. However, if the cache backend ever returns a non-bool truthy value (e.g. some serializers wrap booleans), the `and` chain would produce unexpected types. More importantly, the dataset/sample_weight check is intentionally re-evaluated on every cache hit even though it has no dependency on the cached value's inputs, so the caching only saves the `options.get` and the per-project allowlist scan — but the cache key itself varies by project set, so hit rate for any given key is low. This negates the claimed performance benefit.

title: TableWidgetVisualization rendered with hardcoded empty data on feature-flag branch
body: When the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature flag is enabled, the new branch in `tableResultComponent` renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />` with hardcoded empty values instead of forwarding the actual `result.data`, `result.meta`, `eventView`, `fields`, `location`, `fieldAliases`, `fieldHeaderMap`, etc. that are still computed above the conditional. Anyone with this flag on will see completely empty table widgets in their dashboards. The non-flagged branch correctly renders `<StyledSimpleTableChart ... data={result.data} metadata={result.meta} ... />`, so the new code path appears to be an unfinished placeholder that needs to be wired up to the same `result` data.

title: Analytics event recorded before feature-flag check
body: The new `analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` call is placed before the `features.has("organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble", ...)` gate. Any caller without the feature flag still gets a 404 response, but the analytics event is emitted anyway, so the preprod assemble analytics will be inflated by traffic from orgs/projects that have no access to the feature. The analytics call should be moved after the feature check (and ideally inside the try/else branch that actually enqueues work) so it only counts requests that are processed.

title: Mutating an already-named Django migration to a no-op without its replacement in the same PR
body: The file references `0921_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views_rerevised.py` in its docstring/comment but that migration is not part of this PR. Replacing the body of a migration that is already named and shipped (0917 was generated 2025-04-28, 0920 on 2025-06-03) is dangerous: any environment that recorded an applied state of these migrations will see a hash mismatch when `manage.py migrate` is next run, and any fresh database will silently skip the conversion because 0921 is not present here. Either the coordinating 0921 migration needs to be in this PR, or these files should be left as-is and 0921 should supersede them through the normal Django migration chain (i.e., 0917/0920 must remain non-no-ops, and 0921 must depend on them).

title: Mutating an already-named Django migration to a no-op without its replacement in the same PR
body: Same issue as 0917: the comment refers to `0921_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views_rerevised.py` which is not in this PR, and the migration body has been reduced to `return`. If any environment has applied 0920, Django will refuse to continue and may require manual intervention; if no environment has applied it, this still relies on a migration (0921) that the reviewer cannot inspect, and the corresponding test for the conversion has been removed without a replacement test for 0921.

title: TableWidgetVisualization is rendered with empty columns and empty data when the feature flag is on
body: Inside `tableResultComponent`, when `organization.features.includes('use-table-widget-visualization')` is true, `<TableWidgetVisualization>` is rendered with `columns={[]}` and `tableData={{ data: [], meta: { fields: {}, units: {} } }}`, ignoring the actual `result.data` and `result.meta` (and `fieldAliases`, `fields`, `fieldHeaderMap`, etc. used by the legacy path). For any organization with this feature flag enabled, every table widget in a dashboard will render as an empty table. There is also no test covering the feature-flag-enabled branch. The gated branch should pass the real `result.data`, `result.meta`, and columns derived from `result.meta.fields` (and any `fieldAliases`/`fieldHeaderMap`/`getCustomFieldRenderer`) rather than hard-coded empty values.

title: Analytics recorded before authorization check
body: `analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` is invoked at the top of `post`, before the `features.has("organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble", ...)` gate and before any other validation (schema validation, chunk upload checks, etc.). This means every POST to this endpoint — including unauthorized, malformed, and feature-flag-disabled requests — will be counted in the analytics event, skewing usage data and breaking any downstream dashboards or alerting on this event. The analytics call should be moved to after the feature flag check and ideally after the request has been validated as legitimate.

title: Default for sentry:autofix_automation_tuning changed from "low" to "off" without an opt-in rollout
body: `DEFAULT_AUTOFIX_AUTOMATION_TUNING_DEFAULT` changed from "low" to "off", and the project option default (`src/sentry/projectoptions/defaults.py`) was updated to match. This silently changes behavior for any project that was relying on the previous default of "low". Combined with the existing feature flag handling in `test_project_details.py`/`test_project.py` which now assert the new default, this is a behavior change shipped in the same release as the code rather than a controlled rollout. Projects that have never explicitly set this option will see autofix turned off after deploy, which is a user-visible behavior change that should either require an explicit upgrade step or be gated behind a flag.

title: Visualize constructor signature changed from (yAxes[], options) to (yAxis, options)
body: `Visualize` previously accepted `yAxes: readonly string[]` and stored an array of y-axes per visualize. It now requires a single `yAxis: string`. While the in-tree callers have been updated, this is an exported public class used by getsentry and other downstream consumers. Any external code constructing `new Visualize(["count()", "avg()"], {...})` will now pass an array as the first argument and the class will store the array as a string (TypeScript will likely error or, worse, silently misbehave). Either keep both shapes via a deprecated overload, document this as a breaking change in a changelog/release notes, or guard with a runtime check that throws a clear error for the old shape.

title: get_environment_info swallows all exceptions via bare `except Exception`
body: `get_environment_info` catches `Exception` for the entire `issue.get_recommended_event()` + `recommended_event.get_environment()` block and logs the error as `info` rather than `warning`/`error`. This hides genuine failures (DB outages, programming errors, schema drift) behind a benign-looking info log and degrades the new PR comment feature silently. The try/except should at minimum scope the catch (e.g., only catch expected lookup misses / `Group.DoesNotExist`-style failures) and the unexpected branch should log at warning or re-raise so issues surface in Sentry.

title: dcg_to_slow_conditions now keyed by dcg_ids instead of dcg_to_groups.keys()
body: `get_condition_query_groups` previously computed `dcg_to_slow_conditions` from `event_data.dcg_to_groups.keys()` and looked up `dcg_to_slow_conditions[dcg.id]` for every dcg in `data_condition_groups` (which is fetched from `event_data.dcg_ids`). After the refactor, the slow-conditions dict is built once from `event_data.dcg_ids` and reused in both `get_condition_query_groups` and `get_groups_to_fire`. The new behavior is more correct (it now covers DCGs present in `dcg_ids` but missing from `dcg_to_groups`, which would previously have raised `KeyError`), but it changes the set of condition groups considered "slow". Any DCG that previously was not flagged as slow because it was missing from `dcg_to_groups.keys()` will now be flagged as slow, potentially altering which conditions get sent to Snuba and which workflows fire. Worth verifying with a sample trace that this matches the intended semantics.

title: Fallback column derivation reads meta.fields with no null check
body: When `columns` is not provided, the fallback computes `Object.keys(tableData?.meta.fields).map(...)`. The optional chaining handles `tableData` being undefined but does not handle `tableData.meta` itself being undefined — if a caller passes `tableData` without a `meta` key (or with `meta: undefined`), this throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'fields')`. This becomes very real given that `chart.tsx` is calling this component with `tableData.meta` set, but downstream callers may forget. Use `tableData?.meta?.fields` for the safe default.

title: PR comment template no longer includes the issue culprit/subtitle
body: The previous comment format was `- ‼️ **{title}** \`{subtitle}\` [View Issue]({url})`, which surfaced the issue's `culprit` (the file/function associated with the issue). The new template is `* ‼️ [**{title}**]({url}){environment}\n` and replaces the subtitle with an environment tag. Anyone scanning PR comments to find which file triggered an issue loses that information. If the subtitle was noisy or low-value, that's fine, but this is a deliberate change to user-visible PR content and should be called out in release notes.

title: schedule_webhook_delivery given a 30s processing_deadline_duration
body: `schedule_webhook_delivery` is the parent task that fans out delivery tasks to `drain_mailbox`. 30s is a tight budget for a task that may need to schedule a large batch of webhook deliveries (Redis push, multiple apply_async calls, potentially across many integrations). If the task exceeds 30s the in-flight work is killed by the taskworker, leaving deliveries unscheduled. Consider a more generous budget (e.g., 5–10 minutes consistent with `drain_mailbox`) or chunk the dispatch into smaller batches.

title: Per-error nodestore lookup not batched
body: `fetch_error_details` does `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` which is batched, but for each issue the broader flow calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` (separate Eventstore lookup) inside `fetch_error_details` would be one DB query per error. In `make_seer_request` the actual call passes the full log list at once, so the prompt is fine, but `fetch_error_details` itself iterates and calls `Event.generate_node_id` for each error id; if error_ids is large this is N independent DB reads per call site. Not a blocker but worth a follow-up to batch event lookups.

title: max_segment_id null guard could mask the same bug elsewhere
body: `_make_recording_filenames` now early-returns `[]` when `row["max_segment_id"] is None`, and the TypedDict was widened from `int` to `int | None`. The accompanying test (`tests/sentry/replays/tasks/test_delete_replays_bulk.py`) was updated to match. This is a defensive fix, but a `max_segment_id` of None on a real replay row is data the bulk-delete query should be filtering out upstream (via `WHERE max(segment_id) IS NOT NULL`) rather than producing rows that silently delete nothing. Verify that the Snuba query in `fetch_rows_matching_pattern` excludes or filters these rows so the caller doesn't keep paging through hundreds of empty results.

title: Empty columns/data passed to TableWidgetVisualization behind feature flag
body: When the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature flag is enabled, `TableWidgetVisualization` is rendered with `columns={[]}` and `tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}}`. The real data (`result.data`, `result.meta`, `fields`, etc.) that the prior branch passed to `StyledSimpleTableChart` is dropped on this branch. Any organization with the flag enabled will see a completely empty dashboard table instead of their actual rows. This branch should pass the same columns/tableData derived from `result.meta` and `result.data` that the existing branch uses.

title: Visualize API silently breaks multi-y-axis support and changes stacking behavior
body: The `Visualize` constructor now takes a single `yAxis: string` instead of `yAxes: readonly string[]`, and `this.stack = 'all'` is now unconditional. Previously, bar charts with multiple y-axes rendered with `stack === undefined` (unstacked), and `Visualize.replace({yAxes: [...]})` could mutate the y-axis list. Any saved view, link, or component that constructs `new Visualize([...])` or `replace({yAxes: [...]})` will silently produce wrong data or fail. Additionally, callers of `Visualize.fromJSON(json)` previously received a single `Visualize`; the new signature returns `Visualize[]`. Code that did `Visualize.fromJSON(x).replace(...)` will break (`.replace` is undefined on an array). This is a breaking change to a user-facing feature and should be called out in the PR description / release notes.

title: Renaming analytics event 'replay.view_html' to 'replay.view-html' breaks downstream consumers
body: `trackAnalytics('replay.view_html', ...)` is renamed to `trackAnalytics('replay.view-html', ...)`. The internal type registry in `replayAnalyticsEvents.tsx` is updated to match, but any external dashboards, alerts, or saved queries that filter on the old `replay.view_html` event name will silently stop receiving data. Renaming a published analytics event key is an API contract break and should be deprecated, not renamed silently, or at minimum called out clearly in the release notes.

title: Analytics recorded before feature flag check, inflating metrics
body: `analytics.record('preprod_artifact.api.assemble', ...)` is invoked unconditionally at the top of `post()` before the `features.has('organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble', ...)` check. Requests from organizations that don't have the feature enabled will still emit analytics events, polluting the metric with traffic that never reached the assemble path. The record call should happen after the feature flag passes (or guarded by the same condition).

title: Broad `except Exception` in get_environment_info silently swallows errors
body: `get_environment_info` wraps its entire body (including `issue.get_recommended_event()` and `recommended_event.get_environment()`) in `except Exception`, only logs at info level, and returns an empty string. If anything in the recommended-event / environment lookup regresses, this will silently drop environment info from every GitHub/GitLab suspect-PR comment with no alert. At minimum, narrow the catch to the specific exceptions that can be raised (e.g. `Group.DoesNotExist`, `Environment.DoesNotExist`) and/or log at warning/error level.

title: ParameterizationRegexExperiment removed without deprecation
body: The `ParameterizationRegexExperiment` class is removed from `__all__`, the `ParameterizationExperiment` union type alias no longer includes it, and the option `grouping.experiments.parameterization.traceparent` is deleted. Any external consumer or downstream test that still references `ParameterizationRegexExperiment` will fail with `ImportError` or `TypeError`. If this class is genuinely unused, this is fine, but the public export should be removed deliberately and a deprecation cycle would be safer given `__all__` is exported.

title: fetch_error_details pairs zipped IDs with nodestore values that may be out of order or duplicated
body: `fetch_error_details` does `for event_id, data in zip(error_ids, events.values())`, relying on `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids).values()` to return entries in the same order as `node_ids`. If `nodestore.backend.get_multi` returns a mapping whose iteration order does not strictly match the request order (some cache backends do not guarantee this), or if `error_ids` contains duplicates and the implementation deduplicates internally, then `event_id` and `data` will be mismatched: the wrong title/timestamp/message will be associated with the wrong event id when feeding error context to the LLM. Iterate `events` by explicit node_id lookup (e.g. `[events.get(nid) for nid in node_ids]`) to make ordering explicit.

title: Removal of 'browser_report_received' info log not covered by remaining tests
body: The previous endpoint logged `logger.info('browser_report_received', extra={'request_body': request.data})` for every accepted request. The new endpoint removes this log. The test file drops `test_logs_request_data_if_option_enabled` and the new `test_basic` does not assert any logger.info behavior. If the original intent of the endpoint was to capture raw browser reports (the PR description for the original feature indicated GCP forwarding), this log loss should be intentional and documented, or the test asserting the log should be retained.

title: noise_config added to DBQueryInjectionVulnerabilityGroupType without comment
body: A `noise_config = NoiseConfig(ignore_limit=5)` is added to `DBQueryInjectionVulnerabilityGroupType` without any inline comment explaining why this group type is being treated as noisy at a 5-event limit. Group-type noise configs are product decisions that affect alerting/grouping behavior and should be reviewed; at minimum a comment should explain the rationale so future maintainers don't remove it by mistake.

title: MatchedRow.max_segment_id type change lacks test for the None branch
body: `MatchedRow` is updated so `max_segment_id: int | None`, and `_make_recording_filenames` short-circuits when it is `None`. The corresponding test change only flips an existing fixture from `0` to `None` to exercise the early return, but does not assert that no deletion request is made when `max_segment_id` is `None` (no chunks produced, archive-only path). A regression that deletes despite `None` would not be caught by the existing test as-is.

title: User mismatch check bypassed when Integration record missing
body: In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, when `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `Integration.DoesNotExist`, the code returns `pipeline.next_step()` without performing the GitHub user mismatch validation (the very check this PR adds). This means if the webhook-created Integration has been deleted (or hasn't arrived yet due to timing), any GitHub user who knows a valid installation_id can complete the OAuth flow and proceed to build_integration, defeating the central security check of this PR. The `except Integration.DoesNotExist` branch should still perform the user validation, or alternatively should verify that `github_authenticated_user` was set by OAuthLoginView before allowing progress.

title: Unguarded metadata['sender'] access can raise KeyError/TypeError
body: The expression `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` will raise `KeyError` if `sender` is absent from metadata, or `TypeError` if `sender` is `None`/not a dict. Looking at `build_integration`, `sender` is only added when present in state (`if state.get("sender"):`), so older installations or webhook-created Integrations without sender info would crash with a 500 instead of producing the intended error page. The code should defensively check `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` before comparing.

title: safe_urlopen not wrapped in try/except for OAuth token exchange
body: `safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` can raise on network errors or non-2xx GitHub responses, but only `safe_urlread`/`parse_qsl` are wrapped in try/except. A failure during the POST to GitHub's access_token endpoint will surface as an unhandled 500 rather than the intended "Invalid installation request." error page. The call should be inside the try block (or a separate try/except) so transient GitHub failures yield the same user-facing error as a missing/invalid token.

title: Misleading comment about OrganizationIntegration
body: The comment `# OrganizationIntegration does not exist, but Integration does exist.` precedes a `try: Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id, status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE)` that does not consult OrganizationIntegration at all. The previous block already handled OrganizationIntegration via `installations_exist`; this block only checks for an active Integration. The comment should be reworded (e.g., "Active Integration already exists from a prior install; verify it belongs to the same GitHub user.") to match what the code actually does.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the 404 path
body: The test stubs `/app/installations/{installation_id}` to return 404, then issues a callback with state `"ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"` which does NOT match the pipeline signature `"9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3"`. The OAuthLoginView returns the generic error before ever reaching GitHubInstallation or build_integration, so the mocked 404 is never hit. With the correct state the test would also fail because no webhook was sent to create the Integration row, so GitHubInstallation's `Integration.DoesNotExist` branch returns `pipeline.next_step()` and build_integration is never called. The intended 404 behavior of `build_integration` (raising `IntegrationError("The GitHub installation could not be found.")`) is now untested.

title: No dedicated test for OAuth state CSRF mismatch
body: The only state-mismatch coverage is incidental inside `test_installation_not_found`, and even there it's combined with a missing-Integration path. There is no isolated test verifying that OAuthLoginView rejects a callback whose `state` query param differs from `pipeline.signature` and renders the failed-install template. A targeted regression test would protect this CSRF-style check from future refactors.

title: No test for missing access_token from GitHub
body: OAuthLoginView returns the generic error when `"access_token" not in payload` (covering GitHub returning an error response or empty body), but there is no test stubbing `https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token` to return e.g. `error=bad_verification_code` and asserting the pipeline terminates with the failed-install template. This branch is uncovered.

title: No test for get_user_info returning no login
body: OAuthLoginView also returns the generic error when `"login" not in authenticated_user_info`, but the only stub for `/user` returns a valid login. There is no test covering GitHub returning an error body from `/user` (e.g., missing scope or 401), which should likewise surface the failed-install page rather than a 500.

title: safe_urlopen exception not caught in OAuthLoginView
body: The `safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` call at line 423 sits outside the `try`/`except Exception` block at lines 425-429. If `safe_urlopen` raises (e.g. DNS failure, connection refused, TLS error, or any non-success path where it does not return a response object), the exception propagates up and the user gets a 500 instead of the intended "Invalid installation request." page. The current try/except only guards `safe_urlread`, `decode`, and `parse_qsl`. Move `safe_urlopen` inside the `try` block so all failure paths return `error(request, self.active_organization)`.

title: get_user_info exception not handled
body: `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` at line 434 is not wrapped in any exception handler. If the GitHub `/user` call raises (network error, non-2xx that the helper propagates, malformed JSON, missing keys, etc.), the exception bubbles up and the user sees a 500 error rather than the documented "Invalid installation request." failure page. Wrap the call so any exception results in the same `error(request, self.active_organization)` return path used for the other failure cases.

title: User-mismatch check bypassed when Integration record is not yet present
body: In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, the `except Integration.DoesNotExist:` branch at lines 479-481 returns `pipeline.next_step()` immediately, so the new OAuth-authenticated-user vs. sender check at lines 501-505 is never executed. GitHub's install webhook and the user redirect are independent, so when the redirect arrives before the webhook (or the webhook is delayed/retried), the `Integration` row does not exist yet, this branch is taken, and the pipeline proceeds to `build_integration`, which creates the `OrganizationIntegration` for the attacker's installation linked to the victim's Sentry org with no sender comparison. The whole purpose of this PR (validating the GitHub user that authorised the app with the user that installed it) is defeated in that race window. The check should be enforced (e.g. wait/retry for the Integration record and require `metadata["sender"]["login"]` before continuing) instead of silently advancing.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the installation-not-found path
body: The rewritten `test_installation_not_found` (line 379) issues its OAuth callback with `state="ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"` (line 392), which does not match the pipeline signature `"9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3"`. As a result the test bails out in `OAuthLoginView` with the state-mismatch error and never reaches `GitHubInstallation.dispatch` / `build_integration`, where the `IntegrationError("The GitHub installation could not be found.")` is raised. The 404 stub on `/app/installations/{id}` is therefore never exercised, and after this PR there is no test covering the actual installation-not-found failure path. The second GET should use the correct pipeline-signature state so the OAuth step succeeds and the code path under test is actually hit.

title: OAuth authorize URL built with f-string instead of urlencode
body: The redirect at line 408 (`f"{...}?client_id={github_client_id}&state={state}&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}"`) concatenates query parameters with raw f-string interpolation instead of `urlencode`. `pipeline.signature`, the GitHub OAuth `client_id`, and the absolute `redirect_uri` could in principle contain reserved characters (`&`, `=`, `#`, `+`, spaces, unicode). Any such character would either be misinterpreted by GitHub (silently corrupting `state` or `redirect_uri`) or be used to tamper with the query string. Use `urlencode` (or `urllib.parse.urlencode`) to construct the query parameters, matching the safer practice used elsewhere in the file.

title: Webhook signature in test_github_user_mismatch won't match the modified payload
body: The test mutates webhook_event["installation"]["id"] and webhook_event["sender"]["login"] and then re-serializes with json.dumps(webhook_event), but it sends the hard-coded signature sha1=d184e6717f8bfbcc291ebc8c0756ee446c6c9486. That signature was computed over the original bytes of INSTALLATION_EVENT_EXAMPLE; modifying any field changes the HMAC input, so the GitHub webhook endpoint will reject the request with a non-2xx response. The test will fail at `assert resp.status_code == 204`, the Integration record is never created, and the subsequent user-mismatch branch in GitHubInstallation is therefore never exercised. The new security check is added without a working test that proves it actually rejects a mismatched sender.

title: KeyError/TypeError if integration metadata has no 'sender'
body: GitHubInstallation.dispatch() compares pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") to integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]. The webhook handler only writes the sender key when the webhook payload provides one, and build_integration only copies it when state.get("sender") is truthy, so pre-existing integrations (and any future flow where the webhook does not include a sender) can have no "sender" key, or a None value. Subscripting None or accessing a missing key raises TypeError/KeyError, which surfaces as an unhandled 500 to the user instead of the intended "Invalid installation request." page. The access should use a safe lookup such as integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login") and treat a missing sender as a mismatch (or a separate error).

title: safe_urlopen to GitHub token endpoint is outside the try/except
body: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch(), safe_urlread and parse_qsl are wrapped in `try/except Exception` so any decode/parse failure yields an empty payload and triggers the error page. The preceding `req = safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` call is NOT inside that try block, so any network error, DNS failure, timeout, or non-2xx from safe_urlopen propagates out of dispatch and crashes the request as a 500 instead of returning the error page. The same problem applies to the immediately following `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` call at line 434, which is also outside the try block. Both should be wrapped so all token-exchange failures produce the same user-visible error response.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the 404 branch
body: The test name and the responses.replace(...status=404) suggest it is verifying the path where get_installation_info returns 404 (which should produce "The GitHub installation could not be found."). In the new flow, the first GET (with only installation_id) hits OAuthLoginView, which binds the id and redirects to GitHub OAuth without ever calling get_installation_info. The second GET uses state='ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05' which cannot equal pipeline.signature, so the response is the generic state-mismatch error page ("Invalid installation request.") rather than the installation-not-found error. The build_integration 404 branch is therefore no longer covered by any test, and the renamed assertion no longer checks what the test name implies.

title: No audit log when authenticated GitHub user does not match installation sender
body: The new check that rejects an installation when the OAuth-authenticated GitHub login differs from integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] is exactly the attack scenario this PR is designed to catch (a Sentry user trying to claim a GitHub app installation that was installed by a different GitHub identity). The branch only renders an error page and silently drops the request. A warning/error log entry containing the Sentry org, the installation_id, the authenticated login, and the recorded sender should be emitted so security teams can detect and investigate these attempts.

title: Dataclass default `queued=timezone.now()` is evaluated once at class definition
body: In `AssignmentSource`, the field `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a classic Python dataclass pitfall: the default expression is evaluated once when the decorator runs, not per instance. Every `AssignmentSource` constructed without an explicit `queued` argument will share the same timestamp (the time the module was first imported). It should be `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)` (with `field` imported from `dataclasses`). The field is currently unused in the sync logic so the impact is low, but it is incorrect and will surprise anyone who later relies on `queued` for ordering, TTL, or debugging.

title: `from_dict` silently swallows all errors and returns None
body: `AssignmentSource.from_dict` uses a bare `except (ValueError, TypeError)` and returns `None` for any malformed payload. This is unsafe because the only signal callers get is `None`, which is treated identically to "no assignment source was provided", meaning `should_sync` will happily allow the outbound sync to proceed. Concrete risks: (a) forward-compatibility — if a new required field is added to `AssignmentSource` later, every in-flight Celery task whose `assignment_source_dict` predates the change will silently deserialize to `None`, re-enabling the very sync cycle this PR is trying to fix; (b) corruption of task payloads will be invisible. The method should at minimum log the malformed payload, or raise so the caller can decide (e.g., retry vs. drop) instead of silently dropping the cycle-prevention signal.

title: `sync_status_outbound` abstract signature adds `assignment_source` that is never passed anywhere
body: The abstract method `sync_status_outbound` is updated to take `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`, but no caller in this PR (or visible in the diff) ever passes it. The `sync_assignee_outbound` task only invokes `sync_assignee_outbound`, not `sync_status_outbound`. This is misleading: the PR description claims to break "issue sync cycles" (plural) and the new signature implies status sync cycles are being addressed, but the status cycle is not actually broken — inbound `sync_status_inbound` still triggers `sync_status_outbound` without any source guard. Any concrete implementation that does not already accept `**kwargs` will also break if a future caller does pass `assignment_source`. Either remove the parameter from the abstract signature until the status-side fix is implemented, or implement and thread the assignment_source through the status path so the cycle is actually closed.

title: Typo in test method name: `test_from_dict_inalid_data`
body: The test method `test_from_dict_inalid_data` contains a spelling error — "inalid" should be "invalid". This will surface in test reports and any test-runner output that uses the method name.

title: AssignmentSource.queued default evaluated once at class definition time
body: The dataclass field `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a well-known Python dataclass pitfall: `timezone.now()` is called once when the class body executes (at module import), not each time an `AssignmentSource` is constructed. Every instance created without an explicit `queued` will share the same import-time timestamp, so `queued` no longer represents "when this assignment source was queued". Fix by importing `field` from `dataclasses` and writing `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. The current test only asserts `queued is not None`, which masks the bug. The field is not yet consumed by any logic, but it is part of the persisted payload and any future use for TTL, deduplication, or staleness checks will be wrong.

title: Test name typo: `inalid_data`
body: Test method `test_from_dict_inalid_data` has a typo (`inalid` instead of `invalid`). The name shows up in test runner output and failure messages, making the suite harder to read and conflating a misspelling with a real bug during triage.

title: Test name `test_from_dict_empty_array` actually exercises an empty dict
body: The test is named `test_from_dict_empty_array` but passes `data: dict[str, Any] = {}` (an empty dict). If the intent is to assert behavior on an empty mapping, the name should reflect that; otherwise readers will look for an empty-list case that does not exist. This is the kind of misleading test name that causes future contributors to add a second, redundant test for the wrong shape.

title: AssignmentSource.queued default is evaluated at class definition time, not per instance
body: In the AssignmentSource dataclass, `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` evaluates `timezone.now()` exactly once when the module is imported, and that single value becomes the default for every instance created without an explicit `queued` argument. Every AssignmentSource produced by `from_integration` (and every one reconstructed by `from_dict` when the serialized payload omits `queued`) will therefore share the same timestamp — the process startup time, not the actual time the assignment was queued. This silently breaks the semantic of the field and any future logic that relies on it (ordering, staleness checks, debugging). Use `dataclasses.field(default_factory=lambda: timezone.now())` so a fresh timestamp is computed per instance.

title: Outbound deassign cycle-break path is not covered by tests
body: The PR adds `test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration` to verify that outbound `assign` is suppressed when the AssignmentSource matches the target integration. There is no symmetric test for outbound `deassign` (`GroupAssignee.objects.deassign(group, assignment_source=...)`) being suppressed. The `deassign` method also forwards `assignment_source` to `sync_group_assignee_outbound`, so the cycle-break logic on the unassignment path is exercised by no test, and a regression there would silently re-introduce the sync loop on unassign events.

title: No test verifies inbound change still propagates to other integrations on the same group
body: The PR description claims the change 'should still allow other integrations to propagate changes outward', but the new tests only assert that the source integration is suppressed. There is no test that links a single group to two different integrations and confirms that an inbound change from integration A still triggers an outbound sync to integration B. Without that test, a future change that, for example, compares `sync_source` against the group or organization instead of the integration_id could silently break multi-installation setups.

title: Typo in test name: 'inalid' should be 'invalid'
body: The test method `test_from_dict_inalid_data` at line 13 contains a typo ('inalid' instead of 'invalid'). The misspelled name makes the test harder to find via search and reduces code quality. Rename it to `test_from_dict_invalid_data`.

title: sync_status_outbound signature accepts assignment_source but no caller or implementation passes it
body: The abstract method `sync_status_outbound` is updated to accept `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`, but neither any caller in this PR nor any concrete implementation is updated to pass it. The status-sync path is left in an inconsistent state: the parameter is declared but unused. If the intent is to apply the same cycle-break to status syncs, the wiring (callers + concrete implementations) is incomplete and the fix is half-done; if the intent is only a placeholder, the parameter should not be added in this PR. Either finish the wiring or revert this signature update so future maintainers are not misled.

title: test_dedupe expected occurrence is built with wrong group_key, breaking equality assertion
body: In TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe, build_mock_occurrence_and_event is called with group_key='val1' and value=6 to populate the expected_result, but evaluate_group_key_value is then invoked with expected_result.group_key ('group_key') and value=10. Because build_mock_occurrence_and_event sets fingerprint via handler.build_fingerprint(group_key), the expected IssueOccurrence gets fingerprint [f'{detector_id}:val1'] while the one produced inside evaluate_group_key_value (via build_occurrence_and_event_data -> build_mock_occurrence_and_event) gets [f'{detector_id}:group_key']. IssueOccurrence is constructed positionally as a dataclass, so the fingerprints are part of __eq__; the assertion comparing the result to expected_result will fail. The call should be build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, 'group_key', 10, PriorityLevel.HIGH) so the expected and actual occurrences match. The same copy/paste-style hardcoding of 'val1'/6 also appears in other tests in this file (e.g. test_results_on_change) where it happens to be harmless because the evaluate call uses 'val1' too, but it is fragile.

title: get_state_data raises KeyError when counter_names is empty
body: In StatefulDetectorHandler.get_state_data, when self.counter_names is an empty list the 'if self.counter_names:' block is skipped, leaving counter_updates = {}. The subsequent loop then executes 'counter_updates=counter_updates[gk]' on this empty dict, which raises KeyError for every group_key. Since counter_names is declared as an abstract list[str] property and a handler is permitted to legitimately return [] (no counters to track), this is a real latent bug. The fix is to initialize counter_updates to {gk: {} for gk in group_keys} before the if block (or to default to {} inside the DetectorStateData construction when no counter data is available).

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler cannot be instantiated: abstract methods unimplemented
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is defined as 'class MetricAlertDetectorHandler(StatefulDetectorHandler[QuerySubscriptionUpdate]): pass' but StatefulDetectorHandler declares several @abc.abstractmethod methods that it does not implement: counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and the newly-added build_occurrence_and_event_data. Calling MetricAlertDetectorHandler(detector) will raise TypeError. The TODO comment marks this as deliberate placeholder work, but the class is still exported (referenced from MetricAlertFire.detector_handler) so any caller that triggers detector.detector_handler on a MetricAlertFire GroupType will crash with a non-obvious TypeError rather than a clear 'not implemented' error. Consider either raising NotImplementedError in a custom __init__/__new__ or wiring this through a registry entry that is left unset until the abstraction is implemented.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now uninstantiable
body: After this change, MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler with an empty body (`pass`). StatefulDetectorHandler declares four abstract methods (`counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and `build_occurrence_and_event_data`) which the subclass does not implement. As a result, instantiating `MetricAlertDetectorHandler(detector)` raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract methods ...`. Previously the class inherited from `DetectorHandler` and provided a concrete stub `evaluate` that returned `[]`, so it could be instantiated and registered. Because `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler = MetricAlertDetectorHandler`, any code path that resolves the handler for this group type (now or once the feature is wired up) will fail. This is a behavior regression and should be fixed before merging, e.g. by keeping the stub `evaluate`, marking the class `NotImplementedError`-only, or using `# type: ignore[abstract]` along with an explicit raise.

title: build_mock_occurrence_and_event called with wrong value for group_2
body: In `test_state_results_multi_group`, the data packet has `"group_vals": {"group_1": 6, "group_2": 10}` but the mock for group_2 is built with `value=6` (`build_mock_occurrence_and_event(detector.detector_handler, "group_2", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)`). The mock currently ignores the value parameter so the test passes, but the inconsistency masks a real bug if `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` ever starts using `value` (e.g., to populate evidence_data). The test should pass `10` to match the data packet.

title: build_mock_occurrence_and_event called with stale value=6 across tests
body: `test_results_on_change` (line ~488) and `test_dedupe` (line ~508) call `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)` while their input data packets contain values `100` and `8` respectively. The mock does not use the value today, so the tests pass, but the inconsistency is the same kind of copy/paste mismatch as the one above and would silently desynchronize if the helper ever started using `value`. Pass the actual values from the data packet (100 and 8) for clarity and to keep the helper faithful.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler cannot be instantiated (abstract methods not implemented)
body: The class `MetricAlertDetectorHandler(StatefulDetectorHandler[QuerySubscriptionUpdate])` body is just `pass`. With this PR, `StatefulDetectorHandler` adds `build_occurrence_and_event_data` as an `@abc.abstractmethod`, and it still requires the pre-existing abstract members `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, and `get_group_key_values`. None of these are implemented on `MetricAlertDetectorHandler`, so attempting to instantiate it (e.g., via `Detector.detector_handler` when `MetricAlertFire` is the group type, since `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler = MetricAlertDetectorHandler`) will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract methods ...`. The TODO comment hints this is a placeholder, but previously the class extended `DetectorHandler` and implemented `evaluate` returning `[]`, so it was actually instantiable — this PR regresses that. Either the new abstract method needs a default (e.g. raise `NotImplementedError`), or this stub class should be made `StatefulDetectorHandler`-ready (or removed from the registry) before merge.

title: get_monitor_environment_context returns the un-modified monitor.config instead of the local copy it built
body: The function builds a local `config` by copying `monitor_environment.monitor.config`, then conditionally rewrites `config["schedule_type"]` to the human-readable display string via `monitor_environment.monitor.get_schedule_type_display()`. The return dict, however, uses `"config": monitor_environment.monitor.config` — the original dict — discarding the local `config` entirely. Consequence: every occurrence event published to Kafka contains the raw `schedule_type` enum value (e.g. `"crontab"`) in the monitor context instead of the localized display string ("Every minute", "Every hour", etc.) the surrounding evidence display strings use. Downstream issue/event UIs that read this context will render the wrong/ugly value for `schedule_type`. The return should use the local `config` variable. This bug existed in the pre-refactor `mark_failed.py` and was carried over unchanged into the new module.

title: get_monitor_environment_context returns unmodified config
body: The function copies `monitor_environment.monitor.config` into a local `config` variable and mutates it (e.g. replacing `schedule_type` with its display string via `get_schedule_type_display()`), but the returned dict references the original `monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead of the modified `config`. As a result, the schedule_type value in the monitor context included with issue events is the raw enum/config value (e.g. `1`) rather than the human-readable display string (`Crontab`). The bug existed in `mark_failed.py` prior to this refactor and was carried verbatim; since this refactor splits the logic into a new module, fixing it now would correct the monitor context data shown to users in monitor incident events.

title: Docstring typos and inaccurate singular example
body: The docstring for `get_failure_reason` contains typos (`humam readible` should be `human readable`) and the singular example (`A failed check-in was detected`) does not match the actual output produced by `SINGULAR_HUMAN_FAILURE_MAP` (`An error check-in was detected`, `A missed check-in was detected`, `A timeout check-in was detected`). Since this refactor relocates the function into a new module, fixing the docstring now will prevent the mistakes from being propagated to anyone consuming the new module.

title: Unused logging import and module logger left behind by refactor
body: After the extracted logic moved into incidents.py, `import logging` on line 4 and `logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)` on line 11 are dead code in mark_failed.py — the module no longer emits any log statements. A refactor that removes the only consumers of this logger is the natural place to clean it up; leaving it in is misleading and will trip unused-import linters.

title: Unused logger definition in the new module
body: `logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)` on line 25 is defined but never referenced anywhere in the new incident_occurrence.py (the imports of `logging` on line 3 exist solely to support this dead definition). It should be removed together with the now-unused `import logging` so the new module is consistent with mark_failed.py's behavior.

title: get_monitor_environment_context modifies a config copy it never returns
body: In `get_monitor_environment_context`, `config = monitor_environment.monitor.config.copy()` on line 160 and `config['schedule_type'] = monitor_environment.monitor.get_schedule_type_display()` on line 162 are dead code: the dict returned on line 168 uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` (the original) instead of the modified local `config`. Consequence: the `monitor.config` payload sent in issue events via Kafka always contains the raw `schedule_type` enum value and never the human-readable display string the code clearly intended to substitute. The bug is preserved verbatim from the pre-refactor mark_failed.py, but hoisting the function into its own module is the right place to fix it — either return `config` or drop the unused local.

title: record_stored_segments now invoked per flusher buffer instead of once on writer
body: The pre-change code called `self.buffer.record_stored_segments()` once per `submit()` on the writer buffer. The new code iterates `for buffer in self.buffers.values(): buffer.record_stored_segments()`, which is once per flusher process. With multiple flusher processes this multiplies invocations by N, and crucially drops the call on the actual writer buffer (the original `buffer` argument is no longer stored on `self`). If `record_stored_segments` is a metric emission that tags state, has side effects in Redis, or otherwise isn't idempotent across processes, this is a metric/state regression. Even if it is just a gauge, the cardinality and emission frequency for downstream metrics change.

title: Dead helper _create_process_for_shard is never called
body: The newly introduced `_create_process_for_shard(shard)` is never invoked anywhere in the module. It is a leftover that duplicates the work of `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` but is unreachable. Leaving dead public-looking methods around risks future callers assuming restart-by-shard works when the mapping actually restarts whole processes.

title: Killed processes are not joined; replace-by-key can leak zombies
body: In `_ensure_processes_alive`, the old process is killed (when it is a `multiprocessing.Process`) and then immediately replaced in `self.processes[process_index]` by a brand-new process without joining the previous one. The previous process object loses its last reference and becomes a zombie until its finalizer runs. In `join()` the loop calls `process.terminate()` on the still-stored entries but again never joins, leaving zombies for `terminate`d processes. Over many restart cycles this can pile up zombie PIDs and consume resources; combined with the spawn context it is also easy to lose visibility into why flusher processes vanished.

title: Restart path leaves the previous thread (test mode) running with stale buffer
body: `_ensure_processes_alive` only kills `multiprocessing.Process` instances; `threading.Thread` instances (created when `produce_to_pipe` is set, e.g. in tests) are explicitly not killed. The new process/thread is then started with a fresh `SpansBuffer`, but the old thread keeps running against its original buffer and continues to call the (now stale) `produce_to_pipe`. In a unit test this can produce phantom messages or assertions against the wrong buffer; in any future deployment that uses threading it would silently leak work. Either always join both kinds, or explicitly document that thread mode is single-shot.

title: process_restarts accumulates across the lifetime of the consumer
body: `self.process_restarts[process_index]` is incremented on every unhealthy detection and never reset. Combined with the `>` comparison (which lets the count reach `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS + 1 == 11` before raising), any flusher process that crashes 12 times over the consumer's lifetime (including rare, isolated crashes months apart) will permanently take the consumer down with `RuntimeError`. The counter should reset after the process has been healthy for some interval, and the comparison should be `>=` if the intent is exactly `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` restarts.

title: if not process: continue is dead code
body: `self.processes[process_index]` is always assigned a `multiprocessing.Process` or `threading.Thread` instance in `_create_process_for_shards`; both are truthy. The `if not process: continue` guard can never fire and should be removed (or replaced with the actual invariant you want to enforce).

title: Class docstring claims one process per shard but default caps processes at 1
body: The class docstring now reads 'Creates one process per shard for parallel processing.' But the constructor computes `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, and the new CLI flag `flusher_processes` defaults to 1, so the actual production default is one shared process for all shards. The docstring (and the PR description: 'make the flusher spawn a process per redis shard') overstates the behavior at default settings. Either reword the docstring/helper text to reflect the 'up to N processes, defaulting to 1' semantics, or change the default to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)` to actually deliver 'one process per shard' out of the box.

title: --flusher-processes help text and default contradict the PR description
body: The new `--flusher-processes` option defaults to `1` and its help string says 'Maximum number of processes for the span flusher. Defaults to 1.' The PR description says 'let's make the flusher spawn a process per redis shard.' With the default of 1, every shard will be multiplexed onto a single process (because `num_processes = min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` collapses to 1). Operators who read the help text will not realize they have to set `--flusher-processes=<num_shards>` to actually get the documented one-process-per-shard layout. Either set the default to the shard count, or document the trade-off in the option help and in the SpanFlusher docstring.

title: join() never calls terminate on hung threads and can deadlock the consumer
body: In `join()`, the wait loop only sleeps until `process.is_alive()` is false or the deadline elapses, and only calls `process.terminate()` for `multiprocessing.Process`. A hung `threading.Thread` (which happens any time `produce_to_pipe` is set) will block `join()` until the deadline. Worse, the loop terminates by calling `process.terminate()` only on the entry currently iterated, with no `process.join()` afterwards; any process that survives past the deadline (e.g. spawn-context process that ignores SIGTERM) will be left as a zombie. Add explicit `join(timeout)` after `terminate()` for both kinds, and a fallback to `_stopped` polling for threads.

title: Added time.sleep(0.1) is monkeypatched to a no-op
body: The test does `monkeypatch.setattr('time.sleep', lambda _: None)` and then immediately calls `time.sleep(0.1)` with a comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change.' Because of the monkeypatch that call is a no-op, so the comment is misleading and the test does not actually yield to let the (now threaded) flusher catch up on the new drift. The earlier `step.poll()` does not flush either. The test currently still passes because the spawn-context flusher thread races quickly, but this is a latent flake and the comment lies about behavior. Either remove the no-op sleep, drop the comment, or use `event.wait`/an actual non-patched sleep.

title: test_flusher_processes_limit only checks structure, not correctness of shared-shard flushing
body: The new test creates 4 partitions, sets `flusher_processes=2`, and only asserts that `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `max_processes == 2`, `num_processes == 2`, and `sum(len(shards)) == 4`. It never submits a single message, never produces a KafkaPayload, and never verifies that shards are actually distributed (e.g. that processes share shards correctly, that the buffer the flusher uses is the right one, that segments from every shard eventually flush). The most important behavioral claim of the PR — that multiple shards sharing one flusher process still works — is not tested.

title: test_backpressure relies on a sleep that is not patched and is likely flaky
body: `append` uses `sleep` imported via `from time import sleep`, which is a local name bound at import time and is *not* affected by `monkeypatch.setattr('time.sleep', ...)`. So `sleep(1.0)` actually blocks for a real second on each produced payload, while the inner flusher's own `time.sleep(1)` is patched to a no-op. After the 0.1s real sleep, the flusher thread is still blocked inside the very first `append` call and `messages` is empty, so `assert messages` is racing against the producer. The test happens to pass today only because the flusher has not yet produced when the assertion runs, but the assertion is timing-dependent and the comment/help text does not warn about this. Use a sentinel (e.g. set a flag on the first call) instead of sleeping for a wall-clock second, or monkeypatch the local symbol.

title: Distribution test does not verify per-process assignment
body: The test `test_flusher_processes_limit` asserts only that the total number of shards assigned across all processes equals 4 (`total_shards = sum(len(shards) for shards in flusher.process_to_shards_map.values()) == 4`). This passes even if the modulo distribution is broken — for example, all four shards could be assigned to a single process, or a shard could be duplicated across processes — as long as the total counts to 4. The test never submits spans, so it does not exercise the actual per-process flushing of shared shards either. There should be explicit assertions like `assert flusher.process_to_shards_map == {0: [0, 2], 1: [1, 3]}` and a round-trip test that submits spans on each partition and verifies they get flushed.

title: Vestigial time.sleep suggests flaky timing dependency
body: `test_basic` now calls `time.sleep(0.1)` between `step.poll()` and `step.join()` with the comment "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change". Since the test already does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at the top of the function, this sleep is a no-op (it just invokes the patched lambda) and provides no actual scheduling guarantee. This is a code smell indicating that the test depends on wall-clock timing that is no longer being controlled. If the test was flaky without this sleep, the root cause should be fixed by polling for the expected condition instead of sleeping.

title: Dead method _create_process_for_shard
body: The method `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` is defined but never called anywhere in the codebase. The restart path in `_ensure_processes_alive` always uses `_create_process_for_shards` to bring back the whole process (and therefore all shards mapped to it). Either delete the dead method, or use it as a true per-shard restart hook so that one bad shard doesn't take down its siblings sharing the same process.

title: Dead-branch check `if not process`
body: Inside `_ensure_processes_alive` the loop guards with `if not process: continue`. `self.processes` is a `dict[int, SpawnProcess | Thread]` and is only ever assigned live objects in `_create_process_for_shards`, so this guard can never be true and serves no purpose. The subsequent `if not process.is_alive():` already covers dead processes, so this line should be removed to avoid misleading readers.

title: Inconsistent metric tag names for the same flusher
body: The same flusher uses two different tag keys for the shard identifier: `metrics.timer("spans.buffer.flusher.produce", tags={"shard": shard_tag})` at line 185 but `metrics.timer("spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce", tags={"shards": shard_tag})` at line 199. Existing dashboards that key off one of these tag names will silently break or split when the producer switches to multiprocess mode. Pick one key ("shard" since `flusher_unhealthy` already uses that) and use it consistently.

title: Off-by-one in MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS allows one extra restart
body: In `_ensure_processes_alive`, the check `if self.process_restarts[process_index] > MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` happens *before* `self.process_restarts[process_index] += 1`. With `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS = 10`, the sequence is 0,1,...,10 (pass), 11 (fail). That means the consumer tolerates 11 restarts of a given process before giving up, not 10 as the constant name suggests. Either increment before the check or use `>=` so the documented limit matches behavior.

title: max_processes=0 silently becomes 'one process per shard'
body: `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats `0` the same as `None` because `0 or X` evaluates to `X`. A caller that explicitly passes `0` (e.g., a test, or a future config switch) gets the opposite of what they asked for. Use `if max_processes is not None else len(...)` so `0` is honored as "no flusher processes".

title: --flusher-processes default of 1 contradicts PR goal
body: The CLI option defaults to 1 and the help text reads 'Defaults to 1'. With `flusher_processes=1` the flusher remains a single process handling all assigned shards, exactly matching the prior behavior and contradicting the PR description 'make the flusher spawn a process per redis shard'. The factory falls back to `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, so passing 0 would auto-scale but the CLI default of 1 silently disables the new behavior. The default should be 0 (auto), or the help text/help should clearly indicate operators must opt in to get the multi-process behavior described.

title: max_processes=0 falls through to len(assigned_shards) via `or`
body: `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats 0 as falsy, so callers that explicitly pass 0 (a common sentinel meaning 'auto/unbounded') get silently coerced to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`. While 0 is not currently exposed via the CLI default (which is 1), this is a footgun for any future caller (and for the planned 'auto' default). It also makes the check indistinguishable from `None`. Use an explicit `if max_processes is None` check.

title: Memory backpressure check likely over-aggregates Redis global memory
body: In the old single-buffer code, `self.buffer.get_memory_info()` returned one set of Redis memory stats. The new code iterates `for buffer in self.buffers.values(): memory_infos.extend(buffer.get_memory_info())` and sums `used`/`available` across all of them. Because every SpansBuffer in `self.buffers` queries the same underlying Redis cluster, each call returns the same global `used`/`available` values; summing N copies multiplies the apparent memory by N. With the new default of N flushers (one per shard), the threshold would trip at roughly `max_memory_percentage / N` of real usage, causing the consumer to hard-pause way before Redis is actually full. Either aggregate once (deduplicating per Redis cluster) or change `get_memory_info` to report per-shard stats before summing.

title: Per-process backpressure raises on any one process, halting the consumer
body: The old code had a single `backpressure_since` for the lone flusher process; raising MessageRejected on that flag paused the consumer for the whole pipeline. The new code raises MessageRejected if *any* one of the per-process backpressure flags is over threshold. With the new shard-per-process layout a single hot shard can now trip backpressure and stop ingestion entirely, even when the other shards have plenty of headroom. The original code also fetched the `backpressure-seconds` option only when needed; the new code fetches it on every submit (small perf regression). Consider only signalling backpressure when *all* processes are stuck, or aggregating by Redis instance.

title: Dead method _create_process_for_shard defined but never called
body: The new code defines `def _create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` with logic that looks up which process owns a shard and restarts that process. It is never invoked from anywhere in the module (restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards` directly via `_ensure_processes_alive`). It is misleading dead code that should be removed or actually wired into per-shard restart paths.

title: test_basic relies on time.sleep(0.1) for flusher to drain
body: The test was changed to add an unconditional `time.sleep(0.1)` between setting `current_drift` and `step.join()`. With `produce_to_pipe` set, the flusher now runs as a thread whose loop has a `time.sleep(1)` (defanged by the monkeypatch to `lambda _: None`) and is gated by `stopped.value` only being set in `join()`. The 0.1s sleep is a band-aid for a race: if the thread is not yet past the `buffer.flush_segments` call when `join()` runs, the test fails with no messages. The test should deterministically wait for the flusher (e.g., poll on a counter or a barrier) instead of relying on wall time, and the change from `@pytest.mark.django_db` to `@pytest.mark.django_db(transaction=True)` should be justified in a comment.

title: test_flusher_processes_limit does not verify shared-process flushing works
body: The new test only asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `flusher.max_processes == 2`, `flusher.num_processes == 2`, and that `sum(len(shards) for shards in ... ) == 4`. It does not actually send any spans through `submit()`, so the multi-process/sharing code path (round-robin shard distribution, per-shard SpansBuffer instances, per-process backpressure/health values, per-shard metric tags) is never exercised. Add a case that submits spans into shards handled by each of the two threads and asserts each produced its expected message with the correct `shard` tag.

title: Thread flusher not joined on shutdown when produce_to_pipe is set
body: In `join()`, the loop waits for `process.is_alive()` to become False and then only calls `process.terminate()` when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. For the test path (`produce_to_pipe is not None`), the workers are `threading.Thread` daemons, so they have no `terminate()`. The code only signals them via `stopped.value`, but the main loop may exit before the thread observes the flag (especially with the monkeypatched `time.sleep`). Daemon threads will be killed when the interpreter exits, but in-process this can leak work in-flight in Redis (e.g., `done_flush_segments` not called), leaving dangling 'flushing' segment keys. Consider an explicit thread shutdown with a small bounded wait, or document the test-only restriction.

title: Inner join loop ignores remaining_time after first wait
body: Inside `join()`, the per-process loop computes `remaining_time = deadline - time.time()` once before the `while process.is_alive()` loop, but never recomputes `deadline` inside that inner loop. After each `time.sleep(0.1)` the comparison `deadline > time.time()` is still correct (it uses absolute deadline), so the loop does terminate, but the initial `remaining_time` check is dead — it is computed and then never consulted again. Harmless but confusing; either remove the pre-check or actually use it to cap the total per-process wait.

title: Unbounded queue with no backpressure can exhaust memory
body: In FixedQueuePool.__init__, the queues are created as `queue.Queue()` with no maxsize, making them unbounded. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit (line 293) calls `work_queue.put(work_item)` which never blocks. If a particular group is slow (e.g., a subscription whose handler hangs), all items for that group accumulate in its dedicated queue without limit. Unlike the existing `BatchStep`/`RunTask` strategies, this new strategy provides no backpressure: the main thread keeps fetching from Kafka and calling submit, so memory can grow without bound until the consumer OOMs. The PR description acknowledges that 'there's still a chance of individual items backlogging a queue' but does not bound the queue or block submit when queues are full.

title: get_committable_offsets iterates O(max_offset) not O(outstanding)
body: In OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets, the loop `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1):` iterates over every offset in the numeric range, even those that were never added (e.g., gaps from compaction, filtered payloads, or pre-existing committed offsets). For a partition with min_offset=0 and max_offset=1_000_000 and only a few outstanding offsets, this is ~1 million iterations per call, and the commit loop calls this once per second per partition. It should iterate over the sorted `all_offsets` set (O(k log k) where k is the number of seen offsets) and break on the first outstanding/missing one.

title: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join silently drops timeout argument
body: `def join(self, timeout: float | None = None) -> None: self.close()` ignores the `timeout` parameter entirely. Arroyo's ProcessingStrategy contract allows callers to pass a join timeout (e.g., during shutdown sequencing). Silently ignoring it means callers cannot bound how long join blocks, and the strategy will always wait the full internal 5.0s for the commit thread plus however long queue_pool.shutdown takes.

title: FixedQueuePool.shutdown 5s join can drop in-flight work
body: `worker.join(timeout=5.0)` only waits 5 seconds, and the worker is a daemon so it is killed on process exit. If a `result_processor` call takes longer than 5 seconds (which is exactly the kind of slow item this PR is designed to isolate), the join times out, the daemon thread is abandoned, and any work it was holding is never reported as completed/comitted. The fix is either to use a configurable/longer timeout, to join the strategy's commit thread only after all queues drain (e.g., call `wait_until_empty` first), or to set `immediate=True` on `q.shutdown()` and document the data-loss tradeoff.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the wrong behavior
body: The test sets `mock_processor_call.side_effect = [Exception('Processing failed'), None]` and then asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`. But OrderedQueueWorker.run catches the exception in the inner `except Exception` and still calls `offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` in the `finally`, so offset 100 is marked completed. Offset 101 also completes. Both are contiguous, so the commit loop will commit offset 102 (101+1). The assertion as written would fail in the correct behavior, and the assertion is trivially true when `len == 0` regardless of what happened. The test should instead assert the committed offset reflects both completed messages (e.g., `committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102`) to actually verify the 'errors don't block other commits' intent.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_graceful_shutdown does not verify graceful behavior
body: The test submits 5 messages and then immediately calls `factory.shutdown()` without waiting for processing, asserting only `factory.queue_pool is None`. This does not verify that the 5 submitted messages are processed before shutdown, that no offsets are lost, or that the shutdown is actually graceful. Combined with the 5s join timeout in FixedQueuePool.shutdown, this test will pass even if shutdown drops all in-flight work.

title: Kafka integration test depends on private StreamProcessor internals
body: The test drives the consumer by calling `processor._run_once()` in a loop and `processor._shutdown()` at the end. These are private arroyo methods (leading underscore) and are not part of the public API; they can change between arroyo releases without notice, which would silently break this test. It also relies on `override_settings(KAFKA_TOPIC_OVERRIDES=...)` and creates real Kafka topics in a `requires_kafka` test, so it is expensive and fragile. A more robust integration test would use the public `run()` method or otherwise not depend on underscore-prefixed methods.

title: Unreachable queue.ShutDown handler in inner try
body: The inner `try` block in OrderedQueueWorker.run only wraps `sentry_sdk.start_transaction(...)` and `self.result_processor(...)`. `queue.ShutDown` can only be raised by `queue.Queue.get()` or `queue.Queue.put()`, neither of which is called inside this inner try. The `except queue.ShutDown: break` on lines 142-143 is therefore dead code and can be removed (or, if a put call is later added inside the inner try, the comment should explain why).

title: Assert failure leaves partition stuck forever
body: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, the assert `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` is performed before accessing `message.value`. If it fails (or any other error occurs before we can safely read `message.value`), the `except Exception` handler re-checks `isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` — which is the same condition that just failed — and silently does nothing. The offset for that message is never added to the tracker, so it stays outstanding and blocks every future commit for that partition in `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets` (which iterates only up to the highest completed offset). The consumer will hang on this partition indefinitely, with only a log line as evidence. The error should either be re-raised so arroyo/DLQ can handle it, or the offset must be marked complete unconditionally (even if `BrokerValue` can't be read) by carrying the partition/offset before the assert.

title: Graceful shutdown drops in-flight queue items
body: `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets `worker.shutdown = True` for every worker and then calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. Because `OrderedQueueWorker.run` checks `while not self.shutdown` *before* calling `self.work_queue.get()`, workers exit the loop as soon as the flag is observed and never drain items that were already in their queue. Those items have offsets recorded as outstanding in `OffsetTracker`, but since `complete_offset` is never called, they will never be committed and the messages will be re-delivered after restart. The `wait_until_empty` helper exists on the same class but is never invoked, indicating the intent was to drain but the implementation doesn't. Either remove the `wait_until_empty` helper or call it (with a bounded timeout) before flipping the shutdown flag.

title: Hash-based group assignment is not stable across restarts
body: `FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group` uses Python's built-in `hash()`, which is randomized per process under the default `PYTHONHASHSEED`. The class docstring promises 'consistent hashing' and 'Each group is consistently assigned to the same queue'. Within a single process lifetime the assignment is stable (since workers/queues live in memory), but after any restart the same `group_key` can map to a different queue index — directly contradicting the docstring. This is misleading to future maintainers and would break correctness if the pool is ever extended to persist queue assignments or run across processes. Use a stable hash (e.g. `hashlib.sha1(group_key.encode()).hexdigest()`, `zlib.crc32`, or `hashlib.md5`) and update the docstring to reflect the actual guarantee.

title: Docstring claims natural backpressure but queue is unbounded
body: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` docstring states 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up'. However, the queues are constructed via `queue.Queue()` (see `FixedQueuePool.__init__`), which is unbounded. Producers (the arroyo consumer thread calling `submit`) will never block, so a slow worker group causes unbounded memory growth. Either pass `maxsize` to `queue.Queue(maxsize=...)` to actually provide backpressure, or correct the docstring.

title: Worker shutdown flag is a non-atomic bool
body: `OrderedQueueWorker.shutdown` is a plain `bool` attribute written by the main thread (in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown`) and read by the worker thread. While CPython's GIL makes this safe in practice, it is not portable and is not thread-safe by Python's memory model. Use `threading.Event` (`self._stop_event`) and `self._stop_event.is_set()` instead, matching the pattern already used by `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.shutdown_event`.

title: num_queues is not validated
body: `FixedQueuePool.__init__` accepts `num_queues: int = 20` without checking it is positive. If a caller (or the new `thread-queue-parallel` mode) passes `max_workers=0` or a negative value, the loop creates no queues/workers, and the first call to `submit` raises `IndexError` from `self.queues[queue_index]` deep in `FixedQueuePool.submit`. Validate `num_queues >= 1` (and ideally a sensible upper bound) at construction time so misconfiguration fails loudly and early.

title: Offset tracker scans full range per partition every second
body: `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets` is called once per second from `_commit_loop` and, for each partition, computes `min(all_offsets)` and `max(all_offsets)` and then iterates the full range `range(start, max_offset + 1)`. With a partition that has, say, 10k outstanding offsets, every commit tick performs O(10k) set lookups plus two O(n) set scans. For a backlog scenario this is O(n) per second per partition. Track `min_offset` and `max_offset` incrementally (e.g. on `add_offset`) and stop as soon as the first gap is hit instead of recomputing the extremes every call.

title: Worker thread can die silently on unexpected get() error
body: `OrderedQueueWorker.run` only catches `queue.ShutDown` around `self.work_queue.get()`. Any other exception raised by `get()` (e.g. an OS-level error, a future Python version change) propagates out of `run()` and kills the daemon thread silently — items remaining in that queue will never be processed and their offsets will never be marked complete, permanently blocking that partition's commits. Wrap the call in a broader `except Exception` that logs and either retries or exits cleanly, and consider asserting the worker is still alive from a supervisor.

title: Integration test relies on arroyo private internals
body: `test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit` drives the consumer by calling `processor._run_once()` in a loop and `processor._shutdown()` at the end. The leading underscore marks these as private arroyo APIs; their names/signatures are not part of arroyo's public contract and can change without warning, breaking this test (and the CI signal it provides) on an arroyo upgrade. Use the public `StreamProcessor.run()` method (which blocks until the consumer stops) instead, with a bounded stop condition or shutdown timeout, so the test exercises the same path real deployments use.

title: Kafka integration test only waits 5 seconds for 5 messages
