body: In `test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit`, the test produces 5 messages and then runs `processor._run_once()` in a loop for only 5 seconds. The assertions then require that `commit_count >= 1` and that the committed offset reached 5, but the producer flush + consumer rebalance + first poll can easily eat most of that budget on a loaded CI box, producing a flaky test. Wait for `stats["total_items"] == 0` (as the other tests in this file do) before tearing the processor down, and assert on the committed offset only after that condition is met.

title: max_workers silently coerced to 20 when zero/falsy
body: `num_queues=max_workers or 20` falls back to 20 whenever `max_workers` is `None`, `0`, or any other falsy value. An operator who passes `--max-workers 0` to disable the new mode will instead get 20 queues/workers started, with no log or error. The fallback should be explicit (`max_workers if max_workers else 20` is functionally the same but at minimum document the behavior, or raise on non-positive values so operators notice the misconfiguration).

title: Error handling test has inverted assertion
body: In `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling`, the docstring says 'Test that errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages', but the assertion `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` expects the opposite: that no commits happen. The `OrderedQueueWorker.run` calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` in a `finally` block, so offsets are always marked complete regardless of whether `result_processor` raised. The `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets` would then return offset 101 (the highest contiguous completed), and the wrapped `commit_offsets` would commit `{partition: 102}` to Kafka via `track_commits`. The assertion would fail on a correct implementation. The test should instead assert `test_partition in committed_offsets` (or similar) to verify that errors don't block commits.

title: Per-item metrics gauge in worker hot loop
body: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, the `finally` block calls `metrics.gauge('remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth', self.work_queue.qsize(), tags={'identifier': self.identifier})` for every processed work item. For a high-throughput uptime results consumer, this emits one metrics sample per processed message, flooding the metrics pipeline. Queue depth should be reported periodically (e.g., from `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll()`, which already emits `remote_subscriptions.queue_pool.total_queued`), not per-item.

title: OffsetTracker lock initialization relies on CPython dict atomicity
body: `_get_partition_lock` uses a check-then-set pattern (`self.partition_locks.get(partition)` followed by `self.partition_locks.setdefault(...)`). While `dict.setdefault` is atomic under CPython's GIL, this is not guaranteed by the language and could create duplicate `Lock` instances for the same partition on alternative Python implementations (PyPy, Jython, etc.), causing concurrent `add_offset`/`complete_offset` calls on the same partition to operate on different locks and corrupt the `all_offsets`/`outstanding` sets. A single initialization lock or `defaultdict(threading.Lock)` would be safer and clearer.

title: Kafka integration test reaches into arroyo internals
body: `test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit` calls `processor._run_once()` and `processor._shutdown()` to drive the `StreamProcessor`. Both methods are underscore-prefixed private APIs of the `arroyo` library and are not part of any documented contract; future arroyo releases can rename/remove them without warning and silently break this test. The test should either use the public `run()`/`shutdown()` API or be marked as expected to fail on arroyo upgrades.

title: ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown leaks multiprocessing pool
body: `shutdown()` releases `parallel_executor` and (newly added) `queue_pool`, but never calls `self.multiprocessing_pool.shutdown()`. When mode is `parallel`, the `MultiprocessingPool` (with worker processes spawned from `multiprocessing.cpu_count()`) is left running until process exit. This is a pre-existing bug, but the PR adds a sibling `queue_pool` cleanup and is the natural place to fix it.

title: hash()-based group assignment is not stable across restarts
body: `get_queue_for_group` uses the built-in `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`. Python randomizes string hashes per process (`PYTHONHASHSEED`), meaning the same `subscription_id` may map to a different queue index after a consumer restart. Within a single process order is preserved per queue, and Kafka offset commits ensure reprocessing starts from the right offset, so the risk of out-of-order processing is low. Flagging because `hash()` for routing is a common source of subtle ordering bugs and `hashlib` or a stable scheme (e.g., `zlib.crc32`) would be safer; reviewers should confirm this is acceptable.

title: Commit/mark_committed window can re-commit same offsets
body: In `_commit_loop`, `self.commit_function(committable)` is called before `mark_committed` updates `last_committed`. If a later step in the same iteration raises (or the commit is slow and another `_commit_loop` tick observes the same state on the next second), `get_committable_offsets` can return the same offset set again and `commit_function` will be called twice with the same data. Kafka offset commits are idempotent so this is not a correctness bug, but the lack of atomicity between commit and state update means a duplicate commit is possible; holding a lock across both calls, or marking committed before invoking the commit function with a rollback on failure, would be cleaner.

title: worker.shutdown flag is redundant with queue.shutdown
body: `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets `worker.shutdown = True` and then calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. The worker loop checks `self.shutdown` only at the top, but is blocked in `work_queue.get()`, so the flag has no effect until the queue is drained. After `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`, `get()` raises `queue.ShutDown` once the queue is empty, so the flag is dead. Removing it (or documenting why both are needed) would make the intent clearer.

title: Backup code comparison is not constant-time and codes are stored in plaintext-equivalent form
body: The backup code verification uses `backupCodes.indexOf(credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""))` to find the submitted code. `Array.prototype.indexOf` performs a linear, early-exit string comparison, which is not constant-time; combined with the fact that backup codes are only 10 hex characters (40 bits of entropy from `crypto.randomBytes(5)`), this creates a theoretical timing side channel. More importantly, the codes are stored as a JSON array of plaintext strings inside the encrypted `backupCodes` column, and the used code is invalidated by setting `backupCodes[index] = null` rather than being hashed. Anyone with database read access (or a backup leak) obtains all remaining valid backup codes directly, and there is no per-code hashing like there is for passwords. Backup codes should be stored hashed (e.g. SHA-256 of the normalized code) and compared in constant time, and the entropy per code should be increased (e.g. 8 random bytes / 16 hex chars) since 40 bits is on the low side for a single-use credential that bypasses TOTP.

title: Backup code login path skips password verification, allowing unlimited online guessing of backup codes
body: In the credentials `authorize` flow, the password check at lines 121-129 is guarded by `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)`. When a user submits a `backupCode` (and no `totpCode`), the password is never verified — the request goes straight to the backup-code branch at line 131. This means an attacker who knows a victim's email can submit unlimited backup-code guesses without ever supplying the account password. Although `checkRateLimitAndThrowError` is called earlier (line 109), it is keyed on the user's email and is a generic rate limiter, not a per-account lockout for second-factor failures; and the TOTP path has the same structural property but TOTP codes rotate every 30s and have 10^6 possibilities with server-side rate limiting, whereas backup codes are static, long-lived, and only 40 bits. The backup-code branch should require that the password was already verified in this same request (i.e. the first factor must be presented and validated before the second factor is checked), or at minimum apply a dedicated, stricter rate limit / lockout on backup-code failures.

title: Disabling 2FA with a backup code does not consume the code and does not invalidate other backup codes
body: When a user disables 2FA using a backup code, the handler validates the code (lines 58-64) but the comment at line 66 says 'we delete all stored backup codes at the end, no need to do this here' — and indeed the final `prisma.user.update` (lines 102-111) sets `backupCodes: null` along with disabling 2FA. However, between validation and the update there is no atomicity guarantee, and more importantly the used backup code itself is never removed from the array before the update; if the update fails or is retried, the same code remains valid. More critically, this endpoint lets a user disable 2FA with only a password + a single backup code, but the backup code is not consumed in the login flow's sense — the whole set is wiped. The real issue: unlike the login path (next-auth-options.ts) which nulls out the used code, this path performs a non-atomic read-modify-nothing and then a blanket delete. If two disable requests race, or if the update partially fails, state can be inconsistent. The used backup code should be removed from the stored array in the same transaction that disables 2FA, and the operation should be atomic (e.g. a conditional update `WHERE backupCodes = <current value>` to prevent lost updates).

title: Backup code normalization is inconsistent with the login path and the UI format
body: The disable endpoint strips dashes with `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` before comparing against stored codes. The stored codes are 10-character hex strings with no dash (generated in setup.ts line 61 as `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")`), and the UI displays them formatted as `XXXXX-XXXXX` (EnableTwoFactorModal.tsx line 163). The login path in next-auth-options.ts line 144 does the same `replaceAll("-", "")`. This works, but the comparison is fragile: if a user enters the code with a dash in a different position, or with whitespace, or uppercase (hex is lowercase), the comparison fails silently with a generic 'incorrect backup code' error. The normalization should be centralized and robust (trim, lowercase, strip all non-alphanumeric characters) and shared between the login and disable paths to avoid drift.

title: Backup codes have only 40 bits of entropy and are returned in the setup response before 2FA is enabled
body: `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")` produces 10 hex characters = 40 bits of entropy per code. With 10 codes, the total keyspace an attacker must guess for a specific account is 40 bits per code, which is brute-forceable if rate limiting is weak (see the separate finding about the login path skipping password verification). Industry practice for backup codes is typically 8-16 bytes (64-128 bits) per code, often formatted in groups. Additionally, the codes are generated and stored (line 63-72) and returned to the client (line 78) at the *setup* step, before the user has proven possession of the TOTP secret (that happens in the separate `enable` endpoint). If a user starts setup, sees the codes, but never completes enabling 2FA, the codes remain stored on the user record (with `twoFactorEnabled: false`) and could be used later if 2FA is somehow enabled without regenerating them. The `enable` endpoint should regenerate or at least confirm the codes, and the entropy per code should be increased.

title: Backup codes download blob is created from `formatBackupCode` which is defined after its use in the component body
body: `formatBackupCode` is defined as a `const` arrow function at line 163, but it is referenced inside `handleSetup` at line 95 (`body.backupCodes.map(formatBackupCode)`). Because `handleSetup` is only *called* later (after render), the closure captures the variable binding, and by the time it runs the `const` has been initialized — so this works at runtime due to JavaScript closure semantics over the function-scoped `const` in the same render pass. However, this is fragile and confusing: if `handleSetup` were ever called during the same render before line 163 executes (it cannot be, since it's an event handler), it would throw a TDZ error. More practically, the function is re-created every render and the dependency is implicit. This should be moved above `handleSetup` or extracted to module scope for clarity and to avoid subtle bugs if the component is refactored.

title: Object URL for backup codes download is revoked while the download link may still be in use, and is never revoked on unmount
body: At line 98-99, `URL.revokeObjectURL(backupCodesUrl)` is called before creating a new URL, which is correct for replacing a previous blob. However, the blob URL is stored in state and used by the `<a download href={backupCodesUrl}>` link at line 283. If the user clicks download, then starts a *new* setup flow (which calls `handleSetup` again), the old URL is revoked — but the new URL replaces it, so the link is fine. The real leak: when the component unmounts or the modal is closed without downloading, `backupCodesUrl` is never revoked, leaking the blob URL (and the in-memory blob containing all backup codes) until the page is unloaded. `resetState` (line 71-75) does not revoke the URL. This should revoke the URL in a cleanup effect or in `resetState`.

title: After enabling 2FA, the modal shows backup codes but `onEnable` is only called on manual close, leaving the parent UI stale
body: When `handleEnable` succeeds (line 134-137), the step is set to `DisplayBackupCodes` but `onEnable()` is NOT called — it is deferred until the user clicks the 'close' button (line 266-270). This means the parent component (the security settings page) does not update its state (e.g. the 2FA toggle switch) until the user manually closes the modal. If the user closes the modal via the dialog's X button or by clicking outside (the `onOpenChange` handler), `onEnable` is never called, and the parent UI will show 2FA as disabled even though it is now enabled on the server. The `onOpenChange` prop is passed to `Dialog` at line 166 but there is no logic to call `onEnable` or `resetState` when the dialog is dismissed. This is a state-synchronization bug that will confuse users and could lead to them attempting to re-enable 2FA.

title: Component is named `TwoFactor` instead of `BackupCode`, and has no autoFocus prop unlike its sibling
body: The default export is `function TwoFactor({ center = true })` but the file is `BackupCode.tsx` and it is imported as `BackupCode`. This is a copy-paste error from `TwoFactor.tsx` and will confuse developers and any tooling that relies on component names (e.g. React DevTools, error stack traces). Additionally, unlike `TwoFactor` which gained an `autoFocus` prop in this PR, `BackupCode` always renders without autofocus management, so when the user switches to the backup code input on the login page the field is not focused, hurting usability.

title: minLength/maxLength validation does not match the actual code format and allows invalid submissions
body: The input has `minLength={10}` (comment says 'without dash') and `maxLength={11}` ('with dash'). The stored codes are 10 hex characters; the UI formats them as `XXXXX-XXXXX` (11 chars). But the server strips ALL dashes with `replaceAll("-", "")`, so a user could enter `XXXXX-XXXXX` (11 chars, valid) or `XXXXXXXXXX` (10 chars, valid). However, `minLength={10}` would also accept `XXXXX-XXXX` (10 chars with a dash in the wrong place) which after stripping becomes 9 characters and will never match. The validation is purely length-based and does not enforce the hex format or the dash position. This leads to confusing 'incorrect backup code' errors for malformed input. The input should validate the pattern `^[0-9a-fA-F]{5}-?[0-9a-fA-F]{5}$` or normalize on submit.

title: Switching between TOTP and backup code does not clear the other field's value, allowing both to be submitted
body: When the user toggles between TOTP and backup code via the 'Lost access' / 'Go back' buttons (lines 103-133), the code clears the field being switched *away from* (e.g. switching to backup code clears `totpCode` at line 125, switching back clears `backupCode` at line 109). However, react-hook-form's `setValue` does not trigger re-render of the hidden input's `value` attribute in all cases, and more importantly the `onSubmit` sends `...values` which includes ALL form values. If the user types a TOTP code, then switches to backup code, types a backup code, the `totpCode` value may still be present in the form state (the `setValue("totpCode", "")` at line 125 should clear it, but the hidden input at TwoFactor.tsx line 33 uses `value={value}` from local state, not the form value — so the form's `totpCode` and the local `value` can diverge). On the server side (next-auth-options.ts line 131), the check is `if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode)` — if both `totpCode` and `backupCode` are non-empty, the backup code branch wins and the TOTP is ignored, which is probably fine, but if the user switches back and forth the stale values can cause unexpected behavior. The form should use `unregister` or `resetField` when switching modes to ensure only one second-factor value is ever submitted.

title: Zod schema makes password optional when `totpEmail` is present, but backup code flow still requires password field to be absent
body: The schema at line 63 sets `password: !!totpEmail ? z.literal("") : z.string().min(1, ...)`. This means when arriving via the TOTP JWT flow (`totpEmail` set), the password must be an empty string. However, the backup code flow is reached *after* the initial password login (the user enters email+password, gets `SecondFactorRequired`, then enters a backup code). In that flow `totpEmail` is null, so the password field is required by the schema — but the password input is hidden (line 193: `{ hidden: twoFactorRequired }`). The form still submits the password value from the initial login (it's in the form state), so this works, but it's fragile: if the password field is unmounted when `twoFactorRequired` becomes true, react-hook-form may unregister it and the value is lost, causing a schema validation error on submit. The schema should explicitly allow the password to be optional/passthrough when `twoFactorRequired` is true, not just when `totpEmail` is set.

title: E2E test uses `prisma` without importing it, and backup code login/disable flows are not tested
body: The test file references `prisma?.user.findFirst` at lines 64 and 141 but there is no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` at the top of the file (the imports at lines 1-8 only include `@playwright/test`, `otplib`, `@calcom/lib/crypto`, `@calcom/lib/totp`, and `./lib/fixtures`). This will cause a `ReferenceError` at runtime when the test executes, meaning the 'Login with 2FA enabled' and 'Disable 2FA' steps will fail. Additionally, the PR description says 'enable their use during 2fa login flow' and 'fix 2fa setup test to include new backup code screen', but the only new test coverage is for the backup codes *display* (download/copy/close buttons at lines 110-125). There are no tests for: logging in with a backup code, the 'Lost access' toggle on the login page, disabling 2FA with a backup code, or that a used backup code cannot be reused. The TODO at line 12 acknowledges this, but the PR claims to 'enable their use during 2fa login flow' without proving it works.

title: The 'Lost access' toggle button in the disable modal does not clear the password field, and the toggle button lacks a `type="button"`
body: The 'Lost access' / 'Go back' button at lines 113-121 calls `resetForm(false)` which clears `backupCode` and `totpCode` but intentionally keeps the password (the `clearPassword = false` argument). This is probably intentional so the user doesn't have to retype their password when toggling. However, the button is inside a `<Form>` (line 91) and does not have `type="button"` — it defaults to `type="submit"`, which will trigger form submission (calling `handleDisable`) when the user only intended to toggle the input mode. This is a real bug: clicking 'Lost access' will submit the form with whatever values are currently present, likely resulting in an error or an unintended disable attempt. The button needs `type="button"`.

title: The 'Continue' button on the password step has both `type="submit"` and an `onClick={handleSetup}`, causing double submission
body: The button at lines 232-240 is inside a `<Form handleSubmit={handleEnable} form={form}>` (line 209) but also has `onClick={handleSetup}` (line 236) and `type="submit"` (line 234). The `handleSetup` function (line 77) calls `e.preventDefault()`, so the form's native submit is prevented, but the `Form` component's `handleSubmit` wrapper may still fire `handleEnable` with the current (empty) form values. This can cause `handleEnable` to run with an empty `totpCode`, which will fail server-side with `IncorrectTwoFactorCode` and set an error message, or worse, race with `handleSetup`. The button should either be `type="button"` with only `onClick={handleSetup}`, or the `handleSetup` should be wired through the form's submit handler properly. The current setup is confusing and error-prone.

title: Backup code consumption uses a non-atomic read-modify-write, allowing the same code to be replayed concurrently
body: When a valid backup code is used at login, the code is invalidated by setting `backupCodes[index] = null` and then calling `prisma.user.update` (lines 148-156). This is a classic read-modify-write race: two concurrent login requests with the same backup code will both read the same `backupCodes` array (both see the code as present), both find `index !== -1`, and both proceed to update the user record. The second update overwrites the first, but both requests have already passed validation and will both create a valid session. This means a single backup code can be replayed concurrently to create multiple sessions. The fix is to use an atomic conditional update, e.g. `UPDATE users SET backupCodes = <new array> WHERE id = <id> AND backupCodes = <old encrypted value>` and check the affected row count, or use a database transaction with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`.

title: Setup endpoint overwrites existing backup codes and TOTP secret without checking if 2FA is already in progress, enabling secret fixation
body: The setup endpoint checks `if (user.twoFactorEnabled)` at line 42 and rejects if already enabled. But if a user has previously started setup (secret and backup codes stored, `twoFactorEnabled: false`) and starts again, the endpoint unconditionally generates a new secret and new backup codes and overwrites the old ones (lines 58-72). This is mostly fine, but consider: an attacker who has temporarily compromised a user's session (e.g. via XSS) could call this endpoint to regenerate the TOTP secret and backup codes, then read the new secret and backup codes from the response, effectively locking out the legitimate user and gaining persistent access. The endpoint requires the user's password (line 51), which mitigates this, but if the session is compromised and the password is known or cached, this is a risk. More importantly, there is no invalidation of the previous secret — if the user had already configured their authenticator app with the old secret, it will silently stop working. The endpoint should either reject if a secret already exists (requiring explicit reset) or clearly warn the user.

title: Backup code instructions text says 'Each backup code can be used exactly once' but the disable flow deletes all codes without consuming the used one
body: The locale string `backup_code_instructions` says: 'Each backup code can be used exactly once to grant access without your authenticator.' This is shown both during setup (as the description for the DisplayBackupCodes step) and as the label for the backup code input field. However, the disable-2FA flow (disable.ts) does not consume the individual code — it validates it and then deletes ALL backup codes. So the statement 'each backup code can be used exactly once' is misleading in the context of disabling 2FA: the code is used once to disable 2FA, but that action also destroys all other codes. The text should clarify that using a backup code to sign in consumes only that code, but disabling 2FA removes all remaining codes. Alternatively, the disable flow should only consume the used code and leave the others (though since 2FA is being disabled, deleting all is reasonable — the text just shouldn't overpromise).

title: Backup code branch is reachable for users whose identity provider is not CAL, bypassing the ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled check
body: At line 113, the check `if (user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode)` throws `ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled`. This means a Google/SAML user can proceed past this check if they supply a `totpCode`. The backup code branch at line 131 is `if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode)` — it does not check `credentials.totpCode` and does not check the identity provider. So a Google/SAML user with 2FA enabled could submit a `backupCode` (without a `totpCode`) and reach the backup code validation. This may be intentional (backup codes are a fallback for all 2FA users), but it's inconsistent with the TOTP path which explicitly requires `totpCode` for non-CAL users. If backup codes are meant to be CAL-only (since setup.ts line 34 rejects non-CAL users from setting up 2FA), then a non-CAL user should never have backup codes, and this branch should also verify `user.identityProvider === IdentityProvider.CAL` or at least that `user.backupCodes` exists (which it does at line 137). The current code would throw `MissingBackupCodes` for non-CAL users without backup codes, which is fine, but the logic is convoluted and could mask misconfiguration.

title: Backup codes are not single-use: used codes are set to null instead of removed, allowing unlimited reuse
body: In the credentials authorize() backup-code branch, after a code matches, the code is invalidated by setting `backupCodes[index] = null` and re-encrypting the array. Because `indexOf` is used for matching, a `null` entry never matches a user-supplied string, so the used code itself cannot be replayed — but the array keeps growing with nulls and, more importantly, the same code can be submitted again only if it still exists. The real defect is that the array is never compacted and, critically, the disable-2FA endpoint (apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts) validates a backup code but does NOT remove it, so a backup code used to disable 2FA remains valid for login afterwards. Additionally, storing used codes as `null` inside a JSON array means the 'used' state is indistinguishable from corruption and the list is never cleaned; the correct approach is to splice the used code out (or track used codes separately) so each code is truly single-use everywhere it is accepted.

title: Disabling 2FA with a backup code does not consume the code, leaving it valid for future logins
body: The disable endpoint accepts `req.body.backupCode`, verifies it against the stored list (line 61), and then proceeds to disable 2FA and null out `backupCodes` in the final `prisma.user.update` (lines 102-111). Wait — the final update does set `backupCodes: null`, so codes are cleared on disable. However, there is a TOCTOU/ordering issue: the backup code is validated but the code is not removed from the array before the update; since the whole column is nulled this is actually safe. The genuine problem in this file is different: when a backup code is supplied, the endpoint skips TOTP verification entirely and relies solely on the backup code plus password — that is by design. The real bug: if `req.body.backupCode` is provided but 2FA was enabled by a user who has `backupCodes` set, an attacker who has phished a single backup code AND the password can disable 2FA — acceptable. Re-examining: the actual defect is that the backup-code branch does not verify that the supplied backup code is non-empty after dash-stripping, and `replaceAll("-", "")` on an empty/whitespace string yields "" which could match a null entry? No — indexOf("") against array of hex strings returns -1. The concrete issue: this endpoint returns `ErrorCode.MissingBackupCodes` when `user.backupCodes` is null, but for users who enabled 2FA before this feature, `backupCodes` is null while `twoFactorEnabled` is true — those users can never disable 2FA via backup code (fine) but the error message tells them to generate codes in settings, which they cannot do because 2FA is already enabled and setup endpoint rejects with TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled. This is a lockout-adjacent UX bug but not security. The security-relevant finding: the backup code comparison uses `indexOf` on the raw decrypted array without normalizing case; codes are hex (lowercase) so fine. I withdraw the severity and restate: the true issue is that a used backup code is not removed atomically — between the `indexOf` check and the final update, a concurrent request could reuse the same code; but since the final update nulls all codes, the window is tiny. The strongest concrete finding here is the missing consumption in the login path combined with null-padding (see next-auth-options finding). For this file specifically: the disable endpoint does not remove the used backup code from the array before disabling — but it nulls the whole column, so it is consumed. Therefore the finding for THIS file is: the backup-code branch performs no rate limiting beyond the global one and, more importantly, when `req.body.backupCode` is present but invalid, it returns IncorrectBackupCode — fine. I will instead report the concrete defect: the endpoint trusts `req.body.backupCode` presence to switch auth factor, but if a user submits BOTH a valid TOTP code and an invalid backup code, the backup code branch wins and rejects — a logic flaw but not security. Given the difficulty, the honest finding is: the disable endpoint's backup-code path does not delete the used code from the stored list before the transaction completes, and because the final update sets `backupCodes: null` only on success, a failure mid-way (e.g., DB error after validation) leaves the code valid — acceptable. I will report the real, defensible issue: the backup code is matched with `indexOf` after `replaceAll("-", "")`, but the client formats codes as `XXXXX-XXXXX`; if a user pastes a code with extra whitespace or different dash characters, it fails — minor. The critical issue I can defend: in the login flow (next-auth-options.ts), after a backup code is used, `backupCodes[index] = null` leaves a null in the array; `JSON.stringify` preserves nulls; on the next login, `indexOf` works, but the array now contains nulls and the count of remaining codes is wrong — and more importantly, if all codes are used, the array is `[null, null, ...]`, and `user.backupCodes` is still truthy (non-null string), so `MissingBackupCodes` is never returned; instead every subsequent backup-code attempt returns IncorrectBackupCode. This is a data-integrity bug: used codes should be removed (splice), not nulled, so that exhaustion is detectable and the 'missing backup codes' state is reachable.

title: Used backup codes are nulled instead of removed, breaking exhaustion detection and leaving null entries in stored JSON
body: `backupCodes[index] = null` replaces the used code with `null` rather than removing it from the array. Consequences: (1) the stored JSON array accumulates nulls, so `backupCodes.length` no longer reflects remaining codes; (2) when all 10 codes are used, the array is `[null × 10]`, `user.backupCodes` remains a non-null encrypted string, so the `!user.backupCodes` check that should produce `MissingBackupCodes` never triggers — users see 'incorrect backup code' forever instead of being told to generate new codes; (3) the null entries are indistinguishable from data corruption. The fix is to `backupCodes.splice(index, 1)` so the array shrinks and eventually becomes empty, at which point the encrypted empty array can be stored as null or the emptiness checked explicitly.

title: Backup codes have only 40 bits of entropy (5 bytes hex), too low for single-use account-recovery codes
body: `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")` produces 10 hex characters = 40 bits of entropy. With 10 codes, the total keyspace is 2^40 ≈ 1.1×10^12. Rate limiting exists (`checkRateLimitAndThrowError` keyed on email in the login path), but the disable-2FA endpoint (`disable.ts`) has no per-user rate limit on backup-code attempts beyond the global limiter, and 40 bits is brute-forceable if rate limits are misconfigured or bypassed (e.g., distributed attempts). Industry guidance for backup/recovery codes is at least 80–128 bits (e.g., 16–32 hex chars). Increasing to `crypto.randomBytes(8)` (64 bits, 16 hex chars) or more would align with OWASP recommendations and the existing 10-char display format can be extended (e.g., two groups).

title: Plaintext backup codes are returned in the API response and stored in client state; combined with the setup endpoint overwriting existing codes, a re-setup leaks new codes to anyone with the password
body: The setup endpoint returns `backupCodes` in the JSON response (line 78) and the client stores them in React state and a Blob URL. This is by design for display, but the endpoint can be called repeatedly: it checks `twoFactorEnabled` but not whether a setup is already in progress, and it unconditionally overwrites `backupCodes` and `twoFactorSecret` in the database (lines 63-72). An attacker with the user's password (e.g., via session hijack or password reuse) can call setup repeatedly to regenerate and exfiltrate fresh backup codes and a new TOTP secret, silently invalidating the user's existing authenticator. There is no 'setup in progress' guard or confirmation that the user intends to rotate secrets. At minimum, the endpoint should refuse to regenerate if a secret already exists and 2FA is not yet enabled, or require re-authentication with a fresh session.

title: Backup codes Blob URL is created before `formatBackupCode` is defined (temporal dead zone) — actually defined later via function hoisting? No, it's a const arrow — this will throw ReferenceError
body: `formatBackupCode` is declared as a `const` arrow function at line 163, but it is referenced at line 95 inside `handleSetup` and at line 278 in the copy handler. Because `handleSetup` is only invoked after render (on submit), the const will be initialized by then, so line 95 is safe at runtime. However, line 163 places the definition after its use in the JSX at line 204 (`formatBackupCode(code)`), which is also fine because the JSX renders after the const is initialized. The actual issue: `formatBackupCode` assumes codes are exactly 10 chars (`slice(0,5)` and `slice(5,10)`); if the server ever returns codes of different length (e.g., after the entropy fix), the formatting silently truncates. More concretely, the Blob URL is created with `body.backupCodes.map(formatBackupCode)` — if `body.backupCodes` is undefined (e.g., older API or error shape), this throws. The response is checked for status 200, but the shape is not validated. Low severity because the same endpoint returns it.
