As written, zod will treat these computed properties as literal key names (the stringified schema objects) rather than catch-alls, so `minimumTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(response)` will strip/reject almost every real token response (any response containing `expires_in`, `refresh_token`, `token_type`, etc. will fail or be stripped), causing `parseRefreshTokenResponse` to throw "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" for every synced refresh. The intent (require `access_token`, allow arbitrary extra fields) should be expressed as `z.object({ access_token: z.string() }).passthrough()` (or `.catchall(z.unknown())`).

title: Missing refresh_token is silently replaced with the literal string "refresh_token"
body: When the parsed token response has no `refresh_token`, the code sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` — the literal string. This placeholder is then merged into the stored credential (e.g. office365calendar `o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }`, zoom `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token`). On the next refresh, the service will send `refresh_token=refresh_token` to the provider, which will fail with `invalid_grant`, permanently breaking the credential instead of preserving the previous refresh token. The correct behavior when a provider omits `refresh_token` (common — many providers only return it on the first consent) is to keep the existing refresh token from the stored credential, not to fabricate one.

title: Function returns a Zod SafeParseResult but callers treat it inconsistently (some read `.data`, some read `.success`)
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the whole `SafeParseResult` object. Callers use it inconsistently: `googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` line 97 does `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema)` and passes the SafeParseResult (not `.data`) to `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })` — persisting `{ success: true, data: {...} }` instead of the credential object, corrupting the stored credential. `salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts` line 90-94 correctly checks `.success`, and `office365calendar` line 263-264 uses `tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data`. The function should either return the parsed data directly (throwing on failure, which it already does) or all callers must be audited; returning the raw SafeParseResult invites exactly this class of bug.

title: Credential sync endpoint is called without authentication, TLS validation is not enforced, and the response is trusted blindly
body: When `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is set, `refreshOAuthTokens` POSTs `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` to that endpoint with no authentication header, no signature, and no verification that the response actually corresponds to the requested user/app. Any party who can reach the Cal.com instance can point `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` (or an attacker who can influence env) at a server they control and have Cal.com store arbitrary `access_token`/`refresh_token` values into users' credentials — and conversely, the sync endpoint receives a list of which users use which apps. The request should carry a shared secret (e.g. `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`) and the response should be validated (schema + user binding) before being persisted. Also, the returned `Response` is passed to callers that call `.json()`/`.data` on it without checking `response.ok`, so a 4xx/5xx from the sync endpoint yields `undefined` tokens that are then written into credentials (see googlecalendar: `token.access_token` would throw, but hubspot/zoho write `tokenInfo.data` which would be an error body).

title: Type mismatch: function returns a fetch Response in one branch and the provider's parsed body in the other
body: `refreshOAuthTokens` returns `response` (a `Response` object) when syncing, but returns `await refreshFunction()` — which for most callers is the provider's parsed body or an axios response — in the normal path. Callers handle this inconsistently: `googlecalendar` does `const token = res?.data` (works for the googleapis `res` shape but for a fetch `Response`, `.data` is `undefined`, so `token.access_token` throws and the credential is marked invalid); `hubspot` assigns the result to `HubspotToken` and reads `.expiresIn`/`.accessToken` directly (a `Response` has neither, so `hubspotRefreshToken.expiryDate = Math.round(Date.now() + undefined * 1000)` = NaN and `setAccessToken(undefined)`); `zoho-bigin`/`zohocrm` read `tokenInfo.data` (undefined on a `Response`). The abstraction leaks two incompatible shapes; the function should normalize (e.g. always return the parsed JSON body) so every caller works in both modes.

title: Synced refresh response is read as `res?.data` but refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response, so `token` is undefined and the credential update throws
body: In `refreshAccessToken`, `const res = await refreshOAuthTokens(...)` then `const token = res?.data`. In the normal (non-sync) path `res` is `fetchTokens.res` (a GaxiosResponse, which has `.data`) — fine. But in the credential-sync path `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `fetch` `Response` object, which has no `.data` property, so `token` is `undefined` and `token.access_token` throws a TypeError. The catch block then treats any error message other than "invalid_grant" by returning the stale `myGoogleAuth`, so the token is never refreshed and every subsequent API call fails with 401 until the credential is manually fixed. The response must be normalized (e.g. `await res.json()` when it is a `Response`) before reading `.data`.

title: Stored credential key is replaced with the Zod SafeParseResult wrapper object instead of the parsed data
body: `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema);` — `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns a `SafeParseResult` (`{ success, data }`), not the parsed value. This object is then passed to `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`, persisting `{ success: true, data: { ...tokens } }` as the credential key. On the next load, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` in `googleAuth` will fail because the stored shape no longer matches, breaking the integration. It must be `parseRefreshTokenResponse(...).data` (and since the helper already throws on failure, `.data` is safe).

title: parseRefreshTokenResponse already throws on invalid responses; the subsequent `.success` check is dead code and the merge can still persist a placeholder refresh_token
body: `const tokenResponse = parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseJson, refreshTokenResponseSchema);` — the helper throws `"Invalid refreshed tokens were returned"` when parsing fails, so `tokenResponse.success` is always `true` here and the `tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data` guard is dead. More importantly, when the provider omits `refresh_token`, the helper injects the literal string `"refresh_token"` (see parseRefreshTokenResponse finding), and line 264 merges that into `o365AuthCredentials`, overwriting the real refresh token and permanently breaking future refreshes. The merge should preserve the existing `refresh_token` when the response doesn't include one.

title: handleErrorsJson is called on the value returned by refreshOAuthTokens, which may be a parsed body rather than a Response
body: `const responseJson = await handleErrorsJson(response);` assumes `response` is a fetch `Response`. In the sync path `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a `Response` (ok), but in the normal path it returns the result of the inner fetch — which here is also a `Response`, so this works — however the type contract of `refreshOAuthTokens` is `any` and other callers pass axios responses. If the contract is normalized to "parsed body" (as recommended in the refreshOAuthTokens finding), this call site breaks. The two paths must be reconciled so `handleErrorsJson` always receives a `Response`.

title: Salesforce getClient now refreshes the token on every instantiation and overwrites the stored credential, and prisma is not imported
body: The diff adds a full token-refresh block inside `getClient` (lines 75-99) that runs on every service construction — i.e. on every calendar operation — POSTing to Salesforce with the stored `refresh_token` and then `prisma.credential.update(...)`. Two problems: (1) `prisma` is used at line 96 but is never imported in this file (no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` in the shown content), which is a compile/runtime error (`ReferenceError: prisma is not defined`) the first time any Salesforce calendar operation runs; (2) unconditionally refreshing on every `getClient` call discards the access-token caching/expiry logic that previously lived in the jsforce connection, causing an extra token request per operation and — because Salesforce rotates refresh tokens — can invalidate the stored refresh token if the update races with another concurrent operation. The refresh should happen only when the stored access token is expired, and `prisma` must be imported.

title: Refreshed Salesforce credential is persisted without the original refresh_token when the response omits it, and without expiry_date
body: Line 98 writes `key: { ...accessTokenParsed.data, refresh_token: credentialKey.refresh_token }`. `accessTokenParsed.data` comes from `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, which (a) injects the literal string `"refresh_token"` when the field is absent — here it is then overwritten with the real one, so that specific issue is mitigated — but (b) the `salesforceTokenSchema` has no `expires_in`/`expiry_date` field, so the stored credential never records when the new access token expires. The jsforce connection is constructed with `accessToken: credentialKey.access_token` (the OLD token, line 106) rather than the freshly fetched `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`, so the very first API call after a refresh uses a stale access token and fails with 401. The new access token must be used for the connection.

title: Synced refresh response is passed to handleErrorsJson which expects a Response; expiry_date becomes NaN when syncing
body: `const responseBody = await handleErrorsJson<ITokenResponse>(response);` — in the sync path `response` is a fetch `Response` (fine), but the code then computes `responseBody.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + (responseBody?.expires_in || 0) * 1000)`. The credential-sync contract (per `parseRefreshTokenResponse` and the PR description) is that the sync endpoint returns only the access token and an expiry timestamp, not `expires_in`. So `expires_in` is undefined, `expiry_date` becomes `Date.now()`, and `isExpired` (line 56, `expiryDate < Math.round(+new Date())`) immediately treats the fresh token as expired, causing an infinite refresh loop on every API call. The adapter must handle the sync response shape (absolute expiry) distinctly from the Microsoft token shape (relative `expires_in`).

title: HubSpot refresh treats the refreshOAuthTokens return value as a HubspotToken, but in sync mode it is a fetch Response — expiryDate becomes NaN and the credential is corrupted
body: `const hubspotRefreshToken: HubspotToken = await refreshOAuthTokens(...)` then `hubspotRefreshToken.expiryDate = Math.round(Date.now() + hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn * 1000)`. In the normal path the inner function returns the HubSpot SDK token object (has `expiresIn`), but in the credential-sync path `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a `fetch` `Response` object, which has no `expiresIn` — so `expiryDate` is `NaN`, `hubspotRefreshToken.accessToken` is `undefined`, and the credential is updated with `key: { ...Response-ish garbage }` (line 198), destroying the stored HubSpot credential. `hubspotClient.setAccessToken(undefined)` then breaks all subsequent calls. The sync response must be parsed (`await response.json()`) and mapped to the HubspotToken shape before use.

title: zoho-bigin passes credentialId (a number) as the userId argument to refreshOAuthTokens
body: `refreshOAuthTokens(fn, "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` — the third parameter of `refreshOAuthTokens` is `userId: number | null`, but the call site passes `credentialId` (the credential's primary key), not `credential.userId`. In sync mode the request to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` will therefore send `calcomUserId=<credentialId>`, which is the wrong identifier — the self-hoster's app store keys credentials by Cal.com user id, so the sync endpoint will look up (or create) tokens for a non-existent user and return an error/empty payload, breaking token refresh for every zoho-bigin user. The call must pass `credential.userId` (the `CredentialPayload` is available in `refreshAccessToken`'s closure via the class, but the method signature only receives `credentialId` and `credentialKey`; the method should also receive the credential or its userId).

title: Token refresh result is used without checking HTTP status; axios errors and sync-mode Response objects are both mishandled
body: `const tokenInfo = await refreshOAuthTokens(async () => await axios.post(...), ...)` then `if (!tokenInfo.data.error)`. In the normal path `tokenInfo` is an axios response (`.data` is the body — ok), but axios throws on non-2xx by default so the `else` branch logging `tokenInfo.data` is only reachable for 2xx responses containing an `error` field. In the sync path `tokenInfo` is a `Response` and `tokenInfo.data` is `undefined`, so `!tokenInfo.data.error` throws a TypeError (`Cannot read properties of undefined`) which is uncaught in `refreshAccessToken` and propagates to `getToken`, failing the whole calendar operation. The response must be normalized and its HTTP status checked.

title: Zoho CRM refresh swallows all errors and leaves this.accessToken stale/undefined, then API calls proceed with an invalid token
body: `refreshAccessToken` wraps everything in try/catch and on error only does `this.log.error(e)` — it does not rethrow, does not invalidate the credential, and does not set `this.accessToken`. `getToken` resolves successfully regardless, so `createEvent`/`updateEvent`/`deleteEvent` proceed to call the Zoho API with an empty or stale `this.accessToken`, producing confusing 401/NO_AUTH errors instead of a clear "credential invalid" signal. Additionally, in sync mode `zohoCrmTokenInfo` is a `Response` and `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data` is `undefined`, so `!zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error` throws inside the try and is swallowed by the same catch. The refresh must surface failures (or mark the credential invalid) rather than silently continuing.

title: Lark refresh passes the fetch Response to handleLarkError which expects a Response in normal mode but the sync path also returns a Response — however the normal path previously returned a Response too; the real issue is handleLarkError is not applied consistently and errors are not surfaced
body: `const resp = await refreshOAuthTokens(async () => await fetch(...), "lark-calendar", credential.userId)` then `const data = await handleLarkError<RefreshTokenResp>(resp, this.log)`. In the normal path `resp` is the `fetch` `Response` (same as before the change — ok). In the sync path `resp` is also a `Response` — ok by luck. But `handleLarkError` presumably throws on non-OK Lark responses; in sync mode a non-200 from the sync endpoint (e.g. 404 for unknown user) will be interpreted as a Lark API error and its body parsed as `RefreshTokenResp`, yielding `data.data.refresh_token === undefined`, which is then written into the credential (lines 91-96), wiping the user's Lark tokens. The sync response must be validated (ok status + expected shape) before its fields are persisted.

title: Webex refresh passes the refreshOAuthTokens result to handleWebexResponse, which clones/reads it as a Response; in sync mode the body shape differs and expiry_date is never set from the sync payload
body: `const responseBody = await handleWebexResponse(response, credential.id);` — `handleWebexResponse` (line 270) expects a fetch `Response` and returns `responseClone.json()`. In the normal path `response` is a `Response` (ok). In the sync path it is also a `Response` (ok), but the sync endpoint returns only `{ access_token, expiry_date }` (per the PR contract), which does not match `webexRefreshedTokenSchema` (requires `scope`, `token_type`, `refresh_token`, `refresh_token_expires_in`). `parsedToken.success` will therefore be false and the adapter rejects with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" — meaning Webex token refresh is permanently broken whenever credential syncing is enabled. The sync response must be mapped onto the webex token shape (preserving the existing refresh token and computing expiry) instead of being validated against the provider schema.

title: Zoom refresh validates the sync endpoint response against the Zoom provider schema, which the sync payload does not satisfy
body: `const parsedToken = parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseBody, zoomRefreshedTokenSchema);` — when credential syncing is enabled, `parseRefreshTokenResponse` uses `minimumTokenResponseSchema` (only requires `access_token`), so `parsedToken.data` will contain only the fields the sync endpoint returned (e.g. `access_token` and an expiry). But lines 119-122 then unconditionally read `newTokens.refresh_token` and `newTokens.expires_in` — both `undefined` for a sync response — so `key.refresh_token` is set to `undefined` (wiping the stored refresh token) and `key.expiry_date` becomes `NaN`, permanently breaking the Zoom credential. The code must preserve the existing `refresh_token` and derive `expiry_date` from the sync payload's absolute expiry when present.

title: handleZoomResponse is called on the refreshOAuthTokens result, which in sync mode is a Response but in normal mode is also a Response; however the sync body lacks Zoom's error field so invalid_grant handling is bypassed
body: `const responseBody = await handleZoomResponse(response, credential.id);` — `handleZoomResponse` throws on non-OK responses and returns the parsed JSON. In sync mode, if the sync endpoint returns 200 with an error payload or a non-JSON body, `responseClone.json()` may throw or return an unexpected shape; the subsequent `if (responseBody.error)` check (line 98) assumes the Zoom error shape. A sync endpoint that returns `{ "error": "user_not_found" }` with 200 would be treated as a Zoom `invalid_grant` only if the string matches; otherwise it falls through to schema validation and rejects with a generic error, and the credential is never invalidated even though the user's tokens are gone. The sync path needs explicit status/shape validation.

title: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is a string-or-undefined value, not a boolean, and is truthy for an empty-string secret
body: `export const APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED = process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY;` — this evaluates to `string | undefined`, not `boolean`. It is used in boolean contexts (`if (!APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED)`), which works, but the exported name and type imply a boolean and the value can be the empty string `""` (falsy, ok) or the secret string itself (truthy). More subtly, the flag does not include `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, so `refreshOAuthTokens`/`parseRefreshTokenResponse` check `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` — meaning the webhook endpoint is enabled whenever the secret+key are set even if no sync endpoint is configured, which is presumably intended, but the flag should be an explicit boolean (`!!(...)`) and the webhook handler should additionally verify that the encryption key is non-empty before decrypting (see the app-credential.ts finding about the `|| ""` fallback).

title: New credentials created by the webhook are not marked with any indication they are externally managed, and team credentials are not supported
body: The webhook always creates/updates a credential with `userId: reqBody.userId` and never sets `teamId`. Self-hosters syncing credentials for users who belong to teams will have the credential attached to the user rather than the team, so team event types that resolve credentials by `teamId` will not see the synced credential. Conversely, a webhook caller can attach a credential to any user id (the endpoint trusts `userId` after only checking the user exists), which is by design for this feature but means the endpoint is a full credential-write primitive for arbitrary users — combined with the weak secret check, this is a significant privilege. At minimum the created credential should be validated against the app's expected key schema (see earlier finding) and the behavior for team-owned apps should be documented/handled.

title: Sync request sends credentials lookup parameters as URLSearchParams without a Content-Type header or any authentication
body: The POST body is `new URLSearchParams({ calcomUserId, appSlug })` but no `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded` header is set (fetch sets it automatically for URLSearchParams bodies in modern runtimes, so this is mostly fine), and — more importantly — no authentication or shared secret is sent, so the sync endpoint cannot verify the caller is really this Cal.com instance (see the security finding). Also `appSlug` values passed by callers are inconsistent: googlecalendar passes `"google-calendar"`, office365video passes `"msteams"`, zoom passes `"zoomvideo"` — the sync endpoint must know this exact mapping; the PR description does not document the canonical slug list, which will cause silent mismatches for self-hosters.

title: Unrelated hardcoded redirect URI change bundled into the rename commit
body: The diff changes `const redirectUri = WEBAPP_URL + `/api/integrations/${appConfig.slug}/callback`` to the literal ``WEBAPP_URL + `/api/integrations/zoho-bigin/callback` ``. If `appConfig.slug` is not exactly `"zoho-bigin"` this changes the OAuth redirect URI and breaks the Zoho Bigin install flow (the redirect URI must match the one registered in the Zoho console). This change is unrelated to the credential-sync feature and should be reverted or justified.

title: parseRefreshTokenResponse accepts `any` response and an unused schema parameter in sync mode
body: The signature is `(response: any, schema: z.ZodTypeAny)`. In sync mode the `schema` argument is completely ignored (only `minimumTokenResponseSchema` is used), so callers pass provider-specific schemas that are silently discarded — meaning a sync endpoint returning extra/malformed fields is accepted as long as `access_token` is a string. The `any` type also disables type checking at every call site. The function should type the response as `unknown` and, in sync mode, still validate the minimal shape strictly (and ideally require an expiry field, since the whole point of the sync contract is to return token + expiry).

title: appStoreMetadata lookup uses the DB app slug but the credential is written with appMetadata.slug — mismatch for apps whose metadata slug differs from the DB slug
body: `const appMetadata = appStoreMetadata[app.slug as keyof typeof appStoreMetadata];` then the credential is created/updated with `appId: appMetadata.slug`. If `appStoreMetadata`'s key differs from `appMetadata.slug` (the lookup key vs the inner slug), the credential's `appId` will not match the `app.slug` that was validated to exist, and downstream credential resolution (which filters by `appId`) will not find it. The code should assert `appMetadata.slug === app.slug` or use `app.slug` consistently for the credential write.

title: New env vars added to globalEnv include secrets that should not be listed as build-time env for all packages
body: `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, and `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` were added to `globalEnv`. `globalEnv` in turbo affects cache hashing for every task in every package; listing server-only secrets there is not itself a leak (turbo does not print values), but it means builds of unrelated packages (website, ai, embed) will be invalidated when these secrets rotate and implies they are needed at build time for those packages, which they are not. More importantly, the web app's build env list (`@calcom/web#build` `env` array, lines 27-38) was NOT updated to include these variables, so production builds may not have them available at runtime in some deployment setups that rely on the turbo env allowlist. The web build env should include the four new variables (at least the ones read at runtime: `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME`, `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`).

title: Comment says to generate the webhook secret with `openssl rand -base64 32` but the encryption key comment says 24 bytes; the webhook secret has no length requirement and 32 is fine, but the two comments are inconsistent about which key is which
body: The `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` comment says `openssl rand -base64 32` (44 chars, ~256 bits — fine for a shared secret) while `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` says "must be 32 bytes for AES256" and `openssl rand -base64 24` (24 bytes = 192 bits, which is AES-192, not AES-256; 32 bytes needs `openssl rand -base64 32` or `openssl rand 32 | base64`). The encryption key comment is wrong: base64 of 24 random bytes is 24 bytes of key material = AES-192, not AES-256 as claimed. If `symmetricDecrypt` requires a 32-byte key, self-hosters following the comment will get a key of the wrong length. The comment should say `openssl rand -base64 32` for a 32-byte (AES-256) key, matching the existing `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY` guidance at line 90.

title: Team-owned credentials (userId null) silently fall back to the provider refresh path even when syncing is enabled, causing inconsistent behavior
body: `if (APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT && userId)` — when `userId` is null (team credential), the function takes the `else` branch and calls `refreshFunction()`, i.e. it refreshes directly against the provider using the stored refresh token. But the entire premise of the feature (per the PR description) is that the self-hoster's app store is the source of truth and the Cal.com instance may not even have valid client secrets for the provider. For team credentials the refresh will fail (or worse, succeed against a provider the self-hoster has decommissioned), and the two code paths diverge. The function should either support team credentials in the sync call (e.g. pass `teamId`) or explicitly throw/log when syncing is enabled but the credential is team-owned, rather than silently falling back.

title: refreshOAuthTokens is called with credential.userId which may be null for team credentials, silently disabling sync for team Google calendars
body: `refreshOAuthTokens(fn, "google-calendar", credential.userId)` — `credential.userId` is `number | null`. For team-owned Google Calendar credentials `userId` is null, so the sync branch is skipped and the code falls back to refreshing directly against Google with the stored refresh token. For self-hosters using this feature, team credentials will not be synced and will break once the self-hoster rotates/decommissions the Google OAuth client. This should be surfaced (log/throw) rather than silently falling back, consistent with the refreshOAuthTokens finding.

title: Webhook secret comparison is not constant-time and fails open when env vars are unset
body: The webhook secret check uses a plain `!==` string comparison between `req.headers[...]` and `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. Two problems: (1) it is vulnerable to timing attacks, so a remote attacker could theoretically recover the secret byte-by-byte; (2) if `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` is unset (empty string) and the attacker sends an empty header value, `undefined !== undefined` is false... actually `req.headers[...]` would be `undefined` and `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` would be `undefined`, so `undefined !== undefined` is `false`, meaning the check passes and the endpoint is left open. Note `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` is `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` which is falsy when unset, so the 403 guard at line 19 does protect against the unset case — but the comparison should still use a constant-time comparison (e.g. `crypto.timingSafeEqual`) and explicitly reject when either value is missing, rather than relying on the indirect guard. Additionally, the header name is read from an env var (`CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME`) which an attacker-controlled deployment misconfiguration could weaken; the secret value itself must never be logged or echoed.

title: Zod parse errors and JSON.parse throw unhandled 500s instead of 400s
body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` (line 31) and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` (line 57) throw on invalid input. In a Next.js API route an uncaught throw results in an unhandled 500 with a stack trace potentially leaked to the caller, instead of a clean 400 Bad Request. A caller sending a malformed body or a payload that fails decryption/parsing gets a 500. Use `.safeParse` and return 400, and wrap the decrypt/parse in try/catch returning 400 'Invalid encrypted payload'.

title: Decryption uses empty-string fallback key when CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY is unset
body: `symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY || "")` falls back to an empty string key. If the env var is accidentally unset in a deployment where `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` was computed at build time (it is a module-level constant evaluated once at import), the endpoint would attempt to decrypt attacker-supplied ciphertext with a known empty key. Depending on the `symmetricDecrypt` implementation this could either throw or, worse, succeed for payloads encrypted with an empty key, letting an attacker write arbitrary credential keys. The handler should explicitly verify `process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is present and non-empty before decrypting and return 500/403 otherwise.

title: findFirst-then-create/update race can create duplicate credentials or lose updates
body: The handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` and then either `update` or `create` based on the result. Two concurrent webhook calls for the same user+app can both observe 'no credential' and both create, producing duplicate credentials (the schema apparently allows multiple credentials per user+app since the code comments 'Can't use prisma upsert as we don't know the id'). Conversely two concurrent updates can interleave. There is no transaction or unique constraint enforced here. This is a data-integrity risk: duplicate credentials for the same app/user cause ambiguous credential selection downstream (other code uses `findFirst`, so behavior becomes nondeterministic). Wrap in `prisma.$transaction` with serializable isolation, or add a unique constraint on (userId, appId) where appId is non-null and use upsert.

title: Created credential is not validated against the app's credential schema and may overwrite team credentials semantics
body: When creating a new credential the handler sets `key: keys` where `keys` is the raw `JSON.parse` of the decrypted payload — an unvalidated `any`. Unlike the OAuth callback paths (which validate via zod schemas like `googleCredentialSchema`), this webhook writes arbitrary JSON into `credential.key`. A malformed payload (e.g. missing `refresh_token`, wrong types) will be persisted and later crash or misbehave the CalendarService/VideoApiAdapter that parses it. The handler should validate `keys` against the app's credential schema (the app metadata should expose it) before persisting. Also note the update path (line 73-80) overwrites the entire `key`, discarding fields like `expiry_date`/`email` that some services rely on — it should merge or validate.

title: Endpoint does not restrict HTTP method
body: The handler does not check `req.method`. Any HTTP verb (GET, PUT, DELETE, ...) reaching this route will be processed as a credential write. A GET request with a valid secret in the header and a body would still mutate the database, and GET requests may be logged by proxies/caches with the secret header. Restrict to POST (return 405 otherwise).

title: Credential sync endpoint is called over plain fetch with no authentication, TLS validation is implicit, and response is trusted blindly
body: When `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is set, `refreshOAuthTokens` POSTs `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` to that endpoint and returns the raw `Response`. Problems: (1) there is no authentication on this outbound call — any party that can guess/observe the endpoint URL could... actually the endpoint is server-configured, so the risk is that the *response* is fully trusted: the sync endpoint returns the new access token, and callers write it directly into the credential. If the endpoint is misconfigured to an http:// URL or is compromised/MITM'd, an attacker can inject arbitrary access tokens into users' credentials (token substitution → account takeover of the third-party integration). (2) The response is never checked for `response.ok`; a 500 HTML error page would flow into `response.json()` downstream and throw confusing errors, or worse, in callers like HubSpot the raw response object is used as a token. The function should enforce https, check `response.ok`, and callers should validate the parsed body.

title: Sync endpoint response shape mismatch: callers expect provider-shaped bodies, not the raw fetch Response
body: `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `Response` object from the sync endpoint, but callers treat the return value inconsistently. In `googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` line 94 the caller does `const token = res?.data;` — a fetch `Response` has no `.data`, so `token` is `undefined` and `token.access_token` throws a TypeError whenever the sync path is active. Similarly `office365calendar` passes the Response into `handleErrorsJson(response)` which expects a Response (ok there), but `hubspot` assigns the Response to `hubspotRefreshToken: HubspotToken` and reads `.expiresIn`/`.accessToken` off it — undefined. The sync endpoint contract (returning JSON with access_token/expiry) is incompatible with the provider SDK response shapes (`.res.data`, axios `.data`, etc.) that the non-sync path returns. The abstraction leaks: each caller must handle two different shapes. `refreshOAuthTokens` should normalize: parse the sync endpoint's JSON and return a provider-equivalent shape, or callers must branch on which path was taken.

title: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses invalid zod index-signature syntax and will never validate as intended
body: The schema declares `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()` as if they were index signatures. In Zod, computed keys in an object literal are just literal property names (the string `"string"`... actually `z.string().toString()` evaluates to `"string"`), so the schema is effectively `{ access_token: string, "string": number, ... }` — it requires a property literally named `"string"` of type number and does NOT act as a catch-all. As written, `minimumTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(response)` will fail for any real token response that lacks a numeric property named `string`, causing `parseRefreshTokenResponse` to throw 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned' whenever credential sharing is enabled. The intent (passthrough with numeric expiry fields) needs `.passthrough()`/`.catchall()` or an explicit shape. This breaks the entire sync-refresh path for Google/Office365/Zoom/Salesforce.

title: Missing refresh_token is silently replaced with the literal string 'refresh_token', destroying the stored credential
body: When the parsed response has no `refresh_token`, the code sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` — the literal string. OAuth providers often omit `refresh_token` on refresh responses (returning a new one only occasionally), and the correct behavior is to KEEP the existing refresh token. Instead, this overwrites the stored credential's refresh token with the garbage string `"refresh_token"`. The next refresh attempt will send `refresh_token="refresh_token"` to the provider, which will reject it with `invalid_grant`, permanently bricking the user's integration until they re-install. Callers like `googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` then persist this corrupted key via `prisma.credential.update`. The function must not fabricate a refresh token; it should leave it absent and let callers merge with the existing credential (as `salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts` correctly does with `refresh_token: credentialKey.refresh_token`).

title: Return type is inconsistent: throws on failure but callers also check `.success`, and the success value shape differs between branches
body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws `new Error("Invalid refreshed tokens were returned")` when parsing fails (line 21-23), yet callers such as `salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts` (line 90-94) and `zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts` (line 104-110) and `office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` (line 263-264) treat the return value as a zod SafeParse result and check `.success` / access `.data`. Since the function throws instead of returning `{ success: false }`, those `.success` checks are dead code and the `if (!accessTokenParsed.success)` branch in Salesforce is unreachable — a parse failure surfaces as an uncaught exception instead of the intended rejection path. The contract is muddled: either return the SafeParseResult (never throw) or throw consistently and fix all callers. As written, error handling in callers is broken.

title: Sync-path token refresh reads `.data` off a fetch Response, causing TypeError and breaking Google Calendar when credential sharing is enabled
body: In `refreshAccessToken`, `refreshOAuthTokens(...)` returns either the provider SDK's `fetchTokens.res` (a GaxiosResponse with `.data`) or, when sync is enabled, a raw fetch `Response` (which has no `.data`). Line 94 does `const token = res?.data;` then line 95 `googleCredentials.access_token = token.access_token;`. On the sync path `token` is `undefined` and `token.access_token` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`. This exception is caught by the surrounding try/catch (line 103), which checks `if (message !== "invalid_grant") return myGoogleAuth;` — so it silently returns the auth client with the OLD expired access token, and every subsequent Google Calendar API call fails with 401 until the credential is reinstalled. The sync path for Google Calendar is completely broken.

title: HubSpot refresh treats fetch Response as HubspotToken; sync path corrupts credentials with undefined fields
body: When credential sync is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw fetch `Response`, but line 177 assigns it to `hubspotRefreshToken: HubspotToken` and line 192 reads `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` and line 202 `hubspotRefreshToken.accessToken` — all `undefined` on a Response object. Line 192 computes `expiryDate = Math.round(Date.now() + undefined * 1000)` = `NaN`, and the credential is updated with `key: hubspotRefreshToken as any` — persisting a Response-serialized object (or garbage) over the user's real HubSpot tokens, destroying the integration. Additionally `hubspotClient.setAccessToken(undefined)` breaks all subsequent API calls. The non-sync path returns the HubSpot SDK token object directly (not a Response), so the two branches have incompatible shapes.

title: Lark refresh passes fetch Response into handleLarkError which expects a Response on the normal path but the sync path response body is never parsed correctly
body: `refreshOAuthTokens` on the sync path returns the raw `Response` from the sync endpoint, and line 84 passes it to `handleLarkError<RefreshTokenResp>(resp, this.log)`. On the normal path `resp` is the Lark API `fetch` Response, so `handleLarkError` presumably calls `resp.json()`. The sync endpoint returns a minimal JSON `{ access_token, expiry }` (per the PR description: 'The response should only contain the access token and expiry date'), which lacks the Lark envelope `{ code, data: { refresh_token, refresh_expires_in, access_token, expires_in } }` that lines 86-96 read (`data.data.refresh_expires_in`, `data.data.refresh_token`, etc.). So even if parsing succeeds, `data.data` is undefined and the credential update writes `undefined` tokens, or `handleLarkError` throws. The Lark sync path cannot work with the documented sync-endpoint contract.

title: Office365 refresh silently proceeds with unvalidated token data when parse fails
body: Line 263-264: `const tokenResponse = parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseJson, refreshTokenResponseSchema); o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...(tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data) };`. But `parseRefreshTokenResponse` THROWS on parse failure rather than returning `{success: false}` (see separate finding), so the `.success` check is dead. Worse, if it did return a failure result, the spread `...(false && ...)` spreads `false`, which is a no-op — so the code would continue with the OLD (expired) credentials and persist them, silently failing to refresh. The previous code logged the zod error; that logging was removed in this diff. A failed refresh now either throws an unhandled error or silently keeps expired tokens. The refresh result must be checked and an error thrown/logged when invalid.

title: MS Teams refresh: sync path returns Response but handleErrorsJson expects Response — however the sync endpoint's minimal JSON lacks refresh_token, permanently overwriting it with undefined
body: On the sync path, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the sync endpoint's `Response`. `handleErrorsJson<ITokenResponse>(response)` will parse its JSON body. Per the PR's stated contract, the sync endpoint returns only an access token and expiry — no `refresh_token`. Line 84-95 then computes `expiry_date` from `expires_in` (which the minimal schema in `parseRefreshTokenResponse` treats as a generic number property, so it may be absent → `expiry_date = Date.now() + 0`) and writes `key: responseBody` to the database. The stored credential loses `refresh_token`, `email`, `scope`, `token_type`, etc. The next refresh reads `o365AuthCredentials.refresh_token` = undefined and sends `refresh_token=undefined` to Microsoft, which rejects it — permanently breaking the Teams integration. The refresh must merge the new access token into the existing credential and preserve the refresh token (as Salesforce does).

title: Webex refresh: sync-path Response body lacks refresh_token_expires_in required by webexRefreshedTokenSchema, so validation always fails on sync path
body: When sync is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the sync endpoint Response whose JSON (per contract) contains only access token + expiry. `handleWebexResponse` parses it, then line 88 validates with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema` which requires `refresh_token: z.string()` and `refresh_token_expires_in: z.number()`. The minimal sync response has neither, so `parsedToken.success` is false and line 89-91 rejects with 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned' — the Webex credential can never be refreshed via sync, and the rejection propagates up through `getToken()` breaking meeting creation. The schema for the sync path must make refresh_token optional and preserve the existing one.

title: Zoom refresh: parseRefreshTokenResponse throws instead of returning SafeParseResult, making the `.success` check dead and changing error semantics
body: Line 104: `const parsedToken = parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseBody, zoomRefreshedTokenSchema);` then line 108 `if (!parsedToken.success)`. But `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws `new Error("Invalid refreshed tokens were returned")` on failure (it never returns `{success: false}`), so `parsedToken.success` is always `true` when the function returns, and the explicit rejection branch is unreachable. A malformed Zoom refresh response now surfaces as a thrown Error from `parseRefreshTokenResponse` rather than the intended `Promise.reject(new Error("Invalid refreshed tokens were returned"))` — functionally similar but the dead code indicates the contract mismatch (see separate finding on parseRefreshTokenResponse). Additionally, on the sync path the minimal response (access_token + expiry only) lacks `refresh_token`, `token_type: "bearer"`, and `scope`, so `zoomRefreshedTokenSchema` validation fails and Zoom sync refresh always errors.

title: Zoho Bigin refresh passes credentialId (a number) as the userId argument to refreshOAuthTokens
body: Line 85-94: `refreshOAuthTokens(async () => ..., "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` — the third parameter is `credentialId` (the credential's database id), but `refreshOAuthTokens`'s signature is `(refreshFunction, appSlug, userId: number | null)` and it sends `calcomUserId: userId.toString()` to the sync endpoint. The sync endpoint expects the Cal.com user id, not the credential id. The self-hoster's app store will look up the wrong user (or none) and return the wrong tokens — or fail. This is a data-integrity/security issue: tokens for user A could be written into user B's credential if ids collide across tables. The call should pass `credential.userId` (the CredentialPayload has `userId`), matching every other caller.

title: Zoho Bigin refresh: sync-path Response has no `.data`, so tokenInfo.data is undefined and the credential update writes undefined
body: On the sync path `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw fetch `Response`, but line 96 reads `tokenInfo.data.error` and line 98 `tokenInfo.data.expires_in` — a Response has no `.data`, so `tokenInfo.data` is `undefined` and `tokenInfo.data.error` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'error')`. This exception is NOT caught (the try/catch was removed in this refactor — the old code had no try/catch either but the shape matched), so the refresh crashes and the Bigin integration breaks whenever sync is enabled. The non-sync path returns an axios response with `.data`. The two shapes are incompatible.

title: Zoho CRM refresh: sync-path Response has no `.data`; tokenInfo.data is undefined and refresh silently no-ops or crashes
body: Line 204-216: `refreshOAuthTokens` on the sync path returns a fetch `Response`, but line 217 reads `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error` and line 219 `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.expiryDate = ...` / line 233 `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.access_token`. A Response has no `.data`, so `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data` is `undefined` and `!zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error` throws TypeError, which IS caught by the try/catch at line 238 and merely logged (`this.log.error(e)`) — so the refresh silently fails, `this.accessToken` is never updated, and all subsequent Zoho CRM API calls use the stale/empty access token. The sync path for Zoho CRM is broken and fails silently.

title: Salesforce now refreshes the token on EVERY getClient call and overwrites the credential, even when the access token is still valid
body: The diff adds an unconditional `fetch("https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token", { grant_type: "refresh_token", ... })` at the top of `getClient`, followed by `prisma.credential.update`. Previously `getClient` just constructed a jsforce Connection from the stored credential (jsforce itself refreshes lazily when needed). Now every construction of the SalesforceCalendarService (which happens per booking/availability check) triggers a Salesforce token refresh and a DB write. Consequences: (1) massive increase in outbound calls and DB writes (performance/rate-limit risk — Salesforce refresh tokens can also be single-use/rotating, so concurrent refreshes can invalidate each other); (2) the update at line 96-99 writes `{ ...accessTokenParsed.data, refresh_token: credentialKey.refresh_token }` — but `accessTokenParsed.data` from the strict `salesforceTokenSchema` does NOT include `instance_url`... actually the schema requires `instance_url`, ok — but it drops any extra fields and, critically, if the refresh fails (`!response.ok`) it throws HttpError 400 which breaks all Salesforce operations; (3) there is no expiry check — a valid token is refreshed anyway. The refresh should only happen when the token is expired, and ideally reuse the `refreshOAuthTokens` helper for consistency.

title: Salesforce error check uses `response.statusText !== "OK"` instead of `!response.ok`
body: Line 86: `if (response.statusText !== "OK") throw new HttpError({ statusCode: 400, message: response.statusText });`. `Response.statusText` for a successful fetch is typically the empty string `""` (fetch spec: statusText is often empty for HTTP/2 and not guaranteed to be "OK"), so this condition is true even for successful responses and throws a 400 with an empty message — breaking Salesforce entirely. It should be `if (!response.ok)`. (Also note the jsforce Connection constructed at line 101 uses `credentialKey.access_token` — the OLD token — not the freshly refreshed `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`, so even when the refresh succeeds the client is built with a stale token.)

title: Salesforce jsforce Connection is built with the stale access token, not the freshly refreshed one
body: Lines 101-108 construct `new jsforce.Connection({ ..., accessToken: credentialKey.access_token, refreshToken: credentialKey.refresh_token })` using `credentialKey` (the credential as loaded at construction time), even though lines 75-99 just fetched a NEW access token (`accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`) and persisted it. The connection therefore uses the old (possibly expired) access token. jsforce will attempt its own refresh using `refreshToken`, which may work, but if the Salesforce refresh token rotates on use (Salesforce can invalidate old refresh tokens), the just-used refresh token in the DB update (line 98 keeps the old refresh_token) may already be invalid, and the connection's token is stale. The Connection should be built with `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`.

title: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is a string-or-undefined value, not a boolean, and is truthy-checked inconsistently
body: `export const APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED = process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY;` evaluates to `string | undefined` (the value of the second env var when both are set, or `undefined`/empty string). It is used in boolean contexts (`if (!APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED)`, `if (APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT)`) which works, but: (1) if `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET=""` (empty string, as shipped in `.env.example` with `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET=""`), the expression is `"" && ...` = `""` (falsy) — ok; but (2) the exported value leaks into client bundles potentially (constants.ts is imported widely) exposing whether the secret is set (not the value, but still); (3) more importantly, the webhook handler at `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` line 19 relies on this module-level constant, which is evaluated at import time — if env vars are loaded after module evaluation (e.g., in some Next.js runtime configurations), the flag could be stale. It should be an explicit boolean: `!!(process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY)` and ideally the handler should read the env vars directly at request time.

title: appStoreMetadata lookup uses app.slug from DB but credential is written with appMetadata.slug — mismatch for apps whose DB slug differs from metadata slug
body: The handler looks up `prisma.app.findUnique({ where: { slug: reqBody.appSlug } })` and then `appStoreMetadata[app.slug]`. It then writes the credential with `appId: appMetadata.slug` and `type: appMetadata.type`. If the DB `App.slug` differs from the metadata slug (e.g. DB stores `google-calendar` but metadata key is `google-calendar` — fine; but for apps like `msteams` vs `office365video`, or `zoom` vs `zoomvideo`), the credential's `appId`/`type` may not match what the app's service code queries for. The lookup should be done directly on `appStoreMetadata[reqBody.appSlug]` and the DB app check should be a secondary validation, or the code should assert `app.slug === appMetadata.slug`. As written, a webhook for slug `msteams` would find the DB app `msteams` but `appStoreMetadata["msteams"]` — if the metadata key is `office365video` — returns undefined → 404, which is safe; but the inverse (metadata key exists but DB slug differs) could write credentials with an appId that no service queries. Verify the slugs align; the double lookup is fragile.

title: Sync endpoint request has no Content-Type header and no timeout; URLSearchParams body without header may be rejected or hang indefinitely
body: The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends `body: new URLSearchParams({...})` but does not set `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`. Per the fetch spec, when the body is a URLSearchParams object, fetch DOES set the content-type automatically — so that part is fine. However there is no `AbortSignal`/timeout: if the sync endpoint hangs, the token refresh (and therefore the booking flow that triggered it) hangs indefinitely. Also there is no `Authorization` header or signature — the endpoint must rely on network-level trust, which should be documented; and the endpoint URL is taken from env without validation (an `http://` URL would send user ids in cleartext). Add a timeout (AbortController), validate the URL scheme is https in production, and check `response.ok` before returning.

title: Google refresh persists the full googleCredentials object but parseRefreshTokenResponse may have replaced refresh_token with the literal string 'refresh_token'
body: Line 97: `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema);` then line 98-101 persists `key`. `parseRefreshTokenResponse` sets `refresh_token = "refresh_token"` (literal) when the parsed response lacks a refresh_token (see separate finding). Google's token refresh response typically omits `refresh_token` (it's only returned on first consent), so on the sync path — where the minimal schema only guarantees `access_token` — the stored credential's refresh_token is overwritten with the garbage literal `"refresh_token"`. The next refresh sends `refresh_token="refresh_token"` to Google → `invalid_grant` → the catch block at line 108 checks `message !== "invalid_grant"` and marks the credential `invalid: true`, permanently disconnecting the user's Google Calendar. This is a critical data-integrity bug in the primary calendar integration.

title: Office365 getToken validates stored credential with refreshTokenResponseSchema which transforms expires_in into an absolute expiry, corrupting the stored shape on read
body: Line 278: `refreshTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(o365AuthCredentials).success && !isExpired(o365AuthCredentials.expires_in)`. The schema (lines 51-57) transforms `expires_in` via `.transform((offset) => Math.round(+new Date()/1000 + offset))` — i.e., it converts a relative offset into an absolute timestamp. But `o365AuthCredentials` is the STORED credential where `expiry_date` holds the absolute expiry (set in the callback: `responseBody.expiry_date = Math.round(+new Date()/1000 + responseBody.expires_in)`) and `expires_in` was deleted. So `safeParse` on the stored credential fails (no `expires_in`... actually `expires_in` is required in the schema — `expires_in: z.number().transform(...)` — and the stored credential has `expiry_date` not `expires_in`), meaning `getToken` ALWAYS takes the refresh path for Office365, refreshing on every call. Wait — the stored credential from the callback has `expiry_date` and no `expires_in`, so `refreshTokenResponseSchema.safeParse` fails → `getToken` always refreshes → every calendar operation triggers a Microsoft token refresh + DB write. This is a performance bug and, combined with the refresh-path issues above, breaks Office365. The validity check should use `expiry_date` (as `isExpired` does at line 279 — but it's gated behind the failed safeParse). The schema should be split into a 'stored credential' schema and a 'refresh response' schema.

title: MS Teams isExpired uses millisecond timestamp against Date.now() but expiry_date is stored in milliseconds while Office365 calendar stores seconds — inconsistent units across the two adapters
body: `const isExpired = (expiryDate: number) => expiryDate < Math.round(+new Date());` — `+new Date()` is milliseconds. The callback (line 66 of callback.ts) sets `responseBody.expiry_date = Math.round(+new Date() / 1000 + responseBody.expires_in)` — SECONDS plus offset, i.e. a seconds-based timestamp stored in `expiry_date`. So `expiry_date` (seconds, e.g. 1.7e9) is always far less than `Date.now()` (milliseconds, 1.7e12), making `isExpired` ALWAYS true → the token is refreshed on EVERY API call, and each refresh (per the sync-path bugs) can destroy the refresh token. This is a pre-existing unit mismatch (the callback stores seconds, the adapter compares against ms) that this PR's refresh changes amplify into a credential-destroying loop. Note the sibling `office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` `isExpired` (line 235-241) compares `expiryDate < Math.round(+new Date() / 1000)` — seconds — but reads `o365AuthCredentials.expires_in` (line 279) which is a relative offset, not the absolute `expiry_date`... the two Office365 adapters are mutually inconsistent about which field holds the absolute expiry and in which unit.

title: HubSpot isTokenValid logic is inverted: returns true when token is expired
body: `const isTokenValid = (token: HubspotToken) => token && token.tokenType && token.accessToken && token.expiryDate && (token.expiresIn || token.expiryDate) < Date.now();` — the final condition is `< Date.now()`, meaning the function returns true only when the expiry is in the PAST (i.e., the token IS expired). Then line 210: `getToken: () => !isTokenValid(credentialKey) ? Promise.resolve([]) : refreshAccessToken(...)`. So when the token is expired, `isTokenValid` returns true → `!isTokenValid` is false → `refreshAccessToken` is called (correct by accident). When the token is VALID (expiry in the future), `isTokenValid` returns false → `!isTokenValid` is true → returns `Promise.resolve([])` — an empty array used as the token! This is inverted logic (pre-existing, not introduced by this PR, but the PR's refresh changes interact with it). The condition should be `> Date.now()` for validity. As written, valid tokens are never used and expired tokens trigger refresh — the net effect happens to work for refresh but `getToken` returning `[]` for valid tokens means `hubspotClient.setAccessToken` is never called with the valid token... actually `refreshAccessToken` calls `setAccessToken` at the end. This is fragile pre-existing logic that the PR should have fixed while touching this code.

title: Zoho CRM isTokenValid is inverted (returns true when expired) — same class of bug as HubSpot
body: `const isValid = token && token.access_token && token.expiryDate && token.expiryDate < Date.now();` — again `< Date.now()` means 'valid' only when expired. Line 244: `getToken: () => (isTokenValid(credentialKey) ? Promise.resolve() : refreshAccessToken(credentialKey))`. When the token is expired, `isTokenValid` returns true → `getToken` resolves WITHOUT refreshing and WITHOUT setting `this.accessToken` (the `isTokenValid` body sets `this.accessToken = token.access_token` only when `isValid` is true, i.e., when expired — so it sets the EXPIRED token). When the token is valid (future expiry), `isTokenValid` returns false → triggers a refresh unnecessarily. The logic is inverted: it should be `token.expiryDate > Date.now()`. Net effect: Zoho CRM uses expired access tokens and refreshes valid ones — API calls fail with 401 until the credential happens to be refreshed by the inverted path. Pre-existing but directly in the code path this PR modifies.

title: Zoom isTokenValid mixes expires_in (seconds offset) and expiry_date (ms timestamp) in a single comparison against Date.now()
body: `const isTokenValid = (token: ZoomToken) => (token.expires_in || token.expiry_date) < Date.now();` — `expires_in` is a relative seconds offset (e.g. 3600) and `expiry_date` is an absolute ms timestamp. The expression prefers `expires_in` when present. The stored credential (from callback line 44-45) has `expiry_date` (ms) and `expires_in` DELETED (`delete responseBody.expires_in`), so `token.expires_in` is undefined and `expiry_date` (ms) is compared to `Date.now()` (ms) — correct. But the schema comment says `expires_in` is 'deprecated, purely for backwards compatibility', and old credentials may still have `expires_in` (a small number like 3600) → `3600 < Date.now()` is always true → token always considered valid → expired tokens are used → 401s. The function name/semantics are also inverted relative to usage at line 137 (`!isTokenValid(credentialKey) ? resolve(access_token) : refresh(...)`) — `isTokenValid` actually returns 'is expired'. Pre-existing confusion, but the PR's refresh changes rely on this check to decide when to call the (broken) sync path.

title: Webex isTokenValid is inverted (returns true when expired)
body: `const isTokenValid = (token: WebexToken) => token.expiry_date < Date.now();` — returns true when the token IS expired. Line 119-121: `return !isTokenValid(credentialKey) ? Promise.resolve(credentialKey.access_token) : refreshAccessToken(...)`. When expired: `isTokenValid` true → `!isTokenValid` false → refresh (correct by accident). When valid: `isTokenValid` false → `!isTokenValid` true → returns the access token (correct by accident). So despite the misleading name the net behavior is correct — but this is fragile and confusing; the function should be renamed `isTokenExpired` or the comparison flipped. Flagging as low severity since behavior is accidentally correct, but it's a trap for future edits in code this PR touches.

title: No tests for the new webhook endpoint or the refresh/sync helpers
body: The PR adds a new public API endpoint (`apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`) that writes OAuth credentials, plus two new shared helpers (`refreshOAuthTokens`, `parseRefreshTokenResponse`) that are now on the token-refresh path of ~10 integrations. The PR description's checklist explicitly states 'I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective or that my feature works'. Given the number of shape-mismatch bugs identified in the refresh path (Response vs SDK response), unit tests for `refreshOAuthTokens` (both branches) and `parseRefreshTokenResponse` (including the missing-refresh_token case) and integration tests for the webhook (auth, decryption, upsert race) are essential before merge.

title: parseRefreshTokenResponse mutates its input argument and returns a SafeParseResult whose `.data` may be the minimum schema shape, losing provider-specific fields
body: When the sync path is active, the function validates against `minimumTokenResponseSchema` (access_token + numeric props only) and returns that parsed data — dropping provider-specific fields like `token_type`, `scope`, `id`, `instance_url` that the strict schema would have required and that callers persist. For example `googlecalendar` line 97 passes the result to `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })` — wait, it passes `googleCredentials` (the merged object), so Google is ok. But `salesforce` line 90-99 persists `accessTokenParsed.data` directly as the credential key — on the sync path this would be the minimal shape `{ access_token, ...numbers }` plus the fabricated `refresh_token: "refresh_token"`, dropping `id`, `issued_at`, `signature`, `token_type`, `scope` that `salesforceTokenSchema` requires and that jsforce may need. The function should merge the minimal parse back into the original response object (preserving all fields) rather than returning the stripped parse result.

title: Office365 refresh: handleErrorsJson on the sync-path Response parses the minimal sync JSON, then parseRefreshTokenResponse throws due to broken minimum schema, and the thrown error is unhandled
body: Line 262: `const responseJson = await handleErrorsJson(response);` — on the sync path `response` is the sync endpoint's Response, so `responseJson` is the minimal `{ access_token, expiry }` object. Line 263 passes it to `parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseJson, refreshTokenResponseSchema)`. Because `minimumTokenResponseSchema` is broken (see separate finding — the computed-key syntax doesn't create an index signature), `safeParse` fails and `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws `Error("Invalid refreshed tokens were returned")`. This throw is NOT caught in `refreshAccessToken` (no try/catch), so it propagates through `getToken()` → `fetcher` → every Office365 calendar operation fails with an unhandled error when credential sync is enabled. The Office365 sync path is entirely broken.

title: Lark refresh: sync-path Response from handleLarkError lacks the Lark envelope; data.data is undefined and credential is overwritten with undefined tokens
body: Even if `handleLarkError` successfully parses the sync endpoint's minimal JSON `{ access_token, <expiry> }` (no Lark `{ code, data: {...} }` envelope), line 84-96 reads `data.data.refresh_expires_in`, `data.data.refresh_token`, `data.data.access_token`, `data.data.expires_in` — all undefined because the sync response has no `data` envelope. Line 91-96 then builds `newLarkAuthCredentials` with `refresh_token: undefined`, `refresh_expires_date: NaN` (Math.round(+new Date()/1000 + undefined)), `access_token: undefined`, `expiry_date: NaN`, and line 98-105 persists this corrupted credential, destroying the user's Lark Calendar integration. The sync path for Lark is broken and destructive.

title: Zoho Bigin refresh: sync-path minimal response lacks expires_in, producing NaN expiryDate; also refresh_token is overwritten with the old one but access_token shape mismatch
body: On the sync path, `tokenInfo` is a fetch Response and `tokenInfo.data` is undefined → TypeError (see separate finding). But even if the shape were normalized to the sync JSON `{ access_token, expiry }`, line 98 computes `tokenInfo.data.expiryDate = Math.round(Date.now() + tokenInfo.data.expires_in)` — the sync contract returns an absolute expiry, not a relative `expires_in`, so `expires_in` is undefined → `expiryDate = NaN`. Line 100 sets `refresh_token` to the old one (good), but `api_domain` and `accountServer` come from `credentialKey` (line 99 sets accountServer from credentialKey — ok), while `api_domain` is never set on the sync path → `token.api_domain` is undefined → all subsequent Bigin API URLs become `undefined/bigin/v1/...`. The Bigin sync refresh path produces a broken credential.

title: refreshOAuthTokens silently falls back to the provider refresh when userId is null, but team/org credentials (teamId set, userId null) then bypass sync entirely with no indication
body: The condition `if (APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT && userId)` means that when a credential belongs to a team (`credential.userId` is null, `teamId` set), the sync endpoint is NOT called and the provider refresh runs instead. For self-hosters using this feature, team credentials will silently diverge from the app store's source of truth — the app store cannot sync team credentials because the sync endpoint is keyed on `calcomUserId`. This may be intentional (the webhook only supports userId), but it is undocumented in the code and the PR description, and creates an inconsistency where some credentials sync and others don't. At minimum, document this limitation or extend the sync protocol to support teamId.

title: Credential update overwrites the entire key, discarding fields the app may need (email, expiry_date, type-specific fields)
body: The update path (lines 72-81) does `prisma.credential.update({ where: { id }, data: { key: keys } })` — replacing the entire `key` JSON with the webhook payload. For apps like Office365/Google whose credential key includes derived fields (`email`, `expiry_date`, `scope`, `token_type`), a sync payload containing only `{ access_token, refresh_token, ... }` will strip those fields. Downstream code that reads `credential.key.email` (e.g., calendar listing uses the stored email) or validates the full schema will break. The update should merge: `key: { ...existingCredential.key, ...keys }`, and ideally validate the merged result against the app's schema. The create path (line 83-90) has the same issue but is less severe.

title: Salesforce credential update drops the old access_token fields and does not preserve refresh token rotation
body: Line 96-99: `data: { key: { ...accessTokenParsed.data, refresh_token: credentialKey.refresh_token } }`. Salesforce's refresh response includes a new `access_token`, `signature`, `issued_at`, `id`, `instance_url`, `scope`, `token_type` — but NOT a new `refresh_token` (Salesforce refresh tokens are typically long-lived and not rotated on every refresh). The code correctly preserves the old refresh_token. However, it also means the update runs on EVERY getClient call (see separate finding), rewriting the credential each time. Additionally, if Salesforce ever DOES rotate the refresh token, this code would discard the new one. The update should only happen when the token actually changed, and should preserve any newly-returned refresh_token if present.

title: MS Teams refresh computes expiry_date from expires_in which the sync endpoint does not return (it returns an absolute expiry), yielding expiry_date = Date.now()
body: Line 84: `responseBody.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + (responseBody?.expires_in || 0) * 1000);`. On the sync path, the endpoint returns an absolute expiry field (per the PR contract: 'The response should only contain the access token and expiry date') — there is no `expires_in`, so `expiry_date = Date.now() + 0` = now. Combined with the inverted `isExpired` check (always true, see separate finding), the token is refreshed on every call and the stored expiry is always 'now'. Even on the normal path, if Microsoft omits `expires_in` (it doesn't, but defensively), the same corruption occurs. The code should use the absolute expiry returned by the sync endpoint when present, falling back to computing from `expires_in`.

title: Zoom refresh on sync path: minimal response lacks refresh_token, but key.refresh_token is overwritten with newTokens.refresh_token (undefined)
body: Line 120: `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token;`. On the sync path, `parseRefreshTokenResponse` validates against the broken `minimumTokenResponseSchema` (see separate finding) — if it somehow passed, `newTokens` would be the minimal shape without `refresh_token`, so `key.refresh_token = undefined`, destroying the stored refresh token. Even on the normal path, `parseRefreshTokenResponse` fabricates `refresh_token = "refresh_token"` when missing (Zoom DOES return a new refresh_token on refresh, so normal path is ok). But the sync path combined with the fabricated/missing refresh_token corrupts the credential. The update should preserve the existing refresh token when the response doesn't include one: `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token ?? key.refresh_token`.

title: Webex refresh overwrites refresh_token unconditionally; sync path (minimal response) would set it to undefined
body: Line 101: `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token;`. On the sync path, `webexRefreshedTokenSchema` requires `refresh_token` — so validation fails and the function rejects (see separate finding). But if the schema were relaxed for sync (as it should be), `newTokens.refresh_token` would be undefined and the stored refresh token would be destroyed. Webex rotates refresh tokens on use, so the normal path is fine, but the sync path must preserve the existing refresh token when the response omits it. Use `newTokens.refresh_token ?? key.refresh_token`.

title: Google refresh on sync path never calls the provider, so googleCredentials.refresh_token is preserved but the sync endpoint's response is not merged into googleCredentials beyond access_token/expiry_date
body: Lines 94-96: on the sync path, only `access_token` and `expiry_date` are copied from the (broken, see finding) token object into `googleCredentials`. The sync endpoint contract returns only those two fields, which is fine for Google. But because `res?.data` is undefined on the sync path (Response has no `.data`), the code throws before reaching this point (see the high-severity finding). Once that's fixed, this merge is correct for Google. No additional issue beyond the shape mismatch already reported.

title: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is read at module scope in constants.ts but refreshOAuthTokens also checks process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT at call time — inconsistent gating between webhook and refresh paths
body: `refreshOAuthTokens` gates on `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT && userId`, while the webhook gates only on `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED`. This means a deployment can have the webhook enabled (secret + encryption key set) but no sync endpoint — in which case credentials can be pushed IN via webhook but token refreshes go direct to the provider. That's a valid configuration. Conversely, if `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is set but the webhook secret is not, refreshes go to the sync endpoint but no credentials can be pushed — the sync endpoint becomes the only source of tokens, which may be intended. The asymmetry is worth documenting but is not a bug per se. Flagging as low/speculative — the main issue is that `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` doesn't include `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, so the name is misleading.

title: Webhook header name is configurable via env var, allowing an operator to accidentally weaken verification (e.g., set to a header an attacker controls like 'user-agent')
body: `req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"]` — the header name is read from an environment variable with no validation. If an operator sets `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME=user-agent` (or any commonly-sent header), the 'secret' check compares the User-Agent header value to `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` — an attacker who knows the secret (or if it's weak) could pass verification by setting User-Agent. More realistically, a misconfiguration could make the check compare against a header that proxies set. The header name should be a hardcoded constant (or at least validated against a whitelist / not a standard header). The env var configurability adds risk without benefit.

title: refreshTokenResponseSchema transforms expires_in into an absolute timestamp, but the same schema is used to validate the STORED credential in getToken where expires_in is absent and expiry_date holds the absolute value
body: The schema at lines 51-57 requires `expires_in` (a relative offset) and transforms it to an absolute timestamp. It is used in two places with different data shapes: (1) line 263 to parse the refresh RESPONSE (which has `expires_in` — correct usage), and (2) line 278 to validate the STORED credential (`o365AuthCredentials`), which has `expiry_date` (absolute, seconds) and NO `expires_in` (deleted in the callback). The second usage always fails safeParse, making the validity check at line 278-281 always take the refresh path (see separate finding). The stored-credential validation should use a separate schema with `expiry_date: z.number()` and optional `expires_in`.

title: HubSpot getToken returns Promise.resolve([]) (empty array) when token is 'valid' per inverted logic — downstream code receives an array instead of a token
body: Line 210: `getToken: () => !isTokenValid(credentialKey) ? Promise.resolve([]) : refreshAccessToken(credentialKey.refreshToken)`. Due to the inverted `isTokenValid` (see separate finding), when the token is actually valid (future expiry), `isTokenValid` returns false, `!isTokenValid` is true, and `getToken` resolves to `[]` — an empty array, not a token. Callers (`createEvent` line 239: `await auth.getToken();`) ignore the return value and rely on `hubspotClient.setAccessToken` being called inside `refreshAccessToken`. So when the token is valid, `setAccessToken` is NEVER called and the hubspotClient uses whatever token was last set (possibly none) — API calls fail with 401. The inverted logic means valid tokens are never applied to the client. This is a pre-existing bug in the gating logic that the PR's changes interact with.

title: Unrelated change: redirectUri hardcoded to 'zoho-bigin' instead of appConfig.slug
body: The diff changes `const redirectUri = WEBAPP_URL + `/api/integrations/${appConfig.slug}/callback`;` to `const redirectUri = WEBAPP_URL + `/api/integrations/zoho-bigin/callback`;`. If `appConfig.slug` is `zoho-bigin` this is a no-op refactor, but if the config slug ever differs (e.g., for a white-label variant), the hardcoded path breaks the OAuth redirect URI registration. This change is unrelated to the credential-sync feature and should be reverted to use `appConfig.slug` for consistency with the callback (which uses `appConfig.slug` at line 36).

title: Fabricated refresh_token value 'refresh_token' is a magic string that will be sent to providers verbatim
body: The literal string `"refresh_token"` used as a placeholder (line 26) is indistinguishable from a real (if unlikely) token value and will be sent to OAuth providers as `refresh_token="refresh_token"` after being persisted (see the high-severity finding on credential destruction). Even as a placeholder it should be obviously-invalid and, more importantly, the field should be left absent so callers can preserve the existing token. This is primarily a symptom of the deeper bug already reported; flagging the magic string explicitly.

title: Three sequential DB queries (user, app, credential) could be reduced, and app metadata lookup duplicates the DB app check
body: The handler performs `prisma.user.findUnique`, `prisma.app.findUnique`, then `prisma.credential.findFirst` sequentially. The user and app lookups are independent and could be parallelized with `Promise.all`. More importantly, the `prisma.app.findUnique` check is redundant with the `appStoreMetadata` lookup — if the slug exists in `appStoreMetadata`, the app is valid for credential purposes; the DB check only confirms the app is installed/enabled in this instance. If the intent is to ensure the app is enabled, the check should also verify the app is not disabled. As written, the three sequential round-trips add latency to a webhook that should be fast. Low severity (webhook volume is low) but worth noting.

title: Pre-existing: getAvailability catch block logs and returns Promise.reject([]) — rejecting with an empty array instead of resolving
body: Line 183-186: `catch (err) { console.log(err); return Promise.reject([]); }`. Rejecting with an empty array (not an Error) is an anti-pattern — callers awaiting this get a rejection whose reason is `[]`, which is truthy-checkable but not an Error instance, breaking error logging/handling upstream. This is pre-existing code not touched by the PR diff, but it's in a file heavily modified by the PR. Flagging as low since it's out of scope but a maintainer reviewing this file should note it.

title: Salesforce parseRefreshTokenResponse throws on failure, making the `if (!accessTokenParsed.success)` check at line 92 unreachable dead code
