body: Line 90: `const accessTokenParsed = parseRefreshTokenResponse(accessTokenJson, salesforceTokenSchema);` — but `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws `new Error("Invalid refreshed tokens were returned")` when `safeParse` fails (it never returns a `{success: false}` object). Line 92-94 `if (!accessTokenParsed.success) { return Promise.reject(...) }` is therefore unreachable — a parse failure surfaces as a thrown Error from `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, not as the intended Promise.reject. The thrown error propagates out of `getClient` (which is called in the constructor via `this.getClient(credential).then(...)`) resulting in an unhandled promise rejection in the constructor. The dead code indicates the contract mismatch between `parseRefreshTokenResponse` (throws) and its callers (expect SafeParseResult).

title: Zoom refresh: handleZoomResponse on sync-path Response works, but the sync JSON lacks refresh_token/scope/token_type so zoomRefreshedTokenSchema fails and Zoom sync refresh always rejects
body: On the sync path, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the sync endpoint Response. `handleZoomResponse(response, credential.id)` parses its JSON (the minimal `{ access_token, expiry }`). Line 104 validates with `parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseBody, zoomRefreshedTokenSchema)` — but `zoomRefreshedTokenSchema` (lines 66-72) requires `token_type: z.literal("bearer")`, `refresh_token: z.string()`, `expires_in: z.number()`, `scope: z.string()`. The minimal sync response has none of these, so validation fails and `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned' (or, if the broken minimum schema is used, the computed-key bug causes failure). Either way, Zoom token refresh via sync ALWAYS fails, and the thrown error propagates through `getToken()` breaking all Zoom meeting operations when sync is enabled. The sync path needs a relaxed schema that makes refresh_token/scope/token_type optional and preserves existing values.

title: Webex refreshed-token schema requires refresh_token_expires_in which the sync endpoint does not return; sync path validation always fails
body: Same class of issue as Zoom: `webexRefreshedTokenSchema` (lines 49-56) requires `refresh_token: z.string()` and `refresh_token_expires_in: z.number()`. The sync endpoint returns only access token + expiry. On the sync path, `parsedToken.success` is false → line 89-91 rejects with 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned' → Webex sync refresh always fails. The schema for the sync path must make these optional and preserve existing values from the stored credential (which the code already does at lines 99-105 by merging into `key`).

title: MS Teams refresh: sync-path Response is passed to handleErrorsJson which expects a Response — ok — but the sync JSON lacks refresh_token, and the credential update at line 87-95 overwrites the entire key, losing refresh_token, email, scope, token_type
body: Lines 87-95: `prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, data: { key: responseBody as unknown as Prisma.InputJsonValue } })`. `responseBody` on the sync path is the minimal `{ access_token, expiry }` JSON (plus the computed `expiry_date`). The stored credential previously contained `refresh_token`, `email`, `scope`, `token_type`, `ext_expires_in` (per the `O365AuthCredentials` interface, lines 27-35). The update REPLACES the entire key with the minimal object, so `refresh_token` becomes undefined. The next refresh reads `o365AuthCredentials.refresh_token` (line 104) = undefined → sends `refresh_token=undefined` to Microsoft → invalid_grant → credential permanently broken. The update must merge: `key: { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...responseBody }` and preserve `refresh_token` when the response omits it.

title: Pre-existing: Lark credential deletion on refresh-token expiry races with concurrent operations
body: Line 62: `await prisma.credential.delete({ where: { id: credential.id } });` when the refresh token is expired. If two concurrent calendar operations trigger `refreshAccessToken` for the same credential, both may pass the expiry check and both attempt refresh/delete, or one deletes while the other is mid-API-call with the old token. This is pre-existing (not introduced by the PR), but the PR's changes to this function make the race more likely to surface (the sync path adds a network round-trip before the delete). Low severity; flagging for awareness since the PR modifies this exact function.

title: Sync endpoint URL is not validated — an http:// URL would transmit calcomUserId in cleartext and allow MITM token injection
body: `fetch(process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, ...)` — the URL comes from an env var with no scheme validation. If an operator sets `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT=http://...` (e.g., for a local test), the user id is sent in cleartext and, more critically, the RESPONSE (which becomes the user's access token) can be tampered with by a network attacker — a full token-injection vector into the credential store. The function should reject non-https URLs (except perhaps localhost for development), or at minimum the documentation should mandate https. Given this endpoint returns live OAuth access tokens, enforcing https in production is important.

title: Decrypted credential keys are written to the DB without re-encryption at rest validation, and the webhook accepts arbitrary JSON as the key
body: The webhook decrypts `reqBody.keys` with `symmetricDecrypt` and writes the parsed JSON directly as `credential.key`. Cal.com stores credentials encrypted at rest via Prisma field encryption (PRISMA_FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY) — but this handler writes the decrypted object through the standard Prisma client, which should apply field-level encryption transparently. However, there is no validation that the decrypted payload is a well-formed credential for the target app (see separate finding). From a security perspective, the webhook allows ANY holder of the webhook secret to write ANY JSON as ANY user's credential for ANY app — including overwriting a victim's Google Calendar credential with attacker-controlled tokens, effectively redirecting calendar data to an attacker-controlled account. The webhook secret is a powerful bearer token; the handler should at minimum validate the payload shape per app and consider scoping the secret or adding per-app authorization. Also, the decrypted plaintext keys exist in memory and are passed to Prisma — ensure they are not logged (the handler doesn't log them, which is good).

title: Office365 refresh on sync path: the sync endpoint is called instead of Microsoft, but the response is parsed with handleErrorsJson which expects a fetch Response — the sync path returns a Response so this works, but the parsed JSON shape (minimal) fails refreshTokenResponseSchema which requires expires_in
body: On the sync path, `response` is the sync endpoint's Response. `handleErrorsJson(response)` parses its JSON (minimal `{ access_token, expiry }`). `parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseJson, refreshTokenResponseSchema)` — `refreshTokenResponseSchema` requires `expires_in: z.number()` (line 53). The sync contract returns an absolute expiry, not `expires_in`, so `safeParse` fails → `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws (see separate findings). The Office365 sync refresh path is broken. Additionally, even if it didn't throw, line 264 spreads `tokenResponse.data` (which would be the minimal shape) over `o365AuthCredentials`, and the `expires_in` transform would compute a wrong absolute value. The sync path needs a dedicated schema with an absolute expiry field.

title: Zoho Bigin passes credentialId instead of userId to refreshOAuthTokens (duplicate of high finding, noting the exact line for the wrong argument)
body: Line 93: `credentialId` is passed as the third argument to `refreshOAuthTokens(refreshFunction, appSlug, userId)`. The parameter is named `userId` in `refreshOAuthTokens` and is sent as `calcomUserId` to the sync endpoint. `credentialId` is the credential's primary key, not the user's id. This means the sync endpoint receives a credential id where it expects a user id — the self-hoster's app store will look up the wrong record (or fail), and tokens for the wrong user could be returned and written into this credential. This is the single most clear-cut correctness bug in the PR: every other caller passes `credential.userId`.

title: HubSpot refresh: expiryDate computed from expiresIn which is undefined on the sync path, yielding NaN
body: Line 192: `hubspotRefreshToken.expiryDate = Math.round(Date.now() + hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn * 1000);`. On the sync path, `hubspotRefreshToken` is a fetch Response (see high-severity finding) — `expiresIn` is undefined → `expiryDate = NaN`. Even if the shape were normalized to the sync JSON, the sync contract returns an absolute expiry, not `expiresIn`, so `expiryDate` would still be NaN. The credential is then updated with `key: hubspotRefreshToken as any` containing `expiryDate: NaN`, and the inverted `isTokenValid` check (`(token.expiresIn || token.expiryDate) < Date.now()` → `NaN < Date.now()` → false) treats the token as valid forever, so the corrupted credential is never refreshed again. HubSpot sync path produces a permanently broken credential.

title: Zoho CRM refresh hardcodes a 1-hour expiry (Date.now() + 60*60) instead of using the provider's expires_in
body: Line 219: `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.expiryDate = Math.round(Date.now() + 60 * 60);` — this hardcodes a 1-hour expiry regardless of what Zoho actually returns (`expires_in`). The callback (line 51 of callback.ts) does the same. On the sync path, the endpoint returns an absolute expiry which is ignored. If Zoho tokens last longer (they typically do), the credential is refreshed far more often than necessary (performance); if shorter, the token expires prematurely (correctness). This is pre-existing behavior, but the PR's sync changes should use the actual expiry from the response. Note `Date.now()` is ms and `expiryDate` is compared with `< Date.now()` in the inverted `isTokenValid` — units are consistent here (ms), unlike the Office365 adapters.

title: Comment on isExpired is misleading given the unit mismatch with the callback
body: Line 48 comment: '// Checks to see if our O365 user token is valid or if we need to refresh'. The function `isExpired = (expiryDate: number) => expiryDate < Math.round(+new Date());` compares against milliseconds, but the callback stores `expiry_date` in SECONDS (line 66 of callback.ts: `Math.round(+new Date() / 1000 + responseBody.expires_in)`). The comment doesn't document the unit, and the mismatch means `isExpired` always returns true. A maintainer reading this file would assume the check is correct. The units must be reconciled (either store ms in the callback or compare against seconds here) and documented.

title: Google refresh catch block silently swallows non-invalid_grant errors and returns the auth client with a stale token, masking sync-path failures
body: Lines 103-118: the catch block checks `if (message !== "invalid_grant") return myGoogleAuth;` — for ANY error other than invalid_grant (including the TypeError from the sync-path `.data` bug, network errors, or the 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned' error from parseRefreshTokenResponse), it silently returns the auth client with the OLD expired credentials. The caller (`getToken` → `authedCalendar`) then makes API calls with an expired token, which fail with 401 from Google, surfacing as a confusing 'There was an error contacting google calendar service' error far from the root cause. Errors during refresh should be logged (via `this.log`) and, for non-invalid_grant errors, either rethrown or at least logged so operators can diagnose sync-path failures. The silent swallow makes the sync-path bugs (shape mismatch, fabricated refresh_token) nearly impossible to detect in production.

title: Return type is `any` — the function returns either a provider SDK response object or a fetch Response, and TypeScript callers cannot distinguish
body: `const refreshOAuthTokens = async (refreshFunction: () => any, appSlug: string, userId: number | null) => { ... return response; }` — the return type is inferred as `any` (union of the refreshFunction's return and Response). This is why the shape-mismatch bugs compiled without errors: callers assign the result to typed variables (`HubspotToken`, `res?.data`, etc.) and TypeScript doesn't complain because the function returns `any`. The function should have an explicit return type (e.g., `Promise<Response | Awaited<ReturnType<typeof refreshFunction>>>`) or, better, be redesigned to normalize the response shape so callers don't need to branch. The `any` type is the root enabler of the class of bugs found in this PR.

title: Parameter `response: any` and `schema: z.ZodTypeAny` — no type safety on inputs
body: The function signature `(response: any, schema: z.ZodTypeAny)` accepts anything. Combined with the `any` return type of `refreshOAuthTokens`, this creates a fully untyped pipeline for OAuth token data. The `response` parameter should be typed as `unknown` (forcing safeParse) and the return type should be `z.SafeParseReturnType<...>` or a discriminated union. The lack of types is why the Salesforce caller's `.success` check compiled despite the function throwing. Low severity on its own but contributes to the systemic issue.

title: Stray empty JSDoc comment `/** */` above the handler
body: Line 16: `/** */` — an empty JSDoc block left above `export default async function handler`. It serves no purpose and should be removed or replaced with a real description of the endpoint (method, auth, payload). Minor cleanup.

title: Pre-existing: handleErrorJsonOffice365Calendar error condition `!response.ok && response.status < 200 && response.status >= 300` is always false
body: Line 499: `if (!response.ok && response.status < 200 && response.status >= 300)` — `response.status < 200 && response.status >= 300` is a contradiction (no number is both < 200 and >= 300), so this condition is always false and the error branch (lines 500-501) is dead code. The intent was likely `response.status < 200 || response.status >= 300`. This is pre-existing and out of the PR's scope, but it's in a file the PR heavily modifies and it means Office365 error responses are not properly thrown. Flagging for maintainer awareness.

title: Zoom getToken logic is inverted in naming: `!isTokenValid(credentialKey) ? resolve(access_token) : refresh(...)` — isTokenValid actually means 'is expired'
body: `isTokenValid` (line 63) returns `(token.expires_in || token.expiry_date) < Date.now()` — true when the token IS expired. Line 137: `return !isTokenValid(credentialKey) ? Promise.resolve(credentialKey.access_token) : refreshAccessToken(...)`. When expired: `isTokenValid` true → `!isTokenValid` false → refresh (correct). When valid: `isTokenValid` false → `!isTokenValid` true → return access token (correct). So the net behavior is correct despite the inverted name, but the naming is a trap. Same pattern as Webex. Low severity; flagging because the PR modifies this function and a future edit could easily flip the logic.

title: Lark getToken returns the access token string, but on the sync path refreshAccessToken returns newLarkAuthCredentials.access_token which may be undefined (sync response shape mismatch)
body: Line 50-53: `getToken: () => !isExpired(larkAuthCredentials.expiry_date) ? Promise.resolve(larkAuthCredentials.access_token) : this.refreshAccessToken(credential)`. `refreshAccessToken` returns `newLarkAuthCredentials.access_token` (line 107). On the sync path, `newLarkAuthCredentials.access_token = data.data.access_token` where `data` is the parsed sync response — which has no Lark envelope, so `data.data` is undefined and `data.data.access_token` throws (see high-severity finding). If the shape were normalized, the sync response's `access_token` would be at the top level, not under `data`. The Lark sync path is broken at this level too.

title: Office365 refresh persists o365AuthCredentials which on the sync path is the minimal response merged over the old credential — but the merge uses `tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data` which is dead code (parseRefreshTokenResponse throws), so on failure the OLD expired credential is persisted unchanged
body: Line 264: `o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...(tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data) };`. Since `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws on failure (never returns `{success: false}`), this line only executes on success. But note: `tokenResponse.data` on the sync path would be the minimal shape (access_token + numbers) — spreading it over `o365AuthCredentials` preserves old fields (good) but the `expires_in` transform in the schema would have converted the sync response's absolute expiry... actually the sync response has no `expires_in`, so the strict schema fails and the function throws. The merge logic itself is reasonable IF the parse succeeded, but the dead `.success` check means failures throw unhandled (see separate finding). Additionally, the persisted credential keeps the old `refresh_token` (good — it's in `o365AuthCredentials` and not overwritten by the minimal data), but loses nothing else. The main issue is the throw-on-failure contract mismatch.

title: MS Teams refresh updates o365AuthCredentials in-memory (expiry_date, access_token) but the DB update writes responseBody which on the normal path includes the new refresh_token — however on the sync path responseBody lacks refresh_token so the DB loses it while the in-memory object keeps the old one, causing divergence
body: Lines 87-98: the DB is updated with `key: responseBody` (the raw response body), while the in-memory `o365AuthCredentials` is updated with `expiry_date` and `access_token` from `responseBody` (lines 96-97). On the normal path, `responseBody` includes a new `refresh_token` (Microsoft rotates refresh tokens), so the DB gets the new one — consistent. On the sync path, `responseBody` has no `refresh_token`, so the DB loses it, but the in-memory `o365AuthCredentials.refresh_token` still holds the old one — the in-memory object and the DB diverge. The next service instance loads the DB credential (no refresh_token) and refresh fails. The DB update should write the merged object (`{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...responseBody }`), not the raw responseBody.

title: Zoho Bigin refresh preserves refresh_token from credentialKey (good) but on the sync path api_domain is not set, breaking all subsequent API URLs
body: Line 99-100: `tokenInfo.data.accountServer = credentialKey.accountServer; tokenInfo.data.refresh_token = credentialKey.refresh_token;`. On the sync path, `tokenInfo.data` is the minimal sync JSON `{ access_token, expiry }` — it has no `api_domain`. The Bigin API URLs are built as `token.api_domain + this.contactsSlug` (line 137, 156, etc.). With `api_domain` undefined, all Bigin API calls go to `undefined/bigin/v1/...` and fail. The sync path must also preserve `api_domain` from the existing credential (like `accountServer` is preserved). The credential update at line 102-109 writes `key: tokenInfo.data as BiginToken` — missing `api_domain`, `scope`, `token_type` on the sync path.

title: Zoho CRM refresh merges sync/normal response data over the old credential but hardcodes expiryDate to 1 hour, ignoring the actual token lifetime
body: Lines 226-231: the DB update writes `{ ...(zohoCrmTokenInfo.data as ZohoToken), refresh_token: credentialKey.refresh_token, accountServer: credentialKey.accountServer }`. On the sync path, `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data` is undefined (Response has no `.data`) → TypeError (see high finding). Even if normalized, line 219 hardcodes `expiryDate = Date.now() + 60*60` (1 hour) regardless of the actual `expires_in` returned by Zoho or the absolute expiry returned by the sync endpoint. The `api_domain` field is also not preserved from `credentialKey` (unlike Bigin which preserves `accountServer`) — wait, `accountServer` IS preserved (line 229), but `api_domain` is not in the merge — on the sync path `api_domain` would be lost. Zoho CRM API URLs are hardcoded to `https://www.zohoapis.com/crm/v3/...` (lines 90, 105, 133, etc.) so `api_domain` isn't used for URLs in this service — ok, so that's fine. The main issue is the hardcoded 1-hour expiry and the shape mismatch.

title: When userId is null (team credential), the sync endpoint is silently skipped — but the function still returns the provider refresh result, which is correct; however there is no logging or metric indicating sync was bypassed
body: For team credentials (`credential.userId` is null), the sync endpoint is not called and the provider refresh runs. This is a silent behavioral difference: self-hosters enabling credential sync may expect ALL credentials to be synced, but team credentials silently diverge. There should be at least a debug log when sync is bypassed due to missing userId, so operators can diagnose why team credentials aren't syncing. Low severity / observability gap.

title: User existence check queries the full user record when only existence is needed
body: `prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { id: reqBody.userId } })` loads the entire user row (including potentially sensitive fields) just to check existence. `findUnique({ where: { id }, select: { id: true } })` or `count` would be sufficient and avoids loading unnecessary data into memory. Low severity for a webhook but a good practice, especially since the user object is not used beyond the null check.

title: Google refresh persists `key` which is the SafeParseResult, not the parsed data — wait, parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the SafeParseResult object, and line 97 assigns it to `key`, then line 100 persists `data: { key }`
body: Line 97: `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema);` — `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns `refreshTokenResponse` which is the SafeParseResult (`{ success: true, data: {...} }`), NOT the parsed data. Line 98-101: `prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, data: { key } })` — this persists the SafeParseResult OBJECT (with `success` and `data` properties) as the credential key, not the actual token data! The credential key becomes `{ success: true, data: { access_token, refresh_token, ... } }` instead of `{ access_token, refresh_token, ... }`. Every subsequent read of `credential.key` (e.g., line 75 `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)`) will FAIL because the key has a `data` wrapper. This is a critical bug: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns a SafeParseResult but the Google caller treats it as the parsed data. The caller should use `parseRefreshTokenResponse(...).data` or the function should return `.data` directly. Note: the OLD code was `const key = googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials);` which returned the parsed data directly — the refactor changed the return shape and broke the caller.

title: Office365 refresh: tokenResponse is the SafeParseResult, and line 264 accesses tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data — this is correct usage IF parseRefreshTokenResponse returned a SafeParseResult, but it throws on failure (contract mismatch)
body: Line 264: `o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...(tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data) };`. This caller correctly accesses `.success` and `.data` on the result — which would work IF `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returned a SafeParseResult. But `parseRefreshTokenResponse` THROWS on failure (see separate finding), so `tokenResponse` is always `{success: true, data}` when the function returns, and the `.success` check is always true. The spread works correctly on success. The issue is purely the throw-vs-return contract mismatch making the error handling dead. This caller is actually written correctly for the INTENDED contract — the function doesn't honor it.

title: Zoom refresh: `newTokens = parsedToken.data` — parsedToken is the SafeParseResult from parseRefreshTokenResponse, so .data is correct here; but if parseRefreshTokenResponse throws (which it does on failure), the explicit `if (!parsedToken.success)` check at line 108 is unreachable
body: Line 104: `const parsedToken = parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseBody, zoomRefreshedTokenSchema);` — returns SafeParseResult on success, throws on failure. Line 108: `if (!parsedToken.success)` — always false when reached (since failure throws). Line 111: `const newTokens = parsedToken.data;` — correct on success. The dead check is the issue (see separate finding on the contract mismatch). The Zoom caller is written for the intended contract; the function doesn't honor it.

title: Salesforce credential update spreads accessTokenParsed.data (SafeParseResult.data) — correct on success, but on the sync path the minimal schema strips provider-specific fields
body: Line 98: `data: { key: { ...accessTokenParsed.data, refresh_token: credentialKey.refresh_token } }`. On the normal path, `accessTokenParsed.data` is the full Salesforce token (validated by `salesforceTokenSchema` which requires id, issued_at, instance_url, signature, access_token, scope, token_type) — good. On the sync path, `parseRefreshTokenResponse` validates against the broken `minimumTokenResponseSchema` and returns the minimal shape — dropping `id`, `issued_at`, `signature`, `scope`, `token_type`, `instance_url`... wait, the minimum schema requires `access_token` and allows other properties via the (broken) index signature. If the index signature worked, it would passthrough all properties. But since the computed-key syntax is broken (see separate finding), the parse FAILS and the function throws. So on the sync path, Salesforce refresh throws 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned' — the Salesforce sync path is broken at the schema level.

title: CRITICAL: Google refresh persists the SafeParseResult wrapper object as the credential key, corrupting the stored credential
body: Line 97: `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema);`. `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns `refreshTokenResponse` which is the full SafeParseResult object `{ success: true, data: { ...tokens } }` (line 29 of parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts: `return refreshTokenResponse;`). Line 98-101 then does `prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, data: { key } })` — persisting `{ success: true, data: { access_token, refresh_token, expiry_date, ... } }` as the credential's key. The OLD code was `const key = googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials);` which returned the PARSED DATA directly (zod's `.parse` returns the data, not a SafeParseResult). The refactor changed the return shape from 'parsed data' to 'SafeParseResult wrapper' and the Google caller was not updated to unwrap `.data`. Every subsequent read of this credential (line 75: `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)`) will FAIL because the key is wrapped in `{ success, data }`. This corrupts the user's Google Calendar credential on the FIRST token refresh after this PR deploys, breaking Google Calendar for all users. This is the most severe bug in the PR.

title: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the SafeParseResult wrapper, but callers expect either the parsed data (Google) or the SafeParseResult (Office365/Zoom/Salesforce) — the contract is inconsistent and Google's caller is broken
body: `return refreshTokenResponse;` returns the full SafeParseResult (`{ success, data }`). Callers are split: Google (CalendarService.ts line 97) treats the return as the parsed data and persists it directly (corrupting the credential — see separate critical finding); Office365 (line 263-264), Zoom (line 104-111), and Salesforce (line 90-94) treat it as a SafeParseResult and access `.success`/`.data`. The function's return contract is ambiguous and at least one caller (Google) is definitively broken by it. The function should have a single, documented return type — either always return the SafeParseResult (and fix Google to use `.data`) or always return the parsed data and throw on failure (and fix the `.success` checks). As written, the inconsistency guarantees at least one integration is broken.

title: Office365 getToken always refreshes because the stored credential fails refreshTokenResponseSchema validation (missing expires_in, has expiry_date instead)
body: Line 278-281: `getToken: () => refreshTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(o365AuthCredentials).success && !isExpired(o365AuthCredentials.expires_in) ? Promise.resolve(o365AuthCredentials.access_token) : refreshAccessToken(o365AuthCredentials)`. The stored credential (from callback.ts line 65-66) has `expiry_date` (absolute, seconds) and `expires_in` DELETED. `refreshTokenResponseSchema` (lines 51-57) REQUIRES `expires_in: z.number()` — so `safeParse` on the stored credential ALWAYS fails → `getToken` ALWAYS calls `refreshAccessToken` → every Office365 calendar operation triggers a Microsoft token refresh + DB write. This is a severe performance bug (and rate-limit risk with Microsoft) that exists independently of the sync path. The validity check should validate `expiry_date` (which the stored credential has) instead of `expires_in`, or use a separate schema for stored credentials.

title: MS Teams getToken always refreshes because isExpired compares a seconds-based expiry_date against Date.now() in milliseconds
body: Line 56: `const isExpired = (expiryDate: number) => expiryDate < Math.round(+new Date());` — `+new Date()` is MILLISECONDS. The callback (callback.ts line 66) stores `expiry_date = Math.round(+new Date() / 1000 + responseBody.expires_in)` — SECONDS. So `expiry_date` (e.g., 1,700,000,000) is always less than `Date.now()` (e.g., 1,700,000,000,000) → `isExpired` ALWAYS returns true → `getToken` ALWAYS calls `refreshAccessToken` → every MS Teams meeting operation triggers a Microsoft token refresh + DB write. Combined with the sync-path bugs (response shape mismatch, refresh_token loss), this means Teams credentials are constantly refreshed and corrupted. The units must be reconciled: either store `expiry_date` in ms in the callback, or compare against `Math.round(+new Date() / 1000)` here. Note the sibling office365calendar adapter (line 235-241) compares against seconds (`Math.round(+new Date() / 1000)`) but reads `expires_in` (a relative offset) instead of `expiry_date` — the two adapters are mutually inconsistent.

title: MS Teams refresh: responseBody.expiry_date computed from expires_in which is deleted on the sync path, and the sync endpoint returns an absolute expiry that is ignored
body: Line 84-85: `responseBody.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + (responseBody?.expires_in || 0) * 1000); delete responseBody.expires_in;`. On the sync path, the endpoint returns an absolute expiry (per the PR contract) — there is no `expires_in`, so `expiry_date = Date.now() + 0` = now. The stored credential's `expiry_date` becomes 'now', which (combined with the always-true `isExpired`) means the token is considered expired immediately and refreshed on every call. The sync endpoint's absolute expiry value is never read. The code should use the absolute expiry from the sync response when present.

title: MS Teams refresh overwrites the entire credential key with responseBody, losing refresh_token on the sync path and email/scope/token_type on both paths if absent
body: Lines 87-95: `prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, data: { key: responseBody as unknown as Prisma.InputJsonValue } })`. On the sync path, `responseBody` is the minimal `{ access_token, expiry, expiry_date }` — the stored credential's `refresh_token`, `email`, `scope`, `token_type`, `ext_expires_in` are all LOST. The next refresh reads `o365AuthCredentials.refresh_token` (line 104) = undefined → sends `refresh_token=undefined` to Microsoft → `invalid_grant` → the credential is permanently broken and the user must re-install MS Teams. Even on the normal path, if Microsoft's response omits any field that the callback originally stored (e.g., `email` is added by the callback, not by Microsoft), that field is lost. The update must merge: `key: { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...responseBody, refresh_token: responseBody.refresh_token ?? o365AuthCredentials.refresh_token }`.

title: MS Teams in-memory credential update only copies expiry_date and access_token, not the new refresh_token from the response
body: Lines 96-97: `o365AuthCredentials.expiry_date = responseBody.expiry_date; o365AuthCredentials.access_token = responseBody.access_token;`. Microsoft rotates refresh tokens on refresh — the new `refresh_token` in `responseBody` is NOT copied to the in-memory `o365AuthCredentials`. The DB update (line 87-95) writes `responseBody` (which includes the new refresh_token on the normal path), so the DB has the new token but the in-memory object has the old one. If the same adapter instance handles multiple operations, the second refresh uses the OLD (now-invalidated) refresh token → `invalid_grant`. The in-memory update should also copy `refresh_token` when present: `o365AuthCredentials.refresh_token = responseBody.refresh_token ?? o365AuthCredentials.refresh_token`.

title: Office365 refresh merge: on the sync path, tokenResponse.data is the minimal shape and spreading it over o365AuthCredentials preserves old fields, but the schema's expires_in transform would corrupt the stored expires_in if it were present
body: Line 264: `o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...(tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data) };`. On the normal path, `tokenResponse.data` has `expires_in` TRANSFORMED to an absolute timestamp (by the schema's `.transform` at line 54-55) — so the merged credential's `expires_in` field becomes an absolute timestamp instead of a relative offset. The stored credential then has `expires_in` as an absolute value, which breaks the `isExpired(o365AuthCredentials.expires_in)` check at line 279 (compares an absolute seconds timestamp against `Math.round(+new Date() / 1000)` — actually that would work by accident since both are seconds... but the field name `expires_in` now holds an absolute value, which is semantically wrong and breaks the `refreshTokenResponseSchema.safeParse` at line 278 which expects `expires_in` to be a relative offset that it transforms AGAIN — double transformation on the next refresh). The schema's transform should only apply to the refresh RESPONSE, not be persisted. The persisted credential should store `expiry_date` (absolute) and delete `expires_in`, as the callback does.

title: Office365 refresh persists o365AuthCredentials which after the merge has expires_in as an absolute timestamp (transformed by the schema), corrupting the stored credential shape
body: Lines 265-272: `prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, data: { key: o365AuthCredentials } })`. After the merge at line 264, `o365AuthCredentials.expires_in` is the TRANSFORMED value (absolute timestamp in seconds, per the schema's `.transform`), not the original relative offset. The stored credential now has `expires_in` as an absolute value. On the next `getToken` call, line 278 `refreshTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(o365AuthCredentials)` — the schema expects `expires_in` to be a relative offset and transforms it AGAIN (adding the current time to an already-absolute timestamp), producing a wildly wrong future expiry. The credential's expiry tracking is corrupted. The refresh should delete `expires_in` after computing `expiry_date` (as the callback does at line 66: `delete responseBody.expires_in`), or the schema should not transform when validating stored credentials.

title: Office365 getToken checks isExpired(o365AuthCredentials.expires_in) — but expires_in is a relative offset (or transformed absolute), not the stored expiry_date; the check should use expiry_date
body: Line 279: `!isExpired(o365AuthCredentials.expires_in)`. The stored credential has `expiry_date` (absolute, seconds) — set by the callback (line 65) and by the refresh (via the schema transform merged at line 264). `expires_in` is either deleted (callback) or a transformed absolute value (after refresh). The `isExpired` function (lines 235-241) compares `expiryDate < Math.round(+new Date() / 1000)` — seconds. So: (1) on first load (callback-shaped credential), `expires_in` is undefined → `isExpired(undefined)` → `!expiryDate` → returns true → always refresh (see separate finding); (2) after a refresh, `expires_in` is a transformed absolute timestamp → `isExpired` compares it correctly by accident. The check should consistently use `expiry_date` (the absolute field), not `expires_in`. The field confusion between `expires_in` (relative) and `expiry_date` (absolute) is the root cause of the always-refresh bug.

title: CRITICAL: Office365 getToken ALWAYS refreshes because safeParse on the stored credential always fails (schema requires expires_in which the callback deletes)
body: Line 278: `refreshTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(o365AuthCredentials).success`. The stored credential (from callback.ts lines 64-66) has `expiry_date` set and `expires_in` DELETED (`delete responseBody.expires_in`). `refreshTokenResponseSchema` (lines 51-57) requires `expires_in: z.number().transform(...)` — a REQUIRED field. So `safeParse` on the stored credential ALWAYS fails → the `&&` short-circuits → `getToken` ALWAYS calls `refreshAccessToken` → EVERY Office365 calendar operation (createEvent, getAvailability, listCalendars, etc.) triggers a Microsoft token refresh + DB write. This is a severe performance bug (N refreshes for N operations, Microsoft rate limits, DB write amplification) that exists on the BASE code path (not just sync). The PR's refactor of `refreshAccessToken` makes this worse because each refresh now also goes through the (broken) `parseRefreshTokenResponse`. The validity check must use a schema that matches the STORED credential shape (with `expiry_date`, without `expires_in`).

title: CRITICAL: MS Teams getToken ALWAYS refreshes because isExpired compares seconds-based expiry_date against millisecond Date.now()
body: Line 56: `const isExpired = (expiryDate: number) => expiryDate < Math.round(+new Date());`. `+new Date()` returns MILLISECONDS (e.g., 1,700,000,000,000). The callback (callback.ts line 66) stores `expiry_date = Math.round(+new Date() / 1000 + responseBody.expires_in)` — SECONDS (e.g., 1,700,000,000). So `expiry_date < Date.now()` is `1.7e9 < 1.7e12` = ALWAYS TRUE → `isExpired` always returns true → `getToken` (line 103-105) ALWAYS calls `refreshAccessToken` → EVERY MS Teams meeting operation triggers a Microsoft token refresh + DB write. Combined with the sync-path bugs (response shape mismatch, refresh_token loss at line 87-95), this means Teams credentials are constantly refreshed and progressively corrupted (refresh_token lost on sync path → invalid_grant → broken integration). The unit mismatch must be fixed: either store `expiry_date` in ms in the callback, or compare against `Math.round(+new Date() / 1000)` here. Note the sibling office365calendar adapter compares against seconds — the two adapters are inconsistent.

title: MS Teams callback stores expiry_date in seconds while the adapter's isExpired expects milliseconds — unit mismatch (callback side)
body: callback.ts line 66: `responseBody.expiry_date = Math.round(+new Date() / 1000 + responseBody.expires_in);` — stores SECONDS. The adapter (VideoApiAdapter.ts line 56) compares `expiryDate < Math.round(+new Date())` — MILLISECONDS. The callback should store `Math.round(+new Date() + responseBody.expires_in * 1000)` (ms) to match the adapter, or the adapter should compare against seconds. The sibling office365calendar callback (line 65) also stores seconds, and its adapter (line 239) compares against seconds — so the calendar adapter is internally consistent while the video adapter is not. The video callback and adapter must be reconciled.

title: Office365 calendar callback stores expiry_date in seconds and deletes expires_in, but the refresh schema requires expires_in — the stored credential can never pass the schema validation used in getToken
body: callback.ts line 65-66: `responseBody.expiry_date = Math.round(+new Date() / 1000 + responseBody.expires_in); delete responseBody.expires_in;`. The stored credential has `expiry_date` (absolute, seconds) and NO `expires_in`. But `refreshTokenResponseSchema` (CalendarService.ts lines 51-57) requires `expires_in: z.number()` — so the stored credential NEVER validates against the schema used in `getToken` (line 278), causing the always-refresh bug (see separate critical finding). The callback and the schema are inconsistent: either the callback should keep `expires_in` (and the schema should not require it for stored credentials), or the schema should validate `expiry_date` instead.

title: refreshTokenResponseSchema conflates the refresh RESPONSE shape (expires_in relative) with the STORED credential shape (expiry_date absolute) — a single schema is used for both, causing the always-refresh bug
body: `refreshTokenResponseSchema` (lines 51-57) is used for two incompatible purposes: (1) parsing the refresh RESPONSE (line 263), where `expires_in` is a relative offset that the schema transforms to an absolute timestamp; (2) validating the STORED credential (line 278), where the credential has `expiry_date` (absolute) and no `expires_in`. Using one schema for both guarantees the stored-credential validation always fails (see critical finding). The schema should be split: `refreshResponseSchema` (with `expires_in` transform) for parsing responses, and `storedCredentialSchema` (with `expiry_date`) for validating stored credentials. This is the root cause of the Office365 always-refresh bug.

title: O365AuthCredentials interface declares ext_expires_in as required number, but the callback never sets it and the sync path doesn't provide it
body: Lines 27-35: `interface O365AuthCredentials { email: string; scope: string; token_type: string; expiry_date: number; access_token: string; refresh_token: string; ext_expires_in: number; }`. The callback (callback.ts lines 64-67) sets `email` and `expiry_date` but never sets `ext_expires_in` — Microsoft's token response DOES include `ext_expires_in`, so it's present on the normal path. On the sync path, the minimal response lacks it, so the stored credential (after the destructive update at line 87-95) has `ext_expires_in: undefined`. The interface should mark `ext_expires_in` as optional (`ext_expires_in?: number`) since it's not guaranteed, or the refresh should preserve it from the existing credential.

title: ITokenResponse interface has expires_in as optional but the refresh code uses it with a fallback of 0, silently setting expiry_date to 'now' when absent
body: Lines 37-46: `interface ITokenResponse { expiry_date: number; expires_in?: number; ... }`. Line 84: `responseBody.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + (responseBody?.expires_in || 0) * 1000);`. If `expires_in` is absent (sync path, or a malformed Microsoft response), `expiry_date = Date.now()` — the token is immediately considered expired. The fallback of 0 silently corrupts the expiry. The code should either throw when `expires_in` is missing on the normal path, or use the absolute expiry from the sync response. At minimum, log a warning when falling back.

title: MS Teams refresh: on the sync path, the sync endpoint's Response is passed to handleErrorsJson which calls response.json() — but the sync endpoint's minimal JSON is parsed correctly; however the response is never checked for response.ok before parsing, so an error response body would be treated as a token
body: `handleErrorsJson(response)` (line 77) — on the sync path, `response` is the sync endpoint's Response. If the sync endpoint returns a 500 with an HTML error page, `handleErrorsJson` would attempt to parse it as JSON and either throw a confusing error or return garbage that gets persisted as the credential key (line 87-95). The sync endpoint's response should be checked for `response.ok` before parsing, and the parsed body should be validated (e.g., must contain `access_token`). Currently, any JSON error body (e.g., `{ error: "user not found" }`) would be persisted as the credential, destroying it. The `refreshOAuthTokens` helper should check `response.ok` and throw a descriptive error.

title: MS Teams refresh: sync endpoint response is trusted as the new credential without validation — a compromised or misbehaving sync endpoint can inject arbitrary tokens
body: The sync endpoint's response body is parsed by `handleErrorsJson` and then persisted directly as the credential key (line 87-95) with only `error`/`error_description` checks (lines 79-82). There is no validation that the response contains a valid `access_token` (string), `refresh_token`, or that the token actually works. A compromised sync endpoint (or a MITM if the URL is http) can return `{ access_token: "attacker-token", ... }` which is persisted as the user's MS Teams credential — redirecting all meeting creation to an attacker-controlled token. The same applies to all other integrations using `refreshOAuthTokens`. The response should be validated against a schema (at minimum: `access_token` must be a non-empty string) before persisting.

title: All integrations: sync endpoint response is trusted as the new credential without schema validation — a compromised sync endpoint can inject arbitrary tokens into any integration
body: This is a systemic issue across all callers of `refreshOAuthTokens`: the sync endpoint's response is treated as the new token and persisted (or merged) into the credential with little or no validation. For MS Teams (VideoApiAdapter.ts lines 77-95), the response body is persisted directly as `key`. For Google (CalendarService.ts lines 94-101), only `access_token` and `expiry_date` are read (and the sync path is broken). For HubSpot (lines 177-202), the Response object itself is persisted. For Zoom/Webex, the response is validated against `zoomRefreshedTokenSchema`/`webexRefreshedTokenSchema` (which fail on the sync path). The sync endpoint is a trust boundary: its response should be validated against a schema (at minimum: `access_token` must be a non-empty string, expiry must be a valid future timestamp) before being persisted. A compromised sync endpoint can inject arbitrary access tokens into users' credentials across all integrations, enabling meeting hijacking and data exfiltration.

title: Sync endpoint response is trusted without validation across all integrations — token injection vector
body: Systemic security issue: `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw sync endpoint Response, and callers persist its parsed body as the user's OAuth credential with minimal validation. The sync endpoint is configured via `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` env var — if this endpoint is compromised, misconfigured, or reached over http, an attacker can return arbitrary `access_token` values that are written into users' credentials for Google Calendar, Office365, Zoom, Webex, HubSpot, Salesforce, Lark, Zoho, etc. This enables: (1) redirecting calendar/meeting traffic to attacker-controlled accounts; (2) exfiltrating calendar data (attacker's token receives event details); (3) persisting garbage that bricks integrations. The `refreshOAuthTokens` helper or each caller must validate the sync response against a schema (non-empty string access_token, valid expiry) before persisting. This is the security corollary of the shape-mismatch bugs: the lack of validation is what makes the shape bugs exploitable rather than just crashy.

title: SECURITY: Sync endpoint response is persisted as credential without validation — token injection across all integrations
body: Consolidated security finding: `refreshOAuthTokens` (packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts) returns the raw `Response` from `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`. Callers persist its parsed body as the user's OAuth credential: MS Teams (VideoApiAdapter.ts lines 77-95, persists `responseBody` directly as `key`), HubSpot (CalendarService.ts lines 177-202, persists the Response object), Google (CalendarService.ts lines 94-101, reads `.data` which is undefined on Response), Zoom/Webex (validated against schemas that fail on sync path). None of the callers validate that the sync response contains a well-formed token (non-empty `access_token` string, valid expiry). A compromised or MITM'd sync endpoint can inject arbitrary access tokens into any user's credential for any integration, enabling calendar data exfiltration and meeting hijacking. The sync response must be validated against a schema before persisting, and the endpoint URL must be https.

title: SECURITY (consolidated): Sync endpoint is an unauthenticated trust boundary whose response becomes users' OAuth credentials
body: The `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is called with no authentication (no signature, no shared secret, no mTLS) — see `refreshOAuthTokens.ts` lines 8-14. Its response is persisted as users' OAuth access tokens across ~10 integrations. This creates a trust boundary where: (1) anyone who can intercept or redirect traffic to the sync endpoint (if http, DNS hijack, or a compromised host) can inject arbitrary tokens; (2) the sync endpoint itself, if compromised, can inject tokens for all users; (3) there is no response validation (see other findings). The design should include: https enforcement, response schema validation, and ideally an authentication mechanism (shared secret header or request signing) so the sync endpoint can verify Cal.com's identity and Cal.com can verify the response's authenticity (e.g., the endpoint signs responses). At minimum, validate the response shape and enforce https.

title: SECURITY (final consolidated): The credential sync architecture lacks response validation and endpoint authentication, creating a token-injection vector across all integrations
body: Final consolidated security finding for the sync architecture introduced by this PR: (1) `refreshOAuthTokens` calls `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` with no authentication and no response validation (packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts lines 8-15). (2) Callers persist the response as users' OAuth credentials with no schema validation (MS Teams: VideoApiAdapter.ts lines 77-95; HubSpot: CalendarService.ts lines 177-202; Google: CalendarService.ts lines 94-101; etc.). (3) The webhook endpoint (apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts) allows writing arbitrary credential JSON for any user given the webhook secret, with no per-app payload validation. (4) The sync endpoint URL is not validated for https. Together, these create multiple token-injection vectors: a compromised sync endpoint, a MITM on an http sync URL, or a leaked webhook secret allows an attacker to replace users' OAuth tokens with attacker-controlled ones, enabling calendar/meeting data exfiltration and account takeover of third-party integrations. Required fixes before merge: validate sync responses against schemas, enforce https on the sync endpoint, add authentication to the sync endpoint call, and validate webhook payloads per app.

title: Authorization check uses AND instead of OR for team admin/owner
body: The permission check computes `isTeamAdminOrOwner = (await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`. A user must be BOTH a team admin AND the team owner to pass this check, which is almost never true (owner is a single user; admins are typically other members). Combined with the later `if (!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer && !isAttendee)` check, this effectively blocks all team admins/owners who are not the booking organizer from adding guests to team bookings. The intent (per the variable name and the UI's `isUserTeamAdminOrOwner` usage elsewhere) is clearly OR. Consequence: legitimate team admins/owners get FORBIDDEN errors when trying to add guests to team event bookings.

title: Any attendee of a booking can add arbitrary guests to it
body: The authorization check allows `isAttendee` — any existing attendee whose email matches `user.email` — to add new guests to the booking. This means a guest invited to a meeting can add unlimited additional people (subject only to email validation and blacklist filtering), turning a 1:1 or small meeting into an open invitation vector and potentially leaking the meeting link/location to arbitrary third parties via the calendar update and emails. Adding attendees should be restricted to the organizer (and team admins/owners), not to attendees. At minimum this needs product-level confirmation; as written it is an authorization weakness.

title: Guest email comparison is case-sensitive; duplicates and blacklist bypass possible
body: The uniqueness filter compares `guest === attendee.email` exactly, and the blacklist comparison lowercases blacklist entries but not the incoming guest emails (`blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)` where `guest` is not lowercased). Email addresses are case-insensitive in practice, so `Guest@Example.com` will be treated as a new guest even if `guest@example.com` is already an attendee, creating duplicate Attendee rows for the same person; likewise a blacklisted address can be re-added by changing case. Normalize emails (e.g. `guest.trim().toLowerCase()`) before comparison and storage.

title: New attendees are created with empty-string names
body: `guestsFullDetails` sets `name: ""` for every added guest. Downstream, emails and calendar events render attendee names, and the UI falls back to showing the email, but other code paths (e.g. `organizer-add-guests-email.ts` line 28 uses `this.calEvent.attendees[0].name` for the subject) may render an empty name, producing broken subject lines like "Guests Added: {{eventType}} with  at {{date}}". Either derive a display name from the email local-part or leave name null and handle nulls consistently.

title: Calendar update uses the acting user's credentials instead of the booking organizer's
body: `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` and `new EventManager({ ...user, ... })` build the calendar update from the session user, not from `booking.user` (whose credentials were already fetched in the initial query include). If a team admin or an attendee (per the flawed authorization above) adds guests, the calendar event update is attempted with the wrong user's credentials — the update may fail, be applied to the wrong calendar, or silently no-op, leaving the external calendar out of sync with the added attendees. The organizer's credentials (`booking.user.credentials`) should be used, matching how other booking-mutation handlers operate.

title: Email-sending failure is swallowed, leaving DB and calendar mutated with no notification
body: The `try { await sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests); } catch (err) { console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails"); }` block catches all email errors and only logs to console. The handler still returns success, so the UI shows "Guests added" even though no emails (including the ICS update with method REQUEST to existing attendees) were sent. Attendees may never learn about the new guests and their calendar entries stay stale. At minimum the error should be surfaced (logged via the project logger with context, and ideally reported to the client); silently succeeding is a data-integrity/UX hazard.

title: No check that the booking is still active/upcoming before adding guests
body: The handler fetches the booking by id and immediately adds attendees without checking `booking.status` (CANCELLED/REJECTED) or whether the booking is in the past. Guests can be added to cancelled or past bookings, which triggers calendar updates and emails for events that no longer exist, and pollutes attendee lists. Other booking mutations (e.g. editLocation) validate booking state; this one should reject cancelled/rejected (and arguably past) bookings.

title: Video call reference lookup uses substring match that can pick the wrong reference
body: `booking.references.find((reference) => reference.type.includes("_video"))` matches any reference type containing "_video" (e.g. could match unexpected app reference types) and takes the first match rather than the primary video reference. If multiple video references exist (rare but possible with multiple video apps), the wrong meeting URL/password could be attached to `evt.videoCallData` and emailed to attendees. Prefer an exact/primary reference selection consistent with how the rest of the codebase resolves the video call URL.

title: sendAddGuestsEmails ignores event-type email-disable metadata and sends full scheduled email to new guests
body: `sendAddGuestsEmails(calEvent, newGuests)` does not accept or check `eventTypeMetadata`, unlike every other send* function in this file (`eventTypeDisableHostEmail` / `eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail`). Event types configured with `disableStandardEmails` will still receive organizer/attendee emails when guests are added. Additionally, new guests receive `AttendeeScheduledEmail` — the full "booking confirmed" email with ICS — rather than a dedicated "you were added" email; combined with the missing metadata check this can spam users who opted out. The function should accept `eventTypeMetadata` and skip disabled recipients, and the new-guest email content should be reviewed.

title: Organizer email subject uses attendees[0].name which may be empty or the wrong person
body: The subject interpolates `name: this.calEvent.attendees[0].name`. Attendee ordering is not guaranteed to put the original booker first, and newly added guests are created with `name: ""` (see handler finding), so the subject can render as "Guests Added: <event> with  at <date>" or name the wrong attendee. Use the booking's primary attendee deterministically (e.g. the attendee that is not one of the newly added guests) or fall back to the email when the name is empty.

title: Client-side validation accepts empty strings and never clears the invalid-email flag on retry with valid input
body: `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` is `z.array(z.string().email())` — an empty string fails `.email()`, so the initial `[""]` default correctly fails validation, but once `isInvalidEmail` is set to true it is only reset when the dialog is closed/cancelled, not when the user fixes the emails and clicks Add again with valid input... actually on success the mutation fires, but if the user fixes the emails and clicks Add, `handleAdd` re-validates and proceeds, yet the red error banner remains visible until success/close because `setIsInvalidEmail(false)` is never called on the success path of validation. Minor UX bug: clear `isInvalidEmail` when validation succeeds. Also, empty-string entries produce a generic error; filtering empty strings before validation would give better UX.

title: "Add guests" action is shown for past, cancelled, and pending bookings with no gating
body: The `add_members` action is unconditionally added to `editBookingActions`, which are rendered via `bookedActions` for confirmed bookings — including past bookings (`isBookingInPast && isConfirmed` renders `bookedActions` at line 554) and, because the server handler also lacks state checks, cancelled bookings. There is no guard preventing the organizer from opening the Add Guests dialog for a booking that already happened or was cancelled. The action should be hidden when `isBookingInPast || isCancelled` (and arguably when `isPending`), matching how other actions are conditionally filtered.

title: Hardcoded English tooltip text and non-localized remove button in shared UI component
body: The `Tooltip content="Remove email"` string is hardcoded English inside a shared `@calcom/ui` component, while the component already imports `useLocale` and uses `t("add_another")` elsewhere. This breaks localization for all consumers of MultiEmail. Use a translation key (e.g. `t("remove_email")`) consistent with the rest of the component.

title: sendAddGuestsEmails is passed raw `guests` (all requested emails) instead of the actually-added `uniqueGuests`
body: The handler filters `guests` down to `uniqueGuests` (excluding existing attendees and blacklisted emails) and only those are inserted into the DB, but then calls `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` with the original unfiltered array. In `email-manager.ts`, `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)` decides whether an attendee gets the "scheduled" email vs the "add guests" email; passing the unfiltered list means an email that was requested but NOT added (because it was already an attendee) will incorrectly receive the full `AttendeeScheduledEmail` ("booking confirmed" email) again. Pass `uniqueGuests` instead.

title: Schema allows unbounded guest array and duplicate emails
body: `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` has no `.min(1)`, no `.max(...)`, and no uniqueness refinement. The client enforces uniqueness, but the API accepts arbitrarily large arrays (potential abuse/DoS via mass attendee creation and mass email sending) and duplicate emails (which would create duplicate Attendee rows since the server-side uniqueness filter only checks against existing attendees, not within the request). Add `.min(1).max(N)` and a uniqueness refinement (or dedupe server-side) to harden the endpoint.

title: Authorization check uses AND instead of OR for team admin/owner, and allows any attendee to add guests
body: The permission check computes `isTeamAdminOrOwner = (await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`, which is only true when the user is BOTH a team admin and a team owner — a condition that is essentially never true (a user has one role per team). Combined with the `isAttendee` check on line 52, this means the effective authorization is: the booking organizer OR ANY existing attendee of the booking. Any attendee (a guest invited to the meeting) can therefore call `viewer.bookings.addGuests` and add arbitrary email addresses to the booking, triggering calendar updates and emails to those addresses. This is a privilege-escalation/authorization flaw: guests should not be able to modify the attendee list. The `&&` should be `||` (matching the intended 'admin or owner' semantics), and the `isAttendee` branch should almost certainly be removed or restricted (e.g., only the organizer or team admin/owner may add guests).

title: Blacklist comparison is case-sensitive while blacklist entries are lowercased
body: `blacklistedGuestEmails` entries are lowercased (line 71), but the guest emails from user input are compared without lowercasing (`blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)` on line 77). A blacklisted address such as `blocked@example.com` can be bypassed by submitting `Blocked@Example.com` (emails are case-insensitive in the local part per common practice and Prisma stores what is given). The guest filter should lowercase `guest` before comparing, e.g. `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest.toLowerCase())`. The same case-sensitivity issue applies to the duplicate-attendee check on line 76 (`guest === attendee.email`), allowing the same person to be added twice with different casing.

title: Attendee creation is not atomic with the duplicate/blacklist filtering — race condition can create duplicate attendees
body: The handler first reads the booking's attendees (line 26), filters out emails already present (line 74-78), and then performs a separate `prisma.booking.update` with `createMany` (lines 92-106). There is no transaction and no unique constraint enforcement shown between the read and the write. Two concurrent `addGuests` calls (or a concurrent booking flow adding the same attendee) can both pass the duplicate check and both insert the same email, producing duplicate Attendee rows for one booking. This corrupts attendee lists, calendar events, and emails. The read-filter-write sequence should be wrapped in an interactive transaction (`prisma.$transaction`) with the duplicate check re-evaluated inside it, or rely on a DB unique constraint on (bookingId, email) with `skipDuplicates`/error handling.

title: Calendar update failure aborts the mutation after attendees were already persisted, leaving DB and calendar out of sync
body: `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` (line 165) is awaited outside any try/catch and outside the DB transaction. If the calendar update throws (network error, invalid credentials, provider failure), the new Attendee rows created at line 92 remain committed in the database, but the mutation returns an error to the client. The booking now has guests in the DB who never received a calendar invite update, and a retry would hit the duplicate filter and report 'emails_must_be_unique_valid'. Either wrap the DB write and calendar update in a transaction with compensating logic, or catch the calendar error and report partial success; as written, failures leave inconsistent state with no rollback.

title: Email sending failure is silently swallowed with only a console.log
body: The `try { await sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests); } catch (err) { console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails"); }` block (lines 167-171) swallows all email errors and still returns `{ message: "Guests added" }` as success. New guests are added to the booking and the calendar is updated, but if the email dispatch fails (SMTP down, template render error), neither the new guests nor the organizer is notified, and the organizer sees a success toast. The error is only written to server logs with no structured logging (the codebase uses `logger` from `@calcom/lib/logger` elsewhere). At minimum this should use the structured logger and ideally surface a degraded-success indication to the caller.

title: No validation that the booking is in a state that permits adding guests (cancelled/past bookings can be modified)
body: The handler fetches the booking by id and only checks existence and caller permission. It never checks `booking.status` (e.g., CANCELLED or REJECTED) or whether the booking is in the past. Adding guests to a cancelled booking resurrects attendee rows, sends 'guests added' emails and calendar REQUEST updates for an event that was cancelled, and mutates historical/past bookings. Other handlers in this router (e.g., editLocation) enforce status constraints. A guard such as rejecting when `booking.status === BookingStatus.CANCELLED` (and arguably when the booking end time is in the past) is needed.

title: Calendar update uses the requesting user's credentials instead of the booking organizer's credentials
body: `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` (line 158) loads the credentials of whoever is calling the mutation, and the `EventManager` is constructed with `...user` (the caller). If the caller is a team admin/owner or (per the flawed check) an attendee rather than the booking organizer, the calendar update for the organizer's event is attempted with the wrong user's credentials — the update may fail, be written to the wrong calendar, or be attributed to the wrong account. Calendar mutations for a booking should use the booking organizer's credentials (the booking already includes `user.credentials` and `user.destinationCalendar` in the query at lines 35-40, which are loaded but never used). The loaded organizer credentials should be passed to the EventManager instead of `ctx.user`'s.

title: sendAddGuestsEmails ignores eventTypeMetadata email-disable settings and sends scheduled email to new guests without their context
body: Unlike every other send* function in this file (e.g., `sendScheduledEmails`, `sendRescheduledEmails`, `sendLocationChangeEmails`), `sendAddGuestsEmails` (line 525) accepts no `eventTypeMetadata` parameter and therefore never checks `eventTypeDisableHostEmail`/`eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail`. Event types configured with `disableStandardEmails` (metadata) will still receive organizer/attendee emails when guests are added, violating the organizer's email preferences. The handler has `booking.eventType` available and should pass `booking.eventType.metadata` through. Additionally, new guests receive `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (line 542) — a full 'booking confirmed' email — which may be misleading since no new booking was created for them; a dedicated 'you were added as a guest' template would be more accurate, but at minimum the metadata-based suppression must be honored.

title: Organizer email subject uses attendees[0].name which may be a newly added guest with an empty name
body: The subject interpolates `name: this.calEvent.attendees[0].name` (line 28). In the handler, newly created guests are inserted with `name: ""` (addGuests.handler.ts line 85), and attendee ordering after `createMany` is not guaranteed to put the original booker first. If a newly added guest (empty name) ends up at index 0, the organizer email subject renders as 'Guests Added: <eventType> with  at <date>' with a blank name. The subject should use the original booker (the attendee that existed before the addition) or fall back to the organizer/team name as the attendee template does (`this.calEvent.team?.name || this.calEvent.organizer.name`).

title: Client-side validation accepts an array containing a single empty string as valid input path is blocked, but empty-string entries in multi-row input are not rejected before submit when combined with valid emails
body: The zod schema `z.array(z.string().email())` (line 26) rejects empty strings, so `handleAdd` correctly blocks submission when any row is empty — but only after the user clicks Add, and the error message shown ('emails_must_be_unique_valid') does not distinguish 'invalid/empty email' from 'duplicate email'. More importantly, `isInvalidEmail` is never reset to `false` when the user subsequently edits the emails to valid values (it is only reset on cancel or success), so after one failed attempt the red error banner stays visible even when the input becomes valid. The error state should be cleared on value change (e.g., in `setMultiEmailValue` wrapper) or recomputed on each submit attempt.

title: MultiEmail mutates/reassigns the `value` prop and uses array index as React key, and removal of the last email hides the input entirely
body: Line 14 reassigns the `value` prop (`value = value || []`), which is a React anti-pattern (props should not be reassigned) though functionally harmless here. More concretely: (1) `key={index}` on line 26 for a list of editable text inputs causes React to reuse DOM/component state incorrectly when a middle row is removed — typing in row 2 after deleting row 1 can show stale values; a stable key (or the field content) should be used. (2) When the user removes the last remaining email via the remove button (lines 39-43), `value` becomes `[]`, and the component renders only the 'add emails' button (lines 77-91) — the label disappears and the UI affordance changes shape, which is disorienting inside the AddGuestsDialog where the dialog starts with `[""]` (one empty row) and the label 'Add Emails' is shown above the input.

title: 'Add guests' action is offered for bookings where it cannot work (recurring series tab removes edit menu, but action also appears for past/cancelled/rejected bookings and non-organizers)
body: The `add_members` action is unconditionally added to `editBookingActions` (lines 194-200), which is only rendered under `bookedActions` → shown when `isConfirmed` (line 549) for upcoming bookings, or for past bookings (line 554). It is therefore offered for past bookings (where the server handler does not reject past bookings — see handler finding) and for cancelled bookings in some render paths. Additionally, the menu is shown to any viewer of the booking list; given the server-side authorization flaw (attendees can add guests), the UI gives no indication of who may use it. At minimum the action should be hidden for past bookings (`isBookingInPast`) and cancelled bookings, consistent with how `cancel` is filtered (lines 249-251).

title: Newly added guests are created with an empty name and the organizer's locale/timezone, and no Attendee-scheduling metadata (no bookingFields responses, no seats handling)
body: New attendees are created with `name: ""` (line 85), so they appear as blank names in the UI attendee list (BookingListItem renders `name || email`, so this is partially mitigated) and in emails. They also inherit the organizer's `timeZone` and `locale` (lines 87-88), which is a reasonable default but means per-attendee translations in `sendAddGuestsEmails` use the organizer's locale for guests. Furthermore, the handler does not consider `seatsPerTimeSlot` (group bookings): adding guests to a seated booking does not create `SeatReference` rows or decrement/increment seat counts, so a booking with seats can exceed its capacity silently. If seats bookings are in scope, seat references must be created and capacity validated; if not, the handler should reject bookings whose eventType has `seatsPerTimeSlot` set.

title: ICS method REQUEST with status CONFIRMED is sent to existing attendees as if the event were (re)confirmed, without indicating what changed
body: The ICS attachment uses `method: "REQUEST"` and `status: "CONFIRMED"` (lines 15-17) with title 'new_guests_added'. For existing attendees this is a calendar update that will re-render the event in their calendar client; because the ICS contains the full updated attendee list, most clients will handle it, but the ICS `title`/`subtitle` ('Added - New guests added to your event' / 'emailed_you_and_any_other_attendees') is used as the event summary in some clients, potentially overwriting the real event title in the attendee's calendar view. The ICS should carry the actual event title (as `AttendeeScheduledEmail` does) rather than the notification title, so calendar clients do not display 'Added - New guests added to your event' as the meeting name.

title: Authorization check uses AND instead of OR for team admin/owner, and allows any attendee to add guests
body: The permission check computes `isTeamAdminOrOwner = (await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`, which is only true when the user is BOTH a team admin AND the team owner — a condition almost nobody satisfies, so legitimate team admins/owners are denied. More importantly, the subsequent check `if (!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer && !isAttendee)` grants the mutation to ANY attendee of the booking (`isAttendee` matches on email alone). This means any guest invited to a meeting can add arbitrary additional attendees to that booking, modify the attendee list on the organizer's calendar event, and trigger emails/calendar updates — an authorization bypass. The intended logic was almost certainly `(isTeamAdmin || isTeamOwner)`, and attendees should not be permitted to add guests at all (only the organizer or team admin/owner).

title: Email comparison for duplicate/blacklist filtering is case-sensitive
body: `uniqueGuests` filters with `guest === attendee.email` and `blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)` using exact string comparison, while `BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS` entries are lowercased. Email addresses are case-insensitive in practice, so `Guest@Example.com` would bypass the blacklist (stored as `guest@example.com`) and would be treated as a new guest even when `guest@example.com` is already an attendee, creating duplicate attendees on the booking. The comparison should normalize case (e.g. `guest.toLowerCase()` on both sides).

title: Guest insertion is not atomic with the duplicate check (race condition)
body: The handler first reads the booking's attendees (line 26), computes `uniqueGuests` by filtering against that snapshot (line 74), and only afterwards performs `prisma.booking.update` with `createMany` (line 92). Two concurrent `addGuests` calls (or a concurrent booking/reschedule flow that adds attendees) can both pass the duplicate check and both insert the same email, producing duplicate Attendee rows for one booking. There is no unique constraint enforcement shown here and no transaction/serializable isolation around the read-check-write sequence. The update should be done in a transaction with a conditional create (e.g. `createMany` with `skipDuplicates` plus a DB unique constraint on (bookingId, email), or re-validate inside the transaction).

title: Calendar update failure is not surfaced and emails are still sent
body: `await eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` is called outside any try/catch. If the calendar update throws (invalid credentials, provider error), the mutation rejects — but the attendees have ALREADY been persisted to the database (line 92), leaving the database and the external calendars permanently out of sync with no retry and no compensating action. Conversely, if it succeeds, email failures are swallowed (lines 167-171). At minimum the DB write and calendar update should be wrapped in a transaction or the calendar failure should trigger a rollback of the attendee creation; silently diverging state is a data-integrity risk.

title: Email send failure is silently swallowed with only a console.log
body: `sendAddGuestsEmails` is wrapped in try/catch that only does `console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails")` and discards the error object. New guests are added to the booking and calendar, but if the notification emails fail, neither the organizer nor the new guests are informed, and there is no logging of the actual error (no `logger.error`, no `safeStringify`), making the failure undiagnosable in production. The error should be logged properly and ideally surfaced or retried.

title: New guests are created with an empty-string name
body: `guestsFullDetails` sets `name: ""` for every added guest. Downstream, the booking UI renders `name || email` so it degrades gracefully, but the Attendee record stores an empty name, and `organizer-add-guests-email.ts` line 28 uses `this.calEvent.attendees[0].name` in the subject — if the first attendee is a nameless added guest, the email subject contains an empty name. Guests should either be created with `name: null`/email-derived placeholder, or the email templates should fall back to the email address.

title: sendAddGuestsEmails ignores eventTypeMetadata email-disable settings and sends wrong email type to new guests
body: Unlike every other sender in this file (`sendScheduledEmails`, `sendRescheduledEmails`, `sendLocationChangeEmails`, etc.), `sendAddGuestsEmails` does not accept or check `eventTypeMetadata`, so it ignores `disableStandardEmails.all.host` / `.attendee` configured on the event type — hosts/attendees who opted out of standard emails will still receive "guests added" emails. Additionally, for attendees whose email is in `newGuests` it sends a full `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (a 'booking confirmed' email with ICS) rather than the `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail` used for existing attendees, so new guests get a misleading 'scheduled' email instead of a 'guests added' notification. The function should take `eventTypeMetadata` and pass it through, and should use `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail` for the new guests.

title: Organizer email subject uses attendees[0].name which may be empty or the wrong person
body: The subject interpolates `name: this.calEvent.attendees[0].name`. `attendees[0]` is not guaranteed to be the booker (the handler builds the attendee list from a DB query with no ordering guarantee, and newly added guests have `name: ""`), so the organizer email subject can render an empty name or the wrong attendee's name. It should use the original booker's name (e.g. the first attendee present before the addition, or a dedicated field) rather than positional `attendees[0]`.

title: videoCallReference type check uses substring match on reference type
