body: `booking.references.find((reference) => reference.type.includes("_video"))` matches any reference type containing `_video` anywhere (e.g. a hypothetical `integrations:zoom_video_recording`), which may not be the actual video call reference for the meeting. Other handlers in the codebase match the specific app type (e.g. `getVideoCallReference` helpers / exact `type === appType`). Using the wrong reference would put an incorrect `videoCallData.url` into the calendar event and emails sent to guests.

title: Client-side validation rejects the initial empty-string entry, blocking submission of a single valid email flow and never clearing the error state on retry with valid input
body: The dialog initializes `multiEmailValue` to `[""]` and the zod schema is `z.array(z.string().email())` with no `.min(1)` and no filtering of empty strings. `z.string().email()` fails on `""`, so if the user types one valid email into the single existing field the array is valid — but if the user clicks "Add another" and leaves the new empty row, validation fails with the generic 'emails must be unique and valid' message even though the entered emails are fine. Also, `isInvalidEmail` is only set to `true` on failure and only reset on cancel/success — once shown, it stays visible even after the user corrects the emails, until submit succeeds. Empty entries should be filtered out before validation and the error should clear when input changes.

title: Calendar update uses the requesting user's credentials rather than the organizer's
body: `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` and `new EventManager({ ...user, ... })` build the calendar update from the session user's credentials. When a team admin/owner (or, per the flawed check, an attendee) adds guests, the calendar event update is attempted with THEIR credentials, not the booking organizer's — the organizer's calendar event may not be updated at all (the acting user may have no access to the organizer's calendar), again leaving DB and calendars inconsistent. The EventManager should be constructed with the booking organizer's user/credentials (the booking already includes `user.credentials` and `user.destinationCalendar`, which are fetched but unused for this purpose).

title: 'Add guests' action is offered for past, cancelled, and pending bookings with no gating
body: The `add_members` action is unconditionally added to `editBookingActions`, which are shown via `bookedActions` for confirmed bookings — including bookings in the past (`isBookingInPast && isConfirmed` renders `bookedActions` at line 554) and the edit menu is removed only for the recurring tab. There is no guard preventing adding guests to a booking that has already ended or been cancelled, and the server handler likewise performs no status check (it happily updates a CANCELLED or past booking). Adding guests to a past/cancelled booking mutates historical data and sends emails/calendar updates for an event that is over. Both the UI action and the handler should be restricted to upcoming, non-cancelled bookings.

title: Booking lookup by id does not scope the query to the user before the permission check, leaking booking existence
body: The booking is fetched by `id` alone and the permission check happens afterwards in application code. While the FORBIDDEN error prevents data exposure, the distinct `NOT_FOUND` vs `FORBIDDEN` responses let an authenticated user enumerate valid booking IDs (a booking that exists returns FORBIDDEN, one that doesn't returns NOT_FOUND). This is a minor information-disclosure / enumeration vector. The query should include an OR-scoped `where` clause (organizer, team membership, or attendee email) so unauthorized users always get NOT_FOUND, consistent with how other booking handlers scope access.

title: Tooltip content is hardcoded English instead of localized
body: The remove-email button uses `<Tooltip content="Remove email">` with a hardcoded English string, while the component already has access to `t` from `useLocale()` (used for `t("add_another")`). All other user-facing strings in this PR are localized via `common.json`; this one is not and has no corresponding locale key. It should use a translation key (e.g. `t("remove_email")`) for consistency and i18n correctness.

title: Handler returns a hardcoded non-localized English message string
body: The handler returns `{ message: "Guests added" }` — a hardcoded English string. Every other bookings handler returns a translation key (e.g. the UI's `markNoShow` flow shows `t(data.message)`), and the client in `AddGuestsDialog.tsx` ignores the returned message in favor of `t("guests_added")`. Returning a raw English sentence breaks the established contract where `message` is an i18n key, and would render untranslated if any client displays it. It should return a locale key such as `"guests_added"`.

title: deleteMany with retryCount > 1 deletes ALL workflow reminders regardless of method, including EMAIL and WHATSAPP reminders
body: The cleanup query at the top of the handler uses `OR: [{ method: SMS, scheduledDate <= now }, { retryCount: { gt: 1 } }]`. The second OR branch has no `method` filter, so it deletes every WorkflowReminder row in the table with retryCount > 1 — including EMAIL and WHATSAPP reminders that may still be legitimately scheduled for the future. This is a data-loss bug: email reminders (which never increment retryCount in this file, but could in other code paths, e.g. scheduleEmailReminders or future changes) or any reminder that has accumulated retries would be silently deleted even though their scheduledDate is in the future and they were never meant to be cleaned up by the SMS cron. The retryCount-based deletion must be scoped to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` (and ideally `scheduled: false`), e.g. `AND: [{ method: SMS }, { OR: [past-due, retryCount > 1] }]`.

title: Reminders with no message or no sendTo are never retried nor deleted, and the retryCount increment is skipped silently
body: The retryCount increment only happens inside `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)` (line 158) or in the catch block. If a reminder has an empty message (e.g. `reminderBody` is empty and template is not REMINDER, so `message` stays null) or `sendTo` is missing (no `smsReminderNumber` on the booking and no `sendTo` on the step), the code falls through without scheduling, without incrementing retryCount, and without any error. The reminder stays `scheduled: false` forever and will be re-fetched and re-processed by every cron run indefinitely — the exact infinite-retry problem this PR claims to fix. A reminder that can never succeed (missing phone number) should either increment retryCount or be marked failed/cancelled so the cleanup query can remove it.

title: retryCount is incremented via read-modify-write (reminder.retryCount + 1), which is racy under concurrent cron invocations
body: The handler reads `retryCount` once in the findMany (line 48-60) and later writes `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` (lines 184 and 195). If two instances of this cron endpoint run concurrently (overlapping cron schedules, multiple serverless invocations, or a long-running loop), both can read the same retryCount value and both write the same incremented value, losing one increment. Worse, the deleteMany cleanup at line 29-45 runs before the loop, so a reminder at retryCount=1 that fails in two concurrent runs could stay at 2 and be retried again rather than deleted. The correct approach is an atomic increment: `data: { retryCount: { increment: 1 } }`, which Prisma supports and which avoids the lost-update race entirely.

title: Off-by-one: PR description says 'after scheduling failed twice we delete', but retryCount > 1 deletes after the second failure is recorded, allowing only one actual retry before deletion on the next run
body: The PR description states 'after scheduling failed twice we delete the workflow reminder'. The implementation deletes rows where `retryCount > 1`, i.e. retryCount >= 2. A reminder starts at retryCount=0. First failure sets it to 1 (still kept, will be retried). Second failure sets it to 2, and the next cron run's deleteMany removes it. So the reminder is attempted at most twice total (initial + one retry) before deletion, not 'failed twice then deleted' as described — the description implies two retries after the initial attempt. Either the threshold should be `gte: 2` with the description clarified, or the code should use `gt: 2` to match the description. The mismatch between documented behavior and actual behavior should be resolved.

title: If the retryCount update inside the catch block itself throws, the error is unhandled and the loop aborts, leaving remaining reminders unprocessed and the response never sent
body: The catch block (line 189) performs `await prisma.workflowReminder.update(...)` to increment retryCount. If that database update fails (transient DB error, connection issue), the exception propagates out of the for-loop, out of the handler, and the request hangs or returns a 500 via defaultHandler — and all remaining unscheduled reminders in `unscheduledReminders` are skipped for this run. There is no try/catch around the retryCount update and no per-reminder error isolation beyond the outer catch. A failure to record a retry should not prevent processing of other reminders; wrap the increment in its own try/catch (or use a transaction) so one bad row doesn't abort the batch.

title: Migration adds a NOT NULL column with DEFAULT 0 to WorkflowReminder without documenting the table rewrite/lock implications on large tables
body: On PostgreSQL 11+, `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN ... NOT NULL DEFAULT 0` is a metadata-only operation and is safe. However, on older PostgreSQL versions (< 11) this rewrites the entire WorkflowReminder table and holds an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the duration, which on a large production table (workflow reminders accumulate per booking) could cause significant lock contention and downtime during migration. The migration should either confirm the minimum supported PG version is >= 11, or use the safe pattern of adding a nullable column, backfilling, then setting NOT NULL in a separate migration. At minimum this risk should be noted for the deploy runbook.

title: deleteMany with retryCount > 1 deletes ALL workflow reminders (including EMAIL and WHATSAPP), not just SMS
body: The cleanup query at the top of the handler uses `OR: [{ method: SMS, scheduledDate <= now }, { retryCount: { gt: 1 } }]`. The second OR branch has no `method` filter, so every WorkflowReminder row in the database with retryCount > 1 is deleted — including EMAIL and WHATSAPP reminders that may be legitimately scheduled and pending. This causes silent loss of email/WhatsApp reminders for all users. The retryCount branch must be scoped to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` (and arguably also `scheduled: false`), e.g. `{ method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, retryCount: { gt: 1 } }`.

title: Reminders with no message or no sendTo are silently skipped and never retried or cleaned up
body: The retry increment only happens inside `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)` (the else branch) or in the catch block. If `message` is empty/null (e.g. workflowStep has neither reminderBody nor template REMINDER) or `sendTo` is missing (e.g. SMS_NUMBER action with no sendTo configured, or booking without smsReminderNumber), the code falls through without scheduling, without incrementing retryCount, and without any error. The reminder stays `scheduled: false` forever and is re-fetched and re-processed by the cron on every run indefinitely — an infinite no-op loop and unbounded DB growth. These cases should either increment retryCount (so the cleanup deletes them) or be logged/handled explicitly.

title: Read-modify-write of retryCount is not atomic; concurrent cron runs can lose increments
body: The handler reads `retryCount` in the findMany (line 58) and later writes `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` (lines 184 and 195) based on that stale read. If the cron job runs concurrently (overlapping invocations, or the same reminder processed twice), both runs read the same value and write the same incremented value, so failures are undercounted and a reminder that failed twice may never reach retryCount > 1, defeating the retry limit. Use an atomic increment (`retryCount: { increment: 1 }`) instead of computing from the fetched value.

title: Cleanup deletes SMS reminders whose scheduledDate has passed even if they were successfully scheduled and are still pending delivery
body: The first OR branch deletes all SMS reminders with `scheduledDate <= now` regardless of the `scheduled` flag. A reminder that was successfully scheduled with Twilio (scheduled: true, referenceId set) but whose scheduledDate has just passed is deleted from the DB before we can confirm delivery/cancellation status. This was pre-existing behavior, but combined with the new retry logic it also means a successfully scheduled reminder is removed at its fire time, so any downstream logic that relies on the WorkflowReminder row (e.g. cancellation when a booking is cancelled/rescheduled) loses the referenceId needed to cancel the Twilio message. The delete should be scoped to `scheduled: false` (or the deletion of past-due rows should only apply to unscheduled/failed reminders).

title: Unscheduled reminders query does not exclude reminders that already exhausted retries
body: The findMany fetches all unscheduled SMS reminders within 7 days without filtering on retryCount. Reminders with retryCount >= 2 are only removed by the deleteMany at the start of the same run; between runs (or if the deleteMany fails/partially fails), they are re-fetched and re-processed, incrementing retryCount further and generating repeated Twilio attempts/log noise. Adding `retryCount: { lte: 1 }` to the where clause makes the retry cap robust and avoids wasted work.

title: Failed retryCount update in catch block is not awaited error-handled; a DB failure here throws out of the loop iteration silently
body: Inside the catch block, the `prisma.workflowReminder.update` call can itself throw (e.g. transient DB error). If it does, the exception propagates out of the for-loop and aborts processing of all remaining reminders in this run, and the outer handler never sends its 200 response (the request hangs until timeout). The update should be wrapped or the loop should be resilient so one bad row doesn't abort the whole batch.

title: deleteMany with retryCount > 1 deletes ALL workflow reminders across all methods, not just SMS
body: The cleanup query at the top of the handler uses `OR: [{ method: SMS, scheduledDate <= now }, { retryCount: { gt: 1 } }]`. The second OR branch has no `method` filter, so it deletes every WorkflowReminder row in the table with retryCount > 1 — including EMAIL and WHATSAPP reminders. Email reminders are scheduled by a different cron job (scheduleEmailReminders) and may legitimately have retryCount > 1 (or the column may be incremented elsewhere), so this change can silently delete email/WhatsApp reminders that are still pending, causing missed notifications. The retryCount-based deletion should be scoped to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` (e.g. nest it inside the first branch or add `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` to the second OR condition).

title: Reminders with no message or no sendTo are never retried and never cleaned up, causing an infinite silent loop
body: The retry increment only happens inside `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)` (the else branch when scheduleSMS returns falsy) or in the catch block. If `message` is null/empty (e.g. workflowStep has neither reminderBody nor template REMINDER) or `sendTo` is missing (no smsReminderNumber on the booking and action is SMS_ATTENDEE), the code falls through without updating the row: `scheduled` stays false and `retryCount` stays 0. The reminder is then re-fetched by the `findMany` on every cron run forever (it matches `scheduled: false` and `scheduledDate <= now + 7 days`), and the deleteMany cleanup never removes it because retryCount never exceeds 1 and — for future-dated reminders — scheduledDate is not past. This is a busy-loop / unbounded row growth issue. The code should either increment retryCount (or delete the reminder) when message/sendTo is missing, or log and skip explicitly.

title: Read-modify-write of retryCount is not atomic; concurrent cron runs can lose increments
body: The handler reads `retryCount` in the initial `findMany` (line 58), then later writes `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` (lines 184 and 195) based on the stale in-memory value. If two instances of this cron endpoint run concurrently (overlapping schedules, multiple pods, or a long-running invocation overlapping the next tick), both read the same retryCount and both write the same incremented value, so a failure is only counted once. Worse, a concurrent run could also mark the reminder `scheduled: true` while another run is mid-failure, leading to inconsistent state. Prisma's atomic `increment` should be used instead: `data: { retryCount: { increment: 1 } }`. The same non-atomic pattern means the `retryCount > 1` deletion threshold can be defeated by overlapping runs, letting permanently-failing reminders (e.g. invalid phone numbers) persist indefinitely — the exact problem this PR is trying to fix.

title: Off-by-one: reminders are deleted when retryCount > 1, i.e. only after the third failure, not the second as described
body: The PR description says 'after scheduling failed twice we delete the workflow reminder', but the cleanup condition is `retryCount: { gt: 1 }`, which only matches retryCount >= 2. A reminder starts at retryCount 0; the first failure sets it to 1 (still kept), the second failure sets it to 2 (deleted on the next cron run). So the reminder is actually attempted three times (initial attempt + 2 retries) before deletion, not twice. Either change the condition to `gte: 1` (delete after the second failure sets retryCount to 1... note this would delete after the first retry) or, to match 'failed twice' semantics with the current increment placement, use `gte: 2`/`gt: 1` and fix the description — but as written the code and description disagree, and the deletion happens one cron cycle later than the retryCount reaches 2, so a reminder with retryCount = 2 is retried once more before being deleted.

title: A failure in the retryCount update inside the catch block is unhandled and aborts the whole cron run
body: Inside the `catch (error)` block, the code awaits `prisma.workflowReminder.update(...)` to increment retryCount. If that database update itself throws (transient DB error, connection issue), the exception propagates out of the catch block, out of the for-loop, and rejects the handler — the `res.status(200).json(...)` at line 201 is never reached and remaining reminders in `unscheduledReminders` are never processed. The same applies to the update in the else branch at line 179. A failure to record the retry should not prevent processing of other reminders; wrap the retryCount update in its own try/catch (or use a non-throwing update) so one bad row doesn't abort the batch.

title: Org authorization condition includes org ID itself in teamIds for team bookings
body: In buildOrgAuthorizationCondition, `teamIds` is constructed as `[options.orgId, ...teamsFromOrg.map((t) => t.id)]` and then used in `("teamId" = ANY(${teamIds})) AND ("isTeamBooking" = true)`. This means bookings whose `teamId` equals the organization's own ID are treated as valid team bookings. In the previous object-notation implementation, the same `teamIds` array was used with `teamId: { in: teamIds }`, so this behavior is preserved from the original code — but it is a semantic question worth verifying: an organization is not a team, and `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized.teamId` for an org-level team booking may legitimately be the org ID (orgs are teams in cal.com's schema with isOrganization=true). If org-level bookings store the org ID in teamId, this is correct; if not, this condition over-grants access to bookings that should not be visible. The test at line 332-343 of the integration test explicitly expects `testData.org.id` in the ANY array, confirming this is intentional, but the security implication (org owners/admins seeing all bookings with teamId = orgId) should be verified against the actual data model.

title: Org user IDs only fetched from child teams, missing direct org members
body: In buildOrgAuthorizationCondition, `userIdsFromOrg` is only populated when `teamsFromOrg.length > 0`, by calling `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds({ teamIds, ... })` where `teamIds` includes the org ID and child team IDs. However, if the organization has direct members (users with membership on the org itself) but no child teams, `teamsFromOrg.length === 0` and `userIdsFromOrg` is set to `[]`, so the `("userId" = ANY(...)) AND ("isTeamBooking" = false)` branch is omitted entirely. This means non-team bookings (isTeamBooking = false) belonging to direct org members would NOT be visible in org-scope insights when the org has no child teams. The condition would only match team bookings, silently dropping individual bookings of org members. This is a data completeness/authorization coverage bug.

title: Filter condition reduce produces unparenthesized first condition when combined
body: In buildFilterConditions, the reduce starts with the first condition unparenthesized: `if (index === 0) return condition;` and subsequent conditions are wrapped as `(${acc}) AND (${condition})`. When there are exactly two conditions (e.g., eventTypeId OR-group and memberUserId), the result is `("eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X) AND ("userId" = Y)` — wait, actually the reduce wraps acc in parens for index > 0, producing `(<first>) AND (<second>)`. For the eventTypeId condition which itself contains an OR without outer parens (`("eventTypeId" = ${id}) OR ("eventParentId" = ${id})`), the first reduce step returns it raw, and the second step wraps it: `(("eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)) AND ("userId" = Y)`. This is actually correct due to the wrapping. However, when getBaseConditions combines auth and filter conditions at line 73 as `(${authConditions}) AND (${filterConditions})`, and the filter condition from a single eventTypeId filter is the raw OR without parens, the final SQL becomes `(<auth>) AND ("eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)` — the AND binds tighter than OR in SQL, so this evaluates as `((<auth>) AND ("eventTypeId" = X)) OR ("eventParentId" = X)`, which completely breaks the authorization: any booking with a matching eventParentId is returned regardless of authorization! This is a critical operator-precedence bug. The test at line 429-431 expects the combined filter to be wrapped in outer parens `(...) AND (...)`, but that test calls getFilterConditions directly with two filters. The single-filter case (line 384-386) returns the raw OR without parens, and getBaseConditions line 73 wraps it as `(${auth}) AND ${filter}` where filter = `("eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)`, producing `(${auth}) AND ("eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)` — due to SQL precedence (AND before OR), this is `((auth) AND eventTypeId=X) OR (eventParentId=X)`, bypassing authorization for any booking whose eventParentId matches. This is a critical security vulnerability.

title: Integration test does not verify authorization bypass with unauthorized bookings
body: The getBaseConditions integration test (lines 437-502) creates a booking owned by the test user and verifies it is returned. However, it does not create any bookings that the user should NOT be able to see (e.g., bookings from other users, other teams, or with matching eventParentId but different authorization scope). Without a negative test case, the test cannot detect authorization bypass bugs such as the SQL operator precedence issue where an unparenthesized OR in filter conditions can escape the authorization AND-clause. The test asserts `expect(results).toEqual([{ id: userBooking.id }])` which would pass even if the query returned additional unauthorized bookings — actually it uses toEqual with an exact array, so it would fail if extra rows were returned. But since no other bookings exist in the test database with matching eventParentId, the precedence bug would not manifest. The test needs to create a booking with the same eventParentId but belonging to a different user/team that the test user is not authorized to see, and assert it is NOT returned.

title: Test 'should return NOTHING for non-owner/admin user' does not verify the user is actually a member of a team in the org
body: The test creates a regular user and adds them as a MEMBER of the organization (testData.org.id), then expects NOTHING_CONDITION. However, the test user created by createTestData (testData.user) is an OWNER of the org. The regularUser is only a MEMBER of the org, not of any team. The test verifies that a non-owner/admin org member gets NOTHING, which is correct. But it does not test the case where a user is an ADMIN (not OWNER) — the service should allow ADMIN. There is no test verifying that an org ADMIN (as opposed to OWNER) gets proper authorization conditions rather than NOTHING. This is a gap in role-based authorization testing. Additionally, the test does not verify behavior for a user who is OWNER/ADMIN of a child team but not of the org — such a user should get NOTHING for org scope, but this edge case is untested.

title: Org scope test does not verify that non-member users' bookings are excluded
body: The 'should build org scope conditions' test (lines 305-346) creates an org with the test user as OWNER, plus two additional teams each with one MEMBER user. It then verifies the generated SQL condition matches an expected Prisma.sql template. However, this test only checks the SQL string structure — it does not execute the query against the database to verify that: (1) bookings from users who are NOT members of any team in the org are excluded, (2) bookings from users in teams outside the org are excluded, (3) the org owner can see all team bookings and all member bookings. Without executing the query with actual data, subtle SQL logic errors (like the operator precedence bug in getBaseConditions) would not be caught. The test is purely structural.

title: Removal of findMany method is a breaking API change for consumers of InsightsBookingService
body: The PR removes the public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method from InsightsBookingService (replaced by `getBaseConditions()` which returns a Prisma.Sql fragment). Any existing code that calls `service.findMany({ select: ..., where: ..., orderBy: ... })` will break at compile time. The PR description does not mention updating any callers. If there are consumers of this service elsewhere in the codebase (e.g., tRPC routers, API handlers), they need to be updated to use `$queryRaw` with `getBaseConditions()` instead. This is a breaking API change that should be verified — either by checking that no callers exist, or by updating them in the same PR. The new pattern of returning raw SQL fragments and requiring callers to use `$queryRaw` is less type-safe than the previous Prisma findMany approach and shifts SQL construction responsibility to callers.

title: Removed caching tests without replacement — caching behavior is now untested
body: The diff removes the entire 'Caching' describe block (tests for 'should cache authorization conditions' and 'should cache filter conditions'). The service still implements caching via `cachedAuthConditions` and `cachedFilterConditions` fields (lines 49-50, 84-95 of insightsBooking.ts). With the caching tests removed, there is no verification that: (1) repeated calls to getAuthorizationConditions/getFilterConditions return the same cached Prisma.Sql object, (2) the cache is properly initialized (undefined check), (3) concurrent calls don't cause race conditions in cache population. The caching logic remains in the production code but is now completely untested. Either the caching should be removed if not needed, or the tests should be updated to work with the new Prisma.Sql return type.

title: ANY() with empty array produces SQL that may behave unexpectedly
body: In buildOrgAuthorizationCondition, `teamIds` always contains at least `options.orgId`, so `ANY(${teamIds})` is never empty. However, in buildTeamAuthorizationCondition (line 201), `userIdsFromTeam` could theoretically be empty if the team has no members, but the code guards with `if (userIdsFromTeam.length > 0)`. In buildOrgAuthorizationCondition line 168, `uniqueUserIds` is guarded by `if (userIdsFromOrg.length > 0)`. So empty arrays are guarded. However, the `ANY()` operator with a JavaScript array in Prisma.sql requires the array to be non-empty; if somehow an empty array reaches `ANY(${{}})`, PostgreSQL would throw a syntax error or return unexpected results. The guards are present, but this is fragile — if the guard logic changes, empty arrays would cause runtime SQL errors. Consider adding an explicit assertion or using a different pattern for empty arrays.

title: Cleanup function may fail if test fails partway through, leaving orphaned test data
body: The cleanup function in createTestData (lines 153-197) performs sequential deletes without try-catch or transaction wrapping. If any delete fails (e.g., foreign key constraint violation because a booking references an eventType that wasn't cleaned up first, or a team has memberships that weren't deleted), subsequent cleanup steps are skipped, leaving orphaned test data in the database. The cleanup order deletes memberships, users, teams, bookings, eventTypes — but if the test created additional data not tracked in the cleanup (like the userEventType and userBooking in the getBaseConditions test, which are cleaned up separately at lines 494-499), a failure in the main cleanup would orphan those too. Tests should use try-finally blocks to ensure cleanup runs even on assertion failure, and the cleanup should be resilient to partial failures.

title: Org scope authorization misses org-level members when org has no child teams
body: In buildOrgAuthorizationCondition, userIdsFromOrg is only populated when teamsFromOrg.length > 0. If the organization has no child teams, userIdsFromOrg is set to [] and the second OR branch ('userId = ANY(...) AND isTeamBooking = false') is omitted entirely. This means direct members of the organization (users with a membership on the org team itself, not on a child team) are excluded from the org-scope query when the org has no sub-teams. The previous Prisma object implementation had the same structural issue only if the query was built the same way, but here the SQL makes the omission explicit and silently drops all non-team bookings for org members. The user ID list should include members of the org team itself (teamIds already includes options.orgId, so MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds should be called with the full teamIds array unconditionally, not only when child teams exist).

title: Org scope includes the org team ID in teamId ANY() list, matching org-level team bookings incorrectly
body: teamIds is built as [options.orgId, ...teamsFromOrg.map(t => t.id)] and used in the condition '("teamId" = ANY(${teamIds})) AND ("isTeamBooking" = true)'. Including the organization's own ID in the teamId list means any booking whose teamId equals the org ID is treated as an authorized team booking. Whether this is intended depends on the data model (whether bookings can have teamId pointing at an organization), but the previous object-based implementation used the same list, so this is a pre-existing semantic question — however, the raw SQL makes it harder to audit. More importantly, the asymmetry with buildTeamAuthorizationCondition (which only uses the specific team ID) suggests the org ID inclusion may be unintentional. This should be verified against the BookingTimeStatusDenormalized schema and the intended authorization semantics.

title: Event type filter SQL has unparenthesized OR, causing incorrect precedence when combined with other conditions
body: The eventTypeId filter is built as Prisma.sql`("eventTypeId" = ${id}) OR ("eventParentId" = ${id})` without wrapping parentheses. When this is combined with other filters via buildFilterConditions' reduce (which wraps as `(${acc}) AND (${condition})`), the OR is actually parenthesized correctly in the multi-filter case. However, when eventTypeId is the ONLY filter, getFilterConditions returns the bare OR expression. If a caller then combines this with authorization conditions via getBaseConditions, it wraps as `(${authConditions}) AND (${filterConditions})`, which is correct. But the test at line 384-386 of the test file expects the bare unparenthesized OR, and any future caller that embeds the filter condition without wrapping (e.g., `WHERE ${filterConditions} AND something_else`) would get wrong precedence: `eventTypeId = X OR eventParentId = X AND something_else` evaluates as `eventTypeId = X OR (eventParentId = X AND something_else)`. The filter builder should wrap multi-clause OR conditions in parentheses for safety, matching defensive SQL construction practices.

title: Removal of findMany method is a breaking API change for all callers of InsightsBookingService
body: The PR removes the public findMany(findManyArgs) method entirely and replaces it with getBaseConditions() which returns a raw Prisma.Sql fragment. Any existing caller that used service.findMany({ select, where, orderBy, ... }) to query BookingTimeStatusDenormalized will now fail to compile or at runtime. The PR description frames this as a test-only change ('updates the InsightsBookingService integration tests'), but the service file diff shows a substantial API removal. Callers must now construct their own $queryRaw queries with the returned SQL fragment, which changes the contract significantly: they lose Prisma's type-safe select/where/orderBy/pagination handling and must hand-write SQL for everything beyond the WHERE clause. This is a breaking change that should be called out explicitly, and all call sites in the codebase must be updated in the same PR (or the old method kept as a wrapper). The PR provides no evidence that callers were migrated.

title: Integration test queries wrong table and lacks assertions on authorization enforcement
body: The getBaseConditions integration test runs `SELECT id FROM "BookingTimeStatusDenormalized" WHERE ${baseConditions}` but the test setup creates bookings via prisma.booking.create — it never creates any BookingTimeStatusDenormalized rows. The test expects results to equal [{ id: userBooking.id }], which would only pass if BookingTimeStatusDenormalized is populated by a database trigger or if the test database has some sync mechanism. If the denormalized table is populated asynchronously or by a separate process, this test is flaky and depends on timing. Additionally, the test only verifies the positive case (authorized user sees their booking). It does not verify that the NOTHING_CONDITION actually blocks unauthorized access at the SQL level, nor that the org/team scope conditions correctly exclude bookings from other teams. The removed 'Caching' describe block also means caching behavior (cachedAuthConditions/cachedFilterConditions) is no longer tested at all, despite the service still implementing it.

title: Prisma.Sql equality comparison via toEqual may not reliably compare SQL fragments
body: The tests use expect(conditions).toEqual(Prisma.sql`...`) to compare Prisma.Sql objects. Prisma.Sql instances are objects with .strings and .values properties (and internal symbols). toEqual does a deep structural comparison, which may pass or fail depending on Prisma's internal representation, symbol properties, and whether the values arrays contain the same references. Two Prisma.sql fragments with identical SQL text and parameters may not be deep-equal if Prisma attaches non-enumerable properties or if the values contain different object identities. This makes the tests brittle: they test Prisma's internal object structure rather than the actual SQL semantics. A more robust approach would compare conditions.strings and conditions.values explicitly, or execute the SQL against the database and compare results. The PR description even notes 'All test expectations now use direct Prisma.sql comparisons instead of inspecting .strings and .values properties' — this is a regression in test quality, not an improvement.

title: NOTHING_CONDITION SQL lacks spaces around equals sign, inconsistent with other SQL fragments
body: The constant is defined as Prisma.sql`1=0` while all other SQL fragments in the file use spaced operators (e.g., '"userId" = ${id}'). This is purely cosmetic but makes the codebase inconsistent. More importantly, the test file defines its own NOTHING_CONDITION = Prisma.sql`1=0` at line 10 rather than importing it from the service, which means if the service's definition changes, the test won't catch it. The constant should be exported from the service and imported in tests.

title: Test cleanup function has inconsistent delete vs deleteMany usage and potential foreign key failures
body: The cleanup function mixes deleteMany and delete for the same models: it uses prisma.booking.deleteMany({ where: { id: booking.id } }) and prisma.eventType.deleteMany({ where: { id: eventType.id } }) but prisma.membership.delete({ where: { id: orgMembership.id } }) and prisma.team.deleteMany for teams. More critically, the cleanup order deletes the booking before the event type (correct), but deletes memberships before teams and users — however, it deletes the main membership via deleteMany({ where: { id: membership.id } }) which is fine, but then deletes orgMembership via delete. The additional memberships are deleted first, then additional users, then additional teams, then booking, eventType, main membership, orgMembership, team, org, user. If any foreign key constraint exists (e.g., Booking references EventType, EventType references User/Team, Membership references User/Team), the order matters. Deleting the user at the end after deleting teams should be fine, but if the booking still references the event type when eventType.deleteMany runs, it could fail. The test creates a booking with eventTypeId and userId, so deleting the event type while the booking exists would violate FK constraints unless cascade is configured. The cleanup deletes booking first (line 176-178), so this is OK, but the pattern is fragile and the deleteMany-with-single-id pattern is misleading — delete would be clearer.

title: Authorization check queries membership without verifying the org exists or belongs to the expected context
body: isOrgOwnerOrAdmin checks MembershipRepository.findUniqueByUserIdAndTeamId({ userId, teamId: orgId }) and verifies role is OWNER or ADMIN. However, it does not verify that the team with id=orgId is actually an organization (isOrganization=true). If a caller passes a regular team's ID as orgId, and the user is an OWNER/ADMIN of that regular team, the authorization check passes and the user gets access to insights scoped to that 'org'. The zod schema only validates that orgId is a number, not that it corresponds to an organization. This could allow privilege escalation if the API layer doesn't separately validate that orgId is an organization. The service should verify that the orgId refers to an actual organization (e.g., by checking team.isOrganization) before granting access.

title: Test for non-owner/admin user only tests MEMBER role, not other non-privileged states
body: The test 'should return NOTHING for non-owner/admin user' creates a user with MembershipRole.MEMBER. It does not test edge cases such as: a user with no membership at all (should also return NOTHING), a user with a membership that is not accepted (accepted: false), or a user who is a member of a child team but not the org. The isOrgOwnerOrAdmin function checks membership.accepted and membership.role, so unaccepted memberships should return NOTHING, but this path is not tested. Missing test coverage for the accepted=false case is notable because the code explicitly checks it.

title: Missing parentheses around OR condition in eventTypeId filter breaks operator precedence when combined with other filters
body: In `buildFilterConditions()`, the eventTypeId condition is built as `Prisma.sql`("eventTypeId" = ${id}) OR ("eventParentId" = ${id})`` without wrapping parentheses. When this is combined with the memberUserId condition via `Prisma.sql`(${acc}) AND (${condition})``, the resulting SQL is `("eventTypeId" = X OR "eventParentId" = X) AND ("userId" = Y)` — wait, actually the reduce wraps each side, so it becomes `(A OR B) AND (C)`. However, when this filter condition is later combined with authorization conditions in `getBaseConditions()` via `Prisma.sql`(${authConditions}) AND (${filterConditions})``, the filterConditions is already parenthesized by the reduce. BUT: if only the eventTypeId filter is present (no memberUserId), `buildFilterConditions` returns the raw `Prisma.sql`("eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)`` WITHOUT any wrapping parentheses (the reduce returns the first element as-is when index === 0). Then in `getBaseConditions()`, this becomes `(${authConditions}) AND ("eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)` — the OR binds looser than AND, so this evaluates as `(${authConditions} AND "eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)`, which completely bypasses the authorization conditions for any booking whose eventParentId matches, regardless of whether the user is authorized to see it. This is a critical authorization bypass. The test at line 384-386 of the integration test only checks the filter condition in isolation and does not catch this, and the combined test at line 429-431 happens to include memberUserId which causes the reduce to add parentheses, masking the bug.

title: Org authorization condition includes org ID itself in teamIds for team bookings, which may not match the denormalized schema semantics
body: In `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition()`, `teamIds` is constructed as `[options.orgId, ...teamsFromOrg.map((t) => t.id)]` and used in `("teamId" = ANY(${teamIds})) AND ("isTeamBooking" = true)`. The org ID itself is included in the teamIds array. In the `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` table, `teamId` for a team booking should reference an actual team ID, not the organization ID. Including the org ID in this ANY array means the condition will match bookings where `teamId` equals the organization ID — but organization-level bookings (if any exist with isTeamBooking=true and teamId=orgId) would be included. More importantly, this differs from the original Prisma object notation which used `teamId: { in: teamIds }` with the same array, so the behavior is preserved from the original. However, the original code also had this same construction, so this is not a regression. The real issue is that the test at line 332-343 expects this exact behavior, confirming the org ID is intentionally included. This may be correct if org-level bookings exist, but it's worth verifying that `teamId` in the denormalized table can actually be an org ID for team bookings. If org-level bookings don't exist with isTeamBooking=true, this is harmless but confusing. Not a bug per se, but the semantics should be documented.

title: Org authorization only fetches users from child teams, missing users who are direct members of the organization
body: In `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition()`, `userIdsFromOrg` is populated only from `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds({ teamIds, ... })` where `teamIds = [options.orgId, ...teamsFromOrg.map((t) => t.id)]`. Wait — actually `teamIds` DOES include `options.orgId`, so it does query memberships for the org itself. Let me re-read... `teamIds` is `[options.orgId, ...teamsFromOrg.map((t) => t.id)]`, and `findAllByTeamIds` is called with these teamIds. So it does include org members. However, there's a subtle issue: `teamsFromOrg` only contains direct children of the org (from `findAllByParentId`). If there are nested teams (teams within teams), their users won't be included in `userIdsFromOrg`. The original Prisma code had the same logic, so this is not a regression. But it means users who are members of nested sub-teams (grandchildren of the org) won't have their individual (non-team) bookings included in org scope results. This may be intentional (only direct teams are considered) or a pre-existing limitation. Not introduced by this PR.

title: NOTHING_CONDITION uses unquoted 1=0 which may not be portable across all SQL dialects
body: The constant `NOTHING_CONDITION = Prisma.sql`1=0`` uses an unquoted integer literal comparison. While this works in PostgreSQL (which cal.com uses), it's slightly unusual. More importantly, when this is embedded in larger queries via `Prisma.sql`(${authConditions}) AND (${filterConditions})``, it becomes `(1=0) AND (...)` which is fine. However, if `NOTHING_CONDITION` is ever used as a standalone WHERE clause without parentheses (e.g., `WHERE ${NOTHING_CONDITION}`), it becomes `WHERE 1=0` which is valid. The concern is minimal for PostgreSQL but the pattern is slightly fragile. Not a real issue for this codebase.

title: Integration test for getBaseConditions does not verify the authorization bypass scenario with eventTypeId-only filter
body: The test `should combine authorization and filter conditions` at line 438-501 only tests the case where BOTH `eventTypeId` AND `memberUserId` filters are provided. As noted in the finding for insightsBooking.ts line 106, when ONLY `eventTypeId` is provided (without `memberUserId`), the filter condition is returned without wrapping parentheses, causing an operator precedence bug in `getBaseConditions()` that bypasses authorization. This test does not cover that scenario. A test should be added that: (1) creates a booking that matches the eventTypeId filter but belongs to a different user (not authorized), (2) calls `getBaseConditions()` with only `eventTypeId` filter, (3) executes the query, and (4) verifies the unauthorized booking is NOT returned. Without this test, the authorization bypass will not be caught.

title: Test uses toEqual for Prisma.Sql comparison which may not correctly compare SQL fragments
body: The tests use `expect(conditions).toEqual(NOTHING_CONDITION)` and `expect(conditions).toEqual(Prisma.sql`...`)` to compare `Prisma.Sql` objects. `Prisma.Sql` is a class instance with `strings` and `values` properties. `toEqual` does a deep equality check, which should compare these properties. However, two `Prisma.sql` template literals with the same strings and values should be equal. The concern is that `Prisma.sql` may have internal state or the `strings` array may be a `readonly string[]` vs `string[]` which could cause `toEqual` to fail or pass unexpectedly. More importantly, the PR description says 'All test expectations now use direct Prisma.sql comparisons instead of inspecting .strings and .values properties' — this is fragile because if Prisma changes the internal representation of `Sql`, these tests will break. The previous approach of inspecting `.strings` and `.values` was more explicit about what was being tested. Additionally, `toEqual` on class instances checks the constructor, so if `Prisma.sql` returns a subclass or different class in different contexts, comparisons may fail. The tests should verify the actual SQL strings and values explicitly rather than relying on object equality of `Prisma.Sql` instances.

title: Changed from `import type { Prisma }` to `import { Prisma }` — verify this doesn't cause runtime import issues
body: The import changed from `import type { Prisma } from "@prisma/client"` to `import { Prisma } from "@prisma/client"`. This is necessary because `Prisma.sql` is a runtime function (template tag), not just a type. However, this means the entire `Prisma` namespace is now imported at runtime, which may increase bundle size slightly. In a server-side context (which this is, given it's in `packages/lib/server/`), this is typically fine. But it's worth verifying that tree-shaking or bundling doesn't cause issues. Not a real problem for server code.

title: New exported type InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions may break existing callers who pass validated options
body: The PR introduces `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions` as the constructor parameter type, which is a looser type (`scope: "user" | "org" | "team"` with optional `teamId`) compared to the previous `InsightsBookingServiceOptions` (the discriminated union from zod). The constructor still validates with `insightsBookingServiceOptionsSchema.safeParse(options)`. This is actually a reasonable pattern (accept loose input, validate internally), but it changes the public API: callers who previously passed a validated `InsightsBookingServiceOptions` (the discriminated union) will still work, but the type signature is now broader. More importantly, if any caller was relying on TypeScript to enforce that `teamId` is present when `scope === "team"`, that compile-time check is now lost — the validation happens at runtime via zod. This is a deliberate design choice but represents an API change that should be documented. Existing callers should be audited to ensure they handle the case where validation fails (options becomes null, resulting in NOTHING_CONDITION).

title: Removal of findMany method is a breaking API change with no migration path documented
body: The PR removes the `findMany(findManyArgs: Prisma.BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedFindManyArgs)` method entirely and replaces it with `getBaseConditions(): Promise<Prisma.Sql>`. This is a breaking API change. Any existing callers of `InsightsBookingService.findMany()` will now fail at compile time (or runtime if using JS). The PR description does not mention updating any callers. A search of the codebase is needed to find all usages of `InsightsBookingService` and verify they've been updated to use `getBaseConditions()` with `$queryRaw` instead. If callers exist and haven't been updated, this PR will break them. Even if no callers exist yet (this may be a new service), the removal of a public method without deprecation is an API break that should be called out. The new pattern requires callers to manually construct `$queryRaw` queries with `getBaseConditions()`, which is more error-prone than the previous `findMany` wrapper that handled the Prisma query construction.

title: Cleanup function has inconsistent delete patterns — some use deleteMany with single ID, others use delete
body: In the `cleanup` function, the cleanup for the main test data uses inconsistent patterns: `prisma.booking.deleteMany({ where: { id: booking.id } })` and `prisma.eventType.deleteMany({ where: { id: eventType.id } })` use `deleteMany` with a single ID filter, while `prisma.membership.delete({ where: { id: orgMembership.id } })` and `prisma.team.deleteMany({ where: { id: team.id } })` mix `delete` and `deleteMany`. Using `deleteMany` with a single ID is less efficient than `delete` (which throws if not found, providing a sanity check). More importantly, `prisma.user.deleteMany({ where: { id: user.id } })` at line 194-196 will fail if the user has related records (bookings, memberships) that haven't been cleaned up yet due to foreign key constraints. The cleanup order matters: bookings and eventTypes are deleted before memberships and users, which is correct. However, the additional users cleanup at line 162-166 uses `prisma.user.delete({ where: { id: user.id } })` which will throw if the user still has memberships — but memberships are deleted first at line 155-159, so this should be fine. The inconsistency between `delete` and `deleteMany` is a code smell but not a bug. The real risk is that if any cleanup step throws, subsequent steps won't run, leaving orphaned test data. Consider wrapping in try/finally or using a transaction.

title: Test 'should return NOTHING for non-owner/admin user' does not clean up regularUser if getAuthorizationConditions throws
body: In the test at line 213-255, a `regularUser` and `membership` are created, then `service.getAuthorizationConditions()` is called. If this call throws (e.g., due to a database error or a bug in the service), the cleanup code at lines 247-254 will not execute, leaving the `regularUser` and `membership` in the database. This is a test hygiene issue that can cause subsequent test runs to fail due to unique constraint violations (e.g., if the same email/username is generated, though the timestamp+random suffix makes this unlikely). More importantly, if the test fails midway, the test data pollution can affect other tests. The `testData.cleanup()` at line 254 is also not guaranteed to run. Consider using `try/finally` or `afterEach` hooks for cleanup.

title: Filter conditions reduce does not wrap the first condition in parentheses, causing precedence issues when combined with auth conditions
body: In `buildFilterConditions()`, the reduce at line 119-122 returns the first condition as-is when `index === 0`: `if (index === 0) return condition;`. This means if there's only one filter condition (e.g., only `eventTypeId`), the returned `Prisma.Sql` is `("eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)` WITHOUT outer parentheses. When this is combined with authorization conditions in `getBaseConditions()` at line 73 via `Prisma.sql`(${authConditions}) AND (${filterConditions})``, the result is `(${authConditions}) AND ("eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)`. Due to SQL operator precedence (AND binds tighter than OR), this evaluates as `(${authConditions} AND "eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)`. This means ANY booking with `eventParentId = X` will be returned, completely bypassing the authorization conditions. This is a critical security vulnerability — an attacker could potentially access bookings they shouldn't see by crafting a filter with just `eventTypeId`. The fix is to always wrap the final filter conditions in parentheses, or ensure the reduce always wraps: `return Prisma.sql`(${acc}) AND (${condition})`` should be applied even for the first element by initializing with a neutral element, or the return should be wrapped: `return Prisma.sql`(${combined})``.

title: deleteCache authorization check misses delegation credentials, allowing cache deletion for credentials the user does not own
body: The handler verifies ownership with `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { id: credentialId, userId: user.id } })`. In cal.com, delegation credentials (service-account based Google Calendar connections) are stored as Credential rows whose `userId` is null (they are linked via `delegatedToId` / `delegationCredentialId`), so this check correctly rejects them. However, the inverse problem exists: a regular user credential can be *delegated to* another user (credential.delegatedToId set, credential.userId still set to the owner). More importantly, the UI passes `connectedCalendar.credentialId` which for delegation-credential-connected calendars is a negative in-memory credential id or a credential belonging to the org, and the `connectedCalendars` query returns calendars the logged-in user can see but does not own. The ownership check only covers `userId`, not team/org membership or delegation relationships, so any authenticated user who can obtain a credentialId (e.g. via the connectedCalendars response of a shared/team context, or by guessing sequential ids combined with a leaked id) can delete another user's calendar cache. Cache deletion forces expensive re-fetches and can be used to degrade availability data (a denial-of-service vector on the calendar-cache feature). The check should verify the credential belongs to the user OR to a delegation credential the user is authorized to manage, and should reject in-memory (negative) credential ids explicitly.

title: deleteCache throws a plain Error instead of a TRPCError, producing an unhelpful 500 INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR to the client
body: When the credential is not found, the handler does `throw new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. In tRPC, a plain Error is converted to an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR with the message stripped in production, so the client's `onError` toast shows a generic "Error deleting cache" and the real reason (authorization failure vs. not found) is lost. Other handlers in this codebase use `TRPCError` with codes like `NOT_FOUND`/`FORBIDDEN`/`UNAUTHORIZED`. This should be `throw new TRPCError({ code: "FORBIDDEN", message: "..." })` (or NOT_FOUND) so the API contract is correct and the UI can distinguish authorization failures.

title: getCacheStatusByCredentialIds includes expired cache rows, so the UI shows a stale 'last updated' timestamp for expired caches
body: The `groupBy` query filters only by `credentialId: { in: credentialIds }` and takes `_max: { updatedAt: true }`. It does not filter on `expiresAt >= now()`, unlike `getCachedAvailability` which requires `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }`. Consequence: after a cache entry expires (CACHING_TIME = 30 days), the connectedCalendars handler still reports a `cacheUpdatedAt`, so the UI shows "Cache Status: Last updated <date>" and offers "Delete cached data" for a cache that is no longer being served. Deleting it is harmless but misleading; worse, the displayed timestamp suggests fresh data when the cache is actually dead, which can mislead users debugging availability issues. The query should add `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }` to the `where` clause.

title: ICalendarCacheRepository is missing deleteManyByCredential even though the mock implements it, making the interface incomplete
body: The mock class `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` implements `deleteManyByCredential()` (calendar-cache.repository.mock.ts line 23), and `CalendarService.unwatchCalendar` deletes cache rows directly via prisma, but the interface `ICalendarCacheRepository` does not declare `deleteManyByCredential`. The new `deleteCache.handler.ts` also bypasses the repository and calls `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany` directly. This means the repository abstraction is incomplete: callers cannot depend on the interface for cache deletion, and the mock's extra method is dead weight that will silently drift. Either add `deleteManyByCredential(credentialId: number): Promise<void>` to the interface and route `deleteCache.handler.ts` (and ideally `unwatchCalendar`) through the repository, or remove the unused mock method.

title: deleteCache mutation does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query, so the cache status UI stays stale after deletion
body: The `deleteCacheMutation` only shows a toast and calls `onSuccess?.()`. The `disconnectMutation` explicitly invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` and `utils.viewer.apps.integrations` in `onSettled`, but the delete-cache mutation does not. After a successful cache deletion, the `connectedCalendars` query still returns the old `cacheUpdatedAt`, so the dropdown continues to show "Cache Status: Last updated ..." and the "Delete cached data" option even though the cache rows were deleted. The component relies on the parent's `onChanged` callback to refetch, but `onChanged` is optional and in `SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper` it is passed through from props without any guaranteed invalidation. The mutation should invalidate `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` (at minimum) in `onSettled`, mirroring the disconnect mutation.

title: Confirmation dialog closes immediately on confirm, before the mutation completes, so failures leave no visible feedback path
body: In both confirmation dialogs, `onConfirm` calls `mutation.mutate(...)` and then unconditionally `setDeleteModalOpen(false)` / `setDisconnectModalOpen(false)`. The dialog closes immediately while the mutation is still in flight. If the mutation fails, the only feedback is the error toast; the user cannot retry from the dialog and there is no pending/loading state on the confirm button. This is a UX robustness issue: a transient network error forces the user to reopen the dropdown and repeat the flow. Consider keeping the dialog open (with a loading state on the confirm button) until the mutation settles, as is common with `ConfirmationDialogContent` usage elsewhere.

title: Hardcoded 'en-US' locale for cache timestamp formatting ignores the user's locale
body: The cache timestamp is formatted with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" })`. The component already uses `useLocale()` for translations, so the user's locale is available but not used here. Non-English users will see dates in US format, inconsistent with the rest of the app which formats dates according to the user's locale. The formatter should use the locale from `useLocale()` (e.g. `const { t, i18n } = useLocale()` and `i18n.language` or the dayjs locale used elsewhere in the codebase).

title: Cache status row is rendered as an interactive DropdownMenuItem with no action, trapping keyboard focus on a non-actionable element
body: The cache status display (lines 84-97) is wrapped in a `<DropdownMenuItem className="focus:ring-muted">` even though it performs no action — it is purely informational. Radix `DropdownMenuItem` is an interactive menu item: it is focusable, responds to Enter/Space, and shows hover/active states, which misleads users into thinking it is clickable. It should be a non-interactive element (e.g. a plain `<div>` with appropriate padding, or `DropdownMenuLabel`/`DropdownMenuSeparator` semantics) so keyboard and screen-reader users are not stuck on a dead item. Nesting a `<div>` inside `DropdownMenuItem` also produces a menu item whose accessible name is the concatenated text, which is acceptable, but the interactivity is the real problem.

title: connectedCalendars now always instantiates CalendarCacheRepository and runs an extra groupBy query even when calendar-cache is disabled
body: The handler unconditionally constructs `new CalendarCacheRepository()` and calls `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds(credentialIds)` on every `connectedCalendars` query. The codebase has a `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` used precisely when the calendar-cache feature is disabled (the mock logs "Skipping ... due to calendar-cache being disabled"), and `CalendarCache.init(null)` elsewhere selects mock vs. real based on configuration. Here the real repository is always used, so every connectedCalendars call — including for users/teams without the calendar-cache feature — pays for an extra `groupBy` DB query. This adds latency to a frequently-called query (it is used with `suspense: true` in the settings UI and onboarding). The handler should use the same feature-detection used by `CalendarCache.init` (e.g. check the team feature flag / `getCalendarCacheRepository()` factory) and skip the query entirely when the feature is disabled, returning `cacheUpdatedAt: null`.

title: credentialIds may contain in-memory delegation credential ids (negative numbers) which are passed to a DB groupBy query
body: `connectedCalendars.map((cal) => cal.credentialId)` can include negative in-memory delegation credential ids (the codebase uses negative ids for in-memory delegation credentials, see `isInMemoryDelegationCredential` and `assertCalendarHasDbCredential` which throws for `credentialId < 0`). These ids are passed straight into `prisma.calendarCache.groupBy({ where: { credentialId: { in: credentialIds } } })`. Prisma will happily query with negative integers (no rows match), so this is not a crash, but it is wasted work and signals the handler does not account for delegation credentials. The `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` call should filter to DB-backed credential ids (e.g. `credentialIds.filter(id => id > 0)`) or the repository should guard, consistent with `assertCalendarHasDbCredential` used elsewhere in the same package.

title: updateManyByCredentialId is called with an empty data object, relying on Prisma @updatedAt side effect with no explicit intent
body: `await SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` passes an empty `data` object. The only effect is that Prisma touches `updatedAt` (because the schema has `@updatedAt` on SelectedCalendar). This is obscure: a reader cannot tell whether the empty object is a bug or intentional. The PR description itself notes "Consider if SelectedCalendar.updatedAt update should be removed." Either make the intent explicit with a comment or pass `{ updatedAt: new Date() }` explicitly, or remove the call if the timestamp is not consumed anywhere (the frontend uses `cacheUpdatedAt` from CalendarCache, not SelectedCalendar.updatedAt).

title: updateManyByCredentialId accepts Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateInput but the only caller passes {}, hiding the fact that it can update arbitrary fields across all of a credential's calendars
body: The new method signature is `updateManyByCredentialId(credentialId: number, data: Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateInput)`. `SelectedCalendarUpdateInput` allows updating any scalar field (externalId, integration, userId, eventTypeId, googleChannelId, etc.) across every SelectedCalendar row for a credential. That is a broad, potentially dangerous primitive (e.g. it could reassign calendars to another userId or change externalId en masse). The only current caller passes `{}`, so the method's real purpose is "touch updatedAt". The signature should be narrowed to reflect actual intent — e.g. `updateManyByCredentialId(credentialId: number)` that internally sets `{ updatedAt: new Date() }`, or accept a restricted `Pick<Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateInput, "updatedAt">` — so future callers cannot accidentally mass-modify integrity-sensitive fields.

title: Migration adds updatedAt with DEFAULT NOW() but the Prisma schema comment claims it provides a value for 'future raw inserts' — the default is not persisted in the schema, so raw inserts after migration will fail
body: The migration uses `ALTER TABLE "CalendarCache" ADD COLUMN "updatedAt" TIMESTAMP(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW();`. In Postgres, `DEFAULT NOW()` is a persistent column default, so raw SQL inserts without `updatedAt` will work. However, the schema comment says "Provide an initial value for legacy rows and future raw inserts" while the Prisma schema defines `updatedAt DateTime @default(now()) @updatedAt` — Prisma's `@default(now())` is applied by the Prisma client, not the database, so the migration's `DEFAULT NOW()` and Prisma's default are two different mechanisms. The real risk: the migration's warning text says the column was added "without a default value. This is not possible if the table is not empty" — but the SQL does provide a default, so the warning is stale/incorrect (likely hand-edited after generation). More importantly, if this migration is ever squashed or the default is dropped, raw inserts break. The migration comment/warning should be corrected to reflect that a default IS provided, and the team should verify the default persists (it does in Postgres, but the misleading warning suggests the migration was manually edited and may not match what `prisma migrate dev` would generate).

title: Stale TODO comment says updatedAt 'doesn't exist yet in CalendarCache table' but the column was just added by this PR
body: Line 116 contains `// TODO: For better tracking we could also want to use updatedAt directly which doesn't exist yet in CalendarCache table`. This PR adds the `updatedAt` column to CalendarCache (schema.prisma + migration). The TODO is now obsolete: `updatedAt` exists and is exactly what `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` uses. The ordering logic in `getCachedAvailability` (orderBy `expiresAt: "desc"`) could now also consider `updatedAt`, or the TODO should be removed/updated so future readers are not misled into thinking the column is missing.

title: sed -i '' is macOS-only and will break on Linux CI/dev machines
body: Line 68 uses `sed -i '' -E "s|^GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=.*|GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=$TUNNEL_URL|" "$ENV_FILE"`. The `-i ''` syntax is the BSD/macOS form of in-place sed; on GNU/Linux `sed -i ''` treats `''` as a file name and fails with "can't read : No such file or directory". Since this is a developer helper script committed to the repo (not a macOS-only tool), it should use a portable form such as `sed -i.bak -E ... && rm -f "$ENV_FILE.bak"` or detect the platform. As written, the script silently corrupts or fails to update `.env` on Linux.

title: Script writes a public tunnel URL into ../.env, potentially committing a webhook endpoint that exposes the local Google Calendar webhook to the internet
body: The script sets `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` in `../.env` to a public `*.tunnelmole.net` URL. The Google Calendar webhook handler at `/api/integrations/googlecalendar/webhook` is protected by `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_TOKEN`, but this script's purpose is to expose a local dev server to Google's push notifications. Risks: (1) the tunnel URL is written into a file that developers may accidentally commit (`.env` is typically gitignored, but `../.env` relative to `scripts/` is the repo-root `.env` — verify it is ignored); (2) the tunnel stays alive for the whole script session, leaving a public route into the developer's machine; (3) the script reuses an already-running tmole (`pgrep -f "tmole $TM_PORT"`) without verifying it belongs to this project, potentially overwriting `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` for an unrelated tunnel. At minimum the script should warn that the tunnel is public and ensure `.env` is gitignored.

title: Fixed w-32 container may clip or misalign the new dropdown trigger compared to the previous DisconnectIntegration button
body: The actions container is `<div className="flex w-32 justify-end">` wrapping `CredentialActionsDropdown`, whose trigger is an icon-only `Button` with `StartIcon="ellipsis"`. The previous `DisconnectIntegration` with `trashIcon` rendered a similarly small icon button, so width is probably fine, but `w-32` (8rem) is a hardcoded width sized for the old control. If `CredentialActionsDropdown` returns `null` (when `!canDisconnect && !hasCache`, e.g. a delegation credential with no cache), the `w-32` div still renders as an empty 8rem-wide block, leaving a visible gap on the right side of every credential card. The wrapper should render nothing (or not fix the width) when the dropdown is absent — e.g. let `CredentialActionsDropdown` own its container, or conditionally render the wrapper div.

title: Cache actions are gated only on integrationType === google_calendar, but any credential with cache rows (e.g. after an integration rename or a different cached provider) would be hidden; conversely the check does not verify the cache feature is enabled
body: `hasCache = isGoogleCalendar && cacheUpdatedAt` means the "Delete cached data" action only appears for Google Calendar credentials that have a non-null `cacheUpdatedAt`. Two issues: (1) The server enriches `cacheUpdatedAt` for ALL credentials (the groupBy is not filtered by integration), so if cache rows ever exist for a non-Google credential (e.g. a future cached provider, or leftover rows), the UI silently hides the delete action while the server still reports a timestamp — the user has no way to clear it. (2) The gating on `integrationType === GOOGLE_CALENDAR_TYPE` is a UI-level assumption that duplicates server knowledge; the server should be the source of truth for whether cache management applies. The condition should be based on `cacheUpdatedAt` presence alone (server-controlled), or the server should only populate `cacheUpdatedAt` for integrations where cache deletion is supported.

title: deleteCache input schema is defined inline instead of a dedicated schema file, inconsistent with sibling procedures
body: The router defines `deleteCache` with an inline `z.object({ credentialId: z.number() })`, while `connectedCalendars` and `setDestinationCalendar` import dedicated schemas (`ZConnectedCalendarsInputSchema`, `ZSetDestinationCalendarInputSchema`) from `./connectedCalendars.schema` and `./setDestinationCalendar.schema`. The codebase convention (visible in the same file) is one schema file per procedure. This inconsistency makes the input schema harder to discover/reuse (e.g. for platform API parity or client-side validation) and will drift from the handler's `DeleteCacheOptions` type, which is declared separately in `deleteCache.handler.ts` with no compile-time link to the zod schema. Create `deleteCache.schema.ts` exporting `ZDeleteCacheInputSchema` and use it in both the router and the handler type (`z.infer<typeof ZDeleteCacheInputSchema>`).

title: Unrelated refactor of findMany (removing satisfies Prisma.SelectedCalendarFindManyArgs) is bundled into this PR
body: The diff changes `findMany` from building `const args = { where, select, orderBy } satisfies Prisma.SelectedCalendarFindManyArgs; return await prisma.selectedCalendar.findMany(args);` to a direct `return await prisma.selectedCalendar.findMany({ where, select, orderBy });`. This change is unrelated to the calendar-cache feature (it removes a type-safety assertion). It is not needed for the feature and slightly reduces type checking strictness; it should be reverted or split into its own PR so reviewers can evaluate it independently.

title: getCacheStatusByCredentialIds does not guard against an empty credentialIds array, issuing a pointless groupBy query
body: When `connectedCalendars` is empty (a user with no connected calendar apps, or all filtered out by `_ensureNoConflictingNonDelegatedConnectedCalendar`), `credentialIds` is `[]` and the handler still calls `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds([])`, which issues `SELECT credentialId, MAX(updatedAt) FROM CalendarCache WHERE credentialId IN () GROUP BY credentialId`. Prisma translates `IN ()` to a `FALSE`/`0 = 1` condition, so the query is cheap but still a round-trip to the DB on every connectedCalendars call for users with no calendars. The repository method (or the handler) should early-return `[]` when `credentialIds.length === 0`.

title: cacheUpdatedAt prop is typed as Date but tRPC serializes dates as strings over the wire with superjson disabled or as Date with superjson — type may mismatch at runtime
body: The prop is `cacheUpdatedAt?: Date | null` and the component does `new Date(cacheUpdatedAt)` before formatting, which works for both Date and string. However, the tRPC `RouterOutputs` type for `connectedCalendars` will type `cacheUpdatedAt` according to the transformer. Cal.com uses superjson, which preserves Date instances, so the type is likely correct. But the defensive `new Date(cacheUpdatedAt)` suggests uncertainty. If the transformer ever changes or the platform atoms package consumes this without superjson, the `Date` type would be a lie and `Intl.DateTimeFormat.format()` would receive a string (which `new Date()` handles, so it works). This is a minor robustness note: either trust the type and drop the `new Date()` wrapper, or type the prop as `Date | string | null` to be explicit. Low severity because the current code handles both.

title: New locale strings are added only to en/common.json; all other locales are missing the keys, causing fallback or raw-key display for non-English users
body: The PR adds 7 new keys (`cache_status`, `cache_last_updated`, `delete_cached_data`, `cache_deleted_successfully`, `error_deleting_cache`, `confirm_delete_cache`, `yes_delete_cache`) only to the English locale file. Cal.com's i18n setup (next-i18next with `ADD_NEW_STRINGS_ABOVE_THIS_LINE_TO_PREVENT_MERGE_CONFLICTS`) expects translations to be contributed for other locales, typically via the `translate-locales` script or Crowdin. Until other locales are updated, non-English users will see either the English fallback or the raw key (depending on `fallbackLng` config). This is a known workflow in the repo, but the PR should either run the translation pipeline or note that translations are pending. At minimum, verify the fallback behavior so users don't see raw keys like `cache_deleted_successfully`.

title: Authorization check only covers direct user credentials, not delegation credentials
body: The handler verifies ownership with `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { id: credentialId, userId: user.id } })`. However, the connectedCalendars UI passes `connectedCalendar.credentialId` for delegation-credential calendars too (the wrapper renders CredentialActionsDropdown for every connected calendar, including those with `delegationCredentialId` set). For a delegation credential, the `Credential` row's `userId` is the organization/service-account owner, not the logged-in user, so `findFirst` returns null and the mutation throws — meaning the feature silently fails for delegated calendars. Conversely, if any code path ever passes a credentialId belonging to a delegation credential owned by the same user id, the subsequent `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany({ where: { credentialId } })` deletes cache rows for that credential without scoping to the requesting user. The delete should additionally verify the credential is a non-delegation credential owned by the user (e.g. also check `delegationCredentialId: null` or resolve the credential through the user's enriched credential list) before deleting cache rows.

title: getCacheStatusByCredentialIds returns stale cache timestamps for expired entries
body: `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups `CalendarCache` rows by `credentialId` and takes `_max.updatedAt` without filtering on `expiresAt`. The cache read path (`getCachedAvailability`) only serves rows where `expiresAt >= now`, so a credential whose cache rows have all expired will still report a non-null `updatedAt` in the UI ('Last updated: ...'), even though no usable cache exists and the next availability lookup will be a cache miss. The `where` clause should include `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }` (or the UI should treat expired timestamps as no cache) so the displayed status reflects actually-serveable cache.

title: getCacheStatusByCredentialIds includes cache rows keyed only by userId (in-memory delegation credentials)
body: The repository's own `getCachedAvailability` documents that for in-memory delegation credentials the cache is queried solely by `userId` + `key` (no `credentialId`), because those credentials have no DB row. `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups strictly by `credentialId`, so cache entries created under the userId-only path (negative/in-memory credential ids) will never be attributed to any credential, and the UI will show no cache status even though cache data exists and is being served. The status query should also aggregate rows where `credentialId` is an in-memory delegation credential id and map them to the user's real credential, or the handler should fall back to a userId-based lookup.

title: connectedCalendars now always instantiates the real CalendarCacheRepository, bypassing the disabled-cache mock
body: The handler unconditionally does `new CalendarCacheRepository()` and calls `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`. The codebase has a `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` used when the calendar-cache feature is disabled (its methods log 'Skipping ... due to calendar-cache being disabled'), and `CalendarCache.init(null)` elsewhere selects mock vs real based on configuration. By hard-instantiating the real repository, every `connectedCalendars` query now performs an extra `calendarCache.groupBy` database round-trip even on deployments/teams where calendar cache is disabled, adding latency to a query that is rendered on the installed-apps page and in onboarding.
