The handler should resolve the repository through the same factory/feature-flag mechanism used by `CalendarCache.init` so the extra query is skipped when the feature is off.

title: Delete-cache confirmation dialog closes immediately and fires mutation without awaiting it
body: In the delete-cache `ConfirmationDialogContent`, `onConfirm` calls `deleteCacheMutation.mutate({ credentialId })` and then synchronously `setDeleteModalOpen(false)`. The dialog therefore closes instantly regardless of whether the mutation succeeds or fails, and there is no pending/loading state on the confirm button. If the mutation fails (e.g. the authorization issue for delegation credentials), the user already saw the dialog close and only gets an error toast, with no way to retry from the dialog. The dialog should stay open while `deleteCacheMutation.isPending` and close only in `onSuccess` (the same pattern should be applied to the disconnect dialog at line 148).

title: Cache deletion does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query, so cache status stays visible after deletion
body: The `deleteCache` mutation's `onSuccess` only shows a toast and calls the optional `onSuccess` prop; it never invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. The parent wrapper passes `onSuccess={onChanged}`, but `onChanged` is an optional callback prop of `SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper` and is not wired to refetch the `connectedCalendars` query inside this component (the query is owned by `SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper` with `suspense: true`). After a successful delete, the cached `cacheUpdatedAt` remains in the query cache, so the dropdown continues to show 'Cache Status / Last updated: ...' and the 'Delete cached data' action for a credential whose cache was just deleted. The mutation should invalidate `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` in `onSettled`/`onSuccess`, mirroring what the disconnect mutation already does.

title: Cache status is shown for any Google Calendar credential with a cacheUpdatedAt, including delegation credentials that cannot be deleted
body: `hasCache = isGoogleCalendar && cacheUpdatedAt` does not consider `delegationCredentialId`. For a delegation-credential Google Calendar connection, the dropdown renders the cache status and the 'Delete cached data' action, but `canDisconnect` is false. Clicking delete will call the `deleteCache` mutation with the delegation credential's id, which (per the handler's `userId: user.id` ownership check) will fail with 'Credential not found or access denied' and show a generic error toast. Either the delete action should be hidden for delegation credentials, or the handler should support deleting cache for credentials the user is authorized to manage.

title: Hardcoded 'en-US' locale for cache timestamp formatting
body: The cache timestamp is formatted with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" })`, ignoring the user's locale from `useLocale()`. Every other user-facing string in the component is localized via `t(...)`, but the date is always rendered in US format, which is inconsistent for international users. The formatter should use the current locale (e.g. from `useLocale()`'s `i18n.language`) instead of the hardcoded 'en-US'. Additionally, `new Date(cacheUpdatedAt)` assumes the tRPC payload deserializes the timestamp to a Date/string; if superjson/date serialization changes, this could render 'Invalid Date'. A safer approach is to format the raw value defensively.

title: updateManyByCredentialId called with empty data object relies on @updatedAt side effect
body: `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` is called with an empty `data` object purely so Prisma's `@updatedAt` bumps `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt`. This is implicit and fragile: `updateMany` with empty data still issues an UPDATE touching every SelectedCalendar row for the credential (a write lock and WAL churn on potentially many rows) just to refresh a timestamp, and if the schema ever drops `@updatedAt` the call silently becomes a no-op while still scanning/updating rows. The repository method should accept an explicit intent (e.g. a dedicated `touchUpdatedAtByCredentialId` that sets `updatedAt: new Date()` explicitly) so the write is self-documenting and doesn't depend on a schema side effect.

title: updateManyByCredentialId does not scope by userId, allowing cross-user updates if misused
body: The new `updateManyByCredentialId(credentialId, data)` filters only on `credentialId`. Credential ids are globally unique so this is safe for the current single caller, but unlike sibling methods (`findManyUserLevel`, `updateUserLevel`, `deleteUserLevel`) it has no user-level guard, and the caller in `CalendarService.fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache` passes `this.credential.id` without re-verifying the credential belongs to the current user context. Any future caller that passes an unvalidated credentialId (e.g. from request input) would mass-update another user's SelectedCalendar rows. The method should either also require/verify `userId` in the where clause or be documented/enforced as internal-only.

title: Authorization failure throws a generic Error instead of a TRPCError, producing a 500
body: When the credential is not found or not owned by the user, the handler throws `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. In tRPC, a plain `Error` is surfaced to the client as an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (500) with the message potentially masked in production, whereas authorization failures should be `TRPCError({ code: "FORBIDDEN" })` (or `NOT_FOUND`) so the client gets a correct 403/404 and the UI can distinguish 'access denied' from a real server error. The current code conflates a client-input/authorization problem with a server failure.

title: Interface and mock declare getCacheStatusByCredentialIds but mock class also has undeclared deleteManyByCredential
body: The mock class `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` implements `deleteManyByCredential()` (line 23 of the mock) which is not part of `ICalendarCacheRepository`, while the real `CalendarCacheRepository` has no `deleteManyByCredential` method — the deletion paths use `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany` directly (e.g. `CalendarService.unwatchCalendar` line 955 and `deleteCache.handler.ts` line 28). This asymmetry means the mock does not actually mirror the real repository's surface: code that calls `repository.deleteManyByCredential(...)` would work against the mock but crash against the real implementation. Either add `deleteManyByCredential` to the interface and implement it in the real repository (and use it in the handler/service), or remove it from the mock so the mismatch is caught at compile time.

title: Migration comment contradicts the actual SQL (default value is provided)
body: The migration's warning comment says 'Added the required column `updatedAt` ... without a default value. This is not possible if the table is not empty.', but the SQL below it adds the column with `NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()`, which is exactly the safe pattern for non-empty tables. The stale Prisma-generated warning is misleading to reviewers and suggests the migration is unsafe when it is not. The comment block should be removed or corrected to reflect that a default is provided.

title: macOS-only sed syntax breaks the script on Linux
body: Line 68 uses `sed -i '' -E ...`, where the empty string argument is the macOS/BSD `sed` syntax for in-place editing without backup. On GNU sed (Linux, CI runners), `sed -i ''` treats `''` as a file name and fails with an error, so the script cannot update `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` on Linux. The script should use a portable form such as `sed -i.bak -E ... && rm -f "$ENV_FILE.bak"` or detect the platform, especially since this is a developer helper that may be run in containers/CI.

title: Developer-only webhook test script committed to the repository root scripts directory
body: This script is a local developer convenience for exposing a webhook URL via Tunnelmole and mutating a `.env` file. Committing it to the shared `scripts/` directory implies it is a supported repo tool, but it hardcodes paths (`../.env`), a fixed port, and a third-party tunneling service, and it writes to a real environment file. It should either be moved out of the repo (e.g. documented in a README/CONTRIBUTING note) or clearly marked as a local-only helper, otherwise it invites accidental execution in shared environments.

title: ConnectedCalendarList receives disableConnectionModification prop but the wrapper computes shouldDisableConnectionModification and never passes it
body: The wrapper computes `shouldDisableConnectionModification = isDisabled || disableConnectionModification` (line 166) and passes it to `SelectedCalendarsSettingsHeading`, but when rendering `ConnectedCalendarList` (line 179-187) it passes the raw `disableConnectionModification` prop and omits the scope-based `isDisabled` component. As a result, when a scope is disabled (`disabledScope === scope`), the heading hides the 'add calendar' control but each `CredentialActionsDropdown` still receives `disableConnectionModification={false}` and remains fully enabled, letting users delete cache / disconnect integrations while the rest of the scope is locked. The wrapper should pass `shouldDisableConnectionModification` (or `isDisabled || disableConnectionModification`) into `ConnectedCalendarList`.

title: cacheUpdatedAt enrichment changes the connectedCalendars output shape without a schema/type guard
body: The handler spreads `...calendar` and adds `cacheUpdatedAt`, changing the tRPC output type of `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. The UI consumes it via `RouterOutputs` inference, so this is type-safe end-to-end, but there is no explicit output schema (`output()` parser) on the procedure and no test pinning the new field. If the enrichment is later removed or renamed, downstream consumers (including platform atoms that are published as a library) will break at runtime rather than at compile time in external consumers. Adding an output schema or at least a handler-level test asserting `cacheUpdatedAt` presence would make the contract explicit.

title: No tests cover getCacheStatusByCredentialIds, deleteCacheHandler, or the CredentialActionsDropdown flow
body: The PR adds a new repository method (`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`), a new tRPC mutation (`deleteCache`) with an authorization check, and a new UI component with destructive actions, but none of the changed files include or reference tests. In particular there is no test verifying that (a) `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` returns the max updatedAt per credential and handles credentials with no cache rows, (b) `deleteCacheHandler` rejects credentialIds not owned by the session user, and (c) the dropdown hides the delete action for delegation credentials. Given the authorization-sensitive nature of `deleteCache`, at minimum a handler-level test for the ownership check is warranted before merge.

title: deleteCache authorization check misses delegation credentials, allowing cache deletion for credentials the user does not own
body: The handler verifies ownership with `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { id: credentialId, userId: user.id } })`. In cal.com, delegation credentials are stored with a different `userId` (the organization/service account owner) while the requesting user accesses them via `delegationCredentialId`. A user who can see a delegated Google Calendar credential in the connected-calendars UI (the UI explicitly renders CredentialActionsDropdown for delegated credentials, passing `delegationCredentialId`) will pass a credentialId that fails this `userId` check, so the mutation throws — but more importantly, the check does not consider credentials the user is authorized to act on through delegation, and conversely the subsequent `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany({ where: { credentialId } })` deletes cache rows purely by credentialId with no scoping to the verified credential beyond the findFirst. If the ownership check is ever broadened (or if a credential row exists where userId matches but the credential is a delegation credential shared across users), any user matching userId could wipe another principal's cache. The authorization must mirror how connectedCalendars resolves credentials (including delegation credentials via `enrichUserWithDelegationCredentialsIncludeServiceAccountKey` / `isDelegationCredential`), and the delete should be scoped to the exact credential record that was verified, not just the raw input id.

title: getCacheStatusByCredentialIds returns cache status for expired cache rows
body: `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` runs `prisma.calendarCache.groupBy({ by: ["credentialId"], where: { credentialId: { in: credentialIds } }, _max: { updatedAt: true } })` with no `expiresAt` filter. Every other read path in this repository (`getCachedAvailability`) filters `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }`. As a result, a credential whose cache rows have all expired (or whose rows were written long ago and never refreshed) will still report a `cacheUpdatedAt` timestamp, so the UI shows "Cache Status: Last updated ..." and offers "Delete cached data" for a credential that effectively has no usable cache. The groupBy should include `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }` in the `where` clause (and ideally aggregate `_max` over non-expired rows only) so the status reflects live cache state.

title: getCacheStatusByCredentialIds includes cache rows belonging to in-memory delegation credentials keyed only by userId
body: The repository's own `getCachedAvailability` documents that in-memory delegation credentials have no valid DB credentialId and that their cache rows are keyed by `userId` + `key` (see the long comment at lines 101-105: "we use in-memory delegation credentials for this which don't have valid credentialId"). `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups strictly by `credentialId`, so for a user whose calendar runs on an in-memory delegation credential, the cache rows exist with `credentialId` unset/null (or a synthetic negative id) and will never be grouped under the real credential id shown in the UI. The connectedCalendars handler then reports `cacheUpdatedAt: null` even though a live cache exists, so the "Delete cached data" action is hidden and the user cannot clear a cache that is actually being served. The status query needs to account for the userId-keyed cache rows used by delegation credentials (or the handler must resolve the effective credential/user pair the same way `getCachedAvailability` does).

title: connectedCalendars handler always instantiates the real CalendarCacheRepository, bypassing the mock when calendar-cache is disabled
body: The handler unconditionally does `new CalendarCacheRepository()` and calls `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`. The codebase provides `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` specifically for when the calendar-cache feature is disabled (its methods log "Skipping ... due to calendar-cache being disabled"), and `CalendarCache.init(null)` elsewhere selects the mock based on configuration. By hard-constructing the real repository, every `connectedCalendars` query — including for users/teams without the calendar-cache feature — now issues an extra `groupBy` DB query against `CalendarCache`. This adds latency to a hot, frequently-polled endpoint for all users and defeats the purpose of the mock. The handler should resolve the repository via the same factory/feature-flag mechanism used by `CalendarCache.init` (e.g. check the team feature flag or use the existing selection logic) so the query is skipped when the feature is off.

title: deleteCache mutation does not invalidate connectedCalendars, so cache status UI stays stale after deletion
body: The `deleteCacheMutation` only shows a toast and calls `onSuccess?.()`. The `disconnectMutation` in the same component explicitly invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` (and `apps.integrations`) in `onSettled`, but the delete-cache mutation has no invalidation. After a successful cache deletion the server returns `{ success: true }` and the `CalendarCache` rows are gone, yet the `connectedCalendars` query still holds the old `cacheUpdatedAt`, so the dropdown continues to show "Cache Status: Last updated ..." and the "Delete cached data" option remains visible/enabled until some unrelated refetch occurs. The mutation needs `onSettled`/`onSuccess` invalidation of `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` (the same query the wrapper reads `cacheUpdatedAt` from) so the UI reflects the deletion immediately.

title: Confirmation dialog closes immediately on confirm, before the mutation completes, with no pending/disabled state
body: In both confirmation dialogs, `onConfirm` fires `mutation.mutate(...)` and then unconditionally calls `setDeleteModalOpen(false)` / `setDisconnectModalOpen(false)` on the same tick. The dialog therefore closes instantly regardless of whether the mutation succeeds or fails, and there is no `isLoading`/pending guard on the confirm button. If the request is slow or fails, the user gets no in-dialog feedback (only a later toast) and can re-open and re-trigger the destructive action while a previous one is still in flight, enabling duplicate deletes/disconnects. The dialog should stay open (with the confirm button disabled/loading) until the mutation settles, then close on success.

title: Cache timestamp is formatted with a hard-coded "en-US" locale instead of the user's locale
body: The cache status line formats `cacheUpdatedAt` with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" })`. The component already uses `useLocale()` for all surrounding strings, so the timestamp is the only piece of user-facing text that ignores the user's locale and timezone conventions (e.g. a user with locale `de` or `ja` still gets a US-formatted date, and the time is rendered in the browser's timezone rather than the user's configured Cal.com timezone). This is inconsistent with the rest of the app's date rendering and will look wrong for non-en users. The formatter should use the locale from `useLocale()` (and ideally the user's timezone, as other parts of the app do).

title: Authorization failure throws a generic Error instead of a typed TRPC error, producing a 500 rather than a 403
body: When the credential is not found / not owned, the handler does `throw new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. In tRPC, a plain `Error` is surfaced to the client as an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (HTTP 500) with the message potentially masked in production, whereas an authorization failure should be a `TRPCError` with code `FORBIDDEN` (or `NOT_FOUND`). The client's `onError` currently just toasts a generic "Error deleting cache", so the user cannot distinguish "you don't have access" from a real server fault, and monitoring/alerting will treat an authz failure as a server error. The handler should throw `new TRPCError({ code: "FORBIDDEN", message: "..." })` (imported from `@trpc/server`) for the not-found/not-owned case.

title: updateManyByCredentialId accepts arbitrary update data and is called with an empty object, relying on Prisma @updatedAt side-effect
body: The new `updateManyByCredentialId(credentialId, data)` passes `data` straight to `prisma.selectedCalendar.updateMany`. Its only caller (`GoogleCalendarService.fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache`) invokes it as `updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})`, i.e. with an empty payload whose sole purpose is to bump `updatedAt` via the Prisma `@updatedAt` attribute. This is implicit and fragile: it depends entirely on the schema's `@updatedAt` behavior, the method name suggests a general-purpose updater, and any future caller passing real fields would silently mass-update every SelectedCalendar row for the credential (including event-type-scoped rows) with no user scoping. Either make the intent explicit (e.g. a dedicated `touchUpdatedAtByCredentialId(credentialId)` that sets `updatedAt: new Date()`), or at minimum constrain the method so it cannot be used as an unscoped mass-update primitive.

title: SelectedCalendar.updatedAt bump in fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache is not transactional with the cache writes and updates rows for all integrations' calendars under the credential
body: `fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache` writes cache entries per event-type group in a loop (`setAvailabilityInCache`) and only afterwards calls `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` to bump `updatedAt` on every SelectedCalendar row with that credentialId. Two issues: (1) the `updatedAt` bump is not atomic with the cache upserts, so a crash mid-loop leaves some cache rows written but `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` stale (or vice versa), giving an inconsistent "last updated" signal; (2) `updateMany({ where: { credentialId } })` matches SelectedCalendar rows regardless of `integration`, so if a credential id were ever shared across integrations it would touch unrelated rows — today it is google-only, but the method itself is unscoped. The PR description itself flags that this `updatedAt` is "not displayed in frontend" and questions whether it should exist at all; if it is kept, it should be scoped to `integration: this.integrationName` and ideally updated in the same flow that writes the cache.

title: Mock class declares deleteManyByCredential which is not part of ICalendarCacheRepository
body: `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` implements `deleteManyByCredential()` (line 23) even though `ICalendarCacheRepository` (the interface it declares to implement) has no such method — the real repository deletes cache via `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany` directly in `GoogleCalendarService.unwatchCalendar` and the new `deleteCacheHandler`, not through the repository interface. This is dead surface area on the mock that suggests a contract that doesn't exist; if the interface later changes, the mock will silently drift. Either add `deleteManyByCredential` to `ICalendarCacheRepository` (and implement it on the real repository, then use it in `deleteCache.handler.ts` and `unwatchCalendar`) so cache deletion goes through the repository abstraction consistently, or remove the stray mock method.

title: credentialIds may contain null/undefined for delegation credentials, producing a useless IN query and wrong cache mapping
body: The handler builds `credentialIds` with `connectedCalendars.map((cal) => cal.credentialId)` and passes them to `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`, which does `where: { credentialId: { in: credentialIds } }`. For delegation-credential calendars, `credentialId` can be null/absent (the codebase uses `isInMemoryDelegationCredential` / negative ids and `delegationCredentialId` instead — see `getConnectedDestinationCalendars.ts` and the repository's own comments about in-memory delegation credentials having no valid credentialId). Passing nulls into a Prisma `in` filter either throws or silently matches nothing, and the resulting `cacheStatusMap` is keyed by real credential ids, so delegated calendars will always get `cacheUpdatedAt: null` even when a userId-keyed cache exists. The handler should filter out non-positive/null credential ids before the query (mirroring `assertCalendarHasDbCredential`'s `credentialId < 0` guard) and handle the delegation-credential case explicitly.

title: macOS-only sed syntax breaks the script on Linux, and it mutates a shared .env file
body: The script uses `sed -i '' -E ...` (line 68), which is the BSD/macOS form of in-place sed; on GNU/Linux `sed -i ''` treats `''` as a file name and fails, so the `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` is never updated on Linux dev machines. Additionally, the script writes directly into `../.env` (a shared, git-ignored but developer-critical file), creating it if missing and overwriting an existing `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` — a destructive side effect for a helper script that should be opt-in. Use a portable in-place approach (e.g. a temp file + `mv`, or `sed -i.bak` with cleanup) and avoid silently creating/overwriting `.env`; at minimum guard the write behind a confirmation or write to a clearly-named override file.

title: Migration warning comment contradicts the actual migration (column is added WITH a default)
body: The migration's header warning states: "Added the required column `updatedAt` to the `CalendarCache` table without a default value. This is not possible if the table is not empty." But the very next statement is `ALTER TABLE "CalendarCache" ADD COLUMN "updatedAt" TIMESTAMP(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW();`, which adds the column WITH a default, so the warning is factually wrong and the migration is safe on non-empty tables. The stale Prisma-generated warning (left over from before the author added `DEFAULT NOW()`) should be removed or corrected, otherwise reviewers and future readers will believe the migration is unsafe and may attempt to rewrite it.

title: Cache status row is rendered as an interactive DropdownMenuItem with no action, trapping clicks and confusing users
body: The cache status display (lines 84-97) is wrapped in a `<DropdownMenuItem className="focus:ring-muted">` even though it performs no action — it is purely informational. In Radix dropdowns, a `DropdownMenuItem` is an interactive, focusable, clickable element; rendering a non-interactive status inside one means clicking the status row closes the menu (standard item behavior) and it can steal keyboard focus from the real actions, which is an accessibility and UX defect. The status should be rendered as a non-interactive element (e.g. a plain `<div>` with appropriate padding, or `DropdownMenuLabel`/`DropdownMenuSeparator` semantics) inside `DropdownMenuContent`, not as a `DropdownMenuItem`.

title: ConnectedCalendarList receives disableConnectionModification but the wrapper computes shouldDisableConnectionModification and never passes it down
body: The wrapper computes `shouldDisableConnectionModification = isDisabled || disableConnectionModification` (line 166) and passes it only to `SelectedCalendarsSettingsHeading` (to hide the "Add" selector). However, `ConnectedCalendarList` is rendered with `disableConnectionModification={disableConnectionModification}` (line 182) — the raw prop — not `shouldDisableConnectionModification`. `isDisabled` is true when `disabledScope === scope`, i.e. when the current scope is locked; in that state the heading correctly hides connection modification, but each `CredentialActionsDropdown` still receives `disableConnectionModification=false` and will render the "Remove App" action, letting users disconnect an integration while the scope is supposed to be read-only. The list should receive `shouldDisableConnectionModification` so the per-credential actions respect the disabled scope.

title: Unused CalendarsRouterHandlerCache type left in the router file
body: The file declares `type CalendarsRouterHandlerCache = { connectedCalendars?: ...; setDestinationCalendar?: ... }` (lines 8-11) but nothing references it — the handlers are imported dynamically inline in each procedure. It's dead code that will drift out of sync as handlers are added (it already omits `deleteCache`). Remove it or actually use it; as-is it's misleading.

title: getCacheStatusByCredentialIds return type uses updatedAt: Date | null but the implementation can return null for credentials with no rows only via absence, not per-row null
body: The interface declares `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds(credentialIds: number[]): Promise<{ credentialId: number; updatedAt: Date | null }[]>`. The implementation maps `prisma.calendarCache.groupBy` results, where `_max.updatedAt` is `Date | null` (null only if all grouped rows have null updatedAt — which cannot happen now that the column is `NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()`). More importantly, credentials with no cache rows are simply absent from the result array, so callers must distinguish "absent" from "present with null". The `| null` in the type is misleading given the NOT NULL column, and the contract would be clearer if the method either returned a status for every requested id (with null for missing) or the type documented that only credentials with rows are returned. The current handler works around this with `cacheStatusMap.get(...) || null`, but the interface should make the absence semantics explicit.

title: CRON cancellation query does not filter by method, so SMS reminders are also picked up and 'cancelled' via SendGrid
body: The new query `prisma.workflowReminder.findMany({ where: { cancelled: true, scheduledDate: { lte: dayjs().add(1, "hour") } } })` selects ALL cancelled reminders regardless of `method`. For SMS reminders, `referenceId` is a Twilio message SID, not a SendGrid batch_id, so the subsequent `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` with `batch_id: reminder.referenceId` will either fail or, worse, attempt to cancel an unrelated SendGrid batch if a SID collides with a batch id. The query must include `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` (and ideally `scheduled: true` / `referenceId: { not: null }`), otherwise SMS reminders marked cancelled are never actually cancelled in Twilio and are deleted from the DB by this job, leaving the scheduled SMS to still be delivered.

title: A single failed SendGrid cancellation aborts the whole loop and skips deletion of remaining cancelled reminders
body: The `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop awaits `client.request(...)` inside a single `try/catch` that wraps the entire loop. If the SendGrid call for the first reminder throws (network error, invalid batch_id, expired batch), the catch swallows it and the loop exits, so no further reminders are cancelled and none of the `workflowReminder.delete` promises (collected in `workflowRemindersToDelete`) are awaited. Cancelled reminders whose scheduled date is within the hour will then remain in the DB with `cancelled: true` and, because the earlier `deleteMany` only removes reminders with `scheduledDate <= now`, they can be re-processed on the next run — but more importantly, reminders later in the list never get their SendGrid scheduled send cancelled, so the emails are still sent. Each reminder's cancellation should be individually try/caught, and the DB delete should only happen after a successful SendGrid cancel (or be retried).

title: WorkflowReminder rows are deleted even when the SendGrid cancellation was never confirmed, and reminders without a referenceId are deleted without any provider call
body: The code unconditionally pushes `prisma.workflowReminder.delete({ where: { id: reminder.id } })` into `workflowRemindersToDelete` right after issuing the SendGrid cancel request, without checking the response and without handling reminders that have `cancelled: true` but `referenceId: null` (e.g. reminders that were never scheduled with SendGrid because they were beyond the 72h window and `scheduled: false`). For those, `batch_id: null` is sent to SendGrid. Deleting the DB row removes the only record that the email still needs to be cancelled, so if the SendGrid request silently fails or the row had no referenceId, the scheduled email will be sent and there is no longer any state to retry the cancellation. The delete should only occur after a successful provider cancellation, and rows without a referenceId should be handled explicitly.

title: deleteScheduledEmailReminder with immediateDelete=true cancels the SendGrid send but never deletes or marks the WorkflowReminder row
body: In `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminderId, referenceId, immediateDelete)`, when `immediateDelete` is true the function calls SendGrid `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` with `status: "cancel"` and then `return`s — it never deletes the `WorkflowReminder` database row nor sets `cancelled: true`. Callers that pass `immediateDelete: true` are `handleNewBooking.ts` (reschedule path, line 968) and `workflows.tsx` (workflow deleted / step deleted, lines 214 and 521). Consequence: after a booking is rescheduled, the old booking's reminder rows remain in the DB with `scheduled: true` and the old `referenceId`. The CRON job `scheduleEmailReminders` only deletes rows with `scheduledDate <= now`, so these stale rows persist; worse, the `unscheduledReminders` query filters on `scheduled: false`, but any code path that re-reads these rows (e.g. a later cancel of the same booking) will attempt to cancel an already-cancelled batch id. The reminder row must be deleted (or marked cancelled) in the `immediateDelete` branch as well.

title: Reminder cancellation calls are not awaited, so the booking-cancel request can complete before reminders are marked cancelled
body: The block `updatedBookings.forEach((booking) => { booking.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { ... deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId); ... }) })` calls the async `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` functions without `await` and without collecting the promises. `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` performs a Prisma `update` (setting `cancelled: true`) and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` performs a Twilio cancel plus a Prisma `delete`. Because these promises are not awaited, the handler proceeds to `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` and returns a 200 while the reminder updates may still be in flight or may fail silently (both functions swallow errors with `console.log`). If the process is under load or the DB write is slow, the response can be sent before `cancelled: true` is persisted; a crash or early return leaves scheduled emails unsuppressed. The promises must be collected and awaited (the previous code did this via `remindersToDelete` / `PrismaPromise` array).

title: Reschedule path does not await reminder cancellations and uses immediateDelete which leaves stale DB rows
body: In the reschedule branch, `originalRescheduledBooking.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true); ... })` is not awaited (the functions are async and perform SendGrid/Prisma/Twilio calls), and the surrounding `try/catch` only catches synchronous errors — any rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection. Additionally, per the `emailReminderManager.ts` finding, the `immediateDelete: true` path never deletes or marks the `WorkflowReminder` row, so the old booking's reminders stay in the DB with `scheduled: true`. Since the old booking is not deleted on reschedule (it is kept for history), these stale rows are never cleaned up by the `scheduledDate <= now` deleteMany in the CRON (they only get removed once their scheduled date passes), and any later operation iterating `workflowReminders` of the old booking will try to cancel an already-cancelled SendGrid batch. The calls must be awaited (e.g. `await Promise.all(...)`) and the reminder rows must be removed.

title: requestReschedule does not await reminder cancellation calls
body: In the `requestReschedule` mutation, `bookingToReschedule.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId); deleteScheduledSMSReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId); })` invokes async functions without `await` and discards the returned promises. `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` performs a Prisma `update` setting `cancelled: true` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` performs a Twilio cancel plus a Prisma `delete`; both swallow errors internally. Because they are not awaited, the mutation can return success before the reminders are actually cancelled/marked, and any failure is silently lost (only a console.log). If the DB update hasn't committed when the request finishes, the CRON job may not see `cancelled: true` in time and the scheduled email/SMS for the old booking slot will still be sent. The promises must be collected and awaited before the mutation returns.

title: Multiple reminder-cancellation loops in the update mutation are not awaited
body: In the `update` mutation there are three separate `forEach` loops that call the async `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` without awaiting them: (1) `remindersToDelete.flat().forEach(...)` around line 376 (event types disabled), (2) `remindersToUpdate.forEach(async (reminder) => {...})` around line 574 (edited steps — the callback is async but forEach still doesn't await it), and (3) the deleted-step branch around line 519. None of the returned promises are collected or awaited, and the mutation proceeds to delete workflow steps / update the workflow and returns. Consequences: the HTTP response can be sent before the Prisma `update({cancelled: true})` / `delete` and Twilio cancels complete; failures are swallowed by the `console.log` inside the manager functions; and because `workflowStep.delete` runs right after, the `workflowReminder` rows (which have `onDelete: Cascade` to the step) may be cascade-deleted by Prisma before the manager's own `delete`/`update` executes, causing the manager's DB writes to fail on a missing row while the SendGrid/Twilio cancellation may or may not have happened — leaving provider-side scheduled sends alive with no DB record to retry. All cancellation promises must be gathered (e.g. `await Promise.all(reminders.map(...))`) before deleting steps.

title: deleteScheduledSMSReminder deletes the DB row even when the Twilio cancellation fails
body: `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` wraps both `twilio.cancelSMS(referenceId)` and `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` in a single try/catch. If `cancelSMS` throws (Twilio API error, already-completed message, invalid SID), the catch logs the error and the Prisma `delete` is never executed — that part is fine — but the inverse is also true: there is no verification that the Twilio cancellation succeeded before the row is removed, and more importantly the function gives callers no signal of failure (it always resolves). Combined with the un-awaited call sites, a failed Twilio cancel is indistinguishable from success, and because the row is deleted on success while the CRON has no equivalent SMS-cancellation path (the new CRON logic only handles EMAIL), a missed Twilio cancellation means the SMS will still be delivered with no DB record left to retry. The function should rethrow or return a status so callers can react, and the CRON should also process cancelled SMS reminders.

title: The 'unscheduled reminders' query can pick up reminders that were just marked cancelled, causing emails for cancelled bookings to be scheduled and sent
body: The query for `unscheduledReminders` filters on `method: EMAIL, scheduled: false, scheduledDate <= now + 72h`. It does not exclude rows with `cancelled: true`. A reminder that was created with `scheduled: false` (scheduled date more than 72h out, see `emailReminderManager.ts` line 184) and later cancelled via `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` (which only sets `cancelled: true` and leaves `scheduled: false`) will match this query on the next CRON run. The job will then create a SendGrid batch, send the email with `sendAt`, and set `scheduled: true` — resurrecting a reminder for a cancelled/rescheduled booking. The query must add `cancelled: { not: true }` (or `cancelled: false` / `OR: [{cancelled: null}, {cancelled: false}]` since the column is nullable).

title: New 'cancelled' column is nullable with no default, so existing and new rows have NULL instead of false
body: The migration adds `"cancelled" BOOLEAN` with no `NOT NULL` and no `DEFAULT false`. The Prisma schema declares `cancelled Boolean?` (nullable). All existing rows get NULL, and new `workflowReminder.create` calls in `emailReminderManager.ts` / `smsReminderManager.ts` do not set `cancelled`, so new rows are also NULL. The CRON query in `scheduleEmailReminders.ts` filters `cancelled: true`, which works, but any future query filtering `cancelled: false` (a natural way to express 'not cancelled') will silently miss all NULL rows, and the `unscheduledReminders` query (which needs to exclude cancelled reminders, see related finding) cannot simply use `cancelled: false`. The column should be `BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false` with a backfill (`UPDATE "WorkflowReminder" SET "cancelled" = false WHERE "cancelled" IS NULL`) and the schema should be `cancelled Boolean @default(false)`.

title: The initial deleteMany removes past-due reminders regardless of cancelled/scheduled state, deleting rows that the new cancellation logic depends on
body: The first statement `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany({ where: { method: EMAIL, scheduledDate: { lte: now } } })` deletes every EMAIL reminder whose scheduled date has passed, including rows with `cancelled: true` that have not yet been processed by the new cancellation block (which runs after this delete). If a reminder was marked cancelled but its scheduled date is already in the past (e.g. the booking was cancelled after the reminder's scheduled send time but before SendGrid actually delivered it, or the CRON was down), this deleteMany removes the row before the cancellation loop can call SendGrid to cancel the scheduled send — so the email is never cancelled at the provider and will still be delivered. The deleteMany should exclude cancelled rows (`cancelled: { not: true }`) or the cancellation block should run before it.

title: Sender ID input is now rendered for EMAIL actions, allowing users to set an SMS sender ID on email steps
body: The refactor changed the wrapper condition from `{(isPhoneNumberNeeded || isSenderIdNeeded) && (...)}` to a separate `isPhoneNumberNeeded` block plus an unconditional `<div className="mt-2 rounded-md bg-gray-50 p-4 pt-0">` that renders either the Sender ID input (when `isSenderIdNeeded`) or the Sender Name input. `isSenderIdNeeded` is initialized to `true` when `step?.action === SMS_NUMBER || step?.action === SMS_ATTENDEE`, but it is only ever set to `false` in the action `onChange` handler — for an existing EMAIL step loaded from the DB, `isSenderIdNeeded` stays `false`, so this is mostly fine; however the sender block is now always rendered even for actions where neither sender ID nor sender name is relevant, and the `isSenderIdNeeded` state is not re-synced when `step` changes (component reuse across steps), so switching between steps in the UI can show the wrong sender field. This is a UI-state regression introduced by the restructuring; the sender block should be gated on `isSenderIdNeeded || !isEmailSubjectNeeded` (or equivalent) and the state should be derived from the current action.

title: CRON cancellation uses wrong SendGrid endpoint and can cancel the wrong batch
body: The new cancellation loop calls `client.request({ url: "/v3/user/scheduled_sends", method: "POST", body: { batch_id: reminder.referenceId, status: "cancel" } })`. Per the PR description, the previously used `DELETE /v3/user/scheduled_sends/${referenceId}` was wrong because it removes the cancel status; the correct SendGrid API to cancel a scheduled send is `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends/{batch_id}` with body `{ status: "cancel" }` — i.e. the batch_id must be in the URL path, not in the request body. As written, the request posts to the collection endpoint with a `batch_id` field in the body, which SendGrid will not interpret as a cancellation of that batch. Additionally, `reminder.referenceId` is typed `string | null` and is passed directly as `batch_id`; if it is null the request is malformed. Consequence: cancelled/rescheduled booking emails are still sent, which is exactly the bug this PR claims to fix. The same wrong-endpoint pattern is used in `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` with `immediateDelete: true` (emailReminderManager.ts lines 213-223), which is called from workflows.tsx when a workflow or step is deleted.

title: Cancellation query does not filter by method, so SMS reminders are treated as SendGrid email batches
body: `remindersToCancel` is queried with only `cancelled: true` and a `scheduledDate` filter — there is no `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` filter. The `cancelled` flag is only ever set by `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` (email path), but the query then uses `reminder.referenceId` as a SendGrid `batch_id` for every matching row. For SMS reminders the `referenceId` is a Twilio message SID, not a SendGrid batch id, so the CRON job would send a bogus cancellation request to SendGrid using a Twilio SID. More importantly, the subsequent `prisma.workflowReminder.delete` removes the row regardless of method, and the missing method filter means the intent (only cancel scheduled emails) is not enforced at the data layer. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` to the `where` clause.

title: Reminder rows are deleted even if the SendGrid cancellation fails, and a single failure aborts the whole loop
body: Inside the `for` loop, `await client.request(...)` is awaited before the delete promise is created. If the SendGrid request throws (network error, 4xx/5xx), the exception propagates to the outer `try/catch`, which logs and swallows it — but any reminders already queued in `workflowRemindersToDelete` are still deleted via `Promise.all`, and all remaining reminders in `remindersToCancel` are never processed. So a transient SendGrid failure causes: (1) rows whose emails were NOT actually cancelled to be deleted from the DB (the email will still be sent by SendGrid and the row is gone so it can never be retried), and (2) all subsequent cancelled reminders in the batch to be skipped entirely. The delete should only be enqueued after a successful cancellation response, and per-reminder errors should be caught individually so one failure doesn't abort the rest.

title: Past-due reminder cleanup deletes cancelled rows before they are processed, and deletes unscheduled rows that were never sent
body: The first statement `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany({ where: { method: EMAIL, scheduledDate: { lte: now } } })` runs BEFORE the cancellation block. Any reminder whose `scheduledDate` has already passed is deleted here without ever being checked against `cancelled` or being sent/cancelled at SendGrid. Two problems: (1) a reminder marked `cancelled: true` whose scheduled date just passed will be deleted by this statement and never reach the cancellation loop, so the SendGrid scheduled send is never cancelled and the email still goes out; (2) an unscheduled reminder (`scheduled: false`) whose date has passed is silently deleted without the email ever being sent (the later `unscheduledReminders` query only picks up dates within 72h in the future, so past-due unscheduled reminders are lost). The cleanup should exclude `cancelled: true` rows (or run after cancellation), and should not delete unscheduled past-due rows without attempting to send them.

title: Reminder cancellation calls are not awaited, so failures are silent and ordering is not guaranteed
body: In the `updatedBookings.forEach(...)` loop, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` are invoked without `await` (and the enclosing `forEach` callback is not async). These functions are async and internally catch errors, so the promises float. Consequences: (1) the handler can return before the `cancelled: true` DB update (or the Twilio cancel / row delete for SMS) has completed, so a crash or early response can leave reminders un-cancelled; (2) unhandled promise rejections are possible if the internal try/catch is bypassed; (3) for SMS reminders, `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` now deletes the DB row immediately, so a non-awaited call racing with the later `prismaPromises`/`apiDeletes` `Promise.all` creates unclear ordering. The loop should be `for...of` with `await`, or the promises should be collected and awaited.

title: Reschedule reminder cancellation is not awaited and uses immediateDelete for email only
body: When rescheduling, `originalRescheduledBooking.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { ... deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true); ... deleteScheduledSMSReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId); })` is not awaited (the callback is not async and the calls are not collected). The surrounding `try/catch` therefore cannot actually catch async failures — it only catches synchronous throws. Additionally, the email path uses `immediateDelete: true`, which performs the (incorrect, see other finding) SendGrid cancel synchronously, while the SMS path deletes the DB row immediately. Because nothing is awaited, the new booking's `scheduleWorkflowReminders` (line 1269) can run concurrently with the old reminders' cancellation, and a failure leaves stale scheduled emails active for the old booking. Await each cancellation (e.g. `await Promise.all(originalRescheduledBooking.workflowReminders.map(...))`).

title: immediateDelete path uses the wrong SendGrid endpoint and never deletes the DB row
body: `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminderId, referenceId, immediateDelete = true)` sends `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` with `{ batch_id: referenceId, status: "cancel" }` in the body. As noted in the PR description, the correct SendGrid cancellation API is `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends/{batch_id}` with `{ status: "cancel" }` — the batch id belongs in the URL path. With the batch_id in the body, SendGrid will not cancel the scheduled send. Furthermore, when `immediateDelete` is true the function `return`s immediately after the API call and never deletes or marks the `workflowReminder` row, so the row stays in the DB with `scheduled: true` and the stale `referenceId`; the CRON cleanup at the top of `scheduleEmailReminders.ts` will eventually delete it only when `scheduledDate` passes, but the SendGrid send itself was never cancelled. This path is used when a workflow or a workflow step is deleted (workflows.tsx lines 214 and 521), meaning deleting a workflow can leave its scheduled emails active. Fix the URL to `/v3/user/scheduled_sends/${referenceId}` and delete/mark the DB row after a successful cancellation.

title: deleteScheduledEmailReminder deletes the row when referenceId is null, losing reminders that were never scheduled at SendGrid
body: When `referenceId` is null the function deletes the `workflowReminder` row outright. A null `referenceId` occurs for reminders created with `scheduled: false` (scheduled more than 72h out, handled later by the CRON job — see the `else if (scheduledDate.isAfter(currentDate.add(72, "hour")))` branch at line 182-193 which creates the row without a referenceId). Deleting such a row on booking cancellation is correct in intent, but the function conflates two cases: a reminder that was never scheduled (safe to delete) and a reminder that WAS scheduled at SendGrid but whose referenceId was lost/not stored. There is no `scheduled` check, so if a row has `scheduled: true` but a null referenceId (data inconsistency), the SendGrid send cannot be cancelled and the row is silently deleted, leaving an orphaned scheduled email. At minimum, guard with `scheduled: false` before deleting, and log when a scheduled reminder has no referenceId.

title: deleteScheduledSMSReminder deletes the DB row even when the Twilio cancellation fails
body: `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` calls `await twilio.cancelSMS(referenceId)` and then unconditionally `await prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` inside the same `try`. If `cancelSMS` throws, the catch block logs the error and the function returns — but because the delete is in the `try` after the cancel, a cancel failure skips the delete (row remains, which is arguably safe). However, the callers in `handleCancelBooking.ts` and `bookings.tsx` no longer delete reminder rows themselves (that logic was removed in this PR), so the ONLY thing standing between a cancelled booking and an SMS being sent is this function's `cancelSMS` call. If Twilio is down or the SID is invalid, the error is swallowed by the `catch` and the reminder row remains `scheduled: true` with a live Twilio SID — the SMS will still be delivered. There is no `cancelled` flag mechanism for SMS (unlike email), so a failed cancellation is unrecoverable and silent. At minimum, the function should rethrow or the callers should be notified, and ideally SMS reminders should also get the `cancelled` flag + CRON-based retry treatment that emails now have.

title: Reminder cancellation in workflow update is not awaited and rows are no longer deleted
body: In the `update` mutation, `remindersToDelete.flat().forEach((reminder) => { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(...); deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...); })` is fire-and-forget (no await, non-async callback). The previous code explicitly deleted the reminder rows via `ctx.prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany` and awaited `Promise.all(deleteReminderPromise)`; that deletion was removed in this PR. Now: (1) for email reminders with a referenceId, only `cancelled: true` is set and the row persists until the CRON job deletes it — but the CRON job only processes rows with `scheduledDate` within the next hour, so rows for bookings further out stay in the DB indefinitely with `cancelled: true` (they will never be sent because the unscheduled-reminders query filters `scheduled: false`, but they accumulate); (2) for email reminders WITHOUT a referenceId, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` deletes the row, but since the call is not awaited, the subsequent `workflowsOnEventTypes.deleteMany` and step updates can run before the delete completes; (3) for SMS reminders the row is deleted inside `deleteScheduledSMSReminder`, again un-awaited. All of these should be collected into a promise array and awaited before proceeding.

title: userWorkflow.steps.map(async ...) is not awaited — step deletions and reminder cancellations race with the rest of the update
body: The block `userWorkflow.steps.map(async (oldStep) => { ... })` (line 505) uses `Array.map` with an async callback and is never awaited. Inside it: reminder cancellations (`deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder`, themselves async and un-awaited), `ctx.prisma.workflowStep.delete`, `ctx.prisma.workflowStep.update`, and `ctx.prisma.booking.findMany` + `scheduleEmailReminder`/`scheduleSMSReminder` calls. Because the outer `map` promise is discarded, the mutation can return (and the final `workflow.update` / `workflow.findFirst` at lines 814-842 can execute) before any of these complete. Consequences: the response can report a workflow state that doesn't yet reflect step deletions; reminder cancellations for deleted/edited steps may not have run before new reminders are scheduled (duplicate emails); and unhandled rejections from the async callbacks are uncaught. This should be `await Promise.all(userWorkflow.steps.map(async ...))` or a `for...of` loop with awaits.

title: Cancelled email reminders for far-future bookings accumulate forever
body: When a workflow is updated and event types are removed, email reminders are now marked `cancelled: true` instead of deleted (line 378). The CRON job `scheduleEmailReminders.ts` only selects cancelled reminders with `scheduledDate <= now + 1 hour` (line 44-51) and deletes them after cancelling at SendGrid. A reminder for a booking that is, say, 30 days out will therefore sit in the DB with `cancelled: true` for 30 days, and — more importantly — the `unscheduledReminders` query (line 80-98) filters `scheduled: false`, so a cancelled-but-still-`scheduled: true` row is never picked up for sending (good), but it is also never cleaned up until its date is within an hour. This is a slow leak of dead rows and means the `cancelled` flag must be checked in every future query that touches workflow reminders. Consider deleting the row immediately when the booking is far in the future and the SendGrid send can be cancelled right away, or adding a cleanup for old cancelled rows.

title: New cancelled column is nullable with no default, so existing and new rows have NULL instead of false
body: The migration adds `"cancelled" BOOLEAN` (nullable, no default) and the Prisma schema declares `cancelled Boolean?`. Every existing row gets NULL, and new reminders created in `scheduleEmailReminder`/`scheduleSMSReminder` (emailReminderManager.ts lines 169-193, smsReminderManager.ts lines 148-172) do not set `cancelled`, so they are also NULL. The CRON query uses `cancelled: true`, which correctly excludes NULL rows in Prisma, but any code doing truthiness checks or `cancelled === false` comparisons will misbehave, and the column wastes storage on NULLs. Prefer `BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false` in the migration and `cancelled Boolean @default(false)` in the schema so the flag has a well-defined value for all rows.

title: Unscheduled-reminders query can pick up cancelled reminders and send them
body: The `unscheduledReminders` query filters `method: EMAIL, scheduled: false, scheduledDate <= now + 72h` but does NOT filter `cancelled: false` (or `cancelled: null`). A reminder that was created with `scheduled: false` (booking more than 72h out) and later cancelled via `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` (which sets `cancelled: true` but leaves `scheduled: false` and keeps the row) will match this query once its `scheduledDate` falls within the 72-hour window. The CRON job will then schedule and send the email via SendGrid even though the booking was cancelled — reintroducing the exact bug this PR is meant to fix, for the >72h cancellation case. The query must add `cancelled: false` (or `NOT: { cancelled: true }`) to the where clause. Note the cancellation block only handles reminders within the next hour, so a reminder cancelled while still >1h out but <72h out is never cancelled at SendGrid and would be sent by this query.

title: Email reminders cancelled via flag but SMS reminders deleted immediately — inconsistent lifecycle and lost audit trail
body: For a cancelled booking, email reminders are now marked `cancelled: true` and left in the DB (deletion deferred to the CRON job), while SMS reminders are deleted immediately by `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` (smsReminderManager.ts line 182). This asymmetry means: (1) the `workflowReminders` relation on the booking behaves differently per method, which can surprise any code inspecting reminders of a cancelled booking; (2) if the Twilio cancel fails, the row is still deleted (the delete is in the same try block after the cancel — actually it is skipped on throw, but the caller doesn't await or check, so the outcome is nondeterministic from the caller's perspective); (3) there is no record that an SMS reminder existed for a cancelled booking. For consistency and recoverability, SMS reminders should follow the same pattern: mark `cancelled: true` and let a CRON job perform the Twilio cancellation (the `scheduleSMSReminders` CRON would need a matching block), or at minimum the delete should only happen after a confirmed successful Twilio cancellation and the call should be awaited.

title: requestReschedule reminder cancellation is not awaited
body: In the `requestReschedule` mutation, `bookingToReschedule.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId); deleteScheduledSMSReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId); })` is fire-and-forget. The previous implementation collected `PrismaPromise`s and awaited `Promise.all(remindersToDelete)`. Now nothing is awaited, so the mutation can complete (and the reschedule email at line 567 can be sent) before the old reminders are actually cancelled/marked. If the process crashes or the DB update fails silently (both delete functions swallow errors internally), the old booking's reminders remain active and the attendee receives reminders for a booking that has been marked `rescheduled: true` / `CANCELLED`. Collect the promises and `await Promise.all(...)`.

title: Marking a reminder cancelled does not clear scheduled/referenceId, leaving stale SendGrid state
body: When a reminder is cancelled via the flag (`prisma.workflowReminder.update({ data: { cancelled: true } })`), the row keeps `scheduled: true` and its `referenceId` (the SendGrid batch id). The CRON job later cancels the SendGrid send and deletes the row, which is fine, but between cancellation and CRON execution the row still claims `scheduled: true`. Any other code that queries scheduled reminders (e.g. to display or count them) will see a cancelled reminder as still scheduled. Consider also setting `scheduled: false` when marking `cancelled: true`, so the row's state is unambiguous, and ensure the CRON cancellation block keys off `cancelled` rather than `scheduled`.

title: Cancellation loop performs a sequential await per reminder inside a for-loop
body: The cancellation loop `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel) { await client.request(...); ... }` serializes all SendGrid cancellation API calls. With many cancelled reminders due within the hour (the exact scenario this PR is fixing — previously cancellations failed after 100 pending), the CRON job (running every 15 minutes) could take a long time and risk overlapping runs or timing out. The deletes are already batched via `Promise.all(workflowRemindersToDelete)`, but the API calls are not. Consider batching the SendGrid requests with limited concurrency (e.g. `Promise.all` over chunks, or a concurrency-limited mapper) so the job completes quickly and predictably.

title: CRON cancellation query does not filter by method or scheduled status, so it cancels SMS reminders and unscheduled reminders
body: The new `remindersToCancel` query selects `prisma.workflowReminder.findMany({ where: { cancelled: true, scheduledDate: { lte: dayjs().add(1, "hour") } } })` without filtering on `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` or `scheduled: true`. The `cancelled` flag is only ever set by `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` (emailReminderManager.ts), but the query will also match SMS reminders whose `cancelled` column happens to be true (e.g. legacy rows or future writers), and it matches reminders that were never scheduled in SendGrid (`scheduled: false`, `referenceId: null`). For those rows the code then calls SendGrid `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` with `batch_id: reminder.referenceId` (which is `null` for unscheduled reminders) and deletes the DB row. Consequences: (1) SMS reminder rows get deleted from the database without the Twilio scheduled message actually being cancelled, so the SMS will still be delivered by Twilio while the DB record is gone; (2) SendGrid is called with a null batch_id, producing API errors that abort the whole cancellation loop (the try/catch wraps the entire for-loop, so one failure prevents all subsequent reminders from being cancelled and deleted); (3) unscheduled (future, CRON-scheduled) email reminders are deleted from the DB, so they will never be scheduled/sent. The query must be restricted to `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL, scheduled: true, referenceId: { not: null }` (and ideally `cancelled: true`), and per-reminder errors should be caught individually so one bad row doesn't block the rest.

title: A single SendGrid failure aborts cancellation of all remaining reminders, re-introducing the 'emails still sent' bug
body: The cancellation loop `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel) { await client.request(...); ... }` is wrapped in a single try/catch around the whole loop. If the SendGrid `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` call throws for any reminder (invalid/expired batch_id, rate limit, network error), the exception exits the loop, the remaining reminders are never cancelled in SendGrid nor deleted from the DB, and the error is only logged. Because the CRON only picks up reminders whose `scheduledDate` is within the next hour, a reminder that fails cancellation once will keep failing (or be skipped) on subsequent runs once its window passes, and the scheduled email is still delivered — exactly the bug this PR is meant to fix. Each reminder's SendGrid call and DB delete must be individually try/caught (or the DB row should only be deleted after a successful cancel, with failures retried on the next run).

title: WorkflowReminder rows are deleted even if the SendGrid cancellation failed
body: In the cancellation loop, `prisma.workflowReminder.delete({ where: { id: reminder.id } })` promises are collected and executed via `Promise.all(workflowRemindersToDelete)` after the SendGrid calls. However, because the SendGrid `await client.request(...)` and the delete-promise creation are interleaved in the same loop inside one try/catch, and because a delete promise is created regardless of whether the preceding SendGrid request for that reminder succeeded (the request is awaited, but if it throws the loop aborts before pushing — yet for reminders processed before the failure their deletes run), the DB row can be removed while the SendGrid scheduled send remains active. More importantly, the delete is unconditional: there is no check that the SendGrid cancel actually succeeded before removing the row, so a transient SendGrid failure (caught by the outer catch) still leaves the DB row deleted for any reminders whose delete promise was already queued, permanently losing the ability to retry the cancellation. The row should only be deleted after a confirmed successful SendGrid cancellation; on failure the row must be kept (with `cancelled: true`) so the next CRON run retries.

title: `immediateDelete` path cancels the SendGrid send but never deletes or updates the WorkflowReminder row, leaking rows and skipping DB cleanup
body: In `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`, when `immediateDelete` is true the function calls SendGrid `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` with `status: "cancel"` and then `return`s — it never deletes the `workflowReminder` row nor marks it cancelled. Callers that pass `immediateDelete: true` are `handleNewBooking.ts` (reschedule path, line 968) and `workflows.tsx` (workflow delete, line 214; step delete, line 521). In the reschedule case the old booking's reminder rows are left in the DB forever with `scheduled: true` and a now-cancelled `referenceId`; the CRON cleanup at the top of `scheduleEmailReminders.ts` only deletes rows whose `scheduledDate <= now`, so these stale rows persist and, worse, if such a row also had `cancelled` set it would be re-processed. In the workflow-delete and step-delete cases, the rows belong to steps that are subsequently deleted via `ctx.prisma.workflowStep.delete` / cascade, but the reminder rows are only removed by the `onDelete: Cascade` on `workflowStep` — however `handleNewBooking.ts` has no such cascade protection for the reschedule path (the old booking is not deleted), so rows leak. The `immediateDelete` branch must also delete the reminder row (or set `cancelled: true` and let the CRON delete it) after a successful SendGrid cancel.

title: Reminder cancellation calls are not awaited, so the handler can return before reminders are marked cancelled
body: The block `updatedBookings.forEach((booking) => { booking.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { if (reminder.method === WorkflowMethods.EMAIL) { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId); } else if (...) { deleteScheduledSMSReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId); } }); });` invokes the async functions without `await` and discards the returned promises. `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` performs a Prisma `update` (setting `cancelled: true`) and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` performs a Twilio cancel plus a Prisma `delete`; none of this is awaited, and the function's own try/catch swallows errors. The handler then proceeds to `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` and returns 200. If the process is under load or the DB write is slow, the HTTP response can be sent before the `cancelled` flag is persisted; a crash or early return in between leaves the scheduled email active and the row not marked, so the CRON will never cancel it and the reminder email is still sent. The same un-awaited pattern exists in `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx` (requestReschedule, lines 488-494) and `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/workflows.tsx` (multiple forEach loops). All reminder-cancellation promises should be collected and awaited (and errors surfaced) before responding.

title: deleteScheduledSMSReminder deletes the DB row even when the Twilio cancellation fails
body: `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` does `if (referenceId) { await twilio.cancelSMS(referenceId); } await prisma.workflowReminder.delete({ where: { id: reminderId } });` inside a single try/catch that only logs. If `twilio.cancelSMS` throws (network error, invalid SID, Twilio outage), the exception jumps to the catch and the Prisma delete is skipped — good — but the caller in `handleCancelBooking.ts` / `bookings.tsx` / `workflows.tsx` never awaits or inspects the promise, so the failure is silently swallowed and the reminder row remains with `scheduled: true`. There is no `cancelled` flag for SMS reminders (the new column is only used for EMAIL), so the CRON has no mechanism to retry the Twilio cancellation: the scheduled SMS will still be sent by Twilio while the system believes cancellation is in progress. Either add a retry path for SMS (e.g. also set `cancelled: true` and have a CRON job cancel Twilio scheduled messages), or at minimum surface/propagate the error so the booking-cancellation flow can report failure. As written, SMS reminders for cancelled bookings can still be delivered with no record that cancellation was attempted.

title: Reschedule path cancels old email reminders with immediateDelete but leaves SMS reminders and DB rows inconsistent, and cancellation is not awaited
body: In the reschedule branch, `originalRescheduledBooking.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { if (reminder.method === WorkflowMethods.EMAIL) { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true); } else if (reminder.method === WorkflowMethods.SMS) { deleteScheduledSMSReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId); } });` has three problems: (1) the calls are not awaited, so the reschedule response can be returned before the SendGrid cancel / Twilio cancel / DB deletes complete; (2) for EMAIL reminders, `immediateDelete: true` cancels the SendGrid send but (per the emailReminderManager finding) never deletes or marks the `workflowReminder` row, so the old booking's reminder rows leak in the DB with `scheduled: true`; (3) the outer try/catch only catches synchronous errors — since the promises are not awaited, any async rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection instead of being logged by the catch. The old booking is not deleted on reschedule, so these stale rows are never cascade-removed. The promises must be collected and awaited, and the reminder rows must actually be removed (or marked cancelled) for both EMAIL and SMS.

title: Unscheduled-reminder scheduling query does not exclude cancelled reminders, so a cancelled reminder can still be scheduled and sent
body: The query that finds reminders to schedule (`prisma.workflowReminder.findMany({ where: { method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL, scheduled: false, scheduledDate: { lte: dayjs().add(72, "hour") } } })`) does not filter on `cancelled`. A reminder that was created with `scheduled: false` (because its scheduledDate was more than 72 hours out, see emailReminderManager.ts line 184) and later cancelled via `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` (which sets `cancelled: true` but leaves `scheduled: false` and keeps the row) will still be picked up by this query once its scheduledDate falls within 72 hours. The CRON will then create a SendGrid batch, send the email with `sendAt`, and mark the row `scheduled: true` — resurrecting a reminder the user cancelled. The `unscheduledReminders` query must add `cancelled: { not: true }` (or `OR: [{ cancelled: false }, { cancelled: null }]`) so cancelled-but-unscheduled reminders are skipped (and ideally deleted).

title: New `cancelled` column is nullable with no default, so existing and new rows have NULL instead of false
body: The migration adds `"cancelled" BOOLEAN` (nullable, no default) and the Prisma schema declares `cancelled Boolean?` (optional). Every existing WorkflowReminder row gets `NULL`, and rows created by `scheduleEmailReminder` / `scheduleSMSReminder` (which do not set `cancelled`) also get `NULL`. All the new logic relies on truthiness checks (`cancelled: true` in the CRON query; `data: { cancelled: true }` on update), which works for the CRON's `where: { cancelled: true }` filter, but any code that checks `reminder.cancelled === false` or treats NULL as false will misbehave, and the column wastes storage on a tri-state where a boolean only needs two. More importantly, the CRON cleanup query `deleteMany({ where: { method: EMAIL, scheduledDate: { lte: now } } })` deletes rows regardless of `cancelled`, which is fine, but the scheduling query (see separate finding) treats NULL as 'not cancelled' — acceptable — yet the schema should be `Boolean @default(false)` with a migration `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN "cancelled" BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false` (or at least `DEFAULT false`) so the invariant 'cancelled is always a concrete boolean' holds and future queries can safely use `cancelled: false`.

title: Reminder deletion in workflow update is fire-and-forget; DB rows can be deleted by later logic while SendGrid sends remain active
body: In the `update` mutation, `remindersToDelete.flat().forEach((reminder) => { if (reminder.method === WorkflowMethods.EMAIL) { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId); } else if (...) { deleteScheduledSMSReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId); } });` calls the async deleters without awaiting them. For EMAIL reminders without a `referenceId` (unscheduled, `scheduled: false`), `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` deletes the row; for those with a `referenceId` it only sets `cancelled: true`. Because nothing is awaited, the mutation continues and eventually returns the updated workflow while these operations are still in flight; if the process crashes or the event loop is saturated, rows may be left in an inconsistent state (e.g. `cancelled` not yet persisted, or row deleted while SendGrid send still active for the SMS path). The same un-awaited `forEach` pattern appears at lines 212 (workflow delete), 519 (step delete), and 574 (step edit). All of these should collect promises and `await Promise.all(...)` before proceeding, and the workflow delete path should await cancellation before `ctx.prisma.workflow.deleteMany` removes the workflow (and cascades the reminder rows), otherwise the cascade can delete reminder rows before the SendGrid/Twilio cancellation has been recorded.

title: deleteScheduledEmailReminder deletes the row when referenceId is null, but for a scheduled reminder whose referenceId was lost the SendGrid send is never cancelled
body: When `referenceId` is null/empty, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` immediately deletes the `workflowReminder` row and returns. For a reminder that was actually scheduled in SendGrid (row has `scheduled: true`) but whose `referenceId` was never persisted or was lost, this deletes the only record of the scheduled send without calling SendGrid to cancel it, so the email will still be delivered. This is a defensive-coding gap: the function should distinguish 'never scheduled' (`scheduled === false`, safe to just delete) from 'scheduled but referenceId missing' (should attempt cancellation by other means or at least log loudly / not silently delete). As written, any data-integrity issue with `referenceId` silently converts into 'reminder email still sent', which is the exact failure mode this PR is fixing.

title: CRON cleanup deletes past-due EMAIL reminders regardless of `scheduled` flag, racing with the scheduling loop
body: The first statement of the handler, `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany({ where: { method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL, scheduledDate: { lte: dayjs().toISOString() } } })`, deletes every EMAIL reminder whose scheduledDate has passed, including rows with `scheduled: true` whose SendGrid send may not have been delivered yet (SendGrid delivers at `sendAt`; clock skew or a slightly early CRON run can delete the row before SendGrid fires). It also deletes rows with `scheduled: false` that the same handler run is about to process further down (the `unscheduledReminders` query uses `scheduledDate <= now + 72h`, which includes past-due unscheduled rows). Deleting a `scheduled: true` row removes the record needed to cancel the send if the booking is cancelled in the window between the delete and the actual SendGrid delivery. The cleanup should be restricted to rows that are actually past and no longer actionable (e.g. `scheduled: true` and `scheduledDate` well in the past, or `cancelled: true`), and should not race with the scheduling query in the same run.

title: forEach with async callback does not await calendar/video deletions before sending reschedule email
body: The code uses `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })`. `Array.prototype.forEach` does not await the promises returned by its callback, so the `await getCalendar(...)` and the subsequent `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` / `deleteMeeting(...)` calls run as fire-and-forget. The function proceeds immediately to `sendRequestRescheduleEmail` (line 143) and returns `true` before the external calendar events and video meetings have actually been deleted. Consequences: (1) the reschedule email can be sent while the old event still exists on the provider's calendar, causing double-booking; (2) errors thrown inside the async callback are not caught by the surrounding `try/catch` (which only catches synchronous throws), so deletion failures are silently swallowed and never logged; (3) the outer `try/catch` around a `forEach` is effectively dead code for async errors. The same pattern exists in `packages/app-store/wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts` line 125 and `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx` line 553. These should be rewritten with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))` so deletions complete (or fail loudly) before the email is sent.

title: forEach with async callback does not await calendar/video deletions before sending reschedule email
body: Identical to the vital reschedule issue: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })` at line 125 does not await the async work. The `await getCalendar(...)` and `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` / `deleteMeeting(...)` calls are fire-and-forget, so `sendRequestRescheduleEmail` at line 143 runs before external events are deleted, and any rejection inside the callback escapes the surrounding `try/catch` (which cannot catch async errors from `forEach`). This can cause the reschedule email to be sent while the old calendar event still exists (double-booking) and silently swallow deletion failures. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))`.

title: forEach with async callback does not await calendar/video deletions in requestReschedule
body: In the `requestReschedule` mutation, `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })` (line 553) does not await the async callback. The `await getCalendar(...)` at line 556 and the `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` / `deleteMeeting(...)` calls are fire-and-forget: the mutation proceeds to `sendRequestRescheduleEmail` (line 570) and then sends webhooks (line 618) without waiting for the old calendar events and video meetings to be deleted. Consequences: the reschedule confirmation email and BOOKING_CANCELLED webhooks can fire while the old event still exists on the external provider (double-booking window), and any error thrown inside the async callback is not caught (there is no try/catch here at all), producing unhandled promise rejections.
