Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))`.

title: getCalendarCredentials calls async getCalendar without await, storing a Promise instead of a Calendar instance
body: `getCalendar` was changed to be `async` (returns `Promise<Calendar | null>`), but `getCalendarCredentials` (line 23-36) is still a synchronous function that does `const calendar = getCalendar(credential);` at line 28 without `await`. As a result, `calendar` is a `Promise`, not a `Calendar` instance, and it is stored in the returned objects as `{ integration: app, credential, calendar }`. Downstream, `getConnectedCalendars` (line 48) does `const calendar = await item.calendar;` which happens to unwrap the promise, masking the bug there — but any other consumer of `getCalendarCredentials` that treats `calendar` as a `Calendar` (e.g. calling `calendar.listCalendars()` or `calendar.createEvent(...)` directly without awaiting) will break at runtime with "calendar.listCalendars is not a function" or operate on a Promise. The function must either become `async` and `await getCalendar(credential)`, or callers must be audited. This is a latent type-safety/runtime break introduced by the async conversion.

title: forEach with async callback does not await per-credential calendar deletions for recurring bookings
body: In the recurring-event cancellation branch, `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... await calendar?.deleteEvent(...) ... })` (lines 460-470) uses `forEach` with an async callback. The promises are never awaited, so `apiDeletes` may be populated after `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` at line 652 has already run (or the deletions may still be in flight when the handler returns). Consequences: external calendar events for recurring bookings may not be deleted before the response is sent, deletion errors become unhandled rejections, and the booking can be reported as cancelled in the DB while the provider-side events remain. Replace with `await Promise.all(credentials.map(async (credential) => { ... }))` and push results into `apiDeletes`, or collect promises and await them before line 652.

title: forEach callback pushes deleteMeeting promises without awaiting them
body: In the legacy video-credential fallback branch, `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach((credential) => { ... apiDeletes.push(deleteMeeting(credential, uidToDelete)); })` (lines 505-511) pushes the promises returned by `deleteMeeting` into `apiDeletes` synchronously. That part is fine because `apiDeletes` is later awaited via `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` at line 652 — however, note that `deleteMeeting` is now `async` and internally awaits `getVideoAdapters`, so the promise is correctly deferred. The real issue is that this `forEach` is not awaited itself, but since it only pushes promises (no `await` inside), it is actually safe. On review, this specific block is correct; the concern is only the adjacent async `forEach` at line 460. No change needed here beyond verifying `apiDeletes` is awaited, which it is at line 652.

title: appStore values are now dynamic-import Promises, breaking all synchronous consumers and the exported type contract
body: The module now exports an object whose every value is a `Promise<typeof import(...)>` (e.g. `applecalendar: import("./applecalendar")`), whereas previously the values were the resolved module namespaces. The default export's type has silently changed from `{ applecalendar: typeof import("./applecalendar"), ... }` to `{ applecalendar: Promise<typeof import("./applecalendar")>, ... }`. Every consumer that does `appStore[key]` and then accesses `.lib`, `.config`, etc. without `await` will now receive a Promise and fail at runtime (e.g. `"lib" in app` on a Promise is false, so integrations will be silently skipped). The PR updates some call sites (`getCalendar.ts`, `videoClient.ts`, payment handlers) but the type contract of the default export is broken for any consumer not updated, and TypeScript may not catch this if consumers use `keyof typeof appStore` indexing with `await` inconsistently. Additionally, `import("./applecalendar")` at module top-level means all app modules are still referenced at build time (defeating some bundling benefits unless the bundler code-splits), and any circular-import or side-effect ordering that previously relied on eager `import * as` evaluation may change. The maintainers should ensure every `appStore[...]` access site is audited and `await`ed, and consider exporting a typed async accessor function instead of a raw object of promises to make misuse a compile error.

title: getVideoAdapters silently skips apps whose dynamic import rejects, with no error handling
body: `const app = await appStore[appName as keyof typeof appStore];` at line 26 awaits a dynamic import inside a `for` loop with no try/catch. If the dynamic import fails (e.g. chunk load error, network failure in production, or a missing/renamed app directory), the entire `getVideoAdapters` promise rejects. Callers like `createMeeting` (line 52) call `await getVideoAdapters([credential])` outside of any try/catch that would handle this specific failure — the `try` block in `createMeeting` starts at line 70, after `getVideoAdapters` at line 52. So a failed chunk load will cause `createMeeting` to throw an unhandled error instead of falling back to Cal Video (the fallback logic at lines 86-97 only catches errors from `firstVideoAdapter?.createMeeting`, not from `getVideoAdapters`). Same for `updateMeeting` (line 111) and `deleteMeeting` (line 144). Consequence: a transient chunk-loading failure breaks meeting creation entirely instead of degrading to the Cal Video fallback. Add a try/catch around the `await appStore[...]` (or around the whole loop) that logs and skips the credential, matching the previous behavior where a missing app simply produced no adapter.

title: getCalendar does not catch dynamic-import rejection; a failed chunk load propagates as an unhandled error
body: `const calendarApp = await appStore[calendarType.split("_").join("") as keyof typeof appStore];` at line 15 awaits a dynamic import with no try/catch. If the import rejects (chunk load failure, network error, missing module), the returned promise rejects. Callers have inconsistent handling: `CalendarManager.createEvent` (line 233) does `const calendar = await getCalendar(credential);` with no try/catch around it, so a chunk failure will throw out of `createEvent` and abort the whole booking creation flow rather than being treated as "calendar not implemented" (which is the function's documented behavior for unknown types, returning `null`). Similarly `EventManager.updateAllCalendarEvents` line 488 and `handleCancelBooking` line 452/481 call `await getCalendar(...)` without guarding against rejection. The function should wrap the `await appStore[...]` in a try/catch that logs and returns `null` (consistent with the existing "not implemented" path), so a transient module-load failure degrades gracefully instead of crashing booking creation/cancellation.

title: getCachedResults awaits all calendar module loads serially with Promise.all before starting availability fetches, adding latency
body: `const calendars = await Promise.all(calendarCredentials.map((credential) => getCalendar(credential)));` at line 142 now awaits all dynamic imports before any `getAvailability` call begins. Previously `getCalendar` was synchronous so this was instant. Now, on a cold start (first request after deploy, or when chunks are not cached), every calendar credential's module must be fetched and evaluated before availability fetching starts, serializing module-load latency ahead of the actual work. This is partially mitigated by `Promise.all` (loads happen in parallel), but the availability fetches (the expensive part) cannot start until all modules are loaded. A better pattern would be to interleave: map each credential to an async function that awaits `getCalendar` and then immediately calls `getAvailability`, all within a single `Promise.all`, so module loading and availability fetching overlap. As written, cold-start latency for the busy-times endpoint increases by the full module-load time.

title: Warn message logs the awaited module object instead of the app type when PaymentService is missing
body: After the change `const paymentApp = await appStore[paymentAppCredential?.app?.dirName as keyof typeof appStore];`, the guard at line 590 checks `"PaymentService" in paymentApp.lib`, and the warning at line 591 is `console.warn(`payment App service of type ${paymentApp} is not implemented`);`. Since `paymentApp` is now the resolved module namespace object (not a string), the log message will print `[object Module]` or similar instead of the app's dirName/type. The same wrong-message pattern exists in `packages/lib/payment/deletePayment.ts` line 18, `packages/lib/payment/handlePayment.ts` line 28, and `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx` line 969. The message should reference `paymentAppCredential?.app?.dirName` (the string) so operators can identify which payment app failed to load.

title: Warn message interpolates the module object instead of the app type string
body: Line 18: `console.warn(`payment App service of type ${paymentApp} is not implemented`);` — `paymentApp` is now the awaited module namespace (an object), so the log will render the app type as `[object Module]` instead of the actual dirName. This makes the warning useless for debugging which payment app is misconfigured. Use `paymentAppCredentials?.app?.dirName` in the message. Same issue in `packages/lib/payment/handlePayment.ts` line 28 and `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx` line 969.

title: Warn message interpolates the module object instead of the app type string
body: Line 28: `console.warn(`payment App service of type ${paymentApp} is not implemented`);` — `paymentApp` is the awaited module namespace object, so the message prints `[object Module]` rather than the payment app's dirName. This obscures which app failed. Interpolate `paymentAppCredentials?.app?.dirName` instead. Same defect in `packages/lib/payment/deletePayment.ts` line 18, `packages/features/bookings/lib/handleCancelBooking.ts` line 591, and `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx` line 969.

title: Warn message interpolates the module object instead of the app type string
body: Line 969: `console.warn(`payment App service of type ${paymentApp} is not implemented`);` — after `const paymentApp = await appStore[...]`, `paymentApp` is the resolved module namespace object, so the warning prints `[object Module]` instead of the payment app's dirName, making it impossible to tell which app is unimplemented. Use `paymentAppCredential?.app?.dirName` in the template string.

title: getCalendar result awaited but deleteEvent call not awaited inside updateAllCalendarEvents merge path
body: In `updateAllCalendarEvents`, the merge path (when `newBookingId` is set) does `const calendar = await getCalendar(calendarCredential);` at line 488 followed by `await calendar?.deleteEvent(oldCalendarEvent.uid, event, oldCalendarEvent.externalCalendarId);` at line 489. The `await` on line 489 is present, so this specific call is fine. However, note that `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` — if `calendar` is `null` (e.g. unknown credential type or failed dynamic import), the expression short-circuits to `undefined` and `await undefined` resolves immediately, silently skipping the deletion of the old calendar event during a booking merge. There is no log or error when the old event fails to be deleted, so a merge can leave an orphaned event on the external calendar. Consider logging when `calendar` is null in this path.

title: No tests cover the async appStore contract; consumers that forget to await will fail silently at runtime
body: The PR converts every `appStore` entry from an eagerly-imported module namespace into a dynamic-import `Promise`. This is a breaking change to the shape of the default export, and the safety of the migration depends entirely on every call site remembering to `await` the indexed value before accessing `.lib` / `.config`. The PR updates the known call sites, but there is no test that exercises `appStore` access patterns (e.g. a unit test asserting `await appStore.googlecalendar` exposes `lib.CalendarService`, or a type-level test that `appStore` values are promises). A consumer that does `const app = appStore[x]; if ("lib" in app)` without `await` will silently skip the integration (the `"lib" in app` check on a Promise is false) with no error. Recommend adding a test that iterates all appStore entries, awaits them, and asserts each resolves to a module with the expected shape, plus a type test ensuring consumers must await.

title: getCalendarCredentials is not async but now stores Promises from getCalendar
body: getCalendar() was changed to be async (returns Promise<Calendar | null>), but getCalendarCredentials (line 23) is still a synchronous function that calls `const calendar = getCalendar(credential)` at line 28 without awaiting it. The resulting `calendar` value is a Promise, not a Calendar instance. This Promise is stored in the returned objects and later consumed by getConnectedCalendars, which does `const calendar = await item.calendar` (line 48) — that part works — but any other consumer of getCalendarCredentials that expects a Calendar instance (e.g. calling calendar.listCalendars() or checking truthiness directly) will break, because a Promise is always truthy and has no Calendar methods. The function signature and all call sites must be audited; at minimum getCalendarCredentials should become async and await getCalendar, or the Promise should be stored deliberately and documented. As written, the type contract is silently violated (a Promise<Calendar|null> is stored where Calendar|null is expected), which TypeScript may not catch depending on the inferred return type, and can cause runtime 'calendar.listCalendars is not a function' errors or, worse, null-calendars being treated as valid (a Promise is truthy, so the `if (!calendar)` guard at line 51 never triggers for a null-returning getCalendar).

title: forEach with async callback does not await calendar/video deletions; errors are swallowed and deletions may not complete
body: The code uses `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })`. Array.prototype.forEach does not await async callbacks, so the surrounding try/catch (lines 124-139) can never catch errors thrown inside the callback — any rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection. More importantly, the function proceeds to send the reschedule email (line 143) and return true without waiting for the calendar events and video meetings to actually be deleted. If the process handles the request and responds before the deletions finish (or crashes), external calendar events and video meetings remain live while the booking is already marked CANCELLED in the database (the prisma.booking.update at line 67 ran earlier), leaving orphaned events on attendees' calendars. The correct pattern is `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))` so deletions complete (or fail loudly) before the function returns.

title: forEach with async callback does not await calendar/video deletions; errors are swallowed and deletions may not complete
body: Identical issue to vital/lib/reschedule.ts: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })` at line 125 does not await the async work. The try/catch around it (lines 124-139) cannot catch async errors (unhandled rejections), and the function sends the reschedule email (line 143) and returns true before calendar/video deletions complete. The booking is already marked CANCELLED in the DB (line 67), so if the process exits or the deletions fail silently, external calendar events and video meetings are orphaned. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))`.

title: requestReschedule mutation fires async deletions via forEach without awaiting them
body: In the requestReschedule mutation, `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })` (line 553) does not await the async callbacks. The mutation then immediately sends the reschedule email (line 570) and webhooks (line 618) and returns, without waiting for the old calendar events and video meetings to be deleted. The booking has already been marked CANCELLED (line 475-485). Consequences: (1) deletion errors are unhandled promise rejections, not surfaced to the user or logged through the normal path; (2) the API responds before external resources are cleaned up, so a crash or early process exit leaves orphaned events on Google/Office calendars and live video meetings for a booking the user believes is cancelled; (3) webhooks fire with BOOKING_CANCELLED before the external cancellation actually happened, so downstream systems see an inconsistent state. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))`.

title: Recurring-booking cancellation path uses forEach(async ...) so calendar deletions are not awaited before the response
body: In the recurring-event branch (bookingToDelete.eventType?.recurringEvent && allRemainingBookings), the code does `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); for (const updBooking of updatedBookings) { ... await calendar?.deleteEvent(...) ... } })` (lines 458-470). forEach does not await async callbacks, so none of the per-booking calendar deletions are awaited. The handler later does `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` (line 652), but the promises pushed inside the forEach callback (line 467, `apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent)`) may not have been pushed yet when Promise.all runs — a classic race: the pushes happen asynchronously after the forEach returns, so apiDeletes can be empty or partially populated at await time. Result: the API returns 'Booking successfully cancelled' and sends cancellation emails (line 654) while recurring calendar events are still being deleted (or never deleted if the process exits), leaving orphaned events on external calendars for bookings already marked CANCELLED in the DB (updateMany at line 360). Convert to `await Promise.all(credentials.filter(...).map(async (credential) => { ... }))` and collect the deletion promises properly.

title: Legacy video-credential fallback path uses forEach to push deleteMeeting promises without awaiting getCalendar-style async work
body: In the legacy branch (no credentialId on the video reference), `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter((credential) => credential.type.endsWith("_video")).forEach((credential) => { ... apiDeletes.push(deleteMeeting(credential, uidToDelete)); })` (lines 505-511). deleteMeeting is now async (it awaits getVideoAdapters which awaits dynamic imports), but it is called synchronously here and its returned promise is pushed — that part is fine for Promise.all at line 652. However, this forEach is purely synchronous push, which is OK, but note the surrounding pattern is inconsistent with the calendar branch which was converted to a for...of loop with await. More importantly, if deleteMeeting rejects (e.g. the dynamic import of the video app fails), the rejection is only handled by Promise.all at line 652 — which is acceptable — but there is no per-credential error isolation, so one failing video credential rejects the whole Promise.all and skips attendee/bookingReference deletes? No — prismaPromises are also in the same Promise.all, so a video deletion failure would cause the entire cancellation to throw after the booking was already marked CANCELLED, leaving attendees and booking references undeleted while emails are never sent. Consider Promise.allSettled or individual catches for apiDeletes so a single integration failure doesn't abort the DB cleanup. (The calendar branches have the same exposure.)

title: appStore values are now dynamic-import Promises; every consumer must await them, and the module shape changed from static namespace objects to Promise<module>
body: The appStore object changed from statically imported module namespaces (`import * as applecalendar from "./applecalendar"`) to dynamic import promises (`applecalendar: import("./applecalendar")`). This is a breaking contract change: `appStore[key]` now evaluates to `Promise<typeof import("./applecalendar")>` instead of the module namespace. The PR updates the known call sites (getCalendar.ts, videoClient.ts, handleCancelBooking.ts, deletePayment.ts, handlePayment.ts, bookings.tsx), but any other file in the monorepo that imports appStore and accesses a key synchronously (e.g. `appStore.stripepayment.lib.PaymentService`, or iterating `Object.values(appStore)` to enumerate apps, or code in packages/app-store/utils.ts, webhooks, or the app installation flows) will now receive a Promise and break at runtime with 'lib is undefined' or similar. Additionally, `await appStore[key]` where key is undefined (e.g. `paymentAppCredential?.app?.dirName` being undefined) evaluates to `await undefined` which is undefined — that path is guarded by the subsequent `!(paymentApp && ...)` check, so it is safe, but the type cast `as keyof typeof appStore` no longer guarantees a module shape. A repo-wide audit of all `appStore[` accesses and all `import appStore from "@calcom/app-store"` sites is required; any missed site is a latent runtime crash. Also note that dynamic import() in a server bundle may interact with bundler code-splitting differently than static imports, potentially increasing cold-start latency on first use of each app.

title: Awaiting appStore[key] with an unknown/invalid key yields undefined, but the guard checks the awaited module — however a rejected dynamic import is unhandled
body: Line 15: `const calendarApp = await appStore[calendarType.split("_").join("") as keyof typeof appStore];`. If calendarType maps to a key not present in appStore (e.g. a credential type like "somecustom_calendar" that has no corresponding app directory, or a typo), `appStore[...]` is undefined and `await undefined` resolves to undefined — the guard at line 16 handles that. But if the key exists and the dynamic import() rejects (e.g. the app's index.ts throws at module-evaluation time, a missing dependency, or a build error in that app package), the rejection propagates out of getCalendar. Callers like CalendarManager.createEvent (line 233) do `const calendar = await getCalendar(credential);` with no try/catch around it — createEvent itself has a .catch on calendar.createEvent but not on getCalendar — so a failing app import would throw out of createEvent/updateEvent/deleteEvent and abort the whole booking flow. Previously, with static imports, a broken app module would fail at server startup (fail-fast); now it fails per-request at runtime. Consider wrapping the await in try/catch and returning null (with a log) so one broken app doesn't take down booking creation for all integrations.

title: getVideoAdapters: a rejected dynamic import for one credential aborts adapter creation for all credentials and is unhandled
body: In getVideoAdapters (lines 21-36), `const app = await appStore[appName as keyof typeof appStore];` is inside a for...of loop with no try/catch. If the dynamic import rejects for any credential (broken app package, missing module), the entire getVideoAdapters call rejects. Callers: createMeeting (line 52) calls `await getVideoAdapters([credential])` outside its try/catch (the try starts at line 70), so a rejection propagates out of createMeeting — EventManager.createVideoEvent returns that promise, and EventManager.create awaits it at line 109 with no catch, so booking creation fails entirely. deleteMeeting (line 144) and updateMeeting (line 111) similarly propagate. Previously, static imports meant a broken app failed at build/startup; now a single bad app credential can fail every booking that touches video. Wrap the per-credential import in try/catch, log, and continue (skip that adapter), matching the previous behavior where a missing 'VideoApiAdapter' in app.lib was simply skipped (line 28 guard).

title: getCachedResults awaits all calendar imports serially per call via Promise.all over getCalendar, but getCalendarCredentials path still has the un-awaited Promise issue; also index-based credential matching is fragile
body: Line 142: `const calendars = await Promise.all(calendarCredentials.map((credential) => getCalendar(credential)));` — this is correct for awaiting. However, the subsequent `calendars.map(async (c, i) => { ... const { type, appId } = calendarCredentials[i]; ... })` relies on index alignment between the filtered `calendarCredentials` array and the `calendars` array. Since Promise.all preserves order, this is fine. The real issue is that getCalendar now performs a dynamic import() per credential per call; dynamic imports are cached by the module system after first load, so this is cheap after warmup, but on a cold server the first getCachedResults call for N calendar credentials will trigger N concurrent chunk loads. This is acceptable, but note that getCalendarCredentials (line 23-36) still has the un-awaited Promise bug (see separate finding), meaning the two code paths are now inconsistent: one stores Promises, one stores resolved instances. Consumers must know which they have.

title: Error message logs the awaited module object instead of the app type string
body: Line 591: `console.warn(`payment App service of type ${paymentApp} is not implemented`);` — `paymentApp` is now the awaited module namespace object (or undefined), not a string. Previously it was also the module object (the old code had the same bug: `appStore[...]` returned a module namespace), so this is a pre-existing defect, but the PR touches this line's context. The message will print something like 'payment App service of type [object Module] is not implemented' or 'undefined', which is useless for debugging. It should log `paymentAppCredential?.app?.dirName` (the intended app identifier) instead. Same pattern exists in packages/lib/payment/deletePayment.ts line 18 and packages/lib/payment/handlePayment.ts line 28 and packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx line 969 — all log `${paymentApp}` which is a module object.

title: Comment 'example: import("./example")' references a non-existent example app and is misleading
body: Line 2: `// example: import("./example"),` — the commented-out example references `./example` which does not exist in the app-store directory (the actual example app is `_example`). The comment is meant to show the pattern for adding a new app, but as written it would mislead a developer into uncommenting a broken import. It should reference `./_example` or be removed. Minor, but it's the only documentation of how to add an app to this store.

title: getCalendar(calendarCredential) may return null and calendar?.deleteEvent is called with a possibly-null credential result; also the await is inside a block that previously relied on synchronous behavior
body: Line 483-489: `const calendarCredential = await prisma.credential.findUnique({...}); const calendar = await getCalendar(calendarCredential); await calendar?.deleteEvent(oldCalendarEvent.uid, event, oldCalendarEvent.externalCalendarId);`. getCalendar returns null if credential is null or has no key — the optional chaining handles that. But note that `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` returns a Promise that is awaited — fine. However, this whole block is inside the `if (newBookingId)` merge path of updateAllCalendarEvents, which is wrapped in a try/catch that returns a synthetic failure result. If the dynamic import inside getCalendar rejects (broken app), the catch at line 516 handles it and returns a failure EventResult — acceptable. The main concern is consistency: this is one of the few places that correctly awaits, showing the pattern the other files should follow. No change needed here, but it confirms the forEach/forEach-async bugs elsewhere are deviations from the intended pattern.

title: Reschedule cleanup in handleNewBooking pushes deleteEvent promises into integrationsToDelete but the surrounding loop may not await getCalendar before pushing
body: The diff shows `const calendar = await getCalendar(credential);` inside what appears to be a for...of or forEach loop around line 885-890. The snippet shows `integrationsToDelete.push(calendar?.deleteEvent(reference.uid, originalBookingEvt, reference.externalCalendarId))`. If this is inside a `forEach` (as the vital/wipemycalother reschedule files do), the await inside a non-async forEach callback would be a syntax error — so it must be a for...of or an async forEach. Given the diff context (`integrationsToDelete.push(deleteMeeting(credential, reference.uid));` on the line before, also without await on deleteMeeting which is fine since it returns a promise), the structure appears to be a for...of loop. However, the file was only shown as 'diff only' — the full context of whether integrationsToDelete promises are awaited before the new booking is confirmed is not visible. If they are awaited via Promise.all later, this is fine; if not, the same orphaned-event race as the other files applies. Flagging for verification: ensure `await Promise.all(integrationsToDelete)` occurs before the handler returns success, otherwise old calendar/video events from the original booking may outlive the rescheduled booking.

title: getCalendarCredentials is not async but now stores Promises from getCalendar
body: getCalendar() was changed to be async (returns Promise<Calendar | null>), but getCalendarCredentials (line 23) is still a synchronous function that calls getCalendar(credential) at line 28 without await. The returned objects now contain { calendar: Promise<Calendar|null> } instead of { calendar: Calendar|null }. The only consumer that was updated is getConnectedCalendars (line 48: `const calendar = await item.calendar;`), but the type contract of getCalendarCredentials is now wrong — any other caller of getCalendarCredentials will receive un-awaited Promises and break (e.g. calling .listCalendars() on a Promise). The function should either be made async with awaited getCalendar calls, or its return type updated and all callers audited. This is a latent type/runtime break for any consumer not updated in this PR.

title: forEach with async callback does not await calendar/video deletions; errors escape the try/catch
body: The code uses `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })` inside a try/catch. forEach does not await async callbacks, so: (1) the try/catch at lines 124-139 can never catch errors thrown by the async body — rejections become unhandled promise rejections; (2) the function returns `true` (line 151) and proceeds to send the reschedule email before the calendar events and video meetings have actually been deleted. If getCalendar or deleteEvent/deleteMeeting fails, the booking is already marked CANCELLED in the DB (line 67-77) but the external calendar event may remain, leaving a ghost event on the user's calendar. The same pattern exists in packages/app-store/wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts line 125 and packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx line 553. These should use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` inside the try/catch.

title: forEach with async callback does not await deletions; try/catch is ineffective
body: Identical to the vital reschedule issue: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` (line 125) does not await the async work. The surrounding try/catch (lines 124-139) cannot catch async errors, and the function returns before calendar/video deletions complete. The booking is marked CANCELLED in the DB before external events are deleted, so a failure in getCalendar/deleteEvent/deleteMeeting leaves orphaned events on external calendars with no error surfaced. Should be `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => {...}))`.

title: requestReschedule: forEach(async ...) fire-and-forget deletes calendar/video events
body: In the requestReschedule mutation, `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })` (line 553) is not awaited. There is no try/catch here at all, so any rejection from getCalendar, calendar.deleteEvent, or deleteMeeting becomes an unhandled promise rejection, and the mutation continues to send the reschedule email (line 570) and webhooks (line 618) before — or regardless of — whether the external calendar events were actually deleted. The booking has already been marked CANCELLED (line 475-485). Result: silent failure to delete external calendar/video events with no error reporting to the user. Should be `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => {...}))` with error handling.

title: Recurring-event cancellation path uses forEach(async ...) without awaiting deletions
body: In the recurring-event cancellation branch (lines 458-470), `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... await calendar?.deleteEvent(...) ... })` is not awaited. The pushed promises into apiDeletes are never awaited in this branch (the inner `deletedEvent` promises are pushed but the outer forEach promise is not tracked), so `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` at line 652 does not include these deletions. Calendar events for recurring bookings may not be deleted before the request completes, and failures are silently swallowed. Should use a for...of loop with await (as done in the adjacent else branch at lines 480-483) or collect promises properly.

title: Legacy video-credential deletion path uses forEach without awaiting deleteMeeting
body: Lines 505-511: `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach((credential) => { ... apiDeletes.push(deleteMeeting(credential, uidToDelete)); })`. deleteMeeting is now async (returns a Promise) and internally awaits dynamic imports via getVideoAdapters. The forEach itself is synchronous so apiDeletes does get populated with the promises, and they are awaited later at line 652 — so this is less severe than the calendar forEach(async) cases. However, the promises are created eagerly inside forEach which is fine, but note deleteMeeting is called with `bookingToDelete?.references?.[0]?.uid ?? bookingToDelete.uid` — for the legacy path this uses the first reference's uid for ALL video credentials, which may be wrong if there are multiple video references, but that is pre-existing behavior. The main residual issue: if deleteMeeting rejects, it is caught by Promise.all at 652 — acceptable. Downgrading: this is mostly OK; the real issue is consistency, but no concrete bug beyond what's already noted. Not reporting as a separate finding — see the forEach(async) findings for the real problems.

title: appStore values are now Promises of modules; all consumers must await, and type inference changes
body: The appStore object changed from statically imported module namespaces to `import()` dynamic import promises. Every property is now `Promise<typeof import('./xxx')>` instead of the module namespace itself. This is an API/contract break for the entire codebase: any file that does `appStore[dirName].lib.SomeService` or `appStore[dirName].something` without await will now operate on a Promise and fail at runtime (e.g. "lib" in app will be false because Promise objects don't have a lib property, or accessing properties returns undefined). The PR updates the known call sites (getCalendar, videoClient, payment handlers), but there may be other consumers across the monorepo (e.g. packages/app-store/utils.ts getApps, webhook handlers, apps/api, etc.) that index into appStore synchronously and were not updated. A repo-wide audit of `appStore[` usages is required; any missed site is a runtime break. Also, the `as keyof typeof appStore` casts now index into a map of Promises, so TypeScript types no longer reflect the awaited module shape, weakening type safety at all call sites.

title: getVideoAdapters silently skips apps when dynamic import fails or app has no VideoApiAdapter, with no error logging
body: In getVideoAdapters (lines 21-36), `const app = await appStore[appName as keyof typeof appStore];` — if the dynamic import rejects (e.g. chunk load failure, missing module), the await throws and the entire getVideoAdapters rejects, propagating up. But more importantly, if `appName` doesn't match any key in appStore (e.g. a credential type like `riverby_video` or `whereby_video` that has no entry, or a typo), `appStore[appName]` is `undefined`, and `await undefined` is `undefined`, so the `if (app && ...)` check silently skips it. Previously with static imports this was a compile-time guarantee; now it's a silent runtime skip. Callers like createMeeting then get `firstVideoAdapter` as undefined and proceed to `firstVideoAdapter?.createMeeting(calEvent)` returning undefined, then fall into the catch block treating it as a failure and falling back to Cal Video — masking the real problem. At minimum, a warning should be logged when a credential type has no matching app in appStore. Also, an import() rejection is not caught here, so one bad app chunk fails all video adapter creation.

title: getCalendar silently returns null when dynamic import fails or app key missing; no error logging for import failures
body: `const calendarApp = await appStore[calendarType.split("_").join("") as keyof typeof appStore];` — if the dynamic import rejects (network/chunk error in serverless, or module resolution failure), the await throws and getCalendar rejects, which propagates to callers. But if the key simply doesn't exist in appStore (unknown calendar type, or a credential type not in the map), `appStore[key]` is undefined, `await undefined` resolves to undefined, and the function logs a warning and returns null. Callers like CalendarManager.createEvent (line 243: `calendar ? await calendar.createEvent(...) : undefined`) then silently treat this as "no calendar" and report success=true with no created event — the booking appears created but no calendar event exists. Previously, unknown types were a compile-time impossibility with static imports. Now any new credential type not added to appStore, or a typo, silently drops calendar event creation. At minimum, import rejections should be caught and logged distinctly from "not implemented".

title: getCachedResults awaits all calendar imports serially via Promise.all but then maps with index-based credential matching that is now safe; however the awaited Promise.all is correct — no issue. Actually this is fine.
body: Line 142: `const calendars = await Promise.all(calendarCredentials.map((credential) => getCalendar(credential)));` correctly awaits all async getCalendar calls and preserves order, so the index-based matching at line 148 (`calendarCredentials[i]`) remains correct. No bug here. Not reporting.

title: Warn message logs the awaited module object instead of the app name when PaymentService is missing
body: Line 591: `console.warn(`payment App service of type ${paymentApp} is not implemented`);` — `paymentApp` is now the awaited module namespace object (after `await appStore[...]`), so the log message will print `[object Module]` or similar instead of the app's dirName. The same pattern exists in packages/lib/payment/deletePayment.ts line 18 and packages/lib/payment/handlePayment.ts line 28 and packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx line 969. The warning is meant to identify which payment app is misconfigured; logging the module object makes it useless for debugging. Should log `paymentAppCredential?.app?.dirName` instead.

title: Warn message logs module object instead of app dirName
body: Line 18: `console.warn(`payment App service of type ${paymentApp} is not implemented`);` — after the change, `paymentApp` is the awaited module namespace (a Module object), not a string. The log will print the stringified module object rather than the app's directory name, making the warning useless for identifying which payment app is not implemented. Should use `paymentAppCredentials?.app?.dirName` in the message. Same issue in handlePayment.ts:28 and handleCancelBooking.ts:591 and bookings.tsx:969.

title: Warn message logs module object instead of app dirName
body: Line 28: `console.warn(`payment App service of type ${paymentApp} is not implemented`);` — `paymentApp` is now the awaited module namespace object, so the warning prints `[object Module]` instead of the app's dirName. Should log `paymentAppCredentials?.app?.dirName`. Same defect in deletePayment.ts:18, handleCancelBooking.ts:591, and bookings.tsx:969.

title: Warn message logs module object instead of app dirName
body: Line 969: `console.warn(`payment App service of type ${paymentApp} is not implemented`);` — after `await appStore[...]`, `paymentApp` is the module namespace object, so the warning prints the module object instead of the payment app's dirName. Should log `paymentAppCredential?.app?.dirName`. Same defect in handlePayment.ts:28, deletePayment.ts:18, and handleCancelBooking.ts:591.

title: updateAllCalendarEvents: getCalendar can return null and calendar?.deleteEvent is awaited but result unused; also credential could be null from prisma
body: Line 483-489: `const calendarCredential = await prisma.credential.findUnique({...}); const calendar = await getCalendar(calendarCredential); await calendar?.deleteEvent(...)`. getCalendar accepts `CredentialPayload | null` and returns null for null/missing credentials, so this is handled with `?.`. However, if the old calendar event deletion fails, the error propagates up to the try/catch at line 436 which catches it and returns a failure result — but by that point, `result.push(updateEvent(...))` promises at lines 468/474 may already be in-flight and their results are discarded because the catch returns a different array. The updateEvent calls are not awaited before the deleteEvent (they're pushed as promises into `result` and only awaited at line 515 `return Promise.all(result)`), but the deleteEvent at line 489 IS awaited inline. If deleteEvent throws, the catch block returns early and the pending updateEvent promises are orphaned (unhandled rejections possible). This is a pre-existing structural issue but the added await makes the throw path more likely to trigger. At minimum, the deleteEvent should be pushed into the result array or wrapped in its own try/catch.

title: All dynamic imports are kicked off eagerly at module load time, defeating the purpose of code splitting for server bundle
body: The appStore object literal calls `import("./applecalendar")`, `import("./caldavcalendar")`, etc. for ALL ~29 apps at module evaluation time. In a server (Node.js/Next.js API) context, this means importing `@calcom/app-store` triggers 29 dynamic import() calls immediately — they are not lazy. While bundlers may split these into separate chunks, on the server all chunks get loaded into memory anyway when the module is first imported, and the promises all start resolving concurrently. The stated goal of the PR ("Async import of the appStore packages") is presumably to reduce initial bundle size / startup time, but eagerly calling import() for every app at module scope means every serverless function / server process that imports appStore (directly or transitively — and it's imported by videoClient, getCalendar, payment handlers, etc., which are on hot paths) will load all app modules. True lazy loading would require wrapping each in a thunk: `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")` and awaiting `appStore[key]()`. As written, this provides no server-side memory/CPU benefit and may increase startup latency due to 29 concurrent module resolutions.

title: Working-hours check in checkIfIsAvailable uses wrong start/end values, making the check ineffective
body: In the newly added working-hours validation inside `checkIfIsAvailable`, both `start` and `end` are computed identically as `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()` (lines 141-142). The `end` should be the slot end time (`slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute()`), not a copy of the start. As written, the condition `start < workingHour.startTime || end > workingHour.endTime` only rejects slots whose start minute-of-day falls outside the working-hours window; it never rejects a slot that starts inside working hours but extends past the end of the working-hours window (e.g. a 60-minute event starting at the last 30 minutes of an availability block). This means the new working-hours guard — which is the mechanism that makes fixed-host date overrides restrict round-robin slots — fails to block slots that overrun the override/working-hours end, so round-robin events can still be booked at times when the fixed host is unavailable. Fix: compute `end` from `slotEndTime`.

title: Date-override day matching in checkIfIsAvailable uses organizer offset with a sign error and ignores the override's own timeZone
body: The new date-override logic computes `const utcOffset = organizerTimeZone ? dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone).utcOffset() * -1 : 0;` and then compares `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD")` against the slot's UTC day. Two problems: (1) `dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone).utcOffset()` already returns the offset of that instant in the organizer zone; negating it and adding it to the UTC instant shifts the date in the wrong direction, so the 'which day does this override belong to' comparison is off by the offset (e.g. an override stored as 2023-05-10T00:00:00Z for a UTC+5:30 organizer is treated as belonging to 2023-05-09). (2) The override objects now carry their own `timeZone` (added to the flattened `dateOverrides` at line 410-416 and to the `TimeRange` type), but `checkIfIsAvailable` never reads `date.timeZone`; it only uses the passed `organizerTimeZone`, which for per-user schedules is `schedule.timeZone`/`userSchedule.timeZone` — the user's profile timezone, not necessarily the schedule's timezone the override was created in. Consequences: overrides can be matched to the wrong calendar day (slots wrongly excluded or wrongly allowed), and the day-boundary logic is inconsistent with the timezone-correct conversion added in `packages/lib/slots.ts` (which uses `override.timeZone`). The day-matching should use the override's own `timeZone` (falling back to `organizerTimeZone`) and the correct offset sign, consistent with the slots.ts conversion.

title: Date-override containment checks in checkIfIsAvailable compare instants with `===` on Dayjs objects and mis-handle blocked (zero-length) overrides
body: In the new date-override block, `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` (line 114) compares two distinct Dayjs object instances with `===`, which is always `false` — object identity, not value equality. The intent (per the surrounding logic: a zero-length override means 'blocked/unavailable all day') is to detect a blocked day, but the comparison never fires, so an all-day 'unavailable' override (start === end) falls through to the range checks and the slot is treated as available during the blocked day. The correct check is `.isSame(...)` (or comparing the underlying timestamps). Additionally, the containment logic returns `true` from the `find` callback when the slot is entirely before the override start or entirely after the override end, which makes `dateOverrides.find(...)` truthy and causes `return false` ('slot is not within the date override') — i.e. any slot on a day that has any override but falls outside the override window is rejected, which is correct only if the override replaces the whole day; combined with the broken zero-length check, blocked days and partial overrides interact incorrectly. The comparisons should use `.isSame()`/`.isBefore()`/`.isAfter()` consistently and the zero-length (blocked) case must be handled explicitly.

title: Selected-slot filtering returns false for users with no selected slot when seats are not enabled, inverting the intended logic
body: In the selectedSlots filtering block, the per-user filter does: `if (!busy?.length && eventType.seatsPerTimeSlot === null) { return false; }`. `busy` here is the list of that user's reserved (non-seat) selected slots. For a round-robin/team event without seats (`seatsPerTimeSlot === null`), a user who has no reserved slot is filtered out (`return false`), so `slot.userIds` ends up empty and the slot is dropped by the following `.filter((slot) => !!slot.userIds?.length)` — even though the user is perfectly available. The condition appears inverted: a user with no busy/selected time should be kept (subject to `checkIfIsAvailable`), and it is users with conflicting selected slots who should be removed. As written, whenever any selected slot exists for the event, all slots whose `userIds` include users without a reservation are removed, which can suppress valid availability (or, conversely, fail to suppress users whose reserved slot conflicts, since those users are still passed to `checkIfIsAvailable` with the reduced `busy` list). This directly affects the round-robin fixed-host scenario this PR targets.

title: Date-override activation window uses UTC day boundaries of the invitee day, mismatching overrides stored in organizer-local dates
body: `activeOverrides` is computed as overrides where `dayjs.utc(override.start).isBetween(startOfInviteeDay, startOfInviteeDay.endOf("day"), null, "[)")`. `startOfInviteeDay` is the invitee's local midnight converted to an instant, and `override.start` is a UTC instant derived from an organizer-local date/time. An override created for '2023-05-10 14:00–18:00' in the organizer's timezone is stored as the corresponding UTC instant; whether it falls inside the invitee-day window `[inviteeMidnight, inviteeMidnight+24h)` depends on the invitee's timezone offset relative to the organizer. For invitees whose day window does not contain the override's UTC start instant (e.g. invitee far behind/ahead of the organizer), the override is silently dropped and the normal working hours are used, so the date override has no effect for those timezones — precisely the timezone bug (#8329) this PR claims to fix. The activation check should be based on the override's calendar date in the organizer's timezone (using `override.timeZone`, now available on `TimeRange`) compared against the invitee day converted to the organizer's timezone, not on raw UTC instants against the invitee-day window.

title: Override-to-invitee offset conversion in getSlots uses the override start instant's offsets, which is wrong across DST boundaries and for multi-day offsets
body: The new override conversion computes `organizerUtcOffset = dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` and `inviteeUtcOffset = dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(timeZone).utcOffset()`, then shifts both `override.start` and `override.end` by the same `offset = inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset` minutes. The offsets are sampled at the override's start instant only; if the override spans a DST transition in either the organizer's or the invitee's timezone, the end time is shifted by the wrong amount, producing slots at the wrong UTC times (off by the DST delta, typically 60 minutes) for part of the override window. Additionally, `dayjs(override.start.toString())` stringifies a Date in the runtime's local timezone before re-parsing, which can shift the instant depending on the server's TZ — it should operate on the Date/UTC value directly (e.g. `dayjs.utc(override.start).tz(...)`). The conversion should compute the offset per endpoint (start and end separately) using `dayjs(override.start).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` style calls on the actual instants.

title: Fixed-host availability check spreads the whole per-user schedule object, so dateOverrides/workingHours are not scoped to that host
body: The fixed-host filter does `checkIfIsAvailable({ time: slot.time, ...schedule, ...availabilityCheckProps, organizerTimeZone: schedule.timeZone })` where `schedule` is the per-user availability object `{ timeZone, workingHours, dateOverrides, busy, user }`. Because `...schedule` spreads `workingHours` and `dateOverrides` from that user's availability, the new working-hours/date-override checks inside `checkIfIsAvailable` are applied per fixed host — which is the intent — but note that `workingHours` from `getUserAvailability` is the user's raw working hours in minutes-since-midnight in the user's timezone, while `checkIfIsAvailable` compares them against `slotStartTime.hour()*60 + slotStartTime.minute()` where `slotStartTime = time.utc()` — i.e. UTC minutes-of-day, not organizer-local minutes-of-day. Unless the organizer is in UTC, the working-hours comparison is shifted by the organizer's UTC offset, so the guard rejects/accepts the wrong slots. The minutes-of-day must be computed in the organizer's timezone (`slotStartTime.tz(schedule.timeZone)`), consistent with how the override day-matching attempts to use the organizer timezone.

title: New timezone test only asserts identical UTC output and does not cover a case where the invitee timezone changes the override day
body: The added test `scheduleForEventOnADayWithDateOverrideDifferentTimezone` requests the same UTC window with `timeZone: Timezones["+6:00"]` (Asia/Dhaka, 30 minutes ahead of the organizer's Asia/Kolkata) and asserts the exact same UTC slot list, with the comment 'it should return the same as this is the utc time'. Because the requested `startTime`/`endTime` window is identical and the override (14:00–18:00 'UTC' in the fixture, interpreted via the schedule timezone) does not cross a day boundary between +5:30 and +6:00, this test cannot detect the day-window/offset bugs described in the slots.ts and slots.ts findings — the override start instant still falls within the invitee-day window and the offset math happens to cancel. A meaningful regression test would use an override near midnight in the organizer's timezone (so that a +6:00 or negative-offset invitee sees it on a different calendar day) and assert the slots shift accordingly, and would also cover a blocked (zero-length) override and a fixed-host round-robin scenario, none of which are present in the added tests.

title: Date override timezone conversion uses the wrong sign for the organizer UTC offset
body: In checkIfIsAvailable, the organizer's UTC offset is applied with a negated sign: `const utcOffset = organizerTimeZone ? dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone).utcOffset() * -1 : 0;` and then `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes")`. Date overrides are stored as UTC instants representing local wall-clock times in the organizer's timezone (e.g. a 14:00 IST override is stored as 08:30 UTC). To compare the override's wall-clock date against the slot's UTC date, the offset must be ADDED (converting the stored UTC instant back to organizer-local wall-clock), not subtracted. Negating it shifts the override by twice the offset (e.g. 11 hours for IST instead of 5:30), so the 'YYYY MM DD' comparison at line 110-112 matches the wrong day for any organizer whose offset is non-zero. Consequence: for round-robin events with fixed hosts, slots on the override day are incorrectly rejected (or slots on adjacent days incorrectly accepted), meaning fixed-host date overrides are not reliably honored — the exact bug this PR claims to fix. The same negated-offset pattern also appears in the working-hours fallback check below it, compounding the error.

title: Equality comparison of Dayjs objects with === never matches, making all-day (unavailable) overrides ineffective
body: Line 114 uses `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` to detect an all-day-unavailable override (start == end). Dayjs objects are compared by reference with ===, so this is always false even when the two instants are identical. As a result, an override that marks a whole day as unavailable (start equals end, the standard representation for a blocked day) falls through to the subsequent range checks, which compare slotStartTime/slotEndTime against a zero-length interval and never return true — so the override is treated as if it doesn't exist and the day's normal working hours are used. Consequence: fixed hosts' all-day unavailability overrides are ignored for round-robin events, allowing bookings on days the fixed host explicitly blocked.

title: Extra closing parenthesis makes the slotStartTime.isAfter check a no-op
body: Line 123 reads `if (slotStartTime.isAfter(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))) {` — there is an unbalanced extra `)` before the opening brace. The condition `slotStartTime.isAfter(...)` is evaluated and its boolean result is discarded (it becomes the expression statement of the if with an empty body effect), and `return true` executes unconditionally whenever the date comparison on line 110 matched. This means any slot on the override's day is treated as 'outside the override' and rejected, regardless of whether it actually falls after the override end. Combined with the sign error above, the override window boundaries are computed incorrectly. Consequence: slots after the override end time on the override day are wrongly excluded (or, depending on the other branches, the whole day's logic misfires), producing incorrect availability for fixed hosts.

title: Working-hours fallback check compares slot start to both startTime and endTime using the same value
body: In the working-hours fallback inside checkIfIsAvailable (lines 139-147), `const start = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute(); const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` — `end` is assigned the slot START in minutes, not the slot end (start + eventLength). The check `if (start < workingHour.startTime || end > workingHour.endTime) return true;` therefore never detects a slot that starts inside working hours but extends past endTime. Consequence: for fixed hosts in round-robin events, slots that overrun the end of the working day are not rejected by this check, so the event can appear bookable at times the fixed host is not actually available (the busy-time check at the end may still catch some cases, but availability-window enforcement is broken).

title: Selected-slot filtering returns false for users with no reserved slots, dropping all round-robin hosts
body: In the selectedSlots filtering block (lines 565-590), for each slot userId the code builds `busy` from that user's reserved (non-seat) selectedSlots and then: `if (!busy?.length && eventType.seatsPerTimeSlot === null) { return false; }`. For a round-robin event (seatsPerTimeSlot === null) where a loose host has no reserved slot at that time, `busy` is empty and the userId is filtered OUT of the slot — even though the host is simply free. This inverts the intended semantics (a host with no reservation should remain available). Consequence: whenever any selected slot exists for the event (selectedSlots.length > 0), all round-robin hosts without a reservation are removed from every slot, which can empty the slot list entirely and make the event appear fully booked. This is a pre-existing logic error in this block that the PR's changes interact with, and it directly affects round-robin availability.

title: Override timezone conversion uses the override's own timeZone field, which is not populated for user-level overrides
body: In getSlots, the override offset is computed as `const organizerUtcOffset = dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset();`. The `timeZone` property on date overrides is only added in this PR to the flattened overrides in slots.ts (packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/slots.ts line 410-416) and to the TimeRange type; it comes from `availability.timeZone` (the user's timezone). However, getSlots is also called from client-side code and other paths where overrides may not carry `timeZone` (the type marks it optional). When `override.timeZone` is undefined, `dayjs(...).tz(undefined)` falls back to the runtime's local timezone, producing an offset based on the server/browser local zone rather than the organizer's zone. Consequence: the invitee-facing slot computation can shift override windows by the wrong amount for any caller that doesn't populate timeZone, reintroducing the timezone bug this PR fixes on those paths.

title: Override start/end minutes computed in two separate dayjs chains can straddle a DST boundary inconsistently
body: Lines 218-223 compute startTime and endTime via two independent expressions: `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, "minute").hour() * 60 + dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, "minute").minute()` and the same for `override.end`. The offset is derived from `override.start` only (line 212-213). If the override window crosses a DST transition in the invitee timezone (or organizer timezone), the offset computed at `override.start` is applied to `override.end` as well, so the end time can be off by the DST delta (typically 60 minutes). Consequence: override windows spanning a DST change produce slots shifted by an hour at the end of the window on the booking page.

title: New timezone test only verifies identical output, not that the override shifts with the invitee timezone
body: The added test 'scheduleForEventOnADayWithDateOverrideDifferentTimezone' (lines 788-804) queries with timeZone Asia/Dhaka (+6:00) and asserts the exact same UTC slots as the IST query, with the comment 'it should return the same as this is the utc time'. Since getSchedule returns slots as UTC ISO strings, identical UTC output across invitee timezones is expected and does not exercise the fix: the PR's second fix is that the override window (defined in organizer local time) must be interpreted in the organizer's timezone and rendered correctly for any invitee timezone. A meaningful test would use an invitee timezone where the override day/window maps to a different UTC day (e.g. a negative-offset zone like America/New_York, where 14:00-18:00 IST is 03:30-07:30 UTC same day but the date-override day boundary shifts), and assert the slots land on the correct UTC day. As written, the test would pass even if the offset logic in packages/lib/slots.ts were wrong by up to several hours, so it provides no regression protection for the timezone fix.

title: No test covers date overrides for fixed hosts in round-robin events, which is the PR's primary fix
body: The PR description states the main fix is that 'date overrides of fixed hosts are taken into account for round-robin events', but the only new/changed test ('Check for Date overrides', line 742) uses a single-user event with `hosts: []` and no `schedulingType: "ROUND_ROBIN"`. The new checkIfIsAvailable date-override/working-hours logic (packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/slots.ts lines 102-151) is only exercised through the fixed-hosts filter path (line 483-499) for round-robin/team events with hosts; no test creates a ROUND_ROBIN event with a fixed host that has a date override and asserts that slots outside the override are removed. Given the sign error, no-op equality, and syntax-level issues in that new code (see other findings), the primary behavior the PR claims to fix is completely untested and would not be caught by CI.

title: Working-hours check in checkIfIsAvailable uses wrong time units and wrong day, making the new working-hours gate ineffective
body: The newly added working-hours gate compares `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()` (minutes since midnight, e.g. 570 for 09:30) against `workingHour.startTime`/`workingHour.endTime`. However, `WorkingHours` (packages/types/schedule.d.ts) defines `startTime`/`endTime` as minutes since midnight in the *organizer's* timezone, while `slotStartTime` is a UTC Dayjs object — so the comparison mixes UTC minutes-of-day with organizer-local minutes-of-day and will reject or accept slots incorrectly across timezones. Additionally, `workingHour.days.includes(slotStartTime.day())` uses the UTC day-of-week of the slot, but `WorkingHours.days` are defined in the organizer's local timezone, so near midnight the wrong weekday can be selected. The consequence is that after this change, slots can be wrongly filtered out (or wrongly kept) for any organizer whose timezone differs from UTC, breaking availability for round-robin/fixed-host events — the exact scenario this PR is meant to fix. Note the same gate is also applied to non-override days, so this affects normal availability, not just date overrides.

title: Date-override matching in checkIfIsAvailable compares organizer-local dates against UTC slot dates, so overrides are matched to the wrong day
body: In `checkIfIsAvailable`, the override day is computed as `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').format('YYYY MM DD')` where `utcOffset = dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone).utcOffset() * -1`, and this is compared to `slotStartTime.format('YYYY MM DD')` where `slotStartTime = time.utc()`. The left side is the override's calendar date expressed in the organizer's timezone (a local date), while the right side is the slot's UTC calendar date. These are different calendars, so for organizers not in UTC the override will be matched against the wrong day (off by the timezone offset), causing slots on the override day to be incorrectly rejected (treated as 'not within the date override') and slots on adjacent days to be incorrectly accepted. The subsequent range checks also mix the organizer-local shifted instants (`date.start + utcOffset`) with UTC slot times, compounding the error. This directly undermines the PR's goal of honoring fixed-host date overrides for round-robin events.

title: Equality check between Dayjs objects in date-override logic never matches, making all-day overrides behave as ranged overrides
body: Line 114 uses `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes') === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, 'minutes')` to detect an all-day (unavailable) override where start equals end. This is a reference equality comparison between two distinct Dayjs instances, which is always false. As a result, an all-day date override (start === end, meaning 'unavailable all day') is not detected as such; the code falls through to the range checks, and since `slotEndTime.isBefore(start) || slotEndTime.isSame(start)` and `slotStartTime.isAfter(end)` can both be false for slots inside that day, `dateOverrides.find(...)` returns undefined while `dateOverrideExist` is true — so the function returns `true` (available) for slots on a day the organizer explicitly marked unavailable. This is a data-integrity/booking-correctness bug: round-robin events can be booked on days the fixed host marked as fully unavailable.

title: Selected-slot filtering returns false when a user has no reserved slot and the event is not a seated event, inverting the intended logic
body: In the `selectedSlots` handling block, the per-user filter does: `if (!busy?.length && eventType.seatsPerTimeSlot === null) { return false; }`. For a non-seated event (`seatsPerTimeSlot === null`) where the user has no reserved (selected) slot, `busy` is empty, so the user is filtered out of `slot.userIds`, and the slot is subsequently dropped by `.filter((slot) => !!slot.userIds?.length)`. That means any slot without a corresponding `selectedSlots` row removes all users and eliminates the slot entirely — the opposite of the intent (a user with no reservation should be considered available). This will incorrectly hide available slots whenever `selectedSlots` exist for the event but not for every user/slot combination.

title: Date-override activation check uses UTC day boundaries against invitee-local day, misclassifying overrides near midnight
body: `activeOverrides` is computed with `dayjs.utc(override.start).isBetween(startOfInviteeDay, startOfInviteeDay.endOf('day'), null, '[)')`. `startOfInviteeDay` is a Dayjs in the invitee's timezone (its underlying instant is the invitee's local midnight), but `dayjs.utc(override.start)` is the override start as a UTC instant. Comparing a UTC instant against an invitee-local day range means an override that starts on the invitee's local day can be excluded (or one from the adjacent UTC day included) whenever the invitee timezone is not UTC — e.g. an override for 00:30–02:00 local in a UTC+6 invitee timezone starts at 18:30 UTC the previous day and fails the `isBetween` check. The override is then silently ignored and the regular working hours are used, so the timezone fix does not apply consistently.

title: Override offset is computed from the override start instant only, ignoring DST differences between start and end
body: The override-to-invitee conversion computes a single `offset = inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset` using `dayjs(override.start...)` and applies that same offset to both `override.start` and `override.end`. If a DST transition occurs between the override start and end (or the offset differs at the end instant), the end time is shifted by the wrong amount, producing an incorrect override window length. The correct approach is to compute the offset separately for the start and end instants (or convert each instant to the invitee timezone independently). Consequence: date overrides spanning a DST change yield wrong slot boundaries in the invitee's timezone.

title: Seat-occupancy merge uses `typeof x !== undefined` instead of a value check, so the branch is effectively dead
body: `if (typeof availabilityCheckProps.currentSeats !== undefined)` is always true (`typeof` always returns a string, which is never `undefined`), so the intended guard — only merge occupied seats into an existing `currentSeats` array — does not work. When `currentSeats` is `undefined`, the `.map` call on line 532 throws a TypeError at runtime whenever `occupiedSeats.length` is non-zero and `currentSeats` was not previously set. This is a latent crash in the seats path introduced by restructuring this block.

title: New timezone test only asserts identical UTC output and does not actually verify timezone-dependent override behavior
body: The added test `scheduleForEventOnADayWithDateOverrideDifferentTimezone` requests the schedule with `timeZone: Timezones['+6:00']` (Asia/Dhaka) but asserts the exact same UTC slot list (`08:30:00.000Z` … `11:30:00.000Z`) and the same `dateString` bucket as the IST request, with the comment 'it should return the same as this is the utc time'. Because `getSchedule` returns slots keyed by the invitee-timezone date and the requested window (`plus1DateStringT18:30Z` to `plus2DateStringT18:29:59Z`) only covers one UTC day, the test cannot distinguish correct from incorrect timezone handling — a regression that ignored the invitee timezone entirely would still pass. The test does not verify that the override date is interpreted in the organizer's timezone and rendered on the correct invitee-local day, which is the behavior the PR claims to fix. A meaningful test would use a window/override where the invitee-local day differs from the UTC day (e.g. an override late in the UTC day that falls on the next local day in Dhaka) and assert the shifted slot set.

title: No test covers date overrides for fixed hosts in round-robin events, which is the primary fix in this PR
body: The PR description states the main fix is that 'date overrides of fixed hosts are taken into account for round-robin events', but the only new/changed test (`Check for Date overrides`) uses a single-user event with `hosts: []` and no `schedulingType: 'ROUND_ROBIN'`. There is no test that creates a round-robin event with a fixed host plus a round-robin host, adds a date override for the fixed host, and asserts that slots outside the override are removed. The `checkIfIsAvailable` changes that implement this behavior (dateOverrides/workingHours/organizerTimeZone parameters and the fixed-host `every` loop) are therefore untested for the round-robin path, leaving the core fix without regression coverage.

title: SQL injection in migration via interpolated host value
body: The migration builds an INSERT statement by string interpolation: `execute "INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, category_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES ('#{h}', #{category_id}, ...)"`. The value `h` comes directly from the `embeddable_hosts` site setting (line 22, `val.split("\n")`), which is admin-controlled free text. A host value containing a single quote (e.g. `x'); DROP TABLE users;--`) breaks out of the string literal and executes arbitrary SQL during `rake db:migrate`. This must use parameterized queries, e.g. `execute("INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, category_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)", h, category_id)` (or `exec_query` with binds). Note the same file's other `execute` calls interpolate only values read from the database itself (category id / setting value), which is lower risk, but the host loop is a direct injection path.

title: update/destroy actions crash with NoMethodError when the host does not exist
body: `update` does `host = EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` and then unconditionally calls `save_host(host)`, which dereferences `host.host = ...`. If no EmbeddableHost matches the id, `host` is nil and the request raises NoMethodError (500) instead of returning a 404. Same problem in `destroy` (line 15-16): `host.destroy` on nil raises. The controller should return `render_json_error`/404 (e.g. `raise Discourse::NotFound` or check `host.nil?`) when the record is missing. This is reachable by any admin via PUT/DELETE /admin/embeddable_hosts/:id with a stale or bogus id, and the Ember client's `destroyRecord().then(...)` would surface an unhandled 500.

title: Mass-assignment of arbitrary params into EmbeddableHost attributes
body: `save_host` assigns `host.host = params[:embeddable_host][:host]` and `host.category_id = params[:embeddable_host][:category_id]` directly from params without strong-parameter filtering or an allowlist. Any additional keys an admin POSTs under `embeddable_host[...]` are ignored only by luck of this explicit assignment, but more importantly there is no validation that `category_id` refers to an existing category before save; combined with `belongs_to :category` (no `validates :category, presence: true` on the model), an admin can set a dangling `category_id`. The model only validates the `host` format. Consider validating the category's existence (or at least that it is present) and using explicit permitted params.

title: before_validation mutates nil host, crashing validation for blank hosts
body: The `before_validation` block calls `self.host.sub!(...)` unconditionally. If `host` is nil (e.g. an admin submits an empty host field, or `EmbeddableHost.new` without a host), `nil.sub!` raises NoMethodError, turning what should be a normal validation failure ("host is invalid") into a 500 error. The controller's `save_host` path (`EmbeddableHost.new` then assign from params) hits this whenever `params[:embeddable_host][:host]` is blank/nil. Guard with `self.host = host.to_s` or `if host.present?` before the substitutions, and add `validates :host, presence: true` so blank input is rejected cleanly.

title: record_for_host does case-insensitive lookup but stores mixed-case hosts, allowing duplicate/conflicting entries
body: `record_for_host` matches with `where("lower(host) = ?", host)` but the column has no uniqueness constraint and the model has no uniqueness validation, so two rows `Example.com` and `example.com` can both exist (the migration even inserts raw setting values without normalization). `host_allowed?` then returns the first match, and `TopicEmbed.import` uses `eh.try(:category_id)` from an arbitrary one of them, so the category chosen for imported topics is nondeterministic. Add `validates :host, uniqueness: { case_sensitive: false }` and a unique index on `lower(host)` (or downcase in before_validation) so lookups are deterministic.

title: Host validation regex is too permissive (allows paths, ports, and long TLDs), enabling referer-spoofing edge cases
body: The format regex `/\A[a-z0-9]+([\-\.]{1}[a-z0-9]+)*\.[a-z]{2,5}(:[0-9]{1,5})?(\/.*)?\Z/i` permits an optional port and an arbitrary trailing path (`(\/.*)?`). However `record_for_host` compares only `uri.host`, ignoring port and path, so a stored host of `example.com:8080` or `example.com/evil` will authorize ANY referer whose host is `example.com` regardless of port/path. That silently widens the embed allowlist beyond what the admin configured (e.g. allowing `http://example.com:8080` or any path on that host). Either strip/normalize to host-only on save (the before_validation already strips scheme and path but not port) and reject ports, or make `record_for_host` compare scheme+host+port consistently. At minimum, the stored value should be normalized to a bare hostname and the regex should not accept `:` or `/`.

title: Removing the 'embeddable hosts not set' guard lets embed/comments leak when no hosts are configured
body: The old code raised `Discourse::InvalidAccess.new('embeddable hosts not set') if SiteSetting.embeddable_hosts.blank?` before checking the referer. The new code only checks `EmbeddableHost.host_allowed?(request.referer)`. `host_allowed?` returns `record_for_host(host).present?`, and `record_for_host` returns `false` when the referer is nil/unparseable — so with zero configured hosts every request is still denied. However, the behavior change is subtle and untested: previously a blank setting was an explicit early failure; now the security of the endpoint depends entirely on `record_for_host` correctly returning false for nil/blank referers (it does via `uri.present?` / `host.present?` checks, and `URI(nil)` raises and is rescued to nil). The spec at spec/controllers/embed_controller_spec.rb line 13-16 ('raises an error with a missing host') covers the no-host case, but there is no test for a nil referer with hosts configured in the 'by topic id' context — actually there is (line 35-38). The real gap: `ensure_embeddable` rescues `URI::InvalidURIError` but `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host` already rescues internally and returns false, so the rescue is dead code; more importantly, if `request.referer` is nil, `URI(nil)` raises `TypeError` (not `InvalidURIError`) inside `record_for_host`... actually `URI(nil)` raises `ArgumentError`/`TypeError` depending on Ruby version — `URI(nil)` raises `TypeError: no implicit conversion of nil into String` in modern Ruby, which is NOT rescued by `rescue nil` modifier? The modifier `rescue nil` catches StandardError; TypeError is a StandardError, so it is caught. OK — but this fragility (relying on exception class coverage) should be replaced with an explicit `return false if host.blank?` guard in `record_for_host`/`host_allowed?`.

title: EmbeddingSerializer serializes an OpenStruct, but has_many :embeddable_hosts with embed: :ids expects an association that OpenStruct does not provide
body: `fetch_embedding` builds `@embedding = OpenStruct.new(id: 'default', embeddable_hosts: EmbeddableHost.all.order(:host))`. `EmbeddingSerializer` declares `has_many :embeddable_hosts, serializer: EmbeddableHostSerializer, embed: :ids`.
