Conversely, a small-dimension but poorly-compressed image may loop unnecessarily. More critically, the loop can exit with `tempfile.size` still > `max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` after 5 attempts, and the upload proceeds anyway via `Upload.create_for` — there is no check that the downsize actually succeeded in bringing the file under the limit, so the original intent (allow large images by auto-reducing them) is not enforced; the upload will then likely fail at the `Upload` model validation level with a confusing error, or worse, bypass the intended size restriction if validation is missing. The loop should verify the result and reject the upload if the file is still too large after downsizing attempts.

title: In-place downsize of tempfile corrupts file and breaks subsequent Upload.create_for which reads tempfile.size
body: `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...)` writes the converted image to the same path as the input. ImageMagick's `convert` with identical input and output paths is undefined/unsafe — it can truncate or corrupt the file because the output file is opened before the input is fully read. Even if it works in some ImageMagick versions, after the loop `tempfile.size` (line 72) is called on the original Tempfile object, which may have a stale cached size from before the in-place modification, causing `Upload.create_for` to record an incorrect filesize in the database. The downsized file should be written to a separate temp path, and the tempfile reference updated, or the size re-read from disk after downsizing.

title: Downsize loop runs on any image upload regardless of user permissions, enabling CPU-exhaustion DoS
body: The downsizing loop executes for every image upload when `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb > 0`, with up to 5 ImageMagick `convert` invocations per upload. ImageMagick conversion is CPU-intensive. A malicious user (or bot) can upload many large images (up to the 10MB download limit for API URL fetches, or whatever the web server accepts for direct uploads) to trigger repeated expensive image processing, consuming server CPU and potentially causing denial of service. There is no rate limiting, no check on image dimensions before processing (a 10MB image could be 20000x20000 pixels, making each convert extremely expensive), and no queueing — this runs synchronously in the request (or deferred job) without bounds on pixel count. The loop should check image dimensions first and reject images that are absurdly large, and/or limit total processing time.

title: API URL download limit changed from max_image_size_kb to hardcoded 10MB, allowing downloads of files that will be rejected or cause processing issues
body: The API URL download limit was changed from `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` to a hardcoded `10.megabytes`. This means the server will now download up to 10MB from an arbitrary user-supplied URL (SSRF surface is pre-existing, but the size limit change matters), and then the downsizing loop attempts to reduce it. If `max_image_size_kb` is set to e.g. 500KB, the server downloads 10MB, then runs up to 5 ImageMagick conversions on a potentially huge image. The hardcoded 10MB also ignores the site's configured maximum image size entirely for the download step. The download limit should remain tied to `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` (or a separate, explicit setting) to avoid downloading files that are far larger than what will be accepted.

title: content_type is nil for API URL uploads, causing Upload.create_for to receive nil content_type
body: When the upload comes via API URL (`file.nil? && url.present? && is_api?`), `content_type` is never assigned (it is only set in the `else` branch at line 60). The downsizing block at line 64 does not set `content_type` either. Then at line 72, `Upload.create_for(..., content_type: content_type, ...)` passes `nil` for content_type. This may cause the Upload record to have a nil or incorrect content_type, affecting how the file is served (MIME type) and potentially breaking image detection or security checks downstream. The content_type should be inferred from the downloaded file (e.g., using `FileHelper` or Marcel/mime-types) when downloading from a URL.

title: Client-side upload size validation hardcoded to 10MB, ignoring site settings and diverging from server-side limit
body: The client-side validation in `validateUploadedFile` now hardcodes `maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024` (10MB), replacing the previous `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`. This means the client will allow uploads up to 10MB regardless of the site's configured `max_image_size_kb` or `max_attachment_size_kb`. If an admin sets `max_image_size_kb` to 500KB, the client will still permit a 9MB upload, which will then be processed by the server (downloaded, downsized up to 5 times) before being rejected or accepted. This wastes server resources and provides a poor user experience (upload appears to proceed, then fails or is unexpectedly downsized). The client-side check should use the site setting, or at minimum the server-side limit should be communicated to the client. The hardcoded value also affects attachments, which may have a different limit.

title: 413 error handler hardcodes 10MB instead of using site setting, showing wrong limit to user
body: In `displayErrorForUpload`, the 413 (Payload Too Large) handler now hardcodes `maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024` instead of `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb`. When the web server (nginx/Apache) rejects an upload with 413, the user sees an error message stating the limit is 10MB, even if the site's actual configured limit is different (e.g., 500KB). This is misleading and was previously using the correct site setting. The hardcoded value should be reverted to use the site setting, or the message should not display a specific limit when it cannot be determined accurately.

title: Shell command injection risk in convert_with via unsanitized file paths
body: The `convert_with` method executes a shell command via backticks: `` `#{instructions.join(" ")} &> /dev/null` ``. The `instructions` array includes `from` and `to` paths that originate from user-controlled data — in the new `uploads_controller.rb` code, `tempfile.path` is passed as both `from` and `to` to `OptimizedImage.downsize`. While Tempfile paths are generally safe (generated by Ruby), the `from` path in other callers (e.g., `OptimizedImage.create_for` line 31: `Discourse.store.path_for(upload)`) derives from upload filenames which are user-controlled. If a filename contains shell metacharacters (e.g., `;`, `` ` ``, `$()`), and the path is not properly escaped in the `convert`/`gifsicle` command construction, this could lead to command injection. The `resize_instructions` and `downsize_instructions` methods interpolate `#{from}` and `#{to}` directly into the command array without shell escaping. This is a pre-existing risk but is amplified by the new code path that passes tempfile paths directly. The instructions should use `Shellwords.escape` on all path arguments, or better, use `Open3`/`system` with array arguments to avoid shell interpretation entirely.

title: Duplicate downsize method definitions with different arities create ambiguity and potential breakage
body: The diff adds a new `downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` method (line 149) while retaining the existing `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` (line 145). Ruby will use the last defined method when arities match, but having two methods with the same name and overlapping arities (both accept 4-5 arguments) is confusing and fragile. The old 4-argument form `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height)` will now call the new method with `dimensions = max_width` and `opts = max_height` (an Integer), causing `"#{max_width}x#{max_height}"` to never be constructed — instead `dimensions` (an Integer) is passed to `optimize`, which passes it to `downsize_instructions` where it is interpolated as `#{dimensions}\>`, producing e.g. `100\>` instead of `100x100\>`. This silently breaks any existing caller using the old 4-argument form. The old method should be removed or renamed, and all callers updated to use the new dimensions-string form.

title: Downsize condition checks FileHelper.is_image?(filename) but filename may be nil or misleading for URL-based uploads
body: For API URL uploads, `filename = File.basename(URI.parse(url).path)` (line 56). If the URL has no path (e.g., `http://example.com`), `URI.parse(url).path` returns `""`, and `File.basename("")` returns `""`. Then `FileHelper.is_image?("")` likely returns false, so downsizing is skipped — but the downloaded content might actually be an image. Conversely, if the URL path ends with `.png` but the content is not an image (or is a malicious file), `is_image?` returns true and ImageMagick will attempt to process it. The check should be based on the actual file content (magic bytes) or the downloaded file's detected type, not just the filename extension from the URL. Additionally, `FileHelper.is_image?` may not exist or may behave differently than expected — the code should verify the method exists and handles edge cases.

title: Downsize loop runs in deferred job without timeout, potentially blocking worker for extended period
body: When `synchronous` is false (the default for non-API requests), `create_upload` runs inside `Scheduler::Defer.later` (line 19). The downsizing loop can invoke ImageMagick up to 5 times on a large image. ImageMagick `convert` on a very large image (e.g., 10000x10000 pixels) can take tens of seconds or minutes per invocation. There is no timeout on the `convert_with` shell command (line 161 in optimized_image.rb: `` `#{instructions.join(" ")} &> /dev/null` ``), so a single malicious upload could tie up a background worker for an extended period, potentially causing job queue backup. The shell command should have a timeout (e.g., using `Timeout.timeout` around the backtick execution, or ImageMagick's own `-limit` options), and the overall downsizing operation should be bounded.

title: Downsize loop uses file size as proxy for image dimensions, causing infinite/ineffective resizing for already-small large files
body: The new downsize loop in `create_upload` checks `tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` and repeatedly calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...)`. However, `OptimizedImage.downsize` with a percentage string ("80%") resizes the image dimensions by 80%, not the file size. For many image formats (especially PNG, or already-compressed JPEGs), reducing dimensions by 80% may not reduce file size below the limit, or the file may already be under the size limit while having huge dimensions. The loop will run up to 5 times doing nothing useful, or worse, for a large-dimension but small-file-size image (e.g., a mostly-blank PNG), it won't trigger at all even though the image dimensions are enormous. The feature's stated goal is to 'automatically downsize large images' — meaning large dimensions — but the condition checks file size, not width/height. This is a logic mismatch: the guard should check actual image dimensions (e.g., via `FastImage` or ImageMagick `identify`) against a max dimension setting, not file size against `max_image_size_kb`. Consequence: the feature fails to achieve its purpose for dimension-heavy images, and wastes CPU running ImageMagick up to 5 times on files that won't shrink below the size threshold.

title: In-place downsize of tempfile corrupts file and breaks subsequent Upload.create_for which reads tempfile.size
body: The code calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...)` — using the same path for both `from` and `to`. ImageMagick's `convert` cannot safely read and write the same file in-place; this typically results in a corrupted, truncated, or empty output file. After this loop, line 72 calls `Upload.create_for(current_user.id, tempfile, filename, tempfile.size, ...)` which reads `tempfile.size` — but the tempfile's size on disk has been changed by the in-place ImageMagick operation, and the Ruby `Tempfile` object's cached size may be stale or the file may be corrupted. Additionally, `Upload.create_for` will read the file content from `tempfile` — if ImageMagick corrupted it, the upload will store a broken image. The correct approach is to downsize to a new temp file and replace the original, or use a separate output path. Consequence: uploaded images may be corrupted, truncated, or fail to process, leading to broken uploads and potential data integrity issues.

title: Shell command injection risk via filename in OptimizedImage.downsize path
body: The `OptimizedImage.downsize` method ultimately calls `convert_with` which executes a shell command via backticks: `` `#{instructions.join(" ")} &> /dev/null` ``. The `from` and `to` paths are `tempfile.path`, which is a system-generated temp path and safe. However, the `filename` variable (derived from `file.original_filename` or `File.basename(URI.parse(url).path)`) is used in `FileHelper.is_image?(filename)` on line 64, and while it's not directly passed to the shell here, the broader pattern of using user-controlled filenames in ImageMagick commands is dangerous. More critically, if `FileHelper.is_image?` returns true for a crafted filename containing shell metacharacters (e.g., `image.png; rm -rf /`), and if that filename were ever used in a path passed to `convert`, it would be a command injection. In this specific code path, `tempfile.path` is used (safe), but the `filename` is still user-controlled and passed to `Upload.create_for`. The `downsize_instructions` method interpolates `from` and `to` directly into the command without escaping. While `tempfile.path` is safe here, this is a fragile pattern. The real concern: if `FileHelper.download` on line 55 returns a tempfile whose path includes user-controlled components, or if the code is refactored to use `filename` in the path, this becomes exploitable. The current code uses `tempfile.path` which is safe, but the overall design of passing unescaped paths to shell commands is a security risk.

title: API URL download size limit changed from max_image_size_kb to 10MB, bypassing configured limit
body: The diff changes `FileHelper.download(url, SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes, ...)` to `FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)`. This means API clients can now download files up to 10MB regardless of the `max_image_size_kb` site setting. While the subsequent downsize loop attempts to reduce images, non-image files (or images that fail to downsize) will now be accepted up to 10MB, whereas before they were limited to `max_image_size_kb`. This is a behavioral change that bypasses the configured upload size limit for API URL fetches. If `max_image_size_kb` is set to, say, 2MB, an API client could previously only fetch 2MB files; now they can fetch 10MB files. The downsize loop only applies to images (`FileHelper.is_image?(filename)`), so non-image attachments fetched via URL are now subject to a much higher limit. Consequence: server storage exhaustion, bandwidth abuse, and violation of the site's configured upload policy.

title: Synchronous ImageMagick processing in request cycle blocks web worker and risks timeout
body: The downsize loop runs synchronously inside `create_upload`, which is called directly in the `create` action (line 16) for synchronous API requests, or inside `Scheduler::Defer.later` for async requests. For synchronous API requests (`is_api? && params[:synchronous]`), this means up to 5 ImageMagick `convert` operations run in the web request thread, each potentially taking seconds for large images. This blocks the web worker, increases response latency, and can cause request timeouts. Even for async requests, running 5 sequential ImageMagick operations in a deferred job ties up a background worker for an extended period. ImageMagick operations on large images (e.g., 50MP photos) can take 10-30 seconds each, meaning up to 150 seconds of processing per upload. Consequence: degraded server performance, worker pool exhaustion, and potential request timeouts for synchronous API uploads.

title: Downsize loop condition uses `>` instead of `>=`, allowing files exactly at limit to skip processing
body: The while loop condition is `tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes`. If a file is exactly `max_image_size_kb` in size, it will not be downsized. While this may be intentional (files at the limit are acceptable), the `Upload.create_for` on line 72 will still validate the file size against the limit. If the validation uses `>` as well, this is consistent; if it uses `>=`, there's an inconsistency. More importantly, the loop's purpose is to reduce files that exceed the limit, and using `>` means files exactly at the limit pass through — which is fine — but the real issue is that the loop doesn't account for the fact that `Upload.create_for` may have its own size validation that could reject the file if the downsize didn't reduce it enough. The loop exits after 5 attempts regardless of whether the file is still too large, and then `Upload.create_for` is called with the still-oversized file, which will likely fail validation. There's no check after the loop to verify the file is now within limits, and no error handling if downsize fails to reduce the file sufficiently.

title: No error handling if OptimizedImage.downsize fails — upload proceeds with original oversized file
body: `OptimizedImage.downsize` returns a boolean (true/false) via `convert_with`, but the return value is ignored in the loop on line 67. If ImageMagick fails (e.g., corrupt image, unsupported format, missing binary), `downsize` returns false, but the loop continues decrementing `attempt` and retrying. After 5 failed attempts, the loop exits and `Upload.create_for` is called with the original, still-oversized tempfile. `Upload.create_for` will then likely reject the upload due to size validation, but the user gets a generic validation error rather than a meaningful message about why the image couldn't be processed. Additionally, if `downsize` partially succeeds (reduces dimensions but not enough to get under the size limit), the loop exits after 5 attempts and the upload fails. There's no logging of downsize failures, making debugging difficult. Consequence: poor user experience with cryptic errors, and wasted processing on files that cannot be downsized.

title: Hardcoded 10MB max upload size ignores site setting, breaking configurable upload limits
body: The diff changes `var maxSizeKB = Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'];` to `var maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024; // 10MB`. This hardcodes the client-side upload size limit to 10MB, completely ignoring the site's configured `max_image_size_kb` and `max_attachment_size_kb` settings. If a site admin sets `max_image_size_kb` to 2MB, the client will still allow users to select files up to 10MB, only to have them rejected by the server (or worse, accepted by the new downsize logic). This creates a mismatch between client-side validation and server-side limits. The error message shown to users (`post.errors.file_too_large` with `max_size_kb: 10240`) will also be wrong — it will tell users the limit is 10MB when the actual server limit may be much lower. Consequence: confusing user experience, wasted bandwidth uploading files that will be rejected, and incorrect error messages. The same hardcoding appears on line 246 for the 413 error handler.

title: Hardcoded 10MB in 413 error handler shows wrong limit to users
body: The 413 (Payload Too Large) error handler now uses `var maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024; // 10 MB` instead of `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb`. When a web server (nginx, Apache) rejects an upload with 413, the error message shown to the user will state the limit is 10MB, regardless of the actual configured `max_image_size_kb`. If the site has configured a 2MB limit, users will see 'file too large (max 10240 KB)' when the real limit is 2048 KB. This is misleading and confusing. The original code correctly used the site setting. Consequence: incorrect error messaging, user confusion about upload limits.

title: Downsize instructions use `-resize` with `\>` flag but percentage string "80%" doesn't work as expected with `\>`
body: The `downsize_instructions` method generates: `convert #{from}[0] -gravity center -background transparent -resize #{dimensions}\> #{to}`. When `dimensions` is "80%" (as passed from `uploads_controller.rb` line 67), the command becomes `convert input.png[0] -gravity center -background transparent -resize 80%\> output.png`. The `\>` flag in ImageMagick means 'only shrink an image with dimensions larger than the corresponding width and/or height argument'. When combined with a percentage like "80%", the behavior is: resize to 80% only if the image is larger than 80% of its original size — which is always true, so it effectively just resizes to 80%. However, the `\>` flag is designed for absolute dimensions (e.g., `1000x1000\>`), not percentages. Using it with a percentage is semantically incorrect and may produce unexpected results across ImageMagick versions. The intent in the controller is to reduce file size by 80%, but `-resize 80%` reduces dimensions by 80%, not file size. The `\>` flag is irrelevant here and may cause confusion. More importantly, the controller passes "80%" as `dimensions`, but the `downsize` method signature expects `max_width, max_height` or a `dimensions` string. The overload resolution works, but the semantics are muddled. Consequence: unpredictable resizing behavior, and the feature doesn't reliably reduce file size.

title: Shell command execution with unescaped file paths enables command injection
body: `convert_with` executes `` `#{instructions.join(" ")} &> /dev/null` `` where `instructions` includes `from` and `to` paths interpolated directly without shell escaping. While `tempfile.path` in the current controller code is system-generated and safe, this method is a public class method (`OptimizedImage.downsize`, `OptimizedImage.resize`) that accepts arbitrary `from` and `to` paths. Any caller passing a user-controlled filename (e.g., an upload filename containing `; malicious_command` or `$(malicious_command)`) would result in shell command injection. The `instructions` array is built by joining strings with spaces, and paths are not quoted or escaped. For example, if `from` is `/tmp/upload; rm -rf /;.png`, the shell command becomes `convert /tmp/upload; rm -rf /;.png[0] ...` which executes `rm -rf /`. This is a critical security vulnerability if any code path passes user-controlled filenames to these methods. The current controller code uses `tempfile.path` (safe), but the method itself is unsafe by design. Consequence: arbitrary command execution if any caller passes untrusted input as file paths.

title: Method overload ambiguity: two `downsize` methods with different arities may cause confusion
body: The class now has two `self.downsize` methods: one at line 145 taking `(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` and one at line 149 taking `(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`. Ruby resolves these by arity — 4 arguments (plus opts) vs 3 arguments (plus opts). The controller calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: ...)` which matches the 3-argument version (line 149). However, this overload pattern is fragile: if someone calls `downsize(from, to, 800, 600)` they get the first version which formats as "800x600"; if they call `downsize(from, to, "800x600")` they get the second version. The two methods have different semantics — one takes separate width/height, the other takes a dimension string. This is confusing API design. The original code had a single `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` that called `dimensions(width, height)` internally. The refactoring introduced this overload to support passing a percentage string directly, but it creates an inconsistent API. Consequence: potential bugs if callers mix up the calling conventions, and reduced code clarity.

title: Downsize loop modifies tempfile in-place, but `content_type` variable may be undefined for URL-based uploads
body: In the `create_upload` method, `content_type` is only assigned in the `else` branch (line 60: `content_type = file.content_type`). For API URL-based uploads (line 54-56), `content_type` is never assigned. The downsize loop on lines 64-70 runs for both branches (it only checks `tempfile` and `filename`). After the loop, line 72 calls `Upload.create_for(current_user.id, tempfile, filename, tempfile.size, content_type: content_type, ...)`. For URL-based uploads, `content_type` is `nil` (undefined local variable becomes nil in Ruby when referenced). This was the case before the change too, but the downsize loop now processes URL-based image uploads, potentially modifying the tempfile. If `Upload.create_for` uses `content_type` to determine how to process the file, passing `nil` for a downsized image could cause issues. Additionally, after in-place downsizing, the file's actual content type may change (e.g., ImageMagick might output a different format), but `content_type` remains whatever it was (or nil). Consequence: incorrect content type stored in the database, potential processing errors in `Upload.create_for` or downstream thumbnail generation.

title: `tempfile.size` after in-place modification may be stale or incorrect, causing wrong filesize stored in Upload
body: After the downsize loop modifies the tempfile in-place via ImageMagick, line 72 calls `Upload.create_for(current_user.id, tempfile, filename, tempfile.size, ...)`. The `tempfile.size` call returns the size of the file on disk at that moment. However, Ruby's `Tempfile` (and `File`) objects may cache file size or have buffered state. More critically, if ImageMagick's `convert` wrote to the same path, the file size on disk has changed, but if there are any file handles open or OS-level caching, `tempfile.size` might not reflect the actual current size. Additionally, `Upload.create_for` likely reads the file content and may compute its own size or SHA1 — if it uses the passed `tempfile.size` parameter for validation or storage, a stale or incorrect value could cause the upload to be rejected or stored with wrong metadata. The correct approach is to re-stat the file after modification or use a new tempfile. Consequence: incorrect file size stored in the `uploads` table, potential validation failures, and broken download/display of uploads.

title: unsubscribe action crashes with NoMethodError when no TopicUser record exists
body: In TopicsController#unsubscribe, `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil (a user who has never interacted with the topic has no TopicUser row). The very next line calls `tu.notification_level`, which raises NoMethodError on nil, producing a 500 error instead of unsubscribing. The code should use `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, params[:topic_id], notification_level: ...)` (which creates the row if missing, as done in #set_notifications) or handle the nil case explicitly.

title: unsubscribe action does not verify the user can see the topic
body: TopicsController#unsubscribe builds `TopicView.new(params[:topic_id], current_user)` but never calls `guardian.ensure_can_see!` on the topic. TopicView.new may raise Discourse::InvalidAccess for inaccessible topics, but the action also mutates the current user's TopicUser notification level before any visibility check is guaranteed, and unlike #show it does not clean up notifications or handle InvalidAccess. A user who cannot see a topic (e.g. a restricted-category topic) can still hit /t/:id/unsubscribe and toggle their notification state for it. The topic should be fetched and `guardian.ensure_can_see!(topic)` called before mutating TopicUser.

title: unsubscribe toggle logic silently does nothing for muted users and mislabels the action
body: The toggle in #unsubscribe is `if tu.notification_level > regular then regular else muted end`. For a user whose level is already `muted` (0), the condition is false, so the level is set to `muted` again — the link never restores notifications for muted users, it only ever mutes or downgrades. Additionally, the email copy says 'stop receiving notifications about this particular topic', but for watching/tracking users the action only downgrades to regular (they still get emails), which contradicts the promise in the email and the client-side text 'You will stop receiving notifications'. The intended behavior (mute when above regular, restore to regular when muted) is not implemented.

title: unsubscribe renders the full topic show response, leaking topic content and preloading it
body: After mutating the notification level, #unsubscribe calls `perform_show_response`, which serializes the entire TopicView (all posts the guardian can see) and, for HTML requests, calls `store_preloaded("topic_#{id}", ...)` and renders :show. The unsubscribe endpoint is meant to be a lightweight landing page reached from an email link; rendering the full topic leaks the topic body to anyone with the URL (subject only to normal guardian checks, which are not explicitly performed here) and does heavy work. It should render a minimal confirmation instead of the full topic payload.

title: check_xhr is skipped for unsubscribe, allowing non-XHR state-changing GET
body: `skip_before_filter :check_xhr, only: [:show, :unsubscribe, :feed]` permits the state-changing `unsubscribe` action to be triggered by a plain GET request from any context, including via CSRF-style link prefetching or cross-site /link tags (the endpoint is same-origin but a cross-site GET from a browser is still possible since no CSRF token is required for GET). Combined with the missing visibility check, this makes the notification-level mutation triggerable by simple navigation. A POST/PUT route or an explicit confirmation would be safer.

title: topic-unsubscribe route creates a record in the store that is never cleaned up and fetches data needlessly
body: The route's model hook calls `this.store.createRecord("topic", { id: params.id })`, which inserts a new (unsaved, id-only) Topic record into the Ember Data store, then immediately overwrites it via `topic.updateFromJson(json)` from `PostStream.loadTopicView`. Creating a store record for an id-only object pollutes the identity map (a later real fetch of the same topic id may return this stub), and `loadTopicView` duplicates the normal topic-loading path. The route should use `this.store.find('topic', params.id)` or the standard topic model hook instead of createRecord.

title: afterModel sets a nested property path that Ember cannot observe on a plain object
body: `topic.set("details.notificationReasonText", null)` assumes `topic.details` is an Ember object; if `details` is a plain JS object (as serialized topic details typically are in this codebase), setting a nested path on it will not be tracked and may silently fail or throw depending on the Ember version. The intent (hide the notification reason text on the unsubscribe page) is not reliably achieved.

title: Misspelled property name stopNotificiationsText
body: The computed property is named `stopNotificiationsText` (missing the 'a' in 'Notifications'), and the template references `{{{stopNotificiationsText}}}` so it works, but the misspelling will confuse future maintainers and any external references. It should be renamed to `stopNotificationsText` in both the controller and the template.

title: Triple-stache output of stopNotificiationsText injects the topic title as raw HTML
body: The template renders `{{{stopNotificiationsText}}}` (unescaped). The string is built from `I18n.t("topic.unsubscribe.stop_notifications", { title: this.get("model.fancyTitle") })`. `fancyTitle` is HTML-escaped server-side (ERB::Util.html_escape in Topic#fancy_title), but I18n interpolation does not re-escape, and any locale override or future change to the title source would inject raw HTML into the page. The locale string itself contains `{{title}}`, so the title must be escaped before interpolation (e.g. via `Em.I18n` with escaped params or by escaping in the controller) rather than relying on the server-side escaping surviving the round trip.

title: dropdown-button renderString interpolates unescaped values into HTML (XSS)
body:
renderString builds HTML by string concatenation: `buffer.push("
  • ")` and `buffer.push("" + row.title + "")` etc. None of `id`, `row.title`, `row.description`, `row.styleClasses`, `this.get('text')`, `title`, or `longDescription` are HTML-escaped. Any caller that passes user-controlled data (e.g. topic titles, category names) into dropDownContent/text will produce an XSS vulnerability. The component should escape all interpolated values (e.g. with a Handlebars escape or _.escape) before pushing them into the buffer.

title: unsubscribe_url passed to emails points to a login-required page with no key, so email clients cannot use it
body: `send_notification_email` sets `unsubscribe_url: post.topic.unsubscribe_url`, which is `#{Discourse.base_url}/t/#{slug}/#{id}/unsubscribe`. The TopicsController#unsubscribe action is behind `ensure_logged_in`, so a recipient opening the link from an email (typically not logged in, or in a mail client with no Discourse session) is bounced to the login page and the unsubscribe never happens. Unlike the digest's `@unsubscribe_key` (DigestUnsubscribeKey), there is no per-user token authenticating this URL. Either the route must accept an authenticated key (like email/unsubscribe/:key) or the link must be removed; as shipped the 'stop receiving notifications about this particular topic' link in every notification email is broken for logged-out users.

title: List-Unsubscribe header still points to user preferences, not the per-topic unsubscribe URL
body: In `header_args`, when `add_unsubscribe_link` is set the `List-Unsubscribe` header is set to `<#{template_args[:user_preferences_url]}>` — the generic preferences page — even though the PR adds a per-topic `unsubscribe_url` to template_args. Mail clients that expose a one-click unsubscribe (RFC 2369/8058) will therefore send users to preferences rather than actually unsubscribing from the topic, and the header does not reflect the new per-topic capability. The header should use `template_args[:unsubscribe_url]` when present (falling back to user_preferences_url), and ideally include a `mailto:` alternative per RFC 8058.

title: body appends unsubscribe text unconditionally when add_unsubscribe_link is set, even if body is nil
body: `body` does `body = @opts[:body]` then, when `@opts[:add_unsubscribe_link]` is true, executes `body << "\n"`. If `@opts[:body]` is nil (callers that rely on a template, e.g. `template: 'user_notifications.signup'`, pass no :body), this raises NoMethodError on nil. The guard should check that body is present (or initialize it to a String) before appending.

title: unsubscribe_link placeholder only substituted in html_part, not in the plain-text body template
body: The HTML email template now contains `%{unsubscribe_link}`, and `html_part` substitutes it via `html_override.gsub!("%{unsubscribe_link}", ...)`. However the plain-text path (`MessageBuilder#body`) appends `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` directly, which is fine, but any other HTML template that contains `%{unsubscribe_link}` and is rendered through a path that does not go through `html_part`'s gsub (or templates rendered before this change) will leak the literal `%{unsubscribe_link}` placeholder to recipients. The substitution should be centralized so both HTML and text bodies get the placeholder replaced consistently.

title: unsubscribe_link locale string promises per-topic unsubscribe that requires login
body: The new locale text says 'To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, [click here](%{unsubscribe_url}).' but the target URL requires an authenticated session (see TopicsController#unsubscribe ensure_logged_in) and has no per-user token, so recipients opening it from email are redirected to login and the promised action does not occur. The copy overpromises; either fix the endpoint to work logged-out (token-based) or reword the copy.

title: No test verifies the per-topic unsubscribe_url appears in the email body or List-Unsubscribe header
body: The spec adds `unsubscribe_url: "/t/1234/unsubscribe"` to the builder under test but only asserts that the List-Unsubscribe header is present and that the body contains the user_preferences_url. Nothing asserts that the body contains the per-topic unsubscribe URL (via the updated `unsubscribe_link` locale string) nor that the List-Unsubscribe header uses it. The core behavior of this PR — the per-topic unsubscribe link in notification emails — is untested, and the header assertion would still pass with the old preferences-only header.

title: No controller/request specs for the new unsubscribe endpoint
body: The PR adds a new `unsubscribe` action and two new routes (`t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe`, `t/:topic_id/unsubscribe`) but includes no specs covering: the nil TopicUser case, the toggle behavior for muted vs watching users, the slug-mismatch 301 redirect, the login requirement, or the response format. Given the endpoint mutates notification state and is linked from every notification email, request specs are needed before merge.

title: topicUnsubscribe route is registered as a top-level route instead of nested under the topic resource
body: `this.route('topicUnsubscribe', { path: '/t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe' })` is declared outside the `this.resource('topic', ...)` block, so it does not inherit the topic resource's model/controller context. The route's model hook therefore cannot use `this.modelFor('topic')` and must re-fetch the topic itself (which it does via createRecord/loadTopicView). Nesting it under the topic resource (`this.route('unsubscribe', { path: '/unsubscribe' })` inside the resource) would give it the parent topic model for free and match the server route structure.

title: unsubscribe_url uses url (absolute) but is named like relative_url and is interpolated into emails inconsistently
body: `unsubscribe_url` is defined as `"#{url}/unsubscribe"` where `url` is the absolute URL (`Discourse.base_url`-prefixed, see Topic.url). It is passed to the mailer as `unsubscribe_url` and interpolated into the locale string, which is correct for emails, but the name suggests a relative URL like `relative_url`. More importantly, `Topic#url` appends a post number only when > 1, so this is fine, but any caller expecting a path (e.g. for a redirect) would get an absolute URL. The naming should be clarified (e.g. keep it but document it is absolute) to avoid misuse.

title: CSS override `bottom: initial` is invalid and does not achieve the intended dropdown positioning
body: The new `.topic-unsubscribe .notification-options .dropdown-menu { bottom: initial; }` uses `initial` as a value for `bottom`. `initial` resets a property to its initial value, which for `bottom` is `auto` — but the intent appears to be to stop the dropdown menu from being positioned above the button (the notification-options component normally uses `bottom: 100%`-style drop-up styling). `bottom: initial`/`auto` will not reliably produce the desired drop-down behavior across browsers and likely leaves the menu mispositioned on the unsubscribe page. The rule should be verified against the actual notification-options markup and given an explicit value.

title: unsubscribe action crashes with NoMethodError when no TopicUser record exists
body: In TopicsController#unsubscribe, `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil (a user who has never interacted with the topic has no topic_users row). The code then unconditionally calls `tu.notification_level` and `tu.save!`, raising NoMethodError on nil and returning a 500. The unsubscribe link is sent in notification emails to any notified user, including users who never opened the topic, so this path is reachable in production. The code should use `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, params[:topic_id], notification_level: ...)` (which creates the row if missing, as done in #set_notifications) or guard for nil.

title: unsubscribe action does not verify the user can see the topic
body: TopicsController#unsubscribe builds `TopicView.new(params[:topic_id], current_user)` but never calls `guardian.ensure_can_see!` on the topic. TopicView.new may not raise for topics in restricted categories the user cannot access (unlike #show, which rescues Discourse::InvalidAccess). The action then mutates the user's TopicUser notification level and calls perform_show_response, which serializes the topic view — potentially leaking topic existence/content (title, excerpt via @description_meta) for topics in secure categories to unauthorized logged-in users. Compare with #toggle_mute and #clear_pin which call `guardian.ensure_can_see!(@topic)`.

title: unsubscribe toggles notification level instead of unsubscribing, and mutates state on a GET request
body: The unsubscribe endpoint is a GET route (config/routes.rb lines 440-441) that permanently mutates the user's TopicUser notification_level (a side effect on GET, which breaks web semantics, makes the link prefetchable/crawlable, and means email scanners or browser prefetchers silently change user state). Worse, the toggle logic is wrong for an 'unsubscribe' action: if the user is watching/tracking (level > regular) it sets level to regular — i.e. clicking 'stop receiving notifications about this topic' leaves the user at 'regular', which still sends emails for this topic. The intent (per the email copy 'stop receiving notifications about this particular topic') is to set the level to muted. The else-branch muting only happens when the user is already at regular or muted, so a watching user who clicks unsubscribe keeps receiving notifications.

title: unsubscribe renders the full topic show response, leaking topic content and tracking a visit
body: After mutating notification state, #unsubscribe calls perform_show_response, which renders the full topics/show template with the preloaded TopicViewSerializer (all posts the user can see, topic metadata) and sets @description_meta from the topic excerpt. The Ember route (topic-unsubscribe.js.es6) only needs the topic's id/title/notification state, not the entire topic payload. This both leaks more data than the unsubscribe page needs and is wasteful. It also means the unsubscribe URL behaves like a topic view (canonical URL, meta description), which is incorrect for a state-changing endpoint.

title: Unsubscribe route fetches the full topic view instead of the lightweight unsubscribe endpoint
body: The route's model hook calls `PostStream.loadTopicView(params.id)`, which loads the entire topic (all posts) — the same heavy request as viewing the topic — even though the server-side unsubscribe action (TopicsController#unsubscribe) already performs the state change when the URL is hit. The Ember route is registered at /t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe, but the browser first hits the Rails route (GET topics#unsubscribe) which mutates state and renders the show template with preloaded data; the Ember app then re-fetches the full topic view client-side. This doubles the work and loads the whole post stream just to display a one-line confirmation page. The route should rely on the preloaded topic data from the server render (like topic-from-params does via modelFor) or fetch a minimal topic payload.

title: Typo in property name stopNotificiationsText
body: The computed property is named `stopNotificiationsText` (missing 'i' in 'Notifications'), and the template references `{{{stopNotificiationsText}}}` so it works, but the misspelling will confuse future maintainers and any external references. Rename to `stopNotificationsText` in both the controller and the template.

title: Triple-stache rendering of stopNotificiationsText injects the topic title as raw HTML
body: The template renders `{{{stopNotificiationsText}}}` (unescaped). The controller builds this string via `I18n.t("topic.unsubscribe.stop_notifications", { title: this.get("model.fancyTitle") })`, and the locale string is "You will stop receiving notifications for {{title}}." — the tags require unescaped output, but so does the interpolated topic title. `fancyTitle` is HTML-escaped server-side (Topic#fancy_title calls ERB::Util.html_escape), but I18n interpolation in the JS client does not re-escape, and any markup that survives in fancyTitle (e.g. entities produced by SmartyPants rendering, or double-encoding edge cases) is injected raw into the DOM. This is an XSS risk if fancyTitle ever contains unescaped content (e.g. via plugins or serializer changes). Safer: keep the in the template and interpolate the title with escaped {{ }}, e.g. `You will stop receiving notifications for {{model.fancyTitle}}.` in the template itself.

title: unsubscribe_url passed to email template args is never defined for digest and other non-notification emails
body: send_notification_email now always passes `unsubscribe_url: post.topic.unsubscribe_url` into email_opts, and the locale string `unsubscribe_link` (server.en.yml) now interpolates `%{unsubscribe_url}`. Email::MessageBuilder#body and #html_part call `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` whenever `add_unsubscribe_link` is true. Any email built with add_unsubscribe_link: true but without an unsubscribe_url opt (e.g. the digest mailer, which sets add_unsubscribe_link via build_email defaults — check digest path in user_notifications.rb which does not go through send_notification_email) will raise I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument when rendering the unsubscribe link. The digest email (UserNotifications#digest) does not pass unsubscribe_url, so digest emails with the unsubscribe footer will fail to build/send.

title: List-Unsubscribe header still points only to user preferences, not the per-topic unsubscribe URL
body: header_args sets `result['List-Unsubscribe'] = "<#{template_args[:user_preferences_url]}>"` when add_unsubscribe_link is set. The PR adds a per-topic unsubscribe_url to template_args, but the List-Unsubscribe header (the machine-readable one-click unsubscribe used by Gmail etc.) still points to the generic preferences page. For one-click unsubscribe (RFC 8058 / Gmail's unsubscribe button) to actually stop topic notifications, the header should use the per-topic unsubscribe_url when present: `result['List-Unsubscribe'] = "<#{template_args[:unsubscribe_url] || template_args[:user_preferences_url]}>"`. As written, mail clients offering 'unsubscribe' will send users to preferences instead of stopping topic emails, and the feature is only half-wired.

title: respond_instructions placeholder emitted inside the context-posts block
body:
The template renders `
%{respond_instructions}
` both inside the `if context_posts.present?` block (line 6) and again unconditionally at line 19. When context posts exist, the respond instructions appear twice in the HTML email. The first occurrence (inside the context block, before the 'previous discussion' posts) appears to be a leftover from the re-indentation; it should be removed so instructions appear only once at the bottom.

title: unsubscribe_link locale text says 'these emails' for the per-topic link
body: The first sentence of the expanded unsubscribe_link text reads 'To unsubscribe from these emails, visit your [user preferences](%{user_preferences_url}).' followed by 'To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, [click here](%{unsubscribe_url}).' The first sentence is now inaccurate/misleading in notification emails: the preferences link unsubscribes from all notification emails, not 'these emails' (the topic-specific ones). Reword to e.g. 'To unsubscribe from all emails, visit your [user preferences](...).' so users don't think the preferences link only affects the current topic's emails.

title: afterModel sets a nested property path that Ember.set may not observe correctly
body: `topic.set("details.notificationReasonText", null)` sets a nested path on the topic model. In this Ember version, setting a nested path via a single set() call works, but the topic's `details` object comes from updateFromJson and may be a plain object; also the intent (per the comment 'hide the notification reason text') is to suppress the notification banner on this page. If `details` is undefined at that point (updateFromJson may not have created it), set() will throw or silently fail. Safer to guard: `if (topic.get('details')) { topic.set('details.notificationReasonText', null); }` or set the whole details object. Without a test this is unverified behavior.

title: No test verifies the per-topic unsubscribe_url appears in the email body or List-Unsubscribe header
body: The spec adds `unsubscribe_url: "/t/1234/unsubscribe"` to the message_with_unsubscribe builder, but the assertions only check that the List-Unsubscribe header is present and that the body contains the user_preferences_url. Nothing asserts that the body contains the per-topic unsubscribe URL (the new locale string interpolates %{unsubscribe_url}), nor that the header uses it. Given the mailer change and the locale change, a regression that drops unsubscribe_url from template_args (raising I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument) or renders the wrong link would not be caught. Add assertions that `message_with_unsubscribe.body` includes '/t/1234/unsubscribe' and that the rendered unsubscribe_link text contains it.

title: unsubscribe added to skip_before_filter :check_xhr, allowing non-XHR state changes
body: The PR adds :unsubscribe to `skip_before_filter :check_xhr`. check_xhr exists to reject non-XHR requests to JSON API endpoints; skipping it for unsubscribe means the endpoint accepts plain browser GETs (which is required for email links, so this is intentional), but it also means the action must handle HTML and JSON formats itself — which it does via perform_show_response's respond_to. This is acceptable for an email-link endpoint, but note the action is also now reachable via direct navigation and will render the full topic page HTML; combined with the missing guardian check (separate finding) this widens exposure. No code change strictly required, but the security review of the HTML path should be deliberate.

title: dropdown-button title is concatenated into HTML without escaping
body:
renderString now conditionally pushes `"

" + title + "

"` where title comes from `this.get('title')`. Previously the title was always rendered (same injection), so this is not a regression, but the value is interpolated raw into an HTML string buffer. If any caller passes a user-controlled title (e.g. a topic title), this is an XSS vector. The surrounding code also interpolates row.title, row.description, and id unescaped (lines 44-47), so the component generally assumes trusted input. Worth noting as a latent XSS risk, especially since the new unsubscribe page embeds this component via topic-notifications-button.

title: unsubscribe action crashes with NoMethodError when no TopicUser record exists
body: In TopicsController#unsubscribe, `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil (a user who has never interacted with the topic has no topic_users row). The very next line calls `tu.notification_level`, which raises NoMethodError on nil and produces a 500 error. The unsubscribe link is sent in notification emails to any recipient, including users who never opened the topic, so this path is reachable in normal use. The code should use `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, params[:topic_id], notification_level: ...)` (which creates the row if missing, as done in #set_notifications) or guard against nil.

title: unsubscribe action does not verify the user can see the topic
body: TopicsController#unsubscribe builds `TopicView.new(params[:topic_id], current_user)` but never calls `guardian.ensure_can_see!` on the topic. TopicView.new may raise Discourse::InvalidAccess for restricted topics, but for topics the user cannot see the action still mutates TopicUser state and renders the show response via perform_show_response, leaking topic existence/content (title, excerpt via @description_meta) to users without access. Compare with #show, which rescues Discourse::InvalidAccess, and with other actions like #toggle_mute that call `guardian.ensure_can_see!(@topic)`. An explicit `guardian.ensure_can_see!(@topic_view.topic)` is needed before mutating or rendering.

title: unsubscribe toggles notification level instead of unsubscribing, and does not record the change reason
body: The unsubscribe endpoint is linked from notification emails as 'stop receiving notifications about this particular topic', but the implementation toggles between `regular` and `muted` depending on the current level: a user at `watching`/`tracking` is set to `regular` (still notified), and a user at `regular` is set to `muted`. So a watching user clicking the email link will keep receiving notifications, and the page text ('You will stop receiving notifications for ...') is false for them. Additionally, the update bypasses `TopicUser.change`, so `notifications_changed_at` and `notifications_reason_id` are not set and no MessageBus `notification_level_change` event is published, leaving the client UI out of sync. The action should set the level explicitly (muted) via TopicUser.change.

title: unsubscribe is a state-changing GET request
body: The route `get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe" => "topics#unsubscribe"` (config/routes.rb lines 440-441) makes a mutating operation (changing the user's notification level) reachable via GET. Email clients, link previewers, and crawlers prefetch GET URLs, so merely opening/previewing the unsubscribe link in an email can silently change the user's notification state. This also breaks the `check_xhr` skip semantics and makes the action non-idempotent from a crawler's perspective. The state change should be a POST/PUT (with the GET page rendering the confirmation UI), or at minimum the mutation should require an explicit confirmation.

title: check_xhr is skipped for unsubscribe, allowing non-XHR state changes
body: `skip_before_filter :check_xhr, only: [:show, :unsubscribe, :feed]` disables the CSRF/XHR check for the unsubscribe action. Combined with the GET route, this means the notification-level mutation can be triggered by any cross-site GET request (e.g., an tag on a third-party page pointing at the unsubscribe URL) while the victim is logged in, since no CSRF token is required for GET. This is a CSRF risk on a state-changing endpoint.

title: Route creates a new topic record with only an id, producing an invalid/partial model
body: The model hook does `this.store.createRecord("topic", { id: params.id })` and then `topic.updateFromJson(json)`. createRecord pushes a brand-new (unsaved, empty) record into the Ember Data store; updateFromJson then mutates it. This leaves a phantom 'new' topic record in the store (isNew remains true, and it is not properly materialized as a loaded record), which can confuse other code that queries the store for topic id, and the record lacks the slug needed by the template/controller (stopNotificiationsText uses model.fancyTitle, which will be undefined). The correct pattern is `this.store.find('topic', params.id)` or pushing the JSON via store.pushPayload, not createRecord.

title: PostStream.loadTopicView is not a known API and the route ignores slug/access errors
body: `PostStream.loadTopicView(params.id)` is called without any evidence this static method exists on the PostStream model in this codebase (the model exposes instance methods like refresh; topic loading normally goes through the store or Discourse.Topic). If it does not exist, the route's model hook throws and the unsubscribe page fails to load. Additionally, the promise rejection is unhandled, so a 404/403 for a topic the user cannot see results in an unhandled error rather than a proper error page.

title: Typo in property name stopNotificiationsText
body: The computed property is named `stopNotificiationsText` (missing the 'a' in 'Notifications'), and the template references `{{{stopNotificiationsText}}}` so it works, but the misspelling will confuse future maintainers and any external references. It should be renamed to `stopNotificationsText` in both the controller and the template.

title: Triple-stache rendering of stopNotificiationsText injects the topic title as raw HTML
body: The template renders `{{{stopNotificiationsText}}}` (unescaped). The string is built from `I18n.t("topic.unsubscribe.stop_notifications", { title: this.get("model.fancyTitle") })`. `fancyTitle` is HTML-escaped server-side (ERB::Util.html_escape in Topic#fancy_title), but I18n interpolation does not re-escape interpolated values, and the locale string itself wraps {{title}} in <strong> tags. If fancyTitle ever contains markup that survives escaping (e.g., via SmartyPants entities or a title containing encoded entities that get double-unescaped), or if the translation is overridden, this becomes an HTML injection vector in the unsubscribe page. The title should be passed through Ember's escaping (double-stache with a separate escaped binding) rather than triple-stache of a pre-interpolated string.

title: dropdown-button renderString interpolates unescaped values into HTML (XSS)
body:
renderString builds HTML by string concatenation: `buffer.push("
  • ")` and `buffer.push("" + row.title + "")` etc. None of `id`, `row.title`, `row.description`, `row.styleClasses`, `this.get('text')`, `title`, or `longDescription` are HTML-escaped. Any caller that passes user-controlled data (topic titles, category names, usernames) into these fields gets HTML/XSS injection in the dropdown. The change in this PR (adding the `title` field) expands the attack surface. All interpolated values should be escaped (e.g., with a Handlebars escape or _.escape) before being pushed into the buffer.

title: unsubscribe_url passed to email template args is never used by the text body path consistently
body: `send_notification_email` now passes `unsubscribe_url: post.topic.unsubscribe_url` into email_opts, which flows into template_args. The HTML path substitutes it via the `%{unsubscribe_link}` placeholder in the locale string, but the plain-text body path in Email::MessageBuilder#body appends `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` — this works only because template_args includes unsubscribe_url. However, other callers of build_email with `add_unsubscribe_link: true` (e.g., the digest mailer, which sets its own @unsubscribe_key and does not pass unsubscribe_url) will now render the new locale text with a missing `%{unsubscribe_url}` interpolation, producing a broken link ('... [click here]().') or an I18n missing-interpolation error in digest emails. The digest path (UserNotifications#digest) must also supply an unsubscribe_url or the locale must be split.

title: List-Unsubscribe header still points only to user preferences, not the per-topic unsubscribe URL
body: header_args sets `result['List-Unsubscribe'] = "<#{template_args[:user_preferences_url]}>"` when add_unsubscribe_link is set. Now that a per-topic `unsubscribe_url` is available in template_args (passed by UserNotifications#send_notification_email), the List-Unsubscribe header — the one-click unsubscribe mechanism used by Gmail and other mail clients — still directs users to the generic preferences page instead of the topic-specific unsubscribe URL. For one-click unsubscribe to actually stop notifications for the topic (and to satisfy RFC 8058 List-Unsubscribe semantics for this feature), the header should use `template_args[:unsubscribe_url]` when present, falling back to user_preferences_url.

title: Unsubscribe link placeholder only substituted in html_override path; plain-text emails rely on body method
body:
The template now includes `
%{unsubscribe_link}
`, which is only substituted in MessageBuilder#html_part (via html_override.gsub!). For notification emails that use the template-based text body (no html_override), the `%{unsubscribe_link}` placeholder is appended by MessageBuilder#body, so the HTML template change is consistent for the html_override path. However, the template is also rendered directly in UserNotifications#send_notification_email via UserNotificationRenderer for the non-template-HTML path — in that path the `%{unsubscribe_link}` and `%{respond_instructions}` placeholders are NOT substituted before being passed as html_override... actually they are substituted later by html_part's gsub!, so this is fine; but note the renderer output is passed as html_override and gsub! mutates it in place, which is acceptable. No concrete defect beyond the digest-path gap noted separately; flagging only that the placeholder substitution depends on add_unsubscribe_link being set, and any email using this template without that flag will leak the literal '%{unsubscribe_link}' text into the HTML.

title: Route ordering change for moderator-liked/summary may shadow or alter existing URL matching
body: The diff reorders routes: `t/:slug/:topic_id/moderator-liked` was moved after `t/:topic_id/wordpress`, and the `summary` routes had their constraints changed from `{topic_id: /\d+/, post_number: /\d+/}` to `{topic_id: /\d+/}`. The constraint change for `t/:slug/:topic_id/summary` and `t/:topic_id/summary` removes the post_number constraint that was previously (incorrectly) present, which is fine, but the reordering means `t/:topic_id/wordpress` is now matched before `t/:slug/:topic_id/moderator-liked`; since the wordpress route only matches a two-segment path (`t/:topic_id/wordpress`), a URL like `/t/some-slug/123/moderator-liked` has three segments and will not be captured by it, so behavior is preserved. However, the new `t/:topic_id/unsubscribe` route placed before `t/:topic_id/summary` is fine, but `t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe` placed before `put "t/:slug/:topic_id"` is fine for GET. The main risk: `get "t/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` (line 441) will also match `/t/123/unsubscribe` where 123 could be a slug-less id — intended. No concrete breakage found, but the reordering was unnecessary churn that increases review risk; the summary constraint change should be verified against existing tests.

title: unsubscribe_url uses absolute url (includes base_url) while other URL helpers use relative or base_uri
body: `unsubscribe_url` is defined as `"#{url}/unsubscribe"` where `url` is `self.class.url id, slug, post_number` = `"#{Discourse.base_url}/t/#{slug}/#{id}"` — an absolute URL including the host. This is used in `TopicsController#unsubscribe` for `redirect_to @topic_view.topic.unsubscribe_url` (fine for redirects) and in `UserNotifications#send_notification_email` as `unsubscribe_url: post.topic.unsubscribe_url` for the email link (fine, emails need absolute URLs). However, the Ember route path is `/t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe` and the controller redirects to `unsubscribe_url` when the slug is missing — the absolute URL works. The inconsistency: `relative_url` uses `Discourse.base_uri` while `url` uses `Discourse.base_url`; if base_uri differs from base_url (e.g., behind a proxy with a different path prefix), unsubscribe_url built from `url` may be wrong for redirects. Minor, but the method should be consistent with how it's consumed.

title: No test verifies the per-topic unsubscribe_url appears in the email body or List-Unsubscribe header
body: The spec adds `unsubscribe_url: "/t/1234/unsubscribe"` to the message_with_unsubscribe builder, but the existing assertions only check that the List-Unsubscribe header is present and that the body matches the user_preferences_url. There is no assertion that the body contains the per-topic unsubscribe URL (via the updated `unsubscribe_link` locale string with `%{unsubscribe_url}`), and no assertion that the List-Unsubscribe header uses the topic URL. Without these, the core feature of this PR (per-topic unsubscribe link in emails) is untested; a regression that drops unsubscribe_url from template_args or breaks the locale interpolation would pass CI.

title: Read-modify-write of TopicUser notification_level is not atomic
body: `tu.notification_level` is read, then conditionally assigned, then `tu.save!` — a classic read-modify-write race. Two concurrent requests (e.g., the user clicking the email link while also changing notification state in the UI via set_notifications) can interleave, and the last writer wins, potentially clobbering a `watching` level set by the other request. `TopicUser.change` exists precisely to do an atomic UPDATE ... WHERE and should be used instead of find_by + save!.

title: topicUnsubscribe route is registered as a top-level route, not nested under the topic resource
body: `this.route('topicUnsubscribe', { path: '/t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe' })` is declared outside the `this.resource('topic', ...)` block, so the route is named `topicUnsubscribe` rather than `topic.unsubscribe`, and it will not receive the parent `topic` route's model (the route's own model hook must re-fetch the topic, which it attempts via PostStream.loadTopicView). This means the topic is loaded twice (once by the parent resource if it were nested, once here) and the controller hierarchy differs from other topic sub-pages. It should be nested inside the topic resource as `this.route('unsubscribe', { path: '/unsubscribe' })` so it inherits the topic model and matches the server-side URL structure.

title: Race condition in BlockedEmail.should_block? increments match_count non-atomically
body: should_block? does a read-modify-write of match_count (record.match_count += 1; record.save) without any locking or atomic SQL. Two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email can both read the same match_count and both write match_count+1, losing an increment. Worse, the method performs a write (save) during what is called from a validation path (EmailValidator#validate_each), meaning every validation of a user record triggers a database UPDATE on blocked_emails — including validations that never persist the user, inflating match_count with phantom matches and adding an unexpected write inside a read/validation flow. Use an atomic update (e.g. BlockedEmail.where(email: email).update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now)) or move the statistics update out of the validation path.

title: should_block? performs a database write during validation and does not normalize the email
body: BlockedEmail.should_block?(email) is invoked from EmailValidator#validate_each on every user validation where the email changed. It unconditionally saves match_count/last_match_at even when the user record is never saved (e.g. other validations fail), corrupting the match statistics. Additionally, the lookup BlockedEmail.where(email: email) is case-sensitive and not stripped, while user emails are stored downcased/stripped elsewhere (e.g. Email.downcase in users_controller#change_email); 'User@Example.com' and 'user@example.com' would be treated as different emails, letting a blocked address bypass the block by varying case. The lookup should use Email.downcase(email).strip (or an equivalent normalization) and the statistics update should be atomic and separated from the pure predicate.

title: Blocked-email check is skipped when the value is nil, causing a NoMethodError instead of a clean validation failure
body: EmailValidator#validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?(value) whenever record.errors[attribute] is blank. When the email attribute is nil (User only runs this validator if :email_changed?, but a change to nil is possible, and other models may use the validator without a presence check ordering guarantee), should_block?(nil) executes BlockedEmail.where(email: nil).first, which is harmless, but the guard `record.errors[attribute].blank?` means the blocked check runs even when the whitelist/blacklist checks already failed — that part is intended — however the real issue is that with a nil value the validator adds no 'blocked' error and, more importantly, the validator assumes `value` responds to the operations in should_block?; combined with the missing presence ordering, a nil email reaches BlockedEmail.should_block? and the method's `record && record.action_type == actions[:block]` path is fine, but any non-string value (e.g. an array from a malformed param) would raise inside the validator. The validator should guard `if value.present? && record.errors[attribute].blank? && BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`.

title: Switching email validation from a custom validate method to the `email: true` validator changes error messages and drops the whitelist/blacklist error key
body: The old code used `validate :email_validator, if: :email_changed?` which ran the custom email_validator that added errors with the specific I18n key :'user.email.not_allowed' (and now :'user.email.blocked'). The new code uses `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`, which delegates to EmailValidator — but EmailValidator only adds the domain whitelist/blacklist and blocked checks; it does NOT perform any email format validation. There is no built-in Rails `email` validator in this era of Rails/Discourse (the `email: true` option expects an EmailValidator class whose validate_each must do the format check), so this validator as written never rejects malformed emails like 'not-an-email' — a regression from the previous behavior where format checking existed elsewhere, and the client-side JS (Discourse.Utilities.emailValid) is the only remaining format gate, which is trivially bypassable. The EmailValidator must also validate email format (e.g. using the existing Email::VALID_REGEX or Mail::Address parsing) or the format check must be restored.

title: Uniqueness validation on email is now case-sensitive, allowing duplicate accounts with differently-cased emails
body: The old code used `validates_uniqueness_of :email` and the new code uses `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true`. Both are case-sensitive by default in Rails, but the previous custom email_validator path and the rest of the codebase normalize emails (Email.downcase is used in users_controller#change_email and User.find_by_username_or_email). More importantly, the database has a UNIQUE index on users.email (index_users_on_email UNIQUE per the schema comment), which in PostgreSQL is case-sensitive, so 'Foo@bar.com' and 'foo@bar.com' can both be inserted, creating two accounts that downstream code (which downcases before lookup) will treat as the same person — enabling account impersonation/confusion in email-based lookups, password resets, and the DiscourseHub nickname matching. The uniqueness validation should be case-insensitive (e.g. uniqueness: { case_sensitive: false } or a custom validator comparing Email.downcase), and ideally the DB index should be on a downcased expression.

title: Error response now leaks user attribute values (name, username, email) back to the client on failed signup
body: The create action's failure branch now renders `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` in the JSON response. Combined with the client change that pushes result.values.email into rejectedEmails, this echoes back attacker-supplied input. While the values are attacker-supplied in the normal signup flow, this response shape is also produced for any validation failure — including uniqueness failures where the email may belong to an existing account. Returning the submitted email in a structured `values` field alongside `errors` makes it easier for scripts to enumerate which emails are already registered (the errors hash already reveals this via the uniqueness error, but the explicit values echo normalizes the probing interface). More concretely, the client code at create_account_controller.js line 274-275 pushes result.values.email into rejectedEmails whenever result.errors.email is present, which means a user who typos an email that is already taken gets that email permanently stuck in their rejectedEmails list client-side, and the server is now explicitly designed to return these values. The values echo should be removed or limited; the client should not need server-echoed values to know which email was rejected since it already has it in accountEmail.

title: rejectedEmails check compares raw email without normalization and permanently blocks the email client-side
body: The new check `this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email)` compares the raw accountEmail string against previously rejected emails. Emails are case-insensitive in practice, so 'User@Example.com' and 'user@example.com' are different strings; a user whose email was rejected once (e.g. for being already registered) will not be blocked from re-submitting the same address with different casing, and conversely the rejectedEmails entry is pushed from result.values.email (server-normalized or not) which may not string-match the client's accountEmail. Additionally, once an email is pushed into rejectedEmails it can never be removed, so a transient server error (e.g. DiscourseHub failure) that returns errors.email will permanently prevent that email from being used in this session even after the underlying issue is resolved. The comparison should be case-insensitive (compare downcased) and the push should use the client's own accountEmail value.

title: Missing trailing newline at end of file
body: The file ends without a newline character (the diff shows '\ No newline at end of file'). This is a minor style issue but can cause problems with some tools and patch application.

title: EmailValidator spec does not test the whitelist/blacklist behavior that the validator implements
body: The spec only covers the BlockedEmail.should_block? branch. The validator's primary responsibility (moved from User#email_validator) is enforcing SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist and email_domains_blacklist, but there are no tests exercising those settings — neither that a whitelisted domain passes, a non-whitelisted domain fails with :'user.email.not_allowed', nor that the blacklist blocks matching domains. Since this logic was moved out of the User model (where it presumably had coverage) into a new validator, the move is untested for its main purpose. Add contexts that set SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist / email_domains_blacklist and assert the appropriate errors.

title: should_block? spec does not cover case-insensitivity or whitespace, which the implementation does not handle
body: The spec only tests exact-match emails. Given that user emails are downcased/stripped elsewhere in the codebase, should_block? should be tested (and implemented) to handle 'Block@SpamFromHome.org' matching a stored 'block@spamfromhome.org'. Without such a test the case-sensitivity gap in BlockedEmail.should_block? (see separate finding) will persist. Add a test that a differently-cased or whitespace-padded email still matches a blocked record.

title: Enum.new is not a standard Rails/Discourse API; actions may not behave as an integer-backed enum
body: BlockedEmail.actions uses Enum.new(:block, :do_nothing). If Enum is a Discourse core class that maps symbols to integers (as the action_type integer column and the fabricator's BlockedEmail.actions[:block] assignment suggest), this is fine, but the model relies on it without requiring or documenting it, and the migration stores action_type as a plain integer with no constraint. If Enum is not loaded in all contexts (e.g. rake tasks, console), BlockedEmail.actions will raise NameError. Verify Enum is required/available and consider using Rails' built-in enum (Rails 4.1+) or a constant hash with a validation that action_type is in the allowed set.

title: Race condition in BlockedEmail.should_block? read-modify-write of match_count
body: should_block? loads the record, increments match_count in memory, and saves it. Two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email can both read match_count = 0, both write 1, losing one increment. More importantly, the save is a full-record UPDATE with no locking, so under concurrent load the statistics (match_count, last_match_at) can be silently lost. Use an atomic SQL update (e.g. BlockedEmail.where(email: email).update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now)) or lock the row, and re-read the action_type after the update.

title: should_block? performs a write during validation, and its return value is wrong when no record exists
body: BlockedEmail.should_block? is called from EmailValidator.validate_each (lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13), i.e. during User validation, yet it mutates the database (increments match_count, sets last_match_at, saves). This means a mere validation attempt — including failed validations, GET-triggered checks, or User.new(...).valid? in a console — permanently writes to blocked_emails. Also, when no record exists, `record` is nil and the method returns nil (falsy) — fine — but when a record exists with action_type :do_nothing, it still performs the write even though the email will not be blocked, inflating match_count for emails that are explicitly allowed. The statistics write should be moved out of the validation path (e.g. into the controller after a failed signup, or done atomically and only when actually blocking).

title: Email matching is case-sensitive; blocked emails can be bypassed with case variation
body: should_block? does `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` with no downcasing or normalization. The users table stores email as given (User validates uniqueness on the raw email string), and the signup form sends whatever the user typed. An attacker who adds a BlockedEmail entry for 'spam@example.com' can trivially bypass it by registering 'SPAM@example.com' or 'Spam@Example.com'. The lookup must normalize: `BlockedEmail.where(email: Email.downcase(email)).first` (the codebase already has Email.downcase used in users_controller.rb:269), and ideally the email column should be stored downcased on create (before_validation). Without this the entire blocklist feature is ineffective.

title: Blocked-email check is skipped when the email is blank or nil
body: validate_each receives `value` which is the raw attribute. If value is nil (email not yet assigned) or an empty string, `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` is still called with nil/'' — for nil, `where(email: nil).first` returns nil so it is harmless, but the guard `record.errors[attribute].blank?` means the blocked check only runs when no other error exists. More importantly, the validator never checks that value is a syntactically valid email before doing the domain regex match: `value =~ regexp` on line 21 will raise NoMethodError (undefined method =~ for nil) if value is nil when a whitelist/blacklist setting is present, crashing validation with a 500 instead of a validation error. Add `return if value.blank?` at the top of validate_each.

title: Domain whitelist/blacklist regex is injectable and matches substrings
body: email_in_restriction_setting? builds a Regexp directly from the SiteSetting value: `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` after only escaping dots.
