The setting is admin-controlled so the injection risk is limited to admins, but the bigger correctness/security bug is that the pattern is unanchored: '@(example\.com)' matches 'user@sub.example.com' AND 'user@notexample.com' (substring match, no boundary). A blacklist entry for 'example.com' will also block 'myexample.com', and a whitelist entry for 'example.com' will wrongly admit 'user@evilexample.com'. The domain list should be split on commas/whitespace and each domain anchored: Regexp.new("@#{Regexp.escape(domain)}$", true) per domain, matching any of them. This is a real bypass/false-positive issue for the email restriction feature that this PR relocates into the validator.

title: Changing email validation from separate presence/uniqueness validators to combined `validates` alters error messages and hash shape returned to the client
body: The old code used `validates_presence_of :email` and `validates_uniqueness_of :email`, which add errors like 'Email can't be blank' and 'Email has already been taken'. The new `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true` produces the same default messages, so that part is equivalent — but the PR also adds `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice(...)` to the create failure response in users_controller.rb. The client (create_account_controller.js:274) checks `result.errors && result.errors.email` — with to_hash, errors.email is an array of message strings, which works — but the change from the previous response shape (message only) is an API contract change for any other API consumer, and `user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` echoes back the submitted email verbatim, including any HTML/script content, into a JSON response that the client pushes into rejectedEmails and re-renders; ensure the client treats it as text (it does, via Ember binding) but note the response now includes raw user input. The bigger issue: uniqueness validation on email is not case-insensitive — 'User@Example.com' and 'user@example.com' are treated as different by `validates :uniqueness_of`, yet the DB unique index on users.email is also case-sensitive, so this is consistent, but the BlockedEmail lookup (see separate finding) is what must be case-insensitive.

title: Error response now includes raw submitted attributes (name, username, email) without sanitization
body: The create failure path now returns `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")`. These are the raw, un-sanitized params the user submitted (set via User.new_from_params). The values are echoed back in the JSON response and the JS client pushes result.values.email into rejectedEmails and compares it against the email input. While Ember escapes on render, returning raw user input in an API response is an unnecessary reflection vector; at minimum the email should be the normalized/downcased form. Consider returning only what is needed (the email) and normalizing it.

title: rejectedEmails comparison is case-sensitive, so a rejected email can be re-submitted with different casing
body: The client-side check `this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email)` compares the exact string. If the server rejected 'Spam@Example.com', the user can immediately retype 'spam@example.com' (or any case variation) and the client-side check passes; the form will be re-submitted and only fail again server-side. The comparison should be case-insensitive (compare downcased values), matching the server-side normalization the BlockedEmail lookup should have (see related finding). Also note the server returns the email in result.values.email — if the server normalizes differently than the client, the client-side rejection will never trigger.

title: blocked_emails.email has no length limit and no normalization; unique index is case-sensitive
body: t.string :email with no limit defaults to 255 in most adapters, but there is no downcasing on store and the unique index on email is case-sensitive (default PostgreSQL behavior). Combined with the case-sensitive lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block?, entries 'Spam@x.com' and 'spam@x.com' are treated as distinct rows, defeating the blocklist. The migration should either add a functional unique index on lower(email) or enforce downcasing in the model's before_validation, and the model should normalize on lookup.

title: No test for case-insensitive matching of blocked emails
body: The spec suite for BlockedEmail covers default action_type, statistics updates, and both action types, but never tests that should_block? matches an email regardless of case (e.g. record 'block@spam.org' vs query 'BLOCK@SPAM.ORG'). Given that email case-insensitivity is a real-world requirement (and the current implementation is case-sensitive, which is a bug), this is exactly the scenario that needs a regression test. Add a test asserting BlockedEmail.should_block?('BLOCK@SPAMFROMHOME.ORG') returns true when the stored record is lowercase.

title: EmailValidator spec does not test the whitelist/blacklist domain logic that was moved into it
body: The spec only stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and checks the blocked path. The validator also contains the relocated email_domains_whitelist / email_domains_blacklist logic (lines 4-12), which is security-relevant (it is the only thing preventing signups from blacklisted domains). There are no tests covering: whitelist present and email not in whitelist → error; whitelist present and email in whitelist → no error; blacklist present and email in blacklist → error; blacklist present and email not in blacklist → no error. Since this PR moves that logic from User into EmailValidator, the existing User model specs (if any) may no longer exercise it. Add specs for the domain restriction branches.

title: Blocked-email validation only runs when email_changed?, so existing users changing other attributes bypass the blocklist, and email changes are not checked against BlockedEmail
body: `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` means the custom EmailValidator (which includes the BlockedEmail.should_block? check) only runs when the email attribute has changed. This is intentional for the signup path, but it means: (1) any code path that creates or saves a User with an email that matches a BlockedEmail entry but where email_changed? is false (e.g. an admin editing a user, or a user whose email was set before the blocklist entry was added and who re-saves) will not be blocked; (2) more critically, the change_email flow in UsersController (users_controller.rb:265-286) creates an EmailToken for a new email but never validates the new email against BlockedEmail — a blocked user can change their email to another blocked address via the preferences flow, because EmailToken creation does not run User email validation. The blocklist must also be enforced in the change_email path (and ideally in EmailToken creation), not only on User save with email_changed?.

title: Missing newline at end of file
body: The file ends without a trailing newline (the diff shows '\ No newline at end of file'). This is a minor style issue but can cause problems with some tools and diffs.

title: should_block? has a read-modify-write race condition on match_count
body: BlockedEmail.should_block? loads the record, increments match_count in Ruby, and saves. Two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email can both read match_count = 0, both write 1, losing one increment. More importantly, the save is not atomic and there is no locking; under concurrent load the statistics (match_count/last_match_at) that the feature exists to maintain will be silently wrong. Use an atomic SQL update (e.g. BlockedEmail.where(email: email).update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now)) or update_counters, and do the existence/action_type check in the same query to avoid a TOCTOU window where a record is deleted between the read and the save.

title: should_block? performs a write (save) during validation, mutating state on every check
body: BlockedEmail.should_block? is called from EmailValidator#validate_each, which runs inside User validation. Every validation of a user whose email matches a blocked record performs a database UPDATE (incrementing match_count and setting last_match_at), even when the user record is never saved (e.g. other validations fail, or the object is built and discarded). This pollutes the match statistics with phantom hits and means a single signup attempt can increment the counter multiple times (valid? is called in UsersController#create before save, and again inside save). Statistics gathered this way are unreliable, and the write inside a validator is a surprising side effect that can also fail and raise inside validation.

title: Email matching is exact and case-sensitive; blocked emails are trivially bypassed
body: should_block? does BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first with no normalization. User emails are stored via Email.downcase elsewhere in the codebase (e.g. UsersController#change_email uses Email.downcase(params[:email]).strip), but the validator passes the raw value. A blocked address 'Spam@Example.com' stored in blocked_emails will not match a signup with 'spam@example.com' (or with surrounding whitespace), so the block is trivially bypassed by changing case. The lookup should downcase/strip the email (Email.downcase(email).strip) before querying, consistent with how the rest of the app canonicalizes emails.

title: BlockedEmail.should_block? is called even when the email value is nil or malformed
body: validate_each receives `value` without any format check. The User model applies `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` — but there is no built-in email format validator in this codebase (the old code only checked domain whitelist/blacklist), and more importantly validator ordering is not guaranteed: EmailValidator can run when value is nil (presence failure) or a string with no '@'. BlockedEmail.should_block?(nil) will issue a query with nil and, worse, the domain-regexp path calls value =~ regexp which raises TypeError/NoMethodError on nil. Guard with `if value.present?` before calling should_block? or doing the regexp match.

title: Domain whitelist/blacklist regex is injectable and matches substrings
body: email_in_restriction_setting? builds Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true) directly from the SiteSetting value after only escaping dots. The setting is admin-controlled, but the regex is unanchored: a blacklist entry 'example.com' matches 'user@notexample.com' and 'user@example.com.evil.org' because '@(example\.com)' matches anywhere in the string. Conversely a whitelist entry 'example.com' accepts 'user@sub.example.com' only by accident of substring matching and also accepts 'user@xexample.com'. The pattern should be anchored to the end of the domain: /@(#{domains})\z/i (or split on commas and compare the domain part exactly). As written, both the blacklist (bypassable) and whitelist (over/under-permissive) behave incorrectly.

title: Replacing validates_presence_of/uniqueness_of with validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true changes error messages and breaks the client contract
body: The old code used validates_presence_of :email and validates_uniqueness_of :email, which produce the standard Rails messages 'Email can't be blank' and 'Email has already been taken'. The new combined `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true` produces the same default messages, but the uniqueness validator now runs even when email is blank (it did before too, actually) — the real contract change is that the previous custom email_validator added the localized I18n.t(:'user.email.not_allowed') message, and the new EmailValidator adds I18n.t(:'user.email.blocked'). The client (create_account_controller.js) reads result.errors.email and result.values.email to push into rejectedEmails. However, the controller change in users_controller.rb now returns `errors: user.errors.to_hash` — in this Rails version (3.x, given skip_before_filter and render nothing: true) errors.to_hash returns {attribute => [messages]}, so result.errors.email is an array, and the JS checks `result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values` — an empty array is truthy in JS but a present array is fine; the actual breakage: when the email is blocked, the JS pushes result.values.email into rejectedEmails and shows I18n.t('user.email.invalid') — but the server message 'is not allowed.' is more informative and is discarded. More concretely: `user.errors.to_hash` on Rails 3.2 returns a hash of arrays; combined with `values: user.attributes.slice(...)` this leaks the raw attribute values back, which is intended, but the JS only handles the case where errors.email exists — for non-email failures (e.g. username taken) errors.email is undefined and nothing is pushed, which is correct. The genuine regression: the previous behavior returned only `message` with full_messages joined; clients that parsed the message string now get a different shape, and any other consumer of UsersController#create (e.g. the omniauth flows, tests) that expected only {success, message} now receives extra keys — additive, but the errors hash shape (arrays vs strings) is undocumented and the JS truthiness check on an array works only by luck.

title: Error response shape change: errors.to_hash returns arrays, but message still uses full_messages; inconsistent and leaks attribute values
body: The create failure path now returns `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")`. In Rails 3.x, ActiveModel::Errors#to_hash returns {attribute => [msg, ...]} (arrays). The accompanying `message` still embeds full_messages.join("\n"). The JS client checks `result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values` — an array like ["is not allowed."] is truthy so it works, but this is fragile. Additionally, echoing back `values` including the email the user just typed is fine, but returning the full errors hash exposes all validation messages (including password length hints) in a structured form to any client, and the shape (hash of arrays) is not what the JS I18n-based display expects — the JS ignores result.errors content entirely and shows a generic 'user.email.invalid'. The response contract is now internally inconsistent: message is human-readable joined text, errors is structured arrays, and the client only uses errors as a boolean flag.

title: rejectedEmails check is case-sensitive and does not strip whitespace
body: The client-side check `this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email)` compares the raw typed email against the server-returned rejected value. If the user types 'Spam@Example.com' after 'spam@example.com' was rejected, contains() returns false and the email passes client validation, only to be rejected again by the server — a confusing UX loop. The comparison should normalize case (and whitespace) on both sides, e.g. compare email.toLowerCase().trim() against a lowercased rejectedEmails list.

title: rejectedEmails is populated from result.values.email, but the server may not include values when the failure is not email-related; also the pushed value is never cleared
body: In createAccount's failure handler, `if (result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values)` pushes result.values.email into rejectedEmails. Two problems: (1) result.values.email is the server-echoed attribute, which for a blocked email is the same string the user typed, so this works — but if the server ever returns errors.email without values (e.g. the ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid rescue path returns only {success, message}, no errors/values), the guard correctly skips; however the guard `result.errors.email` is an array — if the email error array is empty (shouldn't happen) it's still truthy. (2) More importantly, rejectedEmails is never cleared when the user changes the email to a different, valid address — but since the check is `contains(email)`, a different email won't match, so that's fine. The real issue: the pushed value comes from result.values.email which is user.attributes['email'] — the raw, non-downcased attribute. If the user retries with the same email but different case, the contains() check fails (see case-sensitivity finding) and the server rejects again, pushing a duplicate entry into rejectedEmails (Em.A allows duplicates), growing the array unboundedly across retries.

title: blocked_emails.email has no length limit and no downcasing; unique index is on raw value
body: The email column is t.string :email with no limit (defaults to 255 in most adapters, but the users table uses string(256)) and, critically, the unique index is on the raw email string. Since BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact match on the raw value, storing 'Spam@Example.com' and 'spam@example.com' creates two distinct rows and the block only catches one casing. The migration should either add a downcased unique column (e.g. email_lower) or enforce downcasing in the model before_validation, and the lookup should use the normalized form. Without normalization the feature's core guarantee (blocking an email address) is broken by trivial case variation.

title: No test for case-insensitive matching or for the write-during-validation side effect
body: The BlockedEmail spec covers default action_type, nil last_match_at, should_block? true/false, and match_count increment, but never tests that 'BLOCK@spamfromhome.org' matches a record created with 'block@spamfromhome.org' — the exact bypass described above. It also never tests that should_block? is safe to call with nil or a non-email string. Given the model performs a save inside should_block?, a test asserting the counter increments exactly once per signup (not once per validation pass) is missing; UsersController#create calls user.valid? and then user.save (which re-validates), so match_count would increment twice per blocked signup attempt — the spec's `change { match_count }.by(1)` only passes because it calls should_block? directly once.

title: EmailValidator spec never exercises the whitelist/blacklist paths and stubs away the real integration
body: The spec only tests the BlockedEmail branch by stubbing BlockedEmail.should_block?. It never tests the email_domains_whitelist or email_domains_blacklist behavior that the validator also implements (moved from User#email_validator), nor does it test that the validator handles a nil value, a value without '@', or that it adds the correct I18n message. Since this validator replaced the inline User#email_validator, the domain restriction behavior — the original purpose of that code — is now completely untested, and a regression in the regex (see the anchoring finding) would not be caught.

title: Email format is no longer validated anywhere; only domain restrictions and blocked-list are checked
body: The old User model had `validate :email_validator, if: :email_changed?` which checked domain whitelist/blacklist but notably did NOT check format either — however the new code replaces it with `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`, which relies on a validator named `email` resolving to EmailValidator. The new EmailValidator (lib/validators/email_validator.rb) does NOT validate email format at all — it only checks domain restrictions and the blocked list. So `validates :email, email: true` invokes EmailValidator, which never rejects 'not-an-email'. There is no EmailFormatValidator or built-in :email validator in this Rails version, so the `email: true` option either resolves to the custom EmailValidator (which ignores format) or raises ArgumentError for an unknown validator. Either way, syntactically invalid emails are no longer rejected at the model layer — the only format check left is the client-side Discourse.Utilities.emailValid. This is a functional regression: the server now accepts malformed emails like 'foo' (no @) as long as they aren't blocked and no domain restriction matches.

title: Missing trailing newline at end of file
body: The file ends without a newline ('\ No newline at end of file' in the diff). Minor, but it will show up in diffs and some linters flag it.

title: Enum.new is not a standard Rails/ActiveSupport API; actions may not behave as expected
body: The code uses `Enum.new(:block, :do_nothing)` and `BlockedEmail.actions[:block]`. ActiveSupport does not provide a top-level `Enum` class with this interface (there is no `Enum.new` that returns a hash-like object supporting `[:block]` returning a comparable value). Unless the app defines a custom Enum class elsewhere, this will raise NameError at load time, or if some gem provides it, the semantics of `actions[:block]` returning an integer stored in action_type (an integer column) need verification. The fabricator and specs use BlockedEmail.actions[:block] and compare with ==, and the migration defines action_type as integer — if Enum returns symbols, the comparison `record.action_type == actions[:block]` (integer == symbol) is always false and should_block? would never block. This needs verification that Enum exists and returns integers matching the column type.

title: XSS via unescaped URL interpolation in imported_from link
body: TopicEmbed.import builds an HTML anchor by interpolating the attacker-controlled `url` parameter directly into an href attribute and link text: `"#{url}"`. The url is only checked with a loose regex (`/^https?\:\/\//`) and is never HTML-escaped. A URL such as `http://x/' onmouseover='alert(1)` or one containing `'>

title: Raw HTML from external feeds stored and rendered without sanitization
body: TopicEmbed.import creates posts with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` and `skip_validations: true`. In app/models/post.rb (lines 130-137), `cook` short-circuits and returns `raw` unchanged when cook_method is raw_html, bypassing the entire Markdown pipeline and Sanitize-based HTML cleaning that normally applies to all user content. The `contents` come straight from an external RSS/Atom feed (app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb line 35: `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)`) or from a remote page fetched by ruby-readability (import_remote, line 48). Any script, event handler, or iframe in the feed content is persisted verbatim into `posts.cooked` and rendered unescaped via `<%= raw post.cooked %>` in app/views/embed/best.html.erb line 19 and in the standard topic view. This allows a compromised or malicious feed (feed_polling_url is an admin setting, but embed_url values come from third-party sites via the public /embed/best endpoint) to inject arbitrary JavaScript into the forum — a stored XSS. Imported HTML must be passed through Sanitize with a whitelist before being stored.

title: Referer host check compares against embeddable_host, allowing any path on that host and being spoofable
body: ensure_embeddable validates only that `URI(request.referer).host == SiteSetting.embeddable_host`. Two problems: (1) The Referer header is fully client-controlled — an attacker can send any Referer (or a page on the allowed host can be an open redirect / contain attacker content), so this check does not actually prove the embed is on the configured site; combined with `X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL` (line 28) this lets any third-party page iframe the endpoint. (2) The comparison is exact-host equality, so `evil-eviltrout.com.attacker.com` style suffixes fail but subdomains like `anything.eviltrout.com` pass if embeddable_host is a registrable domain, and conversely if embeddable_host is set to a bare hostname any subdomain matches. More importantly, the check should validate that the referer's host is the configured host (or a subdomain of it) AND that the embed_url host matches the same configured host — currently embed_url is never validated against embeddable_host in the controller, so the controller will happily enqueue retrieval of arbitrary URLs (see TopicRetriever, which does check, but only inside the job). The referer check should be a suffix match on the registrable domain and the embed_url should be validated server-side in the controller before enqueueing.

title: X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL is not a valid header value and disables framing protection
body: The controller sets `response.headers['X-Frame-Options'] = "ALLOWALL"`. ALLOWALL is not a recognized X-Frame-Options directive (valid values are DENY and SAMEORIGIN); browsers ignore unknown directives, so this header provides no protection and, worse, signals intent to allow framing from anywhere. Since the endpoint renders user-generated post content (including the unsanitized raw_html posts created by TopicEmbed), any site can embed it. If framing from the configured host only is intended, the correct approach is to omit X-Frame-Options and rely on CSP `frame-ancestors`, or set it conditionally. At minimum the invalid value should be removed or replaced with a real mechanism.

title: postMessage origin check uses indexOf substring match, which is bypassable
body: The message handler validates the sender with `if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }`. This is a substring check: if discourseUrl is `https://forum.example.com`, then origins like `https://forum.example.com.evil.com`, `https://evil.com/?x=forum.example.com`, or `https://notforum.example.com` (contains the string) all pass the check. A malicious page can therefore post a `discourse-resize` message and set the iframe height to an arbitrary value (e.g. a huge height to break the host page layout, or 0 to hide content). The check must be an exact origin comparison: `if (e.origin !== discourseUrl) { return; }` (after normalizing discourseUrl to an origin).

title: postMessage targetOrigin is the raw Referer header, enabling message leak to attacker-controlled origins
body: The layout sends the resize message with `parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')`. The targetOrigin is the full Referer URL supplied by the client. If the page is somehow framed by an attacker (see the ALLOWALL / referer-check findings), the height data is sent to that origin; more subtly, per the postMessage spec a full URL targetOrigin is matched against the origin, but using a client-controlled header as targetOrigin is fragile and, combined with the missing/invalid X-Frame-Options, means the only thing standing between an attacker and receiving these messages is the referer check. Additionally, `request.referer` is interpolated into a JavaScript string literal without escaping — a Referer containing a quote or `</script>` would break out of the script context (reflected XSS in the embed frame). The targetOrigin should be a fixed, server-derived origin (the configured embeddable host), and the value must be JS-escaped (e.g. via `json_escape` / `javascript_tag`).

title: raw post.cooked rendered in embed view
body:
The view renders `
<%= raw post.cooked %>
`. In the main Discourse UI, cooked post HTML is produced by the Markdown pipeline which sanitizes dangerous markup; here `raw` bypasses any escaping. For posts created through TopicEmbed this cooked content is entirely unsanitized external HTML (see the TopicEmbed raw_html finding), so any script in an imported article executes in the context of the Discourse origin inside the embed iframe. Even for normal cooked posts, re-rendering with `raw` in a separate layout that lacks the standard CSP/onebox protections weakens the XSS posture. The embed view should render cooked content through the same sanitization used elsewhere, and imported raw_html posts must never reach this template unsanitized.

title: import mutates the caller's contents string via <<
body: Line 13 does `contents << "\n<hr>..."`, which mutates the String object passed in by the caller. In app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb line 35 the content is `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` — a fresh string, so it's mostly harmless there, but in app/models/topic_embed.rb import_remote line 52, `doc.content` (the Readability result) is passed and then mutated; any caller reusing the string (e.g. computing the sha1 before/after, or the Disqus importer in lib/tasks/disqus.thor) will see the appended footer. Note also that `content_sha1` on line 16 is computed AFTER the mutation, so the stored hash includes the footer — meaning an update comparison is consistent, but the mutation of a caller-owned object is a hidden side effect that can corrupt data if the same string is reused (e.g. the spec at spec/models/topic_embed_spec.rb line 40 calls import twice with different literals, masking the issue). Use `contents = contents + ...` or `<<` on a dup.

title: Check-then-act race in TopicEmbed.import allows duplicate topics for the same URL
body: import does `embed = TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` and then, if blank, creates a topic/post/TopicEmbed inside a transaction. There is a unique index on embed_url (db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb line 11), but the existence check happens before the transaction and outside any locking, so two concurrent imports of the same URL (e.g. PollFeed running hourly while a user hits /embed/best and enqueues RetrieveTopic, or two Sidekiq workers) can both see `embed.blank?`, both create topics, and the second `TopicEmbed.create!` will raise ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique — leaving an orphaned topic+post created by PostCreator (the transaction wraps it, so it rolls back, but the failure is unhandled and the job has retry: false in poll_feed.rb line 12, so the item is silently lost). The correct pattern is to attempt the create and rescue RecordNotUnique, or lock/upsert. At minimum the job should handle the race gracefully.

title: PollFeed crashes on malformed feed or missing item fields; retry disabled means items are lost
body: `SimpleRSS.parse open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` performs a blocking, unvalidated HTTP fetch with no timeout, no error handling, and no content-type check; `rss.items.each` then dereferences `i.link`, `i.id`, `i.content` without nil checks. A feed that is temporarily down, returns HTML instead of RSS, or has an item without content raises an exception. Because the job declares `sidekiq_options retry: false` (line 12), the exception kills the run and the hourly recurrence simply tries again next hour — but any transient failure also means the whole feed is skipped, and `open()` on an `https` URL with a bad cert, or a redirect loop, will hang the Sidekiq worker indefinitely (no open-uri timeout/redirect limit). The job should rescue parse/network errors, use a timeout, and validate item fields before calling TopicEmbed.import.

title: CGI.unescapeHTML on feed content corrupts HTML entities and double-unescapes
body:
`content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` unescapes HTML entities in the feed content before it is stored as raw_html. RSS content is already HTML (often entity-encoded, e.g. `<p>` for a literal `

` in a code sample, or `&` for a literal `&`). Unescaping turns `<script>` into a real `

title: feed_key is defined but never used — Last-Modified/ETag caching is dead code
body: The job defines `feed_key` (a Redis key `feed-modified:<sha1 of url>`) but nothing in the file ever reads or writes it. The apparent intent was to send If-Modified-Since / track the feed's Last-Modified header and skip re-parsing unchanged feeds, but `poll_feed` unconditionally does `SimpleRSS.parse open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` every hour and re-imports every item (TopicEmbed.import does dedupe by content_sha1, so it's not catastrophic, but every item's content is re-hashed and compared each hour, and the HTTP fetch always happens). Either implement the conditional GET using feed_key or remove the dead method; as written it misleads maintainers into thinking conditional requests are happening.

title: invalid_host? returns true when embeddable_host is blank, but comparison is exact-host and case-sensitive
body: `SiteSetting.embeddable_host != URI(@embed_url).host` compares the configured host string directly to the URI host. If embeddable_host is configured as `http://eviltrout.com` (with scheme) or `Eviltrout.com` (mixed case) or `eviltrout.com/` (trailing slash), the comparison fails for perfectly valid embed URLs and retrieval is silently skipped; conversely `www.eviltrout.com` vs `eviltrout.com` mismatches. The setting is documented as "Host that can embed the comments" (config/locales/server.en.yml), so it should be normalized (strip scheme, downcase, strip port) before comparison, and the embed_url host should be compared as a suffix of the configured registrable domain. As written, misconfiguration silently disables the entire feature.

title: Calling Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({}) synchronously inside RetrieveTopic defeats the purpose of the async job and can recurse
body: perform_retrieve runs `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` inline when feed polling is enabled. RetrieveTopic is itself a Sidekiq job enqueued from the embed controller; running the entire hourly feed poll synchronously inside it means a single embed request can trigger a full feed fetch and import of every item, blocking the RetrieveTopic worker for a long time (PollFeed does unbounded HTTP fetches with no timeout). Worse, PollFeed imports items via TopicEmbed.import, which is fine, but if any code path enqueues RetrieveTopic from within PollFeed processing there is potential for long chains; more practically, the design intent (per the class comment "First check RSS if that is enabled") is to check whether the feed already contains the URL, not to run the whole poll. This should instead query the feed (or a cached copy) for the specific embed_url, or enqueue PollFeed asynchronously and return, letting the loading page's 30-second reload pick up the result.

title: fetch_http performs an unvalidated server-side request to a user-influenced URL (SSRF surface)
body: fetch_http calls `TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, @embed_url)`, which does `open(url).read` (app/models/topic_embed.rb line 48). The URL originates from the `embed_url` query parameter of the public `/embed/best` endpoint (app/controllers/embed_controller.rb line 9). The only validation is `invalid_host?`, which checks `URI(@embed_url).host == SiteSetting.embeddable_host`. This still allows SSRF-style abuse within the allowed host (e.g. `http://eviltrout.com:22/`, `http://eviltrout.com/admin/internal-endpoint`, `http://user:pass@eviltrout.com/`, or `file://` if the host string is ever misconfigured to match), and `open()` follows redirects by default, so a URL on the allowed host that redirects to `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` (cloud metadata) or an internal service will be fetched and its content imported as a post. open-uri must be restricted: validate scheme is http/https, resolve and reject private/loopback/link-local IPs, disable redirects or re-validate each hop, and set timeouts.

title: import_remote fetches arbitrary URLs with open() — no scheme, redirect, or private-network restrictions
body: `Readability::Document.new(open(url).read, ...)` uses Kernel#open (open-uri) on a URL that, via TopicRetriever/RetrieveTopic, is ultimately derived from the public embed_url parameter, and via PollFeed from feed item links/ids (`url = i.id if url.blank? || url !~ /^https?\:\/\//` in poll_feed.rb line 33 — note this fallback accepts ANY string as a URL, including `file:///etc/passwd`, which open-uri will happily open). There is no scheme whitelist, no redirect limit, no timeout, and no protection against requests to internal/private IP ranges. This is a full SSRF primitive: an attacker who can influence a feed item id/link (or an embed_url on the allowed host that redirects) can make the server read local files (`file://`) or internal HTTP services and import the response body as a forum post, leaking internal data. The fetch must be hardened (scheme whitelist, redirect re-validation, IP range blocking, timeouts).

title: Feed item id used as URL without any validation enables file:// and internal URL fetch
body: `url = i.link; url = i.id if url.blank? || url !~ /^https?\:\/\//`. When an RSS item has no link (or a non-http link), the item's `id` (often a GUID, which in many feeds is a URN like `urn:uuid:...`, a tag URI, or — in attacker-controlled feeds — an arbitrary string such as `file:///etc/passwd` or `http://169.254.169.254/`) is used as the URL and passed to TopicEmbed.import → import_remote → `open(url)`. TopicEmbed.import line 11 does check `url =~ /^https?\:\/\//` and returns nil otherwise, which blocks file:// at that layer — but only for the import path; the regex is also loose (matches `https://` anywhere at the start, accepts `https://` followed by anything). The deeper issue is that poll_feed hands unvalidated feed data to a URL fetcher; the id fallback should be removed or strictly validated, and the fetch layer must enforce scheme/IP restrictions regardless (defense in depth).

title: RetrieveTopic job is enqueued on every cache miss with no deduplication, enabling job flooding
body: When no TopicEmbed exists for the embed_url, the controller enqueues `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)` and renders the loading page, which auto-reloads every 30 seconds (app/views/embed/loading.html.erb line 10). Each reload re-enters `best`, finds no embed (the job may still be running or throttled), and enqueues another RetrieveTopic job. TopicRetriever has a 60-second Redis throttle (`retrieved_recently?`), but that only prevents the actual fetch — the jobs still pile up in Sidekiq, and each one performs DB queries and, for staff users (`no_throttle: user.try(:staff?)`), bypasses the throttle entirely. A popular embed (or a bot hitting /embed/best?embed_url=... directly with a valid Referer) can enqueue thousands of jobs. The controller should check the throttle key (or use a single enqueue-per-URL lock) before enqueueing, and the loading page should back off.

title: TopicView is built with current_user, leaking private topic data into the public embed
body: `TopicView.new(topic_id, current_user, {best: 5})` passes the current user. The embed endpoint is meant to be loaded in an iframe on a third-party site; the iframe request will typically carry the Discourse session cookie of whatever user happens to view the host page (cookies are sent on iframe requests depending on SameSite settings). If that user is a staff member or a member of a restricted category, TopicView will include posts/topics they can see but anonymous visitors cannot, and the rendered HTML (including post content from restricted categories) is served to the third-party page. The embed view must always be built as an anonymous/system user (e.g. `TopicView.new(topic_id, nil, ...)` or a dedicated embed user) and should verify the topic is publicly visible before rendering. As written, restricted/private post content can be exfiltrated by embedding a URL.

title: Update path revises the post but never updates the topic title
body: When content changes, import revises the post via PostRevisor with the new contents, but the topic title (from the feed item's `i.title`) is never updated — only the initial creation uses `title`. A feed that renames an article leaves the Discourse topic with the stale original title forever. Additionally, `embed.update_column(:content_sha1, content_sha1)` skips validations/callbacks (acceptable here) but if the PostRevisor revision fails silently (revise! returns false when raw is unchanged — though sha1 differs so raw differs — or raises), the sha1 is still updated only after revise! returns, which is correct, but there is no transaction wrapping the revise + update_column, so a crash between them leaves the post updated but the sha1 stale, causing a redundant re-revision next poll (harmless but noisy). The title update is the real gap: PollFeed passes `i.title` on every run but import ignores it on the update path.

title: absolutize_urls only handles root-relative URLs and mishandles protocol-relative and default ports
body: absolutize_urls rewrites only hrefs/srcs that `start_with?('/')`. Protocol-relative URLs (`//cdn.example.com/x.jpg`) and scheme-relative paths (`http://other.com/...` is fine, but `//host/path` is left as-is and will resolve against the Discourse origin when rendered, breaking images/links). Also, the port logic `prefix << ":#{uri.port}" if uri.port != 80 && uri.port != 443` appends the port for https URLs on port 80 or http URLs on port 443 incorrectly (e.g. `https://host:80/` would get `:80` appended even though URI normalizes... actually URI keeps explicit ports, so `https://eviltrout.com:80/` yields prefix `https://eviltrout.com:80` which is wrong-ish but functional). More importantly, relative URLs like `images/foo.jpg` (no leading slash) are not absolutized at all and will 404 when rendered from the Discourse origin. The method should use URI.join semantics for all relative references, not just root-relative ones.

title: Avatar img src uses ERB interpolation inside a single-quoted HTML attribute without escaping
body: `` interpolates the avatar URL into a single-quoted attribute with no HTML escaping. small_avatar_url is derived from the user's uploaded avatar or gravatar; an admin/user-controlled avatar URL containing a single quote would break out of the attribute. Rails' `image_tag` (used correctly on lines 8 and 26) escapes properly; this raw img tag should use `image_tag(post.user.small_avatar_url)` or at least `h()` the value. Low severity because avatar URLs are largely system-generated, but it's an inconsistency with the rest of the file and a latent injection point if avatar URLs ever become user-supplied strings.

title: Controller spec expects TopicRetriever to be used, but the controller enqueues a job instead
body: The test "tells the topic retriever to work when no previous embed is found" stubs `TopicRetriever.expects(:new)` and `retriever.expects(:retrieve)`, but the controller (app/controllers/embed_controller.rb line 15) never calls TopicRetriever directly — it calls `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)`. The spec would fail against the actual implementation (TopicRetriever.new is never invoked in the controller), meaning either the spec is wrong or the controller was changed after the spec was written and the test suite is red. A correct test would expect `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)` (or `Jobs.expects(:enqueue).with(:retrieve_topic, ...)`). This is exactly the kind of spec that gives false confidence — it documents an implementation that doesn't exist.

title: Update-path spec doesn't verify the content_sha1 changed or that a revision was created
body: The "Supports updating the post" test only asserts `post.cooked.should =~ /new contents/`. It doesn't verify that the TopicEmbed's content_sha1 was updated (so the next poll with the same content won't re-revise), that a PostRevision was created, or that the returned post is the same post (same id) as the original. A regression where import creates a second topic on update (the race condition described in the concurrency finding) would still pass this test as long as cooked contains the new text. The test should assert `post.id == original_post.id`, `TopicEmbed.count == 1`, and the updated sha1.

title: discourse_expires_in 1.minute is applied even to the loading page, causing rapid re-fetch churn
body: `discourse_expires_in 1.minute` sets a 1-minute HTTP cache on both the rendered topic view and the loading page. For the loading page this is mostly harmless, but combined with the 30-second auto-reload in loading.html.erb, a shared/CDN cache could serve a stale loading page for up to a minute after the topic has actually been imported, making the embed appear stuck. More importantly, caching the rendered best view for only 1 minute means every embed impression after the first minute hits the Rails stack and rebuilds a TopicView (an expensive operation) — for a high-traffic embed this is a significant load multiplier. The cache duration should be longer for the success path (the content changes only when the topic changes) and the loading page should send no-cache headers so the reload actually re-queries.

title: no_throttle is granted based on the user_id passed from the controller, which is the iframe viewer's identity
body: `TopicRetriever.new(args[:embed_url], no_throttle: user.try(:staff?))` — the user_id comes from `current_user.try(:id)` in the embed controller, i.e. whichever Discourse user's browser loaded the third-party page. Any staff member who visits a page containing an embed (or an attacker who socially engineers a staff member to a page with many distinct embed_urls) gets the 60-second throttle disabled, allowing unbounded fetch/import of arbitrary URLs on the allowed host. The throttle bypass should not be tied to the viewer's identity at all; if staff bypass is desired it should be a server-side decision, and the throttle key should also incorporate the URL (it does) but the bypass should be removed or gated on a server-controlled flag.

title: cook_method default of 1 does not match Post.cook_methods enum ordering
body: The migration sets `default: 1, null: false` for posts.cook_method. Post.cook_methods is `Enum.new(:regular, :raw_html)` (app/models/post.rb lines 63-65). Discourse's Enum assigns values starting at 1 in declaration order (regular=1, raw_html=2) — so default 1 = regular, which is correct. However, this is fragile: the migration hardcodes the integer 1 instead of referencing the enum, and the schema comment in post.rb doesn't list cook_method at all (the annotate block at the bottom of post.rb is missing the new column). If the enum order ever changes, existing rows silently change meaning. The migration should use a comment documenting the mapping, and the model's schema annotation should be regenerated to include cook_method. More importantly, `Post#cook` (line 133) compares `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` — for legacy rows defaulted to 1 this is regular, fine, but there's no DB check constraint tying the value to the enum, so a bad value (0, 3) silently falls through to the regular cook path.

title: cook_method raw_html bypasses all cooking/sanitization with no guard on who can set it
body: `cook` returns `raw` verbatim when `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. The only setter is PostCreator line 216 (`post.cook_method = @opts[:cook_method] if @opts[:cook_method].present?`), and PostCreator is a public API used by controllers with user-supplied opts in many places. Any code path that passes user-controlled opts through to PostCreator (e.g. a plugin, the API, or a future controller) can set cook_method to raw_html and store arbitrary unsanitized HTML. There is no Guardian check restricting raw_html to staff/import contexts. The raw_html path should be gated (e.g. only settable when the acting user is staff or via an explicit import flag checked against the guardian), and the value should be validated against the enum on assignment.

title: skip_validations option now skips post validations on revise, but the raw_html cook_method is never re-applied on revision
body: The diff changes `@post.save` to `@post.save(validate: !@opts[:skip_validations])`, which is needed for the import update path. However, when TopicEmbed.import revises a raw_html post (topic_embed.rb line 36), PostRevisor.update_post sets `@post.raw = @new_raw` and saves; the before_save callback in post.rb (line 321) recomputes `self.cooked = cook(raw, ...)` only `unless new_record?` — for an existing raw_html post, cook returns raw, so cooked is correctly set to the new raw. That part works. The subtle issue: `skip_validations` now bypasses Validators::PostValidator for ALL revisions when the option is passed, including length/entropy/spam checks — acceptable for the import path, but the option is a general-purpose footgun now available to any caller of PostRevisor. It should be named/scoped to the import use case or documented. Low severity since only TopicEmbed passes it today.

title: Loading page reloads unconditionally every 30s with no cap, hammering the server for never-imported URLs
body: The loading view does `setTimeout(function() { document.location.reload(); }, 30000)` with no maximum retry count and no backoff. If the URL can never be imported (host not actually embeddable, fetch fails, user not found — TopicRetriever.fetch_http returns silently if embed_by_username is blank), the iframe reloads forever, each time enqueueing another RetrieveTopic job (see the controller finding). A single abandoned embed tab generates 2 requests/minute indefinitely plus a Sidekiq job each time. The reload should stop after N attempts and show a permanent message with a link to start the discussion on the forum.

title: Embed route has no rate limiting and is unauthenticated
body: `get 'embed/best' => 'embed#best'` is a public, unauthenticated route with no rate limit. Combined with the job-enqueue-per-miss behavior and the TopicView construction on hit, it's an easy DoS/amplification vector: an attacker can request /embed/best?embed_url=<unique-string> with a spoofed Referer matching embeddable_host, each request enqueuing a Sidekiq job and (for existing topics) building a full TopicView. There is no RateLimiter usage in EmbedController. The endpoint should be rate limited per IP (and per embed_url), and the referer check should be supplemented with a per-IP limiter since the Referer is trivially spoofable.

title: URL validation regex is too loose and inconsistent with the rest of the codebase
body: `return unless url =~ /^https?\:\/\//` accepts strings like `https://` (nothing after), `https://?x`, `https:// evil.com`, and `https://example.com/redirect?to=javascript:...`. It also uses escaped colons (`\:`) which are unnecessary in a regex. Elsewhere the codebase uses the same loose pattern (poll_feed.rb line 33), so the inconsistency is systemic, but the import path is the security boundary: a URL like `https://eviltrout.com@evil.com/` (userinfo trick) passes the regex and URI parsing will treat evil.com as the host — which then fails invalid_host? in TopicRetriever, but TopicEmbed.import is also called directly from PollFeed with feed-supplied URLs that bypass TopicRetriever's host check entirely. The URL should be parsed with URI() and validated: scheme in [http, https], host present, and host matching the expected domain.

title: PollFeed spec requires the wrong dependency and never tests poll_feed itself
body: The spec requires `jobs/regular/process_post` (line 2) — an unrelated job — instead of `jobs/scheduled/poll_feed`, and all four tests only exercise the `execute` guard conditions by mocking `poll_feed`. There is no test that poll_feed actually parses a feed, handles a missing user, handles a malformed feed, or calls TopicEmbed.import with the right arguments. The require of process_post suggests a copy-paste error and means the spec may not even load the class under test in some configurations. The spec should require the correct file and include tests for poll_feed's behavior (using a stubbed SimpleRSS.parse / fakeweb, both of which are available in the Gemfile).

title: Disqus import rewritten to TopicEmbed.import_remote but reply posts are created with raw HTML cooked content and no cook_method
body: The diff replaces the old PostCreator-based topic creation with `TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], title: t[:title])`, then creates reply posts with `attrs = { ..., raw: p[:cooked], cooked: p[:cooked], ... }` (lines 160-165). The Disqus `message` field is HTML from the export; setting both raw and cooked to that HTML and creating via PostCreator means the post goes through the normal Markdown cook pipeline (cook_method defaults to regular), which will mangle the HTML (Markdown-processed HTML often renders incorrectly), and the before_save callback recomputes cooked from raw anyway. The replies should either be created with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` (matching the imported topic) or converted to Markdown. As written, imported Disqus replies will be double-processed and likely display broken markup. Also, `Date.parse(p[:created_at])` will raise on malformed dates, aborting the whole import with no error handling.

title: Disqus import creates users from unvalidated author emails with no approval
body: `post_user = User.create!(email: email, username: UserNameSuggester.suggest(email))` creates a full user account for every distinct author email in the Disqus export, with no validation of the email beyond `Email.downcase`, no check against the email blacklist (which is explicitly cleared on line 141: `SiteSetting.email_domains_blacklist = ""`), and no approval/trust gating. A malicious Disqus export (the import file is operator-supplied, but exports can be crafted) can create thousands of accounts with arbitrary email addresses, which then appear as post authors. These auto-created users have trust level 0 but can still be spam vectors (they exist, can be messaged, appear in user lists). The import should use a dedicated import user or staged/unapproved accounts, and the blacklist should not be globally disabled for the duration.

title: Referer host comparison doesn't handle missing port/scheme normalization and is case-sensitive
body: `URI(request.referer || '').host != SiteSetting.embeddable_host` — URI#host returns a downcased host without port, but SiteSetting.embeddable_host is compared as a raw string. If the admin enters `Eviltrout.com` or `eviltrout.com:80` or `http://eviltrout.com` in the setting, the comparison fails for every request and the feature is entirely broken (all requests raise InvalidAccess). The setting should be normalized once (downcase, strip scheme/port) before comparison, or the comparison should parse the setting as a URI too. The spec (embed_controller_spec.rb) only tests with an exact lowercase match, so this misconfiguration is untested.

title: Script assumes #discourse-comments exists; throws if the host page lacks it
body: `document.getElementById('discourse-comments')` can return null if the host page doesn't include the expected div (typo, different embed snippet version, CSP-modified DOM), and `comments.appendChild(iframe)` on line 12 then throws a TypeError, breaking the entire script. The embed snippet should be documented as requiring the div, but the script should guard: `if (!comments) { return; }`. Low severity (host-page integration issue), but it silently breaks embedding with no error message.

title: import_remote fetches the full page with no timeout, size limit, or redirect limit
body: `Readability::Document.new(open(url).read, ...)` reads the entire response body into memory with open-uri defaults: no open_timeout/read_timeout, no redirect limit (open-uri follows up to 10 redirects by default), and no maximum size. A slow or huge page on the allowed host (or an allowed-host URL redirecting to a multi-GB file) will hang the Sidekiq worker and consume unbounded memory. The fetch should use explicit timeouts, a redirect cap with re-validation, and a maximum content length.

title: TopicRetriever spec never tests the actual retrieval, throttling, or host validation logic end-to-end
body: All tests mock `perform_retrieve` or `retrieved_recently?`, so the spec verifies only the wiring of `retrieve` (that it calls perform_retrieve unless invalid_host?/retrieved_recently?). It never tests that invalid_host? correctly parses URIs, that retrieved_recently? actually uses Redis setnx/expire correctly (the throttle could be broken and no test would catch it), that perform_retrieve checks TopicEmbed existence, or that fetch_http looks up the embed user. The Redis throttle in particular is concurrency-sensitive logic that deserves a real test (mock_redis is available in the Gemfile).

title: XSS via unescaped URL interpolation into raw HTML post content
body: TopicEmbed.import builds the 'imported from' footer by interpolating the caller-supplied `url` directly into an HTML anchor: `"#{url}"`. The post is then created with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`, which (per Post#cook in app/models/post.rb line 133) returns `raw` verbatim with no sanitization. A URL containing a single quote (e.g. `http://x/' onmouseover='alert(1)`) or HTML like `http://x/'>

title: Raw HTML from remote feeds is stored and rendered without sanitization
body: TopicEmbed.import creates posts with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`, and Post#cook (app/models/post.rb line 133) returns `raw` unchanged for that method, bypassing the entire Markdown/sanitization pipeline. The `contents` come from an external RSS/Atom feed (Jobs::PollFeed passes `i.content.scrub` — `scrub` only replaces invalid byte sequences, it does not sanitize HTML) or from `Readability::Document` output in import_remote. Any script, event handler, or iframe in the feed content is stored verbatim in `cooked` and rendered unescaped via `<%= raw post.cooked %>` in app/views/embed/best.html.erb line 19 and in the regular topic view. A compromised or malicious feed source yields stored XSS against every viewer of the imported topic. The content must be passed through Sanitize (as the normal cooking pipeline does) before being stored.

title: Referer host check compares against a single configured host, allowing bypass and enabling unauthorized embedding
body: ensure_embeddable validates only that `URI(request.referer).host == SiteSetting.embeddable_host`. Two problems: (1) the Referer header is fully client-controlled — an attacker can simply send a request with a forged `Referer: http://<embeddable_host>/` header (e.g. via curl) and pass the check, so this is not an authorization boundary at all; (2) the check is an exact string match against one host, so subdomains or any other legitimate embedding host are rejected, and conversely any page on the configured host (including attacker-controlled paths if the host serves user content) is accepted. Combined with the fact that the endpoint renders full topic content (TopicView with posts) for any `embed_url` whose host matches `embeddable_host` (see TopicRetriever#invalid_host?), this exposes forum content to scraping and enables the iframe to be embedded from arbitrary pages on that host. The referer check should be treated as defense-in-depth only; access control must not rely on it.

title: X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL is an invalid value and disables framing protection
body: The controller sets `response.headers['X-Frame-Options'] = "ALLOWALL"`. ALLOWALL is not a valid X-Frame-Options directive (valid values are DENY and SAMEORIGIN, plus the obsolete ALLOW-FROM uri). Browsers ignore unrecognized values, so this header provides no protection and signals intent to allow framing from anywhere. Since the whole point of the referer check is to restrict which sites may frame this content, the header should either be removed (relying on the referer check) or set to a real value; as written it is dead code that gives a false sense of security. Additionally, modern browsers enforce framing via CSP frame-ancestors, which is not set here.

title: postMessage origin check uses indexOf, which is bypassable
body: The message handler validates the sender with `if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }`. `String#indexOf` performs a substring match, so an origin like `http://evil.com/?x=http://discourse.example.com` (or `http://discourse.example.com.evil.com` if discourseUrl lacks a scheme/trailing slash) contains the discourse URL as a substring and passes the check. A malicious page could then send a `discourse-resize` message with an arbitrary height, resizing the iframe to hide or distort content (a clickjacking/UX-integrity issue; the data is only a height so impact is limited, but the check is still wrong). The origin must be compared exactly: `e.origin !== discourseUrl` (after normalizing both to origins).

title: postMessage targetOrigin is the raw Referer header, enabling message leakage to attacker-controlled origins
body: The layout sends the resize message with `parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')`. The targetOrigin is taken verbatim from the client-controlled Referer header. If the Referer is not a valid origin (e.g. a full URL with a path, or an attacker-supplied value), the browser behavior is undefined/lenient in older engines, and more importantly the referer is attacker-controlled, so the height data (and the fact that the embed loaded) can be posted to an origin the site operator never intended. targetOrigin should be a fixed, known origin — the configured `SiteSetting.embeddable_host` (normalized to scheme://host) — not the request's Referer. Also note `request.referer` is interpolated into a JS string literal without escaping; a Referer containing a quote would break out of the string (minor, since the value is also attacker-controlled, but it is a JS injection point).

title: URL scheme validation regex is over-permissive and inconsistent
body: `return unless url =~ /^https?\:\/\//` — the escaped colons (`\:`) in a regex are just literal colons, so this works, but the pattern is not anchored at the end and accepts strings like `http://` followed by anything, including `http://evil.com" onmouseover=...` (relevant given the XSS in the same method) and `https:///path`. More importantly, the same check is duplicated (with slightly different escaping) in Jobs::PollFeed line 33 (`url !~ /^https?\:\/\//`) and TopicRetriever relies on URI parsing instead. There is no shared URL validator, so the three call sites can disagree about what is a valid embed URL. A single strict validator (scheme http/https, parseable URI, present host) should be used everywhere.

title: import mutates the caller's contents string in place
body: `contents << "\n<hr>\n..."` appends to the String passed in by the caller. In Jobs::PollFeed, `content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` is a fresh string so it is mostly harmless there, but in TopicEmbed.import_remote, `doc.content` (the Readability document's content) is passed directly and gets the footer appended to it; any reuse of that string afterwards sees the mutated value. More subtly, the `content_sha1` is computed AFTER the mutation (line 16), which is correct for change detection, but the in-place mutation of an argument is a hidden side effect that violates the method's contract and will surprise callers (e.g. the disqus.thor importer or tests that reuse `contents`). Use `contents = contents + ...` or `<<` on a dup.

title: Content-hash comparison uses the mutated string but the update path can silently skip revisions
body: On update, `if content_sha1 != embed.content_sha1` triggers a PostRevisor revision. But `content_sha1` is computed from `contents` AFTER the 'imported from' footer was appended (line 13), while the stored hash was computed the same way on insert, so far so good. However, if the remote article's URL changes (e.g. trailing slash differences, http→https, redirects), a NEW TopicEmbed row is created for what is the same article, producing a duplicate topic — there is no canonicalization of `embed_url` (the unique index on embed_url then also silently allows near-duplicate URLs). Conversely, if only the footer link text changed, every row would be revised. The embed_url should be canonicalized (normalized URI: lowercase host, strip fragment, default ports, trailing slash) before lookup/insert.

title: Feed polling fetches an admin-configured URL with open-uri without scheme/SSRF restrictions
body: `SimpleRSS.parse open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` uses Kernel#open on a URL. While the setting is admin-controlled, `open` on a string starting with `|` executes a shell command (the classic open-uri/Kernel#open pipe vulnerability) — if the setting value ever begins with `|` (or is otherwise attacker-influenced via a compromised admin UI, import, or YAML injection), this is remote command execution. Even restricting to http(s), there is no protection against SSRF to internal addresses (169.254.169.254, localhost services). The code should use `URI.parse` + `Net::HTTP`/`open-uri`'s `URI.open` equivalent with an explicit scheme whitelist (http/https only) and ideally block private/link-local IP ranges.

title: import_remote fetches arbitrary URLs server-side (SSRF) with no scheme or host restrictions
body: `Readability::Document.new(open(url).read, ...)` fetches `url` server-side. `url` originates from the `embed_url` request parameter (EmbedController#best → Jobs::RetrieveTopic → TopicRetriever → import_remote) and from RSS item links in PollFeed. TopicRetriever#invalid_host? restricts the host to `SiteSetting.embeddable_host`, but: (1) that check is bypassable — see the controller finding — and PollFeed passes `i.link`/`i.id` from the feed with only a `^https?://` regex check, so a malicious feed can make the server fetch `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` or internal services; (2) `open` has the pipe-command issue noted above. The fetch must be restricted to http/https and the resolved IP must be validated against private ranges, and the embeddable_host check must actually be enforced on this path.

title: i.content can be nil, causing NoMethodError on .scrub
body: `content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` — SimpleRSS items do not guarantee a `content` element (it is optional in RSS 2.0; `content:encoded` may be absent, and Atom entries may only have `summary`). When absent, `i.content` is nil and `.scrub` raises NoMethodError, aborting the whole hourly poll (and since `sidekiq_options retry: false`, the failure is silent until someone notices missing imports). Guard with `i.content.to_s.scrub` or skip items without content.

title: feed_key is defined but never used — Last-Modified/ETag caching is dead code
body: `feed_key` builds a Redis key `"feed-modified:<sha1 of url>"` but nothing in the job ever reads or writes it. The apparent intent (per the key name) was to send a conditional GET (If-Modified-Since / If-None-Match) and skip re-parsing unchanged feeds, but `open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` is unconditional. Every hour the full feed is downloaded and every item is re-imported (TopicEmbed.import does dedupe by content hash, so no duplicate topics, but the work is wasted). Either implement the conditional fetch using feed_key or remove the dead method.

title: invalid_host? treats a blank embeddable_host as matching any host
body: `SiteSetting.embeddable_host != URI(@embed_url).host` — when `embeddable_host` is blank/nil (the default in config/site_settings.yml is `''`), `nil != "eviltrout.com"` is true, so invalid_host? returns true and retrieval is blocked. That part is fine. But the check is an exact host string comparison with no normalization: `http://EvilTrout.com/...` (case), `http://eviltrout.com:80/...` (explicit default port — URI#host drops the port so this actually matches), or `http://eviltrout.com./...` (trailing dot, which DNS resolves to the same host) will mismatch or match inconsistently. Host comparison must be done on the normalized, downcased host (and the same normalization must be applied in EmbedController's referer check and in TopicEmbed URL canonicalization), otherwise the allowlist is both bypassable (trailing-dot / case tricks against some resolvers) and brittle.

title: RetrieveTopic triggers a full synchronous PollFeed run inside the request job
body: perform_retrieve calls `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` inline when `feed_polling_enabled?`. PollFeed downloads and parses the entire RSS feed and imports every item (each import creates/revises posts). This runs inside the RetrieveTopic Sidekiq job, so a single embed request for a URL not yet in the feed can trigger a full feed crawl and bulk import — potentially minutes of work and dozens of post creations — while the user's embed request is waiting (the controller already rendered 'loading', but the job is blocked and Sidekiq workers are consumed). Worse, every distinct embed_url hit within the throttle window can re-trigger this. The poll should be enqueued as its own job (`Jobs.enqueue(:poll_feed)`) rather than executed inline, and the per-URL retrieval should not depend on a full feed scan.

title: RetrieveTopic job is enqueued on every cache-miss request with no deduplication
body: When no TopicEmbed exists for the URL, the controller enqueues `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)` and renders 'loading'. The loading page reloads every 30 seconds (app/views/embed/loading.html.erb), and each reload enqueues ANOTHER RetrieveTopic job. TopicRetriever has a 60-second Redis throttle (`retrieved_recently?`) that mitigates duplicate work, but: (1) the throttle key is per-URL and setnx-based, so the first job sets it and subsequent jobs bail — OK — but the throttle only lasts 60s while the loading page reloads every 30s indefinitely, so after 60s a new job is enqueued and the cycle repeats for as long as the topic is missing (e.g. the remote page is down or the import keeps failing), hammering the remote site and the job queue; (2) many concurrent viewers of the same not-yet-imported URL each enqueue jobs. There should be a longer-lived 'import in progress / failed' marker (e.g. a Redis key with a TTL of minutes, or a DB flag) so the job is enqueued at most once per N minutes per URL.

title: EmbedController renders a TopicView for any user (including anonymous) without checking topic access
body: `@topic_view = TopicView.new(topic_id, current_user, {best: 5})` — TopicView is constructed with `current_user`, which is nil for anonymous requests (the embed iframe is loaded cross-origin from the embedding site, so no Discourse session cookie is sent). Whether TopicView enforces access for nil users depends on its internals, but the embed endpoint then renders `post.cooked` raw for every post returned. If the embedded topic is in a restricted category, is a private message, or is otherwise not publicly visible, its content is exposed to anyone who knows/guesses the embed_url — and embed_urls are the external article URLs, which are often public. The controller must verify the topic is publicly visible (e.g. `Guardian.new(nil).can_see?(topic)` / topic.category.read_restricted check) before building the view, and return 404 otherwise.

title: post.user can be nil, causing NoMethodError when rendering an embed
body: The view calls `post.user.small_avatar_url` and `post.user.username` unconditionally. Posts whose author has been deleted (user_id retained but user row gone, or anonymous/system posts) will raise NoMethodError on nil, breaking the whole embed render (500). Guard with `post.user.present?` or use the existing `post.user` serializer pattern (e.g. `BasicUserSerializer`) / `post.username` (Post#username delegates to user.username and would also fail, so an explicit nil check or `try` is needed).

title: absolutize_urls only handles root-relative URLs and mishandles protocol-relative and default ports
body: The method rewrites only `href`/`src` values starting with `/`. Protocol-relative URLs (`//cdn.example.com/x.png`) and scheme-relative paths (`images/foo.png`) are left as-is, so images/links break when the content is viewed on the Discourse origin. Also, the port logic `prefix << ":#{uri.port}" if uri.port != 80 && uri.port != 443` appends the port for https URLs on port 80 or http URLs on port 443 incorrectly (it checks the numeric port against both schemes' defaults regardless of the actual scheme), and `URI#port` returns the default port when none is specified, so `http://host:80` gets no port (fine) but `https://host:443` also gets none (fine) — the real bug is non-default ports on the 'wrong' scheme and the fact that `uri.port` for a URI without an explicit port returns 80/443, making the condition mostly moot. Use `uri.origin` (Ruby 2.x) or build the prefix from scheme+host+optional non-default port, and handle `//`-prefixed and relative URLs via `URI.join`.

title: no_throttle is granted based on the requesting user's staff status, but the job runs asynchronously and the check is per-request
body: `TopicRetriever.new(args[:embed_url], no_throttle: user.try(:staff?))` — the throttle bypass is decided by whichever user happened to trigger the embed request. A staff member viewing the embed page bypasses the 60s throttle, so a staff user (or anyone who can get a staff account to load the page) can force repeated retrievals of the same URL, each performing an outbound HTTP fetch to the embeddable host (a self-DoS / amplification vector against the configured host). The throttle should be keyed on the URL only (as it is), and the staff bypass should either not exist or be rate-limited separately; at minimum the bypass should not be derived from an untrusted request parameter path.

title: Controller spec expects TopicRetriever to be used synchronously, but the controller enqueues a job
body: The test 'tells the topic retriever to work when no previous embed is found' stubs `TopicRetriever.expects(:new).returns(retriever)` and expects `retrieve` to be called during `get :best`. But the controller (app/controllers/embed_controller.rb line 15) calls `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)` — it never instantiates TopicRetriever in the request. In test mode `queue_jobs` is false (config/site_settings.yml developer.queue_jobs test: false), which may execute the job inline, but the spec does not stub Jobs.enqueue and does not assert on the enqueued job; if the job runs inline the mock expectation may pass by accident, and if jobs are queued the expectation fails. The spec should assert `Jobs.expects(:enqueue).with(:retrieve_topic, ...)` instead of mocking TopicRetriever, otherwise it is testing an implementation the controller does not have and will break or silently mislead.

title: Update-path test does not verify the stored content_sha1 is updated, and update is not isolated from creation
body: The 'Supports updating the post' test calls `TopicEmbed.import(user, url, title, "muhahaha new contents!")` and only asserts `post.cooked =~ /new contents/`. It does not verify that `embed.content_sha1` was updated (line 37 of the model uses `update_column`, which skips validations/callbacks — a regression there would go unnoticed), does not verify no second TopicEmbed row was created (the unique index would raise, but the test would surface it only as an error, not an assertion), and because the `let!(:post)` creation runs first, the test depends on ordering. A follow-up import with the SAME content should also be tested to confirm no revision occurs (the `content_sha1 != embed.content_sha1` guard).

title: Spec requires the wrong job file and never tests poll_feed itself
body: `require_dependency 'jobs/regular/process_post'` is unrelated to Jobs::PollFeed (which lives in app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb) — likely a copy-paste. More importantly, the spec only tests the `execute` guard conditions; `poll_feed` (the actual feed parsing, item URL fallback, content scrubbing, and TopicEmbed.import call) has no coverage at all, including the nil `i.content` crash and the URL fallback logic (`url = i.id if url.blank? || url !~ /^https?\:\/\//`). Add specs with a stubbed SimpleRSS feed covering: item with link, item with only id, item with no content, and verification that TopicEmbed.import is called with the right arguments.

title: topic_embeds migration uses force: true, which drops an existing table
body: `create_table :topic_embeds, force: true` — `force: true` drops the table if it already exists. In a migration this is dangerous: on any environment where the table was already created (e.g. by a previous partial run, a restored backup, or a plugin), running this migration silently destroys all topic_embeds rows (the mapping between external URLs and topics), after which every embed re-imports content as new topics. Migrations should use `create_table :topic_embeds` without force (the same applies to the unrelated change in 20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb, which also switched to `force: true`).

title: cook_method raw_html bypasses sanitization for any post that sets it, with no guard on who can set it
body: Post#cook returns `raw` verbatim when `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`, and PostCreator (lib/post_creator.rb line 216) copies `@opts[:cook_method]` onto the post whenever present. There is no validation restricting `raw_html` to trusted callers (e.g. staff or the embed importer): any code path that passes user-controlled `raw` together with `cook_method: raw_html` (or any future caller that forwards a request param into opts) stores and renders unsanitized HTML. The `cook_method` option should be stripped from user-facing PostCreator invocations (whitelist it to internal importers only), and ideally raw_html posts should still pass through Sanitize with a strict whitelist before being stored in `cooked`.

title: Embed view renders post.cooked with raw, relying entirely on the cooking pipeline for safety
body:
`
<%= raw post.cooked %>
` renders cooked HTML unescaped. This is consistent with the main forum, but combined with the raw_html cook method (see the TopicEmbed findings) it means imported feed content is rendered with zero sanitization in this iframe, which is embedded on third-party sites. The embed surface should be treated as higher risk: at minimum, posts shown here should be re-sanitized on output, and raw_html posts should never be displayed without a Sanitize pass.

title: Embed route is defined before the /t/:id routes and lacks a format constraint
body: `get 'embed/best' => 'embed#best'` is placed in the middle of the routes (line 245), before the topic routes. It does not conflict with existing routes, but it also has no `format: false` / constraints, so `/embed/best.json` or `/embed/best.xml` would match and run the controller (params[:embed_url] required, so it would 400 — minor). More relevant: the route is not constrained to GET-only semantics beyond the verb, and there is no rate limiting at the routing layer; combined with the per-request job enqueue finding, this endpoint is an easy amplification target. Consider `get 'embed/best' => 'embed#best', format: false` and Rack::Attack throttling on /embed/.

title: discourse_expires_in is called even when rendering 'loading', caching a page that tells the client to reload
body: `discourse_expires_in 1.minute` runs unconditionally at the end of `best`, including when the 'loading' template is rendered (line 16). The loading page contains a script that reloads after 30 seconds; caching it for 1 minute via the browser/CDN means a user whose import completes 5 seconds later still sees the cached loading page and waits for the reload. The loading response should be marked no-cache (or a very short expiry), while the successful embed view can be cached for 1 minute.

title: Disqus importer now depends on TopicEmbed.import_remote fetching t[:link], but never passes created_at and loses the permalink post
body: The refactored import calls `TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], title: t[:title])` and no longer creates the original permalink post (`raw: "[[Permalink](#{t[:link]})]"` with `created_at: Date.parse(t[:created_at])` was removed). Consequences: (1) the topic's created_at is now the import time, not the original thread creation date — topic ordering and 'new' lists are wrong for all imported threads; (2) the explicit permalink back to the Disqus thread is gone (import_remote's Readability extraction may or may not include it); (3) `import_remote` ignores any created_at option — TopicEmbed.import has no created_at parameter at all, so there is no way to preserve dates.
