The importer should pass `created_at` through TopicEmbed.import (add an opts parameter forwarded to PostCreator, which already supports `created_at`).

title: Disqus importer creates users with User.create! which can raise and abort the whole import
body: `post_user = User.create!(email: email, username: UserNameSuggester.suggest(email))` — the bang version raises on validation failure (duplicate email race, invalid username suggestion, etc.), and the exception is not rescued inside the `parser.threads.each` loop, so one bad author email aborts the entire import mid-way (the `ensure` restores settings but all remaining threads are lost, and already-created topics remain — a partial import with no idempotency). Use `User.create` and skip/fallback to the default user on failure, or rescue and log per-post.

title: embed_by_username lookup will NoMethodError on nil if the setting is blank
body: `User.where(username_lower: SiteSetting.embed_by_username.downcase)` — `execute` guards with `SiteSetting.embed_by_username.present?`, but `poll_feed` is a public method also invoked directly from TopicRetriever (lib/topic_retriever.rb line 41: `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` — that goes through execute, so guarded). However `feed_key` and `poll_feed` are public and the guard lives only in `execute`; any direct call to `poll_feed` (or a future refactor moving the guard) with a blank setting raises NoMethodError on nil.downcase. Move the blank check into poll_feed or use `SiteSetting.embed_by_username.to_s.downcase`.

title: PostRevisor revision of an imported post does not preserve cook_method, so the update is re-cooked as Markdown
body: On update, `PostRevisor.new(post).revise!(user, absolutize_urls(url, contents), skip_validations: true, bypass_rate_limiter: true)` sets a new `raw` (HTML). PostRevisor#update_post assigns `@post.raw = @new_raw` and saves; the Post `before_save` callback (app/models/post.rb line 321) recomputes `self.cooked = cook(raw, ...)` unless new_record?. `cook` checks `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` — the post retains cook_method raw_html from creation, so cooked == raw. OK in the current flow. BUT: PostRevisor never touches cook_method, and if the post's cook_method were ever reset (e.g. by an edit through the normal UI, which doesn't set cook_method but also doesn't clear it — actually it persists), the HTML raw would be run through the Markdown pipeline and mangled. More importantly, the revision path relies on the column persisting; there is no test pinning that an updated imported post still has cook_method raw_html and cooked == raw. The spec gap is noted in the topic_embed_spec finding; additionally, `update_column(:content_sha1, ...)` skips callbacks — acceptable here, but if the revise! fails (returns false because raw unchanged — impossible here since contents changed) the hash would still be updated, desyncing hash from content. Guard: only update the hash if the revision actually happened.

title: Script assumes #discourse-comments exists; throws if the host page lacks it
body: `document.getElementById('discourse-comments')` returns null if the embedding page does not include the expected div, and `comments.appendChild(iframe)` then throws TypeError, leaving a broken embed. The embed snippet should be documented to require the div, and the script should fail gracefully (or create the container) when it is missing.

title: postMessage resize only fires on window.onload and never on content changes
body: The iframe height is sent once on `window.onload`. If the embed content grows after load (images loading, fonts, the loading→content transition when the topic finishes importing and the page reloads — that case is covered by reload, but late-loading avatars/images in best.html.erb are not), the iframe keeps its initial height and content is clipped (scrolling is disabled via `iframe.scrolling = "no"` in embed.js). A ResizeObserver or periodic height check should be used, or at minimum re-send after images load.

title: cook_method default of 1 assumes Enum ordering that is not enforced at the DB level
body: `add_column :posts, :cook_method, :integer, default: 1, null: false` — the default 1 is meant to be `Post.cook_methods[:regular]` (Enum.new(:regular, :raw_html) → regular=1? Discourse's Enum typically starts at 1, so regular=1, raw_html=2). This is correct only if Enum assigns 1 to the first key; the migration hardcodes 1 with no comment or check constraint, so if the Enum definition is reordered, existing rows silently point at the wrong method. Add a comment documenting the mapping, or better, verify in a data migration that the value matches Post.cook_methods[:regular].

title: TopicRetriever spec never tests perform_retrieve, fetch_http, or the Redis throttle
body: All specs stub out `perform_retrieve` or `retrieved_recently?`; the actual retrieval logic (the exists? check, the PollFeed delegation, fetch_http user lookup and import_remote call) and the `retrieved_recently?` Redis setnx/expire logic are completely untested. The throttle is security-relevant (prevents hammering the remote host), so a regression that removes the expire or inverts the setnx result would go unnoticed. Add specs using mock_redis (already a test dependency) for retrieved_recently?, and stub TopicEmbed.import_remote / Jobs::PollFeed for perform_retrieve/fetch_http.

title: Referer-based host check is trivially bypassable and inconsistent with embeddable_host semantics
body: ensure_embeddable compares URI(request.referer).host to SiteSetting.embeddable_host with exact string equality. The Referer header is fully client-controlled, so any site can send a forged Referer matching embeddable_host and load the embed endpoint in an iframe. Additionally, embeddable_host is documented as 'Host that can embed the comments from this Discourse forum' (a single host), but the check requires an exact host match with no subdomain handling, and a blank referer yields URI('').host == nil which fails closed only by accident. The endpoint also sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL, which is not a valid X-Frame-Options directive value (valid values are DENY and SAMEORIGIN), so browsers ignore it and framing is unrestricted. The real protection is the referer check, which is spoofable; combined with the fact that the action enqueues a server-side fetch (Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, embed_url: ...)) of an arbitrary attacker-supplied URL, this allows an attacker to make the Discourse server issue requests to arbitrary hosts (SSRF) by embedding the iframe with a forged Referer. The embed_url is later fetched by TopicRetriever/TopicEmbed.import_remote via open(url).

title: Arbitrary embed_url triggers server-side fetch of attacker-controlled URL (SSRF)
body: The best action takes params[:embed_url] with no validation and enqueues Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, embed_url: embed_url). RetrieveTopic passes it to TopicRetriever, which only checks that URI(embed_url).host equals SiteSetting.embeddable_host. An attacker who controls any page on the embeddable host (or can spoof the Referer as noted above) can supply embed_url values pointing at internal addresses (e.g. http://embeddable_host@169.254.169.254/... or URLs whose host string matches but resolve internally, or simply use the embeddable host as a proxy to fetch internal paths). TopicEmbed.import_remote then calls open(url).read, causing the server to fetch and parse the response, and the fetched content is stored as a post. There is no scheme restriction beyond the implicit http(s) of open-uri, no blocklist of private IP ranges, and no restriction on ports. This is a server-side request forgery vector that also creates topics from the fetched content.

title: Imported RSS/feed content is stored and rendered as raw HTML without sanitization (stored XSS)
body: TopicEmbed.import appends an 'imported from' footer to the feed-supplied contents and creates the post with cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]. In app/models/post.rb, cook returns raw unchanged when cook_method == raw_html, bypassing the entire Markdown rendering/sanitization pipeline (PrettyText/cook normally sanitizes HTML). The resulting post.cooked is then rendered in app/views/embed/best.html.erb line 19 with <%= raw post.cooked %>, and also rendered normally elsewhere in the forum. The content comes from an RSS/ATOM feed (Jobs::PollFeed passes i.content through CGI.unescapeHTML) or from an arbitrary fetched page (import_remote via ruby-readability, which whitelists only a few tags/attributes but still passes through and including javascript: URLs potentially, and import() is also called directly with unsanitized content). Because cook_method raw_html skips sanitization, any

title: import mutates the caller's contents string in place
body: TopicEmbed.import does contents << "\n<hr>..." which mutates the String object passed by the caller. In Jobs::PollFeed, content is built per item so impact is limited, but in TopicEmbed.import_remote, doc.content is passed and mutated; more importantly the content_sha1 is computed AFTER the mutation (line 16), which is consistent, but any caller that reuses the same string across calls (e.g. computing its own hash beforehand, or the Disqus thor task) will see the string changed. This is a hidden side effect that can corrupt data or cause incorrect change detection (content_sha1 comparisons) for callers that pre-compute hashes. The method should dup the string before appending.

title: URL validation regex is too permissive and inconsistent with the rest of the code
body: The guard `return unless url =~ /^https?\:\/\//` accepts URLs like 'http://' followed by anything, including 'http://<script>' or 'http:///path', and does not reject whitespace/control characters. Elsewhere the codebase uses the same loose pattern (poll_feed.rb line 33, topic_retriever invalid_host?), but TopicEmbed.import is the final gate before open(url) and post creation. A URL such as 'http://example.com/\nSet-Cookie: ...' or one containing spaces can be passed to open-uri. More importantly, the regex does not anchor the end and allows e.g. 'http://host\t.evil.com' style tricks depending on URI parsing differences between the regex check and URI()/open-uri. A stricter validation (URI.parse with scheme whitelist and host presence) should be used before the URL is fetched or stored.

title: import_remote fetches arbitrary URL with open() and no redirect/size limits
body: TopicEmbed.import_remote calls open(url).read with no timeout, no redirect limit, no content-size limit, and no scheme/IP restrictions. Combined with the SSRF surface described in the controller finding, a malicious embed_url can cause the Sidekiq worker to hang indefinitely (no timeout on open-uri), follow redirects to internal hosts, or download unbounded content into memory (read with no limit) causing memory exhaustion. ruby-readability then parses the entire document. At minimum open-uri timeouts (open(url, read_timeout:, open_timeout:) or a redirect cap and maximum body size) should be enforced.

title: PollFeed crashes the whole job when the feed is unreachable or malformed; no error handling and feed_key is dead code
body: poll_feed calls SimpleRSS.parse(open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)) with no rescue. If the feed URL is down, returns invalid XML, or open-uri raises (SocketError, Errno::ECONNREFUSED, OpenURI::HTTPError, etc.), the exception propagates out of execute. The job is declared sidekiq_options retry: false, so a single transient failure permanently skips that run (until the next hourly recurrence) and, worse, any items already processed in the loop before the exception are committed (TopicEmbed.import runs per item with its own transaction) while the rest are lost — there is no per-item error isolation either, so one bad item (e.g. i.content being nil causing NoMethodError on .scrub at line 35) aborts processing of all remaining items. Additionally, feed_key (lines 20-22) is defined but never used anywhere, indicating intended caching/last-modified logic was never wired up. The job should rescue per-item errors, rescue overall fetch errors, and use feed_key or remove it.

title: i.content can be nil causing NoMethodError; i.link/i.id handling is fragile
body: Line 35 calls i.content.scrub without a nil check. SimpleRSS items frequently have nil content (e.g. RSS 2.0 items with only a description, or Atom entries without content), which raises NoMethodError and aborts the entire poll_feed loop as described above. Similarly i.title can be nil and is passed to TopicEmbed.import as the topic title, which will fail topic title validation (though skip_validations: true is set, downstream TopicCreator may still misbehave) or produce a broken topic. The code should guard with i.content.to_s and fall back to i.description, and handle missing titles.

title: postMessage origin check uses indexOf (substring match) allowing origin spoofing
body: The handler validates the message origin with `if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }`. indexOf performs a substring check, not an origin comparison: an attacker page at https://evil.com/?x=discourseUrl-value or at a host containing the discourse URL as a substring (e.g. https://discourse.example.com.evil.com when discourseUrl is https://discourse.example.com) will pass the check because e.origin contains the discourseUrl string. The correct check is to compare against the parsed origin of discourseUrl (e.g. new URL(discourseUrl).origin === e.origin). Because the handler sets iframe.height from e.data.height, a spoofed message can resize the iframe arbitrarily (UI redress / covering page content). The iframe src is also constructed from discourseEmbedUrl which is attacker-influenced via the embedding page, but the origin check flaw is the concrete bug here.

title: postMessage targetOrigin is the raw Referer header, enabling message leak to attacker-controlled origins
body: The layout sends the resize message with `parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')`. The targetOrigin is the full Referer URL string, not an origin. Per the postMessage spec, if targetOrigin is not '*' or '/', it must be an origin (scheme://host[:port]); a full URL with a path is compared as a string prefix against the parent's origin, so 'http://eviltrout.com/some/page' will NOT match the parent origin 'http://eviltrout.com' and the message will silently not be delivered (functional bug), but more importantly the value is derived from the client-controlled Referer header. If an attacker can get the iframe loaded with a crafted Referer (or the referer is an attacker-influenced URL), the height data is posted to that origin. The targetOrigin should be derived server-side from SiteSetting.embeddable_host (the validated host), not from request.referer. Also note request.referer is interpolated into a JS string literal without escaping — a Referer containing a quote would break out of the string (though browsers constrain header characters, it is still incorrect to interpolate unescaped).

title: Unescaped attribute interpolation for avatar URL and username
body: Line 16 uses `` with raw ERB interpolation inside a single-quoted HTML attribute, and line 17 outputs `<%= post.user.username %>` (this one is escaped by default, fine). small_avatar_url is generally a Discourse-generated URL, but if it is nil (user without avatar) the src becomes empty; more importantly, interpolating into an attribute without the asset/URL helpers and without escaping is fragile — a URL containing a single quote would break out of the attribute. The codebase convention is to use double-quoted attributes with standard <%= %> escaping (which escapes quotes as "). This should be ``.

title: raw post.cooked renders unsanitized HTML in the embed iframe (stored XSS sink)
body: Line 19 renders `<%= raw post.cooked %>`. For posts created via TopicEmbed.import, cooked is the raw feed HTML because cook_method raw_html bypasses sanitization (see post.rb finding). Even for normal cooked posts, Discourse's cooked HTML is sanitized for the main app, but the embed view is a separate, minimal layout; rendering raw cooked here means any content that survived (or bypassed) sanitization is rendered in the iframe. Combined with the raw_html import path, this is the sink that turns feed-controlled HTML into executed script in the forum origin. The embed view should render cooked through the same sanitization guarantees as the main app (which it nominally does for regular posts) and must never render raw_html-cooked posts without sanitization; at minimum, posts with cook_method raw_html should be sanitized before display.

title: cook_method raw_html bypasses all cooking/sanitization for post content
body: The new cook method returns raw verbatim when cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html], skipping post_analyzer.cook which is where Markdown rendering and HTML sanitization (via Sanitize) occur. Any code path that sets cook_method to raw_html (TopicEmbed.import, and the Disqus thor task which sets cooked directly) therefore stores completely unsanitized HTML in the cooked column. cooked is treated as trusted, pre-sanitized HTML throughout Discourse (rendered with raw in many views, used in excerpts, feeds, emails, and the new embed view). There is no compensating sanitization anywhere on this path. This is a stored-XSS primitive: whoever can influence content imported via RSS/feed or Disqus import controls cooked HTML rendered to all users. The raw_html path must sanitize (e.g. with Sanitize using Discourse's whitelist) before storing, or the feature should be removed.

title: TopicEmbed.import creates topics with skip_validations: true, bypassing title/post validation and spam checks
body: PostCreator.new is called with skip_validations: true, which disables post validation (save(validate: false) in PostCreator#save_post) and skips SpamRulesEnforcer (PostCreator#create only enforces spam rules when !@opts[:skip_validations]). Feed-supplied titles (which can be nil, empty, extremely long, or contain control characters) and feed-supplied raw content therefore bypass min/max title length, min post length, max post length, and all spam rules. This allows the feed to create malformed topics (e.g. nil/empty title, oversized posts exceeding max_post_length) and to spam the forum with content that would normally be rejected. The import path should validate titles and enforce length limits, or at minimum sanitize/truncate the title and enforce max_post_length.

title: PostRevisor.revise! with skip_validations can fail silently and leaves embed.content_sha1 updated even if revision failed
body: In the update branch, revisor.revise!(user, ..., skip_validations: true, bypass_rate_limiter: true) is called and its return value is ignored. PostRevisor#revise! returns false when the raw hasn't changed (should_revise?) and update_post calls @post.save(validate: false) whose failure is not checked (save returns false but no exception, and revise! still returns true). After this, embed.update_column(:content_sha1, content_sha1) unconditionally updates the stored hash. If the revision failed to persist (validation skipped but a DB constraint failed, or save returned false), the embed now claims the new content_sha1 while the post still holds the old content, so future polls will never detect the change again (permanent divergence). The return value of revise! should be checked and the sha1 update should happen only on success, ideally inside the same transaction.

title: Check-then-create race on embed_url allows duplicate topics despite unique index
body: import does TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first and then, if blank, creates a topic/post/TopicEmbed inside a transaction. There is a TOCTOU race: two concurrent imports (e.g. PollFeed running hourly plus RetrieveTopic jobs triggered by embed requests, or multiple Sidekiq workers) can both observe embed.blank? and both create topics. The unique index on embed_url (migration 20131217174004) will cause the second TopicEmbed.create! to raise ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique, rolling back the second transaction — but the first transaction may have already committed, so the net effect is an exception in the job (which for PollFeed has retry: false, so it's lost) and potentially confusing partial behavior. The code should rely on the unique index (rescue RecordNotUnique and re-read) or use a unique constraint check at creation time rather than a pre-check.

title: Host validation compares embeddable_host to URI host with exact equality, no scheme/port normalization
body: invalid_host? returns true unless SiteSetting.embeddable_host == URI(@embed_url).host. This means an embed_url of 'http://embeddable_host:8080/x' or 'https://embeddable_host/x' passes as long as the host string matches, and more importantly the check does not restrict the scheme — 'file://embeddable_host/...' would have host 'embeddable_host'? (URI('file://embeddable_host/etc/passwd').host is 'embeddable_host'), and open-uri supports file:// URLs, so TopicEmbed.import_remote's open(url) could read local files if a file:// URL with matching host passes. Actually open-uri does support file:// ; URI('file://embeddable_host/etc/passwd').host == 'embeddable_host' so invalid_host? is false and the file would be fetched and imported. The validation must whitelist the scheme (http/https only) and ideally normalize/compare ports.

title: Throttle key uses raw embed_url in Redis key without namespacing/escaping
body: retrieved_key = "retrieved:#{@embed_url}" interpolates the full URL into a Redis key. URLs can contain characters that are legal in Redis keys but make keys unbounded in length (Redis keys can be up to 512MB, but very long keys waste memory) and there is no collision-safety concern here since the full URL is the key. More relevantly, the throttle is per-URL and setnx+expire is not atomic with the subsequent work: if the process crashes after setnx but before perform_retrieve completes, the URL is throttled for 60s with no topic created, and the embed shows 'loading' until the next request after expiry. This is acceptable behavior, but the key should be hashed (e.g. Digest::SHA1) to bound key size, consistent with feed_key's approach in poll_feed.rb.

title: no_throttle is set from user.try(:staff?) but the user lookup can return nil and the throttle bypass applies to any staff user id passed in args
body: The job accepts args[:user_id] from the enqueued args and looks up the user; if that user is staff, no_throttle is true, disabling the 60-second retrieval throttle. The controller passes current_user.try(:id), so a staff user browsing the embed repeatedly bypasses throttling — that's intended. However, the job trusts args[:user_id] without verifying the requester is actually that user (jobs are enqueued server-side so this is fine in the current call path), but the RetrieveTopic job is a regular (non-scheduled) job that any code path can enqueue with an arbitrary user_id; combined with the SSRF surface, a staff user_id disables throttling for arbitrary URL fetches. This is a minor trust-boundary note; the main issue is that the throttle bypass is keyed off a user-supplied id in a job payload.

title: TopicView.new is called with current_user which may be nil, and no topic access check is performed
body: When a topic_id is found, the controller builds TopicView.new(topic_id, current_user, {best: 5}) and renders the posts in best.html.erb. current_user is nil for anonymous iframe requests (the embed is loaded cross-site in an iframe where cookies may not be sent depending on browser settings). More importantly, there is no check that the topic is publicly visible: TopicEmbed.topic_id_for_embed returns any topic id for the URL, including topics in restricted categories, private messages, or deleted/hidden topics. TopicView with an anonymous user normally filters posts by guardian permissions, but the embed controller does not verify the topic is accessible to anonymous users, and the embed view renders post.cooked, usernames, and avatar URLs directly. If an embed_url maps to a topic in a restricted category (e.g. via feed import misconfiguration or a leaked URL), the embed endpoint leaks its content to anyone who knows the embed_url. The controller should verify the topic is visible to anonymous users (e.g. guardian.can_see?(topic) with anonymous user) before rendering.

title: discourse_expires_in 1.minute caches the loading page and topic view for anonymous users without varying on embed_url
body: The action sets discourse_expires_in 1.minute, which sets a short public cache TTL. The response content depends entirely on the embed_url query parameter. If a shared/CDN cache caches the response without including the query string in the cache key (or if the framework's expires_in sets Cache-Control: public), one user's embed_url response could be served to another user requesting a different embed_url, leaking topic content across embed URLs. Rails' discourse_expires_in typically sets Cache-Control: public, max-age=60 with no Vary on the query param. The response should be marked private/no-cache (the content is per-URL and per-user), or at minimum Vary on the embed_url parameter.

title: Controller spec expects TopicRetriever to be used directly, but the controller enqueues a job instead
body: The test 'tells the topic retriever to work when no previous embed is found' sets TopicRetriever.expects(:new).returns(retriever) and retriever.expects(:retrieve), then performs get :best. But the controller code calls Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...) — it never instantiates TopicRetriever. This test would fail against the actual implementation (TopicRetriever.new is never called), meaning the spec does not match the code and provides false confidence. Either the controller should call TopicRetriever directly (synchronously) or the spec should expect Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...) with the right args. As written, the test suite is broken/misleading for this behavior.

title: Spec asserts exact HTML serialization that depends on Nokogiri version behavior
body: The test asserts post.cooked.start_with?("hello world new post hello ") — an exact string match on Nokogiri's fragment.to_html output (attribute quoting, tag self-closing style, attribute order). Nokogiri's HTML serialization is not guaranteed stable across versions (e.g. libxml2 version differences change attribute quoting and void-element serialization), so this test is brittle and can fail for reasons unrelated to the code under test. It should assert on parsed structure (e.g. Nokogiri::HTML.fragment(post.cooked).at_css('a')['href']) instead of exact string prefix matching.

title: Migration uses force: true which drops an existing table
body: create_table :topic_embeds, force: true will DROP the table if it already exists, destroying all data. The companion migration 20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb was also changed to add force: true. Using force: true in a migration is dangerous: if this migration is ever run on a database where the table already exists (e.g. re-running after a partial failure, or on a restored backup), it silently destroys all topic_embeds/top_topics data. Migrations should be idempotent without force, or use create_table ... unless table_exists?. The change to add force: true to the existing create_top_topics migration is an unrelated and risky modification.

title: Disqus import rewritten to use TopicEmbed.import_remote but reply posts are created with raw HTML cooked and no cook_method, breaking rendering
body: The import now calls TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], title: t[:title]) to create the topic, then creates reply posts with attrs = { topic_id:, raw: p[:cooked], cooked: p[:cooked], created_at: } via PostCreator.new(post_user, attrs).create. The Disqus export's p[:cooked] is HTML (from the Disqus message field). Setting cooked directly while raw is also HTML means the post's raw is HTML treated as Markdown source; on any later edit/revision, Post#cook will run the Markdown pipeline over HTML, and the before_save callback (post.rb line 321: self.cooked = cook(raw, ...) unless new_record?) will re-cook on update, mangling the HTML. Also, unlike the topic post (which gets cook_method raw_html via import), these reply posts have default cook_method regular, so cooked and raw diverge and the stored cooked is unsanitized HTML rendered with raw elsewhere — the same stored-XSS issue as the feed import, plus content corruption on edit. The reply posts should either be created with cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html] (and sanitized) or, preferably, with raw set to the HTML and cooked left to be generated by the normal pipeline after sanitization.

title: Disqus import creates users with User.create! without password/username validation and can create duplicate/spam accounts
body: For each Disqus post with an author_email, the importer does User.where(email: email).first and, if missing, User.create!(email: email, username: UserNameSuggester.suggest(email)). This creates forum accounts for arbitrary email addresses found in a Disqus export, without activation, without trust level restrictions, and with auto-generated usernames. Combined with the fact that these users' posts are created with the unsanitized cooked HTML, this both pollutes the user table (unactivated accounts that count toward stats, can be emailed, appear in user lists depending on settings) and amplifies the XSS issue. The importer should use a single designated user (options[:post_as]) for all replies, or create users via the proper signup/approval flow, and should not create accounts from untrusted export data.

title: URL fallback regex allows non-http schemes to be treated as valid item URLs
body: url = i.id if url.blank? || url !~ /^https?\:\/\// — when the link is blank or not http(s), the code falls back to i.id, which for Atom feeds is often a URN (e.g. 'urn:uuid:...') or an arbitrary string. TopicEmbed.import then rejects it (returns nil unless url =~ /^https?\:\/\//), so the item is silently skipped — but the intent appears to be to use i.id as a fallback URL, which will almost never be a valid http URL. This means Atom feeds whose entries lack a proper <link href> are silently dropped. The fallback is ineffective; the code should skip items without a valid http(s) link rather than passing a URN to import.

title: Script assumes #discourse-comments element exists; throws if missing
body: The IIFE immediately does document.getElementById('discourse-comments') and later comments.appendChild(iframe) without a null check. If the embedding page includes this script without a #discourse-comments div (a trivial integration mistake), the script throws a TypeError and the embed never renders, with no error message. A null check with a console warning would make integration failures diagnosable.

title: Loading page reloads every 30 seconds indefinitely, causing repeated job enqueues
body: The loading view reloads the page every 30 seconds via setTimeout. Each reload hits EmbedController#best, which (while no TopicEmbed exists) enqueues another Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...) every 30 seconds per viewing browser. TopicRetriever throttles actual fetches to once per 60s per URL for non-staff, but each reload still enqueues a job (jobs pile up in Sidekiq) and each request re-renders. For a popular embed whose source is slow or permanently failing, this creates a self-inflicted load amplification: N viewers → 2N jobs/minute. The reload loop should back off, or the controller should not enqueue a job when one is already pending/in-progress (e.g. check a Redis key set by RetrieveTopic).

title: Embed route is defined before the catch-all topic routes, shadowing nothing but placed inconsistently; no rate limiting on the endpoint
body: The route get 'embed/best' => 'embed#best' is placed after the topics/private-messages routes but before the 't/:id' topic routes. It does not conflict, but the endpoint is publicly accessible, performs a DB lookup and enqueues a job per request, and has no rate limiting at the Rack/Rails level (the only throttle is inside TopicRetriever for the fetch, not for the endpoint itself). An attacker can hammer /embed/best?embed_url=... to fill the Sidekiq queue with RetrieveTopic jobs (each of which does a Redis setnx and a DB exists? check). Rack::Attack or a controller-level rate limit should protect this endpoint.

title: absolutize_urls only handles root-relative URLs, not other relative forms, and mishandles protocol-relative URLs
body: absolutize_urls rewrites href/src only when they start_with?('/'). Relative URLs like 'images/foo.jpg' or '../foo' are left relative, so in the rendered post they resolve against the Discourse forum's origin instead of the source site — broken images/links. Protocol-relative URLs ('//cdn.example.com/x.jpg') start with '/' and are incorrectly rewritten to 'http://sourcehost//cdn.example.com/x.jpg' (double slash after host), producing a broken URL. The method should use URI.join(uri, href) to correctly resolve all relative forms, and skip absolute and protocol-relative URLs.

title: PollFeed spec only tests execute gating; poll_feed itself (the actual feed parsing and import) is untested
body: The spec only verifies that execute calls poll_feed when settings are present and doesn't when they're missing. The poll_feed method — which contains the actual logic (user lookup, SimpleRSS parsing, URL fallback, CGI.unescapeHTML, TopicEmbed.import loop) — has no tests. Given that poll_feed has known fragility (nil i.content, fetch errors, malformed feeds), tests should cover: successful import of items, skipping items with invalid URLs, behavior when the feed is unreachable, and behavior when embed_by_username doesn't exist. The require_dependency at line 2 also loads 'jobs/regular/process_post' which is unrelated to PollFeed (copy-paste error) and should be 'jobs/scheduled/poll_feed'.

title: X-Frame-Options set to invalid value ALLOWALL
body: response.headers['X-Frame-Options'] = "ALLOWALL" — ALLOWALL is not a valid X-Frame-Options directive (the spec defines only DENY and SAMEORIGIN; ALLOW-FROM is deprecated/unsupported). Browsers ignore invalid X-Frame-Options values, so this header provides no framing protection and gives a false sense of security. Since the embed is intended to be framed by the embeddable host, the correct approach is to omit X-Frame-Options (or use CSP frame-ancestors with the specific embeddable host), relying on the referer check — but the referer check itself is spoofable as noted. At minimum the invalid header should be removed or replaced with a CSP frame-ancestors directive listing SiteSetting.embeddable_host.

title: PostRevisor#update_post ignores save failure, allowing silent data loss on revision
body: update_post calls @post.save(validate: !@opts[:skip_validations]) and ignores the return value. If save fails (e.g. a DB-level error, or with validations enabled a validation failure), revise! still returns true and the caller (TopicEmbed.import) proceeds to update embed.content_sha1, marking the content as updated when it wasn't. This is a general data-integrity bug in PostRevisor affecting all revision paths, introduced/exposed by this PR's change to pass skip_validations through. The method should check the save result and raise or return false on failure so callers don't record success.

title: import_remote passes unsanitized readability output to import which stores it as raw_html
body: import_remote extracts doc.content via ruby-readability with a tag/attribute whitelist (div p code pre h1-h3 b em i strong a img; attributes href src). While this strips

title: CGI.unescapeHTML on feed content can reintroduce HTML entities that alter stored markup
body: content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub) unescapes HTML entities in the feed content before it is stored as raw_html. If the feed contains <script>alert(1)</script> (escaped HTML, common in RSS content:encoded fields that are double-escaped), unescapeHTML converts it to literal <script>alert(1)</script>, which is then stored as raw_html and rendered unsanitized (see post.rb finding). This actively converts safe escaped content into executable HTML. The unescapeHTML call should be removed; if the feed double-escapes, the correct fix is to not unescape and let the raw_html sanitization (which should exist) handle it.

title: Update test does not verify content_sha1 is updated or that unchanged content does not create a revision
body: The 'Supports updating the post' test only checks that post.cooked matches /new contents/. It does not verify that the TopicEmbed.content_sha1 was updated (so future identical imports don't re-revise), nor that importing the same content twice does not create a new post revision (the should_revise? guard in PostRevisor). These are core behaviors of the import method (change detection via content_sha1) and should be asserted: after a second import with identical content, post.version should be unchanged; after import with new content, embed.content_sha1 should equal Digest::SHA1 of the new contents.

title: update_column skips callbacks/updated_at and is not transactional with the revision
body: embed.update_column(:content_sha1, content_sha1) performs a direct SQL UPDATE outside any transaction wrapping the PostRevisor.revise! call. If the process crashes between revise! committing and update_column running, the embed retains the old sha1 and the next poll will re-revise the post (creating a spurious revision). Conversely if update_column runs but the revision transaction rolled back (it can't here since revise! is called first, but ordering matters), the sha1 would be wrong. The sha1 update should be inside the same transaction as the revision, or revise! should be wrapped with the update in a Topic.transaction block.

title: Calling Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({}) synchronously inside TopicRetriever is wrong layering and can recurse/deadlock
body: perform_retrieve invokes Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({}) directly (synchronously) when feed_polling_enabled is set, instead of enqueueing the job. This runs the entire feed poll (fetching and importing every item in the feed) inside the RetrieveTopic job, which was triggered by a single embed request. Consequences: (1) the RetrieveTopic job can run for a very long time (Sidekiq timeout), (2) it duplicates work — PollFeed is also scheduled hourly, so every embed request re-polls the entire feed, (3) if the feed contains the embed_url, this creates a nested import while the outer import for the same URL may also be in flight, hitting the race described in the TopicEmbed finding, and (4) it's a layering violation — jobs should enqueue other jobs (Jobs.enqueue(:poll_feed)) rather than instantiating and executing them inline. The correct behavior is Jobs.enqueue(:poll_feed) or to not invoke PollFeed from here at all.

title: skip_before_filter :check_xhr and :preload_json may not exist / are Rails-version dependent
body: The controller skips check_xhr and preload_json before filters. If these filters are not defined on ApplicationController in all supported Rails versions (the Gemfile dual-boots Rails 3.2 and Rails 4), skip_before_filter raises ArgumentError ('no such filter') at load time, breaking the controller. The codebase uses skip_before_filter elsewhere, but the existence of check_xhr and preload_json should be verified for both boot modes; using skip_before_filter with `if:` or `unless:` guards, or skip_filter with raise: false (Rails 4.1+), would be safer. This is a potential boot failure on one of the supported Rails versions.

title: Unrelated whitespace-only change removes trailing newline at end of file
body: The diff for this migration only removes trailing whitespace on line 2 and removes the final newline at end of file (line 33: 'end' with no trailing newline). This is an unrelated change to a historical migration that should not be modified (migrations are immutable once run in production). Removing the trailing newline and touching an already-shipped migration adds noise and risk (e.g. checksum-based migration verification in some setups) with no benefit. The file should be left unchanged.

title: Missing trailing newline at end of file
body: The file ends without a trailing newline (line 69 '}' with \ No newline at end of file). This is a minor style issue that can cause noisy diffs when the file is later edited (the last line appears modified). Not a functional problem but should be fixed for consistency with the rest of the codebase.

title: Missing trailing newline at end of file
body: The file ends without a trailing newline. Same minor consistency issue as other new files; should end with a newline.

title: Missing trailing newline at end of file
body: The file ends without a trailing newline. Minor consistency issue.

title: Missing trailing newline at end of file
body: The file ends without a trailing newline. Minor consistency issue.

title: Referer host comparison does not handle www prefix, subdomains, or ports, causing legitimate embeds to be rejected
body: URI(request.referer).host returns the host without port. If SiteSetting.embeddable_host is configured as 'eviltrout.com' but the embedding page is served from 'www.eviltrout.com', or the referer includes a non-default port (URI(...).host strips the port, so 'eviltrout.com:8080' yields host 'eviltrout.com' — actually that matches), the exact string comparison fails and the embed is rejected with 'invalid referer host'. Conversely if embeddable_host includes 'www.' it won't match the bare domain. The comparison should normalize both sides (strip leading 'www.', compare registrable domains or use a configured exact match with documentation). As written, the feature is brittle to common configuration variations and the failure mode (Discourse::InvalidAccess) is a 403 that breaks the embed with no diagnostic.

title: topic_id_for_embed does not validate or normalize the embed_url before lookup
body: TopicEmbed.topic_id_for_embed(embed_url) passes the raw param directly to a WHERE clause. The controller passes params[:embed_url] unvalidated. While SQL injection is prevented by ActiveRecord's parameter binding, the lookup is exact-string: 'http://example.com/page' and 'http://example.com/page/' or 'https://example.com/page' are treated as different embeds, so the same article embedded with different URL spellings creates duplicate topics (each triggering a separate fetch/import). The embed_url should be normalized (scheme/host lowercase, strip fragment, strip trailing slash, default ports) before lookup and storage to dedupe. This is both a data-integrity issue (duplicate topics) and a fetch-amplification issue.

title: Header layout breaks: .title float removed but flexbox applied to wrong element, orphaning .valign-helper and breaking vertical centering
body: The diff removes `float: left` from `.title` and adds `@include flexbox()` / `@include align-items(center)` to `.contents`, but the actual flex children in the header DOM are `.title`, `.panel`, and `.icons` — not `.contents` itself. The `.valign-helper` element (lines 21-25) is a legacy inline-block vertical-centering hack that only works with `display: inline-block` siblings; once `.contents` becomes a flex container, `.valign-helper` becomes a flex item with `height: 100%` and `vertical-align: middle` (which is ignored in flex layout), producing an unexpected extra flex item that shifts the logo and other items. Additionally, `.panel` uses `margin-left: auto` combined with `@include order(3)` to push right, but `.icons` and `.login-button` still use `float: left` (lines 43, 54) — floats are ignored on flex items, so the login buttons and icons will no longer float left as intended and will instead participate in flex layout in DOM order, likely stacking incorrectly or overlapping. The `.title` selector itself was removed from the stylesheet entirely (the diff deletes the `.title { float: left; }` block), so any remaining `.title` styling is lost. This is a visual regression that breaks the header layout across all browsers.

title: `@include order(2)` applied to `.extra-info-wrapper` without a flex container parent — order property has no effect and may cause layout regression
body: The diff adds `@include order(2)` to `.extra-info-wrapper` (line 30), but the `order` CSS property only applies to flex items or grid items. There is no `@include flexbox()` applied to any ancestor of `.extra-info-wrapper` in this file or in the provided diff — its parent (`#topic-title` or the topic header container) is not converted to a flex container. Without a flex/grid parent, `order: 2` (and all its prefixed variants emitted by the mixin) is completely ignored by browsers. Meanwhile, the diff removes the `&.bullet { margin-top: 5px; }` rule from `.badge-wrapper` inside `.extra-info-wrapper` (lines 33-35), which was providing vertical spacing for bullet-style category badges. The net effect is that the intended reordering does nothing, and the removed margin-top causes bullet badges in the extra-info area to lose their top spacing, misaligning them vertically with adjacent content. The change is both ineffective (order without flex parent) and harmful (removed margin).

title: Flexbox added to .small-action but child floats not cleared — mixed float/flex layout causes misalignment
body: The diff adds `@include flexbox()` and `@include align-items(center)` to `.small-action` (lines 264-265), making it a flex container. However, its children still use `float: left`: `.topic-avatar` has `float: left` (line 270), `.small-action-desc .avatar` has `float: left` (line 298), and the `button` has `float: right` (line 309). In a flex container, `float` is ignored on flex items — the computed value of `float` becomes `none` for flex items per the CSS Flexbox spec. This means: (1) the `float: right` on the button no longer pushes it to the right edge; it becomes a flex item placed in DOM order, likely appearing to the left of where it should be; (2) the `float: left` on avatars is neutralized, which may be fine for layout but changes the intended wrapping behavior; (3) the trailing `clear: both` (line 312) on `.small-action` itself is meaningless on a flex container. Additionally, the diff changes `.small-action-desc` padding from `0.5em 0 0.5em 4em` (which reserved space for the floated avatar) to `0 1.5%`, and removes `padding-top: 4px` from `> p` — these spacing changes were tuned for the old float-based layout and will produce incorrect spacing now that the avatar is a flex item without its reserved left padding. The `.custom-message p` margin change from `5px 0` to `0` (line 292) further removes vertical spacing that was compensating for the old layout.

title: `order` mixin emits invalid prefixed properties: `-ms-flex-order` and `-webkit-order` are not valid CSS
body: The `order` mixin (lines 125-131) emits five properties: `-webkit-box-ordinal-group`, `-moz-box-ordinal-group`, `-ms-flex-order`, `-webkit-order`, and `order`. Two of these are invalid: (1) `-ms-flex-order` — the correct IE10 flexbox property is `-ms-flex-order` only in the context of the old 2009/2012 IE flexbox implementation, but the standard IE10 property for the 2012 spec is `-ms-flex-order` is actually correct for IE10... however, `-webkit-order` (line 129) is NOT a valid property — WebKit never shipped a prefixed `order` property; Safari supported unprefixed `order` from the start of its flexbox implementation (Safari 6.1+/7 with `-webkit-flex`). Similarly, `-moz-box-ordinal-group` is for the old 2009 Firefox flexbox (`display: -moz-box`), which is fine as a fallback, but `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` correctly maps to old WebKit flexbox. The real issue: `-webkit-order` is invalid and will be dropped by browsers, and more importantly, `-ms-flex-order` expects an integer but the mixin passes `$val` directly — for the header use case `@include order(3)`, IE10's `-ms-flex-order` uses 1-based ordinal groups where the default is 0, so `order(3)` in IE10 would place the panel after items with default order 0, which may not match the intended visual order of 1,2,3 in modern browsers. The mixin also lacks `-ms-flex-item-align` or other IE10-specific corrections. Invalid properties in the output CSS increase stylesheet size and can confuse CSS validators/linters; the IE10 ordinal mismatch can cause the header panel to appear in the wrong position in IE10.

title: `align-items` mixin emits both `-ms-flex-align` and `-ms-align-items` — `-ms-align-items` is invalid
body: The `align-items` mixin (lines 117-123) emits `-ms-flex-align` (correct for IE10) and `-ms-align-items` (line 121). The property `-ms-align-items` is not a valid CSS property — IE10 only supports `-ms-flex-align` for the 2012 flexbox spec; there is no `-ms-align-items` prefixed property. This invalid property will be ignored by browsers, adding dead weight to the compiled CSS. It should be removed. Additionally, the mixin emits `-webkit-box-align` (for old 2009 flexbox) which expects different keyword values (e.g., `start`, `end`, `center`, `baseline`, `stretch`) — passing `center` works for both old and new specs, but `baseline` in old Webkit flexbox has different behavior; however, since the only usage in this PR is `align-items(center)` and `align-items(baseline)`, the `baseline` value in `-webkit-box-align` (line 118) may render differently in old Safari (6.0) versus modern browsers, potentially causing vertical misalignment of bullet badges in `badges.css.scss` line 57.

title: `@include order(3)` on `.panel` assumes sibling order values 1 and 2 exist, but no other flex items have explicit order — visual order may not match DOM order intent
body: The diff adds `@include order(3)` to `.panel` (line 39) and relies on `margin-left: auto` to push it right. In flexbox, `order` changes the visual ordering of flex items. The default `order` value is 0 for all flex items. By setting `.panel` to `order: 3`, it will be placed after all items with `order: 0` (the default) — which includes `.title`, `.icons`, `.login-button`, etc. — regardless of their DOM position. This means `.panel` will always render last among the flex items, which may be the intent (pushing the user panel to the right). However, combined with `margin-left: auto`, the behavior is redundant and potentially conflicting: `margin-left: auto` on a flex item absorbs free space and pushes the item (and subsequent items) to the right, but `order: 3` already places it last. If there are other flex items after `.panel` in the DOM with default `order: 0`, they would appear BEFORE `.panel` visually despite being after it in the DOM — this is an accessibility concern (visual order ≠ DOM order, confusing screen reader users) and may cause unexpected layout if the header DOM structure changes. The `order` property should be used sparingly; using `margin-left: auto` alone would achieve the right-alignment without reordering.

title: Replacing raw `display: inline-flex` with `@include inline-flex()` adds old-spec fallbacks that change rendering in legacy browsers
body: The diff replaces `display: inline-flex; align-items: baseline;` (raw modern CSS) with `@include inline-flex()` and `@include align-items(baseline)` (lines 55-57). The `inline-flex()` mixin (mixins.scss lines 108-114) emits `display: -webkit-inline-box; display: -webkit-inline-flex; display: -moz-inline-box; display: -ms-inline-flexbox; display: inline-flex;`. The old-spec fallbacks `-webkit-inline-box` and `-moz-inline-box` use the 2009 flexbox model, which has different sizing and alignment behavior than modern flexbox. In old Safari (6.0) and old Firefox (pre-22), the badge wrapper will render using the 2009 box model, where `align-items: baseline` (via `-webkit-box-align: baseline`) behaves differently — specifically, baseline alignment in old flexbox aligns to the first line of text, which may cause the bullet badge's colored dot and category text to misalign vertically compared to modern browsers. Since the original code used unprefixed `inline-flex` (which old browsers simply ignore, falling back to the `display: inline-block` from `.badge-wrapper` line 22), the visual result in old browsers was a simple inline-block badge. The mixin change makes old browsers attempt flexbox layout with the old spec, potentially introducing visual bugs in legacy browsers that were previously rendering correctly with inline-block fallback.

title: inline-flex mixin emits invalid -moz-inline-box and missing standard fallback ordering
body: The `inline-flex()` mixin outputs `display: -moz-inline-box` (line 111), which is not a valid value for the `display` property in Firefox's old flexbox implementation (Firefox only supported `-moz-box`, never `-moz-inline-box`), so that declaration is dropped. More importantly, the mixin places the prefixed values before the standard `inline-flex` (line 113), which is correct, but it omits `display: -webkit-inline-flex` ordering issues aside, the real problem is that `-moz-inline-box` is invalid CSS that will be ignored, and older Firefox versions that only support `-moz-box` will fall back to `display: block`-like behavior for `.badge-wrapper.bullet` elements, breaking the intended inline-flex layout in those browsers. The invalid `-moz-inline-box` declaration should be removed or replaced with `-moz-inline-flex` (which Firefox never supported either, so the mixin should just use `-webkit-inline-box`, `-ms-inline-flexbox`, and `inline-flex`).

title: order mixin uses -moz-box-ordinal-group which is incompatible with flexbox order semantics
body: The `order()` mixin (lines 125-131) emits `-moz-box-ordinal-group: $val` (line 127). The old Firefox flexbox implementation (`-moz-box`) uses `-moz-box-ordinal-group` with 1-based integer values, while the standard `order` property (and `-webkit-order`, `-ms-flex-order`) uses 0-based integers. Passing the same `$val` (e.g., `3` from header.scss line 39, `2` from topic.scss line 30) to both properties means Firefox's old flexbox will interpret the value differently (off-by-one), causing `.panel` and `.extra-info-wrapper` to appear in the wrong visual order in old Firefox versions. The mixin should either not emit `-moz-box-ordinal-group` at all (since `-moz-box` is ancient and rarely targeted), or adjust the value for that property (e.g., `$val + 1`).

title: Header layout breaks because .panel uses margin-left:auto with order(3) but .title was removed without replacement flex item
body: The diff removes the `.title { float: left; }` rule entirely (lines 16-18 of the diff) and adds `@include flexbox()` + `@include align-items(center)` to `.contents`, but there is no remaining flex item to push `.panel` to the right via `margin-left: auto`. The `.panel` rule (lines 35-40) now has `margin-left: auto` and `@include order(3)`, expecting other flex items (like a `.title` element) to exist as siblings. However, the `.title` selector was deleted from the SCSS, meaning the HTML element with class `title` (the site title/logo area) is no longer styled as a flex item and, more critically, the `margin-left: auto` on `.panel` only works if there are other flex items taking up space. Without the `.title` being a flex item (or any other left-side content), the header layout will collapse or misalign: the logo/title area will not be pushed left, and `.panel` will not be pushed right as intended. The `.title` rule removal appears to be an accidental deletion rather than intentional—the original code had `.title { float: left; }` to position the title, and the flexbox conversion should have kept equivalent styling (e.g., making `.title` a flex item with appropriate flex properties) rather than deleting it entirely.

title: Login/signup buttons and icons still use float:left inside flex container, causing layout breakage
body: The `.contents` element is now a flex container (line 17: `@include flexbox()`), but its children `.login-button, button.sign-up-button` (lines 42-47) and `.icons` (lines 53-61) still use `float: left`. In a flex container, `float` is ignored on flex items—floated children become flex items and their float property has no effect. This means the login/signup buttons and the icon list will no longer float left as intended; instead they will be laid out as flex items in DOM order, potentially breaking the header layout. The `float: left` declarations on these elements are now dead code and the visual layout will differ from the pre-flexbox version. These elements need to be converted to proper flex item styling (e.g., using `margin-right: auto` or flex `order` properties) or the flex container approach needs to account for them.

title: small-action flex container conflicts with floated children and button float:right
body: The `.small-action` element is now a flex container (lines 264-265: `@include flexbox()` + `@include align-items(center)`), but its children `.topic-avatar` (line 270: `float: left`), `.small-action-desc .avatar` (line 298: `float: left`), and `button` (line 309: `float: right`) all use `float`. As with the header issue, `float` is ignored on flex items, so these floats have no effect. The `button { float: right; }` (line 309) was intended to push the button to the right side of the small-action bar, but in a flex container this will not work—the button will appear in DOM order (after `.small-action-desc`) rather than being pushed right. The layout of small-action posts (like "X moved this topic" or "X closed this topic") will be broken, with the action button appearing in the wrong position. The flex conversion needs to use `margin-left: auto` on the button or `order` properties instead of relying on floats.

title: order(2) applied to .extra-info-wrapper without a flex container parent
body: The `.extra-info-wrapper` element has `@include order(2)` (line 30), but the `order` property only has an effect on flex items (children of a flex container). Looking at the surrounding code, `.extra-info-wrapper` appears to be a sibling of `#topic-title` (which contains `.title-wrapper` with `float: left`), and there is no parent element with `display: flex` that contains `.extra-info-wrapper` as a direct child. The `#topic-title` element itself is not a flex container in this file. Without a flex container parent, `order: 2` is completely ignored, and the intended reordering (presumably to place the extra info/badges after the title) will not happen. This is either a missing flex container on the parent (e.g., `#topic-title` should have `@include flexbox()`) or the `order` property is being applied to the wrong element. The layout intent is broken.

title: Removal of .badge-wrapper.bullet margin-top breaks vertical alignment in extra-info-wrapper
body: The diff removes the `&.bullet { margin-top: 5px; }` rule from `.extra-info-wrapper .badge-wrapper` (lines 33-35 of the new file, removed in the diff). This margin was providing vertical spacing/alignment for bullet-style category badges within the extra-info area. Without it, bullet badges in the topic extra-info wrapper will sit flush against the top of their container, potentially misaligning with the topic title text. The flexbox conversion of the parent (if it were a flex container) might handle alignment via `align-items`, but since the parent is not actually a flex container (see separate finding about `order(2)`), this margin removal causes a visible regression in badge positioning.

title: flexbox mixin missing -moz-flex standard unprefixed old syntax and -ms-flexbox needs display: -ms-flexbox
body: The `flexbox()` mixin (lines 100-106) emits `display: -moz-box` (line 102) for old Firefox, but Firefox's old flexbox implementation also supported `display: -moz-flex` as an intermediate unprefixed-ish value before the standard `flex`. More critically, the mixin does not include `display: -ms-flexbox` correctly—it does include it on line 103, but the ordering places `-ms-flexbox` before `-webkit-flex` and `flex`, which is fine. However, the mixin is missing `display: -moz-flex` which was supported in Firefox 18-20 as a transitional value. This is a minor compatibility gap for very old Firefox versions. Additionally, the `-ms-flexbox` value is for IE10, which uses the 2009 flexbox spec with different property names (e.g., `-ms-flex` instead of flex properties), so the `align-items` and `order` mixins' `-ms-flex-align` and `-ms-flex-order` properties may not work correctly with IE10's implementation.

title: Padding change from em-based to percentage-based may cause inconsistent spacing
body: The `.small-action-desc` padding was changed from `padding: 0.5em 0 0.5em 4em` (which provided 0.5em top/bottom and 4em left padding to clear the floated avatar) to `padding: 0 1.5%` (line 280). The percentage-based horizontal padding (`1.5%`) is relative to the width of the containing block, not the element itself, which can produce very different spacing depending on container width. The original `4em` left padding was specifically designed to clear the 45px-wide floated avatar (`.topic-avatar` with `width: 45px` on the `i` element, plus `padding: 5px 0`). With `padding: 0 1.5%`, on narrow containers the left padding may be insufficient to clear the avatar, causing text to overlap or wrap incorrectly under the avatar. The avatar is still floated (line 270: `float: left`), so the text needs adequate left padding to avoid overlapping it.

title: inline-flex mixin emits invalid -moz-inline-box value
body: The `inline-flex()` mixin (lines 108-114) outputs `display: -moz-inline-box`, which is not a valid CSS value. Firefox's old flexbox implementation only supported `display: -moz-box` (block-level), not an inline variant. This invalid declaration is simply dropped by browsers, but it indicates the mixin was written incorrectly and provides no Firefox fallback for inline-flex. The correct old-Firefox value would be `-moz-inline-box` only if it existed (it doesn't); the practical fix is to remove the invalid line or use `-moz-box` with `display: table` workarounds. As written, Firefox users on old versions get no flexbox behavior for `.badge-wrapper.bullet` elements that use this mixin.

title: order mixin emits invalid -moz-box-ordinal-group value
body: The `order()` mixin (lines 125-131) outputs `-moz-box-ordinal-group: $val` where `$val` is passed as `3` or `2` from callers. The old Firefox flexbox specification (`-moz-box`) uses `-moz-box-ordinal-group` with **integer** values starting at 1, which is correct, but the mixin also emits `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` and `-moz-box-ordinal-group` with the same value. However, the real problem is that `-ms-flex-order` expects an **integer** but the mixin passes the raw value through; more critically, the old `box-ordinal-group` property in WebKit/Gecko expects values starting from 1, and passing `3` without ensuring other flex items have explicit orders (defaulting to 0 in some implementations) can cause inconsistent ordering across browsers. The header layout relies on `@include order(3)` for `.panel` (header.scss line 39) and `@include order(2)` for `.extra-info-wrapper` (topic.scss line 30), but without explicit orders on sibling elements, the visual order may differ between browsers that support different flexbox specification drafts.

title: Header layout breaks: floated children inside flex container lose float behavior
body: The `.contents` element is now a flex container (lines 17-18: `@include flexbox(); @include align-items(center);`), but its children `.login-button, button.sign-up-button` (line 42-47) and `.icons` (line 53-61) still use `float: left`. In a flex container, `float` has no effect on flex items — the items become flex items and floats are ignored. This means the login/signup buttons and the icon list will no longer float left as intended; instead they will be laid out as flex items in DOM order, potentially breaking the header layout. The `.panel` element uses `margin-left: auto` (line 37) which works in flexbox to push it right, but the floated elements that were supposed to appear on the left side of the header will now participate in flex layout without their float positioning, likely causing them to appear in unexpected positions or stack incorrectly. The `float: left` declarations on lines 43 and 54 are now dead code that misleads about the actual layout behavior.

title: Dead .valign-helper CSS remains after switching to flexbox alignment
body: The `.valign-helper` class (lines 21-25) uses the old inline-block vertical alignment hack (`display: inline-block; height: 100%; vertical-align: middle;`). Since `.contents` now uses `@include flexbox()` with `@include align-items(center)` (lines 17-18), this helper element is no longer needed for vertical centering — flexbox handles alignment natively. If any HTML still contains `.valign-helper` elements, they will now become flex items and may introduce unwanted spacing or layout artifacts. The CSS should be removed, and any corresponding HTML elements should be cleaned up. Leaving this dead CSS creates confusion and potential layout bugs if the element is still present in templates.

title: Flexbox on .small-action breaks internal float-based layout of children
body: `.small-action` is now a flex container (lines 264-265: `@include flexbox(); @include align-items(center);`), but its children `.topic-avatar` (line 267-277) uses `float: left` (line 270), `.small-action-desc .avatar` uses `float: left` (line 298), and `button` uses `float: right` (line 309). In a flex container, floats on flex items are ignored — these elements become flex items and their float declarations have no effect. The `.topic-avatar` was floated left to position the avatar, `.avatar` inside `.small-action-desc` was floated left to wrap text, and the `button` was floated right to push it to the end. With flexbox, these floats are ignored, so: (1) the avatar may not align properly with the description text, (2) the button will not be pushed to the right edge (flex items default to start alignment unless `margin-left: auto` or `justify-content` is used), and (3) the text wrapping around the floated avatar inside `.small-action-desc` will break because the avatar is no longer floated within that block. The `clear: both` on line 312 is also meaningless in a flex container. This will visibly break the small action post layout (e.g., "X closed this topic" messages).

title: Padding change on .small-action-desc removes left offset for avatar, breaking alignment
body: The `.small-action-desc` padding was changed from `padding: 0.5em 0 0.5em 4em` (which provided a 4em left padding to clear the floated avatar) to `padding: 0 1.5%` (line 280). The old 4em left padding was specifically designed to make room for the `.topic-avatar` which is 45px wide plus padding. With the new `1.5%` horizontal padding, the description text will overlap with the avatar image because there is no longer sufficient left padding to clear the avatar. Even if the avatar were properly positioned (which it isn't, due to the flexbox/float conflict noted separately), the text would not have the intended spacing from the avatar. The `margin-top: 5px` removal (line 281) also changes vertical rhythm. This change assumes flexbox will handle spacing between items, but without `margin` or `padding` on the avatar or gap properties (which aren't in the mixins), the text will collide with the avatar.

title: @include order(2) on .extra-info-wrapper has no effect without a flex container parent
body: The `.extra-info-wrapper` element has `@include order(2)` applied (line 30), but the `order` property only works on flex items — i.e., direct children of a flex container. There is no evidence in the changed files that the parent of `.extra-info-wrapper` is a flex container. The `#topic-title` element (lines 1-23) uses `float: left` on `.title-wrapper` (line 4) and does not have `@include flexbox()`. Without a flex container parent, `order: 2` is completely ignored, and the element will render in its normal DOM order. If the intent was to reorder elements within `#topic-title` using flexbox, the parent `#topic-title` or its wrapper needs `@include flexbox()` first. As written, this change is a no-op and the intended reordering (if any) will not happen.

title: Removal of .badge-wrapper.bullet margin-top breaks vertical alignment in extra-info-wrapper
body: The `.extra-info-wrapper .badge-wrapper.bullet` previously had `margin-top: 5px` (removed in the diff) to vertically align the bullet badge with surrounding text. This margin was specifically targeting the bullet style within the extra-info context. With the margin removed and no replacement vertical alignment mechanism (the parent is not a flex container as noted in the order(2) finding), the bullet badge will sit higher than intended, misaligned with the topic title text. The `line-height: 1.5` on line 32 applies to the wrapper but does not compensate for the missing top margin on the inline-flex badge element. This will cause visual misalignment of category badges in the topic header extra info area.

title: inline-flex mixin on .badge-wrapper.bullet may cause inconsistent baseline alignment across browsers
body: The `.badge-wrapper.bullet` now uses `@include inline-flex()` with `@include align-items(baseline)` (lines 55-57). The `align-items: baseline` in flexbox aligns items based on their first baseline, but the children include `.badge-category-parent-bg` and `.badge-category-bg` which are empty inline-block elements with `content: "\a0"` (a non-breaking space). The baseline of an empty inline-block with only a non-breaking space may be inconsistent across browsers — some may use the bottom margin edge as the baseline. Combined with the invalid `-moz-inline-box` in the mixin (noted separately), Firefox may fall back to different behavior. The previous implementation used `display: inline-flex; align-items: baseline;` directly, which had the same cross-browser concerns but at least didn't emit invalid CSS. The mixin conversion doesn't fix any browser compatibility issue and may introduce new ones due to the invalid vendor prefix.

title: include_website_name is not a predicate method, so the attribute is always serialized
body: The method is named `include_website_name` (without a trailing `?`), but ActiveModel::Serializers only calls `include_<attr>?` predicate methods to decide whether to include an attribute. Because no `include_website_name?` method exists, the serializer falls back to always including `website_name`. This means `website_name` is serialized even when `website` is blank/nil, producing a JSON payload with `website_name: null` for every user with no website. The guard `website.present?` inside the method is dead code in this context. The method should be renamed to `include_website_name?` (matching the pattern used by `include_email?`, `include_stats?`, etc. in the same file).

title: website_name logic is incorrect for subdomain relationships and can produce wrong display text
body: The `website_name` method attempts to show the full path when the website host matches the instance host, but the branching logic is flawed. In the `elsif` branch (line 144), it compares `website_host.split('.')[1..-1].join('.')` with `discourse_host.split('.')[1..-1].join('.')` — this strips the first label from both hosts and compares the remainders. For `website_host = 'forums.example.com'` and `discourse_host = 'example.com'`, the lengths differ (3 vs 2) so this branch is skipped, but for `website_host = 'a.b.example.com'` and `discourse_host = 'c.b.example.com'` (both length 4), it would incorrectly treat them as the same site. More importantly, the final `else` branch (line 149) checks `discourse_host.ends_with?('.' + website_host)`, which correctly handles `forums.example.com` ending with `.example.com`, but the middle branch's length-equality requirement means cases like `website_host = 'www.example.com'` (3 labels) vs `discourse_host = 'example.com'` (2 labels) fall through to the else branch and are handled correctly only by accident. The logic is convoluted and the comment on line 148 ('example.com == forum.example.com') describes the else branch but the condition actually tests the reverse (instance is subdomain of website). Consider simplifying to a single check: show the path when `website_host == discourse_host || discourse_host.ends_with?('.' + website_host)`.

title: URI(website.to_s) is parsed multiple times in website_name
body: The `website_name` method calls `URI(website.to_s)` three separate times (lines 138, 143, 146, 149) to extract the host and path. Each call re-parses the URL string. This is wasteful — the parsed URI object should be computed once and reused. While the performance impact is negligible for a single serialization, it's called for every user in list views (e.g., user directory, admin user list), so the redundant parsing adds up. Extract `uri = URI(website.to_s) rescue nil` once at the top and use `uri.host` and `uri.path` throughout.

title: Website link uses unescaped href attribute that could allow javascript: URLs
body: The template renders `<a href={{model.website}} ...>` where `model.website` comes directly from user profile data (user-controlled input). While the server-side `website` field is presumably validated on save, the serializer returns the raw `user_profile.website` value without any scheme validation. If a user can set their website to `javascript:alert(1)` (depending on server-side validation in the user profile update path, which is not shown in this PR), clicking the link would execute arbitrary JavaScript in the context of the Discourse site. The `website_name` display text is safely derived from the host, but the `href` uses the raw URL. The server should enforce http/https scheme on the website field, or the serializer should sanitize it. At minimum, this is a defense-in-depth concern — the href should be validated to start with `http://` or `https://`.

title: Untrusted attributes test does not include website_name, so the TL0/anonymous privacy leak is not caught
body: The test on line 11 defines `untrusted_attributes` as `%i{bio_raw bio_cooked bio_excerpt location website profile_background card_background}` but does NOT include `:website_name`. Since `website_name` was added to the `untrusted_attributes` list in the serializer (line 109 of user_serializer.rb), it should be included in this test to verify that TL0 users' website names are hidden from anonymous viewers. Without this, the test passes even if the `untrusted_attributes` mechanism is broken for `website_name`, and a privacy regression (leaking a TL0 user's website path to anonymous users) would go undetected. Additionally, because `include_website_name` is not a proper predicate (see separate finding), the attribute may be serialized even when `website` is blank, which this test also fails to catch.

title: No test for website_name when website is blank or nil
body: The spec only tests `website_name` when a website is filled out (line 67+). There is no test verifying that `website_name` is absent (or null) when `user_profile.website` is blank. Given the `include_website_name` predicate bug (it's not a real predicate), this case is important to test — it would catch the bug where `website_name` is always serialized even for users with no website. A test like `expect(json).not_to have_key(:website_name)` when website is nil would be appropriate.

title: JSDoc comment for profileBackground was incorrectly changed from websiteName
body: The diff changed the JSDoc `@property` annotation from `websiteName` to `profileBackground` on the `profileBackground` computed property. This appears to be an accidental edit — the original `@property websiteName` was already wrong (it should have been `profileBackground` for this method), but the change in this PR is unrelated to the website_name feature. While the fix is technically correct (the doc now matches the method name), it's an unrelated change bundled into this PR. More importantly, the original code had a `websiteName` computed property in the controller (removed in this PR) that had no JSDoc, and this model file never had a `websiteName` property — so the original `@property websiteName` on `profileBackground` was a pre-existing copy-paste error. The fix is correct but should have been a separate commit/PR.

title: include_website_name is not a predicate method, so the attribute is always serialized
body: The method is defined as `def include_website_name` (no trailing `?`), but ActiveModel::Serializers only calls `include_<attr>?` predicate methods to decide whether to include an attribute. Because no `include_website_name?` method exists, the serializer falls back to always including `website_name`. This means `website_name` is serialized even when `website` is blank/nil, and — more importantly — it bypasses the `untrusted_attributes` guard: for a TL0 user viewed anonymously, `website` is correctly omitted (the spec at line 11-15 asserts `website` is not in the JSON), but `website_name` will still be present in the JSON, leaking the user's website host/path to anonymous viewers. The `untrusted_attributes :website` declaration at line 109 is therefore ineffective for the derived `website_name` value. Fix: rename the method to `def include_website_name?` (with the question mark), which will both make the conditional work and make the `untrusted_attributes` mechanism apply correctly (it defines `include_website_name?` returning false when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)`).

title: Subdomain-sibling comparison is wrong: it compares only the second label, not the registrable domain
body: The branch handling hosts with the same number of labels (e.g. `www.example.com` vs `forum.example.com`) compares `website_host.split('.')[1..-1].join('.')` with `discourse_host.split('.')[1..-1].join('.')`. For `a.b.example.com` vs `c.d.example.com` (both 4 labels), this compares `b.example.com` vs `d.example.com` and would incorrectly conclude the domains differ even though both are subdomains of `example.com`. Conversely, for `foo.co.uk` vs `bar.co.uk` (both 3 labels, public suffix `co.uk`), it compares `co.uk` == `co.uk` and treats them as the same site, wrongly showing the full path for an unrelated domain. The intent (per the comment 'www.example.com == forum.example.com') is to detect sibling subdomains of a common parent, but the implementation neither strips to the registrable domain nor handles multi-part public suffixes. Consequence: `website_name` shows the full URL path for unrelated domains that happen to share a second-level label (privacy/display bug), and fails to show the path for legitimate sibling subdomains with deeper nesting. A correct implementation needs a public-suffix-aware comparison (e.g. using the `public_suffix` gem if available in Discourse) or a simpler, well-defined rule.

title: Parent-domain check uses ends_with? on a string, which matches unrelated suffixes
body: The final branch checks `discourse_host.ends_with?("." << website_host)`.
