body: The `translate` method (line 67-77) does `load_locale(config.locale) unless @loaded_locales.include?(config.locale)`. If `@loaded_locales` has never been initialized (i.e., this is the first call to `translate` in the process and `ensure_loaded!` was not called first), `@loaded_locales` is nil, and calling `.include?` on nil raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'include?' for nil:NilClass`. The `ensure_loaded!` method added in this PR does `@loaded_locales ||= []` before the check, but `translate` does not. In the normal request flow, `ApplicationController#set_locale` calls `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` which calls `I18n.ensure_loaded!` which initializes `@loaded_locales`, so by the time `translate` is called, `@loaded_locales` is set. However, there are many code paths where `I18n.translate` is called outside of a request cycle: background jobs, rake tasks, initializers, mailers, and model callbacks. Any of these that call `I18n.t` before the first web request will crash with NoMethodError. The `translate` method should also guard with `@loaded_locales ||= []` or use the same pattern as `ensure_loaded!`.

title: I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! called on every request, causing repeated fallback chain computation and DB lookups
body: `set_locale` is a `before_filter` that runs on every request. Line 159 calls `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!`, which invokes `FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded!`. This method calls `self[I18n.locale]` which computes `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact`. `SiteSetting.default_locale` is a site setting that may hit the database or a cache on every call. Then for each locale in the resulting array, it calls `I18n.ensure_loaded! l`, which checks `@loaded_locales.include?(locale)` and potentially calls `load_locale`. While `load_locale` is idempotent (returns early if already loaded), the `ensure_loaded!` call still iterates over the fallback chain and performs the `SiteSetting.default_locale` lookup on every single request. This is unnecessary overhead: once a locale is loaded, it stays loaded for the process lifetime (until `reload!`). The `ensure_loaded!` call should be moved to a place where it runs once per locale change, or the `FallbackLocaleList` should cache the computed fallback chain per locale, or `set_locale` should only call `ensure_loaded!` when the locale actually changes.

title: Pluralization module included into I18n::Backend::Simple instead of I18n.backend, inconsistent with Fallbacks inclusion pattern
body: Line 5 does `I18n::Backend::Simple.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Pluralization)` while line 9 does `I18n.backend.class.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks)`. These are inconsistent: one includes into the class directly, the other into the instance's class. If `I18n.backend` is not an instance of `I18n::Backend::Simple` (e.g., if Rails or another gem has wrapped it), the Pluralization module will be included into `Simple` but the Fallbacks module will be included into whatever class `I18n.backend` actually is. This means Pluralization might not be active on the actual backend instance. The correct approach is to include both modules into `I18n.backend.class` (or better, into `I18n::Backend::Base` so all backends get them), or use `I18n::Backend::Simple.include(...)` consistently for both. The previous `config/initializers/pluralization.rb` (removed in this PR) used `I18n::Backend::Simple.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Pluralization)`, so the behavior for Pluralization is preserved, but the inconsistency with Fallbacks is a code smell that could cause subtle bugs if the backend class changes.

title: Comment 'order: after 02-freedom_patches.rb' is not a recognized Rails initializer directive and may not enforce load order
body: The first line of the initializer is `# order: after 02-freedom_patches.rb`. Rails initializers in `config/initializers/` are loaded in alphabetical order by default. There is no built-in Rails mechanism that reads an `# order:` comment to control load order. If the intent is to ensure this initializer runs after `02-freedom_patches.rb` (which likely loads the translate_accelerator patch), the file should be named with a prefix that sorts after it (e.g., `03-i18n.rb` or similar), or the dependency should be handled explicitly. Since the file is named `i18n.rb`, it will load after `02-freedom_patches.rb` alphabetically (digits sort before letters in ASCII), so the order is accidentally correct, but the comment is misleading and suggests a non-existent feature. If someone renames the file or the freedom patches file, the load order could break silently, causing `I18n.backend.class.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks)` to run before the translate_accelerator patch has reopened `I18n::Backend::Simple`, potentially leading to method resolution issues.

title: Fallbacks module included into wrong backend class, breaking I18n fallback behavior
body: The initializer does `I18n.backend.class.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks)`. At initializer time, `I18n.backend` is an instance of `I18n::Backend::Simple` (the default backend), so this includes Fallbacks into `I18n::Backend::Simple` itself. However, the translate_accelerator freedom patch reopens `I18n::Backend::Simple` and the app's actual translation path goes through the patched `I18n.translate` which calls `translate_no_cache` (the original `I18n.translate`). The Fallbacks module works by overriding `translate` on the backend to walk the fallback chain; including it into the backend class does not make `I18n::Backend::Simple#translate` perform fallback lookups unless the backend's `translate` is the Fallbacks-aware one. More importantly, `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` must be included into the backend *instance's* class and it expects `I18n.fallbacks` to respond to `[](locale)` returning an array — which `FallbackLocaleList` does — but the standard, supported way is `I18n::Backend::Simple.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks)` combined with `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` (which the PR removes from all environment configs). Because the PR deletes `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` from production.rb, profile.rb, and cloud66 production.rb, Rails will not enable the fallbacks machinery, and the custom `ensure_loaded!` in `FallbackLocaleList` (called from `ApplicationController#set_locale` via `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!`) preloads locale files, but the actual translation lookup will not fall back — missing translations in the user's locale will return 'translation missing' strings instead of falling back to the site default locale or English. The consequence: users with partially-translated locales see raw 'translation missing: xx.key' messages in the UI. The fix is to keep `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` in the environment configs (or set `I18n::Backend::Simple.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks)` and ensure the fallbacks config flag is set), and include Fallbacks into `I18n::Backend::Simple` (the class), not `I18n.backend.class` (which is fragile and equivalent only by accident at boot).

title: FallbackLocaleList#[] can return nil elements and does not guard against nil locale, causing NoMethodError or broken fallback chains
body: `FallbackLocaleList#[]` builds `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact`. If `locale` is nil (e.g., `I18n.locale` is nil in some code path before `set_locale` runs, such as background jobs, mailers, or initializers that call `I18n.t` before any request), the array becomes `[nil, :en_default, :en].uniq.compact` — compact removes nil so it is safe there — but `SiteSetting.default_locale` may itself be nil or blank during early boot or in test environments before the settings table is seeded, and calling `.to_sym` on nil raises `NoMethodError`. Additionally, `FallbackLocaleList` subclasses `Hash` but never populates itself; `I18n.fallbacks = FallbackLocaleList.new` relies entirely on the overridden `[]`, which is fine, but `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` internally may call other Hash methods (e.g., `key?`, `fetch`, `each`) that will behave incorrectly on an empty Hash subclass. The consequence: a `NoMethodError` on nil during boot or in edge cases, or fallbacks silently not working because the Fallbacks module iterates the hash rather than calling `[]`. The class should not subclass Hash; it should be a plain object responding to `[]`, and `SiteSetting.default_locale` should be guarded (e.g., `SiteSetting.default_locale.to_s.to_sym` with a fallback to `:en`).

title: New ensure_loaded! method has a race condition: check-then-act on @loaded_locales without holding LOAD_MUTEX
body: The added `I18n.ensure_loaded!(locale)` method does `@loaded_locales ||= []` then `load_locale locale unless @loaded_locales.include?(locale)`. The `include?` check and the subsequent `load_locale` call are not atomic. `load_locale` itself acquires `LOAD_MUTEX`, but the `unless @loaded_locales.include?(locale)` guard is evaluated outside the mutex. In a multi-threaded server (Puma/Unicorn with threads), two threads can both observe that the locale is not loaded and both call `load_locale`. Inside `load_locale`, the mutex serializes them, and the second thread will see `@loaded_locales.include?(locale)` is true after acquiring the mutex and return early — so the actual file loading is protected. However, the `@loaded_locales ||= []` initialization is itself racy: if `@loaded_locales` is nil and two threads call `ensure_loaded!` concurrently, both may assign a new array, and one thread's `<<` in `load_locale` could be lost, causing a locale to be considered unloaded and re-loaded repeatedly, or worse, the array reference seen by `translate` (line 68: `load_locale(config.locale) unless @loaded_locales.include?(config.locale)`) may be a stale array missing entries. The consequence: duplicate translation file loading (performance degradation) and potential `nil` errors if `@loaded_locales` is read as nil in `translate` before assignment completes. The fix: initialize `@loaded_locales = []` at class load time (e.g., in the module body or via `reload!`), and make `ensure_loaded!` delegate entirely to `load_locale` (which already handles the mutex and the include? check internally), i.e., just `def ensure_loaded!(locale); load_locale(locale); end`.

title: translate method reads @loaded_locales without nil guard and without mutex, inconsistent with ensure_loaded!
body: `I18n.translate` (line 67-68) does `load_locale(config.locale) unless @loaded_locales.include?(config.locale)`. If `translate` is called before `ensure_loaded!` or `reload!` has ever run, `@loaded_locales` is nil and `nil.include?` raises `NoMethodError`. The original code had the same latent issue but it was masked because `load_locale` was only called from `translate` itself after `@loaded_locales` was initialized elsewhere; the new `ensure_loaded!` method initializes `@loaded_locales` lazily with `||=`, but `translate` does not. In a fresh process where the first I18n call is `I18n.t` (e.g., from an initializer or rake task before any request triggers `set_locale`), this will crash. The consequence: `NoMethodError: undefined method 'include?' for nil:NilClass` on first translation lookup in a fresh process. The fix: add `@loaded_locales ||= []` at the start of `translate`, or better, initialize `@loaded_locales = []` as a class-level constant default and reset it in `reload!`.

title: I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! called on every request in set_locale before_filter, causing repeated work
body: `set_locale` is a `before_filter` that runs on every request. The added line `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` calls `FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded!`, which iterates `self[I18n.locale]` (up to 3 locales) and calls `I18n.ensure_loaded! l` for each. `I18n.ensure_loaded!` (the new method in translate_accelerator.rb) checks `@loaded_locales.include?(locale)` and calls `load_locale` if not loaded. `load_locale` acquires `LOAD_MUTEX` on every call, even when the locale is already loaded (the `return if @loaded_locales.include?(locale)` check is inside the mutex). So every request acquires a global mutex up to 3 times (once per fallback locale), serializing all requests across all threads for the duration of the check. Under high concurrency, this becomes a significant bottleneck. The consequence: unnecessary mutex contention on every request, reducing throughput. The fix: check `@loaded_locales.include?(locale)` before acquiring the mutex in `load_locale` (double-checked locking), or cache the result of `ensure_loaded!` per locale in the FallbackLocaleList, or move the `ensure_loaded!` call to only run when the locale changes (e.g., compare with a thread-local or request-local cached value).

title: FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded! calls I18n.ensure_loaded! which does not exist in stock i18n gem, creating hidden coupling and potential NoMethodError
body: `FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded!` calls `I18n.ensure_loaded! l`. This method is only defined by the freedom patch in `lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb`. The initializer comment says `# order: after 02-freedom_patches.rb`, implying it relies on load order. However, initializers in Rails are loaded alphabetically, and `config/initializers/i18n.rb` will load after `02-freedom_patches.rb` only if that file exists in `config/initializers/` — but `translate_accelerator.rb` is in `lib/freedom_patches/`, not `config/initializers/`. The freedom patches are typically loaded via `config/initializers/02-freedom_patches.rb` which requires files from `lib/freedom_patches/`. If the load order is not guaranteed (e.g., if `02-freedom_patches.rb` is renamed or the require mechanism changes), `I18n.ensure_loaded!` will be undefined and `set_locale` will raise `NoMethodError` on every request. Even if load order is currently correct, this is fragile coupling. The consequence: potential `NoMethodError: undefined method 'ensure_loaded!' for I18n:Module` on every request if load order breaks. The fix: either define `ensure_loaded!` directly on `I18n` in the initializer itself (not relying on the freedom patch), or add an explicit `require 'freedom_patches/translate_accelerator'` at the top of the initializer, or guard with `I18n.respond_to?(:ensure_loaded!)`. Better: move the `ensure_loaded!` definition into the initializer or a core lib file that is guaranteed to load before initializers.

title: Pluralization module included into I18n::Backend::Simple but Fallbacks included into I18n.backend.class — inconsistent and fragile backend patching
body: Line 5 does `I18n::Backend::Simple.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Pluralization)` — patching the class directly. Line 9 does `I18n.backend.class.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks)` — patching whatever class the current backend instance is. These are inconsistent patterns. If the backend is not `I18n::Backend::Simple` (e.g., if a chain backend, cache backend, or custom backend is configured elsewhere), the Fallbacks module is included into the wrong class and Pluralization is included into a class that may not be used. The consequence: fallbacks or pluralization silently not working depending on backend configuration. The fix: use `I18n::Backend::Simple.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks)` for consistency, matching the Pluralization line and the removed `pluralization.rb` initializer pattern.

title: Denial cache key omits identity type, allowing cross-identity authorization bypass
body: The denial cache key is built as userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, userUID, action, name, parent) and does not include the identity type (user vs service account vs anonymous vs render). The same userUID string can be used with different identity types (e.g. 'user:test-uid' vs 'service-account:test-uid' both yield UserUID 'test-uid' after ParseTypeID). If a check for one identity type is denied and cached, a subsequent check for a different identity type with the same UID, action, name and parent will hit the denial cache at line 117 and be incorrectly denied — or conversely, the design invites key collisions between distinct principals. More importantly, the denial is cached for the raw subject UID without binding to the resolved internal user ID, so any future change in how subjects map to UIDs, or any two distinct principals sharing a UID string across identity types, produces wrong authorization decisions. The key must include checkReq.IdentityType (and ideally the resolved internal user ID from UserIdentifiers) to be safe.

title: Cached permission check treats 'not allowed' as cache miss and re-queries, but denial is only cached after DB requery — TOCTOU window combined with stale allow cache
body: In Check(), when getCachedIdentityPermissions returns cached permissions (line 123) and checkPermission returns allowed=false (line 125-135), the code does NOT write a denial-cache entry; it falls through to re-query the DB (line 139). This means a user repeatedly probing resources they cannot access will never populate the denial cache from the cached-permissions path — every request re-runs the full DB permission query (getUserPermissions), defeating the stated purpose of the denial cache and creating a DB load amplification vector for denied users. Additionally, because the positive permCache entry is only refreshed when getUserPermissions runs, a permission revocation is not reflected until the permCache TTL (30s) expires AND the denial path is taken; there is no invalidation of permCache or permDenialCache when permissions change, so a user whose permissions were just granted will be denied for up to shortCacheTTL (30s) via the denial cache, and a user whose permissions were revoked will be allowed for up to shortCacheTTL via permCache. The PR's stated goal (creator can access newly created dashboard) is undermined by the denial cache: if the creator's first check happens before the permission row is visible/committed, the denial is cached for 30s and the creator is locked out.

title: Denial cache is populated even when the denial is due to a transient error or missing resource, locking out legitimate access
body: At line 153-155, whenever checkPermission returns allowed=false after a fresh DB query, the denial is cached unconditionally with s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true). checkPermission returns false not only for genuine lack of permission but also when the requested resource does not exist yet (e.g. a dashboard/folder being created, or a race where the permission row hasn't been committed). Because the PR's stated motivation is 'allow users to fetch newly created dashboards and folders', caching a denial for a resource that was just created (and whose permission grant may not yet be visible) will cause the creator to be denied for up to shortCacheTTL (30 seconds). There is no distinction between 'resource not found' and 'permission denied', and no cache invalidation hook when a new permission is created. This directly contradicts the PR's goal and introduces a user-facing lockout window.

title: Denial cache key uses raw name/parent strings without escaping, risking cache key collisions
body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, userUID, action, name and parent with '_' separators (cache.go line 30-32). None of these fields are escaped or length-delimited. A resource name or folder UID containing '_' (which is common for Grafana UIDs) can produce identical cache keys for different (name, parent) pairs — e.g. name='a_b', parent='c' and name='a', parent='b_c' both produce '..._a_b_c'. A denial cached for one combination will incorrectly deny a different resource. This is a correctness bug in the authorization decision cache.

title: permissionCacheUsage metric is incremented as 'false' (cache miss) even when the cache was hit but the permission check returned not-allowed
body: At line 137, s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", checkReq.Action).Inc() is executed unconditionally after the cached-permissions block, including the case where getCachedIdentityPermissions succeeded (cache hit) but checkPermission returned allowed=false. In that case the permission cache WAS used (hit), but the metric records a miss. This misreports cache effectiveness and will mislead operators tuning cache TTLs. The metric should only be incremented as a miss when getCachedIdentityPermissions actually returned an error (cache.ErrNotFound).

title: Denial cache is keyed on request-supplied Name and ParentFolder before verifying the resource exists, enabling cache pollution / memory exhaustion
body: The denial cache key includes checkReq.Name and checkReq.ParentFolder, which are arbitrary attacker-controlled strings from the CheckRequest (validated only for non-empty namespace/subject/action). An attacker (or a misbehaving client) can issue Check requests with many distinct random Name values for an action they are denied, each generating a unique permDenialCache entry with shortCacheTTL (30s). With an unbounded local cache (cache.NewLocalCache with no size limit configured in rbac.go line 88), this allows unbounded memory growth in the authz service — a denial-of-service vector. The cache implementation (authlib cache.NewLocalCache) has no max-entries bound, so this is a real memory exhaustion risk.

title: In-proc authz client uses NoopCache, silently disabling client-side caching and changing behavior vs remote mode
body: In ProvideAuthZClient, the in-proc path now constructs the authzlib client with authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{}) (line 103), replacing the previous newRBACClient which used a real 30s local cache. NoopCache.Get always returns cache.ErrNotFound and Set is a no-op. This means the in-proc client never caches Check responses client-side. While the PR description says this is intentional ('remove the use of authLib cache when running authZ service in-proc'), the consequence is that every Check/List call from Grafana's own API server now goes through the full gRPC in-proc round trip plus the server-side cache logic, with no client-side short-circuit. Combined with the server-side denial cache issues above, this changes the latency and load profile of the in-proc path. More critically, if the server-side caches are cold or bypassed (e.g. for render service identity which always returns cache.ErrNotFound from getCachedIdentityPermissions), every request hits the DB. This is a performance regression that should be acknowledged and the NoopCache behavior documented, or a bounded cache should be used instead.

title: Denial cache Set is not protected by singleflight, allowing stampede and inconsistent state
body: The positive permission path uses singleflight (s.sf.Do) to deduplicate concurrent DB queries for the same userPermKey (line 380). However, the denial cache write at line 154 (s.permDenialCache.Set) and the denial cache read at line 117 are not coordinated with singleflight or with the positive cache population. Two concurrent Check requests for the same denied resource can both miss the denial cache, both query the DB, and both write denial entries — a minor stampede. More significantly, there is a race between the positive permCache.Set inside getUserPermissions (line 406) and the denial cache: a request that queries the DB and finds no permission writes a denial entry, while a concurrent request that queried slightly earlier may have populated permCache with a scope map; subsequent requests will hit the denial cache and be denied even though permCache contains a (possibly stale) allow. The two caches can hold contradictory state with no reconciliation, and the denial cache takes precedence (checked first at line 117), so a stale denial can override a fresh allow.

title: Denial cache test does not verify that a denial is actually cached after a DB denial, nor that the denial expires / is invalidated
body: TestService_CacheCheck's 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' subtest (line 973) manually seeds the denial cache and verifies a deny, but there is no test that verifies the production code path at service.go line 153-155 actually writes a denial entry when a DB query returns not-allowed. The existing 'should deny user without permission' test in TestService_Check (line 756) checks the response but does not assert that s.permDenialCache now contains an entry. Without this assertion, a regression that removes or breaks the denial-cache write would not be caught. Additionally, there is no test covering the cross-identity-type key collision issue (same UID, different identity types) or the cache-key collision issue from unescaped '_' in names.

title: Denial cache does not include Group/Resource/Verb, only the mapped action — potential mismatch if action mapping changes
body: The denial cache key uses checkReq.Action (the mapped internal action string, e.g. 'dashboards:read') but not the original Group/Resource/Verb. If the mapper's translation from (group, resource, verb) to action ever changes (e.g. a verb is remapped to a different action), old denial cache entries keyed on the old action string would no longer match new requests, causing cache misses (safe) — but more importantly, if two different (group, resource, verb) tuples map to the same action string, a denial for one would incorrectly deny the other. Currently the mapper appears to produce unique actions per verb, so this is low risk, but the key should include the original request fields for robustness and debuggability.

title: Denial cache key omits identity type, allowing cross-identity authorization bypass
body: The denial cache key is built as userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, userUID, action, name, parent) using only the raw userUID string from the request subject (checkReq.UserUID), without including checkReq.IdentityType. The same UID string can be used with different identity types (e.g. 'user:123', 'service-account:123', 'anonymous:123' all yield UserUID '123' after ParseTypeID). A denial cached for one identity type (say an anonymous user or a service account with UID '123') will be returned for a real user with the same numeric UID, causing Check() to return Allowed:false at line 117-121 without ever consulting permissions. Conversely, and more dangerously, the key does not distinguish identities, so a denial entry created for identity type A is treated as authoritative for identity type B. The consequence is incorrect authorization decisions (denials for legitimate users, or stale denials applied to different identities sharing a UID string). The key must include the identity type (and ideally the resolved internal user ID from UserIdentifiers rather than the raw subject UID).

title: Denial cache is populated even when the permission check failed due to a transient error path, and denials are never invalidated on permission grants
body: At line 153-155, whenever the freshly-fetched permissions from the DB produce allowed==false, the denial is written to permDenialCache with a 30s TTL (shortCacheTTL). There is no invalidation when permissions are granted, revoked, or when a dashboard/folder is created. Combined with the client-side change in rbac.go that disables the authlib client cache (NoopCache) for in-proc mode, the server-side denial cache becomes the only cache in the path, so a user who is denied once (e.g. before a dashboard is created, or before a permission is assigned) will continue to receive Allowed:false for up to 30 seconds even after the grant/create succeeds. This directly undermines the PR's stated goal ('allow users to fetch newly created dashboards and folders'): a creator who first hits a Check that is denied (e.g. a pre-creation existence probe, or a check for a parent folder they don't yet have) will have that denial cached and subsequent checks for the newly created resource will be short-circuited at line 117-121. The denial cache must either be keyed to avoid caching denials for resources that may not exist yet, be invalidated on resource creation/permission changes, or only cache denials when the resource is confirmed to exist.

title: Cached-permission path silently swallows errors from getCachedIdentityPermissions, masking identity-resolution failures
body: In Check(), the call to s.getCachedIdentityPermissions (line 123) returns an error both for a genuine cache miss (cache.ErrNotFound) and for real failures such as GetUserIdentifiers failing (e.g. DB error resolving the user, line 356-359). The code at line 124 treats any error as 'cache miss' and proceeds to getIdentityPermissions, which will call GetUserIdentifiers again and may succeed or fail. While this is partly intentional (fallback), the error from the cached path is completely discarded: if GetUserIdentifiers fails transiently in the cached path but the subsequent getIdentityPermissions succeeds via a different code path, metrics and logs won't reflect the failure; more importantly, for anonymous users the cached path returns cache.ErrNotFound on miss and the code then re-queries, which is fine, but for users the double lookup of GetUserIdentifiers (once in getCachedIdentityPermissions, once in getUserPermissions) doubles the identity-store load on every cache miss. The error handling should distinguish cache.ErrNotFound from other errors so that genuine identity-resolution failures are surfaced rather than silently retried.

title: Denial cache key uses raw request Name/ParentFolder without normalization, causing cache-key collisions and incorrect denials
body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, userUID, action, name and parent with '_' separators (cache.go line 30-32). Because the components are joined with a plain underscore and none of them are escaped or length-prefixed, distinct (name, parent) pairs can produce identical keys: e.g. name='a_b', parent='c' and name='a', parent='b_c' both yield '..._a_b_c'. A denial cached for one resource will then be returned for a different resource, causing incorrect authorization denials. The same ambiguity exists between action/name/parent boundaries (e.g. action='dashboards:read', name='x' vs action='dashboards', name='read_x' — though action is constrained by the mapper, name and parent are arbitrary user-controlled strings). The key construction must use an unambiguous encoding (e.g. length-prefixing, JSON, or a separator that cannot appear in the components).

title: Denial cache is keyed on the request's userUID string, not the resolved internal user identifier, allowing UID-reuse confusion
body: The denial cache key uses checkReq.UserUID, which is the raw UID portion parsed from the subject (e.g. 'user:test-uid' -> 'test-uid'). However, GetUserIdentifiers (line 452-479) explicitly supports looking up users by numeric internal ID when the UID parses as an integer (line 465-468: 'Assume that numeric UID is user ID'). This means the same subject UID string can resolve to different internal users depending on whether it is treated as a UID or an internal ID, and across namespaces the same UID string may map to different internal IDs. The positive permission cache (userPermCacheKey) is keyed on the resolved userIdentifiers.UID (line 360, 379), but the denial cache is keyed on the unresolved request UID. If a user's UID is changed, or if a numeric subject is interpreted as an internal ID in one request and a UID in another, denial entries will be applied to the wrong resolved identity. The denial cache should be keyed on the resolved UserIdentifiers (both UID and internal ID) exactly like permCache, not on the raw request subject.

title: Denial cache hit increments permissionCacheUsage metric with 'true' even though no permission cache was consulted
body: On a denial-cache hit (line 117-121), the code increments s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("true", checkReq.Action) (line 118), labeling it as a permission cache hit. However, the permCache (the actual permission cache) was never consulted on this path — only permDenialCache was. This mislabels denial-cache hits as permission-cache hits in the permissionCacheUsage metric, making the metric unable to distinguish between the two cache types and corrupting any dashboards/alerts built on it. A separate metric label or counter should be used for denial-cache hits.

title: Denial-cache test does not cover the core security property: denial entries must not leak across identity types or resources
body: The new test 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' (line 973-995) only verifies that a denial entry causes a denial. It does not test the critical negative cases that this PR's key design makes possible: (1) a denial cached for identity type 'anonymous' with UID '0' must not deny a 'user:0' or 'service-account:0' subject (same UID string, different identity type — see the key-construction issue); (2) a denial for (name='a_b', parent='c') must not deny (name='a', parent='b_c') given the ambiguous underscore-joined key; (3) a denial cached before a permission grant must stop applying after the grant (invalidation). Without these tests, the cross-identity and collision bugs in the denial cache key would pass CI. Tests should be added that assert a denial entry for one identity type / one resource does not affect a different identity type / resource.

title: Denial cache is consulted before the (cheap) resolved-identity cache, adding a cache lookup on every allowed request
body: The denial cache lookup (line 116-121) happens before getCachedIdentityPermissions, which itself first checks idCache (a long-TTL, 2-minute cache) before permCache. For the common case of an allowed request, this adds an extra cache Get (permDenialCache) on every Check call, even though the denial cache only ever contains entries for denied requests. Since denials are expected to be rarer than allows, the ordering could be reversed (check permCache first, and only consult permDenialCache on a permCache miss or a negative checkPermission result) to avoid the extra lookup on the hot allowed path. This is a minor performance concern given the local in-memory cache, but it is a real extra allocation and map lookup on every authorization check.

title: Denial cache key omits identity type, allowing cross-identity denial cache collisions
body: userPermDenialCacheKey (pkg/services/authz/rbac/cache.go:30-32) builds the denial cache key from namespace, userUID, action, name and parent, but not from the identity type. In Service.Check (service.go:116) the key is computed from checkReq.UserUID, which is the raw UID portion of the subject. Two different identity types can share the same UID string (e.g. subject 'user:abc' and 'service-account:abc' both yield UserUID 'abc'; anonymous and render subjects are also validated to produce a UID). A denial cached for one identity type is then returned as a denial for a different identity type with the same UID, incorrectly denying access. The key must include checkReq.IdentityType (and the same fix applies wherever the denial key is constructed).

title: Denial cache is populated from stale cached permissions, permanently denying access after a permission grant
body: In Service.Check (service.go:123-155), when getCachedIdentityPermissions returns a cached permission map, checkPermission is evaluated against it; if the result is 'not allowed', the code falls through to re-query the DB (good), but the denial is then cached at line 154 based on the fresh DB result. However, the more serious issue is the ordering combined with the denial cache check at line 116-121: once a denial entry exists for (namespace, userUID, action, name, parent), every subsequent Check for that exact tuple returns Allowed:false for up to shortCacheTTL (30s) without ever consulting the permission cache or the DB. If a permission is granted (e.g. the creator is assigned a role on the dashboard they just created, which is the exact scenario this PR targets), the user is still denied until the denial entry expires, and — because the denial cache is checked before the permission cache — the newly granted permission is never observed during that window. Additionally, when the cached permission map exists but the specific resource is not in it (line 124-136), the code re-queries the DB, but if the DB query also returns not-allowed, the denial is cached even though the earlier cached-permission miss may have been caused by a stale negative; combined with the fact that permCache entries are only refreshed on the getUserPermissions path, a denial recorded against a stale permission snapshot can outlive the snapshot. The denial cache should be invalidated (or not written) when permissions change, and the TTL should be treated as a security-relevant bound; at minimum the denial entry must be keyed consistently with the permission cache generation so a permission update clears it.

title: Cached-permission miss silently swallows real errors from getCachedIdentityPermissions
body: In Service.Check (service.go:123-137), getCachedIdentityPermissions is called and its error is only checked with 'if err == nil'. Any non-cache-miss error — for example a failure in GetUserIdentifiers (service.go:356-359, which can return a store error wrapped as 'could not get user internal id') or an 'unsupported identity type' error — is silently discarded and treated as a cache miss, causing an unnecessary DB round-trip and, more importantly, masking genuine failures. The same pattern exists in Service.List (service.go:180-192). The code should distinguish cache.ErrNotFound (a legitimate miss) from other errors and propagate the latter, e.g. 'if err == nil { ... } else if !errors.Is(err, cache.ErrNotFound) { return deny, err }'. As written, a transient store error in GetUserIdentifiers is hidden and the request proceeds to getIdentityPermissions, which will fail again with a less specific error path and inflate error metrics.

title: Denial cache key uses raw user-supplied name/parent without namespacing, enabling cache-key collisions and unbounded cache growth
body: userPermDenialCacheKey (cache.go:30-32) concatenates namespace, userUID, action, name and parent with '_' separators and no escaping or length bound. Because name and parent (folder UID) are attacker/user-controlled strings that may themselves contain '_' (and arbitrary characters), distinct tuples can produce identical keys — e.g. name='a_b', parent='c' collides with name='a', parent='b_c' — so a denial cached for one resource is returned for a different resource. This both causes incorrect denials (a security-relevant correctness bug) and, since every distinct (user, action, resource, folder) tuple creates a new cache entry with a 30s TTL, allows unbounded growth of the denial cache (memory exhaustion) by issuing Check requests for many distinct resource names. The key should use a collision-free encoding (e.g. length-prefixed fields or a hash) and the resource/folder inputs should be validated/bounded.

title: Denial cache is keyed on userUID before identity resolution, but permission cache is keyed on resolved UID — inconsistent identity handling between the two caches
body: The denial cache key at service.go:116 uses checkReq.UserUID, which is the UID string parsed directly from the request subject (validateSubject, service.go:282-300). The positive permission cache, by contrast, is keyed on the resolved userIdentifiers.UID returned by GetUserIdentifiers (service.go:360, 379). GetUserIdentifiers (service.go:452-479) treats a purely numeric userUID as a user ID and looks it up by ID, meaning the same subject can resolve to a canonical UID that differs from the raw subject UID (e.g. subject 'user:123' resolves via ID lookup and the canonical UID may be a different string). Consequently the denial cache and the permission cache operate on different identity spaces: a denial recorded under the raw subject UID will not be cleared or correlated with permission-cache entries stored under the canonical UID, and two different subjects that resolve to the same user (one by UID, one by numeric ID) will produce different denial keys for the same effective identity, fragmenting the denial cache and — worse — allowing a denial recorded for one subject form to be missed (or incorrectly applied) for another form of the same user. The denial key should be computed from the resolved userIdentifiers.UID, consistent with userPermCacheKey.

title: Denial cache is not invalidated when permissions are granted or revoked, causing stale denials and stale allows
body: The new permDenialCache (service.go:58, 85, 116-121, 153-155) has no invalidation path anywhere in the codebase: nothing calls permDenialCache.Delete (the cacheWrap type does not even expose a Delete method, cache.go:46-92), and no permission mutation hook (role assignment, dashboard ACL change, team membership change) clears it. A denial cached at line 154 persists for shortCacheTTL (30s) regardless of any subsequent permission change. This is a fail-closed cache, so the practical impact is bounded by the 30s TTL, but within that window a user who is granted access (the exact 'creator cannot access newly created dashboard' scenario this PR is meant to fix — e.g. the creator is granted a role after a first denied check) will continue to be denied, and conversely the positive permCache entries (also 30s TTL, also never explicitly invalidated) can serve stale allows. For an authorization service this is a data-integrity risk: the caches must be invalidated (or the denial cache keyed by a permissions generation/epoch) on any permission mutation, otherwise authorization decisions can be wrong for up to the TTL in both directions.

title: permissionCacheUsage metric is incremented twice on the cached-permission path, double-counting cache hits
body: In Service.Check, when getCachedIdentityPermissions succeeds and checkPermission returns allowed, s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage is incremented at line 132; but line 137 unconditionally increments permissionCacheUsage with 'false' (cache miss) after the if-block whenever the cached path did not return early — including the case where the cached permissions existed but the specific resource was not in them and the code correctly falls through to the DB. More importantly, the metric semantics are now wrong: line 137 reports a cache miss even when the permission map was found in cache (the miss was only for the specific resource scope, not the permission cache). The 'false' increment should only happen when getCachedIdentityPermissions actually returned cache.ErrNotFound, and the resource-level miss should either not count as a permission-cache miss or be tracked with a distinct label. As written, dashboards/metrics for cache hit ratio are corrupted.

title: Denial-cache test does not cover the core security property: a denial must not outlive a permission grant, and denial keys must be identity-type- and resource-specific
body: TestService_CacheCheck (service_test.go:893-996) covers allow-from-cache, DB fallback on miss, DB fallback on outdated cache, and deny-on-explicit-denial-entry, but it never tests the dangerous interactions introduced by this PR: (1) that a denial entry for one resource does not deny a different resource (the key-collision issue from the unescaped '_' concatenation in userPermDenialCacheKey); (2) that a denial entry recorded for one identity type/subject form does not deny a different identity type with the same UID; (3) that after a denial is cached, a subsequent grant (permission added to the store) is honored once the denial expires or is otherwise invalidated — i.e. the test suite gives no confidence that the denial cache cannot lock a user out after a legitimate grant. Given that the denial cache is a fail-closed authorization cache with no invalidation path, these cases are exactly the regressions most likely to cause real-world lockouts and should be tested.

title: Denial-cache test seeds permCache with a 'false' value that checkPermission would never produce, weakening the test's realism
body: In the 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' subtest (service_test.go:982), the permission cache is seeded with map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}. The production code only ever stores 'true' values in the scope map (getScopeMap, service.go:569-579, sets permMap[perm.Scope] = true), so a 'false' entry is not a state the code can produce. The test therefore does not exercise the real code path it claims to prove ('allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked') — with a realistic seed of {"dashboards:uid:dash1": true} the test would actually verify that the denial cache takes precedence over a positive cached permission, which is the property that matters. As written, the assertion passes trivially and would also pass if the denial-cache check were accidentally removed and the 'false' value were treated as a denial.

title: GrafanaRuleListItem in FilterView is rendered without a React key
body: In the 'grafana' case of the rules.map() switch, <GrafanaRuleListItem> is returned without a key prop, while the 'datasource' and default cases both use key={key}. React will warn about missing keys in lists and may incorrectly reuse/reorder list item components when the filtered rule list changes (e.g. when filters change or new pages load), which can cause stale UI state (open menus, hover state) to be attached to the wrong rule. The computed `key` from getRuleKey() is available in scope and should be passed as key={key}.

title: Grafana rule list key has a stray trailing '}' and omits rule type
body: getGrafanaRuleKey() returns `grafana-${namespace.uid}-${groupName}-${rule.uid}}` — note the extra closing brace at the end. It also does not include the rule type, unlike getDataSourceRuleKey() which includes rule.type. The stray '}' is harmless for uniqueness but is clearly a typo; more importantly, if a rule with the same uid could appear as both an alerting and recording rule (unlikely but possible during type transitions), keys could collide. At minimum the typo should be fixed.

title: Federated rule group detection removed from useAllRulerRuleAbilities, making federated rules appear editable/deletable
body: The old useAllAlertRuleAbilities computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` and treated federated rules as immutable (MaybeSupportedUnlessImmutable = NotSupported), preventing Update/Delete/Pause on federated rule groups. The refactored useAllRulerRuleAbilities (which useAllAlertRuleAbilities now delegates to) hardcodes `const isFederated = false` with a TODO, because it no longer receives the CombinedRuleGroup. As a result, for cloud (Mimir/GEM) federated rule groups, the Update, Delete, Pause, Restore and DeletePermanently abilities are now computed as if the rules were mutable — the UI will show Edit/Delete/Pause actions for federated rules that cannot actually be modified through the ruler API. This is a permissions/authorization regression: users will be offered actions that will fail server-side (or worse, if the backend permits it, allow modification of federated rules). The groupIdentifier passed in does not carry source_tenants information, so the immutability check must be restored by passing the group (or an isFederated flag) into useAllRulerRuleAbilities.

title: useAllRulerRuleAbilities treats ruler-unavailable rules as supported when called without a ruler rule (list view path)
body: In useAllRulerRuleAbilities, `MaybeSupported = loading ? NotSupported : isRulerAvailable`. When AlertRuleMenu calls useRulerRuleAbilities(rulerRule, ...) in the list view, rulerRule is undefined (the ruler API is no longer called in the list view). useIsRuleEditable(rulesSourceName, undefined) presumably returns isRulerAvailable=false, so ruler-based abilities correctly evaluate to unsupported — but this means for cloud rules in contexts where the ruler rule is absent, the ruler abilities silently return [false, false] and the component relies entirely on the OR with grafana abilities. For cloud rules the grafana hook is passed skipToken, so canEdit/canDelete etc. depend solely on useRulerRuleAbilities with rule=undefined. If useIsRuleEditable returns isRulerAvailable=true even when rule is undefined (e.g. based on data source features rather than the specific rule), the abilities would be computed with isEditable/isRemovable=false — fine — but the 'supported' flag would be true, which combined with any future change could show actions. More concretely: the semantics of 'supported' for a rule that was never fetched from the ruler are wrong; the hook should return NotSupported for all actions when rule is undefined, rather than deriving support from data source ruler availability. This is fragile and the AlertRuleMenu OR-logic only accidentally produces correct results.

title: Pause menu item is gated on rulerRule being a Grafana rule, so pausing is never available in the list view where rulerRule is undefined
body: The Pause menu item renders only when `canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) && groupIdentifier.groupOrigin === 'grafana'`. In the alert list view (the whole point of this PR), rulerRule is undefined because ruler API requests were removed, so rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(undefined) is false and the Pause action is never shown for Grafana-managed rules — even when the user has pause permission (grafanaPauseSupported && grafanaPauseAllowed is true). Additionally, MenuItemPauseRule requires a rulerRule prop (`rule={rulerRule}`) which would be undefined. The pause action must be reworked to work from the promRule (GrafanaPromRuleDTO has isPaused and folderUid/uid) in the list view, otherwise pausing alert rules is silently removed from the list view UI.

title: Delete menu item requires rulerRule, so Delete is never available in the list view where rulerRule is undefined
body: The Delete menu item renders only when `canDelete && rulerRule`, and its onClick calls handleDelete(rulerRule, groupIdentifier). In the alert list view, rulerRule is undefined (ruler API calls removed), so the Delete action is never rendered for any rule — including cloud rules where canDelete is computed purely from ruler abilities with rule=undefined. This removes the ability to delete alert rules from the list view entirely. The delete flow (useDeleteModal / DeleteModal) needs to support deletion by identifier (ruleSourceName + uid) without a RulerRuleDTO, as RuleActionsButtons.V2 already does via getEditableIdentifier.

title: DeclareIncidentMenuItem receives an empty url and promRule.name without null check
body: shouldShowDeclareIncidentButton checks `prometheusRuleType.alertingRule(promRule) && promRule.state === PromAlertingRuleState.Firing`, but prometheusRuleType.alertingRule only checks rule.type === 'alerting' — it does not guarantee promRule is defined (the type guard accepts `rule?: Rule`). If promRule is undefined, `promRule.state` throws a TypeError. In the list view promRule is always provided for grafana rules, but AlertRuleMenu is also used from the rule viewer where promRule may be absent while rulerRule is present; in that case shouldShowDeclareIncidentButton would crash. The guard must check promRule is defined before accessing promRule.state, and DeclareIncidentMenuItem is passed url={''} which produces a broken incident link.

title: Silence drawer is gated on rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule), so silencing never opens in the list view where rule (ruler rule) is undefined
body: The silence drawer renders only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) && showSilenceDrawer`, and SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer receives `rulerRule={rule}`. In the list view, RuleActionsButtons is rendered with only promRule (no ruler rule — see GrafanaRuleListItem which passes only promRule), so `rule` is undefined, the condition is false, and clicking 'Silence notifications' in the AlertRuleMenu sets showSilenceDrawer=true but no drawer ever opens. The silence flow must be adapted to work with GrafanaPromRuleDTO (which has uid, folderUid, name) instead of requiring a RulerGrafanaRuleDTO.

title: handleDelete uses identifier-based delete modal but AlertRuleMenu's internal delete path still expects a ruler rule
body: RuleActionsButtons passes `handleDelete={() => showDeleteModal(identifier, groupIdentifier)}` to AlertRuleMenu, but AlertRuleMenu's Props declare `handleDelete: (rule: RulerRuleDTO, groupIdentifier: RuleGroupIdentifierV2) => void` and its Delete menu item calls `handleDelete(rulerRule, groupIdentifier)`. This is a type mismatch: the menu will call the handler with (rulerRule, groupIdentifier) while the handler ignores its arguments and uses the closure `identifier`. It happens to work because the handler ignores arguments, but the Props contract is wrong and the Delete menu item is additionally gated on `rulerRule` being truthy (see separate finding), so in the list view the menu's Delete item never renders and this handler is effectively dead code from the menu. The AlertRuleMenu Props should be changed to `handleDelete: () => void` (or the menu should use the identifier), and the gating fixed.

title: Removing the ruler fetch eliminates 'Creating'/'Deleting' rule states from the group list
body: The previous implementation matched ruler rules against prom rules and rendered rules that exist only in the ruler with RuleOperation.Creating, and rules that exist only in Prometheus (already removed from ruler but not yet propagated) with RuleOperation.Deleting via RuleOperationListItem. The new implementation renders only promResponse rules, so: (1) a newly created rule will not appear in the list until Prometheus evaluates it (previously it appeared immediately with a 'Creating' indicator), and (2) a deleted rule disappears from the list immediately instead of showing a 'Deleting' state until propagation completes. This is a deliberate product change perhaps, but it also means the 'Creating'/'Deleting' UI states and the matchRules consistency warning (which logged when a ruler rule had no Prometheus counterpart) are gone entirely. If the intent was only to remove per-rule ruler requests, the group-level ruler fetch (one request per group, already cached/prefetched) could have preserved these states. At minimum this behavioral regression should be called out and confirmed as intended; the removed tests in GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx ('should render rule with url and creating state when only ruler rule exists', 'should render delete rule operation list item when only prom rule exists') confirm the states are no longer supported.

title: Error handling only covers missing promResponse, not query errors
body: The component checks `if (!promResponse)` to show an error Alert, but useGetGrafanaGroupsQuery's error state is not checked. If the Prometheus groups request fails (network error, 500), promResponse will be undefined and the generic 'Failed to load rules' alert shows — acceptable — but with RTK Query, a failed request followed by a successful retry or a cached undefined could mask errors; more importantly, the previous implementation distinguished ruler vs prom errors (RulerRuleLoadingError). Now a transient prom error permanently shows the error Alert with no retry mechanism other than the polling interval refetch. Consider checking `error` from the query and only showing the Alert when there's no data after loading completes.

title: Redundant double type check for alerting rules
body: The component first checks `prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` (which already verifies rule.type === PromRuleType.Alerting plus folderUid/uid presence), then inside computes `const promAlertingRule = rule && rule.type === PromRuleType.Alerting ? rule : undefined;` — repeating the same type check. The inner check is redundant; `rule` can be used directly. Not a bug per se, but it suggests confusion about the type narrowing and could mask a mismatch if the two checks ever diverge.

title: View link omits returnTo parameter that the old GrafanaRuleListItem included
body: The old GrafanaRuleListItem (in deleted GrafanaRuleLoader.tsx) built the href with `createRelativeUrl('/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view', { returnTo })` using createReturnTo(), so navigating back from the rule view returned to the list with filters intact. The new GrafanaRuleListItem builds `createRelativeUrl('/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view')` without returnTo. This breaks the 'return to list' UX: after viewing a rule, the back navigation loses the list filter/scroll state. The returnTo should be restored.

title: skipToken sentinel exported and threaded through public ability hooks is a fragile API contract
body: A module-level Symbol `skipToken` is exported and accepted by useGrafanaPromRuleAbility/useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities to mean 'skip this rule'. Callers must remember to pass skipToken when the rule is not a Grafana prom rule (e.g. `prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(promRule) ? promRule : skipToken`). If a caller passes undefined instead, useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined) runs the full hook (folder fetch, config status query) and returns abilities computed for a non-existent rule — mostly [false, false] but with wasted queries and potentially wrong 'supported' flags (e.g. Silence supported=true with allowed=false). The skipToken pattern is error-prone; a cleaner contract would be to accept `GrafanaPromRuleDTO | undefined` and return all-unsupported abilities for undefined, or split into a separate hook used only when the rule is known to be Grafana-managed. At minimum, passing a non-Grafana prom rule (not skipToken) would compute abilities against getRulesPermissions('grafana') incorrectly.

title: Grafana prom rule Silence ability drops the 'not a recording rule' check present in the ruler-based hook
body: In useAllRulerRuleAbilities, Silence ability comes from useCanSilence(rule), which returns [false, false] when the rule is a Grafana recording rule (`isGrafanaRecording` check). In the new useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities, Silence is `[silenceSupported, canSilenceInFolder && isAlertingRule]` where isAlertingRule = prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) — this checks type === 'alerting', so recording rules are excluded from the allowed side but `silenceSupported` (the first tuple element) is true for recording rules. Since Ability = [supported, allowed] and consumers check `supported && allowed`, recording rules still won't show silence. However the 'supported' flag being true for recording rules is semantically wrong and any consumer that only checks `supported` (or uses the tuple loosely) would incorrectly enable silence for recording rules. The ruler-based useCanSilence also verified the rule is a Grafana-managed alerting rule; the prom-based version should mirror that by gating both elements on isAlertingRule.

title: useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities marks rules as supported while folder permissions are still loading, and never reflects ruler availability
body: In useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities, `MaybeSupported = loading ? NotSupported : AlwaysSupported` — unlike the ruler-based hook which uses isRulerAvailable. For Grafana-managed rules this is mostly fine (Grafana always has a ruler), but combined with useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable: when the folder is still loading, `loading` is true so MaybeSupported=false — good. However when `!rule || !folderUID`, useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable returns `{isEditable: false, isRemovable: false, loading: false}` — so MaybeSupported becomes AlwaysSupported=true even though there is no rule. Abilities for a non-existent rule then report supported=true (e.g. Duplicate: [true, rulesPermissions.create]). Any caller that checks only the supported flag (or ORs abilities across rule types as AlertRuleMenu does) could surface actions for a rule that doesn't exist. The hook should return all-NotSupported abilities when rule is undefined, similar to how useCanSilence returns [false,false] for missing rules.

title: Test asserts exactly 4 menu items but Delete is missing from the menu in the list view (test passes only because Delete is broken)
body: The test 'should render correct menu actions when More button is clicked' asserts `menuItems.length` is 4 (silence, copy link, duplicate, export) and never asserts that Delete is present, even though the test's beforeEach grants AlertingRuleDelete permission and folder delete permission. Given that AlertRuleMenu gates the Delete item on `rulerRule` being defined (which is undefined in this list view), Delete is silently absent. The test therefore enshrines the broken behavior: a user with delete permission cannot delete a rule from the list. The test should assert the Delete menu item is present (and add a negative-permission case), which would currently fail and expose the bug.

title: Permission-denied test only checks the Edit button, not the More menu actions
body: The test 'should not render edit button when user lacks edit permissions' overrides folder access control to deny update/delete but only asserts the Edit link is absent and the More button is present. It does not verify that the Delete menu item is hidden in the More menu when delete permission is denied (the beforeEach granted delete permission, and this test denies it via setFolderAccessControl). Since the menu's delete/pause/silence visibility depends on the new useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities hook, a regression that shows Delete (or Pause) to unauthorized users would not be caught.

title: Test names say 'Should not render' but the mock grants the permission (isEditable: true)
body: The tests are titled 'Should not render Edit button for users with the update permission' and mock useIsRuleEditable to return { isEditable: true }, then assert the Edit button is NOT in the document. Either the test titles are wrong (they should say 'without the update permission' and mock isEditable: false), or the assertions are inverted. As written, the tests assert that a user WITH edit permission does not see the Edit button — which contradicts the intended RBAC behavior and would only pass if the Edit button is broken for authorized users. The mock values and titles are inconsistent; one of them must be fixed, otherwise the test validates the wrong behavior.

title: beforeEach calls jest.resetAllMocks() after setting up mocks, and mock setup order is fragile
body: The beforeEach calls jest.clearAllMocks(), jest.restoreAllMocks(), jest.resetAllMocks() and then sets default mock return values. jest.resetAllMocks() resets mock implementations, so setting defaults afterwards is correct, but jest.restoreAllMocks() only affects spies created with jest.spyOn — combined with the module-level jest.mock('../../hooks/useAbilities'), the triple-reset pattern is redundant and confusing. More importantly, several tests then override only some of the five mocked hooks (e.g. the Grafana 'Should not render Delete button' test sets useAlertRuleAbility and useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities but relies on the beforeEach default [false,false] for useRulerRuleAbilities). Because AlertRuleMenu ORs ruler and grafana abilities, a test that intends 'no delete permission' could accidentally pass or fail depending on which hook path the component takes. The tests would be more robust if each test explicitly mocked all hooks it depends on, or if the component under test used a single ability source.

title: Stale comment about preloading ruler rules
body: The comment above the populateCache block still says 'This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules, but it improves the UX / Because the user waits a bit longer for the initial load but doesn't need to wait for each group to be loaded' — but the ruler prefetch (alertRuleApi.util.prefetch('getGrafanaRulerGroup', ...)) was removed in this PR. The comment now describes behavior that no longer exists and should be updated to reflect that only the Prometheus groups cache is populated.

title: useAllAlertRuleAbilities marked @deprecated but still used by useAlertRuleAbility/useAlertRuleAbilities which are not deprecated
body: useAllAlertRuleAbilities is annotated '@deprecated Use {@link useAllRulerRuleAbilities} instead', but the non-deprecated public hooks useAlertRuleAbility and useAlertRuleAbilities (used by RuleActionsButtons and others) still call it internally. The deprecation is misleading: consumers of useAlertRuleAbility cannot migrate to useAllRulerRuleAbilities without also reimplementing the groupIdentifier.fromCombinedRule mapping. Either deprecate the whole CombinedRule-based API surface consistently or remove the misleading annotation.

title: RuleActionsButtons receives promRule typed as Rule but GrafanaRuleListItem passes GrafanaPromRuleDTO; pause/delete/silence actions in the menu are broken for list-view Grafana rules
body: GrafanaRuleListItem renders <RuleActionsButtons promRule={rule} groupIdentifier={groupIdentifier} compact /> where rule is GrafanaPromRuleDTO. RuleActionsButtons passes promRule to AlertRuleMenu, which uses it for grafana abilities (correct), but the menu's Pause item requires rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) (undefined in list view → hidden), Delete requires rulerRule (undefined → hidden), and the silence drawer in RuleActionsButtons requires rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) where rule is the ruler rule prop (undefined → drawer never opens). Net effect: in the new list view, Grafana-managed rules lose Pause, Delete, and Silence actions from the UI even for fully authorized users. This is the core functional regression of removing the ruler from the list view; the actions must be reimplemented against GrafanaPromRuleDTO/identifier-based APIs.

title: GrafanaRuleListItem in FilterView is missing the React key prop
body: In FilterViewResults, the 'grafana' case renders <GrafanaRuleListItem rule={rule} groupIdentifier={groupIdentifier} namespaceName={...} showLocation={true} /> without a key prop, while the 'datasource' and default cases correctly use key={key}. React will warn about missing keys in lists and may cause incorrect reconciliation when the filtered rule list changes (e.g., rules reordering or being removed while loading more pages), potentially leading to stale UI state being attached to the wrong rule rows.

title: Extra closing brace in getGrafanaRuleKey produces malformed key
body: getGrafanaRuleKey returns `grafana-${namespace.uid}-${groupName}-${rule.uid}}` — there is a trailing `}` with no matching opening brace. This produces keys like 'grafana-uid-group-ruleuid}' which are still unique so functionally mostly harmless, but it is clearly a typo that makes keys inconsistent with the datasource key format and could confuse debugging; it should be `grafana-${namespace.uid}-${groupName}-${rule.uid}`.

title: Federated rule group check silently disabled in useAllRulerRuleAbilities, allowing edit/delete of federated rules
body: The old useAllAlertRuleAbilities computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` from the CombinedRuleGroup, and federated rules were treated as immutable (no edit/delete/duplicate). The refactored useAllRulerRuleAbilities (lines 242-245) hardcodes `const isFederated = false;` with a TODO comment, and its signature only receives the RulerRuleDTO and groupIdentifier — it has no access to the group's source_tenants. As a result, for cloud (Mimir/Cortex) federated rule groups, Update/Delete/Duplicate/Pause abilities are no longer suppressed by immutability, and the UI will offer edit/delete actions on federated rules that the backend ruler will reject (or worse, the permission checks that previously gated these actions are bypassed at the UI level). This is a real authorization/UX regression for multi-tenant federated setups.

title: useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities treats Grafana rules as always supported, hiding actions while folder permissions load
body: In useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities, `MaybeSupported = loading ? NotSupported : AlwaysSupported` (line 309). Unlike the ruler-based hook, there is no isRulerAvailable concept, so once loading is false every action is 'supported'. However, `loading` here comes from useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable, which returns `loading: false` when `!rule || !folderUID` (line 355) — i.e., when the rule is undefined (skipToken case) or folderUid is missing, loading is false and abilities are computed with isEditable=false/isRemovable=false. That part is fine, but the deeper issue is that `useFolder` loading state only covers the folder fetch; if the folder fetch fails or returns no folder, `isEditable`/`isRemovable` are false while `MaybeSupported` is true, so e.g. Duplicate (which only checks rulesPermissions.create, not folder metadata) is shown even when folder-scoped permissions are unknown. More importantly, the asymmetry with the ruler hook (which gates on isRulerAvailable) means Grafana rules in the list view will show action buttons based purely on global permissions, ignoring folder-scoped RBAC for Duplicate — a permission-UI inconsistency.

title: skipToken sentinel is a module-level Symbol shared across hook instances, enabling cross-component cache confusion
body: skipToken is a single module-level Symbol used as a sentinel to mean 'do not compute abilities for this rule'. useGrafanaPromRuleAbility/useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities map skipToken to `undefined` and then call useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined), which returns abilities computed for an undefined rule: isEditable=false, isRemovable=false, but Duplicate = toAbility(AlwaysSupported, rulesPermissions.create) and View = toAbility(AlwaysSupported, rulesPermissions.read) — i.e., [true, <global-permission>]. In AlertRuleMenu, canDuplicate/canExport etc. are OR-ed between ruler and grafana abilities, so for cloud rules (where rulerRule is undefined and useRulerRuleAbilities returns [false,false]... actually useAllRulerRuleAbilities(undefined,...) returns MaybeSupported=false) the grafana side with skipToken yields Duplicate=[true, create-permission] even though promRule is a cloud rule, not a Grafana rule. Wait — AlertRuleMenu only passes promRule to useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities when prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(promRule) is true, so skipToken is used for cloud rules and abilities are computed for undefined. For undefined rule: Duplicate supported=true, allowed=rulesPermissions.create (global AlertingRuleCreate). So canDuplicate = (ruler: false) || (grafana-undefined: true && create) = true for cloud rules if the user has global create permission — but duplicating a cloud rule via the grafana identifier path would be wrong. Actually handleDuplicateRule uses `identifier` which for cloud rules comes from getEditableIdentifier → ruleId.fromRulerRuleAndGroupIdentifierV2 — but rule (rulerRule) is undefined in the list view for cloud rules... This needs verification, but the core design smell is real: passing skipToken still computes and returns 'supported' abilities for a non-existent rule, and consumers OR them with ruler abilities, which can incorrectly enable actions. The sentinel should short-circuit to [false, false] instead of computing abilities for undefined.

title: Pause menu item requires rulerRule, but the list view no longer fetches ruler rules, so Pause is never available for Grafana rules in the list
body: The Pause menu item is gated on `canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) && groupIdentifier.groupOrigin === 'grafana'` (line 123) and renders <MenuItemPauseRule rule={rulerRule} .../>. In the new list view, GrafanaRuleListItem renders RuleActionsButtons with only promRule (no rulerRule), so rulerRule is undefined in AlertRuleMenu. rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(undefined) returns false (isGrafanaRulerRule checks typeof rule === 'object'), so the Pause menu item never renders in the list view even when canPause is true (computed via the grafana prom-rule abilities). Additionally, MenuItemPauseRule requires a RulerGrafanaRuleDTO to pause the rule via the ruler API — with ruler data removed from the list view, pausing from the list is broken for Grafana-managed rules. Either the pause action needs a prom-rule-based implementation (e.g., PATCH via prometheusApi) or the menu item must be hidden consistently; as written, the ability check says 'can pause' but the UI silently omits the action, and the OR-ed canPause logic gives a false signal.

title: Delete menu item requires rulerRule, so Delete is never available in the list view where ruler rules are no longer fetched
body: The Delete menu item is gated on `canDelete && rulerRule` (line 165) and calls handleDelete(rulerRule, groupIdentifier). In the new list view (GrafanaRuleListItem → RuleActionsButtons.V2 → AlertRuleMenu), only promRule is passed; rulerRule is undefined. Therefore the Delete menu item never renders in the alert list, even for users with delete permission — canDelete may be true (via grafanaDeleteAbility from useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities) but the `&& rulerRule` condition suppresses the item. Conversely, in RuleActionsButtons.V2 the delete flow is wired via handleDelete={() => showDeleteModal(identifier, groupIdentifier)} which uses the identifier, not the rulerRule object — so the menu's handleDelete signature (rule: RulerRuleDTO, groupIdentifier) is incompatible with the list view. This is a functional regression: users cannot delete Grafana-managed rules from the list view. The GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx test 'should render correct menu actions' expects exactly 4 menu items and notably does NOT include delete in its assertions (silence, copyLink, duplicate, export) — consistent with delete being broken/hidden, and the test enshrines the broken behavior.

title: Silence drawer only opens for ruler rules; silencing is broken for Grafana rules in the list view
body: The silence drawer is rendered only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) && showSilenceDrawer` (line 104), where `rule` is the RulerRuleDTO. In the list view, RuleActionsButtons is rendered with only promRule (GrafanaRuleListItem passes `promRule={rule}` and no `rule` prop), so `rule` is undefined, rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(undefined) is false, and clicking 'Silence notifications' in the AlertRuleMenu sets showSilenceDrawer=true but no drawer ever opens — the click appears to do nothing. Meanwhile the menu item itself is shown because canSilence is computed from grafanaSilenceAbility (prom-rule based). This is a broken user flow: the Silence action is advertised but non-functional in the list view. The GrafanaGroupLoader test asserts the silence menu item is present, but no test verifies the drawer actually opens from the list view.

title: getIsProvisioned prefers ruler rule provenance over prom rule provenance, inconsistent with the ruler-less list view
body: getIsProvisioned(rule, promRule) returns isProvisionedRule(rule) if a ruler rule exists, otherwise isProvisionedPromRule(promRule). In the list view only promRule exists, so provisioning status comes from promRule.provenance. The new GrafanaPromRuleDTOBase type adds `provenance?: string` (unified-alerting-dto.ts line 135), so this works, but the two sources can disagree (ruler provenance vs prom provenance), and the duplicate flow (RedirectToCloneRule with isProvisioned) will behave differently between the list view and the rule details view for the same rule. More importantly, isProvisionedPromRule checks `prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(promRule) && Boolean(promRule.provenance)` — for cloud prom rules provenance is undefined so it returns false, which is correct. The risk is divergence between the two code paths; a single source of truth should be used.

title: Removing the ruler fetch eliminates 'Creating' and 'Deleting' transient states from the group list
body: The old GrafanaGroupLoader fetched both the Prometheus groups and the ruler group, matched them by UID, and rendered: (a) ruler rules without a prom counterpart as 'Creating' (RuleOperation.Creating), and (b) prom rules without a ruler counterpart as 'Deleting' (RuleOperationListItem with RuleOperation.Deleting). The new implementation only fetches promResponse and renders only prom rules. Consequences: (1) A rule that was just created (ruler has it, Prometheus hasn't evaluated/propagated it yet) will not appear in the list at all until Prometheus picks it up — the user gets no feedback that creation is in progress. (2) A rule being deleted may linger as a normal-looking row (or disappear abruptly) instead of showing a 'Deleting' state. (3) The RulesTable.test.tsx still contains tests for 'Creating'/'Deleting' states (lines 151-200) but those test RulesTable with CombinedRule objects, not this loader — the GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx had its 'creating state' and 'deleting state' tests removed (see diff: 'should render rule with url and creating state when only ruler rule exists' and 'should render delete rule operation list item when only prom rule exists' were deleted). This is a deliberate product decision perhaps, but it removes user-facing state feedback and the PR description does not mention it; at minimum the removed tests indicate lost coverage of previously supported behavior.

title: isProvisioned derived from promRule.provenance, but GrafanaRuleListItem also accepts an operation prop that is never passed by callers
body: GrafanaRuleListItem accepts an optional `operation?: RuleOperation` prop and passes it to AlertRuleListItem, but neither caller (GrafanaGroupLoader line 70-77 nor FilterView line 157-162) passes `operation`. Since the ruler-based matching that produced Creating/Deleting operations was removed, the prop is dead code. Additionally, isProvisioned is computed as Boolean(provenance) from the prom rule — the newly added provenance field on GrafanaPromRuleDTOBase. If the Prometheus API does not actually populate provenance on rule DTOs (it's an optional field added in this PR), provisioned rules will incorrectly appear editable/deletable in the list. This needs verification against the backend API contract.

title: Menu test asserts exactly 4 items but Delete is silently missing — test enshrines broken delete flow
body: The test 'should render correct menu actions when More button is clicked' grants AlertingRuleDelete permission and folder delete permission in beforeEach, then asserts the menu contains silence, copyLink, duplicate, export and `expect(menuItems.length).toBe(4)`. Given the delete permission is granted, a correct implementation would show 5 items (including Delete). The assertion of exactly 4 items passes only because AlertRuleMenu gates Delete on `canDelete && rulerRule` and rulerRule is undefined in the list view (see AlertRuleMenu.tsx line 165). The test therefore locks in the regression where Delete is unavailable from the list view despite the user having delete permissions. The test should either assert Delete is present (and the component fixed) or explicitly document/verify the intended behavior.

title: Test names say 'Should not render' but mocks grant the permission — assertions are inverted relative to test intent
body: The tests are named 'Should not render Edit button for users with the update permission' and mock useIsRuleEditable to return isEditable: true (i.e., the user HAS update permission), then assert the Edit button is NOT in the document. The test names and the mocked state contradict each other: either the name should be 'without the update permission' (matching RulesTable.test.tsx naming) or the mock should return isEditable: false. As written, the test passes but its name misleads future maintainers about what is being verified. Same issue for the Delete test (line 74) and the cloud rule tests (lines 89, 100).

title: useAllAlertRuleAbilities marked @deprecated but still exported and used; deprecation direction contradicts new hooks
