body: useAllAlertRuleAbilities is marked `@deprecated Use {@link useAllRulerRuleAbilities} instead`, but useAllRulerRuleAbilities takes (rule: RulerRuleDTO | undefined, groupIdentifier) while useAllAlertRuleAbilities takes a CombinedRule and internally derives the groupIdentifier via groupIdentifier.fromCombinedRule. The deprecation message points to a hook with a different, lower-level signature, which is not a drop-in replacement. Meanwhile useAlertRuleAbility (singular, line 179) still uses useAllAlertRuleAbilities and is NOT deprecated, and RuleActionsButtons.V2 still calls useRulerRuleAbility directly. The deprecation is misleading and the migration path is unclear; either provide a proper replacement wrapper or remove the @deprecated tag.

title: Stale comment about preloading ruler rules remains after ruler prefetch was removed
body: The comment at lines 81-82 says 'This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules, but it improves the UX / Because the user waits a bit longer for the initial load but doesn't need to wait for each group to be loaded'. The ruler prefetch (alertRuleApi.util.prefetch('getGrafanaRulerGroup', ...)) was removed in this PR (see diff), so the comment now describes behavior that no longer exists. The comment should be updated to describe the Prometheus group cache population only.

title: Error handling only covers missing promResponse; a failed Prometheus query with error but no data shows the generic error Alert, but a failed query that returns data=undefined with isLoading=false is conflated with 'no data'
body: The component checks `if (!promResponse)` to show an error Alert, but RTK Query returns `data: undefined` both when the query failed AND potentially during refetching/polling edge cases. The old code checked `!rulerResponse && !promResponse`. More importantly, the query error object (promResponse error from useGetGrafanaGroupsQuery) is never inspected — the component destructures only { data, isLoading }, so an HTTP error (e.g., 403, 500) results in data=undefined and the generic 'Failed to load rules' Alert without the actual error message. The old GrafanaRuleLoader surfaced rulerRuleGroupError/promRuleGroupError via RulerRuleLoadingError. Error detail is lost in the new implementation.

title: Federated rule group detection removed from ruler abilities, allowing edit/delete of federated rules
body: In useAllRulerRuleAbilities, the previous implementation computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` from the CombinedRule's group, and treated federated rules as immutable (`immutableRule = isProvisioned || isFederated || isPluginProvided`), which prevented Update/Delete/Pause/Duplicate on federated rule groups. The new implementation hardcodes `const isFederated = false` with a TODO comment. Since useAllRulerRuleAbilities now only receives a RulerRuleDTO and a groupIdentifier (which contains no source_tenants information), federated Mimir rule groups will no longer be detected as immutable. This means users may be shown Edit/Delete/Pause/Duplicate actions for federated rules that cannot actually be modified through the ruler API, and clicking them will produce failed API calls or, worse, the UI will incorrectly report the user as permitted to modify rules they cannot. The ability check no longer matches the server-side enforcement for federated groups.

title: Update/Delete abilities for ruler rules no longer check ruler availability correctly when rule is undefined
body: In useAllRulerRuleAbilities, `MaybeSupported = loading ? NotSupported : isRulerAvailable`. When the list view no longer fetches ruler rules, `rule` is undefined and `useIsRuleEditable(rulesSourceName, undefined)` is called. The behavior of useIsRuleEditable with an undefined rule is not shown, but if it returns isRulerAvailable=true (e.g., based on data source features rather than an actual ruler rule), then for cloud (data source) rules in contexts where AlertRuleMenu still calls useRulerRuleAbilities(rulerRule=undefined, ...), the Update/Delete abilities could incorrectly report supported=true. Combined with the OR logic in AlertRuleMenu (`canDelete = (deleteSupported && deleteAllowed) || (grafanaDeleteSupported && grafanaDeleteAllowed)`), a false positive from the ruler path could enable actions. The ruler ability path should return NotSupported when rule is undefined, but the current code relies on useIsRuleEditable's behavior with undefined input which is not guaranteed to be conservative.

title: Pause menu item only renders when rulerRule exists, but canPause can be true from promRule abilities alone
body: The Pause menu item is gated on `canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) && groupIdentifier.groupOrigin === 'grafana'`. However, `canPause` is computed as `(pauseSupported && pauseAllowed) || (grafanaPauseSupported && grafanaPauseAllowed)`. In the list view where rulerRule is undefined (ruler API removed), `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(undefined)` returns false, so the Pause menu item will NEVER render even when the user has pause permission via the Grafana prom rule abilities (grafanaPauseSupported && grafanaPauseAllowed). This is a functional regression: the pause action is available in the abilities check but the menu item is unreachable for Grafana-managed rules in the list view. The MenuItemPauseRule component also requires a rulerRule prop, so it cannot be rendered without ruler data — the pause feature is effectively broken in the list view for Grafana rules.

title: Delete menu item requires rulerRule, but canDelete can be true from promRule abilities alone
body: The Delete menu item is gated on `canDelete && rulerRule`. `canDelete` is computed as `(deleteSupported && deleteAllowed) || (grafanaDeleteSupported && grafanaDeleteAllowed)`. In the list view where rulerRule is undefined (ruler API removed per the PR description), `rulerRule` is undefined so the Delete menu item will NEVER render, even when the user has delete permission via the Grafana prom rule abilities. Additionally, `handleDelete(rulerRule, groupIdentifier)` is called with an undefined rulerRule, which would crash or misbehave if the menu item could render. This is a functional regression: users cannot delete Grafana-managed rules from the list view's action menu. The delete flow needs to be reworked to work without a rulerRule (e.g., using the promRule identifier), or the menu item gating needs to be fixed.

title: DeclareIncidentMenuItem accesses promRule.state without null check
body: `shouldShowDeclareIncidentButton` is computed as `(!isOpenSourceEdition() || isLocalDevEnv()) && prometheusRuleType.alertingRule(promRule) && promRule.state === PromAlertingRuleState.Firing`. The `prometheusRuleType.alertingRule(promRule)` check returns false when promRule is undefined (it checks `typeof rule === 'object'`), so short-circuit evaluation prevents the `promRule.state` access. However, this relies on the implementation detail of prometheusRuleType.alertingRule. More importantly, at line 134, `<DeclareIncidentMenuItem title={promRule.name} url={''} />` accesses `promRule.name` — while shouldShowDeclareIncidentButton being true implies promRule is defined (due to the alertingRule check), this is fragile. Also `url={''}` passes an empty string as the URL, which is likely a bug — the share URL or rule URL should be passed instead. An empty URL for the incident declaration will produce a broken link.

title: Silence drawer only renders for ruler rules, but silence can be triggered from promRule-only context
body: The silence drawer is gated on `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) && showSilenceDrawer`. In the list view where `rule` (rulerRule) is undefined, `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(undefined)` returns false, so `SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer` will NEVER render even when the user clicks 'Silence notifications' in the AlertRuleMenu (which can be shown based on promRule abilities via `canSilence`). Additionally, `SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer` requires a `rulerRule` prop — passing undefined would be a type error. This means the silence action is advertised in the menu but clicking it does nothing (the drawer never opens) for Grafana-managed rules in the list view. This is a functional regression.

title: Delete modal handler uses identifier but delete flow may not work without rulerRule
body: `handleDelete={() => showDeleteModal(identifier, groupIdentifier)}` passes the identifier to the delete modal. The `useDeleteModal` hook and DeleteModal component are not shown in the diff, but previously the delete flow relied on having a rulerRule to construct the delete request. With the ruler API removed from the list view, the delete modal may attempt to fetch or operate on a ruler rule that doesn't exist in the cache. If DeleteModal internally fetches the ruler rule by identifier, it will fail or show an error for Grafana-managed rules in the list view. This needs verification — the delete flow must work using only the promRule/identifier without requiring ruler API data.

title: Rule view link missing returnTo parameter that was present in the old implementation
body: The old GrafanaRuleLoader's GrafanaRuleListItem used `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`, { returnTo })` where `returnTo = createReturnTo()`. The new GrafanaRuleListItem uses `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`)` without the returnTo parameter. This means when a user navigates from the rule list to a rule's view page and then back, they will not return to the list view with the same scroll position/filter state — they will land on the default view. This is a UX regression: the back navigation behavior is broken compared to the old implementation.

title: Redundant type check in alerting rule branch
body: `const promAlertingRule = rule && rule.type === PromRuleType.Alerting ? rule : undefined;` — this check is redundant because the enclosing `if (prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule))` already guarantees that `rule.type === PromRuleType.Alerting` (isGrafanaPromAlertingRule checks `isAlertingRule(rule)` which checks `rule.type === PromRuleType.Alerting`). The `rule &&` part is also unnecessary since rule is a required prop. This is dead code that could confuse readers, though it doesn't cause a bug.

title: Creating/Deleting rule states are no longer shown because ruler data is not fetched
body: The old GrafanaGroupLoader fetched both Prometheus groups and Ruler groups, matched them, and displayed 'Creating' state for ruler rules without a Prometheus counterpart, and 'Deleting' state for Prometheus rules without a Ruler counterpart (via RuleOperationListItem). The new implementation only fetches Prometheus groups (`useGetGrafanaGroupsQuery`) and renders only `promResponse.data.groups.at(0)?.rules`. Rules that are being created (exist in ruler but not yet in Prometheus) or being deleted (exist in Prometheus but removed from ruler) will no longer be shown in the list at all. This is a functional regression: users will not see rules in transitional Creating/Deleting states, which was an intentional UX feature. The tests for these states were removed (the old tests 'should render rule with url and creating state when only ruler rule exists' and 'should render delete rule operation list item when only prom rule exists' were deleted).

title: Missing key prop on GrafanaRuleListItem in FilterView usage
body: In FilterView.tsx line 157, `<GrafanaRuleListItem rule={rule} groupIdentifier={groupIdentifier} namespaceName={ruleWithOrigin.namespaceName} showLocation={true} />` is rendered without a `key` prop. The surrounding `rules.map()` uses `key` for other branches (DataSourceRuleLoader gets `key={key}`, UnknownRuleListItem gets `key={key}`), but the GrafanaRuleListItem branch is missing the key. React will warn about missing keys in lists, and reconciliation may be inefficient. The `key` variable is available in scope (destructured from ruleWithOrigin at line 152) and should be passed as `key={key}`.

title: Extra closing brace in Grafana rule key template literal
body: `return `grafana-${namespace.uid}-${groupName}-${rule.uid}}`;` — there is an extra `}` at the end of the template literal before the closing backtick. This produces keys like `grafana-uid-groupname-ruleuid}` with a trailing `}`. While this doesn't break uniqueness (the extra character is consistent), it's clearly a typo and produces malformed keys. It should be `grafana-${namespace.uid}-${groupName}-${rule.uid}`.

title: useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities calls useFolder for every rule, causing N+1 folder fetches in list view
body: `useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable` calls `useFolder(folderUID)` for each rule. In the alert list view with ~80 rules, this means up to 80 calls to useFolder. If useFolder fetches folder data via API (not cached), this results in N+1 requests. The old implementation used `useIsRuleEditable(rulesSourceName, rule)` which likely had similar behavior, but the new hook is called from AlertRuleMenu and RuleActionsButtons for every rule in the list. If folders are cached by RTK Query, this is fine, but if not, this is a significant performance regression. The comment in the old code ('This hook is being called a lot in different places... In some cases multiple times for ~80 rules') suggests this was a known concern. Additionally, `useGrafanaRulesSilenceSupport` calls `useGetGrafanaAlertingConfigurationStatusQuery` for every rule — this is an RTK Query hook so it should be cached/deduplicated, but worth verifying.

title: skipToken pattern violates Rules of Hooks — useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities is always called even when skipToken is passed
body: The `skipToken` pattern is used to conditionally skip the `useGrafanaPromRuleAbility`/`useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` hooks when the rule is not a Grafana prom rule. However, looking at the implementation: `useGrafanaPromRuleAbility(rule, action)` calls `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(rule === skipToken ? undefined : rule)` unconditionally. This means `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` is ALWAYS called, which internally calls `useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable(undefined)`, `useAlertingAbility`, `useGrafanaRulesSilenceSupport`, and `useCanSilenceInFolder(undefined)`. These hooks are always executed regardless of skipToken. The skipToken only affects the `rule` parameter passed to useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities (undefined vs actual rule), not whether the hooks run. This is actually fine for Rules of Hooks (hooks are always called in the same order), but the skipToken pattern is misleading — it doesn't actually skip any hook execution, it just passes undefined. The real concern is that `useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable(undefined)` calls `useFolder(undefined)` and `useGrafanaRulesSilenceSupport()` calls an API query — these run for EVERY rule in the list, including cloud rules where they're irrelevant. For cloud rules, this means unnecessary folder lookups and potentially unnecessary API calls.

title: Test names are inverted — 'Should not render Edit button for users with the update permission' tests the wrong scenario
body: The test at line 63 is named 'Should not render Edit button for users with the update permission' but it mocks `useIsRuleEditable.mockReturnValue({ loading: false, isEditable: true })` — i.e., the user HAS the update permission (isEditable: true). The assertion is `expect(ui.actionButtons.edit.query()).not.toBeInTheDocument()` — expecting the Edit button NOT to be rendered. This is contradictory: if the user has update permission (isEditable: true), the Edit button SHOULD be rendered. Either the test name is wrong (should be 'without the update permission') or the mock/assertion is wrong. The same issue exists at lines 74, 89, and 100. These tests are either testing the wrong thing or have inverted names, making them unreliable as regression tests.

title: Test mocks useGrafanaPromRuleAbility but the component uses useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities (plural)
body: In the 'Grafana rules action buttons' tests, `mocks.useGrafanaPromRuleAbility.mockImplementation(...)` is set up (singular hook), but the AlertRuleMenu component uses `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` (plural). The test also mocks `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` separately. The singular hook mock is unnecessary for these tests since RuleActionsButtons.V2 uses `useGrafanaPromRuleAbility` (singular) for the Edit button check, but the test setup is confusing — it mocks both singular and plural hooks with similar logic. If RuleActionsButtons.V2 is the component under test, the singular mock is relevant; if AlertRuleMenu is also rendered (via the More button), the plural mock is relevant. The test setup is overly complex and potentially fragile, but not necessarily wrong.

title: Test asserts exactly 4 menu items but Delete is missing from the expected list despite delete permissions being granted
body: The test 'should render correct menu actions when More button is clicked' grants delete permissions (`AccessControlAction.AlertingRuleDelete` in both grantUserPermissions and setFolderAccessControl) and asserts `expect(menuItems.length).toBe(4)` with expected items: Silence, Copy link, Duplicate, Export. However, Delete is NOT in the expected list despite delete permissions being granted. Looking at AlertRuleMenu, the Delete menu item requires `canDelete && rulerRule` — since rulerRule is undefined in the list view (per the PR's goal of removing ruler API calls), the Delete item will not render. So the test passes with 4 items, but this actually documents the bug: Delete is silently missing from the menu even when the user has delete permission. The test should either expect Delete to be present (and fail, revealing the bug) or explicitly document that Delete is not available in the list view. As written, the test masks the regression.

title: Test 'should not render edit button when user lacks edit permissions' doesn't revoke global permissions
body: The test overrides folder access control to deny editing (`setFolderAccessControl({ [AccessControlAction.AlertingRuleUpdate]: false, ... })`), but the `beforeEach` grants global permissions via `grantUserPermissions([AccessControlAction.AlertingRuleUpdate, ...])`. The `useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable` hook checks `ctx.hasPermissionInMetadata(rulesPermissions.update, folder)` — this checks folder-scoped permissions in metadata, not global permissions. However, if the permission check falls back to global permissions when folder metadata doesn't have the permission, the test might not actually deny edit access. The test asserts the edit button is not present, but if the global permission grants edit access regardless of folder metadata, the test would fail — or if it passes, it might be because the folder metadata check correctly overrides. This is unclear from the code shown and the test may not be testing what it claims.

title: Stale comment about ruler preload after removing ruler prefetch
body: The comment at lines 81-82 says 'This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules, but it improves the UX / Because the user waits a bit longer for the initial load but doesn't need to wait for each group to be loaded'. However, the ruler prefetch code (`alertRuleApi.util.prefetch('getGrafanaRulerGroup', ...)`) was removed in this PR. The comment now refers to preloading ruler rules that are no longer being preloaded. The comment should be updated to reflect that only Prometheus groups are cached now, or removed entirely.

title: Misleading comment '// duplicate' on useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable call
body: Line 289 has the comment `// duplicate` after `const { isEditable, isRemovable, loading } = useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable(rule); // duplicate`. This comment is unclear — it might mean the hook is a duplicate of useIsRuleEditable, or that the call is duplicated. It should be clarified or removed.

title: UnknownRuleListItem missing key prop when used as fallback
body: The fallback `return <UnknownRuleListItem ruleName={name} groupIdentifier={groupIdentifier} ruleDefinition={rule} />;` at line 70 doesn't include a `key` prop. While this is the return value of a component (not directly in a list), if GrafanaRuleListItem is rendered in a list (which it is, in GrafanaGroupLoader and FilterView), the parent should provide the key. The parent components do provide keys (GrafanaGroupLoader uses `key={promRule.uid}`, FilterView should use `key={key}` but doesn't — see separate finding). This is not a bug in this file per se, but the component doesn't enforce or document key requirements.

title: copyToClipboard doesn't handle clipboard write failure
body: `navigator.clipboard?.writeText(text).then(() => { appEvents.emit(AppEvents.alertSuccess, ['URL copied to clipboard']); });` — there is no `.catch()` handler. If the clipboard write fails (e.g., permission denied, document not focused), the promise rejects and an unhandled promise rejection occurs. The user gets no feedback that the copy failed. A `.catch()` should be added to show an error message.

title: runSplitQuery mutates the caller's request.targets via applyTemplateVariables, causing double interpolation and shared-state corruption
body: runSplitQuery now calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, ...) on each target. In the Loki datasource, applyTemplateVariables mutates the passed query object in place (it modifies query.expr and query.step on the original object) rather than returning a copy. Because `request.targets` objects are passed by reference, this mutates the caller's original DataQueryRequest targets. Consequences: (1) when runShardSplitQuery delegates to runSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts line 163), the sub-request targets get interpolated a second time — variables already replaced are re-processed, and any variable whose interpolated value itself contains a variable-like token (e.g. a dashboard variable whose value is '$__interval' or text containing '$var') will be corrupted by double interpolation; (2) the original request object held by the panel/explore is permanently modified, so re-running the query, switching tabs, or the datasource's own metrics/tracking see already-interpolated expressions; (3) the `request` object is also spread into grouped requests (`{ ...request, targets }`) and `request.queryGroupId = uuidv4()` is assigned (line 303), further mutating shared state. The fix is to interpolate on a copy of each query (e.g. `.map((query) => datasource.applyTemplateVariables({ ...query }, ...))`) and to avoid mutating the incoming request.

title: runShardSplitQuery mutates request.targets in place and double-interpolates when delegating to runSplitQuery
body: runShardSplitQuery maps request.targets through datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters). applyTemplateVariables mutates the query object it receives (it rewrites query.expr/query.step in place), so the original request.targets array elements are modified. The interpolated `queries` are then passed to splitQueriesByStreamShard, and each shard sub-request is built as `{ ...request, targets: interpolateShardingSelector(targets, shardsToQuery) }` (line 154) and handed to runSplitQuery (line 163), which — after this PR — interpolates every target again via applyTemplateVariables. This is a double interpolation of the same query objects: any variable value that itself contains a '$'-prefixed token gets re-expanded, producing corrupted LogQL (e.g. a variable value of '$__rate_interval' or a label value containing '$foo' would be substituted again). Additionally, because the objects are shared, the caller's original request is permanently mutated. The interpolation should be done on cloned query objects, and runSplitQuery should not re-interpolate queries that were already interpolated (or runShardSplitQuery should pass the raw targets and let runSplitQuery do the single interpolation).

title: Shard sub-requests spread the original request, re-introducing hidden/empty targets that were filtered out
body: runShardSplitQuery filters targets (removing hidden and empty-expr queries) into `queries` and passes only those to splitQueriesByStreamShard. However, inside runNextRequest the sub-request is built as `{ ...request, targets: interpolateShardingSelector(targets, shardsToQuery) }` — the spread copies the original `request` object, but `targets` is correctly replaced. The problem is that `request` itself was already mutated upstream: runShardSplitQuery's `.map(applyTemplateVariables)` mutated the original target objects in place, and querySplitting.runSplitQuery additionally assigns `request.queryGroupId = uuidv4()` on the request object it receives (which is this same subRequest). More importantly, since the original request.targets objects were mutated in place, any code holding the original request (panel state, query inspector, tracking) now sees interpolated expressions. Also, because the sub-request spreads `request`, properties like `targets` are overridden but the mutation of the shared target objects means the 'filtered' hidden/empty queries in the original request.targets array are also interpolated (they are the same object references), wasting work and mutating queries that should have been skipped. Targets should be cloned before interpolation and the request should not be mutated.

title: runSplitQuery mutates the caller's request by assigning request.queryGroupId
body: Line 303 does `request.queryGroupId = uuidv4();` on the DataQueryRequest passed in by the caller. When runSplitQuery is invoked from runShardSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts line 163), the `request` is the shard sub-request object created via `{ ...request, targets }` — a shallow copy, so this assignment is contained. But when runSplitQuery is called directly with the panel's original request object, the caller's request is mutated: queryGroupId is overwritten on every invocation. If the same request object is re-used (e.g. re-run, or by the datasource's query() wrapper which may call runSplitQuery and also read request properties), the queryGroupId changes between calls and any code that captured the original request (tracking, request cancellation keyed by requestId/queryGroupId) sees inconsistent state. The request should be treated as immutable; the queryGroupId should be set on a copied request object.

title: applyTemplateVariables is called with request.filters, but the shard-splitting path and other callers may not populate filters consistently; interpolation now happens before querySupportsSplitting checks
body: The new code calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters) at the very start of runSplitQuery, before the queries are partitioned by querySupportsSplitting (which checks isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) for $__range). Previously interpolation happened later (inside runQuery per sub-request), so the $__range check in querySupportsSplitting operated on the raw expression. Now it operates on the interpolated expression. If a query uses $__range, applyTemplateVariables will replace $__range with the full range string (e.g. '5m'/'1h' computed from the whole request range), and isQueryWithRangeVariable will no longer detect it — so the query will incorrectly be treated as splittable and split into 1-day chunks, each of which then gets an incorrect $__range value (the comment on lines 285-286 explicitly warns about this: 'Queries with $__range variable should not be split because then the interpolated $__range variable is incorrect because it is interpolated on the backend with the split timeRange'). The splittability check must run on the pre-interpolation expression, or $__range must be excluded from interpolation before splitting. This is a real correctness regression for queries using $__range with time-based query splitting enabled.

title: Test 'Interpolates queries before running' asserts applyTemplateVariables called 5 times, encoding the double-interpolation behavior as expected
body: The test at line 112 asserts `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)`. With 1 target and 5 shard groups (4 shard groups + empty shard group), this means applyTemplateVariables is called once per shard sub-request — i.e. the query is interpolated 5 times (once in runShardSplitQuery plus once per runSplitQuery delegation, or once per group). This bakes the repeated/double interpolation into the test suite as the expected behavior. If interpolation is idempotent for simple variables this passes, but it (a) wastes work, and (b) confirms that non-idempotent interpolations (variables whose values contain variable syntax) will be corrupted. The test should assert interpolation happens exactly once per unique query, and a regression test should be added for a variable value containing '$'-syntax to prove double interpolation does not occur.

title: New interpolation test does not cover the $__range splitting-exclusion regression
body: The added test 'Interpolates queries before execution' only verifies that $__auto and $step are replaced in expr and step. It does not cover the interaction with querySupportsSplitting: a query containing $__range must still be excluded from time splitting even though interpolation now happens before the check. Without a test asserting that a query like 'rate({a="b"}[$__range])' is NOT split into multiple runQuery calls (i.e. runQuery called once with the full range), the regression described in querySplitting.ts lines 285-286 (interpolated $__range no longer detected, query incorrectly split, wrong $__range per chunk) would not be caught.

title: runSplitQuery mutates the caller's request.targets via applyTemplateVariables, causing double interpolation and corrupted queries when called from shard splitting
body: runSplitQuery now maps request.targets through datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, ...). In the Loki datasource, applyTemplateVariables performs template variable interpolation in-place on the query object (it mutates query.expr and other fields, as evidenced by the shardQuerySplitting test mocks which do `query.expr = query.expr.replace(...)` and return the same object). runShardSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts:48-54) already interpolates the targets with applyTemplateVariables and then passes a subRequest built from the original `request` object into runSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts:163). Because the subRequest spreads `...request` but shares the same target object references, runSplitQuery interpolates the already-interpolated queries a second time. Consequences: (1) variables that expand to text containing `$`-like patterns or already-interpolated values can be re-interpolated, corrupting the LogQL expression; (2) `$__interval`/`$__range`-style variables are computed against the split sub-range on the second pass, producing wrong step/range values; (3) any variable whose interpolated output resembles a variable name gets expanded again. The shard-splitting path therefore executes queries with doubly-interpolated expressions. Fix: either make applyTemplateVariables return a copy (non-mutating), or have runSplitQuery/runShardSplitQuery operate on cloned targets so interpolation happens exactly once per query execution path.

title: Shard-split sub-requests re-interpolate already-interpolated targets inside runSplitQuery, and the shard selector can be corrupted by the second interpolation pass
body: runShardSplitQuery interpolates targets once (line 49-52) and groups them by their interpolated stream selector (getSelectorForShardValues on the interpolated expr). It then builds subRequest = { ...request, targets: interpolateShardingSelector(targets, shardsToQuery) } (line 154) and calls runSplitQuery(datasource, subRequest, ...) (line 163). runSplitQuery now unconditionally re-applies datasource.applyTemplateVariables to those targets (querySplitting.ts:296-299). Since interpolateShardingSelector injects a matcher like `__stream_shard__=~"20|10"` into the expression, a second interpolation pass runs template expansion over an expression that already contains interpolated content. If any template variable's value contains characters that look like LogQL or variable syntax, or if applyTemplateVariables is non-idempotent (e.g. it appends/replaces based on current content), the shard matcher or the user's query can be corrupted, causing queries to hit the wrong shards or fail to parse. Additionally, the shard grouping was computed from the once-interpolated selector, but execution uses a twice-interpolated expression, so grouping and execution can diverge. The two splitting layers must agree on a single interpolation point; as written, the shard path interpolates twice.

title: runSplitQuery mutates the caller's request object (request.queryGroupId) and, via shared target references, the caller's targets
body: Line 303 does `request.queryGroupId = uuidv4()`, mutating the DataQueryRequest passed in by the caller. When runSplitQuery is invoked from runShardSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts:163), the subRequest is a shallow copy `{ ...request, targets }`, so this assignment writes queryGroupId onto the shard-splitting request object as well. Combined with the in-place mutation performed by applyTemplateVariables on the shared target objects (see related finding), the caller's request and targets are modified as a side effect of running a split query. This is a data-integrity hazard: the same request object may be reused by the datasource for subsequent queries (e.g. streaming/refresh), and mutated targets (interpolated expr, step) would then be re-interpolated or sent with stale values. The function should clone the request (`{ ...request, queryGroupId: uuidv4() }`) and ensure targets are not mutated in place.

title: New interpolation test does not cover the shard-splitting double-interpolation path or non-idempotent variables
body: The added test 'Interpolates queries before execution' (lines 75-88) only verifies that runSplitQuery interpolates `$__auto` and `$step` once when called directly. It does not cover the composition with runShardSplitQuery, where targets are interpolated by runShardSplitQuery and then interpolated again by runSplitQuery. There is no test asserting that a query executed through the shard-splitting path is interpolated exactly once, nor a test with a variable whose interpolated value contains `$`-syntax or LogQL special characters (which would expose re-interpolation corruption). The shard test at shardQuerySplitting.test.ts:84-101 uses a mock datasource whose applyTemplateVariables is the real implementation backed by a `replace` stub, but its assertions only check the final expr/step, and the mock's replace is idempotent, so double interpolation would not be detected. A regression test that runs a query with a non-idempotent variable through runShardSplitQuery and asserts the executed expression is interpolated exactly once is missing.

title: Test expectation changed from 1 to 5 applyTemplateVariables calls without verifying per-shard-group interpolation correctness
body: The test 'Interpolates queries before running' (line 110-112) now asserts `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)`. This reflects that interpolation moved from once-per-request (the old interpolateVariablesInQueries call) to once-per-target inside runShardSplitQuery plus additional calls inside runSplitQuery for each shard sub-request. The count of 5 is incidental (depends on shard grouping internals) and the test does not assert that each executed sub-request's expression was interpolated exactly once and not re-interpolated. If runSplitQuery's new interpolation causes double interpolation on this path, this test would still pass because the mock's replacement is idempotent. The test should assert on the executed expressions (which it partially does) with a non-idempotent mock, or explicitly verify single interpolation per executed query.

title: runSplitQuery interpolates queries twice when called from shard splitting, causing double interpolation of variables
body: runSplitQuery() now maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables() at line 296-299. However, runShardSplitQuery() in shardQuerySplitting.ts already interpolates all targets via applyTemplateVariables() at line 49-52 before calling runSplitQuery() (line 163). This means when shard splitting is enabled, every query is interpolated twice. For most variables this is idempotent, but for variables whose interpolated output itself contains variable-like syntax (e.g. a variable value containing '$__rate_interval', or a multi-value variable formatted with a regex/glob that produces '$'-prefixed text), the second pass will re-interpolate and corrupt the query. It also doubles the cost of template variable resolution (which can involve async variable lookups in some datasource implementations) and breaks the invariant that interpolation happens exactly once per query. The fix is to remove the interpolation from runSplitQuery() (or make runShardSplitQuery pass un-interpolated targets), keeping interpolation at exactly one layer — the entry point of the splitting pipeline.

title: runSplitQuery mutates the caller's request object and interpolated targets are shared by reference with sub-requests
body: runSplitQuery() calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, ...) on each target of request.targets. Depending on the datasource implementation, applyTemplateVariables may mutate the query object in place (the shardQuerySplitting test mock at shardQuerySplitting.test.ts:56-59 does exactly this: `query.expr = query.expr.replace(...)`). Since request.targets objects are passed by reference, this mutates the original request the caller (e.g. the datasource query() pipeline or Explore) holds. Additionally, at line 303 `request.queryGroupId = uuidv4()` mutates the caller's request object, and at lines 315/337/344 the code spreads `{ ...request, targets }` — the targets arrays contain the same query object references, so later mutations (e.g. adjustTargetsFromResponseState creates new objects, but interpolateShardingSelector in the shard path mutates expr) can leak across sub-requests. The consequence is that a query issued once can have its expr permanently rewritten (e.g. '$__auto' replaced with '5m'), so a subsequent refresh of the same panel would interpolate an already-interpolated query, producing wrong results or double-interpolation artifacts. The function should clone targets before interpolation (e.g. `.map((query) => datasource.applyTemplateVariables({ ...query }, ...))`) and avoid mutating the passed-in request.

title: Switch from interpolateVariablesInQueries to applyTemplateVariables changes the interpolation contract (scopedVars/filters handling and per-query vs per-request semantics)
body: runShardSplitQuery() previously called datasource.interpolateVariablesInQueries(request.targets, request.scopedVars), which is the standard Grafana datasource API that interpolates a batch of queries and returns new query objects. The change replaces it with a per-query call to datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters). Two contract differences matter: (1) applyTemplateVariables receives request.filters, which interpolateVariablesInQueries does not — for Loki this is used for ad-hoc filter interpolation, so behavior changes for queries issued with ad-hoc filters; whether that is intended needs verification, and the previous behavior (no filter interpolation in the shard path) may have been deliberate. (2) applyTemplateVariables is documented to return a new query object, but the Loki implementation and the test mocks mutate and return the same object; combined with the shared references described in the querySplitting.ts finding, this creates cross-request contamination. The PR should either keep using interpolateVariablesInQueries (which handles the batch correctly) or ensure applyTemplateVariables results are cloned. At minimum, the behavioral change around request.filters must be intentional and covered by a test with ad-hoc filters present.

title: querySupportsSplitting checks for $__range on the interpolated expr, but interpolation of $__range happens per split sub-range later, so the guard no longer matches the original intent
body: querySupportsSplitting() (line 282-289) excludes queries containing the $__range variable from time splitting, with the comment that $__range is interpolated on the backend with the split time range and would be incorrect. Previously this check ran on the raw, un-interpolated expr, so a query literally containing '$__range' was detected. Now that runSplitQuery() interpolates targets first (line 296-299), the expr passed to querySupportsSplitting has already had template variables replaced. If the user's query contains '$__range', applyTemplateVariables will typically replace it with a concrete duration (e.g. '1d') based on the full request range — so isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) will no longer find '$__range' and the query will be incorrectly included in time splitting. Each split sub-request would then carry a range duration computed from the full range rather than the sub-range, producing wrong results for exactly the queries this guard was written to protect. The range-variable check must run on the original, un-interpolated expr (i.e. partition before mapping through applyTemplateVariables, or check the raw targets in parallel).

title: New shard-splitting interpolation test does not cover the double-interpolation path between runShardSplitQuery and runSplitQuery
body: The new test 'Interpolates queries before execution' (lines 84-101) creates a datasource whose replace() substitutes $__auto and $step, then asserts the final runQuery expr. However, runShardSplitQuery calls runSplitQuery internally (shardQuerySplitting.ts:163), and runSplitQuery now also calls applyTemplateVariables. The test's mock datasource is created via createLokiDatasource({ replace, getVariables }) — if applyTemplateVariables on that mock delegates to replace(), the query is interpolated twice in this test, but the assertions only check the final string, which happens to be stable under double replacement ('5m' contains no variables). There is no test asserting that applyTemplateVariables is called exactly once per query across the shard+split pipeline, and no test with a variable whose value itself contains a variable-like token, which would expose the double-interpolation bug. A test should assert the call count of applyTemplateVariables (or use a non-idempotent replacement) to lock in single interpolation.

title: New interpolation test does not verify that hidden/empty queries are filtered before interpolation, nor that interpolation errors are handled
body: The new test 'Interpolates queries before execution' (lines 75-88) only covers the happy path for a single visible, non-empty query. The interpolation was inserted after the .filter() calls, which is correct, but there is no test confirming that hidden or empty queries are not passed to applyTemplateVariables (avoiding unnecessary variable lookups and side effects), and no test for what happens when applyTemplateVariables throws or returns a query with an empty expr after interpolation (e.g. a variable that resolves to an empty string) — such a query would flow into isLogsQuery/partitioning and be sent to Loki as an empty selector. Given the PR's stated goal is to move interpolation to the start of the process, the edge cases of that reordering (interpolation exceptions aborting the whole split pipeline, empty post-interpolation exprs) should be covered.

title: MetricsMiddleware shares mutable `next` field across all wrapped clients, causing data race and cross-request client confusion
body: NewMetricsMiddleware creates a single *MetricsMiddleware instance (`imw`) and then mutates its `next` field inside the ClientMiddlewareFunc closure: `imw.next = next; return imw`. Because the same `imw` pointer is returned for every invocation of the middleware function, all plugin clients wrapped by this middleware share the same `next` field. The middleware factory is invoked once per plugin client (per plugin/process), so the last client to be wrapped overwrites `next` for all previously wrapped clients. This is a data race if clients are created concurrently, and even when created sequentially it means every wrapped client will call whichever `next` was assigned last — requests for plugin A will be forwarded to plugin B's client. The consequence is that plugin requests are routed to the wrong plugin backend (data integrity/security issue: queries for one data source can be sent to another plugin), and concurrent client construction triggers the Go race detector. The correct pattern (used by the other middlewares in this package, e.g. LoggerMiddleware and ContextualLoggerMiddleware) is to construct a new middleware struct per invocation: `return &MetricsMiddleware{pluginMetrics: ..., pluginRegistry: ..., next: next}`. The metrics registration part (newMetricsMiddleware) can stay shared, but the per-client state must not be.

title: Test function still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware after rename to MetricsMiddleware
body: The test function is still named `TestInstrumentationMiddleware` even though the middleware under test was renamed to `MetricsMiddleware` and the file was renamed to `metrics_middleware_test.go`. The test should be renamed to `TestMetricsMiddleware` for consistency with the renamed code; leaving the old name makes it harder to locate the tests for the renamed component and is inconsistent with the stated goal of the PR (better naming and consistency).

title: Logger name 'plugin.instrumentation' no longer matches the renamed middleware
body: The logger middleware is still constructed with the logger name `log.New("plugin.instrumentation")` even though the instrumentation middleware was renamed to metrics middleware and the contextual logging was moved out of it. The logger name should be updated (e.g. `plugin.metrics` or similar) to reflect the actual component, otherwise log filtering/queries by logger name will be misleading. This is a leftover from the rename.

title: ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add contextual attributes for SubscribeStream, PublishStream, and RunStream
body: The new ContextualLoggerMiddleware only calls instrumentContext (which adds endpoint/pluginId/dsName/dsUID/uname contextual log attributes) for QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, and CollectMetrics. For SubscribeStream, PublishStream, and RunStream it passes the context through unchanged. Previously (in the old InstrumentationMiddleware) the same three streaming methods also did not instrument the context, so this is not a regression, but it means streaming plugin requests will lack the contextual logger attributes that the PR description says were moved to the LoggerMiddleware. If the intent is for all plugin requests to have contextual logging, these three methods should also call instrumentContext with the appropriate endpoint constant. At minimum this inconsistency should be a conscious decision; as written, log lines emitted during streaming requests will be missing pluginId/endpoint/dsName/dsUID/uname fields.

title: LoggerMiddleware now depends on ContextualLoggerMiddleware ordering but drops traceID from log output
body: The logRequest method previously appended `traceID` (from tracing.TraceIDFromContext) to the log params; that code was removed in this PR. The traceID is still recorded as a Prometheus exemplar in MetricsMiddleware, but it is no longer present in the 'Plugin Request Completed' log line. Correlating a log line with a trace (and with the exemplar-bearing metrics) now requires joining on other fields. If dropping traceID from logs was intentional it should be called out; otherwise it is a regression in observability. Additionally, the logger now relies on `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)` picking up contextual attributes that are only present if ContextualLoggerMiddleware runs earlier in the chain (it does in pluginsintegration.go), but LoggerMiddleware itself has no guard or documentation that it must be placed after ContextualLoggerMiddleware — if the ordering is ever changed, the pluginId/endpoint/dsName/dsUID/uname fields silently disappear from these log lines.

title: FromContext silently discards the receiver's existing context when the context logger is not a *log.ConcreteLogger
body: grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext calls d.l.FromContext(ctx) and type-asserts the result to *log.ConcreteLogger. If the assertion fails it returns d.New() — a logger with only the receiver's own base context — completely ignoring the contextual attributes stored in the provided ctx. This means that whenever the logger stored in the context is not the concrete infra logger type (e.g. a wrapped logger, a logger from a different package, or a logger created via log.New with a different wrapper), all contextual attributes (pluginId, endpoint, dsName, dsUID, uname, traceID, etc.) are silently dropped. The method should fall back to something that preserves the context-derived logger, e.g. return a wrapper around d.l.FromContext(ctx) result without the type assertion, or at minimum document the limitation. As written, the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware + LoggerMiddleware combination can silently lose all contextual log fields depending on which logger implementation ends up in the context.

title: MetricsMiddleware shares a single mutable instance across all clients, causing a data race on the `next` field
body: NewMetricsMiddleware creates one MetricsMiddleware instance (imw) and then, inside the ClientMiddlewareFunc closure, assigns `imw.next = next` every time the middleware is applied. In Grafana, the middleware chain is applied per plugin client (potentially many times, concurrently during plugin initialization and request handling). Multiple goroutines can therefore write to the same `imw.next` field simultaneously, and a request being served by one client can observe another client's `next` (or a partially written pointer), causing requests to be routed to the wrong plugin client or a fatal concurrent map/pointer race. The previous InstrumentationMiddleware had the same pattern, but the rename is a good opportunity to fix it. The middleware should return a new MetricsMiddleware per invocation (e.g., `return &MetricsMiddleware{pluginMetrics: imw.pluginMetrics, pluginRegistry: pluginRegistry, next: next}`) so each decorated client has its own immutable `next`.

title: QueryData dereferences req without a nil check, unlike the LoggerMiddleware
body: MetricsMiddleware.QueryData iterates `req.Queries` and reads `req.PluginContext` without first checking `req == nil`. The sibling LoggerMiddleware explicitly guards every method with `if req == nil { return m.next... }`, and the SDK's plugins.Client contract allows nil requests in some paths/tests. A nil *backend.QueryDataRequest will cause a nil pointer dereference panic inside the middleware, crashing the request goroutine. Add the same nil guard used in logger_middleware.go (lines 63-65, 77-79, 90-92, 104-106) before accessing req fields.

title: CallResource dereferences req without a nil check
body: MetricsMiddleware.CallResource reads `req.PluginContext` and `req.Body` without checking `req == nil`, unlike LoggerMiddleware.CallResource which guards with `if req == nil`. A nil *backend.CallResourceRequest will panic with a nil pointer dereference. Add the same nil guard before accessing req fields.

title: CheckHealth dereferences req without a nil check
body: MetricsMiddleware.CheckHealth reads `req.PluginContext` without checking `req == nil`, unlike LoggerMiddleware.CheckHealth which guards with `if req == nil`. A nil *backend.CheckHealthRequest will panic with a nil pointer dereference. Add the same nil guard before accessing req fields.

title: CollectMetrics dereferences req without a nil check
body: MetricsMiddleware.CollectMetrics reads `req.PluginContext` without checking `req == nil`, unlike LoggerMiddleware.CollectMetrics which guards with `if req == nil`. A nil *backend.CollectMetricsRequest will panic with a nil pointer dereference. Add the same nil guard before accessing req fields.

title: MetricsMiddleware swallows the downstream response when request-size instrumentation fails
body: In QueryData (and CallResource), if `instrumentPluginRequestSize` returns an error (which happens whenever the plugin is not found in the registry, i.e. `plugins.ErrPluginNotRegistered`), the middleware returns `nil, err` immediately without ever calling `m.next.QueryData`. This means a plugin that is temporarily missing from the registry causes all its requests to fail outright, instead of just skipping the size metric. The request should still be forwarded to the next client; only the metric observation should be skipped (or logged). The same issue exists in CallResource at line 161. This is a behavior regression risk: previously the instrumentation middleware did not gate the request on registry lookup success for the size metric path in the same way, and more importantly, failing the actual plugin request because a metric could not be recorded is incorrect — metrics must never break the request path.

title: instrumentPluginRequest returns early on registry lookup failure, skipping the request entirely
body: instrumentPluginRequest calls `m.pluginTarget(ctx, pluginCtx.PluginID)` and returns the error immediately if the plugin is not registered, without invoking `fn(ctx)`. This means the actual plugin request (`m.next.QueryData/CallResource/CheckHealth/CollectMetrics`) is never executed when the plugin is missing from the registry — the middleware turns a metrics-labeling problem into a hard request failure. Metrics collection must not prevent the underlying request from running. The correct behavior is to still execute `fn(ctx)` and return its result, only skipping (or defaulting) the metric observation when the target cannot be resolved.

title: ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not instrument SubscribeStream, PublishStream, or RunStream contexts
body: The new ContextualLoggerMiddleware only enriches the context for QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, and CollectMetrics. SubscribeStream, PublishStream, and RunStream pass the context through unchanged, so any logging performed downstream for streaming requests loses the pluginId/endpoint/dsName/dsUID/uname contextual attributes that the old InstrumentationMiddleware provided (it had the same gap, but the PR's stated goal is to move that behavior, and the LoggerMiddleware now relies on `FromContext(ctx)` to pick up these attributes). If streaming requests are expected to log with the same context, instrumentContext should be applied there too; otherwise the behavior change should be called out.

title: LoggerMiddleware now depends on middleware ordering to include plugin context, and silently loses traceID
body: The PR moves contextual attributes (pluginId, endpoint, dsName, dsUID, uname) out of LoggerMiddleware into ContextualLoggerMiddleware, and LoggerMiddleware now calls `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)` to pick them up. This only works if ContextualLoggerMiddleware runs before LoggerMiddleware in the chain — which it does in pluginsintegration.go (line 160 before 161), but the coupling is implicit and fragile: any reordering, or any other caller of NewLoggerMiddleware that doesn't include NewContextualLoggerMiddleware first, silently drops pluginId/endpoint/dsName/dsUID/uname from the 'Plugin Request Completed' log line. Additionally, the old code appended `traceID` from `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` to the log params; that field was removed entirely and is not provided by instrumentContext, so trace IDs are no longer present in plugin request logs — a regression in log/telemetry correlation. Either restore the traceID param in LoggerMiddleware or document the loss.

title: Logger name 'plugin.instrumentation' is now misleading after the rename to MetricsMiddleware
body: The logger passed to NewLoggerMiddleware is still named `log.New("plugin.instrumentation")`. Since the PR renames InstrumentationMiddleware to MetricsMiddleware and moves contextual logging out of it, the logger name should be updated (e.g. `plugin.requests` or `plugin.metrics`) to avoid confusion in log aggregation and dashboards that filter on the `plugin.instrumentation` logger name. Existing alerting/queries referencing the old logger name will also silently stop matching if the name is changed, so this should be coordinated, but leaving the stale name contradicts the PR's stated goal of 'better naming and consistency'.

title: Test function still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware after rename
body: The test function is still named `TestInstrumentationMiddleware` even though the file was renamed to metrics_middleware_test.go and the type under test is now MetricsMiddleware. Rename to `TestMetricsMiddleware` for consistency with the rename. More importantly, the test suite has no coverage for: (1) nil request handling (the middleware lacks nil guards — see related findings), (2) behavior when the plugin is not registered in the registry (the middleware currently fails the request — see related findings), and (3) the shared-instance race in NewMetricsMiddleware. These gaps hide real bugs introduced/preserved by this refactor.

title: FromContext silently discards the context's logger when the type assertion fails
body: grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext calls `d.l.FromContext(ctx)` and type-asserts the result to `*log.ConcreteLogger`. If the assertion fails (e.g., the context carries a different logger implementation, or infra log's FromContext returns a different type in some code path), the method falls back to `d.New()`, which returns a logger with only the wrapper's existing context — completely discarding whatever logger/attributes were stored in the provided ctx. This means the contextual attributes added by ContextualLoggerMiddleware (via log.WithContextualAttributes) can be silently dropped, producing log lines missing pluginId/endpoint/etc. with no error or indication. At minimum this fallback should be more defensive (e.g., preserve the infra logger from context without the ConcreteLogger assertion, or log a warning).

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a brand-new logger, discarding the passed context and any recorded state
body: TestLogger.FromContext ignores its ctx argument and returns `NewTestLogger()`, a completely fresh logger. Any test that uses FromContext to verify that contextual attributes (e.g., those added by ContextualLoggerMiddleware) propagate into log output will silently pass or fail incorrectly because the returned logger has none of the context's attributes and none of the recorded logs of the original. The fake should either record the received context (e.g., store it in a field) or return a logger that captures FromContext calls, so tests can assert on context propagation. As written, it makes the new FromContext-based logging path effectively untestable with this fake.

title: MetricsMiddleware shares a single mutable instance across all clients, causing a data race on the `next` field
body: NewMetricsMiddleware creates one MetricsMiddleware instance (imw) and then, inside the returned ClientMiddlewareFunc closure, assigns `imw.next = next` every time the middleware is applied. The middleware factory is invoked once per plugin client (per plugin process/connection), so multiple goroutines concurrently execute `imw.next = next` on the same shared struct while other goroutines read `m.next` in QueryData/CallResource/etc. This is a data race: the last writer wins, so requests for one plugin can be routed to another plugin's client, sending queries/health checks/resources to the wrong backend plugin. The correct pattern (used by the other middlewares in this package, e.g. LoggerMiddleware and ContextualLoggerMiddleware) is to construct a new middleware struct per invocation: `return &MetricsMiddleware{pluginMetrics: imw.pluginMetrics, pluginRegistry: pluginRegistry, next: next}`. The metrics/registry can be shared, but the per-client `next` must not be.

title: QueryData and CallResource dereference req without a nil check, unlike the other methods
body: MetricsMiddleware.QueryData iterates `req.Queries` and CallResource reads `req.Body`/`req.PluginContext` without first checking `req == nil`. Every other middleware in this package (LoggerMiddleware, ContextualLoggerMiddleware) guards each method with `if req == nil { return m.next.X(ctx, req) }` before touching the request, and the previous version of this middleware relied on callers passing non-nil requests. A nil request (which the SDK and other middlewares explicitly tolerate) will now cause a nil-pointer panic inside the metrics middleware, crashing the request path instead of being passed through. Add the same nil guards used in logger_middleware.go to QueryData and CallResource (and for consistency, CheckHealth/CollectMetrics, which also dereference req.PluginContext).

title: instrumentPluginRequest returns early on pluginTarget error, silently skipping request execution
body: instrumentPluginRequest calls m.pluginTarget(ctx, pluginCtx.PluginID) and returns the error immediately if the plugin is not found in the registry, before invoking `fn(ctx)`. The same early-return exists in instrumentPluginRequestSize. This means that when the plugin registry lookup fails (e.g. plugin not yet registered, registry temporarily unavailable, or a race during plugin startup/removal), the middleware does not call m.next at all: QueryData returns (nil, ErrPluginNotRegistered), CallResource returns the error without forwarding the request, and CheckHealth/CollectMetrics return (nil, err). Previously the instrumentation middleware always executed the wrapped client and only enriched the context; now a registry miss turns into a hard failure of the plugin request. The request should still be forwarded to the next client (metrics can be skipped or recorded with an 'unknown' target), otherwise a registry hiccup breaks all plugin traffic. Note the existing test only covers the happy path where the plugin is registered, so this regression is untested.

title: SubscribeStream, PublishStream and RunStream do not add contextual logger attributes, unlike all other endpoints
body: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware (which replaced the context-enrichment responsibility of the old InstrumentationMiddleware) only calls instrumentContext for QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth and CollectMetrics. SubscribeStream, PublishStream and RunStream pass the context through unchanged, so log lines emitted during streaming requests lack the endpoint/pluginId/dsName/dsUID/uname attributes that the previous InstrumentationMiddleware provided for those same code paths (the old middleware enriched the context inside instrumentPluginRequest, which was not used by the stream methods either, but the LoggerMiddleware previously logged pluginId/endpoint/uname/dsName/dsUID/traceID for every request type it wrapped). Since the LoggerMiddleware no longer includes pluginId/endpoint/uname/dsName/dsUID in its log params (they were removed in logger_middleware.go), streaming requests now produce 'Plugin Request Completed'-style logs (where applicable) and any downstream contextual logging without any plugin identity, making it impossible to correlate stream logs to a plugin or data source. Either instrument the context in the three stream methods as well, or document why streaming is excluded.

title: LoggerMiddleware now depends on context enrichment that only happens if ContextualLoggerMiddleware is ordered before it; ordering coupling is undocumented and fragile
body: logRequest now calls m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...) instead of m.logger.Info(...), and the pluginId/endpoint/uname/dsName/dsUID/traceID log parameters were removed from logParams. Those attributes are now expected to come from the contextual logger stored in the context by ContextualLoggerMiddleware.instrumentContext (via log.WithContextualAttributes). This only works because pluginsintegration.go happens to place NewContextualLoggerMiddleware() immediately before NewLoggerMiddleware() in the middleware chain. The coupling is implicit: LoggerMiddleware silently produces logs without plugin identity if the chain is reordered, if ContextualLoggerMiddleware is removed, or if LoggerMiddleware is used standalone (it is an exported constructor, NewLoggerMiddleware, so any other caller composing middlewares gets degraded logs with no error). Additionally, the traceID parameter was dropped entirely from the log output — the old code appended "traceID" from tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false); the new code relies on the contextual logger, but instrumentContext does not add a traceID attribute, so trace correlation in plugin request logs is lost. At minimum this ordering dependency should be documented on NewLoggerMiddleware, and the traceID regression should be fixed (e.g. keep appending traceID in logRequest, or add it in instrumentContext).

title: Test function still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware after rename to MetricsMiddleware
body: The test file was renamed from instrumentation_middleware_test.go to metrics_middleware_test.go and the constructor call was updated to newMetricsMiddleware, but the top-level test function is still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware. This is inconsistent with the rename performed throughout the PR (type MetricsMiddleware, NewMetricsMiddleware, newMetricsMiddleware) and will show up as 'TestInstrumentationMiddleware' in test output/CI reports, which is confusing now that no InstrumentationMiddleware exists. Rename it to TestMetricsMiddleware.

title: No test coverage for the new early-return behavior when the plugin is not registered, nor for nil requests
body: The metrics middleware tests only exercise the happy path: a registered plugin and non-nil requests. Two new behaviors introduced by this PR are untested: (1) instrumentPluginRequest/instrumentPluginRequestSize return plugins.ErrPluginNotRegistered without invoking the wrapped client when the plugin is missing from the registry — the test always registers the plugin via pluginsRegistry.Add, so the request-blocking behavior described in the code is never asserted; (2) QueryData/CallResource dereference req without nil checks — there is no test passing a nil request, so the panic risk is unguarded. Add a subtest with an empty/unregistered plugin registry asserting that the next client is NOT called (or, if the intended behavior is to forward anyway, fix the code and test that), and nil-request tests for QueryData and CallResource.

title: TestLogger.FromContext discards the context and returns a fresh logger, losing contextual attributes
body: TestLogger.FromContext(_ context.Context) returns NewTestLogger(), a brand-new logger with no accumulated context, ignoring the passed context entirely. The real implementation (grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext in logger.go) extracts the contextual logger from the context so that attributes added via log.WithContextualAttributes (e.g. by ContextualLoggerMiddleware) are preserved. The fake does not capture or expose those attributes, so any test using TestLogger together with the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware/LoggerMiddleware FromContext path cannot assert on the contextual attributes (endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, uname) that the middleware injects — the fake silently drops them. If tests are expected to verify the contextual logging behavior, the fake should record the context (e.g. store it or extract attributes) rather than discarding it; otherwise tests will give false confidence that contextual logging works.

title: Logger name 'plugin.instrumentation' no longer matches the renamed middleware
body: The LoggerMiddleware is still constructed with log.New("plugin.instrumentation"), even though the PR renames the instrumentation middleware to MetricsMiddleware and moves contextual logging elsewhere. Log lines emitted by the logger middleware will carry the logger name 'plugin.instrumentation', which is now misleading (the middleware is named LoggerMiddleware and the metrics middleware is MetricsMiddleware). This affects log filtering/alerting/dashboards that key on the logger name. Rename to something consistent, e.g. log.New("plugin.logger") or "plugin.requests", and check for any existing log queries/alerts referencing 'plugin.instrumentation'.

title: Device limit check is a TOCTOU race that allows exceeding the configured limit
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice first calls CountDevices and then, if count < deviceLimit, performs an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT/ON DUPLICATE KEY. Between the COUNT and the INSERT there is no transaction, lock, or atomic guard, so N concurrent requests can all observe count = limit-1 and all insert new devices, exceeding the configured anonymous device limit. The limit is a resource-protection control (preventing unbounded growth of the anon_device table from anonymous traffic), so a race that lets it be bypassed defeats the feature's purpose. The check-then-act should be made atomic (e.g. a transaction with a locking read, or a conditional INSERT that fails when the count is at the limit, or a unique constraint plus retry logic).

title: updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached for any device that does not match the time window, not only when the limit is actually reached
body: updateDevice runs UPDATE ... WHERE device_id = ? AND updated_at BETWEEN (now-30d) AND (now+1m) and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached whenever rowsAffected == 0. rowsAffected is 0 both when (a) the device does not exist or its updated_at is outside the window, and (b) the device exists but was not updated. Case (a) is the normal path for a brand-new device when the limit is reached: the caller (CreateOrUpdateDevice) only calls updateDevice when count >= deviceLimit, so a new device ID will never match the WHERE clause and will always get ErrDeviceLimitReached — which is the intended rejection. However, the error is also returned when the UPDATE fails to match for reasons unrelated to the limit (e.g. clock skew pushing updated_at outside the +1m future bound, or a device whose updated_at is older than 30 days but still counted differently by CountDevices). More importantly, the error name/semantics conflate 'device not found / not updatable' with 'limit reached', and callers such as client.go treat any ErrDeviceLimitReached as a hard authentication failure. If the UPDATE matches 0 rows for a transient reason, a legitimate returning device is rejected as if the limit were reached. The function should distinguish 'no such device' from other failures and only surface ErrDeviceLimitReached when the limit is genuinely the cause.

title: Returning ErrDeviceLimitReached from Authenticate breaks anonymous authentication entirely once the limit is hit
body: In Anonymous.Authenticate, when TagDevice returns anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached the code does `return nil, err`, aborting authentication. Since TagDevice is called synchronously on every anonymous request, once the device count reaches the configured limit every subsequent anonymous request — including from already-registered devices whose UPDATE would succeed — is evaluated in CreateOrUpdateDevice: count >= limit triggers updateDevice, which succeeds for existing devices, so existing devices keep working. But the failure mode is still wrong for the intended UX: the whole point of a configurable limit is to cap the number of tracked devices, not to lock out anonymous access. Returning an error from Authenticate causes the authn pipeline to fail the request (typically a 401/500), turning a telemetry/storage limit into a denial of service for anonymous users. The correct behavior is to log and continue authenticating (as was done for all other TagDevice errors), letting the limit only affect whether new devices are recorded. As written, an operator who sets device_limit will break anonymous access for any device not already in the table, which is almost certainly not the intended semantics.

title: TagDevice is now called synchronously with the request context, removing the previous timeout isolation
body: The diff removes the goroutine with `context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 2*time.Minute)` and instead calls `a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, ...)` directly with the incoming request's context. Previously the DB write was bounded by an independent 2-minute timeout and ran off the request path; now a slow or hung database (the new code adds a COUNT query plus an UPDATE/INSERT on every anonymous request when a limit is configured) will block authentication and is bounded only by the request context. Under DB latency or lock contention this adds the anon_device write latency to every anonymous request's critical path and can cause request timeouts. If the synchronous call is intentional (needed to propagate ErrDeviceLimitReached), it should still be wrapped in its own timeout so a DB stall cannot take down anonymous authentication.

title: TagDevice now returns errors that were previously swallowed, changing behavior for all callers
body: TagDevice previously logged tagDeviceUI failures at Debug level and returned nil; the diff adds `return err` after the debug log. TagDevice is a public method (marked FIXME: unexport and remove interface) on AnonDeviceService and is part of the anonymous.Service interface used by the authn client. Now any store error (DB down, unsupported driver, or ErrDeviceLimitReached) propagates to callers. In client.go this is handled, but the change silently alters the contract for any other caller of anonymous.Service.TagDevice and for the post-login untag path expectations; combined with the synchronous call this means transient DB errors now fail anonymous authentication instead of being logged. At minimum this contract change should be called out and all callers audited; the previous behavior (best-effort tagging) was deliberate.

title: Every CreateOrUpdateDevice call now performs an extra COUNT query when a limit is configured
body: When deviceLimit > 0, CreateOrUpdateDevice unconditionally runs CountDevices (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM anon_device WHERE updated_at BETWEEN ...) before every insert/update. This is a full table scan/range count on every anonymous request that reaches the store (the local cache in impl.go mitigates repeats per instance for ~29 minutes, but multi-instance deployments and cache misses all pay it). On large anon_device tables this adds meaningful per-request DB load. Consider caching the count with a short TTL, using an approximate count, or only checking periodically rather than on every write.

title: No test covers the update path for an existing device when the limit is reached
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a second, different device is rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached when the limit is 1. It does not verify the intended behavior that an already-registered device can still update itself (updateDevice succeeding) once the limit is reached — the path that keeps existing anonymous users working. Without that test, a regression that rejects existing devices too (e.g. the rowsAffected==0 semantics described in updateDevice) would not be caught. Add a case: create device A with limit 1, then call CreateOrUpdateDevice again with the same device ID and assert NoError and that updated_at changed.

title: Tests construct the service with setting.NewCfg() whose AnonymousDeviceLimit is 0, so the limit path is untested at the service layer
body: Both tests call ProvideAnonymousDeviceService(..., store, setting.NewCfg(), ...). setting.NewCfg() leaves AnonymousDeviceLimit at its zero value, so ProvideAnonDBStore receives deviceLimit=0 and the limit logic in CreateOrUpdateDevice is disabled. The service-level tests therefore never exercise the limit, the synchronous error propagation from TagDevice, or the ErrDeviceLimitReached handling. The store-level test covers the store in isolation, but there is no test that a configured limit causes TagDevice to return ErrDeviceLimitReached through the service (including the local-cache interaction, which caches the key before the store call and would suppress the error on repeat calls within 29 minutes).

title: New device_limit setting has no documentation, sample config entry, or validation
body: cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit is read from auth.anonymous device_limit with MustInt64(0) (0 = unlimited). There is no corresponding entry in conf/sample.ini or docs, no validation that rejects negative values (a negative limit would make `s.deviceLimit > 0` false, silently disabling the limit — arguably fine, but undocumented), and no default.ini documentation. Operators cannot discover the setting. Additionally, the frontend DTO exposes it as a non-omitempty int64, so it is always serialized as 0 when unset, which is consistent with the TS type `number | undefined` only because 0 is falsy-checked in the store; worth confirming the frontend treats 0 as unlimited.

title: updateDevice time window uses device.UpdatedAt (caller-supplied) rather than the server clock, and the +1 minute future bound is fragile
body: The WHERE clause bounds updated_at by device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) and .Add(time.Minute). device.UpdatedAt is set by the caller (impl.go uses time.Now(), but the store API accepts any Device). If a caller passes a stale or future UpdatedAt, the window shifts accordingly and the UPDATE can match or miss unexpectedly. The comment in impl.go notes MySQL second-precision motivated the +1 minute fudge, but basing the window on the row's own updated_at value (which for an existing row is the previous update time, not now) means the BETWEEN window is [device.UpdatedAt-30d, device.UpdatedAt+1m] — for a returning device whose stored updated_at is, say, 10 days ago and whose new UpdatedAt is now, the stored row's updated_at (10 days ago) falls inside [now-30d, now+1m], so it matches; this works, but it is subtle and undocumented. Using the server clock (time.Now()) for the window would be clearer and immune to caller-supplied timestamps.

title: Device limit enforcement is racy: check-then-act allows exceeding the configured limit
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice first calls CountDevices and only falls back to updateDevice when count >= deviceLimit, otherwise it performs an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT. This is a classic TOCTOU race: under concurrent anonymous requests (the normal case for a public Grafana instance), many goroutines can observe count < limit simultaneously and all insert new devices, exceeding AnonymousDeviceLimit. The limit is a security/abuse-control feature (bounding anonymous device rows), so silently exceeding it defeats its purpose. The count and insert are not performed in a single transaction or with any locking, so there is no atomicity. A correct implementation would enforce the limit atomically (e.g., conditional INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < limit, or a transaction with locking/serializable isolation), or at minimum treat the limit as best-effort and document it.

title: updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached for any device that does not exist or is outside the time window, not only when the limit is reached
body: updateDevice runs an UPDATE ... WHERE device_id = ? AND updated_at BETWEEN ? AND ? and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached whenever RowsAffected == 0.
