RowsAffected is 0 both when the device does not exist (a brand-new device hitting a full table) and when the device exists but its updated_at is outside the [now-30d, now+1m] window (e.g., an expired device that the periodic cleanup has not yet removed, or clock skew). In both cases the caller (client.go Authenticate) treats ErrDeviceLimitReached as a hard failure and rejects the anonymous request, so legitimate first-time visitors can be denied access even though the device table is not actually full. The error conflates 'device not found / stale' with 'limit reached'; the update path should distinguish these (e.g., fall back to insert when the row is missing, or return a distinct error) instead of failing authentication.

title: Anonymous authentication is now performed synchronously on the request path with no timeout, and device-limit errors abort authentication entirely
body: The previous implementation ran TagDevice in a goroutine with a 2-minute timeout (context.WithTimeout) precisely so that slow or failing device tagging would not block or break request authentication. This PR removes the goroutine and the timeout and calls a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, ...) synchronously with the request context. Two consequences: (1) every anonymous request now pays the latency of a COUNT(*) query plus an INSERT/UPDATE against the database on the critical auth path, adding DB load and latency to all anonymous traffic; (2) when TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached (which, per the updateDevice issue, can happen for brand-new devices), Authenticate returns nil, err and the anonymous user is completely denied access — turning a telemetry/abuse-control limit into a full authentication outage for new visitors. The limit should degrade gracefully (log and continue serving the anonymous identity) rather than rejecting the request, and the DB work should not be on the synchronous auth path without a timeout.

title: TagDevice now propagates store errors that were previously only logged, changing error semantics for all callers
body: TagDevice previously logged tagDeviceUI failures at Debug level and returned nil; the PR adds `return err` after the debug log. Combined with the synchronous call in client.go, any transient DB error (connection pool exhaustion, timeout, deadlock) now propagates up through Authenticate. In client.go only ErrDeviceLimitReached is treated as fatal, but other callers of TagDevice (and any future callers) now receive errors they did not before, and the local-cache set in tagDeviceUI (line 87) happens before the DB write, so a failed write still marks the device as cached for ~29 minutes, suppressing retries. The change silently alters the contract of a public-ish method (marked FIXME: Unexport) without updating its other call sites or tests to cover the new error propagation.

title: Every anonymous request now runs an unconditional COUNT(*) over the anon_device table before insert
body: When deviceLimit > 0, CreateOrUpdateDevice executes `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM anon_device WHERE updated_at BETWEEN ? AND ?` on every single call, before deciding whether to insert or update. On a busy instance with anonymous access enabled this turns each request into a full-table range scan (there is no index on updated_at shown in the changed files), adding per-request DB load that scales with the number of devices. The count is also only needed to decide the insert-vs-update branch; a cheaper design would attempt the upsert and only consult the count when a conflict/limit condition is actually hit, or maintain the count incrementally. As written this is a per-request O(n) query on the hot path of every anonymous request.

title: Device-limit test only covers the 'new device rejected' case, not the 'existing device still updated when limit reached' case
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit creates one device with limit=1, then tries to create a second, different device and asserts ErrDeviceLimitReached. It never verifies the intended behavior that motivated updateDevice: when the limit is reached, an already-known device should still be updated (its updated_at refreshed) rather than rejected. Without that case, the updateDevice path (including its WHERE updated_at BETWEEN ? AND ? window and its RowsAffected==0 -> ErrDeviceLimitReached mapping) is untested, and a regression that rejects known devices when the table is full would pass CI. A test should create device A, fill the limit, then re-tag device A and assert success and a refreshed updated_at.

title: New device_limit setting has no default documentation, no validation, and no sample config entry
body: cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit is read via anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0). There is no validation that the value is non-negative (a negative value silently disables the limit because database.go checks `s.deviceLimit > 0`, which may be intended but is undocumented), no entry in conf/sample.ini or docs describing the setting, and no default.ini documentation of its meaning (max number of anonymous devices tracked in the last 30 days). Since this is a user-facing configuration knob that changes authentication behavior (rejecting anonymous users when reached), it needs documentation and a sane guard (e.g., reject or clamp negative values with a warning) so operators do not misconfigure it.

title: anonymousDeviceLimit typed as `number | undefined` but backend always serializes an int64 (0 when unset)
body: The Go DTO declares `AnonymousDeviceLimit int64 `json:"anonymousDeviceLimit"`` with no omitempty, so the backend always sends a JSON number (0 when the setting is unset/default). The TypeScript type `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined` and the runtime default `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined` imply the field may be absent, but it never is; consumers checking `config.anonymousDeviceLimit === undefined` to detect 'not configured' will never see undefined, they will see 0. The frontend type should be `number` (matching the always-present JSON), or the Go field should be a pointer with omitempty if absence is meaningful. As written the `| undefined` is misleading and any frontend logic branching on undefined is dead code.

title: Device limit enforcement has a TOCTOU race that allows exceeding the configured limit
body: In CreateOrUpdateDevice, the device count is checked with CountDevices and then, if count < deviceLimit, a separate INSERT ... ON CONFLICT statement is executed in a different database session. There is no transaction, lock, or atomic conditional insert guarding the limit, so concurrent requests can all observe count < limit and all insert new devices, exceeding AnonymousDeviceLimit. The limit is a security/abuse-control feature (bounding anonymous device rows), so a race that lets an attacker create unbounded device rows defeats its purpose. The check-then-act should be made atomic (e.g., a single conditional INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < limit, or a transaction with an appropriate lock/unique constraint strategy), or the limit must be enforced with a DB-level guarantee.

title: When the device limit is reached, existing devices are silently blocked from updating, breaking legitimate returning devices
body: When count >= deviceLimit, CreateOrUpdateDevice calls updateDevice, which only UPDATEs a row if that device_id already exists AND its updated_at is within the expiration window. If the limit is reached and a returning device's row has expired (older than anonymousDeviceExpiration) or was deleted, rowsAffected == 0 and the function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. The consequence is that once the limit is full, legitimate returning devices whose rows have aged out can never refresh their updated_at, so they are permanently rejected instead of replacing an expired row. The intended behavior for a limit is presumably to allow updates to existing (non-expired) devices and reject only genuinely new devices; expired rows should be evicted/replaced rather than causing a hard failure for the returning device.

title: Returning ErrDeviceLimitReached from Authenticate fails the entire anonymous authentication, causing a denial of service for all anonymous users
body: Anonymous.Authenticate now returns (nil, err) when TagDevice returns anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached. Because this is the authn client for anonymous access, once the device limit is reached every anonymous request from a new/expired device will fail authentication entirely, so anonymous access (dashboards, login page behavior for anonymous org) breaks for all new visitors rather than just being denied device tagging. The device limit is meant to bound device-tracking rows, not to disable anonymous authentication. The correct behavior is to log/metric the limit-reached condition and still return the anonymous identity (as was done for other TagDevice errors), so anonymous access keeps working while new device rows are refused.

title: TagDevice is now called synchronously with the request context, removing the previous timeout and panic isolation
body: The previous implementation ran TagDevice in a goroutine with context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 2*time.Minute) and a recover() guard, so a slow or panicking device-tagging path could not block or crash request handling. The new code calls a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, ...) synchronously on the request's context with no timeout and no panic recovery. A slow database (CountDevices + INSERT) now adds latency directly to every anonymous request, and a panic in the tagging path will propagate into the authn client. This is a performance and robustness regression for the request path.

title: TagDevice now returns errors that were previously only logged, changing the contract for all callers
body: TagDevice previously logged tagging failures at Debug level and returned nil; it now returns the error from tagDeviceUI. This changes the function's contract: callers that treated TagDevice as best-effort (e.g., the anonymous authn client, which previously only warned) now receive errors. Combined with the client.go change, any store error (not just ErrDeviceLimitReached) now propagates out of Authenticate only for the limit case, but other callers of TagDevice (including tests and any other device-kind callers) now see new error returns. The mixed handling (return error here, but client only special-cases ErrDeviceLimitReached and otherwise warns) is inconsistent and the interface comment 'FIXME: Unexport and remove interface' suggests this surface needs a deliberate decision rather than an incidental behavior change.

title: Every device tag performs an extra COUNT(*) query before insert, doubling database work on the anonymous request path
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice now runs CountDevices (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM anon_device WHERE updated_at BETWEEN ...) on every call when deviceLimit > 0, before the upsert. Since TagDevice is invoked on anonymous requests (previously in a background goroutine, now synchronously), this adds a full table scan/count over the anon_device table to each request. On instances with many anonymous devices this is a meaningful per-request cost and can degrade under load. The count should be cached, made conditional/atomic with the insert, or otherwise avoided on the hot path.

title: No test covers that an existing device can still be updated when the limit is reached
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a second, different device is rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached when the limit is 1. It does not verify the intended positive case: that re-tagging the SAME device (an update of an existing row) still succeeds when count >= deviceLimit. That update path (updateDevice succeeding for an existing device) is central to the feature and is currently untested, so a regression that rejects returning devices would not be caught.

title: New device_limit setting has no validation and no documentation of its semantics (0 = unlimited)
body: cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit is read with anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0). There is no validation that rejects negative values, and the semantics of 0 (unlimited, since the check is deviceLimit > 0) are not documented in the config. A negative value would silently behave as unlimited (because of the > 0 guard), which is likely not what an operator intends. The setting should either validate the value (reject negatives) or document the 0/negative behavior, and the new [auth.anonymous] device_limit option should be documented in the configuration docs.

title: anonymousDeviceLimit typed as 'number | undefined' but backend always serializes an int64 (0 when unset)
body: The Go DTO declares AnonymousDeviceLimit int64 with json tag "anonymousDeviceLimit" (no omitempty), so the backend always sends a JSON number (0 when the limit is not configured). The frontend type 'number | undefined' implies the field may be absent, but it will in practice always be present as a number; consumers checking for undefined will never see it. The type should be 'number' to match the actual wire contract, or the backend should use a pointer with omitempty if absence is meaningful.

title: Debug-level log statements left in production cleanup path, logging full ID lists at Error level
body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags call r.log.Error(...) on every batch (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579) with the full list of annotation/tag IDs and the SQL condition. These are not error conditions — they are informational progress messages. Logging at Error level will spam error-level log aggregation/alerting every cleanup cycle (which now runs every minute, see cleanup.go change), and dumping potentially thousands of IDs per batch into logs is a log-volume and potentially sensitive-data concern. These should be log.Debug (or removed), not log.Error.

title: Cleanup job interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute without explanation
body: The diff changes the cleanup ticker from time.Minute * 10 to time.Minute * 1. The PR description says nothing about changing the schedule; it only claims to split the annotation cleanup queries to avoid deadlocks. Running the entire cleanup suite (temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history — including two EnforceRowLimitInQueryHistory passes over up to 200k/150k rows) every minute instead of every 10 minutes is a 10x increase in background database load and directly contradicts the PR's stated goal of reducing lock contention on MySQL. If this change is intentional it must be called out and justified in the PR description; if it is accidental (e.g., leftover from local testing), it must be reverted. Either way it is a real behavioral change a maintainer must consciously approve.

title: SQLite large-batch path interpolates IDs into SQL and keys the decision off configured batch size, not actual ID count
body: In deleteByIDs, when the database is SQLite and cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999, the IDs are string-interpolated directly into the DELETE statement instead of being bound as parameters. Two problems: (1) the decision is based on the configured batch size, but the actual number of IDs in a batch is what matters — a batch size of 1000 with only 500 matching rows still takes the interpolation path unnecessarily, and conversely the guard only protects when the config exceeds 999, while SQLite's real limit (SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER) can be lower on older builds or when other statements in the same connection consume variables; the safe check is len(ids) > limit, not cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > limit. (2) Although the values are int64s fetched from the database itself (so not attacker-controlled), building SQL by string concatenation is a fragile pattern that will break or become a SQL-injection vector if this helper is ever reused with non-integer IDs. The condition should be `len(ids) > sqliteParameterLimit` and the interpolation should be replaced by chunking the DELETE into multiple statements of at most 999 bound parameters each.

title: Cleanup by MaxCount no longer deletes annotation_tag rows, orphaning tags
body: The old implementation deleted from the annotation table with a single DELETE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT ...), and the annotation_tag rows were removed by CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags in a separate pass. The new implementation has the same structure (delete annotations by IDs, then CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags cleans tags), so tags are still eventually removed — but only if CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags runs. More importantly, the MaxAge and MaxCount loops in CleanAnnotations now delete annotation rows in one session and rely on a later, separate job invocation for tag cleanup; between the two, annotation_tag rows reference deleted annotations. The test asserts affectedAnnotationTags == affectedAnnotations*2, which only passes because the test's ProvideCleanupService.Run presumably calls both cleaners. This is acceptable only if the caller always runs CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags after CleanAnnotations; the repository API does not enforce or document this ordering, so any caller that invokes CleanAnnotations alone (the method is exported on xormRepositoryImpl and used directly in TestIntegrationOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst) leaves orphaned tag rows. The tag deletion should be coupled to the annotation deletion (delete tags for the fetched IDs in the same batch loop) rather than relying on a separate sweep.

title: MaxCount cleanup condition is not idempotent across batches: OFFSET-based selection re-selects already-kept rows and can loop forever or delete the wrong rows
body: The MaxCount branch builds its condition as `annotationType ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT/OFFSET(batchSize, MaxCount)` — i.e., it selects rows at offset MaxCount, keeping the newest MaxCount rows overall. After deleting that batch, the next iteration re-runs the same query; the rows just deleted are gone, so the query now returns the next batchSize rows past the new MaxCount-th row — this part is correct. However, the loop termination relies on deleteByIDs returning 0 affected rows. If a concurrent insert adds a new annotation between the SELECT and the DELETE, the next iteration's SELECT returns a non-empty ID set whose DELETE still affects rows, which is fine; but if the DELETE affects 0 rows (e.g., rows were deleted by another process between SELECT and DELETE), untilDoneOrCancelled sees affected == 0 and stops — correct. The real issue: the OFFSET is applied to a table whose contents change between iterations, and the ORDER BY id DESC with OFFSET MaxCount is only correct if no rows with id greater than the current MaxCount-th row are inserted concurrently; a concurrent insert of a newer annotation shifts the window and causes older-than-necessary rows to be kept or, combined with the fetch-then-delete race, can cause the loop to keep selecting a non-empty batch that deletes 0 rows only if IDs collide — which cannot happen. The concrete defect is subtler: because fetchIDs and deleteByIDs are separate statements, a concurrent insert between them does not cause incorrect deletion, but a concurrent DELETE of the selected IDs causes the loop to terminate early (affected == 0) even though more excess annotations remain, silently under-deleting. The previous single-statement DELETE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT ...) was atomic per batch and did not have this early-termination-on-race behavior. The loop should distinguish 'no rows matched the SELECT' (done) from 'rows matched but DELETE affected 0' (retry or continue), e.g., by returning len(ids) == 0 as the termination signal rather than affected == 0.

title: New large-batch SQLite test inserts 40003 rows with hard-coded IDs, which will collide across subtests sharing the same test database
body: createTestAnnotations now assigns explicit IDs (ID: int64(i + 1)) and each subtest in TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp calls it against the same fakeSQL database, relying on t.Cleanup to delete all rows after each subtest. The cleanup deletes from annotation and annotation_tag, so IDs are reset between subtests — but the cleanup runs after the subtest, and if a subtest fails mid-way (require.NoError aborts), t.Cleanup still runs, so this is mostly safe. The actual gap: the new test case with 40003 annotations and batch size 32767 exercises the SQLite interpolation path in deleteByIDs, but it only runs on SQLite (db.InitTestDB default) and is skipped in -short mode; there is no test covering the fetch-then-delete race, the early-termination-on-zero-affected case, or the MaxCount OFFSET window behavior under concurrent inserts. More importantly, the test asserts affectedAnnotations == 40000 but with MaxCount=1 and 40003 rows, the loop must run ceil((40003-1)/32767) = 2 iterations; the second iteration selects OFFSET 1 LIMIT 32767 from the remaining 32768 rows, deleting 32767, leaving 1 — the math works, but the test does not verify that the surviving annotation is the newest one (highest ID), which is the actual contract of MaxCount cleanup. TestIntegrationOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst covers ordering for MaxCount=1 with 3 rows, but not at batch scale.

title: fetchIDs interpolates table name and condition into SQL via fmt.Sprintf
body: fetchIDs builds its query with fmt.Sprintf(`SELECT id FROM %s WHERE %s`, table, condition). The table name and condition are currently only called with hard-coded literals from within this file, so there is no exploitable injection today, but the function is a general-purpose helper whose signature invites future callers to pass user-influenced values. The condition strings themselves embed cutoffDate via %v and annotationType (a caller-supplied string parameter to CleanAnnotations) directly into SQL. annotationType is passed from the cleanup service as a constant (alertAnnotationType etc.), but CleanAnnotations is an exported method and nothing validates annotationType against a whitelist; a future caller passing user input would get SQL injection. At minimum, annotationType should be validated against a known set, and fetchIDs/deleteByIDs should not accept raw SQL fragments as parameters.

title: Cleanup progress is logged at Error level instead of Info/Debug
body: In CleanAnnotations (and the equivalent MaxCount and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags loops), every batch logs 'Annotations to clean by time' / 'cleaned annotations by time' / 'Tags to clean' / 'cleaned tags' via r.log.Error(...). These are routine progress messages for a normal background cleanup operation, not errors. Logging them at Error level will spam error-level logs and alerting/observability pipelines on every cleanup cycle, and makes it impossible to distinguish real failures from normal operation. They should be logged at Info or Debug level (the surrounding cleanup service already logs a Debug summary of affected rows).

title: Log statement includes a stale 'err' value that is always nil at that point
body: The log call `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err)` is placed after `if err != nil { return 0, err }`, so `err` is always nil when the log line executes. The same pattern appears in the MaxCount branch (line 554) and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags (line 576). The 'err' key is dead/misleading log output; it should be removed or the log moved before the error check.

title: MaxAge cleanup condition interpolates annotationType and cutoffDate directly into SQL
body: The batch condition is built with fmt.Sprintf(`%s AND created < %v ORDER BY id DESC %s`, annotationType, cutoffDate, ...) and passed to fetchIDs, which concatenates it into `SELECT id FROM annotation WHERE <cond>`. annotationType is a caller-supplied string (alertAnnotationType/dashboardAnnotationType/apiAnnotationType constants today, but the function signature accepts any string) and is interpolated unquoted and unvalidated into the WHERE clause. If annotationType ever contains SQL syntax (e.g. via a future caller or config), this is a SQL injection vector; at minimum it is fragile string-built SQL. The value should be validated against a whitelist of known type expressions or passed as a bound parameter.

title: SQLite workaround interpolates IDs into SQL and keys off configured batch size rather than actual ID count
body: In deleteByIDs, when the database is SQLite and `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999`, the IDs are string-interpolated directly into the DELETE statement (`DELETE FROM %s WHERE id IN (%s)`). Two problems: (1) the decision is based on the configured batch size, not on len(ids) — if the config is >999 but a batch returns fewer IDs (e.g. the final partial batch, or the MaxCount offset path), the code still takes the interpolation path unnecessarily; conversely the guard is correct only because fetchIDs is bounded by the same config. (2) Although the values are int64s produced by the database itself (so not attacker-controlled), building SQL by string concatenation is a fragile pattern that defeats the purpose of parameterized queries and will break if IDs ever become non-numeric. The condition should be `len(ids) > sqliteParameterLimit`, and the IDs should be chunked into multiple parameterized DELETEs of ≤999 parameters each rather than interpolated.

title: MaxCount cleanup can loop forever or over-delete when rows are concurrently inserted
body: The MaxCount branch selects IDs with `ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT/OFFSET MaxCount, BatchSize` and deletes them, repeating until a batch affects 0 rows. The termination condition is `affected == 0` from the DELETE. Two issues: (1) If annotations are being inserted concurrently with higher IDs, each iteration selects a fresh window past MaxCount and deletes it, so the loop keeps deleting newly inserted annotations indefinitely — the loop only stops when a full batch window contains no rows, which under sustained insert load may never happen within the 9-minute cleanup timeout, and it will delete annotations that were just created and should be kept (the newest MaxCount are preserved only relative to the snapshot at each iteration, but new inserts above the cutoff keep getting deleted). The old single-statement version had the same windowing semantics per execution but was bounded to one statement per run; the new untilDoneOrCancelled loop makes it unbounded. (2) If a concurrent transaction deletes some of the selected IDs between fetchIDs and deleteByIDs, RowsAffected < len(ids) but > 0, so the loop continues — that part is fine — but if ALL selected IDs vanish concurrently, affected == 0 and the loop exits early even though more excess annotations remain. The loop should be bounded (e.g. a max iteration count or a deadline check) and the select should be re-evaluated consistently.

title: Non-atomic select-then-delete can orphan annotation_tag rows when annotations are deleted between the two statements
body: The new cleanup deletes annotations by ID in one statement (deleteByIDs on 'annotation') but never deletes the corresponding annotation_tag rows in the same operation. The old code had the same gap for CleanAnnotations (tags were handled by CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags), so this is pre-existing, but the PR's stated goal is data integrity during cleanup and the test now asserts tag counts. Between the annotation DELETE and the next CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags run, annotation_tag rows reference deleted annotations (orphans), and any concurrent reader joining annotation_tag to annotation simply won't see them — acceptable — but if the process crashes between the two, orphans persist until the next cycle. More importantly, within a single Run() the annotation cleanup and orphan-tag cleanup are separate jobs, so tags for annotations deleted by MaxAge/MaxCount cleanup are only removed later. This should be documented or the tag deletion should be batched alongside (e.g. delete tags by annotation_id IN (...) before deleting the annotations).

title: Orphaned-tag cleanup matches annotation_tag.id, but the orphan condition references annotation_id
body: CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags builds the condition `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM annotation a WHERE annotation_id = a.id)` and fetches `SELECT id FROM annotation_tag WHERE <cond>`. The subquery correlates `annotation_id` (a column of annotation_tag) with `a.id`, which works because the outer query's annotation_tag columns are in scope. However, the fetched `id` is annotation_tag's own primary key, and deleteByIDs deletes `WHERE id IN (...)` on annotation_tag — that is consistent. The subtle issue is that the condition relies on implicit column scoping (`annotation_id` unqualified resolves to the outer annotation_tag), which is correct but fragile; it should be qualified as `at.annotation_id` with an alias for clarity and to avoid ambiguity if the schema changes. Not a functional bug today, but worth fixing while touching this code.

title: Cleanup job interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The diff changes `ticker := time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)` to `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)` in CleanUpService.Run. This is unrelated to the stated PR goal (splitting annotation cleanup queries to avoid MySQL deadlocks) and has major operational impact: every cleanup job — temp file cleanup, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, user invites, short URLs, query history (including two EnforceRowLimitInQueryHistory passes over 200k/150k row limits) — now runs every minute instead of every 10 minutes. On large instances this multiplies background DB load tenfold, increases lock contention with user traffic (the very problem this PR tries to reduce for annotations), and shortens the effective cleanup cadence assumptions elsewhere. If this change is intentional it must be called out in the PR description and justified; as an unexplained side change it should be reverted.

title: New large-batch test only runs on SQLite and does not exercise the parameterized path for other dialects
body: The new test case 'should not fail if batch size is larger than SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER' creates 40003 annotations with batch size 32767. The SQLite-specific interpolation path in deleteByIDs is only taken when `r.db.GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite`; CI integration tests run against SQLite by default, so the test exercises the interpolation branch. However, there is no test covering the parameterized branch with a batch size above 999 on MySQL/Postgres (where SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER does not apply but MySQL has its own max_allowed_packet / placeholder considerations), and no unit test for deleteByIDs chunking behavior. Given the change is motivated by MySQL deadlocks, the deadlock-avoidance behavior itself (separate SELECT and DELETE statements, no shared transaction) is not covered by any concurrency test.

title: Test helper now assigns explicit IDs to annotations, which may mask auto-increment behavior differences across databases
body: createTestAnnotations was changed to set `ID: int64(i + 1)` explicitly on each annotation and to batch-insert with InsertMulti. Explicit primary keys bypass the database auto-increment sequence. On MySQL/Postgres, inserting explicit IDs does not advance the auto-increment counter, so subsequent inserts by the application (which rely on auto-increment) could collide with these test IDs or behave differently than production. More relevant to this PR: the cleanup orders by `id DESC`, and with explicit IDs the test data's ID ordering exactly matches insertion ordering, which is also what auto-increment would produce — so the tests don't catch any divergence. This is acceptable for a test fixture, but the helper should reset the auto-increment sequence after inserting explicit IDs (or use auto-generated IDs) so the fixture doesn't leave the table in a state that breaks later tests in the same database.

title: fetchIDs builds SQL by concatenation and rejects empty condition only at runtime
body: fetchIDs constructs `SELECT id FROM <table> WHERE <condition>` via fmt.Sprintf with caller-provided table and condition strings. The empty-condition guard is a runtime error return rather than a compile-time constraint. All current callers pass constant strings, so this is safe today, but the function is a generic SQL-string builder; a future caller passing user-influenced input would have an injection point. Consider making the condition a structured type or at minimum documenting that callers must pass only static SQL fragments.

title: Cleanup logs at Error level on every successful batch, flooding logs
body: In CleanAnnotations (and the MaxCount branch at line 554, and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags at line 576), the code calls r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", ...) unconditionally after fetchIDs succeeds, passing "err", err which is always nil at that point. This logs every batch of a routine background cleanup job at Error level, including the full list of IDs and the SQL condition. On any instance with annotations configured for cleanup, this will emit an Error-level log line per batch per cleanup cycle (every minute, per the cleanup.go ticker change), which will flood logs, trigger alerting on error-rate dashboards, and obscure real errors. These should be Debug-level logs (matching the style used elsewhere in cleanup.go, e.g. logger.Debug("Deleted excess annotations", ...)), and the always-nil "err" key should be removed.

title: Cleanup job ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute without justification
body: The diff changes `ticker := time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)` to `time.Minute * 1` in CleanUpService.Run. This is unrelated to the stated deadlock fix and increases the frequency of ALL cleanup jobs (temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history) by 10x. Each cycle now runs every minute with a 9-minute timeout, meaning jobs can overlap with themselves if a cycle takes longer than a minute, and it multiplies database load from every cleanup job. The PR description says nothing about changing the schedule. If this was intentional it needs to be called out and justified in the PR description; otherwise it should be reverted to 10 minutes.

title: SQLite large-batch path interpolates IDs into SQL and keys off configured batch size rather than actual ID count
body: In deleteByIDs, when the database is SQLite and cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999, the IDs are string-interpolated directly into the DELETE statement. Two problems: (1) the guard checks the configured batch size, not len(ids) — the actual number of IDs in this batch. If the batch size is configured above 999 but a particular batch returns fewer IDs (e.g. the final partial batch, or a batch where concurrent deletes already removed rows), the parameterized path would have been safe and correct, but more importantly the inverse is also possible: the condition is on configuration, so any code path that passes more IDs than the configured batch size (there is none today, but the function's contract is about len(ids)) would exceed SQLite's variable limit and fail. The check should be `len(ids) > sqliteParameterLimit`. (2) The interpolated values come from fetchIDs which selects id from the database, so they are int64s and not injectable in practice — but building SQL by string concatenation of values is fragile and the fmt.Sprint(ids[0]) / loop pattern is O(n²) due to repeated string concatenation in a loop (each fmt.Sprintf allocates a new string of growing size). For a 32767-element batch this is ~500MB of intermediate allocations. A strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt into a []byte would be linear. The test at cleanup_test.go line 98 exercises this path with 40000 IDs, so the quadratic behavior is real and measurable.

title: MaxAge cleanup condition embeds cutoffDate via %v into SQL and relies on annotationType string without validation
body: The condition strings are built with fmt.Sprintf(`%s AND created < %v ORDER BY id DESC %s`, annotationType, cutoffDate, ...) and passed to fetchIDs, which concatenates them into `SELECT id FROM annotation WHERE %s`. annotationType is a caller-supplied string (alertAnnotationType, dashboardAnnotationType, apiAnnotationType constants today, but the function is exported on the repository and takes an arbitrary string). There is no allowlist, so any future caller passing user-influenced input would have a SQL injection vector. Additionally, cutoffDate is interpolated with %v rather than passed as a bound parameter — it is an int64 computed from timeNow() so it is not injectable, but it bypasses the parameterization that the rest of the codebase uses and would break if the value were ever a string. Both annotationType and cutoffDate should be validated/parameterized: annotationType should be checked against a known set (or mapped to a column predicate server-side), and the cutoff should be a `?` placeholder with the value in args.

title: CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags fetches annotation_tag.id, but annotation_tag has no id column — cleanup of orphaned tags is broken
body: CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags builds the condition `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM annotation a WHERE annotation_id = a.id) ...` and calls fetchIDs(ctx, "annotation_tag", cond). fetchIDs unconditionally generates `SELECT id FROM annotation_tag WHERE ...`. The annotation_tag table (see the annotationTag struct at line 663-666 and the tag-creation code) is a join table with columns annotation_id and tag_id only — it has no `id` column. The original code deleted via `DELETE FROM annotation_tag WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM (SELECT id FROM annotation_tag ...))`, which had the same problem, but the old code's outer DELETE referenced `id` too, so this may have been silently broken before as well; regardless, the new code makes the SELECT fail outright with "no such column: id" on every run, meaning CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags always returns an error and orphaned tags are never cleaned. The correct approach is to select the composite key (annotation_id, tag_id) pairs, or delete with a WHERE NOT EXISTS clause directly (which does not need the fetch-then-delete split for correctness, only to avoid the MySQL deadlock pattern — and a plain `DELETE FROM annotation_tag WHERE NOT EXISTS (...)` with LIMIT is the deadlock-prone form, so selecting the pair keys and deleting by them is the right fix). fetchIDs and deleteByIDs need to support composite keys, or this job needs its own query/delete pair keyed on (annotation_id, tag_id).

title: fetchIDs-then-deleteByIDs is not atomic: annotations deleted between SELECT and DELETE leave orphaned annotation_tag rows, and RowsAffected-based loop termination can spin
body: The new cleanup splits the old single-statement DELETE into a SELECT of IDs followed by a separate DELETE. These run in separate sessions (separate WithDbSession calls), so there is no transaction or lock continuity. Consequences: (1) If an annotation is deleted by another path (e.g. the Delete API, or a concurrent cleanup worker) between fetchIDs and deleteByIDs, the DELETE affects 0 rows for that ID — fine — but the annotation_tag rows for it are handled by a different mechanism (CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags), which per the separate finding is broken, so tags leak. (2) More subtly, untilDoneOrCancelled terminates when a batch returns affected == 0. If fetchIDs returns N IDs but deleteByIDs reports 0 rows affected (all concurrently deleted), the loop terminates even though fetchIDs would still return those same IDs on the next call if the rows still existed — this is actually correct behavior. But the reverse hazard: if deleteByIDs partially fails (some IDs deleted, then error), the error propagates and the loop stops, which is correct. The real issue is that the annotation rows and their annotation_tag rows are deleted by two different jobs (CleanAnnotations deletes annotation rows; CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags deletes tag rows), with no coordination, so between the two jobs running, the database contains annotations with tags whose annotation row is gone. Any reader joining annotation_tag to annotation (e.g. GetTags at line 439-458, which INNER JOINs annotation) will simply not see them, which is benign, but the window is unbounded because the two jobs run at different times in the cleanup cycle. The PR description acknowledges under-deletion on concurrent inserts but does not address the tag-orphan window; given CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags is broken (no id column), the orphans are permanent. At minimum, CleanAnnotations should delete the annotation_tag rows for the IDs it deletes in the same batch loop.

title: Table-driven tests share one database and hard-code sequential IDs, so tests are order-dependent and will collide
body: TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp calls db.InitTestDB(t) once outside the subtests, then each subtest calls createTestAnnotations(t, fakeSQL, ...) which assigns IDs explicitly as int64(i+1) starting from 1. The t.Cleanup deletes all rows after each subtest, but explicit ID assignment combined with shared state means: (1) if the annotation table's auto-increment/identity counter is not reset by DELETE FROM, the next subtest's explicit IDs (1..N) may collide with the sequence's next value on databases where explicit insert of an ID below the sequence value is allowed but later auto-inserts collide — on Postgres, inserting explicit IDs does not advance the sequence, so a later auto-insert (e.g. from a different test running in the same package against the same test DB, or if cleanup ordering changes) will fail with a duplicate key. (2) The tests cannot be run with t.Parallel() and are fragile against any other test in the package that inserts annotations. The explicit ID assignment was added to support the new fetch-then-delete logic (deterministic IDs), but it should either use a per-subtest ID offset, or reset the sequence in cleanup, or use unique high ID ranges per subtest.

title: SQLite large-batch test creates 40003 annotations, making the test suite slow without a short-mode guard for the heavy case
body: The test case "should not fail if batch size is larger than SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER for SQLite >= 3.32.0" inserts 40003 annotations plus 80006 annotation_tag rows via InsertMulti in batches of 500 (160+ SQL statements), then runs the cleanup which fetches and deletes 40000 IDs. This is by far the most expensive test in the file and runs on every non-short test run on every database backend (the test does not check the DB type — it runs the SQLite-specific code path only when the test DB is SQLite, but the 40003-row setup runs regardless of backend). On MySQL/Postgres CI this adds significant time for a test that only exercises the SQLite interpolation branch. The setup should be skipped (t.Skip) when the test database is not SQLite, since the code path under test (deleteByIDs SQLite branch) only executes on SQLite.

title: fetchIDs builds SQL before validating the condition, constructing a misleading error path
body: fetchIDs does `sql := fmt.Sprintf(`SELECT id FROM %s`, table)` first, then checks `if condition == ""` and returns an error. The SQL string is built and then discarded when the condition is empty. This is harmless functionally but the ordering is backwards — the guard should come first — and more importantly the guard only checks for an empty string, not for a condition that is syntactically dangerous. Since the condition is concatenated raw into the WHERE clause (see the injection finding), the empty-string check is the only validation. The function should validate its inputs before building SQL, and the condition parameter should be documented as raw SQL that must never contain user input.

title: Async legacy writes capture the request context, which is cancelled when the HTTP request returns
body: In Create (and identically in Delete at line 110, Update at line 135, and DeleteCollection at line 163), the goroutine that performs the asynchronous legacy write derives its context from the incoming request context via context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...). In Kubernetes apiserver handlers, the request context is cancelled as soon as the HTTP handler returns. Since the legacy write is launched in a goroutine and the function returns immediately after, the parent ctx is almost certainly already cancelled (or will be cancelled within microseconds) by the time d.Legacy.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection runs. The 10-second timeout is therefore meaningless: the derived context is dead on arrival, so every asynchronous legacy write will fail immediately with context.Canceled. This defeats the entire purpose of mode 3 (writing to legacy 'just as a safe measure') — legacy will silently never receive any writes, and because errors are only recorded as metrics (recordLegacyDuration) and never logged, the divergence between unified storage and legacy will be invisible. The goroutine should use a detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) to preserve values, or context.Background() with the logger re-attached) so the legacy write actually executes.

title: Create records a legacy-duration metric on a storage failure path
body: In Create, when d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) (line 45). This records a 'legacy' operation duration/error even though no legacy operation was attempted — the failure was in unified storage. This corrupts the legacy-write error/duration metrics that operators would use to detect legacy divergence, making storage failures appear as legacy failures. The correct call is d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...) (as done in Delete at line 103 and DeleteCollection at line 156). The same copy-paste mistake exists in Update at line 129, where a storage update failure is recorded via d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage).

title: Delete records storage duration with the object name instead of the kind
body: In Delete, the success-path metric is recorded as d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) (line 106), passing the object name as the 'kind' label, whereas every other method (Create line 48, Get line 73, List line 89, Update line 132, DeleteCollection line 159) passes options.Kind. This makes the storage duration metric series for deletes inconsistent with all other operations: the kind label will contain per-object names (unbounded cardinality — a metrics cardinality explosion and a label schema break), and dashboards/alerts grouping by kind will not see delete traffic. It should be options.Kind.

title: DeleteCollection records the legacy write result with the storage metric recorder
body: In the DeleteCollection goroutine, the result of d.Legacy.DeleteCollection is recorded with d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy) (line 166). This is the legacy write's outcome being reported as a storage metric, so legacy delete-collection failures are invisible in the legacy metrics and storage metrics are polluted with legacy results. It should be d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy), consistent with the other methods (Create line 56, Delete line 113, Update line 140).

title: Delete builds a contextual logger but then discards it when attaching to the context
body: In Delete, the code creates log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method) and then calls ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) (line 97), attaching the un-enriched d.Log instead of log. As a result, the name/kind/method values are never present in the context logger, and the error log at line 102 ('unable to delete object in storage') lacks the structured fields that all the other methods include. It should be klog.NewContext(ctx, log).

title: Unbounded goroutine creation with no backpressure for async legacy writes
body: Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection each spawn a fire-and-forget goroutine per request to write to legacy storage, with no worker pool, queue, or concurrency limit. Under load (e.g. a bulk import or a delete-collection storm), every request spawns a goroutine that holds the request's object, options, and validation closures and performs a legacy DB write with a 10s timeout. This can exhaust goroutine/memory/DB-connection resources and, combined with the context-cancellation bug above, leaves large numbers of doomed goroutines. At minimum the legacy write should be dispatched through a bounded worker queue (or the mode should document/limit this), and the goroutines should not retain request-scoped objects longer than necessary.

title: Async legacy Create reuses the caller's object, which the storage layer may have mutated (resourceVersion/uid set)
body: In Create, the same obj pointer passed to d.Storage.Create is later passed to d.Legacy.Create in the goroutine (line 55). Unified storage Create typically mutates the object in place to set metadata such as resourceVersion, uid, and creationTimestamp before returning. The legacy store generally expects the original client-supplied object (legacy SQL stores assign their own ids/resource versions, and some legacy implementations reject or misbehave when resourceVersion is set on create). Writing the storage-mutated object to legacy can cause spurious conflicts, wrong uid mapping between the two stores, or legacy-side validation errors — and because the write is asynchronous and its error is only counted in a metric, the two stores will silently diverge. The legacy write should receive a deep copy of the object as it was before the storage Create mutated it (or the storage-mutated fields should be reset), so both stores persist equivalent but independently-versioned objects.

title: Async legacy Update replays the request's UpdatedObjectInfo, which may re-run create/update validation against a stale or already-applied object
body: In Update, the same objInfo (a rest.UpdatedObjectInfo closure supplied by the apiserver handler) is passed both to d.Storage.Update and, asynchronously, to d.Legacy.Update (line 139). UpdatedObjectInfo is typically single-use: the apiserver's update handler resolves it once (often caching the resolved object and the pre-update 'old' object for updateValidation). Calling UpdatedObject a second time — later, in a goroutine, after the storage update has already changed the stored object — can return a different/stale object, re-run createValidation/updateValidation against the post-storage-update state, or fail outright (many UpdatedObjectInfo implementations are not safe to invoke twice or concurrently). The previous (pre-async) implementation in this file resolved the object once via objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old) and wrapped it in an updateWrapper precisely to avoid this. The async version should capture the resolved object once (as the old code did with updateWrapper) and pass that to legacy, not the raw objInfo.

title: Mode 3 tests never assert that the asynchronous legacy write actually happens, and would pass even if it never runs
body: All Mode 3 unit tests (TestMode3_Create, TestMode3_Delete, TestMode3_Update, TestMode3_DeleteCollection) exercise the dual writer and assert only on the unified-storage result. Because the legacy write now runs in a detached goroutine, the tests return before (or regardless of whether) d.Legacy.* is invoked; the mocks' legacy expectations are set up but never asserted with m.AssertCalled / AssertExpectations, and there is no synchronization (e.g. waiting on a channel or Eventually) to observe the async call. Consequently the tests cannot detect the critical regression where the legacy write never executes (e.g. due to the request-context cancellation bug in dualwriter_mode3.go): they would still pass. Each test that sets up setupLegacyFn should wait for and assert the legacy call (e.g. assert.Eventually on a mock call count, or a WaitGroup/channel in the mock), and there should be a test asserting that a legacy failure does not affect the returned result (the intended mode-3 semantics).

title: TestMode3_Get creates a fresh prometheus registry, unlike the other Mode 3 tests which share the package-level registry
body: TestMode3_Get declares a local p := prometheus.NewRegistry() (line 119) while every other Mode 3 test (and the Mode 1 tests) use the shared package-level var p = prometheus.NewRegistry() declared in dualwriter_mode1_test.go. This inconsistency is harmless today only because NewDualWriter presumably tolerates an already-registered/unregistered registry, but it means the metrics asserted or scraped in the Get test come from a different registry than the rest of the suite, and if any test ever registered collectors on p it would behave differently. For consistency and to avoid future double-registration panics, the local declaration should be removed and the shared p used (this is the same cleanup that was applied to dualwriter_mode1_test.go in this PR, where the duplicate local registry was deleted).

title: Mode 3 integration tests cannot detect divergence because legacy writes are asynchronous and the legacy API is checked immediately
body: The new 'with dual write (file, mode 3)' and 'with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)' subtests (lines 132-144 and 191-204) run the shared doPlaylistTests helper, which performs CRUD via the k8s API and then immediately reads via the legacy /api/playlists endpoints (e.g. getFromBothAPIs at line 610, and the legacy search at line 523). In mode 3 the legacy write happens in a background goroutine after the k8s response is returned, so the legacy read can race ahead of the legacy write and observe a missing/stale playlist, producing flaky failures — or, worse, if the async write is broken (see the context-cancellation finding), the test may still pass intermittently because nothing waits for the legacy write to land. The mode-3 subtests need synchronization: after each k8s write, poll the legacy API (require.Eventually) until the legacy write is visible before asserting equality, so the test both (a) tolerates the intended async delay and (b) actually verifies that the legacy write eventually happens.

title: Create records legacy duration metric on storage failure path
body: In DualWriterMode3.Create, when d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) instead of d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...). This records a storage failure as a legacy-storage duration metric, corrupting the legacy/storage latency metrics dashboards. The same wrong-metric bug exists in Update (line 129), which calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) when d.Storage.Update fails.

title: Delete records storage duration with 'name' instead of 'kind' as the resource label
body: In DualWriterMode3.Delete, the success path calls d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage), passing the object name (e.g. a UID) as the resource/kind label, while every other method passes options.Kind. This produces a high-cardinality, inconsistent metric label (one time series per object name) and breaks aggregation by kind. The failure path on line 103 correctly uses options.Kind, so the two paths are also inconsistent with each other.

title: DeleteCollection goroutine records storage metric instead of legacy metric
body: In DualWriterMode3.DeleteCollection, the asynchronous legacy write goroutine calls d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy) (line 166) instead of d.recordLegacyDuration(...). Legacy delete-collection latency and error rates are therefore recorded into the storage metric, making it impossible to monitor legacy write health for delete-collection, and double-counting storage durations.

title: Async legacy writes capture and reuse the request context after the handler returns
body: Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection all spawn goroutines that use the incoming request ctx (via context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)) after the request handler has returned. The parent context is typically cancelled as soon as the HTTP request completes, so the derived 10-second timeout context is cancelled almost immediately, meaning the 'asynchronous safe-measure' legacy write will usually be aborted right away and effectively never run (or run with an already-cancelled context). This defeats the stated purpose of mode 3 ('write to unified storage and then asynchronously write to legacy as a safe measure') and silently drops the legacy write. A detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or context.Background() with values preserved) should be used for the background legacy write.

title: Create passes the caller's mutable object to the async legacy write, allowing data races with the caller
body: In DualWriterMode3.Create, the same obj runtime.Object is passed both to d.Storage.Create (synchronously) and captured by the goroutine for d.Legacy.Create. The unified storage layer typically mutates the object in place (setting ResourceVersion, UID, defaults, managedFields). After Create returns, the caller (and the API machinery that serializes the response) may read or further mutate obj while the background goroutine is concurrently passing it to Legacy.Create. This is a data race on a shared object and can also cause the legacy store to receive an object whose ResourceVersion/UID was set by the unified store, which legacy create may reject or mishandle. A deep copy of the object should be made before handing it to the goroutine.

title: Update passes the shared UpdatedObjectInfo to the async legacy write, causing a data race and double evaluation
body: In DualWriterMode3.Update, the same objInfo rest.UpdatedObjectInfo is passed to d.Storage.Update and then captured by the goroutine for d.Legacy.Update. UpdatedObjectInfo.UpdatedObject is typically invoked lazily by each store; calling it twice (once per store) re-runs user-supplied transformation/validation logic concurrently with the request goroutine, and any state inside objInfo (or the underlying object it closes over) is shared unsynchronized between the two calls — a data race. The previous (pre-PR) implementation explicitly solved this by resolving objInfo.UpdatedObject once against the storage object and wrapping it in an updateWrapper with the already-computed object for the legacy call. That pattern was removed; the async legacy Update should receive a pre-resolved, immutable object (e.g. via an updateWrapper holding the object returned by Storage.Update) rather than the live objInfo.

title: Delete builds a log context from d.Log instead of the enriched per-request logger
body: In DualWriterMode3.Delete, line 96 creates log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method), but line 97 then does ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log), discarding the enriched logger. All subsequent log.Error calls in this method (and the klog logger in the async goroutine, which inherits ctx) lack the name/kind/method fields, unlike every other method in the file. It should be klog.NewContext(ctx, log).

title: Async legacy Delete may run after the object was already deleted, and NotFound is not handled
body: In DualWriterMode3.Delete, the legacy delete runs asynchronously with no handling of NotFound. Because the unified delete already succeeded and returned to the client, a subsequent immediate re-create of the same name (a common pattern: delete then create) can race with the in-flight legacy delete, causing the legacy delete to remove the newly created legacy object — the two stores diverge and the legacy copy of the re-created resource is silently lost. Additionally, if the legacy delete returns NotFound (e.g. the object never existed in legacy), the error is recorded as a legacy failure metric even though it is an expected condition. The previous implementation explicitly tolerated apierrors.IsNotFound for both stores; that handling was dropped.

title: Unbounded goroutine creation with no backpressure or panic recovery for async legacy writes
body: Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection each spawn an unbounded goroutine per request to perform the legacy write, with no worker pool, queue, or rate limiting. Under load (especially DeleteCollection, which is a single request fanning out to a legacy delete-collection), this can spawn a large number of concurrent goroutines hammering the legacy store, and a panic inside any of these goroutines (e.g. in legacy storage code or the mock in tests) crashes the whole Grafana process since there is no recover(). At minimum, panics in the async path should be recovered and logged; ideally the async writes should go through a bounded worker queue.

title: Legacy write failures are silently swallowed (only a metric, no log)
body: In all four async write paths (Create line 55-56, Delete line 112-113, Update line 139-140, DeleteCollection line 165-166), a failure of the legacy write is only recorded via d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, ...); there is no log.Error call. Since the whole point of the legacy write in mode 3 is to be a 'safe measure' keeping the legacy store in sync, silent failures mean operators have no log trail when the legacy store diverges from unified storage — divergence that will become user-visible the moment reads switch to unified-only or the legacy store is still being read by legacy APIs. Each async path should log the error (with kind/name) in addition to recording the metric.

title: Mode 3 unit tests never assert that the async legacy write actually happens
body: All Mode 3 tests (TestMode3_Create, TestMode3_Delete, TestMode3_Update, TestMode3_DeleteCollection) call the dual writer and immediately assert on the returned object/error. Because the legacy write now runs in a fire-and-forget goroutine, the tests return before (or regardless of whether) the legacy mock is invoked, so they cannot detect a regression where the legacy write is never executed, is cancelled immediately (the request-context cancellation issue), or races. The tests also never call m.AssertExpectations, so the setupLegacyFn expectations (e.g. line 30-32, 313-315) are not even verified. The tests should synchronize with the goroutine (e.g. a WaitGroup/channel in the mock, or assert with Eventually/AssertNumberOfCalls after a wait) and assert the legacy store was called exactly once.

title: TestMode3_Get shadows the package-level registry p with a local one, inconsistent with sibling tests
body: TestMode3_Get declares a local p := prometheus.NewRegistry() (line 119) while all other Mode 3 tests use the shared package-level var p (declared in dualwriter_mode1_test.go line 27). This is inconsistent and, more importantly, the shared package-level registry p is registered/used across many tests in the package; if NewDualWriter registers metrics on it, running tests in the same package can panic with 'duplicate metrics collector registration' depending on test order. The mode1 test file was changed in this PR to remove a shadowing local registry (dualwriter_mode1_test.go diff removes p := prometheus.NewRegistry()), suggesting the intent is to use the shared p everywhere — TestMode3_Get should be aligned.

title: Mode 3 integration test is inherently racy: it asserts legacy API state immediately after k8s writes that are only asynchronously propagated
body: doPlaylistTests (shared by the new 'mode 3' subtests at lines 132-144 and 191-204) performs k8s CRUD and then immediately reads through the legacy API expecting the data to be there — e.g. 'Do CRUD via k8s (and check that legacy api still works)' creates playlists via client.Resource.Create (line 496) and immediately checks /api/playlists (line 523-531); it updates via k8s (line 539) and immediately calls getFromBothAPIs (line 547) which GETs /api/playlists/<uid> (line 623-627); it deletes via k8s (line 572) and the subsequent legacy reads must reflect the deletion. In mode 3 the legacy write happens in a background goroutine after the k8s response returns, so these assertions race with the async legacy write and will flake (and, given the request-context cancellation issue, may fail deterministically). The mode 3 test runs need to poll/wait (require.Eventually) for legacy convergence instead of asserting immediately, otherwise the new mode 3 subtests are a source of CI flakiness.

title: Create returns the storage-created object but the async legacy create may fail, leaving stores permanently divergent with no reconciliation
body: In mode 3, Create returns success to the client as soon as the unified store write succeeds; the legacy write is best-effort and its failure is only counted in a metric. There is no retry, no dead-letter, and no reconciliation mechanism, so any legacy failure (including the systematic cancellation of the request context described above) permanently leaves the object missing from the legacy store. Since legacy APIs (e.g. /api/playlists) still read from the legacy store during migration, the object will be invisible to legacy consumers with no error surfaced to the user or operator beyond a metric. This is a data-integrity risk inherent to the design; at minimum the PR should document the divergence window/risk and provide an operational runbook, and ideally the async write should be retried or queued durably rather than fire-and-forget.

title: Create records legacy duration metric on storage failure path
body: In DualWriterMode3.Create, when d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) (line 45) instead of d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...). This mislabels a unified-storage failure as a legacy-storage failure in the Prometheus metrics, corrupting the dual-writer observability for mode 3. The same wrong-metric pattern appears in Update at line 129 (d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) on the storage error path).

title: Delete records storage duration with the object name instead of the kind
body: In DualWriterMode3.Delete, the success-path metric call at line 106 is d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage), passing the object name as the metric label where every other method (and the error path at line 103, which uses options.Kind) passes options.Kind. This produces a high-cardinality, inconsistent label value (one time series per object name) and breaks label consistency with the error-path series for the same operation.

title: DeleteCollection async goroutine records storage metric instead of legacy metric
body: In DualWriterMode3.DeleteCollection, the asynchronous legacy write goroutine (lines 161-167) calls d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy) at line 166, but it measured the Legacy.DeleteCollection call. It should call d.recordLegacyDuration(...). As written, legacy delete-collection latency/errors are recorded into the storage-duration metric (inflating storage timings and hiding legacy failures), and no legacy-duration metric is ever emitted for this operation.

title: Delete builds a log value but injects the wrong logger into the context
body: In DualWriterMode3.Delete, line 96-97: log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method) is created, but line 97 then does ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log), discarding the enriched logger and putting the base logger (without name/kind/method) into the context. All subsequent log.Error calls in this method (and the async goroutine, which inherits ctx) therefore lack the name/kind/method fields, unlike Create/Get/List/Update which correctly use klog.NewContext(ctx, log).

title: Async legacy writes capture and mutate the request context after the handler returns
body: All four write paths (Create line 50-57, Delete line 108-114, Update line 134-141, DeleteCollection line 161-167) spawn a goroutine that derives a new context from the incoming request ctx via context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...). The parent request context is cancelled as soon as the HTTP handler returns (the apiserver cancels the request context when the response is written), so the derived 10-second timeout context is typically already cancelled — or will be cancelled imminently — when the goroutine runs. The legacy write then fails immediately with context.Canceled (silently, since the error is only recorded as a metric), meaning the 'safe measure' async write to legacy storage will usually never actually happen. The goroutine should use a detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or context.Background()) with its own timeout, not a child of the request context.

title: Async legacy Create reuses the same object pointer that unified storage may have mutated
body: In Create, the same obj runtime.Object is passed to d.Storage.Create (line 42) and then captured by the goroutine for d.Legacy.Create (line 55). Storage implementations commonly mutate the passed object in place (setting ResourceVersion, UID, defaults, managedFields). The async legacy write therefore receives the post-storage-mutation object rather than the original user input, and there is a data race: the goroutine reads obj while the caller/serializer may still be using the returned object. The legacy write should operate on a deep copy of the original object taken before the storage call.

title: Async legacy Update replays the caller's UpdatedObjectInfo against a stale/racing object
body: In Update, the goroutine (lines 134-141) passes the caller's objInfo (rest.UpdatedObjectInfo) to d.Legacy.Update. UpdatedObjectInfo is typically a one-shot wrapper around the request body that computes the updated object from the old object on each call; replaying it asynchronously after the storage update has completed means the legacy store receives an object computed from a potentially stale read, and concurrent requests for the same resource can interleave so the legacy write applies an older revision after a newer one (last-writer-wins inversion). The previous synchronous implementation avoided this by resolving the updated object once (via updateWrapper) before writing to both stores. At minimum the updated object should be resolved once and a deep copy passed to the legacy goroutine.

title: Async legacy Delete ignores NotFound, causing metric noise and hiding real divergence
body: In Delete, the async goroutine calls d.Legacy.Delete and records any error (including NotFound) as a legacy failure via d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, ...). In mode 3 the unified store is the source of truth; if an object exists in unified storage but was never written to legacy (e.g. created before mode 3 was enabled, or a previous async legacy write failed), every delete of such an object will permanently record a legacy error metric even though the delete itself succeeded. The previous implementation explicitly tolerated apierrors.IsNotFound from the legacy delete. NotFound from the legacy store should be filtered out (or at least not counted as an error) in the async path.

title: Unbounded goroutine creation with no backpressure or panic recovery on async legacy writes
body: Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection each spawn an unbounded goroutine per request to write to legacy storage, with no worker pool, queue, or rate limiting. Under load (especially DeleteCollection, which is a single request fanning out one goroutine per collection delete), this can exhaust goroutine/memory resources and hammer the legacy store. Additionally, none of the goroutines recover from panics: a panic inside d.Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection (or inside the metrics recording) will crash the whole Grafana process, since an unrecovered panic in any goroutine terminates the program. Both a bounded queue and a defer/recover (with error logging) are needed.

title: Create returns the storage-created object but the async legacy write can fail silently, creating permanent divergence
body: In mode 3 the design intent (per the PR description) is that legacy writes are 'just a safe measure'. However, the async goroutine in Create (lines 50-57) swallows the legacy error entirely: it only records a metric, never logs it. If the legacy write fails (timeout, DB error, context cancellation as noted in the context finding), the API returns success, the object exists only in unified storage, and no log entry, alert, or retry exists — the failure is invisible except as a metric data point. At minimum the legacy error should be logged (log.Error) in the goroutine, and ideally surfaced via a dedicated 'dual writer divergence' metric/alert. The same silent-swallow pattern applies to Delete (line 112), Update (line 139) and DeleteCollection (line 165).

title: Mode 3 tests never assert that the async legacy write actually happens
body: All Mode 3 unit tests (TestMode3_Create, TestMode3_Delete, TestMode3_Update, TestMode3_DeleteCollection) call the dual writer and immediately assert on the returned object/error. Because the legacy write now runs in a fire-and-forget goroutine, the tests return before (or race with) the goroutine executing. None of the tests wait for or assert that Legacy.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection was invoked (e.g. via m.AssertCalled, m.AssertNumberOfCalls, or a WaitGroup/channel), so a regression that never calls the legacy store at all would pass the test suite. The tests also cannot catch the request-context-cancellation bug because context.Background() is never cancelled. Tests must synchronize with the goroutine (e.g. a WaitGroup injected into the mock, or eventually-style polling with assert.Eventually on mock call counts).

title: TestMode3_Get shadows the shared registry variable with a local one, unlike the other Mode 3 tests
body: TestMode3_Get declares a local p := prometheus.NewRegistry() (line 119) while every other Mode 3 test uses the package-level shared registry p declared in dualwriter_mode1_test.go (line 27). This inconsistency is harmless today only because NewDualWriter presumably tolerates re-registration or the metrics are created per-registry, but it makes the test setup diverge from its siblings and can mask duplicate-registration panics or metric-collision issues that the shared-registry tests would catch. It should use the shared p like the other tests (the corresponding cleanup removing the shadow in dualwriter_mode1_test.go suggests the shared registry is the intended pattern).

title: Test name says 'not implemented' for a List error case that is implemented
body: The first TestMode3_List case is named "error when listing an object in the unified store is not implemented" (line 145), but List is implemented in mode 3 (dualwriter_mode3.go lines 79-92) and the test simply verifies that a storage List error is propagated. The stale name (copied from the old TODO-era test) misleads readers into thinking List is unimplemented. It should be renamed to something like "error when listing objects in the unified store fails".

title: Mode 3 integration tests cannot detect async legacy-write divergence because assertions run immediately
body: The new mode 3 subtests ("with dual write (file, mode 3)" line 132, "with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)" line 191, "with dual write (etcd, mode 3)" line 287) reuse doPlaylistTests, which performs CRUD via the k8s API and then immediately reads via the legacy API (e.g. getFromBothAPIs at line 610, and the legacy /api/playlists search at line 523). Because mode 3 writes to legacy asynchronously in a goroutine, these legacy reads race with the async write: the legacy API may be queried before the goroutine has committed, producing flaky failures (or, worse, the test passes while the async write later fails silently). The mode 3 tests need to poll/wait (e.g. require.Eventually on the legacy read) to tolerate the async delay, otherwise the suite will be flaky and will not actually validate that the legacy copy converges.

title: TOCTOU race: cache check and cache write are not atomic, allowing duplicate work and stale reads in dev mode
body: The fast-path read (lines 41-43) and the write (line 69) are protected by separate lock acquisitions, so the check-then-act sequence is not atomic. In dev mode (cfg.Env == setting.Dev), the fast path is skipped entirely and every concurrent caller acquires the write lock and re-reads the manifest from disk, which is wasteful but not incorrect. More importantly, in non-dev mode, two goroutines can both observe ret == nil, both take the write lock sequentially, and both perform the file read; the second overwrites the first result. This is not a data race (the mutex does protect the variable), but it is a TOCTOU logic flaw: the double-checked locking pattern is incomplete because the second check of entryPointAssetsCache inside the write lock is missing. The consequence is redundant disk I/O and CDN requests under concurrency, and in dev mode every request hits the filesystem. The fix is to re-check entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the write lock (standard double-checked locking), or use sync.Once for the non-dev path.

title: Cache is populated even when reading the manifest fails, poisoning the cache with nil and a non-nil error
body: Line 69 unconditionally assigns `entryPointAssetsCache = result` before returning, even when `result` is nil due to an error from readWebAssetsFromFile (line 60) or readWebAssetsFromCDN (line 56). On the next call in non-dev mode, the fast path at line 45 checks `ret != nil`, so a nil cache entry means the error is not cached and the read is retried — that part is benign. However, if `err != nil` but `result != nil` (which cannot happen with the current code paths, but the contract is fragile), a partially-initialized or error-associated result would be cached. More concretely, the function returns `entryPointAssetsCache, err` (line 70) rather than `result, err`; this is equivalent today but couples the return value to the global, making the function's behavior depend on global state mutation order. If a future change makes readWebAssetsFromFile return a non-nil result alongside an error, that broken result would be permanently cached for the process lifetime in non-dev mode, causing all subsequent requests to receive invalid assets with no error. The cache assignment should be conditional on err == nil.

title: HTTP response status code is never checked in readWebAssetsFromCDN
body: readWebAssetsFromCDN (line 85) performs an HTTP GET via http.DefaultClient.Do (line 90) but never checks response.StatusCode. If the CDN returns a 404, 500, or any non-2xx status, the body is still passed to readWebAssets (line 97), which will attempt to JSON-decode an HTML error page or empty body. This will produce a confusing 'failed to read assets-manifest.json' error rather than a clear 'CDN returned status 404' error, making production debugging difficult. Additionally, the response body is closed but the error from Close is ignored (acceptable), and there is no limit on response body size, which could allow a malicious or misconfigured CDN to exhaust memory. A status check like `if response.StatusCode != http.StatusOK { return nil, fmt.Errorf(...) }` should be added before reading the body.

title: Typo in error message: 'asssets-manifest' should be 'assets-manifest'
body: The error message at line 119 reads 'could not find entrypoints in asssets-manifest' — 'asssets' is a typo (three s's). This message is returned to callers and may appear in logs or API responses when the manifest file is malformed. It should read 'assets-manifest' to match the actual filename referenced elsewhere in the file (e.g., line 60, line 77).

title: Cache check-then-act race allows concurrent manifest reloads and duplicate work
