body: GetWebAssets performs a read-lock check of entryPointAssetsCache (lines 41-43), releases the lock, and then re-acquires a write lock (line 48) to recompute the cache. Between the RUnlock and Lock, another goroutine can also pass the nil check and enter the write-lock section, so multiple goroutines can concurrently execute readWebAssetsFromFile/readWebAssetsFromCDN and overwrite entryPointAssetsCache. This is not a data race on the pointer itself (the mutex does protect the read/write of the variable), but it is a check-then-act race: in non-dev environments the cache is supposed to be computed once, yet N concurrent first-callers will all perform file I/O (or an HTTP request to the CDN) and each will assign the global. Consequences: wasted work, potential thundering-herd file/HTTP load on startup, and last-writer-wins assignment of the cache. The fix is a double-checked locking pattern: after acquiring the write lock, re-check `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` before doing the expensive work.

title: Error from asset loading is discarded when cache is assigned and returned
body: At line 69-70, `entryPointAssetsCache = result` is assigned unconditionally and then `return entryPointAssetsCache, err` returns both the (possibly nil) result and the error. If readWebAssetsFromFile fails (e.g., assets-manifest.json missing or malformed), result is nil and err is non-nil, but the nil result is still stored into the package-level cache. On the next call in a non-dev environment, the fast path at line 45 (`cfg.Env != setting.Dev && ret != nil`) will see ret == nil and retry — which is arguably intended — but in dev mode the cache is overwritten with nil on every failed call, and more importantly the function returns a nil *dtos.EntryPointAssets together with a non-nil error while having mutated global state. Callers that ignore the error (or that only check the returned pointer) could dereference nil. Additionally, if a previous successful result existed and a later reload fails, the good cached value is clobbered with nil. The assignment should be conditional on err == nil (or result != nil), e.g. `if err == nil { entryPointAssetsCache = result }`.

title: CDN read error is silently overwritten by file read, losing the original error
body: Lines 55-67: when `cdn != ""`, `result, err = readWebAssetsFromCDN(ctx, cdn)` is called. If that fails, err is set and result is nil, then line 59 `if result == nil` falls through to readWebAssetsFromFile, which overwrites err. If the file read succeeds, the CDN error is completely lost and the function returns success — fine for fallback semantics, but if the file read also fails, the returned error describes only the file failure, not the CDN failure, making it impossible to diagnose why CDN loading was attempted and failed. More subtly, the CDN path is currently dead code (cdn is hardcoded to "" at line 54), so this error-masking behavior is latent. If/when the CDN is enabled, the error handling should preserve or wrap both errors (e.g., using errors.Join or logging the CDN error) rather than silently discarding it.

title: Error from CDN read is discarded when falling back to file read
body: In GetWebAssets, when `cdn != ""` the code calls `readWebAssetsFromCDN` and assigns the result to `err`, but then at line 59 the condition `if result == nil` unconditionally overwrites `err` by calling `readWebAssetsFromFile`. If the CDN read failed with a meaningful error (network failure, malformed manifest, etc.), that error is silently lost and replaced by the file-read error (or nil if the file read succeeds). This makes debugging CDN failures impossible and can mask the real cause when the file fallback also fails or when the CDN error would have been more informative. The original `err` from the CDN path should be preserved or combined (e.g., using errors.Join or returning the CDN error when the file fallback also fails).

title: Cache is populated even when asset loading failed, poisoning subsequent calls
body: At line 69, `entryPointAssetsCache = result` is executed unconditionally, even when `result` is nil due to an error from `readWebAssetsFromFile` (or the CDN path). On the next call in a non-dev environment, the fast path at lines 41-47 checks `ret != nil` — since the cache is nil, it will retry, which is acceptable. However, the more serious issue is that when `readWebAssetsFromFile` returns a non-nil result but also a non-nil error (which shouldn't happen per the function signature contract, but the code doesn't guard against it), or more importantly: if `result` is nil and `err` is non-nil, the cache remains nil and every subsequent request in production will re-attempt the expensive file read (or CDN fetch) on every call, causing repeated disk I/O or network requests under load. There is no negative caching or error short-circuiting. Additionally, if a transient error occurs (e.g., file temporarily unavailable), the system will hammer the filesystem on every request until success, with no backoff or caching of the failure state.

title: TOCTOU race between cache check and lock acquisition allows duplicate work
body: The double-checked locking pattern at lines 41-49 has a benign race: between the RUnlock at line 43 and the Lock at line 48, another goroutine may have already populated the cache. This goroutine will then acquire the write lock and redundantly re-read the assets from disk/CDN, even though the cache is now valid. This is not a correctness bug (the mutex ensures memory safety), but it means that under high concurrency during cold start, multiple goroutines can simultaneously perform expensive I/O operations (file reads, potential CDN fetches) instead of just one. A proper double-checked locking pattern would re-check the cache after acquiring the write lock: `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock(); if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Unlock(); return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }; defer entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Unlock()`. This would prevent thundering-herd duplicate work.

title: Return value reads cache variable instead of local result, which is equivalent but confusing
body: Line 70 returns `entryPointAssetsCache` (the global) rather than the local `result` variable. While functionally equivalent since line 69 just assigned `result` to the global, this is fragile: if the assignment at line 69 were ever changed or reordered, the return value would diverge from what was just computed. More importantly, returning the global after releasing the lock (via defer) means the caller receives a pointer to shared mutable state without any guarantee that another goroutine won't mutate it (though dtos.EntryPointAssets appears to be treated as immutable after construction). Returning the local `result` would be clearer and safer: `return result, err`.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false, making the feature-flag check dead code and the flag non-functional
body: The function `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then immediately returns `false` in both branches (`if enabled { return false }` followed by `return false`). This means the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle has no effect: SQL expressions are always rejected with "sqlExpressions is not implemented" regardless of whether the flag is enabled. The intent of the security fix is to disable SQL expressions by default while allowing operators to re-enable them via the existing feature flag (as documented in the linked PR #81666). As written, the flag is dead code and the check `if !enabled { return ... }` at the call site (line 129-132) is misleading. The function should return `h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` (i.e., return true only when the flag is enabled), so that the gate actually respects the toggle. Without this fix, operators who legitimately need SQL expressions (and have the flag enabled) cannot use them, and the code misrepresents the security posture.

title: Stub DB methods return 'not implemented' errors, so SQL expressions fail at runtime even if the reader gate is bypassed
body: The new `pkg/expr/sql/db.go` replaces the real DuckDB-backed implementation (`github.com/scottlepp/go-duck/duck`) with a stub `DB` type whose `TablesList`, `RunCommands`, and `QueryFramesInto` methods all return `errors.New("not implemented")`. `TablesList` is called from `NewSQLCommand` (pkg/expr/sql_command.go line 30) and `QueryFramesInto` from `SQLCommand.Execute` (line 100). This means that even if the `enableSqlExpressions` gate in `pkg/expr/reader.go` were corrected to allow SQL expressions when the feature flag is enabled, any SQL expression query would fail at runtime: `NewSQLCommand` would return a BadRequest error ("error reading SQL command") because `sql.TablesList` returns "not implemented", and `Execute` would set `rsp.Error` to "not implemented". The PR description says the goal is to move the security fix into the repo while keeping the feature flag functional, but this stub makes the feature completely non-functional rather than gated. Either the DuckDB dependency should be retained behind the flag, or the stub should be clearly documented as permanently disabling the feature (in which case the flag check in reader.go should be removed entirely rather than kept as dead code).

title: Results overwritten when frame has zero rows: NoData result is immediately replaced by empty TableData
body: In `SQLCommand.Execute`, when `frame.Rows() == 0` the code sets `rsp.Values` to a `mathexp.NoData{Frame: frame}` (lines 110-114), but then unconditionally overwrites `rsp.Values` with `mathexp.TableData{Frame: frame}` at lines 116-118. The `NoData` branch is therefore dead code and the intended "no data" semantics (which typically signal to the frontend/alerting that the query returned no data points, distinct from an empty table) are lost. This is a pre-existing bug in the file (not introduced by this diff), but it is in the direct path of the SQL expression feature being modified by this PR, and it means the `if frame.Rows() == 0` block should either be removed or the unconditional assignment should be made conditional (`else`).

title: SQL string escaping by doubling single quotes is insufficient and leaves an injection path if TablesList is ever reachable
body: `TablesList` builds a DuckDB command via `fmt.Sprintf("SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')", rawSQL)` after only replacing single quotes with doubled single quotes (`strings.Replace(rawSQL, "'", "''", -1)`). This escaping does not account for backslash escapes (DuckDB/SQL string literals interpret `\'` as an escaped quote, so a payload ending in a backslash can break out of the string literal), and it is applied to user-controlled SQL before it is passed to `RunCommands`. In the current state this code path is unreachable in production because `NewSQLCommand` is gated off in `pkg/expr/reader.go` and the stub `DB.RunCommands` returns "not implemented", but the function remains exported and callable, and the escaping is a classic SQL-injection anti-pattern. If the feature flag gate is fixed (see related finding) or if this function is called from any other path, an attacker-controlled `rawSQL` value could inject arbitrary DuckDB commands (which, per CVE-2024-9264, can lead to RCE/LFI via DuckDB extensions and file access). The correct fix is to not build SQL by string concatenation at all — use a parameterized query or pass the SQL text via a bound parameter — and to ensure this code is unreachable unless the feature is explicitly enabled.

title: Error message 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' is misleading — the feature exists but is disabled
body: When SQL expressions are rejected, the error returned to the caller is `fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")`. This message is inaccurate: the SQL expression feature is implemented (see `pkg/expr/sql_command.go` and `pkg/expr/sql/`), it is deliberately disabled/gated as a security measure (CVE-2024-9264). Telling users it is "not implemented" will cause confusion and incorrect troubleshooting (users may believe the query type is unsupported rather than disabled by configuration). The message should say something like "SQL expressions are disabled" or "sqlExpressions feature is disabled" so that operators understand they need to enable the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle (and accept the security implications) to use it.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false regardless of feature flag state
body: The function `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then unconditionally returns `false` in both branches. This means SQL expressions are permanently disabled even when the `sqlExpressions` feature flag is explicitly enabled by an administrator. The intent (per the PR description and the CVE-2024-9264 fix) is to disable SQL expressions by default for security, but the implementation makes the feature flag non-functional: there is no configuration under which SQL expressions can be turned on. If the goal is a hard kill-switch, the feature-flag check should be removed entirely and the function deleted; if the goal is a default-off flag, the function should return the value of `h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` (or its negation, depending on flag semantics). As written, the dead conditional is misleading and the flag documented in the linked docs has no effect.

title: Misleading error message when SQL expressions are rejected
body: When SQL expressions are disabled, `ReadQuery` returns `fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")`. This message is factually wrong: SQL expressions are implemented (see `pkg/expr/sql_command.go` and `pkg/expr/sql/`), they are deliberately disabled as a security measure for CVE-2024-9264. Returning "not implemented" to API consumers will cause confusion and may lead users to believe the feature is simply unavailable rather than intentionally disabled for security. The error should state that SQL expressions are disabled (e.g., "sqlExpressions are disabled" or reference the feature flag), so users and support staff understand the actual reason and know how to look for the relevant configuration.

title: Stub DB methods return "not implemented" errors that are reachable and mishandled
body: The new `pkg/expr/sql/db.go` replaces the real DuckDB-backed implementation with a stub whose `TablesList`, `RunCommands`, and `QueryFramesInto` all return `errors.New("not implemented")`. These stubs are still wired into live code paths: `pkg/expr/sql/parser.go:TablesList` calls `duckDB.RunCommands(...)` (line 26) and `pkg/expr/sql_command.go:NewSQLCommand` calls `sql.TablesList(rawSQL)` (line 30), and `SQLCommand.Execute` calls `db.QueryFramesInto(...)` (line 100). Although `pkg/expr/reader.go` currently blocks the `QueryTypeSQL` path, the older/unmarshal path via `UnmarshalSQLCommand` (pkg/expr/sql_command.go:51) still constructs `SQLCommand` through `NewSQLCommand`, which will now always fail with a generic "error reading SQL command" wrapping the "not implemented" error from the stub. If any code path reaches `SQLCommand.Execute` (e.g., the legacy expression pipeline that does not go through `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery`), it will hit `db.QueryFramesInto` and return the "not implemented" error to the user as a query failure. The stub should either be removed along with the dead SQL command code, or the SQL command construction/execution paths should be fully removed rather than left as landmines that produce confusing errors.

title: Dead code: rsp.Values is overwritten when frame has zero rows
body: In `SQLCommand.Execute`, when `frame.Rows() == 0` the code sets `rsp.Values` to a `mathexp.NoData` value (lines 110-114), but then unconditionally overwrites `rsp.Values` with `mathexp.TableData{Frame: frame}` at lines 116-118. The `NoData` branch is therefore dead code and has no effect. This is a pre-existing bug (not introduced by this diff), but it is in a file touched by this security fix and affects the behavior of the SQL expression path: empty results are returned as an empty table rather than as NoData, which may affect how the frontend renders empty SQL expression results. The `if frame.Rows() == 0` block should either be removed or the unconditional assignment should be made conditional (e.g., `else`).

title: SQL string is interpolated into a DuckDB command without parameterization, relying on a naive quote-escaping heuristic
body: `TablesList` builds a DuckDB command via `fmt.Sprintf("SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')", rawSQL)` after only replacing single quotes with doubled single quotes (`strings.Replace(rawSQL, "'", "''", -1)`). This is a hand-rolled escaping scheme that is applied to user-supplied SQL before it is sent to the database engine. While the SQL expression path is currently disabled by the reader, this function remains reachable via `NewSQLCommand`/`UnmarshalSQLCommand` (see pkg/expr/sql_command.go:30), which does not check the feature flag. The escaping only handles single quotes and does not account for other SQL injection vectors (e.g., backslash escapes depending on DuckDB string literal semantics, or the fact that the input is itself SQL being embedded inside another SQL statement). This is exactly the class of vulnerability that CVE-2024-9264 addressed. Since the DuckDB dependency is being removed and the stub returns "not implemented", the cleanest fix is to delete this function and the entire SQL expression execution path rather than leave an unsafe string-interpolation helper in the codebase. If the code is kept, the raw SQL must never be embedded into another SQL statement via string formatting.

title: Malformed comment on indirect dependency line
body: Line 463 reads `github.com/fxamacker/cbor/v2 v2.7.0 // indirect; indirect0.0.0-20240809095826-8eb5495c0b2a`. The comment contains a corrupted version string (`indirect0.0.0-20240809095826-8eb5495c0b2a`) that appears to be a merge/rebase artifact where a version string was accidentally concatenated with the `// indirect` marker. This is a malformed `go.mod` comment. While Go tooling ignores trailing comments on require lines, this is clearly unintended text that should be cleaned up to just `// indirect` (the version is already specified in the require directive itself).

title: enableSqlExpressions is dead code that always returns false, making the feature-flag check meaningless
body: The function `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns `false` in both branches. This means the feature flag `sqlExpressions` is never actually consulted: SQL expressions are unconditionally disabled regardless of whether the flag is enabled. The intent (per the PR description, which says the flag 'still exists in the codebase') appears to be to keep the flag as an escape hatch, but as written the flag has no effect. If the flag is meant to re-enable SQL expressions for users who explicitly opt in, the function should return `h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` (or the inverse logic corrected); if SQL expressions are meant to be permanently disabled, the flag check and the misleading function should be removed entirely rather than left as dead code that gives the false impression the flag still controls behavior.

title: Error message 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' is misleading and leaks internal naming
body: When SQL expressions are rejected, the code returns `fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")`. This message is wrong on two counts: (1) SQL expressions ARE implemented — they are deliberately disabled for security reasons (CVE-2024-9264, RCE/LFI via DuckDB), so telling users the feature is 'not implemented' misinforms them about why their query fails and what to expect; (2) it exposes the internal camelCase feature-flag name `sqlExpressions` to end users. The message should clearly state that SQL expressions are disabled, e.g. 'SQL expressions are disabled' or reference the security advisory, so users understand this is a deliberate security restriction rather than a missing feature.

title: Stub DB methods return generic 'not implemented' errors instead of a clear security-disabled message
body: The new stub `DB` type in `pkg/expr/sql/db.go` returns `errors.New("not implemented")` from `TablesList`, `RunCommands`, and `QueryFramesInto`. These stubs exist to replace the DuckDB-backed implementation that was removed for security reasons (CVE-2024-9264). However, 'not implemented' is misleading: the functionality was deliberately removed/disabled for security, not merely left unimplemented. Any code path that reaches these methods (e.g. `NewSQLCommand` in `pkg/expr/sql_command.go` line 30 calls `sql.TablesList`, which will now always fail with 'not implemented') will surface a confusing error. In `NewSQLCommand`, this error is caught and converted to a generic 'error reading SQL command' BadRequest, which hides the real reason. The stubs should return an error that clearly states SQL expressions are disabled for security reasons, so that any path that bypasses the reader-level guard produces an understandable, non-misleading failure rather than a generic 'not implemented'.

title: NewSQLCommand can still be reached and now always fails with a misleading error after DuckDB removal
body: `NewSQLCommand` (and `UnmarshalSQLCommand`, which calls it) still calls `sql.TablesList(rawSQL)` at line 30 to extract table names from the SQL. After this PR, `sql.TablesList` is backed by the stub `DB` whose `RunCommands` returns `errors.New("not implemented")`, so `TablesList` will always return an error. Consequently `NewSQLCommand` will always fail with `errutil.BadRequest("sql-invalid-sql", ... "error reading SQL command")`. The reader-level guard in `pkg/expr/reader.go` blocks the `QueryTypeSQL` path, but `UnmarshalSQLCommand` is a separate entry point (used by the legacy/transform path) that is NOT guarded by `enableSqlExpressions` — it calls `NewSQLCommand` directly. This means: (1) any caller of `UnmarshalSQLCommand` gets a confusing 'error reading SQL command' for every SQL query, with no indication that SQL expressions are disabled; (2) the table-extraction logic is now dead/broken code that always errors. The legacy path should either be guarded with the same disabled check (returning a clear 'SQL expressions are disabled' error) or removed, rather than left calling into a stub that always fails with an opaque message.

title: Dead code: rsp.Values is unconditionally overwritten after the NoData branch
body: In `SQLCommand.Execute`, when `frame.Rows() == 0` the code sets `rsp.Values = mathexp.Values{mathexp.NoData{Frame: frame}}` (lines 110-114), but then immediately and unconditionally overwrites it at lines 116-118 with `rsp.Values = mathexp.Values{mathexp.TableData{Frame: frame}}`. The `NoData` assignment is therefore dead code and has no effect. This is a pre-existing bug (not introduced by this PR), but it is in a file central to this change and means empty SQL query results are returned as an empty `TableData` frame rather than `NoData`, which may affect downstream handling of empty results. It should be fixed by adding a `return` or `else` so the `NoData` branch is actually reachable, or by removing the dead branch.

title: SQL string escaping via single-quote doubling is insufficient and the code path is now unreachable dead code
body: `TablesList` builds a DuckDB command with `fmt.Sprintf("SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')", rawSQL)` after only replacing single quotes with doubled single quotes (`strings.Replace(rawSQL, "'", "''", -1)`). This is a fragile, incomplete escaping approach for embedding arbitrary SQL inside a SQL string literal (it does not handle backslashes or other escape sequences that DuckDB's parser may interpret). More importantly, after this PR the function is backed by a stub `DB` whose `RunCommands` always returns an error, so this code path is now unreachable in production — it is dead code that still contains the unsafe string-interpolation pattern. If this code is retained for future re-enablement, the escaping must be fixed (e.g. via proper parameterized queries or a robust escaping function); as it stands, leaving unsafe SQL string construction in the tree is a hazard if the stub is ever replaced with a real implementation. Ideally this function should be removed along with the DuckDB dependency, or clearly marked as disabled.

title: Malformed go.mod comment on fxamacker/cbor line corrupts the require directive annotation
body: Line 463 reads: `github.com/fxamacker/cbor/v2 v2.7.0 // indirect; indirect0.0.0-20240809095826-8eb5495c0b2a`. The trailing comment is malformed — it appears to be a merge/rebase artifact where `// indirect` was concatenated with a version string `indirect0.0.0-20240809095826-8eb5495c0b2a`, producing nonsense text. While Go tooling ignores trailing comments on require lines, this is clearly a corruption (likely from an automated tool that appends `// indirect` and collided with an existing comment) and should be cleaned up to just `// indirect` (or the correct annotation). It indicates the go.mod was not properly regenerated/verified after the dependency removal.

title: No test coverage for the SQL-expression disabled guard or the stub DB behavior
body: This PR adds a security-critical guard (`enableSqlExpressions` returning false, causing `QueryTypeSQL` to be rejected) and replaces the DuckDB-backed `DB` with a stub that always errors. Neither change appears to be accompanied by tests: there is no test asserting that a `QueryTypeSQL` query is rejected with the disabled error, no test asserting that `UnmarshalSQLCommand`/`NewSQLCommand` fail gracefully (or are blocked) now that `sql.TablesList` always errors, and no test for the new stub `DB` methods. Given this is a security fix for CVE-2024-9264 (RCE/LFI), a regression test that verifies SQL expressions cannot be executed through both the `ReadQuery` path and the `UnmarshalSQLCommand` path is important to prevent the vulnerability from being reintroduced if the guard is accidentally removed or bypassed.

title: Init is called from NewResourceServer with a context that is cancelled on Stop, but Init's search.init spawns a goroutine using context.Background() while the watcher uses the cancellable ctx
body: NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) at construction time using the server's long-lived cancellable context (created at line 229). Inside Init, s.search.init(ctx) is called with this same ctx. In search.go's init (line 202), a new context.Background() is used for WatchWriteEvents, which is fine, but the initial index build (s.build -> s.storage.ListIterator) runs with the server ctx. More importantly, the ordering change in Init (search.init before initWatcher) combined with eager initialization means that if the process is shutting down or the context is cancelled during startup, the index build will fail with context cancelled — the exact problem the PR description says it is fixing for gRPC calls, now moved to startup. Additionally, because Init is now called inside NewResourceServer, any caller that constructs a ResourceServer but never starts it (e.g., tests, or code paths that create the server for validation) will now block on a full index build, which can be very slow on large datasets and has no timeout. This is a behavioral change that can cause startup hangs or test timeouts.

title: Init uses sync.Once but initErr is read/written without synchronization after Once.Do, and Stop writes initErr concurrently
body: The server struct has `once sync.Once` and `initErr error` (lines 288-289). Init (line 293) uses s.once.Do to set initErr, which is safe for the first call. However, Stop (line 320) writes `s.initErr = fmt.Errorf("service is stopping")` without any lock and without going through once.Do. If Stop is called concurrently with Init (e.g., during startup while the index is building), or if Init is called again after Stop (the once prevents re-execution but the read of s.initErr at line 317 is unsynchronized relative to Stop's write), this is a data race on initErr. The previous lazy-init pattern called Init on every gRPC method, making concurrent access more likely; now with eager init the window is smaller but Stop can still race with the in-flight Init. The initErr field should be protected by a mutex or atomic, or Stop should not write to it.

title: Stop overwrites initErr and returns nil even when lifecycle.Stop failed, losing the error and returning inconsistent state
body: In Stop (lines 320-342), when s.lifecycle.Stop(ctx) returns an error, stopFailed is set to true and initErr is updated to include the error. However, the function then calls s.cancel() and at line 336-338, if stopFailed is true it returns s.initErr (the error). But if stopFailed is false, it overwrites initErr with "service is stopped" and returns nil. The problem: Stop sets `s.initErr = fmt.Errorf("service is stopping")` at line 321 unconditionally at the start. This means any subsequent call to Init (which is now only called once from NewResourceServer, but could be called by other code paths or tests) will return "service is stopping" even if initialization had previously succeeded. More critically, the initErr field is being used both as the initialization error cache and as a general "server state" error, which is confusing and error-prone. After a successful Init followed by Stop, calling Init again (if once is bypassed or in tests) returns a stale "service is stopping" error rather than the original init result.

title: Removing the global lock from BuildIndex creates a race where two concurrent builds for the same key both create indexes and one overwrites the other, losing documents
body: The PR removes the `b.cacheMu.Lock()` / `defer b.cacheMu.Unlock()` that previously wrapped the entire BuildIndex function (lines 88-90 in the diff), and replaces it with a lock only around the final cache insertion (lines 137-139). This means two concurrent calls to BuildIndex for the same NamespacedResource key can both execute simultaneously: both will create a new bleve index (line 98 or 104), both will run the builder callback to populate documents, and both will then write to b.cache[key]. The second write overwrites the first. The consequence: (1) wasted work building the same index twice, (2) the first index may still be in use by a reader (obtained via GetIndex before the second build completed) while the second build replaces it in the cache — the old index is now orphaned but still referenced, causing stale reads, (3) for file-based indexes (line 98), both builds will try to create/open the same directory path `filepath.Join(b.opts.Root, key.Namespace, ...)`, which can cause bleve.New to fail or corrupt the on-disk index because two bleve instances are writing to the same directory. The original code prevented this by holding the lock for the entire build. The PR description says 'finer grain locking' but the implementation does not add any per-key locking — it simply removes the lock entirely except for the map write. This is a regression that will cause data loss and index corruption under concurrent access to the same key.

title: TotalDocs iterates over b.cache without holding cacheMu, racing with concurrent BuildIndex writes
body: TotalDocs (lines 144-154) iterates over `b.cache` map directly without acquiring `b.cacheMu.RLock()`. Since BuildIndex now writes to b.cache at line 138 (with lock) but the map is being read here without lock, this is a concurrent map read/write race that can cause a panic (fatal error: concurrent map read and map write) or return incorrect counts. This function is called from search.go line 216 during init logging, and potentially from metrics. The GetIndex method correctly uses RLock (lines 61-62), but TotalDocs does not.

title: totalBatchesIndexed is incremented inside a goroutine without synchronization, causing a data race and incorrect count
body: In init (lines 186-193), `totalBatchesIndexed++` is executed inside `group.Go(func() error { ... })` closures. Multiple goroutines (limited by s.initWorkers) can execute this concurrently. The variable totalBatchesIndexed is a plain int declared at line 177, not an atomic. This is a data race that can cause lost updates and incorrect values. The Go race detector will flag this. The consequence is incorrect telemetry (the span event at line 199 reports wrong namespace count) and potential undefined behavior. It should use atomic.Int64 or be incremented after group.Wait() by using len(stats).

title: Watch event goroutine in init has no shutdown mechanism and leaks, and uses context.Background() ignoring cancellation
body: In init (lines 202-213), after building indexes, a goroutine is started that reads from `events` channel and calls s.handleEvent. This goroutine runs forever with no way to stop it: it uses `watchctx := context.Background()` (line 202) which is never cancelled, and the for loop (lines 208-212) has no exit condition (no select on ctx.Done() or a done channel). When the server is stopped (server.Stop calls s.cancel()), this goroutine continues running, leaking. Additionally, the events channel from s.storage.WatchWriteEvents(watchctx) is never closed by this code, so the goroutine blocks forever on `<-events`. This is a goroutine leak that will accumulate if the server is restarted (e.g., in tests or during reconfiguration). The goroutine should select on a done channel or the server's context.

title: IndexMetrics.IndexedKinds is incremented/decremented without nil check in handleEvent, unlike other IndexMetrics usages
body: In handleEvent (lines 262-271), `IndexMetrics.IndexedKinds.WithLabelValues(evt.Key.Resource).Inc()` and `.Dec()` are called without checking if IndexMetrics is nil. Every other usage of IndexMetrics in this file (lines 217, 282, 367) checks `if IndexMetrics != nil` first. If IndexMetrics is nil (e.g., in tests or if metrics registration failed), this will panic with a nil pointer dereference. The nil check is missing here, creating an inconsistency that can cause crashes.

title: History and Origin methods dereference s.search without nil check after Init removal
body: After removing the lazy `s.Init(ctx)` calls from all gRPC methods, the History (line 924) and Origin (line 929) methods now directly call `s.search.History(ctx, req)` and `s.search.Origin(ctx, req)` without checking if s.search is nil. The Search method (line 916) correctly checks `if s.search == nil` first. If the server was created without search configured (opts.Search.Resources == nil, line 250), s.search will be nil, and calling History or Origin will panic with a nil pointer dereference. Previously, the Init call would have run but not prevented this either — however, the Search method's nil check suggests this is a known case that must be handled. History and Origin need the same nil check.

title: NewResourceServer now blocks on full index build with no timeout, changing the constructor contract from fast to potentially very slow
body: NewResourceServer (line 182) now calls s.Init(ctx) at line 258, which calls s.search.init(ctx) which builds indexes for all namespaces with count > initMinSize. This can take minutes on large datasets. The constructor previously returned quickly and initialization was deferred to first use. Now any caller of NewResourceServer will block until the index is built. This is a significant API contract change: (1) callers may have timeouts on construction, (2) the context passed (line 229, derived from context.Background() with claims) has no deadline, so a hung index build will block forever, (3) tests that construct a ResourceServer will now pay the full index build cost even if they don't need search. The PR description asks 'Does anything else depend on initializing US lazily?' — this change breaks that assumption for all callers. A timeout or async initialization with readiness check should be considered.

title: Latency calculation uses evt.ResourceVersion as a timestamp, but ResourceVersion is a monotonically increasing counter, not a unix timestamp
body: In handleEvent (line 278), `latencySeconds := float64(time.Now().UnixMicro()-evt.ResourceVersion) / 1e6` assumes evt.ResourceVersion is a unix timestamp in microseconds. However, looking at the SQL backend (backend.go line 763), ResourceVersion is generated as `max(res.CurrentEpoch, res.ResourceVersion+1)` where CurrentEpoch is the SQL server's microsecond timestamp. So it is a timestamp, but only when the SQL server clock is used. The comment in server.go line 906-907 says 'resource version is a unix timestamp in microseconds'. This is fragile: if the backend implementation changes or if ResourceVersion is ever a simple counter, this calculation will produce nonsensical (potentially negative or huge) latency values. The code should use an explicit timestamp field on the event rather than overloading ResourceVersion.

title: bleveIndex.Write and Flush are not thread-safe but can be called concurrently from watch event handler and search
body: The bleveIndex struct (lines 156-169) has a `batch *bleve.Batch` field with comment 'only valid in single thread' (line 166). After BuildIndex completes and Flush is called (line 132), batch is set to nil (line 202). However, the same index can now be accessed concurrently: (1) the watch event handler in search.go handleEvent calls index.Write (line 257) and index.Delete (line 266), (2) Search calls can happen concurrently via idx.Search. The Write method (lines 172-187) checks `if b.batch != nil` but after Flush, batch is nil so it calls `b.index.Index(...)` directly. Bleve's Index.Index is thread-safe, but the batch field access is not protected. More critically, if a Write happens while another Write is in progress (both see batch==nil), they both call b.index.Index concurrently which is safe in bleve, but the batch field is never re-initialized after Flush, so all writes go through the slower direct Index path. The original code held the cacheMu lock during BuildIndex which prevented concurrent access during build, but now that lock is removed, and the watch handler can call Write on an index that is still being built by another goroutine (if getOrCreateIndex returns an index that is mid-build). Actually, getOrCreateIndex calls build which calls BuildIndex which now inserts into cache only at the end, so a concurrent getOrCreateIndex for the same key will not find it in cache and will start a second build — see the race finding above. Once both builds complete, the second overwrites the first in cache, but the first index may have pending writes from the watch handler that are now lost.

title: NewResourceServer calls s.Init(ctx) with a context that is never cancelled on construction failure, leaking the watcher goroutine and resources
body: NewResourceServer creates a cancelable context (ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)) at line 229 and stores it on the server struct (s.ctx, s.cancel). It then calls s.Init(ctx) at line 258, which starts the watcher (initWatcher) and, via searchSupport.init, spawns a goroutine reading from the storage event channel. If Init fails (e.g., search index build error or WatchWriteEvents error), NewResourceServer returns nil, err at line 261 — but it never calls s.cancel(). The server object is discarded, so the cancel function is unreachable, and the background goroutines started by initWatcher (the broadcaster goroutine piping events from s.backend.WatchWriteEvents(s.ctx)) keep running forever with a context that will never be cancelled. This is a goroutine/resource leak on every failed startup, and in HA or repeated-restart scenarios it will accumulate pollers holding DB connections. Fix: call s.cancel() (or defer it) before returning the error when Init fails.

title: Init is now only called from the constructor, but remains exported and uses sync.Once with a shared initErr that Stop() overwrites, creating a data race and broken re-init semantics
body: The PR removes all lazy s.Init(ctx) calls from the gRPC handlers (Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search, History, Origin, IsHealthy, PutBlob, GetBlob) and instead calls s.Init(ctx) once in NewResourceServer. However, Init (line 293) is still an exported method on the server type, still guarded by s.once, and still writes to the shared s.initErr field. Meanwhile Stop() (line 320) unconditionally writes s.initErr = fmt.Errorf("service is stopping") without any synchronization. If any external caller (or future code) invokes Init concurrently with Stop, or calls Init after Stop, there is an unsynchronized read/write race on s.initErr. More importantly, the once.Do means that if Init is called again after Stop (e.g., a caller retries Init on the same server instance), it will return the stale initErr from the first run — but Stop has since overwritten initErr with "service is stopping"/"service is stopped", so the semantics are now muddled: a second Init returns whatever Stop last wrote. Since Init is now effectively an internal startup step, it should be unexported (init) or the initErr handling should be made race-free and Stop should not clobber the field that Init's once.Do closure reads.

title: totalBatchesIndexed is incremented inside concurrent errgroup goroutines without synchronization — data race and incorrect metric
body: In searchSupport.init, totalBatchesIndexed is declared as a plain int at line 177 and incremented at line 189 inside group.Go(func() error { ... totalBatchesIndexed++ ... }) for each namespace. The errgroup runs up to s.initWorkers concurrent goroutines (group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers) at line 179), so multiple goroutines increment the same variable concurrently with no mutex or atomic. This is a data race (undefined behavior under the Go memory model) and will also produce an incorrect count in the span event at line 199 (attribute.Int("namespaced_indexed", totalBatchesIndexed)). Fix: use atomic.Int64, or compute the count as len(stats) after group.Wait() since every stat entry spawns exactly one goroutine.

title: searchSupport.init starts a second, unbounded event-watching goroutine that duplicates the server's broadcaster watcher and never terminates
body: searchSupport.init (line 172) calls s.storage.WatchWriteEvents(watchctx) at line 203 with watchctx := context.Background() (line 202) and spawns a goroutine at line 207 that loops forever reading from the events channel and calling s.handleEvent. This is separate from the server's own initWatcher (server.go line 752) which also calls s.backend.WatchWriteEvents(s.ctx) and feeds a broadcaster. The searchSupport goroutine uses context.Background(), which is never cancelled — not by server.Stop() (which only calls s.cancel() on the server's own ctx), and not by any lifecycle hook. When the server shuts down, this goroutine keeps running, keeps consuming events from the storage backend's poller, and keeps mutating the search index. Additionally, both the server's broadcaster and this searchSupport goroutine independently call WatchWriteEvents on the same SQL backend, which spawns two poller goroutines (backend.go line 566) polling the same resource_history table — doubling DB load and potentially racing on index writes. The searchSupport watcher should use the server's cancellable context (s.ctx) and be tied to the server lifecycle, or the event handling should be unified with the existing broadcaster.

title: Event watcher goroutine does not check channel closure — blocks forever on closed channel and never exits
body: The goroutine at line 207 does `for { v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v) }`. The events channel returned by WatchWriteEvents is closed by the SQL backend's poller when it exits (backend.go line 572: defer close(stream)). Receiving from a closed channel returns nil immediately and forever, so once the channel is closed this goroutine will spin in a tight infinite loop calling s.handleEvent(watchctx, nil) — which will panic on nil pointer dereference at line 226 (evt.Type) or at minimum burn CPU. The loop should be `for v := range events` or check `v, ok := <-events; if !ok { return }`.

title: Removing the coarse lock from BuildIndex introduces a race: two concurrent builds for the same key can both create indexes and leak one, and GetIndex can return a partially-constructed index
body: The PR removes the function-wide b.cacheMu.Lock() from BuildIndex (previously lines 88-89) and replaces it with a short lock only around the cache insertion at lines 137-139. This means two concurrent callers of BuildIndex for the same NamespacedResource key (which happens: searchSupport.init spawns concurrent builds via errgroup, and getOrCreateIndex can also trigger builds from concurrent Search/handleEvent calls) will both execute bleve.New/bleve.NewMemOnly, both run the builder writing documents, and both insert into b.cache — the second insertion silently overwrites the first. The overwritten bleve.Index is never closed, leaking file handles/disk state (for file-based indexes, the on-disk directory is left behind and will be reopened by a subsequent build, potentially corrupting or duplicating data). Additionally, between the builder writing documents (line 126) and the cache insertion (line 138), another goroutine calling GetIndex will not find the index and will start its own duplicate build. The original coarse lock prevented duplicate builds for the same key; the fix requires per-key locking (e.g., a sync.Map of in-flight builds keyed by NamespacedResource, or a keyed mutex) so that concurrent builds for the same key are deduplicated, while builds for different keys proceed in parallel.

title: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without holding cacheMu — data race with concurrent BuildIndex insertions
body: TotalDocs (line 144) ranges over b.cache with no lock. BuildIndex now writes to b.cache under b.cacheMu.Lock() at lines 137-139, and GetIndex reads under RLock. Since BuildIndex can run concurrently (the whole point of the PR's finer-grained locking), TotalDocs racing with a cache insertion is a concurrent map read/write — a fatal runtime error in Go (concurrent map iteration and map write). TotalDocs is called from searchSupport.init at line 216 (s.search.TotalDocs()) after group.Wait(), but also potentially from metrics or other paths concurrently with getOrCreateIndex-triggered builds. Fix: acquire b.cacheMu.RLock() around the iteration.

title: bleveIndex.Write/Delete/Flush mutate shared batch state with no synchronization — unsafe for concurrent watch-event handling
body: bleveIndex.Write (line 172) checks b.batch != nil, calls b.batch.Index(...), and may call b.index.Batch(b.batch) and b.batch.Reset(). Delete (line 190) errors if batch != nil. Flush (line 198) calls b.index.Batch(b.batch), b.batch.Reset(), and sets b.batch = nil. These fields are documented as "only valid in single thread" (line 166) but after the PR's change, handleEvent in search.go can be invoked concurrently: the searchSupport.init goroutine (line 207) calls handleEvent in a single goroutine, but getOrCreateIndex (line 287) can trigger build() concurrently with handleEvent for the same key, and once the index is in the cache, multiple watch events for the same namespace could be processed... actually the searchSupport event loop is single-goroutine, but the index returned by BuildIndex is placed in the cache before Flush is called by searchSupport.build (line 372: index.Flush() after BuildIndex returns). Between BuildIndex returning (line 140) and searchSupport.build calling Flush (search.go line 372), the index is in the cache with b.batch still non-nil; a concurrent Search on that index is fine, but a concurrent handleEvent Write would see batch != nil and try to batch.Index into a batch that build() is about to Flush and nil out — a race on b.batch. More critically, after Flush sets b.batch = nil, concurrent Write calls go directly to b.index.Index which is safe, but the transition itself (Flush setting batch=nil while Write reads batch) is unsynchronized. The bleveIndex needs a mutex protecting batch, or the batch must be fully flushed and nilled inside BuildIndex before the index is published to the cache.

title: Stop() overwrites initErr with a generic error, losing the original initialization error and breaking error reporting for callers that check Init after Stop
body: Stop() unconditionally sets s.initErr = fmt.Errorf("service is stopping") at line 321 and later s.initErr = fmt.Errorf("service is stopped") at line 339, overwriting whatever initErr was set during Init. Since Init uses sync.Once and returns s.initErr, any caller that calls Init after Stop (or concurrently) will get "service is stopped" instead of the real initialization error. More importantly, the lifecycle is now: NewResourceServer calls Init synchronously; if it fails, the constructor returns an error and the server is never used — so Stop is never called on a failed-init server. But for a successfully initialized server that is later stopped, if any code path still calls Init (it's exported), it gets the once-cached value... which Stop has clobbered. The initErr field is being used for two purposes (init result and stop status) without synchronization. Separate the concerns: keep initErr immutable after once.Do, and use a separate atomic/bool for stopped state.

title: IndexMetrics.IndexedKinds is incremented/decremented without nil check in handleEvent, unlike other IndexMetrics usages in the same file
body: In handleEvent, IndexMetrics.IndexedKinds.WithLabelValues(evt.Key.Resource).Inc() (line 263) and .Dec() (line 271) are called without checking if IndexMetrics is nil. Every other use of IndexMetrics in this file (lines 217, 282, 367) guards with `if IndexMetrics != nil`. If IndexMetrics is nil (which can happen if metrics registration failed or in tests), handleEvent will panic with a nil pointer dereference when processing ADDED or DELETED watch events. This is inconsistent and a latent crash. Fix: add the same nil guard, or better, initialize IndexMetrics to a no-op default so nil checks are unnecessary.

title: Moving Init from lazy per-request to constructor changes the failure contract: NewResourceServer now blocks on full index build and can fail startup, but callers may not expect constructor to do heavy I/O
body: Previously, Init was called lazily on the first gRPC request (Create/Update/Read/List/Watch/Search/etc.), so NewResourceServer returned quickly and the server could start serving requests (returning init errors per-request) even if index building was slow or failed. Now NewResourceServer calls s.Init(ctx) synchronously at line 258, which calls searchSupport.init — this builds the entire search index (potentially minutes for large datasets) and starts watchers before the constructor returns. Consequences: (1) The gRPC server registration/startup path now blocks on index build; if the caller has a startup timeout, the process may be killed before the server is ready. (2) If index build fails, NewResourceServer returns an error and the entire ResourceServer fails to construct — previously the server would start and only Search requests would fail. (3) The ctx passed to Init is the server's internal background-derived context (line 229), not a startup timeout context — so a hung index build hangs the constructor forever with no cancellation. Callers of NewResourceServer need to be audited to ensure they can tolerate a long-blocking, failure-prone constructor; ideally Init should be called with a startup deadline context, or the constructor should return the server immediately and Init be called separately by the module lifecycle with proper timeout handling.

title: Removing the global lock from BuildIndex creates a race where concurrent builds for the same key return different indexes and leak one
body: The PR removes the `b.cacheMu.Lock()` held for the entire `BuildIndex` and only locks the final `b.cache[key] = idx` write. Two goroutines can now concurrently call `BuildIndex` for the same `NamespacedResource` key (e.g. `searchSupport.init` spawns one goroutine per namespace via errgroup, and `getOrCreateIndex` can also trigger `build` for the same key from a Search request or a watch event). Both will create separate bleve indexes (memory or on-disk), both will run the full builder, and the second one to finish will overwrite `b.cache[key]`, orphaning the first index. The orphaned index is never closed, leaking file handles/memory, and worse, callers that already obtained the first index (e.g. an in-flight `Search` or the `handleEvent` goroutine holding `index` from `getOrCreateIndex`) will write/delete documents into an index that is no longer reachable via `GetIndex`, so watch-event updates are silently lost and search results become inconsistent. Additionally, for the file-based path, two concurrent `bleve.New(dir, ...)` calls on the same directory can corrupt the on-disk index. The fix requires per-key locking (e.g. a `singleflight.Group` keyed by `NamespacedResource`, or a map of per-key mutexes) so that only one build happens per key and concurrent callers wait for and share the same index.

title: TotalDocs iterates the cache map without holding cacheMu, racing with concurrent BuildIndex writes
body: `TotalDocs()` ranges over `b.cache` with no lock, while `BuildIndex` now writes `b.cache[key] = idx` under `b.cacheMu.Lock()`. Concurrent map iteration and map write in Go is a fatal runtime error ("concurrent map iteration and map write"), which can crash the process. `TotalDocs` is called from `searchSupport.init` (search.go line 216) after `group.Wait()`, but also potentially from metrics/health paths while other goroutines (watch event handlers calling `getOrCreateIndex` -> `build` -> `BuildIndex`) are still inserting into the map. The map must be accessed under `cacheMu.RLock()` in `TotalDocs`.

title: totalBatchesIndexed is incremented from multiple goroutines without synchronization, producing a data race and wrong metric
body: In `searchSupport.init`, `totalBatchesIndexed++` (line 189) is executed inside `group.Go(func() error {...})` closures running concurrently under `errgroup` with `SetLimit(s.initWorkers)`. `totalBatchesIndexed` is a plain local `int` captured by the closures; concurrent increments are a data race (undefined behavior per the Go memory model) and the value reported in the span event `namespaced_indexed` (line 199) will be wrong/racy. Use `atomic.Int64`/`atomic.AddInt64` or compute the count as `len(stats)` after `group.Wait()`.

title: Watch event goroutine has no shutdown path and leaks; channel receive on a closed/nil channel can spin or block forever
body: In `searchSupport.init`, after building indexes, a goroutine is started that loops `for { v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v) }` using `watchctx := context.Background()`. There is no cancellation tied to server shutdown (`server.Stop` only calls `s.cancel()` on the server's own context, which is not the one used here), so this goroutine and the underlying `WatchWriteEvents` poller goroutine in the SQL backend run forever after shutdown, leaking goroutines and DB pollers. Additionally, when the events channel is closed by the backend (e.g. `poller` does `defer close(stream)` when `b.done` fires), receiving from a closed channel returns `nil` immediately and forever, so `handleEvent` will be called in a tight infinite loop with `evt == nil`, causing a nil-pointer dereference panic at `evt.Type` (line 226) — or at minimum a busy-loop. The loop must select on a cancellable context and check `v, ok := <-events` to break on close.

title: NewResourceServer now blocks on Init, but Init's search index build uses a context that is cancelled by Stop, and more importantly the server is returned already-initialized while callers may still rely on lazy behavior; the bigger issue: Init is called with the server's long-lived ctx, but search.init spawns a watcher on context.Background() that outlives it — combined with the removal of per-request Init calls, any Init failure is now permanent and there is no retry path
body: `NewResourceServer` now calls `s.Init(ctx)` synchronously (line 258) and returns an error if it fails. `Init` uses `sync.Once`, so if initialization fails (e.g. transient DB error during `GetResourceStats` or `WatchWriteEvents`), `s.initErr` is set permanently and every subsequent `Init` call returns the same cached error with no way to retry — and since the per-request `s.Init(ctx)` guards were removed from Create/Update/Delete/Read/List/Watch/Search/etc., a transient startup failure now permanently bricks the server for its lifetime instead of being retried on the next request. Previously the lazy per-request `Init` calls meant a failed init would be retried on the next gRPC call (sync.Once only runs the function once, but initErr was only set inside the Once... actually with Once the error is also sticky, but the request would at least surface it). More concretely: the reviewer note asks "Does anything else depend on initializing US lazily?" — the answer is that tests and callers that construct a `ResourceServer` with a backend that is not yet ready (e.g. DB not migrated) will now fail at construction time rather than at first request, which may break startup ordering in `pkg/server` module initialization. At minimum, the sticky-error-with-no-retry behavior after a transient failure should be documented or fixed (e.g. reset the Once on failure).

title: Stop() overwrites initErr with a plain error and returns nil on success path, losing the real stop error semantics; also Stop is not idempotent and races with in-flight requests that no longer check Init
body: `Stop` sets `s.initErr = fmt.Errorf("service is stopping")` unconditionally, then if the lifecycle stop fails it overwrites with "service stopeed with error" (note the typo "stopeed"), and on the success path it sets `s.initErr = fmt.Errorf("service is stopped")` but returns `nil`. Since the per-request `s.Init(ctx)` checks were removed from all gRPC handlers, a request that arrives after `Stop` has been called will no longer see the "service is stopping/stopped" error from `Init` — it will proceed to use `s.backend`, `s.broadcaster` (which may be nil if Init never ran, or closed channels after cancel), and `s.search` (whose watch goroutine may be dead). In particular `Watch` dereferences `s.broadcaster` (line 798 `s.broadcaster.Subscribe`) — if `Stop` is called before `Init` completes (or Init failed), `s.broadcaster` is nil and `Watch` panics with a nil pointer dereference. The removal of the Init guards means handlers must now defensively check server state, or `Init` must remain callable/idempotent from handlers.

title: History and Origin dereference s.search without nil check after Init guards were removed
body: `History` (line 924) and `Origin` (line 929) call `s.search.History(...)` / `s.search.Origin(...)` directly. `Search` (line 916) correctly checks `if s.search == nil`. If the server is constructed with `opts.Search.Resources == nil` (search not configured), `s.search` is nil, and a `History` or `Origin` gRPC call will panic with a nil pointer dereference. Previously the `s.Init(ctx)` call at the top of these methods did not protect against this either, but the nil-deref is now unconditional for these two methods. Add the same nil check as `Search`.

title: IndexMetrics.IndexedKinds is incremented/decremented without nil check in handleEvent, unlike other IndexMetrics uses
body: In `handleEvent`, lines 263 and 271 call `IndexMetrics.IndexedKinds.WithLabelValues(...).Inc()/.Dec()` without checking `IndexMetrics != nil`, while other uses in the same file (lines 217, 282, 367) guard with `if IndexMetrics != nil`. If `IndexMetrics` is nil (e.g. in tests or when metrics are not registered), a watch event for an ADDED/DELETED resource will panic with a nil pointer dereference. Add the nil guard for consistency and safety.

title: bleveIndex.Write/Delete/Flush mutate shared batch state with no locking, but indexes are now reachable via the cache before Flush completes and can be used concurrently
body: `bleveIndex` documents `batch` as "only valid in single thread" (line 166), and `Write` mutates `b.batch` (lines 175-184), `Flush` sets `b.batch = nil` (line 202), and `Delete` errors if `b.batch != nil` (line 191). Previously the whole `BuildIndex` was under `cacheMu.Lock()`, so the index was not visible in `b.cache` until after `builder(idx)` and `idx.Flush()` completed, guaranteeing single-threaded use during the build. Now the index is only published to the cache at the end, which is correct for the build itself, BUT `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` can return the same index to concurrent callers (Search + handleEvent), and `handleEvent` calls `index.Write(doc)` / `index.Delete(...)` from the watch goroutine while a `Search` may be reading. More critically, if `getOrCreateIndex` is called twice concurrently for the same key (see the BuildIndex race finding), two different `bleveIndex` instances exist, but even with a single instance, `Write` after `Flush` sets `b.batch = nil` and then calls `b.index.Index(...)` directly (line 186) — bleve's `Index.Index` is safe for concurrent use, but the `b.batch` field check-then-use in `Write` is not atomic: a concurrent `Flush` (from a rebuild) could set `b.batch = nil` between the `if b.batch != nil` check and `b.batch.Index(...)`, causing a nil dereference. The struct needs a mutex protecting `batch` or the batch must be removed after build.

title: searchSupport.init starts its own WatchWriteEvents consumer, but server.initWatcher also starts one via the broadcaster — duplicate event streams and double-indexing
body: `searchSupport.init` (line 203) calls `s.storage.WatchWriteEvents(watchctx)` and consumes events directly to update the search index. Separately, `server.Init` calls `s.initWatcher()` (server.go line 310) which calls `s.backend.WatchWriteEvents(s.ctx)` again (server.go line 755) to feed the broadcaster for client watches. For the SQL backend, each `WatchWriteEvents` call starts an independent poller goroutine polling the DB every 100ms, so the database is polled twice and two independent event streams are maintained. This doubles DB load and is wasteful; the search index updates should ideally be driven from the server's broadcaster (single event stream) rather than a second direct `WatchWriteEvents` subscription. At minimum this duplication should be acknowledged; functionally it works but is a performance/correctness smell (the two pollers may see events at different times, causing the index to lag behind the watch stream).

title: Conditional UI passkeys are no longer offered on the initial login form when a user is already set (re-authentication), breaking passkey re-authentication
body: In UsernamePasswordForm.authenticate(), the call to webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) was moved outside the `else` branch and is now guarded by isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()), which returns `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null`. Previously the WebAuthn conditional-UI data was set up whenever passkeys were enabled and no user was set. The new guard has two problems: (1) during re-authentication (prompt=login) the user IS already set in the context, so the condition is true and fillContextForm runs — but the intent of the original code was to enable the conditional UI on the username form when NO user is known yet; (2) more importantly, the companion change in challenge(context, error, field) (line 137) uses the same isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()) guard, so after a failed password attempt during re-authentication the WebAuthn conditional-UI attributes are re-populated only when a user is set — which is the re-authentication case — but the initial challenge path and the UsernameForm skip logic interact such that the passkey conditional UI is not offered where it should be. Concretely, the re-authentication tests added in this PR (e.g. PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest.webauthnLoginWithExternalKey_reauthentication) assert that the webauthn form IS present after prompt=login, and the code only works because the user is set; however for the UsernameForm flow (PasskeysUsernameFormTest) the new `!isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` check in UsernameForm.authenticate() (line 47) — where isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is inherited from UsernamePasswordForm and requires user != null — means that when a user is set the UsernameForm no longer short-circuits, which is intended, but the symmetric change in UsernamePasswordForm means the conditional UI is now keyed on 'user is set' rather than 'passkeys enabled and no user identified', inverting the original semantics ('setup webauthn data when the user is not already selected'). The comment at line 114 ('setup webauthn data when passkeys enabled') contradicts the guard which additionally requires user != null. This inverts the original behavior and will suppress the passkey conditional UI on the first-step login form in flows where the user is pre-set (e.g. organization authenticator or IdP brokering sets the user before the username/password form), preventing passwordless passkey login for those users. The guard should be `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()` (matching the original condition) for the no-user case, and the user != null requirement should only apply where re-authentication display of authenticators is intended.

title: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() used in UsernameForm.authenticate() has inverted semantics — it requires a non-null user, so the skip is never bypassed when it should be
body: UsernameForm.authenticate() now calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` (inherited from UsernamePasswordForm, line 160-162), which is defined as `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null`. The purpose of the new check is to NOT skip the username form during re-authentication when passkeys conditional UI is enabled, so that the user can authenticate with a passkey. But the method requires `user != null` — and the enclosing `if` already guarantees `context.getUser() != null`, so the added condition reduces to `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()` only when a user is set. The actual intent (per the PR title 'Fixing Re-authentication with passkeys' and the new tests) is to keep showing the form when passkeys are enabled so the conditional UI can authenticate the already-known user. However the method name and implementation ('isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)' returning true only when user != null) is being used in two different places with opposite meanings: in UsernamePasswordForm it gates fillContextForm (where user != null means 're-authentication, show passkeys'), while in UsernameForm it gates 'do not skip the form'. Because the method conflates 'passkeys enabled' with 'a user is present', any future caller that invokes it with a null user (e.g. to decide whether to render the conditional UI on a fresh login) will get false even when passkeys are enabled, which is wrong. The method should be split into `isPasskeysEnabled()` (feature/realm check) and the user-presence check should be done explicitly at each call site. As written, the logic happens to work for the current call sites but the semantics are inverted relative to the method name and the original code comment ('setup webauthn data when the user is not already selected'), which is a latent bug and makes the re-authentication behavior fragile.

title: New shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators() indirection is a no-op refactor that obscures the original condition
body: The change replaces `if (user != null)` with `if (shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators(context))` where the new protected method (lines 128-130) simply returns `context.getUser() != null`. This is a pure refactor with no behavioral change for WebAuthnAuthenticator itself; its only purpose is to allow WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator to override it to return false. That is a reasonable extension point, but the default implementation duplicates the existing `user` local variable check (line 98 already fetched `UserModel user = context.getUser()`), so the method could simply be `return user != null` if passed the user, or the call site could keep using the local. Not a bug, but the indirection adds a second source of truth for the same condition and the javadoc ('Typically during 2-factor authentication') does not document the override contract used by WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator to suppress the authenticator list during conditional UI.

title: createErrorResponse() calls setupReauthenticationInUsernamePasswordFormError() unconditionally, hiding the username field even for first-time (non re-authentication) logins after a passkey error
body: WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator.createErrorResponse() now calls AuthenticatorUtils.setupReauthenticationInUsernamePasswordFormError(context) on every passkey error. That utility (AuthenticatorUtils.java lines 125-133) sets LoginFormsProvider.USERNAME_HIDDEN=true and REGISTRATION_DISABLED=true only when the auth note USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH is 'true'. The note is set in UsernamePasswordForm.authenticate() only when context.getUser() != null (line 102). However, this authenticator is also used from UsernameForm flows and potentially other flows where the note may be stale: the note is removed in UsernamePasswordForm.authenticate() only in the `else` branch (line 104), but if a previous authentication attempt in the same authentication session set the note (e.g. user was identified, then the flow restarted or a different authenticator ran), the note can persist and cause the username field to be hidden on a subsequent error page even though the current challenge is for a fresh login where the user must type their username. More concretely: in the UsernameForm flow (PasskeysUsernameFormTest), after the user submits a username, the PasswordForm runs; if a passkey error occurs there, createErrorResponse() is invoked and — because the note was never set in that flow (UsernameForm does not set USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH) — the utility correctly does nothing. But in the UsernamePasswordForm flow, if the user first fails a password (note set, username hidden), then the passkey conditional UI errors, the error page keeps the username hidden — which is intended. The risk is that the note is session-scoped and not cleared when the authentication session restarts the flow (e.g. after a 'try again' or restart), so a stale 'true' note can hide the username on a fresh login form. The utility should be defensive, but more importantly the note lifecycle is not reset when the user is cleared (context.clearUser() in AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator.badPasswordHandler clears the user but not the note), so a user who fails password (note set), then somehow gets the user cleared and re-enters a username, would see a hidden username field with no way to correct it. This is a real UX/data-integrity edge case introduced by relying on a note that is not cleared in lockstep with the user.

title: Static import from browser package into util package creates a package cycle (browser -> util -> browser)
body: AuthenticatorUtils (in org.keycloak.authentication.authenticators.util) now statically imports USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH from org.keycloak.authentication.authenticators.browser.AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator. AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator already imports AuthenticatorUtils (line 24: `import org.keycloak.authentication.authenticators.util.AuthenticatorUtils;` and uses AuthenticatorUtils.dummyHash and getDisabledByBruteForceEventError). This creates a circular package dependency: browser -> util (existing) and util -> browser (new). Java allows this, but it is a layering violation: the util package should not depend on the browser package. The constant USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH was changed from protected to public (AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator line 58) solely to enable this import. The constant is an implementation detail of the username/password form authenticators; it should either remain in the browser package and be accessed via a public method on AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator (e.g. a static helper `isUserAlreadySetBeforeUsernamePasswordAuth(context)` which already exists as a protected instance method at line 257), or be moved to a neutral location. The new public visibility also widens the API surface of a class in the services module unnecessarily.

title: reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey test uses inverted assertion logic that always passes (findElement expected to return null but findElement never returns null)
body: In reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey (lines 291-296 and 312-317), the test asserts the absence of the webauthn form with: `MatcherAssert.assertThat(driver.findElement(By.xpath("//form[@id='webauth']")), nullValue()); fail("Not expected to have webauthn button");` wrapped in try/catch(Exception). Selenium's findElement throws NoSuchElementException when the element is absent — it never returns null. So when the element is correctly absent, findElement throws, the assertThat line is never reached, the exception is caught by the catch block and the test passes. When the element is present, findElement returns a WebElement, assertThat(element, nullValue()) fails with an AssertionError — but AssertionError is an Exception, so it is ALSO caught by the catch block and the test passes. The test therefore passes regardless of whether the webauthn button is present or absent; it cannot detect the regression it is meant to guard (passkeys UI shown during re-authentication when passkeys are disabled). The correct pattern (used elsewhere in the same file, e.g. PasskeysUsernameFormTest line 202) is `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, () -> driver.findElement(...))`. The same broken pattern is repeated at lines 312-317 for the re-authentication page. Both assertions are ineffective.

title: reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey logs in with only a password on the re-authentication page, but the page has a hidden username field — login() with a single argument may submit an empty username
body: In reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey, after the prompt=login re-authentication page is shown (line 305-311), the test calls `loginPage.login(getPassword("test-user@localhost"))` (line 320) with only the password argument. On a re-authentication page the username field is hidden (USERNAME_HIDDEN=true) and the form submits the attempted username via a hidden input. The single-argument login() helper typically fills only the password field and submits. Whether this works depends on the login page object's implementation of the single-argument login and on the hidden username field being populated with the correct attempted username. The preceding successful password login at line 299 uses the two-argument form `loginPage.login("test-user@localhost", getPassword(...))`. The re-authentication call at line 320 relies on the hidden field carrying the username. If the hidden field is not populated (e.g. because the re-authentication page was rendered without the attempted username note, or because the hidden input is empty), the form submits an empty username and authentication fails with USER_NOT_FOUND rather than succeeding. The test then asserts a successful login event (lines 325-329), so it would catch a failure — but the test is fragile: it depends on the hidden-field population behavior that this very PR is changing (the note USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH and the hidden-field setup). The test should either assert the attempted username is present (like PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest.passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey does with getAttemptedUsername()) or use an explicit two-step submit. As written, if the hidden username is empty the test fails for the wrong reason (empty username) rather than validating the intended behavior.

title: webauthnLoginWithExternalKey_reauthenticationWithPasswordOrPasskey submits a different user's password and only checks the error message, not the event or the preserved username
body: In webauthnLoginWithExternalKey_reauthenticationWithPasswordOrPasskey, the test performs a failed re-authentication by submitting the password of a DIFFERENT user ('test-user@localhost', line 377 and 404) while the re-authentication context has the registered user set. It asserts only `Assert.assertEquals("Invalid password.", loginPage.getInputError())`. It does not assert: (1) that a LOGIN_ERROR event with INVALID_USER_CREDENTIALS was emitted (other tests in the file do, e.g. lines 153-157), (2) that the attempted username is still the original user (getAttemptedUsername()), which is the key invariant this PR is about (the username must remain hidden and unchanged after a failed password during re-authentication), and (3) that the user context was not cleared (the subsequent passkey login at line 386 succeeds as the original user, which implicitly checks this, but only for the passkey path). The second failed-password attempt (line 404) is followed by a successful password login with the correct user's password (line 410) — but because the user context may have been cleared by the failed attempt (AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator.badPasswordHandler clears the user when clearUser is true; during re-authentication USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH is set so clearUser is false, but this is exactly the behavior under test), the test does not verify that the username field remained correctly populated. Without asserting getAttemptedUsername() after the failed attempt, a regression that clears the user or empties the hidden username would only surface as a confusing downstream failure. The test should assert the attempted username and the error event after each failed password attempt.

title: Unused import NoSuchElementException remains after the test assertion was changed to expect the element to be present
body: PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest.passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey previously asserted `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, () -> driver.findElement(...))` (the old behavior where the webauthn form was absent after username submission). The PR changed both assertions (lines 200 and 211) to `MatcherAssert.assertThat(driver.findElement(By.xpath("//form[@id='webauth']")), Matchers.notNullValue())`, so NoSuchElementException is no longer referenced anywhere in the file. The import `org.openqa.selenium.NoSuchElementException` (line 51) is now unused. This is a minor cleanliness issue (unused import) that will cause checkstyle/IDE warnings; it should be removed. Note that PasskeysUsernameFormTest still uses NoSuchElementException (line 202) so its import is still needed there.

title: Conditional passkeys UI is now enabled during re-authentication with a known user, breaking the re-authentication contract
body: In `authenticate()`, the WebAuthn conditional-UI form data is now set up whenever `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())` is true, which includes the case where `context.getUser() != null` (re-authentication, e.g. prompt=login). Previously the code only called `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` in the `else` branch, i.e. only when no user was set.
