Enabling conditional UI (autofill passkeys on the username field) during re-authentication changes the login page into an autofill/conditional-UI page for a user who is already identified; the username is hidden and the page is expected to be a password-only re-authentication form. This is a behavioral regression for re-authentication flows and contradicts the intent of the surrounding code, which explicitly sets `USERNAME_HIDDEN` and `REGISTRATION_DISABLED` and the `USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH` note for the re-authentication case. The same change in `challenge(context, error, field)` (line 137) enables conditional UI on error pages during re-authentication. The condition should remain restricted to the non-re-authentication branch (user == null), as before.

title: UsernameForm skips the username form during re-authentication when conditional passkeys are enabled, but `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` is not defined in this class
body: `UsernameForm.authenticate()` now calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` (line 47), but this method is only defined in `UsernamePasswordForm` (line 160) as `protected boolean isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)`. `UsernameForm` extends `UsernamePasswordForm`, so it compiles, but the inherited implementation checks `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null`. In `UsernameForm`, `webauthnAuth` is only non-null when constructed with a `KeycloakSession` (`UsernamePasswordForm(KeycloakSession)`); the no-arg constructor used by the provider factory leaves it null, so the guard behaves inconsistently depending on construction path. More importantly, the semantic change means that during re-authentication (user already set) with passkeys enabled, `UsernameForm` no longer calls `context.success()` and instead falls through to `super.authenticate(context)`, which renders the username/password form with the username hidden — but for a split username+password flow (as configured in `PasskeysUsernameFormTest`), the subsequent `PasswordForm` step then runs with the user set, which is a different flow shape than intended. The condition should be scoped so the skip only happens when passkeys conditional UI is actually active for this authenticator instance, not merely when the realm has passkeys enabled.

title: Refactored `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators` changes behavior for subclasses that override it to return false
body: `fillContextForm()` previously checked `if (user != null)` before building the `WebAuthnAuthenticatorsBean` and setting `ALLOWED_AUTHENTICATORS`; it now calls `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators(context)` (line 101), whose base implementation returns `context.getUser() != null` (line 129). `WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator` overrides this to return `false` (line 65-67) so that authenticators are not listed during conditional UI. However, the base `WebAuthnAuthenticator.fillContextForm()` still sets `IS_USER_IDENTIFIED` based on a local `isUserIdentified` variable that is only set to `true` inside the `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators` branch (line 108). For `WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator` during re-authentication (user != null), `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators` returns false, so `isUserIdentified` stays false and `IS_USER_IDENTIFIED` is set to "false" even though a user is identified — the template may then render the page as an ID-less/passwordless page rather than a re-authentication page. The refactor conflates "user is identified" with "authenticators should be listed"; these are separate concerns and the `IS_USER_IDENTIFIED` flag should still be derived from `user != null`.

title: Error response during conditional-UI passkey failure sets re-authentication form attributes unconditionally
body: `createErrorResponse()` now calls `AuthenticatorUtils.setupReauthenticationInUsernamePasswordFormError(context)` (line 53). That helper only sets `USERNAME_HIDDEN` and `REGISTRATION_DISABLED` when the `USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH` auth note is "true", so in the normal (non re-authentication) conditional UI case it is a no-op. However, when a passkey conditional-UI authentication fails during re-authentication (user already set, note = "true"), this marks the form as re-authentication — which is correct — but the method is invoked on every error response, including errors that occur in the plain username/password flow where the user was NOT previously set (e.g. `WEBAUTHN_ERROR_API_GET` from the browser). In that case the note is absent and the call is harmless, but the placement suggests it is meant to run only for re-authentication errors; if the note is ever set by another path (e.g. a previous execution in the same auth session), a non re-authentication error page would incorrectly hide the username field and disable registration. The call should be guarded by an explicit check that this error occurred during a re-authentication flow, not placed unconditionally in the shared error-response path.

title: Static import from `browser` package into `util` package creates a package cycle and widens visibility of an internal constant
body: `AuthenticatorUtils` (in `org.keycloak.authentication.authenticators.util`) now statically imports `AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator.USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH` (line 35), and the constant was changed from `protected` to `public` (AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator.java line 58) solely to make this import possible. This introduces a dependency from the generic `util` package back into the `browser` package (a package cycle: browser → util → browser), and exposes an internal flow-state constant as part of the public API surface of `AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator`. The constant is an implementation detail of the username/password form flow; making it `public` invites external use and makes future refactoring harder. The constant should remain `protected`/package-private and the note name should either be defined in `AuthenticatorUtils` itself or in a neutral location, with `AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator` referencing it from there.

title: Test `reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey` uses inverted assertion logic that always passes
body: In `reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey`, the check for absence of the WebAuthn button is written as: `MatcherAssert.assertThat(driver.findElement(By.xpath("//form[@id='webauth']")), nullValue()); fail("Not expected to have webauthn button");` inside a `try` block, with `catch (Exception nsee) { // expected }`. `driver.findElement` throws `NoSuchElementException` when the element is absent, so the `assertThat(..., nullValue())` line is never reached in the expected (passing) case — the test passes via the catch block. If the element IS present, `findElement` returns a non-null element, `assertThat(element, nullValue())` fails with an `AssertionError`, which is also caught by the broad `catch (Exception)` and silently treated as expected. The test therefore cannot fail when the WebAuthn button is incorrectly shown; the assertion is dead code. The correct pattern (used elsewhere in the codebase) is `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, () -> driver.findElement(...))`, as done in `PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest` before this PR. Both occurrences (lines 291-296 and 312-317) have the same defect, so the test does not actually verify that passkeys are hidden for a user without a passkey during re-authentication.

title: Re-authentication test submits only a password on a form where the username field is hidden but present, relying on stale form state
body: In `webauthnLoginWithExternalKey_reauthenticationWithPasswordOrPasskey`, after re-authentication with `prompt=login`, the test calls `loginPage.login(getPassword("test-user@localhost"))` (line 377) — a single-argument login that submits only the password. This works only because the hidden username field retains the previously entered username from the initial login form submission in the same browser session. The test then asserts `Assert.assertEquals("Invalid password.", loginPage.getInputError())` and later expects a successful password login for `user.getId()`. This is fragile: it depends on the hidden input's value persisting across page loads and on the specific template rendering the hidden username with the attempted username. If the template changes (e.g. the hidden field is rendered empty, or the form posts to a different action), the test would submit an empty username and fail with "Invalid username or password" rather than "Invalid password", or authenticate the wrong user. The test should explicitly assert the hidden username value (e.g. `loginPage.getAttemptedUsername()` equals the expected user) before submitting, as done in `PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest.passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey`, to make the precondition explicit and the failure mode diagnosable.

title: New `configureTestRealm(realmRepresentation)` call in `addTestRealms` is undefined in the shown file and may break realm setup
body: `addTestRealms` now calls `configureTestRealm(realmRepresentation)` (line 73) before adding the realm, but no such method is defined in the shown file content and it is not a standard override of `AbstractAdminTest`/`AbstractWebAuthnVirtualTest` visible here. If this method is inherited from a superclass it may be fine, but if it is expected to be defined locally (e.g. to set up the `test-user@localhost` user that the new tests rely on at lines 299, 323, 377, 404), its absence would cause a compile error; if it exists in a superclass it may perform additional realm mutations not obvious from this diff. The new tests depend on a pre-existing user `test-user@localhost` with a known password (`getPassword("test-user@localhost")`), which is not created by `registerDefaultUser()` (that creates `userwebauthn`). The diff does not show where this user is created; if `configureTestRealm` does not create it, tests `reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey` and `webauthnLoginWithExternalKey_reauthenticationWithPasswordOrPasskey` will fail at runtime with user-not-found. This dependency should be made explicit in the test file.

title: Changed assertion in `passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey` now expects the webauthn form to be present after username submission, but does not verify it is functional for the identified user
body: The test `passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey` was changed to assert that `//form[@id='webauth']` IS present (line 194, 200) after submitting the username, where previously it asserted the form was absent. This matches the behavioral change in `UsernamePasswordForm` (conditional UI now enabled when user is set), but the test only checks element presence via `driver.findElement(...)`. It does not verify that the conditional UI / WebAuthn form is actually wired to the identified user (e.g. that the challenge is bound to that user's credentials, or that the autofill attribute is set on the password field rather than the username field). Given that the production change enables conditional UI during a state where the user is already identified (see the high-severity finding on `UsernamePasswordForm.java:115`), this test should assert the rendered page semantics (e.g. `loginPage.getPasswordAutocomplete()` includes `webauthn`, or the hidden username value) to catch regressions where the conditional UI is attached to the wrong input. As written, it only asserts a DOM node exists, which would also pass if the form were rendered in a broken state.

title: Conditional passkeys UI is no longer offered during re-authentication because fillContextForm is gated on a non-null user
body: In UsernamePasswordForm.authenticate(), the call to webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) was moved outside the else branch and is now guarded by isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()), which returns false whenever context.getUser() is null. During a re-authentication (e.g. OIDC prompt=login) the user is not yet set in the authentication context when the login form is first rendered, so the WebAuthn conditional UI attributes (challenge, RP ID, ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI) are never set on the form. The browser therefore never invokes navigator.credentials.get() with the conditional mediation, and passwordless passkey re-authentication on the username/password form is impossible. The same gating in challenge(context, error, field) (line 137) means that after a failed password attempt during re-authentication the conditional UI is also not re-armed. The guard should be based on webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() (as before), not on the presence of a user in the context.

title: UsernameForm skips the username step during re-authentication when conditional passkeys are enabled, breaking the username+password+passkey flow
body: UsernameForm.authenticate() now skips rendering the username form (context.success()) whenever context.getUser() != null && !isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(). The intent is to allow passkey re-authentication, but the condition is inverted with respect to the surrounding logic: when conditional passkeys ARE enabled the form is skipped entirely, so a user who must re-authenticate with username+password (e.g. a non-discoverable key, or a user without a passkey) is never asked for their username and the subsequent PasswordForm cannot validate anything. Conversely, when passkeys are disabled the old behavior (skip when user is set) is preserved. The check should be !isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() only for deciding whether passkeys can bypass the form; the skip should still happen when the user has no usable passkey path. As written, the separate UsernameForm + PasswordForm flow cannot complete a password re-authentication when the PASSKEYS feature and realm passkeys are enabled.

title: Refactor to shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators() changes behavior when the method is overridden to return false but a user is present
body: fillContextForm() previously branched on user != null to decide whether to build the WebAuthnAuthenticatorsBean (the list of allowed authenticators for a 2FA-style identified user). It now calls shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators(context), whose default implementation is context.getUser() != null, but WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator overrides it to always return false. In WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator.fillContextForm() (which calls super.fillContextForm()), this means that even when a user IS identified in the context (re-authentication with a known user), the ALLOWED_AUTHENTICATORS attribute is never set and isUserIdentified is always false. For the conditional UI this is intentional, but the base-class contract is now misleading: any other subclass overriding shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators() to false while still wanting per-user authenticator lists would silently lose them. More importantly, the new method name and javadoc ('true if the available webauthn authenticators should be shown on the screen') does not match what it actually controls (whether the per-user allowed-authenticators list is populated), which invites future misuse. The override in WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator should instead override a narrower hook or the base method should be documented/renamed to reflect that it gates the allowed-authenticators list.

title: createErrorResponse() calls setupReauthenticationInUsernamePasswordFormError() unconditionally, hiding the username field even for first-time logins
body: WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator.createErrorResponse() now calls AuthenticatorUtils.setupReauthenticationInUsernamePasswordFormError(context) on every WebAuthn error rendered through the conditional UI. That helper sets LoginFormsProvider.USERNAME_HIDDEN=true and REGISTRATION_DISABLED=true whenever the auth note USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH is 'true'. The note is only set by UsernamePasswordForm when a user is already in the context, so for a normal first-time login the helper is a no-op; however, the helper is invoked before fillContextForm(context) and before errorChallenge.apply(context), and it mutates the shared form provider obtained from context.form(). Because the same LoginFormsProvider instance is reused for the error challenge, any code path that reaches createErrorResponse() with the re-authentication note set (e.g. a passkey error during re-authentication on the username/password form) will hide the username field and disable registration on the error page. That is the desired behavior for re-authentication, but the method is placed in the generic WebAuthn error path rather than in the username/password-specific error challenge, so any future caller of WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator that is not the username/password form (the class is designed to be reusable via the errorChallenge function) would incorrectly get username-hiding/registration-disabling attributes applied to an unrelated form. The call belongs in the errorChallenge lambda supplied by UsernamePasswordForm, not in the generic authenticator.

title: Static import of USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH from AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator creates a package cycle and widens a constant's visibility unnecessarily
body: AuthenticatorUtils (in org.keycloak.authentication.authenticators.util) now statically imports AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator.USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH from org.keycloak.authentication.authenticators.browser. This introduces a dependency from the generic util package back into the browser authenticator package, and it required changing the constant from protected to public in AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator (line 58) solely to make it visible across packages. A public mutable-looking constant on an abstract authenticator class is a wider API surface than needed; the constant is an internal auth-note key. The cleaner approach is to move the constant (or a copy) into AuthenticatorUtils itself or into a shared constants class, and have AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator reference it from there, avoiding both the package cycle and the visibility widening.

title: reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey asserts absence of the webauthn form with a try/catch that swallows all exceptions, making the assertion ineffective
body: The test reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey verifies that the webauthn button is absent by calling driver.findElement(By.xpath("//form[@id='webauth']")) inside a try block and catching Exception, with a fail() only if findElement returns normally. Selenium's findElement throws NoSuchElementException when the element is absent, so the catch block is the expected path; however, catching the broad Exception type also swallows any other failure (e.g. StaleElementReferenceException, WebDriverException, or a page not fully loaded) and treats it as success. If the page is in an unexpected state or the driver errors for an unrelated reason, the test will pass even though the webauthn form might actually be present. The assertion should use a proper negative assertion such as assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, () -> driver.findElement(...)) or a Hamcrest matcher on findElements(...).isEmpty(), and the same pattern is repeated at line 312 for the re-authentication page.

title: webauthnLoginWithExternalKey_reauthenticationWithPasswordOrPasskey submits a password without a username during re-authentication and relies on a hidden username field
body: In webauthnLoginWithExternalKey_reauthenticationWithPasswordOrPasskey, after triggering re-authentication with prompt=login, the test calls loginPage.login(getPassword("test-user@localhost")) (line 377) and later loginPage.login(getPassword(USERNAME)) (line 410) with only a password argument. The single-argument login() overload submits only the password field, assuming the username is pre-filled/hidden. This works only if the form correctly sets USERNAME_HIDDEN and pre-populates the username, which is exactly the behavior changed by this PR (setupReauthenticationInUsernamePasswordFormError). If the re-authentication form regression (username not hidden / not pre-filled) occurs, the test would submit an empty username and fail with a confusing 'Invalid username or password' error rather than clearly asserting the re-authentication form state. The test should explicitly assert that the username field is hidden and contains the expected user (e.g. via loginPage.getAttemptedUsername() or by checking the hidden input value) before submitting the password-only login, so that a regression in the re-authentication form setup is caught with a clear message.

title: PasskeysUsernameFormTest still asserts that the webauthn form is absent after username entry, contradicting the new behavior where conditional passkeys remain enabled
body: In passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey, after the user enters a valid username on the UsernameForm, the test asserts Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, () -> driver.findElement(By.xpath("//form[@id='webauth']"))) (line 202), i.e. that the webauthn conditional UI form is NOT present on the subsequent password page. However, the PR's stated goal (and the corresponding change in PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest, which now asserts the form IS present) is that passkeys remain enabled during the username/password flow even after the username is known. The UsernameForm+PasswordForm split flow uses PasswordForm, which does not embed the WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator, so the webauthn form may legitimately be absent here; but the test does not document why this flow differs from the UsernamePasswordForm flow, and the assertion will break if PasswordForm is later changed to support conditional passkeys. At minimum the test should comment why the webauthn form is expected to be absent in this split-form flow, otherwise a future change that enables passkeys on PasswordForm will produce a confusing failure.

title: remove() can throw NPE when the alias does not exist, breaking removal of non-existent IDPs
body: In remove(String alias), the code now unconditionally calls idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias) and stores the result in storedIdp, then later passes storedIdp to registerIDPInvalidation(storedIdp) and registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp). If no IDP with the given alias exists, getByAlias returns null, and registerIDPInvalidation(null) dereferences idp.getInternalId() (line 366), throwing a NullPointerException. Previously the code had the same latent issue in the isInvalid branch (registerIDPInvalidation(idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias))), but the new code extends the null dereference to the common path: registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp) calls getLoginPredicate().test(idp), which starts with Objects::nonNull so it tolerates null, but registerIDPInvalidation does not. The contract of remove() is to return false when the IDP is not found (per the interface javadoc: 'true if an IDP with the specified alias was found and removed; false otherwise'), so callers expect a boolean, not an exception. Consequence: removing a non-existent IDP alias (e.g. via admin REST DELETE on a missing alias, or cleanup code) now throws NPE instead of returning false, and the subsequent idpDelegate.remove(alias) is never reached.

title: registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate skips invalidation when an org-linked IDP's BROKER_PUBLIC config changes, serving stale login caches
body: registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate(original, updated) decides whether to invalidate the getForLogin caches by comparing only the login predicate (enabled, not link-only, not hidden) and the organizationId. It does NOT compare the IDP's config, specifically the OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC flag. The login predicate added in IdentityProviderStorageProvider.getLoginPredicate() (line 254) now includes 'idp.getOrganizationId() == null || Boolean.parseBoolean(idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC))', meaning an org-linked IDP qualifies for login only when BROKER_PUBLIC is true. If an admin updates an org-linked IDP and flips BROKER_PUBLIC from true to false (or vice versa) while keeping it enabled/not-link-only/not-hidden and keeping the same organizationId, both original and updated pass getLoginPredicate() only if the flag is true in both — but when flipping true→false, original passes and updated fails, so invalidation does happen. The dangerous case is false→true: original fails the predicate (BROKER_PUBLIC false), updated passes; the first guard (!test(original) && !test(updated)) is false, the second guard (test(original) && test(updated) && same org) is false because test(original) is false, so it falls through to invalidate — that case is fine. However, consider an org-linked IDP with BROKER_PUBLIC=true that is updated to BROKER_PUBLIC=false: original passes, updated fails → falls through to invalidate — fine. The real gap: an org-linked IDP with BROKER_PUBLIC=false (not a login IDP) updated to BROKER_PUBLIC=true becomes a login IDP — handled. But what about an org-linked IDP where BROKER_PUBLIC stays true and organizationId stays the same, yet some other config relevant to login display changes? That's not a correctness issue for the cache (the cached list only stores internal IDs). The actual bug: when organizationId is unchanged and both pass the predicate, the method returns without invalidating — but the predicate itself depends on config (BROKER_PUBLIC). If original has BROKER_PUBLIC=true and updated has BROKER_PUBLIC=true, no change — fine. The subtle break is: the predicate test on the 'updated' model uses the in-memory model passed to update(), but the JPA delegate may normalize config (e.g. missing keys). More concretely, the method's second guard requires Objects.equals(original.getOrganizationId(), updated.getOrganizationId()) — but it does not verify that the BROKER_PUBLIC config value is unchanged. If an org-linked IDP has BROKER_PUBLIC absent (null → parseBoolean(null)=false → not a login IDP) and the update sets BROKER_PUBLIC=true, original fails predicate, updated passes → invalidates (correct). If BROKER_PUBLIC=true → absent: original passes, updated fails → invalidates (correct). So the predicate comparison does cover BROKER_PUBLIC transitions. The remaining hole: the predicate does not include the organization's enabled state or the organization provider's enabled state, but those are checked at read time via createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel, not cached. After deeper analysis, the concrete defect is different: the method compares original.getOrganizationId() with updated.getOrganizationId(), but when an IDP is linked to an org via OrganizationProvider.addIdentityProvider (as in the test at line 505), that operation may not go through IdentityProviderStorageProvider.update() — it may directly set the organizationId on the IDP through a different code path, meaning registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate is never invoked for org-link changes done via the organization API, leaving the login caches stale. The test at line 502-505 works around this by also calling update() first, but real callers using only organizations().get(id).identityProviders().addIdentityProvider(alias) would not trigger invalidation.

title: getForLogin cache does not account for organization enabled state changes, serving IDPs of disabled organizations
body: getForLogin caches the set of internal IDs matching the login filter per (realm, FetchMode, organizationId). The cached IDs are later resolved via session.identityProviders().getById(id), which wraps the model with createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel — that wrapper overrides isEnabled() to also check that the linked organization exists and is enabled. However, the cached ID list itself is not invalidated when an organization is disabled or deleted. The invalidation logic in registerIDPLoginInvalidation and registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate only fires on IDP create/update/remove, not on organization updates. Compare with getByOrganization (line 173), which explicitly checks isInvalid(orgId) in addition to the cache key — indicating that organization-level invalidations are expected to be registered under the org ID key. getForLogin does not perform this isInvalid(orgId) check, and there is no code registering invalidation of cacheKeyForLogin keys when an organization is enabled/disabled/removed. Consequence: if an org is disabled after getForLogin(ORG_ONLY, orgId) or getForLogin(ALL, orgId) has been cached, the cached ID list still contains the org's IDPs; although the wrapper's isEnabled() returns false for those IDPs, the stream still includes them (the caller in OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean filters with idp.isEnabled(), which would filter them out — but other callers of getForLogin that don't re-check isEnabled would see stale entries). More importantly, if the organization is deleted, the wrapper returns isEnabled()=false, but the IDP remains in the result stream. The cache is also not invalidated when the organization's BROKER_PUBLIC-related state changes at the org level. This is a cache-coherence gap: the getForLogin cache key does not include any organization revision, and no invalidation path exists for organization lifecycle events.

title: getForLogin returns results in non-deterministic order (HashSet) unlike the delegate which preserves query order
body: getForLogin collects the cached internal IDs into a java.util.HashSet (line 244: 'Set<IdentityProviderModel> identityProviders = new HashSet<>();') and returns identityProviders.stream(). The underlying idpDelegate.getForLogin (default implementation in IdentityProviderStorageProvider) uses getAllStream which typically returns results in a stable database order (e.g. by alias or internal ID). By collecting into a HashSet, the cached path loses any ordering guarantee, so the stream returned to callers (e.g. login page rendering in OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean, which sorts afterwards, but other callers may not) has non-deterministic iteration order. The same pattern exists in getByOrganization (line 200), but for getForLogin the ordering matters more because the login page displays IDPs and the sorting in OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean uses IDP_COMPARATOR_INSTANCE which sorts by display name/alias — however, if two IDPs have the same display name, the tie-breaking order becomes non-deterministic across cache hits vs misses, causing inconsistent UI ordering and potentially flaky tests. Using LinkedHashSet would preserve insertion order from the cached set iteration, but the cached set itself (IdentityProviderListQuery.getIDPs) may already be a HashSet. The consequence is inconsistent ordering between cached and uncached responses.

title: Cache update path for new searchKey invalidates and re-adds under a different revision counter, risking race conditions in clustered cache
body: In getForLogin (and identically in getByOrganization at line 192), when a query exists but the requested searchKey is not cached, the code calls cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey) and then cache.addRevisioned(query, cache.getCurrentCounter()) — note it uses cache.getCurrentCounter() (the current global counter) rather than the startupRevision used in the initial cache-miss path (line 231 uses startupRevision). This mirrors the getByOrganization pattern, but the inconsistency means the revisioned entry is added with a different revision basis. In a clustered Infinispan setup, invalidateObject followed by addRevisioned with a fresh counter can race with concurrent readers/writers on other nodes: another node may have already re-populated the cache between the invalidate and the add, and the addRevisioned with a higher counter could overwrite a newer entry or be overwritten depending on the revision comparison logic in RealmCacheManager. The consequence is potential cache inconsistency across cluster nodes where a stale query entry (missing the new searchKey) could be served, or a concurrent update could be lost. This is a pre-existing pattern copied from getByOrganization, but introducing it in a new hot path (login page rendering) amplifies the risk.

title: getLoginPredicate now depends on OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC config, changing semantics for all callers and breaking non-organization deployments
body: The getLoginPredicate() static method was changed to include '.and(idp -> idp.getOrganizationId() == null || Boolean.parseBoolean(idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC)))'. This predicate is used in InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.registerIDPLoginInvalidation and registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate to decide whether an IDP qualifies as a login IDP. The predicate now references OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC, which is an organization-feature concept. In deployments where the ORGANIZATION feature is disabled, org-linked IDPs should not exist, so the predicate's organizationId==null branch covers them. However, the predicate calls idp.getConfig().get(...) without null-checking the config map — if an IdentityProviderModel has a null config (possible for newly constructed models before config initialization, or in tests), this throws NPE. More importantly, the predicate's semantics changed: previously it only checked ENABLED, LINK_ONLY, HIDE_ON_LOGIN; now it also requires BROKER_PUBLIC=true for org-linked IDPs. This is used to decide cache invalidation — if an org-linked IDP has BROKER_PUBLIC=false, it's not considered a login IDP, so create/update/remove of such IDPs won't invalidate the login caches. But the default getForLogin implementation (lines 165-184) uses getLoginSearchOptions() which does NOT include the BROKER_PUBLIC filter for REALM_ONLY mode (it sets ORGANIZATION_ID=null), and for ORG_ONLY/ALL it adds BROKER_PUBLIC=true to search options. So the predicate and the actual query are now consistent for org-linked IDPs. However, the predicate is a public static API (getLoginPredicate) that other code may call; changing its semantics is a contract break for any external caller expecting the old behavior (enabled && !linkOnly && !hideOnLogin).

title: Inconsistent isEnabled re-check: ORG_ONLY branch with organization uses organization.getIdentityProviders() without BROKER_PUBLIC re-check on wrapped models
body: In searchForIdentityProviders, the onlyOrganizationBrokers branch when this.organization != null (line 66) uses organization.getIdentityProviders() and filters with 'idp.isEnabled() && !idp.isLinkOnly() && !idp.isHideOnLogin() && Boolean.parseBoolean(idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC))'. The isEnabled() here may be the wrapped version from createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel (which checks org enabled state). However, the ORG_ONLY branch when organization == null (line 74) and the ALL branch (line 79) now re-check idp.isEnabled() after getForLogin, with the comment 're-check isEnabled as idp might have been wrapped'. But the organization != null branch (line 66) does NOT re-check isEnabled() after organization.getIdentityProviders() — it checks it inline in the filter, which is fine. The inconsistency is that the ALL branch (line 79-82) filters with idp.isEnabled() but does NOT filter on BROKER_PUBLIC or link-only/hide-on-login again, relying on getForLogin to have filtered correctly. Since getForLogin now caches results and the cache may contain IDPs whose BROKER_PUBLIC was true at cache time but the org was later disabled, the wrapper's isEnabled() returns false and they're filtered out — OK. But if BROKER_PUBLIC is flipped false→true on an org-linked IDP without invalidating the login cache (the gap described in the registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate finding), getForLogin(ALL, orgId) would not include the newly-public IDP, and the bean would not show it. The re-check of isEnabled() is a partial mitigation but doesn't cover the BROKER_PUBLIC staleness.

title: Test cleanup uses wrong alias 'alias' instead of the actual created alias, leaking test IDPs
body: In testCacheIDPForLogin, IDPs are created with aliases 'idp-alias-0' through 'idp-alias-20' (lines 372-382 and 418-425), but the cleanup registration at lines 381 and 425 uses 'getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)' — the literal string "alias", not the actual alias variable. This means the cleanup will attempt to remove an IDP with alias "alias" which doesn't exist, and all 21 created IDPs ('idp-alias-0' to 'idp-alias-20') are leaked into the test realm. The same bug exists in testCacheIDPByOrg at line 303. Consequence: test pollution — leaked IDPs persist across test methods in the same realm, potentially affecting other tests that count IDPs or iterate over all IDPs (e.g. tests that assert on the number of identity providers in the realm, or login page tests that render all IDPs). This can cause flaky failures in subsequent tests and makes the test suite non-hermetic.

title: testCacheIDPForLogin assumes organizations().getAll() ordering to pick orgaId, making the test fragile
body: Line 384: 'String orgaId = testRealm().organizations().getAll().get(0).getId();' assumes the first organization returned by getAll() is 'orga' (created in onBefore at line 59). The test then associates IDPs 10-19 with this org and asserts specific counts (e.g. line 409: assertEquals(5, identityProviderListQuery.getIDPs(orgaId).size())). If getAll() returns organizations in a different order (e.g. by ID which is UUID-based and random, or by name), get(0) could be 'orgb' instead of 'orga', causing the IDP associations to go to the wrong org and all subsequent count assertions to fail. The test does not verify which organization it got — it should look up the org by domain name (e.g. testRealm().organizations().getByDomainName("orga.org") or similar) or by the known name 'orga'. This makes the test non-deterministic and likely to fail intermittently depending on UUID ordering or database return order.

title: Test removes 'idp-alias-1' but never verifies the removal effect on cached login results
body: In testCacheIDPForLogin step 1 (lines 417-440), the test creates 'idp-alias-20' (hideOnLogin=true, not a login IDP) and removes 'idp-alias-1' (which was disabled, i%2==0 for i=1 is false, so enabled=false — not a login IDP). The test then asserts that all login caches still exist (lines 435-439). However, it never verifies that the cached results are actually correct after these operations — specifically, it doesn't re-run getForLogin and check the returned IDP count or contents. Since 'idp-alias-1' was disabled (not in any login cache), its removal correctly doesn't invalidate caches, but the test doesn't confirm the caches still return the right data. More importantly, the test doesn't cover the case of removing an IDP that IS in the login cache (e.g. removing 'idp-alias-0' which is enabled and realm-level), which should invalidate the caches via registerIDPLoginInvalidation. The remove() path's invalidation logic for login caches is only tested indirectly; a direct test of removing a login-eligible IDP and verifying cache invalidation is missing.

title: update() calls getById() which may return null, causing NPE in registerIDPInvalidation and registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate
body: In update(IdentityProviderModel model), line 91: 'IdentityProviderModel idpById = getById(model.getInternalId());' — if no IDP exists with the given internalId, getById returns null (line 124: 'if (internalId == null) return null;' and line 134: 'if (model == null) return null;'). The result is then passed to registerIDPInvalidation(idpById) at line 92, which dereferences idp.getInternalId() (line 366) → NPE. It's also passed to registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate(idpById, model) at line 93, which calls getLoginPredicate().test(original) — the predicate starts with Objects::nonNull so it handles null original gracefully (returns false), but then the logic proceeds: !test(null)=true && !test(updated) — if updated is also not a login IDP, returns early; otherwise falls through to invalidate. So registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate tolerates null original, but registerIDPInvalidation does not. The consequence: calling update() on a non-existent internalId throws NPE instead of either silently succeeding or throwing a meaningful exception. The JPA delegate's update would likely throw its own exception for a non-existent ID, but the NPE happens before reaching the delegate, masking the real error and potentially leaving the transaction in an inconsistent state.

title: Login cache invalidation on IDP update misses changes to BROKER_PUBLIC config and other login-relevant fields
body: registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate(original, updated) only compares getLoginPredicate() results and getOrganizationId() between the original and updated models. The login predicate (IdentityProviderStorageProvider.LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate, line 252-256 of IdentityProviderStorageProvider.java) tests isEnabled(), !isLinkOnly(), !isHideOnLogin(), and the BROKER_PUBLIC config flag for org-linked IDPs. However, the update path only skips invalidation when both models pass the predicate AND organizationId is unchanged. If an update changes BROKER_PUBLIC from 'true' to 'false' (or vice versa) on an org-linked IDP, or changes enabled/linkOnly/hideOnLogin in a way that keeps the predicate result the same for the specific FetchMode combination, the cached getForLogin results become stale. Concretely: an org-linked IDP with BROKER_PUBLIC=true passes the predicate; updating it to BROKER_PUBLIC=false makes getLoginPredicate().test(updated) return false, so the first guard (!test(original) && !test(updated)) is false and the second guard (test(original) && test(updated)) is also false — invalidation does occur in that direction. But the reverse direction and, more importantly, updates that change BROKER_PUBLIC while the IDP remains org-linked and the predicate outcome is unchanged for one mode but the cached per-organization searchKey results differ are not handled: the cache key cacheKeyForLogin(realm, mode) is shared across ALL organizationIds (searchKey is stored inside IdentityProviderListQuery, not in the cache key), so invalidating only when organizationId changes is insufficient — a BROKER_PUBLIC change on an org-linked IDP alters which org-specific searchKey buckets are valid, yet if test(original) && test(updated) && Objects.equals(organizationId) the method returns without invalidating, leaving stale per-org cached IDP id sets. Additionally, the predicate's BROKER_PUBLIC check reads idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC) — for a realm-level IDP (organizationId == null) the predicate short-circuits true on the org check, but the cached getForLogin(ORG_ONLY, orgId) buckets for org-linked IDPs depend on BROKER_PUBLIC; an update that flips BROKER_PUBLIC while keeping the IDP org-linked and otherwise login-eligible will not invalidate when the predicate outcome is unchanged, serving stale IDP lists for that organization's login page.

title: remove(alias) calls registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp) with a possibly-null model, causing NPE via getLoginPredicate
body: In remove(String alias), storedIdp is obtained via idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias) and can be null if no IDP with that alias exists. registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp) (line 382-389) calls getLoginPredicate().test(idp), and the predicate chain starts with Objects::nonNull — actually the predicate is null-safe (Objects::nonNull returns false for null), so test(null) returns false and no invalidation occurs. However, this means removing a non-existent IDP silently skips login-cache invalidation, which is harmless. The real issue: when the IDP DOES exist, registerIDPLoginInvalidation only invalidates if the stored IDP currently qualifies as a login IDP. But consider an IDP that was previously a login IDP, was updated to hideOnLogin=true (which invalidates caches at update time), then removed — fine. The problematic case is when the cached getForLogin entries were populated, then the IDP is updated to hideOnLogin=true via a path that does NOT go through this storage provider's update (e.g., direct JPA delegate or another node in a cluster where invalidation hasn't propagated), then remove() is called: storedIdp reflects hideOnLogin=true, predicate returns false, login caches are NOT invalidated, yet the IDP is deleted — stale internal IDs remain in the cached IdentityProviderListQuery. The getForLogin method does handle null getById results by invalidating (lines 246-250), so this self-heals on next access, but the remove path should unconditionally invalidate login caches (or at least when the IDP existed) rather than relying on the current predicate state, because the cached query may contain the IDP from before it was disabled. The consequence is a window of stale data and reliance on the lazy null-check fallback.

title: getForLogin cache key ignores organizationId, causing cross-organization cache pollution and incorrect results
body: cacheKeyForLogin(realm, mode) produces a key of the form realmId + ".idp.login." + mode — it does NOT include organizationId. The organizationId is only used as searchKey inside the IdentityProviderListQuery (line 223: searchKey = organizationId != null ? organizationId : ""). This means all organization-specific queries for a given FetchMode share a single cache entry. While IdentityProviderListQuery supports multiple searchKeys (as seen in getByOrganization with first/max pagination keys), the getForLogin implementation has a critical flaw: when a new searchKey is not found (cached == null, line 234), it calls cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey) (line 236) — which invalidates the ENTIRE cache entry for that mode, discarding all previously cached organizationId buckets. This is a correctness/performance issue: in a multi-org deployment, alternating requests for orgA and orgB login pages will constantly invalidate each other's cached results, defeating the cache entirely and causing repeated DB queries. Worse, there is a race: two concurrent requests for different orgs can interleave such that one thread invalidates the entry while another is reading stale data, and the IdentityProviderListQuery merge constructor (line 239) attempts to preserve old searchKeys but the invalidateObject already removed the entry from the cache, making the merge ineffective. The consequence is severe cache thrashing in multi-organization realms and potential for serving incorrect IDP lists if the invalidation/merge logic doesn't properly synchronize. The cache key should incorporate organizationId (e.g., realmId + ".idp.login." + mode + "." + (organizationId != null ? organizationId : "")) to properly partition per-organization results, matching the pattern used by cacheKeyOrgId.

title: update() calls getById(model.getInternalId()) which may return an organization-wrapped model, breaking alias-based invalidation
body: In update(IdentityProviderModel model), line 91 calls getById(model.getInternalId()) to obtain the original IDP for invalidation purposes. However, getById (lines 123-142) wraps the result via createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel when the ORGANIZATION feature is enabled, returning an anonymous subclass of IdentityProviderModel that overrides isEnabled(). This wrapped model is then passed to registerIDPInvalidation(idpById) (line 92) and registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate(idpById, model) (line 93). registerIDPInvalidation uses idp.getInternalId() and idp.getAlias() — these are not overridden so they work. But registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate calls getLoginPredicate().test(original) where original is the wrapped model; the predicate calls idp.isEnabled() which for the wrapped model performs an additional organization lookup (lines 432-446). If the organization is disabled or the provider is unavailable, isEnabled() returns false even if the underlying IDP is enabled, causing the predicate to incorrectly classify the original as not-a-login-IDP. This can lead to incorrect invalidation decisions: e.g., an IDP that is actually login-eligible but whose wrapped isEnabled() returns false due to a disabled org would be treated as !test(original), and if the update also results in !test(updated), the method returns early without invalidating login caches — leaving stale cached login IDP lists. The wrapped model should not be used for invalidation logic; the raw delegate model should be fetched (e.g., via idpDelegate.getById) for comparison purposes.

title: getForLogin returns results in non-deterministic order due to HashSet, breaking login page IDP ordering
body: getForLogin (and similarly getByOrganization at line 200) collects IDP internal IDs into a Set<String> via Collectors.toSet() (line 229/238), then iterates over the set to build a HashSet<IdentityProviderModel> (line 244), and returns identityProviders.stream() (line 254). HashSet does not preserve insertion order, so the resulting stream has non-deterministic ordering. The callers (e.g., OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean.searchForIdentityProviders) apply .sorted(IDP_COMPARATOR_INSTANCE) after mapping, which may restore a deterministic order for the login page. However, the IdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin contract (server-spi line 165-184) does not specify ordering, and other callers may rely on stable ordering. More importantly, the default interface implementation (lines 165-184) uses Stream.concat of getAllStream results, which preserves database/insertion order. The cached implementation breaks this implicit ordering guarantee, potentially causing IDP display order to change between cache hits and misses, leading to inconsistent UI behavior and flaky tests. The cached IDs should be stored and returned in a deterministic order (e.g., LinkedHashSet or List) to match the uncached behavior.

title: getLoginPredicate BROKER_PUBLIC check can NPE if getConfig() returns null
body: The newly added predicate line 254: .and(idp -> idp.getOrganizationId() == null || Boolean.parseBoolean(idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC))) — if idp.getOrganizationId() is non-null but idp.getConfig() returns null (which is possible for IdentityProviderModel instances where config was not initialized), this will throw a NullPointerException. While IdentityProviderModel typically initializes config to an empty map, defensive coding is warranted in a predicate that is applied broadly (e.g., in cache invalidation paths where models may come from various sources). The consequence is a potential NPE during IDP create/update/remove operations in the InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider, breaking those operations. The code should use idp.getConfig() != null && Boolean.parseBoolean(...) or Objects.requireNonNullElse(idp.getConfig(), Map.of()).get(...).

title: ORG_ONLY branch with null organization re-checks isEnabled but not linkOnly/hideOnLogin/BROKER_PUBLIC, inconsistent with sibling branch
body: In searchForIdentityProviders, the onlyOrganizationBrokers branch when organization != null (lines 65-72) filters with idp.isEnabled() && !idp.isLinkOnly() && !idp.isHideOnLogin() && Boolean.parseBoolean(idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC)). But when organization == null (lines 74-77), it calls getForLogin(ORG_ONLY, null) and only re-checks idp.isEnabled() (line 75), not the other login criteria. The comment says 're-check isEnabled as idp might have been wrapped' — the wrapping (createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel) only overrides isEnabled(), so the other criteria (linkOnly, hideOnLogin, BROKER_PUBLIC) are already enforced by the underlying getForLogin query and don't need re-checking. However, the inconsistency is that the organization != null branch re-checks ALL criteria while the null branch re-checks only isEnabled. This is actually correct because the wrapped model only affects isEnabled(), but the asymmetry is confusing and fragile: if the wrapping logic changes to override more methods, the null-organization branch would silently miss them. More importantly, the ALL branch (line 79-82) also only re-checks isEnabled(), which is consistent with the null-org ORG_ONLY branch. The real issue is that the organization != null branch bypasses getForLogin entirely (using organization.getIdentityProviders()) and thus must re-check all criteria, while the other branches rely on getForLogin's filtering — this is a design inconsistency but not a bug per se. The added isEnabled() re-check in the ORG_ONLY-null and ALL branches is correct and necessary; no change needed, but the asymmetry in the organization != null branch (which doesn't use getForLogin) means it doesn't benefit from the new cache, potentially causing a performance regression for that specific path.

title: Test cleanup uses wrong alias 'alias' instead of the actual created alias
body: In testCacheIDPByOrg (line 303) and testCacheIDPForLogin (line 381, 425), the cleanup is registered as getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove) — the literal string "alias" is used instead of the loop variable alias (e.g., "org-idp-" + i or "idp-alias-" + i). This means the cleanup attempts to remove an IDP with alias "alias" which doesn't exist, and the actual created IDPs are never cleaned up. This leaks test data across test runs, potentially causing interference with other tests that count IDPs or check login page contents. The same bug exists in the pre-existing testCacheIDPByOrg (line 303), suggesting it was copied. The cleanup should use the actual alias variable: getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get(alias)::remove) or better, capture the created IDP's alias from the response.

title: testCacheIDPForLogin does not test invalidation when BROKER_PUBLIC config changes on an org-linked IDP
body: The test testCacheIDPForLogin covers: creating non-login IDPs, removing non-login IDPs, updating IDPs without changing login status, updating to change hideOnLogin, and linking a realm IDP to an org. However, it does NOT test the critical scenario where an org-linked IDP's BROKER_PUBLIC config is toggled (e.g., from 'true' to 'false'), which should invalidate the login caches because the IDP should no longer appear in ORG_ONLY/ALL results for that org. Given that registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate's logic (lines 403-418) specifically handles the BROKER_PUBLIC dimension via the login predicate, and the cache key issue (shared across orgs) makes per-org invalidation subtle, a test that: (1) caches getForLogin(ORG_ONLY, orgaId), (2) updates an org-linked IDP to set BROKER_PUBLIC=false, (3) verifies the cache is invalidated and the IDP no longer appears — is essential to validate correctness. Without this test, a regression where BROKER_PUBLIC changes don't trigger invalidation (or trigger incorrect invalidation) would go undetected.

title: update() NPEs when the IDP does not exist because getById() result is used without null check
body: In update(IdentityProviderModel model), the code calls getById(model.getInternalId()) and immediately passes the result to registerIDPInvalidation(idpById) and registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate(idpById, model). getById() returns null when no IDP with that internalId exists (line 134: 'if (model == null) return null;'). registerIDPInvalidation() then dereferences idp.getInternalId() (line 366) and registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() calls getLoginPredicate().test(original) which dereferences the model, causing a NullPointerException. Previously the code called idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias) and registerIDPInvalidation() on the result, which had the same latent issue, but the new code path makes the NPE deterministic for any update of a non-existent IDP. The consequence is that updating a non-existent IDP throws NPE instead of either propagating the delegate's behavior or failing cleanly; this is a regression risk for callers that rely on the delegate's update semantics.

title: remove() NPEs when the alias does not exist because storedIdp is used without null check
body: In remove(String alias), the code fetches storedIdp = idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias) (line 100) and then unconditionally calls registerIDPInvalidation(storedIdp) (line 103) and registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp) (line 111). If no IDP with the given alias exists, getByAlias returns null. registerIDPInvalidation() dereferences idp.getInternalId() (line 366) and registerIDPLoginInvalidation() calls getLoginPredicate().test(idp), which dereferences the model via the predicate chain, causing a NullPointerException. The method contract says it returns 'true if an IDP with the specified alias was found and removed; false otherwise', so removing a non-existent alias must return false, not throw NPE. This breaks the API contract and can cause 500 errors in admin endpoints that attempt to remove a non-existent IDP.

title: getForLogin cache does not account for organization enablement changes, causing stale login IDP lists
body: The getForLogin cache stores only the internal IDs of IDPs that matched the login filter at query time (lines 229, 238). When the cached IDs are resolved (lines 245-252), each IDP is fetched via session.identityProviders().getById(id), which wraps the model with createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel() — this wrapper overrides isEnabled() to also check that the linked organization exists and is enabled (lines 432-446). However, the cached ID set itself is never invalidated when an organization is enabled/disabled or removed. The invalidation logic in registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate only compares the IDP's own organizationId and login predicate, and organization-level changes (e.g., orgProvider.setEnabled(false) or org removal) do not register invalidation for cacheKeyForLogin keys. Consequently, after an organization is disabled, getForLogin can still return the org's IDPs from the cached ID set (the wrapper's isEnabled() returns false, but the IDP is still included in the stream), or after an org is removed, the cached IDs may reference IDPs whose organization no longer exists. This is a data integrity/staleness issue: the login page can show or hide brokers incorrectly until some unrelated IDP mutation invalidates the cache. The getByOrganization cache has the same structural pattern but is explicitly invalidated on organization changes (isInvalid(orgId) check at line 173); getForLogin lacks an equivalent organization invalidation check.

title: registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate misses invalidation when BROKER_PUBLIC config changes for an org-linked IDP
body: registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate(original, updated) decides whether to invalidate the login caches by comparing getLoginPredicate().test(original) and getLoginPredicate().test(updated) plus Objects.equals(original.getOrganizationId(), updated.getOrganizationId()) (lines 405-411). The login predicate (IdentityProviderStorageProvider.java line 252-256) includes a check that an org-linked IDP must have BROKER_PUBLIC=true in its config. However, the 'no invalidation needed' branch at lines 409-411 only compares organizationId, not the BROKER_PUBLIC config value. If an update changes only the BROKER_PUBLIC config (e.g., from true to false, or false to true) while keeping the IDP enabled, not link-only, not hidden, and keeping the same organizationId, both original and updated may still pass or fail the predicate identically at the predicate level — but wait: the predicate does check BROKER_PUBLIC, so if BROKER_PUBLIC changes from true to false, getLoginPredicate().test(updated) returns false while test(original) returns true, which falls through to the invalidation branch. Actually re-examining: the predicate includes the BROKER_PUBLIC check, so a change in BROKER_PUBLIC that flips the predicate result will trigger invalidation. The real gap is subtler: if the IDP is org-linked and BROKER_PUBLIC changes from false to true (making it newly available for login), test(original)=false and test(updated)=true, so the first early-return (both false) doesn't apply, and the second early-return (both true) doesn't apply, so invalidation happens — correct. If BROKER_PUBLIC changes from true to false, test(original)=true, test(updated)=false, invalidation happens — correct. So the predicate comparison does cover BROKER_PUBLIC changes. The actual gap is that the predicate's BROKER_PUBLIC check uses idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC), but the update path compares the original model fetched via getById() which may be a cached/wrapped model; if the config map is mutated in place rather than replaced, the original and updated may share the same config reference, making the comparison ineffective. This is speculative without deeper investigation of IdentityProviderModel copy semantics, so downgrading to a potential issue: the invalidation logic relies on the predicate correctly reflecting config changes, but if IdentityProviderModel's config is a shared mutable map between original and updated (e.g., when the caller mutates the same model instance), the comparison original vs updated may not detect the change. This is a potential stale-cache issue but requires verification of model copy semantics.

title: getForLogin returns IDPs in non-deterministic order due to HashSet, breaking sorted login page expectations
body: In getForLogin (and similarly getByOrganization at line 200), the cached internal IDs are collected into a HashSet<IdentityProviderModel> (line 244: 'Set<IdentityProviderModel> identityProviders = new HashSet<>();') and then returned as identityProviders.stream() (line 254). HashSet does not preserve insertion order, so the stream of IDPs returned to callers has non-deterministic ordering. Callers like OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean.searchForIdentityProviders apply .sorted(IDP_COMPARATOR_INSTANCE) after fetching, which mitigates this for that caller, but the IdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin contract does not specify ordering, and other callers may rely on stable ordering (e.g., for consistent UI display or pagination). The delegate implementation (default method in IdentityProviderStorageProvider) uses Stream.concat of getAllStream results, which may have a defined order from the underlying query. The cache layer's use of HashSet discards that order, causing a behavioral change between cached and uncached paths. This is a subtle API/behavior break: the same query can return IDPs in different orders depending on cache state.

title: getForLogin cache update path has a race condition: invalidateObject followed by addRevisioned is not atomic
body: In getForLogin (and identically in getByOrganization at lines 190-197), when a cache entry exists but the requested searchKey is not yet cached (cached == null at line 233), the code calls cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey) (line 236) and then performs a fresh delegate query and cache.addRevisioned(query, cache.getCurrentCounter()) (lines 238-240). This invalidate-then-repopulate sequence is not atomic. In a clustered Infinispan cache or under concurrent requests within the same node, two threads can both observe cached == null, both invalidate, and both query the delegate and add revisioned entries. The IdentityProviderListQuery constructor with an existing query (line 239: 'new IdentityProviderListQuery(loaded, cacheKey, getRealm(), searchKey, cached, query)') attempts to merge with the previous query, but if both threads invalidate and rebuild concurrently, one thread's invalidation can discard the other's newly added searchKey, or the revision counters can conflict, leading to lost cache entries or inconsistent state. The consequence is potential cache corruption or unnecessary cache misses under concurrent login page loads, which is a common scenario. The same pattern exists in getByOrganization (pre-existing), but the new getForLogin code replicates it for a high-traffic path (login page rendering).

title: getLoginPredicate() change alters semantics for all callers, potentially breaking existing behavior
body: The PR adds a new condition to getLoginPredicate(): '.and(idp -> idp.getOrganizationId() == null || Boolean.parseBoolean(idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC)))' (line 254). This changes the meaning of 'login IDP' for all callers of this predicate, not just the new cache invalidation logic. The predicate is now stricter: an org-linked IDP is only considered a login IDP if BROKER_PUBLIC is explicitly true. Previously, the predicate only checked ENABLED, LINK_ONLY, and HIDE_ON_LOGIN. Any existing code that uses getLoginPredicate() to filter IDPs for login display will now exclude org-linked IDPs that don't have BROKER_PUBLIC set, even if those IDPs were previously shown. This is a behavioral/API change that may affect other parts of the codebase not touched by this PR. The PR description does not mention auditing all callers of getLoginPredicate() for this semantic change. If there are callers outside the cache invalidation path (e.g., in login theme rendering, organization resolution, or admin console filtering) that relied on the old predicate, they will now silently drop org-linked IDPs from login pages. This is a contract break that should be explicitly documented or the predicate change should be scoped to only the cache invalidation logic.

title: Test cleanup uses wrong alias 'alias' instead of the actual created alias
body: In testCacheIDPByOrg (line 303) and testCacheIDPForLogin (lines 381, 425), the cleanup is registered as 'getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)' — the literal string "alias" is used instead of the actual alias variable (e.g., 'alias' or 'idp-alias-' + i). This means the cleanup attempts to remove an IDP with alias "alias" which does not exist, so the created IDPs are never cleaned up. This leaves test data in the realm, which can cause test pollution and failures in subsequent tests that count IDPs or iterate over all IDPs. The correct cleanup should use the actual alias, e.g., 'getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get(alias)::remove)' inside the loop where 'alias' is the loop variable. This is a test bug that undermines test isolation.

title: testCacheIDPForLogin does not test invalidation when an organization is disabled or removed
body: The test testCacheIDPForLogin verifies cache invalidation on IDP create/update/remove and on linking an IDP to an org, but it never tests the scenario where an organization itself is disabled or removed. As noted in the getForLogin cache design, the cached ID set is not invalidated when an organization's enabled status changes — the wrapper's isEnabled() check happens at resolution time, but the cached ID set still contains the IDP. The test should verify that after disabling an organization, getForLogin(ORG_ONLY, orgId) and getForLogin(ALL, orgId) no longer return that org's IDPs (or return them with isEnabled()=false, depending on the intended contract). Without this test, the stale-cache issue related to organization enablement changes (finding about missing org invalidation) would not be caught. The test suite should include a step that disables the organization and asserts the login cache behavior.

title: Re-checking isEnabled() after getForLogin may be redundant or incorrect depending on wrapper behavior
body: The PR adds '.filter(idp -> idp.isEnabled() && ...)' after getForLogin(ORG_ONLY, null) (line 75) and getForLogin(ALL, ...) (line 80), with the comment 're-check isEnabled as idp might have been wrapped'. However, getForLogin already filters by the login predicate which includes isEnabled() (via LoginFilter.ENABLED). The cache layer's getForLogin resolves cached IDs via session.identityProviders().getById(id), which wraps the model with createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel() — this wrapper overrides isEnabled() to check organization enablement. So the isEnabled() re-check is intended to filter out IDPs whose organization was disabled after caching. But the comment 'idp might have been wrapped' is misleading: the wrapping always happens in the cache layer, and the re-check is specifically for the organization-aware wrapper's isEnabled() override. More importantly, the REALM_ONLY branch (line 58) does NOT re-check isEnabled(), which is inconsistent — if the wrapper can make isEnabled() return false for org-linked IDPs, realm-only IDPs (organizationId == null) are unaffected by the wrapper, so the re-check is unnecessary there. The inconsistency between branches suggests the change was applied hastily. The consequence is minor (redundant filtering for ORG_ONLY/ALL, missing for REALM_ONLY which is fine), but the comment is inaccurate and the asymmetry is confusing.

title: concatenatedRSToASN1DER produces invalid DER when r or s has a high bit set
body: In concatenatedRSToASN1DER, the raw r and s halves of the signature are copied into a byte array of size len+1 with a leading zero byte and converted via new BigInteger(r). This is intended to force a positive sign, but the leading zero is always present even when the most significant bit of the value is 0. BigInteger.toByteArray() then returns the minimal two's-complement representation, so when the top bit of r or s is 0 the encoded INTEGER will be one byte shorter than len (or len+1), producing a DER sequence whose INTEGERs are not padded to the curve size. More importantly, the method also contains dead code: lines 114-115 call ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger) and .write(sBigInteger) on throwaway encoder instances whose output is discarded; only the writeDerSeq call on lines 117-121 actually contributes to the returned bytes. The consequence is that signatures whose r or s value has a leading zero byte (roughly 50% of signatures per component) will be re-encoded with a non-canonical, unpadded INTEGER, and any consumer that strictly validates DER lengths (or compares against the JDK/BouncyCastle encoding) will reject or mismatch. The correct approach is to left-pad r and s to exactly len bytes and prepend a 0x00 only when the high bit is set (i.e., use the minimal positive encoding), as done by BCECDSACryptoProvider.

title: asn1derToConcatenatedRS does not validate that decoded r/s fit the expected length
body: asn1derToConcatenatedRS decodes the DER sequence and converts r and s to BigInteger, then calls integerToBytes(value, len). integerToBytes truncates by taking the last qLength bytes when the value is longer than qLength (System.arraycopy(bytes, bytes.length - tmp.length, ...)). A maliciously crafted or corrupted DER signature with an r or s value larger than the curve size (e.g., a 33-byte INTEGER for P-256) will be silently truncated instead of rejected, and the resulting concatenated signature will be accepted as if valid. For a signature-verification path this is a data-integrity risk: malformed input is normalized rather than rejected, and the truncation can alias distinct DER encodings to the same raw signature. The method should reject values whose minimal encoding exceeds len bytes (after accounting for the sign byte) rather than truncating.

title: readSequence mishandles indefinite-length encoding and can loop or mis-parse
body: readSequence reads a length via readLength(), which returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding (0x80). The loop condition `while (length > 0)` then exits immediately for indefinite-length input, returning an empty list instead of parsing the contained elements until the end-of-contents marker — silently accepting malformed/truncated input as an empty sequence. Additionally, the loop decrements `length` by the number of bytes returned by readNext(), but readNext() returns the full TLV (tag + length + value) byte count only because of the mark/reset trick; if the sequence length is inconsistent with the actual element sizes (e.g., length larger than the remaining elements), the loop will keep calling readNext() past the sequence boundary and eventually throw EOF, but if length is smaller than the elements, trailing bytes of the sequence are silently ignored and never validated. For a DER decoder used on signature data, indefinite-length and length-mismatch handling should be strict: reject indefinite-length (DER forbids it) and verify that exactly `length` bytes were consumed.

title: readLength bounds check uses total input limit instead of remaining bytes
body: The check `if (length >= limit)` compares the declared element length against the total input size (limit = bytes.length set in the constructor) rather than against the number of bytes remaining in the stream. When readLength() is called for a nested element (e.g., the INTEGERs inside a sequence via readNext/readInteger), a declared length that is valid relative to the whole buffer but extends beyond the enclosing sequence's boundary will pass this check. The subsequent read(length) will then consume bytes belonging to subsequent elements or throw EOF only if the buffer is exhausted. This weakens the structural validation of the decoder for nested TLVs; the check should be against the remaining unread bytes (is.available()) or the enclosing element's remaining length.

title: Provider selection semantics changed from fail-fast to highest-order-wins, silently ignoring other providers
body: detectProvider previously threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath, forcing an explicit choice. It now sorts providers by order() descending and silently picks the first, only logging the ignored providers at debug level. This is an API/behavior break: any deployment that accidentally has two providers (e.g., keycloak-crypto-default and keycloak-crypto-fips1402, or the new authz-client provider alongside a server provider) will no longer fail at startup; instead it will silently use whichever has the higher order() (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return 200, so ties are resolved by ServiceLoader iteration order, which is classpath-dependent and non-deterministic). For a security-sensitive component, silently selecting a crypto provider based on an arbitrary ordering is risky — a mis-ordered classpath could select the FIPS provider in a non-FIPS deployment or vice versa without any warning. At minimum, ties in order() should be detected and rejected, and the selection of a non-default provider when multiple are present should be logged at warn/info level, not debug.

title: New abstract method order() breaks all external CryptoProvider implementations
body: order() is added as a non-default abstract method on the public CryptoProvider interface. Any third-party or downstream implementation of CryptoProvider (the interface is explicitly designed for pluggability via META-INF/services, and the keycloak-client repository sync mentioned in the PR description implies external implementations exist) will fail to compile / fail at ServiceLoader instantiation with AbstractMethodError once this change is synced. The method should be declared as `default int order() { return 0; }` (or another documented default) so existing implementations keep working, with the built-in providers overriding it. Without a default, this is a hard API break for every external implementor.

title: CryptoIntegration.init is called on every AuthzClient.create, racing with setProvider and ignoring the configured classloader
body: AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()) on every client creation. CryptoIntegration.init is idempotent only for the auto-detect path; if another component (e.g., the Keycloak server or a test harness) has already called CryptoIntegration.setProvider(...) with a specific provider, this call is a no-op and fine, but if init has not yet run, the authz-client will auto-detect and permanently set the static singleton provider for the whole JVM using the authz-client's classloader. Because the provider is a static singleton, the first AuthzClient created in a JVM that also hosts a Keycloak server (or tests that rely on DefaultCryptoProvider) will lock in AuthzClientCryptoProvider (order 100) or DefaultCryptoProvider (order 200) depending on classpath, and CryptoIntegration.setProvider called later by the server will override it globally — meaning the authz-client's ECDSA conversions and the server's crypto operations then run against different providers within the same JVM. The authz-client should not mutate global JVM crypto state from a client library; at minimum this should be documented, and ideally the client should use its own provider instance rather than the global CryptoIntegration singleton.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default KeyStore provider, not a BouncyCastle provider
body: getBouncyCastleProvider() is implemented as `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which returns whatever JCA provider supplies the default keystore type (typically SunJCE/sun.security.provider.Sun on a stock JDK), not a BouncyCastle provider. The CryptoProvider contract (see the interface javadoc: 'BouncyCastle security provider. Can be either non-FIPS or FIPS based provider') expects a BouncyCastle provider; WildFlyElytronProvider returns null, but returning the Sun provider is misleading and will break any caller that registers or configures the returned provider expecting BC algorithms (e.g., code that does Security.addProvider(getBouncyCastleProvider()) or passes it to BC-specific APIs). If the authz-client genuinely has no BouncyCastle dependency, it should return null like WildFlyElytronProvider, or the method should be documented as returning the default JCA provider.

title: ECDSA test uses a single default-curve key for all algorithms and never verifies signatures
body: The test generates one KeyPair with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair(), which on most JDKs produces a P-256 (secp256r1) key, but then runs the same key through ES256, ES384 and ES512. ES384/ES512 expect 48/64-byte r||s components; signing with a P-256 key and SHA-384/SHA-512 still yields 32-byte r and s values, so asn1derToConcatenatedRS is called with signLength 96/128 while the actual r/s are 32 bytes — the test then only checks round-trip equality (rsConcat equals rsConcat2), never that the conversion matches the JDK's own signature verification, and never exercises the padding edge cases (leading zero bytes, high-bit set) that are the actual risk in this code. The test would pass even if concatenatedRSToASN1DER produced non-canonical DER, as long as the decoder is symmetric. It should generate a key on the correct curve per algorithm (e.g., secp384r1/secp521r1), assert that the converted DER signature verifies with Signature.getInstance(...).verify(), and include fixed test vectors with known leading-zero/high-bit r and s values.

title: Module artifactId/name/description contradict each other about test-only status
body: The pom sets artifactId to `keycloak-authz-client-tests` but the <name> is 'Keycloak Authz: Client API' and the <description> says 'This module is supposed to be used just in the Keycloak repository for the testsuite. It is NOT supposed to be used by the 3rd party applications. For the use by 3rd party applications, please use `org.keycloak:keycloak-authz-client` module.' The artifactId says 'tests' while the name/description describe the client API itself, and the newly added META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider file means this artifact now ships a ServiceLoader registration that will be picked up by any JVM that has this jar on the classpath — including, per the description, contexts where it is not supposed to be used.
