If this module is truly test-only it should not be producing a service registration consumed at runtime; if it is the real client artifact, the artifactId/name are wrong. Either way the packaging metadata is inconsistent with the new runtime-visible service file.

title: concatenatedRSToASN1DER produces invalid DER for r or s with high bit set
body: In concatenatedRSToASN1DER, the raw r and s halves of the signature are copied into a byte array of size len+1 with a leading zero byte (System.arraycopy(signature, 0, r, 1, len)) and then converted via new BigInteger(r). This always yields a positive BigInteger whose toByteArray() includes the leading zero byte, so the encoded INTEGER is always len+1 bytes long. That is correct only when the original value had its high bit set (requiring a sign-padding zero). When the high bit is clear, DER requires the minimal encoding without the leading zero; the extra 0x00 makes the INTEGER non-minimal and therefore invalid DER. Strict verifiers (and RFC 6979/JWS interop with other implementations) will reject signatures produced by this method whenever r or s has a clear high bit, which happens with probability ~1/2 per component. The correct approach is new BigInteger(1, Arrays.copyOfRange(signature, 0, len)) (signum 1, magnitude only), letting BigInteger.toByteArray() add the sign byte only when needed. Note the two throwaway ASN1Encoder.create().write(...) calls on lines 114-115 are dead code and should be removed.

title: integerToBytes truncates the most significant bytes when the value is larger than the target length
body: integerToBytes(BigInteger s, int qLength) handles the case qLength < bytes.length by copying the LAST qLength bytes (System.arraycopy(bytes, bytes.length - tmp.length, tmp, 0, tmp.length)). For an ECDSA r or s value, the magnitude can legitimately be up to qLength+1 bytes because BigInteger.toByteArray() prepends a 0x00 sign byte when the high bit is set; in that case dropping the leading zero is correct. But if the value is genuinely larger than qLength (e.g. a malformed/forged DER signature where r or s >= curve order, which is exactly the input an attacker controls when verifying a JWT), this silently truncates the most significant bytes and returns a wrong-length, wrong-value r/s instead of rejecting the signature. asn1derToConcatenatedRS is used on the verification path, so a crafted DER signature with oversized integers would be silently mangled rather than rejected, and the resulting concatenated value fed to the JCA verifier. The method should throw (e.g. IOException) when bytes.length > qLength + 1, or when the value does not fit in qLength bytes, instead of truncating.

title: readSequence mishandles indefinite-length encoding and can loop forever / mis-parse
body: readLength() returns -1 for the indefinite-length form (0x80, line 133-135), but readSequence() (line 49) treats the returned length as a plain int and loops while (length > 0), decrementing by the size of each element. With length == -1 the loop condition is true and length only grows more negative as elements are consumed, so the loop never terminates on well-formed input and will keep calling readNext() until it throws EOFException from an exhausted stream — i.e. indefinite-length SEQUENCE encodings (valid BER, produced by some libraries) are rejected with a confusing EOF error rather than parsed or cleanly rejected. Additionally, readSequence never checks that the declared length matches the bytes actually consumed, and readNext() computes element size as content length plus the bytes consumed for tag+length via mark/reset, which double-counts nothing but also does not validate against the remaining sequence length, so a sequence whose declared length disagrees with its contents is silently accepted. For a signature-verification path, accepting structurally inconsistent DER is undesirable; at minimum the indefinite-length case must be rejected explicitly with a clear IOException.

title: Out-of-bounds length check uses the total input size instead of the remaining bytes
body: In readLength(), the sanity check for long-form lengths is `if (length >= limit)` where limit is the total length of the whole input byte array (set in the constructor), not the number of bytes remaining at the current read position. A nested element deep inside a larger structure can therefore declare a length up to the full input size even though far fewer bytes remain, and the check passes; the subsequent read(length) then fails only later with a generic EOF IOException. This weakens the early corruption detection the check is meant to provide (the comment says 'out of bounds length found'). The check should compare against the bytes remaining (limit minus bytes already consumed), e.g. track position and compare length > remaining.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default KeyStore provider, not a BouncyCastle provider
body: getBouncyCastleProvider() is implemented as KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which returns whatever JCA provider supplies the default keystore type (typically SunJCE/SunJSSE on a stock JDK), not a BouncyCastle provider. The CryptoProvider contract (see the interface javadoc: 'BouncyCastle security provider. Can be either non-FIPS or FIPS based provider') and callers such as code that registers or queries CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getBouncyCastleProvider() expect an actual BouncyCastle provider instance. The WildFlyElytronProvider precedent returns null when no BC provider exists; this implementation should either return null (documenting that the authz client has no BC provider) or return a real BouncyCastleProvider, not an unrelated JCA provider. Returning the keystore provider can cause callers to register/query the wrong security provider.

title: Provider selection semantics inverted relative to the documented order() contract
body: CryptoProvider.order() is documented as 'The higher number has preference over the lower number', and the PR description says the Keycloak testsuite keeps using DefaultCryptoProvider via ordering. But detectProvider() sorts with Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed() and then picks foundProviders.get(0). Comparator.reversed() sorts descending, so get(0) is the provider with the LOWEST order value — the opposite of the documented contract. Concretely: AuthzClientCryptoProvider.order() == 100 and DefaultCryptoProvider.order() == 200, so when both are on the classpath (exactly the scenario this PR creates for the authz-client module, which depends on keycloak-core and is used in the testsuite where DefaultCryptoProvider is present), the authz client provider (100) wins over DefaultCryptoProvider (200), contradicting both the javadoc and the stated intent that the testsuite keeps using DefaultCryptoProvider. Either remove .reversed() or fix the javadoc; as written the code and documentation disagree and the wrong provider is selected.

title: Adding abstract method order() to CryptoProvider breaks all external implementors (API break)
body: order() is added to the CryptoProvider interface as a plain abstract method with no default implementation. CryptoProvider is a public SPI in keycloak-common that third parties can implement (it is loaded via ServiceLoader from META-INF/services). Any existing external implementation of CryptoProvider will fail to compile/load against this change with AbstractMethodError at runtime when order() is called (CryptoIntegration.detectProvider now calls CryptoProvider::order on every loaded provider). This is a breaking API change to a published interface. It should be a default method (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) to preserve backward compatibility, matching how getSupportedRsaKeySizes() and getSupportedKeyStoreTypes() are already defined as defaults in the same interface.

title: CryptoIntegration.init is only called from one create() overload; other factory methods leave crypto uninitialized
body: CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()) is added only to create(Configuration). The other public factory methods create() (line 60) and create(InputStream) (line 72) delegate to create(Configuration) so they are covered, but any code path that constructs AuthzClient without going through these factories, or any other entry point in the authz-client that uses CryptoIntegration.getProvider() (e.g. ECDSA signature verification of tokens via the crypto provider), will hit 'Illegal state. Please init first before obtaining provider' if init was never called. More importantly, init() is a global static one-shot: once any other component in the same JVM (e.g. the Keycloak server in the testsuite) has initialized CryptoIntegration with a different classloader, the authz client's later init() call is a no-op and the AuthzClientCryptoProvider service file is never loaded for the client's classloader, so the client silently uses whatever provider was detected first. The initialization should be tied to the classloader actually used by the authz-client classes and be robust to prior initialization, or the provider should be resolved per-classloader rather than globally.

title: Test uses a default 256-bit EC key for ES384/ES512, so the ES384/ES512 paths are not actually exercised
body: The test constructor generates the key pair with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair(), which on a standard JDK produces a 256-bit (secp256r1) key. It then signs with Signature.getInstance(JavaAlgorithm.getJavaAlgorithm(algorithm.name())) — for ES384 that is SHA384withECDSA and for ES512 SHA512withECDSA — but the signature length is still determined by the 256-bit curve, so algorithm.getSignatureLength() (96/132 bytes for ES384/ES512) does not match the actual r||s size (64 bytes). asn1derToConcatenatedRS then splits the DER into halves of signLength/2 = 48/66 bytes, which does not correspond to the real r and s, and concatenatedRSToASN1DER re-encodes with the wrong lengths. The round-trip assertion may still pass because both directions use the same wrong length, masking the mismatch, but the test never validates behavior with a real P-384/P-521 key and never verifies the produced DER against Signature.verify, so it does not prove correctness for ES384/ES512. The test should generate a key on the matching curve (e.g. secp384r1/secp521r1 via ECGenParameterSpec) per algorithm, and ideally assert that the converted signature verifies with the public key.

title: Round-trip test never verifies the converted signature cryptographically and misses the high-bit-set case
body: The test only asserts that asn1derToConcatenatedRS(concatenatedRSToASN1DER(x)) == x. It never checks that the DER produced by concatenatedRSToASN1DER is accepted by Signature.verify (the actual consumer of this conversion in JWT verification), nor that the concatenated form verifies via a JCA Signature using the raw r||s (e.g. SHA256withECDSAinP1363Format). Because of the leading-zero bug in concatenatedRSToASN1DER (see separate finding), the produced DER is non-minimal whenever r or s has a clear high bit; a round-trip through the same buggy code hides this, but a real verifier would reject it. The test should include Signature.verify over the re-encoded DER and should force coverage of both high-bit-set and high-bit-clear r/s values (e.g. by looping over multiple signatures until both cases occur, since each occurs with ~50% probability).

title: Module artifactId/name/description say 'tests' but the module now contains production code and a service provider
body: The pom declares artifactId keycloak-authz-client-tests and the description states 'This module is supposed to be used just in the Keycloak repository for the testsuite. It is NOT supposed to be used by the 3rd party applications.' This PR adds production classes (AuthzClientCryptoProvider, ASN1Encoder/Decoder) and a META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider service registration to this module, and AuthzClient.create() now calls CryptoIntegration.init, meaning the service file will be picked up by ServiceLoader whenever this jar is on the classpath. Shipping a CryptoProvider service registration in a module explicitly documented as testsuite-only is contradictory: if the jar leaks onto a 3rd-party or server classpath, the AuthzClientCryptoProvider (which throws UnsupportedOperationException for most operations) can be selected and break crypto operations. Either the provider classes should move to the real keycloak-authz-client artifact (as the PR description says the changes will later be synced to keycloak-client), or the pom description must be updated; as written the module's stated purpose and its new contents conflict.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default KeyStore provider instead of a BouncyCastle provider
body: The method is documented in CryptoProvider to return 'BouncyCastle security provider. Can be either non-FIPS or FIPS based provider', but the implementation returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which is the JCA provider backing the default keystore type (typically SunJCE/SunJSSE on a stock JVM), not BouncyCastle. Any caller that relies on CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getBouncyCastleProvider() to obtain a BC provider (e.g. to register it, look up BC services, or pass it to BC-specific APIs) will get the wrong provider. The WildFlyElytronProvider returns null in this case, which at least signals 'no BC provider'; returning an unrelated provider is misleading and can cause subtle failures. Either return null like WildFlyElytronProvider, or actually return a BouncyCastleProvider instance.

title: concatenatedRSToASN1DER creates throwaway ASN1Encoder instances and can produce non-DER output
body: In `concatenatedRSToASN1DER`, lines 114-115 call `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger)` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger)` purely for side-effect-free discarded results; the actual encoding is done again at lines 117-121. The discarded calls are dead code. More importantly, the conversion from the fixed-length concatenated R||S form to BigInteger is lossy in a way that breaks DER: `new BigInteger(r)` where `r` is a `len+1` byte array with a leading zero byte is fine, but if the top bit of R is set, `BigInteger.toByteArray()` in `ASN1Encoder.write(BigInteger)` will prepend a 0x00 sign byte — that is correct DER. However, if R's top bit is NOT set, no sign byte is added, which is also correct. The real issue is the dead code plus the fact that the method does not validate that `signature.length == signLength`; if a caller passes a signature shorter than signLength, `System.arraycopy(signature, len, s, 1, len)` throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, and if longer, trailing bytes are silently ignored. Compare with the sibling implementations (BCECDSACryptoProvider, ElytronECDSACryptoProvider) which use BC's ASN1 utilities. At minimum remove the dead encoder calls and validate input length.

title: integerToBytes silently truncates the most significant bytes of R or S when the DER integer is longer than the field length
body: In `asn1derToConcatenatedRS`, `integerToBytes(BigInteger s, int qLength)` handles the case `qLength < bytes.length` by copying the LAST `qLength` bytes (`System.arraycopy(bytes, bytes.length - tmp.length, tmp, 0, tmp.length)`), i.e. it keeps the least-significant bytes and drops the most-significant ones. For an ECDSA signature this is a signature-malleability/validation hazard: a DER-encoded integer whose value exceeds the curve field size (e.g. R or S >= n, or with extra leading zero/sign bytes making the byte array longer than expected) will be silently truncated instead of rejected. A verifier using this conversion could accept a signature whose R/S components were altered (the high bytes dropped), and the round-trip is not faithful. The correct behavior is to reject values that do not fit in `qLength` bytes (after stripping at most one leading 0x00 sign byte), as done by strict implementations. Note the truncation branch also mis-handles the legitimate DER case of a single leading 0x00 sign byte: for a 32-byte field with a 33-byte array (0x00 || 32 bytes), it would drop the leading zero correctly, but for a 33-byte array where the value genuinely needs 33 bytes it silently corrupts the value.

title: readSequence() mishandles indefinite-length encoding and can loop forever or mis-parse
body: `readLength()` returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding (0x80, line 133-135). `readSequence()` then enters `while (length > 0)` — with length == -1 the loop body never executes and it returns an empty list, silently accepting a malformed/truncated sequence instead of failing. Conversely, `readNext()` adds the header size to the content length (`length += reset()`), but `readSequence()` decrements `length` by `bytes.length` which already includes the header bytes, so the accounting is inconsistent between the two paths. For the DER-encoded ECDSA signatures this provider parses, indefinite length is illegal in DER, so it should be rejected with an IOException rather than treated as an empty sequence. As written, a crafted signature using indefinite-length encoding would be parsed as an empty sequence and then fail later with a confusing 'Invalid sequence with size different to 2' error, or worse, be misinterpreted.

title: readLength() bounds check uses total input limit instead of remaining bytes
body: The check `if (length >= limit)` compares the declared content length against the TOTAL input size (`limit = bytes.length` set in the constructor), not against the number of bytes remaining after the tag and length octets have been consumed. A nested TLV (e.g. the INTEGERs inside the ECDSA SEQUENCE, parsed via `readNext()` on a sub-array) can therefore declare a length that runs past the end of its enclosing element but still be `< limit` of the outer buffer, and `read(length)` will happily read bytes belonging to the following sibling element or throw a misleading EOF. For the top-level sequence this is partially mitigated because `readSequence` re-slices via `readNext`, but for `readInteger()` called directly on a sub-array (as done in `asn1derToConcatenatedRS`: `ASN1Decoder.create(seq.get(0)).readInteger()`), the limit is the sub-array length, which is correct — however the general contract of the class is wrong and any future use on a stream position mid-buffer will over-read. The check should be `length > is.available()` (bytes remaining), not `length >= limit`.

title: asn1derToConcatenatedRS does not validate that the DER integers fit the expected signature length and does not reject negative/oversized values
body: The method decodes R and S from the DER sequence and converts them with `integerToBytes(value, len)` where `len = signLength / 2`. It never checks that `rBigInteger` or `sBigInteger` are non-negative or `< n` (the curve order), nor that their minimal byte encoding fits in `len` bytes. Combined with the truncation behavior in `integerToBytes` (see separate finding), a maliciously crafted DER signature with oversized or negative integers (BigInteger can be negative if the high bit of the content is set) will be silently truncated or sign-mangled and produce a fixed-length byte array that a caller may then feed to a raw ECDSA verifier. This is a signature-validation weakness: the conversion layer should reject any R/S that is negative or does not fit in `len` bytes after DER decoding, rather than truncating.

title: Provider selection semantics changed from fail-fast to silent highest-order-wins, which can silently pick a different provider than before
body: Previously, `detectProvider` threw `IllegalStateException` when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath ('Multiple crypto providers loaded...'). Now it sorts by `order()` descending and silently picks the first, only logging the ignored providers at DEBUG level. This is a behavioral/API contract change: any deployment that accidentally had two providers on the classpath (e.g. keycloak-crypto-default and keycloak-crypto-fips1402, or the new authz-client provider alongside the default one) previously failed fast at startup; now it will silently select one based on the arbitrary `order()` values (DefaultCryptoProvider=200, FIPS1402Provider=200, WildFlyElytronProvider=200, AuthzClientCryptoProvider=100). Note that Default, FIPS and Elytron all return the SAME order (200), so when more than one of those is present the choice is determined by ServiceLoader iteration order, which is classpath-dependent and non-deterministic across environments — reintroducing exactly the ambiguity the old fail-fast behavior was designed to prevent. The PR description says the testsuite still uses DefaultCryptoProvider, but with equal orders there is no guarantee which one wins. Either give the server providers distinct, documented orders, or keep failing when multiple providers share the top order.

title: order() added as an abstract method, breaking all third-party CryptoProvider implementations
body: Adding `int order();` as a non-default method to the `CryptoProvider` interface is a breaking change for any external implementation of this interface (the interface is public API in keycloak-common, and the PR itself notes the authz-client will be synced to the separate keycloak-client repository where third parties may implement or have implemented CryptoProvider). Any existing custom CryptoProvider will fail to compile / fail at runtime with AbstractMethodError once this change is synced. Consider making it a `default` method (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) to preserve backward compatibility, matching how `getSupportedRsaKeySizes()` and `getSupportedKeyStoreTypes()` are already defaulted in the same interface.

title: CryptoIntegration.init called from AuthzClient.create can race with server-side initialization and pick the wrong provider
body: `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)` now calls `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())`. `CryptoIntegration.cryptoProvider` is a static singleton initialized once per JVM/classloader. In the Keycloak testsuite (and any app server) where the authz-client jar is on the same classpath as the server, the first caller to trigger `init` wins: if an AuthzClient is created before the server initializes its crypto stack, the classloader passed is the authz client's classloader and the newly-registered `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` (order 100) competes with `DefaultCryptoProvider` (order 200). Because the server providers all share order 200 and the authz provider has order 100, the server provider should win — but only if it is visible to that classloader. If the authz-client is loaded by a child classloader that does NOT see the server's crypto provider jars, `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` will be selected and the static `cryptoProvider` will be permanently set to the authz provider for the whole JVM, after which the server's own `CryptoIntegration.init` is a no-op (`if (cryptoProvider == null)`) and the server silently uses the authz provider, whose methods mostly throw `UnsupportedOperationException('Not supported yet.')`. This is a real initialization-order hazard introduced by initializing a global singleton from a client entry point; the authz client should either use its own isolated provider instance rather than the global singleton, or the ordering must guarantee the server provider always wins regardless of init order.

title: Test uses a single default EC key (P-256) for ES384 and ES512, so those cases do not actually exercise the intended curve sizes
body: The test constructor generates one key pair with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, which on a standard JVM produces a P-256 (secp256r1) key. `testES384` and `testES512` then sign with `SHA384withECDSA`/`SHA512withECDSA` using that P-256 key and pass `algorithm.getSignatureLength()` (96 and 128 bytes respectively) to the conversion methods. The conversions are length-driven, so the round-trip assertion will pass, but the test never verifies behavior with a P-384 or P-521 key, where R/S are 48/64 bytes and the DER integers are more likely to have leading zero bytes or high-bit-set values (the edge cases the conversion code must handle). The test gives false confidence for ES384/ES512. It should generate a key pair on the matching curve (e.g. `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` + `ECGenParameterSpec("secp384r1")` / `"secp521r1"`) per algorithm, and ideally also assert that the DER output verifies with `Signature.getInstance(...).initVerify(publicKey)` to prove the encoding is actually correct, not just self-consistent.

title: Round-trip test only proves self-consistency, not correctness against a real verifier
body: The test asserts `rsConcat` equals `rsConcat2` after a DER->concat->DER->concat round trip through the new provider. This proves the two conversion methods are inverses of each other, but both methods are new code in this PR; a shared bug (e.g. both dropping the same leading zero byte, or both mis-sizing the arrays) would cancel out and the test would still pass. The test should additionally verify the produced DER signature with a standard JCA verifier (`Signature.getInstance(javaAlg).initVerify(keyPair.getPublic())`), and verify that the concatenated form matches what a known-good implementation (e.g. the existing `BCECDSACryptoProvider` or `ElytronECDSACryptoProvider`) produces for the same signature, to prove interoperability rather than self-consistency.

title: getKeyStore ignores the NoSuchProviderException path and uses default provider lookup
body: `getKeyStore(KeystoreFormat format)` returns `KeyStore.getInstance(format.name())` using the default JCA provider lookup, ignoring the `NoSuchProviderException` declared in the interface signature (it can never be thrown as written). More importantly, the default keystore type/provider may not support all `KeystoreFormat` values (e.g. PKCS12 is fine, but BKS/BCFKS require BouncyCastle providers which this provider does not register — see the related getBouncyCastleProvider issue). The default `getSupportedKeyStoreTypes()` in CryptoProvider filters by calling `getKeyStore(format)` and catching exceptions, so unsupported formats will be silently filtered, but callers invoking `getKeyStore` directly will get a KeyStoreException at runtime rather than a clear signal. Given the provider's purpose (authz client), either restrict to formats the default JVM supports and document it, or register a BouncyCastle provider and use it explicitly.

title: Per-client permission lookup uses client.getId() as resource name, but resources are keyed by client ID resolved through resolveClient
body: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the per-client resource is looked up with resourceStore.findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()). However, AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource (AdminPermissionsSchema.java lines 93-95 and 175-184) creates client resources with the name set to resolveClient(session, id), which returns client.getId() — the internal ID. This is consistent only if the permission was created with the internal client ID. But the test PermissionClientTest.testManageOnlyOneClient creates the permission with myclient.getId() (the internal ID from the admin client representation), so it works there. The real problem: when a permission is created via the REST API using the clientId (e.g. 'myclient') rather than the internal UUID, getOrCreateResource resolves it to the internal ID and creates the resource named by the internal ID — consistent. However, if a resource already exists under a different name (e.g. created by an older flow or by name), findByName with client.getId() will miss it and silently fall through to the all-clients resource, potentially granting broader permissions than intended or denying narrower ones. More critically, the fallback logic at lines 217-221 calls getResourceTypeResource and then findByResource(server, resource) — if resource is null (no 'Clients' type resource exists), findByResource will NPE or misbehave. Also, the evaluation uses resource.getScopes() which for a per-client resource includes ALL scopes of the Clients type (set in getOrCreateResource line 106), meaning a permission granting only 'view' on a specific client will still evaluate against all scopes — but the code then filters by expectedScopes, so this is OK. The core issue is the fragile name-based lookup mixing internal IDs and the null-resource dereference risk at line 219 when getResourceTypeResource returns null.

title: Potential NullPointerException when all-clients resource does not exist
body: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), when no per-client resource is found, the code calls AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) which can return null (it returns null if supportsAuthorizationSchema is false or if the resource type resource doesn't exist in the store — see AdminPermissionsSchema.java lines 116-134). The very next line calls authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) with this potentially-null resource. If the 'Clients' all-resource was never created (e.g., realm admin permissions were enabled but init() didn't run, or the resource was deleted), this will throw a NullPointerException, causing a 500 error instead of a clean permission denial. The same pattern exists in hasPermission(String scope) at line 244-247 where a null check IS performed, showing the inconsistency — the per-client variant is missing the null guard.

title: Unused private method getEvaluationContext and unused imports indicate dead code
body: The private method getEvaluationContext(ClientModel authorizedClient, AccessToken token) at lines 262-272 is never called anywhere in the class. It also references ClientModelIdentity and DefaultEvaluationContext. Additionally, imports for Scope (line 27), TOKEN_EXCHANGE (line 46), and the logger (line 51) are unused — logger is declared but never used, and TOKEN_EXCHANGE is statically imported but never referenced. This dead code suggests the token-exchange evaluation path was planned but not implemented, yet canExchangeTo simply throws UnsupportedOperationException. If token exchange is expected to work in V2, this is a functional gap; if not, the dead code should be removed to avoid confusion.

title: canExchangeTo throws UnsupportedOperationException, breaking token exchange for V2 admin permissions
body: The method canExchangeTo(ClientModel authorizedClient, ClientModel to, AccessToken token) throws UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2"). This is an interface method from ClientPermissions (inherited via ClientPermissionEvaluator). If any code path in the V2 admin permissions flow calls canExchangeTo (e.g., during token exchange operations involving admin clients), it will throw an unchecked exception resulting in a 500 error rather than a proper authorization denial. The same applies to exchangeToPermission and all the *Permission(ClientModel) methods that throw UnsupportedOperationException. If these are intentionally unsupported in V2, the interface contract should be documented or the methods should return safe defaults (false/null) rather than throwing, to avoid breaking callers that may invoke them generically.

title: Event listener feature check uses ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) instead of ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2
body: In registerListener, the event handling is now wrapped in `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))` — this is the V1 feature flag. However, the evaluator factory methods in this same class (lines 39-71) check `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2)` to decide whether to use MgmtPermissionsV2. When V2 is enabled (and V1 is not, which is the expected configuration since V2 is the newer feature), this listener will NOT execute, meaning that when a client/role/group is removed, setPermissionsEnabled will never be called to clean up permissions. This leaves orphaned permission resources in the authorization store when clients are deleted in V2-enabled realms. The check should be for ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 (or both, if V1 cleanup is still needed).

title: getScope NPE when resourceType is not in schema
body: In getScope(KeycloakSession session, ResourceServer resourceServer, String resourceType, String id), line 214 calls SCHEMA.getResourceTypes().get(resourceType).getScopes() without first checking if getResourceTypes().get(resourceType) returns null. If a caller passes a resourceType that is not "Users" or "Clients" (e.g., a custom type or a typo), this will throw a NullPointerException. The method is called during policy/permission creation validation, so a malformed request with an invalid resourceType would cause a 500 error instead of a clean 400 validation error. A null check should be added, throwing a ModelValidationException with a descriptive message.

title: getResourceName only handles Users resource type, not Clients
body: The method getResourceName(KeycloakSession session, Policy policy, Resource resource) at lines 304-326 only handles the USERS resource type (lines 310-322), returning "All users" for the type-level resource or the username for user resources. For the newly added CLIENTS resource type, it falls through to `return resource.getDisplayName()` (line 325). This means client resources will display their internal ID (since resources are named by client.getId() per resolveClient) rather than a human-readable clientId. This affects the admin UI/console display of permissions — admins will see UUIDs instead of client IDs when viewing client permissions. A corresponding branch for CLIENTS.getType() should resolve the client and return client.getClientId(), similar to the USERS branch.

title: canView() calls canViewClientDefault() which is not defined in ClientPermissionsV2 and may not exist in parent
body: The method canView() at line 86-88 calls `canViewClientDefault()`. This method is not defined in ClientPermissionsV2, and based on the class hierarchy (extends ClientPermissions), it must be inherited from ClientPermissions. However, the name suggests it checks a default/fallback view permission. If ClientPermissions.canViewClientDefault() relies on V1 permission resources (like viewPermission(client) which throws UnsupportedOperationException in V2), this could throw at runtime. The method should be verified to work correctly in the V2 context — if it depends on V1-specific permission lookups, it should be overridden in ClientPermissionsV2 to use the V2 evaluation path.

title: Test accesses list index 1 without verifying list size, potential IndexOutOfBoundsException
body: In testManageOnlyOneClient, line 148 does `clientResource.getDefaultClientScopes().get(1)` and line 174 does `defaultClientScopes.get(1)` without first asserting the list has at least 2 elements. If the realm has fewer than 2 default client scopes, this will throw IndexOutOfBoundsException, causing a test failure that is unrelated to the permission logic being tested. The test should assert the list size before accessing index 1, or use a safer access pattern.

title: getClientsWithPermission evaluates permissions for every client resource individually (N+1 evaluation problem)
body: The method getClientsWithPermission(String scope) at lines 125-145 iterates over all resources of type CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE using resourceStore.findByType, and for each resource calls hasGrantedPermission(resource, scope), which in turn calls root.evaluatePermission(...) — a full policy evaluation. This means for a realm with N clients that have individual permission resources, N separate policy evaluations are performed. Each evaluation may involve loading policies, roles, and other data from the store. For realms with many clients, this is an O(N) policy evaluation problem that could be slow. The V1 implementation (ClientPermissions) likely uses a more efficient bulk approach. Consider batching evaluations or using a single evaluation context with multiple resources.

title: Per-client permission lookup uses client.getId() as resource name, but resources are created with the client ID resolved by resolveClient, causing a mismatch and potential authorization bypass or denial
body: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the per-client resource is looked up with resourceStore.findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()). However, AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource (server-spi-private/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/AdminPermissionsSchema.java, lines 93-95 and 175-184) creates client resources using resolveClient(session, id), which returns client.getId() — the internal model ID. The lookup here also uses client.getId(), so for a ClientModel obtained from the realm this matches. But the fallback logic is broken: when the per-client resource is null, the code loads the 'all-clients' type resource and then checks authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource).isEmpty() — if there are ANY policies attached to the all-clients resource (even policies that do not grant the requested scope to this admin, or policies of unrelated types), evaluation proceeds against the all-clients resource. The subsequent evaluatePermission call evaluates ALL scopes of that resource and returns true if the requested scope appears in ANY granted permission. This means an admin with, e.g., only a 'view' permission on all-clients would pass hasPermission(client, MANAGE) only if manage is granted — that part is OK — but the real issue is the fallback check findByResource(...).isEmpty() is only an optimization; the deeper problem is that when a per-client resource exists, permissions defined ONLY on the all-clients resource are never evaluated, so a negative/positive interplay between per-client and all-clients permissions is inconsistent with the Users implementation. More concretely: if a per-client resource exists but has no permission granting the scope, the method returns false WITHOUT falling back to the all-clients resource, whereas when no per-client resource exists it does fall back. This asymmetry means creating a resource for a client (e.g., by granting any permission on it) silently disables all-clients permissions for that client, which is a data-integrity/authorization-semantics bug. Additionally, if the all-clients resource is null (getResourceTypeResource returns null), findByResource(server, null) is called with a null resource, which will likely throw an NPE or behave unexpectedly instead of returning false.

title: Null resource passed to policyStore.findByResource when the Clients type resource does not exist
body: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), when the per-client resource is not found, the code calls AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and immediately passes the result to authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) without a null check. getResourceTypeResource returns null when the resource type resource has not been created (e.g., admin permissions were enabled but init() was not run, or the resource was deleted). Passing null to findByResource will cause a NullPointerException (or store-specific failure) instead of the intended graceful 'return false'. The sibling method hasPermission(String scope) at line 244-247 correctly checks 'if (resource == null) return false;', showing the per-client variant is missing the same guard.

title: Permission evaluation grants access if the requested scope appears in any granted permission, ignoring resource/scope binding semantics
body: hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope) builds a ResourcePermission with resource.getScopes() (ALL scopes of the resource) and then iterates over the resulting permissions, returning true if the expected scope name appears in permission.getScopes(). This conflates 'the admin was granted some permission that includes this scope' with proper evaluation. In Keycloak's authorization model, a Permission's scopes represent the scopes for which access was GRANTED after policy evaluation; iterating them is the pattern used by UserPermissionsV2, so this is consistent. However, the evaluation is performed with root.evaluatePermission(...) which evaluates in the context of the current admin — but the ResourcePermission is constructed with the resource's full scope set, meaning the evaluation engine will evaluate policies for all scopes and the result may include scopes granted by policies attached to the resource that are not actually the requested scope. The loop then matches by scope name only. This is the same approach as the Users V2 implementation, so it is likely intentional; the concrete defect is that when the per-client resource exists, the all-clients fallback is skipped entirely (see related finding), so a permission defined on the 'Clients' type resource is ignored for any client that has its own resource — an authorization-semantics inconsistency that can deny legitimate access or, combined with the fallback check only testing policy existence, grant access based on unrelated policies.

title: getEvaluationContext is dead code and mutates a possibly-immutable map
body: The private method getEvaluationContext(ClientModel authorizedClient, AccessToken token) is never called anywhere in the class (all token-exchange related methods throw UnsupportedOperationException). Additionally, it calls super.getBaseAttributes() and then attributes.put(...) — if DefaultEvaluationContext.getBaseAttributes() returns an immutable map, this would throw UnsupportedOperationException at runtime. Since the method is unused, it should be removed; leaving unused, broken code in a security-sensitive permission evaluator is a maintenance hazard and may confuse future maintainers into wiring it up incorrectly.

title: Unused static import TOKEN_EXCHANGE and unused logger/scope imports
body: The class has 'import static org.keycloak.services.resources.admin.permissions.AdminPermissionManagement.TOKEN_EXCHANGE;' (line 46) which is never referenced, an unused 'logger' field (line 51), and unused imports including org.keycloak.authorization.model.Scope (line 27). These are harmless but indicate the class was scaffolded from a template and not cleaned up; the unused TOKEN_EXCHANGE import in particular suggests token-exchange support was planned but is explicitly unsupported (canExchangeTo throws).

title: registerListener now gates V1 cleanup behavior behind ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ, breaking permission cleanup when only V2 is enabled
body: The diff wraps the entire event-handling body in 'if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))'. Previously the listener unconditionally disabled permissions on role/client/group removal. ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is a separate feature flag from ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (the V2 evaluator is selected when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, see AdminPermissions.evaluator). With V2 enabled but V1 disabled, RoleRemovedEvent, ClientRemovedEvent, and GroupRemovedEvent will no longer trigger setPermissionsEnabled(..., false), leaving stale fine-grained permissions referencing deleted roles/clients/groups. This is a data-integrity regression: orphaned permissions remain active and may grant access based on policies referencing non-existent entities. The guard should either be removed (the cleanup is harmless when permissions are disabled) or check for either feature flag.

title: getScope throws NullPointerException when resourceType is not in the schema
body: In getScope(KeycloakSession session, ResourceServer resourceServer, String resourceType, String id), when supportsAuthorizationSchema is true, the code calls SCHEMA.getResourceTypes().get(resourceType).getScopes() without checking whether getResourceTypes().get(resourceType) returns null. If a caller passes a resourceType that is not 'Users' or 'Clients' (e.g., a custom type, or null), this throws a NullPointerException instead of a meaningful ModelValidationException. The sibling method throwExceptionIfResourceTypeOrScopesNotProvided (line 196) explicitly validates 'SCHEMA.getResourceTypes().get(rep.getResourceType()) == null', showing the intended contract; getScope violates it. This NPE would surface as a 500 error rather than a 400 validation error when creating a scope permission with an invalid resource type through a path that reaches getScope before the other validation.

title: getResourceName only handles the Users resource type; Clients resources fall through to displayName which may be null
body: getResourceName(KeycloakSession session, Policy policy, Resource resource) resolves a human-readable name only for USERS resource type policies (returning 'All users' or the username). For a policy with resourceType 'Clients', the method skips the if-block and returns resource.getDisplayName(). Resources created by getOrCreateResource are created via resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId()) without setting a display name, so getDisplayName() returns null for client resources. Any admin UI or API listing permissions for Clients resource-type policies will show a null/empty resource name instead of the client ID or clientId, degrading the admin experience and potentially breaking UI rendering that assumes a non-null name.

title: testManageOnlyOneClient assumes at least 2 default client scopes and indexes get(1) without verifying size
body: In testManageOnlyOneClient, the pre-permission negative check does 'ClientScopeRepresentation clientScopeRep = clientResource.getDefaultClientScopes().get(1);' — but this call is expected to FAIL with ForbiddenException before the permission is granted (the admin has no permission yet), so getDefaultClientScopes() throws and get(1) is never reached; the variable clientScopeRep is then unused in that block. Later, after granting MANAGE, the test does 'List<ClientScopeRepresentation> defaultClientScopes = clientResource.getDefaultClientScopes(); ... ClientScopeRepresentation clientScopeRep = defaultClientScopes.get(1);' — this assumes the client has at least 2 default client scopes. If the test realm's client has fewer than 2 default scopes (depends on realm config), this throws IndexOutOfBoundsException and the test fails for an unrelated reason. The test should assert the list size before indexing, or use get(0). The same pattern appears in testConfigureOnlyOneClient at line 234/242 using get(0), which is safer but still assumes a non-empty list.

title: testViewAllClients creates a client with null representation and only asserts FORBIDDEN, not validating the actual rejection reason
body: In testViewAllClients, the final negative check does 'realmAdminClient.realm(realm.getName()).clients().create(null)' and asserts the response is 403 FORBIDDEN. Passing a null ClientRepresentation is an unusual API call; the server may reject it with 400 Bad Request before even reaching the authorization check, depending on JAX-RS/RESTEasy null-body handling. If the server returns 400 instead of 403, the test fails for a reason unrelated to the permission logic being tested. The intent is clearly to verify that a view-only admin cannot create clients; a valid minimal ClientRepresentation (like the one used in testManageAllClients) should be passed instead so the 403 is attributable to the authorization layer.

title: onAfter cleanup only removes scope permissions, leaving created user policies and clients behind
body: The @AfterEach onAfter method removes all scope permissions via permissions.findAll(...).forEach(p -> permissions.findById(p.getId()).remove()), but the tests create UserPolicyRepresentations via createUserPolicy (which registers realm cleanup callbacks) and, in testManageAllClients, create and delete a 'newClient'. The createUserPolicy helper does register a realm.cleanup() callback to remove the policy, so policies are cleaned up at realm teardown. However, testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient creates client roles ('myclient-role', 'myclient-subRole') via realm.admin() without registering cleanup, and these persist in the managed realm across tests within the same class if the realm is reused. If the test framework reuses the realm across test methods (ManagedRealm lifecycle), the second run of testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient would fail because the roles already exist. The test should register cleanup for the created roles, e.g., realm.cleanup().add(r -> ...remove roles...).

title: getClientsWithPermission returns resource names (internal client IDs) rather than client IDs, producing unusable identifiers
body: getClientsWithPermission(String scope) iterates resources of type CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE and adds resource.getName() to the granted set. Per AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource and resolveClient, the resource name for a client is the client's internal model ID (client.getId()), not the clientId. Callers of getClientsWithPermission (e.g., admin endpoints that filter or search clients by permission) expect to receive identifiers they can use to look up clients — typically the client ID used in admin APIs. Returning internal model IDs (UUIDs) instead of clientIds makes the result unusable for API consumers and inconsistent with the rest of the admin API where clients are addressed by their model ID in URLs but by clientId in search. The Users V2 equivalent (UserPermissionsV2.getUsersWithPermission) has the same pattern with user IDs, which is consistent there because users are addressed by ID; for clients, the resource name is the internal ID, so the method should either return the internal IDs consistently (and document it) or map them back to clientIds. At minimum, the semantics should be verified against actual callers.

title: canView() delegates to canViewClientDefault() which is a V1 method with different semantics, potentially bypassing V2 permission checks
body: canView() is implemented as 'return canViewClientDefault() || hasPermission(AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW);'. canViewClientDefault() is inherited from ClientPermissions (V1) and checks the caller's realm-management roles (view-clients / manage-clients) via root.hasOneAdminRole. This is intentional for backward compatibility (admins with realm-management roles retain access). However, canViewClientDefault() in the V1 implementation may also consult the client's own permission settings or other V1 state that is explicitly unsupported in V2 (isPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException). If canViewClientDefault() internally calls isPermissionsEnabled or resource() on the client, it would throw UnsupportedOperationException at runtime for V2. The method should be verified to only use role checks; otherwise V2 evaluation could crash. This is a speculative but concrete risk given that multiple other inherited methods throw UnsupportedOperationException.

title: hasPermission(ClientModel, scope) looks up resource by client.getId() but resources are stored under the client's internal ID, and the fallback NPEs when no all-clients resource exists
body: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the per-client resource is looked up with resourceStore.findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()). However, AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource() creates client resources with the name returned by resolveClient(), which is client.getId() (the internal UUID), so this lookup is consistent with creation. The real bug is the fallback path: when the per-client resource is null, the code calls AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and then immediately calls authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) without a null check. getResourceTypeResource() returns null when the 'Clients' all-resource does not exist (e.g., the admin permissions client was created before this schema change, or the resource was deleted), causing a NullPointerException instead of returning false. This turns a normal 'no permission' case into a 500 error for every admin API call that checks a client-scoped permission (canManage/canView/canConfigure/canMapRoles on a specific client).

title: Fallback to all-clients resource checks policies on the wrong resource when a per-client resource exists but has no matching permission
body: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), when a per-client resource exists (resource != null), the method evaluates permissions only on that single resource and never falls back to the 'Clients' all-resource-type resource. This is inconsistent with the Users V2 implementation and with the documented semantics ('Also if the caller has a permission to ... all clients' in ClientPermissionEvaluator javadoc). Consequence: an admin granted 'manage' on the 'Clients' resource type (all clients) will be denied manage on any specific client that happens to have a per-client resource created (e.g., because another admin previously created a permission for that client), even though the all-clients permission should grant access. The fallback is only consulted when the per-client resource is entirely absent, so behavior depends on whether an unrelated per-client resource exists — a data-integrity/authorization-correctness bug.

title: getEvaluationContext is dead code and mutates a possibly-immutable map
body: The private method getEvaluationContext(ClientModel, AccessToken) is never called anywhere in the class (dead code). Additionally, it calls super.getBaseAttributes() and then attributes.put(...) — if DefaultEvaluationContext.getBaseAttributes() returns an immutable map, this would throw UnsupportedOperationException. Since the method is unused it should be removed; leaving it invites confusion and a latent bug if someone wires it up later.

title: Unused static import TOKEN_EXCHANGE and unused logger/scope imports
body: The class statically imports AdminPermissionManagement.TOKEN_EXCHANGE (line 46) but never uses it, because canExchangeTo() just throws UnsupportedOperationException. The Logger field (line 51) is also never used, and imports for Scope (line 27) and EvaluationContext usage are only for the dead getEvaluationContext method. These should be cleaned up.

title: registerListener now checks ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) instead of ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2, disabling permission cleanup when only V2 is enabled
body: The listener added in registerListener() previously ran unconditionally. The change wraps the event handling in Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ) — the V1 feature flag. But the evaluator factory methods in this same class (lines 40-71) select MgmtPermissionsV2 when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled. If a deployment enables only the V2 feature (ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2) and not V1, the listener body never executes: when a role, client, or group with permissions enabled is removed, setPermissionsEnabled(..., false) is never called, leaving stale authorization settings (resource servers / permissions) for deleted objects. The guard should check the V2 feature (or both), matching the evaluator selection logic.

title: getScope() throws NullPointerException when resourceType is not in the schema
body: In getScope(session, resourceServer, resourceType, id), when supportsAuthorizationSchema() is true, the code calls SCHEMA.getResourceTypes().get(resourceType).getScopes() without checking that getResourceTypes().get(resourceType) is non-null. throwExceptionIfResourceTypeOrScopesNotProvided() validates the resource type for ScopePermissionRepresentation, but getScope may be called from other paths (e.g., policy evaluation or scope resolution during permission creation/update flows) with an arbitrary or null resourceType, producing an NPE instead of a ModelValidationException. A null check with a proper validation error is needed.

title: getResourceName only resolves display names for Users, not Clients
body: getResourceName(session, policy, resource) has a branch for USERS that maps the resource name (user id) back to the username and returns 'All users' for the type resource, but there is no equivalent branch for CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE. For client resources, the method falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), which is null for resources created by getOrCreateResource (only the name is set). As a result, any admin UI/API listing permissions for Clients resource type will show null/empty resource names instead of the clientId, degrading the admin experience. A CLIENTS branch resolving the client by id (via resolveClient) and returning client.getClientId() (and 'All clients' for the type resource) should be added.

title: testManageOnlyOneClient assumes at least 2 default client scopes and reuses an index after mutation
body: In testManageOnlyOneClient, the pre-permission negative check does clientResource.getDefaultClientScopes().get(1) and later, after granting MANAGE, it fetches defaultClientScopes again and uses get(1) to remove and then re-add as optional. This assumes the realm has at least two default client scopes and that the list ordering/content is stable across the remove/add operations. If the managed realm has fewer than 2 default client scopes, the test fails with IndexOutOfBoundsException; after removeDefaultClientScope, the previously obtained clientScopeRep may no longer be a default scope, making addOptionalClientScope(clientScopeRep.getId()) semantically wrong (it adds a scope that may already be optional). The test should capture the scope id before removal and assert list sizes explicitly.

title: testViewAllClients creates a client with a null representation
body: In testViewAllClients, the negative check for client creation calls realmAdminClient.realm(...).clients().create(null) and asserts a 403. Passing a null ClientRepresentation is not a meaningful 'create a client' attempt — the server may reject it with 400 before ever reaching authorization checks, making the assertion pass for the wrong reason (or fail depending on JAX-RS null-entity handling). The test should pass a valid ClientRepresentation (like testManageAllClients does with newClient) to genuinely verify that VIEW does not grant create.

title: testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient grants CONFIGURE on the client but never verifies it, and mixes user-type and client-type permissions without asserting their distinct effects
body: In testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient, the permission created for myclient includes MAP_ROLES, MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE and CONFIGURE scopes, but the test only exercises role-mapping operations. CONFIGURE is granted presumably because viewing the client's roles requires canView/canConfigure, but the test never asserts that CONFIGURE alone would (or would not) allow the operations, nor does it verify that the USERS-type MAP_ROLES permission (granted on myadmin) is actually what authorizes the user role-mapping call versus the CLIENTS-type MAP_ROLES. Without a negative control (e.g., removing the USERS permission and showing the user-role mapping fails), the test cannot distinguish which permission is being exercised, weakening its value as a regression test for the new Clients resource type.

title: getClientsWithPermission evaluates permissions per resource with no caching, causing N policy evaluations
body: getClientsWithPermission(String scope) iterates all resources of type 'Clients' via resourceStore.findByType and, for each resource, calls hasGrantedPermission(), which performs a full root.evaluatePermission(...) policy evaluation (loading policies, evaluating the policy chain) for every single client resource. For a realm with many clients this is O(N) full authorization evaluations in a single admin request (e.g., when listing clients the admin can manage), which can be very slow and does not scale. The Users V2 equivalent has the same shape, but for Clients the resource count is typically much larger. At minimum this should be noted; ideally evaluation should be batched or the method should evaluate the type-level resource once and only fall back to per-resource checks when needed.

title: hasPermission(ClientModel, scope) silently returns false for cross-realm admins, but canView(ClientModel) composes checks that can mask missing per-client authorization
body: hasPermission(ClientModel, String) returns false when !root.isAdminSameRealm(). That is correct as a deny. However, canView(ClientModel client) first returns true if canView() (realm-wide view) OR canConfigure(client) is true. canConfigure(client) returns true if canManage(client) is true. This composition is fine, but note that canManage(ClientModel) checks root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS) — a realm-management role check that ignores whether the admin is from the same realm as the target client in a cross-realm admin setup. In V2 the FGAP permissions are realm-scoped to the admin permissions client of the admin's realm; if MgmtPermissionsV2 is constructed with a different target realm (the (session, realm, adminsRealm, admin) constructor), hasOneAdminRole may still return true based on the adminsRealm roles while the resource server used for evaluation (root.realmResourceServer()) belongs to a different realm, mixing realms. The class should consistently use the target realm's resource server and reject cross-realm role checks, as the Users V2 implementation does via isAdminSameRealm() guards in every method.

title: Exit code change from 4 to 3 for recreate upgrade breaks documented contract and existing automation
body: The PR changes RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE from 4 to 3 (and introduces FEATURE_DISABLED = 4). This is a breaking change to the exit-code contract of the `update-compatibility check` command: any existing CI/CD pipeline or script that was written against the already-released behavior (where exit code 4 meant 'rolling upgrade not possible') will now misinterpret the result. Exit code 3 previously had no meaning for this command, and 4 is now reused for a different condition (feature disabled). The docs in docs/guides/server/update-compatibility.adoc are updated to match the new values, but the change silently invalidates automation built against the previous release. If this command has already shipped in a released version, the exit code for 'recreate upgrade' must not be changed; a new code should be added instead (e.g., keep 4 for recreate and use 5 for feature-disabled), or the change must be clearly called out as breaking in release notes.

title: Feature check runs before config validation, so --features=rolling-updates is never actually honored for the check itself
body: In `run()`, the code checks `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ROLLING_UPDATES)` before `validateConfig()` is called. The `--features` option is a runtime configuration option that is only applied to the Profile during configuration processing (which happens in validateConfig()/the Quarkus config phase). At the point of the check, the Profile reflects only the persisted/optimized build-time configuration, not the `--features=rolling-updates` CLI flag passed on the command line. This means a user running `kc.sh update-compatibility check --file=x.json --features=rolling-updates` on a server where the feature is not enabled in the build will still get 'feature not enabled' and exit code 4, even though they explicitly passed the flag — contradicting the documentation (docs/guides/templates/kc.adoc) which shows the command being run with `--features=rolling-updates` appended. The feature gate therefore cannot be satisfied via CLI at all for non-optimized invocations, making the documented usage in kc.adoc and update-compatibility.adoc incorrect. The check should either be performed after configuration is applied, or the feature flag should be read from the parsed CLI options directly.

title: Same premature feature check: --features=rolling-updates passed on the CLI is ignored by the gate
body: Identical issue to UpdateCompatibilityCheck: `run()` checks `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ROLLING_UPDATES)` before `validateConfig()` processes the `--features` CLI option. Since the Profile is only updated with CLI-provided feature flags during configuration processing, a user who runs `kc.sh update-compatibility metadata --features=rolling-updates` (exactly as documented in docs/guides/templates/kc.adoc line 53 and docs/guides/server/update-compatibility.adoc line 63) on a default build will always be rejected with 'The preview feature rolling-updates is not enabled' and exit code 4. The documented command therefore cannot work as written unless the feature was enabled at build time, which contradicts the purpose of the docs showing the flag being passed at invocation time.

title: No test verifies the exit code for the feature-disabled path (exit code 4)
body: The new test `testFeatureNotEnabled` asserts only the error message via `cliResult.assertError(...)`, but never asserts the exit code. The whole point of introducing `CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED = 4` is to give automation a machine-readable signal (documented in update-compatibility.adoc exit-code table). Without asserting `cliResult.exitCode() == 4`, a regression that returns a different code (e.g., the generic picocli error code 1 or 2) would not be caught. The test should assert the exit code equals `CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED` for both the `metadata` and `check` subcommands. Additionally, there is no test asserting exit code 3 for the recreate/incompatible path (testWrongVersions only asserts the error message), leaving the changed exit-code contract untested.

title: Test parameterization with null strategy no longer exercises the feature-disabled path, and the feature is now always enabled
body: In `createInitialDeployment`, when `updateStrategy == null` the method returns early (line 105-107) before the `ROLLING_UPDATES` feature is enabled (lines 112-115). Previously the null-strategy case configured the update spec via the `unsupported` stanza; now the null case gets neither an update spec nor the feature. The test names (`testImageChange-{0}`, `testCacheMaxCount-{0}`) and the comment on line 64 ('changing the image to non-existing will always use the recreate upgrade type') suggest the null case is meant to represent the default/legacy behavior, but with the feature flag now being a hard requirement for the operator's update strategies (per the new CAUTION in advanced-configuration.adoc: 'the feature rolling-updates must be enabled. Otherwise, the Keycloak Operator will fail'), the null-strategy deployment may fail outright rather than exercise the intended default path. The test does not assert that the initial deployment actually becomes ready before the upgrade is triggered, so a failure of the initial deployment would surface as a confusing timeout. Either the null case should also enable the feature (to test default strategy behavior with the feature on), or a separate test should verify the operator fails when the feature is missing — currently neither is covered.

title: CAUTION block claims the Operator will fail without the feature, but the surrounding text and table describe the strategy as optional with a default
body: The new CAUTION block states 'While on preview stage, the feature rolling-updates must be enabled. Otherwise, the {project_name} Operator will fail.' However, the NOTE block immediately below (lines 461-466) says 'During this preview stage, the update strategy defaults to mimicking Keycloak 26.1 or older behavior' and the table lists `<not set>` (default) as a valid value that 'Mimics Keycloak 26.1 or older behavior'. These two statements are contradictory: if the operator fails without the feature, there is no default behavior to mimic; if there is a working default, the operator does not fail. The docs need to clarify whether existing deployments without the feature continue to work (legacy behavior) or are rejected, and the example YAML (lines 468-482) only shows the feature enabled together with a strategy, giving no example of a CR without the feature. This ambiguity will cause users to either unnecessarily enable a preview feature or, conversely, hit unexpected failures.

title: CAUTION says commands fail without the feature, but the documented command examples pass --features=rolling-updates which (per the code) does not satisfy the gate
body: The guide's CAUTION block (lines 12-16) states the feature 'must be enabled. Otherwise, the commands will fail.' Yet every command example in the guide (via the kc.adoc macro, line 63 and 83) appends `--features=rolling-updates` at invocation time. As implemented in UpdateCompatibilityCheck/UpdateCompatibilityMetadata, the feature check reads the Profile before CLI options are applied, so passing `--features=rolling-updates` on the command line does not enable the feature for the check — the command will still fail with exit code 4. The documentation therefore instructs users to do something that does not work. The docs should state that the feature must be enabled at build time (e.g., `kc.sh build --features=rolling-updates`) or the code should be fixed so the CLI flag is honored (see related finding). Until one or the other is resolved, the guide is incorrect.

title: New ROLLING_UPDATES preview feature gates operator and CLI behavior but has no versioned key or dependency declaration, and preview features are auto-enabled by the preview profile
body: ROLLING_UPDATES is declared as Type.PREVIEW, which means it is automatically enabled for all users running with `--profile=preview` (see isEnabledByDefault, line 316-325). This feature gates significant operational behavior: the Keycloak Operator's update strategies (documented as causing the operator to fail if not enabled) and the update-compatibility CLI commands. Auto-enabling an operator-affecting feature for every preview-profile user is a broad blast radius for a preview feature; users who enable the preview profile for unrelated features (there are many other PREVIEW features) will silently get the rolling-updates behavior change in the operator. Consider whether this should be PREVIEW_DISABLED_BY_DEFAULT (which exists in the Type enum precisely for 'Preview features, which are not automatically enabled even with enabled preview profile') so that it must be explicitly enabled, matching the docs' emphasis that it 'must be enabled'.

title: Exit code change from 4 to 3 for recreate upgrade breaks documented contract and existing automation
body: The constant RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE is changed from 4 to 3 in this PR. The accompanying documentation in docs/guides/server/update-compatibility.adoc (lines 128-130) is updated to say exit code 3 means 'Rolling Upgrade is not possible. The deployment must be shut down before applying the new configuration.' and exit code 4 means the feature is disabled. However, this is a breaking change to the exit-code contract of the `update-compatibility check` command: any existing CI/CD pipeline or script written against the previous release (where 4 meant 'recreate upgrade required') will now misinterpret exit code 3 as an unexpected error (picocli software error is 1, usage error is 2, and scripts commonly treat any non-0/3/4 code as failure) and, worse, will treat exit code 4 as a distinct 'feature disabled' case only if they were updated. Since the tool is explicitly documented as 'fully scriptable' and 'GitOps friendly' with consumers relying on exit codes, silently renumbering an existing exit code (rather than only adding the new code 4) breaks backward compatibility for anyone already using the command. The renumbering should be avoided (keep RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE = 4 and use a new code such as 5 for FEATURE_DISABLED), or at minimum the change must be called out as a breaking change in release notes; as written, the docs present the new numbering as if it were always the contract.

title: Feature check runs before configuration validation, so --features=rolling-updates is never actually parsed for the check itself
body: In UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run() (and identically in UpdateCompatibilityMetadata.run()), the guard `if (!Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ROLLING_UPDATES))` is evaluated at the very start of run(), before `validateConfig()` is called. Profile.isFeatureEnabled reads the statically initialized Profile (Profile.getInstance()), which is only configured from CLI options/environment during the normal Keycloak configuration/validation phase. The `--features` option is a standard Keycloak CLI option processed by the configuration machinery; whether it has been applied to the Profile singleton at the point run() executes depends on command initialization order in the Quarkus CLI framework. The distribution test UpdateCommandDistTest passes `--features=rolling-updates` as a CLI argument and expects the command to proceed, which suggests the option is honored, but the ordering is fragile: if Profile is initialized lazily or the feature option is applied after run() begins (e.g., when running via `kc.sh update-compatibility ... --features=rolling-updates` in a non-optimized or build-affected mode), the check would incorrectly report the feature as disabled and exit 4 even though the user explicitly enabled it. The feature check should be performed after validateConfig() (which triggers full option processing) or the enabled-features state should be read from the parsed command options rather than the global Profile singleton, to make the gating deterministic.

title: No test asserts the exit code for the feature-disabled path (exit code 4)
body: The new testFeatureNotEnabled test only asserts that the error message 'Unable to use this command. The preview feature 'rolling-updates' is not enabled.' appears in the CLI output; it never asserts the process exit code. The whole point of introducing CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED = 4 (and documenting it in docs/guides/server/update-compatibility.adoc lines 132-134 as the contract for scripts) is that automation can branch on exit code 4. Without an assertion such as `assertEquals(4, cliResult.exitCode())` (or the equivalent CLIResult API), a regression that exits with 0, 1, or 2 instead of 4 would not be caught, and the documented scripting contract would silently break. The test should assert the exit code equals CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED.

title: Test parameterization silently skips enabling the rolling-updates feature when updateStrategy is null
body: In createInitialDeployment(UpdateStrategy updateStrategy), when updateStrategy is null the method returns early at line 105-107 (`if (updateStrategy == null) { return kc; }`) before the code at lines 112-115 that sets the FeatureSpec with Profile.Feature.ROLLING_UPDATES.getKey(). The parameterized test upgradeStrategy() supplies both null and UpdateStrategy.RECREATE, so the null case (testImageChange-null and testCacheMaxCount-null) runs without the rolling-updates feature enabled in the Keycloak CR. Given that the operator documentation added in this PR (docs/guides/operator/advanced-configuration.adoc lines 446-450) states that 'the feature rolling-updates must be enabled. Otherwise, the Keycloak Operator will fail', the null-strategy test case is exercising a deployment configuration that the operator is documented to reject, and the test's expectations (e.g., eventuallyRollingUpgradeStatus for testCacheMaxCount-null) may be passing for the wrong reason or masking a validation failure. Either the null case should also enable the feature (so both parameters test the strategy behavior with the feature on), or the test should explicitly assert the operator's behavior when the feature is missing. As written, the test coverage for the default (no update strategy) path does not match the documented requirement.

title: Exit code table formatting is broken: rows 0-3 are missing the leading pipe, producing a malformed AsciiDoc table
body: In the exit-code table (lines 116-135), the first four rows begin with `m|0`, `m|1`, `m|2`, `m|3` while the newly added row begins with `m|4` — all are missing the leading `|` cell delimiter that AsciiDoc tables require (a cell must start with `|`). Only the header row `|===` / `|Exit Code |Description` and the final row use the correct `|` prefix. As a result the rendered table will be malformed: the `m|N` rows will not be parsed as table rows at all (the `m` is an unintended literal prefix), so exit codes 0 through 3 will render as plain paragraph text outside the table, and only the header and the new exit-code-4 row will appear as a table. The rows should be `m|0` corrected to `|0` (i.e., `|m|0` style consistent with the last row: a leading `|` followed by the `m` cell marker). This makes the documented exit-code contract — which scripts depend on — visually broken in the published guide.

title: Exit code change from 4 to 3 for recreate-upgrade breaks documented contract and existing automation
body: The constant RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE is changed from 4 to 3 in this PR. The public documentation in docs/guides/server/update-compatibility.adoc (lines 128-130) documents exit code 3 as 'Rolling Upgrade is not possible. The deployment must be shut down before applying the new configuration.' and exit code 4 as the new feature-disabled case. However, this is a breaking change to the exit-code contract of the `update-compatibility check` command: any existing CI/CD pipeline or script written against the previously released behavior (where exit code 4 meant 'recreate upgrade required') will now misinterpret exit code 4 as 'feature disabled' and exit code 3 as 'recreate upgrade'. Since the tool is explicitly documented as 'fully scriptable' and consumers 'should rely only on the exit code of the check command', silently renumbering an already-published exit code is an API/contract break. The recreate-upgrade code should keep its existing value (4) and the feature-disabled case should use a new, unused code (e.g., 5), or the change must be called out as a breaking change in release notes.

title: Feature check runs before configuration validation, so --features=rolling-updates is never honored
body: In UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run() (and identically in UpdateCompatibilityMetadata.run()), the guard `if (!Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ROLLING_UPDATES))` is evaluated at the very start of run(), before `validateConfig()` is called. The `--features` CLI option is processed during configuration parsing/validation, which happens in validateConfig() (invoked via super.validateConfig() further down). This means Profile.isFeatureEnabled() reflects only the features from the persisted/optimized configuration or environment, not the `--features=rolling-updates` flag passed on the command line. Consequently, a user running `kc.sh update-compatibility check --file=... --features=rolling-updates` (exactly the invocation shown in docs/guides/templates/kc.adoc line 53 and used throughout UpdateCommandDistTest) would still get 'Unable to use this command. The preview feature rolling-updates is not enabled.' and exit code 4, unless the feature was already enabled via KC_FEATURES environment variable or a prior build. The tests pass only because the distribution test harness may set the feature through the environment/build.
