Returning resource UUIDs means the group-membership filter for user search will never match any real group, so admins restricted to viewing members of specific groups will see an empty user list even though they have view-members permission. The code should resolve the group id from the resource name (the name is the group id per resolveGroup) rather than using the resource id.

title: V1 getGroupIdsWithViewPermission matches resources by type 'Group' but V2 schema uses 'Groups'
body: In GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (line 313), the V1 implementation iterates `resourceStore.findByType(server, "Group", ...)`. The V1 GroupPermissions.initialize sets `groupResource.setType("Group")` (line 117), so this is correct for V1. However, GroupPermissionsV2 extends GroupPermissions and overrides getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (line 106) to use `AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE` ("Groups"), which is correct for V2. The base-class method remains for V1 only, which is fine, but note that the base class method at line 315 does `resource.getName().substring(RESOURCE_NAME_PREFIX.length())` to recover the group id from the V1 resource name prefix 'group.resource.' — this is V1-specific and correct. No bug in V1 itself; the finding is that the type string "Group" is hard-coded and diverges from the schema constant, which is a maintenance hazard but not a runtime defect. Downgrading to low: this is only a latent inconsistency, not an active bug.

title: hasPermission falls back to all-users resource for any user id without verifying the resource belongs to a user
body: In UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission(UserModel user, ...) (lines 94-133), when `resourceStore.findByName(server, user.getId())` returns null, the code falls back to the 'Users' resource-type resource and evaluates it. The guard `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource).isEmpty()` only checks that some policy exists on the all-users resource. This is the intended fallback for users without a dedicated resource, and user.getId() is used as the resource name consistently with AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveUser. However, the same pattern as in GroupPermissionsV2 applies: the fallback is applied unconditionally for any user whose resource is missing, which is correct, but the method also accepts `user == null` to explicitly query the all-users resource. The risk is that `canView(UserModel)`/`canManage(UserModel)` etc. are called with a user whose id happens to collide with a resource name of a different type (e.g. a group id or client id, since resource names are not namespaced per type in the store lookup — findByName searches by name only). If a group resource was created with name equal to some user's id (unlikely but possible since group ids and user ids are both UUIDs from the same id space in some stores), findByName would return the group resource and permissions would be evaluated against the wrong resource type. The V2 schema does set resource.setType(type) for resource-type resources but per-object resources created via getOrCreateResource do not set a type, so findByName cannot disambiguate. This is a defense-in-depth concern; the practical impact is low because ids are UUIDs. Reporting as medium because the fallback logic in both UserPermissionsV2 and GroupPermissionsV2 relies solely on name equality without type verification.

title: Null resource from getResourceTypeResource is dereferenced without a null check
body: In UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission (line 109), `resource = AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.USERS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` can return null when the 'Users' resource-type resource does not exist (AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource returns null for unknown types or missing resources). Line 111 then calls `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` which will throw a NullPointerException when resource is null. This occurs when the admin permissions client exists but the schema resources have not been initialized (e.g. realm.isAdminPermissionsEnabled() true but AdminPermissionsSchema.init not yet run, or the resource was manually deleted). The result is a 500 error instead of a clean permission denial. A null check returning false is required.

title: Group-based user filtering is now applied even when the admin has global view-users permission
body: In UsersResource.searchForUser (lines 445-454), the previous code only set the `UserModel.GROUPS` session attribute (which restricts the user search to members of groups the admin can view) when `!auth.users().canView()`. The new code unconditionally calls `auth.groups().getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` and sets the session attribute whenever the returned set is non-empty. In GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (V1, line 298-320) the method returns an empty set when `root.users().canView()` is true, so V1 behavior is preserved. However, in GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (line 106-107) the guard is also `if (root.users().canView()) return Collections.emptySet();` — so for admins with the view-users role the set is empty and no restriction is applied. But for admins who have *only* fine-grained permissions (no view-users role) and have been granted view on the all-users resource (Users resource type with VIEW scope), `root.users().canView()` in V2 (UserPermissionsV2 inherits UserPermissions.canView, which checks admin roles then hasPermission(VIEW_SCOPE, MANAGE_SCOPE) on the Users resource) returns true, so getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns empty — OK. The problem case: an admin with view-users role in V1 — canView() true, empty set, fine. The actual regression: the condition `if (!groupIds.isEmpty())` sets the session attribute, and later `toRepresentation` calls `usersEvaluator.grantIfNoPermission(session.getAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS) != null)`. Previously, when the admin had global canView(), the GROUPS attribute was never set, so grantIfNoPermission(false) was called and per-user canView filtering was applied normally. Now, if getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns a non-empty set for an admin who actually has global view (which should not happen given the guards, but the V2 override at GroupPermissionsV2 line 107 checks `root.users().canView()` — and UserPermissionsV2 does not override canView(), so it uses UserPermissions.canView which checks admin roles and the V1-style Users resource permission; in V2 the Users resource-type resource is different from the V1 'Users' resource, so hasPermission(MgmtPermissions.VIEW_SCOPE...) looks up resourceStore.findByName(server, "Users") — in V2 the resource-type resource is named "Users" as well (USERS_RESOURCE_TYPE = "Users"), so it may actually find the V2 resource-type resource and evaluate V2 permissions against it using V1 scope names 'view'/'manage' which do exist in the V2 schema. This cross-wiring means canView() may return true in V2 via the V1 code path, and then getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns empty — consistent. The real issue is subtler: the removal of the `!auth.users().canView()` guard means that for an admin with global view-users role, if getGroupIdsWithViewPermission erroneously returns a non-empty set (e.g. due to the resource-id vs group-id bug in GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, which adds resource ids that are not group ids), the user search would be restricted by a bogus group filter, hiding users the admin should see. Combined with the grantIfNoPermission(session.getAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS) != null) call, setting the attribute also flips grantIfNoPermission to true, which changes the semantics of UserPermissions.hasPermission: when the Users resource does not exist, `grantIfNoPermission && expectedScopes.contains(MANAGE_SCOPE) && expectedScopes.contains(VIEW_SCOPE)` grants permission. This is a behavior change for admins with global view: previously grantIfNoPermission stayed false; now it can become true if the group-ids set is non-empty, potentially granting manage+view when no Users resource exists. This is a security-relevant behavior change that depends on the group-ids set being correct.

title: Group-based user filtering applied unconditionally, changing behavior for admins with global view
body: Same pattern as UsersResource.searchForUser: BruteForceUsersResource.searchForUser (lines 144-153) now unconditionally calls `auth.groups().getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` and sets `session.setAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS, groupIds)` when non-empty, whereas the old code only did so when `!auth.users().canView()`. Combined with `toRepresentation` calling `usersEvaluator.grantIfNoPermission(session.getAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS) != null)` (line 159), this changes the grantIfNoPermission flag for admins who have global view-users permission but for whom getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns a non-empty set. In V2, GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns resource ids (not group ids — see separate finding), so the set can be non-empty with bogus ids, causing (a) the user search to be filtered by non-existent groups (returning no users), and (b) grantIfNoPermission to be set to true, which in UserPermissions.hasPermission (line 501) grants manage+view when the Users resource is absent. For an admin with the view-users role this is a functional regression (no users returned) and a potential security issue (grantIfNoPermission flipped). The `!auth.users().canView()` guard should be restored, or getGroupIdsWithViewPermission must reliably return an empty set for admins with global view.

title: Removal of canViewGlobal bypass in getSubGroups changes listing semantics
body: In GroupResource.getSubGroups (lines 170-181), the filter was changed from `g -> canViewGlobal || auth.groups().canView(g)` to `auth.groups()::canView`. The old code allowed an admin with global view (view-users/manage-users role) to list all subgroups regardless of per-group permissions; the new code requires per-group canView(g) for every subgroup. In V1, GroupPermissions.canView(GroupModel) (line 254-264) returns true if canView() (global) is true, so V1 behavior is preserved. In V2, GroupPermissionsV2.canView(GroupModel) (line 56-62) also returns true if the admin has MANAGE_USERS/VIEW_USERS roles. So for admins with global roles, behavior is unchanged. However, for admins with only fine-grained permissions, the old code's `canViewGlobal` was `auth.groups().canView()` — the same global check — so the old code was effectively `canView() || canView(g)`, and the new code is just `canView(g)`. In V2, canView(g) does NOT fall back to the all-groups resource permission for a specific group unless the group resource exists or the all-groups resource has policies — actually GroupPermissionsV2.canView(GroupModel) calls hasPermission(group.getId(), VIEW, MANAGE), which falls back to the all-groups resource. So an admin with VIEW on the Groups resource type can view all subgroups — same as before. The change is effectively a no-op for V2 and V1 given the implementations, but it removes a redundant check. Not a bug per se; the real concern is that `requireView(group)` on line 176 already ensures the parent group is viewable, and the per-subgroup filter now relies entirely on canView(g) which in V2 falls back to all-groups — consistent. Low severity, likely no functional change; reporting because the removal of the global bypass could affect custom GroupPermissionEvaluator implementations that do not implement the fallback in canView(GroupModel).

title: Removal of canViewGlobal bypass in getGroups non-hierarchy path
body: In GroupsResource.getGroups (lines 109-115), when populateHierarchy is false, the filter changed from `g -> canViewGlobal || groupsEvaluator.canView(g)` to `groupsEvaluator::canView`. Same analysis as GroupResource.getSubGroups: for V1 and V2 built-in evaluators, canView(g) already incorporates the global check, so behavior is preserved for built-in implementations. Custom implementations of GroupPermissionEvaluator that return false from canView(GroupModel) for groups without explicit per-group permission but true from canView() would now filter out all groups in the non-hierarchy path. This is an API contract change for the GroupPermissionEvaluator interface: the interface documentation for canView(GroupModel) says 'Or if it has a permission to VIEW or MANAGE the group', which implies per-group, while canView() is global. The old code explicitly OR-ed the two; the new code relies on implementations to do the fallback internally. Since GroupPermissionsV2.canView(GroupModel) does fall back to the all-groups resource, the built-in behavior is correct, but the contract is now implicit. Low severity.

title: V1 getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns empty set only when users().canView(), ignoring manage-users-only admins
body: In GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (line 298-320, V1 implementation), the first guard is `if (root.users().canView()) return Collections.emptySet();`. UserPermissions.canView() (line 297-307) returns true if the admin has MANAGE_USERS or VIEW_USERS role. So an admin with only manage-users (which implies view) gets an empty set — correct, no restriction needed. But the old removed method getGroupsWithViewPermission() (the no-arg version, removed in this PR) had the guard `if (root.users().canView() || root.users().canManage()) return Collections.emptySet();`. The new method only checks canView(). Since canView() already includes MANAGE_USERS (line 298: `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS, AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS)`), the manage check is redundant. So no bug here. However, the method name changed from getGroupsWithViewPermission() to getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() and the return semantics changed from Set<String> of group ids (extracted via substring of resource name) — the V1 implementation at line 315 does `granted.add(resource.getName().substring(RESOURCE_NAME_PREFIX.length()))` which correctly extracts the group id from the V1 resource name 'group.resource.<id>'. This is correct for V1. No bug; retracting this finding.

title: canViewMembers now accepts MANAGE_MEMBERS scope, expanding view-members permission
body: In GroupPermissions.canViewMembers (line 330-341), the V1 implementation was changed from `hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE)` to `hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE, MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE)`. This means an admin with only the 'manage-members' scope on a group is now considered able to view members. This is a deliberate design decision (manage implies view) and is consistent with the interface documentation added in GroupPermissionEvaluator (line 120-125: 'Or if it has a permission to VIEW_MEMBERS or MANAGE_MEMBERS of the group'). The same pattern is applied in GroupPermissionsV2.canViewMembers (line 83-87). This is consistent and documented; not a bug. However, note that the V1 method requireViewMembers (line 323-327) now calls canViewMembers(group) instead of the removed getGroupsWithViewPermission(group). The old getGroupsWithViewPermission(GroupModel) checked `root.users().canView() || root.users().canManage()` first; the new canViewMembers checks `root.users().canView()` only (line 331). Since canView() includes MANAGE_USERS, this is equivalent. No bug; retracting.

title: canViewByGroup now uses canViewMembers which includes MANAGE_MEMBERS, expanding group-based user view
body: In UserPermissions.canViewByGroup (line 587-590), the predicate changed from `root.groups()::getGroupsWithViewPermission` (removed) to `root.groups()::canViewMembers`. The V1 GroupPermissions.canViewMembers now accepts both VIEW_MEMBERS and MANAGE_MEMBERS scopes (see separate finding). The old getGroupsWithViewPermission(GroupModel) (removed) checked `hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE, MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE)` — actually the old removed method at line 295-308 (in the diff context) checked `hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE, MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE)` as well? The diff shows the old getGroupsWithViewPermission(GroupModel) was removed and its logic replaced. Looking at the old code (from the diff, the removed method getGroupsWithViewPermission(GroupModel group) had `return hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE, MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE);` — wait, the diff shows the removed method's body was: `if (root.users().canView() || root.users().canManage()) return true; ... return hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE, MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE);`. Actually the diff context shows the removed method returned `hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE, MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE)` — no, looking at the diff more carefully: the removed `getGroupsWithViewPermission(GroupModel group)` method's last line was `return hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE, MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE);`? The diff shows the removed method ended with `return hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE, MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE);` — actually the diff shows the old canViewMembers had `return hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE);` and the new has `return hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE, MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE);`. And the old getGroupsWithViewPermission(GroupModel) (removed entirely) had `return hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE, MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE);`? The diff is ambiguous. Regardless, the new canViewByGroup uses canViewMembers which accepts MANAGE_MEMBERS — meaning an admin with manage-members on a group can now view all users in that group's hierarchy via the user search. This is consistent with the documented semantics ('Or if it has a permission to VIEW_MEMBERS of the group chain the user is associated with' — the doc says VIEW_MEMBERS only, but the implementation accepts MANAGE_MEMBERS too). The interface doc for UserPermissionEvaluator.canView(UserModel) (line 100-101) says 'Or if it has a permission to VIEW_MEMBERS of the group chain' — it does not mention MANAGE_MEMBERS. So the implementation is more permissive than documented. This is a doc/implementation mismatch; the behavior (manage implies view) is likely intended but the doc is incomplete. Low severity doc defect.

title: canMapRoles and canManageGroupMembership now accept MANAGE scope in addition to the specific scope
body: In UserPermissionsV2, canMapRoles(UserModel) (line 77-83) was changed from `hasPermission(user, null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MAP_ROLES)` to `hasPermission(user, null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE, AdminPermissionsSchema.MAP_ROLES) || canManageByGroup(user)`. Similarly canManageGroupMembership (line 86-92) changed from `hasPermission(user, null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE_GROUP_MEMBERSHIP)` to `hasPermission(user, null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE_GROUP_MEMBERSHIP) || canManageByGroup(user)`. Previously, canMapRoles checked `if (canManage(user)) return true;` first — and canManage(user) already accepts MANAGE scope. So the old code already granted map-roles if the admin had MANAGE on the user. The new code inlines this by adding MANAGE to the hasPermission scopes. The behavioral difference: the old code's `canManage(user)` also included `canManageByGroup(user)` (via UserPermissions.canManage(UserModel) line 260-262: `return canManage() || canManageByGroup(user);`). The new code adds `|| canManageByGroup(user)` explicitly, so group-based manage is still covered. The net effect is the same: MANAGE on the user (direct or via group) grants map-roles. However, the new code also grants map-roles if the admin has MANAGE on the *all-users* resource (via the fallback in hasPermission), which the old code also did via canManage(user) → canManage() → hasPermission(MANAGE_SCOPE) on the Users resource. So no privilege escalation. But note the interface documentation for canMapRoles (UserPermissionEvaluator line 137-145) says 'Or if it has a permission to MANAGE the user or MAP_ROLES of the user' — consistent. No bug; the change is a refactoring that preserves semantics. Retracting.

title: Removal of AdminRoles.ADMIN from canView/canManage checks
body: In UserPermissionsV2.canView(UserModel) (line 47-53) and canManage(UserModel) (line 56-62), the admin role checks were changed from `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.ADMIN, AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS, AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS)` to `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS, AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS)` (and MANAGE_USERS only for canManage). The realm-admin role (AdminRoles.ADMIN, i.e. 'admin' role of the realm) is no longer explicitly checked. In Keycloak, the 'admin' role (realm admin) typically has all realm-management client roles including manage-users and view-users, so hasOneAdminRole(MANAGE_USERS, VIEW_USERS) would still return true for a realm admin because the admin role has those composite roles. However, hasOneAdminRole checks direct or composite role membership; the 'admin' role is a composite that includes manage-users and view-users, so it should still pass. But if a custom setup grants the 'admin' role without the composite including manage-users (unusual), the check would fail. More importantly, the V1 UserPermissions.canView() (line 297-307) also only checks MANAGE_USERS and VIEW_USERS, not ADMIN. So V2 now matches V1. The removal of ADMIN from the explicit check is consistent with V1 and relies on the composite nature of the admin role. Low severity; likely no functional change for standard realm admins.

title: canMapRole now checks MANAGE_USERS role directly instead of canManageDefault()
body: In RolePermissions.canMapRole (line 302), the check `if (root.users().canManageDefault()) return checkAdminRoles(role);` was replaced with `if (root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS)) return checkAdminRoles(role);`. The removed UserPermissions.canManageDefault() was `return root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS);` — identical. So no functional change. However, in V2, UserPermissionsV2.canManage() (inherited from UserPermissions) also checks fine-grained permissions (hasPermission(MANAGE_SCOPE)), not just the role. The old code used canManageDefault() which only checked the role, deliberately bypassing fine-grained user permissions for role mapping. The new code also only checks the role. So V2 admins with fine-grained manage-users permission (but not the manage-users role) still cannot map roles via this early-return path; they would fall through to the per-role permission check. This preserves the old behavior. No bug.

title: canList() logic reordered but equivalent
body: In GroupPermissions.canList (line 148-150), the implementation changed from `canView() || root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS, AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS, AdminRoles.QUERY_GROUPS)` to `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.QUERY_GROUPS) || canView()`. Since canView() already checks VIEW_USERS and MANAGE_USERS, the new version is `QUERY_GROUPS || VIEW_USERS || MANAGE_USERS` — identical set. No functional change. Not a bug; style only. Retracting.

title: getScope throws NullPointerException when resourceType is not in the schema
body: In AdminPermissionsSchema.getScope (lines 229-244), when supportsAuthorizationSchema is true, the code does `SCHEMA.getResourceTypes().get(resourceType).getScopes()` without checking that `getResourceTypes().get(resourceType)` is non-null. If a caller passes a resourceType that is not one of 'Clients', 'Groups', 'Users' (e.g. a legacy resource type or a typo), getResourceTypes().get(resourceType) returns null and .getScopes() throws NullPointerException. The method is called during policy/scope validation; a null resourceType or an unsupported type would cause a 500 error instead of a ModelValidationException. A null check with a proper ModelValidationException should be added, similar to throwExceptionIfResourceTypeOrScopesNotProvided which does validate the resource type.

title: getOrCreateResource throws IllegalStateException for unknown resource types instead of returning null
body: In AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource (lines 92-131), the switch on resourceType now throws IllegalStateException for unknown types (line 111: `default -> throw new IllegalStateException("Resource type [" + resourceType + "] not found.")`). The old code set name = null for unknown types and then threw IllegalStateException at line 115 with a more descriptive message including the id. The new behavior throws earlier with a less informative message and, more importantly, changes the exception path: callers that previously received an IllegalStateException with the id context now receive one without it. Also, if resourceType is null, the switch will throw a NullPointerException (switch on null). The old code handled null resourceType by falling through to name = null and then the IllegalStateException. A null check on resourceType should be added before the switch.

title: GroupPermissionsV2 throws UnsupportedOperationException for management methods that are still called by GroupResource
body: GroupPermissionsV2 throws UnsupportedOperationException for isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, viewMembersPermission, manageMembersPermission, manageMembershipPermission, viewPermission, managePermission, resource, and getPermissions (lines 167-210). However, GroupResource.getManagementPermissions (line 321-330) and setManagementPermissionsEnabled (line 354-365) call `permissions.groups().isPermissionsEnabled(group)`, `permissions.groups().resource(group)`, `permissions.groups().getPermissions(group)`, and `permissions.groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, ...)`. These endpoints are guarded by `ProfileHelper.requireFeature(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)` (the V1 feature), not ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. If both features are enabled (V2 implies V1 feature flag in Keycloak's profile hierarchy? Actually ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is a separate feature; when V2 is enabled, AdminPermissions.management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, whose groups() returns GroupPermissionsV2). So when V2 is enabled and an admin calls GET /admin/realms/{realm}/groups/{id}/management/permissions, GroupResource.getManagementPermissions calls auth.groups().requireView(group) (fine) but then `AdminPermissions.management(session, realm)` returns MgmtPermissionsV2, and `permissions.groups().isPermissionsEnabled(group)` throws UnsupportedOperationException → 500 error. The endpoint should either be guarded to require the V1 feature only (and return an error when V2 is active) or the V2 implementation should provide meaningful behavior. This is a runtime 500 for a documented admin endpoint when the V2 feature is enabled.

title: UserPermissionsV2 throws UnsupportedOperationException for management methods still called by admin endpoints
body: UserPermissionsV2 throws UnsupportedOperationException for isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, getPermissions, resource, managePermission, viewPermission, manageGroupMembershipPermission, mapRolesPermission, adminImpersonatingPermission, userImpersonatedPermission (lines 152-199). These methods are part of UserPermissionManagement interface and are called by admin endpoints such as UsersResource (e.g. the management/permissions endpoints on the realm users resource). When V2 is enabled, AdminPermissions.management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, whose users() returns UserPermissionsV2. Any admin REST endpoint that calls these management methods (e.g. GET /admin/realms/{realm}/users/management/permissions) will hit UnsupportedOperationException and return a 500 error. The endpoints should be guarded by the V1 feature flag or the V2 implementation should provide the V2-equivalent behavior (e.g. returning the resource-type resource and scope permissions). This is a functional regression for the permissions management API when V2 is enabled.

title: registerListener feature check moved outside the listener registration, changing behavior when feature is disabled at runtime
body: In AdminPermissions.registerListener (lines 73-99), the `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)` check was moved from inside the listener's onEvent method to wrap the manager.register call. Previously, the listener was always registered but only acted when the feature was enabled (checked per-event). Now, the listener is only registered if the feature is enabled at registration time. Since Profile features are static at server startup, this is functionally equivalent in practice. However, if registerListener is called before the profile is fully initialized (unlikely), the check could evaluate incorrectly. More importantly, the V2 feature ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 also needs this listener (for cleaning up permissions when groups/users/roles are removed). The check only tests ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1). If V2 is enabled but V1 is disabled (possible if V2 is a separate feature flag), the listener would not be registered, and group/role/client removal events would not clean up V2 permissions, leaving orphaned resources and policies. The check should be `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ) || Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2)` or simply check for V2 as well.

title: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission does not check root.users().canManage() — manage-only admins get restricted
body: In GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (line 106-107), the guard is `if (root.users().canView()) return Collections.emptySet();`. UserPermissions.canView() (inherited by UserPermissionsV2) returns true if the admin has MANAGE_USERS or VIEW_USERS role, or has VIEW/MANAGE permission on the Users resource. An admin with only the manage-users role has canView() true (since canView checks MANAGE_USERS), so they get an empty set — correct. But an admin with fine-grained MANAGE permission on the Users resource type (but not VIEW) — UserPermissions.canView() checks `hasPermission(MgmtPermissions.VIEW_SCOPE, MgmtPermissions.MANAGE_SCOPE)` which accepts MANAGE as sufficient for view, so canView() returns true. So manage-only fine-grained admins also get empty set. The V1 removed method getGroupsWithViewPermission() had `if (root.users().canView() || root.users().canManage()) return Collections.emptySet();` — the canManage() check was redundant since canView() includes manage. So no functional difference. However, the V2 override does not check `root.users().canManage()` separately; if a future change makes canView() not include manage, this would break. Not a current bug. Retracting.

title: Double semicolon in field declaration
body: Line 68: `private final GroupRepresentation topGroup = new GroupRepresentation();;` — there is an extra semicolon after the field declaration. This is a minor style issue (empty statement) and does not affect functionality, but it is a code smell that should be cleaned up.

title: Test uses try-with-resources on Response but also calls ApiUtil.handleCreatedResponse which closes the response, causing double-close
body: In GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest.onBefore (lines 71-79), the code does `try (Response response = realm.admin().groups().add(topGroup)) { ... topGroup.setId(ApiUtil.handleCreatedResponse(response)); ... }`. ApiUtil.handleCreatedResponse (in test-framework/core/src/main/java/org/keycloak/testframework/util/ApiUtil.java) now uses try-with-resources on the response (line 9: `try (response)`), which closes the response when the method returns. The outer try-with-resources in the test will then attempt to close the already-closed response. While closing an already-closed JAX-RS Response is generally idempotent (no exception), it is a resource management smell. More importantly, in testManageAllGroups (line 165), `String testGroupId = ApiUtil.handleCreatedResponse(realmAdminClient.realm(realm.getName()).groups().add(group));` — the response is not in a try-with-resources here, so handleCreatedResponse closing it is correct. But in onBefore and testManageGroup (line 195-199) and testViewGroups (line 261-265), the response is both in a try-with-resources and passed to handleCreatedResponse which closes it. The double-close is harmless for most JAX-RS implementations but the pattern is inconsistent: either use try-with-resources and extract the id manually, or use handleCreatedResponse without try-with-resources. The ApiUtil change to close the response makes the test code's try-with-resources redundant and potentially confusing.

title: handleCreatedResponse now closes the response, which is a contract change for callers that manage the response themselves
body: ApiUtil.handleCreatedResponse was changed to use try-with-resources on the Response (line 9: `try (response)`), which closes the response before returning. Previously, the method called `response.close()` explicitly at the end (old code line 12: `response.close();`), so the behavior is the same — the response was always closed. The change is purely a refactoring to use try-with-resources. However, callers that pass a response they intend to use after calling handleCreatedResponse (e.g. reading the status again or using the response object) would now get an already-closed response. Looking at the test usages, some callers wrap the response in try-with-resources and then call handleCreatedResponse (double close, harmless), and some call handleCreatedResponse directly (correct). The contract is unchanged (response was always closed), but the method name 'handleCreatedResponse' does not imply it closes the response; a caller might not expect the side effect. This is a minor API design concern, not a bug.

title: hasPermission evaluates the all-groups resource for any group id, enabling cross-group permission leakage when resource names collide
body: In GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission(String groupId, String... scopes) (lines 130-165), the resource lookup is `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)`. Resource names in the V2 admin permissions client are not namespaced by type: per-group resources are created with the group id as the name (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup returns group.getId()), per-user resources with the user id, per-client resources with the client id. Since group ids, user ids, and client ids are all UUIDs generated by the same id generator, collisions are practically impossible, but the lookup does not verify the resource type. If a resource with the same name exists but belongs to a different type (e.g. a user resource whose id equals a group id — theoretically possible in stores that reuse ids), the permission evaluation would use the wrong resource. More concretely, the fallback to the all-groups resource (line 144) is applied whenever the specific resource is not found, which means any group id that has not yet had a resource created (resources are created lazily via getOrCreateResource when permissions are defined) will be authorized based on the all-groups permission. This is the intended fallback, but it means that an admin with VIEW on the Groups resource type can view *any* group, including groups they should not have access to if per-group permissions were intended to restrict them. The fallback is by design in V2 (resource-type permissions apply to all objects of that type), so this is not a bug per se. However, the lack of type verification in findByName means that if a group id happens to match a user resource name (both are UUIDs), the group permission check would evaluate the user resource's permissions. This is a defense-in-depth issue; the resource store should be queried with type filtering (findByNameAndType or similar) to prevent cross-type permission leakage.

title: grantIfNoPermission is set based on session attribute that may be set by group filtering, changing permission semantics
body: In UsersResource.toRepresentation (line 456-468), `usersEvaluator.grantIfNoPermission(session.getAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS) != null)` sets the grantIfNoPermission flag on the UserPermissionEvaluator based on whether the GROUPS session attribute was set. The GROUPS attribute is set in searchForUser (line 448-451) whenever `auth.groups().getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` returns a non-empty set. Previously, this attribute was only set when `!auth.users().canView()` — i.e., when the admin did NOT have global view permission. Now it is set unconditionally (whenever the group-ids set is non-empty). In UserPermissions.hasPermission (line 490-521), when the Users resource does not exist (`resource == null`), the method returns `grantIfNoPermission && expectedScopes.contains(MANAGE_SCOPE) && expectedScopes.contains(VIEW_SCOPE)`. This means: if the admin has no global view (so the group filter was applied) AND the Users resource doesn't exist, the admin is granted both manage and view on all users returned by the filtered search. This is the intended behavior for group-restricted admins. But now, with the unconditional setting, an admin who HAS global view (canView() true) but for whom getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns a non-empty set (which should not happen given the guards, but could happen if the V2 implementation returns resource ids instead of group ids — see separate finding — or if there's a logic error) would have grantIfNoPermission set to true. Then, if the Users resource doesn't exist, hasPermission would grant manage+view even though the admin already has global view — no escalation. The real risk: an admin with NO global view and NO group permissions — getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns empty set, attribute not set, grantIfNoPermission false — correct. An admin with group view permissions — attribute set, grantIfNoPermission true — if Users resource doesn't exist, they get manage+view on users in their groups — this is the intended design (group-restricted admins can manage users in their groups). The change from conditional to unconditional setting only matters if getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns non-empty for an admin with global view, which the guards prevent. So the practical impact is limited to the V2 resource-id bug. Medium severity because it's a fragile coupling: the grantIfNoPermission flag is a security-sensitive toggle that depends on a session attribute set by a different subsystem.

title: Scope name constants duplicated between GroupPermissions and AdminPermissionsSchema
body: GroupPermissions defines private constants MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP_SCOPE = "manage-membership" (line 50), MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE = "manage-members" (line 51), VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE = "view-members" (line 52). AdminPermissionsSchema defines the same values as public constants MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP (line 69), MANAGE_MEMBERS (line 70), VIEW_MEMBERS (line 71). The duplication means that if the schema scope names change, the V1 GroupPermissions constants must be updated separately. This is a maintenance hazard, not a runtime bug. Low severity style/maintainability issue.

title: GroupPermissionsV2 extends GroupPermissions but overrides almost all behavior, inheriting only unused V1 helpers
body: GroupPermissionsV2 extends GroupPermissions (line 37) but overrides canView(), canView(GroupModel), canManage(), canManage(GroupModel), canViewMembers, canManageMembers, canManageMembership, getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, and throws UnsupportedOperationException for all management methods. The inherited methods that are still used: requireList, requireManage, requireView, requireManageMembership, requireManageMembers, requireViewMembers, getAccess, canList (inherited from GroupPermissions line 148-150 which calls canView() — overridden, so OK). The V1-specific fields resourceStore and policyStore are protected and used by the V2 hasPermission method. The inheritance is primarily to reuse the require* methods and getAccess. This is a reasonable design, but the class inherits many V1-specific methods (initialize, deletePermissions, groupResource, hasPermission(GroupModel...), hasPermission(Resource...)) that are either overridden or unused. The private V1 hasPermission methods (lines 393-435) are not accessible from V2 (private), so V2 defines its own hasPermission(String, String...). The protected fields resourceStore and policyStore are used. No bug, but the inheritance hierarchy is fragile: changes to GroupPermissions V1 logic (e.g. canList, getAccess) will affect V2. Low severity design concern.

title: groups() method returns GroupPermissionsV2 but the field type and superclass method signature use GroupPermissions
body: In MgmtPermissionsV2.groups() (lines 58-62), the method returns `GroupPermissions` (the superclass method signature in MgmtPermissions presumably returns GroupPermissions). The field `groupPermissions` is typed as `GroupPermissionsV2` (line 27). The method creates `new GroupPermissionsV2(session, authz, this)` and returns it as GroupPermissions. This is fine for polymorphism. However, the superclass MgmtPermissions.groups() likely returns a GroupPermissions instance (V1). The override correctly returns a V2 instance. No bug. The constructor of GroupPermissionsV2 takes (KeycloakSession, AuthorizationProvider, MgmtPermissions) — the `authz` field in MgmtPermissions must be accessible (protected). No issue.

title: getResourceName only handles USERS resource type, not GROUPS or CLIENTS
body: In AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceName (lines 328-350), when supportsAuthorizationSchema is true, the method only handles the USERS resource type (line 334: `if (USERS.getType().equals(resourceType))`). For GROUPS and CLIENTS resource types, it falls through to `return resource.getDisplayName();` (line 349). For group resources, the resource name is the group id (per resolveGroup), and getDisplayName() would return null or the name depending on the resource implementation. This means that in the admin UI or any consumer of getResourceName, group resources would display as null or empty instead of the group name. The method should be extended to resolve group names (similar to resolveUser which looks up the user and returns the username) and client names. This is a functional gap for the new Groups resource type: the display name resolution is incomplete. Low severity because it affects display only, but it is a missing feature for the newly added Groups resource type.

title: canView() global check accepts VIEW scope, but canManage() also accepts VIEW scope — manage granted by view permission
body: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() (lines 64-71), the fallback is `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)` — the same scopes as canView() (line 52). This means an admin with only the VIEW scope on the Groups resource type is considered to have global manage permission. This is clearly wrong: canManage() should only accept MANAGE (and possibly VIEW if manage-implies-view is intended, but the reverse — view implies manage — is a privilege escalation). Compare with canManage(GroupModel) at line 79 which correctly uses only `AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE`. The global canManage() should be `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`. This bug grants manage-group rights (create groups, delete groups, manage any group) to admins who only have view permission on the Groups resource type. High severity security issue.

title: Resource lookup by group id uses findByName without verifying the resource type is 'Groups'
body: In GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission (line 141), `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)` looks up a resource by name only. In the V2 admin permissions client, resources for users, groups, and clients all live in the same resource store and are looked up by name (which is the object id). There is no type filter in the lookup. If a user id and a group id were ever the same (both are UUIDs, collision probability negligible but not zero in custom id generators), or if a resource with the same name exists for a different type (e.g. a client resource created with a name equal to a group id), the permission evaluation would use the wrong resource. The V2 schema does set resource.setType(type) for resource-type resources (in init, line 274: `resource.setType(type)`), but per-object resources created via getOrCreateResource do NOT set a type (getOrCreateResource creates the resource with `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId())` and only updates scopes, never sets type). So per-group resources have no type set, and findByName cannot disambiguate. The lookup should use findByName with type verification or the resource should have its type set when created. Medium severity defense-in-depth issue.

title: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission adds resource.getId() but consumers expect group ids
body: In GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (lines 106-128), the lambda at line 122-124 does `granted.add(groupResource.getId())`. The resource's getId() is the internal resource UUID, not the group id. In V2, per-group resources are created by AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource with the group id as the resource *name* (resolveGroup returns group.getId(), and the resource is created with that name). The resource id is a separate UUID. Consumers of getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (UsersResource.searchForUser line 448-451, BruteForceUsersResource.searchForUser line 147-150) set `session.setAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS, groupIds)` and the user provider filters users by group membership using these ids. Since the returned ids are resource UUIDs, not group ids, the filter will never match any actual group membership, and admins restricted to viewing members of specific groups will see no users in the user search. The fix: extract the group id from the resource name (which is the group id per resolveGroup), e.g. `granted.add(groupResource.getName())` since the name IS the group id for V2 group resources.

title: hasPermission resource lookup by user id uses findByName without type verification, and fallback to all-users resource may grant unintended access
body: In UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission (lines 94-133), `resourceStore.findByName(server, user.getId())` looks up a resource by name (the user id). Per-user resources in V2 are created with the user id as the name (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveUser returns user.getId()). The lookup does not verify the resource type. If a resource with the same name exists for a different type (group or client), the wrong resource would be used. Additionally, the fallback to the all-users resource (line 109) is applied whenever the specific user resource is not found. This means an admin with a permission on the Users resource type (all users) is granted that permission for ANY user, even users for which a more restrictive per-user permission might be intended. This is the intended V2 design (resource-type permissions apply to all objects of that type unless overridden by per-object permissions). However, the fallback only checks `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource).isEmpty()` — if there is ANY policy on the all-users resource, the evaluation proceeds. If that policy grants, say, VIEW, then the admin can view any user. This is correct. But if the admin has a per-user permission that DENIES view (negative policy), and no all-users permission exists, the fallback would not trigger (no policies on all-users resource), and the per-user resource would be found and evaluated — correct. The issue is that the fallback does not consider per-user deny policies when falling back: if a user has a per-user resource with a deny policy, findByName would find it and the fallback would not be used — correct. So the logic is sound. The main concern is the lack of type verification in findByName, same as the group case. Medium severity defense-in-depth.

title: canManage() accepts VIEW scope — view-only admins get global group manage permission (duplicate of line 70 finding, confirming severity)
body: This finding confirms and emphasizes the critical bug at GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() line 70: `return hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE);`. The method name is canManage() and it is used by GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup via `auth.groups().requireManage()` (GroupsResource line 181). An admin with only the 'view' scope on the Groups resource type (all-groups permission) will pass this check and be able to create top-level groups. Additionally, canManage() is called by GroupPermissions.canManage(GroupModel) (inherited, line 234-244) as `if (canManage()) return true;` — so a view-only admin can manage ANY group. This is a direct privilege escalation: view → manage. The fix is to change line 70 to `return hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE);`.

title: V1 GroupPermissions.canManage(GroupModel) calls canManage() which in V2 is overridden with the VIEW-scope bug
body: In GroupPermissions.canManage(GroupModel group) (lines 234-244), the first check is `if (canManage()) return true;`. In V2, GroupPermissionsV2 overrides canManage() (line 64-71) with the buggy implementation that accepts VIEW scope. So when V2 is active, an admin with only VIEW on the Groups resource type calls canManage(anyGroup) → canManage() returns true (due to the VIEW-scope bug) → the admin can manage any group. This is the propagation path of the canManage() bug into per-group manage checks. The V1 canManage() (line 274-276) only checks the MANAGE_USERS role, so V1 is not affected. The fix must be in GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() (line 70) as identified in the primary finding.

title: canManageMembership accepts MANAGE scope in addition to MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP — manage-group implies manage-membership
body: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManageMembership (lines 96-103), the check is `hasPermission(group.getId(), AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP)`. This means an admin with the MANAGE scope on a group (full group management) can also manage membership (add/remove users) of that group. This is consistent with the interface documentation (GroupPermissionEvaluator line 112-117: 'Or if it has a permission to MANAGE the group or MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP of the group'). The V1 GroupPermissions.canManageMembership (line 358-366) also checks `if (canManage(group)) return true;` first, so V1 also grants manage-membership to group managers. Consistent. Not a bug.

title: canViewMembers accepts MANAGE_MEMBERS scope — manage-members implies view-members
body: In GroupPermissionsV2.canViewMembers (lines 82-87), the check is `hasPermission(group.getId(), AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW_MEMBERS, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE_MEMBERS)`. This means an admin with manage-members can also view members. This is consistent with the interface documentation (line 120-125) and with V1 behavior (V1 canViewMembers now also accepts MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE). Not a bug; manage implies view is a standard pattern.

title: canMapRoles accepts MANAGE scope — manage-user implies map-roles
body: In UserPermissionsV2.canMapRoles (lines 76-83), the check is `hasPermission(user, null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE, AdminPermissionsSchema.MAP_ROLES) || canManageByGroup(user)`. This means an admin with MANAGE on a user can also map roles for that user. This is consistent with the interface documentation (UserPermissionEvaluator line 137-145: 'Or if it has a permission to MANAGE the user or MAP_ROLES of the user'). The old code also had `if (canManage(user)) return true;` which granted map-roles to managers. Not a bug.

title: canManageGroupMembership accepts MANAGE scope — manage-user implies manage-group-membership
body: In UserPermissionsV2.canManageGroupMembership (lines 85-92), the check is `hasPermission(user, null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE_GROUP_MEMBERSHIP) || canManageByGroup(user)`. This means an admin with MANAGE on a user can also manage that user's group membership. This is consistent with the interface documentation (line 153-161) and with the old code (`if (canManage(user)) return true;`). Not a bug.

title: Resource name for group is the group id, but getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns resource id — mismatch breaks user search filtering
body: This finding consolidates the data flow issue: AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup (line 181-186) returns group.getId() as the resource name. getOrCreateResource creates the resource with this name. GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission looks up resources by `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)` — correct, since the name is the group id. But GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (line 122-124) adds `groupResource.getId()` (the resource's internal UUID) to the returned set, not the group id (which is the resource name). The consumers (UsersResource.searchForUser, BruteForceUsersResource.searchForUser) use these ids to filter users by group membership via `session.setAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS, groupIds)`. Since the ids are resource UUIDs, not group ids, the user search filter will not match any users. This breaks the feature where an admin with view-members permission on specific groups can see users in those groups. The fix: in getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, add `groupResource.getName()` (which is the group id) instead of `groupResource.getId()`.

title: NullPointerException when the Groups resource-type resource does not exist
body: In GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission (line 144), `resource = AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` can return null (AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource returns null when the resource type is unknown or the resource is not found, lines 133-151). Line 147 then calls `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` — if resource is null, this throws NullPointerException. This happens when the admin permissions client exists (server non-null) but the 'Groups' resource-type resource has not been created (e.g. AdminPermissionsSchema.init has not run, or the resource was deleted). The NPE surfaces as a 500 error. A null check returning false is needed.

title: NullPointerException when the Users resource-type resource does not exist
body: In UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission (line 109), `resource = AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.USERS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` can return null. Line 111 then calls `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` — if resource is null, NullPointerException. Same issue as the Groups case. A null check returning false is needed.

title: UnsupportedOperationException from management methods breaks GroupResource management/permissions endpoints when V2 is enabled
body: GroupPermissionsV2 throws UnsupportedOperationException for isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, resource, getPermissions, and all permission accessor methods (lines 167-210). GroupResource.getManagementPermissions (GroupResource.java line 321-330) calls `permissions.groups().isPermissionsEnabled(group)`, `permissions.groups().resource(group).getId()`, and `permissions.groups().getPermissions(group)`. GroupResource.setManagementPermissionsEnabled (line 354-365) calls `permissions.groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, ref.isEnabled())`. These endpoints are guarded by `ProfileHelper.requireFeature(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)` (V1 feature). When V2 is enabled (ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2), AdminPermissions.management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, whose groups() returns GroupPermissionsV2. If the V1 feature is also enabled (which it typically is when V2 is enabled, since V2 is built on top of V1), the endpoints are accessible and will throw UnsupportedOperationException → 500 error. The endpoints should either be guarded to reject V2 explicitly, or GroupPermissionsV2 should implement these methods using the V2 schema (e.g. isPermissionsEnabled could check if any scope permission exists for the group resource type). This is a functional break of the admin permissions management API for groups when V2 is active.

title: UnsupportedOperationException from management methods breaks UsersResource management/permissions endpoints when V2 is enabled
body: UserPermissionsV2 throws UnsupportedOperationException for isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, getPermissions, resource, managePermission, viewPermission, manageGroupMembershipPermission, mapRolesPermission, adminImpersonatingPermission, userImpersonatedPermission (lines 152-199). These are called by the realm-level users management/permissions endpoints (e.g. GET/PUT /admin/realms/{realm}/users/management/permissions). When V2 is enabled, AdminPermissions.management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, whose users() returns UserPermissionsV2. The endpoints are guarded by ProfileHelper.requireFeature(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ) (V1). If V1 is enabled alongside V2, the endpoints are accessible and will throw UnsupportedOperationException → 500. This is a functional break of the users permissions management API when V2 is active.

title: registerListener only checks V1 feature flag, missing V2 — permission cleanup listener not registered when only V2 is enabled
body: In AdminPermissions.registerListener (line 74), the guard is `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))`. The listener cleans up permissions when roles, clients, or groups are removed (lines 78-95). When V2 (ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2) is enabled, permissions are stored in the admin permissions client's resource server using the V2 schema. If V2 is enabled but V1 is disabled (possible if V2 is a standalone feature flag), the listener would not be registered, and removing a group would leave orphaned resources and policies in the V2 admin permissions client. Even if V2 typically implies V1, the check should explicitly include V2: `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ) || Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2)`. The listener's onEvent calls `management(cast.getKeycloakSession(), realm).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(cast.getGroup(), false)` — in V2, GroupPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException (line 173-175), so even if the listener is registered, it would throw when a group is removed in V2. This is a second bug: the listener is not V2-aware. The listener should either be updated to handle V2 (e.g. delete the group's resource and associated policies directly) or the V2 setPermissionsEnabled should be implemented.

title: setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException, breaking group removal cleanup listener in V2
body: GroupPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled (lines 172-175) throws UnsupportedOperationException. This method is called by AdminPermissions.registerListener's onEvent when a GroupModel.GroupRemovedEvent occurs (AdminPermissions.java line 94: `management(cast.getKeycloakSession(), cast.getRealm()).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(cast.getGroup(), false)`). When V2 is enabled and a group is deleted, the listener fires and calls setPermissionsEnabled(false), which throws UnsupportedOperationException. This exception would propagate up through the event listener, potentially causing the group deletion to fail or leaving the transaction in an inconsistent state. In V2, group permissions are stored as resources and policies in the admin permissions client; when a group is deleted, the corresponding resource and its associated policies should be cleaned up. The V2 implementation should either implement setPermissionsEnabled to delete the group's resource and policies, or the listener should be updated to handle V2 cleanup differently (e.g. by directly deleting the resource via the resource store). This is a data integrity issue: orphaned resources and policies accumulate in the admin permissions client when groups are deleted in V2.

title: setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException, but no user-removal listener exists — orphaned user resources in V2
body: UserPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled (lines 156-159) throws UnsupportedOperationException. Unlike groups and roles, there is no UserRemovedEvent listener in AdminPermissions.registerListener that calls users().setPermissionsEnabled. However, when a user is deleted in V2, the per-user resource (created lazily by getOrCreateResource when a permission is defined for that user) remains in the admin permissions client as an orphan. The V1 implementation had a listener for roles and clients but not users (users permissions were realm-wide in V1, not per-user). In V2, per-user resources exist, so user deletion should clean them up. The absence of a user-removal listener combined with the UnsupportedOperationException in V2 means orphaned user resources accumulate. This is a data integrity issue. A UserRemovedEvent listener should be added (similar to GroupRemovedEvent) that deletes the user's resource and associated policies from the admin permissions client.

title: getOrCreateResource does not set resource type on per-object resources, preventing type-based lookups
body: In AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource (lines 92-131), when a new resource is created for a specific object (group, user, client), the code does `resource = resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId())` (line 121) and then `resource.updateScopes(...)` (line 123), but never calls `resource.setType(resourceType)`. The resource-type resources created in init() do set the type (line 274: `resource.setType(type)`). Per-object resources have no type set. This means that `resourceStore.findByType(server, "Groups", ...)` (used in GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission line 121) will NOT find per-group resources, because they have no type. Wait — GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)` which searches for resources of type "Groups". But per-group resources created by getOrCreateResource do NOT have type "Groups" set — they have no type at all. So findByType would only find the resource-type resource (the 'Groups' all-groups resource), not individual group resources. This means getGroupIdsWithViewPermission would only ever return the resource id of the all-groups resource (if it has view-members permission), not individual group ids. This is a critical bug: the method is supposed to return ids of groups with view permission, but it will only find the all-groups resource (if it has the right type) and return its id. Actually, looking at init() line 271-276, the resource-type resources are created with `resource.setType(type)` where type is the resource type name (e.g. "Groups"). So findByType(server, "Groups") finds the all-groups resource. Per-group resources have no type, so they are not found. Therefore getGroupIdsWithViewPermission only returns the all-groups resource id (if it has view-members permission), which is wrong — it should return individual group ids. The fix: getOrCreateResource should set the resource type on per-object resources (e.g. `resource.setType(resourceType)` after creation), so that findByType can find them.

title: Per-object resources are created without a type, breaking findByType queries used by getGroupIdsWithViewPermission
body: In AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource (lines 118-128), when a new per-object resource is created (line 121: `resource = resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId())`), the resource type is never set. Only the resource-type resources created in init() have their type set (line 274). GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (line 121) uses `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)` to find all group resources with view permission. Since per-group resources have no type, findByType will NOT return them — it will only return the 'Groups' resource-type resource (the all-groups resource). This means getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns at most one id (the all-groups resource id), and never the ids of individual groups that have view-members permissions. This completely breaks the feature where an admin with view-members permission on specific groups can see users in those groups via the user search. The fix: in getOrCreateResource, after creating the resource, call `resource.setType(resourceType)` so that per-object resources are typed and can be found by findByType.

title: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses findByType but per-group resources have no type set — method returns wrong results
body: GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (line 121) calls `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)`. As established in the AdminPermissionsSchema finding, per-group resources created by getOrCreateResource do NOT have their type set (only resource-type resources have type set in init()). Therefore findByType(server, "Groups") will only match the 'Groups' resource-type resource (the all-groups resource), not individual group resources. The method will return the resource id of the all-groups resource (if it has view-members permission) instead of the ids of individual groups. This breaks the user search filtering for group-restricted admins. The fix requires both: (1) getOrCreateResource must set the resource type on per-object resources, and (2) getGroupIdsWithViewPermission must extract the group id from the resource name (not the resource id).

title: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission adds resource.getId() instead of the group id (resource name)
body: In GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (line 122-124), the lambda adds `groupResource.getId()` to the granted set. The resource id is an internal UUID, not the group id. In V2, per-group resources are created with the group id as the resource NAME (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup returns group.getId(), and getOrCreateResource creates the resource with that name). The consumers of getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (UsersResource.searchForUser line 448-451, BruteForceUsersResource.searchForUser line 147-150) set `session.setAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS, groupIds)` and the user provider filters users by group membership using these ids. Since the returned ids are resource UUIDs, not group ids, the filter will never match any users. The fix: add `groupResource.getName()` (which is the group id) instead of `groupResource.getId()`.

title: CRITICAL: canManage() accepts VIEW scope — any admin with view permission on Groups resource type gets full manage rights over all groups
body: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() at line 70 returns `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`. This means the VIEW scope is treated as sufficient for the global manage check. The method is called by: (1) GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup via `auth.groups().requireManage()` (GroupsResource.java line 181) — allows creating top-level groups; (2) GroupPermissions.canManage(GroupModel) line 234 `if (canManage()) return true;` — allows managing ANY group (update, delete, add children, map roles). An attacker (or misconfigured admin) with only a 'view' scope permission on the Groups resource type (e.g. a scope permission granting VIEW on the 'Groups' resource to a user policy) gains the ability to create, update, and delete any group in the realm. This is a complete privilege escalation from view to manage. The fix: change line 70 to `return hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE);`.

title: canView() accepts both VIEW and MANAGE scopes — manage implies view (correct), but combined with canManage() bug creates confusion
body: GroupPermissionsV2.canView() at line 52 returns `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`. Accepting MANAGE for view is correct (manage implies view). However, the same scope list is used in canManage() (line 70), which is the bug. The canView() implementation itself is correct. This finding is to note that the scope list in canView() is correct and should not be changed when fixing canManage().

title: canManage(GroupModel) correctly uses only MANAGE scope — confirms the canManage() global bug is an isolated mistake
body: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(GroupModel) at line 79 correctly uses `hasPermission(group.getId(), AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)` — only the MANAGE scope. This confirms that the canManage() global method at line 70 using VIEW+MANAGE is an isolated mistake (likely a copy-paste from canView()). The per-group manage check is correct; only the global manage check is wrong.

title: hasPermission fallback to all-groups resource applies even when a specific group resource exists but has no policies
body: In GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission (lines 130-165), the logic is: look up resource by groupId; if not found, fall back to all-groups resource. But if the resource IS found (a per-group resource exists), the code proceeds directly to evaluate permissions on that resource (line 152). It does NOT fall back to the all-groups resource if the per-group resource has no policies granting the requested scopes. This means: if an admin has a permission on the all-groups resource (e.g. VIEW on Groups resource type) AND a per-group resource exists for a specific group (created when a permission was defined for that group), the per-group resource is evaluated. If the per-group resource has no policies granting VIEW, the evaluation returns no permissions, and hasPermission returns false — even though the all-groups permission should grant view. This is a semantic question: in V2, should a per-group resource's existence override the all-groups permission? The current implementation says yes (per-group resource takes precedence, no fallback). This could be intended (per-group permissions override resource-type permissions) or a bug (resource-type permissions should apply unless explicitly overridden). The interface documentation and V2 design suggest that resource-type permissions apply to all objects of that type, and per-object permissions are additional. The current implementation makes per-object resources act as a complete override — if a per-group resource exists, the all-groups permission is ignored for that group. This could lead to unexpected denials: an admin with VIEW on all groups creates a per-group permission for a specific group (e.g. MANAGE for a different admin), and suddenly the first admin loses VIEW on that group because the per-group resource exists but doesn't grant VIEW. This is a design decision that should be documented; if unintended, the fallback should also apply when the per-group resource evaluation yields no matching scopes.

title: hasPermission fallback to all-users resource applies even when a specific user resource exists but has no matching policies
body: Same pattern as GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission: in UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission (lines 94-133), if a per-user resource exists (found by findByName), the code evaluates permissions on that resource only (line 116-118). It does NOT fall back to the all-users resource if the per-user resource evaluation yields no matching scopes. This means a per-user resource acts as a complete override of the all-users permission. If an admin has VIEW on all users (Users resource type) and a per-user resource exists for a specific user (created when a permission was defined for that user), the admin's VIEW permission on all users is ignored for that user — the evaluation only considers the per-user resource. If the per-user resource has no VIEW-granting policy, the admin cannot view that user, despite having VIEW on all users. This is likely unintended: resource-type permissions should apply to all objects unless explicitly overridden by a deny. The current implementation makes any per-object resource a complete override. This could cause unexpected permission denials.

title: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission guard checks root.users().canView() but should also check canManage() for admins with manage-only fine-grained permission
body: In GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (line 107), the guard is `if (root.users().canView()) return Collections.emptySet();`. UserPermissions.canView() (inherited by UserPermissionsV2) returns true if the admin has MANAGE_USERS or VIEW_USERS role, OR has VIEW/MANAGE permission on the Users resource (V1-style check using MgmtPermissions.VIEW_SCOPE/MANAGE_SCOPE on the 'Users' resource). In V2, an admin with fine-grained MANAGE permission on the Users resource type would have canView() return true (since canView accepts MANAGE scope). So manage-only fine-grained admins get an empty set — correct. But what about an admin with fine-grained MANAGE on the Users resource type but the V1 'Users' resource doesn't exist (V2 uses a different resource)? UserPermissions.canView() calls hasPermission(MgmtPermissions.VIEW_SCOPE, MgmtPermissions.MANAGE_SCOPE) which looks up `resourceStore.findByName(server, USERS_RESOURCE)` where USERS_RESOURCE = "Users". In V2, the resource-type resource is also named "Users" (USERS_RESOURCE_TYPE = "Users"), so findByName would find the V2 resource-type resource. The scopes 'view' and 'manage' exist in the V2 schema. So canView() would evaluate V2 permissions using V1 code — this cross-wiring works by accident because the resource name and scope names match. But it's fragile. The guard should ideally use the V2-aware canView() (which UserPermissionsV2 inherits from UserPermissions, not overridden). Actually UserPermissionsV2 does NOT override canView() (the no-arg version) — it only overrides canView(UserModel). So root.users().canView() in V2 uses the V1 implementation, which checks admin roles and then V1-style hasPermission on the 'Users' resource. This works by accident as described. Not a bug per se, but fragile.

title: V1 getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses findByType with hard-coded "Group" type string
body: In GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (line 313), the V1 implementation uses `resourceStore.findByType(server, "Group", ...)`. The type string "Group" is hard-coded and matches the type set in V1 initialize() (line 117: `groupResource.setType("Group")`). This is correct for V1. The V2 schema uses "Groups" (GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE). The hard-coded string is a maintenance hazard but not a bug. Low severity.

title: V1 getGroupIdsWithViewPermission extracts group id via substring of resource name prefix
body: In GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (line 315), the V1 implementation extracts the group id via `resource.getName().substring(RESOURCE_NAME_PREFIX.length())` where RESOURCE_NAME_PREFIX = "group.resource.". This is correct for V1 resources which are named "group.resource.<groupId>". The V2 implementation (GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission) does NOT use this prefix — it uses the resource id directly (which is wrong, see separate finding). The V1 code is correct. Low severity note about the divergence between V1 and V2 id extraction strategies.

title: hasPermission does not verify that the resource found by name is actually a group resource (type check missing)
body: In GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission (line 141), `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)` returns any resource with that name, regardless of type. In the V2 admin permissions client, resources for users, groups, and clients coexist. If a user resource happens to have the same name as a group id (both are UUIDs), the group permission check would evaluate the user resource's permissions. While UUID collisions are extremely unlikely, the lack of type verification is a defense-in-depth gap. The resource store supports type filtering (findByType), and per-object resources should have their type set (see AdminPermissionsSchema finding about missing setType). The lookup should be `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)` followed by a type check, or a type-aware lookup method should be used.

title: hasPermission does not verify that the resource found by name is actually a user resource (type check missing)
body: Same issue as GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission: UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission (line 105) uses `resourceStore.findByName(server, user.getId())` without type verification. If a group or client resource has the same name as a user id, the wrong resource would be used. Defense-in-depth gap; the fix is to set resource types on per-object resources and use type-aware lookups.

title: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns empty set for admins with global view, but the method is also used to set grantIfNoPermission — coupling creates fragile security logic
body: The getGroupIdsWithViewPermission method serves two purposes: (1) filtering users by group membership in user search, and (2) indirectly controlling the grantIfNoPermission flag in UsersResource.toRepresentation (line 459: `usersEvaluator.grantIfNoPermission(session.getAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS) != null)`). When the method returns an empty set (admin has global view), the GROUPS attribute is not set, and grantIfNoPermission remains false. When it returns a non-empty set (admin has group-restricted view), the attribute is set, and grantIfNoPermission becomes true. This coupling means that any bug in getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (e.g. returning resource ids instead of group ids, or returning non-empty for admins with global view) directly affects the grantIfNoPermission security flag. The method's contract should be clearly documented, and the coupling should be made explicit or refactored to avoid fragile security logic.

title: GroupPermissionsV2 inherits from GroupPermissions but the V1 hasPermission methods are private and inaccessible
body: GroupPermissionsV2 extends GroupPermissions (line 37). The V1 hasPermission methods in GroupPermissions are private (lines 393-435: hasPermission(GroupModel, String...), hasPermission(GroupModel, EvaluationContext, String...), hasPermission(Resource, EvaluationContext, String...)). Since they are private, GroupPermissionsV2 cannot reuse them and defines its own hasPermission(String groupId, String... scopes) (line 130). This is fine, but the inheritance means GroupPermissionsV2 also inherits the V1 initialize(), deletePermissions(), groupResource(), and other private methods that are never called in V2. The protected fields resourceStore and policyStore are used. The design could be improved by extracting a common base class or using composition, but this is a style concern, not a bug.

title: GroupPermissionsV2 throws UnsupportedOperationException for GroupPermissionManagement methods, but the class implements GroupPermissionManagement via GroupPermissions
body: GroupPermissionsV2 extends GroupPermissions which implements GroupPermissionEvaluator and GroupPermissionManagement. GroupPermissionsV2 overrides the management methods (isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, viewMembersPermission, manageMembersPermission, manageMembershipPermission, viewPermission, managePermission, resource, getPermissions) to throw UnsupportedOperationException. This means that any code path that calls these methods on a GroupPermissionsV2 instance will get an exception. The GroupResource management/permissions endpoints (getManagementPermissions, setManagementPermissionsEnabled) call these methods when V2 is active, resulting in 500 errors. The V2 design should either implement these methods using the V2 schema (e.g. isPermissionsEnabled could check if any scope permission exists for the group) or the endpoints should be guarded to return a meaningful error when V2 is active. Throwing UnsupportedOperationException is not a user-friendly API behavior.

title: UserPermissionsV2 throws UnsupportedOperationException for UserPermissionManagement methods, breaking users management/permissions endpoints
