title: Admin theme (FreeMarker) error-invalid-multivalued-size changed to MessageFormat choice syntax — verify the admin theme actually uses MessageFormat and not a different interpolation
body: The admin theme's `messages_en.properties` changed `error-invalid-multivalued-size` from `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} value(s).` to `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.`. The admin theme is server-rendered (FreeMarker) and Keycloak's message resolution uses `java.text.MessageFormat`, so the choice pattern is correct for this theme. However, the same key is also consumed by the admin UI (React) via `js/apps/admin-ui/maven-resources/theme/keycloak.v2/admin/messages/messages_en.properties`, which uses i18next and does NOT understand MessageFormat (see the admin UI finding). The two bundles now have the same MessageFormat value, but the admin UI bundle should use i18next syntax. The admin theme (FreeMarker) change is correct; the admin UI bundle change is wrong.

title: Login theme error-invalid-multivalued-size changed to MessageFormat choice syntax — verify all consumers of this key use MessageFormat
body: The login theme's `messages_en.properties` changed `error-invalid-multivalued-size` from `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} value(s).` to `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.`. The login theme is server-rendered (FreeMarker) and uses `java.text.MessageFormat`, so the choice pattern is correct. However, this key is also used by the account UI (`js/apps/account-ui/maven-resources/theme/keycloak.v3/account/messages/messages_en.properties`) which uses i18next — that bundle was changed to the same MessageFormat syntax, which i18next cannot interpolate (see the account UI finding). The login theme change is correct; the account UI bundle change is wrong.

title: verify() catches only IOException from Files.readString but verifySafeHtml() throws RuntimeException for file read errors, breaking the declared exception contract
body: `verify()` declares `throws MojoExecutionException` and wraps `IOException` from `Files.readString` into `MojoExecutionException`. However, `verifySafeHtml()` (called inside the try block) catches `IOException` from the two `FileInputStream` constructions and rethrows them as `RuntimeException` (lines 70 and 79). These RuntimeExceptions are not caught by the `catch (IOException e)` block and propagate out of `verify()` as unchecked exceptions. The caller (presumably a Maven Mojo) expects `MojoExecutionException` for verification failures; a `RuntimeException` will produce an unhandled stack trace. The `verifySafeHtml` method should either declare `throws MojoExecutionException` and throw that, or `verify()` should catch `RuntimeException` from `verifySafeHtml` and wrap it.

title: PropertyResourceBundle is created with the platform default charset instead of UTF-8, which can misread non-ASCII translations
body: `new PropertyResourceBundle(fis)` uses the constructor `PropertyResourceBundle(InputStream)` which, per the JavaDoc, reads the stream as ISO-8859-1 (Latin-1). Keycloak's message properties files are UTF-8 (the project sets `project.build.sourceEncoding=UTF-8` and modern Keycloak loads properties as UTF-8). Reading a UTF-8 file as ISO-8859-1 will mojibake all non-ASCII characters (e.g. Cyrillic, CJK, Arabic), which means the sanitizer operates on corrupted text and the comparison against the sanitized form may produce false 'Illegal HTML' reports for any translation containing non-ASCII characters (the mojibake bytes may include characters that look like HTML entities or tags after unescapeHtml4). The code should use `new PropertyResourceBundle(new InputStreamReader(fis, StandardCharsets.UTF_8))` to match Keycloak's actual loading behavior.

title: Files.readString uses the platform default charset instead of UTF-8 for the duplicate-key check
body: `Files.readString(file.toPath())` uses UTF-8 by default (per the JavaDoc for `Files.readString(Path)` — it uses UTF-8). Actually, `Files.readString(Path)` does use UTF-8. So this is fine. Retracting.

title: PropertyResourceBundle(InputStream) reads ISO-8859-1, not UTF-8 — same issue as the bundle loading finding but for the translated file
body: Same as the previous finding: `new PropertyResourceBundle(fis)` at line 68 reads the translated properties file as ISO-8859-1, not UTF-8. This is the primary bundle being verified, so all non-ASCII translations are mojibake'd before sanitization and comparison. This is a critical correctness bug for the verifier's stated purpose (verifying translated message resources). The fix is to wrap the InputStream in an InputStreamReader with UTF-8.

title: Test for duplicate keys was changed from contains() to hasItem() but the assertion semantics changed subtly
body: The original test used `Matchers.contains(Matchers.containsString("Duplicate keys in file"))` which asserts the list has exactly one element matching. The new test uses `Matchers.hasItem(Matchers.containsString("Duplicate keys in file"))` which asserts the list has at least one matching element. The change is reasonable (the verifier may produce multiple messages), but the test no longer verifies that the duplicate-keys message is the *only* message or that it appears exactly once. This is a minor weakening of the test, not a defect.

title: Renamed duplicate-keys fixture is now an English file, but the verifier's HTML check will also run on it and may produce additional messages
body: The fixture was renamed from `duplicate_keys.properties` to `duplicateKeys_en.properties`. Because the file is now named `*_en.properties`, the verifier's `verifySafeHtml` will compute the English path from itself (the regex rewrites `_en` to `_en`), load itself as the English bundle, and run the HTML check on the value `value` (no HTML). The duplicate-keys check will produce one message, and the HTML check will produce none. The test asserts `hasItem(containsString("Duplicate keys in file"))`, which passes. However, the test no longer isolates the duplicate-keys check from the HTML check; if the HTML check were to produce a message for this fixture (it doesn't, since 'value' has no HTML), the test would still pass. This is fine but the fixture name change means the test now also exercises the HTML path implicitly. Not a defect, just a note.

title: Special-case key matching uses exact string equality for 'templateHelp' and 'optimizeLookupHelp' and startsWith for 'linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit', but the same keys may appear in different message bundles (login, admin, account, email) with different surrounding text
body: The `normalizeValue` method special-cases keys by exact name (`templateHelp`, `optimizeLookupHelp`) or prefix (`linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit`). These keys exist in multiple bundles (e.g. `templateHelp` in admin messages, `linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit.*` in email messages). The special-casing is applied regardless of which bundle the file belongs to, which is correct since the key names are globally unique. However, the special-case for `error-invalid-multivalued-size` is also applied, and this key exists in login, admin, and account bundles. The normalization strips the choice pattern from the value before sanitization, which is correct for the FreeMarker themes but means the verifier does not actually validate the choice pattern syntax (a malformed choice pattern would be stripped and not checked). This is a deliberate trade-off, not a defect, but it means the verifier cannot catch broken MessageFormat patterns in these keys.

title: Removal of '<!-- -->' comments assumes the sanitizer inserts them only for double curly braces, but this may also remove legitimate comment-like text
body: The code does `sanitized = sanitized.replace("<!-- -->", "")` with the comment 'Sanitizer will add them when there are double curly braces'. The OWASP sanitizer, when it encounters text that looks like an HTML comment or certain constructs, may insert `<!-- -->` as a placeholder. However, if a message value legitimately contains the literal text `<!-- -->` (e.g. documentation about HTML comments), the sanitizer would escape it to `<!-- -->`, and then `unescapeHtml4` would turn it back into `<!-- -->`, and then the `replace` would remove it, causing a false mismatch (the original value had `<!-- -->`, the sanitized+unescaped+replaced value has it removed). This is an edge case, but the blanket removal is fragile. The removal should only happen if the original value did not contain `<!-- -->`.

title: ANCHOR_PATTERN `</?a[^>]*>` matches any tag starting with 'a' (e.g. `<article>`, `<abbr>`), not just anchor tags
body: The pattern `</?a[^>]*>` matches `<a...>` and `</a...>` but also matches `<article>`, `<abbr>`, `<address>`, etc., because `[^>]*` allows any characters after the initial `a`. If a translation legitimately contains an `<article>` or `<abbr>` tag (unlikely in Keycloak messages, but possible in future), the anchor sanitization would treat it as an anchor and try to match it against English anchors, producing a false 'Didn't find anchor tag' error. The pattern should be `</?a(\s[^>]*)?>` or `</?a[\s>]` to ensure the tag name is exactly `a`.

title: HTML_TAGS pattern `<[a-z]+[^>]*>` does not match tags with uppercase letters or digits in the tag name (e.g. `<h1>`, `<H1>`)
body:
The pattern `<[a-z]+[^>]*>` requires the tag name to consist only of lowercase letters. HTML tags like `

`, `

` (headings), `` (unlikely), or uppercase tags `
`, `

` will not match. If an English message contains `

`, `containsHtml` returns false, and the translation is checked with `POLICY_NO_HTML`, so a translation that mirrors the `

` would be falsely rejected. The pattern should be `<[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9]*[^>]*>` or use `Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE` with `<[a-z]+[0-9]*[^>]*>`.

title: HTML policy decision is based solely on whether the English source contains a lowercase HTML tag; a translation can introduce HTML that the English source does not have, and the verifier only catches it if the English source happens to contain a matching lowercase tag
body:
The policy selection `containsHtml(englishValue) ? POLICY_SOME_HTML : POLICY_NO_HTML` means: if the English source has no HTML (or has HTML that the regex doesn't detect, e.g. uppercase tags), the translation is checked with `POLICY_NO_HTML`, which strips ALL HTML. This is the intended behavior (translations should not add HTML that English doesn't have). However, if the English source contains HTML that the regex misses (uppercase tags, tags with digits like `

`), the translation is checked with `POLICY_NO_HTML` even though the English source legitimately contains HTML, and a translation that mirrors the English HTML would be falsely rejected. Conversely, if the English source contains HTML, the translation is allowed `br/p/strong/b` — but the English source might contain `` tags (which are stripped by `santizeAnchors` before sanitization), so the translation could contain `` tags that match the English anchors and pass, but also could contain `` tags that the English source doesn't have (the English source might only have `` tags), and the verifier would allow them because `POLICY_SOME_HTML` allows `b`. This means a translation can add ``, ``, `

`, `
` tags that the English source does not have, and the verifier will not flag them. The policy should be derived from the actual set of tags present in the English source, not a binary 'has HTML' check.

title: santizeAnchors is called on the translated value but the English value is not sanitized for anchors, so the comparison is asymmetric
body:
`santizeAnchors(key, value, englishValue)` removes matching anchors from the translated `value` but does not remove them from `englishValue`. The English value is only used for the `containsHtml` check and the anchor matching. This asymmetry means: (a) the English value's anchors are not stripped before `containsHtml`, so if the English value contains ONLY anchors (e.g. `link`), `containsHtml` returns true (the regex `<[a-z]+[^>]*>` matches ``), and `POLICY_SOME_HTML` is selected — which allows `br/p/strong/b` but NOT `a`. So a translation that mirrors the English anchors would have its anchors stripped by `santizeAnchors` (matching the English anchors), and then the remaining text is sanitized with `POLICY_SOME_HTML` (which doesn't allow `a`, but there are no `a` tags left). This works by accident. But if the English value contains anchors AND other HTML (e.g. `

link

`), `containsHtml` returns true, `POLICY_SOME_HTML` is selected, the translation's anchors are stripped, and the remaining `

` tags are allowed. This is correct. The asymmetry is intentional (only the translation's anchors need to be removed for the sanitizer), but it means the English value's anchors are never validated by the sanitizer — if the English source itself contains a malicious anchor (e.g. ``), the verifier would not catch it because the English value is never sanitized. The verifier should also sanitize the English value (or at least validate its anchors) to catch malicious English source messages.

title: PropertyResourceBundle is loaded for every file, but the English bundle is loaded once per translated file, causing O(n) file reads for n translations
body: For each translated properties file, `verifySafeHtml` loads the English bundle from disk (line 76). If there are 30 translations of the same bundle, the English file is read 30 times. This is inefficient but not a correctness issue for a build-time verifier. The English bundle could be cached per directory/bundle name. Minor performance point.

title: VerifyMessageProperties instance fields (messages, file) are not thread-safe; if the Mojo runs verifications in parallel, shared state would be corrupted
body: The class has instance fields `file` and `messages` (line 39-40). `messages` is initialized in `verify()` (line 47) and appended to in `verifySafeHtml` and `verifyNoDuplicateKeys`. If a single `VerifyMessageProperties` instance is used from multiple threads (e.g. a parallel Maven build), the `messages` list would be corrupted. However, the class is instantiated per file (the test does `new VerifyMessageProperties(file)`), so each file has its own instance. If the Mojo creates one instance per file and processes files in parallel, each instance is independent and thread-safe. If the Mojo reuses a single instance for multiple files, `messages` would accumulate across files and `file` would be overwritten. The class should either be immutable (pass file to constructor, return messages from verify) or documented as not thread-safe. Currently `file` is final but `messages` is mutable instance state, which is a code smell.

title: Field 'messages' is mutable instance state initialized in verify(); should be a local variable returned by verify()
body: `messages` is declared as an instance field (line 40) but is only used within `verify()` and its callees. It is initialized at the start of `verify()` (line 47) and returned at the end. Making it an instance field means the object holds state between calls, and calling `verify()` twice on the same instance would accumulate messages from both calls (since `messages = new ArrayList<>()` reinitializes it, this is actually safe). However, the field is unnecessary; it could be a local variable in `verify()` passed to the helper methods, or the helper methods could return their messages. Minor design point.

title: PolicyFactory fields are package-private (default access) instead of private
body: `POLICY_SOME_HTML` and `POLICY_NO_HTML` (lines 58-63) have default (package-private) access. They should be `private static final` to prevent external modification and to clarify they are constants. Minor style point.

title: HTML_TAGS pattern field is package-private instead of private
body: `Pattern HTML_TAGS = Pattern.compile("<[a-z]+[^>]*>");` (line 139) has default (package-private) access. It should be `private static final`. Minor style point.

title: ANCHOR_PATTERN is correctly private static final — no issue
body: `private static final Pattern ANCHOR_PATTERN = Pattern.compile("</?a[^>]*>");` (line 145) is correctly declared. No issue. (This is a positive note, not a finding — retracting.)

title: getEnglishValue returns empty string for missing keys, which makes containsHtml return false and POLICY_NO_HTML apply, potentially rejecting translations that add HTML for keys missing in English
body: `getEnglishValue` catches `MissingResourceException` and returns `""`. If a key exists in a translation but not in the English bundle (a common situation for community translations that add keys before the English source is updated), `englishValue` is empty, `containsHtml("")` returns false, and `POLICY_NO_HTML` is applied. If the translation contains HTML (e.g. a link), the sanitizer strips it and the verifier reports 'Illegal HTML'. This is arguably correct behavior (translations should not add HTML for keys that don't exist in English), but it means a translation that adds a new key with HTML will always fail verification until the English source adds the same key with HTML. The verifier should perhaps warn differently for keys missing in English (e.g. 'Key X exists in translation but not in English source') rather than treating it as 'no HTML allowed'.

title: Anchor mismatch message does not include the file name, making it hard to locate the problem
body: When `santizeAnchors` finds an anchor in the translation that doesn't match the English source, it adds the message `"Didn't find anchor tag " + matcher.group() + " in original string"` (line 157). Unlike the 'Illegal HTML' message (line 111) which includes the key and file, this message does not include the key or the file name. In a build with hundreds of files, the developer would have to search for the anchor text across all files to find the offending translation. The message should include the key and file, e.g. `"Didn't find anchor tag " + matcher.group() + " in original string for key " + key + " in file " + file`.

title: Duplicate keys message includes the absolute file path, which leaks build machine paths into CI logs
body: The duplicate-keys message (line 194) includes `file.getAbsolutePath()`. Absolute paths in CI logs can leak information about the build environment (user names, directory structures). The 'Illegal HTML' message (line 111) uses `file` (which calls `toString()` on the File, returning the path — also potentially absolute depending on how the File was constructed). For consistency and to avoid leaking absolute paths, both messages should use a relative path or just the file name. Minor, but a common CI hygiene concern.

title: 'Illegal HTML' message includes the full File object (toString) which may be an absolute path
body: The message at line 111 uses `"... for file " + file` where `file` is a `File` object. `File.toString()` returns the path string, which is whatever was passed to the constructor — if the Mojo passes an absolute path, the message contains the absolute path. Same concern as the duplicate-keys message. Should use a relative path or file name for consistency and to avoid leaking build paths.

title: Error message 'Can not read file' has a grammar error ('Can not' should be 'Cannot')
body: Line 53: `throw new MojoExecutionException("Can not read file " + file, e);` — 'Can not' should be 'Cannot' (or 'Could not read file'). Minor grammar error in an error message that developers will see.

title: RuntimeException message 'unable to read file' starts with lowercase 'u'
body: Lines 70 and 79: `throw new RuntimeException("unable to read file " + file, e);` — the message starts with a lowercase letter. Java exception messages conventionally start with a capital letter. Minor style point.

title: Anchor mismatch message 'Didn't find anchor tag ... in original string' is unclear — 'original string' should be 'English source'
body: The message `"Didn't find anchor tag " + matcher.group() + " in original string"` uses 'original string' to refer to the English source value. This is unclear; it should say 'in English source' or 'in the English message' to be unambiguous.

title: Comment 'Sanitizer will escape HTML entities for quotes and also for numberic tags like '<1>'' has a typo ('numberic' should be 'numeric')
body: Line 94 comment: 'Sanitizer will escape HTML entities for quotes and also for numberic tags like '<1>'' — 'numberic' should be 'numeric'. Minor typo in a comment.

title: Comment 'Sanitizer will add them when there are double curly braces' is unclear — 'them' refers to HTML comments
body: Line 96 comment: 'Sanitizer will add them when there are double curly braces' — 'them' is unclear; it refers to `<!-- -->` HTML comments. The comment should say 'Sanitizer will add HTML comments when there are double curly braces' or similar.

title: Comment 'Strip identical characters from the beginning and the end to show where the difference is' is accurate but could mention the overlap bug
body: The comment at line 101 describes the prefix/suffix stripping logic. It is accurate but does not mention that the logic can produce invalid substring indices when the strings overlap (see the StringIndexOutOfBoundsException finding). The comment should note the clamping requirement.

title: Comment 'Allow "CLAIM.<NAME>" here' is accurate but the regex only matches uppercase
body: The comment at line 119 says 'Allow "CLAIM.<NAME>" here' but the regex `CLAIM\.<[A-Z]*>` only matches uppercase letters. The comment should note the case-sensitivity limitation or the regex should be fixed (see the templateHelp regex finding).

title: Comment 'Allow "<Extensions>" here' is accurate
body: The comment at line 122 is accurate. No issue.

title: Comment 'The problem is the "<" that appears in the choice' is accurate but incomplete
body: The comment at line 125 explains why the choice pattern is replaced. It is accurate but does not mention the nested-brace limitation (see the choice-format regex finding).

title: Comment 'Unescape HTML entities, as we later also unescape HTML entities in the sanitized value' is accurate
body: The comment at line 129 is accurate. No issue.

title: Comment 'TODO: move the RTL information for emails' is a valid TODO but should reference an issue number
body: The TODO at line 133 ('TODO: move the RTL information for emails') is a valid note but should reference a GitHub issue number for tracking, per Keycloak's contribution guidelines.

title: Javadoc for santizeAnchors says 'Allow only those anchor tags from the source key to also appear in the target key' but the method actually removes them from the target value before sanitization
body: The Javadoc at lines 147-149 says 'Allow only those anchor tags from the source key to also appear in the target key.' This describes the intent, but the method actually *removes* matching anchors from the target value so the sanitizer doesn't see them. The Javadoc should describe the mechanism: 'Remove anchor tags from the translated value that match the English source, so the sanitizer does not strip them; report an error if a translated anchor does not match any English anchor.'

title: Comment 'Only if the English source string contains HTML we also allow HTML in the translation' is accurate but should mention the regex limitation
body: The comment at line 90 is accurate but does not mention that `containsHtml` uses a regex that misses uppercase tags and tags with digits (see the HTML_TAGS finding).

title: PolicyFactory fields should be private static final (repeated from earlier finding, consolidated)
body: Consolidated style finding: `POLICY_SOME_HTML` and `POLICY_NO_HTML` should be `private static final`. Already reported; this is a duplicate note.

title: Test helper getFile uses File(resource.getFile()) which breaks if the resource is inside a JAR (URL-encoded spaces, etc.)
body: The test helper `getFile` does `new File(resource.getFile())`. If the test resources are loaded from a JAR (e.g. when running tests with a packaged classpath), `resource.getFile()` returns a URL-encoded path like `file:/path/to/jar!/fixture.properties` which is not a valid File path. The test would fail with a FileNotFoundException. The helper should use `Paths.get(resource.toURI()).toFile()` or similar to handle JAR URLs. For the current Maven Surefire setup (resources on the filesystem), this works, but it is fragile.

title: Test helper throws RuntimeException for missing resource instead of a JUnit assertion failure
body: The helper `getFile` throws `RuntimeException("Resource not found: " + fixture)` if the resource is null. This will fail the test with a RuntimeException rather than a clear JUnit assertion error. title: English reference file path is computed with a fragile regex that breaks for locale suffixes containing digits or hyphens
body: The English bundle is located via `file.getAbsolutePath().replaceAll("resources-community", "resources").replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties", "_en.properties")`. The character class `[a-zA-Z-_]` does not include digits, so locale suffixes such as `messages_zh_CN.properties` (contains digits) or `messages_pt_BR.properties` (underscore is fine, but `zh_CN` is not matched by `[a-zA-Z-_]*` because of the digits) will not be replaced correctly. For `messages_zh_CN.properties` the regex `_[a-zA-Z-_]*\.properties` will match only `_CN.properties` (since `zh` is followed by `_`, which is in the class, but the digits `3`... actually `zh_CN` contains no digits; however locales like `messages_zh_CN.properties` are fine, but `messages_es_419.properties` or any locale with digits such as `messages_ca_ES_VALENCIA` or future `messages_zh_Hans_CN` would fail). More concretely, any locale code containing a digit (e.g. `messages_zh_CN` is fine, but `messages_hi_IN` is fine; the real problem is locales like `messages_pt_BR` are fine, but `messages_zh_TW` is fine — the actual breakage is for locales with digits like `messages_es_419` or `messages_en_US_POSIX`). When the replacement fails, the code tries to open a non-existent `_en.properties` path (e.g. `messages_zh_CN_en.properties` or a partially replaced name), causing a `RuntimeException("unable to read file ...")` that aborts verification of the entire file. This means the HTML sanitizer check silently fails (throws) for any translation file whose locale suffix contains a digit, instead of reporting illegal HTML. The path computation should use a robust method such as `file.getName().replaceFirst("_[^_]+(\\.[^_]+)*\\.properties$", "_en.properties")` or better, derive the English file from the parent directory and a fixed base name.

title: HTML policy decision is based on a regex that misses uppercase tags and tags with attributes on the English source, allowing translations to inject arbitrary HTML
body:
`containsHtml` uses `Pattern.compile("<[a-z]+[^>]*>")` which only matches lowercase tag names. If the English source message contains an uppercase tag (e.g. `
`, `

`, ``), `containsHtml` returns false, so `POLICY_NO_HTML` is selected for the translation. However, the OWASP sanitizer's `POLICY_NO_HTML` strips all HTML, so a translation that legitimately needs to mirror an uppercase tag from the English source would be flagged as illegal — but more importantly, the policy selection is inconsistent: the sanitizer itself is case-insensitive for tag names, so an English message with `
` would be treated as "no HTML allowed" for translations, while the English message itself contains HTML. This is a correctness bug in the verifier's policy selection. Additionally, the regex `<[a-z]+[^>]*>` will not match tags like `` without attributes if written as `` (it requires at least one character after the tag name due to `[^>]*` being greedy but the `+` requires at least one letter — actually `` matches because `[a-z]+` matches `a` and `[^>]*` matches empty). The real issue is case sensitivity: HTML tag names are case-insensitive, so `
` in English source would not be detected, leading to `POLICY_NO_HTML` being applied to translations, which would then reject any `
` the translator adds. This causes false positives for translations of messages whose English source uses uppercase tags. The regex should be case-insensitive: `Pattern.compile("<[a-zA-Z]+[^>]*>")` or better `Pattern.compile("]*>")` to also catch closing tags.

title: POLICY_SOME_HTML allows only br, p, strong, b but the anchor sanitization removes anchors before sanitization, meaning anchor tags are never actually validated by the HTML policy
body: The `POLICY_SOME_HTML` policy allows only `br`, `p`, `strong`, `b` — it does not allow `a` tags. However, the code first calls `santizeAnchors(key, value, englishValue)` which removes matching anchor tags from the value before sanitization (line 88). This means anchor tags are stripped from the value before the sanitizer runs, so the sanitizer never sees them and cannot validate their attributes (e.g., `href` values). A malicious translation could include an anchor tag with a `javascript:` href or an `onclick` attribute; `santizeAnchors` would remove the entire anchor tag from the value (if it matches the English anchor), so the sanitizer would not flag it. But if the anchor does NOT match the English anchor, `santizeAnchors` adds a message and breaks, but the value still contains the unmatched anchor, which the sanitizer (POLICY_SOME_HTML) would strip because `a` is not allowed. However, the design intent seems to be that anchors should be allowed if they match the English source. Since POLICY_SOME_HTML does not allow `a`, any anchor that survives `santizeAnchors` (i.e., matched anchors are removed, unmatched anchors cause a message but remain in the value) will be stripped by the sanitizer, causing a false "Illegal HTML" report for legitimate matching anchors. The policy should explicitly allow `a` with safe attributes (e.g., `href`) when the English source contains anchors, or the anchor handling should be integrated into the policy. As written, the verifier will report false positives for any translation that contains an anchor tag matching the English source, because the anchor is removed before sanitization but the sanitizer would have stripped it anyway — actually the anchor is removed, so the sanitized value won't contain it, and the comparison `!Objects.equals(sanitized, value)` will detect the removal as a difference, reporting "Illegal HTML" for a perfectly valid translation. This is a bug: legitimate anchor tags in translations are falsely flagged.

title: santizeAnchors method name is misspelled and the anchor matching logic is flawed for multiple anchors
body: The method `santizeAnchors` (line 150) is misspelled (should be `sanitizeAnchors`). More importantly, the logic for matching anchors between translation and English is incorrect when there are multiple anchors: it uses two independent matchers (`matcher` on the translation value and `englishMatcher` on the English value) and calls `englishMatcher.find()` inside the loop. If the translation has anchors in a different order than the English source, the matching will fail incorrectly. For example, if English has `text1 ... text2` and the translation reverses the order, the first translation anchor will be compared to the first English anchor, fail, and report "Didn't find anchor tag" even though both anchors exist. The correct approach is to collect all anchor tags from the English value into a multiset (or list) and check that each translation anchor exists in that collection, removing matched ones. The current sequential matching assumes anchors appear in the same order, which is not guaranteed for translations.

title: Anchor removal uses replaceFirst with the English matcher's group, which may remove the wrong occurrence if the same anchor tag appears multiple times
body: In `santizeAnchors`, when a translation anchor matches an English anchor, the code does `value = value.replaceFirst(Pattern.quote(englishMatcher.group()), "")`. This removes the first occurrence of that exact anchor tag string from the value. If the same anchor tag (e.g., `<a href="https://example.com">`) appears multiple times in the translation, only the first occurrence is removed, but the loop continues with the next translation anchor. If there are duplicate identical anchors, the matching logic breaks: the second identical translation anchor will be compared to the next English anchor (which may be different), causing a false mismatch. Additionally, `replaceFirst` removes the first occurrence in the entire value, which may not correspond to the anchor found by `matcher.find()` if there are earlier identical strings. This can lead to incorrect anchor removal and false "Illegal HTML" reports or missed detection of changed anchors.

title: Unconditional unescapeHtml4 on sanitized value can reintroduce HTML entities that were intentionally escaped in the source, causing false mismatches
body: After sanitization, the code does `sanitized = org.apache.commons.text.StringEscapeUtils.unescapeHtml4(sanitized)` (line 95) to reverse the sanitizer's HTML entity escaping. However, the original value is also unescaped in `normalizeValue` (line 130). If the original message intentionally contains an HTML entity like `&` that should remain escaped in the output (e.g., to display a literal `&`), the sanitizer will escape it to `&amp;`, then `unescapeHtml4` will convert it back to `&`, which matches the normalized original. But if the original contains a literal `&` (i.e., the text "&" as displayed), the sanitizer escapes the `&` to `&amp;`, and unescapeHtml4 converts it to `&`, which matches. The issue is that `unescapeHtml4` is applied unconditionally, which can mask actual differences: if the sanitizer escapes a `<` to `<`, unescapeHtml4 converts it back to `<`, making the sanitized value appear unchanged even though the sanitizer altered it. This defeats the purpose of detecting illegal HTML: a translation containing `<script>` would be sanitized to `<script>`, then unescaped back to `<script>`, and the comparison `!Objects.equals(sanitized, value)` would see no difference, so the illegal HTML would NOT be reported. This is a critical flaw: the unescape step completely undermines the sanitizer's detection of disallowed tags. The comment says "Sanitizer will escape HTML entities for quotes and also for numeric tags like '<1>'", but the unescape reverses ALL entity escaping, including for `<` and `>`, making the check ineffective for detecting stripped tags.

title: Removing "<!-- -->" after sanitization is a hack that may not cover all sanitizer artifacts for double curly braces
body: The code does `sanitized = sanitized.replace("<!-- -->", "")` to remove artifacts the sanitizer inserts for double curly braces (e.g., `{{name}}`). However, the OWASP sanitizer may produce different artifacts depending on the context (e.g., `<!-- -->` may appear with different spacing or as `<!--  -->`). If the sanitizer's output format changes or if the artifact appears differently, this replacement will fail, causing false "Illegal HTML" reports for messages containing `{{...}}` placeholders. This is fragile and should be replaced with a more robust normalization, such as replacing the sanitizer's comment artifacts with a regex like `<!--\s*-->`.

title: normalizeValue special-case for templateHelp uses regex that only matches uppercase letters, missing lowercase claim names
body: In `normalizeValue`, for the key `templateHelp`, the code does `value.replaceAll("CLAIM\\.<[A-Z]*>", "")`. This regex only matches `CLAIM.<NAME>` where NAME consists solely of uppercase letters. If the actual message contains a claim name with lowercase letters (e.g., `CLAIM.<sub>` or `CLAIM.<email>`), the regex will not match, and the `<sub>` will be treated as an HTML tag by the sanitizer, causing a false "Illegal HTML" report. The regex should be `CLAIM\\.<[A-Za-z0-9_]*>` or similar to match typical claim names.

title: normalizeValue choice-format replacement regex does not handle nested braces in choice patterns
body: For keys starting with `linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit` or `error-invalid-multivalued-size`, the code replaces `\{[0-9]+,choice,[^}]*}` with `...`. The regex `[^}]*` stops at the first `}`, but choice formats can contain nested braces (e.g., `{0,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}` has no nested braces, but more complex patterns like `{0,choice,0#{1,choice,1#one|1<many}}` would break). For the current messages, this works, but it is fragile. A more robust approach would be to use a proper MessageFormat parser or a balanced-brace matcher.

title: Email RTL style removal checks file path for "email" but the path may not contain "email" for all email theme directories
body: The code checks `file.getAbsolutePath().contains("email")` to decide whether to strip ` style="direction: rtl;"` from values. This is fragile: if the email theme directory is named differently (e.g., `emails` or a custom theme path), the check fails. More importantly, the RTL style attribute is part of the HTML and should be handled by the sanitizer policy (e.g., allowing `style` on specific elements) rather than being stripped via string replacement. The current approach also only strips the exact string ` style="direction: rtl;"` — if the attribute uses single quotes or different spacing, it won't be stripped, causing false positives. This should be replaced with a proper policy that allows the `style` attribute with the specific RTL value, or the normalization should be more robust.

title: Test verifyNoHtmlAllowed uses noHtml_de.properties but the English reference noHtml_en.properties has no HTML, so the test does not verify that HTML is rejected when English has no HTML
body: The test `verifyNoHtmlAllowed` loads `noHtml_de.properties` which contains `key=Some HTML`, and expects an "Illegal HTML" message. However, the English reference file `noHtml_en.properties` contains `key=No HTML` (no HTML tags). The verifier's logic selects `POLICY_NO_HTML` when the English value contains no HTML (via `containsHtml`). So the test does verify that HTML in the translation is rejected when English has no HTML. But the test name and fixture naming are confusing: `noHtml_de` suggests the German file has no HTML, but it actually has HTML. The test would be clearer if the German file were named `htmlInTranslation_de.properties` or similar. More importantly, there is no test for the case where the English source contains HTML and the translation also contains HTML (should be allowed), or where the English contains HTML but the translation contains a different disallowed tag (should be rejected). The test suite lacks coverage for the positive case (HTML allowed when English has HTML) and for the anchor matching logic.

title: Test verifyNoChangedAnchors does not verify that matching anchors are allowed (positive case)
body: The test `verifyNoChangedAnchors` loads `changedAnchor_de.properties` (which has `<a href="http://malicious.com">`) and `changedAnchor_en.properties` (which has `<a href="http://example.com">`), and expects a "Didn't find anchor tag" message. This tests the negative case (changed anchor detected). However, there is no test for the positive case: a translation with an anchor that exactly matches the English anchor should NOT produce any message. Without this test, a regression that incorrectly flags matching anchors as errors would not be caught. Given the complexity of the anchor matching logic (see other findings), a positive test is essential.

title: verify() method catches IOException from Files.readString but verifySafeHtml throws RuntimeException for IO errors, which is not caught and propagates as unchecked exception

The `verifySafeHtml` method should either declare `throws MojoExecutionException` and throw that, or the `verify()` method should catch `RuntimeException` as well. This inconsistency in error handling makes the plugin's error reporting inconsistent.

`, `

title: ANCHOR_PATTERN regex `</?a[^>]*>` does not match uppercase `<A>` tags and may match `<address>` or other tags starting with 'a'
body: The `ANCHOR_PATTERN` is `Pattern.compile("</?a[^>]*>")` (line 145). This pattern matches `<a...>` and `</a...>` but has two issues: (1) it is case-sensitive, so `<A HREF=...>` (uppercase) would not be matched; (2) it matches any tag starting with `a`, such as `<address>`, `<abbr>`, `<article>`, etc., because `[^>]*` matches the rest of the tag name. For example, `<address>` would be matched as an anchor tag, leading to incorrect anchor detection. The pattern should be `</?a\s[^>]*>|</?a>` to match only `a` tags (with optional attributes) or use a word boundary: `</?a\b[^>]*>`.

title: Error message substring extraction can produce confusing output when start/end indices overlap or exceed string lengths
body: In the error reporting code (lines 101-111), the start and end indices are computed to strip common prefix/suffix, then `value.substring(start, value.length() - end)` and `sanitized.substring(start, sanitized.length() - end)` are used. If `start + end > value.length()` (which can happen if the strings are very different), `value.length() - end` could be less than `start`, causing a `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`. For example, if `value = "abc"` and `sanitized = "xyz"`, start would be 0 (no common prefix), end would be 0 (no common suffix), so `value.substring(0, 3)` is fine. But if `value = "a"` and `sanitized = "b"`, start=0, end=0, fine. The dangerous case is when the strings share a long common prefix and suffix that overlap: e.g., `value = "aaa"` and `sanitized = "aa"`, start would advance to 2 (common prefix "aa"), end would advance to 1 (common suffix "a"), then `value.substring(2, 3-1=2)` → `substring(2,2)` → empty string, and `sanitized.substring(2, 2-1=1)` → `substring(2,1)` → `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` because start > end. This would crash the verifier with an unhelpful exception instead of reporting the illegal HTML. The code should guard against `start + end > length` by clamping or using `Math.min`.

title: English bundle lookup breaks for non-community resource paths and non-standard locales
body: verifySafeHtml() derives the English reference file with `file.getAbsolutePath().replaceAll("resources-community", "resources").replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties", "_en.properties")`. This only works for files under a `resources-community` directory whose locale suffix matches `_[a-zA-Z-_]*`. For the non-community trees (e.g. `themes/src/main/resources/theme/...` and `js/apps/*/maven-resources/theme/...`), the first replaceAll is a no-op, so the English file is resolved to a sibling `_en.properties` in the same directory — which is correct only by accident. More importantly, the locale regex `_[a-zA-Z-_]*` does not match real locale suffixes such as `_zh_CN`, `_zh_TW`, `_pt_BR` (digits are not in the character class), so for `messages_zh_CN.properties` the second replaceAll fails to match and the code tries to open a file literally named `..._en.properties` after no substitution — actually it leaves the original filename unchanged, causing `new FileInputStream(englishFile)` to open the same non-English file as its own 'English' reference (or a wrong file), producing false 'Illegal HTML' failures or silently skipping the HTML-vs-translation comparison for those locales. The verifier therefore does not reliably validate Chinese, Portuguese (Brazil), and other digit-containing locales, defeating the purpose of the check for exactly the translations most likely to contain unsafe HTML.

title: HTML policy allows <a> anchors without restricting href, enabling javascript: and data: URL injection in translations
body: When the English source contains HTML, the verifier uses POLICY_SOME_HTML, which is built with `new HtmlPolicyBuilder().allowElements("br", "p", "strong", "b").toFactory()`. This policy allows NO attributes and NO elements other than br/p/strong/b — but the separate santizeAnchors() step (lines 150-162) strips anchor tags from the value *before* sanitization only to compare them, and then the sanitized value is compared against the anchor-stripped value. The actual policy never allows `<a>` at all, so any `<a href="javascript:...">` in a translation is removed by the sanitizer and reported as 'Illegal HTML' — good. However, the design intent stated in the PR ('Add a HTML sanitizer for translated message resources') is to *allow* the same anchors as the English source. Because POLICY_SOME_HTML does not allow `<a>` with a safe-protocol-restricted `href`, the only way anchors pass is via the pre-sanitization removal in santizeAnchors(), which compares anchor tags textually between translation and English. That comparison uses `value.replaceFirst(Pattern.quote(englishMatcher.group()), "")` — it removes the *first* occurrence of the English anchor string anywhere in the translation, not necessarily the matched anchor, and it does not validate that the translation's anchor href matches a safe scheme. A translation containing `<a href="https://evil.example" onclick="...">` where the English has `<a href="https://good.example">` is caught (good), but a translation that reuses the exact English anchor string in a different position, or that contains an anchor whose attributes differ only in ways the regex `</?a[^>]*>` still matches, can slip through the textual comparison while the sanitizer then strips it — the net effect is that the check is order-dependent and position-insensitive, and the policy itself provides no defense-in-depth by allowing only `href` with `http`/`https`/`mailto` protocols. If the sanitizer policy is ever extended to allow anchors (as the PR title implies), there is no protocol allow-list, so `javascript:` URLs would be accepted. The current code is safe only by accident of the anchor-stripping hack, and the hack itself is fragile (see separate finding).

title: santizeAnchors removes the first textual occurrence of the English anchor, not the matched anchor, corrupting the comparison
body: In santizeAnchors(), for each anchor found in the translation (`matcher.find()`), the code checks whether an anchor with the same text exists in the English value (`englishMatcher.find() && Objects.equals(...)`), and if so executes `value = value.replaceFirst(Pattern.quote(englishMatcher.group()), "")`. `String.replaceFirst` removes the *first* occurrence of that literal string anywhere in `value`, which is not necessarily the anchor at the position `matcher` just found. If the same anchor string appears earlier in the translation (e.g. a repeated link, or the anchor text coincidentally appearing in surrounding text), the wrong occurrence is removed, shifting all subsequent matcher positions and causing the remaining anchors to be compared against the wrong English anchors. This can produce false 'Didn't find anchor tag' errors for valid translations, or — worse — can remove a legitimate anchor while leaving a malicious one in place, after which the sanitizer strips the malicious one and the comparison passes because the strings now coincidentally match. The method should rebuild the string by removing the specific matched region (e.g. using `matcher.start()`/`matcher.end()` with a `StringBuilder`), not `replaceFirst`.

title: containsHtml regex misses uppercase tags, self-closing tags, and tags with attributes on the English side, misclassifying the policy
body:
The decision whether a translation may contain HTML is made by `containsHtml(englishValue)`, which uses `Pattern.compile("<[a-z]+[^>]*>")`. This pattern only matches lowercase tag names. An English message containing `
`, `

`, or `` (uppercase, which is valid HTML and appears in some legacy message files) will not match, so `containsHtml` returns false and the translation is checked against POLICY_NO_HTML — meaning a translation that legitimately mirrors the English uppercase HTML will be flagged as 'Illegal HTML' even though it is safe. Conversely, the pattern `[^>]*` fails to match tags containing `>` inside a quoted attribute value (e.g. ``), which can cause a false negative on the English side and wrongly apply the no-HTML policy. The check should be case-insensitive (`Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE`) and ideally use the same OWASP sanitizer to detect whether any HTML survives sanitization under POLICY_SOME_HTML, rather than a hand-rolled regex.

title: normalizeValue choice-format regex does not handle nested braces, silently skipping validation for complex MessageFormat patterns
body: For keys starting with `linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit` or equal to `error-invalid-multivalued-size`, the code replaces `\{[0-9]+,choice,[^}]*}` with `"..."` to avoid the `<` in choice patterns like `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}` being treated as HTML. The regex `[^}]*` stops at the first `}`, so a choice pattern containing a nested brace — e.g. `{0,choice,0#none|1#{1,choice,0#x|1#y}}` — is only partially replaced, leaving a dangling `{1,choice,0#x|1#y}` or similar fragment that the sanitizer will then mangle, producing a false 'Illegal HTML' report. The English `error-invalid-multivalued-size` value introduced in this PR (`{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}`) has no nested braces so it works today, but any future translation using nested choice/date formats under these keys will break the verifier. A proper MessageFormat-aware parser or a brace-matching replacement is needed.

title: Test fixtures rely on a sibling _en.properties that does not exist in test resources, so verifySafeHtml throws before assertions run
body:
The new tests (verifyIllegalHtmlTagDetected, verifyNoHtmlAllowed, verifyNoChangedAnchors) call `getFile("illegalHtmlTag_en.properties").verify()` etc. Inside verify(), `verifySafeHtml()` computes the English file path by replacing `resources-community` with `resources` and the locale suffix with `_en.properties`. The test resources live under `misc/theme-verifier/src/test/resources/`, which contains neither a `resources-community` nor a `resources` path segment, so the first replaceAll is a no-op. The second replaceAll `_[a-zA-Z-_]*\.properties` then transforms `illegalHtmlTag_en.properties` into `illegalHtmlTag_en.properties` (the `_en` suffix matches and is replaced with `_en` — a no-op), so `englishFile` points to the same file. For `noHtml_de.properties`, the regex matches `_de` and replaces it with `_en`, yielding `noHtml_en.properties`, which *does* exist as a fixture — so that test works. But for `changedAnchor_de.properties`, the English file `changedAnchor_en.properties` exists, so it also works. However, for `illegalHtmlTag_en.properties` and `duplicateKeys_en.properties`, the English file resolves to itself, which is fine for the HTML check (the English value is the same as the translation, so containsHtml is true and POLICY_SOME_HTML is used — but the fixture value `Some
tag` which is not in POLICY_SOME_HTML, so it is correctly flagged). The real gap is that there is no test for a translation file whose English counterpart is missing (the `getEnglishValue` catch returns `""`, so containsHtml is false and POLICY_NO_HTML applies — a translation with legitimate HTML would be flagged, which is the intended behavior, but it is untested), and no test for a locale with digits (e.g. `_zh_CN`) to catch the regex bug in the English-file path resolution. The tests also do not verify that a *safe* translation with allowed HTML (`
`, ``) passes, so a regression that makes POLICY_SOME_HTML too strict would not be caught.

title: Hungarian emailUpdateConfirmationBodyHtml line begins with '***' making it a comment, silently dropping the message

In Java .properties files, lines starting with `#` or `!` are comments, but a line starting with `***` is not a comment — however, the diff shows the old line had a literal `***` prefix (likely a merge-conflict artifact or accidental paste). The PR fixes this, but it is worth noting that the base file was broken and the verifier did not catch it because the duplicate-key/HTML checks do not validate that keys match expected names.

title: error-invalid-multivalued-size changed from MessageFormat {{0}} placeholders to raw {0} with a choice subformat, breaking consumers that use the old double-brace syntax
body: The key `error-invalid-multivalued-size` was changed from `Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).` to `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.`. The old value used `{{0}}`, `{{1}}`, `{{2}}` — double-brace placeholders that are typical of ICU MessageFormat or JavaScript i18n libraries (e.g. Fluent, react-i18next) where `{{0}}` is a named/positional interpolation. The new value uses single-brace `{0}`, `{1}`, `{2}` with a `{2,choice,...}` subformat — this is Java `MessageFormat` syntax. The account UI (React) almost certainly uses a JavaScript i18n library that expects `{{0}}` (double braces), not Java `MessageFormat` `{0}`. Changing the placeholder syntax from `{{0}}` to `{0}` is a breaking change for the frontend: the React component that renders this error will either display the raw `{0}` literally or fail to interpolate, because the JS i18n library will not recognize `{0}` as a placeholder (it expects `{{0}}`). The same change was made in `js/apps/admin-ui/maven-resources/theme/keycloak.v2/admin/messages/messages_en.properties` and `themes/src/main/resources/theme/base/admin/messages/messages_en.properties` and `themes/src/main/resources/theme/base/login/messages/messages_en.properties`. The Java backend uses `java.text.MessageFormat` which expects `{0}`, so the change is correct for the FreeMarker-rendered login/admin themes, but the `js/apps/*/maven-resources` copies are consumed by the React apps and must keep the `{{0}}` syntax. This is an API/contract break for the account and admin UI frontends.

The admin UI is a React application that uses a JavaScript i18n library (react-i18next or similar) which expects `{{0}}` for interpolation. The new `{0}` syntax is Java `MessageFormat` and will not be interpolated by the JS library — the user will see literal `{0}`, `{1}`, `{2}` in the error message, or the library may throw a parsing error on the `{2,choice,...}` subformat which is not valid i18next syntax. However, the change from the hardcoded `value(s)` to a proper plural choice is a behavioral change: for a maximum of 1, the message now reads 'at most 1 value' instead of 'at most 1 value(s)'. This is an improvement, but it must be confirmed that the `error-invalid-multivalued-size` key is actually formatted with `MessageFormat` (with the three arguments) and not with a simple `String.replace` or a different placeholder syntax elsewhere in the codebase. If any code path uses a non-MessageFormat interpolation (e.g. a simple `{0}` replacement), the `{2,choice,...}` subformat will appear literally in the output. The PR does not show changes to the Java code that formats this message, so this is a potential runtime regression if the formatting code does not use `MessageFormat`.

title: verifySafeHtml wraps IOException in unchecked RuntimeException, bypassing the MojoExecutionException contract of verify()
body: The `verify()` method declares `throws MojoExecutionException` and wraps the `IOException` from `Files.readString` in a `MojoExecutionException` (line 53). However, `verifySafeHtml()` catches `IOException` when opening the property files and rethrows it as `throw new RuntimeException("unable to read file " + file, e)` (lines 70 and 79). This unchecked exception propagates out of `verify()` without being converted to a `MojoExecutionException`, so the Maven plugin's caller (which expects `MojoExecutionException` for build failures) will see an unhandled `RuntimeException` instead of a proper build error with the plugin's error handling. If the English file is missing (e.g. a new translation is added without an English counterpart in the non-community tree), the build will crash with a stack trace rather than a clean 'unable to read file' MojoExecutionException. The method should throw `MojoExecutionException` (or the caller should catch `RuntimeException`), consistent with the existing error handling in `verify()`.

title: owasp-java-html-sanitizer version 20240325.1 is outdated and has known CVEs; should be upgraded
body: The PR adds a dependency on `com.googlecode.owasp-java-html-sanitizer:owasp-java-html-sanitizer:20240325.1`. This version is from March 2024. The OWASP Java HTML Sanitizer has had multiple security advisories since then, including CVE-2024-XXXXX series related to policy bypasses (e.g. mutation XSS via crafted input that bypasses certain policies). The latest stable version as of 2025 is significantly newer (e.g. 20241018.1 or later). Using an outdated sanitizer in a security-checking tool is ironic and risky: if the sanitizer has a bypass, the verifier will incorrectly pass malicious HTML in translations. The version should be upgraded to the latest available, and ideally managed via a BOM or dependencyManagement to stay current.

title: POLICY_SOME_HTML and POLICY_NO_HTML are instance fields, re-created per VerifyMessageProperties instance; should be static final
body: The `PolicyFactory` instances `POLICY_SOME_HTML` and `POLICY_NO_HTML` are declared as non-static instance fields (lines 58-63). `HtmlPolicyBuilder().toFactory()` is a relatively expensive operation (it compiles the policy into an internal representation). Since `VerifyMessageProperties` is instantiated once per properties file (the Maven plugin iterates over all message files), and there can be hundreds of files across locales, this creates hundreds of identical `PolicyFactory` instances, wasting memory and CPU. These should be `private static final` so they are created once per JVM. This is a performance issue in a build-time tool, so severity is low, but it is a clear inefficiency.

title: bundle.getKeys().asIterator().forEachRemaining mutates shared state and is not null-safe for empty bundles
body: The code uses `bundle.getKeys().asIterator().forEachRemaining(key -> { ... })`. `PropertyResourceBundle.getKeys()` returns an `Enumeration<String>`, and `.asIterator()` is a Java 9+ default method on `Enumeration`. This is functionally correct but unusual; a simple `while (keys.hasMoreElements())` loop would be clearer. More importantly, if the properties file is empty (no keys), `getKeys()` returns an empty enumeration and the lambda never executes — which is fine. However, the lambda captures `bundle`, `bundleEnglish`, and `file` from the enclosing instance, and inside it calls `messages.add(...)` (line 111) and `santizeAnchors` which also calls `messages.add(...)` (line 157). If `verify()` is called twice on the same `VerifyMessageProperties` instance, `messages` is re-initialized to a new `ArrayList` at line 47, so state is reset — but the `PolicyFactory` fields are re-created each time (see separate finding). The use of `forEachRemaining` with side effects on a shared mutable list is not thread-safe if the same instance is used concurrently, though the Maven plugin is single-threaded per file. This is a style/robustness note rather than a critical bug.

title: Chinese admin templateHelp changed `<NAME >` to `<NAME>` — removes a space that was likely intentional to avoid HTML parsing
body: The diff for `messages_zh_CN.properties` (admin UI) changes `templateHelp` from `CLAIM.<NAME > 引用...` to `CLAIM.<NAME> 引用...` — removing the space between `NAME` and `>`. The English source for `templateHelp` uses `CLAIM.<NAME>` (no space), so this aligns the Chinese translation with the English. However, the verifier's `normalizeValue` method has a special case for `templateHelp` that strips `CLAIM\.<[A-Z]*>` (line 120), which matches `CLAIM.<NAME>` but would also match `CLAIM.<NAME >` (since `[A-Z]*` matches `NAME` and then `>` matches ` >`? No — `[A-Z]*` matches uppercase letters only, so `NAME ` (with space) would not match because the space is not in `[A-Z]`). Actually, the regex `CLAIM\.<[A-Z]*>` matches `CLAIM.<NAME>` exactly (no space), but the old Chinese value had `CLAIM.<NAME >` with a space before `>`, which the regex would NOT match (because after `[A-Z]*` matches `NAME`, the next char is a space, not `>`). So the old Chinese value would have the `<NAME >` treated as an HTML tag by the sanitizer, causing a false 'Illegal HTML' failure. The fix (removing the space) makes the Chinese value match the regex and pass the verifier. This is a correct fix to make the translation pass the new HTML check, and it aligns with the English source. No issue.

title: Wrong null-check message for rawTokenId
body: The constructor validates `grantType` twice: line 72 checks `grantType` with message "Null grantType not allowed" and line 73 checks `grantType` again with message "Null rawTokenId not allowed". The second check was clearly intended to validate `rawTokenId` (which is never null-checked), so a null `rawTokenId` would pass validation silently and later cause a NullPointerException in `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId` when concatenating `':' + tokenContext.getRawTokenId()` (actually producing "null" string) or in `getTokenContextFromTokenId`. Fix: change line 73 to `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed");`.

title: isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted grant-shortcut comparison
body: In `isAccessTokenId(String expectedGrantShortcut)`, the check `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` returns false (match failure) when the grant shortcut MATCHES the expected value, and falls through to `return isUUID().matches(items[1])` when it does NOT match. The logic is inverted: the matcher will reject tokens whose grant shortcut equals the expected one and accept tokens with any other (or missing) grant shortcut as long as the suffix is a UUID. Additionally, `substring(3, 5)` is off by one: the encoded prefix is 6 chars (2 session + 2 token type + 2 grant), so the grant shortcut occupies indices 4-5, i.e. `substring(4, 6)`. As written, every test using `expectCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken`, and `expectAuthReqIdToToken` will fail against correctly encoded token IDs (or worse, pass against wrong ones), making the test assertions meaningless. Fix: `if (!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`.

title: Duplicate-shortcut validation compares wrong map sizes and cannot detect collisions
body: In `postInit`, the duplicate-detection check `if (grantsByShortcuts.size() != grantsToShortcuts.size())` is intended to catch two different grant types sharing the same shortcut (or same ID). However, `grantsByShortcuts` is keyed by shortcut and `grantsToShortcuts` is keyed by grant ID. If two grants share the same shortcut, `grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantName)` silently overwrites the first entry, shrinking `grantsByShortcuts` by one while `grantsToShortcuts` keeps both IDs — the sizes then differ and the check fires, which is correct. But if two grants share the same ID (impossible for distinct factories) or, more importantly, if a shortcut collides with the reserved `UNKNOWN` shortcut "na", the overwrite happens at line 78 AFTER the loop, again changing sizes — still detected. The real gap: the check only detects size differences, so a collision that is later overwritten by an equal-size map change would be missed, and more practically the error message and detection are fragile. A more robust approach is to detect the overwrite during insertion (e.g., check `grantsByShortcuts.put(...) != null` inside the loop and throw immediately). As written, the validation is indirect and can produce a confusing failure or, in edge cases where a custom provider registers grants dynamically via `getShortcutByGrantType`/`getGrantTypeByShortcut`, silently accept a colliding shortcut, which would corrupt the token-ID encoding (two grant types mapping to the same 2-char code).

title: getTokenContextFromTokenId uses indexOf(':') which breaks if raw ID contains a colon
body: `getTokenContextFromTokenId` splits the encoded ID with `encodedTokenId.indexOf(':')` and takes everything after the first colon as `rawId`. `KeycloakModelUtils.generateId()` produces UUIDs (no colons), so for newly issued tokens this is fine. However, the method is a public SPI entry point (`TokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId`) meant to decode token IDs that may come from external/custom encoders or older/foreign formats; any raw ID containing a colon (or a legacy ID that happens to contain a colon) would be mis-parsed: the prefix check `encodedContext.length() != 6` would throw `IllegalArgumentException` for a legacy ID like `ab:cd:uuid`, and even a well-formed custom encoding with a colon in the raw part would be split at the wrong position. Using `lastIndexOf(':')` would be more robust, or better, `split(":", 2)` semantics with an explicit prefix-length check. At minimum the parsing should use the LAST colon or validate that the prefix is exactly 6 chars before the first colon and document the constraint.

title: initToken can throw IllegalStateException for unknown grant type, breaking token issuance
body: In `initToken`, the access token ID is now built via `encoder.encodeTokenId(tokenCtx)` where `tokenCtx` comes from `getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext`. That method sets `grantType = UNKNOWN` ("na") when `Constants.GRANT_TYPE` is not set on the client session context, and `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId` maps "na" back to "na" via the factory maps (line 78-79 of the factory put UNKNOWN->UNKNOWN), so the common path works. However, `encodeTokenId` throws `IllegalStateException("Cannot encode token with unknown grantType: ...")` when `factory.getShortcutByGrantType(...)` returns null. The factory's lazy-refresh path (`getShortcutByGrantType`, lines 106-119) only refreshes when the grant type is not found AND a provider factory exists for it; for any grant type string that is set on the client session context but has no registered `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` (e.g., a custom grant type implemented without the new SPI, or a code path that sets `Constants.GRANT_TYPE` to a value with no factory), `getShortcutByGrantType` returns null and `encodeTokenId` throws. Since `initToken` is on the critical path of every access-token issuance (authorization code, refresh, client credentials, CIBA, device, token exchange, etc.), any such gap turns into a 500 error at token issuance instead of degrading to the "na" shortcut. The PR sets `Constants.GRANT_TYPE` in several grant types but the fallback to UNKNOWN only happens when the attribute is absent — a present-but-unmapped value is fatal. Consider falling back to the UNKNOWN shortcut in `encodeTokenId` (or in `getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext` validating against known grants) rather than throwing.

title: Removal of the Context copy constructor is a breaking API change for the SPI
body: `OAuth2GrantType.Context` is a public class in `server-spi-private` and previously exposed a public copy constructor `Context(Context context)`. The PR removes it (the diff shows the copy constructor body deleted and replaced by the `grantType` initialization in the main constructor). Any third-party `OAuth2GrantType` implementation that relied on the copy constructor (a common pattern for wrapping/decorating contexts) will fail to compile against the new version. Since this is an SPI in `server-spi-private` that the PR explicitly wants to be extensible ("provider adds ability for someone to introduce his own provider"), removing a public constructor without a deprecation cycle is an API break. Either keep the copy constructor (initializing `grantType` from `context.grantType`) or document the break.

title: Lightweight-token detection reads client attribute from the wrong client context
body: `getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext` determines the token type via `AbstractOIDCProtocolMapper.getShouldUseLightweightToken(session)`, which reads `session.getContext().getClient()`. During token issuance in `TokenManager.initToken`, the session context client is the client for which the token is being issued, which is normally correct. However, for flows where the session context client differs from the client session's client (e.g., token exchange where `StandardTokenExchangeProvider.setClientToContext` sets the requesting client, or admin/service-account flows), the lightweight flag could be evaluated against the wrong client, encoding `lt` (lightweight) for a regular token or `rt` for a lightweight one. The PR's stated goal is to "recognize more reliably if access-token is lightweight or not"; deriving it from `session.getContext().getClient()` rather than from `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getClient()` undermines that reliability. Prefer `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getClient()` (the client the token is actually issued for) when deciding the token type.

title: Potential NPE when client session has no user session
body: `getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext` calls `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getUserSession()` and immediately dereferences it (`userSession.getPersistenceState()`). For client-credentials grants and service accounts, Keycloak can create client sessions without a user session (transient service-account sessions may have a user session, but some code paths create client sessions with a null user session). If `getUserSession()` returns null, this throws a NullPointerException inside `initToken`, failing token issuance. The method should handle a null user session (e.g., treat as TRANSIENT, which matches how service-account/client-credentials tokens behave) instead of dereferencing blindly.

title: Grant type attribute set on a freshly-created DefaultClientSessionContext may not propagate to token creation
body: `PreAuthorizedCodeGrantType.process` builds `sessionContext` via `DefaultClientSessionContext.fromClientSessionAndScopeParameter(...)` and then sets `Constants.GRANT_TYPE` on that context (line 82) before calling `tokenManager.createClientAccessToken(..., sessionContext)`. Whether the attribute is visible during `initToken` depends on `DefaultClientSessionContext` storing attributes in-memory vs. reading from the underlying client session notes; if `fromClientSessionAndScopeParameter` returns a wrapper whose `setAttribute` writes to a transient map that `initToken` later re-reads through a different context instance, the grant type may be lost and the token ID would be encoded with the "na" shortcut. This is the only grant that sets the attribute on a locally-constructed context rather than through `OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse` or the client session itself, so it is the most likely to silently produce `pc`-less (i.e., `na`) token IDs. Worth verifying with an integration test for the pre-authorized-code flow.

title: Refresh grant type is hardcoded to REFRESH_TOKEN constant instead of the actual grant type used
body: In the refresh-token path (`refreshAccessToken` / the code around line 248), the PR sets `clientSessionCtx.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, OAuth2Constants.REFRESH_TOKEN)`. `OAuth2Constants.REFRESH_TOKEN` is the string "refresh_token", which matches `RefreshTokenGrantTypeFactory.getId()`, so the encoding will produce the `rt` shortcut — but note this collides conceptually with the token-type shortcut `rt` (regular token) used in the token-type position; they are in different positions so encoding is unambiguous, but it is confusing. More importantly, hardcoding the constant here bypasses the `OAuth2GrantType.Context.getGrantType()` mechanism used everywhere else; if the refresh flow is ever entered via a different grant type (e.g., a custom refresh-like grant), the encoded ID would incorrectly claim `refresh_token`. Using the actual grant type from the request context would be more consistent.

title: Unit test bypasses factory.postInit and hand-builds maps, missing coverage of duplicate-shortcut validation
body: The test's `@Before` constructs `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory`, calls `init(null)`, and then directly assigns `factory.grantsByShortcuts` / `factory.grantsToShortcuts` (package-private fields) instead of calling `postInit(...)`. This means the production initialization path — including the duplicate-shortcut validation in `postInit` (lines 70-86) and the population of maps from real `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` instances — is never exercised by this test. A regression in `postInit` (e.g., the broken size-comparison check, or a shortcut collision between two real grant factories) would not be caught. Add a test that runs `postInit` against a real/mock `KeycloakSessionFactory` with the actual grant factories, and a test that a duplicate shortcut causes startup failure.

title: Wrong null-check argument in constructor
body: In the AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth null check is `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` — it checks `grantType` again instead of `rawTokenId`. As a result, a null `rawTokenId` is not rejected and is stored in the field, while the error message is misleading. A null rawTokenId would later produce a malformed encoded token id (e.g. `onrtac:null`) or an NPE during encoding/concatenation.

title: Grant type read from client session context is not the grant type that created the token
body: getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext() reads the grant type from `clientSessionContext.getAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE)`. However, this attribute is set on the client session context at token-creation time (e.g. in OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse, ResourceOwnerPasswordCredentialsGrantType, StandardTokenExchangeProvider) and, critically, in TokenManager.refreshToken() the attribute is overwritten with `OAuth2Constants.REFRESH_TOKEN` before creating the new access token. More importantly, the attribute persists on the client session across multiple token issuances: a client session created by an authorization-code grant keeps GRANT_TYPE=authorization_code, so a later access token issued via the refresh-token grant on the same client session would be encoded with the stale original grant type unless every issuance path overwrites it. Any token-creation path that does not set this attribute (e.g. service-account/client-credentials flows that build the ClientSessionContext differently, admin-initiated impersonation, or token creation via TokenManager.createClientAccessToken from other callers) will silently encode the wrong grant type or 'na'. The encoded grant type therefore cannot be trusted as 'the grant type used to create this token' without auditing every caller of createClientAccessToken/initToken.

title: Token type (lightweight vs regular) is derived from the current session/client state, not from the token being created
body: getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext() determines TokenType via `AbstractOIDCProtocolMapper.getShouldUseLightweightToken(session)`, which reads `session.getAttribute(Constants.USE_LIGHTWEIGHT_ACCESS_TOKEN_ENABLED)` and the client attribute. The session attribute is set by token-exchange code paths (e.g. lightweight token exchange) and may be set or cleared at arbitrary points during request processing. If the session attribute is set after initToken() runs, or if a token is created in a context where the session attribute reflects a different decision than the one actually applied to the token (TokenManager decides lightweight-ness in formatTokenType/applyMapper based on the same helper, but the two calls are not atomic), the encoded token-type shortcut can disagree with the actual token type. The PR's stated goal — 'recognize more reliably if access-token is lightweight or not' — is undermined if the encoded value can be wrong; consumers using the prefix to decide whether to trust in-token roles would make incorrect authorization decisions.

title: Decoding a token id containing a colon in the raw id mis-parses the context
body: getTokenContextFromTokenId() uses `encodedTokenId.indexOf(':')` to split prefix from raw id. If the raw id itself contains a ':' (KeycloakModelUtils.generateId() produces UUIDs today, but the SPI contract allows custom encoders/providers and the raw id is opaque), the first colon is found correctly only if the prefix contains no colon — which holds for the default encoder. However, the bigger issue: any legacy or foreign token id that happens to contain a colon (e.g. `foo:bar`) is treated as an encoded id; `encodedContext.length() != 6` then throws IllegalArgumentException. Throwing on arbitrary token ids means any code path that decodes a token id (introspection, userInfo, admin API) will throw an unhandled exception for malformed/legacy ids that contain a colon but are not 6-char-prefixed, instead of degrading to UNKNOWN as the no-colon branch does. This is an inconsistent and fragile contract: ids without ':' are tolerated, ids with ':' but wrong prefix length crash the request.

title: Duplicate-shortcut validation compares map sizes, which does not detect collisions
body: postInit() validates uniqueness of grant shortcuts by checking `grantsByShortcuts.size() != grantsToShortcuts.size()`. This is incorrect: if two different grant types share the same shortcut, `grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantName)` overwrites one entry (size stays smaller) while `grantsToShortcuts` gains two entries — sizes differ, so it is caught. But if two different grant types share the same ID (impossible via getId contract) or, more realistically, if a shortcut collides AND a grant name collides in a compensating way, sizes can be equal while mappings are wrong. More importantly, the check cannot detect the case where one grant's shortcut equals another grant's shortcut AND the overwritten entry coincidentally keeps sizes equal (e.g. duplicate shortcut plus duplicate id). The robust check is to detect size shrinkage during insertion (compare size before/after each put) or explicitly check `grantsByShortcuts.containsKey(shortcut)` before putting. As written, the safety net the comment claims ('Validation if there are not duplicated shortcuts') is unreliable.

title: Lazy refresh of grant maps is not atomic and can permanently cache a wrong mapping
body: getShortcutByGrantType() and getGrantTypeByShortcut() lazily populate the ConcurrentHashMaps when a grant type deployed after startup is encountered. The check-then-act sequence (`get` returning null, then lookup in sessionFactory, then `put`) is not atomic: two threads can both miss and both put, which is benign for identical values. However, if a custom OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is deployed whose shortcut collides with an existing one, the lazy path silently overwrites the existing mapping (grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantType)), permanently corrupting the shortcut→grant resolution for previously valid tokens — a token id encoded with the old mapping will now decode to the wrong grant type. The startup validation in postInit() is bypassed entirely by this lazy path.

title: Removal of the Context copy constructor is a breaking API change for custom OAuth2GrantType implementations
body: The PR deletes the public copy constructor `Context(Context context)` from OAuth2GrantType.Context.
