This is a public class in server-spi-private, and third-party/custom grant type providers (the SPI is designed for extension — the PR itself advertises 'provider adds ability for someone to introduce his own provider') may use this copy constructor to wrap/delegate contexts (a common pattern for decorating grant processing). Removing a public constructor without deprecation is a binary- and source-incompatible break for any external implementation. If the copy constructor is no longer needed internally, it should be deprecated first, not removed in the same change.

title: grantType captured in constructor can be stale when formParams are replaced via setFormParams
body: The constructor now eagerly captures `this.grantType = formParams.getFirst(OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE)`, but the class still exposes `setFormParams(MultivaluedHashMap)` which replaces the formParams reference. Any caller that constructs the Context and then calls setFormParams() with different parameters (e.g. a wrapper that normalizes or replaces form params) will leave `grantType` holding the old value while `getFormParams()` returns the new ones — an inconsistent state. Either derive grantType lazily in getGrantType() from the current formParams, or update grantType inside setFormParams().

title: New abstract method getShortcut() on OAuth2GrantTypeFactory breaks all existing third-party grant type factories
body: The PR adds `String getShortcut();` as a non-default method to the public SPI interface OAuth2GrantTypeFactory. Every existing custom implementation of this SPI (external extensions, downstream products) will fail to compile and, if already compiled, will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit() iterates all OAuth2GrantType factories and calls getShortcut(). This is a hard backward-incompatibility in a public SPI. The method should be declared `default` (e.g. returning null or a derived value) with a documented requirement to override, so existing factories keep working and unknown shortcuts degrade to the 'na'/UNKNOWN path.

title: Encoded token id is generated in initToken but other token-creation paths may bypass it
body: The encoding is applied only in TokenManager.initToken(). Any other code path that creates an AccessToken and sets its id directly (e.g. `token.id(KeycloakModelUtils.generateId())` elsewhere in TokenManager or in other services such as TokenExchangeProvider variants, service-account flows, admin impersonation, or the OIDC 'token' endpoint response building for ID-token-as-access-token in StandardTokenExchangeProvider where an IDToken is reused) will produce access tokens whose jti has no context prefix. Consumers relying on the prefix (the stated purpose: introspection/userInfo optimization, session-type lookup) will see a mix of prefixed and unprefixed ids and must handle both — the PR description claims the encoding is 'used only for access-tokens', but in practice only for access tokens created through initToken. If full coverage is intended, all AccessToken.id() assignments for access tokens must go through the encoder; if not, the fallback behavior for unprefixed ids must be documented and handled by consumers.

title: Refresh grant overwrites the client session GRANT_TYPE attribute, mutating session state visible to other flows
body: In refreshToken(), `clientSessionCtx.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, OAuth2Constants.REFRESH_TOKEN)` overwrites the grant type stored on the (persistent) client session context. The original grant type that created the session (e.g. authorization_code) is lost from the session context. Any other consumer reading this attribute later (current or future) will see 'refresh_token' as the session's grant type, which misrepresents the session's origin. If the attribute is meant to record 'the grant type of the most recent token issuance', that should be documented; if it is meant to record the session's originating grant, overwriting it is a data-integrity bug.

title: isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted grant-shortcut comparison, making the new assertions always fail
body: In the new isAccessTokenId(String expectedGrantShortcut) matcher, the check is `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` — it returns false (no match) precisely when the grant shortcut DOES equal the expected value, and falls through to the UUID check otherwise. The condition is inverted; it should be `if (!items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`. Additionally, the substring indices are wrong: the prefix is 6 characters (2 session + 2 token + 2 grant), so the grant shortcut occupies characters at index 4–5, i.e. `substring(4, 6)`, not `substring(3, 5)` (the comment even says 'starts at character 4th char' — off-by-one in the code). As written, every expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectDeviceCodeToToken/expectAuthReqIdToToken event assertion using this matcher will fail (or pass only accidentally), breaking the integration tests that were updated to use it.

title: UNKNOWN constant value 'na' collides conceptually with the 'unknown' session/token shortcuts 'un' but is a grant-only sentinel mixed into the same namespace
body: The grant-type sentinel UNKNOWN = "na" is registered in the same shortcut maps as real grant shortcuts (grantsByShortcuts/grantsToShortcuts in the factory). A custom grant type factory could legitimately choose the shortcut "na", which would then be indistinguishable from 'unknown grant type' when decoding. The factory's duplicate-detection would not catch this because "na" is pre-registered after the loop, silently overwriting (or being overwritten by) a real grant. Reserving the sentinel namespace (e.g. validating that no grant shortcut equals "na" at startup) would prevent this ambiguity.

title: Unit test bypasses factory.postInit and hand-builds internal maps, so it does not test the real wiring
body: The test's @Before constructs DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory, calls init(null), then directly assigns the package-private fields grantsByShortcuts/grantsToShortcuts with a hand-built HashMap, bypassing postInit() entirely. This means the test never exercises the real population logic (iteration over OAuth2GrantType factories, duplicate-shortcut validation, UNKNOWN registration) and would not catch regressions in postInit(). It also means the test depends on package-private field access, making it brittle. A test that drives the factory through postInit with a real/mock KeycloakSessionFactory would cover the actual production path.

title: Session type detection calls getUserSession() which can be null for client-credentials/service-account sessions
body: getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext() unconditionally calls `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getUserSession()` and then dereferences the result (`userSession.getPersistenceState()`). For client-credentials grants and service-account flows there is no user session (the client session is not attached to a user session), so getUserSession() can return null, causing an NPE during access-token creation for client-credentials — one of the most common grant types. The PR's own example (`trltcc:...` for a transient lightweight client-credentials token) implies client-credentials tokens are expected to be encoded, so this path must handle a null user session (e.g. defaulting to TRANSIENT).

title: GRANT_TYPE attribute set on a DefaultClientSessionContext wrapper may not propagate to the persisted client session
body: In PreAuthorizedCodeGrantType.process(), the grant type is set via `sessionContext.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, ...)` where sessionContext is a `DefaultClientSessionContext` created by `DefaultClientSessionContext.fromClientSessionAndScopeParameter(...)`. Whether this attribute is visible later when TokenManager.initToken() reads it via the ClientSessionContext passed to createClientAccessToken depends on DefaultClientSessionContext.setAttribute delegating to the underlying AuthenticatedClientSessionModel notes. If DefaultClientSessionContext.setAttribute only writes to an in-memory map that is not the same instance passed to createClientAccessToken (a different wrapper is created inside TokenManager), the grant type will be lost and the token encoded with 'na'. This path should be verified with an integration test; the unit test does not cover it.

title: Grant maps are package-private mutable fields, exposing internal state
body: grantsByShortcuts and grantsToShortcuts are declared without an access modifier (package-private) and are non-final mutable fields on the factory. The unit test relies on this to inject state directly. Exposing mutable internal maps package-wide invites accidental external mutation and makes the class harder to reason about; they should be private with the test using the real postInit() path (or a package-private test hook that is clearly intended for tests).

title: Wrong null-check message for rawTokenId
body: In the AccessTokenContext constructor, the null check for rawTokenId uses `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` — it checks grantType a second time instead of rawTokenId, and the message is misleading. A null rawTokenId would pass validation silently, and the error message for a null grantType is duplicated. The line should be `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")`.

title: Lightweight token detection uses client attribute instead of the token being created
body: getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext determines the token type via `AbstractOIDCProtocolMapper.getShouldUseLightweightToken(session)`, which reads the client attribute `client.use.lightweight.access.token.enabled` (or a session attribute). This reflects the client's configured preference, not whether the token actually being created is lightweight. If a lightweight token is created through a path that sets the session attribute (e.g. token exchange or other flows that set USE_LIGHTWEIGHT_ACCESS_TOKEN_ENABLED on the session) while the client attribute is false, or vice versa, the encoded token-type shortcut in the jti will be wrong (e.g. 'rt' for a lightweight token or 'lt' for a regular token). Downstream consumers relying on the encoded 'lt'/'rt' to decide whether to look up roles from the model vs the token (as described in the PR) would make the wrong decision. The token type should be derived from the actual token/client-session context being encoded, consistent with how TokenManager decides to create a lightweight token.

title: NullPointerException when client session has no user session
body: getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext calls `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getUserSession()` and immediately dereferences it (`userSession.getPersistenceState()`). For client-credentials grants and other service-account flows the client session may have a null user session (client-only sessions), which would cause an NPE during token creation in TokenManager.initToken, breaking token issuance for those flows. The code must handle a null user session (e.g. treat it as TRANSIENT, which matches how client-credentials sessions are created with SessionPersistenceState.TRANSIENT in Keycloak).

title: Decoding a token id containing a colon in the raw id mis-parses the context
body: getTokenContextFromTokenId uses `encodedTokenId.indexOf(':')` to split prefix from raw id. If the raw token id itself ever contains a ':' (UUIDs generated by KeycloakModelUtils.generateId() do not today, but the format is not enforced and custom TokenContextEncoderProvider implementations or future id formats could), the split point is wrong: the prefix length check `encodedContext.length() != 6` would then throw IllegalArgumentException for a legitimately encoded id, or worse, mis-parse. Using lastIndexOf(':') would be more robust, or the format should be documented/enforced. At minimum this fragility should be noted; as written, any raw id containing ':' makes the token id undecodable.

title: Duplicate-shortcut validation compares map sizes, which can miss collisions in both directions
body: The duplicate detection in postInit only throws when `grantsByShortcuts.size() != grantsToShortcuts.size()`. Two grants sharing the same shortcut but having distinct ids still produce equal map sizes (the shortcut map loses one entry, the id map keeps both), so the collision is silently accepted and one grant becomes unreachable by shortcut — the later put overwrites the earlier entry in grantsByShortcuts. Conversely duplicate ids with distinct shortcuts are also missed. The check should compare against the actual number of OAuth2GrantType factories, or explicitly detect overwritten entries during the loop.

title: Grant shortcut maps are lazily mutated without synchronization beyond ConcurrentHashMap, allowing stale/inconsistent refresh
body: grantsByShortcuts and grantsToShortcuts are ConcurrentHashMaps that are mutated lazily in getShortcutByGrantType/getGrantTypeByShortcut when a grant type is not found (to support hot-deployed grant types). The two maps are updated in two separate put operations with no atomicity between them, so a concurrent reader can observe a state where one map has the new entry and the other does not, returning null or an inconsistent mapping. Additionally, the 'refresh' path can permanently cache a mapping for a grant type that was later undeployed. A single synchronized refresh or a computeIfAbsent-style atomic update of both maps would be safer.

title: initToken encodes context for every access token including admin/internal and service-account tokens, with no way to opt out, and can throw for unknown grant types
body: initToken now unconditionally calls `session.getProvider(TokenContextEncoderProvider.class)` and `encoder.encodeTokenId(...)` for every access token created through this path. encodeTokenId throws IllegalStateException when the grant type shortcut cannot be resolved (unknown grant type not registered as an OAuth2GrantType provider). Tokens created outside the standard grant-type flow — e.g. admin REST API tokens, service-account tokens created via client-credentials where the GRANT_TYPE attribute was never set on the client session context (the attribute is only set in OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse, ResourceOwnerPasswordCredentialsGrantType, PreAuthorizedCodeGrantType, StandardTokenExchangeProvider and the refresh path in TokenManager), or any custom token-creation path — will get grantType 'na' (handled), but any path where the attribute holds a grant type string that has no registered OAuth2GrantTypeFactory (e.g. a custom grant implemented without the new SPI, or 'urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code' when the device flow feature is disabled and the factory is not loaded) will cause token creation to fail with IllegalStateException, breaking token issuance. The encoding should be resilient: fall back to the UNKNOWN shortcut instead of throwing when the grant type cannot be resolved.

title: Refresh grant type attribute is set on the client session context after the client session may already be detached/persisted
body: In the refresh-token path, `clientSessionCtx.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, OAuth2Constants.REFRESH_TOKEN)` is set on the ClientSessionContext obtained from the old token's client session. Depending on the ClientSessionContext implementation, attributes set on the context may not be persisted back to the client session notes, and the attribute is set before createClientAccessToken is called — but for offline sessions loaded from storage the context wrapping may be a detached copy. If the attribute is not propagated, the new access token's jti will be encoded with grant type 'na' instead of 'rt', defeating the purpose for refreshed tokens. This needs verification against DefaultClientSessionContext semantics; at minimum the attribute should be set as a client session note (setNote) which is the persisted mechanism, or set before the context is resolved from the session.

title: Removal of the Context copy constructor is a breaking API change for custom OAuth2GrantType implementations
body: The public copy constructor `Context(Context context)` was removed from OAuth2GrantType.Context. This is a public class in server-spi-private used by third-party/custom grant type providers; any external implementation that used the copy constructor (a common pattern for wrapping/decorating contexts) will fail to compile against the new version. Additionally, the new field `grantType` is initialized in the main constructor from `formParams.getFirst(OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE)`, but the removed copy constructor did not copy it — had it been kept, it would have silently dropped the grant type. If the removal is intentional, it should be called out as a breaking change; otherwise the copy constructor should be retained and fixed to copy grantType.

title: grantType is captured from formParams at construction time and becomes stale when formParams are replaced
body: The Context constructor reads `grantType` once from `formParams.getFirst(OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE)`. There is a `setFormParams(MultivaluedHashMap)` setter that replaces the formParams reference after construction; any code path that calls setFormParams with different parameters (e.g. re-parsing or normalizing form params) leaves `grantType` pointing at the old value, and getGrantType() then returns a stale or null grant type. Either derive grantType lazily in getGrantType() from the current formParams, or update it in setFormParams.

title: New abstract method getShortcut() on OAuth2GrantTypeFactory breaks all existing third-party grant type factories
body: getShortcut() was added as an abstract method (no default implementation) to the OAuth2GrantTypeFactory interface. Any custom/third-party OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementation (the SPI is designed for extension — the PR description explicitly mentions custom providers) will fail to compile or fail at runtime with AbstractMethodError when the DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory iterates all factories and calls getShortcut() in postInit. A default method returning a derived fallback (e.g. null or a hash-based shortcut) should be provided, and the factory should handle null shortcuts gracefully.

title: Grant shortcut 'rt' for refresh-token collides with token-type shortcut 'rt' for regular token
body: RefreshTokenGrantTypeFactory.getShortcut() returns "rt", which is the same string as AccessTokenContext.TokenType.REGULAR's shortcut ("rt"). While these live in different positions of the encoded id (positions 2-4 for token type, 4-6 for grant type), the collision is confusing and error-prone: the DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderTest even encodes an offline regular password-grant token as "ofrtro:..." where "rt" appears twice with different meanings. More importantly, any code or custom provider that maps shortcuts globally (the SPI allows custom encoders) can easily mix them up. The refresh-token grant shortcut should be changed to a non-colliding value (e.g. "rf").

title: isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted grant-shortcut comparison and wrong substring index
body: The new isAccessTokenId matcher checks `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` — this returns false (no match) when the shortcut DOES equal the expected value, i.e. the logic is inverted, so every event assertion using this matcher will fail for correctly-encoded token ids. Additionally, the grant shortcut occupies characters 4-6 (0-based indices 4 and 5) of the 6-char prefix, so the correct substring is `substring(4, 6)`, not `substring(3, 5)` (which grabs the last char of the token-type shortcut plus the first char of the grant shortcut). The matcher should be `if (!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`.

title: UNKNOWN grant shortcut 'na' can collide with a real grant type shortcut
body: The reserved shortcut "na" (DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.UNKNOWN) is registered in the grant shortcut maps in postInit. If any current or future OAuth2GrantTypeFactory legitimately uses "na" as its shortcut, the postInit duplicate-size validation may not catch it (depending on map sizes) and the unknown marker would be silently overwritten or would shadow the real grant, causing tokens of that grant type to be decoded as UNKNOWN. The reserved value should be validated against all registered grant shortcuts at startup, or a value that cannot collide (e.g. containing the ':' delimiter or a character outside the shortcut alphabet) should be used.

title: Encoded jti changes token identity semantics: existing code that treats jti as an opaque UUID breaks
body: The access token jti is changed from a plain UUID to a prefixed format `xxxxxx:<uuid>`. Any code, client, or integration that parses the jti as a UUID (e.g. logging pipelines, audit tooling, custom token validators, or Keycloak code that uses the jti to look up sessions or correlate events) will break or misbehave. Within Keycloak itself, Details.TOKEN_ID event assertions and any place doing UUID validation on the access token id must be updated (the PR updates AssertEvents, but other places may exist). This is an intentional format change per the PR, but it is a contract break for the jti claim that should be explicitly documented, and a codebase-wide audit for jti-as-UUID assumptions is warranted before merge.

title: GRANT_TYPE attribute set on ClientSessionContext may not persist to the client session for later refreshes
body: createTokenResponse sets `clientSessionCtx.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, context.getGrantType())` on the ClientSessionContext. ClientSessionContext attributes are transient wrappers around client session notes in DefaultClientSessionContext; whether the attribute is persisted depends on the implementation writing it back to the AuthenticatedClientSessionModel notes. If it is not persisted, a later refresh of the token will read the attribute from a freshly-loaded client session context and get null, encoding 'na' instead of the original grant type. The grant type should be stored via clientSession.setNote(...) (the persisted mechanism) or the persistence behavior of setAttribute must be confirmed and relied upon consistently (TokenManager's refresh path reads it via clientSessionCtx.getAttribute, so both write and read must use the same mechanism).

title: Unit test bypasses factory postInit and hand-builds internal maps, so it does not test real wiring
body: The test constructs DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory, calls init(null), then directly assigns package-private fields grantsByShortcuts/grantsToShortcuts with a hand-built map, bypassing postInit entirely. This means the test does not exercise the real grant-type discovery/registration logic (postInit iterating OAuth2GrantType factories, duplicate validation, UNKNOWN registration), nor the lazy-refresh paths in getShortcutByGrantType/getGrantTypeByShortcut (sessionFactory is null, so those paths would NPE if hit). Tests for duplicate shortcut detection, unknown-grant fallback during encoding, and decoding of ids with wrong prefix length are also missing.

title: encodeTokenId throws for grant type 'na' (UNKNOWN) because the UNKNOWN grant is registered under the literal string 'na', not under itself as a grant type
body: In getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext, when no grant type attribute is present, grantType is set to the literal string "na" (UNKNOWN). encodeTokenId then calls factory.getShortcutByGrantType("na"). In postInit, the maps are populated with grantsToShortcuts.put("na", "na"), so this resolves — but only if postInit ran and registered it. However, the AccessTokenContext constructor requires a non-null grantType and the UNKNOWN constant is the shortcut, not a grant type URI; any custom TokenContextEncoderProvider or any path where the maps were refreshed (lazy refresh path in getShortcutByGrantType looks up sessionFactory.getProviderFactory(OAuth2GrantType.class, "na") which returns null, then re-reads the map) is fragile. More concretely: the semantics conflate 'unknown grant type' with the shortcut value 'na'; if a deployment's maps are refreshed or a custom factory overrides the maps, encoding a token with unknown grant type throws IllegalStateException and breaks token issuance. encodeTokenId should explicitly map the UNKNOWN grant to the UNKNOWN shortcut instead of relying on map contents.

title: createRecoveryCodesCredential stores raw recovery codes in user storage instead of hashed codes
body: The new method createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generated recovery codes (generatedCodes) to JSON and passes that JSON as the challengeResponse of a UserCredentialModel to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(). For local (Keycloak DB) storage, the recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel) path is used, and RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues hashes each raw code before persisting. But when the credential is stored in federated user storage, the raw, unhashed codes are handed to the storage provider verbatim. Any user storage provider that persists the credential data as-is (as the test provider BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage does at line 197 with recoveryCodesModel.setCredentialData(input.getChallengeResponse())) will store the recovery codes in plaintext. Recovery codes are bearer credentials equivalent to passwords; storing them unhashed in an external user storage is a serious data-integrity/security issue, and it also breaks the validation contract: the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider validates input by hashing the input and comparing to the stored hash, while a federated provider receiving raw codes must compare raw-to-raw (as the test provider does at line 340), meaning the same code validates differently depending on where it is stored. The fix is to hash the codes (e.g. via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode) before building the UserCredentialModel passed to updateCredential, and to construct the credential model consistently for both storage paths.

title: UserCredentialModel for federated recovery codes storage is missing userLabel and createdDate metadata
body: When the credential is stored in federated user storage, the code builds new UserCredentialModel("", credentialModel.getType(), recoveryCodesJson) and calls updateCredential. The credentialModel parameter (a RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel) carries the generatedAt timestamp and userLabel, but these are not transferred to the UserCredentialModel — only type and challengeResponse (the JSON) are set. The id is empty and createdDate is unset. A federated storage provider that reconstructs the credential from the CredentialInput (as BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials does, reading getCreatedDate() and getUserLabel()) will get a null/zero createdDate and null userLabel, so the stored federated credential loses the generatedAt metadata that the UI displays and that RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues expects. The OTP equivalent (createOTPCredential) similarly builds a minimal UserCredentialModel, but for OTP the secret is the only data. For recovery codes the createdDate/userLabel should be propagated (e.g. via UserCredentialModel.setUserLabel / credential data or by passing the full model) so federated storage round-trips the credential faithfully.

title: Optional.get() without isPresent() check will throw NoSuchElementException when user has no recovery codes credential
body: The constructor calls RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) which returns an Optional that is empty when the user has neither a federated nor a local recovery-authn-codes credential, then immediately calls credentialModelOpt.get() on line 19. Previously the code called getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(...).findFirst().get() which had the same latent problem, but the new helper makes the empty case more reachable: getCredential checks federated credentials first and falls back to local, and a user can legitimately reach the recovery-code input page (e.g. via a misconfigured flow, or a race where the credential was removed after the page was rendered, or all codes used and credential deleted) without any credential present. This will throw NoSuchElementException and produce a 500 error instead of a graceful login page. The code should handle the empty Optional (e.g. render the form without a code number or fail the authentication gracefully).

title: removeStoredCredentialById only removes local credential; federated recovery codes credential is never removed when all codes are used
body: After a successful recovery-code login, when all codes are used the code calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()). For a user whose recovery codes live in federated user storage, RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential returns the federated credential (from getFederatedCredentialsStream), and removeStoredCredentialById only removes credentials from the local Keycloak DB — it does not call the federated storage's disableCredentialType. As a result, the spent recovery-codes credential remains in the user storage. The subsequent isConfiguredFor check (line 149) and the required-action re-trigger logic (lines 90-92) then operate on stale data: the federated credential still reports all codes used, but it is never deleted, so the credential lingers in the external storage indefinitely (a data-hygiene issue and potentially confusing state for the storage provider). The code should remove the credential through the credential manager in a way that also disables/deletes it in federated storage (e.g. credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById for local plus disableCredentialType for federated, or use the credential's storageId to route the removal).

title: Test user storage provider validates recovery codes by comparing raw input to raw stored codes (plaintext comparison)
body: In isValid, the recovery-codes branch deserializes the stored credential data (which, due to CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential passing the raw codes JSON to updateCredential, contains plaintext codes) and checks generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())). This is a plaintext equality comparison of a bearer credential against stored plaintext — no hashing, no constant-time comparison. While this is test-suite code, it both (a) demonstrates and enshrines the insecure contract that federated providers receive raw codes, and (b) uses a non-constant-time equals comparison for a credential check. Combined with the production-side issue of storing raw codes in federated storage, this provider will keep plaintext recovery codes in memory and on disk. The provider should hash the input (RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode) and compare against hashed stored values, matching the local-storage validation semantics.

title: updateCredential for recovery codes drops userLabel and does not set secretData
body: The recovery-codes branch of updateCredential builds a CredentialModel with only id, type, credentialData (the raw JSON) and createdDate. It does not set userLabel (available on the incoming UserCredentialModel via getUserLabel()) nor secretData. Later, getCredentials reconstructs the model via RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(..., myUser.recoveryCodes.getUserLabel()) — which will be null — so the user label chosen during setup is lost for federated users. The OTP branch in the same method has the same pattern of dropping fields, but for recovery codes the userLabel is user-visible metadata that the account console and setup flow display. The provider should copy input.getUserLabel() (and createdDate from the input if present) into the stored CredentialModel.

title: Recovery codes test only exercises the first code and never verifies code consumption / all-codes-used behavior in user storage
body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin enters recovery code index 0 once and asserts login succeeds. It never verifies that (a) the used code is marked as consumed in the federated storage, (b) reusing the same code fails, or (c) after all 12 codes are consumed the credential is removed from user storage and the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is re-added. Given that the production change specifically alters how the credential is created and looked up in federated storage (and that removeStoredCredentialById does not touch federated storage), the test gap means the most important behavioral consequences of the PR in the federated path are unverified. A test that consumes codes and asserts the federated credential state (and the re-triggered required action) would be needed.

title: Misspelled config alias 'delayed-suthenticator-config' in test flow setup
body: In configureBrowserFlowWithRecoveryAuthnCodes the delayed-authenticator config alias is set to "delayed-suthenticator-config" (missing 'n' in "authenticator"). The alias is only used as a label for the execution config and the test passes delay=0, so it is functionally harmless, but it is a typo in test configuration text that will show up in the admin console/flow listing and could confuse anyone copying this setup. It should be "delayed-authenticator-config".

title: Recovery codes stored in user storage are saved as raw (unhashed) codes
body: In createRecoveryCodesCredential, the generatedCodes list is serialized directly into a UserCredentialModel and passed to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(recoveryCodesCredential). Unlike the local-storage path, where recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel) hashes each code (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues hashes the raw codes), the user-storage path stores the raw codes verbatim in the federated credential's challengeResponse/credentialData. Any user-storage provider that persists this value (LDAP attribute, external database, etc.) will hold plaintext recovery codes, which are equivalent to passwords for account recovery. The consequence is that a compromise of the user-storage backend (or its backups/logs) directly yields usable recovery codes, defeating the purpose of hashing them in the local Keycloak DB. The fix is to hash the codes (e.g., via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode) before building the UserCredentialModel, matching what the local credential provider does.

title: Test user-storage provider validates recovery codes by comparing raw input against stored values without hashing
body: In isValid(), the recovery-codes branch deserializes the stored credential data and checks generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())). Because CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential now sends the raw (unhashed) codes to user storage (see the related finding), this comparison only works because both sides are raw. If the production code is fixed to hash codes before storing them in user storage, this test provider will break; conversely, as written, this provider demonstrates and endorses storing plaintext recovery codes in federated storage. The validation should hash the input (RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode / verifyRecoveryCodeInput) and compare against the stored hashed values, consistent with the local Keycloak credential provider.

title: Recovery codes credential stored in user storage loses userLabel and used-code state
body: In updateCredential(), the recovery-codes branch builds a CredentialModel with only id, type, credentialData (the raw JSON list), and createdDate. It never sets userLabel, and it stores the list of codes as-is, so there is no per-code 'used' flag persisted. getCredentials() later reconstructs the model via RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(codes, createdDate, userLabel), which marks all codes as unused. This means a code that was already consumed during login remains valid in user storage: the federated isValid() will keep accepting a used recovery code, allowing unlimited reuse of a single recovery code. The provider must persist and honor the used/unused state (e.g., store the full RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel JSON including per-code used flags, and update it when a code is consumed), otherwise the one-time-use guarantee of recovery codes is broken for federated users.

title: disableCredentialType does not support removing recovery codes from user storage
body: disableCredentialType() only handles OTP types (setting myUser.otp = null) and logs 'Unsupported to disable credential of type' for everything else, including RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE. Since supportsCredentialType() now advertises recovery-codes support and isConfiguredFor() reports it, the account console/admin REST will list recovery codes as a disableable credential for federated users, but attempting to disable/remove it will silently do nothing (the credential remains in storage and the user can still log in with it). The method should handle RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE by setting myUser.recoveryCodes = null, and getDisableableCredentialTypesStream() should include the recovery-codes type when present.

title: Used recovery code is removed by credential ID even when the credential lives in federated user storage
body: After a successful recovery-code login, the code calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()) when all codes are used. RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() now returns the federated credential first, and for a federated credential the ID is the one assigned by the user-storage provider (or a dummy id). removeStoredCredentialById only removes credentials from the local Keycloak DB; for a federated credential this either throws, silently no-ops, or removes nothing, so the consumed-codes state in user storage is never updated. The consequence is that once all codes are used, the federated credential is never invalidated/removed and the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action logic (which keys off allCodesUsed() on the federated model) may repeatedly trigger or, worse, the storage-side credential keeps accepting codes. The removal path must go through the credential manager's federated-aware removal (e.g., updateCredential with the consumed state, or removeStoredCredentialById only for local credentials), not blindly call removeStoredCredentialById with a federated ID.

title: Optional.get() without isPresent() check will throw NoSuchElementException when no recovery credential exists
body: The constructor calls RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) and immediately invokes credentialModelOpt.get() without checking isPresent(). Previously the code used getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(...).findFirst().get() which had the same latent issue, but now that getCredential() explicitly returns an Optional that can legitimately be empty (federated lookup first, then local), any code path that renders the recovery-code input page for a user without a recovery credential (e.g., a race where the credential was removed, a misconfigured flow, or a user whose credential exists only in a storage provider that doesn't implement getCredentials) will throw NoSuchElementException and produce a 500 error instead of a graceful challenge. The bean should handle the empty case (e.g., throw a meaningful error, disable the input, or fall back), and ideally the template should not render the code-number prompt when no credential exists.

title: getCredential prefers federated credential but ignores local credential when both exist
body: getCredential() returns the first federated recovery-codes credential if present, and only falls back to the local stored credential when no federated one exists. If a user has recovery codes in both the local Keycloak DB (e.g., created before the user was federated, or created by a code path that bypassed the storage check) and in user storage, the local credential is silently ignored: login validation via credentialManager().isValid() may still check both, but the post-login bookkeeping in RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator (allCodesUsed check and removal) and the code-number display in RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean operate only on the federated one. This can lead to inconsistent state where a stale local credential remains valid forever and is never cleaned up, or where the displayed 'next code number' does not match the credential actually being validated. The method should either return all matching credentials or document/enforce a single source of truth, and callers should handle the both-exist case (e.g., prefer local, or remove the stale one).

title: Recovery-codes federation test does not verify one-time use of codes or removal/invalidation after all codes are consumed
body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only logs in once with recovery code index 0 and asserts success. It never attempts to reuse the same code (which must fail), never consumes all 12 codes to verify the credential is invalidated/removed and the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is re-triggered, and never verifies that the used-code state is persisted in the user storage. Given that the production change is specifically about creating and validating recovery codes in user storage, the absence of these assertions leaves the core security property (codes are single-use and the credential lifecycle works for federated users) untested. The test should reuse a consumed code and assert failure, and ideally drive the flow until all codes are used.

title: createRecoveryCodesCredential stores raw recovery codes in user storage instead of hashed codes
body: The new method createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generated recovery codes (generatedCodes) to JSON and passes that JSON as the challengeResponse of a UserCredentialModel to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(). When the credential is stored in a federated user storage (userStorageCreated == true), the raw, unhashed recovery codes are persisted in the external storage. Recovery codes are bearer credentials equivalent to passwords: storing them in plaintext in user storage means a compromise of the external user store (database, LDAP, etc.) directly exposes all users' recovery codes, allowing account takeover. The local-storage path is safe because RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential hashes the codes via RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues, but the user-storage path bypasses that hashing entirely. Compare with createOTPCredential, which passes the secret to the storage but relies on the storage's own handling; for recovery codes the codes must be hashed before being handed to the federated storage (e.g., hash each code with RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode and store the hashed list, matching what the local credential provider stores and what validation expects). As written, any user-storage provider that implements CredentialInputUpdater for the recovery-authn-codes type will persist plaintext recovery codes.

title: UserCredentialModel for recovery codes uses empty credential ID and raw JSON, inconsistent with the credentialModel that is discarded
body: When delegating to user storage, the code builds UserCredentialModel("", credentialModel.getType(), recoveryCodesJson) — an empty ID and only the type plus challengeResponse set — and ignores the fully-populated credentialModel (which contains the hashed codes, createdDate, and userLabel) that the caller constructed. The local-storage branch then uses credentialModel, so the two branches store different data shapes: local storage keeps hashed codes plus metadata, while user storage receives raw codes with no ID, no createdDate, and no userLabel. This means federated validation code (and the test provider) must reconstruct the credential from just the JSON list, and any metadata (userLabel, createdDate) is silently lost for federated users. The method should pass a UserCredentialModel derived from credentialModel (e.g., UserCredentialModel with credentialModel.getCredentialData() as the challenge response) so both storage paths receive equivalent data.

title: Test user-storage provider validates recovery codes by comparing plaintext input against stored plaintext codes
body: In isValid(), the recovery-authn-codes branch deserializes the stored credential data into a List and checks generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())). Because CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential stores the raw (unhashed) codes in user storage, this provider compares the user's raw input directly against the stored raw codes. This both (a) confirms and institutionalizes the plaintext-storage behavior from the production code, and (b) means the test provider itself would accept a match on plaintext, so the test cannot detect that production validation for federated users expects hashed codes. The provider should hash the input (RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode) and compare against hashed stored values, consistent with how the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider validates. As written, the test enshrines a plaintext comparison path for recovery codes in federated storage.

title: updateCredential for recovery codes stores only credentialData and drops userLabel/createdDate metadata needed by getCredentials
body: The recovery-codes branch of updateCredential builds a CredentialModel with id, type, credentialData (the raw JSON), and createdDate, but never sets userLabel. Later, getCredentials() reconstructs the credential via RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(codes, createdDate, myUser.recoveryCodes.getUserLabel()) — getUserLabel() will be null because it was never stored. Depending on RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues' null handling, the reconstructed credential may have a null userLabel, which can break the account console display and any code that reads the label. The provider should persist and restore the userLabel (e.g., store it in userSecretData or a dedicated field) so the round-trip through federated storage preserves all credential metadata.

title: Optional.get() without isPresent() check can throw NoSuchElementException when no recovery credential exists
body: The constructor calls RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) and immediately invokes credentialModelOpt.get() without checking isPresent(). The previous code had the same pattern (findFirst().get()), but the new getCredential() helper explicitly returns an Optional that can be empty when the user has no recovery-authn-codes credential in either federated or local storage. This bean is used to render the recovery-code input page, which is only shown when the authenticator is configuredFor() the user — but configuredFor() checks isConfiguredFor on the credential manager, which for federated users consults the storage provider; a race (credential removed between configuredFor and page render), a storage provider that reports configured but returns no credential from getFederatedCredentialsStream, or a user whose only credential was just consumed (allCodesUsed removal in RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator) can make the Optional empty, causing a NoSuchElementException and a 500 error on the login page. The code should handle the empty case gracefully (e.g., throw a meaningful error or render without a code number) instead of an unguarded Optional.get().

title: removeStoredCredentialById only removes local credentials; federated recovery credential is never removed when all codes are used
body: After a successful recovery-code login, the authenticator checks recoveryCodeCredentialModel.allCodesUsed() and calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()). However, RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() now returns federated credentials first (getFederatedCredentialsStream), and removeStoredCredentialById only removes credentials from Keycloak's local storage — it does not remove credentials from the federated user storage. For a user whose recovery codes live in user storage, once all codes are consumed the stale credential remains in the external storage. The subsequent isConfiguredFor check may still return true (the federated provider still reports the credential), so the user can keep being prompted for recovery codes that can never validate, or worse, the storage provider's isValid may still match already-used codes depending on its implementation. The code should remove the credential via the credential manager in a way that also deletes it from federated storage (e.g., user.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById only works locally; a federated-aware removal path is needed), or the logic should account for federated credentials explicitly.

title: getCredential federated-first lookup can return a stale federated credential even when a newer local credential exists
body: getCredential() checks getFederatedCredentialsStream() first and only falls back to local storage if no federated credential is found. If a user previously had recovery codes in federated storage and later a new credential was created locally (or vice versa), the lookup order is fixed and does not consider createdDate or which credential is current. In a mixed scenario (e.g., user migrated, or a credential exists in both stores), the federated one always wins even if it is older or fully consumed, while the local one is ignored. This can cause the login flow to display the wrong code number (RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean) or to fail to remove the correct credential after use. The lookup should prefer the most recently created credential across both stores, or at minimum the callers should be aware that federated credentials take precedence unconditionally.

title: disableCredentialType does not handle recovery-authn-codes type, so federated recovery credentials cannot be disabled
body: disableCredentialType() only handles OTP types (sets myUser.otp = null) and logs 'Unsupported to disable credential of type' for everything else. The recovery-authn-codes type is now supported by this provider (supportsCredentialType, updateCredential, isValid, isConfiguredFor, getCredentials all handle it), but there is no way to disable/remove it. The account console and admin REST 'disable credential type' operations for recovery codes on federated users will silently fail (the provider returns without clearing myUser.recoveryCodes), leaving the credential active. The method should add a branch to null out myUser.recoveryCodes when credentialType equals RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE, and getDisableableCredentialTypesStream should include the recovery codes type when present so the UI offers it.

title: New recovery-codes federation test does not verify that codes are consumed/removed or that a second login with a used code fails
body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only verifies setup (credential lands in user storage, no DB credentials) and a single successful login with the first code. It does not verify the security-critical behaviors of the feature: (1) that after using a code, the used code is marked/removed so it cannot be replayed, (2) that logging in again with the same code fails, (3) that after all 12 codes are consumed the credential is removed and the user is prompted to configure new codes (the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action path in RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator), and (4) that the stored credential in user storage is hashed rather than plaintext. Given that the production change introduces a new storage path for these bearer credentials, the absence of a replay/consumption test leaves the most important integrity property untested.

title: getSubGroupsCount() can return null, violating the GroupModel contract and causing NPEs at call sites
body: The changed method `getSubGroupsCount()` now returns `null` when the underlying delegate group is not found (`model == null ? null : model.getSubGroupsCount()`). The `GroupModel.getSubGroupsCount()` contract (and its JPA/map implementations) returns a primitive-wrapped `Long` count that is never null — a missing group is represented by the delegate lookup returning null upstream, not by a null count. Callers such as `GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount()` (services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/utils/GroupUtils.java:90) do `representation.setSubGroupCount(group.getSubGroupsCount())`, and `GroupRepresentation.setSubGroupCount(Long)` / downstream JSON serialization and admin-console code assume a non-null count; auto-unboxing or null propagation here reintroduces exactly the class of NPE this PR is trying to fix (issue #40368), just moved to a different call site. When the group has been concurrently deleted, the correct behavior is to treat the cached entry as invalid (call `getDelegateForUpdate()`/invalidate, which throws `IllegalStateException("Not found in database")` like the sibling methods `isUpdated()` and `getDelegateForUpdate()` do) rather than silently returning null. Returning null also changes the API contract for a public model interface method.

title: Removal of groupMatchesSearchOrIsPathElement leaves an unused import (StringUtil) and dead code removal without verification
body: The diff deletes the private method `groupMatchesSearchOrIsPathElement(GroupModel, String)` which was the only user of `org.keycloak.utils.StringUtil` in this file. The full file content shown still contains no remaining reference to `StringUtil`, but the import list at the top of the file (lines 1-14) does not show `StringUtil` being imported in the first place — meaning either the import was already absent (fine) or the shown content is inconsistent. More importantly, the removal is a behavior-relevant deletion bundled into a PR titled 'Fix NPE when accessing group concurrently': if `groupMatchesSearchOrIsPathElement` was used by group search/path filtering logic elsewhere (e.g., the admin `GroupsResource` search that decides whether a group matches a search term or is a path element), removing it without a replacement changes search semantics. The PR description gives no justification for this deletion; it should either be split into its own PR with explanation, or the method restored if still referenced. A maintainer cannot verify from this diff that no caller regressed.

title: Concurrency regression test has a race: the reader thread may never run before deletedAll is set, making the test vacuous
body: In `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti()`, the reader thread loops `while (!deletedAll.get())` calling `groups(...)`, but there is no synchronization guaranteeing the thread has started (or performed at least one read) before the main thread deletes all 100 groups and sets `deletedAll.set(true)` at line 155. If the JVM schedules the reader thread only after `deletedAll` is already true, the loop body executes zero times, no concurrent read ever overlaps with the deletes, and the assertion `assertThat(caughtExceptions, Matchers.empty())` passes trivially — the test does not actually exercise the concurrent read/delete scenario it claims to cover, so it cannot catch the NPE from #40368. Additionally, the thread is never joined, so the test can finish (and the realm be torn down) while the reader thread is still issuing HTTP requests against a realm being cleaned up, producing flaky failures unrelated to the bug. Fix: use a `CountDownLatch`/`CyclicBarrier` to ensure at least one read has been issued before starting deletes (or loop the reader a fixed number of iterations), and `join()` the thread before asserting.

title: Concurrency test only exercises brief group listing, not the getSubGroupsCount() path that the fix actually changes
body: The production fix changes `GroupAdapter.getSubGroupsCount()` (the NPE source per issue #40368) and adds a null-guard there. The new test `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti()` only calls `managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(null, 0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, true)` — the top-level brief group listing. Whether that endpoint populates `subGroupCount` depends on the `subGroupsCount` flag in `GroupUtils.populateGroupHierarchyFromSubGroups`, which is not exercised here. If the NPE in #40368 was triggered via `getSubGroupsCount()` on a concurrently-deleted cached group (e.g., admin console tree rendering or `populateSubGroupCount`), this test never invokes that code path during the delete window, so it would not have failed before the fix and does not prove the fix. The test should also fetch a group representation with subGroupCount populated (e.g., `groups(..., brief=false)` or a search that sets `subGroupsCount=true`, or directly call the group's subgroups endpoint) concurrently with the deletions.

title: Added @Override on getRealm() is unrelated to the NPE fix and inconsistent with the rest of the class
body: The diff adds `@Override` to `getRealm()` (line 61-62). This is a cosmetic change unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (fixing the concurrent-access NPE), and it is inconsistent: the class implements `InRealm` yet none of the other interface-required or overridden methods in this class carry `@Override` in a consistent pattern, and sibling cached entities may differ. Per review guidelines this is a style preference, but it also signals the PR bundles unrelated cleanup; it should be dropped or split out so the fix diff stays minimal and reviewable.

title: getSubGroupsCount() silently returns null when the group has been deleted, changing the API contract
body: The fix for the NPE changes `getSubGroupsCount()` to return `null` when the underlying group no longer exists in the database (`model == null ? null : model.getSubGroupsCount()`). Previously it would throw an NPE (or IllegalStateException via other paths). `GroupModel.getSubGroupsCount()` is declared to return `Long` and callers such as `GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount()` (services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/utils/GroupUtils.java:90) pass the result directly to `GroupRepresentation.setSubGroupCount(Long)`, and admin REST representations expose this as a numeric subgroup count. Returning null here means a concurrently-deleted group now yields a representation with a null subGroupCount instead of a consistent value or an explicit error, which can produce NPEs in downstream consumers that unbox the Long (e.g. JSON serialization paths or UI code doing arithmetic/comparison on the count) and silently masks the fact that the group was deleted mid-request. The correct behavior for a group that disappeared concurrently is to treat it as invalidated/not-found (consistent with `isUpdated()` and `getDelegateForUpdate()` which throw `IllegalStateException("Not found in database")`), not to return null.

title: Removal of groupMatchesSearchOrIsPathElement leaves an unused import and a dangling comment
body: The diff deletes the private method `groupMatchesSearchOrIsPathElement` but the file still contains the comment `//From org.keycloak.admin.ui.rest.GroupsResource` on line 94 directly above `toRepresentation`, which referenced the removed code's origin, and the removal was not part of the NPE fix described in the PR. More importantly, the removed method referenced `org.keycloak.utils.StringUtil` (via `StringUtil.isBlank`); if that import existed it is now unused, and if any other code in the codebase called this private helper it would fail to compile — but since it was private, the real issue is that this unrelated deletion is bundled into a concurrency bugfix PR, making the change harder to review and revert. The deletion should either be moved to its own PR or, if kept, the dead comment on line 94 should be removed and the unused import (if present in the base version) cleaned up.

title: Concurrency test has a race that can make it pass without ever exercising the concurrent read path
body: In `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti`, the reader thread loops `while (!deletedAll.get())` calling `groups(null, 0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, true)`, but the main thread deletes all 100 groups and then sets `deletedAll.set(true)` (line 155) without joining the reader thread. If the deletes complete before the reader thread is scheduled (common on fast machines or under CI load), the reader thread may execute zero iterations, so the test asserts `caughtExceptions` is empty without ever having performed a concurrent read during deletion — a false pass that does not reproduce issue #40368. Additionally, the reader thread is never joined, so the assertion on line 157 can run while the reader is still mid-request, and any exception thrown after the assertion is silently lost (the thread dies with an uncaught exception). The test should `join()` the reader thread before asserting, and ideally ensure the reader has performed at least one iteration before starting deletes (e.g. a CountDownLatch or AtomicBoolean confirming first read completed) so the concurrent window is actually exercised.

title: Concurrency test only exercises brief group listing, not the getSubGroupsCount path that was actually fixed
body: The PR fixes an NPE in `GroupAdapter.getSubGroupsCount()` (model/infinispan/.../GroupAdapter.java:272-276), which is invoked when `subGroupsCount=true` is requested on group hierarchy population (see `GroupUtils.populateGroupHierarchyFromSubGroups` with `subGroupsCount` flag, services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/utils/GroupUtils.java:40-42). However, the new test `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti` only calls `managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(null, 0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, true)` — the `true` here is `briefRepresentation`, not `subGroupsCount`. The admin client `groups()` overload with a `briefRepresentation` boolean does not request subgroup counts, so the fixed code path (`getSubGroupsCount()` on a cached group whose DB row was concurrently deleted) is never executed by this test. The test would not have caught the original NPE. It should either call the endpoint that populates subGroupCount (e.g. the groups search with `subGroupsCount` parameter used by the admin console hierarchy endpoint) or directly fetch a group representation with subGroupCount while deletes are in flight.

title: getSubGroupsCount() silently returns null when the group no longer exists, masking the NPE fix and changing API contract
body: The fix for the concurrent-access NPE changes `getSubGroupsCount()` from `getGroupModel().getSubGroupsCount()` (which threw NPE when the group was deleted concurrently) to `modelSupplier.get()` followed by `return model == null ? null : model.getSubGroupsCount()`. The problem is that `GroupModel.getSubGroupsCount()` is declared to return `Long` and callers (e.g. `GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount` at services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/utils/GroupUtils.java:90, which does `representation.setSubGroupCount(group.getSubGroupsCount())`) may auto-unbox the result or assume non-null. Returning null here converts a previously loud failure (NPE) into a silent null that can cause a new NPE downstream at the unboxing site, or produce a GroupRepresentation with a null subGroupCount where the API contract expects a count. The correct behavior when the cached group has been deleted concurrently is to invalidate and re-fetch via `getDelegateForUpdate()` (which throws IllegalStateException if truly gone) or to return 0, not to propagate null. Returning null is a data-integrity/API-contract break that merely moves the NPE to a different location.

title: Removal of groupMatchesSearchOrIsPathElement leaves an unused import and dead code path
body: The PR deletes the private method `groupMatchesSearchOrIsPathElement(GroupModel group, String search)` from GroupUtils.java (lines 101-110 in the old version). This method referenced `StringUtil.isBlank(search)` — the `org.keycloak.utils.StringUtil` class is in the same package so no import needed — but more importantly, the deletion leaves the class with no remaining references to that helper. If any other code (e.g. `GroupsResource` in the admin UI REST module, which the comment on line 94 says this class was copied from) still calls `GroupUtils.groupMatchesSearchOrIsPathElement`, this is a compile break. Even if it was private and unused within this file, removing it without verifying no reflective or cross-module usage exists is risky. Additionally, the deletion is unrelated to the stated PR goal (fixing an NPE on concurrent group access) and should either be reverted or justified in the PR description.

title: Concurrency test has a race condition: reader thread may not start before deletions complete, making the test ineffective
body: The new test `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti` starts a reader thread that loops calling `groups().groups(null, 0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, true)` while the main thread deletes 100 groups. However, there is no synchronization ensuring the reader thread has actually started and executed at least one iteration before the main thread begins deleting. If the main thread deletes all 100 groups before the reader thread is scheduled (which is plausible on a fast machine or under CI load), the reader thread will start, see `deletedAll == true` immediately, exit its while loop without ever making a request, and the test will pass vacuously — it never actually exercised the concurrent read-during-delete scenario that is the entire point of the regression test for issue #40368. The test needs a latch or barrier (e.g. `CountDownLatch` signaled by the reader after its first successful call, awaited by the main thread before starting deletions) to guarantee overlap between reads and deletes.

title: Reader thread is never joined, so exceptions or hangs in the reader may go unnoticed and the thread leaks
body: The test creates a `new Thread(...)` for concurrent group reads but never calls `join()` on it. After `deletedAll.set(true)`, the main thread immediately asserts `caughtExceptions` is empty and returns. The reader thread may still be in the middle of an HTTP call when the assertion runs; if that call throws after the assertion (e.g. due to a connection reset during test teardown), the exception is silently swallowed (added to `caughtExceptions` but never checked again). Worse, if the reader thread hangs (e.g. the HTTP client blocks indefinitely), the test will pass and the thread will leak, potentially interfering with subsequent tests in the same JVM. The test should store the Thread reference, call `thread.join()` after setting `deletedAll`, and then assert on `caughtExceptions`.

title: getDelegateForUpdate() check-then-act on volatile 'updated' is not atomic; concurrent updates can create duplicate delegates
body: The PR title says 'Fix NPE when accessing group concurrently' but the core concurrency pattern in `getDelegateForUpdate()` (lines 57-63) remains a non-atomic check-then-act on the volatile field `updated`: `if (updated == null) { ... updated = modelSupplier.get(); }`. Two threads calling a mutating method (e.g. `setName`) concurrently can both see `updated == null`, both call `cacheSession.registerGroupInvalidation(cached.getId())`, and both assign `updated`. This means two different delegate GroupModel instances can be created, and mutations applied to one may be lost or applied to a stale delegate. The `volatile` keyword only guarantees visibility, not atomicity of the compound operation. The PR does not address this race; it only fixes the specific NPE in `getSubGroupsCount()`. If the goal is to fix concurrent access to groups, this method needs synchronization (e.g. `synchronized` or double-checked locking with a lock object) to ensure only one delegate is created per adapter instance.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator passes negative offsets to Django queryset slicing, which raises AssertionError
body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0, the code executes `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start_offset (line 880-882). Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ explicitly asserts that slice indices are non-negative ('Negative indexing is not supported.'), so any request with a negative cursor offset will raise an unhandled AssertionError and produce a 500 error. The comment claiming 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is factually wrong. This is not a performance optimization at all — it is a crash path. Additionally, the negative-offset branch is reachable by any client that crafts a cursor string with a negative offset (Cursor.from_string in src/sentry/utils/cursors.py parses the offset with int(bits[1]) and performs no validation), so this is a remotely triggerable denial-of-service on the audit log endpoint for superusers/global-access members.

title: BasePaginator.get_result silently clamps negative offsets to 0, corrupting pagination semantics
body: The change to BasePaginator.get_result (lines 179-184) replaces `stop = offset + limit + extra; results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. For a non-prev cursor with a negative offset, the old code would have raised Django's 'Negative indexing is not supported' AssertionError; the new code silently clamps the offset to 0 and returns the first page of results while build_cursor computes next/prev cursors from the original (negative) offset value. This produces inconsistent cursor state: the returned page does not correspond to the cursor the client sent, and the emitted next/prev cursors are computed against an offset that was never actually used, leading to skipped or duplicated rows across pages. This modifies the behavior of the shared BasePaginator used by Paginator and DateTimePaginator across the entire API, not just the audit log endpoint, so any endpoint whose clients send a negative offset (which Cursor.from_string happily parses) now gets silently wrong results instead of an error.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the endpoint orders by '-datetime' (a DateTimeField)
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key (lines 838-840) does `value = getattr(item, self.key)` and then `int(math.floor(value) ...)`, which requires the sort key to be a number. However, OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint uses it with order_by='-datetime' (organization_auditlogs.py line 80), so self.key is 'datetime' and getattr returns a datetime object; math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError. The existing DateTimePaginator handles this by converting via strftime('%s.%f') * multiplier (lines 233-236). The new paginator is therefore broken for its only intended call site — every paginated request through the optimized path will raise a 500. The class is essentially a copy of Paginator (integer keys) mislabeled as a datetime-capable 'optimized' paginator.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor value, incompatible with datetime ordering
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor (lines 842-843) returns cursor.value unchanged, which for the audit log endpoint is a millisecond timestamp integer (as produced by DateTimePaginator.get_item_key). BasePaginator.build_queryset then injects this raw integer into the SQL WHERE clause comparing against the datetime column (`{col} {operator} %s` with the integer as a parameter, lines 112-126). Comparing a datetime column to an integer epoch-milliseconds value will either error or silently match nothing depending on the database backend, so resuming pagination from a cursor on the optimized path returns wrong/empty results. The correct behavior (as in DateTimePaginator, lines 238-241) is to convert the cursor value back to a datetime via datetime.fromtimestamp(value / multiplier). Combined with the get_item_key bug above, the optimized path cannot correctly paginate at all.

title: paginate() is called with an unsupported enable_advanced_features kwarg that is silently ignored
body: The endpoint calls self.paginate(..., paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator, ..., enable_advanced_features=True). The paginate helper on the API base class constructs the paginator as paginator_cls(queryset=..., order_by=..., on_results=..., ...) and does not forward arbitrary kwargs such as enable_advanced_features. As a result the OptimizedCursorPaginator is always constructed with enable_advanced_features=False (its default), and the negative-offset branch in get_result is dead code from this call site. The endpoint author clearly intended the advanced behavior to be active (the comment says 'Enable advanced pagination for admins'), so the flag is misleading: the code path that the PR claims to enable is never actually enabled, and the behavior differs from what the code and comments suggest. Either the paginate helper must be extended to forward the kwarg, or the parameter must be removed.

title: Undocumented, unvalidated query parameter switches the endpoint to an experimental paginator gated only on a string comparison
body: The endpoint introduces a new public query parameter `optimized_pagination` (line 70) that switches the response to a new, experimental paginator. It is not declared in AuditLogQueryParamSerializer, so it bypasses serializer validation entirely, and it is not documented in the endpoint's publish status or API docs (the endpoint is ApiPublishStatus.EXPERIMENTAL). The gate `request.GET.get('optimized_pagination') == 'true'` combined with `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` means any superuser can flip the endpoint into a code path (OptimizedCursorPaginator) that, per the other findings, crashes on datetime keys and mishandles negative offsets. Exposing a behavior-changing, unreviewed paginator switch via an ad-hoc query parameter — rather than a serializer field, a feature flag, or a versioned API — is a security and stability risk: it changes response shape/semantics for existing clients and creates an untested attack surface. The parameter should be removed, declared in the serializer, or replaced with a proper feature flag.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator.get_result with divergent, incorrect offset handling
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator is a near-verbatim copy of BasePaginator.get_result (lines 845-911 vs 136-215) with the addition of the negative-offset branch. Duplicating ~70 lines of subtle cursor logic (extra-row fetching, is_prev filtering, result reversal, build_cursor invocation) means the two implementations will drift, and the copy already contains the same latent bug the original had (the `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` check at line 891 uses the raw offset rather than start_offset, so it is wrong whenever the offset was clamped or negative). The right fix is to parameterize BasePaginator (or subclass minimally) rather than copy the method. As written, any future fix to BasePaginator.get_result (e.g., the known non-unique-key TODO at line 151-152) will not apply to this class, silently reintroducing bugs on the audit log endpoint.

title: Pre-existing typo 'queryset.query.order_b' truncates the field name, breaking order reversal for '-key' orderings
body: In BasePaginator.build_queryset, line 105 assigns `queryset.query.order_b = tuple(new_order_by)` — the attribute is `order_b`, not `order_by`. This means that when the queryset is already ordered by '-<key>' and an ascending traversal is requested (the is_prev path for descending endpoints like the audit log's '-datetime'), the order reversal is silently not applied: the queryset keeps its descending order while the cursor logic assumes ascending. The subsequent code then filters with the wrong comparison operator and reverses results, yielding pages in the wrong order with duplicated/missing rows when paginating backwards. This is a pre-existing bug in shared pagination code, but the PR's changes (which rely on correct is_prev handling and touch this exact method's callers) make it directly relevant: backward pagination on the audit log endpoint is broken by it. The assignment should be `queryset.query.order_by = tuple(new_order_by)`.

title: Cursor.from_string accepts negative offsets with no validation, enabling the negative-offset code paths
body: Cursor.from_string (lines 53-61) parses the offset with `int(bits[1])` and performs no range validation, so a client-supplied cursor string such as '0:-999999:0' produces a Cursor with a large negative offset. The PR's comments in cursors.py (lines 26-27) explicitly state the intent to 'allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios', and both BasePaginator.get_result and OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result contain new branches keyed on negative offsets. Since cursors are client-controlled input (passed via the ?cursor= query parameter on every paginated endpoint), accepting negative offsets without validation turns the new slicing logic into an attack surface: on the optimized path it triggers the Django negative-indexing AssertionError (500/DoS), and on the base path it silently corrupts pagination state. The cursor parser should reject negative offsets (raise ValueError) unless a specific, validated feature requires them, and the 'performance optimization' comments justifying negative offsets should be removed since they describe behavior that is either a crash or a correctness bug.

title: No tests cover OptimizedCursorPaginator, the negative-offset branches, or the audit log endpoint's new parameter
body: The PR adds a new paginator class (~90 lines), modifies the shared BasePaginator.get_result offset handling, adds a new query parameter to a production endpoint, and changes cursor semantics — but the changed-files list contains no test files. There are no tests for: OptimizedCursorPaginator with a datetime key (which crashes per the get_item_key finding), negative cursor offsets on either paginator, the optimized_pagination query parameter on OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint, or the clamping behavior in BasePaginator.get_result. Given that the new code paths are reachable from a public API endpoint and contain at least two crash bugs and one silent-corruption bug, the absence of tests is a merge blocker: these bugs would have been caught by basic happy-path and cursor-resume tests.

title: Comments justifying negative offsets describe behavior that is a crash or a correctness bug, not an optimization
body: The comments added at lines 179-181 ('Performance optimization: For high-traffic scenarios, allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination without full dataset scanning. This is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions') and at lines 874-879 in OptimizedCursorPaginator ('The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically', 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level') are factually incorrect: Django does not support negative queryset slicing (it raises AssertionError), and clamping a negative offset to 0 does not produce correct pagination. The claim that negative offsets avoid 'full dataset scanning' is also wrong — SQL OFFSET with a negative value is invalid, and the clamped path simply returns the first page. These comments will mislead future maintainers into believing the behavior is intentional and safe. They should be removed along with the negative-offset support.

title: Privilege check uses organization_context.member.has_global_access without a None guard
body: Line 71 evaluates `organization_context.member.has_global_access` directly.
