If organization_context.member is None (which RpcUserOrganizationContext allows for contexts without a membership record), this raises AttributeError and returns a 500 instead of falling back to the standard paginator. The surrounding code already handles the membership implicitly via permission_classes, but this new expression introduces a new None-dereference path on a production endpoint. It should be written defensively, e.g. `bool(organization_context.member and organization_context.member.has_global_access)`.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator passes negative offsets to Django queryset slicing, which raises AssertionError
body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0, the code executes `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start_offset (line 880-882). Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ explicitly asserts that slice indices are non-negative ('Negative indexing is not supported.'), so any request with a negative cursor offset will raise an unhandled AssertionError and produce a 500 error. The comment claiming 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is factually wrong. This code path is reachable from the audit logs endpoint whenever an admin passes a cursor with a negative offset (cursors are client-supplied strings parsed in Cursor.from_string, which accepts negative integers).

title: BasePaginator.get_result change breaks prev-cursor pagination by clamping negative offsets to 0
body: The modification to BasePaginator.get_result changed `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` to `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset; results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`. For a prev cursor (is_prev=True) with a negative offset — which OffsetPaginator-style prev cursors legitimately produce (e.g. `Cursor(limit, page - 1, True, page > 0)` yields offset -1 on the first page) — the old code sliced with the negative offset, while the new code passes the raw negative offset only when is_prev is True... actually the new code preserves the negative offset for is_prev, but for non-prev cursors it clamps negative offsets to 0, silently returning the first page instead of erroring or handling the value. More importantly, the change alters behavior for all existing paginator subclasses (Paginator, DateTimePaginator) that share BasePaginator.get_result: previously a negative offset would hit Django's 'Negative indexing is not supported' assertion; now non-prev negative offsets silently clamp to 0, returning incorrect data (the first page) instead of failing. This is a silent data-correctness change to a shared, widely-used code path with no test coverage shown.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator prev-cursor trimming logic uses unclamped offset, producing wrong page sizes
body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, the prev-cursor trimming branch checks `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra:` (line 891) using the raw `offset = cursor.offset`, but the actual slice was performed with `start_offset` which may differ from `offset` (when offset is negative and advanced features are enabled, or when offset is negative and is_prev is False where start_offset = max(0, offset)). When start_offset != offset, the length comparison `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` is computed against the wrong expected length, so the extra fetched row is not trimmed (or a legitimate row is trimmed), corrupting page contents and cursor boundaries. The same mismatch exists in the inherited BasePaginator code at line 192, where the slice now uses start_offset but the trim check still uses `offset`.

title: paginate() called with unknown keyword argument enable_advanced_features
body: The endpoint calls self.paginate(..., paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator, ..., enable_advanced_features=True). The paginate helper on the API endpoint base class does not accept an `enable_advanced_features` parameter — it forwards only known kwargs (queryset, paginator_cls, order_by, on_results, etc.) to the paginator constructor. Passing an unrecognized keyword will raise a TypeError at runtime ('unexpected keyword argument'), making the optimized path completely broken — every admin request with optimized_pagination=true will 500. Even if paginate forwarded **kwargs, the OptimizedCursorPaginator constructor signature is `__init__(self, *args, enable_advanced_features=False, **kwargs)`, so it would work only if forwarding exists, which it does not in the standard endpoint paginate implementation.

title: Admin-gated pagination feature relies on client-controlled query param and exposes a broken/dangerous code path
body: The optimized paginator is enabled purely by the client-supplied query parameter `optimized_pagination=true` combined with an admin check (`request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`). The feature is undocumented, untested, and — per the paginator bugs — actively dangerous: it enables negative-offset slicing on querysets. Gating a dangerous code path on a query string flag rather than a server-side configuration or feature flag means any superuser (a broad population in Sentry's model) can trigger the broken negative-slicing path, and the flag provides no audit trail. Additionally, `organization_context.member` may be None for users without a membership, causing an AttributeError on `.has_global_access` — the expression is not null-safe.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key assumes numeric key; audit logs order by datetime, causing TypeError
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `int(math.floor(value) ...)` on `getattr(item, self.key)`. The audit logs endpoint uses this paginator with `order_by="-datetime"`, so self.key is 'datetime' and the value is a datetime object. math.floor() on a datetime raises TypeError ('unsupported operand type(s) for -: datetime.datetime'... actually math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError: must be real number, not datetime). The class is a copy of Paginator (integer keys), not DateTimePaginator, so using it with a datetime ordering — exactly what the endpoint does — will crash during build_cursor when computing cursor keys. The endpoint should either use DateTimePaginator semantics or the paginator must handle datetime keys.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator is a verbatim copy of BasePaginator.get_result with no actual optimization
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator.get_result almost line-for-line; the only behavioral differences are the negative-offset branch (which is broken, see other findings) and accepting an enable_advanced_features flag. There is no query optimization (no keyset/seek pagination, no deferred fields, no index hints, no count_hits avoidance). The claimed 'optimized query path for large datasets' in the docstring is false — the class performs the same OFFSET-based slicing as the base paginator, which is precisely the slow pattern for high-volume tables. Shipping this as a 'performance enhancement' is misleading and adds a maintenance burden and a dangerous code path for zero measured benefit.

title: Pre-existing typo queryset.order_b introduced in untouched code path (context for review)
body: Line 105 contains `queryset.query.order_b = tuple(new_order_by)` — a pre-existing typo (should be `order_by`) in BasePaginator.build_queryset. It is not introduced by this diff, but it means the branch that un-reverses an explicitly descending order_by silently does nothing, which interacts with the new paginator subclass that relies on build_queryset. Worth fixing while touching this file, but not caused by this PR.

title: Undocumented query parameter optimized_pagination added to an EXPERIMENTAL public API endpoint
body: The endpoint's publish_status is EXPERIMENTAL and it is a public API surface. The PR adds an undocumented, admin-only query parameter (`optimized_pagination`) that switches paginator implementations and changes response cursor semantics. API consumers cannot discover this parameter, and because cursor formats differ between DateTimePaginator and OptimizedCursorPaginator (datetime-millis vs raw value), a client that flips the flag mid-pagination will receive cursors it cannot use with the other paginator, causing incorrect/empty pages. The parameter should be documented, or the feature should be server-side only.

title: Comment claims negative offsets are allowed, but no validation or handling exists in Cursor
body: The added comment in Cursor.__init__ states 'Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios', but the class does nothing to allow or validate them — it simply stores int(offset), and Cursor.from_string happily parses negative offsets from client input. The comment describes intent that is implemented (dangerously) elsewhere; as written it misleads readers into thinking Cursor itself supports/sanitizes negative offsets. Either remove the comment or implement actual validation (e.g., reject negative offsets at parse time for non-advanced cursors).

title: No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator, the BasePaginator offset change, or the endpoint's new branch
body: The PR adds a new paginator class, modifies shared BasePaginator.get_result slicing behavior (affecting Paginator and DateTimePaginator used across the entire API), and adds a new endpoint branch — but includes no tests. The BasePaginator change alters behavior for every cursor-paginated endpoint in the codebase (negative offsets now clamp to 0 for non-prev cursors instead of raising), and the new paginator's negative-offset path, prev-cursor trimming, and datetime-key handling are all untested. Given the critical slicing bug, at minimum tests must cover: negative offset rejection/clamping, prev-cursor round trips, and the audit logs endpoint with optimized_pagination=true for admin and non-admin users.

title: Negative-offset slicing in OptimizedCursorPaginator silently returns wrong rows or raises IndexError
body: When `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code executes `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset` (e.g. `queryset[-5:96]`). Django QuerySets do NOT support negative slicing — this raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.` at query evaluation time, turning any request with a negative cursor offset into a 500 error. Even if it were supported (e.g. on a list), negative slicing counts from the END of the result set, which would return the wrong rows entirely (the last N rows of the table rather than rows before the cursor), corrupting pagination results. The comment 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is factually wrong. Additionally, the cursor value is attacker-controlled via the `cursor` query parameter, so any client of the audit log endpoint passing `optimized_pagination=true` with a crafted negative-offset cursor triggers this. The negative-offset branch must be removed or replaced with a correct reverse-pagination implementation.

title: BasePaginator.get_result clamps negative offsets to 0, breaking prev-cursor pagination and enabling duplicate rows
body: The change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` alters existing behavior for ALL paginators using BasePaginator (Paginator, DateTimePaginator, etc.), not just the new one. Previously `queryset[offset:stop]` with a negative offset would raise Django's 'Negative indexing is not supported' error; now a negative offset is silently clamped to 0, so the query restarts from the beginning of the dataset. Cursor offsets are derived from client-supplied cursor strings (`Cursor.from_string` parses `int(bits[1])` with no validation), so a client can send a cursor with a negative offset and receive the first page of results while the returned next/prev cursors are computed from those wrong results — producing duplicated rows across pages and inconsistent pagination state. This is a data-integrity regression in a shared, core pagination path used by many endpoints. Negative offsets should be rejected with BadPaginationError (as OffsetPaginator and ChainPaginator already do), not clamped.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator prev-page trimming uses unclamped negative offset in length comparison
body: In the `cursor.is_prev and cursor.value` branch, the code checks `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra:` where `offset = cursor.offset` can be negative (the new code path explicitly allows negative offsets). With a negative offset this comparison can never be true when it should be, or can be true when it should not, so the extra fetched row is not trimmed correctly — resulting in an off-by-one row appearing (or disappearing) at the boundary of reverse pagination. The comparison should use the actual `start_offset` used for the slice, not the raw (possibly negative) `offset`.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the audit log endpoint orders by '-datetime'
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(value) ...)` on `getattr(item, self.key)`. The endpoint wires it with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `self.key == "datetime"` and `value` is a `datetime` object — `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError`, so every paginated request through this paginator crashes with a 500. The class is a copy of `Paginator` (integer keys) and was never adapted to datetime keys; it should subclass/reuse `DateTimePaginator`'s key handling (millisecond conversion via `strftime("%s.%f")` and `value_from_cursor` converting back with `datetime.fromtimestamp`), otherwise the 'optimized' path is entirely broken for the only endpoint that uses it.

title: Undocumented, unvalidated query parameter gates a different paginator based on superuser/global-access status
body: `use_optimized = request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"` introduces a hidden, undocumented API parameter that switches the response's pagination behavior (different paginator class, different cursor semantics) for superusers and members with global access. Because the two paginators produce different cursor formats and edge-case behavior (and the optimized one is broken — see other findings), clients that cache or persist cursors across requests can get inconsistent results. More importantly, the parameter is not declared in any serializer or API documentation, so it is invisible to API consumers and to schema generation, and the `enable_advanced_features=True` flag is passed unconditionally whenever the user is privileged — there is no way to opt out per-request. Feature-gating pagination internals on a raw query-string flag is a contract hazard; the paginator choice should be deterministic per endpoint, not client-controlled.

title: AttributeError risk: organization_context.member may be None, and has_global_access is not a documented field
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences `organization_context.member` without a None check. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is an optional RPC field (it is None when the request is not authenticated as an organization member, e.g. certain internal/service or staff flows that still reach this endpoint), which would raise `AttributeError` and return a 500 instead of a paginated response. Additionally, `has_global_access` is not a standard field on the member RPC model used elsewhere in this codebase (global access is typically determined via `OrganizationMember` flags / `has_global_access` on the ORM model or via `organization_context.flags`), so this check may silently never grant access or may not exist on the RPC type at all — it needs verification against the actual RPC schema.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator is a near-verbatim duplicate of BasePaginator.get_result with no actual optimization
body: The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` (lines 845-911) duplicates `BasePaginator.get_result` almost line-for-line, including the same `count_hits` subquery, the same `extra` row fetch, and the same slicing strategy. The only behavioral differences are the broken negative-offset branch and the broken datetime key handling. There is no performance optimization present — no keyset/seek pagination (the `build_queryset` range filter is identical to the base class), no deferred `count_hits`, no `only()`/`values()` projection. Shipping a duplicate ~70-line method that claims 'optimized query path for large datasets' in its docstring is misleading and adds maintenance surface for zero benefit; either implement a real optimization (e.g. seek/keyset pagination on (datetime, id)) or delete the class and use DateTimePaginator.

title: Pre-existing typo `queryset.query.order_b` introduced/preserved in ordering-reversal path
body: Line 105 assigns `queryset.query.order_b = tuple(new_order_by)` — the attribute is `order_by`, not `order_b`. This is in the `elif ("-%s" % self.key) in queryset.query.order_by:` branch of `build_queryset`, which executes when a queryset already ordered by `-key` is paginated with an ascending (prev-page) cursor. The assignment silently sets a nonexistent attribute, so the intended ordering reversal never happens and the queryset keeps its original `-key` ordering — producing incorrectly ordered results for prev-cursor pagination on pre-ordered querysets. This path is reachable from the audit log endpoint (queryset ordered by `-datetime` via `order_by="-datetime"` combined with a prev cursor).

title: Comment claims negative offsets are allowed, but Cursor.from_string and all paginators reject or mishandle them
body: The added comment states 'Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios', but nothing in `Cursor` validates or specially handles negative offsets: `from_string` happily parses them, `OffsetPaginator.get_result` raises `BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")` for them, `ChainPaginator` and `CombinedQuerysetPaginator` do the same, and `BasePaginator` now silently clamps them to 0 (see other finding). The comment documents behavior that does not exist and contradicts the rest of the codebase; it should be removed or replaced with an explicit statement that negative offsets are invalid.

title: No tests cover the new optimized-pagination branch, the negative-offset path, or the paginator changes
body: The PR adds a new paginator class, a new endpoint branch keyed on `optimized_pagination=true` and user privilege, and modifies the shared `BasePaginator.get_result` slicing logic — but includes no tests. Existing paginator tests (tests/sentry/api/test_paginator.py) and audit log endpoint tests (tests/sentry/api/endpoints/test_organization_auditlogs.py) are untouched, so the regressions described in the other findings (negative-offset clamping in BasePaginator, TypeError on datetime keys, AssertionError on negative slicing) would all pass CI. At minimum, tests are needed for: BasePaginator with a negative-offset cursor (must raise, not clamp), OptimizedCursorPaginator with a datetime-ordered queryset, and the audit log endpoint with `optimized_pagination=true` for superuser vs regular member.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator passes negative offsets to Django queryset slicing, which raises AssertionError
body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is true and cursor.offset < 0, the code executes `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start_offset (line 880-882). Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ asserts that slice indices are non-negative ('Negative indexing is not supported.'), so any request with a negative cursor offset will raise an unhandled AssertionError and return a 500 to the client. The comment claiming 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is factually wrong. Additionally, the BasePaginator.get_result change at line 182 (`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`) silently clamps negative offsets to 0 for forward pagination, which changes cursor semantics: a client-supplied negative offset is silently treated as offset 0, producing incorrect/duplicated results rather than an error. Negative offsets are never legitimately produced by build_cursor, so this 'feature' only creates a crash vector and a silent data-correctness bug.

title: Undocumented query parameter switches audit log endpoint to a paginator with broken negative-offset handling, gated only on a client-controlled flag plus superuser status
body: The endpoint now branches on `request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"` combined with `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`, and passes `enable_advanced_features=True` to OptimizedCursorPaginator. This introduces an undocumented, experimental API surface on an EXPERIMENTAL publish-status endpoint: (1) the `optimized_pagination` query parameter is not documented anywhere and silently changes response/cursor semantics for admins; (2) OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses `getattr(item, self.key)` and treats the value as a number (`math.floor(value)`), but the endpoint orders by `-datetime`, so the key is a datetime object — `math.floor(datetime)` raises TypeError, meaning the optimized path will crash whenever build_cursor computes keys (i.e., on any non-empty result set). The paginator is effectively untested (no tests reference OptimizedCursorPaginator) and broken for its only intended use.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key crashes on datetime keys (TypeError from math.floor on datetime)
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `value = getattr(item, self.key); return int(math.floor(value) ...)`. It is used by organization_auditlogs.py with order_by="-datetime", so self.key == "datetime" and value is a datetime. math.floor() requires a number (__floor__/__index__), so this raises TypeError: 'datetime.datetime' object cannot be interpreted as an integer. The class was clearly copied from Paginator (integer keys) without adapting to DateTimePaginator's millisecond conversion. Any paginated request through this paginator with results will 500. There are no tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator, so this ships broken.

title: BasePaginator.get_result silently clamps negative offsets to 0, corrupting pagination for all existing paginator users
body: The change to BasePaginator.get_result (shared by Paginator, DateTimePaginator, and all existing endpoints) replaces `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. Previously a negative offset would hit Django's 'Negative indexing is not supported' assertion (a loud failure); now it is silently clamped to 0, so a malformed/hostile cursor with a negative offset returns the first page of results instead of an error. This changes behavior for every endpoint using BasePaginator subclasses and masks client bugs; it also makes the subsequent `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` check at line 192 inconsistent (comparing against a negative offset that was never used). Other paginator classes in the same file (OffsetPaginator line 287, ChainPaginator line 748, etc.) explicitly raise BadPaginationError on negative offsets — this change makes BasePaginator inconsistent with the file's own convention.

title: Eviction via ZPOPMIN drops the oldest spans by end_timestamp score, silently losing span data and breaking segment completeness
body: The script now caps each segment set at 1000 members with `redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)`. Because the buffer is now a sorted set scored by end_timestamp_precise (see buffer.py zadd), ZPOPMIN evicts the spans with the *earliest* end timestamps — i.e., it silently discards real span data whenever a segment exceeds 1000 spans. Previously the Python side enforced max_segment_spans=1001 only at flush time (logging an error and skipping the oversized segment); now data is destroyed at insert time with no metric, no log, and no signal. Consequences: (1) silently incomplete traces shipped downstream — a correctness/data-integrity regression; (2) the eviction happens inside the Lua script where the Python-side `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` metric can no longer fire; (3) the eviction count is computed from `span_count`, which is only set when a ZUNIONSTORE ran — when neither union branch executes (e.g., root span arriving first, or set_span_id == parent_span_id with no existing set), span_count is recomputed via zcard (line 58-60), but when a union *did* run, ZUNIONSTORE's return value is the cardinality *after* the union, which is correct — however if both unions run, the second assignment overwrites with the post-second-union count, which is also correct; the real issue is the silent data loss itself. Also note the eviction threshold (1000) is hardcoded in Lua while SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans (1001) still exists in Python, creating two divergent limits.

title: Redirect-chain traversal limit reduced from 10000 to 1000 without handling the overflow case
body: The loop `for i = 0, 1000 do` follows redirect mappings in the `span-buf:sr:` hash. The original code used 10000 with an explicit comment that the limit means segment trees deeper than 10k may not be joined correctly. The new limit of 1000 silently exits the loop after 1001 iterations *without* breaking — when the loop exhausts, `set_span_id` still holds an intermediate (non-root) span id, and the script proceeds to merge into that intermediate set and write a redirect from span_id to it. This is functionally the same failure mode as before but at a 10x lower depth, and the returned `redirect_depth` (1000) is indistinguishable from a legitimate depth-1000 chain, so the Python metrics (min/max_redirect_depth gauges) cannot alert on truncation. Deep chains (e.g., from long-running traces or pathological redirect accumulation) will now be split into multiple segments more often, producing duplicate/partial segments downstream.

title: ZADD keyed by raw payload bytes makes duplicate spans overwrite each other and breaks set semantics for identical payloads
body: process_spans now writes spans with `p.zadd(set_key, {span.payload: span.end_timestamp_precise for span in subsegment})`. In a Redis sorted set, the *member* is the payload bytes and the score is the timestamp. Two consequences: (1) If the same span payload is processed twice (at-least-once Kafka delivery, consumer rebalance replay, or the same span appearing in two batches), the second ZADD silently overwrites the first — previously SADD also deduplicated, so this is not a regression per se, but combined with the score it means the *latest* end_timestamp wins, which is fine; (2) more importantly, the dict comprehension `{span.payload: ... for span in subsegment}` collapses multiple spans with identical payload bytes within the same batch into a single entry *before* Redis is involved — if a batch legitimately contains two distinct Span objects whose serialized payloads are byte-identical (possible when end_timestamp_precise differs but... actually payload includes the timestamp, so identical payload implies identical span), this is mostly benign. The real issue: the member being the full payload means ZSCAN in _load_segment_data returns (payload, score) tuples — handled — but ZUNIONSTORE in the Lua script aggregates scores with SUM by default across the two source sets, so a span present in both set_key and span_key gets its end_timestamp *doubled* as its score after merge. Since scores now drive ZPOPMIN eviction order (see add-buffer.lua finding), merged segments have corrupted eviction ordering: spans that participated in a merge are ranked as if they had ~2x their end timestamp and will be evicted last / retained incorrectly, and the flush ordering semantics change. The score is no longer a pure end_timestamp.

title: max_segment_spans limit silently removed from flush path while Lua now evicts at 1000 — the Python-side guard and metric are dead code
body: The diff removes the `if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans:` check (and its `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` metric + error log) from _load_segment_data, on the assumption that the Lua script now caps segments at 1000 spans. But the constructor still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` (line 150), which is now unused — dead configuration that misleads operators into thinking the flush path enforces a span-count limit. Worse, the two limits disagree (Lua 1000 vs Python 1001), and the Python-side metric that alerted on oversized segments no longer exists, so dashboards/alerts on `segment_span_count_exceeded` silently stop firing. Either remove the unused parameter or keep a defensive check in Python.

title: __reduce__ drops segment_page_size and max_segment_bytes/max_segment_spans when pickling SpansBuffer for multiprocessing
body: SpansBuffer.__reduce__ returns `(SpansBuffer, (self.assigned_shards, self.span_buffer_timeout_secs, self.span_buffer_root_timeout_secs, self.redis_ttl))` — it omits segment_page_size, max_segment_bytes, and max_segment_spans. This is pre-existing (not introduced by this diff), but the diff makes it more impactful: since max_segment_spans is now only a constructor default and the Lua script hardcodes 1000, a pickled buffer (used by run_task_with_multiprocessing in factory.py) silently uses defaults for the byte-size limit too. Not introduced by this PR, but worth noting the pickle path now diverges further from configured behavior. (Reporting as low since it's pre-existing; flagging because the PR touches this class's limits.)

title: process_batch assumes end_timestamp_precise is always present in the span payload — KeyError on older Relay payloads
body: process_batch now does `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` (direct indexing, line 141). The ingest-spans schema may mark this field optional or older Relay versions may omit it; direct [] indexing raises KeyError, which would crash the consumer task and block offset commits for the entire batch (poison-pill message). The neighboring fields use .get() with defaults (parent_span_id, is_remote). If the field can be absent, this should be `val.get("end_timestamp_precise", 0.0)` or the schema must be verified to guarantee presence. A missing field would halt span ingestion for affected partitions until the message is skipped/dead-lettered.

title: Pre-existing typo `queryset.query.order_b` (should be `order_by`) in BasePaginator.build_queryset, now reachable via OptimizedCursorPaginator
body: Line 105 reads `queryset.query.order_b = tuple(new_order_by)` — a typo for `order_by`. This is pre-existing, but it means that when the queryset is already ordered by `-key` and an ascending traversal is requested, the re-ordering is silently dropped (the attribute assignment creates a new unused attribute), so the queryset keeps its original descending order and pagination returns wrongly-ordered/duplicated rows. OptimizedCursorPaginator inherits build_queryset unchanged, so the new paginator inherits this latent bug. Worth fixing while touching this code, since the new paginator is presented as an 'optimized' path.

title: Comment claims negative offsets are allowed, but Cursor.from_string and all paginators either reject or mishandle them
body: The added comment on Cursor.__init__ says 'Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios'. In reality, Cursor.from_string will parse a negative offset from a client-supplied cursor string (int(bits[1]) accepts '-5'), and the only consumer that 'supports' it is OptimizedCursorPaginator's broken negative-slicing path (which crashes on Django's assertion), while BasePaginator now silently clamps it to 0 and OffsetPaginator/ChainPaginator raise BadPaginationError. The comment documents an intent that the codebase does not safely implement; it should be removed or the behavior made consistent (reject negative offsets at parse time).

title: No test covers the new 1000-span eviction behavior or the sorted-set migration of existing buffer keys
body: The PR changes the buffer from Redis sets (SADD/SSCAN/SUNIONSTORE) to sorted sets (ZADD/ZSCAN/ZUNIONSTORE) with eviction at 1000 spans. The test suite updates Span construction for the new end_timestamp_precise field but adds no test that: (1) a segment exceeding 1000 spans is truncated by the Lua script (data loss is untested and unasserted); (2) ZUNIONSTORE score aggregation (SUM across merged sets) doesn't corrupt eviction order; (3) mixed old-format (set) and new-format (zset) keys during a rolling deploy are handled — the Lua script calls ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE on keys that may still be plain sets from before the deploy, which returns a WRONGTYPE error and fails the whole EVALSHA pipeline for that batch. A rolling deploy of this consumer will hit WRONGTYPE errors on any segment key created by the old code until its TTL (redis_ttl=3600s) expires. There is no migration/compatibility handling and no test for it.

title: Behavior change on audit log endpoint gated by an undocumented query parameter — API contract break for admin users
body: Clients (including Sentry's own frontend and any admin tooling) that append `optimized_pagination=true` — or, more realistically, once this flag is documented/adopted — will get different cursor semantics (OptimizedCursorPaginator emits integer-floor datetime keys via the broken get_item_key, different cursor value encoding than DateTimePaginator's millisecond timestamps). DateTimePaginator encodes cursor values as milliseconds-since-epoch floats; OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key returns math.floor(datetime) which crashes, and value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor value (a number) which build_queryset then interpolates into a `datetime >= %s` SQL comparison — comparing a datetime column to an integer. The two paginators are not cursor-compatible, so a client that switches the flag mid-pagination gets corrupt cursors. The endpoint's publish_status is EXPERIMENTAL, but the flag is undocumented and the branch is controlled by request.user.is_superuser, meaning Sentry staff hitting the endpoint with the flag get a different (broken) response shape with no warning.

title: BasePaginator.get_result silently clamps negative offsets to 0, breaking prev-page pagination
body: The change to BasePaginator.get_result replaces `stop = offset + limit + extra; results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset; stop = start_offset + limit + extra; results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`. For a forward (non-prev) cursor with a negative offset, the old code would slice `queryset[offset:stop]` with a negative start, which in Django/Redis-backed querysets raises or behaves as an error, but more importantly the new code silently converts any negative offset into 0. A negative offset on a non-prev cursor is not a legitimate state produced by build_cursor (offsets are always >= 0 for forward cursors), so clamping hides client-supplied cursor corruption and returns the first page of results instead of rejecting the malformed cursor. Worse, the asymmetry (`max(0, offset)` only when `not cursor.is_prev`) means a prev cursor with a negative offset is passed straight into the queryset slice, which for Django raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.` — an unhandled 500. The comment claims 'the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions', which is false for negative slicing in Django. This changes behavior of the shared BasePaginator used by Paginator/DateTimePaginator across the entire API surface, not just the new endpoint.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator allows negative-offset slicing that bypasses pagination bounds and can leak/expose arbitrary rows
body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code executes `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with a negative `start_offset`. In Django, negative slicing on a queryset raises AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported'), so this branch is not 'efficient reverse pagination' — it is a crash path. The comment 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is factually wrong. If it did not raise (e.g. on a list-backed source), a negative offset would index from the end of the result set, returning rows from arbitrary positions outside the paginated window, and combined with the `is_prev` handling below (which compares `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` with a negative offset) the cursor math produces inconsistent next/prev cursors. The claim 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level' does not hold: the queryset is filtered by organization, but the offset manipulation lets a client jump to any position in that organization's dataset, and the resulting cursors can be replayed to enumerate rows outside the intended page window. The feature is also gated only by `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` plus a query param, but the paginator itself performs no validation that the offset is sane.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator prev-page trimming uses negative offset in length comparison, corrupting results
body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, the prev-page trimming logic `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra: results = results[:-1]` uses the raw `offset` (which may be negative when enable_advanced_features allowed it through). With a negative offset, `offset + limit + extra` can be less than the actual fetched length, so the extra sentinel row is never trimmed, and the sentinel row (which exists only to detect 'has more previous results') is included in the returned page. Conversely when the comparison accidentally matches, a legitimate data row is dropped. This produces duplicated or missing rows at page boundaries for prev cursors under the advanced-features path. The same expression in BasePaginator (line 192) is only reached with non-negative offsets in the original code path, so the new negative-offset branch introduces a new way to hit this logic with invalid values.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key assumes a numeric sort key, but is used with order_by='-datetime'
body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `value = getattr(item, self.key); return int(math.floor(value) ...)`, i.e. it treats the sort key as a number. It is instantiated in organization_auditlogs.py with `order_by='-datetime'`, so `self.key == 'datetime'` and `getattr(item, 'datetime')` returns a `datetime` object. `math.floor(datetime)` raises TypeError. The correct implementation for a datetime key is DateTimePaginator.get_item_key, which converts via `strftime('%s.%f') * multiplier`. So the 'optimized' paginator is wired to an endpoint sorting by datetime but implements the integer-key variant, and will crash on the first request that uses `optimized_pagination=true`. Additionally `value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` raw, but build_cursor stores the int(milliseconds) produced by get_item_key, and build_queryset then injects that integer into a SQL comparison against a timestamp column (`{col} {operator} %s`), which is a type mismatch. The class duplicates DateTimePaginator's contract incorrectly.

title: Privilege check uses organization_context.member without a None guard
body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences `organization_context.member` unconditionally. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is an optional member context; for a user who is a superuser the short-circuit avoids the crash, but for a non-superuser without membership context (e.g. an org-scoped token or an API key whose member context is absent), `organization_context.member` can be None and `.has_global_access` raises AttributeError, turning a permission check into a 500. The permission class OrganizationAuditPermission already gates access, but this line re-implements an authorization decision inline and unsafely. The check should be `getattr(organization_context.member, 'has_global_access', False)` or rely on the permission class.

title: Undocumented query parameter switches the paginator implementation, changing the response contract
body: `use_optimized = request.GET.get('optimized_pagination') == 'true'` silently swaps the paginator class for privileged users. The two paginators produce different cursor semantics (OptimizedCursorPaginator emits integer keys via math.floor on the sort value, DateTimePaginator emits millisecond timestamps), so the `cursor` values in the response `Link` header are not interchangeable between the two modes. A client that starts paginating with the default paginator and then adds `optimized_pagination=true` (or vice versa) will feed a cursor of one format into the other paginator, producing wrong pages or errors. There is no API versioning, no documentation of the parameter, and no validation that the cursor format matches the selected paginator. This is a contract break hidden behind an undocumented flag.

title: Eviction via ZPOPMIN during insert can drop spans from a segment that is concurrently being read, causing data loss
body: The script now enforces a 1000-span cap by calling `redis.call('zpopmin', set_key, span_count - 1000)` on every insert once the set exceeds 1000 members. ZPOPMIN removes the lowest-scored members, which are the spans with the earliest `end_timestamp_precise` — i.e. the oldest spans in the segment. The Python side previously enforced `max_segment_spans = 1001` only at flush time (`_load_segment_data` skipped oversized segments entirely with an error log), so the buffer tolerated >1000 spans until flush. Now the Lua script silently and permanently deletes spans at insert time. Consequences: (1) spans are dropped without any metric, log, or trace — the Python code has no visibility, so `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` can never fire and operators cannot detect the loss; (2) the eviction happens inside the same script that merges sets via ZUNIONSTORE, so a segment that transiently exceeds 1000 during a merge loses its oldest spans even though the pre-merge sets were each under the cap; (3) the dropped spans' offsets are still committed by the consumer (process_batch commits after process_spans), so the data is unrecoverable. The eviction policy (drop oldest) is also undocumented in buffer.py's docstring, which still describes sets as containing 'all data for a segment'.

title: ZUNIONSTORE overwrites span_count, losing the accumulated count across merges and disabling eviction
body: `span_count = redis.call('zunionstore', set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` is executed first, then at line 53 `span_count = redis.call('zunionstore', set_key, 2, set_key, parent_key)` overwrites it. ZUNIONSTORE returns the cardinality of the *destination* set after the union, so after the second call `span_count` reflects only the result of merging set_key with parent_key — which is the full destination cardinality, so in the common case it is actually correct. However, when the second branch is skipped (set_span_id == parent_span_id, or parent_key is empty), span_count retains the value from the first ZUNIONSTORE, which is also the destination cardinality — again correct. The real bug: when *neither* branch executes (is_root_span is true, or span_key is empty, and parent_key is empty/equal), span_count stays 0 and line 58-60 falls back to `zcard(set_key)`, which is correct. But when the first branch executes and the second also executes, the intermediate value is discarded — fine. The actual defect is subtler: ZUNIONSTORE with duplicate members across the two source sets keeps the *maximum* score (default aggregate), and since scores are end_timestamp_precise, a span present in both set_key and parent_key keeps its max timestamp — but the Python side writes each payload via ZADD in process_spans *before* the Lua script runs, and the Lua script merges pre-existing sets; a payload that exists in both the freshly-ZADDed set_key and the old parent_key is deduplicated, so span_count (destination cardinality) is accurate. The genuine issue is that `span_count` from ZUNIONSTORE counts *members*, but eviction at line 62-64 uses `zpopmin` which removes by score order; if the segment legitimately contains exactly 1000 spans and a merge adds 0 new members, span_count == 1000 and no eviction occurs — correct. The bug is that when the first ZUNIONSTORE runs and the second does not, and the destination already had >1000 members from prior inserts that were never evicted (e.g. the cap was just deployed), span_count is the post-merge cardinality and eviction triggers — correct. After careful analysis the count logic is mostly sound, BUT: `zunionstore` returns the number of elements in the destination *after* the union, and the destination `set_key` may contain members from the initial ZADD batch that were added by the Python pipeline *before* EVALSHA runs (process_spans does ZADD for all subsegment spans first, then EVALSHA per span). For a root span, the script skips the first merge but the set_key already contains the root span payload from the Python ZADD; span_count stays 0, then line 59 `zcard` counts it — correct. The remaining real defect: when `is_root_span` is false and `span_key` has members, the first ZUNIONSTORE merges set_key (which already contains the current batch's payloads for this parent group, added by Python) with the span's own child set. The Python ZADD used `set_key = span-buf:s:{project_and_trace}:{parent_span_id}` where parent_span_id is the *grouping* parent from `_group_by_parent`, which may differ from the Lua script's resolved `set_span_id` after redirect chasing. So the Python ZADD writes to a key that the Lua script may then merge or abandon, and the Lua script's `set_key` (resolved via redirects) may not contain the just-ZADDed payloads, making `span_count` undercount and eviction unreliable. This is a real correctness hazard introduced by mixing the Python-side ZADD keying with the Lua-side redirect-resolved keying.

title: Redirect-chasing loop limit reduced from 10000 to 1000 without handling overflow
body: The loop `for i = 0, 1000 do` previously ran to 10000. If a redirect chain exceeds 1000 hops, the loop exits with `set_span_id` still pointing at an intermediate span ID rather than the root of the chain. The script then proceeds to write the redirect mapping `hset(main_redirect_key, span_id, set_span_id)` and merge sets under this non-terminal `set_span_id`, creating a segment key that is not the canonical root. The original comment acknowledged the 10k limit ('theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly'); the new code has the same flaw at 1/10th the depth with no comment, no metric, and no error. Deep span trees (long chains of parent_span_id links arriving out of order across many batches) can now silently produce fragmented segments that are flushed separately, duplicating trace segments downstream. The Python side tracks `min_redirect_depth`/`max_redirect_depth` metrics but the Lua side returns `redirect_depth = i` which will read 1000 on overflow, indistinguishable from a legitimate depth-1000 chain.

title: max_segment_spans enforcement removed from flush path, leaving only silent Lua-side eviction
body: `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans: int = 1001`, but `_load_segment_data` no longer references it — the block that skipped segments exceeding `max_segment_spans` (with a `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric and an error log) was deleted. The only remaining enforcement is the Lua script's hard-coded 1000-member ZPOPMIN eviction. This means: (1) the configurable `max_segment_spans` parameter is now dead code — changing it has no effect, misleading operators; (2) there is no longer any flush-time safety net if the Lua eviction is bypassed (e.g. an older script SHA cached in Redis via `_ensure_script`, or a segment that grows between the last insert and the flush via a concurrent consumer on a different partition); (3) the `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric that dashboards/alerts may rely on will never increment, so silent span loss is invisible. The constructor parameter should either be removed or the flush-time check restored.

title: ZADD uses payload bytes as member with end_timestamp_precise as score, but Lua merges assume set semantics that break with duplicate payloads
body: process_spans now does `p.zadd(set_key, {span.payload: span.end_timestamp_precise for span in subsegment})`. In a Redis sorted set, the *member* is the payload bytes and the score is the timestamp. If two spans in the same subsegment have identical payload bytes (same span_id, same trace_id, same project, same end_timestamp_precise — e.g. a retried delivery of the same span within one batch, or two spans that differ only in fields not serialized identically), the dict comprehension `{span.payload: ...}` collapses them into a single ZADD entry, silently dropping one span from the buffer. The previous SADD-based code had the same dedup property, but the Lua script's ZUNIONSTORE merge path now also deduplicates by member, and the eviction count (`zcard`) counts unique payloads, not logical spans. More critically, the Lua script's `zpopmin` eviction removes by lowest score (earliest end_timestamp_precise); if a duplicate payload arrives with a *different* score, ZADD updates the score but keeps one member, so the buffer can hold one member where two logical spans existed. The Python `_group_by_parent` does not deduplicate, so the count of spans processed (`num_spans` metric) will not match the number of members in Redis, and the flush output will contain fewer spans than were ingested, with no error. The score-based dedup is a semantic change from the set-based buffer that is not accounted for in the flush logic or metrics.

title: __reduce__ drops segment_page_size, max_segment_bytes, and max_segment_spans when pickling SpansBuffer
body: `__reduce__` returns `(SpansBuffer, (self.assigned_shards, self.span_buffer_timeout_secs, self.span_buffer_root_timeout_secs, self.redis_ttl))`, omitting `segment_page_size`, `max_segment_bytes`, and `max_segment_spans`. When the buffer is pickled for multiprocessing (the factory uses `run_task_with_multiprocessing` with `partial(process_batch, buffer)`), the child process reconstructs SpansBuffer with default values for the omitted parameters. If an operator has configured non-default `segment_page_size` or `max_segment_bytes`, the child consumer silently uses defaults, causing inconsistent flush behavior (different page sizes, different size limits) between processes. This is a latent data-integrity/config-drift bug.

title: end_timestamp_precise is read with val['end_timestamp_precise'] and will KeyError on older payloads
body: process_batch constructs `Span(..., end_timestamp_precise=val['end_timestamp_precise'], ...)` using direct key access. The ingest-spans schema may not guarantee `end_timestamp_precise` on every payload (older Relay versions, or spans that only carry `end_timestamp`). A missing key raises KeyError inside process_batch, which runs in the arroyo processing strategy; the exception will cause the batch to fail and the consumer to crash-loop or skip offsets depending on the strategy's error handling, stalling span ingestion. The neighboring fields use `val.get('parent_span_id')` and `val.get('is_remote')` defensively; `end_timestamp_precise` should similarly use `val.get('end_timestamp_precise')` with a fallback (e.g. to `end_timestamp` or the message timestamp) or the schema should be validated. The test payloads all include the field, so the tests do not cover the missing-key path.

title: Comment claims negative offsets are allowed, but no validation or handling exists in Cursor
body: The added comment on `self.offset = int(offset)` states 'Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios', but the Cursor class performs no validation and no downstream code in cursors.py handles negative offsets specially — `_build_next_values` and `_build_prev_values` do arithmetic (`offset + limit`) that assumes non-negative offsets, and `Cursor.from_string` will happily parse a negative offset from a client-supplied cursor string (`int(bits[1])`). The comment documents an intent that is not implemented here and that, as implemented in OptimizedCursorPaginator, is unsafe. The comment should be removed or the class should explicitly reject negative offsets.

title: No test covers the Lua-side 1000-span eviction or the removal of the flush-time max_segment_spans check
body: The test suite for the spans buffer (test_basic, test_deep, test_deep2, test_parent_in_other_project, etc.) exercises segments of 4-5 spans. No test inserts more than 1000 spans into a single segment to verify the ZPOPMIN eviction behavior, no test verifies that the oldest spans (lowest end_timestamp_precise) are the ones evicted, and no test verifies that a segment exceeding max_segment_spans at flush time is handled (since that check was removed). Given that the eviction silently drops data and the flush-time safety net was deleted, the absence of a test means a regression that loses spans (e.g. evicting the wrong members, or evicting below 1000) would not be caught. A test should insert >1000 spans with distinct timestamps into one segment and assert exactly which spans survive and that the count metric/log reflects the loss.

title: Pre-existing typo queryset.query.order_b (missing _by) in BasePaginator.build_queryset
body: Line 105 reads `queryset.query.order_b = tuple(new_order_by)` — the attribute is `order_by`, not `order_b`. This is a pre-existing bug (not introduced by this diff), but it is in the exact method that OptimizedCursorPaginator inherits and that the new endpoint exercises. When the branch is hit (order_by key present as '-key' in query.order_by and asc is true), the assignment silently sets a nonexistent attribute and the queryset keeps its original ordering, producing incorrectly ordered pages. Because the new OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates this code path via inheritance and the audit logs endpoint sorts by '-datetime', this latent bug directly affects the new feature. It should be fixed as part of this change since the new paginator relies on build_queryset behaving correctly.

title: BasePaginator.get_result allows negative offsets for is_prev cursors, breaking pagination invariants
body: The change replaces `stop = offset + limit + extra; results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. For `is_prev` cursors, `start_offset` is now the raw (possibly negative) `cursor.offset`. Django QuerySets raise `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` when sliced with a negative start, so any client-supplied prev cursor with a negative offset (e.g. `cursor=1700000000.0:-1:1`) will crash the request with a 500 instead of returning an empty page or a BadPaginationError. Even before that, the subsequent logic `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra: results = results[:-1]` (line 192) uses the raw negative `offset`, so the row-trimming arithmetic is wrong for negative offsets. Other paginators in this same file (OffsetPaginator line 287, MergingOffsetPaginator line 351, CombinedQuerysetPaginator line 701, ChainPaginator line 748, CallbackPaginator line 804) all explicitly reject negative offsets with `raise BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`; this change silently removes that guard for the BasePaginator path used by DateTimePaginator and Paginator, which paginate most list endpoints. The comment claiming 'the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions' is factually wrong — Django does not handle negative slice starts.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator negative-offset branch crashes on Django negative slicing and mis-trims results
body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, the branch `if self.enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0:` sets `start_offset = cursor.offset` (a negative number) and executes `list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`. Django ORM raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.` for negative slice starts, so any request that reaches this paginator with a negative cursor offset (which the endpoint enables via `optimized_pagination=true` for superusers/global-access members) will 500. Additionally, the following block `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra: results = results[:-1]` (line 891) compares against the raw negative `offset`, so even if the slice did not crash, the extra-row trimming for prev cursors would be computed against the wrong value, potentially dropping a legitimate row or keeping the sentinel row. The claim in the comment that 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is incorrect.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key assumes a numeric sort key, but is used with order_by="-datetime"
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `value = getattr(item, self.key); return int(math.floor(value) ...)`, which requires the sort key to be a number. However the only caller, `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint.get` in src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_auditlogs.py line 80, instantiates it with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `self.key == "datetime"` and `getattr(item, "datetime")` returns a `datetime` object. `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime` inside `build_cursor` (sentry/utils/cursors.py line 122/137/197), so the optimized path will crash on the first page whenever it returns any results. The class should either subclass DateTimePaginator's key handling (multiplier=1000, strftime-based) or the endpoint should not use it with a datetime ordering. As written, `optimized_pagination=true` from an admin on the audit log endpoint is a guaranteed 500.

title: Endpoint passes enable_advanced_features=True to self.paginate, which does not forward it to the paginator constructor
body: The endpoint calls `self.paginate(..., paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator, ..., enable_advanced_features=True)`. `paginate` (in sentry/api/base.py) constructs the paginator as `paginator_cls(queryset, order_by=..., max_limit=..., on_results=...)` and only forwards a fixed set of kwargs; `enable_advanced_features` is not among them, so it is either swallowed or raises a TypeError depending on the paginate implementation. Consequently `OptimizedCursorPaginator.enable_advanced_features` stays at its default `False`, and the 'advanced' negative-offset path is never actually enabled — the flag is dead configuration that misleads readers into thinking a special mode is active. Either thread the kwarg through `paginate` or remove it from the call.

title: Undocumented query parameter switches audit log endpoint to a different paginator based on client input
body: `use_optimized = request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"` lets any client toggle which paginator implementation serves the audit log endpoint. The two paginators have different cursor semantics (OptimizedCursorPaginator treats the cursor value as a raw integer key rather than a millisecond timestamp like DateTimePaginator), so a client can craft a cursor string that is valid for one paginator and silently misinterpreted by the other, producing wrong pages, skipped or duplicated audit rows, or (combined with the negative-offset bug) errors. The endpoint is marked `ApiPublishStatus.EXPERIMENTAL` and the parameter is undocumented; an unversioned, undocumented behavior switch on an audit/compliance endpoint is an API-contract hazard. The paginator choice should be a server-side configuration, not a per-request query parameter.

title: Eviction via zpopmin during insert can drop spans that were just added, silently losing trace data
body: The new block `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000) end` evicts the lowest-scored members of the sorted set whenever a segment exceeds 1000 spans. Because members are scored by `end_timestamp_precise` (set in src/sentry/spans/buffer.py line 198), `zpopmin` removes the spans with the *earliest* end timestamps — which are exactly the spans that arrived first and are most likely to be the root/oldest spans of the segment. Dropping them means the flushed segment is missing spans, and if the evicted span was the segment root, the `span-buf:hrs:` flag logic (lines 66-70) may still claim a root span exists (or vice versa), producing a corrupted segment that is emitted to the `buffered-spans` topic and ingested as an incomplete trace. This is silent data loss in the tracing pipeline. Additionally, `span_count` is only assigned from `zunionstore` return values; when neither union branch runs (e.g. root span arriving into an empty set), `span_count` falls back to `zcard` (line 59), which is correct, but when a union runs the count reflects post-union cardinality — however if both unions run, the second `zunionstore` overwrites `span_count` with the cardinality after the second union only, which is still the full set size, so the eviction bound itself is consistent; the core issue is that eviction during insert destroys segment completeness. The previous code enforced the span-count limit at flush time (buffer.py `_load_segment_data` skipped oversized segments with an error metric), which preserved data integrity by refusing to emit rather than truncating. Note also that the flush-time `max_segment_spans` check was removed in this PR (see buffer.py diff), so oversized segments are no longer detected or logged at flush time either — the only enforcement is now this destructive in-place eviction.

title: zunionstore overwrites span_count with partial cardinality when both union branches execute
body: Line 47 `span_count = redis.call("zunionstore", set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` and line 53 `span_count = redis.call("zunionstore", set_key, 2, set_key, parent_key)` both assign to `span_count`. ZUNIONSTORE returns the cardinality of the *destination* set after the union. When both branches execute (a non-root span whose own span_key exists AND whose resolved parent_key exists and differs), the second assignment overwrites the first; the destination cardinality after the second union is the full set size, so in that specific case the value is still correct. However, when only the first branch executes, `span_count` is the cardinality after merging span_key into set_key — correct. When only the second executes, it is the cardinality after merging parent_key — correct. The real problem is subtler: `zunionstore` with default (non-WEIGHTS) aggregation *sums* scores for duplicate members. Since members are span payloads (unique per span), duplicates across the two source sets would only occur if the same payload was already in set_key, in which case its score becomes the sum of two end_timestamp_precise values — corrupting the score used for eviction ordering and for any score-based reads. The previous code used `sunionstore` (set semantics, no scores), which was immune to this. The migration from SET to ZSET changes the merge semantics: re-adding an already-present payload now doubles its score instead of being a no-op.

title: Redirect-chain depth limit reduced from 10000 to 1000 without handling the overflow case
body: The loop `for i = 0, 1000 do ... end` previously ran to 10000. If a redirect chain exceeds the loop bound, the loop exits with `set_span_id` still pointing at an intermediate span ID rather than the chain root, and the script proceeds to `hset`/`zunionstore` against a non-root key. The original comment acknowledged this ('theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly'); reducing the limit to 1000 makes the failure 10x more likely for deep span trees (long-lived traces with thousands of nested spans), and the resulting split segments would be flushed as separate segments, breaking trace assembly. There is no detection or metric when the loop exhausts. Either keep the higher bound, or detect exhaustion and fall back to using the last resolved ID consistently (and log/metric it).

title: zadd with payload as member means duplicate span payloads collapse and scores are overwritten, not summed, on re-ingest
body: The buffer now stores spans in a sorted set keyed by payload: `p.zadd(set_key, {span.payload: span.end_timestamp_precise for span in subsegment})`. With ZADD's default behavior (no XX/GT/LT flags), re-adding an existing member *updates* its score rather than creating a duplicate. For at-least-once Kafka delivery, the same span payload redelivered after a consumer restart will simply update its score — which is benign — but the Lua script's ZUNIONSTORE (add-buffer.lua lines 47/53) *sums* scores for members present in both source sets, so a payload that exists in both `set_key` and `span_key`/`parent_key` gets a doubled `end_timestamp_precise` score. That corrupted score then drives `zpopmin` eviction ordering (evicting the wrong spans) and is never corrected. The previous SET-based implementation was idempotent under re-ingest and union. This is a data-integrity regression for the dedup/merge path.

title: Removal of the max_segment_spans flush-time guard leaves only destructive in-insert eviction to bound segment size
body: The diff removes the block in `_load_segment_data` that checked `if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans:` and skipped the segment with `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded")` and an error log. The constructor still accepts `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` (line 150) and stores it (line 158), but it is now completely unused — dead configuration. Previously, an oversized segment was detected at flush time and *skipped* (with a metric), preserving the invariant that emitted segments never exceed the span limit. Now the only enforcement is the Lua script's `zpopmin` eviction during insert, which silently truncates the segment (see the add-buffer.lua finding). The safety net that turned a data-integrity problem into a visible, measurable error has been removed while its configuration knob remains, which is misleading. Either restore the flush-time check (as a defense in depth) or remove the now-unused `max_segment_spans` parameter and document that eviction is the sole mechanism.

title: __reduce__ drops segment_page_size, max_segment_bytes, and max_segment_spans when pickling SpansBuffer
body: `__reduce__` returns `(SpansBuffer, (self.assigned_shards, self.span_buffer_timeout_secs, self.span_buffer_root_timeout_secs, self.redis_ttl))` — it omits `segment_page_size`, `max_segment_bytes`, and `max_segment_spans`. The factory (src/sentry/spans/consumers/process/factory.py) uses `run_task_with_multiprocessing(partial(process_batch, buffer), ...)`, which pickles the buffer to worker processes. Any non-default values for those three parameters are silently reset to defaults (100, 10 MiB, 1001) in workers. This was already the case for the first two before this PR, but the PR makes `max_segment_spans` newly dead (see related finding), compounding the confusion. The pickle round-trip should include all constructor parameters that affect behavior.

title: process_batch assumes end_timestamp_precise is always present in the span payload
body: `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` uses direct key access on the parsed SpanEvent. The schema type `SpanEvent` (sentry_kafka_schemas.schema_types.ingest_spans_v1) may mark this field optional, and Relay/older producers may omit it; a missing key raises `KeyError`, which would fail the entire batch in `process_batch` and, because offsets are only committed after successful processing (CommitOffsets is downstream of the flusher), cause the consumer to retry the batch indefinitely — a poison-pill that stalls the spans consumer partition. The neighboring fields use `.get()` with defaults (`val.get("parent_span_id")`, `val.get("is_remote")`), showing the codebase's convention for optional fields. Use `val.get("end_timestamp_precise") or <fallback>` (e.g. the message timestamp already computed as `timestamp`) or validate the schema. The test payloads all include the field, so this path is untested for absence.

title: Comment claims Cursor offsets may be negative, but no validation or handling exists and other paginators reject them
body: The added comment 'Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios' on `self.offset = int(offset)` implies the Cursor class now supports or handles negative offsets. In reality the class does nothing special — it just stores the int — and every paginator that consumes cursors either crashes on negative offsets (Django negative slicing, per the paginator.py findings) or explicitly rejects them with BadPaginationError. The comment documents an intention that the code does not implement and that the rest of the pagination stack contradicts; it will mislead maintainers into thinking negative offsets are a supported, safe feature.

title: Pre-existing typo queryset.query.order_b (missing _by) in BasePaginator.build_queryset
body: Line 105 reads `queryset.query.order_b = tuple(new_order_by)` — the attribute is `order_by`, so this silently sets a new, meaningless attribute and leaves the ordering unchanged. This is a pre-existing bug (not introduced by this PR), but it sits directly in the code path that the new OptimizedCursorPaginator inherits and that the modified `get_result` exercises for prev-cursors on already-ordered querysets, so the PR's changes interact with it: when a prev cursor is used on a queryset already ordered by `-key`, the intended order reversal never happens. Worth fixing while touching this file, since the PR's stated goal is correct bidirectional pagination.

title: No test covers the new 1000-span eviction path in add-buffer.lua
body: The PR adds eviction logic (`if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin ...`) to the Lua script and removes the flush-time `max_segment_spans` guard, but tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py contains no test that ingests more than 1000 spans into a single segment and asserts which spans survive eviction or that the segment remains complete/consistent. All existing tests use 4-5 spans per trace. Given that eviction drops the lowest-scored (earliest end_timestamp) members — potentially including the segment root — the behavior of the eviction path (which spans are dropped, whether the hrs flag stays consistent, whether flushed output is a truncated segment) is completely unverified. A test should ingest >1000 spans with distinct end_timestamp_precise values and assert the surviving set and the emitted segment contents.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates ~70 lines of BasePaginator.get_result instead of overriding a hook
body: The new class copies the entire `get_result` body from `BasePaginator` (lines 136-215) and adds one conditional branch for negative offsets. Any future fix to the shared logic (e.g. the `order_b` typo, cursor trimming edge cases, hits handling) must be applied in two places or the paginators diverge. The negative-offset behavior could be a small override or a parameter on BasePaginator. As a standalone duplication it is a maintenance hazard rather than an immediate bug, but it already diverges: the copy retains the `max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` line from the modified base, so the two implementations will drift as the base evolves.

title: Cache key uses Python's randomized hash(), causing cache misses and cross-process inconsistency
body: The cache key is built with `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. Python's `hash()` for tuples of ints is deterministic within a process but the string representation is embedded in a cache key shared across processes/workers (and potentially a shared Redis/memcached backend via `sentry.utils.cache`). More importantly, `hash()` output can differ between processes when `PYTHONHASHSEED` randomization affects str/bytes hashing (tuple hash of ints is stable, but relying on `hash()` for a persistent cache key is fragile and non-portable), and the key is not human-inspectable. Consequence: cache entries may never be hit across workers, silently defeating the stated 60-second caching optimization, and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (line 73) computes the same key so invalidation works only within the same process/seed. Use a stable serialization such as `":".join(map(str, sorted(project_ids)))` instead.

title: Allowlist check compares project IDs against an option that may contain project slugs, and ignores the organization
body: `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` reads `options.get("issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist", [])` and checks `project_id in allowlist`. Sentry options of this kind are typically configured with project slugs or a mixed list, not numeric IDs; if the allowlist contains slugs (or org-scoped values), the membership test will always fail or, worse, could accidentally match if the option is keyed differently. Additionally, the `organization` parameter is accepted but never used, so an allowlist configured per-organization cannot be honored, and a global allowlist would incorrectly apply to every organization. Consequence: upsampling may be silently disabled (safe) or incorrectly enabled for organizations whose projects coincidentally match IDs from another org's allowlist (unsafe — wrong counts). The option value's expected type/scope must be validated and the organization must be part of the check.

title: Upsampled count assumes sample_weight is populated for every event, producing wrong counts when it is not
body: `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` rewrites `count()` to `upsampled_count() as count`, which the discover dataset (src/sentry/search/events/datasets/discover.py, added SnQLFunction `upsampled_count`) implements as `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. The docstrings claim "we rely on the database schema to ensure sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects, so no additional null checks are needed". In ClickHouse/Snuba, `sum()` over a column with NULL/missing values yields NULL (or 0 with default settings), and events ingested before the allowlist was enabled, events from Relay configs that don't set sample_weight, or non-sampled error events will not have a meaningful sample_weight. Consequence: `count()` silently returns 0 or NULL instead of the true event count for allowlisted projects — a data-integrity bug that under-reports error volumes in the events-stats API. The transformation must use `sum(coalesce(sample_weight, 1))` (or equivalent) or the eligibility check must guarantee sample_weight presence per event.

title: Column transformation only matches the exact string "count()" and misses equivalent forms
body: The transform lowercases and strips the column, then compares `column_lower == "count()"`. Real queries produce columns such as `count() as count`, `count()` with an alias, `count_unique(...)` is fine, but also `count()` embedded in equations or with different spacing like `count( )`, or the API's `yAxis=count()` may arrive as `count()` — however any aliasing (`count() as cnt`), whitespace inside the parens, or a trailing alias will not match and will be passed through untransformed. Consequence: mixed queries (e.g. `yAxis=count()&yAxis=count() as total`) would upsample one series and not the other, producing inconsistent, incomparable counts within a single response. The matcher should parse the aggregation (e.g. regex `^count\(\s*\)(\s+as\s+\w+)?$`) and preserve the alias.

title: Discover-dataset eligibility is decided by naive substring match on the raw query string
body: `_is_error_focused_query` returns True whenever the substring `event.type:error` appears anywhere in `request.GET["query"]`. This is trivially bypassed and also produces false positives: a query like `event.type:transaction AND message:"event.type:error"`, or `!event.type:error`, or a negated/quoted occurrence, will be treated as error-focused. Consequence: transaction events (which have no `sample_weight`) get their `count()` rewritten to `sum(sample_weight)`, yielding wrong/zero counts for transaction series on the discover dataset. Eligibility must be based on the parsed search query (the resolved event-type filter), not substring matching.

title: Errors dataset is unconditionally upsampled even for queries that include non-error or transaction events
body: `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns True for the entire `errors` dataset module without inspecting the query. The errors dataset can still be queried with filters that exclude error events or with `event.type:transaction` (the endpoint itself supports dataset=errors with arbitrary queries, and the dashboard split logic in organization_events_stats.py issues `({query}) AND !event.type:transaction` and `event.type:transaction` sub-queries against `discover`). If any non-error rows can appear in the result set, `sum(sample_weight)` will miscount them. Consequence: incorrect counts whenever the errors dataset query is not strictly error-only. The check should apply the same parsed-query validation used for discover, or at minimum exclude transaction event types.

title: Upsampling decision uses the outer `dataset` variable instead of the actually-scoped dataset, breaking dashboard split queries
body: Inside `_get_event_stats`, the eligibility check calls `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` using `dataset` captured from the enclosing `get()` scope. However `_get_event_stats` is invoked with `scoped_dataset` (line 210), which the dashboard-widget factory (lines 372-435) sets to `discover` for split error/transaction sub-queries even when the outer `dataset` is `metrics_enhanced_performance`. Consequence: for a metrics-enhanced widget, the error sub-query executed against `discover` will be evaluated with `dataset=metrics_enhanced_performance`, which `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` treats as "other dataset" and returns False — so upsampling is silently skipped for exactly the error queries the feature targets (or conversely applied based on the wrong dataset). The check must use `scoped_dataset`, not `dataset`.

title: Upsampling transformation is applied only to y-axis columns, not to `selected_columns`/group-by or equations, producing inconsistent results
body: The transformation rewrites `query_columns` (the y-axes) but `top_events_timeseries` is still called with `selected_columns=self.get_field_list(...)` and `equations=self.get_equation_list(...)` untransformed. If a user requests `yAxis=count()` together with `field=count()` or an equation referencing `count()`, the equation/selected column will compute a plain `count()` while the timeseries computes `upsampled_count()`, and the two will disagree. Consequence: top-events responses can return a `count` in the series that does not match the per-item `count` in the selected columns, corrupting the API contract. All count() aggregations in the query (y-axes, equations, and any selected aggregate columns) must be transformed consistently.

title: invalidate_upsampling_cache is defined but never called, so allowlist changes leave stale cache entries for up to 60s
