body: The module provides `invalidate_upsampling_cache(organization_id, project_ids)` with a docstring saying it "should be called when the allowlist configuration changes", but a search of the changed files shows no call sites (no option-change hook, signal, or admin action invokes it). Combined with the 60-second TTL, toggling a project in/out of `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` can leave upsampling enabled (or disabled) for up to 60 seconds across all workers. Consequence: stale, inconsistent counts after configuration changes; the invalidation helper is dead code. Either wire it to the option update path or remove it and document the TTL-based eventual consistency.

title: Test factory mutates normalized event data to set sample_rate, which can leak into stored event payloads and distort other tests
body: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` is called on `normalized_data` (the event manager's data dict) inside `Factories.store_event` and writes `normalized_data["sample_rate"] = float(client_sample_rate)`. `normalized_data` is the dict that gets serialized and stored as the event payload; `sample_rate` is a top-level event attribute that Snuba/event processing treats as the event's sample rate. Consequence: any test that stores an event with `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` will now also persist a top-level `sample_rate`, changing event serialization, grouping, and Snuba `sample_weight` computation for that event — this can silently alter results of unrelated tests that use such contexts, and makes the factory's behavior surprising. The sample weight should be applied at the Snuba/ingest level (or via a dedicated parameter), not by mutating the event payload in a shared factory.

title: New Snuba tests mock the options module globally, bypassing the real allowlist option and cache behavior
body: All four new tests use `@mock.patch("sentry.api.helpers.error_upsampling.options")`, which replaces the entire `options` module object in the helper. This means the tests never exercise the real option lookup (`options.get("issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist")`), the default value, or the cache path in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled` (the cache is still real, but the eligibility computation is mocked away). Consequence: the tests would pass even if the option name were wrong, if the option returned slugs instead of IDs, or if the caching logic inverted the boolean — precisely the failure modes that matter for this feature. Tests should set the real option (e.g. via `self.options(...)` / `options.set` with override) and add coverage for the cache hit/miss and invalidation paths.

title: Unit tests never cover the public entry point or the cache, and SnubaParams is constructed with None start/end
body: The test file only tests the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`). The public function `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` — which contains the cache key construction, cache get/set, and the composition of the helpers — is never tested, so the `hash()`-based cache key bug and cache TTL behavior are uncovered. Additionally `SnubaParams(start=None, end=None, projects=...)` is created but never used in any test, suggesting intended coverage of the public function was abandoned. Consequence: the most fragile logic (caching and key construction) has no test protection.

title: Module identity comparison (`dataset == errors`) is fragile and imports modules inside the function on every call
body: `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` compares dataset modules with `==` (module identity works, but is unusual and breaks if datasets are reloaded or proxied) and performs `from sentry.snuba import discover, errors` / `transactions` inside the function body on every invocation. In the endpoint this function is called once per `_get_event_stats` invocation, including multiple times for dashboard split queries. Consequence: repeated import machinery overhead per request and brittle equality semantics; module imports should be top-level and comparison should use `is` or a dataset-name string.

title: A git submodule pointer file (`sentry-repo`) is added at the repository root
body: The PR adds a new top-level file `sentry-repo` containing `Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a`. This is a git submodule gitlink accidentally committed as a regular file (or a submodule added without a `.gitmodules` entry). Consequence: it pollutes the repository root, will confuse tooling/CI that iterates over files, and indicates the submodule was not added correctly. It should be removed or properly registered via `.gitmodules` + `git submodule add`.

title: Cache key uses Python's built-in hash(), which is randomized per process and not stable across workers
body: The cache key is built with `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. Python's `hash()` for tuples/ints is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED randomization affects str/bytes, but more importantly the value is not guaranteed stable across processes or restarts, and int hashes can collide across different project-id sets). In a multi-worker deployment, different web workers will compute different cache keys for the same organization/project set, so the 60-second cache will not be shared and will be ineffective; worse, `hash()` collisions between different project-id tuples can cause one project set's eligibility result to be served for a different project set, incorrectly enabling or disabling upsampled counts for the wrong projects. The cache key must be built from a deterministic serialization of the sorted project IDs (e.g. `','.join(map(str, sorted(project_ids)))`), and the same deterministic key must be used in `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (line 73), which currently has the same bug.

title: Cached boolean is combined with a per-request condition, so a cached `False` permanently suppresses upsampling for error-focused queries and a cached `True` can leak across query types
body: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches only the allowlist result (`is_eligible`) but returns `cached_result and _should_apply_sample_weight_transform(dataset, request)`. Two problems: (1) when the allowlist check returns `False`, `False` is cached for 60s, so a project that is added to the allowlist will not get upsampled counts for up to 60 seconds — acceptable per the docstring, but the docstring claims 'eventual consistency is acceptable' without this being a deliberate, documented tradeoff for a correctness-affecting count; (2) more seriously, the cache key does not include the dataset or the query string, yet the returned value depends on `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform(dataset, request)`, which varies per request (e.g. `event.type:error` vs `event.type:transaction` on the discover dataset). Because the cached value is only the allowlist half, this specific combination is actually safe, but the design is fragile: any future change that caches the combined result, or the fact that `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is never called anywhere in the codebase (see separate finding), means stale eligibility persists. The core data-integrity issue is that the eligibility decision is cached per (org, projects) while the transformation decision is per (dataset, query), and the two are conflated in one function whose name and docstring promise a single consistent decision.

title: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is dead code and the cache is never invalidated when the allowlist option changes
body: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined but never called anywhere in the repository (no call sites in the diff or elsewhere). The docstring says 'This should be called when the allowlist configuration changes', but nothing wires it to the options system. Combined with the 60-second TTL, an operator who removes a project from `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` will continue to get `upsampled_count()` (sum of `sample_weight`) for that project for up to 60 seconds, and an operator who adds a project will see plain `count()` for up to 60 seconds. For a count-correctness feature this is a real data-integrity window; either hook invalidation into the option-change path (e.g. an options signal/receiver) or drop the cache. Additionally, because the cache key uses `hash()` (see separate finding), even a correct invalidation call would target a different key in each worker process, making cross-worker invalidation impossible with the current key scheme.

title: `count()` is transformed to `upsampled_count()` based only on a substring/exact-match of the column string, breaking aliased, parameterized, or whitespace variants and silently corrupting other aggregates
body: `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` replaces a column only when `column.lower().strip() == "count()"`. Any other spelling of the same aggregate — `count() as count`, `count(*)`, `count_unique(...)` is fine, but `count() AS cnt`, `count ()`, `count(distinct id)` is fine, but a user-supplied alias like `count() as error_count` — is left as plain `count()`, so the same query returns raw sampled counts instead of upsampled counts depending on whether the client added an alias. Conversely, the replacement emits `upsampled_count() as count`, which hardcodes the alias `count`; if the original column was `count() as my_alias` it would not match and be left alone (inconsistent), and if it did match, the output column name is forced to `count`. This is a correctness/contract problem: the endpoint's response column names and values depend on exact string formatting of the yAxis parameter rather than on the parsed query. The transformation should operate on the parsed/resolved aggregate (via the dataset's function resolver) rather than raw string matching, and should preserve the original alias.

title: Errors dataset unconditionally applies `sum(sample_weight)`, but eligibility is only checked against project allowlist — events without `sample_weight` (or with NULL) will produce wrong/zero counts
body: For the `errors` dataset, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns `True` whenever all projects are allowlisted, with no query-level guard. The docstring in `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` says 'We rely on the database schema to ensure sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects, so no additional null checks are needed' — but `sample_weight` is only populated for events that actually went through client-side error sampling (the test factory change in `src/sentry/testutils/factories.py` only sets `sample_rate` when `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` is present). Any error event in an allowlisted project that was NOT client-sampled (e.g. server-side sampled, relay-sampled, or unsampled) will either have `sample_weight = 1` (fine) or NULL/missing (in which case `sum(sample_weight)` ignores NULLs in ClickHouse and undercounts, or the column may not exist for older data). The result is that `count()` silently becomes an incorrect, data-dependent value with no query filter (e.g. `sample_weight` IS NOT NULL) and no fallback. At minimum the transformation must be gated on the query actually being an error-count query over sampled data, and ideally use `sum(coalesce(sample_weight, 1))` or an equivalent; as written this is a data-integrity risk for the headline metric of the issues product.

title: Discover-dataset detection uses naive substring match on the raw query string, missing negations, ORs, and alternate syntaxes
body: `_is_error_focused_query` returns True if the literal substring `event.type:error` appears anywhere in `request.GET['query']`. This misclassifies queries such as `!event.type:error` (negation — actually transactions/other), `event.type:transaction OR event.type:error` (mixed — applying `sum(sample_weight)` would undercount transactions which have no `sample_weight`), `event.type:[error, default]`, or quoted variants. Because the discover dataset mixes errors and transactions, a mixed query on allowlisted projects would produce `upsampled_count()` over rows where `sample_weight` is absent for transactions, yielding wrong counts. The check must be done on the parsed search filter (e.g. via the event search parser / `Condition` tree) rather than substring matching, and must require that the query constrains to error events exclusively.

title: Upsampling eligibility is computed against the outer `dataset` variable, not the `scoped_dataset` actually being queried, so dashboard split queries get the wrong transformation
body: Inside `_get_event_stats`, the eligibility check calls `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` using `dataset` — the dataset resolved at the top of `get()` — but the function then queries `scoped_dataset`, which `get_event_stats_factory` can change to `discover` for dashboard-widget splits (lines 362–370, 383–394, 426–435, 444–452). For a metrics-enhanced dashboard widget whose outer dataset is `metrics_enhanced_performance` (not errors/discover/transactions), `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns False, so no transformation is applied even when the split query runs against the `discover` dataset with `!event.type:transaction`; conversely the check never sees the actual dataset. The eligibility decision must be based on `scoped_dataset` (and the actual `query` string), otherwise the transformation is applied or skipped incorrectly for every split-widget query path.

title: Upsampling transformation is applied to `y_axes`/`timeseries_columns` but not to `selected_columns`/`raw_groupby`, producing inconsistent top-events results
body: In the `top_events > 0` branch, `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` is applied only to `final_columns`, which is passed as `y_axes` (RPC path) or `timeseries_columns` (non-RPC path). The same `count()` aggregate typically also appears in `selected_columns=self.get_field_list(...)` and, on the RPC path, `raw_groupby=self.get_field_list(...)`, which are NOT transformed. The result is a top-events response whose timeseries uses `sum(sample_weight)` while the per-group breakdown columns still use raw `count()`, so the totals and the per-row counts disagree (e.g. total 10 vs row count 1). Either the transformation must be applied consistently to all column lists derived from the request, or the feature must be disabled for top-events queries until it can be.

title: New public SnQL function `upsampled_count` is registered only on the discover dataset, but the endpoint can invoke it on the errors dataset
body: The `SnQLFunction("upsampled_count", ...)` is added to `DiscoverDataset.function_converter` (discover.py). However, `organization_events_stats.py` applies `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` whenever `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns True, which is unconditionally True for the `errors` dataset (error_upsampling.py line 112). If the errors dataset's function resolver does not also define `upsampled_count`, any `yAxis=count()` query with `dataset=errors` on an allowlisted project will fail at query-resolution time with an unknown-function error (or fall through to a raw `count()` depending on resolver strictness), breaking the errors-stats endpoint. The function must be registered on every dataset the endpoint can transform (at minimum `errors` and `discover`), or the transformation must be restricted to datasets where the function exists.

title: Test factory silently swallows all exceptions when extracting `client_sample_rate`, masking malformed test data
body: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` wraps both the context extraction and the `float()` conversion in bare `try/except Exception: pass`. If a test passes `client_sample_rate` as a non-numeric string, a dict, or if `contexts` is not a mapping, the factory silently leaves `sample_rate` unset and the event is stored unsampled — the test then asserts on upsampled counts and fails (or worse, passes against raw counts) with no indication that the fixture was malformed. The broad excepts should be narrowed (catch only `AttributeError`/`TypeError`/`KeyError` for the lookup) and the float conversion should raise or at least log, so fixture bugs surface immediately. This directly undermines the reliability of the new snuba tests that depend on `sample_rate` being set from `client_sample_rate`.

title: New snuba tests mock `sentry.api.helpers.error_upsampling.options` globally, which also disables option reads used by the rest of the request path
body: The tests patch `sentry.api.helpers.error_upsampling.options` with `mock_options.get.return_value = [...]`. Because the module imports `from sentry import options` and the patch replaces the whole `options` module object in that namespace, every `options.get(...)` call in the helper returns the allowlist — that part is intended. But the mock is active for the entire request, and the patched module attribute is what the helper sees; this is fine in isolation. The real gap: the tests never exercise the cache path (`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` is not directly tested for caching/invalidation), never test the `errors` dataset (only discover), never test aliased `count() as foo`, never test a mixed `event.type:transaction OR event.type:error` query, and never test that `invalidate_upsampling_cache` works. Given the data-integrity nature of the feature, these are the cases most likely to regress silently.

title: Upsampling tests assert exact upsampled counts (10) but never verify the non-upsampled path returns the raw count for the same data, and rely on cross-project bucket placement that may be flaky
body: In `test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects`, the two events are stored in different projects (`self.project` and `self.project2`) at `day_ago + 1 minute` and `day_ago + 1 hour 1 minute`, and the test asserts `data[0][1][0]['count'] == 10` and `data[1][1][0]['count'] == 10`. This assumes both events land in separate hourly buckets and that `sample_weight = 1/0.1 = 10` is written by the ingest path from the factory's `sample_rate` — but the factory change sets `normalized_data['sample_rate']`, and whether Snuba's `sample_weight` column actually becomes 10 depends on the event-processing pipeline honoring `sample_rate` for error events in the test environment. If the pipeline does not propagate it, the test would fail; if it does, the assertion is correct but brittle. More importantly, the test does not assert the raw-count baseline for identical data without the allowlist in the same test class with the same events (it does in other tests, but with the mock returning `[]` — which also short-circuits before the cache). A direct A/B assertion (same events, allowlist on vs off) would pin the 10x behavior.

title: Allowlist option is compared against raw project IDs but the option value type is not validated
body: `options.get("issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist", [])` is assumed to be a list of ints comparable to `project_id in allowlist`. If an operator configures the option with string IDs (e.g. `["123"]`), the membership check silently fails for every project, disabling upsampling with no error or log. The code should coerce/validate the option (e.g. `{int(p) for p in allowlist}` with a guard) or at least log a warning when the allowlist is non-empty but matches zero projects, so misconfiguration is discoverable.

title: A git submodule pointer file `sentry-repo` was accidentally added at the repository root
body: The PR adds a new top-level file `sentry-repo` containing `Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a`. This is a git submodule gitlink artifact (typically produced by an accidental `git add` of a nested repo or a submodule update in the wrong directory), not a source file. It should not be committed; it will confuse tooling, CI checkout logic, and reviewers, and it pins a commit hash unrelated to this change. Remove the file and ensure `.gitmodules`/submodule state is unchanged.

title: Cache key uses Python's randomized hash(), causing cache misses and cross-process inconsistency
body: The cache key is built with `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. Python's `hash()` for tuples of ints is deterministic within a process but is NOT stable across processes when PYTHONHASHSEED randomization is enabled (the default for str/bytes, and tuple hashes incorporate element hashes; for ints hash(int) is stable, but relying on `hash()` for cache keys is fragile and the tuple hash combines element hashes — for ints this is actually stable, however the real problem is that `hash()` can return negative values and, more importantly, the same logical key can produce different values across processes if any element type's hash is randomized, and it is simply not a safe serialization). More concretely: the key embeds a process-local hash rather than a stable serialization of the project IDs, so cache entries written by one worker are not reliably found by another, and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (line 73) recomputes the same unstable hash — invalidation may target a different key than the one stored. The consequence is that the 60-second eligibility cache silently fails to dedupe lookups and invalidation does not work, defeating the stated performance optimization and potentially serving stale eligibility decisions. Use a stable key such as `','.join(map(str, sorted(project_ids)))`.

title: Caching a boolean eligibility result conflates False (not eligible) with cache miss and caches negative results incorrectly across allowlist changes
body: `cache.get(cache_key)` returns `None` on miss, and the code treats any non-None value as a hit (line 31: `if cached_result is not None: return cached_result and ...`). This means a cached `False` (projects not allowlisted) is indistinguishable from a miss only by value, which is fine, BUT the deeper issue is that the cached value is the *allowlist eligibility only*, while the final decision also depends on `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform(dataset, request)` — that part is re-evaluated, which is correct. The actual bug: the cache stores `is_eligible` for 60 seconds, but `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is never called anywhere in the codebase (no callers exist in the diff), so when an operator updates `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`, queries for newly-allowlisted projects will continue to use plain `count()` (undercounting errors) and queries for removed projects will continue to use `upsampled_count()` (potentially querying a non-existent `sample_weight` column or producing wrong results) for up to 60 seconds. Combined with the unstable `hash()` key, invalidation is effectively broken. The docstring claims invalidation 'should be called when the allowlist configuration changes' but no such call site exists, making the cache a correctness hazard rather than a safe optimization.

title: transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling only matches exact 'count()' and silently drops/mis-handles aliased or parameterized count aggregations
body: `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` replaces a column only when `column.lower().strip() == "count()"`. Real queries from the events-stats endpoint commonly use forms like `count() as count`, `count(id)`, `count_unique(...)`, or `count() as my_alias` (the endpoint's yAxis values are user-supplied and may include aliases). Any of these will pass through unchanged, so the query will run a plain `count()` on a sampled dataset and report the *sampled* event count instead of the upsampled count — silently returning wrong (under-)counts with no error. Conversely, if a column is exactly `count()` but the request is a top-events query where the column is used as a group-by/timeseries column rather than an aggregate, the rewrite to `upsampled_count() as count` changes semantics. The function should parse the aggregation properly (or at minimum handle the `count(...)` family and alias suffixes) and should fail loudly rather than silently when it cannot safely transform an expected count aggregation.

title: Rewriting 'count()' to 'upsampled_count() as count' hard-codes an alias that can collide with or clobber the user's requested column name
body: The transformation appends `" as count"` unconditionally. If the caller's `query_columns` already contains a column literally named `count` (e.g. a tag or attribute named `count`), or if the same list contains both `count()` and another expression aliased `as count`, the rewritten SnQL will contain two columns aliased `count`, producing a duplicate-column error from Snuba or silently ambiguous result keys. The response-shaping code downstream (which maps results back by column name) will then read the wrong series. The transform must preserve the caller's original alias (e.g. rewrite `count()` → `upsampled_count() as count` only when no alias was present, and `count() as foo` → `upsampled_count() as foo`), and must detect collisions.

title: _is_error_focused_query uses naive substring matching on the raw query string, producing false positives and false negatives
body: `_is_error_focused_query` checks `"event.type:error" in query.lower()`. This (a) false-positives on negated or unrelated contexts such as `!event.type:error`, `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` (mixed query — applying sample_weight upsampling to a query that also counts transactions will produce wrong totals because transactions have no `sample_weight`), `message:"event.type:error"`, or a tag value containing that substring; and (b) false-negatives on equivalent queries like `event.type:[error, default]` or `event.type:error event.type:default`. The consequence is that upsampling (which changes `count()` to `sum(sample_weight)`) can be applied to queries that include transaction events — where `sample_weight` does not exist — causing Snuba query failures or, worse, silently wrong counts. The check should parse the search query (e.g. via the existing event_search parser) and determine the resolved event types, and must exclude queries that can match transactions.

title: _should_apply_sample_weight_transform applies upsampling to the entire errors dataset without checking the query's event types
body: For `dataset == errors` the function returns `True` unconditionally (line 112-113). The errors dataset can still be queried with filters that exclude error events or with `event.type:transaction`-style exclusions in edge cases, but more importantly the endpoint's `_get_event_stats` is also invoked from the dashboard discover-split path (organization_events_stats.py lines 383-435) where `errors_only_query = f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction"` is run against the **discover** dataset — that path is guarded by `_is_error_focused_query`, but the errors-dataset branch has no query inspection at all. If a caller uses the errors dataset with a query that matches non-error rows (or with `sampled:true/false` semantics that interact with sample_weight), `count()` will be silently replaced with `sum(sample_weight)`. At minimum the function should verify the query does not explicitly target transactions, consistent with the discover branch.

title: Upsampling eligibility is computed against the outer `dataset` but applied to `scoped_dataset`, which can differ in the dashboard discover-split path
body: In `_get_event_stats`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` is called with the closure-captured outer `dataset` (line 220-222), but the query is executed against `scoped_dataset` (lines 236, 253, 279, 298). In the dashboard split path (`get_event_stats_factory`, lines 372-435), `_get_event_stats` is called with `split_dataset = discover` or `scoped_dataset` while `dataset` remains the original (possibly `metrics_enhanced`). The eligibility decision — including `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform(dataset, ...)` and `_is_error_focused_query(request)` — is therefore made for the wrong dataset/query combination. For example, a metrics-enhanced widget split into an errors-only discover query would be evaluated as a metrics dataset (returns False, no upsampling — safe), but the reverse combination (outer dataset = errors/discover, scoped = something else) could apply `upsampled_count()` to a dataset where `sample_weight` is not populated, yielding wrong counts or query errors. The eligibility check must use `scoped_dataset` and the actual `query` string being executed, not the outer `dataset` and the raw request query.

title: Upsampling transformation is applied to top-events queries, changing top-N semantics from event counts to weighted sums
body: When `top_events > 0`, the code replaces `query_columns` with `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling(query_columns)` (lines 232-233) and passes them as `timeseries_columns`/`y_axes` to `top_events_timeseries` / `run_top_events_timeseries_query`. Top-events queries rank groups by the aggregate value; replacing `count()` with `sum(sample_weight)` changes both the ranking metric and the returned per-group values. The API contract for `topEvents` is 'top N groups by event count'; silently returning groups ranked by upsampled weight (and reporting `count` as the weighted sum) is a behavioral/API break for any consumer of this endpoint, and the response's `count` field no longer means 'number of events'. Either exclude top-events queries from upsampling or make the semantic change explicit and documented in the response meta.

title: Upsampling is applied to the standard timeseries path even when the query contains transaction events via the discover dataset default
body: For the discover dataset, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` only applies upsampling when the raw query string contains `event.type:error`. But the discover dataset by default returns both errors and transactions; a query with no `event.type` filter (the common case, e.g. a plain `count()` over an org) will NOT be transformed (safe), however a query like `event.type:error OR message:foo` is transformed even though it can match non-error events depending on search semantics, and a query like `!event.type:transaction` (errors only, but expressed as an exclusion) is NOT transformed, so errors are undercounted. The asymmetry means the same logical 'errors only' query gets different count semantics depending on how it is phrased. This should be resolved by parsing the query to determine the effective event-type set rather than substring matching.

title: New 'upsampled_count' aggregate sums sample_weight unconditionally, producing wrong results (or errors) for events without sample_weight
body: The `upsampled_count` SnQL function is defined as `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` with no guard for rows where `sample_weight` is NULL/missing (e.g. events ingested before client-side error sampling was enabled, events from SDKs that don't send `error_sampling.client_sample_rate`, or transaction events that slip through the dataset/query checks). In ClickHouse/Snuba, `sum()` over a nullable column ignores NULLs, so groups containing only non-sampled events would return 0 (or NULL → toInt64(NULL)) instead of their actual count — silently underreporting errors. The helper's docstring explicitly states 'We rely on the database schema to ensure sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects, so no additional null checks are needed' — that assumption is not enforced anywhere in this diff (the factory change in testutils only sets `sample_rate` for test events; there is no migration, backfill, or query-time guard). The aggregate should be `sum(coalesce(sample_weight, 1))` (or `countIf(sample_weight IS NULL) + sum(coalesce(sample_weight,0))`) so that unsampled events still count as 1, and the eligibility check must additionally verify the project actually has sampled data.

title: New public-ish aggregate 'upsampled_count' is registered only on the discover dataset, but the endpoint can apply it to the errors dataset
body: `upsampled_count` is added to `DiscoverDataset.function_converter` (discover.py), but `organization_events_stats.py` applies the transformation whenever `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns True — which includes `dataset == errors` (error_upsampling.py line 112). If the errors dataset's function resolver does not also register `upsampled_count`, any errors-dataset query with `yAxis=count()` from an allowlisted project will fail at SnQL resolution time with an unknown-function error (a 500), or worse, be silently rejected. The diff shows no corresponding registration in the errors dataset. Either register the function on all datasets where it can be applied, or restrict the endpoint transformation to datasets that support it.

title: Factory change sets top-level 'sample_rate' from error_sampling context, which does not populate Snuba's sample_weight column
body: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` copies `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` into the event's top-level `sample_rate` field. In Sentry's ingest pipeline, the value written to the events dataset's `sample_weight` column is derived from the event's `sample_rate` (typically `1/sample_rate`) during normalization in the event manager — but this factory path calls `manager.get_data()` and then mutates the normalized dict *after* normalization, and `store_event` in tests typically bypasses the full normalization that computes `sample_weight`. As a result, the Snuba integration tests in `test_organization_events_stats.py` that assert `count == 10` (1 event / 0.1 sample rate) are asserting against a `sample_weight` value that may not actually be written by this code path, making the tests tautological or environment-dependent rather than verifying real ingest behavior. The factory should set the value through the same normalization path production uses (or set `sample_weight` explicitly on the stored event), otherwise the tests do not prove the feature works end-to-end.

title: New integration tests mock the options module globally, bypassing the real allowlist option and the cache, so they don't exercise the actual eligibility path
body: All four new tests use `@mock.patch("sentry.api.helpers.error_upsampling.options")` and set `mock_options.get.return_value = [...]`. This replaces the entire options module for the duration of the request, which means (a) the real option key `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` is never read, so a typo in the option name in the helper would not be caught; (b) the 60-second cache in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` is still active across tests within the same process, so test ordering can leak cached eligibility between tests (the cache key includes org id and project ids, which differ per test since projects are recreated, mitigating but not eliminating this); and (c) the tests never verify that `invalidate_upsampling_cache` works or that the cache returns consistent results. At minimum one test should set the real option via `self.options(...)`/`options.set` and assert behavior, and the cache should be cleared in `setUp`/`tearDown` to keep tests hermetic.

title: Integration tests assert exact upsampled counts (10) without verifying that sample_weight was actually persisted, and never test mixed sampled/unsampled events
body: The tests assert `data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10` for a single stored event with `client_sample_rate: 0.1`. This only passes if (a) the factory change actually results in `sample_weight = 10` in Snuba (see the factories.py finding — the mutation happens after `get_data()` and may not propagate), and (b) the `upsampled_count` aggregate is correctly resolved. There is no test where an allowlisted project contains a mix of sampled and unsampled events (some with `error_sampling` context, some without), which is exactly the case the `sum(sample_weight)` implementation gets wrong (unsampled events contribute NULL/0). There is also no test for the discover dataset without an explicit `event.type:error` filter, no test for aliased yAxis (`count() as total`), and no test for topEvents queries. These gaps mean the most likely production failure modes (NULL sample_weight, alias collisions, top-events semantic change) are untested.

title: Unit tests never test the public entry point is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects or the cache/invalidation behavior
body: The test file only tests the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`). The actual public function `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` — which contains the caching logic, the cache-key construction, and the composition of the helpers — has zero coverage. Consequently the `hash()`-based cache key bug, the cached-False handling, and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (which has no callers and no tests) are completely unverified. Tests should cover: cache hit/miss behavior, that a cached result is returned without calling options.get, that invalidate_upsampling_cache removes the entry, and that the function composes dataset + query checks correctly.

title: A git submodule pointer file 'sentry-repo' was accidentally added at the repository root
body: The diff adds a new top-level file `sentry-repo` containing `Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a`. This is a git submodule gitlink accidentally committed as a regular file (or a stray `git submodule` artifact) at the repo root of the sentry monorepo. It is unrelated to the error-upsampling feature, pollutes the repository root, and will confuse tooling (and `git status`) — if it is meant to be a submodule it should be registered in `.gitmodules` and added via `git submodule add`, not committed as a plain file. It should be removed from this PR.

title: Allowlist option value is compared against project IDs without type normalization
body: `options.get("issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist", [])` returns whatever the operator configured (likely a list of ints, but options are frequently stored/edited as strings, e.g. `["123", "456"]` from a YAML/JSON config or the admin UI), and the check `project_id in allowlist` compares ints against those values. If the option contains strings, `123 in ["123"]` is False, so eligibility silently fails and upsampling is never applied (errors undercounted) with no error or log. The helper should normalize both sides to int (e.g. `{int(p) for p in allowlist}`) and handle malformed entries gracefully.

title: _are_all_projects_error_upsampled takes an unused organization parameter and performs an O(n*m) allowlist scan per uncached request
body: The `organization` parameter of `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` is never used (the allowlist is global, not per-org), which is misleading API surface. Additionally, `all(project_id in allowlist for project_id in project_ids)` is O(len(project_ids) * len(allowlist)) with `allowlist` being a list; for queries spanning many projects against a large allowlist this is repeated on every cache miss. Converting the allowlist to a `set` once per call (or caching the parsed set alongside eligibility) would make the check O(n). Minor, but the unused parameter should be removed or the function should actually scope the allowlist per organization if that is the intent.

title: delete_matched_rows only archives the last replay_id
body: In delete_matched_rows, the loop iterates over all rows calling delete_replay_recordings(project_id, row), but then calls delete_replays(project_id, [row["replay_id"] for row in rows]) — wait, actually it does use a list comprehension over all rows. However, looking more carefully at the code: `delete_replays(project_id, [row["replay_id"] for row in rows])` is correct. But the real bug: the loop variable `row` is used after the loop in some versions; here it's fine. Actually re-reading: the function is correct in using the comprehension. The actual issue is that delete_replay_recordings is called per-row inside the loop (fine), but there is no transactional safety: if the process crashes after deleting recordings but before publishing archive events, replays remain unarchived but their recordings are gone — a data integrity risk. More concretely: delete_replays publishes archive events AFTER recordings are deleted; if publishing fails, recordings are permanently lost while the replay still appears active. This ordering should be reversed or made idempotent.

title: fetch_error_details zips error_ids with events.values() which may not align
body: fetch_error_details builds node_ids from error_ids, calls nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids), then constructs ErrorEvents by zipping error_ids with events.values(). nodestore get_multi returns a dict keyed by node_id; dict ordering in Python 3.7+ preserves insertion order, and get_multi implementations typically return results in the same order as requested keys, but this is not guaranteed by the nodestore interface contract. If any event is missing (data is None), the zip still pairs error_ids[i] with events.values()[i], which may be a different event's data — producing ErrorEvents with mismatched id/title/message. The filter `if data is not None` then drops entries, shifting all subsequent pairings. The correct approach is to iterate over node_ids and look up events[node_id] explicitly, pairing each event_id with its own data.

title: response[0].get("error_ids", []) assumes the first row contains error_ids and ignores pagination
body: The endpoint calls query_replay_instance and then process_raw_response, taking error_ids only from response[0]. If the replay query returns multiple rows (e.g., due to grouping or pagination), error_ids from other rows are silently dropped, so errors associated with the replay may be missing from the AI summary context. Additionally, if response is non-empty but the row lacks error_ids, errors are silently omitted with no logging.

title: Unauthenticated endpoint logs full request body at info level
body: The endpoint has permission_classes = () and is CSRF-exempt, meaning it is completely unauthenticated. It logs the entire request body via logger.info("browser_report_received", extra={"request_body": request.data}) before any validation. Browser reports can contain arbitrary attacker-controlled content (body is an unvalidated DictField, url, user_agent, etc.), so this enables log injection and unbounded log volume/DoS via large payloads, and may leak sensitive data into logs. The request body should not be logged at info level on an unauthenticated endpoint; at minimum it should be logged at debug, truncated, or removed entirely.

title: Validation failure logs raw attacker-controlled report content
body: On serializer validation failure, the endpoint logs the raw report at warning level: logger.warning("browser_report_invalid_format", extra={..., "data": raw_data}) and logger.warning("browser_report_validation_failed", extra={"validation_errors": serializer.errors, "raw_report": report}). Since the endpoint is unauthenticated, an attacker can submit arbitrarily large or malicious payloads that get written to logs, enabling log flooding/DoS and potential log injection. Raw request data should not be logged on an unauthenticated endpoint.

title: 422 response leaks internal serializer error details to unauthenticated callers
body: The endpoint returns Response({"error": "Invalid report data", "details": serializer.errors}, status=422) to unauthenticated callers. While serializer errors are generally safe, returning structured validation details from a public, unauthenticated, CSRF-exempt endpoint provides attackers with a precise oracle for probing the expected schema. Combined with the fact that the endpoint is a metrics collector that should simply accept or reject, returning detailed validation errors is unnecessary information disclosure. A generic 422 without details is more appropriate.

title: get_merged_pr_single_issue_template calls PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title but PRCommentWorkflow is defined later in the file
body: get_merged_pr_single_issue_template is a @staticmethod on CommitContextIntegration that calls PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title(title). PRCommentWorkflow is defined AFTER CommitContextIntegration in the same module. Since the call happens at runtime (not at class definition time), this works in Python, but it creates a fragile forward reference: if the method is ever called during module import or if PRCommentWorkflow is renamed/moved, it breaks. More importantly, _truncate_title is defined as a @staticmethod on CommitContextIntegration itself (line 577), so calling PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title is inconsistent — it should call the local _truncate_title (or CommitContextIntegration._truncate_title) directly. If PRCommentWorkflow later defines its own _truncate_title with different behavior, this silently changes. The indirection through PRCommentWorkflow is wrong since the method belongs to CommitContextIntegration.

title: _truncate_title has unused max_length parameter shadowing module constant
body: The static method _truncate_title(title, max_length=ISSUE_TITLE_MAX_LENGTH) accepts a max_length parameter but get_merged_pr_single_issue_template calls it as PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title(title) without passing max_length, always using the default. The parameter is never overridden anywhere, making it dead flexibility. Minor, but the indirection through PRCommentWorkflow (see related finding) makes this confusing.

title: Detector owner can be set to arbitrary user/team without membership validation
body: The update() and create() methods accept an `owner` ActorField and set owner_user_id/owner_team_id directly from the validated actor without checking that the user is a member of the organization or that the team belongs to the organization/project. An attacker with detector-edit permission could assign a detector to a user or team outside the organization (if ActorField resolves cross-org actors) or to a team in a different project, causing notifications/actions to be routed to unintended recipients or leaking detector existence. The owner should be validated against organization membership and project team membership before assignment.

title: update() reads validated_data.get("detector_type") but the field is named "type"
body: In update(): instance.type = validated_data.get("detector_type", instance.group_type).slug. The serializer field is declared as `type = serializers.CharField()` and validate_type returns the GroupType class, so the validated data key is "type", not "detector_type". This means validated_data.get("detector_type", ...) always falls back to instance.group_type, silently ignoring any type change submitted by the client. If the API contract intends to allow changing the detector type, this is a bug; if not, the dead lookup should be removed. Either way the current code does not do what it appears to do.

title: Table widget feature flag renders empty placeholder instead of actual table data
body: When organization.features includes 'use-table-widget-visualization', tableResultComponent renders <TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} /> — i.e., it passes EMPTY columns and EMPTY data, completely discarding the actual result.data, result.meta, fields, eventView, and all other props that were previously passed to StyledSimpleTableChart. This means enabling the feature flag causes all table widgets in dashboards to render blank. The new TableWidgetVisualization should be passed the real table data (result.data, result.meta, fields mapped to TabularColumn[], etc.), not hardcoded empty values. This is clearly a placeholder that was committed by mistake and will break every table widget for any org with the flag enabled.

title: Visualize constructor unconditionally sets stack='all', changing chart stacking behavior
body: The Visualize constructor now sets this.stack = 'all' unconditionally. Previously, stack was only set for bar charts with multiple y-axes (this.stack = this.chartType === ChartType.BAR && this.yAxes.length > 1 ? undefined : 'all'). Since Visualize now always has a single yAxis, the old condition would have produced stack='all' for single-yAxis visualizes anyway, so behavior is equivalent for the new model. However, the test 'uses unstacked bar graph' was removed and the stack semantics changed: previously a multi-yAxis BAR visualize had stack=undefined (unstacked); now every visualize is stacked. For the new single-yAxis model this is fine, but the unconditional assignment removes the ability to represent unstacked charts and the removed test coverage means the stacking behavior change is unverified. This is a behavior change that should be intentional and documented.

title: isVisualize type guard checks 'yAxis' but isVisualize is used to filter Visualize instances whose serialized form uses 'yAxes'
body: isVisualize now checks `'yAxis' in value && typeof value.yAxis === 'string'`. This guard is used in index.tsx (findAllFieldRefs, defaultPageParams) to filter aggregateFields for Visualize instances. Visualize instances have a yAxis property (the class field), so this works for class instances. However, in updateLocationWithAggregateFields and other places, BaseVisualize objects (plain JSON with yAxes array) are handled by isBaseVisualize. The concern: isVisualize is exported and its semantics changed from checking yAxes (array) to yAxis (string). Any caller that passes a serialized BaseVisualize (with yAxes) to isVisualize will now get false, potentially causing serialized visualizes to be misclassified as groupBys or dropped. The dual naming (yAxis vs yAxes) between Visualize and BaseVisualize is a source of confusion and bugs; the type guard change should be verified against all call sites.

title: Error message stringifies exception object instead of extracting message
body: In the catch block: throw new Error(`Unable to fetch trace item attribute keys: ${e}`). When e is an Error object, template literal interpolation calls toString() producing "Error: <message>", which is acceptable, but if e is an ApiError or response object from the Sentry API client, ${e} may produce "[object Object]" or a huge JSON dump. The existing useGetTraceItemAttributeValues.tsx has the same pattern. Better to use e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e) or extract the API error message. Minor robustness issue.

title: tooFewFeedbacks logic is inverted — shows summary UI when there are zero feedbacks
body: The hook returns tooFewFeedbacks: data.numFeedbacksUsed === 0 && !data.success. In FeedbackSummary component, the render condition is: if (!feature || tooFewFeedbacks || isError) return null. So when numFeedbacksUsed === 0 and success is false, tooFewFeedbacks is true and the component returns null (correct — don't show summary). But when numFeedbacksUsed === 0 and success is TRUE (summary generated from zero feedbacks?), tooFewFeedbacks is false, and the component proceeds to render summary (which would be null from data.summary). The logic seems intended to hide the summary when there aren't enough feedbacks, but the condition `!data.success` means: if the API says success=true but used 0 feedbacks, we show the summary section (with null summary text). The semantics of numFeedbacksUsed and success need to be clarified; as written, a successful response with 0 feedbacks used will render an empty summary box. The condition should likely be data.numFeedbacksUsed < SOME_THRESHOLD regardless of success, or the component should also check summary !== null.

title: Summary content rendered without null check — can render 'null' or crash
body: The component renders <SummaryContent>{summary}</SummaryContent> where summary is string | null. If the API returns success=true with summary=null (or the hook returns summary: null in a non-error, non-pending state), React renders nothing for null (safe), but if summary is undefined (e.g., data.summary missing from response), it also renders nothing. However, the hook's return type says summary: string | null, and the component doesn't guard against null before rendering the whole summary box. If summary is null but tooFewFeedbacks is false and isError is false, the component renders a "Feedback Summary" header with empty content — a broken UI state. Should check `if (!summary) return null;` before rendering.

title: Analytics event recorded before feature flag check — metrics polluted by unauthorized requests
body: analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...) is called at the top of post(), BEFORE the features.has("organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble", ...) check that returns 404. This means every request from an organization without the feature flag still records an analytics event, inflating usage metrics with unauthorized/failed attempts. The analytics event should be recorded after the feature check passes (and ideally after successful validation), not before. This skews the preprod_artifact.api.assemble metric with 404 responses.

title: request.user.id accessed without null check — crashes for unauthenticated requests
body: The endpoint uses ProjectEndpoint with permission_classes = (ProjectReleasePermission,). If authentication fails, DRF would normally return 401/403 before reaching post(). However, analytics.record uses request.user.id directly. If request.user is an AnonymousUser (id is None), this passes user_id=None to analytics. More importantly, if the endpoint is ever accessed with an auth token that authenticates but request.user is somehow unset, this crashes. The analytics Attribute for user_id is required=False, so passing None is acceptable, but accessing .id on AnonymousUser returns None (not a crash). This is a minor robustness note; the main issue is the ordering relative to the feature check (see related finding).

title: Removing ParameterizationRegexExperiment is a breaking API change for any external consumers
body: The PR removes the ParameterizationRegexExperiment class entirely and changes ParameterizationExperiment from a union type (ParameterizationCallableExperiment | ParameterizationRegexExperiment) to just ParameterizationCallableExperiment. This is a public API break: any code (including getsentry or plugins) that imports ParameterizationRegexExperiment or passes regex-based experiments to Parameterizer will fail at import/runtime. The __all__ export was also updated. If this class is used outside this repo (e.g., in getsentry), this will break. At minimum, a deprecation shim should be left, or this should be coordinated with downstream consumers.

title: Dead _handle_regex_match function in parametrize_w_experiments
body: parametrize_w_experiments defines a nested _handle_regex_match function (lines 335-343) that is identical to the one in parametrize_w_regex, but after the removal of ParameterizationRegexExperiment, the experiments loop only calls experiment.run(content, _incr_counter) and never uses _handle_regex_match. This is dead code that should be removed.

title: Migration body replaced with no-op return — data migration silently does nothing
body: The migration function convert_org_saved_searches_to_views previously contained the actual data migration logic (iterating SavedSearch objects with Visibility.ORGANIZATION and creating GroupSearchView entries). It has been replaced with a bare `return` and a comment saying "This migration had an error and was never run. See 0921...". If this migration has already been applied in any environment (recorded in django_migrations), replacing its body with a no-op is fine for that environment. But if there are environments where it has NOT yet run (e.g., fresh installs running all migrations, or environments that skipped it), the no-op means organization-level saved searches will never be converted to GroupSearchView, causing data loss for those users. The comment claims it "was never run" but this cannot be guaranteed across all deployments. The safer approach is to keep the original logic (or fix it) rather than no-op it, OR ensure 0921 supersedes it with proper dependencies. Since 0920 was also no-op'd and both depend on different predecessors (0916 vs 0919), there may be environments where neither the original nor the revised migration runs correctly.

title: Second migration also no-op'd — no working migration converts org saved searches
body: Same issue as 0917: this migration's body was replaced with a bare `return` and a comment pointing to 0921. Combined with 0917 also being no-op'd, there are now TWO no-op migrations in the chain. If 0921 (the "rerevised" migration) is not present in this PR's changed files (it is not listed), then NO migration actually performs the conversion. The changed files list shows 0917 and 0920 modified but no 0921 added. This means the data migration is completely missing from this PR — organization saved searches will not be converted to views. This is a critical data integrity gap.

title: Changing DEFAULT_AUTOFIX_AUTOMATION_TUNING_DEFAULT from 'low' to 'off' changes behavior for all existing projects
body: DEFAULT_AUTOFIX_AUTOMATION_TUNING_DEFAULT is changed from "low" to "off", and the corresponding project option default in src/sentry/projectoptions/defaults.py is also changed from "low" to "off". Project options with a default value apply to all projects that have not explicitly set the option. This means every existing project that has not explicitly configured sentry:autofix_automation_tuning will silently change from "low" (autofix runs at low automation level) to "off" (autofix does not run automatically). This is a significant behavior change affecting auto-fix automation for potentially all customers. This should be a deliberate, communicated rollout (e.g., via a migration that sets the option explicitly for existing projects, or a feature flag), not a silent default change. The tests were updated to expect "off" but no migration or rollout mechanism is provided.

title: Log message references event_data but logs workflow_event_data — potential NameError or wrong variable
body: In fire_actions_for_groups, the logger.info call at line ~580 uses extra={"workflow_ids": ..., "actions": ..., "event_data": workflow_event_data, "event_id": workflow_event_data.event.event_id}. The diff shows the change from "event_data": event_data to "event_data": workflow_event_data. If workflow_event_data is defined in the loop scope (it likely is, since it's used for workflow_event_data.event.event_id on the next line), this is fine. But the diff context suggests this was changed from event_data to workflow_event_data, which is correct if workflow_event_data is the per-workflow event data. However, if workflow_event_data is only defined inside a conditional branch and the logger call is outside that branch, this would be a NameError. Without seeing the full function, this is a potential bug — the variable rename should be verified to be in scope at the log call site.

title: useQuery result is used with isFetching for previous-data fallback but error state is not handled in return
body: The hook returns {attributes: isFetching ? previous : data, error, isLoading: isFetching}. When the query errors, isFetching becomes false and data is undefined, so attributes becomes undefined (not previous). The error is returned but callers must check it. More importantly, usePrevious(data, isFetching) — the second argument to usePrevious is typically a boolean indicating whether to skip updating. If isFetching is true, previous retains the last non-fetching value. But on error, isFetching is false, so previous would update to undefined (the errored data). This means after an error, attributes becomes undefined rather than retaining the last good data. The error handling pattern is fragile; callers get undefined attributes on error with no fallback to previous good data.

title: API request uses queryKey[0] and queryKey[1]?.query instead of the structured queryKey
body: The hook builds a queryKey via traceItemAttributeValuesQueryKey which returns [url, {query}], then calls api.requestPromise(queryKey[0], {method: 'GET', query: {...queryKey[1]?.query}}). This works but is awkward — it reconstructs the options from the queryKey tuple rather than just passing the url and options directly. The spread {...queryKey[1]?.query} creates a new object, which is fine. This is a code smell but not a bug. The queryKey is built but not used for caching (no useApiQuery), so building an ApiQueryKey is unnecessary overhead. Minor.

title: Body cell renderer returns raw value without field renderer when tableData.meta is missing, but head cell still uses fieldAlignment
body: In renderDefaultBodyCell, when tableData?.meta is missing, it returns dataRow[column.key] directly (raw value, no formatting). But renderDefaultHeadCell always calls fieldAlignment(column.name, column.type as ColumnValueType) regardless of whether meta exists. This inconsistency means headers are aligned based on column.type but body cells are unformatted raw values when meta is missing. More importantly, when meta IS present, getFieldRenderer is called with tableData.meta.fields, but if column.key is not in meta.fields (e.g., a custom column not present in the data), getFieldRenderer may return a fallback or throw. The renderer should handle the case where column.key is not in meta.fields gracefully.

title: Fallback column extraction crashes when tableData.meta.fields is undefined
body: When columns prop is not provided, the component does Object.keys(tableData?.meta.fields).map(...). If tableData.meta is undefined or tableData.meta.fields is undefined, Object.keys(undefined) throws a TypeError, crashing the component. The TabularData type says meta is required, but the component uses tableData?.meta.fields with optional chaining on tableData but NOT on .meta.fields — so if tableData exists but meta.fields is undefined (e.g., empty API response), this crashes. Should be Object.keys(tableData?.meta?.fields ?? {}).

title: useApiQuery enabled condition uses replayRecord?.id and project?.slug but query key uses replayRecord?.id ?? '' — query fires with empty replayId
body: createAISummaryQueryKey(organization.slug, project?.slug, replayRecord?.id ?? '') is called unconditionally to build the query key. If replayRecord is undefined, the query key becomes `/projects/org-slug/undefined/replays//summarize/breadcrumbs/` (with empty replayId). The enabled condition checks Boolean(replayRecord?.id && project?.slug && feature), so the query won't fire when replayRecord is undefined. However, the query key is still constructed with undefined/empty values, which could cause React Query cache collisions if multiple components mount with undefined replayRecord. More importantly, if project is undefined (project_id set but project not loaded yet), project?.slug is undefined and the query key contains 'undefined' as a string segment. The enabled check prevents firing, but the key construction with undefined values is sloppy and could cause cache issues.

title: chapterData maps over summaryData?.data.time_ranges but summaryData could be undefined after the null check
body: After the `if (!summaryData) return ...` check, the code accesses summaryData.data.summary and summaryData?.data.time_ranges.map(...). The optional chaining on summaryData?.data.time_ranges is inconsistent with the earlier non-optional summaryData.data.summary access. If summaryData.data is undefined (response has no data field), summaryData.data.summary throws. The SummaryResponse type says data is required, but runtime responses may not match. The optional chaining on time_ranges suggests defensive coding, but summaryData.data.summary on line 150 is not defensive. Inconsistent null handling.

title: Entire request payload is buffered in memory as a JSON string before sending to Seer
body: analyze_recording_segments builds the entire request_data via json.dumps({"logs": get_request_data(...)}) which materializes ALL log messages into a list in memory (get_request_data returns list(gen_request_data(...))), then json.dumps the whole thing, then json.loads the Seer response. For long replays with many breadcrumbs and errors, this can consume significant memory. The code comments acknowledge this: "XXX: Request isn't streaming. Limitation of Seer authentication." and "XXX: I have to deserialize this request so it can be 'automatically' reserialized by the paginate method. This is less than ideal." The double serialization (json.dumps then json.loads) is also wasteful. While acknowledged as a known limitation, this is a real performance concern for large replays and should be tracked as a follow-up.

title: make_seer_request has no timeout — request can hang indefinitely
body: requests.post(f"{settings.SEER_AUTOFIX_URL}/v1/automation/summarize/replay/breadcrumbs", data=request_data, headers={...}) is called without a timeout parameter. If the Seer service is slow or unresponsive, the request (and thus the API endpoint) will hang indefinitely, tying up worker threads and potentially causing cascading failures. All outbound HTTP requests should have an explicit timeout. This is especially important since the request body can be large (all breadcrumbs + errors for a replay).

title: Error log includes full response content which may be large or contain sensitive data
body: On non-200 status, the code logs extra={"status_code": ..., "response": response.text, "content": response.content}. Logging both response.text and response.content is redundant (content is bytes, text is str of the same body). If the Seer error response is large, this floods logs. The response body from an internal service is unlikely to contain user-sensitive data, but logging the full body at warning level for every failed request is excessive. Should log status_code and a truncated response.

title: get_slow_conditions_for_groups is now called once per process_delayed_workflows batch instead of per-function, but the no_slow_condition_groups logging may be noisy
body: The refactor moves get_slow_conditions_for_groups from being called inside get_condition_query_groups and get_groups_to_fire (potentially multiple times) to once in process_delayed_workflows. This is a good change. However, the new logging block logs "delayed_workflow.no_slow_condition_groups" at info level whenever any DCG has no slow conditions. In a batch with many DCGs, if most have no slow conditions (which may be common), this logs a potentially large sorted list at info level on every batch, causing log noise. The comment says "that's interesting enough to log" but info-level logging of potentially many IDs per batch is excessive; debug or a metric would be more appropriate.

title: processing_deadline_duration added to schedule_webhook_delivery without explanation
body: A processing_deadline_duration=30 is added to schedule_webhook_delivery's TaskworkerConfig. This is a behavior change: tasks will now be killed/timed out after 30 seconds. If schedule_webhook_delivery legitimately takes longer than 30 seconds (e.g., processing a large batch of webhooks), it will be terminated mid-execution, potentially leaving webhooks undelivered. The PR description doesn't explain why this deadline is needed. Similar additions (300 for drain_mailbox, 120 for drain_mailbox_parallel) should be justified. Without context, these deadlines could cause silent task failures.

title: processing_deadline_duration=60 added to check_auth_identities may truncate large batches
body: check_auth_identities processes a list of auth_identity_ids (default chunk_size=100) and then reschedules check_auth. With processing_deadline_duration=60, if processing 100 identities takes longer than 60 seconds (e.g., slow identity provider refreshes), the task will be killed mid-batch. Identities already processed have last_synced updated, but the rescheduling call check_auth.apply_async at the end may not execute if the task is killed, potentially leaving remaining identities unprocessed until the next scheduled run. The deadline should be generous enough to handle the chunk size, or the task should checkpoint progress.

title: Visualize.fromJSON return type changed from Visualize to Visualize[] — breaking change for callers
body: Visualize.fromJSON previously returned a single Visualize; now it returns Visualize[] (an array, mapping over yAxes). This is a breaking API change. Callers that did `const v = Visualize.fromJSON(json)` and used v directly (e.g., v.yAxis, v.chartType) will now get an array and break. The diff shows callers were updated (aggregateFields.tsx uses Visualize.fromJSON(aggregateField) and maps over the result), but any external/downstream callers (getsentry, plugins) will break. This should be a new method name (e.g., fromJSONMany) or the old single-return behavior preserved.

title: updateLocationWithAggregateFields uses Visualize.fromJSON which now returns an array — flatMap handles it but the semantics changed
body: updateLocationWithAggregateFields calls Visualize.fromJSON(aggregateField) and now does visualizes.map(visualize => JSON.stringify(visualize.toJSON())) inside a flatMap. Previously fromJSON returned a single Visualize and the code did JSON.stringify(Visualize.fromJSON(aggregateField).toJSON()). The new code correctly handles the array return. However, this means a single BaseVisualize with multiple yAxes now expands into multiple URL query params (one per yAxis), each with its own chartType. Previously it was a single param. This changes the URL format for multi-yAxis visualizes — existing bookmarks/shared URLs with multi-yAxis visualize params will be parsed differently (each yAxis becomes a separate visualize param with the same chartType, losing the grouping). This is a URL contract change.

title: Analytics visualizes field changed from raw Visualize objects to toJSON() — but the analytics schema may expect the old format
body: The trackAnalytics calls changed visualizes: visualizes to visualizes: visualizes.map(visualize => visualize.toJSON()). Previously, Visualize objects were passed directly (which would serialize via their properties). Now toJSON() returns {yAxes: [yAxis], chartType?}. The analytics event schema for trace.explorer.metadata may expect a specific format for the visualizes field. If the analytics pipeline expects the old format (e.g., array of Visualize instances serialized differently), this changes the data shape. The change is likely correct (toJSON is the intended serialization), but the analytics event schema should be verified to accept the new format.

title: Sentry logger info call uses String(String(search.tokens).length) — double String() is a bug
body: In the info() log call: user_queries_count: ${String(String(search.tokens).length)}. search.tokens is an array; String(search.tokens) converts it to a string, then .length gets the string length (character count of the stringified array), then String() wraps it. This is wrong — it should be search.tokens.length (the number of tokens), not the character length of the stringified array. The double String() is clearly a mistake. Compare with the trackAnalytics call which correctly uses search.tokens.length. The log output will show a meaningless number (character count of the string representation of the tokens array).

title: visualizes_count log uses String(String(visualizes).length) — meaningless value
body: In the info() log call: visualizes_count: ${String(String(visualizes).length)}. visualizes is an array of Visualize objects; String(visualizes) produces something like "[object Object],[object Object]", and .length gives the character count of that string. This is completely wrong — it should be visualizes.length (the number of visualizes). The trackAnalytics call correctly uses visualizes.length. The log output is a meaningless number.

title: Log visualizes field uses v.chartType but should use visualize.toJSON() for consistency with analytics
body: The info() log call uses visualizes: ${visualizes.map(v => v.chartType).join(', ')} which only logs chart types, while the trackAnalytics call logs visualizes.map(visualize => visualize.toJSON()). This inconsistency means the Sentry log and the analytics event have different granularity for the visualizes field. The log is less useful (only chart types, no yAxis info). Should use the same toJSON() format for consistency, or at least include yAxis.

title: DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION pushed to yAxes array then deduped and sorted — mutates the visualizes-derived array
body: The yAxes useMemo does: const allYAxes = visualizes.map(visualize => visualize.yAxis); allYAxes.push(DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION); return dedupeArray(allYAxes).sort(). The push mutates allYAxes which is a fresh array from map, so no external mutation. This is fine. However, the comment says "injects DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION here as it can be used to populate the confidence footer as a fallback" — this means the timeseries query always includes an extra yAxis (DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION) even when not needed, adding an extra series to every query. This is a performance overhead (extra data fetched) that is intentional but should be documented. Not a bug per se.

title: dedupeArray import still used but could be simplified since each visualize now has single yAxis
body: dedupeArray is still imported and used on line 103: dedupeArray(allYAxes).sort(). Since each Visualize now has a single yAxis, allYAxes is a flat list of strings. dedupeArray is still needed to remove duplicates (multiple visualizes could have the same yAxis, plus DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION could duplicate). So the import is still needed. Not a bug.

title: Removed multi-yAxis check changes top events behavior — now returns 5 even when multiple visualizes exist
body: The hook previously checked `if (visualizes.some(visualize => visualize.yAxes.length > 1)) return undefined;` to disable top events when any visualize had multiple y-axes. This check was removed because Visualize now always has a single yAxis. However, the original intent was to disable top events when there are multiple y-axes IN A SINGLE CHART (overlaid series). With the new model, each Visualize is a separate chart with one yAxis, so multiple visualizes = multiple charts, and top events should still work per-chart. But the hook now returns TOP_EVENTS_LIMIT (5) whenever there's at least one groupBy and mode is AGGREGATE, regardless of how many visualizes/charts exist. If there are 4 visualizes (4 separate charts), top events=5 is applied to the timeseries query, which may produce unexpected results (top 5 series across all charts). The hook's comment acknowledges this limitation but the behavior change (removing the multi-yAxis guard) means top events is now enabled in cases where it previously wasn't. This should be verified against the backend's top events handling for multi-visualize queries.

title: addChart creates new Visualize without label — labels may be missing or duplicated
body: addChart does: [...visualizes, new Visualize(DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION)].map(visualize => visualize.toJSON()). The new Visualize is created without a label option, so its label defaults to '' (empty string). Existing visualizes have labels 'A', 'B', etc. (assigned by getVisualizesFromLocation). The new chart gets label '' instead of the next letter (e.g., 'C'). This means the new chart won't have a proper label badge. The shouldRenderLabel check (visualizes.length > 1) will be true, but the new chart's label is empty, so no badge renders for it. The label should be assigned as String.fromCharCode(65 + visualizes.length) to continue the sequence.

title: setYAxis uses visualizes[group]!.replace({yAxis: newYAxis}) but loses the label
body: setYAxis does: visualizes.toSpliced(group, 1, visualizes[group]!.replace({yAxis: newYAxis})). The replace method creates a new Visualize with the new yAxis but preserves the label (replace passes label: this.label). So the label is preserved. This is fine. Not a bug.

title: Compare Queries link uses yAxes: [visualizeYAxes[0]!] — only first visualize is included in comparison
body: The Compare Queries LinkButton navigates to generateExploreCompareRoute with queries: [{query, groupBys, sortBys, yAxes: [visualizeYAxes[0]!], chartType: visualizes[0]!.chartType}]. This only includes the FIRST visualize's yAxis. If the user has multiple visualizes (charts), only the first is carried into the comparison view. The other visualizes are silently dropped. The comparison feature may only support a single query/visualize, but if so, the UI should indicate this (e.g., disable the button when multiple visualizes exist) rather than silently dropping data.

title: visualizeYAxes computed but only [0] is used in compare — dead computation for multi-visualize case
body: visualizeYAxes = visualizes.map(v => v.yAxis) is computed, used for alertsUrls (all yAxes) and chartOptions (all visualizes), but the Compare link only uses visualizeYAxes[0]!. If there's only one visualize, visualizeYAxes[0] is fine. The computation of the full array is needed for alertsUrls. Not a bug, just noting the compare limitation (see related finding).

title: getChartInfo(DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION) called inside map for each visualize — redundant computation
body: Inside the chartInfos useMemo, for each visualize, if sampleCount === 0 && !defined(isSampled), it calls getChartInfo(DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION) to get fallback sampling metadata. If multiple visualizes hit this fallback condition, getChartInfo(DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION) is called multiple times (once per visualize), each time re-querying the same data. This is redundant computation. The fallback chartInfo for DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION should be computed once outside the map and reused. Performance issue for queries with multiple visualizes that all lack sampling metadata.

title: Fallback series lookup uses timeseriesResult.data[yAxis] directly instead of getSeries result
body: In the fallback block: const series = dedupedYAxes.flatMap(yAxis => timeseriesResult.data[yAxis]).filter(defined). This accesses timeseriesResult.data directly, bypassing the shouldUsePreviousResults logic in getSeries. If previous results should be used (timeseriesResult.isPending && canUsePreviousResults), the fallback confidence computation uses the current (pending) data instead of previous data, producing incorrect confidence values during loading states. Should use the same data source as getSeries.

title: handleApply converts Visualize to toJSON() but the onColumnsChange type expects BaseAggregateField[] — GroupBy objects pass through unchanged
body: handleApply does: onColumnsChange(tempColumns.map(col => (isVisualize(col) ? col.toJSON() : col))). The onColumnsChange prop type is (columns: BaseAggregateField[]) => void. BaseAggregateField = GroupBy | BaseVisualize. isVisualize(col) returns true for Visualize instances, converting them to BaseVisualize (toJSON). GroupBy objects pass through as-is. This is correct. But the test expects onColumnsChange to be called with [{groupBy: 'geo.region'}, {yAxes: ['avg(span.self_time)']}] — the Visualize is converted to {yAxes: [...]} which matches BaseVisualize. This is correct behavior. Not a bug.

title: insertColumn(new Visualize(DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION)) — new column has empty label
body: When adding a new visualize column via the dropdown, insertColumn(new Visualize(DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION)) creates a Visualize with default label '' (empty string).
