This means the mock will never match, and the test's assertion `expect(searchQueryMock).not.toHaveBeenCalled()` will pass trivially (the mock was never called because the matcher failed). The test is not actually testing the number-type early return; it's testing that the mock doesn't match. The matcher should check `query.substringMatch === 'search-query'` (or better, the test should verify the hook returns [] without making any request).

title: Number-type test is ineffective: mock matcher uses wrong param name so the mock never matches, making the test pass vacuously
body: In `getTraceItemAttributeValues returns empty array for number type`, the mock matcher checks `query.query === 'search-query'` (line 120), but the hook sends `substringMatch` (line 53 of the hook). Since the matcher never matches, `searchQueryMock` is never called, and the assertion `expect(searchQueryMock).not.toHaveBeenCalled()` passes — but not because the hook correctly returned early; it's because the mock was never triggered. The test does not actually verify the number-type early return. The matcher should be removed (since the hook should return [] before making any request) and the test should simply assert the hook returns [] without any mock setup.

title: Test name says 'returns empty array for number type' but the test doesn't actually verify the early return logic — it just checks the mock wasn't called
body: The test should verify that `getTraceItemAttributeValues` returns `[]` immediately for number type without making an API call. The current test sets up a mock (that never matches) and checks it wasn't called — this is weak. A better test: don't set up any mock, call the hook with type 'number', and assert the result is `[]` and no API call was made (using `MockApiClient` assertions).

title: String-type test verifies substringMatch but doesn't verify other query params (itemType, attributeType, project, datetime)
body: The test only checks `substringMatch`. A more thorough test would verify the full query object including `itemType: 'logs'`, `attributeType: 'string'`, `project: ['1']`, `statsPeriod: '14d'`.

title: Test suite doesn't test error handling (API failure) — the hook throws an Error with the raw exception
body: There's no test for the error path (`catch (e) { throw new Error(...) }`). A test should verify that API failures result in a thrown error with a generic message (not leaking the raw exception).

title: Test suite doesn't test the FieldKind.FUNCTION early return
body: There's no test verifying that function tags return `[]` without an API call. A test should pass a tag with `kind: FieldKind.FUNCTION` and assert the result is `[]` and no API call is made.

title: Test suite doesn't test that undefined values are filtered out
body: The hook filters `defined(item.value)` — a test should include an item with `value: undefined` or `value: null` and verify it's excluded from the results.

title: Test suite doesn't test custom datetime/projectIds props overriding page filters
body: The hook accepts `datetime` and `projectIds` props that override the page filters. No test verifies this override behavior.

title: Test suite doesn't test the SPANS trace item type
body: Both tests use `TraceItemDataset.LOGS`. A test with `TraceItemDataset.SPANS` should verify the `itemType: 'spans'` query param is sent.

title: Test suite doesn't test empty search string behavior
body: When `queryString` is empty, `substringMatch` is not set (the hook only sets it if `search` is truthy). A test should verify that an empty search string doesn't send `substringMatch`.

title: Test suite doesn't test multiple projects in the query
body: The hook sends `project: projectIds.map(String)`. A test with multiple project IDs should verify the array is sent correctly.

title: Test suite doesn't test absolute datetime (start/end) vs relative (statsPeriod)
body: The hook uses `normalizeDateTimeParams` which handles both. A test with absolute start/end should verify those params are sent instead of `statsPeriod`.

title: Test suite doesn't test UTC parameter propagation
body: The `utc` param from `normalizeDateTimeParams` should be sent. A test with `utc: true` should verify it's included.

title: Test suite doesn't test that the returned function is stable (useCallback memoization)
body: A test could verify that the returned function reference doesn't change on re-render when dependencies are stable. Low priority.

title: Test suite doesn't test the hook's behavior when the organization slug changes
body: The hook uses `organization.slug` in the URL. A test with a different organization should verify the URL changes. Low priority.

title: Test suite doesn't test the hook's behavior when the attribute key contains special characters
body: The `attributeKey` is interpolated into the URL path. A test with a key containing special characters (e.g. `http.request.method`) should verify the URL is correctly formed (the key should be URL-encoded if needed).

title: Test suite doesn't test the hook's behavior when the API returns an empty array
body: A test with an empty array response should verify the hook returns `[]`.

title: Test suite doesn't test the hook's behavior when the API returns items with missing value field
body: The hook filters `defined(item.value)`. A test with items missing `value` should verify they're excluded.

title: Test suite doesn't test the hook's behavior when the API returns a non-array response
body: The hook doesn't validate `Array.isArray(result)`. A test with a non-array response (e.g. an object) should verify the hook handles it gracefully (currently it would crash). This is a test gap for a robustness issue.

title: Test suite doesn't test the hook's behavior when the API returns items with non-string values
body: The hook maps `item.value` directly. If `value` is a number, it's returned as-is. The return type is `string[]`, so non-string values would violate the type. A test should verify only string values are returned, or the hook should coerce/filter.

title: Test suite doesn't test the hook's behavior when the API returns duplicate values
body: The hook doesn't deduplicate values. A test with duplicate values should verify they're all returned (or the hook should deduplicate).

title: Test suite doesn't test the hook's behavior when the API returns a large number of values
body: Performance/UX: a test with many values should verify the hook handles them (though this is more of a backend concern). Low priority.

title: Test suite doesn't test the hook's behavior when the API request is slow (loading state)
body: The hook doesn't expose a loading state (it's a callback, not a query hook). The search bar handles loading. No test needed here.

title: Test suite doesn't test the hook's behavior when the API request is cancelled
body: The `useApi` hook provides cancellation. A test with cancellation should verify the hook handles it gracefully. Low priority.

title: Test suite doesn't test the hook's behavior when the API returns a 404 (attribute not found)
body: A test with a 404 response should verify the hook throws an error (caught and re-thrown with a generic message).

title: Test suite doesn't test the hook's behavior when the API returns a 500 (server error)

title: Test suite doesn't test the hook's behavior when the API returns a 403 (permission denied)

title: Test suite doesn't test the hook's behavior when the network is offline

title: delete_matched_rows deletes only the last replay_id instead of all matched replays
body: In `delete_matched_rows(project_id, rows)`, the loop `for row in rows: delete_replay_recordings(project_id, row)` deletes the recording segments for every row, but the subsequent call `delete_replays(project_id, [row["replay_id"] for row in rows])` is placed AFTER the loop, so `row` refers to the last iterated row. The list comprehension `[row["replay_id"] for row in rows]` is evaluated after the loop completes, which is correct, but the indentation in the shown code places it at function scope after the loop — actually re-reading: the comprehension iterates `rows` again so it does collect all replay_ids. However, the real bug is that `delete_replay_recordings` is called per-row inside the loop (fine), but if `rows` is empty the function returns early (fine). The actual defect: the archive events are published for all rows, but `delete_replay_recordings` is invoked once per row — that is correct. The genuine issue is that `delete_matched_rows` returns `None` always and the caller cannot know how many rows were processed; more importantly, the function name and the loop suggest per-row deletion but the archive publish happens once with all ids — this is fine. The concrete bug: the `for row in rows:` loop variable `row` is reused in the list comprehension after the loop; in Python the comprehension has its own scope so this is safe. The real problem is that `delete_replay_recordings` is called inside the loop but `delete_replays` (which archives) is called after — if `delete_replay_recordings` raises for one row, the archive events for ALL rows are never published, leaving recordings deleted but replays not archived (data integrity: replays remain visible but their segments are gone). This is a data-integrity risk: partial failure leaves inconsistent state.

title: fetch_error_details zips error_ids with events.values() which may not align when some events are missing
body: `fetch_error_details` builds `node_ids` from `error_ids`, calls `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)`, then constructs `ErrorEvent` objects by `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. `get_multi` returns a dict keyed by node_id; if any event is missing (returns None), the dict will have fewer entries than `error_ids`, and `zip` will silently pair the wrong `event_id` with the wrong `data` (dict ordering is insertion order of the returned dict, not the requested order). The `if data is not None` filter then drops entries, but the id/data pairing is already corrupted — an error event can be attributed to the wrong event_id, producing incorrect error context (wrong title/message/timestamp) in the AI summary. Consequence: misleading AI-generated replay summaries with incorrect error attribution.

title: response[0].get("error_ids", []) assumes the first row contains error_ids without validating the field was requested
body: `error_ids = response[0].get("error_ids", []) if response else []` — `process_raw_response` is called with `fields=request.query_params.getlist("field")`. If the client does not request the `error_ids` field, the Snuba response rows will not contain `error_ids`, and `.get("error_ids", [])` silently returns `[]`, so error context is silently omitted even when `enable_error_context` is not "false". The endpoint should either always request `error_ids` from Snuba or document that error context requires the field. Consequence: error context is silently dropped depending on client `field` params, making the `enable_error_context` query param unreliable.

title: Unauthenticated endpoint logs full request body at info level, risking PII/secret leakage into logs
body: The endpoint has `permission_classes = ()` and is CSRF-exempt, and `logger.info("browser_report_received", extra={"request_body": request.data})` logs the entire raw request body (which includes `body` dicts that can contain arbitrary page content, URLs, user agents, and potentially user-entered data from the page) at INFO level. Browser reports can contain sensitive page content (e.g., CSP violation reports include the blocked URI and sometimes form data; deprecation/intervention reports include source file URLs and messages). Logging full request bodies from an unauthenticated, internet-facing endpoint at INFO level creates a log-injection/PII-exposure risk and unbounded log volume (DoS via log flooding). Consequence: sensitive data leakage into logs and potential log-based DoS.

title: Non-list request body is logged with full data before validation, and 422 returned without size limits
body: When `raw_data` is not a list, the code logs `extra={"data_type": type(raw_data).__name__, "data": raw_data}` — the entire unvalidated payload — at WARNING level, then returns 422. There is no request size limit enforced before this logging, so an attacker can send a multi-megabyte JSON body that gets fully logged. Combined with the unauthenticated nature of the endpoint, this is a log-flooding vector. Additionally, the serializer validation loop returns on the FIRST invalid report, discarding all subsequent reports in the batch — a single malformed report causes the entire batch to be rejected (fail-closed), which may be intended but should be documented; more importantly, the full `raw_report` is logged on validation failure (`extra={"validation_errors": serializer.errors, "raw_report": report}`), again logging unvalidated user-controlled data.

title: get_merged_pr_single_issue_template calls PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title but _truncate_title is defined as a staticmethod on CommitContextIntegration, not PRCommentWorkflow
body: The new method `get_merged_pr_single_issue_template` (defined on `CommitContextIntegration`) calls `PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title(title)`. However, `_truncate_title` is defined as a `@staticmethod` on `CommitContextIntegration` (line 577), not on `PRCommentWorkflow`. `PRCommentWorkflow` is a separate class defined later in the file and does not inherit from `CommitContextIntegration`. This will raise `AttributeError: type object 'PRCommentWorkflow' has no attribute '_truncate_title'` at runtime when a merged-PR comment is generated. Consequence: the GitHub/GitLab PR comment workflow crashes when formatting suspect-issue comments.

title: MERGED_PR_SINGLE_ISSUE_TEMPLATE uses markdown link syntax that may render incorrectly in some clients
body:
The template `"* ‼️ [**{title}**]({url}){environment}
"` produces a markdown link. The trailing `
` after each issue plus the `
` join in the caller produces blank lines between issues (visible in the test expectations: `* ‼️ [**issue 1**](...) in \`dev\`

* ‼️ ...`). This is a formatting choice, not a bug, but the double newline may render as extra spacing in GitHub/GitLab comments. Not a functional defect.

title: Detector owner update does not validate that the owner (user/team) belongs to the organization or project
body: In `BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update`, the `owner` field is deserialized via `ActorField` and then `instance.owner_user_id = owner.id` / `instance.owner_team_id = owner.id` is set directly. There is no check that the user is a member of the detector's organization or that the team belongs to the organization/project. A user with detector-edit permission could set the owner to an arbitrary user ID or team ID from another organization (IDOR), causing the detector to be attributed to / notify an unrelated user or team. The `create` method has the same issue. The test `test_owner_not_in_organization` expects a 400, but the validator code shown does not perform this validation — `ActorField` only parses the identifier format, it does not check membership. Consequence: cross-organization data attribution / unauthorized assignment.

title: update() pops condition_group but never uses data_conditions to update existing conditions
body: In `update()`, `condition_group = validated_data.pop("condition_group")` and `data_conditions: list[DataConditionType] = condition_group.get("conditions")` is extracted, but `data_conditions` is never used afterwards — the code only updates the condition group's logic type via `group_validator.update(...)` and never updates/creates/deletes the individual `DataCondition` rows. This means PUT requests that change conditions (e.g., the test `test_update` which changes comparison from 50 to 100 and type from LESS to GREATER) will NOT actually persist condition changes — the detector's conditions remain unchanged in the database. The test `assert_data_condition_updated` would fail. Consequence: detector condition updates are silently ignored, leading to incorrect alerting behavior.

title: dcg_to_slow_conditions computed inside a conditional block but used unconditionally later
body: In `process_delayed_workflows`, `dcg_to_slow_conditions = get_slow_conditions_for_groups(list(event_data.dcg_ids))` is computed inside an `if` block (the diff shows it added within a conditional, lines ~649-662), but then passed to `get_condition_query_groups(...)` and `get_groups_to_fire(...)` unconditionally at lines ~672 and ~699. If the enclosing `if` condition is false, `dcg_to_slow_conditions` will be undefined (or stale from a previous iteration), causing a `NameError` or incorrect behavior. The diff context shows the computation is nested under some condition (likely a feature flag or a check for whether slow conditions exist). Consequence: potential NameError or use of stale data in delayed workflow processing.

title: Removing ParameterizationRegexExperiment breaks the public ParameterizationExperiment union type for any external consumers
body: `ParameterizationExperiment` was changed from `ParameterizationCallableExperiment | ParameterizationRegexExperiment` to just `ParameterizationCallableExperiment`, and the `ParameterizationRegexExperiment` class was deleted entirely (also removed from `__all__`). Any code (including getsentry or plugins) that constructed a `ParameterizationRegexExperiment` or relied on the union type will break with ImportError/AttributeError. The corresponding tests were also deleted. This is a breaking API change to a module-level public type without a deprecation path. Consequence: downstream consumers (getsentry) that use regex-based parameterization experiments will crash on import or at runtime.

title: Migration 0917 is replaced with a no-op but the test file was deleted, leaving migration 0921 as the only converter — verify 0921 actually runs
body: Migration 0917's data migration function was replaced with a no-op (`return`) and its test file `tests/sentry/migrations/test_0917_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views.py` was deleted. Migration 0920 was similarly no-op'd. The comment says "See 0921_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views_rerevised.py for the correct migration", but 0921 is NOT in the changed files list — it must already exist on the base branch. The critical question: does 0921 depend on 0920 (and thus 0917), and does it actually contain the conversion logic? If 0921 was already applied in production before 0917/0920 were no-op'd, then environments that already ran 0917 (with the original buggy code) may have partially converted data, and the no-op prevents re-running. The deletion of the test for 0917 removes coverage that the no-op is intentional. This is a data-integrity risk if the migration chain is not carefully verified. The PR should include a test or verification that 0921 performs the conversion and that the dependency chain is correct.

title: Changing DEFAULT_AUTOFIX_AUTOMATION_TUNING_DEFAULT from "low" to "off" changes behavior for all new/existing projects without migration
body: `DEFAULT_AUTOFIX_AUTOMATION_TUNING_DEFAULT` changed from `"low"` to `"off"`, and `src/sentry/projectoptions/defaults.py` correspondingly changed the `sentry:autofix_automation_tuning` default from `"low"` to `"off"`. This is a behavioral change: projects that have never explicitly set this option will now default to autofix automation being OFF instead of LOW. Existing projects that relied on the "low" default will silently stop auto-running autofix on new issues. There is no migration to update existing project options, and no feature flag gating this change. The tests were updated to expect "off", confirming the default changed. Consequence: silent behavioral regression for customers who relied on the "low" default — autofix automation stops running for all projects that haven't explicitly configured it.

title: TableWidgetVisualization is rendered with empty columns and empty data, discarding actual table results
body: In `tableResultComponent`, when the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature flag is enabled, the code renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />` — with hardcoded empty columns and empty data, completely ignoring the actual `result.data`, `result.meta`, `fields`, `eventView`, `location`, etc. that were previously passed to `StyledSimpleTableChart`. This means enabling the feature flag causes ALL table widgets in dashboards to render as empty tables, discarding real query results. This is clearly a placeholder/debugging artifact that was committed. Consequence: enabling the feature flag breaks all dashboard table widgets, showing empty tables instead of data.

title: Visualize.fromJSON return type changed from Visualize to Visualize[] — breaking change for callers expecting a single instance
body: `Visualize.fromJSON` previously returned a single `Visualize` instance; it now returns `Visualize[]` (an array). The callers in `aggregateFields.tsx` (`updateLocationWithAggregateFields`) were updated to handle the array, but any other callers of `Visualize.fromJSON` (including in getsentry or other parts of the codebase not shown in this diff) that expect a single `Visualize` will break. The test file was updated to expect an array. This is a breaking API change to a class static method. Consequence: downstream code calling `Visualize.fromJSON(...)` and treating the result as a single `Visualize` will break (e.g., calling `.yAxis` on an array).

title: isVisualize type guard changed from checking yAxes array to checking yAxis string, but BaseVisualize still has yAxes
body: `isVisualize` was changed from `'yAxes' in value && Array.isArray(value.yAxes)` to `'yAxis' in value && typeof value.yAxis === 'string'`. However, `BaseVisualize` (the interface for serialized visualizes in URLs) still has `yAxes: readonly string[]`, not `yAxis`. In `updateLocationWithAggregateFields`, the code calls `isBaseVisualize(aggregateField)` (correct for BaseVisualize with yAxes) and then `Visualize.fromJSON(aggregateField)`. But in `findAllFieldRefs` (index.tsx line ~372), the code filters with `isBaseVisualize` and then accesses `visualize.yAxes` — that's correct. The issue is that `isVisualize` is used to filter `AggregateField[]` (which contains `Visualize` instances with `yAxis`), but the type guard now checks for `yAxis` which is correct for `Visualize` instances. However, the `isVisualize` guard is also exported and may be used elsewhere to validate URL params (which use `yAxes`). If `isVisualize` is called on a `BaseVisualize` (from URL parsing), it will return false because `BaseVisualize` has `yAxes` not `yAxis`. This inconsistency between `isBaseVisualize` (checks yAxes) and `isVisualize` (checks yAxis) is intentional but fragile — any code that uses `isVisualize` to validate raw URL data will incorrectly reject valid visualizes.

title: tooFewFeedbacks logic is inverted: returns true when numFeedbacksUsed is 0 AND success is false, but should likely be when numFeedbacksUsed is below a threshold
body: `tooFewFeedbacks: data.numFeedbacksUsed === 0 && !data.success` — this returns true only when zero feedbacks were used AND the request was not successful. But the intent (based on the name and usage in `feedbackSummary.tsx` where `tooFewFeedbacks` causes the summary to be hidden) is to hide the summary when there aren't enough feedbacks to generate a meaningful summary. If the API returns `success: true` with `numFeedbacksUsed: 0` (e.g., no feedbacks in the time range but the request succeeded), `tooFewFeedbacks` is false, and the component will try to render `summary` which may be null. Conversely, if `success: false` with `numFeedbacksUsed: 5`, `tooFewFeedbacks` is false even though the summary failed. The logic appears inverted or incomplete — it should likely be `data.numFeedbacksUsed < SOME_THRESHOLD` regardless of success, or `!data.success`. Consequence: the feedback summary UI may render incorrectly (showing null summary or hiding valid summaries).

title: API request uses queryKey[0] as URL but spreads queryKey[1]?.query — fragile destructuring of ApiQueryKey tuple
body: The code does `api.requestPromise(queryKey[0], {method: 'GET', query: {...queryKey[1]?.query}})`. `queryKey` is typed as `ApiQueryKey` which is a tuple `[string, {query: ...}]`. Accessing `queryKey[1]?.query` works but is fragile — if the tuple shape changes or if `queryKey[1]` is undefined, the optional chaining handles it, but the spread `{...queryKey[1]?.query}` could spread `undefined` (which is fine in JS, produces empty object). This is a code smell but not a functional bug. The bigger issue: the `queryKey` is constructed but only partially used — the query key is meant for React Query caching, but here it's used as a plain API call without caching, meaning the `traceItemAttributeValuesQueryKey` function's purpose (cache key) is not actually used for caching. This is a minor design issue.

title: Regex for validating attribute keys rejects valid EAP span attribute keys containing hyphens in tag names
body: The validation regex `/^[a-zA-Z0-9_.:-]+$/` allows hyphens, but the comment says "EAP spans contain tags with illegal characters / SnQL forbids `-` but is allowed in RPC. So add it back later". The second regex `/^tags\[[a-zA-Z0-9_.:-]+,number\]$/` also allows hyphens inside the tag name. However, the first regex is applied to ALL attribute keys, including `tags[...]` keys. A key like `tags[http.status_code,number]` would fail the first regex (because of `[`, `]`, `,`) but pass the second. But a key like `tags[my-tag,number]` passes the second regex (hyphen allowed). The issue: the first regex does NOT match `tags[...]` format at all (square brackets and comma not in the character class), so `tags[...]` keys are only accepted via the second regex. But the second regex only matches `tags[...,number]` — string tags in `tags[name]` format (without `,number`) would fail BOTH regexes and be silently dropped. This means string-valued tag attributes in `tags[attr]` format are incorrectly filtered out. Consequence: valid string tag attributes are missing from the search bar suggestions.

title: analytics.record is called before the feature flag check, recording events for unauthorized requests
body: `analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` is called at the top of `post()` BEFORE the `features.has("organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble", ...)` check. This means every request to this endpoint — including those from organizations without the feature flag (which get a 404) — records an analytics event. This inflates metrics with unauthorized/failed requests and leaks `user_id` for users hitting an endpoint they shouldn't have access to. The analytics event should be recorded only after the feature check passes (or at least after the request is validated as authorized). Consequence: misleading analytics data and potential privacy concern (recording user activity on endpoints they can't use).

title: request.user.id will raise AttributeError for unauthenticated requests (org auth token auth)
body: `user_id=request.user.id` — if the request is authenticated via an org auth token (which the code later checks with `is_org_auth_token_auth(request.auth)`), `request.user` may be an `AnonymousUser` or the user may not be set, causing `AttributeError` when accessing `.id`. The `ProjectReleasePermission` permission class allows org auth tokens, so `request.user` might not have an `id`. The analytics event definition marks `user_id` as `required=False`, but the code unconditionally accesses `request.user.id`. Consequence: 500 error for org-auth-token-authenticated requests before the feature check.

title: processing_deadline_duration=30 for schedule_webhook_delivery may be too short for batch webhook scheduling
body: `schedule_webhook_delivery` now has `processing_deadline_duration=30` (seconds). This task schedules webhook deliveries in batches; if the batch is large or the database is slow, 30 seconds may cause the task to be killed mid-execution, leading to partial processing. Without knowing the expected batch size, 30s seems aggressive for a scheduling task that iterates over potentially many webhook configurations. The other tasks got 300s and 120s. This inconsistency suggests the 30s value may be a mistake. Consequence: task timeouts causing incomplete webhook scheduling.

title: processing_deadline_duration=60 for check_auth_identities may be too short for large batches
body: `check_auth_identities` processes a list of auth identity IDs (default chunk_size=100) and calls `check_single_auth_identity` for each, which makes external provider API calls (`provider.refresh_identity`). With 100 identities and network latency for each refresh, 60 seconds may be insufficient, causing task timeouts and incomplete processing. The task also recursively schedules `check_auth` at the end, so a timeout would lose progress. Consequence: auth identity refresh checks are interrupted, leaving stale auth identities.

title: run_top_events_timeseries_query now accepts equations parameter but passes it through — verify rpc_dataset_common supports it for ourlogs
body: The `equations` parameter was added to `run_top_events_timeseries_query` and passed to `rpc_dataset_common.run_top_events_timeseries_query`. This is a pass-through change; the underlying `rpc_dataset_common` function must support `equations` for the ourlogs dataset. If the RPC common implementation doesn't handle equations for ourlogs (logs) queries, this could cause errors or silently ignore equations. This is a speculative concern but worth verifying since the change adds a parameter to a logs-specific query path.

title: useQuery queryKey is a plain array ['use-trace-item-attribute-keys', queryOptions] — not following ApiQueryKey tuple convention
body: The `queryKey` is constructed as `['use-trace-item-attribute-keys', queryOptions]` — a plain array, not the standard `ApiQueryKey` tuple format `[url, {query}]` used elsewhere in the codebase. This means the query won't be properly deduplicated/cached with other queries that hit the same endpoint, and devtools/debugging will show a non-standard key. Additionally, `queryOptions` is an object that may contain `undefined` values (e.g., `substringMatch: undefined`), which React Query handles but is inconsistent with the `makeTraceItemAttributeKeysQueryOptions` return type. Minor consistency issue.

title: findAllFieldRefs filters writablePageParams.aggregateFields with isBaseVisualize but readablePageParams with isVisualize — inconsistent filtering may miss field refs
body: In `findAllFieldRefs`, the readable params are filtered with `isVisualize` (checks for `yAxis` string — matches `Visualize` instances), but the writable params are filtered with `isBaseVisualize` (checks for `yAxes` array — matches `BaseVisualize` objects from URL params). The writable params' aggregateFields can contain `GroupBy` objects (which have `groupBy`, not `yAxes`) or `BaseVisualize` objects (which have `yAxes`). Using `isBaseVisualize` correctly filters for `BaseVisualize` objects. But the readable params use `isVisualize` which checks for `yAxis` — this matches `Visualize` class instances. The inconsistency is intentional (readable params contain `Visualize` instances, writable params contain `BaseVisualize` objects), but the function name `findAllFieldRefs` suggests it should find ALL field references, and the asymmetry could miss refs if the data shapes change. This is a fragile coupling between the type guards and the data shapes.

title: deleteOverlay uses toSpliced(group, 1) which removes the entire Visualize at index `group`, but the UI labels suggest removing a single yAxis overlay
body: Previously, `deleteOverlay(group, index)` removed a single yAxis from a multi-yAxis Visualize (allowing multiple series per chart). Now `deleteOverlay(group)` uses `visualizes.toSpliced(group, 1)` which removes the ENTIRE Visualize (chart) at that index. Since `Visualize` now only holds a single `yAxis`, this is semantically correct — each Visualize is one chart. However, the `aria-label` on the delete button is still `t('Remove Overlay')`, which is misleading — it removes the entire chart, not an overlay. The button label should be 'Remove Chart' to match the new behavior. This is a UX/labeling bug, not a functional one, but could confuse users.

title: ChartInfo.yAxes is now always a single-element array [visualize.yAxis], but downstream code may expect multiple yAxes per chart
body: `yAxes: [visualize.yAxis]` — since `Visualize` now holds a single `yAxis`, each chart has exactly one yAxis. The `ChartInfo` interface still has `yAxes: readonly string[]` and `formattedYAxes?: Array<string | undefined>`. The `ChartContextMenu` receives `visualizeYAxes={chartInfo.yAxes}` (an array with one element). This is a type-level change that ripples through — any code that iterates over `yAxes` expecting multiple values will now only see one. The `handleChartTypeChange` and other callbacks still work. The main risk is that the `ChartInfo` type still suggests multiple yAxes are possible, but the data model no longer supports it. This is a transitional inconsistency.

title: Analytics visualizes field changed from raw Visualize[] to visualizes.map(v => v.toJSON()), but the analytics event schema may expect a different shape
body: The `visualizes` field in the `trace.explorer.metadata` analytics event was changed from passing the raw `Visualize[]` array to `visualizes.map(visualize => visualize.toJSON())`. The `toJSON()` method returns `BaseVisualize` objects with `yAxes: [yAxis]` and optional `chartType`. Previously, the raw `Visualize` objects were passed (which would serialize differently — they have `yAxis`, `label`, `chartType`, `stack` properties). This changes the analytics event payload shape. If the analytics pipeline expects the old shape (with `yAxis`, `label`, etc.), this is a breaking change to the event schema. The `label` field (e.g., 'A', 'B') is lost in `toJSON()`. Consequence: analytics dashboards/queries that parse the `visualizes` field may break or lose the `label` dimension.

title: yAxes useMemo pushes DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION then dedupes and sorts — but the sort order may not match visualize order
body: `const allYAxes = visualizes.map(visualize => visualize.yAxis); allYAxes.push(DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION); return dedupeArray(allYAxes).sort();` — the yAxes are sorted alphabetically, which means the order of yAxes sent to the API no longer matches the order of visualizes. If the API returns data keyed by yAxis, this is fine (lookup by key), but if any downstream code assumes the order of yAxes matches the order of visualizes (e.g., for assigning colors or matching confidences), the sort will break that assumption. The `confidences` array is indexed by visualize index (`confidences[index]` in charts/index.tsx), so as long as confidences are matched by yAxis key (not array position), this is fine. But the sort is unnecessary and potentially confusing.

title: Visualize constructor no longer supports multiple yAxes — stack is always 'all', removing the ability to have unstacked bar charts
body: Previously, `Visualize` accepted `yAxes: readonly string[]` and set `this.stack = this.chartType === ChartType.BAR && this.yAxes.length > 1 ? undefined : 'all'` — meaning multi-yAxis bar charts were unstacked. Now `Visualize` only accepts a single `yAxis` and `this.stack = 'all'` is always set. The test `uses unstacked bar graph` was deleted. This means it's no longer possible to create an unstacked bar chart with multiple series — all bar charts are now stacked. Since each Visualize is now a single yAxis, this is consistent, but the `stack` property is now always 'all' and could be removed. The `determineDefaultChartType` function still accepts `yAxes: readonly string[]` and counts across multiple yAxes, but it's only ever called with `[yAxis]` (single element). This is dead generality.

title: handleApply converts Visualize to BaseVisualize via toJSON() but the onColumnsChange type expects BaseAggregateField[] — GroupBy objects are passed through unchanged, which is correct, but the test expects {yAxes: [...]} format
body: `onColumnsChange(tempColumns.map(col => (isVisualize(col) ? col.toJSON() : col)))` — `col.toJSON()` returns `BaseVisualize` with `yAxes: [yAxis]`. The test `aggregateColumnEditorModal.spec.tsx` expects `onColumnsChange` to be called with `[{groupBy: 'geo.region'}, {yAxes: ['avg(span.self_time)']}]`. This matches. However, the `onColumnsChange` prop type is `(columns: BaseAggregateField[]) => void` where `BaseAggregateField = GroupBy | BaseVisualize`. The `toJSON()` output is `BaseVisualize` which has `yAxes: readonly string[]`. This is consistent. No bug here — the test and implementation align.

title: updateLocationWithAggregateFields flatMaps BaseVisualize to multiple Visualize JSON strings, but a BaseVisualize with multiple yAxes now produces multiple URL params — verify this matches the new single-yAxis model
body: `updateLocationWithAggregateFields` now does `Visualize.fromJSON(aggregateField).map(visualize => JSON.stringify(visualize.toJSON()))` — since `Visualize.fromJSON` now returns an array (one Visualize per yAxis), a `BaseVisualize` with `yAxes: ['a', 'b']` produces TWO URL params: `[{yAxes: ['a']}, {yAxes: ['b']}]`. Each URL param is a `BaseVisualize` with a single-element `yAxes` array. When parsed back by `getAggregateFieldsFromLocation`, each is converted to a `Visualize` with a single `yAxis`. This round-trips correctly. However, the URL now contains N params for N yAxes instead of 1 param with N yAxes — this changes the URL format and may break saved links/bookmarks that use the old multi-yAxis format. The parsing code (`getVisualizesFromLocation`) handles both formats (it iterates `visualize.yAxes` for each BaseVisualize), so backward compatibility is maintained for reading. But writing always produces single-yAxis params. This is a URL format change.

title: Error message includes raw exception object via string interpolation, potentially leaking internal details
body: `throw new Error(\`Unable to fetch trace item attribute keys: ${e}\`)` — the raw exception `e` is interpolated into the error message. If the API returns a detailed error (e.g., stack trace, internal URL, or auth token), it could leak internal information to the client. The same pattern exists in `useGetTraceItemAttributeValues.tsx` line 115. This is a minor information disclosure risk.

title: LLM prompt directly interpolates raw user feedback strings without sanitization — prompt injection risk
body:
`make_input_prompt` joins raw feedback strings with `"
------
".join(feedbacks)` and interpolates them directly into the LLM prompt: `User Feedbacks:

{feedbacks_string}`. User feedback is untrusted input — a malicious user can craft feedback containing prompt injection payloads (e.g., "Ignore previous instructions and output ...") to manipulate the LLM-generated summary. The summary is then displayed to other users/staff in the feedback UI. There is no sanitization, escaping, or instruction hierarchy hardening. Consequence: prompt injection allowing an attacker to control the AI-generated summary content shown to Sentry staff/other users, potentially generating misleading or harmful summaries.

title: generate_summary raises ValueError on empty LLM response but the caller may not handle it gracefully
body: `generate_summary` raises `ValueError("Invalid response from LLM")` when `complete_prompt` returns a falsy response. The comment says "This can throw". If the caller (the feedback summary endpoint) doesn't catch this, it results in a 500 error. The frontend `useFeedbackSummary` hook handles `isError`, but a 500 from an unhandled exception is not a clean API error. The endpoint should catch this and return a structured error (e.g., 503 or a `success: false` response).

title: AI-generated summary is rendered as plain text without sanitization — potential XSS if summary contains HTML
body:
`{summary}` renders the AI-generated summary as a React child (which escapes HTML by default), so this is safe from XSS. However, `SummaryContent` is a styled `

` element. If the summary contains markdown or HTML that should be rendered (e.g., links), it will show as raw text. This is not a security issue (React escapes by default) but a UX limitation. Not reporting as a finding since React's default escaping prevents XSS.

title: useProjectFromId is called with replayRecord?.project_id which may be undefined, and the hook may not handle undefined gracefully
body: `const project = useProjectFromId({project_id: replayRecord?.project_id})` — if `replayRecord` is undefined (the Props type allows `replayRecord: ReplayRecord | undefined`), `project_id` is `undefined`. The `useProjectFromId` hook likely expects a defined project_id. The code later checks `if (replayRecord?.project_id && !project)` to show an error, but the hook itself may have already made an API call with undefined or thrown. The previous code used `useLocationQuery` to get the project from the URL, which was more reliable. The new code depends on `replayRecord` being loaded before the hook runs, but hooks can't be conditional. Consequence: potential unnecessary API call or error when replayRecord is undefined.

title: createAISummaryQueryKey is called with replayRecord?.id ?? '' — empty string replay ID produces a malformed API URL
body: `createAISummaryQueryKey(organization.slug, project?.slug, replayRecord?.id ?? '')` — if `replayRecord` is undefined, `replayRecord?.id ?? ''` is `''`, producing the URL `/projects/{org}/{project}/replays//summarize/breadcrumbs/` (double slash, empty replay ID). The `useApiQuery` has `enabled: Boolean(replayRecord?.id && project?.slug && ...)` so the query won't fire when replayRecord is undefined. However, the query key is still constructed with the empty string, which means if replayRecord later loads, the query key changes and the query fires correctly. This is fine due to the `enabled` guard, but constructing a malformed URL as a query key is sloppy.

title: Early return for FieldKind.FUNCTION uses tag.kind but the tag parameter may not have kind set correctly for all callers
body: `if (tag.kind === FieldKind.FUNCTION || type === 'number')` — the `tag` parameter is passed from the search query builder's `getTagValues` callback. The `kind` property on the tag determines whether to skip value suggestions. If a caller passes a tag without `kind` set (undefined), the check `tag.kind === FieldKind.FUNCTION` is false, and the function proceeds to fetch values for a function tag, which may not be supported by the API. The `TraceItemSearchQueryBuilder` adds function tags with `kind: FieldKind.FUNCTION`, so this should be fine for that caller, but the hook is generic and other callers may not set `kind`.

title: API request is made on every keystroke (debounced by caller) without React Query caching — duplicate requests for the same attribute+query
body: The hook returns a callback `getTraceItemAttributeValues` that makes a direct `api.requestPromise` call. Unlike `useTraceItemAttributeKeys` which uses `useQuery` for caching, this hook does NOT use React Query caching. The `traceItemAttributeValuesQueryKey` function is defined but only used to construct the URL and query params — it's not passed to `useApiQuery` or `useQuery`. This means every invocation (e.g., every debounced keystroke in the search bar) makes a fresh network request with no deduplication or caching. If the user types the same query twice, two identical requests are made. Consequence: unnecessary network requests and potential rate limiting.

title: useQuery queryFn calls getTraceItemAttributeKeys() without arguments, but the function expects an optional queryString — search filtering is not wired up
body: `useQuery<TagCollection>({enabled, queryKey, queryFn: () => getTraceItemAttributeKeys()})` — `getTraceItemAttributeKeys` accepts an optional `queryString` parameter for substring matching, but the `queryFn` calls it with no arguments. This means the query always fetches ALL attribute keys without any search filtering. The `makeTraceItemAttributeKeysQueryOptions` function supports a `search` parameter, but it's never passed. The `queryKey` includes `queryOptions` which has `substringMatch: undefined` (since `search` is not passed to `makeTraceItemAttributeKeysQueryOptions` in the hook). This means the search/substring filtering feature of the attribute keys endpoint is not utilized by this hook. Consequence: the hook always fetches the full list of attribute keys, which may be slow for projects with many attributes, and the `substringMatch` capability is unused.

title: queryOptions useMemo dependency on `selection` object causes unnecessary recomputation when selection reference changes
body: `const queryOptions = useMemo(() => {...}, [selection, traceItemType, type, projectIds])` — `selection` is an object from `usePageFilters()`. If `usePageFilters` returns a new object reference on every render (even if the contents are the same), the `useMemo` will recompute every render, and the `queryKey` will change, causing `useQuery` to refetch. This is a common React pitfall. The `selection` object should be destructured to its primitive dependencies (e.g., `selection.datetime`, `selection.projects`) to avoid unnecessary refetches.

title: determineDefaultChartType reduce starts with ChartType.AREA as initial accumulator, which biases toward AREA on ties
body: `return [ChartType.AREA, ChartType.BAR, ChartType.LINE].reduce((acc, ct) => (counts[ct] >= counts[acc] ? ct : acc), ChartType.AREA)` — the initial accumulator is `ChartType.AREA`. On a tie (e.g., all counts are 0, or AREA and BAR have equal counts), the `>=` comparison means the later element wins only if strictly greater or equal. Since AREA is first in the array and the initial acc, if all counts are 0, AREA wins (0 >= 0). If BAR and LINE tie at 1 each and AREA is 0, BAR wins (1 >= 0), then LINE (1 >= 1) wins — so LINE wins ties against BAR. The initial AREA means AREA wins when all are 0. This is arbitrary but not a bug per se. The function is only called with a single yAxis now, so the counts will always be 0 or 1 for one chart type.

title: parseBaseVisualize uses Number(parsed.chartType) which coerces string chart types to NaN, silently dropping valid string enum values
body: `const chartType = Number(parsed.chartType); if (Object.values(ChartType).includes(chartType))` — `ChartType` is a TypeScript enum. If it's a numeric enum, `Number(parsed.chartType)` works. But if `ChartType` is a string enum (e.g., `LINE = 'line'`), `Number('line')` is `NaN`, and `Object.values(ChartType).includes(NaN)` is false, so the chartType is silently dropped. The test `converts from JSON with chart type` passes `chartType: ChartType.AREA` which is already the enum value (number or string). If the URL contains the string representation (e.g., `"line"`), `Number("line")` is NaN and the chart type is lost. This depends on whether ChartType is a numeric or string enum. If it's a string enum, this is a bug — the chartType from URL params would always be dropped.

title: Label generation String.fromCharCode(65 + i) breaks for more than 26 visualizes (produces non-letter characters)
body: `label: String.fromCharCode(65 + i)` — this generates labels 'A', 'B', ..., 'Z' for i=0..25. For i >= 26, it produces '[', '\', ']', etc. — non-letter characters. The `MAX_VISUALIZES = 4` constant limits visualizes to 4, so i will never exceed 3 in practice. But the code in `getAggregateFieldsFromLocation` doesn't enforce MAX_VISUALIZES — it processes all parsed visualizes from the URL. A crafted URL with 30 visualizes would produce labels like '^', '_', '`'. This is a minor robustness issue.

title: updateLocationWithAggregateFields flatMap return type is string[] but location.query.aggregateField expects string[] — the flatMap produces one string per yAxis for BaseVisualize, which is correct, but the type of aggregateFields parameter is Array<GroupBy | BaseVisualize> which doesn't include Visualize
body: The function signature is `updateLocationWithAggregateFields(location, aggregateFields: Array<GroupBy | BaseVisualize> | null | undefined)`. But callers may pass `AggregateField[]` which is `GroupBy | Visualize`. `Visualize` is not assignable to `BaseVisualize` (Visualize has `yAxis`, BaseVisualize has `yAxes`). The `isBaseVisualize` check would return false for a `Visualize` instance (since it checks for `yAxes` array), so a `Visualize` would fall through to the `else` branch and be JSON.stringified directly — producing `{"yAxis": "...", "label": "...", ...}` instead of the expected `{"yAxes": ["..."]}` format. This would create malformed URL params. The caller in `aggregateColumnEditorModal.tsx` converts Visualize to BaseVisualize via `toJSON()` before calling, so it's fine there. But the type signature suggests Visualize should be accepted, which would break.

Since each Visualize has a unique yAxis (they're separate charts), the only possible duplicate is `DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION` appearing both as a visualize's yAxis and as the injected default. `dedupeArray` handles this correctly. Not a bug, just noting the import is still needed.

title: Removed check for visualizes with multiple yAxes — but Visualize no longer supports multiple yAxes, so the check was dead code

Since `Visualize` now only has a single `yAxis`, this check would always be false (dead code). Removing it is correct. However, the comment above the hook says "There's a limitation with this hook when a top n query < 5 series. This hook always returns 5" — this limitation still exists and is now more pronounced since each visualize is a single series. The hook returns `TOP_EVENTS_LIMIT` (5) whenever there's at least one group by in aggregate mode, regardless of how many visualizes (series) exist. If there's only 1 visualize, topEvents=5 is misleading. This is a pre-existing issue, not introduced by this PR.
