body: The thread-queue-parallel tests (test_thread_queue_parallel, test_thread_queue_parallel_preserves_order, test_thread_queue_parallel_concurrent_subscriptions) use a polling loop `for _ in range(max_wait): ... if stats['total_items'] == 0 and mock_processor_call.call_count == 2: break; time.sleep(0.1)` followed by `assert mock_processor_call.call_count == 2`. If processing is slow or broken, the loop exhausts max_wait iterations (50 * 0.1s = 5s) and falls through to the assert, which will then fail — so it does not pass vacuously. However, there is no diagnostic on timeout (the assert message is bare), and the pattern relies on wall-clock timing (0.1s sleeps, 5s budget) which is flaky under CI load: a heavily loaded CI runner can easily exceed 5s for two messages, causing intermittent failures. The tests should use an Event set by the mocked processor (as the queue_consumer unit tests correctly do with process_complete_event.wait(timeout=5.0)) instead of polling call_count, which is both deterministic and gives a clear failure. The same polling pattern is repeated in test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_commit, test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling, and test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts offsets are NOT committed after a processing exception, but the implementation completes offsets in a finally block, so the test contradicts the code
body: The test sets mock_processor_call.side_effect = [Exception('Processing failed'), None], submits two messages, waits, then asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`. However, OrderedQueueWorker.run wraps result_processor in try/except/finally, and the finally block unconditionally calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)`. So even when processing raises, the offset is marked complete, and the commit thread will commit it. The test's assertion is therefore wrong relative to the implementation: after both messages are processed (one raising, one succeeding), offsets 100 and 101 are both completed, and the commit thread will commit offset 102 (101+1). The assertion `test_partition not in committed_offsets` will fail once the commit loop runs (within ~1s). Either the test is wrong (it should expect the offset to be committed, matching the at-least-once semantics where a failed message is skipped and its offset committed), or the implementation is wrong (failed messages should not have their offsets committed, requiring DLQ/retry semantics). Given the ResultProcessor.__call__ already swallows exceptions internally (logs and returns normally), the worker-level exception path is mostly unreachable in production, but the test as written will fail against the actual code. This needs to be reconciled: the test should assert the actual intended behavior.

title: wait_until_empty polls qsize() every 10ms; qsize() is O(1) but the polling loop is only used in tests and is a busy-wait
body: FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty busy-polls get_stats() (which calls qsize() on every queue and sums) every 10ms until timeout. queue.Queue.qsize() is documented as approximate and, more importantly, checking qsize()==0 does not mean all items have been processed — a worker can have taken an item off the queue (qsize drops to 0) and still be processing it. So wait_until_empty can return True while work is still in flight, giving a false sense of completion. It is only used in tests, but if used in production shutdown paths it would be incorrect. It should instead join on unfinished_tasks (queue.task_done / queue.join) or check the OffsetTracker's outstanding set, and the method should be documented as only checking queue depth, not in-flight work.

title: Python's built-in hash() is randomized per process, breaking consistent group-to-queue assignment across restarts and workers
body: FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group uses `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`. In Python 3, `hash()` of strings is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED randomization), so the same group key maps to different queue indices in different processes and across restarts. This breaks the core ordering guarantee: two messages for the same subscription can be processed concurrently by different workers (if the consumer runs with multiple processes via --processes, each process has its own pool and different hash seeds), and after a restart a group can move to a different queue, allowing out-of-order processing of the same subscription. The docstring claims 'Each group is consistently assigned to the same queue' but this is only true within a single process. Use a stable hash (e.g., md5/sha1 of the key, or zlib.crc32) instead.

title: get_committable_offsets iterates a range from min to max offset per partition on every commit cycle
body: OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets computes `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1)` and checks set membership for every integer in that span. Kafka offsets are monotonically increasing and can be far apart (e.g., after a long-running consumer, offsets in the millions with sparse in-flight items), so each 1-second commit-loop iteration can iterate over millions of integers per partition, holding the per-partition lock the entire time. This blocks add_offset/complete_offset calls from worker threads (stalling processing) and burns CPU. The algorithm should instead sort the completed offsets and walk only the actual tracked offsets (e.g., iterate over sorted(all_offsets) and stop at the first outstanding one), which is O(k log k) in the number of tracked offsets rather than O(max_offset).

title: OffsetTracker.partition_locks dict is read and written without synchronization, allowing duplicate locks for the same partition
body: _get_partition_lock does `self.partition_locks.get(partition)` followed by `self.partition_locks.setdefault(partition, threading.Lock())` with no lock protecting the dict itself. Multiple worker threads can race on first access to a partition: thread A's get() returns None, thread B's get() returns None, and both create separate Lock objects — one wins in the dict, the other thread uses its own orphaned lock. All subsequent synchronization for that partition is then split across two locks, so add_offset/complete_offset/get_committable_offsets/mark_committed are not mutually exclusive, which can corrupt the offset sets (e.g., mark_committed pruning all_offsets while get_committable_offsets iterates it) and produce incorrect commit decisions — potentially committing offsets for messages still being processed (data loss on crash). Guard creation with a single global lock (e.g., `with self._locks_guard: return self.partition_locks.setdefault(partition, threading.Lock())`).

title: Worker exceptions are swallowed and the offset is still marked complete, causing silent message loss
body: In OrderedQueueWorker.run, when result_processor raises, the exception is only logged ('Unexpected error in queue worker') and the finally block unconditionally calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)`. The offset is therefore treated as successfully processed and becomes committable, so the failed message is never retried and is silently dropped once the offset is committed. Note that ResultProcessor.__call__ in result_consumer.py also swallows exceptions internally, so most processing failures never even reach this handler — either way the message is lost. This is a data-integrity bug for a Kafka consumer whose contract is at-least-once delivery. On exception the offset should remain outstanding (or the item should be retried / sent to a DLQ), not completed.

title: submit() exception handler marks the offset complete, committing messages that were never processed
body: In SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit, the except block logs 'Error submitting message to queue' and then calls add_offset + complete_offset for the message. If the decoder or grouping_fn raised, the message was never enqueued or processed, yet its offset is immediately marked complete and will be committed — permanently skipping that message. The same pattern is used for the `result is None` path (lines 301-304), which is arguably intentional for undecodable messages, but applying it to unexpected exceptions in submit converts a transient failure into silent data loss. The offset should be left outstanding (blocking commits for that partition, surfacing the problem) or the message routed to a DLQ, not completed.

title: close() can commit offsets for items still queued, and shutdown discards in-flight work without committing or requeuing
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event, joins the commit thread (which stops committing), then calls queue_pool.shutdown(). FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True and calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) — with Python's queue.ShutDown semantics, workers finish the item they are currently processing but any items still sitting in the queues are abandoned, and their offsets remain outstanding (never committed, which is safe) — but worse, close() joins the commit thread BEFORE draining the queues, so offsets for items that complete during pool shutdown are never committed even though they were processed. On the next start those messages are reprocessed (at-least-once, acceptable), but the ordering of operations is wrong: the pool should be drained (wait_until_empty) and a final commit performed before the commit thread is stopped. Also, terminate() shuts down the pool without waiting for in-flight items at all. For a consumer whose purpose is exactly-once-ish ordered processing, shutdown should drain queues and flush final offsets.

title: join() ignores its timeout argument and delegates to close(), which is not a graceful join
body: ProcessingStrategy.join(timeout) is expected to wait up to `timeout` for the strategy to finish processing outstanding work. Here join() discards the timeout and calls close(), which (per the close() issues above) stops the commit thread and shuts down workers with a hard 5s join each, abandoning queued items. Arroyo's StreamProcessor uses join during shutdown to allow in-flight work to complete; this implementation makes join equivalent to an abrupt terminate and ignores the caller's timeout, so shutdown behavior does not match the ProcessingStrategy contract.

title: FixedQueuePool is created once per factory but create_with_partitions can be called multiple times, sharing one pool across strategies
body: ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ creates a single FixedQueuePool (with its worker threads and OffsetTracker) when mode == 'thread-queue-parallel'. create_with_partitions then returns a new SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy wrapping that same pool each time it is called. Arroyo calls create_with_partitions per partition-assignment epoch (e.g., on rebalance), so multiple strategy instances can share one pool and one OffsetTracker. Each SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy also spawns its own commit thread calling commit_function with its own `commit` closure — two commit threads can commit interleaved offset maps from the shared tracker, and shutdown() on the factory sets self.queue_pool = None while previously created strategies still reference the pool, leading to double shutdown and commits from stale strategies. The pool should be created per create_with_partitions call (or the factory should guard against reuse), not per factory instance.

title: ResultProcessor.__call__ swallows all exceptions, so failed results are treated as processed and their offsets committed
body: ResultProcessor.__call__ wraps handle_result in a try/except that only logs ('Failed to process message result'). Since OrderedQueueWorker treats the return of result_processor as success and completes the offset, any exception in handle_result (DB errors, assertion failures, etc.) results in the message being acknowledged and committed — silent data loss with no retry and no DLQ routing. This is the queue-mode equivalent of a poison message being dropped. Failures should propagate (so the offset stays outstanding and the partition stalls, surfacing the issue) or be routed to the DLQ policy that the StreamProcessor already supports.

title: Sentry transaction name hardcodes 'monitors.' prefix for a generic remote-subscriptions component
body: OrderedQueueWorker.run creates a transaction named f"monitors.{self.identifier}.worker_{self.worker_id}". This module lives in sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers and is generic infrastructure (also used by uptime via ResultsStrategyFactory), but the metric/transaction namespace is hardcoded to 'monitors.', so uptime results processed through this path will be tagged as monitors.* in Sentry/metrics, polluting dashboards and making the identifier misleading. The prefix should be derived from the identifier or made configurable.

title: wait_until_empty only checks queue size, not outstanding (in-flight) items
body: FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty returns True when get_stats()['total_items'] == 0, i.e., all queues are empty. But an item that has been popped by a worker and is currently being processed is no longer counted in qsize(), so wait_until_empty can return True while work is still in flight. Callers using this to assert 'all work done' (as the tests do implicitly via stats checks) can race with in-flight processing. It should also check that the OffsetTracker has no outstanding offsets (or expose outstanding counts in get_stats).

title: test_different_groups_distributed can pass even if all groups hash to one queue (weak assertion on hash distribution)
body: The test asserts len(queue_indices) == 3 after hashing 20 group keys with num_queues=3. With Python's randomized string hash this usually passes, but it is probabilistic and, more importantly, it validates distribution rather than the actual requirement — consistent assignment per key (covered by the other test) and correct modulo behavior. If hash() were replaced with a broken function returning a constant, this test would catch it, but as written it is flaky-by-construction (a fixed hash seed could theoretically map all 20 keys to fewer than 3 buckets) and does not test the property that matters for correctness (stability across processes), which is untestable in-process. Consider asserting on a deterministic hash function instead once the implementation is fixed.

title: New thread-queue-parallel tests poll with fixed iteration counts and no failure message on timeout
body: The new tests (test_thread_queue_parallel, test_thread_queue_parallel_preserves_order, test_thread_queue_parallel_concurrent_subscriptions, test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_commit, test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling, test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps) use `for _ in range(max_wait): ... time.sleep(0.1)` loops and then assert on results without first asserting the loop actually observed the expected condition. If processing is merely slow (CI under load), the loop exits after max_wait iterations (5 seconds) and the subsequent assert produces a confusing failure, or worse, in test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling the loop breaks only when the condition holds but the final asserts tolerate `len(committed_offsets) == 0` — meaning the test can pass without ever verifying that commits are correctly withheld. The loops should assert the wait condition succeeded (e.g., `assert stats['total_items'] == 0 and ... , 'timed out waiting'`) before proceeding, so slow runs fail loudly at the wait rather than at a downstream assert, and the error-handling test should deterministically verify the no-commit behavior.

title: Python's built-in hash() is randomized per process, breaking consistent queue assignment across restarts and workers
body: FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group uses `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`. In Python 3, hash() of strings is salted with a per-process random seed (PYTHONHASHSEED), so the same group key maps to different queues in different processes and across restarts. This breaks the documented guarantee that 'each group is consistently assigned to the same queue' whenever the consumer runs with multiple processes (the uptime consumer supports --processes), and also means a group's messages can be split across queues within a single process only by luck of the seed. Ordering within a group is therefore not actually guaranteed in multi-process deployments, and a slow item can still clog a queue because the group-to-queue mapping is unstable. Use a stable hash such as hashlib.md5/sha1 of the encoded key, or zlib.crc32.

title: OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets is O(max_offset - min_offset) per partition and can scan millions of offsets
body: get_committable_offsets iterates `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1)` and checks membership in the all_offsets set. Kafka offsets are monotonically increasing and can be in the millions or billions. If a partition has a long-lived gap (e.g., an offset that is never completed because its message was submitted to a queue whose worker died, or an offset added via the exception path in submit() that is never completed), every call to get_committable_offsets — which runs every second in the commit loop — will iterate from the gap to max_offset. With a gap at offset 1000 and current offset 10,000,000, this is a ~10M-iteration loop holding the per-partition lock every second, stalling add_offset/complete_offset for that partition and burning CPU. The algorithm should track a sorted structure or a 'highest contiguous completed offset' pointer instead of scanning the full range.

title: OffsetTracker.partition_locks dict is read and written without synchronization, causing a race on lock creation
body: _get_partition_lock does `self.partition_locks.get(partition)` followed by `self.partition_locks.setdefault(partition, threading.Lock())` with no lock protecting the dict itself. Two threads (e.g., two queue workers completing offsets for a newly-seen partition, or the commit loop calling get_committable_offsets while a worker calls add_offset) can race: both can see no lock, both create a Lock, and one overwrites the other in the dict. The two threads then hold different locks for the same partition, so the mutual exclusion the class documents ('Thread-safe for concurrent access with per-partition locks') is broken, allowing concurrent mutation of all_offsets/outstanding for that partition. In CPython dict operations are atomic so this won't corrupt the dict, but the lock identity is not stable, defeating the locking. Guard creation with a single global lock.

title: Worker exceptions are swallowed and the offset is still marked complete, causing silent message loss
body: In OrderedQueueWorker.run, when result_processor raises, the exception is caught, logged with logger.exception, and then the finally block unconditionally calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)`. This marks the failed message as processed, so the commit loop will commit past it and the message is never retried or sent to a DLQ. The class docstring claims 'Only commits offsets after successful processing', but the code commits offsets after failed processing too. For the uptime results consumer this means a transient error in handle_result (e.g., a DB hiccup) permanently drops that uptime result, corrupting uptime/downtime calculations. The offset should only be completed on success; on failure the offset should remain outstanding (blocking commits for that partition, which is the safe behavior) or the message should be routed to a DLQ/retried.

title: submit() asserts message.value is BrokerValue, crashing on FilteredPayload messages instead of filtering them
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit does `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` before checking the decoded result. Arroyo uses FilteredPayload for messages that were filtered upstream (e.g., by a filter step or topic filtering); the decoder explicitly handles FilteredPayload by returning None (see result_consumer.decode_payload which asserts `not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)` and the test test_handles_invalid_messages which submits a FilteredPayload message). With assertions enabled (the default in production Python unless -O is used), submitting a FilteredPayload message raises AssertionError, which is caught by the broad `except Exception` and logged, but then the except block itself checks `isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` and skips offset tracking — so the offset is never added nor completed. If a FilteredPayload ever arrives with an offset in the middle of a partition, that offset is simply absent from all_offsets, which is fine for the contiguous-commit scan only if no later offset depends on it; but more importantly the assert makes the intended 'skip filtered messages' path unreachable and turns a routine filtered message into an exception log. The isinstance check should come first and return early for non-BrokerValue messages.

title: close() can drop in-flight work and commit offsets for unprocessed messages during shutdown
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event, joins the commit thread with a 5s timeout, then calls queue_pool.shutdown(). FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True and calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) on each queue. Python's queue.Queue.shutdown(immediate=False) (PEP 703-style shutdown, available in Python 3.13) causes get() to raise ShutDown only after the queue is drained, but the worker loop checks `while not self.shutdown` before each get(); once shutdown is set, a worker blocked in get() will still wake on the next item, but a worker that has just finished an item and sees shutdown=True exits immediately, abandoning any remaining items in its queue. Those abandoned items' offsets remain in outstanding forever, but close() does not wait for queues to drain, and the commit thread may have already committed earlier offsets. The result is that on consumer shutdown, queued messages are silently dropped (never processed, never committed — safe for commits but lost for processing) and, worse, terminate() calls queue_pool.shutdown() without stopping the commit thread first, so the commit thread can commit offsets while workers are being torn down. Arroyo's shutdown sequence expects strategies to finish processing submitted messages in join(); this implementation discards them. close()/join() should drain queues (wait_until_empty or join each queue) before shutting down workers, and terminate() should stop the commit thread before the pool.

title: Offset is added to the tracker after the item is already in the queue, creating a window where the offset is untracked
body: FixedQueuePool.submit calls `self.offset_tracker.add_offset(...)` and then `work_queue.put(work_item)`. Between these two calls, a worker can pick up the item and process it, calling complete_offset for an offset that has not yet been added. complete_offset does `self.outstanding[partition].discard(offset)`, which is a no-op if the offset isn't present, and then when add_offset runs it adds the offset to both all_offsets and outstanding — leaving a permanently outstanding offset that blocks all future commits for that partition (the contiguous scan in get_committable_offsets will stop at this offset forever). This is a real race because workers are actively consuming from the queue while submit is called from the main consumer thread. add_offset must happen before the item becomes visible to workers, i.e., before work_queue.put.

title: thread-queue-parallel mode silently ignores num_processes, so --processes has no effect and each process gets its own queue pool
body: In ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__, the 'thread-queue-parallel' branch creates a FixedQueuePool with `num_queues=max_workers or 20` but never uses num_processes. The uptime consumer's CLI (uptime_options in src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py) exposes --processes, and StreamProcessor will fork N processes each running this factory. Each process creates its own FixedQueuePool with its own OffsetTracker and its own commit thread calling the same `commit` handle. Because each process only sees the messages assigned to its Kafka partitions, per-process offset tracking is fine, but the group-to-queue mapping (hash-based, see separate finding) is per-process randomized, and more importantly the operator's mental model of '--processes P, --max-workers W gives P*W parallelism' is wrong: each process independently spawns W queue workers, so total threads = P*W, and the queue count per process is W regardless of P. At minimum this should be documented; more likely num_processes should be rejected or used to scale num_queues. Also, the commit thread in each process commits via the arroyo Commit handle, which is per-partition-assignment, so this is not a correctness bug for commits, but it is a configuration contract break.

title: shutdown() shuts down the queue pool but the SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's commit thread and strategy are never closed
body: ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown() and sets self.queue_pool = None, but the SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy instances created by create_thread_queue_parallel_worker hold their own reference to the queue_pool and run their own commit thread (started in __init__). Shutting down the pool from the factory does not set the strategy's shutdown_event, so the commit thread keeps running (it is a daemon thread, so it dies with the process, but it will keep calling commit_function on a shut-down pool's offset tracker every second until process exit). Additionally, if create_with_partitions is called multiple times (arroyo calls it on rebalance), each call creates a new SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy with a new commit thread, all sharing the same queue_pool — so N rebalances produce N commit threads all committing the same offsets, and none of them are stopped by factory.shutdown(). The factory should track created strategies and close them, or the strategy should be created once and reused.

title: Sentry transaction name hardcodes 'monitors.' prefix for a generic remote-subscriptions component
body: OrderedQueueWorker.run creates a sentry_sdk transaction named f"monitors.{self.identifier}.worker_{self.worker_id}". This module lives in sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers and is generic infrastructure (used by the uptime consumer with identifier 'uptime'), but the transaction name hardcodes the 'monitors.' prefix, so uptime queue workers will report transactions named 'monitors.uptime.worker_N'. This pollutes transaction naming/metrics grouping (transactions are grouped by name) and makes dashboards/alerts on 'monitors.*' include uptime queue workers. The prefix should be derived from the identifier or made configurable, matching the pattern used in result_consumer.py which also hardcodes 'monitors.' but at least is in the monitors-adjacent path.

title: test_different_groups_distributed asserts all 3 queues are used by 20 groups, which is probabilistic and can flake
body: test_different_groups_distributed submits 20 group keys and asserts `len(queue_indices) == 3`, i.e., that all 3 queues receive at least one group. With hash(group_key) % 3, the probability that 20 keys miss at least one bucket is 3 * (2/3)^20 ≈ 0.09% per run — small but non-zero, and because Python's hash() is salted per process, the distribution varies run to run, so this will flake occasionally in CI. Worse, the test is also validating the unstable hash() behavior (see the hash randomization finding). The test should either use enough keys to make the probability negligible (e.g., 100+ keys) and assert `>= 2` or `== 3` with a fixed-seed hash, or mock/patch the hash function. As written it both flakes and enshrines the non-deterministic mapping.

title: New thread-queue-parallel tests poll with fixed iteration counts and no failure message, producing slow, flaky, or silently-passing tests
body: The new tests (test_thread_queue_parallel, test_thread_queue_parallel_preserves_order, test_thread_queue_parallel_concurrent_subscriptions, test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_commit, test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling, test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps) all use a `for _ in range(max_wait): ... time.sleep(0.1)` polling loop and then assert the expected condition afterward. If the loop exhausts max_wait iterations without the condition becoming true, the loop simply exits and the subsequent assert fails — but with max_wait=50 and 0.1s sleeps that's a 5-second wait per test before failing, and for the offset-commit tests max_wait=20 (2 seconds) may be too short on a loaded CI machine because the commit loop only runs every 1.0 second (shutdown_event.wait(1.0) in _commit_loop), so a commit can legitimately take >1s and the test will flake. Additionally, several loops break out of the for loop without any indication of whether the condition was met, and the asserts afterward are the only failure signal. These should use a proper wait helper (e.g., a loop with a deadline and a descriptive failure message, or pytest's wait-for-condition utilities) with a timeout comfortably larger than the 1-second commit interval.

title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the wrong condition for its stated purpose
body: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling sets mock_processor_call.side_effect = [Exception("Processing failed"), None] and then asserts `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`. Because both messages go to the same subscription (self.subscription.subscription_id), they land in the same queue and are processed serially by one worker. The first raises, the second succeeds. Due to the bug where complete_offset is called in the finally block even on exception (see separate finding), both offsets are marked complete and the commit loop WILL commit offset 102 (101+1) for test_partition. The assertion `test_partition not in committed_offsets` will therefore fail once the commit loop runs (within ~1s), meaning this test is currently expected to fail or is only passing because the commit loop hasn't fired within the polling window — i.e., the test encodes the desired behavior but the implementation does not provide it, and the test's loose `or` condition plus short polling window masks the discrepancy. The test should deterministically wait for the commit loop to run and assert the correct behavior (offsets NOT committed past a failed message), which will fail until the worker error-handling bug is fixed.

title: Backup-code login can bypass password check
body: In `authorize`, password is only verified when `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)`. The new branch `if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode)` is taken even when a dummy `totpCode` is also supplied. An attacker who knows only the victim email and one static backup code can send `password=wrong, totpCode=anything-truthy, backupCode=valid` — the password check is skipped because `totpCode` is truthy, the backup code validates, and login succeeds. This turns a second-factor backup code into a password replacement and defeats the first factor.

title: Backup code matching is fragile and type-unsafe
body: The code does `credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` and `indexOf` with no trimming, case normalization, or type check. A correct code pasted with trailing newline/space (e.g. from the downloaded `cal-backup-codes.txt` file) or typed in uppercase will not match the lowercase hex stored from `setup.ts` and login fails. If `backupCode` is a non-string (array/object from a crafted request) `replaceAll` throws a TypeError, producing a 500 instead of an IncorrectBackupCode 400. Same pattern exists in `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts`.

title: Password check can be skipped with backup code + dummy totpCode
body: In packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts authorize() verifies the password only when `!credentials.totpCode` (line 121), but verifies a backup code whenever `credentials.backupCode` is truthy (line 131). An attacker who obtains a single valid backup code can send `backupCode=<valid>` plus `totpCode=<any-non-empty-string>`; the first check is skipped because totpCode is truthy, the second branch succeeds on the backup code alone, and login returns without ever verifying the password. Stolen backup codes (which users download as plaintext `cal-backup-codes.txt`) therefore become password-equivalent. Require password verification for CAL users on every credentials login, independent of which second factor is supplied.

title: Backup-code consume is non-atomic read-modify-write
body: In packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts the backup-code login does read-decrypt-indexOf then a separate `prisma.user.update` that writes `backupCodes[index]=null` back (lines 139-156). Two concurrent logins with the same code can both read the same array, both find the same index, and both succeed before either write nulls it, allowing single-use codes to be reused. Use an atomic transaction/conditional update so consumption cannot race.

title: Backup-code matching only strips dashes, crashes on non-string
body: In apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts line 61 (same pattern in next-auth-options.ts line 144) the code does `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` and `indexOf` against lowercase hex codes generated in setup.ts. It does not trim whitespace/newlines from copy-paste, does not case-fold uppercase hex, and assumes a string so an array/object value throws TypeError resulting in a 500 instead of a 400 IncorrectBackupCode. Valid user-entered codes are rejected and malformed input crashes the handler. Normalize with String(), trim(), toLowerCase() and validate type before comparing.

title: API throws instead of returning JSON error
body: In apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts the new backup-code branches (and existing secret branches) do `throw new Error(ErrorCode.InternalServerError)` when the encryption key is missing or the secret is corrupt (lines 51,77,82,90). An uncaught throw in a Next.js API route returns HTML 500, not the `{error: ErrorCode}` JSON the frontend expects (`await response.json()` then fails), so callers get `something_went_wrong` via exception path and logs lose structured handling. Return `res.status(500).json({error: ...})` like the other branches.

title: No test for login or disable with backup code
body: In apps/web/playwright/login.2fa.e2e.ts the PR only tests backup-code download/copy UI after enable and leaves `TODO: add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup`. The security-critical paths added here — login via `credentials.backupCode` including single-use invalidation (`backupCodes[index]=null`), and disable via backup code — have zero automated coverage, so regressions like reuse, wrong-code handling, or MissingBackupCodes would ship undetected. Add e2e tests that log in with a backup code, verify it cannot be reused, and disable 2FA with a backup code.

title: Backup-code login can bypass password check
body: In packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts password verification is guarded by `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)`. The new branch `if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode)` takes precedence when a backupCode is supplied. An attacker who obtains a valid backup code can send both `totpCode: 'x'` (any non-empty value to make the password check false) and `backupCode: <valid>` and authorize() will skip verifyPassword entirely and log in on backup-code alone. Backup codes are meant as a second factor replacing TOTP, not as a replacement for the password. Consequence: leakage of a backup code (downloaded file, screenshot, copy) alone yields account takeover without the password.

title: Backup code match is case/whitespace sensitive
body: In packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts line 144 and apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts line 61 the code does `backupCodes.indexOf(credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""))`. It only strips dashes. Generated codes are lowercase hex from crypto.randomBytes().hex, displayed as XXXXX-XXXXX. User-typed uppercase, surrounding spaces, or other whitespace will not match and returns IncorrectBackupCode for a valid code. It also calls .replaceAll without verifying the value is a string, so a non-string payload throws. Consequence: legitimate backup codes are rejected on manual entry, locking out users who lost their authenticator.

title: Backup codes stored reversibly instead of hashed
body: In apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts backup codes are persisted as `symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes))` and later decrypted for comparison in next-auth-options.ts and disable.ts. Unlike the TOTP secret which must be reversible, backup codes could be one-way hashed like passwords. With the current design anyone who reads the users table and obtains CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY recovers all 10 usable backup codes in plaintext. Consequence: larger blast radius on DB plus key disclosure; violates single-use credential best practice.

title: Backup-code consume is non-atomic and reusable under race
body: In packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts the backup-code flow does read-decrypt-indexOf then `backupCodes[index]=null` then a separate prisma.user.update to re-encrypt. Two concurrent authorize() calls with the same code can both read the same array, both find the same index, and both succeed before either write nulls it. Consequence: the exactly-once guarantee claimed in backup_code_instructions is violated; one backup code can be used twice.

title: Throws instead of returning 500 on crypto failures
body: In apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts missing encryption key, missing twoFactorSecret, and secret-length mismatch do `throw new Error(ErrorCode.InternalServerError)` inside a Next.js API handler instead of `return res.status(500).json(...)`. The same file also does unguarded `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))`. A throw escapes the handler, yields an unhandled 500 HTML response instead of the JSON error contract the UI expects, and can crash/log stack. Consequence: client cannot parse body.error, shows generic failure, and observability is degraded. This pattern is newly added for the backup-code path.

title: No test for backup-code login or disable
body: In apps/web/playwright/login.2fa.e2e.ts the PR adds only download/copy/close assertions for the backup-code screen and leaves `TODO: add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup`. The new security-critical paths - login with backupCode in next-auth-options.ts including single-use invalidation, and disable with backupCode - have zero automated coverage. Consequence: regressions like reuse, password bypass, or normalization bugs will not be caught before merge.

title: Crash on Google Meet fallback when destinationCalendar is empty
body: File packages/core/EventManager.ts line 119 does `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"` where `mainHostDestinationCalendar` comes from `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? []`. When destinationCalendar is null, undefined, or empty array the destructured value is undefined, so accessing `.integration` throws TypeError. Previously `evt.destinationCalendar?.integration` was safe. Any Meet-location booking without a destination calendar will crash event creation instead of falling back to Cal Video.

title: updateEvent fallback can never match, sends undefined calendarId
body: File packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts line 256 computes `externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. When `externalCalendarId` is falsy the else-branch searches for a calendar whose externalId equals that same falsy value, which never matches, so `selectedCalendar` becomes undefined. The subsequent `calendar.events.update({ calendarId: selectedCalendar })` then gets undefined instead of falling back to the destination calendar, causing Google update/reschedule to fail.

title: deleteEvent fallback can never match
body: File packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts line 317 has the same pattern as updateEvent: `externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. With no externalCalendarId the find predicate compares against null/undefined and returns undefined, so deletion falls back to "primary" even when a specific destinationCalendar exists, deleting from the wrong calendar or failing to delete the collective host's event.

title: Patch after create omits primary fallback
body: File packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts insert uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"` but the follow-up `calendar.events.patch({ calendarId: selectedCalendar })` at line 169 uses the raw value without fallback. When no destination matches the credential, the create succeeds on primary but the patch sends undefined calendarId and fails to add the hangoutLink description.

title: Stale credential reused across calendar references in update
body: File packages/core/EventManager.ts declares `credential` once outside the `for (const reference of calendarReference)` loop and then assigns `credential = this.calendarCredentials.filter(...)[0]` inside. If a later reference's credential is not found in memory and not found in DB, `credential` is not reset to undefined and still holds the previous iteration's credential. The code then calls `updateEvent(credential, ...)` with the wrong user's credential, updating the wrong calendar or crashing on undefined on the first iteration.

title: Inverted IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED condition for org slug
body: File packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/organizations/create.handler.ts line 151 changed `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`. The old code stored `slug` when billing was disabled; the new code stores `slug` when billing is enabled and omits it when disabled, the exact opposite. This unrelated change inverts organization creation semantics: direct slug vs requestedSlug handling is swapped, breaking org provisioning.

title: Webhook expectations still assert null destinationCalendar
body: File apps/web/playwright/webhook.e2e.ts line 119 and line 373 still assert `destinationCalendar: null` for BOOKING_CREATED and BOOKING_REQUESTED, while the type changed to `DestinationCalendar[]` and the code now emits `[]` when empty. Only the BOOKING_REJECTED case was updated to `[]`. The two remaining assertions encode the old contract and will fail against the new payload, leaving the webhook API break uncovered.

title: Inverted IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED slug logic
body: In create.handler.ts the spread was changed from `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})` and `requestedSlug` similarly. The old code included `slug` when billing was disabled and `requestedSlug` when enabled; the new code does the opposite. As a result organizations will be created with the wrong slug/requestedSlug fields, breaking org creation/routing. This change is unrelated to destinationCalendar and inverts behavior.

title: Crash when destinationCalendar is empty on Meet fallback
body: In EventManager.ts `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` can be undefined when there is no destination calendar, but the next line does `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"` without optional chaining. Any booking without a destinationCalendar with location Google Meet will throw TypeError and fail booking creation. It must be `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.

title: updateEvent fallback calendarId can never resolve
body: In GoogleCalendarService.updateEvent the fallback is `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` in the branch where `externalCalendarId` is falsy. Searching for `externalId === externalCalendarId` when externalCalendarId is null/undefined will never match, so calendarId becomes undefined and `calendar.events.update` is called with undefined calendarId. Reschedule/update without an explicit externalCalendarId will fail instead of falling back to the first destinationCalendar.

title: deleteEvent fallback calendarId can never resolve
body: In GoogleCalendarService.deleteEvent the fallback is `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` in the branch where `externalCalendarId` is falsy. That predicate can never be true, so calendarId is undefined and the code falls back to "primary" even when the event has an explicit destinationCalendar. Deleting collective/secondary-host events can hit the wrong calendar or silently succeed on primary without deleting the real event.

title: Collective team calendars dropped when organizer has no calendar
body: In handleNewBooking.ts evt.destinationCalendar is built as `eventType.destinationCalendar ? [...] : organizerUser.destinationCalendar ? [...] : null`, then later `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` for COLLECTIVE. When both are missing the value is null, the optional push is a no-op, so teamDestinationCalendars collected from hosts are lost. EventManager then sees no destinationCalendar and falls back to a single calendar, so additional collective hosts never get calendar events. Initialize to [] instead of null.

title: Webhook expectations left as null after type changed to array
body: CalendarEvent.destinationCalendar was changed from single object/null to array, and one BOOKING_REJECTED expectation was updated to `[]`. The BOOKING_CREATED expectation at line 119 and BOOKING_REQUESTED at line 373 still expect `destinationCalendar: null`. The webhook payload will now be `[]`, so those e2e assertions will fail and the breaking API contract change (null -> []) is not consistently documented/tested.

title: Google updateEvent fallback can never resolve
body: In updateEvent, file packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts line 254, selectedCalendar is computed as `externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. When externalCalendarId is falsy the else-branch searches for `externalId === externalCalendarId` which is falsy, so it never matches and selectedCalendar becomes undefined. The previous code fell back to `event.destinationCalendar.externalId`. The result is calendarId undefined passed to `calendar.events.update`, causing update failures.

title: Google deleteEvent fallback can never resolve
body: In deleteEvent, file packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts line 315, calendarId is computed as `externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. When externalCalendarId is missing the fallback compares against the same missing value, never matches, and yields undefined, so deletion falls back to "primary" instead of the stored destination calendar. This deletes from the wrong calendar or silently misses the event.

title: Crash when destinationCalendar is empty with Google Meet location
body: In file packages/core/EventManager.ts line 119, code does `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? []; if (evt.location === MeetLocationType && mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== ...)`. If destinationCalendar is null, undefined, or empty, the destructured value is undefined and accessing `.integration` throws TypeError. This crashes booking creation for events with no destination calendar. It needs optional chaining.

title: Null destinationCalendar drops collective hosts calendars
body: In file packages/features/bookings/lib/handleNewBooking.ts around line 1063, evt.destinationCalendar is built as `eventType.destinationCalendar ? [...] : organizerUser.destinationCalendar ? [...] : null`. When both are missing it is null, but later code does `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` for COLLECTIVE events. Optional chaining on null skips the push, so the collected team/host destination calendars are silently lost and only the organizer calendar (or none) is used, defeating the multi-host fix.

title: Non-Google calendars ignore per-credential calendar for multi-host
body: In file packages/lib/CalendarService.ts line 156 and similarly packages/app-store/office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts line 73 and packages/app-store/larkcalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts line 128, createEvent only uses the first entry `[mainHostDestinationCalendar] = event.destinationCalendar`. EventManager now loops over each destination and calls createEvent with the host-specific credential and externalId, but these services ignore the credentialId/externalId and always write to the first host's externalId. For collective events the second host's event is created in the wrong calendar or fails, while only GoogleCalendarService was updated to select by credentialId.

title: Recurring cancel only deletes organizer calendars
body: In file packages/features/bookings/lib/handleCancelBooking.ts around line 449, when cancelling all remaining recurring bookings the code iterates `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(c => c.type.endsWith("_calendar"))` to delete each updatedBooking reference. For collective events created with multiple hosts, references now belong to other hosts' credentials which are not in the organizer's credential list, so those calendar events are never deleted and leak on external calendars.

title: Webhook expectations still expect null destinationCalendar
body: In file apps/web/playwright/webhook.e2e.ts line 119 (BOOKING_CREATED) and line 373 (BOOKING_REQUESTED) the expected payload still asserts `destinationCalendar: null`, while the type was changed to `DestinationCalendar[]` and other code now emits `[]`. Only the BOOKING_REJECTED case was updated. The stale expectations will fail and mask the contract break for webhook consumers changing from null/object to array.

title: Missing prisma import causes ReferenceError
body: File packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts calls prisma.credential.update at line 96 but never imports prisma. Any execution of getClient will throw ReferenceError: prisma is not defined, breaking all Salesforce operations after this PR.

title: Refreshed Salesforce connection still uses expired token
body: File packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts fetches a new access token into accessTokenParsed but then constructs jsforce.Connection with accessToken: credentialKey.access_token and instanceUrl from the old credential. The refresh is persisted but never used, so calls continue with the expired token and will keep failing.

title: Minimum token schema uses invalid computed keys
body: File packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts defines minimumTokenResponseSchema with computed keys [z.string().toString()]. That evaluates to a literal property name like the stringified Zod object, not a catch-all. The schema does not mean access_token plus any expiry field; it requires a nonsense property. Use z.object({access_token: z.string()}).passthrough() or catchall instead. As written sync-mode validation will reject valid provider responses or accept wrong shapes.

title: Placeholder refresh_token overwrites real refresh token
body: File packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts mutates parsed data with refresh_token = "refresh_token" when missing. Callers like Office365 spread tokenResponse.data over stored credentials, so the real refresh_token is permanently replaced by the literal string "refresh_token". Subsequent normal refreshes will fail and the credential is corrupted.

title: Stores SafeParse wrapper instead of credential key
body: File packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts assigns const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(...) which returns a Zod SafeParse result {success, data}. It then stores that wrapper as prisma.credential key. Previously it stored googleCredentialSchema.parse output directly. Stored Google credentials will now be {success:true, data:{...}} instead of token fields, breaking googleCredentialSchema.parse on next load.

title: Sync path returns raw fetch Response incompatible with callers
body: File packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts returns a raw fetch Response when credential sync is enabled, but callers expect different shapes: Google expects res.data, HubSpot expects a HubspotToken object, Lark/Office365 expect fetch or axios responses with specific helpers. For example Google does res?.data then token.access_token which will be undefined for a fetch Response, and HubSpot stores the Response object as the credential key. The abstraction leaks provider-specific response types and breaks refresh when enabled. It also never checks response.ok or parses JSON.

title: Unhandled validation/decrypt errors and missing method check
body: File apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts calls appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse, symmetricDecrypt, and JSON.parse without try/catch and accepts any HTTP method. Invalid body, wrong encryption key, or non-JSON payload throws uncaught and returns 500 instead of 400, and GET requests can hit the endpoint. A maintainer would want method restriction to POST and proper 400 handling.

title: Passes credentialId as userId to sync endpoint
body: File packages/app-store/zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts calls refreshOAuthTokens with credentialId as the third argument, but that parameter is userId and is sent as calcomUserId. The sync endpoint will receive the credential row id instead of the Cal.com user id, so it cannot resolve the correct user tokens. Should pass credential.userId like other integrations.

title: Sync refresh overwrites credential with partial token
body: File packages/app-store/office365video/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts stores the sync-endpoint responseBody directly as the credential key. When sync is enabled the endpoint returns only access_token/expiry, so email, refresh_token, scope and other fields are deleted from the DB. The code also derives expiry_date from expires_in which will be missing, yielding Date.now() and immediate expiry. This permanently loses the refresh token.

title: Wrong appSlug sent to credential sync endpoint
body: File packages/app-store/zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts calls refreshOAuthTokens with appSlug "zoomvideo" while the credential is created with appId "zoom". The sync endpoint keyed by appSlug will not match, so Zoom refresh via sync will fail or update the wrong app. Should be "zoom" for consistency with other adapters that send appId.

title: Google refresh stores Zod SafeParse wrapper as credential key
body: In GoogleCalendarService refreshAccessToken, `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema)` returns a SafeParse result `{ success, data, error }`, not the parsed tokens. The code then does `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`, persisting the wrapper object as the credential key. The previous code used `googleCredentialSchema.parse()` which returns the data directly. After one refresh every Google credential becomes `{success:true,data:{...}}` and subsequent `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` will fail or produce wrong credentials, breaking Google Calendar sync.

title: Dummy refresh_token overwrites real refresh token
body: parseRefreshTokenResponse does `if (!data.refresh_token) data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. When credential-sync is enabled the external endpoint intentionally returns only access_token+expiry with no refresh_token. The literal string "refresh_token" is then merged/spread into the credential and persisted (e.g. Office365, Google, Zoom paths), permanently destroying the real refresh_token in the DB. Later non-synced refreshes will send the literal string as the refresh token and fail.

title: Minimum token schema uses computed nonsense keys and strips tokens
body: minimumTokenResponseSchema is declared with `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` as keys. Those expressions evaluate to a fixed string like the Zod type's toString output, not a wildcard/record. Zod objects strip unknown keys by default, so in sync mode the schema effectively keeps only `access_token` and drops `expiry_date`/`expires_in`/`refresh_token` etc. Callers that spread `tokenResponse.data` back into the credential therefore lose expiry data or must rely on the dummy placeholder, causing immediate re-refresh loops or invalid credentials.

title: Sync path always returns fetch Response but callers expect other shapes
body: refreshOAuthTokens returns a `fetch` Response when syncing, otherwise returns whatever `refreshFunction()` returns. Google expects `fetchTokens.res` with `.data` (`const token = res?.data`), HubSpot expects a HubSpot token object directly, Zoho/Zoho-Bigin expect an axios response with `.data`. In sync mode Google gets `res.data === undefined` and crashes on `token.access_token`, HubSpot stores a Response object as tokens (expiresIn becomes NaN), Zoho/Bigin crash on `tokenInfo.data.error` because fetch Response has no `.data`. Only callers that already use fetch + handleErrorsJson keep working. The abstraction is type-incompatible.

title: Salesforce service uses prisma without importing it
body: SalesforceCalendarService.getClient calls `await prisma.credential.update(...)` but the file never imports `prisma` from `@calcom/prisma`. At runtime `prisma` is an undefined reference and every Salesforce calendar operation throws ReferenceError. This is a newly added code path that runs on every getClient call, so Salesforce integration is completely broken.

title: Salesforce connection uses stale tokens after refresh
body: getClient fetches new tokens into `accessTokenParsed.data` and persists them, but then constructs `new jsforce.Connection({ ... accessToken: credentialKey.access_token, refreshToken: credentialKey.refresh_token })` from the old `credentialKey` instead of the refreshed values. The current request therefore authenticates with the expired token that just triggered the refresh, so the refresh has no effect for this call and will be repeated on every call.

title: Salesforce refresh failure check uses statusText instead of ok
body: The new Salesforce refresh does `if (response.statusText !== "OK") throw`. `statusText` is implementation-dependent and often empty with undici/node-fetch, and Salesforce can return non-OK bodies with 200 or OK text with errors. The correct check is `!response.ok`. As written the code can throw on successful refreshes or miss failed refreshes and then try to parse an error page as tokens.

title: Bigin passes credentialId as calcomUserId to sync endpoint
body: BiginCalendarService.refreshAccessToken takes `(credentialId, credentialKey)` and calls `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoho-bigin", credentialId)`. The third parameter is documented as `userId` and other services pass `credential.userId`, and the sync endpoint receives it as `calcomUserId`. Bigin therefore sends the credential primary key where the remote expects a user id, so the remote will look up the wrong user or fail. It should pass the credential's userId, not the credential id.

title: Credential webhook has no method check and unhandled parse/decrypt errors
body: The handler accepts any HTTP method (including GET) to create/overwrite credentials, does `schema.parse(req.body)` without try/catch so invalid bodies throw 500 instead of 400, and does `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` without error handling. A wrong encryption key, corrupted payload, or non-JSON plaintext crashes the endpoint with 500 and can leak stack traces. It should restrict to POST, return 400 on validation/decryption failures, and not expose internal errors.

title: Outbound credential-sync request sends no auth and ignores failures
body: The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends only `calcomUserId`+`appSlug` as URLSearchParams with no Content-Type, no webhook secret, and no signature, so the self-hosted endpoint cannot authenticate that the request came from Cal.com. The code also never checks `response.ok` before returning, so 4xx/5xx HTML error pages are passed to token parsers and treated as token refresh failures, which can incorrectly mark credentials invalid.

title: minimumTokenResponseSchema is invalid and rejects all synced tokens
body: File packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts defines minimumTokenResponseSchema with computed keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()]. That does not create a catch-all/passthrough schema; it creates literal properties named by Zod's toString output that must be numbers. With APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED the code therefore validates every external refresh response against the wrong shape, strips unknown fields like expiry_date/refresh_token, and will fail with Invalid refreshed tokens were returned. Use .passthrough() or .catchall(z.unknown()) instead.

title: Injects dummy refresh_token literal corrupting stored credentials
body: File packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts overwrites a missing refresh_token with the literal string refresh_token. When the external credential-sync endpoint returns only access_token+expiry, this dummy value is persisted to the credential. Subsequent native refreshes or validations that require a real refresh token will then use refresh_token and fail, and the DB no longer holds the true refresh token.

title: Sync path returns raw fetch Response breaking callers expecting tokens
body: File packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts returns the raw fetch Response when credential syncing is enabled, but returns whatever refreshFunction returns otherwise. Callers are inconsistent: Google expects res.data, HubSpot expects a HubspotToken object, ZoHo expects axios {data}, while Office365/Webex/Zoom/Lark expect a fetch Response for handleErrorsJson/handleWebexResponse/handleZoomResponse/handleLarkError. There is no .json() parsing, no response.ok check, no Content-Type header, and no auth secret sent, so half the integrations crash or store undefined tokens when sync is on.

title: Google refresh uses res.data on fetch Response and stores Zod wrapper
body: File packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts does const res = await refreshOAuthTokens(...); const token = res?.data. When sync is enabled res is a fetch Response which has no .data, so token is undefined and token.access_token throws. It then does const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials,...) which returns a SafeParse result {success,data}, and stores that wrapper object as prisma.credential key instead of .data, corrupting the credential with {success,data} shape.

title: HubSpot refresh expects token object but gets fetch Response
body: File packages/app-store/hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts assigns const hubspotRefreshToken = await refreshOAuthTokens(...). In sync mode that value is a fetch Response, not a HubspotToken. The next lines read hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn/accessToken and call prisma.credential.update with the Response object, storing garbage and setting expiryDate to NaN, breaking HubSpot auth when sync is enabled.

title: Passes credentialId as userId and expects axios shape from fetch
body: File packages/app-store/zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts calls refreshOAuthTokens(..., zoho-bigin, credentialId) where the third parameter is defined as userId:number|null. It sends the credential primary key as calcomUserId to the external endpoint, so the external system looks up the wrong user. It then reads tokenInfo.data.error/access_token, but the sync path returns a fetch Response with no .data, causing a crash or storing undefined.

title: ZoHo CRM refresh reads .data from fetch Response
body: File packages/app-store/zohocrm/lib/CalendarService.ts wraps its axios call with refreshOAuthTokens and then reads zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error/access_token. When sync is enabled refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response, not an axios response, so .data is undefined and the code throws when setting expiryDate or persists an invalid key.

title: Uses prisma without importing it
body: File packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts calls prisma.credential.update at line 96 but has no import of @calcom/prisma. This throws ReferenceError: prisma is not defined on every Salesforce getClient call, breaking all Salesforce calendar operations after this PR.

title: Checks response.statusText instead of response.ok
body: File packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts does if (response.statusText !== OK) throw. statusText is implementation-dependent and often empty with undici/node-fetch, so successful token refreshes can be rejected, and error bodies are discarded. Check !response.ok or status codes instead.

title: Creates jsforce connection with stale tokens after refresh
body: File packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts fetches new tokens into accessTokenParsed and persists them, but then constructs new jsforce.Connection with instanceUrl/accessToken/refreshToken from the old credentialKey instead of the refreshed values. The client therefore continues to use the expired access token until the next instantiation.

title: Wrong appSlug sent to credential sync endpoint
body: File packages/app-store/zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts calls refreshOAuthTokens(..., zoomvideo, ...). The Zoom app slug/appId used elsewhere is zoom (type zoom_video, appId zoom). An external sync endpoint keyed by appSlug will not match zoomvideo, so synced refreshes for Zoom will miss or require a special case.

title: Webhook accepts any method and throws 500 on bad body
body: File apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts has no req.method check, so GET/PUT/DELETE with the webhook secret can create/overwrite credentials. It also uses appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body) without try/catch, so invalid bodies throw an unhandled exception resulting in 500 instead of 400, and symmetricDecrypt/JSON.parse on line 57 can similarly throw.

title: Non-atomic findFirst then create/update allows duplicates
body: File apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts does findFirst by userId+appId then separate update or create without a transaction or upsert on a unique constraint. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same user/app can both miss and both create, leaving duplicate credentials. It also stores arbitrary decrypted JSON as key with no schema validation per app type.

title: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is string not boolean
body: File packages/lib/constants.ts defines APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED as process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY, which evaluates to a string or undefined, not a boolean. Consumers treat it as a flag; leaking secret-adjacent values and confusing type-checks. Coerce with Boolean() or !!.

title: Team permission check requires admin AND owner instead of OR
body: In addGuests.handler.ts isTeamAdminOrOwner is computed as `await isTeamAdmin(...) && await isTeamOwner(...)`. A user who is a team admin but not an owner (or vice versa) will get false and be denied unless they are also the organizer/attendee. The consequence is legitimate team admins cannot add guests while the intent was admin-or-owner access.

title: Original guests list sent to email sender instead of filtered list
body: The handler filters `guests` into `uniqueGuests` (removing existing attendees and blacklisted emails) for DB creation, but then calls `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` with the unfiltered input. Existing/blacklisted addresses that were not created will be treated as new guests inside sendAddGuestsEmails and receive AttendeeScheduledEmail instead of AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, sending wrong content to wrong people.

title: Calendar update uses requester's credentials instead of organizer's
body: In addGuests.handler.ts credentials are loaded with `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` and EventManager is built from `...user` where user is the caller. When the caller is an attendee or team admin rather than the booking owner, the calendar update runs with the wrong user's OAuth credentials/calendars. The consequence is updateCalendarAttendees fails or mutates the wrong calendar while the DB was already updated.

title: Blacklist and duplicate checks are case-sensitive and bypassable
body: In addGuests.handler.ts blacklisted emails are lowercased but compared as `blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)` without lowercasing `guest`, and existing-attendee comparison is `guest === attendee.email`. An attacker can bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS with different casing (e.g. Blocked@x.com vs blocked@x.com) and create duplicate attendees differing only by case, defeating the blocklist and uniqueness intent.

title: DB write committed before calendar update with no rollback
body: In addGuests.handler.ts `prisma.booking.update` with `createMany` executes before `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)`. If the calendar call throws, the function throws after guests are already persisted, leaving DB and calendar/email out of sync. A client retry will then fail with emails_must_be_unique_valid because the guests now exist, with no way to recover atomically.

title: Unbounded guests array enables spam and DoS
body: ZAddGuestsInputSchema in addGuests.schema.ts is `z.array(z.string().email())` with no max length, uniqueness, or normalization. Combined with per-attendee getTranslation and per-attendee email sending in the handler, a caller authorized as attendee/organizer can submit hundreds of arbitrary addresses in one call, creating many Attendee rows and triggering mass outbound emails. This is a spam and resource-exhaustion vector that needs a limit and dedup.

title: Validation error flag never cleared on retry
body: In AddGuestsDialog.tsx handleAdd sets `setIsInvalidEmail(true)` on failed validation but never sets it back to false when validation later succeeds. Once shown, the emails_must_be_unique_valid error persists even after the user fixes the emails, confusing users into thinking input is still invalid.

title: Unsafe attendees[0] access can crash email rendering
body: In organizer-add-guests-email.ts the subject uses `this.calEvent.attendees[0].name` with no guard. If a booking has zero attendees the property access throws TypeError inside getNodeMailerPayload. Because the handler already persisted the new attendees before sending mail, this crash leaves the booking updated but emails unsent while the API still reports success due to swallowed email errors.

title: Team admin/owner check uses AND instead of OR
body: In addGuests.handler.ts the authorization check computes isTeamAdminOrOwner as (await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...)). A user is rarely both admin AND owner, so legitimate team admins or owners who are not the organizer/attendee will be rejected with FORBIDDEN, while the intent was to allow either role. It should be ||. Consequence: team management cannot add guests unless they are also the booking owner.

title: Blacklist and duplicate checks are case-sensitive and bypassable
body: In addGuests.handler.ts blacklisted emails are lowercased when loaded from BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS, but the incoming guest value is compared without lowercasing: !blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest). Similarly existing attendees are compared with guest === attendee.email. An attacker can bypass the blacklist and create duplicate attendee rows by changing case (e.g. Foo@bar.com vs foo@bar.com). The server also does not deduplicate duplicates within the request itself. Consequence: blacklist ineffective and duplicate Attendee records.

title: Unbounded guests array allows email/DB spam
body: In addGuests.schema.ts the input is z.array(z.string().email()) with no min/max length, uniqueness, or normalization. A single authorized caller (including any existing attendee) can submit hundreds/thousands of emails in one request. The handler then creates that many Attendee rows, updates the calendar, and fans out to sendAddGuestsEmails for every attendee. Consequence: DB bloat, calendar API abuse, and mass unsolicited email (spam/DoS) from the victim organizer's booking.

title: Sends emails using unfiltered guests list instead of uniqueGuests
body: In addGuests.handler.ts the handler filters input into uniqueGuests (removing existing attendees and blacklisted addresses) for the DB insert, but then calls sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests) with the original unfiltered array. In email-manager.ts newGuests.includes(attendee.email) is used to decide between AttendeeScheduledEmail for new guests vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail for old attendees. Consequence: a re-submitted existing attendee in a mixed request is misclassified as new and gets the wrong invitation email, and blacklisted addresses influence routing.

title: No validation of booking status or time before adding guests
body: In addGuests.handler.ts after loading the booking the handler only checks existence and permission, then immediately inserts new Attendee rows, updates the external calendar via EventManager, and sends emails. It never rejects cancelled, rejected, or already-ended bookings. The UI also exposes the action for past confirmed bookings. Consequence: guests can be added to cancelled/past events, corrupting calendar state and sending confusing add-guest emails for events that will never happen.

title: Calendar update uses requestor credentials instead of organizer credentials
body: In addGuests.handler.ts the booking query eagerly loads booking.user.credentials and destinationCalendar, but they are never used. Instead credentials are loaded with getUsersCredentials(ctx.user) where ctx.user is the caller, who may be any attendee, and EventManager is constructed from the caller. The calendar event is owned by the organizer, not the attendee. Consequence: when an attendee adds guests the calendar update runs with the wrong account's tokens and will fail or update the wrong calendar, leaving external calendars out of sync with the DB.

title: Team admin/owner check uses AND instead of OR
body: File packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts line 46 computes isTeamAdminOrOwner as (await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...)). This requires the caller to be both admin and owner at once, so a user who is only an admin or only an owner fails the check. Consequence: legitimate team admins/owners get FORBIDDEN and cannot add guests; the intent was clearly OR.

title: Duplicate emails inside request create duplicate attendees
body: File packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts line 74 filters guests only against existing booking.attendees, and packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.schema.ts does not enforce uniqueness. If guests is [a@x.com, a@x.com] neither matches an existing attendee, so both pass the filter and createMany inserts two Attendee rows with the same email. Consequence: duplicate attendee records, duplicate emails/calendar invites, broken attendee lists. Client-side uniqueness in AddGuestsDialog can be bypassed by direct API calls.

title: Email routing uses raw input instead of filtered guests
body: File packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts line 168 calls sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests) with the original input instead of uniqueGuests. Guests that were already attendees or blacklisted and therefore not inserted are still treated as newGuests in packages/emails/email-manager.ts newGuests.includes(...), so existing attendees incorrectly receive the new-guest AttendeeScheduledEmail instead of AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, and filtered addresses affect classification. Consequence: wrong email content sent to existing attendees.

title: Blacklist check is case-sensitive and bypassable
body: File packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts line 70 lowercases BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS but line 77 compares raw guest without lowercasing or trimming, and line 76 compares guest === attendee.email exactly. Consequence: Guest@blocked.com bypasses a blacklist entry for guest@blocked.com, and Foo@Bar.com duplicates foo@bar.com, defeating the blocklist and duplicate suppression.

title: DB write commits before calendar update with no rollback
body: File packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts line 92 prisma.booking.update inserts new attendees, then line 165 eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees updates external calendars. If the calendar update throws, the DB rows remain while calendars are stale, with no transaction or compensation. Consequence: database and Google/Outlook calendars diverge; retrying adds confusion and there is no cleanup path.

title: Calendar update uses requester credentials instead of organizer
body: File packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts line 158 loads getUsersCredentials(ctx.user) and builds EventManager from the requesting user, even though the booking query already fetched booking.user.credentials (the organizer). If a team admin or attendee adds guests, the update runs against the requester's calendars, not the organizer's. Consequence: calendar attendee update fails or mutates the wrong calendar, so added guests never appear on the real event.

title: Add-guests emails ignore standard-email disable flags
body: File packages/emails/email-manager.ts line 525 sendAddGuestsEmails never checks eventTypeDisableHostEmail/eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail or host/attendee disabled flags, unlike sendScheduledEmails, sendRescheduledEmails, sendLocationChangeEmails. Consequence: users/event types that disabled standard emails still get organizer/attendee add-guests emails, violating user preference and spamming attendees.

title: Invalid-email error state never cleared on retry/success
body: File apps/web/components/dialog/AddGuestsDialog.tsx sets isInvalidEmail true on failed validation but neither handleAdd on success nor onSuccess resets it to false (only cancel does). Consequence: after fixing emails and submitting, the Errors must be unique and valid banner stays visible during/after a successful add and on next open, confusing users.

title: List items keyed by index cause wrong row after delete
body: File packages/ui/form/MultiEmail.tsx line 26 uses key={index} for controlled EmailField rows while deletion splices the array. Consequence: React reuses DOM nodes by position, so removing a middle email can show the wrong value in the wrong row, lose focus, or preserve stale validation state.

title: Add-guests offered for past/cancelled bookings
body: File apps/web/components/booking/BookingListItem.tsx line 193 adds the additional_guests edit action unconditionally, and bookedActions including edit_booking are still rendered for past confirmed bookings. Consequence: users can open AddGuestsDialog and insert attendees on ended or cancelled events, producing meaningless DB rows, calendar writes, and emails for events that already happened.

title: Retry-count delete clause deletes non-SMS reminders
body: In scheduleSMSReminders.ts the deleteMany uses OR: [{method:SMS, scheduledDate<=now}, {retryCount:{gt:1}}].
