The first request from a new device over the limit is rejected, but for the next 29 minutes TagDevice sees the cache entry and returns nil, so Anonymous.Authenticate succeeds for the same over-limit device. The cache should only be populated after a successful store write (or evicted on error).

title: Device-limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert race
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice runs CountDevices in one DB session, drops back to application code, and then inserts in a separate session with no transaction, unique constraint enforcement, or inter-instance lock. Concurrent requests (including from multiple Grafana instances sharing one database) when the count is limit-1 can all observe count < limit and all insert, exceeding the configured limit. The count check and insert/update need to be atomic, e.g. performed in a single transaction with appropriate locking.

title: Provider signature changes are not reflected in the generated Wire code
body: ProvideAnonDBStore changed from (db.DB) to (db.DB, int64) and ProvideAnonymousDeviceService changed from accepting anonstore.AnonStore to db.DB, but no wire_gen.go/wire set file is updated in this PR. The checked-in generated server wiring still calls these providers with the old arguments, so the server package will not compile until wire is regenerated and the generated file is committed.

title: No test covers an already-known device being allowed when the limit is reached
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a second, new device is rejected. It does not verify the other half of the new contract in updateDevice: that re-tagging the existing device while count >= limit succeeds and updates it, nor that an expired device is rejected. A regression in the UPDATE ... BETWEEN window or in dialect-specific RowsAffected handling would incorrectly lock out legitimate existing anonymous devices and would not be caught.

title: New device_limit option is not declared in defaults/sample config or docs
body: AnonymousDeviceLimit is read from auth.anonymous device_limit, but the PR adds no entry to conf/defaults.ini or conf/sample.ini and no documentation for [auth.anonymous] device_limit. Operators have no discoverable way to learn the option exists, its unit/scope (distinct devices seen in 30 days), or that 0 means unlimited, so the headline configurable feature is effectively undocumented.

title: Rejected device is cached before the limit check, allowing it to bypass the limit on retry
body: tagDeviceUI inserts the device into localCache via SetDefault before calling anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. If CreateOrUpdateDevice then returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, the cache entry remains, so the anonymous client's next request from the same device hits the cache at line 83, TagDevice returns nil, and Authenticate grants access even though the device was never admitted. The limit is therefore only enforced for the first attempt within the 29-minute cache TTL. The cache entry must only be set after a successful store, or deleted on error.

title: Device-limit enforcement has a count-then-insert race that admits devices beyond the limit
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice performs CountDevices and then, in a separate DB session, inserts the new device if count < deviceLimit. There is no transaction, lock, or unique admission constraint tying the count to the insert, so two (or more) concurrent first-time requests on the same or different Grafana instances can all observe count == limit-1 and all insert, exceeding the configured limit. Under a burst of new anonymous devices the limit is not reliably enforced.

title: Provider signature changed without updating Wire-generated dependency injection
body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now takes db.DB instead of anonstore.AnonStore and constructs the store itself via ProvideAnonDBStore(sqlStore, cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit) (line 43), and ProvideAnonDBStore itself now requires an int64. The checked-in Wire injector (pkg/server/wire_gen.go and the anonymous WireSet) is not updated in this PR, so it still passes an AnonStore to this constructor and cannot supply the new int64 argument to ProvideAnonDBStore; the server package will fail to compile / wire generation will fail until the injector is regenerated and updated.

title: Anonymous authentication is now synchronously blocked on device-store database calls
body: Authenticate previously tagged the device in a background goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout context; it now calls TagDevice synchronously with the request context. Every cache-miss anonymous request now waits on a COUNT query plus an INSERT/UPDATE (and, when at the limit, a second UPDATE) before an identity is returned, so slow or contended database calls directly add latency to, or stall until request cancellation, all anonymous page/API loads. Only ErrDeviceLimitReached needs to be decided synchronously; the previous decoupling for ordinary tagging latency has been removed.

title: updateDevice uses generic '?' placeholders unlike the Postgres-specific upsert path
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice carefully uses $1..$5 placeholders for Postgres in its INSERT ... ON CONFLICT statement, but the new updateDevice (used for every request once the limit is reached) hardcodes '?' placeholders. On Postgres deployments this UPDATE will fail with a syntax/placeholder error instead of updating an already-admitted device, so existing anonymous devices are rejected with a database error as soon as the limit is reached, while SQLite/MySQL continue to work. The update statement needs dialect-specific placeholders like the insert path.

title: Rejected device is cached as tagged, so a retry bypasses the limit
body: tagDeviceUI calls localCache.SetDefault(key, ...) before anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds. When the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, TagDevice/Authenticate deny that first request, but the device ID remains cached for the cache's 29-minute default lifetime. The next request hits the cache at line 83 and returns nil without touching the store, so Anonymous.Authenticate succeeds even though the device was never recorded and the limit is still reached. The limit therefore only denies the first attempt per device per instance; clients just retry to get in. The cache must only be populated after a successful store, and must be evicted on error.

title: Device limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert and can be exceeded concurrently
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts active devices and then, in a separate DB session, inserts a new device if count < deviceLimit. There is no transaction, lock, or unique constraint enforcement tying the count to the insert, so many concurrent first-time requests from different devices can all observe count == limit-1 and all insert, exceeding the configured limit. Under anonymous traffic (the exact load this feature limits) the cap is therefore not reliably enforced; enforcement needs to be serialized/atomic in the store.

title: Provider signature changed without regenerating Wire injection
body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now takes db.DB instead of anonstore.AnonStore, and ProvideAnonDBStore now takes an extra int64 argument, but no pkg/server/wire.go / wire_gen.go changes are included. Grafana builds from the checked-in generated wire_gen.go, which still constructs AnonDBStore with one argument and passes it to ProvideAnonymousDeviceService where a db.DB is now expected, so the server package will not compile / DI is stale until `make wire` (or equivalent) is run and the generated file committed.

title: Tagging moved from async background work to the synchronous auth path
body: Previously TagDevice ran in a goroutine with a 2-minute background-context timeout and panic recovery; now Authenticate blocks on TagDevice (a CountDevices query plus an insert/update on cache miss) using the request context. This adds database latency to anonymous authentication, makes auth fail/slow when the store is slow, ties DB writes to request-context cancellation, and removes the panic recovery around tagging. Combined with the per-instance 29-minute cache, cache misses across many instances will also amplify DB load. If synchronous enforcement is required, it needs a bounded timeout/context handling rather than the raw request context.

title: Existing device inactive for >30 days is treated as over-limit instead of an existing device
body: When count >= deviceLimit, updateDevice only updates rows whose updated_at is within the last 30 days (anonymousDeviceExpiration). Devices are only deleted after 61 days (keepFor in impl.go), so a known device returning after 30-61 days still exists in anon_device but its UPDATE matches 0 rows and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, denying a previously registered device. The stated intent ('if device limit is reached, only update devices') is not met for this window; existence should be checked separately from the 30-day activity window.

title: anonymousDeviceLimit contract mismatch: Go always sends 0, frontend type expects undefined for unset
body: AnonymousDeviceLimit is a plain int64 without omitempty, so an unconfigured instance (limit 0 = unlimited in the backend) serializes as anonymousDeviceLimit: 0. The frontend declares it `number | undefined` and GrafanaBootConfig defaults it to undefined to mean unset. Consumers cannot distinguish 'unlimited/0' from an explicitly configured value via the declared type, and any frontend logic checking for undefined to mean 'no limit' will never see it from a real server. Use a pointer/omitempty or document 0 as the unlimited sentinel consistently.

title: Cleanup ticker interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute for all jobs
body: The ticker in CleanUpService.Run is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, but this ticker drives srv.clean(), which runs every cleanup job (expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, and query history), not just annotation cleanup. This increases the frequency and database/filesystem load of all of those jobs tenfold without any justification in the PR description and can worsen the MySQL contention the PR is trying to reduce.

title: Normal cleanup batches are logged at Error level with full ID lists
body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags call r.log.Error for every batch (including successful batches, an empty final batch, and cases where the logged err is nil at line 534). Routine successful cleanup will therefore generate error-level log noise/alerts, and including the entire ids slice (potentially tens of thousands of IDs with a large batch size) makes each message very large. These should be Debug/Info-level summaries without dumping all IDs.

title: Split fetch/delete can over-delete annotations kept by the MaxCount rule
body: For MaxCount cleanup, fetchIDs selects IDs using LIMIT batch OFFSET MaxCount at one instant, then deleteByIDs deletes those IDs in a separate statement/session without rechecking that they are still beyond MaxCount. If annotations that were within the newest MaxCount are deleted concurrently between the fetch and the delete, some fetched annotations may no longer be excess and should now be retained, but they will still be deleted. The previous single DELETE evaluated the excess condition atomically in one statement.

title: Placeholder-limit workaround only handles SQLite
body: deleteByIDs builds one '?' placeholder per ID for every non-SQLite database, bounded only by AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize. The new large-batch test uses a batch size of 32767; on databases with prepared-statement placeholder limits (notably PostgreSQL's 65535 limit is only about twice that, and deployments can configure an even larger batch size), a sufficiently large configured batch will now fail with a parameter-limit error, whereas the previous subquery DELETE did not pass IDs as parameters at all. The check also uses the configured batch size rather than len(ids). Either inline IDs or chunk deletes based on the actual ID count for all dialects with limits.

title: Cleanup ticker interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute without justification
body: The cleanup service ticker is changed from time.Minute*10 to time.Minute*1. This is unrelated to splitting the annotation DELETE queries and makes all cleanup jobs, including the annotation scan/delete batches, run 10x more often. On large installations this increases database load and, because a cleanup run can take up to the 9-minute timeout while ticks are buffered, can cause back-to-back cleanup runs. Restore the 10-minute interval unless the change is intentional and justified.

title: Normal cleanup progress is logged at Error level with full ID lists
body: Lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576 and 579 use r.log.Error for routine, successful batch operations, including when err is nil and when no IDs were found. They also embed the entire ids slice, which can contain tens of thousands of IDs when AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is large. In production this will flood error logs, trigger error-based alerting for non-errors, and create very large log lines every batch. These messages should be Debug (or Info at most), should not log a nil err as an error, and should log counts rather than full ID lists.

title: deleteByIDs can exceed database bind-parameter limits for non-SQLite databases
body: deleteByIDs builds a single DELETE ... WHERE id IN (?, ?, ...) with one placeholder per fetched ID, and only special-cases SQLite when the configured batch size exceeds 999. AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is operator-configurable and unbounded here; on PostgreSQL/MySQL a large value (the new test itself uses 32767) can approach or exceed the driver's bind-parameter limit (e.g. 65535 on PostgreSQL), causing cleanup to fail every run, whereas the previous subquery DELETE had no host-parameter limit. Chunk deletes by len(ids) against a safe per-dialect limit instead of relying only on the SQLite/configured-batch-size check.

title: Cleanup ticker shortened from 10 minutes to 1 minute for all jobs
body: The ticker interval was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, but this ticker drives CleanUpService.clean(), which runs every cleanup job (expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, and query history), not just annotation cleanup. Nothing in the PR description justifies a 10x increase in frequency for all of these jobs. This will increase database and filesystem load on every Grafana instance and shorten the effective timeout/interference window between full cleanup passes; it looks like a leftover local-testing change and should be reverted or scoped/justified separately.

title: Routine cleanup batches are logged at Error level with full ID lists
body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log every batch at Error level (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579), including on success paths where err is nil, and they include the complete ids slice and SQL condition. With the configured batch size this can dump tens of thousands of IDs into error logs once per batch until cleanup finishes, creating false error alerts/on-call noise, high log volume and serialization cost, and obscuring real failures. These progress messages should be Debug (or Info without the ID list), with Error reserved for the returned error path.

title: Placeholder-limit workaround only handles SQLite and keys off configured batch size
body: deleteByIDs inlines IDs only when the database is SQLite and cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999; otherwise it emits one '?' placeholder per ID. PostgreSQL and MySQL also have bind-parameter limits (65535), so a user who raises annotation_cleanupjob_batchsize above that (the new test itself encourages very large batches such as 32767) will now get 'too many parameters' failures from the DELETE and cleanup will error on every cycle, whereas the previous subquery DELETE had no host-parameter limit. The guard should be based on len(ids) and the actual dialect's parameter limit, chunking or inlining as needed per database.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the cancelled request context
body: Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection all launch `go func()` blocks that derive their timeout with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` from the incoming request context. The Kubernetes request context is cancelled as soon as the handler returns the storage result, which happens immediately after spawning the goroutine, so the legacy write will almost always run with an already-cancelled context and fail/abandon. A detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) before adding the timeout) is required, otherwise mode 3 silently does not perform the legacy writes it exists to perform as a safety net.

title: Independent goroutines give no ordering for legacy writes
body: Every write spawns an unsynchronised goroutine for the legacy store. A Create goroutine, a subsequent Update goroutine and a Delete goroutine for the same object can be scheduled or complete out of order (legacy latency is variable up to the 10s timeout): an update can run before the create it depends on and fail as not-found, or a delayed create can run after a delete and resurrect a deleted object in legacy storage. Mode 3 therefore can leave legacy permanently diverged from unified storage; legacy writes need to be serialised/queued per resource or otherwise ordered.

title: Async legacy calls race on objects shared with the returned response
body: Create passes the same `obj` pointer to Storage.Create and then to the background Legacy.Create while returning `created` to the caller, and Update passes the same `objInfo` (line 139) to both Storage.Update and the background Legacy.Update. The API server may serialise/mutate the returned object, and UpdatedObjectInfo.UpdatedObject may be invoked a second time against a different old object, concurrently with the first call and with response handling. This is a data race and can make the legacy copy differ from the object written to unified storage; the legacy goroutine needs its own deep copy / the precomputed updated object (as the previous updateWrapper approach provided).

title: Storage failures are recorded as legacy metrics
body: In Create, when d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) with the storage start time, and Update does the same at line 129. Storage failures are therefore attributed to the legacy duration metric (with the wrong latency) and no failing storage duration is recorded, corrupting the dual-writer dashboards/alerts used to judge migration safety. These should call recordStorageDuration. Conversely DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine at line 166 calls recordStorageDuration for the legacy call, the mirror-image mistake.

title: Delete records object name in the metric kind label
body: On successful Delete the code calls d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage), passing the object `name` where every other call site passes options.Kind as the kind label. This creates one metric series per deleted object name (unbounded label cardinality in Prometheus) and makes per-kind aggregation impossible. It should pass options.Kind like the error path at line 103.

title: Legacy write failures are never logged
body: The background goroutines in Create, Delete (line 112), Update (line 139) and DeleteCollection (line 165) discard the legacy error except for a duration metric; the previous synchronous implementation logged these errors. Combined with the fire-and-forget design, an operator has no log signal (with kind/name) that legacy has diverged from unified storage and no way to know which objects need reconciliation. The error branch should log via the request-scoped logger before recording the metric.

title: Mode 3 tests never verify the async legacy write happens
body: The Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection tests register legacy mock expectations but return and assert on the storage result immediately, without waiting for the spawned goroutine or calling AssertExpectations/AssertCalled on the legacy mock (both mocks also share a single testify mock.Mock, so expectations cannot even distinguish the two stores). The tests pass even if the legacy write is removed entirely, and if the goroutine fires after the test finishes it can race with later tests using the shared mock and shared example objects. Tests need a synchronisation point (channel/WaitGroup in the mock or Eventually-style assertion) proving legacy is invoked with the right arguments.

title: New mode 3 integration cases are flaky because legacy visibility is now asynchronous
body: The added 'mode 3' subtests reuse doPlaylistTests, which creates/updates/deletes via the k8s API and then immediately asserts the objects are visible (and later gone) through the legacy /api/playlists endpoints. In mode 3 the legacy write is performed by a fire-and-forget goroutine started before the response returns, so there is no guarantee it has completed when the very next legacy request is made. These subtests will intermittently fail (missing/extra/stale playlists) unless the legacy assertions poll/wait for eventual consistency.

title: Async legacy writes use the request-scoped context and will usually be cancelled
body: Create, Update, Delete and DeleteCollection all launch the legacy write in a goroutine using `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where ctx is the incoming request context (Create line 51, Update line 135, Delete line 110, DeleteCollection line 163). The handler returns immediately after spawning the goroutine, at which point the apiserver cancels the request context, which cancels the derived timeout context. The legacy 'safety net' writes will therefore routinely fail with context-canceled before they run, silently diverging legacy storage from unified storage exactly as mode 3 is meant to prevent. The goroutine needs a detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or a background context preserving values) with its own timeout.

title: Async legacy Create races with the caller on the same object
body: Create passes the exact same `obj` to Storage.Create, then hands that same object to Legacy.Create in a background goroutine while returning `created` (which typically aliases obj) to the caller. The apiserver will read/serialize/mutate the returned object concurrently with the legacy store reading and mutating the same object (e.g. setting resource version, name, timestamps), which is a data race and can corrupt the response or the legacy write. The legacy goroutine must be given a DeepCopy of the object (ideally made before Storage.Create mutates it), not the shared pointer.

title: Async legacy Update reuses the same UpdatedObjectInfo already consumed by unified storage
body: Update passes the identical `objInfo` instance to Storage.Update and then, asynchronously, to Legacy.Update. The previous implementation computed the updated object once and passed legacy an updateWrapper around that fixed object; now Legacy.Update will call objInfo.UpdatedObject a second time, against the legacy store's old object and after the request has returned. UpdatedObjectInfo implementations are not guaranteed to be idempotent or safe to invoke twice (they may apply deltas, bump fields, or capture request-scoped state), so the legacy write can store different content than unified storage, or fail spuriously. Legacy should receive a wrapper carrying the already-computed/returned object, as before.

title: Storage failures in Create/Update are recorded as legacy durations
body: When Storage.Create fails, line 45 calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) for the time spent in storage, and Update does the same at line 129. No storage-duration sample is recorded and the legacy histogram is polluted with a failure/duration for an operation that never touched legacy storage. Dashboards/alerts on dual-writer latency and error rate per store will misattribute unified-storage failures to legacy. These should call recordStorageDuration(true, ...).

title: Delete records the object name in the metric kind label and DeleteCollection mislabels its legacy metric
body: On successful Delete, line 106 calls recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, ...) passing the object `name` where every other call site passes options.Kind as the kind label. This produces unbounded metric cardinality (one series per deleted object name) and breaks kind-based aggregation. Separately, the legacy DeleteCollection goroutine at line 166 calls recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration, so legacy delete-collection latency/errors are never recorded and storage gets a spurious second sample. Fix line 106 to options.Kind and line 166 to recordLegacyDuration.

title: Async legacy failures are never logged
body: In all four async legacy goroutines the error is used only to set the metric's error flag (e.g. Create lines 55-56) and is otherwise discarded, with no log.Error via the request logger. Since mode 3 returns success to the client regardless, operators get no diagnosable record of which object failed to reach legacy storage or why; divergence will be discovered only via missing data. Log the error with the object name/kind inside each goroutine before recording the metric.

title: Mode 3 tests never verify the async legacy writes and share one mock for both stores
body: The new Mode 3 tests construct legacyStoreMock and storageMock over a single shared testify mock.Mock, so a Storage call can be satisfied by an expectation registered for Legacy and vice versa (e.g. the TestMode3_Create 'storage fails' case at lines 37-44 registers only a Create expectation via setupLegacyFn yet the error surfaces from the Storage.Create call). The tests also return immediately without waiting for or asserting the background legacy goroutines (no AssertCalled/Eventually on Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection), so the defining behavior of mode 3 - the async legacy write - is untested, and stray goroutines can fire mock calls after the subtest ends, causing flaky cross-test interference under -race. Use separate mocks per store and synchronize/assert the legacy call in each test.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and can be cancelled on return
body: Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection launch legacy writes in goroutines using context.WithTimeoutCause derived from the incoming request ctx. That parent context is owned by the API-server request and may be cancelled as soon as the handler returns the unified-storage result, racing with or cancelling the legacy write. The 10s timeout does not detach the goroutine from the parent. Consequently the supposedly protective legacy copy can silently never be written, especially for slower legacy stores. The legacy context should be detached (for example context.WithoutCancel/background-derived) while preserving values, with only the new timeout applied.

title: Legacy goroutines race with the caller on the shared object
body: Create passes the same `obj` pointer to Storage.Create and then to the asynchronous Legacy.Create, while immediately returning `created` to the caller. The caller/serializer and the legacy store can therefore read or mutate the same underlying object concurrently (for example resource version, UID or timestamps set by a store). Update similarly shares `objInfo` with an asynchronous legacy call after the synchronous storage update has already consumed it. This is a data race and can produce corrupted or inconsistent legacy writes; the legacy goroutine needs its own deep copy/computed object.

title: Mode 3 update no longer passes the storage-computed object to legacy
body: Update now passes the original `objInfo` directly to Legacy.Update. A registry Update implementation recomputes the new object by calling objInfo.UpdatedObject against the old object it loads from legacy storage, so legacy recomputes the update against a different (possibly missing or stale) old object instead of applying the exact object already committed to unified storage, as the previous updateWrapper-based implementation did. This can make the asynchronous legacy update fail (for example NotFound/conflict) or diverge from unified storage while the API call reports success. The computed/returned storage object should be wrapped and passed to legacy.

title: Several dual-writer metrics are recorded against the wrong store or label
body: When Storage.Create fails, Create calls recordLegacyDuration (line 45) for elapsed storage time; Update does the same on storage failure (line 129). Delete records a successful storage duration using `name` instead of `options.Kind` as the kind label (line 106), creating wrong/high-cardinality series. DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine calls recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration (line 166). Dashboards/alerts based on these metrics will attribute failures and latency to the wrong backend and cannot be used to verify mode 3 legacy health.

title: Asynchronous legacy failures are not logged
body: The legacy goroutines in Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection only feed a duration metric and discard the error otherwise. The previous synchronous implementation logged legacy failures with object context. If the legacy safety copy fails in mode 3, operators have no log message identifying the kind/name/error to reconcile the divergence; only an aggregate metric counter changes. Each goroutine should log the returned error (without relying on the possibly-cancelled request logger).

title: Mode 3 tests never wait for or verify the asynchronous legacy writes
body: Tests configure legacy mock expectations (for example Create at lines 30-32 and Update at lines 313-315) but return/assert immediately after the dual-writer call and never synchronize with the goroutine or call AssertCalled/AssertExpectations for the legacy mock. The tests therefore pass even if the legacy write is removed, cancelled, or never executes, and leaked goroutines can instead race with later tests using the shared mock/example objects. Tests need a synchronization/wait mechanism and explicit assertions that each legacy method was invoked (and that failures are handled).

title: Mode 3 integration test synchronously asserts legacy visibility after async writes
body: The new mode 3 scenarios reuse doPlaylistTests, which creates/updates/deletes through the k8s API and immediately checks the legacy playlist API (for example the legacy list/get checks inside doPlaylistTests). Because mode 3 now performs legacy writes in fire-and-forget goroutines, there is no happens-before guarantee that the legacy row exists when those assertions run. This makes the new file/unified-storage mode 3 integration cases flaky and can also hide eventual-consistency behaviour that needs polling with a timeout instead of immediate equality assertions.

title: Write lock is taken without re-checking the cache
body: In non-Dev mode, concurrent callers that all observe a nil cache under the read lock will queue on the write lock. After the first caller populates entryPointAssetsCache, each queued caller still re-reads and re-parses assets-manifest.json and replaces the cache because the non-nil check is not repeated after acquiring Lock. This serializes redundant file I/O under the exclusive lock during the initial request burst and blocks fast-path readers; re-check entryPointAssetsCache after Lock (for non-Dev) and return it if populated.

title: No concurrent test covers the claimed race fix
body: The change adds mutex synchronization around the package-global entryPointAssetsCache but adds no test exercising concurrent GetWebAssets calls (e.g. run with -race against a temporary assets-manifest.json). Without such a regression test, a future refactor that accesses the cache outside entryPointAssetsCacheMu would not be caught by CI.

title: Cache is not rechecked after acquiring the write lock
body: Two concurrent non-Dev callers can both observe a nil cache at line 41, then serialize on the write lock. The second caller does not recheck entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the lock at line 48, so it reloads assets-manifest.json despite the first caller having populated the cache. More importantly, if that redundant reload fails, line 69 assigns its nil result over the valid cache and the caller returns an error instead of the already-available assets. Add a non-Dev cache recheck inside the write lock before reloading.

title: No concurrent regression test for the claimed data-race fix
body: The change introduces mutex protection for entryPointAssetsCache but adds no test that calls GetWebAssets concurrently, ideally repeatedly under `go test -race` with both cache-miss and cache-hit paths. Without such a test, a future change that accesses the global outside entryPointAssetsCacheMu or mutates the shared returned value would not be caught by CI as a race regression.

title: Cache is not rechecked after acquiring the write lock
body: After the initial RLock check misses, every concurrent caller waits for the write lock and then unconditionally reloads assets-manifest.json and overwrites entryPointAssetsCache, even if another goroutine populated the cache while it was waiting. Because the file I/O is also performed while holding the exclusive lock, a cold-cache burst in non-Dev mode serializes redundant disk reads and blocks fast-path readers instead of only the first caller loading and the rest reusing the newly cached value. Recheck entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring Lock (when cfg.Env != Dev) and return it if non-nil.

title: No concurrent regression test for the data-race fix
body: This change adds synchronization around the global entryPointAssetsCache but adds no test that calls GetWebAssets concurrently, so the original race would not be reproduced or guarded against in CI (including with the race detector). A test should exercise parallel GetWebAssets calls on a cold cache (and, if feasible, in Dev mode where the cache is rewritten) against a temporary assets-manifest.json so a missing or incorrectly scoped lock fails under -race.

title: Legacy SQL command path is not explicitly disabled
body: UnmarshalSQLCommand is a separate entry point from ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery and does not check whether SQL expressions are disabled; it still calls NewSQLCommand. SQL is currently blocked only incidentally because sql.TablesList now fails when the stub DB returns 'not implemented', producing a misleading 'error reading SQL command' BadRequest. This defense-in-depth gap means restoring or replacing the stub DB implementation would silently re-enable the vulnerable SQL path through this entry point without any explicit feature/security gate. Add the same explicit rejection here (and for direct NewSQLCommand/SQLCommand execution) rather than relying on the stubbed database to fail.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false and can dereference a nil toggle source
body: enableSqlExpressions computes enabled as the negation of IsEnabledGlobally, returns false when that value is true, and also returns false otherwise, so the feature-toggle check is dead logic that always disables SQL while obscuring the intent. It also dereferences h.features unconditionally for SQL queries; an ExpressionQueryReader constructed with a nil FeatureToggles (as test or auxiliary callers may do) will now panic instead of returning an error. Simplify this to an explicit unconditional return false (with a security comment) or handle a nil toggle source.

title: No regression test covers disabling SQL expressions
body: The PR changes the SQL query path to reject QueryTypeSQL and stubs out the SQL database, but adds or updates no tests. There is no test proving that a SQL expression is rejected even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled, nor tests covering NewSQLCommand/UnmarshalSQLCommand and SQLCommand.Execute failing closed with the stubbed DB. Without these, a future refactor of the reader, command unmarshalling, or DB stub could accidentally re-enable the CVE-2024-9264 attack surface without CI noticing.

title: Legacy SQL-command path bypasses the new SQL-expression gate
body: UnmarshalSQLCommand creates a SQLCommand via NewSQLCommand without checking enableSqlExpressions or the sqlExpressions feature toggle, unlike the new check in ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery. This legacy unmarshalling path therefore is not explicitly disabled; it currently fails only incidentally because sql.TablesList now delegates to the stub DB and errors. If the DuckDB-backed DB implementation is restored or replaced, this path would re-enable SQL expressions (the CVE-2024-9264 surface) without passing the gate. Gate or reject SQL in UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand as defense-in-depth.

title: Disabled-SQL check can panic on a nil FeatureToggles
body: enableSqlExpressions unconditionally calls h.features.IsEnabledGlobally even though it always returns false. If an ExpressionQueryReader is constructed without feature toggles (nil interface, e.g. in tests or other direct constructions), a SQL-type query now panics with a nil dereference instead of returning the intended 'not implemented' error. Since the result is unconditionally disabled, return false without dereferencing h.features.

title: enableSqlExpressions has inverted, dead logic
body: The helper computes enabled := !IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions), then returns false both when that value is true and in the fallthrough, so the flag and the branch are dead and the naming is inverted. This is misleading for a security-sensitive gate: a future editor following the variable name could easily re-enable the vulnerable path by 'fixing' the apparent inversion. Replace it with an explicit unconditional return false (with a comment referencing the removal), or remove the helper.

title: Stub DB breaks existing SQL tests with no updated/disabled tests
body: NewInMemoryDB's RunCommands and QueryFramesInto now always return 'not implemented', so the package-level TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/parser.go always errors and NewSQLCommand always rejects queries. The PR adds no test verifying SQL expressions are rejected, and does not update or skip the existing parser/SQL-command tests that expect DuckDB-backed table extraction and execution to succeed, leaving them failing against this stub. Update/skip those tests and add a regression test that a SQL expression is rejected regardless of the feature toggle.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false through inverted dead logic
body: enableSqlExpressions computes enabled as !IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions), returns false when that value is true, and also returns false when it is false. The feature flag therefore has no effect and the branching is misleading: a maintainer trying to re-enable SQL expressions by restoring the flag check can easily invert the logic and either keep the feature permanently disabled or accidentally enable the unsafe DuckDB path. The helper should directly express the intended temporary disable (return false with a clear comment) or correctly return the flag value once the stub is removed.

title: Legacy SQL command entry point is not explicitly disabled
body: UnmarshalSQLCommand still accepts SQL expressions and calls NewSQLCommand without any feature-flag or disabled-feature check. It is only blocked incidentally because sql.TablesList now calls the stub DB and errors, producing a generic 'error reading SQL command' BadRequest. This leaves two different disable behaviours for SQL expressions (explicit rejection in ExpressionQueryReader versus an incidental parsing failure here), and if the stub DB's RunCommands/TablesList is ever partially restored this legacy path would again create executable SQLCommands without passing through the reader's guard. The legacy unmarshalling path should reject QueryTypeSQL explicitly as well.

title: No tests cover SQL-expression rejection and existing SQL tests are not updated
body: The PR disables SQL expressions in ReadQuery and stubs pkg/expr/sql.DB so TablesList, RunCommands, and QueryFramesInto always return 'not implemented', but it adds no test asserting that a SQL expression is rejected even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled, and it does not update or skip the pre-existing tests that exercise TablesList/SQLCommand execution against DuckDB. Those existing tests will now fail against the stub, while the security-critical rejection path itself remains unprotected against regression. Add a reader test for the disabled SQL type and skip/remove/update the DuckDB-dependent tests accordingly.

title: Concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key now race and leak/conflict
body: BuildIndex no longer holds cacheMu while checking/creating/building the index, and only locks briefly to store the finished index at line 137-139. GetIndex therefore returns nil for the whole duration of an in-flight build, so two concurrent Search/getOrCreateIndex calls (or init plus a watch event) for the same NamespacedResource both build an index. For file-backed indexes both call bleve.New on the same directory and can fail with lock/already-exists errors; for memory indexes both do the full scan and the later store silently overwrites and leaks the earlier unclosed bleve index. The old whole-build lock also made concurrent builders serialize. A per-key build lock/singleflight, or double-checked locking around cache insertion, is needed.

title: TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu
body: TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without taking cacheMu.RLock. With the finer-grained locking in this PR, BuildIndex now inserts into b.cache (line 137-139) while other work is in flight, and searchSupport.init calls TotalDocs after it has already started the watch goroutine that can trigger further builds. Concurrent map iteration and map write in Go can panic with 'concurrent map iteration and map write' and is a data race. TotalDocs must snapshot or iterate the cache under RLock.

title: init worker goroutines race on totalBatchesIndexed and err
body: searchSupport.init launches up to initWorkers goroutines via errgroup, and each goroutine does totalBatchesIndexed++ (line 189) and assigns to the shared outer err variable (line 190: '_, _, err = s.build(...)') without synchronization. Concurrent increments can be lost (so the span attribute is wrong) and concurrent writes to err are a data race that go test -race will flag; a failing build's error can also be overwritten by a concurrent successful write before it is returned to errgroup. Use an atomic counter and a goroutine-local err variable returned from the closure.

title: NewResourceServer now blocks on full index build and fails construction on search/watch errors
body: NewResourceServer now synchronously calls s.Init(ctx), which builds every search index (searchSupport.init scans all namespaces over initMinCount) and starts the watcher before returning. Previously construction was cheap and initialization happened lazily on the first gRPC call, so callers could construct the server and serve non-search endpoints (Read, IsHealthy, blob) even if index building was slow or the watch/stats backend was unavailable. Now a slow or failing GetResourceStats/WatchWriteEvents makes NewResourceServer hang for the whole index build or return an error for the entire server, and the background context used has no timeout, so startup can block indefinitely. This is the lazy-initialization dependency the PR description asks about and should be confirmed against all constructors/callers (including tests using fake backends without watch/stats support), or startup should remain non-blocking with readiness reported separately.

title: Postgres storage-server integration test is skipped rather than fixed
body: The PR adds a blanket skip for GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres in TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer, the only integration test exercising the storage-server target end to end. Since this PR changes ResourceServer startup/initialization, losing the postgres run removes coverage for exactly the changed startup path on a supported backend; the stated failure ('not working with postgres in Drone') is left uninvestigated and could hide a real postgres-specific initialization regression introduced here.

title: Concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key are no longer serialized
body: BuildIndex now only holds cacheMu while inserting the finished index, and GetIndex uses a short RLock that returns nil while another goroutine is still building. Two concurrent getOrCreateIndex/Search/init calls for the same NamespacedResource can therefore both invoke BuildIndex, both call bleve.New/NewMemOnly (for file-backed indexes, both on the same directory path), both run the expensive builder, and then overwrite each other in b.cache. The losing bleve index is never closed, leaking file handles/directory locks, and concurrent file-backed creation can fail startup/search with index-lock/already-exists errors instead of sharing the one in-progress build as the old whole-build lock effectively did.

title: TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu
body: TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without acquiring cacheMu.RLock. With BuildIndex now inserting into b.cache from many concurrent init workers and from lazy getOrCreateIndex builds, that unlocked iteration can race with a concurrent map write, which is a data race and can cause a fatal Go runtime 'concurrent map iteration and map write' panic that crashes the process. TotalDocs should snapshot or iterate under RLock (taking care not to hold it while calling out if that can re-enter).

title: init errgroup goroutines race on shared err and totalBatchesIndexed
body: Inside searchSupport.init, each errgroup goroutine executes totalBatchesIndexed++ and assigns to the outer err variable captured from 'stats, err := ...' via '_, _, err = s.build(...)'. With SetLimit(initWorkers) running builds concurrently this is a data race: increments can be lost (wrong 'namespaced_indexed' span attribute) and per-namespace build errors can overwrite each other before 'return err', masking a failed namespace build or reporting another namespace's error. Use a local err per goroutine and an atomic/mutex-protected counter.

title: NewResourceServer performs uncancellable init with the server's background context
body: NewResourceServer now synchronously calls s.Init(ctx) where ctx is the internally created context.Background()-derived watcher context (no caller context, deadline, or cancellation is accepted by the constructor). Building every search index can take arbitrarily long, and a caller that wants to abandon/shut down startup cannot cancel it and has no server handle yet on which to call Stop (which is the only place that cancels this ctx). Startup can thus hang indefinitely inside the constructor; previously a slow/failed init surfaced on the first RPC with that RPC's cancellable context.

title: History and Origin panic when search is not configured
body: When opts.Search.Resources is nil (or the search backend is nil) NewResourceServer leaves s.search nil, yet History (line 925) and Origin (line 930) unconditionally dereference s.search, unlike Search which returns 'search index not configured'. After this PR removed the per-RPC Init guards, a History/Origin gRPC call to a server constructed without search will nil-pointer panic and crash the handler/process instead of returning an error.

title: Concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key now race and can corrupt or leak indexes
body: BuildIndex no longer holds cacheMu while building, and it unconditionally inserts b.cache[key]=idx at the end without checking whether another goroutine already built the same NamespacedResource. searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex does GetIndex (nil while a build is in flight) then BuildIndex, and searchSupport.init builds many keys in parallel, so two callers for the same key can now run bleve.New/NewMemOnly concurrently: for file-backed indexes both use the same directory path (bleve.New fails or contends on an existing/open index), for memory indexes one index is silently overwritten and the other leaked (with duplicate IndexTenants increments), and writes/searches can be split across the two instances. Previously the whole-build lock serialized this. A per-key build lock/singleflight or an existing-entry check under cacheMu before returning is needed.

title: TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu while builds now insert concurrently
body: TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without acquiring cacheMu.RLock. With the finer-grained locking in this PR, BuildIndex now inserts into b.cache (line 138) concurrently with any TotalDocs call outside the init path, which is a Go data race and can panic with 'concurrent map iteration and map write'. TotalDocs should take cacheMu.RLock (and note DocCount on an index being flushed concurrently may also need care).

title: init errgroup goroutines race on totalBatchesIndexed and the shared err variable
body: Inside group.Go, totalBatchesIndexed++ (line 189) and `_, _, err = s.build(...)` (line 190) mutate variables captured from the enclosing scope without synchronization. Multiple workers run concurrently (and this PR makes their index builds actually parallel), so increments are lost and, more importantly, one goroutine's failure can be overwritten by another's nil error (or vice versa) before `return err` is read, causing init to report success despite a failed namespace build or a spurious failure. Use a local err per goroutine returned to errgroup and an atomic/mutex-protected counter.

title: NewResourceServer now blocks on full index building and discards the server on init failure without cleanup
body: NewResourceServer unconditionally calls s.Init(ctx) with the internal background context (no timeout), so constructing a ResourceServer now synchronously builds every search index (GetResourceStats plus a full ListIterator scan per namespace) before any caller can serve or health-check it; construction that was previously cheap/lazy and only failed on first use now fails or hangs process startup, including for embedders that create the server but never serve unified-storage traffic. On init error it returns nil without calling s.cancel() or lifecycle Stop, even though search.init may already have started its background WatchWriteEvents goroutine (search.go uses context.Background()), leaking that goroutine and its backend poller.

title: Handlers no longer consult initErr, so requests are served after Stop marks the server stopped
body: Every handler previously called s.Init(ctx), which (via sync.Once) returned s.initErr on subsequent calls; Stop() overwrites s.initErr with 'service is stopping/stopped', so post-Stop requests were rejected. With all per-handler Init calls removed, Create/Read/List/Search/etc. proceed against the backend after Stop has cancelled s.ctx and stopped the lifecycle, producing confusing backend errors or partially working requests instead of a clear stopped error. Either keep an explicit stopped/initErr check in handlers or gate serving elsewhere.

title: Call to non-existent no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() does not compile
body: UsernameForm.authenticate() calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments, but the only method added to its superclass UsernamePasswordForm is isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) at UsernamePasswordForm.java:160. No no-arg overload exists in UsernamePasswordForm, AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator, or elsewhere in the changed code, so this file fails compilation and the whole services module cannot build.

title: Passkey form data is no longer populated on the initial login page
body: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel) now requires user != null, and authenticate() at line 115 uses it as the only gate for webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context). On a first (non-re-authentication) login context.getUser() is null precisely because the user has not been identified yet, which is the discoverable/passkey-autofill case conditional UI exists for. Previously fillContextForm was called in the user==null branch. The new code therefore renders the initial username/password page without challenge/RP/conditional-UI attributes and without the webauthn form, breaking passwordless discoverable-key login from UsernamePasswordForm (existing tests such as webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey and passwordLoginWithExternalKey expect the webauthn form on the first page). The same inverted gate in challenge(error,field) at line 137 drops passkey data from error pages when no user is set. The fix should populate conditional-UI data both when no user is identified yet and when a user is re-authenticating, not flip from one to the other.

title: Re-authentication skip is disabled for all users when realm passkeys are enabled, even users with no passkey
body: Assuming the intended check is the realm-level isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()), it only tests that passkeys are enabled for the realm and a user is present; it never checks that this user actually has a passwordless WebAuthn credential. Consequently, during re-authentication (e.g. prompt=login) in the split UsernameForm+PasswordForm flow, users who previously were silently skipped through UsernameForm because they have no linked IdP will now always be stopped at the username form, even though they cannot use a passkey and must manually submit the (hidden-username) form to reach the password step. This is a behaviour regression for non-passkey users in passkey-enabled realms; the skip should only be suppressed when the current user could actually authenticate with a passkey.

title: Call to non-existent no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() does not compile
body: UsernameForm.authenticate() calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments, but the only method inherited from UsernamePasswordForm is isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) at UsernamePasswordForm.java:160 and no no-arg overload exists in UsernameForm, UsernamePasswordForm, or AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator. This is a compilation failure. It should be called as isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()).

title: Requiring a known user breaks initial discoverable-passkey login
body: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel) now requires user != null, and authenticate() at line 115 and challenge(context,error,field) at line 137 use it to decide whether to call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context). On the initial login page no user is known yet, which is exactly the discoverable/resident-key passkey flow that identifies the user from the credential, so fillContextForm is never called, the conditional-UI challenge/autocomplete data is not rendered, and passwordless login from UsernamePasswordForm is broken. The same applies after a failed initial password attempt, where bad-password handling clears the user before challenge() re-renders the form. Previously fillContextForm was called when the user was not yet selected. The guard should be based on passkeys being enabled, not on a user already being present; the known-user check is only relevant to showing that user's authenticators.

title: Always hiding WebAuthn authenticators defeats the no-credential guard for known users
body: shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators() now unconditionally returns false, so WebAuthnAuthenticator.fillContextForm() never builds WebAuthnAuthenticatorsBean and never takes its empty-authenticators early return at WebAuthnAuthenticator.java:104-107. Combined with UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() checking only the realm passkeys flag and user != null (not whether that user is configured for a passwordless credential), a re-authenticating user with no passkey credential will still be rendered the conditional-UI/WebAuthn form even though no credential can succeed. This contradicts the stated expectation in PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest.reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey that users without a passkey should not see WebAuthn elements; that test only covers realm-level passkeys disabled, not the passkeys-enabled/user-without-credential case.

title: Call to isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() does not compile
body: UsernameForm.authenticate() calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments, but the only method added to its superclass UsernamePasswordForm is isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user). There is no no-arg overload in UsernamePasswordForm or any other superclass, so this file will fail compilation and the whole change cannot build. The call should be e.g. isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()).

title: Passkey conditional UI is no longer set up for anonymous (initial) login
body: authenticate() now only calls webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) when isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()) is true, and that helper requires user != null. On the initial login page no user has been identified yet, so context.getUser() is null, fillContextForm() is never called, and no WebAuthn challenge/RP/conditional-UI attributes are put on the login form. This inverts the previous behaviour (fill when passkeys are enabled and the user is not already selected) and breaks discoverable/passwordless passkey login from the first page, which existing tests such as webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey rely on. The same inverted condition at line 137 in challenge(context, error, field) also drops passkey data from error challenges shown to anonymous users after a failed attempt once the user is cleared.

title: Login-cache invalidation compares an organization-aware original with a raw updated model
body: update() obtains the original through getById(), which returns createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(): its isEnabled() also returns false when the linked organization is disabled. The updated model passed by callers is normally the raw model. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() therefore evaluates LoginFilter.ENABLED against different semantics for the two models. For example, for an enabled public broker in a disabled organization whose BROKER_PUBLIC is changed from true to false, the wrapped original already fails the login predicate because isEnabled() is false, and the raw updated model also fails it because it is no longer public, so both are treated as 'not a login IdP' and no invalidation is registered. The stale cached getForLogin list can then expose the now-private broker after the organization is re-enabled. The original's underlying IdP fields, not the organization-aware isEnabled(), must be used for this comparison.

title: New login predicate can NPE on an IdP model with null config
body: getLoginPredicate() now unconditionally calls idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC) for every organization-linked IdP. IdentityProviderModel.setConfig() allows the config map to be replaced, including with null, and previously this predicate only called simple boolean getters. The Infinispan provider now invokes this predicate from create(), update(), and remove() invalidation handling, so an org-linked model with a null config can fail those operations with a NullPointerException instead of being created, updated, or removed. The predicate should treat a null config as not public.

title: New test cleanup removes a literal alias instead of the created IdPs
body: Each loop iteration creates an IdP aliased "idp-alias-" + i but registers cleanup as testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove, using the literal string "alias" rather than the created alias (the same mistake is repeated for idp-alias-20 at line 425). Cleanup therefore does not remove the twenty created providers and may attempt to remove a non-existent provider, leaving state that can pollute subsequent tests using the shared test realm and mask or cause cache-count failures.

title: Login-cache invalidation can be skipped for IdPs linked to a disabled organization
body: registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate compares getLoginPredicate() on the original and updated models, but the original model comes from getById() and is wrapped by createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(), whose isEnabled() also returns false when the linked organization (or organizations for the realm) is disabled. The JPA delegate used by getForLogin() nevertheless included that IdP in the cached ID set based on its stored enabled flag. Therefore, while the organization is disabled, changing a login-relevant field such as hideOnLogin, linkOnly, or enabled to make the IdP ineligible makes both predicates evaluate to false (or otherwise appear unchanged), so no login-cache invalidation is registered. The stale ID remains cached and, once the organization is re-enabled, getForLogin() can return an IdP that the uncached JPA query would no longer return to callers that do not re-check those flags.

title: New test registers cleanup for a literal "alias" instead of the created IdPs
body: In testCacheIDPForLogin the cleanup is registered as testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove rather than using each created alias ("idp-alias-" + i, and similarly "idp-alias-20" at line 425). This attempts to remove a provider literally named "alias" and does not clean up the 21 providers created by the test, leaving them in the shared test realm to potentially affect other tests in the class and masking failures from the cleanup call itself.

title: getForLogin cache ignores organization-level invalidations
body: The login cache is keyed only by realm and FetchMode and getForLogin only checks isInvalid(cacheKey). Unlike getByOrganization (which also checks isInvalid(orgId)), it never checks whether the requested organizationId has been invalidated. Organization-side changes that register an invalidation for the organization id (organization update/removal and broker association changes performed through the organization provider rather than through IdentityProviderStorageProvider.create/update/remove) therefore do not evict the cached realm+mode IdentityProviderListQuery. The cached ID set keeps being served until an unrelated IdP mutation invalidates the login key, so brokers can remain visible for an organization they no longer belong to, or remain missing after being linked, on login pages.

title: getLoginPredicate can NPE on identity providers with a null config map
body: The new predicate unconditionally calls idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC) for every org-linked identity provider. IdentityProviderModel allows the config to be set to null (e.g. models built/imported from representations without config), so evaluating this predicate during the new create/update/remove invalidation in InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider will throw NullPointerException and fail the whole IdP operation, whereas the previous predicate only inspected enabled/linkOnly/hideOnLogin. The config access needs a null guard (treat missing config as not public).

title: Cached getForLogin loses the delegate's result ordering
body: On a cache hit the method collects the cached internal IDs into a HashSet and returns identityProviders.stream(), so the order of the returned stream is hash iteration order of UUID strings instead of the order produced by the JPA delegate (which getAllStream returns in its deterministic query order). Any caller of getForLogin that does not explicitly re-sort (the login bean does, but the storage provider contract gives no sorting guarantee to other callers) will now see identity providers in a different, unstable order than before this caching was added.

title: Test cleanup removes a literal "alias" provider instead of the created providers
body: Both cleanup registrations in testCacheIDPForLogin use testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias") rather than the alias of the provider just created ("idp-alias-" + i, and similarly at line 425). The cleanup therefore targets a non-existent provider and the 20+ identity providers created by the test are left behind in the shared test realm, making the test suite order-dependent and potentially polluting other cache/count assertions; the cleanup should capture the per-iteration alias.

title: New abstract order() method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: CryptoProvider is a public extension interface, but order() is added as an abstract method. Every existing implementation outside the three updated in this PR (custom server providers, downstream/client-repo implementations, mocks and test doubles) will fail to compile until it adds order(). This is an avoidable source/binary contract break for an ordering feature: order() should be a default method with a documented default priority, with built-in providers overriding it as needed.

title: Equal-order providers are silently and nondeterministically selected instead of rejected
body: detectProvider() sorts by order() descending and unconditionally returns the first provider. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so when more than one is on the classpath the winner depends on ServiceLoader encounter/classpath order. Previously this configuration failed fast with 'Multiple crypto providers loaded'; now Keycloak can silently run with DefaultCryptoProvider instead of the FIPS provider (or vice versa), defeating an operator's explicit FIPS configuration and hiding a misconfiguration. Ties for the highest order should remain an error, or the mutually exclusive full providers need distinct, intentional priorities.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns an arbitrary non-BouncyCastle provider
body: The CryptoProvider contract states getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the (FIPS or non-FIPS) BouncyCastle provider, but this implementation returns the provider of the JVM default KeyStore type (typically SUN/SunJSSE for PKCS12). Any caller that uses the returned provider for BC-only algorithms, keystore types or provider-name assumptions will get NoSuchAlgorithm/NoSuchProvider failures or silently different crypto behaviour. Like WildFlyElytronProvider, it should return null if no BC provider exists, or throw UnsupportedOperationException, rather than misidentify an unrelated JCA provider as BouncyCastle.

title: ECDSA test never verifies the produced DER signature and does not test provider ordering
body: test() only checks DER->RS->DER->RS self-consistency using the same custom ASN.1 encoder/decoder pair, and generates a single default EC key pair regardless of whether ES256, ES384 or ES512 is under test. A mutually compensating encoder/decoder defect, or DER that JCA rejects, would still pass, and the central new behaviour of this PR (CryptoIntegration choosing between AuthzClientCryptoProvider order 100 and a full provider order 200, including tie handling) has no test at all. The test should verify asn1Des with Signature.verify() using a curve-appropriate key pair, and CryptoIntegration selection should be covered directly.

title: New order() method is abstract and breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
body: CryptoProvider is an extensible interface, but order() was added as an abstract method instead of a default method. Any CryptoProvider implementation compiled against an earlier Keycloak version will throw AbstractMethodError when CryptoIntegration calls order() during sorting, and source code for such implementations will no longer compile. Adding a default implementation (for example returning a neutral order) would preserve compatibility while allowing built-in providers to override it.

title: Equal-order providers are selected silently and nondeterministically
body: detectProvider() now sorts only by order() and silently ignores every provider after the first, replacing the previous fail-fast error for multiple providers. DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, and WildFlyElytronProvider all return order 200, so if more than one is on the classpath the winner depends on ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order rather than configuration. In particular a non-FIPS provider could be selected where FIPS operation is required, silently weakening the intended security posture.

title: AuthzClient installs the stub crypto provider as a global first-wins singleton
body: AuthzClient.create(Configuration) calls CryptoIntegration.init(), and CryptoIntegration only initializes its static cryptoProvider once. When no higher-order provider is present this permanently installs AuthzClientCryptoProvider for the whole JVM, but that provider throws UnsupportedOperationException for PemUtils, CertificateUtils, signatures, ciphers, key factories, EC parameters, and most other CryptoProvider operations; a later attempt to initialize a full provider such as DefaultCryptoProvider will be ignored because the static provider is already set. Authz-client features or other Keycloak client code in the same process that need those operations will therefore fail unexpectedly.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns an unrelated JCA provider
body: The CryptoProvider contract for getBouncyCastleProvider() is to return the BouncyCastle (or BCFIPS) provider, but this implementation returns the provider of the JVM default KeyStore type (typically SUN or SunJSSE). Callers that use the returned provider by name or for BouncyCastle-specific algorithms/services will fail or behave as if BouncyCastle were available when it is not. The Elytron provider already establishes the pattern of returning null when no BouncyCastle provider exists; returning an unrelated provider is more misleading and error-prone.

title: ECDSA test uses one P-256 key for all curves and never verifies the converted signature
body: The test generates a single default EC key pair (P-256 on standard JDKs) and then uses it for ES256, ES384, and ES512, and only asserts that DER-to-RS followed by RS-to-DER and back returns the same bytes. A self-consistent round trip can pass even if the DER output is not acceptable to a real verifier or if R/S padding/length handling for P-384 and P-521 is wrong. The test should generate a key pair on the curve matching each algorithm and verify that a signature converted to ASN.1 DER verifies with the JDK Signature object (and vice versa).

title: Ignored crypto providers are still instantiated and mutate global security state
body: detectProvider streams the whole ServiceLoader before sorting, so every CryptoProvider on the classpath is constructed, not just the winner. DefaultCryptoProvider registers BouncyCastle with Security.addProvider and FIPS1402Provider inserts BCFIPS/BCJSSE at positions 1-3 and modifies security properties. Previously the multiple-provider case threw and aborted startup; now execution continues with the losing providers' global side effects still installed, which can pollute a FIPS deployment with a non-FIPS provider (or vice versa) while CryptoIntegration reports only the selected provider.

title: Equal order() values make provider selection classpath-order dependent
body: DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order() 200. When any two of them are present, the reversed sort leaves their relative order to ServiceLoader/classpath enumeration order, which is not a defined contract, and the previous explicit 'multiple providers' failure is gone. The JVM can therefore silently start with e.g. the Elytron provider (whose getBouncyCastleProvider() returns null) instead of the default/FIPS provider depending on jar ordering.

title: New abstract order() method breaks all external CryptoProvider implementations
body: order() is added as an abstract interface method rather than a default method. Any CryptoProvider implementation outside the four updated in-tree classes will fail to compile against this version, and already-compiled implementations will throw AbstractMethodError when CryptoIntegration sorts providers by CryptoProvider::order. A default order (e.g. 100) would let existing implementations keep working.

title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns an unrelated JCA provider
body: The method contract is to return the BouncyCastle (or BCFIPS) provider, but this implementation returns the provider of the default KeyStore type (e.g. SunJSSE/SUN for PKCS12). Callers that use the returned provider by name/capability for signatures, key factories or certificate handling will silently get a non-BC provider with different algorithms and behaviour, instead of an honest null (as WildFlyElytronProvider returns) or an unsupported-operation signal.

title: ECDSA test uses one P-256 key pair for ES384/ES512 and never verifies a signature
body: The constructor generates a single default (P-256) EC key pair, yet testES384 and testES512 pass it with signature lengths of 96 and 132 bytes, so the conversions are exercised on zero-padded/truncated values rather than real P-384/P-521 signatures. The only assertion is that asn1derToConcatenatedRS and concatenatedRSToASN1DER round-trip to the same bytes; swapped or otherwise invalid R/S encodings would also pass. The test should generate a key pair per named curve and verify the DER-encoded result with Signature.verify against the public key.

title: Existing FGAPv2 realms never receive the new Clients resource type or scopes
body: init() returns immediately whenever realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is non-null. Realms that enabled admin permissions before this change therefore keep only the Users all-resource resource and the old scope set; they never get the Clients all-resource resource or the new configure/map-roles-client-scope/map-roles-composite scopes. Creating a Clients scope permission in such a realm can fail while resolving scopes, and client permission evaluation that falls back to the Clients resource type has no resource to evaluate, so the new feature is broken for upgraded/existing realms rather than only for newly initialized ones.

title: hasPermission can dereference a null all-clients resource
body: When no resource exists for the specific client, the code loads the all-clients resource via AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource() and immediately passes it to policyStore.findByResource() and later calls resource.getScopes(). getResourceTypeResource() can return null (for example when the Clients all-resource resource is absent, as in realms initialized before this resource type existed). That turns a normal permission check into a NullPointerException/500 instead of returning false, potentially breaking client admin endpoints for the whole realm.

title: setPermissionsEnabled now throws for callers reached through MgmtPermissionsV2
body: MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() now always returns ClientPermissionsV2, whose setPermissionsEnabled() and isPermissionsEnabled() throw UnsupportedOperationException. Generic management callers still invoke these methods, notably AdminPermissions.registerListener() on ClientRemovedEvent/RoleRemovedEvent/GroupRemovedEvent via AdminPermissions.management(), which selects MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever the V2 feature is enabled even though the listener only checks the V1 feature flag. If both FGAP features are enabled, deleting a client/role/group can fail with UnsupportedOperationException instead of performing the old cleanup/no-op, and other generic client-permission endpoints that probe isPermissionsEnabled() risk the same 500.

title: getResourceName does not translate Clients resources
body: getResourceName() only special-cases the Users resource type: it returns 'All users' for the all-users resource and resolves a user ID to a username, throwing if the user is missing. Clients resources fall through to resource.getDisplayName(). Resources created by getOrCreateResource() are created with the client ID as the resource name and no display name, and the all-clients resource is named 'Clients'. As a result, permission/resource representations for the new Clients type will expose a null/blank display name (or raw UUID) instead of 'All clients' or the client's clientId, unlike the Users behavior this feature mirrors.

title: Existing FGAPv2 realms never receive the new Clients resource type or scopes
body: init() returns immediately whenever realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is non-null. Realms that enabled admin permissions before this change therefore keep only the Users resource and the old scope set: the Clients all-resource resource and the configure, map-roles-client-scope, and map-roles-composite scopes are never created for them. Client permissions cannot be created or evaluated correctly in such upgraded realms until the admin-permissions client is recreated.

title: Possible NullPointerException when the Clients type resource does not exist
body: In hasPermission(ClientModel, String), when no per-client resource exists the code loads the Clients type resource and immediately passes it to findByResource(server, resource). getResourceTypeResource() can return null, for example in a realm created before the Clients type existed or if the type resource was not provisioned, so this dereference/query with a null resource can throw instead of simply denying the permission.

title: Resource display names are not resolved for the Clients resource type
body: getResourceName() translates Users resources to 'All users' or the user's username, but has no equivalent Clients branch. Client resources therefore fall through to resource.getDisplayName(), which for resources created by getOrCreateResource is based on the internal client UUID and for the type resource is the raw type name, so permission/resource listings for clients show opaque identifiers instead of 'All clients' or the clientId.

title: getClientsWithPermission returns the all-clients pseudo-resource as a client id
body: resourceStore.findByType(server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...) also returns the type resource whose name is literally 'Clients', created at schema initialization. If the caller is granted the scope on all clients, hasGrantedPermission succeeds for that resource and granted.add(resource.getName()) inserts 'Clients' into a set whose contract (Set<String> getClientsWithPermission) is client identifiers, while no actual client ids are added for clients that have no per-client resource yet. Callers filtering clients by id will miss those clients and may treat 'Clients' as an id.

title: Role-mapping checks lose the traditional manage-clients admin fallback
body: canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles (line 97), and canMapClientScopeRoles (line 102) return only hasPermission(client, <fgap-scope>). Unlike canManage(ClientModel), canConfigure, canManageClientScopes, and canView(ClientScopeModel) in the same class, they never check root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS) (directly or via canManage(client)). A realm admin holding the normal manage-clients role can manage and configure a client under FGAPv2 but is denied mapping that client's roles, composite roles, and client-scope roles unless a separate FGAP permission is also created.

title: Removal listener still runs V2-unsupported operations when both FGAP features are enabled
body: The listener is now guarded only by Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (v1). AdminPermissions.management() prefers MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever the v2 feature is enabled, so with both v1 and v2 features enabled a ClientRemovedEvent still reaches ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled(), which unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException, instead of the event being skipped. The guard needs to exclude the case where v2 takes precedence (v1 enabled and v2 not enabled).

title: Possible NullPointerException when the all-Clients resource is missing
