The key also relies on Python's built-in `hash()` of the project tuple rather than a stable, collision-resistant encoding of the project IDs (e.g. joining the sorted IDs), so distinct project sets can collide/share an eligibility decision within a process.

title: upsampled_count sums sample_weight without coalescing missing weights to 1
body: The new aggregate is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` with no `coalesce(sample_weight, 1)`/`ifNull` handling. The transform in error_upsampling.py applies it to every `count()` for an allowlisted project, including events ingested before client error sampling existed or sent by SDKs that did not set a client sample rate, whose `sample_weight` can be NULL. In ClickHouse `sum` over NULLs yields NULL/0 rather than counting those events as weight 1, so historical/unsampled errors silently disappear from upsampled timeseries instead of being counted once.

title: Internal upsampled_count function is exposed as a public query function
body: Unlike the neighbouring private internal function (which sets `private=True`), `upsampled_count` is registered without `private=True`, so any API user can send `upsampled_count()` directly as a y-axis/field on discover queries for arbitrary, non-allowlisted projects. That bypasses the all-projects-allowlisted and errors-only gating in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` and returns misleading weighted counts (or errors on datasets without `sample_weight`); it should be marked private so only the server-side column transformation can invoke it.

title: Upsampling eligibility uses the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset
body: _get_event_stats receives scoped_dataset, which can differ from the closure dataset during dashboard discover-split handling (e.g. an errors-only call is made with discover while the outer dataset is metrics/discover, or vice versa). is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects is nevertheless passed the outer dataset, so eligibility is decided for the wrong dataset: error split results can miss upsampling and transaction/metrics split results can be decided from the wrong dataset context. Pass scoped_dataset to the eligibility check.

title: Substring check treats negated and mixed-type queries as error-only
body: _is_error_focused_query returns True whenever the raw query contains the substring 'event.type:error', including '!event.type:error' (which excludes errors) and mixed queries such as 'event.type:transaction OR event.type:error'. In those cases count() is replaced by sum(sample_weight), a column that is not meaningful for transactions/default events, so results will be wrong or undercounted. The check needs to use the parsed search query and only apply when the query provably restricts to error events.

title: Error-focus detection reads request.GET instead of the actual query being executed
body: _is_error_focused_query ignores the query argument passed through _get_event_stats and only inspects request.GET['query']. Callers that synthesize or modify the query (for example the dashboard split path builds '(query) AND !event.type:transaction' for the errors-only probe) therefore get eligibility decided from a different query than the one sent to Snuba, so genuinely error-only split queries are not upsampled unless the original GET parameter happens to contain 'event.type:error'. Pass the effective query string into the eligibility decision.

title: upsampled_count is enabled for the errors dataset but only registered on Discover
body: _should_apply_sample_weight_transform always returns True for the errors dataset, causing count() to be rewritten to 'upsampled_count() as count', but the new SnQLFunction is only added to DiscoverDatasetConfig.function_converter in discover.py; the errors dataset config is untouched. A request with dataset=errors on an allowlisted project will therefore send an unregistered function to the errors query builder and fail validation instead of returning stats. Register upsampled_count for the errors dataset (and any other dataset for which the transform is enabled) or restrict the transform to datasets that define it; the added Snuba tests never exercise dataset=errors.

title: sum(sample_weight) drops events that have no sample weight
body: The upsampled_count aggregate is a bare sum(sample_weight) wrapped in toInt64. Events in allowlisted projects that were ingested without error sampling (or before sample_weight was populated) have a NULL/0 sample_weight, so they contribute nothing and can make an entire bucket NULL/0 instead of counting once, silently under-reporting historical and unsampled errors. The aggregate should treat a missing weight as 1 (e.g. sum(coalesce/ifNull(sample_weight, 1))) so unsampled events count normally.

title: Stray nested-repository pointer file committed
body: This adds a top-level file named 'sentry-repo' whose entire content is 'Subproject commit a5d2909...', i.e. an accidental gitlink/submodule artifact without any .gitmodules entry. It is unrelated to the upsampling feature, pollutes the repository root, and can confuse tooling that scans the tree. Remove the file before merging.

title: Feature-flagged table widget renders empty data instead of the query result
body: When the organization has the 'use-table-widget-visualization' feature, tableResultComponent renders TableWidgetVisualization with hardcoded columns=[] and tableData containing data: [] and empty meta. It discards result.data, result.meta, fields, aliases, custom renderers, and loading state computed immediately above. Every dashboard table widget for such an organization will therefore show an empty table with no columns instead of its actual data.

title: Error events are interleaved using mismatched timestamp units
body: gen_request_data compares error_events timestamps directly against recording-segment event timestamps. fetch_error_details takes the timestamp from nodestore event data, which is in seconds since epoch, while rrweb/replay segment events use milliseconds since epoch. Consequently every error timestamp is numerically far smaller than every breadcrumb timestamp, so all errors are emitted before the first breadcrumb regardless of when they actually occurred, corrupting the chronological context sent to Seer for summarization.

title: Missing nodestore events misalign error IDs with event data
body: fetch_error_details zips error_ids with events.values() from nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids). get_multi only returns entries for node IDs that exist (and keyed by node ID, not error ID), so if any error event is missing from nodestore, subsequent event payloads are paired with the wrong error_ids and are not dropped even though their own ID is absent. The resulting ErrorEvent objects carry incorrect ids, and the list comprehension's 'if data is not None' cannot detect the misalignment.

title: Hidden span attributes are only hidden while searching
body: The new HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES filter ('is_segment', 'project_id', 'received') is applied only in the branch taken when searchQuery is non-empty. When no search text is entered, sortedAndFilteredAttributes returns sortAttributes(attributes) unfiltered, so the supposedly hidden attributes remain visible in the default attributes list and are only removed after the user starts typing.

title: Browser report age/timestamp mutual-exclusion validation is incomplete and falsy-sensitive
body: validate_timestamp and validate_age only reject the other field when its value is truthy in initial_data, so a report with timestamp plus age=0 (or age plus timestamp=0, though timestamp also has min_value) can pass, and because both fields are required=False a report with neither age nor timestamp also passes. This accepts payloads that conform to neither the Working Draft (timestamp) nor the Editor's Draft (age) reporting format the serializer claims to enforce, allowing malformed reports to be counted as valid.

title: Table widget renders empty data when feature flag is enabled
body: When the organization has the use-table-widget-visualization feature, tableResultComponent renders TableWidgetVisualization with columns={[]} and tableData containing data: [] and empty meta, instead of converting result.data/result.meta and the widget fields into tabular data. Any dashboard table widget for such an organization will therefore show an empty table with no columns, losing the previously displayed query results.

title: Error events can be paired with the wrong error IDs when nodestore results are missing
body: fetch_error_details builds node_ids from error_ids but then zips error_ids with events.values() from nodestore.backend.get_multi. get_multi is keyed by node_id and may omit missing events, so if any event is absent the remaining values shift and are paired with the wrong event_id. This can attach the wrong title, message, and timestamp to an error in the Seer summary request, or drop/misattribute errors silently.

title: Error timestamps are compared against replay segment timestamps in different units
body: gen_request_data compares error_events timestamps, which come from the stored event payload as epoch seconds, directly against replay segment event timestamps, which are rrweb timestamps in epoch milliseconds. Because milliseconds are roughly 1000x larger, all errors will be yielded before the first breadcrumb regardless of their actual chronological position, so the AI summary receives error context in the wrong order.

title: Hidden span attributes are only hidden while searching
body: The new HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES list (is_segment, project_id, received) is applied only in the branch taken when searchQuery is non-empty. When searchQuery is empty, sortedAndFilteredAttributes returns sortAttributes(attributes) unchanged, so the supposedly hidden internal attributes remain visible in the default attributes list and only disappear after the user types a search query.

title: Mutual-exclusion validation for age/timestamp misses age=0
body: validate_timestamp and validate_age check self.initial_data.get('age')/get('timestamp') for truthiness. A report containing timestamp plus age=0 (a valid freshly-generated report age) will pass both validators even though the serializer intends to reject reports that mix the Working Draft timestamp field with the Editor's Draft age field, weakening the spec validation added in this change.

title: Feature-flagged table widget discards all actual table data
body: When the organization has 'use-table-widget-visualization', tableResultComponent renders TableWidgetVisualization with hardcoded columns=[] and tableData={data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}} instead of converting result.data/result.meta/fields from the query result. Because an empty array is not nullish, TableWidgetVisualization also does not derive columns from meta. Any dashboard table widget for such an org therefore renders an empty table and loses its data, title handling, custom field renderers, field aliases, and loading behavior.

title: Hidden span attributes are only hidden while searching
body: HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES ('is_segment', 'project_id', 'received') is only applied in the branch that runs when searchQuery is non-empty; when the search box is empty sortedAndFilteredAttributes returns sortAttributes(attributes) unfiltered. The attributes the change intends to hide therefore remain visible in the default Attributes view and only disappear after the user types a search query.

title: Reports with neither age nor timestamp pass validation
body: BrowserReportSerializer declares both age and timestamp as required=False, and validate_age/validate_timestamp only reject the case where the other field is present in initial_data. A report containing neither field is accepted even though the two supported Reporting API specs each require one of them, and a report with age=0 plus a timestamp also passes because the checks use truthiness (self.initial_data.get('age') / .get('timestamp')) rather than presence. Malformed reports are then counted in metrics as valid browser reports.

title: Error events are interleaved using mismatched timestamp units
body: gen_request_data compares error_events timestamps directly against replay segment event timestamps. Error timestamps come from nodestore event data, which stores timestamp as seconds since epoch, while rrweb/replay segment event timestamps are milliseconds since epoch. Every error timestamp (~1.7e9) is therefore always less than every segment timestamp (~1.7e12), so all errors are emitted before the first breadcrumb regardless of when they occurred, producing a chronologically wrong log sequence for the Seer summary. The new unit test masks this by using second-scale timestamps for the fake segment events.

title: Analytics event is recorded before the feature-flag check
body: analytics.record('preprod_artifact.api.assemble', ...) runs unconditionally at the start of post(), before the organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble feature check that returns 404 and before request-body validation that can return 400. Assemble events are therefore recorded for organizations without the feature and for malformed requests that never assemble anything, polluting the analytics used to measure adoption of this endpoint.

title: AI summary shows 'Project not found' while the project is still loading
body: The new guard `if (replayRecord?.project_id && !project)` runs before the isPending check. useProjectFromId returns undefined while its project request is in flight, so on first render for a valid replay the tab immediately renders the 'Project not found. Unable to load AI summary.' error instead of a loading state; the error is incorrect and flashes (or sticks if the summary query's enabled state is tied to the same render cycle) for projects that do exist.

title: Sender validation is bypassed when the Integration does not exist yet
body: When Integration.objects.get() raises DoesNotExist, GitHubInstallation immediately calls pipeline.next_step() without comparing pipeline state 'github_authenticated_user' against the GitHub user who installed the app. That row is normally created asynchronously by the GitHub installation webhook, so completion races the webhook: a user who reaches this step before the webhook is processed (or if it is delayed/lost) finishes the pipeline and build_integration() creates the integration from the installation_id alone. This defeats the PR's stated guarantee that the authenticated GitHub user must match the app installer whenever the webhook has not already created the Integration.

title: Sender check crashes for integrations whose metadata has no sender
body: The new check unconditionally indexes integration.metadata['sender']['login']. Integrations created through this pipeline itself do not get a sender (build_integration only sets metadata['sender'] from state['sender'], which this pipeline never binds; test_basic_flow asserts metadata without 'sender'), and older integrations likewise may lack it. If such an Integration exists but has no OrganizationIntegration (e.g. the org link was removed and the installation is retried/moved to another org), installations_exist is False, this branch is reached, and a KeyError/TypeError produces a 500 instead of completing or showing the installation-failed page.

title: Token exchange and user lookup exceptions escape as 500s instead of the failure page
body: safe_urlopen() on line 423 is called outside the try/except (which only covers safe_urlread/parse_qsl), and get_user_info() on line 434 is also unguarded. A network error, timeout, or HTTP error from GitHub's token endpoint, or a failed /user request for a bad/expired token, will therefore raise out of OAuthLoginView.dispatch and return a 500. This contradicts the PR description that a wrong or reused 'code' (and by extension a failed token/user exchange) should show the 'Invalid installation request' error page.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the installation-not-found path
body: The rewritten test's second request uses state 'ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05', which fails OAuthLoginView's pipeline-signature check before GitHubInstallation/build_integration ever queries GitHub for the installation. The assertion of 'Invalid installation request.' therefore passes via the state-mismatch branch, and the stubbed 404 from /app/installations/{id} and the 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' handling in build_integration are no longer covered by any test.

title: Sender check crashes when integration metadata has no sender
body: GitHubInstallation unconditionally evaluates integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]. Integrations created before sender was recorded, created through build_integration when state has no sender, or otherwise lacking that nested key will raise KeyError/TypeError here instead of rendering the installation-failed page. This produces a 500 and blocks legitimate attempts to attach an existing orphaned Integration (no OrganizationIntegration) to an organization.

title: Authenticated-user check is bypassed when the Integration row does not yet exist
body: When Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id) raises DoesNotExist, GitHubInstallation returns pipeline.next_step() without comparing pipeline state github_authenticated_user to the installer. Because the GitHub webhook that creates the Integration (with sender metadata) is asynchronous and can lag the user's redirect, an attacker who knows/guesses an installation_id and authenticates to GitHub as a different user can complete the pipeline in that window; build_integration only fetches /app/installations/{id}, which contains no sender to validate against, so the PR's mismatch protection is race-dependent and ineffective for fresh/racing installs.

title: Token exchange and user lookup failures are not converted to the error page
body: safe_urlopen at line 423 is outside the try/except (only safe_urlread/parse_qsl is guarded), and get_user_info(payload["access_token"]) at line 434 is also unguarded. A network error, GitHub HTTP error, invalid/reused code causing a failed /user call, or a missing code (e.g. user denies authorization, so code is None and form-encoding/exchange can fail) will raise and return a 500 instead of the documented 'We could not verify the authenticity...' installation-failed response.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the installation-not-found path
body: The updated test_installation_not_found drives the setup endpoint with state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05, which fails OAuthLoginView's pipeline-signature check and renders 'Invalid installation request.' before GitHubInstallation/build_integration ever calls get_installation_info. The stubbed 404 for /app/installations/{id} and the IntegrationError 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' path therefore have no coverage, so a regression in that handling would not be caught.

title: Sender check crashes for integrations without sender metadata
body: integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] assumes every pre-existing Integration has metadata['sender'] as a dict with 'login'. Integrations created through the normal pipeline do not guarantee this: build_integration only sets metadata['sender'] when state.get('sender') is present, and no pipeline view binds 'sender', so pipeline-created integrations lack it. If such an integration later exists without an OrganizationIntegration (e.g. removed from one org and reinstalled on another), this line raises KeyError/TypeError and returns a 500 instead of the friendly installation-failed page or a successful reinstall.

title: Authenticated-user check is bypassed when Integration row does not yet exist
body: When Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id) raises DoesNotExist, dispatch returns pipeline.next_step() without comparing pipeline state 'github_authenticated_user' to the installer. The sender check at lines 500-505 therefore only runs if the installation webhook has already created the Integration row. An attacker who knows/guesses a predictable GitHub installation_id and starts the claim flow before the webhook is processed (or where the webhook never creates the row) can complete installation as any authenticated GitHub user, defeating the validation this PR is meant to add; build_integration fetches only account info, not the installing user, so no later check compensates.

title: Token exchange and user-info calls can raise unhandled exceptions
body: safe_urlopen at line 423 is outside the try/except (which only covers safe_urlread/parse at lines 425-429), and get_user_info(payload['access_token']) at line 434 is also unguarded. A network error, TLS error, or non-2xx/invalid response from GitHub's /user endpoint will propagate as an unhandled 500 instead of rendering the intended 'Invalid installation request' error page described in the PR for bad/reused codes and verification failures.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the 404 path
body: The rewritten test first requests setup with only installation_id, which now just redirects into the new OAuthLoginView, and then requests setup with a deliberately wrong state value, so it fails at the state-signature check in OAuthLoginView before build_integration/get_installation_info is ever reached. The assertion for 'Invalid installation request.' therefore passes even if the GitHub 404 handling in build_integration is broken, leaving that behavior untested under the new flow.

title: AssignmentSource.queued is evaluated once at import time
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` calls timezone.now() when the dataclass class is defined, not when an instance is created. Every AssignmentSource created without an explicit queued value therefore shares the process import timestamp. If queued is intended to record when an assignment was queued (e.g. for future staleness/debouncing checks or observability), it will be wrong by however long the process has been running. Use field(default_factory=timezone.now) instead.

title: to_dict() puts a raw datetime into Celery task kwargs, breaking the round-trip
body: assignment_source.to_dict() uses dataclasses.asdict(), so the `queued` value passed in the sync_assignee_outbound Celery kwargs is a datetime object, not a JSON-native value. Sentry Celery tasks serialize kwargs as JSON, so enqueueing can fail with a serialization error on exactly the inbound-assignment path this PR enables (propagating synchronously out of GroupAssignee.assign/deassign via sync_group_assignee_outbound), and where a serializer does coerce datetimes it arrives at AssignmentSource.from_dict as a string, silently violating the declared datetime type since from_dict performs no parsing/validation. Serialize queued to an ISO string in to_dict and parse it back in from_dict, or drop it from the wire format; the added tests use eager tasks and a direct to_dict assertion, so they never exercise this round-trip.

title: Task unconditionally passes new assignment_source kwarg to all installations
body: sync_assignee_outbound now always calls installation.sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source), even when it is None, while the abstract IssueSyncIntegration.sync_assignee_outbound signature was not updated to declare this parameter (it still only documents **kwargs). Any installation whose concrete sync_assignee_outbound does not accept **kwargs/an assignment_source parameter will raise TypeError at runtime, causing the task to retry and the outbound sync to fail; the new test mocks ExampleIntegration.sync_assignee_outbound, which accepts arbitrary kwargs, so it cannot catch such an incompatibility. Either declare the parameter on the abstract method and update implementations, or only pass it when supported/non-None.

title: No test for deassign suppression or for propagation to a different integration
body: The only cycle-suppression test covers assign() where the source integration matches the single linked integration, asserting the outbound call is skipped. There is no equivalent test for deassign() with a matching AssignmentSource, and no test where an assignment sourced from one integration still syncs outbound to a different linked integration, which is the behavior the should_sync comment claims to preserve. A regression that suppresses all outbound syncs whenever any assignment_source is present, or that fails to suppress deassign cycles, would pass the current suite.

title: queued timestamp is evaluated once at class definition
body: AssignmentSource declares `queued: datetime = timezone.now()`, which Python evaluates once when the class is defined rather than for each instance. Every AssignmentSource created after process start will therefore carry the import/startup time instead of its actual creation time. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so each assignment source gets a fresh timestamp.

title: AssignmentSource.to_dict() puts a datetime into Celery task kwargs
body: sync_group_assignee_outbound passes `assignment_source.to_dict()` directly as an apply_async kwarg, and to_dict() uses dataclasses.asdict(), so `queued` remains a datetime object. Sentry/Celery task arguments must be serializable (JSON); enqueueing an inbound-triggered assignment can therefore fail to serialize, or in other transports round-trip queued as a string that AssignmentSource.from_dict() never parses back to datetime. Serialize queued with isoformat() in to_dict() and parse it in from_dict() to make the round-trip safe.

title: Task unconditionally passes new assignment_source kwarg to all installations
body: The task now calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)` for every issue-sync installation, but the abstract sync_assignee_outbound signature in IssueSyncIntegration was not updated to declare this parameter. Any concrete integration (including out-of-tree or legacy implementations) whose sync_assignee_outbound accepts only external_issue/user/assign (and no **kwargs) will raise TypeError on every outbound assignee sync, breaking syncs that worked before. Update the abstract contract and all implementations, or only pass the kwarg to implementations that accept it.

title: AssignmentSource queued datetime is placed in Celery task kwargs
body: assignment_source.to_dict() returns the raw datetime object for `queued` (dataclasses.asdict does not convert it), and that dict is passed directly as a sync_assignee_outbound Celery kwarg. Sentry tasks use serializable primitive kwargs, so in production this either fails to enqueue/serialize or is degraded to a string by the JSON encoder, unlike the eager self.tasks() test path which can pass the object through in-process. The new inbound-to-outbound path can therefore error or lose the intended type exactly when an external webhook triggers an assignment.

title: queued default is evaluated once at import time
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated when the dataclass class is defined, not when each AssignmentSource is created. Every source created by a long-lived worker/web process will share the process-import timestamp instead of its actual queue time. Use field(default_factory=timezone.now) so each assignment source records when it was created.

title: from_dict does not restore or validate the queued/integration fields after serialization
body: from_dict blindly does cls(**input_dict). If `queued` has been serialized to an ISO string for transport, it is stored back as a str despite the declared datetime type; similarly integration_id is not coerced/validated. Any current or future logic that compares, formats, or expires based on `queued`, or compares integration_id as an int, can then behave incorrectly or raise, while the tests only cover dicts that omit `queued` entirely.

title: No test proves a different integration still receives outbound sync, or that deassign is blocked for the source
body: The new matching-source test only covers assign with a single linked integration and asserts that integration is not called. It does not cover the stated intended behavior that other integrations still propagate the change, nor the deassign/unassign path with a matching assignment_source. A regression that blocks all outbound syncs for any non-None source, compares the wrong integration id, or only fixes assign would pass the added tests while breaking cross-integration sync or leaving the unassign cycle intact.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and cannot be instantiated
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now extends StatefulDetectorHandler but implements none of its abstract members (counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and the newly added build_occurrence_and_event_data). Detector.detector_handler does `group_type.detector_handler(self)`, so any Detector with type `metric_alert_fire` will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class ...` instead of the previous no-op handler returning an empty result. process_detectors has no exception handling around handler construction/evaluation, so this can abort processing for the whole batch.

title: Stateful evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate now returns `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, but its docstring at line 230 still says it returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult. This misdocuments the new contract that this PR is explicitly changing for callers and subclass authors.

title: Mock occurrence builder ignores value so tests cannot verify value propagation
body: build_mock_occurrence_and_event accepts `value` but never uses it when constructing the IssueOccurrence or event_data. Consequently the new build_occurrence_and_event_data hook's most important input is unverified: several tests even build the expected occurrence with the wrong value (e.g. test_state_results_multi_group builds group_2's expected occurrence with 6 instead of the packet value 10, and TestEvaluate builds expectations with 6 for packet values 100/8) yet still pass. A regression that passed the wrong value to the hook would not be caught.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler can no longer be instantiated
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler but implements none of its abstract members (counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and the newly added build_occurrence_and_event_data). Python will raise TypeError when Detector.detector_handler tries to instantiate it via group_type.detector_handler(self). Previously it implemented evaluate() and returned [], so process_detectors could handle it; now processing a metric-alert detector will crash process_detectors instead of being skipped or producing no results.

title: Occurrence tests do not verify the evaluated value passed to the hook
body: build_mock_occurrence_and_event ignores its value argument when constructing the IssueOccurrence and event_data, so tests cannot detect evaluate_group_key_value passing the wrong value to build_occurrence_and_event_data. This is visible here: group_2 has packet value 10 but the expected occurrence is built with value 6, and the assertion still passes. A regression passing e.g. the dedupe value or another group's value would go uncaught.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler can no longer be instantiated
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler but implements none of its abstract members (counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and the newly added build_occurrence_and_event_data) and only contains `pass`. Detector.detector_handler unconditionally does `group_type.detector_handler(self)`, so any detector of type metric_alert_fire will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class ...` instead of returning the previous no-op `evaluate() -> []`. That exception propagates out of process_detectors and breaks processing for the whole data packet, not just this detector.

title: TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe builds expected occurrence for the wrong group key
body: The expected occurrence is built with `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, ...)`, but evaluate_group_key_value is then called with group_key "group_key" and value 10. build_mock_occurrence_and_event derives the occurrence fingerprint from the supplied group_key via handler.build_fingerprint(), so the expected occurrence has fingerprint `<detector_id>:val1` while the occurrence actually produced inside evaluate_group_key_value has fingerprint `<detector_id>:group_key`. The DetectorEvaluationResult equality comparison therefore cannot match and this test fails / does not verify the dedupe path as intended; the helper should be called with "group_key".

title: StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: The signature of StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate was changed in this PR to return `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, and the implementation builds a dict, but the docstring at line 230 still says it 'returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult'. This misdocuments the new contract that callers such as process_detectors now rely on (they call .values() on the result).

title: Converted monitor config is discarded in environment context
body: get_monitor_environment_context copies monitor.config into the local `config` variable and converts `config["schedule_type"]` to its display value, but the returned context uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead of the converted `config`. The conversion therefore has no effect and the occurrence context continues to contain the raw schedule_type value rather than the intended display value.

title: Converted monitor config is discarded in occurrence context
body: get_monitor_environment_context copies monitor.config into `config` and replaces config['schedule_type'] with get_schedule_type_display(), but the returned context uses monitor_environment.monitor.config instead of the converted `config`. The conversion is therefore dead code and occurrences will contain the raw schedule_type value rather than the intended display value.

title: Hung spawn flusher is never killed before being replaced
body: Flusher workers are created with multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, whose objects are SpawnProcess/BaseProcess instances, not instances of multiprocessing.Process. The isinstance check therefore never passes in production, so a worker detected as hung is not killed before _create_process_for_shards starts its replacement. The hung worker can keep polling and flushing the same Redis shards concurrently with the new worker, causing duplicate buffered-segment production and races between flush_segments/done_flush_segments, while the reference to the leaked worker is overwritten in self.processes.

title: join() never terminates spawn flusher processes
body: For the same reason as the restart path, isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is false for processes created through the spawn context (and for the threading.Thread workers used when produce_to_pipe is set, terminate is inapplicable). After join() waits until its deadline for workers that ignore the shared stopped flag, the terminate call is skipped, so shutdown can return while daemon flusher processes are still alive flushing segments and producing to Kafka; they are only cleaned up implicitly when the parent process exits.

title: Invalid --flusher-processes values are silently remapped or crash obscurely
body: The CLI option added for process-spans accepts any integer and SpanFlusher performs no positive-value validation. Passing 0 is silently changed by `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` into one process per shard, the opposite of an operator's explicit request, while a negative value makes num_processes negative, builds an empty process_to_shards_map, and then fails with a KeyError on `i % self.num_processes` during shard assignment instead of a clear configuration error at startup.

title: Invalid flusher process counts are silently accepted
body: SpanFlusher does not validate max_processes. An explicit 0 is converted by `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` into one process per shard, silently ignoring the configured limit and potentially spawning far more processes than intended. A negative value produces `num_processes <= 0`, an empty process-to-shards map, and therefore no flusher processes at all; submit() then finds no unhealthy processes to report while spans continue to be committed after being written to Redis but are never flushed. The CLI option in sentry.consumers accepts any integer, so this invalid configuration is reachable via --flusher-processes.

title: Restarted flusher is started without waiting for the old process to exit
body: When a process is unhealthy, _ensure_processes_alive() calls process.kill() but never join()s it before _create_process_for_shards() immediately starts a replacement for the same shards and overwrites self.processes[process_index]. kill() only signals termination, so the old and new flushers can briefly run concurrently against the same Redis shards, racing flush_segments()/done_flush_segments() and potentially producing the same segment twice to Kafka. The lost handle also prevents the caller from later confirming or reaping that specific child. The replacement should be started only after the killed process has been joined/reaped.

title: Comma-joined shard metric tag corrupts multi-shard tags
body: When one process handles multiple shards, shard_tag is built as a comma-joined string such as '0,2' and emitted as a single metrics tag value (also for segment_size_bytes and wait_produce). Comma is the separator between tags in StatsD/DogStatsD-style encoding, so the backend can parse this as an extra valueless tag instead of one shard tag, breaking per-shard filtering and creating malformed tag sets. The wait_produce metric also inconsistently uses the key 'shards' while the others use 'shard'. Metrics should be emitted per shard or use a separator that is valid in a single tag value.

title: New multi-flusher test never verifies flushing or the spawn path
body: test_flusher_processes_limit only asserts process counts and shard-map totals, then joins; it never submits a span and never asserts that a process shared by multiple shards actually flushes a segment for each of its shards. All consumer tests also pass produce_to_pipe, which forces SpanFlusher into its threading.Thread branch, so the production spawn branch (run_with_initialized_sentry, pickling the per-shard SpansBuffer, and the new shards argument to SpanFlusher.main) is not exercised at all. A regression that breaks spawned flushers or drops all but one shard in a shared process would pass the new tests.

title: Invalid flusher process counts are not rejected and can disable flushing
body: The CLI accepts any integer for --flusher-processes and SpanFlusher performs no validation. A negative value makes num_processes negative at line 60, producing an empty process_to_shards_map and spawning no flusher at all, while submit() finds no backpressure values and continues accepting spans into Redis indefinitely. A value of 0 passed programmatically is also silently changed by `max_processes or len(...)` into one process per shard instead of being rejected or honored. The process count should be validated as >= 1 at the CLI/factory/flusher boundary.

title: join() stops terminating remaining flusher processes after the deadline expires
body: join() sets the shared stopped flag and then iterates over all flusher processes, but if waiting for an early process consumes the deadline, the `break` at lines 339-341 exits the loop before terminate() is attempted for every later process. Those daemon flusher processes can therefore keep polling Redis and producing segments after the strategy has supposedly joined, including after a rebalance or shutdown, and can compete with a replacement flusher for the same shards. All processes should be terminated even when the waiting deadline has already expired.

title: Restarting a hung threaded flusher creates a duplicate flusher for the same shards
body: When produce_to_pipe is used, flushers are threading.Thread objects. _ensure_processes_alive() detects a hang, but the kill at lines 253-257 is skipped because a thread is not a multiprocessing.Process, and _create_process_for_shards() then starts a second thread for the same shards while the hung thread may later resume. Both threads can call flush_segments(), produce the same segment, and call done_flush_segments() for the same shards, risking duplicate buffered segments. Overwriting self.processes[process_index] also loses the only handle to the old thread, so join() can no longer wait for or stop it.

title: Multi-process flusher test never verifies that shared-process shards actually flush
body: test_flusher_processes_limit only asserts the number of processes and that four shard ids appear in process_to_shards_map; it submits no spans and asserts no produced segment for any shard. A regression in the shard-subset SpansBuffer construction, the new SpanFlusher.main() argument order, or flushing when multiple shards share one process/thread would therefore still pass. The test should push spans for shards handled by both processes and assert the flushed output.

title: Queues are unbounded despite claimed backpressure
body: FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with the default maxsize=0 (unbounded), and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() never blocks or rejects. The docstring at lines 253-254 promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but under a slow result_processor the Arroyo processor will keep submitting messages indefinitely, growing memory without bound and building a huge outstanding-offset set (also delaying commits past max.poll.interval). Bound the queues and make submit() apply backpressure, or remove the claim and add another flow-control mechanism.

title: Shutdown abandons queued-but-unprocessed items
body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown=True for every worker before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False). OrderedQueueWorker.run() re-checks `while not self.shutdown` after each item, so a worker that finishes its current item exits even if its queue still holds pending items (which immediate=False was supposed to drain). Those items are never processed and their offsets stay outstanding forever in this process; graceful shutdown silently drops in-flight work (only redelivery on restart saves it, and only if offsets were not already marked complete). Don't set the flag until queues are drained, or have workers exit only when the queue is empty and shut down.

title: close() stops the commit loop before workers drain
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread first, and only then calls queue_pool.shutdown(). Any items the workers finish during pool shutdown therefore complete their offsets after the last _commit_loop iteration, so those offsets are never passed to commit_function. Arroyo will consider the strategy closed and will not poll again, so successfully processed messages are redelivered and reprocessed on restart. Drain the pool first (and run a final commit pass), then stop the commit thread.

title: Queue pool is created once in the factory but killed by each strategy close
body: FixedQueuePool is constructed a single time in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ (line 133) and the same instance is handed to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy from create_with_partitions(). Arroyo calls create_with_partitions() again after a rebalance/revocation, but the previous strategy's close()/terminate() calls queue_pool.shutdown(), which shuts down the shared queues and joins the workers. The next strategy reuses that dead pool: work_queue.put() raises queue.ShutDown, which SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() catches and converts into add_offset+complete_offset, so messages are silently dropped yet committed. Create a fresh pool per create_with_partitions() call (or make the pool restartable and don't shut it down in strategy close).

title: submit() marks messages complete and committable on any error
body: The bare `except Exception` in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() logs and then does add_offset()+complete_offset() for the message regardless of where the failure occurred - e.g. grouping_fn raising, or FixedQueuePool.submit() failing after add_offset() when putting onto a shut-down queue. Combined with OrderedQueueWorker.run() completing offsets in its `finally` block even when result_processor raises (line 148-149), this contradicts the documented 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and turns transient/poison failures into committed, never-retried message loss instead of letting Arroyo/DLQ handle them. Only skip-and-commit for explicitly undecodable/filtered payloads; propagate or leave outstanding other failures.

title: Kafka commit function is invoked from a background thread
body: _commit_loop runs on a dedicated daemon thread and calls self.commit_function(committable) (which is Arroyo's Commit callable built in create_thread_queue_parallel_worker) concurrently with the StreamProcessor main thread that owns submit()/poll()/close(). Arroyo commit callbacks are expected to be invoked from the processing thread during submit/poll/join; racing them against processor-driven commits and shutdown can corrupt/interleave offset state and commit offsets for partitions that have since been revoked. Perform commits from poll() on the strategy thread, using the tracker only to compute committable offsets.

title: Committable-offset scan is O(range) every second per partition
body: get_committable_offsets() runs min()/max() over the full all_offsets set and then iterates range(start, max_offset+1) with set lookups, and mark_committed() rebuilds the whole set - all repeated every 1s by _commit_loop for every partition. With a backlog (made likely by the unbounded queues), a single slow offset pins a large outstanding set, so each tick rescans an ever-growing range, giving quadratic behaviour and burning a thread. Track the next-expected offset and a completed set per partition instead of rescanning the whole window.

title: hash() is not a stable consistent hash for group assignment
body: get_queue_for_group() uses Python's builtin hash(group_key) % num_queues and documents it as 'consistent hashing'. For str keys hash() is randomised per process via PYTHONHASHSEED, so the group->queue mapping changes on every restart and differs between concurrently running consumer processes; it is also a plain modulo, so changing num_queues (--max-workers) remaps nearly every group. This defeats any cross-restart/cross-process affinity expectations and makes queue distribution non-reproducible in tests/operations. Use a stable digest (e.g. hashlib.md5/sha1 of the key) modulo num_queues.

title: wait_until_empty reports empty while items are still being processed
body: wait_until_empty() (and poll()'s total_queued gauge) rely on queue.qsize(), but OrderedQueueWorker removes an item from the queue via get() before it starts processing it. The method therefore returns True while the last item(s) - one per queue - are still in-flight and their offsets not yet completed, so any caller using it as a drain/flush barrier (as shutdown-style tests do) can proceed/commit/tear down too early. Track in-flight counts (e.g. queue.task_done()/join() or an explicit counter incremented on submit and decremented in the worker's finally).

title: Queues are unbounded, so the new strategy provides no backpressure
body: FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with no maxsize and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() always enqueues and returns successfully, never raising MessageRejected. Despite the class docstring claiming natural backpressure, Arroyo will keep consuming from Kafka while workers fall behind, accumulating messages and WorkItem/result objects in memory indefinitely when one queue is slow or stuck, risking OOM instead of pausing consumption.

title: Closing a strategy permanently kills the shared queue pool that the factory reuses
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() calls queue_pool.shutdown(), which shuts down the queues and workers. That pool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and reused by create_thread_queue_parallel_worker() on every create_with_partitions() call (e.g. after a Kafka rebalance, when Arroyo closes the old strategy and creates a new one for the new assignment). Submits to the now-shutdown queues raise queue.ShutDown, which submit() catches at line 317 and then marks the offset complete, so messages for the new assignment can be committed without ever being processed. The factory only clears queue_pool in its own shutdown(), not when a strategy is closed.

title: Failed work items are marked complete and their offsets are committed
body: OrderedQueueWorker.run() logs any exception from result_processor but unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset() in the finally block, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() similarly marks offsets complete when decoding/grouping/enqueueing fails. The commit loop then treats those offsets as processed and commits them, contradicting the documented 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' guarantee: transient processing failures or poison messages are silently dropped and will not be redelivered.

title: Kafka offsets are committed from a background thread instead of the Arroyo processor thread
body: _commit_loop runs on its own thread and invokes commit_function, which in result_consumer.py calls Arroyo's Commit callable. Arroyo strategies are expected to invoke commit from the strategy's submit/poll/close calls on the StreamProcessor thread; calling it concurrently from this thread races StreamProcessor's own offset/assignment handling and can commit offsets against a stale or revoked assignment. Additionally, each strategy instance created for a rebalance spawns another commit thread over the same shared OffsetTracker, so two threads can race get_committable_offsets()/mark_committed() and double-commit.

title: close() stops the commit loop before draining queues, discarding commit progress
body: close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread before calling queue_pool.shutdown() to drain pending work. Workers then finish processing queued items and mark offsets complete, but no commit loop remains to commit those offsets and close() performs no final commit flush. On every graceful shutdown/rebalance, all work completed during the drain is therefore reprocessed on restart, causing duplicate result processing.

title: Offset scan is O(offset range) every second while a queue is blocked
body: get_committable_offsets() iterates range(start, max_offset + 1) for every partition on every 1-second commit loop iteration. The strategy's stated purpose is to survive a slow item blocking a queue; in exactly that case all later offsets accumulate in all_offsets/outstanding, so each poll rescans an ever-growing range (quadratic overall) and the sets grow without bound for as long as one offset is stuck, wasting CPU and memory.

title: OffsetTracker is never reset when partitions are revoked or reassigned
body: OffsetTracker keeps all_offsets, outstanding and last_committed forever, with no hook to clear a partition when Arroyo revokes it or when create_with_partitions is called with a new assignment. Stale outstanding offsets from a previous assignment block commits for a reassigned partition, and if offsets restart below the stale last_committed value (consumer-group reset, topic recreation, or reassignment with an earlier starting offset from the partitions mapping, which the strategy ignores), get_committable_offsets() can never advance past last_committed and commits silently stall.

title: Failed work items are marked complete and their offsets are committed
body: OrderedQueueWorker catches every exception from result_processor, logs it, and then unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset() in the finally block. The commit loop can therefore commit past a message whose processing failed, so it will never be retried or sent to a DLQ. This directly contradicts the strategy docstring claiming it only commits offsets after successful processing and can silently lose uptime results.

title: Unbounded queues provide no backpressure despite the documented guarantee
body: FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() never blocks or raises MessageRejected when workers fall behind. Arroyo will keep submitting messages as fast as Kafka delivers them, accumulating decoded WorkItems (including the original Kafka message) in memory indefinitely, growing OffsetTracker sets for uncommittable partitions as well. A slow subscription or downstream outage therefore risks OOM and massive reprocessing on restart rather than natural backpressure as claimed in the class docstring.

title: Shared queue pool is destroyed by the first strategy close and reused after rebalance
body: The FixedQueuePool (and its worker threads and OffsetTracker) is created once on the factory and handed to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy created by create_with_partitions(). Arroyo creates/closes strategies on partition assignment and rebalance; SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() shuts down that shared pool, and queue.Queue.put() on a shut-down queue raises ShutDown. The next assignment reuses the same dead pool (factory only nulls it in factory.shutdown(), not on strategy close), so subsequent messages fail to enqueue, are swallowed by submit()'s broad except handler, and are marked complete without processing. The shared OffsetTracker also retains last_committed across assignments, so a partition reassigned at a lower offset can never be committed again.

title: Close stops committing before queued work is drained
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread before shutting down the pool, and it never waits for queues to empty. FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown=True before calling queue.shutdown(immediate=False), so a worker that finishes its current item exits at the loop condition instead of draining remaining queued items. Consequently queued items are abandoned on graceful shutdown and any items workers do finish after the commit thread stops never have their offsets committed, causing avoidable duplicate reprocessing and violating the graceful-shutdown expectation.

title: Group-to-queue assignment uses Python's randomized hash()
body: get_queue_for_group() uses the built-in hash() on a string group key. For strings, hash() is randomized per interpreter process via PYTHONHASHSEED, so the same subscription maps to different queues in different processes and across restarts. That breaks the documented consistent-assignment/ordering guarantee whenever work for a group moves between consumer processes or the consumer restarts, and makes distribution non-reproducible; a stable digest (e.g. hashlib/md5, as used elsewhere in the uptime consumer) should be used instead.

title: Submit swallows grouping/decoder failures and marks the offset complete
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() wraps decoding, grouping and enqueueing in one broad except that logs the error and then add_offset()+complete_offset()s the message. Any failure in grouping_fn (or an enqueue failure such as a shut-down queue) therefore makes the message eligible for offset commit even though it was never processed, silently dropping it instead of surfacing the failure to Arroyo for retry/DLQ handling.

title: Supplying a dummy totpCode skips password verification for backup-code login
body: Password verification only runs when credentials.totpCode is empty (line 121), but the new backup-code branch at line 131 runs whenever credentials.backupCode is present regardless of totpCode. A direct credentials request containing a valid backupCode plus any non-empty totpCode value therefore skips password verification entirely and never validates the dummy TOTP, so a stolen backup code alone becomes a single-factor full login credential instead of a second factor after the password.

title: Backup-code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write and allows parallel reuse
body: The code reads and decrypts the backup-code array, checks indexOf, then writes back the array with that entry nulled (lines 139-156) with no transaction, conditional update, or locking. Two concurrent login requests using the same code can both pass the index check before either update commits, so a code advertised as usable exactly once can be replayed in parallel sessions.

title: Backup codes are unreachable for Google/SAML users in the external TOTP flow
body: Authorize throws ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled whenever identityProvider is not CAL and credentials.totpCode is empty (line 113). Users redirected from Google/SAML via loginWithTotp who choose 'Lost access' submit a backupCode with an empty totpCode, so they are rejected before the new backup-code branch at line 131 is ever reached, making backup-code recovery unusable for non-CAL 2FA users.

title: Backup-code comparison is case-sensitive and only strips dashes
body: Codes are generated as lowercase hex in setup.ts, but login (line 144) and the disable endpoint only remove '-' characters before an exact indexOf match. A user who types the code in uppercase (as suggested by the 'XXXXX-XXXXX' placeholder) or with surrounding spaces will be told the code is incorrect even though they entered the right code, and may burn attempts or get locked out of recovery.

title: Users who enabled 2FA before this feature can never obtain backup codes
body: Setup rejects any user with twoFactorEnabled=true with TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled (lines 42-44), and no other endpoint or UI in this PR generates or regenerates backup codes. Existing 2FA users therefore have backupCodes=null, get MissingBackupCodes at login/disable, and are told by the new 'missing_backup_codes' message to generate them in settings, which is impossible without fully disabling and re-enabling 2FA.

title: Backup code can bypass password verification when combined with a dummy TOTP code
body: Password verification is skipped whenever credentials.totpCode is present (line 121), while the backup-code branch at line 131 is selected solely from credentials.backupCode and never validates totpCode. An attacker who obtains only one backup code can therefore call the credentials provider directly with any password, a non-empty dummy totpCode, and that backup code: the password check is bypassed and only the backup code is checked, turning a second factor into a single-factor login. Password verification must not depend on totpCode, or must be explicitly required in the backup-code branch as it is in the normal form flow.

title: Backup-code comparison is case-sensitive while users are shown uppercase-style codes
body: Setup generates codes with crypto.randomBytes(5).toString('hex') (lowercase a-f) in apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts, but login only strips '-' before indexOf, and the input placeholder is 'XXXXX-XXXXX' suggesting uppercase entry. A user who transcribes or types a code in uppercase (e.g. 'ABC12-DEF34') will always get IncorrectBackupCode even though it is the correct code. The same case-sensitive pattern exists in apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts line 61. Normalize input with toLowerCase() (and trim) before comparison in both places.

title: Single-use backup code can be replayed by concurrent login requests
body: Authorize reads user.backupCodes, checks indexOf, then writes back the array with that entry nulled as a separate non-atomic update. Two concurrent authorize calls with the same backup code can both read the pre-consumption value, both pass the check, and both log in before either update lands, violating the documented 'each backup code can be used exactly once' guarantee. Consumption needs an atomic/transactional compare-and-update (or row locking) so only one request can claim a code.

title: Parent is only notified of enabled 2FA if the user clicks the backup-codes Close button
body: Previously handleEnable called onEnable() as soon as the enable request succeeded; now it only advances to DisplayBackupCodes, and onEnable() is invoked solely from the backup-codes-close button (line 269). If the user dismisses the dialog any other way (Dialog close control / onOpenChange, Escape, backdrop), 2FA is already enabled server-side but the parent settings page is never told, so the 2FA switch/state remains stale (showing disabled) until a reload and can invite a confusing re-setup attempt that the API rejects with TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled. Notify the parent on successful enable, or on any close from the DisplayBackupCodes step.

title: No test exercises login or disable with a backup code, including single-use rejection
body: The PR adds backup-code authentication to the credentials authorize flow and to the disable endpoint, but the only added e2e coverage downloads/copies the codes during setup; the file itself notes 'TODO: add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup'. Core security behavior — successful login with a valid code, rejection of a wrong code, rejection when reusing an already-consumed code, and disabling 2FA with a code — is unverified, so a regression in consumption/normalization would ship unnoticed.

title: Backup code can bypass password verification with a dummy TOTP field
body: Password verification is skipped whenever credentials.totpCode is non-empty, without exempting the new backup-code path. An attacker calling the credentials endpoint directly with a valid backup code, any non-empty totpCode value, and no/wrong password therefore skips verifyPassword, then enters the backupCode branch (which never validates the dummy totpCode) and is authenticated. A backup code, intended only as a second factor, becomes a single-factor passwordless login credential.

title: Single-use backup codes can be replayed concurrently
body: Consumption is a non-atomic read-check-update: two simultaneous logins with the same backup code can both read the stored array, both find the code at the same index, and both authenticate before either request writes back the array with that entry nulled. The documented 'exactly once' property of backup codes is therefore not enforced under concurrent requests; the code should be consumed with an atomic/conditional update or lock.

title: Backup code comparison does not normalize letter case
body: Codes are generated as lowercase hex (crypto.randomBytes(5).toString('hex')) and the only normalization applied to user input is stripping '-'. A user who types or pastes their code in uppercase (a natural way to transcribe XXXXX-XXXXX codes) gets IncorrectBackupCode even though the code is correct. The same flaw exists in apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts line 61. Input should be lowercased (and trimmed) before comparison in both places.

title: Backup codes are persisted and returned before TOTP setup is verified
body: Setup writes the encrypted backup codes (and TOTP secret) to the user row and returns the plaintext codes in the setup response before the user has proven possession of the authenticator by completing the enable step. If setup is abandoned, valid backup codes for a not-yet-enabled account remain stored in the database, and the codes are already exposed to any client/script that called setup, even though the UI only displays them after enabling. Codes should be generated/confirmed at enable time, or at minimum not persisted until enable succeeds.

title: No test exercises logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code
body: The new e2e coverage only downloads/copies the codes during setup; the file itself notes 'TODO: add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup'. The security-critical behaviors added in this PR — login with a backup code, rejection of a wrong code, single-use invalidation on reuse, missing-codes handling for pre-existing 2FA users, and disabling 2FA with a backup code — have no automated verification, so regressions or bypasses in next-auth-options.ts and disable.ts would ship undetected.

title: Crash when Google Meet event has no destination calendar
body: The code destructures `evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` into `mainHostDestinationCalendar`, which is `undefined` when the array is empty or null, then accesses `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining. Callers now routinely pass `destinationCalendar: []` (and handleNewBooking can pass `null`), so any booking whose location is Google Meet with no destination calendar throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` instead of falling back to Cal Video as before (`evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`).

title: Google update/delete no longer fall back to the destination calendar
body: In `updateEvent` (line 254-256) and identically in `deleteEvent` (line 315-317), the fallback is `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`, evaluated only when `externalCalendarId` is falsy. Comparing each `externalId` to a falsy/undefined value never matches, so `selectedCalendar`/`calendarId` becomes `undefined` (update passes `calendarId: undefined` to Google; previously it used `destinationCalendar.externalId`). Updates for bookings without an externalCalendarId in their reference will fail or target no calendar. The find should match on `credentialId`, mirroring `createEvent`.

title: Unrelated inverted slug condition in organization creation
body: This file has nothing to do with destination calendars, but the change flips `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`. Previously the org slug was only set directly when team billing was disabled (and otherwise only stored as `requestedSlug` in metadata pending billing setup); now the slug is set precisely when billing IS enabled and withheld when it is not, inverting the provisioning flow and potentially creating organizations with a claimed slug before billing is configured, or without a slug afterwards.

title: Video booking references lose their credentialId on creation
body: `referencesToCreate` now maps every result with `credentialId: isCalendarType ? result.credentialId : undefined`. Before, non-calendar results used `result.credentialId`. Dedicated video meetings (e.g. Zoom/Meet via createVideoEvent) are not `_calendar` results, so their BookingReference rows are now created with `credentialId: undefined`. Later update/cancel flows look up the video credential by `reference.credentialId` (e.g. handleCancelBooking only deletes the meeting when it is present), so video meetings for new bookings can no longer be updated or deleted.

title: Non-Google services ignore credentialId and always use the first host's calendar
body: EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents now calls `createEvent(credential, event, destination.externalId)` once per destination, and Google was updated to select the calendar matching `credentialId`, but Lark (line 128-129, also createAttendees line 164), Office365 (CalendarService.ts line 73) and CalDAV (packages/lib/CalendarService.ts line 156) still take only `event.destinationCalendar[0]`. For a collective event, the second host's credential is therefore used to write to the first host's `externalId` calendar, which that credential does not own, causing failures or writes attempted against the wrong calendar — the multiple-host support claimed by this PR only works for Google Calendar.

title: Recurring-series cancellation deletes events once per reference, repeatedly
body: The calendar-reference handling was changed from a single `find` to a `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)` loop, but the recurring-event branch inside it (lines 444-468) already iterates ALL of the organizer's calendar credentials and ALL updated bookings. With a collective booking that now has multiple calendar references, the whole series deletion is re-executed once per reference, issuing duplicate `deleteEvent` calls for every instance (and pushing duplicates into `apiDeletes`), multiplying external API calls and error surface on every recurring cancellation.

title: Possible crash when destinationCalendar is empty for Google Meet events
body: The code destructures the first element of evt.destinationCalendar (falling back to an empty array) and then accesses mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration without optional chaining. When destinationCalendar is null or empty, mainHostDestinationCalendar is undefined, so a booking with location integrations:google:meet and no destination calendar throws a TypeError instead of falling back to Cal Video as the previous evt.destinationCalendar?.integration check did.

title: updateLocation creates booking references losing externalCalendarId and credentialId
body: updateLocation now maps externalCalendarId from result.externalId and credentialId from result.credentialId, but CalendarManager.updateEvent's returned EventResult never sets either field (unlike createEvent which was updated to set them). editLocation.handler persists these referencesToCreate via references.create, so after a location change the new calendar booking reference has undefined externalCalendarId/credentialId, breaking subsequent update/cancel lookups that rely on those fields.

title: Google updateEvent can no longer resolve the destination calendar
body: When externalCalendarId is falsy, selectedCalendar is computed by finding a destination calendar whose externalId equals externalCalendarId (null/undefined/empty), which can never match, so calendarId is passed as undefined to calendar.events.update. Previously it fell back to event.destinationCalendar.externalId. Updates/reschedules for Google bookings without a stored externalCalendarId will therefore fail or target no calendar instead of the booking's destination calendar.

title: Google deleteEvent deletes from primary instead of destination calendar
body: The same impossible find (cal.externalId === externalCalendarId when externalCalendarId is falsy) replaces the previous fallback to event.destinationCalendar.externalId. deleteEvent then falls back to 'primary', so cancelling a booking whose event lives on a non-primary destination calendar leaves the real event undeleted and may attempt deletion on the wrong calendar.

title: Google createEvent uses first host's calendar email for every host's event
body: createEvent correctly selects the target calendar by matching credentialId, but the organizer attendee email still uses mainHostDestinationCalendar (the first array element) regardless of credentialId. For collective events, events created on the second host's Google calendar carry the first host's externalId as organizer email, which mismatches the authenticated calendar and can be rejected by Google or show the wrong organizer.

title: Lark createEvent ignores which destination credential is being processed
body: EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents now calls createEvent once per destination calendar/credential, but Lark's createEvent still always uses the first destinationCalendar entry. For a collective event with multiple Lark hosts it will repeatedly create the event on the main host's calendar (duplicates) and never on the other hosts' calendars; its signature also ignores the new credentialId parameter added to the Calendar interface.

title: Office365 createEvent ignores which destination credential is being processed
body: EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents now calls createEvent once per destination calendar/credential, but Office365's createEvent still always uses the first destinationCalendar entry for the events URL. For a collective event with multiple Office365 hosts it will repeatedly create the event on the main host's calendar (duplicates) and never on the other hosts' calendars.

title: CalDAV createEvent ignores which destination credential is being processed
body: EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents now calls createEvent once per destination calendar/credential, but the CalDAV/iCal base service still filters calendars by only the first destinationCalendar entry. For a collective event with multiple CalDAV hosts it will repeatedly create the event on the main host's calendar (duplicates) and never on the other hosts' calendars.

title: Recurring cancellation issues duplicate delete calls per calendar reference
body: The new outer loop iterates over every calendar reference, and inside the recurring branch it again iterates over all of the user's calendar credentials and all updated bookings, picking only the first calendar reference of each. With multiple hosts/references (the collective case this PR adds) the same recurring events are deleted multiple times (references x credentials), causing redundant API calls and spurious 404/410 errors that can surface as cancellation failures.

title: Possible TypeError when destinationCalendar is empty or null for Google Meet events
body: The code destructures `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` and then accesses `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining. If destinationCalendar is null or an empty array (possible when neither the event type nor organizer has a destination calendar, as handleNewBooking can set it to null), mainHostDestinationCalendar is undefined and evaluating the Google Meet fallback throws a TypeError, breaking booking creation instead of falling back to Cal Video. It should use `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.

title: Google updateEvent loses destination-calendar fallback
body: When externalCalendarId is falsy, `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)` compares externalIds against undefined/null and therefore never matches, so selectedCalendar becomes undefined. Previously it fell back to the destination calendar's externalId. calendar.events.update is then called with calendarId undefined, so updates for bookings without an externalCalendarId on the reference fail instead of updating the destination calendar. The fallback should be the first/matching destination calendar, not a find against the falsy argument.

title: Google deleteEvent loses destination-calendar fallback and may delete from primary
body: When externalCalendarId is falsy, the find compares each destination calendar's externalId to that falsy value and returns undefined, so deleteEvent falls back to `primary`. Previously it used the stored destination calendar. Cancelling a booking whose event lives on a non-primary destination calendar will therefore target the wrong calendar (or 404/be silently resolved) and leave the actual event undeleted.

title: Office365 createEvent always uses first host's destination calendar for every host
body: EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents now calls createEvent once per destination calendar/credential, passing the matching credential, but Office365 (like Lark and CalDAV implementations) ignores the credentialId/externalId argument and uses only `event.destinationCalendar[0]`. For a collective event with multiple hosts, the second host's credential is used to create an event on the first host's calendar ID, causing 404/authorization failures or a duplicate event on the wrong calendar rather than an event on the second host's calendar. The per-credential destination must be selected by credentialId.

title: Lark createEvent always uses first host's destination calendar for every host
body: EventManager loops over all destination calendars and creates one event per credential, but Lark's createEvent still derives calendarId solely from `event.destinationCalendar[0]`. A collective booking's additional hosts therefore attempt creation on the organizer's Lark calendar with their own credentials, which fails or writes to the wrong calendar, so the multi-host fix does not work for Lark. It needs to pick the destination whose credentialId matches the credential used for this call.

title: Team destination calendars are silently dropped when evt.destinationCalendar is null
body: evt.destinationCalendar is initialized to null when neither eventType nor organizerUser has a destination calendar, and team calendars are added via `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`. With null, the optional-chain push is a no-op, so for a collective event where only non-organizer hosts have destination calendars, those calendars are lost and EventManager falls back to creating only one event on the first generic calendar credential. Initializing to [] or assigning the team array would preserve them.

title: Non-credential destinations create events without storing externalCalendarId/credentialId correctly
body: In the branch where a destination has no credentialId, createAllCalendarEvents calls `createEvent(c, event)` without passing destination.externalId (unlike the credentialId branch at line 370). EventResult.externalId is therefore undefined, and referencesToCreate stores externalCalendarId undefined for that calendar event. Subsequent reschedule/cancel/update operations cannot address the specific external calendar the event was created on and may target primary/the wrong calendar.

title: Recurring cancellation deletes the first calendar reference for every credential and repeats per outer reference
body: Inside the new loop over all bookingCalendarReference entries, the recurring branch maps over all organizer calendar credentials and for each updated booking uses `updBooking.references.find(ref => ref.type.includes('_calendar'))`, i.e. always the first calendar reference regardless of the credential being iterated or the outer reference. With multiple hosts/references this issues duplicate deleteEvent calls with mismatched credential/uid/externalCalendarId pairs, potentially failing to delete some hosts' events and repeatedly deleting others.

title: Uses prisma without importing it
body: The newly added refresh block calls prisma.credential.update, but this file never imports prisma (imports are jsforce, rrule, zod, CalEventParser, constants, HttpError, logger, types, getAppKeysFromSlug and parseRefreshTokenResponse). Any construction of SalesforceCalendarService will fail type-checking/compilation or throw ReferenceError at runtime when this line executes, breaking the Salesforce integration entirely.

title: Stores SafeParse wrapper object as the credential key
body: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the full zod SafeParse result ({success, data}), not the parsed data. This line assigns that result to `key` and persists it via prisma.credential.update({data:{key}}), whereas previously googleCredentialSchema.parse returned the credential object itself. The stored key becomes {success:true,data:{...}}, so the next googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key) in googleAuth will fail and Google Calendar credentials become unusable after the first refresh, even when credential sharing is disabled.

title: Minimum token schema strips expiry and provider-specific fields
body: minimumTokenResponseSchema only declares access_token plus computed keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()], which are literal object-string keys, not wildcards.
